note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Homophone: sole (a fish, or the bottom of your foot or shoe, or "only": the sole survivor). "Not a soul" means "no one" — it is not about religion there.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (church) Anglican describes the Church of England and the churches around the world that grew from it, such as the Church of Ireland, the Scottish Episcopal Church, the Episcopal Church in the USA, and the Anglican Church of Australia. 2) An Anglican is a member of one of these churches.
its sense in the lessons: The Anglican Communion is a worldwide family of churches led spiritually by the Archbishop of Canterbury. Anglican churches have bishops and priests (men and, in many places, women), use the Book of Common Prayer and hymns, and are both Catholic and Protestant in style. In England, the local parish church is usually Anglican. Phrases: the Anglican Church, an Anglican vicar, Anglican cathedral.
examples from the lessons: Our village church is Anglican, and the vicar is called Reverend Sarah. | The Archbishop of Canterbury leads the Anglican Communion. | Anglicans sing hymns and say prayers from a prayer book. | My Aussie cousins go to the Anglican church in Sydney. | Westminster Abbey hosts Anglican services. | In America, Anglicans are called Episcopalians.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital A. Comes from Latin "Anglia" (England). "Church of England" is the English branch; Anglicanism is the whole tradition. Not the same as Catholic, though services may look similar.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An anniversary is the day exactly one or more years after an important event, which people remember or celebrate. 2) A wedding anniversary is the day each year when a married couple remembers their wedding. 3) A sad anniversary is the day remembering a death or disaster.
its sense in the lessons: Families celebrate wedding anniversaries with cards or a meal; schools and towns mark anniversaries of their founding. On the anniversary of a loved one's death, families may visit the grave or light a candle. In maths, counting anniversaries is counting whole years: an event, then its first, second, third anniversary. Phrases: wedding anniversary, silver/golden anniversary, the anniversary of, happy anniversary.
examples from the lessons: It's Mum and Dad's wedding anniversary, so we made them a card. | Nan and Grandpa had a golden anniversary party for fifty years of marriage. | The school celebrated the anniversary of its opening. | On the anniversary of Grandad's death, we visited his grave. | Happy anniversary! | The town marked the anniversary of the flood with a minute's silence.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; plural anniversaries (y → ies). Spelling: double n, -ersary. A birthday is a person's own anniversary of being born, but we just say "birthday". Silver = 25 years, golden = 50 years, diamond = 60 years of marriage.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An atheist is a person who believes there is no God or gods. 2) As an adjective, atheist describes such a person or view.
its sense in the lessons: In RE and ethics lessons, pupils learn that people hold many views: theists believe in God, atheists do not, and agnostics say they cannot know. Atheists can be kind and moral, just as religious people can; respect for different beliefs is part of school values. Phrases: be an atheist, an atheist view, atheists and believers.
examples from the lessons: My uncle is an atheist, but he still comes to our carol service. | An atheist does not believe in any god. | Atheists and Christians talked politely in the debate. | She became an atheist when she was older. | In ethics class, an atheist and a Muslim pupil shared their views. | Being an atheist doesn't mean you have no values.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: an atheist (use "an"). Noun for the belief: atheism. Spelling: a-the-ist (Greek "a" = without, "theos" = god). Not the same as agnostic (not sure) or humanist (a non-religious view based on reason and kindness).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A humanist is a person who lives by reason, science and kindness rather than religion, believing people can be good and make life meaningful without God. 2) (history) A humanist was a scholar of the Renaissance who studied the writings of ancient Greece and Rome. 3) As an adjective, humanist describes these ideas, like a humanist wedding or funeral.
its sense in the lessons: In RE many UK schools teach humanism alongside religions. Humanists hold ceremonies such as weddings, baby namings and funerals without prayers. In history lessons, Renaissance humanists brought back old books and ideas. Phrases: humanist ceremony, humanist wedding, humanist funeral, Humanists UK.
examples from the lessons: My aunt had a humanist wedding in a garden. | Humanists believe we should be kind because people matter. | The humanist speaker talked about Grandma's life at the funeral. | Erasmus was a famous Renaissance humanist. | In RE we compared Christian and humanist views of right and wrong. | A humanist uses reason and evidence to make choices.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a humanist. Noun humanism. Not the same as "humanitarian" (someone who helps people in need) or "humane" (kind, especially to animals).

part of speech: noun (a payslip, payslips) — US pay stub
meaning for a pupil: 1) (money) A payslip is a paper or digital note that an employer gives a worker with their pay, showing how much they earned and what was taken off for tax and other things.
its sense in the lessons: In adult life a payslip shows gross pay (before deductions), tax, national insurance or similar, pension, and net pay (take-home pay). Banks ask for payslips before giving a mortgage. In maths lessons pupils may work out net pay: gross pay minus deductions. Phrases: monthly payslip, check your payslip, gross and net pay on a payslip.
examples from the lessons: Mum checked her payslip to see if her overtime was paid. | The payslip showed tax taken off her wages. | The bank asked for three payslips. | Gross pay 2,000 minus deductions 400 gives net pay 1,600 on the payslip. | Dad's first payslip from his new job made him smile. | In America it's called a pay stub.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word (payslip); also written pay slip. Countable. Maths: net pay = gross pay − deductions. US/Canada: pay stub.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (Bible) An apostle is one of the twelve men Jesus chose to be his closest followers and send out to spread his teaching, such as Peter, James and John; Paul is also called an apostle. 2) An apostle is a strong supporter who spreads a new idea, as in "an apostle of clean energy".
its sense in the lessons: In RE, the Apostles spread Christianity after Pentecost; the Acts of the Apostles in the Bible tells their story. The Apostles' Creed is a short statement of Christian belief. Phrases: the twelve apostles, the Apostles' Creed, the Acts of the Apostles, an apostle of something.
examples from the lessons: Peter was one of the twelve apostles. | The apostles travelled far to tell people about Jesus. | Paul wrote many letters to churches and is called an apostle. | We said the Apostles' Creed in assembly. | The Twelve Apostles are also tall rocks on the coast of Australia. | She is an apostle of recycling and nags everyone to do it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: an apostle (use "an"). The t is silent: say "uh-POS-ul". Adjective apostolic. Disciples are followers; apostles are those "sent out".

meaning for a pupil: 1) (religion) Buddhism is a religion and way of life that follows the teaching of the Buddha (Siddhartha Gautama), who taught how to end suffering through wisdom, kindness and meditation.
its sense in the lessons: In RE pupils learn the Four Noble Truths and the Eightfold Path, the idea of karma and rebirth, and the goal of enlightenment (nirvana). Buddhists meditate, keep the Five Precepts (such as not harming living things), and visit temples with statues of the Buddha. Buddhism is common in Thailand, Sri Lanka, Japan, Tibet and other places. Phrases: Theravada Buddhism, Zen Buddhism, the teachings of Buddhism.
examples from the lessons: Buddhism began in India long ago. | In Buddhism, meditation helps calm the mind. | Lin's family follows Buddhism and visits the temple. | Buddhism teaches kindness to all living things. | We learned the Eightfold Path in our lesson on Buddhism. | Many Buddhists do not eat meat.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always capital B. A follower is a Buddhist; adjective Buddhist. Buddhists do not usually worship the Buddha as a god; they honour him as a teacher. Spelling: double d, then h — Buddhism.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (Bible) A covenant is a solemn promise or agreement between God and people, such as God's covenant with Noah (the rainbow), with Abraham, and with Moses and the Israelites. 2) (law, formal) A covenant is a formal written agreement, for example a rule in a house deed or a promise to give money to a charity.
its sense in the lessons: In RE the rainbow is the sign of God's covenant with Noah never to flood the earth again; circumcision is a sign of the covenant with Abraham; the Ark of the Covenant held the Ten Commandments. Christians speak of the "new covenant" through Jesus. Adults may sign a covenant when buying land or giving to charity. Phrases: make a covenant, keep the covenant, the Ark of the Covenant, the new covenant.
examples from the lessons: God made a covenant with Noah and put a rainbow in the sky. | The Israelites promised to keep the covenant. | The Ark of the Covenant was carried by priests. | Christians call the time of Jesus the new covenant. | The house has a covenant saying no shops may be built there. | A covenant is more serious than an ordinary promise.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Say "KUV-uh-nunt". Related to "convene" (come together). In everyday talk people usually say "agreement" or "promise"; covenant is solemn or formal.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Cremation is burning a dead person's body to ashes, as a respectful way of saying goodbye instead of burying it. 2) A cremation is the ceremony or event when this happens, often at a crematorium after a funeral service.
its sense in the lessons: In family life, after a death, relatives choose burial or cremation; the ashes may be kept in an urn, buried, or scattered in a special place. Hindus and Sikhs usually cremate; many Christians and humanists choose either; Jewish and Muslim tradition usually prefers burial. Phrases: burial or cremation, the cremation service, scatter the ashes, crematorium.
examples from the lessons: Grandpa wanted a cremation, so his ashes are by the sea. | The cremation took place at the crematorium after the church service. | We scattered Nan's ashes in her favourite garden. | In Hinduism, cremation is the usual custom. | The family talked gently about whether to choose burial or cremation. | After the cremation, people shared stories over tea.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable for events; uncountable for the practice. Verb cremate (cremated). Place: crematorium. A sad but normal part of life; talk about it gently.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Ethical means morally right, fair and honest. 2) Ethical means about right and wrong, as in "an ethical question". 3) Ethical shopping means buying things made fairly, without harming workers, animals or nature.
its sense in the lessons: In ethics lessons pupils decide if an action is ethical: is it fair, honest, kind, and what are the consequences? Adults talk about ethical businesses, ethical banks and fair-trade chocolate. Phrases: an ethical choice, an ethical problem, ethical shopping, it's not ethical to…
examples from the lessons: Is it ethical to keep the extra change the shop gave you? | The class debated an ethical question about animals. | We buy fair-trade bananas because they're more ethical. | Copying a friend's homework isn't ethical. | The doctor faced a hard ethical decision. | Our school tries to run an ethical tuck shop.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb ethically; opposite unethical. Noun ethics. Note: ethical (right and wrong) is different from "ethnic" (about cultures and peoples).

part of speech: noun, plural (the Israelites; singular an Israelite)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (Bible) The Israelites were the people of ancient Israel, the descendants of Jacob (also called Israel) and his twelve sons, whose story is told in the Hebrew Bible. 2) An Israelite is one person of that people.
its sense in the lessons: In RE the Israelites are slaves in Egypt, led out by Moses in the Exodus, wander in the desert for forty years eating manna, and then settle in the Promised Land. They are the ancestors of the Jewish people. Today's citizens of the modern state of Israel are called Israelis, not Israelites. Phrases: the twelve tribes of the Israelites, lead the Israelites, the Israelites in Egypt.
examples from the lessons: Pharaoh made the Israelites build cities. | Moses led the Israelites across the Red Sea. | The Israelites ate manna in the desert. | God gave the Israelites the Ten Commandments. | The walls of Jericho fell when the Israelites shouted. | The twelve tribes of the Israelites came from Jacob's sons.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital I. Plural noun as in the input. Trap: Israelites (ancient Bible people) vs Israelis (people of the modern country). Also called Hebrews in some stories.

part of speech: proper noun (Judas); noun (a Judas — a traitor)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (Bible) Judas Iscariot was one of Jesus' twelve disciples who betrayed him to the authorities for thirty pieces of silver, giving him away with a kiss. 2) A Judas is anyone who betrays a friend; it is a strong insult. 3) (Bible) Another disciple, Jude (Judas son of James), had the same name but was faithful.
its sense in the lessons: In Easter lessons the story of Judas shows betrayal and regret: he later felt terrible about what he had done. In everyday speech "a Judas kiss" means a show of friendship that hides betrayal. Phrases: Judas Iscariot, a Judas kiss, thirty pieces of silver, you Judas!
examples from the lessons: Judas betrayed Jesus with a kiss in the garden. | Judas was paid thirty pieces of silver. | Peter denied Jesus, but Judas betrayed him. | "You Judas!" shouted Sam when his friend told the secret. | After the betrayal, Judas was full of sorrow. | The traitor's handshake was a Judas kiss.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital J. Calling someone "a Judas" is a strong, hurtful insult. The input is lower case, but in texts it is a name. Many Jewish names come from Judah; do not use "Judas" against any group.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Ownership is the fact of owning something — having it as yours by right, like a house, a dog, or a bike. 2) Taking ownership of a task means accepting it as your own responsibility and doing it well.
its sense in the lessons: In adult life ownership of a house comes after a mortgage is paid; documents prove ownership of a car. In law and custody talk, ownership of things is split after a divorce. In school, teachers praise pupils who "take ownership" of their learning. In stories, arguments over ownership start many quarrels. Phrases: home ownership, proof of ownership, change of ownership, take ownership of.
examples from the lessons: The papers showed the farmer's ownership of the field. | The shop is under new ownership. | Home ownership is a dream for many families. | Our class took ownership of the vegetable garden. | The two boys argued about the ownership of the football. | Dog ownership means walking it every day.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Verb own; person owner. "-ship" makes a noun of state (friendship, membership). Owning something brings responsibilities, especially for pets.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (church) Presbyterian describes Protestant churches that are run by elders (presbyters) chosen by the members, not by bishops; the Church of Scotland is Presbyterian. 2) A Presbyterian is a member of such a church.
its sense in the lessons: Presbyterian churches come from the teaching of John Calvin and John Knox; they are common in Scotland, Northern Ireland, the USA, Canada, Australia, New Zealand and Korea. Services are plain, with Bible reading, sermon and psalms. Phrases: the Presbyterian Church, a Presbyterian minister, Presbyterian elders.
examples from the lessons: The Church of Scotland is a Presbyterian church. | Our Presbyterian minister preaches a short sermon. | My gran is a Presbyterian from Belfast. | Presbyterian churches are led by elders, not bishops. | The Presbyterian kirk has white walls and clear windows. | In Korea there are many big Presbyterian churches.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital P. Long word: pres-by-TEER-ee-un. Noun for the system: Presbyterianism. "Kirk" is the Scottish word for church.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal, law) Restitution is giving back something that was stolen or lost to its owner, or paying for damage you caused. 2) (ethics) Restitution is making things right after doing wrong, by repairing or repaying.
its sense in the lessons: In ethics lessons pupils learn that saying sorry is good, but restitution goes further: if you broke a window, you help pay for it. In law, a judge may order an offender to make restitution. In the Bible, Zacchaeus the tax collector promised to pay back four times what he had cheated. Phrases: make restitution, pay restitution, restitution for damage.
examples from the lessons: The judge ordered the boys to make restitution for the broken fence. | Zacchaeus made restitution by paying back four times as much. | Saying sorry is a start, but restitution is fixing it. | The museum made restitution of the stolen paintings. | She did extra chores as restitution for breaking the lamp. | Restitution helps the victim, not just the wrongdoer.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable; formal. Everyday words: paying back, making up for, making amends. In maths word problems "four times what he took" means multiply.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Sung is the form of "sing" used after have, has, had and be: "I have sung", "It was sung". 2) As an adjective, sung means performed by singing rather than speaking, as in "a sung service" or "sung prayers".
its sense in the lessons: In grammar lessons pupils learn sing, sang, sung (like ring, rang, rung; drink, drank, drunk). In church, a sung Mass or sung Eucharist has the prayers sung by choir and people. Phrases: have sung, was sung, sung Mass, unsung hero (a hero no one praises).
examples from the lessons: We have sung that song three times today. | The anthem was sung at the start of the match. | Happy Birthday was sung loudly by the whole class. | On Sundays there is a sung Mass at eleven. | The choir had sung beautifully. | The lollipop lady is an unsung hero of our school.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: past simple is sang ("I sang"); past participle is sung ("I have sung"). Wrong: "I have sang", "I sung yesterday" (said in some dialects, but not in school English). "Unsung" means not praised.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (religion) Christianity is the religion based on the life and teaching of Jesus Christ; Christians believe Jesus is the Son of God, who died and rose again, and they follow the Bible. 2) Christianity can also mean Christian people and churches as a whole.
its sense in the lessons: In RE pupils learn the main festivals (Christmas, Easter, Pentecost), the sacraments (baptism, communion), the Bible, prayer, and the many churches (Catholic, Orthodox, Protestant). Christianity is the largest religion in the world. Phrases: convert to Christianity, the history of Christianity, Christianity and other faiths.
examples from the lessons: Christianity began with Jesus and his disciples. | The cross is the main symbol of Christianity. | Saint Patrick brought Christianity to Ireland. | In Christianity, Easter is the most important festival. | We visited a church to learn more about Christianity. | Christianity teaches love of God and neighbour.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always capital C. A follower is a Christian; adjective Christian. Spelling: the h after C is silent ("kris-tee-AN-it-ee").

part of speech: adjective (divine, more divine); verb (divine, divines, divined, divining — to guess, to find water)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (religion) Divine means of God or a god, or coming from God, as in "divine love" or "divine help". 2) (informal) Divine means wonderful or delicious: "This cake is divine!" 3) To divine is to guess or discover something by a feeling; water divining is looking for water underground with a stick.
its sense in the lessons: In RE, Christians speak of Jesus as both human and divine; Hindus speak of many forms of the divine. In everyday talk a grown-up might say a chocolate pudding is "simply divine". Science pupils may hear that water divining has not been shown to work in fair tests. Phrases: divine intervention, divine love, the divine, simply divine.
examples from the lessons: Christians believe Jesus is divine. | The hymn praised God's divine love. | "Your soup is divine!" said Aunty Pat. | Some people say the rescue was divine intervention. | She divined from his face that something was wrong. | Water divining hasn't been proved by scientific tests.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb divinely; noun divinity (also RE in some schools). "Divine" as "delicious" is a bit posh and old-fashioned. Say "dih-VINE".

meaning for a pupil: 1) Equality is being equal: when people have the same rights, chances and respect, whatever their sex, skin colour, religion, disability or background. 2) (maths) Equality is when two amounts are the same; a statement with an equals sign, like 3 + 4 = 7, is an equality.
its sense in the lessons: In citizenship and history lessons, pupils learn about fights for equality: votes for women, civil rights, equal pay. In ethics, equality is a key part of fairness, though fairness sometimes means giving extra help to those who need it (equity). In maths, an equality must balance on both sides. Phrases: equality of opportunity, gender equality, racial equality, fight for equality.
examples from the lessons: Martin Luther King Jr fought for equality for Black Americans. | Our school values equality and respect. | Equality means everyone gets a fair chance. | In maths, 5 + 5 = 10 is an equality. | The sign = shows equality between two sides. | Women marched for equality at work.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Adjective equal; verb equal / equalise. Maths: equality (=) vs inequality (<, >). Equality is not exactly equity: equality gives everyone the same; equity gives each what they need to have a fair chance.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A firecracker is a small firework that explodes with a loud bang, often in a string of many. 2) (informal) A firecracker is a lively, energetic, quick-tempered person.
its sense in the lessons: At Chinese New Year and Diwali, people set off firecrackers to celebrate; in the USA they are popular on Independence Day. In safety lessons pupils learn: only adults should light fireworks, never pick up one that did not go off, and keep pets indoors. Phrases: set off firecrackers, a string of firecrackers, light a firecracker.
examples from the lessons: The firecrackers went bang-bang-bang at the New Year parade. | Dad lit the firecracker and stepped back. | Never hold a firecracker in your hand. | The dog hid under the bed when the firecrackers started. | Our new teacher is a real firecracker, full of energy. | Red paper from firecrackers covered the street.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; one word. UK children more often say "banger" or "firework". Fireworks are dangerous: burns and hearing damage happen every year. In many places it is against the law for children to buy them.

part of speech: verb (past and past participle of find: found); verb (found, founds, founded, founding — to start)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Found is the past of "find": "I found my keys." 2) To found something is to start or set up an organisation, school, city or company: "She founded a charity." 3) "Found" as an adjective means something that was lost and is found: "Lost and found". 4) "Be found to be" (formal) means turned out to be after checking.
its sense in the lessons: In stories "found" is everywhere: someone lost something and found it, or found a clue. In history, people founded towns, schools and churches; the person is the founder. Lost-property boxes at school are labelled "lost and found". Phrases: found out (discovered the truth), found it, lost and found, founded by.
examples from the lessons: I found a pound coin under the sofa! | We found out who ate the cake. | Saint Columba founded a monastery on Iona. | The school was founded by a group of nuns. | Check the lost and found box for your jumper. | The answer was found to be correct.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Two verbs share this spelling: find → found → found (irregular), and found → founded → founded (regular, "to start"). Trap: "founded" is NOT the past of find. "Find out" (discover) → "found out".

part of speech: noun (a gospel, gospels; the Gospel); adjective (gospel music)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (Bible) The Gospels are the four books of the New Testament — Matthew, Mark, Luke and John — that tell the life, teaching, death and rising of Jesus. 2) (church) The gospel is the "good news" of Jesus that Christians share. 3) Gospel (music) is a joyful style of Christian music with roots in African American churches. 4) (informal) "Gospel truth" or "take it as gospel" means something completely true.
its sense in the lessons: In church, the Gospel reading is often read standing, as a mark of respect. Gospel choirs sing with clapping and strong harmonies. In everyday talk, "Don't take everything you read online as gospel" means check it. Phrases: the Gospel of Luke, the gospel truth, gospel choir, preach the gospel.
examples from the lessons: Matthew, Mark, Luke and John are the four Gospels. | The priest read from the Gospel of John. | The gospel choir made everyone clap along. | It's the gospel truth — I didn't touch your sweets! | Don't take every website as gospel. | The disciples went out to preach the gospel.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital G often for the books or the Christian message; small g for music and "gospel truth". The word comes from Old English "good news". Countable for the books.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (religion) Judaism is the religion of the Jewish people, who believe in one God who made a covenant with Abraham and gave the Torah to Moses.
its sense in the lessons: In RE pupils learn about the synagogue, the rabbi, the Torah, the Sabbath (Shabbat), kosher food, and festivals such as Passover, Hanukkah, Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur. Judaism is one of the oldest religions; Christianity and Islam both grew from its roots. Phrases: Orthodox Judaism, Reform Judaism, convert to Judaism, the teachings of Judaism.
examples from the lessons: Judaism teaches that there is one God. | The Torah is the most holy book in Judaism. | In Judaism, Shabbat begins on Friday evening. | We visited a synagogue to learn about Judaism. | Rachel's family follows Reform Judaism. | Judaism has many festivals with special foods.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always capital J. A follower is a Jew; adjectives Jewish and Judaic. Say "JOO-day-iz-um". Being Jewish can mean faith, culture or family heritage — not all Jewish people are religious.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (health) A prescription is a note from a doctor (GP) saying which medicine a patient needs, which you take to a chemist or pharmacy to get it. 2) The medicine itself, given on a doctor's order, can be called a prescription. 3) (formal) A prescription is a firm rule or piece of advice about what should be done.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, after seeing the GP you may pick up a prescription at the pharmacy; some medicines need a prescription and some can be bought freely. Glasses need a prescription from an optician. In safety lessons pupils learn never to take someone else's prescription medicine. Phrases: write a prescription, fill a prescription (US), on prescription, prescription glasses, repeat prescription.
examples from the lessons: The doctor wrote me a prescription for ear drops. | Mum took the prescription to the chemist. | These tablets are only available on prescription. | Grandpa has a repeat prescription every month. | Never take medicine from someone else's prescription. | My new prescription glasses make the board clear.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Verb prescribe (prescribed). Trap: prescribe (a doctor orders) vs proscribe (to ban). Do not confuse with "subscription" (paying regularly for a magazine or app).

part of speech: noun, plural (Quakers; singular a Quaker); also the Religious Society of Friends
meaning for a pupil: 1) (church) Quakers are members of a Christian group called the Religious Society of Friends, who worship mostly in silence, believe there is "that of God" in every person, and work for peace, equality and honesty. 2) (old, informal) The name comes from a joke that they "quake" (tremble) before God.
its sense in the lessons: In RE and history lessons, pupils learn that Quakers have no priests; at a Meeting for Worship anyone may stand and speak if they feel moved. Quakers campaigned against slavery and war, and helped refugees. Quaker families started firms like Cadbury's and Rowntree's chocolate. Phrases: Quaker meeting, Quaker meeting house, a Quaker school.
examples from the lessons: Quakers sit together in silence during their meetings. | The Quakers were among the first to speak out against slavery. | The Cadbury family were Quakers. | Quakers refuse to fight in wars. | There is a small Quaker meeting house in our town. | Quakers believe every person has something of God inside them.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital Q. Plural as in the input; singular a Quaker. They often call themselves "Friends". Pennsylvania was started by a Quaker, William Penn. "Quaker Oats" is a brand name, not a church.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (work, UK, Ireland, Australia) Redundancy is losing your job because the employer no longer needs that job — for example when a factory closes — not because of anything you did wrong. 2) (money) Redundancy pay is money given to a worker who is made redundant. 3) (formal) Redundancy is having more of something than is needed, like spare parts kept "just in case" or repeated words.
its sense in the lessons: In adult life a parent may be "made redundant"; families then cut spending and the parent writes a new CV. Children may hear euphemisms like "let go" or "laid off" (US). In engineering, redundancy is good: a spare engine or backup computer keeps things safe. In writing lessons, redundancy means saying the same thing twice ("a free gift"). Phrases: be made redundant, redundancy pay, voluntary redundancy, face redundancy.
examples from the lessons: Dad was made redundant when the factory closed. | Mum got redundancy pay to help until she finds work. | Hundreds of workers faced redundancy. | It wasn't his fault — it was redundancy, not the sack. | Planes have redundancy: if one system fails, another takes over. | "Return back" has redundancy, because return already means go back.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural redundancies (y → ies). Adjective redundant. US/Canada say "laid off" or "layoffs". Redundancy is different from being sacked or fired (losing a job for doing something wrong).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (church) A sacrament is a holy ceremony in Christian churches, which Christians believe is an outward sign of God's grace (love and help) given to people. 2) The Blessed Sacrament (Catholic) is the bread blessed at Mass, which Catholics believe is Jesus' body.
its sense in the lessons: Catholic and Orthodox churches count seven sacraments: baptism, confirmation, Eucharist (Holy Communion), confession (reconciliation), anointing of the sick, marriage and holy orders. Most Protestant churches count two: baptism and the Lord's Supper. Quakers and the Salvation Army do not hold outward sacraments. Phrases: the seven sacraments, receive a sacrament, the Blessed Sacrament.
examples from the lessons: Baptism is the first sacrament for many Christians. | Catholics have seven sacraments. | Marriage is a sacrament in the Catholic Church. | The priest carried the Blessed Sacrament in procession. | Our RE teacher explained the sacrament of confirmation. | Most Protestant churches celebrate two sacraments.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Adjective sacramental. Spelling: sacra + ment (one c, one m before -ent). Related to "sacred" (holy).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Sorrow is a deep feeling of sadness, especially because of a loss, death or disappointment. 2) A sorrow is a thing that makes you very sad. 3) (formal) Sorrow is also feeling truly sorry for something wrong you did, as in "sorrow for sin".
its sense in the lessons: In stories, sorrow often follows a death or parting; writers show it by tears, silence or a heavy heart. At funerals people "share in your sorrow". In church, being sorry for sins is called sorrow or repentance. Phrases: in sorrow, great sorrow, joys and sorrows, drown your sorrows (try to forget sadness, often by drinking), more in sorrow than in anger.
examples from the lessons: The whole village felt sorrow when the old teacher died. | Her eyes were full of sorrow. | Life has joys and sorrows. | He showed real sorrow for what he had done. | "We share in your sorrow," said the card. | The song was slow and full of sorrow. | Losing the dog was a great sorrow to the family.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly uncountable; countable for particular sad things ("many sorrows"). Adjective sorrowful. It is a stronger, more formal word than "sadness". Not the same as "sorry", though related in meaning.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A trader is a person who buys and sells goods to make money, such as a market trader. 2) (money) A trader is a person who buys and sells shares, money or other goods on a stock market. 3) (history) Traders carried goods like spices, silk and furs between faraway lands.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, traders travel the Silk Road, and Viking traders sail to new lands. In everyday life, market traders call out prices and give change; in maths problems, traders buy at one price and sell at a higher one, and the difference is profit. Phrases: market trader, street trader, sole trader (a one-person business), fur trader.
examples from the lessons: The market trader sold apples three for a pound. | Viking traders sailed far to sell furs. | A trader buys low and sells high to make a profit. | The fruit trader gave me an extra orange. | Traders on the Silk Road carried silk from China. | Dad is a sole trader who runs his own plumbing business.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Verb trade (traded). Maths: profit = selling price − buying price; if the trader sells for less, it is a loss. Trap: trader vs traitor (a person who betrays) — they sound a little alike.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (church) A creed is a short statement of the main things a religion believes, said together in a service; the Apostles' Creed and the Nicene Creed are said in many churches. 2) A creed is any set of beliefs or principles someone lives by.
its sense in the lessons: In church, Christians stand and say the Creed: "I believe in God, the Father almighty, creator of heaven and earth…". In ethics and citizenship, "people of every race and creed" means of all religions and beliefs. Phrases: the Apostles' Creed, the Nicene Creed, say the creed, of every creed.
examples from the lessons: We said the Apostles' Creed at the start of assembly. | The Creed begins "I believe in God". | Our club welcomes people of every race and creed. | Kindness to animals is her creed. | The congregation stood for the Creed. | The Nicene Creed is said in many churches.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. The word comes from Latin "credo" (I believe), like "credit" and "incredible". Capital C when naming a church creed.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Mercy is kindness or forgiveness shown to someone you could punish or hurt. 2) (church) Christians, Jews and Muslims believe God is full of mercy, forgiving people who turn back to him. 3) A mercy is a lucky thing that you are thankful for: "It's a mercy nobody was hurt." 4) "At the mercy of" means in the power of someone or something.
its sense in the lessons: In stories a hero shows mercy to a beaten enemy; a cruel king shows none. In church services people pray "Lord, have mercy". In news, "a mercy mission" brings help to people in danger. Phrases: have mercy, show mercy, beg for mercy, at the mercy of, it's a mercy that, mercy me (old exclamation).
examples from the lessons: The king showed mercy and let the prisoner go. | "Lord, have mercy," prayed the people. | The little boat was at the mercy of the waves. | It's a mercy the rain stopped before the match. | The robber begged for mercy. | Blessed are the merciful, for they will be shown mercy. | The helicopter flew a mercy mission to the island.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly uncountable; plural mercies in "small mercies" (things to be glad about). Adjective merciful, merciless. Mercy is not the same as justice: justice gives what is fair; mercy gives more kindness than is deserved.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (Bible) Pontius Pilate was the Roman governor of Judea who questioned Jesus, found no fault in him, yet allowed him to be crucified, and then washed his hands to show he took no blame.
its sense in the lessons: In Easter lessons Pilate's story shows a leader who knows what is right but gives in to the crowd. "Washing your hands of something" (refusing responsibility) comes from this story. Christians name him in the Creed: "suffered under Pontius Pilate". Pilates (the exercise) is a different word, from a man named Joseph Pilates.
examples from the lessons: Pilate asked Jesus, "Are you the king of the Jews?" | Pilate said, "I find no fault in this man." | The crowd shouted, and Pilate gave in. | Pilate washed his hands in front of the people. | The Creed says Jesus "suffered under Pontius Pilate." | Mum does Pilates on Tuesdays — that's an exercise, not the governor!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital P; a name. Input is lower case. Trap: Pilate (governor, said "PIE-lut") vs Pilates (exercise, said "pih-LAH-teez") vs pilot (flies a plane).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A shipwreck is when a ship is destroyed or sinks at sea, by a storm, rocks or an accident. 2) A shipwreck is also the broken remains of a sunken ship. 3) To be shipwrecked is to be on a ship that is wrecked, often ending up on a shore or island.
its sense in the lessons: In stories like Robinson Crusoe and in the Bible (Paul's shipwreck on Malta), shipwreck starts an adventure of survival. In history and science lessons, divers study shipwrecks like the Titanic and the Mary Rose. In safety lessons, life jackets and lifeboats save people. Phrases: survive a shipwreck, be shipwrecked, the wreck of, a shipwreck diver.
examples from the lessons: Robinson Crusoe was shipwrecked on a lonely island. | Divers explored the shipwreck on the sea bed. | Paul survived a shipwreck on the way to Rome. | The lighthouse helps prevent shipwrecks on the rocks. | After the shipwreck, the sailors swam to shore. | Fish now live inside the old shipwreck.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; one word. Shorter form: wreck. Verb is usually passive: "They were shipwrecked." Spelling: ship + wreck (silent w).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (church, Bible) To anoint is to put holy oil on someone's head or body as a sign of blessing, healing, or being chosen by God, for example as a king or priest. 2) (informal) To anoint someone is to choose them for an important role, like "anointed as the next captain".
its sense in the lessons: In the Bible, the prophet Samuel anointed David as king; "Messiah" and "Christ" both mean "the anointed one". In church, oil is used at baptism, confirmation, ordination and for the sick (anointing of the sick). A British monarch is anointed at the coronation. Phrases: anoint with oil, the anointed one, anointing of the sick.
examples from the lessons: Samuel anointed David with oil to show he would be king. | The priest anointed the sick woman and prayed for her. | A woman anointed Jesus' feet with perfume. | The new king was anointed in the abbey. | The coach anointed Maya as our new captain. | "Christ" means "the anointed one".
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: anointed. Noun anointing. Spelling: one n after a, one n at the end: a-n-o-i-n-t. Formal word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (church) Baptists are members of Protestant Christian churches that baptise only believers old enough to choose, usually by full immersion in water, and in which each local church largely runs itself.
its sense in the lessons: Baptists are a big group in the USA (including the Southern Baptists), and are found in Wales, England, Australia, Canada and Africa. Famous Baptists include Martin Luther King Jr. Baptist services include hymns, Bible reading, sermon and prayer. Phrases: Southern Baptists, the Baptists down the road, Baptists and Methodists.
examples from the lessons: Baptists believe people should choose to be baptised. | Many Baptists live in the southern United States. | The Baptists held a picnic after the baptism in the river. | Baptists and Methodists sang together at the town service. | Martin Luther King Jr's father was also a Baptist minister. | Baptists usually baptise by putting people right under the water.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital B; plural of Baptist. John the Baptist is a single Bible person, not a member of these churches.

part of speech: verb (past participle of beat: beaten); adjective (beaten)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Beaten is the form of "beat" after have or be: lost to someone in a game ("We were beaten 3–0"). 2) Beaten means hit many times: "The traveller was beaten by robbers." 3) Beaten (cooking) means mixed hard with a fork or whisk: "beaten eggs". 4) Beaten (adjective) can mean tired and defeated, or flattened by walking, as in "a beaten path".
its sense in the lessons: In sport and stories, being beaten is losing; good players learn from it. In the parable of the Good Samaritan the traveller is "beaten and left half dead". In cooking lessons, recipes ask for beaten eggs. Phrases: be beaten, beaten up (rude violence), off the beaten track (in a quiet, faraway place), can't be beaten (the best).
examples from the lessons: We were beaten by the other school, but we played well. | Robbers left the man beaten by the side of the road. | Add two beaten eggs to the flour. | We walked along a beaten path through the woods. | Our cottage was off the beaten track. | This pizza can't be beaten! | Hitting people is never right; nobody should be beaten.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb forms: beat, beats, beat (past), beaten (past participle), beating. Trap: "We beat them" (past) vs "We were beaten" (passive). In sports scores, the first number is usually the winner's.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A certificate is an official paper that proves something is true, like a birth certificate, a certificate of baptism, or a certificate for passing an exam. 2) A certificate is a prize paper given for an achievement, like a swimming certificate or a star-of-the-week certificate. 3) (film) A certificate is the age rating of a film, such as PG or 12.
its sense in the lessons: In school, pupils get certificates in assembly for good work, attendance or swimming badges. In adult life, important certificates are kept safe: birth, marriage and death certificates, exam certificates for a CV, and house papers. A film's certificate tells parents which ages it suits. Phrases: birth certificate, death certificate, get a certificate, award a certificate, a PG certificate.
examples from the lessons: I got a certificate for swimming twenty-five metres. | Mum keeps our birth certificates in a folder. | The head gave out certificates in Friday assembly. | You need your exam certificates when you apply for a job. | The film has a 12 certificate, so I'm too young. | The baptism certificate shows the church's name.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Say "ser-TIF-ik-ut". Verb certify (to state officially). Keep certificates safe; copies may need to be official.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Confirmation is a message or proof that something is true or definitely happening, like a booking confirmation. 2) (church) Confirmation is a Christian ceremony in which a young person or adult, usually already baptised, confirms their faith for themselves, often with a bishop laying hands on them and praying.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, adults get confirmation emails for orders, tickets and appointments. In science, an experiment that matches the prediction gives confirmation. In church life, Catholic children often have confirmation at around ten to fourteen, choosing a saint's name; Anglicans and Lutherans also confirm young people. Phrases: booking confirmation, get confirmation, confirmation of, confirmation class, be confirmed.
examples from the lessons: We got an email confirmation for the cinema tickets. | The teacher waited for confirmation that the trip was on. | My sister's confirmation is at the cathedral with the bishop. | At confirmation, Ciara chose the name Brigid. | The test result gave confirmation of our guess. | Confirmation classes are on Wednesday evenings.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable or uncountable. Verb confirm (confirmed). In the church sense people say "be confirmed": "I was confirmed when I was eleven."

part of speech: proper noun (Eden, the Garden of Eden); noun (an Eden — a paradise)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (Bible) The Garden of Eden was the beautiful garden where, in Genesis, God put the first people, Adam and Eve, before they disobeyed by eating the forbidden fruit and had to leave. 2) An Eden is any very beautiful, peaceful place, like a paradise.
its sense in the lessons: In RE the story of Eden is about trust, temptation and choices; the serpent tempts Eve and Adam to eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. Writers call a lovely garden or island "an Eden". The Eden Project in Cornwall is a famous garden in giant domes. Phrases: the Garden of Eden, a little Eden, east of Eden.
examples from the lessons: God placed Adam and Eve in the Garden of Eden. | The serpent tempted Eve in Eden. | After eating the fruit, Adam and Eve had to leave Eden. | Nan's garden in summer is a little Eden. | We visited the Eden Project and its rainforest dome. | The island looked like an Eden of palm trees and blue sea.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital E. The input is lower case, but the word is a name. The Bible says "fruit", not "apple" — the apple is a later picture tradition.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (church) Episcopal means about bishops, or led by bishops, as in "episcopal churches". 2) (church) The Episcopal Church is the Anglican church in the USA; the Scottish Episcopal Church is the Anglican church in Scotland.
its sense in the lessons: In RE, churches are sorted by how they are led: episcopal (by bishops: Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican), presbyterian (by elders), and congregational (each congregation decides). In the USA and Scotland, "Episcopalian" is the word for an Anglican. Phrases: the Episcopal Church, Scottish Episcopal Church, episcopal visit.
examples from the lessons: The Episcopal church on our street has a red door. | In the USA, Anglicans are called Episcopalians. | The Scottish Episcopal Church has its own bishops. | Catholic and Orthodox churches are episcopal, because bishops lead them. | The bishop made an episcopal visit to our parish. | Presbyterian churches are not episcopal.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital E for the church names, small e for the general adjective. Noun for a member: Episcopalian. From Greek "episkopos" (overseer), which also gives "bishop".

meaning for a pupil: 1) Equity is fairness: treating people so each has what they need for a fair chance, not just exactly the same. 2) (money) Equity in a house is the part of its value that the owner truly owns — the price minus what is still owed on the mortgage. 3) (money) Equities are shares in companies. 4) (law, UK) Equity is a part of the law that lets judges act fairly where strict rules would be unjust.
its sense in the lessons: In school and ethics, equity means e.g. a ramp for a wheelchair user, or extra reading help, so everyone can join in. In adult money talk, as the mortgage is paid, home equity grows. In maths, equity = value − debt: a house worth 300 thousand with 200 thousand owed has 100 thousand equity. Phrases: equity and fairness, home equity, negative equity (owing more than the house is worth), equality and equity.
examples from the lessons: Equity means giving each pupil the help they need. | The taller boxes for shorter children showed equity, not just equality. | As they pay the mortgage, Mum and Dad's equity grows. | Negative equity means the house is worth less than the loan. | Grandpa invests in equities. | The judge used equity to reach a fair decision.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable in the fairness sense. Maths: equity = value of asset − amount owed. Trap: equity (fair to each person's needs) vs equality (the same for everyone). Adjective equitable (fair).

part of speech: adjective (faithful, more faithful); noun (the faithful — plural)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Faithful means loyal and true — always staying with and supporting a person, a team or a promise. 2) (church) Faithful means firmly believing in God and keeping your faith; "the faithful" are the believers. 3) Faithful means exact and true to the original: "a faithful copy". 4) A faithful husband or wife is loyal to their partner and does not love someone else.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, a faithful dog or friend sticks by the hero; the reader trusts them. In church, "O come, all ye faithful" is a famous carol. In the Bible, Jesus says "Well done, good and faithful servant". Old Faithful is a geyser in the USA that erupts regularly. Phrases: faithful friend, faithful servant, remain faithful, the faithful, ever faithful.
examples from the lessons: The faithful dog waited every day at the station. | Grandad was a faithful supporter of his football club for life. | "O come, all ye faithful," sang the choir. | The faithful filled the church for Easter. | Her drawing was a faithful copy of the painting. | Ruth stayed faithful to Naomi and went with her.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb faithfully: letters to someone you don't know end "Yours faithfully" (UK). Noun faithfulness. Opposite unfaithful. Spelling: faith + ful (one l).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (church) A godparent is a person chosen by a child's family to promise at the child's baptism to help them grow up in the Christian faith, and to be a special adult friend through life. A woman is a godmother; a man is a godfather.
its sense in the lessons: In family life godparents often send birthday presents, come to big events and give advice. In some families they would care for the child if the parents died. In fairy tales a fairy godmother grants wishes (Cinderella). Humanist and non-religious families sometimes choose "guide parents" or "supporting adults". Phrases: be a godparent, my godmother, my godfather, fairy godmother, godchild.
examples from the lessons: My godmother always sends me a book for my birthday. | Uncle Joe was chosen to be my baby cousin's godparent. | The godparents held the baby at the font. | Cinderella's fairy godmother turned a pumpkin into a coach. | My godfather took me to my first football match. | Godparents promise to help the child learn about faith.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; one word. The child is a godchild (goddaughter, godson). Not a legal guardian unless chosen in a will. "Godfather" can also mean a crime boss in films — a different use.

part of speech: noun (a goody, goodies); exclamation (goody!, goody gumdrops); noun (goody-goody)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) Goodies are nice things, especially treats such as sweets, cakes or small presents: "a bag of goodies". 2) (informal) A goody is a good character in a story or film, the opposite of a baddie. 3) (informal, childish) "Goody!" is a happy shout meaning "great!" 4) (informal, unkind) A goody-goody is a child who always tries to look good to grown-ups, in a smug way.
its sense in the lessons: Party bags are full of goodies; children play "goodies and baddies". Saying "goody-goody" to someone is mildly teasing and can hurt. Phrases: goody bag, goodies and baddies, oh goody!, goody two-shoes (a too-perfect person).
examples from the lessons: Every guest got a goody bag at the party. | Gran brought a box of goodies from the bakery. | In the film, the goodies win in the end. | "We're having pizza tonight." "Oh goody!" | He's such a goody-goody, always telling the teacher. | Let's play goodies and baddies in the park.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural goodies (y → ies). Also spelled "goodie". All senses are informal or childish. "Goody two-shoes" and "goody-goody" are teasing, so use kindly or not at all.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A hospice is a special home or hospital where people who are very ill and are not expected to get better are cared for kindly and kept comfortable until they die. 2) Hospice care can also be given at home by hospice nurses. 3) (history) A hospice was once a house where travellers or pilgrims could rest, often run by monks.
its sense in the lessons: In family life a grandparent may move to a hospice near the end of life; staff focus on comfort, pain relief and family time, not on cure. Children's hospices care for very ill children and their families, with play rooms and gardens. Schools often raise money for local hospices. Phrases: hospice care, a children's hospice, hospice nurse, in a hospice.
examples from the lessons: Grandma spent her last weeks in a peaceful hospice. | The hospice nurses were so kind to our family. | Our school ran a sponsored walk for the children's hospice. | The hospice has a garden where families can sit. | Hospice care helps people feel comfortable, not alone. | Long ago, monks ran a hospice for travellers in the mountains.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Say "HOS-pis". Related: hospital, hospitality (all from Latin for "guest"). A hospice is not a place of failure: its aim is comfort and dignity. Euphemisms like "passed away peacefully at the hospice" are common in death notices.

part of speech: noun (a martin, martins — bird); proper noun (Martin — name)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A martin is a small bird of the swallow family, such as the house martin, which builds a mud nest under the roofs of houses and flies south in winter. 2) Martin is a common boy's first name and a surname. 3) (church) Saint Martin of Tours was a soldier who cut his cloak in half to share with a freezing beggar; he is remembered for kindness.
its sense in the lessons: In science and nature lessons, house martins, sand martins and purple martins are watched in spring and summer; they catch insects in the air and migrate. In history, Martin Luther began the Protestant Reformation, and Martin Luther King Jr led the civil rights movement for equality. Phrases: house martin, sand martin, Saint Martin, Martin Luther King Jr.
examples from the lessons: House martins built a mud nest under our roof. | The martins flew south when the weather turned cold. | Sand martins nest in holes in river banks. | Saint Martin shared his cloak with a poor man. | Martin Luther King Jr dreamed of equality for all. | Martin from next door helped us fix the fence.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Small m for the bird; capital M for the name. Countable for the bird (martins). A martin is related to the swallow but has a shorter tail; the house martin has a white patch on its back.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Misconduct is bad or wrong behaviour, especially by a person at work or in a responsible job who breaks the rules. 2) (law, work) Gross misconduct is very serious wrong behaviour, such as stealing or violence at work, that can get someone sacked at once.
its sense in the lessons: In adult life, a worker can be dismissed for misconduct (that is not redundancy, which is not their fault). In sport, a player may be fined or banned for misconduct. In school, behaviour policies may use "misconduct" for serious rule-breaking. Phrases: gross misconduct, professional misconduct, accused of misconduct, sacked for misconduct.
examples from the lessons: The footballer was banned for misconduct. | The worker lost his job for gross misconduct after stealing money. | The doctor was investigated for professional misconduct. | Cheating in the exam counts as misconduct. | The club fined the player for misconduct towards the referee. | Misconduct is when someone breaks the rules of their job.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable, formal. Prefix mis- means "badly or wrongly" (misbehave, mistake, misspell). Everyday words: bad behaviour, wrongdoing. Say "mis-KON-dukt".

meaning for a pupil: 1) (church) Pentecostal describes Christian churches that put strong weight on the Holy Spirit's gifts — such as healing, lively praise and speaking in tongues — like the disciples at Pentecost. 2) A Pentecostal is a member of such a church. 3) Pentecostal can also mean about the feast of Pentecost.
its sense in the lessons: Pentecostal churches are among the fastest-growing in the world, strong in Africa, Latin America, the USA and in many cities of the UK. Services often have loud music, hand-raising, clapping and prayer for healing. Phrases: Pentecostal church, Pentecostal worship, a Pentecostal pastor.
examples from the lessons: Kofi's family goes to a Pentecostal church with a big band. | Pentecostal worship is lively, with clapping and dancing. | The Pentecostal pastor prayed for the sick. | Pentecostals believe the Holy Spirit still gives gifts today. | Our town's Pentecostal church meets in an old cinema. | The name Pentecostal comes from the feast of Pentecost.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital P. Noun for the movement: Pentecostalism. "Speaking in tongues" means praying in a language the speaker has not learned, which Pentecostals believe is a gift of the Spirit.

part of speech: noun (a plague, plagues; the plague); verb (plague, plagues, plagued, plaguing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A plague is a serious disease that spreads quickly and kills many people; "the plague" usually means bubonic plague, the Black Death of the Middle Ages, spread by fleas on rats. 2) (Bible) The ten plagues were the disasters God sent on Egypt in Exodus — such as frogs, locusts, darkness and the death of the firstborn — so Pharaoh would free the Israelites. 3) A plague of something is a huge, annoying number of it: "a plague of wasps". 4) To plague someone is to keep bothering or troubling them.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, the Great Plague and the village of Eyam, which shut itself off to stop the spread, show courage and how germs spread. In science, pupils learn plague is caused by bacteria and can now be treated with antibiotics. In everyday talk, "avoid it like the plague" means stay right away. Phrases: the plague, a plague of locusts, the ten plagues, avoid like the plague, plagued by.
examples from the lessons: The plague spread through the city, carried by fleas on rats. | The fourth plague was swarms of flies. | Locusts came in a plague and ate the crops. | The village of Eyam stayed apart so the plague would not spread. | Our picnic was plagued by wasps. | I avoid spiders like the plague. | He was plagued by worries before the test.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable (plagues), but "the plague" for the disease. Say "playg" — the -ue is silent (like vague, league). Verb forms plagued, plaguing.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (law) Probation is when a person who broke the law is allowed to stay out of prison but must behave well and meet regularly with a probation officer for a set time. 2) (work) Probation is a trial time at the start of a new job, when the employer checks that the new worker is suitable. 3) (school, US) Academic probation is a warning time for a student whose marks or behaviour are too poor.
its sense in the lessons: In adult life, a new teacher or nurse may be "on probation" for the first months. In law, probation gives offenders a chance to change instead of prison; breaking the rules can mean being sent to prison. Phrases: on probation, probation officer, a probation period, put on probation, break probation.
examples from the lessons: The young man was put on probation instead of going to prison. | He meets his probation officer every week. | Mum is still on probation at her new job. | After the probation period, she got a permanent contract. | If he breaks the rules of his probation, he could go to prison. | Our new puppy is "on probation" until it stops chewing shoes!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Adjective probationary ("probationary period"). Related to "prove" and "probe" (test). Probation (outside prison with rules) is different from parole (early release from prison with rules).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (church, history) The Reformation was the time, about five hundred years ago in Europe, when some Christians broke away from the Roman Catholic Church and started Protestant churches. 2) A reformation is a big change that makes something better, especially a person's behaviour or a system. 3) (formal) The act of reforming something, putting it right again.
its sense in the lessons: In history and religious education lessons the Reformation explains why there are Catholic and Protestant churches, and names like Martin Luther come up. In everyday or story language a «reformation» of a person means they changed their bad ways. Phrases: «the Protestant Reformation», «a complete reformation», «a reformation of character».
examples from the lessons: We learned that the Reformation split the Church in Western Europe. | Martin Luther is famous for starting the Reformation in Germany. | After the Reformation, many churches held services in English instead of Latin. | The new head teacher brought about a reformation of the school rules. | The story tells of a thief's reformation into an honest man. | The town hall needed a total reformation of the way it spent money. | Our RE teacher drew a timeline of the Reformation on the board.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital R for the historical event: «the Reformation». As a common noun it is countable: «a reformation». Do not confuse with «re-formation» (forming again, as a band re-forming). Related: reform (verb and noun), reformer, Protestant. Christians of different churches tell the story of the Reformation in different ways; be fair to both sides.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A refugee is a person who has had to leave their home country because of war, danger or being treated cruelly, and who has gone to live somewhere safer. 2) More loosely, anyone who has had to escape from a place: «refugees from the flood».
its sense in the lessons: In geography, history and citizenship lessons refugees come up in topics on war, migration and human rights. In stories, a refugee child often has to learn a new language and make friends in a new school. Phrases: «refugee camp», «refugee status», «asylum seeker», «flee as a refugee», «welcome refugees».
examples from the lessons: A new girl in our class is a refugee from a country at war. | The family lived in a refugee camp for two years. | Refugees often leave with only what they can carry. | Our school collected warm coats for refugees. | Many people became refugees after the earthquake destroyed their towns. | The book tells the story of a refugee boy crossing the sea. | Countries have laws that protect refugees.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one refugee, two refugees; stress on the last part: ref-u-GEE. A refugee is not the same as a migrant: a migrant may move by choice (for work), a refugee has to flee. An asylum seeker is someone who has asked for protection and is still waiting for an answer. Speak respectfully: refugees are ordinary people in a hard situation.

part of speech: verb (snoop, snoops, snooped, snooping); noun (a snoop, snoops)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To snoop is to look secretly around a place or into someone's private things to find out about them. 2) A snoop is a person who snoops, someone nosy. 3) (informal) To snoop on someone is to spy on them or watch what they do.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life snooping means poking into things that are not yours, like reading someone's diary or looking in drawers; it is seen as rude. In stories detectives and nosy neighbours snoop to find clues. Phrases: «snoop around», «snoop on someone», «snoop through», «a nosy snoop».
examples from the lessons: Stop snooping in my bag! | My little brother snooped around my room while I was out. | The detective snooped through the old letters looking for a clue. | Our neighbour is such a snoop; she always watches from her window. | I caught him snooping on my phone. | The cat snooped about the kitchen for scraps. | Apps should not snoop on what children do online.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly informal. Past: snooped. Usually negative: calling someone a snoop is a mild insult. Similar: pry, nose about, spy. «Snoopy» is the name of a famous cartoon dog, and «snoopy» (adjective) means nosy.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Your spouse is the person you are married to: your husband or your wife. 2) (formal, law) The word used on forms and in law for a married partner, whatever their sex.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday talk people say husband, wife or partner; «spouse» is the word on official forms, in law and in stiff writing. Children meet it in forms, stories about weddings and family trees. Phrases: «spouse or partner», «his spouse», «a surviving spouse» (one whose husband or wife has died).
examples from the lessons: The form asks for your name and your spouse's name. | Each guest may bring their spouse to the dinner. | In the law, a spouse can inherit money when their husband or wife dies. | My aunt and her spouse live in Dublin. | The king's spouse is called the queen consort. | Spouses often share a bank account. | The teacher wrote «spouse» on the family-tree worksheet.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable, formal. Plural: spouses. Not used for a boyfriend or girlfriend who is not married to you (that is «partner»). Gender-neutral: a spouse may be a husband or a wife.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) A stakeholder is a person or group who is affected by something, such as a plan or a business, and so cares how it turns out. 2) (business, money) Someone who owns a share in a company or has money in it. 3) (old use) A person who holds the money that people have bet, until the winner is known.
its sense in the lessons: In school and business talk «stakeholders» are everyone with an interest: pupils, parents and teachers are the stakeholders of a school. It is a stiff, office or exam word. Phrases: «key stakeholders», «consult the stakeholders», «all stakeholders».
examples from the lessons: Parents, pupils and teachers are all stakeholders in the school. | The council talked to local stakeholders before building the park. | A shop's stakeholders include its workers, customers and owners. | The report was sent to every stakeholder. | Farmers are big stakeholders in decisions about water. | Our project plan lists the stakeholders and what each one wants. | The company must listen to its stakeholders, not only its bosses.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable, formal and business-like; in plain speech say «people who care about it» or «people affected». Often in the plural. Not the same as a shareholder (who owns shares), though shareholders are one kind of stakeholder.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) The taxman is the government office that collects taxes, spoken of as if it were one person. 2) A person who collects taxes for the government.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday talk adults say «the taxman» when they mean the tax office (in the UK, HMRC; in the USA, the IRS). In old stories and the Bible a taxman (tax collector) was often disliked. Phrases: «pay the taxman», «owe the taxman», «the taxman takes a cut».
examples from the lessons: Dad grumbled that the taxman takes a big part of his pay. | You must tell the taxman how much money you earn. | In the story, the taxman came to the village every spring. | Mum owes the taxman a little money this year. | The shop has to keep records for the taxman. | In the Bible, Zacchaeus was a taxman who changed his ways. | Everyone has to pay the taxman, even famous people.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal; plural «taxmen». Usually «the taxman», like a nickname for the tax office. Formal word: tax collector or tax authority. Not rude, but often said with a grumble.

part of speech: noun (a tenant, tenants); verb (tenant, tenants, tenanted — rare, formal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A tenant is a person who pays rent to live in a house or flat, or to use land or a building, that belongs to someone else (the landlord). 2) (law) Anyone who has the right to use a property for a time. 3) (rare, formal) To tenant a place is to live in it as a tenant.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday adult life families are either owners or tenants (renters); tenants pay rent each month to a landlord. In maths problems a tenant's rent is a regular payment to add up. In history and stories, tenant farmers worked land owned by a lord. Phrases: «tenant and landlord», «the previous tenants», «a tenant farmer», «tenants' rights».
examples from the lessons: We are tenants, so we pay rent to the landlord. | The new tenants moved in next door yesterday. | A tenant must look after the flat and pay the rent on time. | The landlord fixed the boiler for his tenants. | If a tenant pays four hundred pounds a month, how much is that in a year? | Long ago, tenant farmers gave part of their crops to the lord. | The shop is empty and needs a new tenant.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Opposite: landlord (or landlady). In the USA people also say «renter». Do not confuse «tenant» with «tenet» (a belief or principle). Maths: rent per month × 12 = rent per year.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (church) The Trinity is the Christian belief that there is one God who is three persons: the Father, the Son (Jesus) and the Holy Spirit. 2) A trinity is any group of three things or people that belong closely together.
its sense in the lessons: In religious education Christians believe in the Holy Trinity, and it is shown with symbols such as the shamrock or a triangle; Trinity Sunday is a feast in the church year. Many churches, schools and colleges are named Trinity. In everyday writing «a trinity» is a set of three. Phrases: «the Holy Trinity», «Trinity Sunday», «Trinity College», «an unholy trinity» (three bad things together, joking).
examples from the lessons: Christians believe in the Trinity: Father, Son and Holy Spirit. | Saint Patrick is said to have used a shamrock to explain the Trinity. | Our church is called Holy Trinity Church. | The priest preached about the Trinity on Trinity Sunday. | Reading, writing and maths are the trinity of basic skills. | The triangle on the window stands for the Trinity. | Wind, rain and cold were the trinity that ruined our picnic.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital T for the Christian belief. Countable when it means any set of three. Jews and Muslims do not believe in the Trinity; Christians say it is a mystery that is hard to explain fully. Related: triple, trio, tri- (three).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Universal means true for, done by or belonging to everyone or everything, in every place. 2) Something universal works in all cases: a universal remote works with any TV. 3) Belonging to the whole universe: universal laws of nature. 4) (formal) A universal is an idea or quality that is the same everywhere.
its sense in the lessons: In science, laws such as gravity are called universal because they work everywhere. In citizenship lessons people talk about «universal human rights» and «universal suffrage» (everyone can vote). In everyday life a universal charger or plug fits many devices. Phrases: «universal truth», «universal language», «a universal favourite», «universal credit» (a UK benefit).
examples from the lessons: Smiling is a universal sign of being happy. | Gravity is a universal force: it pulls on everything with mass. | Music is sometimes called a universal language. | Dad bought a universal charger that fits all our phones. | Every child has the universal right to an education. | Chocolate ice cream is a universal favourite in our class. | Universal Credit is money from the government that helps some families in the UK.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective; adverb «universally». Starts with a «you» sound, so we say «a universal», not «an universal». Something «universal» is not always true just because many people say it; check. Related: universe, universally, university (a different meaning, a place of study).

part of speech: noun (a vat, vats); noun (VAT, uncountable — UK, money)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A vat is a very large tank or barrel for holding liquids, used in factories, breweries and dye works. 2) (UK, money) VAT (value added tax) is a tax added to the price of most things you buy in shops; you say each letter, V-A-T, or «vat».
its sense in the lessons: In stories and factories vats hold wine, beer, cheese milk or dye; in cartoons a villain may fall into a vat. In the UK and Ireland VAT is part of the price in shops, and in maths problems you may need to add VAT as a percentage. Phrases: «a vat of», «plus VAT», «including VAT», «VAT at twenty per cent».
examples from the lessons: Grapes are crushed in big wooden vats. | The factory had huge vats of chocolate. | The workers stirred the cloth in a vat of blue dye. | The price is fifty pounds plus VAT. | VAT in the UK is usually twenty per cent of the price. | If a toy costs ten pounds before VAT at twenty per cent, it costs twelve pounds with VAT. | Books and children's clothes have no VAT in the UK.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «vat» (tank) is countable: two vats. «VAT» (tax) is written in capitals and is uncountable. The USA has sales tax, not VAT. Maths: price with VAT = price × (1 + rate); twenty per cent VAT means multiply by 1.2. Do not confuse with «vet» (animal doctor).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Worldwide means happening or found in all parts of the world. 2) As an adverb, worldwide means all over the world: «sold worldwide».
its sense in the lessons: In geography and science, things like climate change, pandemics and the internet are worldwide. In everyday life a worldwide shop delivers to any country. Phrases: «worldwide famous», «a worldwide problem», «known worldwide», «the World Wide Web» (written as three words).
examples from the lessons: Football is popular worldwide. | The flu spread worldwide in a few months. | The book sold millions of copies worldwide. | Plastic in the oceans is a worldwide problem. | The World Wide Web lets people share pages worldwide. | This company has shops worldwide. | Our school took part in a worldwide day of reading.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word, no hyphen (sometimes «world-wide» in older writing). Same form for adjective and adverb. Similar: global, international, all over the world.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Anonymous means made, given or done by someone whose name is not known or not told. 2) A person who is anonymous is not named or not known. 3) Something plain and dull with nothing special about it can be called anonymous: «an anonymous grey building».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life you may see an anonymous letter, an anonymous gift to a charity, or an anonymous survey where you do not write your name. Online safety lessons teach that people can be anonymous online, so you cannot always know who they are. In poetry books «Anonymous» or «Anon.» means the poet's name is unknown. Phrases: «remain anonymous», «an anonymous donor», «an anonymous tip».
examples from the lessons: Someone left an anonymous note on my desk. | An anonymous donor gave the hospital a lot of money. | The survey is anonymous, so do not write your name. | The poem was written by Anonymous. | The man wanted to stay anonymous, so the paper did not print his name. | Online, people can be anonymous, so be careful who you talk to. | The office was in an anonymous grey building.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective; adverb «anonymously»; noun «anonymity». Spelling: a-n-o-n-y-m-o-u-s; stress on the second part: a-NON-y-mous. Short form «Anon.». Being anonymous online does not make bad behaviour all right.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An appraisal is a careful judgement of how good, useful or valuable something or someone is. 2) (work) A meeting at work where a manager talks with a worker about how well they are doing. 3) (money) An official judgement of how much something, such as a house or a ring, is worth.
its sense in the lessons: In adult work life many people have a yearly appraisal with their boss. When a family buys or sells a house, an expert makes an appraisal of its value. In school, teachers make an appraisal of your work. It is a formal word; plain words are «review», «judgement», «valuation». Phrases: «a performance appraisal», «a fair appraisal», «an appraisal of the damage».
examples from the lessons: Mum has her appraisal at work next week. | The expert gave an appraisal of the old painting. | The bank wanted an appraisal of the house before lending money. | The coach gave an honest appraisal of our game. | After the storm, the council made an appraisal of the damage. | My teacher's appraisal of my story was very kind. | The ring's appraisal said it was worth a lot.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable, formal. Verb «appraise» (to judge the value). Do not confuse «appraise» with «apprise» (to tell someone) or «praise» (to say good things); an appraisal can be bad as well as good.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (church, Bible) The Ascension is the event when, Christians believe, Jesus rose up into heaven forty days after he rose from the dead. 2) (formal) An ascension is the act of rising or going up. 3) (formal) Coming to a high position, such as a king coming to the throne (more often «accession»).
its sense in the lessons: In religious education, Ascension Day is a Christian feast day; the story is told in the Gospel of Luke and the Acts of the Apostles. Ascension Island is a small island in the Atlantic. In formal writing «ascension» means going up, like a balloon's ascension. Phrases: «Ascension Day», «the Ascension of Jesus», «the ascension of a balloon».
