examples from the lessons: Christians remember the Ascension of Jesus on Ascension Day. | The Bible says Jesus was taken up into a cloud at his Ascension. | Our church window shows the Ascension. | We watched the slow ascension of the hot-air balloon. | Ascension Island is in the middle of the Atlantic Ocean. | The climbers' ascension of the mountain took three days. | The vicar explained the Ascension to the children.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital A for the Christian feast. In everyday words, «ascent» is more common for climbing or rising. Related: ascend (verb), ascent. «Accession» is the usual word for a king or queen coming to the throne.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A chronic illness or problem lasts a long time or keeps coming back. 2) A chronic habit is one a person has had for a long time and cannot stop: «a chronic liar». 3) (UK, informal) Very bad: «The film was chronic».
its sense in the lessons: In health and science lessons «chronic» illnesses like asthma or diabetes are long-lasting, opposite to «acute» ones that come suddenly and pass. In news, «chronic shortages» are problems that never go away. In British slang, «chronic» means awful. Phrases: «chronic pain», «chronic illness», «a chronic shortage», «chronically ill».
examples from the lessons: Grandad has chronic back pain. | Asthma is a chronic illness, but medicine helps. | The town has a chronic shortage of doctors. | He is a chronic worrier and frets about everything. | My little sister is a chronic nail-biter. | That match was chronic; we lost ten nil! (UK, informal) | Chronic tiredness can be a sign that you need to see a doctor.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective; adverb «chronically». Opposite in medicine: acute. Trap: chronic does NOT mean «very serious»; it means «long-lasting». The «ch» sounds like «k»: KRON-ik. Related: chronicle, chronology (all about time).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (Bible, church) The Crucifixion is the death of Jesus on a cross, which Christians remember on Good Friday. 2) A crucifixion is a cruel way of killing someone by fixing them to a cross, used by the Romans long ago. 3) A painting or statue showing Jesus on the cross.
its sense in the lessons: In religious education the Crucifixion is the centre of the Easter story: Christians believe Jesus died on the cross and rose again three days later. In history lessons, the Romans used crucifixion as a punishment. In art, many churches have a crucifixion picture. Phrases: «the Crucifixion of Jesus», «Good Friday», «a painting of the Crucifixion».
examples from the lessons: On Good Friday Christians remember the Crucifixion. | The Gospels tell the story of the Crucifixion. | The Romans used crucifixion to punish slaves and rebels. | The museum has a famous painting of the Crucifixion. | After the Crucifixion, Jesus was buried in a tomb. | Christians believe the Crucifixion shows how much God loves people. | We read about the Crucifixion in our Easter assembly.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital C for the death of Jesus. Verb: crucify (crucified). Related: cross, crucifix (a cross with a figure of Jesus on it). Speak about it respectfully; it is a sad and holy story for Christians.

part of speech: noun (envy, uncountable); verb (envy, envies, envied, envying)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Envy is the unhappy feeling of wanting something that someone else has, like their toys, skills or luck. 2) To envy someone is to wish you had what they have. 3) Someone or something that is «the envy of» others is admired and wanted by them. 4) (church) Envy is one of the seven deadly sins in Christian teaching.
its sense in the lessons: In ethics and stories, envy is a feeling that can make people unkind or jealous; fairy tales like Snow White show its harm. In everyday talk «I envy you» can also be friendly: «I envy your holiday!». Phrases: «green with envy», «the envy of the class», «full of envy», «I don't envy you» (I would not like to be in your place).
examples from the lessons: She felt envy when her friend got a new bike. | I envy you; you get to go to the beach! | The queen was green with envy of Snow White's beauty. | Our new playground is the envy of other schools. | I don't envy him; he has three tests tomorrow. | Christians list envy among the seven deadly sins. | He tried to turn his envy into hard work.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun (uncountable) and verb; past «envied». Adjective: envious. Envy vs jealousy: envy is wanting what another has; jealousy is often fear of losing what you have (but people often mix them). «Green with envy» is an idiom; nobody turns green.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (church) The Epiphany is a Christian feast that remembers the wise men (the Magi) visiting the baby Jesus; it falls twelve days after Christmas. 2) An epiphany is a sudden moment when you understand something important. 3) (formal) A sudden appearance or showing of something.
its sense in the lessons: In religious education the Epiphany marks the end of the twelve days of Christmas; in some countries children get presents then. In stories and in writing about learning, a character «has an epiphany» when they suddenly see the truth. Phrases: «the feast of the Epiphany», «have an epiphany», «a sudden epiphany».
examples from the lessons: Christians celebrate the Epiphany, when the wise men brought gifts to Jesus. | We take down the Christmas decorations at the Epiphany. | In Spain, children get presents at the Epiphany. | I had an epiphany: the answer was right in front of me! | The scientist had an epiphany in the bath. | After reading the letter, the girl had an epiphany about her friend. | The Epiphany is sometimes called Twelfth Night or Three Kings' Day.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital E for the feast. Plural «epiphanies». Stress: e-PIPH-a-ny. The «ph» sounds like «f». Related: «a eureka moment» means much the same as an epiphany.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A furnace is a very hot enclosed fire or oven used to melt metal, make glass or burn things. 2) (USA, Canada) The heater in a house that warms the air or water for the whole home. 3) A very hot place: «The classroom was a furnace today».
its sense in the lessons: In science and history lessons blast furnaces melt iron from rock to make steel, and furnaces made the Industrial Revolution possible. In North American homes, the furnace is the heating system in the basement. In the Bible, Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego were thrown into a fiery furnace and were not harmed. Phrases: «blast furnace», «a fiery furnace», «hot as a furnace».
examples from the lessons: The iron was melted in a huge furnace. | Our furnace broke, so the house was cold all night. (USA) | Glassblowers heat the glass in a furnace. | The car was like a furnace after sitting in the sun. | In the Bible story, three men walked unharmed in the fiery furnace. | Coal kept the old furnaces burning day and night. | Never go near a furnace without an adult; it can burn you badly.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: furnaces. In the UK a home heater is usually called a boiler; in the USA and Canada, a furnace. Pronunciation: FUR-nis. Safety: furnaces are dangerous and only for trained workers.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A gnome is a tiny old man in fairy tales who lives under the ground and guards treasure. 2) A garden gnome is a small painted statue of a bearded little man with a pointed hat, put in gardens for fun. 3) (informal) A small, odd-looking person (can be unkind).
its sense in the lessons: In stories and fantasy games gnomes live in burrows, mines or forests and are often clever and secretive. In everyday life many British and European gardens have gnome statues. Phrases: «garden gnome», «the gnomes of Zurich» (an old joke name for Swiss bankers).
examples from the lessons: Grandma has three garden gnomes by her pond. | In the story, a gnome guarded a cave of gold. | The gnome had a long white beard and a red pointed hat. | Someone stole our gnome and sent us photos of it on holiday! | Gnomes, elves and fairies live in the magic forest of the book. | I painted a little clay gnome in art class. | The gnome whispered a secret to the girl.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The «g» is silent: say «nome». Countable: gnomes. Gnomes are not real; they come from folk tales. Calling a real person a gnome is rude.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Greed is wanting much more of something, such as money, food or power, than you need or than is fair. 2) (church) Greed (also called avarice) is one of the seven deadly sins in Christian teaching.
its sense in the lessons: In ethics, stories and fables greed often leads to trouble: King Midas wanted everything to turn to gold, and the dog with the bone lost it by being greedy. In everyday life greed means not sharing, taking more than your share. Phrases: «out of greed», «pure greed», «greed for money», «greed is good» (a famous line meant to be shocking).
examples from the lessons: The king's greed made him unhappy in the end. | He ate all the sweets out of greed. | Greed for gold made the pirates fight each other. | Sharing is the opposite of greed. | Christians count greed as one of the seven deadly sins. | The fable shows how greed can make you lose everything. | Some people cut down forests out of greed for money.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: no plural. Adjective: greedy; adverb: greedily. Related: greedy guts (UK informal, a person who eats too much). Wanting things is normal; greed is wanting too much and not caring about others.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A haven is a safe, peaceful place where people or animals can rest or be protected. 2) (old use) A harbour where ships can shelter. 3) A tax haven is a country where people put money to pay less tax (money).
its sense in the lessons: In stories and in science, a nature reserve is a haven for wildlife; a library can be a haven of quiet. In everyday life parents want home to be a safe haven. Place names like Newhaven or New Haven come from the harbour meaning. Phrases: «safe haven», «a haven of peace», «a haven for wildlife», «tax haven».
examples from the lessons: The garden pond is a haven for frogs. | Our treehouse is a haven from my noisy brothers. | The ship found a haven from the storm. | The library is a quiet haven at lunchtime. | The island is a haven for seabirds. | Some rich people keep money in tax havens. | Home should be a safe haven for every child.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Do not confuse with «heaven» (the sky, or where God is, Christians believe). Pronunciation: HAY-ven. Similar: refuge, shelter, sanctuary.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Hinduism is the main religion of India and Nepal, one of the oldest religions in the world; Hindus worship one supreme reality, Brahman, often through many gods and goddesses such as Vishnu, Shiva and Lakshmi. 2) The way of life and beliefs of Hindus, including ideas like karma, dharma (duty) and reincarnation.
its sense in the lessons: In religious education Hinduism is taught as one of the major world religions: Hindus worship at a mandir (temple) and at home, celebrate Diwali and Holi, and read holy texts such as the Vedas and the Bhagavad Gita. Many Hindus live in the UK, the USA, Canada and Australia too. Phrases: «in Hinduism», «Hindu gods», «Hindu festivals».
examples from the lessons: Hinduism is one of the oldest religions in the world. | In Hinduism, Diwali is the festival of lights. | Many Hindus believe in reincarnation, being born again. | We visited a Hindu temple, called a mandir. | The idea of karma comes from Hinduism and other Indian religions. | Ganesh, the god with an elephant's head, is loved in Hinduism. | Our class learned about Hinduism, Islam, Judaism and Christianity.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always capital H: Hinduism; a follower is a Hindu (plural Hindus); adjective Hindu. Do not confuse Hindu (religion) with Hindi (a language) or Indian (a nationality): not all Indians are Hindus. Speak of beliefs fairly: «Hindus believe…».

part of speech: noun (a honeymoon, honeymoons); verb (honeymoon, honeymoons, honeymooned, honeymooning)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A honeymoon is a holiday that a newly married couple take together just after their wedding. 2) The honeymoon (period) is the happy, easy time at the start of something new, like a new job or a new leader, before problems begin. 3) To honeymoon is to go on a honeymoon.
its sense in the lessons: In stories about weddings, the couple leave for their honeymoon after the party. In news and adult talk, a new prime minister or teacher has a «honeymoon period». Phrases: «go on honeymoon», «on their honeymoon», «the honeymoon is over», «honeymoon suite».
examples from the lessons: After the wedding they went on honeymoon to Italy. | My aunt sent us a postcard from her honeymoon. | The hotel gave them the honeymoon suite. | They honeymooned on a quiet island. | The new coach had a short honeymoon before we started losing. | When the puppy chewed the sofa, the honeymoon was over! | Mum and Dad showed us photos from their honeymoon.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Use «a honeymoon» (the h is pronounced). «The honeymoon is over» is an idiom: the easy start has ended. Mostly about married couples; a holiday before a wedding is not a honeymoon.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (Islam) An imam is the person who leads prayers in a mosque and often teaches and gives advice to Muslims. 2) (Islam, especially Shia) A title for an important religious leader descended from the Prophet Muhammad's family.
its sense in the lessons: In religious education an imam leads Friday prayers at the mosque, gives a talk (sermon), and helps families with weddings and funerals. In the UK, USA and Australia many mosques have an imam who visits schools. Phrases: «the imam of the mosque», «the imam led the prayers».
examples from the lessons: The imam led the prayers at the mosque on Friday. | The imam visited our school to talk about Islam. | Muslims stand in rows behind the imam when they pray. | The imam gave a talk about kindness to neighbours. | The family asked the imam to help with the wedding. | An imam studies the Qur'an for many years. | Our RE class asked the imam questions about Ramadan.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: imams. Pronounced ih-MAHM. Not the same as a priest: Muslims believe anyone knowledgeable may lead prayer. Begins with a vowel sound, so «an imam».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Jonathan is a common boy's first name. 2) (Bible) In the Old Testament, Jonathan was the son of King Saul and the loyal best friend of David.
its sense in the lessons: In religious education the friendship of David and Jonathan is a famous Bible example of loyal, loving friendship: Jonathan helped David escape when Saul wanted to kill him. In everyday life Jonathan is a common name, short forms Jon or Jonny. In stories it is just a character's name.
examples from the lessons: Jonathan is the new boy in our class. | In the Bible, Jonathan loved David like a brother. | Jonathan warned David to run away from King Saul. | We call him Jon for short. | Jonathan scored the winning goal. | The story of David and Jonathan teaches us about true friendship. | Jonathan Swift wrote «Gulliver's Travels».
note for the reader of a maths problem: A name, so always with a capital J. The name comes from Hebrew and means «God has given». Spellings vary: Jonathan, Jonathon, Johnathan.

part of speech: noun (an MOT, MOTs — UK); noun (a mot, mots — rare: a bon mot)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (UK) An MOT is a yearly test that cars more than a few years old must pass to show they are safe to drive on the road. 2) (rare, from French) A mot or «bon mot» is a clever, witty remark.
its sense in the lessons: In British and Irish everyday life (where Ireland calls it the NCT), parents take the car for its MOT; if it fails, it must be repaired. The letters come from the old Ministry of Transport. In books for adults, «a bon mot» is a clever saying. Phrases: «take the car for its MOT», «pass the MOT», «fail the MOT», «MOT certificate».
examples from the lessons: Dad's car failed its MOT because of a broken light. | The car is due for its MOT next month. | The garage does MOTs on Saturdays. | You cannot legally drive an old car without a valid MOT. | Mum was pleased the car passed its MOT. | The writer was famous for his witty bons mots. | The MOT checks the brakes, tyres and lights.
note for the reader of a maths problem: In the car sense it is written in capitals, «MOT», and each letter is said: an M-O-T (so «an», because M is said «em»). Plural: MOTs. Used in the UK; other countries have their own car safety tests. In «bon mot», the t is silent: bon MOH.

meaning for a pupil: 1) If one thing outweighs another, it is more important or bigger in effect: «The good points outweigh the bad». 2) To be heavier than something else.
its sense in the lessons: In ethics, science and decision-making lessons, people weigh benefits against risks: the benefits of a vaccine outweigh the risks. In maths and science, one object can outweigh another on a balance. Phrases: «the benefits outweigh the risks», «the pros outweigh the cons», «far outweigh».
examples from the lessons: The fun of the trip outweighs the long drive. | The benefits of exercise far outweigh the effort. | A full bag of sand outweighs a bag of feathers. | The doctor said the good of the medicine outweighs the side effects. | My worries were outweighed by excitement. | Does the cost outweigh the benefit? | The elephant outweighs every other land animal.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb, past «outweighed». Spelling: out + weigh (with the silent «gh»). Not the same as «outnumber» (more in number). The thing that wins comes first: «A outweighs B» means A is bigger or more important.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (church) Penance is something a person does to show they are sorry for a sin, such as saying prayers or doing a good deed, especially after confession in the Catholic Church. 2) (church) Penance is also the name of the sacrament of confession (also called reconciliation). 3) Something unpleasant you have to put up with, as if as a punishment: «Waiting in the queue was a penance».
its sense in the lessons: In religious education, Catholic children learn about confession, where a priest may give a penance, often a few prayers. In everyday talk, «do penance» means doing something hard to make up for a wrong. Phrases: «do penance», «as a penance», «the sacrament of penance».
examples from the lessons: After confession the priest gave her a penance of three prayers. | He cleaned the kitchen as a penance for breaking the cup. | In the Middle Ages, some people walked to holy places to do penance. | Catholics also call confession the sacrament of penance. | Listening to my brother's music was a real penance. | Lent is a time of prayer and penance for many Christians. | She did penance by giving her pocket money to charity.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly uncountable («do penance»), countable when it means a particular task («a penance»). Related: penitent, repent. Penance is not the same as punishment from a court; it is chosen to show sorrow.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Penitent means feeling and showing that you are sorry for doing wrong. 2) (church) A penitent is a person who confesses their sins to a priest or does penance.
its sense in the lessons: In religious stories and in ethics lessons a penitent person admits a wrong and wants to make it right; the father in the Prodigal Son story welcomes back his penitent son. In formal writing, «penitent» describes a sorry look or voice. Phrases: «a penitent sinner», «penitent tears», «look penitent».
examples from the lessons: The penitent boy said sorry to his grandmother. | The puppy looked penitent after chewing the shoe. | The priest listened kindly to the penitent. | She wrote a penitent letter to her friend. | In the Bible story, the penitent son came home to his father. | Penitents in the old church wore plain clothes. | He was truly penitent and promised not to lie again.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective and noun; formal. Adverb: penitently. Opposite: unrepentant. Related: penance, repent. Do not confuse with «penitentiary» (an old word for a prison, mainly USA).

part of speech: noun (a petition, petitions); verb (petition, petitions, petitioned, petitioning)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A petition is a written request, signed by many people, asking someone in power to do or change something. 2) To petition someone is to make a formal request to them, often with a petition. 3) (law) A formal written request to a court. 4) (church) A prayer that asks God for something.
its sense in the lessons: In citizenship lessons, pupils learn that a petition is a peaceful way to ask for change, such as a new crossing near school. Online petitions collect signatures. In church, the prayers of petition ask God for help. Phrases: «sign a petition», «start a petition», «petition the council», «a petition for divorce» (law).
examples from the lessons: We started a petition for a new zebra crossing. | Over five hundred people signed our petition. | The children petitioned the head teacher for a longer break. | The petition was handed to the mayor. | In church we prayed petitions for the sick. | Mum signed an online petition to save the library. | The court received a petition from the family.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun and verb; past «petitioned». A petitioner is a person who makes a petition. Maths: count the signatures and compare with a target (e.g. «we need a thousand; we have six hundred, so we need four hundred more»).

part of speech: noun (a poll, polls; the polls); verb (poll, polls, polled, polling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A poll is a survey in which many people are asked the same question to find out what most of them think. 2) The polls are an election, the time when people vote: «go to the polls». 3) To poll people is to ask them questions in a survey. 4) (formal) The number of votes in an election. 5) (old use) The head; a «poll tax» is a tax that every person must pay.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and data lessons, children take a class poll (for example favourite fruit), then make a tally chart and bar chart. In the news, opinion polls show who might win an election. Phrases: «opinion poll», «take a poll», «exit poll», «polling station», «go to the polls».
examples from the lessons: We took a poll to choose the class pet. | The poll showed that most pupils like pizza best. | Grown-ups vote at a polling station. | The country goes to the polls next month. | The newspaper polled a thousand people. | An exit poll asks people how they voted as they leave. | Twelve of the twenty-five children voted for a hamster in the poll.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun and verb, past «polled». In maths, results of a poll can be shown as numbers, fractions or percentages: 12 out of 25 is 48 per cent. A poll asks some people, not everyone, so it can be wrong. Do not confuse with «pole» (a long stick) or «Pole» (a person from Poland).

part of speech: noun (probate, uncountable); verb (probate, probates, probated — USA)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (law) Probate is the official legal process that checks that a dead person's will is real, so that their money and belongings can be shared out as the will says. 2) (USA, law) To probate a will is to prove it in court.
its sense in the lessons: This is an adult, legal word children meet when a grandparent dies and the family talks about the will. A probate court or office deals with it, and it can take months. Phrases: «grant of probate», «go through probate», «probate court».
examples from the lessons: After Grandad died, Mum had to deal with probate. | The house cannot be sold until probate is finished. | The lawyer applied for probate of the will. | Probate can take many months. | The probate court checked that the will was real. | Aunt Jo explained probate to me at the kitchen table. | Without probate, the bank will not hand over the money.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable in British use. Formal and legal. Related: will, executor (the person who carries out the will), inheritance. Do not confuse with «probation» (a time of being tested or watched, e.g. after a crime).

meaning for a pupil: 1) To repent is to feel truly sorry for something wrong you have done and to want to change. 2) (church, Bible) To turn away from sin and turn back to God: in the Gospels John the Baptist and Jesus called people to repent. 3) (formal) To regret a choice: «He repented of his decision».
its sense in the lessons: In religious education, repentance is a key idea in Christianity, Judaism and Islam: saying sorry to God and to the person hurt, and changing. In stories, a villain may repent at the end. Phrases: «repent of your sins», «repent and be forgiven», «repent at leisure» (from «marry in haste, repent at leisure»).
examples from the lessons: The thief repented and gave the money back. | John the Baptist told the people to repent. | She repented of the mean things she had said. | Christians believe God forgives those who truly repent. | The giant repented and became the village's friend. | Marry in haste, repent at leisure, says the old proverb. | He did not repent until he saw how sad his friend was.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb, past «repented». Noun: repentance; adjective: repentant (opposite: unrepentant). Often «repent of» something. Repenting is more than saying sorry: it means wanting to change.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (UK, Australia, NZ) A rota is a list showing who has to do a job and when, so that people take turns. 2) A regular turn-by-turn system of doing a job.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life schools have rotas for tidying up, watering plants or class monitors; families make a washing-up rota; workers have shift rotas. In the USA people say «roster» or «schedule». Phrases: «a cleaning rota», «on the rota», «a duty rota», «draw up a rota».
examples from the lessons: Our class has a rota for feeding the fish. | I'm on the washing-up rota tonight. | Mum made a rota so we take turns with the dog. | The nurses' rota shows who works at night. | The teacher drew up a rota for playground jobs. | Check the rota to see whose turn it is. | If four children share a rota of eight days, each child has two turns.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: rotas. Mainly British, Irish, Australian and NZ English; American English uses «roster» or «schedule». Maths: share jobs equally by dividing days by people.

part of speech: noun (Scripture, the Scriptures; a scripture, scriptures)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (church, Bible) Scripture (or the Scriptures) means the holy writings of the Bible for Christians. 2) (religion) The holy writings of any religion, such as the Qur'an, the Torah or the Vedas. 3) (old use, UK schools) A school subject for Bible study, now called Religious Education.
its sense in the lessons: In religious education Christians read Scripture in church services; Jews read the Hebrew scriptures; Muslims recite the Qur'an. In stories, a preacher quotes Scripture. Phrases: «Holy Scripture», «a passage of scripture», «quote Scripture», «according to scripture».
examples from the lessons: The vicar read a passage from Scripture. | Christians call the Bible the Holy Scriptures. | Hindu scriptures include the Vedas. | The Torah is the most important scripture for Jews. | My grandmother can quote Scripture from memory. | Long ago, monks copied the scriptures by hand. | We compared stories from the scriptures of different religions.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Often with a capital S for the Bible. Uncountable («Scripture says…») or countable («the scriptures of Hinduism»). Adjective: scriptural. Related: verse, gospel, testament.

part of speech: noun (a testament, testaments; the Old Testament, the New Testament)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (Bible) The Old Testament and the New Testament are the two main parts of the Christian Bible: the Old Testament has the Hebrew scriptures, and the New Testament tells of Jesus and the early Church. 2) A testament to something is clear proof of it: «The bridge is a testament to their hard work». 3) (law) A will, especially in the phrase «last will and testament».
its sense in the lessons: In religious education pupils learn which stories are in the Old Testament (Noah, Moses, David) and which in the New Testament (the Gospels, Paul's letters). In formal writing «a testament to» shows proof. Phrases: «Old Testament», «New Testament», «a testament to», «last will and testament».
examples from the lessons: Noah's ark is a story from the Old Testament. | The New Testament begins with the four Gospels. | Her medal is a testament to years of practice. | The old castle stands as a testament to the builders' skill. | Grandad wrote his last will and testament. | Jews call their holy book the Tanakh, which Christians call the Old Testament. | Our class read a parable from the New Testament.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capitals for the parts of the Bible. «A testament to» (proof) is formal. Related: testimony (what a witness says), testify. Do not confuse «testament» with «test».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (religion) Ahimsa is the idea of not harming any living thing, in thought, word or action; it is an important teaching in Hinduism, Jainism and Buddhism. 2) Non-violence as a way of life and of working for change.
its sense in the lessons: In religious education ahimsa is taught with Indian religions: many Jains and Hindus are vegetarian because of it, and Jain monks may sweep the path so as not to step on insects. In history lessons, Mahatma Gandhi used ahimsa (non-violence) in India's struggle for freedom. Phrases: «the principle of ahimsa», «practise ahimsa».
examples from the lessons: Ahimsa means doing no harm to any living thing. | Because of ahimsa, many Jains do not eat meat. | Gandhi used ahimsa to protest peacefully. | Some monks walk carefully to avoid hurting insects, following ahimsa. | Our class talked about how ahimsa is like being kind to animals. | Ahimsa is a word from Sanskrit, an old language of India. | Buddhists, Hindus and Jains all value ahimsa.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A word from Sanskrit; uncountable; often in italics in books. Stress: a-HIM-sa. Meaning in English: non-violence, harmlessness.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (church) An archbishop is a very senior bishop who is in charge of the bishops and churches in a large area. 2) (church, UK) The Archbishop of Canterbury is the leading bishop of the Church of England.
its sense in the lessons: In religious education and history lessons archbishops appear as leaders in the Catholic, Anglican and Orthodox churches; they wear special robes and a tall hat called a mitre. The Archbishop of Canterbury crowns British kings and queens. Phrases: «the Archbishop of Canterbury», «the Archbishop of Dublin», «an archbishop's palace».
examples from the lessons: The Archbishop of Canterbury crowned the king. | An archbishop leads the bishops of a large area. | The archbishop visited our cathedral at Easter. | Thomas Becket was an archbishop killed in his cathedral long ago. | The archbishop wore a tall hat called a mitre. | Our school choir sang for the archbishop. | Archbishop Desmond Tutu worked for fairness in South Africa.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: archbishops. Capital A before a name or place: «Archbishop of York». «Arch-» means chief, as in archangel, archenemy. Order in many churches: priest, bishop, archbishop.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A Buddhist is a person who follows Buddhism, the religion based on the teachings of the Buddha, Siddhartha Gautama. 2) Buddhist means to do with Buddhism: a Buddhist temple, Buddhist monks.
its sense in the lessons: In religious education Buddhists follow the Buddha's teachings about ending suffering through the Eightfold Path, meditation and kindness; many live in Asia, and also in the UK, USA, Canada and Australia. Buddhist monks often wear orange or maroon robes. Phrases: «a Buddhist monk», «a Buddhist temple», «Buddhist teachings».
examples from the lessons: My friend's family are Buddhists. | We visited a Buddhist temple with a big golden statue. | Buddhist monks shave their heads and wear robes. | Buddhists try to be kind to all living things. | Many Buddhists meditate every day. | Buddhists celebrate Wesak, the Buddha's birthday. | The Buddhist teacher told us a story about patience.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always capital B. «Buddhist» is the person and the adjective; «Buddhism» is the religion; «the Buddha» is its founder. Spelling: double d then h: B-u-d-d-h-i-s-t. Buddhists do not usually worship the Buddha as a god; they honour him as a teacher.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (church) A christening is a church ceremony in which a baby is baptised, given its Christian name and welcomed into the Church. 2) The first use of a new thing, such as a ship's launch or new shoes (joking).
its sense in the lessons: In everyday family life a christening is a happy event: the baby wears white, godparents make promises, water is poured on the baby's head, and there is often a party after. In stories, a fairy may come to a royal christening (Sleeping Beauty). Phrases: «christening gown», «christening party», «christening cake», «godparents at a christening».
examples from the lessons: We went to my baby cousin's christening on Sunday. | The baby wore a long white christening gown. | At the christening the vicar poured water on her head. | My aunt and uncle are my godparents from my christening. | In Sleeping Beauty, the bad fairy came to the christening. | We had cake and sandwiches after the christening. | The new ship's christening was done by breaking a bottle on it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Verb: christen (the «t» is silent: KRIS-en). Christening and baptism are almost the same; «baptism» is the general church word, also for adults. Some churches baptise only older believers, not babies.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (law, money) A claimant is a person who says they have a right to something, such as money, land or a benefit, and asks for it officially. 2) (UK) A person who receives or asks for government benefit money. 3) (old use) A person who says they should be king or queen: a claimant to the throne.
its sense in the lessons: In adult life and the news, a claimant fills in forms to claim money from insurance or from the government; in court a claimant brings a case. In history, two claimants to the throne might fight. Phrases: «benefit claimant», «a claimant to the throne», «the claimant's case».
examples from the lessons: Each claimant must fill in a long form. | The insurance company paid the claimant for the flood damage. | The claimant asked the court for money. | In history, there were two claimants to the throne. | Benefit claimants get help from the government. | The lost dog had three claimants, but only one had a photo! | The claimant said the land had been his grandmother's.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable, formal. Related: claim (verb, noun). In UK courts «claimant» replaced the older word «plaintiff» (still used in the USA).

meaning for a pupil: 1) To commemorate an important event or person is to remember and honour them, often with a ceremony or a special object. 2) A statue, plaque or stamp that commemorates something is made to help people remember it.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons and in everyday life people commemorate wars, heroes and famous events: Remembrance Day commemorates soldiers who died, and churches commemorate saints on their feast days. Phrases: «commemorate the dead», «a plaque to commemorate», «a coin commemorating».
examples from the lessons: We wear poppies to commemorate the soldiers who died in wars. | A statue was built to commemorate the brave nurse. | The new stamp commemorates a famous scientist. | Christians commemorate the Last Supper on Maundy Thursday. | The school planted a tree to commemorate its old head teacher. | The town holds a parade to commemorate its founding. | A blue plaque commemorates the writer who lived here.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb, past «commemorated». Noun: commemoration; adjective: commemorative («a commemorative mug»). Spelling: two m's at the start (comm-), one m in the middle (-mem-). Formal; plain words: remember, honour, mark.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A creator is a person who makes or invents something new, such as a story, game, character or video. 2) (religion) The Creator is God, who Christians, Jews and Muslims believe made the world and everything in it.
its sense in the lessons: In art, computing and media lessons a creator makes things: a game's creator, a content creator online. In religious education the creation stories in Genesis show God as the Creator. Phrases: «the creator of», «content creator», «God the Creator», «creator of the universe».
examples from the lessons: J.K. Rowling is the creator of Harry Potter. | The creator of the game made it in his bedroom. | Christians believe God is the Creator of heaven and earth. | My cousin is a video creator online. | Mary Shelley's Frankenstein is about a creature and its creator. | Every creator needs time to try ideas. | The prayer thanks the Creator for the beauty of the world.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Capital C when it means God. Related: create, creation, creative, creature. Spelling ends in -or, not -er.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (church) A denomination is one of the separate groups or branches of a religion, especially Christianity, such as Catholic, Anglican, Methodist or Baptist. 2) (money, maths) The value printed on a coin or banknote: a five-pound note and a ten-pound note are different denominations. 3) (formal) A name or kind of unit.
its sense in the lessons: In religious education pupils learn that Christians belong to different denominations that share beliefs about Jesus but worship in different ways. In maths and money problems, «denomination» means the value of coins and notes. Phrases: «Christian denominations», «coins of every denomination», «notes in small denominations».
examples from the lessons: Methodists and Baptists are two Christian denominations. | Our town has churches of many denominations. | The bank gave Dad the money in small denominations. | Coins come in denominations such as 1p, 2p, 5p, 10p, 20p and 50p. | Which denomination is the biggest coin you have? | Christians of all denominations came to the joint service. | The machine accepts notes of every denomination.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable, formal. Adjective: denominational («a non-denominational school»). Do not confuse with «denominator», the bottom number of a fraction. Maths: knowing denominations helps you make change, e.g. 50p = two 20p coins + one 10p coin.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To establish something is to start or set it up so that it lasts, such as a school, a business or a rule. 2) To establish a fact is to find it out or prove it for sure. 3) To establish yourself is to become accepted or well known in a place or job. 4) (formal) To establish a relationship or contact is to make it.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, the Romans established towns; in science, experiments establish facts; in everyday life a shop sign may say «established» with the year it opened. In the Church of England, «the established church» means the official state church. Phrases: «establish a rule», «establish the facts», «well established», «established church».
examples from the lessons: The school was established a long time ago. | The police tried to establish what happened. | Our experiment established that plants need light. | She soon established herself as the best goalkeeper in the team. | The settlers established a small village by the river. | The club established a new rule about phones. | The Church of England is the established church in England.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb, past «established». Noun: establishment (also «the Establishment», the powerful people in a country). Formal; plain words: set up, start, find out, prove.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Gentleness is the quality of being kind, calm and careful, not rough or harsh. 2) Softness or mildness: the gentleness of a breeze or a slope.
its sense in the lessons: In ethics and religious education gentleness is a virtue; Christians list it among the «fruit of the Spirit» in Paul's letter to the Galatians. In everyday life gentleness is needed with babies, pets and people who are upset. Phrases: «with gentleness», «great gentleness», «gentleness and kindness».
examples from the lessons: She held the baby bird with great gentleness. | The vet treated the frightened dog with gentleness. | Gentleness is a strength, not a weakness. | Christians count gentleness among the fruit of the Spirit. | The teacher spoke with gentleness to the crying boy. | I like the gentleness of the summer breeze. | Grandpa's gentleness made everyone feel safe.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: no plural. From the adjective «gentle» + -ness; adverb «gently». Opposite: roughness, harshness.

part of speech: noun (the Gospels; a gospel, gospels; gospel music)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (Bible) The Gospels are the first four books of the New Testament, by Matthew, Mark, Luke and John, which tell the life and teaching of Jesus. 2) (church) The gospel is the Christian message, the «good news» about Jesus. 3) Gospel (music) is a lively style of Christian singing from African American churches. 4) (informal) «Gospel» or «gospel truth» means something completely true.
its sense in the lessons: In religious education pupils compare the four Gospels and read stories such as the parables and the Nativity. In music lessons, gospel choirs sing with clapping and strong voices. In everyday talk «take it as gospel» means believe it totally. Phrases: «the four Gospels», «the Gospel of Luke», «gospel choir», «the gospel truth», «take something as gospel».
examples from the lessons: The four Gospels tell the story of Jesus. | The Gospel of Luke has the story of the Good Samaritan. | The priest read from one of the Gospels. | Our school has a gospel choir. | «Gospel» comes from an old word meaning «good news». | Don't take everything online as gospel. | Matthew, Mark, Luke and John are called the Gospels.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually capital G when it names the books: the Gospels; plural of «gospel». Uncountable when it means the music or the message. A «gospel truth» is a strong saying, not always literally true.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Hatred is a very strong feeling of disliking someone or something, much stronger than ordinary dislike. 2) A hatred of something is a strong dislike of it: «a hatred of spiders».
its sense in the lessons: In ethics, history and citizenship lessons, hatred between groups can lead to bullying, violence and war, and laws forbid stirring up hatred. Religions teach to replace hatred with love and forgiveness. In everyday talk «a hatred of» can be light: a hatred of broccoli. Phrases: «full of hatred», «hatred of», «racial hatred», «love and hatred».
examples from the lessons: Hatred can grow if people do not talk to each other. | He looked at the bully with hatred. | Martin Luther King said hatred cannot drive out hatred; only love can. | My sister has a hatred of spiders. | Laws in many countries forbid spreading hatred against groups of people. | The story ends with the two families letting go of their hatred. | Kind words can help stop hatred.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable; «a hatred of» is also used. Related: hate (verb, noun), hateful. Spelling: hat-red, not «hatered». Stronger than «dislike».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Humanity means all the people in the world together, the human race. 2) Humanity is also kindness and care for others: «She showed great humanity». 3) The state of being human. 4) The humanities are school and university subjects about people and culture, such as history, languages and religious studies.
its sense in the lessons: In history and citizenship lessons we talk about «crimes against humanity» and things that help all humanity, like medicine. In ethics lessons humanity means kindness. In secondary school, «humanities» are a group of subjects. Phrases: «all humanity», «an act of humanity», «crimes against humanity», «the humanities».
examples from the lessons: Clean water is important for all humanity. | The nurse treated the enemy soldier with humanity. | Landing on the Moon was a great step for humanity. | History and geography are humanities subjects. | The story shows the humanity of the robot, who cares for the little girl. | War crimes are crimes against humanity. | Science can help humanity live longer.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable; «the humanities» (plural) are subjects. Related: human, humane (kind), humanitarian (helping people in need). Do not confuse humane (kind) with human.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Immersion is putting something completely under water or another liquid. 2) (church) Baptism by immersion means dipping a person fully under water, as some churches do. 3) Being deeply involved in something, such as learning a language by living in it: «language immersion». 4) (UK, Ireland) An immersion (heater) is an electric heater in a water tank that heats hot water.
its sense in the lessons: In science, immersion of an object in water shows whether it floats or sinks and lets you measure volume. In religious education Baptist churches baptise by full immersion. In schools, «immersion» classes teach children wholly in another language (French immersion in Canada, Irish in Gaelscoileanna). Phrases: «total immersion», «French immersion», «turn on the immersion».
examples from the lessons: Immersion in water makes a sponge heavy. | We measured the stone's volume by immersion in a jug of water. | Some churches baptise by full immersion in a pool. | My cousin goes to a French immersion school in Canada. | Turn on the immersion if you want a hot bath. (UK, Ireland) | The book's immersion in the world of dragons kept me reading. | Total immersion is a fast way to learn a language.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly uncountable. Verb: immerse; adjective: immersive. Science maths: the rise in water level when an object is fully immersed equals the object's volume (e.g. water rises from 200 ml to 250 ml, so the object is 50 cubic centimetres).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (religion) In Hinduism, Buddhism, Jainism and Sikhism, karma is the idea that a person's actions, good or bad, bring results back to them, in this life or a future life. 2) (informal) The idea that good or bad things happen to you because of how you behaved: «That's karma!».
its sense in the lessons: In religious education karma is taught with rebirth (reincarnation) in Indian religions. In everyday English people use «karma» loosely, often as a joke when someone who did wrong has bad luck. Phrases: «good karma», «bad karma», «instant karma», «karma will get you».
examples from the lessons: Hindus believe karma follows a person into their next life. | Buddhists try to do good actions to make good karma. | He laughed at me and then tripped; that's karma! (informal) | Helping others is said to bring good karma. | The idea of karma means our actions matter. | Instant karma: the boy who took the last cake dropped it. | Our RE teacher explained karma with a story about a kind farmer.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. A Sanskrit word meaning «action». The everyday joke sense («karma got him») is looser than the religious meaning; in the religions karma is not a magic punishment but the result of actions.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (Judaism) Kosher food is food that is allowed by Jewish law, prepared in the right way; for example, meat and milk are not eaten together, and pork is not eaten. 2) A kosher shop, kitchen or restaurant sells or makes kosher food. 3) (informal) Genuine, honest or acceptable: «Is this deal kosher?».
its sense in the lessons: In religious education pupils learn the Jewish food laws (kashrut) from the Torah. Many supermarkets have kosher sections. In informal speech, «not kosher» means suspicious or not allowed. Phrases: «kosher food», «keep kosher», «a kosher kitchen», «not quite kosher».
examples from the lessons: Many Jewish families keep kosher. | A kosher kitchen has separate dishes for meat and milk. | Pork is not kosher. | The school canteen offers kosher meals. | We bought kosher bread at the Jewish bakery. | Something about the email didn't seem kosher, so we deleted it. (informal) | Fish with fins and scales are kosher.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective (also used as a verb in kitchens, «to kosher a pot», rare). Similar idea in Islam: halal; kosher and halal rules are alike in some ways and different in others. The informal sense is common in British and American speech.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A maid is a woman whose job is to clean and do housework in a hotel or someone's house. 2) (old use) A maid is a girl or young unmarried woman: «a fair maid». 3) A bridesmaid or maid of honour is a girl or woman who helps the bride at a wedding.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and history lessons, rich families had maids and servants; in fairy tales a «maid» is a young woman. In hotels today, room cleaners are sometimes called maids, though «housekeeper» is more polite. Phrases: «maid of honour», «housemaid», «old maid» (old-fashioned, unkind), «Maid Marian» (from Robin Hood).
examples from the lessons: The hotel maid cleaned our room every morning. | In the old house, a maid lit the fires at dawn. | The milk maid carried two buckets on a pole. | My sister will be the maid of honour at the wedding. | Maid Marian was Robin Hood's friend. | The story tells of a poor maid who married a prince. | Long ago, many girls went into service as maids.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: maids. Homophone: «made» (past of make) sounds the same. «Old maid» is old-fashioned and unkind; also a card game. Today «cleaner» or «housekeeper» is the more respectful job title.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (Bible) Manna was the special food that, the Bible says, God sent from heaven each morning to feed the Israelites in the desert after they left Egypt. 2) Something good and unexpected that you need very much: «manna from heaven».
its sense in the lessons: In religious education the story in the book of Exodus tells how the people gathered manna each day, but only as much as they needed. In everyday speech «manna from heaven» means a lucky help just when you need it. Phrases: «manna from heaven», «like manna».
examples from the lessons: In the desert the Israelites ate manna every morning. | The Bible says manna tasted like wafers made with honey. | The people were told to gather only enough manna for one day. | The surprise money was manna from heaven for the poor family. | For the hungry walkers, the café was like manna. | Moses told the people that the manna came from God. | The rain was manna from heaven for the dry farms.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Do not confuse with «manner» (a way of doing) or «mana» (magic power in games, and a word in Polynesian cultures). Christians sometimes link manna with the bread of Holy Communion.

part of speech: noun (maternity, uncountable); adjective (maternity — before a noun)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Maternity is the state of being a mother. 2) As an adjective it means to do with having a baby: maternity clothes, a maternity ward. 3) (work) Maternity leave is time off work that a mother gets before and after her baby is born, often with maternity pay.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday adult life a teacher may go on maternity leave and a supply teacher takes the class. Hospitals have maternity wards where babies are born. Phrases: «maternity leave», «maternity ward», «maternity pay», «maternity clothes». The father's version is «paternity».
examples from the lessons: Our teacher is going on maternity leave next month. | My little brother was born in the maternity ward. | Mum wore maternity clothes before the baby came. | Some mothers get maternity pay while they look after their babies. | The maternity unit is on the second floor. | When the baby is born, the dad may take paternity leave. | She returned to work after a year of maternity leave.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly used before another noun (maternity leave). Related: maternal (motherly), mother. Opposite for fathers: paternity. Formal; children usually say «having a baby».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (church) A nun is a woman who has promised to give her life to God and lives in a religious community called a convent, following rules of prayer and work. 2) (religion) Buddhist and some other religious traditions also have nuns.
its sense in the lessons: In religious education nuns take vows of poverty, chastity and obedience; many teach, nurse or care for poor people. Some nuns wear a long dress and a veil called a habit. In stories like «The Sound of Music», Maria starts out as a young woman preparing to be a nun. Phrases: «become a nun», «a convent of nuns», «a nun's habit», «Sister Mary» (how nuns are called).
examples from the lessons: The nuns ran a school for girls. | A nun is often called «Sister». | Mother Teresa was a nun who cared for the poor in India. | Some nuns wear a black and white habit. | The nuns pray together many times each day. | My great-aunt became a nun when she was young. | Buddhist nuns shave their heads and wear robes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: nuns. Homophone: «none» (not any) sounds the same. The male equivalent is a monk (or friar); the leader of a convent is an abbess or Mother Superior.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (church) To ordain someone is to make them a priest, minister or rabbi in a special religious ceremony. 2) (formal) To ordain something is to order or decide it officially, as a king or law does. 3) (formal) To decide what will happen, as if by God or fate: «It was ordained that they would meet».
its sense in the lessons: In religious education a bishop ordains new priests; some churches ordain women and some do not. In old stories and formal writing a king may ordain a new law. Phrases: «be ordained a priest», «ordained minister», «divinely ordained».
examples from the lessons: The bishop ordained three new priests. | My uncle was ordained a minister last summer. | Some churches ordain women as priests. | The king ordained that a feast be held. | The ceremony to ordain a priest is called ordination. | She felt it was ordained that she would become a nurse. | An ordained minister can lead a wedding service.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb, past «ordained». Noun: ordination. Formal word. Related: order, ordinance (a law).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Overtime is extra time that someone works after their normal working hours. 2) Overtime is also the money paid for that extra work. 3) (sport, USA, Canada) Extra time added to the end of a game when the score is tied. 4) Working overtime (informal): working very hard: «My brain is working overtime».
its sense in the lessons: In adult work life and in maths money problems, overtime is often paid at a higher rate, such as «time and a half». In North American sport, a game «goes into overtime»; in the UK, football has «extra time». Phrases: «work overtime», «do overtime», «overtime pay», «go into overtime».
examples from the lessons: Dad worked overtime to finish the job. | Mum gets extra money for doing overtime. | The hockey game went into overtime. | My imagination was working overtime last night. | Nurses often work overtime during busy weeks. | If Sam earns ten dollars an hour and fifteen dollars for each hour of overtime, how much does he get for two hours of overtime? | The shop pays overtime at time and a half.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable noun; also an adverb («work overtime»). Maths: «time and a half» means pay × 1.5; «double time» means pay × 2. UK football says «extra time», North American sports «overtime».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (church) A pastor is a Christian minister who leads a church and cares for its people, especially in Protestant churches. 2) (rare) To pastor a church is to be its pastor.
its sense in the lessons: In religious education and everyday life in the USA, Canada and Australia many church leaders are called «Pastor», as in «Pastor John». The word comes from the Latin for «shepherd», because the pastor looks after the people like a shepherd looks after sheep. Phrases: «the church pastor», «Pastor Smith», «youth pastor».
examples from the lessons: The pastor gave a talk about forgiveness. | Pastor Jones visited Grandma in hospital. | Our youth pastor runs the Friday club. | The word «pastor» means shepherd. | Martin Luther King Jr. was a pastor in Alabama. | The pastor baptised the new members. | The pastor said a prayer before the meal.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Capital P as a title: Pastor Ruth. Related: pastoral (caring for people; also about farms and countryside). Similar words: minister, vicar, priest, reverend (different churches use different words).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A philosopher is a person who thinks and writes about big questions, such as what is true, what is right and wrong, and what life means. 2) A person who stays calm and thoughtful about life's troubles: «Grandad is a bit of a philosopher».
its sense in the lessons: In history and ethics lessons, famous philosophers include Socrates, Plato and Aristotle of ancient Greece and Confucius of China. In «philosophy for children» lessons, pupils become little philosophers by asking «why?» and giving reasons. Phrases: «a Greek philosopher», «the philosopher's stone» (a magic stone in stories).
examples from the lessons: Socrates was a philosopher who asked lots of questions. | Philosophers ask: what makes an action right or wrong? | In P4C our class acted like philosophers. | The philosopher's stone in the story turns metal into gold. | Plato was a student of Socrates and a great philosopher. | Grandma is a philosopher about bad weather: «It'll pass». | Some philosophers think animals have rights.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: philosophers. Related: philosophy, philosophical. Spelling: «ph» sounds like «f»: fi-LOS-o-fer. «Philosopher» comes from Greek for «lover of wisdom».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A planner is a person who plans things, such as events, holidays or towns. 2) A planner is a book, diary or app where you write plans and dates for things you need to do. 3) (UK) A town planner works for the council deciding where new buildings and roads may go.
its sense in the lessons: In school, pupils use a homework planner (homework diary) to write down tasks and teachers sign it. In everyday life a wedding planner organises weddings; town planners decide land use. Phrases: «homework planner», «wedding planner», «town planner», «a good planner».
examples from the lessons: Write your homework in your planner. | The wedding planner chose the flowers. | My mum is a great planner; she never forgets anything. | Town planners decided where the new park would go. | I use a planner app to track my football practices. | The teacher checks our planners every Friday. | The party planner booked a magician.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: planners. Related: plan, planning. Spelling: double n.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (Bible, church) The Resurrection is the rising of Jesus from the dead on the third day after his crucifixion, which Christians celebrate at Easter. 2) A resurrection is the act of coming back to life. 3) A return of something that was forgotten or gone: «the resurrection of an old toy craze».
its sense in the lessons: In religious education, Christians believe the Resurrection is the heart of their faith; Easter Sunday celebrates it, and the empty tomb is its sign. In everyday language «resurrection» can mean bringing something old back into use. Phrases: «the Resurrection of Jesus», «resurrection of the dead», «Easter and the Resurrection».
examples from the lessons: Christians celebrate the Resurrection on Easter Sunday. | The women found the tomb empty on the morning of the Resurrection. | Christians believe in the resurrection of the dead at the end of time. | The Easter eggs remind some Christians of new life and the Resurrection. | The film was a resurrection of an old cartoon. | The fashion for yo-yos had a resurrection. | Our class painted pictures of the Resurrection story.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital R for the Resurrection of Jesus. Verb: resurrect. Spelling: double r, double r: r-e-s-u-r-r-e-c-t-i-o-n. Speak of beliefs as «Christians believe».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (church) A schism is a split in which a religious group divides into two separate groups because of disagreements. 2) (formal) Any serious split between members of a group.
its sense in the lessons: In history and religious education the Great Schism split the Church into the Catholic Church in the West and the Orthodox Church in the East; the Reformation caused further schisms. In formal writing a club or political party can have a schism. Phrases: «the Great Schism», «a schism in the church», «cause a schism».
examples from the lessons: The Great Schism divided the Christian Church into East and West. | The argument caused a schism in the chess club. | A schism split the party into two groups. | Historians study why the schism happened. | The schism lasted for hundreds of years. | The new rule led to a schism among the members. | Christians today try to heal old schisms.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable, formal. Pronunciation: SKIZ-um or SIZ-um, both are used. Adjective: schismatic. Similar: split, division, rift.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Sikhism is a religion founded in the Punjab region of India by Guru Nanak; Sikhs believe in one God and follow the teachings of the ten Gurus and their holy book, the Guru Granth Sahib.
its sense in the lessons: In religious education pupils learn that Sikhs worship in a gurdwara, where a free kitchen called the langar feeds everyone; many Sikhs wear the five Ks, such as the kara (steel bracelet) and kesh (uncut hair), and men often wear a turban. Sikhs live in the UK, Canada, the USA and Australia. Phrases: «in Sikhism», «Sikh temple (gurdwara)», «the Sikh Gurus».
examples from the lessons: Sikhism was founded by Guru Nanak. | In Sikhism, everyone is equal before God. | We visited a gurdwara and ate in the langar. | The holy book of Sikhism is the Guru Granth Sahib. | Many Sikh men wear a turban. | Sikhism teaches sharing, honest work and remembering God. | Vaisakhi is an important festival in Sikhism.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital S: Sikhism; a follower is a Sikh (plural Sikhs), pronounced «seek» in many places or «sick» in the Punjab. Sikhs are not Hindus or Muslims; it is a separate religion.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Temptation is the feeling of wanting to do something, especially something you know is wrong or not good for you. 2) A temptation is a thing that makes you want to do it: «Cake is a big temptation». 3) (Bible, church) The Temptation is the story of Jesus being tempted by the devil in the desert.
its sense in the lessons: In ethics lessons and stories, characters face temptation, like Edmund in Narnia with Turkish delight. In religious education, the Lord's Prayer says «lead us not into temptation», and Lent remembers Jesus' forty days in the wilderness. Phrases: «resist temptation», «give in to temptation», «a strong temptation», «lead us not into temptation».
examples from the lessons: I resisted the temptation to open my present early. | The sweets on the table were a big temptation. | He gave in to temptation and ate the last biscuit. | In the Bible, Jesus resisted temptation in the desert. | The Lord's Prayer says, «Lead us not into temptation». | Leaving your homework until the last minute is a common temptation. | The shop puts sweets at the till as a temptation for children.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable for the feeling, countable for a thing that tempts. Verb: tempt; adjective: tempting. Temptation itself is not wrong; giving in to it may be.

part of speech: noun (a tithe, tithes); verb (tithe, tithes, tithed, tithing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (church) A tithe is one tenth of what a person earns or grows, given to the church or to God. 2) (history) Long ago, farmers had to give a tithe of their crops to the local church. 3) To tithe is to give a tithe.
its sense in the lessons: In religious education, some Christians today still give a tenth of their income to their church; the idea comes from the Old Testament. In history lessons, tithe barns stored the grain farmers gave to the church. In maths, a tithe is ten per cent. Phrases: «pay a tithe», «tithe barn», «give a tithe».
examples from the lessons: A tithe is one tenth of what you have. | Long ago, farmers gave a tithe of their crops to the church. | The village still has an old tithe barn. | Some Christians tithe their wages. | If Lucy has thirty pounds and gives a tithe, she gives three pounds. | The Bible tells of Abraham giving a tithe to the priest Melchizedek. | Tithes were stored in big barns.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun; regular verb, past «tithed». Rhymes with «scythe». Maths: a tithe = 1/10 = 10 per cent; divide by 10.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Verse is writing in the form of poetry, with lines and often rhythm and rhyme. 2) A verse is a group of lines in a poem or song (a stanza), often followed by a chorus. 3) (Bible) A verse is one short numbered part of a chapter in the Bible or other holy book.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons pupils write verse and learn that a song has verses and a chorus. In religious education people look up Bible verses by book, chapter and verse number. Phrases: «in verse», «the first verse», «chapter and verse» (all the exact details), «free verse», «blank verse».
examples from the lessons: We sang the first verse and then the chorus. | The poem has four verses. | Shakespeare wrote many plays in verse. | Our teacher asked us to find a Bible verse about kindness. | The verse John 3:16 is famous among Christians. | She can quote chapter and verse from the rule book. | Free verse is poetry without rhyme.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable when it means poetry in general, countable for a part of a poem, song or holy book. Do not confuse with «versus» (against). Bible references: book, chapter, verse.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A vineyard is a piece of land where grapevines are grown, usually to make wine. 2) (Bible) In Jesus' parables, a vineyard is often a picture of God's people or the world, as in the parable of the workers in the vineyard.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons, vineyards grow in sunny places such as France, Italy, California and South Australia. In religious education, several parables are set in a vineyard. Phrases: «work in the vineyard», «the workers in the vineyard», «a hillside vineyard».
examples from the lessons: Rows of grapes grew in the sunny vineyard. | We visited a vineyard on our holiday in France. | The workers picked grapes in the vineyard. | In the parable, every worker in the vineyard got the same pay. | South Australia has many famous vineyards. | Vineyards often grow on hillsides that face the sun. | Naboth's vineyard is an Old Testament story about greed.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Pronunciation: VIN-yard (the «e» is silent). Related: vine, vintage, wine.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Virtue is goodness and right behaviour. 2) A virtue is a good quality in a person, such as honesty, kindness, patience or courage. 3) A virtue of something is a good point or advantage: «The virtue of this bike is that it's light». 4) «By virtue of» (formal) means because of.
its sense in the lessons: In ethics and religious education pupils learn virtues such as honesty, fairness and courage; Christians speak of faith, hope and love (charity) as virtues. Proverbs: «Patience is a virtue». Phrases: «patience is a virtue», «make a virtue of necessity», «by virtue of».
examples from the lessons: Honesty is an important virtue. | Patience is a virtue, my gran always says. | The story shows the virtue of courage. | Christians speak of faith, hope and love as the three great virtues. | One virtue of this tent is that it's easy to put up. | She won the prize by virtue of her hard work. | Kindness is a virtue everyone can practise.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable (goodness) and countable (a good quality). Adjective: virtuous. Opposite: vice. Do not confuse «virtue» with «virtual» (seeming real but not really, like virtual reality).

part of speech: noun (a vow, vows); verb (vow, vows, vowed, vowing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A vow is a serious promise, often a solemn or religious one. 2) To vow is to promise firmly that you will do something. 3) (church) Wedding vows are the promises a couple make when they marry; monks and nuns take vows to God.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, a hero vows to rescue a friend; in religious education monks and nuns take vows of poverty, chastity and obedience. At weddings the couple exchange vows. Phrases: «take a vow», «make a vow», «break a vow», «wedding vows», «vow to do something».
examples from the lessons: The knight made a vow to protect the king. | She vowed never to tell the secret. | At the wedding they said their vows. | The monks took vows of silence. | I vowed to practise the piano every day. | Breaking a vow is a serious thing. | The friends vowed to stay in touch.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun and regular verb, past «vowed». Pronunciation rhymes with «now». Stronger and more solemn than an ordinary «promise». Do not confuse with «vowel» (a, e, i, o, u).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Vulnerable means easily hurt, harmed or attacked, in body or feelings. 2) Vulnerable people are those who need extra protection, such as young children, very old people or people who are ill. 3) (formal) Open to something bad: «vulnerable to colds».
its sense in the lessons: In safety and citizenship lessons, adults protect vulnerable children; online safety lessons explain how people can make you vulnerable by learning private details. In science, some animals are vulnerable to extinction. Phrases: «vulnerable to», «vulnerable children», «feel vulnerable», «a vulnerable species».
examples from the lessons: Babies are very vulnerable and need care. | The castle's weak gate made it vulnerable to attack. | I felt vulnerable when I told everyone my secret. | Old people are more vulnerable to the flu. | Pandas are a vulnerable species. | Never share your password; it makes you vulnerable online. | The charity helps vulnerable families.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective. Noun: vulnerability. Spelling: v-u-l-n-e-r-a-b-l-e (do not forget the «l» after «vu»). Opposite: invulnerable, protected, safe. Being vulnerable (sharing feelings) can also be brave.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A wilderness is a wild area of land that people have not changed, with no towns, farms or roads. 2) (Bible) The wilderness is the desert where, the Bible says, the Israelites wandered for forty years and Jesus fasted for forty days. 3) In the wilderness (idiom): left out, without power or importance for a time.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and science lessons wildernesses include forests, mountains and deserts where animals live freely; national parks protect them. In religious education, Lent remembers Jesus' forty days in the wilderness. In stories, characters get lost in the wilderness and must survive. Phrases: «in the wilderness», «wilderness area», «a voice crying in the wilderness».
examples from the lessons: Bears live deep in the Canadian wilderness. | The explorers crossed the frozen wilderness. | Moses led the people through the wilderness. | Jesus spent forty days in the wilderness. | Our garden became a wilderness when nobody weeded it. | The team spent years in the wilderness before winning again. | A wilderness guide taught us to read a compass.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable (plural «wildernesses»), often «the wilderness». Pronunciation: WIL-der-ness (short «i», unlike «wild»). Related: wild.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Something addictive makes people want it again and again until they cannot easily stop, such as cigarettes, alcohol or some drugs. 2) (informal) Very enjoyable so that you keep wanting more: «This game is so addictive».
its sense in the lessons: In health and safety lessons pupils learn that nicotine in cigarettes and vapes and some drugs are addictive, harming the body and making it hard to stop. In everyday talk people call games, snacks or TV shows addictive as a joke. Phrases: «highly addictive», «addictive substance», «an addictive game».
examples from the lessons: Nicotine in cigarettes is very addictive. | Vapes can be addictive, so they are not for children. | This puzzle game is really addictive! | Some apps are designed to be addictive. | Doctors warn that sugary drinks can feel addictive. | Crisps are addictive; I can't stop at one! | Addictive drugs can damage your brain and body.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective. Related: addict (a person), addiction (the illness), addicted (to). The joking sense is mild; real addiction is a serious health problem that people need help with.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Antisemitism is hatred of, prejudice against or unfair treatment of Jewish people because they are Jewish.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons antisemitism is studied in the Holocaust, when the Nazis murdered millions of Jews; in citizenship lessons pupils learn that antisemitism is a form of racism and is wrong, and that laws protect people from it. Phrases: «fight antisemitism», «antisemitic remarks», «stand up against antisemitism».
examples from the lessons: Antisemitism is hatred of Jewish people. | The Holocaust was the worst example of antisemitism in history. | Our school teaches that antisemitism, like all racism, is wrong. | Someone painted antisemitic words on a wall, and the police came. | Learning about Anne Frank helps us understand antisemitism. | Many people marched to stand against antisemitism. | Calling out antisemitism is part of being a good citizen.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Spelling varies: antisemitism, anti-Semitism. Adjective: antisemitic; a person who holds these views is an antisemite. Related ideas: racism, prejudice, discrimination, Islamophobia.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A birthright is something that a person has a right to just because they were born into a certain family, country or position. 2) (Bible) In the Old Testament, the birthright was the special share the eldest son got from his father; Esau sold his birthright to his brother Jacob for a bowl of stew.
its sense in the lessons: In religious education the story of Esau and Jacob shows someone trading something precious for something small. In citizenship talk, freedom or education may be called every child's birthright. Phrases: «sell your birthright», «a birthright citizen», «freedom is our birthright».
examples from the lessons: Esau sold his birthright for a bowl of soup. | Education should be every child's birthright. | The prince's birthright was to become king. | Being able to speak your own language is a birthright. | Jacob tricked his brother out of his birthright. | In some countries citizenship is a birthright if you are born there. | Don't sell your birthright for a quick treat.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. One word: birth + right. «Sell one's birthright for a mess of pottage» is an old saying from the Esau story: to give up something precious for something small.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To commit a crime or a wrong act is to do it: «commit a crime», «commit a sin». 2) To commit to something is to promise to give your time and effort to it. 3) To commit someone to prison or hospital is to send them there officially. 4) (computing) To save changes officially, for example in a program. 5) To commit something to memory is to learn it by heart.
its sense in the lessons: In news, law and safety lessons, people commit crimes; in ethics lessons people commit sins or mistakes. In sport and school, committing to a team means turning up and trying hard. Phrases: «commit a crime», «commit to», «commit to memory», «committed (devoted)», «commit suicide» (now people prefer «die by suicide»).
examples from the lessons: The thief committed a crime and was caught. | She committed to practising every day. | Please commit these spellings to memory. | The judge committed him to prison. | The team is fully committed to winning. | Christians pray to be forgiven for sins they have committed. | Don't commit to too many clubs at once.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb; double the t: committed, committing. Nouns: commitment (a promise), committee (a group). Adjective «committed» means very loyal and hard-working. Speak gently about suicide; a trusted adult can help anyone who feels very sad.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (church) A congregation is the group of people gathered in a church, synagogue or mosque for worship. 2) The members of a particular church or religious community. 3) (formal) Any gathering of people or animals.
its sense in the lessons: In religious education the congregation sings, prays and listens to the sermon; the priest or minister leads them. In everyday life the word is used for members of a local church. Phrases: «the congregation stood», «a large congregation», «a congregation of birds» (rare).
examples from the lessons: The congregation sang a hymn together. | The vicar welcomed the congregation. | Our church has a small but friendly congregation. | The rabbi spoke to the congregation in the synagogue. | The congregation stood up when the bride came in. | The whole congregation said «Amen». | A congregation of seagulls gathered on the beach.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: congregations. In British English it can take a plural verb («the congregation were singing»). Related: congregate (to gather).

meaning for a pupil: 1) To covet something is to want very much something that belongs to someone else. 2) (Bible) «You shall not covet» is the last of the Ten Commandments, telling people not to long for their neighbour's house, wife or belongings. 3) A coveted prize or place is one that many people want.
its sense in the lessons: In religious education and ethics the commandment against coveting teaches contentment. In everyday and sports writing a «coveted trophy» is one everyone wants. Phrases: «covet your neighbour's», «a coveted prize», «coveted place».
