examples from the lessons: The Ten Commandments say, «You shall not covet». | He coveted his friend's new bike. | The gold cup is the most coveted prize in the league. | She won a coveted place in the school orchestra. | Coveting what others have can make you unhappy. | The dragon coveted the king's treasure. | Try to be thankful instead of coveting.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: coveted, coveting (one t). Noun/adjective: covetous. Formal or biblical; plain words: want badly, envy. Not the same as «cover».

part of speech: noun (a craving, cravings); form of verb (crave, craves, craved, craving)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A craving is a very strong wish for something, especially a food or drink. 2) A strong need for an addictive thing, like a smoker's craving for a cigarette. 3) Craving is also the -ing form of «crave», to want something very strongly.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life people have cravings for chocolate or pizza; pregnant mothers are said to have unusual cravings. In health lessons cravings are part of addiction. In Buddhism, craving (wanting) is taught as a cause of suffering. Phrases: «a craving for», «satisfy a craving», «crave attention».
examples from the lessons: I have a craving for ice cream. | Mum had cravings for pickles when she was expecting the baby. | Smokers feel cravings when they try to stop. | He is craving attention from his friends. | Buddhists teach that craving leads to suffering. | After the run I was craving water. | A glass of milk stopped my craving for something sweet.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun. Verb «crave» is regular: craved. Usually «a craving for» something. Stronger than «want».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A deadline is the latest time or day by which something must be done or handed in. 2) (old use) A line in a prison that prisoners must not cross.
its sense in the lessons: In school, homework and projects have deadlines; in adult work life people «meet» or «miss» deadlines. In maths problems you may count how many days are left before a deadline. Phrases: «meet a deadline», «miss a deadline», «a tight deadline», «extend the deadline», «the deadline is Friday».
examples from the lessons: The deadline for the project is Friday. | I finished my story just before the deadline. | Mum works late when she has a deadline. | The teacher extended the deadline by two days. | If you miss the deadline, you lose marks. | Newspapers have strict deadlines each night. | We had a tight deadline to build the model.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. One word. Maths: if the deadline is in 10 days and the work needs 2 days per part for 4 parts, you need 8 days and have 2 to spare. Planning helps you meet deadlines.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Disobedience is refusing or failing to do what a person in charge, a rule or a law tells you. 2) (formal) Civil disobedience means breaking a law peacefully on purpose to protest that it is unfair.
its sense in the lessons: In ethics and religious education, the story of Adam and Eve is about disobedience; in school, disobedience breaks class rules. In history lessons, Rosa Parks and Gandhi used civil disobedience. Phrases: «act of disobedience», «civil disobedience», «punished for disobedience».
examples from the lessons: The dog was told off for its disobedience. | Disobedience to the rules can lead to a detention. | Adam and Eve's disobedience is told in the book of Genesis. | Rosa Parks' act of civil disobedience helped change unfair laws. | The soldier was punished for disobedience. | The story shows how disobedience got the boy into trouble. | Peaceful disobedience can be brave when a law is unfair.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Opposite: obedience. Related: disobey (verb), disobedient (adjective). «Dis-» means not.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An employer is a person or company that pays people to work for them.
its sense in the lessons: In adult work life, the employer pays wages and the employee (worker) does the job; in money lessons pupils learn about wages, contracts and holiday pay. Phrases: «my employer», «a big employer», «employer and employee», «equal opportunities employer».
examples from the lessons: Mum's employer gave her a day off for her birthday. | The hospital is the biggest employer in our town. | An employer must pay workers fairly. | The employer interviewed five people for the job. | Dad's employer let him work from home. | Employers must keep workers safe. | If an employer pays ten pounds an hour for eight hours, the worker earns eighty pounds.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Opposite: employee (the worker). Related: employ, employment, unemployed. Ending -er = the one who does it; -ee = the one it is done to.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An engagement is an agreement to marry someone; a couple who are engaged usually wear or give an engagement ring. 2) (formal) An arrangement to meet someone or be somewhere: «a dinner engagement». 3) Engagement is being interested and taking part: «pupils' engagement in lessons». 4) A battle or fight between armies.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday family life an engagement party celebrates a couple who plan to marry. In school reports teachers talk about engagement in learning. In history lessons an engagement can mean a battle. Phrases: «engagement ring», «announce their engagement», «a prior engagement», «student engagement».
examples from the lessons: My cousin showed us her engagement ring. | They announced their engagement at the family dinner. | The engagement lasted a year before the wedding. | I'm sorry, I have a prior engagement on Saturday. | The teacher praised our class's engagement in the project. | The naval engagement lasted all day. | We went to my aunt's engagement party.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable for a promise to marry, a meeting or a battle; uncountable for «taking part». Related: engage, engaged (also: busy, as a phone line in the UK). An engagement can be «broken off».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Fame is being known about and talked about by very many people.
its sense in the lessons: In history and stories people win fame for great deeds; in everyday life film stars, singers and footballers have fame. In ethics lessons pupils discuss whether fame makes people happy. Phrases: «rise to fame», «find fame», «fame and fortune», «claim to fame», «hall of fame».
examples from the lessons: She found fame as a singer. | Fame and fortune do not always bring happiness. | The footballer's rise to fame was very fast. | My town's claim to fame is a giant pumpkin. | His fame spread across the country. | The scientist did not want fame; she wanted to help people. | Our school has a hall of fame for top readers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: no plural. Adjective: famous; infamous means famous for something bad. «Claim to fame» is an idiom for the one thing someone or something is known for.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Favouritism is unfairly treating one person or group better than others, for example a teacher always choosing the same pupil or a parent giving one child more.
its sense in the lessons: In ethics lessons and family stories favouritism causes jealousy, as in the Bible story of Joseph, whose father gave him a special coat. In school and sport, fair adults try not to show favouritism. Phrases: «show favouritism», «accuse someone of favouritism», «no favouritism».
examples from the lessons: The coach was accused of favouritism. | Jacob's favouritism towards Joseph made his brothers jealous. | A good teacher avoids favouritism. | Mum says there is no favouritism in our house. | Favouritism can make people feel left out. | The other workers complained about favouritism. | Picking teams by drawing names stops favouritism.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. British, Irish, Canadian and Australian spelling «favouritism»; American «favoritism». Related: favourite, favour. Liking someone is fine; favouritism is treating them unfairly better.

part of speech: noun (glory, uncountable; glories); verb (glory, glories, gloried — glory in)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Glory is great fame, honour and praise won by doing something important or brave. 2) (church) Glory is the great praise and worship given to God, and God's greatness and splendour. 3) Great beauty: «the glory of the sunset». 4) To glory in something is to enjoy it with great pride.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and sport, heroes win glory; in church, people sing «Glory to God» and «Glory be to the Father». In everyday talk «glory days» are happy past times. Phrases: «in all its glory», «blaze of glory», «glory to God», «crowning glory», «glory days».
examples from the lessons: The team won glory in the final. | The choir sang «Glory to God in the highest». | We watched the sunrise in all its glory. | The soldiers fought for glory. | Her long hair is her crowning glory. | He gloried in his win. | Grandad talks about his glory days in the football team.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable; plural «glories» for great things. Adjective: glorious; verb «glorify». «Glory hunter» (UK, informal) is someone who supports only winning teams.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Governance is the way a country, organisation or school is run and controlled, including who makes decisions and how.
its sense in the lessons: In citizenship lessons and adult news, «good governance» means fair, honest, open running of a country or company. School governors look after a school's governance. It is a stiff formal word; plain words: running, management, rule. Phrases: «good governance», «school governance», «corporate governance».
examples from the lessons: The report looked at the governance of the school. | Good governance means leaders are honest and fair. | The charity changed its governance after problems. | Citizens have a say in the governance of their country by voting. | The company's governance is checked every year. | Students learned about local governance from the mayor. | Weak governance can let money be wasted.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable, formal. Related: govern, government, governor. Different from «government» (the group of people in charge).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A governor is a person who is chosen or elected to be in charge of a region, such as a state of the USA or an Australian state. 2) (UK) A school governor is a volunteer on the board that helps run a school. 3) (UK) The governor of a prison or a bank is its head. 4) (old use) A governor-general represents the king or queen in countries like Canada, Australia and New Zealand. 5) (informal, UK, old) «Guv'nor» means boss.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and citizenship lessons, each US state has a governor; Australian states have governors too. In British schools, parents can become school governors. In history, a colonial governor ran a colony for another country. Phrases: «state governor», «school governor», «the Governor of the Bank of England», «Governor-General».
examples from the lessons: The governor of California gave a speech. | My mum is a school governor. | The prison governor visited each cell. | The Governor-General of Canada opened the new park. | The governor signed the new law. | In history, the governor ruled the colony for the king. | The school governors met to plan the budget.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: governors. Capital G before a name or title: Governor Smith. Related: govern, government, governance. In the UK, «governess» is a different (old) word for a woman who taught children at home.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (Islam) Halal means allowed by Islamic law; it is used especially for food, such as meat from animals killed in the correct way, and no pork or alcohol. 2) A halal shop or restaurant sells halal food. 3) (Islam) Halal can mean anything allowed in Islam; the opposite is haram (forbidden).
its sense in the lessons: In religious education pupils learn that many Muslims eat only halal food. Many school canteens and supermarkets in the UK, USA, Canada and Australia offer halal options. Phrases: «halal meat», «halal food», «is it halal?», «halal butcher».
examples from the lessons: My friend eats only halal meat. | The school canteen has a halal option every day. | Pork is never halal. | We bought chicken at the halal butcher. | Many Muslims check if sweets are halal because some gelatine comes from pigs. | The restaurant sign says «Halal». | In Islam, halal means what is allowed and haram means what is forbidden.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective, sometimes noun. Pronunciation: ha-LAL. Similar idea in Judaism: kosher (but the rules are not identical). Not «Hallal». Be respectful of food rules at parties and school trips.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A handover is the act of passing something, such as a job, power or a place, from one person or group to another. 2) (work) A meeting where a worker tells the next worker what they need to know, such as nurses at the end of a shift. 3) (sport) Passing the baton in a relay race (more often called the changeover).
its sense in the lessons: In adult work life, nurses and doctors do a handover between shifts; in history, a handover of power or a territory (for example, a colony to another country) is a big event. In relay races, the handover of the baton must be smooth. Phrases: «a smooth handover», «handover of power», «shift handover».
examples from the lessons: The nurses had a handover at seven o'clock. | The handover of the keys happened at the new house. | The new head teacher had a long handover with the old one. | Our relay team practised the baton handover. | The handover of power was peaceful. | After the handover, the new owners moved in. | The teacher wrote handover notes for the supply teacher.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun, one word. The verb is two words: «hand over» («Please hand over your phones»). Similar: changeover, transfer.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (Bible, church) Hosanna is a shout of praise to God; the crowds shouted «Hosanna!» when Jesus rode into Jerusalem on Palm Sunday. 2) A hosanna is a shout or song of praise or joy.
its sense in the lessons: In religious education the Palm Sunday story tells of people waving palm branches and calling «Hosanna to the Son of David!»; it is sung in many church services and hymns. Its first meaning in Hebrew was «save us, please». Phrases: «Hosanna in the highest», «sing hosanna», «shouts of hosanna».
examples from the lessons: The crowd shouted «Hosanna!» as Jesus rode in on a donkey. | On Palm Sunday we sing «Hosanna in the highest». | The choir sang a joyful hosanna. | Children waved palm leaves and called «Hosanna!». | «Hosanna» comes from Hebrew words meaning «save us». | The hymn ends with a great hosanna. | The vicar explained the meaning of hosanna.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Often capital H in church texts. Spelling: one s, double n: h-o-s-a-n-n-a. Mostly used in church; it sounds odd in everyday talk.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Humanism is a way of thinking that says people can live good, meaningful lives using reason, kindness and science, without believing in God or a religion. 2) (history) Humanism was a movement about six hundred years ago, in the Renaissance, that brought back the learning of ancient Greece and Rome and put people at the centre of study.
its sense in the lessons: In religious education, humanism is taught as a non-religious worldview: humanists celebrate weddings and funerals without religious words and try to make the best of this one life. In history lessons Renaissance humanists studied old books and art. Phrases: «humanist values», «a humanist wedding», «Renaissance humanism».
examples from the lessons: Humanism is a way of living without religion. | Humanists believe people should be kind because it helps others. | My uncle had a humanist wedding. | Renaissance humanism brought back interest in Greek writers. | Our RE class compared humanism with Christianity. | Humanism puts reason and science at the centre. | Many humanists work for charities.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. A follower is a humanist; adjective humanist or humanistic. Do not confuse with «humanitarian» (helping people in need) or «humane» (kind). Speak of views fairly: «Humanists believe…».

meaning for a pupil: 1) An icon is a small picture on a computer, tablet or phone screen that you click or tap to open an app or do something. 2) (church) An icon is a holy painting of Jesus, Mary or a saint, especially in Orthodox churches, used to help prayer. 3) An icon is a very famous person or thing that stands for an idea or time: «a fashion icon», «a national icon».
its sense in the lessons: In computing lessons pupils click icons and design their own. In religious education, Orthodox Christians pray before icons and light candles. In everyday talk, a famous singer or a landmark like the Sydney Opera House is an icon. Phrases: «click the icon», «a pop icon», «a cultural icon», «an icon of Saint Nicholas».
examples from the lessons: Click the printer icon to print your work. | The Orthodox church was full of golden icons. | Grandma kisses the icon of Mary when she prays. | The Eiffel Tower is an icon of Paris. | She is a fashion icon for many young people. | Tap the camera icon to take a photo. | The red double-decker bus is a London icon.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; «an icon» (starts with a vowel sound). Adjective: iconic (very famous and typical). Spelling: i-c-o-n, not «ikon» (an old spelling still seen for church icons).

meaning for a pupil: 1) An idol is a person who is greatly admired and loved by many people, such as a pop star or sports star. 2) (religion, Bible) An idol is a statue or picture that is worshipped as a god; the Bible forbids worshipping idols. 3) Anything treated as more important than it should be: «Money became his idol».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life children have idols such as footballers and singers; TV shows pick «pop idols». In religious education, the Ten Commandments say not to make or worship idols, and the golden calf story shows the Israelites worshipping one. Phrases: «a pop idol», «my childhood idol», «worship idols», «a golden idol».
examples from the lessons: My idol is a famous footballer. | The singer was the idol of millions of fans. | The Israelites made a golden calf as an idol. | The Ten Commandments forbid worshipping idols. | The explorer found a stone idol in the jungle temple. | Don't make money your idol. | She met her idol and got an autograph.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; «an idol». Homophone: «idle» (lazy, not working) sounds the same. Related: idolise (to admire greatly), idolatry (worship of idols).

meaning for a pupil: 1) An inn is a small hotel or pub, often in the countryside or an old building, where travellers can eat, drink and stay the night. 2) (Bible) In the Christmas story, there was no room for Mary and Joseph at the inn in Bethlehem, so Jesus was born where animals were kept.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and history lessons, travellers on horseback stopped at inns; in nativity plays a child plays the innkeeper. In everyday life many British pubs are called «The Something Inn». Phrases: «stay at an inn», «there was no room at the inn», «innkeeper», «roadside inn».
examples from the lessons: We had lunch at an old inn in the village. | There was no room at the inn for Mary and Joseph. | In the nativity play, I was the innkeeper. | The tired travellers stopped at an inn for the night. | The Good Samaritan took the hurt man to an inn. | The Red Lion Inn has a big fireplace. | The inn had rooms upstairs and a bar below.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: inns. Homophone: «in» (preposition) sounds the same. Old-fashioned word; today «hotel», «pub» or «B&B» are common.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (religion) In Judaism, the Messiah is a future king from the family of David whom God will send to bring peace and rescue the Jewish people. 2) (church) Christians believe that Jesus is the Messiah (the Christ). 3) A messiah is any leader people hope will save them or solve their problems (sometimes said with doubt).
its sense in the lessons: In religious education, pupils learn that «Messiah» comes from a Hebrew word meaning «anointed one», and «Christ» is the Greek word for the same; Jews are still waiting for the Messiah, while Christians believe he came in Jesus. In music, Handel's «Messiah» is famous at Christmas and Easter. Phrases: «the promised Messiah», «Handel's Messiah», «a would-be messiah».
examples from the lessons: Christians believe Jesus is the Messiah. | Jewish people believe the Messiah has not yet come. | «Christ» is the Greek word for «Messiah». | Our choir sang the Hallelujah chorus from Handel's «Messiah». | The prophets spoke of a Messiah from the family of David. | Fans treated the new coach like a messiah. | The shepherds were told that the Messiah was born.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital M for the religious meaning. Adjective: messianic. Pronunciation: me-SY-ah. Say beliefs fairly: «Christians believe…», «Jews believe…».

part of speech: noun (a minority, minorities; minority as an adjective)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A minority is the smaller number or part of a group, less than half. 2) A minority (group) is a group of people who are different in race, religion, language or culture from most people in a country. 3) (law) The time when a person is still a child in law (under eighteen in most places).
its sense in the lessons: In maths and data lessons, «a minority» means fewer than half: if 8 of 30 pupils like sprouts, they are a minority. In citizenship lessons, laws protect the rights of minorities. In voting, the minority loses but should still be respected. Phrases: «in the minority», «a small minority», «ethnic minority», «minority language», «minority government».
examples from the lessons: Only a minority of the class wanted to stay inside. | People who like broccoli are in the minority here. | Welsh is a minority language in the UK. | The law protects religious minorities. | A small minority of fans behaved badly. | If 12 out of 30 children chose red, red was the choice of a minority. | The party formed a minority government.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; plural «minorities». Opposite: majority (more than half). Maths: a minority is less than 50 per cent of the whole; with exactly half, there is no majority or minority. A minority is not less important.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (church) A monk is a man who has given his life to God and lives in a religious community called a monastery, following rules of prayer, work and simple living. 2) (religion) Buddhist monks and monks in other religions live a similar life of prayer, study and meditation.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, monks copied books by hand, made medicine and ran schools; Vikings raided monasteries such as Lindisfarne. In religious education monks take vows such as poverty and obedience; Buddhist monks wear saffron or maroon robes. Phrases: «a Buddhist monk», «a Benedictine monk», «live like a monk».
examples from the lessons: The monks prayed together seven times a day. | Long ago, monks copied the Bible by hand. | A Buddhist monk taught us how to meditate. | The Vikings attacked the monks at Lindisfarne. | Monks grew herbs to make medicine. | The monk wore a brown robe tied with a cord. | Friar Tuck was a monk-like friar in the Robin Hood stories.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: monks. Female equivalent: nun. Related: monastery (where monks live), monastic, abbot (head monk). Do not confuse with «monkey».

meaning for a pupil: 1) To mourn is to feel and show deep sadness because someone has died. 2) To mourn something is to feel sad that it is gone or lost: «We mourned the end of the holidays».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life families mourn when someone dies; there is a funeral and sometimes people wear black. In religious education, different faiths have customs for mourning, like Jewish sitting shiva. In stories a character mourns a lost friend. Phrases: «mourn the death of», «mourn for», «in mourning», «a period of mourning».
examples from the lessons: We all mourned when Grandpa died. | The whole country mourned the queen. | The family wore black to show they were in mourning. | The girl mourned for her lost cat. | Jesus said, «Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted». | Jewish families mourn together for seven days, called shiva. | It is natural to cry when you mourn.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb, past «mourned». Noun: mourning, mourner. Homophone: «morning» sounds very similar but «mourning» (sadness) has a «u». Mourning has no time limit; people grieve in different ways.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Mustard is a hot-tasting yellow or brown paste or sauce made from the seeds of the mustard plant, eaten with meat and hot dogs. 2) The mustard plant has small yellow flowers and tiny seeds. 3) A dark yellow colour. 4) (UK, informal) «Keen as mustard» means very eager. 5) «Cut the mustard» (informal) means be good enough.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday food, mustard goes on sandwiches and hot dogs. In science, children grow cress and mustard seeds on wet paper. In religious education, Jesus' parable of the mustard seed says the kingdom of God grows from something tiny into something big. Phrases: «mustard seed», «English mustard», «keen as mustard», «cut the mustard».
examples from the lessons: Dad puts mustard on his hot dog. | We grew mustard and cress on cotton wool. | The mustard seed is tiny, but the plant grows big. | Jesus told the parable of the mustard seed. | She wore a mustard-yellow jumper. | English mustard is very hot! | The new player is keen as mustard.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable (no plural). Idioms: «keen as mustard» (UK), «cut the mustard» (good enough). Mustard is hot in taste, not in temperature.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To overhear something is to hear what other people are saying without them knowing, or without meaning to listen.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, a character often overhears a secret plan and the adventure begins. In everyday life you might overhear grown-ups talking; listening on purpose is eavesdropping. Phrases: «overhear a conversation», «I couldn't help overhearing», «be overheard».
examples from the lessons: I overheard Mum planning my surprise party. | In the story, the boy overheard the pirates' plan. | Sorry, I couldn't help overhearing your conversation. | Speak quietly so you are not overheard. | She overheard her name in the staff room. | The spy overheard the soldiers talking. | We overheard the teacher say there would be a quiz.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular verb: overhear, overheard, overheard (like hear, heard). Overhearing is usually by accident; «eavesdropping» is listening on purpose.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who helps people or groups stop fighting and make friends again. 2) (Bible) In the Bible, Jesus says «Blessed are the peacemakers», and Christians believe peacemakers do God's work. 3) (informal) Someone in a family or class who often calms arguments down.
its sense in the lessons: In stories the peacemaker steps between two sides and helps them listen; in school it names a pupil who helps settle playground quarrels; in church it comes from the Beatitudes in the Sermon on the Mount. Phrases: «play the peacemaker», «act as peacemaker», «a natural peacemaker».
examples from the lessons: My sister is the peacemaker when my brothers argue. | The teacher asked Ava to be the peacemaker at the football game. | «Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called children of God.» | A good peacemaker listens to both sides first. | The two kings sent a peacemaker to stop the war. | Grandad always played the peacemaker at family dinners. | Being a peacemaker takes patience and courage.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun, one word, plural peacemakers. A peacemaker is not the same as a person who simply keeps quiet; the peacemaker works to fix the quarrel. Related: peace, make peace, peaceable, peacekeeper (a soldier who keeps peace after a war).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A journey to a holy place for religious reasons, such as Christians going to Jerusalem or Muslims going to Mecca. 2) A trip to a place that is very special to you, such as a famous writer's house or a sports ground. 3) (formal) A long life journey thought of as a search for something good.
its sense in the lessons: In religion lessons a pilgrimage shows faith in action: people walk or travel far to pray in a special place (Lourdes, Canterbury, Santiago, Mecca for the hajj). In stories it means a long meaningful trip. Phrases: «go on a pilgrimage», «make a pilgrimage to», «place of pilgrimage».
examples from the lessons: Many Christians go on a pilgrimage to Jerusalem. | In The Canterbury Tales the travellers are on a pilgrimage. | The hajj is the pilgrimage to Mecca that Muslims try to make once in their lives. | Dad made a pilgrimage to the old football ground where he watched his first match. | Pilgrims on the pilgrimage walked for many days. | Lourdes in France is a famous place of pilgrimage. | Our class read about a pilgrimage across Spain.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun. A person on a pilgrimage is a pilgrim. Spelling: pil-gri-mage, ends in -age. Do not confuse with «pilgrim» (the person) or with the Pilgrims who sailed to America.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (church) To give a religious talk, called a sermon, to people, usually in a church. 2) To tell others strongly that something is right and that they should do it: «preach kindness». 3) (informal, disapproving) To give advice or tell people what is right in an annoying, bossy way: «Stop preaching at me!»
its sense in the lessons: In church life the priest, minister or pastor preaches a sermon; in the Bible Jesus and the apostles preach the good news. In everyday life «preach» can be a complaint about someone lecturing others. Phrases: «preach a sermon», «preach the gospel», «practise what you preach» (do what you tell others to do), «preach to the converted» (tell people what they already believe), «preaching to the choir».
examples from the lessons: The vicar preached about forgiveness on Sunday. | Jesus preached to crowds by the lake. | Mum always says we should practise what we preach. | Don't preach at me, I know I made a mistake. | The coach preaches teamwork every training session. | John the Baptist preached in the desert. | Telling our class to recycle was preaching to the converted.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: preached, preaching. A person who preaches is a preacher; the talk is a sermon. «Preach to» someone, «preach about» something. In the informal sense it is often unkind, like «lecture».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (Bible) The prodigal son is the young man in Jesus's story who wastes his father's money, comes home sorry, and is welcomed with love. 2) (formal) Spending money or things too freely and wastefully. 3) (noun, humorous) Someone who comes back home after being away a long time, especially after doing wrong: «the prodigal returns».
its sense in the lessons: In religion lessons the parable of the prodigal son teaches forgiveness: the father runs to hug the son who came back. In everyday speech people joke «the prodigal returns» when someone comes home late or after a long absence. Phrases: «the prodigal son», «prodigal with money».
examples from the lessons: Jesus told the story of the prodigal son to show God's love. | The prodigal son spent all his money and ended up feeding pigs. | His father threw a party when the prodigal came home. | «Look, the prodigal returns!» said Gran when my cousin finally visited. | The king was prodigal with gold and soon the treasury was empty. | Our teacher asked who we felt sorry for in the story of the prodigal son. | The older brother was angry about the feast for the prodigal.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Many people think «prodigal» means «coming back home», but its real meaning is «wasteful»; the son is called prodigal because he wasted money. Not usually used for people today except in the phrase. Noun prodigality (formal).

part of speech: adjective (reborn); past participle of the rare verb rebear (be reborn)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Born again; made to live again or start a new life. 2) (church) Christians who say they are «born again» or «reborn» believe they have started a new life of faith in Jesus. 3) (belief) In Hinduism and Buddhism, people believe a soul can be reborn in a new body after death. 4) Full of new energy or hope, as if starting again: «The old park was reborn.»
its sense in the lessons: In stories something «reborn» comes back to life, like a phoenix rising from the ashes, or a town rebuilt after a storm. In religion lessons it links to baptism and to beliefs about rebirth (reincarnation). Phrases: «be reborn», «feel reborn», «reborn as».
examples from the lessons: The phoenix burned up and was reborn from the ashes. | After the holiday Dad said he felt reborn. | Many Christians say they were reborn when they were baptised. | Hindus believe a soul is reborn many times. | The old cinema was reborn as a theatre. | In spring the garden seems reborn. | In the game your character is reborn at the last checkpoint.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Used mostly with «be»: «was reborn», «is reborn». Noun: rebirth. «Born-again» is the usual adjective for Christians: «a born-again Christian». Not «reborned».

part of speech: noun (a repayment, repayments; also uncountable repayment)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (money) Paying back money that you borrowed. 2) (money) One of a set of regular amounts paid back on a loan, such as the monthly payment on a mortgage or car. 3) Doing something in return for help or harm: «in repayment for your kindness».
its sense in the lessons: In adult life repayments are paid on loans, mortgages and credit cards, usually with extra money called interest. In maths word problems, repayments are equal parts of a total: a 600 dollar loan repaid in 6 repayments means 100 dollars each (if there is no interest). Phrases: «monthly repayments», «make a repayment», «loan repayment», «miss a repayment».
examples from the lessons: Mum and Dad make a mortgage repayment every month. | The loan has twelve monthly repayments. | If you miss a repayment, the bank may charge more. | Tom gave Sam two chocolate bars in repayment for the pen. | Each repayment is 50 pounds. | The repayments on the car are quite high. | She finished the last repayment and owned the bike outright.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable for single payments («three repayments»), uncountable for the idea («repayment of the loan»). Verb: repay (repaid). In maths: total paid = repayment × number of repayments; with interest, the total paid is more than the money borrowed.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (Jewish faith) The special meal and service held at home on the first night (or first two nights) of the Jewish festival of Passover. 2) The order of the evening, where the family reads the story of the Exodus from the Haggadah and eats symbolic foods.
its sense in the lessons: In religion lessons the seder teaches how Jewish families remember God freeing the Israelites from slavery in Egypt. Foods on the seder plate include matzah (flat bread), bitter herbs, salt water and a roasted bone; the youngest child asks four questions. Phrases: «the seder plate», «a Passover seder», «hold a seder».
examples from the lessons: Rachel's family holds a seder on the first night of Passover. | At the seder the youngest child asks the four questions. | The seder plate has bitter herbs to remember slavery. | They eat matzah at the seder. | We visited a friend's seder and listened to the story of Moses. | The seder ends with songs and hopes for next year in Jerusalem.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Hebrew word meaning «order». Often written with a capital S. Plural seders (or sedarim in Hebrew). Not to be confused with «cedar» (a tree), which sounds a little similar.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (law) A special kind of court or group of officials who decide on a particular kind of problem, such as work disputes or tax arguments. 2) (law) A court set up to judge serious crimes, such as war crimes. 3) Any group with the power to judge someone.
its sense in the lessons: In adult life a worker who thinks they were sacked unfairly may take their case to an employment tribunal. In history lessons tribunals judged leaders after wars. In stories it can sound frightening: someone stands before a tribunal. Phrases: «employment tribunal», «go to a tribunal», «war crimes tribunal», «appear before a tribunal».
examples from the lessons: Uncle Dan took his old boss to an employment tribunal. | The tribunal decided he had been dismissed unfairly. | After the war, a tribunal judged the leaders. | Three judges sat on the tribunal. | The tribunal will give its decision next week. | In the story the hero had to stand before a tribunal of elders.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun, stress on the second syllable: try-BYOO-nal. A tribunal is smaller and more specialised than an ordinary court. Formal word; children rarely use it.

part of speech: fragment / prefix (un-); abbreviation (UN); French and Spanish word (un, «a/one»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) As «un-» at the start of a word, it means «not» or «the opposite of»: unhappy (not happy), unkind, unlock (do the opposite of lock). 2) UN (written in capitals) stands for the United Nations, a group of nearly all the countries of the world that works for peace. 3) In French and Spanish, «un» means «a» or «one». 4) (informal, dialect) In some speech «'un» is a clipped «one»: «a good 'un», «the little 'uns».
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons pupils learn that un- builds opposites; in maths, «un» is part of words like «unequal» and «unknown» (the number we are looking for). On the news «the UN» is the United Nations. In UK speech «a good 'un» means a good person. Phrases: «the UN», «UN peacekeepers», «a good 'un».
examples from the lessons: Add un- to «happy» and you get «unhappy». | The door was unlocked, so we went in. | The UN sends peacekeepers to troubled places. | In French, «un chat» means «a cat». | Grandad says our dog is a good 'un. | The little 'uns are playing in the sandpit. | Find the unknown number in the sum.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Not a normal word on its own in English. Do not confuse prefix un- with in-/im-/dis- (incorrect, impossible, dislike): each word takes its own. «Unlock» undoes an action; «unhappy» means «not». UN is said as two letters: «you-en».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Being joined together as one, or people agreeing and working together. 2) (maths) The number one; «unity» is an old word for 1. 3) (church) Christians pray for the unity of the church, meaning all believers together as one family.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and on the news unity means a team, family or country standing together. In maths, very old or advanced books say «unity» for 1. In church life it links to ecumenism, when different churches work together. Phrases: «in unity», «national unity», «a show of unity», «unity is strength».
examples from the lessons: The team showed real unity in the final. | Unity is strength: together we can do more. | The country needed unity after the storm. | The churches held a service for Christian unity. | The class flag was a sign of our unity. | In old maths books, unity means the number one. | There was no unity in the group; everyone wanted something different.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable. Adjective: united; verb: unite. Do not confuse with «uniformity», which means everything is the same; unity can include different people working together.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who believes that we cannot know for sure whether God exists, so they do not say yes or no. 2) (adjective) Not sure or not deciding about something: «I'm agnostic about pineapple on pizza.» 3) (computers) Working with any kind of system: «a device-agnostic app» works on any phone or computer.
its sense in the lessons: In religion and ethics lessons agnostic is set beside believer (theist) and atheist (someone who believes there is no God); pupils learn to respect all three. In everyday and computer talk it means «not choosing a side». Phrases: «an agnostic», «I'm agnostic about…», «platform-agnostic».
examples from the lessons: My uncle says he is an agnostic: he doesn't know if God is real. | An atheist says there is no God; an agnostic says we can't be sure. | Our class learned that Christians, atheists and agnostics can still be good friends. | I'm agnostic about whether cats or dogs are better. | The game is platform-agnostic, so it runs on any console. | She grew up agnostic but later went to church.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Use «an» because it starts with a vowel sound: «an agnostic». Noun for the belief: agnosticism. Trap: agnostic is not the same as atheist. From Greek «a-» (not) + «gnosis» (knowledge).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A time of training when a young person learns a trade or job by working with a skilled worker, often while being paid a small wage. 2) Any period of learning a skill from someone more experienced.
its sense in the lessons: In adult life, school leavers can do an apprenticeship to become plumbers, electricians, chefs, hairdressers or engineers, learning on the job and at college. In stories and history, boys and girls were sent to masters for an apprenticeship. Phrases: «do an apprenticeship», «start an apprenticeship», «serve an apprenticeship», «apprenticeship scheme».
examples from the lessons: My cousin is doing an apprenticeship as an electrician. | In old times a boy might serve a long apprenticeship with a blacksmith. | Her apprenticeship lasts four years. | During his apprenticeship he earned a small wage and went to college one day a week. | The bakery offers an apprenticeship to school leavers. | She finished her apprenticeship and became a qualified chef.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun. The person is an apprentice. Spelled with -ship at the end, like friendship. «Serve an apprenticeship» is a fixed phrase.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Saying who wrote, made, said or did something: giving credit. 2) Saying what caused something: «the attribution of the flood to heavy rain». 3) (formal) A quality that someone is thought to have.
its sense in the lessons: In school it matters when using pictures, quotes or facts from other people: you must give attribution (say where it came from) and not copy as if it were yours. In art and history experts argue about the attribution of a painting to a painter. Phrases: «with attribution», «without attribution», «give attribution», «correct attribution».
examples from the lessons: Always add an attribution when you use a photo from the internet. | The quote had no attribution, so we didn't know who said it. | The attribution of this painting to a famous artist is not certain. | Our teacher showed us how to write an attribution under a picture. | Copying words without attribution is called plagiarism. | The museum changed the attribution after new tests.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly uncountable, sometimes countable. Verb: attribute (to) — «The poem is attributed to an unknown writer.» Stress: at-tri-BU-tion. Do not confuse with «attributes» (qualities) or «contribution».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A machine or person that blows air, such as a leaf blower, a snow blower or a fan heater. 2) (UK, informal, old-fashioned slang) The telephone: «Get on the blower to the plumber.» 3) Someone who blows something: a glass-blower shapes hot glass by blowing into it. 4) (in «whistle-blower») A person who tells the public or the authorities about wrongdoing in a company or organisation.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life people use leaf blowers in autumn and snow blowers in winter (Canada, the northern USA). In British TV and stories «on the blower» means on the phone. On the news a whistle-blower is a worker who reveals cheating or danger. Phrases: «leaf blower», «on the blower», «glass-blower», «whistle-blower».
examples from the lessons: The neighbour's leaf blower is very noisy. | In Canada we clear the drive with a snow blower. | Grandad said, «I'll get on the blower and ring the doctor.» | We watched a glass-blower make a blue vase. | A whistle-blower told the newspaper the factory was unsafe. | The hand dryer is a hot-air blower.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun. «Blower» for the phone is old-fashioned UK slang; children may hear it from grandparents. «Whistle-blower» is often written with a hyphen.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (Hindu belief) In Hinduism, Brahman is the one ultimate reality or supreme spirit behind everything; Hindus believe all gods and all things come from Brahman. 2) A member of the highest priestly group (caste) in traditional Hindu society; also spelled Brahmin. 3) A breed of cattle with a big hump on its shoulders, found in India, the USA and Australia.
its sense in the lessons: In religion lessons Brahman is the central idea of God in Hinduism, often explained through many gods such as Brahma, Vishnu and Shiva being forms of it. In farming in Australia and Texas, Brahman cattle cope well with heat. Phrases: «Brahman cattle», «Brahmin priests».
examples from the lessons: Hindus believe Brahman is in everything. | Our teacher explained that Brahman is not the same as the god Brahma. | Brahmin priests lead prayers at the temple. | Brahman cattle have a hump and big floppy ears. | Farmers in Queensland raise Brahman cattle because they cope with the heat. | Many Hindus see their gods as faces of the one Brahman.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: Brahman (the ultimate reality), Brahma (a god, the creator) and Brahmin (a priestly caste) are different words. Usually capitalised. «Boston Brahmin» (USA) means an old rich family.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A woman on her wedding day, or a woman who has just got married. 2) (church, Bible) Christians sometimes call the church «the bride of Christ», a picture of Jesus's love for his people.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and family life the bride wears a special dress and walks up the aisle; her partner is the groom (bridegroom). In church weddings the bride and groom make promises (vows). Phrases: «bride and groom», «the bride's father», «bride-to-be», «the bride wore white», «here comes the bride».
examples from the lessons: The bride wore a long white dress. | The bride and groom cut the cake together. | My aunt will be a bride next spring. | The flower girl walked in front of the bride. | Everyone stood up when the bride came in. | In the fairy tale the princess became the prince's bride. | The bride's father made a funny speech.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun. Adjective: bridal (bridal dress). A bridesmaid helps the bride. The man is the groom or bridegroom. Not to be confused with «bribe» (money given to make someone do wrong) or «pride».

part of speech: noun (chanting, uncountable); present participle of chant (chant, chants, chanted, chanting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Singing or saying words over and over on one or a few notes, often in religious worship. 2) A crowd shouting the same words again and again, at a football match or protest. 3) (school) Saying something together in rhythm to learn it, like times tables.
its sense in the lessons: In church life monks sing Gregorian chant; in Buddhism and Hinduism people chant mantras such as «Om». At sports matches fans chant the team's name. In class pupils may chant times tables («three fours are twelve»). Phrases: «the crowd was chanting», «chanting slogans», «chanting monks».
examples from the lessons: The monks were chanting in the old abbey. | The crowd kept chanting the player's name. | We learned the times tables by chanting them. | Buddhist monks start the day with chanting. | Protesters were chanting «Save our park!» | Soft chanting came from the temple.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Chanting» can be a noun (uncountable) or the -ing form of the verb «chant». A chant (countable) is one set of words that is chanted. Do not confuse with «enchanting», which means charming or magical.

part of speech: present participle and adjective of clarify (clarify, clarifies, clarified, clarifying)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Making something clearer or easier to understand, by explaining it more. 2) (cooking) Making a liquid, such as butter or soup, clear by removing the bits in it. 3) (adjective) Helping to make something clear: «a clarifying question».
its sense in the lessons: In school pupils ask clarifying questions when they don't understand the task: «Do you mean the total or the difference?» In maths, clarifying the question before solving stops mistakes. In cooking, clarified butter has the white milky part taken out. Phrases: «a clarifying question», «clarifying the rules», «clarified butter».
examples from the lessons: Can I ask a clarifying question, please? | The teacher was clarifying the rules of the game. | Thanks for clarifying that; now I understand. | Clarifying the question first helps you solve it. | Mum is clarifying butter for the curry. | The coach drew a picture, clarifying where everyone should stand.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: clarify → clarifies, clarified (y changes to i), but clarifying keeps the y. Noun: clarification. Formal-ish; in everyday speech people say «explain» or «make clear».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A spoken description of an event, such as a football match or race, given while it happens on TV or radio. 2) A set of written notes that explain a book, such as a Bible commentary. 3) Opinions and remarks about something: «social commentary».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life children hear sports commentary; in church a Bible commentary explains verses. In English lessons pupils write commentaries on poems or give a running commentary of a science experiment. Phrases: «live commentary», «running commentary» (non-stop comments), «Bible commentary», «a commentary on».
examples from the lessons: We listened to the radio commentary of the match. | The commentary got very excited when she scored. | Stop giving a running commentary on everything I do! | The vicar uses a Bible commentary to prepare sermons. | The film has a director's commentary. | The cartoon is a commentary on how people waste plastic.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural commentaries. The person is a commentator; the verb is «commentate» (sport) or «comment». Stress: COM-men-tary (in the USA often COM-men-tair-ee).

meaning for a pupil: 1) The good feeling of being with friends or others and not being alone. 2) Friendly company that someone or something gives you, such as a pet or a neighbour.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, lonely characters long for companionship; in everyday life people get companionship from friends, pets and clubs. Old people who live alone may get companionship from visitors. In ethics lessons it shows why visiting and including others matters. Phrases: «for companionship», «need companionship», «companionship of friends».
examples from the lessons: Gran got a cat for companionship. | The old sailor missed the companionship of his crew. | Dogs give great companionship. | We visit Mr Jones to give him some companionship. | Clubs offer companionship as well as games. | The two travellers enjoyed each other's companionship.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: not «a companionship». Comes from companion (a friend you go along with). Similar: friendship, company. «Company» can mean companionship too: «I like your company.»

meaning for a pupil: 1) A strong feeling of sympathy and sadness for someone who is suffering, together with wanting to help them. 2) (church, ethics) Kindness and care shown to people in need; Christians believe Jesus showed compassion to the sick and poor.
its sense in the lessons: In ethics and religion lessons compassion is a key value: the Good Samaritan shows compassion to the hurt man. In stories a character's compassion makes them help others even when it is hard. Phrases: «show compassion», «feel compassion for», «with compassion», «full of compassion», «out of compassion».
examples from the lessons: The nurse treated every patient with compassion. | Jesus felt compassion for the hungry crowd. | Showing compassion means helping, not just feeling sorry. | The Good Samaritan stopped out of compassion. | She felt compassion for the lost puppy. | Our school collects food for families, as an act of compassion.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Adjective: compassionate. Similar: empathy (understanding feelings), pity (feeling sorry, sometimes from above). Compassion adds the wish to help.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To burn the body of a person who has died, until only ashes are left, as a way of saying goodbye instead of burying them. 2) (informal, joking) To burn food very badly: «You've cremated the toast!»
its sense in the lessons: In adult life, when someone dies their family may choose for the body to be cremated at a crematorium, then keep or scatter the ashes. Many Hindus and many Christians choose cremation; some faiths prefer burial. Phrases: «be cremated», «cremated remains», «scatter the ashes».
examples from the lessons: Grandpa was cremated, and we scattered his ashes by the sea. | Some families choose to bury, and some to cremate. | Hindus usually cremate their dead. | Her ashes are in a small box after she was cremated. | Dad cremated the sausages on the barbecue! | The funeral was followed by a short service at the crematorium.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Noun: cremation; the place is a crematorium. Usually passive: «He was cremated.» A sensitive word: be gentle when using it about real people.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (church) A belief or set of beliefs taught by a church or religion, such as the Christian doctrine of the Trinity. 2) (formal) A set of ideas or rules that a government, army or group follows. 3) (law) A rule or principle that courts follow.
its sense in the lessons: In religion lessons pupils learn that different churches agree on some doctrines and disagree on others. On the news a «doctrine» can be a country's plan for how it acts. Phrases: «Christian doctrine», «church doctrine», «the doctrine of», «teach a doctrine».
examples from the lessons: The doctrine of the Trinity says God is Father, Son and Holy Spirit. | Different churches have different doctrines about baptism. | The priest explained the church's doctrine. | The leader's doctrine was to never give up land. | Students of law learn about legal doctrines. | Christians believe the doctrine of the resurrection.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable and uncountable. Adjective: doctrinal. Formal word. Related: dogma (a belief that must be accepted without question), creed (a short statement of beliefs).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (church) The movement or effort to bring different Christian churches together, so they understand each other, pray together and work together. 2) (wider sense) Friendship and cooperation between different religions or groups.
its sense in the lessons: In religion lessons ecumenism explains why Catholic, Protestant and Orthodox Christians might hold a shared service or work together on charity. The Week of Prayer for Christian Unity is an ecumenical event. Phrases: «spirit of ecumenism», «ecumenical service», «ecumenical movement».
examples from the lessons: Ecumenism means Christians from different churches working together. | Our town held an ecumenical service on Good Friday. | The two vicars believe strongly in ecumenism. | Ecumenism helps churches focus on what they share. | The Pope spoke about ecumenism and unity. | The local food bank is run in a spirit of ecumenism.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Adjective: ecumenical (ek-yoo-MEN-ical). Pronunciation: ee-KYOO-men-ism or ek-YOO-men-ism. Usually about Christian churches; for different faiths people say «interfaith».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Coming from or to do with Egypt, a country in north-east Africa. 2) A person from Egypt. 3) To do with ancient Egypt: pharaohs, pyramids, mummies and hieroglyphs. 4) (Bible) In the Bible, the Egyptians were the people who kept the Israelites as slaves until Moses led them out.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons children study the ancient Egyptians, the Nile, the pyramids and mummies. In maths, Egyptian fractions and the ancient Egyptian way of multiplying appear in puzzles. In religion lessons the Exodus story features Pharaoh and the Egyptians. Phrases: «ancient Egyptians», «Egyptian pyramids», «Egyptian hieroglyphs», «the Egyptian army».
examples from the lessons: The ancient Egyptians built huge pyramids. | We made Egyptian masks in art class. | My friend's mum is Egyptian. | Egyptian writing used pictures called hieroglyphs. | The Egyptian army chased the Israelites to the Red Sea. | Egyptian fractions are written as sums of fractions with 1 on top.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always capital E. «An Egyptian» (vowel sound). Pronunciation: ih-JIP-shun. Myth: the pyramids were not built by slaves as old films show; most workers were paid labourers.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Eight times as much or as many: «The price rose eightfold.» 2) Having eight parts. 3) (Buddhism) The Noble Eightfold Path is the Buddha's teaching of eight ways to live well: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness and right concentration.
its sense in the lessons: In religion lessons the Eightfold Path is shown as a wheel with eight spokes and is how Buddhists believe suffering can end. In maths «eightfold» means multiply by 8: if 5 grows eightfold, it becomes 40. Phrases: «the Noble Eightfold Path», «increase eightfold», «an eightfold rise».
examples from the lessons: Buddhists follow the Noble Eightfold Path. | The Eightfold Path is drawn as a wheel with eight spokes. | The number of visitors grew eightfold. | If 3 grows eightfold, you get 24. | The Buddha taught the Eightfold Path after his enlightenment. | Our class made a poster of the eightfold path.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word. Like twofold, threefold, tenfold. Math trap: «grew eightfold» means «became 8 times as big», not «grew by 8».

meaning for a pupil: 1) The ability to understand and share the feelings of another person, as if you were in their place. 2) Feeling with someone, not just for them.
its sense in the lessons: In school and ethics lessons empathy is taught as a key skill: imagine how the other person feels before you act. In stories characters with empathy notice when someone is sad. Phrases: «show empathy», «have empathy for», «feel empathy», «put yourself in someone's shoes».
examples from the lessons: Empathy means putting yourself in someone else's shoes. | She showed empathy when her friend's dog died. | Good doctors have empathy for their patients. | Reading stories can help us build empathy. | He lacked empathy and laughed when Tom fell. | Our teacher asked us to show empathy to the new boy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Adjective: empathetic or empathic; verb: empathise/empathize (with). Trap: sympathy means feeling sorry for someone; empathy means feeling what they feel. Both are kind.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Lasting for ever, without beginning or end. 2) (church) Christians believe God is eternal and that believers will have eternal life with God after death. 3) (informal) Seeming to go on for ever, often annoyingly: «his eternal complaining». 4) Always true or always there: «eternal truths», «an eternal optimist».
its sense in the lessons: In religion lessons eternal describes God and heaven: «eternal life», «the Eternal City» (Rome). In everyday talk it means «never-ending» or is used with humour. Phrases: «eternal life», «eternal love», «eternal flame», «eternal rest», «an eternal optimist».
examples from the lessons: Christians believe God is eternal. | Jesus promised eternal life to those who believe. | The car journey felt eternal! | Rome is called the Eternal City. | An eternal flame burns at the war memorial. | My dad is an eternal optimist; he always thinks it'll be sunny. | They swore eternal friendship.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective, not used with «more». Noun: eternity. Similar: everlasting, endless. «Eternal rest» (euphemism) is said about people who have died.

part of speech: noun (an ex, exes; informal); prefix (ex-); preposition (ex, Latin)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) A person's former husband, wife, girlfriend or boyfriend: «my mum's ex». 2) As a prefix «ex-», it means «former» or «no longer»: ex-teacher, ex-president, ex-wife. 3) (money, formal) «ex» means «without»: «ex VAT» means without the tax. 4) The letter X.
its sense in the lessons: In adult life, after a divorce or break-up, people call their former partner «my ex». In news and stories «ex-» shows who someone used to be. In maths, «x» (said «ex») is often the unknown number. Phrases: «my ex», «his ex-wife», «ex-pupil», «ex-boyfriend».
examples from the lessons: Dad still gets on well with his ex. | My aunt's ex came to the party. | Mr Lee is an ex-soldier. | She is an ex-pupil of our school. | The ex-champion now trains young swimmers. | In the sum 3 + x = 7, «ex» stands for 4.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal as a noun; plural exes. As a prefix it needs a hyphen: ex-wife. Trap: do not confuse with «x» the letter used in algebra, which sounds the same. Sensitive word in family talk.

part of speech: verb (flutter, flutters, fluttered, fluttering); noun (a flutter, flutters)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To move wings quickly and lightly, or to fly with quick small movements, like a butterfly. 2) To move gently and quickly back and forth in the air, like a flag or leaves. 3) (of the heart) To beat fast and unevenly because of excitement or nerves. 4) (noun, UK informal) A small bet: «have a flutter on the horses». 5) (noun) A state of excitement: «in a flutter».
its sense in the lessons: In science and nature stories butterflies, moths and birds flutter. In stories a nervous character's heart flutters. In UK and Irish everyday talk a «flutter» is a small, fun bet on a horse race. Phrases: «flutter about», «flutter your eyelashes», «have a flutter», «in a flutter».
examples from the lessons: The butterfly fluttered from flower to flower. | The flags fluttered in the wind. | My heart fluttered when they called my name. | Leaves fluttered down to the ground. | Grandad has a little flutter on the Grand National. | The baby bird fluttered its wings but couldn't fly yet. | She was all in a flutter before the show.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: fluttered. Double t. «A flutter» (bet) is UK/Ireland informal. Similar: flap (bigger, slower), flicker (light), quiver.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (computers) A set of letters and numbers in one design and size, such as Arial or Times New Roman. 2) (church) A large stone or wooden basin in a church that holds the water for baptism. 3) (formal) A source of something: «a font of knowledge» (also «fount»).
its sense in the lessons: In school ICT lessons pupils choose a font, font size and colour for their work. In church life babies are baptised at the font, usually near the church door. Phrases: «font size», «change the font», «bold font», «the baptismal font», «a font of wisdom».
examples from the lessons: Change the font to make the title bigger. | Use font size 14 for your story. | The baby was baptised at the font. | The old stone font is the oldest thing in the church. | Comic Sans is a fun font. | Grandma is a font of knowledge about birds.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Two separate meanings come from two old words. «A font of knowledge» and «a fount of knowledge» are both used. In computers a «typeface» is the design and a «font» is strictly one size and style, but most people use them the same.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A sweet-smelling gum (resin) from certain trees in Arabia and Africa, burned to make perfumed smoke. 2) (Bible) One of the three gifts the wise men gave the baby Jesus, with gold and myrrh; Christians see it as a sign that Jesus is God, since it was burned in worship.
its sense in the lessons: In religion lessons and nativity plays frankincense is one of the Magi's gifts. In church life some churches burn incense in worship. In science, it is an example of a resin from tree sap. Phrases: «gold, frankincense and myrrh».
examples from the lessons: The wise men brought gold, frankincense and myrrh. | Frankincense smells sweet when it burns. | In the nativity play I carried the frankincense. | Frankincense comes from the sap of a tree. | The church filled with the smell of frankincense. | People have traded frankincense for thousands of years.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: not «a frankincense». Pronounced FRANK-in-sense. «Incense» is the general word for anything burned to smell nice. Often listed with gold and myrrh.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To collect information bit by bit, often with effort: «I gleaned a few facts from the leaflet.» 2) (old farming, Bible) To gather the grain left in a field after the harvesters have finished; in the Bible, Ruth gleaned in Boaz's field, and farmers were told to leave the edges for the poor.
its sense in the lessons: In school pupils glean facts from texts, charts and sources in history or science. In religion lessons the law of gleaning shows care for the poor and foreigners. Phrases: «glean information from», «glean facts», «glean in the fields».
examples from the lessons: We gleaned some facts about owls from the book. | Ruth gleaned barley in the field of Boaz. | The detective gleaned clues from the muddy footprints. | Farmers left grain at the edges so the poor could glean. | What can you glean from this graph? | I couldn't glean much from his short answer.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: gleaned. Usually with «from». Fairly formal word in the information sense. A person who gleans is a gleaner.

part of speech: noun (a groom, grooms); verb (groom, grooms, groomed, grooming)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A man on his wedding day, or a man who has just got married; also called the bridegroom. 2) A person whose job is to look after horses: feeding, brushing and cleaning them. 3) (verb) To brush and clean an animal's fur or coat, or (for animals) to clean themselves. 4) (verb) To make yourself neat and tidy: «well-groomed». 5) (verb) To prepare someone for a job: «groomed to be captain». 6) (safety) When an adult wrongly makes friends with a child to trick and harm them, this is called grooming; children should tell a trusted adult if someone online or nearby asks for secrets.
its sense in the lessons: At weddings the bride and groom make their promises. At stables a groom cares for horses. In science monkeys groom each other. In online safety lessons children learn that grooming is a danger sign: secrets, gifts and asks to meet should be told to a trusted adult. Phrases: «bride and groom», «groom a horse», «well-groomed», «groomed for».
examples from the lessons: The bride and groom danced first. | The groom brushed the horse until it shone. | Cats groom themselves with their tongues. | Monkeys groom each other to stay clean and friendly. | He was always well-groomed for school. | The young player is being groomed for the first team. | If an online stranger asks you to keep secrets, tell an adult: it could be grooming.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun, regular verb. Bridegroom is the full form. Noun for the activity: grooming. «Grooming» in safety lessons is a serious word; it is never the child's fault.

part of speech: noun (the hajj, Hajj; also hadj, haj)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (Islam) The pilgrimage to the holy city of Mecca in Saudi Arabia that every adult Muslim who is healthy and can afford it should make at least once in their life. 2) It is one of the Five Pillars of Islam, the main duties of Muslims.
its sense in the lessons: In religion lessons pupils learn that on the hajj Muslims wear simple white clothes (ihram), walk around the Kaaba seven times, and pray at Mount Arafat; afterwards comes the festival of Eid al-Adha. It shows that all believers are equal before God. Phrases: «go on hajj», «make the hajj», «perform hajj».
examples from the lessons: My friend's grandfather went on hajj last summer. | The hajj is one of the Five Pillars of Islam. | Millions of Muslims make the hajj to Mecca. | Pilgrims on the hajj wear plain white clothes. | During the hajj, people walk around the Kaaba seven times. | A man who has made the hajj is sometimes called Hajji.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Arabic word. Often written with a capital H. Spelled hajj, haj or hadj. Pronounced «hadge». Not to be confused with other trips: it is a religious duty, done at a set time of the Islamic year.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Cruel, unkind or too strict: «a harsh punishment», «harsh words». 2) Very difficult to live in: «a harsh winter», «a harsh desert». 3) Unpleasant to the senses: too loud, bright or rough: «harsh light», «a harsh voice». 4) (slang) Unfair or a bit mean: «That's harsh, mate!»
its sense in the lessons: In stories harsh weather and harsh rulers make life hard for characters. In science lessons «harsh environments» like deserts and the Arctic show how animals adapt. In everyday kid talk «harsh!» means «that's unfair». Phrases: «harsh conditions», «harsh reality», «harsh words», «be harsh on someone».
examples from the lessons: The punishment was too harsh for such a small mistake. | Polar bears live in a harsh climate. | The harsh light hurt my eyes. | Don't be so harsh on your little brother. | «You got detention for that? Harsh!» | The coach's harsh words made him cry. | Camels can survive harsh desert conditions.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular comparison: harsher, harshest. Noun: harshness. Opposites: gentle, mild, soft. Spelling: one s, then h.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Coming to live in a new country from another country. 2) The place at an airport or border where officials check passports and visas: «go through immigration». 3) The rules and the government department that control who may come to live in a country.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and history lessons immigration explains how people moved to the USA, Canada, Australia, New Zealand and the UK, making them mixed and varied countries. In adult life people talk about immigration rules and visas; at airports travellers queue at immigration. Phrases: «go through immigration», «immigration officer», «immigration rules».
examples from the lessons: Many families in our class came here through immigration. | We waited a long time at immigration at the airport. | The immigration officer checked our passports. | Immigration helped build cities like Toronto and Sydney. | Ellis Island was where immigration to New York was checked. | Grandma remembers her immigration to Australia by ship.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Person: immigrant; verb: immigrate (to). Trap: immigration = coming IN to a country; emigration = going OUT of your country. A person moving is both an emigrant (from the old country) and an immigrant (in the new).

part of speech: past tense and past participle of imprison (imprison, imprisons, imprisoned, imprisoning); adjective (imprisoned)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Put in prison as a punishment, or kept in prison. 2) Kept somewhere and not able to get out, like a trapped animal or a princess in a tower. 3) (figurative) Unable to escape a feeling or situation: «imprisoned by fear».
its sense in the lessons: In history and stories people are imprisoned for crimes, or unfairly for their beliefs; in the Bible Joseph and Paul were imprisoned. In ethics lessons pupils discuss fair punishment and people imprisoned for speaking up. Phrases: «be imprisoned for», «wrongly imprisoned», «imprisoned in a tower».
examples from the lessons: The thief was imprisoned for two years. | Joseph was imprisoned in Egypt, though he had done nothing wrong. | The princess was imprisoned in a high tower. | Nelson Mandela was imprisoned for a very long time before becoming president. | The bird felt imprisoned in its small cage. | Paul wrote letters while he was imprisoned.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: imprison, imprisoned. Noun: imprisonment. Usually passive: «He was imprisoned.» Similar: jailed, locked up (informal).

part of speech: adjective (joyful, more joyful, most joyful); adverb joyfully
meaning for a pupil: 1) Very happy, or full of joy. 2) Causing joy: «joyful news». 3) (church) Used in hymns and prayers for happy praise of God: «Make a joyful noise to the Lord».
its sense in the lessons: In stories a joyful scene ends a sad journey: a joyful reunion, a joyful wedding. In church life Christmas and Easter are joyful festivals; Psalm 100 says «Make a joyful noise». Phrases: «joyful news», «a joyful occasion», «joyful singing».
examples from the lessons: The children gave a joyful shout when it snowed. | It was a joyful day when the puppy came home. | The church choir sang a joyful carol. | «Make a joyful noise unto the Lord.» | Everyone was joyful at the news. | The families had a joyful reunion at the airport.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelled with one l at the end: joyful, not «joyfull». Noun: joy, joyfulness. Similar: happy, glad, cheerful, delighted.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A small thing you keep to help you remember a person, place or time. 2) A gift given so the person will remember the giver.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and family life a keepsake can be a photo, a lock of hair, a shell from a holiday, or a ring from a grandparent who has died. It tells the reader the thing is precious for its memories, not its price. Phrases: «as a keepsake», «a treasured keepsake», «keepsake box».
examples from the lessons: Gran gave me her old brooch as a keepsake. | I keep the shell as a keepsake of our beach holiday. | The ticket is a keepsake from my first concert. | She kept his letters as keepsakes. | Our class made keepsake boxes for our memories. | After Grandpa passed away, each grandchild chose a keepsake.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable, one word. Similar: memento, souvenir (a souvenir is often bought on a trip; a keepsake is more personal).

meaning for a pupil: 1) An illness caused by germs (bacteria) that harms the skin and nerves, so people can lose feeling in their hands and feet. 2) (Bible) In the Bible, «leprosy» meant several skin diseases; people with it had to live apart, and Jesus healed lepers.
its sense in the lessons: In religion lessons Jesus touching and healing lepers shows his compassion for people that others avoided. In science and health, leprosy today can be cured with medicine and is hard to catch. Phrases: «suffer from leprosy», «cure leprosy», «leprosy mission».
examples from the lessons: Jesus healed ten men who had leprosy. | Leprosy can now be cured with medicine. | In old times people with leprosy had to live outside the town. | Leprosy harms the nerves, so people may not feel pain. | Father Damien cared for people with leprosy in Hawaii. | Charities still help people with leprosy around the world.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Person: leper (today «person with leprosy» is kinder). Myth: fingers and toes do not just «fall off»; injuries happen because people cannot feel pain. It is not easily caught by touching.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A strong boat kept on the coast that goes out to rescue people in danger at sea. 2) A small boat carried on a ship, used to escape if the ship sinks.
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons and stories the lifeboat crew rescue swimmers and sailors in storms; in the UK and Ireland the RNLI runs lifeboats, often with volunteers. The Titanic story is famous because there were not enough lifeboats. Phrases: «launch the lifeboat», «lifeboat crew», «lifeboat station», «lifeboat drill».
examples from the lessons: The lifeboat rescued two fishermen in the storm. | The Titanic did not have enough lifeboats for everyone. | My uncle is a volunteer on the lifeboat crew. | We visited the lifeboat station by the harbour. | The passengers climbed into the lifeboats. | Every ship has a lifeboat drill.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable, one word. Similar: life raft (a floating raft), lifejacket (worn to float). Do not confuse with lifeguard (a person watching swimmers on a beach or at a pool).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Mecca (also spelled Makkah) is the holiest city of Islam, in Saudi Arabia; it is where the Prophet Muhammad was born and where Muslims go on the hajj. 2) Muslims everywhere face towards Mecca when they pray. 3) (a mecca, lower case) A place that many people with the same interest love to visit: «Paris is a mecca for artists.»
its sense in the lessons: In religion lessons Mecca is the centre of Islam, with the Kaaba in the Great Mosque. In everyday speech «a mecca for…» means a favourite place for a group. Phrases: «face Mecca», «pilgrimage to Mecca», «a mecca for».
examples from the lessons: Muslims face towards Mecca when they pray. | Millions travel to Mecca for the hajj. | The Kaaba stands in the middle of the Great Mosque in Mecca. | The Prophet Muhammad was born in Mecca. | That shop is a mecca for comic fans. | The beach town is a mecca for surfers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital M for the city. Some Muslims prefer the name Makkah, and some dislike the casual use «a mecca for…», so use it with care. Pronounced MEK-a.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A sweet-smelling, bitter gum (resin) from a small thorny tree in Arabia and Africa, used in perfumes, medicines and incense. 2) (Bible) One of the three gifts the wise men gave the baby Jesus, with gold and frankincense; Christians see it as a sign of his death, because myrrh was used to prepare bodies for burial.
its sense in the lessons: In nativity plays and religion lessons myrrh is the «sad» gift that points to Jesus's death. In history, ancient Egyptians used myrrh when making mummies. Phrases: «gold, frankincense and myrrh».
examples from the lessons: The third wise man brought myrrh. | Myrrh is a resin from a thorny tree. | Gold, frankincense and myrrh were gifts for a king. | Myrrh was used to prepare bodies for burial. | The Egyptians used myrrh for their mummies. | In the carol, myrrh's «bitter perfume» speaks of sorrow.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Strange spelling: m-y-r-r-h; pronounced «mur», rhymes with «fur». Silent h at the end.

part of speech: verb (neglect, neglects, neglected, neglecting); noun (neglect, uncountable)
