meaning for a pupil: 1) To not give enough care or attention to someone or something you should look after. 2) To forget or fail to do something: «He neglected to tell us.» 3) (noun) The state of not being cared for. 4) (law, safety) When parents or carers do not give a child food, safety, warmth or care, this is called neglect, and adults like teachers must help.
its sense in the lessons: In stories a neglected garden or house is overgrown and broken; a neglected animal is thin and sad. In ethics and adult-life lessons neglect is a serious wrong that social workers protect children from. In school, neglecting homework means not doing it. Phrases: «neglect your duties», «fall into neglect», «child neglect», «neglected to mention».
examples from the lessons: The old house had been neglected for years. | Don't neglect your teeth: brush them twice a day. | The dog was rescued from neglect. | He neglected to mention he had broken the window. | The garden fell into neglect. | Teachers must report it if they think a child suffers neglect. | She neglected her homework and got behind.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Noun is the same word. Adjectives: neglected, neglectful. «Neglect to do» means «fail to do». Do not confuse with «negligent» (careless, in law) or «negligible» (very small).

part of speech: adjective (noble, nobler, noblest); noun (a noble, nobles)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Good, brave and honest; acting in a way that shows a fine character: «a noble deed». 2) Belonging to a high social rank, such as lords, dukes and princes. 3) (noun) A person of high rank in old times; a lord or lady. 4) Impressive and grand: «a noble horse». 5) (science) Noble gases (helium, neon, argon…) hardly react with anything; noble metals like gold do not rust.
its sense in the lessons: In stories a noble knight helps the weak; nobles live in castles and serve the king. In religion lessons the Buddha's teachings are called the Noble Truths and the Noble Eightfold Path. In science «noble gas» is a special term. Phrases: «a noble cause», «noble family», «noble gas», «noble savage» (old, unfair idea).
examples from the lessons: It was noble of you to share your lunch. | The nobles met at the king's castle. | She was born into a noble family. | Helping the poor is a noble cause. | Neon is a noble gas used in bright signs. | The knight did a noble thing and saved the village. | Buddhists follow the Four Noble Truths.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparison: nobler, noblest. Adverb: nobly. Noun: nobility (both the quality and the rank). The «noble» rank and the «noble» character are different senses; a noble by rank may not act nobly.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Following or obeying a law, rule or custom: «observance of the rules». 2) (church, religion) Keeping a religious day or practice, such as resting on the Sabbath or fasting in Ramadan. 3) A ceremony or ritual held to mark a special day: «religious observances».
its sense in the lessons: In religion lessons observance describes how believers keep holy days and customs: Jewish observance of the Sabbath, Muslim observance of Ramadan, Christian observance of Lent. In formal writing «strict observance» means following rules exactly. Phrases: «religious observance», «strict observance», «observance of the Sabbath».
examples from the lessons: Observance of the Sabbath means resting on that day. | Her family's religious observance includes daily prayer. | The school closed in observance of the holiday. | Strict observance of the rules kept everyone safe. | Fasting is an important observance in Ramadan. | Different churches have different observances in Lent.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal word. Countable for single customs, uncountable for the idea. Verb: observe (sense «keep, follow»). Trap: observance is not «observation» (watching carefully); a scientist makes observations, a believer keeps observances.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal, law) Being the father of a child. 2) (adult life) «Paternity leave» is time off work that a father gets when his baby is born. 3) (formal) Where an idea or work came from; who started it.
its sense in the lessons: In adult life dads take paternity leave to look after a new baby; in law a «paternity test» shows who a child's father is, sometimes in custody cases. In stories it may be a secret about who someone's father is. Phrases: «paternity leave», «paternity test», «paternity pay».
examples from the lessons: Dad took two weeks of paternity leave when my sister was born. | A paternity test can show who a baby's father is. | His workplace gives good paternity pay. | The court looked at the question of paternity. | Mum had maternity leave and Dad had paternity leave. | In the story, the boy's paternity was a mystery.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Formal; in everyday speech people say «being a dad». Related: paternal (fatherly, or on the father's side: «paternal grandmother»). Opposite on the mother's side: maternity, maternal.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Keeping on trying to do something even when it is hard, or when you fail at first. 2) (church) Christians speak of perseverance in faith: keeping faith through hard times.
its sense in the lessons: In school perseverance is a learning value: practise reading, keep going with tricky maths, don't give up. In stories heroes succeed through perseverance. In Bible lessons Paul writes that suffering produces perseverance. Phrases: «show perseverance», «with perseverance», «perseverance pays off», «award for perseverance».
examples from the lessons: She learned to ride her bike through perseverance. | Our class has a star for perseverance. | Perseverance pays off: keep practising! | The spider's perseverance inspired Robert the Bruce. | It took great perseverance to finish the marathon. | Learning the piano needs patience and perseverance.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Verb: persevere (with, in). Stress: per-se-VEER-ance. Spelling trap: perseverance (no «r» after the second e): not «perserverance». Similar: persistence, determination, grit.

part of speech: noun (a pew, pews); interjection (pew, also pee-yew, informal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (church) A long wooden bench with a back, where people sit in a church. 2) (informal, UK) A seat: «Take a pew» means «sit down». 3) (interjection, informal) A sound people make about a bad smell: «Pew! What stinks?»
its sense in the lessons: In church life families sit in the pews; the front pews are for the wedding or funeral family. In British everyday speech «take a pew» is a friendly way to say «have a seat». Children say «pew!» (or «pee-yew») at a smell. Phrases: «take a pew», «the front pew», «church pews».
examples from the lessons: We sat in the front pew at the wedding. | The old church pews are hard to sit on. | «Come in and take a pew,» said Grandad. | Hymn books are kept in a shelf on the back of each pew. | «Pew! Who left their socks here?» | The family filled three pews at the christening.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Rhymes with «few». «Take a pew» is UK informal. The smell word is also spelled «phew» or «pee-yew» (US); «phew» more often means relief («Phew, we made it!»).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) A very valuable silvery-white metal that does not rust and is heavier than gold; its chemical symbol is Pt. 2) (adjective) Made of platinum: «a platinum ring». 3) (adjective) Very pale silver-blonde in colour: «platinum blonde». 4) (music) A «platinum record» is a prize for an album or song that sells a very great number of copies.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons platinum is a metal element used in jewellery, car parts and lab equipment because it does not react easily. In music news a song «goes platinum». Phrases: «platinum ring», «platinum blonde», «go platinum», «platinum jubilee» (seventy-year celebration).
examples from the lessons: Platinum is rarer than gold. | Mum's wedding ring is made of platinum. | The singer's album went platinum. | Platinum does not rust or tarnish. | Her hair was dyed platinum blonde. | Platinum is used in parts that clean car exhaust fumes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Stress: PLAT-in-um. Not a «platinum» coin in everyday money. A platinum jubilee marks seventy years of something, after gold (fifty) and diamond (sixty).

part of speech: noun (preaching, uncountable); present participle of preach
meaning for a pupil: 1) (church) Giving religious talks or sermons; the work of a preacher. 2) The message that is preached: «Jesus's preaching about the kingdom of God». 3) (informal, disapproving) Telling others what is right in a bossy, lecturing way: «I'm tired of his preaching.»
its sense in the lessons: In church life preaching is a main part of a service, and some churches are famous for good preaching. In Bible lessons Jesus's preaching in Galilee drew crowds. In everyday talk, «stop preaching» complains about someone lecturing. Phrases: «preaching the gospel», «stop preaching», «preaching to the converted», «lay preaching».
examples from the lessons: The minister's preaching was simple and kind. | Jesus began preaching in Galilee. | Mum said, «Less preaching, more helping!» | John Wesley travelled the country preaching. | She's preaching to the converted: we already recycle. | Street preaching happens in the town square on Saturdays.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable as a noun. The verb is preach (preached). A person who preaches is a preacher. In the bossy sense, similar to «lecturing» or «moralising».

meaning for a pupil: 1) The daughter or granddaughter of a king or queen. 2) The wife of a prince. 3) In fairy tales, a royal girl or young woman, often the heroine. 4) (informal, sometimes teasing) A girl or woman who is treated as very special or acts spoiled: «Don't be such a princess.»
its sense in the lessons: In stories princesses appear in fairy tales (Snow White, Cinderella, the Princess and the Pea), sometimes waiting to be rescued, often today rescuing others. In real life the UK and other countries have royal princesses. Phrases: «fairy-tale princess», «Princess Royal», «princess and the pea», «spoiled princess».
examples from the lessons: The princess lived in a tall castle. | In this story the princess saves the prince from the dragon. | Princess Anne is the king's sister. | My little sister dressed up as a princess for the party. | «You're my little princess,» said Dad. | «Don't be such a princess, you can carry your own bag!»
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural princesses (add -es). Capital P before a name: Princess Diana. Male: prince. The teasing sense can be unkind.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Doing something or paying something to make up for a wrong or damage you caused. 2) (law, history) Money a country or company must pay after a war or a wrong to help those who were harmed: «war reparations». 3) (church) Christians speak of making reparation for sin: making amends after confession.
its sense in the lessons: In ethics lessons reparation means putting right what you did wrong: say sorry, pay for the broken window, fix things. In history countries paid reparations after wars. In schools «restorative» approaches ask pupils to make reparation to people they hurt. Phrases: «make reparation», «pay reparations», «reparation for».
examples from the lessons: He made reparation by mowing the lawn of the neighbour whose window he broke. | After the war the country had to pay reparations. | Saying sorry is a start, but reparation means fixing it too. | The company paid reparation to the families who were harmed. | In the story the thief returned the gold as reparation. | Making reparation can help heal friendships.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal. «Reparations» (plural) is mostly about money after wars or great wrongs. Similar: amends («make amends»), compensation. Do not confuse with «repair» (fixing things) or «preparation».

part of speech: noun (a saviour, saviours; US spelling savior)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who saves someone or something from danger or harm. 2) (church) The Saviour (capital S) is a name Christians use for Jesus Christ, because they believe he saves people from sin and death. 3) (informal) Something that helps a lot just in time: «This umbrella was a saviour!»
its sense in the lessons: In religion lessons and at Christmas, carols and Bible readings call Jesus the Saviour («a Saviour has been born to you»). In stories and sport the saviour rescues the town or wins the match at the last moment. Phrases: «our Saviour», «the saviour of the team», «a real saviour».
examples from the lessons: Christians believe Jesus is the Saviour of the world. | «Today in the town of David a Saviour has been born to you.» | The goalkeeper was the saviour of the match. | The firefighter was the family's saviour. | That spare pencil was a lifesaver, a real saviour! | The new owner was the saviour of the old cinema.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK, Ireland, Australia, NZ: saviour; USA: savior (Canada uses both). Capital S for Jesus. Related verb: save. Do not confuse with «savour» (to enjoy the taste).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (Jewish faith) The most important Jewish prayer, which begins «Hear, O Israel: the Lord is our God, the Lord is one.» 2) It comes from the book of Deuteronomy in the Bible and is said every morning and evening by many Jews.
its sense in the lessons: In religion lessons the Shema shows the Jewish belief in one God and in loving God with all your heart, soul and strength. Its words are written inside the mezuzah on doorposts and in tefillin. Jesus quoted it as the greatest commandment. Phrases: «say the Shema», «recite the Shema».
examples from the lessons: Many Jewish children learn the Shema when they are very young. | The Shema begins «Hear, O Israel». | The words of the Shema are kept in a mezuzah on the door. | Jews say the Shema in the morning and at night. | Jesus quoted the Shema when asked about the greatest commandment. | The rabbi explained what the Shema teaches about one God.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Hebrew word meaning «Hear!». Usually with «the» and a capital S. Pronounced «shmah» or «sheh-MAH».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Looking after something carefully on behalf of someone else, or for the future. 2) (church) Christians believe God made the world and gave people stewardship of it: the duty to care for the earth, animals and gifts, not waste them. 3) (money, formal) Managing money or a business carefully and responsibly.
its sense in the lessons: In religion and science lessons stewardship links to caring for the environment: recycling, saving energy, protecting animals. In church life «stewardship» also means giving time, talents and money wisely. Phrases: «stewardship of the earth», «good stewardship», «under the stewardship of».
examples from the lessons: Christians believe humans have stewardship of God's creation. | Planting trees is good stewardship of the land. | The club grew under the stewardship of its new coach. | Our eco-club teaches stewardship of the school garden. | Stewardship means looking after what is not only ours. | The church talked about stewardship of time and money.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Comes from steward (a person who looks after a house, ship or estate for someone). Formal word. Similar: care, guardianship.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Not noticed, found or discovered. 2) Not found by a test or a machine: «The illness went undetected.»
its sense in the lessons: In stories a spy, thief or hidden animal moves undetected; in science, tiny things may be undetected without a microscope. In health and safety, a leak or illness can go undetected for a long time, which is why tests and alarms matter. Phrases: «go undetected», «remain undetected», «slip past undetected».
examples from the lessons: The cat crept past the dog undetected. | The spy slipped into the castle undetected. | A gas leak can go undetected without an alarm. | The tiny germs were undetected until the microscope was used. | His mistake remained undetected until the teacher checked. | The rabbit stayed undetected under the bush.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually after verbs like go, remain, stay, slip: «went undetected». Opposite: detected, discovered. From detect (find, notice) + un- (not).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (Bible) Uriah the Hittite was a loyal soldier in King David's army; David took Uriah's wife Bathsheba and had Uriah sent to the front of the battle, where he was killed. 2) A man's name. 3) Uriah Heep is a sly, falsely humble villain in Charles Dickens's novel David Copperfield.
its sense in the lessons: In religion and ethics lessons the story of David and Uriah shows how even a great king did a terrible wrong, and how the prophet Nathan made David face his sin; David then repented. Phrases: «Uriah the Hittite», «a Uriah Heep» (a creepy, fake-humble person).
examples from the lessons: Uriah was a brave soldier in David's army. | King David sent Uriah to the front of the battle. | The prophet Nathan told David a story to show he had wronged Uriah. | David was sorry for what he had done to Uriah. | Uriah Heep keeps saying he is «very 'umble». | Uriah would not go home while his fellow soldiers were in danger.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A name, always with capital U. Pronounced yoo-RYE-uh. «Uriah Heep» is used to describe a person who pretends to be humble but is scheming.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal, old-fashioned) Very great anger. 2) (Bible, church) The wrath of God is God's anger at evil and sin, described in many Bible stories. 3) (humorous) Somebody's anger when you have done something wrong: «Mum's wrath».
its sense in the lessons: In Bible lessons and old stories wrath is used for kings, gods and storms. In ethics wrath is one of the seven deadly sins (also called anger). In everyday speech children use it jokingly: «I'll face my teacher's wrath.» Phrases: «the wrath of God», «face someone's wrath», «incur the wrath of», «The Grapes of Wrath».
examples from the lessons: The king's wrath was terrible. | The prophets warned of God's wrath against injustice. | We fled before we could face the wrath of the farmer. | Wrath is one of the seven deadly sins. | I'll face Mum's wrath if I'm late again! | «Do not let the sun go down on your wrath.»
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Pronounced «roth» (UK) or «rath» (US). Adjective: wrathful. Old or formal; in normal speech say «anger» or «fury». Not the same as «wreath» (a ring of flowers).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (Islam) The giving of a fixed part of one's wealth each year to the poor and needy; it is one of the Five Pillars of Islam. 2) For most savings it is one-fortieth (2.5 per cent) of the wealth a Muslim has kept for a full year above a set minimum.
its sense in the lessons: In religion lessons zakat teaches that wealth comes from God and must be shared; it helps the poor, the sick and those in debt. In maths, zakat is a percentage problem: 2.5% of 400 pounds is 10 pounds. Phrases: «pay zakat», «give zakat», «zakat al-fitr» (a gift of food before Eid).
examples from the lessons: Zakat is one of the Five Pillars of Islam. | My friend's family pays zakat every year. | Zakat helps the poor and needy. | If you have 800 pounds of savings, the zakat is 20 pounds. | Before Eid, Muslims give zakat al-fitr so everyone can celebrate. | Zakat means «purifying» because giving cleans the heart of greed.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Arabic word; also spelled zakah. Uncountable. Maths: zakat = wealth × 2.5 ÷ 100 = wealth ÷ 40. Different from sadaqah, which is extra voluntary charity.

part of speech: adjective (addicted); past participle of addict (rare as a verb)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Not able to stop taking a harmful drug, alcohol or tobacco, because the body and mind need it. 2) Not able to stop doing something, such as gambling or gaming, even when it causes harm. 3) (informal, light) Liking something very much: «I'm addicted to this song!»
its sense in the lessons: In health and safety lessons pupils learn that nicotine, alcohol and some drugs can make people addicted, and that addiction is an illness people can get help for. In adult-life lessons a family member may be addicted and need support. In everyday talk children say they are «addicted» to a game or a snack. Phrases: «addicted to», «become addicted», «get addicted».
examples from the lessons: Smoking can make you addicted to nicotine. | My uncle was addicted to alcohol but got help and recovered. | Some people become addicted to gambling. | I'm totally addicted to this book series! | Games can be fun, but be careful not to get addicted. | Doctors and support groups help people who are addicted.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always «addicted to» something (not «addicted with»). Person: an addict; illness: addiction; adjective for things: addictive («Sugar can be addictive»). Trap: addicted (the person) vs addictive (the thing that causes it).

part of speech: noun (an apprentice, apprentices); verb (be apprenticed to)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A young person who learns a trade or skill by working with a skilled worker, usually for a set time and a small wage. 2) A beginner learning from an expert in any field. 3) (verb, passive) «be apprenticed to» means to be sent to work and learn under a master.
its sense in the lessons: In adult life apprentices train as builders, mechanics, hairdressers and chefs. In stories the apprentice learns from a wizard, a blacksmith or a ship's captain (The Sorcerer's Apprentice). Phrases: «an apprentice electrician», «apprentice to», «be apprenticed to».
examples from the lessons: My brother is an apprentice plumber. | In the story the wizard's apprentice caused a flood. | She was apprenticed to a dressmaker. | Apprentices learn by watching and doing. | The apprentice swept the workshop floor every morning. | After four years the apprentice became a master carpenter.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. «An apprentice» (vowel sound). The training period is an apprenticeship. In stories the apprentice often makes a mistake when the master is away.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (law, UK) An official who has the legal power to take goods from someone's home, or make them leave it, when they have not paid money they owe. 2) (law, US) An officer who keeps order in a courtroom. 3) (history) In old times, a man who managed a lord's land and farm workers.
its sense in the lessons: In adult-life lessons bailiffs appear when a family is in debt; they may come to take things to pay what is owed, which can be very worrying. In US court scenes on TV the bailiff says «All rise». In history lessons the medieval bailiff ran the manor. Phrases: «send in the bailiffs», «the bailiffs came», «court bailiff».
examples from the lessons: The bailiffs came to take the car because the bills were not paid. | The bailiff in the courtroom asked everyone to stand. | In the castle, the bailiff checked that the peasants worked. | Families in debt can get advice so the bailiffs don't come. | The bailiff knocked on the door with a letter from the court. | In the story, the cruel bailiff took the farmer's cow.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Spelled with double f at the end. In Scotland the similar officer is a sheriff officer. Sensitive word in talk about money troubles.

part of speech: verb (bluff, bluffs, bluffed, bluffing); noun (a bluff, bluffs); adjective (bluff)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (verb) To pretend you are stronger, braver, cleverer or have better cards than you really do, to trick someone. 2) (noun) A trick of pretending like this: «It was just a bluff.» 3) (noun) A steep cliff or high bank, especially by a river or the sea. 4) (adjective) Friendly and honest but rather direct and loud: «a bluff old farmer».
its sense in the lessons: In games like poker players bluff to win; in stories a hero bluffs past guards. «Call someone's bluff» means to make them prove what they claim. In geography a bluff is a steep slope by a river (common in the USA and Canada). Phrases: «call someone's bluff», «it's a bluff», «bluff your way through».
examples from the lessons: He said he had a dog at home, but he was bluffing. | I called her bluff and she admitted she had no ticket. | In card games you can bluff to make others give up. | The house stood on a bluff above the river. | The guard believed the bluff and let them in. | Grandad is a bluff man who says what he thinks. | Don't try to bluff your way through the test; study!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Several unrelated meanings; context shows which. «Double bluff»: telling the truth so that people think you are lying.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The feeling or inner voice inside you that tells you what is right and wrong, and makes you feel bad when you do wrong. 2) (church, ethics) Christians and many others believe the conscience helps us know God's law; they examine their conscience before confession. 3) «In all conscience» (formal) means «honestly, fairly».
its sense in the lessons: In ethics lessons pupils learn to listen to their conscience; a «guilty conscience» makes you feel bad after doing wrong, a «clear conscience» means you have done nothing wrong. In stories Jiminy Cricket is Pinocchio's conscience. Phrases: «guilty conscience», «clear conscience», «prick of conscience», «on your conscience», «conscience-stricken», «examine your conscience».
examples from the lessons: My conscience told me to give the money back. | He had a guilty conscience after lying to his mum. | She went to bed with a clear conscience. | Jiminy Cricket was Pinocchio's conscience. | Before confession, Catholics examine their conscience. | His conscience was bothering him, so he said sorry. | I couldn't, in all conscience, take the last cake.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: con-science (like «science»). Pronounced KON-shuns. Do not confuse with «conscious» (awake, aware) or «consciousness». Adjective: conscientious (hard-working and careful).

part of speech: verb (construct, constructs, constructed, constructing); noun (a construct, constructs)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To build or make something, such as a house, bridge or model. 2) (maths) To draw a shape accurately using a ruler, compasses and protractor: «Construct a triangle with sides 5 cm, 6 cm and 7 cm.» 3) To put together ideas or words: «construct a sentence», «construct an argument». 4) (noun, formal) An idea or thing made by people's minds rather than found in nature.
its sense in the lessons: In maths lessons «construct» is a key instruction: use exact tools, not freehand. In science and technology pupils construct models, circuits and bridges. In English they construct sentences and paragraphs. Phrases: «construct a triangle», «construct a model», «well constructed», «construct a sentence».
examples from the lessons: Workers constructed a new bridge over the river. | Construct an angle of 60 degrees using a protractor. | We constructed a model volcano. | Can you construct a sentence using the word «because»? | The bird constructed its nest from twigs. | Money is a human construct.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb stress: con-STRUCT; noun stress: CON-struct. Noun for the activity: construction. More formal than «build». In maths, «construct» means draw accurately, while «sketch» means draw roughly.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (church) An area with many churches and parishes, looked after by a bishop. 2) The church community and offices of that area.
its sense in the lessons: In church life, Anglican and Catholic churches belong to a diocese; the bishop's main church is called the cathedral. Church schools may belong to a diocese and say «diocesan». Phrases: «the Diocese of…», «diocesan school», «bishop of the diocese».
examples from the lessons: Our parish is part of the diocese of Dublin. | The bishop visits every church in his diocese. | The cathedral is the main church of the diocese. | Our school is a diocesan school. | The diocese has more than a hundred parishes. | Young people from the whole diocese met for a festival.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; plural dioceses. Pronounced DY-uh-sis. Adjective: diocesan. A parish is smaller (one church area); an archdiocese is a big important one led by an archbishop.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (money) The money a person gets for working: wages or salary. 2) (money) The profit a business makes. 3) Money you get from any work, like pocket money for chores.
its sense in the lessons: In adult life and maths problems, earnings are money in: «His earnings are 20 dollars an hour; how much for 8 hours?» (multiply: 160 dollars). Business news talks of company earnings. Phrases: «weekly earnings», «total earnings», «earnings per hour», «average earnings».
examples from the lessons: Mum's earnings went up when she got a new job. | My earnings from washing cars were 15 pounds. | If you earn 6 dollars an hour, your earnings for 5 hours are 30 dollars. | The company reported big earnings. | She saved half her earnings. | Taxes are taken from your earnings.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always plural in this sense: «my earnings are», not «my earning is». Verb: earn (earned). In maths, total earnings = rate × time; earnings minus spending = savings.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A man who rules an empire, a group of many countries or lands, such as the Roman emperors. 2) (Bible) Caesar Augustus was the Roman emperor when Jesus was born. 3) The emperor penguin is the biggest kind of penguin.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons pupils learn about Roman, Chinese and Japanese emperors. In stories «The Emperor's New Clothes» shows a vain ruler fooled into wearing nothing, and a child tells the truth. In science, emperor penguins live in Antarctica. Phrases: «Roman emperor», «the Emperor's New Clothes», «emperor penguin».
examples from the lessons: Julius Caesar's adopted son became the first Roman emperor. | The emperor ruled many lands. | In the story, a child shouted that the emperor had no clothes. | Emperor penguins huddle together to keep warm. | China was once ruled by emperors. | The emperor ordered a census of the whole world.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «An emperor» (vowel sound). Female: empress. The land is an empire. An emperor is usually more powerful than a king.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To give someone a job, thing or person to look after because you trust them: «She entrusted me with her keys.» 2) (church, Bible) Christians «entrust» themselves or the dead to God, meaning they put them into God's care.
its sense in the lessons: In stories a king entrusts a secret message to a brave messenger; in school a teacher entrusts the class pet to a pupil for the holidays. In funerals people pray «we entrust our sister to God's mercy». Phrases: «entrust somebody with something», «entrust something to somebody».
examples from the lessons: The teacher entrusted me with the class hamster. | The king entrusted the secret to his best knight. | Parents entrust their children to the school each day. | She entrusted her money to the bank. | In the parable, the master entrusted his gold to his servants. | We entrust our grandmother to God's loving care.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Two patterns: «entrust someone WITH something» or «entrust something TO someone». Formal; in everyday speech people say «trust someone with». Also spelled intrust (rare, old).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (church) The Christian service in which bread and wine are blessed and shared to remember Jesus's Last Supper; also called Holy Communion, the Mass or the Lord's Supper. 2) The bread and wine themselves, which many Christians believe become, or show, the body and blood of Christ.
its sense in the lessons: In religion lessons pupils learn that Christians celebrate the Eucharist because Jesus said «Do this in remembrance of me». Different churches understand it differently, but most see it as the heart of worship. Children may make their First Holy Communion. Phrases: «celebrate the Eucharist», «receive the Eucharist», «Sunday Eucharist».
examples from the lessons: On Sunday the family went to the Eucharist. | The priest blessed the bread and wine at the Eucharist. | Christians believe Jesus gave the Eucharist at the Last Supper. | Catholics call the Eucharist the Mass. | She received the Eucharist for the first time at her First Communion. | «Eucharist» comes from a Greek word meaning «thanksgiving».
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually with a capital E and «the». Pronounced YOO-ka-rist. Adjective: eucharistic. Different churches use different names: Mass (Catholic), Holy Communion (Anglican, many Protestant), Divine Liturgy (Orthodox).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A short story, often with animals that talk, that teaches a lesson called a moral, like Aesop's «The Tortoise and the Hare». 2) A story that is not true, a myth or legend. 3) (informal) A lie or made-up claim: «His story about the shark was pure fable.»
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons pupils read fables and find the moral («Slow and steady wins the race»). Writers like Aesop and La Fontaine are famous for fables. In everyday talk «fable» can mean something that is not true. Phrases: «Aesop's fables», «the moral of the fable», «fact and fable».
examples from the lessons: «The Tortoise and the Hare» is a famous fable. | The moral of the fable is «Don't tell lies». | Aesop wrote many fables about animals. | We wrote our own fable about a greedy fox. | In the fable, the ant works hard while the grasshopper plays. | His tale of seeing a dragon was just a fable.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Adjective: fabled (famous in stories) and fabulous (wonderful, first meant «like a fable»). Difference: a fable teaches a moral; a fairy tale has magic; a parable (like Jesus's) teaches a spiritual lesson with people, not talking animals.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Being loyal and true to someone, keeping your promises. 2) (church, Bible) God's faithfulness means God keeps his promises and never leaves his people; Christians try to show faithfulness to God. 3) Staying true to a partner in marriage. 4) Being exact and accurate: «faithfulness to the original book».
its sense in the lessons: In religion lessons faithfulness is a fruit of the Spirit and a quality of Ruth and of Noah; hymns praise «Great is thy faithfulness». In stories the faithful dog Greyfriars Bobby shows faithfulness. Phrases: «God's faithfulness», «faithfulness in marriage», «faithfulness to a friend».
examples from the lessons: The dog's faithfulness touched everyone. | Ruth showed faithfulness to Naomi. | The hymn «Great Is Thy Faithfulness» praises God. | Faithfulness means keeping your promises. | The film was praised for its faithfulness to the book. | Married people promise faithfulness to each other.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Adjective: faithful; adverb: faithfully («Yours faithfully» ends formal UK letters). Similar: loyalty. Opposite: unfaithfulness, betrayal.

part of speech: noun (a feud, feuds); verb (feud, feuds, feuded, feuding)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A long, bitter quarrel between two people, families or groups, often lasting for many generations. 2) (verb) To have such a long quarrel: «The two families feuded for years.»
its sense in the lessons: In stories and history famous feuds include the Hatfields and McCoys in the USA and the Montagues and Capulets in Romeo and Juliet. In ethics lessons feuds show how revenge keeps a quarrel alive, and forgiveness can end it. Phrases: «a family feud», «a bitter feud», «end a feud», «feud with».
examples from the lessons: The two families had a feud that lasted generations. | Romeo and Juliet's families were in a bitter feud. | The neighbours feuded over the fence. | Nobody remembered how the feud started. | The feud ended when both sides forgave each other. | The singers had a public feud online.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun; regular verb. Pronounced «fyood». Similar: quarrel (shorter), vendetta (revenge feud). Often «a feud between X and Y» or «a feud with somebody».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Burning or full of fire: «a fiery furnace». 2) Bright red or orange like fire: «a fiery sunset», «fiery red hair». 3) Quick to get angry or very passionate: «a fiery temper», «a fiery speech». 4) Very hot and spicy: «a fiery curry».
its sense in the lessons: In Bible lessons Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego were thrown into the fiery furnace and saved by God. In stories a fiery dragon breathes flames and a fiery character loses their temper fast. Phrases: «fiery furnace», «fiery temper», «fiery red», «fiery chilli».
examples from the lessons: The dragon gave a fiery roar. | Three young men were thrown into the fiery furnace. | The sky was fiery orange at sunset. | Our captain has a fiery temper. | This sauce is really fiery! | The leader gave a fiery speech.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: fiery (not «firey»), although it comes from «fire». Comparison: fierier, fieriest (rare). Similar: blazing, flaming, hot-tempered.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (Bible) The angel Gabriel is a messenger of God; Christians remember that he told Mary she would have a baby, Jesus, and told Zechariah about John the Baptist. 2) (Islam) Muslims believe the angel Jibril (Gabriel) brought the words of the Qur'an to the Prophet Muhammad. 3) A boy's or man's name.
its sense in the lessons: In religion lessons and nativity plays the angel Gabriel appears to Mary (the Annunciation). In the Jewish Bible Gabriel helps Daniel understand his visions. Phrases: «the angel Gabriel», «Archangel Gabriel».
examples from the lessons: The angel Gabriel visited Mary in Nazareth. | Gabriel said, «Do not be afraid.» | In the nativity play I was the angel Gabriel. | Muslims believe Jibril, or Gabriel, brought the Qur'an to Muhammad. | Gabriel also appeared to Zechariah in the Temple. | My friend Gabriel sits next to me in class.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A name, always with capital G. Pronounced GAY-bree-ul. Often called an archangel (chief angel), like Michael.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Being happy to give money, time, help or things to others, more than is expected. 2) Being kind and fair in judging people: «generosity of spirit».
its sense in the lessons: In ethics and religion lessons generosity is a key virtue: the widow's mite, the Good Samaritan, zakat in Islam and charity in all faiths. In stories generous characters share food and gifts. Phrases: «thank you for your generosity», «act of generosity», «generosity of spirit», «show generosity».
examples from the lessons: Thank you for your generosity, said the charity leader. | The widow's small gift showed great generosity. | His generosity helped pay for the new playground. | Sharing your sweets is an act of generosity. | She is known for her generosity to strangers. | Generosity makes both the giver and the receiver happy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Adjective: generous; adverb: generously. Stress: jen-uh-ROS-i-tee. Opposite: meanness, selfishness, greed.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Very unpleasant and deserving to be hated: «a hateful thing to say». 2) Full of hate, showing hate towards others: «hateful messages». 3) (informal, old-fashioned) Horrible, nasty: «this hateful rain».
its sense in the lessons: In ethics and online safety lessons hateful comments are unkind words meant to hurt people because of who they are; pupils learn to report them. In stories a hateful villain is cruel. Phrases: «hateful words», «hateful comments», «a hateful person».
examples from the lessons: Calling him names was a hateful thing to do. | The website removes hateful comments. | The villain in the play was truly hateful. | She regretted her hateful words and said sorry. | If you see hateful messages online, tell an adult. | What a hateful, rainy day!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelled with one l at the end. Similar: horrible, nasty, spiteful. Related: hate, hatred (noun). Strong word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The Holocaust (capital H) was the murder of about six million Jewish people, and many others such as Roma, disabled people and gay people, by the Nazis in Germany and lands they controlled during the Second World War. 2) (lower case) A huge destruction and killing, especially by fire or nuclear war: «a nuclear holocaust». 3) (Bible, old) A sacrifice that was completely burned.
its sense in the lessons: In history and ethics lessons pupils learn about the Holocaust so that people remember the victims and stand against hatred, prejudice and bullying. Holocaust Memorial Day remembers them. The diary of Anne Frank tells one girl's story. Phrases: «Holocaust survivor», «Holocaust Memorial Day», «remember the Holocaust», «nuclear holocaust».
examples from the lessons: We read The Diary of Anne Frank to learn about the Holocaust. | A Holocaust survivor came to speak to our school. | Six million Jews were murdered in the Holocaust. | Holocaust Memorial Day helps us remember. | The Holocaust shows where hatred can lead. | The film warned of a nuclear holocaust.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital H for the historical event. In Hebrew it is called the Shoah. A very serious word: do not use it for small things. Denying the Holocaust is wrong and is a crime in some countries.

part of speech: adjective (humble, humbler, humblest); verb (humble, humbles, humbled, humbling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Not proud; not thinking you are better or more important than other people. 2) Simple, poor or ordinary: «a humble cottage», «from humble beginnings». 3) (verb) To make someone feel less proud, or to beat a strong opponent: «The small team humbled the champions.» 4) (church, Bible) Christians believe God loves the humble; «humble yourself» means put God and others first. 5) (formal, polite) Used to be polite about yourself: «In my humble opinion…».
its sense in the lessons: In ethics and religion lessons humility is a virtue: Jesus washed his disciples' feet and was born in a humble stable. In stories a humble hero does not boast. In sport news a big team is «humbled» by a small one. Phrases: «humble beginnings», «humble pie» («eat humble pie»: admit you were wrong), «in my humble opinion» (IMHO), «humble yourself».
examples from the lessons: Even after winning, she stayed humble. | Jesus was born in a humble stable. | He came from humble beginnings and became a doctor. | The little club humbled the league leaders. | I had to eat humble pie when I lost the bet. | «In my humble opinion, pizza is the best food.» | God lifts up the humble.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparison: humbler, humblest. Noun: humility (not «humbleness», though it exists). Pronounced HUM-bul (some say UM-bul). Trap: humble does not mean weak; humble people can be strong and brave.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (church) The Incarnation is the Christian belief that God the Son became a human being, Jesus, born of Mary. 2) A person or thing that shows a quality perfectly: «She is the incarnation of kindness.» 3) One of the lives or forms of someone or something: «in a past incarnation», «the latest incarnation of the phone». 4) (Hindu belief) A form in which a god appears on earth, such as Krishna as an incarnation (avatar) of Vishnu.
its sense in the lessons: In religion lessons, Christmas celebrates the Incarnation: Christians believe «the Word became flesh». In Hinduism avatars are incarnations of gods. In everyday speech «a past incarnation» jokes about someone's earlier job or life. Phrases: «the Incarnation», «the incarnation of evil», «in a former incarnation».
examples from the lessons: At Christmas Christians celebrate the Incarnation. | Christians believe Jesus is God's incarnation as a man. | Hindus see Krishna as an incarnation of Vishnu. | The villain was the incarnation of evil. | In a past incarnation, our teacher was a chef. | This is the newest incarnation of the game.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital I for the Christian belief. Adjective: incarnate («the devil incarnate», «God incarnate»). From Latin «in carne», in the flesh. Related: reincarnation (being born again in a new body).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who owns or runs an inn, a small hotel or pub where travellers can eat, drink and sleep. 2) (Bible, nativity) In the Christmas story, the innkeeper says there is no room at the inn, so Mary and Joseph stay where the animals are.
its sense in the lessons: In nativity plays a child plays the innkeeper who sends Mary and Joseph to the stable. In the parable of the Good Samaritan the Samaritan pays the innkeeper to care for the hurt man. In old stories innkeepers serve travellers and hear news. Phrases: «the kind innkeeper», «no room at the inn».
examples from the lessons: In the nativity play I was the innkeeper. | The innkeeper said, «There is no room at the inn.» | The Good Samaritan gave the innkeeper two coins. | The innkeeper served the travellers hot soup. | The old innkeeper knew every story in the village. | The kind innkeeper let them sleep in the stable.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable, one word, double n. «An innkeeper» (vowel sound). Today people say «landlord» (UK pub) or «hotel owner». The Bible does not actually name an innkeeper in the Christmas story; the character comes from plays.

meaning for a pupil: 1) What you plan or mean to do: your aim or purpose. 2) (law, ethics) What you meant to happen: in ethics and law it matters whether harm was done on purpose or by accident. 3) (church) A special purpose or person that a prayer or Mass is offered for: «Mass for the intentions of…». 4) (old-fashioned) «His intentions» can mean whether a man plans to marry someone.
its sense in the lessons: In ethics lessons pupils weigh intentions against consequences: «She meant well.» In school a teacher may share a «learning intention» (what pupils will learn). In stories a character's good or bad intentions drive the plot. Phrases: «good intentions», «with the intention of», «have no intention of», «learning intention», «the road to hell is paved with good intentions».
examples from the lessons: My intention was to help, not to make a mess. | I have no intention of going to bed early! | She went to the shop with the intention of buying bread. | Our learning intention today is to add fractions. | He had good intentions but forgot. | The priest offered the Mass for the intentions of the sick. | The judge asked about the man's intention.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Verb: intend; adjective: intentional (on purpose); adverb: intentionally. «Have no intention of + -ing», not «to». Similar: aim, plan, purpose.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (jeans, plural) Trousers made of strong cotton cloth called denim, usually blue: «a pair of jeans». 2) (jean, as an adjective) Made of denim: «a jean jacket». 3) (noun, old) A strong cotton cloth like denim. 4) Jean is a name: in English usually a woman's name (rhymes with «seen»); in French it is a man's name (said «zhahn»), like John.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life jeans are what children wear to school on «non-uniform day» and at weekends. In reading «Jean» may be a character's name. Phrases: «a pair of jeans», «blue jeans», «jean jacket», «skinny jeans».
examples from the lessons: I wore my new jeans to the party. | These jeans are too long; Mum will turn them up. | He has a blue jean jacket. | Aunt Jean makes the best scones. | Jean-Luc is a French boy in our class. | My jeans got a hole in the knee.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Clothes word is nearly always plural: «my jeans are», «a pair of jeans». «Jean» alone is mostly used before another noun (jean jacket) or as a name. Homophone: «gene» (part of our DNA) sounds the same as Jean in English.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who has leprosy, an illness of the skin and nerves. 2) (Bible) In Bible times lepers had to live apart and call out «Unclean!»; Jesus touched and healed lepers. 3) (figurative) A person that others avoid or reject: «He was treated like a leper.»
its sense in the lessons: In religion lessons Jesus healing ten lepers, with only one coming back to say thank you, teaches gratitude; touching the leper shows compassion for outcasts. Today people prefer to say «a person with leprosy», because «leper» can be hurtful. Phrases: «treated like a leper», «the ten lepers», «leper colony».
examples from the lessons: Jesus healed ten lepers. | Only one leper came back to thank Jesus. | Jesus touched the leper, and he was healed. | In old times lepers lived outside the town. | After the argument he felt like a leper at school. | Father Damien worked in a leper colony.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. The illness is leprosy. Today «a person with leprosy» is kinder and more correct. Do not confuse with «leopard» (big spotted cat).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (Bible) A member of the Israelite tribe of Levi, whose men served in the Temple, helping the priests, singing and caring for holy things. 2) (Bible) In Jesus's parable of the Good Samaritan, a Levite walks past the hurt man without helping, as a priest also did.
its sense in the lessons: In religion lessons the Levite in the Good Samaritan story shows that being religious is not enough; you must also show love to your neighbour. In Old Testament stories Levites carried the Ark of the Covenant. Phrases: «the priest and the Levite», «the tribe of Levi».
examples from the lessons: The Levite saw the hurt man and passed by on the other side. | Moses and Aaron came from the tribe of Levi. | Levites helped the priests in the Temple. | The priest and the Levite did not help, but the Samaritan did. | The Levites carried the Ark of the Covenant. | The book of Leviticus is named after the Levites.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital L. Pronounced LEE-vite. Related: Leviticus (a book of the Bible). Used almost only in Bible contexts.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A long open box or trough that horses and cattle eat from. 2) (Bible, Christmas) The manger in which Mary laid the baby Jesus, because there was no room at the inn.
its sense in the lessons: In nativity plays and carols («Away in a Manger») the manger stands for Jesus's humble birth; Christians see it as God coming in poverty. On farms a manger holds hay or feed. Phrases: «away in a manger», «lying in a manger», «dog in the manger» (someone who won't let others have what they themselves cannot use).
examples from the lessons: Mary laid the baby Jesus in a manger. | We sang «Away in a Manger» at the carol service. | The cows ate hay from the manger. | Our nativity scene has a tiny wooden manger. | Don't be a dog in the manger: if you're not using the ball, let us play. | The shepherds found the baby lying in a manger.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Pronounced MAYN-jer. Not related to «mango» or «manager» (but it looks similar to «manager», so read carefully).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Quiet, gentle and patient; not easily angry and not wanting to argue. 2) (often disapproving) Too quiet and ready to do what others say: «meek and timid». 3) (Bible) Jesus said «Blessed are the meek, for they shall inherit the earth»; Christians see meekness as gentle strength, not weakness.
its sense in the lessons: In religion lessons the Beatitudes praise the meek; Jesus called himself «gentle and humble in heart», and Moses was called very meek. In stories a meek character may surprise everyone by being brave. Phrases: «meek and mild», «the meek shall inherit the earth», «meekly obey».
examples from the lessons: «Blessed are the meek, for they shall inherit the earth.» | The meek little mouse squeaked a thank you. | He meekly said sorry and sat down. | She seemed meek, but she stood up to the bully. | Moses was a very meek man, the Bible says. | Don't be so meek; tell the teacher your idea!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparison: meeker, meekest. Noun: meekness. Trap: in the Bible, meek is a good thing (gentle and self-controlled); in everyday speech it can mean too weak. Similar: gentle, mild, humble.

part of speech: adjective (merciful, more merciful, most merciful); adverb mercifully
meaning for a pupil: 1) Showing mercy: kind and forgiving to someone you could punish or harm. 2) (church, Bible) Christians believe God is merciful, forgiving people who are sorry; Muslims call God «the Most Merciful». 3) Bringing relief from something bad: «a merciful release», «mercifully short».
its sense in the lessons: In religion lessons «Blessed are the merciful, for they will be shown mercy» is a Beatitude; the Islamic phrase «In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful» begins most chapters of the Qur'an. In stories a merciful king spares his enemy. Phrases: «merciful God», «a merciful act», «mercifully short».
examples from the lessons: God is merciful and forgives those who are sorry. | The merciful king let the prisoner go free. | «Blessed are the merciful.» | The talk was mercifully short. | Be merciful to animals. | Muslims begin with «In the name of God, the Most Merciful».
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelled with one l at the end. Noun: mercy. Opposite: merciless, cruel. «Mercifully» can mean «luckily, thankfully»: «Mercifully, it stopped raining.»

meaning for a pupil: 1) Not necessary, and often causing harm or waste that could have been avoided: «needless suffering». 2) «Needless to say» means «as you would expect» or «it is obvious that…».
its sense in the lessons: In stories and the news, «needless» warns that something bad did not have to happen: needless deaths, needless waste. In everyday talk «needless to say» introduces something obvious. Phrases: «needless to say», «needless waste», «needless risk», «needlessly cruel».
examples from the lessons: It was needless to leave the lights on all night. | Needless to say, we were very hungry after the long walk. | Wearing a helmet prevents needless injuries. | The fight caused needless pain. | He worried needlessly; the test was easy. | Throwing away good food is a needless waste.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Do not confuse with «needy» (poor, needing help) or «needles» (sewing pins, plural). «Needless to say» is a fixed phrase, often at the start of a sentence.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Doing what you are told by someone in charge, or following rules and laws. 2) (church, Bible) Christians believe obedience to God means following God's commands; Abraham and Mary are examples. 3) (animals) Training a dog to follow commands: «obedience classes».
its sense in the lessons: In ethics lessons pupils discuss when obedience is right and when it is wrong to obey (for example, if someone asks you to do something harmful). In religion lessons Noah's obedience in building the ark and Jesus's obedience to the Father are key. Phrases: «in obedience to», «blind obedience», «dog obedience classes», «vow of obedience».
examples from the lessons: Our puppy is going to obedience classes. | Noah built the ark in obedience to God. | Monks and nuns make a vow of obedience. | The soldiers showed complete obedience. | Blind obedience can be dangerous if the order is wrong. | Obedience to safety rules keeps everyone safe.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Adjective: obedient; verb: obey; opposite: disobedience. Pronounced oh-BEE-dee-ence. Spelling: -ence ending.

part of speech: adjective (peaceable, more peaceable, most peaceable); adverb peaceably
meaning for a pupil: 1) Not wanting to fight or argue; liking peace. 2) Calm and without fighting: «a peaceable meeting». 3) (church, Bible) The «peaceable kingdom» is Isaiah's picture of a world where the wolf lives with the lamb.
its sense in the lessons: In stories a peaceable village or a peaceable giant is gentle; in religion lessons the peaceable kingdom shows the hope of perfect peace. In law «peaceable protest» is protest without violence. Phrases: «peaceable kingdom», «peaceable people», «settle peaceably».
examples from the lessons: The giant was peaceable and kind. | The neighbours settled their argument peaceably. | Isaiah wrote of a peaceable kingdom where the lion and lamb lie down together. | Our cat is a peaceable creature. | The crowd was peaceable and calm. | Try to solve things in a peaceable way.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Similar to «peaceful», but «peaceable» is more about people who avoid fights; «peaceful» is used more for calm places and times («a peaceful garden»). Formal or old-fashioned.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal, law) Lasting for ever or for an endless time; mostly in the phrase «in perpetuity» (for ever). 2) (money) A payment that goes on for ever.
its sense in the lessons: In law, money and adult life, papers say land, a grave or a right is given «in perpetuity», meaning it can never end. In stories it sounds grand and serious. Phrases: «in perpetuity», «for perpetuity».
examples from the lessons: The land was given to the town in perpetuity. | The grave is kept in perpetuity. | The charity owns the park in perpetuity. | The rights to the song belong to her in perpetuity. | They promised to protect the forest in perpetuity. | A perpetuity pays the same amount every year, for ever.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Very formal; in everyday speech say «for ever». Pronounced per-pe-TYOO-i-tee. Related: perpetual (never-ending), perpetuate (make something continue).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Cruel and unfair treatment of a person or group, especially because of their religion, race, beliefs or who they are. 2) (church, history) The persecution of the early Christians by some Roman emperors, and the persecution of many faith groups through history and today.
its sense in the lessons: In religion and history lessons pupils learn about persecution of Christians, Jews, Muslims and others, and about people fleeing persecution as refugees. In ethics, it teaches standing up for others. Phrases: «flee persecution», «religious persecution», «suffer persecution», «face persecution».
examples from the lessons: The early Christians suffered persecution in Rome. | Many refugees flee persecution in their countries. | Religious persecution is when people are hurt for their faith. | The Pilgrims left England partly to escape persecution. | Saint Paul at first led the persecution of Christians. | Bullying a group because of who they are is a kind of persecution.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable usually. Verb: persecute; person: persecutor. Trap: do not confuse with «prosecution» (taking someone to court for a crime). Pronounced per-se-KYOO-shun.

part of speech: noun (a picket, pickets); verb (picket, pickets, picketed, picketing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A pointed wooden stake, used in a fence: a «picket fence». 2) (work) A group of workers on strike who stand outside their workplace to protest and ask others not to go in: a «picket line». 3) (verb) To stand outside a place to protest. 4) (old, army) A small group of soldiers on guard.
its sense in the lessons: In adult-life lessons pickets appear when workers strike for fair pay: «Don't cross the picket line.» In stories and in the USA, a white picket fence stands for a neat family home. Phrases: «picket line», «white picket fence», «cross a picket line», «on the picket line».
examples from the lessons: The house has a white picket fence. | The nurses stood on the picket line in the cold. | Workers picketed the factory gates. | Mum said she would not cross the picket line. | The picket held signs asking for fair pay. | One picket in the fence was broken.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun; regular verb (picketed, picketing; one t). «Picket line» is the line of striking workers. Not to be confused with «pickle» or «ticket».

meaning for a pupil: 1) The sharp metal blade of a plough that cuts into the soil. 2) (Bible) «They shall beat their swords into ploughshares» (Isaiah and Micah) is a picture of peace: weapons are made into farm tools.
its sense in the lessons: In religion lessons and peace talks, «swords into ploughshares» means stopping war and using things to help people grow food. In history and farming lessons a ploughshare is part of the plough pulled by oxen or horses. Phrases: «swords into ploughshares», «beat swords into ploughshares».
examples from the lessons: «They shall beat their swords into ploughshares.» | The farmer sharpened the ploughshare before spring. | A statue outside the United Nations shows a man beating a sword into a ploughshare. | The ploughshare cut deep into the soil. | The prophets dreamed of a time when weapons become ploughshares. | Old ploughshares were made of iron.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK, Ireland, Australia, NZ spelling: plough (said «plow»); US: plow, plowshare. Countable. Mostly used today in the Bible phrase.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (maths) How likely something is to happen, given as a number from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain), or as a fraction or percentage. 2) The chance that something will happen: «There's a high probability of rain.» 3) (formal) «In all probability» means «very likely».
its sense in the lessons: In maths lessons probability uses words like impossible, unlikely, even chance, likely, certain. A fair coin has probability 1/2 of heads; a dice has probability 1/6 of rolling a 3. Probability = number of ways it can happen ÷ total number of equally likely outcomes. Weather forecasts give the probability of rain. Phrases: «the probability of», «high/low probability», «in all probability», «probability scale».
examples from the lessons: The probability of getting heads is one half. | What is the probability of rolling a six on a dice? | There's a high probability of snow tomorrow. | In all probability, the bus will be late. | Draw an arrow on the probability scale to show «unlikely». | If a bag has 3 red and 1 blue marble, the probability of red is 3/4. | The probability of an impossible event is 0.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable and uncountable. Adjective: probable; adverb: probably. In maths, probability is never less than 0 or more than 1; all the probabilities of the possible outcomes add up to 1. Trap: «probably» (likely) is not «certainly».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To proscribe something is to forbid it officially, by a law or a rule. 2) (formal, law) To proscribe a group or a person is to name them as banned or outlawed, so that joining or helping them is a crime.
its sense in the lessons: A stiff word of laws, rules and exam texts; a pupil meets it in history (books or groups that were proscribed), in school rules written in formal style and in news about banned organisations. It tells the reader that an authority has said «no» and that breaking it brings punishment. Phrases: «proscribed by law», «a proscribed group», «proscribed substances».
examples from the lessons: The rules proscribe the use of phones during the exam. | The old law proscribed meetings of more than ten people. | The government proscribed the group after the attacks. | Some books were proscribed in that country, so people read them in secret. | Doping is proscribed in all sports. | Running in the corridors is proscribed, the notice said, in very grown-up words. | Membership of a proscribed organisation is a crime.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: proscribed, proscribing; the noun is «proscription». Big trap: do not mix it up with «prescribe» (a doctor prescribes medicine = orders it to be used). Proscribe = forbid, prescribe = order or recommend; they are nearly opposites. In everyday talk people say «ban» or «forbid» instead.

part of speech: noun (a ram, rams; RAM, computer memory); verb (ram, rams, rammed, ramming)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A ram is a male sheep, usually with big curled horns. 2) To ram something is to hit or push it very hard, often on purpose. 3) To ram something into a place is to push it in with force, so it is squashed and tight. 4) RAM (said «ram») is a computer's working memory, which holds what the computer is using right now. 5) (old) A battering ram is a heavy log once used to smash castle doors.
its sense in the lessons: On the farm and in nature lessons a ram is the father sheep (the mother is a ewe, the baby a lamb). In stories and news, a car or ship rams another — a violent crash. In computing lessons RAM is measured in gigabytes. Phrases: «ram into», «ram something home» (make a point very clearly), «rammed» (UK slang, very crowded).
examples from the lessons: The ram lowered its horns and charged at the fence. | A ewe and a ram stood in the field with their lambs. | The thief rammed the gate with a stolen van. | He rammed all his clothes into the small bag. | The teacher rammed home the rule: always check your answer. | My laptop has eight gigabytes of RAM. | The soldiers used a battering ram to break down the door. | The shop was absolutely rammed on Saturday. (UK slang)
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb doubles the m: rammed, ramming. RAM stands for «random access memory» and is written in capitals; it is not the same as storage (the hard drive). Do not confuse ram (male sheep) with «lamb» (baby sheep) or «ewe» (female sheep). «Rammed» meaning very full is informal UK talk.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To remarry is to get married again, after a divorce or after a husband or wife has died. 2) To remarry someone is to marry the same person again after being divorced from them.
its sense in the lessons: A word of adult life and family stories: a child may learn that a parent has remarried, so there is now a stepmother or stepfather and maybe stepbrothers or stepsisters. Churches have their own rules about remarriage. Phrases: «remarry after a divorce», «never remarried».
examples from the lessons: After the divorce, Dad remarried and I got a stepsister. | Grandma never remarried after Grandad died. | My aunt remarried last spring and we all went to the wedding. | They divorced but later remarried each other. | Some churches will not let divorced people remarry in church. | Mum said she might remarry one day, but not yet.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Change y to i: remarries, remarried, but remarrying keeps y. The noun is «remarriage». «Re-» means again, as in redo, rewrite. Remarrying does not stop a parent being your parent; the new partner is a step-parent.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Repentance is being truly sorry for something wrong you have done and wanting to change and not do it again. 2) (church, Bible) Repentance is turning away from sin and back to God; Christians believe God forgives those who truly repent.
its sense in the lessons: In religious education, Bible stories and sermons repentance is a key idea: John the Baptist called people to repent, and the prodigal son came home in repentance. In stories about ethics it tells the reader a character has changed inside, not just said «sorry». Phrases: «show repentance», «a sign of repentance», «repentance and forgiveness».
examples from the lessons: The boy's tears showed real repentance. | The judge noted that the man showed no repentance for the crime. | Christians believe repentance means turning back to God. | John the Baptist preached repentance by the river Jordan. | The prodigal son came home full of repentance. | Saying sorry is easy; repentance means you also change. | Lent is a time of prayer and repentance for many Christians.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: no «a repentance» or «repentances». The verb is «repent», the adjective «repentant» (and «unrepentant» = not sorry at all). Repentance is deeper than an apology: it includes the wish to change. Spelling: -ance, not -ence.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Something restorative makes you feel healthy, strong or calm again. 2) (school, law) Restorative ways of dealing with wrongdoing bring the person who did harm and the person harmed together to talk, put things right and mend the relationship, rather than only punishing. 3) (old) A restorative is a drink or medicine that gives you strength back.
its sense in the lessons: In many schools «restorative conversations» or «restorative justice» replace plain punishment after a fight or bullying: both sides talk about what happened, how it felt and how to make it right. In health and everyday talk a walk, a sleep or a cup of tea can be restorative. Phrases: «restorative justice», «restorative practice», «a restorative sleep».
examples from the lessons: A long sleep can be very restorative after a busy week. | The walk by the sea was restorative for Mum. | After the fight, the teacher held a restorative meeting with both boys. | Restorative justice lets the victim tell the offender how the crime hurt them. | In our school we use restorative questions: What happened? Who was hurt? | The nurse gave him a hot sweet drink as a restorative. (old-fashioned)
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comes from «restore» (to put back as it was). Stress on «stor»: re-STOR-a-tive. It is mostly an adjective; the noun use is old-fashioned. Restorative does not mean «no consequences»: the wrongdoer must still face what they did and help put it right.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Sahib is a respectful word, like «sir» or «master», used in India and Pakistan, especially in the past when Britain ruled India. 2) In Sikh use, Sahib is added to holy names as a sign of great respect, as in Guru Granth Sahib, the Sikh holy book.
its sense in the lessons: A word met in stories and history about British India, where servants called British officers «sahib», and in religious education about Sikhism (Guru Granth Sahib, Harmandir Sahib, the Golden Temple). It tells the reader about respect, rank and sometimes the unfairness of colonial times. Phrases: «memsahib» (a respectful word for a European woman in old India).
examples from the lessons: The servant bowed and said, «Yes, sahib.» | In the old story, the sahib lived in a large house with many servants. | Sikhs treat the Guru Granth Sahib as a living teacher. | The Golden Temple is also called Harmandir Sahib. | Grandfather remembered when people still said «sahib» to British officers. | The memsahib ordered tea on the veranda.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A borrowed word from Hindi and Urdu, said «SAH-ib» or «sahb». Usually written with a capital when it comes after a name (Guru Granth Sahib). Used today about colonial times, it can sound old-fashioned or show an unequal relationship, so it is not a casual word for «sir».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A scholar is a person who studies one subject very deeply and knows a great deal about it, like a professor. 2) A scholar is a pupil or student who has won a scholarship, money to pay for their studies. 3) (old, informal) A scholar is any pupil or schoolchild, or someone who is good at learning.
its sense in the lessons: In history and religious education, scholars are experts who study old books, languages and the Bible; in stories a scholar is a wise, bookish person. A school may call its prize-winning pupils «scholars». Phrases: «a Bible scholar», «a classical scholar», «a scholar of history», «no scholar» (not good at book learning).
examples from the lessons: She is a scholar of ancient Egypt. | Bible scholars study the old languages of the Bible. | The scholar spent years reading old letters in the library. | He became a music scholar at the big school. | Dad laughs and says he was never much of a scholar. | Scholars argue about who wrote the poem. | The young scholars filed into the hall for prize day.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a scholar, two scholars. Related words: «scholarly» (careful and learned), «scholarship» (a grant of money for study, or deep learning itself). A scholar is not the same as a «schoolboy» today, though in older English and in some countries it can mean any pupil.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A selfless person thinks about other people's needs and happiness more than their own. 2) A selfless act is something done to help others without wanting anything back.
its sense in the lessons: A word of ethics, stories and religious education: heroes, nurses, firefighters and saints are praised for selfless acts. It tells the reader a character puts others first. In assemblies and church, selfless love and service are taught as good things. Phrases: «a selfless act», «selfless love», «selfless service».
examples from the lessons: The firefighter's selfless courage saved the family. | Mum is selfless; she always gives us the bigger slice. | Giving your lunch to the hungry boy was a selfless thing to do. | Nurses did selfless work during the long winter of illness. | Christians believe Jesus showed selfless love. | Her selfless help at the food bank was thanked in assembly.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The noun is «selflessness», the adverb «selflessly». Trap: the opposite is «selfish», not «selfful». Selfless does not mean having no self; it means not putting yourself first. Being selfless does not mean letting others hurt you.

part of speech: noun (a shortlist, shortlists); verb (shortlist, shortlists, shortlisted, shortlisting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A shortlist is a small list of the best people or things, chosen from a bigger group, from which the final winner will be picked. 2) To shortlist someone or something is to put them on that list.
its sense in the lessons: Used for prizes, jobs and competitions: a book is shortlisted for an award, a person is shortlisted for a job interview. In school, poems or posters may be shortlisted for a competition. It tells the reader that something is close to winning but has not won yet. Phrases: «on the shortlist», «make the shortlist», «be shortlisted for».
examples from the lessons: Three stories made the shortlist for the writing prize. | My poster was shortlisted, but it did not win. | The company shortlisted five people for interview. | We drew up a shortlist of names for the new puppy. | The book has been shortlisted for a big award. | Out of fifty songs, the judges chose a shortlist of six.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Also written «short list» or «short-list». Regular verb: shortlisted, shortlisting. Being shortlisted is good news but not winning; the final choice comes after. Do not confuse it with «a short list» meaning just a list that is not long.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A smoker is a person who smokes cigarettes, cigars or a pipe, usually often. 2) A smoker is a box or oven used for cooking meat or fish slowly in smoke. 3) (beekeeping) A smoker is a small can that puffs smoke to calm bees.
its sense in the lessons: In health lessons smokers are people at risk of lung disease and heart disease; signs say «no smoking», and «passive smoking» harms people nearby. In stories, a smoker coughs, smells of smoke or stands outside. Phrases: «a heavy smoker», «a non-smoker», «an ex-smoker», «a smoker's cough».
examples from the lessons: Grandad was a smoker but he gave up years ago. | Smokers are more likely to get lung disease. | The doctor asked, «Are you a smoker?» | Mum is a non-smoker and hates the smell. | We cooked the fish in a smoker in the garden. | The beekeeper puffed the smoker to calm the bees. | A heavy smoker smokes many cigarettes a day.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a smoker, smokers. From «smoke» + «-er» (the person who does it). «Non-smoker» means someone who does not smoke. Trap: a «smoker's cough» is a cough from smoking, not a cough of any smoke. Children should know smoking is harmful and is not allowed for them by law in many countries.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal, UK) Soppy means too soft and sentimental, full of love-talk or easy tears, in a way that some people find silly. 2) (informal, UK) A soppy person is silly, weak or soft-hearted, too easily upset or too sweet. 3) (rare) Soppy can mean very wet and soaked.
its sense in the lessons: Children use it about films with kissing, cards with hearts and grown-ups who get misty-eyed: «That film is so soppy!» It tells the reader a character finds love or feelings a bit embarrassing, or teases someone gently. Phrases: «soppy film», «don't be soppy», «go all soppy».
examples from the lessons: Ugh, this film is too soppy, they keep kissing. | My big sister wrote a soppy poem about her boyfriend. | Don't be soppy, it's only a little scratch. | Dad goes all soppy when he sees baby photos. | The card was full of soppy hearts and flowers. | Our dog is a soppy old thing who loves cuddles. | The grass was soppy after the storm. (rare)
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mainly British and Irish; Americans more often say «sappy» or «mushy». Comparison: soppier, soppiest. It is a teasing word, not rude, but calling someone soppy can hurt if they are really sad. Related: «sop» (bread soaked in liquid).

part of speech: noun (a stereotype, stereotypes); verb (stereotype, stereotypes, stereotyped, stereotyping)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A stereotype is a fixed, too-simple idea about what all people of one group are like, for example that all girls like pink or all old people are slow. 2) To stereotype people is to judge them by such an idea instead of as the person they really are. 3) A stereotype is a character in a story who is not real or deep but is made from such a simple idea.
its sense in the lessons: In PSHE, citizenship and ethics lessons stereotypes are linked with prejudice and unfair treatment; pupils learn to spot them in adverts, books and jokes. In English lessons a «stereotypical» villain or princess is a flat character. Phrases: «a gender stereotype», «break the stereotype», «fit the stereotype», «challenge stereotypes».
examples from the lessons: It is a stereotype that boys don't cry. | The advert used the old stereotype of the grumpy teenager. | Don't stereotype people because of where they come from. | She broke the stereotype by becoming the first female captain of the team. | In our book, the witch is a stereotype: ugly, cruel and cackling. | Stereotypes can make people feel left out. | He was stereotyped as lazy, but he worked harder than anyone.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: stereo-type, with «e» after r. Adjective «stereotypical», adverb «stereotypically». A stereotype is not the same as a fact about a group: even if some people fit it, many do not, so it is unfair to judge any one person by it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A thinker is a person who thinks deeply and carefully, especially about important or difficult ideas. 2) A thinker is a famous philosopher or writer whose ideas changed how people see the world. 3) A thinker is anyone who thinks in a certain way, as in «a quick thinker» or «a creative thinker».
its sense in the lessons: In school, teachers praise «independent thinkers» and «critical thinkers» who ask questions and check reasons; in history and RE, great thinkers like Socrates are studied. In stories, a thinker is the quiet clever one who works out the plan. Phrases: «a deep thinker», «a free thinker», «a quick thinker», «great thinkers».
