examples from the lessons: Ella is a deep thinker who asks big questions. | Socrates was one of the greatest thinkers of ancient Greece. | A quick thinker grabbed the rope and saved the dog. | Our teacher wants us to be critical thinkers. | The famous statue «The Thinker» shows a man resting his chin on his hand. | He is a slow thinker but a careful one. | Great thinkers have argued about right and wrong for thousands of years.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a thinker, thinkers. From «think» + «-er». «Thinker» usually sounds like praise, but «a muddled thinker» or «a wishful thinker» are not. Do not confuse with «thicker» (more thick).

part of speech: pronoun (thou; thee, thy, thine — old forms)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (old, Bible) Thou is an old word for «you» when speaking to one person, as the subject of a sentence: «Thou art» = «you are». 2) (church) Thou is still used in old prayers and hymns to speak to God, as in the Lord's Prayer: «Our Father, which art in heaven». 3) (informal) «Thou» can also be short for «a thousand», used by some adults about money.
its sense in the lessons: Pupils meet thou in the King James Bible, old hymns, Shakespeare, poems and fairy tales; it tells the reader that the language is old or holy. It goes with old verb forms ending in -st or -t: thou art, thou hast, thou shalt, thou dost. Phrases: «thou shalt not» (the Ten Commandments), «holier than thou» (someone who acts morally better than others).
examples from the lessons: «Thou shalt not steal,» says one of the Ten Commandments. | «Where art thou?» called the knight. | The old hymn says, «How great thou art.» | In Shakespeare's play, the girl says, «Thou art my friend.» | Stop being so holier-than-thou about it! | Thou, thee, thy and thine are old ways of saying you and your. | The car cost him twenty thou. (informal, money)
note for the reader of a maths problem: Old forms: thou (subject, like «I»), thee (object, like «me»), thy (before a word, like «my»), thine (alone, like «mine»). Verbs change: thou art, thou hast, thou didst. In old English «thou» was actually the friendly or intimate form, not the polite one. Rhymes with «now». The money sense «thou» means a thousand.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A tribe is a group of families and people who share the same ancestors, language, customs and way of life, often with their own leader. 2) (Bible) The tribes of Israel were the twelve family groups said to come from the twelve sons of Jacob. 3) (informal) A tribe is any big group of people who belong together or like the same things, such as fans or a large family. 4) (science) In biology, a tribe is a group of related plants or animals.
its sense in the lessons: In history and geography, pupils learn about tribes of ancient Britain, Native American nations and First Nations, Aboriginal peoples, and Māori iwi. In RE, the twelve tribes of Israel. In everyday talk, «a tribe of kids» means many children. Phrases: «tribal», «the twelve tribes», «a tribe of».
examples from the lessons: The Iceni were a tribe in ancient Britain led by Queen Boudica. | Each tribe had its own chief and customs. | The Bible tells of the twelve tribes of Israel. | Our cousins arrived like a whole tribe, loud and hungry. | Football fans are a tribe of their own. | Many Native American peoples prefer to be called nations rather than tribes. | Lions, tigers and other big cats belong to the same tribe of cats in biology.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a tribe, tribes; adjective «tribal». Be careful and respectful: many peoples prefer their own names (nation, iwi, First Nation, people), and «tribe» can sound old-fashioned or rude when used about whole countries. The informal sense («my tribe») is friendly.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Something trivial is small and not important, not worth worrying about. 2) (maths) A trivial case or answer is the simplest, most obvious one, that needs no real work, for example x = 0. 3) Trivial facts are odd little facts that are fun but not important, as in a quiz (trivia).
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and stories, people argue over trivial things and later feel silly. In maths, «trivial» means easy or obvious, and a «trivial solution» is often zero. In quizzes, «trivia» means little facts. Phrases: «a trivial matter», «trivial details», «trivialise» (make something serious seem small).
examples from the lessons: They had a big argument about something trivial. | Don't worry about trivial mistakes like a missing comma. | Her worry seemed trivial, but to her it was big. | In maths, x = 0 is the trivial answer to x × 5 = x × 3. | The quiz was full of trivial facts about famous people. | It is not a trivial problem; it will take hours to solve. | Losing a pencil is trivial compared with losing your dog.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The noun is «triviality»; related «trivia» (little facts, uncountable). Trap: what seems trivial to one person may be serious to another, so be kind. In maths, «not trivial» or «non-trivial» means it needs real thought.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A trough is a long narrow open box that holds water or food for farm animals like pigs, cows or horses. 2) (science) A trough is the low point between two waves, or between two high points on a graph. 3) (weather) A trough is a long area of low air pressure, which often brings rain. 4) A trough is a low or bad time, after a good one, as in «peaks and troughs». 5) (informal) To have your snout in the trough means to take more money or benefits than you should.
its sense in the lessons: On the farm, animals drink from a trough. In science lessons about waves (sound, light, water), the crest is the top and the trough is the bottom; the height from the middle to the crest is the amplitude. On line graphs, the lowest dips are troughs. Phrases: «peaks and troughs», «water trough», «feeding trough».
examples from the lessons: The pigs pushed their noses into the trough. | The horse drank from the stone trough by the gate. | The boat sank into the trough between two huge waves. | Label the crest and the trough on your wave diagram. | The graph shows peaks in summer and troughs in winter. | A trough of low pressure will bring rain tomorrow. | Business has its peaks and troughs.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Said «troff» (rhymes with off), not «trow» or «true». Plural: troughs. Opposite of trough on a wave is «crest» (or «peak»). Spelling trap: ough is said many ways — tough, through, though, trough, bough.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Undiscovered means not yet found or known about by anyone. 2) Undiscovered can mean not yet famous or noticed, as an undiscovered talent.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography, scientists believe there are many undiscovered species in the deep sea and the rainforest; in stories, undiscovered treasure, islands and secrets drive adventures. It tells the reader something exists but is still hidden. Phrases: «undiscovered species», «remain undiscovered», «an undiscovered talent».
examples from the lessons: There may be thousands of undiscovered insects in the rainforest. | The pirates' treasure remained undiscovered for hundreds of years. | The deep ocean is full of undiscovered creatures. | Our secret den stayed undiscovered all summer. | She was an undiscovered singer until the talent show. | The planet was undiscovered until astronomers saw it through a telescope.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Un-» means not: not discovered. Trap: «undiscovered» does not mean nonexistent — it exists but nobody has found it. Not the same as «uncovered» (with its cover taken off, or found out).

meaning for a pupil: 1) An unforgiving person does not forgive people easily and keeps blaming them for wrongs they did. 2) An unforgiving place, weather or task is very hard and does not allow any mistakes, as an unforgiving desert or an unforgiving mountain.
its sense in the lessons: In ethics and RE, being unforgiving is contrasted with forgiveness, which Christians and many faiths teach as good; in Bible parables an unforgiving servant is punished. In adventure stories and geography, deserts, seas and cliffs are unforgiving — a small mistake can be deadly. Phrases: «unforgiving heat», «an unforgiving climate», «the unforgiving servant».
examples from the lessons: He was unforgiving and never spoke to his brother again. | In the parable, the unforgiving servant would not cancel a small debt. | The desert is unforgiving; without water you cannot survive. | The mountain was unforgiving to climbers who did not plan well. | Exams can feel unforgiving: one wrong answer loses the mark. | She tried not to be unforgiving when her friend apologised.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Un-» + «forgiving». Do not confuse with «unforgivable», which describes a wrong that is too bad to forgive. Unforgiving describes the person (or place); unforgivable describes the act.

part of speech: noun (a wig, wigs); verb (wig out — slang)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A wig is a covering of real or false hair worn on the head to hide baldness, for a costume or to change how someone looks. 2) (law, UK) In some countries judges and barristers wear white wigs in court as part of their uniform. 3) (slang, wig out) To wig out means to become very upset or panic.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, rich people in old times wore powdered wigs; in plays and dressing-up, children wear funny wigs. People who lose hair through illness, such as cancer treatment, may wear a wig. Phrases: «put on a wig», «a powdered wig», «wig out», «flip your wig» (go crazy, slang).
examples from the lessons: The actor wore a long blonde wig in the play. | Judges in England still wear white wigs in some courts. | Rich men in old portraits wore powdered wigs. | My aunt wore a wig while she was having treatment for cancer. | I bought a rainbow wig for the fancy-dress party. | Don't wig out, we'll find your homework. (slang) | The wind blew the clown's wig right off.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a wig, wigs. Be kind: people may wear wigs because of illness, so laughing at them is hurtful. «Earwig» is an insect, not a wig. The slang «wig out» and «flip your wig» are informal.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A workload is the amount of work a person or group has to do in a certain time. 2) (computing) A workload is the amount of work a computer or machine has to do.
its sense in the lessons: In school and adult life people talk about a heavy or light workload: lots of homework, a busy job, too many tasks for teachers or nurses. It tells the reader whether someone is stressed or has time. Phrases: «a heavy workload», «reduce the workload», «share the workload», «a manageable workload».
examples from the lessons: Our homework workload is much bigger this year. | Teachers have a heavy workload at report time. | We shared the workload so the project was fair. | Mum's workload doubled when her colleague left. | The new computer can handle a bigger workload. | A heavy workload can make people tired and stressed.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually countable but often used with «a» or «the»: a heavy workload. One word: workload, not «work load». Maths link: if a workload is shared equally, divide the total work by the number of people.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An allegation is a statement that someone has done something wrong or illegal, said without proof yet. 2) (law, formal) An allegation is a claim made in court or to the police that must be investigated and proved.
its sense in the lessons: In the news and adult life, allegations of cheating, bullying or crime are made and then checked by teachers, police or courts. It tells the reader that the wrongdoing is claimed but not proved. Phrases: «make an allegation», «deny the allegation», «allegations of bullying», «a serious allegation».
examples from the lessons: The player denied the allegations of cheating. | The police are looking into an allegation of theft. | She made a serious allegation against her boss. | The school takes every allegation of bullying seriously. | The allegations turned out to be false. | Newspapers must be careful when printing allegations.
note for the reader of a maths problem: An allegation: starts with a vowel sound, so «an». Verb «allege», adjective «alleged», adverb «allegedly» (said to be true but not proved). Trap: an allegation is not a fact or a verdict; a person is innocent until proven guilty. Spelling: double l, then -egation.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (church) An altar is a holy table at the front of a church where the priest or minister prepares communion (the bread and wine). 2) (religion, history) An altar is a table or stone where people in old religions offered gifts or sacrifices to God or gods. 3) (idiom) To sacrifice something on the altar of something is to give it up for that thing.
its sense in the lessons: In RE and church life the altar is the focus of the church, often with a cloth, candles and a cross; couples stand before the altar at a wedding. In Bible stories Abraham, Noah and Elijah built altars. Phrases: «at the altar», «altar boy», «altar server», «lead someone to the altar» (marry them).
examples from the lessons: The priest stood at the altar and blessed the bread and wine. | The bride and groom walked up to the altar. | Candles and flowers were placed on the altar. | In the Bible, Noah built an altar after the flood. | My brother is an altar server at Sunday Mass. | The ancient Greeks made offerings at altars to their gods.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Homophone trap: «altar» (holy table) and «alter» (to change) sound the same. Remember: an altAr is a tAble. Countable: altars. Use «an altar» because it begins with a vowel sound.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (church) A blessing is a prayer asking God to protect and do good to someone or something, or God's favour itself; Christians believe blessings come from God. 2) A blessing is something good that you are glad and thankful for. 3) A blessing is permission or approval, as in «with my parents' blessing». 4) A blessing in disguise is something that seems bad at first but turns out good.
its sense in the lessons: In church the priest gives a blessing at the end of the service; families say a blessing (grace) before meals; people say «count your blessings» to mean be thankful. In stories it tells the reader something good or approved has happened. Phrases: «count your blessings», «a mixed blessing», «a blessing in disguise», «give your blessing».
examples from the lessons: The priest gave a blessing at the end of the service. | We say a blessing before dinner. | Good friends are a real blessing. | Missing the bus was a blessing in disguise, because we met Grandma on the way. | She married him with her father's blessing. | Count your blessings: you have a home and people who love you. | A big dog in a small flat is a mixed blessing.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a blessing, blessings. From the verb «bless» (bless, blessed). «Bless you!» is said after a sneeze. A «mixed blessing» has good and bad sides. Christians believe God's blessing is a gift, not a reward to be bought.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A bridesmaid is a girl or woman who helps the bride on her wedding day and walks with her at the ceremony. 2) (idiom) «Always the bridesmaid, never the bride» means always nearly winning but never quite winning.
its sense in the lessons: A word of weddings and family life: a girl may be a bridesmaid at her aunt's or cousin's wedding, wearing a special dress and carrying flowers. The main one is the chief bridesmaid or maid of honour; a little one is a flower girl. Phrases: «chief bridesmaid», «maid of honour», «bridesmaid dress».
examples from the lessons: I was a bridesmaid at my aunt's wedding. | The bridesmaids wore pale blue dresses. | My sister is the chief bridesmaid. | The little bridesmaid scattered petals up the aisle. | Bridesmaids help the bride get ready on the big day. | Our team was always the bridesmaid, never the bride, until this year's final.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: bridesmaids. One word: bride + s + maid. The male helper of the groom is the «best man»; boys may be «pageboys» (UK) or «ring bearers». «Maid of honour» is the head bridesmaid.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Broadband is a fast internet connection that can send a lot of information at once, used in homes, schools and offices. 2) (science) Broadband describes something that uses or covers a wide range of frequencies.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life families pay for broadband, and it can be slow, fast or «down». In computing lessons, pupils learn that speed is measured in megabits per second (Mbps). Phrases: «broadband connection», «fibre broadband», «the broadband is down», «superfast broadband».
examples from the lessons: Our broadband stopped working, so we couldn't stream the film. | Mum is paying for faster broadband. | Fibre broadband uses cables made of glass. | The village still has slow broadband. | Many schools have broadband in every classroom. | The broadband speed is 50 megabits per second.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable in the internet sense: «the broadband», «our broadband», not «a broadband» usually. Mostly British; Americans often just say «the internet» or «high-speed internet». Maths link: download time = file size ÷ speed (watch the units: bits vs bytes, 8 bits = 1 byte).

part of speech: noun (a buffet, buffets); verb (buffet, buffets, buffeted, buffeting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A buffet (said «BUFF-ay» or «boo-FAY») is a meal where food is set out on a table and people serve themselves. 2) A buffet is a café or carriage on a train or at a station where you can buy food. 3) To buffet (said «BUFF-it») is to hit or push something again and again, like strong wind or waves. 4) (old) A buffet is a side cabinet for dishes.
its sense in the lessons: Parties, weddings and hotels often have a buffet; «all-you-can-eat buffet» means you pay once and eat as much as you like. In stories and weather reports, boats and people are buffeted by wind and waves. Phrases: «buffet lunch», «buffet car», «buffeted by the wind».
examples from the lessons: At the party there was a buffet with sandwiches and cake. | We helped ourselves from the buffet. | The hotel serves a breakfast buffet. | Dad bought tea from the buffet car on the train. | The little boat was buffeted by the waves. | Strong winds buffeted the tent all night. | It was an all-you-can-eat buffet, so my brother had four plates.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Two pronunciations, two meanings: food = «BUFF-ay» (the t is silent), hitting = «BUFF-it». Verb forms: buffeted, buffeting (single t). Polite buffet manners: take a fair share, use the serving spoons, don't touch food you won't take.

part of speech: verb (chant, chants, chanted, chanting) — past form; noun (a chant, chants)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Chanted is the past form of «chant»: they said or sang the same words again and again in a rhythm, often loudly together. 2) (church) Chanted can mean sung on one or a few notes, as monks chant psalms and prayers. 3) Chanted can describe words said together as a crowd, at a football match or a protest.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, crowds chanted names, children chanted rhymes in the playground, and protesters chanted slogans. In school, pupils chanted times tables. In RE, monks and nuns chanted prayers, and many faiths use chanting in worship. Phrases: «chanted his name», «chanted slogans», «chanted the times tables».
examples from the lessons: The crowd chanted the team's name. | We chanted the seven times table until we knew it. | The monks chanted psalms in the dark chapel. | The children chanted a skipping rhyme in the playground. | Protesters chanted, «Save our park!» | The fans chanted and clapped all through the match.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: chant, chanted, chanting. «Chanted» is past tense: they chanted. The noun is «a chant». Do not confuse with «enchanted» (put under a magic spell, or delighted).

part of speech: verb (clang, clangs, clanged, clanging) — -ing form; adjective (clanging); noun (the clanging)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Clanging is making a loud ringing sound of metal hitting metal, like a bell, a pan or a gate. 2) A clanging sound is loud, harsh and ringing. 3) (idiom, informal) A clanger or a clanging mistake is a big, embarrassing mistake (from «drop a clanger»).
its sense in the lessons: In stories, clanging bells, gates and pans set the scene: a clanging fire bell, a clanging prison door. In science lessons about sound, metal objects clang when they vibrate. It tells the reader the noise is loud and metallic. Phrases: «clanging bells», «the clanging of pots», «clang shut».
examples from the lessons: The fire engine came clanging down the street. | The iron gate was clanging in the wind. | I heard the clanging of pots and pans in the kitchen. | The school bell was clanging loudly. | The heavy door clanged shut behind the prisoner. | The clanging of the hammer on the metal hurt my ears.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Clang is an onomatopoeia (a word that sounds like its noise), like bang and ding. Regular verb: clanged, clanging. «Drop a clanger» (UK) means make an embarrassing mistake.

part of speech: noun (a commission, commissions); verb (commission, commissions, commissioned, commissioning)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A commission is an official group of people chosen to find out about something or to run something, like a road safety commission. 2) (money) A commission is money paid to a salesperson as a part (a percentage) of what they sell. 3) To commission something is to ask an artist, writer or builder to make it for you and pay them. 4) (army) A commission is an officer's official rank. 5) Out of commission means broken or not working.
its sense in the lessons: In money and maths problems, commission is a percentage of sales: 10% commission on a sale of £500 is £50. In the news, commissions investigate events. Artists and composers are commissioned to make new works. Phrases: «earn commission», «on commission», «out of commission», «commission a painting».
examples from the lessons: The shop assistant earns commission on every phone she sells. | She gets 5% commission, so on £200 of sales she earns £10. | The government set up a commission to look into the flooding. | The town commissioned a statue of the famous nurse. | The lift is out of commission, so we took the stairs. | The artist got a commission to paint the mayor. | He received his commission as an officer in the army.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: double m, double s: co-MM-i-SS-ion. Maths: commission = rate × sales, e.g. 8% of 300 = 0.08 × 300 = 24. Related: «commissioner» (a member or head of a commission). Do not confuse with «omission» (leaving something out).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Conception is the moment when a baby starts to grow inside its mother, when a sperm joins an egg. 2) A conception is an idea or understanding of something, how you picture it in your mind. 3) Conception is the start or the first forming of a plan or an idea. 4) (church) The Immaculate Conception is a Catholic belief that Mary, the mother of Jesus, was free from sin from the start of her life.
its sense in the lessons: In science and sex education lessons, conception is the start of pregnancy. In thinking and maths, pupils may have a «misconception» — a wrong idea. In projects and art, the conception is the first idea. Phrases: «from conception to birth», «a clear conception of», «misconception», «from its conception».
examples from the lessons: Pregnancy lasts about nine months from conception to birth. | A baby begins to form at conception. | He had no conception of how big the ocean really is. | From its conception, the park was meant for children. | It is a common misconception that bats are blind. | Catholics celebrate the Immaculate Conception of Mary.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The verb is «conceive»; the adjective «conceptual». Trap: «misconception» means a wrong idea, not a failed pregnancy. Catholic trap: the Immaculate Conception is about Mary's own beginning, not the birth of Jesus, which many people confuse.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To condemn something is to say strongly and publicly that it is wrong or bad. 2) (law) To condemn someone is to give them a punishment in court, as in «condemned to death». 3) To condemn someone to something is to force them into a bad situation. 4) To condemn a building is to say officially that it is not safe to use and must be knocked down or closed. 5) (church) In Christian teaching, to condemn is to judge someone guilty of sin; Christians believe Jesus came to save, not to condemn.
its sense in the lessons: In the news, leaders condemn attacks and unfair acts. In history, prisoners were condemned; in stories, a condemned house is falling down. In ethics, pupils learn to condemn the act but not hate the person. Phrases: «condemn the attack», «condemned to death», «a condemned building», «strongly condemn».
examples from the lessons: The head teacher condemned the bullying in assembly. | World leaders condemned the attack. | The prisoner was condemned to death in the old days. | The old flats were condemned and pulled down. | His injury condemned him to a season on the bench. | Jesus told the woman, «Neither do I condemn you.» | We should condemn cruelty to animals.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The final n is silent: «con-DEM». It comes back in «condemnation» (con-dem-NAY-shun). Regular verb: condemned, condemning. A condemned person is someone sentenced to punishment, often death. Do not confuse with «contempt» (looking down on someone).

meaning for a pupil: 1) To confide in someone is to tell them a secret or a private worry because you trust them. 2) To confide something is to say it privately, as a secret. 3) (formal) To confide something to someone is to give it into their care.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and PSHE lessons, children confide in a trusted adult, friend or teacher about problems like bullying; it shows trust. Safety lessons say: if someone hurts you, confide in a grown-up you trust. Phrases: «confide in», «confided that», «a confidant».
examples from the lessons: She confided in her best friend about the bullying. | You can always confide in your teacher if something is wrong. | He confided that he was scared of the dark. | Grandma confided a family secret to me. | I don't confide in people who spread gossip. | The king confided the treasure to his loyal knight. (formal)
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: confided, confiding. Say «confide in someone», not «confide to someone» for the trusting sense. Related: «confidence», «confidential» (secret), «confidant» (a person you confide in). Safety note: secrets that hurt someone should be told to a trusted adult, even if you promised.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Consistency is always acting, working or happening in the same way, steady and reliable. 2) Consistency is how thick, smooth or runny something is, like a liquid or mixture. 3) (maths, logic) Consistency means that facts or rules do not contradict each other.
its sense in the lessons: In cooking and science, pupils describe the consistency of mixtures: runny, thick, lumpy, smooth. In sport and school, teachers praise consistency in effort and results. In maths and stories, an answer or a story must show consistency — no contradictions. Phrases: «the consistency of paste», «show consistency», «lack of consistency».
examples from the lessons: Stir the batter until it has a smooth consistency. | The paint was the consistency of thick cream. | The team won because of their consistency all season. | Consistency is important when you train a puppy. | The teacher checked my story for consistency: the dog can't be brown and then white. | Her work shows great consistency.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly uncountable. Adjective «consistent», adverb «consistently». Spelling: -ency, not -ancy. In science experiments, «consistent results» mean repeated tests give the same or similar answers, which makes them more reliable.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A coward is a person who is too afraid to do what is right, brave or necessary, or who runs away from danger or difficulty. 2) (insult) Calling someone a coward is a strong insult meaning they have no courage.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and legends, the coward runs away while the hero stays; in ethics lessons pupils learn that bullies can be cowards, picking on weaker people. It also teaches that being afraid is normal; acting rightly in spite of fear is bravery. Phrases: «a coward's way out», «cowardly», «don't be a coward».
examples from the lessons: The bully was a coward who only picked on small children. | The cowardly lion in the story was really brave in the end. | He called me a coward because I wouldn't jump off the wall. | Telling the truth when it is hard is the opposite of being a coward. | The soldier was not a coward; he stayed to help his friends. | Running away from the fight was not cowardly; it was sensible.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a coward, cowards. Adjective «cowardly», noun «cowardice». Trap: «cowardly» looks like an adverb but is an adjective (a cowardly act). Not every fear is cowardice: walking away from danger can be wise. Do not confuse with «cower» (to crouch down in fear).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A crematorium is a building where the body of a person who has died is burned to ashes, often with a funeral service in a small chapel there. 2) (euphemism, family) «Going to the crematorium» is a gentle way adults speak of attending a cremation service for someone who has died.
its sense in the lessons: A word of adult life and family loss: a child may go with the family to a service at the crematorium, and later the ashes may be scattered or buried. It tells the reader someone has died and the family is saying goodbye. Phrases: «the crematorium chapel», «a service at the crematorium», «cremation».
examples from the lessons: Grandad's funeral service was held at the crematorium. | We sat quietly in the crematorium chapel. | After the crematorium, everyone went back to Auntie's house. | The ashes were collected from the crematorium a week later. | The crematorium had a peaceful garden with roses. | Some people choose burial, and others choose cremation at a crematorium.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: crematoriums or crematoria. Related: «cremate» (verb), «cremation» (noun). Americans also say «crematory». Some faiths prefer burial; many Christians accept cremation. Talk about it gently: it is a place of sadness and respect.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A cymbal is a round flat metal plate used as a musical instrument, hit with a stick or clashed against another cymbal to make a loud ringing crash. 2) (music) A hi-hat is a pair of cymbals on a drum kit worked with the foot.
its sense in the lessons: In music lessons cymbals belong to the percussion family; in an orchestra or band they make big crashing sounds. In stories, cymbals clash in parades and celebrations; in the Bible (Psalm 150) people praise God with loud cymbals. Phrases: «crash cymbal», «clash the cymbals», «hi-hat cymbal».
examples from the lessons: The drummer crashed the cymbal at the end of the song. | Clash the cymbals together when I nod. | Cymbals are part of the percussion section. | The noise of the cymbals made the baby jump. | The psalm says, «Praise him with loud cymbals.» | My little brother wants a drum kit with real cymbals.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Homophone trap: «cymbal» (music instrument) and «symbol» (a sign, like + or a heart) sound the same. Remember: a cYmbal is played by a drummer — Y like a drumstick. Countable: cymbals.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Dampness is a slight wetness, being a little wet in a way that is often unpleasant. 2) Dampness is wet air or wet walls in a building, which can cause mould and smell.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about materials and weather, dampness shows water in the air (humidity) or in materials. In homes, dampness causes mould on walls, which is bad for health, especially breathing. In stories, dampness creates a cold, gloomy setting. Phrases: «rising damp», «the dampness of the cellar», «signs of dampness».
examples from the lessons: The dampness in the cellar made everything smell musty. | Black mould grew because of the dampness on the wall. | I could feel the dampness of the grass through my jeans. | Dampness in a house can make asthma worse. | The cave was cold and full of dampness. | We used a fan to dry out the dampness after the flood.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: no «a dampness». From «damp» + «-ness». Damp means a little wet; «soaked» or «drenched» means very wet. The UK also says «damp» as a noun: «There's damp in the bedroom».

part of speech: noun (a decree, decrees); verb (decree, decrees, decreed, decreeing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A decree is an official order given by a ruler, a government or a court. 2) To decree something is to order it officially. 3) (Bible) In the Bible, Caesar Augustus sent out a decree that everyone must be counted, which is why Mary and Joseph went to Bethlehem. 4) (law) A decree can be a court's decision, as in a divorce decree.
its sense in the lessons: In history and RE pupils meet decrees of kings, emperors and popes; in the Christmas story the decree sends the family to Bethlehem. In stories a king decrees a feast or a law. Phrases: «issue a decree», «by royal decree», «decree that».
examples from the lessons: The king issued a decree that all dogs must wear bells. | By royal decree, the day was a holiday. | «In those days a decree went out from Caesar Augustus,» the reader began. | The emperor decreed that a new road should be built. | The court gave its final decree on the divorce. | Mum decreed that there would be no screens at dinner. (humorous)
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stress on the second syllable: de-CREE. Verb forms: decreed, decreeing (keep both e's). Do not confuse with «degree» (a unit of temperature or angle, or a university qualification).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Deliverance is being rescued or set free from danger, suffering or evil. 2) (church, Bible) In Christian and Jewish teaching, deliverance means God saving people, as when God led the Israelites out of slavery in Egypt. Christians pray «deliver us from evil».
its sense in the lessons: A stiff and religious word: in Bible stories (the Exodus, Daniel in the lions' den) and hymns, deliverance means God's rescue. In adventure stories it means the moment of rescue after long danger. Phrases: «deliverance from slavery», «pray for deliverance», «a day of deliverance».
examples from the lessons: The Israelites celebrated their deliverance from Egypt. | The sailors prayed for deliverance from the storm. | Passover remembers God's deliverance of the Israelites. | The rescue boat was their only hope of deliverance. | Daniel's deliverance from the lions amazed the king. | The prisoners waited many years for deliverance.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable and formal. From «deliver» (to rescue, as well as to bring parcels). Trap: deliverance is not «delivery» (bringing a parcel or giving birth). The Lord's Prayer says «deliver us from evil» — save us from evil.

part of speech: noun (a deluge, deluges); verb (deluge, deluges, deluged, deluging)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A deluge is a very heavy fall of rain or a great flood. 2) A deluge is a huge amount of something arriving at once, like letters, questions or emails. 3) To be deluged with something is to get far too much of it at once. 4) (Bible) The Deluge is another name for the great flood in the story of Noah.
its sense in the lessons: In weather and geography lessons, a deluge causes flooding; in stories it soaks the characters. In everyday life a teacher is deluged with questions, a shop with customers. In RE, the Deluge is Noah's flood. Phrases: «a deluge of rain», «a deluge of emails», «deluged with complaints».
examples from the lessons: The deluge flooded the streets in minutes. | We got caught in a deluge on the way home from school. | The teacher was deluged with questions about the trip. | After the advert, the shop received a deluge of orders. | The story of the Deluge tells how Noah built the ark. | The river burst its banks after three days of deluge.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Said «DEL-yooj». Verb forms: deluged, deluging. A deluge is more than a shower: it is a downpour. Similar: downpour, torrent, flood.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (church) Denominational means belonging to or run by one particular branch of a religion, such as Catholic, Anglican, Methodist or Baptist. 2) Non-denominational means open to all Christians or all faiths, not belonging to one church.
its sense in the lessons: In school life, a denominational school (or «faith school») is linked to a church, such as a Catholic or Church of England school. In RE, pupils learn that Christianity has many denominations which share beliefs about Jesus but differ in worship and leadership. Phrases: «denominational school», «non-denominational», «denominational differences».
examples from the lessons: Our school is a denominational school linked to the Catholic church. | The hospital chapel is non-denominational, so anyone can pray there. | There are small denominational differences in how churches baptise. | The service was non-denominational and welcomed people of all faiths. | Many denominational schools have assemblies with prayers. | Denominational groups worked together to help the homeless.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «denomination» (a branch of a religion; also the value of a coin or note — a £20 denomination). Adjective only. Trap: in money, «denomination» means the value of a note or coin, which has nothing to do with church.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Discourtesy is rude, impolite behaviour that shows a lack of respect for other people. 2) A discourtesy is one rude act, such as ignoring someone or not saying thank you.
its sense in the lessons: A stiff, polite-sounding word used in formal letters, school reports and old stories: «It would be a discourtesy to arrive late.» It tells the reader someone was impolite, said in a careful grown-up way. Phrases: «an act of discourtesy», «a discourtesy to», «discourteous».
examples from the lessons: It would be a discourtesy to leave without saying goodbye. | The knight saw the insult as a great discourtesy. | Interrupting the speaker is a discourtesy. | The manager apologised for the discourtesy of his staff. | Not replying to the invitation was a small discourtesy. | Ignoring a visitor is a discourtesy in any culture.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal word; in everyday talk people say «rudeness». Opposite: «courtesy» (politeness). Adjective «discourteous». Can be uncountable (rude behaviour) or countable (a discourtesy, discourtesies).

part of speech: adjective (early, earlier, earliest); adverb (early, earlier, earliest)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Earliest is the superlative of «early»: the first one in time, or the one that comes before all the others. 2) The earliest time or moment is the soonest possible one. 3) At the earliest means not before this time, and possibly later.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons pupils learn about the earliest humans, the earliest writing and the earliest towns. In maths and timetables, the earliest train is the first one; in time problems you compare times to find the earliest. Phrases: «at the earliest», «the earliest possible», «from my earliest memory», «earliest times».
examples from the lessons: The earliest train leaves at six in the morning. | My earliest memory is of a red balloon. | The earliest people made tools from stone. | Who woke up earliest today? | We can finish the project by Friday at the earliest. | Cave paintings are some of the earliest art we know. | Which runner finished earliest? She had the shortest time.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparison: early, earlier, earliest; change y to i before -er and -est. Maths trap: the earliest time is the smallest time on the clock in the same day, and in races the earliest finisher has the shortest time. «At the earliest» means «not sooner than», the opposite of «at the latest».

meaning for a pupil: 1) An elector is a person who has the right to vote in an election. 2) (USA) An elector is a member of the Electoral College, who formally chooses the President. 3) (history) An Elector was one of the princes who chose the Holy Roman Emperor.
its sense in the lessons: In citizenship lessons electors are voters: in many countries adults over a certain age are electors and their names are on the electoral roll. Phrases: «the electorate» (all the voters together), «the electoral roll», «the Electoral College».
examples from the lessons: Every elector gets one vote. | The electors queued at the polling station. | Candidates try to win the support of electors. | In the USA, electors from each state choose the President. | The Elector of Saxony was a powerful prince. | Only adults can be electors in a general election.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: an elector, electors («an» because of the vowel sound). Related: «elect», «election», «electorate», «electoral». In everyday talk people say «voter». Not the same as «electrician» or «electric».

meaning for a pupil: 1) An emotion is a strong feeling such as happiness, sadness, fear, anger, love or surprise. 2) Emotion is strong feeling in general, as when someone speaks «with emotion».
its sense in the lessons: In PSHE lessons pupils name emotions, learn that all emotions are normal and learn safe ways to manage anger or worry; «emotional literacy» means understanding feelings. In stories, a character's emotions show in faces, voices and actions. Phrases: «show emotion», «mixed emotions», «hide your emotions», «full of emotion».
examples from the lessons: Fear is a powerful emotion. | It's okay to show your emotions. | She felt mixed emotions: happy to move, sad to leave her friends. | His voice shook with emotion as he read the poem. | We drew faces to show different emotions. | Animals like dogs show emotions too. | Writers use actions to show a character's emotions.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable for one feeling (an emotion, emotions); uncountable for feeling in general (with emotion). Adjective «emotional», adverb «emotionally». Trap: feelings are not bad or good in themselves; what we do with them matters.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Enforcement is making sure that people obey a law or a rule, and punishing those who do not. 2) (law) Law enforcement means the police and other officers whose job is to make people obey the law.
its sense in the lessons: In citizenship lessons and the news, enforcement explains how laws work: speed cameras, parking wardens and the police enforce rules. Phrases: «law enforcement», «enforcement officer», «strict enforcement», «enforcement of the rules».
examples from the lessons: Law enforcement officers arrived at the scene. | Speed cameras help with the enforcement of speed limits. | The new rule needs proper enforcement, or nobody will follow it. | Enforcement of the school phone ban is the teachers' job. | The council is strict about the enforcement of parking rules. | Without enforcement, a law is just words on paper.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. From the verb «enforce» (enforce a law). «Law enforcement» is common in American English for the police. Spelling: en-force-ment.

part of speech: adjective (essential; more essential, most essential); noun (an essential, essentials)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Something essential is completely necessary; you cannot manage without it. 2) Essential means the most basic and important part of something. 3) Essentials are the things you really need, like food, water and warm clothes. 4) (science) Essential oils are strong-smelling oils taken from plants.
its sense in the lessons: In science, pupils learn that water, food, air and shelter are essential for living things. In everyday life and safety, a first-aid kit is essential on a trip. In maths, essential information in a word problem is what you need to solve it. Phrases: «essential for», «it is essential that», «the bare essentials», «essential oils».
examples from the lessons: Water is essential for all living things. | It is essential to wear a helmet when you cycle. | Pack only the essentials: a coat, a drink and your lunch. | Sleep is essential for good health. | The essential part of the story is the friendship between the two girls. | Underline the essential information in the maths problem. | Lavender essential oil smells lovely.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb «essentially» (basically). Trap: «essential» means really needed, stronger than «useful» or «important». As a noun, mostly plural: the essentials. Spelling: -tial, not -cial.

part of speech: noun (fumes — usually plural); verb (fume, fumes, fumed, fuming)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Fumes are smoke, gas or strong smells that are unpleasant or harmful to breathe, like car exhaust or paint fumes. 2) To fume is to be very angry, often quietly or while waiting. 3) To fume is to give off smoke or gas. 4) (informal, UK) «I'm fuming» means I'm really angry.
its sense in the lessons: In science and safety lessons, harmful fumes from cars, fires and chemicals are a danger; open windows when painting. In stories, a character fumes with anger: «She fumed all the way home.» Phrases: «exhaust fumes», «paint fumes», «toxic fumes», «fuming with anger», «running on fumes» (almost out of fuel or energy).
examples from the lessons: The car's exhaust fumes made me cough. | Open the window; the paint fumes are strong. | The firefighters wore masks against the toxic fumes. | Dad fumed when the train was late again. | I was fuming when my brother broke my model! | The chemical began to fume when it touched the water. | I'm running on fumes after that long day.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a noun, usually plural: fumes. Verb is regular: fumed, fuming. «Fuming» is a strong but not rude word for angry. Safety: never breathe fumes from chemicals or burning plastic; tell an adult.

part of speech: adjective (hallowed); verb (hallow, hallows, hallowed, hallowing — old)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (church) Hallowed means holy, made holy, or treated with great respect for God. 2) Hallowed means greatly respected and honoured because of its history, as a hallowed football ground. 3) (Bible, old) To hallow is to make holy or to honour as holy, as in the Lord's Prayer: «hallowed be thy name».
its sense in the lessons: Pupils meet it in the Lord's Prayer, said in many schools and churches: «Our Father, who art in heaven, hallowed be thy name» — may God's name be treated as holy. In sport and history, «hallowed ground» is a place with a special, respected past, like a famous stadium or a war cemetery. Related: Halloween (the eve of All Hallows, All Saints' Day).
examples from the lessons: «Hallowed be thy name,» we said together in assembly. | The cemetery is hallowed ground. | Playing at the hallowed stadium was the player's dream. | The old church felt hushed and hallowed. | Halloween comes from «All Hallows' Eve», the night before All Saints' Day. | The poem is one of the hallowed classics of English literature.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Said «HAL-ode», two syllables. In the Lord's Prayer, «hallowed be thy name» is old English for «may your name be holy». «Halloween» is a short form of «All Hallows' Even». Not the same as «hollow» (empty inside).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A headstone is a stone set at the head of a grave, with the name of the person who died and often a short message. 2) (building) A headstone can also mean the main stone of a building, the keystone or cornerstone.
its sense in the lessons: A word of family life, history and graveyards: families choose a headstone for someone who has died; in history lessons pupils read old headstones to learn about people of the past. It tells the reader about death, memory and respect. Phrases: «carved on the headstone», «a marble headstone», «lay flowers by the headstone».
examples from the lessons: We put flowers by Grandma's headstone. | The headstone said, «Loved by all who knew her.» | In history, we read the names on the old headstones in the churchyard. | Some headstones were so old that the words had worn away. | The family chose a simple grey headstone. | A little angel was carved on the headstone.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Also called a «gravestone» or «tombstone». Graveyards are places of respect: don't climb on headstones or run between graves. Headstones often say when the person was born and when they died, which helps historians.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal, law) Hereby means «by this statement, letter or document» — the words themselves make something happen. 2) (formal) It is used in official announcements, certificates and old-fashioned speeches.
its sense in the lessons: A stiff legal and ceremonial word: certificates, contracts and proclamations use it — «I hereby declare the fete open». Children use it playfully to sound important. It tells the reader that saying or signing these words makes it so. Phrases: «I hereby declare», «you are hereby», «I hereby promise».
examples from the lessons: I hereby declare this library open! | You are hereby invited to my birthday party. | We hereby agree to share the toys fairly. | «I hereby name this ship Explorer,» said the queen. | The certificate says: «This hereby certifies that Sam can swim twenty-five metres.» | I hereby promise to tidy my room every Saturday. (playful)
note for the reader of a maths problem: Very formal; everyday English does not need it. It usually goes before the verb: «I hereby declare». Related formal words: herewith, hereafter, whereby. Do not confuse with «nearby».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A historian is a person who studies history and writes about the past, using evidence such as documents, objects and buildings. 2) (school) A historian is anyone who does the work of history, like pupils asking questions about the past and checking sources.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons pupils «think like historians»: they look at primary and secondary sources, ask who made them and why, and compare different accounts. It tells the reader that knowledge of the past comes from evidence. Phrases: «a local historian», «historians believe», «a military historian», «an art historian».
examples from the lessons: Historians study letters and diaries to learn about the past. | A local historian showed us old photos of our town. | Historians disagree about why the war began. | Today we are historians, looking at clues from Roman Britain. | The historian wrote a book about the Victorian railways. | Historians use evidence, not guesses.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Both «a historian» and «an historian» are seen; «a historian» is more common today. Related: history, historic (important in history), historical (about history). Trap: a historian is not the same as a «storyteller»; historians must check evidence.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Humbly means in a modest way, not thinking you are better or more important than others. 2) Humbly means in a very polite, respectful way, especially when asking for something or saying sorry. 3) (church) In prayers and hymns, people come to God humbly, with humble hearts.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, servants and polite characters speak humbly to kings; in RE and church life, people pray humbly, as in «we humbly pray». In ethics, winners who thank others humbly are admired. Phrases: «humbly ask», «humbly apologise», «humbly beg your pardon», «live humbly».
examples from the lessons: The winner humbly thanked her team. | «I humbly ask for your forgiveness,» said the knight. | We humbly pray for those who are ill. | He lived humbly in a small cottage. | The servant bowed humbly before the queen. | She humbly admitted she had made a mistake.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «humble» + «-ly» (the e drops: humble → humbly). Noun «humility». Being humble is not saying you are useless; it means knowing your worth without boasting.

part of speech: verb (impress, impresses, impressed, impressing); noun (an impress — rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To impress someone is to make them admire you or feel strongly that something is very good. 2) To impress something on someone is to make them understand clearly how important it is. 3) To impress a mark or pattern is to press it into something soft. 4) (history) To impress men was to force them to serve in the navy.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life children try to impress friends, teachers or judges; in stories a character impresses the king with a clever answer. Parents impress on children the importance of road safety. Phrases: «be impressed by», «impress on», «try to impress», «make an impression».
examples from the lessons: She impressed the judges with her singing. | I was really impressed by your story. | He tried to impress his friends by doing a wheelie. | Mum impressed on us that we must never talk to strangers online. | We impressed leaves into the clay to make patterns. | The new pupil's maths impressed the whole class. | In old times, sailors were impressed into the navy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: impressed, impressing. Nouns: «impression», «impressiveness»; adjective «impressive». «Impressed by» or «impressed with» both work. Trap: trying too hard to impress can make you look silly.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Injustice is unfairness: a situation where people are not treated equally or are not given what they deserve. 2) An injustice is a particular unfair act, such as punishing the wrong person.
its sense in the lessons: In ethics, history and RE lessons, pupils learn about injustices such as slavery, unequal rights and poverty, and people who fought injustice, like Martin Luther King. In stories, injustice drives the plot: the hero is wrongly blamed. Phrases: «a sense of injustice», «fight injustice», «a great injustice», «do someone an injustice» (judge them unfairly).
examples from the lessons: Martin Luther King fought against the injustice of racism. | It was an injustice to blame Tom for the broken window. | She felt a burning sense of injustice. | Slavery was a terrible injustice. | Many people work to end injustice in the world. | You do him an injustice: he is kinder than you think.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Can be uncountable (injustice in general) or countable (an injustice, injustices). Opposite: «justice». Adjective «unjust». The prophets in the Bible often spoke out against injustice to the poor.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An instance is one example or one case of something happening. 2) «For instance» means «for example». 3) (formal) «In the first instance» means at first, as the first step. 4) (computing) An instance is one copy of a program or object that is running.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons pupils give instances (examples) to support a point; teachers say «for instance». In maths, an instance of a pattern is one case of it. In formal writing: «in this instance» (in this case). Phrases: «for instance», «in this instance», «in the first instance», «an instance of».
examples from the lessons: There are many animals that live in the desert, for instance camels. | This is one instance of kindness I will never forget. | In this instance, the teacher let us off. | Please contact the office in the first instance. | Give an instance of a time when you were brave. | Each instance of rudeness was written down.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: instances. «For instance» = «for example» (comma before and after in a sentence). Do not confuse with «instants» (very short moments) — they sound almost the same.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Interfaith means between or among people of different religions, like Christians, Jews, Muslims, Hindus, Sikhs and Buddhists. 2) An interfaith event brings different faiths together to meet, talk, pray or work for good causes.
its sense in the lessons: In RE and community life, interfaith services, weeks and projects help people of different beliefs understand and respect each other. In schools pupils visit different places of worship. Phrases: «interfaith dialogue», «an interfaith service», «interfaith week», «interfaith council».
examples from the lessons: The town held an interfaith service for peace. | Leaders from many religions met for interfaith dialogue. | During Interfaith Week we visited a mosque, a synagogue and a gurdwara. | The interfaith group runs a food bank together. | Interfaith friendship helps people respect each other's beliefs. | The interfaith council meets every month.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective, usually before a noun (an interfaith event). «Inter-» means between, as in international. Sometimes written «inter-faith». Interfaith does not mean all religions are the same; it means people of different faiths meet with respect.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Islamic means belonging to or connected with Islam, the religion of Muslims, who believe in one God (Allah) and follow the teachings of the Prophet Muhammad and the Qur'an. 2) Islamic describes art, buildings, law, history and culture shaped by Islam, such as Islamic patterns or Islamic architecture.
its sense in the lessons: In RE, history and art lessons, pupils learn about Islamic beliefs, the five pillars, Islamic art with geometric patterns, and the Golden Age of Islamic science (algebra and the numbers we use came through Islamic scholars). Phrases: «Islamic art», «Islamic patterns», «Islamic festivals», «Islamic world».
examples from the lessons: Islamic art often uses beautiful geometric patterns. | Eid is an important Islamic festival. | We visited a museum of Islamic history. | Islamic scholars in Baghdad made great discoveries in maths and astronomy. | The mosque has fine Islamic tiles and a dome. | In maths, we drew Islamic star patterns with a compass.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always written with a capital I: Islamic. A person who follows Islam is a «Muslim» (not «an Islamic»); use «Islamic» for things, ideas and culture, «Muslim» for people (Muslim families). Be respectful: most Muslims are peaceful people of faith.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (Bible) An Israelite was a member of the ancient people of Israel, the descendants of Jacob, whose stories are told in the Hebrew Bible (the Old Testament). 2) Israelite describes things belonging to that ancient people.
its sense in the lessons: In RE pupils meet the Israelites in stories of Moses, the Exodus from Egypt, the crossing of the Red Sea, the Ten Commandments and the journey to the Promised Land. Jews today see the Israelites as their ancestors. Phrases: «the Israelites in Egypt», «the twelve tribes of the Israelites».
examples from the lessons: Moses led the Israelites out of slavery in Egypt. | The Israelites wandered in the desert for forty years. | God gave the Israelites manna to eat. | The Israelites crossed the Red Sea on dry land. | Pharaoh would not let the Israelites go. | The Israelites were made up of twelve tribes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always with a capital I. Trap: «Israelite» (the ancient Bible people) is not the same as «Israeli» (a citizen of the modern state of Israel). Christians and Jews read the stories of the Israelites in the Bible.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A jackpot is the biggest prize in a game, lottery or competition, often a large amount of money. 2) (informal) To hit the jackpot is to have great luck or success, or find exactly what you wanted.
its sense in the lessons: In money talk and adult life, jackpots are won in lotteries and gambling; in maths lessons about chance, pupils learn that the probability of winning a jackpot is very small. In everyday talk, «we hit the jackpot» means great luck. Phrases: «hit the jackpot», «win the jackpot», «a rollover jackpot».
examples from the lessons: She won the lottery jackpot and gave money to charity. | The jackpot this week is a million pounds. | We hit the jackpot at the car boot sale: a whole box of comics for a pound. | The fruit machine paid out the jackpot. | The chance of winning the jackpot is tiny. | When the jackpot isn't won, it rolls over to the next game.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word: jackpot. Maths note: the chance of winning a big lottery jackpot can be less than one in millions, so most players lose money. Gambling is for adults only and can become a serious problem.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Judgement is the ability to make good, sensible decisions. 2) A judgement is an opinion you form after thinking about something. 3) (law) A judgement is the official decision of a judge or court. 4) (church, Bible) The Last Judgement or Judgement Day is when, Christians believe, God will judge all people at the end of time.
its sense in the lessons: In safety and everyday life, children are told to «use your judgement» (think sensibly). In ethics, pupils learn not to make quick judgements about people. In RE, pupils meet the Day of Judgement. Phrases: «good judgement», «pass judgement», «against my better judgement», «a snap judgement», «Judgement Day».
examples from the lessons: Use your judgement before crossing the road. | Against my better judgement, I ate the fifth cake. | Don't make judgements about people by their clothes. | The judge gave her judgement after hearing both sides. | Christians believe in a final Day of Judgement. | Her good judgement kept the team safe on the mountain. | It was an error of judgement to leave the door open.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: British «judgement», American «judgment» (no e); in UK law «judgment» is often used too. Both are correct. Verb «judge», adjective «judgemental» (judging others too quickly).

part of speech: verb (lament, laments, lamented, lamenting); noun (a lament, laments)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To lament is to show or say strongly that you are very sad or sorry about something, often someone's death. 2) A lament is a sad song, poem or piece of music about loss or death. 3) To lament something is to complain or regret that it happened or is missing.
its sense in the lessons: In RE and the Bible, the Book of Lamentations and David's lament for Saul show grief; in literature and music, a lament (like bagpipe laments) expresses sorrow. In formal writing, people lament changes («many lament the loss of the village shop»). Phrases: «lament the loss of», «the late lamented» (who has died, or is gone), «a lament for».
examples from the lessons: The villagers lamented the death of their kind old doctor. | A piper played a lament at the funeral. | David sang a lament for his friend Jonathan. | Grandad laments that children don't play outside anymore. | The poem is a lament for the lost forests. | Many readers lamented the end of the series.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stress on the second syllable: la-MENT. Noun «lamentation», adjective «lamentable» (very bad, regrettable — formal). Regular verb: lamented. A lament is not a complaint about something small; it is deep sorrow or strong regret.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Lifelong means lasting or continuing for all of someone's life. 2) Lifelong describes something that has been true for a very long time, since childhood.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and stories people have lifelong friends, lifelong dreams and lifelong illnesses. In school, «lifelong learning» means learning that goes on after school, all through life. Phrases: «lifelong friend», «lifelong learner», «a lifelong fan», «a lifelong condition».
examples from the lessons: They met at nursery and became lifelong friends. | Grandad is a lifelong fan of the local football team. | Diabetes can be a lifelong condition. | Our school wants us to be lifelong learners. | It was her lifelong dream to see the Northern Lights. | Learning to swim is a lifelong skill.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective, usually before a noun (a lifelong friend). Not the same as «lifetime» (a noun: in my lifetime) or «long-lived» (living a long time). One word, no hyphen.

part of speech: noun (Maundy) — used in Maundy Thursday and Maundy money
meaning for a pupil: 1) (church) Maundy Thursday is the Thursday before Easter, when Christians remember the Last Supper of Jesus with his disciples and how he washed their feet. 2) (UK) Maundy money is special silver coins that the British king or queen gives to older people on Maundy Thursday. 3) (church) The Maundy is the ceremony of washing people's feet, done to remember Jesus' example of serving others.
its sense in the lessons: In RE and church life, Maundy Thursday is part of Holy Week, before Good Friday and Easter Sunday. The word comes from Latin «mandatum», «commandment», because Jesus said, «Love one another». Some churches wash feet that day. Phrases: «Maundy Thursday», «Maundy money», «the Maundy service».
examples from the lessons: On Maundy Thursday we remember the Last Supper. | The priest washed people's feet at the Maundy service. | Maundy Thursday comes just before Good Friday. | The king gave Maundy money to elderly people. | Jesus washed his disciples' feet to show they must serve one another. | Holy Week includes Palm Sunday, Maundy Thursday, Good Friday and Easter Sunday.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always with a capital M and used mostly in the phrases «Maundy Thursday» and «Maundy money». It is not used on its own in everyday talk. Said «MAWN-dee». Maundy money coins are real coins but are kept, not spent.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To meditate is to sit quietly and focus your mind, often on your breathing, to feel calm and peaceful. 2) (church, religion) To meditate is to think deeply and prayerfully about God or a holy text; Buddhists, Hindus and Christians all meditate in their own ways. 3) (formal) To meditate on something is to think about it seriously for a long time.
its sense in the lessons: In PSHE and well-being lessons, children meditate or do «mindfulness» to calm worries and anger. In RE, pupils learn Buddhist meditation and Christian prayerful reading of the Psalms. Phrases: «meditate on», «meditate for ten minutes», «guided meditation».
examples from the lessons: We meditate for five minutes after lunch to calm down. | The monk meditated in silence for hours. | The psalm says to meditate on God's law day and night. | When I feel angry, I meditate and count my breaths. | Buddhists meditate to train their minds. | She meditated on what her grandmother had said.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: meditated, meditating. Noun «meditation». Trap: do not confuse with «medicate» (give medicine) or «mediate» (help two sides agree). Meditating is not sleeping; you stay awake and calm.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (church, Bible) The Nativity is the birth of Jesus in Bethlehem, as told in the Gospels; Christians celebrate it at Christmas. 2) A nativity play is a play, often done by children at school or church, that tells the Christmas story. 3) A nativity scene is a model or picture of the stable with Mary, Joseph, baby Jesus, shepherds, wise men and animals. 4) (formal) Nativity can mean anyone's birth.
its sense in the lessons: In schools in the UK, Ireland and elsewhere, children act in the nativity play as Mary, Joseph, angels, shepherds, kings or sheep. In church, a crib or nativity scene is set up at Christmas. In art lessons, pupils study famous paintings of the Nativity. Phrases: «nativity play», «nativity scene», «the Nativity story».
examples from the lessons: I was a shepherd in our school nativity play. | The nativity scene showed baby Jesus lying in a manger. | The Nativity is told in the Gospels of Matthew and Luke. | My little brother was a sheep in the nativity and forgot to say «baa». | Families came to watch the children's nativity. | The painting shows the Nativity with angels above the stable.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Use capital N for the birth of Jesus (the Nativity) and small n for the play (a nativity). Christians believe Jesus is the Son of God born as a baby; the Nativity is part of that belief. In art, a «Nativity» is a painting of the scene.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Obligatory means something you must do because a rule or law says so; it is not a free choice. 2) (humorous) Obligatory can describe something that always happens and is expected, as in «the obligatory selfie».
its sense in the lessons: A stiff word of rules and exams: «Attendance is obligatory». In school and sport, wearing a uniform or helmet may be obligatory. In everyday talk it can be playful: «the obligatory family photo». Phrases: «obligatory for all pupils», «it is obligatory to», «the obligatory».
examples from the lessons: Wearing a seatbelt is obligatory in the car. | Swimming lessons are obligatory for every pupil. | School uniform is obligatory, the rules said. | Helmets are obligatory on the climbing wall. | Then came the obligatory photo with Grandma. (humorous) | The trip is not obligatory; you can choose.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal word; in everyday talk «compulsory» or «you have to». Opposite: «optional» or «voluntary». Related: «obligation», «obliged». Stress: o-BLIG-a-tory.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Ooh is a sound people make to show surprise, delight, interest or admiration. 2) Ooh can show pain or worry, as when something hurts or looks dangerous. 3) «Oohs and aahs» means sounds of wonder from a crowd.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday talk and stories, characters say «Ooh!» when they see something lovely, tasty or surprising, like fireworks or cake. Writers use it to show a feeling quickly. Phrases: «ooh and aah», «Ooh, that's nice!», «Ooh, that hurts».
examples from the lessons: Ooh, look at those fireworks! | Ooh, is that chocolate cake? | Ooh, that must have hurt! | The crowd oohed and aahed at the acrobats. | Ooh, I've just had a brilliant idea. | «Ooh,» said Gran, «what a lovely surprise!»
note for the reader of a maths problem: An interjection (an exclamation), not a full word with forms; it can be used as a verb in «oohed and aahed». Spelling varies: ooh, oooh. Not the same as «oh» (a short surprise) or «ouch» (pain). Informal, used in speech and dialogue.

part of speech: noun (an ornament, ornaments); verb (ornament, ornaments, ornamented, ornamenting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) An ornament is a small object used to make a room, a shelf or a Christmas tree look nice, rather than for a practical use. 2) Ornament is decoration added to something to make it beautiful, like carving on a building. 3) To ornament something is to decorate it. 4) (music) An ornament is extra notes added to decorate a tune.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and Christmas traditions, families hang ornaments (baubles) on the tree; grandparents have china ornaments on shelves. In art and history, buildings and furniture have ornament. In stories, a broken ornament causes trouble. Phrases: «Christmas tree ornaments», «a china ornament», «garden ornament».
examples from the lessons: We hung shiny ornaments on the Christmas tree. | The cat knocked a china ornament off the shelf. | Grandma's house is full of little ornaments. | The church door was carved with beautiful ornament. | We made paper ornaments in art class. | The garden had a stone frog as an ornament.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable for objects (an ornament, ornaments), uncountable for decoration in general. Adjective «ornamental», «ornate» (very decorated). Spelling: or-na-ment, not «ornement».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (money) An overdraft is when a bank lets you take out more money from your account than you have in it, so you owe the bank money. 2) (money) An overdraft is the amount of money owed in this way.
its sense in the lessons: A word of adult life and money: parents may talk about being «in their overdraft» or «overdrawn» at the end of the month; banks charge fees or interest. In maths, an overdraft is a negative balance: if you have £50 and spend £80, the balance is −£30. Phrases: «go into an overdraft», «an overdraft limit», «pay off the overdraft».
examples from the lessons: Mum said we were nearly in our overdraft, so no takeaway this week. | The bank gave Dad an overdraft of £500. | He had £40 and spent £60, so he had a £20 overdraft. | Overdrafts can be expensive because banks charge fees. | They worked hard to pay off their overdraft. | Her overdraft limit is £200, so she can't spend more.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: an overdraft. Related: «overdrawn» (adjective: my account is overdrawn). Maths link: overdraft = money spent − money in account; the balance is a negative number. An overdraft is borrowed money, not free money.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Something overdue has not arrived, happened or been done by the time it was expected or needed. 2) An overdue library book has not been returned by the day it was due. 3) (money) An overdue bill has not been paid in time. 4) Overdue can mean something that should have happened long ago, as in «a change that is long overdue». 5) A baby that is overdue has not been born by the expected time.
its sense in the lessons: In school life and libraries, overdue books get a reminder or a fine. In money and adult life, overdue bills cost extra. In maths, if a payment is overdue by some days, you may add a fee for each day. Phrases: «long overdue», «overdue books», «an overdue bill», «overdue for».
examples from the lessons: My library book is overdue, so I must return it today. | The train is twenty minutes overdue. | The bill is overdue and there's a late fee. | A holiday for Mum is long overdue! | The baby was a week overdue. | The rule change was long overdue. | The fine is ten pence for each day the book is overdue.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective; it can come after the verb (the book is overdue) or before a noun (an overdue book). «Over» + «due». Not the same as «overdo» (to do too much). Maths: total fine = daily fine × number of overdue days.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To paralyse someone is to make them lose the ability to move part or all of their body, through injury or illness. 2) To paralyse something is to stop it working or moving normally, as snow can paralyse a city. 3) To be paralysed with fear means to be so frightened that you cannot move or act.
its sense in the lessons: In science and health lessons, damage to the spine or nerves can paralyse; some spiders and snakes paralyse their prey with venom. In stories, characters are «paralysed with fear». In the news, strikes or storms paralyse transport. Phrases: «paralysed from the waist down», «paralysed with fear», «paralyse the city».
examples from the lessons: The accident paralysed his legs, so he uses a wheelchair. | The spider's venom paralyses the fly. | Heavy snow paralysed the city for three days. | She was paralysed with fear when she saw the bear. | The power cut paralysed the trains. | Some illnesses can paralyse muscles for a short time.
note for the reader of a maths problem: British spelling «paralyse», American «paralyze». Noun «paralysis», adjective «paralysed» or «paralytic». Be respectful: people who are paralysed can live full lives; say «a person who uses a wheelchair», not unkind names.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (church) A parish is an area that has its own church and priest or vicar, and the people who live there. 2) (UK, local government) A parish is a small area, often a village, with its own local council called a parish council. 3) (church) The parish can mean all the people who belong to a church.
its sense in the lessons: In church life and RE, the parish priest looks after the parish; there are parish halls, parish newsletters and parish fêtes. In UK history and geography, old records list births and marriages in parish registers. In Louisiana, USA, a parish is like a county. Phrases: «parish church», «parish priest», «parish council», «parish hall».
examples from the lessons: Our parish church is the oldest building in the village. | The parish priest visits people who are ill. | The parish hall is used for Brownies and toddler groups. | The whole parish came to the summer fête. | The parish council voted to build a new playground. | Old parish registers help us find out about our ancestors.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: parishes. Adjective «parochial» (of a parish; also, narrow-minded). A person who belongs to a parish is a «parishioner». Do not confuse with «perish» (to die).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Patchy means appearing in some places but not others, in uneven patches, like patchy fog or patchy grass. 2) Patchy means not complete or not good everywhere — some parts good, some poor, as in patchy knowledge.
its sense in the lessons: In weather forecasts, «patchy rain» or «patchy fog» means some areas get it and others don't. In school reports, «patchy work» means uneven effort or results. In everyday life, a phone signal can be patchy. Phrases: «patchy rain», «patchy fog», «patchy signal», «patchy knowledge».
examples from the lessons: There will be patchy rain this afternoon. | The phone signal is patchy in the countryside. | The lawn was patchy after the dry summer. | His knowledge of the times tables is still patchy. | Patchy fog made driving slow. | The paint job looked patchy, so Dad did a second coat.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparison: patchier, patchiest. From «patch» (a small area). Not rude or strong; it means uneven, not bad everywhere.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (maths) A percentage is a number written as a part of 100, using the sign %, as 25% means 25 out of every 100. 2) A percentage is a part or share of something, as in «a large percentage of the class». 3) (informal) There's no percentage in it means there's no benefit.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, pupils find percentages of amounts (10% of 50 = 5), change fractions into percentages (½ = 50%) and use them in shopping problems with discounts and price rises. In science, results are shown as percentages; in news, survey results. Phrases: «a high percentage», «percentage increase», «percentage of».
examples from the lessons: Fifty percent is the same as a half. | What percentage of the class has a pet? | The percentage of water in the human body is about 60%. | A 20% discount on £10 saves £2. | A small percentage of pupils walk to school. | We turned our test scores into percentages. | The battery is at a low percentage, so charge it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Use «percentage» for the idea and «percent» (or «per cent» in British English) with a number: 30 percent, a high percentage. Maths: to find P% of an amount, multiply by P and divide by 100. A percentage can be more than 100% (a price can rise by 150%). «Percentage points» compare percentages: from 20% to 30% is 10 percentage points.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Popularity is being liked, enjoyed or supported by many people. 2) Popularity is how many people use or choose something, as in the popularity of a sport.
