its sense in the lessons: In school life children notice popularity among friends; in ethics, pupils learn that kindness matters more than being popular. In maths and data lessons, bar charts show the popularity of foods or pets. Phrases: «grow in popularity», «a popularity contest», «gain popularity», «lose popularity».
examples from the lessons: Football has huge popularity in many countries. | We made a bar chart to show the popularity of different fruits. | The new game grew in popularity very quickly. | The king lost popularity when he raised taxes. | It's not a popularity contest; choose the best person for the job. | The popularity of cycling rose when the new path opened.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. From «popular». Trap: popularity does not mean something is good or right. Maths link: in a survey, the most popular choice is the mode (the one chosen most often).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A provider is a person or company that supplies something people need, such as electricity, internet or health care. 2) A provider is a person who earns money to support a family. 3) (formal) A provider can be any person or group that gives a service, like a childcare provider.
its sense in the lessons: In adult life families pay internet providers and energy providers. In stories and family life, a parent may be called the main provider. In RE, Christians believe God is the provider of all good things. Phrases: «internet provider», «service provider», «health care provider», «the main provider».
examples from the lessons: Our internet provider is changing the router. | Dad is the main provider in our family since Mum is studying. | The health care provider sent a letter about my check-up. | The energy provider raised its prices. | The nursery is a good childcare provider. | Christians thank God as the provider of their daily bread.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: providers. From «provide» + «-er». The «main provider» or «breadwinner» can be anyone in a family. «ISP» means Internet Service Provider.

part of speech: noun (prudence — uncountable; also a girl's name, Prudence)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Prudence is being careful and sensible, thinking ahead so you avoid risks and mistakes. 2) (money) Prudence is being careful with money, not wasting it and saving for the future. 3) (church, ethics) In Christian teaching, prudence is one of the four cardinal virtues: wisely choosing what is right. 4) Prudence is also a girl's name.
its sense in the lessons: In ethics and RE lessons prudence is a virtue, along with justice, courage and self-control. In money talk, prudence means spending wisely and saving. In fables, the prudent ant saves food for winter while the grasshopper plays. Phrases: «act with prudence», «financial prudence», «prudence and courage».
examples from the lessons: Prudence told her to wait until the ice was thick enough. | The ant showed prudence by storing food for winter. | With prudence, Grandma saved enough for a holiday. | Prudence is one of the four cardinal virtues. | It would be prudence, not cowardice, to turn back in the storm. | The family used their money with prudence.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Adjective «prudent», adverb «prudently». The opposite is «imprudence» or recklessness. Not the same as «prudish» (easily shocked by talk about bodies or love), which comes from «prude».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (church) A pulpit is a raised, enclosed stand in a church, from which the priest or minister gives the sermon. 2) The pulpit can mean preachers or religious teaching in general, as in «from the pulpit».
its sense in the lessons: In RE and church visits, pupils learn the parts of a church: altar, font, lectern, pulpit and pews. In stories, a preacher speaks fiercely from the pulpit. Phrases: «from the pulpit», «climb into the pulpit», «a bully pulpit» (a strong position to speak from, USA).
examples from the lessons: The vicar climbed the steps into the pulpit. | The minister preached from the pulpit every Sunday. | The old pulpit was carved from dark oak. | From the pulpit, the priest asked people to help the flood victims. | On our church visit we saw the font, the altar and the pulpit. | The pulpit was high so everyone could hear.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: pulpits. Said «PUL-pit» (the first u like in «pull»). A «lectern» is a stand for reading the Bible; a pulpit is for preaching, though small churches may use one for both.

part of speech: noun (reading, readings); verb (-ing form of read)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Reading is looking at written words and understanding them. 2) A reading is a piece of writing read aloud to people, as in church or at a wedding. 3) A reading is the number shown on a measuring instrument, like a thermometer or meter. 4) A reading is the way you understand something, an interpretation. 5) (UK) Reading is also the name of a town in England, said «RED-ing». 6) (law) A reading is a stage when a new law is discussed in parliament.
its sense in the lessons: In school, reading is a core subject: reading books, reading comprehension, reading aloud. In church, people read readings from the Bible. In science, pupils take readings from thermometers, scales and rulers. Phrases: «reading book», «take a reading», «the first reading», «a reading age», «light reading».
examples from the lessons: Reading every evening helps you learn new words. | My reading book is about a talking fox. | The first reading in church was from the Book of Isaiah. | Take a reading from the thermometer every hour. | The meter reading shows how much electricity we used. | My reading of the poem is that it is about loneliness. | We drove through Reading on the way to London.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Reading» the activity is uncountable; a reading (Bible passage, measurement) is countable. Pronunciation trap: «reading» (REE-ding) as the activity, but the town is «RED-ing». Science: always write the unit with a reading (21 °C, 3.5 kg).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (church) A rector is a priest in charge of a parish in the Church of England, the Episcopal Church or the Catholic Church. 2) (school) In some schools, colleges and universities, especially in Scotland and some other countries, the rector is the head. 3) The house a rector lives in is the rectory.
its sense in the lessons: In church life and stories set in English villages, the rector leads services, visits the sick and runs the parish. In RE, pupils learn different names for church leaders: vicar, rector, priest, minister, pastor. Phrases: «the parish rector», «the rectory», «the Rector of the university».
examples from the lessons: The rector welcomed everyone at the church door. | The rector visited Grandma in hospital. | We had the fête in the rectory garden. | The new rector is a woman who loves gardening. | In Scotland, the rector of the school gave out the prizes. | The rector read the banns for the wedding.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Related: «rectory» (his or her house). Rector, vicar and minister are similar jobs with different names in different churches. A rector can be a man or a woman in many Anglican churches.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Regardless means without paying attention to problems, warnings or difficulties; anyway. 2) Regardless of something means without being affected by it, as in «everyone is welcome regardless of age».
its sense in the lessons: In ethics and citizenship, people should be treated fairly regardless of race, religion or gender. In stories, a character carries on regardless of danger. In maths, some rules work regardless of the numbers chosen. Phrases: «regardless of», «carry on regardless».
examples from the lessons: Everyone can join the club regardless of age. | It was raining, but we went to the beach regardless. | The rules apply to everyone, regardless of who they are. | He kept running regardless of the pain in his leg. | Regardless of the order you add numbers, the total is the same. | She treated everyone kindly, regardless of what they could give her.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: «irregardless» is a common mistake; the correct word is «regardless». Regardless of = no matter. Maths: addition gives the same answer regardless of order (3 + 5 = 5 + 3), but subtraction does not.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Remarriage is getting married again after a divorce or after a husband or wife has died. 2) A remarriage is a second (or later) marriage.
its sense in the lessons: A word of family life and adult life: after a parent's remarriage, a child may get a step-parent, step-siblings and a «blended family». In RE, churches have different teachings on remarriage after divorce. Phrases: «remarriage after divorce», «a happy remarriage».
examples from the lessons: After Dad's remarriage, I got two stepbrothers. | Some churches do not allow remarriage after divorce. | Her remarriage made the whole family happy. | Remarriage can bring big changes for children. | Grandma's remarriage at seventy surprised everyone. | The book is about a family learning to get along after a remarriage.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable and uncountable. From «re-» (again) + «marriage»; verb «remarry». Spelling: double r in the middle: re-ma-rr-iage.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A reputation is what people generally think about someone or something, based on what they have done in the past. 2) A reputation for something means being known for it, good or bad.
its sense in the lessons: In ethics, stories and adult life, a good reputation takes years to build and can be lost quickly; lying and cheating damage reputation. Schools, shops and companies care about their reputation. In stories, a character «with a reputation» is known for something, often bad. Phrases: «a good reputation», «a reputation for», «damage your reputation», «live up to your reputation».
examples from the lessons: The bakery has a reputation for the best bread in town. | Cheating would ruin his reputation. | She has a reputation for being fair and kind. | The school has an excellent reputation. | The old house had a reputation for being haunted. | It takes years to build a good reputation and seconds to lose it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a reputation, reputations. Related: «reputable» (trusted), «disreputable» (not trusted). Trap: a reputation is people's opinion, which may be wrong; it is not the same as a person's real character.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A resolution is a firm decision to do or not do something, such as a New Year's resolution. 2) Resolution is solving or ending a problem, argument or conflict. 3) (formal) A resolution is an official decision voted for by a group, like a council or the United Nations. 4) (science, computing) Resolution is how sharp and detailed a picture or screen is, measured in pixels. 5) (stories) The resolution is the part at the end of a story where the problem is solved.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons, a story has an opening, build-up, problem, resolution and ending. In PSHE, conflict resolution means solving fights fairly. At New Year, people make resolutions. In computing, screens and photos have high or low resolution. Phrases: «New Year's resolution», «conflict resolution», «high resolution», «pass a resolution».
examples from the lessons: My New Year's resolution is to read more books. | The teacher helped us find a resolution to the argument. | In the resolution, the lost dog finds its way home. | The council passed a resolution to build a new park. | This photo has a high resolution, so it's very clear. | She faced the hard climb with great resolution. | Conflict resolution means listening to both sides.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable in most senses. Related: «resolve» (verb: to decide or solve; noun: determination), «resolute» (determined). Computing: resolution is often given as width × height in pixels, e.g. 800 × 600.

part of speech: verb (retake, retakes, retook, retaken, retaking); noun (a retake, retakes)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To retake a test or exam is to take it again, often because you failed or want a better mark. 2) A retake is a second try at a test, or a scene in a film filmed again. 3) To retake a place is to capture it again after losing it.
its sense in the lessons: In school and adult life, students retake exams; «resits» is the British word in many schools. In film-making and drama, a retake is shooting a scene again. In history, armies retake towns or castles. Phrases: «retake an exam», «a retake of the scene», «retake the castle».
examples from the lessons: She failed her driving test but will retake it next month. | I need to retake the spelling test. | The actor forgot his lines, so they did a retake. | The army retook the castle after a long siege. | Retakes are allowed if you are ill on the day. | After three retakes, the scene was perfect.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular like «take»: retake, retook, retaken. Stress: verb re-TAKE, noun RE-take. British schools also say «resit». A retake is a second chance, not a punishment.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Richly means in a beautiful, expensive or lavish way, as richly dressed or richly decorated. 2) Richly means fully and well, as in «richly deserved». 3) Richly means in large amounts or with strong colour, flavour or detail.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, kings and queens are richly dressed in velvet and gold; churches and palaces are richly decorated. In ethics and praise, «richly deserved» means fully earned. In descriptive writing, «richly coloured» paintings use strong colours. Phrases: «richly deserved», «richly decorated», «richly rewarded», «richly coloured».
examples from the lessons: The queen was richly dressed in silk and jewels. | The church was richly decorated for Christmas. | Her prize was richly deserved after so much hard work. | The cake was richly flavoured with chocolate and cherries. | His kindness was richly rewarded. | The book is richly illustrated with colourful pictures.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «rich» + «-ly». «Richly» does not only mean «with lots of money»; «richly deserved» means completely deserved. Comparison: more richly, most richly.

part of speech: noun (ridicule — uncountable); verb (ridicule, ridicules, ridiculed, ridiculing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Ridicule is unkind laughing at someone or something to make them look silly or stupid. 2) To ridicule someone is to make fun of them in a cruel or mocking way.
its sense in the lessons: In ethics and anti-bullying lessons, ridicule is a form of bullying that hurts feelings and stops people from trying. In stories, inventors and dreamers are ridiculed at first and later proved right. Phrases: «face ridicule», «hold up to ridicule», «an object of ridicule», «be ridiculed for».
examples from the lessons: The other children ridiculed him for his old shoes. | She faced ridicule but never gave up her dream. | The inventor's idea was met with ridicule, but it worked. | Ridicule can hurt more than a push. | Don't ridicule someone for making a mistake. | His silly hat made him an object of ridicule.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable as a noun. Adjective «ridiculous» (silly, laughable). Stress: RID-i-cule. Spelling: ridicule, not «redicule». Making fun of someone to hurt them is bullying.

part of speech: noun (a robe, robes); verb (robe, robes, robed, robing — formal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A robe is a long, loose piece of clothing that covers the body, worn for special ceremonies, by judges, priests, kings and graduates. 2) A robe is a bathrobe or dressing gown worn at home after a bath or before getting dressed. 3) (formal) To be robed is to be dressed in a robe.
its sense in the lessons: In RE and church life, priests and choirs wear robes; in the Bible Joseph had a «robe of many colours». In history and stories, kings, wizards and judges wear robes. In everyday life, «robe» is often an American word for dressing gown. Phrases: «a judge's robe», «a long white robe», «bathrobe», «robed in».
examples from the lessons: The judge wore a black robe. | The choir walked in, wearing white robes. | Joseph's father gave him a beautiful robe. | The wizard swept his robe around him and vanished. | I put on my robe after my bath. | The king was robed in red velvet.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: robes. Often plural in ceremony (robes of office). British «dressing gown» = American «robe» or «bathrobe». Not to be confused with «rob» (to steal).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A selfish person thinks mostly about themselves and what they want, and does not care enough about other people. 2) A selfish act is one done only for your own good, at others' expense.
its sense in the lessons: In ethics, PSHE and stories, selfishness is shown as wrong: the selfish giant who would not share his garden, the child who will not share sweets. Pupils learn that sharing and taking turns are the opposite. Phrases: «selfish behaviour», «a selfish giant», «don't be selfish».
examples from the lessons: It's selfish to eat all the sweets yourself. | The Selfish Giant would not let the children play in his garden. | He was too selfish to share his toys. | Taking the last seat when Grandma was standing was selfish. | Being selfish can lose you friends. | She realised she had been selfish and said sorry.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparison: more selfish, most selfish. Noun «selfishness», adverb «selfishly». Opposite: «selfless», «unselfish», «generous». Trap: taking care of yourself (rest, saying no to danger) is not the same as being selfish.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Signification is the meaning of a word, sign or symbol. 2) (formal) Signification is the act of showing or signalling something.
its sense in the lessons: A rare and very stiff word, used in old books, language study and philosophy. It tells the reader about what a word or sign means. In everyday talk people say «meaning». Phrases: «the signification of a word», «true signification».
examples from the lessons: The scholar explained the signification of the old word. | Each colour in the flag has its own signification. | In the old book, the signification of the dream was explained by a wise man. | Words can change their signification over hundreds of years. | The priest explained the signification of the candle at Easter. | He did not understand the full signification of the sign.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal and rare. Not the same as «significance» (importance), though related: both come from «signify» (to mean or show). Use «meaning» in normal writing.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (old, Bible) A sluggard is a very lazy person who does not want to work or get up. 2) (humorous) Sluggard can be used jokingly for someone who sleeps late or moves slowly.
its sense in the lessons: Pupils meet it in the Bible's Book of Proverbs: «Go to the ant, you sluggard; consider its ways and be wise» — the ant works hard and prepares, so we should too. In stories and joking talk, a sluggard lies in bed while others work. Phrases: «go to the ant, thou sluggard».
examples from the lessons: «Go to the ant, you sluggard,» says the proverb. | Get out of bed, you sluggard! (joking) | The sluggard's garden was full of weeds. | The fable shows the hard-working ant and the sluggard grasshopper. | Proverbs warns that the sluggard will go hungry. | He was no sluggard; he worked from dawn to dusk.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Old-fashioned; today people say «lazybones» or «slacker». Related: «sluggish» (slow, without energy), «slug» (a slow, slimy animal). A sluggard is a person, not an animal.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) Specs is short for «spectacles», meaning glasses that people wear to see better. 2) (informal) Specs is short for «specifications», a detailed description of how something is made or what it can do, like a computer or phone.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday talk, children say «Where are my specs?» or «Grandad's specs». In technology and adult life, people compare the specs of phones, cars or game consoles: memory, screen size, speed. Phrases: «reading specs», «put on your specs», «check the specs», «high specs».
examples from the lessons: Grandad can't read without his specs. | I left my specs on the bus! | She got new pink specs from the optician. | The new tablet has amazing specs: a big screen and lots of memory. | Before buying, Dad checked the specs of the laptop. | My specs steamed up when I came in from the cold.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always plural and informal: «my specs are», not «my spec is». For glasses, formal word is «spectacles». For technology, «specifications» or «tech specs». A «spec» alone can mean «speculation» («on spec» = without being asked or sure).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Stripy means having stripes — long thin lines or bands of different colours.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and children's books, there are stripy jumpers, stripy socks, stripy tigers and stripy deckchairs. In science, animals have stripy fur or skin for camouflage, like zebras and tigers. In art and maths, stripy patterns can repeat. Phrases: «stripy jumper», «stripy tail», «red and white stripy».
examples from the lessons: I'm wearing my stripy socks today. | The zebra's stripy coat helps confuse lions. | The bee has a black and yellow stripy body. | We sat on stripy deckchairs at the beach. | The tiger's stripy fur hides it in the long grass. | My little sister drew a stripy rainbow snake.
note for the reader of a maths problem: British and Australian informal word; also spelled «stripey». «Striped» is more formal and more American. Comparison: stripier, stripiest. Stripes on a pattern often repeat, which makes them a simple example of a pattern in maths.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A tragedy is a very sad event that causes great suffering, damage or death, like a terrible accident or disaster. 2) A tragedy is a serious play or story that ends sadly, often with the death of the main character, as in Shakespeare's Romeo and Juliet. 3) (informal) Tragedy can be used jokingly for something small that seems sad, like dropping your ice cream.
its sense in the lessons: In history and the news, tragedies like shipwrecks, wars and floods are remembered with respect. In English lessons, pupils study tragedy and comedy as kinds of drama. In everyday talk, children may joke «What a tragedy!» about small losses. Phrases: «a terrible tragedy», «a Shakespearean tragedy», «end in tragedy», «tragedy struck».
examples from the lessons: The sinking of the Titanic was a great tragedy. | The town held a minute's silence after the tragedy. | Romeo and Juliet is one of Shakespeare's most famous tragedies. | Tragedy struck when the bridge collapsed. | The day out ended in tragedy. | I dropped my ice cream — what a tragedy! (joking)
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: tragedies. Adjective «tragic», adverb «tragically». Opposite in drama: «comedy». Be careful with the joking sense: around people who have suffered a real tragedy, it can sound unkind.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To unclip something is to open or remove a clip so that it comes loose or apart, like a seatbelt, a dog's lead or a hair clip.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and safety, children unclip their seatbelt only when the car has stopped, unclip a bike helmet, or unclip a dog's lead in the park. In stories, it shows a small action of freeing or opening. Phrases: «unclip the seatbelt», «unclip the lead», «unclip your helmet».
examples from the lessons: Don't unclip your seatbelt until the car stops. | I unclipped the dog's lead and she ran across the field. | She unclipped her helmet and shook out her hair. | Unclip the lid to open the lunch box. | He unclipped his badge and gave it to the teacher. | The climber unclipped from the rope at the top.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double p in the past: unclipped, unclipping. «Un-» means the opposite of the action: clip → unclip, like do → undo. Safety: in a moving car, keep your seatbelt clipped.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An uneventful time is one when nothing special, exciting or bad happens. 2) An uneventful trip or operation goes smoothly, with no problems.
its sense in the lessons: Used in stories to show calm before something happens, or to say a journey or recovery went fine; often in «an uneventful day», «the flight was uneventful»; in news and doctors' talk it is good news.
examples from the lessons: It was an uneventful Monday at school. | The flight home was long but uneventful. | Grandpa's operation was uneventful, and he is resting now. | After an uneventful morning, the storm hit at lunchtime. | The camping weekend was pleasantly uneventful. | Nothing happened at all; it was the most uneventful holiday ever.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Built from un- + eventful («full of events»). Not always boring: often it means «safe, no trouble». Opposite: eventful.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unjust means not fair or not right, especially when someone is treated badly without a good reason. 2) (law) An unjust law or punishment goes against fairness and people's rights.
its sense in the lessons: Used in ethics lessons, history (unjust laws, slavery) and stories about wrongs being put right; phrases: «an unjust punishment», «unjust treatment», «it is unjust that…».
examples from the lessons: It was unjust to blame Mia for the broken window. | The whole class was kept in, which felt unjust. | People marched against the unjust law. | The story is about a king who was cruel and unjust. | Martin Luther King spoke out against unjust treatment. | Is it unjust to punish everyone for one person's mistake?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: just (fair). Noun: injustice (not «unjustice»). Adverb: unjustly. Stronger and more formal than «unfair».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unrelated things have no link or connection with each other. 2) Unrelated people are not part of the same family.
its sense in the lessons: Used in science and maths to say two facts or numbers do not affect each other; in everyday talk to change topic («on an unrelated note»); in stories for strangers who look alike.
examples from the lessons: My headache is unrelated to the test; I just slept badly. | The two fires were unrelated. | Liam and Leo share a surname but are unrelated. | On an unrelated note, who wants pizza? | Ignore the unrelated information in the word problem. | The teacher said the question was unrelated to today's lesson.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Often followed by «to»: unrelated to something. In maths word problems, unrelated numbers are distractors: do not use them in the sum.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To vacate a place is to leave it so that it is empty for someone else. 2) (formal) To vacate a job or seat is to give it up.
its sense in the lessons: Seen on signs and notices («Please vacate the room by…»), in hotels, flats and offices; in safety drills it means everyone must leave a building.
examples from the lessons: Please vacate your seats when the bell rings. | Guests must vacate their rooms by eleven o'clock. | The family had to vacate the flat when the lease ended. | Everyone vacated the building during the fire drill. | The captain vacated his post to become coach. | The hall must be vacated for cleaning.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal word; in everyday talk say «leave» or «move out». Related: vacant (empty), vacancy, vacation (US: holiday).

part of speech: noun (a valentine, valentines; Valentine as a name)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A valentine is a card or small gift sent on Valentine's Day to show love or liking, often without signing your name. 2) Your valentine is the person you send it to or love. 3) Valentine is also a name, for example Saint Valentine, a Christian saint.
its sense in the lessons: Used around Valentine's Day: in schools children make cards; phrases «be my valentine», «a secret valentine», «Valentine's Day».
examples from the lessons: I made a valentine with red hearts and glitter. | Will you be my valentine? | Sam got a valentine but did not know who sent it. | Our class made valentines for the people in the care home. | Mum and Dad are each other's valentines. | Saint Valentine is remembered by many churches.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Write «Valentine's Day» with a capital V and an apostrophe. The card is often written with a small v: a valentine. Sending one secretly is a custom, not a rule.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To venerate someone or something is to treat them with very deep respect. 2) (church) Some Christians venerate saints, relics or icons: they honour them, but believe only God is worshipped.
its sense in the lessons: Used in religion lessons (saints, holy places), history (ancestors, heroes) and formal writing; noun veneration.
examples from the lessons: Many people venerate their grandparents' wisdom. | The village venerates the old oak tree. | Catholics and Orthodox Christians venerate the saints. | The pilgrims kissed the icon to venerate it. | Ancient Egyptians venerated cats. | Scientists still venerate Newton's work.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal word; everyday «respect» or «honour» is softer. Trap: venerate (honour) is not the same as worship (give the love and praise owed to God), as churches use the words. Adjective: venerable (old and respected).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A warden is a person whose job is to look after a place or the people in it, like a park, a hall of residence or a nature reserve. 2) A prison governor in the US is called a warden. 3) A traffic warden (UK) checks cars are parked legally. 4) (church) A churchwarden helps run a parish.
its sense in the lessons: Seen in many jobs: park warden, game warden, fire warden at school (the person who checks everyone is out in a drill), traffic warden; in stories, the prison warden.
examples from the lessons: The park warden told us not to feed the ducks. | Our teacher is the fire warden for this floor. | The traffic warden gave Dad a parking ticket. | The game warden protects the animals from hunters. | The prisoners stood in line while the warden walked past. | The hostel warden locks the doors at night.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a warden, two wardens. Do not confuse with «warder» (old UK word for a prison guard) or «guardian».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Absolute means total, complete, as much as possible: absolute silence. 2) Certain and not changing: an absolute rule. 3) (maths) The absolute value of a number is its distance from zero, always positive or zero. 4) An absolute ruler has complete power. 5) (informal) Used for force: an absolute disaster, an absolute legend.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: absolute value |−5| = 5; in science: absolute zero (the coldest possible temperature); in everyday talk to make a word stronger; in history: absolute monarchs.
examples from the lessons: There was absolute silence during the test. | The absolute value of minus seven is seven. | Nothing can be colder than absolute zero. | The king had absolute power. | That party was an absolute disaster! | You're an absolute star for helping. | Safety is an absolute must on the trip.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Not used with «more» or «very». In maths |x| means absolute value: |−3| = 3 and |3| = 3; distances use it so they are never negative. Adverb: absolutely.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Completely, totally: absolutely right. 2) Used as a strong «yes» when you agree: «Absolutely!» 3) With «not» or «nothing», a strong «no»: absolutely not, absolutely nothing. 4) (informal) Used to make a feeling stronger: absolutely starving.
its sense in the lessons: Very common in talk to agree warmly or to stress a word; in maths problems «absolutely certain» means probability 1.
examples from the lessons: Are you coming? — Absolutely! | You are absolutely right. | I'm absolutely starving. | Absolutely not, you can't go out in this storm. | There was absolutely nothing left in the fridge. | The sunset was absolutely beautiful. | Make absolutely sure the tap is off.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: absolute + ly, keep the e (absolutely). Stress is on «lute»: ab-so-LUTE-ly. Overused in speech; in writing choose a precise word.

part of speech: noun (an abstention, abstentions; uncountable for the habit)
meaning for a pupil: 1) An abstention is when someone chooses not to vote, neither for nor against. 2) (formal) Abstention is choosing not to do or have something you might want, like food or alcohol.
its sense in the lessons: Used in class elections and councils («ten for, five against, two abstentions»); in religion for fasting or giving things up in Lent.
examples from the lessons: The vote was twelve for, eight against, with three abstentions. | Ruby's abstention meant the result was a tie. | Abstention from sweets during Lent was hard for Tom. | The council counted the abstentions separately. | There were no abstentions; everyone voted. | In the class vote for the trip, there was one abstention.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: abstain (abstain from voting). In maths of votes: abstentions are counted but usually do not add to either side, so for + against + abstentions = everyone who was there.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An adjudicator is a person who judges a contest, such as a music, dance or speaking competition, and decides who wins. 2) (formal, law) A person who officially decides a disagreement between people.
its sense in the lessons: Used at school music festivals, eisteddfods, debating and drama contests; in adult life for disputes about work or money.
examples from the lessons: The adjudicator gave our choir first place. | Each dancer bowed to the adjudicator. | The adjudicator wrote helpful comments on my sheet. | An independent adjudicator settled the argument between the builder and the family. | The debate adjudicator explained why our team lost. | The adjudicator listened to every reader before choosing.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: adjudicate. Similar: judge, referee (sport), umpire. Spelling: ad-ju-di-ca-tor, ends in -or.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Adoptive describes the family who adopts a child: adoptive parents, adoptive mother. 2) An adoptive home or country is one you choose and come to belong to.
its sense in the lessons: Used gently in family talk and stories about adoption; the adopted child is «adopted», the parents are «adoptive».
examples from the lessons: Ella loves her adoptive parents very much. | His adoptive mum came to the school play. | Canada became her adoptive country. | The adoptive family welcomed the puppy too. | Many children grow up happy with adoptive families. | Her adoptive brother taught her to ride a bike.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: the parents are adoptive, the child is adopted. Do not say «adopted parents» in careful writing. Adoptive parents are real parents in law and in love; birth parents are the ones who gave birth.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (church, Bible) The Annunciation is when, as the Bible tells, the angel Gabriel came to Mary to say that she would be the mother of Jesus. 2) The church feast that remembers this. 3) (formal, rare) An announcement.
its sense in the lessons: Used in religion lessons, Christmas story teaching, church calendars and art: many famous paintings are called «The Annunciation».
examples from the lessons: The Annunciation is told in the Gospel of Luke. | In the painting of the Annunciation, the angel holds a lily. | Our church keeps the feast of the Annunciation in spring. | Mary said yes to God at the Annunciation, Christians believe. | We acted out the Annunciation in the nativity play. | Gabriel's words at the Annunciation begin «Hail Mary» in many prayers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually with a capital A and «the». Spelling: double n twice: an-NUN-ci-a-tion. Related verb: announce.

part of speech: verb (appeal, appeals, appealed, appealing); noun (an appeal, appeals)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To appeal for something is to ask for it strongly, often from the public: appeal for help. 2) If something appeals to you, you like it or find it attractive. 3) (law) To appeal is to ask a higher court or person to change a decision. 4) In sport, players appeal to the umpire or referee. 5) Noun: a request, a charity collection, or the attractive quality of something.
its sense in the lessons: In news (police appeal for witnesses), charities (a school appeal for the food bank), sport (cricket appeal «Howzat!»), law and fairness; phrases «appeal to», «lose its appeal», «on appeal».
examples from the lessons: The police appealed for witnesses. | Our school appeal raised money for flood victims. | Camping doesn't appeal to me. | The game lost its appeal after a week. | The bowler appealed, but the umpire said not out. | The family will appeal against the court's decision. | I appealed to Mum to let me stay up.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: appealing (attractive). «Appeal to» = attract, or ask someone; «appeal against» (UK) / «appeal» (US) a decision. Double p, single l, but appealed, appealing.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To appoint someone is to choose them officially for a job or role. 2) (formal) To appoint a time or place is to decide it: at the appointed time.
its sense in the lessons: Used for jobs in school (appoint a new head teacher, class captain) and government; noun appointment (a job given, or a time to see the doctor or dentist).
examples from the lessons: The school appointed a new head teacher. | Mrs Lee appointed Zoe as team captain. | We met at the appointed time. | The council appointed a new mayor. | She was appointed to look after the class pet. | Who appoints the judges?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: appointment, which also means a booked meeting (a dentist appointment). Opposite feeling: disappointed (not about appointing!). Double p.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Arbitrary means chosen by chance or by someone's wish, not for a good reason or rule. 2) (maths) An arbitrary number is any number you pick, used to show a rule works for all. 3) Unfair power used without rules: an arbitrary punishment.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: «take an arbitrary point», «an arbitrary whole number»; in ethics and fairness: arbitrary rules feel unjust; in everyday talk for random choices.
examples from the lessons: The order of the names was arbitrary. | Pick an arbitrary number and double it. | The rule seemed arbitrary to the pupils. | It was an arbitrary punishment with no warning. | The starting point on the line is arbitrary. | Giving prizes by height is arbitrary.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced AR-bi-tra-ry (UK often AR-bi-tree). In maths «arbitrary» means «any one, whichever you choose», so a fact shown for an arbitrary number is true for all of them. Adverb: arbitrarily.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An assignment is a piece of work a teacher gives you to do, often at home or over several days. 2) A job or task someone is given at work. 3) (formal) Giving something to someone or putting it in a place: the assignment of seats.
its sense in the lessons: Very common at school (hand in your assignment, due date), in jobs (a reporter's assignment) and in spy stories (a secret assignment); in computing, assigning a value to a variable.
examples from the lessons: Our science assignment is about volcanoes. | Hand in your assignments on Friday. | The reporter was on assignment in Kenya. | The spy accepted a dangerous assignment. | I finished the maths assignment early. | The assignment of tables was done by drawing names.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: assign. Countable. Spelling: the g is silent: as-SIGN-ment. Similar: homework (uncountable: no «a homework»), task, project.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To bestow something on someone is to give it to them, especially an honour, gift or title.
its sense in the lessons: Used in fairy tales (the fairy bestowed a gift on the baby), ceremonies, awards and religious language (God bestows blessings, Christians believe).
examples from the lessons: The queen bestowed a knighthood on the scientist. | The fairy godmother bestowed three wishes. | The school bestowed a special prize on the caretaker. | Praise was bestowed on the brave firefighter. | The title was bestowed upon him by the king. | Many Christians thank God for the blessings he bestows.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal and old-fashioned; everyday «give» or «award». Pattern: bestow something on/upon someone.

part of speech: noun (a blindfold, blindfolds); verb (blindfold, blindfolds, blindfolded, blindfolding); adjective/adverb (blindfold)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A blindfold is a cloth tied over someone's eyes so they cannot see. 2) To blindfold someone is to put such a cloth over their eyes. 3) Doing something blindfold means doing it without seeing.
its sense in the lessons: In party games (pin the tail on the donkey, blind man's buff), science tasting tests (taste with a blindfold), trust games, and stories with kidnappers.
examples from the lessons: Put on the blindfold and guess the fruit. | We blindfolded Jack for pin the tail on the donkey. | She can solve the puzzle blindfold. | The blindfolded player tried to catch us. | In the taste test, each child wore a blindfold. | The kidnappers blindfolded the hero.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: blind + fold, not «blindfolded» as the noun. Safety: never run while blindfolded; a partner should guide you.

part of speech: verb (brag, brags, bragged, bragging); noun (a brag)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To brag is to talk proudly about yourself, what you have or what you did, in a way that annoys others. 2) A brag is such a boast.
its sense in the lessons: Used in friendship stories and lessons about kindness and good manners; phrases «brag about», «bragging rights».
examples from the lessons: Stop bragging about your new bike. | He bragged that he scored all the goals. | Nobody likes it when you brag. | The winners had bragging rights for a week. | She never brags, even though she is top of the class. | «I'm the fastest!» was his usual brag.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double the g: bragged, bragging. Similar: boast, show off. A person who brags is a braggart (old) or «show-off».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Bronze is a hard brown-gold metal made by mixing copper and tin. 2) A bronze is a medal for third place. 3) A statue or object made of bronze. 4) Bronze is a reddish-brown colour, like a suntan.
its sense in the lessons: In history (the Bronze Age), science (alloys), sport (bronze medal for third), art (bronze statues).
examples from the lessons: She won bronze in the swimming race. | Bronze is made from copper and tin. | People in the Bronze Age made tools from bronze. | A bronze statue stands in the park. | Gold, silver and bronze go to first, second and third. | His skin looked bronze after the beach holiday.
note for the reader of a maths problem: In science, bronze is an alloy (a mix of metals), not a pure element. In rankings: bronze = third place. Do not confuse with brass (copper and zinc).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A captive is a person or animal that has been caught and is kept somewhere and not allowed to leave. 2) Captive means kept and not free: captive animals. 3) A captive audience must listen because they cannot leave.
its sense in the lessons: In history and adventure stories (taken captive, held captive), in science about zoos and wildlife (captive breeding), and in Bible stories (the people taken captive to Babylon).
examples from the lessons: The pirates took the sailors captive. | The prince was held captive in a tower. | Captive pandas are bred in zoos to save the species. | The captives escaped at night. | On the long bus ride, Dad had a captive audience for his jokes. | The Bible tells of the Israelites held captive in Babylon.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun captivity (in captivity). Captor = the one who holds the captive. Captivate means to charm, not to capture.

part of speech: noun (a career, careers); verb (career, careers, careered, careering)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A career is the job or kind of work someone does for a long part of their life, often getting better at it. 2) Your career at school is your time there. 3) To career is to move fast and out of control: the bike careered down the hill.
its sense in the lessons: Used in careers lessons and careers days, talk about grown-ups' jobs («a career in nursing»), and in stories for wild movement.
examples from the lessons: She wants a career as a vet. | Careers day helped me think about jobs. | Grandpa had a long career as a train driver. | Dad changed careers and became a teacher. | The runaway trolley careered across the car park. | The footballer's career ended after his injury.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stress: ca-REER. US spells it the same. Do not confuse with «carer» (someone who looks after a sick person) or «courier».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Carpentry is the skill or job of making and fixing things from wood, like tables, doors and roof frames. 2) The woodwork itself: the carpentry in the old church.
its sense in the lessons: Used in design and technology lessons, jobs talk (a carpenter), Bible stories (Joseph and Jesus were carpenters, the Gospels say) and safety (tools, goggles).
examples from the lessons: Uncle Ben learned carpentry at college. | Carpentry needs careful measuring. | We did some simple carpentry in DT. | The carpentry in this house is beautiful. | Jesus learned carpentry from Joseph, Christians believe. | Wear goggles when you do carpentry.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: no «a carpentry». Person: carpenter. In maths problems carpentry means measuring lengths and cutting: «measure twice, cut once».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A casserole is a dish of meat, vegetables or beans cooked slowly in the oven in liquid. 2) A casserole dish is the deep pot with a lid it is cooked in.
its sense in the lessons: Used in cooking lessons, family dinners and community kindness (bringing a casserole to a neighbour who is ill or grieving); US «hotdish» in some areas.
examples from the lessons: Mum made a chicken casserole for tea. | Put the casserole in the oven for two hours. | The neighbours brought a casserole when Gran was ill. | Carry the casserole dish with oven gloves. | The bean casserole was warm and filling. | We need a bigger casserole dish.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Safety: casserole dishes stay hot for a long time. In maths recipes: double the casserole = double every ingredient.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (church, formal) Chastity means not having a sexual relationship, or only within marriage, as a religious or moral choice. 2) (formal) Being pure and simple in style.
its sense in the lessons: Used in religion lessons about promises made by monks and nuns (poverty, chastity and obedience) and in old stories about virtue; a word pupils meet in church life.
examples from the lessons: Monks and nuns make promises of poverty, chastity and obedience. | In the old story, the knight was praised for his chastity. | Chastity is one of the virtues many Christians try to live by. | The nun spoke kindly about her vow of chastity. | Some young Christians promise chastity until they marry. | The poem calls chastity a white flower.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Adjective: chaste. A grown-up topic: use it respectfully; it describes a choice about relationships, not anything about clothing.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Chemotherapy is a treatment for cancer that uses strong medicines to kill the sick cells. 2) It can make people tired and sometimes lose their hair for a while.
its sense in the lessons: Met in adult life seen by a child (a parent or grandparent having chemo), health lessons and kind talk; usually shortened to «chemo».
examples from the lessons: Grandma is having chemotherapy for her cancer. | Chemotherapy made Mr Hall very tired. | His hair grew back after chemo. | The nurse explained how chemotherapy works. | Our class made cards for a teacher during her chemo. | Some people have chemotherapy in hospital, some at a clinic.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Informal: chemo. Hair loss is not catching, and you cannot catch cancer from someone. It often helps people get better, but not always.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (church) A churchwarden is a volunteer in a parish (especially Church of England and Anglican churches) who helps look after the church building, its money and services. 2) (old) A long clay pipe for smoking.
its sense in the lessons: Used in church life: the churchwarden welcomes people, counts the collection, helps the vicar; in village stories.
examples from the lessons: The churchwarden unlocked the church for the choir. | Mrs Patel is a churchwarden at St Mary's. | The churchwardens counted the collection after the service. | Each parish chooses two churchwardens. | The churchwarden helped fix the leaking roof. | Our churchwarden rings the bell on Sunday mornings.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word. Not a priest: a lay (non-clergy) helper. Also written «church warden» sometimes.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To cite something is to mention it as an example or reason. 2) To cite a book or website is to name it as where you got your information or to quote from it. 3) (law) To cite someone is to name them officially in a court case.
its sense in the lessons: In school projects: cite your sources; in debates: cite evidence; in news and law.
examples from the lessons: Remember to cite the websites you used. | She cited three reasons for wanting a dog. | The judge cited an earlier case. | The report cites a study about sleep. | Can you cite an example from the text? | He was cited for bravery.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Homophones: cite, sight (seeing), site (a place, a website). Noun: citation.

part of speech: noun (a cock, cocks); verb (cock, cocks, cocked, cocking)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A cock is an adult male chicken (a rooster); also the male of some other birds. 2) To cock your head or ear is to tilt it or lift it, often to listen. 3) To cock a gun is to get it ready to fire. 4) (rude) A slang word for a man's private part; also a rude insult. 5) (UK, informal, old) A friendly word: «All right, cock?»
its sense in the lessons: In farm stories and fables (the cock crowed at dawn), the Bible (the cock crowed when Peter denied Jesus), dog behaviour (cocked its head); the rude sense is heard in rough talk and should not be used at school.
examples from the lessons: The cock crowed at sunrise. | The dog cocked its head when I whistled. | Before the cock crows, Peter will deny Jesus, the Bible says. | The hens and the cock live in the back garden. | He cocked an ear to listen at the door. | (rude) The older boys called him a cock, and the teacher stepped in.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Many people prefer «rooster» (US) or «cockerel» (UK, a young cock) to avoid the rude sense. Words like cockpit, cockroach, cocktail, peacock are fine. Phrase «cock-a-doodle-doo» is the rooster's sound.

part of speech: verb form (commute, commutes, commuted, commuting); noun (commuting, uncountable)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Commuting is travelling the same way regularly between home and work or school. 2) (law) Commuting a punishment is making it less severe. 3) (maths) Operations that commute give the same answer in either order.
its sense in the lessons: Adult life (Dad's commuting by train), maths (adding commutes: 3 + 5 = 5 + 3), news about traffic and rush hour.
examples from the lessons: Mum spends an hour commuting each day. | Commuting by bike keeps Dad fit. | The trains are full of people commuting to the city. | Commuting is tiring when the roads are busy. | Addition and multiplication are commuting operations. | He is commuting from the country to London.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Person: commuter. In maths the commutative law: a + b = b + a and a × b = b × a, but subtraction and division do not commute (5 − 3 is not 3 − 5). In journey problems: a commute counts twice a day, there and back.

part of speech: verb form (compensate, compensates, compensated, compensating); adjective (compensated)
meaning for a pupil: 1) If you are compensated, you are given money or something else to make up for a loss, harm or work. 2) If one thing compensated for another, it balanced or made up for it.
its sense in the lessons: Adult life (workers compensated for extra hours, families compensated after a flood), law and fairness, science (the body compensated for the cold).
examples from the lessons: The family was compensated for the damage to their house. | Passengers were compensated for the late train. | His speed compensated for his size. | Workers are compensated for overtime. | She was not compensated for her help. | The good ending compensated for the slow start.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pattern: be compensated for something. Noun: compensation. In money problems: the compensation is the amount paid to make up the loss.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Competence is the ability to do something well enough or properly. 2) (formal) A skill someone has: core competences.
its sense in the lessons: Used in reports, jobs and school assessment (competence in reading), law (competence to make decisions) and safety (only competent people use the machines).
examples from the lessons: She showed great competence on the football pitch. | Swimming competence is checked before the trip. | The pilot's competence kept everyone safe. | Reading competence improves with practice. | The court questioned his competence to manage money. | Her competence with computers helped the whole class.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: incompetence. Adjective: competent. Do not confuse with «competition». Also spelled «competency» (plural competencies).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Competent means able to do something well enough or properly. 2) (law) Allowed or able by law to decide or act.
its sense in the lessons: In school reports (a competent reader), jobs (a competent driver), safety and law.
examples from the lessons: She is a competent swimmer now. | We need a competent adult to supervise. | The doctor was calm and competent. | He's a competent cook but not a great one. | Is he competent to sign the papers? | Only a competent adult should use the chainsaw.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Competent» can sound like «OK, good enough», not «excellent». Opposite: incompetent. Pattern: competent at/in something.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To concur is to agree with someone or with an opinion. 2) (formal) To happen at the same time.
its sense in the lessons: Exam voice and formal writing, judges and committees («the other judges concurred»), science reports.
examples from the lessons: I concur with your answer. | The doctors concurred that he needed rest. | All the judges concurred. | Do you concur with the author's view? | The two events concurred. | (formal) The committee concurred with the head teacher's plan.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; everyday «agree». Double r: concurred, concurring. Noun: concurrence. Adjective: concurrent (happening together).

meaning for a pupil: 1) To contribute is to give money, time or help together with other people. 2) To contribute to something is to help cause it. 3) To contribute an idea is to share it in a discussion.
its sense in the lessons: School (contribute to the class discussion, contribute to the food bank), science (smoking contributes to illness), team work.
examples from the lessons: Everyone contributed a pound for the gift. | Please contribute your ideas. | Litter contributes to pollution. | She contributed three goals to the win. | Lack of sleep contributed to his grumpiness. | We all contributed food for the picnic.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stress: con-TRIB-ute. Noun: contribution. In maths problems: «each child contributes 2 dollars» means add or multiply: total = number of children × 2.

part of speech: noun (counsel, uncountable; counsel = lawyer); verb (counsel, counsels, counselled/counseled, counselling/counseling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Counsel is advice. 2) To counsel someone is to give them advice, especially about a problem or feelings. 3) (law) Counsel is a lawyer who speaks for someone in court.
its sense in the lessons: Used about school counsellors, help after sad events, law (counsel for the defence) and the Bible (wise counsel).
examples from the lessons: She gave me wise counsel. | A teacher counselled him after his dog died. | Counsel for the defence stood up. | The Bible praises those who listen to good counsel. | Families are counselled through hard times. | Keep your own counsel means keep quiet about it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Homophone: council (a group that runs a town). UK: counselled, counsellor; US: counseled, counselor. Plural for lawyers stays «counsel».

part of speech: noun (a cradle, cradles); verb (cradle, cradles, cradled, cradling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A cradle is a small bed for a baby, often one that can rock. 2) The place where something began: the cradle of civilisation. 3) To cradle something is to hold it gently in your arms. 4) A frame that holds something, like a phone cradle.
its sense in the lessons: Used in lullabies («Rock-a-bye baby… down will come baby, cradle and all»), history (cradle of civilisation), and stories and care: «from the cradle to the grave».
examples from the lessons: The baby slept in a wooden cradle. | She cradled the kitten in her arms. | Mesopotamia is called the cradle of civilisation. | Rock the cradle gently. | He cradled his sore arm. | Put the phone back in its cradle.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. «From the cradle to the grave» = all your life. Similar: crib, cot (UK).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A criterion is a rule or standard used to judge or decide something. 2) Success criteria are the steps a teacher says show you did the task well.
its sense in the lessons: In school (success criteria), science (criteria for an experiment), competitions and jobs.
examples from the lessons: The main criterion was neat handwriting. | Read the success criteria before you start. | What criteria will the judges use? | Price was one criterion for choosing a bike. | The essay met all the criteria. | Kindness is one criterion for the class award.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural is criteria; «a criteria» is a common mistake. From Greek, like phenomenon/phenomena.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Criticism is saying what is wrong or bad about someone or something. 2) A criticism is one point about what is wrong. 3) (formal) Judging books, art or music: literary criticism.
its sense in the lessons: In school (constructive criticism helps you improve), in news (the plan faced criticism), in books and film reviews.
examples from the lessons: She took the criticism well. | Constructive criticism helps you learn. | The new rule got a lot of criticism. | My only criticism is that the story was too short. | Teachers give criticism kindly. | The film received good and bad criticism.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: critic + ism. Verb: criticise (UK) / criticize (US). Criticism is not always nasty: «constructive criticism» means helpful advice.

part of speech: noun (a crow, crows); verb (crow, crows, crowed (or crew, old), crowing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A crow is a large black bird with a loud harsh call. 2) To crow (of a rooster) is to make its loud morning cry. 3) To crow is to boast happily about winning. 4) «As the crow flies» means in a straight line.
its sense in the lessons: In nature and science (crows are clever birds), fables (The Crow and the Pitcher), farm stories, maths distance («as the crow flies»).
examples from the lessons: A crow sat on the fence cawing. | The rooster crowed at dawn. | Stop crowing about your score. | Crows can use sticks as tools. | The town is ten miles away as the crow flies. | In the fable, the crow dropped stones into the jug.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Crow's feet = small lines near the eyes. «Crow over» = boast. In maths, «as the crow flies» is the straight-line distance, shorter than by road.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To dawdle is to walk or do something too slowly, wasting time.
its sense in the lessons: Common in parents' and teachers' talk («Don't dawdle!»), school mornings, stories.
examples from the lessons: Don't dawdle, we'll miss the bus! | He dawdled on his way to school. | Stop dawdling and finish your breakfast. | She dawdled behind, looking at shop windows. | The tortoise didn't dawdle; it kept going. | If you dawdle in the shop, the ice cream will melt.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal. Person: dawdler. Similar: dilly-dally, loiter.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (church) A deacon is a church minister below a priest, or in many Protestant churches a member chosen to help with services, care and practical work. 2) (Bible) In the Bible, the first deacons were chosen to help share food fairly.
its sense in the lessons: Church life and religion lessons: the deacon reads the Gospel, helps at communion, visits the sick.
examples from the lessons: The deacon read the Gospel at mass. | Mr Jones is a deacon at our chapel. | Deacons visit people who are ill. | Stephen was one of the first deacons, the Bible says. | She was ordained as a deacon. | The deacon helped give out communion.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Order in some churches: deacon, priest, bishop. A female deacon is sometimes called a deaconess.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Deceit is making someone believe something that is not true, to trick them. 2) A deceit is a trick or lie.
its sense in the lessons: In ethics lessons, fairy tales (the wolf's deceit), Bible stories (Jacob's deceit), and friendship talk about honesty.
examples from the lessons: The wolf's deceit fooled Little Red Riding Hood. | Friendships can't last with deceit. | His deceit was discovered. | Jacob won his father's blessing by deceit, the Bible tells. | She hated lies and deceit. | Honesty is the opposite of deceit.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: «ei» after c: deceit, deceive. Adjective: deceitful. Verb: deceive.

part of speech: verb form (decree, decrees, decreed, decreeing); noun decree
meaning for a pupil: 1) If a ruler or government decreed something, they gave an official order. 2) (Bible, old) Something decreed is fixed and must happen.
its sense in the lessons: History and Bible stories («Caesar Augustus decreed that all the world should be counted»), fairy tales, law.
examples from the lessons: The king decreed a holiday for all. | Caesar Augustus decreed that everyone must be counted. | The council decreed that dogs must be on leads. | It was decreed that no one could leave. | The queen decreed a feast. | The emperor decreed that the bridge be built.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past of decree: decreed (three e's in a row). Noun: a decree. Formal and old-fashioned.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A deity is a god or goddess.
its sense in the lessons: In religion and history lessons (Greek, Roman, Egyptian, Hindu deities), myths and stories.
examples from the lessons: Zeus was the chief deity of the Greeks. | The Egyptians had many deities. | Ganesh is a Hindu deity with an elephant head. | The temple was built for a sea deity. | Christians believe there is one God, not many deities. | Thor was a Norse deity of thunder.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced DAY-i-ty or DEE-i-ty. Plural: deities. Respect: say «Hindus worship…» not «fake gods».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Deliberation is careful and long thinking or talking about something before deciding. 2) Doing something with deliberation means slowly and carefully, on purpose. 3) (law) The jury's deliberations are their discussions before the verdict.
its sense in the lessons: In law (jury deliberation), school councils, ethics dilemmas, stories.
examples from the lessons: After much deliberation, we chose the blue one. | The jury began its deliberations. | He placed the last brick with great deliberation. | The class council's deliberation took an hour. | She chose her words with deliberation. | The judges' deliberation over the cake contest was long.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: deliberate (de-LIB-er-ate). Adjective deliberate (on purpose). Often plural in law.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To demote someone is to move them to a lower rank, job or level. 2) In sport, to move a team down a league (UK: relegate).
its sense in the lessons: Adult life (being demoted at work), sport, games and computer rankings.
examples from the lessons: He was demoted from captain to player. | The manager demoted her after the mistake. | Pluto was demoted to a dwarf planet. | Losing three games could demote us. | The officer was demoted for bad behaviour. | The coach threatened to demote anyone who skipped practice.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: promote. Noun: demotion. Pluto example: scientists reclassified it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A denial is saying that something is not true. 2) Denial is refusing to give something, or saying no: denial of rights. 3) Being «in denial» means not accepting a painful truth. 4) (Bible) Peter's denial is when he said he did not know Jesus.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and news (he issued a denial), feelings (in denial about grief), ethics (denial of rights), the Easter story.
examples from the lessons: The minister made a firm denial. | Despite his denial, the crumbs were on his face. | She was in denial about losing the race. | Denial of food is cruel. | Peter's denial happened before the cock crowed. | Denial is one stage of grief.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: deny (denied). Self-denial = giving up things you want.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To deprive someone of something is to take it away or not let them have it.
its sense in the lessons: In science (plants deprived of light), ethics (depriving people of rights), health (sleep-deprived), punishment talk.
examples from the lessons: Plants deprived of light turn yellow. | You'll be deprived of screen time if you lie. | Many children are deprived of education. | Sleep-deprived drivers are dangerous. | The war deprived them of their homes. | Being sent to bed early deprived him of the film.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pattern: deprive someone of something. Adjective: deprived (poor, lacking basics). Noun: deprivation.

part of speech: verb form (dip, dips, dipped, dipping); adjective (dipped)
meaning for a pupil: 1) If you dipped something, you put it into a liquid and took it out quickly. 2) If something dipped, it went down a little: the temperature dipped. 3) Dipped headlights are car lights angled down.
its sense in the lessons: Cooking (biscuits dipped in milk), science (temperature dipped), maths graphs (the line dipped), art (brush dipped in paint).
examples from the lessons: She dipped her biscuit in her tea. | The temperature dipped below zero. | He dipped his toe in the pool. | The sun dipped behind the hills. | I dipped my brush in the blue paint. | Sales dipped in winter.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double p in dipped, dipping. In graphs and maths «dipped» means decreased a bit, then may go up.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A disadvantage is something that makes things harder or less good. 2) To be at a disadvantage is to have less chance than others. 3) To disadvantage someone is to put them in a worse position.
its sense in the lessons: In writing (advantages and disadvantages), sport, fairness and society (disadvantaged children).
examples from the lessons: One disadvantage of a dog is the cost. | Being short is a disadvantage in basketball. | We were at a disadvantage without our goalie. | List the advantages and disadvantages. | Some families are disadvantaged by poverty. | Playing away from home can be a disadvantage.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: advantage. Adjective: disadvantaged.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Discretion is being careful not to tell secrets or upset people. 2) Discretion is the freedom to decide what to do: at the teacher's discretion. 3) (formal) Viewer discretion means take care, some things may upset you.
its sense in the lessons: School rules (at the head's discretion), adult life, TV warnings («viewer discretion advised»).
examples from the lessons: Please use discretion with this secret. | Homework extensions are at the teacher's discretion. | The nurse acted with discretion. | Viewer discretion is advised. | Leave the tip to your discretion. | The doctor treated the family's news with discretion.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: discreet (careful, not discrete = separate). Spelling: dis-CRE-tion.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Disloyal means not loyal: not supporting or being faithful to your friends, family, team or country.
its sense in the lessons: Ethics and friendship stories, history (disloyal knights), sport.
examples from the lessons: It was disloyal to tell her secret. | The disloyal soldier joined the enemy. | Don't be disloyal to your team. | He felt disloyal for cheering the other side. | A disloyal friend is not a true friend. | Gossiping about your friends is disloyal.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: disloyalty. Opposite: loyal.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To disobey is to not do what a person, rule or law tells you to do.
its sense in the lessons: Home and school rules, fairy tales and Bible stories (Adam and Eve disobeyed God, the Bible says), safety.
examples from the lessons: The dog disobeyed and ran into the road. | Don't disobey the lifeguard. | Adam and Eve disobeyed God, Genesis tells. | She was punished for disobeying. | It is dangerous to disobey safety signs. | The puppy disobeyed every command.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: disobedience; adjective: disobedient. Past: disobeyed (keep y).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Disruption is something that stops a thing from going on normally. 2) A disruption is one such interruption.
its sense in the lessons: School behaviour (disruption in class), travel (disruption to trains), weather and news.
examples from the lessons: The snow caused disruption to the buses. | Talking caused disruption in the lesson. | There may be disruption on the trains. | The fire alarm was a big disruption. | We apologise for the disruption. | Road works mean disruption for drivers this week.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: disrupt; adjective: disruptive.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A divider is something that separates a space or things into parts: a room divider. 2) A file divider separates sections in a folder. 3) Dividers are a maths tool like compasses with two points, for measuring distances on maps.
its sense in the lessons: School folders, maths tools (dividers on maps), homes and offices.
examples from the lessons: Put a divider between maths and English notes. | A screen divider split the classroom. | Use dividers to measure the map distance. | The road had a concrete divider. | Each section had a coloured divider. | Dad put up a divider so the twins had their own space.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Do not confuse with divisor (the number you divide by in maths).

part of speech: noun (a dope, dopes; dope, uncountable); verb (dope, dopes, doped, doping); adjective (dope — slang)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) A dope is a silly or foolish person. 2) (slang) Dope is an illegal drug, especially cannabis. 3) Doping is giving drugs to an athlete or animal to cheat in sport or to make someone sleepy. 4) (slang, US) Dope means great or cool. 5) (informal) The dope on something is the inside information about it.
its sense in the lessons: Heard in teasing among friends, in sport news (doping scandals, drug tests), in safety lessons about drugs, and in slang; tells the reader someone is being silly, cheating or using drugs.
examples from the lessons: Don't be such a dope, the door says «pull»! | Athletes are tested to stop doping. | The cyclist was banned for doping. | The police found dope in the car. | (slang) Those trainers are dope! | Give me the dope on the new teacher. | The racehorse had been doped, so it was disqualified.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mild insult but still unkind. «Dopey» = sleepy or silly (one of the seven dwarfs). Doping in sport is cheating and is banned; illegal drugs are dangerous and against the law.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To encompass something is to include it or cover all of it. 2) (formal) To encompass a place is to surround it completely.
its sense in the lessons: Exam and formal voice (the topic encompasses history and geography), science (a habitat encompassing forests and lakes), descriptions in stories (darkness encompassed them).
examples from the lessons: The project encompasses maths, art and science. | The national park encompasses mountains and lakes. | Her job encompasses teaching and coaching. | Thick fog encompassed the village. | The school's rules encompass behaviour online too. | The word «pet» encompasses dogs, cats and fish.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; everyday words: include, cover, surround. Spelling: en + compass; third person encompasses (double s + es).

meaning for a pupil: 1) To endure is to bear or suffer something hard or painful without giving up. 2) To endure is to last for a long time.
its sense in the lessons: Stories of courage and hardship, science (materials that endure), history, faith (the Bible speaks of love that endures).
examples from the lessons: The explorers endured terrible cold. | She endured the pain bravely. | Their friendship endured for life. | Love endures all things, the Bible says. | I couldn't endure another boring film. | Pyramids have endured for thousands of years.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: endurance. Adjective: enduring (lasting).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Enjoyment is the feeling of pleasure you get when you like doing something.
its sense in the lessons: Reading for enjoyment, sport, holidays, writing about feelings.
examples from the lessons: I read for enjoyment. | The children shouted with enjoyment. | Rain didn't spoil our enjoyment. | Music brings her great enjoyment. | Fishing gives Grandpa a lot of enjoyment. | The puppy's enjoyment of the snow was clear to see.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Verb: enjoy.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To enslave people is to make them slaves: owned by others and forced to work without pay or freedom. 2) To enslave someone is to control them so completely that they are not free, like a habit.
its sense in the lessons: History lessons (enslaved Africans, the slave trade, abolition), ethics (slavery is deeply wrong), Bible (the Israelites enslaved in Egypt), and everyday talk about habits.
examples from the lessons: The Israelites were enslaved in Egypt, the Bible tells. | Millions of Africans were enslaved and taken across the Atlantic. | Harriet Tubman helped enslaved people escape to freedom. | It is wrong to enslave anyone. | Don't let video games enslave you. | Enslaved workers had no wages and no rights.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Historians often say «enslaved people» rather than «slaves» to show they were people first. Noun: enslavement; opposite: free, liberate, emancipate.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To entitle someone to something is to give them the right to have or do it. 2) To entitle a book, film or poem is to give it a title. 3) (adjective entitled) Someone who acts entitled thinks they deserve special treatment.
its sense in the lessons: Rights and fairness (every child is entitled to education), money and shopping (entitled to a refund), books and art (a poem entitled…), behaviour talk (an entitled attitude).
examples from the lessons: This ticket entitles you to one free drink. | Every child is entitled to go to school. | You are entitled to a refund if it's broken. | Her poem is entitled «The Sea». | Being captain doesn't entitle you to boss others around. | He acts so entitled, expecting everyone to wait for him.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pattern: entitle someone to something / be entitled to something. Noun: entitlement. Both «titled» and «entitled» are fine for names of books.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Ethically means in a way that is right and fair. 2) From a moral point of view.
its sense in the lessons: Ethics lessons, shopping (ethically sourced), science (ethically tested).
examples from the lessons: The coffee is ethically sourced. | We must behave ethically. | Ethically, it was the right choice. | They acted ethically. | Is it ethically right to test on animals? | The scientists treated the animals ethically.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: ethical. Opposite: unethically.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Evolution is how living things change over a very long time, from one generation to the next. 2) The slow change and development of anything: the evolution of phones.
its sense in the lessons: Science lessons (evolution of animals, Darwin), technology, history.
examples from the lessons: Darwin studied the evolution of finches. | Evolution explains how whales came from land animals. | The evolution of cars has been fast. | Fossils show evolution over time. | Many Christians believe God works through evolution. | The theory of evolution was put forward by Charles Darwin.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: evolve. Not the same as one animal changing in its life.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (law) An executor is the person named in a will to carry out what it says after the person who made it has died: sharing out money and things. 2) (formal) A person who carries out a plan or task.
its sense in the lessons: Adult life as a child sees it (a relative sorting out Grandpa's things after he passed away), law and money lessons (wills, inheritance).
examples from the lessons: Aunt Jane is the executor of Grandpa's will. | The executor shared out the money as the will said. | Mum was chosen as executor because she is careful. | The executor sold the house and paid the bills. | You should pick an executor you trust. | The executor read the will to the family.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced ig-ZEK-yu-tor. It comes from «execute» in its sense «carry out», not the sense «kill». Related: will, inheritance, heir.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An exemption is official permission not to do something that others must do. 2) (money) A tax exemption means you do not have to pay a certain tax.
its sense in the lessons: School (exemption from PE with a note, exemption from a uniform rule for religious reasons), money and law (tax exemptions), formal notices.
examples from the lessons: Tom has an exemption from PE because of his broken arm. | Charities get an exemption from some taxes. | There is no exemption from the safety rules. | She asked the head for an exemption from the uniform rule. | The exemption lasts until his leg heals. | Exemptions are given only with a parent's letter.
