note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: exempt (exempt from something). Spelling: ex-EMP-tion, with a p.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Expense is the amount of money something costs. 2) An expense is something you have to pay for. 3) Expenses are money a worker spends for the job and is paid back for. 4) At someone's expense means they paid for it, or that a joke made them look silly.
its sense in the lessons: Money lessons and adult life (household expenses, travel expenses), maths (income minus expenses), stories and jokes (laughing at someone's expense).
examples from the lessons: The new roof was a huge expense. | Food is the family's biggest expense. | Mum's work pays her travel expenses. | They laughed at my expense. | The trip was paid for at the school's expense. | Spare no expense for the party! | Keep a list of your weekly expenses.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: expensive. Do not confuse with «expanse» (a wide area). In maths: money left = income − expenses.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Expressly means clearly and directly, so there is no doubt. 2) (formal) Expressly means specially, for one particular purpose.
its sense in the lessons: Formal rules and signs (expressly forbidden), law, and in stories when a parent clearly told a child something.
examples from the lessons: Smoking is expressly forbidden on school grounds. | I expressly told you not to touch the cake! | The room was built expressly for music lessons. | The rules expressly say no phones in exams. | This book was written expressly for children. | The sign expressly warns against swimming.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal. Everyday: clearly, specially. Related: express (to say clearly).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A fad is something, like a toy, game, fashion or food, that becomes very popular suddenly and is then quickly forgotten. 2) A fad diet is a popular way of eating that promises quick results but is often not healthy.
its sense in the lessons: Playground crazes (loom bands, fidget spinners), fashion, health lessons (fad diets), adults' talk («it's just a fad»).
examples from the lessons: Fidget spinners were a big fad. | Mum says my slime collection is just a fad. | Every term there is a new playground fad. | Fad diets promise too much. | The dance was a fad that lasted one summer. | Is this game a fad or here to stay?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Similar: craze, trend. A fad is short; a trend can last longer.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (UK, slang) A fag is a cigarette. 2) (UK, informal) A fag is a boring or tiring job: what a fag! 3) (UK, old) At some old boarding schools, a fag was a younger boy who did jobs for an older one. 4) (offensive) A hateful slur against gay men, mostly American; never use it.
its sense in the lessons: Heard in UK rough talk (going out for a fag), health lessons about smoking, old school stories; the slur appears in bullying, which schools stop.
examples from the lessons: (UK slang) Uncle Mick went outside for a fag. | There were fag ends all over the pavement. | (UK) Washing up after a party is such a fag. | Smoking fags damages your lungs. | In the old story, the young boy had to be a fag for the prefects. | Calling someone a hateful name is bullying; tell a teacher.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The cigarette sense is British slang; in the USA the word is mainly the slur, so avoid it. «Fag end» = cigarette end, or the last bit of something. Related: fagged out (UK, very tired).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Fidelity is being faithful and loyal to a person, a promise or a belief, especially to a husband or wife. 2) Fidelity is how exactly something copies or follows the original: high-fidelity sound, fidelity to the book.
its sense in the lessons: Used in church weddings and ethics (promises of fidelity), stories of loyal dogs and knights, and about music and films (hi-fi, a film's fidelity to the novel).
examples from the lessons: The couple promised fidelity to each other at their wedding. | The dog's fidelity to its master was famous. | Christians believe God shows fidelity to his people. | The film shows great fidelity to the book. | Hi-fi is short for high fidelity. | Fidelity to your word matters to a good friend.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Opposite: infidelity (unfaithfulness, often in marriage). Related: faithful. The dog name «Fido» comes from the same Latin root (faithful).

part of speech: adjective (forbidding; more forbidding); verb form (forbid, forbids, forbade, forbidden, forbidding)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Forbidding means looking unfriendly, frightening or dangerous: a forbidding castle. 2) Forbidding is the -ing form of forbid: telling someone they must not do something.
its sense in the lessons: In stories to set a scary mood (forbidding mountains, a forbidding look), in rules and signs (a sign forbidding swimming), in Bible stories (God forbidding the fruit).
examples from the lessons: The castle looked dark and forbidding. | The head teacher gave us a forbidding stare. | There is a sign forbidding dogs on the beach. | The forbidding cliffs rose above the sea. | Mum is forbidding sweets before dinner. | The forest seemed forbidding at night.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Two different uses: adjective (unfriendly-looking) and verb form (not allowing). Forms of forbid: forbid, forbade (say «for-BAD»), forbidden.

part of speech: noun (a formulation, formulations; uncountable for the process)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A formulation is the way an idea, rule or question is put into words. 2) Formulation is the making or planning of something, like a plan or rule. 3) A formulation is a mixture with a fixed recipe, like a medicine or cream.
its sense in the lessons: Exam and science voice (the formulation of a hypothesis), maths (a different formulation of the same problem), medicine labels (a new formulation).
examples from the lessons: The formulation of the question confused the class. | The scientist worked on the formulation of a new theory. | This cough syrup is a children's formulation. | Try a different formulation of the problem. | The formulation of the school rules took weeks. | A clear formulation makes a problem easier to solve.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal. Verb: formulate. In maths, restating a word problem (a new formulation) can make the sum clearer without changing the numbers.

part of speech: noun (a frazzle); verb (frazzle, frazzles, frazzled, frazzling); adjective (frazzled)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) To be worn to a frazzle is to be completely tired out. 2) (informal) Burnt to a frazzle means burnt until black and crisp. 3) To frazzle someone is to make them tired, nervous and stressed.
its sense in the lessons: Everyday family talk (Mum is frazzled after a long day), cooking jokes (the toast is burnt to a frazzle), stories about busy days.
examples from the lessons: By Friday the teacher was worn to a frazzle. | Dad burnt the sausages to a frazzle. | The noisy party frazzled Grandma. | She looked frazzled after moving house. | Exams can frazzle your nerves. | The twins wore their babysitter to a frazzle.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal. Most common as the adjective «frazzled» (tired and stressed). Similar: exhausted, worn out.

part of speech: noun (a gathering, gatherings); verb form (gather, gathers, gathered, gathering)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A gathering is a group of people who meet together, often for a special reason. 2) Gathering is collecting things together, like food or information. 3) (formal, rare) A gathered fold in cloth.
its sense in the lessons: Family gatherings, church gatherings, history (hunter-gatherers), science (gathering data), weather (gathering clouds = a storm is coming).
examples from the lessons: We have a big family gathering at Christmas. | The church held a gathering after the service. | Early people lived by hunting and gathering. | We are gathering data for our science project. | Storm clouds were gathering. | The gathering sang together around the fire.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Gathering» is countable as a meeting (a gathering, gatherings). In safety: «gathering point» is where you meet in a fire drill.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (church) A godfather is a man who promises at a child's baptism or christening to help bring the child up in the Christian faith and care for them. 2) The founder or most important early person of something: the godfather of rock. 3) (informal) The boss of a criminal gang, from the film «The Godfather».
its sense in the lessons: Church life (baptism, christening), family (Uncle Tom is my godfather), music and history (godfather of something), crime films.
examples from the lessons: My godfather gave me a Bible when I was baptised. | Uncle Joe is my godfather and sends me birthday cards. | At the christening, the godfather held the baby. | He is called the godfather of punk music. | In the film, the godfather ran the gang. | Godparents promise to pray for the child.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Godfather and godmother together are godparents; the child is a godson or goddaughter. The gang-boss sense comes from films and is informal.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (church) A godmother is a woman who promises at a child's baptism or christening to help bring the child up in the Christian faith and care for them. 2) A fairy godmother is a magic helper in fairy tales, like in «Cinderella», or anyone who helps you unexpectedly.
its sense in the lessons: Church life (baptism), family, fairy tales (Cinderella's fairy godmother), everyday jokes («I need a fairy godmother»).
examples from the lessons: My godmother came to my first communion. | Aunt Sophie is my godmother. | Cinderella's fairy godmother turned a pumpkin into a coach. | The godmother promised to help the child grow in faith. | She was like a fairy godmother to the charity. | I have two godmothers and one godfather.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: godmothers. Godparents = godmothers and godfathers. A godmother does not have to be a relative.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To govern is to rule a country, state or group officially. 2) To govern something is to control or decide how it happens: rules govern the game. 3) (formal) To control your feelings: govern your temper.
its sense in the lessons: Citizenship and history lessons (who governs the country), science (laws that govern motion), games and sport (rules that govern play).
examples from the lessons: The prime minister and parliament govern the country. | Rules govern how the game is played. | Gravity governs how planets move. | Try to govern your temper. | The queen governed for many years. | A council governs our town.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Nouns: government, governor. In grammar, «govern» is also used for words that control another word's form (advanced).

part of speech: verb form (govern, governs, governed, governing); adjective (governed)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Governed is the past of govern: ruled or controlled. 2) The governed are the people who are ruled.
its sense in the lessons: Citizenship and history (a country governed by a king), science (motion governed by laws), rules of games.
examples from the lessons: The island was governed by Britain. | The game is governed by strict rules. | The planets' paths are governed by gravity. | Democracy needs the consent of the governed. | The school is governed by a board. | He governed his temper well.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past and past participle: governed. «The governed» (noun) = the people ruled.

part of speech: adjective (grave, graver, gravest); noun (a graver — tool)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Graver means more serious or more worrying: a graver danger. 2) A graver is a sharp tool for cutting lines into metal, wood or stone (an engraving tool).
its sense in the lessons: Formal writing and news (a graver problem), doctors' talk, art and craft (engraving).
examples from the lessons: The flood was a graver danger than the wind. | The doctor's face grew graver. | Nothing could be graver than lying under oath. | The artist cut the lines with a graver. | The situation is graver than we thought. | Lying would only make things graver.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative of grave (serious): grave, graver, gravest. Not related in meaning to a «grave» for burial (same spelling, different word).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Greece is a country in south-east Europe, by the Mediterranean Sea, with many islands; its capital is Athens. 2) Ancient Greece was the world of the ancient Greeks, famous for the Olympics, myths, democracy and great thinkers.
its sense in the lessons: History lessons (Ancient Greece, the Olympics, gods and myths), geography (islands, the Mediterranean), food and holidays.
examples from the lessons: We are learning about Ancient Greece this term. | The first Olympic Games were held in Greece. | Greece has thousands of islands. | Athens is the capital of Greece. | My cousins went on holiday to Greece. | The myths of Greece tell of Zeus and Athena.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always with a capital G. Adjective and people: Greek, the Greeks. Language: Greek. Do not confuse with «grease» (fat, oil), which sounds the same.

part of speech: noun (a gymnasium, gymnasiums or gymnasia; short: gym)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A gymnasium is a large room or building with equipment for sport and exercise. 2) In some countries (Germany, Ukraine, the Netherlands) a gymnasium is a kind of secondary school. 3) In ancient Greece, a place where young men trained and studied.
its sense in the lessons: School (PE in the gymnasium, assemblies), sport, history (Greek gymnasium), other countries' schools.
examples from the lessons: PE is in the gymnasium today. | The school gymnasium has ropes and climbing bars. | Assembly was held in the gymnasium. | In Germany, my cousin goes to a gymnasium. | Greek athletes trained in the gymnasium. | The gymnasium smelled of floor polish.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually shortened to «gym». Plural: gymnasiums or gymnasia. The school sense is a false friend for English learners.

part of speech: noun (Hebrews — proper noun; Hebrew, the Hebrews)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (Bible) The Hebrews were the ancient people of Israel, the people of Abraham, Isaac, Jacob and Moses. 2) (Bible) Hebrews is the name of a letter (epistle) in the New Testament of the Bible. 3) Hebrew is also the language of the Jewish people and of modern Israel.
its sense in the lessons: Religion lessons (the Hebrews in Egypt, the Exodus), church readings («a reading from the Letter to the Hebrews»), history and languages.
examples from the lessons: The Hebrews were slaves in Egypt, the Bible tells. | Moses led the Hebrews out of Egypt. | Today's reading is from Hebrews. | The Letter to the Hebrews talks about faith. | Much of the Old Testament was first written in Hebrew. | The Hebrews crossed the Red Sea, the story says.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital H. The book name «Hebrews» takes a singular verb («Hebrews says…»). Related: Hebrew (language), Jewish, Israelite.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A homeland is the country where you or your family were born or come from. 2) A homeland is the land a people or nation see as their own.
its sense in the lessons: Geography and history (refugees far from their homeland), stories about migration, news.
examples from the lessons: She missed her homeland after moving to Canada. | Many refugees hope to return to their homeland. | Ireland is the homeland of my grandparents. | The poem is about love for one's homeland. | The tribe returned to their homeland. | Our class mapped each family's homeland.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Similar: home country, motherland, fatherland. It carries strong feelings of belonging.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An impediment is something that gets in the way or makes progress hard. 2) A speech impediment is a difficulty in speaking, like a stammer or a lisp. 3) (church, law) An impediment to marriage is a legal reason two people cannot marry.
its sense in the lessons: Formal writing (an impediment to learning), health (speech impediment, said kindly), church weddings («if anyone knows of any impediment…»).
examples from the lessons: Lack of money was an impediment to the plan. | He has a slight speech impediment. | Speech therapy helped her impediment. | The priest asked if anyone knew of an impediment to the marriage. | Fallen trees were an impediment to the rescue. | Shyness need not be an impediment.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal. Verb: impede (to slow down or block). Be kind: a speech impediment is not a sign of low intelligence.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Incomplete means not finished or with some parts missing.
its sense in the lessons: School (incomplete homework, incomplete sentences), maths (incomplete tables, missing numbers), science (incomplete data).
examples from the lessons: Your homework is incomplete. | This puzzle is incomplete; three pieces are missing. | «Ran to the» is an incomplete sentence. | Fill in the incomplete table. | The data was incomplete, so we repeated the test. | The house was still incomplete when they moved in.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: complete. Noun: incompleteness. In maths an incomplete pattern or table asks you to find the missing values.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To inherit money, a house or things is to receive them from someone after they die. 2) To inherit a feature is to get it from your parents through your genes: inherit blue eyes. 3) To inherit a problem or job is to take it over from someone before you.
its sense in the lessons: Science (inherited characteristics, genes), adult life and law (wills, inheritance), stories (the youngest son inherited a cat), Bible («the meek shall inherit the earth»).
examples from the lessons: She inherited her grandmother's ring. | I inherited my dad's curly hair. | Children inherit genes from both parents. | In the story, the miller's son inherited only a cat. | The new coach inherited a losing team. | Blessed are the meek, for they shall inherit the earth.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: inheritance; person: heir. In science: inherited features (eye colour) come from parents; learned skills (riding a bike) are not inherited.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An inheritance is money, property or things you receive from someone who has died. 2) Inheritance is the passing of features from parents to children through genes. 3) Something passed down from the past: our cultural inheritance.
its sense in the lessons: Science (genetic inheritance), money and law (a will, inheritance tax), stories and Bible (the prodigal son asked for his inheritance).
examples from the lessons: He spent his inheritance on a farm. | The prodigal son asked for his inheritance early. | Inheritance explains why you look like your parents. | The house was her inheritance from her uncle. | Folk songs are part of our inheritance. | The family argued over the inheritance.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable or uncountable. Related: heir, heritage, inherit. In money problems, an inheritance shared equally is divided by the number of heirs.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An instalment is one of several parts of a payment, paid at different times. 2) An instalment is one part of a story or series that comes out bit by bit.
its sense in the lessons: Money and adult life (pay for a car in instalments), maths problems (equal instalments), books, TV and comics (the next instalment).
examples from the lessons: They paid for the sofa in ten instalments. | The next instalment of the comic comes out on Friday. | Each instalment is fifty dollars. | The book was first printed in weekly instalments. | We are watching the final instalment tonight. | Grandad paid off the loan in monthly instalments.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK: instalment; US: installment (double l). In maths: total cost = number of instalments × amount of each instalment.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An intrusion is when someone comes into a place or situation where they are not wanted or allowed. 2) Intrusion into someone's private life is not respecting their privacy. 3) (science) An intrusion is rock that pushed into other rock while melted.
its sense in the lessons: Privacy lessons and internet safety (intrusion into private life), stories (an intrusion in the night), news, geology.
examples from the lessons: Sorry for the intrusion, but dinner is ready. | Reading her diary was an intrusion into her privacy. | The alarm sounds if there is an intrusion. | The reporters' intrusion upset the family. | Granite can form an intrusion in older rock. | The noise was an unwelcome intrusion.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: intrude; adjective: intrusive; person: intruder.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Islamophobia is hatred, fear or unfair treatment of Muslims or of Islam.
its sense in the lessons: Ethics and citizenship lessons about prejudice and respect, news, anti-bullying talk.
examples from the lessons: Islamophobia is a kind of prejudice. | The school spoke out against Islamophobia. | Calling a girl names because of her headscarf is Islamophobia. | People of many faiths work together against Islamophobia. | The news reported a rise in Islamophobia. | Respect for all faiths helps stop Islamophobia.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually with a capital I. Similar words for other prejudices: antisemitism (against Jews), racism. Disagreeing with ideas is different from hating people.

part of speech: noun (jade, uncountable; a jade); adjective (jade — colour)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Jade is a hard green stone used to make jewellery and carvings. 2) Jade is also a green colour. 3) (old) A jade was a worn-out horse; jaded means tired and bored. 4) Jade is a girl's name.
its sense in the lessons: Science (rocks and minerals), history and art (Chinese jade carvings), colours, names.
examples from the lessons: Grandma wears a jade bracelet. | The museum has old Chinese jade carvings. | She painted her room jade green. | Jade is a very hard stone. | My friend Jade sits next to me. | The jade statue shone in the light.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable as a stone. Adjective «jaded» (tired of something) comes from the old horse meaning.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Jealously means in a jealous way: feeling upset that someone has what you want. 2) Jealously can also mean very carefully, protecting something: a jealously guarded secret.
its sense in the lessons: Stories about feelings and friendship, family (a sibling looking jealously at a new toy), Bible stories (Cain and Joseph's brothers).
examples from the lessons: He looked jealously at his brother's new bike. | The dragon jealously guarded its gold. | The recipe is a jealously guarded secret. | Joseph's brothers watched him jealously. | She stared jealously at the trophy. | The cat jealously watched the new puppy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: jealous; noun: jealousy. Jealous is often mixed up with envious; envy is wanting what someone else has.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) Jittery means nervous and shaky, often because you are worried or have had too much caffeine.
its sense in the lessons: Feelings talk before tests, shows and races; stories; science (caffeine makes people jittery).
examples from the lessons: I felt jittery before my piano exam. | Too much coffee makes Mum jittery. | The horses were jittery during the storm. | The new player was jittery in his first match. | Everyone was jittery waiting for the results. | A deep breath helps when you feel jittery.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal. Noun: the jitters («I've got the jitters»). Similar: nervous, jumpy, on edge.

part of speech: noun (Karen — a name; a karen, karens — slang)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Karen is a girl's or woman's first name. 2) (slang, rude) A karen is a mocking word for a woman who complains loudly, acts as if she has the right to everything and demands to "speak to the manager". 3) (slang) As a verb-like joke, people sometimes say someone is "being a Karen" when they make a big fuss over something small.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and school Karen is usually just a name, like Sarah or Emma. On the internet and in teenage talk, "a Karen" is a label for a rude, demanding adult; it tells the reader the person is entitled and makes trouble for shop workers. Phrases: "being a Karen", "speak to the manager", "full Karen mode".
examples from the lessons: My aunt Karen lives in Dublin and keeps chickens. | Karen won the spelling bee in our class. | (slang) A woman in the café shouted at the waiter and asked for the manager, and my brother whispered, "Total Karen." | (slang) Don't be such a Karen about the cold chips, Mum, they're fine. | (slang) The video showed a karen yelling at a teenager working the till. | Mrs Hill says calling people "Karen" is unkind to everyone who has that name.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a name it starts with a capital letter: Karen. As slang it is often written "a Karen" or "a karen", plural "Karens". The slang sense is rude and unfair to real people called Karen, so many teachers ask pupils not to use it. It is not a polite word for an adult in a formal letter.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A lamppost is a tall post in a street or park with a light at the top that comes on when it gets dark. 2) Lampposts are also used to hold signs, posters and bins.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life lampposts light roads and paths at night and help people see where they are going; in safety lessons children learn to walk where it is well lit. In stories a lamppost may mark a meeting place (as in the Narnia story, where the lamppost stands in a snowy wood). Phrases: "under the lamppost", "lean against a lamppost", "lost dog poster on a lamppost".
examples from the lessons: We met under the lamppost at the corner of our street. | A poster about a lost cat was taped to the lamppost. | The lampposts come on when it gets dark. | In the book, Lucy finds a lamppost glowing in the snowy wood. | Dad bumped into a lamppost while looking at his phone. | The council is replacing old lampposts with bright LED ones. | There are twelve lampposts along the path, one every 20 metres.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one lamppost, two lampposts. Also written "lamp post" or "lamp-post"; all three are correct. It is the same thing as a streetlight or street lamp. In a maths problem about lampposts in a row, remember the gaps: 5 lampposts in a straight line make 4 gaps between them.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A landowner is a person or group that owns land, especially a large area such as a farm, an estate or fields. 2) (law, money) A landowner has the right to decide how the land is used, and may rent it to others.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons landowners were often rich and powerful, and poor people worked their land; in geography, landowners decide whether fields are farmed or built on. In everyday news a landowner may give or refuse permission for a path or a new house. Phrases: "wealthy landowner", "private landowner", "with the landowner's permission".
examples from the lessons: The landowner let us camp in his field for the night. | In the Middle Ages most farmers rented their fields from a landowner. | You need the landowner's permission to fish in this river. | The landowner planted hundreds of trees on her hill. | In the story, a greedy landowner threw the family off the farm. | Australia's biggest landowners run huge cattle stations. | The council talked with three landowners about building the new school.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a landowner, landowners. It is a compound of land + owner. A landowner may be a person, a family, a company or a church. Do not confuse with "landlord", who rents a house or flat to a tenant; a landowner owns the land itself (a landowner can also be a landlord).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Lasagne is an Italian dish made of flat sheets of pasta in layers with meat or vegetable sauce and cheese, baked in an oven. 2) Lasagne is also the name of the wide flat pasta sheets themselves.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life lasagne is a family dinner, a school-dinner favourite and a dish people bring to friends who are ill or have a new baby. In maths it is used for sharing problems (cut a lasagne into equal pieces) and in science for layers. Phrases: "a slice of lasagne", "vegetable lasagne", "layers of lasagne".
examples from the lessons: We had lasagne for tea on Friday. | Mum made a vegetable lasagne with spinach and cheese. | Grandad cut the lasagne into eight equal pieces. | Rock layers are stacked like a lasagne, with the oldest at the bottom. | The lasagne was so hot that the cheese burnt my tongue. | Our neighbours brought round a lasagne when the baby was born. | You need nine lasagne sheets for three layers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: British and Irish English usually spell it "lasagne"; American English often spells it "lasagna". Both are correct. Usually uncountable (some lasagne, a piece of lasagne), but you can say "a lasagne" for one whole dish. In a sharing problem, if a lasagne is cut into 12 equal pieces and you eat 3, you have eaten 3/12 = 1/4 of it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A lectern is a tall stand with a sloping top on which a speaker puts notes or a book while standing up to read or speak. 2) (church) In a church a lectern holds the big Bible, and a reader reads the Bible passages from it.
its sense in the lessons: In school a lectern may stand on the stage in the hall for assemblies and speeches; in church it is where the Bible readings are read aloud, often shaped like an eagle. In stories a lectern shows a formal speech or a lesson. Phrases: "step up to the lectern", "stand at the lectern", "eagle lectern".
examples from the lessons: The head teacher stood at the lectern to give out the prizes. | I put my speech on the lectern and took a deep breath. | In our church the lectern is a brass eagle holding the Bible on its wings. | My sister read the first reading from the lectern on Sunday. | The professor leaned on the lectern while he talked. | The president walked up to the lectern with a microphone on it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a lectern, lecterns. Do not confuse it with a "pulpit": in many churches the pulpit is a raised, enclosed place for preaching the sermon, while the lectern is a stand for reading. Do not confuse with "lecture" (a talk); a lecturer often uses a lectern.

part of speech: noun (a magnolia, magnolias; magnolia — a colour); adjective (magnolia walls)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A magnolia is a tree or bush with large, beautiful white, pink or purple flowers that often open in spring before the leaves. 2) Magnolia is also a pale creamy-white colour, often used for painting walls. 3) The flower of this tree is also called a magnolia.
its sense in the lessons: In science and nature lessons magnolias are a flowering plant and one of the oldest kinds of flowering tree; in everyday life they grow in gardens and parks. In the UK, "magnolia" paint is famous as a plain, safe wall colour, so "magnolia walls" can mean a boring room. Phrases: "magnolia tree", "in bloom", "painted magnolia".
examples from the lessons: The magnolia in our front garden is covered in pink flowers. | Magnolia flowers are big and smell sweet. | The new flat had magnolia walls everywhere. | We painted the hall magnolia because Dad didn't like bright colours. | Bees crawled into the magnolia blossoms. | Magnolias are some of the oldest flowering plants on Earth. | Petals from the magnolia covered the path like snow.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable for the tree or flower (magnolias); uncountable for the colour. The word comes from a person's name (a French botanist called Magnol). Magnolia trees are famous in the southern USA; "Magnolia State" is a nickname for Mississippi.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The Mahabharata is a very long ancient poem from India, written in Sanskrit, telling the story of a great war between two families of cousins, the Pandavas and the Kauravas. 2) It is one of the holy books of Hinduism and contains many stories and teachings, including the Bhagavad Gita.
its sense in the lessons: In religious education lessons the Mahabharata is taught as a sacred Hindu text, full of lessons about duty, honesty, family and right and wrong; Hindus believe it teaches how to live a good life. In literature it is called an epic, like the Iliad, and is one of the longest poems ever written. Phrases: "the epic Mahabharata", "stories from the Mahabharata".
examples from the lessons: In RE we read a story from the Mahabharata about five brothers. | The Mahabharata is one of the longest poems in the world. | Priya's grandmother tells her stories from the Mahabharata at bedtime. | The Bhagavad Gita is a part of the Mahabharata. | The Mahabharata tells of a great battle between cousins. | Hindus believe the Mahabharata teaches about duty and doing what is right.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It is a proper name, so it takes a capital letter and usually "the": the Mahabharata. Spelled in English in a few ways (Mahabharata, Mahābhārata). Do not confuse it with the Ramayana, the other great Hindu epic, which tells the story of Rama and Sita.

part of speech: adjective (malicious, more malicious, most malicious); adverb maliciously
meaning for a pupil: 1) Malicious means wanting to hurt someone or do harm on purpose. 2) A malicious act, word or rumour is one meant to harm or upset someone. 3) (computers) Malicious software or a malicious link is made to damage a computer or steal information.
its sense in the lessons: In stories a malicious character is cruel on purpose, which tells the reader they are a villain. In computing and online safety lessons children learn not to click malicious links or download malicious files. In law, damaging something on purpose can be called "malicious damage". Phrases: "malicious gossip", "malicious rumour", "malicious software (malware)", "malicious intent".
examples from the lessons: The witch gave a malicious smile and locked the door. | Someone spread a malicious rumour that Tom had cheated. | Don't open emails from strangers; they may contain malicious links. | The website was attacked by malicious software. | It was an accident, not a malicious act. | (formal) The court found that the damage to the car was malicious. | Her malicious comments made the new girl cry.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It is a stronger word than "mean" or "nasty": it shows a real wish to harm. Opposite: kind, well-meaning, harmless. Noun: malice ("He did it out of malice"). "Malware" is short for "malicious software". Do not confuse with "mischievous", which means naughty in a playful way, not truly wanting harm.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A mattress is the large, thick, soft pad that you lie on in a bed. 2) An air mattress is a plastic one you fill with air, for camping or for floating on water.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life you sleep on a mattress; in science lessons a mattress is an example of a soft material and of springs. In safety lessons, mattresses must not be put near heaters, and babies should sleep on a firm mattress. Phrases: "a new mattress", "spring mattress", "air mattress", "under the mattress".
examples from the lessons: My mattress is so soft I sink into it. | We blew up an air mattress for my cousin to sleep on. | The old mattress was too lumpy, so we bought a new one. | My little brother jumped on the mattress until Mum told him to stop. | In the story, the princess could feel a pea under twenty mattresses. | Inside the mattress there are hundreds of metal springs. | People used to hide money under the mattress.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a mattress, two mattresses (add -es). Spelled with double t and double s. The mattress is the soft part; the bed is the whole thing with its frame. "Mattress" also appears in fixed jokes like "hiding money under the mattress", which means keeping savings at home instead of a bank.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Matzah is a flat, thin, crispy bread made only from flour and water, without yeast, so it does not rise. 2) Jewish people eat matzah during the festival of Passover to remember the Exodus, when the Israelites left Egypt in a hurry and had no time to let their bread rise.
its sense in the lessons: In religious education matzah is taught as part of Passover and the Seder meal, where it reminds Jewish people of the escape from slavery in Egypt told in the Bible (the book of Exodus). In cooking it is an unleavened bread, which also teaches how yeast makes bread rise. Phrases: "a piece of matzah", "matzah ball soup", "unleavened bread".
examples from the lessons: At the Seder meal, the family broke a piece of matzah. | Matzah is flat because it has no yeast in it. | Jewish people eat matzah during Passover. | Rachel's grandma makes matzah ball soup. | The Israelites left Egypt so quickly that their bread had no time to rise. | Matzah tastes like a big plain cracker. | In science we compared bread with yeast and matzah without it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Also spelled matzo, matza or matzoh; the plural can be matzahs, matzos or matzot. Usually uncountable (some matzah), but "a matzah" can mean one sheet. "Unleavened" means made without yeast. Christians recall that the Last Supper took place at Passover time.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A mediator is a person who helps two people or groups who disagree to talk calmly and reach an agreement. 2) (law, money) A mediator can be a trained, fair person who helps settle arguments about divorce, children, money or work without going to court. 3) (church) Christians believe that Jesus is the mediator between God and people.
its sense in the lessons: In school, some pupils are trained as peer mediators who help classmates sort out playground quarrels. In adult life and law, mediators help parents agree on custody or help workers and bosses agree. In stories a mediator brings peace between enemies. Phrases: "act as a mediator", "peer mediator", "a neutral mediator".
examples from the lessons: Our teacher acted as a mediator when Sam and Jack fell out. | Ella is a peer mediator at lunchtime. | Mum and Dad saw a mediator to agree who the children would live with. | A good mediator listens to both sides and doesn't take sides. | The two countries asked a mediator to help them make peace. | (church) The vicar said that Christians believe Jesus is the mediator between God and people. | The union and the company met with a mediator to end the strike.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a mediator, mediators. Verb: mediate; noun for the process: mediation. A mediator does not decide who is right; a judge or referee does. The key quality of a mediator is being fair (neutral) to both sides.

part of speech: verb (meow, meows, meowed, meowing); noun (a meow, meows); interjection (Meow!)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A meow is the soft crying sound a cat makes. 2) To meow is to make this sound. 3) (slang) People sometimes say "meow" after someone makes a catty, spiteful remark, as a joke.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and early reading, "meow" is a sound word (onomatopoeia) showing that a cat is speaking. In everyday life cats meow to ask for food or to be let in. Phrases: "the cat meowed at the door", "a little meow".
examples from the lessons: The kitten meowed until I gave it some milk. | "Meow!" said the cat, rubbing against my legs. | We heard a sad meow from under the shed. | Our cat meows at the door every morning to be let out. | In music class we sang a song with lots of meows in it. | (slang) "Your hair looks like a bird's nest." "Ooh, meow!"
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelled "meow" in American English and often "miaow" or "miaou" in British English; all mean the same. It is an onomatopoeia, a word that sounds like the noise it names, like "woof" and "moo". Past: meowed.

part of speech: noun (merit, merits — a merit; uncountable merit); verb (merit, merits, merited, meriting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Merit is the quality of being good and deserving praise or a reward. 2) The merits of something are its good points. 3) (school) A merit is a point, star or certificate a pupil gets for good work or good behaviour. 4) To merit something is to deserve it.
its sense in the lessons: In school, merits are part of reward systems: pupils collect merits for effort, kindness or good homework. In adult life, people are chosen "on merit" when they are picked because they are the best, not because of who they know. In formal writing you "weigh the merits" of ideas. Phrases: "on merit", "merit award", "the merits and drawbacks", "worthy of merit".
examples from the lessons: I got a merit for my story about the dragon. | Jake has twenty merits this term. | Each idea has its merits. | She was chosen for the team on merit, not because her dad is the coach. | Your drawing merits a place on the wall. | (formal) The proposal was judged on its merits. | Ten merits earn you a bronze certificate.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a quality it is uncountable ("a work of great merit"); as a school reward it is countable ("three merits"). The verb is formal: "This merits a reward" = "This deserves a reward". Adjective: meritorious (formal). In maths problems about merits, they are usually counted like points: if 10 merits make a certificate, 35 merits make 3 certificates with 5 left over.

part of speech: noun (Mike — a name; a mike, mikes — informal); verb (mike up — informal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Mike is a boy's or man's first name, short for Michael. 2) (informal) A mike is a microphone, the device that picks up your voice so it can be made louder or recorded. 3) (informal) To mike someone up is to fix a small microphone on them. 4) In the radio alphabet, Mike stands for the letter M.
its sense in the lessons: In school, a mike is used in assemblies, plays and school radio; you speak clearly into the mike. Pilots and police say "Mike" for M when spelling over the radio. Phrases: "speak into the mike", "the mike is on", "open mike night", "mike drop".
examples from the lessons: Mike is my best friend from football. | Please speak into the mike so the people at the back can hear. | The mike squeaked loudly when the head teacher tapped it. | The sound team miked up all the actors before the play. | My uncle played guitar at an open-mike night. | "M for Mike," said the pilot over the radio. | (slang) She finished her speech, dropped the mike and walked off.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a name it takes a capital letter. "Mike" for microphone is also spelled "mic" (pronounced the same). "Mike drop" is slang for ending something boldly after a great point. "For the love of Mike!" is an old exclamation of annoyance.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Mischief is naughty behaviour that is usually playful and not very harmful, like playing tricks. 2) Mischief can also mean harm or trouble caused on purpose. 3) A wish to tease or play tricks, as in "a look of mischief".
its sense in the lessons: In stories, children and animals "get up to mischief"; it tells the reader the character is cheeky and fun but causes trouble. In everyday life parents warn children to keep out of mischief. In the UK "Mischief Night" is a night of pranks in some places. Phrases: "get up to mischief", "keep out of mischief", "make mischief", "full of mischief", "a twinkle of mischief".
examples from the lessons: The puppy got into mischief and chewed my slippers. | Grandma gave us jobs to keep us out of mischief. | His eyes were full of mischief as he hid the teacher's chalk. | The twins are always up to mischief. | The goblins made mischief in the village every night. | She gave me a look of mischief before pouring water on Dad. | (formal) The rumours were spread to make mischief between the two families.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: you say "some mischief", not "a mischief" or "mischiefs". Spelled "mischief", with -ief. The adjective is "mischievous", pronounced MIS-chi-vus with three syllables; saying "mis-CHEE-vee-us" with an extra syllable is a common mistake.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Mutually means felt or done by each of two or more people towards the other, or shared by both. 2) In maths, "mutually exclusive" events cannot both happen at the same time.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life two friends can be mutually helpful, and people find a "mutually agreed" time to meet. In maths and probability, mutually exclusive outcomes (like getting heads and tails on one coin flip) cannot happen together. In formal writing, "mutually beneficial" means good for both sides. Phrases: "mutually agreed", "mutually beneficial", "mutually exclusive", "mutually respectful".
examples from the lessons: We mutually agreed to share the last biscuit. | The two schools have a mutually helpful friendship. | Bees and flowers have a mutually beneficial relationship. | (maths) Rolling a 2 and rolling a 5 on one throw are mutually exclusive. | They are mutually respectful even though they disagree. | (formal) The meeting was cancelled by mutual agreement — the two sides mutually decided to stop. | Being tired and being happy are not mutually exclusive.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: mutual ("a mutual friend" means a friend you both have). In probability, if A and B are mutually exclusive, P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B); for example, on a dice P(1 or 2) = 1/6 + 1/6 = 2/6. "Mutually" needs two or more sides; one person cannot do something mutually alone.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (church) Nicene describes something connected with Nicaea, an ancient city in what is now Turkey, where Christian leaders met in a great council. 2) (church) The Nicene Creed is a short statement of what Christians believe about God the Father, Jesus Christ and the Holy Spirit; many churches say it together at services.
its sense in the lessons: In church life and religious education the word is almost always seen in "the Nicene Creed", which begins "We believe in one God". Saying it together is a way for Christians of many churches (Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican and others) to declare the same faith. Phrases: "the Nicene Creed", "the Council of Nicaea".
examples from the lessons: On Sunday the whole church stood to say the Nicene Creed. | The Nicene Creed begins, "We believe in one God, the Father, the Almighty." | Our RE teacher explained that the Nicene Creed was agreed by a council of bishops. | Christians believe what the Nicene Creed says about the Trinity. | Many churches around the world use the Nicene Creed. | Grandma knows the Nicene Creed by heart.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It is a proper adjective, so it takes a capital letter: Nicene. Pronounced NY-seen. It is used almost only in "the Nicene Creed" and "the Nicene Council". A "creed" is a statement of beliefs. Do not confuse it with the Apostles' Creed, another, shorter Christian creed.

part of speech: noun (nonsense — uncountable); interjection (Nonsense!); adjective (nonsense words, nonsense poems)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Nonsense is words or ideas that are silly, untrue or have no meaning. 2) Nonsense is also silly or annoying behaviour, as in "Stop this nonsense!". 3) "Nonsense!" is said to disagree strongly with something. 4) Nonsense words and nonsense poems are made up for fun and do not have real meanings.
its sense in the lessons: In reading lessons children read nonsense words (like "blim" or "zort") to practise phonics, and enjoy nonsense poems by Edward Lear and Lewis Carroll. In everyday life a parent may say "That's nonsense" to calm a fear or reject an excuse. In science, a claim with no evidence may be called nonsense. Phrases: "talk nonsense", "utter nonsense", "stuff and nonsense", "no-nonsense", "make nonsense of".
examples from the lessons: Don't talk nonsense — monsters don't live under your bed. | "Jabberwocky" is a famous nonsense poem. | In phonics we read nonsense words like "plim" and "groft". | "I'm too old to play." "Nonsense! Come and join in." | That's enough of this nonsense; sit down, please. | The idea that goldfish remember only three seconds is nonsense. | Our coach is a no-nonsense woman who expects hard work.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: "a lot of nonsense", not "a nonsense" (though British people sometimes say "it makes a nonsense of the rules"). "No-nonsense" is an adjective meaning practical and strict. Similar words: rubbish (UK), rot, baloney (US, informal), codswallop (UK, informal), crap (rude).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Numbness is the state of not being able to feel something in a part of your body, for example after cold or an injection. 2) Numbness can also mean feeling no emotions for a while, often after shock or sad news.
its sense in the lessons: In science and health lessons numbness is a symptom: cold, pressure or a dentist's injection can stop nerves sending messages. In safety, numbness from cold can be a sign of frostbite, and sudden numbness can be a sign to get help quickly. In stories, numbness after bad news shows a character is in shock. Phrases: "numbness in my fingers", "a feeling of numbness", "pins and needles".
examples from the lessons: After the dentist's injection, the numbness in my lip lasted two hours. | I felt numbness in my toes after playing in the snow. | Sitting cross-legged too long caused numbness in my leg. | When she heard Grandad had passed away, she felt a strange numbness. | The numbness wore off and then my arm started to tingle. | Doctors ask about numbness to check if nerves are hurt.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Adjective: numb (the b is silent: "num"). So "numbness" is said NUM-ness. Numbness is not the same as pain; often when numbness wears off, you feel "pins and needles". Sudden numbness on one side of the face or body in an adult is an emergency; call for help.

part of speech: noun (an offering, offerings); verb form (offering — from offer)
meaning for a pupil: 1) An offering is something you give, especially as a gift. 2) (church) An offering is money people give in a church service, or a gift given to God; in the Bible people brought offerings such as animals, grain or the first fruits of the harvest. 3) Offering is the -ing form of the verb "offer": giving someone the chance to take something. 4) An offering can be something made available to buy or watch, like a new film or a menu choice.
its sense in the lessons: In church, the offering is collected in a plate or bag while a hymn is sung, and the money supports the church and the poor. In the Bible, Cain and Abel bring offerings to God. In other religions people also make offerings of flowers, food or light. In everyday life "offering" is often just the verb: "offering help". Phrases: "take up the offering", "peace offering", "harvest offering", "burnt offering".
examples from the lessons: During the hymn, two people passed round the offering plate. | I put my pocket money in the offering at church. | In the Bible, Abel's offering was the best of his lambs. | Hindus may place flowers as an offering in the temple. | I gave my sister a chocolate as a peace offering after our fight. | Thank you for offering to help with the washing up. | The café's newest offering is a strawberry milkshake.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable as a noun: an offering, offerings. Be careful: "offering" is both a noun ("the offering") and part of the verb ("I am offering you a sweet"). A "peace offering" is a gift to make friends again after a quarrel. Related: "to offer up a prayer" (church).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Officially means in a way that is approved by people in charge, according to the rules or the law. 2) Officially can mean in public, according to what has been announced, even if the truth may be different. 3) (informal) Officially is used for fun to mean "really and truly", as in "I'm officially starving".
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life something becomes official when someone in charge says so: a school is officially opened, a record is officially broken. In news, "officially" contrasts with what really happens ("officially he resigned, but really he was pushed out"). Children use it jokily to make a big statement. Phrases: "officially opened", "officially announced", "officially, …", "it's official".
examples from the lessons: The new library was officially opened by the mayor. | Summer is officially here — the pool is open! | Our team is officially the champion of the league. | Officially the shop closes at six, but they often stay open later. | The record was not officially counted because the wind was too strong. | (informal) I've eaten four pancakes, so I'm officially full. | She is now officially a teenager.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: official; noun: an official (a person with an important job). Spelled with double f and double l. In formal writing "officially" means by the proper authority; in casual speech it is often just an intensifier.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (church) Ordination is the ceremony in which a person is made a priest, minister, deacon or rabbi, usually by a bishop or other leader. 2) (church) Ordination is also the state of being ordained, of being given the role of a minister.
its sense in the lessons: In church life an ordination service is a big, joyful event; Christians believe the person is called by God to serve, and a bishop lays hands on their head and prays. In news, people sometimes discuss who may be ordained in different churches. Phrases: "ordination service", "the ordination of women", "after his ordination".
examples from the lessons: My cousin's ordination took place in the cathedral. | At the ordination, the bishop laid his hands on her head and prayed. | After his ordination he became the vicar of a small village church. | Families came from far away to see the ordination. | Some churches allow the ordination of women and some do not. | The new priest wore white for his ordination.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: ordain ("she was ordained a priest"). Do not confuse with "ordinal", which in maths means a number that shows position (first, second, third), and do not confuse with "ordinary". "Ordinance" is also a different word (a rule or law).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Overboard means over the side of a boat or ship and into the water. 2) (informal) To go overboard means to do too much of something, to be too excited or too extreme.
its sense in the lessons: In stories about the sea, "Man overboard!" is shouted when someone falls off a ship. In water safety lessons, children learn to wear life jackets so they float if they fall overboard. In everyday life, "Don't go overboard" means don't overdo it, for example with decorations or spending. Phrases: "fall overboard", "throw overboard", "man overboard", "go overboard".
examples from the lessons: The pirate threw the treasure map overboard. | "Man overboard!" shouted the captain. | Always wear a life jacket in case you fall overboard. | A big wave washed the bucket overboard. | Mum went overboard with the Christmas lights this year. | Don't go overboard with the glitter — a little is enough. | (informal) They threw the old plan overboard and started again.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It is an adverb, so you "fall overboard" (no "the"). "Throw something overboard" can also mean to get rid of an idea completely. The opposite direction is "on board" or "aboard" (on the ship).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Partial means not complete; only part of something. 2) Partial means unfairly supporting one side or person more than another. 3) (informal) To be partial to something means to like it a lot, as in "I'm partial to a scone".
its sense in the lessons: In science, a partial eclipse is when only part of the Sun or Moon is covered. In maths and money, a partial payment or refund is only part of the full amount. In fairness and ethics lessons a referee or judge must not be partial. In older or polite speech, people say they are "partial to" a food. Phrases: "partial eclipse", "partial refund", "partial success", "partial to", "impartial".
examples from the lessons: We saw a partial eclipse of the Sun through special glasses. | The shop gave us a partial refund because the box was damaged. | The plan was only a partial success. | A judge must not be partial to either side. | Grandpa is rather partial to a slice of chocolate cake. | The flood caused partial damage to the school. | There was only a partial answer to question five, so I got 2 marks out of 4.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposites: for "not complete" the opposite is "complete" or "total"; for "unfair" the opposite is "impartial" (fair). Adverb: partially ("partially sighted" = can see only partly). In maths problems, a "partial" amount is a fraction of the whole: a partial refund of £6 on a £10 toy means £4 was kept.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Participation is taking part in an activity or event. 2) Participation can also mean how many people take part.
its sense in the lessons: In school, participation in lessons, sports and clubs is encouraged, and reports may mention "class participation". In everyday life and citizenship lessons, participation in voting and community events helps society work. In maths and data, participation can be measured as a number or percentage of people. Phrases: "active participation", "participation in", "thanks for your participation", "participation rate".
examples from the lessons: Thank you all for your participation in Sports Day. | Our teacher wants more participation in class discussions. | Participation in the school choir has doubled this year. | Everyone got a participation medal for running the race. | Voting is a way of participation in a democracy. | (formal) Participation in the survey is voluntary. | If 18 of 24 pupils joined the trip, the participation was 75%.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: "more participation", not "participations". Verb: participate (in something); a person who takes part is a participant. In maths: participation rate = people who took part ÷ people who could take part, often as a percentage (18 ÷ 24 = 0.75 = 75%).

meaning for a pupil: 1) To penalise someone is to punish them for breaking a rule or law, for example with a penalty, a fine or lost points. 2) To penalise can also mean to put someone at an unfair disadvantage.
its sense in the lessons: In sport, a referee penalises a player for a foul by giving a free kick or penalty. In school, pupils may be penalised for late homework by losing marks. In law and money, people are penalised with fines. In ethics and fairness, a rule may unfairly penalise some people. Phrases: "be penalised for", "penalise heavily", "unfairly penalised".
examples from the lessons: The referee penalised the team for a high tackle. | You will be penalised if you hand in your project late. | Drivers are penalised for speeding. | The judges penalised the dancer for stepping off the stage. | (formal) The new rule penalises families who live far from school. | In the quiz, wrong answers are penalised with minus one point. | He was penalised two points for poor spelling.
note for the reader of a maths problem: British, Irish, Australian and New Zealand spelling: penalise; American and often Canadian spelling: penalize. Noun: penalty. In maths problems, a penalty is usually subtracted: if you get 12 points and are penalised 3, you have 12 − 3 = 9.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To persecute people is to treat them cruelly and unfairly for a long time, especially because of their religion, race, beliefs or who they are. 2) To persecute someone can also mean to keep annoying or bothering them.
its sense in the lessons: In history and religious education, the early Christians were persecuted by Roman rulers, and many groups (such as Jews) have been persecuted through history; this tells the reader about injustice and suffering. In the Bible, Saul persecuted Christians before he became the apostle Paul. In ethics lessons pupils learn that persecution is wrong. Phrases: "persecuted for their faith", "flee persecution", "persecute minorities".
examples from the lessons: Many families fled their country because they were persecuted for their religion. | (Bible) Before he became Paul, Saul persecuted the followers of Jesus. | The early Christians were persecuted by Roman emperors. | People should never be persecuted for the colour of their skin. | Refugees often escape from being persecuted. | The bullies persecuted him with nasty messages for weeks.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: persecution; a person who persecutes is a persecutor. Do not confuse with "prosecute", which means to accuse someone in a court of law: the police and lawyers prosecute criminals, but cruel rulers persecute innocent people.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To persuade someone is to make them agree to do something or believe something by giving good reasons or by asking nicely. 2) To persuade can also mean to convince someone that something is true.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons pupils write persuasive texts (letters, adverts, speeches) using reasons, facts and strong words to persuade the reader. In everyday life children try to persuade parents to let them have a pet or stay up late. Phrases: "persuade someone to do something", "persuade someone that", "be persuaded", "persuasive writing".
examples from the lessons: I persuaded Mum to let me have a puppy. | Can you persuade your brother to come to the park? | The advert tries to persuade you to buy the toy. | We wrote letters to persuade the council to build a skate park. | She persuaded me that the film was worth seeing. | No one could persuade him to eat broccoli. | A good speech uses facts to persuade people.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Patterns: "persuade someone to do something" or "persuade someone that …". Noun: persuasion; adjective: persuasive. "Persuade" means you succeeded; if you tried but failed, say "tried to persuade". Do not confuse with "pursue" (to chase or follow).

part of speech: noun (a philistine, philistines; the Philistines — Bible); adjective (philistine)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (Bible) The Philistines were an ancient people who lived along the coast of Canaan and were often at war with the Israelites; Goliath was a Philistine. 2) A philistine is a person who does not care about or understand art, music, books or culture. 3) As an adjective, philistine means not caring about art and culture.
its sense in the lessons: In Bible stories the Philistines are enemies of Israel in the stories of Samson and of David and Goliath. In everyday and formal speech, calling someone a philistine is an insult meaning they ignore beauty and learning. Phrases: "the Philistines", "a Philistine giant", "a complete philistine".
examples from the lessons: (Bible) David killed Goliath, the Philistine giant, with a sling and a stone. | (Bible) Samson fought against the Philistines. | The Philistines lived on the coast near Gaza. | My uncle calls anyone who doesn't like opera a philistine. | Only a philistine would paint over that beautiful old mural. | "Museums are boring," said Ben. "You philistine!" laughed his sister.
note for the reader of a maths problem: For the ancient people it takes a capital letter: the Philistines. For the insult it is often lower case: a philistine. The insult is unfair to the real ancient people, whose art and pottery were skilled. The name Palestine is thought to come from the same word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Philosophy is the study of big questions about life, knowledge, right and wrong, the mind and what is real, by thinking carefully and arguing with reasons. 2) A philosophy is a particular set of ideas from a thinker or group, like the philosophy of Plato. 3) A person's philosophy is their way of thinking about how to live or work, as in "My philosophy is to always try my best".
its sense in the lessons: In some schools children do "philosophy for children" (P4C), where they discuss questions like "Is it ever OK to lie?" and give reasons. In ethics lessons philosophy helps think about dilemmas. In everyday life people say "my philosophy" to explain their personal rules. Phrases: "study philosophy", "a philosophy of life", "my philosophy is", "Greek philosophy".
examples from the lessons: In philosophy club we discussed whether animals can think. | Socrates was a famous teacher of philosophy in ancient Greece. | My grandad's philosophy is "never give up". | She is studying philosophy at university. | The coach's philosophy is that every player gets a turn. | Philosophy asks questions like "What makes something fair?" | Different religions and philosophies have different ideas about happiness.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable for the subject ("I love philosophy"); countable for a set of ideas ("two philosophies"). Plural: philosophies (y → ies). A person who studies it is a philosopher; adjective: philosophical. The word comes from Greek and means "love of wisdom".

part of speech: noun (a pit, pits); verb (pit, pits, pitted, pitting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A pit is a large hole in the ground, dug by people or made naturally. 2) A pit is a coal mine (UK). 3) (US, Canada) A pit is the hard stone in the middle of some fruits, like a peach or cherry. 4) In motor racing, the pits are the place beside the track where cars stop for fuel and new tyres. 5) (slang, UK) A very messy room or place can be called a pit. 6) To pit one person against another is to make them compete or fight. 7) The pit of your stomach is the deep inside of your belly, where you feel fear.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons pits are coal mines where miners (and once even children) worked; in science, pits and craters form in rock and on the Moon. In stories a pit can be a trap, and in the Bible Joseph's brothers threw him into a pit. In everyday life, "the pits" means the very worst. Phrases: "fire pit", "sand pit", "orchestra pit", "the pits", "a sinking feeling in the pit of my stomach", "pit against".
examples from the lessons: The workers dug a deep pit for the new pond. | (Bible) Joseph's brothers threw him into a dry pit. | My great-grandad worked down the pit in Wales. | (US) Be careful not to swallow the cherry pit. | The racing car came into the pits for new tyres. | The final pitted our school against last year's champions. | I had a horrible feeling in the pit of my stomach before the test. | (informal) Losing the match in the last minute was the pits. | (slang, UK) Your bedroom is a total pit — tidy it!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: a pit, pits. Past of the verb: pitted (double t). A "pitted" olive has had its stone removed; "pitted" skin or metal has many small holes. In British English the fruit centre is usually a "stone", in American English a "pit". "The pits" (plural, informal) means terrible.

part of speech: adjective (progressive, more progressive); noun (a progressive, progressives); adverb progressively
meaning for a pupil: 1) Progressive means happening or developing step by step over time. 2) Progressive ideas or people support new ideas and changes in society, especially to make things fairer. 3) (grammar) The progressive form of a verb shows an action going on, like "I am running" or "she was singing". 4) (health) A progressive illness gets gradually worse. 5) (money) A progressive tax takes a bigger share from people who earn more.
its sense in the lessons: In grammar lessons pupils learn the present progressive (also called continuous): am/is/are + -ing. In history and citizenship, progressive reformers fought for votes for women and an end to child labour. In medicine and family life, a grandparent may have a progressive illness. Phrases: "present progressive", "progressive ideas", "a progressive school", "progressive illness".
examples from the lessons: I am eating is in the present progressive. | The music got progressively louder. | She is very progressive and supports new ideas. | My grandma has a progressive illness that makes her more forgetful each year. | The school has a progressive approach to learning outside. | (money) In a progressive tax system, people who earn more pay a bigger share. | Progressive reformers helped end child labour in factories.
note for the reader of a maths problem: In grammar, "progressive" and "continuous" mean the same thing. In politics it is the opposite of "conservative" (keeping things as they are), but neither word is simply good or bad. Adverb: progressively ("progressively harder" = harder at each step). In maths, "progressive" changes follow a pattern, like a sequence that grows by 3 each time.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Propriety is behaving in a correct, polite and proper way, following the rules of good manners and morals. 2) (formal) The proprieties are the rules of polite behaviour in society.
its sense in the lessons: In old novels and history, propriety was very important, especially for girls and women, who were told what was "proper". In adult life, propriety means acting honestly and correctly at work and in public office, and people question "the propriety" of a decision when it may be unfair. Phrases: "a sense of propriety", "with propriety", "question the propriety of".
examples from the lessons: In the old story, the governess was very strict about propriety. | Victorian children were taught propriety at the dinner table. | (formal) The newspaper questioned the propriety of the mayor giving the job to his son. | She behaved with complete propriety at the funeral. | (formal) The judge must act with propriety at all times. | Running around shouting in the museum was not the height of propriety!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. It is a formal word; in everyday speech people say "good manners" or "doing the proper thing". Do not confuse with "property" (things you own) or "proprietor" (an owner of a shop or business). Opposite: impropriety (improper behaviour).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A proverb is a short, well-known saying that gives advice or states a truth about life, like "Look before you leap". 2) (Bible) Proverbs is a book of the Old Testament full of wise sayings, many linked with King Solomon.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons pupils learn proverbs and explain what they mean, because their meaning is not literal. In everyday life, grandparents and teachers use proverbs to give advice. In church, readings from the book of Proverbs teach about wisdom, honesty and hard work. Phrases: "as the proverb says", "an old proverb", "the Book of Proverbs".
examples from the lessons: Don't count your chickens before they hatch is a proverb. | My nan has a proverb for everything. | "Many hands make light work" means that a job is easier when people help. | We wrote our own proverbs in class. | (Bible) The book of Proverbs says that a gentle answer turns away anger. | Every language has its own proverbs. | The proverb "Actions speak louder than words" means what you do matters more than what you say.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a proverb, proverbs. Adjective: proverbial ("the proverbial needle in a haystack" means "as in the saying"). A proverb is different from an idiom: a proverb is a complete sentence with advice, an idiom is a phrase with a special meaning ("under the weather"). The Bible book is "Proverbs" with a capital P.

part of speech: adjective (qualified, more qualified, well-qualified); verb form (qualified — past of qualify)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Qualified means having passed the exams or training needed to do a job, like a qualified nurse. 2) Qualified means having the right skills or knowledge to do something. 3) In sport, qualified means having won a place in the next part of a competition. 4) (formal) A qualified answer or agreement is limited, not complete, as in "qualified approval".
its sense in the lessons: In adult life you need to be qualified to be a teacher, doctor, electrician or swimming coach; in safety, only qualified people should fix gas or electrics. In sport, a team "has qualified for the final". In formal writing, "a qualified success" means only partly successful. Phrases: "fully qualified", "qualified for", "highly qualified", "a qualified success".
examples from the lessons: My mum is a qualified nurse. | Only a qualified electrician should fix the wiring. | Ireland qualified for the World Cup. | The lifeguard is qualified in first aid. | I'm not qualified to give advice about cars! | Our team qualified for the final by winning three games. | (formal) The school trip was only a qualified success because it rained all day.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past of qualify: qualified (y → ied). Opposite: unqualified. "Qualified for" a competition or job; "qualified as" a nurse. "Qualified" is about having passed training; "qualifications" are the certificates and exams themselves.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A quizmaster is the person who asks the questions in a quiz, keeps the score and says who has won.
its sense in the lessons: In school, a teacher or pupil may be the quizmaster in a class quiz or end-of-term quiz; in everyday life, pub quizzes and TV quiz shows have quizmasters. In stories the quizmaster may be strict or funny. Phrases: "the quizmaster's question", "act as quizmaster".
examples from the lessons: Mr Patel was the quizmaster at our end-of-term quiz. | The quizmaster read out the scores after each round. | I want to be the quizmaster next time! | The quizmaster gave a clue because no one knew the answer. | On the TV show, the quizmaster wore a shiny suit. | Our team argued with the quizmaster about question seven.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a quizmaster, quizmasters. It is a compound of quiz + master and can be used for a woman or a man. In the USA a TV quizmaster is often called a "host" or "quiz show host".

part of speech: noun (recompense — uncountable); verb (recompense, recompenses, recompensed, recompensing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Recompense is money or something else given to make up for harm, loss or trouble someone has suffered. 2) (formal) Recompense can also be a reward for work or effort. 3) (formal) To recompense someone is to pay or reward them for loss, work or trouble.
its sense in the lessons: It is a stiff, formal word used in letters, law and exam texts; in everyday speech people say "compensation", "payback" or "pay". In the Bible some older translations use "recompense" to mean reward or punishment for what someone has done. Phrases: "in recompense for", "as recompense", "without recompense".
examples from the lessons: (formal) The airline offered a free ticket as recompense for the lost luggage. | (formal) He worked for years without recompense. | (formal) The company recompensed the families for the damage to their homes. | In recompense for breaking the window, Tom washed the neighbour's car. | (Bible) The old Bible says that God will give each person recompense for their deeds. | (formal) The volunteers asked for no recompense.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal and uncountable as a noun. Everyday words with similar meaning: compensation, payment, reward, making up for. Do not confuse with "recompose" or "repay"; recompense is usually for loss or work, while "repay" means to pay back money you borrowed.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A referral is the act of sending someone to another person or place that can help them better, especially from a family doctor to a specialist. 2) A referral is also the letter or note that does this. 3) (money, business) A referral is when a customer recommends a shop or service to someone else, sometimes for a reward.
its sense in the lessons: In health and adult life, a GP gives a referral to a hospital specialist. In school, a teacher may make a referral to a school nurse, counsellor or speech therapist. In shops and apps, "refer a friend" schemes give rewards for referrals. Phrases: "get a referral", "a referral to", "referral letter", "self-referral".
examples from the lessons: The doctor gave my brother a referral to an eye specialist. | We are waiting for a referral letter from the hospital. | My teacher made a referral to the speech therapist. | The dentist sent a referral to the orthodontist about my teeth. | The gym gives you a free month for every referral. | Most of the shop's new customers come from referrals.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a referral, referrals. Verb: refer ("the doctor referred me"), past: referred (double r). Spelled with double r and one l: referral. In UK health care, you usually need a referral from a GP to see a specialist.

part of speech: noun (a reformer, reformers; the Reformers — church history)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A reformer is a person who works to change something, such as laws, schools, prisons or society, to make it better and fairer. 2) (church) The Reformers were Christian leaders, such as Martin Luther and John Calvin, who wanted to change and renew the Church, leading to the Protestant churches.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, reformers campaigned against slavery, child labour and cruel prisons; for example, Elizabeth Fry worked to improve prisons. In church history, the Reformation was started by the Reformers. In stories a reformer often faces opposition. Phrases: "social reformer", "prison reformer", "the Protestant Reformers".
examples from the lessons: Elizabeth Fry was a prison reformer who helped women in jail. | Lord Shaftesbury was a reformer who fought to stop children working in mines. | (church) Martin Luther was one of the great Reformers. | The new head teacher is a reformer who wants to change everything. | Reformers campaigned for the vote for women. | Many reformers were inspired by their Christian faith.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a reformer, reformers. Verb: reform (to change for the better); noun: reform. "The Reformation" (capital R) is the time when the Protestant churches split from the Roman Catholic Church. Do not confuse "reform" (improve) with "re-form" (form again).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Refuge is safety or shelter from danger, trouble or bad weather. 2) A refuge is a place that gives this safety, like a shelter for animals, a mountain hut or a safe house for people escaping violence. 3) (church, Bible) Christians and Jews pray that God is their refuge, meaning a safe place to trust.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and news, people "seek refuge" in another country, and a person given refuge may be called a refugee. In nature lessons, a wildlife refuge protects animals. In safety, a refuge on a busy road (a traffic island) is a safe place to stop when crossing. In the Psalms, God is called "my refuge and my strength". Phrases: "take refuge", "seek refuge", "a place of refuge", "wildlife refuge", "women's refuge".
