examples from the lessons: We took refuge under a tree when the storm started. | The family sought refuge in another country after the war. | The bird reserve is a refuge for wild geese. | (Bible) The psalm says, "God is our refuge and strength." | Climbers sheltered in a mountain refuge for the night. | Wait on the traffic refuge in the middle of the road. | The library was her refuge when the playground got too noisy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable for the idea ("take refuge"), countable for a place ("two refuges"). A refugee is a person who has to flee their country to find refuge. Pronounced REF-yooj. Do not confuse with "refuse" (rubbish, or to say no).

part of speech: noun (a reign, reigns); verb (reign, reigns, reigned, reigning)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To reign is to rule a country as a king, queen or emperor. 2) A reign is the period of time during which a king or queen rules. 3) To reign can mean to be the strongest feeling or thing in a place, as in "Silence reigned". 4) In sport, the reigning champion is the one who won last time and still holds the title.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons pupils learn about the reigns of kings and queens and put them on timelines. In the Bible and church, Christians speak of God reigning and of the reign (kingdom) of God. In stories, "chaos reigned" means everything was in a mess. Phrases: "reign over", "during the reign of", "reigning champion", "reign supreme", "reign of terror".
examples from the lessons: Queen Victoria reigned for a very long time. | During the reign of King Henry VIII, England broke away from the Pope. | The lion reigns over the jungle in the story. | When the teacher walked in, silence reigned. | Our school is the reigning champion of the county quiz. | (church) Christians sing that Christ will reign for ever. | Chaos reigned in the kitchen while Dad made pancakes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Homophones: reign (to rule), rain (water from the sky), rein (the strap used to control a horse). A common trap is "free rein": it comes from horses, so it is spelled "rein", not "reign". The g is silent. In timeline maths, the length of a reign = year it ended − year it began.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Reincarnation is the belief that after a person or animal dies, their soul is born again in a new body. 2) A reincarnation is the new life or new person someone is believed to have become. 3) (informal) A reincarnation can be a new version of an old thing, like an old song made new.
its sense in the lessons: In religious education, reincarnation is taught as a belief in Hinduism, Buddhism and Sikhism: for example, Hindus believe the soul (atman) is reborn many times and that karma affects the next life. Christians believe in resurrection and eternal life, not reincarnation. In stories and films, characters may claim to remember past lives. Phrases: "believe in reincarnation", "the cycle of reincarnation", "a past life".
examples from the lessons: Hindus and Buddhists believe in reincarnation. | In RE we learned that reincarnation means the soul is born again in a new body. | Some people believe the Dalai Lama is the reincarnation of the one before him. | My friend joked that her cat is the reincarnation of a grumpy old king. | Christians believe in resurrection rather than reincarnation. | The new film is a reincarnation of an old cartoon.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable for the belief; countable for one new life. Verb: reincarnate; adjective: reincarnated. It is a belief, not a scientific fact, so in writing say "Hindus believe …". Do not confuse with "resurrection", rising from death in the same (changed) body, which Christians believe happened to Jesus.

part of speech: verb (rejoice, rejoices, rejoiced, rejoicing); noun rejoicing
meaning for a pupil: 1) To rejoice is to feel or show great joy or happiness. 2) (church, Bible) To rejoice in God is to be glad and praise God, as in "Rejoice in the Lord always".
its sense in the lessons: In church and the Bible, "rejoice" is a common word in hymns, psalms and Christmas carols ("Rejoice! Rejoice! Emmanuel"). In stories, a whole village rejoices when the dragon is defeated or a lost child comes home. In everyday speech it sounds rather formal or old-fashioned; people more often say "celebrate" or "be over the moon". Phrases: "rejoice at", "rejoice in", "rejoice over", "there was great rejoicing".
examples from the lessons: The whole village rejoiced when the lost girl was found. | (Bible) "Rejoice in the Lord always," wrote Saint Paul. | We sang "Rejoice" at the carol service. | (Bible) In the parable, the shepherd rejoiced when he found the lost sheep. | There was great rejoicing when the war ended. | The fans rejoiced as the final whistle blew. | (formal) We rejoice at the news of your recovery.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: rejoiced, rejoicing. The noun "rejoicing" is uncountable ("much rejoicing"). It is a formal or church word; in everyday talk say "be very happy" or "celebrate".

meaning for a pupil: 1) Reliability is how much you can trust someone or something to do what they should, every time. 2) (science, maths) The reliability of a test or experiment is how much the results stay the same when you repeat it.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, doing an experiment several times and getting similar results shows reliability; scientists repeat measurements and take the average. In everyday life, the reliability of a car, a bus service or a friend is very important. In shopping, people compare the reliability of products. Phrases: "reliability of results", "improve reliability", "known for its reliability".
examples from the lessons: We repeated the test three times to check the reliability of our results. | Grandad's old car is famous for its reliability. | The bus company has poor reliability; buses are often late. | Her reliability makes her a great team captain. | (formal) The reliability of the data was questioned. | The new phone was tested for reliability by dropping it many times.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Adjective: reliable; verb: rely (on). In science, reliable results are close to each other when repeated; this is not the same as accurate (close to the true value). A watch that is always 5 minutes slow is reliable but not accurate. Opposite: unreliability.

part of speech: noun (a rental, rentals; rental — uncountable); adjective (rental car, rental property)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A rental is something you pay to use for a time, like a car, flat or bike, but do not own. 2) Rental is the money you pay for this, or the act of renting.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life families take a rental car on holiday, or live in a rental flat. In maths word problems, rental prices are often per hour or per day, which practises multiplication. In adult life and money, many people rent their home rather than buy it. Phrases: "car rental", "rental car", "bike rental", "rental agreement", "rental income".
examples from the lessons: We picked up a rental car at the airport. | The bike rental costs £5 an hour. | Our flat is a rental, so we can't paint the walls. | The ski rental shop was very busy. | We watched a film rental on the TV. | (money) The rental agreement says no pets. | If a boat rental costs $12 per hour, three hours cost $36.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable for a thing rented ("two rentals"); also used as an adjective ("rental car"). Verb: rent. In the USA "rental" is very common; in the UK people also say "hire" ("car hire"). In maths: total rental cost = price per time × time, sometimes plus a fixed fee.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A renter is a person who pays money to live in a house or flat, or to use something, that belongs to someone else. 2) A renter can also be someone who hires a car or other item for a short time.
its sense in the lessons: In adult life and money, renters pay rent to a landlord each month instead of buying a home. In news, there are stories about renters' rights and rising rents. In maths problems, renters pay a set amount per month. Phrases: "first-time renter", "renters' rights", "renter and landlord".
examples from the lessons: We are renters, so our landlord fixes the boiler. | Many young people are renters because houses cost so much. | The renters must give a month's notice before they leave. | (law) New laws protect renters from unfair evictions. | The bike shop asks every renter to wear a helmet. | If a renter pays £800 a month, they pay £9,600 in a year.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a renter, renters. In British English the more common word for someone renting a home is "tenant"; "renter" is very common in American English. The owner is the "landlord" or "landlady". Do not confuse with "rental" (the thing or payment).

meaning for a pupil: 1) To repay money is to pay back money that you borrowed. 2) To repay someone is to do something for them in return for help or kindness they gave you. 3) To repay something such as effort can mean to be worth it, as in "The hard work repaid itself".
its sense in the lessons: In money lessons, if you borrow from a friend or a bank you must repay it, often with interest. In stories, a character may repay a kindness, like the mouse that frees the lion. In ethics, repaying good with good is fairness; repaying evil with good is mercy. Phrases: "repay a loan", "repay a debt", "repay a kindness", "how can I ever repay you?".
examples from the lessons: I'll repay the £5 I borrowed on Friday. | How can I ever repay you for your help? | In the fable, the mouse repaid the lion by chewing through the net. | My parents are still repaying the loan for our house. | (Bible) Jesus taught not to repay evil with evil. | Your practice has repaid you with a great performance. | If you borrow £20 and repay £4 a week, it takes 5 weeks.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular past: repaid (not "repayed"). Noun: repayment. In maths: weeks to repay = total borrowed ÷ amount paid each week (20 ÷ 4 = 5). If there is interest, you repay more than you borrowed.

part of speech: verb (reseal, reseals, resealed, resealing); adjective resealable
meaning for a pupil: 1) To reseal something is to close or seal it again after it has been opened. 2) To reseal can also mean to put a new seal or protective coat on something, like a floor, bath edge or road.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life you reseal food packets to keep food fresh; resealable bags have a zip. In science, resealing a container stops air and germs getting in. In jobs at home, adults reseal the edges of a bath or a wooden deck to keep water out. Phrases: "reseal the bag", "resealable pack", "reseal the bath".
examples from the lessons: Please reseal the cereal bag so it doesn't go stale. | This pack of cheese is resealable. | Dad resealed the edge of the bath to stop leaks. | After the inspection, the officer resealed the box. | The road was resealed with new tar. | Make sure you reseal the paint tin tightly.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It is re- (again) + seal. Regular verb: resealed. "Resealable" means it can be closed again; you often see "Reseal after opening" or "Resealable" on packets.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A resignation is when someone officially leaves their job by choice. 2) A resignation is also the letter or announcement saying that you are leaving a job. 3) Resignation is calmly accepting something bad that you cannot change, as in "a sigh of resignation".
its sense in the lessons: In adult life and news, a leader or worker may hand in their resignation. In stories, "a look of resignation" shows a character has given up hope of changing something. Phrases: "hand in your resignation", "letter of resignation", "call for his resignation", "with resignation".
examples from the lessons: The football manager handed in his resignation after the team lost again. | She wrote a letter of resignation to her boss. | People called for the minister's resignation. | "Fine, I'll do my homework," he said with resignation. | The head teacher's resignation surprised everyone. | We accepted the rainy weather with resignation and played board games.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: resign; you resign "from" a job. Note: "resign" (leave a job) is pronounced ri-ZINE, but "re-sign" (sign again, like a footballer signing a new contract) is pronounced ree-SINE. Being "let go" or "sacked" is different from resigning: in resignation you choose to leave.

part of speech: verb (retell, retells, retold, retelling); noun retelling
meaning for a pupil: 1) To retell a story is to tell it again, often in your own words. 2) A retelling is a new version of an old story.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons, pupils retell stories orally or in writing to show they understand the order of events; story maps help. In books, a retelling gives a fresh version of a fairy tale or myth. Phrases: "retell the story", "retell in your own words", "a modern retelling".
examples from the lessons: Retell the story of the Three Little Pigs in your own words. | Grandma retold the tale of how she met Grandad. | We used a story map to retell "The Gruffalo". | The film is a modern retelling of Cinderella. | Can you retell what happened at break time? | The myth has been retold many times.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular, like "tell": retell, retold, retold. Noun: retelling. To retell is not to copy word for word; it means giving the main events in order using your own words.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A reversal is a change to the opposite direction, order or result. 2) A reversal can be a sudden change of fortune, often from good to bad. 3) (law) A reversal is when a decision is changed by a higher authority.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, reversal can mean undoing an operation (inverse operations, like reversing ×2 with ÷2) or reversing the order of digits. In science, a reversal of a process (melting then freezing) shows a reversible change. In stories and sports, a reversal is a big turnaround. Phrases: "a complete reversal", "role reversal", "reversal of fortune", "a policy reversal".
examples from the lessons: The team made an amazing reversal in the second half. | In the play there was a role reversal: the children were in charge and the parents obeyed. | The new rule was a reversal of the old one. | The reversal of 47 is 74. | Freezing melted ice again is a reversal of the change. | (law) The higher court ordered a reversal of the decision. | Losing his job was a sad reversal of fortune.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a reversal, reversals. Verb: reverse; adjective: reversible. In maths: reversing the digits of 52 gives 25, and 52 − 25 = 27 (a multiple of 9, true for every two-digit number). Reversing an operation is using its inverse.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Rightly means correctly or truly. 2) Rightly means fairly, for a good reason, as in "She was rightly proud". 3) "Rightly or wrongly" means whether it is right or wrong.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and stories, "rightly" shows the speaker agrees that a feeling or action is justified. In formal writing, "rightly so" adds approval. Phrases: "rightly so", "quite rightly", "rightly or wrongly", "if I remember rightly".
examples from the lessons: She was rightly proud of her gold medal. | If I remember rightly, the party starts at four. | The goal was rightly disallowed. | He complained, and rightly so — the food was cold. | Rightly or wrongly, they decided to go out in the storm. | People were quite rightly upset when the park closed.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It comes from "right" + -ly. In many sentences "right" and "rightly" differ: "answer it right" (correctly, informal) vs. "rightly praised" (with good reason). "Rightly" is not used for the direction right.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Rightness is the quality of being morally right, good or fair. 2) Rightness is also the quality of being correct or suitable.
its sense in the lessons: In ethics and religious education, people discuss the rightness or wrongness of actions, for example whether telling a lie to protect a friend is right. In formal writing it also means fit or suitable: "the rightness of the choice". Phrases: "the rightness of", "a sense of rightness", "rightness and wrongness".
examples from the lessons: We debated the rightness of keeping animals in zoos. | She was sure of the rightness of her decision. | (formal) The judge thought carefully about the rightness of the punishment. | There was a feeling of rightness when all the puzzle pieces fit. | Philosophers ask what gives an action its rightness. | He never doubted the rightness of standing up to the bully.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. It is a fairly formal word; in everyday speech you'd say "whether it is right". Opposite: wrongness. Related: righteousness (a church word for being good in God's eyes).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A rite is a religious or serious ceremony that is done in a fixed way, like baptism or a funeral. 2) A rite of passage is a ceremony or event that marks a big change in someone's life, like becoming an adult, or a first experience that everyone goes through.
its sense in the lessons: In religious education, pupils learn about rites such as baptism, confirmation, bar and bat mitzvah, weddings and funerals; Catholics speak of "the last rites" for the dying. In everyday life, things like losing your first tooth or your first day at secondary school can be called rites of passage. Phrases: "rite of passage", "last rites", "funeral rites", "sacred rites".
examples from the lessons: Baptism is a Christian rite of welcome into the church. | (church) The priest gave Grandad the last rites. | Starting secondary school is a rite of passage. | Every culture has its own funeral rites. | The bar mitzvah is a Jewish rite for a boy becoming an adult. | Learning to ride a bike is a childhood rite of passage.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a rite, rites. Homophones: rite (ceremony), right (correct, or the opposite of left), write (put words on paper), wright (maker, as in "playwright"). Related: ritual. Do not write "right of passage" for "rite of passage".

meaning for a pupil: 1) A role is a part that an actor plays in a film, play or show. 2) A role is a job, position or purpose someone or something has, like the role of a captain. 3) A role is how important something is in a situation, as in "play a big role".
its sense in the lessons: In drama, pupils get roles in the school play and do role play to act out situations; in safety lessons, role play helps practise saying no. In science, things have roles (the role of the heart is to pump blood). In everyday life a role model is someone you look up to. Phrases: "play a role", "the lead role", "role play", "role model", "take on a role", "role reversal".
examples from the lessons: I got the role of the wolf in the school play. | What is the role of the heart in the body? | My big sister is my role model. | In role play, we practised what to do if a stranger asks us to go with them. | Exercise plays an important role in staying healthy. | Her role in the team is goalkeeper. | Mum took on the role of class rep this year.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a role, roles. Homophone: roll (a bread roll, or to turn over and over). "Role" for a part; "roll" for movement or bread. Some old texts spell it "rôle".

part of speech: adjective (Russian); noun (a Russian, Russians; Russian — the language)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Russian means coming from or connected with Russia, the very large country that stretches from Eastern Europe across northern Asia. 2) A Russian is a person from Russia. 3) Russian is the main language of Russia, written in the Cyrillic alphabet.
its sense in the lessons: In geography, Russia is the largest country in the world by area, and has many time zones. In languages, Russian is a Slavic language and uses Cyrillic letters. In stories, Russian folk tales include Baba Yaga and the firebird; Russian dolls (matryoshka) fit one inside another. Phrases: "Russian doll", "speak Russian", "Russian roulette" (a dangerous gamble).
examples from the lessons: My friend's mum speaks Russian. | Russian is written in the Cyrillic alphabet. | We opened the Russian doll and found five more inside. | The Russian winter is very cold. | Baba Yaga is a witch in Russian fairy tales. | A Russian dancer came to perform at our school.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It is a proper adjective and noun, so it takes a capital letter: Russian. The country is Russia. Russian dolls are used in maths and language as an image of things nested inside each other. Do not confuse Russian with the languages of neighbouring countries like Ukrainian or Belarusian, which are separate languages.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (money) A salaried person is paid a fixed amount of money every year, usually in monthly payments, rather than being paid for each hour worked. 2) A salaried job is a job that pays a salary.
its sense in the lessons: In adult life and money lessons, workers can be salaried (fixed pay, often for office jobs, teachers, managers) or paid hourly wages (often for shop or factory work). In maths, a yearly salary can be divided by 12 to find the monthly pay. Phrases: "salaried staff", "a salaried job", "salaried employee".
examples from the lessons: My mum is salaried, so she gets the same pay every month. | Teachers are salaried workers. | He left his hourly job for a salaried position. | Salaried staff do not usually get paid for overtime. | If a salaried worker earns £24,000 a year, she gets £2,000 a month.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective from the noun "salary". A "wage" is usually paid by the hour or week; a "salary" is a fixed yearly amount. In maths: monthly pay = yearly salary ÷ 12; weekly pay ≈ yearly salary ÷ 52.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A sceptic is a person who doubts whether something is true and wants to see evidence before believing it. 2) A sceptic may doubt a particular idea, like "a climate sceptic", or doubt religious beliefs.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, a healthy sceptic asks for evidence, tests claims and checks sources; online safety teaches pupils to be sceptical of fake news. In stories, the sceptic is the one who does not believe in ghosts until they see one. Phrases: "a bit of a sceptic", "remain a sceptic", "sceptical about".
examples from the lessons: My dad is a sceptic about adverts that promise miracles. | Scientists should be sceptics until there is good evidence. | Tom was a sceptic about ghosts until he heard the noise in the attic. | Be sceptical of websites that don't say who wrote them. | Even the sceptics were impressed by the magician. | She remained a sceptic about the new diet.
note for the reader of a maths problem: British spelling: sceptic, sceptical; American spelling: skeptic, skeptical. Pronounced SKEP-tik (the c is hard, like k). Do not confuse with "septic" (infected with germs, as in a septic wound or septic tank), which sounds different.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A sceptre is a decorated rod or staff carried by a king or queen at ceremonies as a sign of their power. 2) The sceptre can also mean royal power itself.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons and on visits to see crown jewels, pupils see sceptres with jewels and crosses on top. In stories and the Bible, a king holds out his sceptre; in the book of Esther, the king holds out his gold sceptre to Queen Esther to show she may approach. Phrases: "the royal sceptre", "orb and sceptre", "crown and sceptre".
examples from the lessons: The king held the sceptre in his right hand. | The crown, orb and sceptre were kept in the Tower of London. | (Bible) The king held out his gold sceptre to Queen Esther. | The queen in our play had a sceptre made of a painted stick. | The sceptre had a huge diamond at the top. | In the story, whoever held the magic sceptre ruled the land.
note for the reader of a maths problem: British spelling: sceptre; American spelling: scepter. Pronounced SEP-ter (the c is silent). Countable: a sceptre, sceptres. Do not confuse with "spectre" (a ghost).

part of speech: verb (scold, scolds, scolded, scolding); noun scolding (a scolding)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To scold someone is to speak to them angrily because they have done something wrong. 2) A scolding is an angry telling-off. 3) (old-fashioned) A scold was a person, especially a woman, who often nagged or complained.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and stories, parents and teachers scold children for being naughty; it tells the reader someone is in trouble but not punished harshly. In the UK people more often say "tell off", in Australia "growl at". Phrases: "scold someone for", "get a scolding", "a good scolding".
examples from the lessons: Mum scolded me for leaving my muddy boots on the carpet. | The teacher scolded the boys for running in the corridor. | I got a scolding for being late home. | The farmer scolded the dog for chasing the sheep. | "You should know better!" scolded Grandma. | (Australia, informal) Dad growled at us — he really scolded us for fighting.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: scolded. Pattern: "scold someone for doing something". Everyday synonyms: tell off (UK), give out to (Ireland, informal: "Mam gave out to me"), chew out (US, informal). It is milder than punish: scolding is only words.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Scratchy cloth or material feels rough and makes your skin itch. 2) A scratchy sound or voice is rough, harsh or crackly, like an old record. 3) A scratchy throat feels sore and dry. 4) Scratchy writing or drawing is made of rough, untidy lines.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on materials, wool or straw may be described as scratchy, while silk is smooth. In everyday life, children complain about scratchy jumpers or labels, and a scratchy throat can be the start of a cold. In stories, a scratchy voice may belong to a witch or an old radio. Phrases: "scratchy jumper", "scratchy throat", "scratchy old record".
examples from the lessons: This wool jumper is too scratchy to wear. | I've got a scratchy throat, so I might be getting a cold. | The old record made a scratchy sound. | The witch spoke in a scratchy voice. | The label in my shirt is scratchy. | His handwriting was small and scratchy. | Hay feels scratchy on your legs.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative: scratchier, scratchiest (y → ier/iest). It comes from "scratch" + -y. Opposite: smooth, soft. Related: itchy (wanting to scratch), which is about feeling, while scratchy is about the material.

part of speech: noun (a script, scripts; script — handwriting); verb (script, scripts, scripted, scripting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A script is the written words of a play, film or TV show, telling actors what to say and do. 2) A script is a writing system or style of handwriting, like the Latin, Cyrillic or Arabic script, or joined-up "script" handwriting. 3) (computers) A script is a small program, a list of instructions for a computer. 4) To script something is to write the words for it or plan it in detail.
its sense in the lessons: In drama lessons pupils read scripts, learn their lines and write playscripts with stage directions. In handwriting lessons in the USA, "script" or "cursive" means joined-up writing. In computing, children may write scripts in Scratch. In stories and real life, "following the script" means doing what was planned. Phrases: "learn the script", "film script", "write a script", "go off script", "scripted".
examples from the lessons: I learned my lines from the script for the school play. | The script says, "Enter the giant, stage left." | Arabic script is written from right to left. | In Scratch, we built a script to make the cat dance. | The interview felt scripted, not natural. | The comedian went off script and made everyone laugh. | We wrote a script for our own puppet show.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a script, scripts. A person who writes film scripts is a scriptwriter or screenwriter. "Scripture" (holy writing, like the Bible) comes from the same old word for "writing". A playscript has character names on the left and stage directions in brackets.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Sex is being male or female; people and most animals are born one sex or the other, decided by their body. 2) A sex is one of these two groups, as in "both sexes". 3) Sex is also a private, physical act of love between adults, which is how babies can be made.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons sex is about biology: animals and plants have male and female parts, and reproduction makes new living things. Forms may ask your sex (male or female). In health and relationships lessons, older pupils learn that sex is a private, grown-up thing; in safety lessons, children learn that their body is private and that they should tell a trusted adult if anyone makes them uncomfortable. Phrases: "the opposite sex", "both sexes", "single-sex school", "sex education".
examples from the lessons: Some fish can change their sex. | You can tell the sex of a lion by its mane. | Our school is a single-sex school for girls. | The form asks for your name, age and sex. | In science, we learned how flowers have male and female parts. | Sex education is part of health lessons for older pupils. | Male and female birds of the same kind can look very different.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable for the act and the idea; countable for the groups ("the two sexes"). Adjective: sexual; "sexist" means treating people unfairly because of their sex. Many people use "gender" for the roles and identity people have in society, and "sex" for the body. It is a private topic: if anyone talks to a child about sex in a way that feels wrong, the child should tell a trusted adult.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A shamrock is a small green plant with three round leaves on each stem, like clover. 2) The shamrock is a symbol of Ireland, worn on Saint Patrick's Day.
its sense in the lessons: In Irish life and church, the story says Saint Patrick used a shamrock to explain the Holy Trinity: three leaves but one plant, as Christians believe in three persons — Father, Son and Holy Spirit — in one God. On Saint Patrick's Day, people around the world wear shamrocks and green. In nature lessons it is a kind of clover. Phrases: "a sprig of shamrock", "wear the shamrock".
examples from the lessons: On Saint Patrick's Day, Granny pinned a shamrock to my coat. | A shamrock has three leaves. | (church) Saint Patrick used the shamrock to teach about the Trinity. | The Irish rugby team has a shamrock on its shirts. | We drew shamrocks on cards for our pen pals in Ireland. | Four-leaf clovers are rare; a shamrock has only three leaves.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a shamrock, shamrocks, though people also say "a bunch of shamrock". It is not the same as a "four-leaf clover", which is a lucky rarity; the shamrock has three leaves. The word comes from the Irish "seamróg", meaning little clover.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A sheaf is a bundle of stalks of wheat, barley or other grain, tied together after cutting at harvest. 2) A sheaf of papers is a thick pile or bundle of papers.
its sense in the lessons: In harvest festival at school and church, a sheaf of wheat or a bread shaped like one is often displayed to give thanks for the harvest. In the Bible, Joseph dreams that his brothers' sheaves bow down to his sheaf, and Ruth gathers grain behind the harvesters. In everyday life a teacher may carry a sheaf of papers. Phrases: "a sheaf of wheat", "a sheaf of papers", "bringing in the sheaves" (hymn).
examples from the lessons: The farmer tied the wheat into sheaves. | (Bible) Joseph dreamed that his brothers' sheaves bowed down to his. | A sheaf of corn stood by the altar at the harvest festival. | Mr Lee came in carrying a sheaf of test papers. | In the old days, sheaves were stacked in the field to dry. | The baker made a loaf shaped like a sheaf of wheat.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular plural: sheaves (f → ves), like leaf → leaves, loaf → loaves. Countable. In a maths problem: if each sheaf has 40 stalks and there are 6 sheaves, there are 240 stalks.

part of speech: noun (Shona — a people and a language; Shona — a girl's name); adjective (Shona)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The Shona are a people of southern Africa who live mainly in Zimbabwe. 2) Shona is the language of the Shona people, one of the official languages of Zimbabwe. 3) Shona (or Shonagh) is also a girl's first name, mainly in Scotland and Ireland.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and languages, Shona is one of the most widely spoken Bantu languages, and Shona sculpture in stone is famous. Great Zimbabwe, the ancient stone city, is linked with the ancestors of the Shona. In everyday life in Scotland, Shona is a common name. Phrases: "the Shona people", "speak Shona", "Shona sculpture".
examples from the lessons: My friend's dad speaks Shona and English. | "Mhoro" means "hello" in Shona. | Shona is spoken by millions of people in Zimbabwe. | We saw beautiful Shona stone carvings at the museum. | Shona from Glasgow is the best swimmer in our club. | The Shona people built great stone walls long ago.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Proper noun, so it takes a capital letter: Shona. "Shona" can mean the people (the Shona) or their language (Shona). Names of languages and peoples always take capitals in English.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) A signatory is a person, group or country that has signed an official agreement, contract or treaty. 2) (formal, money) A signatory on a bank account is a person allowed to sign cheques and approve payments.
its sense in the lessons: In history and news, countries are signatories to treaties, such as agreements on human rights or the environment. In adult life and law, both sides of a contract are signatories. In clubs and charities, two signatories may be needed to pay money. Phrases: "signatory to", "the signatories of the treaty", "authorised signatory".
examples from the lessons: (formal) Over a hundred countries are signatories to the treaty. | All the signatories must sign on the last page. | Both my parents are signatories on the house contract. | (money) The club treasurer is a signatory on the bank account. | (formal) The signatories agreed to protect the rainforest. | Every pupil in the class became a signatory to our class charter.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a signatory, signatories (y → ies). It is formal; the everyday verb is "sign" and the noun "signature" is your name written in your own way. Do not confuse "signatory" (the person) with "signature" (the written name).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Slavery is the cruel system in which people are owned by other people, forced to work for no pay and have no freedom. 2) Slavery is also the state of being a slave. 3) Slavery can describe very hard work or control that feels like being owned, as in "modern slavery".
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons pupils learn about slavery in the ancient world, the transatlantic slave trade that took African people to the Americas, and the abolitionists such as William Wilberforce, Frederick Douglass and Harriet Tubman who fought to end it. In the Bible, the Israelites escape slavery in Egypt in the Exodus, remembered at Passover. In ethics, slavery is a clear example of a great wrong. In news, "modern slavery" means people forced to work today. Phrases: "the abolition of slavery", "escape from slavery", "modern slavery", "freed from slavery".
examples from the lessons: Slavery is against the law in every country today. | Harriet Tubman led many people out of slavery. | (Bible) Moses led the Israelites out of slavery in Egypt. | William Wilberforce campaigned to end slavery in the British Empire. | At Passover, Jewish families remember the escape from slavery. | Modern slavery still happens, and police work to stop it. | Frederick Douglass wrote about his life in slavery.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. A person held in slavery is a slave, though many historians now say "an enslaved person" to show it was done to them; the verb is "enslave". "Abolition" means ending slavery by law, and an abolitionist worked for that.

part of speech: noun (snogging — uncountable); verb form (snog, snogs, snogged, snogging); noun (a snog)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (slang, UK, Ireland, Australia) Snogging is kissing for a long time, usually between a couple who are in love or going out together. 2) (slang) A snog is one such long kiss.
its sense in the lessons: It is a casual, cheeky word used by teenagers and adults, and in funny children's books about older siblings ("Yuck! They're snogging!"). It is not used in formal writing. Phrases: "caught snogging", "a quick snog", "snogging on the sofa".
examples from the lessons: (slang) My big sister was snogging her boyfriend at the bus stop. | (slang) "Eww, they're snogging!" shouted my little brother at the film. | (slang) The teachers caught two Year 11s snogging behind the gym. | (slang) There's too much snogging in this film. | (slang) He gave her a snog at the end of the party.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It is informal and mainly British, Irish, Australian and New Zealand slang; Americans say "making out". The past is "snogged" (double g). Children use it mostly to tease. In formal writing say "kissing".

meaning for a pupil: 1) A snooper is a person who secretly looks into other people's private business, looks around where they should not, or spies. 2) A snooper can also be someone officially checking up on people, like an inspector (often said in a disapproving way).
its sense in the lessons: In stories, a snooper peeks through windows or reads someone's diary, which tells the reader they are nosy. In online safety, snoopers are people or apps trying to see your private information. Phrases: "nosy snooper", "keep snoopers out".
examples from the lessons: Our neighbour is a snooper who watches everyone through her curtains. | Keep your password secret from snoopers. | The detective caught the snooper reading the letters. | My little brother is a snooper — he looked in my diary! | The house had a lock to keep snoopers out. | (informal) The newspaper called the tax inspectors "snoopers".
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a snooper, snoopers. Verb: snoop (snooping, snooped). Similar words: nosy parker (UK, informal), busybody, spy. Do not confuse with "snooker", a game played with balls and cues.

part of speech: verb (snort, snorts, snorted, snorting); noun (a snort, snorts)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To snort is to push air out loudly through your nose, making a rough sound. 2) People snort when they laugh suddenly or to show they do not believe or like something. 3) Animals like pigs and horses snort. 4) (slang, drugs) To snort a drug is to sniff a powder up the nose; this is dangerous and illegal.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, "she snorted" shows a character is laughing in surprise or is scornful ("Huh! As if!"). In nature lessons, horses snort to clear their noses and show feelings. In safety lessons older pupils learn that drugs can be snorted and that this is very harmful. Phrases: "snort with laughter", "give a snort", "snort in disgust".
examples from the lessons: The pig snorted as it searched for food. | Tom snorted with laughter and milk came out of his nose. | "You? Win the race?" she snorted. | The horse snorted and stamped its hoof. | Dad gave a snort when he saw the price. | The bull snorted and lowered its head.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: snorted. Countable noun: a snort. When writing dialogue, "snorted" is a good word instead of "said" to show disbelief or a sudden laugh. Do not confuse with "snore", the noise when you sleep.

part of speech: noun (sobbing — uncountable); verb form (sob, sobs, sobbed, sobbing); adjective (sobbing child)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Sobbing is crying loudly with short, noisy breaths, because you are very sad or upset. 2) To be sobbing is to cry in this way.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, sobbing shows deep sadness, like after a pet dies or a child is lost; it tells the reader the feeling is strong. In everyday life, adults comfort a sobbing child with a hug. Phrases: "burst into sobbing", "sobbing uncontrollably", "sob your heart out", "a sob story".
examples from the lessons: We heard sobbing from the bedroom. | The little girl was sobbing because she had lost her mum in the shop. | He sobbed when his dog passed away. | The sobbing stopped when Grandma gave her a hug. | I sobbed my heart out at the end of the film. | (informal) Don't give me that sob story — you just forgot your homework!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: sob, sobbed, sobbing (double b). "Sobbing" is stronger and noisier than "crying"; "weeping" is quieter and more formal; "whimpering" is small, weak cries. A "sob story" (informal) is a sad tale told to get sympathy.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A specialist is a person who knows a great deal about one subject or does one kind of work very well. 2) (health) A specialist is a doctor who treats one part of the body or one kind of illness, like a heart specialist. 3) As an adjective, specialist means for one particular purpose or for experts, as in "specialist equipment".
its sense in the lessons: In health, a GP sends you to a specialist with a referral. In school, specialist teachers teach music, PE or languages. In science and careers, specialists study one field deeply. Phrases: "a specialist in", "see a specialist", "heart specialist", "specialist shop", "specialist knowledge".
examples from the lessons: The doctor sent me to a skin specialist. | Our music lessons are taught by a specialist teacher. | She is a specialist in sharks. | The divers used specialist equipment to explore the wreck. | We bought my bike at a specialist cycle shop. | A specialist came to fix the old church clock.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a specialist, specialists. Verb: specialise (UK) / specialize (US). Opposite: a generalist (someone who knows about many things), such as a GP who treats all kinds of illness. In the USA, "specialist" is also a rank in the army.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A spillage is an amount of liquid or other stuff that has spilled out by accident. 2) Spillage is the act of spilling, as in "oil spillage".
its sense in the lessons: In science labs and in school dinners, a spillage must be wiped up quickly to stop slips; there may be a "spillage kit". In safety, signs warn of a spillage on the floor. In geography and news, oil spillages from ships harm sea birds and beaches. Phrases: "clean up a spillage", "oil spillage", "chemical spillage", "report any spillage".
examples from the lessons: Please tell a teacher about any spillage in the lab. | There was a milk spillage in the dinner hall. | A yellow sign warned of a spillage on the shop floor. | The oil spillage killed hundreds of seabirds. | The cleaners mopped up the spillage straight away. | The lorry crashed and caused a spillage of paint on the road.
note for the reader of a maths problem: More formal than "spill", which is the everyday word ("a spill", "I spilled my juice"). It can be countable (a spillage) or uncountable (prevent spillage). In the UK the past of spill is "spilled" or "spilt"; in the USA usually "spilled".

meaning for a pupil: 1) Spotless means completely clean, without any dirt or marks. 2) Spotless can also mean without any mistake or fault, as in "a spotless record".
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, parents ask for a spotless room or kitchen; restaurants and hospitals must be spotless for hygiene. In stories, a spotless house can show a very neat character. In sport or law, a spotless record means no mistakes or crimes. Phrases: "spotlessly clean", "a spotless record", "keep it spotless".
examples from the lessons: After an hour of cleaning, the kitchen was spotless. | The nurse's uniform was spotless. | My nan keeps her house spotless. | Our team has a spotless record this season: no defeats. | The windows were so spotless that the bird flew into them. | (informal) My bedroom is never spotless, but it's tidy enough.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It is spot (a mark) + -less (without), so "without spots". "Spotlessly clean" is a common phrase. Opposite: dirty, grubby, filthy. Be careful: a spotless dog is not one without spotty fur; the word almost always means clean.

part of speech: noun (a steelworks — same form for singular and plural)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A steelworks is a factory where steel is made from iron and other materials, using huge furnaces.
its sense in the lessons: In history and geography lessons, steelworks were very important in industrial towns, such as Sheffield and Port Talbot in the UK, Pittsburgh in the USA, and Newcastle and Wollongong in Australia; their closing often caused job losses and redundancy. In science, steel is made by removing carbon and other impurities from iron. Phrases: "work at the steelworks", "the old steelworks", "a steelworks closure".
examples from the lessons: My grandad worked at the steelworks for forty years. | The steelworks glowed orange at night. | The town was sad when the steelworks closed. | In science we learned how a steelworks turns iron into steel. | There are two steelworks near the coast. | The old steelworks is now a museum.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Same form for one and many: "a steelworks", "two steelworks"; it can take a singular or plural verb ("the steelworks is/are closing"). Similar words: ironworks, gasworks. A person who works there is a steelworker.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A storey is one floor or level of a building. 2) "Multi-storey" describes a building with many floors, like a multi-storey car park.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and maths, buildings are described by storeys: a two-storey house, a ten-storey block of flats. In maths problems, you may multiply storeys by height per storey. In stories, a giant may be "three storeys tall". Phrases: "a two-storey house", "multi-storey car park", "on the top storey".
examples from the lessons: We live in a two-storey house. | The library is on the top storey of the building. | The multi-storey car park was full. | The giant was as tall as a three-storey building. | The new block of flats has twelve storeys. | If each storey is 3 metres high, a 5-storey building is about 15 metres tall.
note for the reader of a maths problem: British, Irish, Australian and New Zealand spelling: storey, plural storeys. American spelling: story, plural stories — the same as a tale! So in American books "a three-story house" means floors, not tales. In maths: total height ≈ number of storeys × height of one storey. In the UK the "ground floor" is the bottom; in the USA that is the "first floor".

meaning for a pupil: 1) A submission is something you hand in to be judged or checked, like a piece of homework, a competition entry or a form. 2) Submission is the act of handing something in. 3) Submission is giving in or obeying someone more powerful, as in "beaten into submission". 4) (formal, law) A submission is an argument or statement given to a judge or committee.
its sense in the lessons: In school, submission of homework or projects has a deadline, and many online systems have a "submit" button. In competitions, entries are submissions. In stories and history, a defeated army is forced into submission. In some churches, submission to God's will means humble trust. Phrases: "submission date", "deadline for submissions", "in submission", "into submission".
examples from the lessons: The deadline for submission of your project is Friday. | The poetry competition received two hundred submissions. | My submission to the art contest was a painting of a fox. | The wrestler forced his opponent into submission. | The dog lay on its back in submission. | (formal) The lawyer made a submission to the judge. | (church) The monks lived in humble submission to God.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: submit, submitted, submitting (double t). Adjective: submissive (too ready to obey). Countable for things handed in; uncountable for giving in. "Submit" in online forms means "send".

meaning for a pupil: 1) A successor is a person who takes over a job, title or position after someone else leaves it, like the next king or the next head teacher. 2) A successor is something that comes after and replaces something else, like a newer model of a phone. 3) (maths) The successor of a whole number is the number that comes right after it.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, a king's successor is usually his eldest child; in the Bible, Joshua was the successor of Moses and Elisha the successor of Elijah. In maths, the successor of 9 is 10 (add one), and the predecessor of 9 is 8. In everyday life a new phone model is the successor of the old one. Phrases: "successor to", "a worthy successor", "name a successor".
examples from the lessons: Prince Charles was the successor to Queen Elizabeth. | (Bible) Joshua was chosen as the successor of Moses. | The head teacher's successor starts next term. | The new game is the successor to last year's hit. | (maths) The successor of 99 is 100. | The king had no son, so there was no clear successor. | She is a worthy successor to the old captain.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a successor, successors. Opposite: predecessor (the one who came before). Verb: succeed (to follow after); noun: succession. In maths, successor of n = n + 1; predecessor of n = n − 1. Do not confuse with "success" (doing well), though the words are related.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Symbolically means in a way that uses a symbol to stand for an idea, rather than in a real or practical way. 2) In maths, symbolically means using signs and letters, like + and x, instead of words.
its sense in the lessons: In religious education, actions are done symbolically: in baptism water symbolically washes away sin, and Christians share bread and wine symbolically or as a sacrament to remember Jesus. In stories and poems, a storm may symbolically show a character's anger. In maths, a word problem can be written symbolically, like "x + 3 = 7". Phrases: "symbolically important", "act symbolically", "written symbolically".
examples from the lessons: The dove symbolically stands for peace. | At the end of the year we symbolically handed the class key to the next year group. | (church) In baptism, water symbolically washes the person clean. | In the story, the dark forest symbolically shows the girl's fear. | We wrote the problem symbolically as 3 × n = 12. | Planting a tree was a symbolically important start for the new school.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: symbolic; noun: symbol; verb: symbolise (UK) / symbolize (US). Something done symbolically matters for its meaning, not its practical effect: cutting a ribbon symbolically opens a building. Spelled with -ically: symbolic + -ally.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Synonymous words have the same or nearly the same meaning, like "big" and "large". 2) If one thing is synonymous with another, people think of them together because they are so closely connected, as in "Paris is synonymous with romance".
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons, pupils find synonymous words (synonyms) to make writing more interesting, using a thesaurus. In everyday and formal writing, "synonymous with" links a person or place with a quality. Phrases: "synonymous with", "almost synonymous".
examples from the lessons: Happy and "glad" are synonymous. | Finland is almost synonymous with saunas. | The name Einstein is synonymous with genius. | In maths, "add" and "plus" are synonymous. | For my brother, holidays are synonymous with ice cream. | (formal) In this text, "the authorities" and "the police" are synonymous.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: synonym (a word with the same meaning). Opposite word type: antonym (opposite meaning). Pattern: "synonymous with". Spelled with a y in the middle: syn-ON-y-mous. Few words are exactly synonymous; most synonyms differ a little in register or shade (e.g. "kid" is informal, "child" is neutral).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Technically means according to the exact rules or facts, even if it doesn't seem that way in everyday life, as in "Technically, a tomato is a fruit". 2) Technically means relating to skill or method, as in "technically brilliant". 3) Technically can mean connected with machines, science or technology.
its sense in the lessons: In science, "technically" is used for strict definitions (technically a spider is not an insect). In sport and music, a performance can be technically perfect. In everyday arguments, children say "technically" to win a point using the exact rules. Phrases: "technically speaking", "technically correct", "technically possible".
examples from the lessons: Technically, a tomato is a fruit because it has seeds. | Technically speaking, a spider is not an insect. | The dancer is technically brilliant. | "You said I couldn't eat the biscuits — technically, I only ate one!" | It's technically possible to walk there, but it would take all day. | The film was technically impressive with amazing special effects.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: technical. "Technically" often signals that the next point is true by strict rules but may not be what people mean in normal talk, so it can sound like a clever excuse. Spelled with -ically.

part of speech: noun (a terrace, terraces); verb (terrace, terraced, terracing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A terrace is a flat area next to a house, café or hotel where people can sit outside. 2) (UK) A terrace is a row of houses joined together in a line; these are terraced houses. 3) A terrace is one of a set of flat steps cut into a hillside for growing crops. 4) (UK, Ireland) The terraces are the wide steps in a sports ground where fans stand to watch.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons, terraces on hillsides (like rice terraces in Asia) stop soil being washed away and give flat ground for farming. In history and everyday British life, terraced houses were built for factory workers. In football, fans chant on the terraces. Phrases: "terraced house", "rice terraces", "on the terraces", "roof terrace".
examples from the lessons: We had lunch on the terrace in the sunshine. | We live in a terrace of red-brick houses. | Rice terraces climb up the hills like giant steps. | The fans on the terraces sang loudly. | The hotel has a roof terrace with a pool. | Farmers terraced the hillside to grow tea.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a terrace, terraces. "Terraced house" (UK) = "row house" (US); "end terrace" is the house at the end of the row. In some street names, "Terrace" is part of the address (e.g. "Victoria Terrace") and takes a capital letter.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Thankfulness is the feeling of being grateful and glad for something good that you have or that someone has done for you.
its sense in the lessons: In church and religious education, thankfulness to God is shown in prayers, grace before meals and harvest festival. In everyday life and wellbeing lessons, children may keep a thankfulness or gratitude journal. In stories, thankfulness shows a kind, humble character. Phrases: "a feeling of thankfulness", "with thankfulness", "thankfulness for".
examples from the lessons: She felt deep thankfulness when her lost dog came home. | We wrote notes of thankfulness to the dinner ladies. | (church) Harvest festival is a time of thankfulness for food. | His heart was full of thankfulness for his friends. | Saying grace before meals shows thankfulness. | Thankfulness can make people feel happier.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Adjective: thankful; a similar noun is "gratitude", which is more common in formal writing. "Thankfulness" is a little softer and often used in church and in feelings. Opposite: ingratitude, ungratefulness.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) A theory is a well-tested explanation of how something in nature works, supported by a lot of evidence, like the theory of evolution or the theory of gravity. 2) A theory is an idea someone has to explain something, which may or may not be true, as in "I have a theory about who ate the cake". 3) Theory is the ideas and rules of a subject, as opposed to practice, like music theory. 4) "In theory" means what should happen if things go as planned, though they might not.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, pupils learn that a scientific theory is not just a guess: it has been tested many times. In stories, a detective forms a theory about the crime. In music lessons, theory means notes, scales and rhythm rules. Phrases: "in theory", "come up with a theory", "test a theory", "theory and practice", "conspiracy theory".
examples from the lessons: Darwin's theory of evolution explains how living things change over time. | I have a theory that the cat ate the fish fingers. | In theory, the bus comes every ten minutes, but it never does. | The detective tested her theory by checking the footprints. | I passed my music theory exam. | Scientists test a theory by doing experiments. | (informal) Some people believe in silly conspiracy theories.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: theories (y → ies). Adjective: theoretical. A common trap: in everyday talk "just a theory" means a guess, but in science a theory is a strong, tested explanation. A "hypothesis" is the smaller idea you test in an experiment.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A touchy person gets upset or annoyed very easily. 2) A touchy subject is one that needs to be talked about carefully because it can upset people.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and stories, "touchy" describes someone in a bad mood or sensitive about something, which tells the reader to be careful around them. In adult life, money, religion or someone's weight can be touchy subjects. Phrases: "touchy about", "a touchy subject", "touchy-feely" (informal: showing feelings a lot).
examples from the lessons: Dad is a bit touchy about his bald patch. | Be careful — Mia is touchy today because she lost the match. | Money is a touchy subject in our house. | Why are you so touchy? I was only joking! | The cat is touchy and scratches if you stroke its tummy. | (informal) Our new teacher is very touchy-feely and hugs everyone.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative: touchier, touchiest. It is informal; more formal words are "sensitive" or "irritable". "Touchy" does not mean "likes touching"; that is "touchy-feely" (informal).

part of speech: verb (tow, tows, towed, towing); noun (a tow, tows)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To tow something is to pull it behind a vehicle or boat, using a rope, chain or bar. 2) A tow is the act of towing, as in "give someone a tow". 3) "In tow" means following closely behind, as in "with three children in tow".
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, a breakdown truck tows a broken-down car, and cars tow caravans and trailers. In road safety and parking, a car parked illegally can be towed away. In science, towing is a pulling force. Phrases: "tow truck", "tow away", "give someone a tow", "in tow", "tow rope".
examples from the lessons: The tow truck towed our car to the garage. | Dad's car tows the caravan on holiday. | If you park there, your car will be towed away. | The tractor gave the stuck car a tow out of the mud. | Mum arrived with all five of us in tow. | The boat towed the water-skier across the lake.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: towed. Homophone: toe (on your foot). Trap: it is "in tow" (following), not "in toe"; but "toe the line" (obey rules) uses toe. A tow truck is also called a breakdown truck (UK) or wrecker (US).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Twofold means having two parts or two sides, as in "a twofold problem". 2) Twofold means twice as much or twice as many, as in "a twofold increase".
its sense in the lessons: In maths and science, a twofold increase means the amount doubles. In formal writing, "The reason is twofold" means there are two reasons. Phrases: "a twofold increase", "twofold purpose", "the reason is twofold", "increase twofold".
examples from the lessons: The number of pupils in the club has increased twofold, from 10 to 20. | The purpose of the trip was twofold: to learn and to have fun. | The problem is twofold — no money and no time. | (formal) Prices have risen twofold in a short time. | Our garden produced a twofold harvest of tomatoes this year.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Written as one word: twofold. Similarly: threefold (three times), tenfold (ten times). In maths, "a twofold increase" means multiply by 2 (10 becomes 20), so the increase is 10 (100%). Be careful: some people use "a twofold increase" loosely, but strictly it means doubling.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unpopular means not liked by many people or by most people. 2) An unpopular decision, rule or idea is one many people disagree with.
its sense in the lessons: In school, an unpopular rule might be a ban on football at break. In stories, an unpopular character has few friends or is disliked. In history and news, rulers and laws can be unpopular. Phrases: "unpopular with", "deeply unpopular", "an unpopular decision".
examples from the lessons: The new uniform was very unpopular with the pupils. | Broccoli is unpopular in our house. | The king became unpopular when he raised taxes. | It was an unpopular decision, but it was the right one. | Being unpopular for a while is better than being unkind. | The film was unpopular at first but is now loved.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It is un- (not) + popular. Noun: unpopularity. Pattern: "unpopular with someone". In ethics lessons, pupils learn that doing the right thing can sometimes be unpopular.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unrestricted means without limits, rules or controls; free to do, have or use as much as you want.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, an unrestricted view means nothing blocks what you see; unrestricted internet access means no filters, which is why schools use filters for safety. In money and adult life, an unrestricted ticket can be used at any time. Phrases: "unrestricted access", "unrestricted view", "unrestricted use".
examples from the lessons: We had an unrestricted view of the stage from the front row. | The library gives unrestricted access to its books for members. | Children should not have unrestricted internet use. | The ticket is unrestricted, so you can travel at any time. | The dogs had unrestricted run of the farm. | (formal) The museum allows unrestricted entry on Sundays.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It is un- (not) + restricted. Opposite: restricted, limited. Verb: restrict; noun: restriction. Spelled with two r's in "restricted" separated: un-re-strict-ed.

part of speech: verb (urge, urges, urged, urging); noun (an urge, urges)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To urge someone to do something is to try hard to persuade them, or to tell them strongly that they should. 2) An urge is a strong wish or need to do something, often suddenly. 3) To urge an animal on is to make it move faster.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, characters urge each other on ("Run!") or feel a sudden urge to laugh or explore. In health and safety, adults urge children to wear helmets; news says "Police urge drivers to slow down". In everyday life, you may have the urge to go to the toilet. Phrases: "urge someone to", "have an urge to", "a sudden urge", "resist the urge", "urge on".
examples from the lessons: The teacher urged us to check our answers. | I had a sudden urge to sing. | The police urge drivers to take care on icy roads. | The crowd urged the runners on to the finish. | I resisted the urge to eat the last cookie. | Mum urged me to wear a coat. | The rider urged her horse forward.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: urged. Pattern: "urge someone to do something". Adjective: urgent (needing action quickly); noun: urgency. "Urge" is stronger than "ask" or "advise".

meaning for a pupil: 1) Vengeance is harming someone because they have harmed you or someone you love; revenge. 2) (informal) "With a vengeance" means very strongly or much more than usual, as in "It rained with a vengeance".
its sense in the lessons: In stories and films, a character may swear vengeance, which tells the reader the plot is about revenge. In ethics and church, people learn that seeking vengeance often makes things worse; in the Bible, "Vengeance is mine, says the Lord" teaches that people should not take revenge themselves, and Jesus taught to love enemies. Phrases: "take vengeance", "swear vengeance", "seek vengeance", "with a vengeance".
examples from the lessons: The hero swore vengeance on the dragon that burnt his village. | (Bible) Saint Paul wrote, "Do not take revenge … for it is written, 'Vengeance is mine,' says the Lord." | Vengeance doesn't fix anything; it just makes the fight longer. | The rain came back with a vengeance. | She forgave him instead of seeking vengeance. | The cold came back with a vengeance just when spring had started.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Similar: revenge (more common in everyday speech), retaliation. Adjective: vengeful. Spelled with -geance. "Avenge" is the verb (to punish someone for a wrong done to another), as in "avenge his brother".

part of speech: noun (a viewing, viewings; viewing — uncountable); verb form (viewing — from view)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A viewing is an occasion when you look at something, especially a house you might buy or rent, a film, or a show. 2) Viewing is the act of watching, especially TV or films, as in "family viewing". 3) A viewing is a time before a funeral when people come to see the body of the person who has died, to say goodbye. 4) Viewing is the -ing form of "view": looking at.
its sense in the lessons: In adult life, families go to viewings of houses or flats before buying or renting. In everyday life, TV programmes are labelled "family viewing" or "not suitable for younger viewers". In family life, a funeral viewing lets loved ones say goodbye. In science, a viewing platform helps you watch birds or the stars. Phrases: "a house viewing", "viewing platform", "family viewing", "essential viewing", "private viewing".
examples from the lessons: We went to three house viewings on Saturday. | The programme is good family viewing. | From the viewing platform we saw the whole city. | This documentary is essential viewing for anyone who loves animals. | Before the funeral, there was a viewing at the funeral home. | Viewing the eclipse directly can hurt your eyes. | The museum held a private viewing of the new paintings.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable for an event (a viewing, viewings); uncountable for watching in general. A "viewer" is someone who watches. Safety trap: never view the Sun directly, even during an eclipse; use special glasses or a pinhole viewer.

part of speech: noun (a virgin, virgins; the Virgin Mary — church); adjective (virgin)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (church) The Virgin Mary is the mother of Jesus; Christians believe she conceived Jesus by the power of the Holy Spirit while still a virgin. 2) A virgin is a person who has never had sex. 3) As an adjective, virgin means never used, touched or spoiled, as in "virgin snow" or "virgin rainforest". 4) Extra virgin olive oil is the purest, best kind, made from the first pressing of olives.
its sense in the lessons: In church and at Christmas, the word appears in carols and prayers about Mary ("the Virgin Mary", "born of a virgin"), and in the Nicene Creed. In geography and science, virgin forest has never been cut down. In cooking, labels say "extra virgin olive oil". In health lessons for older pupils, the meaning about sex is explained privately and respectfully. Phrases: "the Virgin Mary", "virgin forest", "virgin snow", "extra virgin olive oil".
examples from the lessons: (church) At Christmas we sing about Jesus being born of the Virgin Mary. | There is a statue of the Virgin Mary in our church. | We were the first to walk on the virgin snow. | Virgin rainforest has never been cut down by people. | Mum cooks with extra virgin olive oil. | (Bible) Matthew's Gospel says Mary was a virgin when Jesus was born. | The Virgin Islands are a group of islands in the Caribbean.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable as a noun. With Mary it takes a capital letter: the Virgin Mary, the Virgin. Noun: virginity. The meaning about sex is private and grown-up; in most school texts the word means "the Virgin Mary" or "untouched".

meaning for a pupil: 1) A warrior is a brave fighter or soldier, especially in old times or in stories. 2) A warrior can be someone who fights hard for a cause or keeps going through difficult things, like an "eco-warrior" or a child bravely fighting an illness.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, pupils learn about Viking, Celtic, Maori and Samurai warriors; in stories and myths, warriors go on quests. In everyday life, children with serious illnesses are sometimes called "little warriors". In the Bible, David was a great warrior king. Phrases: "a brave warrior", "warrior queen", "eco-warrior", "weekend warrior" (informal).
examples from the lessons: Boudicca was a warrior queen who fought the Romans. | The Vikings were fierce warriors. | The Maori haka was once a warrior's challenge before battle. | (Bible) King David was a mighty warrior. | My cousin is a little warrior; she never gives up in hospital. | The eco-warriors camped in the trees to save the forest. | The warrior lifted her shield and charged.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a warrior, warriors. Spelled with double r: warrior. Related: war. Similar words: fighter, soldier (a soldier is in an army; a warrior is often from older times or stories). "Weekend warrior" (informal) is someone who does sport or DIY only at weekends.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Wonderfully means in a very good, pleasing or delightful way. 2) Wonderfully can also mean very or extremely, in a good way, as in "wonderfully warm".
its sense in the lessons: In everyday speech and stories, "wonderfully" adds strong praise: a show was wonderfully funny, the weather was wonderfully sunny. In writing lessons it is a lively adverb to describe how something was done. Phrases: "wonderfully well", "wonderfully kind", "wonderfully done".
examples from the lessons: You sang wonderfully at the concert. | The bath was wonderfully warm after the cold walk. | Grandma is wonderfully kind to everyone. | The plan worked wonderfully. | The cake was wonderfully gooey in the middle. | The children behaved wonderfully on the trip.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It is wonderful + -ly; note the double l: wonderfully. Similar: brilliantly, marvellously (UK) / marvelously (US), beautifully. Do not confuse with "wondering" (thinking about something).

part of speech: verb form (worship, worships, worshipped, worshipping — past of worship); adjective (worshipped)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (church) Worshipped is the past of "worship": to show love, praise and honour to God or a god, by praying, singing and attending services. 2) Worshipped can mean loved and admired very much, as in "a worshipped footballer". 3) (Bible) In the Bible, people who worshipped idols (statues of false gods) were told to turn back to God.
its sense in the lessons: In religious education, pupils learn that Christians worshipped in churches, Jews in synagogues, Muslims in mosques and Hindus in temples. In history, ancient Egyptians worshipped many gods, like Ra the Sun god. In everyday life, fans "worship" celebrities. Phrases: "worshipped God", "worshipped as a god", "worshipped the ground he walked on".
examples from the lessons: The early Christians worshipped in each other's homes. | The ancient Egyptians worshipped the Sun god, Ra. | (Bible) The Israelites worshipped a golden calf while Moses was on the mountain. | The family worshipped at the local synagogue every Saturday. | The younger boys worshipped the captain of the team. | She worshipped the ground her grandmother walked on.
note for the reader of a maths problem: British spelling: worshipped, worshipping (double p); American spelling often worshiped, worshiping (one p). Both correct. A place of worship is any building where people worship. Saying a person "worshipped" a pop star is exaggeration, not religion.

part of speech: noun (a worshipper, worshippers); US spelling: worshiper
meaning for a pupil: 1) (church) A person who worships, who prays to and praises God or a god, especially in a church, mosque, synagogue or temple. 2) A person who loves and admires someone or something very much, almost as if it were holy, like a sun worshipper or a hero worshipper.
its sense in the lessons: Used in stories and lessons about religion to mean the people at a service: worshippers fill the church, kneel, sing and pray. In everyday talk it is used playfully for great fans: a sun worshipper loves lying in the sun. Phrases: fellow worshippers, regular worshipper, sun worshipper, hero worship.
examples from the lessons: The worshippers stood up to sing the first hymn. | Hundreds of worshippers came to the cathedral at Christmas. | The mosque was full of worshippers on Friday. | Gran is a regular worshipper at St Mary's. | My aunt is a real sun worshipper and lies on the beach all day. | The worshippers bowed their heads as the priest prayed. | Fellow worshippers brought food to the family after the funeral.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one worshipper, two worshippers. UK spelling doubles the p (worshipper); US often writes worshiper. The verb is worship (worships, worshipped, worshipping). Do not confuse worship (to praise God) with warship (a ship for war). Respectful word; it says nothing bad about the person.

part of speech: noun (abundance; usually uncountable, an abundance of)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A very large amount of something, more than enough. 2) The state of having plenty, being rich in things such as food or water.
its sense in the lessons: Used in science for nature (an abundance of fish, plants growing in abundance), in geography for resources, and in everyday life for having plenty. In stories it paints a picture of riches or plenty, often the opposite of a famine. Phrases: an abundance of, in abundance, abundance of food.
examples from the lessons: There was an abundance of apples in the orchard this autumn. | Wild flowers grow in abundance by the river. | The rainforest has an abundance of animals and plants. | Our class had an abundance of ideas for the school fair. | After the long drought, the rains brought abundance to the farms. | Fresh water is found in abundance in Canada. | The teacher said we had an abundance of time, so no need to rush.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: abundant; adverb: abundantly. Opposite: scarcity, shortage, lack. Usually "an abundance of" + noun. Formal-sounding; in plain talk say "lots of" or "plenty of". In maths it means a large amount but gives no exact number.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To agree to a request or demand, often after first not wanting to. 2) (formal) To take up an important job or position, especially to become king or queen (accede to the throne). 3) (formal, law) For a country to join an agreement or an organisation.
its sense in the lessons: A stiff, formal word met in history lessons, news and exam texts. It is almost always followed by "to": accede to a request, accede to the throne. In stories it shows someone giving way to pressure. Plain words: agree, give in, become king or queen.
examples from the lessons: The head teacher finally acceded to our request for a longer break. | The king's daughter acceded to the throne when he died. | The company would not accede to the workers' demands. | After much arguing, Dad acceded and let us keep the puppy. | The country acceded to the treaty and became a member. | The council acceded to the parents' wish for a crossing guard. | She refused to accede to their threats.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always "accede to" something. Formal: in speech people say "agree to" or "give in to". Do not confuse with exceed (go beyond) or concede (admit or give up). The noun is accession (the accession of a new queen).

part of speech: noun (accordance; used almost only in the phrase in accordance with)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Agreement; "in accordance with" means following, obeying or matching a rule, wish or plan. 2) (formal) Being in agreement with something.
its sense in the lessons: A formal word found in rules, letters from school, signs and exam texts: "in accordance with school policy" means "following the school's rules". It tells the reader that something was done the official or correct way. Phrases: in accordance with the rules, in accordance with the law, in accordance with her wishes.
examples from the lessons: The fire drill was carried out in accordance with the safety rules. | In accordance with Grandma's wishes, we scattered flowers at the beach. | Uniform must be worn in accordance with school policy. | The experiment was done in accordance with the instructions. | Parking is allowed only in accordance with the signs. | The money was shared in accordance with the plan. | The building was checked in accordance with the law.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable, nearly always in the fixed phrase "in accordance with". Plain alternatives: following, according to, in line with. Do not mix it up with "according to" (which means "as said by": according to the teacher...). Related: accord, accordingly.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal, money) To grow or build up little by little over time, especially money such as interest. 2) (formal) To come to someone as a benefit or result over time.
its sense in the lessons: A formal word used mostly in money and banking: interest accrues on savings, debts accrue. In maths problems about interest it means the amount gets bigger as time goes on. Also used in exam texts for slowly gaining advantages or points. Phrases: interest accrues, accrued interest, benefits accrue to.
examples from the lessons: Interest accrues on the money in your savings account each month. | The late fees accrued until the library book was returned. | Points accrue every time you shop at that store. | Benefits accrue to those who practise every day. | She accrued a lot of holiday time at work. | Unpaid bills can accrue quickly. | The accrued interest was added to the total.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; in speech say "build up" or "add up". Often used with money and interest. In a maths problem, "accrued interest" is the extra money added on top of the starting amount. Spelling: double c, ends in -ue. Related noun: accrual.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal, law) To make an official decision about a disagreement or a legal case, as a judge does. 2) To be the judge of a competition, deciding who wins, such as in music, debating or sport.
