its sense in the lessons: Used in law to mean deciding a case, and at school for judging contests: a teacher adjudicates the spelling bee. It tells the reader that someone has the power to decide fairly. Phrases: adjudicate a dispute, adjudicate a competition, adjudicate on, adjudicate between.
examples from the lessons: A judge will adjudicate the case next month. | Mrs Patel adjudicated the school debating contest. | Three experts adjudicated the piano competition. | The referee had to adjudicate between the two teams. | The court adjudicated in favour of the family. | Who will adjudicate at the singing contest? | It is hard to adjudicate when both sides seem right.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; plain words: judge, decide. The person is an adjudicator; the noun is adjudication. Stress on "-ju-": a-JOO-di-cate. Not the same as "judge" in every sentence: you adjudicate a dispute but you judge a person's character.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (Bible, church, law) When a married person has a loving, romantic or sexual relationship with someone who is not their husband or wife. 2) (Bible) One of the sins named in the Ten Commandments: "You shall not commit adultery."
its sense in the lessons: Met in Bible lessons and religious education as one of the Ten Commandments, and in adult life as a reason for divorce. It tells the reader that a marriage promise has been broken. Christians believe marriage is a lifelong promise of faithfulness. Phrases: commit adultery, the commandment against adultery.
examples from the lessons: The seventh commandment says, "You shall not commit adultery." | The teacher explained that adultery means breaking the promise of marriage. | In the story, the king's adultery brought great trouble to his family. | Many religions teach that adultery is wrong. | Adultery can be one reason a marriage ends in divorce. | The Bible tells how King David committed adultery and later was sorry. | The vicar spoke about faithfulness and the harm adultery causes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: no plural. The verb phrase is "commit adultery". A person who does it is an adulterer. It has nothing to do with "adult" meaning grown-up in the ordinary sense, although the words look alike. A serious, grown-up topic; talk about it respectfully.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Saying firmly that something is true or that you agree with it. 2) Words of support or encouragement that help someone feel good about themselves. 3) (law) A promise to tell the truth, made instead of a religious oath.
its sense in the lessons: Used in school well-being lessons for positive sayings ("I am brave"), in debates for agreeing, and in law for a solemn non-religious promise. It tells the reader that someone is confirming or supporting something. Phrases: positive affirmation, daily affirmations, a nod of affirmation, in affirmation.
examples from the lessons: She gave a nod of affirmation when I asked if she was ready. | Our class writes a positive affirmation on the board each morning. | "I can do hard things" is a good affirmation. | The coach's words were an affirmation that we had played well. | In court, he made an affirmation instead of swearing on the Bible. | The award was an affirmation of all her hard work. | Mum's hug was all the affirmation I needed.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: affirmations. Verb: affirm. Adjective: affirmative ("an affirmative answer" means yes). Do not confuse with "information". Opposite idea: denial.

part of speech: adjective (only after a verb: be aflame, set aflame)
meaning for a pupil: 1) On fire, burning with flames. 2) Glowing brightly with colour as if burning, like autumn leaves or a sunset. 3) Full of a strong feeling, such as anger or excitement.
its sense in the lessons: A poetic, story-telling word. It paints a picture of fire, bright colour or strong feeling. Used in descriptions of sunsets, autumn trees and fires. Phrases: set aflame, aflame with colour, cheeks aflame.
examples from the lessons: The old barn was aflame within minutes. | The sky was aflame with red and orange at sunset. | In autumn the maple trees are aflame with colour. | Her cheeks were aflame with embarrassment. | The dragon set the castle aflame. | The crowd was aflame with excitement. | The hills looked aflame in the evening light.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Used after a verb (the house was aflame), not before a noun: we say "a burning house", not "an aflame house". Like other a- words: afloat, asleep, alive. More poetic than "on fire".

meaning for a pupil: 1) Again from the beginning, in a new way. 2) Once more, newly.
its sense in the lessons: Used in stories and instructions when someone starts something over: start afresh, look at it afresh. It tells the reader there is a new start or a fresh view. Common in school when work goes wrong and you begin again. Phrases: start afresh, begin afresh, look at something afresh.
examples from the lessons: I made a mess of my drawing, so I started afresh. | After the argument, the friends decided to begin afresh. | The family moved to Australia to start life afresh. | Look at the problem afresh tomorrow and you might see the answer. | The snow had fallen afresh in the night. | Let's read the question afresh and check each step. | The new term is a chance to start afresh.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb, so it describes the verb (start afresh). Similar: anew, again, from scratch. A little formal or bookish; in speech people say "start again" or "start over" (US).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Something that you think of, say or add later, after the main thing is done. 2) Something added without much care, treated as less important.
its sense in the lessons: Used in stories and writing lessons: a sentence added as an afterthought comes at the end. It tells the reader that something was not planned. In everyday talk it can be a little unkind: "the little room was an afterthought". Phrases: as an afterthought, an afterthought to, no afterthought.
examples from the lessons: As an afterthought, she grabbed her umbrella. | He added a P.S. to the letter as an afterthought. | The garden seemed like an afterthought to the builders. | "And bring a snack," Mum said as an afterthought. | Safety should never be an afterthought. | The last line of the poem was an afterthought. | The small extra room was built as an afterthought.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: afterthoughts. Written as one word. Often in the phrase "as an afterthought". Do not confuse with "second thoughts" (changing your mind).

part of speech: noun (an airplane, airplanes); UK and Australia: aeroplane
meaning for a pupil: 1) A flying machine with wings and engines that carries people or goods through the air. 2) (informal) A toy model of such a machine, including a paper airplane.
its sense in the lessons: Used in everyday life about travel and in science lessons about flight, air, lift and forces. In stories, a trip by airplane is a big journey. Phrases: by airplane, get on an airplane, paper airplane, airplane mode (on a phone).
examples from the lessons: We flew to see Grandma in a big airplane. | The airplane took off from the runway. | I folded a paper airplane in class and it flew across the room. | In science we learned how wings help an airplane fly. | Put your phone in airplane mode during the flight. | The airplane landed safely in the storm. | My little brother wants to be an airplane pilot.
note for the reader of a maths problem: US spelling is airplane; British, Irish, Australian and New Zealand English usually say aeroplane, and everyone says plane. Use "an" (an airplane) because it starts with a vowel sound. Plural: airplanes. Travel phrase: "by plane", not "by the airplane".

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person or thing that shares out or gives out parts of something, such as money, places or jobs. 2) (computing) Part of a computer program that hands out memory space when it is needed.
its sense in the lessons: A formal and technical word. In everyday or school use it means the one who divides things up; in computing it is the code that gives out memory. In maths problems, it is the one who shares an amount into parts. Phrases: memory allocator, seat allocator.
examples from the lessons: The allocator gave each team a room for the project. | The teacher acted as the allocator of jobs for the class trip. | A memory allocator gives programs the space they need. | The ticket allocator made sure every family got two seats. | The money allocator divided the budget between the clubs. | The computer's allocator ran out of free memory. | Who is the allocator of the parking spaces?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: allocators. From the verb allocate (to share out for a purpose); noun allocation. Rare in everyday talk; children mostly meet "allocate" and "allocation". Not the same as "alligator"!

meaning for a pupil: 1) (church) Giving money, food or help to poor people, especially as a religious duty. 2) Charity given out of kindness to people in need.
its sense in the lessons: Met in religious education: Christians, Muslims and others believe giving to the poor pleases God. In Lent, Christians often practise prayer, fasting and almsgiving. In Islam, giving to the poor (zakat) is one of the Five Pillars. Phrases: prayer, fasting and almsgiving.
examples from the lessons: During Lent, our church encourages prayer, fasting and almsgiving. | Almsgiving means sharing what you have with people who are poor. | The children collected tins for the food bank as an act of almsgiving. | Many faiths teach that almsgiving is a duty. | In the story, the rich man was praised for his almsgiving. | Almsgiving should be done quietly, Jesus taught, not to show off. | The monks lived simply and spent their money on almsgiving.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. From "alms" (old word for gifts to the poor; pronounced "ahmz", the l is silent) + giving. Old-fashioned and religious in tone; in everyday talk people say "giving to charity".

part of speech: noun (an ambition, ambitions; also uncountable ambition)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A strong wish to do or become something special, like a big goal for the future. 2) The drive to be successful, powerful or rich; when there is too much of it, it can make people selfish.
its sense in the lessons: Used in everyday life and school when talking about dreams and goals ("My ambition is to be a vet"). In stories it can be good (a hero's ambition) or dangerous (a villain's greedy ambition, as in Macbeth). Phrases: life's ambition, lifelong ambition, achieve an ambition, full of ambition, lack of ambition.
examples from the lessons: My ambition is to play football for my country. | Her lifelong ambition was to visit Australia. | He finally achieved his ambition of climbing the mountain. | The teacher said our class is full of ambition. | The king's ambition made him cruel to his people. | Write about your greatest ambition in your diary. | Too much ambition can make you forget your friends.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable for a particular goal (my ambitions), uncountable for the quality (she has a lot of ambition). Adjective: ambitious (an ambitious plan). Starts with a vowel sound, so "an ambition". Not always positive: "blind ambition" is a warning.

part of speech: adjective (amended); also the past tense and past participle of the verb amend (amend, amends, amended, amending)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Changed a little to correct or improve it, especially a rule, law, plan or piece of writing. 2) (law) Officially altered by adding or changing parts, like an amended law.
its sense in the lessons: Used for rules, timetables, laws and homework: an amended timetable has small changes. It tells the reader that a first version was fixed or improved. Phrases: amended version, amended rules, as amended, amended timetable.
examples from the lessons: The school sent home an amended timetable for the sports day. | She handed in an amended copy of her story. | The law was amended to protect wildlife. | Here are the amended rules for the game. | The teacher amended my mark after checking again. | The amended plan includes a wet-weather option. | Please read the amended letter carefully.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Amend means to change slightly to improve; the noun is amendment. Do not confuse amend with "emend" (correct a text; rare) or with "mend" (fix something broken). "Make amends" means to make up for something wrong you did. In maths, an amended answer is a corrected one.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A collection of short sayings or pieces of writing chosen from a writer or teacher. 2) The Analects: the famous book of sayings of Confucius, a wise teacher in ancient China.
its sense in the lessons: Met in religious education and history when learning about Chinese thought: The Analects of Confucius teach kindness, respect for parents, good manners and learning. It tells the reader they are reading wise sayings. Phrases: The Analects of Confucius.
examples from the lessons: The Analects are sayings of the Chinese teacher Confucius. | We read a line from The Analects about treating others well. | In The Analects, Confucius says that learning should be a joy. | Our teacher showed us a page of The Analects in Chinese. | The Analects teach respect for parents and older people. | Many people in China still quote The Analects. | The Analects is a book of short wise sayings.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural form, but often treated as the name of one book ("The Analects is..." or "are..."). Usually with a capital A. A rare, specialised word; pronounced AN-a-lects.

part of speech: verb (analyse, analyses, analysed, analysing); US spelling: analyze
meaning for a pupil: 1) To look at something closely and carefully, part by part, to understand it. 2) (science, maths) To study data, results or a sample to find patterns or what it is made of. 3) (school) To examine a poem, story or text to explain how it works and what it means.
its sense in the lessons: Very common in school: analyse the data, analyse a poem, analyse the results of an experiment. It tells the reader to think carefully, not just look quickly. In maths, analyse a graph means read it and explain the patterns. Phrases: analyse the results, analyse data, carefully analyse.
examples from the lessons: We analysed the results of our plant experiment. | Analyse the graph and say which month was the wettest. | The scientist analysed the water to see if it was clean. | In English we analysed how the poet uses rhyme. | The coach analysed the video to see where we went wrong. | Let's analyse the problem step by step. | The police analysed the fingerprints on the glass.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK, Irish, Australian, NZ spelling: analyse; US and often Canada: analyze. Noun: analysis (plural analyses); person: analyst; adjective: analytical. Exam questions saying "analyse" want reasons and detail, not just a description.

part of speech: noun (Latin; used almost only in "per annum")
meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal, money) A year; "per annum" means each year or for every year.
its sense in the lessons: Met in money and maths problems: a salary or interest rate is often given "per annum" (p.a.). It tells the reader the amount is for one year. Phrases: per annum, p.a.
examples from the lessons: The bank pays 3% interest per annum. | Her salary is fifty thousand pounds per annum. | The club charges twenty dollars per annum to join. | The tree grows about 30 centimetres per annum. | If the rent is 1,200 per annum, how much is it per month? | The rate is written as 5% p.a. on the poster. | The farm produces ten tonnes of wheat per annum.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Latin for "year", used in "per annum". Abbreviation: p.a. Formal; plain English is "a year" or "each year". In maths: to change a per annum amount to per month, divide by 12; to per week, divide by 52. Related: annual, anniversary.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Without giving your name, so nobody knows who you are. 2) In a way that hides who someone is.
its sense in the lessons: Used in everyday life and stories for gifts, letters, tip-offs and online posts: someone donated money anonymously. It tells the reader the person's name is a secret. Also used in safety lessons: you can report bullying anonymously. Phrases: give anonymously, donate anonymously, report anonymously, remain anonymous.
examples from the lessons: Someone anonymously left flowers at the school gate. | The money was donated anonymously to the hospital. | You can report problems anonymously in the class box. | The letter was sent anonymously, with no signature. | She liked to help people anonymously. | The survey was filled in anonymously so we could be honest. | Online, some people post anonymously and say unkind things.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: anonymous ("an anonymous letter"); noun: anonymity. Stress: a-NON-i-mus-ly. Short form "anon" in old poems means the author is unknown. Online, being anonymous does not mean you cannot be traced; stay kind and safe.

part of speech: preposition (anti); prefix (anti-); noun (an anti, antis — informal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Against; opposed to something ("They are anti the new road"). 2) (prefix anti-) A word part meaning against or opposite, as in antisocial, antibiotic, anticlockwise. 3) (informal) A person who is against something.
its sense in the lessons: Mostly met as a prefix in school words: anticlockwise (maths), antibiotic and antibodies (science), anti-bullying week. As a word on its own it is informal and means "against". Phrases: anti-bullying, anticlockwise, anti-slip, antifreeze.
examples from the lessons: My dad is anti the idea of a phone before I am twelve. | Turn the dial anticlockwise to open it. | It is anti-bullying week at our school. | The doctor gave me an antibiotic for the infection. | Put the anti-slip mat in the bath. | Antifreeze stops the water in the car from freezing. | Mum is a bit anti fizzy drinks.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a prefix it is sometimes joined with a hyphen (anti-bullying), sometimes not (antisocial). Pronounced AN-tee (UK) or AN-tie (US). Do not confuse anti- (against) with ante- (before: anteroom) or with "auntie" (aunt). In maths, anticlockwise (UK) = counterclockwise (US).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (noun) An old object, usually a hundred years old or more, valued because it is old, rare or beautiful. 2) (adjective) Old and valuable, like antique furniture. 3) (adjective, informal) Very old-fashioned (said as a joke).
its sense in the lessons: Used in everyday life (antique shops, Grandma's antique clock) and history lessons about objects from the past. In stories, an antique often holds a secret or a memory. Phrases: antique shop, antique dealer, antique furniture, priceless antique.
examples from the lessons: Grandma has an antique clock that ticks loudly. | We visited an antique shop full of old toys. | The antique vase was worth a lot of money. | Please do not sit on that chair; it is an antique. | Dad's phone is so old it's practically an antique! | The museum shows antique tools from farms. | She inherited antique jewellery from her great-aunt.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced an-TEEK. Countable as a noun: antiques. Use "an antique". Not the same as "antic" (a silly act) or "ancient" (very very old, for things like pyramids). Old does not always mean valuable.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Behaving in a way that harms or annoys other people in the community, like vandalism or shouting late at night. 2) Not wanting to be with other people; unfriendly or shy of company.
its sense in the lessons: Used in safety and citizenship lessons (antisocial behaviour like graffiti or litter) and in everyday talk for someone who keeps to themselves. It tells the reader someone is not behaving well toward others, or does not want company. Phrases: antisocial behaviour, antisocial hours (work late at night), feeling antisocial.
examples from the lessons: Dropping litter in the park is antisocial behaviour. | The police were called because of antisocial noise in the street. | I'm feeling a bit antisocial today, so I'll stay in my room. | Nurses often work antisocial hours. | Writing graffiti on walls is antisocial. | My cat is very antisocial and hides when guests arrive. | The school talks about how to stop antisocial behaviour.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Can be written antisocial or anti-social. Two meanings: harmful to others, or just not sociable; context tells which. In UK news, "antisocial behaviour" means nuisance crime. Being quiet or shy is not the same as being harmful.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Large or important enough to be noticed or measured. 2) Big enough to matter.
its sense in the lessons: A formal word in science and exam texts: an appreciable difference, an appreciable amount. It tells the reader the change is real and noticeable, not tiny. Phrases: appreciable difference, appreciable amount, appreciable effect.
examples from the lessons: There was an appreciable difference in the plants given sunlight. | The new road has made an appreciable change to traffic. | It took an appreciable amount of time to finish. | The extra practice made an appreciable improvement in her reading. | The temperature dropped appreciably after sunset. | There was no appreciable change in the results. | An appreciable number of pupils walk to school.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; plain words: noticeable, considerable. Do not confuse with "appreciative" (feeling or showing thanks). In maths or science, an appreciable change is big enough to measure, but no exact size is given.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Taking something for yourself, often without permission or without the right to. 2) (money, law) Money that is officially set aside for a particular use, like a government budget. 3) Using parts of someone else's culture, art or ideas as your own, sometimes without respect (cultural appropriation).
its sense in the lessons: A formal word met in news, law, money and art lessons. It tells the reader something was taken or set aside for a purpose. Phrases: appropriation of funds, cultural appropriation, budget appropriation.
examples from the lessons: The appropriation of the land angered the farmers. | The council made an appropriation for a new playground. | The treasurer was accused of the appropriation of club money. | People discussed whether the costume was cultural appropriation. | Congress approved the appropriation for schools. | The museum talked about the appropriation of other people's treasures. | An appropriation is money saved for one job only.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: appropriate (ap-PRO-pree-ate, to take). Do not confuse with the adjective "appropriate" (ap-PRO-pree-it, meaning suitable). Formal word; context decides whether it means taking unfairly or setting aside.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To think that something or someone is good, right or acceptable ("approve of"). 2) To officially agree to a plan, request or idea and allow it to happen. 3) To say yes to something after checking it, like approving a design.
its sense in the lessons: Used in everyday life (parents approve of friends or plans), school (the head approves a trip), and adult life (a bank approves a loan). It tells the reader someone gives permission or a good opinion. Phrases: approve of, approve a plan, approved by, seal of approval.
examples from the lessons: My parents approve of my new friend. | The head teacher approved the class trip to the zoo. | Mum doesn't approve of eating in front of the TV. | The council approved the plans for a new library. | This toy has been approved as safe for small children. | The bank approved the loan for the house. | I hope the teacher approves my project idea.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Approve of + person or thing = think it is good; "approve" + plan = officially allow. Noun: approval. Opposite: disapprove (of), reject. Past: approved.

part of speech: adjective (approving); also the present participle of approve; adverb: approvingly
meaning for a pupil: 1) Showing that you think something is good or right, like an approving smile or nod. 2) (verb form) In the act of officially agreeing to something.
its sense in the lessons: Used in stories to describe a look, nod or smile that shows someone is pleased. It tells the reader that a character likes what they see. Phrases: an approving nod, an approving look, nodded approvingly.
examples from the lessons: The teacher gave me an approving nod. | Dad smiled in an approving way when I tidied my room. | The crowd made approving noises. | Grandma looked at my drawing with an approving eye. | The coach nodded approvingly as we passed the ball. | The council is approving new rules this week. | Her approving words made me feel proud.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: disapproving. As an adjective it goes before a noun (an approving look). "-ing" form of approve: drop the final e and add -ing.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person whose people come from the Arabic-speaking countries of the Middle East and North Africa, such as Egypt, Saudi Arabia or Morocco. 2) (adjective) To do with Arabs or the Arab world, like Arab culture. 3) An Arab horse, a beautiful breed known for speed and strength.
its sense in the lessons: Used in geography and history lessons about the Middle East and North Africa, and in stories. It names a people and their culture, not a religion. Phrases: the Arab world, Arab countries, Arab culture, an Arab horse.
examples from the lessons: Many Arab families live in our city. | We learned about the Arab world in geography. | Arab scholars long ago helped develop algebra. | My friend Layla's family is Arab and speaks Arabic at home. | The Arab horse is famous for its speed. | Arab countries stretch from Morocco to Oman. | Our class tasted food from different Arab countries.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always written with a capital A: Arab. Related: Arabic (the language; also Arabic numerals 0–9), Arabian (Arabian Peninsula, Arabian Nights). Not all Arabs are Muslim, and most Muslims are not Arab. Use it respectfully as a name for a people.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Behaving as if you are more important, cleverer or better than other people. 2) Too much pride that makes someone rude or not willing to listen.
its sense in the lessons: Used in stories about proud characters who look down on others and often learn a lesson. In ethics and religious lessons, arrogance is seen as a fault, the opposite of humility. Phrases: full of arrogance, the arrogance of, sheer arrogance.
examples from the lessons: The hare's arrogance made him lose the race to the tortoise. | His arrogance made it hard for others to like him. | She spoke with arrogance, as if nobody else knew anything. | The king's arrogance led to his downfall. | Being confident is good, but arrogance is not. | It was pure arrogance to think he couldn't lose. | Many stories teach that arrogance comes before a fall.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Adjective: arrogant; adverb: arrogantly. Opposite: humility, modesty. Not the same as confidence: confidence is believing in yourself, arrogance is thinking you are better than others. Spelled with double r.

part of speech: noun (assent; uncountable); verb (assent, assents, assented, assenting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Agreement or permission, especially official agreement. 2) (verb, formal) To agree to something. 3) (law, UK) Royal Assent: the monarch's official approval that turns a bill into a law.
its sense in the lessons: A formal word in history, law and exam texts. In stories it shows someone agreeing, often with a nod. In UK citizenship lessons, a bill gets Royal Assent to become an Act. Phrases: give assent, nod of assent, Royal Assent, assent to.
examples from the lessons: She nodded her assent. | The bill received Royal Assent and became law. | The head teacher gave her assent to the plan. | Everyone assented to the new rules of the game. | Without his parents' assent, he could not join the trip. | The king assented to the treaty. | A murmur of assent went round the room.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; plain word: agreement, agree. Homophone trap: assent (agreement) sounds like ascent (going up, a climb). Opposite: dissent. Usually "assent to" something.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person whose job is to judge or measure how good, big or valuable something is, such as work, damage or property. 2) (school) Someone who checks and marks exams or coursework. 3) (law, money) An official who works out how much tax or insurance money is due.
its sense in the lessons: Used in school (an assessor checks exams or a school inspection), in insurance (a loss assessor checks damage after a flood or fire), and in tax. It tells the reader someone is judging fairly by a standard. Phrases: insurance assessor, loss assessor, independent assessor.
examples from the lessons: An assessor came to watch our lesson. | The insurance assessor looked at the flood damage. | The assessor marked our projects using a checklist. | A tax assessor works out how much a house is worth. | The judges and assessors met after the competition. | The assessor said our playground was safe. | An independent assessor checked the results.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: assessors. From the verb assess (to judge, measure); noun assessment. Double s twice: a-ss-e-ss-or. Not the same as "accessor" or "successor".

meaning for a pupil: 1) The belief that there is no God or gods. 2) Not believing in any god.
its sense in the lessons: Met in religious education when learning about different beliefs. Atheists base their ideas of right and wrong on reason, kindness and human values. Compare with theism (believing in God) and agnosticism (not being sure). Phrases: atheism and religion, a belief in atheism.
examples from the lessons: Atheism is the belief that there is no God. | In RE we learned about atheism as well as world religions. | Some people choose atheism, and others choose a faith. | My uncle's atheism doesn't stop him enjoying Christmas with us. | Atheism and religion both try to answer big questions. | We should respect people's beliefs, including atheism. | An atheist might say that people can be good without God.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Person: an atheist; adjective: atheist or atheistic. Prefix a- means "without" + theism (belief in God). Not the same as agnostic (someone who says they do not know). Talk about it respectfully, as with any belief.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To fix or join one thing to another, such as with glue, a clip or string. 2) To add a file to an email or message. 3) To feel love or fondness for someone or something (be attached to). 4) To link something like importance or blame to something ("attach importance to").
its sense in the lessons: Used in everyday life (attach a label), school (attach the picture to your page), computing (attach a file), and feelings (attached to a pet). Phrases: attach to, attached file, be attached to, no strings attached.
examples from the lessons: Attach the label to your coat with a safety pin. | Please attach your homework to the email. | The trailer is attached to the back of the car. | I'm very attached to my old teddy bear. | Glue the leaves and attach them to the poster. | Our teacher attaches great importance to neat handwriting. | You get a free gift with no strings attached.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelled with one t and -ach (not -atch): attach. Noun: attachment (an email attachment; a strong attachment to someone). Opposite: detach. "No strings attached" means with no hidden conditions.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To show or prove that something is true. 2) (formal, law) To state officially, often in writing, that something is true, like a witness signing a document. 3) (formal) To be clear evidence of something ("The trophies attest to her skill").
its sense in the lessons: A formal word in law, history and exam texts. It tells the reader there is proof or a witness. Often "attest to". Phrases: attest to, can attest, as attested by.
examples from the lessons: I can attest that she worked very hard. | The full shelf of trophies attests to her skill. | Two witnesses attested the signature on the will. | Old maps attest to a village here long ago. | Many parents can attest to the teacher's kindness. | The doctor attested that he was too ill to travel. | Footprints in the mud attest that a fox passed by.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; plain words: prove, show, confirm, swear. Often "attest to" + noun. Do not confuse with "test" or "contest". Noun: attestation.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To make something bigger, stronger or better by adding to it. 2) (music) To make a musical interval larger (augmented chord).
its sense in the lessons: A formal exam-voice word: augment your income, augment the team. In maths it hints at adding to an amount. In technology, augmented reality adds pictures to the real world on a screen. Phrases: augment income, augmented reality, augment with.
examples from the lessons: She augments her pocket money by washing cars. | The team was augmented by two new players. | Augmented reality games add creatures to the real world on your screen. | The museum augmented its collection with new fossils. | Exercise can augment your strength. | The farmer augmented the soil with compost. | The choir was augmented by singers from another school.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; plain words: increase, add to, boost. Noun: augmentation. In maths word problems, "augmented by 5" means "increased by 5" (add 5). Stress: awg-MENT.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Official permission to do something. 2) A document or code that gives that permission.
its sense in the lessons: Used in school (a note giving authorisation for a trip), adult life (banks, passwords, payments) and safety (only staff with authorisation may enter). It tells the reader someone has been allowed. Phrases: without authorisation, give authorisation, authorisation code, written authorisation.
examples from the lessons: You need your parents' authorisation to go on the trip. | No entry without authorisation. | The bank sent an authorisation code to Mum's phone. | Only staff with authorisation can open this door. | The head gave authorisation for the fire drill. | He used the computer without authorisation and got in trouble. | Please sign this form to give your authorisation.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK, Australia, NZ spelling often -isation; US and Canada -ization. Verb: authorise/authorize. Similar: permission, approval. Countable for documents (authorisations), uncountable for the idea.

part of speech: verb (authorise, authorises, authorised, authorising); US spelling: authorize
meaning for a pupil: 1) To give official permission for something to happen. 2) To give someone the power or right to do something.
its sense in the lessons: Used in school (the head authorises a day off), money (authorise a payment) and law. It tells the reader someone in charge said yes. Phrases: authorised by, authorised person, authorise a payment, unauthorised absence.
examples from the lessons: The head teacher must authorise any day off school. | Dad authorised the payment on his phone. | Only authorised people may enter the lab. | The council authorised the new bike lanes. | Missing school without a reason is an unauthorised absence. | She was authorised to speak for the class. | Who authorised this purchase?
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK spelling: authorise; US: authorize (both are fine in UK, but stay consistent). Noun: authorisation; opposite adjective: unauthorised. Similar: permit, allow, approve.

part of speech: noun (an autograph, autographs); verb (autograph, autographs, autographed, autographing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A famous person's signature, written for a fan to keep. 2) (verb) To sign your name on something, such as a book, photo or shirt, for someone. 3) (formal) A piece of writing in the author's own hand.
its sense in the lessons: Used in everyday life when meeting famous people, at book signings and in end-of-year autograph books where friends sign. It tells the reader someone values a personal signature. Phrases: get an autograph, autograph book, signed and autographed.
examples from the lessons: I got the footballer's autograph on my shirt! | The author autographed copies of her new book. | At the end of term we all signed each other's autograph books. | He queued for an hour to get an autograph. | This autographed photo is very special. | Can I have your autograph, please? | The singer autographed my ticket.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: autographs. "Auto" means self, "graph" means writing. A signature on a form is not usually called an autograph; autograph is for fans and keepsakes.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To say something openly and firmly, to declare it. 2) (formal) To admit or confess something openly.
its sense in the lessons: An old-fashioned, formal word met in stories and exam texts. It tells the reader someone states a belief or feeling openly. The adjective "avowed" (an avowed enemy) means openly declared. Phrases: avow your love, avowed enemy, avowed aim.
examples from the lessons: The knight avowed his loyalty to the king. | She avowed that she had never seen the stolen ring. | He was an avowed fan of the team. | The two families were avowed enemies. | They avowed their love in front of everyone. | The avowed aim of the club is to help animals. | He avowed his mistake and apologised.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal and literary; plain words: declare, state, admit. Noun: avowal. Do not confuse with vow (a solemn promise) or allow.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A man who is not married and never has been. 2) (school) A first university degree, such as a Bachelor of Arts (BA) or Bachelor of Science (BSc). 3) (informal) A bachelor pad is a flat where an unmarried man lives.
its sense in the lessons: Used in everyday talk about family and adult life, and in talk about university (a bachelor's degree). In stories, a bachelor uncle often lives alone. Phrases: bachelor's degree, Bachelor of Science, a confirmed bachelor, bachelor party (US).
examples from the lessons: My uncle is a bachelor who lives with three cats. | My sister is studying for a bachelor's degree in science. | She has a Bachelor of Arts in history. | The prince was the most famous bachelor in the land. | The bachelor finally married at fifty. | Dad's friends threw him a bachelor party before the wedding. | A bachelor's degree usually takes three or four years.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: bachelor has no t (not "batchelor"). For a woman, the old word was spinster, now rarely used; people just say "single". The degree is spelled with an apostrophe: bachelor's degree.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (law, UK, Ireland, Australia, NZ) A lawyer who speaks for people in the higher courts and argues their case in front of a judge. 2) In some countries, the word for lawyer is attorney or counsel.
its sense in the lessons: Met in adult life and stories about courts. In the UK and Ireland, a solicitor does most legal paperwork, and a barrister argues in court, often wearing a wig and gown. Phrases: defence barrister, barrister-at-law, called to the bar.
examples from the lessons: The barrister stood up and spoke to the jury. | My cousin is training to be a barrister. | The barrister wore a white wig and a black gown. | In court, the barrister asked the witness questions. | Her barrister said she was innocent. | Barristers must study the law for many years. | The barrister won the case for the family.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: barristers. In the USA and Canada people usually say lawyer or attorney. Do not confuse with "barista" (a person who makes coffee). Spelled with double r and one s.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Doing good, being kind and generous to others. 2) (formal, church) The goodness and kindness of God or of a generous person.
its sense in the lessons: A formal word in ethics, religion and exam texts. In ethics, beneficence means acting for the good of others, an important rule for doctors. Christians believe in the beneficence of God. Phrases: an act of beneficence, the beneficence of God.
examples from the lessons: The hospital was built through the beneficence of a rich family. | Doctors follow the principle of beneficence, which means doing good for the patient. | Christians speak of the beneficence of God. | Her beneficence helped many poor children. | The story praises the king's beneficence. | Beneficence means more than not doing harm; it means helping. | The town remembered his beneficence with a statue.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal and rare; plain words: kindness, generosity, goodness. Related: beneficent, benefit, benefactor. Do not confuse with "benevolence" (wishing good), which is very close in meaning.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (law, formal) To leave money or belongings to someone in your will, so they get them after you die. 2) (formal) To pass something on to people who come later, like ideas or traditions.
its sense in the lessons: Met in stories and adult life about wills and inheritance. It tells the reader someone gave something to be received after their death. Also used for passing down ideas. Phrases: bequeath to, bequeathed by.
examples from the lessons: Great-grandpa bequeathed his gold watch to my dad. | She bequeathed her house to the animal shelter. | The ancient Greeks bequeathed us many ideas. | In his will, he bequeathed his books to the library. | The painting was bequeathed to the museum. | What would you like to bequeath to future generations? | The farm was bequeathed to the youngest son.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; plain words: leave, hand down. The noun for the gift is a bequest. Pronounced bi-KWEETH. Used with "to": bequeath something to someone.

part of speech: adjective (bereaved); noun (the bereaved — people who are grieving)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Having lost a close family member or friend because they died. 2) (noun, the bereaved) People whose loved one has recently died.
its sense in the lessons: Used gently in adult life, news and church: the bereaved family, support for the bereaved. It tells the reader someone is grieving. Schools and churches offer care for bereaved children. Phrases: bereaved family, recently bereaved, support for the bereaved.
examples from the lessons: The bereaved family thanked everyone for their kind messages. | Our class made cards for a bereaved classmate. | The vicar comforted the bereaved at the funeral. | Recently bereaved people may feel sad for a long time. | The charity helps bereaved children. | We should be gentle with someone who is bereaved. | The bereaved mother planted a tree in her son's memory.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A respectful, gentle word. Noun: bereavement (the loss). "The bereaved" can mean one or many people. Related verb bereave (rare). Not the same as "brave".

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) The act of giving something, such as an honour, gift or title, to someone.
its sense in the lessons: A rare, formal word met in stories about kings, awards and ceremonies. It tells the reader that something special was given. Phrases: the bestowal of an honour, bestowal of a title.
examples from the lessons: The bestowal of the medal took place in the great hall. | The knight knelt for the bestowal of his title. | Everyone clapped at the bestowal of the award. | The bestowal of gifts was part of the ceremony. | The queen's bestowal of honours is a yearly event. | The story ends with the bestowal of a crown. | The bestowal of blessings was the last part of the service.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal and rare. Verb: bestow (to give, usually something special: bestow an honour on someone). Plain words: giving, award, presentation.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (Bible) To do with the Bible or found in the Bible, like biblical stories. 2) (informal) Very great or huge, like a flood in the Bible ("rain of biblical proportions").
its sense in the lessons: Used in religious education (biblical stories, biblical times) and, as a joke or exaggeration, in everyday life ("the flood was biblical"). It tells the reader about the Bible or about something enormous. Phrases: biblical times, biblical story, of biblical proportions.
examples from the lessons: We read the biblical story of Noah's Ark. | In biblical times people travelled by donkey and on foot. | The rain was of biblical proportions; the whole street flooded. | The play was based on a biblical story. | Many famous paintings show biblical scenes. | My dad's beard is getting biblical! | The vicar explained the biblical meaning of the parable.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually written with a small b, though "Bible" has a capital B. Pronounced BIB-li-cal. The informal meaning of "huge" is a joke; context tells you which meaning is meant.

part of speech: noun (bickering; uncountable); also the -ing form of bicker (bicker, bickers, bickered, bickering)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Arguing about small, unimportant things, again and again. 2) (verb form) Squabbling in a petty way.
its sense in the lessons: Used in everyday life and stories about brothers, sisters and friends who argue over silly things. It tells the reader the argument is small and annoying, not serious. Phrases: constant bickering, stop bickering, bickering over.
examples from the lessons: Stop bickering, you two! | My brother and I were bickering about who got the front seat. | The constant bickering made the car trip feel long. | They were bickering over the last biscuit. | After a while the bickering turned into laughter. | Mum is tired of all the bickering at bedtime. | The friends bickered but soon made up.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable as a noun. Verb: bicker; past bickered. Similar: squabbling, quarrelling (UK spelling), arguing. Bickering is smaller and sillier than a real fight.

part of speech: verb (bind, binds, bound, binding); noun (a bind — informal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To tie something tightly with string, rope or cloth. 2) To hold things together or make people feel close and united. 3) To make someone keep a promise or obey a rule or law. 4) To fix the pages of a book together inside a cover. 5) (noun, informal) A difficult situation; "in a bind" means in trouble. 6) (noun, UK informal) A boring or annoying task ("What a bind!").
its sense in the lessons: Used in stories (tie the prisoner's hands), first aid (bind a wound), science (flour and egg bind the mix), law and promises (bound by the rules). Phrases: in a bind, bind together, bound by, bound book.
examples from the lessons: The pirates bound his hands with rope. | Bind the wound with a clean bandage. | The egg will bind the ingredients together. | Friendship binds the class together. | We are bound by the rules of the game. | Our class poems were bound into a book. | I'm in a bit of a bind: I forgot my homework. | Washing up every night is such a bind. (UK informal)
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular: bind, bound, bound (not "binded"). "Bound" also means "certain" (it's bound to rain) and "going to" (bound for London). Noun: binding (book cover); adjective binding (a binding promise must be kept).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) To do with living things and how they grow and work, or with biology, the study of them. 2) Related by birth, not by adoption or marriage (biological parents). 3) (cleaning) Containing natural enzymes that break down dirt, as in biological washing powder.
its sense in the lessons: Used in science lessons (biological processes, biological weapons), adult life and family talk (a biological father), and on household products. It tells the reader something is about life, bodies or birth. Phrases: biological parents, biological clock, biological washing powder, biological science.
examples from the lessons: Growing and breathing are biological processes. | Sam lives with his adoptive family but knows his biological mother. | Biology is the study of biological life. | Mum uses non-biological washing powder for my skin. | Plants and animals are biological; rocks are not. | Scientists study the biological effects of pollution. | Your biological clock tells you when to sleep.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced by-o-LOJ-i-cal. From biology (study of life). A biological parent is the one whose genes you have; adoptive and step-parents are real parents too. Not the same as "bionic" or "organic".

meaning for a pupil: 1) (of eyes) Tired, watery or unable to see clearly, especially after sleep or crying. 2) Not clear, blurry.
its sense in the lessons: Used in stories and everyday life to describe someone just waking up or very tired. It paints a picture of rubbing tired eyes. Phrases: bleary-eyed, bleary eyes.
examples from the lessons: I came down for breakfast bleary-eyed. | His eyes were bleary after the long night. | The baby looked up with bleary eyes. | Dad was bleary after the late flight. | Through bleary eyes I saw the clock say six. | The children were bleary after the sleepover. | Her eyes were bleary from crying.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually about eyes or people who are tired. "Bleary-eyed" with a hyphen. Similar: sleepy, blurry. Not the same as "blurry" for photos, though close.

part of speech: noun (a blob, blobs); verb (blob, blobs, blobbed, blobbing — informal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A small round lump of a thick liquid, like paint, glue or jam. 2) A shape or thing that is hard to see clearly, without a clear outline. 3) (verb, informal) To put small lumps of something somewhere.
its sense in the lessons: Used in art lessons (a blob of paint), cooking (a blob of cream) and science (a blob of jelly). In stories it can describe a strange shape or a slimy monster. Phrases: a blob of glue, blob of cream, just a blob.
examples from the lessons: Put a blob of glue on each corner. | I dropped a blob of jam on my shirt. | The jellyfish looked like a clear blob in the water. | Through the fog the house was just a grey blob. | Add a blob of cream to the top of the pudding. | The slimy blob monster crept across the floor. | She blobbed paint onto the paper to make flowers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: blobs. Informal word; in science you may say "drop" or "lump". Past of the verb: blobbed (double b).

part of speech: verb (blurt, blurts, blurted, blurting) — usually "blurt out"
meaning for a pupil: 1) To say something suddenly, without thinking first, often something you should have kept secret.
its sense in the lessons: Used in stories and everyday life when someone speaks too quickly: they blurt out the answer or a secret. It tells the reader the words came out without control. In class, blurting out answers means not putting your hand up. Phrases: blurt out, blurt out the answer, blurt out a secret.
examples from the lessons: Tom blurted out the answer before the teacher finished. | She blurted out the secret about the surprise party. | "I broke it!" he blurted. | Try not to blurt out; put your hand up. | I blurted out the first thing that came into my head. | He blurted out that he was scared. | Oops, I blurted out the ending of the film.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually used with "out". Regular verb: blurted. Similar: burst out, let slip. Blurting is not lying; it is saying things too quickly.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A hat tied under the chin with ribbons, worn by babies or by women in the past. 2) (UK, Ireland, Australia, NZ) The metal cover over the engine at the front of a car (US: hood). 3) (Scotland) A soft flat cap worn by men.
its sense in the lessons: Used in history lessons (Victorian women in bonnets), everyday car talk in the UK and Australia (open the bonnet), and baby clothes. Phrases: Easter bonnet, under the bonnet, a bee in your bonnet (an idea you keep thinking about).
examples from the lessons: The baby wore a white bonnet in the sun. | Dad opened the bonnet to check the oil. | We made Easter bonnets with paper flowers. | In the old photo, Grandma's grandma wore a bonnet. | Steam came out from under the bonnet. | She has a bee in her bonnet about tidy desks. | The Victorian girl tied her bonnet under her chin.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: bonnets. Car meaning differs: UK bonnet = US hood; UK boot = US trunk. "A bee in your bonnet" is an idiom, not a real bee.

part of speech: noun (a bookie, bookies) — informal, short for bookmaker
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) A person or company that takes bets on races and games and pays out money to winners. 2) (informal, UK) The bookie's: a betting shop.
its sense in the lessons: Met in adult life and stories about horse racing, football betting and gambling. It tells the reader money is being bet. In safety and money lessons, gambling is shown as risky because most people lose. Phrases: the bookies' favourite, at the bookie's, bookies' odds.
examples from the lessons: Grandad put a small bet on a horse at the bookie's. | The bookies said that team was most likely to win. | That horse is the bookies' favourite. | There's a bookie's shop on the high street. | The bookie paid out ten pounds to the winner. | Gambling with a bookie can lose you a lot of money. | The odds at the bookie's changed before the race.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal, clipped from bookmaker. Countable: bookies. "The bookie's" (with apostrophe) means the betting shop. Gambling is only for adults. Has nothing to do with books for reading.

part of speech: noun (a breast, breasts); verb (breast — formal or literary)
meaning for a pupil: 1) One of the two soft round parts on the front of a woman's chest that can make milk to feed a baby. 2) The front of the chest of a person or animal. 3) (cooking) The meat from the chest of a bird, like chicken breast. 4) (literary) The heart, as a place of feelings ("hope in his breast"). 5) (verb) To reach the top of a hill or push through something with your chest.
its sense in the lessons: Used in science and health lessons (mammals feed babies breast milk), cooking (chicken breast), swimming (breaststroke) and old stories and poems for the chest or heart. Phrases: breastfeed, breaststroke, chicken breast, robin redbreast, make a clean breast of it (confess everything).
examples from the lessons: Mammals feed their babies with milk from the breast. | We had chicken breast with vegetables for tea. | The robin has a red breast. | I learned breaststroke at swimming lessons. | She held the kitten to her breast. | He decided to make a clean breast of it and tell the truth. | The runners breasted the hill and saw the finish line.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: breasts. Pronounced BREST (rhymes with rest). A normal science and body word, not rude; use it calmly and correctly. Idiom "make a clean breast of it" = confess everything.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (church, Bible) Fellow members of a church or religious group, used to address them in old or formal language ("Dearly beloved brethren"). 2) (old-fashioned) Brothers. 3) Members of the same group or profession.
its sense in the lessons: Met in the Bible, old hymns, church services and history. It tells the reader the speaker sees others as family in faith. Some church groups call themselves Brethren. Phrases: dearly beloved brethren, brethren in Christ.
examples from the lessons: The preacher began, "My dear brethren." | In the Bible, Joseph forgave his brethren. | The monks prayed with their brethren every morning. | He greeted his brethren at the church meeting. | The farmers helped their brethren in the next valley. | The old hymn calls all Christians brethren. | The judge was respected by her legal brethren.
note for the reader of a maths problem: An old plural of brother, now used mostly in church or formal speech. Ordinary plural today: brothers. It can include women in church use (like "brothers and sisters"). Pronounced BRETH-ren.

part of speech: noun (a bribe, bribes); verb (bribe, bribes, bribed, bribing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Money or a gift given to someone to make them do something dishonest or unfair, such as break a rule. 2) (verb) To offer someone money or a gift to make them do what you want, often wrongly. 3) (informal, joking) A treat given to get a child to do something ("a sweet as a bribe").
its sense in the lessons: Used in stories, law and ethics lessons (bribing a judge or police officer is a crime) and jokingly in family life. It tells the reader someone is trying to buy a decision. Phrases: take a bribe, offer a bribe, bribe someone with.
examples from the lessons: The guard took a bribe and let the thief go. | It is against the law to bribe a police officer. | Mum bribed us with ice cream to tidy our rooms. | The judge refused the bribe. | I won't take a bribe, said the referee. | My little brother can be bribed with stickers. | Offering a bribe can lead to prison.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: bribery (the crime). Verb bribe, bribed (drop e, add -ed). A reward for good work is not a bribe; a bribe is to make someone do something unfair. In families the word is often used as a joke.

part of speech: noun (a bugger, buggers); verb (bugger — rude); exclamation (bugger! — rude)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (rude, UK, Australia, Ireland) A swear word said when something goes wrong ("Bugger! I missed the bus"). 2) (rude) An annoying or difficult person or thing ("This lid is a bugger to open"). 3) (informal, UK, Australia, affectionate) A cheeky person, often a child ("You little bugger!"). 4) (rude, UK) "Bugger off" means go away; "bugger all" means nothing; "bugger up" means spoil.
its sense in the lessons: Heard in real speech in the UK, Ireland, Australia and NZ as mild-to-strong swearing; children should not use it at school. In stories it shows a character is cross or rough-spoken. In Australia it can sound almost friendly. Phrases: bugger off, bugger all, bugger it, silly bugger, lucky bugger.
examples from the lessons: Bugger! Dad said when he dropped the plate. (rude) | This jar is a bugger to open. (rude) | "Bugger off and leave me alone!" the old man shouted. (rude) | We got bugger all done today. (rude) | "You cheeky little bugger," Grandad laughed. (affectionate, rude) | Don't say "bugger" at school; it is a swear word. | "Lucky bugger won the raffle again," said Uncle Pete. (rude)
note for the reader of a maths problem: A swear word: rude, especially in formal places; do not use it with teachers. Milder in Australia and New Zealand than in the UK, and rare and odd-sounding in the USA. Polite replacements: "Oh no!", "bother", "darn". Countable: buggers.

part of speech: noun (a burden, burdens); verb (burden, burdens, burdened, burdening)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A heavy load that you carry. 2) A difficult duty, worry or problem that is hard to deal with. 3) (verb) To give someone a heavy load or a worry. 4) (law) Burden of proof: the duty to show that something is true.
its sense in the lessons: Used in stories (a donkey carrying a burden), feelings (worries as a burden), adult life (money burdens, debts) and law (burden of proof). It tells the reader someone carries something heavy, in the body or the mind. Phrases: a burden to, ease the burden, burden of proof, a weight off my shoulders.
examples from the lessons: The donkey carried a heavy burden up the hill. | She didn't want to be a burden to her family. | Sharing a worry with a friend eases the burden. | Homework felt like a burden this week. | Don't burden yourself with too many clubs. | In court, the burden of proof is on the person who accuses. | Debt can be a heavy burden for a family.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: burdens. Adjective: burdensome. Similar: load, weight, strain. "Beast of burden" means an animal that carries loads, like a donkey or camel.

part of speech: adjective (burdened); also past tense and past participle of burden
meaning for a pupil: 1) Carrying a heavy load. 2) Weighed down by worries, duties, debts or problems.
its sense in the lessons: Used in stories and adult life to describe someone weighed down, like a family burdened with debt or a hiker burdened with a heavy pack. Phrases: burdened with, burdened by, heavily burdened.
examples from the lessons: The hikers were burdened with heavy backpacks. | He felt burdened by the secret. | Families can be burdened with debt. | The camel was burdened with goods for the market. | She was burdened with too much work. | Don't feel burdened; we'll help you. | The old tree was burdened by snow.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Followed by "with" (things) or "by" (worries). Opposite: unburdened, free. Pronounced BUR-dend.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A terrible event that causes great damage, loss or suffering, like an earthquake or a flood. 2) (informal, joking) A small accident or mess made to sound big ("It's a calamity: I've lost my pencil!").
its sense in the lessons: Used in geography and news (natural calamities), stories (a great calamity struck the kingdom) and jokingly in everyday life. It tells the reader something really bad, or comically bad, happened. Phrases: natural calamity, a calamity struck, Calamity Jane (a nickname for someone who has many accidents).
examples from the lessons: The flood was a calamity for the whole village. | A great calamity struck the kingdom. | Spilling the paint on the carpet was a calamity. | Earthquakes are natural calamities. | Oh no, what a calamity, we've run out of milk! | The war brought calamity to many families. | Losing the map was a calamity on our hike.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: calamities (y becomes ies). Adjective: calamitous. Similar: disaster, catastrophe. Sometimes used as a joke for small problems; context tells you.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The act of calling off something that was planned, such as a match, flight or appointment. 2) A place or booking that becomes free because someone else cancelled it. 3) (maths) Removing the same number or factor from the top and bottom of a fraction, or terms that make zero, to simplify.
its sense in the lessons: Used in everyday life (cancellation of a train or match because of weather), in money (cancellation fees) and in maths (cancellation in fractions). Phrases: last-minute cancellation, cancellation fee, wait for a cancellation.
examples from the lessons: The cancellation of the school trip was a big disappointment. | Snow caused the cancellation of all flights. | We got a dentist appointment because of a cancellation. | There is a cancellation fee if you change your booking. | In maths, cancellation makes 6/8 into 3/4. | The cancellation was announced on the radio. | The concert's cancellation upset the fans.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelled with double l in both UK and US: cancellation. But the verb past form differs: UK cancelled, US canceled. In maths, cancelling means dividing top and bottom by the same number; the value of the fraction stays the same.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (church) A song or hymn with words from the Bible, sung in church services, such as the Magnificat. 2) (literary) A song of praise.
its sense in the lessons: Met in church life and choir: canticles are sung at morning and evening prayer. It tells the reader about a holy song of praise. Phrases: the canticle of Mary, sing the canticles.
examples from the lessons: The choir sang a canticle at evening prayer. | The Magnificat is the canticle of Mary. | We learned a canticle for the Christmas service. | The monks sang canticles before dawn. | A canticle is like a psalm sung in church. | The organist played softly before the canticle. | St Francis wrote the Canticle of the Sun.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: canticles. A church word; similar: hymn, psalm, chant. A psalm comes from the Book of Psalms; a canticle comes from other parts of the Bible.

part of speech: noun (a carriageway, carriageways) — mainly UK, Ireland, Australia, NZ
meaning for a pupil: 1) The part of a road that vehicles drive on. 2) One side of a big road; a dual carriageway has two lanes each way with a strip in the middle.
its sense in the lessons: Used in road safety lessons and news (traffic on the northbound carriageway) and in everyday UK travel. It tells the reader about the main road surface. Phrases: dual carriageway, single carriageway, northbound carriageway, the carriageway was closed.
examples from the lessons: Never walk on the carriageway; stay on the pavement. | We drove along a dual carriageway to the beach. | A lorry broke down on the southbound carriageway. | Cyclists should keep to the edge of the carriageway. | Both carriageways were closed after the crash. | The fox ran across the carriageway. | A dual carriageway has a barrier down the middle.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: carriageways. Mostly UK, Irish, Australian and NZ English; in the USA people say "lanes" or "divided highway". From "carriage" (old word for a vehicle) + way.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (church) A summary of the main beliefs of a Christian church, set out as questions and answers, used to teach the faith. 2) (church) Lessons in which children or new members learn these beliefs. 3) A set of questions asked one after another, like a test.
its sense in the lessons: Met in church life: children learn the catechism before First Communion or Confirmation. It tells the reader someone is learning the beliefs of their faith. Phrases: the Catholic catechism, learn the catechism, catechism class.
examples from the lessons: My cousin goes to catechism class on Saturdays. | The catechism asks, "Who made you?" | She learned the catechism before her Confirmation. | The priest taught the catechism to the children. | Our church gives every family a copy of the catechism. | Grandma still remembers her catechism from long ago. | Mum put me through a catechism of questions about where I'd been.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced KAT-a-kiz-um. Countable. Related: catechist (teacher of it), catechise. The last sense is a playful use for many questions.

part of speech: noun (caution; a caution, cautions); verb (caution, cautions, cautioned, cautioning)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Great care to avoid danger or mistakes. 2) A warning, like a sign saying "Caution: wet floor". 3) (law, UK) An official warning from the police instead of a charge. 4) (verb) To warn someone to be careful or not to do something again.
its sense in the lessons: Used in safety (caution signs, use caution when crossing), science (take caution with chemicals), law and stories. It tells the reader to slow down and be careful. Phrases: with caution, caution: wet floor, err on the side of caution, throw caution to the wind.
examples from the lessons: Use caution when crossing the road. | The sign said "Caution: wet floor." | Handle the glass beakers with caution. | The police gave him a caution for shouting in the street. | The teacher cautioned us not to run in the corridor. | She threw caution to the wind and jumped into the lake. | It's best to err on the side of caution and take a coat.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable for the care (with caution), countable for a warning (a caution). Adjective: cautious; adverb cautiously. "Throw caution to the wind" means stop being careful. "Err on the side of caution" means choose the safer way.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Done or made to celebrate something happy, like a birthday or a win.
its sense in the lessons: Used in everyday life and stories: a celebratory cake, a celebratory dance, a celebratory meal after a match. It tells the reader there is joy about something good. Phrases: celebratory meal, celebratory mood, celebratory drink.
examples from the lessons: We had a celebratory pizza after winning the match. | The team did a celebratory dance on the pitch. | There was a celebratory mood in the classroom on the last day. | Dad baked a celebratory cake when I passed my swimming test. | The players poured celebratory water over the coach. | A celebratory cheer went up from the crowd. | The village held a celebratory party when the bridge opened.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Goes before a noun (a celebratory meal). Pronounced SEL-a-bray-tor-ee (UK) or se-LEB-ra-tor-ee (US). Related: celebrate, celebration.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person or team that tries to beat the champion or winner in a competition. 2) A person who questions whether something is right or true.
its sense in the lessons: Used in sport and games (the challenger fights the champion), in elections (a challenger tries to win a seat), and in debate. It tells the reader who is trying to take the top place. Phrases: the challenger to, a new challenger, strong challenger.
examples from the lessons: The young challenger beat the champion in the final. | A new challenger has entered the chess club. | The challenger trained hard for the boxing match. | She was a strong challenger for the title. | In the election, the challenger won more votes. | Every challenger must pass three tests. | The challenger questioned the referee's decision.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: challengers. From challenge. Opposite role: champion, holder. Does not always mean the person is rude; it means they compete or question.

part of speech: noun (a champ, champs — informal); verb (champ, champs, champed, champing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) Short for champion, a winner. 2) (informal) A friendly word for someone who did well ("Good job, champ!"). 3) (verb) To bite or chew noisily, as horses do. 4) Champing (or chomping) at the bit: very impatient and eager to start.
its sense in the lessons: Used in everyday talk and sport, often by parents and coaches to praise a child. Also used in stories about horses. Phrases: world champ, you're a champ, champing at the bit.
examples from the lessons: She's the new spelling champ! | Well done, champ, you scored a goal! | Dad called me a champ for helping. | The horse champed at its hay. | We were champing at the bit to go outside. | The boxing champ held up his belt. | You're a real champ for carrying all the bags.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal shortening of champion. Used kindly as a nickname. "Champing at the bit" is also said "chomping at the bit". Not the same as chimp (a chimpanzee).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person or thing that changes something. 2) A machine that changes things, like a coin changer that gives you smaller coins. 3) Game changer: something that changes a situation in a big way.
its sense in the lessons: Used mostly in phrases: game changer, money changer, coin changer, nappy changer (a changing table). In stories about the Bible, Jesus turned over the tables of the money changers. Phrases: game changer, money changer, coin changer.
examples from the lessons: The new playground slide was a game changer for our break times. | Put a note in the coin changer to get coins. | Jesus drove the money changers out of the temple. | The internet was a real game changer. | My bike's gear changer is broken. | A good teacher can be a life changer. | The baby changer is in the toilets.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: changers. Mostly used in compound phrases. "Game changer" is informal. From the verb change + -er (the one who does it).

part of speech: noun (a chant, chants); verb (chant, chants, chanted, chanting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Words or a phrase repeated over and over in a rhythm, often by a crowd. 2) (church) A simple tune used to sing prayers or psalms, like plainchant or Gregorian chant. 3) (verb) To say or sing words again and again in a rhythm.
its sense in the lessons: Used in sport (fans chant), protests, playground games, and church music. In school, children chant times tables to learn them. It tells the reader there is a strong repeated rhythm. Phrases: football chant, chant a name, Gregorian chant, chant times tables.
examples from the lessons: The fans chanted the team's name. | We chant our times tables every morning. | The monks sang a slow chant in the chapel. | "We want more!" chanted the crowd. | The playground chant goes "one, two, buckle my shoe". | The protesters chanted for change. | Gregorian chant is very old church music.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: chants. Regular verb: chanted. Not the same as "shout" (a chant is repeated with rhythm). Some football chants are rude; not all are school-friendly.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A two-wheeled cart pulled by horses, used in ancient times for war and racing. 2) (literary) Any grand carriage.
its sense in the lessons: Met in history lessons (Romans, Egyptians, Celts like Boudicca), Bible stories and myths. It tells the reader about ancient battles or races. Phrases: chariot race, war chariot, Swing Low, Sweet Chariot (a famous song).
examples from the lessons: The Romans raced chariots in the Circus Maximus. | Boudicca rode into battle in a chariot. | In the Bible, Elijah was taken up in a chariot of fire. | The Egyptian king stood in his golden chariot. | Two horses pulled the chariot. | We made a model chariot in history class. | The crowd cheered as the chariots raced round the track.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: chariots. Pronounced CHA-ree-ot. The driver is a charioteer. An old word for history and stories, not for modern cars.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who chooses. 2) Beggars can't be choosers: a saying meaning when you need help, you must accept what you are given.
its sense in the lessons: Mostly met in the saying "beggars can't be choosers". Also used for the person who picks in games ("the chooser picks the team"). Phrases: beggars can't be choosers, the chooser picks.
examples from the lessons: Beggars can't be choosers, so I ate the cold pizza. | The chooser picks the first player for the team. | I'm the chooser today; we'll watch a cartoon. | We only had blue paint left, but beggars can't be choosers. | Each chooser gets one sticker. | Who is the chooser for the next game? | The chooser of the winning name gets a prize.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: choosers. From choose + -er. Rare outside the saying. Note spelling: choose (double o), chooser.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To do with a choir or sung by a choir. 2) (school) Said or spoken by a group together, like choral reading or a choral speaking of a poem.
its sense in the lessons: Used in music and church (choral music, choral society) and school (choral reading of a poem). It tells the reader that many voices are together. Phrases: choral music, choral society, choral speaking, choral reading.
examples from the lessons: The church holds a choral concert every Christmas. | Our class did a choral reading of the poem. | Grandma sings in a choral society. | Choral music filled the cathedral. | The choral group practised every Tuesday. | We won the choral speaking prize at the festival. | Evensong is a choral service.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced KOR-al. Do not confuse with coral (sea creatures and their reef), which sounds almost the same, or with chorale (a hymn tune). Related: choir, chorus.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) To move round and round inside something and come back, like blood around the body. 2) To pass from person to person or place to place, like news, money or a letter. 3) To move around a party and talk to many people.
its sense in the lessons: Used in science (blood circulates, air circulates), school (a letter is circulated to parents), money and news (rumours circulate). It tells the reader something moves around. Phrases: blood circulates, rumours circulate, circulate a letter, circulate around the room.
examples from the lessons: The heart pumps blood to circulate around the body. | A letter was circulated to all parents. | Open the window to let the air circulate. | Rumours circulated about a new teacher. | Old coins still circulate in some countries. | At the party Mum circulated and talked to everyone. | Water circulates through the pipes to the radiators.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Noun: circulation (blood circulation; the circulation of a newspaper). In science, the circulatory system is the heart, blood and blood vessels.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To do with a town or city and its official life, like a civic centre or civic building. 2) To do with being a citizen and the duties of people in a community, like voting or helping.
its sense in the lessons: Used in citizenship lessons (civic duty, civic pride) and in town life (civic centre, civic leaders). It tells the reader something belongs to or serves the community. Phrases: civic duty, civic pride, civic centre, civic leaders, civics (a school subject).
examples from the lessons: Voting is a civic duty. | The concert is in the civic centre. | The town showed great civic pride after the cleanup. | Picking up litter is a small civic act. | The mayor and other civic leaders opened the park. | In civics class we learned how laws are made. | The museum is a civic building, owned by the town.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Goes before a noun. "Civics" is the study of citizenship (a school subject, mainly US). Related: city, citizen, civil. Not the same as civil (polite; or not military).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Being clear and easy to understand. 2) Being clear to see through or see well, like clean water or a sharp picture. 3) Clear thinking, when you understand something well.
its sense in the lessons: Used in writing lessons (write with clarity), science and photography (clarity of water or image), and in feelings ("a moment of clarity"). It tells the reader that something is clear. Phrases: for clarity, with clarity, moment of clarity, clarity of thought.
examples from the lessons: Write your answer with clarity so the teacher can follow it. | The clarity of the lake let us see the fish. | The new TV has amazing picture clarity. | For clarity, use a ruler for your graph. | After a good sleep I had more clarity about the problem. | The teacher explained with great clarity. | Diamonds are judged by their clarity.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Adjective: clear; verb: clarify. Opposite: confusion, vagueness. "For clarity" means "to make it clear".

meaning for a pupil: 1) Being clean or keeping things clean. 2) The habit of keeping yourself and your home clean.
its sense in the lessons: Used in health, hygiene and science lessons (cleanliness stops germs), in kitchens and hospitals, and in the old saying "Cleanliness is next to godliness". It tells the reader about hygiene and care. Phrases: personal cleanliness, cleanliness and hygiene, cleanliness is next to godliness.
