examples from the lessons: Cleanliness helps stop germs spreading. | The restaurant got top marks for cleanliness. | Grandma always said cleanliness is next to godliness. | Hospitals need great cleanliness. | Personal cleanliness means washing and brushing your teeth. | The cat's cleanliness surprised us; it licks itself all day. | Cleanliness in the kitchen keeps food safe.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced KLEN-li-ness (the first part sounds like "clen", not "clean"). Uncountable. Related: clean, cleanly. Similar: hygiene, tidiness.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Working together with others to make or do something. 2) A piece of work made by people working together. 3) (history, negative) Helping an enemy who has taken over your country, especially in a war.
its sense in the lessons: Very common in school (group work, collaboration on projects), science (scientists' collaboration) and music (a collaboration between singers). In history, collaboration can mean helping the enemy, which is seen as wrong. Phrases: in collaboration with, close collaboration, a collaboration between.
examples from the lessons: Our class mural was a collaboration between all the pupils. | The project was made in collaboration with the local museum. | Good collaboration means listening to each other. | The two singers released a collaboration. | Scientists around the world worked in collaboration. | Collaboration helps us solve bigger problems. | In the war, collaboration with the enemy was punished.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable for the idea, countable for a piece of work (a collaboration). Verb: collaborate; person: collaborator. Similar: teamwork, cooperation. Spelling: double l, one b.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (adjective) Done or shared by all members of a group together. 2) (noun) A group of people who work together and share what they make or own. 3) (grammar) A collective noun is a word for a group, like a flock of sheep, a team or a herd.
its sense in the lessons: Used in grammar lessons (collective nouns: a pride of lions, a swarm of bees), citizenship (collective decisions) and everyday life (collective effort). Phrases: collective noun, collective effort, collective responsibility, a farmers' collective.
examples from the lessons: Flock is a collective noun for sheep. | It was a collective effort to clean the beach. | The class made a collective decision to raise money for the zoo. | A pride of lions is a collective noun. | The artists formed a collective and shared a studio. | We felt a collective sigh of relief when the test ended. | A murder of crows is a funny collective noun.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb: collectively. With collective nouns, UK English often uses a plural verb (the team are winning), US uses singular (the team is winning). Related: collect, collection.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An event, ceremony or thing that helps people remember and honour a person or an important event. 2) The act of remembering someone or something with respect.
its sense in the lessons: Used in history, citizenship and church: Remembrance Day, Anzac Day and memorials are commemorations of people who died in wars. It tells the reader that people are remembering with respect. Phrases: in commemoration of, a service of commemoration, commemoration ceremony.
examples from the lessons: A statue was built in commemoration of the brave nurse. | The school held a commemoration for soldiers who died in the wars. | Anzac Day is a commemoration in Australia and New Zealand. | We planted a tree in commemoration of our old head teacher. | The church holds a commemoration of the saint every year. | The stamps were printed in commemoration of the anniversary. | The commemoration ended with two minutes of silence.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: commemorate; adjective: commemorative (a commemorative coin). Spelling: double m then one m: co-mm-e-m-oration. Similar: memorial, remembrance. A serious, respectful word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To praise someone or something, especially officially or in public. 2) (formal) To recommend something as good. 3) (church) To give someone into the care of another, especially into God's care ("I commend her to God").
its sense in the lessons: Used in school reports and awards (commended for effort), news (a firefighter commended for bravery), and church prayers. It tells the reader someone is praised. Phrases: highly commended, commend for, commend to God.
examples from the lessons: The head teacher commended the class for their good behaviour. | Her poem was highly commended in the competition. | The firefighter was commended for his bravery. | I would commend this book to anyone who loves animals. | At the funeral the priest commended her soul to God. | The coach commended our teamwork. | The judges commended every entry.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; plain words: praise, recommend. "Highly commended" is a prize just below the winners. Noun: commendation. Do not confuse with command (give an order) or comment.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Deserving praise, worthy of being admired.
its sense in the lessons: Used in school reports, speeches and exam texts: commendable effort, commendable honesty. It tells the reader that the action was good, even if the result was not perfect. Phrases: commendable effort, highly commendable, commendable courage.
examples from the lessons: Your effort this term has been commendable. | It was commendable of him to return the lost wallet. | She showed commendable patience with the little ones. | The team made a commendable effort in the rain. | The report praised the school's commendable work on safety. | His honesty was commendable. | That's a commendable idea; let's try it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; plain words: praiseworthy, good, admirable. Related: commend, commendation. Often used for effort or behaviour rather than talent.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (church) The part of a funeral when the body is buried or cremated, with a final prayer. 2) (law) Officially sending someone to prison, court or a hospital. 3) Promising yourself firmly to something (more often: commitment).
its sense in the lessons: Met in church and adult life (the committal service at the graveside) and in law (committal to trial). It tells the reader about a serious formal step. Phrases: committal service, committal to prison, committal for trial.
examples from the lessons: After the church service, the family went to the cemetery for the committal. | The vicar read the words of committal at the graveside. | The judge ordered his committal to prison. | The case was sent for committal to a higher court. | The committal was short and quiet. | Only close family went to the committal. | During the committal the coffin was lowered into the grave.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: committals. Formal; mostly used for funerals and law. Not the same as "commitment" (a promise or dedication) or "acquittal" (being found not guilty). Spelling: double m, double t.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (adjective) Ordinary and happening often, not surprising. 2) (noun) Something ordinary and common. 3) (noun) A remark said so often that it is no longer interesting.
its sense in the lessons: Used in history and science (things that were rare are now commonplace, like phones), and in stories to show something is normal. Phrases: commonplace now, a commonplace event, become commonplace.
examples from the lessons: Mobile phones are now commonplace. | Snow is commonplace in Canada in winter. | Seeing kangaroos is commonplace in parts of Australia. | Electric cars are becoming commonplace. | In the old days, walking miles to school was commonplace. | Rain is a commonplace in Ireland. | It is commonplace for pupils to have a school email.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Written as one word. Similar: ordinary, common, usual, everyday. Opposite: rare, unusual, extraordinary.

part of speech: adjective (compelling); also the -ing form of compel (compel, compels, compelled, compelling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) So interesting or exciting that you want to keep watching or reading. 2) So strong or convincing that you have to believe or agree, like a compelling reason or argument. 3) (verb form) Forcing someone to do something.
its sense in the lessons: Used in reading lessons (a compelling story), debates and science (compelling evidence), and in formal texts. It tells the reader something is very strong or gripping. Phrases: compelling evidence, compelling reason, compelling story, compelling argument.
examples from the lessons: The book was so compelling I couldn't put it down. | There is compelling evidence that exercise is good for you. | She gave a compelling reason for being late. | The film's story was compelling from start to end. | His argument was compelling, so we agreed. | The detective found compelling proof. | Hunger was compelling them to keep looking for food.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb compel = force (be compelled to do something). Adverb: compellingly. Similar: gripping, convincing, persuasive. Spelling: double l in compelling, compelled.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Wanting very much to win or to do better than others. 2) Involving competition, like competitive sports. 3) (money) As good as or cheaper than others, like competitive prices.
its sense in the lessons: Used in sport, school (competitive games), and shops (competitive prices). It tells the reader about trying to win or being equal to rivals. Phrases: competitive sport, very competitive, competitive prices, competitive spirit.
examples from the lessons: My brother is very competitive, even at board games. | Football is a competitive sport. | The shop has competitive prices. | Getting into that school is very competitive. | Our class has a competitive spirit on sports day. | Being competitive is fine, but be a good loser too. | The team played a competitive match against the champions.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: compet-i-tive (not "competative"). Noun: competition; verb: compete; person: competitor. Adverb: competitively. Opposite: uncompetitive, cooperative.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Obeying a rule, law, request or order. 2) The habit of doing what other people want, sometimes too easily.
its sense in the lessons: A formal word used in law, business and safety (compliance with safety rules), and in exam texts. It tells the reader whether people follow the rules. Phrases: in compliance with, compliance with the law, safety compliance.
examples from the lessons: All toys must be in compliance with safety rules. | The school checked compliance with the uniform policy. | Compliance with the law is everyone's duty. | The inspector made sure of the restaurant's compliance with hygiene rules. | He nodded in compliance. | Compliance with seatbelt laws saves lives. | The company was fined for lack of compliance.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Verb: comply (comply with); adjective: compliant. Formal; plain words: obeying, following the rules. Not the same as "compliment" (praise) or "complement" (something that completes).

meaning for a pupil: 1) One of the parts that something is made of, especially a machine or a system. 2) (science) A part of a circuit, such as a bulb, battery, wire or switch. 3) (maths) A part of something larger, like the parts of a vector.
its sense in the lessons: Used in science (circuit components), technology and design (computer components), maths, and everyday life (the components of a healthy diet). Phrases: electrical component, key component, component parts, components of a circuit.
examples from the lessons: A bulb, a wire and a battery are components of a circuit. | The car factory makes engine components. | Exercise is an important component of a healthy life. | Draw the circuit using the right component symbols. | The kit has all the components you need to build the robot. | Each component must be checked for safety. | Listening is a key component of good teamwork.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: components. Stress: com-PO-nent. Similar: part, piece, element, ingredient. In maths and science, components together make the whole.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Being calm and in control of your feelings, especially in a difficult or stressful moment.
its sense in the lessons: Used in stories and sport: a player keeps her composure under pressure; someone loses composure and cries. It tells the reader how calm a character is. Phrases: keep your composure, lose your composure, regain composure.
examples from the lessons: She kept her composure even when the crowd booed. | He lost his composure and started to cry. | After a deep breath, I regained my composure. | The goalkeeper showed great composure in the penalty shootout. | The teacher spoke with composure during the fire alarm. | It's hard to keep your composure when you're very nervous. | The pilot's composure kept the passengers calm.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Adjective: composed (calm). Similar: calmness, self-control. Not related in meaning to "compose" a song, though it comes from the same root.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A very strong wish to do something that is hard to stop, even when you know you shouldn't. 2) Being forced to do something by a rule or by another person ("under compulsion").
its sense in the lessons: Used in stories and health (a compulsion to check things), in adult life (a compulsion to gamble), and in law (no compulsion to attend). It tells the reader about a strong force inside or outside a person. Phrases: under compulsion, a compulsion to, no compulsion.
examples from the lessons: I felt a compulsion to look in the box. | There is no compulsion to join the club; it's your choice. | He had a compulsion to wash his hands again and again. | She signed the paper under compulsion. | The compulsion to eat sweets can be strong. | Some people have a compulsion to gamble, which can harm their family. | Attendance at school is a legal compulsion for children.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: compulsory (must be done, like compulsory homework) and compulsive (can't stop doing it). Verb: compel. Do not mix up compulsory (a rule) with compulsive (a habit you can't stop).

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a way that proves something completely and leaves no doubt. 2) In a final way that settles the matter.
its sense in the lessons: Used in science, maths and detective stories: the test proved conclusively. It tells the reader that the answer is certain. Phrases: prove conclusively, show conclusively, conclusively won.
examples from the lessons: The experiment showed conclusively that plants need light. | The fingerprints proved conclusively who took the cake. | The team won conclusively, ten goals to nil. | Scientists cannot yet say conclusively why this happens. | The video showed conclusively that the ball crossed the line. | The test results conclusively ruled out an infection. | We can't conclusively say who won until we count again.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: conclusive (conclusive proof); noun: conclusion. Opposite: inconclusively. In maths, a proof that works for all cases shows something conclusively; one example alone does not.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Depending on something else happening first; only true or allowed if a condition is met. 2) (grammar) A sentence or verb form with "if", like "If it rains, we will stay in." 3) (maths, computing) A conditional statement says "if this, then that".
its sense in the lessons: Used in grammar lessons (conditional sentences), computing and maths (if-then statements), and everyday life (a conditional offer, "your pocket money is conditional on doing chores"). It tells the reader something only happens if something else does. Phrases: conditional on, conditional offer, conditional sentence, conditional love.
examples from the lessons: My trip to the park is conditional on finishing my homework. | "If you heat ice, it melts" is a conditional sentence. | In coding, a conditional tells the computer what to do if something is true. | She got a conditional offer from the university. | The prize is conditional on good behaviour. | Use the conditional: "I would help if I could." | Parents' love should not be conditional on good marks.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually "conditional on" (or "upon") something. Opposite: unconditional (no conditions, like unconditional love). Adverb: conditionally. In maths logic: "if P, then Q" does not mean "if Q, then P".

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) The act of giving someone an honour, a title, a degree or a right in an official way. 2) (formal, rare) The act of talking things over with others; this sense is usually said as «conferring» or «conference».
its sense in the lessons: A stiff, official word met in exam texts, school prize-giving reports and news about universities and awards. It tells the reader that something was given by someone with authority, not just handed over. Phrases: «the conferral of a degree», «conferral of citizenship», «conferral of an award». In everyday speech people say «giving» or «being given» instead.
examples from the lessons: The conferral of degrees takes place in the great hall. | Her conferral of the gold medal was the proudest moment of the evening. | The conferral of citizenship came after a long wait and a short ceremony. | After the conferral of the title, the knight stood up and bowed. | The school board approved the conferral of a special award on the lollipop lady. | Grandad keeps a photo of the conferral of his apprenticeship certificate. | The conferral of honorary membership surprised the old coach.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comes from the verb «confer» (to give officially; also to discuss). Countable but mostly used in the singular with «of»: «the conferral of …». Formal; in a story for children «giving» or «awarding» sounds more natural. Do not confuse with «conference» (a meeting) or «referral» (sending someone on to another doctor or service).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Tiny pieces of coloured paper thrown into the air at weddings, parties and parades. 2) Anything that falls or lies about in many tiny bright bits, like confetti: «a confetti of petals». 3) Small sugar sweets or sprinkles used to decorate cakes (sometimes called «confetti sprinkles»).
its sense in the lessons: Used in stories about weddings, birthdays, sports wins and New Year parties; it tells the reader the scene is happy and noisy. In school, art lessons use paper confetti for collage; science teachers warn that plastic or glitter confetti harms nature, so many places now use paper or dried-petal confetti. Phrases: «throw confetti», «a confetti cannon», «covered in confetti», «confetti everywhere».
examples from the lessons: The guests threw confetti over the bride and groom. | There was confetti in my hair for days after the party. | The winning team was showered with confetti on the stage. | We made confetti with a hole punch and old magazines. | The church asks people to use only paper confetti. | Mum sighed when she saw the confetti all over the carpet. | Autumn leaves fell like confetti in the wind. | The cupcakes were topped with rainbow confetti sprinkles.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: say «some confetti», «a handful of confetti», never «a confetti» or «confettis». It takes a singular verb: «The confetti was everywhere». It comes from Italian, where the word first meant small sweets thrown at carnivals. Glitter is not the same as confetti: glitter is tiny shiny plastic bits.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To take something away from someone, usually as a punishment or because a rule says it is not allowed, often keeping it for a while. 2) (law) For police or the government to take someone's property officially, for example because it was used in a crime.
its sense in the lessons: Very common in school life: a teacher may confiscate a phone, sweets or a toy during class and give it back at the end of the day. In news and stories, police or customs officers confiscate illegal goods, weapons or stolen things. It tells the reader that someone in charge took something by right of a rule. Phrases: «confiscate a phone», «have something confiscated», «confiscated by customs».
examples from the lessons: The teacher confiscated my phone because it rang in maths. | If you bring that slime to class again, I'll confiscate it. | My yo-yo was confiscated until home time. | Customs officers confiscated the fruit at the airport because of the rules on pests. | Police confiscated the stolen bikes. | Dad threatened to confiscate the games console if we kept fighting. | The referee confiscated the ball from the boys who kept kicking it at the windows.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: confiscated, confiscating. Often used in the passive: «It was confiscated». To confiscate is not the same as to steal: the person taking it has the right to do so under the rules. Stress on the first syllable: CON-fis-cate.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The act of taking something away from someone because of a rule or as a punishment. 2) (law) The official taking of property by police, a court or the government.
its sense in the lessons: Used in school rules («Phones seen in class are liable to confiscation»), in news about police and customs, and in history lessons where kings or governments took land from people. It tells the reader that the taking was official and had a reason. Phrases: «confiscation of property», «face confiscation», «risk confiscation».
examples from the lessons: The school rules say that toys in class may lead to confiscation. | The confiscation of his skateboard made Sam sulk all afternoon. | The court ordered the confiscation of the money from the robbery. | In history we read about the confiscation of land from farmers. | Sweets brought into the exam room face confiscation. | After the third confiscation, Mia stopped bringing her cards to school.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun form of «confiscate». Countable (one confiscation, two confiscations) but often used without a/an: «risk confiscation». Formal; in speech children usually say «it got taken off me» (UK) or «it got taken away».

part of speech: noun (congratulation, congratulations) — almost always plural; interjection (Congratulations!)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Congratulations: words you say to show you are happy for someone who has done well or had good news. 2) Congratulations! — an exclamation said to someone on their success or happy event. 3) (formal, singular) The act of congratulating someone: «a letter of congratulation».
its sense in the lessons: Used on cards, in speeches, assemblies, sports days and family news (a new baby, a wedding, passing a test). It tells the reader that someone is praised and others share their joy. Phrases: «Congratulations on …», «Congratulations to …», «send my congratulations», «a card of congratulation», «Congrats!» (informal). Sometimes said sarcastically when someone did something silly: «Well, congratulations, you broke it.»
examples from the lessons: Congratulations on winning the spelling bee! | Congratulations to Year 5 for the best attendance this term. | Please give my congratulations to your sister on her new baby. | We all signed a card of congratulation for our teacher's wedding. | The head teacher read out a list of congratulations in assembly. | "I passed my swimming test!" "Congrats, that's brilliant!" | Oh, congratulations, you've spilt juice on the homework again (sarcastic). | The mayor sent a letter of congratulation to the winning team.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The everyday form is the plural «congratulations», even to one person. Use «on» for the thing done: «congratulations on your win», and «to» for the person: «congratulations to Ben». Spelling trap: it is «congratulations» with a T in the middle, not «congradulations» (people mix it up with «graduation»). «Congrats» is informal.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To join two or more things together so they touch or are linked: «connect the wires». 2) To link to a network, the internet, a phone line or a power supply. 3) To see or show that two ideas, facts or events are related: «connect the clues». 4) For a train, bus or plane to meet another so that you can change from one to the other. 5) To feel close to and understand someone: «She really connects with children». 6) (informal, sport) To hit something well: «He connected with the ball».
its sense in the lessons: In science, pupils connect wires, bulbs and batteries to make a circuit; in maths they connect dots, points and lines to draw shapes; in reading they connect ideas and clues. In everyday life we connect to Wi-Fi, connect a phone charger, connect with friends. Safety: never connect things to the mains yourself, and never connect the two ends of a battery directly. Phrases: «connect to», «connect with», «connect the dots», «connected to the internet», «stay connected».
examples from the lessons: Connect the battery to the bulb with two wires. | Connect the dots in order to see the picture. | The tablet won't connect to the Wi-Fi. | Can you connect the clues and find who took the cake? | This bridge connects the two halves of the town. | Our train connects with the ferry at the harbour. | Grandma connects with every child she meets. | He finally connected with the ball and it flew into the net. | Join the points A, B and C to connect them into a triangle.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Use «connect A to B» or «connect A and B» for joining things, «connect with» for people or for meeting transport. Opposite: «disconnect». Noun: «connection». The double N is a common spelling trap: c-o-n-n-e-c-t.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A place or thing where two things are joined: «a loose connection in the wire». 2) A link to the internet, a phone network or a power supply: «a bad connection». 3) A link between ideas, facts or events: «There is a connection between sleep and good marks». 4) A train, bus or plane that you change to on a journey: «We missed our connection». 5) A feeling of closeness and understanding between people. 6) Connections (plural): people you know who can help you: «He got the job through connections».
its sense in the lessons: In science: a broken connection stops the current in a circuit, so the bulb goes out. In reading and history: pupils explain the connection between a cause and its result. In everyday life: Wi-Fi connection, missing a connection at a station, feeling a connection with a friend or a pet. Phrases: «in connection with» (formal: about), «make a connection», «lose connection», «have connections».
examples from the lessons: The bulb did not light because of a loose connection. | Our internet connection keeps dropping during the video call. | Can you see the connection between the two stories? | We ran to catch our connection to Dublin. | Ella felt a special connection with the old horse. | The police want to speak to a man in connection with the robbery. | His uncle has connections at the football club. | Draw a line to show the connection between each word and its picture.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. «In connection with» is formal and means «about» or «linked to». British older spelling «connexion» is now rare. Do not confuse with «collection». Double N, then -ction.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Protecting nature — animals, plants, forests, seas — so it is not damaged or lost. 2) Using something carefully so that less is wasted: «water conservation», «energy conservation». 3) Looking after old buildings, paintings and objects so they last. 4) (science) The rule that some amounts stay the same in a closed system, such as «conservation of energy» or «conservation of mass».
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography lessons: conservation of habitats, endangered animals, rainforests and oceans; saving water and electricity at home. In maths and science for older pupils: «conservation of mass» means that when ice melts or things mix, the total mass stays the same. In everyday life: conservation areas, national parks, museum conservation. Phrases: «wildlife conservation», «conservation area», «conservation project», «water conservation».
examples from the lessons: Conservation helps save tigers and turtles from dying out. | Our class joined a conservation project to plant trees by the river. | Turning off the tap while brushing your teeth is water conservation. | The old mill is in a conservation area, so it cannot be knocked down. | Experts worked on the conservation of the old painting. | Conservation of energy means energy is never lost, only changed into another form. | The ranger told us about koala conservation in the bush. | When the ice melted, the mass was the same — that shows conservation of mass.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly uncountable. Related words: «conserve» (verb), «conservationist» (a person who works to protect nature). Do not confuse with «conversation» (talking) — the letters r and v swap places — or with «conservative» (wanting things to stay the same; also a political party).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To send goods to someone, often to be sold or delivered. 2) (formal) To put someone or something in an unpleasant place or state, often to get rid of it: «consigned to the bin». 3) (formal) To hand something over to someone's care: «consign the child to her aunt's care».
its sense in the lessons: A formal word met in older stories, history books and exam texts. Phrases: «consign to the rubbish bin», «consign to history» (to make something belong to the past and be forgotten), «consign to the scrapheap», «consigned to the attic». It tells the reader that something was sent away or put aside, often for good.
examples from the lessons: The old toys were consigned to the attic. | The broken chair was consigned to the skip. | The farmer consigned his apples to a shop in the city. | The king consigned the traitor to the dungeon. | Phones without buttons consigned old ones to history. | The orphan was consigned to the care of her grandmother. | My first drawing was consigned to the bin, but Mum rescued it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. The G is silent: con-SINE. Noun: «consignment» (a load of goods sent). Formal; in speech say «send», «put away» or «throw out». The pattern is usually «consign something/someone to something».

meaning for a pupil: 1) To plan secretly with other people to do something bad or against the law. 2) (of events) To happen together in a way that causes a bad result, as if planning it: «Everything conspired to make us late». 3) (playful) To plan something together in secret, such as a surprise.
its sense in the lessons: In history and stories: people conspire against a king, a teacher, or a hero; in the Bible, enemies conspire against kings and prophets. In everyday talk, «the weather conspired against us» means bad luck happened. It tells the reader there is a secret plan or bad luck piling up. Phrases: «conspire against», «conspire to do», «conspire with».
examples from the lessons: The guards conspired to free the prisoner. | The villains conspired against the queen. | Rain and traffic conspired to make us miss the start of the match. | My brother and I conspired to surprise Mum with breakfast in bed. | In the story, the foxes conspire with the crows to steal the eggs. | Everything seemed to conspire against our picnic. | The twins were caught conspiring in whispers behind the shed.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Noun: «conspiracy» (a secret plan by a group); a person who conspires is a «conspirator». «Conspiracy theory» is a belief that a secret group is behind events, often without good evidence — be careful with such claims and check facts.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A meeting with an expert, such as a doctor or lawyer, to get advice. 2) The act of asking people for their views before making a decision: «after consultation with parents». 3) (formal) The act of looking something up in a book or source: «consultation of the map».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: a doctor's consultation, a vet consultation, a consultation with a lawyer about a will or custody. At school and in towns: a consultation asks parents, pupils or residents what they think about a plan (a new playground, new uniform). It tells the reader that people were asked before deciding. Phrases: «in consultation with», «public consultation», «a free consultation», «consultation period».
examples from the lessons: Mum had a consultation with the doctor about her bad back. | The council held a public consultation about the new skate park. | The school changed the uniform after consultation with parents. | The vet charged for a short consultation. | The plan was made in consultation with the pupils. | Dad booked a consultation with a lawyer. | The consultation lasted twenty minutes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Verb: «consult» (consult a doctor, consult a dictionary). Formal; in speech people say «appointment» for the doctor and «asking people» for the other sense. «In consultation with» means «working together with and asking».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (adjective, formal) Depending on something else happening first: «The trip is contingent on good weather.» 2) (noun) A group of people who belong to a larger group, sent or gathered together: «a contingent of soldiers», «the Irish contingent». 3) (adjective, formal) Possible but not certain; that may or may not happen.
its sense in the lessons: A formal exam word. In maths word problems or rules, «contingent on» means «only if»: the prize is contingent on getting all answers right. In news and sport, «a contingent» is a group: «the school's contingent at the parade». Phrases: «contingent on», «contingent upon», «a large contingent of».
examples from the lessons: Our trip to the zoo is contingent on everyone bringing a signed form. | Your pocket money is contingent upon tidying your room. | A contingent of firefighters marched in the parade. | The Scottish contingent cheered loudest at the games. | His place in the team is contingent on passing his fitness test. | A small contingent of parents stayed to help clear up.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective use goes with «on» or «upon». Noun is countable. Related: «contingency» (a possible future event; «a contingency plan» = a backup plan). Formal; in speech say «depends on» or «a group of». Logic: «A is contingent on B» means no B, no A.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) The state of going on or lasting; continuing: «the continuance of the old custom». 2) (law, mainly US) A delay of a court case to a later time, asked for by one side.
its sense in the lessons: A stiff, formal word met in older books, speeches and legal news. In everyday talk people say «continuing» or «carrying on». Phrases: «the continuance of», «ask for a continuance» (law, US). It tells the reader that something is carrying on, or in law that a case is put off.
examples from the lessons: The villagers hoped for the continuance of the old harvest fair. | The club's continuance depends on new members joining. | The lawyer asked the judge for a continuance. | The judge granted a continuance so the witness could arrive. | The continuance of peace was all the people wanted. | Money from the cake sale ensured the continuance of the library.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly uncountable, though in the law sense «a continuance». Close words: «continuation» (the next part, or carrying on), «continuity» (staying the same without breaks). In everyday English «continuation» is far more common.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To break a law, rule or agreement. 2) (formal, rare) To go against or disagree with an idea or statement.
its sense in the lessons: A formal exam and legal word. It appears on notices («Anyone contravening these rules will be asked to leave»), in news about companies breaking laws, and in school policies. It tells the reader that a rule was broken in an official sense. Phrases: «contravene the rules», «contravene the law», «in contravention of» (noun form).
examples from the lessons: Parking on the zigzag lines outside school contravenes the rules. | The factory contravened safety laws and had to pay a fine. | Pupils who contravene the phone policy will have phones confiscated. | The referee said the tackle contravened the rules of the game. | Feeding the animals contravenes the zoo's rules. | Building the wall so high contravened the planning law.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Noun: «contravention». Formal; in speech say «break» or «go against». Pattern: «contravene + rule/law» (no preposition).

part of speech: adjective (convinced); past form of the verb convince (convince, convinces, convinced, convincing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (adjective) Completely sure that something is true: «I'm convinced the cat ate my sandwich.» 2) (verb, past) Made someone believe something or agree to do something: «She convinced me to join the choir.» 3) (adjective, before a noun) Firm in a belief: «a convinced Christian», «a convinced vegetarian».
its sense in the lessons: In stories, «convinced» shows what a character strongly believes — sometimes wrongly, which makes the story funny or exciting. In science, a good scientist is convinced only by evidence. In everyday life, children convince parents to let them stay up. Phrases: «be convinced that», «be convinced of», «not convinced» (doubtful), «convince someone to do something».
examples from the lessons: I'm convinced there is a monster under my bed. | Tom was convinced that he had left his bag on the bus. | She convinced her parents to get a puppy. | The teacher wasn't convinced by my excuse. | After the experiment, we were convinced that plants need light. | Grandpa is a convinced fan of the local team. | Are you convinced, or do you need more proof?
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Convinced» (sure) vs «convincing» (making others sure): «I am convinced» but «a convincing story». «Convince someone of something» / «convince someone that …». «Not convinced» is a polite way to say «I doubt it». Being convinced does not make a thing true — check the evidence.

part of speech: verb (coo, coos, cooed, cooing); noun (a coo, coos); interjection (Coo! — UK, old-fashioned)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (verb) For a pigeon or dove to make its soft, low, round sound. 2) (verb) To speak softly and lovingly, as people do to babies: «She cooed over the baby.» 3) (noun) The soft sound a dove makes, or a baby's happy sound. 4) (UK, old-fashioned, informal) «Coo!» — an exclamation of surprise, like «Wow!»
its sense in the lessons: In nature lessons, pigeons and doves coo; babies coo before they learn to talk. In stories, adults «coo over» babies, puppies and kittens, showing tenderness. Phrases: «coo over», «bill and coo» (old-fashioned: for lovers to kiss and whisper).
examples from the lessons: The pigeons cooed on the roof all morning. | The baby cooed and kicked her legs. | Aunt Sally cooed over the new kittens. | We heard the soft coo of a dove in the garden. | "Who's a lovely boy?" cooed Nan to the puppy. | Coo, look at the size of that cake! | The doves were cooing in the church tower.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: cooed, cooing. Sounds like «coup» (a sudden seizure of power — the P is silent) — a homophone. Do not mix up with «cue». Animal sounds: doves coo, owls hoot, crows caw.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To match or be the same as something, or to fit together: «The numbers correspond to the pictures.» 2) To be like or equal to something else in another system: «The British «year 6» roughly corresponds to the American «fifth grade».» 3) To write letters or emails to someone over time.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, sides and angles that correspond are in matching positions in two shapes; each number in a table corresponds to a value. In reading, answers must correspond to questions. In everyday and historical life, pen pals correspond. Phrases: «correspond to», «correspond with», «correspond closely».
examples from the lessons: Each letter corresponds to a number in this code. | Your answer does not correspond with what the question asked. | The dots on the map correspond to the schools in our town. | I correspond with a pen pal in New Zealand. | The two girls corresponded for many years. | In similar triangles, the angles that correspond are equal. | The tally marks should correspond to the numbers in the chart.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. «Correspond to» = match; «correspond with» = match or write letters to. Nouns: «correspondence» (letters; a match), «correspondent» (a news reporter in a place, or a letter writer). Adjective: «corresponding».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Matching or connected with something else: «Write each word next to its corresponding picture.» 2) Happening at the same time or in the same way as something else: «the corresponding week last term». 3) (maths) In the same position in two shapes or on two lines: «corresponding angles», «corresponding sides». 4) (verb form) Writing letters or matching: «We have been corresponding by email.»
its sense in the lessons: In maths: corresponding angles are equal when a line crosses two parallel lines; corresponding sides of similar shapes are in the same ratio. In science graphs, each time has a corresponding temperature. In everyday use: a price rise and a corresponding fall in sales. Phrases: «the corresponding …», «corresponding to», «a corresponding increase».
examples from the lessons: Match each animal to its corresponding home. | Find the corresponding angle in the second triangle. | The corresponding sides of the two squares are 2 cm and 4 cm. | Sales rose, with a corresponding rise in profit. | Each question has a corresponding answer at the back of the book. | When the temperature fell, there was a corresponding drop in visitors. | Look at the corresponding page in your workbook.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective usually before the noun with «the»: «the corresponding number». Maths: corresponding angles on parallel lines are equal; corresponding sides of similar shapes grow by the same scale factor (if one side doubles, every corresponding side doubles). Adverb: «correspondingly».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Costing no money; free. 2) (formal) Done without any loss, harm or effort: «a costless mistake».
its sense in the lessons: A rare, slightly formal word, met in economics, maths and exam texts. In everyday speech people say «free» or «at no cost». It tells the reader that nothing has to be paid or lost. Phrases: «almost costless», «not costless».
examples from the lessons: Walking to school is costless and good for you. | Borrowing a book from the library is costless. | The mistake was costless because we noticed it in time. | Smiling at people is costless but makes them happy. | Nothing in life is completely costless. | The plan looked costless, but it took a lot of time.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Made from «cost» + «-less» (without). It does not mean «priceless» (worth a huge amount) or «worthless» (worth nothing). In maths problems, a costless item adds 0 to the total cost.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person elected to sit on a council, especially a town, city or local council, to make decisions for the area. 2) (more general) A member of any council, such as a school council: «a school councillor».
its sense in the lessons: In citizenship and social studies: councillors run local services such as bins, parks, libraries and roads; people vote for them. At school: pupils may be elected class or school councillors. In news and everyday life: you can write to your councillor about a broken streetlight. Phrases: «local councillor», «city councillor», «school councillor», «elected councillor».
examples from the lessons: Our local councillor came to open the new playground. | I was voted school councillor for my class. | Write to your councillor about the potholes. | The councillors voted to build a new library. | My aunt is a city councillor in Melbourne. | The school councillors asked for more benches in the yard. | A councillor visited our class to talk about democracy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: British/Australian/NZ spelling «councillor»; American «councilor». Homophone trap: «counsellor» (US «counselor») is a person who gives advice, such as a school counsellor. A council makes decisions; counsel is advice. Capital C before a name as a title: «Councillor Patel».

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a secret or hidden way, so that others do not notice. 2) (formal) Not openly shown or admitted: «covertly unhappy».
its sense in the lessons: Used in spy stories, mysteries and news about secret agents or police; in classroom stories, a child might covertly pass a note. It tells the reader that something is done secretly. Opposite: «openly», «overtly».
examples from the lessons: She covertly passed a note to her friend under the desk. | The detective covertly watched the house. | Spies covertly gathered information. | Tim covertly slipped the sprouts to the dog. | The cameras covertly filmed the badgers at night. | He covertly checked his phone during the film. | The rabbit covertly nibbled the lettuce while the farmer slept.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from «covert» (secret, hidden). Pronounced KUV-ert-lee or KOH-vert-lee. Opposite: «overtly». Do not confuse with «covet» (to want something that belongs to someone else).

part of speech: noun (crib, cribs); verb (crib, cribs, cribbed, cribbing — informal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (noun, US/Canada) A baby's bed with high barred sides (UK: «cot»). 2) (noun, UK/Ireland/Australia) A model of the stable where Jesus was born, with figures of Mary, Joseph, the baby and animals, set up at Christmas (also «nativity scene»; US «crèche»). 3) (noun) A wooden box or rack that holds food for animals; a manger. 4) (verb, informal) To copy someone else's work and pretend it is yours; to cheat. 5) (noun, informal) A sheet of answers or notes used to cheat (a «crib sheet»), or a quick summary of facts. 6) (noun, slang, US) Someone's house or home: «Welcome to my crib.» 7) (noun) Short for «cribbage», a card game.
its sense in the lessons: In family life: the baby sleeps in a crib (US) or cot (UK). In church life: at Christmas many churches and homes set up a crib, and children may take part in the crib service. At school: cribbing (copying) in a test is cheating and is punished. Slang: «crib» for home is used by teenagers and in songs. Phrases: «crib sheet», «crib from», «the Christmas crib», «crib death» (US for cot death).
examples from the lessons: The baby is fast asleep in her crib. | At Christmas we put the crib under the tree with little wooden sheep. | The children placed baby Jesus in the crib at the crib service. | The cows ate hay from the crib in the barn. | Don't crib your answers from Jack — do your own work. | He was caught with a crib sheet in his pencil case. | "Come round to my crib after school," said my cousin (slang). | Grandad taught us to play crib.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb with a doubled B: cribbed, cribbing. UK «cot» = US «crib» for a baby's bed; but in the UK, «crib» is mostly the Christmas nativity scene. Christians believe the baby Jesus was laid in a manger because there was no room at the inn. The slang «crib» (home) is informal — not for school writing.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Sounding rough, low and hoarse, especially because of a sore throat or a cold. 2) Sounding like the croak of a frog or crow.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and health: a croaky voice is a sign of a cold, a sore throat or too much shouting at a match. In stories, an old witch or a tired character may have a croaky voice. Phrases: «a croaky voice», «sound croaky», «feel croaky».
examples from the lessons: I've got a cold and my voice is all croaky. | After cheering at the match, Dad was croaky for two days. | "Who's there?" asked a croaky voice. | The frog gave a croaky call from the pond. | She sounded croaky on the phone, so I knew she was ill. | Drink some warm honey and lemon for your croaky throat.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative «croakier», superlative «croakiest». Made from «croak» (the deep sound of a frog or crow). Close words: «hoarse» (not «horse»!), «husky», «raspy». Informal, «croak» can also mean to die (slang, not polite).

meaning for a pupil: 1) To kill someone by nailing or tying them to a cross and leaving them to die — a cruel punishment used in ancient times, especially by the Romans. 2) (Bible, church) Used of Jesus: Christians believe Jesus was crucified and rose again on the third day. 3) (informal) To criticise someone very harshly or punish them badly: «The newspapers crucified the manager.» 4) (informal, sport) To beat someone very heavily.
its sense in the lessons: In religious education and church life: the Gospels tell how Jesus was crucified; Good Friday remembers his death, Easter his rising. In history: the Romans crucified rebels and slaves. In everyday informal talk: «My mum will crucify me if I'm late!» means she will be very angry (an exaggeration). Phrases: «was crucified», «crucified under Pontius Pilate», «crucify someone for something».
examples from the lessons: The Romans crucified criminals as a warning to others. | Christians believe Jesus was crucified on Good Friday and rose again on Easter Sunday. | The creed says he was crucified under Pontius Pilate. | Two thieves were crucified beside Jesus. | Mum will crucify me if I lose another coat! | The critics crucified the new film. | We got crucified six–nil in the final.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular spelling: y changes to i before -es and -ed: crucifies, crucified; but «crucifying». Nouns: «crucifixion» (the act), «crucifix» (a cross with the figure of Jesus on it). Talk about the religious meaning respectfully. The informal sense is an exaggeration, not a real threat.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In old royal courts, a trusted servant whose job was to pour and serve wine to the king, and often to taste it first to check it was not poisoned. 2) (Bible) Used of Nehemiah, who was cupbearer to the Persian king, and of Pharaoh's cupbearer in the story of Joseph.
its sense in the lessons: Met in Bible stories, history and fairy tales about castles and kings. It tells the reader that the person was very close to the king and trusted. In the story of Joseph, Pharaoh's cupbearer and baker had dreams in prison; Joseph explained them, but the cupbearer forgot him for two years.
examples from the lessons: Nehemiah was cupbearer to King Artaxerxes. | Pharaoh's cupbearer told Joseph about his dream of a vine. | The cupbearer tasted the wine before handing it to the king. | Only the most trusted servant could be the royal cupbearer. | The cupbearer promised to remember Joseph, but he forgot. | In the play, Sam was the cupbearer with a golden goblet.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable compound of «cup» + «bearer» (one who carries). Older Bibles sometimes say «butler» for the same servant. Pronounced CUP-bair-er. A historical word; not used for modern jobs.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal, UK/Australia/NZ/Ireland) A cup of tea. 2) (informal, less often) A cup of any hot drink, such as coffee.
its sense in the lessons: Very common in everyday British, Irish, Australian and New Zealand speech: adults offer visitors a cuppa, and «putting the kettle on» is a way to welcome and comfort people. In stories it shows a cosy, friendly or calm moment, or comfort after bad news. Phrases: «fancy a cuppa?», «put the kettle on for a cuppa», «a nice cuppa», «a cuppa and a biscuit». Safety: kettles and hot tea can burn — children should ask an adult.
examples from the lessons: Fancy a cuppa? I'll put the kettle on. | Nan sat down with a cuppa and a biscuit. | After the long walk, everyone wanted a hot cuppa. | Mum always makes a cuppa when she's had bad news. | Let's have a quick cuppa before we leave. | The builders stopped for a cuppa at ten. | Grandad's idea of breakfast is toast and a strong cuppa.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal: fine in speech and stories, not in formal writing. It comes from «cup of» said quickly. Countable: «two cuppas». In the US people rarely say it; Americans say «a cup of coffee». Spelling: double P.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (of an illness or injury) Able to be cured or made completely better. 2) (of a problem) Able to be fixed or put right.
its sense in the lessons: Used in health and science lessons and in family news about illness: doctors may say an illness is curable, which brings hope. It tells the reader there is a way to get better. Opposite: «incurable». Phrases: «easily curable», «curable with medicine», «if caught early, it is curable».
examples from the lessons: Most ear infections are easily curable with medicine. | The doctor said Grandpa's illness is curable. | Many diseases that were once deadly are now curable. | Head lice are annoying but curable. | Shyness is curable — with a bit of practice. | If it is found early, the illness is often curable.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Made from «cure» + «-able»: the e is dropped. Opposite «incurable». «Curable» (can be cured) is different from «treatable» (can be helped or controlled, even if not fully cured). Do not confuse with «durable» (lasting a long time).

part of speech: verb (dab, dabs, dabbed, dabbing); noun (a dab, dabs); adjective (a dab hand — UK informal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (verb) To touch something lightly and quickly several times, often with a cloth or sponge: «dab your eyes». 2) (verb) To put on a small amount of something with light touches: «dab paint on the paper». 3) (noun) A small amount of something: «a dab of glue». 4) (noun) A light, quick touch. 5) (noun, informal) A dance move where you drop your head into the bent arm while the other arm points out. 6) (UK informal) «a dab hand at» — very good at something. 7) (noun) A small flat sea fish. 8) Dabs (UK slang, old) fingerprints.
its sense in the lessons: In art lessons, children dab paint with sponges to make textures; in first aid, you dab a cut gently with a clean cloth, not rub it. In cooking, «a dab of butter». In the playground, «doing the dab» was a popular dance move. Phrases: «a dab of», «dab at», «dab on», «a dab hand at».
examples from the lessons: Dab the cut gently with a clean tissue. | She dabbed her eyes with a hanky at the end of the film. | Dab blue paint on with a sponge to make the sky. | Put a dab of glue on each corner. | Add a dab of butter to the hot potatoes. | The footballer did a dab to celebrate his goal. | Grandma is a dab hand at knitting. | We caught a little dab off the pier.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb with a doubled B: dabbed, dabbing. To dab is gentler than to rub or wipe. «Dab hand» is British, informal. «Dab» (fish) is a flatfish. Do not confuse «dab» with «dub» (to give a name, or to add voices to a film).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Hard work and loyalty to a task or a purpose over a long time: «Her dedication to swimming won her the medal». 2) Words at the start of a book, song or piece of music that say who it is for: «The dedication reads "For my mum"». 3) (church) A ceremony to give a building, such as a church, or a person to God or to a holy purpose: «the dedication of the new church», «a baby dedication». 4) The act of naming something in honour of someone: «the dedication of a bench to Grandad».
its sense in the lessons: In school and sport: teachers praise dedication — practising, coming every week, not giving up. In books and music: a dedication shows love and thanks. In church life: some churches hold a dedication service when a church building opens, or a baby dedication where parents promise to bring up a child in the faith. In everyday life: a bench or a tree with a plaque in memory of someone. Phrases: «dedication to», «with great dedication», «a dedication service».
examples from the lessons: The coach praised the team's dedication. | It takes dedication to learn the violin. | The dedication in the book said "For Rosie, who loves stories." | The bishop led the dedication of the new church. | At the baby dedication, the parents promised to raise their son in the faith. | The radio played a song dedication for Grandma's birthday. | There was a short dedication when the bench was named after Mrs Kelly. | Nurses show great dedication to their patients.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable in senses 2–4, often uncountable in sense 1 («great dedication»). Verb: «dedicate» (dedicate a book to someone; dedicate yourself to something). Adjective: «dedicated» (very committed; also used only for one purpose: «a dedicated bike lane»).

part of speech: noun (default, defaults); verb (default, defaults, defaulted, defaulting); adjective (default)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (computing) The setting or choice that a computer, phone or game uses unless you change it: «the default font». 2) What happens or is chosen automatically when nobody decides otherwise: «by default». 3) (money, law) Failure to pay back money you owe, or failure to do what you promised: «default on a loan». 4) (sport, law) «by default» or «win by default» — to win because the other side did not turn up or could not play. 5) (verb) To fail to pay a debt or do a duty; or for a computer to go back to a setting.
its sense in the lessons: In computing lessons: default settings, default passwords (change them for safety!), default answers. In maths and logic: the default value is what is assumed if nothing else is given. In adult money talk: if people default on their mortgage, they may lose their home. In sport: a team can win by default when the other team does not come. Phrases: «by default», «default setting», «default on a loan», «win by default», «in default of» (formal: without).
examples from the lessons: The default language on the tablet is English. | Change the default password to keep your account safe. | We won the match by default because the other team didn't turn up. | If you don't choose a colour, the game picks blue by default. | The company defaulted on its loan and the bank took the building. | The printer always defaults to black and white. | My default lunch is a cheese sandwich. | When nobody volunteered, Sam became the leader by default.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stress: de-FAULT (often DEE-fault for the noun in the US). Regular verb. «Default on» a payment. «By default» can be neutral (automatically) or slightly negative (not by choice, only because nothing else happened). In maths problems, a default value is the starting value used when none is given.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) The act of putting something off until a later time; a delay that is allowed: «the deferral of the exam». 2) (formal) An official permission to start something later, such as a place at university or school.
its sense in the lessons: A formal word met in letters from schools, universities, banks and governments. It tells the reader that something was officially delayed, not cancelled. Phrases: «a deferral of payment», «ask for a deferral», «grant a deferral», «deferral of entry».
examples from the lessons: Sophie asked for a deferral of her university place for a year. | The bank allowed a deferral of the loan payments. | The school agreed to a deferral of the test because so many pupils were ill. | A deferral is not the same as a cancellation. | His deferral was granted, so he can start next term. | The council announced a deferral of the building work.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. From the verb «defer» (to put off; also to give way to someone's opinion: «defer to your elders»). Note the double R: deferred, deferring, deferral (but «deference», «deferment» with one R). Formal; in speech say «putting it off» or «delay».

part of speech: noun (a delegate, delegates — pronounced DEL-i-gut); verb (delegate, delegates, delegated, delegating — pronounced DEL-i-gate)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (noun) A person chosen to speak, vote or act for a group, especially at a meeting or conference. 2) (verb) To give part of your work, power or a task to someone else to do for you. 3) (verb, formal) To choose someone to act for a group.
its sense in the lessons: In school: a class delegate goes to the school council meeting; a leader learns to delegate jobs in group work. In news and politics: delegates at a conference or the United Nations. At home: parents delegate chores to children. Phrases: «delegate to», «delegate tasks», «a delegate to the conference».
examples from the lessons: Each class chose one delegate for the school council. | Delegates from many countries met to talk about the oceans. | A good captain knows how to delegate jobs. | Mum delegated the washing-up to me. | The teacher delegated the job of handing out books to Priya. | Our delegate reported back to the class. | The manager delegated the planning to her team.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The noun and verb are spelled the same but pronounced differently: noun «DEL-i-gut», verb «DEL-i-gayt». Noun: «delegation» (a group of delegates; or the act of delegating). When you delegate, you are still responsible for checking the job.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The act of removing something, such as words from a text or a file from a computer. 2) Something that has been removed: «I made several deletions in my essay». 3) (science) The loss of a part of a gene or chromosome.
its sense in the lessons: In computing: deletion of files, messages and photos (a deleted file may still be in the bin or backup). In writing lessons: editing includes deletions — crossing out unneeded words. In online safety: asking for deletion of something posted about you. Phrases: «deletion of», «permanent deletion», «make a deletion».
examples from the lessons: The deletion of the file was an accident. | After a few deletions, my story was much shorter and clearer. | Ask an adult about deletion of photos posted online. | The app asks you to confirm the deletion. | Permanent deletion means you cannot get it back. | The teacher marked the deletion with a neat line through the word.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Verb: «delete». Opposite ideas: «addition», «insertion». In computing, «deleted» does not always mean gone forever — things can often be recovered, so think before you post.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Based on democracy: a system where people choose their leaders by voting and have equal rights. 2) Fair, where everyone has an equal say in a decision: «a democratic vote in class». 3) (US politics, capital D) Belonging to the Democratic Party.
its sense in the lessons: In citizenship and history lessons: democratic countries hold free elections; ancient Athens is called the birthplace of democracy. At school: choosing the class pet's name by a show of hands is a democratic decision. Phrases: «democratic country», «democratic vote», «democratic process», «democratic rights».
examples from the lessons: We made a democratic decision: everyone voted on the trip. | In a democratic country, people choose their leaders. | The school council is a democratic way to share ideas. | Voting by secret ballot is part of a democratic election. | The teacher wanted the class rules to be democratic. | Free speech is important in a democratic society.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: «democracy»; person: «democrat» (Democrat with a capital D in US politics). Opposite ideas: «undemocratic», «dictatorship». In maths, a democratic vote is decided by the majority: more than half of the votes wins.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To say publicly and strongly that something or someone is wrong, bad or evil. 2) To tell the authorities that someone has done something wrong, often to get them punished: «He denounced his neighbour to the police».
its sense in the lessons: In news and history: leaders denounce violence, unfair laws or cruelty; in some dark times of history, people were forced to denounce friends and family. In the Bible, prophets denounced kings who did wrong. In ethics lessons: it can be brave to denounce bullying. Phrases: «denounce as», «publicly denounce», «denounce someone to the authorities».
examples from the lessons: The mayor denounced the attack on the mosque. | The prophet denounced the king for his greed. | Pupils denounced the bullying in a school assembly. | The spy was denounced to the police. | Many people denounced the plan as unfair. | The church leaders denounced the cruelty to refugees.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Noun: «denunciation» (note the spelling change: «-nunc-», not «-nounc-»). Stronger than «criticise». Do not confuse with «renounce» (to give up something, such as a right or belief) or «announce» (to tell people news).

part of speech: adjective (dependent, more dependent); noun (US: a dependent, dependents; UK also «dependant»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (adjective) Needing someone or something for support, help or money: «Babies are dependent on their parents.» 2) (adjective) Decided by or changing with something else: «Our trip is dependent on the weather.» 3) (adjective) Needing a drug or substance and finding it hard to stop. 4) (noun) A person, usually a child, who relies on someone else for money and care: «He has three dependants.» 5) (maths, science) A «dependent variable» is what you measure, which changes when you change something else.
its sense in the lessons: In science investigations: the dependent variable is what you measure (how tall the plant grows), and the independent variable is what you change (amount of water). In maths, one quantity can be dependent on another (cost depends on how many you buy). In everyday and adult life: children are dependents; tax forms ask about dependants. Phrases: «dependent on», «dependent upon», «heavily dependent», «financially dependent».
examples from the lessons: Young children are dependent on their parents. | Our picnic is dependent on the weather. | In our experiment, the dependent variable was the height of the bean plant. | Many towns are dependent on tourism. | Dad listed us as dependants on the form. | The total cost is dependent on how many tickets we buy. | Some animals are dependent on one kind of food.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Use «dependent on» (not «of»). Spelling trap: the adjective is always «dependent»; the noun is «dependant» in British English and «dependent» in American. Opposite: «independent». Verb: «depend»; noun: «dependence».

part of speech: adjective (depleted); past form of the verb deplete (deplete, depletes, depleted, depleting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Reduced in amount so that there is not much left; used up: «depleted supplies». 2) (sport) Weakened because many members are missing: «a depleted team». 3) (science) With part of something removed: «ozone-depleted», «depleted soil».
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography: depleted fish stocks, depleted soil, depleted water in a reservoir, the depleted ozone layer — showing harm to nature and why conservation matters. In sport news: a depleted squad because of injuries. In everyday life: depleted energy after a long day. Phrases: «badly depleted», «depleted stocks», «depleted supplies».
examples from the lessons: After the party, our snack supplies were badly depleted. | The fish in the sea are depleted because of overfishing. | A depleted team still managed to win the match. | Farmers rest the land so the soil is not depleted. | By the end of the camp, our water was depleted. | I felt depleted after the long swimming race.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb «deplete». Noun: «depletion». Formal; in speech say «used up», «running low». Do not confuse with «completed». In maths problems, «depleted by 20 litres» means 20 litres less than before.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To remove a ruler or leader from power, often by force. 2) (law) To give evidence under oath, especially in a written statement outside court; or to question someone in this way.
its sense in the lessons: In history and Bible lessons: kings and queens were deposed; in the Bible, God «has brought down rulers from their thrones» (from Mary's song). In news: a president can be deposed by a revolution or a vote. Phrases: «depose a king», «the deposed leader», «be deposed from power».
examples from the lessons: The people deposed the cruel king. | The deposed queen fled to another country. | The general tried to depose the president. | In the story, the wicked uncle deposed the rightful prince. | The lawyer deposed the witness in his office. | Rulers who ignore the people risk being deposed.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Noun: «deposition» (removing a ruler; or a sworn statement). Do not confuse with «dispose» (to get rid of something) or «deposit» (to put down; money in a bank). Formal word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unkind laughter or comments that show you think someone or something is stupid or worthless; mocking. 2) The state of being laughed at: «an object of derision».
its sense in the lessons: In stories and history: an idea or person may be met with derision at first, before being proven right (inventors, explorers). In ethics and school life: derision is a form of bullying — laughing at someone hurts. In the Bible, people held Jesus up to derision at the cross. Phrases: «with derision», «an object of derision», «hoots of derision», «met with derision».
examples from the lessons: The crowd greeted the referee's decision with derision. | His idea was met with derision, but later it made him famous. | She ignored the derision of the older boys. | The giant laughed in derision at the tiny knight. | The poor singer became an object of derision. | Derision can hurt more than a push.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Related: «deride» (verb, to mock), «derisive» (showing derision), «derisory» (so small it is laughable: «a derisory offer»). Formal; in speech say «mocking» or «laughing at».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Showing that you think someone or something is stupid or worthless; mocking: «a derisive laugh». 2) (less common) Deserving to be laughed at; ridiculous (better said «derisory»).
its sense in the lessons: Used in stories to describe a sneering laugh, snort or comment from a bully or villain. It tells the reader the character is unkind or scornful. Phrases: «a derisive laugh», «a derisive snort», «derisive comments».
examples from the lessons: The bully gave a derisive laugh. | "You? Win a race?" she said with a derisive snort. | The crowd made derisive noises at the other team. | Derisive comments online can be a kind of bullying. | The witch's derisive cackle echoed in the cave. | He ignored their derisive looks and kept practising.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb: «derisively». Close but different: «derisory» usually means «too small to be taken seriously» («a derisory pay rise»). Formal; in speech say «mocking», «sneering».

meaning for a pupil: 1) The process of becoming worse in quality, condition or health. 2) (science) The slow breaking down of materials, such as wood rotting or metal rusting.
its sense in the lessons: In science: deterioration of materials over time — rust, rot, fading. In health and family life: a doctor may notice a deterioration in a patient's condition. In geography and history: deterioration of buildings, roads, or relations between countries. Phrases: «deterioration in», «deterioration of», «rapid deterioration», «a sudden deterioration».
examples from the lessons: There has been a deterioration in the weather, so the match is cancelled. | The nurse watched for any deterioration in Grandma's health. | The deterioration of the old bridge made it unsafe. | Rust causes the deterioration of iron gates. | Teachers noticed a deterioration in his handwriting. | Damp led to the deterioration of the books in the shed.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: «deteriorate» (to get worse). Spelling: de-te-ri-o-ra-tion; many people wrongly say «deteoration» — keep the «-ior-». Opposite: «improvement».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Harm or damage: «to the detriment of your health» means harming your health. 2) (formal) Something that causes harm.
its sense in the lessons: A formal exam word. It appears in phrases: «to the detriment of», «without detriment to», «to someone's detriment». It tells the reader that something causes harm or a loss. In health lessons: too much screen time may be to the detriment of sleep.
examples from the lessons: He played games all night, to the detriment of his homework. | Eating only sweets is to the detriment of your teeth. | The new road was built to the detriment of the woodland. | You can enjoy sport without detriment to your studies. | Shouting at the team worked to the coach's detriment. | Pollution is a detriment to the health of rivers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal and uncountable; mostly used in the fixed phrases above. Adjective: «detrimental» (harmful). In speech say «harm», «damage».

meaning for a pupil: 1) To invent or plan something clever or new, usually after careful thinking: «devise a plan». 2) (law, old) To leave property to someone in a will.
its sense in the lessons: In science and design lessons: pupils devise experiments, fair tests and models. In maths: devise a method or a strategy to solve a problem. In stories: heroes and villains devise schemes and escape plans. Phrases: «devise a plan», «devise a way to», «devise a test», «of your own devising».
examples from the lessons: Devise a fair test to see which paper towel is strongest. | The children devised a plan to rescue the kitten. | Can you devise a quicker way to add these numbers? | The prisoner devised a clever escape. | Our class devised a new game for wet playtime. | Scientists devised a machine to clean the ocean. | The puzzle was of her own devising.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb ends in -ise in both British and American English (never «devize»). Do not confuse with the noun «device» (a machine or tool): «I devised a device». Pronounced dih-VIZE.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To eat something quickly and hungrily, often all of it. 2) To read, watch or take in something eagerly and quickly: «She devoured the book». 3) To destroy something completely: «The fire devoured the forest». 4) (of a feeling) To fill someone completely: «devoured by jealousy».
its sense in the lessons: In science: predators devour their prey (food chains). In stories and fairy tales: wolves, dragons and giants devour; the Bible says the devil «prowls around like a roaring lion looking for someone to devour». In reading: children devour books they love. Phrases: «devour a meal», «devour books», «devoured by flames».
examples from the lessons: The hungry boys devoured the pizza in minutes. | The lion devoured its prey. | Ellie devoured the whole series of books in a week. | The fire devoured the old barn. | In the story, the wolf wanted to devour Little Red Riding Hood. | The caterpillars devoured our cabbages. | He was devoured by curiosity about the locked box.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Stronger than «eat»: it shows speed and greed. Pronounced dih-VOW-er. Do not confuse with «devout» (very religious).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Causing a disadvantage; not helpful; putting someone in a worse position: «a disadvantageous deal».
its sense in the lessons: A formal exam word used in maths word problems about deals, in history and in news. It tells the reader that something makes things harder or worse for someone. Phrases: «disadvantageous to», «disadvantageous for», «a disadvantageous position».
examples from the lessons: Starting the race at the back was disadvantageous. | The swap was disadvantageous to me: I gave three cards for one. | Living far from school can be disadvantageous for sport clubs. | The wind was disadvantageous for the team playing towards the river. | The rules were disadvantageous for smaller schools. | It is disadvantageous to skip breakfast before a test.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Long word: dis-ad-van-TAY-jus. Opposite: «advantageous». Everyday words: «unhelpful», «worse», «bad for». Noun: «disadvantage». In a maths problem, a disadvantageous deal means you lose value — check by comparing the numbers.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To not believe that someone or something is true; to refuse to believe. 2) To not have faith in something, especially in God (formal, older use).
its sense in the lessons: In stories: a character may disbelieve a strange tale or warning, often wrongly. In the Bible: Thomas disbelieved that Jesus had risen until he saw him (that's why he is called «Doubting Thomas»). In everyday life: people disbelieve tall stories. Phrases: «disbelieve someone», «disbelieve the story».
examples from the lessons: The villagers disbelieved the boy who cried wolf. | Thomas disbelieved the news until he saw Jesus himself. | I have no reason to disbelieve you. | The teacher disbelieved my excuse about the dog eating my homework. | Many people disbelieved the explorer's tales. | She was disbelieved at first, but the evidence proved her right.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Noun: «disbelief» («in disbelief» = not able to believe it). More common in speech: «not believe». Spelling: «ie» after b-e-l (i before e except after c).

meaning for a pupil: 1) The act of cutting off a supply, such as electricity, gas, water, phone or internet. 2) A break in a link between things: «a disconnection in the circuit». 3) A feeling of not being close to or in touch with other people or things.
its sense in the lessons: In science: a disconnection in a circuit stops the current. In everyday adult life: families who cannot pay the bills may face disconnection of their power or water. In computing: internet disconnection. In feelings: some people feel a disconnection from friends after moving. Phrases: «disconnection from», «face disconnection», «a sense of disconnection».
examples from the lessons: A disconnection in the wire made the buzzer stop. | The game froze after an internet disconnection. | The company warned of disconnection if the bill was not paid. | After moving schools, Leo felt a disconnection from his old friends. | Check every joint for a disconnection. | Too much screen time can cause disconnection from family.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Verb: «disconnect». Opposite: «connection». Double N from «connect».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A feeling of having lost confidence or hope, so you do not want to try any more. 2) Something that makes people less likely to do something: «Fines are a discouragement to dropping litter». 3) The act of trying to stop someone from doing something.
its sense in the lessons: In school and sport: discouragement after failing a test or losing a match; teachers help pupils overcome it. In ethics: a fine or a rule can be a discouragement to bad behaviour. In stories: heroes face discouragement but keep going. Phrases: «a feeling of discouragement», «despite discouragement», «discouragement to».
