examples from the lessons: Despite discouragement from others, she kept practising. | After losing again, Ben felt deep discouragement. | The fence is a discouragement to burglars. | Our coach turned our discouragement into determination. | Small setbacks are no reason for discouragement. | High prices are a discouragement to buying sweets.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable or uncountable. Verb: «discourage»; opposite «encouragement». The «-ou-» spelling of «courage» stays: dis-cour-age-ment.

part of speech: noun (discourse, discourses); verb (discourse, discourses, discoursed, discoursing — formal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Serious talk or discussion between people; the way people talk and write about a subject: «public discourse». 2) (formal) A long, serious speech or piece of writing on a subject, such as a sermon. 3) (verb, formal) To talk or write at length about something: «He discoursed on the stars». 4) (language study) Any stretch of language longer than a sentence: conversation or connected text.
its sense in the lessons: A formal exam word met in English, history and church texts. In church: a «discourse» can mean a long sermon or teaching, such as Jesus' discourses in the Gospels. In news: «political discourse». Phrases: «public discourse», «a discourse on», «discourse about».
examples from the lessons: The professor gave a long discourse on volcanoes. | Polite discourse means listening as well as talking. | Grandad discoursed on the old days for an hour. | In the Gospel, Jesus' discourse at the Last Supper is long and tender. | Bad language has no place in classroom discourse. | The book is a discourse on kindness.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal word. Pronounced DIS-corse (noun), dis-CORSE (verb, sometimes). In speech say «talk», «discussion» or «speech». Do not confuse with «discus» or «course».

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a way that is not honest; by lying, cheating or stealing. 2) (law) With the intention of cheating someone or taking what is not yours.
its sense in the lessons: In ethics and school life: getting marks dishonestly (copying) or winning a game dishonestly (cheating). In law and news: obtaining money dishonestly is a crime. In stories: villains act dishonestly. Phrases: «act dishonestly», «obtained dishonestly», «behave dishonestly».
examples from the lessons: He won the game dishonestly by peeking at the cards. | The money was obtained dishonestly. | She answered dishonestly when Mum asked who broke the vase. | Acting dishonestly can lose you your friends. | The man dishonestly claimed the lost wallet was his. | If you score points dishonestly, they don't really count.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from «dishonest». The H is silent: dis-ON-est-lee. Opposite: «honestly». Note: «Honestly!» can also be an exclamation of annoyance, but «dishonestly» never is.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Behaviour that is not honest, such as lying, cheating or stealing. 2) The quality of being a person who is not honest.
its sense in the lessons: In ethics and religious education: honesty is a key value; dishonesty breaks trust; the Ten Commandments say «You shall not steal» and «You shall not bear false witness». In school: academic dishonesty (cheating, copying) has consequences. In law and adult life: dishonesty at work can lead to being sacked. Phrases: «an act of dishonesty», «accused of dishonesty».
examples from the lessons: Copying in a test is dishonesty. | The team was punished for dishonesty in the race. | Dishonesty breaks trust between friends. | He was sacked for dishonesty at work. | The story teaches that dishonesty always comes out in the end. | She was ashamed of her dishonesty and said sorry.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «an act of dishonesty», not «a dishonesty». Silent H. Opposite: «honesty».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Not being loyal: failing to support or be faithful to a friend, family, team, country or cause. 2) A disloyal act.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and history: disloyalty to a king can be called treason; in the Bible, Judas' betrayal and Peter's denial are famous stories of disloyalty, and Peter was forgiven. In friendships: telling a friend's secret is disloyalty. Phrases: «disloyalty to», «an act of disloyalty», «accused of disloyalty».
examples from the lessons: Telling her secret to everyone was an act of disloyalty. | The king punished the knight for disloyalty. | Peter wept bitterly over his disloyalty to Jesus. | Switching to the other team felt like disloyalty. | The captain would not forgive disloyalty. | Sam's disloyalty hurt more than losing the game.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly uncountable; countable for single acts. Adjective: «disloyal»; opposite «loyalty». Stronger words: «betrayal», «treachery».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To speak about someone or something in a way that shows you think they are not important or not good; to belittle.
its sense in the lessons: A formal exam word. In ethics and school life: disparaging others' work or background is unkind. In news: politicians may disparage opponents. It tells the reader that someone is putting others down. Phrases: «disparage someone's efforts», «not to disparage».
examples from the lessons: Don't disparage your sister's drawing — she tried her best. | The critic disparaged the new film. | He disparaged his rival's ideas without listening to them. | It is wrong to disparage people because of where they come from. | Without wishing to disparage the cook, the soup was cold. | She never disparages other teams, even when they lose.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Noun: «disparagement». Adjective: «disparaging». Formal; in speech say «put down», «run down», «belittle». Pronounced dis-PARR-ij.

part of speech: adjective (disparaging, more disparaging); present participle of disparage
meaning for a pupil: 1) Showing that you think someone or something is not good or not important; insulting in a quiet way: «disparaging remarks».
its sense in the lessons: In stories and ethics: disparaging comments hurt feelings and can be bullying. In news: «disparaging remarks» about a group of people are often reported and criticised. Phrases: «disparaging remarks», «disparaging comments», «a disparaging look».
examples from the lessons: He made disparaging remarks about her clothes. | The coach would not allow disparaging comments about the other team. | She gave my sandcastle a disparaging look. | Disparaging words can hurt as much as a push. | The review was very disparaging about the new restaurant. | Grandma never says anything disparaging about anyone.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb: «disparagingly». Formal; in speech say «rude», «mean», «putting people down». Do not confuse with «disparate» (very different from each other).

part of speech: adjective (displeased, more displeased); past form of displease
meaning for a pupil: 1) Annoyed or unhappy about something someone has done. 2) (verb, past) Made someone feel annoyed or unhappy.
its sense in the lessons: A rather formal or polite word, used in stories for kings, teachers and parents: «The queen was most displeased». In the Bible, God or a king may be displeased with wrongdoing. In everyday life it is a gentle way to say angry. Phrases: «displeased with», «displeased at», «displeased about», «not displeased» (secretly quite pleased).
examples from the lessons: The teacher was displeased with our noisy behaviour. | The king was displeased and sent the jester away. | Mum looked displeased when she saw the muddy floor. | The coach was displeased at our late arrival. | The cat seemed displeased about its bath. | Grandad was not displeased when we offered to wash the car.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Use «displeased with» a person or result, «displeased at/about» an event. Opposite: «pleased». Milder and more formal than «angry».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A feeling of being annoyed or not satisfied with someone or something.
its sense in the lessons: Rather formal. Used in stories and news: someone shows displeasure with a frown, a sigh or a letter of complaint. In the Bible and old texts: «the king's displeasure» was a danger. Phrases: «show displeasure», «express displeasure», «to someone's displeasure», «incur someone's displeasure».
examples from the lessons: The crowd showed its displeasure by booing. | Much to my displeasure, it rained all through the holiday. | The head teacher expressed her displeasure at the mess. | The cat showed its displeasure by turning its back. | Parents wrote letters to show their displeasure about the new rules. | No one wanted to incur the king's displeasure.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Formal; in speech say «annoyance», «being cross». Opposite: «pleasure». Pronounced dis-PLEZH-er.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Too large or too small compared with something else; not in a fair or sensible proportion: «a disproportionate punishment».
its sense in the lessons: In maths: proportion and ratio — a disproportionate share is more (or less) than the fair share. In ethics and law: a punishment should fit the wrongdoing; a disproportionate one is unfair. In science and drawing: a figure with disproportionate parts (a head too big for the body). Phrases: «disproportionate to», «a disproportionate amount», «disproportionately large».
examples from the lessons: Missing a whole term of football for being late once seemed a disproportionate punishment. | The giant had disproportionate hands, far too big for his body. | A disproportionate number of the sweets went to Sam. | The cost of the repair was disproportionate to the value of the old bike. | The drawing looks odd because the legs are disproportionate. | Small schools spend a disproportionate amount on heating.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal. Adverb: «disproportionately». Opposite: «proportionate». In maths problems: if a share is disproportionate, it does not match the ratio given — e.g. 3 children sharing equally should each get one-third.

part of speech: adjective (disqualified); past form of disqualify (disqualify, disqualifies, disqualified, disqualifying)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Officially stopped from taking part in or winning a competition because you broke a rule. 2) (law) Not allowed to do something, such as drive or hold a job, because of a rule or a court decision.
its sense in the lessons: In sport and school competitions: a runner who starts too early, a swimmer who touches the wrong way, a team that cheats is disqualified. In adult life and news: a driver can be disqualified from driving. Phrases: «disqualified from», «disqualified for», «be disqualified».
examples from the lessons: The runner was disqualified for a false start. | Our team was disqualified because we had too many players. | She was disqualified from the spelling bee for using a dictionary. | The judge disqualified him from driving for a year. | The cake was disqualified because a grown-up had made it. | If you push in the race, you'll be disqualified.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Disqualify» changes y to i: disqualifies, disqualified. Noun: «disqualification». Use «disqualified from» an event and «for» the reason. Spelling: q is followed by u.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To spread information, news or ideas widely to many people. 2) (science, formal) To spread or scatter widely, as seeds or a disease.
its sense in the lessons: A formal exam word. In science: research results are disseminated in journals; seeds are disseminated by wind and birds. In news and online safety: false news can be disseminated quickly — check before sharing. In church history: early Christians disseminated the Gospel across the Roman world. Phrases: «disseminate information», «widely disseminated».
examples from the lessons: The school disseminates news to parents by email. | Wind disseminates dandelion seeds far and wide. | Fake news can be disseminated very quickly online. | The scientists disseminated their findings at a conference. | Missionaries disseminated the Gospel in many lands. | Leaflets were disseminated to every house.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Noun: «dissemination». Formal; in speech say «spread», «share». Double S, single M: dis-SEM-in-ate.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Something that takes your attention away from what you should be doing: «Phones are a distraction in class». 2) Something fun that takes your mind off worries; an amusement. 3) (formal) A state of great worry or confusion: «driven to distraction».
its sense in the lessons: At school: distractions such as noise, phones or chatting make learning hard; teachers remove distractions. Safety: distraction while crossing roads or driving causes accidents. In stories: a character may cause a distraction so another can escape. Phrases: «a welcome distraction», «drive someone to distraction», «cause a distraction», «without distraction».
examples from the lessons: Phones are a big distraction during homework. | The dog barking was a distraction during the test. | While Tom caused a distraction, Mia grabbed the key. | Playing football was a welcome distraction from his worries. | The noise from the road drives Mum to distraction. | Never let anything be a distraction when you cross the road. | We need a quiet room without distractions.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Verb: «distract»; adjective: «distracted» (not paying attention). Do not confuse with «destruction» (destroying) or «detraction».

meaning for a pupil: 1) The quality of being God or a god; being divine. 2) A god or goddess: «Roman divinities». 3) (school, university) The study of religion and God; theology: «a Doctor of Divinity». 4) (sweets, US) A soft white sweet made with egg whites and sugar (also «divinity fudge»).
its sense in the lessons: In religious education: Christians believe in the divinity of Jesus — that he is both God and man; other faiths and ancient peoples had their own divinities. In history: Greek and Roman divinities like Zeus and Jupiter. At universities: divinity schools train church ministers. Phrases: «the divinity of Christ», «divinity school», «a pagan divinity».
examples from the lessons: Christians believe in the divinity of Jesus. | The Romans worshipped many divinities. | My uncle studied divinity before becoming a vicar. | Zeus was the king of the Greek divinities. | The Egyptian temple was built for a sun divinity. | She made divinity sweets for the church bake sale.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable for «a god», uncountable for the quality or subject. Adjective: «divine». Talk about beliefs respectfully: «Christians believe…», «The Greeks believed…».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Power or control over people, land or things: «have dominion over». 2) A land or territory ruled by a king or government. 3) (history) «Dominion» was the name for some self-governing countries of the British Empire, such as Canada, Australia and New Zealand. 4) (Bible) In Genesis, God gives people dominion over the animals, which many Christians understand as a duty to care for creation.
its sense in the lessons: In history: kings ruled over dominions; Canada was once called the Dominion of Canada. In religious education: the Genesis account of dominion, and the idea of stewardship (looking after the earth). Phrases: «dominion over», «under the dominion of», «Dominion Day».
examples from the lessons: The king had dominion over all the land. | In Genesis, God gives people dominion over the fish, birds and animals. | Many Christians believe dominion means caring for creation, not harming it. | Canada was once called a Dominion. | The emperor's dominions stretched across the sea. | The dragon held dominion over the mountain.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal and historical. Countable for a land. Related words: «dominate», «domain». Pronounced doh-MIN-yun.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person or group that gives money, goods or help to a charity or a cause. 2) (medicine) A person who gives blood, an organ or another part of the body to help someone else: «a blood donor», «an organ donor». 3) (science) Something that gives up a part, such as an atom giving an electron.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and ethics: donors give to charities, school fundraisers, food banks. In health: blood donors and organ donors save lives; people can choose to register as organ donors. In news: big donors give money to political parties. Phrases: «blood donor», «organ donor», «anonymous donor», «generous donor».
examples from the lessons: An anonymous donor gave the school a new piano. | Grandad is a blood donor and gives blood twice a year. | The donor card says she wants to help others after she dies. | Thanks to a kidney donor, my cousin is healthy again. | The charity thanked all its donors. | The food bank depends on generous donors.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Verb: «donate»; noun: «donation». Opposite: «recipient» (the one who receives). Spelling: -or, not -er.

part of speech: noun (doom — uncountable); verb (doom, dooms, doomed, dooming)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (noun) Death, ruin or a terrible fate that cannot be avoided. 2) (verb) To make something certain to fail or suffer: «The plan was doomed from the start». 3) (noun, informal) «doom and gloom» — a feeling that everything will go wrong. 4) (old, Bible) Judgement, especially the Last Judgement: «Doomsday» or «the crack of doom».
its sense in the lessons: In stories and films: heroes face doom; villains plot doom; «impending doom» builds suspense. In history: the Domesday Book (an old English survey; not about the end of the world). In everyday talk: «doom and gloom» about the weather or tests; «doomscrolling» (reading lots of bad news online). Phrases: «doomed to fail», «sense of doom», «spell doom for», «prophet of doom».
examples from the lessons: The ship was doomed when it hit the iceberg. | The knight rode bravely to meet his doom. | Too much rain could spell doom for the picnic. | A feeling of doom came over me before the test. | Stop the doom and gloom — it might be sunny tomorrow! | Without water, the plants were doomed. | The dragon roared, "Your doom is near!"
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable noun. Regular verb: doomed. «Doomed» (adjective) means sure to fail or die. Informal «doomscrolling» is a modern word. The Domesday Book is spelled differently.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who earns money by working. 2) (UK informal) Something that brings in money: «a nice little earner».
its sense in the lessons: In adult life and money lessons: the main earner in a family; low and high earners; «breadwinner» is a similar word. In maths problems: comparing what two earners make per hour or per week. Phrases: «main earner», «high earner», «low earner», «wage earner», «a nice little earner».
examples from the lessons: Mum is the main earner in our house. | High earners pay more tax. | The lemonade stand was a nice little earner. | Both earners in the family work night shifts. | If one earner makes £10 an hour and works 5 hours, he earns £50. | The ice-cream van is a good earner in summer.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. From «earn» (get money for work, or deserve). «A nice little earner» is British, informal. In maths: earnings = rate × hours (or × days).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Connected with the Christian church or its clergy (priests, ministers, bishops): «ecclesiastical buildings», «ecclesiastical law».
its sense in the lessons: A formal word met in history, church life and architecture: ecclesiastical robes, ecclesiastical courts, ecclesiastical history. It tells the reader that something belongs to the church. Phrases: «ecclesiastical history», «ecclesiastical court», «ecclesiastical architecture».
examples from the lessons: The bishop wore his ecclesiastical robes. | The museum has a room of ecclesiastical silver. | The old church is a fine example of ecclesiastical architecture. | In the past, ecclesiastical courts judged church matters. | The library holds many ecclesiastical records. | Ecclesiastical music filled the cathedral.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Long formal word: ih-klee-zee-AS-tik-ul. Related: «ecclesiastic» (a churchman), «Ecclesiastes» (a book of the Bible). In speech say «church» as an adjective: «church music».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Working well; producing the result you want, especially of a medicine or treatment.
its sense in the lessons: A formal exam and medical word. It tells the reader that something truly works. In science: scientists test whether a treatment is efficacious with fair tests. Phrases: «efficacious in», «highly efficacious», «efficacious against».
examples from the lessons: The new medicine proved efficacious against the cough. | Rest and fluids are efficacious for a cold. | The scientists tested whether the cream was efficacious. | A warm bath was efficacious in calming the baby. | The spray was efficacious against greenfly. | Practice is the most efficacious way to learn tables.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal. Noun: «efficacy». Close words: «effective» (works), «efficient» (works without waste). In speech say «works well», «effective». Pronounced ef-ih-KAY-shus.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) The power to produce the result you want, especially of a medicine, treatment or method.
its sense in the lessons: A formal word used in science and medicine, and in exam texts. Scientists measure the efficacy of medicines in careful trials. Phrases: «the efficacy of», «proven efficacy», «test the efficacy».
examples from the lessons: Doctors tested the efficacy of the new vaccine. | We doubted the efficacy of his homemade cure. | The efficacy of the method was shown by better test results. | Studies prove the efficacy of hand washing against germs. | Scientists compared the efficacy of two sun creams. | The efficacy of prayer is a matter of faith for many.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable, formal. Adjective: «efficacious». Do not confuse with «efficiency» (doing something without waste of time or energy). Stress: EF-ih-kuh-see.

part of speech: adjective (elaborate, more elaborate) — pronounced ih-LAB-er-it; verb (elaborate, elaborates, elaborated, elaborating) — pronounced ih-LAB-er-ate
meaning for a pupil: 1) (adjective) Having many parts or details; carefully planned and complicated: «an elaborate costume». 2) (verb) To give more details or explain more: «Can you elaborate on your answer?» 3) (verb, formal) To develop a plan or idea in detail.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons: teachers ask pupils to elaborate — add detail and examples to answers. In art and design: elaborate patterns, costumes, cakes. In stories: an elaborate plan or trick. Phrases: «elaborate on», «an elaborate plan», «elaborate decorations».
examples from the lessons: The princess wore an elaborate gown with gold stitching. | Can you elaborate on why you think the character is sad? | The thieves made an elaborate plan to steal the jewels. | Grandma baked an elaborate three-layer cake. | The cathedral has elaborate carvings. | "Please elaborate," said the teacher, "your answer is too short." | The magician's trick was very elaborate.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The adjective and verb are spelled the same but sound different (adjective ends «-it», verb ends «-ate»). Verb takes «on»: «elaborate on something». Noun: «elaboration». Opposite of the adjective: «simple», «plain».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A picture or object that stands for a country, group, team or idea: «The maple leaf is the emblem of Canada». 2) Something that represents a quality: «The dove is an emblem of peace». 3) A badge with such a picture.
its sense in the lessons: In history, citizenship and geography: national emblems (the rose of England, the thistle of Scotland, the shamrock of Ireland, the kangaroo of Australia, the silver fern of New Zealand, the bald eagle of the USA). In church life: the cross, the fish and the dove are Christian emblems. At school: the school emblem on uniforms. Phrases: «national emblem», «the emblem of», «school emblem».
examples from the lessons: The maple leaf is Canada's national emblem. | The dove is an emblem of peace. | Our school emblem is an owl holding a book. | The shamrock is an emblem of Ireland. | The cross is the main emblem of Christianity. | The team's emblem is printed on every shirt. | The silver fern is a famous emblem of New Zealand.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Adjective: «emblematic» (being a typical example or symbol). Close words: «symbol», «logo», «badge», «crest».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Special importance or attention given to something: «The school puts emphasis on reading». 2) Extra force given to a word or syllable when speaking, to show it matters: «Put the emphasis on "not"». 3) In writing, a way of showing importance, such as bold or italic print.
its sense in the lessons: In English: emphasis in speaking (stress) and writing (bold, italics, underlining, capital letters, exclamation marks). In school life: the emphasis of a lesson is its main point. Phrases: «put/place emphasis on», «with emphasis», «a strong emphasis», «the emphasis is on».
examples from the lessons: Our coach puts a lot of emphasis on teamwork. | "I did NOT break it," she said with emphasis. | In this lesson, the emphasis is on fractions. | Italics are used for emphasis in the story. | The word "photograph" has the emphasis on the first part. | The school places emphasis on kindness.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «emphases» (em-fuh-seez). Verb: «emphasise» (UK) / «emphasize» (US); adjective: «emphatic». Use «emphasis on», never «emphasis about».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A group of countries or lands ruled by one ruler or government, often an emperor or empress. 2) A very large business or group of businesses controlled by one person or company: «a toy empire». 3) (informal) An area that someone controls: «The kitchen is Dad's empire».
its sense in the lessons: In history: the Roman Empire, the British Empire, the Ottoman, Aztec and Inca empires; empires rise and fall. In the Bible: the Roman Empire ruled the land where Jesus lived. In business news: media empires. Phrases: «rise and fall of an empire», «build an empire», «the Roman Empire».
examples from the lessons: The Roman Empire built roads across Europe. | Jesus was born when the Roman Empire ruled Judea. | She built a pizza empire from one small shop. | The British Empire once ruled many lands around the world. | The empire fell after many wars. | My little brother's empire is the sandpit.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Capital letter in names: «the Roman Empire». A ruler is an «emperor» (man) or «empress» (woman). Adjective: «imperial». The «Empire State Building» is in New York.

part of speech: adjective (empowered, more empowered); past form of empower (empower, empowers, empowered, empowering)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Feeling strong, confident and in control of your life. 2) Given the power, right or permission to do something, especially officially: «The police are empowered to arrest».
its sense in the lessons: In school and personal development: pupils feel empowered when they have a voice (school council, choosing projects). In law and news: officials empowered to make decisions. Phrases: «feel empowered», «empowered to do», «empowered by».
examples from the lessons: Learning to swim made Amy feel empowered. | The school council is empowered to choose new games for the yard. | Police officers are empowered to stop cars. | Speaking up in class left him feeling empowered. | The judge is empowered to decide the case. | Girls in the club felt empowered to try coding.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb «empower». Noun: «empowerment». Common in modern talk about confidence; a little formal. «Empowered to do something» = allowed and able to do it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To put someone or something in danger; to make harm likely. 2) To threaten something so that it might be lost or die out: «Pollution endangers wildlife».
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography: «endangered species» are animals and plants that might die out (tigers, pandas, kakapo). In safety lessons: behaviour that endangers others (running by the pool, playing near roads). In law: «endangering life» is a serious crime. Phrases: «endanger lives», «endangered species», «endanger health».
examples from the lessons: Running by the pool can endanger you and others. | Plastic in the ocean endangers turtles. | Pandas are an endangered species. | The driver endangered lives by speeding near the school. | Cutting down forests endangers many animals. | Don't endanger yourself trying to rescue someone in deep water — call for help.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Adjective «endangered» (in danger of dying out). Noun idea: «danger». Spelling: en + danger.

part of speech: noun (endeavour, endeavours); verb (endeavour, endeavours, endeavoured, endeavouring) — formal
meaning for a pupil: 1) (noun, formal) A serious effort or attempt to do something: «a new endeavour». 2) (verb, formal) To try hard to do something: «We endeavour to help all pupils». 3) (noun) Hard work towards a goal: «human endeavour».
its sense in the lessons: A formal exam and school-report word: «He endeavours to do his best». In history: Captain Cook's ship was called the Endeavour; space endeavours. Phrases: «endeavour to», «in all your endeavours», «human endeavour», «make every endeavour».
examples from the lessons: We endeavour to answer every letter. | Climbing the mountain was a great endeavour. | Good luck in all your future endeavours! | Captain Cook sailed the Endeavour to Australia and New Zealand. | The space station is a triumph of human endeavour. | She endeavoured to finish the race despite her sore knee.
note for the reader of a maths problem: British spelling «endeavour»; American «endeavor». Formal; in speech say «try», «effort». Verb takes «to + verb»: «endeavour to help». Pronounced en-DEV-er.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The ability to keep going through something long, hard or painful without giving up. 2) (sport) The ability to keep up physical effort for a long time; stamina. 3) The ability of something to last for a long time without breaking.
its sense in the lessons: In PE and science: endurance sports (long-distance running, swimming, cycling); building endurance by training; heart and lungs. In stories and history: the endurance of explorers like Shackleton (his ship was called Endurance). In the Bible: patience and endurance in hard times. Phrases: «test of endurance», «endurance race», «beyond endurance», «build endurance».
examples from the lessons: Running a marathon takes great endurance. | Shackleton's crew showed amazing endurance on the ice. | Swimming helps build endurance. | The long car journey was a test of endurance. | The pain was beyond endurance. | The rope's endurance was tested by the heavy boat. | Endurance means not giving up when things get hard.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Verb: «endure»; adjective: «enduring» (lasting). Close word: «stamina». Not the same as «speed»: a sprinter needs speed, a marathon runner needs endurance.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To make sure that people obey a law or rule. 2) To make something happen by force or strong pressure: «enforced silence».
its sense in the lessons: In citizenship: police enforce laws; referees enforce rules in sport; teachers and lunchtime staff enforce school rules. In adult life: courts enforce payment of debts. Phrases: «enforce the law», «enforce a rule», «strictly enforced», «law enforcement».
examples from the lessons: The police enforce the speed limit near schools. | The referee enforced the offside rule. | The no-phone rule will be strictly enforced. | Lifeguards enforce the "no running" rule at the pool. | The court enforced the payment. | A rule is useless if nobody enforces it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Noun: «enforcement» («law enforcement» = police and similar). Do not confuse with «reinforce» (make stronger). Spelling: en + force.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To make something better, stronger or more attractive; to improve the quality or value. 2) (computing, images) To make a picture or sound clearer: «enhance the photo».
its sense in the lessons: In science and computing: enhance an image, enhance sound. In school: enhance your writing with adjectives and detail; enhance learning with trips. In everyday life: spices enhance flavour. Safety and ethics: «performance-enhancing drugs» are banned in sport. Phrases: «enhance quality», «enhance the flavour», «enhanced by».
examples from the lessons: A pinch of salt enhances the flavour. | Adding adjectives can enhance your writing. | The detective enhanced the photo to see the number plate. | The new playground enhanced the school grounds. | Lights enhance the beauty of the Christmas tree. | Performance-enhancing drugs are against the rules in sport.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Noun: «enhancement». Formal; in speech say «improve», «make better». Spelling: en + hance (not «enhanse»).

meaning for a pupil: 1) The act of making something bigger. 2) A photo that has been printed or made bigger. 3) (maths) A transformation that makes a shape bigger or smaller by a scale factor, keeping its shape the same. 4) (medicine) A part of the body that has become larger than normal: «enlargement of the heart».
its sense in the lessons: In maths: enlargement by a scale factor — every length is multiplied by the same number (scale factor 2 doubles each side; area becomes 4 times bigger). In art and photography: enlargements of photos. In everyday life: enlargement of a building or a school. Phrases: «scale factor of enlargement», «centre of enlargement», «an enlargement of».
examples from the lessons: Draw an enlargement of the triangle with scale factor 3. | Mum framed an enlargement of our wedding photo. | The enlargement of the library gave us more room. | In an enlargement, the angles stay the same. | The centre of enlargement is the point the shape grows from. | The doctor noticed an enlargement of his tonsils.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Verb: «enlarge». Maths: with scale factor k, lengths are multiplied by k, area by k × k, and angles do not change. A scale factor between 0 and 1 makes the shape smaller (still called an enlargement in maths).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) A feeling of hate or strong dislike between people or groups; being enemies.
its sense in the lessons: Used in history, Bible and stories: enmity between nations, families or rivals; in Genesis, God puts enmity between the serpent and the woman. In ethics: forgiveness can end enmity; Jesus taught «love your enemies». Phrases: «enmity between», «long enmity», «bitter enmity».
examples from the lessons: There was bitter enmity between the two families. | The enmity between the kingdoms lasted for generations. | Their enmity ended when they shook hands. | God put enmity between the serpent and the woman. | Jealousy grew into enmity. | Forgiveness can turn enmity into friendship.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal, mostly uncountable. Related to «enemy». Opposite: «friendship», «amity». In speech say «hatred», «being enemies».

part of speech: verb (entail, entails, entailed, entailing); noun (an entail — law, old)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (verb) To include or need something as a necessary part or result: «The job entails a lot of travel». 2) (logic) If A entails B, then whenever A is true, B must also be true. 3) (noun, law, old) A rule that property must pass down to certain heirs, often eldest sons, as in old English novels.
its sense in the lessons: A formal exam word. In everyday talk: «What does the job entail?» = what do you have to do? In maths and logic: «entail» means «it follows that». In history and old novels: entailed estates. Phrases: «what does it entail?», «entail risk», «entail cost».
examples from the lessons: What does being class monitor entail? | Owning a dog entails walking it every day. | The trip will entail an early start. | Building the shed entailed a lot of work. | If a number ends in 0, that entails it can be divided by 10. | The house was entailed, so it went to a cousin, not the daughters.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Formal; in speech say «involve», «mean», «need». Do not confuse with «entrails» (insides of an animal). In logic, «A entails B» does not mean «B entails A».

meaning for a pupil: 1) To say words clearly and carefully, sounding each part. 2) (formal) To state an idea, plan or belief clearly: «enunciate a principle».
its sense in the lessons: In English and drama lessons: actors, readers and speakers learn to enunciate so the audience can hear. In church: readers enunciate Bible readings clearly. In formal writing: leaders enunciate policies. Phrases: «enunciate clearly», «enunciate each word».
examples from the lessons: Please enunciate so everyone at the back can hear. | The actor enunciated every word of the poem. | When you read in church, enunciate clearly and slowly. | The head teacher enunciated the new rules at assembly. | Practise tongue twisters to help you enunciate. | She enunciated "thank you" very carefully in Irish.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Noun: «enunciation». Formal; in speech say «speak clearly». Do not confuse with «announce» or «pronounce» (to say a word in a certain way). Pronounced ih-NUN-see-ate.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Wanting something that someone else has, and feeling unhappy or annoyed that you do not have it; jealous.
its sense in the lessons: In ethics and religious education: envy is one of the «seven deadly sins» in Christian teaching; the Ten Commandments say «You shall not covet». In stories: an envious sister or neighbour causes trouble (Cinderella's stepsisters, Joseph's brothers). In everyday life: feeling envious of someone's new bike is normal, but acting on it badly is not. Phrases: «envious of», «envious looks», «green with envy».
examples from the lessons: Tom was envious of his friend's new bike. | Joseph's brothers were envious of his special coat. | She cast envious looks at the girl with the puppy. | I'm a bit envious that you're going to the beach. | Being envious made him unhappy all day. | The envious stepsisters were cruel to Cinderella.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Use «envious of» someone or something. Noun: «envy». «Envious» and «jealous» are close: envy = wanting what others have; jealousy can also mean fear of losing what you have. «Green with envy» = very envious.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To imagine or picture something that might happen in the future. 2) (formal) To expect or plan something: «We envisage finishing by summer».
its sense in the lessons: A formal exam and news word, common in British English (Americans often say «envision»). In school: «envisage the scene» in creative writing. In planning: «The council envisages a new park». Phrases: «envisage a future», «it is envisaged that».
examples from the lessons: Can you envisage living on Mars? | The architect envisaged a school full of light. | I never envisaged that we would win the cup. | It is envisaged that the new bridge will open next year. | Close your eyes and envisage a quiet beach. | The plan envisages more trees on every street.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal, mainly British. Regular verb. In speech say «imagine», «picture», «expect». American «envision» means the same.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (noun) A long poem or story about the adventures of heroes, often in ancient times, such as the Odyssey or Beowulf. 2) (noun) A long film or book about big, exciting events. 3) (adjective) Very big, long, brave or impressive: «an epic journey». 4) (adjective, slang) Really great, amazing: «That party was epic!» 5) (adjective, slang) «epic fail» — a huge, funny failure.
its sense in the lessons: In English and history: epic poems (the Iliad, the Odyssey, Beowulf, Gilgamesh), heroes and quests. In everyday and children's slang: «epic» for anything brilliant. Phrases: «an epic journey», «epic battle», «epic fail» (slang), «of epic proportions».
examples from the lessons: Beowulf is an old English epic about a hero who fights a monster. | Homer's Odyssey is an epic poem. | The explorers made an epic journey across the ice. | We watched an epic film about knights and dragons. | That water fight was epic! (slang) | Falling in the pond in my new clothes was an epic fail. | The final was an epic battle that went to penalties.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun. The slang senses («epic!», «epic fail») are informal — not for formal writing. Do not confuse with «epoch» (a long period of time). Adjective form also «epical» (rare).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To make a mistake or be wrong: «To err is human». 2) (formal, old, church) To do wrong; to sin: «We have erred and strayed like lost sheep». 3) «err on the side of» — to choose the safer of two choices: «err on the side of caution».
its sense in the lessons: A formal and old word. Common sayings: «To err is human, to forgive divine» (it is natural to make mistakes; forgiving is God-like). In church: some old prayers say «we have erred and strayed». In safety: «err on the side of caution» = choose the safer option. Phrases: «to err is human», «err on the side of caution», «erring child».
examples from the lessons: To err is human, to forgive divine. | If you're unsure whether the ice is safe, err on the side of caution and stay off. | The judge erred in his decision. | In the old prayer we say, "We have erred and strayed from your ways like lost sheep." | The erring pupil said sorry. | It is better to err on the side of kindness.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: erred, erring. Pronounced «ur» (rhymes with «fur»), sometimes «air». Related nouns: «error», «erratum». Do not confuse with the hesitation sound «er» or «erm».

part of speech: adjective (evangelical, more evangelical); noun (an evangelical, evangelicals)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (church) Evangelical describes Christians and churches that put great weight on the Bible, on a personal faith in Jesus and on telling others the good news. 2) (church) An evangelical is a person who belongs to this kind of Christianity. 3) Very keen and eager to persuade others about something you believe in, like a cause or a hobby.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and lessons on church life it tells the reader what kind of church or believer someone is: lively worship, Bible study, sharing faith. In everyday talk «evangelical about» means wildly enthusiastic: «evangelical about recycling». Phrases: evangelical church, evangelical Christian, evangelical zeal.
examples from the lessons: Our neighbours go to an evangelical church on the corner. | Evangelical Christians believe that each person can have a personal friendship with God. | The evangelical preacher spoke about the good news of Jesus. | Many evangelicals read the Bible every day. | My uncle is evangelical about cycling and tells everyone to get a bike. | She was almost evangelical about her new vegetable diet. | The evangelical youth group sang songs at the summer camp.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comes from «evangel», an old word for the gospel, the «good news». Capital letter is optional but common when naming a group. Not the same as «evangelist» (a person who preaches the gospel, or one of the four Gospel writers). The everyday sense «very keen» is a bit of a joke-comparison; it is not about religion.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Easy to see or understand; clear and obvious. 2) (formal) Shown by the facts, so that people can be sure of it.
its sense in the lessons: In science and maths it means something you can see from the results or the diagram: «it is evident from the table that…». In stories it tells the reader that a feeling or fact is plain to everyone: «her joy was evident». Phrases: it is evident that, self-evident, become evident, evident from.
examples from the lessons: It was evident that the dog had eaten the cake. | Her excitement was evident from her huge smile. | It is evident from the graph that plants grow faster in sunlight. | The damage from the storm was evident everywhere in the town. | His nervousness became evident when his voice shook. | The answer was evident once we drew a picture of the problem. | It is self-evident that you cannot be in two places at once.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Related words: evidently (adverb), evidence (noun, the facts that prove something). Do not mix «evident» (clear) with «evidence» (proof). «Self-evident» means so obvious that it needs no proof. It is a slightly formal word; in speech people often say «clear» or «obvious».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (law) To kill someone as a punishment ordered by a court or ruler. 2) (formal) To carry out a plan, an order or a task. 3) To perform a movement or skill well, such as a dance step or a dive. 4) (computers) To run a program or a command.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons it means putting a person to death as punishment, for example kings and traitors long ago. In sport, dance and computing it means doing or running something exactly: «execute a perfect cartwheel», «the computer executes the code». Phrases: execute a plan, execute an order, be executed for, execute a program.
examples from the lessons: The gymnast executed a perfect backflip. | The team executed their plan and won the match. | When you press Enter, the computer executes the command. | In history we learned that the king was executed long ago. | The soldiers executed the general's orders at once. | The skater executed a tricky jump on the ice. | The robot will execute each step in order.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Nouns: execution (the act of executing), executive (a manager in a company), executioner (the person who carried out death sentences). An «executor» is the person who carries out the wishes in someone's will. The killing sense is serious and sad; in sport and computing the word is neutral and common.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To be a typical example of something. 2) (formal) To give an example to show what you mean.
its sense in the lessons: In English and exam questions it appears as «Which sentence best exemplifies…?» meaning «Which is the best example of…?». In stories and essays it shows that a person or thing is a perfect example of a quality. Phrases: exemplify a quality, is exemplified by.
examples from the lessons: Her kindness exemplifies the spirit of our school. | This poem exemplifies the use of rhyme. | Can you exemplify your point with a story? | The old castle exemplifies how people built long ago. | His hard work exemplified what a good team player does. | Which sentence best exemplifies a simile? | The rainforest exemplifies a habitat full of life.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Related: example, exemplary (excellent, a model for others). Spelling: y changes to i before -es and -ed: exemplifies, exemplified. It is a formal word; in speech people say «is a good example of» or «shows».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Getting bigger in size, amount or space. 2) (science) The way a material takes up more space when it gets warmer. 3) The growth of a business, a town or an empire into new places. 4) (maths) Writing a number or an expression out in a longer form, such as 345 = 300 + 40 + 5.
its sense in the lessons: In science it describes heat making solids, liquids and gases expand: railway tracks have gaps for expansion. In maths «expanded form» or «expansion» means writing a number as a sum of its place values, or multiplying out brackets. In history and business it means growing into new lands or markets. Phrases: rapid expansion, expansion of the town, thermal expansion.
examples from the lessons: The expansion of the balloon showed that the air inside was getting warmer. | Bridges have small gaps to allow for expansion on hot days. | The expansion of the school means we will get a new library. | Write 4,562 in expanded form: 4,000 + 500 + 60 + 2. | The company's expansion brought new jobs to the town. | The Roman Empire's expansion covered many lands. | Water's expansion when it freezes can crack a pipe.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: expand; adjective: expansive (wide, open, or friendly and chatty). The opposite is contraction. Spelling: -sion, not -tion. In maths, expansion does not change the value: 345 and 300 + 40 + 5 are equal.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Quick and efficient; done fast and without wasting time.
its sense in the lessons: Mostly used in formal letters, business and law: «an expeditious reply». In stories it can make a character sound stiff or official. Phrases: in an expeditious manner, expeditious delivery.
examples from the lessons: We thank you for your expeditious reply. | The council promised an expeditious repair of the road. | The most expeditious way to the station is by train. | The judge asked for an expeditious end to the case. | The nurse dealt with the queue in an expeditious way. | An expeditious tidy-up meant we could go out to play sooner.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb: expeditiously. Related to «expedite» (to speed something up), not directly to «expedition» (a long journey), although they share a root. A formal word; in everyday speech say «quick» or «fast».

part of speech: verb, past form of exploit (exploit, exploits, exploited, exploiting); adjective (exploited)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Treated unfairly by someone who uses you for their own gain, for example made to work hard for very little pay. 2) Used fully and well, such as a resource or a chance. 3) (computers) A weakness in a program that has been used by someone to break in.
its sense in the lessons: In history and ethics lessons it describes workers, children or countries treated unfairly. In geography it describes natural resources that have been used: «the forest was exploited for wood». In games and computers it means a weakness was used. It tells the reader that someone took advantage. Phrases: exploited workers, feel exploited, be exploited by.
examples from the lessons: Long ago, many children were exploited in factories and mines. | The workers felt exploited because they were paid so little. | The team exploited every chance to score. | The coal under the hills was exploited for a hundred years. | The hacker exploited a weakness in the website. | She felt exploited when her friends only called her for help with homework. | Wind power is not yet fully exploited in some countries.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Base verb: exploit; noun: exploitation. «An exploit» (stress on EX-) can also mean a brave or exciting deed: «tales of his exploits». The verb is stressed on -PLOIT. The unfair sense is the most common and is negative; the resource sense is neutral.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To uncover something so it can be seen. 2) To leave someone or something without protection from danger, weather or sunlight. 3) To show the truth about a bad person or a secret. 4) To let someone meet or try something new: «expose children to music». 5) (photography) To let light reach the film or sensor in a camera.
its sense in the lessons: In science and safety it is about being left open to sun, cold, germs or chemicals: «do not expose skin to strong sun». In stories it often means revealing a liar or a cheat. In school it means giving children new experiences. Phrases: be exposed to, expose a lie, expose the truth, exposed skin.
examples from the lessons: Low tide exposes the rocks on the beach. | Do not expose the seedlings to frost. | The journalist exposed the cheating company. | Our teacher exposes us to music from many countries. | Hikers can get sick if they are exposed to the cold for too long. | The detective exposed the thief's lies. | Too much light will expose the whole film.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: exposure (being exposed; also the danger of cold weather: «die of exposure»). «Exposé» with an accent (ex-POH-zay) is a news story that reveals a scandal. «Exposed» also means open to wind: «an exposed hill».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A clear and full explanation of an idea or a subject. 2) (stories) The beginning part of a story that introduces the characters, the setting and the background. 3) A big public show or fair where things are displayed, also called an expo. 4) (music) The first part of a piece where the main tunes are played.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons the exposition is the first stage of a story plan (exposition, rising action, climax, falling action, resolution). In church life a preacher may give an exposition of a Bible passage, meaning an explanation. «Expo» is a big show. Phrases: story exposition, a clear exposition of, world exposition.
examples from the lessons: The exposition of the story tells us that the girl lives on a farm. | Our teacher gave a clear exposition of how volcanoes work. | The minister's exposition of the psalm helped us understand it. | Thousands of people visited the science exposition. | In the exposition we meet the hero and learn about his problem. | The book starts with a long exposition before anything exciting happens.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Related verb: expound (to explain in detail). The short form «expo» is used for fairs and shows. Not the same as «exposure» or «exhibition», though an exhibition and an exposition can both mean a public show.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Covering a large area. 2) Large in amount or very thorough and detailed. 3) (farming) Using a lot of land with little work or money per field, opposite of intensive farming.
its sense in the lessons: It tells the reader that something is big or wide-ranging: extensive damage, extensive research, extensive gardens. In geography, extensive farming means big farms with few workers per area, like sheep stations. Phrases: extensive knowledge, extensive damage, extensive grounds.
examples from the lessons: The storm caused extensive damage to the town. | The castle has extensive gardens with a maze. | She has an extensive collection of shells. | The scientists did extensive tests on the new medicine. | His extensive knowledge of dinosaurs amazed the class. | The fire spread over an extensive area of forest. | Sheep stations in Australia are a kind of extensive farming.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb: extensively. Related: extend, extension, extent. Opposite: limited, slight; in farming, intensive. It does not mean «expensive» — watch the spelling: exTENsive vs exPENsive.

part of speech: adjective (external); noun (externals — plural, the outward appearance)
meaning for a pupil: 1) On the outside, or coming from the outside. 2) Coming from another place or person, not your own school or group: «an external examiner». 3) (medicine) For use on the outside of the body only, not to be swallowed.
its sense in the lessons: In science it describes the outside of a body or object: external organs, external walls. In safety it appears on medicine labels: «For external use only» means do not swallow it. In maths, an external (exterior) angle is outside a shape. Phrases: external wall, external use only, external examiner, external factors.
examples from the lessons: The skin is the body's external covering. | This cream is for external use only. | Paint the external walls of the shed. | The external angle of a triangle is outside the shape. | An external examiner came to mark our music test. | External noise from the road made it hard to sleep. | Insects have an external skeleton called an exoskeleton.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: internal. Adverb: externally. «For external use only» is an important safety warning. Also «exterior» means outside, mostly for buildings and angles. «Externals» means the outward look of things.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A lie or a made-up story pretending to be true. 2) The making or building of something, especially from many parts in a factory.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and ethics it tells the reader that something said is false on purpose: «the whole story was a fabrication». In technology and design lessons it means making things: metal fabrication. Phrases: a complete fabrication, pure fabrication, steel fabrication.
examples from the lessons: His story about meeting a famous footballer was a complete fabrication. | The newspaper said the claims were fabrication. | The factory does the fabrication of car parts. | Her excuse was pure fabrication; she simply forgot her homework. | Steel fabrication takes skill and safety gear. | The witness admitted that his story was a fabrication.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: fabricate (to make up a lie, or to build). In the lie sense it is a stronger and more formal word than «lie». Countable when it means one invented story; uncountable when it means the activity of making things.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A natural ability of the body or mind, such as sight, hearing or memory. 2) A group of departments in a university, such as the Faculty of Science. 3) (US) All the teachers of a school or university. 4) A special skill or talent for something: «a faculty for languages».
its sense in the lessons: In stories about old people it often appears as «in full possession of her faculties», meaning her mind still works well. In American schools «the faculty» means the teachers. Phrases: mental faculties, faculty of hearing, faculty members, faculty for.
examples from the lessons: Grandpa is ninety but still has all his faculties. | The faculty of sight lets us see colours. | The faculty held a meeting about the school play. | My sister studies in the Faculty of Arts. | She has a faculty for remembering names. | Faculty and students cheered at the graduation.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: faculties (y to ies). In the UK, «staff» is usual for teachers in a school; «faculty» is mostly US or university. Not linked to «factory».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (UK, informal) Fussy about food, liking only a few things and refusing many others. 2) (informal) Following short-lived fashions or crazes.
its sense in the lessons: Used by British parents and grandparents about picky eaters: «a faddy eater». In stories it shows a child who will not eat vegetables. Phrases: faddy eater, faddy about food.
examples from the lessons: My little brother is a faddy eater and only eats pasta. | Don't be faddy; try one bite of the carrots. | Grandma said children today are too faddy about food. | The cat is so faddy that it only eats one brand of fish. | He went through a faddy phase of eating only yellow food. | The new diet seemed faddy and silly.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mainly British. Comes from «fad» (a short-lived craze). In US English people say «picky» instead. Spelling: double d.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a frightened or worried way. 2) (old-fashioned, UK) Very or extremely: «fearfully clever».
its sense in the lessons: In stories it shows how a character acts when scared: «she looked fearfully at the door». In old-fashioned British talk it can simply mean «very». Phrases: look fearfully, whisper fearfully, fearfully sorry.
examples from the lessons: The kitten peeped fearfully out from under the bed. | He whispered fearfully, «Did you hear that noise?» | The children looked fearfully at the dark cave. | She stepped fearfully onto the wobbly bridge. | I'm fearfully sorry for being late, said the old gentleman. | The little boy held his mother's hand fearfully during the storm.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: fearful (afraid, or causing fear). Similar: nervously, anxiously. Opposite: bravely, boldly, fearlessly. The «very» sense sounds old-fashioned and posh.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To pretend to feel something or to be ill, tired or asleep when you are not.
its sense in the lessons: In stories it tells the reader that a character is acting, not truly feeling: «she feigned sleep». Animals can feign death to escape danger. Phrases: feign illness, feign surprise, feign interest, feign sleep.
examples from the lessons: Tom feigned a headache so he would not have to go swimming. | The possum feigned death to trick the dog. | She feigned surprise, but she already knew about the party. | He feigned interest in his aunt's holiday photos. | The cat feigned sleep while watching the mouse. | Don't feign illness; tell the truth about the test.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced like «fain» — the g is silent. Spelling: ei. Homophone: «feint» (a fake move in sport) sounds almost the same and is related. A slightly formal word; in speech people say «pretend».

part of speech: verb, past form of feign (feign, feigns, feigned, feigning); adjective (feigned)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Pretended; shown on the outside but not truly felt. 2) Past form of feign: having pretended to feel or be something.
its sense in the lessons: In stories it warns the reader that a feeling is fake: «feigned surprise», «feigned innocence». It helps readers notice when a character is hiding the truth. Phrases: feigned interest, feigned surprise, feigned illness, with feigned calm.
examples from the lessons: She gasped with feigned surprise when she opened the present she had already seen. | He feigned illness to miss the spelling test. | With feigned innocence, the dog sat next to the chewed shoe. | The spy spoke with feigned calm. | Her feigned smile did not fool her best friend. | The fox feigned sleep until the hens came close.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced «faind», the g is silent. Opposite: genuine, real, sincere. Used before a noun as an adjective: a feigned yawn.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal, slang) A man or a boy; a spelling of «fellow» that shows how people say it. 2) (informal) A boyfriend: «her fella».
its sense in the lessons: Used in friendly, casual speech, especially in Ireland, Australia, the UK and the US. In stories it shows chatty, relaxed characters: «Good on ya, fella». It can also be used for a male animal: «that little fella». Phrases: young fella, little fella, old fella, her fella.
examples from the lessons: Hey, fella, you dropped your hat! | That little fella is my puppy, Max. | The young fella next door helped carry our shopping. | My aunt is bringing her new fella to dinner. | Come on, fellas, the game is starting! | The old fella at the shop always gives us a sweet.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: fellas. Also spelt «feller». The standard word is «fellow». It is friendly and informal, not rude, but not for written school work.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A friendly feeling of sharing and belonging among people with the same interests. 2) A group or club of people who share an aim or belief. 3) (church) Christians meeting together, sharing faith, prayer and friendship. 4) A special job or paid place for a researcher at a university.
its sense in the lessons: In church life «fellowship» means believers spending time together, often with tea after the service. In stories it shows a team bound by friendship, as in «The Fellowship of the Ring». Phrases: Christian fellowship, fellowship meal, sense of fellowship, research fellowship.
examples from the lessons: After the service there is tea and fellowship in the church hall. | The fellowship of the campers made the trip special. | Christians believe fellowship with others helps their faith grow. | The nine heroes formed a fellowship to destroy the ring. | She won a fellowship to study at a university. | Our youth fellowship meets on Friday evenings.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «fellow» + «-ship». Can be countable (a fellowship = a group, a university post) or uncountable (the feeling). Similar: friendship, companionship.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Invented or made up; not real or true. 2) Used as a false name or detail to trick people.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons it describes made-up characters and places in stories. In safety and law it describes fake names or false details used to cheat. Phrases: fictitious character, fictitious name, entirely fictitious.
examples from the lessons: Sherlock Holmes is a fictitious detective. | The story takes place in a fictitious town by the sea. | The thief gave a fictitious name to the police. | All the characters in this book are fictitious. | The scammer used a fictitious address. | Her excuse about the dog eating her homework was fictitious.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Related: fiction (stories that are made up), fictional (in a story). «Fictional» usually means part of a story; «fictitious» often hints at a lie. Spelling: -titious, with two i's after the first t.

part of speech: ordinal number, adjective (fiftieth); noun (a fiftieth, fiftieths)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Coming as number 50 in a row or order. 2) (maths) One of fifty equal parts of something, written 1/50.
its sense in the lessons: In maths it is the ordinal of 50 and also a fraction: one fiftieth = 1/50 = 0.02 = 2%. In everyday life it is used for birthdays and anniversaries: «Grandpa's fiftieth». Phrases: fiftieth birthday, fiftieth anniversary, one fiftieth.
examples from the lessons: Dad is having a party for his fiftieth birthday. | She came fiftieth out of two hundred runners. | One fiftieth of 100 is 2. | Our school is celebrating its fiftieth anniversary. | This is the fiftieth time I've asked you to tidy your room! | Two fiftieths make one twenty-fifth.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Short form: 50th. Spelling: fifty changes y to ie: fiftieth. Pronounced with three syllables: FIF-tee-eth. As a fraction 1/50: divide by 50. Do not confuse with «fifteenth» (15th).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A soft, sweet fruit with many tiny seeds inside, shaped like a small pear. 2) The tree that this fruit grows on. 3) (Bible) The fig tree appears in many Bible stories; Adam and Eve made clothes from fig leaves. 4) (abbreviation) «Fig.» is short for «figure», a numbered picture or diagram in a book. 5) (informal, old-fashioned) Something worth nothing: «I don't give a fig».
its sense in the lessons: In science and textbooks «Fig. 3» means look at picture number 3. In cooking and nature lessons it is a fruit, fresh or dried. In Bible stories Jesus told a parable about a fig tree. Phrases: fig tree, fig leaf, dried figs, see Fig. 2, not care a fig.
examples from the lessons: We ate fresh figs on holiday in Greece. | The fig tree in the garden gives lots of fruit. | Look at Fig. 4 to see the parts of a flower. | In the Bible, Adam and Eve covered themselves with fig leaves. | Dried figs are sweet and chewy. | He doesn't care a fig about football.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: figs. «Fig.» with a full stop is an abbreviation of «figure» and is read aloud as «figure». A «fig leaf» can also mean something used to hide an embarrassing fact.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Used with a meaning different from the usual, word-for-word one, to make a picture in the mind: «a heart of gold» is figurative. 2) (art) Showing real people or things that you can recognise, not abstract shapes.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons «figurative language» means similes, metaphors, personification and idioms. It tells the reader not to take the words literally. Phrases: figurative language, figurative meaning, in a figurative sense.
examples from the lessons: «It's raining cats and dogs» is figurative language. | Poets use figurative language to paint pictures with words. | «He has a heart of stone» has a figurative meaning: he is unkind. | The teacher asked us to find three figurative phrases in the poem. | She paints figurative pictures of people at the beach. | The figurative meaning of «break the ice» is to start a friendly chat.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: literal (the plain, word-for-word meaning). Adverb: figuratively. Related noun: figure of speech. A common trap: «I literally died laughing» is really figurative.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a figurative way, not with the plain word-for-word meaning. 2) Used in the phrase «figuratively speaking» to show you are using an image, not a fact.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons it helps explain idioms and metaphors: «figuratively, he is a lion» means he is brave. It is the opposite of «literally». Phrases: figuratively speaking, both literally and figuratively.
examples from the lessons: Figuratively speaking, my brain is full after that test. | «She is a shining star» is meant figuratively. | He was figuratively walking on air after the win. | The climbers reached the top, both literally and figuratively. | When Mum says the house is a zoo, she means it figuratively. | Can you explain this sentence figuratively and literally?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: literally. A common mistake is to say «literally» when you mean «figuratively». Spelling: figurative + -ly.

part of speech: noun (finance, finances); verb (finance, finances, financed, financing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (money) The management of money, especially by governments, banks and businesses. 2) Money that is used to pay for a project or a purchase. 3) (verb) To provide the money for something.
its sense in the lessons: In adult life and economics lessons it describes how money is handled, borrowed and spent. In stories about grown-ups: «Mum works in finance». Buying a car «on finance» means borrowing money and paying it back in parts. Phrases: personal finance, finance a project, on finance, minister of finance.
examples from the lessons: My aunt works in finance at a big bank. | The school needs finance to build a new playground. | The bake sale helped finance our class trip. | They bought the car on finance and pay each month. | The government's minister of finance plans the budget. | Learning about personal finance helps you save money.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: financial. Pronounced FY-nance or fi-NANCE; both are fine. «Finances» (plural) means the money a person or group has. «Fiancé» (engaged partner) is a different word.

part of speech: noun, plural of finance (finances); verb, third person of finance (finances)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (money) The money that a person, family, business or country has and how it is managed. 2) Third person form of the verb finance: pays for something.
its sense in the lessons: In adult life it means how much money a family has and how they spend it: «our finances are tight this month». In stories it shows worry or comfort about money. Phrases: family finances, sort out your finances, his finances are in a mess, the bank finances.
examples from the lessons: Mum and Dad talk about the family finances every Sunday. | The club's finances are healthy, so we can buy new kits. | After he lost his job, their finances were tight. | Grandad helps me keep my finances in order with a piggy bank. | The council finances the local library. | Good finances mean spending less than you earn.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually plural in this sense: «my finances are…», with a plural verb. Related: financial, financially. In maths problems about finances, think of money in and money out.

part of speech: noun (fingerprint, fingerprints); verb (fingerprint, fingerprints, fingerprinted, fingerprinting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The pattern of tiny lines on the tip of each finger, or the mark it leaves on a surface. 2) (verb) To take a record of someone's fingerprints, for example by the police. 3) A special mark that shows who made something or where it came from.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons pupils study loops, whorls and arches and learn that every person's fingerprints are different. In detective stories fingerprints help to catch a thief. Phones can unlock with a fingerprint. Phrases: leave fingerprints, take fingerprints, fingerprint scanner, dust for fingerprints.
examples from the lessons: The detective found fingerprints on the window. | No two people have the same fingerprints, not even twins. | I unlock my mum's tablet with my fingerprint. | Press your finger on the ink pad to make a fingerprint. | The police fingerprinted the suspect. | There are sticky fingerprints all over the fridge door!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Compound noun: finger + print. Identical twins share DNA but still have different fingerprints. Fingerprints form before birth and do not change as you grow, only get bigger.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The first child born to a family; the eldest child. 2) (Bible) In the Bible the firstborn son had special rights and duties, and the firstborn of Egypt are part of the Passover story.
its sense in the lessons: In family stories it tells the reader who is the eldest child. In Bible lessons it appears in the stories of Esau and Jacob, and of the Passover in Egypt; Jesus is called Mary's firstborn son. Phrases: firstborn son, firstborn child, her firstborn.
examples from the lessons: Emma is the firstborn, so she is the oldest of the three. | The king's firstborn son would one day become king. | In the Bible, Esau was Isaac's firstborn son. | Our cat's firstborn kitten is the biggest. | Being the firstborn means you often help with the little ones. | The Passover story tells about the firstborn of Egypt.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Can be written firstborn or first-born. Opposite idea: youngest, last-born. Not about birthday order in a class, only about children of the same parents.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who catches fish, as a job or for fun; a fisherman or fisherwoman. 2) An animal that catches fish, such as a kingfisher or an otter. 3) A North American forest animal like a large weasel, also called a fisher cat.
its sense in the lessons: Used in stories and the Bible: Jesus called Peter and Andrew, who were fishers, to be «fishers of men». It is a word that includes both men and women who fish. Phrases: fishers of men, fisher folk.
examples from the lessons: The fishers mended their nets on the beach. | Jesus said to Peter and Andrew, «Follow me, and I will make you fishers of men.» | The kingfisher is a clever little fisher. | A fisher is a dark furry animal that lives in the forests of Canada. | The old fisher told stories about the sea. | Fishers go out early when the sea is calm.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: fishers. «Fisherman» is more common in everyday English; «fisher» is neutral for any gender. Also a common surname (Fisher). Not the same as «fissure» (a crack).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Speaking, reading or writing a language easily, smoothly and well. 2) Moving or working smoothly, without stopping or stumbling.
its sense in the lessons: In school it describes reading and language skills: «read fluently», «speak French fluently». It tells the reader that someone is skilled and confident. Phrases: speak fluently, read fluently, fluently bilingual.
examples from the lessons: My friend speaks Spanish and English fluently. | By Year 4 most children read fluently. | She played the tune fluently without one mistake. | He explained the answer fluently to the whole class. | After living in Japan, Dad can speak Japanese fluently. | The dancer moved fluently across the stage.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: fluent; noun: fluency. Fluency in reading means accurate, fast and with expression. Not the same as «fluidly», though both suggest smoothness.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Able to be forgiven; not so bad that you cannot excuse it.
its sense in the lessons: In ethics and stories it helps judge how bad a mistake is: a small accident is forgivable, cruelty is harder to forgive. It shows that a character's mistake can be pardoned. Phrases: a forgivable mistake, perfectly forgivable, easily forgivable.
examples from the lessons: Forgetting your lunch is a forgivable mistake. | Spilling the paint was forgivable because it was an accident. | Some lies are less forgivable than others. | Her nervousness on the first day was perfectly forgivable. | Breaking a promise to your friend is hard but still forgivable. | Christians believe that every sin is forgivable if a person is truly sorry.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: unforgivable. Related: forgive, forgiveness. Spelling: drop the e of «forgive» before -able.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To choose to go without something you would like, or to give up a chance.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and ethics it shows a sacrifice: «she forwent her dessert so her brother could have it». In church life people may forgo treats during Lent. Phrases: forgo a treat, forgo a chance, forgo payment.
examples from the lessons: She decided to forgo her pocket money to help the charity. | We will forgo the trip to the park because of the rain. | Many Christians forgo chocolate during Lent. | He forwent the last cake so his sister could have it. | The team agreed to forgo a break to finish the project. | You may forgo the second helping if you are full.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Also spelt «forego», but «forego» can also mean «go before» (the foregone conclusion). Past forms are rare and formal: forwent, forgone. In speech people say «go without» or «give up».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Something that must be done because of rules or custom, often a small step that does not change the result: «just a formality». 2) Polite, stiff and correct behaviour, as at an important ceremony. 3) An official step, such as signing forms at a border.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life it describes paperwork and rules: «passport formalities». In stories, «it's only a formality» tells the reader that something is sure to happen. It also describes how stiff or relaxed an event is. Phrases: just a formality, a mere formality, without formality, legal formalities.
examples from the lessons: Signing the form is just a formality; you are already in the team. | The formality of the wedding made the little boy nervous. | At the airport we went through the usual formalities. | Let's skip the formalities and start the game. | Asking Dad was a formality; he always says yes. | The headteacher spoke with great formality at assembly.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: formalities. Adjective: formal; opposite: informality. «A mere formality» is a common phrase meaning something easy and certain.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (maths) A rule written with letters and symbols that tells you how to work something out: area = length × width. 2) (science) A short way to write what a chemical is made of, using letters and numbers: H2O is water. 3) A set of steps or a recipe that brings a certain result: «a formula for success». 4) Powdered milk made for feeding babies. 5) A class of motor racing, such as Formula One.
its sense in the lessons: In maths a formula lets you put numbers in place of letters and get the answer; for example perimeter of a square = 4 × side. In science chemical formulas show the elements in a substance. In family life, babies may drink formula from a bottle. Phrases: use the formula, the formula for, baby formula, a magic formula, Formula One.
