examples from the lessons: The formula for the area of a rectangle is length times width. | Using the formula, a square with sides of 5 cm has a perimeter of 20 cm. | The chemical formula for water is H2O. | The baby drinks formula from a bottle. | There is no magic formula for getting good at piano; you have to practise. | Formula One cars are incredibly fast. | Write the formula, then put in the numbers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: formulas (everyday and US) or formulae (more formal, UK science). Verb: formulate (to plan or express carefully). In maths problems, a formula tells you exactly which operations to do with the numbers.

part of speech: ordinal number, adjective (fortieth); noun (a fortieth, fortieths)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Coming as number 40 in a row or order. 2) (maths) One of forty equal parts of something, written 1/40.
its sense in the lessons: In maths it is the ordinal of 40 and a fraction: one fortieth = 1/40 = 0.025. In family life it is used for birthdays and anniversaries: «Mum's fortieth». Phrases: fortieth birthday, fortieth anniversary, one fortieth.
examples from the lessons: We had a surprise party for Mum's fortieth birthday. | He finished fortieth in the cross-country race. | One fortieth of 80 is 2. | Our town is having its fortieth summer fair. | The fortieth day after Easter is when Christians remember Jesus going up to heaven. | Four fortieths equal one tenth.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Short form: 40th. Spelling trap: forty and fortieth have NO u (not «fourty»). Three syllables: FOR-tee-eth. As a fraction 1/40: divide by 40.

part of speech: noun (founder, founders); verb (founder, founders, foundered, foundering)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who starts a school, company, club, charity or city. 2) (verb) Of a ship: to fill with water and sink. 3) (verb) Of a plan: to fail or come to nothing. 4) (verb) Of a horse: to go lame, or to stumble.
its sense in the lessons: In history it names the person who began something: «the founder of the school». In stories at sea, a ship that founders is sinking. In business news, plans founder when they fail. Phrases: founder of, co-founder, Founder's Day, founder on the rocks.
examples from the lessons: The founder of our school was a kind teacher. | Every year we celebrate Founder's Day. | She is the co-founder of a children's charity. | The little boat foundered in the storm. | Their plan foundered because nobody had enough money. | The founder of the club still comes to every meeting.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Related: found (to start something), foundation. Do not confuse «founder» (sink, fail) with «flounder» (to struggle clumsily; also a flat fish). The noun is common; the verb is mostly in stories and the news.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Four times as much or as many. 2) Having four parts or four kinds.
its sense in the lessons: In maths it means multiply by 4: «a fourfold increase» from 10 gives 40. In science and news it describes how much something has grown. Phrases: a fourfold increase, rise fourfold, fourfold symmetry.
examples from the lessons: The number of birds in the park has risen fourfold. | A fourfold increase from 5 is 20. | The price of tickets went up fourfold. | The plan had a fourfold aim: learn, play, share and grow. | A square has fourfold symmetry; it looks the same after each quarter turn. | Sales of ice cream grew fourfold on the hot day.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Similar words: twofold, threefold, tenfold. In maths, «a fourfold increase» usually means the new amount is 4 times the old one (×4), not «old + 4 times». Be careful in word problems.

part of speech: verb (fulfil, fulfils, fulfilled, fulfilling) — US spelling fulfill
meaning for a pupil: 1) To do what you promised or what is needed: «fulfil a promise». 2) To make a dream, wish or hope come true. 3) To meet a need or a requirement. 4) To make someone feel happy and satisfied with what they do. 5) (Bible) Of a prophecy: to come true, as Christians believe Jesus fulfilled the prophecies.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and ethics it is about keeping promises and doing duties. In stories a character fulfils a dream or a quest. In Bible lessons, «this was to fulfil what the prophet said» means it came true. Phrases: fulfil a promise, fulfil a dream, fulfil your duty, fulfil the requirements.
examples from the lessons: He fulfilled his promise and visited his grandma every week. | She fulfilled her dream of swimming in the sea. | This job fulfils me; I love helping people. | Your project must fulfil all the rules on the sheet. | Christians believe Jesus fulfilled the words of the prophets. | The knight fulfilled his quest and returned home.
note for the reader of a maths problem: British spelling: fulfil, fulfils, but fulfilled, fulfilling (double l before -ed and -ing). American spelling: fulfill. Noun: fulfilment (UK) / fulfillment (US). Adjective: fulfilling (making you happy).

part of speech: verb, past form of fulfil (fulfil, fulfils, fulfilled, fulfilling); adjective (fulfilled, more fulfilled)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Done or carried out as promised or needed. 2) Of a dream or hope: made to come true. 3) (adjective) Happy and satisfied because your life or work is meaningful. 4) (Bible) Of a prophecy: having come true.
its sense in the lessons: In stories it shows a promise kept or a dream realised. As an adjective it describes a feeling of deep satisfaction: «she felt fulfilled as a teacher». In church readings: «the scripture was fulfilled». Phrases: a promise fulfilled, feel fulfilled, a fulfilled life.
examples from the lessons: The promise was fulfilled when Dad took us to the beach. | Grandma felt fulfilled after years of helping at the food bank. | His wish was fulfilled when the puppy arrived. | All the conditions of the bet were fulfilled. | Christians believe the old prophecies were fulfilled in Jesus. | She led a long and fulfilled life.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double l in both UK and US spelling. Opposite as an adjective: unfulfilled (feeling something is missing). As a verb, a past form; as an adjective it often follows «feel».

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a way that is about how something works or what it does, not how it looks. 2) For practical purposes; in effect: «functionally the same».
its sense in the lessons: In design and technology it means about how well something works: «functionally, the old phone is fine». In science and maths it can say two things act the same. Phrases: functionally the same, functionally equivalent, functionally useless.
examples from the lessons: The two kettles look different but are functionally the same. | Functionally, the old bike still works well. | The broken phone is functionally useless. | The room was designed functionally, with lots of storage. | A calculator and a phone app are functionally equivalent for adding numbers. | Functionally speaking, the bridge is safe, though it looks old.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: functional (working; practical). Noun: function. «Functionally illiterate» means a person who cannot read well enough for everyday life.

part of speech: noun (fund, funds); verb (fund, funds, funded, funding)
meaning for a pupil: 1) An amount of money saved or collected for a special purpose. 2) (plural, funds) Money that is available to spend. 3) A large supply of something: «a fund of stories». 4) (verb) To give the money that pays for something.
its sense in the lessons: In school and everyday life it appears in fundraising: «the school fund», «raise funds for the roof». In adult life: savings fund, pension fund. In maths problems it may be the total money collected. Phrases: raise funds, school fund, short of funds, a fund of jokes, fund a project.
examples from the lessons: We are raising funds for a new playground. | The class put the money from the bake sale into the trip fund. | The charity is short of funds this winter. | Grandpa has a fund of funny stories. | The council will fund the new swimming pool. | Our school fund paid for the visiting author.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Related: funding, fundraising, fundraiser. «Funds» with s means money in general. In word problems, «the fund had £200 and they added £50» means 200 + 50.

part of speech: verb, past form of fund (fund, funds, funded, funding); adjective (funded, well-funded)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Paid for by money from a person, group or government. 2) Given enough money to work: «well-funded», «underfunded».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday and adult life it says who pays for something: «the library is funded by the council». In news, «underfunded» schools or hospitals do not get enough money. Phrases: funded by, publicly funded, well-funded, underfunded, fully funded.
examples from the lessons: The new park was funded by the town council. | Our trip was partly funded by the parents' association. | Public libraries are funded by taxes. | The project was fully funded, so building could start. | The hospital is underfunded and needs more nurses. | The research was funded by a big charity.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually used with «by» to name the payer. Opposite idea: unfunded, underfunded. Related noun: funding.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) The act of helping something to move forward or succeed.
its sense in the lessons: Used in formal and legal writing: «in furtherance of the plan». In stories it can make a speaker sound official. Phrases: in furtherance of, the furtherance of science.
examples from the lessons: The money was spent in furtherance of education. | The club exists for the furtherance of chess in our town. | The scientist worked for the furtherance of medicine. | All actions must be in furtherance of the charity's aims. | The council's plan is for the furtherance of safe cycling.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: no «a», no plural. Related verb: further (to help move forward). A formal word; in speech say «to help» or «to support».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A garden or pot plant with bright red, pink, white or purple flowers and round, often furry leaves. 2) A wild plant of the same family, also called cranesbill.
its sense in the lessons: In nature and science lessons, geraniums are often used to study plant growth, cuttings and leaves. In everyday life they sit on window sills and balconies. Phrases: pot of geraniums, red geraniums, geranium cuttings.
examples from the lessons: Grandma keeps red geraniums on her window sill. | We took cuttings from the geranium and grew new plants. | The geranium leaves smell like lemon when you rub them. | Water the geraniums when the soil is dry. | Wild geraniums grow along the edge of the field. | The bees visited the pink geraniums all afternoon.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: geraniums. Pronounced je-RAY-nee-um. Many garden «geraniums» are really pelargoniums, a close relative, but everyone calls them geraniums.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Willingly and happily; with pleasure. 2) In a pleased way.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday talk it is a polite way of agreeing: «I'll gladly help». In stories it shows a character's willingness. Phrases: gladly help, I would gladly, gladly accept.
examples from the lessons: I'll gladly help you carry those bags. | She gladly shared her sweets with everyone. | The dog gladly jumped into the car. | We would gladly come to your party. | He gladly accepted the prize. | Christians are encouraged to give gladly, not because they must.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: glad. Opposite: unwillingly, reluctantly. A bit polite and formal; in speech people also say «happily» or «sure».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A feeling of being happy and joyful.
its sense in the lessons: Found in stories, poems, hymns and the Bible: «serve the Lord with gladness». It tells the reader of a warm, gentle joy. Phrases: with gladness, full of gladness, joy and gladness.
examples from the lessons: Her heart was full of gladness when her brother came home. | The children sang with gladness on the last day of school. | The psalm says, «Serve the Lord with gladness.» | There was great gladness in the village after the rain came. | He felt a quiet gladness as he watched the sunrise. | Joy and gladness filled the room at the wedding.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: no plural. Slightly old-fashioned or poetic; in everyday speech people say «happiness» or «joy». Opposite: sadness, sorrow.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Dark or dim, with very little light. 2) Sad and without hope; in low spirits. 3) Expecting bad things to happen: «a gloomy forecast».
its sense in the lessons: In stories it sets a dark, sad mood: «a gloomy castle», «a gloomy day». In weather talk it means grey and cloudy. It also describes a person's mood. Phrases: gloomy weather, a gloomy face, feel gloomy, gloomy news.
examples from the lessons: It was a gloomy, rainy afternoon. | The old house was gloomy and full of shadows. | Why do you look so gloomy? Cheer up! | The weather forecast for the weekend is gloomy. | Tom felt gloomy after losing the match. | The gloomiest room in the castle was the dungeon.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: gloom; adverb: gloomily. Comparative: gloomier, gloomiest (y to i). Opposite: bright, cheerful, sunny.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Happening slowly and little by little over time, not suddenly. 2) Of a slope: rising or falling gently, not steeply.
its sense in the lessons: In science it describes slow changes: «a gradual change in temperature», erosion, growth. In maths it describes gentle slopes and steady increases. In everyday life it describes slow improvement. Phrases: gradual change, gradual increase, a gradual slope, gradual improvement.
examples from the lessons: There was a gradual change in the colour of the leaves. | The path has a gradual slope, so it is easy to walk up. | Her reading showed gradual improvement over the term. | The river caused gradual erosion of the bank. | The gradual rise in temperature melted the snow. | Learning to swim is a gradual process.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb: gradually. Opposite: sudden, abrupt, steep. Related: gradient (how steep a slope is), grade.

part of speech: noun (graffiti; uncountable, or plural of graffito)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Words or pictures painted, sprayed or scratched on walls, trains or other public places, usually without permission. 2) Street art: large, colourful paintings on walls, sometimes made with permission.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and citizenship lessons it raises questions of right and wrong: graffiti on other people's property is against the law (vandalism), but some cities have legal walls for street art. In stories it shows a run-down place or a rebellious character. Phrases: spray graffiti, covered in graffiti, graffiti artist, remove graffiti.
examples from the lessons: The bus shelter was covered in graffiti. | The council cleaned the graffiti off the school wall. | A graffiti artist painted a beautiful mural with permission. | Writing graffiti on someone's wall is against the law. | There was graffiti on the old train carriage. | Our class designed a graffiti-style poster for art.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually treated as uncountable: «the graffiti was removed». Spelling: double f, single t: graffiti. The singular «graffito» is very rare. From Italian.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal or informal) Free of charge; without having to pay.
its sense in the lessons: Used in shops and adverts or as a jokey word in speech: «you get the second one gratis». It tells the reader no money is needed. Phrases: for gratis, gratis and for nothing.
examples from the lessons: The museum lets children in gratis. | Buy one cake and get another gratis. | He fixed my bike gratis because we are friends. | Programs that are free to use are sometimes called gratis software. | The drinks at the party were gratis. | You can have this old toy gratis.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From Latin. Pronounced GRAH-tis or GRAT-is. «For gratis» is common but repeats the idea. The usual word is «free». Not the same as «gratitude» (thankfulness), though related in origin.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Being very important, powerful, skilled or famous. 2) Being very good, wise or noble in character. 3) Great size.
its sense in the lessons: In history and stories it describes famous leaders, artists and athletes: «the greatness of Shakespeare». In church life people speak of the greatness of God. Phrases: achieve greatness, signs of greatness, greatness of God, true greatness.
examples from the lessons: The coach saw signs of greatness in the young player. | The greatness of the pyramids amazed the travellers. | True greatness is about helping others, not just winning. | Christians praise the greatness of God in their songs. | The poet wrote about the greatness of the ocean. | Some people are born to greatness, others work hard for it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. From «great» + «-ness». Similar: excellence, importance, glory. Opposite: smallness, ordinariness.

part of speech: verb (grin, grins, grinned, grinning); noun (a grin, grins)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To smile widely, often showing your teeth. 2) (noun) A wide, happy or cheeky smile. 3) Phrase «grin and bear it»: to put up with something unpleasant without complaining.
its sense in the lessons: In stories a grin shows joy, mischief or cheekiness: «he grinned from ear to ear». «Grin and bear it» is an idiom for being patient. Phrases: grin from ear to ear, a cheeky grin, a big grin, wipe that grin off your face.
examples from the lessons: Max grinned when he saw the birthday cake. | She had a cheeky grin on her face. | He grinned from ear to ear after scoring a goal. | The Cheshire Cat's grin stayed after the cat disappeared. | The injection hurt, but I had to grin and bear it. | Wipe that grin off your face and tidy your room!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: grinned; -ing: grinning (double n). A grin is usually wider than a smile. Do not mix up with «grind» or «groan».

part of speech: verb, -ing form of grin (grin, grins, grinned, grinning); adjective (grinning)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Smiling widely, often showing the teeth. 2) (adjective) Having a big smile: «a grinning face».
its sense in the lessons: In stories it shows a character who is very pleased, amused or cheeky. Often in phrases like «grinning from ear to ear», «grinning like a Cheshire cat». Phrases: stop grinning, grinning faces, grinning broadly.
examples from the lessons: The children were grinning as they ran into the sea. | Why are you grinning like that? | He walked in grinning from ear to ear. | A grinning pumpkin sat on the doorstep. | She stood grinning at the top of the climbing frame. | The photo shows our whole class grinning.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double n before -ing: grinning. «Grinning like a Cheshire cat» means smiling very widely, from «Alice in Wonderland».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (law) A person who is legally responsible for looking after a child who is not their own, for example when the parents have died or cannot care for the child. 2) A person or thing that protects or guards something. 3) (church) In some Christian beliefs, a guardian angel is an angel who watches over each person.
its sense in the lessons: In school letters «parent or guardian» means the adult who looks after the child. In stories guardians protect treasure, kingdoms or forests. In adult life and law it is about who cares for a child. Phrases: parent or guardian, legal guardian, guardian angel, guardian of the forest.
examples from the lessons: Please ask your parent or guardian to sign this form. | After her parents died, her aunt became her guardian. | The dog is the guardian of the farm. | Many Christians believe in a guardian angel who watches over them. | The tall trees are the guardians of the valley. | The museum is the guardian of the town's history.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun for the role: guardianship. Related: guard. A guardian need not be a relative. In ethics and law lessons, a guardian has many of the same duties as a parent.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The part of a telephone that you hold to your ear and mouth. 2) A mobile phone. 3) A hand-held remote control or device.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday and technology talk it means a phone or the part of a phone you hold. Shops say «handset» for mobile phones. Phrases: mobile handset, pick up the handset, cordless handset.
examples from the lessons: Grandma picked up the handset and said hello. | The shop sells the newest mobile handsets. | Put the cordless handset back on its base to charge it. | My dad's old handset still works. | The TV handset is lost under the sofa again. | Speak clearly into the handset.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Compound: hand + set. More technical than «phone»; children usually say «phone» or «mobile».

part of speech: noun (harp, harps); verb (harp, harps, harped, harping)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A large musical instrument with many strings stretched on a tall frame, played by plucking with the fingers. 2) (Bible) In the Bible King David played the harp (lyre) and wrote psalms. 3) (verb, informal) «Harp on» means to keep talking about the same thing in a boring or annoying way. 4) (informal) A harmonica, sometimes called a mouth harp or blues harp.
its sense in the lessons: In music lessons it is a string instrument in the orchestra. It is a symbol of Ireland and appears on Irish coins. In Bible stories David played the harp to calm King Saul. «Harp on» is everyday speech for nagging. Phrases: play the harp, harp music, harp on about, Irish harp.
examples from the lessons: She plays the harp in the school orchestra. | The harp makes a soft, rippling sound. | In the Bible, David played the harp for King Saul. | The Irish harp is a symbol of Ireland. | Stop harping on about your new trainers! | Angels are often drawn with harps.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: harps. A person who plays it is a harpist. «Harp on» is informal and a little critical. Not the same as «harpoon».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Proud and unfriendly, acting as if you are better than other people.
its sense in the lessons: In stories it describes snobbish characters, often queens, princesses or rich people: «a haughty look». It tells the reader the character looks down on others. Phrases: a haughty look, a haughty voice, haughty manner.
examples from the lessons: The haughty princess would not talk to the servants. | She gave me a haughty look and walked away. | The cat sat on the wall, haughty and proud. | His haughty manner made him few friends. | «I never eat cheap food,» she said in a haughty voice. | The Bible says that a haughty spirit comes before a fall.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced HAW-tee; the gh is silent. Noun: haughtiness; adverb: haughtily. Similar: arrogant, snooty, stuck-up. Opposite: humble, modest.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Extremely sad, usually because someone you love has died or left, or because of a great disappointment.
its sense in the lessons: In stories it shows deep sadness: when a pet dies, a friend moves away, or a dream fails. It tells the reader the character's grief is strong. Phrases: be heartbroken, heartbroken by, left heartbroken.
examples from the lessons: Lily was heartbroken when her old dog died. | He was heartbroken when his best friend moved to another country. | The team were heartbroken after losing the final. | Grandpa was heartbroken after Grandma passed away. | She was heartbroken to find her sandcastle washed away. | The heartbroken boy cried all night.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Related: heartbreak (noun), heartbreaking (causing great sadness). Stronger than «sad» or «upset». It does not mean anything is wrong with the actual heart.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) From now on; from this time into the future.
its sense in the lessons: Used in formal announcements, laws, old stories and the Bible: «henceforth all generations shall call me blessed». It tells the reader a rule or change starts now. Phrases: henceforth known as, henceforth and forever.
examples from the lessons: Henceforth, all pupils must wear their hats in the sun. | The village, henceforth known as Riverbend, grew quickly. | The king declared that henceforth there would be no more taxes. | Henceforth, I will always check my answers. | In the Bible Mary says that henceforth all generations will call her blessed.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Very formal and a bit old-fashioned. In speech say «from now on». Related: hence (therefore; from here). Also «henceforward» with the same meaning.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) In this document, place or thing; in here.
its sense in the lessons: Used in legal papers, official letters and formal writing: «the information contained herein». In stories it can make writing sound like an old law. Phrases: contained herein, herein lies.
examples from the lessons: The rules stated herein apply to all players. | Herein lies the secret of the treasure. | Please read the instructions contained herein. | The answers to the puzzle are herein. | Herein lies the problem: we have only one key.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Very formal. Related: therein (in that), hereby (by this). «Herein lies…» means «this is where … is found». In speech say «in here» or «in this».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A pen with bright see-through ink, used to mark important words in a text. 2) A make-up product that makes parts of the face look brighter.
its sense in the lessons: In school, pupils use highlighters to mark key words, facts and answers when reading. It helps with study and revision. Phrases: yellow highlighter, highlighter pen, use a highlighter.
examples from the lessons: Use a yellow highlighter to mark the key words. | My pencil case has five different highlighters. | She highlighted the main facts with a pink highlighter. | Don't highlight every line, or nothing stands out. | The highlighter ran out of ink halfway through the page. | My big sister puts highlighter on her cheeks.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: highlight; noun: highlight (the best part, «the highlight of the trip»). Plural: highlighters. Highlighting too much makes it less useful.

part of speech: noun (hoard, hoards); verb (hoard, hoards, hoarded, hoarding)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A large store of money, food or valuable things, often kept secret. 2) (verb) To collect and keep a lot of something, often more than you need, and hide it away. 3) (history) A buried treasure of old coins or objects found by archaeologists.
its sense in the lessons: In stories dragons sit on a hoard of gold; squirrels hoard nuts for winter. In history lessons, hoards of Roman or Viking coins are found by metal detectors. In ethics, hoarding food when others need it is seen as selfish. Phrases: a hoard of gold, hoard food, treasure hoard, secret hoard.
examples from the lessons: The dragon slept on a hoard of gold. | Squirrels hoard nuts for the winter. | A farmer found a hoard of Roman coins in his field. | My brother has a hoard of sweets under his bed. | People hoarded toilet paper when they were worried. | Don't hoard the crayons; share them with the table.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Homophone: «horde» (a large crowd, «a horde of children»). Hoard = stored things; horde = crowd of people. Noun: hoarder (a person who hoards).

meaning for a pupil: 1) An evergreen bush or tree with shiny, prickly dark green leaves and bright red berries in winter. 2) Its branches used to decorate homes and churches at Christmas.
its sense in the lessons: In nature lessons it is an evergreen plant that keeps its leaves in winter; birds eat its berries. At Christmas it decorates houses, wreaths and cards; in the carol «The Holly and the Ivy» Christians link it to Jesus. Phrases: holly and ivy, a sprig of holly, holly berries, holly wreath.
examples from the lessons: We decorated the front door with a holly wreath. | Holly leaves are shiny and prickly. | Birds eat the red holly berries in winter. | The carol «The Holly and the Ivy» is sung at Christmas. | Be careful picking holly; the leaves are sharp. | A sprig of holly sat on top of the Christmas pudding.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: hollies. Holly berries are poisonous to people; do not eat them. Also a girl's name (Holly). Do not confuse with «holy» (sacred), which has one l.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Being friendly, welcoming and generous to guests or strangers. 2) Food, drink and entertainment given to guests. 3) The business of hotels, restaurants and cafés, called the hospitality industry.
its sense in the lessons: In ethics and church life, hospitality — welcoming strangers — is an important value; the Bible tells of Abraham welcoming three visitors. In adult life «hospitality» is a type of job. Phrases: show hospitality, warm hospitality, thank you for your hospitality, hospitality industry.
examples from the lessons: Thank you for your kind hospitality; we loved staying with you. | The village was famous for its hospitality to travellers. | The Bible teaches Christians to show hospitality to strangers. | My cousin works in hospitality at a big hotel. | The family's hospitality made us feel at home. | The team enjoyed the hospitality of the other school after the match.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Adjective: hospitable (welcoming); opposite: inhospitable (unwelcoming, also of harsh places like deserts). Related to «hospital» and «host» in origin.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unfriendly, angry behaviour or feelings towards someone. 2) Strong opposition to an idea or plan. 3) (plural, hostilities, formal) Fighting in a war.
its sense in the lessons: In stories it shows enemies or people who dislike each other: «the hostility between the two families». In history lessons «hostilities ended» means the fighting stopped. Phrases: open hostility, show hostility, hostility towards, the end of hostilities.
examples from the lessons: There was hostility between the two rival teams. | The new boy felt the hostility of the older children at first. | The plan to close the park met with hostility from the town. | Hostilities ended when both sides signed a peace treaty. | The cat looked at the puppy with hostility. | Kindness can slowly melt hostility.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: hostile (unfriendly, or of an enemy). Opposite: friendliness, goodwill. The plural «hostilities» is mainly about war.

part of speech: noun (hound, hounds); verb (hound, hounds, hounded, hounding)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A dog used for hunting, such as a foxhound or bloodhound, with a strong sense of smell. 2) (informal) Any dog. 3) (verb) To chase or bother someone again and again: «hounded by reporters». 4) (informal, in compounds) A person who is very keen on something: «a news hound».
its sense in the lessons: In stories hounds track people and animals by smell; «The Hound of the Baskervilles» is a famous detective story. As a verb it describes pestering: «she hounded her mum for a phone». Phrases: hunting hound, pack of hounds, hound someone, be hounded by.
examples from the lessons: The hounds followed the scent through the woods. | A bloodhound can follow a trail many hours old. | Our old hound sleeps by the fire. | The famous singer was hounded by photographers. | He hounded his dad for weeks until he got a new bike. | The detective story is about a giant hound on the moor.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: hounds. A group is a «pack of hounds». As a verb it is negative: hounding someone means not leaving them in peace.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who owns or rents a house and is responsible for it.
its sense in the lessons: Used in official letters, news and adult life: «the council has written to all householders». In maths and money problems a householder pays bills, rent or a mortgage. Phrases: local householders, every householder.
examples from the lessons: The council sent a letter to every householder about recycling. | Householders must keep the footpath outside their house clear. | Each householder pays a water bill. | The householder came out to see why the dog was barking. | Many householders put solar panels on their roofs.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Compound: house + holder. A formal word; in speech people say «homeowner» or «the people who live there». Related: household (all the people living in a home).

part of speech: verb (howl, howls, howled, howling); noun (a howl, howls)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Of a wolf or dog: to make a long, loud, sad cry. 2) Of a person: to cry loudly in pain, anger or sadness. 3) Of the wind: to blow hard with a loud, wailing sound. 4) To laugh very loudly: «howl with laughter». 5) (noun) A long, loud cry.
its sense in the lessons: In stories it creates a spooky or wild mood: wolves howling at the moon, the wind howling in a storm. It can also show strong laughter or crying. Phrases: howl at the moon, howl with laughter, howling wind, a howl of pain.
examples from the lessons: The wolves howled at the full moon. | The wind howled around the house all night. | The baby howled when she dropped her ice cream. | We howled with laughter at the funny film. | There was a howl of pain when he stubbed his toe. | Our dog howls whenever the fire engine goes past.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Related: howler (an obvious, funny mistake, especially UK). Similar: wail, yowl, bay. «Howling» can also mean very great: «a howling success».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) A husband, said in a friendly, joking or loving way.
its sense in the lessons: Used in casual speech and messages, mostly by wives about their husbands: «my hubby». In stories it shows a chatty, warm character. Phrases: my hubby, the hubby.
examples from the lessons: I'll ask my hubby to fix the fence. | Mrs Jones and her hubby went on holiday to Spain. | «Hubby's cooking tonight,» said Mum with a wink. | Her hubby always brings her flowers on Fridays. | The hubbies were all watching the football.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: hubbies. Short for «husband». Informal; do not use it in school writing. The female version is sometimes «wifey», also informal.

part of speech: verb (huff, huffs, huffed, huffing); noun (a huff)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To breathe out loudly and heavily, often because you are tired or annoyed. 2) (noun, informal) A bad mood, usually after being offended: «in a huff». 3) (informal) «Huff and puff»: to breathe hard, or to complain and make a fuss without doing much.
its sense in the lessons: In stories «he left in a huff» tells the reader a character went off sulking. In «The Three Little Pigs» the wolf says «I'll huff and I'll puff and I'll blow your house down». Phrases: in a huff, go off in a huff, huff and puff.
examples from the lessons: She went off in a huff because she lost the game. | The wolf huffed and puffed and blew the house down. | He was huffing and puffing by the top of the hill. | Don't get in a huff; it was only a joke. | Grandpa huffed and turned back to his newspaper. | My little sister is in a huff because she can't stay up late.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: huffy (easily offended or sulky). «In a huff» is informal. Similar: sulk, strop (UK).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Kind and gentle, causing as little pain as possible to people or animals.
its sense in the lessons: In ethics and animal welfare it describes kind treatment: «a humane way to catch a mouse». In history it describes fair laws. Phrases: humane treatment, a humane trap, humane society.
examples from the lessons: The farmer uses a humane trap that does not hurt the mouse. | Animals should always be treated in a humane way. | The new law made prisons more humane. | The vet is kind and humane. | A humane society helps look after lost and hurt animals. | It is humane to give injured birds water and quiet.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced hyoo-MAYN, stress on the second part. Do not confuse with «human» (a person). Opposite: inhumane, cruel. Noun: humanity (kindness; also all people).

meaning for a pupil: 1) All people together; the human race.
its sense in the lessons: In science, history and church life it means everyone in the world: «the history of humankind». Christians believe God created humankind. Phrases: all humankind, the future of humankind, for the good of humankind.
examples from the lessons: The invention of the wheel helped all humankind. | Scientists study the history of humankind. | Christians believe that God made humankind in His image. | Clean water is important for the future of humankind. | Landing on the moon was a giant leap for humankind. | Music belongs to all humankind.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable; no «a». Also «mankind» (older), «humanity», «the human race». «Humankind» includes everyone and is often preferred today.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To make someone feel very ashamed, foolish or small, especially in front of other people.
its sense in the lessons: In ethics and stories it describes unkind behaviour, bullying, or embarrassing moments. It tells the reader a character's pride has been badly hurt. Phrases: humiliate someone in public, feel humiliated, a humiliating defeat.
examples from the lessons: The bully tried to humiliate him in front of the class. | She felt humiliated when everyone laughed at her mistake. | Losing ten–nil was a humiliating defeat. | It is cruel to humiliate someone for being different. | The coach never humiliates players when they make mistakes. | He was humiliated when his trousers split on stage.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: humiliation. Adjective: humiliating (causing shame), humiliated (feeling shame). Stronger than «embarrass». Related to «humble» and «humility» but negative.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The quality of being humble: not thinking you are better or more important than others. 2) (church) A virtue Christians value, following Jesus, who washed his disciples' feet.
its sense in the lessons: In ethics and church lessons it is a good quality: knowing your limits, admitting mistakes, serving others. In stories it shows a hero who does not boast. Phrases: show humility, with humility, a lesson in humility.
examples from the lessons: Even though she won the prize, she spoke with great humility. | Humility means listening to others and admitting your mistakes. | Jesus showed humility when he washed his disciples' feet. | The champion's humility made everyone like him. | Losing the game was a lesson in humility. | It takes humility to say «I was wrong».
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Adjective: humble. Opposite: pride, arrogance. Do not confuse with «humiliation» (being made to feel ashamed). Humility is chosen and good; humiliation is done to you and hurts.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a funny way that makes people smile or laugh.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons it describes a writer's or speaker's tone: «the poem is written humorously». In stories it shows a character joking. Phrases: speak humorously, humorously written.
examples from the lessons: Grandpa told the story humorously, and we all laughed. | The book humorously describes a cat's day. | He humorously suggested we hire an elephant to carry our bags. | The teacher humorously called the messy desk «a work of art». | She humorously answered, «Only on Tuesdays!»
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: humorous; noun: humour (UK) / humor (US). Spelling trap: «humorous» drops the u even in British English: humour but humorous.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who says that others should behave in a good way but does not behave that way themselves, or pretends to be good when they are not. 2) (Bible) Jesus called some religious leaders hypocrites for praying to be seen rather than from the heart.
its sense in the lessons: In ethics and stories it describes someone whose actions do not match their words. In Bible lessons Jesus warned against being a hypocrite. Phrases: a hypocrite, call someone a hypocrite, don't be a hypocrite.
examples from the lessons: He tells us not to eat sweets, but he eats them all the time — what a hypocrite! | It would be hypocritical to shout at others for shouting. | Jesus told people not to pray like the hypocrites, just to be seen. | She didn't want to be a hypocrite, so she started recycling too. | Calling someone a hypocrite is a strong accusation. | The story's hero discovers the king is a hypocrite.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun for the quality: hypocrisy. Adjective: hypocritical. Spelling: hypo-crite, with y. Pronounced HIP-o-krit.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (Bible, church) Worshipping idols, meaning statues or objects treated as gods, which the Bible forbids. 2) Loving or admiring something or someone far too much, as if it were a god.
its sense in the lessons: In Bible lessons it appears in the story of the golden calf and in the Ten Commandments: «You shall have no other gods before me». Christians believe putting money, fame or anything above God is a kind of idolatry. In everyday talk it means extreme admiration. Phrases: guilty of idolatry, the sin of idolatry.
examples from the lessons: In the Bible, the Israelites fell into idolatry when they worshipped the golden calf. | The Ten Commandments forbid idolatry. | Christians believe loving money more than God is a kind of idolatry. | The prophets warned the people against idolatry. | Some people's love of football is almost idolatry.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Related: idol (a statue worshipped as a god; also a famous star), idolise/idolize (to admire very much). Pronounced eye-DOL-a-tree.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Not knowing about something; without information: «ignorant of the rules». 2) Without much education or knowledge in general. 3) (informal, UK and Ireland) Rude or bad-mannered, for example not saying hello: «Don't be so ignorant!»
its sense in the lessons: In ethics and stories it shows that someone did something wrong because they did not know. In UK and Irish speech it often means rude. Saying someone is ignorant can be insulting, so be careful. Phrases: ignorant of, an ignorant comment, wilfully ignorant.
examples from the lessons: I was ignorant of the rule, so I didn't know I couldn't run in the hall. | The settlers were ignorant of the dangers of the desert. | It is not a crime to be ignorant; it just means you have more to learn. | That was an ignorant comment about other countries. | Don't be ignorant — say thank you to the driver! (UK) | People long ago were ignorant of germs.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: ignorance. Related: ignore (to pay no attention to) — not the same! «Ignorant» means not knowing; «ignore» means choosing not to notice. Calling someone ignorant can be rude.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The Roman numeral for 2, written ii or II. 2) Used in lists and in names to show «the second»: «Elizabeth II», «part ii», «World War II».
its sense in the lessons: In maths Roman numerals: I = 1, II = 2, III = 3, IV = 4, V = 5. In books and lists it numbers sections: (i), (ii), (iii). After a name it means «the second»: «Henry II» is read «Henry the Second». Phrases: part II, question (ii), Elizabeth II.
examples from the lessons: The Roman numeral II means 2. | Answer question (ii) on the worksheet. | Queen Elizabeth II is read as «Queen Elizabeth the Second». | Chapter II begins on page 20. | On the clock face, II stands where the 2 should be. | III minus II equals I.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Not a word but a number written with letters. Small letters (i, ii, iii) are often used for sub-parts of a question. After a king's or queen's name, say «the Second». In Roman numerals II + II = IV, not IIII (though some clocks show IIII).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Good at thinking of new, clever or creative ideas. 2) Showing creativity and new ideas: «an imaginative story».
its sense in the lessons: In school, teachers praise imaginative writing, art and play. In stories it describes creative children and inventors. Phrases: an imaginative story, imaginative play, imaginative ideas, highly imaginative.
examples from the lessons: Mia wrote an imaginative story about a talking teapot. | Imaginative play helps young children learn. | He found an imaginative way to fix the broken kite. | The artist's paintings are bright and imaginative. | Be imaginative and invent your own monster. | The class came up with imaginative ideas for the school fair.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Related: imagine, imagination, imaginary (not real). Do not confuse «imaginative» (creative) with «imaginary» (made up, not real): an imaginary friend; an imaginative child.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To copy the way someone speaks, moves or behaves. 2) To make something look or sound like something else. 3) To follow someone as an example: «imitate your heroes».
its sense in the lessons: In school, young children learn by imitating adults; in music and drama pupils imitate sounds. In nature some animals imitate others to stay safe (mimicry). In church life Christians try to imitate Jesus. Phrases: imitate a voice, imitate a sound, try to imitate.
examples from the lessons: Parrots can imitate human voices. | My brother imitates the teacher's voice to make us laugh. | Young children imitate what they see adults do. | Some harmless flies imitate wasps to scare off birds. | The clarinet imitates the cuckoo in this piece of music. | Christians try to imitate Jesus in kindness.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: imitation, imitator. Similar: copy, mimic. Imitating to mock someone can be unkind.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A copy of something, often a fake that looks like the real thing. 2) Copying someone's voice or actions, often to be funny. 3) (adjective) Not real but made to look real: «imitation leather».
its sense in the lessons: In shops it means a cheaper copy: imitation gold, imitation fur. In drama and games it is copying someone's voice. The saying «Imitation is the sincerest form of flattery» means copying someone shows you admire them. Phrases: a cheap imitation, do an imitation of, imitation jewellery.
examples from the lessons: The ring is only an imitation; it isn't real gold. | He does a great imitation of a chicken. | Babies learn to talk by imitation. | The chair is covered in imitation leather. | It was a poor imitation of the famous painting. | «Imitation is the sincerest form of flattery,» said Gran.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: imitate. Opposite of an imitation: the real thing, the original, genuine. Countable for a copy; uncountable for the act of copying.

meaning for a pupil: 1) About to happen very soon, often something bad or dangerous.
its sense in the lessons: In news, weather and safety it warns of something close: «a storm is imminent», «imminent danger». In stories it builds tension. Phrases: imminent danger, imminent arrival, in imminent danger, an imminent storm.
examples from the lessons: Dark clouds showed that rain was imminent. | The firefighters said the house was in imminent danger. | The baby's arrival is imminent. | An announcement about the new playground is imminent. | The ship's captain warned of an imminent storm. | With the bell imminent, everyone packed their bags.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: imminence. Do not confuse with «eminent» (famous and respected) or «immanent» (present within). Similar: impending, approaching.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) The body's ability to fight off a disease so that you do not catch it. 2) (law) Protection from being punished or from a law: «diplomatic immunity». 3) Freedom from something unpleasant.
its sense in the lessons: In science and health lessons it explains vaccines and how the immune system protects us after we have had some illnesses. In law and news, some people have immunity from being charged. In games it can mean being safe from being out. Phrases: build up immunity, immunity to a disease, diplomatic immunity, herd immunity.
examples from the lessons: Vaccines help your body build immunity to diseases. | After chickenpox, most people have immunity for life. | Ambassadors have diplomatic immunity. | Washing hands and sleeping well support your immunity. | In the game, the person holding the ball has immunity. | Herd immunity happens when enough people are protected from a disease.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: immunities (rare). Adjective: immune («immune to measles»). Verb: immunise / immunize (to give a vaccine). Immunity does not always last forever.

meaning for a pupil: 1) About to happen soon, often something unpleasant or important.
its sense in the lessons: In stories it creates suspense: «a feeling of impending doom». In news and weather it describes events close at hand. Phrases: impending doom, impending storm, impending visit, impending danger.
examples from the lessons: The dark sky warned of an impending storm. | There was a feeling of impending doom in the haunted house. | Everyone was nervous about the impending exams. | The impending visit of the inspector made the teachers busy. | The animals sensed the impending earthquake. | News of the impending wedding spread fast.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Used before a noun. Similar: imminent, upcoming, approaching. «Impending doom» is a fixed, often jokey phrase. From the verb «impend», which is rare.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Having faults or mistakes; not perfect. 2) (grammar) The imperfect tense describes past actions that were going on or happened often, as in French and Spanish, or «I was reading» in English.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and ethics it reminds us that everyone makes mistakes: «we are all imperfect». In shops «imperfect» goods have small faults and are cheaper. In language lessons it is a past tense. Phrases: an imperfect world, imperfect but useful, the imperfect tense.
examples from the lessons: The vase is slightly imperfect, so it was half price. | Nobody is perfect; we are all imperfect. | Her English is imperfect, but she speaks it bravely. | Christians believe that God loves people even though they are imperfect. | In French lessons we learned the imperfect tense. | The plan was imperfect, but it worked.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: imperfection. Opposite: perfect. Prefix im- means «not» (like impossible, impatient). In grammar, «imperfect» is a tense name, not a judgement.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An unfair or unwelcome demand on someone's time, help or kindness. 2) The act of making a rule, tax or punishment apply to people. 3) (UK, old-fashioned school) An extra piece of written work given as a punishment.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday polite talk: «I hope it's not an imposition» means «I hope I'm not asking too much». In history and law it describes rules or taxes put on people. Phrases: an imposition on, the imposition of a tax, not an imposition.
examples from the lessons: I hope it's not an imposition to ask you to feed the cat. | Staying for a whole week would be an imposition on our hosts. | The imposition of a new tax made people angry. | The teacher gave him an imposition of a hundred lines. | Helping you is no imposition at all. | The imposition of a curfew kept everyone indoors.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: impose (to force something on someone; «I don't want to impose» means «I don't want to be a bother»). Countable.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (law) To put someone in prison or keep them locked up. 2) To trap or keep someone or something somewhere so they cannot leave.
its sense in the lessons: In history and law it describes people sent to prison for crimes, or unfairly for their beliefs. In stories villains imprison heroes in towers. In the Bible Paul and Peter were imprisoned. Phrases: be imprisoned for, imprisoned in, wrongly imprisoned.
examples from the lessons: The thief was imprisoned for three years. | The wicked queen imprisoned the princess in a tower. | In the Bible, Paul was imprisoned for preaching. | The bird felt imprisoned in its small cage. | Some people have been wrongly imprisoned. | The snow imprisoned us in the cabin for two days.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: imprisonment. Prefix im- here means «in», not «not». Similar: jail, lock up, detain. Opposite: release, free.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A sudden wish to do something without thinking about it first. 2) (science) A signal that travels along a nerve, or a short push or burst of force. 3) A reason or force that makes something happen.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and money talk, «buying on impulse» means buying something you did not plan to. In science, nerve impulses carry messages from the brain. In stories it shows hasty actions. Phrases: on impulse, act on impulse, impulse buy, nerve impulse, resist the impulse.
examples from the lessons: On impulse, she jumped into the pool with her clothes on. | He felt a sudden impulse to laugh during assembly. | Sweets near the till are for impulse buying. | Nerve impulses travel from your fingers to your brain. | Try to resist the impulse to shout out the answer. | Acting on impulse can sometimes get you into trouble.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: impulsive (doing things without thinking). Countable. «Impulse» stresses the first syllable: IM-pulse.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Not wise or sensible; likely to cause trouble.
its sense in the lessons: Used in safety warnings and formal advice: «it is inadvisable to swim after a big meal». It tells the reader something is a bad idea. Phrases: it is inadvisable to, highly inadvisable.
examples from the lessons: It is inadvisable to go out in a thunderstorm. | Climbing the cliff without a rope is highly inadvisable. | It would be inadvisable to leave your bike unlocked. | The doctor said it was inadvisable to play football with a sprained ankle. | Eating wild mushrooms is inadvisable unless an expert checks them.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal. Opposite: advisable (sensible). Prefix in- means «not». In speech say «not a good idea» or «unwise».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Not being able to do something, especially because of illness, injury or weakness. 2) (law, money) Being unable to work because of illness or disability; some countries pay incapacity benefit.
its sense in the lessons: In adult life and law it describes a person who cannot work or care for themselves. In formal writing it means lacking the ability: «an incapacity to listen». Phrases: incapacity to work, incapacity benefit, mental incapacity.
examples from the lessons: Grandad's incapacity after his fall meant he needed help at home. | She received support during her incapacity to work. | His incapacity to keep a secret got him into trouble. | Long illness can lead to incapacity. | The law has rules for people with mental incapacity.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal. Related: incapable (not able), incapacitate (to make someone unable), incapacitated. Opposite: capacity, ability.

part of speech: noun (incense; uncountable); verb (incense, incenses, incensed, incensing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (church) A substance, often made from tree gum, that gives off a sweet-smelling smoke when it is burned, used in worship. 2) The smoke itself. 3) (verb, stress on -CENSE) To make someone extremely angry.
its sense in the lessons: In church life incense is burned in many Catholic and Orthodox services; the smoke rising is a sign of prayers going up to God. In the Bible the wise men brought frankincense to baby Jesus. As a verb it shows strong anger in stories: «he was incensed». Phrases: burn incense, incense sticks, be incensed by.
examples from the lessons: The priest swung the incense burner during the service. | The church smelled of incense. | The wise men brought gold, frankincense and myrrh. | Incense smoke rose slowly towards the ceiling. | She was incensed when someone kicked over her sandcastle. | The unfair rule incensed the whole class.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Two pronunciations: noun IN-sense, verb in-SENSE. The verb is strong: incensed means furious. Frankincense is a special kind of incense from trees in Arabia and Africa.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To stir up or encourage people to do something bad or violent, or to feel angry. 2) (law) To urge someone to commit a crime, which can itself be a crime.
its sense in the lessons: In history and law it describes people who encourage riots or hatred. In ethics it shows how words can lead others to harm. Phrases: incite violence, incite a riot, incite hatred.
examples from the lessons: The man was arrested for inciting a riot. | Posting hateful messages can incite violence. | The villain incited the crowd to storm the castle. | Words can incite hatred, so choose them with care. | He incited his friends to break the rules.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: incitement. Do not confuse with «insight» (deep understanding) — they sound similar. Usually about bad actions.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Being included or making someone part of a group. 2) Making sure everyone, including people with disabilities or from different backgrounds, can take part and feel welcome. 3) Something that is included or added.
its sense in the lessons: In school and ethics it is an important value: every child belongs and can join in. In maths and science it may mean something being part of a set or list. Phrases: inclusion of, social inclusion, a policy of inclusion.
examples from the lessons: Our school values the inclusion of every child. | Inclusion means making sure nobody is left out at playtime. | The inclusion of a ramp means wheelchair users can get in. | Her inclusion in the team made her very happy. | The book's inclusion of maps helps the reader. | Christians believe everyone is welcome at God's table, a picture of inclusion.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: include; adjective: inclusive. Opposite: exclusion. «Inclusive» in maths can mean the end numbers count: 1 to 5 inclusive means 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Not important; too small to matter.
its sense in the lessons: In formal writing and stories it tells the reader that a detail does not matter: «an inconsequential remark». In science and maths it can describe a tiny difference that makes no real change. Phrases: inconsequential details, an inconsequential mistake.
examples from the lessons: Don't worry about the inconsequential details; focus on the main idea. | The scratch on the car was inconsequential. | They chatted about inconsequential things like the weather. | The difference of one gram is inconsequential in this recipe. | What seemed an inconsequential choice changed the whole story. | Her mistake was inconsequential and did not affect the result.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal. Opposite: important, significant, consequential. From «consequence» with the prefix in- (not). Similar: trivial, minor, unimportant.

part of speech: noun (an incumbent, incumbents); adjective (incumbent; incumbent on/upon someone)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) The incumbent is the person who holds an official job right now, such as a president, mayor or member of parliament. 2) (formal) Incumbent on or upon you means it is your duty: if it is incumbent on you to do something, you must do it. 3) (church) The incumbent of a parish is the priest or vicar in charge of it.
its sense in the lessons: Mostly heard in news about elections: «the incumbent mayor», «the incumbent won again», «defeat the incumbent». In exam and formal writing: «it is incumbent upon all pupils to…». In church life, the vicar or rector of a parish is its incumbent. It tells the reader who already holds the post, as opposed to the challenger who wants it.
examples from the lessons: The incumbent mayor is standing for election again. | The challenger beat the incumbent by two hundred votes. | It is incumbent upon every visitor to sign the book at the front desk. | The incumbent president gave a speech on television. | The parish has had the same incumbent for many years. | As class captain, it was incumbent on Mia to help new pupils. | Voters were unhappy with the incumbent government.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal word; children rarely say it. As an adjective it usually comes before a noun («the incumbent leader») or in the phrase «incumbent on/upon». Do not confuse with «encumber» (to weigh down). Opposite in elections: challenger.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An incurable illness cannot be cured: doctors cannot make it go away, though they may help the person feel better. 2) An incurable habit or quality is so strong that it will never change: an incurable optimist always hopes for the best.
its sense in the lessons: In health and science lessons and in family life: «an incurable disease», «sadly, the illness is incurable». Used kindly and humorously about character: «an incurable chatterbox», «an incurable romantic». It tells the reader something cannot be fixed or changed.
examples from the lessons: The vet said the old dog's illness was incurable. | Grandad has an incurable disease, but medicine helps him feel comfortable. | My sister is an incurable chatterbox. | Scientists are working hard to find treatments for incurable illnesses. | Dad is an incurable optimist about the weather. | Some illnesses that were once incurable can now be cured. | She was incurably curious about everything.
note for the reader of a maths problem: in- + cure + -able = cannot be cured. «Incurable» does not always mean deadly: many incurable conditions, like some allergies, can be managed for life. Opposite: curable.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Indifference is not caring or not being interested in something or someone. 2) (formal) A matter of indifference is something that makes no difference to you either way.
its sense in the lessons: In stories it describes a cold or bored character: «she shrugged with indifference». In ethics lessons, indifference to people who suffer is seen as a fault: «indifference to the poor». It tells the reader a person shows no feeling, neither for nor against.
examples from the lessons: The cat looked at the new toy with complete indifference. | His indifference to his homework worried his teacher. | She hid her hurt behind a mask of indifference. | We should not show indifference when someone is being bullied. | Which seat I sit in is a matter of indifference to me. | The crowd's indifference made the singer sad.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: say «indifference», not «an indifference». Adjective: indifferent. Indifference is not the same as hatred: it is a lack of any strong feeling. Followed by «to» or «towards»: indifference to pain.

meaning for a pupil: 1) If you are indifferent to something, you do not care about it or are not interested in it. 2) Not very good; only ordinary or rather poor: an indifferent meal.
its sense in the lessons: In stories: «he seemed indifferent to the danger», a character who does not care. In reviews and reports (sense 2): «the food was indifferent», «an indifferent player». Often followed by «to»: indifferent to the cold.
examples from the lessons: The cat was indifferent to the dog barking outside. | Tom seemed indifferent to winning or losing. | How can you be indifferent when your friend is sad? | The hotel was lovely, but the food was indifferent. | He is an indifferent swimmer but a great runner. | She answered in an indifferent voice. | Most people were indifferent to the new rule.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Use «to», not «about», in formal writing: indifferent to praise. Trap: «indifferent» does not mean «different»; it means «not caring» or «so-so». Noun: indifference.

meaning for a pupil: 1) One at a time, separately, not as a group. 2) In a way that fits each single person or thing: each cake was individually decorated.
its sense in the lessons: In school: «work individually, then share with a partner»; «the teacher spoke to us individually». In shops and maths: items «individually wrapped» or «sold individually» (one by one, not in a pack). It tells the reader each one is treated alone.
examples from the lessons: The teacher marked each test individually. | First work individually, then compare answers with your partner. | The chocolates are individually wrapped. | The coach spoke to each player individually after the match. | The pens cost 50p individually or £2 for a pack of five. | Each costume was individually made by hand. | Individually, the ants are tiny, but together they are strong.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: individual; noun: an individual (one person). In maths, «sold individually» means price per single item; compare it with the pack price to find the better deal (e.g. 5 × 50p = £2.50, so the £2 pack saves 50p). Spelling: double l.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Not costing a lot of money; cheap, but in a polite or positive way.
its sense in the lessons: In shopping and money lessons and in adverts: «an inexpensive gift», «an inexpensive way to have fun». It sounds nicer than «cheap», which can also mean poor quality.
examples from the lessons: We found an inexpensive present for Grandma. | A picnic in the park is an inexpensive day out. | These pencils are inexpensive but good. | The café serves tasty, inexpensive food. | Walking to school is free, and the bus is inexpensive. | It is inexpensive to grow herbs on a windowsill.
note for the reader of a maths problem: in- + expensive = not expensive. «Inexpensive» is polite and positive; «cheap» can also suggest low quality («cheap plastic»). Do not mix up with «priceless» (worth so much that no price is enough).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Never wrong; never making a mistake. 2) Always working or always succeeding: an infallible method. 3) (church) Catholics believe the Pope is infallible when he solemnly teaches on faith and morals; this is called papal infallibility.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday talk: «nobody is infallible», «Mum's infallible cure for hiccups». In science: no test or person is infallible, so we check results. In church history lessons: the Catholic teaching of papal infallibility.
examples from the lessons: Nobody is infallible; everyone makes mistakes sometimes. | Grandma has an infallible recipe for pancakes. | The detective's memory was almost infallible. | Even computers are not infallible. | Catholics believe the Pope is infallible only in special solemn teachings, not in everything he says. | There is no infallible way to win at games of chance.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal word. Opposite: fallible (able to make mistakes). Trap: papal infallibility does not mean Catholics think the Pope never sins or never makes ordinary mistakes. Spelling: double l.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An inhabitant is a person who lives in a place, such as a town, island or country. 2) An animal that lives in a particular place or habitat: the inhabitants of the pond.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and maths: «the town has 5,000 inhabitants», «the inhabitants of the island». In science: animals that are inhabitants of a habitat. It tells the reader who lives somewhere.
examples from the lessons: The village has only three hundred inhabitants. | The first inhabitants of the island were fishermen. | Frogs and newts are inhabitants of the pond. | The inhabitants of the town came out to watch the parade. | How many inhabitants does your city have? | The castle's only inhabitants now are bats.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Verb: inhabit (to live in). Trap: «inhabited» means people live there; «uninhabited» means nobody lives there; «inhabitable» and «habitable» both mean fit to live in. In maths problems, number of inhabitants = population.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Being a natural, basic part of something, so it cannot be taken away: an inherent danger, an inherent quality.
its sense in the lessons: In formal writing and exams: «there are risks inherent in climbing», «inherently dangerous». In science: a property inherent in a material. It tells the reader the quality belongs to the thing itself, not added from outside.
examples from the lessons: There is an inherent danger in playing near deep water. | Curiosity is inherent in young children. | Every sport has some inherent risk. | Kindness seemed inherent in her nature. | Glass is inherently fragile. | The plan had an inherent problem: it cost too much.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal word. Usually «inherent in» something: risks inherent in the job. Do not confuse with «inherit» (to receive from someone who has died); they are not the same word family in meaning. Synonyms: built-in, natural, basic.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Inheriting money, a house or things means receiving them from someone after that person has died. 2) Inheriting a feature, like blue eyes or curly hair, means getting it from your parents or family through your body. 3) Inheriting a problem or job means taking it over from the person before you.
its sense in the lessons: «Inheriting» is the -ing form of «inherit». In family life and law: inheriting from a will. In science: children inheriting features from their parents (genes). At school and work: inheriting an old desk or a messy project.
examples from the lessons: She is inheriting her grandmother's piano. | You might be inheriting your dad's red hair. | Plants grown from seeds are inheriting features from the parent plants. | The new teacher is inheriting a very lively class. | They were inheriting the farm after their uncle died. | Inheriting a fortune did not make him happy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: -ing form: drop nothing, just add -ing (inherit → inheriting). Noun: inheritance; the person who inherits is an heir. Trap: you inherit from a person; you do not «inherit» someone. Do not confuse with «inhibit» (to hold back).

part of speech: verb (initiate, initiates, initiated, initiating); noun (an initiate, initiates)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To initiate something is to start it or make it begin: initiate a conversation. 2) To initiate someone into a group is to let them join, often with a special ceremony. 3) To initiate someone into something is to teach them the basics of it. 4) (noun) An initiate is a person who has just been allowed to join a group or learn its secrets.
its sense in the lessons: In formal and exam language «initiate» means «start»: «initiate a plan», «initiate contact». In stories and history: initiation ceremonies into clubs, tribes or secret societies. In computers: initiate a download.
examples from the lessons: The head teacher initiated a new reading scheme. | Who initiated the argument? | Pupils can initiate a class project. | The club initiated new members with a funny song. | Grandpa initiated me into the secrets of fishing. | The new initiates were nervous at their first meeting. | Press the button to initiate the countdown.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb is said in-ISH-ee-ate; noun is said in-ISH-ee-it. Noun for the act: initiation; adjective: initial (first). Formal: in everyday talk say «start» or «begin».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (law) An injunction is an order from a court telling someone that they must or must not do something. 2) (formal) A firm warning or instruction: his mother's injunction to be home before dark.
its sense in the lessons: Heard in news and adult life: «the court granted an injunction», «she got an injunction to stop him coming near the house». In formal writing: an injunction against something. It tells the reader an official order has been given.
examples from the lessons: The court issued an injunction to stop the building work. | The company got an injunction against the protesters. | Breaking an injunction can lead to a fine. | Mum's injunction was clear: no screens after bedtime. | The judge refused to grant an injunction. | An injunction can protect a person from someone who has been threatening them.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Typical verbs: grant, issue, seek, break an injunction. Do not confuse with «junction» (where roads meet) or «conjunction» (a joining word like «and»).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Insincerity is saying or showing feelings you do not really have; not being honest about what you feel.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and ethics lessons: a character who smiles or praises falsely shows insincerity. Phrases: «with obvious insincerity», «the insincerity of his apology». It tells the reader that the words do not match the true feelings.
examples from the lessons: Everyone could hear the insincerity in his apology. | Her praise was full of insincerity. | I hate insincerity; just tell me what you really think. | The prince saw through the courtier's insincerity. | There was no insincerity in the little girl's thank-you card. | His big smile hid his insincerity.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Adjective: insincere; opposite: sincerity, sincere. Note: insincerity is about feelings; a lie about facts is dishonesty, though both are untruthful.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (money) To insure something is to pay a company a small amount regularly so that, if it is lost, damaged or stolen, the company pays you money. 2) (money) To insure a person means to buy insurance that pays out if they are ill, hurt or die. 3) To protect against a bad result: practising insures against mistakes (more often spelled «ensure» or «insure against» in US English).
its sense in the lessons: In adult life and money lessons: insure the car, insure the house, travel insurance. In stories: «Luckily the house was insured». It tells the reader there is a plan to pay for loss.
examples from the lessons: Dad insures the car every year. | Is your bike insured against theft? | They insured the house against fire and floods. | We insured our luggage before the holiday. | The violin is insured for a lot of money. | Mum pays a monthly sum to insure our home. | Wearing a helmet is one way to insure against injury.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: insurance; the money you pay is a premium. Trap: «insure» (cover with insurance) vs «ensure» (make sure) vs «assure» (tell someone confidently). In UK English «ensure» is used for «make sure»; in US English «insure» is sometimes used for it too. Maths: a premium is paid often (e.g. monthly), and the payout is only made if something goes wrong.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Clear enough to be understood: an intelligible answer, intelligible speech.
its sense in the lessons: In formal and exam language: «make your writing intelligible», «the message was barely intelligible». In science and technology: a radio signal that is intelligible. It tells the reader whether something can be understood.
examples from the lessons: His handwriting was hardly intelligible. | Speak slowly so your speech is intelligible. | The radio message was crackly but intelligible. | The teacher made the hard idea intelligible to everyone. | After the storm the phone line was barely intelligible. | Write your answer in clear, intelligible sentences.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal word. Opposite: unintelligible. Trap: «intelligible» means understandable, not clever; a clever person is «intelligent».

meaning for a pupil: 1) On purpose; meaning to do it, not by accident.
its sense in the lessons: In school and playground fairness: «Did you push him intentionally?» In ethics and law: doing harm intentionally is treated more seriously than doing it by accident. It tells the reader the action was planned or wanted.
examples from the lessons: She didn't break the vase intentionally; it slipped. | He intentionally left the door open for the cat. | The referee said the foul was done intentionally. | Never hurt an animal intentionally. | I intentionally kept the surprise secret. | The page was left blank intentionally.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: intentional; noun: intention. Opposites: accidentally, by accident, unintentionally. Synonyms: on purpose, deliberately. Spelling: double n and double l.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To interpret something is to explain or decide what it means: interpret a poem, interpret a graph. 2) To interpret is to translate aloud what someone says from one language into another as they speak. 3) To interpret music, a role or a dance is to perform it in your own way.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and science: interpret a graph, chart or results — say what the numbers show. In English lessons: interpret a poem or a character's actions. In everyday life: an interpreter helps people who speak different languages, or uses sign language. In church: people interpret Bible passages.
examples from the lessons: Can you interpret what this bar chart shows? | I interpreted her smile as a yes. | A teacher interpreted for the new pupil from Poland. | People interpret this poem in many different ways. | The scientist interpreted the results carefully. | Each pianist interprets the music a little differently. | He interpreted the silence as anger.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: interpretation; person: an interpreter. Trap: an interpreter works with speech; a translator works with written text. Past: interpreted (not «interpretated»). In maths, «interpret» means read off values and say what they mean in words.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (grammar) Interrogative means used to ask a question: an interrogative sentence ends with a question mark. 2) (grammar, noun) An interrogative is a question word, such as who, what, where, when, why, which or how. 3) (formal) An interrogative look or tone seems to be asking a question.
its sense in the lessons: In English grammar lessons: the four sentence types are statement (declarative), question (interrogative), command (imperative) and exclamation. Interrogative pronouns: who, whom, whose, which, what.
examples from the lessons: «Where is my bag?» is an interrogative sentence. | Who, what and why are interrogatives. | Turn the statement into the interrogative form. | An interrogative sentence ends with a question mark. | She gave me an interrogative look. | Write three interrogative sentences about the story.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Related: interrogate (to question hard, like police), interrogation. Grammar trap: «I wonder where he is.» is a statement, not interrogative, even though it has «where».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Intimidation is frightening someone, often with threats, so that they do what you want or are too scared to act.
its sense in the lessons: In school safety and anti-bullying lessons: intimidation is a form of bullying. In law and news: «voter intimidation», «witness intimidation». It tells the reader someone is using fear as a weapon.
examples from the lessons: Intimidation is a kind of bullying and is never okay. | The big boys used intimidation to take the younger children's ball. | Tell a teacher if you face intimidation online. | The witness refused to speak because of intimidation. | There was no intimidation; she agreed freely. | Police are investigating claims of intimidation.
