note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Verb: intimidate; adjective: intimidating (scary, e.g. an intimidating exam). Trap: «intimidating» can also just mean impressive and a bit scary, without anyone meaning harm. Do not confuse with «intimate» (very close and private).

meaning for a pupil: 1) To intrude is to go into a place or join a situation where you are not wanted or not invited. 2) To intrude on something is to disturb it or spoil it: the noise intruded on our peace.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday manners: «Sorry to intrude, but…» is a polite way to interrupt. In safety: an intruder is someone who enters a home or school without permission. It tells the reader someone is crossing a boundary.
examples from the lessons: I'm sorry to intrude, but your mum is on the phone. | Please don't intrude when someone is praying. | We felt we were intruding on a private family moment. | The traffic noise intruded on our picnic. | Reporters should not intrude on people's grief. | A fox intruded into the hen house.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: intrusion; person: intruder; adjective: intrusive. Usually followed by «on», «upon» or «into». Polite phrase: «I hope I'm not intruding.»

meaning for a pupil: 1) Involvement is taking part in something: your involvement in the school play. 2) Involvement can mean being connected to something, often something wrong: his involvement in the robbery. 3) Strong interest or feeling for something, or (formal) a close relationship with someone.
its sense in the lessons: In school reports: «good involvement in class discussions». In news and stories: police check a person's involvement in a crime. In community life: parent involvement in the school.
examples from the lessons: Thank you for your involvement in the charity run. | Parents' involvement helps children learn. | The detective proved the butler had no involvement in the theft. | Her involvement with the drama club began in Year 3. | He denied any involvement. | Sport needs the involvement of the whole team.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly uncountable. Verb: involve; adjective: involved. Common phrase: «involvement in» an activity, «involvement with» a group or person. Spelling: keep the e — involve + ment = involvement.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Not connected with what is being talked about or done, so it does not matter here.
its sense in the lessons: In maths word problems: some numbers are irrelevant and should be ignored. In writing and debates: keep to the point, leave out irrelevant details. In everyday talk: «That's irrelevant!» It tells the reader the information does not help.
examples from the lessons: The colour of the bus is irrelevant to how fast it goes. | Cross out the irrelevant information in the question. | Your age is irrelevant; anyone can join. | Stick to the topic and leave out irrelevant details. | Whether it rained is irrelevant to the answer. | His excuse was completely irrelevant.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: relevant. Spelling trap: irRELevant (r-r-e-l-e-v-a-n-t), not «irrevelant». In maths, spotting irrelevant numbers is a key skill: «Sam has 3 red pens and is 9 years old; how many pens?» — his age is irrelevant.

part of speech: verb (itemise, itemises, itemised, itemising; US itemize)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To itemise is to make a list of things one by one, often with the price or amount of each.
its sense in the lessons: In money lessons and adult life: an itemised bill or receipt shows each thing you bought and its cost. In school: itemise the equipment you need. It tells the reader everything is listed separately.
examples from the lessons: The shop gave us an itemised receipt. | Please itemise everything you spent on the trip. | Dad checked the itemised phone bill. | The teacher itemised the things we must bring to camp. | An itemised list makes packing easier. | The plumber itemised the parts and the labour.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK spelling -ise, US spelling -ize (itemize); both are correct. From «item» (one thing in a list). Maths: the total of an itemised bill is the sum of all the item prices; check it by adding them up.

part of speech: noun (a jingle, jingles); verb (jingle, jingles, jingled, jingling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A jingle is a light ringing sound made by small metal things, like keys, coins or little bells, knocking together. 2) To jingle is to make or cause that sound. 3) A jingle is a short, catchy tune or song used in an advert on radio or TV.
its sense in the lessons: At Christmas: «Jingle Bells», sleigh bells jingling. In stories: the jingle of keys tells the reader someone is coming. In media lessons: advertising jingles are easy to remember.
examples from the lessons: I heard the jingle of Mum's keys at the door. | The coins jingled in my pocket. | We sang «Jingle Bells» at the Christmas concert. | The cat's bell jingles when she moves. | That advert jingle is stuck in my head! | The ice-cream van's jingle played down the street. | He jingled the money in his hand.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun. Past: jingled. Compare sounds: jingle (light metal), clink (glass or metal touching), clang (loud metal), tinkle (very light, high).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Kinship is being related to someone by family: being part of the same family by birth or marriage. 2) A feeling of being close to someone because you share something, like interests or troubles.
its sense in the lessons: In history, geography and social studies: kinship groups, clans and extended families. In stories: «she felt a kinship with the lonely boy». In law: kinship care is when a child is looked after by a grandparent or other relative.
examples from the lessons: Kinship was very important in the old Scottish clans. | Ella felt a kinship with the other new pupils. | The two tribes were joined by kinship and marriage. | Gran looks after my cousin; it's called kinship care. | There is a special kinship between twins. | Sharing a hobby can create a strong kinship.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. From «kin» (family): «next of kin» means your closest relative. Old-fashioned: «kith and kin» means friends and family.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Lateness is being late; arriving or happening after the right or expected time. 2) The fact that it is late in the day or night: because of the lateness of the hour.
its sense in the lessons: In school: lateness is recorded in the register and may lead to a warning. In formal language: «Please excuse my lateness», «apologies for the lateness of this reply».
examples from the lessons: Lateness is marked in the class register. | The teacher spoke to Ben about his lateness. | Please excuse my lateness; the bus broke down. | Because of the lateness of the hour, we went straight to bed. | The train company apologised for the lateness of the service. | Repeated lateness can mean missing important lessons.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Adjective: late. Opposite: punctuality. Trap: «lately» does not mean «in a late way»; it means «recently».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Leadership is being the leader of a group, team or country. 2) Leadership is the ability to lead people well: to guide, decide and help others work together. 3) The leadership is the group of people who lead an organisation or party.
its sense in the lessons: In school: leadership skills, leadership roles like class captain or prefect. In history and citizenship: a country under someone's leadership. In sport: the captain shows leadership.
examples from the lessons: The team won the cup under her leadership. | Being a school prefect helps you learn leadership. | Good leadership means listening to others. | The party's leadership met to plan the campaign. | He showed real leadership when the tent fell down. | Leadership is not just giving orders. | The class voted for Ava because of her leadership skills.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly uncountable. From leader + -ship (as in friendship, membership). Phrases: «under the leadership of», «take the leadership», «leadership qualities».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (law) Legislation is a law or a set of laws made by a parliament or government. 2) (law) The process of making laws.
its sense in the lessons: In citizenship and history lessons: parliament passes legislation; new legislation on school safety or the environment. In news: «the government introduced legislation to…». It tells the reader that something is made official by law.
examples from the lessons: New legislation bans smoking in cars with children. | Parliament debated the legislation for weeks. | The legislation protects wild birds and their nests. | Some countries have strict legislation about plastic bags. | Making legislation is the job of parliament. | The legislation will come into force next year.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: say «a piece of legislation» or «a law», not «a legislation». Related: legislate (verb), legislator (person), legislature (the law-making body, e.g. parliament, Congress).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Liberation is setting people or a place free from someone who controlled or imprisoned them, such as an enemy army. 2) Liberation is gaining equal rights and freedom for a group of people. 3) A feeling of being free from worries or rules.
its sense in the lessons: In history: the liberation of a city or country at the end of a war, the liberation of prisoners from camps. In social studies: movements for liberation and equal rights. In everyday speech: «Finishing the exams was a liberation!»
examples from the lessons: The people cheered at the liberation of their town. | Soldiers helped in the liberation of the prisoners. | Women's liberation fought for equal rights. | Leaving the plaster cast felt like liberation. | The film tells the story of the city's liberation. | Christians believe Jesus brings liberation from sin.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly uncountable. Verb: liberate; person: liberator. Synonyms: freeing, release, freedom. Related: liberty.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Liberty is freedom: the right to live, speak and act as you choose without being controlled or imprisoned unfairly. 2) At liberty means free, not in prison; or (formal) allowed to do something: I am not at liberty to say. 3) A liberty is a cheeky or rude act; taking a liberty means doing something without permission.
its sense in the lessons: In history and citizenship: the Statue of Liberty, liberty and justice, the fight for liberty. In everyday life (UK): «What a liberty!» or «He took liberties» about cheeky behaviour. Formal: «I took the liberty of booking a table» means I did it without asking first.
examples from the lessons: The Statue of Liberty stands in New York harbour. | People have fought hard for liberty. | The escaped tiger is still at liberty. | I'm not at liberty to tell you the secret. | I took the liberty of borrowing your pen. | Eating my last biscuit — what a liberty! | Liberty includes the freedom to speak your mind.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: liberties. Phrases: at liberty, take liberties, take the liberty of. Synonym: freedom; «liberty» is more formal and often used for rights.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To lighten something is to make it less heavy: lighten your bag. 2) To lighten is to make or become brighter or paler in colour: the sky lightened. 3) To lighten a mood or a job is to make it easier or happier: a joke lightened the mood. 4) Lighten up (informal) means relax and stop being so serious.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: lighten the load, lighten the mood. In art: lighten a colour by adding white. In stories: «Her face lightened when she saw him.» Informal: «Lighten up!»
examples from the lessons: Take out some books to lighten your schoolbag. | The sky lightened as the sun came up. | Add white to lighten the blue paint. | Grandpa's jokes lightened the mood. | Helping each other lightens the work. | Oh, lighten up — it's only a game! | Her face lightened when she heard the good news.
note for the reader of a maths problem: -ing form: lightening (no extra n). Trap: «lightening» (making lighter) vs «lightning» (the flash in a storm). Opposite: darken, or for weight: make heavier.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Lightness is being not heavy. 2) Lightness is being bright or pale in colour. 3) Lightness is a gentle, cheerful, easy feeling or way of moving: lightness of heart, lightness of step.
its sense in the lessons: In science: the lightness of a feather or of a material. In art: the lightness or darkness of a colour. In stories: a dancer's lightness, or a lightness in someone's voice when they are happy.
examples from the lessons: The lightness of the bike makes it easy to carry. | The ballet dancer moved with great lightness. | Feel the lightness of this feather. | Add white to increase the lightness of the colour. | There was a lightness in her voice after the good news. | The cake had a wonderful lightness.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Opposite: heaviness (weight), darkness (colour). Do not confuse with «lighting» (lamps) or «lightning» (storm flash).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Linen is a strong, cool cloth made from the flax plant. 2) Linen (or household linen) means sheets, pillowcases, tablecloths and towels, even when they are made of cotton. 3) (church) The white cloths used on the altar for communion are called altar linens.
its sense in the lessons: In history: the ancient Egyptians wrapped mummies in linen. In everyday life: bed linen, a linen cupboard, table linen. In science and technology: flax fibres are spun into linen thread.
examples from the lessons: Mum keeps the sheets in the linen cupboard. | My summer shirt is made of linen. | The ancient Egyptians wove fine linen. | Please change the bed linen on Saturday. | The linen tablecloth was white and crisp. | Linen comes from the stems of the flax plant. | The priest folded the white linen on the altar.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «some linen», «a linen shirt». Used as an adjective: linen sheets. Phrase: «wash your dirty linen in public» means talk about private family problems where others can hear.

part of speech: noun (logging, uncountable); verb form (log, logs, logged, logging)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Logging is the work of cutting down trees and taking the wood away to sell. 2) Logging (from «log») is writing down information in a log or record: logging the weather each day. 3) Logging in (or on) means entering your name and password to start using a computer or website; logging out (or off) means leaving it.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and science: logging of rainforests and its effect on animals. In school computing: logging in and logging out. In science: logging results in a table or data logger.
examples from the lessons: Logging has destroyed large parts of the rainforest. | The logging trucks carried huge tree trunks. | We are logging the temperature every hour. | Remember logging out after you use the school computer. | I'm having trouble logging in. | The captain was logging the ship's speed. | Careful logging can let a forest grow back.
note for the reader of a maths problem: -ing form doubles the g: log → logging, logged. Person who cuts trees: a logger (US also lumberjack). «Log in» is two words as a verb; «login» is a noun (your login details).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A lover of something is a person who likes it very much: an animal lover, a book lover, a music lover. 2) (adult) A lover is a person someone loves in a romantic way and is in a close relationship with, especially when they are not married.
its sense in the lessons: Most often in children's life: «nature lover», «chocolate lover», «dog lover». In stories and poems: young lovers, star-crossed lovers (Romeo and Juliet). Sense 2 is adult and usually about a secret or unmarried relationship.
examples from the lessons: My aunt is a great animal lover. | This book is perfect for lovers of adventure stories. | Dad is a football lover. | Romeo and Juliet are the most famous lovers in plays. | The two lovers walked hand in hand by the river. | Calling all chocolate lovers: free samples today!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Safe for children in sense 1 (a lover of something). In sense 2 it can suggest a secret relationship; «boyfriend», «girlfriend» or «partner» are more usual everyday words.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Lovesick means so much in love, often with someone who does not love you back, that you feel sad, dreamy and cannot think of anything else.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, songs and comedies: a lovesick teenager sighing, a lovesick knight writing poems. Often a bit humorous. It tells the reader a character is miserable or silly because of love.
examples from the lessons: The lovesick boy wrote poems about the girl next door. | My big brother has been lovesick all week. | The lovesick puppy followed her everywhere. | In the story, the lovesick knight could not eat or sleep. | Stop sighing like a lovesick teenager! | The song is about a lovesick sailor far from home.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Compound: love + sick. It is not a real illness. Similar informal phrases: «head over heels», «have a crush on».

part of speech: noun (madam, madams; mesdames as a very formal plural)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (polite) Madam is a polite way to speak to a woman whose name you do not know, used by shop staff, waiters and in letters: «Dear Madam». 2) Madam is used before a title when speaking to a woman in an important job: Madam Chair, Madam President. 3) (UK, informal) A little madam is a girl who is bossy, cheeky or spoilt.
its sense in the lessons: In shops and restaurants: «Can I help you, madam?» In formal letters: «Dear Sir or Madam». At home (UK): «Don't you speak to me like that, young madam!»
examples from the lessons: «Can I take your coat, madam?» asked the waiter. | I began my letter with «Dear Sir or Madam». | Thank you, Madam Speaker. | Gran called my sister a little madam when she sulked. | «This way, madam,» said the usher. | Excuse me, madam, you dropped your glove.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Matching word for men: sir. «Ma'am» is a short form, very common in the USA and used for the Queen or King's family in the UK. Do not say «Madam Smith» in everyday English; use «Mrs/Ms Smith».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A maxim is a short, wise saying that gives a rule about how to behave or live.
its sense in the lessons: In English and ethics lessons: maxims like «Honesty is the best policy» or «Look before you leap». In stories: a character who lives by a maxim. Close to proverb and motto.
examples from the lessons: Grandma's favourite maxim is «Waste not, want not». | «Treat others as you would like to be treated» is a famous maxim. | My dad lives by the maxim «Better safe than sorry». | We wrote our own maxims for the classroom wall. | The old maxim says «Practice makes perfect». | Each chapter begins with a maxim.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Similar: proverb (traditional saying), motto (a rule chosen by a person or group), saying. Do not confuse with «maximum» (the most).

part of speech: noun (a meaning, meanings); adjective in «well-meaning»; verb form (mean, means, meant, meaning)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The meaning of a word or sign is what it stands for or expresses. 2) The meaning of something is its purpose or importance: the meaning of life, a life full of meaning. 3) The hidden message or idea behind something: the meaning of a poem or a dream. 4) «Meaning» is also the -ing form of «mean»: I've been meaning to call you (planning to).
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons: look up the meaning of a word in a dictionary; words with more than one meaning. In maths: the meaning of a symbol (+ means add). In religion and ethics: the meaning of life, the meaning of a parable. Phrase: «I've been meaning to…» = I've wanted and planned to.
examples from the lessons: What is the meaning of «enormous»? | Some words have more than one meaning. | The red light has a clear meaning: stop! | We discussed the meaning of the poem. | Helping others gives her life meaning. | Jesus told parables with a deeper meaning. | I've been meaning to tidy my room all week. | A shrug can have many meanings.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable (meanings). Related: meaningful (important), meaningless (with no meaning or point), well-meaning (with good intentions). Maths: knowing the meaning of each symbol (=, <, >, ÷) is key to reading problems.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Meanness is being unkind or nasty to others. 2) Meanness is not wanting to share or spend money; being stingy.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and ethics lessons: a character's meanness to others. In the UK «mean» often means stingy, so meanness can be about money; in the USA it mostly means unkindness.
examples from the lessons: The bully's meanness made the little ones cry. | Scrooge was famous for his meanness with money. | There was no meanness in her; she shared everything. | We talked about how meanness hurts feelings. | His meanness meant he never bought anyone a drink. | Kindness is the cure for meanness.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Double n: mean + ness. From «mean» (unkind; UK also stingy). Do not confuse with «meaning» or «means» (a way, or money).

meaning for a pupil: 1) To mediate is to help two people or groups who disagree to talk and find an agreement, without taking sides. 2) (formal) To be the means by which something passes or happens between two things.
its sense in the lessons: In school: peer mediators help pupils settle playground arguments. In news and law: someone mediates between two countries or in a family dispute. In church: Christians believe Jesus mediates between God and people.
examples from the lessons: A teacher mediated between the two friends after their fight. | Our school trains pupils to mediate playground quarrels. | Another country offered to mediate in the dispute. | The coach mediated between the angry players. | A good mediator listens to both sides. | Christians believe Jesus mediates between God and humans.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: mediation; person: mediator. Mediating is not deciding who wins (that is judging); it is helping both sides agree. Do not confuse with «meditate» (to think quietly).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Medication is medicine: pills, liquids, creams or injections that a doctor gives to treat an illness or stop pain. 2) Being on medication means taking medicine regularly.
its sense in the lessons: In health and safety lessons: only take medication given by a parent, doctor or school nurse; keep medication away from small children. In everyday life: «Grandad takes his medication with breakfast.» It is a slightly more formal word than «medicine».
examples from the lessons: The nurse keeps our medication in a locked cupboard. | Never take someone else's medication. | Dad is on medication for his high blood pressure. | Read the label before giving any medication. | The doctor changed her medication. | Some medications make you sleepy. | Keep all medication out of reach of children.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Can be uncountable (some medication) or countable (several medications). Synonyms: medicine, drug (but «drugs» can also mean illegal substances). Safety: in maths problems about doses, the dose is often per kilogram of body weight or per day; never guess real doses.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Membership is being a member of a club, group or organisation. 2) The membership is all the members of a group, or how many there are. 3) A membership is the right to use a club, gym or library, often paid for with a fee.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: library membership, gym membership, swimming club membership. In maths: membership fees, how much a year's membership costs compared with paying each time. In citizenship: membership of a country in a group of nations.
examples from the lessons: My library membership card lets me borrow ten books. | The club's membership has grown to two hundred. | Mum pays for a family membership at the zoo. | Membership of the chess club is free. | Is membership open to everyone? | Her membership runs out at the end of the month.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From member + -ship. Maths: compare a membership fee with pay-per-visit — e.g. £30 membership vs £4 a visit: after 8 visits (£32) the membership is cheaper.

part of speech: verb (memorise, memorises, memorised, memorising; US memorize)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To memorise something is to learn it so well that you can remember it exactly without looking.
its sense in the lessons: In school: memorise times tables, spellings, a poem or lines in a play. In church: memorise a Bible verse or prayer. It tells the reader someone learnt something by heart.
examples from the lessons: I memorised my seven times table. | We have to memorise a poem for the assembly. | She memorised her lines for the school play. | Try to memorise your home phone number. | He memorised the way to the park. | Children memorise the Lord's Prayer in Sunday school.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK -ise, US -ize; both correct. Phrase: «learn by heart» means the same. Memorising is not the same as understanding; good learners do both. In maths, memorising number facts (like 7 × 8 = 56) makes harder sums faster.

part of speech: adjective (mere, merest; merely adv.); noun (a mere, meres — old or poetic)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Mere means only, just, no more than: a mere child, a mere five minutes. It makes something sound small or unimportant. 2) The merest means the smallest possible: the merest touch. 3) (old, poetic, place names) A mere is a lake or pond, as in some English place names.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and formal writing: «a mere boy beat the giant», «the mere thought of spiders makes me shiver». In maths problems: «it costs a mere £2» stresses that the amount is small.
examples from the lessons: It was a mere five minutes' walk to school. | She was a mere child when she learnt to swim. | The mere sight of the dentist's chair scared him. | It cost a mere fifty pence. | At the merest noise, the rabbit ran away. | The walk took us around the mere.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Only used before a noun: «a mere child» (not «the child is mere»). Adverb: merely (only). In maths, «a mere 3» still equals 3; the word adds feeling, not a different number.

part of speech: noun (Methodism, uncountable; Methodist noun and adjective)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (church) Methodism is a Christian Protestant church movement started by John and Charles Wesley in England, known for warm preaching, hymn singing, Bible study and helping the poor.
its sense in the lessons: In history and religion lessons: Methodism spread among working people in towns and mining villages and to America. Methodists meet in chapels or churches; Charles Wesley wrote many hymns still sung today.
examples from the lessons: My grandparents belong to the Methodist church. | Methodism began as a movement within the Church of England. | Methodism is known for its hymn singing. | John Wesley rode on horseback to preach Methodism. | Many Welsh villages have an old Methodist chapel. | Methodism teaches care for the poor.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Proper noun: written with a capital M (Methodism, Methodist). The name came because early members were very methodical (orderly) in prayer and study. Do not confuse with «method» (a way of doing something).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A monarch is a king or queen (or emperor or empress) who rules a country, usually because they were born into the royal family. 2) A monarch (butterfly) is a large orange-and-black butterfly of North America that travels very long distances.
its sense in the lessons: In history and citizenship: the British monarch, absolute monarchs, a monarchy (a country with a monarch). In science (USA, Canada): monarch butterflies migrating to Mexico.
examples from the lessons: The monarch opened Parliament with a speech. | Henry the Eighth was a famous English monarch. | The country's monarch has little real power today. | Monarch butterflies fly thousands of kilometres. | A monarch usually inherits the throne. | We made a timeline of all the monarchs we studied.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Related: monarchy (system or country), monarchist. «Mon-» comes from Greek «one»: one ruler. Said MON-ark.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a way that is about right and wrong behaviour: morally right, morally wrong. 2) In a way that is good and honest: to act morally.
its sense in the lessons: In ethics and religion lessons: «Is it morally right to tell a white lie?» In stories and debates: something can be legal but morally wrong. Phrase: «morally bound/obliged» means you feel it is your duty.
examples from the lessons: Stealing is morally wrong. | Is it morally right to keep money you find? | She felt morally bound to tell the truth. | The knight always tried to act morally. | Something can be allowed by law but still be morally wrong. | We discussed a morally difficult choice.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: moral; noun: morals (rules of right and wrong), morality. Trap: «morale» (with e) means team spirit, not right and wrong.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A motto is a short sentence or phrase that sums up the beliefs or aims of a person, school, family or country.
its sense in the lessons: In school: the school motto is often on the badge, sometimes in Latin. In history: family mottos on coats of arms. In everyday life: «My motto is: always be kind.»
examples from the lessons: Our school motto is «Learn, Grow, Shine». | The Scouts' motto is «Be Prepared». | Many school mottos are in Latin. | My grandad's motto is «Never give up». | The family motto was written under the coat of arms. | Let's choose a motto for our team.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: mottos or mottoes (both correct). Similar: slogan (often for adverts), maxim (wise saying).

part of speech: noun (muck, uncountable); verb (muck, mucks, mucked, mucking)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Muck is dirt, mud or something wet and dirty. 2) Muck is animal dung (poo), often spread on fields as manure. 3) (UK, informal) Muck about/around means to behave in a silly way and waste time. 4) (UK, informal) Muck up means to spoil or do something badly; muck in means to help with the work; muck out means to clean an animal's stable.
its sense in the lessons: On farms and in nature: muck in the farmyard, mucking out the pony. At home: «Take off your boots, they're covered in muck!» In school (UK): «Stop mucking about!» It is an informal, everyday word.
examples from the lessons: Your trainers are covered in muck! | The farmer spread muck on the field. | We took turns to muck out the stables. | Stop mucking about and finish your work. | I mucked up my spelling test. | Everyone mucked in to tidy the hall after the party. | Wipe the muck off the window.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal, mostly UK and Ireland. Uncountable: «some muck». Adjective: mucky (dirty). Phrasal verbs with about/around/up/in/out each have their own meaning. Not rude, just casual.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A multitude is a very large number of things or people. 2) (formal, Bible) The multitude means a huge crowd of people; or ordinary people in general.
its sense in the lessons: In formal writing: «a multitude of reasons», «a multitude of colours». In Bible stories: Jesus fed the multitude with five loaves and two fish. Phrase: «cover a multitude of sins» means hide many faults.
examples from the lessons: There is a multitude of stars in the night sky. | The coral reef is home to a multitude of fish. | Jesus fed the multitude with five loaves and two fish. | We had a multitude of reasons to be happy. | Multitudes gathered to hear him speak. | A big coat can cover a multitude of sins.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal word; everyday: lots, loads, a huge number. «A multitude of» + plural noun. In maths it does not give an exact number; it just means very many.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) A municipality is a town or city (or district) that has its own local government. 2) The local government of a town or city: the council.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and citizenship: municipalities run local services such as bins, parks, libraries and water. Common in Canada, Ireland, Australia and many other countries.
examples from the lessons: The municipality repaired the playground. | Each municipality collects its own rubbish. | Our town became a municipality long ago. | The municipality decided to plant more trees. | There are many small municipalities in the region. | The library is run by the municipality.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal word; everyday UK words: council, town, city. Adjective: municipal (municipal pool, municipal park). Plural: municipalities.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Mutual means felt or done by each of two or more people towards the other: mutual respect, mutual help. 2) Mutual means shared by two or more people: a mutual friend, a mutual interest.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: «We met through a mutual friend.» In ethics: mutual respect, mutual trust. In business and money: a mutual agreement. Phrase: «The feeling is mutual» means I feel the same about you.
examples from the lessons: The two teams showed mutual respect. | Jack and Ella met through a mutual friend. | Their friendship was based on mutual trust. | We have a mutual love of football. | «I like you.» «The feeling is mutual!» | The decision was by mutual agreement.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Mutual» means two-way. Trap: some say «common friend», but «mutual friend» (a friend of both people) is the usual phrase. Adverb: mutually (mutually helpful).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Mysterious means strange and hard to explain or understand. 2) A mysterious person keeps secrets or does not tell much about themselves.
its sense in the lessons: In stories: mysterious noises, a mysterious stranger, a mysterious letter — they build suspense and make the reader want to find out more. In science: something mysterious may be explained later by experiments.
examples from the lessons: A mysterious parcel arrived with no name on it. | We heard mysterious footsteps in the attic. | The mysterious stranger wore a long black cloak. | The cookies disappeared mysteriously. | Scientists study mysterious objects in space. | She smiled in a mysterious way and said nothing. | The old house looked dark and mysterious.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: mystery. Spelling: mysterIOUS (drop the y → i: mystery → mysterious). Synonyms: strange, puzzling, secretive.

part of speech: noun (a naan, naans; also nan, naan bread)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Naan is a soft, flat bread, often shaped like a teardrop, baked in a hot oven, eaten with curry in Indian, Pakistani and other South Asian food.
its sense in the lessons: In food and culture lessons: foods from around the world. In everyday life (UK, Ireland, Australia): ordering naan with a takeaway curry; garlic naan, peshwari naan.
examples from the lessons: I dipped my naan in the curry. | We ordered two garlic naans. | Naan is baked inside a hot clay oven called a tandoor. | Dad made pizza on naan bread. | The naan was warm and buttery. | Would you like rice or naan with your meal?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Also spelled «nan». Trap: «nan» or «nana» is also an informal UK word for grandmother; context tells you which. Countable (two naans) or uncountable (some naan).

part of speech: verb form (nap, naps, napped, napping); noun (a nap)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Napping means sleeping for a short time, especially during the day. 2) Caught napping (informal) means caught not paying attention or not ready.
its sense in the lessons: In family life: the baby is napping, Grandad napping in his chair. In science: many animals nap during the day. Phrase: «caught napping» in sport or tests means unprepared.
examples from the lessons: Shh, the baby is napping. | Grandad was napping in front of the TV. | Cats spend much of the day napping. | The goalkeeper was caught napping and let in a goal. | I like napping after a long swim. | Our dog is napping in the sun.
note for the reader of a maths problem: -ing form doubles the p: nap → napping, napped. Noun: a nap (have/take a nap). Similar: doze, snooze, kip (UK informal), forty winks.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Needy people are poor and do not have enough money, food or things they need. 2) The needy means poor people as a group. 3) (informal) A needy person wants a lot of attention, help or comfort from others.
its sense in the lessons: In ethics, church life and charity: help the needy, give to needy families, food banks. In everyday talk: «My puppy is so needy — he follows me everywhere.»
examples from the lessons: Our school collected food for needy families. | The church gives warm meals to the needy. | Christians believe they should care for the needy. | Children in needy areas may have no books at home. | My little brother is very needy when he is tired. | The charity helps needy children all over the world.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «The needy» takes a plural verb: the needy are helped. Be respectful: many people prefer «people in need». The informal «needy» (clingy) can sound unkind about a person.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To negate something is to cancel it out or make it have no effect. 2) (formal) To negate a statement is to deny it or say it is not true. 3) (grammar) To negate a sentence is to make it negative, for example by adding «not».
its sense in the lessons: In formal and exam writing: «eating a cake negates the effect of the run». In grammar: «I like peas» negated is «I don't like peas». In maths and logic: negating a number gives its opposite (5 → -5).
examples from the lessons: Eating junk food can negate the good of exercising. | One rude word can negate a hundred kind ones. | Negate the sentence by adding «not». | The new evidence negated his story. | In maths, negating 7 gives -7. | The rain negated all our watering.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal word; everyday: cancel out, undo. Noun: negation; adjective: negative. Maths: the negation of a number has the same size but the opposite sign.

part of speech: adjective (neglected); verb form (neglect, neglects, neglected, neglecting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Neglected means not looked after or cared for: a neglected garden, a neglected dog. 2) Neglected is the past form of «neglect»: he neglected his homework means he did not do it or did not give it attention. 3) (law) A neglected child is one whose parents or carers do not give them the food, care or safety they need.
its sense in the lessons: In stories: a neglected old house with broken windows. In science: a neglected plant wilts. In safety and law: neglect of children or animals is wrong and can be reported.
examples from the lessons: The neglected garden was full of weeds. | The rescue centre took in a neglected horse. | He neglected his piano practice all week. | The castle had been neglected for centuries. | A neglected child may need help from social workers. | Don't let your pets feel neglected.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: neglect; adjective: neglectful (about the person who neglects). Neglect is not always on purpose, but it still causes harm. If you think a child or animal is neglected, tell a trusted adult.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (UK, Australia) A newsreader is a person who reads the news on television or radio.
its sense in the lessons: In media lessons and everyday life: the newsreader on the evening news. In the USA the usual word is «news anchor» or «newscaster».
examples from the lessons: The newsreader announced the football results. | My aunt works as a newsreader on local radio. | The newsreader spoke clearly and calmly. | We pretended to be newsreaders in drama class. | The newsreader smiled at the end of the bulletin. | A newsreader must practise reading aloud.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Compound: news + reader. US: news anchor, newscaster. Note: «news» is uncountable and takes a singular verb: the news is on.

meaning for a pupil: 1) NI is short for Northern Ireland, part of the United Kingdom. 2) (UK) NI is short for National Insurance, money taken from wages to pay for state pensions and benefits. 3) (science) Ni is the chemical symbol for the metal nickel. 4) In the old film «Monty Python and the Holy Grail», the Knights Who Say «Ni!» shout it as a silly word.
its sense in the lessons: In geography: NI on maps and in addresses. In money (UK): an NI number on a payslip. In chemistry: the symbol Ni in the periodic table. As a lowercase fragment it may also appear from Spanish «ni» (nor) or Ni in names.
examples from the lessons: Belfast is the capital of NI. | Every worker in the UK has an NI number. | Ni is the symbol for nickel. | The postcode area BT is in NI. | Coins can contain Ni (nickel). | NI contributions help pay for state pensions.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Not an ordinary English word; always check the context. Abbreviations are usually in capitals (NI); chemical symbols have a capital first letter and small second letter (Ni).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (history, church) Nicaea was an ancient city in what is now Turkey (today the town of İznik). 2) (church) The Council of Nicaea was a famous meeting of Christian bishops held there, called by the Roman emperor Constantine; it wrote the Nicene Creed, a statement of what Christians believe about God.
its sense in the lessons: In religion and history lessons: the Council of Nicaea and the Nicene Creed, which many churches still say aloud in services. It tells the reader about early church history.
examples from the lessons: The Council of Nicaea met in an ancient city in Turkey. | Bishops travelled from many lands to Nicaea. | The Nicene Creed is named after Nicaea. | Many churches still say the Nicene Creed on Sundays. | Emperor Constantine called the council at Nicaea. | Nicaea is now a town called İznik.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Proper noun: capital N. Said nye-SEE-uh. Adjective: Nicene (the Nicene Creed). A common myth says the Council of Nicaea chose which books go in the Bible; it did not.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) Nocturnal animals are active at night and sleep during the day. 2) Happening at night: a nocturnal walk, nocturnal noises.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons: nocturnal animals like owls, bats, hedgehogs, foxes, badgers and possums have special senses for the dark. Opposite: diurnal (active in the day). In stories: nocturnal adventures.
examples from the lessons: Owls are nocturnal birds. | Hedgehogs are nocturnal, so you see them at night. | Bats use sound to find food on their nocturnal flights. | Possums in Australia are nocturnal. | Our hamster is nocturnal and runs on its wheel all night. | We went on a nocturnal walk to see the stars. | Many desert animals are nocturnal to avoid the heat.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: diurnal (active by day); crepuscular means active at dawn and dusk. From Latin «nox» (night). Trap: not all animals that come out at night are fully nocturnal.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Offensiveness is the quality of being rude or hurtful, so that it upsets or insults people. 2) Being very unpleasant to the senses: the offensiveness of a smell.
its sense in the lessons: In ethics and online safety lessons: the offensiveness of a joke or comment. In media: films are rated partly for the offensiveness of the language. It tells the reader how much something hurts or insults.
examples from the lessons: The offensiveness of his joke shocked the class. | People complained about the offensiveness of the advert. | Swear words are graded by their offensiveness. | She did not see the offensiveness of what she said. | The offensiveness of the smell made us hold our noses. | We discussed the offensiveness of name-calling.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. From offensive (rude) + -ness. Related: offend, offence (UK) / offense (US). Trap: «offensive» in sport means attacking, but «offensiveness» is almost always about rudeness.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (church) To officiate at a wedding, funeral or service is to lead it as a priest, minister or official. 2) (sport) To officiate a match is to be the referee, umpire or judge.
its sense in the lessons: In church life: «The vicar officiated at my cousin's wedding.» In sport: referees and umpires officiate games. It tells the reader who is in charge of a ceremony or game.
examples from the lessons: The minister officiated at the funeral. | Father Michael will officiate at the wedding. | Two referees officiated the basketball game. | A registrar officiated at the town hall wedding. | Who is officiating today's match? | The bishop officiated at the confirmation service.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal word. Usually «officiate at» a ceremony; in sport «officiate» or «officiate at» a match. Person who officiates: an official (referee, priest, registrar).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Orderly means tidy and well arranged: an orderly desk. 2) Orderly means calm and well behaved, without pushing: an orderly queue. 3) (noun) An orderly is a person who helps in a hospital, carrying things and moving patients, or a soldier who helps an officer.
its sense in the lessons: In school and safety: leave the building in an orderly way during a fire drill; make an orderly line. In hospitals: orderlies help nurses. It tells the reader things are calm and organised.
examples from the lessons: Please walk out in an orderly line. | The fire drill was quick and orderly. | Her pencils were in an orderly row. | The crowd waited in an orderly queue. | A hospital orderly pushed the wheelchair. | Keep your notes neat and orderly.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Though it ends in -ly, «orderly» is an adjective, not an adverb: say «in an orderly way», not «they left orderly». Opposite: disorderly. From «order».

part of speech: verb (organise, organises, organised, organising; US organize)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To organise something is to plan and arrange it: organise a party, a trip or a game. 2) To organise things is to put them in order: organise your pencil case. 3) To organise people is to get them to work together for a goal, such as a club or a protest.
its sense in the lessons: In school: organise your work, your time, a class event or a fundraiser. In everyday life: organise a birthday party. In maths and science: organise data in a table or chart.
examples from the lessons: We organised a cake sale for charity. | Organise your books by size. | Mum organised a surprise party for Dad. | Organise your results in a table. | The class organised a litter pick in the park. | She is good at organising her time. | Who is organising the school trip?
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK -ise, US -ize; both correct. Noun: organisation (a group, or the act of organising); adjective: organised (tidy and good at planning). Opposite: disorganised.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Ornamental means used to decorate and make something look nice, rather than for a practical use.
its sense in the lessons: In gardens and nature: ornamental plants, ornamental ponds, ornamental fish. In art and history: ornamental carvings on old buildings and churches. It tells the reader something is there for beauty.
examples from the lessons: The garden has an ornamental pond with goldfish. | The fireplace is only ornamental; it doesn't work. | Ornamental cherry trees have pretty flowers but no fruit. | The church door has ornamental carvings. | Ornamental grasses sway in the wind. | That sword is ornamental, not for fighting.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From ornament (a decoration, like a Christmas tree ornament). Opposite: practical, useful, functional.

part of speech: noun (an orphan, orphans); verb (orphan, orphans, orphaned, orphaning — usually passive)
meaning for a pupil: 1) An orphan is a child whose parents have both died. 2) To be orphaned is to become an orphan. 3) An orphan animal has lost its mother. 4) (printing, computing) An orphan is a single line or word left alone at the top or bottom of a page.
its sense in the lessons: In stories: many famous characters are orphans, such as Harry Potter, Anne of Green Gables and Oliver Twist. In ethics and church life: caring for orphans. In nature: orphaned animals are raised in rescue centres.
examples from the lessons: Anne Shirley was an orphan who went to live on a farm. | The orphan was looked after by her aunt. | Harry Potter was orphaned as a baby. | The zoo is raising an orphaned baby elephant. | The Bible tells believers to care for orphans and widows. | An orphanage was once a home for orphans.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Starts with a vowel sound: «an orphan». Place: orphanage. Today children without parents usually live with relatives or foster families, not in orphanages. Said OR-fun.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An outcast is a person who is not accepted by other people and is pushed out of a group or society.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and ethics lessons: a character treated as an outcast because they are different; the lesson is often about kindness and inclusion. In the Bible: Jesus spent time with outcasts, such as lepers and tax collectors.
examples from the lessons: The ugly duckling felt like an outcast. | Nobody should be made an outcast at school. | Jesus welcomed outcasts and sinners. | After the argument, he felt like an outcast. | The story is about an outcast who becomes a hero. | Lepers were once treated as outcasts.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Stress on OUT. Similar: outsider (but «outsider» is milder and can be chosen). Opposite: insider, member.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An outsider is a person who does not belong to a group, or is not accepted by it. 2) An outsider is someone from another place or organisation, not part of it. 3) (sport, betting) An outsider is a person, team or horse that is not expected to win.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and social lessons: feeling like an outsider at a new school. In sport: «The outsider won the race!» In work: bringing in an outsider to look at a problem.
examples from the lessons: On my first day at the new school, I felt like an outsider. | The village did not welcome outsiders. | Our team was the outsider, but we won the cup! | An outsider can sometimes see the problem more clearly. | The horse was a complete outsider. | Try to include anyone who looks like an outsider.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Opposite: insider. Compare: outcast (pushed out by others), outsider (just not part of the group). In betting maths, an outsider has long odds: a small chance of winning.

part of speech: verb (overcharge, overcharges, overcharged, overcharging); noun (an overcharge)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (money) To overcharge someone is to ask them to pay more money than the correct price. 2) To overcharge a battery is to put too much electricity into it.
its sense in the lessons: In money and maths lessons: check your change and receipt so you are not overcharged. In everyday life: «The shop overcharged us by £2.» In science: overcharging batteries can damage them.
examples from the lessons: The café overcharged us for the drinks. | Check your receipt to make sure you weren't overcharged. | We were overcharged by fifty pence. | The shopkeeper said sorry for overcharging. | Don't overcharge your tablet battery. | The taxi driver tried to overcharge the tourists.
note for the reader of a maths problem: over- + charge. Opposite: undercharge. Maths: overcharged amount = price paid − correct price (e.g. paid £7, correct £5 → overcharged by £2).

part of speech: verb (overspend, overspends, overspent, overspending); noun (an overspend)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (money) To overspend is to spend more money than you have or than you planned. 2) (money, noun) An overspend is the amount spent above the plan or budget.
its sense in the lessons: In money and maths lessons: keeping to a budget, not overspending your pocket money. In news: a council or hospital overspend. It tells the reader the money went over the limit.
examples from the lessons: I overspent at the fair and had no money left for the bus. | The school overspent on the new playground. | Make a list so you don't overspend. | The overspend was £300. | Mum says not to overspend at Christmas. | The club had to cut costs after overspending.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: overspent (not «overspended»). Maths: overspend = amount spent − budget (e.g. budget £20, spent £26 → overspend of £6). Opposite: underspend.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To overturn is to turn over, or make something turn over, so the bottom is on top: the boat overturned. 2) (law) To overturn a decision is to change it officially and say it was wrong: the judge overturned the ruling. 3) To overturn an idea is to show it is wrong or replace it.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and news: overturned boats, cars or tables. In law and citizenship: overturning a verdict or a ban. In science: new discoveries can overturn old ideas. In the Bible: Jesus overturned the tables of the money changers in the Temple.
examples from the lessons: The canoe overturned and we fell into the lake. | The wind overturned our tent. | Jesus overturned the tables of the money changers. | The court overturned the unfair decision. | The lorry overturned on the motorway. | New fossils overturned the old idea.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: overturned. Similar: capsize (for boats), tip over, knock over. In law the opposite is uphold (keep the decision).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) Panicky means feeling or showing sudden great fear or worry, so that you cannot think calmly.
its sense in the lessons: In stories: a panicky voice, a panicky crowd. In everyday life and safety: «I felt panicky when I lost Mum in the shop» — the advice is to stop, breathe and find a safe adult.
examples from the lessons: I felt panicky when I couldn't find my ticket. | The panicky horse ran round the field. | Her voice sounded panicky on the phone. | Take deep breaths if you feel panicky. | The crowd became panicky when the lights went out. | He gets panicky before tests.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: panic + k + y (panicky), just like panicked, panicking. Noun and verb: panic. Informal.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (church) Papal means to do with the Pope, the head of the Roman Catholic Church.
its sense in the lessons: In religion and history lessons: papal visits, the papal palace, papal letters, papal authority. It tells the reader something belongs to or comes from the Pope.
examples from the lessons: Crowds gathered to see the papal visit. | The papal flag is yellow and white. | The Vatican holds the papal palace. | The papal letter was read in all the churches. | In history, papal power was very great in Europe. | The papal car is sometimes called the Popemobile.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Said PAY-pul. From Latin «papa» (father). Related: Pope, papacy (the Pope's office). Trap: do not confuse with «paper».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Paramount means more important than anything else.
its sense in the lessons: In formal and safety language: «Safety is paramount», «children's welfare is paramount». It tells the reader what must come first.
examples from the lessons: On a school trip, safety is paramount. | The welfare of the child is paramount. | Honesty is of paramount importance. | For the climbers, good ropes were paramount. | In a fire, getting out quickly is paramount. | Clean water is paramount for health.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; everyday: most important, top. Usually after a verb («safety is paramount») or in «of paramount importance». Not used with «more» or «most».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (church) A parishioner is a person who lives in a parish or belongs to its church.
its sense in the lessons: In church life: the vicar or priest visits parishioners; parishioners help with the church fete, flowers and food bank. It tells the reader about the members of a local church community.
examples from the lessons: The priest greeted every parishioner at the door. | Parishioners decorated the church for the harvest festival. | Many parishioners came to the carol service. | Mrs O'Brien is a parishioner who arranges the flowers. | The vicar visits sick parishioners at home. | Parishioners raised money to fix the church roof.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «parish», the area served by one church and priest. Said pa-RISH-uh-ner.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A PC is a personal computer, often a desktop or laptop computer, especially one that is not an Apple Mac. 2) (UK) PC stands for Police Constable, the lowest rank of police officer: PC Jones. 3) PC (or «politically correct») describes language or behaviour that tries not to offend groups of people; sometimes said in a mocking way. 4) pc (lowercase) can mean per cent or piece in short notes.
its sense in the lessons: In computing lessons: using a PC. In stories and news (UK): PC Smith helped the lost child. In everyday talk: «That's not very PC» means that might offend people.
examples from the lessons: I did my homework on the PC. | Our classroom has six PCs. | PC Patel visited our school to talk about road safety. | Turn off the PC before you go home. | He said the joke wasn't PC. | The price went up by 5 pc.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually written in capitals: PC. Plural: PCs. Women police officers are also «PC» (WPC is old-fashioned). Read the context to know which meaning is used.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Pecuniary means to do with money.
its sense in the lessons: Mostly in law and formal writing: «pecuniary gain» (getting money), «pecuniary loss», «pecuniary interest». Children rarely meet it except in exam language.
examples from the lessons: He gained no pecuniary benefit from helping. | The court looked at the pecuniary loss. | She had no pecuniary interest in the shop. | Volunteers work for no pecuniary reward. | The trouble was pecuniary: they had no money. | Pecuniary matters were handled by the treasurer.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Very formal; everyday word: financial, money. From Latin «pecunia» (money).

meaning for a pupil: 1) To penetrate something is to go into it or through it, often with effort: the nail penetrated the wood. 2) To penetrate a group or market is to get into it successfully. 3) (formal) To penetrate an idea or mystery is to understand it.
its sense in the lessons: In science: light penetrates water, X-rays penetrate the body, roots penetrate the soil. In stories: «her eyes could not penetrate the darkness». In geography: sunlight penetrates the rainforest floor only in places.
examples from the lessons: Sunlight cannot penetrate the deep ocean. | The roots penetrated deep into the soil. | The cold penetrated through his thin coat. | X-rays penetrate skin but not bone. | The torch could not penetrate the thick fog. | Rain penetrated the old roof.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: penetration; adjective: penetrating (a penetrating look or sound is sharp and strong). Formal; everyday: go through, get into.

part of speech: noun (pepperoni, uncountable; a slice of pepperoni)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Pepperoni is a spicy dried sausage, usually made of pork and beef, sliced thin and often put on pizza.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: «A pepperoni pizza, please!» In maths: fractions and counting with pizza and pepperoni slices. In food lessons: pepperoni is a processed meat.
examples from the lessons: I'd like a pepperoni pizza. | Count the slices of pepperoni on the pizza. | She picked the pepperoni off her pizza. | Pepperoni is a little bit spicy. | We put pepperoni and cheese on our homemade pizza. | There were twelve pepperoni slices, shared equally among four pieces.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable; count it as «slices of pepperoni». Spelling: double p, one r, ends in -i. Note: in Italy, «peperoni» means peppers (vegetables), not sausage. Maths: 12 slices ÷ 4 pieces = 3 slices each.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (church, old) Perdition is everlasting punishment after death, often meaning hell, in old Christian language. 2) (old, formal) Complete ruin or disaster.
its sense in the lessons: In old Bible translations, hymns and classic stories: «the road to perdition». Today it sounds old-fashioned or dramatic. It tells the reader about a terrible fate.
examples from the lessons: The preacher warned against the road to perdition. | In the old story, the pirate feared eternal perdition. | Old hymns sometimes speak of perdition. | Gambling led him to perdition. | Christians believe Jesus came to save people from perdition. | The book calls greed the path to perdition.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Old-fashioned, uncountable. Similar: damnation, hell, ruin. Not used in everyday speech.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal, law) A perpetrator is a person who does something wrong or harmful, especially a crime.
its sense in the lessons: In news, police reports and detective stories: «the perpetrator was caught», «police are looking for the perpetrators». In anti-bullying talk: the perpetrator and the victim. It tells the reader who did the bad act.
examples from the lessons: Police are searching for the perpetrator. | The perpetrator of the prank owned up. | Who was the perpetrator of this mess? | The detective found the perpetrator. | Bullying hurts both the victim and, in the long run, the perpetrator. | The perpetrators were sent to prison.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal. Verb: perpetrate (do something wrong). Everyday words: culprit, wrongdoer. Spelling: per-pe-tra-tor. Do not confuse with «perpetual» (lasting for ever).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Persistence is going on trying to do something even when it is hard or other people want you to stop. 2) Persistence is something continuing for a long time: the persistence of the rain.
its sense in the lessons: In school: persistence is praised in learning — keep going when maths is difficult. In science: Thomas Edison's persistence in testing light bulbs. In nature: the persistence of a smell or pollution.
examples from the lessons: With persistence, she learnt to ride her bike. | His persistence paid off when he solved the puzzle. | The spider showed great persistence rebuilding its web. | Persistence is more important than talent. | We were annoyed by the persistence of the rain. | Learning an instrument takes persistence.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Adjective: persistent; verb: persist. Synonyms: perseverance, determination, grit. Spelling: -ence, not -ance.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A persistent person keeps on trying and does not give up easily. 2) Something persistent goes on for a long time or keeps coming back: a persistent cough, persistent rain.
its sense in the lessons: In school reports: a persistent learner. In health: «See a doctor if you have a persistent cough.» In weather: persistent rain. Sometimes negative: a persistent salesman who will not leave.
examples from the lessons: She is a persistent and hard-working pupil. | The persistent rain spoiled our picnic. | A persistent cough should be checked by a doctor. | The persistent fly kept landing on my sandwich. | He was persistent and finally got a reply. | Persistent lateness can get you into trouble.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: -ent, not -ant. Noun: persistence; verb: persist. Can be praise (keeps trying) or complaint (will not stop).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (Jewish faith) Pesach is the Hebrew name for Passover, a spring festival when Jewish people remember how God freed the Israelites from slavery in Egypt, as told in the Book of Exodus.
its sense in the lessons: In religion lessons: families hold a Seder meal, read the story from a book called the Haggadah, eat matzah (flat bread without yeast) and other symbolic foods. In Christian lessons: the Last Supper took place at Passover time.
examples from the lessons: Jewish families celebrate Pesach in spring. | At Pesach, people eat matzah, flat bread made without yeast. | The youngest child asks four questions at the Pesach Seder. | Pesach remembers the escape from slavery in Egypt. | Before Pesach, homes are cleaned of all bread with yeast. | The Last Supper took place around the time of Pesach.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Proper noun, capital P. Said PAY-sakh (with a throaty «kh»). English name: Passover. The festival lasts seven or eight days.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (church, formal) Petitionary means asking for something; petitionary prayer is prayer that asks God for help or for something needed, for yourself or for others.
its sense in the lessons: In religion lessons: types of prayer — praise (adoration), thanks (thanksgiving), saying sorry (confession) and asking (petitionary or intercessory prayer). It tells the reader that the prayer or letter is a request.
examples from the lessons: Petitionary prayer asks God for help. | «Please make Grandma better» is a petitionary prayer. | We learnt about thanksgiving and petitionary prayers. | The Lord's Prayer includes petitionary lines like «Give us this day our daily bread». | The king received a petitionary letter from the villagers. | Some petitionary prayers are for other people.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal. From «petition» (a request). Prayer for others is often called intercession or intercessory prayer.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A pillar is a tall, strong post of stone, wood or metal that holds up part of a building or stands as a monument. 2) A pillar of smoke, fire or cloud is a tall column of it. 3) A pillar of a community or group is an important person or idea that supports it: a pillar of the church.
its sense in the lessons: In history: Greek and Roman temples with pillars. In the Bible: God led the Israelites by a pillar of cloud by day and a pillar of fire by night; Lot's wife became a pillar of salt. In religion: the Five Pillars of Islam. Phrase (UK): «from pillar to post» means from one place to another without rest.
examples from the lessons: The temple roof stood on tall stone pillars. | A pillar of smoke rose from the bonfire. | God led the Israelites with a pillar of cloud. | Grandpa was a pillar of the community. | The Five Pillars of Islam are the main duties of Muslims. | In the UK, post boxes used to be called pillar boxes. | We were sent from pillar to post.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Similar: column (often round and decorated), post. Phrase: «pillar of strength» = someone who supports others in hard times.

part of speech: noun (a ping, pings); verb (ping, pings, pinged, pinging)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A ping is a short, high, ringing sound, like a bell or a phone alert. 2) To ping is to make that sound. 3) (informal) To ping someone is to send them a quick message: ping me later. 4) (computing) A ping is a test signal sent to check if a computer can be reached and how fast it answers.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: the microwave pings when food is ready; your phone pings with a message. In computing and games: low ping means a fast connection. In informal talk: «I'll ping you an email.»
examples from the lessons: The microwave pinged and the soup was hot. | My phone pinged with a message from Gran. | The bell gave a loud ping. | Ping me when you're home. | The game is slow because my ping is high. | A stone pinged against the window.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: pinged. Informal for messaging. Related sound words: ding, beep, buzz. In UK sport and table tennis talk, «ping-pong» is table tennis.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Pitta (or pita) is a flat round or oval bread from the eastern Mediterranean and the Middle East that can be opened into a pocket and filled with food.
its sense in the lessons: In food lessons and everyday life: a pitta filled with falafel, salad or hummus; pitta bread in lunchboxes; Greek gyros wrapped in pitta.
examples from the lessons: I had a pitta filled with chicken and salad. | Cut the pitta open to make a pocket. | We dipped pitta bread in hummus. | Toast the pitta so it puffs up. | Mum packed a cheese pitta for my lunch. | Falafel tastes great in a warm pitta.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK spelling usually «pitta», US spelling «pita». Countable (two pittas) or «pitta bread» (uncountable). Pitta is not pizza: it has no topping and opens into a pocket.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A plunger is a tool with a rubber cup on a stick, used to clear a blocked sink or toilet by pushing and pulling. 2) A plunger is a part that slides in and out of a tube, like in a syringe, a cafetière (French press) or a pump.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: unblocking a toilet with a plunger. In science: the plunger of a syringe pushes liquid or air; experiments with air pressure. In cooking: a cafetière plunger pushes the coffee down.
examples from the lessons: Dad used a plunger to unblock the sink. | Push the plunger slowly to squeeze out the water. | The nurse pressed the syringe plunger. | Press the plunger on the cafetière to make the coffee. | The plunger made a loud sucking sound. | Pull back the plunger to fill the syringe with air.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. From «plunge» (push or dive in). It works by changing air or water pressure.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal, mainly UK) A little fat, short and soft-looking. 2) (informal) Soft and fleshy, of hands, fingers or a face.
its sense in the lessons: Used in stories to describe a chubby person, pet or a baby's hands, often in a fond or teasing way; it can hurt if said about someone's body to their face. Phrases: «podgy little fingers», «a podgy puppy», «a bit podgy».
examples from the lessons: The baby grabbed my finger with her podgy hand. | Our cat got podgy after the neighbours kept feeding her. | He was a podgy boy with red cheeks and a big grin. | The puppy's podgy tummy wobbled as it ran. | Grandad patted his podgy belly after Christmas dinner. | "Don't call him podgy, it's unkind," Mum said. | The teddy had a podgy face and button eyes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal, mostly British; American English says «pudgy». Comparative «podgier», superlative «podgiest». Talking about someone's weight can be rude, so it is kinder to keep such words for babies, animals and toys. Not a maths word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Writing in which words are chosen for their sound, rhythm and pictures, often set out in short lines and sometimes rhyming. 2) Poems as a group, or the poems of one writer or country. 3) A quality of beauty and grace in something that is not writing: «the poetry of her dancing».
its sense in the lessons: In school English pupils read poetry, learn it by heart, spot rhyme, rhythm, similes and repetition, and write their own. A «poetry recital» or «poetry slam» is a performance. In church the Psalms are poetry from the Bible. Phrases: «write poetry», «a book of poetry», «poetry in motion».
examples from the lessons: We are studying poetry in English this week. | Her poetry is full of the sea and the wind. | Each pupil read a poem at the poetry assembly. | The Psalms are some of the oldest poetry in the Bible. | Not all poetry rhymes; some is free verse. | Watching the gymnast was like poetry in motion. | Grandma keeps a book of Irish poetry by her bed. | He won a prize in the school poetry competition.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Poetry» is uncountable: say «some poetry» or «a poem», never «a poetry» or «poetries». A poet writes poems; the whole art is poetry. Do not confuse with «poultry» (chickens and ducks). Myth: poems do not have to rhyme.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) A sign or warning that something important, often bad, is going to happen. 2) (literary) A strange or wonderful thing that seems to carry a message. 3) (formal) Serious meaning or importance: «a matter of great portent».
its sense in the lessons: Found in fairy tales, myths and old stories: a comet, a black cat or a storm seen as a portent of doom. Science teaches that such signs do not really foretell the future. Phrases: «a portent of doom», «an evil portent», «portents of change».
examples from the lessons: The villagers believed the comet was a portent of war. | Dark clouds rolled in like a portent of the storm to come. | In the story, a raven on the roof was taken as a portent. | The first falling leaves are a portent of autumn. | Ancient kings asked wise men to read the portents in the sky. | Scientists explain eclipses; they are not portents of anything. | The empty classroom felt like a portent of trouble.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: «a portent», «portents». Related adjective «portentous» (seeming to warn of something; also pompous and overly serious). Stress on the first part: POR-tent. Superstition: an eclipse or a black cat is not a real warning; that is a myth.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a hopeful, good or approving way: «She answered positively.» 2) (emphatic) Really, completely, truly: «It was positively freezing.» 3) Certainly, without any doubt: «I positively know he was there.» 4) (maths, science) In the positive direction or with a plus charge: «a positively charged particle».
its sense in the lessons: Teachers praise children who «think positively» and «respond positively» to advice. In science, protons are positively charged; in maths, a number above zero is positive. In talk, «positively» makes an adjective stronger: «positively delicious». Phrases: «think positively», «react positively», «positively charged».
examples from the lessons: Try to think positively before the test. | The coach reacted positively to our new idea. | The soup was positively delicious. | It was positively freezing at the bus stop this morning. | A proton is positively charged. | I can positively say I locked the door. | The class spoke positively about the trip. | The magnet's end is positively charged in this picture.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from «positive». The emphatic sense («positively huge») is informal. In maths and science «positive» means greater than zero or with a plus sign; «positively correlated» means both go up together. Opposite: «negatively».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Something that might happen or might be true. 2) The chance that something can happen: «There is a possibility of rain.» 3) A choice or option you could take. 4) possibilities (plural) The good things that something could become: «The old shed has possibilities.»
its sense in the lessons: In maths, pupils list all the possibilities (outcomes) of rolling a dice or tossing a coin to find probability. In everyday talk and safety it means something to plan for: «the possibility of a fire». Phrases: «a strong possibility», «rule out the possibility», «within the realms of possibility», «endless possibilities».
examples from the lessons: There is a possibility of snow tomorrow. | We listed every possibility when we rolled two dice. | Is there any possibility we can stay up late? | The detective did not rule out the possibility of a second thief. | Moving to Canada is a real possibility for our family. | A blank page is full of possibilities. | Tossing a coin has two possibilities: heads or tails. | Always think about the possibility of a slippery floor.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; plural «possibilities» (y becomes ies). Adjective «possible», adverb «possibly». In maths problems, «how many possibilities» asks you to count all the outcomes; if each is equally likely, probability = favourable possibilities divided by all possibilities.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A hole in the surface of a road or path, made by weather and traffic. 2) A deep hole or cave in rock, often made by water, that people may climb down. 3) (informal) A hidden problem that could cause trouble.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life potholes damage bikes and cars, so cyclists must watch for them, especially when puddles hide them. Councils fill potholes. «Potholing» (UK) is exploring caves. Phrases: «hit a pothole», «fill in a pothole», «avoid the potholes».
examples from the lessons: Dad's car hit a pothole and the tyre went flat. | Watch out for potholes when you ride your bike. | The pothole filled with rain and looked like a puddle. | The council finally fixed the potholes on our street. | The explorers climbed down a deep pothole in the hills. | There are a few potholes in the plan, but we can fix them. | My scooter wobbled when it hit a pothole.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable, one word. A «pothole» on roads is common in UK, US, Canada, Australia, NZ and Ireland. Safety: a puddle can hide a deep pothole, so ride around puddles carefully. «Potholing» (caving) is mainly British; Americans say «caving» or «spelunking».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Almost, nearly: «The jar is practically empty.» 2) In a sensible, useful, real-life way: «Think practically about what to pack.» 3) In practice, as things really are, not in theory.
its sense in the lessons: Very common in everyday talk to mean «almost»: «I practically fell asleep.» In school it can also mean doing something with your hands rather than on paper: «a practically minded child». Phrases: «practically nothing», «practically everyone», «practically speaking».
examples from the lessons: The bus was practically empty. | I've practically finished my homework. | Practically everyone in the class has a pet. | Practically speaking, we can't fit ten people in the car. | She is very practically minded and can fix anything. | It cost practically nothing at the car-boot sale. | We were practically running to get to school on time.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb of «practical». The «almost» sense is informal but very common. Spelling: practic-al-ly, with «-ally». Do not confuse with «practice» (noun in UK; verb is «practise» in UK). In maths, «practically» is not exact: «practically 100» is not 100.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Done to stop something bad from happening, before it happens. 2) (formal) Done just in case, to be safe, even if the danger may not be real.
its sense in the lessons: Used in safety and news: a «precautionary measure», a «precautionary evacuation», taking a child to hospital «as a precautionary step». It tells the reader there may be no real harm yet. Phrases: «as a precautionary measure», «a precautionary approach».
examples from the lessons: As a precautionary measure, the school closed early because of the storm. | The nurse kept him in for a precautionary check. | The fire alarm sounded, and we left the building as a precautionary step. | The lifeguard closed the beach as a precautionary move after a shark was seen. | We packed spare batteries as a precautionary thing. | Precautionary signs warned of thin ice on the pond.
