note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective from «precaution» (a step taken to stay safe). It goes before a noun: «a precautionary measure». Fairly formal, often in notices and news. Spelling: pre-caution-ary. Not a maths word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) A rule or principle telling people how to behave or think. 2) (church, Bible) A command or teaching from God or a religious teacher. 3) (law, UK) An official written order.
its sense in the lessons: Found in ethics, religion and old books: «the precepts of Jesus», «moral precepts» like «be kind» and «tell the truth». In Buddhism there are «five precepts». Phrases: «moral precepts», «follow the precepts», «by example rather than precept».
examples from the lessons: Treat others as you want to be treated is a famous precept. | Christians believe the precepts of the Bible guide how to live. | Buddhists follow five precepts, such as not harming living things. | Our teacher taught us more by example than by precept. | Honesty is the first precept of our school rules. | The old book was full of wise precepts. | The monks lived by strict precepts.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal word; in everyday talk say «rule» or «principle». Countable. Stress: PREE-sept. Do not confuse with «concept» (an idea) or «percept».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Exact and correct in every small detail. 2) Very careful and accurate in doing things. 3) Used to stress that you mean exactly this one: «at that precise moment».
its sense in the lessons: In maths and science, precise measurements give exact numbers with the right units; pupils are asked to be precise with a ruler or a thermometer. In writing, precise words make meaning clear. Phrases: «to be precise», «at that precise moment», «precise instructions».
examples from the lessons: Please give a precise answer, not a guess. | The recipe needs precise amounts of flour and sugar. | The line is 7.4 centimetres long, to be precise. | At that precise moment, the bell rang. | A surgeon must be very precise. | Use precise words to describe your character. | The clock gives the precise time.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb «precisely», noun «precision». In science, «precise» (repeated measurements close together) is different from «accurate» (close to the true value). In maths, a precise answer may need decimals; «round to one decimal place» makes it less precise. Do not confuse with «concise» (short).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (money) An amount paid regularly for insurance. 2) An extra amount paid on top of the usual price. 3) adjective Of high quality and usually more expensive: «premium ice cream». 4) at a premium Hard to find and so in great demand: «Space is at a premium in our flat.» 5) put a premium on Treat something as very important.
its sense in the lessons: In adult life, families pay a «monthly premium» for car, house or health insurance. In shops «premium» on labels means the dearer, better kind; «premium petrol». In maths problems, a premium is an extra amount you add. Phrases: «insurance premium», «pay a premium», «at a premium», «premium quality».
examples from the lessons: Mum pays an insurance premium every month for the car. | Premium tickets cost more but you sit at the front. | We bought the premium ice cream for the party. | Seats were at a premium at the school concert. | Our coach puts a premium on teamwork. | Dad filled up with premium petrol. | You pay a premium for fruit that is out of season.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «premiums». Stress: PREE-mee-um. In maths: if a ticket costs £20 plus a £5 premium, the total is £25. «Premium» on a label is marketing; it does not always mean better. An insurance premium is paid even if nothing goes wrong.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (church) An elder or leader of a local church in the early Christian Church. 2) (church) In some churches, a priest; in Presbyterian churches, an elder who helps lead the congregation.
its sense in the lessons: Met in church history, Bible study and the names of churches: the Presbyterian Church is named after presbyters (elders) who lead it together. In the New Testament presbyters looked after the first Christian communities. Phrases: «the presbyters of the church», «ordained a presbyter».
examples from the lessons: In the early Church, presbyters cared for the believers in each town. | The Bible says Paul met the presbyters of the church in Ephesus. | Our church is Presbyterian, which means it is led by elders. | A presbyter helped the bishop with services. | The new presbyter was ordained on Sunday. | In some churches the word presbyter means the same as priest.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal and churchy; everyday words are «elder» or «priest». The word «priest» actually comes from «presbyter». Related: «Presbyterian», «presbytery» (a group of elders, or a priest's house in Catholic use).

meaning for a pupil: 1) To think something is true without being sure, because it seems likely. 2) (law) To treat something as true until it is proved wrong: «innocent until proved guilty». 3) (formal) To be bold or rude enough to do something you have no right to do: «Don't presume to tell me what to do.» 4) presume on/upon To take unfair advantage of someone's kindness.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and talk: «I presume you've done your homework.» Famous line: «Dr Livingstone, I presume?» In law a person is «presumed innocent». In science, a guess you treat as true until tested is close to an assumption. Phrases: «I presume», «presumed dead», «presumed innocent».
examples from the lessons: I presume you're hungry after the long walk. | The sailors were presumed lost at sea, but they came home. | In court, everyone is presumed innocent until proved guilty. | Don't presume to boss me around! | We presumed the shop was open, but it was shut. | "You're the new girl, I presume?" said the teacher. | She never presumed on her friends' kindness.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: presumed, presuming. Noun «presumption», adjective «presumptuous» (too bold). Close to «assume»; «presume» suggests more reason to believe it. In maths word problems, do not presume facts that are not given.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To win or be stronger in the end after a struggle. 2) To be common or usual in a place or time. 3) prevail on/upon (formal) To persuade someone to do something.
its sense in the lessons: In stories good often «prevails over» evil. In geography, the «prevailing wind» is the wind that blows most often in a place. In formal speech: «Common sense prevailed.» Phrases: «justice prevailed», «prevailing wind», «prevail upon someone».
examples from the lessons: In the end, good prevailed over evil. | The prevailing wind in Ireland blows from the west. | Calm prevailed after the storm. | Our team prevailed after extra time. | She prevailed on her dad to let her keep the kitten. | Fairness must prevail in every game. | Sunny weather prevailed for the whole holiday.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular: prevailed, prevailing. «Prevailing» as an adjective means the most common: «prevailing opinion». Noun «prevalence», adjective «prevalent». Formal; everyday words are «win» or «be common».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (church) The job and calling of being a priest. 2) (church) All the priests of a church or religion together. 3) (Bible, church) Christians believe in «the priesthood of all believers»: every believer can speak to God directly.
its sense in the lessons: Used in church life: a young man may «enter the priesthood» or «train for the priesthood» at a seminary. In the Bible, the priesthood of Aaron served in the Temple. Phrases: «enter the priesthood», «called to the priesthood», «the Catholic priesthood».
examples from the lessons: My uncle decided to enter the priesthood. | He trained for the priesthood for six years. | In the Bible, Aaron and his sons held the priesthood. | The priesthood of the church met to pray. | Some churches allow women in the priesthood and some do not. | She felt called to the priesthood when she was young.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable with «the». Built from «priest» + «-hood» like «childhood». Different churches and faiths have different rules about who can be a priest; speak about them respectfully.

part of speech: noun (a privilege, privileges); verb (privilege, privileges, privileged, privileging)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A special right or advantage that only some people have. 2) Something that makes you feel honoured and lucky: «It was a privilege to meet her.» 3) An advantage some people have in life because of money, family or where they were born. 4) (law) A legal right, such as keeping some talk secret. 5) verb To treat one person or thing as more important than others.
its sense in the lessons: At school, privileges are rewards: staying in at break, being a monitor, golden time; bad behaviour can mean losing privileges. In ethics, pupils talk about privilege and fairness. Phrases: «lose your privileges», «an honour and a privilege», «a privileged background», «screen privileges».
examples from the lessons: Year 6 pupils have the privilege of using the big field. | If you misbehave, you will lose your screen privileges. | It was a privilege to sing in the cathedral. | Driving is a privilege, not a right. | Some children grow up with more privilege than others. | The headteacher said it was a privilege to lead our school. | The prefects' privileges include their own common room.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: privi-LEGE, no «d» (not «priviledge»). Countable for special rights; uncountable for advantage in life. Adjective «privileged» (lucky, with advantages). A privilege can be taken away; a right should not be.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Done or given for a trial time, to see if a person is good enough before they are made permanent. 2) (law) Connected with probation, when someone who broke the law is watched instead of sent to prison.
its sense in the lessons: In adult life a new worker often has a «probationary period» of a few months. A new teacher may be a «probationary teacher». In law, «probationary» links to the probation officer who checks on someone. Phrases: «probationary period», «probationary teacher», «probationary licence».
examples from the lessons: Mum is in her probationary period at her new job. | Our new teacher is still probationary. | After a three-month probationary period, he got a permanent contract. | New drivers in some places have a probationary licence. | The club gave him probationary membership. | During the probationary year, nurses are checked often.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective from «probation». Goes before the noun: «a probationary period». Fairly formal. Not «probational».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) The act of getting or buying something, especially goods for a company or government. 2) (business) The department or job of buying things for a big organisation.
its sense in the lessons: An adult and business word: schools, hospitals and armies have «procurement» to buy books, beds or vehicles. In news: «defence procurement», «public procurement». Children meet it in adult talk about work. Phrases: «the procurement process», «procurement officer».
examples from the lessons: Dad works in procurement for the hospital. | The procurement of new laptops for the school took months. | The council has rules for the procurement of school buses. | The army's procurement office ordered new boots. | Food procurement was hard during the long winter. | She is a procurement manager for a supermarket.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; in everyday talk say «buying» or «getting». Verb «procure» (formal: to obtain). Usually uncountable.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A high level of skill or ability in something. 2) A test or badge showing that you have reached a certain level: «a swimming proficiency badge».
its sense in the lessons: In school: «reading proficiency», «proficiency in maths». Scouts and Guides earn proficiency badges; cyclists may take a «cycling proficiency» test (UK). Exams of English test language proficiency. Phrases: «proficiency in», «a proficiency test», «level of proficiency».
examples from the lessons: She showed great proficiency in French. | I passed my cycling proficiency test at school. | The swimming club gives proficiency badges. | Proficiency in reading helps with every subject. | His proficiency on the violin grew with practice. | The test measures your proficiency in English.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «great proficiency», not «a proficiency» (except «a proficiency test/badge»). Adjective «proficient (in/at)». Preposition: «proficiency in» something. Formal; everyday words are «skill» or «ability».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who makes a promise. 2) (law, formal) The person in an agreement who promises to do something (also spelled «promisor»).
its sense in the lessons: Rare word, used in stories, ethics lessons and law: a «good promiser» keeps promises; «a great promiser» may make many and keep few. In ethics, the promiser has a duty to the person promised. Phrases: «a promiser of great things», «the promiser and the promisee».
examples from the lessons: He was a big promiser but a poor doer. | A good promiser always keeps their word. | In the contract, the promiser agrees to pay the money. | The king was a promiser of gifts he never gave. | Don't be a promiser if you can't keep it. | The promiser must do what was promised.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Rare; usually we say «someone who makes promises». Built from «promise» + «-er». In law the spelling «promisor» is common, and the other person is the «promisee». Saying «promise» means keeping it is an ethical duty.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal, law) The official public announcement of a new law or rule, so it comes into force. 2) (formal) Spreading an idea or belief widely among people. 3) (church) The official announcement of a teaching by a church.
its sense in the lessons: Exam and law word: «the promulgation of a law», «the promulgation of a new constitution». In church history, the promulgation of a teaching by the Pope or a council. Children rarely use it; in stories a king may order the promulgation of a decree.
examples from the lessons: The promulgation of the new law was read in the town square. | The promulgation of the rules came after months of debate. | The church announced the promulgation of a new prayer book. | The king ordered the promulgation of his decree across the land. | Teachers help in the promulgation of good ideas. | After its promulgation, the law applied to everyone.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Very formal. Verb «promulgate». Stress: prom-ul-GAY-shun. Everyday words: «announcing», «spreading».

meaning for a pupil: 1) In the right size, amount or degree compared with something else; fair and not too much. 2) (maths) Growing or shrinking in the same ratio as something else: «proportionate to».
its sense in the lessons: In maths, two amounts are proportionate when one is always the same multiple of the other: «cost is proportionate to weight». In ethics and law, a punishment should be «proportionate to» the wrong. Phrases: «proportionate to», «a proportionate response», «disproportionate».
examples from the lessons: The punishment should be proportionate to what you did. | Your pocket money is proportionate to the jobs you do. | The cost of the apples is proportionate to their weight. | Doubling the recipe needs a proportionate amount of eggs. | Shouting at a tiny mistake is not a proportionate response. | Her pay was proportionate to her hours.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite «disproportionate» (too big or too small). Also «proportional», which is the usual word in maths. In maths problems: if y is proportionate to x, then y = kx; doubling x doubles y. Adverb «proportionately».

part of speech: noun (a prospect, prospects); verb (prospect, prospects, prospected, prospecting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The possibility that something will happen: «There is little prospect of rain.» 2) An event you expect: «the prospect of a holiday». 3) prospects (plural) Chances of success in the future, especially in a job. 4) A person likely to be chosen, or a good player for the future. 5) (literary) A wide view of land. 6) verb To search land for gold, oil or minerals.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and talk: «the prospect of a day at the beach», «a bright young prospect» in sport. In history and geography: gold prospectors searched in California, Australia and the Yukon. In adult talk: «job prospects». Phrases: «in prospect», «the prospect of», «good prospects», «prospect for gold».
examples from the lessons: The prospect of a snow day made us all cheer. | There is no prospect of the rain stopping soon. | She is the club's brightest prospect. | Good exam results improve your job prospects. | Miners came to prospect for gold in the hills. | From the hilltop we had a fine prospect of the valley. | I don't like the prospect of a long car journey.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stress: noun PROS-pect; verb pros-PECT or PROS-pect. Someone who prospects is a «prospector». Do not confuse with «perspective». Plural «prospects» often means future chances.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Likely or expected to be or become something in the future: «prospective parents». 2) (formal) Going to happen or take effect in the future.
its sense in the lessons: Used in adult life and school: «prospective pupils» visit on open day; «prospective buyers» look at a house. It tells the reader the person is not yet that thing. Phrases: «prospective students», «prospective buyers», «prospective parents».
examples from the lessons: Prospective pupils toured the school on open day. | The prospective buyers looked round our house. | She met her prospective in-laws for the first time. | The coach watched the prospective players at trials. | Prospective parents asked about the lunch menu. | The prospective changes to the timetable were explained.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Goes before a noun. Different from «perspective» (a point of view) — a common confusion. Formal; in everyday talk say «future» or «possible».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Lasting a long time, often longer than expected or wanted. 2) (verb form) Past of «protract», to make something last longer.
its sense in the lessons: News and formal writing: «a protracted illness», «protracted talks», «a protracted war». In maths, a «protractor» measures angles — a different meaning from the same root (drawing out). Phrases: «a protracted struggle», «protracted negotiations».
examples from the lessons: After protracted talks, the teachers agreed a deal. | Grandpa recovered from a protracted illness. | The protracted rain ruined our camping trip. | The two countries fought a protracted war. | The meeting was protracted and boring. | The protracted argument went on all afternoon.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; everyday words are «long» or «drawn-out». Usually about something unpleasant. Not to be confused with «protractor», the tool for measuring angles in degrees.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A large part of a country with its own local government, like Ontario in Canada. 2) the provinces (UK, plural) All of a country outside the capital city. 3) An area of knowledge or responsibility: «Cooking is Dad's province.» 4) (church) A group of dioceses under an archbishop.
its sense in the lessons: In geography Canada has ten provinces and three territories; Ireland has four old provinces (Leinster, Munster, Connacht, Ulster); South Africa and China have provinces. Phrases: «the province of Quebec», «in the provinces», «outside my province».
examples from the lessons: Canada is made up of provinces and territories. | Ontario is the most populous province of Canada. | Ireland has four provinces, including Munster. | My cousins live out in the provinces, far from London. | Gardening is Granny's province. | That question is outside my province, ask the science teacher. | The archbishop leads the church province.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Adjective «provincial» (of a province; also, rudely, narrow-minded or not like the big city). Canada: «provinces»; Australia: «states»; USA: «states». Northern Ireland is sometimes called «the Province».

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a careful, sensible way that avoids risk. 2) (money) Carefully with money, saving instead of wasting.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and ethics: a wise character acts prudently. In money talk adults «spend prudently» or «invest prudently». Prudence was one of the old virtues taught in church and ethics. Phrases: «act prudently», «spend prudently».
examples from the lessons: She prudently saved half of her birthday money. | The sailors prudently returned to harbour before the storm. | He prudently checked the ice before stepping on it. | Spend prudently, and you'll have money for the trip. | The captain prudently ordered everyone to wear life jackets. | We prudently packed raincoats.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb of «prudent»; noun «prudence». Formal-ish; everyday words: «carefully», «wisely». Do not confuse with «prudish» (easily shocked).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Short for «postscript»: an extra note added at the end of a letter or email after the signature. 2) (UK schools) Sometimes short for other things, such as «primary school», or a part number like «PS4» for a games console.
its sense in the lessons: Children write «PS» at the bottom of letters and cards: «PS Give the dog a hug from me.» A second extra note is «PPS». Phrases: «PS I love you», «PPS».
examples from the lessons: Love, Gran. PS Don't forget your scarf! | I forgot to say it, so I added a PS. | PS The party starts at three. | Her letter had a PS and a PPS. | Write a PS to remind them about the money. | He got a PS4 for his birthday.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually written in capitals: «PS» or «P.S.». It comes from Latin «post scriptum», «written after». No real need for a PS in an email you can edit, but people still use it for a friendly extra. Not a word on its own.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (church, Bible) A book containing the Psalms from the Bible, used for worship. 2) (church) A version of the Psalms set out to be sung or said in services.
its sense in the lessons: Church life: choirs sing from the psalter; old psalters were beautifully hand-painted by monks. In history lessons children may see a famous illuminated psalter in a museum. Phrases: «a medieval psalter», «the parish psalter».
examples from the lessons: The choir sang from the psalter. | The monks copied the psalter by hand. | We saw an old psalter with gold pictures at the museum. | Gran keeps her psalter next to her prayer book. | The Psalms in the psalter are songs and prayers. | Each page of the psalter had a decorated letter.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Silent «p»: pronounced «SAWL-ter». Same silent «p» as «psalm». Countable. A «psalm» is one song; the «psalter» is the book of them.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Arriving or doing something at the agreed time, not late. 2) Happening exactly on time: «a punctual train».
its sense in the lessons: School values punctuality: being punctual for registration and lessons. Reports may say «always punctual». Trains and buses are praised when punctual. Phrases: «be punctual», «punctual to the minute».
examples from the lessons: Please be punctual for the school trip. | Our teacher is always punctual. | The bus was punctual this morning for once. | Being punctual shows respect for others. | He's never punctual, he's always five minutes late. | My report said I was polite and punctual.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun «punctuality», adverb «punctually». Do not confuse with «punctuation». In maths time problems: punctual means arriving exactly at the stated time, not early or late.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A language spoken in the Punjab region of India and Pakistan, and by many people in the UK, Canada and elsewhere. 2) A person from the Punjab region. 3) adjective Connected with the Punjab, its people, food or culture.
its sense in the lessons: In multicultural classes some children speak Punjabi at home; it is one of the most spoken languages in the UK and Canada. Punjabi food (like samosas and naan) and bhangra music are popular. Many Sikhs are Punjabi. Phrases: «speaks Punjabi», «Punjabi food».
examples from the lessons: My friend Harpreet speaks Punjabi at home. | We learned to count to ten in Punjabi. | Punjabi is written in two different scripts. | The restaurant serves Punjabi food. | Her grandparents are Punjabi. | Bhangra is lively Punjabi dance music.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A proper noun: always a capital letter, «Punjabi» (the input is lower case only by format). Also spelled «Panjabi». Plural «Punjabis» for people. Written in Gurmukhi script in India and Shahmukhi script in Pakistan.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Only, simply, for no other reason: «I did it purely for fun.» 2) Completely, entirely: «a purely made-up story». 3) In a clean, pure way, without anything mixed in.
its sense in the lessons: Common in explanations: «purely by chance», «purely for fun», «purely an accident». It tells the reader there is just one reason. In science, «purely» can mean with nothing mixed in. Phrases: «purely by chance», «purely and simply», «purely for».
examples from the lessons: We met purely by chance at the park. | I joined the choir purely for fun. | It was purely an accident, I didn't mean to break it. | The story is purely made up. | The water was purely clean after boiling and filtering. | She trained purely and simply because she loved running.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb of «pure»; spelled «purely» (keep the «e»). Close to «only», «simply», «just». «Purely and simply» is a fixed phrase for strong emphasis.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (church) A member of the Religious Society of Friends, a Christian group that worships in silence and believes in peace and simplicity. 2) adjective Connected with the Quakers: «a Quaker meeting».
its sense in the lessons: In church life and history: Quakers meet in a «meeting house», sit in silence and speak when they feel moved. They are known for refusing war, working against slavery and helping prisoners and the poor. Quakers believe there is «that of God in everyone». Phrases: «a Quaker meeting», «Quaker school».
examples from the lessons: Quakers sit together in silence during their meeting. | The Quakers worked hard to end slavery. | She goes to a Quaker school. | Quakers believe in peace and do not fight in wars. | The Quaker meeting house has no altar or pictures. | The famous oats are named Quaker but are not made by Quakers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A proper noun: always «Quaker» with a capital (the input is lower case only by format). Official name: «the Religious Society of Friends», so Quakers are also called «Friends». The name came from people saying they «quaked» (shook) before God. Speak of beliefs respectfully: «Quakers believe…».

part of speech: verb form (ration, rations, rationed, rationing); adjective (rationed)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Past of «ration»: limited the amount of something each person could have, because there was not enough. 2) adjective Given out in fixed, limited amounts: «rationed food». 3) Used carefully in small amounts to make it last: «I rationed my sweets.»
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, food like sugar, butter and meat was rationed during wartime with ration books. In everyday life, families ration screen time or treats; in a drought, water may be rationed. In maths, rationing means sharing a fixed amount equally. Phrases: «strictly rationed», «rationed out».
examples from the lessons: During the war, sugar and butter were rationed. | We rationed our water on the long hike. | Mum rationed the chocolate so it lasted all week. | Screen time is rationed in our house. | The sailors rationed the food until help came. | Petrol was rationed when supplies ran low.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: ration, rationed, rationing. Noun «a ration» (a fixed share). In maths problems: if 12 biscuits are rationed equally over 4 days, that is 12 ÷ 4 = 3 a day. Pronounced RASH-und (UK, also RAY-shund in US).

meaning for a pupil: 1) The state of being prepared and ready for something. 2) Willingness, being happy to do something: «her readiness to help». 3) Quickness: «readiness of wit».
its sense in the lessons: In school: «readiness for school», «readiness for the test». In safety and emergencies: «in readiness for the storm». In stories, characters show readiness to help. Phrases: «in readiness for», «a readiness to», «state of readiness».
examples from the lessons: The boats were kept in readiness for a rescue. | Her readiness to help made her popular. | We packed the bags in readiness for the trip. | The fire crew is always in a state of readiness. | The teacher checked our readiness for the exam. | His readiness to say sorry ended the argument.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. From «ready» (y changes to i: readi-ness). «In readiness for» means prepared for.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal, old) A country ruled by a king or queen; a kingdom. 2) An area of knowledge, activity or interest: «the realm of science». 3) (stories) A world or land, often magical: «the realm of the fairies». 4) (church) Christians speak of «the heavenly realm».
its sense in the lessons: Fairy tales and fantasy books are full of realms. In formal talk «the realm of possibility» means what could happen. In history, a knight defended the realm. Phrases: «the realm of», «within the realms of possibility», «defender of the realm».
examples from the lessons: The king ruled his realm wisely. | The story takes place in a magical realm under the sea. | Flying cars are not in the realm of science fiction any more. | Time travel is outside the realm of possibility. | The knights swore to protect the realm. | In the realm of sport, she is a star.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The «l» is pronounced: «relm». Countable. Fairly formal or literary; everyday words: «kingdom», «area», «world».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A new start or return to life after something has ended or declined. 2) (church) Christians believe in being «born again», a new spiritual life through faith. 3) (religion) In Hinduism and Buddhism, being born again into a new life after death (reincarnation). 4) A revival of an idea, art or place.
its sense in the lessons: In science, spring is a time of rebirth in nature. In history, the «Renaissance» means rebirth of learning. In religion lessons, Christians speak of spiritual rebirth in baptism; Hindus and Buddhists believe in rebirth after death. Phrases: «a rebirth of interest», «spiritual rebirth».
examples from the lessons: Spring is a time of rebirth when flowers return. | The old town saw a rebirth after the new park opened. | Christians believe baptism is a sign of rebirth. | Hindus believe the soul goes through rebirth. | The Renaissance was a rebirth of art and learning. | The phoenix rises from the ashes in a story of rebirth.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Built from «re-» (again) + «birth». Mostly uncountable. Beliefs differ, so say «Christians believe», «Buddhists believe». The «phoenix» is a myth bird symbolising rebirth.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) A statement or argument that shows something said is wrong. 2) (law, debate) A reply that answers the other side's claims.
its sense in the lessons: In school debates, each team gives a rebuttal to the other team's points. In persuasive writing pupils plan a rebuttal (counter-argument). Phrases: «a strong rebuttal», «in rebuttal», «rebuttal speech».
examples from the lessons: In the debate, our team gave a clever rebuttal. | Her rebuttal showed the facts were wrong. | Plan a rebuttal for the other side's best point. | The lawyer's rebuttal convinced the jury. | He wrote a short rebuttal to the letter in the newspaper. | The rebuttal speech came last.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb «rebut» (rebutted, rebutting) — double «t». Formal; everyday words: «answer», «reply», «counter-argument».

part of speech: verb form (reclaim, reclaims, reclaimed, reclaiming); adjective (reclaimed)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Past of «reclaim»: got something back that was yours. 2) adjective Saved and used again instead of thrown away: «reclaimed wood». 3) adjective (land) Made usable again, for example by draining the sea or cleaning polluted land. 4) (formal) Rescued someone from a bad way of life.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography: the Netherlands has land reclaimed from the sea; old mines become reclaimed parks. In recycling lessons, «reclaimed timber» or «reclaimed bricks». In everyday life you reclaim your lost bag. Phrases: «reclaimed land», «reclaimed wood», «reclaim your luggage».
examples from the lessons: We reclaimed our bags at the airport. | The table is made from reclaimed wood. | Much of the Netherlands is reclaimed land. | The old rubbish dump was reclaimed as a nature park. | He reclaimed his title as champion. | Reclaimed bricks were used to build the new playhouse. | She reclaimed the umbrella from lost property.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Noun «reclamation» (spelling changes!). At airports «baggage reclaim» (UK) is where you collect bags; US says «baggage claim».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A memory of something from the past. 2) (uncountable) The ability to remember: «I have no recollection of it.» 3) (church) Calm, quiet prayer and thoughtfulness.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and history lessons: «recollections of the war» from older people. In everyday speech: «to the best of my recollection». Phrases: «have no recollection of», «a vague recollection», «to the best of my recollection».
examples from the lessons: I have a vague recollection of my first day at school. | Grandad shared his recollections of growing up on a farm. | She had no recollection of where she put her keys. | To the best of my recollection, the shop closes at six. | His recollection of the match was different from mine. | The nuns spent the day in quiet recollection.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb «recollect» (formal for «remember»). Countable for single memories, uncountable for the ability. Formal; «memory» is the everyday word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Making friends again after an argument or fight. 2) Making two ideas or facts agree when they seemed different. 3) (church) In the Catholic Church, the sacrament of Reconciliation (confession), where Catholics believe sins are forgiven. 4) (money) Checking that two sets of numbers match, like a bank statement and your own record.
its sense in the lessons: In ethics and PSHE lessons, reconciliation follows conflict: saying sorry and forgiving. In history, «Truth and Reconciliation» in South Africa; reconciliation with Aboriginal people in Australia and First Nations in Canada. In church, children prepare for first Reconciliation. Phrases: «bring about reconciliation», «the sacrament of reconciliation», «National Reconciliation Week» (Australia).
examples from the lessons: After the fight, the two friends had a happy reconciliation. | Mum helped bring about a reconciliation between my brother and me. | Catholics go to Reconciliation to confess their sins. | Australia holds National Reconciliation Week. | Christians believe Jesus brought reconciliation between God and people. | The bank reconciliation showed a mistake of five pounds. | The teacher talked about forgiveness and reconciliation.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb «reconcile». Spelling: re-con-cil-i-a-tion. Reconciliation needs both sides; one person can forgive, but reconciliation means coming back together. Say «Catholics believe» for the sacrament.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To think again about a decision or opinion, possibly to change it. 2) (formal) To look again at a case or plan.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and everyday life: «Please reconsider!» In maths, pupils reconsider an answer that looks wrong. In ethics, people reconsider when they learn new facts. Phrases: «reconsider a decision», «ask someone to reconsider».
examples from the lessons: Please reconsider and come to the party. | After hearing the facts, the judge reconsidered the case. | I reconsidered my answer and found a mistake. | The council will reconsider closing the library. | Dad reconsidered and let us keep the puppy. | She asked the coach to reconsider his choice.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Noun «reconsideration». «Re-» means again. Not the same as «regret».

part of speech: verb (recount, recounts, recounted, recounting); noun (a recount, recounts)
meaning for a pupil: 1) verb To tell a story or describe events in order: «He recounted his adventure.» 2) verb (re-count) To count again. 3) noun A second count of votes in an election when the result is very close. 4) noun (UK schools) A piece of writing that retells events in time order, like a diary or trip report.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons a «recount» is a text type: write a recount of the school trip using time words (first, next, after that). In elections, a recount checks a close result. In maths, recount to check you counted right. Phrases: «write a recount», «demand a recount».
examples from the lessons: Write a recount of your weekend. | Grandma recounted stories of her childhood in Ireland. | I recounted the coins and found one more. | The vote was so close that they had a recount. | The sailor recounted his adventure on the island. | Use time words in your recount: first, then, finally.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Two meanings with different stress: re-COUNT (tell) and RE-count (count again or the noun). Sometimes written «re-count» for counting again. A recount text uses the past tense and time order.

part of speech: verb (recruit, recruits, recruited, recruiting); noun (a recruit, recruits)
meaning for a pupil: 1) verb To find and get new people to join a group, team, army or company. 2) noun A new member, especially of the army or police. 3) verb (informal) To get someone to help you: «I recruited my sister to help clean.»
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life clubs recruit new members; companies recruit workers. In history, armies recruited soldiers with posters. Phrases: «new recruits», «recruit volunteers», «recruitment».
examples from the lessons: The football club is recruiting new players. | The army recruits trained hard at camp. | I recruited my friends to help with the bake sale. | The school wants to recruit more volunteers. | She was recruited as a lifeguard for the summer. | The new recruit was nervous on his first day.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: re-cr-UI-t (the «ui» says «oo»). Noun for the process: «recruitment». Countable noun.

part of speech: verb form (redden, reddens, reddened, reddening); adjective (reddened)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Past of «redden»: became red or made something red. 2) Went red in the face from shame, anger or embarrassment (blushed). 3) adjective Red, often sore: «reddened eyes».
its sense in the lessons: In stories, a character's face «reddened» with embarrassment or anger; skin reddens in the sun (a sign of sunburn, so cover up). The sky reddens at sunset. Phrases: «her cheeks reddened», «reddened with anger».
examples from the lessons: His face reddened when he forgot his lines. | The sky reddened as the sun went down. | Her eyes were reddened from crying. | My arms reddened after a day at the beach without sun cream. | The leaves reddened in autumn. | She reddened with anger at the unfair comment.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb «redden» (double «d»). Safety: reddened skin after sun is an early sign of sunburn. Similar: «blushed», «flushed».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (money) Able to be exchanged for money, goods or a prize: «This voucher is redeemable in any store.» 2) Able to be saved or made good again: «The situation is still redeemable.» 3) (church) Christians believe every person is redeemable, able to be saved by God's grace.
its sense in the lessons: Everyday shopping: vouchers, tokens and coupons are «redeemable» at certain shops and until a set time. In ethics and stories, a villain may turn out to be redeemable. Phrases: «redeemable against», «not redeemable for cash».
examples from the lessons: This gift card is redeemable in any of our shops. | The tokens are not redeemable for cash. | Points are redeemable for prizes. | The coach believed the team was still redeemable after a bad start. | In the story, even the grumpy giant was redeemable. | Christians believe no one is beyond being redeemed.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «redeem» + «-able». Opposite: «irredeemable» (hopeless). In maths money problems, a voucher redeemable for £5 takes £5 off the total.

part of speech: noun (a relapse, relapses); verb (relapse, relapses, relapsed, relapsing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Becoming ill again after seeming to get better. 2) Going back to a bad habit or behaviour after stopping it. 3) verb To fall back into illness or a bad state.
its sense in the lessons: In adult life and health: a patient may «have a relapse». In ethics and habits: someone trying to stop smoking may relapse. In school stories, a child may relapse into old naughty ways. Phrases: «suffer a relapse», «relapse into».
examples from the lessons: Grandpa was getting better but then had a relapse. | After a good week, he relapsed into his old habit of chewing pencils. | The doctor warned her to rest to avoid a relapse. | She relapsed into silence. | A relapse can happen, so keep trying. | He stayed away from sweets for a month before a small relapse.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Same spelling for noun and verb; stress: re-LAPSE (verb), RE-lapse or re-LAPSE (noun). A relapse does not mean failure forever; many people try again and succeed.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Quite, fairly, when compared with others: «a relatively small school». 2) relatively speaking Compared with other things: «Relatively speaking, it's cheap.»
its sense in the lessons: Common in science and maths explanations: «relatively large», «relatively quickly». It tells the reader the size is judged by comparison. Phrases: «relatively easy», «relatively few», «relatively speaking».
examples from the lessons: The test was relatively easy. | Our town is relatively quiet. | Relatively few people came because of the rain. | An ant is relatively strong for its size. | The new phone is relatively cheap. | Relatively speaking, Mars is close to Earth.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb of «relative». Different from «relative» as a family member. In maths, «relatively» means compared with something; check what it is compared with.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Needing or depending on someone or something. 2) Trust that someone or something will help: «reliance on friends».
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography: «reliance on fossil fuels», «reliance on imports». In everyday life: too much reliance on calculators or screens. Phrases: «reliance on», «over-reliance», «self-reliance».
examples from the lessons: Our reliance on cars causes pollution. | Too much reliance on a calculator can make mental maths weaker. | The town's reliance on fishing made it poor when the fish ran out. | Self-reliance means being able to look after yourself. | The team's reliance on one star player was risky. | Babies have total reliance on their parents.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Preposition: «reliance on/upon». Verb «rely», adjective «reliant», «reliable» (can be trusted). «Self-reliance» is a good quality.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To pay someone for work or a service.
its sense in the lessons: Exam and business voice: «Staff will be remunerated for overtime.» Adults use it in contracts and job adverts; children say «pay». Phrases: «well remunerated», «remunerate for».
examples from the lessons: The workers were well remunerated for their extra hours. | Volunteers are not remunerated; they help for free. | The company will remunerate you for travel costs. | Helpers at the fair were remunerated with free ice cream. | How will the babysitter be remunerated?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal word for «pay». Noun «remuneration» (pay, salary). Spelling trap: «remunerate», not «renumerate» (letters often swapped). In maths: if remunerated at £10 an hour for 3 hours, pay = £30.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Making something new, fresh or strong again. 2) Making an agreement, ticket or membership last longer: «library book renewal». 3) (church) Spiritual renewal: Christians believe God renews people's hearts. 4) Rebuilding and improving old parts of a town (urban renewal).
its sense in the lessons: Everyday: renewal of library books, passports, memberships. In science, spring renewal in nature. In church, «renewal of baptismal vows». Phrases: «up for renewal», «urban renewal», «a sense of renewal».
examples from the lessons: My library books are due for renewal. | Mum sent off the passport renewal form. | Spring brings renewal to the garden. | The town centre is going through renewal. | At Easter, Christians speak of new life and renewal. | Our club membership is up for renewal next month.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb «renew». Countable when talking about one act (a renewal); uncountable for the general idea.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To say officially or publicly that you give up a right, title or claim. 2) To stop believing in or supporting something: «renounce violence». 3) (church) To reject evil and sin; in baptism Christians are asked «Do you renounce evil?»
its sense in the lessons: In history, kings renounced the throne; in news, groups renounce violence. In church, at a baptism, parents and godparents renounce evil for the child. In stories, a hero renounces riches to help others. Phrases: «renounce the throne», «renounce violence», «renounce your citizenship».
examples from the lessons: The king renounced the throne to marry the woman he loved. | The group promised to renounce violence. | At the baptism, the godparents renounced evil. | She renounced her share of the money and gave it to charity. | Monks renounce worldly possessions. | He renounced his old bad habits.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Noun «renunciation» (spelling change). Formal; everyday words: «give up», «reject». Different from «announce» and «pronounce».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Fame and respect for doing something well.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and history: «a knight of great renown», «a scientist of world renown». The adjective «renowned» is more common: «renowned for its cheese». Phrases: «of renown», «win renown», «world renown».
examples from the lessons: The knight won great renown in battle. | She is a scientist of world renown. | The town is of renown for its castle. | His paintings brought him renown. | The baker's renown spread across the valley. | Heroes of renown were remembered in songs.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Adjective «renowned (for)». Pronounced ri-NOWN (rhymes with «town»). Formal; everyday word: «fame».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (money, law) To take back goods or a house because the buyer has not kept up the payments they promised.
its sense in the lessons: Adult life seen by a child: if a family cannot pay the mortgage, the bank may repossess the house; a car bought on credit can be repossessed. It is a sad and serious thing for families. Phrases: «the house was repossessed», «repossession order».
examples from the lessons: The bank repossessed the house when the payments stopped. | If you don't pay for the car, the company can repossess it. | Our neighbours were worried their home would be repossessed. | The shop repossessed the sofa after the missed payments. | Losing a job can mean a home is repossessed. | They got help from a charity so their house was not repossessed.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: double «s» twice — re-po-SS-e-SS. Noun «repossession». It happens only after a long time of missed payments, usually with warnings and court steps.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A picture, model or sign that shows or stands for something. 2) Having someone to speak or act for you: «legal representation». 3) Being included and shown fairly: «representation of girls in sport». 4) (maths) A way of showing a number or data: «a bar chart representation». 5) (formal) representations A formal statement or complaint.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, pupils draw a representation of a fraction, bar model or number line. In history and citizenship, «no taxation without representation»; MPs give representation to their area. In art, a painting is a representation of a scene. Phrases: «a visual representation», «legal representation», «fair representation».
examples from the lessons: Draw a representation of 3/4 using a shape. | The map is a representation of our town. | Every person has the right to legal representation. | The class wanted better representation of girls in the football team. | The statue is a representation of a famous queen. | A bar chart is a clear representation of the data.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb «represent», noun for a person «representative». Countable for pictures or models, uncountable for the idea of speaking for people. In maths, a «representation» shows the same value in a different form: 0.5, ½ and 50% are representations of one number.

part of speech: verb (reproach, reproaches, reproached, reproaching); noun (reproach, reproaches)
meaning for a pupil: 1) verb To tell someone, gently or sadly, that you are disappointed in what they did. 2) noun Words or looks showing disappointment or blame. 3) beyond reproach So good that no one can criticise it.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, a parent «looks at someone with reproach». In ethics: «reproach yourself» means feel guilty. In formal talk, «behaviour beyond reproach». Phrases: «a look of reproach», «beyond reproach», «reproach yourself».
examples from the lessons: Mum gave me a look of reproach when I came home muddy. | Don't reproach yourself, it wasn't your fault. | The teacher reproached him for being unkind. | Her honesty is beyond reproach. | His silence was full of reproach. | The dog looked at me with reproach when I ate its biscuit.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: re-pro-ACH. Adjective «reproachful». Softer than «scold». Countable and uncountable as a noun.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Known to be honest, reliable and good; having a good reputation.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday safety: use reputable websites for homework; buy pets from reputable breeders; adults choose reputable builders. Phrases: «a reputable company», «a reputable source».
examples from the lessons: Only use reputable websites for your research. | We bought our puppy from a reputable breeder. | Dad asked a reputable builder to fix the roof. | The news came from a reputable source. | Choose a reputable charity to give to. | A reputable shop gives you a receipt.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stress on the first syllable: REP-yoo-ta-bul. Opposite: «disreputable». Related: «reputation». Online safety: a reputable source is trusted, checked and well known.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A feeling of anger and hurt because you think you have been treated unfairly, often lasting a long time.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and ethics/PSHE lessons: resentment builds when someone feels left out or treated unfairly; forgiveness can let it go. Phrases: «feel resentment», «resentment towards», «bitter resentment».
examples from the lessons: He felt resentment when his brother got a bigger present. | Resentment grew between the two teams after the unfair match. | Talking about it helped her let go of resentment. | Forgiveness can heal resentment. | There was no resentment in her voice. | The children's resentment of the new rule faded.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb «resent», adjective «resentful». Uncountable. Resentment is a natural feeling; talking with someone you trust helps.

part of speech: noun (a resort, resorts); verb (resort, resorts, resorted, resorting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) noun A place where people go on holiday: «a seaside resort», «a ski resort». 2) a last resort The thing you do only when nothing else works. 3) verb resort to To do something, often bad or extreme, because other ways failed: «resort to cheating».
its sense in the lessons: Holiday talk: beach resorts, ski resorts, holiday resorts in Australia or Ireland. In ethics and stories: «resort to violence» is wrong. Phrases: «as a last resort», «resort to», «seaside resort», «holiday resort».
examples from the lessons: We stayed at a seaside resort in the summer. | Calling the fire brigade was a last resort. | Never resort to hitting; use words instead. | The ski resort was packed with families. | She resorted to asking her little brother for help. | As a last resort, we ate cold beans.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced ri-ZORT. Do not confuse with «re-sort» (sort again). «Last resort» is not a holiday place: it means the final choice.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who answers a survey, questionnaire or question. 2) (law) The person who must answer a case in court, especially in a divorce or appeal.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and science, pupils carry out surveys and count respondents: «20 respondents chose pizza». In law, in a divorce or custody case, one parent may be the respondent. Phrases: «survey respondents», «the majority of respondents».
examples from the lessons: We asked 30 respondents what their favourite fruit was. | Most respondents said they walk to school. | Half of the respondents chose the beach. | Each respondent filled in a short form. | In the court case, the respondent had a lawyer. | The survey had 100 respondents.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Spelling ends in «-ent». In maths: percentage of respondents = number choosing an answer ÷ total respondents × 100.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To stop working, usually because you are older. 2) (sport) To stop playing in a game or race, often because of injury. 3) (formal) To go to bed or to a quiet room: «retire for the night». 4) (formal) To go away from a place, like an army moving back.
its sense in the lessons: Adult life seen by a child: Grandma retired from nursing; a retirement party. In sport, a player retires injured or retires from the sport. In old stories, ladies «retire to the drawing room». Phrases: «retire from», «retire early», «retire hurt», «retired teacher».
examples from the lessons: Grandad retired after working at the post office for many years. | The runner had to retire from the race with a sore leg. | The guests retired for the night. | She plans to retire to the seaside. | My retired neighbour grows tomatoes. | The army retired behind the hill.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Noun «retirement», person «retiree». Adjective «retired». «Retiring» can also mean shy. Retired people often receive a pension (money paid regularly).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Able to be given or sent back, often for money back: «returnable bottles». 2) (formal) Must be given back by a certain time: «The form is returnable by Friday.»
its sense in the lessons: In recycling, returnable bottles and cans earn a deposit (in Canada, Australia, Ireland). In shops, goods may be returnable with a receipt. School letters: «Permission slips returnable by Friday.» Phrases: «a returnable deposit», «non-returnable».
examples from the lessons: These bottles are returnable for ten cents each. | The deposit is returnable if you bring the key back. | Sale items are not returnable. | The form is returnable to the office by Friday. | Keep your receipt so the shoes are returnable. | We took the returnable cans back to the shop.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «return» + «-able». Opposite: «non-returnable». In maths money problems: a returnable deposit of £10 is given back, so it does not count in the final cost.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A meeting of people who have not seen each other for a long time. 2) Coming together again after being apart: «a happy reunion». 3) (formal) Joining two things back together, like countries or churches.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: family reunions, school reunions; on the news a lost dog's reunion with its owner. In stories, a long-awaited reunion is a happy ending. Phrases: «family reunion», «class reunion», «a tearful reunion».
examples from the lessons: We had a big family reunion at Grandma's farm. | The lost puppy's reunion with its owner made everyone cry. | My parents went to their school reunion. | The soldiers had a joyful reunion with their families. | After the holidays, the reunion with my friends was fun. | The story ends with a tearful reunion.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced ree-YOON-yun. Countable. Not about being «a union again» in everyday talk; it means meeting again.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Able to be used again, many times, instead of being thrown away.
its sense in the lessons: In science and eco-lessons: reusable water bottles, bags, lunchboxes and nappies reduce waste («reduce, reuse, recycle»). Phrases: «reusable bag», «reusable bottle», «single-use vs reusable».
examples from the lessons: Bring a reusable water bottle to school. | We use reusable bags at the supermarket. | Reusable lunchboxes cut down on plastic. | This rocket is reusable. | The class made reusable wax wraps. | Single-use straws are bad; reusable ones are better.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: «reusable» (no «e» after «s»). Also seen as «re-usable». Opposite: «disposable», «single-use». «Reuse» is different from «recycle»: reusing keeps the thing as it is.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Coming back to life, health, strength or popularity. 2) A new performance of an old play or show. 3) (church) A time when many people turn to faith with new energy; also a lively religious meeting. 4) Bringing someone back to consciousness.
its sense in the lessons: In history and church: the Welsh Revival, revival meetings. In culture: «a revival of interest in vinyl records». In theatre: a revival of an old musical. Phrases: «a revival of», «economic revival», «revival meeting».
examples from the lessons: There has been a revival of interest in board games. | The town enjoyed a revival after the new shops opened. | The theatre put on a revival of an old musical. | The church held a revival meeting with lots of singing. | The flowers made a revival after the rain. | Dance crazes from long ago are having a revival.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb «revive». Countable. In church history, a «revival» is a big growth of faith in a place.

part of speech: verb form (rip, rips, ripped, ripping); adjective (ripping — UK, old-fashioned)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Present participle of «rip»: tearing quickly and roughly. 2) adjective (UK, old-fashioned, informal) Wonderful, excellent: «a ripping adventure». 3) (informal) Moving very fast or strongly: «a ripping current». 4) ripping off (slang) Cheating someone by charging too much; also copying.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: ripping paper, ripping open presents. In old British children's books «a ripping time» means a great time. At the beach, a «rip» current is dangerous. Phrases: «ripping open», «ripping yarn», «ripping someone off».
examples from the lessons: He was ripping open his birthday presents. | The dog is ripping up the newspaper. | "What a ripping adventure!" said Jack in the old story. | Stop ripping pages out of your book! | That shop is ripping people off with high prices. | The wind was ripping through the trees.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double «p» before «-ing»: rip, ripped, ripping. The «wonderful» sense is old-fashioned British, mostly in old books. «Rip-off» (slang) means something overpriced.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The state of a vehicle being safe and fit to be driven on the road.
its sense in the lessons: Adult life and safety: cars need roadworthiness checks — the MOT in the UK, the NCT in Ireland, the WOF in New Zealand, a roadworthy certificate in Australia. Phrases: «roadworthiness test», «certificate of roadworthiness».
examples from the lessons: The car failed its roadworthiness test because of worn tyres. | Mum took the car in for a roadworthiness check. | In Australia, you need a certificate of roadworthiness to sell a car. | Good brakes are part of roadworthiness. | The mechanic checked the van's roadworthiness. | Bald tyres affect a car's roadworthiness.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Adjective «roadworthy». One long compound: road + worthy + ness. Formal, used in official notices.

part of speech: verb (roam, roams, roamed, roaming); noun (a roam — rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To walk or travel around with no fixed plan, often over a wide area. 2) (phones) To use a mobile phone abroad through another network («roaming»). 3) (of eyes or thoughts) To move from place to place.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography: buffalo roam the plains; wild horses roam in Australia. In stories, children roam the woods. With phones, «roaming charges» can cost a lot abroad. Phrases: «free to roam», «roam the streets», «roaming charges».
examples from the lessons: Wild ponies roam across the moor. | We roamed the beach looking for shells. | The dog was free to roam the farm. | Turn off data roaming when you go abroad. | Her eyes roamed around the busy room. | Dinosaurs once roamed the Earth.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Do not confuse with «Rome» (city) — same sound. Safety: children should not roam far without telling an adult.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A round badge made of ribbon, given as a prize, for example at a horse or pet show. 2) A rose-shaped decoration in building or on clothes. 3) (science) A ring of leaves growing from one point near the ground, like a dandelion's.
its sense in the lessons: At shows and gymkhanas, winners get rosettes (red, blue, yellow by place). Political supporters wear rosettes. In science, plants like dandelions grow leaves in a rosette. Phrases: «a red rosette», «win a rosette».
examples from the lessons: My pony won a blue rosette at the show. | Our dog got a rosette for best tail. | The candidates wore party rosettes. | A dandelion's leaves grow in a rosette. | She pinned the rosette to her jacket. | The ceiling has a plaster rosette around the light.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced roh-ZET. Countable. Rosette colours differ by country: in the UK red is first; in the US and Canada blue is often first.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (church) Connected with a sacrament, a holy rite such as baptism or communion. 2) noun (Catholic Church) A blessed object or action, like holy water or a rosary, that Catholics believe helps prayer. 3) Feeling holy or very special.
its sense in the lessons: Church life: «sacramental wine» used in communion; «sacramental life» of a church. Catholics keep sacramentals at home. Phrases: «sacramental bread», «sacramental wine», «the sacramental life».
examples from the lessons: The priest poured the sacramental wine. | Baptism is a sacramental act in many churches. | Holy water is one of the sacramentals in the Catholic Church. | Catholics believe sacramentals help them pray. | The sacramental bread is shared at communion. | The service had a quiet, sacramental feel.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «sacrament». Different churches count different sacraments: Catholics and Orthodox seven, many Protestant churches two (baptism and communion). Speak respectfully: «Christians believe».

part of speech: verb (safeguard, safeguards, safeguarded, safeguarding); noun (a safeguard, safeguards)
meaning for a pupil: 1) verb To protect something or someone from harm or danger. 2) noun Something that protects: «a safeguard against fire». 3) safeguarding (school) Keeping children safe from harm and abuse.
its sense in the lessons: In schools, «safeguarding» is a key rule: every adult must keep children safe and report worries. In everyday life: passwords safeguard your account; laws safeguard rights. Phrases: «safeguard against», «a safeguard for», «safeguarding lead».
examples from the lessons: Passwords safeguard your personal information. | The fence is a safeguard against falling into the river. | Schools have rules to safeguard children. | Laws safeguard our right to free speech. | Seatbelts are an important safeguard. | The museum safeguards old treasures.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. One word. «Safeguarding» in UK schools means child protection: tell a trusted adult if you feel unsafe.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The good feeling you get when you have done something well or got what you wanted. 2) Being pleased with a service, product or result: «customer satisfaction». 3) (formal) Proof or an answer that removes doubt: «to my satisfaction». 4) (formal) Making up for a wrong, like an apology or payment.
its sense in the lessons: In school: «the satisfaction of finishing a puzzle». Shops run «satisfaction surveys»; «satisfaction guaranteed» on labels. In maths surveys, data about satisfaction is often shown as percentages. Phrases: «job satisfaction», «to your satisfaction», «a sense of satisfaction».
examples from the lessons: I felt great satisfaction when I finished the jigsaw. | Customer satisfaction is important to our shop. | The work was done to the teacher's satisfaction. | Satisfaction guaranteed or your money back! | She smiled with satisfaction at her painting. | He got no satisfaction from winning unfairly.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly uncountable. Verb «satisfy», adjective «satisfied», «satisfying». Opposite: «dissatisfaction».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A player who scores a goal or points. 2) A person who keeps the score in a game, especially in cricket. 3) top scorer The player or pupil with the most points or goals.
its sense in the lessons: In sport at school and clubs: «the top scorer in netball», «goal scorer». In cricket, the scorer records every run. In quizzes and tests, «the highest scorer». Phrases: «top scorer», «leading goal scorer», «the official scorer».
examples from the lessons: She was the top scorer in the hockey match. | Our scorer kept track of every run. | The team's leading goal scorer got a trophy. | Who was the highest scorer in the spelling test? | The scorer wrote the points on the board. | He is a natural scorer.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. From «score» + «-er». In maths, a scorer with 3 goals in each of 4 games scored 3 × 4 = 12 goals.

part of speech: verb form (scowl, scowls, scowled, scowling); adjective (scowling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Present participle of «scowl»: making an angry, cross face with lowered eyebrows. 2) adjective Looking angry: «a scowling giant».
its sense in the lessons: In stories, a grumpy character is «scowling at» someone; writers use it to show feelings without telling. Phrases: «scowling at», «a scowling face».
examples from the lessons: The giant was scowling at the children. | Why are you scowling? | She sat scowling in the corner after losing the game. | A scowling face looked out of the window. | He stopped scowling when he saw the cake. | The teacher walked in scowling.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb «scowl». Similar: «frown» (often thinking or worried), but «scowl» is angrier. Show-not-tell tip: «scowling» tells the reader someone is cross.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (history) A person whose job was to write or copy documents by hand, before printing. 2) (Bible) In the New Testament, the scribes were experts in Jewish law. 3) (school) An adult who writes down a pupil's answers in a test. 4) (informal, humorous) A writer or journalist.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, Egyptian scribes wrote hieroglyphs; monks were scribes copying Bibles. In the Bible, Jesus spoke with the scribes and Pharisees. In school, a scribe helps a child who cannot write easily. Phrases: «act as a scribe», «the scribes and Pharisees».
examples from the lessons: Ancient Egyptian scribes wrote on papyrus. | The monk worked as a scribe copying the Bible. | In the Bible, Jesus argued with the scribes. | A scribe helped Sam write his test answers. | You can be the scribe for your group. | The king's scribe wrote down every word.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Related: «scribble», «script». In group work the «scribe» is the person who writes notes.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (church, Bible) Based on or connected with holy writings, especially the Bible.
its sense in the lessons: In church and religion lessons: «a scriptural passage», «scriptural teaching». Other faiths have scriptures too (the Qur'an, the Torah, the Vedas). Phrases: «scriptural reading», «scriptural basis».
examples from the lessons: The vicar read a scriptural passage. | Christians look for scriptural guidance in the Bible. | The song uses scriptural words. | Each faith has its own scriptural texts. | The lesson had a scriptural theme. | The artist painted scriptural scenes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «scripture». Formal. Sometimes with a capital «Scriptural». Speak respectfully: people of different faiths have different scriptures.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who chooses players for a team. 2) A device, knob or switch for choosing a setting. 3) (computing) A tool or rule that picks out items.
its sense in the lessons: In sport, selectors choose the national cricket or rugby team. In everyday life, a «gear selector» or «channel selector». In coding at school, a selector picks out parts of a web page. Phrases: «team selectors», «gear selector».
examples from the lessons: The selectors picked her for the county team. | Turn the selector to «wash». | The cricket selectors announced the squad. | Dad moved the gear selector to reverse. | The selector chose the fastest runners. | Use the colour selector to pick blue.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. From «select». Spelling ends «-or», not «-er».

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a way that thinks about others more than yourself; generously and without wanting a reward.
its sense in the lessons: In ethics and stories: heroes act selflessly; nurses work selflessly. In church, Christians believe Jesus loved selflessly. Phrases: «work selflessly», «give selflessly».
examples from the lessons: The firefighters worked selflessly to save the family. | She selflessly gave her lunch to a hungry friend. | Volunteers help selflessly at the food bank. | He selflessly let the younger children go first. | Christians believe Jesus gave his life selflessly. | Mum selflessly stayed up all night with the sick puppy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb of «selfless». Opposite: «selfishly». Noun «selflessness».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Weak in mind because of old age, especially forgetful or confused. 2) (medicine, old-fashioned) Connected with old age: «senile dementia».
its sense in the lessons: Adult life seen by a child: an elderly relative may become confused. Today doctors say «dementia» rather than «senile», and calling someone senile is unkind. Phrases: «going senile».
examples from the lessons: Great-gran gets confused, but the doctor says it is dementia, not just being senile. | It is rude to call old people senile. | The old dog seemed a bit senile, barking at nothing. | Some people become forgetful as they age, but many stay sharp. | In the story, the old king was senile and easily fooled.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced SEE-nile. Often hurtful; say «has dementia» or «forgetful». Myth: not all old people become senile; many stay clear-minded. Noun «senility».

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a wise, sensible and practical way. 2) In a suitable way for the situation: «dressed sensibly for the rain».
its sense in the lessons: School rules: «walk sensibly in the corridor», «behave sensibly on the trip». Safety: «use scissors sensibly». Phrases: «behave sensibly», «dress sensibly», «sensibly priced».
examples from the lessons: Please walk sensibly in the corridor. | She dressed sensibly for the snowy walk. | Use the equipment sensibly in the science lab. | They behaved very sensibly on the trip. | The shoes are sensibly priced. | He sensibly asked an adult for help.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb of «sensible». False friend: in French and Spanish a similar word means «sensitive», but English «sensibly» means wisely.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Seven times as big or as many. 2) Having seven parts. 3) (Bible) Seven times over, a lot: «avenged sevenfold».
its sense in the lessons: In maths it means multiply by seven: «a sevenfold increase». In the Bible, the number seven is special (complete), and the phrase appears in Genesis. Phrases: «a sevenfold increase», «grew sevenfold».
examples from the lessons: The number of visitors grew sevenfold. | A sevenfold increase from 2 is 14. | The sevenfold path had seven steps. | In the Bible, Cain was promised protection sevenfold. | Prices rose sevenfold in the story. | Their crop grew sevenfold after the rain.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word. Maths: «sevenfold increase» usually means it becomes 7 times as much (× 7). Same pattern: twofold, threefold, tenfold.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To cut right through something, separating it. 2) To end a relationship or connection completely: «sever ties».
its sense in the lessons: In stories and news: a rope severed, a severed cable, a country severing links with another. Safety: a severed wire is dangerous. Phrases: «sever ties», «sever links», «severed finger».
examples from the lessons: The rope was severed by a sharp rock. | The storm severed the power line. | The two countries severed ties. | Don't touch a severed cable. | He severed his friendship with the bully. | The axe severed the branch.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Pronounced SEV-er. Do not confuse with «severe» (very bad, harsh), though «severance» (payment when your job ends) comes from «sever».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (religion) A Jewish festival celebrating the giving of the Torah to Moses on Mount Sinai, and the wheat harvest; also called the Feast of Weeks.
its sense in the lessons: In religion lessons, Shavuot comes seven weeks after Passover. Jewish families decorate with flowers and greenery, read the Book of Ruth and eat dairy foods like cheesecake. Christians' Pentecost is linked in timing. Phrases: «celebrate Shavuot», «the festival of Shavuot».
examples from the lessons: Jewish families celebrate Shavuot with dairy food. | At Shavuot, the synagogue was decorated with flowers. | Shavuot remembers the giving of the Torah. | The Book of Ruth is read at Shavuot. | Shavuot comes seven weeks after Passover. | We learned about Shavuot in RE.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Proper noun with a capital (the input is lower case only by format). Pronounced sha-voo-OT or sha-VOO-ot. Also spelled «Shavuos». Its date moves each year because it follows the Jewish calendar.

part of speech: verb form (shed, sheds, shed, shedding); noun (shedding — uncountable)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Present participle of «shed»: losing hair, skin or leaves naturally. 2) Letting something fall or flow: «shedding tears». 3) Getting rid of something unwanted: «shedding weight», «shedding jobs». 4) (UK) Dropping its load on a road: «a lorry shedding its load».
its sense in the lessons: Science: snakes shed their skin; trees shed leaves in autumn; dogs shed hair. Everyday: «shedding light on» means explaining. Phrases: «shed light on», «shed tears», «shedding hair».
examples from the lessons: Our dog is shedding hair all over the sofa. | The trees are shedding their leaves. | A snake was shedding its old skin. | She was shedding tears of joy. | This book sheds light on the Tudors. | The company is shedding jobs.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Shed» is irregular: shed, shed (past same), shedding (double «d»). Do not confuse with «a shed» (a small hut in the garden).

meaning for a pupil: 1) interjection A word said to make animals or people go away. 2) verb To make someone or something leave by waving your arms and saying «shoo». 3) (informal) shoo-in Someone sure to win.
its sense in the lessons: Everyday: shooing a cat from the kitchen, shooing birds off the picnic. In stories, a cross gran shoos children outside. Phrases: «shoo away», «shoo off», «a shoo-in».
examples from the lessons: Shoo! shouted Gran at the pigeons. | Mum shooed the dog off the sofa. | We shooed the wasps away from our lunch. | The teacher shooed us outside into the sunshine. | She's a shoo-in for the captain's job. | Shoo, cat, get out of the kitchen!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Sounds like «shoe» — homophone trap: «shoe» is what you wear. Past «shooed». Informal.

part of speech: verb form (signal, signals, signalled, signalling — UK; signaled, signaling — US); noun (signalling — uncountable)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Present participle of «signal»: giving a sign, sound or light to send a message. 2) Showing that something is happening: «Dark clouds are signalling rain.» 3) noun The system of signals on a railway or in the body: «railway signalling», «cell signalling».
its sense in the lessons: Safety: cyclists signal by putting out an arm; drivers signal before turning. In history: semaphore and Morse code signalling. In science, nerves send signals. Phrases: «signalling left», «hand signals», «signalling system».
examples from the lessons: The cyclist was signalling left. | The lifeguard is signalling for us to come in. | Dark clouds were signalling a storm. | Railway signalling stops trains from crashing. | Sailors used flags for signalling. | Always check the driver is signalling before you cross.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: UK, Australia, NZ, Ireland, Canada often «signalling» (double l); US «signaling». Both correct in their places.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Honest and true; meaning what you say or feel. 2) Real, not pretend: «a sincere apology». 3) Yours sincerely (UK) A polite ending of a formal letter.
its sense in the lessons: In ethics and PSHE: a sincere apology means you are really sorry. In letter writing lessons: «Yours sincerely» when you know the name. Phrases: «sincere thanks», «a sincere apology», «Yours sincerely».
examples from the lessons: Please accept my sincere apology. | Her thanks were warm and sincere. | He is a sincere friend who never lies. | We send our sincere thanks to the volunteers. | Yours sincerely, Amy Brown. | The card had a sincere message.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb «sincerely», noun «sincerity». Letter rule (UK): «Dear Mrs Smith … Yours sincerely»; «Dear Sir or Madam … Yours faithfully». US: «Sincerely».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (church) Wrong according to God's law or religious teaching; full of sin. 2) (informal, humorous) Very naughty or too much: «a sinfully rich chocolate cake».
