its sense in the lessons: In church and Bible lessons: Christians believe all people are sinful and need forgiveness; confession and repentance follow. In everyday jokes: «sinful desserts». Phrases: «sinful behaviour», «sinfully delicious».
examples from the lessons: Christians believe that people are sinful and need God's forgiveness. | The priest spoke about sinful thoughts. | That chocolate cake is sinfully rich! | The story showed how sinful greed can be. | She felt sinful eating three doughnuts. | In the Bible, people turned away from sinful ways.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «sin» + «-ful». Adverb «sinfully». The humorous sense is light-hearted and not about religion.

part of speech: noun (slag — uncountable; a slag, slags — rude); verb (slag off — UK slang)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) Rocky waste left over when metal is taken from ore. 2) (UK, rude, offensive) An insulting word for a woman; never use it. 3) slag off (UK, slang) To criticise someone rudely behind their back.
its sense in the lessons: In history and geography: slag heaps from old coal mines in Wales and northern England. In real speech children may hear «slag someone off», meaning saying nasty things. The insult is very rude and hurtful. Phrases: «slag heap», «slag off».
examples from the lessons: The old mine left a huge slag heap. | Slag from the furnace was dumped by the river. | Stop slagging off your sister; it's unkind. | He slagged off the referee after the match. | The grey slag looked like rough stone. | Calling someone that word is rude and hurtful.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Rude sense: offensive, can get you in trouble; do not use it. «Slag off» is informal British and Irish slang. The science sense (waste from metal-making) is uncountable.

part of speech: verb (slay, slays, slew, slain; slaying; slang: slayed)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (old, literary) To kill violently, especially in battle or a story. 2) (slang) To do something brilliantly or look amazing: «You slayed that dance!» 3) (informal) To make someone laugh a lot: «That joke slays me.»
its sense in the lessons: In fairy tales and the Bible: knights slay dragons; David slew Goliath. In children's slang today, «slay» means do amazingly. Phrases: «slay the dragon», «you slay», «slayed it».
examples from the lessons: The knight set off to slay the dragon. | In the Bible, David slew the giant Goliath. | You slayed that song at the talent show! | Her costume totally slays. | That cartoon slays me every time. | Many soldiers were slain in the battle.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Two past forms: old sense «slew, slain»; slang sense «slayed». Do not confuse with «sleigh» (sledge pulled by reindeer) — same sound.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To walk or do things while asleep without knowing it. 2) (informal) To move into a bad situation without noticing or thinking: «sleepwalking into trouble».
its sense in the lessons: Science and health: sleepwalking is common in children and usually stops as they grow. Safety: gently guide a sleepwalker back to bed and lock doors. Phrases: «sleepwalk into», «a sleepwalker».
examples from the lessons: My little brother sometimes sleepwalks into the kitchen. | She sleepwalked down the stairs and didn't remember it. | Mum guided me back to bed when I was sleepwalking. | Lock the doors if someone in the house sleepwalks. | The team sleepwalked through the first half. | Sleepwalking is common in children.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb, one word. Noun «sleepwalker». Myth: it is not dangerous to wake a sleepwalker, but it can confuse them, so gently guide them back to bed.

part of speech: verb (slew, slews, slewed, slewing); noun (a slew of, slews); also the past form of «slay» (slay, slays, slew, slain)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A slew of things is a large number or amount of them (informal). 2) To slew is to turn or slide sideways suddenly and out of control, like a car on ice. 3) Slew is the old past form of «slay»: the knight slew the dragon means he killed it (old-fashioned, stories).
its sense in the lessons: In everyday talk and news «a slew of» means «lots of»: a slew of emails, a slew of new games. In stories about cars, boats or bikes «slewed» shows a sudden skid that tells the reader something dangerous is happening. In fairy tales and the Bible-style stories «slew» is the past of «slay» (David slew Goliath). Phrases: a slew of, slew round, slewed across the road.
examples from the lessons: The teacher got a slew of questions after the fire drill. | There is a whole slew of new books in the library. | The car slewed across the icy road and stopped in the ditch. | My bike slewed sideways on the wet leaves. | The boat slewed round in the strong wind. | In the story, the brave prince slew the dragon. | Christians read that young David slew the giant Goliath with a stone. | After the storm we had a slew of broken branches in the garden.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «A slew of» is informal and is followed by a plural noun (a slew of problems). «Slew» (killed) is only in old stories; today we say «killed». Do not confuse with «slough» or «slue» (an American spelling of the turning sense). In maths problems «a slew of» means «many» but gives no exact number.

part of speech: verb (slump, slumps, slumped, slumping); noun (a slump, slumps)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To slump is to sit or fall down heavily because you are tired, ill or sad. 2) To slump also means to fall suddenly by a large amount, like prices or sales. 3) A slump is a time when business, trade or a team does badly (money, sport). 4) A slump is also a sudden fall in numbers or in how well someone is doing.
its sense in the lessons: In stories «slumped» shows the reader that a person is exhausted, upset, ill or fainting (he slumped in his chair). In the news and money lessons a slump is a bad time for business, when people buy less and jobs may be lost. In sport a team in a slump keeps losing. Safety: if someone slumps and will not wake, call an adult or the emergency number. Phrases: slump into a chair, slumped over, a sales slump, in a slump.
examples from the lessons: After the long race, Mia slumped onto the grass. | Grandad slumped in his armchair and fell asleep. | The boy slumped over his desk, too tired to finish. | Sales of ice cream slump in winter. | The team is in a slump and has lost five games in a row. | During the slump, many shops in town closed. | House prices slumped last year. | Sit up straight and don't slump at the table!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past form: slumped. As a noun it is countable: a slump, two slumps. «Slump» (fall heavily) is close to «sag» and «collapse». In maths word problems «sales slumped by 40» means they went down by 40, so subtract.

part of speech: verb (sneer, sneers, sneered, sneering); noun (a sneer, sneers)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To sneer is to smile or speak in an unkind way that shows you think someone or something is not good enough. 2) A sneer is that unkind, mocking smile, often with one side of the lip lifted. 3) To sneer at something is to make fun of it as if it were worthless.
its sense in the lessons: In stories a sneer marks a proud, mean or bullying character; the reader learns the person feels better than others. In lessons about kindness, sneering is a kind of disrespect and a sign of bullying. Phrases: sneer at, with a sneer, a sneering voice.
examples from the lessons: The bully sneered at my old trainers. | «Is that the best you can do?» he said with a sneer. | The villain's face twisted into a sneer. | Don't sneer at other people's drawings. | She sneered when he dropped the ball. | Some people sneered at the idea, but it worked. | His sneer made Tom feel small. | The rich man sneered at the poor farmer.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Use «sneer at» someone or something. Past form: sneered. A sneer is not the same as a grin or a smirk: a grin is friendly; a smirk is a self-pleased smile; a sneer is scornful. Countable noun: a sneer, sneers.

part of speech: adjective (sneering, more sneering); verb form (the -ing form of «sneer»); noun (sneering — uncountable)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Sneering describes a voice, look or remark that is mocking and shows someone thinks others are worthless. 2) Sneering is the -ing form of «sneer»: he was sneering at us. 3) Sneering as a noun is the act of mocking in that unkind way.
its sense in the lessons: In stories a «sneering tone» or «sneering smile» warns the reader that the speaker is proud, cruel or bullying. In lessons on respect, sneering remarks count as unkind words. Phrases: a sneering tone, a sneering remark, sneering at.
examples from the lessons: He answered in a sneering voice. | The sneering boy laughed at my spelling. | Stop sneering at your sister. | Her sneering remark hurt my feelings. | The sneering guard would not let them pass. | There was a lot of sneering when he fell over, but his friends helped him up.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The adverb is «sneeringly». Spelled with double «e» and one «r» before -ing: sneer → sneering. Close words: mocking, scornful, contemptuous.

part of speech: verb (snigger, sniggers, sniggered, sniggering); noun (a snigger, sniggers)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To snigger is to laugh quietly in a rude or unkind way, often at someone's mistake or at something naughty. 2) A snigger is that small, half-hidden laugh. 3) (US) The usual American word is «snicker», which means the same.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and at school sniggering happens behind someone's back; the reader learns that people are mocking, or that a joke is a bit rude. Teachers often stop children from sniggering when someone gets an answer wrong. Phrases: snigger at, a snigger went round the class.
examples from the lessons: The boys sniggered when the teacher tripped. | A snigger went round the class. | Please don't snigger when someone reads aloud. | She heard sniggers from the back row. | He sniggered at the rude word in the book. | Mum told us off for sniggering in church.
note for the reader of a maths problem: British English mostly says «snigger», American English «snicker». Past form: sniggered. Countable noun: a snigger. It is not the same as a giggle: giggling can be friendly; sniggering is usually unkind or cheeky.

part of speech: noun (a sojourn, sojourns); verb (sojourn, sojourns, sojourned, sojourning — formal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A sojourn is a short stay in a place that is not your home (formal). 2) To sojourn is to stay somewhere for a while as a visitor (formal, old-fashioned). 3) (Bible) In the Bible, to sojourn is to live in a land as a stranger or traveller, as Abraham did.
its sense in the lessons: You meet «sojourn» in travel writing, older books, Bible readings and exam texts; in everyday talk people say «stay» or «visit». It tells the reader that the stay was temporary. Phrases: a brief sojourn, a sojourn in the country.
examples from the lessons: After a short sojourn in Scotland, they came home. | The writer spent a sojourn by the sea. | Our sojourn at Gran's farm lasted a week. | The explorers sojourned in the desert for several days. | Christians read that Abraham sojourned in a strange land. | During his sojourn abroad he learned French.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It is a formal word; in normal speech say «stay». Pronounced SOJ-urn (or SO-jurn). Countable noun: a sojourn, sojourns. A sojourn is always temporary, not a move for ever.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A solicitation is a request asking someone for money, help, business or support (formal). 2) Solicitation is the act of asking for something, like donations or votes (formal). 3) (law) Solicitation is also the crime of asking or urging someone to do something illegal.
its sense in the lessons: This is a stiff word met in letters, notices, law and exam texts. A sign saying «No solicitation» means salespeople and collectors must not knock or ask. In money lessons a solicitation for donations is a request from a charity. Phrases: solicitation of funds, no solicitation, a solicitation letter.
examples from the lessons: The charity sent a solicitation for donations. | The sign on the gate says «No solicitation». | The school refused solicitations from companies selling sweets. | He ignored the solicitation in his email. | Solicitation of votes inside the polling station is not allowed. | In law, solicitation means urging someone to commit a crime.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal word; the verb is «solicit» and something not asked for is «unsolicited». Do not confuse with «solicitor», a kind of lawyer (UK, Ireland, Australia). Countable when it means one request; uncountable for the activity.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A speakerphone is a setting on a phone that lets you hear the caller through a loudspeaker, so everyone in the room can listen and talk without holding the phone. 2) A speakerphone is also a phone or device that works this way.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life families put calls on speakerphone so everyone can talk to Grandma. Safety: drivers use speakerphone or hands-free so they don't hold the phone; you should tell the caller if others can hear. Phrases: on speakerphone, put it on speakerphone, switch to speakerphone.
examples from the lessons: Mum put Grandma on speakerphone so we could all say hello. | Can you hear me? I'm on speakerphone. | Dad uses the speakerphone in the car. | Turn off the speakerphone, it's too loud. | The teacher called the head on speakerphone during class. | Let me switch to speakerphone so my brother can hear.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually one word, sometimes «speaker phone». We say «on speakerphone» (not «in»). Related: hands-free, loudspeaker.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Specially means for one particular purpose or person: a cake specially made for your birthday. 2) Specially means in a special or unusual way, done with extra care. 3) Specially is also used in everyday talk to mean «especially», particularly (informal).
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and stories «specially» shows that extra effort was made for someone: specially made, specially designed, specially for you. In school writing teachers often prefer «especially» for «particularly». Phrases: specially for, specially made, specially trained.
examples from the lessons: I made this card specially for you. | The bus is specially built for wheelchairs. | The dogs are specially trained to find people after earthquakes. | Gran cooked a specially big dinner for us. | These shoes are specially designed for running. | I like all fruit, specially strawberries (informal). | The room was specially decorated for the party.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Specially» = for a special purpose (specially made). «Especially» = particularly, above all (I love sport, especially football). In speech they are often mixed up; in careful writing keep them apart. Spelled with double «l».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A spinster is a woman who has never married, usually an older one (old-fashioned). 2) (old use) A spinster was once a woman whose job was spinning thread. 3) In old legal papers spinster was the word for an unmarried woman (law, old).
its sense in the lessons: You meet «spinster» in old novels, fairy tales and legal records. Today it can sound unkind, because it was used to mock women who did not marry; people now just say «a single woman» or «unmarried». The male word «bachelor» is still used more freely. Phrases: an old spinster (unkind), spinster aunt.
examples from the lessons: In the old story, the spinster lived alone with her cats. | Great-aunt Molly was a spinster all her life and loved travelling. | The marriage record called her «spinster» because she had not been married before. | Long ago spinsters spun wool into thread. | Calling someone «an old spinster» is rude. | The book is about two spinster sisters who run a shop.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun. Old-fashioned and sometimes rude; prefer «single woman». The male partner word is «bachelor», but the two words do not carry the same feeling. It comes from «spin» (spinning thread).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Sponsorship is money or support that a person or company gives to pay for an event, team or activity, often to advertise their name. 2) Sponsorship is also money people promise to give to charity if you complete a challenge, like a sponsored walk. 3) Sponsorship can mean officially supporting someone, such as a person moving to a new country or a member joining a club.
its sense in the lessons: In sport and school events, sponsorship explains why a company's logo is on football shirts. At school children collect sponsorship for a sponsored run or read-a-thon. In money lessons sponsorship is a deal: the sponsor pays and gets advertising. Phrases: get sponsorship, sponsorship deal, under the sponsorship of.
examples from the lessons: Our football team got sponsorship from the local bakery. | I raised forty pounds in sponsorship for the charity swim. | The concert was paid for by sponsorship. | The company ended its sponsorship of the race. | My uncle signed a big sponsorship deal. | We need sponsorship to buy new instruments for the band. | Gran gave me sponsorship for every lap I ran.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable (much sponsorship), but «a sponsorship deal» or «sponsorships» is fine. The person or firm that pays is a «sponsor». In maths problems «a sponsorship of 2 pounds per lap» means multiply the laps by 2.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Spontaneous means happening or done suddenly, without being planned. 2) A spontaneous person often does things on the spur of the moment, naturally and freely. 3) (science) Spontaneous describes something that happens by itself without being caused from outside, like spontaneous combustion.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life spontaneous fun is not planned: a spontaneous trip to the beach. In stories it shows a character is lively and free, or a crowd reacts naturally (spontaneous applause). In science «spontaneous» means happening on its own. Phrases: spontaneous applause, a spontaneous decision, spontaneous combustion.
examples from the lessons: The crowd burst into spontaneous applause. | We made a spontaneous trip to the park. | Her laugh was warm and spontaneous. | He is spontaneous and always has new ideas. | The hug was spontaneous, not planned. | Piles of wet hay can catch fire by spontaneous combustion. | Our teacher likes spontaneous questions in class.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelled -taneous: spon-TAY-nee-us. Opposite: planned, deliberate, rehearsed. Myth: «spontaneous human combustion» (people bursting into flames by themselves) is not supported by science.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A sporty person likes sport and is good at it. 2) Sporty clothes look like clothes for sport, casual and bright. 3) A sporty car is fast and looks like a racing car.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday talk and school stories «sporty» describes the child who loves running, football or netball; it tells the reader about the character's hobbies. In shops it describes casual or athletic clothes and fast-looking cars. Phrases: the sporty type, sporty kids, a sporty look.
examples from the lessons: My sister is very sporty and plays three sports. | I'm not sporty, but I like swimming. | He wore a sporty jacket and trainers. | Dad wants a sporty red car. | She is the sportiest girl in our year. | Our school has sporty clubs after school.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative: sportier, sportiest (y → i). Informal word. Not the same as «sportsmanlike» (playing fairly).

meaning for a pupil: 1) To squander something is to waste it foolishly, especially money, time or a chance. 2) To squander a chance or talent is to fail to use it well.
its sense in the lessons: In money lessons squandering means spending money on things you do not need until it is gone. In stories (like the prodigal son in the Bible) it shows a careless character who later regrets it. In sport a team squanders a lead when it loses after being ahead. Phrases: squander money, squander a chance, squander time.
examples from the lessons: He squandered all his pocket money on sweets. | Don't squander your time on silly games. | The team squandered a three-goal lead. | She squandered her chance to win. | In the Bible story, the younger son squandered his father's money. | It's a pity to squander such talent. | They squandered the water during the drought.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past form: squandered. It is stronger than «waste» and shows blame. Opposite: save, use wisely. In maths, «he squandered half of his 20 dollars» means he lost 10, so 10 is left.

part of speech: noun (a stabbing, stabbings); adjective (stabbing — of pain); verb form (the -ing form of «stab»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A stabbing is a crime or attack in which someone is hurt with a knife or sharp object. 2) A stabbing pain is a sudden, sharp pain, as if something pointed is pushing in. 3) Stabbing is the -ing form of «stab»: pushing something pointed into something, like a fork into food.
its sense in the lessons: In the news «a stabbing» is a serious crime; safety lessons teach that knives are dangerous and never to carry one. In health and stories «a stabbing pain» tells the reader the pain is sudden and sharp. At the table children stab peas with a fork. Phrases: a stabbing pain, a stabbing in the street, stabbing at.
examples from the lessons: There was a stabbing in the city, and the police are looking for the attacker. | I felt a stabbing pain in my side after running. | He was stabbing at his food with his fork. | She kept stabbing the button, but the lift did not come. | A stabbing pain in your chest means you should tell an adult at once. | Knife crime and stabbings are very serious.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The noun is countable: one stabbing, two stabbings. The verb doubles the «b»: stab → stabbed, stabbing. Safety: carrying a knife is dangerous and often against the law.

part of speech: verb (past form of «stink»: stink, stinks, stank, stunk)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Stank is the past form of «stink»: it smelled very bad. 2) Stank can also mean (informal) that something was very bad or poor: the film stank.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and funny stories «stank» describes bins, socks, rotten eggs and drains; it makes the reader almost smell the scene. In informal talk it means something was terrible. Phrases: it stank of, stank to high heaven.
examples from the lessons: The bin stank after a week in the sun. | His socks stank after the football match. | The room stank of fish. | The pond stank in the hot weather. | The rotten egg stank so badly we opened the windows. | That joke stank (informal). | The cheese stank, but it tasted great.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Forms: stink – stank – stunk (have stunk). Some people say «stunk» as the past too (it stunk), but «stank» is standard for the simple past. «Stank of» + the smell.

part of speech: adjective (stern, sterner, sternest); noun (the stern, sterns)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Stern means serious and strict, not smiling, like a teacher who wants you to behave. 2) The stern is the back part of a ship or boat. 3) Stern can also describe a hard, serious test or warning: a stern warning.
its sense in the lessons: In stories a stern face or voice tells the reader that someone is strict or angry and expects obedience. On boats children learn stern (back) and bow (front). Phrases: a stern look, a stern warning, from stem to stern (from front to back, all of it).
examples from the lessons: The headteacher gave us a stern look. | Grandpa's voice was stern: «Go to bed now.» | We got a stern warning about running in the corridor. | We sat at the stern of the boat. | The captain stood at the stern and steered. | She is stern but fair. | The ship was cleaned from stem to stern.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb: sternly. The front of a boat is the bow; the back is the stern; left is port; right is starboard. «Stern» (strict) and «stern» (back of a boat) are spelled the same but are different words.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A storehouse is a building where food, goods or supplies are kept. 2) A storehouse of something is a place or person full of a lot of it: a storehouse of knowledge. 3) (Bible) In Bible stories storehouses hold grain for hard times, as in the story of Joseph in Egypt.
its sense in the lessons: In history and Bible lessons storehouses kept grain so people would not starve in famine. In figurative speech a library or a grandparent can be «a storehouse of stories». Phrases: a storehouse of, grain storehouse.
examples from the lessons: The farmers kept the wheat in a big storehouse. | The castle had a storehouse full of food for the winter. | Christians read that Joseph filled the storehouses of Egypt before the famine. | Our library is a storehouse of knowledge. | Gran is a storehouse of old stories. | The squirrels' nest was a little storehouse of nuts.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun. Close words: warehouse, store, barn, granary. «Warehouse» is the modern business word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To submit something is to hand it in or send it so it can be checked or judged, like homework or a form. 2) To submit is to give in and accept someone's power or control. 3) (formal) To submit can also mean to state an opinion politely: I submit that the plan is unfair. 4) (computers) To submit is to click a button that sends what you typed.
its sense in the lessons: At school you submit homework, projects and entries for a competition. Online you press «Submit» to send a form. In stories and history an army or person submits when they stop fighting and obey. In lessons about faith, Christians speak of submitting to God's will. Phrases: submit homework, submit to, submit an application.
examples from the lessons: Please submit your homework by Friday. | I submitted my poem to the writing competition. | Click «Submit» to send your answers. | The rebels finally submitted to the king. | He would not submit to the bully. | We submitted a form to join the swimming club. | The lawyer submitted that the man was innocent (formal).
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double the «t»: submitted, submitting. Noun: submission. «Submit to» = give in to. In formal writing «submit» is a stiff word for «hand in» or «send».

part of speech: verb form (the -ing form of «substantiate»: substantiate, substantiates, substantiated, substantiating); adjective (substantiating evidence)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Substantiating means proving that something is true by giving facts or evidence (formal). 2) As an adjective, substantiating describes evidence or facts that support a claim (formal).
its sense in the lessons: This is the stiff exam and law voice; in everyday speech people say «proving», «backing up» or «supporting». In science, substantiating a claim means showing data that supports it. In law, a claim needs substantiating evidence. Phrases: substantiating evidence, substantiating a claim.
examples from the lessons: The scientist is substantiating her idea with careful tests. | The police need substantiating evidence before they arrest anyone. | He had trouble substantiating his story. | Substantiating a rumour means checking the facts. | Your essay should include substantiating examples. | The detective spent a week substantiating the witness's claims.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal word. Base verb: substantiate; noun: substantiation. The opposite idea is «unsubstantiated» (not proved). Plain words: prove, support, back up.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Successively means one after another, in order, without a break. 2) Successively also means each time in a series, with each one following the last: successively larger numbers.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, numbers that get «successively larger» increase each time (2, 4, 8, 16). In history, kings ruled successively one after the other. In science instructions you add things successively, one at a time. It is a formal word; people often say «one after another» or «in turn». Phrases: successively larger, successively smaller.
examples from the lessons: The numbers 3, 6, 9, 12 get successively bigger. | The team won three matches successively. | The kings ruled the country successively. | The steps get successively harder. | Pour the liquids in successively, not all at once. | The bowls were successively smaller, like Russian dolls.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal adverb. From «successive» (one after the other) and «succession». Do not confuse with «successfully» (with success). In maths «successively doubled» means double, then double the result again.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Suitability is how right or appropriate something or someone is for a purpose, person or situation. 2) Suitability is also how fit someone is for a job or role.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and safety, films and games have age ratings to show their suitability for children. In jobs, employers check a person's suitability. In exam texts «assess the suitability» means judge whether it fits. Phrases: suitability for, check the suitability.
examples from the lessons: The age rating shows the film's suitability for children. | The coach checked the pitch's suitability for the match. | We tested the material's suitability for making a raincoat. | The interview is to see his suitability for the job. | Mum questioned the suitability of the game for my little brother. | Check the suitability of the shoes for walking.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: no plural, no «a». Adjective: suitable; opposite: unsuitable, unsuitability. Followed by «for» (suitability for children).

meaning for a pupil: 1) To supplant someone or something is to take their place, often by being newer or better (formal). 2) To supplant someone can also mean to push them out of their position, sometimes by tricks.
its sense in the lessons: This is a formal word from history, science and the news: computers supplanted typewriters, a new king supplanted the old one. In Bible stories Jacob (whose name is linked with this idea) supplanted his brother Esau. Phrases: be supplanted by.
examples from the lessons: Phones have supplanted letters for most messages. | Cars supplanted horses on the roads. | The new player supplanted the captain in the team. | Christians read that Jacob supplanted Esau and took his blessing. | Plastic bags have been supplanted by cloth bags in many shops. | The invader supplanted the old king.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; plain words: replace, take the place of. Past: supplanted. Often in the passive: be supplanted by.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Supplication is asking for something humbly and seriously, especially from God or a powerful person (formal). 2) (church) A supplication is a humble prayer asking God for help.
its sense in the lessons: You meet «supplication» in church prayers, the Bible, history and older stories. It tells the reader that someone is pleading, often kneeling or with hands raised. Christians speak of prayer and supplication. Phrases: in supplication, prayers and supplications.
examples from the lessons: She raised her hands in supplication. | Christians believe God hears prayers and supplications. | The poor man knelt before the king in supplication. | The prayer book has a supplication for the sick. | The villagers made a supplication for rain. | His voice was full of supplication.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal word. Verb: supplicate; adjective: suppliant. Plain words: plea, prayer, begging. Do not confuse with «supplement» (something added) or «supply».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A surveyor is a person whose job is to measure land and make maps or plans of it. 2) A surveyor is also someone who checks a building to see what condition it is in, often before people buy it (money, UK). 3) A surveyor can be an official who inspects something, like ships.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and maths lessons surveyors use measuring tools, angles and distances to map land. In adult life, people buying a house pay a surveyor to check for damp or cracks. Phrases: land surveyor, building surveyor, a surveyor's report.
examples from the lessons: The surveyor measured the field with a special tool. | The surveyor's map showed where the new road would go. | Before buying the house, Mum and Dad hired a surveyor. | The surveyor found damp in the cellar. | Long ago, surveyors mapped the coastlines. | My aunt is a surveyor and works outdoors a lot.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun. Verb: survey; noun: a survey (a careful look or a set of questions). In maths, surveyors use triangles and angles to find distances they cannot measure directly.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Suspicion is a feeling that someone has done something wrong, without being sure. 2) A suspicion is a feeling or idea that something is probably true. 3) Suspicion is also not trusting someone. 4) A suspicion of something is a very small amount or trace of it: a suspicion of a smile.
its sense in the lessons: In mystery stories suspicion falls on characters, and the reader tries to find who is guilty. In everyday life and safety, if a stranger or a situation makes you feel suspicious, tell a trusted adult. Phrases: under suspicion, arouse suspicion, on suspicion of, have a suspicion that.
examples from the lessons: The detective had a suspicion that the butler was lying. | The man was arrested on suspicion of theft. | Everyone looked at Ben with suspicion when the biscuits disappeared. | I have a suspicion that it will rain. | Her strange story aroused suspicion. | The cat eyed the new dog with suspicion. | There was a suspicion of a smile on his face.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: suspicious; verb: suspect. Countable (a suspicion that...) and uncountable (with suspicion). Spelled with «-cion», not «-sion». A suspicion is not proof.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To sustain something is to keep it going for a long time. 2) To sustain someone is to give them the food, strength or support they need to live. 3) To sustain an injury or damage is to suffer it (formal). 4) To sustain a weight is to hold it up without breaking.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons food and water sustain life, and «sustainable» means using resources so they don't run out. In the news people «sustain injuries» in accidents. In sport you sustain effort or a lead. Phrases: sustain life, sustain an injury, sustained effort.
examples from the lessons: Plants need sunlight to sustain life. | A good breakfast will sustain you until lunch. | The runner could not sustain her speed. | Two people sustained minor injuries in the crash. | The bridge can sustain heavy lorries. | Christians believe God sustains the world. | The class sustained their attention for the whole film.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal word. Past: sustained. Nouns: sustenance (food), sustainability. «Sustain an injury» is a formal way of saying «get hurt».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Symbolic means standing for an idea or thing as a sign or symbol: a dove is symbolic of peace. 2) Symbolic also describes an action done to show feelings or ideas rather than for practical use: a symbolic gesture. 3) (maths) Symbolic means using letters and signs instead of words.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons symbolic things in stories carry hidden meaning: a storm may be symbolic of anger. In church, symbols like the cross and bread and wine are symbolic for Christians. In maths, symbolic language uses signs like + and =. Phrases: symbolic of, a symbolic gesture.
examples from the lessons: The dove is symbolic of peace. | Red roses are symbolic of love. | For Christians, the cross is symbolic of Jesus's death and love. | Planting a tree was a symbolic act for the school. | In the story, the dark forest is symbolic of fear. | In maths we use symbolic notation, like x + 3 = 7. | The handshake was a symbolic end to the quarrel.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Symbolic of» + the idea. Noun: symbol; verb: symbolise (UK) / symbolize (US). Do not confuse «symbol» with «cymbal» (a musical instrument).

meaning for a pupil: 1) The tarsus is the group of small bones in the ankle and upper foot (science). 2) In birds and insects, the tarsus is a part of the leg near the foot. 3) Tarsus is also the name of an old city (now in Turkey); in the Bible, Saint Paul came from Tarsus.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on the skeleton you learn the tarsus (ankle bones), metatarsals (foot bones) and phalanges (toe bones). In Bible lessons Paul is called «Saul of Tarsus». Phrases: Saul of Tarsus, the bones of the tarsus.
examples from the lessons: The tarsus is made of seven small bones. | The heel bone is part of the tarsus. | A bird's tarsus is the thin part of its leg above the toes. | An insect's tarsus helps it grip leaves. | Christians read that Paul was born in Tarsus. | The doctor said the X-ray of my tarsus was fine.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: tarsi. Science word. Related: metatarsal. As a city name it is written with a capital: Tarsus.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A teacup is a cup used for drinking tea, often with a handle and a saucer. 2) A teacup can also be the amount a teacup holds, used in old recipes.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life teacups appear at tea parties and at Gran's house. In stories teacups show politeness and old-fashioned homes. The phrase «a storm in a teacup» (UK; US «a tempest in a teapot») means a lot of fuss about something small. Phrases: a teacup and saucer, a storm in a teacup.
examples from the lessons: Gran poured the tea into her best teacups. | I broke a teacup when I was washing up. | We had a teddy bears' tea party with tiny teacups. | Add one teacup of flour. | Their argument was just a storm in a teacup. | The teacup had a pattern of roses.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word: teacup. Countable. In old recipes a teacup is a rough measure, not exact. Not the same as a mug (bigger, no saucer).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Terminable means able to be ended or stopped, especially a contract or agreement (formal, law). 2) Terminable can describe something that has a limited time and will end.
its sense in the lessons: This is a stiff legal and exam word. In adult life, a job contract or a rental agreement might be «terminable by either side with one month's notice», meaning either person can end it. Children meet it in exam texts rather than in speech. Phrases: terminable at will, terminable on notice.
examples from the lessons: The contract is terminable with one month's notice. | The agreement is terminable if either side breaks the rules. | The lease was terminable at any time. | The job was terminable after the trial period. | Is this deal terminable, or does it last for ever?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal, rare word. Verb: terminate (end); opposite: interminable, which strangely means «seeming to go on for ever, very long and boring» (an interminable speech).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Terribly means very or extremely (informal): I'm terribly sorry. 2) Terribly means very badly or in a way that is awful: he sang terribly. 3) Terribly can mean in a way that causes great suffering: she was terribly hurt.
its sense in the lessons: In polite British speech «terribly» is often just a strong «very»: terribly kind, terribly sorry. In stories it can show how badly something went or how much someone suffered. Phrases: terribly sorry, terribly important, went terribly wrong.
examples from the lessons: I'm terribly sorry for being late. | The plan went terribly wrong. | She was terribly kind to us. | He played the piano terribly. | I miss my friend terribly. | The house was terribly damaged in the flood. | It's not terribly important.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Terribly» as «very» can go before good words too (terribly nice), which surprises learners. «Not terribly» means «not very». Spelled with double «r»: terrible → terribly.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Therapy is treatment to help someone get better from an illness or injury. 2) Therapy is also talking with a trained person about worries and feelings, to feel better in your mind. 3) A therapy is one kind of treatment: speech therapy, physical therapy.
its sense in the lessons: In health lessons and adult life, people go to therapy after an accident, for speech, or for sadness and worry. It tells the reader that someone is getting help, and asking for help is good and brave. Phrases: go to therapy, speech therapy, physiotherapy, in therapy.
examples from the lessons: After breaking her leg, she had therapy to walk again. | My cousin goes to speech therapy to help with his talking. | Talking therapy helped Dad when he felt very sad. | The dog visits the hospital for pet therapy. | Music therapy helps some children relax. | There are many therapies for back pain.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable (go to therapy), countable for kinds (therapies). Person: therapist. Adjective: therapeutic. Going to therapy is normal, like seeing a doctor.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Threefold means three times as much or as many: a threefold increase. 2) Threefold also means having three parts: a threefold plan.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and science problems «threefold» means multiply by three. In stories and church talk «threefold» describes something with three parts. Phrases: increase threefold, a threefold rise.
examples from the lessons: The number of visitors increased threefold. | The price rose threefold, from 2 to 6 pounds. | Our school plan is threefold: read, write, think. | The plant's height grew threefold in a month. | There was a threefold rise in rain this spring. | The prize money has grown threefold.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Maths: «increase threefold» = the new amount is 3 × the old amount (10 → 30), not 10 + 3. Similar: twofold, fourfold, tenfold. One word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Tidiness is being neat and in order, with things put in their right places. 2) Tidiness is also the habit of keeping things neat.
its sense in the lessons: At home and school tidiness means a clean desk, toys put away, and a neat bedroom. In stories it can show a careful, organised character. Teachers sometimes give marks for the tidiness of work. Phrases: tidiness of work, a love of tidiness.
examples from the lessons: Mum praised me for the tidiness of my room. | The teacher gives a star for tidiness. | Tidiness helps you find things quickly. | His tidiness surprised his friends. | Good tidiness in the kitchen keeps it safe. | The tidiness of her handwriting made it easy to read.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Adjective: tidy (tidier, tidiest); verb: tidy up. The «y» changes to «i»: tidy → tidiness. Opposite: untidiness, messiness.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Tiredly means in a tired way, showing that you have little energy.
its sense in the lessons: In stories «tiredly» describes how a character moves or speaks after hard work or a long day; it tells the reader they are worn out. Phrases: smiled tiredly, said tiredly.
examples from the lessons: «Goodnight,» she said tiredly. | He walked tiredly up the stairs. | The runners waved tiredly at the end of the race. | Dad smiled tiredly after his long shift. | The puppy wagged its tail tiredly. | She rubbed her eyes tiredly.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: tired; noun: tiredness. It is a less common adverb; writers also say «wearily».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Tobacco is a plant whose dried leaves are smoked in cigarettes, cigars and pipes, or chewed. 2) Tobacco is also the dried leaves themselves, prepared for smoking.
its sense in the lessons: In health and safety lessons tobacco is harmful: it contains nicotine, which is addictive, and smoking causes lung disease and cancer. It is illegal to sell to children. In history, tobacco was grown on big farms and traded. Phrases: tobacco smoke, tobacco plant, chewing tobacco.
examples from the lessons: Tobacco is very bad for your health. | The shop is not allowed to sell tobacco to children. | Grandad gave up tobacco and feels much better. | The pipe smelled of tobacco. | Tobacco plants have big green leaves. | Tobacco smoke can harm people nearby too.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Spelled with one «b» and double «c»: to-bac-co. Myth: «a few cigarettes don't hurt» — any smoking harms health. Second-hand smoke hurts others.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A token is a round piece of metal or plastic used instead of a coin, for example in games or machines. 2) A token is a card or voucher that you can exchange for goods: a book token (UK). 3) A token of something is a sign or symbol of a feeling: a token of thanks. 4) As an adjective, token means small and done only for show: a token effort. 5) (computers) A token is a piece of text or a code that a program reads or that proves who you are.
its sense in the lessons: In board games you move your token around the board. In money lessons tokens are like vouchers. In stories a ring or flower can be a token of love. Phrases: a token of thanks, by the same token (for the same reason), a token gesture.
examples from the lessons: Put a token in the slot to play the game. | I got a book token for my birthday. | She gave him a flower as a token of thanks. | Move your token three squares forward. | He made only a token effort to tidy his room. | By the same token, you must help too. | The program splits the sentence into tokens.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun. «Token» as an adjective (token effort) means not real or serious. «By the same token» = for the same reason. In language models, a token is a small piece of text.

part of speech: adjective (towny, townier, towniest); noun (a towny, townies — informal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Towny describes someone or something that belongs to the town, not the countryside, or that likes town life (informal). 2) A towny (often spelled townie) is a person from the town, especially as country people or students see them (informal, sometimes unkind).
its sense in the lessons: You meet «towny» in informal speech and stories about life in the country and the town. It often shows a friendly or teasing contrast: a towny child does not know about cows. Phrases: towny folk, a bit towny.
examples from the lessons: The farm kids laughed at the towny boy who was scared of the sheep. | Gran calls us townies when we visit her village. | The towny clothes looked strange in the muddy field. | She is too towny to enjoy camping. | The students and the townies played a football match.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal. The more common spelling for the noun is «townie». Opposite idea: country folk. Can sound teasing.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A tradesman is a person with skilled practical work, such as a plumber, electrician or builder. 2) (UK, old) A tradesman is also a shopkeeper or someone who delivers goods.
its sense in the lessons: In adult life, families call a tradesman to fix leaks or wiring. In old stories, the tradesman's entrance was a back door for deliveries. Today people also say «tradesperson» or «trades worker» to include women. Phrases: a skilled tradesman, the tradesman's entrance.
examples from the lessons: We called a tradesman to fix the boiler. | My uncle is a tradesman; he is an electrician. | The tradesmen arrived early to build the wall. | In the old house there was a tradesman's entrance. | A good tradesman uses the right tools. | Many tradesmen learn their skills as apprentices.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: tradesmen. Gender-neutral form: tradesperson, tradespeople. Australia and New Zealand often say «tradie» (informal).

part of speech: verb form (past and past participle of «transform»: transform, transforms, transformed, transforming); adjective (transformed)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Transformed means changed completely in shape, look or nature. 2) As an adjective, transformed describes something or someone that has been greatly changed, usually for the better. 3) (maths) A transformed shape has been moved, flipped, turned or resized.
its sense in the lessons: In science, a caterpillar is transformed into a butterfly. In maths, shapes are transformed by translation, reflection, rotation and enlargement. In stories a character transformed by kindness has changed inside. Phrases: transformed into, transformed by.
examples from the lessons: The caterpillar transformed into a butterfly. | The old shed was transformed into a playroom. | The princess was transformed into a frog by a spell. | After the holiday, he seemed transformed. | In maths, the triangle was transformed by a rotation. | The snow transformed the garden into a white world.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Use «transformed into» for the new form. Noun: transformation. In maths, a transformation can keep the shape the same size (translation, reflection, rotation) or change its size (enlargement).

part of speech: adjective (transient, more transient); noun (a transient, transients)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Transient means lasting only a short time. 2) A transient person stays in a place only for a short time before moving on. 3) As a noun, a transient is a person who moves from place to place, often without a home (mainly US).
its sense in the lessons: This is a formal word in science, exam texts and adult news. In science a transient change does not last. In stories it describes passing moods or travellers. Phrases: transient pain, transient population.
examples from the lessons: The pain was transient and soon went away. | Happiness can be transient, so enjoy it. | The town has a transient population of tourists. | The hotel was full of transient guests. | A rainbow is a transient sight. | The shelter helps transients who have nowhere to sleep (US).
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal. Plain words: short, brief, passing. Noun: transience. Opposite: permanent, lasting.

part of speech: noun (trash — uncountable); verb (trash, trashes, trashed, trashing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Trash is rubbish, things you throw away (US, Canada). 2) Trash is also something of very poor quality: that film is trash (informal). 3) To trash something is to damage it badly or make a big mess of it (slang). 4) To trash someone or something is to criticise it harshly (informal). 5) (rude) Calling people «trash» is an insult.
its sense in the lessons: In North America children take out the trash and put litter in the trash can; in the UK, Ireland and Australia people say rubbish and bin. In informal speech, «trashed the room» means made a terrible mess. Phrases: take out the trash, trash can, in the trash.
examples from the lessons: Please take out the trash after dinner. | Put the wrapper in the trash can. | My little brother trashed my Lego castle. | The party guests trashed the house. | That TV show is total trash. | The critics trashed the new film. | Don't call people trash; it's unkind.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: no plural (some trash). UK: rubbish, bin; US: trash, garbage, trash can. Calling a person «trash» is a rude insult. Verb forms: trashed, trashing.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unanswered means not answered or not replied to: an unanswered question. 2) Unanswered can describe something not responded to, like a phone call or a challenge.
its sense in the lessons: In school an unanswered question on a test gets no marks. In stories and science, unanswered questions are mysteries still to solve. In church life people sometimes speak of unanswered prayers. Phrases: unanswered questions, left unanswered, an unanswered call.
examples from the lessons: There were two unanswered questions on my test. | The phone rang unanswered. | Some questions about space are still unanswered. | Her letter went unanswered for weeks. | Don't leave any question unanswered. | Some people feel their prayers are unanswered.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Prefix un- (not) + answered. Often after «go», «remain» or «leave»: went unanswered, remained unanswered. Tip: in tests, answer every question; an unanswered one scores zero.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unappealing means not attractive, not nice or not interesting. 2) Unappealing food does not look or smell nice.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life children say food, ideas or jobs are unappealing when they don't want them. In writing it is a polite word for «not nice». Phrases: look unappealing, an unappealing idea.
examples from the lessons: The grey soup looked unappealing. | Homework on a sunny day seems unappealing. | The old toy shop was dark and unappealing. | The idea of walking in the rain was unappealing. | The dish was healthy but unappealing to the children. | The room looked unappealing until we painted it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Prefix un- + appealing. Opposite: appealing, attractive. It is softer than «horrible» or «disgusting».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unborn means not yet born: an unborn baby is still growing inside its mother. 2) Unborn can also mean belonging to the future: generations yet unborn.
its sense in the lessons: In science and family life, an unborn baby grows inside the mother for about nine months. In stories and speeches, «unborn generations» means people of the future. Some ethics and church discussions talk about protecting the unborn. Phrases: an unborn baby, the unborn child, generations yet unborn.
examples from the lessons: Mum's unborn baby kicks when music plays. | The doctor checked the unborn baby with a scan. | We must protect the planet for generations yet unborn. | The unborn calf was healthy. | Smoking can harm an unborn baby. | Christians believe the unborn child is precious to God.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Prefix un- + born. Usually before a noun (an unborn baby). Safety: smoking and alcohol can harm an unborn baby.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unchecked means not controlled or stopped, so it can grow or spread: the fire spread unchecked. 2) Unchecked also means not looked over or tested: unchecked homework. 3) An unchecked box is a box with no tick in it.
its sense in the lessons: In science and safety, a disease or fire left unchecked becomes dangerous. In school, unchecked work may have mistakes. On computers, an unchecked box means the option is off. Phrases: go unchecked, left unchecked, spread unchecked.
examples from the lessons: The weeds grew unchecked in the empty garden. | If left unchecked, the infection can spread. | The fire burned unchecked for hours. | Don't hand in your work unchecked. | Leave the box unchecked if you don't want emails. | His bad temper went unchecked.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Prefix un- + checked. Often after «go» or «left»: went unchecked. A check mark (US) is a tick (UK).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unconditional means without any conditions or limits; complete and not depending on anything. 2) Unconditional love is love that does not change whatever you do.
its sense in the lessons: In family and church talk, unconditional love means loving someone always; Christians believe God's love is unconditional. In history and law, an unconditional surrender means giving up completely. In adult life, an unconditional offer (for example, from a university) does not depend on results. Phrases: unconditional love, unconditional surrender, unconditional offer.
examples from the lessons: Parents give their children unconditional love. | Christians believe God's love is unconditional. | The army made an unconditional surrender. | My dog's love is unconditional. | She got an unconditional offer from the college. | He gave unconditional support to his friend.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Prefix un- + conditional. Opposite: conditional (depending on something). Adverb: unconditionally.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unconsumed means not eaten, drunk or used up (formal). 2) Unconsumed can describe fuel or energy that was not burned or used.
its sense in the lessons: This is a formal word in science, money and exam texts: unconsumed food is leftover food; unconsumed fuel was not burned. In everyday talk people say «uneaten», «unused» or «left over». Phrases: unconsumed food, unconsumed fuel.
examples from the lessons: Unconsumed food was given to the food bank. | The scientists measured the unconsumed fuel. | Half the meal was left unconsumed. | Unconsumed medicine should be taken back to the pharmacy. | The unconsumed electricity was stored in a battery.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal. Prefix un- + consumed. Plain words: uneaten, unused, leftover. In maths, «unconsumed» means what is left, so subtract the used amount from the total.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Undamaged means not harmed or broken; still in good condition.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and stories, something undamaged survived an accident, storm or fall safely. In shops and money, undamaged goods can be returned. Phrases: escape undamaged, left undamaged.
examples from the lessons: The vase fell but was undamaged. | Luckily our house was undamaged by the storm. | The parcel arrived undamaged. | You can return undamaged items to the shop. | The car was undamaged after the bump. | The old church survived the fire undamaged.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Prefix un- + damaged. Opposite: damaged, broken. Similar: unharmed (for people and animals), intact.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The underdog is the person or team that is expected to lose a contest. 2) An underdog is also a person with less power or money than others.
its sense in the lessons: In sport and stories, underdogs who win surprise everyone and make exciting tales (David and Goliath is a famous underdog story). Many people like to support the underdog. Phrases: the underdog, root for the underdog, an underdog story.
examples from the lessons: Our small school was the underdog in the final. | Everyone cheered when the underdog won the race. | I always support the underdog. | David was the underdog against the giant Goliath. | The film is a classic underdog story. | The underdogs played their best game ever.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun, one word. Opposite: the favourite (UK) / favorite (US). «Root for» (US) or «support» the underdog.

part of speech: adjective; also verb form (the -ing form of «underlie»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Underlying means real but hidden; it is the true reason behind something: the underlying cause. 2) Underlying also means lying under something else: the underlying rock.
its sense in the lessons: In science and maths, the underlying rule or pattern explains what you see. In health, an underlying condition is an illness someone already has. In stories, an underlying feeling may be hidden by what characters say. Phrases: underlying cause, underlying problem, underlying condition.
examples from the lessons: The underlying cause of the fire was a broken wire. | Under the soil is the underlying rock. | Look for the underlying pattern in the numbers. | His jokes hid an underlying sadness. | Grandad has an underlying heart problem. | The underlying idea of the story is friendship.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective before a noun. Verb: underlie (underlies, underlay, underlain). Close words: basic, hidden, root.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To undermine something is to make it weaker little by little, often secretly. 2) To undermine someone is to make them less confident or less respected. 3) To undermine also means to dig under something, like a wall or cliff, so it may fall.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and lessons on friendship, undermining someone by teasing or gossip hurts their confidence. In science and geography, the sea undermines cliffs by wearing away the bottom. Phrases: undermine confidence, undermine authority.
examples from the lessons: Constant teasing can undermine a child's confidence. | Waves undermine the cliffs until they fall. | Don't undermine your teacher by talking over her. | The lies undermined their friendship. | Water undermined the old wall. | Eating junk food can undermine your health.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: undermined. Not the same as «underline» (draw a line under words). Close words: weaken, damage.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Undisturbed means not interrupted or bothered: she slept undisturbed. 2) Undisturbed also means not moved or changed: the dust lay undisturbed.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and history, undisturbed places like tombs or forests have been left alone for a long time. In everyday life, «undisturbed» sleep or reading means peaceful. In science, an undisturbed habitat has not been damaged by people. Phrases: sleep undisturbed, leave undisturbed.
examples from the lessons: The baby slept undisturbed all night. | The ancient tomb lay undisturbed for centuries. | Please leave the bird's nest undisturbed. | I like to read undisturbed in my room. | The snow was undisturbed until we ran across it. | The forest remained undisturbed by people.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Prefix un- + disturbed. Opposite: disturbed. Similar: peaceful, untouched.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unduly means more than is right, necessary or reasonable; too much (formal).
its sense in the lessons: This is a formal word used in polite or exam language: don't be unduly worried means don't worry more than you need to. It tells the reader something is too much. Phrases: unduly worried, unduly harsh, not unduly.
examples from the lessons: Don't be unduly worried about the test. | The punishment was unduly harsh. | The teacher was not unduly concerned about the noise. | Prices were unduly high. | He was unduly proud of his small win. | Please don't be unduly alarmed.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal. Adjective: undue (too much). Often «not unduly» = not very much. Plain words: too, overly, excessively.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unequal means not the same in size, amount or value. 2) Unequal also means not fair, when people are treated differently or have different chances. 3) Unequal to a task means not good enough or strong enough for it (formal).
its sense in the lessons: In maths, unequal parts are not the same size; fractions need equal parts. In history and ethics, unequal treatment of people is unfair. Phrases: unequal parts, unequal shares, unequal treatment.
examples from the lessons: The cake was cut into unequal pieces. | Those two lines are unequal in length. | Fractions need equal parts, not unequal ones. | Long ago, women had unequal rights. | It was an unequal fight between the giant and the boy. | He was unequal to the hard job.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Prefix un- + equal. In maths the symbol ≠ means «is not equal to». Halves must be equal parts; unequal pieces are not halves.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unfounded means not based on facts or evidence; not true.
its sense in the lessons: In science and news, unfounded claims have no proof. In everyday life, unfounded fears are worries that turn out to be wrong. It tells the reader a belief was mistaken. Phrases: unfounded rumours, unfounded fears, completely unfounded.
examples from the lessons: The rumour was completely unfounded. | My fears about the new school were unfounded. | The claims were unfounded and untrue. | The teacher said the complaint was unfounded. | Scientists showed the worry was unfounded. | Don't spread unfounded stories.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Prefix un- + founded (based on). Similar: groundless, baseless. Opposite: well-founded.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unhappiness is the feeling of being sad or not happy.
its sense in the lessons: In stories unhappiness can be a character's problem to solve. In lessons on wellbeing, talking about unhappiness to a trusted adult helps. Phrases: cause unhappiness, deep unhappiness.
examples from the lessons: There was unhappiness in the class when the trip was cancelled. | His unhappiness showed on his face. | Losing her pet caused great unhappiness. | Talking to Mum eased his unhappiness. | Bullying causes a lot of unhappiness. | The story ends with the end of unhappiness.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. The «y» of happy becomes «i»: unhappiness. Adjective: unhappy. Opposite: happiness.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Universally means by everyone or everywhere, without exception. 2) Universally also means true or used in all cases.
its sense in the lessons: In science and maths, universally true rules work everywhere. In everyday talk, universally loved means liked by everyone. Phrases: universally accepted, universally known, universally loved.
examples from the lessons: Chocolate is almost universally loved. | The rule is universally accepted. | Gravity works universally. | Smiles are understood universally. | The book was universally praised. | No idea is universally liked.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «universal». Spelled with double «l». Be careful: few things are truly universal; writers often say «almost universally».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unjustified means not fair or not reasonable; without a good reason.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and ethics lessons, unjustified punishment or anger is unfair. In news and law, unjustified claims have no reason behind them. Phrases: unjustified anger, completely unjustified.
examples from the lessons: The punishment was unjustified. | His anger at me was unjustified. | The price rise is unjustified. | The referee's decision seemed unjustified. | Your fears are unjustified. | It was an unjustified attack.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Prefix un- + justified. Opposite: justified, fair. Similar: unfair, unwarranted.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unkindness is being unkind, mean or cruel to others. 2) An unkindness is one unkind act or word.
its sense in the lessons: In lessons on friendship and ethics, unkindness hurts feelings and is the opposite of kindness. In church life Christians may confess unkindness and ask forgiveness. Phrases: an act of unkindness, unkindness to animals.
examples from the lessons: Unkindness can make someone very sad. | She said sorry for her unkindness. | There is no place for unkindness in our class. | Unkindness to animals is wrong. | He remembered every small unkindness. | Kindness wins over unkindness.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable; countable for single acts (an unkindness). Adjective: unkind; opposite: kindness.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unmerited means not deserved, whether good or bad (formal).
its sense in the lessons: In ethics and church talk, Christians speak of God's grace as unmerited favour — a gift not earned. In stories, unmerited punishment is unfair. Phrases: unmerited praise, unmerited favour.
examples from the lessons: The praise was unmerited, because he had copied his work. | The punishment was unmerited. | Christians believe grace is God's unmerited favour. | She felt her prize was unmerited. | His unmerited good luck surprised everyone.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal. Prefix un- + merited (deserved). Similar: undeserved. Opposite: deserved, earned.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unqualified means not having the training, skills or certificate needed for a job. 2) Unqualified also means complete, without limits: an unqualified success.
its sense in the lessons: In adult life and safety, an unqualified electrician may be dangerous. In news and exam texts, «an unqualified success» means a complete success. Phrases: unqualified to, an unqualified success.
examples from the lessons: He is unqualified to fix the wiring. | The party was an unqualified success. | Unqualified drivers must not drive. | She was unqualified for the job. | The teacher gave unqualified praise. | Don't let unqualified people treat your pet.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Two meanings: «without qualifications» or «complete». Opposite of the first: qualified.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To unscrew something is to remove it or open it by turning it. 2) To unscrew is also to take out screws.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, you unscrew bottle lids, light bulbs and jar tops. In design and technology lessons, you unscrew screws with a screwdriver. Phrases: unscrew the lid, unscrew the top.
examples from the lessons: Can you unscrew this jar lid for me? | Dad unscrewed the old light bulb. | She unscrewed the cap of the water bottle. | We unscrewed the shelf from the wall. | Turn left to unscrew. | The lid was too tight to unscrew.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Prefix un- + screw. Remember «lefty loosey, righty tighty». Safety: switch off power before unscrewing light bulbs.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unsolicited means not asked for: unsolicited advice or unsolicited emails.
its sense in the lessons: In adult life and safety, unsolicited emails, calls or messages can be scams. In everyday talk, unsolicited advice is advice someone gives without being asked. Phrases: unsolicited advice, unsolicited mail.
examples from the lessons: Mum gets lots of unsolicited emails. | He gave me unsolicited advice about my hair. | Never click links in unsolicited messages. | The company made an unsolicited offer. | The shop sent unsolicited leaflets. | Unsolicited calls can be annoying.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal. From «solicit» (ask for). Similar: unrequested, unwanted. Safety: be careful with unsolicited messages.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unsuitable means not right or not appropriate for a purpose, person or situation.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, films and games may be unsuitable for children. In safety lessons, unsuitable clothes or shoes can be dangerous. Phrases: unsuitable for, unsuitable clothes.
examples from the lessons: This film is unsuitable for young children. | Flip-flops are unsuitable for hiking. | The weather was unsuitable for flying. | The site is unsuitable for building. | The toy is unsuitable for babies. | He wore unsuitable clothes for the snow.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Prefix un- + suitable. Followed by «for». Noun: unsuitability.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unwillingness means not wanting to do something.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, a character's unwillingness to help may change later. In school, unwillingness to try can hold you back. Phrases: unwillingness to.
examples from the lessons: His unwillingness to share upset his friends. | She showed unwillingness to go to bed. | The team's unwillingness to give up won the game. | Unwillingness to learn makes things harder. | The dog's unwillingness to bathe was funny. | Their unwillingness to listen caused problems.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Followed by «to» + verb. Adjective: unwilling.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Upfront means paid or done in advance, before the work or goods are received (money). 2) An upfront person is honest and open about things.
its sense in the lessons: In money lessons and adult life, paying upfront means paying before you get the goods. In everyday talk, being upfront means saying things clearly and honestly. Phrases: pay upfront, be upfront about.
examples from the lessons: You have to pay upfront for the concert tickets. | The builder wanted half the money upfront. | She was upfront about her mistake. | Be upfront with your friends. | The fee is paid upfront. | He was upfront and told the truth.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Can be written as one word (upfront) or two (up front). In maths, «pay 20 upfront» means subtract 20 first from the total.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Urgency is the need to act quickly because something is important. 2) Urgency is also the feeling that something must be done at once.
its sense in the lessons: In safety and stories, urgency tells the reader there is danger or a deadline. Phrases: a sense of urgency, with urgency, a matter of urgency.
examples from the lessons: There was urgency in her voice. | The doctor acted with urgency. | We need a sense of urgency to finish on time. | The fire was a matter of urgency. | He spoke with urgency. | The urgency of the situation was clear.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Adjective: urgent. Safety: in an emergency, act with urgency and call the emergency number.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An urn is a tall vase, often with a lid, used for decoration or to hold the ashes of a person who has died. 2) An urn is also a large metal container with a tap, used for making and serving tea or coffee.
its sense in the lessons: In church life and family loss, ashes may be kept in an urn after cremation. At school fetes and church halls, a tea urn keeps water hot. Phrases: a tea urn, an urn of ashes.
examples from the lessons: Grandpa's ashes are in an urn on the shelf. | The church hall has a big tea urn. | The ancient Greeks made beautiful urns. | Be careful, the urn is hot. | The urn was filled with flowers. | We poured tea from the urn at the fair.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Homophone: «earn» (to get money for work). Safety: tea urns are very hot.

part of speech: noun (a utility, utilities; also uncountable); adjective (utility)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A utility is a service like water, gas or electricity that people need in their homes. 2) Utility means usefulness (formal). 3) As an adjective, utility describes something practical and useful: a utility room.
its sense in the lessons: In money and adult life, utility bills are payments for water, gas and electricity. In everyday homes, a utility room is for washing machines. In computers, a utility is a small useful program. Phrases: utility bills, utility room, utility vehicle.
examples from the lessons: Mum pays the utility bills each month. | The washing machine is in the utility room. | The tool has great utility. | Utilities include gas, water and electricity. | The company runs the local utilities. | A sport utility vehicle is a big car.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable for services (utilities), uncountable for usefulness. In maths problems, utility bills are often added up.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A vacancy is a job that is free and waiting for someone to fill it. 2) A vacancy is also an empty room in a hotel. 3) Vacancy can mean emptiness or lack of thought (formal).
its sense in the lessons: In adult life, job vacancies are advertised. Hotels show «vacancies» or «no vacancies». In stories, a vacancy in someone's eyes shows emptiness. Phrases: job vacancy, no vacancies.
examples from the lessons: There is a vacancy for a teacher at our school. | The hotel sign said «No vacancies». | Dad applied for a vacancy at the bank. | We found a vacancy at the campsite. | There was a vacancy in his stare. | The club has two vacancies.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Plural: vacancies. Adjective: vacant (empty).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A vandal is a person who deliberately damages or destroys property. 2) (history) The Vandals were a group of people who attacked Rome long ago.
its sense in the lessons: In safety and citizenship lessons, vandals break windows or spray graffiti. Vandalism is a crime. Phrases: vandals broke, attacked by vandals.
examples from the lessons: Vandals broke the bus shelter. | Someone sprayed graffiti; the police are looking for the vandals. | The park bench was damaged by vandals. | The Vandals were an ancient tribe. | Don't be a vandal; respect property. | Vandals smashed the school windows.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Noun for the crime: vandalism; verb: vandalise (UK) / vandalize (US).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Vegetarianism is the practice of not eating meat or fish.
its sense in the lessons: In health and ethics lessons, vegetarianism is a choice for animals, health or the planet. Some faiths and families follow vegetarianism. Phrases: practise vegetarianism, switch to vegetarianism.
examples from the lessons: Vegetarianism is popular in our school. | My aunt chose vegetarianism to protect animals. | Vegetarianism means no meat or fish. | Some religions encourage vegetarianism. | Vegetarianism can be very healthy. | He read about vegetarianism for his project.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Person: vegetarian. Vegans also avoid milk and eggs.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Vehemently means with very strong feeling, especially when disagreeing or denying something.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and news, someone vehemently denies a charge or argues. It tells the reader the feelings are very strong. Phrases: vehemently deny, vehemently oppose.
examples from the lessons: He vehemently denied stealing the cookies. | She vehemently opposed the plan. | The children argued vehemently about the rules. | The mayor vehemently refused. | They vehemently defended their friend. | He shook his head vehemently.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal. Adjective: vehement. Pronounced VEE-uh-ment-lee.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A vendor is a person or company that sells something. 2) A vendor is also someone who sells food or goods in the street. 3) (law, money) The vendor is the person selling a house.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, ice-cream vendors sell at parks. In money and adult life, the vendor sells and the buyer buys. Phrases: street vendor, ice-cream vendor.
examples from the lessons: We bought hot dogs from a street vendor. | The vendor sold balloons at the fair. | The vendor of the house accepted the offer. | Many vendors sell fruit at the market. | The ice-cream vendor rang a bell. | The vendor gave us change.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Also spelled «vender» sometimes. Opposite in sales: buyer, purchaser.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A victor is the winner of a battle, game or contest (formal).
its sense in the lessons: In history and sport stories, the victor wins. Phrases: the victor, emerge the victor.
examples from the lessons: The victor raised the trophy. | Our team was the victor in the final. | The victor of the battle became king. | She emerged the victor. | The victors celebrated. | To the victor go the spoils.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal. Noun: victory; adjective: victorious. Victor is also a boy's name.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Vocal means about the voice or using the voice. 2) A vocal person speaks out strongly and often. 3) Vocals are the singing parts of a song.
its sense in the lessons: In music lessons, vocals are singing. In science, vocal cords make your voice. In news, vocal people speak out. Phrases: vocal cords, vocal about, lead vocals.
examples from the lessons: Your vocal cords make sounds. | She is very vocal about saving animals. | He sang the lead vocals. | The choir did vocal warm-ups. | The crowd was vocal in support. | Parrots are vocal birds.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective; noun usually plural (vocals). Spelled «vocal cords», not «chords».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A voter is a person who votes in an election or is allowed to vote.
its sense in the lessons: In citizenship lessons, voters choose leaders in elections. Children learn that adults over a certain age can vote. Phrases: first-time voters, voter turnout.
