examples from the lessons: Voters chose a new mayor. | My mum is a voter. | First-time voters were excited. | The voters queued at the polling station. | Every voter has one vote. | Voter turnout was high.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Verb: vote. In maths, voter numbers are often counted or compared.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A voucher is a piece of paper or code you can exchange for goods or services, or that gives a discount.
its sense in the lessons: In money lessons, vouchers can save money. Children get gift vouchers for birthdays. Phrases: gift voucher, discount voucher.
examples from the lessons: I got a gift voucher for my birthday. | Use this voucher to get 10% off. | The voucher is for a free ice cream. | Mum used vouchers at the shop. | The book voucher can be spent at any bookshop. | Vouchers have a set value.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. In maths, a voucher's value is subtracted from the price.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To waive a rule, fee or right is to choose not to use it or not to demand it (formal).
its sense in the lessons: In money and law, a fee can be waived, meaning you don't pay it. In school, a rule may be waived for special cases. Phrases: waive a fee, waive a rule, waive the right.
examples from the lessons: The school waived the fee for the trip. | The teacher waived the homework rule this week. | He waived his right to a lawyer. | The bank waived the charge. | The shop waived the delivery cost. | They waived the late fine.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal. Homophone: «wave» (to move your hand). Noun: waiver.

part of speech: noun (wallpaper — uncountable; a wallpaper, wallpapers); verb (wallpaper, wallpapers, wallpapered, wallpapering)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Wallpaper is paper with patterns or colours that is stuck on walls to decorate a room. 2) Wallpaper is also the background picture on a computer or phone screen. 3) To wallpaper is to put wallpaper on walls.
its sense in the lessons: At home, families choose wallpaper for bedrooms. On phones, you change your wallpaper picture. Phrases: put up wallpaper, phone wallpaper.
examples from the lessons: We put up new wallpaper in my bedroom. | The wallpaper has stars on it. | My phone wallpaper is my dog. | Dad wallpapered the hall. | The old wallpaper peeled off. | Choose a wallpaper for the computer.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable for the paper; countable for designs. Verb: wallpapered. One word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Warfare is fighting in a war, or the way a war is fought.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, children learn about different kinds of warfare. Phrases: modern warfare, chemical warfare.
examples from the lessons: Warfare changed when guns were invented. | Ancient warfare used swords and shields. | Chemical warfare is banned. | The book is about warfare at sea. | Warfare causes great suffering. | Knights trained for warfare.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Not «a warfare».

part of speech: noun (a weed, weeds); verb (weed, weeds, weeded, weeding)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A weed is a wild plant growing where it is not wanted. 2) To weed is to pull weeds out of a garden. 3) (slang) Weed is a slang word for cannabis, an illegal drug. 4) (informal, UK) A weed is a thin, weak person.
its sense in the lessons: In gardening and science, weeds compete with crops. In safety, weed as a drug is harmful. Phrases: weed out, pull weeds.
examples from the lessons: We pulled weeds from the vegetable patch. | Dandelions are common weeds. | Grandma weeds the garden every Sunday. | Weed out the bad apples. | Weed is an illegal drug (slang). | He's a bit of a weed (UK, informal).
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable plant noun. Verb: weeded. «Weed out» = remove the unwanted ones. Safety: drugs are dangerous.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Wheresoever means wherever, in any place (old-fashioned, formal).
its sense in the lessons: You meet it in old books, Bible readings and prayers. Today people say «wherever». Phrases: wheresoever you go.
examples from the lessons: Wheresoever you go, I will follow. | The Lord is with you wheresoever you are. | Wheresoever he travelled, he made friends. | Search wheresoever you like. | The king's law reached wheresoever his people lived.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Old-fashioned. Modern word: wherever. Also «wheresoe'er» in poetry.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Willingly means gladly, without being forced.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and lessons on kindness, helping willingly is good. Phrases: willingly help, willingly give.
examples from the lessons: She willingly helped her friend. | He gave his toys willingly. | I'll willingly do the dishes. | The children willingly shared their sweets. | They willingly followed the teacher. | He willingly said sorry.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «willing». Opposite: unwillingly, reluctantly.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Willpower is the strength of mind to control your actions and do what you decide, even when it is hard.
its sense in the lessons: In health and stories, willpower helps people stop bad habits or resist temptations. Phrases: strong willpower, use willpower.
examples from the lessons: It takes willpower not to eat all the sweets. | She showed great willpower when training. | He used willpower to finish his homework. | Willpower helps you keep promises. | My brother has no willpower with chocolate. | With willpower you can learn hard things.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. One word.

part of speech: adjective; verb form (the past form of «wither»: wither, withers, withered, withering)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Withered means dried up and shrunk, like an old plant or flower. 2) Withered can describe old, wrinkled skin or weak limbs.
its sense in the lessons: In science, plants wither without water. In stories, a withered tree or hand shows age or illness; in the Bible Jesus heals a man with a withered hand. Phrases: withered flowers, a withered hand.
examples from the lessons: The flowers withered in the heat. | The withered leaves fell from the tree. | Grandma's hands are withered with age. | Christians read that Jesus healed a man with a withered hand. | The withered plant needed water. | The apple was withered and brown.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past form of «wither». Opposite: fresh, blooming.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Wrongful means unfair, unjust or against the law (formal, law).
its sense in the lessons: In law and news, a wrongful arrest or wrongful dismissal is unfair or illegal. Phrases: wrongful arrest, wrongful dismissal, wrongful death.
examples from the lessons: He sued for wrongful arrest. | The court said it was wrongful dismissal. | The family won a wrongful death case. | The wrongful punishment upset the class. | She fought her wrongful conviction. | The judge corrected the wrongful decision.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal, used in law. Adverb: wrongfully. Plain words: unfair, unlawful.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Wrongfully means unfairly or against the law (formal, law).
its sense in the lessons: In news and law, someone wrongfully accused or wrongfully imprisoned was treated unfairly. Phrases: wrongfully accused, wrongfully convicted.
examples from the lessons: He was wrongfully accused of stealing. | She was wrongfully imprisoned for years. | The worker was wrongfully dismissed. | The dog was wrongfully blamed for the mess. | They were wrongfully punished. | The court freed the wrongfully convicted man.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal. Adjective: wrongful. Do not confuse with «wrongly» (in a mistaken way).

meaning for a pupil: 1) xx stands for two kisses, written at the end of a message or card to show love (informal). 2) XX is the Roman numeral for 20 (maths). 3) (science) XX is the pair of sex chromosomes usually found in girls and women.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, people end friendly notes with «xx». In maths, Roman numerals use X for 10, so XX is 20. In science lessons on genes, XX and XY are chromosome pairs. Phrases: love, xx.
examples from the lessons: Love, Mum xx | See you soon, xx | Happy birthday, Gran! xx | XX is the Roman numeral for twenty. | Chapter XX is the last one. | Most girls have XX chromosomes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal; not used in formal letters. A single «x» is one kiss. Roman numerals: X = 10, XX = 20, XXX = 30.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A zealot is a person who is too strong and fierce in their beliefs, especially in religion or politics. 2) (Bible, history) The Zealots were a group of Jewish people in the time of Jesus who fought against Roman rule.
its sense in the lessons: In history and church lessons, the Zealots opposed the Romans; one of Jesus's disciples was called Simon the Zealot. In news, a zealot is someone extreme. Phrases: a religious zealot, Simon the Zealot.
examples from the lessons: The zealot shouted at everyone who disagreed. | Simon the Zealot was one of Jesus's twelve apostles. | Zealots can be dangerous when they refuse to listen. | He is a zealot about tidiness. | The Zealots fought against Rome. | Don't be a zealot; listen to others.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Noun: zeal (strong enthusiasm); adjective: zealous. Pronounced ZEL-ut.

part of speech: noun (a plait, plaits); verb (plait, plaits, plaited, plaiting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A plait is a length of hair divided into three strands that are crossed over each other again and again to make one neat rope-like piece. 2) A plait is any rope, bread or strip of straw or cloth made in the same crossed way. 3) To plait means to cross three or more strands over each other to make this shape.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life plaits are a common school hairstyle, especially for long hair, and stories use them to show a child getting ready or a tease ("he pulled her plaits"). In art and craft lessons children plait wool, paper strips or ribbon. Phrases: «in plaits», «a French plait», «plait your hair», «a plaited loaf». In stories, pulling someone's plait is a classic picture of teasing or bullying.
examples from the lessons: Mum plaited my hair before school. | Chloe wore her hair in two long plaits. | A boy in the line kept tugging her plait, so she told the teacher. | We plaited three strips of coloured paper to make a bookmark. | Can you do a French plait? | The baker sold a shiny plaited loaf. | Her plait came undone during PE. | Grandma taught me how to plait wool for a bracelet.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: a plait, two plaits. Past: plaited. Mainly British, Irish, Australian and New Zealand English; in American and Canadian English the usual word is «braid» (noun and verb). Pronounced to rhyme with «flat» in the UK (some say «plate»). Do not confuse with «plate» or «pleat» (a fold sewn into a skirt).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) An altercation is a noisy argument or small fight between people, usually in public. 2) (formal, news and police) It is a polite word reporters and police use for a fight or scuffle when they do not want to give details.
its sense in the lessons: You meet this word mostly in news reports, police statements, school incident reports and exam passages, not in children's chat. It tells the reader that people argued loudly or pushed each other, but often hides how bad it was. Phrases: «a verbal altercation» (only words), «a physical altercation» (pushing or hitting), «be involved in an altercation», «an altercation broke out».
examples from the lessons: There was an altercation between two fans outside the stadium. | The report said a brief altercation took place in the playground. | Police were called after a verbal altercation in the car park. | The headteacher wrote that both boys were involved in the altercation. | A physical altercation broke out at the bus stop. | Nobody was hurt in the altercation. | The players had an altercation with the referee.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun. A stiff, formal word: in everyday speech people say «argument», «row» (UK), «fight», «scrap» or «bust-up». Stress on «-CA-»: al-ter-CAY-shun. «Verbal» altercation means only shouting, not hitting. Do not mix it up with «alteration» (a change).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A ponytail is a hairstyle where long hair is pulled back and tied with a band at the back of the head so that it hangs down like a pony's tail. 2) The hair that hangs down in this style.
its sense in the lessons: A very common school and sports hairstyle; schools often ask for long hair to be tied back in a ponytail for PE, science practicals near flames, and swimming, for safety. In stories, a swinging ponytail shows movement or energy, and tugging one is a picture of teasing. Phrases: «in a ponytail», «tie your hair back in a ponytail», «a high ponytail», «a low ponytail», «a hair tie / scrunchie».
examples from the lessons: Lily tied her hair in a high ponytail for netball. | Please put long hair in a ponytail before you light the Bunsen burner. | Her ponytail swung as she ran. | Some boys kept tugging her ponytail, so she moved seats. | My dad has a short ponytail. | She took out her ponytail and brushed her hair. | The horse's real tail was longer than any ponytail.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: one ponytail, two ponytails. Written as one word. Two bunches on each side are «bunches» (UK) or «pigtails». Safety: long loose hair can catch fire or get caught in machines, which is why teachers ask for a ponytail.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An actress is a woman or girl who acts in plays, films or TV shows, pretending to be a character. 2) (informal) Someone who is "a good actress" is good at pretending feelings she does not really have.
its sense in the lessons: Used in talk about films, theatre, school plays and celebrities. Today many women prefer to be called «actor», the same word as for men, so you will see both. Phrases: «a famous actress», «a film actress», «best actress» (an award), «child actress», «leading actress».
examples from the lessons: The actress played a queen in the new film. | My sister wants to be an actress when she grows up. | She won the award for best actress. | The actress learned all her lines in a week. | A child actress played the girl in the story. | Don't believe her tears, she's a good little actress! | The actress waved to the fans outside the theatre.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun; plural «actresses» (add -es after -ss). «An actress» because it starts with a vowel sound. Many people now use «actor» for every gender; «actress» is not rude but is used less. Male form: actor.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A tomboy is a girl who likes doing things that people used to think were only for boys, such as climbing trees, rough games and football, and often prefers jeans to dresses. 2) (dated) It was once used as a criticism of girls who did not behave in a "ladylike" way.
its sense in the lessons: Appears in stories and everyday chat about friendship, fairness and growing up. It tells the reader about a girl's interests and style, not about anything wrong with her. Modern lessons stress that girls and boys may like any games, clothes and hobbies. Phrases: «a bit of a tomboy», «a real tomboy», «tomboyish».
examples from the lessons: Maddie is a tomboy who loves football and climbing trees. | Mum says she was a tomboy as a girl. | Being a tomboy doesn't mean she can't like painting too. | The tomboy in the story beat all the boys in the race. | She hated dresses and called herself a proud tomboy. | Some kids teased her for being a tomboy, but she didn't care. | She had a short, tomboyish haircut.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun; plural «tomboys» (not -ies, because there is a vowel before y). Adjective: tomboyish. Used only of girls. Trap: it is a description, not a judgement; liking football does not make a girl less of a girl. Some people today find the word old-fashioned.

part of speech: noun (a duke, dukes; the Duke of …)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A duke is a man of the highest rank of the nobility below a prince, in Britain and some other countries; he has a title such as "the Duke of York". 2) In history, a duke ruled a small land called a duchy. 3) (old slang, «dukes») Your dukes are your fists, as in "put up your dukes" (get ready to fight).
its sense in the lessons: Used in history lessons, stories about kings and castles, and news about the royal family (for example, princes who are also given the title Duke of Cambridge or Duke of Sussex). It tells the reader the person is very high in rank. Phrases: «the Duke of …», «the Duke and Duchess», «Your Grace» (how you speak to a duke), «put up your dukes».
examples from the lessons: The Duke of Wellington was a famous general. | The duke lived in a huge castle with a hundred rooms. | Prince William is also the Duke of Cambridge. | The Duke and Duchess waved from the carriage. | In the fairy tale, the duke wanted to marry the princess. | "Put up your dukes!" shouted the cartoon boxer. | The duke's land was called a duchy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun; capital D when it is part of a title («the Duke of Kent»), small d otherwise. Female form: duchess. His land: a duchy or dukedom. You address him as «Your Grace», not «Your Majesty» (that is for a king or queen).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A fighter is a person who fights, for example in boxing or martial arts, or in a war. 2) A fighter is someone who does not give up and keeps trying hard against problems or illness. 3) A fighter (fighter plane, fighter jet) is a small fast military aeroplane made to attack other aircraft. 4) A firefighter is a person whose job is to put out fires.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and news it tells the reader that someone is brave or tough, or that someone hits others. Praise use: "She's a real fighter" about a sick person or an athlete who never quits. In history lessons about wars you meet fighter planes and «freedom fighters». Phrases: «a born fighter», «a street fighter», «fighter pilot», «firefighter», «freedom fighter».
examples from the lessons: The boxer was a strong fighter. | Grandad was ill for months, but he's a real fighter. | Two fighter jets flew low over the beach. | The firefighters put out the fire in ten minutes. | Sam wasn't a fighter; he hated hitting anyone. | My little sister is a fighter and never gives up at chess. | The fighter pilot landed the plane safely.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun; formed from «fight» + -er (one who fights). «Firefighter» is one word and is the modern name for a fireman or firewoman. Calling someone «a fighter» can be praise (does not give up) or a worry (gets into fights); the context tells you which.

part of speech: noun (a lookout, lookouts; on the lookout); verb phrase «look out» (look out, looks out, looked out)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A lookout is a person who keeps watch for danger or for someone coming. 2) A lookout is a high place from which you can see far, such as a tower or hilltop point. 3) To be «on the lookout» for something means to watch and search for it. 4) (informal, UK) "That's your lookout" means it is your problem. The two-word verb «look out!» means "Be careful!".
its sense in the lessons: In stories, a lookout often stands guard while others do something (sailors, soldiers, or naughty children). In safety, «Look out!» is a warning shout. On walks and trips, a lookout point gives a view. Phrases: «keep a lookout», «on the lookout for», «stand lookout», «lookout tower», «Look out!».
examples from the lessons: The sailor in the crow's nest was the lookout. | Ben kept a lookout while we built the den. | We climbed to the lookout and saw the whole valley. | Be on the lookout for rabbits in the field. | "Look out! A car is coming!" | The lookout shouted when he saw land. | We're on the lookout for a cheaper bike.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun, written as one word: «a lookout». The warning verb is two words: «Look out!». Do not mix with «outlook» (a view of the future, or someone's attitude).

part of speech: noun (a peer, peers); verb (peer, peers, peered, peering)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To peer means to look very carefully or with difficulty at something, often narrowing your eyes or leaning forward. 2) Your peers are people of the same age, class or level as you, such as your classmates. 3) (UK) A peer is a member of the nobility, such as a lord, who may sit in the House of Lords.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, «peer» shows someone looking hard through fog, darkness or a small gap. In school talk, «peers» means classmates; «peer pressure» is when friends push you to do something, and «peer assessment» is when pupils mark each other's work. In UK citizenship lessons, peers sit in the House of Lords. Phrases: «peer into/at/through», «peer pressure», «peer review», «peer mentor», «your peers».
examples from the lessons: She peered through the keyhole. | Grandpa peered at the tiny writing on the box. | We peered into the dark cave. | Don't give in to peer pressure. | Today we'll do peer marking: swap books with your partner. | He was taller than most of his peers. | A lord is a peer in the House of Lords. | The owl peered down from the branch.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: peer, peered, peering; followed by a preposition (peer at, into, through). Noun: countable (one peer, many peers). Homophone: «pier» (a long platform going out into the sea). Trap: peer (look hard) is not the same as «peek» (quick look) or «peep».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Allegedly means "people say this is true, but it has not been proved". 2) (law, news) It is used by reporters and police so they do not say for certain that someone did something wrong before a court decides. 3) (informal, jokey) People sometimes say "allegedly" after a claim to show they don't quite believe it.
its sense in the lessons: Very common in news, gossip, tabloids and media lessons. It tells the reader that the fact is a claim, not proven, so a careful reader should keep an open mind. In lessons about rumours and fake news, it is a key warning word. Phrases: «allegedly stole», «was allegedly seen», «allegedly said».
examples from the lessons: The man allegedly took the money from the till. | The singer was allegedly seen at the café. | He allegedly broke the window, but nobody saw him do it. | The team allegedly cheated, but the judges are still checking. | "I'm the best footballer in the class – allegedly," laughed Jake. | The report says she allegedly lied about her age. | Allegedly, the shop is closing next month.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from «allege» (claim without proof) and «alleged». Pronounced a-LEJ-id-lee (four syllables). Trap: «allegedly» does NOT mean the thing happened; it means someone says so. In maths or fact questions, a claim marked «allegedly» is not a proven fact.

part of speech: noun, plural (boxers; a pair of boxers); singular «boxer» (a boxer, boxers)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Boxers (boxer shorts) are loose cotton underpants for men and boys that look like short shorts. 2) Boxers are people who fight with their fists in padded gloves in the sport of boxing. 3) A boxer is also a breed of strong, short-haired dog.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life it is mostly about underwear (in a clothes shop, laundry, packing for a trip) or about the sport of boxing. In stories it tells what someone is wearing or that people are fighting in a ring. Phrases: «a pair of boxers», «boxer shorts», «professional boxers», «a boxer dog».
examples from the lessons: He packed five pairs of boxers for the trip. | Dad walked around the house in his boxers. | The two boxers touched gloves before the fight. | Boxers train by skipping and running. | Our neighbour has a boxer called Max. | The boxer won by a knockout. | Boxer shorts are loose; briefs are tight.
note for the reader of a maths problem: For underwear «boxers» is plural like «trousers»: «my boxers are clean», «a pair of boxers». For sport and dogs it is the normal plural of «boxer». Underwear talk can make children giggle; it is not rude, just private.

part of speech: noun (a skirt, skirts); verb (skirt, skirts, skirted, skirting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A skirt is a piece of clothing worn by women and girls that hangs from the waist and has no separate legs. 2) The skirt of a dress or coat is the part below the waist. 3) To skirt something means to go round the edge of it. 4) To skirt (round) a problem or question means to avoid talking about it.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life it is about school uniform (skirt or trousers), shopping and clothes. In stories the verb shows a path going round something, or someone dodging a hard topic. Phrases: «a pleated skirt», «a school skirt», «skirt round the edge», «skirt the issue», «skirting board» (a strip at the bottom of a wall).
examples from the lessons: She wore a grey pleated skirt to school. | Girls may choose a skirt or trousers. | The path skirted the lake. | We skirted round the muddy field. | The politician skirted the question about money. | Her skirt swirled as she danced. | The kilt is a kind of skirt worn by Scottish men. | Mum painted the skirting board white.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: a skirt, skirts. Verb: skirted, skirting; often «skirt (round/around) something». A Scottish kilt looks like a skirt but is traditional men's dress. In some schools anyone may wear a skirt; trousers are always allowed for girls.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A traitor is a person who betrays their country, for example by helping its enemies. 2) A traitor is someone who betrays friends, a team or a group they belonged to, by giving away secrets or changing sides.
its sense in the lessons: In history and stories (spies, wars, kings) the word marks one of the worst crimes. In playground talk children shout "Traitor!" at someone who joins the other team or tells a secret, often half as a joke. Phrases: «a traitor to his country», «turn traitor», «You traitor!», «traitor's gate».
examples from the lessons: The traitor gave the secret plans to the enemy. | Guy Fawkes was called a traitor for his plot against the king. | "Traitor!" Jake joked when his friend joined the other team. | She felt like a traitor for telling Mum the secret. | In the story, the knight's best friend turned out to be a traitor. | Traitors were once taken through Traitors' Gate at the Tower of London. | He was no traitor; he only told the truth to stop someone getting hurt.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun. Related: betray, betrayal, treason (the crime of betraying your country), treacherous. Trap: telling a teacher when someone is in danger is not being a traitor; it is keeping people safe.

part of speech: proper noun (Windsor; the Windsors; Windsor Castle)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Windsor is a town in Berkshire, England, west of London, by the River Thames, home of Windsor Castle. 2) Windsor Castle is a very old castle there and one of the official homes of the British king or queen. 3) Windsor is the family name of the British royal family, "the House of Windsor" or "the Windsors". 4) Windsor is also a city in Ontario, Canada, opposite Detroit.
its sense in the lessons: Met in news about the royal family, history lessons on castles and kings, and geography of England and Canada. It tells the reader a story may be about the royals or a royal place. Phrases: «Windsor Castle», «the House of Windsor», «the Windsors», «a Windsor knot» (a tie knot), «Windsor chair».
examples from the lessons: The king spent the weekend at Windsor Castle. | Windsor is a town on the River Thames. | The Windsors are the British royal family. | The royal wedding took place in a chapel at Windsor. | We went on a school trip to Windsor and saw the guards. | Windsor in Canada is just across the river from Detroit. | Dad tied his tie with a Windsor knot.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A proper noun: always a capital W (here written lower case only because the dictionary lists words that way). Pronounced WIN-zer; the d is almost silent. Do not confuse with «windsurf» or «windscreen».

part of speech: noun (a justification, justifications; justification for something)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A justification is a good reason that shows something is right or fair. 2) Justification is the act of explaining why something was right. 3) (maths, school) A justification is the explanation of how you know an answer is correct. 4) (computers, printing) Justification is lining up text so both edges of a column are straight.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and science, "show your justification" means explain your reasoning, not just give the answer. In ethics lessons, pupils ask whether there is any justification for hitting back, lying or breaking a rule. Phrases: «no justification for», «there is some justification», «in justification», «give a justification».
examples from the lessons: There is no justification for bullying. | Write down your answer and a justification. | His justification was that he was protecting his little brother. | The teacher asked for a justification of each step. | Is there any justification for lying to a friend? | In justification, she said the bus was late. | Use full justification so both sides of the text are straight.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable for the idea («without justification»), countable for a single reason («two justifications»). Verb: justify (justified, justifying); adjective: justified, justifiable. In maths tests, marks often go to the justification, not just the final number.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unnamed means without a name, or whose name is not given. 2) (news) An unnamed person is someone whose name the reporter does not tell, often to protect them.
its sense in the lessons: In news it shows a source or person is kept secret ("an unnamed source said"). In stories it may describe a mysterious stranger or a place without a name. In maths or science, an unnamed point or quantity is one you have not labelled yet. Phrases: «an unnamed source», «an unnamed man», «remain unnamed».
examples from the lessons: An unnamed source told the newspaper about the plan. | The unnamed boy was only nine years old. | We sailed past an unnamed island on the map. | The parent wished to remain unnamed. | The new kitten was still unnamed after a week. | Label the unnamed angle "x". | An unnamed shop owner called the police.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: un- (not) + named. Usually before a noun («an unnamed source») or after «remain/stay/be». Trap: news stories with only unnamed sources are harder to check; a careful reader treats them with care. Close word: «nameless» (more for things that cannot or should not be named).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A waitress is a woman or girl whose job is to bring food and drinks to customers' tables in a café or restaurant and take their orders.
its sense in the lessons: Used in everyday life about cafés, diners and restaurants; often in maths word problems about bills and tips. Many places now use «server» or «waiting staff» for everyone. Phrases: «work as a waitress», «call the waitress», «tip the waitress».
examples from the lessons: The waitress brought us three glasses of lemonade. | My cousin works as a waitress on Saturdays. | We thanked the waitress and left a tip. | The waitress wrote down our order. | Mum asked the waitress for the bill. | The waitress carried four plates at once. | A waitress earns £8 an hour; how much does she earn in 5 hours?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun; plural «waitresses». Male form: waiter. Neutral forms: server, waiting staff. In the USA and Canada tipping (about a sixth to a fifth of the bill) is expected; in the UK, Ireland, Australia and New Zealand it is smaller or optional. In maths problems a "tip" is an extra amount added to the bill, often a percentage.

part of speech: adjective (decent, more decent, most decent); adverb decently
meaning for a pupil: 1) Decent means good enough, of an acceptable or fairly good quality. 2) A decent person is honest, kind and fair to others. 3) Decent means polite and respectable, following what people think is proper. 4) (informal) Are you decent? means "Are you dressed?" (so someone can come in).
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life it praises things or people in a calm way ("a decent meal", "a decent bloke"). In ethics lessons, "the decent thing to do" means the fair, kind choice. In UK and Australian slang, «decent» can mean "really good". Phrases: «a decent person», «do the decent thing», «a decent amount», «decent of you», «Are you decent?».
examples from the lessons: We had a decent lunch at the café. | He's a decent kid; he always helps others. | It was decent of you to share your crisps. | Get a decent night's sleep before the test. | "Can I come in? Are you decent?" "Yes, I'm dressed!" | The decent thing would be to say sorry. | She got a decent mark in maths.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced DEE-sent. Do not confuse with «descent» (going down, di-SENT) or «dissent» (disagreement). Opposite: indecent (rude, improper), which is a strong word. Noun: decency.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Ladylike describes behaviour that people used to think was polite, quiet and proper for a woman or girl, such as sitting neatly and speaking softly. 2) (often old-fashioned or critical) Saying something is "not ladylike" was used to stop girls running, shouting or getting dirty.
its sense in the lessons: Met in older stories and in lessons on fairness and gender. It tells the reader what some people expected of girls; modern lessons point out these rules were unfair, and that good manners are for everyone. Phrases: «not very ladylike», «ladylike behaviour», «sit in a ladylike way».
examples from the lessons: Great-Aunt Edith said climbing trees wasn't ladylike. | She gave a very unladylike burp and laughed. | The girls in the old book were taught to be ladylike. | Maddie didn't care about being ladylike; she wanted to win. | Her grandmother had ladylike manners and a soft voice. | "That's not ladylike!" "Neither is it gentlemanly – it's just rude!"
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective, not an adverb, even though it ends in -like. Opposite: unladylike. The male word is gentlemanly. Trap: «ladylike» is often a judgement about girls; kindness and good manners matter the same for boys and girls.

part of speech: noun (a mime, mimes; mime, uncountable); verb (mime, mimes, mimed, miming)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Mime is acting a story using only movements, faces and gestures, without words. 2) A mime is a performer who does this, often with a white painted face. 3) To mime means to show something with actions instead of words. 4) To mime a song means to move your lips as if singing while a recording plays.
its sense in the lessons: In drama lessons, games such as charades use mime. In stories, a character may mime a message when they cannot speak. In music videos and shows, «miming» to a recording is sometimes called cheating. Phrases: «in mime», «mime artist», «mime a word», «mime along to».
examples from the lessons: We acted out the story in mime. | The mime pretended to be trapped in a glass box. | Mime brushing your teeth. | In charades you have to mime the film title. | The pop star was caught miming at the concert. | She mimed "Call me" through the window. | Our drama teacher showed us how to mime pulling a rope.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: mimed, miming. «Mime» (the art) is uncountable; «a mime» (a performer or a short act) is countable. Rhymes with «time». Do not confuse with «mimic» (copy someone's voice or actions, often to make fun).

meaning for a pupil: 1) An onlooker is a person who watches something happen but does not take part, especially an accident, fight or event in the street.
its sense in the lessons: Used in news and stories about accidents, fights and shows. In lessons about bullying and safety, onlookers (bystanders) are told that they can help by getting an adult or calling for help rather than just watching or filming. Phrases: «a crowd of onlookers», «curious onlookers», «onlookers gathered».
examples from the lessons: A crowd of onlookers gathered round the crashed car. | Onlookers cheered as the firefighters saved the cat. | He was just an onlooker; he didn't join the fight. | Onlookers filmed the scuffle on their phones. | The street performer amazed the onlookers. | An onlooker called the ambulance. | Don't be a silent onlooker when someone is being bullied.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun, one word. Close words: bystander, spectator (who watches a sport or show on purpose), witness (who saw something and can tell what happened). An onlooker is not to blame, but can still help.

part of speech: noun (a recording, recordings; recording, uncountable); verb form of «record» (recording)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A recording is sound or pictures that have been stored so they can be played again, such as a song, video or voice message. 2) Recording is the act of storing sound or pictures. 3) (school, science) Recording means writing down results, such as measurements in a table. 4) It is the -ing form of «record»: "She is recording a song."
its sense in the lessons: In science, «recording results» means writing them clearly in a table or chart. In everyday life, recordings are videos, songs and voice notes; safety lessons warn about recording people without asking. Phrases: «a video recording», «a sound recording», «recording studio», «make a recording», «recording sheet».
examples from the lessons: We listened to a recording of the class play. | The band went into a recording studio. | Use the recording sheet to write down the temperatures. | She is recording a message for Grandma. | Please ask before recording anyone on your phone. | The police checked the camera recording. | This is an old recording of a famous speech.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun stress: re-COR-ding. Note «record» changes stress: a REC-ord (noun) but to re-CORD (verb). Countable when it is one item («two recordings»). Trap: in science, «recording» is not the same as «observing» – you observe, then you record.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A scandal is something wrong or shameful that people find out about and are shocked by, such as a famous person lying or cheating. 2) Scandal is talk and gossip about such things. 3) (informal) "It's a scandal" means something is very unfair or wrong.
its sense in the lessons: Very common in news, tabloids and gossip. In media lessons, children learn that a scandal is often reported loudly and some details may be rumours. Phrases: «cause a scandal», «a political scandal», «a scandal broke», «caught up in a scandal», «It's a scandal that…».
examples from the lessons: The scandal was on the front page of every newspaper. | The footballer was caught up in a cheating scandal. | It's a scandal that the park has no toilets. | The minister lost her job after the scandal. | Tabloids love scandal. | The village was buzzing with scandal about the missing cake. | When the scandal broke, the singer said sorry.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable for one event («two scandals»), uncountable for gossip in general («full of scandal»). Adjective: scandalous; verb: scandalise/scandalize (shock). Not every rumour is a true scandal; check the facts.

part of speech: noun (a scuffle, scuffles); verb (scuffle, scuffles, scuffled, scuffling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A scuffle is a short, confused fight with pushing and grabbing, usually not very serious. 2) To scuffle means to fight in this way. 3) To scuffle (along) means to walk dragging your feet, or to make a scraping noise.
its sense in the lessons: Used in news, school incident reports and stories about fights in the playground or at football matches. It tells the reader the fight was short and messy, not a big battle. Phrases: «a scuffle broke out», «a brief scuffle», «be involved in a scuffle», «scuffle with».
examples from the lessons: A scuffle broke out in the lunch queue. | Two boys scuffled over a football. | There was a brief scuffle, but no one was hurt. | Police broke up a scuffle outside the stadium. | We heard something scuffling in the attic. | He scuffled along in his slippers. | The teacher stepped in before the scuffle got worse.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun; verb scuffled, scuffling. Close words: scrap, tussle, altercation (formal), brawl (bigger and wilder). Not the same as «shuffle» (walk slowly dragging feet, or mix cards), although they sound alike.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (church) An abbey is a building, or group of buildings, where monks or nuns live and pray together, led by an abbot or abbess. 2) An abbey is also a large church that was once part of such a place, such as Westminster Abbey in London.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons (monks, Henry VIII closing the monasteries, castles) and church life lessons. In news, royal weddings and coronations take place at Westminster Abbey. Phrases: «Westminster Abbey», «a ruined abbey», «the abbey church», «Downton Abbey» (a TV series).
examples from the lessons: Monks lived and prayed at the abbey. | We visited the ruins of an old abbey. | Kings and queens are crowned in Westminster Abbey. | The abbey bells rang for evening prayers. | The abbot was in charge of the abbey. | Many abbeys were closed long ago and fell into ruins. | Nuns at the abbey made honey and candles.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun; plural «abbeys» (vowel before y, so just add -s). «An abbey». Leaders: abbot (man), abbess (woman). Close words: monastery (monks), convent or nunnery (nuns), priory (a smaller house).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Balmoral Castle is a large castle in the Highlands of Scotland, a private holiday home of the British royal family. 2) (clothing) A balmoral is a flat Scottish cap, or a kind of laced boot.
its sense in the lessons: Met in news about the royal family, who often spend late summer there, and in geography or history about Scotland. It tells the reader the story is about the royals or Scotland. Phrases: «at Balmoral», «Balmoral Castle», «the Balmoral estate».
examples from the lessons: The royal family spends the summer holidays at Balmoral. | Balmoral Castle is in the Scottish Highlands. | The queen loved walking her dogs at Balmoral. | Balmoral is surrounded by hills, forests and rivers. | Visitors can see the gardens at Balmoral in some months. | The piper wore a balmoral cap.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A proper noun: write it with a capital B (Balmoral). Pronounced bal-MOR-al. It is a private home of the royal family, not a palace owned by the state like Buckingham Palace.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A cadet is a young person training to be an officer in the army, navy, air force or police. 2) A cadet is a child or teenager in a youth club linked to the armed forces, such as Air Cadets or Sea Cadets, which teaches skills, drill and teamwork.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life children may join Army Cadets, Sea Cadets or Air Cadets after school. In stories it tells the reader the character is young, in training and in uniform. Phrases: «police cadet», «air cadets», «cadet force», «naval cadet», «join the cadets».
examples from the lessons: My brother joined the Air Cadets when he was twelve. | The cadets marched in the parade. | She is a police cadet and wants to be a detective. | Sea Cadets learn to sail and tie knots. | The young cadet saluted the officer. | Cadets wear a uniform and polish their boots. | The cadet camp taught first aid and map reading.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun. Stress on the second syllable: ka-DET. Being a cadet is not the same as being a soldier; cadets are learning and are often still at school.

part of speech: noun (a cannonball, cannonballs); verb (informal: cannonball, cannonballed)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A cannonball is a heavy round metal or stone ball that used to be fired from a cannon. 2) (informal) A cannonball is a jump into a swimming pool with your knees tucked up to your chest, which makes a big splash. 3) (informal) To cannonball means to move very fast and with force.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons and pirate stories, cannonballs are fired in battles and sieges. At the swimming pool, a "cannonball" is a fun jump, though lifeguards may stop it when people are near. In science, cannonballs are used to talk about falling objects and gravity. Phrases: «fire a cannonball», «do a cannonball», «cannonball run».
examples from the lessons: The pirates loaded a cannonball into the cannon. | You can still see a cannonball stuck in the old castle wall. | Jake did a cannonball and soaked everyone. | No cannonballs in the shallow end! | The cannonball hit the ship's mast. | A heavy cannonball and a light ball fall at almost the same speed if there is little air. | The dog came cannonballing down the stairs.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun, one word. Trap and myth: a heavier object does not fall much faster than a lighter one of the same shape; air resistance makes the difference. Safety: only cannonball into deep water when no one is near.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (church) A chapel is a small church, or a room for Christian prayer inside a bigger building such as a school, hospital, prison, palace or airport. 2) A chapel is a small part of a large church or cathedral with its own altar. 3) (UK) Chapel is also the church of some Protestant groups, such as Methodists or Baptists, especially in Wales: "We go to chapel."
its sense in the lessons: In church-life lessons, schools with chapels hold services there; in stories, weddings and quiet prayers happen in chapels. Royal weddings have taken place in St George's Chapel at Windsor. Phrases: «school chapel», «a wedding chapel», «go to chapel», «chapel of rest» (where a person who has died lies before the funeral).
examples from the lessons: Our school has a little chapel where we have assembly on Fridays. | They got married in a chapel by the sea. | The hospital chapel is open for anyone who wants to pray or be quiet. | St George's Chapel is at Windsor Castle. | Grandma goes to chapel every Sunday. | The cathedral has many side chapels. | The family visited Grandad at the chapel of rest to say goodbye.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: a chapel, chapels. In UK English «go to chapel» without «the» means attending services there. A chapel is smaller than a church; a cathedral is the main church of a bishop.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A mural is a large picture painted directly onto a wall or ceiling.
its sense in the lessons: In art lessons, classes may design a mural for the playground or corridor. In towns, murals show local history, heroes or nature. In history, cave paintings and church wall paintings are early murals. Phrases: «paint a mural», «a school mural», «a street mural», «a wall mural».
examples from the lessons: Our class painted a mural of the ocean in the hall. | The mural on the bridge shows the town's history. | Artists painted a huge mural of footballers on the side of the building. | The church had old murals of Bible stories. | We planned the mural on paper first. | The mural covered the whole wall.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun. From Latin «murus», wall. A mural is painted on the wall itself, not hung on it like a framed painting. Not the same as graffiti, which is often done without permission.

part of speech: noun (a parody, parodies); verb (parody, parodies, parodied, parodying)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A parody is a funny copy of a song, story, film or style that exaggerates it to make people laugh or to make fun of it. 2) To parody something means to copy it in a funny exaggerated way. 3) A parody of something is a very bad, unfair version of it, as in "a parody of justice".
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons, children read and write parodies of poems and fairy tales, and in media lessons they learn to tell a parody from real news (some fake news sites are parody). Phrases: «a parody of», «a parody song», «parody account», «a parody of justice».
examples from the lessons: We wrote a parody of "Twinkle Twinkle Little Star" about homework. | The comedy show did a parody of the news. | That account is a parody; it isn't really the president. | The film parodies old spy movies. | The trial was a parody of justice. | His parody of the teacher's walk made everyone laugh. | Parody is funny when it is clever, not cruel.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: parodies; verb: parodied, parodying (y → ie before -s/-ed, but stays before -ing). Stress: PAR-o-dee. Close words: spoof, satire, send-up. Trap: a parody can look real, so check before believing or sharing it.

part of speech: noun (a secretary, secretaries; Secretary of State)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A secretary is a person whose job is to help in an office by typing letters, answering the phone, keeping records and arranging meetings. 2) The school secretary works in the school office and deals with visitors, absences, lunch money and phone calls. 3) A Secretary (in government) is the head of a government department, such as the Home Secretary (UK) or the Secretary of State (USA). 4) The secretary of a club writes down what happens at meetings.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday school life the school secretary is who you see when you arrive late or feel ill. In news and citizenship lessons, «Secretary» names top government ministers. Phrases: «school secretary», «Home Secretary», «Foreign Secretary», «Secretary of State», «club secretary».
examples from the lessons: The school secretary phoned my mum when I felt sick. | Hand your letter to the secretary in the office. | The Home Secretary spoke on the news. | My aunt is a secretary at a law firm. | Our club voted Maya as secretary. | The secretary wrote down what was said at the meeting. | The Secretary of State visited Canada.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: secretaries (y → ies). Pronounced SEK-re-tree (UK) or SEK-re-tair-ee (USA). Note the second r: secRetary. Capital S in government titles.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Toughness is being strong and hard to break, bend or damage. 2) Toughness is being brave and strong in your mind, able to put up with pain or hard times. 3) Toughness of meat or food is being hard to cut or chew. 4) (materials science) Toughness is how much energy a material can take before it breaks.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about materials, pupils test toughness and compare it with hardness and strength. In sports and stories, toughness means not giving up. In lessons on fights and courage, children learn that real toughness can mean walking away or standing up for others, not hitting. Phrases: «mental toughness», «show toughness», «toughness test».
examples from the lessons: Rubber boots need toughness to survive the mud. | We tested the toughness of three kinds of paper. | The goalkeeper showed real toughness after the injury. | The toughness of the steak made it hard to chew. | True toughness is staying calm when someone wants a fight. | Glass is hard but has little toughness, so it shatters.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: no «a», no plural. From «tough» + -ness. Science trap: hard is not the same as tough. A diamond and glass are hard (hard to scratch) but can shatter; rubber is not hard but is tough.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Aggression is angry or violent behaviour or feelings that make a person or animal want to attack or hurt others. 2) Aggression is a country or army attacking another without being attacked first. 3) (sport) Aggression can mean playing with great force and energy.
its sense in the lessons: In lessons about behaviour, fights and feelings, pupils learn to notice aggression in themselves and others and to calm down. In science, animals show aggression to protect food or young. In history, «an act of aggression» starts a war. Phrases: «act of aggression», «show aggression», «signs of aggression», «verbal aggression».
examples from the lessons: The dog showed aggression when someone touched its food. | Shouting and pushing are kinds of aggression. | Try deep breaths when you feel aggression building up. | The invasion was an act of aggression. | The players were told to control their aggression on the pitch. | Teasing can lead to aggression if nobody stops it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable (no «an aggression» in ordinary use). Spelling: two g's and two s's – aGGreSSion. Adjective: aggressive; person: aggressor. Being assertive (standing up for yourself calmly) is not aggression.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An alley is a narrow lane or path between or behind buildings. 2) A bowling alley is a building or lane where people play bowling. 3) (informal) Something that is "up your alley" (also "right up your street") is the kind of thing you like.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, alleys can be dark, quiet or a shortcut; in safety lessons children are told to avoid dark alleys alone and to use busy, well-lit routes. In everyday life bowling alleys are a fun place for parties. Phrases: «a back alley», «a dark alley», «bowling alley», «blind alley» (a dead end), «up my alley».
examples from the lessons: The cat ran down the alley behind the shops. | Don't take the dark alley home; use the main road. | We had my birthday party at the bowling alley. | The alley was too narrow for a car. | This puzzle book is right up your alley. | The thief escaped through a back alley. | The plan led us up a blind alley.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun; plural «alleys» (just add -s). Do not confuse with «ally» (a friend or partner in a fight, AL-eye) or «alloy» (a mix of metals). «Alleyway» means the same as alley.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal, news and police) An assailant is a person who attacks someone physically.
its sense in the lessons: A formal word used in news, police reports and court cases, not in everyday chat. It tells the reader someone was attacked and this is the attacker. Phrases: «the assailant fled», «an unknown assailant», «describe the assailant».
examples from the lessons: The assailant ran off before the police arrived. | The victim could not see the assailant's face. | Police are searching for the assailant. | The shopkeeper fought off his assailant. | The two assailants were later arrested. | Witnesses described the assailant as tall with a red hat.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun; formal. Everyday words: attacker, mugger. Related: assail (attack), assault (an attack). Pronounced a-SAY-lent.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Betrayal is breaking someone's trust, for example by telling their secret, lying to them or helping their enemy. 2) A betrayal is one act of this kind. 3) Betrayal of a country is helping its enemies (treason).
its sense in the lessons: In stories, betrayal is a big turning point: a friend tells a secret or changes sides. In ethics lessons, pupils discuss whether telling an adult about danger is betrayal (it is not; it keeps people safe). In Bible lessons, Judas's betrayal of Jesus is a famous story. Phrases: «a sense of betrayal», «an act of betrayal», «feel betrayed».
examples from the lessons: Telling everyone her secret was a betrayal. | She felt a deep sense of betrayal when her friend laughed at her. | In the Bible, Judas's betrayal of Jesus happened for thirty silver coins. | The spy's betrayal cost many lives. | It wasn't a betrayal to tell the teacher that Sam was being hurt. | The film is about friendship and betrayal.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable for one act («two betrayals»), uncountable for the idea. Verb: betray (betrayed, betraying); person: traitor. Trap: telling to keep someone safe is not betrayal; spreading gossip to hurt is.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A bulldog is a breed of strong dog with a short, flat face, a big head, short legs and loose wrinkly skin. 2) (figurative) A bulldog is a person who is very stubborn and brave and never lets go of a task. 3) A bulldog clip is a strong metal clip for holding papers together.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life bulldogs are pets; in British history and cartoons the bulldog is a symbol of Britain's toughness ("the British bulldog"). Many sports teams are called "the Bulldogs". In PE, "British Bulldog" is a rough chasing game some schools no longer allow. Phrases: «British bulldog», «bulldog spirit», «bulldog clip», «French bulldog».
examples from the lessons: Our neighbour's bulldog snores very loudly. | Bulldogs can find it hard to breathe in hot weather. | Use a bulldog clip to keep your worksheets together. | The team mascot is a bulldog. | She tackled the problem like a bulldog and never gave up. | We played British Bulldog until someone fell over. | A French bulldog has big, bat-like ears.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun, one word. Myth: bulldogs are not usually fierce; most are gentle. The name came from long ago, when such dogs were used in a cruel sport with bulls, which is now banned.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Cowardly means not brave, too afraid to face danger, pain or something difficult. 2) A cowardly act is mean and unfair because the person avoids risk, such as attacking someone weaker or hiding behind others.
its sense in the lessons: In stories it is a strong criticism of a character; the Cowardly Lion in The Wizard of Oz is a famous example. In lessons about fights and fear, pupils learn that walking away from a fight is not cowardly, while bullying someone smaller is. Phrases: «a cowardly act», «a cowardly attack», «a cowardly lion».
examples from the lessons: The Cowardly Lion wanted to be brave. | Picking on a younger child is cowardly. | It was cowardly of him to blame his little brother. | Sam thought refusing to fight was cowardly, but his dad said it was wise. | The newspaper called the attack cowardly. | Sending nasty messages without a name is cowardly.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It looks like an adverb (ends in -ly) but it is an adjective: «a cowardly boy». From «coward» + -ly. Noun: cowardice. Opposite: brave, courageous. Trap: feeling scared is not cowardly; everyone feels fear. Courage is doing the right thing anyway.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (law) Defamation is saying or writing something untrue about a person that damages their good name. 2) Defamation in writing is called libel; spoken defamation is called slander.
its sense in the lessons: Met in news, media and law lessons. It tells the reader that someone is accused of spreading damaging lies, and can be taken to court. In lessons about gossip and the internet, pupils learn that posting false rumours can hurt people and even break the law. Phrases: «sue for defamation», «defamation of character», «a defamation case».
examples from the lessons: The actor sued the newspaper for defamation. | Spreading lies online about someone can be defamation. | The judge said the article was defamation because it was not true. | A defamation case can cost a lot of money. | It isn't defamation if what you say is true and fair. | Calling someone a thief without proof could be defamation of character.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Verb: defame; adjective: defamatory. Pronounced def-a-MAY-shun. Trap: the key is «untrue» and «damaging»; an honest opinion or a proven fact is not usually defamation.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A disco is a party or event where people dance to recorded pop music, often with coloured lights. 2) A school disco is an evening dance party for pupils at school. 3) Disco is a kind of dance music with a strong beat, popular long ago and still played at parties.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday children's life, the school disco, a birthday disco or a disco at a holiday camp are exciting events. In stories it shows a party atmosphere. Phrases: «school disco», «disco lights», «disco ball», «go to a disco», «disco music».
examples from the lessons: The school disco is on Friday night. | We danced under the flashing disco lights. | Grandma loves old disco music. | A silver disco ball hung from the ceiling. | Tickets for the disco cost £2 each. | Lily was too shy to dance at her first disco.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable for the event (plural discos), uncountable for the music style. Short for «discotheque». In the USA a school disco is more often called «a school dance».

part of speech: noun (a duchess, duchesses; the Duchess of …)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A duchess is a woman who is married to a duke, or a woman who holds the rank of duke herself. 2) (informal, UK) "Duchess" is sometimes a friendly or teasing way to speak to a woman, especially one who seems grand.
its sense in the lessons: Used in news about the royal family (for example the Duchess of Cambridge or the Duchess of Sussex), in history, and in fairy tales. It tells the reader the woman has a very high rank. Phrases: «the Duke and Duchess», «Duchess of …», «Your Grace».
examples from the lessons: The Duchess visited a children's hospital. | The Duke and Duchess waved to the crowd. | In the story the duchess wore a dress covered in jewels. | A duchess is addressed as "Your Grace". | The duchess opened the new library. | "Mind your step, Duchess," joked the bus driver.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun; plural duchesses. Capital D in titles. Male form: duke. Her lands: a duchy. Spelling: ends in -ess like «princess».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Esteem is great respect and good opinion of someone. 2) Self-esteem is how much you value and respect yourself. 3) (formal) To esteem someone means to respect and admire them a lot.
its sense in the lessons: In PSHE and wellbeing lessons, «self-esteem» is common: feeling good about who you are. In stories or speeches, someone is "held in high esteem" when people respect them. Phrases: «hold someone in high esteem», «self-esteem», «low self-esteem», «a token of our esteem», «highly esteemed».
examples from the lessons: The teacher was held in high esteem by everyone. | Bullying can damage a child's self-esteem. | Praise for effort can help build self-esteem. | The doctor was a highly esteemed scientist. | Please accept this gift as a token of our esteem. | She had low self-esteem until she joined the drama club.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun is uncountable. Verb: esteemed, esteeming (formal). Adjective: esteemed. Do not mix up with «estimate» (a rough guess of a number), which looks similar.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Fierceness is being wild, angry and ready to attack, like a fierce animal. 2) Fierceness is very great strength or force, such as of a storm, fire or competition. 3) Fierceness can mean strong, passionate feeling, such as fierce love or loyalty.
its sense in the lessons: In science and nature lessons it describes predators; in stories it describes animals, warriors, storms and strong-willed characters. Phrases: «the fierceness of the storm», «with fierceness», «the fierceness of the battle».
examples from the lessons: The tiger's fierceness frightened the visitors. | The fierceness of the wind blew the fence down. | She defended her little brother with surprising fierceness. | We were amazed by the fierceness of the competition. | The dog's fierceness was only an act; it was really scared. | The fierceness of the fire made it hard to get close.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. From «fierce» + -ness. Spelling: «ie» as in «fierce» (i before e). Close words: ferocity, intensity.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An intermediary is a person or group who goes between two sides to help them talk, agree or make a deal. 2) (formal adjective) Intermediary means in the middle, between two stages or things.
its sense in the lessons: In lessons about conflict, a teacher or a peer mediator can act as an intermediary between two pupils who have fallen out. In news, countries use intermediaries to help end wars or free hostages. In business, an intermediary connects buyers and sellers. Phrases: «act as an intermediary», «through an intermediary», «a go-between».
examples from the lessons: The teacher acted as an intermediary between the two angry boys. | The countries talked through an intermediary. | An estate agent is an intermediary between the buyer and the seller. | Maya was the intermediary when her friends fell out. | The deal was made through an intermediary. | Caterpillar to butterfly passes through an intermediary stage, the chrysalis.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: intermediaries. A long formal word: everyday words are «go-between» or «middleman». Similar: mediator (helps people solve a quarrel). Related adjective: intermediate (in the middle level).

meaning for a pupil: 1) An intervention is when someone steps in to change what is happening, especially to stop a problem or help. 2) (school) An intervention is extra help given to pupils who need it, such as a reading group. 3) (medicine) A medical intervention is a treatment or operation. 4) (politics) Intervention is when a country gets involved in another country's affairs, sometimes with soldiers.
its sense in the lessons: In school life, teachers' intervention stops fights; "intervention groups" give extra support. In news, governments make interventions in wars or the economy. In lessons about bullying, bystander intervention means helping someone instead of watching. Phrases: «thanks to the intervention of», «early intervention», «military intervention», «intervention group».
examples from the lessons: Thanks to the teacher's quick intervention, nobody got hurt. | I go to a reading intervention group on Tuesdays. | Early intervention can stop small problems getting big. | The doctors said no intervention was needed. | The goal was saved by the goalkeeper's last-second intervention. | Many people argued about the military intervention.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable for single actions («two interventions»), uncountable for the idea. Verb: intervene (intervened, intervening). Spelling: inter- + vention. Stress: in-ter-VEN-shun.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Mistreatment is treating a person or animal cruelly or unfairly, for example hurting them, starving them or not caring for them.
its sense in the lessons: In lessons about rights, safety and animals, mistreatment is something to report to a trusted adult or the RSPCA (UK) or similar groups. In news and history it describes cruelty to workers, prisoners or animals. Phrases: «mistreatment of animals», «suffer mistreatment», «report mistreatment».
examples from the lessons: The farmer was fined for the mistreatment of his horses. | Mistreatment of children is against the law. | The prisoners suffered terrible mistreatment. | If you see mistreatment of an animal, tell an adult. | The charity helps dogs rescued from mistreatment. | Calling names every day is a kind of mistreatment too.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Verb: mistreat (mistreated). Prefix «mis-» means badly or wrongly (mislead, misbehave). Close words: abuse, cruelty, neglect (not caring), ill-treatment.

part of speech: adjective; past form of «muddle» (muddle, muddles, muddled, muddling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Muddled means confused and not thinking clearly. 2) Muddled means mixed up and untidy, in the wrong order. 3) It is the past form of the verb «muddle»: to mix things up or confuse them.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, a muddled answer has steps in the wrong order; teachers ask for clear working. In stories, a muddled character is confused, perhaps tired, old or scared. Phrases: «get muddled», «muddled up», «muddled thinking», «muddle through» (manage somehow).
examples from the lessons: I got muddled and added instead of taking away. | The papers were all muddled up on the floor. | Grandpa gets a bit muddled about names. | Her story was muddled and hard to follow. | He muddled the twins up again. | After the long trip I felt tired and muddled. | We muddled through the quiz without our best player.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: muddle, muddled, muddling. Noun: a muddle (a mess or confusion: «in a muddle»). Mostly British; Americans also say «mixed up». Not the same as «muddy» (covered in mud).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Nameless means having no name or whose name is not known. 2) Nameless means whose name is kept secret on purpose. 3) A nameless feeling (fear, dread) is too strange or strong to describe.
its sense in the lessons: In stories it creates mystery: a nameless stranger, a nameless dread. In news it is like «unnamed». In history, nameless soldiers or workers are people whose names were lost. Phrases: «a nameless fear», «who shall remain nameless» (a joke way of not naming someone).
examples from the lessons: A nameless stranger knocked at the door. | The stray cat was nameless until we called it Biscuit. | Someone, who shall remain nameless, ate all the biscuits! | She felt a nameless fear in the dark wood. | The tomb holds a nameless soldier. | The river was nameless on the old map.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: name + -less (without). «Who shall remain nameless» is a playful phrase meaning "I won't say who, but you know". Close word: unnamed.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal, UK) Posh means very smart, expensive and fancy, like a posh hotel or a posh car. 2) (informal, UK) A posh person is from a rich, upper-class family, or speaks and acts like one. 3) "Talk posh" means to speak in a very proper, upper-class accent.
its sense in the lessons: Very common in British, Irish, Australian and New Zealand speech, sometimes as teasing. It tells the reader about money, class and how people seem. In lessons about kindness, children learn not to judge people by whether they seem posh or not. Phrases: «a posh restaurant», «talk posh», «posh school», «posh nosh» (fancy food), «Posh Spice».
examples from the lessons: We went to a posh restaurant for Grandma's birthday. | The new kid talks a bit posh. | That's a posh car! | They live in a posh part of town. | Mum put on her posh voice on the phone. | We had sandwiches, nothing posh. | Don't tease him for being posh; it isn't his fault.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal; mainly British. Comparatives: posher, poshest. Myth: the story that «posh» comes from "port out, starboard home" on ships is almost certainly not true; nobody knows the real origin. It can sound mocking, so use it kindly.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The prostate is a small gland in men and boys, under the bladder, that helps make fluid used in making babies. 2) (medicine) Prostate problems or prostate cancer are illnesses of this gland, common in older men.
its sense in the lessons: Met in adult life lessons, health talk and news, often when a grandad or older man is ill or having a check-up. It tells the reader the illness is a man's illness. Phrases: «prostate cancer», «prostate gland», «prostate test», «enlarged prostate».
examples from the lessons: Grandad went to hospital to have his prostate checked. | Only men have a prostate. | Prostate cancer is one of the most common cancers in older men. | The doctor said finding it early helps a lot. | Many men walk and run to raise money for prostate cancer research. | An enlarged prostate can make an older man need the toilet often.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable but usually «the prostate». Trap: do not confuse with «prostrate» (lying flat on the ground, face down), which has an extra r. It is a normal body part, not rude; doctors and nurses talk about it plainly.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A pursuer is someone who is chasing or following another person or animal to try to catch them.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, chases and adventure tales, the pursuer is the one chasing; the hero may hide from pursuers. In nature lessons, a predator is the pursuer of its prey. In police news, «escape his pursuers». Phrases: «escape from pursuers», «shake off a pursuer», «in hot pursuit».
examples from the lessons: The fox ran into a hole to escape its pursuers. | The thief looked back at his pursuers. | The rabbit was faster than its pursuer. | The hero hid in a cave until his pursuers had gone. | The cheetah is a fast pursuer but tires quickly. | She shook off her pursuers by climbing over the wall.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun. From «pursue» (to chase, or to work towards a goal) + -er. Related noun: pursuit («in hot pursuit»). Spelling: pursuer has «-suer» at the end.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A thug is a violent, rough person, especially a criminal who hurts people. 2) (informal) People sometimes call someone a thug if they behave in a bullying, aggressive way.
its sense in the lessons: In news, stories and police dramas, thugs are attackers, muggers or troublemakers. In sport, a player who fouls roughly may be called a thug by fans. Phrases: «a gang of thugs», «a hired thug», «act like a thug», «thuggish».
examples from the lessons: A gang of thugs smashed the shop windows. | The newspaper called the attackers cowardly thugs. | Don't act like a thug just because you're bigger. | The thug was caught on camera and arrested. | The fans called the defender a thug after the foul. | In the film, the boss sent two thugs to frighten the shopkeeper.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun; a strong, insulting word. Adjective: thuggish; behaviour: thuggery. Calling a person a thug is name-calling; it is better to describe what they did.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A troublemaker is a person who often causes problems, for example by breaking rules, starting fights or upsetting others on purpose.
its sense in the lessons: Common in school life and stories; a teacher may move a troublemaker to the front. It tells the reader the character tends to misbehave, although stories often show a "troublemaker" has reasons or can change. Phrases: «a real troublemaker», «a bit of a troublemaker», «known as a troublemaker».
examples from the lessons: The teacher sat the troublemaker near her desk. | Jake had been called a troublemaker since infant school. | The troublemakers were sent to the head's office. | She was not a troublemaker; she was just bored. | One troublemaker spoiled the trip for everyone. | Don't label him a troublemaker; give him a chance.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun, one word: trouble + maker. Close words: rascal, rebel, stirrer (UK informal). Trap: labels stick; a child who once caused trouble is not always a troublemaker.

part of speech: noun (a tutor, tutors); verb (tutor, tutors, tutored, tutoring)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A tutor is a teacher who teaches one pupil or a small group, often at home or after school. 2) (UK school) A form tutor is the teacher who looks after a class in secondary school and takes the register. 3) (university) A tutor teaches and guides students. 4) To tutor means to teach someone in this way.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life children may have a maths or reading tutor. In UK schools, «tutor time» or «tutor group» is the start-of-day class meeting. Phrases: «private tutor», «form tutor», «tutor group», «maths tutor», «tutor time».
examples from the lessons: My tutor comes on Wednesdays to help with spelling. | Our form tutor reads the notices every morning. | She tutors younger kids in reading. | A tutor helped him get ready for the test. | We discussed the trip in tutor time. | Big sister tutored me in fractions. | The tutor charges £20 an hour; how much for 3 hours?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun; verb tutored, tutoring. Spelling ends -or (like doctor, actor). Related: tutorial (a lesson, or step-by-step guide such as a video tutorial).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Acceptance is agreeing to take something that is offered, such as a gift, invitation or job. 2) Acceptance is welcoming someone into a group and treating them as one of you. 3) Acceptance is calmly agreeing that something is true or cannot be changed, even if it is sad. 4) An acceptance (letter) is a message saying "yes" to an offer or a place.
its sense in the lessons: In PSHE lessons, acceptance means including people who are different. In stories about loss, acceptance is coming to terms with sad news. In adult life, people get acceptance letters from schools or jobs. Phrases: «acceptance of others», «gain acceptance», «acceptance letter», «acceptance speech».
examples from the lessons: Thank you for your acceptance of our invitation. | She got an acceptance letter from the new school. | The new boy felt acceptance when the team picked him. | Acceptance of others means respecting differences. | After a while, Grandma found acceptance that Grandad had passed away. | The winner gave a short acceptance speech.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable; countable for letters/replies. Verb: accept; adjective: acceptable. Spelling: -ance (not -ence). Do not confuse «accept» (take, agree) with «except» (apart from).

meaning for a pupil: 1) An aggressor is a person, group or country that starts a fight, attack or war.
its sense in the lessons: In history and news, the aggressor is the side that attacked first. In school fights and in lessons about fairness, teachers try to find out who was the aggressor and who was defending. Phrases: «the aggressor», «act as aggressor», «unprovoked aggressor».
examples from the lessons: The teacher asked who was the aggressor in the fight. | In the war, the invading country was the aggressor. | He wasn't the aggressor; he was only defending himself. | The aggressor pushed first and then ran away. | Countries came together to stop the aggressor. | Usually the aggressor is not the one who gets most hurt.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun. From «aggression» (attacking behaviour). Opposite: victim, defender. Spelling: two g's and two s's: aGGreSSor. Trap: the aggressor is not always the one who hits hardest; it is the one who started it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Arnica is a yellow flower that grows in mountains, related to daisies. 2) Arnica is a cream or gel made from this plant that some people put on bruises and sore muscles.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life parents may rub arnica cream on a bruise after a knock. In science lessons, it is an example of a plant used in folk remedies. It is not to be swallowed: the plant is poisonous if eaten. Phrases: «arnica cream», «arnica gel», «rub on arnica».
examples from the lessons: Mum put arnica cream on my bruised knee. | Arnica grows on sunny mountain slopes. | Jake came home covered in bruises, and his nan reached for the arnica. | Never eat arnica; it can make you very ill. | The football coach keeps arnica gel in his bag. | Some people say arnica helps bruises; scientists are still not sure how much.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Pronounced AR-ni-ca. Myth/trap: there is little strong scientific proof that arnica heals bruises faster; homeopathic «arnica» tablets contain almost none of the plant. Safety: use on unbroken skin only, never swallow the plant or cream.
