meaning for a pupil: 1) Bingo is a game where players have cards with numbers, and the winner is the first to cross off all the numbers in a line or on the card as they are called out. 2) (interjection, informal) "Bingo!" means "Yes! I've found it" or "Exactly right".
its sense in the lessons: Bingo is played at fairs, holiday camps, care homes, church halls and classrooms (maths bingo, word bingo). The caller shouts numbers, sometimes with funny rhymes ("legs eleven"). In maths lessons bingo practises number facts and times tables. Phrases: «bingo hall», «bingo card», «play bingo», «full house», «Bingo!».
examples from the lessons: Nan plays bingo at the community hall every Thursday. | We played times-table bingo in maths. | "Seven times eight?" "Fifty-six!" "Bingo!" | Cross off the number if it's on your card. | Bingo! I've found my lost shoe! | The first person to fill the card shouts "House!" | At the care home, the residents love bingo.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable as a game; no «a». As an interjection it is always with an exclamation mark. In maths, bingo numbers are usually 1 to 90 (UK) or 1 to 75 (USA); each number is equally likely to be called.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A bodyguard is a person whose job is to protect an important or famous person from being attacked or harmed. 2) A group of such guards is also called a bodyguard.
its sense in the lessons: In news and stories about royals, presidents and pop stars, bodyguards walk close beside them. In children's play, a big friend may be jokingly called someone's bodyguard. Phrases: «personal bodyguard», «hire a bodyguard», «surrounded by bodyguards».
examples from the lessons: The singer arrived with two bodyguards. | The president's bodyguards wore dark glasses. | The prince's bodyguard walked one step behind him. | My big brother acts like my bodyguard at the park. | A bodyguard must stay calm and alert. | The bodyguard stopped the crowd from pushing.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun, one word: body + guard. Close words: guard, minder (UK informal), security officer.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Clumsily means in an awkward, careless way, so that you knock things over, drop things or move badly. 2) Clumsily means said or done without skill or tact, so that it sounds awkward or rude.
its sense in the lessons: In stories it describes a character tripping, dropping things or saying something awkward. In writing lessons, a sentence that is «clumsily written» needs to be made smoother. Phrases: «clumsily knocked over», «clumsily written», «move clumsily».
examples from the lessons: He clumsily knocked over the paint pot. | The puppy ran clumsily across the slippery floor. | She clumsily tried to say sorry. | This sentence is clumsily written; try making it shorter. | The baby walked clumsily on her first steps. | He clumsily spilled juice all over his homework.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from «clumsy» (y → i + -ly). Noun: clumsiness. Spelling: c-l-u-m-s-i-l-y, with no letter b. Do not write «clumsly».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A confrontation is an angry argument or fight between people or groups who disagree. 2) A confrontation is a meeting where someone faces a person or problem directly, for example to talk about something wrong. 3) (formal) Confrontation is the act of facing up to danger or a difficult situation.
its sense in the lessons: In lessons about fights and conflict, pupils learn how to avoid or calm a confrontation, for example by walking away, using calm words or getting an adult. In stories, a confrontation is often the big moment when the hero faces the villain. In news, it describes clashes between police and protesters or between countries. Phrases: «avoid confrontation», «a face-to-face confrontation», «a confrontation with», «direct confrontation».
examples from the lessons: Sam wanted to avoid a confrontation with the older boys. | The story ends with a confrontation between the knight and the dragon. | There was a confrontation between fans after the match. | The teacher had a calm confrontation with the boy about the broken window. | Walking away from a confrontation can be the bravest choice. | The protest ended in a confrontation with police.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable for one event, uncountable for the idea. Verb: confront (confronted); adjective: confrontational (likes to argue or fight). Stress: con-fron-TAY-shun. A confrontation is not always violent; it can be calm and honest talking.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To contradict someone means to say the opposite of what they have said, showing you think they are wrong. 2) If two facts or statements contradict each other, they cannot both be true. 3) To contradict yourself means to say two things that do not fit together.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and science, a result that contradicts your prediction shows the prediction was wrong; in logic, two statements that contradict cannot both be true. In detective stories, a witness whose stories contradict each other may be lying. In manners lessons, contradicting adults rudely is discouraged, but polite disagreement is fine. Phrases: «contradict each other», «contradict yourself», «don't contradict me».
examples from the lessons: The two witnesses contradicted each other. | "Don't contradict your grandfather," said Mum. | The results of our test contradicted our prediction. | You just contradicted yourself: first you said yes, then no. | The new evidence contradicts his story. | It's fine to contradict someone politely if you have facts. | "All odd numbers end in 1" is contradicted by the number 3.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: contradicted, contradicting. Noun: contradiction; adjective: contradictory. Prefix «contra-» means against, «dict» means say. In maths, one counter-example is enough to contradict a rule that says "all".

meaning for a pupil: 1) Courageous means brave: willing to do something frightening, difficult or dangerous because it is right.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, history and news it praises heroes, rescuers and ordinary people who stand up for others. In lessons on fights and fear, pupils learn that courage can mean saying no, telling the truth or helping someone being bullied, not only fighting. Phrases: «a courageous act», «a courageous decision», «it was courageous of you».
examples from the lessons: The courageous firefighter ran into the burning house. | It was courageous of Lily to tell the truth. | Standing up for the new girl was a courageous thing to do. | The courageous little dog barked at the bear. | She made a courageous decision to try again after falling off her bike. | Being courageous doesn't mean you aren't scared.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: keeps the e after g so it says "j": courAGEous. Pronounced kuh-RAY-jus. Noun: courage; adverb: courageously. Opposite: cowardly. Close words: brave, bold, fearless (but fearless means without fear; courageous means acting despite fear).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal, UK) Daft means silly or foolish. 2) (informal, UK) Daft about something means very keen on it: "She's daft about horses." 3) (informal, UK) A daft idea is one that does not make sense.
its sense in the lessons: Very common in friendly British, Irish, Australian and New Zealand speech; often affectionate, not very rude. Parents and teachers say "Don't be daft!" meaning "That's silly". Phrases: «Don't be daft», «daft as a brush», «daft idea», «daft about».
examples from the lessons: Don't be daft, of course you can come! | That was a daft thing to do. | He's daft about football. | It's a daft idea to swim in a storm. | My dog is as daft as a brush. | "Did you think I was angry?" "Don't be daft!" | We laughed at the daft jokes in the comic.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal, mainly British. Comparatives: dafter, daftest. Mild and usually friendly; saying it to someone in a mean way can still hurt. Close words: silly, foolish, barmy (UK), goofy (US).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Derogatory words or comments show a low opinion of someone and are meant to insult or put them down.
its sense in the lessons: In lessons on respect, bullying and language, pupils learn that derogatory words about people's race, religion, disability, looks or gender are hurtful and not allowed. In dictionaries, «(derogatory)» marks an insulting word. Phrases: «derogatory remarks», «derogatory term», «derogatory comments».
examples from the lessons: The coach was told off for making derogatory remarks. | That word is derogatory; please don't use it. | The dictionary labels some slang as derogatory. | Derogatory comments about someone's skin colour are racist. | She felt hurt by his derogatory joke about her accent. | Posting derogatory comments online is a form of bullying.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective. Pronounced di-ROG-a-tree (UK) or di-ROG-a-tor-ee (USA). Formal word; everyday words: insulting, rude, offensive, put-down. Trap: saying "it's only a joke" does not make a derogatory word harmless.

part of speech: noun (a disgrace; disgrace, uncountable); verb (disgrace, disgraces, disgraced, disgracing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Disgrace is losing other people's respect because you did something very bad or shameful. 2) A disgrace is something or someone so bad that it is shocking: "This mess is a disgrace!" 3) To disgrace someone means to bring shame on them, such as your family or school.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, a character may "fall into disgrace" or be sent away "in disgrace" after doing wrong. Adults often say "It's a disgrace!" when angry about a mess or unfairness. In lessons about little sins, children learn that after a disgrace you can still say sorry and rebuild trust. Phrases: «in disgrace», «a public disgrace», «bring disgrace on», «It's a disgrace!», «fall into disgrace».
examples from the lessons: Your bedroom is a disgrace! | He was sent home in disgrace after the fight. | The cheating brought disgrace on the whole team. | It's a disgrace that the park is full of litter. | She didn't want to disgrace her family. | The disgraced minister left her job. | After the disgrace, he worked hard to earn back their trust.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable for the state of shame («in disgrace»), countable in «a disgrace». Verb: disgraced, disgracing. Adjective: disgraceful. Prefix «dis-» + grace (favour, good name).

part of speech: adjective (durable, more durable, most durable); noun (durables, in money talk)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Durable means strong and lasting a long time without breaking or wearing out. 2) (money) Durables or durable goods are things people buy that last many years, such as fridges and cars.
its sense in the lessons: In science and design lessons, pupils choose durable materials (for example metal or tough plastic for a playground, waterproof fabric for a tent). In shops, "durable" is a selling point. Phrases: «durable materials», «hard-wearing and durable», «a durable peace» (formal, lasting).
examples from the lessons: These boots are durable enough for muddy walks. | Which material is most durable for a lunchbox? | Plastic is durable, which is why it stays in the sea for so long. | The durable bag lasted three years of school. | Stone is a durable building material. | The countries hoped for a durable peace.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective; noun: durability (how long something lasts). Pronounced DYOOR-a-bl. Science trap: durable is not the same as hard or strong; it means it lasts. Plastic's durability is useful but also why plastic pollution is a problem.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Emigration is leaving your own country to go and live permanently in another country.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and history lessons, emigration explains why people moved (for work, safety, families), for example from Ireland and Britain to the USA, Canada, Australia and New Zealand. Often studied with «push and pull factors». Phrases: «mass emigration», «emigration from», «wave of emigration».
examples from the lessons: There was huge emigration from Ireland during the famine. | Emigration to Australia was popular among British families. | Many emigrants left by ship, a journey of many weeks. | Emigration can split families across the world. | Poverty and war are common causes of emigration. | Grandad talks about his emigration from Scotland to Canada.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Verb: emigrate; person: emigrant. Trap: EMIgration = leaving (Exit) your country; IMMigration = coming In to a new country. The same person is an emigrant from one country and an immigrant to another.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To endorse someone or something means to say publicly that you support or approve of them. 2) (money, advertising) A famous person endorses a product when they are paid to recommend it. 3) (law, money) To endorse a cheque or document means to sign it on the back. 4) (UK, law) A driving licence is endorsed when penalty points are added for breaking a driving rule.
its sense in the lessons: In news and adverts, a star may endorse trainers or a politician. In media lessons, pupils learn that celebrity endorsements are often paid and are not proof that a product is good. Phrases: «endorse a candidate», «endorse a product», «fully endorse».
examples from the lessons: The footballer endorses a brand of trainers. | The teachers endorsed the plan for a longer playtime. | Remember: if a star endorses a snack, they are often paid. | The newspaper endorsed the new mayor. | I fully endorse what Maya said. | Dad endorsed the cheque before taking it to the bank.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: endorsed, endorsing. Noun: endorsement. American and British spelling «endorse» is standard (older British «indorse» is rare). Trap: being endorsed by someone famous does not make a product better or healthier.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) "Ew!" is a sound people make to show disgust, when something seems dirty, smelly or gross.
its sense in the lessons: Very common in children's speech, chat and comics, especially in North America but now everywhere. It tells the reader that a character finds something disgusting, like slime, a bug or kissing. In writing, the more w's, the stronger the feeling ("ewwww"). Phrases: «Ew, gross!», «Eww, that's disgusting».
examples from the lessons: Ew! There's a slug in my shoe! | "Ew, gross!" said Chloe when her brother burped. | Eww, this milk smells off. | "They're kissing!" "Ewww!" | Ew, don't touch that, it's sticky. | The class all said "ew" when the teacher showed the worm.
note for the reader of a maths problem: An interjection, not a full word; usually written with an exclamation mark. Pronounced like "eee-oo". Spelling varies (ew, eww, ewww). Similar: yuck, ugh, gross. It is informal, so not used in school essays except in speech marks.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Flatly means completely and firmly, with no doubt: "She flatly refused." 2) Flatly means in a dull, flat voice without feeling or expression.
its sense in the lessons: In stories it shows a character saying a firm "no" or speaking in a bored or sad voice. Phrases: «flatly refused», «flatly denied», «said flatly».
examples from the lessons: He flatly refused to eat the sprouts. | The boy flatly denied breaking the window. | "I don't care," she said flatly. | The team flatly rejected the idea of cheating. | He spoke flatly, as if he were very tired. | Mum flatly said no to a second dog.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from «flat» + -ly. Usually goes before the verb («flatly refused, flatly denied»). It does not mean "in a flat shape"; for that you say «laid flat».

part of speech: noun (a giveaway, giveaways); adjective (informal: giveaway prices); verb phrase «give away» (give, gave, given away)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A giveaway is a thing that is given free, for example a free gift or a prize in a competition. 2) A giveaway (dead giveaway) is a small sign that tells a secret or shows the truth: "Her red face was a giveaway." 3) (informal, adjective) Giveaway prices are very low. 4) The verb «give away» means to give something for free, or to tell a secret by mistake.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, detective tales and everyday life, «a dead giveaway» is a clue that tells you who did it. In shops and online, a giveaway is a free prize or gift. Phrases: «a dead giveaway», «free giveaway», «enter a giveaway», «give away a secret».
examples from the lessons: The chocolate on his face was a dead giveaway. | The comic came with a free giveaway: a toy whistle. | Enter our giveaway to win a bike! | Her smile was a giveaway that she knew the surprise. | Don't give away the ending of the book! | They gave away all the kittens to good homes. | The shop sold the toys at giveaway prices.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The noun is one word: «a giveaway». The verb is two words: «give away» (gave away, given away). Online giveaways can be scams: never share personal details to win a prize.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Illegally means in a way that is against the law.
its sense in the lessons: In news, citizenship lessons and stories, it tells the reader someone broke a law, such as parking illegally, downloading films illegally or selling goods illegally. Phrases: «parked illegally», «illegally downloaded», «entered illegally», «illegally dumped».
examples from the lessons: The car was parked illegally on the zigzag lines outside school. | Films downloaded illegally can carry viruses. | The rubbish was dumped illegally in the woods. | The man was fishing illegally without a licence. | It is against the rules, but is it done illegally? | They illegally sold fireworks to children.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from «illegal» + -ly; il- (not) + legal. Spelling: two l's at the start (iLLegaLLy) and two at the end. Do not confuse with «ill» (sick). «Against the rules» at school is not always «illegal» (against the law of the country).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (law) Liability is being legally responsible for something, especially for paying for damage or harm. 2) (money) Liabilities are money a person or company owes. 3) (informal) A liability is a person or thing that causes problems or puts others at risk: "He's a liability on the team."
its sense in the lessons: In adult life and money lessons, companies list assets (what they own) and liabilities (what they owe). Signs at pools or car parks may say the owners accept "no liability" for loss. In everyday speech, a clumsy or risky person is called a liability. Phrases: «accept liability», «no liability», «a liability to», «assets and liabilities».
examples from the lessons: The shop accepts no liability for lost umbrellas. | The company's liabilities were bigger than its money, so it closed. | The broken ladder is a liability; someone could fall. | With his bad ankle, he was a liability in the match. | The driver admitted liability for the crash. | Debts are liabilities.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: liabilities. Adjective: liable («liable for damage» = responsible; «liable to fall» = likely). In money maths: assets minus liabilities = what you are really worth.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A mantelpiece is the shelf above a fireplace, often with ornaments, clocks, cards or photos on it. 2) The frame around a fireplace.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and stories it is a cosy home detail: birthday cards, Christmas stockings and family photos often sit on the mantelpiece. In detective stories, a clue is often found "on the mantelpiece". Phrases: «on the mantelpiece», «above the mantelpiece».
examples from the lessons: Grandma keeps our school photos on the mantelpiece. | The clock on the mantelpiece struck six. | We hung our Christmas stockings from the mantelpiece. | The birthday cards were lined up along the mantelpiece. | The detective found a key hidden behind a vase on the mantelpiece. | A painting hung above the mantelpiece.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun, one word. Spelling: mantEL (not mantle). American English often says «mantel». Safety: don't put things that can burn, or hang stockings, too close to a lit fire.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A millionaire is a person who has money and property worth at least a million pounds, dollars or other units of money.
its sense in the lessons: Used in stories, news and games ("Who Wants to Be a Millionaire?"). In maths, a million is 1,000,000 (a thousand thousands), which helps pupils feel how big the number is. Phrases: «become a millionaire», «a self-made millionaire», «lottery millionaire».
examples from the lessons: The lottery winner became a millionaire overnight. | He is a self-made millionaire who started with a market stall. | If you saved £1 a day, it would take more than two and a half thousand years to save a million pounds. | The millionaire gave money to the children's hospital. | Being a millionaire doesn't always make you happy. | A million has six zeros.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun. Spelling: two l's and -aire at the end. Related: billionaire (a thousand million). In maths, «a million» = 1,000,000 = 10 × 10 × 10 × 10 × 10 × 10.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A mugshot is a photograph of a person's face, from the front and the side, taken by the police after an arrest. 2) (informal, jokey) Any photo of someone's face, especially an unflattering one.
its sense in the lessons: In news and crime stories, mugshots of suspects are shown. In media lessons on gossip, being shown in a mugshot means someone was arrested, not that they are guilty. Jokingly, people call passport photos or school ID pictures "mugshots". Phrases: «police mugshot», «take a mugshot».
examples from the lessons: The police released the suspect's mugshot. | The robber's mugshot was on the front page. | My passport photo looks like a mugshot! | In the film, the gangster smirked in his mugshot. | A mugshot doesn't prove someone is guilty. | Every member of the club had a mugshot on the noticeboard.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun; one word or two («mug shot»). From «mug», slang for face. Trap: a mugshot shows someone was arrested; a court decides if they are guilty.

part of speech: noun (a navy, navies; the Navy); adjective (navy, navy blue)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A navy is the part of a country's armed forces that fights at sea, with ships, sailors and submarines. 2) Navy (navy blue) is a very dark blue colour.
its sense in the lessons: In history and news, the Royal Navy (UK), the US Navy, the Royal Australian Navy and others defend their countries at sea. In school life, «navy» is a common uniform colour for jumpers and skirts. Phrases: «join the navy», «Royal Navy», «navy blue», «in the navy».
examples from the lessons: My uncle served in the Royal Navy for ten years. | Our school jumper is navy blue. | The navy sent ships to help after the flood. | She wore a navy coat and red boots. | Sailors in the navy learn to swim and tie knots. | The two navies fought a great sea battle.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: navies. Capital N when naming a particular navy (the Royal Navy). As a colour it does not take -s: «navy socks». Adjective for the sea forces: naval («a naval base»), not «navy base» (though US English sometimes uses «Navy base»).

meaning for a pupil: 1) The originator of something is the person who first thought of it, made it or started it.
its sense in the lessons: A formal word used in history, science and news to say who invented or began something, such as an idea, a game or a rumour. In lessons on gossip, pupils try to find the originator of a rumour. Phrases: «the originator of the idea», «the originator of the rumour».
examples from the lessons: Who was the originator of this plan? | The originator of the rumour turned out to be a jealous classmate. | He is the originator of the popular board game. | The originator of the idea got a prize. | Scientists are not sure who was the originator of the joke. | Each new email shows the originator's address.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun. Formal: in everyday talk say «the person who started it», «inventor» or «creator». Related: origin, original, originate.

part of speech: verb form (-ing form of «pin»: pin, pins, pinned, pinning); noun (uncountable, in some uses)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Pinning means fastening something with a pin, for example a badge, a poster or a piece of cloth. 2) Pinning (someone down) means holding a person so they cannot move, for example in a fight or a wrestling match. 3) Pinning the blame on someone means saying they did something wrong, often unfairly. 4) (computers) Pinning means fixing a message or app in place at the top of a screen.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday and school life, pupils pin work on a noticeboard. In stories about fights, pinning someone to the ground is rough and dangerous. In ethics lessons, «pinning the blame» on an innocent person is a common unfair act. Phrases: «pinning up», «pinning down», «pinning the blame on», «pinning your hopes on».
examples from the lessons: She was pinning her painting to the board. | The bigger boy was pinning Sam to the ground until the teacher came. | Stop pinning the blame on your sister! | Mum is pinning up the hem of my trousers. | We're pinning our hopes on the last match. | The wrestler won by pinning his opponent. | I'm pinning that message so everyone sees it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: double n before -ing and -ed (pinning, pinned) because «pin» is a short word ending in one vowel + one consonant. Safety: pinning someone down in play can hurt their chest and breathing; stop if they say stop.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Preventative means meant to stop something bad from happening before it starts, such as illness, damage or crime. 2) A preventative is something used to prevent a problem, such as a medicine or treatment.
its sense in the lessons: In health and science lessons, «preventative medicine» includes vaccines, healthy eating and brushing teeth. In safety and money lessons, preventative steps (like checking a bike) save trouble later. Phrases: «preventative measures», «preventative medicine», «preventative care», «as a preventative».
examples from the lessons: Brushing your teeth is a preventative measure against tooth decay. | The vet gave the dog a preventative treatment for fleas. | Vaccines are preventative medicine. | We took preventative steps and tied down the trampoline before the storm. | Sun cream is a preventative against sunburn. | Regular check-ups are preventative care.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Preventative» and «preventive» mean the same; «preventive» is more common in American English and in science writing. Related: prevent, prevention. Saying "prevention is better than cure" means stopping problems early is better than fixing them later.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To prolong something means to make it last longer.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and everyday life, people prolong a holiday, a visit or a game; in health, medicines may prolong life. In science, keeping food cold prolongs its freshness. Phrases: «prolong the agony», «prolong life», «prolonged» (long-lasting, as in «prolonged rain»).
examples from the lessons: We prolonged our holiday by two days. | Keeping milk in the fridge prolongs its life. | Don't prolong the argument; just say sorry. | The new medicine helped prolong Grandad's life. | Extra time prolonged the football match. | Prolonged rain caused flooding in the valley. | Stop prolonging the agony and tell us who won!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: prolonged, prolonging. Adjective: prolonged (lasting a long time). Formal word; everyday: make longer, drag out, extend. Pronounced pro-LONG.

part of speech: adjective; noun (a reciprocal, reciprocals – in maths)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Reciprocal means given and received in return; done by both people or sides for each other: "a reciprocal friendship". 2) (maths) The reciprocal of a number is 1 divided by that number; a number times its reciprocal equals 1.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, reciprocals are used to divide fractions: to divide by a fraction, multiply by its reciprocal ("flip it"). In ethics and everyday life, «reciprocal» help or respect goes both ways. Phrases: «reciprocal of», «reciprocal arrangement», «reciprocal respect».
examples from the lessons: The reciprocal of 4 is 1/4. | The reciprocal of 2/3 is 3/2. | To divide by 1/2, multiply by its reciprocal, 2. | Our schools have a reciprocal visit: we go to them, then they come to us. | Friendship should be reciprocal; both people care. | 5 × 1/5 = 1, so 1/5 is the reciprocal of 5. | The two countries have a reciprocal agreement on health care.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective, and countable noun in maths. Pronounced ri-SIP-ro-kal. Maths: reciprocal of a/b is b/a; reciprocal of a whole number n is 1/n; zero has no reciprocal (you cannot divide by 0). A number and its reciprocal always multiply to 1. Do not confuse with «opposite» (the opposite of 5 is −5; they add to 0).

meaning for a pupil: 1) To reciprocate is to give or do the same thing back to someone who gave or did it to you. 2) To return a feeling, such as liking or love, that someone has for you. 3) (formal) To answer a kind act, a favour or an invitation with one of your own.
its sense in the lessons: A fairly formal word used in stories about friendship, manners and fairness: it tells the reader that something was returned, or not. In social studies and ethics lessons it links to the idea of «give and take» and treating others as they treat you. Phrases: «reciprocate the favour», «reciprocate feelings», «did not reciprocate».
examples from the lessons: She smiled at the new girl, and the new girl reciprocated with a wave. | When Tom helped me with my maths, I reciprocated by helping him with spelling. | He liked her, but sadly she did not reciprocate his feelings. | They invited us to dinner, so next month we will reciprocate. | Good neighbours reciprocate small kindnesses. | (formal) The school hopes the visiting team will reciprocate the invitation. | If you lend a pencil, a friend will often reciprocate one day.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A verb; the noun is «reciprocation» and the adjective is «reciprocal» (a reciprocal arrangement). Everyday speech usually says «return the favour» or «do the same back». In maths, «reciprocal» (not reciprocate) means 1 divided by a number: the reciprocal of 4 is 1/4.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Refurbishment is the work of repairing, cleaning and redecorating a building or room so it looks and works like new. 2) A refurbishment is one such job, for example on a library, a shop or a school hall. 3) The repairing and cleaning of a used machine, such as a phone or computer, so it can be sold again.
its sense in the lessons: Seen on signs («Closed for refurbishment») and in news about schools, swimming pools and shops. In everyday life a «refurbished» phone or laptop is a used one fixed up and sold cheaper. In stories it tells the reader a place is being made new. Phrases: «closed for refurbishment», «undergo a refurbishment», «a major refurbishment».
examples from the lessons: The swimming pool is closed for refurbishment until after the holidays. | The school library had a refurbishment, and now it has bright beanbags. | The refurbishment of the old cinema took many months. | Mum bought a refurbished laptop because it was cheaper. | During the refurbishment, our class had lessons in the hall. | The museum reopened after a big refurbishment. | Builders carried out the refurbishment of the playground toilets.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From the verb «refurbish» (refurbish, refurbishes, refurbished, refurbishing) and adjective «refurbished». Longer and more formal than «doing up» (UK) or «fixing up» (US). Not the same as «rebuilding»: refurbishment keeps the building and renews the inside.

part of speech: verb (regenerate, regenerates, regenerated, regenerating); adjective (formal, rare: regenerate)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) To regenerate is to grow again after being damaged or lost, as a lizard's tail or a starfish's arm can. 2) To bring new life, jobs and activity to a run-down town or area. 3) To make something new or fresh again, such as a forest after a fire. 4) (computing) To make something again, such as a page or a password. 5) (church) In Christian teaching, to be spiritually reborn; Christians believe God makes a person new.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons it describes living things that regrow body parts (starfish, lizards, flatworms) and forests that grow back. In geography and news it means improving poor neighbourhoods. It tells the reader that something lost or tired is coming back to life. Phrases: «regenerate a limb», «regenerate the town centre», «regenerate tissue».
examples from the lessons: A starfish can regenerate a lost arm. | Some lizards drop their tail and later regenerate it. | Our skin regenerates after a small cut. | The council plans to regenerate the old docks with shops and parks. | After the bushfire, the forest slowly regenerated. | Press the button to regenerate the password. | Humans cannot regenerate a whole arm, but the liver can regrow part of itself.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: «regeneration». Trap: people cannot regrow fingers or legs; only some animals can regrow whole limbs. Not the same as «generate» (make for the first time); «re-» means again.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A registry is an official place or office where records are kept, for example of births, marriages and deaths. 2) An official list or record of things or people, such as a registry of ships or of dogs. 3) (UK) A registry office is where people can get married without a church service. 4) (US) A gift list for a wedding or a new baby, kept at a shop. 5) (computing) A store of settings inside a computer.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life you hear «registry office» in the UK and Ireland, and «baby registry» or «wedding registry» in the USA and Canada. In history and civics it shows how governments keep track of people and property. Phrases: «registry office», «land registry», «wedding registry».
examples from the lessons: My aunt got married at the registry office in town. | Every baby's birth is written in the registry. | The land registry shows who owns each house. | They made a baby registry so friends knew what gifts to buy. | Each racing pigeon is listed in a registry. | The ship's name is in the national registry. | We chose a toaster from the wedding registry.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «registries». Related: «register» (a list, or to sign up), «registrar» (the person in charge of records). In the UK «register office» is the official name, but «registry office» is common speech. Do not confuse with «registration» (the act of signing up).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (medicine) Remission is a time when a serious illness, such as cancer, gets much better or its signs disappear, though it may return. 2) (law, UK) Time taken off a prisoner's sentence for good behaviour. 3) (church) The forgiveness of sins; Christians speak of «the remission of sins». 4) (formal) Cancelling a debt or payment, such as the remission of fees.
its sense in the lessons: Children usually meet it when a grown-up talks about someone who has been ill: «Grandad is in remission» is good news, said gently. In church it appears in prayers and the creed. It tells the reader that something bad has eased but may not be gone forever. Phrases: «in remission», «go into remission», «remission of sins».
examples from the lessons: Aunt Rosie's cancer is in remission, and we are all so happy. | The doctor said the illness had gone into remission. | He was let out early because of remission for good behaviour. | Christians believe Jesus brings the remission of sins. | The school offered remission of fees for families in need. | Even in remission, she still has check-ups with the doctor.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable: «in remission», not «in a remission». «In remission» does not always mean cured; doctors say that only after a long time. Related verb: «remit» (formal). A sensitive word: use it kindly.

part of speech: verb (snub, snubs, snubbed, snubbing); noun (a snub, snubs); adjective (snub nose)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To snub someone is to ignore them or treat them coldly on purpose, to show you do not respect or like them. 2) A snub is an act of ignoring or insulting someone in this way. 3) A snub nose is short and turned up at the end.
its sense in the lessons: A word for playground and friendship stories: it tells the reader someone felt left out or insulted on purpose. In news it is used for leaders or teams who refuse to meet or shake hands. Phrases: «a deliberate snub», «felt snubbed», «snub nose».
examples from the lessons: Jess snubbed me at lunch and sat with other girls. | It felt like a snub when he did not invite me to his party. | The captain snubbed the other team and walked off without shaking hands. | I said hello, but she snubbed me and looked away. | The puppy has a cute snub nose. | Not being picked for the team felt like a snub, but the coach had a reason. | Don't snub new kids; say hi.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double the b: snubbed, snubbing. Snubbing is unkind; if someone simply did not see you, it is not a snub. Similar: «give the cold shoulder», «blank someone» (UK slang), «diss» (slang).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Speculation is guessing about something without knowing all the facts. 2) A speculation is one such guess or idea. 3) (money) Speculation is buying things such as shares, land or houses hoping to sell them later for more money, which is risky.
its sense in the lessons: In news and gossip: «There is speculation that the star will leave the team». In science, a speculation is an idea not yet tested. In money talk it means risky buying. It tells the reader that something is not confirmed. Phrases: «pure speculation», «speculation about», «wild speculation», «fuel speculation».
examples from the lessons: There is a lot of speculation about who will be the new head teacher. | That is just speculation; we don't know for sure. | His absence caused speculation that he was ill. | Scientists' speculation about life on Mars needs evidence. | He lost his savings through speculation on shares. | Stop the wild speculation and wait for the facts.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: «speculate»; adjective: «speculative». Usually uncountable. Trap: speculation in the news is not fact; check for evidence.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Spooky means strange and a bit frightening, as if there might be ghosts. 2) (informal) Spooky can mean strangely surprising, like an odd coincidence. 3) (informal, of an animal) Easily frightened or nervous, as in a spooky horse.
its sense in the lessons: A favourite word for Halloween, ghost stories and dark places: it tells the reader to feel a shiver, often in a fun way. In everyday talk «that's spooky» is said about coincidences. Phrases: «spooky house», «spooky story», «spooky coincidence», «a bit spooky».
examples from the lessons: The old house on the hill looks spooky at night. | We told spooky stories around the campfire. | Our classroom is decorated with spooky bats for Halloween. | It's spooky that we both drew the same picture! | The woods were spooky and silent. | The pony is spooky and jumps at plastic bags. | The spookiest part of the film was the creaking door.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comes from «spook» (informal for ghost; also slang for a spy). Milder and more playful than «terrifying». Spelling: spookier, spookiest (y changes to i). The word «spook» is also an old offensive slur in the US in one sense, so use «spooky» and «spook» meaning ghost only.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A sportsman is a man who plays sport, especially well or as his job. 2) A person who plays fairly, is polite to the other side and accepts losing well. 3) (older use) A man who goes hunting, shooting or fishing for sport.
its sense in the lessons: In PE and sports reports it names athletes; in ethics and stories it praises fair play: «a true sportsman». The quality is «sportsmanship». Phrases: «a good sportsman», «sportsman of the year», «true sportsman».
examples from the lessons: He is a famous sportsman who plays rugby for New Zealand. | A good sportsman shakes hands even after losing. | Dad was a keen sportsman when he was young. | She was named sportsperson of the year. | The coach praised Liam's sportsmanship. | Be a sportsman and help the other player up.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «sportsmen». For women: «sportswoman», «sportswomen»; neutral: «sportsperson», «athlete», «player». Adjective «sporting» (a sporting gesture) and «sportsmanlike». Do not confuse with «sporty» (likes sport).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (UK, Ireland, Australia) A tombola is a game at a fair where people buy tickets and win a prize if their ticket number matches one on a prize. 2) The turning drum that tickets are drawn from in such a game.
its sense in the lessons: A familiar stall at school fêtes, church fairs and Christmas fairs in the UK and Ireland, used to raise money. Prizes are often bottles, sweets and toys given by parents. In maths it is a nice chance and probability example. Phrases: «the tombola stall», «win on the tombola», «tickets ending in 0 or 5».
examples from the lessons: I won a bottle of bubble bath on the tombola! | Mum ran the tombola stall at the school fair. | Tickets ending in 0 or 5 win a prize at our tombola. | The tombola raised money for the new playground. | We spun the tombola and pulled out a ticket. | Please bring a bottle for the tombola. | If 1 ticket in 5 wins, your chance of winning is 1/5.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «tombolas». In the US people say «raffle» or «drawing», though a raffle usually has a few big prizes drawn later, while in a tombola you know straight away. Maths: if 20 of 100 tickets win, the chance of a prize is 20/100 = 1/5.

part of speech: adjective (unimpressed; usually after a verb: be/look/seem unimpressed)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Unimpressed means not thinking that someone or something is good, special or clever. 2) Showing that you are a little annoyed or not pleased, often with a flat look.
its sense in the lessons: Used in stories to show a character's reaction, often funny: a cat, a teacher or a parent looks unimpressed. It tells the reader that someone was not won over. Phrases: «look unimpressed», «be unimpressed by/with», «distinctly unimpressed».
examples from the lessons: The cat looked unimpressed by its new toy. | Mum was unimpressed when she saw the muddy carpet. | The judges seemed unimpressed with his magic trick. | I was unimpressed by the film; it was boring. | Grandpa stayed unimpressed by the new phone. | Our teacher was unimpressed that nobody did the homework.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: «impressed». Followed by «by» or «with». Usually not before a noun. Milder than «angry» or «disgusted».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Verbal means spoken in words, not written down: a verbal warning, a verbal agreement. 2) Verbal means to do with words: verbal skills are skills with language. 3) (grammar) Verbal means to do with verbs. 4) (slang, UK) «Verbals» are insults or rude talk said to someone.
its sense in the lessons: In school it appears in «verbal reasoning» tests (word puzzles, UK), rules about «verbal bullying» (name-calling, threats), and sports («a verbal warning» from the referee). It tells the reader that something was said, not done or written. Phrases: «verbal warning», «verbal abuse», «verbal reasoning», «verbal agreement».
examples from the lessons: The referee gave him a verbal warning. | Name-calling is verbal bullying, and it hurts too. | We practised verbal reasoning for the test. | They made a verbal agreement to share the bike. | She has strong verbal skills and loves debates. | He was told off verbally, not in a letter. | Some fans gave the referee a lot of verbal (UK slang).
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: «verbal» strictly means «in words» (written or spoken), but in everyday use it nearly always means spoken; «oral» means spoken too. «Verbal» is not about verbs only, though in grammar it can be. Adverb: «verbally».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A weatherman is a man who tells people what the weather will be, especially on TV or radio. 2) (informal) Any weather forecaster, or a meteorologist (a scientist who studies weather).
its sense in the lessons: Children see weather forecasts on TV and apps; in science lessons on weather and climate it links to forecasting, maps, symbols and temperatures. Phrases: «the weatherman said», «TV weatherman».
examples from the lessons: The weatherman said it will rain tomorrow. | The TV weatherman pointed to a big cloud on the map. | The weatherman was wrong; it was sunny all day! | I want to be a weatherman and study storms. | The weatherwoman warned about strong winds. | Weathermen use satellites and computers to predict the weather.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «weathermen». For women «weatherwoman»; neutral «weather forecaster», «weather presenter», «meteorologist». Forecasts are predictions, not certainties: «70% chance of rain» means rain is likely, not sure.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Abdominal means to do with the abdomen, the belly part of the body between the chest and the hips. 2) Abdominals (or «abs», informal) are the muscles of the tummy. 3) (science) In insects, abdominal means to do with the abdomen, the back part of the body.
its sense in the lessons: In science it appears in lessons on the human body and insects (head, thorax, abdomen). In PE and health it appears with exercises and with doctors («abdominal pain» means tummy ache). Phrases: «abdominal muscles», «abdominal pain», «abdominal exercises».
examples from the lessons: Sit-ups make your abdominal muscles stronger. | The doctor asked if she had any abdominal pain. | An insect has a head, a thorax and an abdomen; the stinger of a bee is at its abdominal end. | Wear a seat belt low across your hips, not across your abdominal area. | He trained his abs for the race. | Abdominal pain on the right side can be serious, so tell a grown-up.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stress: ab-DOM-in-al. Noun «abdomen». «Abs» is the short, informal form. Doctors say «abdominal» where children say «tummy» or «stomach»; strictly the stomach is just one organ inside the abdomen.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To adjudge is to decide officially that something is true or that someone is something, as a judge or referee does. 2) (law) To give an official decision in a court case.
its sense in the lessons: A stiff word met in sports reports and law: «the ball was adjudged to have crossed the line». It tells the reader that an official made a judgement. Usually used in the passive: «was adjudged». Phrases: «adjudged the winner», «adjudged guilty», «adjudged offside».
examples from the lessons: The goal was adjudged offside. | She was adjudged the winner of the poetry competition. | The court adjudged him guilty. | The referee adjudged that the ball had gone out. | Our project was adjudged the best in the school. | The match was adjudged a draw.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; everyday words are «judge», «decide», «rule». Spelling: adjudge has a d before the j. Related: «adjudicate» (to act as a judge in a contest or dispute) and «adjudicator».

meaning for a pupil: 1) An adolescent is a young person who is growing from a child into an adult, usually aged about 12 to 18; a teenager. 2) Adolescent means to do with this time of life. 3) (disapproving) Adolescent can describe behaviour that is silly or immature, like a teenager showing off.
its sense in the lessons: In health and PSHE lessons it comes with puberty and growing up; doctors and books for parents use it. It tells the reader someone is no longer a little child but not yet an adult. Phrases: «adolescent years», «adolescent health», «adolescent behaviour».
examples from the lessons: An adolescent's body changes a lot during puberty. | My big sister is an adolescent now, and she wants more privacy. | The library has a section for adolescent readers. | Adolescents need plenty of sleep. | The book is about the adolescent years of a famous scientist. | Throwing food was a bit adolescent, Dad said.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Use «an»: an adolescent. Noun for the time of life: «adolescence». More formal than «teenager», «teen», «young person». Not a rude word in its main sense.

part of speech: adjective (affectionate, more affectionate, most affectionate); adverb (affectionately)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Affectionate means showing love and fondness in a gentle way, for example with hugs, kind words or cuddles. 2) An affectionate pet likes to be stroked and stay close to people.
its sense in the lessons: In stories it tells the reader about warm, loving relationships between family members, friends or pets. Pet books describe breeds as «affectionate». Phrases: «affectionate hug», «affectionate nickname», «affectionately known as».
examples from the lessons: Our dog is very affectionate and always wants a cuddle. | Grandma gave me an affectionate hug. | He has an affectionate nickname for his little sister. | The kitten is playful and affectionate. | She smiled affectionately at the baby. | The old teacher was affectionately known as «Mr B».
note for the reader of a maths problem: Use «an»: an affectionate cat. Noun: «affection». Not the same as «affected» (changed by something, or putting on a false manner). Adverb: «affectionately».

part of speech: noun (an Afghan, Afghans; an afghan, afghans); adjective (Afghan)
meaning for a pupil: 1) An Afghan is a person from Afghanistan, a country in Central and South Asia; Afghan means from or to do with Afghanistan. 2) An Afghan hound is a tall dog with long, silky hair. 3) (US, Canada) An afghan is a knitted or crocheted blanket, often colourful. 4) (UK, older use) An Afghan coat is a sheepskin coat with the woolly side inside.
its sense in the lessons: In geography it names the people of Afghanistan and things from there (Afghan food, Afghan rugs). In everyday North American homes an afghan is a blanket Grandma knitted. Capital A for the people and the dog; small a for the blanket.
examples from the lessons: Our new classmate is Afghan and speaks Dari and English. | Afghan food includes rice dishes and flatbread. | The Afghan hound has long, flowing hair. | Grandma crocheted a bright afghan for my bed. | Afghan rugs are famous for their red patterns. | We wrapped up in an afghan to watch the film.
note for the reader of a maths problem: People from Afghanistan: «Afghans» (or «Afghan people»); the money of Afghanistan is the «afghani», a different word. Capital letter for people and the country's things. «An» before Afghan.

part of speech: adjective (aloof); adverb (aloof: stand aloof, keep aloof)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Aloof means unfriendly and distant, keeping away from other people and not joining in. 2) Keeping apart from something on purpose, not getting involved, as in «stay aloof from the argument».
its sense in the lessons: In stories it describes a cool, proud or shy character who keeps to themselves; the reader wonders why. Cat books often call cats aloof. Phrases: «remain aloof», «keep aloof from», «seem aloof».
examples from the lessons: The new boy seemed aloof, but really he was shy. | Cats can be aloof and walk off when you call them. | She stayed aloof from the silly argument. | The princess was cold and aloof with the servants. | He looks aloof, but he is kind once you know him. | Don't judge someone as aloof too quickly.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually after a verb (be, seem, remain aloof). Trap: aloof can be shyness, not pride; the word tells how someone looks to others. Opposite: friendly, outgoing, warm.

part of speech: adjective (amazed); verb form (past of amaze: amaze, amazes, amazed, amazing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Amazed means very surprised, often in a happy way, because something is wonderful or hard to believe. 2) Amazed is also the past form of «amaze»: something amazed you when it surprised you greatly.
its sense in the lessons: Very common in stories and in everyday speech to show strong surprise; it tells the reader a character could hardly believe what happened. In science, pupils are «amazed» by experiments. Phrases: «amazed at/by», «amazed that…», «amazed to see», «I'm amazed».
examples from the lessons: I was amazed by the magic trick. | We were amazed to see a whale near the beach. | She was amazed that she had won the prize. | The fireworks amazed everyone. | Dad looked amazed when I tidied my room. | The class was amazed when the volcano model erupted. | I'm amazed you finished the puzzle so fast!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Amazed (how you feel) vs amazing (what causes the feeling): «I was amazed; the show was amazing». Followed by «at», «by», «to + verb», or «that». Stronger than «surprised». Spelling: drop e and add -ed.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Amazement is the feeling of being very surprised because something is wonderful or hard to believe.
its sense in the lessons: Used in stories to describe reactions: «to her amazement», «in amazement», «stared in amazement». It tells the reader that something surprising has happened. Phrases: «in amazement», «to my amazement», «a look of amazement».
examples from the lessons: We watched in amazement as the rocket took off. | To my amazement, my little brother cleaned his room. | She stared at the giant cake in amazement. | His face was full of amazement. | To everyone's amazement, the shy girl sang a solo. | The crowd gasped in amazement.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: no «an amazement», no plural. Related: amaze (verb), amazed, amazing (adjectives), amazingly (adverb). «To my amazement» goes at the start of a sentence.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Amicable means friendly and without arguments, especially when people could have argued. 2) (law, formal) An amicable agreement or divorce is settled calmly, with both sides agreeing.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and news about disagreements: an «amicable split» means people parted calmly. In family life a child may hear that parents had an «amicable divorce». Phrases: «amicable agreement», «amicable relationship», «settle amicably», «part amicably».
examples from the lessons: The two teams had an amicable chat after the match. | My parents' divorce was amicable, and they are still friends. | We reached an amicable agreement to share the swing. | The neighbours settled the fence argument amicably. | The band split up on amicable terms. | It is better to sort out problems in an amicable way.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; everyday: «friendly». Use «an»: an amicable agreement. Not the same as «amiable» (pleasant, good-natured, about a person), though close.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Anticipation is the excited feeling of waiting for something you expect to happen, especially something nice. 2) Anticipation is also expecting something and getting ready for it: «in anticipation of rain». 3) (formal) Guessing in advance what will happen, as a good goalkeeper does.
its sense in the lessons: In stories it builds excitement before birthdays, holidays or big events; in sport it praises a player who sees what will happen next. Phrases: «in anticipation of», «full of anticipation», «with great anticipation».
examples from the lessons: The children waited for Christmas morning with great anticipation. | We packed umbrellas in anticipation of rain. | The crowd was full of anticipation before the match. | The goalkeeper's anticipation stopped the penalty. | In anticipation of the test, we revised every evening. | The anticipation was almost better than the trip itself.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Verb: «anticipate» (to expect, to get ready for). Not always happy: you can wait with anticipation or with dread. «In anticipation of» means «because we expect».

meaning for a pupil: 1) To applaud is to clap your hands to show that you liked a show, a speech or a performance. 2) To applaud someone or something is to praise them or say they did right.
its sense in the lessons: At school assemblies, plays and concerts the audience applauds. In news and ethics, people «applaud» a brave or kind decision. Phrases: «applaud loudly», «applaud the decision», «stand and applaud».
examples from the lessons: The audience applauded at the end of the school play. | Everyone applauded when Sara scored the goal. | We applaud your hard work this year. | The crowd stood up and applauded. | Teachers applauded the pupils' idea to recycle more. | Please applaud our guest speaker.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: «applause» (uncountable). Spelling: two p's. In everyday speech people say «clap» more often. Formal use: «I applaud your honesty» = I praise it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Applause is the sound of people clapping their hands to show they enjoyed something or agree. 2) Applause is also praise or approval.
its sense in the lessons: At concerts, assemblies and sports events; in stories it tells the reader that something went well. Phrases: «a round of applause», «loud applause», «to applause», «thunderous applause».
examples from the lessons: Let's give our singers a big round of applause! | The applause went on for a long time. | She walked onto the stage to loud applause. | The magician bowed after the applause. | There was polite applause when the head teacher finished. | His brave act earned the applause of the whole town.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «an applause» and «applauses» are wrong; say «a round of applause». Verb: «applaud». Spelling: two p's, ends in -ause.

part of speech: noun (an assault, assaults; also uncountable); verb (assault, assaults, assaulted, assaulting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (law) An assault is a violent attack on a person, or a threat to hurt them; it is a crime. 2) To assault someone is to attack them violently. 3) (military) An assault is an attack by soldiers to capture a place. 4) A strong attack or challenge of another kind: «an assault on the mountain», «an assault on the senses» (very strong sights, sounds and smells).
its sense in the lessons: Met in news, history (battles) and safety talks: hurting someone is assault, and it is against the law. In stories it tells the reader there is danger. Phrases: «charged with assault», «assault on», «an assault course» (UK, an obstacle course for training).
examples from the lessons: The man was arrested for assault. | Hitting someone can be assault, which is a crime. | The soldiers launched an assault on the fort. | The climbers made their assault on the summit at dawn. | The market was an assault on the senses: colours, smells and noise. | Our PE class did an assault course with ropes and walls. | If anyone hurts you, tell a trusted adult or the police.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable and uncountable. Stress on the second part: a-SAULT. A serious word: if someone hits or threatens you, it is never your fault. «Assault course» (UK) = «obstacle course» (US).

part of speech: noun (a bogey, bogeys; also spelt bogy, bogie)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (UK, Ireland, Australia, informal) A bogey is a bit of dried mucus (snot) from inside your nose; Americans say «booger». 2) (golf) A bogey is a score of one more than par on a hole. 3) A bogey (bogeyman) is an imaginary evil spirit or monster used to scare children. 4) Something people fear or worry about: «Maths is my bogey subject». 5) (Australia, slang) A swim or a bath.
its sense in the lessons: In the playground and at home it is the funny, slightly rude word for a bit of snot. In golf on TV it is a score. In stories the bogeyman is a monster under the bed. Phrases: «pick your nose for bogeys», «make a bogey», «bogeyman», «bogey team».
examples from the lessons: Stop picking your bogeys and use a tissue! | My little brother wiped a bogey on the sofa, yuck. | The golfer made a bogey on the fifth hole. | I was scared that the bogeyman lived under the stairs. | Spelling is my bogey; I always find it hard. | That team is our bogey team; we never beat them. | (Australia) Let's go for a bogey in the creek.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «bogeys». The snot meaning is informal, a bit rude but not swearing; at school say «use a tissue». In golf: par 4 hole done in 5 shots = a bogey; in 3 = a birdie. «Bogie» is also a set of wheels on a train.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To budge is to move a little, or to make something heavy or stuck move a little. 2) To change your mind or opinion, or to make someone change theirs: «She won't budge». 3) (informal) «Budge up» or «budge over» means move along to make space for someone.
its sense in the lessons: Usually in negative sentences: «it won't budge», «he wouldn't budge». In stories it shows stubborn things or people. In everyday life «budge up» is said on a bench or sofa (UK, Ireland, Australia). Phrases: «won't budge», «budge an inch», «budge up».
examples from the lessons: The window is stuck and won't budge. | We pushed the car, but it didn't budge. | Mum would not budge: no sweets before dinner. | Budge up so Mia can sit on the bench. | The donkey refused to budge an inch. | Nothing could budge him from his opinion.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly used with «not»: «it won't budge». Past: budged. Not the same as «budget» (a money plan) or «bulge» (swell out).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A bungalow is a house with only one floor, without stairs to an upstairs. 2) (South Asia, older use) A large one-storey house with a veranda. 3) (US) A small, cosy house, often with a low roof and a porch.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and geography lessons about homes: houses, flats, bungalows, cottages. Older people often live in bungalows because there are no stairs. Phrases: «a seaside bungalow», «live in a bungalow».
examples from the lessons: Grandma lives in a bungalow, so she doesn't climb stairs. | Our holiday bungalow had a veranda facing the sea. | A bungalow has all its rooms on one floor. | They moved from a flat into a little bungalow. | The street is full of brick bungalows. | In Australia many old houses are weatherboard bungalows.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «bungalows». The word came into English from India (from a word meaning «from Bengal»). Not the same as a «cottage» (a small country house, often with two floors).

part of speech: verb (bust, busts, bust or busted, busting); noun (a bust, busts); adjective (bust)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) To bust something is to break it: «I bust my bike». 2) A bust is a statue of a person's head, shoulders and chest. 3) A bust is a woman's chest, or its measurement for clothes. 4) (informal) Go bust means a business runs out of money and closes. 5) (slang) To bust someone is to catch them doing wrong or arrest them; a bust is a police raid. 6) (slang) «Busted!» means «you've been caught!».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday talk it is a casual, strong word for «broken» or «caught». In history lessons and museums, busts are statues of famous people. In business news, «the company went bust». Phrases: «go bust», «busted!», «bust a gut» (try very hard), «a drugs bust», «-buster» (ghostbuster, myth-buster).
examples from the lessons: I bust my headphones when I sat on them. | There is a marble bust of the old queen in the museum. | The toy shop went bust and closed. | Busted! I saw you take the last biscuit! | The police made a big drugs bust. | We bust a gut to finish the model on time. | The dressmaker measured her bust, waist and hips.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past form: «bust» (UK) or «busted» (US and informal everywhere). «Bust» for break is informal; in writing use «broke». The chest meaning is polite, not rude. «Busted» can also mean «broken» in US slang: a busted phone.

part of speech: noun (a chap, chaps); verb (chap, chaps, chapped, chapping)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (UK, informal, a bit old-fashioned) A chap is a man or boy, a fellow. 2) Chaps are leather leg coverings worn by cowboys over their trousers. 3) To chap is for skin or lips to become dry, rough and cracked, usually from cold or wind. 4) (Scotland, Northern Ireland) To chap is to knock on a door.
its sense in the lessons: In British stories and older books, «a nice chap», «old chap» are friendly ways to talk about men. In winter health tips: «chapped lips», «lip balm». In westerns, cowboys wear chaps. Phrases: «a decent chap», «old chap», «chapped lips/hands».
examples from the lessons: Mr Davies is a friendly chap who runs the corner shop. | «Well done, old chap!» said Grandpa. | My lips are chapped from the cold wind. | Use hand cream so your hands don't chap. | The cowboy pulled on his leather chaps. | (Scotland) Chap the door and see if he's in.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «chaps». Mostly British; Americans say «guy», Australians «bloke». Double the p: chapped, chapping. «Chap» is not short for «chapter» (that is «chap.» with a full stop in writing).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A cheerer is a person who cheers, shouting loudly to encourage a team or a player. 2) Something or someone that makes others happier.
its sense in the lessons: A rare word; at sports days and matches you more often hear «supporter», «fan» or «cheerleader». It tells the reader that someone is shouting encouragement. Phrases: «loud cheerers».
examples from the lessons: The cheerers waved flags along the race track. | Mum is the loudest cheerer at every football match. | Our class were the best cheerers on sports day. | The cheerers shouted «Go, Ella, go!». | A puppy is a great cheerer-upper on a sad day (informal). | The cheerers clapped for every runner, even the last.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A rare word made from «cheer» + «-er». More common: «fan», «supporter», «cheerleader» (a person in a squad who leads cheering with dances). «Cheerer-upper» is a playful informal word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The coastguard is the organisation that watches the sea near a coast and rescues people and boats in danger. 2) A coastguard is a person who works for it.
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons: if someone is in trouble at sea or on cliffs, call the emergency number (999 or 112 in the UK and Ireland, 911 in the US and Canada, 000 in Australia, 111 in New Zealand) and ask for the coastguard. In stories it tells the reader help is coming. Phrases: «call the coastguard», «coastguard helicopter», «coastguard station».
examples from the lessons: The coastguard rescued two kayakers caught by the tide. | If you see someone in trouble at sea, call for the coastguard. | A coastguard helicopter flew over the beach. | My uncle is a coastguard and watches for ships in danger. | The coastguard warned people to keep away from the cliff edge. | The boat radioed the coastguard for help.
note for the reader of a maths problem: In the US it is «the Coast Guard» (two words, a military service); in the UK and Ireland «the Coastguard» or «coastguard». Lifeguards watch swimmers on beaches; the coastguard deals with the wider sea and coast.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Combative means ready and eager to fight or argue. 2) In sport, combative means playing hard and strongly against the other side.
its sense in the lessons: In stories it describes a character who always picks arguments; in sports reports it praises or criticises a tough player. It tells the reader that someone likes to fight or argue. Phrases: «combative mood», «combative style», «a combative player».
examples from the lessons: The combative goat butted everyone who came near. | He was in a combative mood and argued with everyone. | She is a combative tennis player who never gives up. | The debate became combative and loud. | Our dog is friendly, not combative. | Try not to be combative when someone disagrees with you.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stress: com-BAT-ive (UK) or COM-ba-tive. From «combat» (fighting). Not always bad: in sport it can mean brave and determined. Similar: aggressive, argumentative.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A commendation is official praise or an award given to someone for doing something well or bravely. 2) Commendation is praise in general. 3) (church, formal) A prayer that gives someone into God's care, especially a person who is dying.
its sense in the lessons: In school, a commendation can be a certificate for good work or behaviour; police officers and firefighters get commendations for bravery. It tells the reader that someone has been praised officially. Phrases: «receive a commendation», «a commendation for bravery», «highly commended».
examples from the lessons: Ava got a commendation for her science project. | The firefighter received a commendation for bravery. | Our class earned a commendation for helping at the food bank. | The teacher wrote words of commendation on my report. | His painting was «highly commended» in the competition. | The headteacher read out the commendations in assembly.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: «commend» (to praise formally). «Highly commended» in a competition usually means just below the prizes. Spelling: two m's.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (grammar) The comparative is the form of an adjective or adverb used to compare two things: bigger, taller, more beautiful, better. 2) Comparative means judged by comparing with something else: «comparative comfort», «comparatively easy». 3) Comparative describes a study that compares things: comparative religion.
its sense in the lessons: In English grammar lessons pupils learn comparatives and superlatives (big, bigger, biggest). In maths it links to comparing amounts with «more than», «less than». Phrases: «comparative form», «comparative adjective», «comparatively small».
examples from the lessons: «Taller» is the comparative of «tall». | The comparative of «good» is «better». | After the storm, the calm felt like comparative luxury. | The test was comparatively easy this time. | Write the comparative and superlative of «fast». | Long words use «more»: «more interesting» is a comparative.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Rules: short words add -er (cold → colder), words ending in y change to -ier (happy → happier), long words use «more» (more careful). Irregular: good → better, bad → worse, far → further/farther. Use «than» after a comparative: taller than me. Do not say «more bigger». Superlative: biggest, most careful.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (law) A complainant is a person who makes an official complaint or brings a case to a court, saying they have been wronged. 2) (formal) Anyone who makes a formal complaint, for example to a company or school.
its sense in the lessons: A formal, legal word met in news about trials and complaints. It tells the reader who says they were harmed. Phrases: «the complainant said», «the complainant's lawyer».
examples from the lessons: The complainant told the court what had happened. | The judge listened to both the complainant and the accused. | The complainant asked for the money to be returned. | The company wrote back to each complainant. | In the case, the complainant was a shop owner. | The complainant's name was kept secret.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; in daily speech say «the person who complained». Not the same as «complaint» (what is said) or «complainer» (someone who moans a lot, informal). The other side in a criminal case is «the defendant» or «the accused».

part of speech: verb (compress, compresses, compressed, compressing); noun (a compress, compresses)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To compress something is to press or squeeze it so it takes up less space. 2) (computing) To compress a file is to make it smaller so it is quicker to send or store. 3) To compress words or time is to make them shorter: «compress the story into one page». 4) A compress is a pad of cloth, often cold or warm and wet, pressed on the body to ease pain or swelling.
its sense in the lessons: In science, gases can be compressed (air in a bike tyre or a spray can); springs compress when pushed. In first aid, a cold compress helps a bump or sprain. In computing, files are compressed into zip files. Phrases: «compressed air», «cold compress», «compress a file».
examples from the lessons: When you squash a sponge, you compress it. | The air in a bicycle pump is compressed. | Dad compressed the photos so he could email them. | Put a cold compress on the bruise. | The spring compresses when you press it and springs back. | Gases can be compressed much more than liquids. | We had to compress our story into 100 words.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stress differs: verb com-PRESS, noun COM-press. Noun of the action: «compression». In science: gases compress easily; liquids and solids hardly at all.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Conclusive means proving something completely, so that there is no doubt left. 2) Conclusive describes a final, clear result: a conclusive win.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons it talks about evidence: one test is rarely conclusive; we repeat experiments. In detective stories, conclusive proof catches the thief. Phrases: «conclusive evidence», «conclusive proof», «conclusively prove».
examples from the lessons: The fingerprints were conclusive proof that the cat had walked on the cake. | One test is not conclusive; we need to repeat it. | The team won a conclusive victory, 5–0. | Scientists have conclusive evidence that smoking harms health. | The footage showed conclusively that the ball was in. | The results were not conclusive, so the experiment goes on.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: «inconclusive» (not proving anything for sure). Related to «conclude» and «conclusion». Trap: in science, «conclusive» should be used carefully; a fair test needs repeats.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Condolences are words or messages of sympathy you give to someone when a person they love has died. 2) Condolence is the feeling of sympathy shown at such a time.
its sense in the lessons: Used when someone dies: people send cards of condolence, sign a book of condolence, or say «My condolences». It is a respectful and gentle word. Phrases: «my condolences», «offer condolences», «a letter of condolence», «book of condolence».
examples from the lessons: We sent a card of condolence to our neighbours. | Please accept my condolences on the loss of your grandmother. | The class wrote condolences to their teacher when her father died. | Hundreds of people signed the book of condolence. | He offered his condolences at the funeral. | A short, kind message of condolence can mean a lot.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually plural: «condolences». You «offer», «send» or «express» condolences. Used for a death (or sometimes a big loss), not for small problems. Similar phrase: «I'm so sorry for your loss».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Confidently means in a way that shows you believe in yourself and are not afraid. 2) Confidently means while feeling sure that something is true or will happen.
its sense in the lessons: In school reports and lessons: «speaks confidently», «reads confidently», «uses times tables confidently». In stories it shows a brave, sure character. Phrases: «answer confidently», «walk confidently», «confidently predict».
examples from the lessons: She walked confidently onto the stage. | Tom answered the question confidently. | Now I can confidently swim a whole length. | The weatherman confidently said it would be sunny. | Speak confidently and look at the audience. | He confidently predicted that his team would win.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: «confident»; noun: «confidence». Not the same as «confidentially» (in secret). Confident is not the same as being right: you can say something confidently and still be wrong.

part of speech: verb (-ing form of congregate: congregate, congregates, congregated, congregating)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Congregating means gathering together in a group or crowd in one place. 2) (church) People congregating in a church are coming together to worship; the group is a «congregation».
its sense in the lessons: Used in science (animals congregating at a waterhole), in stories and in rules («No congregating in the corridor»). It tells the reader that many people or animals are coming together. Phrases: «congregating around», «congregating outside».
examples from the lessons: Birds were congregating on the telephone wires before flying south. | Pupils were congregating near the school gates. | Penguins are congregating on the ice to keep warm. | People were congregating outside the church for the wedding. | Fans are congregating in the square before the match. | Please stop congregating in the doorway.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Base verb «congregate»; past «congregated». Noun «congregation» (the people in a church service, or a gathering). A formal word; everyday: «gathering», «crowding». Stress: CON-gre-gate.

part of speech: noun (a conjecture, conjectures; also uncountable); verb (conjecture, conjectures, conjectured, conjecturing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A conjecture is a guess or opinion formed without full proof. 2) To conjecture is to guess or suppose something when you do not have all the facts. 3) (maths) A conjecture is a statement mathematicians think is true but have not yet proved.
its sense in the lessons: In maths lessons pupils make a conjecture from patterns («I think all even numbers end in 0, 2, 4, 6 or 8») and then test it. In stories and news it means a guess. Phrases: «pure conjecture», «make a conjecture», «a matter of conjecture».
examples from the lessons: My conjecture is that the next number in the pattern is 20. | Without evidence, what you say is just conjecture. | Scientists conjectured that the planet had water. | Test your conjecture with more examples. | How the stones got there is still a matter of conjecture. | A famous conjecture says every even number bigger than 2 is the sum of two prime numbers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: In maths, a conjecture becomes a «theorem» when it is proved. One counterexample shows a conjecture is false. Formal; everyday words: «guess», «hunch», «theory».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Convincingly means in a way that makes people believe something is true or real. 2) Convincingly also means clearly and with a big difference: «won convincingly».
its sense in the lessons: In drama and stories: an actor plays a part convincingly. In persuasive writing pupils argue convincingly. In sports reports: the team won convincingly. Phrases: «argue convincingly», «win convincingly».
examples from the lessons: She argued convincingly for a longer break time. | He acted the part of the wolf very convincingly. | Our team won convincingly, 6–1. | The robot moved convincingly like a real dog. | Write convincingly, with good reasons and examples. | He lied so convincingly that we almost believed him.
