note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: «convincing»; verb: «convince». Opposite: «unconvincingly». Trap: something said convincingly is not always true.

part of speech: noun (copyright, copyrights; usually uncountable); verb (copyright, copyrights, copyrighted, copyrighting); adjective (copyright)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (law) Copyright is the legal right of the person who made a book, song, picture, film or program to decide who can copy, sell or use it. 2) To copyright something is to get or claim this right over it.
its sense in the lessons: In school, pupils learn not to copy others' work or pictures without permission, and to give credit to sources. The symbol © shows copyright. Phrases: «under copyright», «copyright holder», «out of copyright», «breach of copyright».
examples from the lessons: The author owns the copyright to her books. | You can't put that song in your video without permission; it is under copyright. | The © sign shows who owns the copyright. | Very old stories are out of copyright, so anyone can print them. | Our class asked permission to use the photo. | Copying a whole website and calling it yours breaks copyright.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: copyright, not «copywrite» (copywriting is writing adverts, a different thing). Copyright does not last forever; after a long time works become «public domain». Plagiarism (passing off someone's work as yours) is wrong even when copying is allowed.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Cowardice is a lack of courage: being too afraid to do what is right or what is needed. 2) A shameful act done because of fear.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and ethics it is the opposite of bravery; it tells the reader a character let others down out of fear. Discussions note that feeling fear is not cowardice; letting fear stop you doing right can be. Phrases: «an act of cowardice», «accuse of cowardice».
examples from the lessons: Running away and leaving his friend was an act of cowardice. | The knight was ashamed of his cowardice. | It isn't cowardice to walk away from a fight. | She overcame her cowardice and told the truth. | Bullying a smaller child is a kind of cowardice. | The soldier was accused of cowardice.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Related: «coward» (a person), «cowardly» (adjective, not an adverb: «a cowardly act»). Spelling: cowardice ends in -ice. Being sensible about danger is not cowardice.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Criminally means in a way that breaks the law and is a crime. 2) (informal) Criminally means shockingly or very badly, as if it should be a crime: «criminally underrated».
its sense in the lessons: In news and law: «criminally responsible», «charged criminally». In everyday talk, it is used jokingly: «That band is criminally underrated». Phrases: «criminally responsible», «criminally negligent», «criminally underrated».
examples from the lessons: He was found criminally responsible for the damage. | The company acted criminally when it dumped waste in the river. | That film is criminally underrated (informal). | The owner was criminally careless with the fire exits. | In some countries, children under a certain age are not criminally responsible. | It's criminally unfair that we have homework on holiday! (joking)
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: «criminal»; noun: «crime», «criminal». The informal meaning is exaggeration (hyperbole), not a real crime.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal, unkind) A crybaby is someone, especially a child, who cries or complains easily over small things. 2) (informal) An adult who moans when things do not go their way.
its sense in the lessons: A playground taunt; in stories it tells the reader someone is being teased for crying. In PSHE lessons, it is a word that can hurt: everyone cries sometimes. Phrases: «don't be a crybaby», «called him a crybaby».
examples from the lessons: The older boys called him a crybaby, which was mean. | «Stop being a crybaby,» said his sister, but he really was hurt. | The footballer acted like a crybaby when the referee gave a foul. | It's okay to cry; it doesn't make you a crybaby. | The toddler is not a crybaby; she's just tired. | Calling someone a crybaby is a kind of teasing.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «crybabies». Informal and unkind; better not to call people this. Spelt crybaby (US) or cry-baby (UK).

part of speech: adjective (decisive, more decisive, most decisive); adverb (decisively)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Decisive describes a person who can make decisions quickly and firmly. 2) Decisive means having the biggest effect on the result: «the decisive goal», «a decisive moment». 3) Decisive means clear, with no doubt: «a decisive victory».
its sense in the lessons: In stories leaders and heroes are decisive; in sports and history the «decisive battle» or «decisive goal» settled the result. Phrases: «decisive moment», «decisive role», «act decisively».
examples from the lessons: Our captain is decisive and makes quick plans. | Her goal in the last minute was decisive. | The battle was decisive and ended the war. | Be decisive: pick a book and start reading! | He acted decisively and called for help. | Winning 10–0 was a decisive victory.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: «indecisive» (unable to decide). Related: decide, decision. Not «decisive» = cutting; that is «incisive».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (medicine) A diagnosis is the decision a doctor makes about what illness or problem someone has, after looking at the signs. 2) Finding out what is wrong with a machine, a car or a system.
its sense in the lessons: In health lessons and doctor visits: the doctor asks questions, checks you, and gives a diagnosis. Mechanics diagnose cars too. It tells the reader that the cause of a problem has been found. Phrases: «make a diagnosis», «an early diagnosis», «the diagnosis was…».
examples from the lessons: The doctor's diagnosis was a sprained ankle, not a break. | An early diagnosis can help people get better faster. | After tests, the diagnosis was asthma. | The mechanic made a quick diagnosis: a flat battery. | My cousin got a diagnosis of dyslexia, and now she gets extra help. | A wrong diagnosis can lead to the wrong medicine.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «diagnoses» (dy-ag-NO-seez). Verb: «diagnose». Adjective: «diagnostic» (a diagnostic test). Do not use search engines to diagnose yourself; see a doctor.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Dignity is the worth that every person has, which means they should be treated with respect. 2) Dignity is a calm, serious and proud way of behaving, even in hard times. 3) Self-respect: feeling that you matter.
its sense in the lessons: In ethics, RE and citizenship lessons, «human dignity» is the idea that every person deserves respect; it is behind human rights. In stories it shows a character staying calm and proud. Phrases: «with dignity», «human dignity», «beneath my dignity», «lose your dignity».
examples from the lessons: Every person deserves to be treated with dignity. | She lost the race but shook hands with dignity. | The nurses helped Grandpa keep his dignity in hospital. | Laughing at someone who fell takes away their dignity. | The old king walked with great dignity. | Slipping on the ice, I lost all my dignity! (joking)
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Adjective: «dignified». Many religions teach that all people have dignity; Christians believe every person is made in the image of God. «Beneath your dignity» = too silly or low for you to do.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Discernible means able to be seen, heard, noticed or understood, even if only just.
its sense in the lessons: A formal word in science and reading: «no discernible difference» in a test, «a discernible shape» in fog. It tells the reader that something can be noticed, often with effort. Phrases: «barely discernible», «no discernible difference», «a discernible change».
examples from the lessons: There was no discernible difference between the two plants. | In the fog, the lighthouse was barely discernible. | A faint smile was discernible on her face. | The change in temperature was hardly discernible. | After a week, there was a discernible improvement in his reading. | The ship became discernible on the horizon.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: discernible (with -ible). Verb: «discern» (to notice, often with effort). Formal; everyday: «noticeable», «visible». Opposite: «indiscernible».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Disciplinary means to do with punishing people who break rules, at school, work or in sport. 2) (formal) To do with a subject of study, as in «interdisciplinary».
its sense in the lessons: In school life: «disciplinary action» means a punishment such as detention or exclusion. In sport, a player may face a «disciplinary hearing». Phrases: «disciplinary action», «disciplinary hearing», «disciplinary record».
examples from the lessons: Fighting in class led to disciplinary action. | The player faced a disciplinary hearing after the match. | The school has a clear disciplinary policy. | He has a clean disciplinary record. | The worker was given a disciplinary warning for being late. | Our project was interdisciplinary: maths, art and science together.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Related: «discipline» (rules and control, or a subject; also verb: to punish). Stress: DIS-ci-plin-ary or dis-ci-PLIN-ary. A formal word used by schools and employers.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Disinterested means fair because you do not gain anything either way; not taking sides. 2) (informal, often thought wrong) Disinterested is also used to mean not interested, bored.
its sense in the lessons: In law, sport and ethics, a «disinterested judge» or referee is fair and does not support one side. In everyday speech many people use it for «uninterested», which careful writers avoid. Phrases: «a disinterested observer», «disinterested advice».
examples from the lessons: A referee should be disinterested and fair to both teams. | We asked a disinterested person to judge the competition. | Her advice was disinterested; she gained nothing from it. | The judge must be disinterested in the case. | He seemed disinterested in the lesson (many say «uninterested» here). | A disinterested witness has nothing to win or lose.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Big trap: «disinterested» (fair, not taking sides) vs «uninterested» (bored, not caring). Teachers and exams prefer: «The judge was disinterested; the bored pupil was uninterested». Noun: «disinterest».

meaning for a pupil: 1) To disperse is to go away in different directions, or to make a crowd do this. 2) To spread something widely over an area. 3) (science) For light, to split into its colours, as in a prism. 4) For fog, cloud or smoke, to thin out and disappear.
its sense in the lessons: In science: seeds are dispersed by wind, water and animals; light is dispersed by a prism into a rainbow. In news: police dispersed a crowd. Phrases: «the crowd dispersed», «seed dispersal», «the fog dispersed».
examples from the lessons: After the match, the crowd slowly dispersed. | Dandelion seeds are dispersed by the wind. | Birds help disperse seeds by eating fruit. | By noon, the fog had dispersed. | A prism disperses white light into the colours of the rainbow. | Police told the gathering to disperse. | The smell dispersed when we opened the window.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: «dispersal» (seed dispersal) or «dispersion» (of light). Opposite: gather, congregate. Spelling: disperse, not «disburse» (which means to pay out money).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) Dissipation is the slow spreading out and loss of something, especially energy, heat or a cloud, until it fades away. 2) Wasting money, time or effort. 3) (old-fashioned, disapproving) Living a wild life of too much drinking and pleasure.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on energy: some energy is «dissipated» as heat and sound, so no machine is perfectly efficient. In weather, clouds and fog dissipate. In older stories, dissipation describes a wasteful, unhealthy life. Phrases: «heat dissipation», «energy dissipation».
examples from the lessons: A car engine loses energy through the dissipation of heat. | The dissipation of the fog made the road safe again. | The fan helps the dissipation of heat from the computer. | The storm weakened, and its dissipation took a day. | In the old novel, the rich young man ruined his health with dissipation. | The dissipation of his savings left him poor.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Verb: «dissipate». In physics, energy is not destroyed when it dissipates; it spreads out, usually as heat. Formal word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A diva is a famous and very talented female singer, especially in opera. 2) (informal, disapproving) A diva is someone who behaves as if they are very important and expects special treatment, making a fuss.
its sense in the lessons: In music lessons, an opera diva; in everyday talk and showbiz stories, «diva behaviour» means demanding and fussy. Phrases: «opera diva», «pop diva», «diva behaviour», «a bit of a diva».
examples from the lessons: The opera diva sang a beautiful song. | She is a pop diva with millions of fans. | Stop being such a diva and help tidy up! | The cat is a diva; she only eats from a clean bowl. | The star refused to go on stage until she had pink roses — real diva behaviour. | He was a bit of a diva about his costume.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «divas». The word comes from Italian for «goddess». The informal meaning is used for anyone, boys and men too, though it is more often said of women; it can be a little unkind.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Dominance is having more power, control or importance than others. 2) In sport, dominance means being much better than other teams over a long time. 3) (science) In genetics, dominance is when one version of a gene shows instead of another.
its sense in the lessons: In science it appears in animal groups (the dominant wolf) and in genetics (dominant and recessive genes, for example eye colour). In sports reports, «total dominance» of a match. In history, the dominance of an empire. Phrases: «total dominance», «dominance over», «a position of dominance».
examples from the lessons: The team showed its dominance by winning every match. | Wolves show dominance with body language. | The dominance of the empire lasted for centuries. | Hand dominance means whether you are left- or right-handed. | The gene for brown eyes shows dominance over the gene for blue eyes. | The big dog tried to show dominance over the puppy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Adjective «dominant»; verb «dominate». Do not confuse with «domination» (taking control, often by force) though they are close. Myth: «alpha wolf» stories are simplified; wild wolf packs are mostly families.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Drowsiness is the feeling of being sleepy and only half awake, with heavy eyelids.
its sense in the lessons: In health and safety: some medicines «may cause drowsiness», so adults must not drive. In stories it tells the reader a character is drifting off. Phrases: «may cause drowsiness», «feeling of drowsiness».
examples from the lessons: This medicine may cause drowsiness. | A warm room and a long film filled me with drowsiness. | Drowsiness while driving is dangerous. | After lunch, a wave of drowsiness came over the class. | Drowsiness is a sign that you need more sleep. | The cat yawned in drowsiness on the windowsill.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Adjective: «drowsy», adverb «drowsily». Spelling: drowsiness (y changes to i). Safety: never drive or use machines when drowsy.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A drummer is a person who plays the drums, for example in a band, orchestra or marching band. 2) (older use) A drummer boy beat a drum for marching soldiers. 3) (US, old-fashioned) A travelling salesman.
its sense in the lessons: In music lessons and school bands; a drummer keeps the beat for everyone. Phrases: «the band's drummer», «drummer boy», «march to the beat of a different drummer» (to do things your own way).
examples from the lessons: My brother is the drummer in the school band. | The drummer kept a steady beat. | The drummer counted «one, two, three, four» before the song. | In old battles, a drummer boy marched with the soldiers. | She wants to be a drummer when she grows up. | He marches to the beat of a different drummer; he does things his own way.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double m: drummer, drumming. Related: drum, drumsticks. The drummer usually sits at the back of the stage with the drum kit.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An endorsement is public support or approval for a person, plan or product. 2) (money) A deal where a famous person is paid to say they use or like a product. 3) (UK, law) A note on a driving licence that shows the driver broke a traffic law. 4) (money) A signature on the back of a cheque.
its sense in the lessons: In news and adverts: celebrities and sports stars get «endorsement deals». In elections, a famous person may give an endorsement to a candidate. It tells the reader that someone has said «yes, I support this». Phrases: «endorsement deal», «a strong endorsement», «celebrity endorsement».
examples from the lessons: The footballer has an endorsement deal with a trainer company. | The mayor gave her endorsement to the new park. | The book got a glowing endorsement from a famous author. | Celebrity endorsements make people want to buy things. | Speeding earned him an endorsement on his licence. | The plan won the endorsement of the whole school council.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: «endorse». Spelt endorsement (UK and US). Trap: an endorsement in an advert is paid; it does not prove the product is good.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Escalation is when something becomes bigger, worse or more serious, step by step, like a fight or a war. 2) A rise in amounts or prices.
its sense in the lessons: In news (escalation of a conflict) and in PSHE lessons on conflict: shouting, then pushing, then fighting is escalation; «de-escalation» means calming things down. Phrases: «escalation of violence», «avoid escalation», «de-escalation».
examples from the lessons: Name-calling led to an escalation, and soon they were pushing. | Leaders met to stop the escalation of the war. | There was an escalation in prices at the shop. | Walking away can prevent escalation. | The teacher stopped the argument before any escalation. | The escalation of the storm forced us inside.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: «escalate». Opposite: «de-escalation». Related: «escalator» (moving stairs), which goes up step by step too.

part of speech: noun (an escort, escorts); verb (escort, escorts, escorted, escorting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To escort someone is to go with them to protect them, guide them or keep them under guard. 2) An escort is a person, group or vehicle that goes with someone for protection or as an honour. 3) (old-fashioned) A person who goes with another to a party or dance as a partner. 4) (adult, euphemism) Someone paid to go out with another person; children usually do not need this sense.
its sense in the lessons: In news and stories: police escorts, soldiers escorting a king, a teacher escorting pupils across the road. It tells the reader someone is being protected or guarded. Phrases: «police escort», «under escort», «escort someone home».
examples from the lessons: A police car escorted the ambulance through traffic. | The teacher escorted the children to the bus. | The queen arrived with an escort of soldiers on horses. | The prisoner was taken to court under escort. | Dad will escort you home after the party. | Two ships escorted the big tanker into the harbour.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stress: verb es-CORT, noun ES-cort. Similar: accompany, guide. «Under escort» means guarded.

part of speech: adjective (esteemed); verb form (past of esteem: esteem, esteems, esteemed, esteeming)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Esteemed means greatly respected and admired. 2) Esteemed is also the past form of «esteem»: to respect someone highly.
its sense in the lessons: A formal, polite word used in speeches, letters and ceremonies: «our esteemed guests», «an esteemed scientist». Sometimes used jokingly in a grand way. Phrases: «highly esteemed», «esteemed colleague», «esteemed guest».
examples from the lessons: We welcome our esteemed guest, the mayor. | She is an esteemed author of children's books. | The old doctor was highly esteemed in the village. | My esteemed brother has finally done the washing up (joking). | The scientist was esteemed for her discoveries. | Esteemed judges, thank you for listening.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; everyday: «respected», «admired». Noun «esteem» (respect), as in «self-esteem» (how much you value yourself). Use «an»: an esteemed visitor.

part of speech: adjective (informal: fab); noun (prefab, fab lab — separate words)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (slang, UK and others) Fab is short for «fabulous»: great, wonderful, brilliant. 2) (informal, technical) A «fab» is a factory that makes computer chips.
its sense in the lessons: A cheerful casual word in everyday talk, texts and comics: «That's fab!» It tells the reader the speaker is very pleased. Often said in the UK, Ireland and Australia. Phrases: «fab idea», «you look fab», «absolutely fab».
examples from the lessons: What a fab party! | You look fab in that costume. | «Fab idea!» said Mum when I suggested pancakes. | We had a fab time at the beach. | The Fab Four is a nickname for a famous old band. | It's a fab book; you should read it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Short for «fabulous». Informal; in a school essay use «wonderful» or «excellent». No comparative usually (not «fabber»).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Faithfully means in a loyal way that can be trusted: keeping promises and staying true. 2) Faithfully means exactly and carefully, without changes: «copied faithfully». 3) (UK, Ireland, Australia) «Yours faithfully» is the polite way to end a formal letter when you begin with «Dear Sir or Madam». 4) (church) Faithfully also means with religious faith and devotion.
its sense in the lessons: In letter-writing lessons, pupils learn «Yours faithfully» and «Yours sincerely». In stories, a faithful dog waits faithfully for its owner. Phrases: «Yours faithfully», «faithfully promise», «faithfully copied», «serve faithfully».
examples from the lessons: The dog waited faithfully at the door every evening. | He promised faithfully to return the book. | She copied the drawing faithfully, line by line. | The old gardener served the family faithfully. | End your letter to «Dear Sir or Madam» with «Yours faithfully». | She went to church faithfully every Sunday.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK rule: «Dear Sir or Madam» → «Yours faithfully»; «Dear Mrs Smith» → «Yours sincerely». In the US «Sincerely» is used for both. Adjective: «faithful»; noun: «faith», «faithfulness».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A feeder is a container that holds food for birds or animals. 2) An animal or person that eats in a particular way: «a messy feeder», «a night feeder». 3) A feeder road, river or school sends people or things into a bigger one: a feeder school sends pupils to a secondary school. 4) A device that feeds material into a machine, like a paper feeder in a printer.
its sense in the lessons: In science and nature at home: bird feeders in the garden help birds in winter. In school life, «feeder schools» send children to a bigger school. Phrases: «bird feeder», «feeder school», «feeder road».
examples from the lessons: We hung a bird feeder outside the classroom window. | Blue tits and robins visit our feeder every morning. | Our primary is a feeder school for the high school. | The baby is a messy feeder! | Caterpillars are hungry feeders that munch leaves all day. | The paper feeder on the printer is jammed.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «feeders». From «feed» + «-er». Keep feeders clean so birds do not get sick.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A footballer is a person who plays football, especially as a job. 2) In the UK and most countries, football means soccer; in the USA, Canada and parts of Australia, «football» can mean American, Canadian, Australian rules football or rugby league, so a footballer can play those games.
its sense in the lessons: In PE, sport and news; many children want to be footballers. Phrases: «professional footballer», «famous footballer», «young footballer».
examples from the lessons: My cousin wants to be a professional footballer. | The footballer scored a header in the last minute. | The footballers ran onto the pitch. | A footballer needs good fitness and teamwork. | She is the best footballer in our school team. | Famous footballers visited the children's hospital.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly British/Irish/Australian word; Americans more often say «soccer player» or «football player». Plural «footballers».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (law) Forfeiture is the losing of property, money or a right as a punishment for breaking a rule or law. 2) (sport) Losing a match because a team broke the rules or did not turn up.
its sense in the lessons: A formal legal word used in news: «forfeiture of assets» (when the police take money or things gained from crime). Phrases: «asset forfeiture», «forfeiture of a deposit».
examples from the lessons: The court ordered the forfeiture of the stolen car. | Breaking the rules led to the forfeiture of the prize. | The deposit is subject to forfeiture if you cancel late. | The criminal faced forfeiture of all his money. | Forfeiture of the match happened because the team had too few players. | Asset forfeiture means taking things bought with crime money.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: «forfeit» (to lose something as a penalty); «forfeit» is also a noun. Spelling: forfeiture (ei, not ie). Very formal; say «losing» in everyday speech.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A forgery is a copy of something such as a painting, a banknote, a document or a signature, made to trick people into thinking it is real. 2) (law) Forgery is the crime of making such false copies.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and news about art, money and crime; detectives find out that a painting is a forgery. In school, copying a parent's signature on a note is forgery and is dishonest. Phrases: «a clever forgery», «guilty of forgery», «the painting is a forgery».
examples from the lessons: The museum found out that the painting was a forgery. | Forging a signature is forgery, which is a crime. | Banknotes have special marks to stop forgery. | He was sent to prison for forgery. | The detective spotted the forgery because the ink was too new. | Signing your mum's name on a school note is forgery, even if it seems small.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «forgeries». Verb «forge» (also means to shape hot metal); person «forger». A «fake» is a looser everyday word. Not the same as «counterfeit», which is used especially for money and goods.

part of speech: verb (past of formulate: formulate, formulates, formulated, formulating); adjective (formulated)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Formulated means carefully thought out and put into words or a plan: «a well-formulated question». 2) (science) Formulated means made according to a special recipe or formula: «a cream formulated for babies». 3) (maths) A rule or problem formulated as an equation is written in mathematical form.
its sense in the lessons: In science and maths: scientists formulated a theory, laws are formulated, a problem is formulated as an equation. In adverts, products are «specially formulated». Phrases: «carefully formulated», «well-formulated», «formulated for».
examples from the lessons: Newton formulated the laws of motion. | The question was clearly formulated, so it was easy to answer. | This toothpaste is formulated for children's teeth. | We formulated a plan to raise money for charity. | The rule was formulated after a playground accident. | The word problem can be formulated as 3 × 7 = 21.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Base verb «formulate»; noun «formulation»; «formula» (plural formulas or formulae) is the recipe or maths rule. In adverts «specially formulated» is a selling phrase, not proof.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A greyhound is a tall, thin dog with long legs that can run very fast, used for racing and hunting and kept as a gentle pet. 2) (US) Greyhound is the name of a well-known long-distance bus company.
its sense in the lessons: In science, greyhounds are famous as the fastest dog breed. In everyday life, many retired racing greyhounds are adopted as calm pets. Phrases: «greyhound racing», «rescue greyhound».
examples from the lessons: A greyhound can run as fast as a car in town. | Our rescue greyhound loves sleeping on the sofa. | Greyhound racing is popular in Ireland and Australia. | The greyhound chased a toy rabbit around the track. | Greyhounds are gentle and quiet dogs. | They travelled across America on a Greyhound bus.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelt greyhound everywhere, even in the US (not «grayhound»). Greyhounds are not always grey. They can reach about 70 kilometres per hour.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Heartbreak is very great sadness, especially when someone you love leaves you, dies, or when you lose something important. 2) A heartbreak is an event that causes such sadness.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, songs and sports reports: heartbreak when a pet dies, a friend moves away, or a team loses in the last minute. It tells the reader a character is deeply sad. Phrases: «heartbreak of losing», «last-minute heartbreak», «heartbreak hotel» (song).
examples from the lessons: Losing our old dog was a real heartbreak. | The team suffered heartbreak in the final minute. | Moving away from her best friend caused great heartbreak. | The song is about heartbreak and love. | There was heartbreak when the school play was cancelled. | Time and friends help heal heartbreak.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Related: «heartbroken» (very sad), «heartbreaking» (causing great sadness). Usually uncountable. Not a medical problem of the heart.

part of speech: verb (heed, heeds, heeded, heeding); noun (heed; uncountable)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To heed advice or a warning is to pay attention to it and do what it says. 2) Heed (noun) means attention: «take heed», «pay no heed».
its sense in the lessons: A slightly old-fashioned or formal word in stories, fables and safety messages: «Heed the warning signs». It tells the reader whether a character listened to good advice. Phrases: «heed the warning», «take heed», «pay heed to», «pay no heed».
examples from the lessons: The sailors did not heed the storm warning. | Heed your teacher's advice and check your work. | Take heed: the ice is thin! | The boy who cried wolf found that no one heeded him. | She paid no heed to the rude comments. | Heed the signs and keep away from the cliff edge.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; everyday: «listen to», «pay attention to». Adjective: «heedless» (careless), as in «heedless of danger». «Heedful» is rare.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Honorary describes a title or position given to someone as an honour, to thank or respect them, without the usual exams, work or pay. 2) (formal) Honorary describes a job done without being paid: «honorary secretary».
its sense in the lessons: In news and school life: an «honorary degree» from a university, an «honorary member» of a club, «honorary citizen» of a town. It tells the reader that a title is a mark of respect. Phrases: «honorary degree», «honorary member», «honorary citizen».
examples from the lessons: The famous author got an honorary degree from the university. | Our lollipop lady was made an honorary member of the school council. | The firefighter was named an honorary citizen. | Grandpa is the honorary president of the football club. | The dog became an honorary member of our class! | An honorary doctor does not treat patients.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: honorary (no u, even in the UK). Do not confuse with «honourable/honorable» (deserving honour, honest). An honorary doctorate does not make someone a medical doctor.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Idleness is being lazy and not working or doing anything useful. 2) Idleness is also simply not being in use or not busy: a machine's idleness.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, fables and sayings, idleness is shown as a fault: «Idleness is the root of all mischief». In ethics and church teaching, laziness (sloth) is one of the old list of sins. Phrases: «a life of idleness», «idle hands».
examples from the lessons: The grasshopper spent the summer in idleness while the ants worked. | His idleness meant his homework never got done. | After weeks of idleness, the factory machines were rusty. | A little idleness on a holiday can be nice. | «Idle hands make mischief,» Grandma says. | Idleness made the long afternoon feel boring.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Adjective «idle», adverb «idly». Do not confuse «idle» with «idol» (a famous person you admire, or a statue worshipped). Resting is not idleness: everyone needs rest.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) In a way that nobody can argue against or prove wrong, because the facts are completely clear. 2) Without any possible doubt; certainly.
its sense in the lessons: Used in the stiff exam voice, in science reports and in detective stories when the evidence is so strong that the question is closed: «the footprints incontrovertibly showed…». It tells the reader that a claim is settled, not just likely. In maths it is close to «proved»: a proof shows something incontrovertibly. Often comes in «incontrovertibly true», «incontrovertibly proved», «incontrovertibly linked».
examples from the lessons: The video incontrovertibly showed that the ball crossed the line. | The experiment proved incontrovertibly that plants need light to grow. | The fingerprints incontrovertibly linked the thief to the broken window. | It is incontrovertibly true that 2 + 2 = 4. | The results were incontrovertibly clear, so the teacher did not ask us to repeat the test. | «You took the last biscuit,» said Mum, «and the crumbs prove it incontrovertibly.» | Scientists have shown incontrovertibly that the Earth goes round the Sun.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A long formal word; in everyday talk people say «without a doubt», «definitely» or «beyond question». Stress: in-con-tro-VER-ti-bly. Do not mix it up with «controversially» (in a way that causes arguments) – it means almost the opposite. Be careful: writers sometimes use it for things that are only very likely; true incontrovertible proof leaves no room for doubt at all.

part of speech: adjective (indistinguishable; not used with «more» in the strict sense, but people say «almost indistinguishable», «nearly indistinguishable»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) So alike that you cannot tell them apart. 2) So faint or unclear that you cannot pick it out or recognise it, for example a shape in fog.
its sense in the lessons: Used about twins, copies, fakes, colours, sounds and samples in science: «the two liquids look indistinguishable, so we need a test». In stories it builds mystery or comedy (twins swapping places). In safety it warns that dangerous things can look like safe ones (some poisonous berries look indistinguishable from edible ones). In maths, «indistinguishable objects» means objects you count as the same (identical balls). Phrases: «indistinguishable from», «almost indistinguishable», «virtually indistinguishable».
examples from the lessons: The twins are indistinguishable until one of them smiles. | This fake note is almost indistinguishable from a real one. | In the fog, the hills were indistinguishable from the sky. | The two salts are indistinguishable by sight, so we tested them with water. | Some mushrooms that can kill you are nearly indistinguishable from safe ones, so never pick wild mushrooms to eat. | Her copy of the painting was indistinguishable from the original. | In the problem, the five red balls are indistinguishable, so swapping them does not make a new arrangement. | His voice on the phone was indistinguishable from his dad's.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Built from in- (not) + distinguish (tell apart) + -able. Use «indistinguishable from», not «to» or «with». Spelling: -guish-, -able. In maths counting problems, indistinguishable things give fewer arrangements than different ones: three identical red counters can be placed in a row in only 1 way, but three different counters in 6 ways.

part of speech: noun (initiation, initiations); from the verb initiate
meaning for a pupil: 1) The act of starting something, such as a plan or a process. 2) A ceremony or test that makes someone a new member of a group, club, team or religion. 3) A first introduction to something new: your initiation into cooking. 4) (church) In some faiths, the rites by which a person joins the community; Christians often speak of baptism as Christian initiation.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and stories it often means the welcome or ritual for a newcomer: a secret club password, the first-day jokes on a team. In safety talk, «initiation» can mean hazing – cruel or dangerous tests forced on new members, which schools and clubs ban. In science, «initiation» is the start of a reaction or process. Phrases: «initiation ceremony», «initiation rite», «initiation into», «the initiation of talks».
examples from the lessons: The Scouts held a little initiation ceremony for the new members. | Our secret club's initiation was learning the password and the handshake. | The coach banned any initiation pranks on the new players. | My first camping trip was my initiation into cooking over a fire. | The initiation of the project took a whole week of planning. | In the story, the boy had to cross the dark wood as part of his initiation. | Christians believe that baptism is the beginning of a person's life in the Church, and it is sometimes called Christian initiation. | If an initiation ever asks you to do something dangerous or humiliating, say no and tell an adult.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable in the ceremony sense (an initiation, two initiations); uncountable for the act of starting (the initiation of talks). Pronounced in-ish-ee-AY-shun. Not the same as «invitation» (being asked to come). Harmful initiation tests are called «hazing» in the USA; they are wrong and often against school rules.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Immediately, with no time at all passing in between. 2) (science) At one exact instant of time, rather than over a period.
its sense in the lessons: A more formal word for «instantly» or «at once». In science it is used for very fast events (light seems to arrive instantaneously over short distances) and for values at one moment («instantaneous speed» is the speed at one exact moment, like on a speedometer). In stories it shows sudden action. Phrases: «almost instantaneously», «happen instantaneously».
examples from the lessons: When I pressed the switch, the light came on instantaneously. | The message reached my friend in Australia almost instantaneously. | The lizard's tongue shot out and caught the fly instantaneously. | Ice cream melts quickly in the sun, but not instantaneously. | The crowd reacted instantaneously when the goal went in. | We see lightning almost instantaneously, but the thunder takes longer to reach us. | Nothing travels truly instantaneously; even light takes time.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stress: in-stan-TAY-nee-us-lee. Spelling trap: -aneous-, not -anious-. «Instantly» is the everyday word. Do not confuse with «simultaneously» (at the same time as something else). In maths and science, speed at an instant (instantaneous speed) can differ from average speed: a car averaging 40 mph may be doing 60 mph at one instant.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To start something or make it happen, such as an inquiry, a plan or changes. 2) To stir up or encourage trouble, a fight or bad behaviour, often while staying in the background.
its sense in the lessons: Used in news, school reports and the exam voice: «the head teacher instigated new rules». In playground stories it often names the one who started the trouble: «Who instigated the fight?». It helps a reader see who is responsible, which matters in fairness and ethics lessons. Related noun: «instigator» (the person who starts it), «instigation» («at his instigation» = because he urged it).
examples from the lessons: The council instigated a plan to make the park safer. | The teacher wanted to know who had instigated the food fight. | Jake didn't throw anything, but he instigated the whole argument. | The school instigated a new reading programme for every class. | Police instigated an investigation after the window was smashed. | She was accused of instigating the trouble on the bus. | The changes were made at the instigation of the parents' group.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: instigated, instigating. The instigator is often blamed more than the others, even if they did less with their own hands. Not the same as «investigate» (to look into something) – a common mix-up: police investigate a fight; a troublemaker instigates it.

part of speech: noun (interception, interceptions); from the verb intercept
meaning for a pupil: 1) The act of stopping or catching something on its way from one place to another. 2) (sport) Catching or taking the ball when the other team passes it, especially in American football, netball, rugby and football. 3) Secretly catching or reading a message, call or letter meant for someone else.
its sense in the lessons: In sport it is a big moment: the defender makes an interception and the game turns. In spy and detective stories it means catching a secret message. In maths, do not mix it up with «intercept», the point where a line crosses an axis. In science and safety: an interception of a dangerous object, like catching a falling cup. Phrases: «make an interception», «interception of messages».
examples from the lessons: The goalkeeper's interception stopped the attack. | Our netball team won because of Sophie's clever interception. | In American football, an interception means the defence catches a pass meant for the other team. | The spy's message never arrived because of an interception. | The interception of the letter gave the detectives their clue. | His quick interception saved the vase from hitting the floor. | The quarterback threw two interceptions in the first half.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: an interception, interceptions. Spelling: -ception (like «reception»). In maths the point where a graph meets an axis is called the «intercept» (y-intercept), not the «interception». Reading someone else's private messages without permission is wrong and can be against the law.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Able to be swapped or exchanged for each other without making any difference. 2) So alike that one could easily replace the other.
its sense in the lessons: Used for parts, words, tools and numbers. In maths, in addition and multiplication the numbers are interchangeable in order: 3 + 5 = 5 + 3 (the commutative law), but in subtraction and division they are not. In English lessons: some words are interchangeable (big and large in many sentences), others are not. In everyday life: interchangeable batteries, lids, Lego pieces. Phrase: «interchangeable with».
examples from the lessons: The heads on this toothbrush are interchangeable. | In this sentence, «big» and «large» are interchangeable. | In addition, the numbers are interchangeable: 4 + 7 is the same as 7 + 4. | In subtraction, the numbers are not interchangeable: 9 − 2 is not 2 − 9. | Lego bricks are interchangeable, so you can build anything. | The players on the team are not interchangeable; each has a special job. | These two chargers look the same, but they are not interchangeable.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: keep the «e» – interchangEable (change + able). Use «interchangeable with». In maths: order is interchangeable in + and ×, not in − and ÷. Words that seem interchangeable often have small differences in meaning or register (kid/child).

part of speech: verb (intimidate, intimidates, intimidated, intimidating); adjectives «intimidating», «intimidated»; noun «intimidation»
meaning for a pupil: 1) To frighten or threaten someone, especially to make them do what you want. 2) To make someone feel nervous, shy or less confident, even without meaning to.
its sense in the lessons: A key word in anti-bullying lessons: bullies intimidate by threats, staring, crowding round someone or online messages. In sport, players try to intimidate opponents with loud shouts. In everyday life, something big or new can be «intimidating»: a new school, a hard test, a big dog. Phrases: «intimidate someone into doing something», «feel intimidated», «an intimidating task».
examples from the lessons: The older boys tried to intimidate him into giving them his lunch money. | Don't let anyone intimidate you – tell a teacher. | The big dog's growl intimidated the postman. | I felt intimidated on my first day at the new school. | The team's haka can intimidate their opponents. | The long maths test looked intimidating, but it was fine. | Intimidating someone online is still bullying.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. «Intimidating» = causing fear (an intimidating teacher); «intimidated» = feeling fear (I was intimidated). Intimidation is a form of bullying and can be a crime among adults. Not related to «intimate» (very close or private), although they look alike.

part of speech: noun (investigation, investigations); from the verb investigate
meaning for a pupil: 1) A careful search for facts to find out the truth about something, such as a crime or an accident. 2) (school/science) A planned experiment or study to answer a question by testing and measuring. 3) (maths) An open task where you explore numbers or shapes to find patterns and rules.
its sense in the lessons: Very common in school: «science investigation» means asking a question, making a prediction, doing a fair test and recording results. In maths, «an investigation» means exploring a problem («How many squares on a chessboard?»). In news and detective stories: a police investigation looks for clues and suspects. Phrases: «carry out an investigation», «under investigation», «an investigation into».
examples from the lessons: Our class did an investigation into which paper towel soaks up the most water. | The police started an investigation after the bike was stolen. | The cause of the fire is still under investigation. | In our maths investigation, we found a pattern in the square numbers. | A good science investigation must be a fair test. | The detective's investigation led her to the old lighthouse. | The school ran an investigation into who had broken the window. | We wrote up our investigation with a method, results and conclusion.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: an investigation, investigations. «Carry out» or «conduct» an investigation (not «make»). «Under investigation» means it is still being studied. Do not confuse with «instigation» (starting trouble). In a fair test, change only one thing at a time and keep everything else the same.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A special anniversary celebrating a number of years, especially of a king's or queen's reign: a silver jubilee is 25 years, a golden jubilee 50, a diamond jubilee 60, a platinum jubilee 70. 2) A time of great celebration and joy. 3) (Bible) In the Old Testament, a special year every fiftieth year when slaves were set free, debts were cancelled and land was returned. 4) (church) In the Catholic Church, a special holy year of pilgrimage and forgiveness.
its sense in the lessons: Common in the UK, Canada, Australia and New Zealand for royal celebrations with street parties, bunting and holidays. Schools, clubs and churches also hold jubilees for their anniversaries. In maths problems, a jubilee is a way of naming a number of years (golden = 50). Phrases: «silver jubilee», «golden jubilee», «diamond jubilee», «jubilee celebrations», «a jubilee street party».
examples from the lessons: Our street had a jubilee party with flags and cakes. | The school celebrated its golden jubilee with a big concert. | A silver jubilee marks twenty-five years. | The town planted trees for the Queen's jubilee. | Grandma kept a jubilee mug in the cupboard. | In the Bible, the year of jubilee was a time when debts were forgiven. | The church held a jubilee service to thank God for fifty years of the parish.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a jubilee, jubilees. Stress: JOO-bi-lee. Numbers: silver = 25, golden = 50, diamond = 60, platinum = 70 years (not the same scheme as wedding anniversaries in every detail, but similar). Do not confuse with «jubilant» (very happy), though both come from joyful ideas.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) Nervous and easily frightened or startled. 2) Moving in sudden jerks; not smooth (a jumpy video). 3) (money) Going up and down quickly and unpredictably, like prices.
its sense in the lessons: In stories it shows a character is scared or on edge: «Everyone was jumpy after the strange noise». About pets: a jumpy horse or cat. About screens: a jumpy picture. In maths graphs, a «jumpy» line rises and falls a lot rather than steadily. Phrases: «feel jumpy», «a bit jumpy».
examples from the lessons: After the ghost story, everyone was a bit jumpy. | The cat is jumpy during fireworks. | I always feel jumpy before a big test. | The video was jumpy because the internet was slow. | The horse was jumpy, so we spoke to it softly. | The graph of the temperature looked jumpy because it changed every hour. | Dad gets jumpy when the car makes a strange noise.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative: jumpier, jumpiest (y → i). Informal word; in formal writing use «nervous» or «anxious». Not the same as «jumping» (actually doing jumps). A jumpy person is not necessarily jumping at all.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A Japanese martial art and sport in which people fight using hands, feet, elbows and knees, with strikes, kicks and blocks. 2) The skills and training of this sport, with coloured belts showing levels.
its sense in the lessons: Many children do karate after school; it teaches discipline, fitness, respect and self-defence. Belts go from white up to black. In stories, a karate expert can be a hero or a comic show-off. Safety: karate is practised with rules, a teacher and control; you should never use moves to hurt people for fun. Phrases: «do karate», «a karate class», «karate chop», «karate kid», «black belt in karate».
examples from the lessons: I do karate on Tuesdays and Thursdays. | She got her yellow belt in karate. | Our karate teacher says respect comes first. | He pretended to do a karate chop on the cardboard box. | Karate came from Okinawa in Japan. | You bow when you enter the karate hall. | Karate is for self-defence, not for starting fights.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «do karate», not «play karate» and not «a karate». Pronounced ka-RAH-tee in English. The person is a «karateka» (rare) or just «someone who does karate». Not the same as judo (throws and holds) or taekwondo (a Korean martial art with many kicks).

part of speech: noun (legging, leggings – almost always plural: a pair of leggings)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Leggings: tight, stretchy trousers, usually for girls and women, worn for sport, dance or everyday. 2) Leggings: warm outer coverings for the legs, worn over trousers in snow, or by soldiers and riders in the past. 3) The singular «legging» means one leg of such a garment, and is rare.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and children's clothes: leggings for PE, dance, under a skirt or dress. In stories from long ago: a cowboy's or soldier's leggings. School uniform rules sometimes mention leggings. Phrases: «a pair of leggings», «black leggings», «leggings and a T-shirt».
examples from the lessons: She wore black leggings to dance class. | I need a new pair of leggings for PE. | My little sister has leggings with stars on them. | In winter I wear leggings under my jeans. | The old soldier wore leather leggings. | One legging had a hole at the knee. | Are leggings allowed with the school uniform?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually plural: «leggings are», «a pair of leggings» (like «trousers», «jeans»). The singular «legging» appears only when talking about one leg. «Tights» cover the feet; leggings stop at the ankle or calf.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To make something smaller, weaker or less: to lessen pain, noise or danger. 2) To become smaller, weaker or less.
its sense in the lessons: Used in science and safety: «A helmet lessens the risk of a head injury», «Insulation lessens heat loss». In feelings: «Talking to a friend lessened her worry». In maths word problems it means a decrease. Phrases: «lessen the risk», «lessen the pain», «lessen the impact», «the wind lessened».
examples from the lessons: Wearing a helmet lessens the danger of hurting your head. | The medicine lessened the pain in my tooth. | The rain lessened, so we went outside. | Talking about it lessened my worry. | Planting trees can lessen flooding. | Turn the music down to lessen the noise. | The number of pupils with colds lessened after the holidays.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: lessened, lessening. Homophone trap: «lessen» (to make less) sounds exactly like «lesson» (a period of teaching). In maths, «lessen by 5» means subtract 5: 20 lessened by 5 is 15. Formal-ish; everyday words are «reduce», «cut down», «ease».

part of speech: noun (mag, mags) – short for magazine; also short for magnitude, magnesium, magnet (rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) A magazine: a thin book with pictures and articles that comes out regularly. 2) (informal, Australia/NZ/UK) Chat or gossip, or to chatter: «have a mag» (old-fashioned). 3) (informal) A magazine for a gun – the part that holds the bullets. 4) (informal) Short for «mag wheel» (a shiny metal car wheel), or for magnitude/magnesium in science shorthand.
its sense in the lessons: Mostly a clipped word in everyday talk: «a comic mag», «a gaming mag», «a football mag». In older Australian and British speech, «to mag» is to chat a lot. In science notes, «Mg» is the symbol for magnesium; «mag» may be written as a shorthand. It tells the reader the speaker is casual.
examples from the lessons: I bought a football mag with my pocket money. | Mum reads a cooking mag on the train. | My brother loves gaming mags. | The school mag has a page of jokes. | Gran and her friend had a good mag over a cup of tea. | The detective found an empty mag on the floor. | Dad's car has new mag wheels.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Clipped informal word; in writing use «magazine». Plural «mags». A «magazine» (the whole word) can also mean a store for weapons or ammunition. Not the same as «mug» or «nag».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal, UK – Wales, the north of England; Ireland) Mother; another word for «mum» or «mam». 2) Sometimes a spelling of «ma'am» (madam), a polite way to speak to a woman, especially in the USA.
its sense in the lessons: Children in Wales, Northern England, Ireland and Scotland may call their mother «Mam». In stories set there, it shows where the family comes from. In the US, «ma'am» is how you politely address a woman or a teacher. Phrases: «my mam», «me mam» (dialect), «yes, ma'am».
examples from the lessons: «Mam, can I go out to play?» | My mam makes the best soup in Cardiff. | «Me mam says I have to be home by six,» said Liam. | Our mam works at the hospital. | «Thank you, ma'am,» said the boy to the lady at the shop. | When I fell over, I shouted for my mam.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regional and informal. Like «Mum», it gets a capital when used as a name («Mam, help!») but not after «my» («my mam»). Other forms: mum (UK), mom (USA, Canada), mummy, mommy, ma. «Ma'am» (with an apostrophe) is a shortened «madam», not a word for mother.

part of speech: verb (manifest, manifests, manifested, manifesting); adjective (manifest); noun (a manifest, manifests)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (verb) To show something clearly, or to appear and become visible: «The illness manifested as a rash». 2) (adjective, formal) Clear and obvious to everyone. 3) (noun) A list of the goods or passengers on a ship, plane or train. 4) (verb, slang/modern) To imagine and hope hard for something so that it might happen, as people say online: «I'm manifesting a snow day». 5) (religion/stories) For a spirit or ghost: to appear.
its sense in the lessons: In science and health it means a sign shows itself: «symptoms manifest». In formal writing «manifest» means «obvious». On ships and planes, the manifest is the official list. In modern talk, «manifesting» means wishing hard – a popular idea, but wishing alone does not make things happen. In ghost stories, a ghost «manifests». Phrases: «manifest itself», «make manifest», «passenger manifest», «manifest destiny» (history).
examples from the lessons: His nerves manifested themselves as a stomach ache. | Her talent for music was manifest from a young age. | The captain checked the ship's manifest. | The passenger manifest listed two hundred people. | «I'm manifesting a pizza for dinner,» joked Chloe. | In the story, the ghost manifested at midnight. | The measles virus manifests as red spots on the skin.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: manifested. Stress: MAN-i-fest. Not the same as «manifesto» (a list of a political party's aims). The modern «manifesting» is a belief; there is no scientific proof that wishing makes things happen, though hope can help you work towards goals.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A sign or way that something shows itself: «Fever is a manifestation of illness». 2) The act of appearing or showing. 3) An appearance of a ghost or spirit, in stories; (religion) a sign of God's presence, as believers describe it.
its sense in the lessons: A formal word in science, health and history: «a manifestation of the problem», «an outward manifestation». In stories: a ghostly manifestation. In church language, some feasts celebrate a manifestation (Epiphany is the manifestation of Jesus to the wise men, Christians believe). Phrases: «a manifestation of», «physical manifestation», «outward manifestation».
examples from the lessons: Sneezing can be a manifestation of hay fever. | His kind letter was a manifestation of his respect. | The rash was the first manifestation of chickenpox. | The villagers claimed they had seen a ghostly manifestation. | Anger can be a manifestation of fear. | Christians believe Epiphany celebrates the manifestation of Jesus to the world. | Litter in the park is one manifestation of a bigger problem.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a manifestation, manifestations. Formal; everyday words are «sign», «show», «appearance». Built from «manifest» + -ation.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Having qualities that people traditionally think of as typical of men or boys, such as a deep voice. 2) Belonging to or suitable for men. 3) (grammar) In languages like French, Spanish, German or Ukrainian, describing nouns and words of a class called «masculine»; in English, words like «he», «king», «actor» are masculine forms.
its sense in the lessons: Used in English and language lessons: in French «le livre» is masculine, «la table» feminine; in English, pairs like king/queen, prince/princess, actor/actress. In everyday talk «masculine» describes styles and qualities, but ideas of what is masculine change between cultures and times; boys and girls can like any colour or hobby. Opposite: «feminine». Phrases: «masculine noun», «masculine form».
examples from the lessons: In French, «le soleil» is a masculine noun. | «Prince» is the masculine form of «princess». | His voice became deeper and more masculine as he grew up. | The room was decorated in a masculine style with dark wood. | In Spanish, most masculine nouns end in -o. | Some people think pink isn't masculine, but anyone can wear pink. | «He» and «him» are masculine pronouns.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: «feminine». Neutral: «neuter» (grammar). Grammatical gender is not about real men or women: in German the word for a girl («Mädchen») is neuter. Careful with stereotypes: what counts as masculine is partly custom, not fact.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To make something bad less serious, less painful or less harmful. 2) (law) To make a wrong action seem less bad, so a punishment may be lighter: «mitigating circumstances».
its sense in the lessons: Exam voice and news: «measures to mitigate climate change», «mitigate the risk of floods». In safety and science: sandbags mitigate flooding. In law and ethics lessons: «mitigating circumstances» are facts that make a person less to blame (for example, they were very young or tricked). Phrases: «mitigate the effects», «mitigate the damage», «mitigating factors».
examples from the lessons: Planting trees can help mitigate flooding. | The new crossing will mitigate the danger to children. | Saying sorry quickly may mitigate your punishment. | Engineers built walls to mitigate the damage from storms. | The judge said there were mitigating circumstances. | We shut the windows to mitigate the noise. | Wearing sun cream mitigates the risk of sunburn.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: mitigated. Formal; everyday words: «reduce», «ease», «soften», «lessen». Common error: «militate against» is a different phrase (to work against) – do not write «mitigate against». Mitigate means to make less bad, not to remove completely.

part of speech: noun (mob, mobs); verb (mob, mobs, mobbed, mobbing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (noun) A large, noisy, often angry crowd that may become violent. 2) (verb) To crowd round someone in a big, excited or aggressive group: fans mob a star. 3) (the Mob) Organised criminals, the Mafia. 4) (informal, Australia) A group of people or animals, also a group of kangaroos or cattle; (Aboriginal English) a person's family, clan or community. 5) (informal, UK) A gang or crowd of friends: «the whole mob».
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons: angry mobs in revolutions. In news: «mob violence». In everyday life: «fans mobbed the singer». In Australia, «a mob of kangaroos» is the correct collective noun, and Aboriginal people may say «my mob» for their people. Safety: in a mob, people can get crushed or do things they would never do alone. Phrases: «angry mob», «mob rule», «mobbed by fans», «flash mob».
examples from the lessons: An angry mob gathered outside the castle gates. | The footballer was mobbed by fans after the match. | We saw a mob of kangaroos in the paddock. | «Which mob are you from?» asked the Aboriginal elder. | The whole mob came round for Sunday lunch. | A flash mob suddenly started dancing in the shopping centre. | In the film, the Mob ran the city's gambling.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb doubles the b: mobbed, mobbing. A mob is usually seen as disorderly; a peaceful crowd is just a «crowd». «Mob rule» means rule by a crowd instead of by law. In Australian and NZ usage it is a normal, friendly word for a group.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The reason why someone does something, especially something secret or wrong. 2) (adjective, science) Causing movement: «motive power» drives an engine.
its sense in the lessons: In detective stories the key question: «Who had a motive?» – the detective looks for means, motive and opportunity. In ethics lessons: good deeds can have selfish motives, and the same act can be judged differently depending on the motive. In science and history: steam gave motive power to trains. Phrases: «a motive for», «hidden motive», «ulterior motive», «the motive behind».
examples from the lessons: The detective asked who had a motive to steal the cake. | Her motive for helping was to win the prize, not to be kind. | The police still don't know the motive for the crime. | What was your motive for getting up so early? | He had an ulterior motive: he wanted to borrow my bike. | Steam engines gave motive power to the first trains. | Kind actions with good motives make the world better.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a motive, motives. Related: «motivation» (the drive to do something) and «motivate». A motive is a reason inside the person; it is not the same as an excuse. «Ulterior motive» = a hidden selfish reason.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A daughter of your brother or sister (or of your husband's or wife's brother or sister). 2) In a family tree, the girl one generation below you on a sideways branch.
its sense in the lessons: Family vocabulary: aunt/uncle and niece/nephew are pairs. If your mum has a brother, you are his niece (if you are a girl) or nephew (if you are a boy). In maths and logic puzzles about family trees, you have to work out the relationships carefully. Phrases: «my niece», «nieces and nephews», «great-niece».
examples from the lessons: My aunt calls me her favourite niece. | Uncle Tom has three nieces and one nephew. | Her niece is coming to stay for the holidays. | I am my mum's brother's niece. | A great-niece is the granddaughter of your brother or sister. | Grandad's niece lives in New Zealand.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: «i before e» – n-i-e-c-e. The male word is «nephew». The pair is aunt/uncle ↔ niece/nephew. Plural «nieces». Do not mix up with «cousin» (your aunt's or uncle's child – your niece's parent is your brother or sister).

part of speech: noun (notification, notifications); from the verb notify
meaning for a pupil: 1) A message or alert on a phone, tablet or computer telling you that something has happened: a new message, a like, an update. 2) (formal) The act of officially telling someone about something, or the letter that does this.
its sense in the lessons: Very common in children's digital life: phone notifications, app alerts. In online-safety lessons: turning off notifications at bedtime helps sleep; never open notifications from strangers or tap suspicious links. Formal sense: a school notification about a trip, a written notification of a change. Phrases: «get a notification», «turn off notifications», «push notification», «written notification».
examples from the lessons: My tablet keeps pinging with notifications. | Turn off notifications before you start your homework. | I got a notification that my game had updated. | Parents received a notification about the school trip. | The library sent a notification that my book was overdue. | She has fifty unread notifications. | Never tap a notification that asks for your password.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a notification, notifications. Built from «notify» (y → i + -cation). Everyday short form: «notif» (slang). Too many notifications can distract you; settings let you control them.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An idea or belief about something, often a vague or mistaken one: «I had a notion that school started at nine». 2) A sudden wish or impulse to do something: «She took a notion to paint her room purple». 3) (US) Notions: small sewing items like buttons, pins and thread. 4) (maths/science, formal) A basic idea or concept: the notion of a number.
its sense in the lessons: In stories it shows a character's thinking: «He had no notion where he was». In school: «the notion of fairness», «the notion of infinity». Phrases: «have no notion», «the notion that», «take a notion» (Ireland, Scotland, US), «a silly notion».
examples from the lessons: I had a notion that the shop was closed on Sundays. | She hadn't the faintest notion what to do. | Where did you get the silly notion that carrots let you see in the dark? | The notion of fairness is important in our class rules. | Gran took a notion to go swimming in the sea. | In maths, the notion of zero took people a long time to invent. | The sewing shop sells buttons, ribbons and other notions.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a notion, notions. Close to «idea», but often vaguer or slightly doubtful. «Have no notion» = have no idea. A «notional» number is one that is imagined or estimated, not real.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To take part or join in an activity or event. 2) (formal) To share in something.
its sense in the lessons: Common in school reports and rules: «He participates well in class discussions», «Everyone can participate in sports day». In the exam voice it replaces «join in» or «take part». In ethics and citizenship lessons: participating in community events. Phrases: «participate in», «participate fully», «active participation», «participants».
examples from the lessons: Everyone in our class participated in the charity run. | She always participates in class discussions. | You don't have to win to participate. | Over a hundred children participated in the science fair. | Will you participate in the school play? | Participants must wear a name badge. | My report says I should participate more in group work.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: participated. Use «participate in» (not «at» or «on»). Everyday equivalent: «take part in», «join in». Noun for the person: «participant»; for the act: «participation». In maths, «participants» often means the people counted in a survey.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) The act of reading something carefully and thoroughly. 2) (formal, often in modern use) A quick look through something; reading it casually.
its sense in the lessons: A stiff formal word found in letters and documents: «for your perusal» means «for you to read». In stories it can give an old-fashioned or comic tone. Today, many people use it loosely to mean a quick read, though the older meaning is a careful read.
examples from the lessons: The letter was left on the desk for her perusal. | After a careful perusal of the map, we found the hidden path. | «I enclose my homework for your perusal,» wrote Ben, trying to sound grand. | A quick perusal of the menu showed there was no pizza. | The teacher's perusal of our stories took all weekend. | The contract needs a full perusal before anyone signs it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun from the verb «peruse» (to read carefully). Usually used with «for your perusal» or «a perusal of». Trap: some people think «peruse» means only «skim quickly»; dictionaries list both, but «read carefully» is the traditional meaning. Formal; everyday word: «read», «look».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who takes photographs, either as a job or as a hobby. 2) The person who took a particular photo.
its sense in the lessons: Everyday jobs: school photographers, wedding photographers, wildlife photographers, press photographers. In art lessons: famous photographers. Online safety: ask before photographing others, and remember a photographer should have permission to share pictures of children. Phrases: «professional photographer», «school photographer», «wildlife photographer».
examples from the lessons: The school photographer took our class picture today. | She wants to be a wildlife photographer and photograph tigers. | The photographer asked us to say «cheese». | A newspaper photographer came to our sports day. | My uncle is a keen amateur photographer. | The photographer waited hours for the perfect sunset. | Who was the photographer of this picture?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stress: pho-TOG-ra-pher (not PHO-to-graph-er). Compare: PHO-to-graph (the picture), pho-to-GRAPH-ic (adjective). Countable: a photographer, photographers.

part of speech: verb (photoshop, photoshops, photoshopped, photoshopping); noun (Photoshop – the program, a trademark)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (Photoshop, noun) A computer program used to edit pictures. 2) (verb, informal) To change a photo digitally, often to make it look better or to fake something that did not happen.
its sense in the lessons: In media and online-safety lessons: many pictures in ads and online are photoshopped, so bodies, faces and events may not look like real life. Fake photoshopped images can spread lies. In art and design lessons: editing photos is a real skill. Phrases: «photoshopped picture», «badly photoshopped», «photoshop out».
examples from the lessons: The magazine photoshopped the model to make her look taller. | That picture of a shark on the motorway is photoshopped. | Dad photoshopped my brother out of the holiday picture as a joke. | Many photos online are photoshopped, so don't compare yourself to them. | My sister learned Photoshop in her design class. | You can tell it's photoshopped because the shadows are wrong. | Can you photoshop a hat onto the dog?
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a program name it takes a capital P (Photoshop), because it is a trademark; as an informal verb it is often written lower case. Doubles the p: photoshopped, photoshopping. Being able to spot edited images is part of checking facts online.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) Having to do with how the bodies of living things work: breathing, heart rate, digestion, growing. 2) Of the body rather than the mind: a physiological reaction is a body reaction.
its sense in the lessons: Used in science and health: «physiological changes» in puberty, «physiological needs» (food, water, sleep, warmth) – the base of Maslow's pyramid of needs. In the exam voice: «a physiological response to fear» (racing heart, sweating). Contrast with «psychological» (of the mind). Phrases: «physiological changes», «physiological needs», «physiological effects».
examples from the lessons: A racing heart is a physiological response to fear. | Food, water and sleep are basic physiological needs. | Exercise causes physiological changes like faster breathing. | Doctors study the physiological effects of being in space. | Blushing is a physiological reaction you can't easily control. | Some illnesses are physiological; others are psychological.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stress: fiz-ee-o-LOJ-i-kul. Spelling: physio-log-ical (ph at the start). Do not confuse with «psychological» (about the mind) or «physical» (more general: of the body or of matter). «Physiology» is the science of how the body works.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (UK, Australia, NZ, Ireland) A public box, often red in the UK, where you put letters to be collected and posted. 2) A private box at your house or a post office where your own mail is delivered (more often «letterbox» or «mailbox»).
its sense in the lessons: Everyday life in Britain and Ireland: red pillar boxes in the UK, green postboxes in Ireland, red in Australia and New Zealand. In the USA and Canada people say «mailbox». In stories, posting a letter to Father Christmas in the postbox. Phrases: «put it in the postbox», «the nearest postbox», «collection times».
examples from the lessons: I put my birthday card to Grandma in the postbox. | The red postbox is at the end of our street. | In Ireland, postboxes are painted green. | The collection time on the postbox says half past five. | We posted our letter to Santa in the postbox. | Is there a postbox near the school?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: postboxes. US/Canadian word: «mailbox». British «letterbox» usually means the slot in your front door. Also written «post box» (two words). Do not put anything dangerous in a postbox.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Deserving praise; good and admirable. 2) (formal) Worth being approved of, even if not completely successful: «a praiseworthy effort».
its sense in the lessons: In school reports and ethics lessons: praiseworthy behaviour, a praiseworthy effort. It often praises the effort or intention rather than the result. In the exam voice it is a polite, slightly formal word. Phrases: «praiseworthy effort», «praiseworthy aim», «highly praiseworthy».
examples from the lessons: Lucy's honesty about the broken window was praiseworthy. | Raising money for the animal shelter is a praiseworthy idea. | It was a praiseworthy effort, even though we lost the match. | The headteacher said the class's behaviour on the trip was praiseworthy. | Helping a lost child is praiseworthy. | Giving up your seat to an old person is a praiseworthy habit.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word: praise + worthy. Similar words: «admirable», «commendable», «creditable». Opposite: «blameworthy». It is mostly used in writing or formal talk.

part of speech: verb (precipitate, precipitates, precipitated, precipitating); noun (a precipitate, precipitates – chemistry); adjective (precipitate – formal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (verb, formal) To make something bad happen suddenly or sooner than expected: «The argument precipitated a fight». 2) (verb, chemistry) For a solid to form and separate out of a liquid during a reaction; (noun) the solid that forms. 3) (verb, science) For water vapour to fall as rain, snow, sleet or hail. 4) (adjective, formal) Done too quickly, without thinking: «a precipitate decision».
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons: mixing two clear liquids can make a cloudy precipitate; «precipitation» is rain, snow and hail in weather lessons. In history and the exam voice: an event «precipitated» a war or a crisis. In stories: a precipitate act is hasty. Phrases: «precipitate a crisis», «a white precipitate», «precipitate into».
examples from the lessons: The rude comment precipitated a big argument. | When we mixed the two liquids, a white precipitate formed. | The storm precipitated a power cut. | Water vapour cools and precipitates as rain. | His precipitate decision to quit the team surprised everyone. | The chalky solid precipitated to the bottom of the test tube. | The loss of his job precipitated the family's move.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: precipitated. Stress differs: verb pre-SIP-i-tate; noun and adjective pre-SIP-i-tut or pre-SIP-i-tate. Related: «precipitation» (rain, snow, sleet, hail), «precipitous» (very steep). The formal adjective «precipitate» (hasty) is rare; «hasty» or «rash» is more common.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Steadily and step by step, more and more over time: «It got progressively colder». 2) In a progressive, forward-looking way (rare).
its sense in the lessons: Used in science, maths and stories for change that keeps growing: progressively harder questions, progressively darker sky. In maths it describes sequences that keep increasing or decreasing. Phrases: «progressively worse», «progressively better», «progressively harder», «progressively more».
examples from the lessons: The questions get progressively harder as you go down the page. | It grew progressively darker as the sun set. | My reading has got progressively better this year. | The noise got progressively louder as the parade came closer. | The path became progressively steeper. | In the sequence 2, 4, 8, 16, the numbers get progressively bigger. | His cough got progressively worse, so he went to the doctor.
