note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: progress + ive + ly (double s). Similar: «gradually», «increasingly», «steadily». In maths it signals a pattern of change, but not which kind: adding the same amount (2, 4, 6, 8) or multiplying (2, 4, 8, 16) are both «progressively bigger».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who performs rap music, speaking words in rhythm and rhyme over a beat. 2) (rare) Something used for knocking, like a door knocker.
its sense in the lessons: In music lessons and everyday culture: rappers write lyrics with rhymes and rhythm; rap began in New York among Black and Latino communities and spread worldwide. In English lessons, rap can teach rhyme, rhythm and poetry. Some rap songs have swearing or adult themes, so many have «clean» versions. Phrases: «a famous rapper», «rapper and producer», «battle rapper».
examples from the lessons: My cousin wants to be a rapper when he grows up. | The rapper performed his new song at the festival. | Our class wrote a rap about the water cycle and Josh was the rapper. | A good rapper needs great rhythm and clever rhymes. | The rapper's lyrics were about growing up in the city. | The old door had a brass rapper shaped like a lion.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double p: rap → rapper (like «run» → «runner»). Homophone trap: «wrapper» (paper round a sweet) sounds the same as «rapper». Do not confuse the musician with the wrapper on a chocolate bar.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To make friends again after a quarrel: «The two friends were reconciled». 2) To make two ideas, facts or needs agree with each other, or show that they can both be true. 3) (reconcile yourself to) To accept something unpleasant that you cannot change. 4) (money) To check that two sets of figures, such as bank records and receipts, match. 5) (church) In Christian teaching, to be brought back into friendship with God; the sacrament of Reconciliation is confession in the Catholic Church.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and ethics lessons: two characters reconcile after a fight; making peace is brave. In maths and money: reconciling accounts means checking that totals match. In formal writing: reconcile different views. In church life: Catholics speak of the Sacrament of Reconciliation, where a person confesses their sins to a priest and is forgiven, as they believe. Phrases: «reconcile with», «be reconciled», «reconcile yourself to», «reconcile the accounts».
examples from the lessons: After a week of not talking, the two friends were reconciled. | Mum and her sister finally reconciled after years apart. | It is hard to reconcile wanting to save money with wanting a new game. | He reconciled himself to missing the trip because he was ill. | Dad reconciled his bank statement with his receipts and found a mistake. | Our story ended with the two kings reconciled and the war over. | Catholics believe that in the Sacrament of Reconciliation, God forgives their sins.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: reconciled. Stress: REC-on-sile. Noun: reconciliation (rec-on-sil-ee-AY-shun). «Reconcile with» a person; «reconcile yourself to» a situation. In money tasks, when two lists are reconciled, the totals must be equal; any difference is a mistake to find.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person whose job is to find out news and tell it in a newspaper, on television, on radio or online. 2) A person who reports or tells about something, for example in a class group.
its sense in the lessons: In media lessons: reporters interview people, check facts and write news stories; good reporters report facts, not rumours. In school: the group «reporter» tells the class what the group found. In stories: a curious reporter digs into a mystery. Phrases: «news reporter», «TV reporter», «sports reporter», «a reporter for».
examples from the lessons: A TV reporter came to film our school garden. | The reporter asked the firefighter how the fire started. | In group work, Amelia was our reporter. | The sports reporter wrote about the final. | Reporters waited outside the court for the verdict. | A good reporter checks facts before writing the story. | I want to be a reporter for the school newspaper.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a reporter, reporters. Related: «report» (the story or the verb), «journalist» (a more general word). A reporter does not decide the news; he or she tells about it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The habit of not saying much, or of keeping your feelings and thoughts to yourself. 2) (sometimes, informal) Unwillingness to do something; reluctance.
its sense in the lessons: In stories it describes quiet, private characters: «Despite his reticence, he was kind». In formal writing: «reticence about discussing money». In everyday life: some people are naturally reticent and need time to share. Phrases: «reticence about», «his usual reticence», «overcome her reticence».
examples from the lessons: Despite her reticence, Mia told the teacher what had happened. | His reticence made some people think he was unfriendly. | Grandad's reticence about the war meant he rarely talked about it. | She overcame her reticence and sang in front of the class. | The detective noticed the witness's reticence. | Reticence is not the same as rudeness; some people are just quiet.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Adjective: «reticent» (quiet, reserved). Stress: RET-i-sense. Traditionally it means «not speaking much»; using it to mean simply «reluctant» is common but some teachers mark it as a mistake.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A situation in which people, teams or groups compete with each other for the same thing, often for a long time. 2) Feelings of competition or jealousy between people, for example between brothers and sisters.
its sense in the lessons: In sport: famous rivalries between teams or countries (England and Australia in cricket). In family life: «sibling rivalry» – brothers and sisters competing for attention. In stories and history: rivalries between kingdoms. Rivalry can push people to do better, but can also cause unkindness. Phrases: «sibling rivalry», «friendly rivalry», «fierce rivalry», «rivalry between».
examples from the lessons: There's a friendly rivalry between the two classes on sports day. | The rivalry between the two football clubs is very old. | Sibling rivalry means Sam and his sister argue about everything. | The rivalry between the two kings led to war. | Their rivalry made both runners faster. | The cricket rivalry between England and Australia is famous. | The twins' rivalry turned into friendship.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a rivalry, rivalries (y → ies). Person: «a rival». Verb: «rival» (to be as good as). Spelling: rival + ry.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Good enough; acceptable, but not excellent. 2) Fulfilling what is needed or expected.
its sense in the lessons: In school reports, «satisfactory» usually means OK – not bad, but with room to improve. In formal writing: «a satisfactory answer», «satisfactory progress». In everyday life: a satisfactory meal or repair. In the stiff exam voice: «the results were satisfactory». Phrases: «satisfactory progress», «less than satisfactory», «a satisfactory explanation».
examples from the lessons: My report said my handwriting was satisfactory. | The plumber's repair was satisfactory, and the tap stopped leaking. | We found a satisfactory answer to the problem. | His behaviour was less than satisfactory. | The test results were satisfactory, but she wanted to do better. | The room was clean and satisfactory for one night. | The teacher wanted a more satisfactory explanation of how the experiment worked.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Not as strong as «satisfying» (giving pleasure): a satisfactory meal is good enough; a satisfying meal makes you happy and full. Opposite: «unsatisfactory». «Less than satisfactory» is a polite way to say «bad». Spelling: satis-fact-ory.

part of speech: verb (scowl, scowls, scowled, scowling); noun (a scowl, scowls)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (verb) To frown in an angry or bad-tempered way. 2) (noun) An angry frown on someone's face.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, a scowl shows a character is cross, grumpy or jealous without words: «The giant scowled down at Jack». It helps readers picture feelings. In drama lessons: practising faces like a scowl and a smile. Phrases: «scowl at», «a deep scowl», «with a scowl».
examples from the lessons: The old man scowled at the children kicking the ball. | She scowled when she lost the game. | «Go away,» he said with a scowl. | The cat gave me a scowl and walked off. | Dad scowled at the bill. | Stop scowling and say thank you. | Her scowl turned into a smile when she saw the cake.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: scowled. Rhymes with «owl». A «frown» can be worried or thinking; a scowl is always cross. «Scowl at» someone.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A feeling or opinion about something: «I share your sentiment». 2) Tender, emotional feelings such as love, pity or nostalgia, sometimes too much: «There's no room for sentiment». 3) (formal) A thought expressed in words, such as in a card: «a lovely sentiment».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: birthday cards have sentiments, «I agree with the sentiment». In English lessons: writers show sentiment through words. In news and the exam voice: «public sentiment», meaning what people feel. Phrases: «public sentiment», «share the sentiment», «a kind sentiment», «sentimental».
examples from the lessons: The card had a lovely sentiment inside. | I share your sentiment: homework should be shorter. | Public sentiment was against closing the library. | She kept her old teddy for sentiment. | Grandma's speech was full of sentiment. | The coach said there was no room for sentiment in picking the team. | It's a nice sentiment, but will it work?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable for opinions (sentiments); uncountable for emotional feeling in general. Adjective: «sentimental» (full of tender feelings, sometimes too much). Spelling: senti-ment.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (adjective) Treating people unfairly or badly because they are a boy or a girl, a man or a woman. 2) (noun) A person who thinks or behaves in this unfair way.
its sense in the lessons: In fairness and ethics lessons: saying «girls can't play football» or «boys can't cry» is sexist. In everyday life: sexist jokes, adverts or rules. Schools teach that everyone should have the same chances whatever their sex. Phrases: «sexist comment», «sexist joke», «that's sexist».
examples from the lessons: Saying girls can't be engineers is sexist. | The class decided the rule about only boys playing football was sexist. | «That's a sexist joke,» said Chloe. | The old advert was sexist because it showed only women cleaning. | It's sexist to say boys shouldn't do ballet. | Connor said he wasn't sexist, but he never passed the ball to the girls.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The idea is «sexism» (noun). A word about fairness; calling something sexist means it treats one sex unfairly. Not a rude word, but a serious charge, so use it carefully and explain why.

part of speech: adjective (shameful, more shameful, most shameful); adverb «shamefully»
meaning for a pupil: 1) Causing shame; so bad or wrong that people should feel ashamed of it. 2) Disgraceful; shocking in a bad way.
its sense in the lessons: In ethics lessons and stories: shameful behaviour, a shameful secret. In news: «a shameful decision». It judges an action, not just a feeling. Phrases: «a shameful thing», «it's shameful that», «shameful behaviour», «a shameful secret».
examples from the lessons: It's shameful to laugh at someone who has fallen over. | Cheating in the test was a shameful thing to do. | The way they treated the new girl was shameful. | He kept the shameful secret for years. | It is shameful that the park is full of litter. | Leaving the dog without water all day was shameful.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Do not confuse with «ashamed» (feeling shame: «I'm ashamed») and «shameless» (feeling no shame when you should). Shameful describes the act; ashamed describes the person.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) A black eye: a bruise round the eye from a punch or a knock. 2) Something or someone that shines, like a shiny coin. 3) A kind of small silver fish (in North America).
its sense in the lessons: In stories about fights and sport, «a shiner» shows someone was hit: «He came home with a shiner». In everyday talk it's informal and a bit funny. In fishing, a shiner is a little silvery fish. Phrases: «a real shiner», «give someone a shiner».
examples from the lessons: Jake came to school with a shiner after the football match. | «Where did you get that shiner?» asked Mum. | He walked into a door and got a shiner. | The boxer had a shiner the next day. | We caught three shiners in the creek. | The new coin was a real shiner.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal; neutral words: «black eye», «bruise». A black eye should be checked by an adult or doctor if vision changes or there is bad pain. Plural: shiners.

part of speech: adjective (simulated); past form of the verb simulate (simulate, simulates, simulated, simulating)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (adjective) Made to look or feel real, but not real; imitation: simulated leather, a simulated fire drill. 2) (adjective, science/computing) Created by a computer model to show what would happen in real life. 3) (verb, past) Pretended: «She simulated surprise».
its sense in the lessons: In science and maths: simulated experiments on a computer, simulated flight for pilots, simulated weather. In safety: simulated emergencies to practise (a fire drill with simulated smoke). In everyday life: simulated fur. Phrases: «a simulated emergency», «simulated flight», «computer-simulated».
examples from the lessons: Pilots train in a simulated cockpit before flying a real plane. | The firefighters ran a simulated rescue at our school. | The bag is made of simulated leather. | We watched a simulated volcano on the computer. | The game uses simulated weather that changes every day. | She simulated surprise when she saw the cake, but she already knew. | The simulated spacewalk took place in a big pool.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past and adjective form of «simulate». Noun: «simulation», «simulator» (machine that simulates). Simulated ≠ fake in a bad sense: simulations are useful for practice and science.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A short, catchy phrase used in advertising or by a group to make people remember a product or an idea: «Every little helps». 2) A short phrase that expresses the aims of a campaign or protest.
its sense in the lessons: In media lessons: slogans in adverts try to persuade us. In citizenship: protest slogans on signs. In school: making a slogan for a recycling campaign or a sports team. Phrases: «a catchy slogan», «advertising slogan», «chant slogans», «come up with a slogan».
examples from the lessons: Our class made a slogan for saving water: «Every drop counts!» | The cereal box had a catchy slogan. | The protesters chanted slogans outside the town hall. | A good slogan is short and easy to remember. | The team's slogan is «Never give up». | Adverts use slogans to make you want things.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a slogan, slogans. Similar: «motto» (a rule to live by, often for a school or family), «catchphrase». Slogans can be persuasive but not always true – think before you believe them.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To ask for something such as money, help or opinions, especially politely or officially. 2) (formal) To try to get business or customers. 3) (law) To ask someone in a public place for something illegal, which adults are forbidden to do.
its sense in the lessons: In formal letters and news: «The school solicited donations», «The council solicited residents' opinions». On signs: «No soliciting» means no selling door to door or asking for money here. In law it can mean asking for something illegal. Phrases: «solicit donations», «solicit feedback», «no soliciting».
examples from the lessons: The charity solicited donations for the flood victims. | The teacher solicited our ideas for the class trip. | The sign on the door said «No soliciting». | The council solicited opinions from people in the town. | It is against the rules to solicit money in the school car park. | The shop solicited feedback from its customers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: solicited, soliciting (no doubled letters). Related: «solicitor» (in the UK, Ireland, Australia and NZ: a kind of lawyer). «Solicit» is formal; everyday words: «ask for», «request». «Unsolicited» = not asked for (unsolicited advice).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Lying flat on your back, face upwards. 2) (formal) Weak, lazy or too willing to accept things without protesting.
its sense in the lessons: In science, PE and first-aid lessons: «supine position» = lying on your back (the opposite of «prone», lying face down). In the formal voice: a supine government does nothing. Phrases: «supine position», «lie supine».
examples from the lessons: The doctor asked the patient to lie supine on the bed. | In yoga, we lay supine and breathed slowly. | The opposite of supine is prone, lying face down. | The cat lay supine in the sun with its paws in the air. | The newspaper called the council supine for doing nothing about the potholes. | For this exercise, start in a supine position with your knees bent.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced SOO-pine (or soo-PINE). Opposite: «prone» (face down). Memory trick: supine has «up» in it – face up. In first aid, an unconscious person who is breathing is usually put in the recovery position, not left supine.

meaning for a pupil: 1) According to what people say or believe, though it may not be true: «The house is supposedly haunted». 2) As something is meant or intended to be: «a supposedly easy test».
its sense in the lessons: Used to show doubt about a claim: in stories, news and science («supposedly cures colds»). Helps readers notice that a fact is not checked. In media lessons: words like «supposedly», «allegedly» and «it is said» signal unproved claims. Phrases: «supposedly true», «supposedly easy».
examples from the lessons: The old house is supposedly haunted. | This cream supposedly makes spots disappear overnight. | The test was supposedly easy, but most of us found it hard. | Supposedly, carrots help you see in the dark, but that's mostly a myth. | He was supposedly ill, but we saw him at the park. | Our teacher is supposedly from Scotland.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: suppos-ed-ly (four syllables: sup-POZE-id-lee). Common error: «supposably» is a mistake in most uses. Similar: «allegedly», «apparently», «reportedly». It signals doubt, so a reader should ask «how do we know?».

part of speech: adjective (tedious, more tedious, most tedious); adverb «tediously»; noun «tedium»
meaning for a pupil: 1) Long, slow and boring; tiring because it goes on and on. 2) (of a person) Annoying because they are boring.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: tedious chores, tedious journeys, tedious homework. In maths: some tasks are tedious, like adding the same number many times; multiplication or a pattern can save effort. In stories: a tedious speech. Phrases: «a tedious job», «tedious and repetitive».
examples from the lessons: Sorting all the socks was a tedious job. | The journey was long and tedious. | Copying out the spelling list ten times is tedious. | Instead of tedious adding, use multiplication. | The speech was so tedious that half the audience fell asleep. | Weeding the garden is tedious but useful. | His tedious jokes made everyone groan.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stress: TEE-dee-us. Similar: «boring», «dull», «monotonous». Formal-ish; children usually say «boring». Noun «tedium» means boredom.

part of speech: adjective (telling, more telling, most telling); also the present participle and gerund of «tell» (tell, tells, told, telling); noun (a telling, tellings)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (verb form) Saying or reporting something: «She is telling a story». 2) (adjective) Showing something important, often more than people meant to show: «a telling remark». 3) (adjective) Having a strong effect: «a telling blow». 4) (noun) The act of telling a story: «In this telling of the tale, the wolf is kind». 5) (phrase) «telling off» = a scolding (UK, Australia); «that's telling him» = a sharp reply; «there's no telling» = no way to know.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and English lessons: a telling detail shows a character's feelings or a clue. In everyday life: «I got a telling-off for being late». In maths problems «telling» can mean what information you are given. Phrases: «telling the time», «telling off», «there's no telling», «a telling sign».
examples from the lessons: Grandad is telling us a story about the war. | She said nothing, but her silence was telling. | The muddy footprints were a telling clue. | I got a telling-off from Mum for leaving my bike out. | There's no telling what the cat will do next. | In this telling of Cinderella, the stepsisters are nice. | We are learning telling the time in class.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Telling» as an adjective is not about speaking: «a telling look» shows something without words. «Telling off» (noun, UK/Aus) = a scolding; the verb is «tell someone off». «Tell» past: told (not «telled»).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (law) A formal statement of what someone saw or knows, given in a court of law. 2) Evidence or proof that something is true: «Her medals are testimony to her hard work». 3) (church) A personal story a Christian tells about how faith changed their life; (Bible) the Ten Commandments are sometimes called the testimony.
its sense in the lessons: In law and detective stories: witnesses give testimony in court and promise to tell the truth. In everyday and formal writing: «a testimony to» = a sign that proves something. In church life: people may share their testimony at a service. Phrases: «give testimony», «a testimony to», «witness testimony».
examples from the lessons: The witness gave testimony in court about the accident. | Her shiny trophies are testimony to years of practice. | The judge listened carefully to each testimony. | At church, Mrs Brown shared her testimony about how faith helped her through illness. | The detective did not believe the man's testimony. | The old bridge is a testimony to the skill of its builders.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: testimony, testimonies (y → ies). Stress: TES-ti-mo-nee. Related: «testify» (to give testimony), «testimonial» (a letter saying someone is good). Lying in testimony in court is a serious crime called perjury.

part of speech: verb (past form of «thin»: thin, thins, thinned, thinning); adjective (thinned)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Made thinner or less thick: «She thinned the paint with water». 2) Became less crowded or less dense: «The crowd thinned». 3) (gardening) Took out some young plants so the others have room to grow. 4) (of hair) Became thinner, with less hair: «His hair thinned as he got older».
its sense in the lessons: In art: thinned paint, thinned glue. In gardening and science: seedlings are thinned. In stories: «The fog thinned», «The crowd thinned out». In cooking: thinned sauce. Phrases: «thinned out», «thinned with water».
examples from the lessons: Mum thinned the gravy with a little water. | The crowd thinned after the fireworks ended. | We thinned the carrot seedlings so they had space. | The fog thinned and we could see the hills. | Grandad's hair has thinned over the years. | The teacher thinned the paint so it would spread easily. | By evening, the traffic had thinned out.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double n: thin → thinned, thinning. Opposite: «thickened». «Thin out» often means to become fewer or less crowded.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Being shy, nervous and easily frightened; lack of courage or confidence.
its sense in the lessons: In stories: a timid character grows brave. In ethics and PSHE lessons: everyone feels shy sometimes; timidity is not a fault, and people can be gentle and brave. In animals: the timidity of deer and rabbits. Phrases: «overcome your timidity», «out of timidity».
examples from the lessons: Out of timidity, Ella didn't put her hand up, though she knew the answer. | The rabbit's timidity kept it hidden in the bushes. | Sam overcame his timidity and asked to join the game. | The teacher was patient with the new boy's timidity. | His timidity disappeared when he talked about dinosaurs. | Timidity is natural in a new place.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Adjective: «timid». Stress: ti-MID-i-tee. Similar: «shyness». Opposite: «boldness», «courage».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Allowing beliefs, customs or behaviour that you may not agree with, without trying to stop them. 2) (history/religion) A government's allowing people to follow different religions freely: religious toleration. 3) The ability to put up with something unpleasant (more often «tolerance»).
its sense in the lessons: In history and religion lessons: laws of religious toleration let people of different faiths worship freely. In citizenship and ethics: living together peacefully needs toleration and respect. Phrases: «religious toleration», «toleration of», «a spirit of toleration».
examples from the lessons: The king's law of religious toleration let people worship as they chose. | Toleration means letting others hold different views. | Our class talked about toleration of other people's beliefs. | The town was known for its toleration of different religions. | Toleration of bullying is never acceptable. | Living together in peace needs toleration and kindness.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. «Tolerance» is the more common word for the quality or attitude; «toleration» is more often the act or policy of allowing. Verb: «tolerate». Toleration is not the same as approval: you can tolerate something you dislike.

part of speech: noun (trend, trends); verb (trend, trends, trended, trending)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (noun) A general direction in which something is changing or developing: «a trend towards healthier eating». 2) (noun) A fashion or craze: «the latest trend». 3) (verb) To move in a general direction. 4) (verb, online) To be talked about a lot online at a particular moment: «trending on social media».
its sense in the lessons: In maths and science: a trend in data is the overall direction on a graph (upwards trend, downward trend); a trend line shows it. In everyday life: fashion and toy trends. Online: trending topics and videos – but popular is not the same as true. Phrases: «a trend towards», «follow the trend», «set a trend», «trending now».
examples from the lessons: The graph shows an upward trend in temperatures. | Fidget spinners were a big trend at our school. | There is a trend towards more children walking to school. | That video is trending on social media. | My sister always follows the latest trends. | Prices have trended down over the last few months. | Look at the data and describe the trend.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun. Verb is regular: trended, trending. In maths, a trend is a general direction; some points may go against it. Trending online can include false stories – check facts. Adjective: «trendy» (fashionable, informal).

part of speech: noun (trolling); verb form of «troll» (troll, trolls, trolled, trolling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (online) Posting rude, mean or upsetting messages on the internet on purpose, to make people angry or to get attention. 2) (fishing) Fishing by pulling a baited line behind a slowly moving boat. 3) (informal) Teasing someone as a joke: «I'm just trolling you».
its sense in the lessons: Online-safety lessons: trolling is a kind of cyberbullying; the advice is not to reply, block, report and tell an adult. Among friends, «trolling» can be playful teasing, but it can hurt. In fishing, trolling is a normal method. Phrases: «internet trolling», «stop trolling», «don't feed the trolls».
examples from the lessons: Trolling people online is a form of bullying. | If someone is trolling you, don't reply – block and report them. | He was trolling the comments with nasty messages. | «Are you trolling me?» she laughed when I said school was cancelled. | We went trolling for salmon from Uncle Jim's boat. | The website removed accounts for trolling.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A «troll» online is a person who trolls; in stories, a troll is a monster under a bridge. Different origins: the fishing «troll» and the monster are different words. «Don't feed the trolls» means don't give them the reaction they want.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An agreement between enemies or opponents to stop fighting or arguing for a time. 2) (informal) A pause in a quarrel, for example between brothers and sisters.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons: the famous Christmas truce in the First World War, when soldiers stopped fighting for a day. In everyday life: «Let's call a truce» ends an argument. In stories: warring kingdoms make a truce. Phrases: «call a truce», «declare a truce», «an uneasy truce», «a truce between».
examples from the lessons: The two armies agreed to a truce. | «Let's call a truce,» said Maddie to her brother. | During the Christmas truce, soldiers played football together. | The cats seem to have made a truce and share the sofa now. | After the argument, the twins had an uneasy truce. | The truce lasted only three days. | The teacher asked the two groups to make a truce and work together.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a truce, truces. A truce is temporary; a «peace treaty» ends a war for good. Rhymes with «loose» and «juice».

meaning for a pupil: 1) In an honest way; telling the truth. 2) (sentence adverb) Used to show you are being honest about your feelings: «Truthfully, I didn't like the film».
its sense in the lessons: In ethics lessons and stories: answering truthfully even when it's hard. In court, witnesses must answer truthfully. In everyday talk «truthfully» or «to be truthful» introduces an honest opinion. Phrases: «answer truthfully», «truthfully speaking», «to be truthful».
examples from the lessons: Please answer the questions truthfully. | Truthfully, I forgot to do my homework. | She told the teacher truthfully what had happened. | Can you truthfully say you didn't eat the last biscuit? | Truthfully, I'm a bit scared of the dark. | The witness promised to speak truthfully. | He answered truthfully, even though he knew he would get in trouble.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: truth + ful + ly (one l in -ful, then -ly: truthfully has double l). Similar: «honestly». Opposite: «untruthfully», «dishonestly».

part of speech: noun (tweet, tweets); verb (tweet, tweets, tweeted, tweeting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (noun) The short, high sound a small bird makes; (verb) to make this sound. 2) (noun) A short message posted on the social media site Twitter (now called X); (verb) to post such a message.
its sense in the lessons: In nature lessons and stories: birds tweet in the morning. In media and online-safety lessons: tweets can be seen by many people and are hard to delete; think before you post. Many social media sites require users to be at least thirteen. Phrases: «tweet about», «send a tweet», «a viral tweet».
examples from the lessons: The little birds tweeted in the tree outside my window. | «Tweet, tweet!» sang the robin. | The footballer tweeted a photo of the trophy. | His tweet went viral and thousands of people saw it. | Think before you tweet, because others can share it. | The news was announced in a tweet. | The baby chicks tweeted for food.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: tweeted. The site was renamed X, but many people still say «tweet» and «Twitter». Onomatopoeia: «tweet» copies the sound of a bird. Similar bird sounds: chirp, cheep, twitter.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Impossible to reach, achieve or get. 2) (of a person, informal) Seeming too far above you to be friends or go out with.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and school: an unattainable goal, unattainable standards. In PSHE: pictures online can show unattainable bodies or lifestyles, often edited. In maths: an unattainable score is one that can't happen with the rules (e.g. 11 out of 10). Phrases: «an unattainable goal», «seemingly unattainable», «unattainable standards».
examples from the lessons: Getting every single question right seemed an unattainable goal. | The top shelf was unattainable without a ladder. | Some adverts show unattainable perfection. | For a beginner, a black belt can feel unattainable, but step by step it's possible. | With only two dice, a score of 13 is unattainable. | The mountain peak looked unattainable in the snow.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Built from un- + attain (reach) + -able. Opposite: «attainable», «achievable». In maths, check what is possible: two ordinary dice give scores 2 to 12, so 1 and 13 are unattainable.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Not deserved; not earned or fair, whether good or bad: an undeserved punishment, an undeserved prize.
its sense in the lessons: In ethics and fairness lessons: undeserved blame or punishment is unfair. In sport: an undeserved win. In stories: a hero gets undeserved praise or a villain undeserved luck. Phrases: «undeserved punishment», «undeserved reputation», «undeserved praise».
examples from the lessons: The detention was undeserved – I wasn't even there. | They won, but it was an undeserved victory. | He got undeserved praise for work his sister did. | The dog has an undeserved reputation for biting. | She felt her bad mark was undeserved. | An undeserved telling-off can feel very unfair.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced un-di-ZERVD. Opposite: «deserved». «Undeserving» is used for people (an undeserving winner). Christians speak of grace as God's undeserved kindness.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (online) To stop following a person or account on social media, so you no longer see their posts.
its sense in the lessons: In online life and safety lessons: you can unfollow accounts that upset you, show harmful content or make you feel bad. Unfollowing is usually not told to the other person, but they may notice. Phrases: «unfollow someone», «unfollow an account».
examples from the lessons: If an account makes you feel bad, you can unfollow it. | She unfollowed the channel because the videos were too scary. | He was upset when his friend unfollowed him. | I unfollowed the page because it was full of adverts. | You can unfollow without blocking. | After the argument, they unfollowed each other.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: unfollowed. Different from «block» (stop someone seeing or contacting you) and «mute» (hide posts without unfollowing). Opposite: «follow».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Not hurt or harmed; without any injury.
its sense in the lessons: In news and safety: «All the passengers were uninjured», «The driver escaped uninjured». In stories: a character walks away uninjured from danger. Phrases: «escape uninjured», «walk away uninjured», «uninjured but shaken».
examples from the lessons: Luckily, everyone on the bus was uninjured. | The cat fell from the tree but landed uninjured. | The rider was uninjured, but the bike was broken. | She escaped from the fire uninjured. | Two people were hurt and five were uninjured. | He was uninjured but very shaken.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Similar: «unhurt», «unharmed». Opposite: «injured». In maths word problems: if 12 people were on a bus and 3 were injured, 12 − 3 = 9 were uninjured.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Not done on purpose; accidental.
its sense in the lessons: In ethics, safety and playground situations: an unintentional push, an unintentional insult. Saying sorry still matters even if it was unintentional. In law, unintentional harm is treated differently from harm done on purpose. Phrases: «completely unintentional», «unintentional mistake».
examples from the lessons: Sorry, it was unintentional – I didn't see you there. | His rude comment was unintentional, but it still hurt. | The broken vase was an unintentional accident. | The joke had an unintentional double meaning. | Even an unintentional mistake should be fixed. | The referee decided the handball was unintentional.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: «intentional», «deliberate», «on purpose». Similar: «accidental». The intention matters in judging blame, but the effect matters too: apologise even when harm was unintentional.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Not having lights switched on; dark: an unlit street. 2) Not set on fire or burning: an unlit candle.
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons: unlit roads and paths are dangerous at night, so wear bright or reflective clothes and use a torch; bikes must have lights. In stories: an unlit house feels spooky. Phrases: «an unlit road», «an unlit candle», «unlit path».
examples from the lessons: The path through the park is unlit, so take a torch. | We walked carefully down the unlit lane. | An unlit candle stood on the table. | Cyclists must not ride on unlit roads without lights. | The old house was unlit and silent. | The bonfire was still unlit when we arrived.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: «lit». «Lit» is a past form of «light» (also «lighted»). «Unlit» has nothing to do with «lit» meaning literature or the slang «lit» (exciting).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Not controlled or held back; free and wild: unrestrained joy, unrestrained anger. 2) Not physically held back or tied: an unrestrained dog, an unrestrained passenger (without a seat belt).
its sense in the lessons: In stories: unrestrained laughter, unrestrained tears. In safety: unrestrained children in cars (no seat belt or car seat) can be badly hurt; unrestrained dogs may run into roads. In formal writing: unrestrained spending. Phrases: «unrestrained joy», «unrestrained passenger».
examples from the lessons: The fans cheered with unrestrained joy. | An unrestrained passenger can be thrown forward in a crash. | The puppy ran unrestrained across the field. | Her unrestrained laughter filled the room. | His unrestrained anger frightened the little ones. | Unrestrained spending left them with no money.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: «restrained». Built from un- + restrain (hold back). In cars, always wear a seat belt: being unrestrained is dangerous and against the law.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Not yet solved, answered or explained: an unsolved mystery, an unsolved problem.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: unsolved problems – some famous puzzles are still unsolved by anyone. In detective stories and the news: unsolved crimes, «cold cases». In science: unsolved questions drive research. Phrases: «an unsolved mystery», «unsolved crime», «remain unsolved».
examples from the lessons: The mystery of the missing cake remains unsolved. | Some maths problems are still unsolved after hundreds of years. | The detective reopened the unsolved case. | Question 5 is still unsolved on my worksheet. | Scientists have many unsolved questions about the universe. | The crime remained unsolved for many years.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: «solved». Often after «remain» or «still». An unsolved problem is not the same as an unsolvable one (impossible to solve).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Not checked or proved to be true or correct.
its sense in the lessons: In media and online-safety lessons: unverified stories, claims and accounts may be false; check reliable sources before sharing. In science: unverified results need more tests. In news: «unverified reports». Phrases: «unverified claims», «unverified reports», «unverified account».
examples from the lessons: The news report was based on unverified rumours. | Don't share unverified stories online. | His claim that he saw a ghost is unverified. | Unverified accounts may be fake. | Scientists repeated the test because the results were unverified. | The rumour about a snow day was unverified, so we still went to school.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: «verified» (checked). Verb: «verify». Unverified does not mean false – it means not yet checked. Treat it with caution.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Having won a battle, game or competition. 2) Showing that you have won: a victorious shout.
its sense in the lessons: In sport, history and stories: the victorious team, the victorious army. Phrases: «emerge victorious», «victorious over», «a victorious return».
examples from the lessons: Our team was victorious in the final. | The victorious army marched home. | She gave a victorious cheer when she finished the puzzle. | The knight emerged victorious from the battle. | After a long game, the blue team was victorious. | The victorious players lifted the cup.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: «victory». Similar: «winning», «triumphant». Opposite: «defeated», «beaten». Stress: vik-TOR-ee-us.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Containing too much water; thin and weak: watery soup. 2) Full of water or wet: watery eyes. 3) Pale, weak in colour or light: a watery sun. 4) Like water or connected with water: a watery grave.
its sense in the lessons: In cooking: watery sauces or tea are too thin. In health: watery eyes in hay fever or a cold. In stories and descriptions: a watery sun in winter, «a watery grave» (drowning at sea). Phrases: «watery eyes», «watery soup», «a watery smile».
examples from the lessons: The soup was watery and tasteless. | My eyes go watery when I chop onions. | A watery sun peeped through the clouds. | She gave a watery smile through her tears. | The paint was too watery to cover the paper. | The pirates were sent to a watery grave.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative: usually «more watery», sometimes «waterier». A watery smile is a weak, tearful one. Related: «waterproof», «watertight» have different meanings.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The state of being healthy, happy and comfortable in body and mind.
its sense in the lessons: Common in schools: «wellbeing lessons», «wellbeing week», «mental wellbeing». It covers sleep, food, exercise, friendships, feelings and asking for help. Phrases: «mental wellbeing», «physical wellbeing», «a sense of wellbeing», «wellbeing of children».
examples from the lessons: Our school has a wellbeing week with yoga and nature walks. | Sleep is important for your wellbeing. | Talking about worries helps your mental wellbeing. | The teacher cares about the wellbeing of every pupil. | Playing outside gives me a sense of wellbeing. | Pets can be good for people's wellbeing.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: no «a», no plural. Spelling: «wellbeing» (common in the UK and Australia) or «well-being» (common in the USA). Not the same as «welfare», which often means help from the state.

part of speech: exclamation (wow); verb (wow, wows, wowed, wowing); noun (a wow – informal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (exclamation) Said when you are surprised, amazed or impressed. 2) (verb, informal) To impress someone greatly: «She wowed the judges». 3) (noun, informal) A great success: «The show was a wow». 4) (sarcastic) Used to show you are not impressed: «Wow, thanks a lot».
its sense in the lessons: Everyday talk and stories: «Wow!» shows amazement. In writing lessons: «wow words» are interesting words that make writing exciting. Sarcastic «wow» can hide annoyance – tone matters. Phrases: «wow factor», «wow the crowd», «wow words».
examples from the lessons: Wow, look at that rainbow! | «Wow, you got full marks!» | The magician wowed the audience. | The new playground has a real wow factor. | Use some wow words in your story to make it exciting. | «Wow, thanks for eating all the chips,» said Lily crossly. | The dancers wowed the judges at the competition.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal; avoid it in formal writing except in quotes. Verb: wowed. Like many exclamations, its meaning depends on the tone of voice. A palindrome: it reads the same backwards.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The quality of being morally wrong or unfair. 2) The quality of being incorrect or not as it should be: «a feeling of wrongness».
its sense in the lessons: In ethics lessons: «the wrongness of stealing», asking why something is wrong. In stories: a feeling of wrongness tells the reader something bad is about to happen. Phrases: «the wrongness of», «a sense of wrongness».
examples from the lessons: She understood the wrongness of what she had done. | There was a strange wrongness about the empty house. | We discussed the wrongness of cheating. | He felt a sense of wrongness when the dog didn't bark. | The wrongness of the answer was clear when we checked it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. A fairly rare word; often «how wrong something is» sounds more natural. Opposite: «rightness». Related: «wrong», «wrongly», «wrongdoing».

part of speech: verb (yelp, yelps, yelped, yelping); noun (a yelp, yelps)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (verb) To give a short, sharp cry, especially of pain, fright or surprise. 2) (noun) A short, sharp cry, especially of a dog or a person.
its sense in the lessons: Animals and stories: a puppy yelps when someone treads on its paw. In stories it shows sudden pain or fright. Phrases: «yelp in pain», «give a yelp», «yelp with surprise».
examples from the lessons: The puppy yelped when I stepped on its tail. | She gave a yelp when the cold water hit her. | «Ouch!» he yelped, holding his toe. | We heard a yelp from the garden. | The fox yelped in the night. | Lily yelped with surprise when the balloon popped.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: yelped. Similar: «squeal», «yowl», «cry out». A «yelp» is short; a «howl» is long. Also the name of a review website, written with a capital Y.

part of speech: article (French; le, la, les) — not an English word
meaning for a pupil: 1) (French) «Le» means «the» in French, used before a masculine word: «le chat» is «the cat». 2) It sounds like «luh» to an English ear, with a short soft vowel. 3) It is not an English word, but you meet it in French names and phrases that English has borrowed.
its sense in the lessons: In French lessons it is one of the first words learnt, with «la» (the, feminine) and «les» (the, plural); every French noun has a gender, and «le» shows that the noun is masculine. In English you meet it in borrowed names and phrases such as «Le Mans», café menus («le menu») and in names of places in Canada (Quebec) and France.
examples from the lessons: In French, «le chat» means «the cat». | Our teacher wrote «le livre» on the board and said it means «the book». | «Le» sounds a bit like «luh». | The Quebec street sign said «Le Vieux-Port». | In French class we sorted words into «le» words and «la» words. | «Le garçon» means «the boy». | The café in our town is called «Le Petit Café».
note for the reader of a maths problem: French, not English. Before a vowel or silent «h», «le» shrinks to «l'»: «l'arbre» (the tree), «l'homme» (the man). Do not confuse it with «la» (feminine the) or «les» (plural the). Gender in French is grammar, not real life: a table is «la table» but a book is «le livre». In English text it is usually in names, so keep the capital: «Le Mans».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A verb is a word that tells what someone or something does, like «run», «eat» or «think». 2) A verb can also tell what someone or something is or has, like «is», «seem» or «have». 3) Every full sentence needs a verb; it is the word that changes for time, like «walk», «walked».
its sense in the lessons: In English grammar lessons pupils find the verb in a sentence, change its tense (past, present, future) and match it to the subject («she runs», «they run»). Teachers call verbs «doing words» and «being words». Phrases: «action verb», «helping verb» (also «auxiliary verb», like «is», «have», «will»), «irregular verb» («go – went»), «verb tense», «modal verb» («can», «must»). In stories, strong verbs («dashed», «whispered») make writing lively.
examples from the lessons: «Jump» is a verb because it is something you can do. | In «The dog barked», the verb is «barked». | Underline the verb in each sentence. | «Is» is a verb too, even though nothing moves. | Choose a stronger verb than «went», like «raced» or «crept». | Irregular verbs change in odd ways: «swim, swam, swum». | A sentence without a verb is not a full sentence. | In «She can sing», «can» is a helping verb and «sing» is the main verb.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one verb, two verbs. Some words can be a verb or a noun: «a run» (noun), «I run» (verb) — look at the job the word does in the sentence. Regular verbs make the past with «-ed» (walked); irregular ones do not (ran, ate, went). A verb must agree with its subject: «he plays», «they play». The adjective is «verbal», which also means «spoken» («a verbal warning»).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A noun is a word that names a person, place, thing or idea, like «girl», «London», «ball» or «happiness». 2) A proper noun is the special name of one person, place or thing and starts with a capital letter, like «Emma» or «Canada». 3) A common noun is a general name, like «dog» or «city», and has no capital unless it starts a sentence.
its sense in the lessons: In English grammar lessons pupils sort nouns into common and proper, countable and uncountable, singular and plural, and concrete (you can touch them: «table») and abstract (ideas: «courage»). Phrases: «noun phrase» («the big red bus»), «collective noun» («a flock of sheep», «a team»), «proper noun», «compound noun» («football»). In stories nouns tell the reader who and what the story is about.
examples from the lessons: «Cat» is a noun because it names an animal. | «Paris» is a proper noun, so it needs a capital letter. | Find all the nouns in this sentence. | «Love» and «fear» are abstract nouns. | «Flock» is a collective noun for a group of birds or sheep. | Add «s» to most nouns to make the plural: «book, books». | In «The old man smiled», the noun is «man». | My teacher calls nouns «naming words».
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one noun, two nouns. Many words are a noun in one sentence and a verb in another: «a drink» (noun) and «to drink» (verb). Some nouns have odd plurals: «child – children», «mouse – mice», «sheep – sheep». Uncountable nouns like «water», «rice», «advice» usually have no plural and take «some», not «a». Pronouns («he», «it») stand in for nouns.

part of speech: noun (a panda, pandas; giant panda, red panda)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A panda (giant panda) is a large black-and-white bear from the mountain forests of China that eats almost only bamboo. 2) A red panda is a smaller, reddish-brown, furry animal with a long ringed tail; it also eats bamboo but is not a close relative of the giant panda. 3) (UK, old-fashioned) A «panda car» was a small police car.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography lessons pandas come up in habitats, food chains, adaptations (a special wrist bone works like a thumb to grip bamboo) and conservation: there are not many wild pandas, and protecting their bamboo forests helped their numbers grow. In everyday life pandas are a symbol of wildlife protection (the WWF logo) and of China, and are favourite soft toys and zoo animals.
examples from the lessons: The panda munched bamboo for most of the day. | Giant pandas live in the mountains of China. | A baby panda is tiny and pink when it is born. | The red panda curled its bushy tail around itself to keep warm. | Our class adopted a panda through a wildlife charity. | Pandas have a special wrist bone that helps them hold bamboo. | There were huge crowds at the zoo to see the new panda cub. | The panda is the symbol of a famous nature charity.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «pandas». A baby is a «cub». Myth: pandas are not lazy — bamboo has little energy in it, so they rest a lot to save energy. The giant panda is a real bear; the red panda is not a bear and is in a family of its own. Pandas are black and white, not black and grey.

part of speech: pronoun (French «il»; Italian «il» is an article) — not an English word
meaning for a pupil: 1) (French) «Il» means «he» or «it» in French: «il mange» is «he eats». 2) (French) In some phrases it means «it» with no real person: «il pleut» is «it is raining». 3) (Italian) In Italian «il» means «the», as in «il gelato» (the ice cream). 4) It is not an English word; to an English ear French «il» sounds like «eel».
its sense in the lessons: In French lessons «il» (he/it) is learnt with «elle» (she/it), «ils» (they, masculine) and «elles» (they, feminine). Common phrases: «il y a» (there is, there are), «il fait beau» (the weather is nice), «s'il vous plaît» (please). In English you might see «il» in Italian food and place names, such as «Il Duomo» or a restaurant called «Il Forno».
examples from the lessons: In French, «il est grand» means «he is tall». | «Il pleut» means «it is raining». | «S'il vous plaît» means «please». | «Il y a un chat» means «there is a cat». | French «il» sounds like the English word «eel». | The Italian restaurant on our street is called «Il Forno». | In French, a thing that is masculine is also called «il».
note for the reader of a maths problem: French or Italian, not English. Do not read «il» as «ill» (sick). In French the «l» is said; in «ils» (they) the «s» is silent, so «il» and «ils» sound the same. Do not confuse it with the prefix «il-» in English words like «illegal» and «illogical», where it means «not».

part of speech: verb (French «est» = is); abbreviation (est. = established, estimated; EST = Eastern Standard Time); suffix «-est»
meaning for a pupil: 1) (French) «Est» means «is» in French: «il est content» is «he is happy»; the «s» and «t» are silent, so it sounds like «eh». 2) (French) «L'est» also means «the east» in French, and then the «st» is said. 3) (abbreviation) «Est.» is short for «established» (when a shop or school began) or «estimated» (a guess that is close). 4) (abbreviation) «EST» means Eastern Standard Time, the clock time in the eastern USA and Canada. 5) «-est» is also an English ending meaning «the most»: «tallest», «fastest».
its sense in the lessons: In French lessons «est» is one of the forms of «être» (to be): «c'est» means «it is» or «that's». On signs and shop fronts «Est.» shows the year a business started. In maths and science «est.» marks an estimate. In grammar lessons the ending «-est» makes superlatives: «big, bigger, biggest».
examples from the lessons: In French, «c'est bon» means «it's good». | «Elle est ma sœur» means «she is my sister». | The bakery sign said «Est.» and then the year it opened. | The table showed «est. 300 people», meaning about 300. | The football match starts at seven o'clock EST. | Add «-est» to make the superlative: «fast, faster, fastest». | French «est» sounds like «eh», not like «east».
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a whole word, «est» is French, not English. In French, «est» (is) and «et» (and) sound the same, «eh», but are different words. In English, «est.» with a dot is an abbreviation, not a word on its own. Spelling trap with «-est»: double the last letter after a short vowel («big – biggest») and change «y» to «i» («happy – happiest»).

part of speech: noun (Mandarin, pinyin; the Ming dynasty); name — not an English word
meaning for a pupil: 1) (Mandarin, pinyin) «Míng» means «bright» or «clear» in Mandarin Chinese and is part of words like «míngtiān» (tomorrow) and «míngzi» (name). 2) (history) The Ming dynasty was a family of emperors who ruled China for nearly three hundred years; it is famous for blue-and-white porcelain and for building much of the Great Wall we see today. 3) (a name) Ming is a Chinese personal name or part of one. 4) (UK slang) «Minging» means disgusting; «ming» is rarely heard on its own. To an English ear it sounds just like it is spelt, «ming».
its sense in the lessons: In Mandarin lessons pupils meet «míngzi» (name: «nǐ jiào shénme míngzi?» = what is your name?) and «míngtiān» (tomorrow). In history lessons «Ming» comes in «Ming dynasty», «Ming vase» and the Great Wall. In stories, «Ming the Merciless» is a villain in an old science-fiction comic.
examples from the lessons: In Mandarin, «míngtiān» means «tomorrow». | «Nǐ jiào shénme míngzi?» means «What is your name?» | The museum had a blue-and-white Ming vase. | Much of the Great Wall that tourists visit was built under the Ming emperors. | My friend Ming sits next to me in maths. | The Ming dynasty came after the Mongol rulers of China. | Pinyin «ming» sounds the same as it looks in English.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Not an English word on its own. In pinyin, the mark on the vowel shows the tone; «míng» has a rising tone, and a different tone can mean a different word. As a dynasty or a person's name it needs a capital: «the Ming dynasty», «Ming». «Ming vase» is often used in stories to mean something very precious and easy to break.

meaning for a pupil: 1) African means from, of or about Africa, the second-largest continent. 2) An African is a person from Africa or whose family comes from Africa. 3) African is also used in the names of animals and plants that live in Africa, like the African elephant.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons pupils learn that Africa has more than fifty countries and many hundreds of languages, the Sahara desert, the Nile river and rainforests, so «African» covers a huge variety of people, foods, music and ways of life. In science «African» appears in animal names: «African elephant», «African wild dog», «African grey parrot». In history lessons «African» comes in the history of ancient kingdoms (Egypt, Mali, Benin) and the slave trade. Phrases: «African American», «South African», «North African».
examples from the lessons: The African elephant is the largest land animal. | Our school celebrated African music with a drumming workshop. | Nigeria and Kenya are both African countries. | Her grandparents are African, from Ghana. | The African savanna has lions, zebras and giraffes. | We read a traditional African folk tale about Anansi the spider. | Many African languages are spoken across the continent. | The African grey parrot is very good at copying words.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always a capital A, because it comes from a place name. Africa is a continent, not a country, so «African» is not one language or one culture — say «Nigerian», «Kenyan», «Egyptian» when you mean one country. «African American» is a person in the USA with African family roots. Be respectful: use it about people as a description, not as a label for a whole group.

part of speech: noun (a plural, plurals; the plural); adjective (plural)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Plural means more than one: «cats» is the plural of «cat». 2) The plural of a word is the form it takes when it means more than one. 3) (formal) Plural can also mean having many kinds or groups living together, as in «a plural society».
its sense in the lessons: In English grammar lessons pupils learn plural rules: add «-s» (dog, dogs), add «-es» after s, x, z, ch, sh (box, boxes), change «y» to «ies» (baby, babies), «f» to «ves» (leaf, leaves), and learn irregular plurals (child – children, mouse – mice, foot – feet, sheep – sheep). Phrases: «singular and plural», «in the plural», «plural noun», «plural verb». In maths word problems, a plural noun shows there is more than one thing.
examples from the lessons: «Cats» is the plural of «cat». | What is the plural of «mouse»? It is «mice». | «Sheep» is the same in the singular and the plural. | Add «-es» to make the plural of «box». | «We» and «they» are plural pronouns. | The plural of «baby» is «babies». | Use a plural verb with a plural subject: «The dogs bark». | The word «scissors» is always plural.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: «singular» (just one). Traps: «data» and «media» are old plurals; «news» looks plural but takes a singular verb («the news is good»). Some words have no plural («water», «furniture»). An apostrophe does not make a plural: write «apples», not «apple's». In maths problems, a plural word does not tell you how many; read the number.

part of speech: adverb (French «ne», part of «ne … pas» = not); abbreviation (NE = north-east) — not an English word
meaning for a pupil: 1) (French) «Ne» is the first half of the French way to say «not»: «je ne sais pas» is «I don't know»; the word goes before the verb and «pas» goes after it. 2) (abbreviation) «NE» means north-east, the direction halfway between north and east, as on a compass or a map. 3) It is not an English word on its own; French «ne» sounds like «nuh».
its sense in the lessons: In French lessons pupils learn the negative «ne … pas» (not), «ne … jamais» (never), «ne … plus» (no more) and «ne … rien» (nothing). In everyday spoken French people often drop «ne» and just say «je sais pas». In geography lessons «NE» is a compass point: «the wind blew from the NE».
examples from the lessons: «Je ne parle pas allemand» means «I don't speak German». | «Il ne mange jamais de viande» means «he never eats meat». | In fast French, people often leave out «ne». | Before a vowel, «ne» becomes «n'»: «je n'aime pas». | The map showed the town to the NE of the lake. | A compass has N, NE, E, SE, S, SW, W and NW. | French «ne» sounds like «nuh».
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a word, French, not English. «Ne» cannot make a sentence negative alone in written French; it needs a partner such as «pas». Before a vowel it becomes «n'». As a direction write «NE» in capitals or «north-east» in full. Do not confuse with «né(e)» (born), as in «née» for a woman's family name at birth.

part of speech: article and preposition (French «des» = some / of the); name (Des, short for Desmond) — not an English word
meaning for a pupil: 1) (French) «Des» means «some» before a plural noun: «des pommes» is «some apples». 2) (French) «Des» also means «of the» or «from the» for plural things: «la maison des enfants» is «the children's house». 3) (a name) Des is a short form of the man's name Desmond. 4) To an English ear French «des» sounds like «day».
its sense in the lessons: In French lessons «des» is learnt with «du» and «de la» (some): «je voudrais des frites» (I would like some chips). It appears in French place names and phrases English borrows: «Champs-Élysées», «Jardin des Plantes». In Ireland and the UK «Des» is a familiar nickname. Also «des res» (UK, informal, jokey) means a «desirable residence», a nice house.
examples from the lessons: In French, «j'ai des bonbons» means «I have some sweets». | «Le jardin des plantes» means «the garden of the plants». | «Des» sounds like «day» in French. | My uncle Des runs the corner shop. | In French, «un chat» is «a cat», and «des chats» is «some cats». | Mum joked that the new house was a real «des res».
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a word, French, not English; the «s» is silent unless the next word starts with a vowel («des amis» sounds like «day-zah-mee»). In English «des-» at the start of a word is a prefix, as in «describe». As a name it takes a capital: «Des».

part of speech: noun (ma, mas — informal: mother); abbreviation (MA = Master of Arts; ma = milliamp); Mandarin pinyin «ma» — mixed
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) «Ma» is a homely word for mother, like «Mum» or «Mom», heard in old stories, in the USA countryside and in Ireland. 2) (Mandarin, pinyin) «Mā» means «mum»; «ma» with no tone is a little word at the end of a sentence that turns it into a question: «nǐ hǎo ma?» (are you well?). 3) (abbreviation) «MA» is a Master of Arts, a university degree. 4) (French) «Ma» means «my» before a feminine noun: «ma mère» is «my mother»; in Italian «ma» means «but».
its sense in the lessons: In stories, «Ma» and «Pa» are what children call their parents in old American tales such as «Little House on the Prairie». In Mandarin lessons pupils learn «māma» (mum) and the question word «ma». In Ireland and Scotland «me ma» means «my mum». In science «mA» is a milliamp, a tiny unit of electric current.
examples from the lessons: «Ma, can I go out to play?» asked the boy in the old story. | Pa fixed the fence while Ma baked bread. | In Mandarin, «nǐ hǎo ma?» means «how are you?» | «Māma» is the Mandarin word for «mum». | My aunt has an MA in history. | The tiny bulb needed only a few mA of current. | «Me ma says I have to be home for tea», said Sean.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As «mother» it is informal and old-fashioned; in a letter or essay write «mother», «mum» (UK, Ireland, Australia, New Zealand) or «mom» (USA, Canada). Capital M when used as a name: «Ma said no». In pinyin the tone mark changes the meaning: «mā» (mum), «mǎ» (horse), «mà» (scold). «MA» and «mA» are abbreviations, not words.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A lemming is a small, furry, short-tailed rodent that lives in cold northern lands such as the Arctic tundra. 2) (figurative) A person who blindly follows the crowd, even into danger, is sometimes called a lemming.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons lemmings come up in Arctic food chains: snowy owls, Arctic foxes and stoats eat them, and lemming numbers rise and fall in big cycles every few years. In everyday talk «like lemmings» means people following each other without thinking. Myth lesson: lemmings do not throw themselves off cliffs on purpose; a nature film long ago faked that scene.
examples from the lessons: The lemming dug a tunnel under the snow. | Snowy owls hunt lemmings on the tundra. | Some years there are huge numbers of lemmings, and other years very few. | Lemmings are related to voles and hamsters. | Everyone rushed to the door like lemmings when the bell rang. | Don't be a lemming — think for yourself. | The Arctic fox pounced on a lemming hiding in the grass.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «lemmings». Myth: lemmings do not commit mass suicide; that idea came from a staged film scene. Calling someone a lemming is a mild insult meaning they follow others without thinking. Spelling: double «m».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A comma is a punctuation mark (,) that shows a short pause or separates parts of a sentence. 2) Commas separate things in a list: «eggs, milk and bread». 3) In numbers, a comma groups digits in threes to make them easy to read: «1,000,000»; in many European countries a comma is used as the decimal point instead.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons pupils use commas in lists, after a fronted adverbial («After lunch, we played»), around extra information («My brother, who is ten, plays chess»), before speech marks and in addresses. Phrases: «Oxford comma» or «serial comma» (a comma before «and» in a list), «comma splice» (two sentences joined only by a comma — a mistake). In maths, commas separate thousands in big numbers in the UK, USA and Australia, and coordinates are written with a comma: (3, 4).
examples from the lessons: Put a comma between the items in a list. | «Let's eat, Grandma!» needs a comma, or it sounds like we are eating Grandma. | After a fronted adverbial, put a comma: «Later that day, it rained.» | My sister, who loves horses, rides every Saturday. | Write ten thousand as 10,000. | The point (2, 5) is two across and five up. | A comma shows the reader where to take a short breath.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «commas». A comma is not a full stop: do not join two complete sentences with only a comma. In maths, «3,5» in France or Germany means three and a half, but in the UK and USA it is «3.5» — the comma and the decimal point swap between countries. Do not confuse «comma» with «coma» (a deep sleep after an illness or injury).

part of speech: noun (gen — UK informal: information; Gen — short for generation; Gen. — General, Genesis); adverb (UK slang «gen» = genuinely)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) «Gen» is short for «generation», as in «Gen Z» or «Gen Alpha», a group of people born around the same time. 2) (UK slang) «Gen» means «genuinely» or «honestly»: «I'm gen tired». 3) (UK, informal, old-fashioned) «The gen» means the information or the facts: «give me the gen». 4) (abbreviation) «Gen.» is short for the army rank General, and «Gen» for the Bible book Genesis.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday talk children hear «Gen Z» and «Gen Alpha» used about age groups, and in games «next-gen» means the newest version of consoles. In UK playground slang «gen» means «for real». In church and Bible lessons, «Gen 1:1» means Genesis, chapter one, verse one — the first verse of the Bible. In history, «Gen.» is a rank written before a name: «Gen. Washington».
examples from the lessons: My older cousin says she is Gen Z. | Children born recently are sometimes called Gen Alpha. | «That was gen the best film ever», said Callum. | The new next-gen console came out at the weekend. | Look up Gen 1:1 — the first verse of the Bible. | Gen. Eisenhower led the soldiers. | Grandad asked for «the gen» on the school trip.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly informal or an abbreviation, not a full word in careful writing; in essays write «generation», «genuinely», «General» or «Genesis». «Gen» is said with a soft «j» sound, like «jen». Do not confuse it with «gene» (part of DNA) or «gem» (a jewel).

meaning for a pupil: 1) DNA is the chemical inside the cells of every living thing that carries the instructions for how it grows, works and what it looks like. 2) DNA is passed from parents to children, which is why children often look like their parents. 3) (figurative) Something's «DNA» is the most basic part of what it is: «kindness is in our school's DNA».
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons DNA comes in inheritance and evolution: DNA is shaped like a twisted ladder called a double helix, it is found in the nucleus of a cell, and genes are small sections of it. In everyday life and stories, DNA tests help doctors, help police solve crimes (DNA from a hair or a drop of blood) and help families find relatives. It stands for deoxyribonucleic acid.
examples from the lessons: DNA is like a recipe book inside every cell. | You got half your DNA from your mum and half from your dad. | DNA is shaped like a twisted ladder called a double helix. | The detectives found DNA on the cup. | Identical twins have almost the same DNA. | Scientists can read the DNA of plants and animals. | Rosalind Franklin's pictures helped scientists see the shape of DNA. | Being curious is part of our family's DNA.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always written in capitals: DNA, said letter by letter, «dee-en-ay». Uncountable: say «DNA», not «a DNA» (but «a DNA test», «a DNA sample» are fine). Genes are parts of DNA; chromosomes are long packed strands of DNA. Myth: DNA does not decide everything — what you eat, learn and do also shapes you.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A chimp is a chimpanzee, a clever, hairy African ape that lives in groups in forests and is one of the closest animal relatives of humans. 2) (informal) People sometimes call a cheeky, silly person a chimp, in a joking way.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons chimps come up in classification (they are apes, not monkeys), animal intelligence (they use sticks as tools to catch termites) and conservation (they are endangered). Jane Goodall is famous for watching wild chimps for many years. In everyday talk «chimp» is just the short, friendly word for chimpanzee.
examples from the lessons: The chimp used a stick to fish for termites. | Chimps live in groups in the forests of Africa. | A baby chimp rides on its mother's back. | Chimps are apes, so they have no tail. | Jane Goodall studied wild chimps for many years. | Stop acting like a chimp and sit down! | The zoo's chimps hooted when the keeper arrived.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «chimps». Informal short form of «chimpanzee»; in a science report use «chimpanzee». Trap: chimps are apes, not monkeys — monkeys usually have tails, apes do not. Myth: humans did not come from chimps; humans and chimps share an ancestor from long ago.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A tusk is a very long, pointed tooth that grows out of the mouth of some animals, such as elephants, walruses, wild boars and narwhals. 2) Tusks are used for digging, fighting, lifting and getting food, and they keep growing through the animal's life.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons tusks come up in adaptations: elephants use tusks to dig for water and strip bark, walruses use them to pull themselves onto the ice. In conservation lessons pupils learn that tusks are made of ivory and that poachers kill elephants for it, so selling ivory is banned or limited in many countries. In stories about mammoths and wild boars, tusks show the animal is strong and dangerous.
examples from the lessons: The elephant lifted the log with its tusks. | Walruses use their tusks to haul themselves onto the ice. | A narwhal's tusk is really one long spiral tooth. | Woolly mammoths had huge curved tusks. | Elephant tusks are made of ivory. | The wild boar's tusks were sharp and curved. | Poachers hunt elephants for their tusks, which is against the law. | Some elephants are born without tusks.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «tusks». A tusk is a tooth, not a horn; horns grow on the head, tusks come out of the mouth. «Tusked» means having tusks. Do not confuse with «task» (a job).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A leopard is a big wild cat with yellow fur covered in dark spots called rosettes; it lives in Africa and parts of Asia. 2) Leopards are strong climbers and often drag their food up into trees to keep it safe from lions and hyenas. 3) «Leopard print» is a pattern on clothes that looks like a leopard's spots.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons leopards come up in camouflage (spots help them hide in the shade), food chains (top predator) and comparing big cats: a cheetah has solid round spots and a slim body, a jaguar has bigger rosettes with dots inside and lives in the Americas. The saying «a leopard can't change its spots» means people do not really change who they are. A black leopard is often called a black panther.
examples from the lessons: The leopard rested on a branch in the afternoon heat. | A leopard's spots help it hide in the long grass. | The leopard dragged its catch up into a tree. | Leopards hunt mostly at night. | A black panther is often a leopard with very dark fur. | Gran wore a leopard-print scarf. | «A leopard can't change its spots», said Dad.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «leopards». Spelling trap: «leo-pard», the «o» is silent; say «LEP-erd». Do not mix up leopard, cheetah and jaguar: cheetahs have simple spots and tear marks on the face; jaguars live in the Americas and have dots inside their rosettes. The young is a «cub».

meaning for a pupil: 1) An atom is the smallest piece of a chemical element, far too small to see even with an ordinary microscope; everything around us is made of atoms. 2) An atom has a tiny centre called the nucleus, with even tinier electrons moving around it. 3) (figurative) «Not an atom of» means not even the tiniest bit: «not an atom of truth».
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons atoms come in materials and chemistry: atoms join together to make molecules (two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom make a water molecule), and different kinds of atom are the elements on the periodic table, like carbon, oxygen and gold. Phrases: «atom bomb» (a nuclear bomb), «split the atom». Atoms are so small that millions would fit across the full stop at the end of this sentence.
examples from the lessons: Everything is made of tiny atoms. | A water molecule has two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom. | Gold is made only of gold atoms. | An atom is mostly empty space. | Scientists use special microscopes to see the shapes of atoms. | The word «atom» comes from a Greek word meaning «cannot be cut». | There wasn't an atom of doubt in her mind.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «atoms»; use «an atom» because it starts with a vowel sound. Adjective «atomic». Trap: the name means «uncuttable», but atoms can be split into smaller parts (protons, neutrons, electrons). An atom is not a cell: cells are in living things and are made of billions of atoms. Do not confuse atom and molecule: a molecule is two or more atoms joined.

part of speech: noun (bamboo — uncountable; a bamboo, bamboos for kinds)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Bamboo is a very tall, fast-growing plant, a kind of giant grass, with hard hollow stems divided into sections. 2) Bamboo is also the strong, light material made from those stems, used for building, furniture, fishing rods and even toothbrushes.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons bamboo comes up as the food of giant pandas and as one of the fastest-growing plants on Earth — some kinds grow almost a metre in a single day. In design and technology and in lessons about the environment, bamboo is a sustainable material because it grows back quickly. In Asian stories and art, bamboo is a sign of strength because it bends in the wind but does not break.
examples from the lessons: Pandas eat bamboo almost all day. | Bamboo is a kind of giant grass. | Some bamboo can grow very fast in a single day. | We grew beans up bamboo canes in the school garden. | My new toothbrush is made of bamboo. | The bamboo stem is hollow inside. | The bamboo bent in the storm but did not snap. | They built a raft from bamboo poles.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable: «some bamboo», «a bamboo cane», «a bamboo forest». Bamboo is a grass, not a tree, even though it can be as tall as a tree. Spelling: double «o» at the end.

part of speech: Mandarin pinyin (méi = not have; měi = beautiful, every; Měiguó = America); name (Mei) — not an English word
meaning for a pupil: 1) (Mandarin, pinyin) «Méi» means «not» or «don't have»: «méiyǒu» is «there isn't» or «I haven't got». 2) (Mandarin, pinyin) «Měi» means «beautiful» and also «every»: «měitiān» is «every day». 3) (Mandarin, pinyin) «Měiguó» means «America», the USA, literally «beautiful country». 4) (a name) Mei is a girl's name, used in China and Japan. To an English ear it sounds like «may».
its sense in the lessons: In Mandarin lessons pupils learn «méi guānxi» (it doesn't matter, no problem), «méiyǒu» (haven't got) and «měitiān» (every day). In stories and anime Mei is a character's name. Heard on the street in Chinatowns and Chinese families, «méiyǒu» is a common short answer meaning «no, there isn't any».
examples from the lessons: In Mandarin, «méi guānxi» means «never mind». | «Wǒ méiyǒu gēge» means «I haven't got an older brother». | «Měitiān» means «every day». | «Měiguó» is the Mandarin name for America. | My friend Mei is learning the violin. | Pinyin «mei» sounds like the English name «May». | «Méiyǒu!» the shopkeeper said — there were none left.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Not an English word. In pinyin the tone mark changes the meaning: «méi» (rising: not have) and «měi» (dipping: beautiful, every) are different words. As a name it takes a capital: «Mei». Do not read it as «me» or «my».
