meaning for a pupil: 1) A lemur is a furry animal with big eyes, a pointed face and usually a long tail, found in the wild only on the island of Madagascar, off the coast of Africa. 2) The best-known kind, the ring-tailed lemur, has a long black-and-white striped tail.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography lessons lemurs come up in islands and habitats (animals that live in only one place), adaptations (big eyes for seeing at night, long tails for balance) and conservation, because many lemurs are endangered when forests are cut down. Lemurs are primates, like monkeys and apes. In films, lemurs are famous from cartoons set in Madagascar.
examples from the lessons: Lemurs live wild only on Madagascar. | The ring-tailed lemur held its striped tail high. | Lemurs sunbathe in the morning to warm up. | A baby lemur clings to its mother's back. | Some lemurs are active at night and have huge eyes. | Lemurs are primates, like monkeys and apes. | Cutting down the forest puts lemurs in danger.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «lemurs». Say «LEE-mer». Lemurs are primates but neither monkeys nor apes. Do not confuse with «lemming» (an Arctic rodent).

part of speech: noun (a reef, reefs); verb (reef, reefs, reefed, reefing — sailing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A reef is a long ridge of rock, sand or coral just under or at the surface of the sea. 2) A coral reef is built over many years by tiny sea animals called corals and is home to huge numbers of fish and other sea creatures. 3) (sailing) To reef a sail means to roll or tie up part of it to make it smaller in strong wind.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography lessons reefs come up in ocean habitats and climate: the Great Barrier Reef off Australia is the largest coral reef system in the world and can be seen from space; warmer, more acidic seas can cause «coral bleaching», when corals turn white and may die. In stories, ships wreck on hidden reefs. In safety lessons, swimmers learn that reefs can be sharp and waves break hard over them.
examples from the lessons: The Great Barrier Reef is off the coast of Queensland, Australia. | Clownfish hide in the anemones on the reef. | The ship hit a reef and sank. | Coral reefs are full of colourful fish. | Warm water can make the reef turn white. | Divers must not touch or break the coral reef. | The sailors reefed the sails as the storm grew stronger.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «reefs» (not «reeves»). Countable: «a reef». Coral is made by animals, not plants, though it looks like rock or plants. Do not confuse with «wreath» (a ring of flowers) or «reek» (a bad smell).

part of speech: adverb (French «pas» = not); noun (a pas — a step in ballet; plural pas); in phrases «faux pas», «pas de deux» — not an English word on its own
meaning for a pupil: 1) (French) «Pas» means «not» in French, used with «ne»: «je ne sais pas» is «I don't know»; in casual French people often just say «pas». 2) (French, ballet) «Pas» means «a step» in dance: a «pas de deux» is a dance for two people. 3) «A faux pas» (from French, meaning «false step») is an embarrassing social mistake, like saying the wrong thing at a party. To an English ear «pas» sounds like «pah».
its sense in the lessons: In French lessons «pas» is part of the negative: «ce n'est pas grave» (it's not a big deal), «pas du tout» (not at all), «pas mal» (not bad). In ballet classes «pas» names steps. In English, «a faux pas» is used in everyday talk for a social blunder. Also, in French «un pas» is a footstep.
examples from the lessons: «Je ne sais pas» means «I don't know». | «Pas mal!» means «not bad!» | «Pas du tout» means «not at all». | In ballet, a «pas de deux» is a dance for two. | Wearing trainers to the wedding was a bit of a faux pas. | French «pas» sounds like «pah», and the «s» is silent. | «Ce n'est pas grave» means «it doesn't matter».
note for the reader of a maths problem: French, not English, except in borrowed phrases like «faux pas» (said «foh pah»). The «s» is silent. Do not confuse with «pa» (informal for father) or «pass».

meaning for a pupil: 1) An antler is one of the two branched, bony horns that grow on the head of a deer, elk, moose or reindeer. 2) Antlers fall off and grow again every year, unlike horns, which stay for life.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons antlers come up in adaptations and life cycles: male deer use antlers to fight other males in the mating season, and the new antlers are covered in soft furry skin called velvet while they grow. Reindeer are the only deer where both males and females have antlers. In stories and Christmas pictures, reindeer pulling Santa's sleigh have big antlers.
examples from the lessons: The stag's antlers had many points. | Deer shed their antlers every year. | The moose had wide, flat antlers. | Both male and female reindeer grow antlers. | Two stags locked antlers in a fight. | The new antlers were covered in soft velvet. | We found an old antler in the woods.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually plural «antlers», because an animal has two. Antlers are bone and fall off each year; horns (on cows, goats, rhinos) are not shed. Do not say a cow has antlers.

part of speech: noun (an ape, apes); verb (ape, apes, aped, aping — to copy)
meaning for a pupil: 1) An ape is a large primate with no tail, such as a gorilla, chimpanzee, bonobo, orangutan or gibbon. 2) (verb, a bit formal) To ape someone means to copy the way they act or talk, often in a silly way. 3) (informal) «Go ape» means to get very excited or angry: «Dad went ape when he saw the mess».
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons pupils learn that apes are different from monkeys: apes have no tail, are usually bigger, and are very clever, using tools and solving problems. Humans are classed as great apes too. In conservation lessons, many apes are endangered because their forests are cut down. In stories «ape» can make a character sound big and clumsy.
examples from the lessons: Gorillas are the largest apes. | An ape has no tail, but most monkeys do. | Orangutans are apes that live in the rainforests of Borneo and Sumatra. | The younger boy aped everything his big brother did. | Stop aping the teacher's voice! | The crowd went ape when we scored. | Chimpanzees are apes that use sticks as tools.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «apes»; «an ape». Trap: apes and monkeys are not the same — check for a tail. Myth: humans did not evolve from today's apes; we share ancestors with them. «Go ape» is slang; avoid it in essays. «Aping» (copying) is a verb.

part of speech: preposition + article (French «au» = to the, at the, in the); symbol (Au = gold); abbreviation (AU = Australia; astronomical unit) — not an English word on its own
meaning for a pupil: 1) (French) «Au» means «to the», «at the» or «in the» before a masculine word: «au parc» is «to the park», «au revoir» is «goodbye». 2) (science) «Au» is the chemical symbol for gold, from the Latin word «aurum». 3) (abbreviation) «AU» is short for Australia (as in web addresses ending .au) and, in space science, for an astronomical unit, the distance from the Earth to the Sun. To an English ear French «au» sounds like «oh».
its sense in the lessons: In French lessons pupils learn «au revoir» (goodbye), «au café» (at the café), «au lait» (with milk). English borrows phrases: «au pair» (a young person from abroad who lives with a family and helps look after the children), «au naturel», «au revoir». In science, «Au» appears on the periodic table for gold.
examples from the lessons: «Au revoir!» means «goodbye!» | «Je vais au parc» means «I'm going to the park». | Our au pair comes from Spain and walks us to school. | On the periodic table, Au stands for gold. | A café au lait is coffee with milk. | French «au» sounds like «oh». | Australian websites often end in «.au».
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a word, French, not English, except in borrowed phrases like «au pair» and «au revoir». «Au» is «à + le» joined; before a feminine word French uses «à la», before plurals «aux». The gold symbol is «Au» with a capital A and small u. Do not read «Au» as «ow».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Dung is the solid waste, or poo, of animals, especially large animals like cows, horses and elephants. 2) Dung is used on farms as manure to help plants grow, and in some places it is dried and burned as fuel.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons dung comes up in food chains and decomposition: dung beetles roll balls of dung, bury it and lay eggs in it, which recycles nutrients back into the soil. In history and geography lessons pupils learn that dried dung is burned for cooking and heating where there is little wood. Phrases: «dung beetle», «cow dung», «dung heap». It is a polite, scientific word, not a rude one.
examples from the lessons: The dung beetle rolled a ball of dung across the sand. | Farmers spread cow dung on the fields to help crops grow. | Elephant dung is full of seeds. | In some villages dried dung is used as fuel. | The smell of horse dung filled the stable. | Scientists study dung to find out what animals eat. | Watch out for the cow dung in the field!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «some dung», «a pile of dung», not «a dung». It is a polite word for animal waste; «poo» is the everyday word, «manure» means dung used on fields. Never touch animal dung with bare hands — wash your hands after farm visits.

part of speech: noun (a republic, republics; the Republic of …)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A republic is a country where the people choose their leaders, and the head of state is usually an elected president, not a king or queen. 2) «Republic» is part of the full name of many countries, such as the Republic of Ireland or the French Republic.
its sense in the lessons: In history and citizenship lessons pupils compare a republic with a monarchy (a country with a king or queen): the USA, France, Ireland and Ukraine are republics; the UK, Canada, Australia and New Zealand have a monarch. In history, ancient Rome was a republic before it had emperors. In the USA, «Republican» is also the name of one of the two main political parties, and in the USA the Pledge of Allegiance mentions «the Republic».
examples from the lessons: The USA is a republic with a president. | Ireland is a republic, but the UK has a king. | The ancient Romans were once a republic. | In a republic, the people vote for their leaders. | Ukraine is a republic. | France became a republic after its revolution. | The Czech Republic is in the middle of Europe.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «republics». Adjective «republican». Capital R when it is part of a name: «the Republic of Ireland». Trap: not every republic is fair or free — some countries call themselves republics but do not have real elections. A «Republican» in the USA is a member of one party, not just someone who likes republics.

part of speech: abbreviation (Br, br., BR) — a fragment, not a word
meaning for a pupil:
1) (abbreviation) «Br» is the chemical symbol for bromine, a dark red liquid element. 2) (abbreviation) «Br.» can be short for «British», «Brother» (a monk or member of a religious order, as in «Br. John») or «branch». 3) (texting) «br» or «brb» is chat shorthand: «brb» means «be right back». 4) (computing) In web pages, «
» is a tag that starts a new line.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons «Br» appears on the periodic table. In church life, «Br.» is written before the name of a religious brother. In online chat, children see «brb». In coding lessons, the HTML tag «br» means «line break». In everyday life it is never said as a word; people say the full form.
examples from the lessons: On the periodic table, Br stands for bromine. | Br. Thomas teaches at the monastery school. | «brb» means «be right back». | We used a br tag to start a new line on our web page. | On old train tickets, «BR» stood for British Rail. | Bromine, Br, is one of only two elements that are liquid at room temperature.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A fragment or abbreviation, not an English word. Read it out as the full word it stands for. Chemical symbols have a capital first letter and a small second one: «Br», not «BR».

part of speech: noun (a dye, dyes; dye — uncountable for the stuff); verb (dye, dyes, dyed, dyeing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A dye is a substance used to change the colour of cloth, hair, food or other things. 2) To dye something means to change its colour by soaking it in, or covering it with, a dye. 3) (science) Dyes can be made from plants, insects or chemicals.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons dye is used in experiments: food dye in water shows how water moves up a celery stalk, and chromatography separates the colours in an ink or dye. In history lessons pupils learn that purple dye was once so rare and costly that only kings and emperors wore it, and that people made dyes from plants such as woad and onion skins. In everyday life people dye their hair, dye Easter eggs and tie-dye T-shirts.
examples from the lessons: We used blue food dye to show water climbing up the celery. | Mum dyed her hair red. | We tie-dyed T-shirts at summer camp. | Onion skins make a yellow-brown dye. | The dye ran in the wash and turned my socks pink. | Long ago, purple dye was worn only by rulers. | We dyed eggs bright colours for Easter.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past «dyed», «-ing» form «dyeing» (keep the «e»). Homophone trap: «dye» (colour) and «die» (stop living); «dyeing» (colouring) and «dying» (about to die) — spell carefully. A dye soaks in; a paint sits on top.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An adjective is a word that describes a noun, telling us more about a person, place or thing, like «big», «red», «happy» or «three». 2) Adjectives can come before a noun («a tall tree») or after verbs like «is» and «seems» («the tree is tall»).
its sense in the lessons: In English grammar lessons pupils find adjectives, use them to make writing more interesting («an expanded noun phrase»: «the gloomy, silent castle»), and learn comparatives and superlatives (big, bigger, biggest; good, better, best). Phrases: «comparative adjective», «superlative adjective», «adjective of size, colour, shape». In maths word problems, adjectives like «each», «every», «more», «fewer» carry number meaning.
examples from the lessons: «Fluffy» is an adjective in «a fluffy kitten». | Add two adjectives to describe the monster. | «Happy» is an adjective; «happiness» is a noun. | The comparative of the adjective «big» is «bigger». | In «The sky is blue», «blue» is an adjective after the verb. | Use an adjective of colour and one of size: «a small green frog». | «Good, better, best» are forms of one adjective.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «adjectives»; «an adjective». English adjectives do not change for plural: «a red car, two red cars» (not «reds cars»). Order trap: in English the usual order is opinion, size, age, shape, colour, origin, material: «a lovely big old round red French wooden table». Do not confuse with adverbs, which describe verbs: «a quick run» (adjective), «run quickly» (adverb).

meaning for a pupil: 1) In grammar, a clause is a group of words that has a verb and usually a subject: «when the bell rang» and «we went outside» are clauses. 2) A main clause makes sense on its own as a sentence; a subordinate clause does not and needs a main clause. 3) (law) A clause is one section or rule in a written agreement or law.
its sense in the lessons: In English grammar lessons pupils join clauses with conjunctions («and», «but», «because», «when») and learn main clauses, subordinate clauses and relative clauses («the boy who won»). Phrases: «main clause», «subordinate clause», «relative clause», «a clause in the contract». In everyday adult life, contracts for phones, homes and jobs have clauses that say what each side must do. «Santa Claus» sounds the same but is a different word.
examples from the lessons: «I went home» is a main clause. | «Because it was raining» is a subordinate clause; it cannot stand alone. | Join the two clauses with «but». | «The dog that barked» has a relative clause: «that barked». | Every clause has a verb. | Dad read every clause of the phone contract before signing. | A comma often comes after a subordinate clause at the start of a sentence.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «clauses». Homophone trap: «clause» (grammar, law) and «claws» (sharp nails of an animal), and «Claus» in «Santa Claus». A clause has a verb; a phrase usually does not («in the morning» is a phrase).

part of speech: slang spelling and foreign word: «da» = the (slang), dad (dialect); Italian/Portuguese «da» = from; Russian «da» = yes — a fragment
meaning for a pupil: 1) (slang) «Da» is a playful spelling of «the», as in «da best»; it copies how some people say «the». 2) (Ireland, Scotland, Northern England, informal) «Da» means dad: «me da». 3) (Russian) «Da» means «yes» in Russian; Ukrainian for «yes» is «tak», not «da». 4) (Italian, Portuguese) «Da» means «from» or «by»: Leonardo da Vinci means «Leonardo from Vinci». 5) (Mandarin, pinyin) «Dà» means «big». To an English ear it sounds like «dah».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday talk in Ireland and Scotland children say «me da» for my dad. In online chat and songs «da» stands for «the». In history and art lessons pupils meet «Leonardo da Vinci». In Mandarin lessons «dà» (big) and «xiǎo» (small) are early words. In stories about the Cold War, a Russian character might say «da».
examples from the lessons: «Me da's picking me up after school», said Aoife. | Leonardo da Vinci painted the Mona Lisa. | «Da» means «yes» in Russian. | In Ukrainian, «yes» is «tak». | In Mandarin, «dà» means «big». | The poster said «Da Best Burgers in Town». | Grandad calls his own father «Da».
note for the reader of a maths problem: Not a standard English word. In writing use «the» and «dad». Do not assume Russian and Ukrainian words are the same: «yes» is «da» in Russian but «tak» in Ukrainian. In names like «da Vinci» the «da» usually keeps a small d.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A rhino, short for rhinoceros, is a very large, heavy, thick-skinned animal with one or two horns on its nose; it lives in Africa and southern Asia and eats plants. 2) (UK, old slang) «Rhino» once meant money, but this is rarely heard now.
its sense in the lessons: In science and conservation lessons rhinos are a key example of endangered animals: poachers kill them for their horns, which are made of keratin, the same stuff as our hair and nails, and have no real medical power. Pupils learn about the white rhino, black rhino (both African) and Indian, Javan and Sumatran rhinos. In stories a rhino is huge, strong and short-sighted.
examples from the lessons: The rhino has two horns on its nose. | Rhinos roll in mud to cool off and protect their skin. | Rhino horn is made of keratin, like your fingernails. | Poachers hunt rhinos, so rangers guard them. | A baby rhino is called a calf. | The black rhino is not really black; it is grey. | The rhino charged across the plain.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «rhinos». Short for «rhinoceros» (plural «rhinoceroses» or «rhinoceros»). Myth: rhino horn does not cure illness. Another trap: white and black rhinos are both grey; «white» may come from a word meaning «wide», describing its wide mouth.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A tentacle is a long, bendy arm-like part on some animals, such as octopuses, squids and jellyfish, used for feeling, grabbing, moving or stinging. 2) (figurative) The «tentacles» of something are the ways it reaches into many places: «the tentacles of the gang».
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons tentacles come up in sea habitats and adaptations: jellyfish and sea anemones sting prey with their tentacles; an octopus has eight arms with suckers (scientists call octopus limbs «arms» and squid have two longer «tentacles»). In safety lessons at the beach, pupils learn not to touch jellyfish, even dead ones, because the tentacles can still sting.
examples from the lessons: The jellyfish trailed long, stinging tentacles. | The octopus wrapped its arms around the crab. | A squid catches food with its two long tentacles. | Sea anemones wave their tentacles to catch tiny fish. | Do not touch a jellyfish on the beach — its tentacles can still sting. | Snails have tentacles on their heads with eyes at the tips. | The monster in the story reached out with slimy tentacles.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «tentacles». Spelling: «-acle», like «miracle». Trap: scientists say an octopus has eight arms, not tentacles; squids have eight arms plus two tentacles. In everyday talk people call all of them tentacles.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A pigment is a substance that gives colour to something, like the green in leaves or the colour of skin, hair and eyes. 2) A pigment is also a coloured powder that is mixed with oil or water to make paint.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons pupils learn that chlorophyll is the green pigment that plants use to catch sunlight in photosynthesis, that leaves change colour in autumn when chlorophyll breaks down, and that melanin is the pigment in human skin, hair and eyes that helps protect from the sun. Chromatography separates the pigments in ink or leaves. In art and history lessons, early artists ground rocks and plants to make pigments for cave paintings.
examples from the lessons: Chlorophyll is the green pigment in leaves. | Melanin is a pigment in our skin. | Cave painters made pigments from red earth and charcoal. | We separated the pigments in a felt-tip pen using wet paper. | The artist mixed the blue pigment with oil. | In autumn the green pigment fades and the yellow shows through. | Some animals have no pigment and are pure white.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «pigments». Adjective «pigmented». A pigment is the colour stuff itself; paint is pigment mixed with a liquid. Do not confuse with «figment» («a figment of your imagination»).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A sensor is a device that notices something, such as light, heat, movement, sound or touch, and sends a signal about it. 2) (science) Living things have natural sensors too, like the eyes, ears and skin.
its sense in the lessons: In science, computing and design lessons sensors are used with micro:bits and robots: a light sensor, a temperature sensor, a motion sensor, a sound sensor. In everyday life sensors are everywhere: automatic doors, smoke alarms, phone screens, car parking sensors, security lights and taps that turn on by themselves. In safety lessons, smoke and carbon monoxide sensors warn people of danger.
examples from the lessons: The automatic door has a sensor that sees you coming. | We used the micro:bit's light sensor to measure brightness. | The security light switched on when the motion sensor saw a cat. | Smoke alarms have a sensor that detects smoke. | The car's parking sensor beeped near the wall. | The robot used a touch sensor to stop at the wall. | Your skin is full of sensors for heat and pain.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «sensors». Spelling trap: «sensor» (a detector) and «censor» (a person who cuts or hides things from films, books or news) sound the same. A sensor detects; it does not decide — a program or brain decides what to do.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An apostrophe is a punctuation mark (') used to show that letters are missing in a shortened word: «don't» means «do not». 2) An apostrophe also shows that something belongs to someone: «Sam's bag». 3) (literature, formal) An apostrophe is also when a speaker in a poem talks directly to someone absent or a thing, like «O Moon!».
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons pupils learn apostrophes for contraction («can't», «it's», «I'm») and for possession («the dog's bone», one dog; «the dogs' bones», more than one dog; «the children's toys»). A common mistake is the «greengrocer's apostrophe», putting an apostrophe in an ordinary plural, like «apple's for sale». Teachers often check «its» and «it's».
examples from the lessons: «Don't» has an apostrophe where the «o» is missing. | This is Mia's coat. | The girls' changing room is on the left. | «It's» means «it is»; «its» means «belonging to it». | Do not use an apostrophe to make a plural: «bananas», not «banana's». | «The children's paintings» uses «'s» because «children» is already plural. | «Who's» means «who is».
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «apostrophes»; «an apostrophe». Say «a-POS-truh-fee». Biggest traps: «its» (no apostrophe) means belonging to it; «it's» means «it is» or «it has». Plurals do not take an apostrophe unless showing possession. For a plural ending in «s», put the apostrophe after the «s»: «the teachers' room».

part of speech: abbreviation (EU = European Union); French «eu» (past form of «avoir»), Portuguese «eu» (= I) — not an English word
meaning for a pupil: 1) (abbreviation) «EU» stands for the European Union, a group of many European countries that work together on trade, travel, laws and money. 2) (French) «Eu» is a form of the verb «avoir» (to have): «j'ai eu» means «I had»; it sounds like «oo» said with rounded lips. 3) (Portuguese) «Eu» means «I» in Portuguese.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and citizenship lessons the EU comes up in talk about countries, borders, trade and the euro (the money many EU countries share). Pupils learn that the UK left the EU, while Ireland is still a member, and that Ukraine has asked to join. In French lessons «eu» appears in the past tense: «j'ai eu peur» (I was scared).
examples from the lessons: France, Germany and Ireland are in the EU. | Many EU countries use the euro. | The UK left the EU after a vote. | Ukraine has applied to join the EU. | In French, «j'ai eu un chien» means «I had a dog». | In Portuguese, «eu» means «I». | The EU flag is blue with a circle of yellow stars.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a word it is French or Portuguese, not English. «EU» in capitals is an abbreviation; say the letters «ee-you». Trap: the EU is not the same as Europe — some European countries (like Norway, Switzerland and the UK) are not in the EU. The euro is the money; the EU is the group.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A capybara is the world's largest rodent, a big, calm, barrel-shaped animal with short brown fur, from South America. 2) Capybaras live in groups near rivers, lakes and swamps and are very good swimmers.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons capybaras come up in classification (they are rodents, like guinea pigs, their close relatives), habitats (wetlands of South America) and adaptations: their eyes, ears and nostrils are on top of their head so they can stay hidden in water, and their feet are slightly webbed. On the internet capybaras are famous for being calm and letting birds and other animals sit on them.
examples from the lessons: The capybara is the largest rodent in the world. | Capybaras love to swim and wallow in water. | A bird sat on the capybara's back. | Capybaras are related to guinea pigs. | Jaguars and caimans hunt capybaras. | The capybaras lay in the sun by the river. | A group of capybaras grazed on the grass.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «capybaras». Say «kap-ee-BAR-uh». It is a rodent, not a pig or a beaver.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A chameleon is a kind of lizard that can change the colour of its skin, has eyes that move separately, and catches insects with a very long, sticky tongue. 2) (figurative) A person who changes their opinions or behaviour to fit in with whoever they are with is called a chameleon.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons chameleons come up in adaptations: eyes that can look in two directions at once, feet and tail that grip branches, and a tongue that shoots out longer than its body. Many live in Madagascar and Africa. Pupils learn that chameleons change colour mostly to show mood, control temperature and signal to other chameleons, not only to hide.
examples from the lessons: The chameleon's tongue shot out and caught a cricket. | A chameleon can look forward and backward at the same time. | The chameleon turned bright when it was angry. | Chameleons grip branches with their feet and curly tail. | Many chameleons live in Madagascar. | He's a real chameleon — he agrees with whoever he's talking to. | The chameleon moved slowly along the branch.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «chameleons». Spelling: «ch» is said like «k»: «ka-MEE-lee-un». Myth: chameleons do not simply copy the colour of whatever they sit on; colour change is mainly about mood, temperature and signals.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A cheetah is a slim, spotted big cat from Africa (and a few in Iran) and the fastest land animal, able to run as fast as a car on a main road for a short burst. 2) Cheetahs have black «tear lines» running from their eyes to their mouth.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons cheetahs come up in adaptations (long legs, bendy spine, big lungs and a long tail for balance when turning) and food chains: they hunt gazelles in the daytime but tire quickly after a short sprint. In maths lessons the cheetah's speed is used in comparing speeds and distance–time problems. Cheetahs are endangered and can purr but cannot roar.
examples from the lessons: The cheetah is the fastest land animal. | A cheetah can only sprint for a short time before it gets tired. | The cheetah chased a gazelle across the plain. | Cheetahs have black tear marks on their faces. | Its long tail helps the cheetah turn quickly. | Cheetahs purr like house cats but cannot roar. | Mum drives at about the speed a cheetah can run.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «cheetahs». Spelling: «chee-tah», with «h» at the end. Do not confuse with «cheater» (someone who cheats) — they sound almost the same. Cheetahs have solid round spots; leopards and jaguars have rosettes.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An orangutan is a large, intelligent ape with long reddish-orange hair and very long arms, which lives in the rainforests of Borneo and Sumatra in South-East Asia. 2) Orangutans spend most of their lives in trees and are the largest tree-living animals.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography lessons orangutans come up in rainforest habitats and conservation: forests are being cut down for farms, including palm oil plantations, so orangutans are critically endangered. Their name comes from Malay words meaning «person of the forest». They make a new nest of leaves to sleep in every night and use leaves as umbrellas.
examples from the lessons: The orangutan swung slowly from branch to branch. | Orangutans live only on the islands of Borneo and Sumatra. | Their name means «person of the forest». | A baby orangutan stays with its mother for years. | Orangutans build a fresh leafy nest each night. | Cutting down the rainforest puts orangutans in danger. | The orangutan held a big leaf over its head like an umbrella.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «orangutans»; «an orangutan». Also spelt «orang-utan». Spelling trap: it ends in «-tan», not «-tang», though some people say «orang-utang». It is an ape, not a monkey.

part of speech: noun (a knight, knights); verb (knight, knights, knighted, knighting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) In the Middle Ages, a knight was a soldier who fought on horseback in armour and served a king, queen or lord. 2) In the UK today, a knight is a man given an honour by the King or Queen for great service, and he is called «Sir»; to knight someone is to give them this honour. 3) In chess, the knight is the piece shaped like a horse's head that moves in an L shape. 4) (figurative) «A knight in shining armour» is someone who comes to rescue another person.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons pupils learn about castles, armour, swords, shields, coats of arms, tournaments and the code of chivalry (being brave, loyal and kind to the weak). In stories, King Arthur and the Knights of the Round Table are famous knights. In chess clubs the knight is the only piece that can jump over others. In UK news, famous people may be knighted.
examples from the lessons: The knight put on his armour and climbed onto his horse. | Knights fought for their lord in battles. | The young page trained for years to become a knight. | The famous scientist was knighted by the King. | In chess, the knight moves in an L shape. | King Arthur's knights sat at a round table. | She called her brother her knight in shining armour.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «knights». The «k» and «gh» are silent: it sounds exactly like «night» (the dark time) — a homophone trap. A woman given the same honour is a «Dame». Past «knighted».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A quill is a pen made from a large bird feather, with the end sharpened and dipped in ink, used for writing long ago. 2) A quill is also a large, stiff feather from a bird's wing or tail. 3) The sharp spines on a porcupine or hedgehog are also called quills.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons pupils learn that before metal nibs and ballpoint pens people wrote with quills made from goose or swan feathers, and that important old documents were written with them. In science lessons porcupine quills are a defence adaptation. In stories, writers and wizards write with quills.
examples from the lessons: People long ago wrote with a quill and ink. | She dipped the quill in the inkpot. | The quill was made from a goose feather. | The porcupine raised its quills to warn the dog. | Hedgehog quills are stiff and sharp. | In the wizard school story, pupils write with quills. | We tried to write our names with a quill in the museum.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «quills». Countable: «a quill». A porcupine cannot shoot its quills — that is a myth; they come out when they stick into an attacker.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Whiskers are the long, stiff hairs that grow near the mouth and nose of animals such as cats, dogs, mice and seals, used for feeling things around them. 2) Whiskers can also mean the hair growing on a man's face. 3) «By a whisker» means by a tiny amount: «we won by a whisker».
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons whiskers are a sense adaptation: a cat's whiskers feel tiny movements in the air and help it judge whether it can fit through a gap; seals use whiskers to find fish in murky water. In everyday talk «by a whisker» means only just. In stories, characters may stroke their whiskers when thinking.
examples from the lessons: The cat's whiskers twitched when it heard the mouse. | Cats use their whiskers to feel if they fit through a gap. | Seals find fish with their whiskers. | Grandad's whiskers tickled when he kissed me. | We won the race by a whisker. | Never cut a cat's whiskers. | The mouse had long whiskers and a pink nose.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually plural «whiskers»; singular «a whisker». Whiskers are not just decoration — cutting them can confuse an animal. «The cat's whiskers» (old-fashioned slang) means something excellent.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A hippo, short for hippopotamus, is a huge, heavy African animal with a wide mouth, short legs and thick skin, which spends most of the day in rivers and lakes. 2) Hippos eat grass, coming out of the water at night to graze.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons hippos come up in adaptations: eyes, ears and nostrils are on top of the head so they can stay under water; their skin makes a reddish liquid that protects against the sun. In safety and geography lessons pupils learn that hippos are among the most dangerous large animals in Africa because they are very territorial. The name means «river horse» in Greek.
examples from the lessons: The hippo yawned and showed its huge teeth. | Hippos spend the day in the water to keep cool. | A hippo can stay under water for several minutes. | Hippos come out at night to eat grass. | The name «hippopotamus» means «river horse». | Hippos may look slow, but they are very dangerous. | A baby hippo is called a calf.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «hippos». Short for «hippopotamus» (plural «hippopotamuses» or «hippopotami»). Myth: hippos do not sweat blood; the red liquid is a natural sunscreen. Hippos cannot really swim; they walk or bounce along the bottom.

part of speech: adjective (lush, lusher, lushest); noun (a lush, lushes — rude, informal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Lush plants or places are green, thick and growing well: «lush grass», «a lush rainforest». 2) Lush can mean rich, comfortable and expensive-looking: «lush velvet curtains». 3) (UK slang, especially Wales and the South West) Lush means lovely, great or delicious: «That cake was lush!»; it can also mean good-looking. 4) (US, rude, informal) A lush is a person who drinks too much alcohol.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and science lessons «lush» describes rainforests, river valleys and wet green land where plants grow well because of rain and warmth. In descriptive writing it makes a scene feel rich and alive. In everyday UK talk, especially in Wales, «lush» is a common word of praise. The «drunk» meaning is unkind; pupils should know it but not use it about people.
examples from the lessons: The rainforest was lush and green. | After the rain, the garden looked lush. | Cows grazed on the lush meadow. | «This pizza is lush!» said Rhys. | The hotel room had lush carpets and soft cushions. | The valley was lush, unlike the dry hills around it. | In the old film, a character was called a lush because he drank too much.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative «lusher», superlative «lushest». The slang «lovely» meaning is friendly and informal — do not use it in a formal essay. The noun «a lush» (a heavy drinker) is rude. Do not confuse with «plush» (soft and fancy).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A molecule is the smallest unit of a substance that still has its properties, made of two or more atoms joined together. 2) A water molecule, for example, is two hydrogen atoms joined to one oxygen atom (H2O).
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons molecules come up in states of matter: in solids molecules are packed tightly and vibrate, in liquids they slide past each other, in gases they move fast and far apart; heating makes them move faster. Pupils learn formulas like H2O (water), CO2 (carbon dioxide) and O2 (oxygen). Molecules are much too small to see, even with an ordinary microscope.
examples from the lessons: A water molecule has three atoms. | When ice melts, its molecules start to move more freely. | Oxygen gas is made of molecules with two oxygen atoms. | Smells reach your nose as tiny molecules floating in the air. | Heating makes molecules move faster. | Carbon dioxide molecules are breathed out by animals. | A single drop of water has more molecules than there are stars we can see.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «molecules». Say «MOL-ih-kyool». Adjective «molecular». An atom is a single particle of an element; a molecule is atoms joined together. Not all substances are made of molecules (metals and salt are made differently), but at primary level «particles» is often used for all of them.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A dynasty is a line of rulers from the same family, where power passes from parent to child over many years, like the Tudors in England or the Ming in China. 2) The time when one family rules is also called a dynasty. 3) (figurative) A family or team that stays powerful or successful for a long time is called a dynasty: «a football dynasty».
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons dynasties are used to divide long histories into periods: ancient Egyptian dynasties of pharaohs, Chinese dynasties (Shang, Han, Tang, Song, Ming, Qing), English royal houses (Tudors, Stuarts, Windsors). In sport and business news, «dynasty» means a family or club winning for many seasons.
examples from the lessons: The Ming dynasty ruled China for nearly three hundred years. | Ancient Egypt had many dynasties of pharaohs. | The Tudor dynasty included Henry VIII and Elizabeth I. | The Great Wall was rebuilt by several Chinese dynasties. | The emperor wanted his son to carry on the dynasty. | That team built a dynasty, winning the cup again and again. | A family of famous actors can be called an acting dynasty.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «dynasties» (y changes to ies). Adjective «dynastic». Say «DIN-uh-stee» (UK) or «DY-nuh-stee» (US). A dynasty is a family line, not one ruler; a single ruler has a reign.

part of speech: verb (Spanish «es» = is; French «es» = (you) are); suffix «-es» (plurals and verbs); symbol (Es = einsteinium) — not an English word
meaning for a pupil: 1) (Spanish) «Es» means «is» in Spanish: «es grande» means «it is big». 2) (French) «Tu es» means «you are» in French; the «s» is silent, so it sounds like «eh». 3) «-es» is also an English ending that makes plurals (box, boxes; bus, buses) and the «he/she» form of some verbs (she watches, he goes). 4) (science) «Es» is the symbol for einsteinium, an element made in laboratories.
its sense in the lessons: In Spanish and French lessons «es» is a form of the verb «to be». In English spelling lessons pupils learn when to add «-es» rather than «-s»: after s, ss, sh, ch, x and z, and after many words ending in «o» (tomatoes, potatoes, heroes). In everyday Spanish heard in the USA, «¿Qué es?» means «what is it?».
examples from the lessons: In Spanish, «Es mi amigo» means «he is my friend». | In French, «tu es gentil» means «you are kind». | Add «-es» to make the plural of «fox»: «foxes». | She «watches» TV — the verb gets «-es» after «ch». | «¿Qué es esto?» means «what is this?» in Spanish. | The plural of «potato» is «potatoes». | Es is the symbol for an element named after Albert Einstein.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a word, Spanish or French, not English. In English «-es» is an ending, not a separate word. Exceptions to the «-es» rule: «pianos», «photos», «videos» take just «-s».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A hyena is a dog-like wild animal from Africa and parts of Asia with strong jaws, a sloping back and, in the spotted kind, a call that sounds like laughing. 2) Hyenas hunt in groups and also eat what other animals leave behind.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons hyenas come up in food chains and as scavengers and predators: spotted hyenas actually hunt most of their own food, and their jaws can crush bones. In stories and cartoons hyenas are often shown as sneaky villains, but that is not fair to real hyenas. Pupils learn that hyenas are more closely related to cats and mongooses than to dogs.
examples from the lessons: The hyena's laugh echoed across the savanna at night. | Spotted hyenas live in big groups called clans. | Hyenas have jaws strong enough to crack bones. | Lions and hyenas often fight over food. | Hyenas hunt zebras and wildebeest as well as scavenging. | In the cartoon, the hyenas were the villain's helpers. | Female spotted hyenas are bigger than the males and lead the group.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «hyenas». Say «hy-EE-nuh». Myths: hyenas are not just scavengers, and they are not dogs — they are a family of their own, closer to cats. Their «laugh» is a call, not happiness.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Indigenous people are the first people known to live in a place, and their descendants, such as Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples in Australia, Māori in New Zealand, First Nations, Inuit and Métis in Canada, and Native Americans in the USA. 2) (science) An indigenous plant or animal is one that grows or lives naturally in a place, rather than being brought there by people: «the kangaroo is indigenous to Australia».
its sense in the lessons: In history, geography and citizenship lessons pupils learn about indigenous cultures, languages and land, how colonists took land and treated indigenous peoples unfairly, and how countries now try to respect and listen to them (for example, an «Acknowledgement of Country» in Australian schools). In science lessons, «indigenous species» is contrasted with «invasive species» brought from elsewhere.
examples from the lessons: Māori are the indigenous people of New Zealand. | Our school begins assemblies by thanking the indigenous people of the land. | Kangaroos are indigenous to Australia. | Many indigenous languages are being taught again to children. | First Nations, Inuit and Métis are indigenous peoples of Canada. | Rabbits are not indigenous to Australia; they were brought by settlers. | We read indigenous stories about how the land was made.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective only; the noun is «indigenous people» or «indigenous peoples» (when meaning many different groups). Often written with a capital: «Indigenous Australians». Say «in-DIJ-uh-nus». Use the names the peoples use for themselves; avoid old words like «natives» used as a noun, which can be hurtful. Synonym in science: «native».

part of speech: adjective (Soviet); noun (a soviet, soviets; the Soviets)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Soviet means of or about the Soviet Union (USSR), a large communist country that existed for most of the last century, made of Russia, Ukraine and other republics, ruled from Moscow. 2) (history) A soviet was a workers' council in Russia; the word means «council» in Russian. 3) «The Soviets» means the government or people of the Soviet Union.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons «Soviet» comes in the Second World War, the Cold War between the USA and the Soviet Union, the space race (the Soviets sent the first satellite, Sputnik, and the first person, Yuri Gagarin, into space) and the end of the Soviet Union, after which Ukraine, Russia and other republics became separate countries. Pupils also learn about the Holodomor, the man-made famine in Soviet Ukraine.
examples from the lessons: Yuri Gagarin was the first person in space, sent by the Soviet Union. | Ukraine was part of the Soviet Union before it became independent. | The Cold War was a long standoff between the USA and the Soviets. | Soviet soldiers fought in the Second World War. | The Soviet Union broke up into fifteen countries. | Under Soviet rule, many people could not speak freely. | The word «soviet» means «council» in Russian.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually a capital S: «Soviet», «the Soviet Union». It is history: the Soviet Union no longer exists. Trap: «Soviet» does not just mean «Russian» — Ukrainians, Georgians, Kazakhs and others lived in the Soviet Union too, and today they are separate countries.

part of speech: noun (a jaguar, jaguars; Jaguar — a car make)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A jaguar is a big, powerful wild cat of Central and South America, with golden fur covered in rosettes that have spots inside them. 2) Jaguars are strong swimmers and hunt in rainforests and swamps, catching capybaras, fish, turtles and even caimans. 3) Jaguar (with a capital J) is a British make of expensive car.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography lessons jaguars come up in Amazon rainforest food chains (top predator) and in comparing big cats: the jaguar is the largest cat in the Americas and has the strongest bite for its size. In history lessons, the Maya and Aztecs honoured the jaguar as a symbol of power. Pupils learn to tell jaguars from leopards: jaguars are stockier and their rosettes have dots in the middle.
examples from the lessons: The jaguar crept silently through the rainforest. | Jaguars are the biggest cats in South America. | Unlike most cats, jaguars love water. | A jaguar's rosettes have little spots inside them. | The jaguar pounced on a caiman by the river. | The ancient Maya carved jaguars on their temples. | My uncle's new car is a Jaguar.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «jaguars». Said «JAG-yoo-ar» (UK) or «JAG-wahr» (US). Jaguars live only in the Americas; leopards live in Africa and Asia — if you see a spotted big cat in Africa, it is not a jaguar.

part of speech: noun (alpha — the Greek letter Α, α); adjective (alpha — first, top); noun (Gen Alpha)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Alpha is the first letter of the Greek alphabet, written Α or α. 2) Alpha can mean the first or the top one: the «alpha» wolf leads the pack. 3) (computing) An alpha version is an early, unfinished test version of a program or game. 4) (informal, slang) An «alpha» is a bossy, confident person who wants to lead. 5) (Bible) «The Alpha and the Omega» means the first and the last, the beginning and the end; Christians use it about God.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and science lessons α is used as a symbol for an angle. The word «alphabet» comes from «alpha» and «beta», the first two Greek letters. In everyday talk children are called «Gen Alpha». In radio and spelling codes «Alpha» stands for the letter A (Alpha, Bravo, Charlie). In nature lessons the idea of strict «alpha» wolves is now thought to be too simple: wild wolf packs are mostly families led by the parents.
examples from the lessons: Alpha is the first letter of the Greek alphabet. | The word «alphabet» comes from «alpha» and «beta». | We labelled the angle α in our maths diagram. | The game is still in alpha, so it has lots of bugs. | Kids born recently are called Gen Alpha. | In the radio alphabet, «A» is «Alpha». | «I am the Alpha and the Omega», says a verse in the Bible.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «alphas» (rare). Trap: the «alpha wolf» idea comes from studies of wolves in zoos; in the wild, the pack leaders are simply the parents. Calling someone «an alpha» is slang. Omega (Ω, ω) is the last Greek letter.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A meerkat is a small, furry animal of the mongoose family that lives in groups in the deserts and dry grasslands of southern Africa. 2) Meerkats are famous for standing up on their back legs to watch for danger.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons meerkats come up in adaptations and teamwork: one meerkat stands guard as a sentry and gives an alarm call when it sees an eagle or jackal, while the others dig for insects, scorpions and lizards. They live in underground burrows, and the dark patches round their eyes cut the glare of the sun. In everyday life meerkats are a favourite zoo animal and a famous advertising character.
examples from the lessons: The meerkat stood on its back legs to look around. | One meerkat keeps watch while the others look for food. | Meerkats live in groups called mobs or gangs. | Meerkats can eat scorpions without getting hurt by the sting. | The meerkats dashed into their burrow when an eagle flew over. | Meerkats live in the Kalahari Desert. | The baby meerkats came out to play in the sun.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «meerkats». It is not a cat; it is a kind of mongoose. A group is called a «mob», «gang» or «clan». Spelling: double «e».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Smallpox was a very serious, catching disease that caused a high fever and spots that turned into blisters, often leaving deep scars or killing people. 2) Smallpox is the first human disease ever wiped out completely from the world, thanks to vaccination.
its sense in the lessons: In history and science lessons smallpox comes up in the story of vaccines: Edward Jenner noticed that milkmaids who caught mild cowpox did not get smallpox, and he made the first vaccine (the word comes from «vacca», Latin for cow). Pupils also learn that diseases like smallpox, brought by Europeans, killed huge numbers of indigenous people in the Americas and Australia. A worldwide vaccination campaign later ended smallpox completely.
examples from the lessons: Smallpox was once one of the deadliest diseases. | Edward Jenner used cowpox to protect people from smallpox. | Thanks to vaccines, nobody catches smallpox any more. | Smallpox left many survivors with scars. | Smallpox brought from Europe killed many Native Americans. | Smallpox was the first disease to be wiped out by people. | Doctors around the world worked together to end smallpox.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «smallpox», not «a smallpox». One word. It is not the same as chickenpox, which is a much milder, common childhood illness. Now only kept in a few laboratories.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The Mediterranean (Sea) is the large sea between southern Europe, North Africa and western Asia. 2) Mediterranean means of or near this sea: Mediterranean countries include Spain, France, Italy, Greece, Turkey and Egypt. 3) A Mediterranean climate has hot, dry summers and mild, wet winters, found around this sea and in places like California and parts of Australia.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons pupils locate the Mediterranean on maps, learn about its climate, tourist beaches and the plants that grow there (olives, grapes, lemons). In history lessons the ancient Egyptians, Greeks, Phoenicians and Romans all traded and fought across the Mediterranean; the Romans called it «our sea». In everyday life, a «Mediterranean diet» means lots of vegetables, fish, olive oil and grains. In news, people fleeing war sometimes cross it in dangerous small boats.
examples from the lessons: We went on holiday to a beach on the Mediterranean. | Italy sticks out into the Mediterranean Sea like a boot. | Olives grow well in the Mediterranean climate. | The Romans sailed all around the Mediterranean. | Perth has a Mediterranean climate. | Doctors say the Mediterranean diet is healthy. | Many refugees have tried to cross the Mediterranean in small boats.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always a capital M. Spelling trap: one «d», one «t» together with double «r»: «Med-i-ter-ran-e-an». Informal short form: «the Med». It is a sea, not an ocean, although it joins the Atlantic Ocean at Gibraltar.

part of speech: noun (informal: a mo = a moment; a mo = a moustache, Australia/NZ); name (Mo); abbreviation (MO, mo.)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal, UK) «A mo» means a moment, a very short time: «half a mo», «wait a mo». 2) (Australia, New Zealand, informal) A mo is a moustache; «Movember» is a November charity month when men grow moustaches. 3) (a name) Mo is a short name, for example for Mohammed, Maureen or Morris. 4) (abbreviation) «mo.» means month; «MO» can mean «modus operandi», a way of doing something, or a medical officer.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday British, Irish, Australian and New Zealand talk, «just a mo» is a common way of asking someone to wait. In Australia and New Zealand, «mo» is the everyday word for moustache. In sport, Mo Farah is a famous British runner and Mo Salah a famous footballer. In maths tables «mo.» can be short for months.
examples from the lessons: «Half a mo, I'm just getting my coat», said Mum. | Wait a mo — I've forgotten my lunch! | Dad grew a mo for charity. | Mo Farah won lots of running races. | My friend Mo is captain of the football team. | The phone plan costs ten pounds per mo. | «He's got a big bushy mo», said Grandpa.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal; in writing use «moment», «moustache» or «month». Plural «mos» (moustaches). Capital M for a name. Do not confuse with «mow» (cut grass) or «more».

meaning for a pupil: 1) An adverb is a word that tells us more about a verb — how, when, where or how often something happens — like «quickly», «yesterday», «here» or «often». 2) Adverbs can also describe adjectives or other adverbs: «very tall», «really slowly».
its sense in the lessons: In English grammar lessons pupils find adverbs, use them to make writing more precise and learn that many adverbs end in «-ly» (quick, quickly; happy, happily). Phrases: «adverb of manner» (how: slowly), «adverb of time» (when: soon), «adverb of place» (where: outside), «adverb of frequency» (how often: always, never), «fronted adverbial». In stories, adverbs like «suddenly» and «silently» build tension.
examples from the lessons: «Quickly» is an adverb in «She ran quickly». | Add an adverb to show how the giant walked: «heavily». | «Yesterday» is an adverb of time. | «Very» is an adverb in «very cold». | Many adverbs end in «-ly». | Suddenly, the lights went out. | «Always» and «never» are adverbs of frequency.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «adverbs»; «an adverb». Not every «-ly» word is an adverb: «friendly», «lovely», «lonely» are adjectives. Not every adverb ends in «-ly»: «fast», «well», «soon», «here». Trap: «good» is an adjective, «well» is the adverb — say «she sings well», not «she sings good».

part of speech: abbreviation (BA = Bachelor of Arts; British Airways); symbol (Ba = barium); Mandarin pinyin «bā» = eight, «ba» = suggestion particle; sheep sound «baa» — a fragment
meaning for a pupil: 1) (Mandarin, pinyin) «Bā» means «eight» in Mandarin; «ba» with no tone goes at the end of a sentence to make a suggestion: «wǒmen zǒu ba» means «let's go». 2) (abbreviation) A BA is a Bachelor of Arts, a first university degree. 3) (abbreviation) BA is short for British Airways, an airline. 4) (science) «Ba» is the chemical symbol for barium. 5) The sound a sheep makes is spelt «baa», not «ba».
its sense in the lessons: In Mandarin lessons pupils count «yī, èr, sān … bā» (one, two, three … eight); eight is a lucky number in Chinese culture because «bā» sounds like a word for getting rich. In science, «Ba» is on the periodic table; barium is used in hospitals to help X-rays show the stomach. On flights and luggage tags, «BA» means British Airways. In nursery rhymes, «Baa, baa, black sheep».
examples from the lessons: In Mandarin, «bā» means «eight». | «Wǒmen zǒu ba» means «let's go». | My aunt has a BA in English. | We flew to London with BA. | Ba is the symbol for barium. | Eight is a lucky number in China. | The sheep said «baa».
note for the reader of a maths problem: A fragment, not an English word. Read abbreviations as letters: «B-A». The sheep sound is spelt «baa». In pinyin, the tone mark matters: «bā» (eight) and «bà» (dad, as in «bàba») are different.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A chimpanzee is an intelligent ape with black hair, long arms and no tail, which lives in groups in the forests and grasslands of central and West Africa. 2) Chimpanzees, together with bonobos, are the closest living animal relatives of humans.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons chimpanzees come up in classification (great apes), evolution (humans and chimpanzees share a common ancestor and much of their DNA), tool use (sticks to fish for termites, stones to crack nuts) and conservation, as they are endangered. Jane Goodall is famous for her long study of wild chimpanzees in Tanzania. In everyday talk they are often called chimps.
examples from the lessons: Chimpanzees live in groups in African forests. | A chimpanzee used a stone to crack open a nut. | Chimpanzees share a lot of their DNA with humans. | Jane Goodall watched wild chimpanzees for many years. | Chimpanzees groom each other to stay friends. | Chimpanzees are apes, not monkeys. | The chimpanzee made a nest of leaves high in a tree.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «chimpanzees». Short informal form: «chimp». Say «chim-pan-ZEE». Myth: humans did not evolve from chimpanzees; both came from a shared ancestor long ago.

part of speech: noun (a grub, grubs — larva; grub — uncountable, slang: food); verb (grub, grubs, grubbed, grubbing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A grub is the young, worm-like form (larva) of some insects, especially beetles, which lives in soil or wood. 2) (informal, UK, Australia, NZ) Grub means food: «Grub's up!» means the meal is ready. 3) (verb) To grub means to dig or search about in the ground or in a messy place: «the pig grubbed for roots». 4) (Australia) A «witchetty grub» is a large grub eaten as traditional bush food by Aboriginal people.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons grubs come up in insect life cycles (egg, larva, pupa, adult) and food chains: birds, hedgehogs and badgers eat grubs. In everyday talk «grub» is cheerful slang for food, especially at camp or at home. In Australian lessons, witchetty grubs are part of bush tucker. The adjective «grubby» means dirty.
examples from the lessons: The bird pulled a fat grub out of the lawn. | A beetle grub lives in rotten wood. | «Grub's up!» called Dad from the kitchen. | The food at camp was good grub. | Witchetty grubs are a traditional Aboriginal bush food. | The hedgehog grubbed around in the leaves for insects. | A grub is the larva stage of a beetle.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «grubs» (insects). As «food» it is informal and uncountable: «some grub». Past «grubbed». «Grubby» (dirty) comes from it. A grub is a larva, not a worm, even though it looks wormy.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A mantis, often called a praying mantis, is a long green or brown insect that holds its spiky front legs together as if praying, and uses them to snatch other insects. 2) Mantises can turn their heads right round to look behind them.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons mantises come up in camouflage (some look like leaves, sticks or even flowers), predators and life cycles. Pupils sometimes keep them in class. The «praying» name comes from the way they fold their front legs. In martial arts there is a «mantis» style inspired by their quick strikes.
examples from the lessons: The praying mantis waited still on the leaf. | The mantis snatched a fly with its front legs. | A mantis can turn its head to look behind it. | Some mantises look just like pink flowers. | The mantis was so well camouflaged we almost missed it. | Baby mantises hatch from a foamy egg case. | It is called a praying mantis because of how it holds its legs.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «mantises» (also «mantids»). Spelling trap: «praying» (with folded legs), not «preying», although mantises do prey on insects — a nice pun to remember. Mantises are harmless to people.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A syllable is a part of a word that has one vowel sound; you can count syllables by clapping a word: «di-no-saur» has three syllables. 2) A word with one syllable, like «cat», is called a one-syllable word or monosyllable.
its sense in the lessons: In English and phonics lessons pupils clap and count syllables to help with reading and spelling long words. In poetry lessons syllables matter for rhythm: a haiku has three lines of five, seven and five syllables. Phrases: «stressed syllable» (the one said strongest: «TA-ble»), «not one syllable» (not a single word: «he didn't say a syllable»).
examples from the lessons: «Elephant» has three syllables: el-e-phant. | Clap the syllables in your name. | «Dog» has one syllable. | A haiku has five syllables in the first line. | In «banana», the middle syllable is stressed. | Break long words into syllables to spell them. | «Hippopotamus» has five syllables.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «syllables». Spelling: double «l», ending «-able». Count vowel sounds, not vowel letters: «cake» has one syllable even with two vowel letters. Do not confuse with «syllabus» (a list of topics for a course).

part of speech: noun (Congo, the Congo — proper noun: a river and two countries)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The Congo is a great river in central Africa, the second-longest in Africa and the deepest river in the world. 2) Congo is part of the names of two countries beside it: the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC, with capital Kinshasa) and the Republic of the Congo (capital Brazzaville). 3) The Congo Basin rainforest is the second-largest rainforest on Earth, after the Amazon.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons pupils locate the Congo River and rainforest, learn about the animals there (gorillas, bonobos, okapis, forest elephants) and the many peoples and languages. In history lessons pupils learn that the Congo was cruelly ruled by the Belgian king Leopold II, whose men forced people to collect rubber. In news, the DRC has long suffered wars, and its mines produce metals used in phones and batteries.
examples from the lessons: The Congo River flows through the rainforest. | The Congo is the deepest river in the world. | Bonobos live only in the Congo rainforest. | Kinshasa is the capital of the Democratic Republic of the Congo. | The Congo rainforest is second only to the Amazon in size. | Metals for phone batteries are mined in the Congo. | Two countries have «Congo» in their names.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always a capital C; usually «the Congo» for the river or region. Trap: there are two countries with «Congo» in the name; the bigger one is the DRC. The adjective is «Congolese». Do not confuse with «conga», a dance.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An anemone is a garden or wild flower with bright petals, often red, purple, pink or white, and a dark centre. 2) A sea anemone is a soft sea animal that looks like a flower; it sticks to rocks and catches food with stinging tentacles.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons sea anemones come up in rock pools and coral reefs: clownfish live safely among their tentacles in a partnership where both help each other. On beach trips pupils find anemones in rock pools; they pull their tentacles in and look like blobs of jelly when the tide is out. In gardens, anemones are spring and autumn flowers. The name comes from Greek for «daughter of the wind».
examples from the lessons: The clownfish hid among the anemone's tentacles. | We found red sea anemones in the rock pool. | A sea anemone is an animal, not a plant. | When the tide went out, the anemones looked like blobs of jelly. | Gran planted purple anemones in her garden. | Sea anemones sting small fish to catch them. | The anemone closed up when I touched it gently.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «anemones»; «an anemone». Say «uh-NEM-uh-nee» — it is a tricky word to say and spell. Trap: a sea anemone looks like a flower but is an animal, related to jellyfish and corals. Do not confuse with «enemy».

part of speech: preposition and pronoun (French «en» = in, to, of it); noun (an en, ens — printing: en dash); in phrases «en route», «en masse» — not an English word on its own
meaning for a pupil: 1) (French) «En» means «in» or «to» with countries and months, and «in» or «by» for ways of travelling: «en France» (in France), «en été» (in summer), «en bus» (by bus). 2) (French) «En» also means «some» or «of it»: «j'en veux» means «I want some». 3) English borrows French phrases: «en route» (on the way), «en masse» (all together in a big group). 4) (printing) An «en dash» (–) is a dash about the width of the letter n. To an English ear French «en» sounds like a nasal «on».
its sense in the lessons: In French lessons «en» comes with countries («je vais en Espagne» – I'm going to Spain), seasons and transport. English phrases with «en» appear in stories and news: «en route to school», «the fans arrived en masse». In English typing, the en dash is used in number ranges: «pages 4–9».
examples from the lessons: «J'habite en Angleterre» means «I live in England». | «En hiver» means «in winter». | We stopped for a snack en route to the beach. | The parents arrived en masse for the school play. | «Tu en veux?» means «do you want some?» | Use an en dash in ranges like «5–10». | French «en» sounds a bit like «on» said through the nose.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a word, French, not English, except in phrases like «en route» and «en masse». Do not confuse with the English ending «-en» (golden, wooden, broken) or with «an».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A sperm is a tiny male cell made by male animals and men; when a sperm joins with an egg cell from a female, a new baby animal or baby human can start to grow. 2) In plants, the male cells that join with egg cells are carried in pollen.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons sperm comes up in life cycles and reproduction: sperm and egg join (fertilisation), and the new living thing gets half its DNA from each parent. Fish and frogs often release eggs and sperm into water; in mammals, including humans, the baby grows inside the mother. Pupils learn this as respectful, plain science. The «sperm whale» is named after the waxy stuff in its head that people long ago wrongly thought was sperm.
examples from the lessons: A baby starts when a sperm and an egg join. | A sperm cell has a long tail to help it swim. | Half of your DNA came from the sperm and half from the egg. | Frogs release eggs and sperm into the pond. | Sperm are much too small to see without a microscope. | The sperm whale is the largest toothed whale.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «sperm» or «sperms»; «a sperm cell» is clear and polite. It is a proper science word, not a rude one. Trap: the sperm whale's name comes from an old mistake and has nothing to do with sperm cells.

part of speech: noun (a spike, spikes); verb (spike, spikes, spiked, spiking)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A spike is a thin, sharp point, like on a fence, a cactus or a hedgehog. 2) A spike is a sudden, sharp rise: «a spike in temperature». 3) (verb) To spike means to rise suddenly, or to stick a sharp point into something. 4) (verb, informal) To spike a drink means to secretly put alcohol or a drug in it, which is dangerous and against the law. 5) Spikes are running shoes with short metal points on the bottom for grip.
its sense in the lessons: In science and maths lessons, a spike on a graph is a sudden peak in the line (a spike in heart rate during exercise). In nature lessons cacti and some animals have spikes for protection. In safety lessons older pupils learn never to leave a drink unattended because someone could spike it. In sport, athletes wear spikes on the track. In volleyball, a spike is a hard downward hit.
examples from the lessons: The cactus is covered in sharp spikes. | The fence had spikes on top to stop people climbing. | There was a spike in the graph when we started running. | The temperature spiked in the afternoon. | Sprinters wear spikes for better grip. | She jumped and spiked the volleyball over the net. | Never leave your drink alone, in case someone spikes it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «spikes». Past «spiked». Adjective «spiky» (with points) — also used for hair and for a grumpy person. In graphs, a spike goes up and back down quickly; a steady climb is not a spike.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An adverbial is a word, phrase or clause that does the job of an adverb, telling us how, when, where or how often something happens: «in the morning», «after lunch», «with a smile». 2) A fronted adverbial is an adverbial placed at the start of a sentence, usually followed by a comma: «Later that day, we went home.»
its sense in the lessons: In English grammar lessons (especially in England), pupils learn to use fronted adverbials to vary how sentences start and to add a comma after them. Adverbials can be single words («Suddenly,»), phrases («Under the bridge,») or clauses («When the bell rang,»). The adjective «adverbial» describes anything that works like an adverb: «an adverbial phrase».
examples from the lessons: «After school» is an adverbial of time. | Start your sentence with a fronted adverbial. | «As quick as a flash, the fox ran off» begins with an adverbial. | Put a comma after a fronted adverbial. | «In the garden» is an adverbial of place. | «With great care, she lifted the egg» uses a fronted adverbial. | An adverbial can be one word or a whole phrase.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «adverbials». An adverb is one word; an adverbial can be a word, a phrase or a clause. Do not forget the comma after a fronted adverbial. Spelling: «ad-verb-ial».

meaning for a pupil: 1) The Vikings were seafaring people from Scandinavia (now Norway, Denmark and Sweden) who long ago sailed far in longships to raid, trade, explore and settle. 2) Viking means of or about the Vikings: «a Viking longship».
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons (especially in the UK and Ireland) pupils learn about Viking raids on monasteries like Lindisfarne, Viking settlements such as York (Jorvik) and Dublin, their gods (Odin, Thor, Loki), runes, sagas and long journeys to Iceland, Greenland and North America. Pupils also learn that most Vikings were farmers and traders, not only fighters. Words like «sky», «egg», «window» and «Thursday» came into English from the Vikings' language.
examples from the lessons: The Vikings sailed across the sea in longships. | Viking raiders attacked the monastery. | The Vikings founded the city of Dublin. | Thursday is named after the Viking god Thor. | Many Vikings were farmers and traders. | We wrote our names in Viking runes. | Viking explorers reached North America long before Columbus.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually a capital V. Myth: Vikings did not wear horned helmets in battle — that idea came from later artists and operas. «Viking» was really what they did (going raiding), not the name of one country.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A boar, or wild boar, is a wild pig with thick, bristly hair and sharp tusks, living in forests in Europe, Asia and North Africa. 2) A boar is also an adult male pig on a farm; the female is a sow. 3) The male of some other animals, like the guinea pig and badger, is also called a boar.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons boars come up in woodland habitats and food webs; they dig up the ground with their snouts looking for roots, nuts, insects and worms. In history and stories, boar hunting was a royal sport, and a boar's head was served at feasts. In some parts of Europe wild boars come into towns looking for food.
examples from the lessons: The wild boar dug in the forest floor with its snout. | A boar has sharp tusks. | The farmer has one boar and ten sows. | Wild boar piglets have stripes on their fur. | Keep away from wild boars; they can be dangerous. | In the old story, the hero hunted a giant boar. | Wild boars live in forests across Europe.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «boars». Homophone traps: «boar» (pig), «bore» (dull, or to make a hole) and «boor» (a rude person). Baby boars are «piglets»; striped wild boar piglets are sometimes called «humbugs» in the UK.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A coyote is a wild animal of the dog family, smaller than a wolf, with grey-brown fur, big ears and a bushy tail, found across North and Central America. 2) (US, slang) A coyote is also a person paid to smuggle people secretly across the border from Mexico into the USA.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons coyotes come up in North American habitats and adaptation: they live in deserts, prairies, forests and even big cities, and eat almost anything — mice, rabbits, fruit and rubbish. They are famous for howling and yipping at night. In Native American stories, Coyote is a clever trickster. In cartoons, Wile E. Coyote always chases the Road Runner and fails.
examples from the lessons: We heard coyotes howling in the desert at night. | Coyotes now live in many cities in North America. | The coyote hunted mice in the field. | A coyote is smaller than a wolf. | In Native American tales, Coyote is a trickster. | In the cartoon, the coyote never catches the Road Runner. | Keep small pets inside at night if coyotes live nearby.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «coyotes». Said «ky-OH-tee» or «KY-ote». Coyotes live only in the Americas; in Australia the wild dog is the dingo, in Africa the jackal. The smuggler meaning is slang.

part of speech: noun (a python, pythons; Python — a programming language)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A python is a large snake that is not venomous and kills its prey by wrapping round it and squeezing; pythons live in Africa, Asia and Australia. 2) Python (with a capital P) is a popular programming language, easy to read, used in schools and by scientists and companies.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons pythons come up in reptiles and predators: they squeeze prey and swallow it whole, then may not eat again for weeks. In Australian lessons, carpet pythons sometimes live in roofs. In computing lessons pupils move from Scratch to Python to write real text code. The language was named after a British comedy show, not after the snake.
examples from the lessons: The python wrapped itself around its prey. | Pythons are not venomous; they squeeze. | A python can swallow an animal bigger than its head. | We found a carpet python in the shed! | In computing, we wrote our first program in Python. | Python code uses indentation to show blocks. | The reticulated python is one of the longest snakes in the world.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «pythons». Capital P for the language. Trap: pythons live in Africa, Asia and Australia; the similar big snakes of the Americas are boas and anacondas. Pythons squeeze to stop breathing and blood flow, not to crush bones.

part of speech: noun (a yak, yaks); verb (informal: yak, yaks, yakked, yakking — to chatter)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A yak is a large, long-haired wild or farm ox that lives in the high, cold mountains of Tibet, the Himalayas and Central Asia. 2) (informal) To yak means to chat or talk on and on about unimportant things.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and science lessons yaks come up in mountain habitats and adaptations: long thick hair, big lungs and a strong heart for thin air. People in the Himalayas use yaks to carry loads, and get milk, butter, meat, wool and dung for fuel from them. In everyday informal talk, «stop yakking» means stop chattering.
examples from the lessons: Yaks carry heavy loads up the mountain paths. | A yak's long hair keeps it warm in the snow. | People in Tibet drink yak butter tea. | The yak herders lived in tents high in the mountains. | Stop yakking and finish your work! | The two friends yakked on the phone for an hour. | Dried yak dung is burned for heat.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «yaks». The verb is informal; past «yakked», «-ing» form «yakking» (double k). Do not confuse with «yuck» (disgusting).

meaning for a pupil: 1) The Mongols are the people of Mongolia and nearby lands in Central and East Asia, traditionally herders who moved with their animals and lived in round felt tents called gers or yurts. 2) (history) Mongol describes the huge empire built by Genghis Khan and his family, the largest joined land empire in history, stretching from China to Eastern Europe.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons pupils learn about Genghis Khan and Kublai Khan, Mongol horse riders and archers, the Silk Road trade they protected, and the attacks on cities such as Kyiv. In geography lessons pupils learn that Mongolia today is a country between Russia and China with grasslands called steppes. Phrases: «Mongol Empire», «Mongol horsemen».
examples from the lessons: Genghis Khan united the Mongol tribes. | The Mongol Empire stretched across Asia and into Europe. | Mongol riders could shoot arrows while galloping. | The Mongols attacked and burned Kyiv. | Many Mongol families still live in round tents called gers. | Kublai Khan was a Mongol ruler of China. | Marco Polo travelled to the court of the Mongol emperor.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital M. «Mongol» is for the people and their history; «Mongolian» is the usual adjective for today's country and language. Warning: an old use of this word with a small m as an insult for people with Down's syndrome is very offensive — never use it that way.
