meaning for a pupil: 1) A snout is the long nose and mouth part that sticks out at the front of some animals' faces, such as pigs, dogs, crocodiles and anteaters. 2) (informal, joking or rude) A snout can mean a person's nose.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons snouts come up in adaptations: a pig's snout digs for food, an anteater's long snout reaches into ant nests, a crocodile's snout shape shows what it eats. In stories and descriptions «snout» helps describe an animal's face. «To have your snout in the trough» (UK, informal) means to be greedy for money or rewards.
examples from the lessons: The pig dug in the mud with its snout. | The anteater pushed its long snout into the ant nest. | The dog sniffed the ground with its wet snout. | A crocodile's snout is long and narrow. | The hedgehog's snout twitched as it smelled a worm. | «Keep your snout out of my business!» snapped the troll.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «snouts». Countable. Calling a person's nose a snout is rude or jokey. Similar words: «muzzle» (a dog's nose and mouth), «beak» (birds), «trunk» (elephants).

part of speech: interjection (UK dialect «ee», Northern England); Scots «ee» = eye (plural «een»); company name (EE); letters «ee» in spelling — a fragment
meaning for a pupil: 1) (UK, Northern England dialect) «Ee!» is a cry of surprise or feeling, like «oh!»: «Ee, it's cold!»; also «ee by gum». 2) (Scots) «Ee» means eye; the old plural is «een». 3) (spelling) «ee» is a common letter pair making the long «ee» sound, as in «tree», «sheep», «green». 4) (a name) EE is a British mobile phone company.
its sense in the lessons: In phonics lessons pupils learn «ee» as a digraph (two letters, one sound): «see», «feet», «bee». In stories set in Yorkshire, Lancashire or the North East of England, characters say «Ee!» or «Ee, lad». In Scots poems and songs, «ee» means eye. In everyday life, EE is a phone network.
examples from the lessons: «Ee, it's grand to see you!» said Grandma from Yorkshire. | «Ee by gum!» is an old Northern English way of saying «my goodness!». | The letters «ee» make the sound in «sheep». | «Bee», «tree» and «free» all have «ee». | In the Scots poem, «ee» means eye. | My mum's phone is on EE.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Not a standard English word on its own; it is dialect, a spelling pattern or a company name. In writing use «oh» or «eye». The long «ee» sound can also be spelt «ea» (sea), «e» (me), «ie» (field) or «y» (happy).

part of speech: noun (an ottoman, ottomans — furniture; the Ottomans); adjective (Ottoman)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (history) The Ottoman Empire was a large, long-lasting empire ruled by Turkish sultans from Istanbul, covering Turkey and lands in south-east Europe, the Middle East and North Africa. 2) Ottoman means of or about that empire; «the Ottomans» are its rulers and people. 3) An ottoman (small o) is a low, padded seat or footstool, often with a lid and storage space inside.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons pupils learn about the Ottomans capturing Constantinople (renaming it Istanbul), the sultans, the Topkapı Palace, coffee houses, and the empire's end after the First World War, when modern Turkey and other countries were formed. In everyday life an ottoman is a piece of furniture in a living room or bedroom.
examples from the lessons: The Ottoman Empire was ruled by sultans. | The Ottomans made Istanbul their capital. | Ottoman armies once reached Vienna. | The Ottoman Empire ended after the First World War. | Put your feet up on the ottoman. | We keep the spare blankets inside the ottoman. | Ottoman palaces were decorated with beautiful tiles.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital O for the empire and people; small o for the furniture. Plural «ottomans». The name comes from Osman, the founder of the ruling family.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A reindeer is a deer of the cold Arctic and northern lands, with thick fur and large branched antlers; in North America wild reindeer are called caribou. 2) In Christmas stories, reindeer pull Santa's flying sleigh, led by Rudolph with his red nose.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons reindeer come up in Arctic adaptations: thick fur, wide hooves that work like snowshoes and help dig for lichen under snow, and eyes that change colour between summer and winter. Both males and females grow antlers. In geography lessons pupils learn that the Sámi people of northern Norway, Sweden, Finland and Russia herd reindeer. At Christmas, reindeer are in songs, cards and stories.
examples from the lessons: The reindeer dug in the snow to find lichen. | Both male and female reindeer have antlers. | In North America, wild reindeer are called caribou. | Rudolph the reindeer has a shiny red nose. | The Sámi people herd reindeer. | Reindeer have wide hooves that help them walk on snow. | We saw a herd of reindeer on our trip to Lapland.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural is the same: «one reindeer, two reindeer» (not «reindeers»). Spelling trap: «rein-», like the reins of a horse, not «rain». In maths word problems «reindeer» can be one or many — read the number word.

part of speech: noun (a spiral, spirals); adjective (spiral); verb (spiral, spirals, spiralled/spiraled, spiralling/spiraling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A spiral is a curve that winds round and round a centre point, getting further away or closer each time, like the shape of a snail shell. 2) A spiral is also a shape that winds upward like a spring or a corkscrew: «a spiral staircase». 3) (verb) To spiral means to move in a spiral, or to get quickly worse or bigger: «prices spiralled». 4) (figurative) «A downward spiral» is when things keep getting worse.
its sense in the lessons: In maths lessons spirals come up in patterns and shapes, and in nature studies in snail shells, sunflower seeds, pine cones and galaxies (our Milky Way is a spiral galaxy). In science, DNA is a double spiral (double helix). In art, pupils draw spirals. In everyday talk «spiral notebook» is a notebook bound with a wire coil. In news, «spiralling costs» means costs going up fast.
examples from the lessons: A snail's shell is a spiral. | We climbed the spiral staircase to the top of the tower. | The Milky Way is a spiral galaxy. | The leaf spiralled down to the ground. | Sunflower seeds grow in spirals. | Write it in your spiral notebook. | Prices spiralled when there was not enough food.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «spirals». UK spelling «spiralled, spiralling»; US «spiraled, spiraling». A circle comes back to where it started; a spiral does not.

part of speech: noun (a titan, titans; Titan — a moon, the Titans in myth)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (myth) The Titans were giant, powerful gods in Greek myths who ruled before Zeus and the Olympian gods defeated them. 2) A titan is a person or thing that is very big, strong or important: «a titan of industry». 3) (science) Titan is the largest moon of the planet Saturn, the only moon with a thick atmosphere.
its sense in the lessons: In history and myth lessons pupils read about the Titans, such as Cronus, Atlas (who held up the sky) and Prometheus (who gave fire to humans). In science lessons Titan is studied as a moon with lakes of liquid methane. The ship Titanic was named for its huge size. In sports news, a match between two great teams is a «clash of the titans».
examples from the lessons: In Greek myths, the Titans fought the Olympian gods. | Atlas was a Titan who held up the sky. | Titan is Saturn's largest moon. | Titan has lakes of liquid methane. | She was a titan of science. | The final was a clash of the titans. | The Titanic was named after the Titans because it was so big.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «titans». Capital T for the myth figures and the moon. Adjective «titanic» (huge). The metal titanium is also named after the Titans.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To evolve means to change slowly, over a very long time and many generations, as living things adapt to their surroundings: «whales evolved from land animals». 2) To evolve also means to develop or change gradually into something more complex or better: «the plan evolved over time». 3) (games) In some games, a character evolves into a new, stronger form.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons «evolve» comes in evolution and inheritance: pupils learn about Charles Darwin, natural selection (living things best suited to their environment survive and have more young), fossils as evidence, and Darwin's finches. In everyday life, languages, ideas, technology and towns evolve. In Pokémon and other games, «evolve» is used loosely for a sudden change, which is different from real evolution.
examples from the lessons: Birds evolved from dinosaurs. | Living things evolve over millions of years. | Darwin explained how animals evolve by natural selection. | Giraffes with longer necks could reach more food, so the species evolved. | The English language keeps evolving. | Our project evolved from a small idea into a big show. | My game character evolved into a dragon.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past «evolved». Noun «evolution». Trap: one animal does not evolve in its lifetime; a species evolves over many generations. Myth: humans did not evolve from monkeys we see today; we share ancestors. Some people believe God created life; Christians hold different views on how creation and evolution fit together.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A falcon is a fast bird of prey with long pointed wings and a hooked beak that catches other birds and small animals. 2) The peregrine falcon is the fastest animal on Earth when it dives through the air.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons falcons come up in food chains, adaptations (sharp eyesight, curved talons, streamlined bodies) and conservation: peregrine falcons nearly died out because of pesticides and have since come back, and now even nest on city skyscrapers and cathedrals. In history lessons, falconry was a sport of kings and nobles, training falcons to hunt. Falcons are also national symbols for some countries.
examples from the lessons: The peregrine falcon dived at amazing speed. | Falcons have sharp talons to catch their prey. | A falcon nests on the tower of our cathedral. | In the Middle Ages, nobles hunted with trained falcons. | The falcon hovered and then swooped down. | Falcons can see a mouse from high in the sky. | We watched the falcon show at the castle.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «falcons». Say «FAL-kun» or «FAWL-kun». Falcons, hawks and eagles are all birds of prey but different groups. «Falconry» is training falcons to hunt; «falconer» is the person.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A spacecraft is a vehicle built to travel in space, with or without people on board, such as a rocket capsule, a space probe, a satellite or a space station. 2) Spacecraft can carry astronauts, explore other planets or orbit the Earth to send back pictures and signals.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons spacecraft come up in space and forces: rockets push spacecraft up against gravity, and once in orbit they keep falling around the Earth. Pupils learn about Apollo spacecraft landing on the Moon, robot rovers on Mars, the Voyager probes leaving the Solar System, and the International Space Station. In stories, spacecraft are often called spaceships.
examples from the lessons: The spacecraft blasted off from the launch pad. | A robot spacecraft landed on Mars. | The astronauts lived on the spacecraft for six months. | Voyager is a spacecraft that has left our Solar System. | Satellites are spacecraft that orbit the Earth. | Two spacecraft docked with the space station. | The spacecraft sent back photos of Jupiter.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural is the same: «one spacecraft, two spacecraft» (not «spacecrafts»). One word. «Spaceship» is the everyday or story word; «spacecraft» is the science word.

part of speech: noun (rouge — uncountable); adjective (French «rouge» = red); verb (rouge — rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (French) «Rouge» means «red» in French: «une pomme rouge» is «a red apple». 2) Rouge is red or pink make-up powder or cream put on the cheeks, now usually called «blusher» or «blush». 3) In the game of roulette, «rouge» means red. To an English ear it sounds like «roozh».
its sense in the lessons: In French lessons «rouge» is one of the colours learnt early, with «bleu», «vert», «jaune» and «noir». In English the make-up meaning is old-fashioned. In history and place names, «Moulin Rouge» (red windmill) is a famous Paris theatre; «Baton Rouge» (red stick) is a city in the USA. In French, colour words usually come after the noun.
examples from the lessons: In French, «rouge» means «red». | «Le drapeau est bleu, blanc et rouge» means «the flag is blue, white and red». | Grandma put a little rouge on her cheeks. | The actor's cheeks were painted with rouge. | Baton Rouge is a city in Louisiana. | «Rouge» sounds like «roozh». | In French we say «un crayon rouge» — the colour goes after the noun.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As «red», French, not English. As make-up it is an English word, uncountable: «some rouge». Do not confuse with «rogue» (a dishonest or naughty person) — the letters are swapped.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A microbe is a living thing too small to see without a microscope, such as a bacterium, a virus or some fungi like yeast. 2) Some microbes cause diseases, but most are harmless and many are useful, helping us digest food, making bread rise and breaking down dead things.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons microbes come up in health and hygiene (washing hands removes harmful microbes, vaccines help the body fight them), food (yeast in bread, bacteria in yogurt and cheese) and decomposition (microbes rot leaves and food). Pupils learn about Louis Pasteur and Alexander Fleming, who found penicillin, a medicine made from a mould that kills bacteria. «Microbe» is the same as «micro-organism» or the everyday word «germ».
examples from the lessons: Microbes are too small to see with your eyes. | Wash your hands to get rid of harmful microbes. | Yeast is a microbe that makes bread rise. | Microbes in the soil break down dead leaves. | Some microbes make us ill, but many help us. | Your stomach is full of helpful microbes. | Louis Pasteur showed that microbes spoil food.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «microbes». Say «MY-krohb». «Germ» usually means a harmful microbe. Trap: antibiotics kill bacteria but do not work against viruses like a cold.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An orca, also called a killer whale, is a large black-and-white sea mammal with a tall back fin; it is actually the biggest member of the dolphin family. 2) Orcas live and hunt in family groups called pods in all the world's oceans, especially cold ones.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons orcas come up in ocean food chains (top predator — they eat fish, seals, penguins and even whales), mammals (they breathe air through a blowhole and feed their young milk) and communication: each pod has its own calls, like a family language. In conservation lessons, pupils learn about pollution and noise in the sea and debates about keeping orcas in marine parks.
examples from the lessons: The orca is the largest kind of dolphin. | Orcas hunt together in pods. | An orca breathes through a blowhole on its head. | We saw an orca's tall black fin from the boat. | Orcas sometimes slide onto beaches to catch seals. | Each orca pod has its own calls. | Another name for the orca is the killer whale.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «orcas»; «an orca». Trap: despite the name «killer whale», an orca is a dolphin, and wild orcas are not known to have killed people. Orcas are mammals, not fish.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A caiman is a reptile of the alligator family that lives in the rivers, lakes and swamps of Central and South America. 2) Caimans have long jaws, tough scaly skin and are usually smaller than alligators and crocodiles, although the black caiman can grow very large.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography lessons caimans come up in Amazon rainforest and wetland habitats and food chains: they eat fish, birds and small mammals, and are hunted by jaguars and anacondas. Pupils compare crocodiles, alligators and caimans: caimans have a bony ridge between their eyes, like the frame of glasses (the spectacled caiman).
examples from the lessons: A caiman floated in the river with only its eyes showing. | Caimans live in South America. | The jaguar caught a caiman on the riverbank. | The spectacled caiman has a ridge between its eyes like glasses. | A caiman is a relative of the alligator. | Caimans lay their eggs in nests of leaves. | The black caiman is the biggest caiman.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «caimans». Also spelt «cayman», as in the Cayman Islands. Say «KAY-mun». Crocodiles, alligators and caimans are related but different reptiles.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The dodo was a large, plump bird that could not fly and lived only on the island of Mauritius in the Indian Ocean; it became extinct after sailors arrived and hunted it, and brought animals that ate its eggs. 2) «As dead as a dodo» means completely gone or finished. 3) (informal) A dodo can mean an old-fashioned or silly person.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons the dodo is the most famous example of extinction caused by humans: it had no natural predators, so it was not afraid of people. Pupils learn how island animals are at risk and why conservation matters. In stories, a Dodo appears in «Alice's Adventures in Wonderland». In everyday talk, «dead as a dodo» means something has totally ended.
examples from the lessons: The dodo lived only on the island of Mauritius. | The dodo could not fly. | Dodos became extinct soon after sailors arrived. | The dodo was not afraid of people, so it was easy to catch. | A Dodo runs a race in «Alice in Wonderland». | That old game is as dead as a dodo. | We saw a model of a dodo in the museum.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «dodos» or «dodoes». Myth: the dodo was not stupid or clumsy; it just had never met dangerous animals. It was a kind of pigeon, a very large one.

part of speech: abbreviation (Fr, Fr., fr — a fragment, not a word)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (church) «Fr» or «Fr.» is short for «Father», the title of a Catholic, Orthodox or Anglican priest: «Fr. Michael». 2) (abbreviation) «Fr» can be short for «French» or «France», and «fr» for French on language menus and web addresses ending «.fr». 3) (slang, texting) «fr» means «for real»: «that's funny fr». 4) (science) «Fr» is the chemical symbol for francium, a rare element. 5) (money) «Fr» was short for «franc», old French money; Swiss francs are still used.
its sense in the lessons: In church life, priests are written «Fr.» before their name in parish newsletters. In online chat, teenagers write «fr» or «fr fr» to mean «for real», «honestly». In computing, «fr» is the language code for French. In science, «Fr» is on the periodic table.
examples from the lessons: Fr. Patrick said Mass on Sunday. | «That's so true fr», she texted. | French websites often end in «.fr». | On the language menu, «fr» means French. | Fr is the symbol for francium. | Write to Fr. Brown at the parish office.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A fragment or abbreviation, not an English word. Read it out in full: «Father», «French» or «for real». The slang «fr» is informal and only for chat.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To inhabit a place means to live in it: «polar bears inhabit the Arctic». 2) (formal) To inhabit can also mean to be present in something: «strange creatures inhabit her stories».
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography lessons «inhabit» is used for where living things and people live: «Which animals inhabit the rainforest?». Related words are «inhabitant» (a person or animal that lives somewhere), «habitat» (the natural home of a living thing) and «uninhabited» (with nobody living there: «an uninhabited island»). In maths and geography, «the town has ten thousand inhabitants» gives its population.
examples from the lessons: Penguins inhabit the cold seas of the southern hemisphere. | Which animals inhabit a pond? | People have inhabited this valley for thousands of years. | The island is not inhabited. | Bats inhabit the old church tower. | The town has twenty thousand inhabitants. | Many creatures inhabit the deep ocean.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past «inhabited». It takes an object directly: «inhabit the forest», not «inhabit in the forest». Trap: «inhabited» means lived in, and «uninhabited» means not lived in — but «inhabitable» and «habitable» both mean fit to live in (here «in-» does not mean «not»). Formal; in everyday talk say «live in».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Plankton are tiny plants and animals that drift in the sea and in lakes, carried by the water; most are too small to see without a microscope. 2) Plant plankton (phytoplankton) make food from sunlight and produce a large share of the oxygen we breathe; animal plankton (zooplankton) include tiny shrimps and baby fish.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons plankton come at the start of ocean food chains: plankton are eaten by small fish and krill, which are eaten by bigger fish, seals and penguins — and the biggest animal of all, the blue whale, eats mostly tiny krill. In environment lessons pupils learn that warming and polluted seas harm plankton. In a famous cartoon, Plankton is a tiny villain.
examples from the lessons: Plankton float in the ocean. | Many whales feed on tiny plankton and krill. | Plankton are at the bottom of the ocean food chain. | Phytoplankton make oxygen from sunlight. | We looked at plankton under the microscope. | The sea glowed at night because of special plankton. | Small fish eat plankton, and bigger fish eat the small fish.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable in everyday use: «plankton», not «a plankton»; it can take a plural verb («plankton are») or singular («plankton is»). Plankton are not one species but many tiny living things. The word comes from Greek for «drifting».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A sac is a small bag-like part inside a plant or animal, often filled with liquid or air, like an egg sac or an ink sac. 2) (science) In a spider, an egg sac is a silk bag holding its eggs; in a squid or octopus, the ink sac squirts dark ink to escape enemies.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons «sac» comes up in life cycles (spider egg sacs, frogspawn), animal defences (the octopus ink sac), the human body (air sacs in the lungs, called alveoli) and plant seeds. It is a science word; in everyday talk people say «bag» or «pouch».
examples from the lessons: The spider guarded its egg sac. | The octopus squirted ink from its ink sac. | Our lungs have millions of tiny air sacs. | Frogs puff up a vocal sac to croak. | The baby spiders hatched from the egg sac. | A bee's sting has a venom sac.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «sacs». Homophone trap: «sac» (a bag in a body) and «sack» (a large bag; or to fire someone from a job). Science writing uses «sac».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A simile is a way of describing something by comparing it to something else using «like» or «as»: «as brave as a lion», «she ran like the wind». 2) Similes help the reader picture something more clearly or feel it more strongly.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons pupils find and write similes in descriptive writing and poetry, and compare them with metaphors. Common similes: «as cold as ice», «as busy as a bee», «as light as a feather», «like a fish out of water». In stories a good fresh simile is better than a tired one.
examples from the lessons: «As white as snow» is a simile. | «He ate like a horse» is a simile using «like». | Write a simile to describe the storm. | «Her eyes shone like stars» is a simile. | A simile uses «like» or «as»; a metaphor does not. | «The classroom was as quiet as a mouse» is a simile. | Try to invent new similes instead of using old ones.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «similes». Say «SIM-ih-lee» (three syllables). Trap: a simile says something is «like» something else; a metaphor says it «is» that thing: «He was a lion in battle» is a metaphor. Not every sentence with «like» is a simile: «I like cake» is not.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A pronoun is a word used instead of a noun, so we don't have to repeat it, like «he», «she», «it», «they», «we», «you» and «I». 2) Possessive pronouns show who something belongs to: «mine», «yours», «hers», «ours», «theirs». 3) Relative pronouns like «who», «which» and «that» join extra information to a noun: «the girl who won».
its sense in the lessons: In English grammar lessons pupils replace nouns with pronouns to avoid repetition, and make sure it is clear who the pronoun means. Phrases: «personal pronoun», «possessive pronoun», «relative pronoun», «reflexive pronoun» («myself», «themselves»). In everyday life some people tell others which pronouns to use for them, such as «she/her», «he/him» or «they/them», and it is kind to use them.
examples from the lessons: «She» is a pronoun in «She is my sister». | Replace «the dog» with a pronoun: «It barked». | «Mine» is a possessive pronoun. | «Who» is a relative pronoun in «the boy who laughed». | «Myself» is a reflexive pronoun. | Too many pronouns can confuse the reader about who is who. | «They» can be used for one person whose gender you don't know.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «pronouns». Traps: «its» (no apostrophe) is the possessive; «it's» means «it is». Use «I» as a subject and «me» as an object: «Sam and I went», «he gave it to Sam and me». «Their», «there» and «they're» sound the same but mean different things.

part of speech: noun (an alkali, alkalis or alkalies); adjective form: alkaline
meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) An alkali is a chemical that is the opposite of an acid; it can cancel out an acid. 2) (science) An alkali dissolves in water and makes a solution with a pH above 7. 3) Strong alkalis, like some oven cleaners, can burn skin and eyes, just like strong acids.
its sense in the lessons: In school science the word comes with acids, pH, indicators and neutralisation: acid + alkali makes a salt and water. Litmus paper turns blue in an alkali, and universal indicator turns blue or purple. In everyday life alkalis are in soap, toothpaste, baking soda and indigestion tablets. Safety: cleaning products with alkalis carry warning signs; wear goggles and gloves. Phrases: «acids and alkalis», «a strong alkali», «a weak alkali», «alkaline batteries».
examples from the lessons: Soap is a mild alkali, so it feels slippery. | We tested the liquids to see which were acids and which were alkalis. | Litmus paper turns blue in an alkali. | An alkali can neutralise an acid. | Indigestion tablets contain a weak alkali that calms stomach acid. | The oven cleaner is a strong alkali, so Mum wears rubber gloves. | Toothpaste is slightly alkaline. | Bicarbonate of soda makes an alkaline solution in water.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «alkalis» (also «alkalies»); the adjective is «alkaline» (alkaline batteries, alkaline soil). Pronounced AL-ka-lie. Trap: an alkali is not «safe» just because it is not an acid; strong alkalis are dangerous too. A base is the wider word; an alkali is a base that dissolves in water. pH 7 is neutral, below 7 acid, above 7 alkali.

part of speech: noun (a humpback, humpbacks); adjective (humpback whale, humpback bridge); also humpbacked (adjective)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A humpback, or humpback whale, is a very large whale with long flippers that is famous for its songs and its leaps out of the water. 2) A humpback bridge is a small bridge that rises steeply in the middle like a hump. 3) (old-fashioned, can be unkind) A humpback was an old word for a person with a curved, bent-over back; today we say a person has a curved spine.
its sense in the lessons: Mostly met in nature lessons and stories about the sea: humpbacks migrate thousands of kilometres, eat krill through baleen plates and sing long songs. Whale watching in Australia, New Zealand, Canada and Ireland often shows humpbacks breaching. In the UK countryside you see road signs for a «humpback bridge». In old fairy tales the word may describe a character; modern writers avoid it as rude. Phrases: «humpback whale», «humpback bridge», «a pod of humpbacks».
examples from the lessons: A humpback leapt right out of the sea and crashed back down. | Humpback whales sing songs that can last for hours. | We saw three humpbacks on the whale-watching trip in Sydney. | Humpbacks have no teeth; they filter krill through baleen. | The car slowed down for the humpback bridge. | A baby humpback is called a calf. | Humpbacks travel to warm waters to have their calves. | The humpback slapped its long white flipper on the water.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «humpbacks». Usually a compound: «humpback whale» (also «humpbacked whale»). Using «humpback» for a person is old and hurtful; say «a person with a curved back». Not to be confused with «hunchback», an old word with the same meaning for people.

part of speech: noun (a variety, varieties; countable and uncountable)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Variety means having many different kinds of things, not all the same: a menu with variety has lots of choices. 2) A variety of things is a number of different kinds of them: «a variety of fruit». 3) A variety is one particular type of something, especially a type of plant or animal: «a new variety of apple». 4) Variety, or a variety show, is entertainment made of many short acts like songs, jokes and magic.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life it praises change and choice: «variety is the spice of life». In science it names a type within a species, like apple varieties. In maths and data, «a variety of» just means several different ones; it gives no exact number. Stories use it to show a busy, colourful scene. Phrases: «a wide variety of», «a variety of reasons», «for variety», «variety show», «variety pack».
examples from the lessons: The school canteen has a good variety of lunches. | Granny grows ten varieties of tomato. | We read a variety of books this term, from comics to poems. | For variety, we had pasta instead of rice. | The talent show was a variety show with singers, dancers and a juggler. | Variety is the spice of life, so let's try something new. | The shop sells a wide variety of pens. | Penguins come in many varieties, from tiny blue ones to huge emperors.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «varieties» (change y to ies). «A variety of + plural noun» usually takes a plural verb: «A variety of birds live here». Adjective: «various» (different kinds); verb: «vary». Trap: «a variety of» does not tell how many in a maths problem; it only says they are different kinds.

part of speech: noun (amber, uncountable for the stone; an amber light); adjective (amber, an amber colour)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Amber is a hard, see-through, golden-yellow stone that formed from the sticky sap of ancient trees over millions of years. 2) Amber is a warm orange-yellow colour, like honey. 3) (UK, Ireland, Australia) The amber light is the middle traffic light between red and green that means «get ready to stop». 4) (UK) An amber warning is a medium-level weather warning: be prepared, take care.
its sense in the lessons: In science and history, amber is famous because insects and plant bits were trapped inside it and preserved as fossils. In road safety lessons, amber means slow down and stop if it is safe; Americans usually call it the yellow light. In weather news, red is the highest warning and amber is the one below. Phrases: «trapped in amber», «amber light», «amber warning», «amber eyes».
examples from the lessons: This piece of amber has a tiny fly trapped inside. | The lights turned amber, so Dad slowed down. | There is an amber warning for heavy snow tomorrow. | Her eyes were a warm amber colour. | Amber is fossilised tree resin, not a real stone made of minerals. | The street lamps gave off an amber glow. | On a pedestrian crossing, a flashing amber light means you may cross with care. | Scientists found a feather from a dinosaur in amber.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable as a material («made of amber»); countable as a light or warning. In the USA the traffic light is usually called «yellow». Myth: in films dinosaurs are cloned from blood in amber mosquitoes; scientists say that cannot really be done because DNA breaks down. Amber is also a girl's name (a name).

part of speech: adverb (Scottish and Northern English: na); short form in casual speech; chemical symbol Na; also a fragment of words like «gonna», «wanna»
meaning for a pupil: 1) (Scotland, Northern England) «Na» means «no» or «not»: «I'm na going». 2) (slang, informal) «Na» or «nah» is a casual way to say «no»: «Na, I'm fine». 3) (science) Na is the chemical symbol for sodium, a soft silvery metal found in salt; it comes from its Latin name, natrium. 4) As a fragment, «na» is the end of words like «gonna» (going to) and «wanna» (want to). 5) (Mandarin, pinyin) «nà» means «that», and «ná» means «to take»; these are not English words.
its sense in the lessons: In chats and stories «na/nah» shows a relaxed, friendly «no». In Scottish stories and songs «na» or «nae» means «not». In science, Na appears in the periodic table and in salt: NaCl is sodium chloride, table salt. If you see «na» after «gon» or «wan» it is clipped speech. Also «N/A» means «not applicable» on forms – a different thing.
examples from the lessons: «Want a biscuit?» «Na, I'm full, thanks.» | Nah, I don't think it'll rain. | «I'm na feart,» said the Scottish lad, meaning «I'm not afraid». | Na is the symbol for sodium on the periodic table. | Table salt is NaCl: one sodium (Na) and one chlorine (Cl). | I'm gon-na be late! | In Mandarin, «nà ge» means «that one». | Write N/A in the box if the question does not apply to you.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly spoken or informal; in careful writing use «no» or «not». The symbol Na always has a capital N and small a. Do not confuse with «nay» (an old word for «no», also used when voting) or «neigh» (the sound a horse makes). «N/A» on forms means «not applicable» or «not available».

part of speech: noun (nous, uncountable; UK, Ireland, Australia, informal); also French pronoun (nous)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (UK, Ireland, Australia, informal) Nous means common sense and practical cleverness: knowing what to do in real life. 2) (philosophy) In old Greek thinking, nous meant the mind or reason. 3) (French) «Nous» is the French word for «we» or «us»; it sounds like «noo» and is not an English word.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday British and Australian talk, someone with nous is sensible and quick to work things out: «He had the nous to call for help». It rhymes with «house» in English (NOWSS). In French lessons «nous» is the «we» form: «nous sommes» = we are, «nous avons» = we have. Phrases: «a bit of nous», «business nous», «the nous to…».
examples from the lessons: Use a bit of nous and take a coat — it's freezing! | She had the nous to write the number plate down. | That footballer has real football nous. | The little lad showed great nous by finding his way home. | In French, «nous sommes amis» means «we are friends». | «Nous» in French sounds like «noo», with a silent s. | Ancient Greek thinkers said nous was the part of us that understands.
note for the reader of a maths problem: English «nous» is uncountable: «a bit of nous», never «nouses». It is informal and not used much in the USA. Trap: the English word rhymes with «house», but the French «nous» sounds like «noo»; they mean different things (common sense vs we).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A roadrunner is a fast bird of the deserts of the south-western USA and Mexico that prefers to run rather than fly. 2) The Road Runner is a cartoon bird who always escapes from a hungry coyote (a name of a character).
its sense in the lessons: In nature lessons about deserts the roadrunner shows how animals adapt: it can run about 30 km per hour, eats lizards, snakes and insects, and is a kind of cuckoo. Children also know it from the old «Road Runner» cartoons, where it says «meep meep». Phrases: «greater roadrunner», «as fast as a roadrunner».
examples from the lessons: A roadrunner dashed across the desert road in front of our car. | Roadrunners can catch and eat small rattlesnakes. | The roadrunner is the state bird of New Mexico. | It can fly, but it would rather run. | In the cartoon, the coyote never catches the Road Runner. | Roadrunners sunbathe in the morning to warm up after cold desert nights. | Our class drew a desert food chain with a roadrunner in it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «roadrunners». Written as one word (also «road runner»). The cartoon name is usually «Road Runner» with capitals. Myth: real roadrunners do not say «meep meep»; they make cooing and clattering sounds.

part of speech: French pronoun and determiner (ce, cet, cette, ces); English abbreviation CE
meaning for a pupil: 1) (French) «Ce» means «this» or «that» or «it»: «ce livre» = this book, «c'est» = it is. It sounds like «suh» and is not an English word. 2) (abbreviation) CE stands for «Common Era», used with years instead of AD; BCE means «Before the Common Era». 3) (abbreviation) A CE mark on toys and electrical goods shows they meet European safety rules.
its sense in the lessons: In French lessons «ce» comes in «c'est» (it is), «qu'est-ce que c'est?» (what is it?) and «ce matin» (this morning). In history lessons CE and BCE mark years on timelines. On toys and chargers, look for the CE mark (in the UK also UKCA) as a sign of a safety check.
examples from the lessons: In French, «c'est mon chien» means «it's my dog». | «Ce garçon» means «this boy». | «Qu'est-ce que c'est?» means «What is it?» | The Romans left Britain in the fifth century CE. | BCE years count down towards year 1 CE. | Check the toy box for a CE safety mark. | French uses «ce» before a masculine noun and «cette» before a feminine one.
note for the reader of a maths problem: French «ce» changes: «cet» before a vowel (cet arbre), «cette» for feminine (cette fille), «ces» for plural. «C'est» is «ce + est». CE and BCE are written in capitals and mean the same years as AD and BC. Not an English word on its own.

part of speech: noun (a mole, moles); also unit «mole» (science, mol)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A mole is a small, furry animal with tiny eyes and big front paws that digs tunnels underground and eats worms. 2) A mole is a small dark spot on someone's skin. 3) A mole is a spy who works secretly inside an organisation and passes on its secrets. 4) (science) In chemistry, a mole is a unit for counting a huge number of tiny particles, used by older students. 5) A mole is also a stone wall built out into the sea to protect a harbour.
its sense in the lessons: In nature lessons moles show life underground: they are almost blind, feel with their noses and leave molehills on lawns. In health lessons, a mole on the skin that changes shape, colour or size should be shown to a doctor; wear sun cream. In spy stories, «the mole» is the traitor inside. Phrases: «make a mountain out of a molehill» (make a small problem seem huge), «blind as a mole», «whack-a-mole».
examples from the lessons: A mole dug a tunnel under our lawn and left little hills of soil. | Moles eat earthworms and can store them for later. | Grandad has a mole on his cheek. | If a mole on your skin changes, show it to a doctor. | In the spy film, there was a mole inside the secret service. | Don't make a mountain out of a molehill — it's only a scratch. | A mole's big paws are like shovels. | The fishing boats sheltered behind the mole in the harbour.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «moles». A mole's heap of earth is a «molehill». Trap: the animal and the skin spot are the same spelling but not connected. «Mole» (Mexican sauce, said MO-lay) is another word. Moles are not completely blind, but they see very little.

part of speech: noun (a stegosaurus, stegosauruses; scientists also write Stegosaurus as a genus name)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A stegosaurus was a large plant-eating dinosaur with two rows of big bony plates along its back and sharp spikes on its tail. 2) The name means «roof lizard» because people once thought its plates lay flat like roof tiles.
its sense in the lessons: In lessons about dinosaurs and fossils, stegosaurus is a favourite example: it lived in the Jurassic period, walked on four legs, had a tiny brain for its big body, and used its spiked tail (called a thagomizer) to defend itself. It lived long before Tyrannosaurus rex, so they never met. Phrases: «a stegosaurus skeleton», «back plates», «tail spikes».
examples from the lessons: The stegosaurus had plates on its back and spikes on its tail. | Stegosaurus ate ferns and low plants. | We saw a stegosaurus skeleton at the Natural History Museum. | A stegosaurus was as long as a bus. | Its brain was surprisingly small, about the size of a dog's. | The plates may have helped it warm up or show off to other stegosauruses. | My little brother's favourite dinosaur toy is a green stegosaurus.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «stegosauruses» (sometimes «stegosauri»). As a scientific name it is written with a capital: Stegosaurus. Say STEG-uh-SORE-us. Myth: it did not have a second brain in its hip. Trap: stegosaurus and T. rex lived millions of years apart; more time separates them than separates T. rex from us.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Feedback is information or comments about how well you have done something, so you can do it better next time. 2) Feedback is what customers or users tell a company or a game maker about what they liked or disliked. 3) Feedback is a loud, high whistling noise when a microphone picks up the sound coming out of its own speaker. 4) (science) In a system, feedback is when the result of something goes back and changes what happens next.
its sense in the lessons: At school teachers give feedback on writing, often as «two stars and a wish» or «what went well, even better if». Pupils give peer feedback to each other: kind, specific and helpful. In everyday life apps ask for feedback with stars or a smiley face. In assemblies, the microphone may squeal with feedback. Phrases: «give feedback», «get feedback», «positive feedback», «constructive feedback», «feedback form».
examples from the lessons: My teacher's feedback said my story had a great opening. | Give your partner kind and useful feedback on their poster. | The shop asked us to fill in a feedback form. | Positive feedback made Leo feel proud. | The microphone made a terrible screech of feedback. | Use the feedback to improve your next draft. | The game makers read players' feedback and fixed the bug. | Your body gives you feedback: when you are tired, you yawn.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: say «some feedback» or «a piece of feedback», not «a feedback» or «feedbacks». Feedback can be good or bad; good feedback still points to next steps. «Constructive feedback» means criticism meant to help.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A flytrap, or Venus flytrap, is a plant whose leaves snap shut like jaws to catch flies and other insects, which it then digests. 2) A flytrap can also be any device that catches flies, like a sticky strip. 3) (slang, humorous) «Flytrap» can jokingly mean a person's open mouth.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons the Venus flytrap is an example of a carnivorous plant: it grows in poor, boggy soil, so it gets extra nutrients from insects. Tiny trigger hairs inside the leaf must be touched twice quickly before it closes. It grows wild only in a small area of North and South Carolina in the USA. Phrases: «Venus flytrap», «snap shut», «carnivorous plant».
examples from the lessons: The Venus flytrap snapped shut on the fly. | Flytraps catch insects because their soil has few nutrients. | Don't poke the flytrap with your finger — it wastes its energy. | Our class grew a flytrap on the windowsill. | The trap reopens after about a week once the insect is digested. | Dad hung a sticky flytrap in the kitchen. | «Shut your flytrap!» said the cartoon pirate rudely.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «flytraps». Usually written «Venus flytrap» with a capital V (named after the goddess Venus). Myth: flytraps do not eat people or large animals; they catch small insects and spiders. Flytraps still make food from sunlight like other plants.

part of speech: noun (a peregrine, peregrines); adjective (peregrine, formal, old = wandering)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A peregrine, or peregrine falcon, is a bird of prey that dives at amazing speed to catch other birds in the air. 2) (formal, old) Peregrine means travelling or wandering from place to place. 3) Peregrine is also a boy's name (a name).
its sense in the lessons: In nature lessons the peregrine falcon is called the fastest animal on Earth: in a dive (a stoop) it can go over 300 km per hour. It is found almost all over the world and nests on cliffs, and also on tall buildings and cathedrals in cities. It nearly died out because of pesticides like DDT, and recovered after they were banned — a conservation success story. Phrases: «peregrine falcon», «in a dive», «bird of prey».
examples from the lessons: A peregrine falcon nests on top of the city cathedral. | The peregrine dived out of the sky and caught a pigeon. | Peregrines are the fastest animals on Earth when they dive. | We watched the peregrine chicks on a webcam. | The word «peregrine» comes from Latin for «a traveller from abroad». | Peregrines nearly died out, but now they are back in many cities. | A female peregrine is bigger than the male.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «peregrines». Often just «peregrine» for the falcon. Trap: the cheetah is the fastest land animal, but the peregrine is the fastest when diving; in level flight other birds can be faster. The related word «pilgrim» comes from the same Latin root.

part of speech: verb (tamp, tamps, tamped, tamping); usually «tamp down»
meaning for a pupil: 1) To tamp something means to press or pat it down firmly so it is packed tight, such as soil around a plant or coffee in a machine. 2) (formal) To tamp down something like feelings or rumours means to try to calm it or reduce it.
its sense in the lessons: In gardening, after planting a seedling you tamp down the soil gently so the plant stands firm. Builders tamp down gravel or concrete. In cafés a barista tamps the coffee. In news writing, «to tamp down fears» means to calm worries. Phrases: «tamp down», «tamp the soil», «tamp it firm».
examples from the lessons: Tamp the soil down around the bean plant with your fingers. | The builder tamped the gravel flat before laying the slabs. | The barista tamped the coffee into the little metal cup. | Grandad tamped the tobacco into his old pipe. | The head teacher tried to tamp down the rumours about the closure. | After filling the hole, we tamped it down with our boots.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: tamped, tamping. Usually with «down». Not to be confused with «stamp» (to bring your foot down hard) or «tamper» (to interfere with something secretly), though a tool for tamping is called a «tamper».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Gender is being a boy or a girl, a man or a woman, especially the roles and ideas people and societies connect with that; some people feel they are both, neither, or not the gender they were thought to be at birth. 2) (grammar) In languages like French, German and Spanish, gender is the group a noun belongs to, such as masculine or feminine, which changes words like «the» and «a». 3) On forms, gender is a box asking whether you are male, female or something else.
its sense in the lessons: In PSHE and relationships lessons, gender comes up when talking about fairness and stereotypes: any gender can like football, dancing, science or cooking. People and countries hold different views about gender identity; lessons ask pupils to be kind and respectful to everyone. In French lessons, «le» is masculine and «la» feminine; grammatical gender often has nothing to do with real boys and girls (a table is feminine in French). In English, gender shows in «he, she, his, her». Phrases: «gender stereotypes», «gender equality», «gender pay gap», «masculine/feminine gender».
examples from the lessons: Any gender can be a scientist or a nurse. | Our class talked about gender stereotypes in toy adverts. | In French, every noun has a gender: «le livre», «la table». | The form asked for my name, age and gender. | Gender equality means girls and boys get the same chances. | In German there are three genders: masculine, feminine and neuter. | Some people say gender and sex mean the same; others use gender for roles and identity.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable when naming kinds (two genders in French), uncountable for the idea. Trap: grammatical gender (le/la) is about words, not about living things. People disagree about how to use the word «gender»; schools teach respect for others either way. «Sex» is the biological word.

part of speech: noun (an Inca, the Incas); adjective (Inca, Incan); usually written with a capital I
meaning for a pupil: 1) The Incas were a people of the Andes mountains in South America who built a huge empire with its capital at Cusco, in today's Peru. 2) The Inca was also the title of their emperor, the ruler of the empire. 3) Inca or Incan describes things from this people and empire: Inca roads, Inca gold.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons the Incas are studied as a great civilization of the Americas: they built Machu Picchu, about 40,000 km of roads with rope bridges, and stone walls so exact that a knife blade cannot fit between the stones. They kept records with knotted strings called quipu, grew potatoes on terraces, and spoke Quechua, which millions still speak. Spanish conquerors led by Francisco Pizarro defeated the empire. Phrases: «the Inca Empire», «the Inca Trail», «Inca gold».
examples from the lessons: The Incas built Machu Picchu high in the Andes. | Inca runners carried messages along stone roads. | The Inca ruled from the city of Cusco. | The Incas recorded numbers with knots on strings called quipu. | Spanish soldiers came looking for Inca gold. | Inca farmers grew hundreds of kinds of potato. | Walkers hike the Inca Trail to reach Machu Picchu.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Write it with a capital: Inca, Incas. Adjective: «Inca» or «Incan». Trap: do not mix up the Incas (Peru, Andes) with the Aztecs (Mexico) and the Maya (Central America). The Incas had no written alphabet as we know it; quipu stored numbers and information.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A flamingo is a tall wading bird with long thin legs, a long bendy neck, pink feathers and a curved beak, that lives in big groups by lakes and lagoons. 2) A plastic flamingo is a pink garden ornament, a joke symbol of fancy American gardens.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons flamingos show how diet changes the body: they are pink because of the pink-coloured food they eat, like tiny shrimps and algae. They feed with their heads upside down, filtering water through their beaks. They often stand on one leg. A group is sometimes called a «flamboyance» of flamingos. Phrases: «stand on one leg like a flamingo», «a flock of flamingos», «pink as a flamingo».
examples from the lessons: A flamingo stood on one leg in the shallow lake. | Flamingos are pink because of the shrimps and algae they eat. | A flock of flamingos flew over the salt lake. | Flamingo chicks are grey and fluffy at first. | The flamingo fed with its head upside down. | We did a balance challenge: stand like a flamingo for one minute! | A group of flamingos can be called a flamboyance.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «flamingos» (also «flamingoes»). Myth: flamingos are not born pink; they turn pink from their food. Scientists are still studying why they stand on one leg; saving body heat and saving energy are two ideas.

part of speech: noun (folk, folks — plural meaning people); adjective (folk music, folk tale)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Folk means people, especially ordinary people: «country folk», «old folk». 2) (informal) Your folks are your parents or family: «my folks». 3) (informal) «Folks» is a friendly way to speak to a group of people: «Hi, folks!» 4) Folk, or folk music, is traditional music of a place, passed down by ordinary people, or modern songs in that style. 5) Folk describes old customs and stories of ordinary people: a folk tale, folk dance.
its sense in the lessons: In English and history lessons folk tales and folk songs are stories and songs passed down by word of mouth, often with no known author, like Jack and the Beanstalk. In music lessons you might dance a folk dance or sing a folk song. In everyday talk «folks» is warm and friendly; «that's all, folks» ends cartoons. Phrases: «folk tale», «folk song», «folk dance», «old folk», «country folk», «ordinary folk».
examples from the lessons: We read a Russian folk tale about a clever girl and a witch. | The old folk in the village remembered the big storm. | My folks are picking me up after school. | «Right, folks, line up please!» said the coach. | Granny loves Irish folk music with fiddles and pipes. | We learned a folk dance from Scotland. | Kind folk helped us push the car. | Many folk tales begin «Once upon a time».
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Folk» is already plural in meaning: «these folk are kind» (not «folks are» in formal writing, though «folks» is common in speech, especially in the USA). The l is silent: say «foke». Folklore = traditional stories and beliefs of a people.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A piranha is a South American river fish with very sharp, triangle-shaped teeth that eats meat as well as plants and fruit. 2) (informal) A piranha can describe a fierce, greedy person who attacks others to get what they want.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography lessons about the Amazon river, piranhas show food chains: they eat fish, insects, seeds and dead animals, and are eaten by river dolphins, caimans and birds. They swim in groups. Films show them as man-eaters, but real attacks on people are rare and usually just bites. Phrases: «a shoal of piranhas», «razor-sharp teeth», «a feeding frenzy».
examples from the lessons: Piranhas live in the Amazon River. | A piranha's teeth fit together like scissors. | The fishermen pulled a piranha out of the river. | Piranhas usually swim in shoals for safety. | Some piranhas eat mostly seeds and fruit. | In the film the piranhas ate everything in seconds, but that is not true to life. | The reporters were like piranhas, all shouting questions at once.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «piranhas». Say pi-RAH-na (some say pi-RAN-ya). Myth: piranhas do not usually strip people to the bone; that idea comes from films and old stories.

part of speech: noun (punctuation, uncountable); verb related: punctuate (punctuates, punctuated)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Punctuation is the set of marks we use in writing, such as full stops, commas, question marks and apostrophes, to make the meaning clear and show where to pause. 2) Punctuation is also the way you use these marks: «Check your punctuation».
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons, punctuation is taught with grammar and spelling (GPS, SPaG): capital letters and full stops, commas in lists, question and exclamation marks, apostrophes for missing letters and possession, speech marks (inverted commas), brackets, dashes, colons, semicolons and hyphens. Good punctuation helps the reader: «Let's eat, Grandma!» vs «Let's eat Grandma!» Phrases: «punctuation marks», «check your punctuation», «correct punctuation».
examples from the lessons: Remember your punctuation: capital letter at the start, full stop at the end. | A question mark is a punctuation mark. | Commas save lives: «Let's eat, Grandma!» | My teacher said my punctuation in speech was excellent. | Use speech marks around the words a character says. | The test had ten punctuation questions. | Without punctuation, the sentence was hard to read. | Americans call a full stop a «period».
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «good punctuation», not «punctuations»; for one mark say «a punctuation mark». In the USA: period (full stop), quotation marks (speech marks). Common traps: «its» (belonging) vs «it's» (it is); no apostrophe in simple plurals (apples, not apple's).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A squad is a small group of people who work or train together, especially a sports team or a group of soldiers or police. 2) A squad is the full group of players a coach can choose a team from. 3) (slang) Your squad is your group of close friends: «me and my squad».
its sense in the lessons: In PE and sport, the school football squad trains together and the coach picks the team from the squad. In news and police stories: «the bomb squad», «the drugs squad», «a firing squad». In slang, «squad goals» means a friend group to admire. Phrases: «the school squad», «make the squad», «squad training», «bomb squad», «flying squad».
examples from the lessons: I made the netball squad this year! | The coach named an eighteen-player squad for the final. | Squad training is on Tuesday after school. | The bomb squad made the old shell safe. | A squad of soldiers marched past. | Me and my squad are going to the park. | The whole squad cheered when Amira scored.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: «a squad, two squads». In British English a squad can take a plural verb: «the squad are training». A squad is usually bigger than a team on the pitch: the team is the players who actually play. Slang sense is informal.

part of speech: noun (a vampire, vampires); also vampire bat
meaning for a pupil: 1) In stories and legends, a vampire is a dead person who rises from the grave at night and drinks the blood of living people. 2) A vampire bat is a real small bat from Central and South America that feeds on the blood of animals. 3) (informal) A vampire can be a person or thing that drains your energy, time or money: «energy vampire».
its sense in the lessons: Vampires appear in spooky stories, Halloween costumes and films; the most famous is Count Dracula, from a book by Bram Stoker. In folk tales vampires fear garlic, sunlight and crosses, and have no reflection — these are made-up beliefs. In science, vampire bats make tiny cuts and lap the blood; they hardly ever bite people. Phrases: «vampire bat», «vampire fangs», «energy vampire».
examples from the lessons: In the story, the vampire only came out at night. | My brother dressed up as a vampire with plastic fangs for Halloween. | Count Dracula is the most famous vampire. | Vampire bats lick up blood from sleeping cows. | Old stories say vampires are scared of garlic. | Phone chargers left plugged in are «energy vampires». | Vampires are not real; they are a legend.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «vampires». Vampires are made-up; vampire bats are real. Trap: vampire bats do not suck blood; they lap it like a cat drinking milk. The word came into English from Slavic languages through German.

part of speech: verb (conquer, conquers, conquered, conquering); nouns: conqueror, conquest
meaning for a pupil: 1) To conquer a country or people means to take control of them by fighting. 2) To conquer a problem or a fear means to deal with it successfully and beat it. 3) To conquer a mountain means to climb to the top of it. 4) To conquer a place can also mean to become very popular there: «The band conquered America».
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons: the Romans conquered much of Britain, the Normans conquered England, the Spanish conquered the Aztecs and Incas — history shows both the winners and the people who lost their land. In personal stories and PSHE: «conquer your fears», like learning to swim. Phrases: «divide and conquer» (split enemies or a big problem into parts), «conquer a fear», «William the Conqueror», «the conquest of…».
examples from the lessons: The Romans conquered most of Britain. | William the Conqueror won the Battle of Hastings. | Maya finally conquered her fear of the dark. | They conquered the mountain in three days. | The Spanish conquered the Aztec Empire. | Divide and conquer: break the big problem into small steps. | Her song conquered the charts all over the world.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: conquered (one r before -ed). Spelling trap: «qu» after «con», and the ending is «-er» (conquer), not «-or»; but the person is a «conqueror» (-or). Say KONG-ker.

part of speech: noun (a jay, jays); also the letter J (jay); also a name (Jay)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A jay is a noisy, colourful bird of the crow family; the Eurasian jay is pinkish brown with bright blue wing patches, and the blue jay of North America is blue and white. 2) «Jay» is how we say and sometimes write the letter J. 3) Jay is also a name (a name).
its sense in the lessons: In nature lessons jays are famous for burying acorns to eat in winter; the forgotten ones grow into oak trees, so jays help plant forests. Their loud screech warns other animals of danger. In North America, the blue jay is a common garden bird. Phrases: «blue jay», «a jay's screech».
examples from the lessons: A jay buried acorns all over the park. | The jay screeched loudly when the cat came near. | Blue jays visited our bird feeder in Toronto. | Jays are clever members of the crow family. | Forgotten acorns hidden by jays grow into new oak trees. | «Jay» is the name of the letter J. | My cousin Jay plays the drums.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «jays». Capital J for the name. Trap: in old American slang «jaywalk» means to cross the road carelessly away from a crossing; that word came from «jay» meaning a silly country person.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A llama is a South American animal like a small camel without a hump, with a long neck and thick woolly coat, kept for carrying loads and for its wool. 2) (Buddhism) A different word, lama (one l), means a Buddhist teacher, like the Dalai Lama.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons about the Andes, llamas carry goods on mountain paths, as they did for the Incas; their wool, meat and dung (as fuel) are useful. Llamas live in herds and may spit when annoyed. Cousins: alpacas (smaller, woollier), guanacos and vicuñas. Phrases: «a herd of llamas», «llama trekking».
examples from the lessons: Llamas carried our bags up the mountain path in Peru. | A llama spat at the farmer when he got too close. | Llamas are related to camels. | The Incas used llamas as pack animals. | Some farms in Britain keep llamas to protect sheep from foxes. | An alpaca is smaller and fluffier than a llama. | We went llama trekking on our holiday.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «llamas». Spelling: double l at the start. Trap: «lama» (one l) is a Buddhist monk or teacher; «llama» is the animal. In Spanish «ll» sounds like «y», so some people say YAH-ma, but English speakers usually say LAH-ma.

part of speech: noun (a mangrove, mangroves; mangrove swamp, mangrove forest)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A mangrove is a tree or shrub that grows in salty water along tropical coasts, with tangled roots that stand above the mud. 2) A mangrove, or mangrove swamp or forest, is an area of coast covered with these trees.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and science lessons mangroves are an important habitat: their roots shelter baby fish, crabs and birds, hold the mud together, protect coasts from storms and tsunamis, and store a lot of carbon. They grow in places like northern Australia, Florida, Indonesia and Bangladesh (the Sundarbans, home of Bengal tigers). Mangroves are being cut down for shrimp farms and building, so people work to protect and replant them. Phrases: «mangrove swamp», «mangrove forest», «mangrove roots».
examples from the lessons: Mangroves can grow in salty sea water. | Baby fish hide among the mangrove roots. | We walked on a boardwalk through the mangroves in Queensland. | Mangrove forests protect the coast from big waves. | Tigers live in the mangrove swamps of the Sundarbans. | Mangroves store lots of carbon in their mud. | Volunteers planted new mangroves along the shore.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «mangroves». Usually countable: «a mangrove», «the mangroves». Mangrove roots that stick up out of the mud help the tree breathe; they are sometimes called breathing roots.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A vulture is a large bird with a bald or nearly bald head that eats the meat of dead animals. 2) (informal) A vulture is a person who waits to take advantage of someone else's trouble or bad luck.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons vultures are scavengers: they clean up dead animals, which stops diseases spreading, so they are important in food chains. They soar high on warm air currents and find food by sight or smell. Many vulture species are in danger because of poison. In stories and news, «like vultures» describes people crowding round to grab something. Phrases: «circling like vultures», «culture vulture» (someone who loves arts, joking).
examples from the lessons: Vultures circled high over the savannah. | A vulture's bald head stays clean when it feeds. | Vultures are nature's clean-up crew. | Without vultures, dead animals would spread disease. | The condor is a kind of New World vulture. | As soon as the shop closed, buyers came like vultures for the cheap stock. | My aunt is a real culture vulture — she visits every museum.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «vultures». Spelling: vul-ture. Trap: vultures rarely kill animals; they mostly eat ones already dead. Old-world vultures (Africa, Europe, Asia) and new-world vultures (Americas) look alike but are not close relatives.

part of speech: noun (baleen, uncountable; baleen plates); adjective (baleen whale)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Baleen is a strong, bendy material growing in long plates from the top jaw of some whales, used like a giant sieve or comb to filter food from sea water. 2) A baleen whale is a whale that has baleen instead of teeth, like the blue whale and the humpback.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, baleen whales take in a huge mouthful of water and push it out through the baleen, trapping krill and small fish. Baleen is made of keratin, the same stuff as our fingernails and hair. In history, people hunted whales for baleen (called «whalebone») to make corsets and umbrella ribs. Phrases: «baleen whale», «baleen plates», «filter feeder».
examples from the lessons: Blue whales are baleen whales. | Baleen is made of the same material as our fingernails. | The whale strained krill through its baleen. | We touched a strip of baleen at the museum; it felt like a stiff hairbrush. | Toothed whales, like dolphins, have no baleen. | In the past, baleen was used to make corsets. | A humpback has hundreds of baleen plates.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable as the material: «baleen», «a plate of baleen». Say ba-LEEN. Trap: old word «whalebone» meant baleen, though baleen is not bone.

part of speech: noun (a bog, bogs); verb (bog down, bogs down, bogged down, bogging down); adjective (boggy)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A bog is an area of soft, wet, spongy ground, often with moss and peat, where your feet can sink. 2) (UK, Ireland, Australia, slang) The bog is the toilet: «I need the bog». 3) To get bogged down means to get stuck in mud, or to get stuck in too many details so you cannot move on. 4) (Australia, slang) To bog in means to start eating hungrily or to start work with energy.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and science, bogs are wetlands: peat bogs store huge amounts of carbon and have preserved old things, even «bog bodies» thousands of years old. Ireland has many bogs where people cut turf (peat) for fires. Safety: keep to paths, as bogs can be deep. In everyday British talk, «bog roll» means toilet paper and «bog-standard» means ordinary. Phrases: «peat bog», «bogged down», «bog-standard», «bog roll».
examples from the lessons: The path crossed a wide, wet bog. | Grandad's boots sank into the bog up to his ankles. | Irish bogs are made of peat that took thousands of years to form. | Can I go to the bog, sir? (slang) | We got bogged down in the mud on the way to the farm. | Don't get bogged down in one hard question — move on and come back. | It's just a bog-standard phone, nothing special. | Dinner's ready — bog in! (Australia)
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: «a bog, bogs». «Bog» for toilet is slang and not polite in class; say «toilet» or «loo». «Bog-standard» is informal UK. The verb is almost always «bog down» or «get bogged down».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A piglet is a baby pig. 2) Piglet is the small, shy pink pig in the Winnie-the-Pooh stories (a name of a character).
its sense in the lessons: In farm and science lessons piglets show life cycles and young animals: a mother pig (sow) can have about 10 piglets in one litter, and they drink her milk. In stories, Piglet is Pooh's anxious but brave friend. Phrases: «a litter of piglets», «the runt of the litter» (the smallest piglet).
examples from the lessons: The sow had twelve piglets. | The piglets squealed as they ran to their mother. | A litter of piglets slept in the straw. | The smallest piglet is called the runt. | Piglet held Pooh's paw on the windy day. | Piglets drink their mother's milk for a few weeks. | We fed the piglets at the city farm.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «piglets». The «-let» ending means small (like booklet, droplet). Animal family: boar (male), sow (female), piglet (baby). Capital P for the Pooh character.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A meteorite is a piece of rock or metal from space that has fallen through the air and landed on the Earth's surface.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about space, three words are taught together: a meteoroid is a small rock travelling in space; a meteor is the streak of light («shooting star») when it burns in our air; a meteorite is the piece that reaches the ground. Many meteorites are older than the Earth itself. A giant one hit the Earth about 66 million years ago and helped wipe out the dinosaurs. Meteorites are often heavy because they contain iron. Phrases: «meteorite impact», «meteorite crater», «iron meteorite».
examples from the lessons: The museum has a meteorite you can touch. | A meteorite made this huge crater in Arizona. | Most meteorites land in the sea, because most of Earth is water. | Scientists found meteorites on the ice in Antarctica. | The meteorite was heavy because it was made mostly of iron. | A meteor that reaches the ground becomes a meteorite. | Some meteorites came from Mars or the Moon.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «meteorites». Trap: meteor (the flash in the sky) vs meteorite (the rock on the ground) vs meteoroid (rock in space); the «-ite» ending is like «rock». Myth: most meteorites are cool or just warm when they land, not red hot.

part of speech: adjective (Norse); noun (the Norse, Old Norse); written with a capital N
meaning for a pupil: 1) Norse describes the people of old Scandinavia (Norway, Denmark, Sweden, Iceland) in the time of the Vikings, and their language, gods and stories. 2) Old Norse is the language the Vikings spoke. 3) The Norse are the people of that time.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons the Norse are the Vikings and their families: farmers, traders, raiders and explorers who reached Britain, Ireland, Iceland, Greenland and even North America. Norse myths tell of gods like Odin, Thor and Loki, the world tree Yggdrasil, and Valhalla. Many English words come from Old Norse, like «sky», «egg», «knife» and «Thursday» (Thor's day). Phrases: «Norse myths», «Norse gods», «Old Norse».
examples from the lessons: Thor is a Norse god of thunder. | We read Norse myths about Odin and Loki. | The Vikings spoke Old Norse. | Norse sailors reached North America long before Columbus. | «Sky» and «egg» came into English from Old Norse. | The Norse believed in a great tree joining nine worlds. | Dublin was founded as a Norse town.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always a capital N. Mostly an adjective: «Norse myths». «Norse» and «Viking» are close but not the same: «Viking» often means the raiders and traders, «Norse» the whole people and culture. Trap: Vikings did not wear horned helmets; that is a myth from later art and opera.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A numeral is a symbol or group of symbols that stands for a number, like 7 or VII. 2) (grammar) A numeral is a word for a number, like «seven» or «seventh».
its sense in the lessons: In maths lessons numerals are how we write numbers: we use Hindu-Arabic numerals (0–9), and pupils also learn Roman numerals (I, V, X, L, C, D, M) seen on clocks, in book chapters and after kings' names (Henry VIII). Phrases: «Roman numerals», «Arabic numerals», «write in numerals» (use digits, not words).
examples from the lessons: Write the number in numerals, not words. | The clock face has Roman numerals. | XIV is the Roman numeral for fourteen. | Our numerals 0 to 9 came to Europe from India through Arab mathematicians. | The Romans had no numeral for zero. | Henry VIII uses the Roman numeral for eight. | «12» is a numeral, «twelve» is a word.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «numerals». A numeral is the written symbol; a number is the amount or value itself; a digit is one single symbol from 0 to 9. So «25» is a numeral made of two digits. Roman numerals: I=1, V=5, X=10, L=50, C=100, D=500, M=1000; a smaller one before a bigger one is taken away (IV=4, IX=9).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A teat is the small, soft part on a female mammal's body that her babies suck to get milk; cows, goats and pigs have teats. 2) A teat is the rubber or plastic top of a baby's bottle that the baby sucks.
its sense in the lessons: In science and farm lessons, teats are how mammals feed their young with milk: a cow is milked from her four teats, piglets each find a teat on the sow. At home, a baby's bottle has a teat. Phrases: «the cow's teats», «bottle teat».
examples from the lessons: The calf drank milk from its mother's teat. | A cow has four teats on her udder. | The farmer milked the goat's teats by hand. | Each piglet found a teat and started to drink. | Mum boiled the bottle teats to keep them clean. | The baby lamb would not take the teat, so we fed it with a syringe.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «teats». Say «teet». It is a normal science and farm word, not rude. In some places people say «nipple» for the human body part and for a bottle teat (USA: «nipple» for bottle). Trap: «teat» is not «treat» or «tit» (a small bird).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A woodpecker is a bird that clings to tree trunks and hammers into the wood with its strong, sharp beak to find insects and to make nest holes.
its sense in the lessons: In nature lessons woodpeckers show adaptations: a strong beak like a chisel, a thick skull that protects the brain, stiff tail feathers to lean on, and a very long sticky tongue to pull out grubs. They also drum on trees to talk to other woodpeckers. In Britain you may see the great spotted woodpecker and the green woodpecker. Phrases: «drumming», «peck holes», «great spotted woodpecker».
examples from the lessons: We heard a woodpecker drumming on the oak tree. | The woodpecker pecked a hole for its nest. | A woodpecker's tongue is long enough to wrap round its skull. | The green woodpecker hops on lawns to eat ants. | Woodpeckers do not get headaches because of their special skulls. | Woody Woodpecker is a cartoon bird. | The woodpecker held on to the trunk with its stiff tail.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «woodpeckers». One word: wood + pecker. There are no woodpeckers in Australia, New Zealand or Madagascar. The drumming is mostly a signal, not feeding.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Canny means clever and careful, especially with money or in business; hard to trick: «a canny shopper». 2) (North-East England, Scotland, informal) Canny means nice, good or pretty: «a canny lass», «it's canny cold». 3) (Scotland) «Ca' canny» means be careful, go gently.
its sense in the lessons: In stories a canny character is shrewd, sensible and quick to spot a trick. In Newcastle and around (Geordie speech), «canny» is an everyday word of praise, and also means «quite»: «canny good» = quite good. Phrases: «a canny move», «canny with money», «canny good» (Geordie).
examples from the lessons: The canny fox did not fall into the trap. | Gran is canny with money and always finds a bargain. | That was a canny move, swapping your queen for two rooks! | «He's a canny lad,» said the man from Newcastle, meaning a nice boy. | It's canny windy today! (Geordie) | The canny shopkeeper raised his prices before the holiday.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative «cannier», superlative «canniest». Opposite: «uncanny» actually means strange and spooky, not «not clever»: an uncanny likeness = a strangely close likeness. Regional senses are informal.

part of speech: noun (a dumpling, dumplings; the input form is the plural)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Dumplings are small balls of dough cooked in boiling water, soup or stew. 2) Dumplings are also little parcels of thin dough with a filling of meat, vegetables or fruit, steamed, boiled or fried, as in Chinese jiaozi, Polish pierogi or Ukrainian varenyky. 3) (informal) «Dumpling» is a fond pet name for a small, chubby child.
its sense in the lessons: Dumplings show how many cultures have similar foods: British suet dumplings in stew, Chinese dumplings at Lunar New Year (said to look like old gold money and bring luck), Japanese gyoza, Ukrainian varenyky with potato or cherries, Jewish kreplach. In cooking lessons pupils may fold dumplings. Phrases: «stew and dumplings», «steamed dumplings», «apple dumplings».
examples from the lessons: Mum made beef stew with fluffy dumplings. | We folded dumplings for Chinese New Year. | Varenyky are Ukrainian dumplings with potato or cherries inside. | The dumplings floated to the top when they were cooked. | We had steamed dumplings at the dim sum restaurant. | Grandma calls the baby her little dumpling. | Each dumpling had a juicy filling.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Singular «dumpling», plural «dumplings». Countable. The word is common in recipes and menus. In Chinese, «jiaozi» and «baozi» are different: baozi are bigger, fluffy buns.

part of speech: verb (gnaw, gnaws, gnawed, gnawing); usually «gnaw at», «gnaw on», «gnaw through»
meaning for a pupil: 1) To gnaw means to bite or chew something again and again, especially something hard, like a dog with a bone or a mouse with wood. 2) If a worry or a feeling gnaws at you, it keeps bothering you for a long time.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, rodents (rats, mice, beavers, squirrels) gnaw because their front teeth never stop growing; gnawing wears them down.
