Beavers gnaw through trees to build dams. In stories, «a gnawing hunger» or «doubt gnawed at her» shows a feeling that will not go away. Phrases: «gnaw on a bone», «gnaw through», «gnaw at someone», «gnawing hunger».
examples from the lessons: The dog gnawed on a bone under the table. | Mice gnawed through the bag of rice. | Beavers gnaw trees down to build dams. | A rabbit needs things to gnaw so its teeth don't grow too long. | Guilt gnawed at Sam after he broke the window. | He felt a gnawing hunger on the long walk. | Don't gnaw your pencil!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Silent g: say «naw» (rhymes with «saw»). Regular verb: gnawed. Other words with silent g: gnome, gnat, gnu, sign. Trap: «gnaw» is not «knaw» or «nor».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A kernel is the soft part inside a nut or the seed inside the hard stone of a fruit. 2) A kernel is a whole seed of a grain such as corn (maize) or wheat: popcorn is made of corn kernels. 3) The kernel of something is its most important central part: «a kernel of truth». 4) (computing) The kernel is the core part of a computer's operating system that controls everything else.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about seeds, a kernel is the part that can grow into a new plant and stores food. In cooking, popcorn kernels pop when heated because the water inside turns to steam. In stories and arguments, «a kernel of truth» means a small true part inside a mostly false story. Phrases: «corn kernels», «popcorn kernels», «a kernel of truth».
examples from the lessons: Popcorn kernels pop when you heat them. | Squirrels crack hazelnuts to eat the kernel. | Each corn cob has hundreds of kernels. | The rumour had a kernel of truth in it. | Wheat kernels are ground into flour. | Some kernels did not pop and stayed hard at the bottom of the bowl. | The computer's kernel controls the memory and the screen.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «kernels». Homophone trap: «kernel» sounds the same as «colonel» (an army officer), spelled very differently.

part of speech: noun (a khan, khans); often a title and a name (Khan)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A khan was a ruler or king among the Mongols, Turks and other peoples of Central Asia; the most famous is Genghis Khan. 2) Khan is a common family name in South Asia and elsewhere (a name). 3) A khan was also an inn where travelling merchants and their camels stayed, on old trade routes like the Silk Road.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, Genghis Khan united the Mongol tribes and built the largest land empire the world had seen, and his grandson Kublai Khan ruled China. The words «khanate» (land ruled by a khan) and «Great Khan» appear in history books. Today «Khan» is a family name of many people, such as footballers, mayors and cricketers. Phrases: «Genghis Khan», «the Great Khan», «Kublai Khan».
examples from the lessons: Genghis Khan led the Mongols across Asia. | The khan's horsemen rode faster than any army. | Kublai Khan ruled China from Beijing. | Marco Polo visited the court of the Great Khan. | Traders rested at a khan on the Silk Road. | My friend's surname is Khan.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually a capital K in names and titles. Say «kahn». Trap: «Khan» the title and «Khan» the surname are the same word in origin but used differently today; never invent details about a real person called Khan.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An oryx is a large antelope of the deserts and dry grasslands of Africa and Arabia, with very long, straight, pointed horns and a pale coat with dark face markings.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons the oryx is an example of desert adaptation: it can go a long time without drinking, getting water from plants and dew, and its pale coat reflects the sun. The Arabian oryx died out in the wild and was brought back from zoo herds — a conservation success. Some people think oryx seen side-on, with horns overlapping, gave rise to unicorn legends. Phrases: «Arabian oryx», «scimitar-horned oryx», «a herd of oryx».
examples from the lessons: An oryx can live in the desert without drinking for weeks. | The oryx has long, straight horns like spears. | The Arabian oryx was saved by breeding them in zoos. | A herd of oryx crossed the dry plain. | The scimitar-horned oryx has curved horns. | From the side, an oryx with one horn hidden looks a bit like a unicorn.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «oryx» or «oryxes». Use «an» before it: «an oryx». Say OR-ix.

part of speech: noun (a pom, poms; Pom, Pommy); short forms: pom-pom, Pomeranian
meaning for a pupil: 1) (Australia, New Zealand, slang) A Pom or Pommy is an English person or a British person; it is a joking word but can sound rude. 2) A pom is short for a pom-pom (pompom), a fluffy ball of wool or a cheerleader's bunch of ribbons. 3) A pom is short for a Pomeranian, a small fluffy dog.
its sense in the lessons: In Australian and New Zealand talk «Pom» is common in sport banter: «the Poms» are the English cricket or rugby team. It can be friendly teasing or unkind, so be careful. In craft lessons you make poms (pom-poms) from wool and card. In cheerleading, cheerleaders wave poms. Phrases: «whingeing Pom» (a joking insult), «the Poms», «wool pom».
examples from the lessons: The Aussies beat the Poms at cricket. (Australia, slang) | «G'day, mate, you a Pom?» asked the man at the beach. | My beanie hat has a red pom on top. | We made woolly poms in art class. | The cheerleaders shook their poms. | Our neighbour's pom barks at everything. (short for Pomeranian)
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «poms». For the nationality it is often written with a capital: Pom, Pommy. It is slang and may offend some English people; do not use it in formal writing. Myth: the story that it stands for «Prisoner of Mother England» is not true; most experts think it came from «pomegranate», rhyming with «immigrant».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Something radioactive gives off strong, invisible energy called radiation because the centres of its atoms are breaking apart. 2) (informal, joking) Radioactive can describe something so unpopular or dangerous that everyone stays away from it.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons radioactivity was discovered by Henri Becquerel and studied by Marie Curie, who found radium and polonium. Radioactive materials are used in nuclear power stations, in hospitals to treat cancer and take scans, and in smoke alarms in tiny safe amounts. They can be dangerous: too much radiation damages living cells, as in the Chernobyl disaster in Ukraine. Safety: warning sign is a yellow-and-black trefoil. Phrases: «radioactive waste», «radioactive material», «half-life».
examples from the lessons: Uranium is radioactive. | Marie Curie studied radioactive elements. | Radioactive waste must be stored safely for thousands of years. | The area around Chernobyl is still radioactive. | Doctors use radioactive substances to find and treat illnesses. | You cannot see, hear or smell radiation, so workers wear special badges to measure it. | In comics, a radioactive spider gave Peter Parker his powers. | After the scandal, the singer was radioactive — no company would hire him. (informal)
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Radioactivity» is uncountable. Myth: radioactive things do not glow green as in cartoons. Trap: «radiation» also includes harmless or useful things like light and radio waves; «radioactive» is about atoms breaking apart. A small amount (background radiation) is around us all the time.

part of speech: noun (a tang, tangs; uncountable for the taste); adjective (tangy); also Tang (a name, Chinese dynasty)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A tang is a strong, sharp taste or smell, like lemon or the sea air. 2) A tang is a hint or trace of something: «a tang of autumn in the air». 3) Tang was a great Chinese dynasty, the Tang dynasty, famous for poetry, art and trade (a name). 4) A tang is the part of a knife blade that fits into the handle. 5) (Mandarin, pinyin) «táng» means sugar or sweets, and «tāng» means soup; these are not English words.
its sense in the lessons: In cooking and describing food, «tang» and «tangy» praise a sharp, fresh taste: lemon, lime, cheese, yoghurt. In stories, «the salty tang of the sea» helps you smell the setting. In history, the Tang dynasty in China was a golden age of the Silk Road. Phrases: «a salty tang», «a citrus tang», «tangy cheese», «the Tang dynasty».
examples from the lessons: The lemonade had a nice sharp tang. | We smelled the salty tang of the sea as we got out of the car. | This cheese is tangy. | There was a tang of smoke in the cold air. | Poets wrote famous poems during the Tang dynasty. | The tang of the knife goes into the wooden handle. | In Mandarin, «tang» with a rising tone means sweets.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable («a tang») or uncountable. Adjective «tangy» is more common in everyday talk. Capital T for the dynasty. Do not confuse with «tank» or «tangle».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A vole is a small, plump rodent like a mouse, with a short tail, small ears and a blunt nose, that lives in fields, woods and riverbanks.
its sense in the lessons: In nature lessons voles are an important part of food chains: owls, kestrels, foxes, weasels and stoats eat lots of them. The water vole is a British riverbank animal that has become rare because of American mink and loss of habitat; Ratty in «The Wind in the Willows» is really a water vole. Phrases: «field vole», «bank vole», «water vole».
examples from the lessons: A barn owl swooped down and caught a vole. | Voles have shorter tails than mice. | Ratty in «The Wind in the Willows» is really a water vole. | Water voles dig burrows in riverbanks. | We found vole tunnels in the long grass. | Voles eat grass, roots and seeds. | The kestrel hovered, looking for voles.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «voles». Trap: a vole is not a mole (a mole digs underground and eats worms) and not exactly a mouse (shorter tail, rounder face). Rhymes with «hole».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A macaw is a large parrot with a long tail, a strong curved beak and very bright feathers, such as red, blue, yellow and green, from the rainforests of Central and South America.
its sense in the lessons: In rainforest lessons macaws show the canopy layer: they crack hard nuts with their beaks, eat clay from riverbanks, and live in pairs that stay together for life. Many are endangered because of forest loss and the illegal pet trade. They can copy sounds and some words. Phrases: «scarlet macaw», «blue-and-gold macaw», «hyacinth macaw».
examples from the lessons: A scarlet macaw flew over the rainforest canopy. | Macaws crack hard nuts with their strong beaks. | The macaw at the zoo said «hello» to us. | Hyacinth macaws are the biggest parrots that can fly. | Macaw pairs often stay together for life. | Many macaws are taken illegally from the wild to be sold as pets. | The macaw's feathers were red, yellow and blue.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «macaws». Say ma-KAW. A macaw is a kind of parrot; not all parrots are macaws.

part of speech: noun (Napoleon, a name; a napoleon — a pastry; a napoleon — an old French gold coin)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (a name) Napoleon Bonaparte was a French general who made himself Emperor of France and conquered much of Europe before he was defeated at the Battle of Waterloo. 2) A napoleon is a layered pastry with cream filling, also called a mille-feuille or vanilla slice. 3) A napoleon was an old French gold coin.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons Napoleon is studied as a brilliant and ambitious leader whose wars changed Europe; he lost in Russia in winter and finally at Waterloo against Britain and Prussia, and was sent to the island of St Helena. He also made a famous set of laws, the Napoleonic Code. In stories, a «Napoleon» is a bossy, power-hungry person; in «Animal Farm», Napoleon is the pig who becomes a tyrant. Phrases: «the Napoleonic Wars», «a Napoleon complex».
examples from the lessons: Napoleon was defeated at the Battle of Waterloo. | Napoleon crowned himself Emperor of France. | Napoleon's army retreated from Russia in the freezing winter. | The Napoleonic Wars lasted many years. | In «Animal Farm», Napoleon is a pig who takes over the farm. | For pudding we had a napoleon with layers of pastry and cream. | Napoleon was sent away to the island of St Helena.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital N for the person. Myth: Napoleon was not especially short; he was about average height for his time, and British cartoons made fun of him as tiny. «A Napoleon complex» is a popular, not scientific, idea that short people act bossy to make up for it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A condor is a very large vulture with huge wings and a bald head, living in the Andes mountains (the Andean condor) or California (the California condor).
its sense in the lessons: In nature lessons the Andean condor is one of the largest flying birds, with wings over 3 metres across; it soars for hours on rising air without flapping. The California condor almost died out — fewer than 30 were left — and was saved by catching them all, breeding them and releasing their young. Condors are scavengers and eat dead animals. Phrases: «Andean condor», «California condor», «soar like a condor».
examples from the lessons: The condor soared over the mountains without flapping. | An Andean condor's wings are wider than a tall man is high. | Condors eat dead animals, like other vultures. | The California condor was saved from extinction. | We saw a condor gliding high above the canyon in Peru. | A condor can live for more than fifty years.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «condors». Say KON-dor. Condors are New World vultures. The Andean condor is a national symbol in several South American countries.

part of speech: noun (Constantinople, a name of a city)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (a name) Constantinople was the old name of the great city on the Bosphorus strait that is now called Istanbul, in Turkey. 2) It was the capital of the Eastern Roman (Byzantine) Empire and later of the Ottoman Empire.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons Constantinople is where Europe meets Asia: the Roman emperor Constantine made it his capital and named it after himself. It was rich and strong for over a thousand years, with huge walls and the great church of Hagia Sophia. The Ottoman Turks captured it, and it became their capital; the name Istanbul became official much later. It was a key city on trade routes between east and west. Phrases: «the fall of Constantinople», «Byzantine Constantinople».
examples from the lessons: Constantinople was named after the emperor Constantine. | The city of Constantinople is now called Istanbul. | Hagia Sophia was the great church of Constantinople. | Constantinople had enormous walls to keep out enemies. | The Ottoman Turks captured Constantinople with huge cannons. | Merchants from many lands traded in Constantinople. | Before it was Constantinople, the town was called Byzantium.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always a capital C. Say kon-stan-ti-NOH-pul. Three names, one city: Byzantium, then Constantinople, then Istanbul. Trap: Istanbul is the largest city in Turkey, but the capital of Turkey today is Ankara.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The Cossacks were communities of free, self-ruling warriors and farmers on the steppes of what is now Ukraine and southern Russia, famous as horsemen. 2) Cossack describes their things: a Cossack hat, a Cossack dance.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons about Ukraine, the Zaporizhzhian Cossacks had their fortress, the Sich, on the Dnipro river, elected their leaders (hetmans), and are a proud symbol of Ukrainian freedom; Bohdan Khmelnytsky was a famous hetman. There were also Don Cossacks in Russia. Cossacks served as soldiers for different rulers, and their history includes both bravery and cruel deeds. The famous Cossack dance (hopak) has high jumps and squatting kicks. Phrases: «Zaporizhzhian Cossacks», «Cossack hat», «Cossack dance».
examples from the lessons: The Cossacks were famous horse riders. | The Zaporizhzhian Cossacks lived on islands in the Dnipro river. | The Cossacks elected their own leader, called a hetman. | In a famous painting, Cossacks laugh as they write a rude letter to the Turkish sultan. | The hopak is a lively Cossack dance from Ukraine. | Grandad wore a tall furry Cossack hat. | Ukraine's national anthem says Ukrainians are of Cossack kin.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually written with a capital C: Cossack, Cossacks. The word comes from a Turkic word meaning «free person». The Ukrainian word is «kozak».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A feeler is a long, thin part on the head of an insect, snail or other small animal, used to touch, smell and sense the world; scientists call insect feelers antennae. 2) (informal) To put out feelers means to quietly try to find out what people think before you decide something.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on minibeasts, ants, beetles, butterflies and snails all have feelers; a snail pulls its feelers in when touched, and its eyes are on the tips of its long top pair. Insects have two feelers. In everyday adult life, «putting out feelers» means asking around carefully. Phrases: «long feelers», «waved its feelers», «put out feelers».
examples from the lessons: The beetle waved its feelers in the air. | When I touched the snail, it pulled its feelers in. | Ants touch feelers to pass messages to each other. | Butterflies have club-shaped feelers. | A snail's eyes are at the ends of its long feelers. | Dad put out feelers to see if any shop had the game in stock.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «feelers». The scientific word is «antenna» (plural «antennae»). Trap: «feeler» is not a person who feels; it is a body part (or the phrase «put out feelers»).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A kea is a large, olive-green mountain parrot from the South Island of New Zealand, with bright orange under its wings, famous for being very clever and cheeky.
its sense in the lessons: In nature lessons about New Zealand, the kea is the world's only alpine (mountain) parrot. Keas solve puzzles, play in the snow, and love to pull apart cars, bags and boots, so they are called «the clown of the mountains». They are endangered and protected. Its name comes from the Māori language and copies its call, «kee-aa». Phrases: «cheeky kea», «kea-proof».
examples from the lessons: A kea pulled the rubber off our car window. | Keas live high in the mountains of New Zealand's South Island. | The kea's wings are bright orange underneath. | Scientists say keas are as clever as some monkeys at puzzles. | Don't leave your boots outside — the keas will steal them! | Keas are protected because only a few thousand are left.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «keas». Say KEE-a. The word is from te reo Māori. Trap: don't feed keas; human food harms them.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A trench is a long, narrow, deep ditch dug in the ground, for pipes, drains or building foundations. 2) In war, trenches are long ditches that soldiers dig and live in to protect themselves from enemy fire, especially in the First World War. 3) An ocean trench is a very deep, long valley in the sea floor, like the Mariana Trench, the deepest place on Earth. 4) A trench coat is a long, belted raincoat.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons trenches are studied with the First World War: soldiers lived in muddy, wet, rat-filled trenches, with «no man's land» between the two sides; diseases like «trench foot» came from wet feet. In geography and science, the Mariana Trench in the Pacific is about 11 km deep, deeper than Mount Everest is tall. Today soldiers in Ukraine also fight from trenches. Phrases: «trench warfare», «in the trenches», «trench foot», «ocean trench».
examples from the lessons: Workers dug a trench to lay the new water pipe. | Soldiers in the trenches wrote letters home. | The trenches were full of mud and rats. | The Mariana Trench is the deepest place in the ocean. | Trench foot was caused by standing in cold water for days. | Detectives in old films wear trench coats. | Between the trenches was a deadly strip called no man's land.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «trenches» (add -es after ch). «In the trenches» can also mean (informal) doing the hard, everyday part of a job. Trap: a trench is long and narrow; a pit or hole can be any shape.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An anglerfish is a fish with a big mouth and sharp teeth that catches prey using a long spine on its head with a glowing or wiggly tip that works like a fishing rod and bait. Many live in the deep, dark ocean.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons the deep-sea anglerfish shows adaptations to darkness: its «lure» glows with light made by bacteria (bioluminescence), and small fish swim towards it and get swallowed. In some kinds the tiny male fuses onto the much larger female for life. The name comes from «angler», a person who fishes with a rod. Phrases: «deep-sea anglerfish», «glowing lure».
examples from the lessons: The anglerfish dangled a glowing lure in the dark. | Small fish swim towards the light and get eaten by the anglerfish. | Anglerfish live in the deep ocean where no sunlight reaches. | The female anglerfish is much bigger than the male. | In the film, a scary anglerfish chased the little fish. | The anglerfish can swallow prey bigger than itself.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural is usually «anglerfish» (like «fish»), sometimes «anglerfishes». One word. In British fish shops, one kind of anglerfish is sold as «monkfish». Use «an» before it.

part of speech: noun (a chilli, chillies; UK, Ireland, Australia, New Zealand spelling); US: chili, chile
meaning for a pupil: 1) A chilli is a small pepper, often red or green, that tastes very hot and spicy. 2) Chilli, or chilli con carne, is a spicy dish made with minced meat, beans, tomatoes and chillies. 3) Chilli powder or flakes are dried, ground chillies used as a spice.
its sense in the lessons: In cooking and food lessons, chillies come from the Americas and spread around the world, now used in Indian, Mexican, Thai, Chinese and Korean food. Their heat comes from a chemical called capsaicin, measured on the Scoville scale. Safety: wash hands after cutting chillies and never rub your eyes; milk soothes a burning mouth better than water. Phrases: «chilli con carne», «sweet chilli sauce», «chilli powder», «hot as chilli».
examples from the lessons: The curry had too much chilli for me. | Dad made chilli con carne with rice. | Wash your hands after chopping chillies! | A glass of milk helps when chilli burns your mouth. | Green chillies are picked before they turn red. | Grandma grows chillies in her greenhouse. | We dipped our spring rolls in sweet chilli sauce.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «chillies». Spelling: UK/Australia «chilli», USA «chili» (and «chile» for the pepper in some places). Homophone trap: «chilly» means cold; «Chile» is a country in South America; «chilli» is the hot pepper. Funny but true: hot chilli makes you feel warm though it is not hot in temperature.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A peasant was a poor farmer or farm worker in the past, especially in the Middle Ages, who worked a small piece of land and often had to give part of the crops to a lord. 2) In some countries today, peasant means a farmer on a small farm who grows food mostly for the family. 3) (rude, insult) Calling someone a peasant means they are uneducated or have bad manners; it is unkind.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons peasants appear in the feudal system: king, barons, knights, peasants (also called serfs or villeins); they lived in small houses with animals, paid taxes, and in the Peasants' Revolt they rose up against unfair taxes. In fairy tales, a clever peasant often tricks a king. In playground talk, «peasant» is used as a snobby insult — not kind. Phrases: «the Peasants' Revolt», «peasant farmers», «peasant life».
examples from the lessons: Most people in medieval England were peasants. | The peasants worked in the lord's fields for three days a week. | In the Peasants' Revolt, peasants marched on London. | The peasant's cottage had one room shared with a cow. | In the fairy tale, a poor peasant married the princess. | «You peasant!» he said — which was very rude. | Peasant farmers in many countries still grow their own food.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «peasants». Spelling: peas-ant, but not related to peas. Trap: «pheasant» (with ph) is a bird; «pleasant» (with l) means nice. In history, a «serf» was a peasant who was not free to leave the land.

part of speech: adjective (Persian); noun (a Persian, Persians; Persian — the language, uncountable; a Persian cat)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Persian describes Persia, the old name for Iran, and its people, history and culture. 2) Persian, also called Farsi, is the main language of Iran, also spoken in Afghanistan (Dari) and Tajikistan (Tajik). 3) A Persian is a person from Persia or Iran. 4) A Persian, or Persian cat, is a cat breed with long fluffy fur and a flat face. 5) A Persian carpet or rug is a hand-woven carpet with rich patterns.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons the Persian Empire of Cyrus the Great and Darius was one of the largest in the ancient world; Persians fought the Greeks at Marathon and Thermopylae. Persian poets like Rumi and Hafez are still loved. The Persian Gulf is the sea between Iran and Arabia. Words like «paradise», «pyjamas» and «chess» have Persian roots. Phrases: «the Persian Empire», «Persian cat», «Persian carpet», «the Persian Gulf».
examples from the lessons: Cyrus the Great ruled the Persian Empire. | The Greeks fought the Persians at the Battle of Marathon. | My neighbour speaks Persian at home. | Our Persian cat has long white fur that needs brushing every day. | The living room has a beautiful Persian rug. | Persian New Year, Nowruz, starts on the first day of spring. | The word «paradise» comes from an old Persian word for a garden.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always a capital P. Persian (the language) is uncountable; Persians (people) is countable. Persian is not Arabic: they are different languages, though Persian uses a form of the Arabic alphabet. Iran was called Persia in English until the twentieth century.

part of speech: noun (polo, uncountable — the sport; a polo, polos — a polo shirt or neck)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Polo is a game played on horseback in which two teams use long-handled wooden mallets to hit a small ball into the other team's goal. 2) Water polo is a team game played in a swimming pool, where swimmers throw a ball into a goal. 3) A polo, or polo shirt, is a short-sleeved cotton shirt with a collar and a few buttons at the neck. 4) A polo neck is a jumper with a high, folded collar round the neck (in the USA a turtleneck).
its sense in the lessons: Polo is one of the oldest team sports, from ancient Persia; it is linked with rich people because horses are expensive. Many schools have a polo shirt as part of the uniform. Water polo is an Olympic sport. Marco Polo was a famous Italian traveller to China (a name). Phrases: «polo shirt», «polo neck», «water polo», «polo match».
examples from the lessons: The polo players galloped after the ball. | Our school uniform is a blue polo shirt and grey trousers. | I joined the water polo club at the swimming pool. | Grandma knitted me a woolly polo neck jumper. | Polo was first played in ancient Persia. | Marco Polo travelled all the way to China. | A polo team has four riders.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The sport is uncountable: «play polo», not «a polo». The shirt is countable: «two polos». Capital P for Marco Polo and for the brand of mint sweets (Polo mints, UK).

part of speech: verb (hypnotise, hypnotises, hypnotised, hypnotising; US: hypnotize); nouns: hypnosis, hypnotist
meaning for a pupil: 1) To hypnotise someone means to put them into a deep, calm, dreamy state in which they pay close attention and may follow suggestions. 2) To be hypnotised by something means to be so fascinated by it that you cannot look away: «hypnotised by the flames».
its sense in the lessons: In stories, cartoons and stage shows a hypnotist swings a watch and says «you are getting sleepy»; this is mostly showbusiness. Real hypnosis (hypnotherapy) is used by some therapists to help people relax or stop habits; people under hypnosis are not asleep and cannot be made to do things against their will. In nature, a snake is said to hypnotise its prey, though really the prey freezes with fear. Phrases: «hypnotised by», «under hypnosis», «stage hypnotist».
examples from the lessons: The magician claimed he could hypnotise anyone in the audience. | The cat was hypnotised by the fish swimming in the tank. | We sat hypnotised by the fireworks. | In the cartoon, the snake hypnotised the boy with its swirly eyes. | Some people see a hypnotist to help them stop smoking. | The music was so beautiful it almost hypnotised me.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK, Ireland, Australia, New Zealand: «hypnotise» (or «hypnotize»); USA and Canada: «hypnotize». Regular verb. Myth: a hypnotised person cannot be forced to do anything they really don't want, and hypnosis is not magic.

part of speech: verb (lag, lags, lagged, lagging); noun (a lag, lags; jet lag, time lag; an old lag)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To lag, or lag behind, means to move or develop more slowly than others, so you fall behind. 2) A lag, or time lag, is a delay between one thing happening and another. 3) (gaming, computers, informal) Lag is a delay in a game or video call, when the screen freezes or jumps because the internet is slow. 4) Jet lag is feeling tired and muddled after flying across many time zones. 5) To lag pipes or a hot-water tank means to wrap them in material to keep the heat in. 6) (UK, slang) An old lag is a person who has been in prison many times.
its sense in the lessons: In PE and stories, someone lags behind on a walk or race. In gaming, «it's lagging» is a common complaint. In science, there is a lag between seeing lightning and hearing thunder because light is faster than sound; in maths, you can use that lag to work out how far away the storm is (about 3 seconds per kilometre). Lagging pipes stops them freezing in winter. Phrases: «lag behind», «jet lag», «time lag», «lag spike».
examples from the lessons: Hurry up, don't lag behind! | The game kept lagging, so I lost the level. | We had terrible jet lag after flying to Australia. | There is a lag between the lightning flash and the thunder. | Dad lagged the pipes in the loft so they wouldn't freeze. | Our class is lagging behind with the project, so we need to work faster. | The video call had a two-second lag.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb doubles the g: lagged, lagging. «Lag» as an internet delay is informal but very common. Trap: «laggy» (informal) means slow and jerky; «lagging» can also be the noun for pipe insulation.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A sauropod was a huge, plant-eating dinosaur with a very long neck, a long tail, a small head and four thick legs like pillars, such as Diplodocus, Brachiosaurus and Argentinosaurus.
its sense in the lessons: In dinosaur lessons sauropods were the biggest animals ever to walk on land: some were longer than three buses and heavier than ten elephants. Their long necks let them reach leaves high up or sweep over a wide area without walking. They laid eggs about the size of a football. The name means «lizard foot». Phrases: «long-necked sauropods», «sauropod footprints», «a herd of sauropods».
examples from the lessons: Diplodocus was a sauropod with a whip-like tail. | Sauropods were the largest animals ever to walk on land. | We saw sauropod footprints in the rock. | A sauropod's head was tiny for its giant body. | Sauropods swallowed leaves without chewing them. | Brachiosaurus was a sauropod that could reach the treetops.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «sauropods». Say SORE-uh-pod. Trap: the blue whale (living today, in the sea) is heavier than any sauropod we know. Sauropods were not the same as the «Brontosaurus» of old books, although Brontosaurus is a sauropod name that scientists have recently brought back.

part of speech: adjective (sulky, sulkier, sulkiest); verb related: sulk (sulks, sulked); adverb: sulkily
meaning for a pupil: 1) Sulky means bad-tempered and silent because you are upset or annoyed, and you want others to notice: «a sulky face». 2) A sulky is also a light two-wheeled cart for one person pulled by a horse in harness racing.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, a sulky character pouts, slams doors, folds arms and refuses to talk, so the reader knows they are upset or feel treated unfairly. In PSHE, pupils learn better ways to show feelings than sulking: name the feeling and talk about it. Phrases: «in a sulky mood», «a sulky teenager», «go off in a sulk» (noun), «sulk about something».
examples from the lessons: Tom was sulky all afternoon because he lost the game. | Don't be sulky — tell me what's wrong. | She gave a sulky shrug and looked away. | My little sister went into a sulk when it was bedtime. | The sulky teenager in the story wouldn't come down for dinner. | He answered sulkily, «Fine. Whatever.» | In harness racing, the driver sits in a sulky behind the horse.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative «sulkier», superlative «sulkiest» (y changes to i). The verb is «sulk»; «a sulk» is also a noun. Sulky is about a quiet, moody mood; angry shouting is not sulking.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A unicorn is a magical animal from stories and legends that looks like a white horse with one long, straight, twisted horn on its forehead. 2) (informal) A unicorn is something rare and wonderful that is very hard to find. 3) (money) A unicorn is a new company that has become worth over a billion dollars.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and myths unicorns stand for purity, magic and wildness; they are the national animal of Scotland and appear on the UK royal coat of arms with the lion. People in the past may have imagined them from narwhal tusks (sold as «unicorn horns»), oryx or rhinos. In science lessons they are a good example of a myth: unicorns are not real. Phrases: «unicorn horn», «as rare as a unicorn».
examples from the lessons: The unicorn galloped through the enchanted forest. | My sister has unicorn pyjamas. | The unicorn is the national animal of Scotland. | Unicorns are made-up animals; they are not real. | Long ago, traders sold narwhal tusks as unicorn horns. | A friend who always shares their sweets is a unicorn! (informal) | The lion and the unicorn are on the royal coat of arms.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «unicorns». Use «a», not «an», because it starts with a «you» sound: «a unicorn». «Uni» means one, as in uniform and unicycle. Trap: a narwhal is real (a whale with a long tusk); a unicorn is a legend.

part of speech: noun (a champion, champions); verb (champion, champions, championed, championing); adjective (champion, UK informal); noun: championship
meaning for a pupil: 1) A champion is a person or team that has won a competition, especially the most important one: «the world champion». 2) A champion of something is a person who fights for it or speaks up for it: «a champion of children's rights». 3) To champion something means to support it and argue for it strongly. 4) (UK, informal, old-fashioned) «Champion!» means excellent, great.
its sense in the lessons: In sport and PE, «champions» win leagues, cups and sports days; a «championship» is a competition for the title. In history and stories, a champion was a knight who fought on behalf of someone else. In PSHE and the news, people champion causes like recycling or kindness. Phrases: «world champion», «reigning champion», «defending champion», «Olympic champion», «a champion of…».
examples from the lessons: Our class were the sports day champions! | She is the world champion at chess. | The defending champions lost in the first round. | Martin Luther King was a champion of equal rights. | Our head teacher champions reading for pleasure. | The knight fought as the queen's champion. | «How was the match?» «Champion!» (UK, informal, Northern) | Liverpool became champions of the league.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «champions». Short informal form: «champ». «Championship» is the competition; «champion» is the winner. Trap: «the reigning champion» is the current one; «a former champion» won before.

part of speech: noun (French: une fille, des filles); not an English word
meaning for a pupil: 1) (French) «Fille» means «girl» or «daughter»: «une petite fille» = a little girl, «ma fille» = my daughter. It sounds like «fee» with a soft y at the end («feey»), and it is not an English word.
its sense in the lessons: In French lessons, «fille» is learned with «garçon» (boy): «Je suis une fille» = I am a girl. «Fille» is a feminine noun, so it goes with «la» and «une». Grown-ups know the phrase «jeune fille» (young lady). Do not mix it up with English «fill» or «file».
examples from the lessons: «Je suis une fille» means «I am a girl» in French. | «C'est ma fille» means «This is my daughter.» | In French, «fille» is feminine: «la fille», «une fille». | The French teacher said «filles» for the girls and «garçons» for the boys. | «Petite-fille» in French means granddaughter. | «La fille du roi» means «the king's daughter».
note for the reader of a maths problem: French only; plural «filles». The «ll» in «fille» sounds like «y», not like an English l. Trap: «fillet» (a boneless piece of meat or fish) and «fill» are different English words.

part of speech: noun (a Geordie, Geordies; Geordie — the dialect); adjective (Geordie)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (UK) A Geordie is a person from Newcastle upon Tyne or Tyneside in North-East England. 2) (UK) Geordie is the strong local accent and dialect spoken there. 3) Geordie is also a Scottish and Northern pet form of the name George (a name).
its sense in the lessons: In lessons about accents and dialects, Geordie is a famous British example with its own words: «howay» (come on), «hinny» and «pet» (dear), «bairn» (child), «canny» (nice, good), «gan» (go), «whey aye» (yes, of course), «nowt» (nothing). Dialect is not wrong English; it is a local way of speaking, and Standard English is used for exams and formal writing. Phrases: «a Geordie accent», «a proud Geordie».
examples from the lessons: My uncle is a Geordie from Newcastle. | She speaks with a strong Geordie accent. | «Howay, man!» is Geordie for «Come on!» | In Geordie, «bairn» means child. | «Whey aye, pet!» said the Geordie bus driver, meaning «Yes, of course, love!» | Geordies are proud of their football team and the Tyne bridges.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually a capital G. Countable for people («two Geordies»), uncountable for the dialect. Trap: not everyone from the North-East is a Geordie; people from Sunderland are called Mackems.

part of speech: noun (ken, uncountable, in «beyond my ken»); verb (Scottish, Northern English: ken, kens, kent or kenned, kenning); also a name (Ken)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (Scotland, Northern England) To ken means to know: «I dinnae ken» = I don't know. 2) (formal, old) Your ken is what you know or understand: «Rocket science is beyond my ken». 3) Ken is a boy's name, short for Kenneth (a name). 4) (Scotland, informal) «Ken» at the end of a sentence means «you know»: «It was brilliant, ken.»
its sense in the lessons: In Scottish stories and poems (like those of Robert Burns) and in Scottish everyday talk, «ken» is very common. In English lessons it shows how dialects keep old words: «ken» is related to «know» and «can». The phrase «beyond my ken» is used in books to say something is outside what a person knows. Phrases: «I dinnae ken», «d'ye ken?», «beyond one's ken».
examples from the lessons: «Dae ye ken where the station is?» asked the old Scottish man. | I dinnae ken what you mean. (Scotland) | It was a great game, ken? | How the universe began is beyond my ken. | Ken is my uncle's name. | «Aye, I ken him fine,» said Granny, meaning she knew him well.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Scottish and old/literary; in standard school writing use «know». Past form «kent» (Scotland) or «kenned». Capital K for the name. Trap: «ken» is not short for «can».

part of speech: noun (a microchip, microchips; also chip); verb (microchip, microchips, microchipped, microchipping — to put a chip in a pet)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A microchip is a very small piece of material, usually silicon, carrying tiny electronic circuits that store information or do calculations inside computers, phones and other machines. 2) A microchip is also a tiny chip, the size of a grain of rice, put under a pet's skin by a vet so a lost pet can be identified. 3) To microchip a pet means to put this chip in.
its sense in the lessons: In computing lessons, microchips (also called integrated circuits or just chips) are the «brains» of devices: processors hold billions of tiny switches called transistors. In everyday life, bank cards, passports and pets have chips. In the UK it is the law to microchip dogs and cats. Phrases: «microchip a dog», «computer chip», «chip and PIN».
examples from the lessons: A phone contains many microchips. | The vet microchipped our new puppy. | The lost cat was returned home because of her microchip. | Microchips are made from silicon, which comes from sand. | One microchip can hold billions of tiny switches. | My bank card has a microchip in it. | Making microchips needs super-clean factories.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «microchips». The verb doubles p: microchipped, microchipping. Often shortened to «chip». Myth: a pet microchip is not a GPS tracker; it cannot show where the pet is, it only gives an ID number when scanned. «Micro» means very small.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A silkworm is the caterpillar of the silk moth, which spins a cocoon of fine silk thread; people use this thread to make silk cloth.
its sense in the lessons: In science and history lessons silkworms show life cycles (egg, caterpillar, cocoon/pupa, moth) and the story of silk: it was first made in ancient China, which kept the secret for a long time, and silk was traded along the Silk Road. Silkworms eat only mulberry leaves. One cocoon can be made of a single thread up to about 1 km long. To get the silk, the cocoons are usually boiled, which kills the pupa — some people prefer «peace silk». Phrases: «silkworm cocoon», «mulberry leaves», «the Silk Road».
examples from the lessons: Silkworms eat only mulberry leaves. | The silkworm spun a white cocoon around itself. | Silk cloth is made from the thread of silkworms. | Ancient China kept silkworms secret for centuries. | Our class watched silkworms turn into moths. | A single silkworm cocoon is made of one very long thread. | Silkworm moths cannot fly.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «silkworms». Trap: a silkworm is not a worm; it is a caterpillar (an insect larva). Silk moths have been kept by people for so long that they can no longer live in the wild.

part of speech: noun (the zodiac; a zodiac sign); adjective (zodiacal, rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The zodiac is a band of twelve star patterns (constellations) across the sky that the Sun, Moon and planets seem to move through during the year. 2) In astrology, the zodiac is divided into twelve signs, such as Aries, Leo and Pisces, and people's «star sign» depends on their birthday. 3) The Chinese zodiac is a cycle of twelve animals, one for each year, like the Rat, Ox, Tiger and Dragon.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about space, the zodiac constellations are real star patterns, but astrology — the belief that star signs control personality and luck — is not science; studies have found no such effect. Horoscopes in magazines are for fun. At Lunar New Year, children learn which Chinese zodiac animal their birth year has and the story of the animals' race across the river. Phrases: «signs of the zodiac», «star sign», «Chinese zodiac».
examples from the lessons: There are twelve signs of the zodiac. | «What's your star sign?» «I'm a Leo.» | The Chinese zodiac has twelve animals. | In the story, the Rat won the zodiac race by riding on the Ox's back. | Astronomers study the stars; astrologers make horoscopes, which are not science. | The zodiac constellations lie along the path of the Sun in the sky.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually «the zodiac». Say ZOH-dee-ak. Trap: astronomy is the science of space; astrology is a belief system, not a science. «Zodiac» comes from Greek for «circle of little animals».

meaning for a pupil: 1) An axolotl is a Mexican salamander, an amphibian that keeps its baby features all its life: feathery pink gills on its head and a tail fin, and lives always in water. It looks as if it is smiling.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons the axolotl is amazing because it can regrow lost legs, tails, and even parts of its heart and brain; scientists study it to learn about healing. In the wild it lives only in lakes and canals near Mexico City and is critically endangered, but many are kept as pets and in labs. The name comes from the Aztec language Nahuatl. Phrases: «Mexican walking fish» (though it is not a fish).
examples from the lessons: An axolotl can grow back a lost leg. | Axolotls breathe with the feathery gills on their heads. | Wild axolotls live only near Mexico City. | Our class pet is a pink axolotl called Bubbles. | The axolotl looks like it is always smiling. | Axolotls are amphibians, not fish. | Scientists study axolotls to understand how bodies heal.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «axolotls». Use «an»: «an axolotl». Say AK-suh-lot-ul. Trap: called the «Mexican walking fish», but it is an amphibian like frogs and newts.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A bonobo is an ape very like a chimpanzee but slimmer, with longer legs and a darker face, that lives only in the rainforests of the Democratic Republic of the Congo in Africa.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons bonobos and chimpanzees are humans' closest living relatives, sharing about 98–99% of our DNA. Bonobo groups are often led by females and settle arguments peacefully with play and friendliness, while chimps can be more aggressive. Bonobos are endangered by hunting and forest loss. Phrases: «great apes», «bonobos and chimpanzees».
examples from the lessons: Bonobos live only in the Congo rainforest. | Bonobos and chimpanzees are our closest animal relatives. | In bonobo groups, females often lead. | Bonobos share food and hug to calm arguments. | The bonobo used a stick as a tool. | Bonobos are endangered because of hunting.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «bonobos». Say bo-NO-bo. Once called the «pygmy chimpanzee», but it is a separate species and not much smaller. Great apes: orangutans, gorillas, chimpanzees, bonobos and humans.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A mongoose is a small, fast, furry animal with a long body and tail, from Africa and Asia, famous for fighting and killing snakes, including cobras.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, the most famous mongoose is Rikki-Tikki-Tavi from Rudyard Kipling's «The Jungle Book», who protects a family from cobras. In science lessons, mongooses are quick and have some resistance to snake venom. Meerkats are a kind of mongoose. When people brought mongooses to islands like Hawaii to kill rats, they also killed native birds — a lesson about invasive species. Phrases: «a band of mongooses».
examples from the lessons: The mongoose darted at the cobra and won the fight. | Rikki-Tikki-Tavi is a brave mongoose in Kipling's story. | Meerkats belong to the mongoose family. | Mongooses brought to Hawaii ate the eggs of rare birds. | A mongoose is quick enough to dodge a snake's strike. | A group of mongooses is called a band.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «mongooses» (not «mongeese»): the word has nothing to do with «goose»; it comes from an Indian language (Marathi «mungūs»).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A musician is a person who plays a musical instrument or sings, especially as a job or with great skill. 2) A musician can also be someone who writes music (a composer).
its sense in the lessons: In music lessons pupils learn about famous musicians and composers, and about different musicians in an orchestra or band: violinists, drummers, pianists, singers. Being a musician takes lots of practice. Buskers are musicians who play in the street for money. Phrases: «a talented musician», «a professional musician», «street musician», «session musician».
examples from the lessons: My aunt is a musician in an orchestra. | The street musician played the guitar outside the station. | Mozart was a brilliant musician from a young age. | Musicians practise for hours every day. | The band has four musicians. | You don't have to be famous to be a musician — anyone who plays can be one.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «musicians». Spelling: music + ian; the c sounds like «sh»: mew-ZISH-un. Similar: magician, electrician, politician.

part of speech: adjective (passive; adverb: passively; noun: passivity); noun (the passive, grammar)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Passive means letting things happen to you without acting, reacting or taking part: «a passive audience». 2) (grammar) The passive, or passive voice, is a way of making a sentence where the thing that something is done to comes first: «The window was broken by Sam», instead of the active «Sam broke the window». 3) Passive smoking means breathing in smoke from other people's cigarettes. 4) (science) Passive means working without extra power or effort, like a «passive house» that stays warm with no heaters.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons (SATs grammar), pupils learn to change active sentences into passive ones; the passive uses «be» + past participle (was eaten, is made, were found) and is common in science reports: «The water was heated». It hides or lowers the doer: «Mistakes were made». In PSHE, being passive is the opposite of standing up for yourself (being assertive). Phrases: «passive voice», «passive smoking», «passive-aggressive» (being unkind in a hidden way).
examples from the lessons: «The cake was eaten by the dog» is in the passive. | Rewrite the sentence in the passive voice. | In science reports we write «The water was heated». | Don't just be passive — join in the discussion! | Passive smoking can harm children's lungs. | She gave a passive-aggressive smile and said «Fine». | Watching TV is passive; building a model is active.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: «active». The passive is made with a form of «be» + past participle: «is cleaned», «was taken», «will be sent»; the doer can be added with «by». Trap: a sentence in the past tense is not automatically passive: «He ate the cake» is active, «The cake was eaten» is passive.

part of speech: noun (a quack, quacks); verb (quack, quacks, quacked, quacking); adjective (quack remedy)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A quack is the loud, harsh sound a duck makes; to quack means to make that sound. 2) A quack is a person who pretends to be a doctor or to have medical skill and sells fake cures. 3) (UK, Australia, slang) «The quack» can be a joking word for a real doctor.
its sense in the lessons: With young children, «quack quack» is the duck sound in songs like «Five Little Ducks». In science and health lessons, a quack sells «cures» that do not work, so we learn to check health claims and trust real doctors and evidence. Phrases: «quack doctor», «quack remedy», «quack medicine», «if it looks like a duck and quacks like a duck, it's a duck».
examples from the lessons: The ducks quacked loudly when we brought bread. | «Quack, quack!» went Mother Duck. | The quack sold bottles of coloured water as medicine. | Don't trust quack cures you see online. | I'm off to see the quack about my cough. (UK, slang) | If it looks like a duck and quacks like a duck, it probably is a duck.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: quacked, quacking. Calling a real doctor «a quack» is joking slang; calling someone a quack in earnest is an accusation of fraud. «Quackery» means fake medicine. Myth: a duck's quack does echo, despite the old story that it doesn't.

part of speech: noun (a raid, raids); verb (raid, raids, raided, raiding); noun: raider
meaning for a pupil: 1) A raid is a sudden attack on a place by soldiers, ships or aircraft. 2) A raid is a surprise visit by police to search a place or arrest people. 3) A raid is when robbers suddenly break in to steal: «a bank raid». 4) (informal) To raid something means to take a lot from it: «raid the fridge», «raid Mum's wardrobe». 5) (gaming) In online games, a raid is when many players team up to beat a big enemy.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, Viking raids on monasteries like Lindisfarne, and air raids in the Second World War (the Blitz, air-raid shelters, sirens) are key ideas. In news, police raid houses. In everyday talk, children raid the biscuit tin. Phrases: «air raid», «police raid», «raid the fridge», «Viking raiders», «dawn raid».
examples from the lessons: The Vikings raided the monastery and stole its gold. | During air raids, families hid in shelters. | Police raided the warehouse and found stolen phones. | My brother raided the fridge at midnight. | Robbers carried out a raid on the jewellery shop. | We joined a raid to beat the dragon boss in the game. | The air-raid siren wailed across the city.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: raided. Sounds like «rayd». Trap: «raid» (attack) and «rayed» are rare homophones; do not confuse with «ride» or «rate».

part of speech: noun (a vent, vents); verb (vent, vents, vented, venting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A vent is a small opening that lets air, smoke, steam or gas go in or out, like an air vent in a room or a car. 2) (science) A volcanic vent is the opening where lava, ash and gas come out; deep-sea vents (hydrothermal vents) let out hot water on the ocean floor. 3) To vent your feelings, especially anger, means to let them out by talking, shouting or crying: «She vented about her day». 4) A vent can also be a slit at the back or side of a coat or jacket.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, volcanoes have a main vent; hydrothermal vents on the sea floor support strange animals like giant tube worms with no sunlight at all. In daily life, keep vents clear, especially on gas heaters, for safety. In PSHE, venting to a trusted person can help feelings, but not by hurting others. Phrases: «air vent», «vent your anger», «give vent to», «hydrothermal vent».
examples from the lessons: Steam came out of the vent in the bathroom. | Lava poured out of the volcano's vent. | Strange creatures live around hot vents on the deep sea floor. | Don't block the air vents on the heater. | After the match, Jack vented to his dad about the unfair referee. | It helps to vent your feelings to a friend. | In the film, the spy crawled through the air vents.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: vented. «Give vent to» means let out strong feelings. Trap: to «vent at» someone means to dump your anger on them, which may be unfair.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A warthog is a wild pig of the African grasslands with a big flat head, long curved tusks, a thin mane and lumpy bumps on its face that look like warts.
its sense in the lessons: In nature lessons about the African savannah, warthogs graze on grass, kneel on their front knees to eat, dig for roots, and back into burrows (often old aardvark holes) so their tusks face out. They are eaten by lions, leopards and hyenas. Pumbaa in «The Lion King» is a warthog. Phrases: «a sounder of warthogs» (a group).
examples from the lessons: The warthog knelt down to eat the short grass. | Warthogs back into their burrows so their tusks face outwards. | Pumbaa from «The Lion King» is a warthog. | A warthog ran with its tail sticking straight up like an aerial. | The bumps on a warthog's face protect it in fights. | Lions sometimes hunt warthogs.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «warthogs». One word: wart + hog. The «warts» are not real warts but thick pads of skin. «Hog» is another word for pig.

part of speech: noun (a buffalo, buffalo or buffaloes or buffalos); verb (buffalo, US informal, rare = to confuse or bully)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A buffalo is a large wild or farmed animal of the cattle family with big curved horns, such as the African buffalo (Cape buffalo) or the water buffalo of Asia. 2) (North America) People often call the American bison a buffalo, though scientists say bison is the correct name. 3) Buffalo is a city in New York State, USA (a name).
its sense in the lessons: In geography and history lessons, the American bison («buffalo») was central to the life of Plains Native Americans, who used every part of it; huge herds were nearly wiped out by hunters, then protected. In Asia, water buffalo pull ploughs in rice fields and give milk (mozzarella was first made from buffalo milk). The African buffalo is one of the «Big Five» on safari. Phrases: «a herd of buffalo», «water buffalo», «buffalo wings» (spicy chicken from Buffalo city).
examples from the lessons: A herd of buffalo crossed the river. | Water buffalo pull ploughs in the rice fields. | The Plains peoples used every part of the buffalo. | The African buffalo is one of the Big Five animals. | Real mozzarella is made with buffalo milk. | The bison is often called a buffalo in America. | We ate buffalo wings at a party — it's chicken, not buffalo!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «buffalo», «buffaloes» or «buffalos»; a group is often just «buffalo». Trap: «buffalo wings» are chicken. Fun fact: «Buffalo buffalo Buffalo buffalo buffalo buffalo Buffalo buffalo» is a real (very confusing) grammatical English sentence.

part of speech: noun (a clump, clumps); verb (clump, clumps, clumped, clumping)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A clump is a small group of plants or trees growing close together: «a clump of daisies». 2) A clump is a lump or mass of something stuck together: «a clump of hair», «clumps of mud». 3) To clump, or clump together, means to stick together in lumps or gather in a group. 4) To clump means to walk with slow, heavy, noisy steps: «He clumped up the stairs in his boots».
its sense in the lessons: In science and nature lessons, plants like grasses and bulbs grow in clumps; in cooking, flour can clump if you don't stir. In stories, «clumping» footsteps tell you someone heavy or tired is walking. Phrases: «a clump of trees», «clump together», «clumping footsteps».
examples from the lessons: A clump of bluebells grew under the tree. | The cat left a clump of fur on the sofa. | Stir the porridge so it doesn't clump. | The children clumped together to keep warm. | We heard Dad clumping upstairs in his wellies. | Clumps of mud fell off my football boots. | The rabbits hid in a clump of long grass.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: clumped. Similar sounding: «clomp» (also heavy walking) and «lump». «Clumpy» describes things that form lumps or heavy shoes.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A finch is a small songbird with a short, strong, cone-shaped beak for cracking seeds, such as a goldfinch, chaffinch or greenfinch.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, Darwin's finches on the Galápagos Islands are a famous example of adaptation and evolution: different islands had finches with different beak shapes suited to different foods, which helped Charles Darwin develop his ideas. In gardens, finches come to bird feeders with seeds. Phrases: «Darwin's finches», «goldfinch», «chaffinch», «a charm of finches» (a group of goldfinches).
examples from the lessons: A goldfinch came to our bird feeder. | Finches crack seeds with their strong beaks. | Darwin studied the finches of the Galápagos Islands. | The chaffinch is one of the commonest birds in Britain. | Each kind of finch had a beak shaped for its food. | A group of goldfinches is called a charm.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «finches» (add -es after ch). Capital F for the surname Finch (e.g. Atticus Finch in a famous novel). Trap: not every small brown bird is a finch; sparrows are a different family.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A porpoise is a sea mammal like a small dolphin, with a short, round snout, a rounded head, a small triangular back fin and flat, spade-shaped teeth.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, porpoises are cetaceans, like whales and dolphins: they breathe air through a blowhole, are warm-blooded and feed their babies milk. The harbour porpoise lives around the coasts of Britain, Ireland and North America and is shy. The vaquita, a tiny porpoise in Mexico, is the most endangered sea mammal in the world, often caught in fishing nets. Phrases: «harbour porpoise», «a pod of porpoises».
examples from the lessons: We saw a porpoise from the ferry. | Porpoises are smaller than most dolphins. | A porpoise breathes through a blowhole on top of its head. | Harbour porpoises live in the cold seas around Britain. | The vaquita is a porpoise that is nearly extinct. | Porpoises hunt fish using echoes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «porpoises». Spelling: por-poise; say POR-pus. Trap: «purpose» (a reason or aim) sounds similar but is a different word. Porpoise vs dolphin: porpoises have rounded snouts and spade-shaped teeth; most dolphins have a beak-like snout and cone-shaped teeth.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A referendum is a vote in which all the voters of a country or area decide one important question directly, usually by answering yes or no.
its sense in the lessons: In citizenship and politics lessons, a referendum is direct democracy: instead of choosing people to decide for them, citizens decide the question themselves. Examples: the Brexit referendum in the UK on leaving the European Union, the Scottish independence referendum, Ireland's referendums to change its constitution, and Australia's referendums. Results can be close and split families and friends, so arguing politely matters. Phrases: «hold a referendum», «vote in a referendum», «referendum result».
examples from the lessons: The country held a referendum on whether to change the voting system. | In a referendum, every voter answers the same question. | The Brexit referendum asked if the UK should leave the European Union. | Ireland must hold a referendum to change its constitution. | The result of the referendum was very close. | Our school had a mini referendum on whether to have a uniform-free day.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «referendums» (most common) or «referenda». Trap: an election chooses people; a referendum decides a question. In maths terms, a referendum is usually won by more than half of the votes cast (a simple majority), though some need more.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Webbed feet or toes have skin joining the toes together, like ducks, frogs and otters, which helps them swim. 2) Webbed can also mean covered with or made like a web.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons webbed feet are a classic adaptation for swimming: they work like paddles, pushing more water. Ducks, geese, swans, penguins, frogs, platypuses and otters have them; divers wear flippers to copy this. Some people are born with slightly webbed toes, which is usually harmless. Phrases: «webbed feet», «webbed toes».
examples from the lessons: Ducks have webbed feet for paddling. | A frog's webbed back feet help it swim fast. | Flippers give divers webbed feet. | The platypus has webbed front feet. | Otters swim well with their webbed paws. | The penguin waddled on its webbed feet.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective only (from «web»). Spelled with double b: webbed. Trap: «webbed» has nothing to do with the World Wide Web; a website is not «webbed».

part of speech: French adjective (bleu, bleue, bleus, bleues); not an English word
meaning for a pupil: 1) (French) «Bleu» means «blue»: «le ciel bleu» = the blue sky. It sounds roughly like «bluh» (lips rounded), and it is not an English word. 2) (cooking) In English menus, «bleu» or «blue» describes a steak cooked very rare, only seared outside. 3) «Cordon bleu» means top-class cooking, and «bleu cheese» is an American spelling of «blue cheese».
its sense in the lessons: In French lessons «bleu» is a colour word learned with «rouge» (red), «vert» (green) and «jaune» (yellow); the French flag is «bleu, blanc, rouge». In French, colour words usually come after the noun and change for feminine and plural: «une robe bleue». Phrases: «bleu, blanc, rouge», «cordon bleu», «bleu cheese».
examples from the lessons: In French, «bleu» means blue. | «Mon sac est bleu» means «My bag is blue». | The French flag is «bleu, blanc, rouge». | «Une voiture bleue» has an extra e because «voiture» is feminine. | Grandad likes his steak «bleu», almost raw. | She trained as a cordon bleu chef. | The menu said «bleu cheese dressing».
note for the reader of a maths problem: French only; forms: bleu (m.), bleue (f.), bleus, bleues. The final «eu» has no exact English sound. Trap: in English write «blue»; «bleu» in English is only in borrowed phrases.

part of speech: noun (abbreviation: Ed., ed., eds.); also a name (Ed); verb ending -ed
meaning for a pupil: 1) «Ed» is short for education: «PE» is physical education, «sex ed» means sex education, «special ed» special education (informal, US). 2) «Ed.» or «ed.» is short for editor or edition in books: «3rd ed.», «ed. by». 3) Ed is a boy's name, short for Edward, Edmund or Edwin (a name). 4) «-ed» is the ending added to regular verbs to make the past tense: play → played.
its sense in the lessons: In school life «Ed» appears in phrases like «driver's ed» and «phys ed» (US, informal). In books and references, «ed.» tells you who edited a book or which edition it is. In grammar lessons, «-ed» marks the past: walked, jumped, wanted; it can sound like /t/ (jumped), /d/ (played) or /id/ (wanted). Phrases: «phys ed», «sex ed», «adult ed», «2nd ed.».
examples from the lessons: We have phys ed on Fridays. (US, informal) | The book's second ed. has new pictures. | Ed. by means the person who edited the book. | My uncle Ed is a firefighter. | Add «-ed» to make the past tense: jump → jumped. | Older students take driver's ed before they drive. (US)
note for the reader of a maths problem: As an abbreviation it is informal or used in references; write «education», «editor», «edition» in full in essays. Capital E for the name. Trap: not all verbs take «-ed»: go → went, see → saw (irregular verbs).

part of speech: verb (huddle, huddles, huddled, huddling); noun (a huddle, huddles)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To huddle means to crowd close together, usually to keep warm, to feel safe or to talk secretly. 2) To huddle can also mean to curl your body up small: «huddled under a blanket». 3) A huddle is a small, close group of people or animals; in sports, a team huddle is when players gather close to plan.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, emperor penguins huddle together through the freezing Antarctic winter, taking turns on the cold outside. In stories, «huddled» shows cold, fear or secrecy: «the children huddled round the fire». In PE and American football, teams go into a huddle to plan the next play. Phrases: «huddle together», «huddle round», «in a huddle», «huddled up».
examples from the lessons: The penguins huddled together to keep warm. | We huddled round the campfire and told stories. | The kittens huddled in a corner of the box. | The team went into a huddle before the second half. | She sat huddled under a blanket during the storm. | The friends huddled in a corner to share a secret. | Sheep huddle against a wall in heavy snow.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: huddled (drop the e, add -d). Often with «together», «round» or «up». Similar: «cuddle» (hug lovingly) — different meaning; «huddle» is about crowding close.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A marmot is a large, plump ground squirrel that lives in mountains and grasslands of Europe, Asia and North America, digs burrows and hibernates through the winter.
its sense in the lessons: In nature lessons marmots show hibernation: they sleep for up to eight months, their heartbeat slowing right down. Alpine marmots in the Alps whistle loudly to warn others of eagles or foxes. The groundhog (woodchuck) of North America is a kind of marmot — on Groundhog Day, Americans and Canadians watch one to «predict» the end of winter, just for fun. Phrases: «Alpine marmot», «sleep like a marmot».
examples from the lessons: A marmot whistled to warn the others of an eagle. | Marmots hibernate in burrows all winter. | We saw marmots sunbathing on rocks in the Alps. | The groundhog is a kind of marmot. | Marmots live in family groups. | A marmot is about the size of a big cat.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «marmots». Say MAR-mut. Myth: the groundhog cannot really forecast the weather; it's a fun tradition.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A palindrome is a word, number or sentence that reads the same backwards as forwards, like «level», «racecar», «12321» or «Was it a car or a cat I saw?»
its sense in the lessons: In English and maths lessons and puzzles, palindromes are fun: words (mum, dad, noon, kayak, civic), names (Anna, Otto, Hannah) and sentences («Never odd or even»), where spaces and punctuation are ignored. In maths, palindromic numbers read the same both ways (121, 4004, 12321); a puzzle: reverse a number and add it to itself again and again until you get a palindrome (e.g. 56 + 65 = 121). Phrases: «palindromic numbers», «a palindrome puzzle».
examples from the lessons: «Level» is a palindrome. | My name, Hannah, is a palindrome. | 12321 is a palindromic number. | «Never odd or even» is a palindrome sentence. | Can you write a palindrome that is a whole sentence? | 47 + 74 = 121, and 121 is a palindrome. | «Kayak» reads the same backwards and forwards. | Madam, in Eden, I'm Adam.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «palindromes». In sentence palindromes, spaces, capitals and punctuation are usually ignored. In maths, a palindromic number has the same digits in reverse order; every one-digit number is a palindrome. Trap: «stressed» → «desserts» is a reversal of two different words (a «semordnilap»), not a palindrome.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Spinach is a dark green leafy vegetable that can be eaten raw in salads or cooked.
its sense in the lessons: In food and health lessons, spinach is a healthy vegetable with vitamins (A, C, K), folate and iron. In cartoons, Popeye the Sailor eats a can of spinach to get super strong. Spinach shrinks a lot when cooked. Phrases: «baby spinach», «spinach leaves», «spinach and ricotta».
examples from the lessons: Mum puts spinach in the pasta sauce. | Popeye eats spinach to get strong. | A big pile of spinach shrinks to a small spoonful when you cook it. | We grew spinach in the school garden. | Baby spinach is nice in a salad. | Spinach has lots of vitamins.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «some spinach», not «a spinach» or «spinaches». Say SPIN-itch. Myth: spinach is not unusually high in iron; an old story says a decimal-point mistake made people think so, but that story is itself doubtful. Also, the iron in spinach is not easy for the body to take in.

part of speech: noun (a tardigrade, tardigrades); also called water bear, moss piglet
meaning for a pupil: 1) A tardigrade is a tiny, eight-legged animal, usually less than 1 millimetre long, that lives in water, moss and soil and can survive extreme conditions.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons tardigrades amaze pupils: you need a microscope to see them; they look like chubby little bears with claws. When their home dries out they curl into a dry «tun» and can survive freezing, boiling, crushing pressure, radiation and even outer space for a while, then come back to life when wet. They live almost everywhere, from mountaintops to the deep sea. The name means «slow walker». Phrases: «water bear», «moss piglet».
examples from the lessons: A tardigrade is smaller than a full stop. | Tardigrades are also called water bears. | We looked for tardigrades in wet moss with a microscope. | Tardigrades survived a trip into outer space. | A dried-out tardigrade can come back to life in water. | Tardigrades have eight stubby legs with claws.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «tardigrades». Say TAR-di-grade. Trap: they are tough, but not indestructible; they can be killed, and they are not really bears or pigs.

part of speech: noun (a teaspoon, teaspoons); also teaspoonful (a teaspoonful); abbreviation tsp
meaning for a pupil: 1) A teaspoon is a small spoon used for stirring tea or coffee and for eating some foods. 2) A teaspoon, or teaspoonful, is the amount a teaspoon holds, used as a measure in cooking and for medicine: about 5 millilitres.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and cooking, recipes use «tsp» (teaspoon) and «tbsp» (tablespoon); 3 teaspoons make 1 tablespoon. A medicine teaspoon is exactly 5 ml; safety: use the measuring spoon or syringe that comes with medicine, not a kitchen spoon, because kitchen spoons vary. A «level teaspoon» is flat on top; a «heaped teaspoon» has a pile. Phrases: «a level teaspoon», «a heaped teaspoon», «tsp».
examples from the lessons: Add one teaspoon of salt to the water. | Stir your tea with a teaspoon. | The medicine dose is one 5 ml spoonful, like a teaspoon. | Three teaspoons make one tablespoon. | The recipe says ½ tsp baking powder. | Use a level teaspoon of sugar, not a heaped one. | If 1 teaspoon holds 5 ml, then 4 teaspoons hold 20 ml.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «teaspoons»; for the amount also «teaspoonful(s)». Abbreviation «tsp» (small t), tablespoon «tbsp» or «Tbsp». Maths: 1 teaspoon = 5 ml, 1 tablespoon = 15 ml (Australia uses a 20 ml tablespoon, so 4 teaspoons).

part of speech: noun and number (a trillion, trillions; two trillion); adjective (trillionth)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A trillion is a million millions: 1,000,000,000,000, or 10 to the power of 12 — a 1 followed by 12 zeros. 2) (informal) «Trillions» means an enormous, uncountable number: «I've told you trillions of times!»
its sense in the lessons: In maths lessons place value grows: thousand (3 zeros), million (6), billion (9), trillion (12). Trillions come up in science and money: the human body has about 30 trillion cells; there are hundreds of billions to trillions of trees on Earth; whole countries' economies are measured in trillions of dollars or pounds. Phrases: «a trillion dollars», «trillions of stars», «one in a trillion».
examples from the lessons: A trillion is a thousand billion. | The human body is made of trillions of cells. | Write one trillion in digits: 1,000,000,000,000. | Counting to a trillion, one number a second, would take over 30,000 years. | Some countries' economies are worth trillions of dollars. | There are trillions of tiny bacteria in your gut. | I've asked you a trillion times to tidy your room! (informal)
note for the reader of a maths problem: After a number, «trillion» has no s: «three trillion», but «trillions of». Today in English a trillion = 10^12 (a million million). Trap: long ago in Britain «billion» meant a million million and «trillion» a million million million; old books may use these. In some other languages (like French «billion») the word means 10^12, so check translations. Maths: 1 trillion = 1,000 billion = 1,000,000 million.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An armadillo is a small mammal from the Americas with a body covered in hard, bony plates like armour, which digs for insects with strong claws.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons armadillos show protection adaptations: their shell is made of bony plates covered in tough skin. Only the three-banded armadillo can roll fully into a ball; others run or dig to escape. The nine-banded armadillo almost always has identical quadruplets. The name is Spanish for «little armoured one». Phrases: «roll up like an armadillo», «nine-banded armadillo», «giant armadillo».
examples from the lessons: The armadillo rolled into a tight ball. | Armadillos dig for ants and termites with their claws. | The name «armadillo» means «little armoured one» in Spanish. | Nine-banded armadillos usually have four identical babies. | An armadillo's shell is made of bony plates. | Armadillos live in Texas and South America. | The giant armadillo is as long as a child is tall.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «armadillos». Use «an»: «an armadillo». Myth: most armadillos cannot roll into a ball; only the three-banded ones can.

part of speech: noun (a critic, critics); related: criticise (UK) / criticize (US), criticism, critical
meaning for a pupil: 1) A critic is a person whose job is to give opinions about films, books, music, food, art or plays, often in newspapers, magazines or online. 2) A critic is someone who says what they think is wrong or bad about a person, idea or plan: «critics of the new rule». 3) (informal) «Everyone's a critic» is a joke said when someone complains about your work.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons, pupils write reviews like a critic: give a star rating and reasons with evidence. In news and politics, critics argue against a decision, and fair reports give both supporters' and critics' views. Being critical can mean thinking carefully («critical thinking»), not only being negative. Phrases: «film critic», «food critic», «a harsh critic», «a fierce critic of», «your own worst critic».
examples from the lessons: The film critic gave the movie five stars. | A food critic visited our local restaurant. | Critics of the plan said it would cost too much. | Don't be your own worst critic — your drawing is good! | «Everyone's a critic!» laughed Dad when we didn't like his soup. | The book was loved by readers but not by critics.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «critics». Say KRIT-ik. Trap: «critic» is a person; «criticism» is what they say; «critique» (cri-TEEK) is a careful written judgement. «Critical» can also mean very serious («in a critical condition»).

meaning for a pupil: 1) An opossum is a North and South American marsupial about the size of a cat, with a pointed white face, bare ears and a long, bare tail that can grip branches. 2) In Australia and New Zealand, «possum» is a different marsupial: a furry tree animal like the brushtail possum.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons opossums are the only marsupials (mammals with a pouch) in North America; babies, born tiny, grow in the mother's pouch and later ride on her back. When scared, an opossum may «play dead» — it falls over, lies still and smells bad — the origin of the phrase «playing possum». In New Zealand, introduced Australian possums are pests that damage forests and birds. Phrases: «play possum», «Virginia opossum».
