examples from the lessons: The opossum hung from the branch by its tail. | A mother opossum carried her babies on her back. | The opossum played dead when the dog sniffed it. | «Playing possum» means pretending to be asleep or dead. | Opossums are the only marsupials in North America. | In Australia, a brushtail possum lived in our roof!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «opossums». Use «an»: «an opossum». In North America people often drop the o and say «possum». Trap: American opossums and Australian possums are different animals, though both are marsupials. Myth: opossums don't hang by their tails to sleep.

part of speech: noun (a premier, premiers); adjective (premier, formal: best, most important)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A premier is the leader of a government, especially a prime minister; in Canada and Australia, a premier leads a province or state government. 2) Premier (adjective) means the best, the most important or the first: «a premier hotel», «the Premier League». 3) A premier league or division is the top level of a sport.
its sense in the lessons: In citizenship lessons in Canada and Australia, the premier of each province or state (e.g. the Premier of Ontario, the Premier of New South Wales) is different from the national prime minister. In sport, the English Premier League is the top football league. Phrases: «the Premier League», «state premier», «premier division».
examples from the lessons: The Premier of Queensland spoke about the floods. | Ontario's premier met the prime minister of Canada. | Our team wants to play in the Premier League one day. | This is the premier event of the school year. | The Chinese premier visited Europe. | The premier division is the highest level of the league.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «premiers». Say PREM-ee-er (UK) or pruh-MEER (US). Trap: «premiere» (with an e at the end) is the first showing of a film or play: «the film's premiere». «Premier» = leader or best; «premiere» = first show.

part of speech: noun (a pufferfish, pufferfish or pufferfishes); also puffer, blowfish
meaning for a pupil: 1) A pufferfish is a fish that can quickly swallow water to blow itself up into a big, round, often spiky ball to scare off predators. Many kinds are very poisonous.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons pufferfish show defence adaptations: puffing up makes them hard to swallow, and many contain a strong poison (tetrodotoxin) that has no known antidote. In Japan, pufferfish (fugu) is eaten as a delicacy, prepared only by specially trained chefs. Some male pufferfish make beautiful circle patterns in the sand to attract females. Phrases: «puff up like a pufferfish», «fugu».
examples from the lessons: The pufferfish blew itself up into a spiky ball. | Many pufferfish are poisonous to eat. | In Japan, only licensed chefs may prepare pufferfish. | A male pufferfish drew a circle pattern in the sand. | Puffing up makes the pufferfish too big for most predators to swallow. | We saw a pufferfish while snorkelling in Australia.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural usually «pufferfish», sometimes «pufferfishes». Also called «blowfish» or «puffer». Safety: never touch or eat a pufferfish you find on a beach.

part of speech: proper noun (Qing — a Chinese dynasty, a name); Mandarin pinyin syllable (qīng, qíng, qǐng, qìng); not an English word
meaning for a pupil: 1) (a name) The Qing was the last dynasty of emperors to rule China, founded by the Manchu people; it ended when China became a republic. 2) (Mandarin, pinyin) «Qing» is a Mandarin syllable whose meaning depends on its tone: «qǐng» = please or to invite, «qīng» = clear or light, «qíng» = feeling or sunny (weather). In pinyin, «q» sounds like English «ch», so «qing» sounds like «ching». It is not an English word.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons the Qing dynasty is the time of China's last emperors, the Forbidden City in Beijing, the Opium Wars with Britain and the Boxer Rebellion; the last emperor, Puyi, became emperor as a small child. In Mandarin lessons, «qǐng» (please) is a polite word: «qǐng zuò» = please sit down, «qǐng wèn» = may I ask. «Qingming» is a festival when families sweep their ancestors' graves. Phrases: «the Qing dynasty», «qǐng wèn», «Qingming Festival».
examples from the lessons: The Qing dynasty was the last royal dynasty of China. | Qing emperors lived in the Forbidden City. | The last Qing emperor was only a little boy when he took the throne. | In Mandarin, «qǐng» means «please». | «Qǐng wèn» means «excuse me, may I ask?» | In pinyin, «q» sounds like «ch», so «Qing» sounds like «Ching». | Families sweep graves at the Qingming Festival.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital Q for the dynasty: «the Qing dynasty» (older spelling «Ch'ing»). In pinyin, tone marks change the meaning, and the q is never followed by a u as in English. Not an English word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A settler is a person who moves to a new place, often far away, to live there for good and make a home. 2) In history, settlers were people who came from another country and took land to farm and build towns, often where other peoples already lived. 3) (rare) Something that settles a matter, like a final point that ends an argument.
its sense in the lessons: In history and geography lessons settlers are the people who arrived in new lands, such as Europeans in North America, Australia and New Zealand; lessons talk about what they built and also about the harm done to the First Nations, Aboriginal and Māori peoples whose land was taken. In stories a settler is often brave, hard-working and poor, living in a log cabin or a hut. Phrases: early settlers, the first settlers, European settlers, settler families, settler colony.
examples from the lessons: The first settlers built their houses out of logs. | My great-great-grandparents were settlers who came to Canada by ship. | The settlers cleared the forest to plant wheat. | Many settlers did not survive their first winter. | The land the settlers farmed had belonged to Aboriginal people for thousands of years. | In our project we wrote a diary as if we were settlers in New Zealand. | The settlers traded tools for food with the local people. | A new settler arrived in the village every spring.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: one settler, two settlers. Comes from the verb «settle» (to make a home somewhere) + «-er» (a person who does it). Do not confuse with «settlement» (the place or village they make) or «settlor» (a law word for someone who sets up a trust). Settlers are not the same as explorers: explorers travel and look around, settlers stay. Remember that «settling» land was often taking it from people who already lived there.

part of speech: noun (a yuan, yuan; plural usually the same: ten yuan)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The yuan is the money of China; one yuan is divided into ten jiao or a hundred fen. 2) The Yuan (with a capital Y) was a dynasty, a family of rulers, that ruled China, started by the Mongol leader Kublai Khan. 3) (Mandarin, pinyin) «yuán» also means «round» or «first, original» in Chinese; as money it sounds like «yoo-AN» to an English ear.
its sense in the lessons: In maths problems about money around the world, prices may be given in yuan instead of dollars or pounds, and you may have to change one currency into another with an exchange rate. In geography and history lessons about China, the Yuan dynasty is the time when the Mongols ruled. Phrases: Chinese yuan, ten yuan, the Yuan dynasty, renminbi (the official name of the money).
examples from the lessons: A bowl of noodles cost twenty yuan in Beijing. | The yuan is the money used in China. | If one pound buys nine yuan, how many yuan do you get for five pounds? | Grandad brought back some yuan notes with Mao's face on them. | Kublai Khan started the Yuan dynasty. | Marco Polo is said to have visited China during the Yuan dynasty. | She paid with her phone, not with yuan coins. | The shop sign showed the price in yuan.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The plural is usually the same: «one yuan, fifty yuan» (not «yuans», though you may see it). Pronounced «yoo-AN». The official name of China's money is «renminbi» (RMB); «yuan» is its unit, a bit like «sterling» and «pound». The symbol is ¥, the same sign as the Japanese yen, so check which country a price is from. In maths: to change yuan to another money, multiply or divide by the exchange rate given in the problem.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An anaconda is a very large snake from South America that lives in and near rivers and swamps. 2) The green anaconda is the heaviest snake in the world; it is not venomous but kills its prey by squeezing it until it cannot breathe, then swallows it whole.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about rainforests and food chains the anaconda is a top predator of the Amazon that eats fish, birds, capybaras and even caimans. In stories and films it is a scary giant snake, though real anacondas almost never attack people. Phrases: green anaconda, giant anaconda, a constrictor snake.
examples from the lessons: An anaconda can stay under water for a long time. | The green anaconda lives in the Amazon rainforest. | Anacondas squeeze their prey instead of biting with venom. | We saw an anaconda sleeping in the warm pool at the zoo. | An anaconda can swallow an animal bigger than its own head. | The anaconda's eyes sit high on its head so it can see above the water. | In the film the anaconda was much bigger than any real snake. | Baby anacondas are born live, not hatched from eggs outside.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: an anaconda (use «an» because it starts with a vowel sound), two anacondas. Trap: the green anaconda is the heaviest snake, but the reticulated python can be longer. Anacondas are constrictors, not venomous snakes: they squeeze, they do not poison. Myth: films show anacondas hunting people, but this is very rare in real life.

part of speech: noun (a conquest, conquests; also uncountable: conquest)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Conquest is taking control of a country, city or people by force, usually in a war. 2) A conquest is a place or land that has been taken this way. 3) Conquest can mean beating a very hard challenge, like the conquest of a mountain or of a disease. 4) (informal, old-fashioned) A conquest can be a person someone has won the love of, said in a boastful way.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons you meet the Norman Conquest of England, the Roman conquest of Britain and the Spanish conquest of the Aztecs and Incas; lessons ask why people conquered others and what happened to the conquered. In science and adventure stories «the conquest of space» or «the conquest of Everest» means a great achievement. Phrases: the Norman Conquest, conquest of, wars of conquest, a new conquest.
examples from the lessons: The Norman Conquest changed the English language for ever. | The Romans began their conquest of Britain with a large army. | Spain's conquest of the Aztec Empire brought terrible suffering. | Climbing Everest was the greatest conquest of his life. | The conquest of smallpox is one of medicine's big wins. | The king boasted about his new conquest. | The conquest of space started with tiny satellites. | Many people died during the conquest.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun from the verb «conquer» (to take by force, or to beat a problem). Pronounced «KONG-kwest». The person who conquers is a «conqueror»; William the Conqueror led the Norman Conquest. Capital C in «the Norman Conquest» because it is the name of an event. Do not mix up «conquest» (the act) and «conquer» (the verb): «They conquered the land» but «The conquest of the land».

part of speech: noun (an eggshell, eggshells); adjective (eggshell colour, eggshell paint)
meaning for a pupil: 1) An eggshell is the hard thin outside cover of an egg, which breaks easily. 2) Eggshell is a very pale off-white colour, like the inside of an egg's shell. 3) Eggshell paint is paint with a soft, slightly shiny finish. 4) «Walking on eggshells» means being very careful not to upset someone who gets angry or hurt easily.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons eggshells are used to show that they are made of calcium carbonate, which fizzes in vinegar, and that a curved shell is surprisingly strong when pushed evenly. In cooking you must not get bits of eggshell in the cake mix; eggshells can go in the compost. The phrase «walking on eggshells» shows a tense feeling at home or in class. Phrases: crack the eggshell, bits of eggshell, eggshell white, walking on eggshells.
examples from the lessons: She picked a bit of eggshell out of the pancake batter. | We put the eggshells in the compost bin. | The chick pecked its way out of the eggshell. | We soaked an egg in vinegar until the eggshell disappeared. | Mum painted the hall in eggshell white. | Everyone was walking on eggshells after the big argument. | An eggshell is mostly made of calcium. | You can grow cress seeds in an empty eggshell.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one eggshell, many eggshells; also written as two words, «egg shell», but «eggshell» is more usual. Fun science fact: an eggshell is hard to crush when you squeeze it from both ends, because the dome shape spreads the push; it breaks easily on an edge. «Walking on eggshells» is an idiom, not about real eggs.

part of speech: noun (a hyphen, hyphens); verb (hyphenate — to join with a hyphen)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A hyphen is a short line (-) used to join words or parts of words together, as in «well-known» or «twenty-one». 2) A hyphen is also used at the end of a line when a word is split and goes on to the next line.
its sense in the lessons: In English grammar and punctuation lessons (and SATs) you learn to use hyphens in compound numbers (thirty-four), in compound adjectives before a noun (a man-eating shark), with some prefixes (re-enter, co-owner) and to avoid confusion (re-cover a sofa versus recover from illness). In writing a hyphen can change the meaning: «a little-used car» and «a little used car» are different. Phrases: use a hyphen, joined by a hyphen, hyphenated word.
examples from the lessons: Twenty-one has a hyphen in it. | Put a hyphen in «well-known» when it comes before a noun. | The word was too long, so the printer split it with a hyphen. | My name is double-barrelled, with a hyphen in the middle. | Is «e-mail» written with a hyphen or without? | A man-eating shark is different from a man eating shark! | Re-enter has a hyphen so the two e's do not run together. | The teacher circled the missing hyphen.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a hyphen, two hyphens. Pronounced «HY-fen». Trap: a hyphen (-) is shorter than a dash (– or —); a hyphen joins words, a dash separates parts of a sentence and has spaces around it in UK style. Do not confuse the hyphen with the minus sign in maths, which looks similar but means subtract. Compound numbers from twenty-one to ninety-nine take a hyphen.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A pendulum is a weight hanging from a fixed point on a string or rod, which swings backwards and forwards. 2) The swinging part of some old clocks, like a grandfather clock, which keeps the clock on time. 3) The idea of something changing from one extreme to the other and back again, like the «pendulum of opinion».
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons pupils make a pendulum with string and a weight, time its swings with a stopwatch and find that the length of the string changes how long one swing takes, while the weight hardly does; it is a classic fair test. In stories a ticking pendulum clock adds a spooky or calm feeling. Phrases: swing like a pendulum, the pendulum swings, pendulum clock, the pendulum of a clock.
examples from the lessons: The pendulum of the grandfather clock swung slowly. | We timed ten swings of the pendulum and divided by ten. | A longer pendulum swings more slowly. | Changing the weight did not change the pendulum's time much. | Galileo noticed a lamp swinging like a pendulum in a church. | The hypnotist swung a watch like a pendulum. | The pendulum of fashion has swung back to wide trousers. | A playground swing is a kind of pendulum.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one pendulum, two pendulums (the Latin plural «pendula» is very rare). Pronounced «PEN-dyoo-lum» or «PEN-juh-lum». In science investigations: to measure the time of one swing more accurately, time ten swings and divide by 10. Trap: many children guess a heavier weight swings faster, but the length of the string matters, not the weight.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A porcupine is a large rodent covered in long sharp spines called quills, which protect it from enemies. 2) There are two main groups: tree-climbing porcupines in the Americas and ground-living ones in Africa, Asia and southern Europe.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about animal adaptations, the porcupine shows defence: its quills come out easily and stick into a predator. In stories a porcupine is prickly, grumpy or hard to hug. Phrases: porcupine quills, prickly as a porcupine.
examples from the lessons: A porcupine raises its quills when it feels scared. | The dog came home with porcupine quills in its nose. | Porcupines eat bark, leaves and fruit. | A baby porcupine is called a porcupette. | The porcupine climbed a tree to escape the fox. | Porcupines cannot shoot their quills, despite the myth. | My little brother's hair stuck up like a porcupine after his nap. | We read a story about a porcupine who wanted a hug.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one porcupine, two porcupines. Myth: porcupines do not shoot or throw their quills; the quills come off when touched. Do not confuse with a hedgehog (smaller, an insectivore not a rodent, with short spines, lives in the UK and Europe) or an echidna (an Australian egg-laying mammal with spines). The name comes from old words meaning «spiny pig», though it is not a pig.

part of speech: noun (a profile, profiles); verb (profile, profiles, profiled, profiling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A profile is the side view of a face or head, especially its outline. 2) A profile is a short description of a person, place or company, telling the main facts about them. 3) On a website, app or game, your profile is the page with your name, picture and information. 4) To profile someone is to write or collect a description of them; in police work it means guessing what kind of person did a crime. 5) «Keep a low profile» means try not to be noticed; a «high profile» means being well known.
its sense in the lessons: In art lessons you draw a portrait in profile, from the side. In online safety lessons you learn to keep your profile private, not to share your address or school, and that a profile picture may not show who someone really is. In geography a «profile» can be a cross-section drawing of a river or hill. Phrases: profile picture, in profile, keep a low profile, high-profile, a profile of.
examples from the lessons: She drew her friend's face in profile. | Set your profile to private so strangers cannot see it. | His profile picture was a cartoon cat. | The newspaper wrote a profile of the new head teacher. | The famous footballer is keeping a low profile after the match. | We drew a profile of the river from its source to the sea. | It was a high-profile case on the news. | Never put your home address on your profile.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: a profile, profiles. Pronounced «PRO-file». As a verb: «The magazine profiled the young inventor.» Online safety: someone's profile can be fake, so a person who says they are ten may not be. «High-profile» before a noun has a hyphen: a high-profile visit.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A rover is a vehicle that drives around on the surface of another planet or the Moon to explore it, like the Mars rovers. 2) A rover is a person or animal that wanders from place to place. 3) Rover is an old-fashioned common name for a pet dog, used in jokes and stories. 4) A Rover Scout is an older member of the Scouts in some countries.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about space, rovers such as Curiosity and Perseverance drive on Mars, take photos, drill rocks and look for signs of water and past life; they are robots controlled from Earth. In stories «Rover» is the dog's name and «a rover» is a traveller with no home. Phrases: Mars rover, lunar rover, a roving reporter.
examples from the lessons: The rover took photos of red rocks on Mars. | Engineers on Earth send instructions to the rover. | A message takes minutes to travel from Earth to the rover. | The lunar rover carried astronauts across the Moon. | We built a model rover out of a shoebox and bottle tops. | The old sailor had been a rover all his life. | «Come here, Rover!» called the farmer. | The rover's wheels got stuck in the sand.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one rover, two rovers. Comes from the verb «rove», meaning to wander. Names of real rovers have capitals (Curiosity, Perseverance). Fact: rovers move very slowly and cannot be steered live with a joystick, because signals take several minutes to reach Mars. Land Rover is a car brand, a name.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An academy is a school or college, often one that trains people in a special skill, such as music, dance, football or the police. 2) In England an academy is a kind of state school paid for by the government but run by a trust instead of the local council. 3) An academy can be a society of famous experts in science or art, such as a national academy of sciences. 4) In ancient Greece the Academy was the school of the philosopher Plato.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life an academy is where you train: a football academy, a dance academy, a drama academy. UK children often go to schools with «Academy» in their names. In history lessons about ancient Greece you meet Plato's Academy. Phrases: football academy, police academy, the Royal Academy, an academy school, the Academy Awards (the Oscars).
examples from the lessons: My cousin trains at a football academy on Saturdays. | Our school became an academy last year. | She won a place at a ballet academy. | Plato taught at the Academy in Athens. | The Academy of Sciences gave her a prize. | The Royal Academy shows paintings in London. | He wants to join the police academy when he grows up. | The film won three Academy Awards.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: an academy (use «an»), two academies (y changes to ies). Pronounced «uh-KAD-uh-mee». Related word: «academic» (about school learning or university). Capital A when part of a name (Riverside Academy). Trap: in the US «academy» often means a private school; in England it is usually a state school with its own trust.

part of speech: noun (alliteration, uncountable; an alliteration, alliterations — an example of it)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Alliteration is when several words close together start with the same sound, like «Peter Piper picked a peck of pickled peppers». 2) An alliteration is one example of this in a poem, story, title or slogan.
its sense in the lessons: In English and poetry lessons alliteration is a technique pupils spot and use to make writing fun to read aloud, memorable or dramatic: «the slithering, slimy snake». Tongue-twisters, brand names (Coca-Cola, PayPal) and cartoon names (Mickey Mouse, Peppa Pig) use it. In reading tests you may be asked to find and name it and say what effect it has. Phrases: use alliteration, an example of alliteration.
examples from the lessons: «Silly Sally swiftly shooed seven sheep» is alliteration. | The poet used alliteration to make the wind sound wild. | Peppa Pig and Donald Duck have alliterative names. | Find two examples of alliteration in the poem. | Our class wrote alliteration about animals: «busy buzzing bees». | Alliteration makes slogans easy to remember. | The headline «Messi's Magic Moment» uses alliteration. | Too much alliteration can make a sentence sound silly.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly uncountable: «The poem uses alliteration.» Adjective: «alliterative». Trap: alliteration is about the first SOUND, not the first letter: «cat» and «king» alliterate (both /k/), but «cat» and «cello» do not. Do not confuse with rhyme (same ending sounds: cat, hat) or assonance (same vowel sounds inside words) or onomatopoeia (words that sound like the noise they name).

part of speech: adjective (casual; more casual, most casual); noun (a casual, casuals — a casual worker, informal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Casual clothes are relaxed, comfortable everyday clothes, not smart or formal ones. 2) Casual means relaxed and not seeming to care much or not making an effort: a casual wave, a casual chat. 3) Casual can mean happening by chance or without a plan: a casual meeting. 4) A casual job or worker is one that is not regular or permanent, done only now and then. 5) (UK, slang) A «casual» can be a member of a football fan group known for wearing designer clothes; and «casual» (gaming slang) is a player who plays just for fun.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life «casual» describes clothes and mood: non-uniform day is a casual day, «smart casual» is a dress code. In stories it shows a character trying to look relaxed: «He gave a casual shrug, but his heart was pounding.» Phrases: casual clothes, dress-down / casual Friday, smart casual, a casual job, casual remark, casual gamer, casually.
examples from the lessons: We can wear casual clothes on Friday for charity. | She tried to sound casual, but she was really nervous. | It was just a casual chat at the bus stop. | Dad has a casual job at the market on Saturdays. | He gave a casual wave as he walked past. | The party is casual, so jeans are fine. | I'm only a casual gamer; I play on weekends. | A casual remark can still hurt someone's feelings.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: casual, more casual, most casual; adverb «casually» (She walked casually away). Pronounced «KAZH-yoo-ul». Do not confuse with «causal» (about cause, as in cause and effect) — the letters u and a are swapped. Also do not confuse with «casualty» (a person hurt or killed in an accident or war; in the UK also the hospital emergency department).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Colouration is the pattern and mix of colours on an animal or plant, such as the stripes of a tiger or the spots on a ladybird. 2) Colouration can mean the way something is coloured in general, including a slight colour or tint.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about adaptation, colouration helps animals survive: camouflage colouration hides them (a stick insect, a snowy owl), and warning colouration tells predators «I am poisonous» (a poison dart frog, a wasp's yellow and black). Some animals copy the warning colours of others (mimicry). Phrases: warning colouration, camouflage colouration, bright colouration, protective colouration.
examples from the lessons: The snake's bright colouration warns birds to stay away. | The moth's colouration matches the tree bark. | Male birds often have brighter colouration than females. | The frog's colouration changes as it grows. | Warning colouration is common in poisonous animals. | The leaf's colouration turned red and gold in autumn. | Scientists studied the colouration of the butterflies' wings. | The fish's colouration helps it hide among the coral.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «Its colouration is green», not «a colouration» in most cases. UK, Ireland, Australia, NZ and Canada usually spell it «colouration» (with u); the US spells it «coloration». Pronounced «kul-uh-RAY-shun». A more formal, science word for «colours and pattern». Related: colour, colourful, discoloured.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A mission is an important job someone is sent to do, often far away, like a space mission or a rescue mission. 2) A mission is a trip by a spacecraft or a team of soldiers, scientists or helpers to do a special task. 3) Someone's mission is the big aim they feel they must achieve: her mission is to save the turtles. 4) (church) A mission is work by a church to spread its faith and help people, or the place, such as a church or hospital, where missionaries work. 5) A group of officials sent to another country, such as a diplomatic mission. 6) (informal) «It was a mission» means a task was really hard work.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons you learn about space missions, like the Apollo missions to the Moon and missions to Mars. In video games, a mission is a task or level to complete. In history and RE you meet Christian missions and missionaries, who Christians believe were sharing the good news of Jesus, though some missions also harmed local cultures. Phrases: on a mission, mission accomplished, mission control, space mission, rescue mission, mission statement.
examples from the lessons: The astronauts trained for years before the mission. | Mission control talked to the crew by radio. | The firefighters went on a rescue mission in the storm. | Her mission is to get everyone in class reading. | The old Spanish mission is now a museum. | Our school has a mission statement on the wall. | I finished the last mission in the game! | Finding a parking space at the beach was a mission (informal).
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a mission, missions. A person sent on a church mission is a «missionary». «Mission accomplished» means the job is done. «Mission impossible» (from a film) means a task that seems impossible. Australia/NZ/UK informal: «It's a mission» means it's a lot of effort.

meaning for a pupil: 1) As a suffix, «-ness» is added to an adjective to make a noun that names a quality or state: kind → kindness, happy → happiness, dark → darkness. 2) As a word, a ness is a headland, a piece of high land sticking out into the sea; it appears in place names like Dungeness, Sheerness and Loch Ness area names. 3) (a name) Loch Ness is a long deep lake in Scotland, famous for the legend of the Loch Ness Monster, «Nessie». 4) (a name) Ness can also be a surname, such as Eliot Ness, an American lawman.
its sense in the lessons: In English grammar lessons -ness is a key suffix for making abstract nouns from adjectives, and spelling rules apply: a final y changes to i (happy → happiness, lazy → laziness), but a final n is kept (sudden → suddenness). In geography a ness is a coastal feature, and Loch Ness is in lessons about Scotland and myths. Phrases: the Loch Ness Monster, Nessie.
examples from the lessons: Add -ness to «kind» to make «kindness». | Happiness is spelt with an i because the y changes. | The darkness made the forest feel scary. | Dungeness is a ness on the coast of Kent. | We read about the legend of the Loch Ness Monster. | Nobody has ever proved that Nessie is real. | Her gentleness made the shy puppy come closer. | «Openness» keeps both n's: open + ness.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a suffix, -ness makes uncountable nouns (kindness, sadness), though some can be countable (a kindness, many illnesses). Spelling: consonant + y becomes i before -ness (busy → business, happy → happiness); words ending in n keep it, so you get double n (keenness, thinness). On its own «ness» is rare outside place names, so if you see it alone it is probably a suffix or a name. The Loch Ness Monster is a legend, not a proven animal.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Reportedly means «according to what people say or what news reports say», when we are not completely sure it is true. 2) It tells the reader the writer is passing on a claim, not stating a proven fact.
its sense in the lessons: In news, media and citizenship lessons «reportedly» is a key signal word: it shows a claim comes from reports, and a careful reader checks other sources before believing it. In history writing it is used for stories that may be legends: «The king reportedly burnt the cakes.» Similar words: allegedly, apparently, supposedly, it is said that.
examples from the lessons: The singer is reportedly planning a new album. | The bridge reportedly cost twice as much as planned. | King Alfred reportedly burnt some cakes while hiding. | The storm has reportedly knocked out power to thousands of homes. | Our team is reportedly getting a new coach. | The spider reportedly escaped from the zoo, but it has not been confirmed. | The prize was reportedly worth a million dollars. | When you read «reportedly», ask: who reported it?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb, so it does not change form. Often comes before the verb (He reportedly said...) or at the start (Reportedly, ...). Pronounced «ri-POR-tid-lee». It does not mean something is false; it means it is not yet proven by the writer. Compare with «allegedly», used especially when someone is said to have done something wrong but it has not been proved.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A shrew is a tiny mammal with a long pointed nose, small eyes and soft fur, that looks a bit like a mouse but eats insects and worms. 2) (old-fashioned, insulting) A shrew was an old word for a bad-tempered woman who often scolds; this use is now seen as unkind.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about food chains and British wildlife the shrew is a small insect-eater that has to eat almost all the time because it burns energy so fast. Owls and cats hunt them. In old stories and the play title «The Taming of the Shrew» the word is used in its old insulting sense. Phrases: pygmy shrew, common shrew, water shrew, shrew-like.
examples from the lessons: A shrew must eat every few hours or it will starve. | The cat brought a dead shrew into the kitchen. | Shrews have pointed noses that twitch all the time. | The pygmy shrew is one of Britain's smallest mammals. | A water shrew can swim and dive for food. | The owl swooped down and caught a shrew. | A shrew is not a mouse; it eats insects, not seeds. | In old books a cross woman was rudely called a shrew.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one shrew, two shrews. Pronounced «shroo». Trap: shrews are not rodents like mice; they are in a different group with moles and hedgehogs (insect-eaters). The adjective «shrewish» means bad-tempered; but «shrewd» (clever and good at judging) is a different word, though it comes from the same old root. Calling a person a shrew is rude.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A sultan is a king or ruler in some Muslim countries, both in history and today, such as the Sultan of Brunei or the Sultan of Oman. 2) In history, the sultans of the Ottoman Empire ruled a huge empire from Istanbul.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons you meet sultans in the Ottoman Empire, in stories of the Crusades (Sultan Saladin) and in tales like «One Thousand and One Nights». A country ruled by a sultan is a sultanate. Phrases: the Sultan of, sultan's palace, sultanate.
examples from the lessons: The sultan lived in a palace with beautiful gardens. | The Sultan of Brunei is one of the world's richest rulers. | Saladin was a famous sultan at the time of the Crusades. | The Ottoman sultans ruled from Istanbul for centuries. | In the story, the sultan listened to a new tale every night. | A country ruled by a sultan is called a sultanate. | The sultan's wife was called the sultana. | Oman is ruled by a sultan.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one sultan, sultans. Capital S when used as a title (Sultan Suleiman). Trap: a «sultana» is a sultan's wife, mother or daughter, but also a kind of dried grape like a raisin (used in cakes and scones) — food, not royalty, in a recipe.

part of speech: adjective (mute); verb (mute, mutes, muted, muting); noun (a mute, mutes)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To mute a sound, phone, TV or video call is to turn its sound off so nothing can be heard; the mute button does this. 2) Mute means silent, not speaking: she stayed mute. 3) Muted colours or sounds are soft, quiet or not bright. 4) A mute on a musical instrument, like a trumpet or violin, is something that makes its sound quieter or different. 5) (old-fashioned, now offensive) Mute was once used for a person who cannot speak; today we say «non-speaking» or «a person who does not speak».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and online classes «mute» is very common: «You're on mute!», «Please mute your microphone.» In stories a character may be «struck mute» with surprise. In music lessons a trumpet mute changes the sound. Phrases: on mute, mute button, mute yourself, mute the TV, muted colours, a mute swan.
examples from the lessons: Please mute your microphone when the teacher is talking. | Dad, you're still on mute! | She muted the TV during the adverts. | He stood mute with shock. | The room was painted in muted greens and greys. | The trumpet player put a mute in his trumpet. | A mute swan is a white swan with an orange beak. | You can mute a group chat if it gets too noisy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb forms: mute, mutes, muted, muting. «On mute» = sound off; «unmute» = turn sound back on. In spelling, a «silent letter» is sometimes called a mute letter (the k in «knee»). Be kind: calling a person «mute» can be hurtful; say they do not speak or use sign language. A mute swan is not silent; it can hiss and snort.

part of speech: noun, a name (NATO, written in capitals; UK also Nato)
meaning for a pupil: 1) NATO stands for the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, an alliance of countries in North America and Europe, including the USA, Canada, the UK and many others, which promise to defend each other if one of them is attacked. 2) The NATO phonetic alphabet is the list of code words for letters (Alpha, Bravo, Charlie...) used by pilots, police and armies so letters are not misheard on the radio.
its sense in the lessons: In citizenship and news lessons NATO comes up when talking about wars, defence and alliances, for example how NATO countries have helped Ukraine after Russia's invasion with weapons and money, while not sending their own armies to fight. The key idea is «an attack on one is an attack on all». The NATO alphabet is fun for spelling names on the phone. Phrases: NATO members, a NATO country, NATO allies, the NATO alphabet.
examples from the lessons: NATO is an alliance of countries that promise to protect each other. | The UK and Canada are both members of NATO. | NATO leaders met to talk about helping Ukraine. | Finland and Sweden joined NATO after Russia invaded Ukraine. | In the NATO alphabet, A is Alpha and B is Bravo. | The pilot spelt the word as «Charlie, Alpha, Tango». | Some people support NATO and some argue against it. | NATO's headquarters are in Brussels in Belgium.
note for the reader of a maths problem: An acronym, said as one word: «NAY-toe». Written NATO (UK newspapers may write Nato). Usually without «the» (NATO says..., members of NATO). It is a defence alliance, not a country and not the same as the United Nations (UN), which nearly all countries belong to. In the input it is in lower case, but it is always a name.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A pelican is a large water bird with a very long beak and a big stretchy pouch of skin under it, which it uses to scoop up fish. 2) (UK) A pelican crossing is a road crossing with traffic lights that people control by pressing a button.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons the pelican shows how a beak is adapted to food: the pouch works like a fishing net, then the water drains out before swallowing. Pelicans live by seas, lakes and rivers in many warm countries, including Australia and the USA. In road safety lessons in the UK, you learn to cross at a pelican crossing and wait for the green man. Phrases: pelican pouch, pelican crossing, brown pelican, Australian pelican.
examples from the lessons: The pelican scooped up a fish in its pouch. | Pelicans fly in long lines just above the waves. | A pelican's beak can hold more than its stomach. | We saw pelicans on the jetty at the beach. | Press the button at the pelican crossing and wait for the green man. | The Australian pelican has the longest beak of any bird. | Brown pelicans dive into the sea from high up. | The pelican shook the water out of its pouch.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one pelican, two pelicans. Pronounced «PEL-ih-kun». A UK pelican crossing (PEdestrian LIght CONtrolled) is different from a zebra crossing (black and white stripes, no lights) and a puffin or toucan crossing (newer types). Myth: pelicans do not keep fish stored in their pouch for later; they swallow quickly.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A servo (short for servomotor) is a small motor that can turn to an exact position and hold it, used in robots, remote-control cars and planes and models. 2) (Australia, informal) A servo is a petrol station, short for «service station».
its sense in the lessons: In computing, robotics and design and technology lessons, pupils program a servo with a micro:bit or Arduino to move a robot arm, open a gate or wave a flag to an exact angle, such as 90 degrees. In Australian everyday talk, you stop at the servo for petrol, snacks and a drink on a road trip. Phrases: servo motor, turn the servo to 90 degrees, stop at the servo (Australia).
examples from the lessons: We programmed the servo to turn to 90 degrees. | The robot's arm moves with two servos. | The remote-control plane uses servos to move its wings. | Our servo buzzed but would not turn because a wire was loose. | (Australia) Let's stop at the servo for a pie. | (Australia) Dad filled up the car at the servo. | A servo can move to an exact angle, but a normal motor just spins. | The servo opened the little door of our model house.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a servo, servos. Pronounced «SER-voh». It is a short, clipped form: servomotor (robotics) or service station (Australian slang). In robotics maths, the servo's position is measured in degrees, usually from 0 to 180. Australian slang often clips words with -o: servo, arvo (afternoon), bottle-o (bottle shop).

part of speech: noun (a spur, spurs); verb (spur, spurs, spurred, spurring)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A spur is a small metal spike or wheel on the back of a rider's boot, used to push a horse to go faster. 2) To spur someone on is to encourage them to try harder or go faster. 3) A spur is something that makes you act: «a spur to action». 4) «On the spur of the moment» means suddenly, without planning. 5) In geography a spur is a ridge of high land that sticks out from a hill or mountain into a valley. 6) A spur is a sharp point on the back of the leg of some birds, such as a rooster. 7) (a name) Spurs is the nickname of Tottenham Hotspur football club and San Antonio Spurs basketball team.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons on rivers you learn about «interlocking spurs», the ridges a young river winds around in a V-shaped valley. In cowboy stories and films riders have jingling spurs. In everyday life, cheering spurs on runners at sports day. Phrases: spur on, on the spur of the moment, spurred into action, interlocking spurs.
examples from the lessons: The cowboy's spurs jingled as he walked. | The crowd's cheers spurred her on to win the race. | On the spur of the moment, we decided to go to the beach. | The river winds between interlocking spurs. | The rooster had sharp spurs on its legs. | The fire spurred the town to build a new fire station. | He supports Spurs, not Arsenal. | Good marks spurred him to work even harder.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb forms: spur, spurs, spurred, spurring (double r before -ed and -ing). Countable noun: a spur, spurs. «On the spur of the moment» is an idiom: no planning. «Spur on» means encourage, often with «to»: «The coach spurred us on to score.»

meaning for a pupil: 1) A suffix is a group of letters added to the end of a word to make a new word or change how it is used, like -ful in «hopeful», -ness in «kindness» or -ed in «jumped». 2) In maths and computing, a suffix can be letters or a number added to the end of a name or code.
its sense in the lessons: In English grammar and spelling lessons (and SATs), suffixes are key: -s and -es make plurals, -ed and -ing change verb tense, -er and -est compare, and -ful, -less, -ness, -ment, -ly, -tion make new words. Spelling rules apply: double the consonant (run → running), drop the e (hope → hoping), change y to i (happy → happiness). Phrases: add a suffix, the suffix -ly, root word and suffix.
examples from the lessons: Add the suffix -ful to «help» to make «helpful». | «-ly» is a suffix that turns «quick» into «quickly». | The suffix -less means «without», as in «homeless». | Underline the suffix in «enjoyment». | Adding -ing to «swim» doubles the m. | The suffix -er can mean «a person who does it», as in «teacher». | When you add the suffix -ness to «happy», y changes to i. | Some words have two suffixes, like «care-ful-ly».
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a suffix, suffixes (add -es after x). Pronounced «SUF-ix». A suffix goes at the END; a prefix goes at the START (un- in «unhappy»). The word you add it to is the root or base word. A suffix can change the word class: «kind» (adjective) → «kindness» (noun).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unique means being the only one of its kind, unlike anything else: every snowflake is unique. 2) Unique to something means found only there: koalas are unique to Australia. 3) (informal) Unique is often used to mean very special or unusual.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons fingerprints, DNA and snowflakes are unique, which is why fingerprints can identify a person. In maths «a unique answer» means there is only one correct answer, and a unique value is one that appears only once. In PSHE lessons «everyone is unique» means each person is special and different. Phrases: unique to, truly unique, a unique chance, unique answer.
examples from the lessons: Every person's fingerprints are unique. | Kangaroos are unique to Australia. | This puzzle has a unique solution. | Our school has a unique garden on the roof. | Everyone is unique, so we should not all be the same. | It was a unique chance to meet a real astronaut. | Each password should be unique so a hacker cannot guess them all. | The museum has a unique fossil found nowhere else.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced «yoo-NEEK». Use «a unique» (not «an»), because it starts with a «you» sound. Strictly, unique means «only one», so careful writers avoid «very unique» or «more unique»; say «very unusual» instead. In maths: «unique» = exactly one; if a problem says the answer is unique, there is only one number that works.

part of speech: noun (a voyager, voyagers; Voyager — a name)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A voyager is a person who goes on a long journey, especially by sea or into space. 2) (a name) Voyager 1 and Voyager 2 are two space probes sent from Earth to visit the outer planets; they have now travelled further than anything else people have made, out beyond the planets.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about space, the Voyager probes flew past Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune and sent back photos, and they carry a golden record with sounds and pictures of Earth in case aliens find them. In history lessons, voyagers sailed across oceans, like the Polynesian voyagers who found New Zealand and Hawaii using the stars. Phrases: ocean voyager, space voyager, the Voyager probes, the Golden Record.
examples from the lessons: Voyager 1 is the most distant human-made object. | The Voyager probes took the first close photos of Neptune. | Polynesian voyagers sailed huge distances using the stars. | The voyager kept a diary of the long sea crossing. | Voyager carries a golden record with music from Earth. | Radio signals from Voyager take many hours to reach us. | The ship's voyagers were glad to see land. | In the story, a young voyager sails to a mysterious island.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a voyager, voyagers. Comes from «voyage» (a long journey, especially by sea or space) + «-er». Pronounced «VOY-ij-er». Capital V when it is the name of the probe. A «voyage» is the trip; a «voyager» is the traveller.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (slang) A bummer is a disappointing or annoying thing or situation: «The rain was a bummer.» 2) (slang) «What a bummer!» or «Bummer!» is said when something goes wrong, like «What a shame!» or «That's annoying!»
its sense in the lessons: Mainly in everyday talk, especially American, Australian and Canadian, among children and adults, to show mild disappointment in a friendly, casual way. It is not rude in the USA, but some older British people think it sounds a bit cheeky, because «bum» is a slang word for bottom in the UK. In stories it makes characters sound casual and relaxed. Phrases: what a bummer, a real bummer, bummer!
examples from the lessons: The trip was cancelled? What a bummer! | It's a bummer that the pool is closed today. | (slang) Bummer, I left my lunch at home. | Losing the final was a real bummer. | «I can't come to your party.» «Aw, bummer.» | Getting a cold on the first day of the holidays is such a bummer. | It's a bummer, but we can try again tomorrow. | The ending of the film was a bit of a bummer.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: a bummer, bummers. Register: informal slang, fine with friends but not in school essays; in formal writing say «a disappointment» or «a shame». Not a swear word in American English, but in Britain «bum» means bottom, so some people find it slightly rude. Do not use it in a serious situation such as someone being ill or dying; it sounds too light.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A conjunction is a word that joins words, phrases or clauses together in a sentence, like and, but, or, because, when, if and although. 2) A conjunction is a time when things come together or happen at the same time: «in conjunction with» means together with. 3) (space) A conjunction is when two planets or a planet and the Moon look very close together in the sky.
its sense in the lessons: In English grammar lessons and SATs pupils learn two kinds: coordinating conjunctions (FANBOYS: for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so) that join equal parts, and subordinating conjunctions (because, when, if, although, while, since, until) that start a subordinate clause. Using conjunctions makes longer, richer sentences. In science, a conjunction of planets is a sight to look out for. Phrases: in conjunction with, coordinating conjunction, subordinating conjunction.
examples from the lessons: «And» and «but» are conjunctions. | Join the two sentences with a conjunction. | «Because» is a subordinating conjunction. | I wanted to play out, but it was raining. | Underline the conjunction in this sentence. | The school works in conjunction with the local library. | Last night there was a conjunction of Jupiter and Venus. | Try not to start every sentence with the same conjunction.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one conjunction, conjunctions. It is a word class (part of speech) like noun or verb. Trap: some words can be a conjunction or a preposition: «after» is a conjunction in «after we ate» (a clause follows) but a preposition in «after lunch». Many teachers say not to start a sentence with «and» or «but», but good writers sometimes do for effect. Mnemonic FANBOYS lists the coordinating ones.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A hornbill is a tropical bird from Africa and Asia with a very large curved beak, often with a hard bump called a casque on top of it.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about rainforests and adaptations, the hornbill eats fruit and spreads seeds, helping the forest grow. Its nesting habit is famous: the female seals herself inside a tree hole with mud, and the male feeds her through a narrow slit. In stories and films (Zazu in «The Lion King» is a hornbill) it is a talkative bird. Phrases: great hornbill, ground hornbill, rhinoceros hornbill.
examples from the lessons: The hornbill has a huge yellow beak. | A hornbill helps the forest by dropping seeds. | The great hornbill lives in the forests of India and Southeast Asia. | The female hornbill stays sealed in her nest while the chicks grow. | Zazu in «The Lion King» is a red-billed hornbill. | The hornbill's casque sits on top of its beak like a helmet. | We heard the loud whoosh of a hornbill's wings. | Some hornbills are endangered because forests are cut down.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one hornbill, hornbills. A compound word: horn + bill (bill = beak). Do not confuse with the toucan of South and Central America, which also has a big colourful beak but is a different family; hornbills live in Africa and Asia.

part of speech: noun, plural of porcupine (one porcupine, two porcupines)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Porcupines are more than one porcupine: large rodents covered in long sharp quills that protect them from predators. 2) There are New World porcupines, which climb trees in the Americas, and Old World porcupines, which live on the ground in Africa, Asia and southern Europe.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about adaptations and defence, porcupines show how animals protect themselves: their quills come loose and stick in an attacker. They eat plants, bark and fruit, and they are mostly active at night. In stories porcupines are prickly or shy characters. Phrases: a family of porcupines, porcupines' quills.
examples from the lessons: Porcupines are covered in thousands of sharp quills. | Porcupines are mostly awake at night. | In winter, North American porcupines chew tree bark. | Porcupines rattle their quills to warn enemies. | Young porcupines are called porcupettes. | Wolves usually leave porcupines alone. | Porcupines are good at climbing trees. | We made porcupines out of clay and cocktail sticks.
note for the reader of a maths problem: This is the plural form; the singular is «porcupine». Possessive plural: «the porcupines' quills» (apostrophe after the s). Myth: porcupines cannot shoot their quills. Porcupines are rodents, unlike hedgehogs and echidnas, which also have spines.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A starling is a common bird with dark shiny feathers that look purple and green in the sun, often covered in small pale spots in winter. 2) A large swirling flock of starlings in the evening sky is called a murmuration.
its sense in the lessons: In science and nature lessons, starlings are known for murmurations: thousands of birds twisting in the sky together without crashing, each bird copying its nearest neighbours. Starlings are clever mimics and can copy car alarms and phone ringtones. They live in Europe and were brought to North America, Australia and New Zealand, where they are now very common and sometimes pests. Phrases: a flock of starlings, a murmuration of starlings, common starling.
examples from the lessons: Starlings gathered on the roof every evening. | We watched a murmuration of starlings over the pier. | The starling copied the sound of a phone ringing. | A starling's feathers shine purple and green in the sun. | Starlings eat insects and grubs from the lawn. | Starlings were brought to New Zealand by settlers. | The starling flew off with a worm in its beak. | Thousands of starlings make shapes in the sky like a cloud.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one starling, starlings. Pronounced «STAR-ling». Not related to «star» in the sky, despite the spelling. In some countries starlings are a pest species because they take nest holes from native birds. A murmuration is the special word for their flock in flight.

part of speech: noun (sulphur, uncountable; US and science spelling sulfur)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Sulphur is a yellow chemical element, a solid that is not a metal; its symbol is S. 2) Sulphur and many of its compounds have a strong smell, like rotten eggs (really the gas hydrogen sulphide), and sulphur burns with a blue flame. 3) Sulphur yellow is a bright pale yellow colour.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons sulphur is found around volcanoes and hot springs, is used to make matches, fireworks, gunpowder and fertilisers, and is in the periodic table. Burning fossil fuels that contain sulphur makes acid rain. In the Bible and old stories, «fire and brimstone» uses an old name for sulphur. Phrases: sulphur dioxide, sulphur smell, sulphur springs, smells of sulphur.
examples from the lessons: Sulphur is a yellow element found near volcanoes. | The hot springs smelled of sulphur. | The symbol for sulphur is S. | Gunpowder contains sulphur, charcoal and saltpetre. | Sulphur burns with a blue flame. | Burning coal can release sulphur, which causes acid rain. | Brimstone is an old word for sulphur. | The match head is coated with chemicals that include sulphur.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «Sulphur is yellow», not «a sulphur». UK, Ireland, Australia and NZ traditionally spell it «sulphur»; the USA and science books worldwide now use «sulfur» (the official chemistry spelling). Both mean the same. The rotten-egg smell is really from sulphur compounds such as hydrogen sulphide; pure sulphur has little smell.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A walrus is a very large sea mammal of the Arctic with long white tusks, whiskers, flippers and a thick layer of fat. 2) (informal) A walrus moustache is a big, thick, drooping moustache like the walrus's whiskers.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about the Arctic and adaptations, the walrus keeps warm with blubber, uses its tusks to pull itself out of the water onto ice and to fight, and finds clams on the sea floor with its sensitive whiskers. Walruses are threatened as sea ice melts with climate change. In poems such as «The Walrus and the Carpenter» it is a funny character. Phrases: a herd of walruses, walrus tusks, walrus moustache.
examples from the lessons: The walrus pulled itself onto the ice with its tusks. | Walruses live in the cold Arctic seas. | A walrus uses its whiskers to find clams on the sea floor. | A thick layer of blubber keeps the walrus warm. | Hundreds of walruses lay together on the beach. | Melting sea ice is making life harder for walruses. | Grandad has a big walrus moustache. | We read «The Walrus and the Carpenter» by Lewis Carroll.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one walrus, two walruses (add -es). Pronounced «WAWL-rus». Both male and female walruses have tusks, which are long teeth. A group is a herd. Do not confuse with seals and sea lions, which are relatives without big tusks.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A weaver is a person whose job or hobby is weaving: making cloth by crossing threads over and under each other on a loom. 2) A weaver (or weaverbird) is a small bird, mostly from Africa, that weaves amazing nests from grass and leaves. 3) Someone who makes up and tells stories can be called a weaver of tales. 4) (a name) Weaver is also a surname.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons weavers worked at home on hand looms until factories with power looms took over in the Industrial Revolution, which made many weavers poor. In science lessons weaver birds show animal building skills, and the male builds a nest to attract a female. In art and DT lessons pupils weave paper or wool on a card loom. Phrases: hand-loom weaver, silk weaver, weaver bird, a weaver of stories.
examples from the lessons: The weaver worked at her loom all day. | Weavers lost their jobs when big factories were built. | The weaver bird tied the grass into a tight knot. | Hundreds of weaver nests hung from the tree like balls. | My aunt is a weaver who makes colourful rugs. | The old storyteller was a great weaver of tales. | Silk weavers made fine cloth for rich people. | We became weavers for a day and made a paper mat.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a weaver, weavers. From the verb «weave» (weave, weaves, wove, woven, weaving) + «-er». Do not confuse with «waver», which means to be unsure or to shake. «Weaving» in traffic means moving in and out between cars.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The Aztecs were a people who built a great empire in what is now central Mexico, with their capital Tenochtitlan built on a lake, until the Spanish conquest. 2) Aztec describes things from their culture: Aztec gods, Aztec pyramids, the Aztec calendar. 3) Aztec is also used for patterns inspired by their art, though this name is sometimes thought to be inaccurate.
its sense in the lessons: In UK and US history lessons the Aztecs are a common topic: their city on the lake with floating gardens (chinampas), their temples and human sacrifice, their markets, chocolate drink, writing with pictures, and the arrival of Hernán Cortés and the Spanish, which ended the empire. Their descendants and language, Nahuatl, are still alive in Mexico today. Phrases: the Aztec Empire, Aztec gods, Aztec warriors, Aztec calendar.
examples from the lessons: The Aztecs built their capital on an island in a lake. | Aztec farmers grew maize on floating gardens. | The Aztecs drank chocolate with chilli in it. | Spanish soldiers led by Cortés conquered the Aztec Empire. | Our class made masks of Aztec gods. | The Aztec calendar stone is carved with a face in the middle. | Words like «chocolate» and «tomato» come from the Aztec language, Nahuatl. | Diseases brought by Europeans killed many Aztec people.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A name, so it takes a capital A: Aztec, the Aztecs (the input is lower case only by format). Pronounced «AZ-tek». Do not mix up the Aztecs (central Mexico), the Maya (southern Mexico and Central America, older) and the Incas (Peru in South America). Many people today say «Mexica» for the people the Aztec capital belonged to.

part of speech: adjective, a name (Baltic; the Baltic Sea, the Baltic states)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The Baltic Sea is a sea in northern Europe, surrounded by countries such as Sweden, Finland, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, Poland, Germany and Denmark. 2) The Baltic states are Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania, three countries on its eastern shore. 3) Baltic describes things from that region: Baltic amber, Baltic languages (Latvian and Lithuanian). 4) (UK, slang) «It's Baltic!» means it is freezing cold.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons the Baltic Sea is a fairly shallow, not very salty sea that freezes in parts in winter. In history and news, the Baltic states were taken into the Soviet Union and became independent again; they are now in the EU and NATO. In everyday British, Irish and Scottish slang, «Baltic» means very cold weather. Phrases: the Baltic Sea, the Baltic states, Baltic amber, it's Baltic out there (UK slang).
examples from the lessons: The Baltic Sea is less salty than the ocean. | Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania are called the Baltic states. | Amber from the Baltic often has tiny insects trapped inside. | Ferries cross the Baltic between Sweden and Finland. | (slang, UK) Shut the door, it's Baltic in here! | (slang, Scotland) It was absolutely Baltic at the bus stop this morning. | Parts of the Baltic freeze over in winter. | Lithuanian is a Baltic language.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A name, so it is written with a capital B: Baltic. Pronounced «BAWL-tik». The slang «it's Baltic» is informal and used mainly in Scotland, northern England and Ireland; in school writing say «very cold» or «freezing». Not to be confused with the Balkans (south-eastern Europe).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A cassowary is a very large flightless bird from the rainforests of north-eastern Australia and New Guinea, with black feathers, a bright blue neck, red wattles and a tall hard crest called a casque on its head.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about Australian animals and rainforests, the cassowary is a key seed spreader: it eats fallen fruit and drops the seeds far away in its droppings. It has sharp dagger-like claws and can be dangerous if people get too close or feed it, so safety signs in Queensland warn drivers and walkers. The father sits on the eggs and raises the chicks. Phrases: southern cassowary, cassowary crossing, be cass-o-wary (a safety pun).
examples from the lessons: The cassowary lives in the rainforests of Queensland. | A cassowary cannot fly, but it can run fast and jump. | Never feed a cassowary; it can kick and hurt you. | The cassowary's blue neck and red wattles are very bright. | Cassowaries help the forest by spreading seeds. | The father cassowary looks after the stripy chicks. | A road sign warned drivers to watch for cassowaries. | The cassowary has a bony helmet called a casque.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one cassowary, two cassowaries (y changes to ies). Pronounced «KASS-uh-wair-ee». It is a ratite, a flightless bird, like the emu, ostrich, rhea and kiwi. Safety: it is one of the few birds that can seriously hurt people, so keep your distance.

part of speech: noun (a cod, cod; plural usually cod); adjective (cod — UK informal, fake)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A cod is a large sea fish with white flesh, eaten a lot as food, especially in fish and chips. 2) (UK, informal) «Cod» before a word means fake or pretend, not real: a cod accent, cod science. 3) COD (cash on delivery) means paying when goods are delivered, in some countries.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday British, Irish, Canadian and Australian life cod is the classic fish in fish and chips. In geography and science lessons, overfishing of cod is a famous example: the Atlantic cod near Newfoundland in Canada collapsed after too much fishing, showing why sustainable fishing matters. Cod liver oil is a vitamin supplement. Phrases: cod and chips, cod liver oil, Atlantic cod, the Cod Wars (UK and Iceland fishing quarrels).
examples from the lessons: Can I have cod and chips, please? | Cod is a fish with flaky white flesh. | Too much fishing made the cod disappear near Newfoundland. | Grandma made us take cod liver oil in winter. | The fishermen caught three huge cod. | (UK, informal) He put on a cod French accent to make us laugh. | Britain and Iceland once argued about cod fishing. | Choose cod with a label saying it was caught sustainably.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The plural is usually the same: one cod, ten cod (like «sheep»); «cods» is used for different kinds. Do not confuse with «COD» (cash on delivery) or the video game short name. «Cod» as «fake» is informal British use.

meaning for a pupil: 1) DDT is a strong chemical insecticide (short for dichlorodiphenyltrichloroethane) that was once sprayed widely to kill mosquitoes, lice and crop pests. 2) DDT was found to harm wildlife, especially birds of prey, whose eggshells became thin and broke; it was banned for farm use in many countries, though small amounts are still used against malaria mosquitoes in some places.
its sense in the lessons: In science and history lessons DDT is a key example of how a chemical can build up along a food chain (bioaccumulation): from insects to fish to eagles and ospreys. Rachel Carson's book «Silent Spring» warned about it and helped start the environmental movement. It also saved many lives by controlling malaria and typhus. Phrases: DDT spray, banned DDT, the effects of DDT.
examples from the lessons: DDT was sprayed on fields to kill insects. | DDT made birds' eggshells too thin. | Rachel Carson wrote about the dangers of DDT. | DDT builds up in animals higher up the food chain. | Many countries banned DDT for farming. | Bald eagles recovered after DDT was banned in the USA. | DDT was once used to kill lice on soldiers. | Some countries still use DDT inside homes to fight malaria.
note for the reader of a maths problem: An abbreviation: always written in capitals, DDT, and said letter by letter, «dee-dee-tee». Uncountable: «DDT is», not «a DDT». The full chemical name is long and hard; pupils are not expected to remember it. It is a good example of a trade-off: helpful against disease, harmful to wildlife.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Eczema is a common skin condition that makes patches of skin dry, red, cracked and very itchy. 2) It often starts in babies and children, may come and go, and can be made worse by things like soap, heat, stress or some foods.
its sense in the lessons: In health lessons and everyday life, eczema is something many children have; it is not catching, so you cannot get it from touching someone. People treat it with creams (emollients), avoiding triggers and not scratching. Being kind about someone's skin is part of PSHE. Phrases: have eczema, eczema flare-up, eczema cream, atopic eczema.
examples from the lessons: My little sister has eczema on her elbows. | Eczema is not catching, so you can still hold hands. | He puts cream on his eczema every night. | Hot baths can make eczema worse. | Her eczema flared up when she was worried about tests. | Try not to scratch eczema, even though it itches. | Some children grow out of their eczema. | The doctor gave her a special cream for her eczema.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «She has eczema», not «an eczema». Pronounced «EK-zuh-muh» (UK) or «eg-ZEE-muh» (US). Spelling trap: e-c-z-e-m-a, with the tricky «cz». Myth: eczema is not caused by being dirty and it is not contagious.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Gunpowder is a black powder that explodes when lit, made from saltpetre, charcoal and sulphur; it was used in old guns and cannons and is still used in fireworks.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons gunpowder was invented in China, first used for fireworks and then weapons, and changed warfare around the world. In the UK, the Gunpowder Plot was a failed plan by Guy Fawkes and others to blow up Parliament and King James I, remembered on Bonfire Night with fireworks. In science lessons it shows a chemical reaction that gives out heat, light and gas very fast. Phrases: the Gunpowder Plot, barrels of gunpowder, keep your powder dry.
examples from the lessons: Gunpowder was invented in ancient China. | Guy Fawkes hid barrels of gunpowder under Parliament. | We remember the Gunpowder Plot on Bonfire Night. | Fireworks use a kind of gunpowder to shoot into the sky. | Pirates kept their gunpowder dry in the ship's hold. | Gunpowder is a mixture of saltpetre, charcoal and sulphur. | Never play with fireworks or anything that contains gunpowder. | The cannon fired with a bang and a puff of gunpowder smoke.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «some gunpowder», «barrels of gunpowder», not «a gunpowder». Compound word: gun + powder. Safety: gunpowder and fireworks are dangerous and only adults should handle them. «Gunpowder tea» is a kind of green tea rolled into little balls, not explosive.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A maze is a puzzle made of paths or passages with walls or hedges, where you have to find the way through without getting lost. 2) A maze is a puzzle drawn on paper where you trace a line from the start to the finish. 3) A maze can be any confusing place or set of things: a maze of streets, a maze of rules.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and computing lessons, mazes are used to practise directions (left, right, forward), giving instructions to robots and Bee-Bots, and solving problems step by step; a famous trick is to keep one hand on a wall. In stories mazes are mysterious places, like the labyrinth of the Minotaur in Greek myth. Phrases: a hedge maze, a corn maze, get lost in a maze, a maze of.
examples from the lessons: We got lost in the hedge maze for half an hour. | Draw a line through the maze to help the mouse find the cheese. | We programmed the robot to get through the maze. | The old town was a maze of narrow streets. | The corn maze at the farm had a scarecrow in the middle. | If you keep your hand on one wall, you may find your way out of the maze. | The Minotaur lived in a maze called the labyrinth. | Filling in the form felt like a maze of questions.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a maze, mazes. Homophone: «maize» (corn, the plant) sounds the same; a «maize maze» is a maze cut into a field of maize! The adjective «amazing» comes from an old meaning of «amaze», to confuse. Wall-following works for simple mazes but not for every maze.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A millipede is a small creature with a long body made of many segments, with two pairs of legs on most segments, that lives in damp soil and leaf litter and eats dead plants.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on minibeasts and habitats, millipedes are found under logs and stones; they are decomposers that break down dead leaves into soil. When frightened they curl into a spiral and may give off a smelly liquid. They are not insects. Phrases: a millipede curled up, minibeast hunt.
examples from the lessons: We found a millipede under the old log. | The millipede curled up into a tight spiral. | Millipedes eat rotting leaves and help make soil. | A millipede moves its legs in waves. | Millipedes like dark, damp places. | Despite its name, a millipede does not have a thousand legs. | We counted the millipede's legs with a magnifying glass. | A millipede is slower than a centipede.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a millipede, millipedes. «Milli-» means thousand and «-pede» means feet, but most millipedes have far fewer than a thousand legs (often under 400; one rare kind has over 1,000). Do not confuse with a centipede: centipedes have one pair of legs per segment, move fast, hunt other animals and can bite; millipedes have two pairs per segment, are slow and eat plants. Neither is an insect (insects have six legs).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A peacock is a large male bird with a long, brilliant blue-green tail with «eye» patterns, which it spreads out in a huge fan to attract females. 2) Strictly, the peacock is the male; the female is a peahen, and both are peafowl. 3) A person who is vain and shows off how they look can be called a peacock. 4) A peacock butterfly is a butterfly with eye spots on its wings.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons the peacock is a famous example of how males show off colourful features to attract a mate, while the plain brown peahen is camouflaged on her nest. Peacocks are the national bird of India. In stories «proud as a peacock» describes someone very pleased with themselves. Phrases: proud as a peacock, peacock feathers, peacock blue, strut like a peacock.
examples from the lessons: The peacock spread its tail in a huge shimmering fan. | A peacock's tail feathers have spots that look like eyes. | The peacock screeched loudly in the park. | The peahen is brown, but the peacock is blue and green. | He strutted around in his new trainers like a peacock. | She was as proud as a peacock of her painting. | We saw a peacock butterfly on the buddleia. | The peacock is the national bird of India.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a peacock, peacocks. Male = peacock, female = peahen, babies = peachicks, all of them = peafowl. Trap: people often call any peafowl a peacock. «Peacock blue» is a bright blue-green colour.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A preposition is a small word that shows how a noun or pronoun is linked to other words, often telling where, when or how: in, on, under, behind, after, with, by, to, from. 2) (formal, rare) A preposition can also mean an idea put forward, but this is very rare; usually «proposition» is used.
its sense in the lessons: In English grammar lessons and SATs pupils find prepositions, use them to describe where things are (the cat under the table) and when things happen (after lunch, on Monday, in the morning), and learn prepositional phrases. In maths, position words like above, below, between and next to are prepositions. Phrases: preposition of place, preposition of time, prepositional phrase.
examples from the lessons: «Under» is a preposition in «under the bed». | Circle all the prepositions in the sentence. | The ball rolled behind the sofa. | We have PE after lunch. | «In», «on» and «at» are tricky prepositions of time. | The book is between the two boxes. | Use a preposition to say where the treasure is hidden. | She walked across the bridge.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a preposition, prepositions. A preposition is followed by a noun, pronoun or noun phrase (its object): «with my friend». Trap: the same word can be a preposition or a conjunction or adverb: «before lunch» (preposition), «before we ate» (conjunction), «I've seen it before» (adverb). Old «rule»: some say never end a sentence with a preposition, but in everyday English «Who are you talking to?» is fine.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A raptor is a bird of prey: a bird that hunts other animals with strong feet, sharp curved claws (talons) and a hooked beak, such as an eagle, hawk, falcon or owl. 2) (informal) A raptor is a short name for some meat-eating dinosaurs, especially velociraptor and its relatives (dromaeosaurs).
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on food chains and birds, raptors are top predators; owls are night raptors, eagles and hawks hunt by day. Raptor centres look after hurt birds of prey. In dinosaur topics and films like «Jurassic Park», «raptors» are fast clever hunters, though real ones were smaller and had feathers. Phrases: birds of prey, raptor centre, raptor talons.
examples from the lessons: Eagles, hawks and owls are all raptors. | The raptor grabbed the mouse with its sharp talons. | We visited a raptor centre and held a barn owl. | Raptors have amazing eyesight for spotting prey. | Peregrine falcons are the fastest raptors when they dive. | In the film, the raptors opened the kitchen door. | Real raptor dinosaurs were covered in feathers. | The raptor circled high above the field.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a raptor, raptors. From Latin «raptor», meaning one who seizes or robs. Trap: film raptors are much bigger than real velociraptors, which were about the size of a turkey. Owls are raptors too, even though they hunt at night.

part of speech: noun (Swahili, uncountable — the language; also Kiswahili); adjective (Swahili)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Swahili is a language spoken by many millions of people in East Africa, especially in Kenya, Tanzania, Uganda and nearby countries; in Swahili itself it is called Kiswahili. 2) The Swahili are also a people of the East African coast, and Swahili describes their culture, such as Swahili cities and Swahili food.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and language lessons Swahili is the most widely spoken language of East Africa, used for trade between people who speak different first languages. Some Swahili words are known in English: «safari» (journey), «jambo» (hello), and «Hakuna matata» (no worries) from «The Lion King». «Asante» means thank you. It is written in the Latin alphabet. Phrases: speak Swahili, Swahili words, the Swahili coast.
examples from the lessons: Swahili is spoken in Kenya and Tanzania. | «Jambo» means hello in Swahili. | The word «safari» comes from Swahili and means journey. | «Hakuna matata» is Swahili for «no worries». | Our teacher taught us to count to ten in Swahili. | «Asante sana» means «thank you very much» in Swahili. | Swahili has borrowed many words from Arabic. | People on the Swahili coast have traded by sea for centuries.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A name, so it is written with a capital S: Swahili. Pronounced «swah-HEE-lee». It is a language and people of Africa, not a country. The word «Swahili» itself comes from Arabic, meaning «of the coasts».
