meaning for a pupil: 1) Vegetation means all the plants that grow in a place, such as trees, bushes, grass and flowers, taken together. 2) (medicine, rare) It can also mean a growth on a part of the body, but pupils will meet only the plant meaning.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons, vegetation is a key word when describing biomes and landscapes: thick vegetation in rainforests, little vegetation in deserts, low vegetation in the tundra. In science, vegetation is food and shelter for animals and holds soil together, which stops erosion and floods. Phrases: thick vegetation, natural vegetation, lush vegetation, sparse vegetation, vegetation cover.
examples from the lessons: The rainforest is full of thick green vegetation. | There is very little vegetation in the desert. | Goats ate all the vegetation on the hill. | The explorers cut their way through dense vegetation. | Vegetation along the river bank stops the soil washing away. | After the bushfire the vegetation slowly grew back. | The map showed the different types of vegetation. | Cold winds mean the tundra has only low vegetation.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «a lot of vegetation», «little vegetation», not «vegetations». Pronounced «vej-uh-TAY-shun». A more formal, geography word for «plants». Related words: vegetable, vegetarian, vegetate (to sit doing nothing). Do not confuse with «vegetable», which means a plant or part of one eaten as food.

part of speech: noun (a velociraptor, velociraptors; Velociraptor — the scientific name)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A velociraptor was a small, fast, meat-eating dinosaur that lived in what is now Mongolia and China; it ran on two legs, had feathers and a large curved claw on each foot.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on dinosaurs and fossils, the velociraptor is famous from films like «Jurassic Park», where it is shown as large and scaly; real fossils show it was about the size of a turkey and had feathers, like birds, which are its distant relatives. A famous fossil shows a velociraptor fighting a protoceratops. Phrases: velociraptor claw, a feathered velociraptor.
examples from the lessons: A velociraptor had a big curved claw on each foot. | Real velociraptors were about the size of a turkey. | Fossils show that velociraptors had feathers. | The name velociraptor means «swift thief». | A velociraptor fossil was found locked in a fight with another dinosaur. | In the film the velociraptors were much bigger than real ones. | The velociraptor ran on two legs and held its tail out straight. | Birds are distant relatives of dinosaurs like the velociraptor.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a velociraptor, velociraptors; often shortened to «raptor». Pronounced «vuh-LOSS-ih-rap-tor». As a scientific genus name it is written with a capital V and in italics: Velociraptor. The name comes from Latin: «velox» (swift) + «raptor» (thief, robber). Myth: the films' velociraptors were really based on a bigger relative.

part of speech: noun (a veto, vetoes); verb (veto, vetoes, vetoed, vetoing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A veto is the right of one person or group to stop a decision or law, even if others agree with it. 2) To veto something is to use that power to say no and stop it. 3) (informal) To veto an idea at home or with friends is just to refuse it: «Mum vetoed the idea of a puppy.»
its sense in the lessons: In citizenship lessons the US President can veto laws passed by Congress, and five permanent members of the United Nations Security Council (the USA, the UK, France, Russia and China) each have a veto, so one «no» can block a decision, for example Russia blocking UN action on its invasion of Ukraine. In everyday life, children and parents «veto» choices for films or dinner. Phrases: use a veto, power of veto, right of veto, veto a plan.
examples from the lessons: The President vetoed the new law. | Russia used its veto at the UN Security Council. | Each of the five permanent members has a veto. | My sister vetoed my idea of pizza for breakfast. | The head teacher has the power of veto over school trips. | One veto is enough to stop the resolution. | Dad vetoed the scary film. | The council could not veto the plan on its own.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun plural: vetoes (with e). Verb: veto, vetoes, vetoed, vetoing. Pronounced «VEE-toe». From Latin, meaning «I forbid». A veto stops something; it does not make a new plan instead.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (a name) Amelia is a girl's first name, very popular in the UK, Australia and other English-speaking countries. 2) (a name) A famous Amelia was Amelia Earhart, an American pilot who was the first woman to fly alone across the Atlantic Ocean and who later disappeared while trying to fly around the world.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and maths word problems Amelia is often just a character's name: «Amelia has 12 stickers.» In history lessons about brave women and flight, pupils learn about Amelia Earhart and the mystery of her disappearance over the Pacific Ocean. Short forms: Millie, Amy, Mia.
examples from the lessons: Amelia sits next to me in class. | Amelia has 24 sweets and shares them equally with 3 friends. | Amelia Earhart was a famous pilot. | Amelia Earhart's plane was never found. | Amelia is one of the most popular girls' names in England. | Amelia's mum calls her Millie for short. | In the story, Amelia finds a secret door in the attic. | We wrote a report about Amelia Earhart's life.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A name, so it always takes a capital A: Amelia. Pronounced «uh-MEE-lee-uh». Not an ordinary English word with a meaning; it is a person's name. Different from «Amalia» and «Emilia», which are similar names.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (a name) Berlin is the capital city of Germany and its largest city. 2) In history, Berlin was divided into East and West Berlin by the Berlin Wall during the Cold War; the Wall came down and Germany became one country again. 3) (rare) A berlin (berline) is an old kind of four-wheeled carriage.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons Berlin is a European capital on the River Spree. In history lessons about the Second World War and the Cold War, pupils learn that the city was split, people were stopped from crossing, and the fall of the Berlin Wall was a time of great joy. In everyday life, Berlin is a place people visit for its museums, the Brandenburg Gate and bits of the Wall. Phrases: the Berlin Wall, East Berlin, West Berlin, the fall of the Berlin Wall.
examples from the lessons: Berlin is the capital of Germany. | The Berlin Wall split the city in two. | People danced on the Berlin Wall the night it opened. | We saw a piece of the Berlin Wall in a museum. | The Brandenburg Gate is a famous sight in Berlin. | Many families were separated when the wall was built across Berlin. | Berlin has more bridges than Venice. | Our class wrote postcards from an imaginary trip to Berlin.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A name, so it takes a capital B: Berlin. Pronounced «bur-LIN». A person from Berlin is a Berliner. Not to be confused with Bern (the capital of Switzerland).

part of speech: noun (a context, contexts; also uncountable: context)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The context of a word or sentence is the words and sentences around it that help you understand what it means. 2) The context of an event is the situation, background or facts around it that help explain why it happened. 3) «Out of context» means taken away from its surroundings, so the meaning is changed or unfair.
its sense in the lessons: In reading lessons pupils use context clues to work out the meaning of a new word: «The arid desert had no water at all» shows that «arid» means very dry. In history lessons, putting events «in context» means understanding the time and place. In media lessons, a quote or video «taken out of context» can be misleading. In maths word problems, the context is the real-life story around the sum. Phrases: in context, out of context, context clues, historical context, in this context.
examples from the lessons: Use the context to guess what the new word means. | In this context, «bat» means an animal, not a cricket bat. | The video was cut and shown out of context. | Our teacher gave us the historical context of the war. | The context of the story is a village during a flood. | Read the sentences around it for context. | His words sounded rude out of context, but he was joking. | Put the number into context: is it a lot or a little?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually a countable noun (different contexts), but often uncountable (some context, more context). Pronounced «KON-tekst». Adjective: «contextual». Many English words have more than one meaning, and only the context tells you which is meant (bank, bat, right, light).

part of speech: noun (a draft, drafts); verb (draft, drafts, drafted, drafting); adjective (draft — not final)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A draft is an early version of a piece of writing, drawing or plan that is not finished and will be improved: a first draft. 2) To draft something is to write or draw the first version of it. 3) (US) A draft is a cold current of air in a room (UK spelling: draught). 4) (US) The draft was a system that made young men join the army; to be drafted is to be chosen for it, and in sports to be picked for a team. 5) (money) A bank draft is a written order to pay money. 6) (US) Draft beer is beer from a barrel (UK: draught).
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons pupils plan, draft, edit and redraft their writing: the first draft is messy and that is normal; then you improve spelling, punctuation and word choice. In email and apps, an unsent message is saved in «Drafts». In American sports news, players are picked in «the draft». Phrases: first draft, rough draft, final draft, redraft, draft email, drafted into the army.
examples from the lessons: Write a first draft, then check it for mistakes. | My rough draft was full of crossings-out. | She drafted a letter to the council about the park. | The email is saved in my Drafts folder. | We redrafted our story to make the ending stronger. | (US) Close the window, there's a draft. | His grandfather was drafted into the army. | The basketball player was picked first in the draft.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: draft, drafts, drafted, drafting. Spelling trap: in UK English a cold wind in a room, a beer from a barrel and the game draughts (checkers) are spelt «draught»; but a piece of writing is «draft» in both UK and US English. US English uses «draft» for all of them.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An electron is a tiny particle, much smaller than an atom, that has a negative electric charge and moves around the nucleus (centre) of an atom. 2) When many electrons flow through a wire, that flow is an electric current.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about electricity and atoms, electrons carry electric current through wires in circuits; metals let electrons flow easily (conductors), while plastic and rubber do not (insulators). Static electricity happens when electrons move from one thing to another, like rubbing a balloon on your hair. Phrases: flow of electrons, negative charge, protons, neutrons and electrons.
examples from the lessons: An electron has a negative charge. | Electrons flow through the copper wire. | An atom has protons and neutrons in the middle and electrons around them. | When you rub a balloon, electrons move onto it. | Electrons are far too small to see, even with a microscope. | Electricity is a flow of electrons in a circuit. | A proton has a positive charge, and an electron has a negative one. | Electrons move easily in metals, so metals conduct electricity.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: an electron (use «an»), electrons. Pronounced «ih-LEK-tron». Related words: electric, electricity, electronic. Simplified pictures show electrons orbiting like planets, but scientists now describe them as clouds around the nucleus. Opposite charges attract: electrons (negative) are attracted to protons (positive).

part of speech: interjection (er — a hesitation sound); also abbreviation (ER, E.R.)
meaning for a pupil: 1) «Er» is a sound people make when they are not sure what to say or are thinking, like «um»: «It's, er, somewhere here.» 2) (US, abbreviation) ER stands for «emergency room», the part of a hospital that treats urgent injuries and illness (UK: A&E). 3) (UK, abbreviation) ER stands for «Elizabeth Regina», Latin for Queen Elizabeth, seen on postboxes. 4) «-er» is also a suffix that makes a person who does something (teacher) or a comparative (bigger).
its sense in the lessons: In stories and play scripts «er» shows a character is nervous, shy, unsure or lying: «Did you eat the cake?» «Er… no.» In speaking lessons pupils learn to use fewer «ers» and «ums» when presenting. In grammar lessons the suffix -er makes comparatives (taller) and nouns (singer). Phrases: er… um…, er, well.
examples from the lessons: «Er, I think I forgot my homework,» said Sam. | He said «er» a lot because he was nervous. | «Where's my phone?» «Er… I haven't seen it.» | Try not to say «er» between every sentence in your talk. | The doctor in the ER fixed his broken arm. | The old postbox had «ER» on it. | The suffix -er turns «fast» into «faster». | Add -er to «paint» to make «painter».
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Er» is not a real word with a meaning; it is a filler sound and has no plural or forms. In British English it is pronounced like «uh» (the r is silent); Americans may write it as «uh». ER and E.R. in capitals are abbreviations. Do not confuse with «err», a formal verb meaning to make a mistake («to err is human»).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A gibbon is a small ape with very long arms and no tail that lives in the rainforests of Southeast Asia and swings quickly from branch to branch through the trees.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about primates and rainforests, gibbons are the fastest tree-swinging animals (this way of moving is called brachiation), and they sing loud songs in the morning, often in pairs, to mark their territory. Many gibbons are endangered because forests are cut down. Phrases: swing like a gibbon, gibbon song, lesser apes.
examples from the lessons: The gibbon swung from branch to branch at high speed. | Gibbons sing loud songs every morning. | A gibbon's arms are longer than its legs. | Gibbons do not have tails. | The gibbon pair sang together to tell others to keep away. | Gibbons live in the forests of Southeast Asia. | Many kinds of gibbons are in danger because of logging. | At the zoo we watched the gibbons swinging on ropes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a gibbon, gibbons. Pronounced «GIB-un». Trap: gibbons are apes, not monkeys, because they have no tails; they are called «lesser apes», smaller than the great apes (gorillas, chimpanzees, orangutans, bonobos). Edward Gibbon was a famous historian, a name.

part of speech: noun (a lichen, lichens; also uncountable: lichen)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A lichen is a living thing that grows in crusty, leafy or bushy patches on rocks, walls, tree bark and gravestones; it is made of a fungus and a tiny alga (or bacteria) living together and helping each other.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, lichens are a famous example of two living things working together (symbiosis): the alga makes food from sunlight, the fungus gives shelter and holds water. Lichens are used to check air quality, because many kinds die where the air is polluted, so lots of lichens mean clean air. They grow very slowly and can live in harsh places like the Arctic, where reindeer eat them. Phrases: covered in lichen, lichen survey, crusty lichen.
examples from the lessons: The old wall was covered in orange lichen. | Lots of lichen on trees shows the air is clean. | Lichen is made of a fungus and an alga living together. | Reindeer eat lichen in winter. | We did a lichen survey around the school grounds. | Lichens grow very slowly, only a few millimetres a year. | Grey lichen spread across the gravestone. | Lichens can grow on bare rock where nothing else can.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable (different lichens) or uncountable (some lichen). Pronounced «LY-ken» (UK and US) or sometimes «LITCH-en». Trap: lichen is not a plant and not a moss, though it may look like one. Moss is a plant; lichen is a partnership of a fungus and an alga.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A mandrill is a large monkey from the rainforests of central Africa; the males have a bright red and blue face and a colourful bottom.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about primates and how animals show off, the mandrill is the world's largest monkey, and the brightest males are the strongest and lead the group. They live in big groups called hordes, eat fruit, seeds and insects, and have big teeth. In stories and films (Rafiki in «The Lion King» is partly a mandrill) it appears as a wise or funny character. Phrases: a horde of mandrills, mandrill's face.
examples from the lessons: The mandrill has a bright red and blue nose. | Mandrills are the biggest monkeys in the world. | A male mandrill shows its long teeth to warn others. | Mandrills live in large groups in African forests. | The brightest male mandrill is the leader of the group. | Rafiki in «The Lion King» looks a bit like a mandrill. | Mandrills store food in their cheek pouches. | We drew the mandrill's colourful face in art class.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a mandrill, mandrills. Pronounced «MAN-dril». A mandrill is a monkey (it has a short tail), not an ape. Do not confuse with a «mandrel» (a tool) or a baboon, its close relative.

part of speech: noun (a roost, roosts); verb (roost, roosts, roosted, roosting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A roost is a place where birds or bats rest or sleep, such as a branch, a perch or a barn. 2) To roost is for birds or bats to settle down to rest or sleep there. 3) «Rule the roost» means to be the boss of a group or a home. 4) «Come home to roost» means that bad things someone did come back to cause trouble for them.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about birds and bats, roosts are where they sleep, often in large groups; bat roosts are protected by law in the UK. Chickens roost on a perch in their coop at night. In stories the idioms show who is in charge or how bad deeds return. Phrases: rule the roost, come home to roost, bat roost, go to roost.
examples from the lessons: The hens went to roost as the sun set. | Hundreds of starlings roost under the pier. | Bats roost in the old church roof. | You must not disturb a bat roost. | In our house the cat rules the roost. | The owl roosts in the hollow tree during the day. | His lies came home to roost when the truth came out. | The parrot has a favourite roost by the window.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: a roost, roosts. Verb: roost, roosts, roosted, roosting. «Rooster» (US, Australia) is a male chicken (UK: cockerel), from the same word. Both idioms are figurative, not about real birds.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A toucan is a tropical bird from Central and South America with black feathers and a huge, brightly coloured beak. 2) (UK) A toucan crossing is a road crossing with lights that both pedestrians and cyclists can use («two can» cross).
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about rainforests and adaptations, the toucan's big beak is light because it is hollow inside; it helps the bird reach fruit on thin branches and lose heat to keep cool. Toucans spread seeds through the forest. In UK road safety lessons, a toucan crossing lets bikes and people cross together. Phrases: toco toucan, keel-billed toucan, toucan crossing.
examples from the lessons: The toucan's beak is bright orange and very big. | A toucan uses its beak to pick fruit. | Toucans live in the rainforests of South America. | Although it looks heavy, a toucan's beak is light and hollow. | The toucan threw a berry up and caught it in its beak. | Toucans sleep with their beaks tucked under their wings. | We crossed the road on our bikes at the toucan crossing. | I painted a toucan with a rainbow beak.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a toucan, toucans. Pronounced «TOO-kan». Do not confuse with the hornbill of Africa and Asia, which looks similar but is not related. The UK «toucan crossing» is a pun on «two can» (people and bikes), not about birds.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (old-fashioned, literary or Bible) A babe is a baby: «a babe in arms», the baby Jesus «the babe in the manger». 2) (informal) «Babe» is a loving name people call their boyfriend, girlfriend, husband, wife or child, like «darling» or «honey». 3) (slang, can be rude) A «babe» is a word for an attractive person, especially a young woman; many people find this disrespectful. 4) «A babe in the woods» means someone innocent who does not know how the world works.
its sense in the lessons: In Christmas carols and Bible stories, «babe» means baby: «Away in a manger, no crib for a bed, the little Lord Jesus laid down his sweet head… the babe». In everyday talk adults may say «Thanks, babe» to a partner. In stories, «a babe in arms» means a very young baby. Phrases: babe in arms, the babe in the manger, babe in the woods, hey babe.
examples from the lessons: The shepherds found the babe lying in a manger. | She was only a babe in arms when they moved to Ireland. | «Thanks, babe,» Mum said to Dad. | (informal) «Night night, babe,» said Mum as she switched off the light. | He was a babe in the woods when it came to money. | The carol tells of the babe born in Bethlehem. | (slang) Calling a stranger «babe» can sound rude. | Babe is also the name of a famous film about a pig.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a babe, babes. Register matters: «babe» meaning baby is old or poetic; as a pet name it is informal and used between people who are close; calling women you don't know «babe» is disrespectful. «Babes» is also UK slang for friends or partners. Not to be confused with «baby», the everyday word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A beluga (or beluga whale) is a white whale of the Arctic with a round head, no back fin, and a very wide range of whistles and clicks; it is sometimes called the «sea canary». 2) A beluga is also a very large fish, a kind of sturgeon, whose eggs are sold as expensive caviar.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about the Arctic and sea mammals, the beluga uses echolocation to find food, can turn its head because its neck bones are not joined, and its white colour hides it among ice. Babies are born grey. Belugas face danger from pollution, noise and melting ice. Phrases: beluga whale, a pod of belugas, beluga caviar.
examples from the lessons: The beluga whale is completely white. | Belugas make so many sounds they are called sea canaries. | A pod of belugas swam up the river. | Baby belugas are grey and turn white as they grow. | A beluga can move its head from side to side. | Belugas have no back fin, which helps them swim under ice. | We sang the song «Baby Beluga» in the nursery. | Beluga caviar comes from a huge fish, not a whale.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a beluga, belugas. Pronounced «buh-LOO-guh». The word comes from Russian «belyi», meaning white. Two different animals share the name: the whale (a mammal) and the sturgeon (a fish); context tells you which.

part of speech: noun (a chihuahua, chihuahuas; Chihuahua — a name)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A chihuahua is a very small breed of dog with big ears and big eyes, the smallest dog breed in the world. 2) (a name) Chihuahua is a large state in northern Mexico and a city there, after which the dog is named.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life chihuahuas are popular pets, often carried in bags; they are lively, loyal and can be noisy and bossy for their size. In geography lessons about Mexico, Chihuahua is the largest state, with deserts and the Copper Canyon. In stories a chihuahua is often a small dog that thinks it is big. Phrases: a tiny chihuahua, a long-haired chihuahua.
examples from the lessons: A chihuahua is small enough to fit in a handbag. | Our neighbour's chihuahua barks at the postman. | The chihuahua shivered, so they put a little coat on it. | Chihuahuas are named after a place in Mexico. | Even though it is tiny, the chihuahua acts like a guard dog. | The chihuahua weighed less than two bags of sugar. | Chihuahua is the biggest state in Mexico. | My aunt's chihuahua sleeps on a cushion by the fire.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a chihuahua, chihuahuas. Pronounced «chi-WAH-wah»; the spelling is hard: c-h-i-h-u-a-h-u-a (the h in the middle is silent). Often spelt with a capital C because it comes from a place name. Small dogs still need walks, training and gentle handling.

part of speech: noun (a curie, curies — a science unit); a name (Curie)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (a name) Marie Curie was a scientist born in Poland who worked in France; she discovered the elements radium and polonium, studied radioactivity, and was the first woman to win a Nobel Prize and the first person to win two in different sciences. Pierre Curie was her husband and work partner. 2) A curie is an old unit for measuring radioactivity, named after the Curies.
its sense in the lessons: In science and history lessons about famous scientists and women in science, Marie Curie is a role model who worked very hard when women were not welcome in science. She did not know how dangerous radioactivity was, and she became ill from it; her notebooks are still radioactive. In the UK, Marie Curie is also the name of a charity that cares for people who are dying. Phrases: Marie Curie, the Curies, Marie Curie nurses.
examples from the lessons: Marie Curie won two Nobel Prizes. | Marie and Pierre Curie discovered radium. | Marie Curie studied radioactivity. | Her notebooks are still radioactive and are kept in lead boxes. | Marie Curie was born in Poland. | The Marie Curie charity helps people at the end of their lives. | Radioactivity can be measured in curies. | We dressed up as Marie Curie for our science day.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a name: capital C, Curie; pronounced «KYOOR-ee». As a unit: small c, symbol Ci; today scientists mostly use the becquerel instead. The element curium is named after the Curies. It is not an ordinary English word you use for something else.

part of speech: noun, a name (Han; the Han, the Han Chinese, the Han dynasty)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (a name) The Han dynasty was a family of emperors who ruled China for about four hundred years, a famous golden age of Chinese history. 2) (a name) The Han Chinese are the largest ethnic group in China and in the world, named after the Han dynasty. 3) (Mandarin, pinyin) «hàn» is a Chinese syllable used in words like «Hànzì» (Chinese characters) and «Hànyǔ» (the Chinese language); it sounds like «hahn». 4) (a name) Han is also a Korean family name, a river in Korea (the Han River in Seoul), and a first name, as in Han Solo from «Star Wars». 5) (old) A han was an inn for travellers in Turkey and the Middle East.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons about ancient China, the Han dynasty made paper, built parts of the Great Wall, started the Silk Road trade with the West and gave its name to the Chinese people and Chinese writing. In Mandarin lessons pupils meet «Hànzì» for Chinese characters. Phrases: the Han dynasty, Han Chinese, Han characters.
examples from the lessons: Paper was invented in China during the Han dynasty. | The Silk Road grew busy in the time of the Han. | Most people in China are Han Chinese. | Chinese characters are called «Hànzì» in Mandarin. | Han emperors sent explorers far to the west. | Han Solo flies the Millennium Falcon in «Star Wars». | The Han River flows through Seoul in South Korea. | We made a timeline of Chinese dynasties, from the Qin to the Han and beyond.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A name, so it takes a capital H: Han. Not an ordinary English word. In pinyin, tone marks may be added (hàn); the Mandarin «a» sounds like the «a» in «father». The Han dynasty came right after the Qin dynasty, which first united China.

part of speech: noun (French: une plage, des plages); also English science word (a plage, plages — rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (French) «Plage» is the French word for «beach»: «la plage» means «the beach»; it sounds like «plahzh» to an English ear and is not an everyday English word. 2) (science, rare) In astronomy a plage is a bright patch in the Sun's atmosphere near a sunspot. 3) In English it may appear in names of seaside places, like Paris-Plages.
its sense in the lessons: In French lessons pupils learn holiday words: «Je vais à la plage» (I am going to the beach), «la mer» (the sea), «le sable» (the sand). In France and Belgium road signs say «Plage» pointing to the beach. In science it is a rare word for bright areas on the Sun. Phrases: à la plage (to/at the beach), la plage (the beach).
examples from the lessons: «Plage» means «beach» in French. | (French) Nous allons à la plage. — We are going to the beach. | The sign in France said «Plage 500 m». | (French) La plage est très belle. — The beach is very beautiful. | We sang a French song about a day at the plage. | In English you say beach, but in French you say plage. | Scientists photographed a bright plage near a sunspot. | (French) Il y a du sable sur la plage. — There is sand on the beach.
note for the reader of a maths problem: In French «plage» is a feminine noun: «la plage», «une plage», plural «les plages». Pronounced «plahzh», with the «g» soft like the «s» in «treasure». Not an English word in everyday life; English speakers say «beach». Do not confuse with «page» or «plague».

part of speech: noun (a po, pos — UK old-fashioned); abbreviation (PO, P.O.); also a name (the Po)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (UK, old-fashioned, informal) A po is a chamber pot: a bowl kept under the bed to wee in at night in the days before indoor toilets. 2) (abbreviation) PO stands for Post Office, as in «PO Box», a box at the post office where letters can be collected; also «purchase order» in business and «petty officer» in the navy. 3) (a name) The Po is the longest river in Italy. 4) (Mandarin, pinyin) «pó» means grandmother on the mother's side in «pópo» (Cantonese and Mandarin speakers also say this), and «pō» means slope; it sounds like «paw». 5) (a name) Po is a character's name, like the red Teletubby and the panda in «Kung Fu Panda».
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons about Victorian and Tudor homes, people used a po or chamber pot at night and emptied it in the morning. In everyday life a PO Box is an address for letters. In geography, the River Po flows across northern Italy to the Adriatic Sea. In stories and cartoons, Po is a name. Phrases: PO Box, chamber pot, the River Po, po-faced (UK: serious and disapproving).
examples from the lessons: In Victorian times, people kept a po under the bed. | Send your entry to PO Box 25. | The River Po flows across northern Italy. | Po is the panda in «Kung Fu Panda». | Po was the smallest Teletubby. | (UK, informal) The teacher looked po-faced when we laughed in assembly. | The chamber pot was also called a po. | The farmland around the Po is very flat and rich.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As «chamber pot», «po» is old and slightly funny; plural «pos». As an abbreviation it is in capitals: PO, P.O. «Po-faced» (UK, informal) means looking very serious and not amused. In pinyin, tones change the meaning; «po» alone is not English. Context tells you which meaning is meant.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A primate is a mammal belonging to the group that includes humans, apes (gorillas, chimpanzees, orangutans, gibbons), monkeys and lemurs; primates usually have hands that can grasp, forward-facing eyes and big brains. 2) (church) A primate is the most senior bishop of a country or region; for example, the Archbishop of Canterbury is called the Primate of All England.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on animal groups (classification), primates are mammals with flexible hands and feet, fingernails instead of claws, good eyesight and clever brains; humans are primates too. Many primates live in rainforests and are endangered. In RE lessons about the Church of England or the Catholic Church, «primate» is a title for a top archbishop. Phrases: non-human primates, great apes, the Primate of All Ireland.
examples from the lessons: Humans, monkeys and apes are all primates. | Primates have hands that can grip things. | Lemurs are primates that live only in Madagascar. | Many primates live in groups and look after their young for a long time. | Chimpanzees are the primates most closely related to humans. | Scientists study primates to learn how they use tools. | (church) The Archbishop of Armagh is the Primate of All Ireland. | Gorillas are the largest primates.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a primate, primates. Pronounced «PRY-mate» for the animal, and also «PRY-mit» for the church title. Trap: «primate» does not mean only monkeys; humans and apes are primates too. Apes have no tails; most monkeys have tails.

part of speech: noun, a name (Qin; the Qin dynasty) and Mandarin pinyin (qín)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (a name) The Qin dynasty was the first family of emperors to join China into one country; its first emperor, Qin Shi Huang, built early parts of the Great Wall, made one system of writing, money and measures, and was buried with the Terracotta Army. 2) (Mandarin, pinyin) «Qin» is a Chinese syllable; «qín» can mean a stringed instrument, like the «guqin», a kind of Chinese zither. In pinyin «q» sounds like «ch», so «Qin» sounds like «chin» to an English ear. 3) (a name) Qin is also a Chinese family name. It is not an English word.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons about ancient China, the Qin dynasty was short but very important: it united warring states, standardised writing and measures, and ruled harshly. The word «China» may come from «Qin». The Terracotta Army of thousands of clay soldiers was found by farmers digging a well. In Mandarin lessons pupils learn that pinyin «q» is said like English «ch». Phrases: the Qin dynasty, Qin Shi Huang, the Qin emperor.
examples from the lessons: The Qin dynasty united China for the first time. | Qin Shi Huang was buried with an army of clay soldiers. | Pinyin «Qin» is pronounced like «chin». | The name «China» may come from the Qin. | The Qin emperor made everyone use the same coins and writing. | The guqin is an old Chinese instrument with seven strings. | Farmers found the Terracotta Army of the Qin emperor while digging a well. | The Qin was followed by the Han dynasty.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A name, so it takes a capital Q: Qin. Not an English word, so do not use it as one. In pinyin «q» is not followed by «u» as in English (queen); it is a «ch» sound. Do not confuse with «Qing», the last Chinese dynasty, many centuries later.

part of speech: noun (a senate, senates; the Senate — a name)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A senate is one of the two parts of the group that makes laws in some countries; in the USA, Australia, Canada, Ireland (Seanad) and others, the Senate is often called the «upper house». 2) In ancient Rome, the Senate was a council of important men who advised and ruled the Roman Republic. 3) In some universities, the senate is the group of senior teachers that runs the university.
its sense in the lessons: In citizenship lessons, the US Congress has two parts: the House of Representatives and the Senate, with two senators from every state; both must agree to make a law. Australia's Parliament also has a House of Representatives and a Senate. In UK Parliament the matching part is the House of Lords. In history lessons about Rome, senators wore togas and Julius Caesar was killed in a meeting of the Senate. Phrases: the US Senate, a senate vote, the Roman Senate, senator.
examples from the lessons: The Senate voted on the new law. | Each US state has two senators in the Senate. | The Australian Senate meets in Canberra. | Julius Caesar was stabbed at a meeting of the Senate. | Roman senators wore white togas with purple stripes. | The bill must pass both the House and the Senate. | The university senate decides on new courses. | In the UK, the House of Lords is a bit like a senate.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a senate, senates; capital S when naming a particular one: the Senate. A member is a «senator». Pronounced «SEN-it». Do not confuse with «Senate» and «Congress»: in the USA, Congress is the Senate plus the House of Representatives together.

part of speech: noun (a shay, shays — old); a name (Shay)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (a name) Shay is a first name, used for boys and girls, from the Irish name Séamus or Séaghdha; it is also a surname. 2) (old-fashioned) A shay is a light, two-wheeled carriage pulled by a horse, a word made from «chaise». 3) (rare) It can be a spelling of «shae» or «Shea», other names.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and maths word problems Shay is usually just a character's name: «Shay ran 3 km.» In old poems and history books a «shay» is a carriage, as in the poem «The Deacon's Masterpiece, or the Wonderful One-Hoss Shay». It is not a common everyday English word today.
examples from the lessons: Shay is the captain of our football team. | Shay has 15 marbles and gives away 6. | My cousin Shay lives in Galway. | The farmer drove to town in his one-horse shay. | In the old poem, the shay fell apart all at once. | Shay and Amelia are partners in the science project. | A shay was a light carriage for one or two people. | Shay's dad is a firefighter.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a name, write it with a capital S: Shay. Pronounced «shay», rhyming with «day». The carriage meaning is old and rare. Do not confuse with «Shea» or «Shae», other spellings of names, or with «chez» (French for «at the home of»).

part of speech: noun (snot, uncountable — informal); also a snot (a rude person, informal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) Snot is the slimy stuff (mucus) that comes out of your nose, especially when you have a cold. 2) (informal, rude) A snot is a rude, proud, cheeky person who thinks they are better than others; the adjective is «snotty».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life «snot» is a common but slightly rude word; in science and health lessons the polite word is «mucus», which traps dust and germs and helps protect your body. Hygiene lessons say «Catch it, bin it, kill it»: sneeze into a tissue, throw it away and wash your hands. In funny stories for children, snot is used for gross-out jokes. Phrases: snotty nose, wipe your snot, snot-nosed, snotty (posh and rude).
examples from the lessons: Use a tissue, not your sleeve, to wipe your snot! | When I have a cold, my nose is full of snot. | The baby had snot running down her face. | Snot traps dust and germs before they get into your lungs. | «Ew, there's snot on the door handle!» | (informal) The doctor calls it mucus, but we call it snot. | (rude) Don't be such a snot to your little brother. | The story had a slimy monster made of snot.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable for the nose stuff: «some snot», not «a snot». Register: informal and a bit rude; in school science writing use «mucus». «Snotty» can mean full of snot or (informal) rude and stuck-up. «Snot-nosed» means young and cheeky (rude).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Soreness is pain, aching or tenderness in a part of the body, such as sore muscles after exercise, a sore throat or a sore knee. 2) (rare, old-fashioned) Soreness can mean being upset or annoyed about something, like still feeling «sore» about losing.
its sense in the lessons: In PE and health lessons, soreness in muscles a day or two after hard exercise is normal and gets better with rest, stretching and water; sharp pain is different and should be told to an adult. In health talk, soreness in the throat is a sign of a cold. Phrases: muscle soreness, a feeling of soreness, some soreness, redness and soreness.
examples from the lessons: I felt some soreness in my legs after the cross-country race. | The cream helped the soreness on her sunburnt shoulders. | Soreness in your throat can mean you are getting a cold. | Stretching after sport can reduce soreness. | The nurse asked if there was any soreness around the cut. | Redness and soreness around a wound can be signs of infection. | His arm had a little soreness after the injection. | The soreness went away after a few days.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «some soreness», not «a soreness» or «soreneses». Made from the adjective «sore» + suffix «-ness». Homophone trap: «sore» (painful) sounds like «saw» (tool, and the past of «see») and «soar» (fly high) in many accents. Soreness is usually a mild ache; severe or lasting pain needs a doctor.

part of speech: noun (a tartan, tartans; also uncountable); adjective (tartan)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Tartan is a pattern of coloured stripes crossing each other at right angles, making squares; it is woven into woollen cloth, especially in Scotland. 2) A tartan is one particular pattern belonging to a Scottish clan (family group), region or organisation. 3) Tartan describes things made of this cloth: a tartan kilt, a tartan scarf.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and history lessons about Scotland, tartan is part of Highland culture: kilts, clans and bagpipes. Each clan, like MacDonald or Campbell, has its own tartan, and some countries and towns have one too. In maths and art, tartan is a fun way to study patterns, symmetry and right angles. Phrases: tartan kilt, clan tartan, the Tartan Army (Scotland's football fans), tartan rug.
examples from the lessons: He wore a tartan kilt at the wedding. | Every Scottish clan has its own tartan. | Grandma wrapped a tartan rug around her knees. | The tartan pattern has lines that cross at right angles. | Our class designed a new tartan for our school. | The Tartan Army sang loudly at the football match. | The shortbread tin was covered in red tartan. | Tartan was once banned in the Scottish Highlands for a time.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable (many tartans, different patterns) or uncountable (a scarf made of tartan). Pronounced «TAR-tun». Americans often call the pattern «plaid»; in Scotland a «plaid» is actually a large piece of tartan cloth worn over the shoulder. Do not confuse with «tartar» (a crust on teeth, or tartare sauce).

part of speech: noun (te — a music note; also spelt ti); also French and Māori word (te)
meaning for a pupil: 1) In tonic sol-fa singing (do, re, mi, fa, so, la, te), «te» is the seventh note of the major scale, just below the top do; it is spelt «ti» in the USA. 2) (French) «te» is a French pronoun meaning «you» or «yourself» to one friend or child, as in «Je t'aime» (I love you, where «te» becomes t') and «Comment tu t'appelles?»; it sounds like «tuh» to an English ear and is not an English word. 3) (Māori, New Zealand) «te» means «the» (for one thing), as in «Te Reo Māori» (the Māori language) and «Aotearoa», «Te Papa» (the museum). 4) (Mandarin) «tè» means special, in «tèbié» (especially).
its sense in the lessons: In music lessons pupils sing the scale «do re mi fa so la te do», as in the song «Do-Re-Mi» from «The Sound of Music» («Tea, a drink with jam and bread» is a pun on «te»). In New Zealand schools, Māori words with «te» are everyday: Te Reo, Te Ika-a-Māui (the North Island). In French lessons «te» is in phrases like «Je te remercie» (I thank you). Phrases: do re mi fa so la te do; Te Reo Māori.
examples from the lessons: Sing up the scale: do, re, mi, fa, so, la, te, do. | «Te» is the note just before the top «do». | In America they spell it «ti». | (Māori) Te Reo Māori is taught in New Zealand schools. | (Māori) Te Papa is the national museum in Wellington. | (French) Je te vois. — I see you. | (French) Comment tu t'appelles? — What is your name? | In the song, «tea» is a pun on the note «te».
note for the reader of a maths problem: Not an everyday English word on its own. In sol-fa, «te» is UK and Commonwealth spelling, «ti» is American. In French «te» changes to «t'» before a vowel (je t'aime). In Māori «te» is for one thing, «ngā» for more than one. Pronounced «tee» for the music note, «tuh» in French, «teh» in Māori.

meaning for a pupil: 1) UTC stands for Coordinated Universal Time, the main world time standard that clocks and computers use; time zones are given as UTC plus or minus some hours. 2) In winter UTC is the same as the time in London (Greenwich Mean Time, GMT). 3) (UK) A UTC is also a University Technical College, a kind of school for pupils aged 14 to 19 focusing on science and engineering.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and maths lessons about time zones, places are «ahead of» or «behind» UTC: Sydney is several hours ahead, New York is several hours behind. Pilots, scientists, weather forecasters and computers use UTC so everyone means the same time. In maths problems you add or subtract hours to work out local time. Phrases: UTC+10, UTC−5, in UTC, time zone.
examples from the lessons: New York is five hours behind UTC in winter. | Sydney is ahead of UTC. | Pilots always use UTC so there is no mix-up. | The rocket launch time was given in UTC. | If it is noon UTC and you live in UTC+2, it is two o'clock where you are. | My computer shows the time zone as UTC+1. | In winter, London time is the same as UTC. | My brother goes to a UTC to study engineering.
note for the reader of a maths problem: An abbreviation: always written in capitals, UTC, said letter by letter «you-tee-see». The letters are in a strange order because it was a compromise between English (CUT) and French (TUT). In maths: «UTC+3» means add 3 hours to UTC to get local time; «UTC−5» means take away 5 hours. Watch out when the answer passes midnight: the day changes too.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In fairy tales and stories, a witch is a woman (and sometimes a man) who has magic powers, often shown with a pointed hat, a broomstick, a black cat and a cauldron. 2) In history, many people, mostly poor or old women, were wrongly accused of being witches and punished or killed in witch hunts. 3) Some people today follow religions such as Wicca and call themselves witches; for them it is about nature and their beliefs, not evil. 4) (rude, insulting) Calling a woman «a witch» means she is nasty or ugly; this is unkind.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and Halloween, witches can be wicked (the witch in «Hansel and Gretel», the White Witch of Narnia) or good (Hermione in «Harry Potter», Meg in «Meg and Mog»). In history lessons, the witch trials in Europe and at Salem in America show how fear and rumours led to innocent people being harmed; «a witch hunt» now means unfairly blaming and attacking someone. In the Bible, King Saul visits the witch of Endor. Phrases: wicked witch, witch hunt, witch's hat, witching hour.
examples from the lessons: The witch flew over the town on her broomstick. | The wicked witch locked Hansel in a cage. | I dressed up as a witch for Halloween. | In the past, innocent women were accused of being witches. | The witch stirred a bubbling cauldron. | The newspaper said the inquiry was a witch hunt. | Witches are not real in the way stories show them. | The White Witch made it always winter in Narnia.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a witch, witches (add -es). Homophone trap: «which» (the question word) sounds the same in many accents: «Which witch is which?» A man in stories is often called a «wizard» or «warlock». Calling a real person a witch is an insult. In history, saying someone was a witch was a false accusation, not a proven fact.

meaning for a pupil: 1) BCE stands for «Before the Common Era», used after a year number to show years counted backwards from the start of the usual calendar; it means the same as BC («before Christ»). 2) Its partner is CE («Common Era»), which means the same as AD.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons BCE is used on timelines for ancient times, such as ancient Egypt, ancient Greece and the Stone Age. Years BCE count down towards zero (a larger number BCE is longer ago), then years CE count up. Some people prefer BCE and CE because they do not name a religion; others use BC and AD. Phrases: years BCE, BCE and CE, in the third century BCE.
examples from the lessons: The pyramids of Giza were built more than two thousand years BCE. | On our timeline, years BCE are on the left. | BCE means the same as BC. | The bigger the number BCE, the longer ago it was. | Ancient Rome was founded many centuries BCE. | Our book uses BCE and CE instead of BC and AD. | Stonehenge was built in the Stone Age, thousands of years BCE. | There is no year zero between 1 BCE and 1 CE.
note for the reader of a maths problem: An abbreviation: written in capitals, BCE (sometimes B.C.E.), and said letter by letter «bee-see-ee». It goes after the year number. Maths trap: for BCE years, counting goes backwards, so to find how many years passed between a year BCE and a year CE, add the two numbers and take away 1 (because there is no year zero); between two years BCE, subtract the smaller from the bigger.

part of speech: noun (a bias, biases; also uncountable); verb (bias, biases, biased, biasing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Bias is an unfair way of favouring one person, side or idea over others, often without good reason: a referee with a bias towards one team. 2) To bias someone or something is to make them unfair or one-sided; «biased» means unfair and one-sided. 3) In maths and science, bias is when results are pushed in one direction by the way you test or collect data, so they are not fair or accurate. 4) In sewing, cutting cloth «on the bias» means cutting diagonally across the threads. 5) In bowls (lawn bowls), the bias is the weight that makes the ball curve.
its sense in the lessons: In media and citizenship lessons pupils learn to spot bias in news, adverts and websites: who wrote it, what side they want you to take, and what is left out. In science and maths, a fair test avoids bias; a survey asking only your friends is biased. In computing lessons, AI can show bias if it learns from unfair examples. Phrases: biased towards, biased against, without bias, unconscious bias, bias in a survey.
examples from the lessons: The referee was accused of bias towards the home team. | This website is biased because it only shows one side. | Ask lots of different people so your survey is not biased. | A coin that lands on heads too often may have a bias. | Try to read the news without bias. | Everyone has some bias, so it helps to check other views. | The advert biased people towards buying the sweets. | AI can copy the bias in the data it learns from.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: countable or uncountable (a bias, biases; some bias). Adjective: biased (spelt with one s in most places; «biassed» is rare). Pronounced «BY-us». «Biased towards» means favouring; «biased against» means unfair against. In maths: a biased dice or coin does not give each result an equal chance, so probabilities like one half or one sixth do not apply.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A hammerhead (or hammerhead shark) is a shark whose head is wide and flat, shaped like the letter T or a hammer, with an eye at each end. 2) The head of a hammer, the heavy metal part you hit with. 3) A hammerhead (hamerkop) is also an African wading bird with a crest at the back of its head.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about oceans and adaptations, the hammerhead's wide head lets it see all around and helps it sense the tiny electric signals of prey, like stingrays hiding in the sand. Some hammerheads swim in big groups called schools. Several kinds are endangered because of overfishing and shark finning. Phrases: great hammerhead, scalloped hammerhead, a school of hammerheads.
examples from the lessons: The hammerhead shark has eyes at both ends of its head. | Hammerheads hunt stingrays on the sea floor. | Divers saw a school of hammerheads. | A hammerhead can sense the electricity made by hidden fish. | The great hammerhead is the biggest kind. | Many hammerheads are caught for their fins. | The hammerhead's head is wide like a T. | The metal hammerhead came loose from the wooden handle.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a hammerhead, hammerheads. Compound word: hammer + head. Most hammerheads are not dangerous to people, though big ones should be treated with respect.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A mane is the long thick hair growing on the neck of some animals, especially horses and male lions. 2) (informal) A mane is a person's long, thick hair: a mane of red hair.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons a male lion's mane protects its neck in fights and shows how strong and healthy it is; darker manes can show older, stronger lions. Horse riders brush and plait the mane. In stories, a hero's flowing mane of hair makes them look wild or strong. Phrases: a lion's mane, a horse's mane, a mane of hair, lion's mane jellyfish.
examples from the lessons: The lion shook its golden mane. | She brushed the pony's mane until it shone. | Only male lions have a mane. | The horse's mane blew in the wind as it galloped. | The singer had a wild mane of curly hair. | We plaited the pony's mane for the show. | A lion's mane jellyfish has long trailing tentacles. | The young lion's mane was still short.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a mane, manes. Homophones: «main» (most important, as in main road) and «Maine» (a US state) sound the same. Do not confuse «mane» (hair) with «main» in writing.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A metaphor is a way of describing something by saying it IS something else, to show what it is like, without using «like» or «as»: «The classroom was a zoo» means it was wild and noisy. 2) A metaphor can be a thing or idea that stands for something else: a journey can be a metaphor for growing up.
its sense in the lessons: In English and poetry lessons (and reading tests), pupils find and explain metaphors and use them to make their own writing vivid: «Her eyes were stars», «Time is money», «He has a heart of stone». Many everyday phrases are hidden metaphors: «a sea of faces», «a storm of applause», «the apple of my eye». Phrases: use a metaphor, a metaphor for, an extended metaphor.
examples from the lessons: «The snow was a white blanket» is a metaphor. | The poet uses a metaphor to compare life to a river. | «He has a heart of gold» is a metaphor; he is very kind. | Explain what the metaphor tells us about the character. | «My brother is a couch potato» is a funny metaphor. | Underline the metaphor in the second line. | The storm in the story is a metaphor for her anger. | «Time is a thief» is a metaphor, because time cannot really steal.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a metaphor, metaphors. Adjective: «metaphorical»; adverb «metaphorically» (not literally). Pronounced «MET-uh-for». The key trap: a metaphor says something IS something else; a simile compares using «like» or «as» («as brave as a lion», «ran like the wind»). Personification gives human actions to things («the wind whispered») and is a special kind of metaphor.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A moa was a very large flightless bird that lived only in New Zealand; the tallest kinds stood taller than a person when reaching up. 2) All moa are now extinct; they died out a few hundred years after people first arrived in New Zealand.
its sense in the lessons: In New Zealand history and science lessons, the moa is a key example of extinction caused by hunting and loss of forest after people arrived. Its only predator before humans was Haast's eagle, the biggest eagle ever, which died out too. Moa bones, eggs and feathers are kept in museums like Te Papa. Phrases: giant moa, moa bones, extinct moa, «gone the way of the moa» (New Zealand: gone for ever).
examples from the lessons: The moa was a giant bird from New Zealand. | Moa could not fly because they had no wings at all. | Haast's eagle hunted moa. | The moa became extinct after people arrived. | We saw a huge moa skeleton at the museum. | Moa ate leaves, twigs and fruit. | (New Zealand) That old phone has gone the way of the moa. | Scientists study moa bones to learn how they lived.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a moa; the plural is moa (in New Zealand, following Māori) or moas. Pronounced «MOH-uh». The word comes from the Māori language. Related to emus and kiwis, which are also flightless birds. Myth: some people claim moa still live in remote forests, but there is no evidence.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Musk is a strong-smelling substance first taken from a gland of the male musk deer, used in making perfumes; today most musk in perfumes is man-made. 2) Musk is any strong, warm, animal-like smell, such as the smell of some animals or plants. 3) Musk is used in names of animals and plants with this smell: musk ox, muskrat, musk rose, musk mallow. 4) (a name) Musk is a surname, for example of a well-known businessman who runs electric car and space rocket companies.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about Arctic animals the musk ox, with its long shaggy coat, forms a circle with others to protect calves from wolves. In history, musk was an expensive trade good on routes from Asia. In news lessons, Musk is a name often in the news about rockets, electric cars and social media, and people have strong and different views about him. Phrases: musk ox, musk deer, muskrat, musky smell.
examples from the lessons: Musk ox live in the cold Arctic tundra. | Some perfumes have a smell of musk. | The musk deer has no antlers but long tusk-like teeth. | The fox left a strong musky smell. | Muskrats build homes in rivers and marshes. | Musk roses smell sweet in summer. | Most musk in perfume today is made in a lab. | The news reported on Musk's latest rocket launch.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «a smell of musk», not «a musk». Adjective: «musky». As a surname it takes a capital M. The musk ox is not really an ox; it is closer to goats and sheep.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A narwhal is a whale of the Arctic Ocean; the male usually has one very long straight spiral tusk growing from his upper lip, which is really a tooth.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about Arctic animals and adaptations, the narwhal's tusk is full of nerves and may help it sense the water and show off to females. Narwhals dive very deep under the ice to catch fish and squid, and Inuit people have hunted them for food for a very long time. In history, sailors sold narwhal tusks in Europe as «unicorn horns». Phrases: the unicorn of the sea, narwhal tusk, a pod of narwhals.
examples from the lessons: The narwhal is called the unicorn of the sea. | A male narwhal has a long spiral tusk. | The narwhal's tusk is actually a tooth. | Narwhals live in the icy Arctic Ocean. | A pod of narwhals came up to breathe through a crack in the ice. | People once sold narwhal tusks as unicorn horns. | Narwhals can dive more than a kilometre deep. | Melting sea ice is a danger for narwhals.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a narwhal, narwhals. Pronounced «NAR-wul». Fact: only some narwhals (mostly males) have a tusk; a few have two. Myth: unicorns are not real, and the «unicorn horns» sold long ago were narwhal teeth.

part of speech: noun (onomatopoeia, uncountable; also an onomatopoeia — an example)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Onomatopoeia is when a word sounds like the noise it describes, such as buzz, bang, sizzle, hiss, splash, cuckoo and woof. 2) An onomatopoeia (or an onomatopoeic word) is one such word.
its sense in the lessons: In English and poetry lessons pupils find and use onomatopoeia to make writing lively and noisy: «The bacon sizzled in the pan.» Comics use it in big letters: POW! CRASH! BOOM! Animal sounds are different in different languages: an English dog says «woof», a French dog says «ouaf», a Ukrainian dog says «hav». Phrases: use onomatopoeia, an onomatopoeic word, sound words.
examples from the lessons: «Buzz» is an example of onomatopoeia. | The poem is full of onomatopoeia: crash, splash, whoosh. | Add some onomatopoeia to make your storm sound real. | The comic showed «KAPOW!» when the hero punched. | «The snake went hiss» uses onomatopoeia. | Can you spell onomatopoeia without looking? | «Tick-tock» copies the sound of a clock. | In Japanese, a cat's meow is «nyan».
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable when talking about the technique: «The poem uses onomatopoeia.» Adjective: «onomatopoeic». Pronounced «on-uh-mat-uh-PEE-uh». Spelling is hard: o-n-o-m-a-t-o-p-o-e-i-a. Do not confuse with alliteration (same first sounds: big bad bear). Many onomatopoeic words can be verbs or nouns: «the bees buzz», «a loud buzz».

part of speech: noun, a name (Panama); also a panama (a hat, panamas)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (a name) Panama is a country in Central America that joins North and South America; its capital is Panama City. 2) (a name) The Panama Canal is a famous canal across Panama that lets ships sail between the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans without going all the way around South America. 3) A panama (or Panama hat) is a light summer hat woven from straw-like leaves; it is actually made in Ecuador.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons Panama is the narrow strip of land between two oceans, and the Panama Canal is a great engineering story: ships are lifted by locks, and it saves thousands of kilometres. Many workers died building it, from disease and accidents. In everyday life a panama is a smart summer hat, worn by cricket fans and grandads. Phrases: the Panama Canal, the Isthmus of Panama, a panama hat.
examples from the lessons: Panama joins North America to South America. | Ships use the Panama Canal to cross from the Atlantic to the Pacific. | Locks lift the ships up and down in the Panama Canal. | The canal saves ships a very long trip around South America. | Grandad wore his panama hat at the cricket. | Panama hats are really made in Ecuador. | Panama City is the capital of Panama. | Many workers died of malaria while building the Panama Canal.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a country it is a name, written with a capital P: Panama. The hat can be written with a small p: a panama. Pronounced «PAN-uh-mah». A person from Panama is Panamanian.

part of speech: noun (a prefix, prefixes); verb (prefix, prefixes, prefixed, prefixing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A prefix is a group of letters added to the start of a word to make a new word with a different meaning, like un- in «unhappy», re- in «redo» or pre- in «preview». 2) To prefix something is to add a word, letters or numbers in front of it. 3) In maths and science, prefixes on units show size: kilo- means a thousand (kilometre), centi- means a hundredth (centimetre), milli- means a thousandth (millimetre). 4) A phone prefix (dialling code) is the numbers you dial before a phone number.
its sense in the lessons: In English grammar and spelling lessons (and SATs), prefixes change meaning but not spelling of the root: un- and dis- and in-/im-/il-/ir- make opposites (unkind, disagree, impossible, illegal, irregular); re- means again; pre- means before; sub- means under; super- means above; anti- means against; auto- means self. In maths lessons, unit prefixes help convert measures. Phrases: add a prefix, the prefix un-, negative prefix.
examples from the lessons: Add the prefix un- to «tidy» to make «untidy». | The prefix re- means «again», as in «rewrite». | «Impossible» uses the prefix im-. | Kilo- is a prefix meaning a thousand, so a kilogram is 1,000 grams. | The prefix sub- means under, like in «submarine». | Circle the prefix in «disappear». | Milli- means one thousandth, so there are 1,000 millimetres in a metre. | To call another country, you prefix the number with its code.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a prefix, prefixes (add -es after x). Pronounced «PREE-fix». A prefix goes at the START; a suffix goes at the END. Spelling trap: adding a prefix does not change the root's letters, so double letters can appear: dis + satisfied = dissatisfied, mis + spell = misspell, un + necessary = unnecessary. In maths: kilo- = ×1,000; centi- = ÷100; milli- = ÷1,000.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A quart is a unit for measuring liquids, equal to a quarter of a gallon, or two pints; it is used mainly in the USA and was used in the UK in the past. 2) «You can't fit a quart into a pint pot» (UK saying) means you cannot fit too much into too small a space.
its sense in the lessons: In maths lessons about measures and converting units, especially in the USA, pupils learn: 2 pints = 1 quart, 4 quarts = 1 gallon. A US quart is a little under a litre (about 0.95 litres); an old British (imperial) quart is bigger, about 1.14 litres, because British pints are bigger. Milk and ice cream in the USA come in quart cartons. Phrases: a quart of milk, quarts and gallons.
examples from the lessons: Mum bought a quart of milk at the store. | There are four quarts in a gallon. | Two pints make one quart. | A quart is about the same as a litre, but a bit less in the US. | How many quarts are in three gallons? | The recipe needs a quart of chicken stock. | Grandma still talks about a quart of milk. | You can't fit a quart into a pint pot.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a quart, quarts. Pronounced «kwort». The name comes from «quarter» because it is a quarter of a gallon. Maths: 1 gallon = 4 quarts = 8 pints. Trap: US and UK quarts are different sizes, so check which one the problem means; most countries use litres instead. Do not confuse with «quartz» (a mineral) or «quarter».

part of speech: noun (a sabre, sabres; US spelling saber); verb (sabre — rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A sabre is a heavy sword with a curved blade and one sharp edge, once used by soldiers on horseback (cavalry). 2) In the sport of fencing, the sabre is one of three weapons (with foil and épée), and points are scored by hitting with the edge or the tip. 3) «Sabre-rattling» means threatening to use force or war to scare others, without actually fighting. 4) A sabre-toothed cat (sabre-toothed tiger) was an extinct big cat with two very long curved teeth.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons sabres were carried by cavalry soldiers and officers; in PE and the Olympics, fencers fight with sabres wearing masks and white suits. In news and citizenship lessons, «sabre-rattling» describes countries making threats. In science lessons about the Ice Age, the sabre-toothed cat (Smilodon) is a famous extinct predator found in tar pits. Phrases: sabre-rattling, sabre-toothed tiger, cavalry sabre, lightsaber.
examples from the lessons: The cavalry officer drew his sabre. | Sabre is the fastest of the three fencing weapons. | The sabre-toothed cat had teeth as long as a ruler. | The two countries were accused of sabre-rattling. | A sabre has a curved blade. | Fossils of sabre-toothed cats were found in tar pits. | She won a medal for sabre fencing. | In «Star Wars» the Jedi fight with lightsabers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a sabre, sabres. Spelling: «sabre» in UK, Ireland, Australia, NZ and Canada; «saber» in the USA (and in «lightsaber»). Pronounced «SAY-ber». «Sabre-rattling» and «sabre-toothed» take hyphens. Trap: the sabre-toothed «tiger» was not closely related to real tigers.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Sodium is a soft, silvery-white metal element with the symbol Na; it is so reactive that it reacts strongly with water, sometimes fizzing and catching fire, so it is never found pure in nature. 2) Sodium is part of many compounds, most famously sodium chloride, which is common table salt; «sodium» on a food label usually means salt in the food.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons sodium is in the periodic table among the alkali metals; teachers show a tiny piece fizzing across water behind a safety screen. In health and food lessons, food labels list sodium or salt, and eating too much can raise blood pressure. Street lights used to glow orange because they used sodium vapour. Phrases: sodium chloride, sodium bicarbonate (baking soda), low sodium, sodium lights.
examples from the lessons: Table salt is made of sodium and chlorine. | Sodium is so soft you can cut it with a knife. | The teacher dropped a tiny piece of sodium into water and it whizzed around. | Too much sodium in food is not good for your heart. | The label shows how much sodium is in the crisps. | Old orange street lights were sodium lamps. | Sodium bicarbonate makes cakes rise. | The symbol for sodium is Na, from its Latin name «natrium».
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «too much sodium», not «a sodium». Pronounced «SOH-dee-um». Symbol trap: sodium is Na, not So or S (S is sulphur). Safety: pure sodium is dangerous and only used by teachers or scientists. On food labels in some countries, the salt amount is about two and a half times the sodium amount.

part of speech: noun (a carcass, carcasses; also spelt carcase in the UK)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A carcass is the dead body of an animal, especially a large one, or one cut up for meat. 2) The carcass of a cooked chicken or turkey is the bones left after the meat is eaten. 3) The carcass of something is its frame or the broken remains: the carcass of an old car or building. 4) (informal, rude or jokey) Someone's carcass can mean their body: «Get your carcass off the sofa!»
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about food chains, scavengers like vultures, hyenas, crows and Tasmanian devils feed on carcasses, and decomposers break down what is left, returning nutrients to the soil. In cooking at home, the turkey carcass is boiled to make soup or stock. In stories a carcass is a grim sign of a hunt or danger. Phrases: an animal carcass, a chicken carcass, the carcass of a whale, pick the carcass clean.
examples from the lessons: Vultures circled above the zebra carcass. | Mum boiled the chicken carcass to make soup. | Hyenas stripped the carcass to the bones. | A whale carcass on the sea floor feeds many creatures. | The rusty carcass of a car lay in the field. | Tasmanian devils eat carcasses, even the bones. | The butcher hung the carcasses in the cold room. | (jokey) «Move your carcass, we're late!» said Dad.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a carcass, carcasses (add -es). Pronounced «KAR-kus». UK spelling «carcase» is also used, especially in the meat trade. Do not confuse with «corpse» (a dead human body). Using «carcass» for a living person's body is informal and jokey or rude.

part of speech: noun (a commonwealth, commonwealths; the Commonwealth — a name)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (a name) The Commonwealth (Commonwealth of Nations) is a group of more than fifty countries, most of which were once part of the British Empire, such as the UK, Canada, Australia, New Zealand, India and many African and Caribbean countries; they work together on trade, education and sport. 2) (a name) A commonwealth is a name for some countries or states: the Commonwealth of Australia, and some US states like Massachusetts and Virginia. 3) A commonwealth is a group of people or a nation working together for the good of all. 4) In English history, the Commonwealth was the time after King Charles I was executed, when England had no king and Oliver Cromwell ruled.
its sense in the lessons: In geography, history and sport lessons, pupils meet the Commonwealth Games, a big sports event every four years for Commonwealth countries, and Commonwealth Day in schools. History lessons discuss how the Commonwealth came from the British Empire and that empire also brought suffering. Phrases: the Commonwealth Games, Commonwealth countries, Commonwealth Day, the Commonwealth of Australia.
examples from the lessons: Canada and Australia are members of the Commonwealth. | The Commonwealth Games are held every four years. | Our school flew flags on Commonwealth Day. | Australia's full name is the Commonwealth of Australia. | Most Commonwealth countries were once ruled by Britain. | Massachusetts is called a commonwealth, not a state. | During the Commonwealth, England had no king. | Athletes from Kenya and Jamaica won medals at the Commonwealth Games.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually a name with a capital C: the Commonwealth. Countable when general: a commonwealth, commonwealths. Compound word: common + wealth (in old English «wealth» meant well-being, so it means «the good of everyone»). Members are free and equal; the King is its symbolic head, but many members are republics with their own presidents.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A cuttlefish is a sea animal related to the squid and octopus, with a wide flat body, eight arms, two long tentacles, a fin around its body and a hard flat shell inside called a cuttlebone. 2) It can change its colour and pattern in a flash to hide or to send messages.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about sea creatures and camouflage, cuttlefish are masters of disguise: special skin cells change their colour and even the texture of their skin. They squirt ink to escape predators. Cuttlebones wash up on beaches and are given to pet birds to peck for calcium. They are clever animals, and are molluscs, not fish. Phrases: giant cuttlefish, cuttlebone, cuttlefish ink.
examples from the lessons: The cuttlefish changed colour to match the rocks. | A cuttlefish squirts ink when it is scared. | We found a white cuttlebone on the beach. | The budgie pecks at its cuttlebone. | Cuttlefish flash stripes of colour to hypnotise their prey. | Giant cuttlefish gather near Whyalla in South Australia. | A cuttlefish has eight arms and two longer tentacles. | Despite its name, a cuttlefish is not a fish.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The plural is usually the same: one cuttlefish, many cuttlefish (cuttlefishes is also used). Trap: it is a mollusc (like squid, octopus and snails), not a fish, even though its name has «fish» in it, just like jellyfish and starfish. The ink, called sepia, was once used for writing and drawing.

part of speech: noun, a name (a Dane, Danes); a Great Dane (a dog)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (a name) A Dane is a person from Denmark. 2) (a name) In history, the Danes were Vikings from Denmark who raided and settled in England, Ireland and other places; part of England under their rule was called the Danelaw. 3) A Great Dane is a breed of very large, tall dog, one of the tallest dogs in the world, gentle despite its size.
its sense in the lessons: In UK history lessons about the Anglo-Saxons and Vikings, the Danes attacked monasteries, King Alfred the Great fought them and later made a deal, and England paid them «Danegeld» to stay away. In everyday life a Great Dane is a giant pet dog (Scooby-Doo is a Great Dane). Phrases: the Danes, a Great Dane, the Danelaw, Danish (the adjective and language).
examples from the lessons: A Dane is someone from Denmark. | The Danes attacked the monastery on the island. | King Alfred fought hard against the Danes. | The Danelaw was the part of England ruled by the Danes. | Our neighbour's Great Dane is taller than me when it stands up. | Scooby-Doo is a Great Dane. | Hans Christian Andersen, who wrote fairy tales, was a Dane. | The Danish language is spoken by Danes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A name, so it takes a capital D: a Dane, the Danes, a Great Dane. The adjective and language is «Danish» (a Danish pastry is a sweet pastry). Do not confuse with «deign» (to lower yourself to do something), which sounds the same, or «Dean» (a name and a title).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Ivory is the hard, creamy-white material that elephant tusks are made of; walrus, narwhal and hippo teeth are also ivory. 2) Ivory is a creamy off-white colour. 3) In the past, piano keys, chess pieces and carvings were made of ivory; «tickle the ivories» (informal) means to play the piano. 4) «An ivory tower» is a place or life far from real-world problems, especially used about clever people who do not understand ordinary life.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography lessons about endangered animals, poachers kill elephants and rhinos (rhino horn is different, made of keratin) for ivory, which is why selling new ivory is banned in most countries, including the UK. In history and art lessons, ivory carvings and old piano keys are shown. Phrases: elephant ivory, ivory trade, ivory poaching, ivory white, ivory tower, Côte d'Ivoire (Ivory Coast).
examples from the lessons: Elephants are killed by poachers for their ivory. | Selling new ivory is against the law in many countries. | The old piano had ivory keys. | She chose an ivory-coloured dress. | The museum has a chess set carved from walrus ivory. | Rangers protect elephants from ivory hunters. | (informal) Grandad likes to tickle the ivories at parties. | Scientists should not live in an ivory tower.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «made of ivory», not «an ivory» (except «ivories», an informal word for piano keys or ivory objects). Pronounced «EYE-vuh-ree». Côte d'Ivoire, the West African country, is French for «Ivory Coast». Plastic and resin «ivory» copies are used today instead of real ivory.

part of speech: noun (a mama, mamas; also mamma, momma)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal, child's word) Mama is a word for mother, often used by young children or in families; it is one of the first words babies say. 2) (informal, US) «Mama» or «momma» is used as an everyday word for mum. 3) (slang) «Mama» can be a friendly or flirty word for a woman, and «big mama» means a large or powerful woman. 4) (French, Spanish, Italian, Ukrainian, Mandarin and many other languages) «mama» or «mamá» or «māma» also means mother in many languages, because babies easily say «ma-ma»; in Ukrainian «мама» (mama) is the everyday word for mum.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, songs and nursery rhymes «mama» is a loving word for mother: «Mama bear», «Hush, little baby, don't say a word, Mama's gonna buy you a mockingbird». In everyday British English «mum» or «mummy» is more usual, in American «mom» or «mommy», in Australia and NZ «mum», in Ireland «mam» or «mammy»; «mama» is common among families from many backgrounds and languages. Phrases: mama bear, mama's boy, mama mia (from Italian «mamma mia», «my mother!» — an exclamation of surprise).
examples from the lessons: The baby's first word was «mama». | «Mama, can I have a biscuit?» | In the story, Mama Bear's porridge was too cold. | (Ukrainian) «Мама» (mama) means mum in Ukrainian. | (Mandarin) «māma» means mum in Chinese. | (informal) He's a real mama's boy who does everything his mum says. | «Mamma mia!» shouted the chef when the pizza burned. | My friend calls her mother Mama, and I call mine Mum.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a mama, mamas. Pronounced «MAH-muh» (US also «muh-MAH» in old British use). Capital M when used as a name: «Thank you, Mama.» but small m with «my»: «my mama». Spellings vary: mama, mamma, momma. Many unrelated languages have a similar word because «ma» is an easy baby sound.
