part of speech: verb (munch, munches, munched, munching); noun (a munch — informal; the munchies — slang)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To munch is to chew food steadily and noisily, often with enjoyment: munch an apple, munch on crisps. 2) (slang) «The munchies» means feeling very hungry for snacks: «I've got the munchies.» 3) (informal) A munch is a snack or a meal: «Let's grab some munch.» 4) (a name) Edvard Munch was a Norwegian painter, famous for the painting «The Scream».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and stories «munch» is a sound-and-action word that shows eating with enjoyment and noise: «The caterpillar munched through the leaves» (as in «The Very Hungry Caterpillar»). It is a good, vivid verb for creative writing instead of «ate». In art lessons pupils copy Munch's «The Scream» to show strong feelings. Phrases: munch on, munch away, munch through, the munchies.
examples from the lessons: The caterpillar munched through five oranges. | We munched popcorn during the film. | The horse munched happily on the hay. | (informal) She munched away on a carrot while she read. | (slang) I always get the munchies after swimming. | The rabbit munched the lettuce in seconds. | Stop munching so loudly! | In art we painted our own version of Munch's «The Scream».
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb forms: munch, munches (add -es), munched, munching. Often with «on» or «through»: «munch on an apple», «munch through a bag of crisps». The painter's name is pronounced «moonk», not like the verb. «The munchies» is informal slang; in an essay write «very hungry».

part of speech: noun (an opera, operas); noun (opera house, opera singer)
meaning for a pupil: 1) An opera is a play in which the actors sing almost all the words, with an orchestra playing music. 2) Opera is this kind of music and theatre in general. 3) An opera house is the building where operas are performed.
its sense in the lessons: In music lessons children learn that opera mixes singing, acting, costumes and an orchestra; famous composers include Mozart, Verdi and Puccini. In stories, going to the opera often shows something grand or fancy. The Sydney Opera House in Australia is a famous building. Phrases: «go to the opera», «opera singer», «soap opera» (a long TV drama series, not sung).
examples from the lessons: We watched a short opera about a magic flute in music class. | The opera singer sang so loudly the whole hall rang. | My nan loves opera and plays it in the kitchen. | The Sydney Opera House has a roof shaped like sails. | In an opera, even the arguments are sung. | Our class wrote a tiny opera about a lost lunchbox. | Mum watches a soap opera every evening.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one opera, two operas. A «soap opera» is a TV drama, not real opera. Do not confuse with «Oprah» (a name). An opera is mostly sung; a musical mixes singing with ordinary spoken talk.

part of speech: noun (a perch, perches; fish plural perch or perches); verb (perch, perches, perched, perching)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A perch is a branch, bar or stick where a bird sits. 2) To perch means to sit on something high or narrow, the way a bird does. 3) To perch something is to put it in a high or wobbly place. 4) A perch is also a freshwater fish with spiny fins that people catch and eat.
its sense in the lessons: In science, birds such as sparrows are called perching birds because their feet grip branches. In stories, a character «perched on a stool» sits lightly or on the edge, often nervous or watchful. Pet budgies have a perch in their cage. Anglers catch perch in lakes and rivers.
examples from the lessons: The parrot hopped onto its wooden perch. | A robin perched on the garden fence. | I perched on the edge of the bed, waiting for news. | His glasses were perched on the end of his nose. | The castle was perched on top of a steep hill. | Dad caught three perch at the lake. | Owls watch for mice from a high perch.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb past: perched. As a fish the plural is often the same: «three perch». «Perched» often means sitting not fully settled. Do not confuse with «porch» (a covered entrance of a house) or «purge».

part of speech: noun (phonics — uncountable, used with a singular verb)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Phonics is a way of learning to read by matching letters and groups of letters to the sounds they make. 2) Phonics also means the lessons and books that teach this.
its sense in the lessons: In early school reading (especially UK, Australia and New Zealand), children learn phonics: «sh» says /sh/, «igh» says /eye/. They blend sounds to read words (c-a-t, cat) and segment words to spell them. The UK has a «phonics screening check» in Year 1. Phrases: «phonics lesson», «sound it out», «blend the sounds».
examples from the lessons: We have phonics every morning before break. | In phonics we learned that «ai» and «ay» make the same sound. | My little brother uses phonics to sound out new words. | Phonics helps you read words you have never seen before. | The teacher held up phonics cards with letters on them. | Not every word follows phonics rules, like «said» and «the».
note for the reader of a maths problem: Ends in -s but is singular: «Phonics is fun», not «are». Words that do not follow the rules are often called «tricky words» or «sight words». Phonics is about sounds, not about the meaning of words.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A plantation is a large farm, usually in a hot country, where one crop such as cotton, sugar, tea, coffee or rubber is grown. 2) A plantation is also an area where many trees have been planted in rows, for example for wood. 3) (history) In the past, many plantations in the Americas used enslaved African people who were forced to work without pay.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, plantations are linked to the slave trade and to the American Civil War; this is taught as a serious wrong. In geography, tea plantations in India or Sri Lanka and palm oil plantations show how farming changes land and forests. In Ireland, «the Plantation of Ulster» was when land was taken and given to settlers from Britain.
examples from the lessons: Tea is grown on huge plantations on green hillsides. | Enslaved people were forced to pick cotton on plantations. | The pine plantation had trees in straight rows. | Cutting forests for palm oil plantations harms orangutans. | We read a story about a girl who escaped from a plantation. | Workers on the coffee plantation pick the beans by hand.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Stress on «-TAY-». A plantation grows one main crop on a large scale; a «farm» can be any size and grow many things. A word with a painful history: speak about it carefully and truthfully.

part of speech: noun (a stunt, stunts); verb (stunt, stunts, stunted, stunting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A stunt is a daring or dangerous action, often done in a film or show, such as jumping a car or falling from a building. 2) A stunt is also a trick done to get attention, like a «publicity stunt». 3) To stunt something means to stop it from growing properly.
its sense in the lessons: In films, stunt performers (stuntmen and stuntwomen) do the dangerous parts so actors stay safe. In safety lessons: «Do not try this at home» — stunts are planned by experts. In science, lack of light or food can stunt a plant's growth. «Pull a stunt» means do something silly or naughty.
examples from the lessons: The stuntwoman jumped from the roof onto a mattress. | Don't try that bike stunt — you'll break your neck! | The skateboarder did a stunt off the ramp. | The plant in the dark cupboard was stunted and pale. | Poor food can stunt a child's growth. | Painting the school statue pink was just a publicity stunt. | If you pull a stunt like that again, you'll be in trouble.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb past: stunted. «Stunted» as an adjective means smaller than it should be. A «stunt double» looks like the actor and does the risky scenes.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Tasmanian means from or about Tasmania, the island state in the south of Australia. 2) A Tasmanian is a person from Tasmania. 3) The Tasmanian devil is a small, fierce black marsupial that lives only in Tasmania. 4) The Tasmanian tiger (thylacine) was a striped marsupial that is now extinct.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and science lessons (especially in Australia), Tasmania is known for wilderness, cold southern weather and unique animals. The Tasmanian devil has a loud screech and strong jaws; many are sick with a face tumour disease, so scientists protect them. The last known Tasmanian tiger died in a zoo long ago.
examples from the lessons: The Tasmanian devil screeched in the dark. | We met a Tasmanian family on the ferry. | Tasmanian apples are sold all over Australia. | The Tasmanian tiger is extinct, but people still claim to see one. | My cousin is Tasmanian and loves bushwalking. | Tasmanian forests have some of the tallest trees in the world.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always written with a capital T. The Tasmanian devil is not a real devil and not a dog; it is a marsupial (it carries babies in a pouch). The cartoon «Taz» spins like a tornado; real devils do not.

part of speech: noun (ti, also spelled te — a music note); fragment
meaning for a pupil: 1) Ti (also te) is the seventh note in the singing scale do, re, mi, fa, so, la, ti, do. 2) Ti is also the name of a plant (the cabbage tree) in New Zealand and the Pacific. 3) As a fragment, «ti» often comes from a longer word cut in the middle, or from «Ti», the chemistry symbol for titanium.
its sense in the lessons: In music lessons, children sing the scale «do re mi fa so la ti do»; ti is just below the top do. In the song from «The Sound of Music» it is «tea, a drink with jam and bread». In chemistry, Ti stands for the metal titanium.
examples from the lessons: Do, re, mi, fa, so, la, ti, do! | Ti is the note right before the high do. | In the song, «ti» sounds like «tea». | The symbol Ti on the periodic table means titanium. | We sang ti a bit too low and the teacher laughed. | A ti tree, or cabbage tree, grows in New Zealand.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Sounds like «tee». Not a common English word on its own. In the UK it is often spelled «te». Do not confuse with «tea» or «tee» (a golf peg), which sound the same.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A verruca is a small hard wart on the bottom of the foot, caused by a virus. 2) In medicine, verruca can mean any wart.
its sense in the lessons: In health lessons and at swimming pools (UK, Ireland, Australia), children learn verrucas spread on wet floors, so you wear flip-flops in changing rooms and do not share towels. Some schools used to make children wear «verruca socks» in swimming. Most verrucas are harmless and go away on their own, though they can hurt when you walk.
examples from the lessons: I've got a verruca on my heel and it hurts when I walk. | Wear flip-flops in the changing room so you don't catch a verruca. | The nurse put special cream on my verruca. | My verruca took months to go away. | She wore a verruca sock to swimming lessons. | You can catch verrucas from wet floors at the pool.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly UK/Irish word; in the USA people usually say «plantar wart». Plural «verrucas» is normal; «verrucae» is the Latin, used by doctors. Not dangerous, but catching.

part of speech: noun (a name, Ada); proper noun (Ada, a programming language); abbreviation (ADA)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Ada is a girl's name (a name). 2) Ada Lovelace was an English mathematician who wrote what is often called the first computer program. 3) Ada is also a programming language named after her. 4) ADA in the USA stands for the Americans with Disabilities Act, a law that protects disabled people.
its sense in the lessons: In computing lessons, Ada Lovelace is remembered as a pioneer; Ada Lovelace Day celebrates women in science. In stories Ada is a character's name. «ADA» on US signs refers to accessibility (ramps, lifts).
examples from the lessons: Ada Lovelace worked with Charles Babbage on his Analytical Engine. | Ada is the youngest girl in our class. | Our coding lesson was about Ada Lovelace and the first program. | The library has a poster of Ada Lovelace. | ADA rules mean the building must have a ramp. | Ada is a programming language used in planes and trains.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A name, so written with a capital A. Not a normal English word. Ada Lovelace was the daughter of the poet Lord Byron.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (Scotland, northern England) A bairn is a child or a baby. 2) (Scotland) «Your bairns» means your children, your own family's kids.
its sense in the lessons: Used in Scottish and Geordie speech, in stories set in Scotland and in Scottish songs. It shows the speaker is Scottish or from the north of England and sounds warm and homely. «Wee bairn» means a little baby.
examples from the lessons: The wee bairn is sleeping, so keep your voice down. | She's got three bairns and a dog. | Come here, bairn, and let me tie your lace. | Gran says all her bairns are grown up now. | The bairns are playing out in the garden. | «Haud yer wheesht, the bairn's sleeping,» said Granny.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regional word (Scots); rhymes with «barn» but with a Scottish r. In standard English say «child» or «baby». Not rude at all; it is affectionate.

meaning for a pupil: 1) «Clon» is not an English word on its own. It is usually a piece of a longer word such as «clone», «cyclone» or «colon», cut off in the middle. 2) In Irish place names «Clon-» (from Irish «cluain», a meadow) begins names such as Clonmel and Clontarf.
its sense in the lessons: You meet «clon» only as part of words: «clone» (an exact copy of a living thing), «cyclone» (a huge storm). In Ireland, «Clon» begins many town names.
examples from the lessons: «Clon» is the start of «clone». | A cyclone is a giant spinning storm. | Clonmel is a town in County Tipperary. | Dolly the sheep was the first mammal cloned from an adult cell. | The game lets you clone your character. | We drove through Clontarf on the way to Dublin.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A fragment, not a word: do not use it alone. Pronounced like «clon» in «Clonmel» (klon).

meaning for a pupil: 1) «Ge» is not an English word on its own. It is a piece of a longer word, for example «age», «gem» or «get». 2) Ge is the chemistry symbol for germanium, a grey element used in electronics. 3) GE can stand for General Electric, an American company, or for «general election» in news talk. 4) In Greek myths, Ge (also Gaia) is the goddess of the Earth (a name).
its sense in the lessons: In phonics, «ge» at the end of a word often sounds like /j/: page, huge, cage. «g» before «e» is often soft (gem, gentle), though not always (get, give).
examples from the lessons: In «page», the letters «ge» make a /j/ sound. | Ge is the symbol for germanium on the periodic table. | Words like «huge» and «cage» end in «ge». | The Greeks called the Earth goddess Ge or Gaia. | Our fridge was made by GE. | «Ge» at the start of «gentle» sounds soft.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A fragment or symbol, not a word. Spelling tip: «-ge» gives a soft g; «-gue» or «-g» keeps it hard (league, bag).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A goby is a small fish that lives near the sea floor, in rock pools or on coral reefs. 2) Some gobies live together with shrimps and share a burrow with them.
its sense in the lessons: In science, gobies are an example of partnership in nature: a blind shrimp digs the burrow and the goby keeps watch for danger. Children find gobies in rock pools at the seaside in the UK, Ireland, Australia and New Zealand.
examples from the lessons: We found a little goby hiding in the rock pool. | The goby darted under a stone. | Some gobies are smaller than your fingernail. | A goby and a shrimp share a burrow on the reef. | The aquarium had bright yellow gobies. | Gobies stick to rocks with fins on their bellies.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: gobies (y to ies). Pronounced «GOH-bee». Not to be confused with «gobi», as in the Gobi Desert, or «go by».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Graphite is a soft, dark grey form of carbon that leaves marks on paper. 2) Graphite is the «lead» in pencils, mixed with clay. 3) Graphite is also used in batteries, as a lubricant and in sports gear like tennis rackets.
its sense in the lessons: In science, graphite and diamond are both pure carbon but with atoms arranged differently: graphite is soft and slippery, diamond is very hard. Graphite conducts electricity, unusual for a non-metal. Thin layers of graphite are called graphene.
examples from the lessons: The «lead» in your pencil is really graphite. | Graphite and diamond are both made of carbon. | Graphite feels slippery because its layers slide. | A circuit with a graphite line can light a small bulb. | His tennis racket is made with graphite. | Use a soft graphite pencil for shading.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Pencils never contained the poisonous metal lead; that is a myth from old times when people thought graphite was lead. «HB», «2B» tell how soft the graphite is.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Greenish means a little bit green, or of a colour close to green. 2) Greenish can describe a face that looks pale and ill, as if about to be sick.
its sense in the lessons: In art and science, «-ish» softens a colour word: greenish, bluish, reddish. In stories, a character who turns «greenish» is feeling sick, e.g. on a boat.
examples from the lessons: The pond water looked greenish and murky. | After the roller coaster, Sam's face went greenish. | The old coin had a greenish crust. | Mix a little yellow into blue for a greenish colour. | The frog's skin was greenish brown. | The bread had greenish mould on it, so we binned it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: No comparative usually. «-ish» means «somewhat». Copper turns greenish when it reacts with air (verdigris).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Lactic means to do with milk. 2) Lactic acid is a substance made when milk goes sour and also made in your muscles during hard exercise.
its sense in the lessons: In science and PE, lactic acid is linked with tired, burning muscles after sprinting. Bacteria turn milk into yogurt by making lactic acid. «Lactose» is the sugar in milk; people who cannot digest it are «lactose intolerant».
examples from the lessons: Lactic acid makes yogurt taste sour. | My legs burned from lactic acid after the race. | Bacteria make lactic acid in milk. | The coach said a cool-down helps your muscles recover. | Lactic means «from milk». | Sauerkraut is made sour by lactic bacteria.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mainly used in «lactic acid». Myth: lactic acid causes muscle soreness the next day — scientists now think next-day soreness is mostly from tiny muscle damage. Do not confuse with «lactose».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A midi is a skirt or dress that reaches the middle of the lower leg. 2) MIDI (Musical Instrument Digital Interface) is a way for electronic instruments and computers to send music notes to each other. 3) Midi is French for «noon» or «south» (French), as in «le Midi», the south of France.
its sense in the lessons: In music technology lessons, a MIDI keyboard plays sounds through a computer. In fashion, «midi skirt» is between mini and maxi. In French lessons, «midi» means midday: «à midi» = at noon.
examples from the lessons: She wore a blue midi dress to the party. | Plug the MIDI keyboard into the laptop. | The game's music was made with MIDI files. | In French, «midi» means twelve o'clock. | Mini, midi, maxi — short, middle, long. | We had lunch at midi in Paris.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced «MID-ee». MIDI is written in capitals when it means the music system. Not the same as «middy».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A mussel is a sea or river shellfish with a long dark blue or black shell in two halves. 2) Mussels are cooked and eaten as food.
its sense in the lessons: In science, mussels are molluscs; they stick to rocks with strong threads and filter water to eat. At the seaside children find mussel beds on rocks. In cooking, mussels are steamed until shells open.
examples from the lessons: Mussels cling to the rocks at low tide. | Dad ordered mussels with chips. | A mussel opens its shell to feed. | Don't eat a mussel that stays closed after cooking. | The rocks were black with mussels. | Mussels clean the water by filtering it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Homophone: «muscle» (the body part) sounds exactly the same. Joke: «Why did the mussel go to the gym? To build muscle.» Countable: one mussel, two mussels.

part of speech: proper noun (Oxford); noun (an oxford, oxfords — a shoe)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Oxford is a city in England, famous for its very old university (a name). 2) The University of Oxford is one of the oldest universities in the world. 3) An oxford is a lace-up leather shoe. 4) An Oxford comma is a comma before «and» in a list (red, white, and blue).
its sense in the lessons: In school, the Oxford Dictionaries and Oxford Reading Tree books are common. In grammar, the «Oxford comma» is a style choice. «Oxford and Cambridge» are the two famous old English universities.
examples from the lessons: Oxford is a city full of old stone colleges. | My cousin studies at Oxford University. | We read Oxford Reading Tree books in Year 1. | He wore black oxfords to the wedding. | Should I use an Oxford comma in this list? | The Oxford dictionary has thousands of words.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually with capital O (a place name). Literally «a ford for oxen» — a place where cattle crossed the river.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Porcelain is a hard, white, shiny material made by baking fine clay at very high heat; also called china. 2) Porcelain means things made of it, like cups, plates, dolls and vases. 3) Porcelain describes skin that is very pale and smooth.
its sense in the lessons: In history, porcelain was invented in China, which is why it is called «china». In science, it is a ceramic: it does not conduct electricity, so it is used in insulators. In stories, a «porcelain doll» is delicate and easily broken.
examples from the lessons: Gran keeps her porcelain teacups in a glass cabinet. | Porcelain was first made in China long ago. | The porcelain vase smashed on the floor. | The toilet and sink are made of porcelain. | She had a porcelain doll with painted cheeks. | Hold it carefully — porcelain breaks easily.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable as the material. Pronounced «POR-suh-lin». Porcelain is finer and harder than ordinary pottery (earthenware).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A proposal is a plan or idea that you put forward for others to think about and agree to. 2) A proposal is when someone asks another person to marry them. 3) (formal) A proposal is a written plan, for example asking for money or permission.
its sense in the lessons: In school councils, pupils make proposals (e.g. a longer break). In stories and films, a marriage proposal often involves kneeling with a ring. In grown-up life, people write proposals for projects. Phrases: «make a proposal», «accept/reject a proposal», «a marriage proposal».
examples from the lessons: Our class council made a proposal for a new bike shed. | He made a proposal on the beach and she said yes. | The teacher liked my proposal for a science project. | The council rejected the proposal to close the park. | Write a short proposal explaining your idea. | The proposal was voted on by the whole school.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: propose. Countable. «Proposal» is a suggestion, not a decision — it still has to be agreed.

part of speech: noun (a pun, puns); verb (pun, puns, punned, punning)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A pun is a joke that uses a word with two meanings, or words that sound the same, to be funny. 2) To pun means to make such a joke.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons, puns are a kind of wordplay used in jokes, riddles, headlines and poems. They often use homophones (flour/flower) or double meanings. Phrases: «no pun intended», «pun intended». People often groan at bad puns.
examples from the lessons: I'm reading a book about anti-gravity — it's impossible to put down. That's a pun! | «Time flies like an arrow; fruit flies like a banana» is a famous pun. | Dad tells terrible puns at dinner. | The headline used a pun on «sole» and «soul». | Why can't a bicycle stand up? Because it's two-tyred — a pun on «tired». | We wrote our own puns in English class.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: punned, punning (double n). Puns need two meanings or two similar sounds; spot both to «get» the joke.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A semicolon is the punctuation mark ; which joins two closely linked full sentences. 2) A semicolon can also separate items in a long list when the items already contain commas.
its sense in the lessons: In grammar lessons (and UK SATs), pupils learn to use a semicolon between two main clauses: «It was raining; we stayed in.» It is stronger than a comma but weaker than a full stop. In computer coding, many languages end each line with a semicolon.
examples from the lessons: It was late; we went home. | A semicolon looks like a dot on top of a comma. | Use a semicolon to join two related sentences. | We visited Paris, France; Rome, Italy; and Dublin, Ireland. | In some code you must end each line with a semicolon. | I love reading; my brother loves football.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Do not use a semicolon before «and/but» joining short clauses, and do not use it to start a list (that's a colon :). Both sides of a semicolon should usually be full sentences.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A wishbone is a forked V-shaped bone between the neck and breast of a chicken, turkey or other bird. 2) It is used in a game where two people pull it and the one who gets the bigger piece makes a wish.
its sense in the lessons: At Christmas or Thanksgiving dinners, children pull the turkey wishbone and make a wish. In science, the wishbone (furcula) helps birds fly. It is a custom and a game, not real magic.
examples from the lessons: We pulled the wishbone after Christmas dinner. | I got the bigger piece of the wishbone, so I made a wish. | Let the wishbone dry before you pull it. | The wishbone helps a bird's wings work. | My sister always wins the wishbone. | What did you wish for with the wishbone?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Wishing on a wishbone is a fun tradition; it does not really make wishes come true.

part of speech: noun (a baba, babas); (Ukrainian, Polish, Russian) noun (baba)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (Ukrainian) «Baba» means grandmother or granny; also an old woman. It sounds like «BAH-bah» and is not an English word. 2) A baba (rum baba) is a small sweet sponge cake soaked in syrup or rum. 3) Baba Yaga is a witch in Slavic fairy tales who lives in a hut on chicken legs (a name). 4) Baby talk: «baba» can mean a baby or a bottle.
its sense in the lessons: In families with Ukrainian, Polish or Russian roots, children call their grandmother «baba» or «babusia». In fairy-tale lessons, Baba Yaga flies in a mortar. In cooking, rum baba is a French-style dessert.
examples from the lessons: We visit Baba every Sunday and she makes varenyky. | «Baba» is the Ukrainian word for granny. | Baba Yaga's hut stood on chicken legs. | The bakery sold a rum baba with cream. | My baby brother points at his bottle and says «baba». | Baba told us stories about her village.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As «granny» it is borrowed from Ukrainian and other Slavic languages, not English. Ukrainian «баба» can also sound rude for «woman» in some contexts, so «babusia» is gentler. «Baba ghanoush» is a Middle Eastern aubergine dip.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A clan is a large group of families who share the same ancestor, especially in Scotland and Ireland. 2) A clan is a big, close family or a group of friends who stick together (informal). 3) In online games, a clan is a team of players.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, Scottish clans such as the MacDonalds had chiefs, tartans and lands. In stories, clans can be rival groups (e.g. cats in «Warriors» books). Informally: «the whole clan came for Christmas».
examples from the lessons: The MacGregor clan had its own tartan. | The whole clan came round for Gran's birthday. | Each clan in the story had a different leader. | He joined a clan in his online game. | Clans in the Highlands sometimes fought each other. | Our family is a noisy clan.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Members of a clan are «clansmen/clanswomen». Do not confuse with «Klan» (the Ku Klux Klan, a hate group in the USA).

part of speech: noun (a frill, frills); in phrase «no frills»
meaning for a pupil: 1) A frill is a strip of cloth with lots of folds sewn on the edge of a dress, curtain or collar for decoration. 2) A frill is also a ruffle-like part on an animal, like the frill around the neck of a frilled lizard. 3) Frills are extra things that are nice but not needed (informal).
its sense in the lessons: In science, the frilled lizard of Australia spreads its neck frill to scare enemies. In everyday life «no-frills» means simple and cheap: a no-frills airline. In stories, frilly dresses show old-fashioned or fancy clothes.
examples from the lessons: Her party dress had a pink frill at the hem. | The frilled lizard opened its frill and hissed. | It's a no-frills hotel, but it's clean. | The curtains had lace frills. | The dinosaur Triceratops had a big bony frill. | I just want a plain cake, no frills.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: frilly. «No frills» = basic, nothing extra.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In Greek myths, a harpy is a monster with the face and body of a woman and the wings and claws of a bird. 2) (rude) Harpy is an insulting word for a woman who is thought to be nasty or bossy. 3) The harpy eagle is a huge, powerful eagle of South American rainforests.
its sense in the lessons: In myth lessons, harpies snatch food and people in stories like Jason and the Argonauts. In science, the harpy eagle hunts monkeys and sloths. As an insult it is unkind and should not be used.
examples from the lessons: The harpies swooped down and stole the king's food. | A harpy eagle can carry off a sloth. | In the story, the hero chased the harpies away. | Calling someone a harpy is rude and unkind. | Harpies had sharp claws and screeched loudly. | The harpy eagle is one of the strongest birds in the world.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: harpies. Insult use is old-fashioned and sexist; know it, don't use it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A hatchling is a baby animal that has just come out of its egg, such as a bird, turtle, snake or crocodile.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on life cycles, «hatch» is when the young breaks out of the egg and «hatchling» names the newborn. Sea turtle hatchlings crawl to the ocean at night, guided by moonlight; beach lights can confuse them.
examples from the lessons: The turtle hatchlings raced towards the sea. | We watched the chick hatchlings in the classroom incubator. | A crocodile mother carries hatchlings in her mouth. | The hatchling was wet and tiny. | Lights on the beach confuse sea turtle hatchlings. | Hatchlings need warmth to survive.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. «-ling» means small or young (duckling, gosling). A hatchling is just hatched; later it becomes a «nestling» or «fledgling» (birds).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Industrial means to do with factories, making goods, and industry. 2) An industrial place has lots of factories. 3) Industrial also describes things that are strong and large enough for factory use, like industrial machines.
its sense in the lessons: In history, the Industrial Revolution was when machines and factories changed how people lived and worked; children worked in mills and mines. In geography, industrial areas, industrial estates and industrial pollution are studied.
examples from the lessons: The Industrial Revolution started in Britain. | Smoke rose from the industrial chimneys. | Dad works on an industrial estate. | Industrial waste polluted the river. | They used an industrial vacuum to clean the hall. | Manchester was a great industrial city.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: industry. Adverb: industrially. Do not confuse with «industrious» (hard-working).

meaning for a pupil: 1) LAN stands for local area network: computers connected together in one building, like a school or house. 2) «Lan» is a name or part of a name (a name), and a fragment of longer words like «land» or «plan». 3) (Mandarin, pinyin) «lán» means blue (蓝). It sounds like «lahn» and is not an English word.
its sense in the lessons: In computing, a LAN connects computers in a school so they share printers and files; a «LAN party» is when friends link computers to play games. In Mandarin lessons, «lán sè» means the colour blue.
examples from the lessons: Our school computers are on a LAN. | The LAN cable plugs into the back of the computer. | They had a LAN party to play games together. | In Mandarin, «lán» means blue. | «Lan» is the start of «lane» and «land». | The internet is bigger than a LAN — it is a network of networks.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually written in capitals: LAN. Not a normal English word on its own.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (French) Madame is the French way of saying «Mrs» or «madam», a polite title for a woman. It sounds like «ma-DAM». 2) In English it is used for a woman's title in fancy or foreign settings, such as «Madame Curie».
its sense in the lessons: In French lessons: «Bonjour, Madame» — hello, madam. In history, Marie Curie is called Madame Curie. In stories, a fortune-teller or ballet teacher is often «Madame». Short form: Mme.
examples from the lessons: «Bonjour, Madame Dupont!» said the children. | Madame Curie won two Nobel Prizes. | Our French teacher likes to be called Madame. | Madame Tussauds is a famous wax museum in London. | «Merci, Madame,» I said to the shopkeeper. | The ballet teacher, Madame Rose, clapped the beat.
note for the reader of a maths problem: French word. Plural: mesdames. English «madam» is spelled without -e; «madame» keeps the French spelling. Capital M when used as a title.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Melanin is the natural dark substance in skin, hair and eyes that gives them their colour. 2) Melanin helps protect skin from the sun's harmful rays.
its sense in the lessons: In science, melanin explains why skin tans in the sun and why people have different skin colours: more melanin makes darker skin. Freckles are spots of extra melanin. People with albinism have very little melanin.
examples from the lessons: Melanin gives your skin its colour. | Freckles are spots with more melanin. | Skin makes more melanin in the sun, so you tan. | Even with lots of melanin, you still need sun cream. | People with albinism have very little melanin. | Melanin also colours your hair and eyes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Skin colour is just the amount of melanin — it says nothing about what a person is like. A tan is the skin protecting itself, a sign of sun damage, not health.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Midsummer is the middle of summer, around the longest day of the year. 2) Midsummer Day or Midsummer's Eve is a traditional festival at that time, especially in northern Europe.
its sense in the lessons: In science, the summer solstice has the most daylight. In literature, «A Midsummer Night's Dream» is a play with fairies. In Sweden people dance round a maypole at Midsummer; in Australia and NZ midsummer falls around Christmas.
examples from the lessons: At midsummer it stays light until very late. | We had a picnic on midsummer's evening. | In Sweden people dance at Midsummer. | In Australia midsummer comes around Christmas. | Stonehenge lines up with the sunrise at midsummer. | The fairies came out on Midsummer's Eve.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: midwinter. The longest day is in different months in the northern and southern hemispheres.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A pangolin is a mammal covered in hard, overlapping scales, which eats ants and termites with a long sticky tongue. 2) When scared, a pangolin rolls up into a tight ball.
its sense in the lessons: In science and conservation lessons, pangolins live in Africa and Asia and are among the most trafficked animals in the world because people illegally hunt them for scales and meat. Their scales are made of keratin, like fingernails.
examples from the lessons: The pangolin curled into a ball to protect itself. | Pangolins eat thousands of ants a day. | Their scales are made of the same stuff as your nails. | Pangolins are in danger because of poaching. | A baby pangolin rides on its mother's tail. | The pangolin licked termites out of the mound.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. It is not a reptile even though it has scales; it is a mammal. Its scales do not cure illness — that belief is a myth.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A parrotfish is a brightly coloured fish of coral reefs with teeth joined into a beak like a parrot's. 2) It scrapes and bites coral to eat the algae on it.
its sense in the lessons: In science, parrotfish keep coral reefs healthy by eating algae. They grind coral and poo out fine white sand, so a lot of beach sand on tropical islands comes from them. Some sleep in a bubble of mucus.
examples from the lessons: The parrotfish crunched on the coral. | Parrotfish make white sand on tropical beaches. | We saw a blue and green parrotfish when snorkelling. | A parrotfish sleeps in a slimy bubble. | Its mouth looks like a parrot's beak. | Parrotfish help keep the reef clean.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural usually «parrotfish». It is a fish, not a bird.

meaning for a pupil: 1) pH is a number that shows how acidic or alkaline a liquid is, on a scale from 0 to 14. 2) The letters «ph» together usually make an /f/ sound, as in phone and elephant.
its sense in the lessons: In science, pH 7 is neutral (pure water), below 7 is acid (lemon juice), above 7 is alkali (soap). Litmus paper or universal indicator changes colour to show pH. In phonics, «ph» is one way to spell the /f/ sound, mostly in words from Greek.
examples from the lessons: Lemon juice has a low pH because it is acidic. | Pure water has a pH of 7. | The indicator turned purple, so the pH was high. | «Ph» in «photo» sounds like f. | We tested the pH of the pond water. | Soap has a pH above 7.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Write it pH (small p, capital H). A LOWER pH number means MORE acidic. Each step is ten times stronger: pH 3 is ten times more acidic than pH 4.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A pterosaur was a flying reptile that lived at the time of the dinosaurs, with wings of skin stretched from a very long finger.
its sense in the lessons: In science and history lessons, pterosaurs like Pteranodon and Quetzalcoatlus flew over the dinosaurs; some were as big as a small plane. They are not dinosaurs and not birds — they are close cousins of dinosaurs. They died out with the dinosaurs.
examples from the lessons: A pterosaur glided over the sea looking for fish. | Quetzalcoatlus was a giant pterosaur. | Pterosaurs had wings made of skin. | A pterosaur is not a dinosaur. | We found a pterosaur in the museum. | Some pterosaurs had big crests on their heads.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The «p» is silent: «TERR-uh-sor». Common trap: calling them «flying dinosaurs». Birds came from dinosaurs; pterosaurs did not become birds.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The retina is the thin layer at the back of the inside of the eye that senses light and sends messages to the brain.
its sense in the lessons: In science, light enters through the pupil, the lens focuses it on the retina, and the optic nerve takes the signal to the brain. The image on the retina is upside down; the brain turns it round. Rods see in dim light; cones see colour.
examples from the lessons: The retina is at the back of your eye. | Light makes a picture on the retina. | Never look at the sun — it can damage your retina. | The optician shone a light to check my retina. | The retina has cells called rods and cones. | The brain flips the picture from the retina.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Plural retinas (doctors also say retinae). Not the same as the iris (the coloured part).

meaning for a pupil: 1) In grammar, singular means one: «cat» is singular and «cats» is plural. 2) (formal) Singular means very unusual or special, one of a kind. 3) The singular is the form of a word for just one thing.
its sense in the lessons: In grammar lessons, pupils change singular nouns into plurals and make verbs agree: «he runs» (singular), «they run» (plural). In maths and science writing, «unit» is singular. In stories, «a singular man» means very strange or remarkable.
examples from the lessons: «Mouse» is singular and «mice» is plural. | Use a singular verb with «everyone». | Write the singular of «children». | She showed singular bravery. | «Is» goes with a singular subject. | «Sheep» is the same in singular and plural.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: plural. Traps: some words look plural but are singular (news, maths); some are the same in both (sheep, fish). «They» can be used for one person whose gender is unknown.

part of speech: noun (a toque, toques) (Canada); noun (a toque — chef's hat)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (Canada) A toque (also tuque) is a knitted winter hat, often with a bobble on top; a beanie. 2) A toque is a tall white hat worn by chefs.
its sense in the lessons: In Canada, everyone says «toque» for a winter hat; in the UK «bobble hat» or «beanie», in Australia «beanie». In cooking stories, the head chef wears a tall white toque.
examples from the lessons: Put your toque on, it's freezing outside! | The chef wore a tall white toque. | My toque has a big red pompom. | In Canada, a toque is just a woolly hat. | I lost my toque at the hockey rink. | The pleats on a chef's toque used to show skill.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced «took» (Canada). Mainly Canadian English for the winter hat.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Zinc is a bluish-white metal, a chemical element (symbol Zn). 2) Zinc is used to coat iron and steel to stop rust. 3) Zinc is a mineral your body needs in small amounts, found in foods like meat, nuts and beans.
its sense in the lessons: In science, zinc is used in batteries and in making brass (with copper). Zinc cream or zinc oxide is a white sun cream, famous on cricketers' noses in Australia. Galvanised buckets and fences are zinc-coated.
examples from the lessons: The bucket is coated with zinc so it won't rust. | Zinc and copper make brass. | The cricketer had white zinc cream on his nose. | Batteries often contain zinc. | Your body needs a little zinc to heal cuts. | Zinc's symbol is Zn.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Spelt with a c. Too much zinc as a supplement can be harmful — follow the label.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An anteater is a South and Central American mammal with a long snout and a long sticky tongue that eats ants and termites. 2) Loosely, other ant-eating animals (like the echidna or pangolin) are sometimes called anteaters.
its sense in the lessons: In science, the giant anteater has no teeth; it rips open termite mounds with strong claws and flicks its tongue up to 150 times a minute. It is an example of an animal adapted to its food.
examples from the lessons: The anteater poked its long nose into the termite mound. | An anteater has no teeth. | The giant anteater has a bushy tail. | Its tongue is longer than my arm! | The baby anteater rode on its mother's back. | Anteaters live in South America.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Use «an»: an anteater. Ant + eater.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Atomic means to do with atoms, the tiny particles everything is made of. 2) Atomic means to do with nuclear energy or nuclear weapons, as in an atomic bomb. 3) An atomic clock is a super-accurate clock using atoms.
its sense in the lessons: In science, the atomic number tells how many protons an element has; the periodic table is ordered by it. In history, atomic bombs were dropped on Hiroshima and Nagasaki at the end of World War Two. Atomic power stations make electricity.
examples from the lessons: Hydrogen has the atomic number 1. | The atomic bomb destroyed a whole city. | An atomic clock loses less than a second in millions of years. | Everything has an atomic structure. | We studied atomic energy in science. | Carbon's atomic number is 6.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: atom. «Atomic» and «nuclear» often mean the same in everyday talk.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Certainty is the feeling of being completely sure about something. 2) A certainty is something that will definitely happen or is definitely true.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, probability uses a scale from impossible to certain: an event with certainty has a probability of 1. In science, we say «with certainty» only when there is strong evidence. Phrases: «with certainty», «it's a certainty», «for a certainty».
examples from the lessons: It is a certainty that the sun will rise tomorrow. | I can't say with certainty who broke the vase. | On the probability line, certainty is at 1. | She spoke with great certainty. | Rolling a number less than 7 on a die is a certainty. | Nothing in the weather forecast is a certainty.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: certain. Opposite: uncertainty. In maths problems, «certain» = probability 1, «impossible» = probability 0.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A cockerel is a young male chicken. 2) In everyday speech it means any male chicken, a rooster.
its sense in the lessons: In farm stories, the cockerel crows «cock-a-doodle-doo» at dawn to wake everyone. In science, hens lay eggs; cockerels do not. In the UK «cockerel» is common; in the USA and Australia «rooster».
examples from the lessons: The cockerel crowed at sunrise. | Our cockerel has a red comb and a long tail. | Hens lay eggs, but cockerels don't. | The weathervane had a metal cockerel on top. | The cockerel chased the cat out of the yard. | Tottenham football club has a cockerel badge.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. US: rooster. Female: hen. Baby: chick. Cockerels crow at many times of the day, not only at dawn.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A dingo is a wild dog of Australia, usually sandy-yellow, which hunts alone or in packs.
its sense in the lessons: In Australian science and geography lessons, dingoes are a top predator; the long Dingo Fence was built to keep them away from sheep. They howl rather than bark. Campers are warned not to feed dingoes (e.g. on K'gari/Fraser Island).
examples from the lessons: A dingo howled in the outback. | Don't feed the dingoes — it's dangerous. | Dingoes hunt kangaroos and rabbits. | The dingo fence is one of the longest fences in the world. | A dingo looks like a sandy dog. | We saw dingo tracks in the sand.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: dingoes (or dingos). Not a pet dog; it is wild.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Enrichment means making something better, richer or more interesting by adding to it. 2) In schools, enrichment means extra activities beyond normal lessons, like clubs, trips and challenges. 3) In zoos, enrichment means toys, puzzles and changes to an animal's home to keep it busy and happy. 4) In science, enrichment can mean adding something useful, like vitamins to food, or making a metal like uranium stronger for fuel.
its sense in the lessons: At school, «enrichment week» or «enrichment clubs» offer cooking, chess or sport. Zoos give animals enrichment like frozen fruit or puzzle feeders. Phrases: «enrichment activities», «enrichment programme».
examples from the lessons: Our school has enrichment clubs on Friday afternoons. | The zookeeper gave the tigers a ball for enrichment. | Enrichment week included a trip to the museum. | Frozen fruit treats are enrichment for the monkeys. | Bread flour has vitamins added as enrichment. | Reading for fun is enrichment for your mind.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Verb: enrich. Not about money, though «rich» is in it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Erroneous means wrong or containing a mistake.
its sense in the lessons: Used in the stiff exam voice, in reports and news: «an erroneous answer», «erroneous belief». In science, an erroneous result is a measurement that went wrong. Everyday speech would just say «wrong» or «mistaken».
examples from the lessons: The report contained erroneous information. | His answer was erroneous because he added instead of subtracting. | It is an erroneous belief that goldfish forget everything in three seconds. | Cross out any erroneous results in your table. | The newspaper corrected its erroneous headline. | An erroneous reading can come from a broken thermometer.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal word; say «wrong» in everyday talk. Pronounced «ih-ROH-nee-us». Related: error. In maths problems, «identify the erroneous step» means find the mistake.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A footstep is one step that someone takes when walking. 2) A footstep is the sound of a step. 3) «Follow in someone's footsteps» means do the same thing they did, such as the same job.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, «footsteps» in the dark build suspense: «I heard footsteps behind me.» The phrase «follow in her mother's footsteps» means to copy a parent's path in life.
examples from the lessons: I heard footsteps on the stairs. | Her footsteps echoed in the empty hall. | He followed in his dad's footsteps and became a firefighter. | Muddy footsteps led to the kitchen. | The footsteps came closer and closer. | The baby took her first footsteps.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually plural. «Footprint» is the mark left; «footstep» is the step or its sound.

part of speech: verb (gallop, gallops, galloped, galloping); noun (a gallop, gallops)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To gallop is to run very fast, the way a horse does, with all four feet off the ground at one moment. 2) A gallop is a horse's fastest way of running, or a ride at that speed. 3) Gallop also means to do something very fast (informal).
its sense in the lessons: In stories, knights and cowboys gallop away. Horse speeds: walk, trot, canter, gallop. In PE, children «gallop» as a movement skill. Informally, «galloping prices» rise very fast.
examples from the lessons: The horse galloped across the field. | We went for a gallop on the beach. | Children galloped around the hall like ponies. | The knight galloped off to save the princess. | The days galloped by during the holidays. | At a gallop, a horse is very fast.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: galloped (one p — not «gallopped»). Order of speeds: walk, trot, canter, gallop.

part of speech: verb (grunt, grunts, grunted, grunting); noun (a grunt, grunts)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To grunt is to make a short low sound in your throat, like a pig. 2) A grunt is that sound. 3) People grunt when lifting something heavy, or to answer without words when they are tired or grumpy. 4) (slang) A grunt is a low-ranking soldier or worker who does hard, boring jobs.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, a grunt shows a character is grumpy, tired or straining. Pigs grunt, and so do tennis players hitting hard. «Grunt work» means boring hard work.
examples from the lessons: The pig grunted in the mud. | Dad grunted as he lifted the sofa. | My brother just grunts when I ask about school. | The tennis player grunted with every shot. | He gave a grunt of agreement. | I got stuck with all the grunt work.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: grunted. Grunting instead of answering can seem rude.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A hornet is a large wasp with a powerful sting, often yellow and brown or black.
its sense in the lessons: In science, hornets build paper nests and catch other insects. In safety lessons: keep away from nests and stay calm; people allergic to stings need help fast. «Stir up a hornet's nest» means cause a lot of trouble and anger.
examples from the lessons: A hornet buzzed around the picnic table. | Hornets build nests made of chewed wood. | Don't swat a hornet — walk away calmly. | His question stirred up a hornet's nest. | The hornet's sting really hurt. | Asian hornets attack honeybees.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. A hornet is a type of wasp, bigger than common wasps. «Hornet's nest» idiom = angry trouble.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Inverted means turned upside down or the other way round. 2) Inverted commas are the punctuation marks ‘ ’ or « » used around speech or a quote; also called speech marks or quotation marks.
its sense in the lessons: In English (UK SATs), pupils punctuate speech with inverted commas: ‘Come here,’ said Mum. In maths, an inverted fraction is turned over (2/3 becomes 3/2) — used when dividing fractions. In science, a lens makes an inverted (upside-down) image.
examples from the lessons: Put inverted commas around what the character says. | The camera made an inverted picture. | Turn the jar inverted on the plate. | To divide by a fraction, multiply by the inverted fraction. | The bat hung inverted from the branch. | The letters on the reflection looked inverted.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: invert. UK schools say «inverted commas»; US says «quotation marks». In maths, «invert» = flip (reciprocal): 4 becomes 1/4.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A juvenile is a young animal or person, not yet an adult. 2) Juvenile means to do with young people, as in a juvenile court. 3) Juvenile also means childish or silly in a way that seems immature (said about grown-ups or older children).
its sense in the lessons: In science, juvenile animals often look different from adults (juvenile gulls are brown). In law, a juvenile is someone under the adult age. Calling behaviour «juvenile» is a criticism.
examples from the lessons: The juvenile eagle had brown feathers. | Juveniles go to a special court. | Stop that — it's so juvenile! | The aquarium had juvenile sharks. | Juvenile fish hide in the seaweed. | Pulling faces at the teacher was juvenile.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced «JOO-vuh-nile». Formal or scientific word for «young».

meaning for a pupil: 1) To knead means to press, fold and stretch dough with your hands to make bread. 2) To knead also means to press and rub muscles, like in a massage. 3) Cats «knead» by pushing their paws in and out on something soft.
its sense in the lessons: In cooking lessons, kneading makes the dough stretchy (it develops gluten) so bread rises. Cats knead blankets when content.
examples from the lessons: Knead the dough for ten minutes. | My hands got sticky from kneading. | The cat kneaded my lap with its paws. | She kneaded her sore shoulders. | Kneading makes the bread soft and springy. | We kneaded the play dough into a ball.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Silent k: sounds the same as «need» (homophone). Spelling: kn-ead.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A lynx is a wild cat of medium size with tufts of black fur on the tips of its ears, a short tail and big furry paws. It lives in forests of North America, Europe and Asia.
its sense in the lessons: In science, the Canada lynx mainly eats snowshoe hares; when hares go down, lynx go down too (predator-prey cycles). There are plans to bring the lynx back to parts of the UK. Lynx is also a brand of deodorant.
examples from the lessons: The lynx crept silently through the snow. | A lynx has tufts on its ears. | Its big paws work like snowshoes. | People want to bring lynx back to Scotland. | The lynx pounced on a hare. | We saw a lynx at the wildlife park.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced «links» (sounds like «links»). Plural lynxes or lynx.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Morocco is a country in north-west Africa, across the sea from Spain (a name). 2) Morocco (small m) is a fine soft leather made from goatskin, used for book covers.
its sense in the lessons: In geography, Morocco has the Atlas Mountains, the Sahara Desert, and cities like Marrakesh, Rabat and Casablanca; people speak Arabic, Berber (Amazigh) and French. Famous for markets (souks), mint tea and tagines.
examples from the lessons: Morocco is in North Africa. | We drank mint tea in Morocco. | The Atlas Mountains are in Morocco. | The old book was bound in red morocco. | Morocco's capital is Rabat, not Casablanca. | Morocco reached the World Cup semi-finals.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital M for the country. Adjective: Moroccan. Trap: the capital is Rabat.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Nasal means to do with the nose. 2) A nasal voice or sound comes partly through the nose, like when you have a cold. 3) In phonics and grammar, nasal sounds are m, n and ng.
its sense in the lessons: In science, nasal passages warm and clean the air you breathe. In health, nasal spray helps a blocked nose. In French lessons, French has nasal vowels (as in «bon», «vin»).
examples from the lessons: He had a nasal voice because of his cold. | Use the nasal spray twice a day. | M and n are nasal sounds. | Hairs in the nasal passages catch dust. | The French word «bon» has a nasal sound. | She had a nasal infection.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective only. Related noun: nose.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A polyp is a small sea animal with a tube-shaped body and a mouth ringed with tentacles; coral and sea anemones are made of polyps. 2) (medicine) A polyp is a small lump that grows inside the body, for example in the nose or gut.
its sense in the lessons: In science, coral reefs are built by millions of tiny coral polyps that make limestone skeletons. Hydra is a freshwater polyp. In health, doctors check and sometimes remove polyps.
examples from the lessons: A coral reef is made of tiny polyps. | Each coral polyp catches food with its tentacles. | The doctor found a small polyp in his nose. | Polyps build their homes from limestone. | A sea anemone is a large polyp. | Coral polyps live with algae inside them.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Pronounced «POL-ip». Coral is an animal, not a plant or a rock.

part of speech: noun (a sewer, sewers); noun (a sewer — person who sews)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A sewer is a large underground pipe or tunnel that carries away dirty water and waste from toilets, sinks and streets. 2) A sewer (said «SOH-er») is also a person who sews.
its sense in the lessons: In history, London's sewers were built to stop diseases like cholera spreading. In science, sewage goes through sewers to treatment works. In stories, sewers are dark tunnels (like the Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles' home).
examples from the lessons: Rainwater runs into the sewer through the drain. | Rats live in the sewers. | The Victorians built huge sewers under London. | The Ninja Turtles live in a sewer. | My nan is a great sewer — she made my costume. | Don't pour fat down the sink, it blocks the sewers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Two pronunciations: «SOO-er» (pipe) and «SOH-er» (one who sews). Waste in it is «sewage». Never go into a sewer — dangerous gases and floods.

part of speech: adjective (subordinate); noun (a subordinate, subordinates); verb (subordinate, subordinated) — formal
meaning for a pupil: 1) In grammar, a subordinate clause is a part of a sentence that has a verb but cannot stand alone, like «because it was raining». 2) A subordinate is a person who has a lower rank and takes orders from someone else at work. 3) (formal) Subordinate means less important than something else.
its sense in the lessons: In UK grammar lessons, pupils learn subordinating conjunctions (because, although, when, if) that start subordinate clauses: «Although it was cold, we went out.» At work or in the army, a boss gives orders to subordinates.
examples from the lessons: «When the bell rang» is a subordinate clause. | Add a subordinate clause starting with «because». | The captain gave orders to his subordinates. | A subordinate clause needs a main clause. | Fun is subordinate to safety on the trip. | Use a comma after a subordinate clause at the start of a sentence.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite of main/superior. Stress: «suh-BOR-din-it» (adjective, noun). The subordinate clause can come first or after the main clause.

part of speech: verb (tout, touts, touted, touting); noun (a tout, touts) (UK); (French) adjective (tout)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To tout means to try hard to sell something or to praise it loudly, so people will buy or believe it. 2) (UK) A tout (ticket tout) is a person who buys tickets for concerts or matches and sells them at a higher price. 3) (French) «Tout» means «all» or «everything», as in «tout le monde» (everybody); it sounds like «too».
its sense in the lessons: In news, a product is «touted as» the best. Outside stadiums, ticket touts sell tickets illegally or at high prices. In French lessons, «tout» and «toute» mean all.
examples from the lessons: He was touted as the next football star. | Ticket touts were selling seats for double the price. | Street sellers touted cheap watches. | «Tout le monde» means everybody in French. | The new game was touted as the best ever. | Don't buy from touts — the tickets might be fake.
note for the reader of a maths problem: English «tout» rhymes with «out»; French «tout» sounds like «too». US: «scalper» for a ticket tout.

part of speech: noun (a bass, basses); adjective (bass); noun (a bass — fish, plural bass)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Bass (said «base») means the lowest notes or sounds in music. 2) A bass is a bass guitar or a double bass, a large string instrument that plays low notes. 3) A bass is a man with a very deep singing voice. 4) A bass (said «bas», to rhyme with «gas») is a kind of fish.
its sense in the lessons: In music lessons, the bass line is the low part that keeps the rhythm; the bass clef is a sign for low notes. In science, low pitch means slow vibrations. Anglers catch bass in lakes and the sea.
examples from the lessons: Turn the bass down — the windows are shaking! | My brother plays bass in a band. | He sings bass in the choir. | We caught a sea bass off the pier. | The bass drum went boom boom. | Low notes are written in the bass clef.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One spelling, two pronunciations: «base» (music) and «bas» (fish). Homophone: bass (music) sounds like «base». Fish plural: bass.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A beagle is a small to medium hunting dog with long floppy ears, short legs and a white, brown and black coat. 2) HMS Beagle was the ship Charles Darwin sailed on to study nature (a name).
its sense in the lessons: Beagles have a great sense of smell; they work at airports sniffing luggage for food. In science, Darwin's voyage on the Beagle helped him think about evolution. Snoopy from Peanuts is a beagle.
examples from the lessons: Our beagle howls when the doorbell rings. | Snoopy is a beagle. | The beagle sniffed every bag at the airport. | Darwin sailed on HMS Beagle. | Beagles love to follow their noses. | A beagle needs lots of walks.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Capital B for the ship's name.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A beast is a large, wild or frightening animal. 2) A beast is a cruel or nasty person. 3) (informal) A beast is something very big, powerful or difficult: «That maths test was a beast.» 4) (slang) Someone who is a beast at something is amazingly good at it.
its sense in the lessons: In fairy tales, «Beauty and the Beast». In the Bible (Bible), «beasts of the field» means animals; in the Book of Revelation «the beast» is an evil figure. In sport slang, «he's a beast» is praise. Phrases: «beast of burden» (an animal that carries loads).
examples from the lessons: The beast roared in the dark forest. | Beauty learned the Beast was kind inside. | That homework was a beast! | She's a beast at football — she scored five goals. | Donkeys are beasts of burden. | The bully was a real beast to the younger kids.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Adjective: beastly (old-fashioned UK for nasty). Slang «beast» can be praise or insult — the tone tells you.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Bolivia is a country in the middle of South America with no coast, high in the Andes Mountains (a name).
its sense in the lessons: In geography, Bolivia has Lake Titicaca (shared with Peru), the huge salt flat Salar de Uyuni, and La Paz, one of the highest capital cities in the world. Many people speak Spanish, Quechua and Aymara. Llamas live there.
examples from the lessons: Bolivia is in South America. | The Uyuni salt flat in Bolivia looks like a giant mirror after rain. | Bolivia has no coastline. | La Paz is very high up, so the air is thin. | People in Bolivia speak Spanish and other languages. | Llamas and alpacas live in Bolivia.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital B. Adjective: Bolivian. Trap: Bolivia has two capitals — Sucre (official) and La Paz (government).

part of speech: noun (a chronicle, chronicles); verb (chronicle, chronicles, chronicled, chronicling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A chronicle is a written record of events in the order they happened. 2) To chronicle means to record events in order. 3) «Chronicle» is a common name for newspapers and story series (The Chronicles of Narnia). 4) (Bible) Chronicles (1 and 2 Chronicles) are books of the Old Testament that tell the history of the kings of Israel and Judah.
its sense in the lessons: In history, monks wrote chronicles like the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle. In English lessons, a chronological report puts events in time order (from the same Greek word «chronos», time).
examples from the lessons: The monks kept a chronicle of every battle. | Her diary chronicles a year at sea. | I'm reading The Chronicles of Narnia. | The book of Chronicles is in the Old Testament. | The film chronicles the life of a famous footballer. | The town newspaper is called the Chronicle.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Related: chronological (in time order). Spelling: chr- like «Christmas» sound /k/.

part of speech: noun plural (clams; singular a clam); verb (clam up, clams up, clammed up)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Clams are shellfish with two hard shells joined by a hinge, which live in sand or mud. 2) Clams are eaten as food, as in clam chowder. 3) To clam up means to suddenly stop talking, often from shyness or fear. 4) (US slang, old) Clams can mean dollars.
its sense in the lessons: In science, clams are molluscs that filter water to feed; giant clams on coral reefs can be huge. At the beach, kids dig for clams. «Happy as a clam» means very happy (US).
examples from the lessons: We dug for clams at low tide. | Clam chowder is a creamy soup. | The giant clams on the reef were bigger than me. | When the teacher asked, he clammed up. | Clams breathe through gills. | That bike cost fifty clams! (slang)
note for the reader of a maths problem: Singular: clam. Clam up: past «clammed». Myth: giant clams do not trap divers.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) Daddy is what young children call their father. 2) (slang) «The daddy of them all» means the biggest or best one.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and everyday life, small children say Daddy; older children usually say Dad. Animals in picture books have «daddy» bears. In the Bible and in prayers, some Christians mention that Jesus called God «Abba», sometimes explained as close to «Daddy».
examples from the lessons: Daddy, can you read me a story? | The baby giraffe walked next to its daddy. | «Daddy's home!» shouted my little sister. | This storm is the daddy of them all. | Daddy Bear had the biggest bowl. | My daddy works nights.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: daddies. Childish and loving; teenagers often say «Dad». Capital D when used as a name: «Hi, Daddy.»

meaning for a pupil: 1) Julian is a boy's name (a name). 2) Julian means to do with Julius Caesar, as in the Julian calendar, the calendar he brought in. 3) Julian of Norwich was an English woman who wrote about God's love (a name).
its sense in the lessons: In history, the Julian calendar was used in Europe before the Gregorian calendar we use today; some Orthodox Christians, for example in parts of Ukraine and Russia, still keep certain feasts by the Julian calendar, so their Christmas falls later. In the Famous Five books, Julian is the eldest child.
examples from the lessons: Julian is the oldest of the Famous Five. | Julius Caesar started the Julian calendar. | My friend Julian is great at chess. | Some churches still use the Julian calendar for feasts. | Julian of Norwich wrote «All shall be well». | The Julian calendar was slightly too long each year.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A name: capital J. The Julian calendar added a leap year every four years without exception, so it slowly drifted from the seasons.

part of speech: noun (lah, also la — a music note); (Singapore, Malaysia — slang) particle
meaning for a pupil: 1) Lah (also la) is the sixth note of the singing scale do, re, mi, fa, so, la, ti, do. 2) (Singapore, Malaysia — slang) «Lah» is a word added at the end of a sentence to make it sound friendly, firm or relaxed: «Come on lah!» It is not standard English. 3) «La-di-dah» (also lah-di-dah) means posh in a showy way (UK, informal).
its sense in the lessons: In music lessons the scale is sung «doh, ray, me, fah, soh, lah, te, doh». In Singapore and Malaysia, «lah» is famous in Singlish talk.
examples from the lessons: Doh, ray, me, fah, soh, lah, te, doh! | «Lah» is the note just after «soh». | «Don't worry lah, it's okay,» said my friend from Singapore. | «Hurry up lah!» shouted his cousin. | She talks all lah-di-dah since her trip. | We sang «lah» on a long high note.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Not a word in standard English on its own. The Singlish «lah» comes from Malay and Chinese speech and has no meaning by itself; it changes the tone.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A matriarch is a woman who is the head of a family or group, often the oldest and most respected. 2) In animal groups like elephants, the matriarch is the old female who leads the herd.
its sense in the lessons: In science, elephant herds are led by a matriarch who remembers where water is in drought. In family stories, the grandmother may be the matriarch whose word is law. Opposite: patriarch.
examples from the lessons: The matriarch led the elephants to the waterhole. | Granny is the matriarch of our family. | Everyone listened to the matriarch's advice. | Killer whale pods are led by matriarchs. | The old matriarch knew every path in the forest. | In the story, the matriarch ruled the family business.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced «MAY-tree-ark». «Matri-» means mother. Opposite: patriarch.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A mermaid is an imaginary sea creature with the head and body of a woman and the tail of a fish. 2) A merman is the male version.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and myths (like «The Little Mermaid» by Hans Christian Andersen), mermaids live under the sea, sing and sometimes lure sailors. Sailors in the past may have mistaken manatees or dugongs for mermaids. Mermaids are not real.
examples from the lessons: The mermaid flicked her shiny tail. | We read «The Little Mermaid» in class. | Sailors told stories of mermaids singing on rocks. | She wants a mermaid cake for her birthday. | A manatee was once mistaken for a mermaid. | The mermaid swam down to the coral castle.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. «Mer» is an old word for sea. Mermaids are imaginary — there is no scientific evidence for them.

part of speech: noun (a muzzle, muzzles); verb (muzzle, muzzles, muzzled, muzzling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A muzzle is the nose and mouth of an animal such as a dog or horse. 2) A muzzle is a cover of straps or wire put over a dog's nose and mouth to stop it biting. 3) The muzzle of a gun is the open end the bullet comes out of. 4) To muzzle someone means to stop them speaking freely.
its sense in the lessons: In pet care and safety, some dogs must wear a muzzle in public. In history and news, governments «muzzle» the press when they stop newspapers reporting. Dog breeds have long or short muzzles.
examples from the lessons: The dog's muzzle was grey with age. | Our greyhound wears a muzzle at the park. | Never point the muzzle of a gun at anyone. | The horse nuzzled me with its soft muzzle. | The rulers tried to muzzle the newspapers. | The vet put a muzzle on the scared dog.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: muzzled. A muzzle does not mean a dog is bad — some just get nervous. Do not confuse with «nuzzle» (rub gently with the nose).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A nebula is a huge cloud of gas and dust in space. 2) Some nebulae are places where new stars are being born; others are what is left after a star dies.
its sense in the lessons: In space science, famous ones are the Orion Nebula (seen with binoculars) and the Crab Nebula (left by an exploding star). Telescopes like Hubble and James Webb take colourful photos of nebulae. The Sun formed from a nebula long ago.
examples from the lessons: The Orion Nebula is a nursery for new stars. | The telescope photo showed a glowing pink nebula. | A nebula is made of gas and dust. | The Crab Nebula came from an exploded star. | Our Sun was born from a nebula. | The nebula looked like a giant space cloud.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural nebulae («NEB-yoo-lee») or nebulas. Latin for «mist». A nebula is not a galaxy (a galaxy has billions of stars).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Pronunciation is the way a word is said out loud. 2) Pronunciation is also how well or how a person says words in a language, including their accent.
its sense in the lessons: In English and language lessons, dictionaries show pronunciation; French, Mandarin and Ukrainian lessons practise pronunciation. English spelling does not always match pronunciation (through, though, tough). People in the UK, USA and Australia have different pronunciations of the same words (tomato).
examples from the lessons: What's the pronunciation of this word? | Her French pronunciation is really good. | «Tomato» has two common pronunciations. | The dictionary shows the pronunciation in brackets. | We practised the pronunciation of new Mandarin tones. | English spelling and pronunciation often don't match.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Famous trap: the verb is «pronounce» (with -ounce), but the noun is «pronunciation» (-nun-, no «o»). Do not write «pronounciation».

meaning for a pupil: 1) To ripen means to become ready to eat, soft and sweet, as fruit and crops do. 2) To ripen something means to make it ripe. 3) A plan or a situation ripens when it becomes ready or right for action.
its sense in the lessons: In science, fruits ripen as they change colour and their starch turns to sugar; bananas give off a gas (ethylene) that ripens other fruit. In farming, wheat ripens before harvest. «Ripen» uses «-en» to mean «become»: ripe → ripen, wide → widen.
examples from the lessons: The tomatoes ripened in the sun. | Put the avocado in a bag with a banana to ripen it. | The wheat ripens in late summer. | Green bananas ripen in a few days. | The apples are ripening on the tree. | Cheese ripens slowly in a cave.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: ripened. Adjective: ripe. Opposite: unripe; too ripe = overripe.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A sequoia is a huge evergreen tree from California; it includes the giant sequoia and the coast redwood. 2) Sequoias are among the biggest and oldest living things on Earth.
its sense in the lessons: In science, the giant sequoia General Sherman is the largest single tree by volume; coast redwoods are the tallest trees. Their thick bark helps them survive forest fires, and some cones only open after fire. Named after Sequoyah, a Cherokee man who made a writing system for his language.
examples from the lessons: The sequoia was so wide we couldn't hug it, even with ten people. | Sequoias can live for thousands of years. | Their bark protects them from fire. | We saw giant sequoias in a national park in California. | A sequoia grows from a seed as small as a flake of oat. | Redwoods and sequoias are cousins.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced «suh-KWOY-uh». The word has all five vowels (a, e, i, o, u) — a fun spelling fact.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Silicon is a chemical element (symbol Si), a grey shiny solid that is the main part of sand and many rocks. 2) Silicon is used to make computer chips and solar panels.
its sense in the lessons: In science, sand is mostly silicon dioxide (silica), used to make glass. In computing, chips are made on thin silicon slices. Silicon Valley in California is a famous area for tech companies.
examples from the lessons: Computer chips are made of silicon. | Sand contains a lot of silicon. | Silicon Valley is home to big tech companies. | Solar panels use silicon to turn sunlight into electricity. | Silicon's symbol is Si. | Glass is made by melting sand rich in silicon.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: «silicon» (the element, chips) is not «silicone» (a soft rubbery material used in baking moulds and sealants).

meaning for a pupil: 1) The som is the money (currency) of Kyrgyzstan and Uzbekistan (money). 2) (Ukrainian) «Som» (сом) means catfish, a big river fish with whiskers; it is not an English word. 3) «Som» is often a fragment of longer words like «some», «somersault» or «blossom».
its sense in the lessons: In maths problems about other countries' money, prices may be given in som. In Ukrainian lessons, «сом» is a fish. In English you usually meet it inside «some» or «handsome».
examples from the lessons: In Kyrgyzstan, bread costs a few som. | «Som» in Ukrainian means catfish. | «Som» is the start of «somersault». | We changed dollars into som at the airport. | The fisherman caught a huge som in the river. | Don't write «som» when you mean «some».
note for the reader of a maths problem: Not a standard English word. Sounds like «som» in «sombre». Common spelling mistake: writing «som» for «some».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A sovereign is a king or queen, the ruler of a country. 2) Sovereign means having the full right to rule itself without control from other countries: a sovereign country. 3) A sovereign is an old British gold coin worth one pound. 4) (formal) Sovereign also means very great or best, as in «a sovereign remedy» (old).
its sense in the lessons: In history and politics lessons, a sovereign state makes its own laws; Ukraine's sovereignty means its right to rule itself without another country taking control. In the UK, the monarch is the sovereign. In the Bible and church, God is sometimes called «Sovereign Lord».
examples from the lessons: The sovereign was crowned in Westminster Abbey. | Ukraine is a sovereign country. | Grandad keeps an old gold sovereign in a box. | Every sovereign state has its own laws. | The sovereign signed the new law. | Christians sometimes pray to «the Sovereign Lord».
