note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: silent g — «SOV-rin». Noun: sovereignty (the right to rule).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A supporter is a person who likes and cheers for a sports team. 2) A supporter is a person who agrees with and helps an idea, a person, a charity or a political party. 3) A supporter can also be something that holds something up, like an athletic support.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday UK, Irish and Australian life: «I'm a Liverpool supporter» (US: «fan»). In politics lessons, candidates have supporters who vote and campaign. Charities thank their supporters.
examples from the lessons: He's been an Arsenal supporter since he was five. | The supporters sang all through the match. | She is a big supporter of animal charities. | The candidate thanked her supporters. | The away supporters cheered loudly. | Supporters raised money for the new hospital.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Verb: support. «Supporter» is a little more formal than «fan».

part of speech: noun plural (togs) (informal; Australia, New Zealand, Ireland, UK)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (Australia, Ireland) Togs are swimming costumes, swimmers. 2) (UK informal) Togs means clothes, especially for a special purpose: «football togs», «your best togs».
its sense in the lessons: Children in Queensland and Ireland pack their togs for swimming lessons. In the UK, «get your togs on» means get dressed. Also «togged up» = dressed up.
examples from the lessons: Don't forget your togs for swimming! | We put our togs on and ran into the sea. | Pack your football togs for PE. | She got togged up for the party. | My togs are still wet from yesterday. | Everyone wore their Sunday togs.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always plural. Informal. Other words for swimwear: swimmers (Australia), cozzie (UK, Australia), bathers, swimsuit, trunks.

part of speech: noun (a vibe, vibes) (informal); verb (vibe, vibes, vibed, vibing) (slang)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) A vibe is the feeling or mood a place, person or thing gives you. 2) (slang) To vibe means to relax and enjoy yourself, often to music. 3) (slang) To vibe with someone means to get on well with them. 4) «Vibes» is short for vibraphone, a musical instrument (rare).
its sense in the lessons: Common in young people's talk: «good vibes», «bad vibes», «the vibe in here is cosy», «just vibing». In stories, a character «gets a weird vibe» when something feels wrong — it can be a warning feeling.
examples from the lessons: This café has a really chill vibe. | I got bad vibes from that dark alley. | We're just vibing to music in my room. | Good vibes only! | I really vibe with my new classmate. | The party had a happy vibe.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal/slang — fine with friends, not in formal writing. Short for «vibration». A «vibe check» means checking how someone feels.

part of speech: noun (a whip, whips); verb (whip, whips, whipped, whipping)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A whip is a long thin rope or strip of leather with a handle, used to hit animals or, in the past, people. 2) To whip means to hit with a whip. 3) To whip cream or eggs means to beat them fast until they are thick and fluffy. 4) To whip means to move or take something very fast: «She whipped out her phone.» 5) (politics) A whip is a person in parliament who makes sure members of their party vote. 6) (slang, US) A whip can mean a car.
its sense in the lessons: In cooking lessons, whipped cream; in history, enslaved people and convicts were whipped as cruel punishment. In stories, a horse rider cracks a whip. In UK politics, «chief whip». Phrases: «whip up» (make quickly), «whip round» (UK, collect money from a group).
examples from the lessons: Whip the cream until it is stiff. | He whipped round to see who was there. | The circus trainer cracked his whip. | Let's have a whip-round for the teacher's present. | Mum whipped up a quick lunch. | Prisoners were whipped in the past.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: whipped (double p). «Whipped cream» not «whip cream» in UK. Whipping people is now illegal in most countries.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A baobab is a huge tree of Africa, Madagascar and Australia with a very fat trunk and short branches that look like roots.
its sense in the lessons: In science, baobabs store water in their trunks for dry seasons and can live for over a thousand years. They are sometimes called «upside-down trees». In «The Little Prince», baobabs are dangerous plants that must be pulled out early. In Australia the boab is a relative.
examples from the lessons: The baobab looked like it was planted upside down. | Baobab trunks store water. | Elephants peel bark from baobab trees. | The Little Prince pulled up baobab sprouts. | Baobab fruit is full of vitamin C. | Some hollow baobabs have been used as shelters.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced «BAY-oh-bab». Countable.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Bold means brave and confident, not afraid to take risks. 2) Bold means strong and easy to see, like bright colours or thick lines. 3) Bold (bold type) is thick, dark print used to make words stand out. 4) (Ireland) Bold means naughty, especially for children: «Don't be bold!» 5) (old) Bold can mean cheeky or rude.
its sense in the lessons: In English and computing lessons, you make headings bold to stand out. In stories, a bold knight or a bold plan shows courage. In Ireland, parents tell a naughty child «you're very bold» — it means badly behaved, not brave.
examples from the lessons: The bold explorer sailed into unknown seas. | Write the title in bold. | She painted the wall a bold red. | «Stop being bold!» Mum said to my little brother. (Ireland) | It was bold of you to ask the head teacher. | The key words in the text are in bold.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb: boldly. Noun: boldness. Irish meaning «naughty» is a common surprise for visitors.

part of speech: noun (borscht — uncountable; a bowl of borscht)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Borscht is a sour soup, usually red from beetroot, eaten in Ukraine and other Eastern European countries. 2) It is often made with cabbage, potatoes, meat and beans and served with sour cream and dill.
its sense in the lessons: In lessons about Ukraine and food, borscht is a national dish of Ukraine; Ukrainian borscht cooking was added to UNESCO's list of cultural heritage in need of protection. Families each have their own recipe. There is also green borscht made with sorrel.
examples from the lessons: Baba makes the best borscht in the world. | Borscht is red because of the beetroot. | We had borscht with sour cream and bread. | Green borscht is made with sorrel leaves. | Every Ukrainian family has its own borscht recipe. | The borscht was so hot I blew on every spoonful.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Borscht» is the common English spelling (from Yiddish); «borshch» is closer to Ukrainian «борщ». Uncountable as food.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (Ukrainian) Borshch (борщ) is the Ukrainian spelling in Latin letters of «borscht», the sour beetroot soup that is a national dish of Ukraine. It sounds like «borshch», with «shch» like the sounds in «fresh cheese» run together.
its sense in the lessons: Used in lessons about Ukraine, Ukrainian cooking and Ukrainian heard on the street. Ukrainian borshch has beetroot, cabbage, potatoes and often meat, served with sour cream, garlic bread (pampushky) and dill.
examples from the lessons: Mum cooked borshch with pampushky. | In Ukraine, borshch is on almost every family's table. | Borshch is the Ukrainian way to write borscht. | We learned to say «borshch» properly. | The borshch was bright red and smelled of dill. | Grandma's borshch takes all morning to cook.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Ukrainian word in Latin letters; English usually writes «borscht». Both mean the same soup.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In grammar, a contraction is a short form made by joining two words with an apostrophe, like «don't» (do not) or «I'm» (I am). 2) In science, contraction means getting smaller or shorter, like a metal shrinking when it cools or a muscle tightening. 3) Contractions are the tightenings of the womb when a baby is about to be born.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons, the apostrophe in a contraction shows where letters are missing: can't = cannot, it's = it is. In science, metals expand when heated and contract when cooled. Muscles move bones by contraction. Contractions are not used in very formal writing.
examples from the lessons: «Won't» is a contraction of «will not». | The apostrophe shows the missing letters in a contraction. | Cold weather causes contraction of the metal rails. | Muscle contraction makes your arm bend. | Mum's contractions started, so they went to the hospital. | Write the contraction for «they are».
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: contract. Trap: «it's» (it is) vs «its» (belonging to it); «you're» vs «your». Opposite of contraction (getting smaller) is expansion.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A conversion is changing something from one form, unit or use to another. 2) In maths, a conversion is changing a measurement into different units, like centimetres to metres. 3) A conversion is a building changed for a new use, like a barn conversion or a loft conversion. 4) (church) Conversion is when a person changes their religion or comes to believe; Christians speak of the conversion of Saint Paul. 5) In rugby, a conversion is a kick at goal after a try, worth two points.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, conversion tables and conversion facts (1 km = 1000 m, 1 kg = 1000 g) are used in problems. In science, energy conversion changes, for example, electrical energy into light. Phrases: «currency conversion», «loft conversion».
examples from the lessons: Use the conversion chart to change inches to centimetres. | The conversion of 3 metres to centimetres is 300. | We live in a barn conversion. | He scored a try and then kicked the conversion. | A light bulb's energy conversion makes heat as well as light. | The story of Saint Paul's conversion is in the Bible.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: convert. In maths problems, «convert» means multiply or divide by the right number: metres to cm × 100; cm to metres ÷ 100. Always check which unit is bigger.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A coot is a black water bird with a white beak and a white patch on its forehead. 2) (informal) An «old coot» is a funny or slightly rude name for a strange or grumpy old man.
its sense in the lessons: In nature lessons, coots live on ponds and lakes in the UK, Europe and Australia and squabble noisily. «As bald as a coot» (UK) means completely bald, because of its white forehead patch.
examples from the lessons: A coot dived under the water for weeds. | The coots were fighting on the pond. | Grandad says he's as bald as a coot. | The coot has a white patch above its beak. | That old coot shouts at everyone who walks past. | Coots build floating nests.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. «Old coot» is mild teasing, a bit rude.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A documentary is a film or TV programme about real people, places and events, giving facts and information. 2) Documentary (adjective) means made of documents, as in «documentary evidence».
its sense in the lessons: In school, classes watch nature documentaries (like those by David Attenborough) and history documentaries. In media lessons, pupils learn that documentaries can still choose what to show, so they are not always neutral. In law, documentary evidence is written proof.
examples from the lessons: We watched a documentary about penguins. | The documentary showed real footage from the war. | Sir David Attenborough makes nature documentaries. | Our class made a short documentary about recycling. | Is this a documentary or a made-up story? | There is documentary evidence that the castle was built by the king.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: documentaries. A documentary is non-fiction but can still have a point of view.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An editor is a person who checks, corrects and improves writing before it is published. 2) An editor is the person in charge of a newspaper, magazine or part of one. 3) An editor is a person who cuts and puts together film or video. 4) In computing, an editor is a program for changing text, pictures or code.
its sense in the lessons: In writing lessons, pupils «edit» their work (check spelling and punctuation) like an editor. The school newspaper has a pupil editor. Coders write in a code editor.
examples from the lessons: The editor fixed all my spelling mistakes. | She is the editor of the school magazine. | The film editor cut the boring parts. | Open the file in a text editor. | The newspaper editor chose the front page story. | Swap your story with a partner and be their editor.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Use «an»: an editor. Verb: edit. Female editors are also just «editor».

meaning for a pupil: 1) An enzyme is a substance made by living things that speeds up chemical changes, for example breaking down food in your stomach.
its sense in the lessons: In science, digestive enzymes in saliva and the stomach break food into small pieces the body can use. Biological washing powders use enzymes to remove stains. Enzymes work best at certain temperatures; too much heat stops them working.
examples from the lessons: Enzymes in your saliva start to digest bread. | Biological washing powder has enzymes that eat stains. | Each enzyme does one special job. | Heat can stop an enzyme from working. | Enzymes help turn milk into cheese. | Pineapple has an enzyme that can make your tongue tingle.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Use «an»: an enzyme. Enzymes are not alive themselves; they are chemicals made by living cells.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An exoplanet is a planet that goes around a star other than our Sun.
its sense in the lessons: In space science, thousands of exoplanets have been found, mostly by spotting a star dimming as a planet passes in front. Scientists look for exoplanets in the «Goldilocks zone», where water could be liquid. No life has been found on any exoplanet so far.
examples from the lessons: Astronomers have found thousands of exoplanets. | An exoplanet orbits a faraway star. | Some exoplanets are giant balls of gas. | Could an exoplanet have life? | The telescope spotted an exoplanet by watching its star dim. | The exoplanet is too far away to visit.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Use «an». «Exo-» means outside (outside our solar system).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A fallacy is a false idea that many people believe. 2) In logic, a fallacy is a mistake in reasoning that makes an argument wrong, even if it sounds convincing.
its sense in the lessons: In ethics and logic lessons, pupils learn fallacies like «everyone does it, so it's right» (bandwagon), attacking the person instead of the argument, and the «gambler's fallacy» (thinking after five heads, tails is «due» — in fact each coin toss is still 50-50). Spotting fallacies helps with news and adverts.
examples from the lessons: It is a fallacy that we only use ten percent of our brains. | «Everyone's doing it» is a fallacy, not a reason. | The gambler's fallacy fools lots of people. | She pointed out the fallacy in his argument. | It's a common fallacy that bats are blind. | Name-calling instead of answering is a fallacy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: fallacies. Adjective: fallacious (formal). In maths probability, past coin tosses do not change the next toss.

part of speech: noun (flesh — uncountable); verb (flesh out, fleshes out, fleshed out)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Flesh is the soft part of the body of a person or animal, between the skin and bones, mostly muscle and fat. 2) Flesh is the soft part of a fruit or vegetable that you can eat. 3) (Bible, church) «The flesh» means the human body and its desires, as opposed to the spirit; «the Word became flesh» means Christians believe God became a human in Jesus. 4) To flesh out an idea or a story means to add more details.
its sense in the lessons: In science, flesh-eating animals are carnivores. In writing lessons, teachers ask pupils to «flesh out» characters. Phrases: «in the flesh» (in person, for real), «flesh and blood» (your own family; a real human).
examples from the lessons: The peach had sweet orange flesh. | Lions eat the flesh of other animals. | I met my favourite author in the flesh! | Flesh out your story with more details. | He's my own flesh and blood. | Christians believe the Word became flesh at Christmas.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Adjective: fleshy. «Flesh-coloured» is an old phrase that wrongly assumes one skin colour — say «skin-coloured» or name the shade.

part of speech: noun (a fossa, fossas; anatomy plural fossae)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A fossa is a slim, cat-like meat-eating animal that lives only in Madagascar, the island's top predator. 2) In anatomy, a fossa is a small hollow or dip in a bone or the body.
its sense in the lessons: In science, the fossa hunts lemurs and climbs trees using its long tail for balance; it appears in the film «Madagascar». It is related to mongooses, not cats.
examples from the lessons: The fossa leapt through the trees after a lemur. | Fossas live only in Madagascar. | A fossa looks like a cat but isn't one. | Its long tail helps it balance on branches. | The doctor pointed to a small fossa in the skull bone. | The fossa is the largest predator on Madagascar.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced «FOSS-uh». Not related to «fossil», though both come from Latin «fodere», to dig.

part of speech: proper noun (Franklin — a name); noun (a franklin, franklins — history, rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (a name) Franklin is a first name and a family name, as in Benjamin Franklin, one of the founders of the United States, and Franklin the Turtle in children's books. 2) (history) In old England, a franklin was a free man who owned land but was not a lord or a knight.
its sense in the lessons: In lessons the word is almost always a name: Benjamin Franklin is famous for his kite experiment with lightning, for inventing bifocal glasses and the lightning rod, and for helping write the Declaration of Independence; his face is on the US hundred-dollar bill. Franklin is also a place name (many US towns) and a character in picture books. In history lessons about the Middle Ages, a franklin is one of the people in Chaucer's Canterbury Tales. Phrases: «Benjamin Franklin», «Franklin the Turtle», «the Franklin expedition» (a lost voyage to the Arctic).
examples from the lessons: Benjamin Franklin flew a kite in a storm to learn about electricity. | Franklin helped write the Declaration of Independence. | My little brother loves the Franklin the Turtle books. | There is a picture of Franklin on the hundred-dollar bill. | We drove through a small town called Franklin. | In Chaucer's story, the franklin loves good food and wine. | Franklin invented the lightning rod to protect houses.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Written with a capital F when it is a name. As an old word for a free landowner (small f) it is rare and only met in history. Do not invent facts about a person called Franklin in a story: read what the text says. Benjamin Franklin did not "discover" electricity; he showed that lightning is electricity.

part of speech: adjective (freshwater — no other forms); noun (fresh water, uncountable)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Freshwater describes water that is not salty, like the water in most rivers, lakes, ponds and streams. 2) Freshwater animals and plants live in water that is not salty: a trout is a freshwater fish. 3) (noun, written as two words) Fresh water is water without salt that people, animals and plants can drink or use.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography, freshwater is the opposite of saltwater (sea water). Pupils learn that only a tiny part of the water on Earth is fresh, and much of that is frozen in ice caps and glaciers, so we must save water. Habitats are sorted into freshwater (ponds, rivers, lakes) and marine (sea). In everyday life it comes up with fishing, aquariums and drinking water. Phrases: «freshwater fish», «freshwater lake», «freshwater habitat», «fresh water supply».
examples from the lessons: A pond is a freshwater habitat. | Trout and perch are freshwater fish. | Most of the Earth's fresh water is frozen in ice. | We cannot drink sea water, we need fresh water. | The freshwater crayfish hides under stones in the stream. | Lake Superior is one of the biggest freshwater lakes in the world. | Our class kept tadpoles in a freshwater tank. | Frogs lay their eggs in freshwater ponds.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As an adjective before a noun it is one word: «a freshwater lake». As a noun phrase it is usually two words: «we need fresh water». Uncountable: «some fresh water», not «a fresh water». Fresh water is not always safe to drink — river water may carry germs. Opposite: saltwater, sea water, marine.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A haiku is a very short poem that comes from Japan, usually with three lines. 2) In English lessons, a haiku often has 5 syllables in the first line, 7 in the second and 5 in the third, 17 syllables in all. 3) A haiku usually paints one small moment, often about nature or a season.
its sense in the lessons: In English and poetry lessons pupils count syllables to write a haiku: 5–7–5. It teaches careful word choice, because there is so little space. A haiku often has a "seasonal word" (snow, blossom, leaves) and a surprise or turn at the end. In maths-like puzzles, you may be asked how many syllables a haiku has (17). Phrases: «write a haiku», «haiku about autumn», «5-7-5 pattern».
examples from the lessons: We wrote a haiku about the first snow. | A haiku has three lines and seventeen syllables. | Count the syllables on your fingers to check your haiku. | Her haiku was about a frog jumping into a pond. | Haiku come from Japan. | The poet wrote a haiku for every season. | My haiku: "Red leaves drift and fall / the wind carries them away / the tree stands alone."
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: «haiku» (same as singular) or «haikus»; both are seen. Say it "HIGH-koo". In Japanese the count is of sound units, not English syllables, so the 5–7–5 rule is a school rule for English, and real poets sometimes break it. A haiku does not need to rhyme. Maths: 5 + 7 + 5 = 17 syllables.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A herring is a small silver fish that lives in big groups in the North Atlantic and other cold seas. 2) Herring is also the fish eaten as food, often smoked (a kipper) or pickled. 3) A red herring is a clue or fact that leads you the wrong way, on purpose or by accident.
its sense in the lessons: In science, herring are an example of a fish that swims in shoals and is eaten by seals, whales and seabirds — a link in a food chain. In history, herring fishing made many coastal towns rich. In stories and mysteries, «a red herring» is a false clue that distracts the reader or detective. In maths problems, a red herring is a number in the question that you do not need. Phrases: «a shoal of herring», «pickled herring», «red herring», «packed like herrings».
examples from the lessons: A shoal of herring flashed silver in the sea. | Grandad eats pickled herring on toast. | A smoked herring is called a kipper. | Puffins and seals eat herring. | The muddy footprint was a red herring; the thief came in through the window. | This word problem has a red herring: the age of the bus driver does not matter. | The fishing boats came back full of herring.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: «herring» or «herrings»; «herring» is common for fish in the sea and as food. «Red herring» is an idiom: it is not a real red fish. In maths word problems, look out for red herrings — extra numbers you should not use.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A homophone is a word that sounds the same as another word but has a different meaning and often a different spelling, like «there», «their» and «they're». 2) Two or more such words are called homophones of each other.
its sense in the lessons: In English and spelling lessons, homophones cause many spelling mistakes, so pupils learn pairs and groups: to/too/two, hear/here, see/sea, knight/night, write/right, bear/bare, peace/piece, which/witch, flour/flower. The meaning of the sentence tells you which spelling to choose. Homophones are also used in jokes and puns. Phrases: «a pair of homophones», «homophone mistakes», «choose the right homophone».
examples from the lessons: «Sea» and «see» are homophones. | «Two», «too» and «to» are a group of homophones. | I wrote «their» instead of «there» — a homophone mistake. | The joke works because «knight» and «night» are homophones. | Circle the correct homophone: The (bare/bear) ate the honey. | Can you think of a homophone for «flour»? | Spell checkers often miss homophone mistakes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Do not mix up with «homograph» (same spelling, maybe different sound: a «bow» to tie, to «bow» your head) or «homonym» (a wider word for same-looking or same-sounding words). Homophones can depend on accent: «aunt/aren't» sound the same in much of England but not in the USA. Spell checkers do not catch them because each spelling is a real word.

part of speech: proper noun (Malacca, also Melaka — a place); noun (malacca — a cane, rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (a name, place) Malacca, also spelled Melaka, is a historic city and state in Malaysia on the west coast of the Malay Peninsula. 2) (place) The Strait of Malacca is a narrow sea passage between Malaysia and the Indonesian island of Sumatra, one of the busiest shipping routes in the world. 3) (rare) A malacca is a walking stick made from a kind of rattan palm.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and history lessons, Malacca is a famous old trading port where spices, silk and tea passed between China, India, the Middle East and Europe; it was ruled in turn by a sultanate, then by the Portuguese, the Dutch and the British. The Strait of Malacca is shown on maps of world trade routes because huge ships carry oil and goods through it. Phrases: «the Strait of Malacca», «the port of Malacca», «a malacca cane».
examples from the lessons: Malacca was a busy port where traders swapped spices and cloth. | Ships carrying oil sail through the Strait of Malacca. | The city is now usually spelled Melaka. | Find the Strait of Malacca on the map between Malaysia and Sumatra. | The old man walked with a malacca cane. | Portuguese and Dutch traders fought over Malacca.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital M for the place. Today Malaysians spell the city «Melaka»; «Malacca» is the older English spelling. Stress: "ma-LACK-a". Not the same as «Molucca» (the Spice Islands in Indonesia).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Malaria is a serious illness that causes high fever, shivering and sweating, and can kill if it is not treated. 2) It is caused by a tiny parasite that gets into the blood when an infected mosquito bites a person.
its sense in the lessons: In science and health lessons, malaria is the classic example of a disease spread by an animal (the mosquito), so pupils learn about life cycles, hot wet climates and how to stay safe: bed nets, insect spray, draining still water, and medicine for travellers. In geography it is linked to tropical countries, mostly in Africa. In history, it slowed down building projects such as the Panama Canal. Phrases: «catch malaria», «malaria nets», «anti-malaria tablets», «malaria vaccine».
examples from the lessons: Malaria is spread by mosquito bites. | Many children in Africa sleep under nets to stop malaria. | Before the trip, Dad took anti-malaria tablets. | Malaria gives you a very high fever. | Mosquitoes lay their eggs in still water, so people drain puddles to fight malaria. | Scientists have made vaccines against malaria. | You cannot catch malaria by touching someone who has it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «malaria», not «a malaria». Myth: the name comes from Italian «bad air», because people once thought bad air from swamps caused it; in fact it is the mosquito. Only some mosquitoes (female Anopheles) spread it. It is treatable and preventable.

part of speech: adjective/prefix (mini — before a noun: a mini quiz); noun (a mini, minis); proper noun (a Mini — a car)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Mini means very small or smaller than usual: a mini pizza, a mini test. 2) As the start of a word (mini-), it means "small": minibus, minibeast, miniskirt, mini-golf. 3) A Mini is a small British car. 4) (informal) A mini is a short skirt (a miniskirt).
its sense in the lessons: In school, mini is everyday talk: «mini whiteboards», «a mini quiz», «minibeasts» (small creatures like woodlice and beetles in science), «a mini project». In maths, «mini» is not a measurement; it only tells you something is small. Phrases: «mini whiteboard», «minibeast hunt», «mini-golf», «mini version», «mini break».
examples from the lessons: Write your answer on your mini whiteboard. | We went on a minibeast hunt and found three snails. | The party had mini sausages and mini muffins. | Our class went to the zoo in a minibus. | Let's have a mini quiz before lunch. | Grandma drove a little red Mini. | We played mini-golf on holiday.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Often joined to the next word (minibus) or with a hyphen (mini-golf), or written separately before a noun (mini quiz). Opposite: maxi, mega, giant. «Mini» comes from «miniature». Capital M for the car brand. Not a number: «mini» does not tell you how small.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A neutron is one of the tiny particles inside the centre (nucleus) of an atom. 2) A neutron has no electric charge — it is neutral, neither positive nor negative.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, the atom is made of protons (positive), neutrons (no charge) and electrons (negative); protons and neutrons sit in the nucleus, electrons move around it. Neutrons are important in nuclear power stations, where they split atoms. A neutron star is what is left after some huge stars explode: very small and very heavy. Phrases: «protons and neutrons», «neutron star», «number of neutrons».
examples from the lessons: An atom has protons, neutrons and electrons. | A neutron has no charge. | Protons and neutrons are packed together in the nucleus. | A neutron star is smaller than a city but heavier than the Sun. | Most hydrogen atoms have no neutrons at all. | Neutrons help split atoms in a nuclear power station.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Easy way to remember: Neutron = Neutral. A proton and a neutron weigh about the same; an electron is much lighter. Maths: number of neutrons = mass number − number of protons. Do not confuse with «neuron», a nerve cell in the brain.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An okapi is a shy African forest animal with a brown body and black-and-white stripes on its legs, like a zebra's. 2) The okapi is the giraffe's closest living relative, and like a giraffe it has a very long, dark tongue.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography lessons, the okapi is an example of a rare animal found only in the rainforests of the Democratic Republic of the Congo; its stripes help it hide in light and shadow (camouflage). It is endangered because of hunting and loss of forest. In animal fact books and zoos it is the "forest giraffe". Phrases: «okapi stripes», «the okapi's tongue», «a rare okapi».
examples from the lessons: The okapi looks like a mix of a zebra and a giraffe. | An okapi can lick its own ears with its long tongue. | Okapis live in the rainforest of the Congo. | The stripes on its legs help the okapi hide among the trees. | We saw an okapi at the zoo. | The okapi is an endangered animal.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Use «an»: «an okapi». Plural: «okapis». Say it "oh-KAH-pee". Trap: it is not a kind of zebra, even with the stripes; it is in the giraffe family.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A panther is a big wild cat, usually a leopard or a jaguar with black fur (a black panther). 2) In North America, a panther is another name for a puma or cougar, as in the Florida panther.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, «panther» is a good example of a word that is not one exact species: black panthers are leopards or jaguars with a lot of dark colour, and if you look closely you can still see their spots. Panthers are carnivores and skilled hunters. In stories, the panther Bagheera in The Jungle Book is wise and calm. Sports teams often use the name. Phrases: «black panther», «Florida panther», «Pink Panther» (a cartoon).
examples from the lessons: A black panther is really a leopard or jaguar with dark fur. | In The Jungle Book, Bagheera is a black panther. | The Florida panther is very rare. | A panther moves silently through the trees. | You can see faint spots on a black panther in bright light. | The panther climbed the tree with its prey.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: «panthers». Myth: there is no separate black panther species. In a story «moved like a panther» means quietly and gracefully. Not the same animal as a lion or tiger.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A pesticide is a chemical used to kill pests — insects, weeds, fungi or small animals that damage crops or gardens. 2) Pesticides include insecticides (for insects), herbicides (for weeds) and fungicides (for moulds and fungi).
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography lessons about farming, pesticides help farmers grow more food, but they can harm bees, birds and rivers, and can travel up food chains. Pupils compare them with natural methods like ladybirds eating aphids and with organic farming. In everyday life and safety: pesticides are poisonous, must be kept away from children and pets, and fruit should be washed. Phrases: «spray pesticides», «pesticide-free», «harmful pesticides».
examples from the lessons: The farmer sprayed pesticide on the potatoes. | Some pesticides can harm bees. | Organic farms use fewer chemical pesticides. | Wash fruit before you eat it to remove pesticide. | Ladybirds are a natural way to control aphids without pesticides. | Keep pesticides locked away from children and pets. | The pesticide washed into the river and harmed the fish.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «-cide» means "killing": pesticide, insecticide, herbicide. Countable for kinds («two pesticides») or uncountable for the stuff («some pesticide»). A pest is something that harms crops or homes; the word sounds like a judgement, but the animal is not "bad", just in the way.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To punctuate writing is to put in punctuation marks, like full stops, commas, question marks and speech marks. 2) To punctuate something also means to interrupt it again and again: the speech was punctuated by cheers. 3) To punctuate can mean to stress a point: he punctuated his words by banging the table.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons, pupils are told to «punctuate your writing correctly» and «punctuate the speech»: capital letters, full stops, commas in lists, apostrophes, and inverted commas round spoken words. In stories, «punctuated by» shows something happening at intervals: silence punctuated by drips. Phrases: «punctuate correctly», «punctuate the sentence», «punctuated by», «punctuated with».
examples from the lessons: Punctuate this sentence: where are you going asked tom | Remember to punctuate your story with full stops and capital letters. | She punctuated the dialogue with speech marks. | The quiet night was punctuated by an owl's hoot. | His talk was punctuated with jokes. | The teacher punctuated each rule by tapping the board. | Can you punctuate the list with commas?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: «punctuation» (uncountable). Spelled with «-uate», like «graduate». The second meaning is common in stories and the exam voice. Do not confuse with «punctual» (on time), though both come from a Latin word for "point".

part of speech: verb, past form (rig, rigs, rigged, rigging); adjective (rigged)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Rigged means unfairly arranged so that a certain person wins: a rigged game, a rigged election. 2) Rigged also means fitted with ropes, sails or equipment: a ship rigged with three masts. 3) Rigged up means made quickly from whatever you have: we rigged up a shelter with a sheet.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and politics talk, «rigged» means cheating — a rigged raffle, a rigged vote; when people say an election was rigged, that is a serious claim that needs proof, and news reports often show it as one side's claim. In stories about ships, a vessel is «rigged» with sails. In design and technology lessons, you «rig up» a model or a circuit. Phrases: «rigged game», «rigged election», «rig up», «the game is rigged».
examples from the lessons: The fairground game was rigged so nobody could win the big teddy. | He shouted that the match was rigged, but the referee was fair. | We rigged up a tent with a blanket and two chairs. | The old ship was rigged with white sails. | Was the raffle rigged? The head teacher's son won again! | They rigged up a pulley to lift the bucket.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double g: rig → rigged, rigging. «Rigging» is also a noun for a ship's ropes. Saying «it's rigged» is an accusation; in a news or politics lesson, ask for evidence. Not the same as «rugged» (rough, strong).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Static means not moving or not changing: a static picture, prices stayed static. 2) Static electricity is an electric charge that builds up on things when they rub together, making hair stand up or giving a small shock. 3) (noun) Static is a crackling noise on a radio or TV, or fuzzy dots on a screen.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, pupils rub a balloon on hair or a jumper to make static electricity, then make it stick to a wall or lift bits of paper; they learn that like charges push apart and opposite charges pull together; lightning is a giant static spark. In maths and graphs, a static number does not change. In PE, «static stretches» are held still. Phrases: «static electricity», «static shock», «static on the radio», «stay static».
examples from the lessons: Rub the balloon on your jumper to make static electricity. | I got a static shock when I touched the car door. | My hair stood up because of static. | The radio only played static in the tunnel. | The number of pupils stayed static all year. | We did static stretches after the race. | Lightning is a huge spark of static electricity.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite of «dynamic» or «moving». The noun «static» (noise) is uncountable. Static shocks are usually harmless; lightning is not. Do not mix up with «statistic» (a number fact) or «statue».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Suspense is the excited or worried feeling of waiting to find out what will happen next. 2) In stories and films, suspense is the tension a writer builds on purpose so that you want to keep reading.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons, pupils learn to «build suspense» in their writing: short sentences, cliffhangers, hints of danger, slowing down time, questions in the reader's mind, sounds in the dark. «Keep someone in suspense» means making them wait for news. Suspense is a key idea for mystery, adventure and ghost stories. Phrases: «build suspense», «keep in suspense», «full of suspense», «the suspense is killing me».
examples from the lessons: The story was full of suspense. | Don't keep me in suspense — who won? | Short sentences can build suspense. Then silence. A creak. | The suspense is killing me! | The film's suspense made us hold our breath. | The author ends each chapter in suspense with a cliffhanger. | We waited in suspense for our test results.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «a lot of suspense», not «a suspense». Adjective: «suspenseful». Spelled with «-ense», not «-ence». Related to «suspend» (to hang): you are left "hanging". Do not confuse with «suspension» (being sent off from school, or a car's springs).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A tapir is a large, plant-eating animal shaped a bit like a pig, with a short, bendy nose (snout) like a tiny trunk. 2) Tapirs live in forests of Central and South America and South-East Asia, and are good swimmers.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, the tapir is an example of a rainforest herbivore; baby tapirs have stripes and spots for camouflage that fade as they grow. The Malayan tapir is black with a white middle, like a blanket. Tapirs are endangered because forests are cut down. Their nearest relatives are horses and rhinos, not pigs. Phrases: «baby tapir», «Malayan tapir», «a tapir's snout».
examples from the lessons: A tapir uses its bendy snout to grab leaves. | Baby tapirs have stripes like a watermelon. | The tapir hid in the river to escape the jaguar. | Tapirs are related to horses and rhinos. | The Malayan tapir is black and white. | Tapirs are in danger because the rainforest is shrinking.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: «tapirs». Say it "TAY-per" (UK and US) or "ta-PEER". Trap: it looks like a pig but is not related to pigs. Spelled with -ir.

part of speech: verb (tarnish, tarnishes, tarnished, tarnishing); noun (tarnish, uncountable)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To tarnish is when metal like silver, brass or copper loses its shine and gets dull or dark, because of the air. 2) To tarnish someone's name or reputation is to make people think less well of them. 3) (noun) Tarnish is the dull, dark layer that forms on metal.
its sense in the lessons: In science, tarnishing is a chemical change: silver reacts with sulphur in the air and goes black; copper goes green over time (like the Statue of Liberty). Pupils clean coins with vinegar and salt to see tarnish come off. In stories and news, «tarnished reputation» means people trust someone less after something bad. Phrases: «tarnished silver», «tarnish a reputation», «polish off the tarnish».
examples from the lessons: Grandma's silver spoons have tarnished. | We cleaned the tarnished pennies with vinegar and salt. | The brass doorknob is covered in tarnish. | Cheating tarnished the team's good name. | Gold does not tarnish easily. | The scandal tarnished the king's reputation.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Third person: «it tarnishes». The noun «tarnish» is uncountable. Gold hardly tarnishes; that is one reason it is valued. Tarnishing is not exactly rust: rust is iron going orange-brown.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A tit is a small, lively bird, such as the blue tit or great tit, common in gardens in the UK and Europe. 2) (rude, slang) Tit is also a rude word for a part of the body; not for school. 3) (UK, slang, mild insult) A tit is a silly or annoying person: «Don't be a tit.» 4) «Tit for tat» means doing something bad back to someone because they did it to you.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons in the UK, blue tits and great tits appear in bird watches, nest-box projects and food chains (they eat caterpillars and seeds). In playground talk in Britain, «you tit» is a mild insult, and the rude meaning of the word is not polite; teachers may tell children off for it. «Tit for tat» is a common phrase in stories about fights and arguments. Phrases: «blue tit», «great tit», «long-tailed tit», «tit for tat», «feel a right tit» (UK, slang: feel stupid).
examples from the lessons: A blue tit is feeding at the bird table. | Great tits nested in our school's nest box. | Long-tailed tits fly around in little flocks. | They kept taking each other's pens — tit for tat. | (UK, slang) "Don't be a tit, give it back!" | (UK, slang) I felt a right tit when I fell off the stage. | Blue tits eat lots of caterpillars in spring.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The bird meaning is perfectly polite. The body meaning (rude) and the insult (UK slang) are not used in class; in a story they show rough talk. American English calls similar birds «chickadees» and «titmice». Plural of the bird: «tits»; the word «titmouse» has the plural «titmice».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (abbreviation) VA is short for Virginia, a state in the United States, in addresses. 2) (abbreviation) In the USA, the VA is the Department of Veterans Affairs, which helps people who served in the armed forces. 3) (French) «Va» is French for "goes" or "go!"; «ça va?» means "how are you?" or "all right?", and sounds like "sa VAH". It is not an English word.
its sense in the lessons: On its own, «va» is not an English word. In geography and addresses it is the postal code for Virginia (Richmond, VA). In French lessons, pupils meet «Ça va?» — «Ça va bien, merci» (I'm fine, thanks); «il va» means "he goes" or "he is going". In electricity, VA (volt-ampere) is a unit on some chargers. Phrases: «ça va», «Richmond, VA», «the VA hospital».
examples from the lessons: (French) "Ça va?" "Oui, ça va bien, merci!" | (French) Il va à l'école — he goes to school. | The letter was sent to Arlington, VA. | (USA) Grandpa gets help from the VA because he was a soldier. | (French) "Va!" shouted the mother — "Go!" | The charger says 500 VA on the label.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As an abbreviation, write it in capitals: VA. In French, «va» comes from the verb «aller» (to go): je vais, tu vas, il/elle va. «Ça va» can be a question (How are things?) or an answer (Fine). Do not read «va» as part of an English sentence unless it is one of these.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A warship is a ship built and armed for fighting in a war, run by a navy. 2) Warships include battleships, aircraft carriers, destroyers, frigates and submarines.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, warships appear in stories of the Vikings' longships, Henry VIII's Mary Rose, the Spanish Armada, Nelson's HMS Victory and the world wars. In news, warships may patrol seas, guard ships carrying food or oil, or rescue people. In design and technology and science, pupils learn why heavy steel ships float (displacement). Phrases: «a fleet of warships», «sink a warship», «enemy warships», «naval warship».
examples from the lessons: The Mary Rose was Henry VIII's favourite warship. | HMS Victory is an old wooden warship you can visit in Portsmouth. | A fleet of warships sailed into the harbour. | The warship had big guns on its deck. | Navy warships helped rescue people after the flood. | A submarine is a warship that travels underwater.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word: «warship». Ships are often called «she» in old-fashioned writing: «she sank». Steel warships float because they push aside (displace) a weight of water equal to their own weight.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An admiral is a very high-ranking officer in a navy who commands many ships (a fleet). 2) A red admiral is a black butterfly with red bands and white spots on its wings, common in gardens.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, admirals lead navies in battles: Admiral Nelson won the Battle of Trafalgar and has a column in Trafalgar Square in London. In science lessons and garden surveys, the red admiral is a butterfly pupils spot on buddleia and nettles (its caterpillars eat nettles). Phrases: «Admiral Nelson», «rear admiral», «vice admiral», «red admiral», «white admiral».
examples from the lessons: Admiral Nelson stands on top of a tall column in London. | The admiral gave orders to the whole fleet. | A red admiral landed on the buddleia bush. | Red admiral caterpillars feed on stinging nettles. | She joined the navy and dreamed of becoming an admiral. | The admiral's flag flew from the biggest ship.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Use «an»: «an admiral». Capital A before a name: «Admiral Nelson». Ranks: rear admiral, vice admiral, admiral, admiral of the fleet. Do not confuse with «admire» or «admirable», which are about liking or respecting someone.

part of speech: noun (a beech, beeches; beech — the wood, uncountable)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A beech is a large tree with smooth grey bark and shiny oval leaves, found in Europe and North America. 2) Beech is also the hard, pale wood of this tree, used to make furniture and toys.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on trees and seasons, beech is easy to recognise by its smooth grey bark; its small three-sided nuts (beechnuts or beech mast) are eaten by squirrels, mice and birds; young beech hedges keep their brown leaves all winter. In design and technology, beech wood is used for spoons, chopping boards and toys. Phrases: «beech tree», «beech wood/beechwood», «beech hedge», «beechnut».
examples from the lessons: A huge beech tree grows in the park. | The beech has smooth grey bark. | Squirrels collect beechnuts in autumn. | Our wooden spoon is made of beech. | The beech hedge keeps its brown leaves in winter. | Bluebells grow in the beech woods in spring.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Homophone trap: «beech» (the tree) and «beach» (sand by the sea) sound the same. Memory trick: a beech has two «e»s like a tree. Plural: «beeches».

part of speech: adjective (Byzantine, byzantine); noun (a Byzantine, Byzantines — history)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (history) Byzantine describes the Byzantine Empire, the eastern part of the Roman Empire, which lasted for about a thousand years after Rome fell, with its capital at Constantinople (now Istanbul). 2) (history, art, church) Byzantine art and churches have gold mosaics, domes and holy pictures called icons. 3) (formal) byzantine (small b) means far too complicated and hard to understand: byzantine rules.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, the Byzantine Empire links ancient Rome to the Middle Ages: Emperor Justinian, the great church of Hagia Sophia, Greek language and Orthodox Christianity. In church and art lessons, Byzantine icons and mosaics are shown. In the formal or exam voice, «byzantine» describes a confusing system, like a maze of rules. Phrases: «the Byzantine Empire», «Byzantine art», «a byzantine system».
examples from the lessons: The Byzantine Empire's capital was Constantinople. | Hagia Sophia is a famous Byzantine church with a huge dome. | Byzantine mosaics shine with tiny pieces of gold glass. | Orthodox Christians still pray with icons in the Byzantine style. | (formal) The club's rules were so byzantine that nobody understood them. | The Byzantines spoke Greek but called themselves Romans.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital B for the empire and its art; small b is common for the "too complicated" sense. Say it "bi-ZAN-teen" or "BIZ-an-tine". People of the time did not call it "Byzantine"; they called themselves Romans — the name was given later by historians.

part of speech: noun (a cannon, cannon or cannons); verb (cannon, cannons, cannoned, cannoning — rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A cannon is a big, heavy gun, usually on wheels or on a ship, that fires large metal balls or shells. 2) To cannon into someone is to crash into them hard while moving fast. 3) A water cannon is a machine that sprays very strong jets of water.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, cannons appear in castles, sieges, pirate ships and old battles; pupils learn that cannons made castle walls less safe. In science, a cannon firing a ball is an example of forces and motion. In stories, «a loose cannon» is a person nobody can control. In everyday talk, children «cannon into» each other in the corridor. Phrases: «fire a cannon», «cannonball», «loose cannon», «water cannon», «cannon into».
examples from the lessons: The pirates fired their cannons at the ship. | A cannonball smashed through the castle wall. | The cannon on the hill fires once a day for the tourists. | He cannoned into me in the corridor and we both fell over. | He is a loose cannon; you never know what he will say. | Firefighters used a water cannon on the burning barn.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: «cannons» or «cannon» (both correct). Homophone trap: «cannon» (gun) and «canon» (a church rule, a list of important books, a priest; also a round in music) sound the same. «Cannonball» is one word; «doing a cannonball» is jumping into a pool with knees hugged.

part of speech: noun (a clam, clams); verb (clam up, clams up, clammed up, clamming up)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A clam is a sea or river animal with a soft body inside two hard shells joined by a hinge; it lives buried in sand or mud. 2) Clams are also eaten as seafood. 3) To clam up means to suddenly stop talking, often because you are nervous or do not want to tell.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, clams are molluscs, like snails and mussels; they filter tiny food from water; the giant clam on coral reefs can be bigger than a child. In stories and everyday life, someone who «clams up» goes quiet when asked questions. «Happy as a clam» (US) means very happy. Phrases: «clam chowder», «giant clam», «clam up», «shut like a clam».
examples from the lessons: We found an empty clam shell on the beach. | Clams dig into the sand when the tide goes out. | The giant clam lives on coral reefs. | Dad ordered clam chowder at the restaurant. | When the teacher asked who broke it, Sam clammed up. | She shut her mouth like a clam and said nothing.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb forms double the m: «clammed», «clamming». Do not confuse with «clammy» (cold and slightly wet: clammy hands). A clam is a mollusc, not a fish.

part of speech: noun (a con, cons); verb (con, cons, conned, conning); prefix (con-)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) A con is a trick to cheat someone, usually to get their money: it was all a con. 2) (informal) To con someone is to trick them into believing something false or giving you something. 3) Cons are the disadvantages of something, as in «pros and cons» (the good points and the bad points). 4) (informal) A con is short for a convict, a person in prison. 5) A con is also a big fan meeting, like a comic con.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and online safety lessons, pupils learn to spot cons: messages saying you won a prize, people asking for passwords or money. In English and persuasive writing, «pros and cons» means weighing up both sides before a decision. Phrases: «a con artist» (a cheat), «con someone out of money», «pros and cons», «comic con».
examples from the lessons: That free phone offer is a con. | A con artist tricked Grandpa out of his savings. | Don't let anyone con you into sharing your password. | Let's list the pros and cons of a school uniform. | One con of a dog is that you have to walk it in the rain. | We dressed up as superheroes for the comic con. | He conned his little sister into doing his chores.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb forms: conned, conning. «Pros and cons»: pros = for, cons = against. «Con» is informal, used in talk and news; in formal writing use «fraud», «scam» or «trick». «Con-» at the start of many words (connect, contain) has nothing to do with cheating.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Dyslexia is a common difference in how the brain works with words, which makes reading, spelling and sometimes writing harder, even for clever people. 2) Someone who has dyslexia is described as dyslexic.
its sense in the lessons: In school, pupils learn that dyslexia has nothing to do with being clever or lazy; many inventors, artists and business people are dyslexic. Helpful things include coloured overlays, clear fonts, extra time in tests, audiobooks and multi-sensory spelling. It is about one in ten people. Phrases: «have dyslexia», «be dyslexic», «dyslexia-friendly font», «support for dyslexia».
examples from the lessons: My friend has dyslexia, so she uses a coloured overlay to read. | Dyslexia makes spelling hard, but he is brilliant at maths. | Many famous artists and scientists have dyslexia. | The teacher printed the worksheet in a dyslexia-friendly font. | Dyslexic pupils can have extra time in tests. | Audiobooks help my cousin who has dyslexia enjoy stories.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «dyslexia», not «a dyslexia». Adjective: «dyslexic». Myth: dyslexia is not «seeing letters backwards» only, and it is not caused by poor teaching or low intelligence. It is not an illness that you catch.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An eyelash is one of the short, curved hairs that grow along the edges of your eyelids. 2) Eyelashes help keep dust, sweat and small insects out of your eyes.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on the body and senses, eyelashes, eyelids and tears protect the eyes. In everyday life, people make a wish when they find a fallen eyelash and blow it away; «without batting an eyelash» (US; UK «eyelid») means without showing surprise or fear. Phrases: «long eyelashes», «flutter your eyelashes», «false eyelashes», «make a wish on an eyelash».
examples from the lessons: An eyelash fell onto my cheek. | Camels have very long eyelashes to keep out the sand. | Eyelashes protect your eyes from dust. | She blew the eyelash off her finger and made a wish. | The doll has long black eyelashes. | He told the lie without batting an eyelash.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word: «eyelash»; also called «lash». Plural «eyelashes» (add -es after -sh). Making a wish on an eyelash is a fun custom, not magic.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Fusion is the joining of two or more things into one: a fusion of music styles. 2) (science) Nuclear fusion is when tiny atoms join together and give out huge amounts of energy, which is how the Sun shines. 3) (science) Fusion can also mean melting, especially of metal or rock. 4) Fusion food mixes cooking from different countries.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, the Sun and stars make light and heat by fusion of hydrogen into helium; scientists try to copy this on Earth for clean energy. In music and food, fusion means a mix of styles, like Indian-British dishes or jazz-rock. In technology, fusion means welding things together. Phrases: «nuclear fusion», «fusion energy», «fusion food», «a fusion of».
examples from the lessons: The Sun makes its energy by nuclear fusion. | Scientists hope fusion will give us clean power one day. | The restaurant serves fusion food: Korean tacos. | The band's music is a fusion of folk and rock. | Welding is a kind of fusion of two metals. | Fusion joins small atoms; fission splits big ones.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: «fuse» (to join or melt). Do not confuse fusion (joining atoms, the Sun) with fission (splitting atoms, today's nuclear power stations). Uncountable for the process; «a fusion of» for a mix.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A glider is a light aircraft with long wings and no engine that flies by riding on air currents. 2) A glider is also any thing or animal that glides, like a paper glider or a sugar glider (a small flying possum). 3) (UK) A glider is a garden swing seat that moves smoothly back and forth (also in the US, a glider chair).
its sense in the lessons: In science and design and technology lessons, pupils make paper or balsa gliders to test wing shapes, weight and air resistance (forces: lift, drag, gravity). Gliders are pulled into the air by a plane or a winch, then slowly come down while rising on warm air (thermals). In nature, sugar gliders, flying squirrels and colugos glide between trees. Phrases: «paper glider», «hang glider», «sugar glider», «launch a glider».
examples from the lessons: We made paper gliders and tested which flew furthest. | A glider has no engine. | The glider rose on warm air above the hills. | A sugar glider can glide from tree to tree. | The hang glider jumped off the cliff and floated over the beach. | Adding a paperclip to the nose made my glider fly better.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: «gliders». A glider still falls slowly overall; it rises only when the air under it rises. A «hang glider» is a different, simpler kind where the pilot hangs under a wing.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Global means about the whole world: a global problem, global warming. 2) Global can mean about the whole of something, not just one part: a global view of the project.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and science lessons, «global warming», «global climate change» and «global trade» show that problems and businesses link countries together. «Global citizen» means someone who cares about the whole world. In computing, a «global variable» can be used everywhere in a program. Phrases: «global warming», «global problem», «go global», «global citizen», «global pandemic».
examples from the lessons: Global warming is making the Earth hotter. | Plastic in the sea is a global problem. | The football World Cup is a global event. | The company went global and opened shops in many countries. | Our school joined a global project with children in Kenya. | The internet is a global network.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Related words: «globe» (a ball-shaped map of the Earth), «globally», «globalisation» (UK) or «globalization» (US). Opposite: local. Not countable.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A grizzly, or grizzly bear, is a large brown bear of North America with a hump on its shoulders and grey-tipped fur. 2) (adjective) Grizzly can mean grey or grey-haired. 3) (UK, informal) A grizzly baby or child is grumpy and whiny.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography lessons, the grizzly is a top predator and an omnivore: it eats salmon, berries, roots and insects; it hibernates in winter. In outdoor safety lessons in Canada and the US, people learn bear safety: make noise, carry bear spray, never feed bears. Phrases: «grizzly bear», «mother grizzly», «a grizzly old man» (grey-haired).
examples from the lessons: A grizzly bear caught a salmon in the river. | Grizzlies sleep through the winter in a den. | Hikers in Canada carry bear spray in case they meet a grizzly. | The grizzly has a big hump on its shoulders. | (UK, informal) The baby was grizzly because she was tired. | A mother grizzly protects her cubs fiercely.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: «grizzlies» (y → ies). Homophone trap: «grizzly» (bear, grey) and «grisly» (horrible, gory: a grisly murder) sound the same. Grizzlies are a kind of brown bear, not a separate species.

part of speech: adjective (gummy, gummier, gummiest); noun (a gummy, gummies)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Gummy means sticky like glue or gum. 2) A gummy smile shows a lot of gum (the pink part above the teeth), and a gummy baby has no teeth yet. 3) A gummy is a chewy sweet, like a gummy bear or gummy worm (US: gummies, also vitamins).
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, gummy bears and gummy worms are sweets; dentists warn that sticky sweets stick to teeth and cause decay, so brush after. In science, «gummy» describes the texture of some materials, like tree sap. In stories, a «gummy grin» shows a baby or an old person without teeth. Phrases: «gummy bears», «gummy smile», «gummy vitamins».
examples from the lessons: I had a bag of gummy bears at the cinema. | The baby gave a big gummy smile. | Grandad took his teeth out and grinned a gummy grin. | The glue went all gummy in the sun. | Gummy sweets stick to your teeth, so brush afterwards. | Mum takes gummy vitamins every morning.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparatives: gummier, gummiest. «Gummy» sweets in the US are often «gummies»; in the UK people also say «jelly sweets». Different from «gooey» (soft and sticky) and «chewy».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A hermit is a person who chooses to live alone, away from other people, often for religious reasons or to think and pray. 2) Someone who hardly ever goes out or meets people is sometimes jokingly called a hermit. 3) A hermit crab is a crab that lives inside an empty shell of another sea animal.
its sense in the lessons: In church and history lessons, hermits were monks or holy people who lived alone in caves, deserts or huts to pray; Christians remember early hermits in the Egyptian desert. In science lessons, the hermit crab moves into bigger shells as it grows. In stories, a hermit is often a mysterious old person in the woods. Phrases: «live like a hermit», «hermit crab», «become a hermit».
examples from the lessons: The hermit lived alone in a cave on the hill. | Long ago, some Christians became hermits to pray in the desert. | A hermit crab looks for a bigger shell when it grows. | Since he started his game, my brother has been a hermit in his room. | In the story, the children met a wise hermit in the forest. | The hermit grew vegetables and rarely spoke to anyone.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: «hermits». Adjective: «hermit-like». A hermit crab's shell is borrowed; it does not grow its own. Calling a person a hermit as a joke is not unkind, but it can be about real loneliness.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A hostage is a person who is held prisoner by someone who will not let them go until they get what they want. 2) To take someone hostage, or hold someone hostage, is to capture and keep them like this.
its sense in the lessons: In history and news, hostages are taken in wars, by kidnappers or by terrorists; it is a crime under the law of every country, and governments work hard to free them. News reports of conflicts say who is being held and what each side says. In stories, a hostage raises the stakes for the hero. Figuratively, «held hostage» can mean controlled by something: «held hostage by the weather». Phrases: «take hostage», «hold hostage», «release the hostages», «hostage crisis».
examples from the lessons: The robbers took two people hostage in the bank. | The hostages were released after many days. | Families waited for news of the hostages. | In the film, the hero rescued the hostage from the castle. | Taking hostages is a serious crime. | (figurative) Our picnic was held hostage by the rain.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: «hostages». Pattern: «take/hold someone hostage» (no «as»). In news, reports often say how many hostages were taken and who says what; stick to what is reported. Not the same as a prisoner of war, who is a soldier captured in a war.

part of speech: adjective (humid, more humid, most humid); noun (humidity, uncountable)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Humid weather is warm and damp because there is a lot of water vapour in the air, so you feel hot and sticky. 2) A humid place, like a rainforest or a bathroom after a shower, has damp air.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and science lessons, rainforests have a hot, humid climate; humidity is measured with a hygrometer and given as a percentage. In everyday life: on humid days sweat does not dry, so you feel hotter; bread goes mouldy faster. Weather forecasts give humidity. Phrases: «hot and humid», «humid climate», «high humidity», «humid summer».
examples from the lessons: The rainforest is hot and humid. | It was so humid that my clothes stuck to me. | Bathrooms get humid after a hot shower. | The weather forecast says humidity is ninety percent today. | Tropical plants like humid greenhouses. | Singapore has a humid climate all year.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: «humidity». Opposite: dry, arid. Not the same as «hot»: a desert is hot but dry; a cold foggy morning can be humid. Say it "HYOO-mid". Maths: humidity is a percentage from 0 to 100.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An idiom is a group of words with a meaning you cannot guess from the separate words, like «it's raining cats and dogs» (it is raining very hard). 2) An idiom can also be the special way a group of people speak or write.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons, pupils collect idioms and explain them: «break a leg» (good luck), «a piece of cake» (very easy), «spill the beans» (tell a secret), «under the weather» (ill), «hit the sack» (go to bed). Idioms make writing lively but can confuse learners of English, because they are not meant literally. Each country has its own (Australia: «flat out like a lizard drinking» — very busy). Phrases: «use an idiom», «explain the idiom», «a common idiom».
examples from the lessons: «It's a piece of cake» is an idiom meaning it's easy. | My Polish friend was puzzled by the idiom «raining cats and dogs». | Can you draw the literal meaning of the idiom «spill the beans»? | «Under the weather» is an idiom for feeling ill. | Idioms are hard to translate into other languages. | «Let the cat out of the bag» is an idiom about telling a secret.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Use «an»: «an idiom». Adjective: «idiomatic» (natural English). Idioms are not literal: nobody's leg breaks in «break a leg». Do not confuse with «idiot». An idiom is different from a simile («as brave as a lion»), though some similes are idioms too.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To ingest is to take food, drink, medicine or another substance into your body by swallowing it. 2) (formal) To ingest information is to take it in and absorb it.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on digestion, ingestion is the first step: food is ingested (eaten), then digested, absorbed and the waste is egested. Safety labels say «harmful if ingested», meaning dangerous to swallow: cleaning products, batteries, some plants. In the exam voice, «ingest» replaces «eat» or «swallow». Phrases: «harmful if ingested», «ingest food», «accidentally ingested».
examples from the lessons: Bleach is harmful if ingested. | Animals ingest food through their mouths. | The dog ingested a sock and had to see the vet. | If a child ingests a battery, go to hospital straight away. | Whales ingest tiny plastic bits from the sea. | Plants do not ingest food; they make it from sunlight.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal word; in everyday talk say «swallow» or «eat». Noun: «ingestion». Opposite in science: «egest» (get rid of waste). Do not confuse with «digest» (break down food inside the body) or «inject» (put in with a needle).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A ligament is a strong, slightly stretchy band in your body that joins one bone to another at a joint, like the knee or ankle. 2) Ligaments hold joints together and stop them bending the wrong way.
its sense in the lessons: In science and PE lessons, pupils learn the parts of the skeleton and joints: bones, muscles, tendons (join muscle to bone), ligaments (join bone to bone) and cartilage. Sports injuries such as a sprained ankle or a torn knee ligament are common; warming up helps. Phrases: «torn ligament», «knee ligament», «damaged ligaments», «sprain a ligament».
examples from the lessons: Ligaments join bone to bone. | The footballer tore a ligament in his knee. | A sprained ankle means a ligament has been stretched too far. | Warming up helps protect your muscles and ligaments. | The doctor said the ligament would heal in six weeks. | Tendons attach muscles to bones, but ligaments attach bones to bones.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Easy trap: tendon (muscle to bone) vs ligament (bone to bone). Say it "LIG-a-ment". Plural «ligaments».

part of speech: proper noun (Mao — a name); Mandarin pinyin (mao)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (a name) Mao usually means Mao Zedong, the leader of the Communist Party who ruled the People's Republic of China from its start until his death. 2) (Mandarin, pinyin) «Máo» (毛) means hair, fur or feather, and is also a small unit of Chinese money: ten mao make one yuan. 3) (Mandarin, pinyin) «Māo» (猫) means cat. It sounds like "mow" (rhymes with "cow"). It is not an English word.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, Mao is a key figure of modern China: he led the Communists to power, and his rule is remembered both for uniting the country and for campaigns in which millions of people died of famine and persecution; historians and Chinese people today judge him in different ways. In Mandarin lessons and on Chinese streets, «máo» is used for money (like ten pence), and «māo» is a cat; the tone changes the meaning. Phrases: «Chairman Mao», «yí kuài wǔ máo» (one yuan fifty).
examples from the lessons: (a name) Chairman Mao led China for many years. | (a name) Mao's picture hangs over the gate in Tiananmen Square in Beijing. | (Mandarin, pinyin) Wǔ máo means five mao, half a yuan. | (Mandarin, pinyin) Wǒ yǒu yì zhī māo — I have a cat. | (Mandarin, pinyin) In Chinese, «máo» can mean fur or feathers. | Historians still argue about Mao's rule.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital M for the person. In pinyin the tone marks matter: māo (cat, high level tone) vs máo (hair, money, rising tone). In speech the money unit is called «máo»; on notes it is written «jiǎo». It is not an English word apart from the name.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A matador is the main bullfighter in a Spanish-style bullfight, the person who tries to kill the bull with a sword. 2) The word comes from Spanish and means "killer".
its sense in the lessons: In geography and culture lessons about Spain, bullfighting is a very old tradition that many people now oppose as cruel to animals; it is banned in some regions and countries. Matadors wear a sparkly "suit of lights" and wave a red cape (muleta). In stories, a matador is a picture of bravery or showing off. Phrases: «the matador's red cape», «matador and bull», «like a matador» (dodging neatly).
examples from the lessons: The matador waved his red cape at the bull. | Many people protest against bullfights because the bull is hurt and killed. | The matador wore a glittering costume. | Dodging the tacklers like a matador, he scored a try. | Bullfighting is banned in some parts of Spain. | The crowd cheered the matador.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: «matadors». Myth: the bull is not angry at the colour red — bulls cannot see red well; it is the cape's movement that makes it charge. A «toreador» is an older word for a bullfighter (from the opera Carmen).

meaning for a pupil: 1) mg is short for milligram, a very small unit of mass: there are 1,000 mg in 1 gram. 2) MG (capitals) is also a British car brand.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and science lessons, mg appears in measurement and conversion: 1 g = 1,000 mg, 1 kg = 1,000,000 mg. On food and medicine labels, mg tells you how much of a vitamin, salt or medicine is in a dose; safety: only adults should give medicine, and never take more than the label says. Phrases: «500 mg tablet», «mg per day», «convert g to mg».
examples from the lessons: This vitamin tablet has 200 mg of vitamin C. | 1 gram is the same as 1,000 mg. | Convert 3 g into milligrams: 3,000 mg. | The label says 5 mg of salt per biscuit. | A grain of rice weighs about 20 mg. | The doctor said to take one 250 mg tablet twice a day.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Write it in small letters with no full stop: «mg»; the plural is also «mg» (5 mg, not 5 mgs). Read it as «milligrams». Maths: to change mg into grams, divide by 1,000; grams to mg, multiply by 1,000. Do not confuse mg (milligram) with ml (millilitre, volume) or kg (kilogram).

part of speech: proper noun (Mickey — a name); noun (the mickey — UK, informal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (a name) Mickey is a first name, short for Michael, and the name of Mickey Mouse, the famous cartoon mouse from Disney. 2) (UK, informal) To take the mickey (out of someone) means to tease them or make fun of them. 3) (informal) Mickey Mouse (as an adjective) means silly, small or not serious: a Mickey Mouse job.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, Mickey Mouse is on toys, clothes and in theme parks. In British, Irish and Australian playground talk, «stop taking the mickey» means stop teasing; teasing that hurts someone is unkind, and teachers deal with it. In a story, it shows friendly banter or meanness depending on tone. Phrases: «Mickey Mouse», «take the mickey», «extract the mickey» (joking).
examples from the lessons: (a name) Mickey Mouse has big round ears. | (a name) My uncle Mickey is a builder. | (UK, informal) Stop taking the mickey out of my haircut! | (UK, informal) Are you taking the mickey? That's a terrible joke. | (informal) It was a Mickey Mouse competition with only three teams. | We met Mickey at Disneyland.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Take the mickey» is UK, Irish and Australian; Americans more often say «make fun of» or «tease». Capital M for the name. «Mickey Mouse» as an adjective is a bit rude about something.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Mimicry is copying the way someone talks, moves or behaves, often to make people laugh. 2) (science) Mimicry is when a living thing looks or sounds like another thing to protect itself or to trick others, like a harmless hoverfly that looks like a wasp.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on adaptation, mimicry helps animals survive: hoverflies copy wasp stripes, some caterpillars look like snakes, the lyrebird copies chainsaws and camera clicks, stick insects look like twigs (that is camouflage, a close idea). In drama and everyday life, mimicry is doing impressions of people; making fun of someone in a hurtful way is unkind. Phrases: «a talent for mimicry», «vocal mimicry», «animal mimicry».
examples from the lessons: The hoverfly's stripes are an example of mimicry. | Parrots are famous for their mimicry of human speech. | The lyrebird's mimicry can copy a car alarm. | His mimicry of the head teacher made the class giggle. | Mimicry helps harmless animals look dangerous. | Some orchids use mimicry to look like bees.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Verb: «mimic, mimics, mimicked, mimicking» (add k before -ed and -ing). Mimicry (looking like another animal) is not the same as camouflage (blending into the background), though both help animals hide or survive.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (French) Monsieur is the French word for "Mr" or "sir", used before a man's name or to speak to a man politely: «Bonjour, monsieur!» 2) In English, «monsieur» is sometimes used in jokes or stories to make a man sound French.
its sense in the lessons: In French lessons, pupils learn polite greetings: «Bonjour, monsieur», «Merci, madame», «Au revoir, mademoiselle»; in France it is polite to add monsieur or madame when greeting a shop keeper. It is written M. before a name: M. Dupont. It sounds like "muh-SYUR" to an English ear. It is a French word, not an English one. Phrases: «Bonjour, monsieur», «Monsieur Dupont», «Mesdames et messieurs» (ladies and gentlemen).
examples from the lessons: (French) Bonjour, monsieur ! | (French) Merci beaucoup, monsieur. | (French) Monsieur Martin is our French teacher. | (French) Mesdames et messieurs, the show is about to begin. | The waiter said, "Your soup, monsieur." | (French) Excusez-moi, monsieur, où est la gare ?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: «messieurs» ("may-SYUR"). Short form: «M.» (not «Mr.»). Women: «madame» (Mrs, Ms), «mademoiselle» (Miss, now old-fashioned). The «on» sounds like "uh", not "on". It is not an English word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Personification is a way of writing that gives human feelings or actions to things that are not human: «The wind howled.» «The sun smiled down.» 2) A personification of something is a person or character who stands for an idea: Father Time is a personification of time.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons, personification is a key figure of speech for poetry and descriptive writing, alongside similes and metaphors; pupils find it in poems («the leaves danced») and use it to make settings come alive.
