In art and history, the statue of Justice holding scales is a personification. Phrases: «use personification», «an example of personification», «the personification of».
examples from the lessons: «The trees whispered secrets» is personification. | Underline the personification in the poem. | «The angry sea swallowed the boat» uses personification. | Father Christmas is a personification of Christmas giving. | The old car coughed and groaned up the hill. | She was the personification of kindness.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: «personify» (personifies, personified). Long word: per-son-i-fi-ca-tion. Different from a simile (uses like/as) and a metaphor (says something is something else); personification is a kind of metaphor that makes things act like people.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A pipistrelle is a very small bat, the commonest kind of bat in Britain and much of Europe. 2) A pipistrelle is so small it could fit in a matchbox, and it eats thousands of tiny insects in a night.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on nocturnal animals and food chains, pupils learn that pipistrelles use echolocation (they send out squeaks and listen to the echoes) to catch midges and mosquitoes. Bats are protected by law in the UK: you must not disturb their roosts. On summer evenings children can see them flitting around streetlights. Phrases: «common pipistrelle», «soprano pipistrelle», «bat detector».
examples from the lessons: A pipistrelle can eat three thousand insects in one night. | We used a bat detector to hear the pipistrelles. | The pipistrelle flew around the streetlight catching moths. | Pipistrelles roost in roofs and old trees. | A pipistrelle weighs less than a pound coin. | Bats like the pipistrelle are protected by law in Britain.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say it "pip-i-STREL". Plural: «pipistrelles». Myth: bats are not blind, and pipistrelles do not get tangled in your hair. Bats are mammals, not birds.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A pixel is one of the tiny coloured dots or squares that make up a picture on a screen or a digital photo. 2) Pixels are also a way of measuring screen or picture size: 1,920 pixels wide.
its sense in the lessons: In computing lessons, pupils learn that every screen image is a grid of pixels, each with a colour made from red, green and blue light; more pixels means a sharper picture (higher resolution). Pixel art draws pictures on squared paper or in a computer grid. In maths, a picture 10 pixels wide and 10 high has 100 pixels (area). Phrases: «pixel art», «megapixel», «pixelated», «screen resolution».
examples from the lessons: Zoom in on the photo and you can see each pixel. | We made pixel art of a cat on squared paper. | My camera takes 12-megapixel photos. | The image went blocky and pixelated when I stretched it. | Each pixel can show millions of colours. | A picture 8 pixels by 8 pixels has 64 pixels in total.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: «pixels». «Megapixel» = one million pixels. «Pixelated» (blurry, blocky). Maths: number of pixels = width × height. Short for "picture element".

meaning for a pupil: 1) A plesiosaur was a large sea reptile that lived at the time of the dinosaurs, with a broad body, four flippers and often a very long neck. 2) Plesiosaurs are now extinct; we know them from fossils.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on fossils and evolution, plesiosaur fossils are famous because Mary Anning found one of the first complete skeletons on the coast at Lyme Regis in England. Pupils learn that plesiosaurs were not dinosaurs but marine reptiles living at the same time. The Loch Ness Monster legend often shows a plesiosaur-like creature, but there is no evidence for it. Phrases: «plesiosaur fossil», «long-necked plesiosaur».
examples from the lessons: Mary Anning found a plesiosaur fossil on the beach. | A plesiosaur swam using four big flippers. | Plesiosaurs ate fish and squid. | The museum has a plesiosaur skeleton with a very long neck. | Plesiosaurs were reptiles, but not dinosaurs. | Some people say the Loch Ness Monster is a plesiosaur, but there is no proof.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say it "PLEE-zee-o-sor". Plural «plesiosaurs». Trap: not a dinosaur — dinosaurs lived on land. The name means "near lizard".

part of speech: adjective (rad — slang); noun (a rad, rads — science, rare); abbreviation (rad)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (slang, mainly US and Australia) Rad means really cool or great: «That skateboard trick was rad!» 2) (science) A rad is an old unit for measuring how much radiation something has absorbed. 3) (maths) rad is short for radian, a unit for measuring angles used in higher maths. 4) (UK, informal) A rad can be short for a radiator.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday talk, especially among skaters and surfers or in old cartoons, «rad» means awesome; it can sound a bit retro now. In maths and science, «rad» is an abbreviation you meet later in secondary school. In a story, «rad» shows a cool, casual character. Phrases: «totally rad», «that's rad».
examples from the lessons: (slang) That's so rad! | (slang) He did a totally rad jump on his BMX. | (slang) Your new shoes are rad. | (maths) A full circle is about 6.28 rad. | (science) Doctors once measured radiation doses in rads. | (UK, informal) Put your wet socks on the rad to dry.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Slang «rad» is short for «radical». Informal; not for formal writing. The maths and science meanings are abbreviations; read «rad» as «radians» or «rads». Do not confuse with «red».

part of speech: noun (Scouse, uncountable; a Scouser, Scousers); adjective (Scouse)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (UK) Scouse is the accent and dialect of people from Liverpool in north-west England. 2) (UK) Scouse is a meat and vegetable stew, a traditional Liverpool dish. 3) (UK, informal) A Scouser is a person from Liverpool.
its sense in the lessons: In lessons about accents and dialects, Scouse is a well-known British accent; words like «la» or «lad» for a friend, «boss» for great, «ta» for thanks, «our kid» for brother or sister. Pupils learn that every accent is a proper way of speaking, and Standard English is a tool for formal writing. In food lessons, Scouse stew gives Liverpool people their nickname. Phrases: «a Scouse accent», «a pan of Scouse», «a proud Scouser».
examples from the lessons: (UK) She has a strong Scouse accent. | (UK) The Beatles were Scousers from Liverpool. | (UK) Nan made a big pot of Scouse for tea. | (UK) "That's boss, la!" is how a Scouser might say "That's great, mate!" | (UK) Scouse stew is made with lamb or beef, potatoes and onions. | (UK) Our teacher is a Scouser and supports Everton.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually with capital S. Scouse is a dialect and accent, not bad English. Rhymes with "house". «Scouser» is the person, «Scouse» the speech or the stew. Some people use «Scouser» proudly; it is not an insult, though tone matters.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (history) Serfdom was a system, mainly in the Middle Ages, in which poor farm workers called serfs were tied to a lord's land and could not leave it. 2) (history) Serfdom means the state of being a serf.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons on the Middle Ages and the feudal system, the king gave land to lords, lords had knights, and serfs (also called villeins) worked the land; serfs had to give the lord crops and work for free and needed permission to marry or move. Serfdom ended in England after the Black Death and the Peasants' Revolt, but lasted much longer in Russia. It was not exactly slavery, because serfs could not be sold apart from the land, but life was hard. Phrases: «end of serfdom», «abolish serfdom», «free from serfdom».
examples from the lessons: Under serfdom, peasants could not leave the lord's land. | Serfdom slowly ended in England after the Black Death. | The Russian tsar abolished serfdom, freeing millions of people. | Serfs paid the lord with work and crops. | The feudal system was built on serfdom. | Many peasants rebelled against serfdom.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Person: «a serf, serfs». Homophone trap: «serf» (a worker tied to land) and «surf» (waves) sound the same. Serfdom is not the same as slavery, but both took away people's freedom.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Siberian means from or about Siberia, the huge, very cold northern part of Russia that stretches from the Ural Mountains to the Pacific Ocean. 2) Siberian is also used in the names of animals and plants from there: Siberian tiger, Siberian husky. 3) (informal) Siberian can mean extremely cold: a Siberian wind.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons, Siberia has the taiga (huge pine forests), the tundra, Lake Baikal (the deepest lake in the world) and some of the coldest towns where people live. In science, the Siberian tiger is the largest cat and is endangered; Siberian huskies pull sleds. In history, Siberia was where Russian rulers sent prisoners. In UK weather news, a «Siberian blast» is freezing air from the east. Phrases: «Siberian tiger», «Siberian husky», «Siberian winter», «the Beast from the East».
examples from the lessons: The Siberian tiger is the biggest cat in the world. | Our neighbours have a Siberian husky with blue eyes. | Siberian winters can reach minus fifty degrees. | Lake Baikal is in southern Siberia. | A Siberian wind made the playground freezing. | Siberian forests are full of pine and birch trees.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital S. Siberia is part of Russia, not a separate country. The Siberian tiger is also called the Amur tiger. Maths: Siberian temperatures are negative numbers — minus 50 is colder than minus 30.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A simulation is a copy of a real situation, made on a computer or with models, so that people can study it or practise safely. 2) A simulation can also be a pretend version of something, like a fire drill or a flight simulator. 3) (formal) Simulation can mean pretending, putting on a false show: a simulation of interest.
its sense in the lessons: In science and computing lessons, pupils use simulations to see things that are too big, small, fast, slow or dangerous to test for real: planets moving, volcanoes, the spread of germs, circuits. Pilots train in flight simulators. In maths, a simulation can repeat a random event (like rolling a dice many times on a computer) to estimate a probability. Games like city builders are simulations too. Phrases: «computer simulation», «flight simulator», «run a simulation».
examples from the lessons: We used a computer simulation to see how the planets orbit the Sun. | Pilots practise emergencies in a flight simulator. | The fire drill is a simulation of a real fire. | The simulation rolled a dice a thousand times. | Scientists run simulations to predict the weather. | My brother plays a farming simulation game.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: «simulate», adjective: «simulated». A simulation is only as good as its rules: it can be wrong if the model is wrong. Not the same as «stimulation» (exciting or waking something up).

part of speech: noun (a span, spans); verb (span, spans, spanned, spanning)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A span is the length of time something lasts: a life span, an attention span. 2) A span is the distance from one end of something to the other: the span of a bridge, a bird's wingspan. 3) To span something is to stretch across it or last over it: the bridge spans the river. 4) A hand span is the distance from the tip of your thumb to the tip of your little finger when your hand is spread out.
its sense in the lessons: In maths lessons on measurement, pupils measure their hand span and use it as a non-standard unit, then compare in centimetres. In science, «life span» (how long an animal lives) and «wingspan» appear in animal facts; in history, a time line can span hundreds of years. In design and technology, a bridge's span is tested with models. Phrases: «life span», «attention span», «wingspan», «hand span», «span the river», «spick and span» (very clean).
examples from the lessons: An albatross has the biggest wingspan of any bird. | Measure your hand span with a ruler. | A mayfly's life span is only a day or two. | The bridge spans the whole river. | Small children have a short attention span. | The story spans three generations of a family. | After tidying, my room was spick and span.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb forms double the n: «spanned», «spanning». «Span» is also an old past form of «spin», now rare. Maths: a span is a length, so measure it in cm or m; a life span is a time, so measure it in years.

part of speech: adjective (Swiss); noun (a Swiss, the Swiss — the people)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Swiss means from or about Switzerland, a small mountain country in the middle of Europe. 2) The Swiss are the people of Switzerland. 3) Swiss is used in names of things: Swiss cheese, Swiss roll, Swiss Army knife.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons, Switzerland has the Alps, lakes, four official languages (German, French, Italian and Romansh) and no coastline; it is famous for staying neutral in wars. In everyday life: chocolate, watches, cheese with holes (like Emmental), the Swiss roll cake, and the Swiss Army knife. Phrases: «Swiss chocolate», «Swiss Alps», «Swiss roll», «Swiss cheese», «Swiss Army knife».
examples from the lessons: Swiss chocolate is famous around the world. | We went skiing in the Swiss Alps. | Grandma made a jam Swiss roll for pudding. | A Swiss Army knife has a blade, scissors and a tiny saw. | Many Swiss people speak German or French. | The Swiss have a red flag with a white cross.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always capital S. The country is «Switzerland», the people «the Swiss», the adjective «Swiss» — there is no word "Switzerlandish". Plural of a person: «a Swiss person, Swiss people». The holes in Swiss cheese come from gas bubbles made by bacteria.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A talon is a long, sharp, curved claw on the foot of a bird of prey, like an eagle, owl or hawk. 2) In stories, talons can be any sharp claws or long fingernails that look frightening.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, talons are an adaptation of predators: an owl or eagle grips and kills prey with its talons and tears food with its hooked beak. In stories, a monster or witch might have «talons» to sound scary. Phrases: «sharp talons», «gripped in its talons», «eagle's talons».
examples from the lessons: The eagle grabbed the fish with its talons. | An owl's talons are very sharp. | The hawk perched on the falconer's glove, which protected his arm from its talons. | The dragon's talons scraped across the rock. | The witch pointed a long, talon-like fingernail at him. | Ospreys have rough talons to hold slippery fish.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: «talons». Usually for birds of prey; for cats and dogs say «claws». Say it "TAL-on".

meaning for a pupil: 1) A volt is the unit used to measure voltage, the "push" that makes electricity flow around a circuit. 2) The short form is V: a 1.5 V battery.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on electricity, batteries (cells) have a voltage marked on them: AA cells are 1.5 volts; more cells in a series give more volts and make a bulb brighter or a buzzer louder. In the UK, mains electricity is about 230 volts, in the USA about 120 volts — dangerous, so never poke anything into sockets. The volt is named after the Italian scientist Alessandro Volta, who made an early battery. Phrases: «1.5-volt battery», «high voltage», «volts and amps».
examples from the lessons: An AA battery gives 1.5 volts. | Two 1.5-volt cells in series make 3 volts. | Mains electricity in Britain is about 230 volts. | The sign said "Danger: high voltage". | The bulb shone brighter when we added another volt. | The volt is named after Alessandro Volta.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Symbol: V (capital). Plural: «volts». Maths: in a series circuit, add the volts of each cell: 1.5 + 1.5 + 1.5 = 4.5 V. «Voltage» is the quantity; «volt» is the unit, like «length» and «metre». Do not confuse with «vault» (a jump or a safe room).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A wrasse is a brightly coloured sea fish with thick lips, found in warm seas and around rocky coasts and coral reefs. 2) The cleaner wrasse is a small wrasse that eats tiny pests off bigger fish.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on habitats and living together, the cleaner wrasse is an example of two animals helping each other: big fish wait at "cleaning stations" and the wrasse eats parasites from their skin and even inside their mouths, getting a meal. Ballan wrasse live around British coasts and rock pools. Many wrasse can change from female to male. Phrases: «cleaner wrasse», «ballan wrasse», «cuckoo wrasse».
examples from the lessons: A cleaner wrasse swam into the big fish's mouth to clean it. | We saw a green wrasse near the rocks while snorkelling. | Wrasse have thick lips and bright colours. | The cuckoo wrasse is blue and orange. | Fish farms use wrasse to eat lice off salmon. | Big fish wait in line for the cleaner wrasse.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say it "rass" (silent w). Plural: «wrasse» or «wrasses». Like many fish names, «wrasse» is used for many different species.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A wren is a tiny brown bird with a short tail that sticks up; it has a very loud song for its size. 2) (a name) Wren is also a family name, as in Sir Christopher Wren, the architect of St Paul's Cathedral in London.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons and bird watches in the UK and Ireland, the wren is one of the commonest birds; it hops in hedges and eats insects and spiders. In history and art lessons, Christopher Wren rebuilt many London churches after the Great Fire of London. In Irish tradition, Wren Day (St Stephen's Day) has the "wren boys" who go door to door in costumes. Phrases: «a jenny wren», «wren's nest», «Christopher Wren».
examples from the lessons: A wren was singing loudly from the hedge. | The wren is tiny but very loud. | Wrens build round nests with a hole in the side. | Christopher Wren designed St Paul's Cathedral. | The wren's tail sticks straight up. | In Ireland, the wren boys dress up on St Stephen's Day.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Silent w: say it "ren". Plural «wrens». Capital W when it is a name. In North America there are other kinds of wrens, such as the house wren and the Carolina wren.

part of speech: noun (an alpaca, alpacas; alpaca — the wool, uncountable)
meaning for a pupil: 1) An alpaca is a South American animal like a small llama, with a long neck and very soft, thick wool. 2) Alpaca is also the soft wool from this animal, used for jumpers, scarves and blankets.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and science lessons, alpacas come from the Andes mountains in Peru, Bolivia and Chile, where people have kept them for thousands of years for wool. They are herbivores, live in herds and can spit when annoyed (more often at each other). Alpaca farms and walks are now popular in the UK, Australia and New Zealand. Phrases: «alpaca wool», «alpaca farm», «llamas and alpacas».
examples from the lessons: The alpaca has a fluffy fringe over its eyes. | Grandma knitted me a scarf from alpaca wool. | Alpacas live high in the Andes mountains. | We went for a walk with alpacas on the farm. | An alpaca is smaller than a llama. | Alpacas hum to talk to each other.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Use «an»: «an alpaca». Plural «alpacas». Trap: alpacas and llamas are cousins, not the same: alpacas are smaller, with shorter pointed ears, and are kept for wool; llamas are bigger and carry loads.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An anagram is a word or phrase made by mixing up all the letters of another word or phrase: «listen» is an anagram of «silent». 2) An anagram puzzle asks you to rearrange the letters to find a hidden word.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons and olympiad puzzles, anagrams train spelling and thinking: «earth» → «heart», «dormitory» → «dirty room». Crosswords and word games use them. In maths, the number of ways to arrange letters is counted with permutations: «cat» has 3 × 2 × 1 = 6 arrangements. Phrases: «solve the anagram», «an anagram of», «anagram puzzle».
examples from the lessons: «Listen» is an anagram of «silent». | Can you find an anagram of «stop»? Pots, spot, tops, post, opts. | The detective solved the anagram and found the secret name. | «Dormitory» is an anagram of «dirty room». | The crossword clue was an anagram. | «Act» and «cat» are anagrams of each other.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Use «an»: «an anagram». A real anagram uses every letter exactly once. Maths: a word with n different letters can be arranged in n × (n−1) × … × 1 ways, but only a few of them are real words. Not the same as a palindrome (reads the same backwards: «level»).

part of speech: fragment/abbreviation (ar, Ar, AR); dialect word (ar — UK)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (UK, dialect) In parts of northern England and the Midlands, «ar» or «arr» means "yes", and «ar» can also mean "our": «ar kid» (my brother or sister). 2) (science) Ar is the chemical symbol for argon, a gas in the air used in light bulbs. 3) (abbreviation) AR is short for Arkansas, a US state, and for augmented reality, where a screen shows computer pictures over the real world. 4) «Arr!» is how pirates talk in films and cartoons. 5) Ar is also the name of the letter R said aloud.
its sense in the lessons: On its own, «ar» is not a standard English word. In dialect lessons, «ar» for "yes" or "our" is heard in Yorkshire, Lancashire and the Black Country. In science, Ar is on the periodic table. In computing, AR games (like catching creatures through a phone camera) show computer images on top of real life. On Talk Like a Pirate Day, children shout «Arr!». Phrases: «ar kid», «AR game», «Ar (argon)».
examples from the lessons: (UK, dialect) "Are you coming?" "Ar, I'm coming." | (UK, dialect) Ar kid's gone to the shops. | (science) The symbol Ar stands for argon. | (computing) We used an AR app to see a dinosaur in our classroom. | "Arr, me hearties!" said the pirate. | (US) Little Rock is the capital of AR, Arkansas.
note for the reader of a maths problem: For argon, capital A and small r: «Ar». For Arkansas and augmented reality, capitals: «AR». Dialect «ar» is informal speech; in formal writing use «yes» and «our». The letter R is spelled out as «ar» only in some dictionaries.

part of speech: noun (an axe, axes; US also ax); verb (axe, axes, axed, axing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) An axe is a tool with a heavy metal blade on a long handle, used for chopping wood or cutting down trees. 2) (informal) To axe something is to cut it or end it suddenly: the TV show was axed. 3) (informal) To axe workers means to sack them or make them lose their jobs. 4) «Have an axe to grind» means to have a private reason, often a grudge, for doing or saying something.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, stone axes, Viking battle-axes and Iron Age tools appear. In everyday safety: axes are sharp and heavy, only for adults. In news and everyday talk, «axed» means cancelled or cut: «the bus route was axed», «jobs axed». In stories, a woodcutter carries an axe. Phrases: «chop with an axe», «battle-axe», «get the axe», «face the axe», «axe to grind».
examples from the lessons: The woodcutter chopped the log with his axe. | Vikings fought with axes and shields. | Stone Age people made axes from flint. | The swimming club was axed because there was no money. | Our favourite show got the axe. | Two hundred jobs were axed at the factory. | He criticised the plan because he had an axe to grind.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Use «an»: «an axe». UK spelling «axe», US «ax» (both «axes» in the plural). Trap: «axes» is also the plural of «axis» (x-axis and y-axis), but said differently: "AX-eez". «Battle-axe» is also a rude old word for a fierce woman.

part of speech: verb (bathe, bathes, bathed, bathing); noun (a bathe — UK, old-fashioned)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To bathe means to wash yourself or someone else in a bath (more US; in the UK people more often say «have a bath»). 2) To bathe a wound or your eyes is to wash them gently with water. 3) (UK) To bathe means to swim in the sea, a river or a lake for fun. 4) To be bathed in light means to be filled or covered with it: the room was bathed in sunlight.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, parents bathe babies and pet owners bathe dogs; in first aid, you bathe a cut or a sting with clean water. In stories and poems, a scene «bathed in moonlight» paints a soft, bright picture. In history, Romans bathed in public baths. In geography, beaches have «bathing water» quality signs. Phrases: «bathe the baby», «bathe a wound», «bathed in light», «bathing suit», «sunbathe».
examples from the lessons: Mum bathed the baby before bed. | Bathe the cut with clean water. | We bathed in the cold sea on Boxing Day. | The garden was bathed in golden sunlight. | The Romans bathed together in big public baths. | Lizards sunbathe on warm rocks.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: «bathe» (verb, rhymes with "save", long a, soft th) vs «bath» (noun or UK verb, short a or "bahth"). UK: «I'll bath the baby» is also common. Forms: bathed, bathing (drop the e). «Bathing» can be from bathe ("BAYTH-ing") or from bath ("BAHTH-ing").

part of speech: noun (beta, betas); adjective (beta — of a version)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Beta (β) is the second letter of the Greek alphabet, after alpha. 2) A beta version of a game, app or program is an early version that is being tested by users before the final one. 3) (science) Beta is used in names, like beta rays (a kind of radiation) and beta-carotene (the orange colour in carrots). 4) (slang) «Beta» is used online as an insult for a weak or shy person; it is unkind.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and science lessons, Greek letters label angles and quantities: α (alpha), β (beta), γ (gamma). «Alphabet» comes from alpha + beta. In computing and gaming, «beta testing» means trying out a new program to find bugs. In science later, beta radiation is one of three kinds (alpha, beta, gamma). The slang meaning is a put-down from online talk; it is not kind. Phrases: «beta version», «beta test», «alpha and beta», «beta-carotene».
examples from the lessons: β is the Greek letter beta. | «Alphabet» comes from the Greek letters alpha and beta. | My brother joined the beta test of a new game. | The app is still in beta, so it has some bugs. | Carrots get their orange colour from beta-carotene. | In the diagram, angle beta is 40 degrees. | (slang) Calling someone «beta» online is a mean put-down.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say it "BEE-ta" (UK) or "BAY-ta" (US). Plural «betas». In maths, β is a label for a number or angle, not a fixed value. «Alpha» (first, top) and «beta» (second, test) often appear together.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A carnivorous animal eats meat, mostly other animals: lions, sharks and eagles are carnivorous. 2) A carnivorous plant catches and digests insects or small animals, like the Venus flytrap or sundew.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on food chains and classification, animals are herbivores (plants only), carnivores (meat only) or omnivores (both); carnivores are often predators with sharp teeth or talons. Carnivorous plants grow in poor, boggy soil and get extra nutrients from insects. Phrases: «carnivorous animal», «carnivorous plant», «carnivore, herbivore, omnivore».
examples from the lessons: Sharks are carnivorous. | A Venus flytrap is a carnivorous plant. | Carnivorous dinosaurs like T. rex had sharp teeth. | Tigers are carnivores, but bears are omnivores. | The sundew is carnivorous: it traps flies on sticky hairs. | Cats are carnivorous, so they need meat in their food.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: «carnivore». Say it "car-NIV-or-us". Related: herbivorous, omnivorous, insectivorous. Myth: carnivorous plants do not eat people — they catch small insects. Some scavengers are carnivorous without hunting.

part of speech: noun (a cob, cobs; cob — building material, uncountable)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A cob, or corncob, is the long middle part of an ear of corn (maize) that the kernels grow on: corn on the cob. 2) A cob is a male swan (a female is a pen, a baby is a cygnet). 3) (UK) A cob is a small round loaf of bread, or in some areas a bread roll. 4) A cob is a strong, short-legged horse. 5) Cob is a mix of clay, straw and water used to build walls of old houses.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, «cob» is the word for a male swan. In food and farming lessons, corn on the cob is sweetcorn cooked whole. In parts of England (the Midlands, the North) «a cob» is a bread roll — the word is part of a famous regional argument (bap, barm, batch, cob, roll, bun). In history and design, cob cottages in Devon have thick earth walls. Phrases: «corn on the cob», «cob loaf», «cob and pen».
examples from the lessons: We ate buttery corn on the cob at the barbecue. | The cob swan hissed to protect the cygnets. | (UK, Midlands) Can I have a cheese cob, please? | The farmer rode a sturdy cob. | Old Devon cottages are made of cob. | The baker sold a big round cob loaf.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «cobs». The meaning depends on where you are and what you are talking about: swans, corn, bread, horses or walls. Swans: cob = male, pen = female, cygnet = young.

part of speech: noun (a comeback, comebacks); verb phrase (come back, comes back, came back, coming back)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A comeback is when someone or something becomes successful or popular again after a bad time: the team made a great comeback. 2) A comeback is a quick, clever reply to an insult or a joke. 3) (written as two words, verb) To come back means to return.
its sense in the lessons: In sport, «a comeback» is when a team losing badly fights back to win or draw; in music and fashion, an old style or star can make a comeback. In playground talk, «a good comeback» is a smart answer; pupils learn that a kind or calm reply is better than a mean one. Phrases: «make a comeback», «stage a comeback», «comeback kid», «a quick comeback».
examples from the lessons: Our team was 3–0 down but made an amazing comeback. | Flared jeans are making a comeback. | The singer's comeback concert sold out. | He had no comeback when she proved him wrong. | Her funny comeback made everyone laugh. | Come back home before dark!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun is one word: «a comeback»; verb is two words: «come back». In maths/sport problems, a comeback means one side's score overtakes the other's: from 0–3 to 4–3 they scored 4 goals in a row.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Cyrillic is the alphabet used to write Ukrainian, Russian, Bulgarian, Serbian, Belarusian, Macedonian, Kazakh, Mongolian and other languages. 2) Cyrillic letters include some that look like English ones (А, О, Т) and others that do not (Ж, Ш, Щ, Ї).
its sense in the lessons: In language lessons, pupils compare alphabets: Latin (English, French), Cyrillic, Greek, Arabic, Chinese characters. Cyrillic was created long ago from Greek letters and named after Saint Cyril, a missionary who with his brother Methodius brought writing to Slavic peoples. Traps for English readers: Cyrillic Р is an "r" sound, Н is "n", С is "s", В is "v". Ukrainian has letters Russian does not, like Ї, Є and Ґ. Phrases: «Cyrillic alphabet», «Cyrillic letters», «written in Cyrillic».
examples from the lessons: Ukrainian is written in the Cyrillic alphabet. | The sign was in Cyrillic, so I could not read it. | The Cyrillic letter Ж sounds like the "s" in "treasure". | Cyrillic was named after Saint Cyril. | In Cyrillic, the letter Р is said like an "r". | We learned to write our names in Cyrillic.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital C. Say it "si-RIL-ik". Trap: some Cyrillic letters look like Latin ones but sound different (Р = r, В = v, Н = n, С = s, У = u). Cyrillic is an alphabet, not a language.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A dagger is a short knife with a pointed blade, made as a weapon for stabbing. 2) (printing) A dagger (†) is a small mark used in books to point to a note, or next to a name to show the person has died.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, daggers appear with Romans, Vikings, knights and pirates. In stories, «look daggers at someone» means to give them a very angry look; «cloak and dagger» means secret and spy-like. Knives and daggers are dangerous; in the UK, Ireland and Australia it is against the law to carry one in public, and school safety lessons explain why. Phrases: «look daggers», «cloak-and-dagger», «at daggers drawn» (ready to fight).
examples from the lessons: The Roman soldier carried a short dagger. | The pirate hid a dagger in his boot. | My sister looked daggers at me when I told Mum. | It was a cloak-and-dagger plan to hide the birthday cake. | The museum has a Viking dagger with a carved handle. | Carrying a knife or dagger in public is against the law.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «daggers». A dagger is shorter than a sword. «Look daggers» is figurative: nobody throws a knife. The † mark is also called an obelus.

part of speech: noun (an eyeball, eyeballs); verb (eyeball, eyeballs, eyeballed, eyeballing — informal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) An eyeball is the round ball of the eye, most of which sits inside your head. 2) (informal) To eyeball someone or something is to look at them hard, often in a challenging or rude way. 3) (informal) To eyeball an amount is to guess it just by looking, without measuring.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on the body, the eyeball has the pupil, iris, lens and retina, and is moved by six muscles. In everyday talk: «eyeball to eyeball» means face to face in an argument; «up to my eyeballs in homework» means very busy. In maths, «eyeballing» is estimating: good for a quick check, but measure for an exact answer. Phrases: «eyeball to eyeball», «up to your eyeballs», «eyeball it».
examples from the lessons: The eyeball is about the size of a large grape. | We looked at a model of the eyeball in science. | The two cats eyeballed each other across the fence. | I'm up to my eyeballs in homework this week. | Don't just eyeball it, measure the line with a ruler. | At Halloween we ate jelly eyeballs.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word. «Eyeball» as a verb is informal. Maths: eyeballing gives an estimate, not an exact measurement.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A fern is a green plant with no flowers and long feathery leaves called fronds. 2) Ferns make new plants from tiny spores, not seeds; the spores grow in brown dots under the fronds.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on plant groups, ferns are an old group of plants that lived before the dinosaurs; giant tree ferns made coal. They like damp, shady places like woods and rainforests. Young fronds unroll from a curl called a fiddlehead. In New Zealand, the silver fern is a national symbol on sports shirts. Phrases: «tree fern», «fern fronds», «silver fern», «fern spores».
examples from the lessons: Ferns grow in the shady part of the wood. | A fern has no flowers and no seeds. | The brown dots under the leaf are spores. | Dinosaurs walked among giant ferns. | The All Blacks have a silver fern on their shirts. | A baby fern frond is curled up like a snail shell.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «ferns». Ferns are not mosses; mosses are smaller and have no real roots. Myth: ferns do not flower at midsummer — that is an old legend.

part of speech: verb (invade, invades, invaded, invading); noun (invasion, invader)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To invade a country or place is to enter it with an army in order to take control of it. 2) To invade can mean to come into a place in large numbers, often unwelcome: ants invaded the kitchen. 3) To invade someone's privacy or personal space is to get too close or poke into things that are theirs.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, invasions shape whole topics: the Romans, Anglo-Saxons, Vikings and Normans invaded Britain; in today's news, Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine is reported as such by most countries and condemned in UN votes. In science, germs and invasive species (like grey squirrels in Britain or cane toads in Australia) «invade» habitats. In everyday life, children learn to respect personal space and privacy. Phrases: «invade a country», «invade someone's privacy», «invasive species», «invaders».
examples from the lessons: The Romans invaded Britain and built roads and towns. | The Vikings invaded from across the North Sea. | Ants invaded our picnic. | Please don't invade my personal space. | Reading my diary is invading my privacy! | Germs invade the body and make us ill. | Cane toads have invaded large parts of Australia.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun forms: «invasion» (the act), «invader» (the person or army). Adjective: «invasive». Drop the e: «invading». In history and news, ask who invaded whom and what each side says.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A lagoon is a stretch of salty or brackish water separated from the sea by a sandbank, a reef or a strip of land. 2) A lagoon can also be the calm water inside a ring-shaped coral island (an atoll). 3) A lagoon can be a pond or pool made by people, for example to hold waste water.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons on coasts, lagoons form behind spits and barrier beaches; Venice is built in a lagoon. In science, lagoons are calm habitats for fish, birds and seagrass. In stories and adventure books, a "blue lagoon" is a calm, beautiful place on a tropical island. Phrases: «blue lagoon», «coral lagoon», «Venice lagoon».
examples from the lessons: The children swam in the calm lagoon. | A coral reef protects the lagoon from big waves. | Venice is built on islands in a lagoon. | Flamingos fed in the shallow lagoon. | The lagoon is separated from the sea by a sandbank. | We paddled a canoe across the lagoon.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «lagoons». Say it "la-GOON". A lagoon is not a lake: a lake is fresh water inland; a lagoon is usually salty and near the sea.

part of speech: noun (a limerick, limericks); proper noun (Limerick — a place)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A limerick is a short, funny poem of five lines, with lines 1, 2 and 5 rhyming together and lines 3 and 4 rhyming together (AABBA). 2) (place) Limerick is a city and county in Ireland.
its sense in the lessons: In English and poetry lessons, pupils read Edward Lear's limericks and write their own, often starting «There once was a…». They practise rhyme scheme (AABBA) and rhythm: longer lines 1, 2, 5 and shorter lines 3, 4. In geography, Limerick is a city on the River Shannon in Ireland. Phrases: «write a limerick», «a silly limerick», «rhyme scheme AABBA».
examples from the lessons: There once was a cat from Peru, / who dreamed he was eating a shoe. / He woke with a fright, / in the middle of the night, / and found that his dream had come true. | Edward Lear wrote many limericks. | A limerick has five lines. | The rhyme scheme of a limerick is AABBA. | Our class wrote limericks about our pets. | Limerick is a city in Ireland on the River Shannon.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Small l for the poem, capital L for the city. Limericks are meant to be silly; some grown-up ones are rude, so school ones are chosen carefully. Count: 5 lines, 3 long and 2 short.

part of speech: noun (a mandate, mandates); verb (mandate, mandates, mandated, mandating — formal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal, politics) A mandate is the authority given to a government or leader by voters to carry out their plans: the party won a strong mandate. 2) (formal) A mandate is an official order or rule saying something must be done: a mask mandate. 3) (formal) To mandate something is to order it officially or make it a rule. 4) (history) A mandate was a territory that the League of Nations put under another country's rule.
its sense in the lessons: In politics and news lessons, after an election, the winners say they have «a mandate» from the people; others may disagree about how strong it is. In the exam voice, «mandate» and «mandatory» (required) appear in rules and instructions. In history, the British Mandate for Palestine is a key topic in understanding Israel and Gaza. In money talk, a «direct debit mandate» lets a bank take payments. Phrases: «win a mandate», «a clear mandate», «government mandate», «mandatory».
examples from the lessons: The new government says it has a mandate to build more homes. | The school mandated that everyone wear a helmet on bikes. | Voters gave the president a strong mandate. | Seat belts in cars are mandated by law. | The British ruled Palestine under a mandate after the First World War. | (money) Dad signed a mandate so the gym could take money from his bank each month.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal word; in everyday talk say «order», «rule» or «permission». Adjective: «mandatory» (must be done, compulsory). Say it "MAN-date". In politics, whether a win gives a mandate is often argued about.

part of speech: noun (a nanny, nannies); adjective use (nanny state — informal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A nanny is a person whose job is to look after a family's children in the family's home. 2) (UK, informal) Nanny is a child's word for grandmother, like nan or nana. 3) A nanny goat is a female goat (a male is a billy goat). 4) (informal, critical) A «nanny state» is a government that people think makes too many rules about how they should live.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, nannies care for children while parents work; in stories (Mary Poppins, Nanny McPhee) nannies are magical or strict. Children call their grandmother Nanny or Nan in many British, Irish and Australian families. In farming and science, nanny and billy goats appear with kids (baby goats). In politics, «nanny state» is a complaint, not a neutral description. Phrases: «nanny goat», «a live-in nanny», «Nanny and Grandad», «nanny state».
examples from the lessons: Our nanny picks us up from school. | Mary Poppins is the most famous nanny in stories. | (UK, informal) I'm going to Nanny's house for tea. | The nanny goat fed her two kids. | The nanny read us a story before bed. | (informal) Some people complain about a «nanny state» when new rules are made.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «nannies» (y → ies). Capital N when used as a name for grandma: «Nanny Pat». Related: «nan», «nana», «gran». A nanny is not the same as a babysitter, who looks after children for a few hours now and then.

part of speech: adjective (persuasive, more persuasive, most persuasive; adverb persuasively)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Persuasive means good at making people agree with you or do what you want: a persuasive speaker. 2) Persuasive writing is writing that tries to make the reader believe something or take an action, like an advert, a letter of complaint or a speech.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons, «persuasive writing» is a main text type: pupils use a clear opinion, reasons with evidence, facts and numbers, rhetorical questions, emotive words, «you», repetition and a strong ending («So join us today!»). In media and online-safety lessons, they learn to spot persuasive tricks in adverts and posts, so they can think for themselves. Phrases: «persuasive letter», «persuasive speech», «persuasive argument», «persuasive techniques».
examples from the lessons: Write a persuasive letter to the head teacher asking for a longer break. | Her speech was so persuasive that everyone voted for her. | Adverts use persuasive language to make us buy things. | A rhetorical question is a persuasive technique. | He gave a persuasive reason for having a class pet. | The poster was bright and persuasive: "Save the bees!"
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: «persuade» (persuaded, persuading); noun: «persuasion». Spelled with «-suas-». Persuasive is not the same as true: a persuasive argument can still be wrong, so check the evidence.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A proboscis is a long, bendy nose or snout, like an elephant's trunk or a tapir's snout. 2) A proboscis is also the long, tube-like mouthpart of some insects, like butterflies and mosquitoes, used for sucking up food.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on adaptation, a butterfly uncoils its proboscis like a straw to drink nectar, then rolls it up; a mosquito uses its proboscis to pierce skin and drink blood. The proboscis monkey of Borneo has a huge, dangly nose. In stories, «proboscis» is a funny, grand word for a big nose. Phrases: «a butterfly's proboscis», «proboscis monkey».
examples from the lessons: The butterfly uncurled its proboscis to drink nectar. | A mosquito bites with its proboscis. | An elephant's trunk is a kind of proboscis. | The proboscis monkey has an enormous nose. | A moth's proboscis can be longer than its body. | The bee pushed its proboscis deep into the flower.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say it "pro-BOSS-iss" (the c is silent). Plural: «proboscises» (also «proboscides» in science). A tricky spelling: -scis.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A rebellion is when a group of people fight against or refuse to obey the people in power, such as a ruler or government. 2) Rebellion is also refusing to obey rules or do what is expected, like a teenager's rebellion against parents.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, famous rebellions include Boudicca's rebellion against the Romans, the Peasants' Revolt, the Jacobite rebellions in Scotland, the Easter Rising in Ireland and the Eureka Rebellion in Australia; pupils ask why people rebelled and what happened afterwards. In stories, a rebellion against an unfair ruler is a common plot. In everyday life, «a bit of rebellion» is breaking small rules. Phrases: «lead a rebellion», «crush a rebellion», «rise in rebellion», «act of rebellion».
examples from the lessons: Boudicca led a rebellion against the Romans. | The king's army crushed the rebellion. | The peasants' rebellion began because of unfair taxes. | Dyeing his hair green was his little act of rebellion. | In the story, the animals started a rebellion against the farmer. | Many rebellions in history ended in failure.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: «rebel» (re-BEL), «rebelled», «rebelling»; person: «a rebel» (REB-el); adjective: «rebellious». Spelled with double l. A rebellion is smaller or less successful than a revolution, which changes who rules.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) A rep is short for a representative: a person chosen to speak or act for a group, like a class rep or a school council rep. 2) (informal) A rep is a salesperson who visits customers for a company: a sales rep. 3) (informal) In exercise, a rep (repetition) is doing a movement once: ten reps of sit-ups. 4) (slang) Rep is short for reputation: he has a rep for being funny. 5) (informal) Rep is short for repertory theatre.
its sense in the lessons: In school, pupils vote for «class reps» or «school council reps» to share their classmates' ideas with teachers; it is a small taste of elections. In PE, «reps» and «sets» organise exercises: 3 sets of 10 reps. In maths, «10 reps in each of 3 sets» means 30 in all. Phrases: «class rep», «sales rep», «reps and sets», «get a rep for».
examples from the lessons: I was voted class rep this year. | The school council reps met the head teacher. | Do three sets of ten reps. | A sales rep came to show the new books. | (slang) He's got a rep for being late. | Our rep asked for more benches in the playground.
note for the reader of a maths problem: All informal short forms; in formal writing use «representative», «repetition» or «reputation». Plural «reps». Maths: total = sets × reps per set.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A rhetorical question is a question asked to make a point or for effect, not to get an answer: «Who wants to live in a world without trees?» 2) (formal) Rhetorical means to do with the art of speaking or writing in a way that persuades or impresses people.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons on persuasive writing and speeches, rhetorical questions make the reader think and agree: «Isn't it time we did something?» Pupils find and use them alongside the rule of three and repetition. In everyday life, «Do you know what time it is?» from a cross parent can be rhetorical — no answer needed. In the formal voice, «rhetoric» can mean fancy speech that may hide a lack of real action. Phrases: «rhetorical question», «rhetorical device», «empty rhetoric».
examples from the lessons: Who would want to drop litter in such a beautiful park? is a rhetorical question. | Add a rhetorical question to your persuasive letter. | "Do you think I'm made of money?" Dad asked — it was rhetorical. | The speaker used rhetorical tricks to excite the crowd. | Don't answer that, it was a rhetorical question! | Is the sky blue? That's rhetorical — of course it is.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say it "ri-TOR-i-kal". A rhetorical question still ends with a question mark. Noun: «rhetoric» (RET-or-ik). Answering a rhetorical question from an angry adult can sound cheeky.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A runway is a long, flat strip of hard ground at an airport where planes take off and land. 2) A runway is also the long, narrow stage that models walk along at a fashion show (also called a catwalk).
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and travel, planes taxi to the runway, speed up and take off; pupils may watch from an airport's viewing area. In science, a plane needs a long runway to build up enough speed to make lift. In maths, runways are long lengths measured in metres or kilometres. In fashion, models walk the runway. Phrases: «take off from the runway», «runway lights», «on the runway», «a new runway».
examples from the lessons: The plane raced down the runway and took off. | The runway lights guide pilots at night. | The airport is building a new runway. | We waited on the runway for twenty minutes. | The model walked down the runway in a gold dress. | This runway is three kilometres long.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word. In the UK the fashion stage is more often called a «catwalk». Not the same as «taxiway», the path planes use to get to and from the runway.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Sediment is sand, mud, stones and other bits that are carried by water, wind or ice and then settle in a layer, for example at the bottom of a river, lake or sea. 2) Sediment is also the bits that sink to the bottom of a liquid, like in a glass of juice or a bottle of medicine.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography lessons, rivers carry sediment downstream and drop it (deposition) where they slow down, forming deltas, beaches and floodplains; over millions of years, layers of sediment press together into sedimentary rock like sandstone, chalk and limestone, where fossils are found. In kitchen science, you see sediment when you let muddy water stand. Phrases: «layers of sediment», «sedimentary rock», «carry sediment», «settle as sediment».
examples from the lessons: The river carried sediment down to the sea. | Layers of sediment slowly turned into rock. | Fossils are found in sedimentary rock. | Leave the muddy water to stand and the sediment will sink. | There was a brown sediment at the bottom of the bottle. | The delta is made of sediment dropped by the river.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly uncountable: «a lot of sediment». Adjective: «sedimentary». Sediment sinks because it is heavier (denser) than water; tiny bits settle more slowly.

part of speech: noun (a shoal, shoals); adjective/verb (shoal, shoals, shoaled, shoaling — rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A shoal is a large group of fish swimming together. 2) A shoal is also a shallow place in a sea or river, often a sandbank, that can be dangerous for boats. 3) (informal, UK) A shoal of things is a large number of them: shoals of letters.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, fish swim in shoals for safety: it is harder for a predator to pick out one fish, and many eyes spot danger. Herring, sardines and mackerel form shoals. In geography and history, ships ran aground on shoals near coasts; lighthouses warn of them. Phrases: «a shoal of fish», «swim in shoals», «run aground on a shoal».
examples from the lessons: A shoal of silver fish flashed past the boat. | Fish swim in shoals to stay safe from sharks. | The dolphins herded the shoal of sardines into a ball. | The ship ran aground on a hidden shoal. | Shoals of mackerel came close to the shore. | The lighthouse warns sailors about the shoals.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A «school» of fish means almost the same; scientists sometimes say a shoal is a loose group and a school moves together. Collective nouns: a shoal of fish, a flock of birds, a herd of cows.

part of speech: noun (a sucker, suckers); verb phrase (sucker someone into — informal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A sucker is a part of an animal that can stick to things by suction, like the round pads on an octopus's arms. 2) A sucker is also a rubber cup that sticks to smooth surfaces when you press it. 3) (informal) A sucker is a person who is easily tricked: «Ha, sucker!» 4) (informal) To be a sucker for something is to like it so much you cannot resist it: I'm a sucker for chocolate. 5) A sucker is also a new shoot growing from the root of a plant, and (US) a lollipop.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, octopuses and squid use suckers to grip and taste; leeches use suckers to feed; some plants spread by suckers. In design and technology, suction cups (suckers) hold things to windows. In everyday and playground talk, calling someone a «sucker» is teasing or mocking. Phrases: «octopus suckers», «a sucker for», «suckered into», «sucker punch» (a sneaky hit).
examples from the lessons: An octopus has two rows of suckers on each arm. | The sucker holds the toy to the window. | (informal) I'm a sucker for funny cat videos. | (informal) He was suckered into paying for everyone's chips. | (informal) "Made you look, sucker!" | Cut off the suckers so the tomato plant grows strong. | (US) The dentist gave me a sugar-free sucker.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «suckers». Calling someone «sucker» is rude teasing. In science, «suction cup» is the more formal name for the rubber kind.

part of speech: noun (a ton, tons); slang (tons of, a ton of)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A ton is a large unit of weight. In the UK an old ton is 2,240 pounds (long ton); in the US a ton is 2,000 pounds (short ton). 2) A tonne, or metric ton, is 1,000 kilograms; in science and maths we usually use this. 3) (informal) A ton or tons of something means a lot of it: I've got tons of homework. 4) (UK, slang) A ton is a hundred: a hundred runs in cricket, a hundred miles an hour, or a hundred pounds.
its sense in the lessons: In maths lessons on measurement, pupils convert: 1 tonne = 1,000 kg, so a 2.5-tonne elephant weighs 2,500 kg; lorry weight limits on bridges are given in tonnes. In everyday talk, «tons of», «weighs a ton» and «like a ton of bricks» mean a lot or very heavy. In cricket, scoring «a ton» is making a century (100 runs). Phrases: «tons of», «weighs a ton», «come down on someone like a ton of bricks», «do a ton» (UK, drive at 100 mph).
examples from the lessons: An elephant can weigh about six tonnes. | 1 tonne is the same as 1,000 kilograms. | This bag weighs a ton! | I've got tons of homework tonight. | (UK, slang) The batsman scored a ton — one hundred runs. | The bridge sign says lorries must weigh less than 7.5 tonnes. | If you're cheeky, the teacher will come down on you like a ton of bricks.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Homophone trap: «ton» and «tonne» sound the same ("tun"), but tonne = 1,000 kg exactly; ton (US) ≈ 907 kg; ton (UK long) ≈ 1,016 kg. In school maths, use tonnes (t). «Tons of» (a lot) is informal and not an exact number. Maths: tonnes → kg, multiply by 1,000.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An udder is the bag-like part that hangs under the belly of a female cow, goat or sheep, where milk is made. 2) Milk comes out of the teats on the udder when a calf drinks or when the animal is milked.
its sense in the lessons: In science and farming lessons, a dairy cow's udder has four teats; farmers milk cows by hand or with milking machines, usually twice a day; the milk is then cooled, tested and taken to the dairy. Pupils learn that cows only make milk after they have had a calf. Phrases: «a full udder», «milk the udder», «cow's udder».
examples from the lessons: The farmer washed the cow's udder before milking. | A cow's udder has four teats. | The calf drank milk from its mother's udder. | Goats have udders with two teats. | The milking machine attaches to the udder. | The cow's udder was full and heavy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Use «an»: «an udder». Plural «udders». Myth: cows do not make milk all the time without having calves. Do not mix up with «utter» (complete, total: utter nonsense; or to speak), which sounds a bit similar.

part of speech: noun (waw, also vav or vau — a letter); fragment
meaning for a pupil: 1) Waw (also spelled vav or vau) is the sixth letter of the Hebrew alphabet; in Hebrew it can sound like "v" or stand for an "o" or "u" sound. 2) (Bible) In some Bibles, Psalm 119 is divided into 22 parts, each headed by a Hebrew letter in order, and the sixth part is headed «Vau» or «Waw». 3) Waw is also the name of the Arabic letter و, which sounds like "w" or a long "oo". It is not an English word.
its sense in the lessons: On its own, «waw» is not an English word. In church and Bible lessons, pupils may notice the Hebrew letter names (Aleph, Beth, Gimel… Waw) above the sections of Psalm 119, a long poem about God's law; Jews and Christians believe the Psalms are holy writing. In language lessons comparing alphabets, waw is a shared letter in Hebrew and Arabic, both written from right to left. Online, «waw» sometimes appears as a misspelling of «wow». Phrases: «the letter waw», «Psalm 119: Waw».
examples from the lessons: (Bible) Psalm 119 has a section headed Waw. | Waw is the sixth letter of the Hebrew alphabet. | In Arabic, the letter waw (و) can sound like "w". | Hebrew and Arabic are written from right to left, and both have a letter waw. | The Hebrew word for "and" starts with waw. | "Waw!" — she meant "wow", but she typed it too fast.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spellings vary: waw, vav, vau. In Hebrew and Arabic, a single waw at the start of a word often means "and". If you see «waw» in a chat message, it is probably a typo or playful spelling of «wow».

part of speech: verb (adore, adores, adored, adoring); adjective (adorable, adoring)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To adore someone is to love them very much: she adores her baby brother. 2) To adore something is to like it very much: I adore chocolate cake. 3) (church) To adore God is to worship and praise him; Christians speak of the shepherds and wise men coming to adore the baby Jesus.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and stories, «adore» is a strong, warm word for love and liking, stronger than «like» or «love». In church lessons and Christmas carols, «O come, let us adore him» means let us worship him. The adjective «adorable» means very cute and lovable (puppies, babies). Phrases: «absolutely adore», «adoring fans», «adore him» (carol), «adorable puppy».
examples from the lessons: I adore my grandma. | She adores horses and draws them all the time. | The puppy was adorable. | The singer waved to her adoring fans. | (church) "O come, let us adore him," we sang at Christmas. | My dad adores old rock music.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Third person: «she adores». Drop the e: «adored», «adoring». Adjective: «adorable» (very cute), «adoring» (full of love). Noun: «adoration». Very strong word — «I adore broccoli» sounds funny if you only like it a little.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Agriculture is farming: growing crops and keeping animals for food, wool and other products. 2) Agriculture is also the science and business of farming.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and history lessons, agriculture began when early people stopped wandering and started growing wheat and keeping animals (the first farmers), which allowed villages and towns to grow. Pupils learn about arable farming (crops), pastoral farming (animals), mixed farming, irrigation, machines, and how agriculture uses land and water. In science, fertilisers and pesticides help crops but can harm the environment. Phrases: «modern agriculture», «organic agriculture», «agricultural land», «agricultural show».
examples from the lessons: Agriculture began when people started to grow crops. | Most of the land in this county is used for agriculture. | Many people in Kenya work in agriculture. | We went to the agricultural show and saw prize cows. | Machines changed agriculture a lot. | Agriculture needs a lot of fresh water.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «agriculture», not «an agriculture». Adjective: «agricultural». Everyday word: «farming». Spelled agri + culture ("field" + "growing").

meaning for a pupil: 1) An algorithm is a list of clear, step-by-step instructions for solving a problem or doing a task. 2) In computing, an algorithm is the set of rules a computer program follows, for example to sort a list or to choose what videos to show you.
its sense in the lessons: In computing lessons, pupils write algorithms for everyday tasks (making a sandwich, brushing teeth), then turn them into code; they learn that steps must be exact and in the right order (sequence), with choices (selection) and repeats (repetition). In maths, column addition and long division are algorithms. In online-safety lessons, apps use algorithms to choose what you see, which can keep you watching for a long time. Phrases: «write an algorithm», «sorting algorithm», «search algorithm», «the algorithm» (on social media).
examples from the lessons: Write an algorithm for making a cup of tea. | An algorithm must be precise, or the robot gets confused. | Long division is an algorithm for dividing big numbers. | The video app's algorithm suggests new videos. | We debugged our algorithm because the steps were in the wrong order. | A sorting algorithm puts numbers in order from smallest to largest.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Use «an»: «an algorithm». Spelled with «-rithm» (no y): not «algorythm». Adjective: «algorithmic». Named after the Persian mathematician al-Khwarizmi. An algorithm is the plan; a program is the plan written in a coding language.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An alliance is an agreement between countries, groups or people to work together or to help and protect each other. 2) An alliance is also the group of countries or people who have made such an agreement.
its sense in the lessons: In history and politics lessons, alliances explain why wars spread: before the First World War, countries were in two big alliances. Today NATO is a military alliance in which members agree to defend each other if attacked. In stories and games, characters form alliances to defeat a common enemy. Phrases: «form an alliance», «make an alliance», «in alliance with», «military alliance», «NATO alliance».
examples from the lessons: The two kingdoms formed an alliance against the invaders. | NATO is an alliance of many countries in Europe and North America. | In the game, we made an alliance with the other team. | The alliance broke when one side cheated. | The countries signed an alliance to protect each other. | In the story, the mice made an alliance with the birds.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Use «an»: «an alliance». Verb: «ally» (to join with); a member is «an ally» (plural «allies»). Spelled with -ance. An alliance is a deal; members can still disagree or leave.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An ammonite is an extinct sea animal with a coiled shell, related to today's octopus, squid and nautilus. 2) An ammonite is also the fossil of this animal, often found in rocks as a stone spiral.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on fossils and rocks, ammonites are among the commonest fossils, found on beaches such as the Jurassic Coast in Dorset and Whitby in Yorkshire, where Mary Anning collected them. They lived in the seas in the time of the dinosaurs and died out at the same time. Their spiral shell is also used in maths lessons to look at spirals. Phrases: «ammonite fossil», «fossil hunting», «coiled ammonite».
examples from the lessons: We found an ammonite fossil on the beach. | An ammonite has a shell shaped like a spiral. | Ammonites died out at the same time as the dinosaurs. | Mary Anning collected ammonites at Lyme Regis. | The museum has an ammonite as big as a car tyre. | Ammonites were related to squid and octopuses.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Use «an»: «an ammonite». Plural «ammonites». In the Bible, «Ammonites» (capital A) were an ancient people living east of the River Jordan — a different meaning.

part of speech: noun (an arc, arcs); verb (arc, arcs, arced, arcing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) An arc is part of the curved line of a circle, or any curved line shaped like this. 2) To arc is to move in a curve: the ball arced through the air. 3) A story arc is the shape a story or a character's change follows from beginning to end. 4) (science) An electric arc is a bright spark that jumps across a gap.
its sense in the lessons: In maths lessons on circles, an arc is part of the circumference; pupils draw arcs with compasses to construct triangles, and learn related words (radius, diameter, chord, sector). In PE and science, a thrown ball travels in an arc. In English, «story arc» or «character arc» describes how events or a character change. Phrases: «draw an arc», «arc of a circle», «in an arc», «story arc», «rainbow arc».
examples from the lessons: Use a compass to draw an arc. | An arc is part of the edge of a circle. | The ball arced high over the goalkeeper's head. | A rainbow is an arc of colours. | The hero's character arc goes from scared to brave. | The welder's arc was so bright we could not look at it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Use «an»: «an arc». Homophone trap: «arc» (curve) and «ark» (Noah's boat) sound the same. Maths: the arc length of a full circle is the circumference; half the circle gives half the length. Do not confuse an arc with an arch (a curved structure like a doorway).

meaning for a pupil: 1) An aspen is a tall, thin tree of the poplar family, with round leaves on long, flat stalks that make them shake and flutter in the slightest wind. 2) Aspen wood is light and soft.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on trees and seasons, aspens are famous for leaves that tremble («quaking aspen») and turn bright gold in autumn. A grove of aspens can grow from one shared root system, so it can be one huge living thing. In stories and poems, «trembling like an aspen leaf» means shaking with fear. Aspen is also a ski town in Colorado, USA. Phrases: «quaking aspen», «trembling aspen», «aspen leaves», «shake like an aspen leaf».
examples from the lessons: The aspen leaves trembled in the breeze. | In autumn, the aspens turned golden yellow. | A whole forest of aspens can grow from one root. | She was shaking like an aspen leaf before her solo. | Beavers like to chew aspen trees. | Aspen bark is pale and smooth.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Use «an»: «an aspen». Plural «aspens». Capital A for the town. The leaves tremble because of their flat stalks, not because the tree is weak.

part of speech: adjective (-bellied, in compounds); verb, past form of «belly» (belly, bellies, bellied, bellying — rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Bellied is used in compound words to describe what kind of belly (tummy) something has: pot-bellied, big-bellied, red-bellied. 2) (rare) Bellied means swelled out in a round shape: the sails bellied in the wind. 3) «Belly-up» means dead (for a fish) or failed (for a business).
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons and bird or animal books, «bellied» is part of names: red-bellied woodpecker, yellow-bellied sapsucker, pot-bellied pig. In stories, a «pot-bellied» man has a round tummy; describing bodies should be kind. «Yellow-bellied» is an old slang insult meaning cowardly. Sailing stories use «the sails bellied out». Phrases: «pot-bellied», «red-bellied», «yellow-bellied», «big-bellied».
examples from the lessons: A red-bellied woodpecker tapped on the tree. | They keep a pot-bellied pig as a pet. | The ship's sails bellied out in the strong wind. | The pot-bellied stove warmed the old cabin. | (old slang) "You yellow-bellied coward!" shouted the cowboy. | The big-bellied jug held lots of water.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Almost always with a hyphen after another word: «pot-bellied», «red-bellied». The base noun is «belly» (plural «bellies»). «Yellow-bellied» is an insult. Say it "BEL-eed".

meaning for a pupil: 1) A bombardier is the member of a bomber aircraft's crew who aims and releases the bombs. 2) (UK, army) A bombardier is a rank in the British Royal Artillery, like a corporal. 3) A bombardier beetle is a beetle that sprays a hot, stinging chemical from its back end to defend itself.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons on the Second World War, bomber crews had a pilot, navigator, gunners and a bombardier. In science lessons, the bombardier beetle is an amazing example of defence: two chemicals mix inside it and burst out boiling hot with a pop. Phrases: «bombardier beetle», «the bombardier aimed».
examples from the lessons: The bombardier aimed at the bridge. | The bomber crew included a pilot, a navigator and a bombardier. | A bombardier beetle sprays hot liquid at ants. | My great-grandad was a bombardier in the Royal Artillery. | The bombardier beetle makes a little popping sound. | Bombardiers trained for many months.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say it "bom-ba-DEER". Plural «bombardiers». Related: «bomb», «bombard» (to attack with many bombs or with questions). In the US Air Force, the word was a crew job, not a rank.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A cockatoo is a large parrot with a crest of feathers on its head that it can raise and lower. 2) Most cockatoos live wild in Australia and nearby islands; many are white, pink, grey or black.
its sense in the lessons: In science and nature lessons cockatoos appear as Australian birds, as examples of parrots, and in talk about pets that live a very long time. In Australian stories a flock of screeching cockatoos is a normal backyard sound. Phrases: «sulphur-crested cockatoo», «pink cockatoo (galah)», «a flock of cockatoos».
examples from the lessons: A cockatoo raised its yellow crest and screeched. | A flock of white cockatoos landed on the school oval in Sydney. | Our neighbour's cockatoo can say «hello» and «good boy». | Cockatoos crack nuts with their strong curved beaks. | Some pet cockatoos live longer than their owners. | The black cockatoo has red feathers in its tail. | In class we compared a cockatoo with a parrot from South America.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one cockatoo, two cockatoos. Stress on the last part: cock-a-TOO. A cockatoo is a kind of parrot, but not every parrot is a cockatoo (cockatoos have crests). Pet cockatoos need a lot of attention and can be very loud.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A colonist is a person who goes to live in a new land that is ruled by their home country, or who settles a new colony. 2) In history it often means the first settlers from Europe in places such as America, Australia or New Zealand.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons colonists are the settlers who started colonies, for example the colonists in the thirteen American colonies, or the British colonists in Australia. Good lessons also say that the land already belonged to Native peoples, so colonists often took land and harmed the people living there. In science fiction there are colonists on Mars or the Moon. Phrases: «early colonists», «British colonists», «colonists and Native Americans».
examples from the lessons: The colonists built small wooden houses near the river. | Many colonists died during the first hard winter. | The colonists traded with the local people for food. | The American colonists did not want to pay taxes to Britain. | Aboriginal people had lived in Australia long before the colonists arrived. | In the story, colonists on Mars grow potatoes in domes. | Our class acted out a meeting between colonists and Native leaders.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one colonist, many colonists. Related words: colony, colonial, colonize (US) / colonise (UK). A colonist is not the same as a tourist (who visits) or an immigrant (who joins an existing country); a colonist settles land claimed by their own country. Do not confuse with «colon» (the punctuation mark or the body part).

part of speech: noun (a color, colors); verb (color, colors, colored, coloring); adjective (color photos, color TV)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Color is what we see when light of different kinds reaches our eyes, such as red, blue, green or yellow. 2) To color something is to fill it in with crayons, pens or paint. 3) A person's color can mean the color of their skin; this is a sensitive topic and should be spoken about with respect. 4) Color can mean interest or liveliness, as in «the story has lots of color». 5) To color something can mean to change how it seems, as in «Her anger colored her judgment». 6) «Colors» can mean the flag of a team, school or army.
its sense in the lessons: This is the American spelling; British, Canadian, Australian, New Zealand and Irish spelling is «colour». In art lessons pupils learn primary colors (red, yellow, blue) and mixing. In science, white light splits into the colors of the rainbow, and some animals use color to hide (camouflage) or warn. In maths, colors are used to sort, make bar charts and in probability with colored counters or marbles. Phrases: «favorite color», «color in», «in color», «show your true colors», «with flying colors» (very well).
examples from the lessons: What is your favorite color? | Color the triangle blue and the square red. | A rainbow has seven colors. | Mix yellow and blue to get the color green. | The leaves change color in the fall. | She passed the test with flying colors. | The bag has 3 red marbles and 2 blue ones; what is the chance of picking each color? | Treat everyone fairly, whatever the color of their skin.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Color» is US spelling; «colour» is UK and Commonwealth spelling; both are correct in their own countries. Past form: colored / coloured. Usually uncountable for the general idea («a lot of color») but countable for kinds («three colors»). Black and white are often called colors in everyday talk. In probability problems, color tells you which group a counter belongs to: count each color to find the chance.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A counterweight is a heavy weight used to balance another weight, so that something heavy is easier to lift or does not tip over. 2) Figuratively, a counterweight is anything that balances something else, such as one idea balancing another.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on forces and levers, a counterweight balances a load, as on a seesaw, a crane, a lift (elevator) or a drawbridge. Cranes have big concrete counterweights at the back so they do not fall over. In history, a trebuchet used a heavy counterweight to throw stones. Phrases: «act as a counterweight», «a counterweight to».
examples from the lessons: The crane has a huge counterweight to stop it tipping. | A lift uses a counterweight so the motor does less work. | The trebuchet's counterweight dropped and the arm flung the stone. | On a seesaw, a heavier child can be a counterweight to two smaller ones. | We used a bag of marbles as a counterweight in our lever experiment. | Grandad's calm voice was a counterweight to all the shouting.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Written as one word. In balance problems the counterweight's turning effect must equal the load's: weight times distance from the pivot is the same on both sides (for example 10 kg at 2 m balances 20 kg at 1 m).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Development is the process of growing or changing and becoming bigger, stronger or more advanced. 2) A development is a new event or piece of news that changes a situation. 3) Development is the building of new houses, roads or businesses on land; a development can also be a group of new buildings. 4) Development is the making of a new product or idea, such as a new game or medicine. 5) (photography) Development is the process that turns old-style film into photos.
its sense in the lessons: In science, pupils study the development of a baby, a frog (from frog spawn to tadpole to frog) or a plant. In history and geography, development means how a country or town grows and gets roads, schools and hospitals; «developing countries» are poorer countries still building these. In news reports «a new development» means something new has happened. Phrases: «child development», «housing development», «software development», «in development», «the latest development».
examples from the lessons: We watched the development of tadpoles into frogs. | Reading helps a child's development. | There has been a new development in the missing dog case. | A new housing development is being built near our school. | The development of the vaccine took many years. | The game is still in development. | Good food and sleep are important for healthy development.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable for the process («growth and development»), countable for events or building sites («two new developments»). Verb: develop; adjective: developed, developing. Spelling trap: no «e» after «develop» (not «developement»).

part of speech: adjective (educated, more educated); verb form (past of «educate»: educated)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Educated describes a person who has learned a lot, especially at school, college or university. 2) As a verb form, «educated» means taught: «She was educated at a school in Dublin». 3) An «educated guess» is a guess based on some knowledge, not a wild guess.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life «well educated» praises someone who knows a lot. In maths and science, pupils are often asked to make an «educated guess» (an estimate or prediction based on what they know) before an experiment or calculation. In history, many children long ago were never educated because they had to work. Phrases: «well educated», «highly educated», «educated guess», «educated at».
examples from the lessons: My grandma was educated at a small village school. | She is a well-educated woman who speaks four languages. | Make an educated guess: how many sweets are in the jar? | Before the experiment, write an educated guess about what will happen. | In the past, many girls were not educated at all. | He was educated at home by his parents.
