note for the reader of a maths problem: Past form of «educate»: educate, educates, educated, educating. Being educated is not the same as being clever or kind; people without school education can be wise. An educated guess in maths is like an estimate: check it afterwards with the real answer.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A gazelle is a small, slim, fast antelope with curved horns that lives in Africa and Asia. 2) People sometimes call a graceful, fast runner a gazelle.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography lessons gazelles are grassland animals of the African savanna, plant eaters (herbivores) that are hunted by cheetahs and lions, often used in food chains. They are famous for speed and for leaping high (pronking). Phrases: «as fast as a gazelle», «Thomson's gazelle», «a herd of gazelles».
examples from the lessons: A herd of gazelles grazed on the savanna. | The cheetah chased the gazelle across the plain. | Gazelles can run very fast and turn quickly. | In the food chain, grass is eaten by the gazelle, and the gazelle is eaten by the lion. | She ran like a gazelle on sports day. | The gazelle leapt high into the air to warn the herd.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one gazelle, two gazelles. Stress: ga-ZELLE. A gazelle is a kind of antelope, not a deer. In food chains it is a primary consumer (eats plants).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A handler is a person who trains and looks after an animal, especially a working dog or horse. 2) A handler is a person whose job is to move or deal with things, such as a baggage handler at an airport or a food handler. 3) A handler can be a person who guides or manages someone famous or important. 4) (computers) A handler is a piece of a program that deals with a certain event, such as a click.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and safety lessons, police dog handlers and sniffer dog handlers work at airports. In health lessons, food handlers must wash their hands. In coding lessons, an «event handler» is the code that runs when you click a button. Phrases: «dog handler», «baggage handler», «food handler», «event handler».
examples from the lessons: The dog handler gave the sniffer dog a treat. | Baggage handlers loaded our suitcases onto the plane. | All food handlers must wear hairnets and wash their hands. | The snake handler showed us a python at the zoo. | The pop star's handlers kept the fans away. | In Scratch, the green flag block is a kind of event handler.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Comes from the verb «handle» (to hold, touch or deal with). Do not confuse with «handle» (the part of a door or cup you hold).

part of speech: noun (a harpoon, harpoons); verb (harpoon, harpoons, harpooned, harpooning)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A harpoon is a long spear with a sharp, hooked point, often tied to a rope, used for catching whales, big fish or seals. 2) To harpoon something is to hit or catch it with a harpoon.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons harpoons appear in stories of whaling ships and in the lives of Inuit hunters who used harpoons to catch seals. In nature lessons pupils learn that commercial whale hunting is now banned in most countries. Phrases: «harpoon gun», «throw a harpoon».
examples from the lessons: The hunter threw his harpoon at the seal. | Old whaling ships carried harpoons and long ropes. | The Inuit carved harpoon points from bone. | The sailor harpooned a huge fish. | Today most countries protect whales from harpoons. | In the museum we saw a rusty harpoon gun.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Stress: har-POON. A harpoon has a barb (hook) so it stays in the animal, unlike a simple spear.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An iguana is a large lizard with a row of spines down its back, found in hot parts of Central and South America and the Caribbean. 2) The marine iguana of the Galapagos Islands is the only lizard that swims and feeds in the sea.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons iguanas are examples of reptiles: cold-blooded, scaly, laying eggs, and needing the sun to warm up. Green iguanas are mostly plant eaters. Charles Darwin saw marine iguanas in the Galapagos. Some people keep iguanas as pets. Phrases: «green iguana», «marine iguana».
examples from the lessons: An iguana lay on the warm rock in the sun. | Iguanas are reptiles, so they are cold-blooded. | The green iguana eats leaves, flowers and fruit. | Marine iguanas dive into the sea to eat seaweed. | My cousin keeps an iguana in a big glass tank. | The iguana's long tail can whip at an enemy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; use «an» (an iguana). Stress: ig-WAH-nuh. Iguanas are lizards, not dinosaurs, although they look a little like small dinosaurs.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Logic is careful, clear thinking where each step follows from the one before, so you reach a sensible answer. 2) Logic is also the study of correct reasoning, a part of maths and philosophy. 3) The logic of something is the reason or sense behind it: «I don't see the logic of that plan». 4) (computers) Logic is the set of rules and true/false steps a computer or program follows.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, logic puzzles ask pupils to use clues to work out who has which pet or what number is hidden; good answers explain each step. In coding, «if … then … else» and «and / or / not» are logic. In everyday life and stories, someone with logic is calm and reasons well; something «against all logic» is surprising or silly. Phrases: «logic puzzle», «use your logic», «the logic behind», «there's no logic in it», «flawed logic».
examples from the lessons: Use logic to solve the puzzle: the cat is not in the red house. | There is no logic in walking home in the rain without your coat. | In coding, logic decides what the robot does next. | Sherlock Holmes solved crimes with logic. | Her logic was good, but one fact was wrong. | We learned about «and», «or» and «not» in logic. | I can't follow the logic of this rule.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «good logic», not «a logic» in everyday speech. Adjective: logical; opposite: illogical. A logical argument can still reach a wrong answer if one starting fact is false. In maths problems, logic means showing each step that leads to the answer.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A manta, or manta ray, is a very large, flat sea fish with wide fins like wings, which glides through warm oceans and eats tiny plankton. 2) A manta is also a kind of blanket or cloak in Spanish-speaking countries (rare in English).
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons manta rays appear in ocean habitats and as filter feeders; they are related to sharks and have skeletons made of cartilage, not bone. They are harmless to people, unlike stingrays, and can be seen by divers on reefs in Australia and other warm seas. Phrases: «manta ray», «giant manta».
examples from the lessons: A manta ray glided over the coral reef. | Manta rays eat plankton, not people. | The giant manta can be wider than a car. | Divers swam beside the gentle mantas. | A manta's skeleton is made of cartilage like a shark's. | We watched mantas leap out of the water on a nature film.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Usually said in full: «manta ray». A manta has no stinging spine, so do not mix it up with a stingray.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Muscular means having big, strong muscles. 2) Muscular means to do with the muscles of the body: «muscular pain», «the muscular system».
its sense in the lessons: In science and PE lessons, the «muscular system» is the set of muscles that move the body together with the skeleton; exercise makes muscles stronger. In stories «muscular» describes a strong character or a strong animal. Phrases: «muscular system», «muscular arms», «muscular build».
examples from the lessons: The weightlifter had muscular arms. | The muscular system and the skeleton work together to move us. | A horse has strong muscular legs. | Swimming makes your back more muscular. | The heart is a muscular organ that pumps blood. | He felt muscular pain after the long run.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective from «muscle». Spelling: muscle has a silent «c», and muscular keeps the «c» but you hear it (MUS-kyoo-lar). Being muscular is not the same as being healthy; fitness also needs the heart and lungs.

part of speech: adjective / preposition-like word (née; also written «nee»; borrowed from French)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Née (often written nee) is used before a woman's family name from birth, to show what her surname was before she married: «Mrs Jane Smith, née Brown». 2) It comes from French, where «née» means «born».
its sense in the lessons: It is a formal, written word found in family trees, history books, old newspapers and death notices; children meet it in family history projects. It tells the reader the woman's maiden name (surname before marriage). A related form «né» is sometimes used for a man's earlier name.
examples from the lessons: Mary Wilson, née Taylor, was my great-grandmother. | The notice read «Ann Kelly (nee O'Brien)». | In our family tree, Nan is listed as Mrs Jones, née Evans. | Née shows the surname someone had when she was born. | The queen's mother was born with another surname, so books write «née» before it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal and written; rare in speech. Pronounced «nay». Not an English word in origin: it is French for «born». Do not confuse with «nay» (an old word for «no») or «neigh» (a horse's sound), which sound the same.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An orb is a ball or round object, especially one that glows. 2) An orb is a golden ball with a cross on top, held by a king or queen at a coronation. 3) (poetic) An orb can mean the sun, the moon, a planet or an eye. 4) (games) In video games, an orb is a glowing ball you collect for points or power.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, the Sovereign's Orb is part of the British crown jewels, held by the monarch at the coronation as a sign of power under God. In stories and poems «orb» sounds grand or magical; in games, orbs give power-ups. Phrases: «a glowing orb», «orb and sceptre».
examples from the lessons: The king held the orb and the sceptre. | A glowing orb floated above the wizard's hand. | The golden orb of the sun sank behind the hills. | Collect ten orbs to unlock the next level. | The crown jewels include a jewelled orb. | In the poem, the moon is called «the silver orb».
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; use «an» (an orb). Literary or special word; in everyday speech people say «ball». Do not confuse with «orbit» (the path round a planet), though both come from the idea of a circle.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A potion is a drink made of mixed liquids that is supposed to have a special effect, such as magic, medicine or poison. 2) In fairy tales and fantasy games, a potion is a magic drink that heals, makes someone sleep, fall in love or change shape.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, witches and wizards brew potions in cauldrons; in games, health potions restore lives. In history, «potions» were old medicines, often useless or dangerous. Safety lessons warn children never to drink or mix unknown liquids, even in a game. Phrases: «love potion», «magic potion», «sleeping potion», «health potion», «brew a potion».
examples from the lessons: The witch stirred a bubbling potion in her cauldron. | Drink the health potion to get your lives back. | In the fairy tale, a sleeping potion put the princess to sleep. | We made a pretend potion with water, glitter and food colouring. | Never drink a «potion» made from things in the cupboard. | Old doctors sold potions that did not really work.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Mostly used in stories, games and history; real medicines are called «medicine», not «potion». Safety: cleaning liquids are poisonous and must never be mixed or tasted.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Resin is a thick, sticky liquid that comes out of some trees, especially pine trees, and becomes hard over time. 2) Resin is also a man-made material, a kind of plastic, that is poured in liquid form and sets hard, used for glue, models and art.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, tree resin protects a tree when its bark is hurt; fossilized resin is amber, which can trap insects for millions of years. In art and craft, epoxy resin is used for jewellery and models. Violinists rub resin called «rosin» on their bows. Phrases: «tree resin», «pine resin», «epoxy resin».
examples from the lessons: Sticky resin oozed from the pine tree's bark. | Amber is old resin that has turned hard. | A tiny insect was trapped inside the resin long ago. | The artist poured clear resin over the flowers. | My hands smelled of pine resin after climbing the tree. | Resin glue sets very hard.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable («some resin»); «resins» means kinds of resin. Not the same as «sap», which is the watery liquid inside a plant. «Rosin» is a special kind of resin for string instruments.

part of speech: noun (roe; also a roe, roes for the deer)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Roe is the mass of eggs inside a female fish, often eaten as food. 2) A roe or roe deer is a small deer of Europe and Asia with a reddish coat; the male is called a roebuck.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, roe is a stage in the life cycle of fish (eggs). In food lessons, cod roe and salmon roe are eaten in many countries; caviar is the roe of the sturgeon. In nature lessons in the UK and Ireland, roe deer live in woods. Phrases: «cod roe», «salmon roe», «roe deer».
examples from the lessons: The salmon laid her roe in the gravel of the river. | Caviar is a very expensive kind of roe. | Grandad likes cod roe on toast. | We saw a roe deer at the edge of the wood. | The orange balls on the sushi were fish roe. | A roe deer is smaller than a red deer.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Fish roe is uncountable («some roe»). Sounds the same as «row» (a line, or to move a boat with oars) and «Roe» in names. Do not confuse with «doe», a female deer.

part of speech: noun (shearing; uncountable); verb form (present participle of «shear»: shearing); adjective (shearing shed)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Shearing is cutting the wool off a sheep, usually once a year. 2) «Shearing» is the -ing form of «shear»: cutting with big scissors (shears) or clippers. 3) (science) Shearing is when forces push parts of something in opposite directions so it slides or breaks, as in a «shearing force».
its sense in the lessons: In Australia and New Zealand shearing is a big part of farm life: shearers work in a «shearing shed» in spring and compete in shearing contests. In science, it explains why materials snap or why the ground slips in earthquakes. Phrases: «sheep shearing», «shearing shed», «shearing season», «shearing force».
examples from the lessons: The farmer is shearing the sheep before summer. | Shearing does not hurt the sheep, like a haircut. | We visited a shearing shed in New Zealand. | A fast shearer can finish a sheep in about a minute. | The strong wind was shearing branches off the trees. | Shearing season is the busiest time on the farm.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb forms: shear, shears, sheared, shearing; past participle sheared or shorn. Homophone trap: «shear» (cut) and «sheer» (very steep, or complete: «sheer luck») sound the same.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To shun someone is to keep away from them on purpose and refuse to talk to them. 2) To shun something is to avoid it: «She shuns the spotlight».
its sense in the lessons: In stories and history, a character may be shunned by a village for being different, which is a kind of bullying. In wellbeing lessons, pupils discuss how being shunned feels and how to include others. In formal writing it means «avoid». Phrases: «shunned by», «shun publicity», «shun the limelight».
examples from the lessons: The other children shunned him because he was new. | In the story, the village shunned the old woman. | Some animals shun bright light and hide during the day. | She shuns fast food and eats healthily. | Being shunned by your friends can feel very lonely. | We should not shun someone just because they are different.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb; double the «n»: shunned, shunning. A bit formal or literary; everyday words are «avoid», «ignore», «leave out». Shunning on purpose to hurt someone is a form of bullying.

part of speech: noun (a sighting, sightings); verb form (-ing form of «sight»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A sighting is an occasion when someone sees something rare, unusual or wanted: a bird, a whale, a UFO or a missing person. 2) «Sighting» is also the -ing form of «sight» (to see or catch sight of), or of aiming a gun or telescope (sighting it).
its sense in the lessons: In nature lessons, birdwatchers record sightings of birds in a log; scientists count sightings to see if animals are rare. In news, police ask for sightings of a missing person or animal. In stories, «UFO sightings» and «ghost sightings» are unproven reports. Phrases: «a rare sighting», «reported sightings», «first sighting», «UFO sighting».
examples from the lessons: There was a rare sighting of a kingfisher by the river. | Our class recorded ten bird sightings in one hour. | Police asked for any sightings of the missing dog. | The first sighting of land made the sailors cheer. | There have been many UFO sightings, but none has been proved. | The tally chart showed sightings of each bird.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. A sighting is a report that someone saw something; it is not proof. Do not confuse with «siting» (choosing the place for something) or «citing» (quoting), which sound the same. In tally and data problems, each sighting counts as one.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Sonar is a way of finding things under water by sending out sound waves and listening for their echoes. 2) Sonar is also the machine that does this, used by ships and submarines. 3) Animals such as bats and dolphins use a natural kind of sonar called echolocation.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about sound, sonar shows that sound travels through water and bounces back as an echo; the time the echo takes tells the distance. Ships use sonar to measure the depth of the sea, find fish or find wrecks. Phrases: «sonar system», «on sonar», «use sonar».
examples from the lessons: The submarine used sonar to find the shipwreck. | Fishing boats use sonar to find shoals of fish. | Bats use a kind of natural sonar to catch moths. | The sonar screen showed a large shape below the ship. | Sonar works by sending out sound and listening for the echo. | Dolphins find food with echolocation, which is like sonar.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. It is short for «sound navigation and ranging». In maths problems: the echo goes there and back, so to find the distance, halve the total distance the sound travels (distance = speed × time ÷ 2).

part of speech: noun (a spout, spouts); verb (spout, spouts, spouted, spouting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A spout is a short tube or lip on a teapot, kettle or jug that liquid is poured out of. 2) A spout is a strong stream of liquid, such as a whale's spout of water and air. 3) To spout is to come or send out liquid in a strong stream. 4) (informal) To spout is to talk a lot, often saying silly or boring things: «He spouts nonsense». 5) «Up the spout» (UK, informal) means ruined or wasted.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, the spout is the part of the teapot or watering can you pour from. In nature lessons, a whale's spout is the cloud of breath it blows out of its blowhole. In stories, a fountain spouts water. Informally, people complain that someone «spouts rubbish». Phrases: «water spout», «spout nonsense», «up the spout».
examples from the lessons: Tea poured from the spout of the teapot. | The watering can has a long spout. | We saw a whale's spout far out at sea. | Water spouted from the broken pipe. | The fountain spouts water high into the air. | He's always spouting nonsense about aliens. | The rain made all our plans go up the spout.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun is countable; verb is regular (spouted). «Spout nonsense» is informal and a bit rude about someone. «Waterspout» (one word) is also a tornado over water.

part of speech: noun (a tee, tees); verb (tee, tees, teed, teeing — usually «tee up», «tee off»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A tee is a small peg, often wooden or plastic, that holds a golf ball up before it is hit. 2) The tee is also the flat area where each hole in golf begins. 3) (informal) A tee is short for a T-shirt. 4) To tee up is to put the ball on a tee, or to get something ready; to tee off is to make the first hit in golf. 5) A tee is also the letter T or a T-shaped thing.
its sense in the lessons: In PE, golf and mini-golf lessons use tees; in tee-ball (T-ball) young children hit a baseball from a stand called a tee. In everyday speech, «tee» means T-shirt. «Teed off» (US slang) means annoyed. «To a T» (sometimes «to a tee») means exactly or perfectly. Phrases: «tee off», «tee up», «tee-ball», «fits to a T».
examples from the lessons: Put the golf ball on the tee. | We met at the first tee. | Dad teed off and the ball flew into the bushes. | He wore a white tee and shorts. | In tee-ball, you hit the ball off a stand. | The coach teed up the next game. | That costume suits you to a tee.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Sounds the same as «tea» (the drink) and «T» (the letter). «Teed off» is slang for «annoyed», not polite in formal writing.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A terminal is a big building at an airport, bus station, train station or port where people start or end their journeys. 2) A terminal is one of the metal ends of a battery or electrical part where wires are joined: the positive and negative terminals. 3) (computers) A terminal is a screen and keyboard used to work with a computer, or a program for typing commands. 4) A terminal illness is one that cannot be cured and will lead to death. 5) Terminal means at the end: «terminal station».
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on circuits, a battery has a positive (+) terminal and a negative (−) terminal, and wires must join them to make a complete circuit. In travel and everyday life, «Terminal 2» at an airport is where you check in. In coding, programmers type commands into a terminal. In health and family talk, «terminal illness» is a sad and serious phrase. Phrases: «airport terminal», «bus terminal», «positive terminal», «terminal illness».
examples from the lessons: Our flight leaves from Terminal 5. | Connect the wire to the positive terminal of the battery. | The bus terminal was busy at night. | She typed the command into the terminal. | Grandpa has a terminal illness, so the doctors are keeping him comfortable. | The ferry terminal has a cafe and a shop.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun; adjective has no comparative. «Terminal» comes from the idea of «end» (terminus). In circuit problems: current flows from the positive terminal round the circuit to the negative terminal. Do not confuse with «terminate» (to end) or «terminus» (the last stop of a line).

meaning for a pupil: 1) The touchline is one of the two long side lines of a football, rugby or hockey pitch; when the ball goes over it, it is out of play. 2) «On the touchline» means at the side of the pitch, where coaches and fans stand.
its sense in the lessons: In PE and sport, especially football (soccer) and rugby in the UK, Ireland, Australia and New Zealand, the ball «goes into touch» over the touchline and play restarts with a throw-in or line-out. Parents cheer «from the touchline». In maths, a pitch's perimeter includes two touchlines and two goal lines. Phrases: «on the touchline», «along the touchline», «touchline ban».
examples from the lessons: The ball rolled over the touchline for a throw-in. | Mum cheered from the touchline. | The winger ran down the touchline and crossed the ball. | The coach paced up and down the touchline. | In rugby, the ball went into touch near the touchline. | The pitch's touchlines are 90 metres long.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; one word. In America, «sideline» is more usual. In perimeter problems, a rectangular pitch has 2 touchlines (the long sides) and 2 goal lines (the short sides): perimeter = 2 × touchline + 2 × goal line.

part of speech: noun (a whit; used mostly in «not a whit», «no whit»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A whit is a very tiny amount; it is used almost only in negative phrases: «not a whit» means not at all. 2) «Whit» is also short for Whitsun or Whit Sunday, the Christian feast of Pentecost (church, UK).
its sense in the lessons: It is an old-fashioned, literary word found in classic stories, the Bible and old poems: «He cared not a whit». In the UK, Whit Sunday or Whitsun is the church feast of Pentecost, when Christians believe the Holy Spirit came to Jesus's followers; «Whit Monday» was a holiday. Phrases: «not a whit», «every whit», «Whit Sunday», «Whitsun».
examples from the lessons: He cared not a whit about the rain. | The new rule did not change things one whit. | The old knight was not a whit afraid. | My little brother is every whit as stubborn as me. | Whit Sunday is also called Pentecost. | In the old days, children had a holiday at Whitsun.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Old-fashioned; modern speech says «not at all», «not a bit». Do not confuse with «wit» (cleverness or humour) or «white». Countable in form but almost never plural.

part of speech: interjection (woof); noun (a woof, woofs); verb (woof, woofs, woofed, woofing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Woof is the sound a dog makes when it barks, written as a word. 2) A woof is one bark. 3) To woof is to bark like a dog. 4) (weaving, also «weft») The woof is the set of threads that run across a piece of woven cloth.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and picture books, «Woof!» shows a dog barking; it is an example of onomatopoeia (a word that sounds like the noise) in English lessons. In design and technology lessons on weaving, the warp threads go up and down and the woof (weft) threads go across. Phrases: «woof woof», «warp and woof».
examples from the lessons: «Woof! Woof!» barked the puppy. | The dog gave a happy woof when we came home. | The big dog woofed at the postman. | «Woof» is an onomatopoeia, like «meow» and «moo». | In weaving, the woof goes over and under the warp. | My baby sister says «woof» every time she sees a dog.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Interjection, often written with an exclamation mark. Different languages write dog barks differently (for example «wau» in German). «Woof» meaning cloth threads is old-fashioned; «weft» is more common. Not to be confused with «wolf».

meaning for a pupil: 1) An ankylosaurus was a large, plant-eating dinosaur covered in thick bony plates, like armour, with a heavy club at the end of its tail. 2) It lived at the end of the age of dinosaurs (the Late Cretaceous), in what is now North America.
its sense in the lessons: In science and dinosaur lessons, the ankylosaurus is the «armoured tank» of dinosaurs: it defended itself from meat eaters such as Tyrannosaurus rex by swinging its tail club. It is used to teach about fossils, adaptations and herbivores. Phrases: «tail club», «armoured dinosaur».
examples from the lessons: The ankylosaurus swung its tail club at the T. rex. | An ankylosaurus was covered in bony plates. | Ankylosaurus ate low plants. | We saw an ankylosaurus skeleton at the museum. | Its armour was an adaptation to keep it safe. | The ankylosaurus was about as long as a bus.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; use «an». Plural «ankylosauruses» (some books say «ankylosaurs» for the whole group). Pronounced ANK-ih-lo-SAW-rus. The name means «fused lizard», because its bones were joined. It did not live at the same time as people.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An arsenal is a big collection of weapons, or a building where weapons are made or stored. 2) An arsenal can mean any big set of tools, tricks or ideas: «an arsenal of jokes». 3) Arsenal is a famous football club in north London, England.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, arsenals stored guns and gunpowder for armies; in news, countries have «nuclear arsenals». In everyday UK talk, «Arsenal» usually means the football club, nicknamed «the Gunners». In sports and games, a player can have «an arsenal of skills». Phrases: «nuclear arsenal», «an arsenal of», «Arsenal fan».
examples from the lessons: The army kept its cannons in the arsenal. | Some countries have large nuclear arsenals. | My brother is a huge Arsenal fan. | The chess player had an arsenal of clever moves. | The teacher has an arsenal of fun maths games. | Arsenal won the match two goals to nil.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; capital A for the football club. The club name was taken from the Royal Arsenal, a weapons factory in London. «Arsenal» is not related to «arsenic» (a poison), though they look alike.

part of speech: proper noun (Bach); noun (a bach, baches — New Zealand)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Bach is the surname of Johann Sebastian Bach, a famous German composer of classical and church music who lived long ago (a name). 2) (New Zealand) A bach is a small, simple holiday house, often by the beach or a lake. 3) (informal, US, old) To bach it means to live alone as a bachelor (rare).
its sense in the lessons: In music lessons, pupils listen to Bach's music, for example his preludes for keyboard and his church music such as cantatas. In New Zealand everyday life, families go «to the bach» for summer holidays; in some parts of the South Island the same kind of house is called a «crib». Phrases: «Bach's music», «go to the bach», «the family bach».
examples from the lessons: We listened to a piece by Bach in music class. | Bach wrote a lot of music for church organs. | Every summer we stay at our bach in the Coromandel. | The bach has no TV, just a deck and the beach. | Johann Sebastian Bach came from a family of musicians. | Gran's bach is by the lake.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The composer's name is said «bahk» (with a throaty sound at the end in German). The New Zealand word is said «batch». Capital B for the composer; lower case for the holiday house. Plural of the house: baches.

part of speech: noun (a beau, beaux or beaus); French word (beau)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (old-fashioned) A beau is a boyfriend or a man who is courting a woman. 2) (French) Beau is a French adjective meaning «beautiful» or «handsome» (masculine form), as in «beau temps» (fine weather); it sounds like English «bow» (the knot) or «bo». 3) Beau can also be a boy's name (a name).
its sense in the lessons: In old novels and historical stories, a young woman's «beau» is the man who wants to marry her. In French lessons, «beau» describes a handsome boy or nice weather: «Il fait beau» means «The weather is fine». Phrases: «her beau», «Il fait beau» (French).
examples from the lessons: In the old story, Lizzie waited for her beau at the dance. | Aunt Sue's new beau brought her flowers. | In French, «Il fait beau» means «It's a nice day». | «Un beau chien» is French for «a handsome dog». | Beau is the name of the boy next door. | Grandma laughed and called Grandpa her old beau.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced «boh», like «bow» (the ribbon). English plural is «beaux» (also said «bohz») or «beaus». In French, the feminine form is «belle», and before a vowel it becomes «bel». Old-fashioned in English; today people say «boyfriend».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A belle is a very beautiful girl or woman, especially the most admired one at a party: «the belle of the ball». 2) (French) Belle is the feminine form of the French adjective «beau», meaning «beautiful»: «une belle maison» (a beautiful house). 3) Belle is also a girl's name, as in the heroine of «Beauty and the Beast» (a name).
its sense in the lessons: In fairy tales and old stories, «the belle of the ball» is the girl everyone wants to dance with. In French lessons, «belle» describes feminine nouns: «la belle rose». Many children know Belle from «Beauty and the Beast». Phrases: «belle of the ball», «Southern belle» (US).
examples from the lessons: Cinderella was the belle of the ball. | Belle loved reading books in the old story. | In French, «belle» means beautiful: «une belle journée». | The town's belle wore a blue silk dress. | «Ma belle» is a French way to say «my beautiful one». | In old American stories, a Southern belle was a rich young woman from the South.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced «bell», like the thing that rings. Old-fashioned in English. In French, «belle» goes with feminine nouns and «beau» with masculine ones. Do not confuse with «bell».

part of speech: proper noun (Chad); noun (a chad, chads); slang (a Chad)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Chad is a large country in north-central Africa; its capital is N'Djamena and much of the north is Sahara desert. 2) Chad is a man's name (a name). 3) A chad is the tiny bit of paper punched out when you make a hole in a card or ballot paper. 4) (slang, internet) A «Chad» is a joke name for a confident, sporty, popular young man.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons, Chad is a landlocked country (no coast) with Lake Chad, a lake that has shrunk a lot. In news and history, «hanging chads» on paper ballots once caused arguments about vote counting in the USA. In online slang, calling someone «a Chad» is teasing and can be mean. Phrases: «Lake Chad», «hanging chad».
examples from the lessons: Chad is a country in Africa with no coastline. | Lake Chad has become much smaller. | My cousin Chad plays rugby. | The hole punch left little chads all over the desk. | Online, some people call a show-off «a Chad». | We found Chad on the map, south of Libya.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital C for the country and the name. The country is landlocked. The slang «Chad» is internet talk and may sound unkind; avoid it in school writing.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Colourless means having no colour at all, like clear water or air. 2) Colourless can mean pale and grey: «a colourless face». 3) Colourless can mean dull and boring, with nothing interesting: «a colourless town».
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, many gases (oxygen, carbon dioxide) and liquids (water) are colourless; pupils learn that colourless is not the same as invisible or safe, as some colourless gases are poisonous. In stories, a colourless person is dull or shy. Phrases: «colourless liquid», «colourless gas», «colourless and odourless».
examples from the lessons: Water is a colourless liquid. | Oxygen is a colourless gas with no smell. | After the shock, her face was colourless. | The old town felt grey and colourless. | Carbon monoxide is colourless and deadly, so homes need alarms. | Mix the colourless solution with the indicator and watch it turn pink.
note for the reader of a maths problem: British spelling «colourless»; US «colorless». Colourless means «no colour», but «clear» and «transparent» mean you can see through it; a colourless liquid is usually clear. Safety trap: a colourless liquid in a bottle may not be water.

part of speech: noun (a crest, crests); verb (crest, crests, crested, cresting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A crest is a bunch of feathers, fur or skin on the top of an animal's head, like a cockatoo's crest or a rooster's comb. 2) The crest of a hill or wave is its top. 3) A crest is a special picture or badge of a family, school, team or town. 4) To crest is to reach the top of a hill or wave. 5) «On the crest of a wave» means very successful at the moment.
its sense in the lessons: In science, crests are animal features, and the crest of a wave is its highest point (the low point is the trough). In history, knights had family crests on shields; schools have crests on uniforms. In geography, the crest is the top of a ridge. Phrases: «school crest», «family crest», «crest of a wave», «crest the hill».
examples from the lessons: The cockatoo raised its yellow crest. | We reached the crest of the hill and saw the sea. | Our school crest has a lion and a book on it. | The surfer rode the crest of the wave. | The knight's shield showed his family crest. | The river crested after days of rain. | In a wave, the crest is the top and the trough is the bottom.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. In science problems about waves: the distance from one crest to the next is the wavelength; the height from the middle line to the crest is the amplitude. Related word: «crested» (having a crest).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Diesel is a kind of heavy fuel made from oil, used in many trucks, buses, trains, tractors and some cars. 2) A diesel is a vehicle or engine that uses diesel fuel. 3) It is named after Rudolf Diesel, the engineer who invented the diesel engine (a name).
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, at a petrol station (US: gas station) you choose petrol or diesel; putting the wrong one in a car can break it. In science and geography lessons, diesel is a fossil fuel that gives out carbon dioxide and pollution, so many towns now want electric buses instead. Phrases: «diesel engine», «diesel fuel», «diesel train», «diesel fumes».
examples from the lessons: Dad filled the van with diesel. | The diesel train rumbled into the station. | Tractors usually run on diesel. | Diesel fumes make the air dirty. | Our school bus is now electric, not diesel. | Never put diesel in a petrol car.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable for the fuel («some diesel»); countable for vehicles («two old diesels»). Capital D only for the inventor's name. Diesel is not the same as petrol (gasoline); the engines are different.

part of speech: noun (a dit, dits); French word (dit); abbreviation-like fragment
meaning for a pupil: 1) In Morse code, «dit» is the spoken name of a short signal (a dot); «dah» is the long one (a dash). 2) (French) «Dit» is a French word meaning «said» or «says»: «il dit» means «he says», «c'est dit» means «that's settled»; to an English ear it sounds like «dee». 3) (UK navy slang) A dit is a story or yarn, as in «spin a dit».
its sense in the lessons: In science and history lessons on communication, children learn to send Morse code: S is «dit dit dit», O is «dah dah dah», so SOS is «dit dit dit, dah dah dah, dit dit dit». In French lessons «dit» appears in reading: «Le chat dit miaou». It is not a common everyday English word.
examples from the lessons: In Morse code, the letter E is just one dit. | SOS is dit-dit-dit, dah-dah-dah, dit-dit-dit. | We tapped dits and dahs on the desk. | In French, «Maman dit non» means «Mum says no». | The old sailor spun a dit about a storm at sea. | A dit is short; a dah is three times as long.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a Morse word, «dit» is a sound name for a dot, not a dictionary word most people use. The French «dit» is not an English word; the final «t» is silent. In Morse timing, a dah lasts as long as three dits.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Earwax is the soft yellow or brown waxy stuff that the body makes inside the ear canal. 2) It protects the ear by catching dust and germs and keeping the skin from drying out.
its sense in the lessons: In science and health lessons, earwax is a natural part of the body that cleans itself; doctors say not to push cotton buds (cotton swabs, Q-tips) into ears, as this can push wax deeper and hurt the eardrum. In funny stories, earwax is a «yucky» detail. Phrases: «build-up of earwax», «ear drops».
examples from the lessons: Earwax helps keep dirt out of your ears. | Never poke cotton buds into your ear to remove earwax. | The doctor put drops in my ear to soften the earwax. | Earwax can be yellow, orange or brown. | Too much earwax can make it hard to hear. | In the story, the troll had earwax as thick as butter.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «some earwax», not «an earwax». Written as one word (also «ear wax»). The body moves earwax out by itself, so most people do not need to clean inside the ear.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Electoral means to do with elections, where people vote to choose leaders or representatives. 2) It is used in phrases such as «electoral roll» (the list of people allowed to vote) and «Electoral College» (the US system for choosing a president).
its sense in the lessons: In politics and citizenship lessons, «electoral» describes how voting works: electoral systems, electoral districts, electoral fraud (cheating in elections). In the USA, the president is chosen by electoral votes from each state. In the UK, Ireland, Canada, Australia and New Zealand, adults put their names on an electoral roll. Phrases: «electoral roll», «Electoral College», «electoral system», «electoral fraud».
examples from the lessons: Mum checked she was on the electoral roll. | The USA uses the Electoral College to pick the president. | Australia has an electoral commission that runs elections. | Electoral fraud means cheating in an election. | Each state gets a number of electoral votes. | Our class made its own electoral rules for choosing a class rep.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective only; no comparative. Related: elect, election, elector, electorate. Stress: e-LEC-tor-al. In maths, electoral results are often given as votes, percentages or seats; a candidate with the most votes may not have more than half.

part of speech: adjective (fatty, fattier, fattiest); noun (a fatty, fatties — rude)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Fatty means containing a lot of fat: «fatty food», «fatty meat». 2) Fatty describes something made of fat: «fatty tissue», «fatty acids». 3) (rude) «Fatty» is an insulting name for a fat person; using it is unkind and hurtful.
its sense in the lessons: In health and food lessons, fatty foods (chips, crisps, burgers) are eaten in small amounts for a balanced diet; some fats are needed. In science, «fatty acids» are parts of fats. In wellbeing lessons, name-calling such as «Fatty» is discussed as bullying. Phrases: «fatty foods», «fatty acids», «fatty meat».
examples from the lessons: Chips and burgers are fatty foods. | Eat fatty foods only now and then. | The dog chewed a fatty bone. | Fish oil contains fatty acids that are good for the brain. | Calling someone «Fatty» is mean and is bullying. | Cut off the fatty part of the bacon.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative: fattier, fattiest (change y to i). As a name for a person it is rude and hurtful. «Fatty» (full of fat) is different from «fat» (a big body), though both come from «fat».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Feathery means covered with feathers. 2) Feathery means light, soft or delicate, like a feather: «feathery clouds», «feathery leaves».
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, birds have feathery bodies; some dinosaurs had feathery coats too. In art and creative writing, «feathery» is a describing word for soft snow, ferns or wispy clouds (cirrus clouds look feathery). Phrases: «feathery leaves», «feathery clouds», «feathery touch».
examples from the lessons: The baby chick was soft and feathery. | Feathery cirrus clouds floated high in the sky. | Carrots have feathery green leaves. | Some dinosaurs were feathery, scientists say. | The snow fell in feathery flakes. | The fern's feathery fronds swayed in the breeze.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective from «feather». Comparative «more feathery» is more common than «featherier». A good word for adding detail in descriptive writing.

part of speech: suffix fragment (-ful); not a word on its own
meaning for a pupil: 1) «-ful» is an ending added to a word to make an adjective meaning «full of» or «having»: careful, hopeful, colourful, helpful. 2) «-ful» added to a container noun makes a noun for an amount: a spoonful, a handful, a cupful. 3) As a separate word «ful» is not English; it is a fragment, a spelling mistake for «full», or part of a broken word.
its sense in the lessons: In spelling lessons, pupils learn that the suffix has only one «l»: «beautiful», not «beautifull», even though «full» has two. When added to a word ending in «y», the y changes to i: beauty → beautiful, pity → pitiful. In maths and cooking, «a spoonful» and «a cupful» are amounts. Phrases: careful, wonderful, thankful, mouthful.
examples from the lessons: Be careful when you cross the road. | Add two spoonfuls of sugar. | She was hopeful about the test. | The garden was full of colourful flowers. | Spell «helpful» with one «l» at the end. | He grabbed a handful of sweets.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Not a word by itself; write «full» when you mean the word. The suffix «-ful» always has one «l». Plural of «spoonful» is «spoonfuls» (not «spoonsful»). Opposite suffix is often «-less»: careful / careless, hopeful / hopeless.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Historical means to do with history or the past: «historical events», «historical facts». 2) Historical describes a person or event that really existed in the past, not only in a legend. 3) Historical describes a story, film or novel set in the past: «a historical novel».
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, pupils study historical sources (old letters, pictures, objects) to find out what happened, and ask whether a person in a legend is historical (really lived). In reading, «historical fiction» mixes real history with made-up characters. Phrases: «historical source», «historical fiction», «historical figure», «historical site».
examples from the lessons: We read a historical novel about the Romans. | Is King Arthur a historical person or a legend? | Old diaries are useful historical sources. | The castle is an important historical site. | She dressed as a historical figure for the school day. | Historical records show the town flooded many times.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Both «a historical» and «an historical» are used; «a historical» is more common today. Do not confuse with «historic», which means very important in history: «a historic day» (one people will remember), «a historical day» (just a day in the past).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A horde is a very large crowd of people or animals, often noisy or out of control. 2) In history, a horde was a large group of nomadic warriors, such as the Mongol horde.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, hordes appear in stories of armies on horseback crossing Asia and Europe. In everyday life, «hordes of tourists», «hordes of shoppers» or «a horde of kids» means a big, busy crowd. In games and fantasy stories, «a horde of zombies or orcs» attacks. Phrases: «hordes of», «a horde of».
examples from the lessons: Hordes of shoppers rushed in when the sale began. | A horde of children ran onto the playground. | The Mongol horde rode across the steppe. | In the game, a horde of zombies attacked the castle. | Hordes of tourists visit the beach every summer. | A horde of ants carried away the crumbs.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Sounds the same as «hoard», which means a hidden store of treasure or food: «a dragon's hoard». Horde = crowd; hoard = stash.

part of speech: noun (a hryvnia, hryvnias or hryvni) — word from Ukrainian
meaning for a pupil: 1) (Ukrainian) The hryvnia is the money (currency) of Ukraine; one hryvnia is made of 100 kopiyky (kopecks). 2) Its sign is ₴ and its short code is UAH.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and geography lessons about money around the world, the hryvnia is Ukraine's currency, as the pound is Britain's and the dollar is America's. Exchange-rate problems may ask how many hryvnias equal one pound or dollar. Ukrainian banknotes show famous people from Ukraine's history and culture. Phrases: «Ukrainian hryvnia», «100 hryvnias».
examples from the lessons: The hryvnia is the currency of Ukraine. | A loaf of bread in Kyiv costs a few hryvnias. | One hryvnia equals 100 kopiyky. | The sign for the hryvnia is ₴. | Our teacher showed us a 200-hryvnia note. | We changed some pounds into hryvnias for the trip.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A Ukrainian word used in English; to an English ear it sounds like «HRIV-nee-uh» (with a breathy «h»). Also spelled «hryvna». In conversion problems: multiply by the exchange rate to change pounds into hryvnias, and divide to change back.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Jasmine is a climbing plant or bush with small white or yellow flowers that smell very sweet. 2) Jasmine tea is green tea flavoured with jasmine flowers; jasmine rice is a sweet-smelling kind of long rice. 3) Jasmine is a girl's name (a name).
its sense in the lessons: In nature and gardening lessons, jasmine is a climbing plant that grows on walls and fences, and its scent attracts moths and bees at night. In food lessons, jasmine rice is common in Thai cooking. Jasmine is also the princess in the story of Aladdin. Phrases: «jasmine tea», «jasmine rice», «scent of jasmine».
examples from the lessons: The jasmine by the door smells lovely in summer. | We had jasmine rice with our curry. | Grandma drinks jasmine tea. | Jasmine flowers are small and white. | My friend Jasmine sits next to me. | The jasmine climbed up the garden wall.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable for the plant in general and the scent; countable for kinds («several jasmines»). Capital J for the name. Pronounced JAZ-min.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A joystick is a lever that you push in any direction to control a video game, a computer or a machine. 2) A joystick is also the control stick of an aeroplane, used by the pilot to steer it.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, children use joysticks on game controllers; in computing lessons, a joystick is an «input device», like a mouse or keyboard. Powered wheelchairs, cranes, drones and robots are also driven with joysticks. Phrases: «move the joystick», «joystick controller».
examples from the lessons: Push the joystick left to make the car turn. | My game controller has two joysticks. | The pilot pulled back on the joystick. | A joystick is an input device. | The crane driver used a joystick to lift the beam. | Grandad steers his electric wheelchair with a small joystick.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; one word. In computing lessons, a joystick is input (information goes into the computer), while a screen is output.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A kenning is a short, two-word phrase that names something in a clever, poetic way instead of using its usual name, such as «whale-road» for the sea or «sky-candle» for the sun. 2) Kennings were used a lot in Old English and Old Norse poems, such as «Beowulf» and Viking sagas.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons, pupils read and write kenning poems: a list of kennings that describe one thing, such as a cat («mouse-catcher», «lap-warmer», «sofa-scratcher»), and the reader guesses what it is. In history lessons about the Anglo-Saxons and Vikings, kennings show how their poets spoke. Phrases: «kenning poem», «write a kenning».
examples from the lessons: «Whale-road» is a kenning for the sea. | Write a kenning poem about your pet. | A dog could be a «ball-chaser» or «postman-scarer». | Viking poets used kennings like «bone-house» for the body. | Our class guessed that «night-light» was a kenning for the moon. | Each line of a kenning poem is two words.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Kennings are usually written with a hyphen: «tree-climber». They are often noun + noun, or noun + a noun made from a verb with -er. A kenning is a kind of metaphor.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A lotus is a water plant with large round leaves and big pink or white flowers that rise above the water in ponds and lakes, mostly in Asia. 2) In some religions, especially Hinduism and Buddhism, the lotus is a holy symbol of purity, because it grows clean and beautiful out of mud. 3) The «lotus position» is a way of sitting cross-legged with each foot on the opposite thigh, used in yoga and meditation. 4) In old Greek stories, the lotus was a magic fruit that made people forget home.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, the lotus is a water plant whose leaves repel water (the «lotus effect»), which inspires self-cleaning materials. In RE lessons, Hindus and Buddhists see the lotus as a symbol; pictures of the Buddha often show him sitting on a lotus. In PE and calm lessons, the lotus position is a yoga pose. Phrases: «lotus flower», «lotus position», «lotus effect».
examples from the lessons: A pink lotus floated on the pond. | Water rolls off lotus leaves in little balls. | Buddhists see the lotus as a sign of purity. | In yoga, we tried to sit in the lotus position. | The lotus grows in mud but its flower is clean. | In the old tale, sailors ate the lotus and forgot to go home.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; plural lotuses. The lotus is different from the water lily, though they look similar. Pronounced LOH-tus.

part of speech: noun-like word (malik, from Arabic and other languages); proper noun (Malik — a name)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Malik is a name, used as a first name or a family name in many Muslim, Arab and South Asian families (a name). 2) In Arabic, Urdu and some other languages, «malik» means «king» or «owner, master»; it is not an English word.
its sense in the lessons: Children meet Malik as the name of classmates, famous people or characters in stories. In RE lessons about Islam, «Al-Malik» (the King) is one of the names Muslims use for God. In English it is used only as a name or a borrowed word. Phrases: «Mr Malik», «Malik's family».
examples from the lessons: My friend Malik plays goalkeeper. | Mrs Malik is our new head teacher. | In Arabic, «malik» means «king». | Malik and his sister walk to school together. | Muslims call God «Al-Malik», which means «the King». | Malik wrote a story about a dragon.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a name, always write it with a capital M. Sounds like «MAH-lik» or «MAL-ik». Do not invent facts about a person called Malik; it is just a name unless a text tells you more.

part of speech: noun (a maw, maws); (Scotland, informal) noun (maw = mum)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A maw is the mouth, jaws or throat of a hungry or fierce animal. 2) A maw is anything that seems to swallow things up, like a big dark hole: «the maw of the cave». 3) (Scotland, informal) «Maw» means mum or mother; «Paw» is dad.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and poems, «maw» makes a monster or animal sound scary and greedy: «the dragon's gaping maw». In descriptive writing, it is a strong word for a dark opening. In Scottish speech, a child may call their mum «Maw». Phrases: «gaping maw», «into the maw of».
examples from the lessons: The crocodile opened its huge maw. | The ship sailed into the dark maw of the storm. | The dragon's maw was full of sharp teeth. | The cave's black maw frightened the explorers. | «Maw, can I go out to play?» asked the boy in Glasgow. | The whale's maw swallowed the tiny fish.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Literary in its main sense; in everyday speech people say «mouth» or «jaws». The Scottish «Maw» (mum) is informal and regional. Rhymes with «saw».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (grammar) A modal, or modal verb, is a helping verb such as can, could, may, might, must, shall, should, will or would, which shows how sure, possible, allowed or necessary something is. 2) (maths) Modal means to do with the mode: the modal value is the one that appears most often in a set of data. 3) (computers) A modal or modal window is a box that pops up on a screen and must be closed before you can go on. 4) (music) Modal means using musical modes, kinds of scale.
its sense in the lessons: In English grammar lessons, modal verbs change meaning: «You must go» (necessary), «You might go» (possible), «You can go» (allowed or able). In maths, the «modal class» or «modal number» is the most common one in a tally chart or list. In apps and websites, a modal pops up to ask «Are you sure?». Phrases: «modal verb», «modal value», «modal class», «modal window».
examples from the lessons: «Must», «should» and «might» are modal verbs. | In «I can swim», «can» is a modal verb. | The modal shoe size in our class is 3. | Find the modal colour from the tally chart. | Close the modal window to go back to the game. | Modal verbs show how sure we are about something.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Modal verbs have no -s for he/she/it («She can», not «She cans») and are followed by a verb without «to» («must go», not «must to go»). In maths: the mode is the value that appears most often; if two values tie, there are two modes. Do not confuse the mode with the mean (average) or median (middle).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Percussion means musical instruments that you play by hitting, shaking or scraping them, such as drums, tambourines, triangles, cymbals and xylophones. 2) The percussion is the part of an orchestra or band that plays these instruments. 3) Percussion means the hitting of one thing against another, a sharp knock (formal).
its sense in the lessons: In music lessons, children play percussion instruments to keep the beat and learn rhythm; percussion is one of the orchestra's four families (strings, woodwind, brass, percussion). «Body percussion» is clapping, clicking and stamping to make music. Phrases: «percussion section», «percussion instruments», «body percussion», «tuned percussion».
examples from the lessons: The drum is a percussion instrument. | In music we played percussion with shakers and drums. | The percussion section sits at the back of the orchestra. | A xylophone is tuned percussion, because it plays notes. | Clap and stamp for body percussion. | My brother has percussion lessons on Saturdays.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «She plays percussion», not «a percussion». Someone who plays it is a percussionist. Tuned percussion (xylophone, glockenspiel) plays notes; untuned percussion (drum, triangle) does not.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A pinhole is a very small hole, like one made by a pin. 2) A pinhole camera is a simple camera made from a box with a tiny hole, and no lens, that makes an upside-down picture inside.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about light, pupils make a pinhole camera from a box or tube with tracing paper at the back: light travels in straight lines through the pinhole, so the picture appears upside down. During a solar eclipse, people use a pinhole viewer to look at the sun safely, never looking straight at it. Phrases: «pinhole camera», «pinhole viewer».
examples from the lessons: We made a pinhole camera from a shoebox. | The picture in the pinhole camera was upside down. | Light shone through a pinhole in the curtain. | Use a pinhole viewer to watch the eclipse safely. | A pinhole in the tyre let the air out slowly. | Light travels in straight lines through the pinhole.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; one word. Safety: never look at the sun directly, not even through a pinhole; a pinhole viewer projects the image onto paper. The picture is upside down because light rays cross at the hole.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A rotor is a part of a machine that turns round and round, such as the blades on top of a helicopter. 2) A rotor is the spinning part inside an electric motor or generator. 3) In a wind turbine, the rotor is the hub with its blades that the wind turns.
its sense in the lessons: In science and design lessons, helicopters fly because their rotor blades push air down; a tail rotor stops the helicopter from spinning. In lessons on energy, wind turbine rotors turn a generator to make electricity. Pupils make paper «helicopters» (spinners) to test rotors and air resistance. Phrases: «rotor blades», «tail rotor», «main rotor».
examples from the lessons: The helicopter's rotor began to spin. | The tail rotor stops the helicopter turning round. | The wind turned the rotor of the turbine. | Inside the motor, the rotor spins very fast. | We dropped paper rotors from the stairs and timed them. | Stay away from the rotor blades when the helicopter lands.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. The word «rotor» is a palindrome: it reads the same backwards. The part of a motor that does not move is called the stator. Related words: rotate, rotation.

part of speech: noun (a snorkel, snorkels); verb (snorkel, snorkels, snorkelled / snorkeled, snorkelling / snorkeling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A snorkel is a short, bent tube that lets you breathe through your mouth while swimming face-down near the surface of the water. 2) To snorkel is to swim using a snorkel and a mask to look at fish and coral.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and holidays, children snorkel on beaches and reefs, such as the Great Barrier Reef in Australia. In science lessons, snorkelling is a way to observe sea life. In safety lessons, children learn to snorkel with an adult, in calm water, and never to go deep with a snorkel. Submarines also have snorkels for air. Phrases: «mask and snorkel», «go snorkelling».
examples from the lessons: I wore a mask and snorkel to look at the fish. | We went snorkelling on the reef. | Blow hard to clear water from your snorkel. | She snorkelled over a turtle. | A snorkel only works near the surface. | Always snorkel with a buddy and an adult nearby.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun. Spelling: UK «snorkelled, snorkelling»; US «snorkeled, snorkeling». A snorkel is not the same as scuba gear, which has an air tank for diving deep.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A steroid is a kind of chemical, made in the body or as a medicine, that can calm swelling or act like hormones. 2) Steroid creams and inhalers are medicines doctors give for eczema, asthma and other illnesses. 3) Steroids (anabolic steroids) are also drugs some people take to build muscles; using them like this is often against sports rules and can harm health. 4) (informal) «On steroids» means much bigger or stronger than usual: «It's like a skateboard on steroids».
its sense in the lessons: In health lessons, children learn that a brown asthma inhaler may contain a steroid medicine that is safe when a doctor prescribes it. In sport and news, athletes can be banned for taking steroids to cheat. Informally, «on steroids» is a funny way to say «extra powerful». Phrases: «steroid cream», «steroid inhaler», «on steroids», «tested for steroids».
examples from the lessons: The doctor gave me a steroid cream for my eczema. | My brown inhaler has a small dose of steroid in it. | The runner was banned for taking steroids. | Taking steroids without a doctor can damage your heart. | This new bike is like a scooter on steroids. | Your body makes some steroids naturally, like hormones.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; often plural «steroids». Medicine steroids from a doctor are not the same as muscle-building steroids misused in sport. Pronounced STEER-oyd or STAIR-oyd.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Sumatran means from or to do with Sumatra, a large island of Indonesia in South-East Asia. 2) A Sumatran is a person from Sumatra. 3) It is used in the names of rare animals that live there: the Sumatran tiger, the Sumatran orangutan, the Sumatran rhinoceros and the Sumatran elephant.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and science lessons, Sumatran animals are examples of critically endangered species whose rainforest home is being cut down, often for palm-oil farms. Pupils learn about protecting habitats and choosing products that do not destroy forests. Phrases: «Sumatran tiger», «Sumatran orangutan», «Sumatran rainforest».
examples from the lessons: The Sumatran tiger is the smallest tiger. | Sumatran orangutans live high in the trees. | Only a few Sumatran rhinos are left in the wild. | The Sumatran rainforest is being cut down for farms. | We adopted a Sumatran tiger at the zoo for our class project. | Sumatran coffee is sold all over the world.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Write with a capital S, because it comes from a place name (Sumatra). Pronounced soo-MAH-tran. «Critically endangered» means a species is at very high risk of dying out.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A thermostat is a device that keeps a room, oven, fridge or machine at a set temperature by switching heating or cooling on and off. 2) The dial or screen you use to set that temperature is also called the thermostat.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, a thermostat is an example of control: it senses temperature and switches heating on when it is too cold and off when it is warm enough. In everyday life, families «turn down the thermostat» to save energy and money. In coding lessons, it is a simple «if … then» rule. Phrases: «turn up / turn down the thermostat», «set the thermostat».
examples from the lessons: Dad turned the thermostat down to save energy. | The thermostat switches the heating on when it gets cold. | The oven's thermostat keeps it at 180 degrees. | Set the thermostat to 20 degrees. | A thermostat in the fish tank keeps the water warm. | If the temperature drops below 18, the thermostat turns the heater on.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Pronounced THER-mo-stat. A thermostat is not a thermometer: a thermometer only measures temperature, while a thermostat also controls it. In temperature problems, the room swings a little above and below the set number.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A tribute is something said, done or given to show respect, thanks or admiration for someone: «a tribute to the nurses». 2) In history, a tribute was money, food or goods that a weaker country or people had to pay to a stronger ruler. 3) A tribute act or tribute band copies the music of a famous band. 4) «To be a tribute to» means to show how good something is: «The garden is a tribute to her hard work».
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, conquered lands paid tribute to the Romans or to other empires. In everyday life and the news, people «pay tribute» to someone who has died or done something brave, with words, flowers or a minute's silence. In stories, a tribute is sometimes a person sent as a payment. Phrases: «pay tribute to», «a fitting tribute», «tribute band», «in tribute to».
examples from the lessons: The school planted a tree as a tribute to our old caretaker. | Fans left flowers in tribute to the singer. | The king demanded tribute from the villages. | Everyone paid tribute to the brave firefighters. | We went to see a Beatles tribute band. | Her neat work is a tribute to her patience.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. «Pay tribute to» is the usual phrase. Do not confuse with «tributary» (a small river that flows into a bigger one).

part of speech: proper noun (Troy); adjective (troy, in «troy weight», «troy ounce»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Troy was an ancient city in what is now Turkey, famous from Greek stories of the Trojan War, in which the Greeks got inside the city by hiding in a giant wooden horse. 2) Troy is a boy's name (a name). 3) Troy weight is an old system for weighing gold, silver and gems; a troy ounce is a little heavier than an ordinary ounce.
its sense in the lessons: In history and reading lessons, the story of Troy and the Trojan Horse is told from old Greek poems; archaeologists found the ruins of a real city there. A «Trojan horse» now also means a trick to get inside, or a computer virus hidden in a harmless-looking file. In maths and money news, gold prices are given per troy ounce. Phrases: «Helen of Troy», «Trojan Horse», «troy ounce».
examples from the lessons: The Greeks hid inside a wooden horse to get into Troy. | Helen of Troy was said to be very beautiful. | Archaeologists dug up the ruins of Troy. | Gold is weighed in troy ounces. | My cousin Troy is in Year 6. | A computer virus called a Trojan horse tricks you into opening it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital T for the city and the name; lower case in «troy weight». Adjective for people of Troy: Trojan. In measurement problems: a troy ounce is about 31 grams, while an ordinary ounce is about 28 grams.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Turkish means from or to do with Turkey (Türkiye), a country partly in Europe and partly in Asia, or its people. 2) Turkish is the language spoken in Turkey and by many people in Cyprus and around the world. 3) It is used in names of foods and things: Turkish delight (a soft sweet dusted with sugar), Turkish coffee, a Turkish bath.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons, pupils learn about Turkey, a country joining Europe and Asia, and its biggest city Istanbul. In everyday life, many towns have Turkish shops and kebab cafes; Turkish delight appears in «The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe». Phrases: «Turkish delight», «speak Turkish», «Turkish food».
examples from the lessons: She speaks Turkish and English at home. | Edmund ate Turkish delight in the story. | We went to a Turkish restaurant for kebabs. | Turkish coffee is very strong and thick. | Istanbul is the biggest Turkish city. | Turkish uses the same alphabet as English with some extra letters.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always capital T. «Turkish» is the adjective and the language; a person is «a Turk» or «a Turkish person». The country now calls itself «Türkiye» in English too. Do not confuse with «turkey», the bird.

meaning for a pupil: 1) UNESCO is a part of the United Nations that works for education, science and culture around the world; its name is short for the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization. 2) It chooses World Heritage Sites: places so special that the whole world should protect them.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and history lessons, UNESCO World Heritage Sites include the Great Wall of China, Stonehenge, the Grand Canyon, the Great Barrier Reef and the Giant's Causeway. UNESCO also helps children get schooling. Phrases: «UNESCO World Heritage Site», «protected by UNESCO».
examples from the lessons: Stonehenge is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. | UNESCO is part of the United Nations. | UNESCO helps more children go to school. | The old town was listed by UNESCO. | The Great Barrier Reef is protected as a UNESCO site. | UNESCO stands for the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization.
note for the reader of a maths problem: An acronym, usually written in capitals: UNESCO. Said as one word: yoo-NESS-ko. Not «a UNESCO»; it is a name. Its headquarters is in Paris, France.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Wifi (also written Wi-Fi) is a way of connecting phones, tablets, computers and other devices to the internet or to each other without wires, using radio waves. 2) In everyday talk, «the wifi» means the wireless internet connection in a place: «The wifi is down».
its sense in the lessons: In computing lessons, wifi is a wireless network that uses a router; pupils learn that data travels as radio signals. In online-safety lessons, children learn not to join unknown public wifi without an adult and to keep the wifi password private. In everyday life, «What's the wifi password?» is a common question. Phrases: «the wifi password», «free wifi», «connect to the wifi», «wifi signal».
examples from the lessons: What's the wifi password? | The wifi isn't working, so I can't watch my show. | The cafe has free wifi. | My tablet connects to the wifi at school. | The wifi signal is weak in my bedroom. | Wifi sends information by radio waves.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «the wifi», not «a wifi». The official spelling is «Wi-Fi», but «wifi» is common. Pronounced WHY-fy. Wifi is not the same as the internet: wifi connects you to a router, which then connects to the internet.

part of speech: noun (an auction, auctions); verb (auction, auctions, auctioned, auctioning — often «auction off»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) An auction is a public sale where things are sold to the person who offers the most money. 2) To auction something (or auction it off) is to sell it at an auction. 3) An online auction is one held on a website, where people bid until a set time ends.
its sense in the lessons: In maths lessons, auction problems compare bids and find the winning (highest) price or how much more one bid was than another. In everyday life, schools hold charity auctions, and paintings, cars and houses can be sold at auction. The person who runs it is the auctioneer, who says «Going, going, gone!». Phrases: «at auction», «auction off», «charity auction», «going, going, gone».
examples from the lessons: The painting was sold at auction. | Our school held an auction to raise money for the library. | Dad bid on a bike in an online auction. | The farm was auctioned off. | The highest bid wins the auction. | «Going, going, gone!» shouted the auctioneer. | At the auction, Ella bid 15 pounds and Tom bid 18; Tom won by 3 pounds.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun; regular verb. In maths problems: the winner pays the highest bid; to find by how much someone won, subtract the second-highest bid. A «bid» is the money someone offers.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A bilby is a small Australian marsupial with long rabbit-like ears, a long pointed nose and silky blue-grey fur. 2) It lives in desert areas, digs burrows and comes out at night.
its sense in the lessons: In science and nature lessons, the bilby is an example of a marsupial (mothers carry babies in a pouch) and of an endangered animal harmed by foxes, cats and rabbits brought to Australia. At Easter in Australia, many children get chocolate «Easter bilbies» instead of bunnies, to help save bilbies. Phrases: «Easter bilby», «greater bilby».
examples from the lessons: The bilby has big ears like a rabbit. | Bilbies dig burrows in the desert. | A mother bilby carries her baby in a pouch. | We got a chocolate Easter bilby. | Foxes and cats are a danger to bilbies. | The bilby comes out at night to look for food.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; plural bilbies (y → ies). A bilby is not a rabbit; it is a marsupial, like a kangaroo. Its pouch opens backwards so dirt does not get in when it digs.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A botanist is a scientist who studies plants: how they grow, where they live and how they are related. 2) Botany is the science that botanists do.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, children act like botanists when they sort leaves, grow seeds and name the parts of a flower. History lessons may mention botanists who travelled on ships to collect plants, such as Joseph Banks on Captain Cook's voyage to Australia. Phrases: «a famous botanist», «plant collector».
examples from the lessons: A botanist studies plants and flowers. | The botanist found a new kind of orchid. | We were botanists for the day and collected leaves. | Botanists work in gardens, labs and rainforests. | The botanist explained how seeds spread. | Joseph Banks was a botanist on a long sea voyage.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Related words: botany (the subject), botanical (adjective, as in «botanical garden»). Stress: BOT-an-ist.

part of speech: noun (a cache, caches); verb (cache, caches, cached, caching)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A cache is a hidden store of things, such as food, weapons or treasure. 2) (computers) A cache is a place in a computer or phone where data is kept for a while so it can be found quickly next time. 3) To cache something is to store it in a cache, hidden or for quick use.
its sense in the lessons: In nature lessons, squirrels and jays make caches of nuts for winter. In computing lessons, a browser cache keeps copies of web pages; «clear the cache» can fix a problem. In geocaching, families use GPS to find hidden boxes called caches. Phrases: «a cache of», «clear the cache», «geocaching».
examples from the lessons: The squirrel buried a cache of acorns. | Police found a cache of stolen phones. | Clear your browser's cache if the page won't load. | The phone caches photos so they load faster. | We found a geocache hidden under a log. | The explorers left a cache of food for the way back.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced «cash», like money. Do not confuse with «cash» (money) or «catch»; and not with French «cachet». Countable noun; regular verb (cached).

part of speech: noun (a carp, carp or carps); verb (carp, carps, carped, carping)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A carp is a large freshwater fish that lives in lakes, ponds and slow rivers; goldfish and koi are kinds of carp. 2) To carp is to keep complaining about small, unimportant things (informal, disapproving): «He's always carping about the food».
its sense in the lessons: In nature lessons, carp are pond and river fish; in Australia, introduced carp are pests that harm rivers. In Asia, koi carp are kept in ornamental ponds. Some families in Europe, including Ukraine and Poland, eat carp at Christmas Eve. In everyday talk, «stop carping» means stop grumbling. Phrases: «koi carp», «carp fishing», «carp about», «carp on».
examples from the lessons: We saw big orange carp in the pond. | Grandad caught a carp in the lake. | Koi are a kind of carp. | In Australia, carp are a pest in the rivers. | Stop carping about the weather! | He carped on about the noise all day.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural of the fish is usually «carp» (one carp, five carp); «carps» is for kinds. The verb is regular and a bit formal or old-fashioned; «moan» and «grumble» are more common.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A cashew is a curved, kidney-shaped nut that grows at the bottom of a fruit called the cashew apple on a tropical tree. 2) The cashew is also the tree that grows these nuts.
its sense in the lessons: In food and health lessons, cashews are a healthy snack, but some children are allergic to nuts, so many schools are «nut-free». In science and geography, cashew trees grow in hot countries such as India, Vietnam and parts of Africa and Brazil; the shell has an oil that burns the skin, so the nuts are roasted or steamed before eating. Phrases: «cashew nuts», «roasted cashews», «nut allergy».
examples from the lessons: Mum added cashews to the stir-fry. | I like salted cashews. | Our school is nut-free, so no cashews in lunchboxes. | Cashews grow under a fruit called the cashew apple. | He is allergic to cashews and carries an EpiPen. | A handful of cashews is a healthy snack.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Pronounced KASH-oo (also ka-SHOO). Safety: nut allergies can be very serious; never share nut snacks with a child who is allergic.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A chromosome is a tiny thread-like structure inside the centre (nucleus) of a living cell, made of DNA, which carries the instructions (genes) for how a living thing grows and works. 2) Humans usually have 46 chromosomes in each cell, in 23 pairs: one of each pair comes from the mother and one from the father.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on inheritance and genetics, chromosomes explain why children look like their parents. The X and Y chromosomes are involved in whether a baby is usually born a boy or a girl. Some people are born with an extra chromosome, as in Down syndrome; they are just as valued as anyone. Phrases: «X chromosome», «Y chromosome», «pairs of chromosomes».
