examples from the lessons: Chromosomes are inside the nucleus of a cell. | People usually have 23 pairs of chromosomes. | Each chromosome carries many genes. | You get half your chromosomes from each parent. | People with Down syndrome have an extra copy of chromosome 21. | We looked at a picture of chromosomes under a microscope.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Pronounced KROH-muh-sohm. In number problems: 23 pairs = 46 chromosomes (23 × 2); an egg or sperm cell has only half, 23. Chromosomes, genes and DNA are linked: DNA makes up genes, and genes sit on chromosomes.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Clockwise means moving round in the same direction as the hands of a clock: from the top to the right, down, to the left and back up. 2) The opposite is anticlockwise (UK, Australia, New Zealand, Ireland) or counterclockwise (US, Canada).
its sense in the lessons: In maths lessons, pupils turn shapes clockwise or anticlockwise by quarter turns (90°), half turns (180°) and three-quarter turns (270°), and give directions on grids. In everyday life, you usually turn a screw or jar lid clockwise to tighten it («righty-tighty, lefty-loosey»). In PE and games, players may pass round a circle clockwise. Phrases: «turn clockwise», «a quarter turn clockwise», «clockwise direction».
examples from the lessons: Turn the shape a quarter turn clockwise. | The children walked clockwise round the circle. | Turn the lid clockwise to close the jar. | If you face north and turn 90° clockwise, you face east. | The hands of a clock always move clockwise. | Stir the mixture clockwise, then the other way.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word. In maths: a full turn is 360°, so a turn of 90° clockwise is the same as 270° anticlockwise. Facing north: a quarter turn clockwise → east; half turn → south; three-quarter turn → west.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A coelacanth is a large, rare, deep-sea fish with thick fleshy fins, a very old kind of fish once thought to have died out with the dinosaurs. 2) It is often called a «living fossil» because it looks much like its fossil relatives from millions of years ago.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on fossils, extinction and evolution, the coelacanth is famous because scientists knew it only from fossils until a fisherman caught a living one off South Africa. Its leg-like fins help show how fish are related to land animals. Phrases: «living fossil», «the coelacanth was rediscovered».
examples from the lessons: The coelacanth was thought to be extinct for millions of years. | A fisherman caught a living coelacanth. | Scientists call the coelacanth a living fossil. | Coelacanths live in deep, dark water near caves. | Its fins move a little like legs. | We saw a model coelacanth at the natural history museum.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Tricky spelling and sound: written «coelacanth», said SEE-luh-kanth (the «oe» sounds like «ee»). «Living fossil» is a nickname; the fish has still changed over time.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A colon is the punctuation mark (:) that introduces a list, an explanation or an example: «You will need: a pen, a ruler and glue». 2) The colon is the main part of the large intestine (large bowel), the tube in the body where water is taken out of food waste. 3) In maths and times, a colon separates numbers: in ratios (2:3) and in clock times (7:30). 4) The colon is the money of Costa Rica (colón).
its sense in the lessons: In English grammar lessons, pupils use colons before lists, before an explanation, and in play scripts after a character's name. In science and health lessons, the colon is part of the digestive system after the small intestine. In maths, the colon in 3:2 is read «three to two» for a ratio. Phrases: «use a colon», «colon before a list», «the large intestine (colon)».
examples from the lessons: Put a colon before the list. | Bring three things: a hat, a drink and sun cream. | The colon is part of the large intestine. | The ratio of boys to girls is 3:4. | School starts at 8:45. | In a play script, write a colon after the name: «Tom: Hello!»
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Not the same as a semicolon (;), which joins two linked sentences. In ratio problems, 2:3 means for every 2 of the first there are 3 of the second, so 5 parts in total. Do not confuse with «colonel» (an army officer) or «colony».

part of speech: noun (confiture, confitures) — French word, rare in English
meaning for a pupil: 1) (French) Confiture is the French word for jam or fruit preserve: «confiture de fraises» means strawberry jam; to an English ear it sounds like «kon-fee-TOOR». 2) In English it is a rare, fancy word used on jars and menus for a jam or sweet preserve.
its sense in the lessons: In French lessons, «la confiture» comes up in breakfast vocabulary: bread, butter and jam (du pain, du beurre et de la confiture). In shops, posh jars may say «confiture». It is not a usual English word; in English people say «jam» (UK) or «jelly» or «preserves» (US). Phrases: «confiture d'abricots» (apricot jam).
examples from the lessons: In French, jam is «la confiture». | «Je voudrais de la confiture» means «I'd like some jam». | The jar said «Confiture de fraises». | We spread confiture on our croissants in Paris. | Confiture is made by boiling fruit with sugar. | The menu offered toast with butter and confiture.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly a French word, not ordinary English. In French it is feminine: «la confiture». False friend trap: it is not «confectionery» (sweets) and not «comfit» exactly, though they come from the same old root.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Continental means to do with a continent, one of the world's large land masses: «continental shelf», «continental climate». 2) (UK, Ireland) Continental means from mainland Europe, as opposed to Britain and Ireland: «continental breakfast», «a continental holiday». 3) (US) Continental can mean to do with the main part of North America, as in «the continental United States» (all states except Alaska and Hawaii).
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons, pupils learn the seven continents and about continental plates that move slowly and cause earthquakes; a «continental climate» has hot summers and cold winters far from the sea. In everyday life, a hotel «continental breakfast» is bread, croissants, jam, cheese and coffee instead of a cooked breakfast. Phrases: «continental breakfast», «continental drift», «continental shelf», «continental Europe».
examples from the lessons: We had a continental breakfast of croissants and jam. | Continental drift means the continents move very slowly. | The continental shelf is the shallow sea floor near the coast. | Moscow has a continental climate with cold winters. | The continental United States does not include Hawaii. | Many British families take holidays on the Continent.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective; no comparative. «The Continent» (capital C) in British English means mainland Europe. The seven continents: Africa, Antarctica, Asia, Australia (Oceania), Europe, North America, South America.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Cowpox is a mild disease of cows that causes sores on their udders and can pass to people, giving them a few small blisters. 2) In history, catching cowpox protected people from the deadly disease smallpox, which led to the first vaccine.
its sense in the lessons: In science and history lessons, Edward Jenner, an English doctor, noticed that milkmaids who had caught cowpox did not get smallpox; he used material from cowpox sores to protect a boy, which began vaccination. The word «vaccine» comes from the Latin word for cow. Today smallpox has been wiped out thanks to vaccines. Phrases: «cowpox and smallpox», «Edward Jenner».
examples from the lessons: Milkmaids who caught cowpox did not get smallpox. | Edward Jenner used cowpox to make the first vaccine. | Cowpox gives cows sores on their udders. | Cowpox is much milder than smallpox. | The word «vaccine» comes from «vacca», Latin for cow. | Our class acted out Jenner's cowpox experiment.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable; one word. Do not confuse with chickenpox, a common children's illness that has nothing to do with chickens. Jenner's experiment would not be allowed today, because it put a child at risk without the safety rules we now use.

part of speech: verb (creak, creaks, creaked, creaking); noun (a creak, creaks)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To creak is to make a long, high, squeaking sound, like an old door, a wooden floor or stairs when they move or are walked on. 2) A creak is that sound. 3) To creak can mean to work badly because of being old or weak: «The old system is creaking».
its sense in the lessons: In stories, especially spooky ones, creaking doors and floorboards build suspense; it is a good onomatopoeia for creative writing. In science lessons on sound, a creak happens when two surfaces rub and vibrate. In everyday life, oiling hinges stops them creaking. Phrases: «creaky door», «creak open», «creaking floorboards».
examples from the lessons: The old door creaked open. | I heard a creak on the stairs. | The floorboards creaked as I tiptoed past. | Dad oiled the gate so it would stop creaking. | The ship's timbers creaked in the storm. | In the dark, every creak made me jump.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Sounds exactly like «creek» (a small stream) — a homophone trap. Adjective: creaky (a creaky door). «Creak» is a long squeak; «crack» is a sudden sharp sound.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Cud is food that a cow, sheep, goat or deer has swallowed and then brings back up from its stomach into its mouth to chew again. 2) «To chew the cud» means to chew food this way; figuratively, it means to think about something slowly and carefully.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, animals that chew the cud are called ruminants; they have a stomach with several parts so they can digest tough grass. In farm visits and stories, cows lie in the field chewing the cud. In the Bible, animals that chew the cud and have split hooves are listed as clean to eat in the old laws (Bible). Phrases: «chew the cud», «chewing the cud».
examples from the lessons: The cow lay in the field chewing the cud. | Sheep and goats chew the cud too. | Animals that chew the cud are called ruminants. | A cow brings grass back up from its stomach as cud. | Grandad sat on the bench chewing the cud about the old days. | In old laws, animals that chew the cud were allowed as food.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «chew the cud», not «a cud». Rhymes with «mud». Do not confuse with «could».

part of speech: adjective (cultivated, more cultivated); verb form (past of «cultivate»: cultivated)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Cultivated land has been dug, planted and looked after for growing crops. 2) A cultivated plant has been grown by people on purpose, not wild: «cultivated strawberries». 3) A cultivated person is well educated, polite and knows about art, music and books. 4) As a verb form, «cultivated» means grew or developed: «She cultivated roses»; «He cultivated a friendship».
its sense in the lessons: In geography and science lessons, cultivated land is farmland; the first farmers cultivated wheat and barley. In history, people moved from hunting and gathering to cultivating crops. In stories, a cultivated character speaks politely and enjoys culture. Phrases: «cultivated land», «cultivated crops», «cultivated manners».
examples from the lessons: The farmers cultivated rice in the wet fields. | Wild strawberries are smaller than cultivated ones. | The cultivated fields stretched for miles. | Long ago, people first cultivated wheat. | Her aunt is a cultivated woman who loves opera. | He cultivated a good friendship with his neighbour.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past form of «cultivate»: cultivate, cultivates, cultivated, cultivating. Opposite of a cultivated plant is a wild one. Related: cultivation (the act of growing crops).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Destiny is what will happen to someone in the future, especially when it seems already decided by fate or a higher power. 2) Someone's destiny can be the important job or role they seem meant to have: «It was her destiny to be a doctor». 3) Destiny is also a power that some people believe controls the future (fate).
its sense in the lessons: In stories, legends and films, a hero often has a destiny to save the kingdom, and the story asks whether people can choose their own destiny. In ethics and RE lessons, pupils discuss free will: some people believe God or fate guides life; others believe we make our own choices. Phrases: «control your own destiny», «it was his destiny», «a sense of destiny», «meet your destiny».
examples from the lessons: The prophecy said it was his destiny to become king. | You can shape your own destiny by working hard. | She felt it was her destiny to help animals. | In the film, the hero fought against his destiny. | Some people believe destiny brings friends together. | The two countries share a common destiny.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable for the idea («a belief in destiny»); countable for one person's future («their destinies»). Similar word: fate. Do not confuse with «destination» (the place you are going to).

part of speech: noun (a fiddle, fiddles); verb (fiddle, fiddles, fiddled, fiddling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A fiddle is a violin, especially when it is used to play folk or country music. 2) To fiddle with something is to keep touching or moving it with your fingers, often because you are nervous or bored. 3) (informal) To fiddle is to cheat, especially by changing figures to get money: «fiddle the books». A fiddle is such a cheat. 4) (UK, informal) «A fiddle» can mean a task that is awkward and fiddly. 5) To play the fiddle is to play the violin.
its sense in the lessons: In music lessons, fiddles are played in Irish, Scottish and country music. In class, teachers say «Stop fiddling with your pencil». In news about money, «fiddling expenses» means cheating. Phrases: «fit as a fiddle» (very healthy), «play second fiddle» (be less important), «fiddle with», «fiddle about / around», «fiddly».
examples from the lessons: She played a jig on her fiddle. | Stop fiddling with your zip and listen. | Grandpa is ninety but as fit as a fiddle. | He fiddled the numbers to pay less tax. | I'm tired of playing second fiddle to my big sister. | It was a real fiddle putting the tiny Lego pieces together. | Irish music often has a fiddle, a flute and a drum.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb (fiddled, fiddling). Adjective «fiddly» (UK) means small and hard to handle. A fiddle and a violin are the same instrument; «fiddle» is the informal name. «Fiddlesticks!» is an old-fashioned mild way to say «nonsense».

part of speech: noun (a forearm, forearms); verb (forearm, forearms, forearmed — rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The forearm is the part of the arm between the elbow and the wrist. 2) (rare) To forearm is to prepare or arm yourself before something happens; it appears in the saying «Forewarned is forearmed», meaning if you know about a danger beforehand, you can be ready for it.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, the forearm has two bones, the radius and the ulna, and muscles that move the hand. In PE and sport, players use their forearms in volleyball and in blocking. In maths, children measure the length of their forearm (from elbow to fingertips is an old measure called a cubit). Phrases: «forewarned is forearmed», «forearm pass».
examples from the lessons: He broke his forearm falling off his bike. | The forearm has two bones: the radius and the ulna. | Hit the volleyball with your forearms. | She had a tattoo on her forearm. | Measure your forearm with a tape measure. | Forewarned is forearmed, so check the weather before the hike.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; one word. Stress: FORE-arm for the noun, fore-ARM for the verb. A cubit (from elbow to fingertip) was about 45 cm in the old days, so it differs a little from the forearm alone.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A gladiator was a man in ancient Rome who fought other men or wild animals in an arena to entertain crowds, often with swords, nets or tridents. 2) A gladiator can mean someone who fights hard in a contest or argument (figurative).
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons on the Romans, gladiators fought in amphitheatres such as the Colosseum; many were slaves, prisoners or criminals, though some became famous. Pupils discuss why crowds enjoyed such cruel games and how attitudes have changed. Phrases: «gladiator fight», «gladiator school», «in the arena».
examples from the lessons: The gladiator fought a lion in the Colosseum. | Many gladiators were slaves. | Gladiators trained at special schools. | Some gladiators used a net and a trident. | The crowd cheered as the gladiators entered the arena. | We made gladiator helmets out of card.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Pronounced GLAD-ee-ay-tur. Myth trap: the thumbs-up or thumbs-down signal for life or death is not certain; historians are not sure which gesture meant what.

part of speech: proper noun (Google); verb (google, googles, googled, googling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Google is a large technology company and its search engine, a website used to find information on the internet (a name). 2) To google something is to search for it on the internet, especially using Google: «I googled the answer». 3) (maths, old) A «googol» (spelled differently) is the number 1 followed by 100 zeros; the company's name was a play on that word.
its sense in the lessons: In computing and online-safety lessons, pupils learn to search well: use good keywords, check that websites are reliable, and know that not everything online is true. In everyday talk, «Just google it» means look it up online. Phrases: «google it», «a Google search», «Google Maps».
examples from the lessons: I googled how tall a giraffe is. | Just google it if you don't know. | Mum used Google Maps to find the way. | Not everything you find on Google is true. | Type your keywords into the search box. | She googled pictures of the planets for her project.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a company name, write Google with a capital G; the verb «google» is often lower case. Regular verb (googled, googling). «Googol» (the number) is spelled with «-ol». Searching is not the same as checking: compare more than one good source.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A graveyard is a piece of land, often around a church, where dead people are buried. 2) A graveyard is a place where old, broken or unwanted things are left: «a car graveyard», «an elephant graveyard». 3) «Graveyard shift» means work done late at night until morning (informal).
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, gravestones in a churchyard graveyard tell us names and ages of people from the past. In church life, Christians bury the dead there with prayers. In spooky stories, graveyards appear at night, though real ones are calm, respectful places. Phrases: «graveyard shift», «in the graveyard», «churchyard».
examples from the lessons: The old church has a graveyard with mossy stones. | We visited Grandad's grave in the graveyard. | Please walk quietly and respectfully in a graveyard. | The ghost story was set in a graveyard at midnight. | Old aeroplanes are kept in a desert graveyard. | Nurses on the graveyard shift work all night.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; one word. Similar words: cemetery (a large burial ground, not always by a church), churchyard (the land around a church). Graveyards are places to remember people, so behave with respect.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A hagfish is a long, eel-shaped sea fish with no jaws and no proper backbone that lives on the deep sea floor and eats dead animals. 2) It is famous for making huge amounts of slime when attacked, which clogs the gills of predators.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on adaptations and food chains, the hagfish is a scavenger (it eats dead animals) and a decomposer-helper on the sea floor; its slime defence is a strange adaptation. It is one of the oldest kinds of fish. Phrases: «hagfish slime», «slime eel».
examples from the lessons: A hagfish can make a bucket of slime in seconds. | The hagfish ate the dead whale on the sea floor. | Hagfish have no jaws. | Sharks spit out hagfish because of the slime. | Hagfish can tie themselves in knots to clean off slime. | Some people call the hagfish a slime eel.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural is usually «hagfish» (like «fish»). It is not a real eel, even though it looks like one.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A herb is a plant whose leaves, seeds or flowers are used to add flavour to food, such as basil, mint, parsley, rosemary and thyme. 2) A herb is a plant used to make medicine or tea, such as chamomile or lavender. 3) (science) A herb is any small plant with a soft stem, not woody like a tree or bush.
its sense in the lessons: In cooking and food lessons, children grow herbs on windowsills and use them in recipes. In history, people made herbal remedies, though not all of them worked. In science, herbs are non-woody plants. Phrases: «fresh herbs», «dried herbs», «herb garden», «herbal tea».
examples from the lessons: Mum grows herbs on the kitchen windowsill. | Add some fresh herbs to the soup. | Mint is a herb that smells fresh. | We planted a herb garden at school. | Grandma makes tea from dried herbs. | Basil is a herb used in pizza sauce.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. British English says «a herb» with the h sounded; American English says «an herb» with a silent h («erb»). Herbal medicines can be strong too: never take any without an adult.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An ichthyosaur was a large sea reptile that lived at the time of the dinosaurs and looked like a dolphin or a fish, with flippers, a long snout and big eyes. 2) It was not a dinosaur but a separate kind of reptile that breathed air and gave birth to live young in the sea.
its sense in the lessons: In science and history lessons, ichthyosaur fossils are famous because Mary Anning, a girl from Lyme Regis in England, found one of the first known skeletons on the beach and became an important fossil hunter. Ichthyosaurs teach about fossils, extinction and how unrelated animals can look alike (they look like dolphins but are reptiles). Phrases: «ichthyosaur fossil», «Mary Anning».
examples from the lessons: Mary Anning found an ichthyosaur fossil on the beach. | An ichthyosaur looked like a dolphin. | Ichthyosaurs breathed air, so they swam up to the surface. | Ichthyosaurs had very large eyes for seeing in deep water. | An ichthyosaur was a sea reptile, not a fish. | We saw an ichthyosaur skeleton in the museum.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; use «an». Pronounced IK-thee-uh-sor. The name means «fish lizard». Trap: ichthyosaurs were not dinosaurs; dinosaurs lived on land.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The Jurassic is a long period in Earth's history, many millions of years ago, in the middle of the age of dinosaurs. 2) Jurassic describes things from that period: «Jurassic rocks», «Jurassic fossils». 3) (informal) Jurassic can mean very old-fashioned, as a joke: «Dad's phone is positively Jurassic».
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on rocks and fossils, the Jurassic comes between the Triassic and the Cretaceous; dinosaurs such as Stegosaurus and Brachiosaurus lived then, as did the first birds. In the UK, the «Jurassic Coast» in Dorset and Devon is full of fossils, where Mary Anning searched. The film «Jurassic Park» made the word famous, but T. rex actually lived later, in the Cretaceous. Phrases: «the Jurassic period», «Jurassic Coast», «Jurassic Park».
examples from the lessons: Stegosaurus lived in the Jurassic. | We found ammonites on the Jurassic Coast. | The Jurassic came after the Triassic. | The first birds appeared in the Jurassic. | These Jurassic rocks are full of fossils. | Grandpa's computer is so slow it's practically Jurassic.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually written with a capital J. Pronounced joo-RASS-ik. Myth trap: Tyrannosaurus rex is not Jurassic; it lived in the later Cretaceous period. People did not live at the same time as dinosaurs.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A kestrel is a small bird of prey, a kind of falcon, with brown feathers and a long tail. 2) It is famous for hovering in one place in the air, beating its wings, while looking down for mice and insects.
its sense in the lessons: In nature lessons in the UK, Ireland and Australia (where the Nankeen kestrel lives), kestrels are often seen hovering beside motorways and fields; they are predators in food chains with voles and mice. Pupils learn words like «bird of prey», «talons» and «hover». Phrases: «a hovering kestrel», «bird of prey».
examples from the lessons: A kestrel hovered above the field. | The kestrel swooped down and caught a mouse. | Kestrels are small falcons. | We saw a kestrel beside the motorway. | In the food chain, the vole is eaten by the kestrel. | A kestrel has sharp talons and a hooked beak.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Pronounced KES-trel. Kestrels hover; most other falcons do not, which helps you tell them apart.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A kingfisher is a small, brightly coloured bird with a big head and a long sharp beak that dives into water to catch fish. 2) Some kingfishers, such as the Australian kookaburra, are large and catch lizards and insects on land.
its sense in the lessons: In nature lessons in the UK and Ireland, the common kingfisher is a bright blue and orange river bird; seeing one is a special sighting. In Australia and New Zealand, kookaburras and sacred kingfishers are kinds of kingfisher. Engineers in Japan copied the kingfisher's beak shape to make a quieter, faster bullet train (biomimicry). Phrases: «a flash of blue», «kingfisher blue».
examples from the lessons: A kingfisher dived into the river and caught a fish. | We saw a flash of blue — a kingfisher! | The kookaburra is a big kingfisher. | Kingfishers nest in tunnels in riverbanks. | The bullet train's nose was copied from a kingfisher's beak. | Kingfishers need clean rivers with lots of small fish.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; one word. A kingfisher is not related to kings; the name means it is a very good «fisher».

part of speech: noun (a loft, lofts); verb (loft, lofts, lofted, lofting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (UK, Ireland, Australia, New Zealand) A loft is the room or space just under the roof of a house, often used for storage (US: attic). 2) A loft is a large flat in an old factory or warehouse, with high ceilings (especially US). 3) A hayloft is the upper floor of a barn where hay is stored. 4) A pigeon loft is a shed for keeping pigeons. 5) To loft a ball is to hit or kick it high into the air.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, families keep boxes of old toys and decorations «up in the loft»; loft insulation keeps homes warm and saves energy (a science and energy topic). In stories, children find secrets in the loft. In sport, a player lofts the ball over a defender. Phrases: «up in the loft», «loft insulation», «loft conversion», «loft ladder».
examples from the lessons: The Christmas decorations are up in the loft. | Dad climbed the loft ladder. | Loft insulation keeps heat in the house. | We turned the loft into a bedroom. | The cat was hiding in the hayloft. | She lofted the ball over the goalkeeper.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. British «loft» is close to American «attic». Related adjective «lofty» means very high or proud. Regular verb (lofted).

part of speech: noun (a louvre, louvres; US «louver»); proper noun (the Louvre)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The Louvre is a famous art museum in Paris, France, in an old royal palace; it is home to the «Mona Lisa» (a name). 2) A louvre is one of a set of sloping slats in a door, window or shutter that let air in but keep out rain or direct light; also called a louvre window or louvred door.
its sense in the lessons: In art and geography lessons, the Louvre is one of the most visited museums in the world, with a glass pyramid entrance and paintings such as the Mona Lisa by Leonardo da Vinci. In design and technology, louvres let air flow through cupboards, cars and sheds. In French lessons, it is said «LOO-vruh». Phrases: «the Louvre Museum», «louvre doors».
examples from the lessons: The Mona Lisa hangs in the Louvre. | The Louvre has a big glass pyramid at the entrance. | We queued for an hour to get into the Louvre. | The cupboard has louvre doors so air can flow. | Tilt the louvres to keep out the sun. | The Louvre was once a palace for French kings.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital L for the museum («the Louvre»). The slats are spelled «louvre» in British English and «louver» in American English. The museum name in English sounds like «LOO-vruh» or «loov».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A lungfish is a freshwater fish that can breathe air with lungs as well as with gills. 2) Some lungfish can survive when their pond dries up by burying themselves in mud and breathing air for months.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on adaptations and evolution, the lungfish is a link between fish and land animals; the Australian lungfish in Queensland is a very old species, and African lungfish survive droughts in mud cocoons. Phrases: «Australian lungfish», «living fossil».
examples from the lessons: The lungfish swims up to gulp air. | When the pond dries out, the lungfish hides in the mud. | Lungfish have lungs and gills. | The Australian lungfish lives in rivers in Queensland. | A lungfish can live for many years. | Scientists study lungfish to learn how animals moved onto land.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural usually «lungfish». One word. Lungfish are fish, not amphibians, even though they breathe air.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A meridian is an imaginary line on the globe or a map that runs from the North Pole to the South Pole; lines of longitude are meridians. 2) The Prime Meridian is the meridian at 0° longitude that passes through Greenwich in London, from which other places are measured east or west. 3) (old, poetic) The meridian is the highest point of the sun at midday, or the peak of something. 4) In Chinese medicine, meridians are believed paths of energy in the body (a belief, not proved by science).
its sense in the lessons: In geography and maths lessons, pupils use meridians (longitude) and parallels (latitude) as a grid to find places; time zones are based on meridians. At Greenwich, visitors stand with one foot each side of the Prime Meridian. Phrases: «the Prime Meridian», «Greenwich Meridian», «lines of longitude».
examples from the lessons: The Prime Meridian passes through Greenwich. | Meridians run from pole to pole. | London is on the 0° meridian. | I stood with one foot in each hemisphere on the meridian line. | Lines of longitude are also called meridians. | Places east of the Prime Meridian are ahead in time.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Meridians (longitude) run north–south; parallels (latitude) run east–west. In maths and time problems: the Earth turns 360° in 24 hours, so every 15° of longitude is about one hour of time difference.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Michael is a common boy's and man's name in English-speaking countries (a name); short forms are Mike, Mick, Mikey and Mickey. 2) (Bible, church) Michael is an archangel in the Bible, who Christians believe leads God's angels against evil; Saint Michael is shown with a sword, defeating a dragon.
its sense in the lessons: Children meet Michael as a classmate's name, in stories and in songs. In RE and church lessons, Saint Michael the Archangel appears in the Bible and in church windows; Michaelmas is his feast day in the church year. Phrases: «Saint Michael», «Michael the Archangel», «Michaelmas».
examples from the lessons: Michael sits next to me in maths. | My uncle Michael is called Mike for short. | Saint Michael is shown defeating a dragon. | In the Bible, Michael is an archangel. | Michael scored the winning goal. | The church is named after Saint Michael.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always a capital M. Tricky spelling: «ae» in the middle, said MY-kul. Do not invent facts about a person called Michael; it is just a name unless the text tells you more.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A millennium is a period of a thousand years. 2) «The millennium» often means the moment when a new thousand years starts in the calendar, celebrated with big parties and fireworks. 3) (Bible, church) The Millennium is a thousand-year reign of Christ described in the Book of Revelation, which Christians understand in different ways.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and history lessons, pupils learn time words: a decade is 10 years, a century is 100 years, and a millennium is 1,000 years; timelines may show several millennia. In science, «over millennia» means over many thousands of years, as rivers carve valleys. Phrases: «a new millennium», «for millennia», «the turn of the millennium».
examples from the lessons: A millennium is a thousand years. | Ten centuries make a millennium. | The pyramids have stood for several millennia. | People celebrated the new millennium with fireworks. | Rivers shape valleys over millennia. | How many decades are in a millennium? One hundred.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: double l and double n: millennium. Plural: millennia (more common) or millenniums. In maths: 1 millennium = 10 centuries = 100 decades = 1,000 years. «Millennial» as a noun means a person born around the end of the last millennium.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Obsidian is a hard, shiny black (or dark) natural glass that forms when lava from a volcano cools very quickly. 2) Obsidian was used long ago to make very sharp knives, arrowheads and mirrors.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on rocks, obsidian is an igneous rock (made from cooled lava) that cooled too fast for crystals to grow, so it is glassy; when it breaks it has very sharp curved edges. In history, the Aztecs and other peoples made tools and mirrors from it. In the game Minecraft, obsidian is a very hard block. Phrases: «obsidian blade», «volcanic glass».
examples from the lessons: Obsidian is black volcanic glass. | Obsidian forms when lava cools very quickly. | Ancient people made sharp arrowheads from obsidian. | The museum had an Aztec mirror made of obsidian. | In Minecraft you need obsidian to build a portal. | Obsidian is an igneous rock.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «a piece of obsidian». Pronounced ob-SID-ee-un. Safety: broken obsidian is sharper than a knife, so handle with care.

part of speech: noun (an opening, openings); verb form (open, opens, opened, opening); adjective (the opening scene)
meaning for a pupil: 1) An opening is a gap or hole that something can pass through. 2) An opening is the start of something, such as a story, film, game or match. 3) An opening is a chance or a free job or place, such as a job opening. 4) The opening of a shop, bridge or show is the event when it first starts to be used. 5) Opening is the -ing form of open: making something open.
its sense in the lessons: In stories the opening is the first part that grabs the reader; teachers ask pupils to write a strong opening. In science, animals and plants have openings (a mouth, a pore). In everyday life: opening hours, opening night, an opening ceremony. In chess and sport the opening is the first moves. Phrases: opening hours, opening line, grand opening, opening ceremony, an opening for (a chance).
examples from the lessons: The mouse squeezed through a small opening in the fence. | The opening of the story begins with a storm. | The shop's opening hours are nine to five. | The Olympic opening ceremony was full of fireworks. | There is a job opening at the library. | She is opening her birthday presents. | The striker saw an opening and scored. | Write an opening sentence that makes the reader curious.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one opening, two openings. As a noun it is the start or a hole; as a verb form it needs be (is opening) or comes after other verbs. Opening hours = the times a place is open. Do not confuse with open (adjective): the door is open, not the door is opening, unless it is moving now.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal, old-fashioned) Pa is a word for father or dad, used mostly in old stories and in some families. 2) (abbreviation) p.a. means per annum, Latin for each year, as in a salary of 30,000 pounds p.a. 3) (science) Pa is the short symbol for pascal, the unit for measuring pressure. 4) (abbreviation) PA can mean a personal assistant (a helper at work) or a public address system (loudspeakers). 5) (New Zealand, Maori) A pa is a Maori village or hill fort, often with fences and ditches.
its sense in the lessons: In old stories, such as books about farm families in America, children call their parents Ma and Pa. In science and weather, Pa (pascal) measures pressure; hPa (hectopascal) is used on weather maps. In everyday life the PA announces things at school or the station. In New Zealand history lessons a pa is a fortified Maori settlement.
examples from the lessons: Pa came home from the fields at sunset. | Ma and Pa sat by the fire and told stories. | The job pays 25,000 pounds p.a. | Air pressure is measured in pascals, written Pa. | The weather map showed 1010 hPa over the city. | The head teacher spoke over the PA system. | We visited an old Maori pa on a hill. | Her PA arranges all her meetings.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pa (dad) is informal and old-fashioned; most children today say dad or daddy. Ma and Pa go together. Pa (pascal) has a capital P because the unit is named after Blaise Pascal. p.a. is usually written with dots and lower-case letters. Do not mix up pa with par (as in golf) or pah (a sound of disgust).

part of speech: noun (a pore, pores); verb (pore, pores, pored, poring — pore over)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A pore is a tiny hole in skin, a leaf or a rock that lets sweat, air or water pass through. 2) To pore over something means to read or study it very carefully for a long time.
its sense in the lessons: In science, skin has pores for sweat, leaves have tiny pores (stomata) for gases, and soil and rock have pores that hold water. In everyday life people talk about clean or blocked pores. In stories a character might pore over a map or an old book looking for a clue. Phrase: pore over.
examples from the lessons: Sweat comes out through tiny pores in your skin. | Leaves breathe through pores on their underside. | Sponges are full of pores. | Water soaks into the pores of the sandstone. | She pored over the treasure map all evening. | Detectives pored over the old letters. | We pored over the instructions before building the model.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: one pore, many pores. The verb is almost always pore over. Homophones: pour (pour water) and poor (having little money) sound the same in many accents. Trap: you pore over a book (study it), you do not pour over it, though people often misspell it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A puma is a large wild cat of North and South America with a plain sandy-brown coat and a long tail. It is also called a cougar or mountain lion.
its sense in the lessons: In science and nature lessons the puma is a predator and a carnivore; it hunts deer and lives in mountains, forests and deserts from Canada to the tip of South America. It cannot roar but can purr, hiss and scream. In stories it is a silent, powerful hunter. Puma is also the name of a sports clothing company.
examples from the lessons: A puma can leap high into a tree. | The puma stalked a deer through the forest. | Pumas live alone except for mothers with cubs. | Puma, cougar and mountain lion are three names for the same cat. | Puma cubs are born with spots that fade as they grow. | Hikers in Canada were warned about a puma nearby.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one puma, two pumas. The same animal has several names: puma, cougar, mountain lion, panther (in Florida). Pumas are not big cats in the scientific sense because they cannot roar. Do not confuse with the jaguar, which has spots.

part of speech: noun (the Renaissance; a renaissance, renaissances); adjective (Renaissance art)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The Renaissance was a time in Europe, from about the 1300s to the 1600s, when art, science and learning grew greatly, starting in Italy. 2) A renaissance is a new burst of interest or energy in something, a rebirth.
its sense in the lessons: In history and art lessons the Renaissance brings names like Leonardo da Vinci, Michelangelo and Galileo; artists studied the human body, used perspective, and scholars read old Greek and Roman books again. The printing press spread ideas. In everyday life a town or a hobby can have a renaissance when it becomes popular again. A Renaissance man or woman is someone good at many things.
examples from the lessons: Leonardo da Vinci was a famous painter of the Renaissance. | During the Renaissance, artists learned to draw with perspective. | The Renaissance began in Italy, in cities such as Florence. | Board games are having a renaissance. | Our old town centre has enjoyed a renaissance with new shops. | She is a real Renaissance woman: she paints, codes and plays the violin.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The word comes from French and means rebirth. When it names the historical period it has a capital R and the: the Renaissance. Spelling trap: double n and double s, renaissance. Usually said ren-AY-sunss (UK) or REN-uh-sahnss (US).

part of speech: noun (shellfish — plural usually the same, shellfish)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Shellfish are water animals with a shell, such as crabs, lobsters, prawns, mussels, oysters and clams, especially when eaten as food.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons shellfish are not true fish: some are crustaceans (crabs, lobsters, shrimps) and some are molluscs (mussels, oysters, scallops). In everyday life and safety, some people have a shellfish allergy, which can be very dangerous, and shellfish must be fresh and cooked properly. Food labels warn about shellfish.
examples from the lessons: Crabs and lobsters are shellfish. | My uncle is allergic to shellfish. | We ate shellfish at the seaside restaurant. | Shellfish live in rock pools and on the sea bed. | The menu says this dish contains shellfish. | Mussels are shellfish that cling to rocks.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable or the plural is the same: some shellfish, many shellfish. Trap: despite the name, shellfish are not fish; they have no backbone. Seafood is a wider word that includes fish too.

part of speech: noun (shipping — uncountable); verb form (ship, ships, shipped, shipping)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Shipping is the sending of goods from one place to another, by sea, air, road or post. 2) Shipping is the cost of sending things you buy, as in free shipping. 3) Shipping means all the ships of an area or country, as in shipping lanes. 4) Shipping is the -ing form of ship: sending something.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, online shops charge for shipping or offer free shipping. In geography, busy shipping lanes cross the oceans and ports handle shipping containers. In the UK the Shipping Forecast on radio gives sea weather. In maths problems shipping is often a cost added to a price.
examples from the lessons: The game costs 20 dollars plus 5 dollars shipping. | The shop offers free shipping on orders over 30 pounds. | The English Channel is full of shipping. | Shipping containers are stacked high at the port. | They are shipping the parcel tomorrow. | Fog can be dangerous for shipping. | Dad listens to the Shipping Forecast at night.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a noun it is uncountable: no a shipping, no shippings. In maths: total cost = price + shipping; free shipping means add 0. Shipping (UK English too) is used for posting goods even when no ship is involved; British people also say postage or delivery.

part of speech: noun (spam — uncountable; Spam); verb (spam, spams, spammed, spamming)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Spam is unwanted messages sent to many people at once, usually emails or texts trying to sell something or trick you. 2) To spam means to send lots of unwanted messages, or to post the same thing again and again. 3) Spam is a brand of tinned cooked pork meat.
its sense in the lessons: In online safety lessons spam often hides scams and phishing links: do not click, do not reply, report or delete it. Email programs have a spam folder or junk folder. In games and chats, spamming means flooding the chat or using the same move again and again. Spam (the meat) is a tinned food from the USA, famous in wartime Britain.
examples from the lessons: My email filter sent the message to the spam folder. | Never click links in spam. | Stop spamming the chat with emojis! | He kept spamming the same attack in the game. | The spam said I had won a prize, but it was a trick. | Grandad remembers eating Spam sandwiches. | Report the account if it sends spam.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spam (messages) is uncountable: some spam, a lot of spam, a spam email. The verb doubles m: spammed, spamming. Spam with a capital S is the meat brand. A spammer is a person who sends spam.

part of speech: verb (spawn, spawns, spawned, spawning); noun (spawn — uncountable: frogspawn)
meaning for a pupil: 1) When fish or frogs spawn, they lay lots of eggs in water. 2) Spawn is the mass of eggs laid by fish, frogs or toads, like frogspawn. 3) To spawn something means to cause many new things to appear, as in the film spawned three sequels. 4) (games) In video games, to spawn means for a player or character to appear in the game world; the spawn point is where they appear.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on life cycles, frogs lay frogspawn in ponds in spring; it hatches into tadpoles. Salmon swim upriver to spawn. In computer games, players spawn and respawn after losing a life. In everyday talk, one popular thing can spawn many copies.
examples from the lessons: Frogs spawn in ponds in early spring. | We saw a clump of frogspawn in the school pond. | Salmon swim up the river to spawn. | The film spawned a whole series of toys. | In the game you spawn next to a castle. | After you lose a life, you respawn at the last checkpoint. | Zombies spawn at night in that game.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spawn as a noun is uncountable: some spawn, not a spawn. Frogspawn is written as one word. Respawn means spawn again. Older and formal use: spawn can sound negative, as in spawn of the devil in old stories.

part of speech: verb (stoke, stokes, stoked, stoking); adjective (stoked — slang)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To stoke a fire means to add fuel such as coal or wood and stir it so it burns more strongly. 2) To stoke a feeling such as fear or anger means to make it stronger. 3) (slang, stoked) If you are stoked, you are very excited and happy, especially in Australia, New Zealand and the USA.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons about steam trains and ships, stokers stoked the furnace with coal. In everyday life people stoke the fire or the barbecue. In news, rumours can stoke fear. Stoked is common surfer and teen slang. Stoke-on-Trent is a city in England famous for pottery.
examples from the lessons: Grandpa stoked the fire before bed. | The stoker shovelled coal to stoke the engine. | Rumours stoked fears that the school would close. | The coach's speech stoked our team spirit. | I'm so stoked about the holidays! (slang) | She was stoked to win the surfing contest. (slang)
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: stoked, stoking. Stoked meaning excited is informal slang; do not use it in a formal essay. Do not confuse with stroke (a gentle touch or an illness) or stock.

part of speech: noun (a strand, strands); verb (strand, strands, stranded, stranding)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A strand is a single thin thread, hair or wire, or one of several twisted together. 2) A strand is one part of a story, plan or argument. 3) To strand someone means to leave them stuck somewhere with no way to leave; they are stranded. 4) (literary) A strand is a beach or the shore.
its sense in the lessons: In science, DNA is made of two strands twisted into a double helix, and ropes are made of strands. In stories, characters get stranded on desert islands or at airports. In school subjects, a course can have several strands (for example the number strand in maths). Whales sometimes strand themselves on beaches.
examples from the lessons: A strand of hair fell across her face. | The rope is made of three strands twisted together. | DNA has two strands. | The storm stranded us at the airport overnight. | The sailors were stranded on a desert island. | A whale was stranded on the beach. | The book weaves several strands into one story.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun. Stranded is the common adjective: stranded on an island. A strand of hair is one hair; strands of spaghetti. The Strand is also a famous street in London.

part of speech: verb form — past participle of sink (sink, sinks, sank, sunk, sinking); adjective (sunk, sunken)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Sunk is a form of sink: gone down under water or below a surface, as in the ship had sunk. 2) (informal) If you are sunk, you are in deep trouble with no way out. 3) Sunk is used for things set lower, as in sunk into the sofa.
its sense in the lessons: In history and stories: the Titanic sank in 1912 and lies sunk on the sea bed; pirate ships are sunk. In science, objects that are denser than water sink. In the game Battleships you say You sunk my battleship. In everyday talk, If we miss the bus, we're sunk.
examples from the lessons: The ship had sunk before help arrived. | The treasure lay in a sunk ship. | My heart sank when I saw the score, and it has sunk lower since. | If we lose the key, we're sunk! (informal) | She sat sunk in the armchair. | The stone has sunk to the bottom of the pond.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Forms: sink (now), sank (past), sunk (after have/has/had): it sank, it has sunk. Common mistake: it sunk yesterday is non-standard; say it sank. Sunken is used before a noun: a sunken ship, sunken treasure.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A survivor is a person or animal that stays alive after something dangerous, such as an accident, war, illness or disaster. 2) A survivor is someone who keeps going strongly through hard times.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons we read about survivors of shipwrecks, wars and earthquakes, and stories told by survivors. In safety lessons, survivors are helped by rescue teams. In nature, survival of the fittest means the creatures best suited to their home survive. In stories the survivor is often the brave hero.
examples from the lessons: Rescuers searched for survivors after the earthquake. | There were only a few survivors of the shipwreck. | She is a cancer survivor. | The survivor told reporters what happened. | Gran is a real survivor; nothing gets her down. | The last survivor of the old fort was a cat.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one survivor, many survivors. Ends in -or, not -er. Related words: survive (verb), survival (noun). Survivor of something: a survivor of the flood.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Tidal describes something to do with the tides, the daily rise and fall of the sea. 2) A tidal river or pool is one where the water level goes up and down with the tide.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and science, tides are caused mainly by the Moon's pull; tidal pools hold sea creatures at low tide; tidal energy makes electricity. A tidal wave is an old name for a giant wave, now usually called a tsunami. In safety lessons, beware tidal currents and check tide times before walking on sand flats.
examples from the lessons: Crabs hide in the tidal pools on the beach. | The Thames is tidal in London. | Tidal power stations use the movement of the sea. | The tidal causeway is only open at low tide. | A tidal surge flooded the coast. | We explored the tidal mudflats with a guide.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective only; no plural. Trap: a tidal wave is not really caused by tides; scientists say tsunami for waves made by earthquakes. Tidal comes from tide (noun) + -al.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Timber is wood that is cut and used for building or making things. 2) Timbers are the large wooden beams of a building or ship. 3) Timber! is a shout made by tree-cutters to warn people that a tree is falling.
its sense in the lessons: In design and technology lessons pupils work with timber. In history, old houses have timber frames and ships were built of timber. In geography, forests produce timber, and cutting too many trees causes problems. In the UK and Australia timber is the usual word; Americans say lumber for cut wood.
examples from the lessons: The shed is built from timber. | Old Tudor houses have black timber frames. | The ship's timbers creaked in the storm. | Logs are taken to the mill to be cut into timber. | Timber! shouted the woodcutter as the tree fell. | The forest is grown for timber.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly uncountable: some timber, a piece of timber. Timbers (plural) means beams. Do not confuse with timbre, a word for the special sound quality of a voice or instrument, which sounds the same. US English often uses lumber.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A toxin is a poison, especially one made by a living thing such as a plant, animal, fungus or germ.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, snakes, spiders, jellyfish and some frogs make toxins; bacteria can make toxins that cause food poisoning. Toxic means poisonous. In safety lessons, do not touch or eat unknown mushrooms, berries or animals. In everyday adverts, people talk about removing toxins from the body, which is often a myth.
examples from the lessons: Some frogs have toxins in their skin. | Bee stings contain a mild toxin. | The bacteria made a toxin that caused food poisoning. | The puffer fish has a deadly toxin. | Plants make toxins to stop animals eating them. | The liver cleans toxins from the blood.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a toxin, toxins. Related: toxic (adjective), toxicity. Myth: detox drinks and foot pads do not really pull toxins out; your liver and kidneys do that. A venom is a toxin that is injected by a bite or sting.

part of speech: noun (a tsar, tsars; also czar, tzar)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A tsar was an emperor of Russia before 1917. 2) (informal) A tsar is a person given strong power over one area by a government, as in a drugs tsar.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, tsars such as Peter the Great and Ivan the Terrible ruled Russia; the last tsar, Nicholas II, lost power in the Russian Revolution in 1917. The tsar's wife was the tsarina. In news, governments appoint tsars for things like energy or schools.
examples from the lessons: Peter the Great was a famous Russian tsar. | The last tsar was Nicholas II. | The tsar lived in a palace in Saint Petersburg. | The tsarina wore a jewelled crown. | The government named a new education tsar. | Bulgaria also had tsars long ago.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelled tsar (UK) or czar (often US); both are said zar. It comes from the Latin name Caesar. Female: tsarina. Plural: tsars.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The tundra is a huge cold, flat, treeless land in the far north (the Arctic) or high on mountains, where the ground below stays frozen all year.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and science lessons the tundra is one of the world's biomes. The deep ground is permafrost; only mosses, lichens, grasses and small shrubs grow. Animals include caribou (reindeer), Arctic foxes, lemmings, musk oxen and snowy owls. It covers parts of Canada, Alaska, Russia and Scandinavia. Climate change is melting the permafrost.
examples from the lessons: Trees cannot grow on the tundra. | Caribou travel across the tundra in huge herds. | In summer the tundra is covered with flowers and mosquitoes. | Lemmings live on the Arctic tundra. | The ground under the tundra is permafrost. | We made a model of the tundra biome in class.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually with the: the tundra. Do not confuse with taiga, the cold forest just south of the tundra. The word comes from the Sami language of northern Europe.

part of speech: adjective (a westerly wind); noun (a westerly, westerlies)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A westerly wind blows from the west. 2) Westerly also means towards the west or in the west, as in a westerly direction. 3) The westerlies are strong winds that blow from the west in the middle parts of the Earth.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and weather forecasts, wind names tell where the wind comes FROM: a westerly comes from the west. Britain and Ireland get mostly westerly winds from the Atlantic, bringing rain. Sailors, pilots and hikers use these words. In New Zealand and southern Australia the westerlies are strong.
examples from the lessons: A westerly wind brought rain from the Atlantic. | The westerlies blow across the southern oceans. | We sailed in a westerly direction. | The most westerly point of Ireland is on the Dingle Peninsula. | Strong westerlies are forecast for tomorrow. | The kite flew well in the westerly breeze.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: a westerly wind comes from the west and blows towards the east. Plural noun: westerlies. Similar words: easterly, northerly, southerly. Westerly is a bit more formal than west wind.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Abandonment is leaving someone or something behind for ever, especially when you should have cared for them. 2) Abandonment is giving up a plan or activity completely, as in the abandonment of the match. 3) (formal) Abandonment is acting wildly and freely without control, as in dancing with abandonment.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, the abandonment of a child or pet is a sad event; animal charities fight pet abandonment. In history, towns and castles fell into ruin after their abandonment. In sport, a match can be abandoned because of rain. In law, abandonment of a child or animal is a crime.
examples from the lessons: Pet abandonment rises after the holidays. | The abandonment of the village left the houses empty. | Rain led to the abandonment of the cricket match. | The orphan in the story felt the pain of abandonment. | The castle fell into ruin after its abandonment. | The team decided on the abandonment of the old plan.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable. Related: abandon (verb), abandoned (adjective). This is a formal word; in everyday talk people say left or given up. Spelling: abandon + ment.

part of speech: noun (an albino, albinos); adjective (an albino rabbit)
meaning for a pupil: 1) An albino is a person or animal born with little or no colour (pigment) in the skin, hair and eyes, so they are very pale or white. 2) Albino describes such an animal or person, as in an albino tiger.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons albinism is caused by genes, which are passed from parents. Albino animals often have pink or red eyes and are easier for predators to see. In respectful everyday talk about people, we say a person with albinism; people with albinism need to protect their skin and eyes from the sun.
examples from the lessons: The zoo has an albino alligator. | An albino rabbit has white fur and pink eyes. | Albino animals are rare in the wild. | A person with albinism may need strong sun cream. | The albino peacock looked like it was made of snow. | Albinism is passed on in genes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: albinos. Respect: for people, say a person with albinism rather than an albino, which can sound hurtful. Albino is not the same as a white breed of animal like a polar bear, which has dark skin and eyes.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Alkaline describes a substance that is the opposite of an acid: it has a pH above 7, such as soap, baking soda or bleach. 2) An alkaline battery is a common kind of battery that uses an alkaline chemical inside.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, the pH scale goes from 0 to 14: acids are below 7, neutral is 7 (pure water), and alkaline is above 7. Indicators such as red cabbage juice or litmus change colour: alkalis turn red litmus blue. Strong alkalis like bleach and oven cleaner can burn skin, so safety goggles and gloves are needed. Some soils are alkaline, which matters to gardeners.
examples from the lessons: Soap is slightly alkaline. | Red litmus paper turns blue in an alkaline solution. | Baking soda makes the water alkaline. | Bleach is strongly alkaline, so handle it with care. | The TV remote uses alkaline batteries. | Some plants grow best in alkaline soil. | Our cabbage indicator turned green in the alkaline liquid.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective only. The noun is alkali (plural alkalis). Opposite: acidic. A substance that is neither is neutral. Trap: alkaline does not mean safe; strong alkalis are as dangerous as strong acids. Myth: alkaline water does not change the pH of your blood.

part of speech: adjective (animated); verb form (animate, animates, animated, animating)
meaning for a pupil: 1) An animated film or cartoon is made from many drawings, models or computer pictures shown quickly so they seem to move. 2) An animated person or talk is lively, excited and full of energy. 3) Animated is the past form of animate: brought to life or made to move.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, animated films, cartoons and series are popular with children; animators make them frame by frame. In art and computing lessons, pupils make simple animations with flip books or code. In stories, someone talks in an animated way when excited.
examples from the lessons: We watched an animated film about talking cars. | Animated cartoons are made from thousands of pictures. | The children had an animated discussion about dinosaurs. | Grandad became animated when he talked about football. | The class animated a clay model for a short film. | The emoji is animated and waves at you.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective and past form of animate. Animation is the noun for the art or the film. Animated does not always mean a cartoon: an animated conversation is a lively one.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Archaeopteryx was a small animal that lived about 150 million years ago and had features of both dinosaurs and birds: feathers and wings, but also teeth, claws and a long bony tail.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about evolution and fossils, Archaeopteryx is a famous link between dinosaurs and birds. Its fossils were found in limestone in Germany. It was about the size of a crow or magpie. Scientists still discuss how well it could fly. Name: Greek for ancient wing.
examples from the lessons: Archaeopteryx had feathers like a bird and teeth like a dinosaur. | The first Archaeopteryx fossil was found in Germany. | Archaeopteryx was about the size of a magpie. | Our museum has a cast of an Archaeopteryx fossil. | Archaeopteryx helps show that birds came from dinosaurs. | Could Archaeopteryx really fly? Scientists still argue about it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As the name of the creature in science it is often written with a capital A and in italics. Said ar-kee-OP-ter-ix. Hard spelling: archae + opteryx. It is not a pterodactyl; pterosaurs were flying reptiles, not birds.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (Scots) Braw means fine, good, lovely or handsome, as in a braw day.
its sense in the lessons: Braw is a Scottish word heard in Scotland and in Scottish stories and songs. Scottish people may say It's a braw day for sunny weather or That's braw for great. In lessons on dialects it shows that English is spoken in many ways.
examples from the lessons: It's a braw day for a walk up the hill. (Scots) | That's a braw jumper you've got on. (Scots) | We had a braw time at the ceilidh. (Scots) | Gran says the view is braw. (Scots) | A braw lad and a bonny lass walked by. (Scots)
note for the reader of a maths problem: Braw is dialect from Scotland and northern England; in standard English say fine, lovely or great. It sounds like the start of brawl without the l. Do not confuse with bra or bro.

part of speech: noun (celery — uncountable; a stick of celery)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Celery is a vegetable with long pale-green crunchy stalks and leafy tops, eaten raw or cooked.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, celery is used in salads, soups and snacks with dips or peanut butter. In science lessons, celery is used in a famous experiment: put a stalk in coloured water and watch the colour travel up its tubes (xylem), showing how plants carry water. In food labels, celery is one of the allergens that must be listed in the UK and Europe.
examples from the lessons: Mum chopped celery for the soup. | Celery is crunchy and full of water. | We put a stick of celery in blue water and the leaves turned blue. | Ants on a log is celery with peanut butter and raisins. | This salad contains celery. | Celery seeds are used as a spice.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: some celery, a stick or a stalk of celery, not a celery. Myth: celery has negative calories is not true; it simply has very few. Celery is a listed allergen.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Chaos is a state of complete confusion and disorder, where nothing is organised. 2) (science, maths) Chaos is when tiny changes at the start lead to huge, hard-to-predict differences later, as in weather. 3) (myth, Bible) In old stories, Chaos was the formless emptiness before the world was made.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: the morning rush can be chaos, a messy bedroom is chaos, traffic chaos after snow. In stories, chaos breaks out when something goes wrong. In science, weather is chaotic, so forecasts get less certain the further ahead they look (the butterfly effect). In Greek myths, Chaos came first, before the gods.
examples from the lessons: The classroom was in chaos when the fire alarm went off. | Snow caused chaos on the roads. | The puppy caused chaos in the kitchen. | After the party the house was total chaos. | The weather is hard to predict because of chaos. | In Greek myths, the world began from Chaos.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: no a chaos, no chaoses. Adjective: chaotic. Said KAY-oss; the ch sounds like k. The opposite is order.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A coastline is the edge of the land where it meets the sea, especially its shape as seen on a map or along a long stretch.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons, coastlines change through erosion (waves wearing away cliffs) and deposition (sand building beaches); features include bays, headlands, cliffs, stacks and spits. Countries are compared by length of coastline. In maths there is a famous puzzle: the more carefully you measure a coastline, the longer it seems (the coastline paradox).
examples from the lessons: Norway has a very long, jagged coastline. | We walked along the rocky coastline. | Waves are wearing away the coastline. | The map shows the coastline of Ireland. | Australia's coastline has beautiful beaches. | Puffins nest along the Welsh coastline.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable, one word: coastline. Coast is the strip of land by the sea; coastline is mainly its shape or edge. Shoreline is similar and can be used for lakes too.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Cohesion is how well the parts of something stick or hold together. 2) (science) Cohesion is the pull between particles of the same kind, such as water molecules sticking to each other. 3) (writing) Cohesion is how well sentences and paragraphs link together so the writing flows. 4) Social cohesion is when people in a group or country get on and work together.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons, pupils improve cohesion with linking words like however, then, as a result, and by using pronouns. In science, cohesion makes water form drops and lets some insects walk on water (surface tension). In everyday life and news, team cohesion and community cohesion mean people sticking together.
examples from the lessons: Water drops form because of cohesion between water molecules. | Use linking words to give your writing cohesion. | The team's cohesion helped them win. | Pond skaters walk on water thanks to cohesion. | The essay lacks cohesion; the ideas jump around. | Festivals can build community cohesion.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Adjective: cohesive. In science, cohesion (same particles sticking together) is different from adhesion (sticking to something else, such as water sticking to glass). A formal school word.

part of speech: adjective (colonial); noun (a colonial, colonials — old use)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Colonial describes things to do with a colony, a land ruled by another, faraway country. 2) Colonial describes the time when a country was a colony, such as colonial America or colonial India, and its buildings and furniture style. 3) (science) Colonial animals live joined together in groups, like corals.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, empires such as Britain, Spain and France ruled colonies; colonial rule brought trade but also conquest, unfair treatment and slavery, and many colonies later fought for independence. In the USA, the Colonial period is before 1776. In Australia, New Zealand and Canada, colonial times are when British settlers arrived, which harmed First Nations, Maori and Aboriginal peoples.
examples from the lessons: India was under British colonial rule for many years. | The thirteen colonial states became the USA. | Colonial houses often have tall white columns. | The museum shows life in colonial Australia. | Colonial powers drew borders across Africa. | Corals are colonial animals.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective from colony. Related: colonist, colonise (UK) or colonize (US), colonialism (the system of ruling colonies). Colonial history is told differently by different peoples, so name the viewpoints.

part of speech: noun (comprehension; a comprehension, comprehensions — school exercise)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Comprehension is understanding: being able to know what something means. 2) (school) A comprehension is a reading exercise where you read a text and answer questions about it.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons, reading comprehension tests check whether you understood a passage, can find facts, and can infer (read between the lines). In everyday life, something beyond comprehension is too strange or huge to understand. Listening comprehension is used in language lessons.
examples from the lessons: We did a comprehension about a lighthouse keeper. | Read the passage, then answer the comprehension questions. | Her comprehension of maths improved a lot. | The size of the universe is beyond comprehension. | Listening comprehension is part of the French test. | Good comprehension means reading carefully.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable for understanding; countable for the school exercise. Verb: comprehend (formal for understand). Related: comprehensible (can be understood). A comprehensive school (UK) is a different meaning: a school for all.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A crested bird or animal has a crest: a tuft of feathers, fur or skin on top of its head. 2) Crested describes things with a decoration or badge (a crest) on them, as in crested notepaper or a crested blazer.
its sense in the lessons: In science and nature, many animals are named for their crests: crested newt, great crested grebe, crested tit, crested penguin, cockatoos. Crests help animals show off or signal. In everyday life in the UK and Ireland, school blazers and jumpers are often crested with the school badge.
examples from the lessons: The great crested grebe dances on the lake in spring. | A crested newt lives in the pond. | Cockatoos are crested parrots. | The crested penguin has yellow feathers above its eyes. | Our school jumper is crested with an owl badge. | The crested lizard raised its frill.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective from crest (noun). Crest also means the top of a hill or wave (the crest of a wave). Crested newts are protected in the UK, so do not disturb them.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Critically means very seriously or dangerously, as in critically ill or critically endangered. 2) Critically means by judging carefully what is good and bad, as in think critically. 3) Critically means in a way that finds fault, as in she spoke critically of the plan.
its sense in the lessons: In science and nature lessons, critically endangered species, such as the Sumatran tiger or kakapo, are at very high risk of dying out. In news, a person critically injured needs urgent hospital care. In school, critical thinking means asking: is it true, who says so, how do they know? This helps spot fake news.
examples from the lessons: The kakapo is critically endangered. | The driver was critically injured in the crash. | Read the advert critically: what is it trying to sell? | Scientists think critically about their results. | The film was critically praised. | The coach spoke critically about our defending.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from critical. Critically acclaimed means praised by critics. Think critically does not mean be negative; it means check carefully.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Cuisine is a style of cooking from a certain country or region, such as Italian cuisine or Indian cuisine. 2) Cuisine is the food served, especially good-quality food, as in the restaurant's cuisine.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and food lessons, pupils taste dishes from different cuisines and learn how climate and history shape what people eat. In everyday life, restaurants and menus advertise their cuisine. French cuisine is famous for sauces and pastries; Japanese cuisine for sushi.
examples from the lessons: Pizza and pasta are part of Italian cuisine. | Mexican cuisine uses lots of beans, corn and chillies. | The town has restaurants with cuisines from all over the world. | We studied Chinese cuisine in food technology. | Australian cuisine has many influences. | The hotel is famous for its fine cuisine.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Said kwi-ZEEN; it comes from French and means kitchen. Countable when talking about types: cuisines of the world. A more formal word than cooking or food.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Diplodocus was a huge plant-eating dinosaur with a very long neck and an even longer whip-like tail that lived about 150 million years ago in North America.
its sense in the lessons: In science and history lessons, Diplodocus is a sauropod, one of the longest land animals ever, about 25 metres long. It swallowed leaves and plants without chewing. A famous cast skeleton nicknamed Dippy stood in the Natural History Museum in London and toured the UK.
examples from the lessons: Diplodocus had a neck as long as a bus. | Diplodocus ate plants, not meat. | Its long tail may have cracked like a whip. | Dippy the Diplodocus visited our city museum. | A Diplodocus was about 25 metres long. | We drew a Diplodocus next to a giraffe to compare sizes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Said dih-PLOD-uh-kus or dip-loh-DOH-kus. Often with a capital D as a genus name. Plural: diplodocuses, though people often say Diplodocus for more than one. It was not a brontosaurus, a different but related dinosaur.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A dory is a flat, thin sea fish; the John Dory is one eaten as food. 2) A dory is a small, light boat with high sides and a flat bottom, used for fishing. 3) Dory is the name of a forgetful blue fish in the animated films Finding Nemo and Finding Dory.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and food, John Dory is a fish on restaurant menus in the UK, Australia and New Zealand; it has a dark spot on each side. In history, fishermen used dories off the coast of Canada and New England. Most children know Dory as the cartoon blue tang fish who says Just keep swimming.
examples from the lessons: We had John Dory and chips at the harbour. | The John Dory has a dark spot on its side. | Fishermen rowed out in a dory. | The dories were stacked on the deck of the big ship. | Dory keeps forgetting things in the film. | Just keep swimming, says Dory.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: dories. John Dory is the usual name for the fish. Dory in the films is a blue tang, not a real dory fish.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To excavate means to dig carefully in the ground to find old things such as buildings, bones or tools. 2) To excavate means to dig out a hole, tunnel or area, for example for building.
its sense in the lessons: In history and archaeology lessons, archaeologists excavate sites like Roman towns, Viking villages or dinosaur fossils, using trowels and brushes and recording every find. In building, diggers excavate foundations. The noun excavation names the dig or the hole.
examples from the lessons: Archaeologists excavated a Roman villa under the car park. | They are excavating the dinosaur bones slowly with brushes. | Workers excavated the ground for the new swimming pool. | The site was excavated last summer. | Our class pretended to excavate a sandpit for buried treasure. | Badgers excavate long tunnels.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: excavated, excavating. Noun: excavation; a person: excavator (also the name of a digging machine). A formal word for dig.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Gluten is a protein found in wheat, barley and rye that makes dough stretchy and helps bread rise.
its sense in the lessons: In food and science lessons, gluten is why bread is chewy. In everyday life and health, people with coeliac disease (celiac in the US) get ill from gluten, so they eat gluten-free food; labels must show it. Some people have other intolerances. Gluten-free food is not healthier for most people.
examples from the lessons: Bread dough is stretchy because of gluten. | My friend has coeliac disease and cannot eat gluten. | This cake is gluten-free. | Wheat, barley and rye contain gluten. | Check the label for gluten. | Rice and potatoes do not contain gluten.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Gluten-free is written with a hyphen before a noun. Said GLOO-ten. Do not confuse with glutton (a greedy eater). Myth: gluten is bad for everyone; it is only a problem for some people.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The grassroots are the ordinary people in a group, club or movement, not the leaders. 2) Grassroots describes something that starts with ordinary people locally, not with people in power, as in grassroots football or a grassroots campaign.
its sense in the lessons: In politics and citizenship lessons, grassroots campaigns are begun by ordinary people, such as a petition to save a park. In sport, grassroots football and rugby mean local clubs where children play. In news, leaders are told to listen to the grassroots.
