examples from the lessons: Grassroots football clubs need volunteers. | The campaign to save the library was a grassroots effort. | Many famous players started at grassroots level. | The party leader listened to the grassroots. | Our recycling scheme began as a grassroots idea. | Grassroots sport keeps children active.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Often written as one word, sometimes grass-roots or grass roots. The literal grass roots (roots of grass) is a different, ordinary meaning. Used as an adjective before a noun: grassroots project.

part of speech: noun (a heading, headings); verb form (head, heads, headed, heading)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A heading is the title at the top of a page, section or piece of writing that tells you what it is about. 2) Heading is the -ing form of head: going towards somewhere, as in heading home. 3) (sport) Heading is hitting the ball with your head in football. 4) A heading is a direction of travel, especially for ships and planes, given in degrees.
its sense in the lessons: In English and non-fiction writing lessons, headings and subheadings organise information and help the reader find things. In everyday life, Where are you heading? means where are you going. In football, young children's heading practice is limited for safety in the UK. In maths and navigation, a heading such as 090 degrees means east.
examples from the lessons: Write a heading at the top of your page. | The leaflet uses headings and bullet points. | We're heading to the beach after school. | The storm is heading towards the coast. | He scored with a great heading of the ball. | The ship changed its heading to the north. | Under each heading, list three facts.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: headings. Head for or head to a place: we are heading for town. Heading in football: limited for under-12s in some countries because of concussion worries.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A honeydew is a kind of melon with smooth pale skin and sweet pale-green flesh. 2) Honeydew is a sweet sticky liquid made by insects such as aphids, which ants like to eat.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, honeydew melon is a fruit in fruit salads. In science lessons, aphids suck plant sap and give out honeydew; ants farm aphids and protect them to get it, an example of animals helping each other. Honeydew makes leaves and cars under trees sticky.
examples from the lessons: We had honeydew melon for pudding. | Honeydew melons are pale green inside. | Ants drink the honeydew made by aphids. | The car under the tree was sticky with honeydew. | Bees sometimes collect honeydew to make honey. | Cut the honeydew into cubes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word. A honeydew or a honeydew melon. The insect honeydew is uncountable. It is not dew and not made by bees, though bees can collect it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A hotspot is a place where there is a lot of a certain activity, such as a tourist hotspot or a crime hotspot. 2) A Wi-Fi hotspot is a place or device that lets you connect to the internet without wires. 3) (science) A hotspot is a place where hot rock rises from deep in the Earth, making volcanoes, as under Hawaii or Iceland. 4) A biodiversity hotspot is an area with very many different kinds of plants and animals that are in danger.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons, hotspots make volcano chains like the Hawaiian islands. In science, rainforests and coral reefs are biodiversity hotspots. In everyday life, phones can be used as a mobile hotspot; in online safety, be careful on public Wi-Fi hotspots and do not share private details. In news, a hotspot can be where an illness spreads fast.
examples from the lessons: The Hawaiian islands formed over a volcanic hotspot. | The café has a free Wi-Fi hotspot. | Mum turned her phone into a hotspot for my tablet. | The beach is a tourist hotspot in summer. | Madagascar is a biodiversity hotspot. | Be careful what you share on public hotspots.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Usually one word, sometimes hot spot. A hotspot is not always hot in temperature; it means a busy or important spot.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (abbreviation) i.e. is short for the Latin id est, meaning that is or in other words; it explains more exactly what was just said. 2) (abbreviation, computing) .ie is the internet ending for websites from Ireland. 3) (spelling) ie is a common pair of letters in English words, as in the rule i before e except after c.
its sense in the lessons: In writing and textbooks, i.e. adds a clearer explanation: the largest planet, i.e. Jupiter. In spelling lessons, children learn i before e except after c (believe, receive), though there are many exceptions (weird, science). Irish websites end in .ie.
examples from the lessons: Bring something to write with, i.e. a pen or pencil. | We meet on the last day of term, i.e. Friday. | Mammals are warm-blooded, i.e. they keep a steady body heat. | The website ends in .ie, so it's from Ireland. | Believe and field follow the ie rule. | Science and weird break the i before e rule.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually written with dots: i.e. Trap: i.e. (that is, exactly this) is different from e.g. (for example, one of many). After i.e. you give the full or exact meaning; after e.g. you give examples. It is not an English word on its own.

part of speech: noun (a kneecap, kneecaps); verb (kneecap, kneecaps, kneecapped, kneecapping — rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The kneecap is the small, flat, roundish bone at the front of your knee. 2) (rare, violent) To kneecap someone means to shoot or hurt them in the knee as a cruel punishment.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on the skeleton, the kneecap's proper name is the patella; it protects the knee joint. In sport and safety, knee pads protect kneecaps when skating or playing goalkeeper. The violent verb meaning appears only in history or news about gangs and conflicts.
examples from the lessons: The kneecap protects the front of your knee joint. | The doctor tapped below my kneecap and my leg jumped. | Wear knee pads to protect your kneecaps. | The proper name for the kneecap is the patella. | She dislocated her kneecap playing netball. | Babies' kneecaps are mostly soft cartilage.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable, one word. Plural: kneecaps. The k in knee is silent: NEE-cap. The verb is rare and describes violence.

part of speech: noun (a lass, lasses) — informal, UK dialect
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal, Scotland and northern England) A lass is a girl or young woman. 2) (informal) Lass is used as a friendly way to talk to a girl or woman, as in Thanks, lass.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday speech in Scotland, Ireland and the north of England, people say lass and lad for girl and boy. In old songs and stories, a lad and a lass fall in love, and bonny lass means pretty girl. The word is friendly and warm, not rude.
examples from the lessons: She's a clever lass. (UK dialect) | Thanks, lass, that's very kind. | The lads and lasses went to the dance. | A bonny lass sang by the river. (Scots) | Our Sarah's a lovely lass. (northern England) | Come here, lass, and tell me what happened.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: lasses. Informal and regional; in standard English say girl or young woman. The boy word is lad. Lassie means the same; Lassie is also a famous dog in films.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A lionfish is a striped red, brown and white sea fish with long fan-like fins and venomous spines.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, the lionfish lives on coral reefs in the Indian and Pacific Oceans. Its stripes warn predators. It has spread into the Atlantic and Caribbean, where it is an invasive species eating many small fish, so divers catch it. In safety, its spines give a very painful sting. It is also eaten as food in some places.
examples from the lessons: The lionfish has long, spiky fins. | A lionfish sting is very painful. | Lionfish are invasive in the Caribbean. | Divers catch lionfish to protect the reef. | The lionfish's stripes warn other animals to stay away. | We saw a lionfish in the aquarium.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural is usually lionfish. It is venomous (it stings), not poisonous to touch the flesh; cooked properly it can be eaten. One word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A mechanism is a set of moving parts in a machine that work together, such as the mechanism of a clock or a lock. 2) A mechanism is a way or system by which something happens or is done, as in the body's mechanism for keeping warm.
its sense in the lessons: In design and technology lessons, pupils learn about mechanisms: levers, gears, pulleys, cams, linkages, and make toys with moving parts. In science, the body has mechanisms such as shivering and sweating. In everyday life, a safety mechanism stops a machine from hurting people. A defence mechanism is how animals or people protect themselves.
examples from the lessons: The clock's mechanism is full of tiny gears. | We made a pop-up card with a lever mechanism. | Shivering is the body's mechanism for warming up. | The lock mechanism was jammed. | A hedgehog's spines are a defence mechanism. | The toy car has a wind-up mechanism.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Said MEK-uh-niz-um; ch sounds like k. Related: mechanical, mechanic (a person who fixes cars), mechanics.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Miserable means very unhappy. 2) Miserable describes something unpleasant that makes you unhappy, such as miserable weather. 3) Miserable describes something very small or poor, as in a miserable amount. 4) (UK, informal) A miserable person is grumpy and never cheerful, as in a miserable old man.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, miserable describes how characters feel when lonely, cold or treated badly. In everyday life, people say the weather is miserable on wet grey days. In English lessons it is a stronger word than sad. Related phrases: feel miserable, look miserable, a miserable day.
examples from the lessons: I felt miserable when I lost my dog. | It's a miserable, rainy day. | Cinderella was miserable doing all the chores. | We got a miserable two points in the quiz. | Don't be so miserable, cheer up! | The cold, miserable camp made everyone want to go home.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective. Noun: misery. Adverb: miserably (we failed miserably). Stronger than sad or unhappy. Misery guts (UK, informal) is a grumpy person.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A moorhen is a black water bird with a red and yellow beak and a white stripe on its side, often seen on ponds, rivers and canals.
its sense in the lessons: In science and nature lessons in the UK, Ireland and other countries, moorhens are common pond birds; they swim with jerking heads and walk on floating plants with long green toes. They build nests near water. In North America a very similar bird is called the common gallinule. Coots are similar but have a white beak.
examples from the lessons: A moorhen swam across the duck pond. | The moorhen has a bright red beak. | Moorhen chicks are fluffy and black. | Moorhens flick their tails when nervous. | We counted three moorhens on the canal. | A moorhen built its nest in the reeds.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Both males and females are called moorhens, though hen usually means female. Moor here comes from an old word for marsh, not moorland. Do not confuse with the coot, which has a white beak and forehead.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) The nucleus is the centre of a cell that holds its DNA and controls it. 2) (science) The nucleus of an atom is its tiny centre, made of protons and neutrons. 3) A nucleus is the central or most important part of a group or thing, as in the nucleus of a team.
its sense in the lessons: In biology lessons, plant and animal cells have a nucleus; bacteria do not. In chemistry and physics, the atom's nucleus holds almost all its mass, with electrons around it; nuclear energy comes from it. In everyday talk, a few key players form the nucleus of a team.
examples from the lessons: The nucleus controls what the cell does. | Plant and animal cells both have a nucleus. | The nucleus of an atom contains protons and neutrons. | We drew the nucleus in the middle of our cell diagram. | Nuclear power comes from splitting the nucleus of atoms. | These five players are the nucleus of the team.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: nuclei (said NEW-klee-eye). Adjective: nuclear. Said NEW-klee-us (UK) or NOO-klee-us (US). Trap: nuclear is often mispronounced nucular.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An oar is a long pole with a flat blade at one end, used to row a boat. 2) (idiom, UK informal) To stick or put your oar in means to give your opinion when it is not wanted.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and sport, rowers pull oars to move a boat; rowing teams race on rivers. In history, Viking longships and Roman galleys used many oars. In safety, boats carry spare oars. An oar is held in an oarlock or rowlock. A paddle (used in canoes) is different: it is held without a fixed place on the boat.
examples from the lessons: He pulled hard on the oars. | The rowing boat has two oars. | Vikings rowed their longships with long oars. | We lost an oar and drifted in circles. | Don't stick your oar in; it's not your argument. (UK informal) | Eight rowers pulled their oars together.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; use an before oar. Homophones: or (this or that) and ore (rock with metal) sound the same in many accents. An oar is fixed to the boat; a paddle is not.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An osprey is a large bird of prey with brown wings and a white underside that dives feet-first into water to catch fish.
its sense in the lessons: In science and nature lessons, ospreys live near lakes, rivers and coasts on every continent except Antarctica. They migrate long distances, for example from Scotland to West Africa. They nearly died out in Britain but have come back, and people watch their nests on webcams. They have special rough feet to grip slippery fish.
examples from the lessons: An osprey dived into the lake and caught a trout. | Ospreys fly to Africa for the winter. | We watched the osprey nest on a webcam. | The osprey carried the fish head-first. | Ospreys returned to Scotland after many years. | An osprey's feet have spikes to grip fish.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; use an: an osprey. Plural: ospreys. Sometimes called a fish hawk or sea hawk.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Plumage is all the feathers of a bird, their colours and patterns.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, male birds often have brighter plumage to attract females, while females are duller to hide on the nest (peacocks, mallards). Birds moult and grow new plumage. Young birds have juvenile plumage. In stories, bright plumage describes beautiful or showy birds.
examples from the lessons: The peacock showed off its colourful plumage. | The male mallard has bright green plumage on its head. | In winter the ptarmigan's plumage turns white. | The parrot's plumage was red, blue and yellow. | Young gulls have brown plumage. | Birds clean their plumage with their beaks.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: no a plumage. Said PLOO-mij. Related: plume (one big feather). A formal word for feathers.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Predation is when one animal (a predator) hunts, kills and eats another animal (its prey).
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on food chains and ecosystems, predation keeps the numbers of prey animals in balance; if predators disappear, prey can become too many. Animals avoid predation with camouflage, speed, shells, warning colours and living in groups. Conservation groups protect nests from predation by foxes or rats.
examples from the lessons: Camouflage helps insects avoid predation. | Predation by foxes is a danger to ground-nesting birds. | Wolves control deer numbers through predation. | Living in herds protects zebras from predation. | Rats on the island caused heavy predation of seabird eggs. | Predation is part of every food chain.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Related: predator (the hunter), prey (the hunted), predatory (adjective). A formal science word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A protester is a person who shows in public that they strongly disagree with something, for example by marching, holding signs or shouting.
its sense in the lessons: In citizenship and history lessons, protesters have changed laws, for example suffragettes for women's votes and civil rights marchers in the USA. In news, protesters march about climate, wars, jobs or prices; in many countries peaceful protest is a right. Some protests turn violent, and police manage crowds.
examples from the lessons: Protesters marched through the city with banners. | The protesters wanted cleaner air. | Suffragettes were protesters for women's right to vote. | Police kept the protesters away from the road. | Some protesters chained themselves to trees. | Thousands of protesters gathered peacefully.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Both spellings are used: protester and protestor. Related: protest (noun and verb). Stress: a PRO-test (noun), to pro-TEST (verb).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Regional means to do with a particular region, an area of a country or the world, as in a regional accent or regional news.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons, countries are divided into regions; regional differences include weather, food and jobs. In everyday life, regional accents and dialects (Geordie, Scouse, Cockney, Texan) show where people come from; regional news covers your area; regional trains link towns. In sport, regional finals come before national ones.
examples from the lessons: She has a strong regional accent. | We watch the regional news after the main news. | The team won the regional final. | Regional dishes include Cornish pasties. | Regional trains stop at every small station. | Weather varies in different regional areas of Australia.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective from region. Opposite or contrast words: local (smaller), national (whole country), international. Regionally is the adverb.

part of speech: noun (a rhinoceros, rhinoceroses or rhinoceros; informal: rhino)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A rhinoceros is a very large, thick-skinned grey animal from Africa or Asia with one or two horns on its nose.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography lessons, there are five kinds of rhino: white and black rhinos in Africa, and Indian, Javan and Sumatran rhinos in Asia. They eat plants. Several are critically endangered because poachers kill them for their horns, which are made of keratin like our fingernails. Conservation and rangers protect them.
examples from the lessons: A rhinoceros has very thick skin. | The black rhinoceros is critically endangered. | Rhino horn is made of keratin, like your hair. | We saw two rhinos on safari. | A baby rhinoceros is called a calf. | Rangers guard the rhinoceroses from poachers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually shortened to rhino. Plural: rhinoceroses, rhinos, or sometimes rhinoceros. Said rye-NOSS-er-us. Myth: rhino horn does not cure illness. A group of rhinos is called a crash.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A safari is a trip to see or photograph wild animals in their natural home, especially in Africa. 2) A safari park is a large park where wild animals roam and visitors drive through. 3) Safari is the name of the web browser on Apple devices.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons, safaris in Kenya, Tanzania and South Africa help pay for protecting wildlife through tourism. In the past, safaris were often hunting trips; today most are for watching. In everyday life, families visit safari parks in the UK. On computers, Safari is a browser.
examples from the lessons: We saw lions and elephants on safari. | They went on a safari in Kenya. | The safari park has giraffes and monkeys. | A safari guide drove the jeep. | Our class planned an imaginary safari across the savanna. | Open the website in Safari.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a safari, safaris. Usually on safari or go on a safari. The word comes from Swahili and means journey. The browser name has a capital S.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Saudi describes Saudi Arabia, a large desert country in the Middle East, or its people, as in a Saudi city. 2) A Saudi is a person from Saudi Arabia.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and religion lessons, Saudi Arabia covers most of the Arabian Peninsula; its capital is Riyadh; it holds Mecca and Medina, the holiest cities in Islam, which millions of Muslims visit on pilgrimage (Hajj). It is very rich in oil. It is ruled by a king, and its laws are strict. In news, it is often just called Saudi.
examples from the lessons: Saudi Arabia is mostly desert. | Riyadh is the Saudi capital. | Millions of Muslims travel to Mecca in Saudi Arabia for the Hajj. | The Saudi football team played in the World Cup. | Saudi Arabia sells a lot of oil. | Her uncle works in Saudi.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always a capital S. Said SOW-dee (rhymes with cloudy) or SAW-dee. The country is named after the Saud family who rule it. Saudi Arabia is in Asia, not Africa.

part of speech: abbreviation (SE, se); French word (se); Spanish word (se)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (abbreviation) SE stands for south-east, the direction halfway between south and east. 2) (abbreviation, UK) SE is the start of postcodes in south-east London, as in SE1. 3) (French) se is a small word meaning himself, herself, itself or themselves, used with some verbs, as in il se lave (he washes himself). It sounds like suh. 4) (Spanish) se is a similar small word in Spanish. It is not an English word.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and maths lessons on compass points, SE is one of the eight main directions: N, NE, E, SE, S, SW, W, NW. In French lessons, se appears in reflexive verbs like se laver (to wash oneself) and s'appeler (to be called). In maps and weather, winds can come from the SE.
examples from the lessons: The wind is blowing from the SE. | Walk SE across the field to reach the stile. | SE is halfway between south and east. | Our cousins live in London SE15. | Il se lave, means he washes himself. (French) | On the compass, SE is at 135 degrees.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a compass direction write SE in capitals; south-east (UK) or southeast (US) in full. In French se becomes s' before a vowel: il s'appelle. Not an English word on its own.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (French, old money) A sou was an old French coin of very little value. 2) (idiom, old-fashioned) Not a sou means no money at all, as in he hasn't a sou. 3) (French) Sous (said soo) also means under in French, as in sous-chef, the cook under the head chef.
its sense in the lessons: In history and old stories, people are poor without a sou to their name. In French lessons, sous means under, and sou means a small coin; both sound like the English word sue. In cooking, a sous-chef is the second chef in a kitchen. It is not an everyday English word.
examples from the lessons: He was so poor he didn't have a sou. | The old woman counted her few sous. | In the story, the beggar asked for a sou. | A sou was worth very little. | A sous-chef helps the head chef. | Sous la table means under the table. (French)
note for the reader of a maths problem: Said soo, like sue. Plural: sous (also said soo). Mostly found in old books and set phrases. It comes from French, not English.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Spongy means soft, squashy and full of tiny holes, like a sponge, so it springs back when pressed. 2) Spongy can describe ground that is soft and wet, or something that has too much give, like spongy brakes.
its sense in the lessons: In science and food lessons, cakes are spongy because air bubbles get trapped; bones have spongy inner parts; moss and marsh ground feel spongy. In materials lessons, pupils describe materials as spongy, hard, rigid or flexible. In everyday life a spongy cake is light and soft.
examples from the lessons: The cake was light and spongy. | Moss feels spongy under your feet. | The inside of a bone is spongy. | The ground near the river was spongy and wet. | Bread dough becomes spongy as it rises. | The old mattress was too spongy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparatives: spongier, spongiest. Adjective from sponge. Not used for people, except in jokes.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (abbreviation) SS before a ship's name stands for steamship, as in the SS Great Britain. 2) (history) The SS was a violent Nazi military and police force in Germany during the Second World War, which ran concentration camps and carried out the Holocaust. 3) (abbreviation) ss can mean screenshot in online chat. 4) (spelling) ss is a double letter in many words, as in miss, class, kiss, often at the end after a short vowel. 5) (abbreviation, church) Ss is short for Saints, as in Ss Peter and Paul.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, the SS Great Britain was a famous early steamship (the Titanic was RMS, Royal Mail Ship); the Nazi SS is studied when learning about the Holocaust, which must be talked about seriously and truthfully. In spelling lessons, the floss rule: double s, f, l, z after a short vowel at the end of short words (miss, off, fill, buzz). In chats, ss means screenshot.
examples from the lessons: The SS Great Britain is a famous ship in Bristol. | We visited the SS Great Britain on a school trip. | The SS ran the Nazi concentration camps. | Miss, class and grass all end in ss. | Send me a ss of the score. (chat slang) | The church is called Ss Peter and Paul.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Not a word on its own; an abbreviation or a letter pattern. The Nazi SS is a very serious topic, never a joke. Spelling rule: after a short vowel at the end of a one-syllable word, s is often doubled (pass, less), but not always (bus, yes).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A supernova is a gigantic explosion of a star at the end of its life, which can shine brighter than a whole galaxy for a short time.
its sense in the lessons: In science and space lessons, very big stars end their lives as supernovae, leaving a neutron star or black hole. Supernovae spread elements like iron and gold into space, so the atoms in our bodies were made in stars. A supernova was seen from Earth in 1054 and made the Crab Nebula.
examples from the lessons: A supernova is the explosion of a huge star. | The Crab Nebula is left over from a supernova. | Supernovae make heavy elements like gold. | For a few weeks the supernova outshone its galaxy. | Our Sun is too small to become a supernova. | Astronomers spotted a new supernova in a distant galaxy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: supernovae (said soo-per-NOH-vee) or supernovas. A nova is a smaller star blast. Our Sun will not become a supernova; it will become a red giant and then a white dwarf.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (Australia, New Zealand) Thongs are flip-flops: simple open sandals with a strap between the toes. 2) A thong is a piece of underwear or swimwear with a very thin strip at the back. 3) A thong is a thin strip of leather used to tie or fasten things.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life in Australia, people wear thongs to the beach; in the UK they are called flip-flops, in New Zealand jandals. In history, leather thongs tied shoes and tools. Because the word means underwear in the UK and USA, it causes funny misunderstandings between countries.
examples from the lessons: Don't forget your thongs for the beach! (Australia) | My thongs broke and I had to walk barefoot. (Australia) | In the UK, thongs are called flip-flops. | The sandal was tied with a leather thong. | The necklace hung on a leather thong. | Kiwis call them jandals, Aussies call them thongs.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; usually plural for footwear: a pair of thongs. Trap: an Australian asking for thongs means flip-flops, not underwear. Said with a hard g at the end: thong rhymes with long.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (a name) Tia is a girl's name. 2) (Spanish and Portuguese) Tía (Spanish) and tia (Portuguese) mean aunt; it sounds like TEE-uh to an English ear. It is not an English word. 3) (abbreviation, medicine) TIA stands for transient ischaemic attack, a mini-stroke.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and classes, Tia may be a character's name. In families with Spanish or Portuguese roots, including many Latino families in the USA, children call their aunt Tía, and their uncle Tío. In health, a TIA is a short warning stroke and needs a doctor at once.
examples from the lessons: Tia sits next to me in class. (a name) | My tía makes the best tamales. (Spanish) | Tía Rosa is visiting from Mexico. (Spanish) | Tio and Tia mean uncle and aunt. | Grandad had a TIA and went to hospital. | Tia scored the winning goal. (a name)
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a name it takes a capital T. In Spanish it is written tía with an accent. Not an English word. TIA in capitals is a medical abbreviation.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal, old-fashioned, from French) Toilette is the process of washing, dressing and doing your hair, as in making her toilette. 2) (French) In French, toilette also means a toilet or washroom (usually toilettes). It sounds like twah-LET. 3) (old-fashioned) A toilette is a woman's elegant outfit.
its sense in the lessons: In old novels and classic stories, rich ladies spent hours at their toilette with maids helping them. In French lessons, Où sont les toilettes? means Where are the toilets? In everyday English today, toilet means the loo, which comes from this word.
examples from the lessons: The lady finished her toilette before the ball. | She made her morning toilette by the window. | Où sont les toilettes? means Where are the toilets? (French) | The cat licked its paws in its careful toilette. | In the old book, the duchess wore a splendid toilette. | The maid helped her mistress with her toilette.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A French word used in formal or old English; in modern English say getting washed and dressed. Do not confuse with toilet (the loo), although the English word toilet comes from it. Eau de toilette is a light perfume.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A treetop is the highest part of a tree, its top branches and leaves.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography lessons on rainforests, the treetops form the canopy where many birds, monkeys and insects live. In stories, characters hide or build treehouses in the treetops. Treetop walks and adventure parks let people walk on high bridges between trees, with harnesses for safety.
examples from the lessons: Monkeys swung through the treetops. | Birds sang from the treetops. | We did a treetop walk on rope bridges. | The wind whistled through the treetops. | Many rainforest animals never leave the treetops. | The squirrel built its drey high in the treetop.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable, one word. Often plural: in the treetops. Similar: canopy (in science).

part of speech: noun (a trump, trumps); verb (trump, trumps, trumped, trumping); name (Trump)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (card games) A trump or trumps is a suit of cards that beats all others in a game. 2) To trump something means to beat it by doing something better, as in she trumped his story. 3) (UK, informal, childish) To trump means to fart. 4) (a name) Trump is a family name; Donald Trump is an American businessman who became President of the United States. 5) (Bible, old) A trump is a trumpet, as in the last trump.
its sense in the lessons: In card games and Top Trumps (a children's card game), a trump card wins. In everyday talk, your trump card is your best secret advantage. In the UK, children giggle at trump meaning fart. In news and citizenship lessons, Donald Trump is a US president; describe him with facts, as different people see him very differently. In the Bible, the last trump is the trumpet sound at the end of time.
examples from the lessons: Hearts are trumps in this game. | Let's play Top Trumps with dinosaur cards. | Her goal trumped all the others. | Our trump card is our fast runner. | Who trumped? It smells! (UK, informal) | Donald Trump was elected US president. (a name) | The Bible speaks of the last trump.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: trumped. Trump as a name has a capital T. Trump meaning fart is childish UK slang, not rude but not polite. Trumped-up charges means false accusations.

part of speech: adjective (varied); verb form (vary, varies, varied, varying)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Varied means made of many different kinds, as in a varied diet. 2) Varied is the past form of vary: changed or was different, as in the temperature varied.
its sense in the lessons: In science and health lessons, a varied diet with many foods keeps you healthy. In English lessons, teachers ask for varied sentence starts and vocabulary to make writing interesting. In maths and science investigations, you change (vary) one thing and see results; results varied means they were not all the same.
examples from the lessons: Eat a varied diet with lots of fruit and vegetables. | Use varied sentence openers in your story. | The weather varied from sunny to stormy. | Our results varied each time we did the test. | The zoo has a varied collection of animals. | Prices varied from shop to shop.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: vary becomes varied (y changes to i before -ed), varies. Do not confuse with various (several different) or variety (noun). In maths, if a number varied, it changed.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Velocity is speed in a particular direction. 2) In everyday use, velocity means speed, especially high speed.
its sense in the lessons: In science and maths lessons, speed tells how fast something goes; velocity tells how fast and which way. Velocity is measured in metres per second (m/s). If you run round a track at the same speed, your velocity keeps changing because your direction changes. Escape velocity is the speed a rocket needs to leave Earth's pull.
examples from the lessons: The ball left the bat at a high velocity. | Velocity is speed in a given direction. | A rocket needs a huge velocity to escape Earth. | The river's velocity was faster in the middle. | We measured the velocity of the toy car in metres per second. | Wind velocity was 50 kilometres per hour from the north.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly uncountable; plural velocities in science. In maths problems, velocity = distance (displacement) divided by time; a negative velocity means moving the opposite way. Speed has no direction; velocity does.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A viper is a kind of venomous snake with long fangs that fold back, such as the adder. 2) (old-fashioned) A viper is a wicked, treacherous person who betrays others.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, vipers include adders, rattlesnakes and puff adders; the adder is Britain's only venomous snake and is shy and protected. In safety, if bitten, stay calm, keep still and get medical help at once. In the Bible and old stories, a brood of vipers or a viper in the nest means a dangerous, deceitful person.
examples from the lessons: The adder is a kind of viper. | Vipers have long fangs that fold back. | Rattlesnakes are vipers from America. | If a viper bites you, get help straight away. | In the story, the king's adviser was a viper. | A viper basked on the warm rocks.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Vipers are venomous (they inject venom), not poisonous to eat. Do not confuse with a wiper (windscreen wiper). The cruel-person meaning is old-fashioned.

part of speech: noun (a whisk, whisks); verb (whisk, whisks, whisked, whisking)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A whisk is a kitchen tool made of curved wires, used to beat eggs or cream quickly. 2) To whisk means to beat food fast with a whisk or fork to add air. 3) To whisk someone or something away means to take them somewhere very quickly.
its sense in the lessons: In cooking and food lessons, you whisk eggs for scrambled eggs and whisk egg whites until stiff for meringues; whisking traps air bubbles. In stories, a car whisks someone away, or a magic wind whisks the hero to another land. A cow whisks its tail to brush off flies.
examples from the lessons: Whisk the eggs and milk together. | Pass me the whisk, please. | Whisk the cream until it is thick. | A taxi whisked them away to the airport. | The magic carpet whisked Aladdin into the sky. | The horse whisked its tail at the flies.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun; regular verb: whisked. Electric whisk = a mixer. Do not confuse with whisky (a strong alcoholic drink) or whiskers.

part of speech: noun (a wizard, wizards); adjective (wizard — old UK slang); interjection
meaning for a pupil: 1) A wizard is a man in stories who has magic powers. 2) A wizard is a person who is extremely good at something, as in a maths wizard. 3) (computing) A wizard is a step-by-step helper in a computer program. 4) (old UK slang) Wizard! meant excellent, in old school stories.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and fairy tales, wizards like Merlin and Gandalf cast spells and give advice; a witch is usually a woman with magic. In everyday life, praise someone as a wizard with numbers or a wizard on the football pitch. On computers, a setup wizard guides you through steps. Old British children's books use wizard! for great.
examples from the lessons: Merlin was a wise old wizard. | The wizard waved his wand and the frog became a prince. | My sister is a wizard at maths. | He's a wizard with a football. | Follow the setup wizard to install the game. | What a wizard idea! (old UK slang)
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Magic in stories is not real. Related: wizardry (great skill or magic). Wizard is usually male; witch is usually female in stories, though some modern stories use wizard for everyone.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal, UK, Australia) Wonky means crooked, not straight or not level. 2) (informal) Wonky means shaky, weak or not working properly, as in a wonky table or wonky Wi-Fi.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, people say the picture is wonky, a wonky tooth, wonky vegetables (odd-shaped vegetables sold cheaply to cut waste). In art and design lessons, a wonky line is not straight; use a ruler. In stories, a wonky old house leans over.
examples from the lessons: That picture on the wall is wonky. | My bike wheel is a bit wonky. | The table's wonky; put a coaster under the leg. | Supermarkets sell wonky carrots cheaply. | He has a wonky smile. | The Wi-Fi is wonky today.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal; in formal writing say crooked, uneven or faulty. Comparatives: wonkier, wonkiest. Not related to Willy Wonka.

part of speech: noun (yen — plural the same); noun (a yen — informal desire)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (money) The yen is the money of Japan; its sign is ¥. 2) (informal) A yen is a strong wish or longing for something, as in a yen to travel.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and geography lessons, problems may change pounds or dollars into yen; one yen is worth very little, so prices in Japan have big numbers (a snack might cost 150 yen). In everyday talk, having a yen for something means really wanting it.
examples from the lessons: The comic book cost 500 yen in Tokyo. | The yen is the currency of Japan. | How many yen do you get for one pound? | I've always had a yen to visit Japan. (informal) | She has a yen for chocolate. (informal) | Japanese coins include a 100-yen coin.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural is the same: one yen, 500 yen (not yens). In maths, a big number of yen is not much money, because one yen is worth less than a penny or a cent. The Chinese yuan has a similar sign but is different money.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Anatomical means to do with the structure of the body of a person, animal or plant, as in an anatomical drawing.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, anatomical diagrams and models show bones, muscles and organs. In history and art, Leonardo da Vinci made famous anatomical drawings. In sport and medicine, anatomical words name body parts exactly. Anatomically correct means shaped like the real body.
examples from the lessons: We labelled an anatomical diagram of the heart. | Leonardo da Vinci made anatomical drawings. | The museum has an anatomical model of the skeleton. | Doctors use anatomical names for bones. | The book has clear anatomical pictures of insects. | Running shoes have an anatomical shape to fit the foot.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective from anatomy (the study of body structure). Adverb: anatomically. A formal science word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Andean describes the Andes, the long chain of mountains along the west of South America, or the people and things from there.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and history lessons, Andean countries include Peru, Bolivia, Ecuador, Chile, Colombia and Argentina. The Inca Empire was an Andean civilisation with Machu Picchu. Andean animals include llamas, alpacas, vicunas and the Andean condor. Andean farmers grow potatoes and quinoa on terraces.
examples from the lessons: The Andean condor is one of the largest flying birds. | Llamas carry loads on Andean paths. | The Incas were an Andean people. | Potatoes first came from the Andean region. | Andean music uses pan pipes. | The Andean mountains are very high and cold.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually with a capital A. Said an-DEE-un or AN-dee-un. Comes from Andes.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An animator is a person who makes animated films, cartoons or computer games by creating moving pictures.
its sense in the lessons: In art, computing and careers lessons, animators draw, model in clay or use computers to make characters move frame by frame; big films need hundreds of animators. Some children learn animation with flip books, stop-motion and coding apps.
examples from the lessons: She wants to be an animator when she grows up. | Animators drew thousands of pictures for the film. | The animator moved the clay model a little for each photo. | Computer animators make characters in games. | Our class became animators for a day. | The animator's job is to make drawings seem alive.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; use an: an animator. Ends in -or. Related: animate, animation, animated.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Antiquity is the distant past, especially the time of ancient Greece and Rome. 2) Antiquities are old objects and buildings from long ago, such as statues, coins and pots. 3) Antiquity means being very old, as in a church of great antiquity.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, classical antiquity means ancient Greece and Rome; museums show antiquities from Egypt, Greece, China and more. In news, stealing and selling antiquities is a crime, and some countries ask museums to return objects taken long ago.
examples from the lessons: The Pyramids were built in antiquity. | The museum is full of Greek antiquities. | Roman roads survive from antiquity. | The church is of great antiquity. | Thieves smuggled antiquities out of the country. | Scholars study the writers of antiquity.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable for the time period; countable (antiquities) for objects. Related: antique (old valuable object), ancient. A formal word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An arum is a plant with arrow-shaped leaves and a hood-like flower around a spike, such as the arum lily or the wild arum (cuckoo pint, lords and ladies).
its sense in the lessons: In science and nature lessons in the UK and Ireland, the wild arum (lords and ladies) grows in woods and hedges; its bright red-orange berries in autumn are poisonous, so do not eat them. In gardens, the white arum lily is common, especially in Australia and New Zealand, where it can be a weed. Some arums smell bad to attract flies.
examples from the lessons: Lords and ladies is a wild arum that grows in hedges. | Arum berries are poisonous. | The white arum lily is popular at weddings. | Flies are attracted to the smelly arum flower. | Don't pick the arum's red berries. | Arum lilies grow wild in parts of Australia.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; an arum. Said AIR-um. Safety: all parts of arum plants are poisonous and can irritate skin and mouth.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An avalanche is a huge mass of snow, ice and rocks that suddenly slides fast down a mountain. 2) An avalanche of something is a sudden very large amount of it, as in an avalanche of letters.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and safety lessons, avalanches happen after heavy snowfall or warm weather on steep slopes; skiers and climbers check avalanche warnings, carry beacons, and rescue dogs search for buried people. In everyday talk, an avalanche of homework or emails means too much at once.
examples from the lessons: An avalanche buried the mountain road. | Skiers must check the avalanche warning. | Rescue dogs found the climber after the avalanche. | Loud noises do not usually start avalanches, despite the films. | We got an avalanche of birthday cards. | The teacher faced an avalanche of questions.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Myth: shouting rarely causes an avalanche; usually it is the weight of snow or a skier. A landslide is similar but of earth and rock.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A baboon is a large monkey from Africa and Arabia with a dog-like face, long jaws and big teeth, living in large groups called troops. 2) (informal, insult) Calling someone a baboon means they are acting rough or silly; it is rude.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, baboons live on the ground in savannas and rocky hills, eat almost anything, and have strong social ranks. Hamadryas baboons were sacred in ancient Egypt. In safety, in parts of South Africa baboons steal food from people and cars, so do not feed them.
examples from the lessons: A troop of baboons crossed the road. | Baboons are monkeys, not apes. | The baboon showed its long teeth. | Baboons in Cape Town sometimes steal picnic food. | Baby baboons ride on their mothers' backs. | Ancient Egyptians honoured baboons.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Baboons are monkeys (they have tails), unlike apes. Calling a person a baboon is an insult.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The Bastille was a fortress prison in Paris; on 14 July 1789 crowds stormed it, starting the French Revolution. 2) (French) bastille means a fort or castle; it sounds like bass-TEEL to an English ear.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, the Storming of the Bastille is the start of the French Revolution, when people rose against the king and his unfair rule. Bastille Day, 14 July, is France's national day, with parades and fireworks. The prison was pulled down; a column stands on the Place de la Bastille.
examples from the lessons: The Storming of the Bastille began the French Revolution. | Bastille Day is celebrated with fireworks in France. | The Bastille held only seven prisoners when it was stormed. | The crowd tore down the walls of the Bastille. | We learned about the Bastille in history. | French people call the day le 14 juillet.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually the Bastille with a capital B. A French word. Said bass-TEEL. The famous date is the main fact; Bastille Day is 14 July.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A bowerbird is a bird from Australia and New Guinea; the male builds a decorated shelter of twigs (a bower) to attract a female.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about animal behaviour, the satin bowerbird collects blue things such as feathers, flowers, bottle caps and pegs to decorate his bower; females choose the best builder. Australian children often see bowerbirds in gardens. It is an example of courtship and of animals using objects.
examples from the lessons: The bowerbird decorated his bower with blue bottle tops. | A male bowerbird builds a bower to impress a female. | Bowerbirds live in Australia and New Guinea. | The satin bowerbird loves anything blue. | The bowerbird stole a blue peg from our washing line. | Scientists study how bowerbirds choose colours.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word. A bower is a shady shelter; the bird is named after the bower it builds. The bower is not a nest; eggs are laid elsewhere.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A calculation is working out an answer using numbers, such as adding, subtracting, multiplying or dividing. 2) Calculation is careful planning or thinking about what will happen, sometimes selfishly, as in cold calculation.
its sense in the lessons: In maths lessons, show your calculations so the teacher can see your method; check calculations with the inverse operation or estimation. Mental calculation is done in your head; written calculation uses methods like column addition. In science, calculations find speed, averages and areas. In stories, a calculating character plans coldly.
examples from the lessons: Show your calculation in the box. | My calculation was wrong; I forgot to carry the ten. | Do the calculation in your head. | The calculator does long calculations quickly. | By my calculation, we'll arrive at six. | Check each calculation with an estimate.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Verb: calculate; tool: calculator; adjective: calculating (crafty). In maths, a calculation must have the numbers and operations right; a mistake in one step changes the final answer.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) The Cambrian was a period of Earth's history about 540 to 485 million years ago, when many kinds of animals with hard shells first appeared in the sea. 2) Cambrian means to do with Wales, as in the Cambrian Mountains, from Cambria, the Latin name for Wales.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about fossils and evolution, the Cambrian explosion was when many animal groups appeared quickly; trilobites are famous Cambrian fossils. The period was named after rocks studied in Wales. In geography, the Cambrian Mountains run through mid-Wales, and the Cambrian Line is a railway.
examples from the lessons: Trilobites lived in Cambrian seas. | Many animal groups appeared in the Cambrian explosion. | There were no animals on land in the Cambrian. | The Cambrian period is named after Wales. | We hiked in the Cambrian Mountains. | Cambrian rocks contain early fossils.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital C. Said KAM-bree-un. Before the Cambrian came the Precambrian; after it came the Ordovician. No dinosaurs lived then; they came hundreds of millions of years later.

part of speech: noun (canvas — uncountable; a canvas, canvases); verb (canvass is a different word)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Canvas is a strong, heavy cloth used for tents, sails, bags and shoes. 2) A canvas is a piece of this cloth stretched on a frame for painting a picture, or the painting itself. 3) (computing) A canvas is the area on screen where you draw or design in an app.
its sense in the lessons: In art lessons, artists paint with oils or acrylics on canvas. In history, ships' sails and soldiers' tents were canvas. In everyday life, canvas shoes and bags are common. In computing lessons, apps like Scratch have a stage or canvas. Under canvas means in a tent, camping.
examples from the lessons: The tent is made of canvas. | The artist painted a sunset on a large canvas. | Van Gogh's canvases are worth millions. | I wear canvas trainers in summer. | Draw your design on the canvas in the app. | We slept under canvas at scout camp.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: canvases. Trap: canvass with double s is a verb meaning to ask people for votes or opinions. Canvas is uncountable for the cloth, countable for paintings.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A caribou is a large deer of North America's Arctic and northern forests with big branching antlers; in Europe and Asia the same animal is called a reindeer.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography lessons, caribou live on the tundra and in the taiga of Canada and Alaska; huge herds migrate hundreds of kilometres; both males and females grow antlers. They are very important to Inuit and other First Nations peoples for food and clothing. Canada's 25-cent coin shows a caribou.
examples from the lessons: Caribou migrate across the tundra in huge herds. | Both male and female caribou grow antlers. | The Canadian quarter shows a caribou. | Caribou dig through snow to eat lichen. | Wolves follow the caribou herds. | Caribou and reindeer are the same species.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural usually the same: caribou. Said KA-ri-boo. Reindeer is the Eurasian (and Christmas) name of the same species.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A catchy tune, song or slogan is easy to remember and stays in your head. 2) (informal) Catchy can describe a name or idea that is attractive and grabs attention.
its sense in the lessons: In music lessons, catchy songs have simple repeated choruses and rhythms. In English and advertising lessons, adverts use catchy slogans and jingles to make you remember a product; pupils learn to spot persuasive tricks. In everyday life, a catchy tune can become an earworm.
examples from the lessons: That song is so catchy I can't stop humming it. | The advert has a catchy jingle. | Think of a catchy title for your poster. | A catchy slogan helps people remember. | The chorus is the catchiest part. | Her band has a catchy name.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparatives: catchier, catchiest. Informal but fine in school writing. An earworm is a catchy tune stuck in your head.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (music) A chord is a group of notes played at the same time, such as C, E and G on a piano. 2) (maths) A chord is a straight line joining two points on a circle or curve. 3) To strike a chord means to remind someone of something or make them feel sympathy.
its sense in the lessons: In music lessons, pupils learn guitar and keyboard chords; major chords sound happy and minor chords sound sad. In maths geometry, a chord joins two points on a circle; the longest chord is the diameter. In everyday talk, a story that strikes a chord feels familiar.
examples from the lessons: She played three chords on the guitar. | C major is an easy chord on the piano. | Minor chords often sound sad. | A chord joins two points on a circle. | The diameter is the longest chord of a circle. | His speech struck a chord with the audience.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Silent h: said kord. Homophone: cord (a string or rope) and vocal cords (often misspelled vocal chords). In maths, a chord through the centre is a diameter.

part of speech: noun (a chorus, choruses); verb (chorus, choruses, chorused, chorusing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The chorus of a song is the part that is repeated after each verse. 2) A chorus is a large group of singers, a choir, or a group who sing and dance together in a show. 3) A chorus of voices or sounds is many of them at once, as in a chorus of birds. 4) To chorus means to say something all together. 5) (drama) In ancient Greek plays, the chorus was a group who commented on the story.
its sense in the lessons: In music lessons, songs have verses and a chorus; the chorus is often the catchiest part. In school plays, children may be in the chorus. In nature, the dawn chorus is birds singing at sunrise. In stories, Yes, Miss! the class chorused. In Greek drama, the chorus explained events.
examples from the lessons: Everyone sang along with the chorus. | The song has three verses and a chorus. | She sings in the school chorus. | We woke to the dawn chorus of birds. | Good morning, Mr Smith! the children chorused. | A chorus of complaints followed the news. | In Greek plays the chorus speaks together.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: choruses. Said KOR-us; ch sounds like k. In chorus means all together. Do not confuse with choir (also a group of singers), though they overlap.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (UK, informal) Chuffed means very pleased and proud, as in I'm chuffed to bits. 2) Chuffed is also the past form of chuff: to make a puffing sound like a steam train.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday British, Irish, Australian and New Zealand speech, chuffed means delighted: chuffed with my test result. Chuffed to bits means extremely pleased. In stories, a little steam engine chuffed along the track.
examples from the lessons: I was chuffed to bits with my certificate. (UK informal) | Dad's dead chuffed with his new bike. (UK slang) | She was chuffed that her team won. | Gran was chuffed with her birthday card. | The little engine chuffed up the hill. | I'm well chuffed! (UK slang)
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal: fine in speech and stories, not in formal essays. Usually after be: I'm chuffed, not a chuffed boy. Dead chuffed and well chuffed are slang ways of saying very chuffed.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A civilisation is a large, organised society with cities, government, writing, laws and culture, such as ancient Egypt or the Maya. 2) Civilisation is the way of life of an advanced society, as in the history of civilisation. 3) (informal) Civilisation can mean towns with comforts, as in back to civilisation after camping.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, pupils study early civilisations: Sumer, ancient Egypt, the Indus Valley, the Shang dynasty in China, ancient Greece, the Maya, the Aztecs and the Incas, and compare their farming, writing, beliefs and buildings. Many began by rivers. Historians now avoid calling some peoples more civilised than others.
examples from the lessons: Ancient Egypt was a great civilisation on the Nile. | The Maya civilisation built huge pyramids. | Many early civilisations grew up near rivers. | Writing helped civilisations keep records. | After a week of camping we were glad to be back in civilisation. | The Indus Valley civilisation had drains and toilets.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK spelling civilisation, US spelling civilization; both are correct. Countable for particular societies. Related: civil, civilised.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A composer is a person who writes music, such as songs, symphonies, operas or film music.
its sense in the lessons: In music lessons, famous composers include Bach, Mozart, Beethoven, Clara Schumann, Florence Price, and film composers like John Williams. Composers write music down in notation or use computers. Pupils become composers when they make up their own tunes.
examples from the lessons: Mozart was a composer who began writing music as a child. | Beethoven was a composer who became deaf. | John Williams is the composer of many film tunes. | Today we are composers: make up a four-bar tune. | The composer conducted the orchestra herself. | Who is your favourite composer?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Verb: compose; noun for the piece: composition. A composer writes the music; a songwriter writes songs; a performer plays it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (maths, logic) A counterexample is one example that shows a general statement is false.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and reasoning lessons, to test a claim like All prime numbers are odd, you look for a counterexample: 2 is prime and even, so the claim is false. One counterexample is enough to prove a statement wrong, but examples alone cannot prove it true. In everyday arguments, a counterexample answers someone who says always or never.
examples from the lessons: 2 is a counterexample to the claim that all primes are odd. | Can you find a counterexample to Every square is a rectangle? (There is none.) | One counterexample shows the rule is false. | A penguin is a counterexample to All birds can fly. | She found a counterexample and won the argument. | Find a counterexample: All numbers ending in 9 are prime. (Answer: 9 itself.)
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable, one word (sometimes counter-example). In maths, one counterexample proves a statement false; but many examples cannot prove it true for all numbers. Statements with all, every, always, never are tested this way.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (US, Canada, Australia, New Zealand) A creek is a small stream or narrow river. 2) (UK) A creek is a narrow inlet where the sea or a river comes into the land. 3) (idiom, slang) Up the creek means in trouble.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons, creeks are small streams that flow into rivers; in Australia, many creeks dry up in summer. In the UK, creeks are muddy inlets on the coast. In everyday North American and Australian life, children play and catch tadpoles in the creek. Safety: creeks can flood fast after rain.
examples from the lessons: We caught tadpoles in the creek behind the house. | The creek dries up in summer. (Australia) | Boats were moored in the creek at high tide. (UK) | Don't cross the creek after heavy rain. | If we miss this bus, we're up the creek! (slang) | The creek joins the big river near town.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Said kreek. Homophone: creak (a squeaky sound). In British English the usual word for a small stream is stream or brook; creek is mostly a sea inlet there.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science, geography) Deposition is when wind, water or ice drops sand, mud or stones it was carrying, building up new land such as beaches and deltas. 2) (law) A deposition is a statement made under oath, written down to be used in court. 3) (formal) Deposition is removing a ruler or leader from power. 4) (science) Deposition is when a gas turns straight into a solid, like frost forming.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons, rivers and the sea erode in one place and deposit material in another: deposition forms beaches, spits, deltas and floodplains. In chemistry, frost forming from water vapour is deposition, the opposite of sublimation. In law and history lessons, a deposition is sworn evidence, and the deposition of a king is his overthrow.
examples from the lessons: Deposition at the river mouth formed a delta. | Waves cause deposition of sand on the beach. | A spit is made by deposition along the coast. | Frost on the window is an example of deposition. | The witness gave a deposition to the lawyers. (law) | The deposition of the king led to a new government. (formal)
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable in science. Related verb: deposit (drop, leave). In geography, the order is erosion, transportation, deposition. A formal school word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Dialogue is the words that characters speak to each other in a story, play or film. 2) A dialogue is a conversation between two or more people. 3) Dialogue is a formal talk between groups or countries to solve a problem.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons, pupils write dialogue using inverted commas (speech marks), starting a new line for each new speaker and using said words like whispered or shouted. In drama, actors learn the dialogue of a script. In news, countries hold a dialogue to make peace. In computing, a dialogue box is a small window that asks a question.
examples from the lessons: Put inverted commas around the dialogue. | Start a new line each time someone new speaks in your dialogue. | The film's dialogue is very funny. | The two countries began a dialogue about peace. | Click OK in the dialogue box. | We acted out a dialogue between a shopkeeper and a customer.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK spelling dialogue; US also dialog, especially in computing. Countable and uncountable. Do not confuse with monologue (one person speaking alone).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A drake is a male duck. 2) (a name) Drake is a family name; Sir Francis Drake was an English sea captain and explorer of the 1500s. Drake is also the stage name of a Canadian rapper.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, the drake mallard has a shiny green head and a curly tail feather, while the female (duck) is brown so she can hide on her nest. In history lessons, Francis Drake sailed around the world and fought the Spanish Armada. Old dragon words: drake is also an old word for a dragon in some stories.
examples from the lessons: The drake has a bright green head. | A drake and a duck swam on the pond with their ducklings. | Female ducks are brown, but drakes are colourful. | Sir Francis Drake sailed around the world. (a name) | Drake played bowls before fighting the Armada, says the story. | The drake quacked more quietly than the female.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Male duck = drake, female = duck, young = duckling. Trap: duck can mean any duck or just the female. Female mallards quack loudly; drakes make a softer, raspy sound.

part of speech: verb (fertilise, fertilises, fertilised, fertilising); US spelling fertilize
meaning for a pupil: 1) To fertilise soil is to add manure, compost or chemicals so that plants grow better. 2) In living things, to fertilise an egg is when a male cell (sperm or pollen) joins a female egg cell so a new animal or plant can start to grow. 3) (formal, rare) To make something richer or more productive, like ideas.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons it comes in plant life cycles (bees carry pollen that fertilises flowers) and animal reproduction (frogs' eggs are fertilised in water). In gardening and farming it means feeding the soil. Phrases: fertilise the lawn, fertilised egg, be fertilised by pollen. It tells the reader a new life is starting or that plants will be helped to grow.
examples from the lessons: Dad fertilises the vegetable patch with compost every spring. | Bees help to fertilise apple blossom by carrying pollen. | A hen's egg from the shop is usually not fertilised, so no chick will hatch. | Farmers fertilise their fields before planting wheat. | In our science book, the fish eggs were fertilised in the river. | Don't fertilise the tomatoes too much or the leaves will burn. | Once the flower is fertilised, it starts to grow a fruit.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK, Australia, NZ and Ireland spell it fertilise; the USA and usually Canada spell it fertilize. The noun is fertiliser (plant food) and fertilisation (the joining of cells). Past form fertilised. Fertiliser chemicals can be poisonous: wash your hands and never eat them.

part of speech: noun (a fleece, fleeces); verb (fleece, fleeces, fleeced, fleecing — informal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The woolly coat of a sheep, or the wool cut from one sheep in one piece. 2) A soft, warm jacket or jumper made of fluffy man-made fabric. 3) (informal) To fleece someone is to cheat them out of money, often by charging far too much.
its sense in the lessons: In farm topics and stories, sheep are sheared and their fleece is spun into wool. In everyday life a fleece is a cosy jacket for cold days or school trips. In money and safety lessons, being fleeced means being cheated. Phrases: a fleece jacket, the Golden Fleece (a Greek myth), get fleeced.
examples from the lessons: The farmer clipped the sheep's fleece in one big piece. | Mary had a little lamb, its fleece was white as snow. | Bring a warm fleece on the school camping trip. | My fleece got covered in dog hair. | The tourists were fleeced by a taxi driver who charged them triple. | In the Greek myth, Jason sailed to find the Golden Fleece. | One fleece can give enough wool to knit a jumper.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one fleece, two fleeces. The verb sense is informal and means cheat; it does not mean to cut wool (that is shear). A fleece jacket is usually made of polyester, not sheep's wool.

part of speech: adjective (fossilised); verb past form of fossilise (fossilise, fossilises, fossilised, fossilising); US spelling fossilized
meaning for a pupil: 1) Turned into a fossil: the remains or print of a plant or animal that has slowly turned to stone over millions of years. 2) (figurative) Old-fashioned and unable to change, like ideas or rules stuck in the past.
its sense in the lessons: In science and history lessons it comes with dinosaurs, ammonites, ancient trees and rocks: a fossilised bone tells the reader the creature lived very long ago. Also fossilised footprints, fossilised poo (coprolite), fossilised wood. In opinion writing, fossilised ideas are ones that never change.
examples from the lessons: We found a fossilised shell on the beach at Lyme Regis. | The museum shows a fossilised dinosaur egg. | Fossilised footprints prove that the animals walked here. | Amber can hold a fossilised insect inside it. | Over millions of years, the tree trunk fossilised into stone. | My uncle says the school rules are fossilised and need updating.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK-style spelling fossilised; US fossilized. Fossilisation takes a very long time, usually thousands to millions of years, not a few years. Not every dead animal becomes a fossil; most rot away.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A small furry rodent with a long tail and strong back legs, from the deserts of Africa and Asia, often kept as a pet.
its sense in the lessons: In children's life it is a common classroom or home pet, like a hamster. In science it shows desert adaptations: gerbils need little water and dig burrows. Stories use it as a small cute pet that must be fed and cleaned out. Phrases: gerbil cage, pet gerbil.
examples from the lessons: Our class gerbil is called Nibbles. | Gerbils love to dig tunnels in deep bedding. | My gerbil drinks very little water because it comes from the desert. | Gerbils are happier living in pairs than alone. | Please close the cage so the gerbil doesn't escape. | The gerbil stood up on its back legs to sniff the air.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one gerbil, two gerbils. Not the same as a hamster: gerbils have long furry tails and are more active by day. In some places, such as California, keeping gerbils is not allowed.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A tall tree with fan-shaped leaves that turn bright yellow in autumn; it is called a living fossil because trees like it grew in the time of the dinosaurs. 2) A medicine or supplement made from its leaves (ginkgo biloba).
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons it is an example of a living fossil and an ancient plant. In everyday life you may see ginkgo trees in city streets and parks. Phrases: ginkgo leaf, ginkgo biloba, maidenhair tree (its other name).
examples from the lessons: The ginkgo in the park turns golden yellow in autumn. | Ginkgo leaves look like little fans. | Ginkgo trees were around when dinosaurs lived. | Some ginkgo trees survived the bomb in Hiroshima. | Grandma takes ginkgo tablets, but you should only take medicine an adult gives you. | The seeds of a female ginkgo tree smell very bad.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelled ginkgo (g-i-n-k-g-o), though many people say and wrongly write gingko. Pronounced GINK-oh. Its seeds can be poisonous raw; do not eat them.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Never dying; living for ever. 2) Remembered or famous for ever, like a great writer or song. 3) (noun) A being, such as a god in a myth, who never dies.
its sense in the lessons: In myths and stories, gods and magical creatures are immortal, and heroes sometimes seek to become immortal. In history and literature, people's work can be called immortal because it will always be remembered. In science, people learn that all living things die, though some tiny animals like a kind of jellyfish can renew themselves. Phrases: the immortal words, immortal soul.
examples from the lessons: The Greek gods were believed to be immortal. | In the story, the vampire was immortal and never grew older. | Nobody is immortal, so we should take care of our health. | The poet's words became immortal. | Achilles was nearly immortal except for his heel. | Christians believe that every person has an immortal soul. | The immortals lived on top of Mount Olympus.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: mortal (will die one day). Noun immortality. The im- means not. Do not mix with immoral (wrong, wicked).

meaning for a pupil: 1) To keep eggs warm so they will hatch, as a bird does by sitting on them or as a machine does. 2) To keep something such as germs, or a sick premature baby, at the right warm temperature so it can grow or be looked after. 3) (medicine) When an illness incubates, it is growing in the body before you feel sick. 4) (formal) To develop an idea or a new company slowly before it is ready.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons classes sometimes incubate chicken or duck eggs and watch them hatch in about three weeks. In health topics, an incubation period is the time between catching a germ and feeling ill. In hospitals, tiny babies may go in an incubator. Phrases: incubate eggs, incubation period.
examples from the lessons: The hen incubates her eggs for about 21 days. | Our class incubated duck eggs and four ducklings hatched. | Scientists incubate bacteria in warm dishes to study them. | The flu virus incubates for a day or two before you feel ill. | Penguin dads incubate the egg on their feet. | She incubated her idea for a book for years before writing it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: incubation; the machine is an incubator. Regular verb: incubated. The eggs must be turned and kept at the right temperature, or they will not hatch.

part of speech: adjective (Indonesian); noun (an Indonesian, Indonesians; Indonesian, the language — uncountable)
meaning for a pupil: 1) From or about Indonesia, a large country in Southeast Asia made of thousands of islands. 2) A person from Indonesia. 3) Indonesian (Bahasa Indonesia), the national language of Indonesia.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons it comes with islands, volcanoes, rainforests, orangutans and Komodo dragons. In languages it is the official language used by many millions. Phrases: Indonesian food, the Indonesian islands, speak Indonesian.
examples from the lessons: Indonesian food often has rice, peanut sauce and spices. | My friend's mum is Indonesian and comes from Bali. | The Indonesian islands include Java, Sumatra and Borneo's southern part. | Komodo dragons live on a few Indonesian islands. | She is learning to say hello in Indonesian: selamat pagi means good morning. | Many Indonesian volcanoes are still active.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always written with a capital I in normal writing. The language is often called Bahasa Indonesia (bahasa means language). Indonesia has more islands than most people guess: more than 17,000.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A large mass of earth, rocks and mud suddenly sliding down a hill or mountain. 2) (politics) A huge win in an election, by far more votes than the others.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and natural hazards lessons it is caused by heavy rain, earthquakes or cutting down trees; it can block roads and bury houses. In safety talk: keep away from steep slopes after storms. In politics and news, a landslide victory means one side won by a lot. Phrases: landslide victory, win by a landslide.
examples from the lessons: After days of rain, a landslide blocked the mountain road. | Tree roots help to stop landslides on steep hills. | The village was evacuated because of the danger of a landslide. | She won the class election by a landslide, with 25 votes out of 28. | Earthquakes can trigger landslides. | Rescue teams searched the mud after the landslide.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Similar words: mudslide (mostly mud), rockfall (falling rocks), avalanche (snow). A landslide win is a figure of speech, not real earth moving.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The leatherback turtle, the largest turtle in the world, a sea turtle whose shell is covered with tough, leathery skin instead of hard plates.
its sense in the lessons: In science and ocean lessons it is an endangered animal that eats jellyfish and can mistake plastic bags for them, so it shows why litter in the sea is dangerous. It swims very long distances and dives very deep. Phrases: leatherback turtle, leatherback sea turtle.
examples from the lessons: The leatherback is the biggest turtle on Earth. | A leatherback can weigh as much as a small car. | Leatherbacks eat mostly jellyfish. | Plastic bags in the sea can kill a leatherback that thinks they are food. | Leatherback mothers come ashore at night to lay eggs in the sand. | The leatherback's shell feels like rubbery leather.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. It is a compound of leather + back. A big leatherback can be about two metres long and weigh several hundred kilograms.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A large kind of grasshopper that sometimes gathers in huge swarms that fly far and eat all the crops. 2) (Bible) Locusts are one of the plagues of Egypt in the Book of Exodus; John the Baptist ate locusts and wild honey. 3) (US, informal) Sometimes used for a cicada, a loud buzzing insect. 4) A kind of tree (the locust tree or carob).
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography it shows how insects can damage farms and cause hunger in parts of Africa and Asia. In Bible lessons it is part of the story of Moses and the plagues. Phrases: a plague of locusts, a swarm of locusts.
examples from the lessons: A swarm of locusts can eat a whole field in one day. | Locusts are a kind of grasshopper. | In the Bible, God sent locusts to cover the land of Egypt. | John the Baptist ate locusts and wild honey. | Farmers in East Africa feared the locust swarms. | Some people around the world eat roasted locusts.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. A swarm can hold millions or even billions of locusts, which is why the numbers in problems about them get huge. In the USA people sometimes wrongly call cicadas locusts.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The main large part of a country or continent, not counting the islands near it.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons it is used to compare islands with the land next to them: Tasmania and mainland Australia, the Isle of Wight and mainland Britain, Vancouver Island and the Canadian mainland. In stories, characters take a ferry from an island to the mainland. Phrases: the mainland, mainland Europe, mainland China, back to the mainland.
examples from the lessons: We took the ferry from the island back to the mainland. | Tasmania is an island south of mainland Australia. | Some Scottish islanders shop on the mainland once a week. | Mainland Europe is just across the sea from Britain. | The storm cut the island off from the mainland. | Kangaroo Island has animals that are rare on the mainland.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually used with the: the mainland. In the UK, mainland Europe is often called the Continent. It is one word, not main land.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A delicate insect with see-through wings and long tails that lives for years as a young nymph in water but, as a flying adult, often lives only a day or less.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons it is a famous example of a short adult life and a life cycle with nymphs; mayfly nymphs in a stream show that the water is clean. In stories and poems it stands for something that lasts a very short time. Phrases: mayfly nymph, as short-lived as a mayfly.
