examples from the lessons: The mayfly lives under water for a year but flies for only one day. | We found mayfly nymphs in the stream, so the water was clean. | Adult mayflies cannot eat because they have no working mouths. | Thousands of mayflies danced above the lake at sunset. | Trout love to eat mayflies. | Her interest in chess was like a mayfly: gone by the next day.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural mayflies (y becomes ies). Despite the name, mayflies are not only seen in May. Myth: they do not all live just 24 hours; some adults live a few minutes, others a couple of days.

meaning for a pupil: 1) So small that it can only be seen through a microscope. 2) (informal) Very, very small.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons it describes germs, bacteria, cells, plankton and dust mites: things too small to see with your eyes. In health lessons it explains why hands can look clean but still carry germs. Phrases: microscopic organisms, microscopic life. In everyday talk, a microscopic slice of cake is a joke for a tiny piece.
examples from the lessons: Bacteria are microscopic living things. | The pond water is full of microscopic creatures. | Germs are microscopic, so wash your hands even when they look clean. | Your body is made of microscopic cells. | My brother gave me a microscopic piece of chocolate. | Under the lens, we saw microscopic hairs on the leaf.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective; the adverb is microscopically. Comes from microscope, the instrument. Opposite: macroscopic or visible to the naked eye.

part of speech: verb (mimic, mimics, mimicked, mimicking); noun (a mimic, mimics); adjective (mimic — rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To copy the way someone talks or moves, often to be funny or to make fun of them. 2) In nature, to look or sound like something else to stay safe or to trick, as some animals do. 3) (noun) A person or animal that is good at copying sounds or actions.
its sense in the lessons: In science it is about animal disguise: a hoverfly mimics a wasp, the lyrebird mimics chainsaws and cameras. In everyday life and kindness lessons, mimicking someone to make fun of them can hurt. In drama, mimicking voices is a skill. Phrases: a good mimic, mimic someone's accent.
examples from the lessons: Parrots can mimic human words. | The lyrebird mimics the sound of a camera shutter. | The hoverfly mimics a wasp so birds leave it alone. | Please don't mimic Sam's voice; it upsets him. | My sister is a brilliant mimic of our teacher. | The stick insect mimics a twig. | Robots can mimic the way people walk.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: add k before -ed and -ing: mimicked, mimicking (not mimiced). Noun: mimicry, the copying in nature. Similar: imitate, copy.

part of speech: adjective (modified); verb past form of modify (modify, modifies, modified, modifying)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Changed a little, usually to make it better or to suit a new purpose. 2) Genetically modified (GM): having its genes changed by scientists. 3) (grammar) A word is modified when another word describes or limits it, as an adjective does a noun.
its sense in the lessons: In design and technology, a modified car or toy has been changed. In science, genetically modified crops are a debated topic. In English grammar, adjectives and adverbs are modifiers. In maths, a modified rule or shape is a changed one. Phrases: slightly modified, genetically modified, modified version.
examples from the lessons: The scientists modified the design so the bridge was stronger. | This is a modified version of the game with easier levels. | Some crops are genetically modified to resist insects. | We modified our paper plane and it flew twice as far. | In the phrase red apple, the noun apple is modified by red. | The rules were modified after the accident.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past form of modify: y changes to ie in modifies and modified. Noun: modification. Modified usually means a small or partial change, not a complete replacement.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Across land, by road or on foot, rather than by sea or by air.
its sense in the lessons: In history and geography it describes long journeys: pioneers travelling overland by wagon in America, explorers crossing Australia, trade routes like the Silk Road. Phrases: travel overland, an overland route, overland journey.
examples from the lessons: The pioneers travelled overland in covered wagons. | We went overland by train from London to Rome instead of flying. | The overland route through the desert took weeks. | Some animals migrate overland, others by sea. | The explorers carried water on their overland trek. | The overland telegraph line crossed Australia.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word. Can be adverb (they travelled overland) or adjective (an overland journey). Opposite: by sea, by air.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A tiny living thing, such as a bacterium, virus or fungus, that can cause disease.
its sense in the lessons: In science and health lessons it explains how illnesses spread and how the immune system, vaccines, soap and cooking food properly protect us. Phrases: harmful pathogens, kill pathogens, spread of pathogens.
examples from the lessons: A pathogen is a germ that makes you ill. | Viruses and bacteria can be pathogens. | Washing your hands removes many pathogens. | Cooking chicken properly kills the pathogens in it. | White blood cells fight pathogens in the body. | Not all bacteria are pathogens; some help us digest food.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Formal science word; in everyday talk people say germ. Adjective: pathogenic. Most microbes are harmless, so pathogen does not mean every germ.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Ground that stays frozen all year round for at least two years in a row, found in very cold places like the Arctic, Siberia, Alaska and northern Canada.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and climate lessons, melting permafrost shows global warming: buildings sink, roads crack, and gases trapped inside escape. Frozen mammoths have been found in permafrost. Phrases: thawing permafrost, permafrost layer.
examples from the lessons: In northern Canada, the ground under the moss is permafrost. | Scientists found a baby mammoth frozen in the permafrost. | Houses in Siberia are built on stilts above the permafrost. | As the climate warms, the permafrost is thawing. | Trees cannot grow deep roots in permafrost. | Thawing permafrost lets out greenhouse gases.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: some permafrost, not a permafrost. From permanent + frost. The top layer may thaw in summer while the ground below stays frozen.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who hunts or catches animals or fish illegally, often rare animals like elephants and rhinos. 2) A pan for poaching (gently cooking) eggs. 3) (sport) A player who scores by waiting near the goal.
its sense in the lessons: In conservation and geography lessons, poachers kill elephants for ivory and rhinos for their horns, so rangers protect parks. In old stories, a poacher steals rabbits or deer from a rich landowner. Phrases: ivory poachers, poacher turned gamekeeper (someone who changes sides).
examples from the lessons: Poachers killed the rhino for its horn. | Park rangers chase poachers away from the elephants. | In the story, the poor man became a poacher to feed his children. | An egg poacher cooks eggs in little cups over water. | The striker is a goal poacher who always finds space. | Dogs help sniff out poachers in Africa.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Verb: poach (to hunt illegally, or to cook gently in water; also to take someone from another team). Poaching wild animals is a crime in most countries.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Mostly; mainly; for the greatest part.
its sense in the lessons: In geography, science and exam writing it summarises data: a region is predominantly forest; the class is predominantly girls. It tells the reader that most, but not all, of something is like this. In maths problems it hints at more than half.
examples from the lessons: The forest is predominantly made up of pine trees. | The town is predominantly English-speaking. | Koalas eat predominantly eucalyptus leaves. | The weather in Ireland is predominantly mild and wet. | Our class is predominantly made up of nine-year-olds. | The book is predominantly about friendship.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; in everyday talk say mostly or mainly. Adjective: predominant. Spelling: pre-dom-in-ant-ly. In numbers, it means more than half, usually much more, but not all.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (of animals and plants) A very small kind of a species, much smaller than its relatives, such as a pygmy hippo, pygmy goat or pygmy marmoset. 2) (often offensive) An old word for members of some peoples in Central Africa who are short; today people prefer to use the names of the peoples themselves, such as the Mbuti or Baka. 3) (informal, insulting) A person thought to be unimportant.
its sense in the lessons: In science and zoo topics, pygmy is part of animal names: pygmy hippo, pygmy seahorse, pygmy shrew, pygmy possum. In geography and history, children learn to name peoples respectfully. Phrases: pygmy hippopotamus, pygmy goat.
examples from the lessons: The pygmy hippo lives in the forests of West Africa. | A pygmy seahorse is smaller than your fingernail. | The farm had three cheeky pygmy goats. | The pygmy marmoset is one of the smallest monkeys. | The pygmy possum sleeps through the cold winter in Australia. | Our guide used the name Baka for the forest people instead of an old label.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural pygmies. Also spelled pigmy. Safe to use for animals; for people, the word is often seen as insulting.

part of speech: noun (a redwood, redwoods; redwood — the wood, uncountable)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A very tall evergreen tree with reddish bark, found mainly in California; coast redwoods are the tallest trees on Earth. 2) The reddish wood from such trees.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and science lessons redwoods are record-breakers: some are over 110 metres tall and over 2,000 years old. They show forests, conservation and fire-resistant bark. Phrases: redwood forest, giant redwood, Redwood National Park.
examples from the lessons: Redwoods are the tallest trees in the world. | We walked among giant redwoods in California. | Some redwoods are older than the Roman Empire. | The redwood's thick bark protects it from fire. | Our garden bench is made of redwood. | You have to tip your head right back to see the top of a redwood.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable for trees, uncountable for wood. The giant sequoia is a related tree that is the biggest by volume, while the coast redwood is the tallest.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unusual or special in a way that makes people notice it and talk about it; amazing or impressive.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, a remarkable person or event stands out. In science and history writing, a remarkable discovery is surprising and important. In school reports, remarkable progress is great praise. Phrases: a remarkable achievement, remarkably good.
examples from the lessons: She made a remarkable recovery after her accident. | It is remarkable that a bee can find its way home. | The boy showed remarkable courage. | What a remarkable view from the top of the hill! | Your handwriting has made remarkable progress this term. | There is nothing remarkable about this ordinary stone.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb: remarkably (remarkably fast). From remark (to notice and say). Usually positive, but it can simply mean surprising.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person whose job is to study something carefully to discover new facts, for example a scientist doing experiments or someone studying history or people.
its sense in the lessons: In science and news lessons, researchers find things out and publish results; children learn to ask who the researchers were and how they tested their idea. Phrases: medical researcher, researchers found that, a team of researchers.
examples from the lessons: Researchers found that dogs can understand many words. | A team of researchers studied the coral reef. | The researcher wore a lab coat and goggles. | Researchers say more sleep helps children learn. | My aunt is a researcher who studies bees. | The researcher asked our class to fill in a survey.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Verb and noun: research (researching, researched; research as a noun is usually uncountable: do some research). Researchers found that is often reported as fact, but one study can be wrong, so check if others agree.

part of speech: noun (a revolt, revolts); verb (revolt, revolts, revolted, revolting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (noun) A fight or protest by many people against their rulers or the people in charge. 2) (verb) To refuse to obey and rise up against the people in power. 3) (verb) To revolt someone is to make them feel disgusted or sick. 4) (informal) Revolting (adjective) means really disgusting.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons revolts happen against kings, empires or unfair taxes, like the Peasants' Revolt in England. In everyday talk revolting food or a revolting smell is disgusting. Phrases: rise in revolt, the Peasants' Revolt, be revolted by.
examples from the lessons: Long ago, thousands of English peasants joined a revolt against unfair taxes. | The people revolted against the cruel king. | The sailors revolted and took control of the ship. | The smell of the bins revolted me. | This school dinner is revolting! | The children staged a small revolt when the trip was cancelled.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: revolted. Similar: rebellion, uprising, mutiny (on a ship or in an army). Revolting usually means disgusting, but it can mean taking part in a revolt.

part of speech: noun (rickets — uncountable, used with a singular verb)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A disease in children that makes bones soft and weak, so legs can bend, usually caused by not getting enough vitamin D, sunlight or calcium.
its sense in the lessons: In health and history lessons rickets shows why vitamin D and sunlight matter; it was common in smoky Victorian cities and is now rare but can still happen. Phrases: suffer from rickets, prevent rickets.
examples from the lessons: Rickets makes children's bones bend. | Victorian children in dark, smoky cities often had rickets. | Sunlight helps your skin make vitamin D, which prevents rickets. | Fish, eggs and fortified milk help stop rickets. | The doctor said rickets is rare today but still happens. | Cod liver oil was given to children to prevent rickets.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Ends in -s but is not a plural: rickets is a disease (not a ricket). Doctors use it for children; the adult illness is called osteomalacia.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A set of actions always done in the same way and order, especially as part of a religious ceremony. 2) Something a person or family always does in the same way, like a habit. 3) (adjective) Done as part of a ceremony or out of habit.
its sense in the lessons: In religion and history lessons, rituals include baptism, prayers, festivals, ancient burial and harvest ceremonies; in church, Christians share rituals such as communion. In everyday life, a bedtime story or a team chant before a match is a ritual. Phrases: a bedtime ritual, religious ritual, ritual dance.
examples from the lessons: Lighting candles is part of the ritual in many churches. | Our bedtime ritual is a bath, a story and a cuddle. | The ancient Egyptians had rituals for burying their kings. | Every Saturday, Dad's ritual is pancakes and the football. | The team does a ritual handshake before each game. | Baptism is an important Christian ritual.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Related: rite (a single ceremony) and ritually (adverb). Not the same as habit, although an everyday ritual can be a habit with a special meaning.

part of speech: adjective (saltwater); noun (saltwater or salt water — uncountable)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Water that has salt in it, like sea water. 2) (adjective) Living in or coming from the sea, not fresh water: saltwater fish, saltwater crocodile.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons it is used to compare freshwater and saltwater habitats and in experiments (an egg floats in salt water). In geography, most of Earth's water is saltwater in oceans. In safety, saltwater crocodiles in northern Australia are very dangerous. Phrases: saltwater crocodile (saltie), saltwater aquarium.
examples from the lessons: Most of the water on Earth is saltwater. | Saltwater fish cannot live in a pond. | An egg floats in salt water but sinks in tap water. | Saltwater crocodiles live in northern Australia; never swim where there are croc signs. | Don't drink saltwater, as it makes you thirstier. | We gargled warm salt water for a sore throat.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As an adjective it is one word (a saltwater fish); as a noun many writers use two words (salt water). Opposite: freshwater. Drinking seawater is dangerous because the salt dries the body out.

part of speech: noun (the Sami, a Sami, Sami); adjective (Sami); also spelled Sámi or Saami
meaning for a pupil: 1) The Sami are an Indigenous people of the far north of Norway, Sweden, Finland and Russia, an area called Sápmi; many have herded reindeer. 2) The Sami languages, spoken by the Sami people. 3) (a name) Sami is also a first name for a person, used in Finland and in Arabic-speaking countries.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and world cultures lessons, the Sami show life in the Arctic, reindeer herding, colourful traditional clothes called gákti and joik songs. Phrases: the Sami people, Sami culture. Use the name Sami, not the old word Lapp, which is seen as rude.
examples from the lessons: The Sami have lived in the far north of Europe for thousands of years. | Some Sami families herd reindeer. | She wore a bright blue Sami dress for the festival. | A joik is a traditional Sami song. | Sami children may learn both Sami and Norwegian at school. | Our pen pal Sami lives in Helsinki.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital S. Spellings Sami, Sámi and Saami are all used. Do not call them Lapps or the region Lapland in a way that ignores the people; Sápmi is their own name for their land.

part of speech: noun (sandpaper — uncountable; a sheet of sandpaper); verb (sandpaper, sandpapers, sandpapered, sandpapering)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Strong paper with sand or grit stuck to one side, used for rubbing wood or other surfaces to make them smooth. 2) (verb) To smooth something by rubbing it with sandpaper.
its sense in the lessons: In design and technology lessons you sandpaper wood before painting it; rough and smooth grades are compared. In science, it is used to show friction. In descriptions, a cat's tongue or a rough cheek feels like sandpaper. Phrases: rub with sandpaper, sandpaper the edges, rough as sandpaper.
examples from the lessons: Use sandpaper to smooth the edges of your wooden box. | Dad sandpapered the old door before painting it. | A cat's tongue feels like sandpaper. | Coarse sandpaper takes off a lot; fine sandpaper makes it really smooth. | Wear a mask when sandpapering, because the dust gets in your nose. | Grandad's chin felt like sandpaper when he hadn't shaved.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable: some sandpaper, a sheet or piece of sandpaper. The verb sand is often used instead: sand the table. Lower grit numbers mean rougher paper.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who saves money instead of spending it all. 2) Something that saves you time, money, space or energy: a time-saver, an energy saver. 3) A screen saver: a moving picture a computer shows when it is not being used. 4) (sport) A goalkeeper or player who saves goals or points.
its sense in the lessons: In money lessons, savers put money in a piggy bank or bank account and may earn interest. In everyday life, a lifesaver is someone or something that helps a lot. Phrases: a good saver, money saver, time-saver, lifesaver.
examples from the lessons: My brother is a good saver; he keeps half his pocket money. | Savers get a little extra money called interest from the bank. | The dishwasher is a real time-saver. | This bulb is an energy saver. | Thanks for the pencil, you're a lifesaver! | The keeper was a great saver of penalties.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Not to be confused with savour (to enjoy a taste slowly) or saviour (someone who rescues; in church, Christians call Jesus the Saviour). In maths problems a saver adds money each week.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An animal that feeds on dead animals or scraps that other creatures have left, such as a vulture, hyena or crab. 2) A person who searches through rubbish for things to use or sell. 3) A scavenger hunt is a game in which you search for a list of things.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons scavengers are part of food chains and help clean up nature by eating dead bodies. In everyday life children play scavenger hunts at parties and on school trips. Phrases: scavenger hunt, nature's clean-up crew.
examples from the lessons: Vultures are scavengers that eat dead animals. | Hyenas are hunters and scavengers. | Seagulls are scavengers that steal chips. | We had a scavenger hunt in the park for leaves, pine cones and feathers. | Crabs are scavengers on the sea floor. | Scavengers help recycle nutrients back into the soil.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Verb: scavenge (scavenged, scavenging). Myth: hyenas do not only scavenge; they hunt most of their food.

part of speech: noun (a scrum, scrums); verb (scrum, scrums, scrummed, scrumming)
meaning for a pupil: 1) In rugby, a way of restarting play in which players from each team pack together with arms linked, push against each other and try to win the ball with their feet. 2) (informal) A crowd of people pushing to get somewhere or something. 3) (work, computing) Scrum is a way teams of programmers plan work in short bursts called sprints.
its sense in the lessons: In sport, scrum is a key rugby word, popular in New Zealand, Australia, Ireland, the UK and South Africa. In everyday talk, a scrum is the crush at the school gate or a sale. Phrases: scrum-half, a media scrum, scrum down.
examples from the lessons: The two rugby teams packed down for a scrum. | The ball was fed into the scrum and our side won it. | There was a scrum at the canteen door when the bell went. | Photographers formed a scrum around the famous singer. | The scrum-half passed the ball out quickly. | In Scrum, the software team meets for a few minutes every day.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Short for scrummage. In rugby league and rugby union the scrum has different numbers of players (6 or 8 per side).

part of speech: noun (a seesaw, seesaws); verb (seesaw, seesaws, seesawed, seesawing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A long board balanced in the middle on which two children sit at opposite ends and go up and down. 2) (verb) To move up and down or back and forth again and again, or to keep changing between two states.
its sense in the lessons: In playground life it is a favourite toy (in the USA also called a teeter-totter). In science and maths it shows balance and levers: a heavier child must sit nearer the middle. In stories, feelings or a score can seesaw. Phrases: on the seesaw, seesawing prices.
examples from the lessons: We went up and down on the seesaw at the park. | Dad is heavier, so he sat nearer the middle of the seesaw to balance it. | A seesaw is a kind of lever. | The score seesawed all game until the last goal. | My mood seesawed between happy and nervous before the concert. | Hold on tight on the seesaw and don't jump off suddenly.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Also written see-saw. Americans also say teeter-totter. In lever problems, weight times distance from the middle must match on both sides for it to balance.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A very large grey bird of the swamps of East Africa with a huge bill shaped like a wooden shoe, which it uses to catch fish, lungfish and even baby crocodiles.
its sense in the lessons: In science and nature lessons, it is a strange-looking bird that stands still for a long time and then strikes; it is threatened by loss of wetlands. Phrases: shoebill stork (a common but inexact name).
examples from the lessons: The shoebill has a bill shaped like a big shoe. | A shoebill can stand still for hours waiting for a fish. | Shoebills live in the swamps of Uganda and South Sudan. | The shoebill clatters its bill to make a noise. | Visitors at the zoo stared at the shoebill's grumpy face. | Shoebills are tall, about as tall as a child.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Often called a shoebill stork, but it is not a true stork. Related: whalehead, another name for it.

part of speech: noun (a sketch, sketches); verb (sketch, sketches, sketched, sketching)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A quick drawing that shows the main shapes without much detail. 2) A short, funny scene in a comedy show or school play. 3) A short description of something with only the main points. 4) (verb) To draw quickly, or to describe in a few words. 5) (slang, US) Sketchy means dodgy, unsafe or suspicious.
its sense in the lessons: In art lessons you sketch with a pencil before painting; in science you sketch what you see under a magnifier. In drama, groups make up sketches. In everyday slang, a sketchy place or website is not trustworthy. Phrases: a rough sketch, sketch out a plan, sketchbook.
examples from the lessons: I made a quick sketch of the tree before painting it. | Sketch the leaf and label its parts. | Our group acted a funny sketch about a lost dog. | She sketched out her plan for the treehouse. | Keep your sketchbook in your bag. | That website looks sketchy, so don't type your password. | The teacher gave a short sketch of the Romans' life.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: sketch, sketches (add -es). Regular verb sketched. Sketchy (informal) can also mean incomplete: sketchy details.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To hit or shock a person or animal so they are dizzy or knocked out for a short time. 2) To surprise or shock someone so much that they cannot think or speak for a moment. 3) Stunning (adjective) means extremely beautiful or impressive.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and news, people are stunned by surprising events. In science, some fish and eels stun prey with electricity. In everyday talk, a stunning view or a stunning goal is amazing. Phrases: stunned silence, stun gun, absolutely stunning.
examples from the lessons: The bird hit the window and was stunned for a minute. | Electric eels can stun fish with a shock. | We were stunned when our team won the cup. | There was a stunned silence after the news. | The view from the mountain was stunning. | The news of the fire stunned the whole town.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double the n: stunned, stunning. Stun guns are weapons and are illegal for ordinary people in many places.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A small meat-eating plant that grows in boggy places and has leaves covered in sticky, shining hairs that trap and digest insects.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons it is an example of a carnivorous plant, like the Venus flytrap, which gets extra food from insects because bog soil is poor. Phrases: carnivorous plant, sticky leaves.
examples from the lessons: A sundew catches flies with its sticky leaves. | The drops on a sundew look like dew in the sun. | Sundews grow in wet, boggy places. | When an insect lands on a sundew, the leaf curls around it. | We grew a sundew on the classroom windowsill. | Sundews and Venus flytraps are both meat-eating plants.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. From sun + dew, because the sticky drops shine. It does not eat people or big animals, only small insects.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A small bird of the swift family living in tropical Asia and Australia, many of which nest in caves and find their way in the dark with clicking sounds (echolocation).
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons it is an example of a bird that uses echolocation like bats. In geography, some swiftlets make nests of their own spit that people collect for bird's nest soup. Phrases: cave swiftlet, edible-nest swiftlet.
examples from the lessons: Swiftlets nest high on the walls of dark caves. | A swiftlet clicks to find its way in the dark. | Some swiftlets build nests from their own spit. | Bird's nest soup is made from swiftlet nests. | Swiftlets catch insects while flying. | The cave was full of the sound of swiftlets.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. The -let ending means small (like piglet, booklet). Swiftlets are not swallows, though they look alike.

part of speech: noun (a thrush, thrushes; thrush — the illness, uncountable)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A songbird with a brown back and a spotted chest, such as the song thrush; the American robin is also a thrush. 2) (medicine) An infection caused by a yeast (a fungus), which makes white patches in the mouth or itching.
its sense in the lessons: In nature lessons the song thrush is known for repeating its song phrases and smashing snail shells on stones. In health topics, thrush is a common, treatable infection, often in babies' mouths. Phrases: song thrush, mistle thrush.
examples from the lessons: A song thrush was singing in the garden at dawn. | The thrush cracked a snail shell on a stone. | Thrushes have speckled chests. | The American robin is actually a kind of thrush. | The baby had thrush, so the doctor gave some medicine. | We saw a mistle thrush eating berries.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The bird is countable (thrushes); the illness is uncountable. Two very different meanings with one spelling.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The Tasmanian tiger or Tasmanian wolf, a striped, dog-like marsupial (pouched animal) that lived in Australia and Tasmania and is believed to have died out; the last known one died in a zoo in Hobart nearly a hundred years ago.
its sense in the lessons: In science and history lessons it is a sad example of extinction caused by hunting, habitat loss and disease. In Australia it is a symbol of Tasmania. Phrases: Tasmanian tiger, last thylacine.
examples from the lessons: The thylacine had stripes on its back like a tiger. | The last known thylacine died in a zoo in Hobart. | Thylacines carried their babies in a pouch. | Farmers hunted thylacines because they thought they killed sheep. | Some people say they have seen a thylacine, but nobody has proved it. | Scientists study old thylacine bones and films.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Pronounced THY-luh-seen. It was not a real tiger or wolf; it was a marsupial. Claims of sightings are unproven.

part of speech: noun (a troll, trolls); verb (troll, trolls, trolled, trolling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) In Scandinavian fairy tales, a big, ugly, often stupid creature that lives in caves, mountains or under bridges. 2) (internet slang) A person who posts nasty or silly messages online on purpose to upset people or start arguments. 3) (verb, slang) To troll is to post such messages, or to tease someone by pretending. 4) (verb) To fish by pulling a baited line slowly behind a boat.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, the troll under the bridge in Three Billy Goats Gruff is famous. In online safety lessons, children learn not to feed the trolls: do not reply, block and report, and tell an adult. Phrases: internet troll, don't feed the trolls, get trolled.
examples from the lessons: The troll lived under the bridge and roared at the goats. | In Norwegian tales, trolls turn to stone in sunlight. | Someone was a troll and wrote mean comments on her video. | Don't feed the trolls; block them and tell a grown-up. | My brother was just trolling me when he said school was cancelled. | Grandpa trolled for fish from the back of the boat.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Regular verb: trolled. Being trolled online is not your fault; screenshot, report and talk to a trusted adult.

part of speech: noun (vas, plural vasa — medical, rare); fragment
meaning for a pupil: 1) (medicine, Latin) A tube or vessel in the body that carries fluid; mostly seen in vas deferens, the tube in a man's body that carries sperm. 2) A fragment of longer words such as vascular (to do with blood vessels) or canvas. 3) (French) Vas is a form of the French verb aller, to go: tu vas means you go or you are going; vas-y means go on! It sounds like va to an English ear. It is not an English word on its own.
its sense in the lessons: In science and health lessons it may appear in the name vas deferens in reproduction topics. In French lessons, vas-y and comment vas-tu (how are you?) are common phrases. Otherwise it is rarely used alone in English.
examples from the lessons: The vas deferens is a tube in the male reproductive system. | Vascular plants have tubes that carry water. | In French, comment vas-tu means how are you. | Vas-y! means go on! in French. | Vas is Latin for vessel. | The word canvas ends with the letters vas.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Not a normal English word on its own; it is Latin (vessel) or French (go). In French the s is silent: vas sounds like va.

part of speech: noun (velvet — uncountable; a velvet, rare); adjective (velvet, velvety)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A soft cloth with a thick, short, fluffy surface on one side, often used for fancy clothes, curtains and cushions. 2) (figurative) Something very soft and smooth, like a voice or skin. 3) The soft furry skin on a deer's new antlers.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and descriptions, velvet suggests richness and softness: a velvet cloak, velvet curtains in a theatre. In science, deer antlers grow covered in velvet. Phrases: red velvet cake, velvety soft, The Velveteen Rabbit (a children's story with velveteen, a similar cloth).
examples from the lessons: The queen wore a long velvet cloak. | The theatre had heavy red velvet curtains. | The puppy's ears felt like velvet. | Mum made a red velvet cake for my birthday. | The young deer's antlers were covered in velvet. | She sang in a soft, velvety voice.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable. Adjective velvety means soft like velvet. Velcro and velour are different things.

part of speech: noun (a watermelon, watermelons; watermelon — the flesh, uncountable)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A large round or oval fruit with a hard green skin and sweet, juicy red or pink flesh with black seeds. 2) The juicy flesh of this fruit as food.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life it is a summer fruit at picnics and barbecues. In science, it shows seeds and that watermelon is about 90 per cent water. In maths, slices of watermelon are used for fractions. Phrases: a slice of watermelon, seedless watermelon.
examples from the lessons: We ate watermelon at the beach on a hot day. | A watermelon is mostly water. | Mum cut the watermelon into eight equal slices. | Don't swallow the seeds, spit them out. | Watermelons grow on long vines on the ground. | A whole watermelon is heavy, so carry it with two hands. | I would like some more watermelon, please.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable for whole fruits (two watermelons), uncountable for the flesh (some watermelon). Myth: swallowing a seed will not make a watermelon grow in your tummy. In fraction problems, a watermelon cut into 8 equal slices gives each slice one eighth.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A small beetle with a long snout, which often eats and damages crops, flour, rice, grain and nuts.
its sense in the lessons: In science and farming topics, weevils are pests that spoil stored food or crops, such as the boll weevil on cotton. In history, sailors' ship biscuits were often full of weevils. In everyday life, finding weevils in flour means throwing it out. Phrases: boll weevil, weevils in the flour.
examples from the lessons: There were weevils in the old bag of flour. | The weevil has a long nose called a snout. | Weevils can damage a whole crop of grain. | Sailors on old ships ate biscuits full of weevils. | Keep rice in a sealed jar so weevils can't get in. | The boll weevil damaged cotton farms in the USA.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Weevils are beetles, so they have six legs and hard wing cases. They are not poisonous, but food with weevils is usually thrown away.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Having no wings.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons it describes animals like ostriches, kiwis, emus (whose wings are tiny and useless), fleas, lice, ants that are workers, and some insects. It tells the reader the creature cannot fly. Phrases: wingless bird, wingless insect.
examples from the lessons: The kiwi is almost wingless and cannot fly. | Fleas are wingless insects that jump. | Worker ants are wingless, but the queen has wings at first. | The wingless toy plane would never fly. | Moas were huge wingless birds in New Zealand. | Silverfish are small wingless insects.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The suffix -less means without (like hopeless, careless). Some birds called flightless still have small wings, so flightless is often more accurate than wingless.

meaning for a pupil: 1) XIV is the Roman numeral for 14: X (10) + IV (4). 2) It is used for numbers in names of kings, popes and chapters, such as Louis XIV (Louis the Fourteenth) of France.
its sense in the lessons: In maths lessons, children learn Roman numerals: I = 1, V = 5, X = 10, and a smaller number before a bigger one is subtracted (IV = 4). In history, kings' names use them. On clocks and buildings Roman numerals appear too. Phrases: Louis XIV, Chapter XIV.
examples from the lessons: XIV means fourteen. | X plus IV makes XIV. | Louis XIV was a famous king of France known as the Sun King. | Turn to Chapter XIV of the book. | Write 14 in Roman numerals: XIV. | XIV minus IV is X.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It is not a word but a number; usually written in capital letters, XIV. It is said as fourteen, or fourteenth after a king's name. Trap: XIV is 14, not 16 (that is XVI).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (US, Canada sometimes) The name of the letter Z in American English. 2) (informal) Zees, or z's, means sleep, as in catch some z's, because cartoons show sleep with zzz.
its sense in the lessons: In spelling and alphabet lessons, Americans say zee and most of the UK, Ireland, Australia, New Zealand and Canada say zed. In comics, zzz shows snoring. Phrases: from A to Z, catch some z's.
examples from the lessons: In the USA, the last letter of the alphabet is called zee. | In Australia we say zed, but my American cousin says zee. | The alphabet song in America ends with x, y and zee. | I'm going to catch some zees before the trip. | Zebra begins with zee in American speech. | Canadians usually say zed, but some say zee.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Zee and zed are the same letter Z, said differently. Not to be confused with the sea or the letter C (see).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A sweet drink made from fruit juice, water and sugar, such as lemonade, orangeade or limeade. 2) (suffix) -ade ends many words: lemonade, parade, blockade, barricade, escapade. 3) (a name) Ade is a short form of the names Adrian or Adeola.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life ade appears mostly inside drink names: lemonade (in the UK often fizzy, in the USA usually still). On its own, ade is rare. In spelling lessons, -ade is a common ending. Phrases: lemonade stand.
examples from the lessons: We sold lemonade at a stand outside our house. | Orangeade is an orange drink, like lemonade. | The menu had a mango ade. | The words parade and lemonade both end in -ade. | Ade is short for Adrian. | Limeade is green and sour.
note for the reader of a maths problem: On its own it is rare; mostly a part of longer words. Lemonade in the UK and Australia is usually a fizzy drink; in the USA it is still lemon juice, water and sugar.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A cartoon or film made by showing many drawings, models or computer pictures one after another so they seem to move. 2) The art or work of making such films. 3) Liveliness and excitement in the way someone talks or moves.
its sense in the lessons: In art and computing lessons children make simple animations with flip books, Scratch or stop-motion clay figures. In everyday life, many films and TV shows are animations. In stories, someone speaking with animation is lively. Phrases: computer animation, stop-motion animation, suspended animation (a state like deep sleep).
examples from the lessons: We made a stop-motion animation with plasticine figures. | Animation needs many pictures every second. | My favourite animation is about a dragon who can't fly. | In Scratch, we coded an animation of a cat dancing. | She told the story with great animation, waving her arms. | A flip book is a simple kind of animation.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable for the art, countable for a single film. Verb: animate; a person who makes animations is an animator. Films often show 24 pictures (frames) per second.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A large group of warships. 2) The Spanish Armada: the great fleet that King Philip II of Spain sent to invade England in the time of Queen Elizabeth I; it was defeated and wrecked by storms. 3) (informal) Any large group of boats or vehicles.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons the Spanish Armada is a famous story about the Tudors, Francis Drake, fire ships and storms. In everyday writing, an armada of boats means a lot of them. Phrases: the Spanish Armada.
examples from the lessons: The Spanish Armada sailed to attack England. | Storms wrecked many ships of the Armada. | The English sent fire ships among the Armada's ships at night. | An armada of little boats rescued the soldiers. | Queen Elizabeth I gave a famous speech when the Armada came. | A colourful armada of yachts sailed into the harbour.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Spanish word for armed fleet. Written with a capital A in the Spanish Armada. Similar: fleet, navy.

part of speech: noun (a bloom, blooms; in bloom); verb (bloom, blooms, bloomed, blooming)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A flower, especially on a plant grown for its flowers. 2) (verb) To produce flowers; to open into flowers. 3) (verb) To grow healthy, happy or confident. 4) (in science) An algal bloom: a sudden big growth of algae in water, sometimes harmful. 5) (UK, informal, old-fashioned) Blooming is a mild swear word meaning very or annoying: blooming cheek!
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, plants bloom in spring and summer and insects visit the blooms. In stories, a shy character blooms into a confident one. In safety, algal blooms can make lakes unsafe for swimming. Phrases: in full bloom, late bloomer, a blooming nuisance.
examples from the lessons: The cherry trees are in full bloom. | Roses bloom in summer. | The cactus bloomed after the rain. | Our new classmate bloomed once she made friends. | Don't swim in the lake: there's a green algal bloom. | My brother is a late bloomer, but now he's great at football. | It's blooming freezing out here!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: bloomed. Similar: blossom (often used for fruit trees). Blooming as a swear word is very mild and a bit old-fashioned in the UK.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The bottlenose dolphin, a common grey dolphin with a short, bottle-shaped snout, often seen near coasts and in shows. 2) A bottlenose whale, a kind of deep-diving whale.
its sense in the lessons: In science and ocean lessons, bottlenose dolphins are clever mammals that use echolocation, whistle to each other and live in groups called pods. Phrases: bottlenose dolphin, a pod of bottlenoses.
examples from the lessons: A pod of bottlenose dolphins swam beside our boat. | Bottlenose dolphins use clicks to find fish. | Each bottlenose has its own signature whistle, like a name. | Bottlenoses breathe air through a blowhole. | We saw bottlenose dolphins in Cardigan Bay. | The bottlenose leapt high out of the water.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly used before dolphin. Dolphins are mammals, not fish. Also spelled bottle-nose.

part of speech: verb (bray, brays, brayed, braying); noun (a bray, brays)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To make the loud, harsh noise of a donkey (hee-haw). 2) (of people) To laugh or talk loudly and unpleasantly. 3) (noun) The sound a donkey makes.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and farm topics, donkeys bray. In descriptions, a braying laugh is loud and annoying. In nativity and Bible stories, a donkey may bray in the stable. Phrases: donkey's bray, braying laugh.
examples from the lessons: The donkey brayed loudly at the gate. | We heard a loud bray from the field. | The man's braying laugh filled the café. | Hee-haw is how we write a donkey's bray. | The donkey brayed when it wanted its dinner. | A trumpet in the band brayed out of tune.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: brayed. Bray is also a seaside town in Ireland (a name).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A tiny piece of bread. 2) Breadcrumbs (plural): very small bits of dried bread used for coating food like fish or chicken before frying. 3) (computing) A breadcrumb trail: a line of links at the top of a website showing where you are, like Home > Science > Plants.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, Hansel and Gretel leave a trail of breadcrumbs to find their way home, but birds eat them. In cooking, food is coated in breadcrumbs. In computing lessons, breadcrumbs help you find your way on a website. Phrases: a trail of breadcrumbs, coated in breadcrumbs.
examples from the lessons: Hansel dropped breadcrumbs to mark the path. | The birds ate all the breadcrumbs. | Dip the fish in egg and then in breadcrumbs. | There were breadcrumbs all over the table after breakfast. | The website's breadcrumbs showed Home > Games > Puzzles. | We fed breadcrumbs to the ducks, but oats are better for them.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable, usually plural (breadcrumbs). Bread itself is uncountable. Feeding a lot of bread to ducks is bad for them.

part of speech: noun (breakers — plural of breaker; a breaker)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Big waves that rise up and crash into white foam on a beach or rocks. 2) A breaker is also a person or machine that breaks things: a record-breaker, an ice-breaker, a circuit breaker (a safety switch). 3) (informal) Breakers can be breakdancers.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and stories about the sea, the breakers roll in and crash on the shore. In safety lessons, big breakers and rip currents can be dangerous, so swim between the flags. In science, a circuit breaker switches off electricity when something goes wrong. Phrases: record-breaker, ice-breaker game, circuit breaker.
examples from the lessons: The breakers crashed on the rocks. | Surfers waited for the big breakers. | Swim between the flags, away from the big breakers. | The ship was smashed by the breakers. | She is a record-breaker in the swimming team. | We played an ice-breaker game on the first day of school. | The circuit breaker tripped and the lights went out.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural of breaker. When used for waves it is nearly always plural. Related: break, broke, broken.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A small clever monkey from Central and South America with a cap of dark fur on its head, known for using tools such as stones to crack nuts. 2) (church) A Capuchin is a member of a Catholic order of friars (monks) who wear brown robes with pointed hoods.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, capuchin monkeys show tool use and intelligence. In church and history topics, Capuchin friars live simply and help the poor; the drink cappuccino is named after the colour of their robes. Phrases: capuchin monkey, Capuchin friar.
examples from the lessons: Capuchin monkeys use stones to crack open nuts. | The capuchin has a dark cap of hair on its head. | Capuchins live in groups in the rainforest trees. | A Capuchin friar wears a brown robe with a hood. | Cappuccino coffee is named after the Capuchin friars. | The capuchin monkey washed its food in the stream.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Capital C for the friars. Pronounced KAP-yoo-chin or kap-oo-CHEEN. Monkeys are wild animals and should not be kept as pets.

part of speech: noun (the Cherokee, a Cherokee, Cherokees; Cherokee — the language); adjective (Cherokee)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The Cherokee are a Native American people, originally from the south-east of what is now the USA, many of whom now live in Oklahoma and North Carolina. 2) The Cherokee language, which has its own writing system created by Sequoyah. 3) (a name) Cherokee is also the name of a car model and of places.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, the Cherokee are known for Sequoyah's syllabary and for the Trail of Tears, when the US government forced them to leave their homelands and many died on the journey. In everyday life, the Cherokee Nation is a modern self-governing nation. Phrases: the Cherokee Nation, the Trail of Tears.
examples from the lessons: The Cherokee are a Native American nation. | Sequoyah created a way to write the Cherokee language. | Thousands of Cherokee people were forced to walk the Trail of Tears. | Today many Cherokee live in Oklahoma. | My friend is learning a few Cherokee words. | The Cherokee Nation has its own government.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always capital C. Both the Cherokee and Cherokees are used for the people. Pronounced CHAIR-uh-kee.

part of speech: noun (a clone, clones); verb (clone, clones, cloned, cloning)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A living thing that is an exact copy of another, with the same genes, made naturally or by scientists. 2) (verb) To make such a copy. 3) (informal) Something or someone that is very like another: a cheap clone of a famous game. 4) (computing) To make an exact copy of a disk, phone or code project.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, Dolly the sheep was the first mammal cloned from an adult cell; gardeners make clones when they take cuttings, and identical twins are natural clones. In everyday talk, clone means copy. In online safety, criminals may clone a phone or bank card. Phrases: Dolly the sheep, clone a project.
examples from the lessons: Dolly the sheep was a clone. | A cutting from a plant grows into a clone of the parent. | Identical twins are a bit like natural clones. | Scientists cloned a mouse in a laboratory. | This game is a clone of a famous one. | We cloned the code from the website. | Criminals cloned his bank card, so he called the bank.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: cloned. A clone has the same genes but is not the same person: it has its own memories and life. Cloning people is not allowed in most countries.

part of speech: verb past form of colonise (colonise, colonises, colonised, colonising); adjective (colonised); US spelling colonized
meaning for a pupil: 1) When a country colonised a land, it took control of it and sent its people to live there, often taking the land from the people already living there. 2) (science) When animals or plants colonise a place, they move in and start living and growing there.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons it comes with empires: Britain colonised Australia, India and parts of Africa and America, which brought great harm to the Indigenous peoples. In science, plants colonise new land after a volcano or fire. Phrases: colonised by, the colonised peoples.
examples from the lessons: Britain colonised Australia and New Zealand. | The land was colonised by Europeans who took it from the people already living there. | Many colonised countries became independent later. | After the fire, grasses quickly colonised the bare ground. | Moss colonised the old wall. | Bacteria colonised the dish of jelly in our experiment.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK spelling colonised, US colonized. Nouns: colony, colonist, colonisation, colonialism. Colonising was often violent and unfair; history books now tell both sides.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To do with Christopher Columbus (as in pre-Columbian, before Columbus reached the Americas). 2) To do with places called Columbia, such as British Columbia in Canada, the District of Columbia (Washington, D.C.) or the Columbia River. 3) Often a misspelling of Colombian, which means from Colombia, the country in South America.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, pre-Columbian means the Americas before European contact (the Maya, Aztecs, Inca). In spelling lessons, children learn the trap: the country is Colombia, and its people and coffee are Colombian. Phrases: pre-Columbian art, British Columbian.
examples from the lessons: The museum shows pre-Columbian gold from Peru. | The Columbian Exposition was a world fair in Chicago. | People from British Columbia are sometimes called British Columbians. | Colombian coffee is from Colombia, spelled with an o. | Pre-Columbian peoples grew maize and potatoes. | The Columbian salmon swim up the Columbia River.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Big spelling trap: Colombia (country) has o-o; Columbia (US places, British Columbia, universities) has o-u. Columbian is not the right word for the people of Colombia.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A calm, happy feeling of being satisfied with what you have, without wanting more.
its sense in the lessons: In wellbeing, PSHE and religion lessons, contentment is a quiet kind of happiness, often linked with being thankful. In stories, a cat purring by the fire shows contentment. In church, Christians are taught to be content with what they have. Phrases: a feeling of contentment, sigh of contentment, a life of contentment.
examples from the lessons: The cat purred with contentment on my lap. | Grandma smiled with contentment as we all ate dinner together. | Contentment doesn't need lots of toys. | He let out a sigh of contentment after a long swim. | Being grateful can bring contentment. | The farmer lived a life of quiet contentment.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Adjective: content (stressed on the second syllable: con-TENT) or contented. Do not mix with content (CON-tent), meaning what is inside something.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A small plant with tiny green leaves that taste peppery, eaten in salads and sandwiches; watercress grows in water.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, children grow cress on damp cotton wool or kitchen roll to test what seeds need (water, warmth, light) and to see plants bend towards light. In everyday life, egg and cress sandwiches are a classic in the UK. Phrases: egg and cress, grow cress, watercress, cress heads.
examples from the lessons: We grew cress on wet cotton wool in an eggshell. | The cress grew towards the window. | Egg and cress sandwiches are my favourite. | Cress tastes a little bit peppery. | Cress in the dark cupboard grew pale and yellow. | Watercress grows in clean, flowing streams.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: some cress, not a cress. Grows fast, in about a week, so it is popular for experiments with fair tests.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A soft, flaky, buttery bread roll shaped like a crescent (a curved moon), first made famous in France and eaten for breakfast. In French, croissant also means crescent or growing.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life it is a breakfast food in cafés and bakeries. In French lessons, it is one of the first French food words children learn, with pain au chocolat and baguette. Phrases: a warm croissant, ham and cheese croissant.
examples from the lessons: I had a warm croissant with jam for breakfast. | The croissant was so flaky it left crumbs everywhere. | In Paris we bought croissants from a bakery. | Croissants are made with lots of butter. | Can I have a chocolate croissant, please? | Croissant means crescent in French because of its shape.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. A French word used in English. English speakers often say KWAH-son or kruh-SONT; in French it is said kwa-SAHN with a nasal sound.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To become darker or to make something darker. 2) To become sad, angry or less hopeful, as a face or mood can. 3) (idiom) Never darken my door again means never come to my house again.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on light, a room darkens when you close the curtains. In stories, the sky darkens before a storm and a character's face darkens with anger. In art, you darken a colour by adding black. Phrases: the sky darkened, darken someone's door.
examples from the lessons: The sky darkened before the storm. | Close the blinds to darken the room for the film. | Add a little black to darken the paint. | His face darkened when he heard the bad news. | The leaves darken in late summer. | As the sun went down, the forest darkened.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: darkened. The -en ending means to make or become (like brighten, soften, harden). Opposite: brighten, lighten.

part of speech: adjective (darkened); verb past form of darken (darken, darkens, darkened, darkening)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Made darker or grown darker, with little light. 2) Past form of darken: the sky darkened.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, a darkened room or darkened street sets a spooky or quiet mood. In science, experiments with torches and shadows happen in a darkened room. Phrases: a darkened room, darkened windows.
examples from the lessons: We watched the film in a darkened room. | The darkened streets felt quiet and spooky. | The sky darkened and it began to rain. | Shadows are easiest to see in a darkened classroom. | The house had darkened windows. | Her mood darkened when she lost the match.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past form and past participle of darken. As an adjective it suggests someone or something made it dark.

part of speech: noun (an encore, encores); exclamation (encore!); verb (encore — rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) An extra song or piece played at the end of a concert because the audience claps and asks for more. 2) (exclamation) Encore! is shouted by an audience to ask for more. 3) (French) Encore means again or still in French; it is a French word used in English.
its sense in the lessons: In music and school concerts, the audience calls for an encore. In everyday talk, as an encore means as something extra after a success. In French lessons, encore une fois means one more time. Phrases: do an encore, for an encore.
examples from the lessons: The crowd shouted Encore! and the band played one more song. | The choir sang a lullaby as an encore. | The magician's encore was the best trick. | In French, encore une fois means one more time. | For an encore, our team won the cup again the next year. | She bowed and came back for an encore.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Pronounced ON-kor in English. In French it means again or still, not necessarily a concert word.

part of speech: noun (a ferret, ferrets); verb (ferret, ferrets, ferreted, ferreting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A small, long, thin furry animal related to the weasel, kept as a pet or once used to chase rabbits out of their holes. 2) (verb) To ferret around or about is to search busily for something. 3) To ferret out is to find something out by careful searching.
its sense in the lessons: In nature topics, ferrets are playful pets that sleep a lot. In history and countryside stories, people used ferrets to hunt rabbits. In everyday talk, ferret about in a drawer means rummage. Phrases: ferret around, ferret out the truth.
examples from the lessons: Our neighbour has two pet ferrets. | The ferret squeezed into the rabbit hole. | Ferrets sleep for many hours a day. | She ferreted around in her bag for her keys. | The detective ferreted out the truth. | A baby ferret is called a kit.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: ferreted. In New Zealand, ferrets are a pest that kills native birds, and keeping them as pets is not allowed.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The leaves of a plant or many trees, all together.
its sense in the lessons: In science and nature lessons, foliage is the green leafy part of plants; animals hide in thick foliage. In geography, autumn foliage turns red and gold in Canada and New England. In art, you draw foliage with light and dark greens. Phrases: autumn foliage, thick foliage, green foliage.
examples from the lessons: The bird hid in the thick foliage. | Autumn foliage in Canada is red and orange. | Giraffes eat foliage from tall trees. | The garden has plants with silver foliage. | The tiger's stripes blend into the foliage. | We drew the foliage with three shades of green.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: no plural, and not a foliage. Spelling and saying trap: FOH-lee-ij (not foilage).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person or animal that collects things, such as food, information or people. 2) Hunter-gatherers: people who live by hunting animals and collecting wild plants, nuts and berries instead of farming.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, Stone Age people were hunter-gatherers before farming began. In geography, a few groups still live partly this way today. In everyday life, a gatherer collects things, for example a news gatherer or a berry gatherer. Phrases: hunter-gatherers, data gatherer.
examples from the lessons: Stone Age people were hunter-gatherers. | Hunter-gatherers moved from place to place to find food. | The honey gatherer climbed the tall tree. | In our group, I was the information gatherer. | Squirrels are busy gatherers of nuts in autumn. | The gatherers came back with baskets of berries.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. From gather (to collect). Hunter-gatherers did not farm or keep crops.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (a name) Geneva is a city in Switzerland on Lake Geneva, where many world organisations such as parts of the United Nations and the Red Cross have their headquarters. 2) The Geneva Conventions: international rules about treating people fairly in war, such as prisoners, the wounded and civilians. 3) (a name) Geneva is also a girl's name and the name of towns in the USA.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons, Geneva is a French-speaking Swiss city with a famous fountain. In citizenship and news lessons, the Geneva Conventions protect people in wars. Phrases: Lake Geneva, the Geneva Conventions.
examples from the lessons: Geneva is a city in Switzerland. | The Red Cross was founded in Geneva. | Lake Geneva is big and blue, with mountains around it. | The Geneva Conventions say prisoners of war must be treated fairly. | Many world leaders meet in Geneva for talks. | People in Geneva mostly speak French.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always capital G. In French it is Genève. Geneva is not the capital of Switzerland; that is Bern.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To do with geography: the study of places, land, seas, countries and people. 2) To do with where things are on Earth.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons, geographic features are mountains, rivers and coasts; a geographic map shows them. In everyday life, the magazine National Geographic is famous for nature photos. Phrases: geographic features, geographic location, the North and South geographic poles.
examples from the lessons: Mountains and rivers are geographic features. | The geographic North Pole is different from the magnetic north pole. | We studied the geographic location of our town. | National Geographic has amazing photos of animals. | Australia is a huge geographic area. | The map shows geographic regions in different colours.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Geographic and geographical mean the same; geographical is more common in the UK. Adverb: geographically.

part of speech: verb (gobble, gobbles, gobbled, gobbling); noun (a gobble — the turkey sound)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To eat something very quickly and greedily. 2) (of a turkey) To make the throaty gobble-gobble sound. 3) To gobble up is to use up or take over something quickly, like money or land.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, parents tell children not to gobble their food. In stories, the wolf gobbles up Grandma. On farms and at Thanksgiving, turkeys gobble. In money talk, fees gobble up savings. Phrases: gobble up, gobble down.
examples from the lessons: Don't gobble your dinner; chew slowly. | The wolf gobbled up Little Red Riding Hood's grandma. | The turkey gobbled at the farmer. | The dog gobbled the sausage before anyone could stop it. | Big companies gobble up little shops. | My game gobbles up all the phone's battery.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: gobbled. Gobbledygook (or gobbledegook) means nonsense language. Eating too fast can make you choke, so chew well.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A picture or symbol used for writing, especially in ancient Egypt, where little drawings of birds, eyes and other things stood for sounds or words. 2) (informal) Writing that is very hard to read.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, children learn that the Rosetta Stone helped people read Egyptian hieroglyphs again. They write their names in hieroglyphs. The Maya of Central America also used glyphs. Phrases: Egyptian hieroglyphs, the Rosetta Stone.
examples from the lessons: Ancient Egyptians wrote with hieroglyphs. | The Rosetta Stone helped scholars read hieroglyphs. | Each hieroglyph can stand for a sound or an idea. | We wrote our names in hieroglyphs on paper scrolls. | Hieroglyphs were carved on the walls of tombs. | My brother's handwriting looks like hieroglyphs!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Also hieroglyphic (adjective, or noun mostly plural: hieroglyphics). Pronounced HY-ruh-glif. Myth: hieroglyphs are not only pictures of things; many stand for sounds.

part of speech: verb (hoot, hoots, hooted, hooting); noun (a hoot, hoots)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (of an owl) To make its long oo sound. 2) To sound a car horn (mainly UK, Australia). 3) To laugh loudly, or to shout in mockery. 4) (informal, noun) A hoot is something or someone very funny: the film was a hoot. 5) (informal) Not give a hoot means not care at all.
its sense in the lessons: In nature lessons, owls hoot at night (the tawny owl's twit-twoo is two owls calling). In everyday life, drivers hoot to warn others. In stories, a funny character is a hoot. Phrases: hoot with laughter, not give a hoot, what a hoot.
examples from the lessons: An owl hooted in the dark woods. | The driver hooted at the cyclist. | We hooted with laughter at the clown. | The school play was an absolute hoot. | He doesn't give a hoot about football. | The train hooted as it came into the station.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: hooted. Hooter is old informal UK slang for a car horn or a nose. In the USA people usually say honk for car horns.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (a name) Islay is an island off the west coast of Scotland, in the Inner Hebrides, famous for whisky distilleries, peat, birds and wild geese. It is said EYE-luh, not iss-lay.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons it is an example of a Scottish island reached by ferry, with peat bogs and many birds. In everyday life adults know it for whisky. Phrases: the Isle of Islay.
examples from the lessons: Islay is an island in Scotland. | We took the ferry to Islay. | Thousands of geese spend the winter on Islay. | Islay is said EYE-luh. | Farmers on Islay cut peat for fires. | Islay has beautiful sandy beaches.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital I. The s is silent. It is a place name, not a common word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An island, especially a small one or one in a name, mainly used in poems and place names.
its sense in the lessons: In geography, place names use isle: the Isle of Man, the Isle of Wight, the British Isles, the Isle of Skye. In poems and songs, isle sounds old and special. Phrases: the British Isles, Emerald Isle (Ireland), treasure isle.
examples from the lessons: The Isle of Wight is off the south coast of England. | We went on holiday to the Isle of Man. | Ireland is called the Emerald Isle. | The pirate's map showed a small isle. | The British Isles include Great Britain, Ireland and many smaller islands. | The poem was about a peaceful green isle.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The s is silent: isle sounds like I'll and aisle (the gap between rows of seats). Homophones: isle, aisle, I'll. Islet means a very small island.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A kind of music that began with African American musicians in New Orleans, USA, with strong rhythms, brass instruments and lots of making up music on the spot (improvisation). 2) (verb, informal) To jazz something up is to make it brighter, livelier or more exciting. 3) (informal, US) And all that jazz means and things like that.
its sense in the lessons: In music lessons, children listen to jazz and learn about Louis Armstrong and Ella Fitzgerald. In everyday life, you can jazz up your bedroom or a cake. Phrases: jazz band, jazz hands, jazz up, and all that jazz.
examples from the lessons: My uncle plays the trumpet in a jazz band. | Jazz began in New Orleans. | Louis Armstrong was a famous jazz trumpeter. | Let's jazz up this boring poster with glitter. | We did jazz hands at the end of the song. | The music teacher played some jazz and asked how it made us feel.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: some jazz, not a jazz. Adjective: jazzy (bright and lively). Double z.

part of speech: noun (a labourer, labourers); US spelling laborer
meaning for a pupil: 1) A person whose job is hard physical work, such as building, digging or farming, usually without special training.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, labourers built canals and railways and worked on farms and in factories. In everyday life, a builder's labourer carries bricks on a building site. In Bible stories, Jesus told a parable about labourers in a vineyard. Phrases: farm labourer, day labourer, builder's labourer.
examples from the lessons: The labourers dug the trench for the new pipe. | My great-grandad was a farm labourer. | Thousands of labourers built the railway. | In the parable, the labourers in the vineyard were all paid the same. | The labourer carried bricks up the ladder. | Labourers often work outside in all weathers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK, Australia, NZ, Ireland and Canada usually spell labourer; the USA spells laborer. Related: labour (work), laboratory (a science room, different meaning).

part of speech: noun (Manila — a name; manila — the paper, uncountable); adjective (manila)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (a name) Manila is the capital city of the Philippines, a country of islands in Southeast Asia. 2) Manila paper or a manila envelope or folder: strong, light brown paper, first made from a plant called Manila hemp.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons, Manila is a huge, busy capital on Manila Bay. In everyday and office life, manila envelopes and folders are the brown ones used for documents. Phrases: Manila Bay, a manila envelope, manila folder.
examples from the lessons: Manila is the capital of the Philippines. | Our teacher keeps our tests in a manila folder. | The letter came in a brown manila envelope. | Manila is on the island of Luzon. | Many people in Manila speak Filipino and English. | Typhoons sometimes hit Manila.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital M for the city, small m for the paper. Sometimes spelled manilla for the paper.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A large, fast ocean fish with a long pointed spear-like nose (a bill) and a tall fin on its back.
its sense in the lessons: In science and ocean lessons, marlin are among the fastest fish and hunt smaller fish with their bills. In stories, The Old Man and the Sea tells of a fisherman and a giant marlin. Phrases: blue marlin, black marlin, striped marlin.
examples from the lessons: A marlin has a long spear-like nose. | The blue marlin is one of the fastest fish in the sea. | The fisherman fought the marlin for hours. | Marlin leap high out of the water. | Marlin swim in warm oceans around the world. | In the film, the clownfish dad is called Marlin.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural marlin or marlins. Not the same as a swordfish, though they look alike. Marlin (a name) is the dad clownfish in Finding Nemo.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To do with machines or worked by machines, with moving parts like gears, levers and wheels. 2) Done without thinking, like a machine, out of habit. 3) Mechanical engineering: designing and building machines.
its sense in the lessons: In science and design lessons, mechanical toys use cams, gears and pulleys; a mechanical problem is something wrong with a machine. In everyday life, a car breakdown may be a mechanical fault. In writing, a mechanical answer is done without thought. Phrases: mechanical pencil, mechanical engineer, mechanical problem.
examples from the lessons: The old clock has mechanical parts inside. | We built a mechanical toy with a cam. | The bus stopped because of a mechanical problem. | My mechanical pencil never needs sharpening. | She answered in a mechanical voice, as if she wasn't listening. | A mechanical engineer designs machines and engines.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb: mechanically. Related: mechanic (a person who fixes cars and machines), mechanism (the working parts).

part of speech: noun (mu — the Greek letter μ); fragment
meaning for a pupil: 1) Mu (μ, M) is the twelfth letter of the Greek alphabet, the Greek m. 2) (science, maths) The symbol μ means micro-, one millionth: a μm (micrometre) is a millionth of a metre. 3) (Mandarin, pinyin) Mù is a Mandarin syllable; with a falling tone it means tree or wood (木), and also eye (目); it sounds like moo to an English ear. 4) (Japanese, Zen) Mu can mean nothing or not having. It is not an ordinary English word.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and science, μ is used for micro- and, for older pupils, for the average (the mean) and friction. In Mandarin lessons, mù (木) is one of the first characters children see: it looks like a tree. In cartoons, a cow says moo, not mu. Phrases: μm, mu-sign.
examples from the lessons: Mu is a letter in the Greek alphabet. | The symbol μm means micrometre. | In Mandarin, mù means tree. | The Chinese character for tree, 木, is said mù. | Alpha, beta and mu are all Greek letters. | Bacteria are measured in μm.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced mew in English (for the Greek letter) and moo in Mandarin. A cow's sound is spelled moo, not mu.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A small deer from Asia, also called a barking deer because it makes a loud bark; it has now spread wild in parts of England.
its sense in the lessons: In nature lessons, the muntjac is an example of an animal brought from abroad that now lives wild and can damage woods and gardens. In the UK, people may see one in parks or hear it barking at night. Phrases: muntjac deer, barking deer.
examples from the lessons: A muntjac ran across the road in front of our car. | Muntjac are small deer about the size of a dog. | The muntjac barked in the woods at night. | Muntjac first came to England from China. | Muntjac eat bluebells and young trees. | Male muntjac have short antlers and little tusks.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural muntjac or muntjacs. Also spelled muntjak. Pronounced MUNT-jak.

part of speech: adjective (muted); verb past form of mute (mute, mutes, muted, muting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Quiet and soft, not loud. 2) (of colours) Soft and not bright. 3) (of feelings or reactions) Not strong; held back. 4) (computing) With the sound turned off, as on a video call or phone.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday and online-lesson life, you are muted when your microphone is off ("you're on mute!"). In art, muted colours are soft greys, browns and pale shades. In news, a muted reaction means people were not very excited. Phrases: on mute, muted colours, muted response.
examples from the lessons: You're muted, so we can't hear you. | The teacher muted everyone during the video call. | The room was painted in muted greens and greys. | The trumpet sounded muted with the cup in it. | The news got a muted reaction from the crowd. | I muted the TV during the adverts.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past form of mute (to turn off sound). Mute as an adjective once described people who could not speak; today that is seen as rude, so say non-speaking instead.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (old-fashioned, formal) Needed or necessary. 2) (informal, UK) The needful is what is needed, often money: Dad will provide the needful. 3) (Indian English) Do the needful means do what is necessary; many English speakers elsewhere find it old-fashioned.
its sense in the lessons: In old books and the Bible, needful means necessary: one thing is needful. In everyday talk, it is rare; children are more likely to say needed or necessary. In emails in India and some other places, please do the needful is common. Phrases: do the needful, the needful.
examples from the lessons: Take only what is needful for the journey. | In the Bible, Jesus told Martha that one thing is needful. | Mum said she'd do the needful and pay for the trip. | Please do the needful and send the form. | Water and food are needful for life. | He packed the needful things in a small bag.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Old-fashioned; in school writing, use necessary or needed. Not the same as needy (poor or wanting attention).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A family of plants that includes some very poisonous ones, such as deadly nightshade, which has shiny black berries. 2) The nightshade family also includes foods like potatoes, tomatoes, peppers and aubergines.
its sense in the lessons: In science and safety lessons, children learn never to eat wild berries because some, like deadly nightshade, are poisonous. In stories, witches and poisoners use nightshade. Phrases: deadly nightshade, woody nightshade, the nightshade family.
examples from the lessons: Deadly nightshade has shiny black berries that are very poisonous. | Never eat berries you find in the wild. | Potatoes and tomatoes belong to the nightshade family. | In the story, the witch brewed a potion with nightshade. | Woody nightshade has purple flowers and red berries. | If someone eats a wild berry, tell an adult and get help at once.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Deadly nightshade is also called belladonna. Even the green parts of potatoes and leaves of tomato plants can be harmful if eaten.

part of speech: noun (nutmeg — the spice, uncountable; a nutmeg, nutmegs); verb (nutmeg, nutmegs, nutmegged, nutmegging — football slang)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A brown spice made by grating the hard seed of a tropical tree, used in cakes, custard and drinks. 2) (football slang, UK) To nutmeg someone is to kick the ball between their legs and run past them; the trick itself is called a nutmeg (or megs).
