its sense in the lessons: In cooking, nutmeg goes in rice pudding, pumpkin pie and eggnog. In history, nutmeg came from the Banda Islands in Indonesia and was once worth more than gold, so countries fought over it. In playground football, a nutmeg is a cheeky trick. Phrases: grated nutmeg, megs!
examples from the lessons: Sprinkle a little nutmeg on the custard. | Nutmeg was once so valuable that people fought wars over it. | Grandma grates nutmeg into her rice pudding. | He nutmegged the defender and scored! | The crowd cheered the nutmeg. | Too much nutmeg can make you ill, so use only a pinch.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The spice is uncountable (some nutmeg); a whole seed is countable (a nutmeg). Verb doubles g: nutmegged. Despite its name, nutmeg is a seed, not a true nut.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A place in a desert where there is water, so plants and trees such as date palms can grow. 2) (figurative) A calm, pleasant place in the middle of a busy or difficult place.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons, oases are water sources in the Sahara or Arabian deserts where travellers and camels stop. In stories, thirsty travellers dream of reaching an oasis. In everyday talk, a quiet library can be an oasis of calm. Phrases: an oasis of calm, desert oasis. Oasis (a name) was also a famous English band.
examples from the lessons: The camels drank at the oasis. | Date palms grow around the oasis. | The travellers walked for days to reach an oasis. | The park is an oasis of green in the busy city. | Our library corner is an oasis of calm. | Some oases have water coming up from under the ground.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural oases (oh-AY-seez), not oasises. Pronounced oh-AY-sis. A mirage of water in a desert is not an oasis: it is a trick of the light.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A strong, illegal drug made from the juice of a kind of poppy, which makes people sleepy and is very addictive and dangerous. 2) Medicines made from it, like morphine, are used by doctors to stop very bad pain.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, the Opium Wars were fought when Britain forced China to allow opium sales. In health and safety lessons, children learn that drugs like opium and heroin are addictive and harmful, and only doctors should give strong painkillers. Phrases: opium poppy, the Opium Wars.
examples from the lessons: Opium comes from the seed pods of a kind of poppy. | Opium is a dangerous and addictive drug. | Britain and China fought the Opium Wars over the opium trade. | Doctors use medicines made from opium to stop terrible pain. | Never take medicine that wasn't given to you by a trusted adult or doctor. | Addiction to opium ruined many lives in history.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Related: opiate, opioid (drugs like it). The red poppies worn for Remembrance are a different kind of poppy.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In ancient Greece and Rome, a priest or priestess through whom people believed the gods gave advice or told the future, or the holy place where this happened, like the Oracle of Delphi. 2) A message or answer given by such an oracle. 3) (informal) A person who knows a lot and is asked for advice.
its sense in the lessons: In history and myths lessons, Greeks travelled to the Oracle at Delphi to ask questions, and its answers were often riddles. In everyday talk, the oracle is the person who knows everything about something. Phrases: the Oracle of Delphi, consult the oracle.
examples from the lessons: The Greeks visited the Oracle at Delphi for advice. | The oracle's answer was a puzzling riddle. | The king asked the oracle if he would win the war. | My sister is the family oracle on dinosaurs. | The oracle was believed to speak the words of the god Apollo. | Ask Grandpa, he's the oracle on football facts.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Adjective: oracular. Ancient people believed oracles spoke for gods; historians today see them as part of their religion and politics. Oracle (a name) is also a computer company.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Soft, dark brown soil made of plants that have half-rotted very slowly in wet, boggy places over thousands of years; it can be dried and burned as fuel.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and science lessons, peat bogs in Ireland, Scotland and Canada store huge amounts of carbon, so protecting them helps the climate. In history, people cut peat for fires, and bog bodies were preserved in peat. In gardening, people now use peat-free compost. Phrases: peat bog, peat-free compost, cut peat.
examples from the lessons: Peat forms very slowly in wet bogs. | In Ireland, families once burned peat on their fires. | Peat bogs store a lot of carbon. | Buy peat-free compost to protect the bogs. | Ancient bodies have been found preserved in peat. | The peat smoke smelled earthy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: some peat, a block of peat. In Ireland peat is also called turf. Pete (a name) sounds the same.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A large bird with a long tail; the males have bright copper, green and red feathers, while females are brown. They are often hunted for food.
its sense in the lessons: In nature lessons, pheasants are common in the British and Irish countryside and often walk across roads. In everyday life, some people hunt and eat pheasant. Phrases: cock pheasant (male), hen pheasant (female).
examples from the lessons: A pheasant ran across the country lane. | The male pheasant has a red face and a long tail. | Hen pheasants are brown so they can hide on their nests. | We heard a pheasant's loud call from the field. | Pheasants were brought to Britain long ago from Asia. | Some people eat pheasant as a special meal.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural pheasants, or pheasant for hunting and food. Spelling: ph sounds like f, and there is an ea: pheasant (FEZ-unt). Do not mix with peasant (a poor farm worker of old times).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A shiny, pale gold-coloured mineral made of iron and sulphur, often called fool's gold because people mistook it for real gold.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about rocks and minerals, pyrite shows that looks can trick you: it is harder and more brittle than gold, and it often forms cubes. In history, gold rush miners were fooled by it. Phrases: fool's gold, iron pyrite.
examples from the lessons: Pyrite is called fool's gold. | The miner shouted with joy, but it was only pyrite. | Pyrite often grows in little cubes. | Real gold is soft, but pyrite is hard and brittle. | Pyrite makes sparks if you strike it with steel. | We found a shiny pyrite crystal at the rock shop.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable as a mineral. Also called iron pyrites. Test: rubbed on rough tile, pyrite leaves a greenish-black streak, while gold leaves a gold streak.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A large machine, especially a nuclear reactor, in which atoms are split to make heat to produce electricity. 2) Any container where chemical reactions take place.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, nuclear reactors in power stations make electricity without burning coal, but their waste is dangerous. In history and news, accidents like Chernobyl in Ukraine show why reactors need safety rules. Phrases: nuclear reactor, reactor core.
examples from the lessons: A nuclear reactor makes heat to produce electricity. | The Chernobyl reactor exploded in Ukraine, and the area around it is still unsafe. | Workers in the reactor wear special suits. | Some submarines are powered by small reactors. | Scientists tested a new reactor design. | The reactor core must be kept cool with water.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. From react (to change when mixed or when something happens). A reactor cannot explode like a nuclear bomb, but accidents can spread dangerous radiation.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A second game or match between the same players or teams, often because the first was close, unfair or lost.
its sense in the lessons: In sport and games at school and home, the loser often asks for a rematch. In stories, a rematch gives a character a chance to win this time. Phrases: demand a rematch, play a rematch, best of three.
examples from the lessons: I lost at chess, so I asked for a rematch. | The two teams will play a rematch next week. | She won the rematch easily. | Rematch! shouted my brother after losing at cards. | The final ended in a draw, so there was a rematch. | Let's have a rematch after lunch.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: rematches (add -es). The prefix re- means again (replay, retry). Can also be used as a verb in sports news: they will rematch.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The way living things make new young of their own kind, such as animals having babies or plants making seeds. 2) A copy of something, especially a painting or piece of old furniture. 3) Making a copy of sound or pictures, like a printed photo.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, reproduction is a life process (like breathing and growing): plants reproduce by seeds, runners and bulbs; animals by eggs or live young. In art and museums, a reproduction is a copy, not the original. Phrases: sexual and asexual reproduction, a reproduction of the Mona Lisa.
examples from the lessons: Reproduction is one of the life processes of all living things. | Plants use seeds for reproduction. | Strawberry plants also use runners for reproduction. | Frogs lay eggs as part of reproduction. | The poster is a reproduction of a famous painting. | This chair is a reproduction, not a real antique.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: reproduce. The reproduction (copy) of a painting is worth much less than the original. Reproduction in humans is taught in later science and in family lessons with care.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A skin infection caused by a fungus (not a worm) that makes red, itchy, ring-shaped patches on the skin or scalp; it spreads by touching and is treated with cream.
its sense in the lessons: In health lessons, ringworm shows how fungal infections spread through sharing towels or touching pets, and why washing helps. Phrases: catch ringworm, ringworm cream.
examples from the lessons: Ringworm is caused by a fungus, not a worm. | The cat had ringworm, so we washed our hands after stroking it. | Ringworm makes a red, itchy ring on the skin. | Don't share towels so ringworm doesn't spread. | The doctor gave him a cream for ringworm. | Athlete's foot is caused by a similar fungus.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Big myth: there is no worm. It is a common and treatable infection, so it is nothing to be ashamed of.

part of speech: fragment or abbreviation (RO, ro — not a word on its own)
meaning for a pupil: 1) «RO» is short for «reverse osmosis», a way of cleaning water by pushing it through a very fine filter. 2) «ro» is the internet code and language code for Romania and the Romanian language (as in a web address ending «.ro»). 3) «ro» is often just a piece of a longer word, such as «ro» in «robot» or «row».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life you may see «RO water» on a water filter or bottle: water cleaned by reverse osmosis. In computing, «.ro» at the end of a web address shows a Romanian website. In science lessons about water, reverse osmosis is one way to make sea water safe to drink. On its own, «ro» is not an English word you would use in a sentence.
examples from the lessons: Our kitchen filter makes RO water. | The RO system takes salt out of sea water. | A website ending in .ro is usually from Romania. | The language code «ro» stands for Romanian. | Some ships use RO machines to make drinking water. | «Ro» here is only the start of the word «robot».
note for the reader of a maths problem: Not an English word on its own: an abbreviation or a fragment. Write «RO» in capitals for reverse osmosis. Do not confuse with «row» (a line of things) or «roe» (fish eggs), which sound the same.

part of speech: noun (a saiga, saigas; also saiga antelope)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A saiga is a kind of antelope that lives on the dry grassy plains of Central Asia, with a big, soft, drooping nose. 2) Its strange nose works like a filter: it warms cold air in winter and keeps out dust in summer.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography lessons the saiga is an example of an animal adapted to harsh steppe weather and of an endangered species: many died from disease and hunting, and people work to protect them. In stories it can stand for wild, wide open land.
examples from the lessons: A saiga has a nose that hangs over its mouth. | Saigas live on the steppes of Kazakhstan and Mongolia. | The saiga's nose filters dust from the air. | Thousands of saigas run together across the plains. | Hunters once killed many saigas for their horns. | Scientists count the saigas every year. | The saiga is listed as an endangered animal. | We saw a picture of a baby saiga in our nature book.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: one saiga, two saigas. Pronounced «SY-guh». Only the males have horns. It is a real animal, not a cartoon or a made-up creature.

part of speech: noun (scaffolding — uncountable; a piece of scaffolding); verb form of «scaffold» (scaffold, scaffolds, scaffolded, scaffolding)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Scaffolding is a frame of metal poles and wooden boards put up against a building so workers can stand on it while they build, paint or repair. 2) In school, scaffolding means the extra help a teacher gives you at the start of learning something, which is taken away step by step as you get better. 3) Scaffolding is any support that holds something up while it is being made.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life you see scaffolding on houses and big buildings being built or mended; safety rules say children must never climb it. In teaching, «scaffolding» describes help such as sentence starters, word banks or worked examples. In stories, a building «covered in scaffolding» tells the reader it is being repaired or built.
examples from the lessons: The church tower is covered in scaffolding. | Builders put up scaffolding to paint the house. | Never climb on scaffolding — it is not a playground. | A pole fell off the scaffolding, so the street was closed. | The teacher gave us scaffolding: the first line of each answer. | Writing frames are a kind of scaffolding for your story. | They took the scaffolding down when the roof was finished. | Workers on the scaffolding wear hard hats and harnesses.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable: «some scaffolding», «a lot of scaffolding», not «a scaffolding»; for one part say «a scaffolding pole». «A scaffold» can also mean an old platform for hanging criminals.

part of speech: verb (screech, screeches, screeched, screeching); noun (a screech, screeches)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To screech is to make a very loud, high, harsh sound, like a scared bird or a person screaming. 2) When tyres or brakes screech, they make a sharp, scraping noise as a car stops suddenly. 3) A screech is one such loud, high, unpleasant sound. 4) «Screech to a halt» means to stop very suddenly, often with that noise.
its sense in the lessons: In stories «screech» tells the reader something sudden, scary or out of control: an owl in the night, brakes before a crash, a frightened person. In road safety, screeching brakes warn that a car is stopping hard. A barn owl is also called a screech owl in some places. Common phrases: «screech to a halt», «let out a screech».
examples from the lessons: The owl screeched in the dark wood. | The car screeched to a halt at the crossing. | My little sister screeched when she saw the spider. | We heard the screech of brakes outside school. | The chalk made a horrible screech on the board. | Parrots screech when they are excited. | The train screeched into the station. | She let out a screech of laughter.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: screeched. Close in meaning to «shriek» and «scream», but «screech» is harsher and more like a scraping noise; machines and birds screech, people shriek or scream more often. «Screech» can be noun or verb.

part of speech: noun (a sen, sen — money unit); abbreviation (Sen. = Senator)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A sen is a small coin or money unit in some Asian countries, for example 100 sen make 1 ringgit in Malaysia; in Japan the sen was an old unit, 100 sen to 1 yen. 2) «Sen.» is short for «Senator», a member of a senate, written before a name, for example in the USA. 3) «sen» can also be a piece of a longer word or a name.
its sense in the lessons: In maths problems with money from Malaysia or Indonesia, sen work like cents: 100 sen = 1 unit. In news from the USA, «Sen.» before a name means that person is a senator. On its own «sen» is rare in everyday English.
examples from the lessons: In Malaysia a sweet costs 50 sen. | One hundred sen make one ringgit. | Old Japanese coins were counted in sen. | Sen. Smith spoke in the Senate today. | Count the coins: 20 sen plus 30 sen is 50 sen. | In the news, «Sen.» means «Senator».
note for the reader of a maths problem: The plural of the coin is also «sen» (50 sen). «Sen.» with a capital and a full stop is an abbreviation, not a word you say; read it «Senator». In money problems, think of sen as cents: 1 = 100 sen.

part of speech: proper noun (Shanghai — a city); verb (shanghai, shanghais, shanghaied, shanghaiing — old, informal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Shanghai is a huge city on the east coast of China, one of the biggest cities in the world, with a famous river front and tall towers. 2) (old, informal) To shanghai someone is to trick or force them into doing something they did not want to do; long ago it meant kidnapping sailors to work on ships.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons Shanghai is an example of a megacity and a busy sea port. The verb is old-fashioned and appears in sea stories and jokes: «I got shanghaied into tidying the classroom» means you were tricked into it. The Chinese name means roughly «on the sea».
examples from the lessons: Shanghai is one of the biggest cities on Earth. | My cousin flew to Shanghai for work. | Shanghai has one of the busiest ports in the world. | The Shanghai Tower is very tall. | In the old story, a sailor was shanghaied onto a ship. | I was shanghaied into helping with the washing-up! | Lots of people in Shanghai speak Shanghainese as well as Mandarin.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Write the city with a capital S. The verb is usually lower case and passive: «be shanghaied». Pronounced «shang-HY». The verb is not rude, just old and jokey.

part of speech: verb (shriek, shrieks, shrieked, shrieking); noun (a shriek, shrieks)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To shriek is to give a short, loud, very high cry, because you are scared, excited, hurt or laughing hard. 2) A shriek is one such cry. 3) To shriek something is to say it in a very high, loud voice.
its sense in the lessons: In stories «shriek» shows strong sudden feeling: fear in a ghost story, delight at a party, pain when someone falls. Phrases: «shriek with laughter», «shriek with delight», «let out a shriek». In the playground, shrieking is common in games of chase.
examples from the lessons: The children shrieked with joy on the roller coaster. | She let out a shriek when the mouse ran past. | «Get off my foot!» he shrieked. | We heard shrieks from the haunted house ride. | The baby shrieked with laughter at the puppy. | A sudden shriek woke the whole house. | The girls shrieked as the cold wave hit them.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: shrieked. Spelling: «i before e» — shr-ie-k. Similar words: scream, screech, squeal; «shriek» is shorter and higher than «scream».

part of speech: noun (a shutter, shutters); verb (shutter, shutters, shuttered, shuttering)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A shutter is a wooden or metal cover on a window that you open and close to keep out light, wind or burglars. 2) In a camera, the shutter is the tiny part that opens for a moment to let light in when you take a photo. 3) To shutter a shop or business is to close it, often for good. 4) A shop shutter is a metal roll-down cover on a shop front.
its sense in the lessons: Everyday: houses in hot countries often have shutters to keep rooms cool. In science lessons about light and cameras, the shutter controls how long light comes in. In news, «shuttered» shops have closed. In stories, banging shutters tell the reader there is a storm or a spooky house.
examples from the lessons: Grandma closes the shutters when the sun is hot. | The shutters banged in the wind all night. | Press the button and the camera shutter clicks. | A fast shutter can photograph a running dog without blur. | The shopkeeper pulled down the metal shutter at six. | Many shops on the high street are shuttered now. | Green shutters made the cottage look pretty.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one shutter, two shutters; often plural for a pair on one window. Regular verb: shuttered. Do not confuse with «shudder» (to shake from fear or cold), which sounds almost the same.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A silverback is a grown-up male gorilla, the leader of a gorilla family, named after the silvery-grey hair on his back. 2) (informal) Sometimes people jokingly call a strong older man who leads a group a silverback.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about animals and habitats, the silverback is the leader who protects the troop, decides where they go and settles quarrels. In nature films and zoo visits children meet the word. The joke sense appears in everyday talk about bosses.
examples from the lessons: The silverback beat his chest to scare off danger. | A silverback can weigh twice as much as a man. | The baby gorillas played near the silverback. | The silverback leads his family through the forest. | Gorillas' hair turns silver when they are about twelve years old. | At the zoo, the silverback sat calmly eating leaves. | Dad is the silverback of our house, Mum joked.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun written as one word. Only adult male gorillas are silverbacks. Gorillas are mostly gentle plant-eaters; the image of the angry monster gorilla in films is a myth.

part of speech: fragment; proper noun (Sion — a town; an old spelling of Zion)
meaning for a pupil: 1) «-sion» is a word ending that makes nouns, as in «television», «decision», «explosion»; it often sounds like «zhun» or «shun». 2) Sion is a town in Switzerland, in the Alps. 3) Sion is an old spelling of Zion, the hill of Jerusalem in the Bible, often used to mean God's city or God's people (as in Sion College, Mount Sion).
its sense in the lessons: In spelling lessons «-sion» and «-tion» are taught together: «decide → decision», «explode → explosion». In church and Bible reading, «Sion» or «Zion» appears in hymns and psalms. On its own «sion» is not an everyday English word.
examples from the lessons: «Television» ends in -sion. | «Decide» becomes «decision». | «Explode» becomes «explosion». | Sion is a town in the Swiss mountains. | The old hymn sings of the hill of Sion. | Spell «confusion» with -sion, not -tion.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly a suffix, not a word. Spelling tip: words ending in «-de» or «-se» often take «-sion» (decide → decision, confuse → confusion); many others take «-tion». With a capital S it is a place name.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A songbird is a small bird that sings tuneful songs, such as a robin, blackbird, thrush, nightingale or wren. 2) (informal) A person, usually a woman, with a lovely singing voice is sometimes called a songbird.
its sense in the lessons: In science and nature lessons songbirds are a big group of perching birds; they sing to mark their territory and to find a mate, mostly in spring mornings (the «dawn chorus»). Gardeners put up feeders and nest boxes to help songbirds. In stories, songbirds show a happy, peaceful morning.
examples from the lessons: A songbird was singing on the fence at dawn. | Robins and blackbirds are songbirds. | We hung a feeder to help the songbirds in winter. | Male songbirds sing to say «this is my patch». | Cats catch many songbirds in gardens. | The concert star was called the nation's songbird. | The dawn chorus is lots of songbirds singing together.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable, one word. Not every bird is a songbird: ducks, owls and eagles are not. Birds that sing are usually the males.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Spherical means shaped like a ball, round in every direction, like a sphere. 2) In maths, a spherical object has every point on its surface the same distance from the centre.
its sense in the lessons: In maths lessons on 3D shapes, a sphere is round like a ball; things like oranges, marbles and planets are roughly spherical. In science, raindrops, bubbles and the Earth are described as nearly spherical. It is a more formal, exact word than «round».
examples from the lessons: A football is spherical. | The Earth is almost spherical but a little flat at the poles. | Bubbles are spherical because of how water pulls on itself. | Marbles are small spherical glass balls. | A circle is flat, but a ball is spherical. | The bead was spherical with a hole through the middle. | Name three spherical things in the classroom.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced «SFERR-ik-ul»; spelt with «ph». «Circular» is for flat shapes (a circle), «spherical» for solid shapes (a sphere) — a common trap. In maths a sphere has 1 curved face, no edges and no vertices.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Springy means bouncy: it goes back to its shape after you press, squash or stretch it, like a spring. 2) A springy walk or step is light, quick and full of energy.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about materials, springy (elastic) materials such as rubber, sponge and coiled metal come back to shape. In cooking, a cake is done when the top feels springy. In stories, a springy step shows someone is happy or excited.
examples from the lessons: The grass felt soft and springy under our feet. | A trampoline is very springy. | The sponge is springy: squeeze it and it pops back. | Press the cake; if it is springy, it is ready. | She walked with a springy step on her birthday. | My curly hair is springy. | Moss on the hill was thick and springy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative springier, superlative springiest (y → i). Close to «bouncy» and «elastic»; the opposite is «stiff» or «squashy».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A stalactite is a long, pointed stone shape that hangs down from the roof of a cave, made very slowly by dripping water that leaves tiny bits of minerals behind. 2) Anything hanging down in that shape, like an icicle, can be called a stalactite.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography lessons about rocks and caves, stalactites form over thousands of years from limestone dissolved in water. They are taught with stalagmites, which grow up from the floor; when they meet they make a column. On cave trips, guides ask you not to touch them, because hand oil stops them growing.
examples from the lessons: A huge stalactite hung from the cave roof. | Stalactites grow only a tiny bit every year. | Water dripped from the tip of the stalactite. | Don't touch the stalactites — they are very old. | When a stalactite meets a stalagmite, it makes a pillar. | Icicles look like stalactites made of ice. | Our class drew stalactites in the cave picture.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Memory trick: stalaCtites hang from the Ceiling (c), stalaGmites grow from the Ground (g). Another trick: «tights come down». Countable: stalactites.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal, law) Statutory means set by law: something written in a statute, a law made by a parliament. 2) (formal) Statutory also means required or official, something that must happen by the rules.
its sense in the lessons: In adult life and the news you meet «statutory sick pay», «statutory rights», «statutory holidays» (in Canada, «stat holidays»). In school, «statutory assessments» are tests the law says must be done, such as some tests in England. It is a stiff, official word, often in letters and exam questions.
examples from the lessons: Schools must give statutory tests in Year 6. | Workers have a statutory right to holidays. | Mum got statutory sick pay when she was ill. | In Canada, Canada Day is a statutory holiday. | The council has a statutory duty to collect rubbish. | Children have statutory protection under the law. | This guidance is advice, not a statutory rule.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal word; in everyday talk say «by law» or «legal». Pronounced «STATCH-u-tree» or «STAT-yoo-tuh-ree». Do not confuse with «statue» (a carved figure) or «stature» (height, importance).

part of speech: verb (strip, strips, stripped, stripping — past form); adjective (stripped)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Stripped is the past of «strip»: took off a covering or layer, such as paint, bark or sheets. 2) Stripped can mean took off your clothes. 3) Stripped of something means something was taken away from someone, often as a punishment («stripped of his medal»). 4) As an adjective, stripped means bare, with the cover taken off («stripped wood»).
its sense in the lessons: Everyday life: we stripped the beds to wash the sheets; old paint was stripped off a door. In sport news a player is «stripped of a title» for cheating. In science, «stripped» wires have the plastic taken off. In stories, trees «stripped bare» by wind show winter or a storm.
examples from the lessons: We stripped the beds on Saturday. | Dad stripped the old paint off the door. | The wind stripped the leaves from the trees. | The runner was stripped of her medal for cheating. | The swimmers stripped off and jumped into the lake. | Goats stripped the bark from the young trees. | The electrician stripped the end of the wire. | The house was stripped of furniture before the move.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double p: strip → stripped, stripping. Do not confuse with «striped» (with stripes, one p): a striped shirt has lines; a stripped bed has no sheets. «Strip off» = take your clothes off.

part of speech: noun (a sturgeon, sturgeons; also sturgeon as a plural)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A sturgeon is a very large, old kind of fish with a long nose and rows of bony plates instead of normal scales, living in rivers and seas of the northern part of the world. 2) Sturgeon is also its meat as food; its eggs are made into caviar.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons sturgeons are «living fossils», a fish group that has existed since the time of the dinosaurs. They are an example of endangered animals, overfished for caviar. Some sturgeons live over 100 years and grow longer than a car.
examples from the lessons: A sturgeon can live for more than a hundred years. | The sturgeon has bony plates along its back. | Caviar is made from sturgeon eggs. | Sturgeons swim up rivers to lay their eggs. | Many sturgeons are in danger because of overfishing. | The beluga sturgeon is one of the biggest fish in rivers. | The museum had a model of a giant sturgeon.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; the plural can be «sturgeons» or «sturgeon». Pronounced «STUR-jun». Not related to «surgeon» (a doctor), though they look alike.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A suffragette was a woman, especially in Britain about a hundred years ago, who campaigned, often with bold protests, for women to have the right to vote in elections. 2) More widely, a suffragette or suffragist is anyone who fought for women's votes.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons the suffragettes (Emmeline Pankhurst and others) are taught as part of how democracy grew in the UK; they marched, chained themselves to railings and were sent to prison. Women in Britain got the vote step by step after their campaigns. New Zealand was the first country where women could vote in national elections. «Suffrage» means the right to vote.
examples from the lessons: The suffragettes wanted women to be allowed to vote. | Emmeline Pankhurst was a famous suffragette. | Some suffragettes were sent to prison for protesting. | Suffragettes wore purple, white and green. | Our class read about suffragettes in history. | The suffragette chained herself to the railings. | Thanks to the suffragettes and others, women in Britain can vote today.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: suffragettes. «Suffrage» means the right to vote; it has nothing to do with «suffer», although they sound similar. «Suffragist» is often used for campaigners who used only peaceful methods.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Territorial means about land or an area that belongs to a country or person («territorial waters»). 2) A territorial animal defends its own area and chases others away from it. 3) A territorial person gets cross when others use what they think is theirs, like their seat or desk.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, robins, cats, dogs and many fish are territorial: they mark and defend a patch. In geography and the news, «territorial waters» are the sea near a country's coast that belongs to it, and «territorial disputes» are arguments between countries about land. In everyday life it describes someone guarding their space.
examples from the lessons: Robins are very territorial and fight other robins. | Our cat is territorial about the garden. | The boat crossed into another country's territorial waters. | The two countries have a territorial dispute about an island. | My brother is territorial about his side of the bedroom. | Dogs bark at the gate because they are territorial. | In Australia, the Northern Territory is a territorial area, not a state.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective from «territory». Stress: «terri-TOR-ee-ul». Being territorial is natural in animals, not a sign that the animal is bad.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Tofu is a soft white food made from soya milk pressed into blocks, eaten a lot in China, Japan and other Asian countries and by vegetarians. 2) Tofu is a source of protein instead of meat.
its sense in the lessons: In food and health lessons tofu is an example of a plant protein made from soya beans, used by vegetarians and vegans. In cooking it can be fried, put in soups or stir-fries; it takes on the taste of the sauce. Children often meet it in school dinners and Asian restaurants.
examples from the lessons: We had tofu in our stir-fry tonight. | Tofu is made from soya beans. | My vegetarian friend eats tofu instead of chicken. | Tofu has hardly any taste on its own. | Crispy fried tofu is my favourite. | Miso soup has little cubes of tofu in it. | Tofu is a good source of protein.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «some tofu», «a block of tofu», not «a tofu». The word comes from Chinese and Japanese. People with a soya allergy must not eat it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Treacherous describes a person who betrays people who trust them, like a traitor. 2) Treacherous ground, roads, water or weather are very dangerous, often in a hidden way, such as icy roads or strong currents.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and history, a treacherous character secretly turns against friends or their country. In safety and weather news, «treacherous conditions» means ice, fog, snow or floods that make travel dangerous. Common phrases: «treacherous roads», «treacherous currents», «a treacherous path».
examples from the lessons: The roads are treacherous after the frost. | Do not swim there — the currents are treacherous. | The climbers crossed a treacherous icy ridge. | The treacherous knight opened the castle gate to the enemy. | Fog made the drive home treacherous. | In the story, the treacherous servant stole the king's ring. | The muddy path down the cliff was treacherous.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced «TRETCH-er-us». Noun: «treachery» (betrayal). Close words: «dangerous», «disloyal». Hidden danger is the key idea: something looks safe but is not.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unconscious means not awake and not able to see, hear or feel, for example after a bad bang on the head or in an operation. 2) Unconscious also means not aware: doing something without knowing or noticing it. 3) (psychology) The unconscious is the part of the mind that has thoughts and feelings you do not notice.
its sense in the lessons: In first aid lessons, if someone is unconscious you call the emergency number (999, 911, 000, 111 or 112, depending on the country), check their breathing and put them in the recovery position. In everyday talk, «an unconscious habit» is one you do without thinking. In stories, a character knocked unconscious wakes up later, confused.
examples from the lessons: He fell off the horse and was knocked unconscious. | If someone is unconscious, call for help at once. | She was unconscious during the operation. | Put an unconscious person who is breathing on their side. | Biting my nails is an unconscious habit. | He was unconscious of the spider on his hat. | The boxer lay unconscious for a minute. | Doctors check how long the patient was unconscious.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: un + conscious, with «sc»: un-con-scious. Opposite: conscious. «Unconscious of» means «not noticing». Being unconscious is not the same as being asleep — you cannot be woken up easily, so it is an emergency.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Uranium is a heavy, silvery, radioactive metal found in rocks, a chemical element with the symbol U and atomic number 92. 2) Uranium is used as fuel in nuclear power stations and in nuclear weapons.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons uranium is an example of an element and of radioactivity: its atoms slowly break apart and give off energy and radiation. In energy lessons, nuclear power stations use uranium to make heat, which boils water to drive turbines. Australia, Canada and Kazakhstan mine a lot of uranium. It is named after the planet Uranus.
examples from the lessons: Uranium is found in some rocks. | Nuclear power stations use uranium as fuel. | Uranium is radioactive, so it must be handled with care. | The symbol for uranium is U. | Canada and Australia mine uranium. | A small amount of uranium can make a lot of energy. | Uranium was named after the planet Uranus.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «some uranium», not «a uranium». Pronounced «yoo-RAY-nee-um». Radioactive does not mean it glows green — that is a cartoon myth.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) A valediction is the act of saying goodbye, or the words you use to say goodbye. 2) (formal) A valediction is a goodbye speech or poem, or the closing words of a letter, such as «Yours sincerely» or «Best wishes».
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons on letter writing, the valediction is the sign-off at the end. In the USA and Canada, the «valedictorian» is the top student who gives the goodbye speech at graduation. In older poems and classics, a valediction is a farewell. In everyday talk people just say «goodbye» or «sign-off».
examples from the lessons: «Yours sincerely» is a polite valediction. | End your letter with a valediction and your name. | The headteacher gave a short valediction at the leaving party. | The poem is a valediction to a friend going away. | A text message rarely has a valediction. | The valedictorian gave a valediction at graduation.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal word; plain English: goodbye, farewell, sign-off. Opposite: «salutation» (the greeting, like «Dear Sam»). Pronounced «val-uh-DIK-shun». Letter rule (UK): «Dear Sir» goes with «Yours faithfully», «Dear Ms Lee» with «Yours sincerely».

part of speech: abbreviation (var, VAR — not an ordinary word)
meaning for a pupil: 1) In computer programming, «var» is a short keyword for «variable», a named box that holds a value (used in JavaScript and other languages). 2) VAR in football (soccer) stands for «video assistant referee»: officials who watch replays on screens to help the referee. 3) «var.» is short for «variety» in plant names, and «var» can be short for «variance» in maths and statistics.
its sense in the lessons: In coding lessons «var score = 0;» makes a variable called score. In football talk, «VAR checked the goal» means the video referee looked at it. In maths, «var» is mostly for older students (variance tells how spread out numbers are). On its own «var» is not a word you say in normal sentences.
examples from the lessons: In JavaScript, «var age = 10;» makes a variable. | The goal was cancelled after a VAR check. | Fans waited while VAR looked at the replay. | The referee went to the VAR screen. | The seed packet says «Rosa var. alba». | Newer JavaScript code uses «let» more than «var».
note for the reader of a maths problem: Abbreviation, not an English word on its own. Write VAR in capitals for the football system, lower case «var» in code. Pronounced «var» or «V-A-R» for football, depending on the country.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A warbler is one of many kinds of small, often greenish or brownish songbirds that eat insects and sing quick, trilling songs, such as the willow warbler or the yellow warbler. 2) (informal) A warbler is a person who sings, especially in a wobbly or not very good way.
its sense in the lessons: In nature lessons warblers are songbirds that often migrate long distances, coming to Britain or North America in spring and leaving in autumn. Birdwatchers learn to tell them apart by their songs. The verb «warble» means to sing with trills and wobbles.
examples from the lessons: A warbler was singing in the willow tree. | Warblers fly to Africa for the winter. | The yellow warbler is common in Canada in summer. | It is hard to see warblers among the leaves. | We heard a warbler but could not spot it. | Grandpa is a cheerful warbler in the shower. | Warblers catch tiny insects to feed their chicks.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: warblers. From the verb «warble» (warbled, warbling). Many warblers look alike; experts often tell them apart by song.

part of speech: verb (wean, weans, weaned, weaning); noun (a wean — Scottish dialect, a child)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To wean a baby or young animal is to slowly stop feeding it only on its mother's milk and start giving it other food. 2) To wean someone off something is to help them slowly stop needing or using it («wean off sugar», «wean off screens»). 3) (Scotland, dialect) A wean is a small child.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about life cycles, mammals feed their young on milk until they are weaned. In everyday life parents talk about weaning a baby onto mashed food, and people try to wean themselves off habits. In Scotland, «the weans» means the kids.
examples from the lessons: Puppies are weaned at about eight weeks. | Mum is weaning the baby onto mashed carrots. | Lambs are weaned from their mothers in summer. | I am trying to wean myself off fizzy drinks. | The doctor weaned him off the medicine slowly. | (Scotland) Get the weans ready for school! | The calf was weaned and moved to the field.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: weaned. Common pattern: «wean somebody off/from something», «wean onto solid food». Sounds like «ween»; the Scottish noun is pronounced «wayn».

part of speech: interjection and word (Mandarin, pinyin «wei» — not an English word); also a Chinese name
meaning for a pupil: 1) (Mandarin, pinyin) «Wei» (喂) is what people say when they answer the phone in Chinese, like «hello?»; it sounds like «way». 2) (Mandarin, pinyin) «Wei» is part of many other Chinese words, for example «wèi» (为) «for», «wèi» (位) a polite counting word for people, and «wèi» (胃) «stomach». 3) (a name) Wei is a common Chinese surname and given name, and the name of old Chinese kingdoms.
its sense in the lessons: In lessons on Mandarin heard on the street, «wei?» is the phone greeting you might hear. In history, the Wei were kingdoms in ancient China. It is not an English word; in English texts it is usually a person's name.
examples from the lessons: «Wei? Ni hao!» — that is how he answered the phone. | «Wei» sounds like the English word «way». | My friend Wei comes from Beijing. | Mr Wei teaches us Mandarin. | In Chinese, «wei» has different meanings for different tones. | The kingdom of Wei was in ancient China.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mandarin in pinyin letters, not English. Pinyin has tones; without the tone mark the meaning is unclear. Names: write Wei with a capital W. Do not confuse with English «way» or «weigh», which sound the same.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An alchemist was a person long ago, in the Middle Ages and before, who tried to turn ordinary metals like lead into gold and to find a medicine that would make people live for ever. 2) In stories, an alchemist is a kind of wizard who mixes strange potions. 3) Figuratively, an alchemist is someone who seems to turn ordinary things into something wonderful.
its sense in the lessons: In history and science lessons alchemists are the early form of chemists: they never made gold, but they invented lab tools and found out about many substances, which helped chemistry begin. In fantasy books and games, alchemists brew potions. The «philosopher's stone» was the magic stone alchemists searched for.
examples from the lessons: The alchemist tried to turn lead into gold. | Alchemists worked with bubbling pots and glass flasks. | Isaac Newton also did experiments as an alchemist. | No alchemist ever really made gold. | In the game, the alchemist sells healing potions. | The chef is an alchemist with leftovers. | Chemistry grew out of the work of alchemists.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: alchemists. The subject is «alchemy». Pronounced «AL-kuh-mist». A myth: alchemists did not succeed in making gold; today we know lead cannot be changed into gold by chemistry.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An amendment is a small change made to a law, rule, plan or piece of writing to correct or improve it. 2) (law, USA) An Amendment is one of the changes added to the United States Constitution, such as the First Amendment about free speech.
its sense in the lessons: In politics lessons, parliaments vote on amendments to new laws. In the USA, children learn about the Bill of Rights, the first ten amendments. In school writing, an amendment is a correction you make to your work. In formal letters: «with amendments».
examples from the lessons: The council made an amendment to the parking rules. | Parliament voted on the amendment. | The First Amendment protects free speech in the USA. | I made a few amendments to my story after reading it again. | The teacher accepted our amendment to the class rules. | There are twenty-seven amendments to the US Constitution. | The amendment changed one word in the law.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: amendments. Verb: «amend» (to change a little). Do not confuse with «amends»: «make amends» means to do something good to make up for a wrong.

part of speech: adverb and adjective (anticlockwise) — UK, Ireland, Australia, NZ; US and Canada say «counterclockwise»
meaning for a pupil: 1) Anticlockwise means turning in the opposite direction to the hands of a clock: from 12 towards 9, then 6, then 3. 2) As an adjective it describes that direction («an anticlockwise turn»).
its sense in the lessons: In maths lessons on turns, angles and rotation, shapes are turned clockwise or anticlockwise by a quarter, half or three-quarter turn. In everyday life you turn many lids and taps anticlockwise to open them («lefty loosey»). In PE and dance, children move round the circle anticlockwise.
examples from the lessons: Turn the jar lid anticlockwise to open it. | Rotate the triangle a quarter turn anticlockwise. | We ran anticlockwise round the track. | The roundabout in the UK goes clockwise, but in the USA traffic goes counterclockwise. | Turn the tap anticlockwise to let the water out. | Draw the arrow showing an anticlockwise turn. | Stir the paint anticlockwise.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Written as one word; some write «anti-clockwise». US/Canada: counterclockwise. In maths a quarter turn = 90 degrees, a half turn = 180, a three-quarter turn anticlockwise is the same as a quarter turn clockwise.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An archaeologist is a scientist who studies how people lived long ago by digging up and examining old things they left behind, such as bones, tools, pots and buildings.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons archaeologists explain how we know about the Stone Age, Romans, Vikings and Egyptians: they dig carefully, record where each find was, and date it. Archaeologists study human remains and things people made; dinosaur bones are studied by palaeontologists instead. In stories, archaeologists explore tombs and lost cities.
examples from the lessons: The archaeologist found a Roman coin in the field. | Archaeologists dig very slowly with small trowels and brushes. | An archaeologist can tell how old a pot is. | Archaeologists found a Viking ship under the ground. | When I grow up I want to be an archaeologist. | The archaeologists marked every find on a map. | Archaeologists study ancient Egypt by looking at tombs.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: UK «archaeologist» (with «ae»); US also «archeologist». Pronounced «ar-kee-OL-uh-jist». Trap: archaeologists do not dig up dinosaurs — that is palaeontology.

meaning for a pupil: 1) ASL stands for American Sign Language, the language of hand signs, faces and body movements used by many Deaf people in the USA and parts of Canada. 2) (internet slang) «asl» is an old chat question meaning «age, sex, location?» — strangers online use it to find out about you.
its sense in the lessons: In lessons about languages and inclusion, ASL is a real language with its own grammar, different from British Sign Language (BSL) and Auslan in Australia. In online safety lessons: if a stranger in a chat asks «asl?», do not answer, and tell a trusted adult — never share your age, where you live or personal details.
examples from the lessons: She is learning ASL to talk with her deaf cousin. | ASL has its own grammar, not the same as English. | In ASL, you can spell names with finger signs. | British Sign Language is different from ASL. | A stranger typed «asl?» in the game chat, so I told my mum. | Never tell strangers online your age or where you live.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Abbreviation, not a word. Write ASL in capitals for the language. Sign languages are not the same in every country: the UK uses BSL, Australia Auslan, New Zealand NZSL. «Deaf» with a capital D means the Deaf community.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Atmospheric means to do with the atmosphere, the layer of air around the Earth or another planet («atmospheric pressure»). 2) Atmospheric also describes a place, picture, film or music that creates a strong mood or feeling, often mysterious, cosy or spooky.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons «atmospheric pressure» is the weight of air pushing down on us, measured with a barometer; scientists study atmospheric gases and pollution. In English lessons, writers use atmospheric description (sounds, light, weather) to set the mood of a story. Everyday: an atmospheric café has candles and soft music.
examples from the lessons: Atmospheric pressure is lower at the top of a mountain. | Scientists measure atmospheric carbon dioxide. | The old castle was dark and atmospheric. | The film has atmospheric music that makes you nervous. | Use atmospheric words like «mist» and «creaking» in your ghost story. | Mars has a very thin atmospheric layer. | The candlelit room felt atmospheric.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective from «atmosphere». Stress: «at-mus-FERR-ik». The two senses are quite different: one is science (air), the other is mood.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An auk is a black-and-white seabird of the cold northern seas, which dives and «flies» underwater to catch fish; puffins, guillemots and razorbills are kinds of auk. 2) The great auk was a big flightless auk, hunted until it became extinct about two hundred years ago.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons auks are an example of birds adapted to the sea, and the great auk is a famous example of extinction caused by people. Auks look a little like penguins but live in the north and most can fly. Seen on cliffs of Scotland, Ireland, Canada and Iceland.
examples from the lessons: Puffins are a kind of auk. | Auks nest on steep cliffs by the sea. | The great auk could not fly. | People hunted the great auk until none were left. | Auks use their wings to swim underwater. | We watched auks diving off the rocks. | Auks live in the north, penguins in the south.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: auks. Rhymes with «hawk» (pronounced «awk»). Myth: auks are not penguins, though they look alike; most auks can fly.

part of speech: verb (babble, babbles, babbled, babbling — -ing form); adjective (babbling); noun (babbling — uncountable)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Babbling is talking quickly in a silly, excited or confusing way, so it is hard to understand or not very sensible. 2) Babbling is the sound babies make — «ba-ba-ba, da-da» — before they can say real words. 3) A babbling brook or stream makes a soft, bubbling, continuous sound as water runs over stones.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on growing up, babbling is a stage of learning to talk, at about 6–9 months. In stories, «a babbling brook» is a peaceful countryside image, and a babbling character is nervous or over-excited. Everyday: «Stop babbling and tell me what happened!»
examples from the lessons: The baby was babbling happily in her cot. | He was so nervous he started babbling. | We sat beside a babbling brook. | Stop babbling and tell me slowly. | Babbling is how babies practise sounds. | The excited children were babbling about the trip. | I could hear the stream babbling under the bridge.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «babble» (drop the e: babbling). Usually a little rude about grown-ups or older children, but kind about babies and streams. Similar: chatter, gabble, prattle.

part of speech: noun (a braid, braids; braid — uncountable trim); verb (braid, braids, braided, braiding)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A braid is hair that has been divided into three or more pieces and twisted over each other into one long rope shape; in the UK this is more often called a plait. 2) To braid is to make hair, rope, string or bread into that shape. 3) Braid is a decorative band of woven thread used on uniforms and curtains.
its sense in the lessons: Everyday life: children braid hair, friendship bracelets and bread (challah). In maths and art, braid patterns are repeating patterns. In history, gold braid on a uniform shows a high rank. US and Canada say «braid» most; UK, Ireland and Australia often say «plait».
examples from the lessons: My sister has two long braids. | Can you braid my hair before school? | We braided three colours of thread into a bracelet. | The baker braided the dough into a loaf. | The captain's coat had gold braid on the sleeves. | Box braids take hours to do. | French braids start at the top of the head.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable for hair (braids), uncountable for the trim (gold braid). Regular verb: braided. UK synonym: plait (pronounced «plat»).

part of speech: noun (cacao — uncountable; a cacao tree, cacao beans)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Cacao is a tropical tree whose seeds, called cacao beans or cocoa beans, are used to make chocolate and cocoa. 2) Cacao also means those beans or the raw powder made from them before much processing.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography lessons cacao is an example of a crop grown near the equator, in West Africa and South and Central America; the beans grow in big pods on the tree trunk. In history, the Maya and Aztecs made a bitter cacao drink. In food shops, «cacao» on a label usually means less processed than «cocoa».
examples from the lessons: Chocolate is made from cacao beans. | The cacao tree grows pods on its trunk. | Ghana and Ivory Coast grow lots of cacao. | The Aztecs drank bitter cacao with chilli. | Cacao beans are dried in the sun. | This bar has seventy per cent cacao. | Each cacao pod holds about forty beans.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced «kuh-KOW» or «kuh-KAY-oh». Cacao and cocoa are nearly the same; cocoa is the usual word for the powder and drink. Not the same as coconut or coca (a different plant).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Capsaicin is the natural chemical in chilli peppers that makes them taste hot and makes your mouth feel like it is burning.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about taste and the body, capsaicin tricks the nerves that sense heat, so your mouth feels hot even though nothing is really burning. Milk helps more than water to calm the burn. In medicine, capsaicin is used in some creams for aches. The «heat» of chillies is measured on the Scoville scale.
examples from the lessons: Capsaicin makes chillies taste hot. | The hottest chillies have the most capsaicin. | Drinking milk helps wash away capsaicin. | Capsaicin is mostly in the white parts and seeds of a chilli. | Birds cannot taste capsaicin, so they eat chilli seeds. | Wash your hands after cutting chillies, because capsaicin stings your eyes. | Some pain creams contain capsaicin.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Pronounced «kap-SAY-sin». Myth: water makes the burn go away — it does not help much, because capsaicin does not mix with water; milk or yoghurt works better.

part of speech: verb (chatter, chatters, chattered, chattering); noun (chatter — uncountable)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To chatter is to talk quickly and a lot about small, unimportant things. 2) When your teeth chatter, they knock together because you are very cold or scared. 3) Birds and monkeys chatter when they make quick, repeated high sounds. 4) Chatter is the sound of people or animals chattering.
its sense in the lessons: In school, «Stop chattering!» means stop talking in class. In science about the body, teeth chattering is shivering that helps warm you up. In stories, chatter fills busy places like the playground or a café; «idle chatter» means unimportant talk.
examples from the lessons: The girls chattered all the way home. | Stop chattering and listen, please. | My teeth were chattering in the freezing sea. | Monkeys chattered in the trees. | The classroom was full of happy chatter. | Magpies chatter loudly in the garden. | There was lots of chatter about the new teacher.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: chattered. Uncountable noun: «a lot of chatter», not «chatters». Similar: babble, natter (UK), chat. «Chatterbox» is a friendly word for someone who talks a lot.

part of speech: verb (clatter, clatters, clattered, clattering); noun (a clatter — usually singular)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To clatter is to make a loud, rattling noise as hard things bang against each other, like falling pans or shoes on stairs. 2) A clatter is that loud, rattling noise. 3) To clatter somewhere is to move noisily («clatter down the stairs»).
its sense in the lessons: In stories, a clatter tells the reader something fell or someone is arriving noisily: dishes, hooves, a dropped tray. In writing lessons it is an example of onomatopoeia, a word that sounds like its meaning. Everyday: the clatter of plates in the school canteen.
examples from the lessons: The pans clattered to the floor. | We heard the clatter of horses' hooves on the road. | He clattered down the stairs in his boots. | The tray fell with a loud clatter. | The train clattered over the bridge. | There was a clatter of cutlery in the dining hall. | The bike clattered when the chain came off.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: clattered. Close to «rattle» and «clang»; «clatter» is many quick bangs. Do not confuse with «clutter» (a messy pile of things).

part of speech: noun (clotting — uncountable); verb (clot, clots, clotted, clotting — -ing form)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Clotting is when blood thickens and becomes a lump at a cut so that bleeding stops. 2) Clotting is when any liquid, like cream or milk, becomes thick and lumpy.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on the body, tiny parts of the blood called platelets help clotting, which forms a scab over a cut. In health, a «blood clot» inside a vein can be dangerous, so doctors watch for it. In cooking, «clotted cream» from Devon and Cornwall is thick cream made by gentle heating.
examples from the lessons: Clotting stops a cut from bleeding for ever. | Platelets in the blood help clotting. | A scab forms after clotting. | Some people's blood has trouble clotting. | Press on the cut to help clotting start. | Clotted cream is thick and yellow. | The milk was clotting in the hot sun.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double t: clot → clotted, clotting. «Clotted cream» is a fixed food phrase (UK). Haemophilia (US hemophilia) is an illness where blood does not clot well.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Coldness is the state of being cold, having a low temperature («the coldness of the water»). 2) Coldness is unfriendly behaviour: not showing warmth, kindness or interest towards someone.
its sense in the lessons: In science, we more often say «cold» or «low temperature», but «the coldness of the ice» appears in descriptions. In stories and in lessons about feelings, a character's coldness shows they are unkind, upset or hiding feelings. Phrase: «treat someone with coldness».
examples from the lessons: The coldness of the sea took my breath away. | I could feel the coldness of the stone floor. | Her coldness hurt his feelings. | He spoke with coldness after the argument. | The coldness of the wind made our ears ache. | The new girl's coldness was really shyness. | After the fight there was a coldness between the friends.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable; formed from «cold» + «-ness». In everyday talk «the cold» is more common for weather («I hate the cold»). Opposite: warmth.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Colossal means extremely large, huge, enormous. 2) (informal) Colossal also means very great in amount or degree («a colossal mistake», «a colossal waste»).
its sense in the lessons: In stories, colossal giants, waves and buildings show huge size. In history lessons the Colossus of Rhodes was a giant statue, one of the Seven Wonders of the ancient world; «colossal» comes from it. In everyday talk «colossal» exaggerates for effect.
examples from the lessons: A colossal wave crashed over the harbour. | The blue whale is a colossal animal. | The pyramids are colossal stone buildings. | We ate a colossal pizza. | Losing the key was a colossal mistake. | The storm did colossal damage. | The giant took colossal steps across the hills.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: col-OSS-al, double s, one l at the end. Strong word: it is bigger than «big» and «large». Similar: enormous, gigantic, huge, massive.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A contagious disease is one that spreads from person to person by touching or being close, such as a cold, flu or chickenpox. 2) A contagious person has an illness they can pass on. 3) A contagious feeling, laugh or yawn spreads quickly from one person to others.
its sense in the lessons: In health lessons, washing hands, covering coughs and staying home when ill stop contagious diseases spreading. Schools ask parents to keep contagious children at home. In everyday talk, «Her laugh is contagious» means it makes others laugh too.
examples from the lessons: Chickenpox is very contagious. | Stay at home while you are contagious. | Wash your hands to stop contagious germs. | Her smile is contagious. | Yawns are contagious — I just yawned too! | The doctor said I am no longer contagious. | His excitement was contagious, and soon we were all cheering.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Similar to «infectious»; in everyday talk they are used almost the same way. Not every illness is contagious: a broken arm or diabetes cannot be caught. Spelling ends in «-gious».

part of speech: noun (cornflour — uncountable) — UK, Ireland, Australia, NZ; US and Canada say «cornstarch»
meaning for a pupil: 1) Cornflour is a fine white powder made from maize (corn), used in cooking to make sauces, soups and gravy thicker. 2) In the US, «corn flour» can also mean flour ground from whole corn, which is different.
its sense in the lessons: In cooking at home and school, a spoon of cornflour mixed with cold water thickens a sauce. In science lessons, cornflour mixed with water makes «oobleck», a strange slime that is hard when you hit it and runny when you pour it — a non-Newtonian fluid. Recipes from the US will say «cornstarch».
examples from the lessons: Mix the cornflour with cold water before adding it to the gravy. | Cornflour makes the sauce thick and shiny. | We made slime with cornflour and water. | The oobleck went hard when I punched it. | US recipes call cornflour «cornstarch». | Cornflour is gluten-free. | Dust the table with cornflour so the icing does not stick.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «a tablespoon of cornflour». Trap: UK «cornflour» = US «cornstarch»; US «cornmeal» is something else (yellow and gritty). Always mix it with cold water first, or it goes lumpy.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Corundum is a very hard natural mineral made of aluminium oxide; rubies and sapphires are coloured kinds of corundum.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about rocks and minerals, corundum scores 9 on the Mohs scale of hardness, second only to diamond (10). Because it is so hard, crushed corundum is used to make sandpaper and grinding tools (emery). Red corundum is ruby; blue and other colours are sapphire.
examples from the lessons: Rubies and sapphires are both corundum. | Corundum is harder than almost any other mineral. | On the Mohs scale, corundum is 9 and diamond is 10. | Emery boards for nails contain corundum. | Pure corundum has no colour. | The museum showed a big red crystal of corundum.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Pronounced «kuh-RUN-dum». A trap: ruby and sapphire are the same mineral, just different colours caused by tiny amounts of other metals.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Curds are the thick white lumps that form when milk goes sour or is made to separate; they are used to make cheese. 2) Curd is a thick, creamy spread made with fruit juice, sugar, eggs and butter, as in lemon curd. 3) Curd can mean soft cheese, like cottage cheese, or bean curd (tofu).
its sense in the lessons: In science and cooking lessons, adding something sour such as lemon juice or rennet to milk makes it separate into curds (solid) and whey (liquid) — an example of a change that cannot be undone. In nursery rhymes, Little Miss Muffet ate «her curds and whey». In Canada, cheese curds go on poutine.
examples from the lessons: Little Miss Muffet ate her curds and whey. | Add lemon juice and the milk turns into curds. | Cheesemakers press the curds into blocks. | I love lemon curd on toast. | Poutine is chips with gravy and cheese curds. | Squeaky cheese curds are a snack in Canada. | Bean curd is another name for tofu.
note for the reader of a maths problem: For the milk lumps it is often plural: curds. «Lemon curd» is uncountable. Do not confuse with «curdle» (the verb: milk curdles) or «Kurd» (a person of the Kurdish people), which sounds the same.

part of speech: adjective (Danish); noun (Danish — the language; a danish, danishes — a pastry)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Danish means from Denmark or to do with Denmark and its people. 2) Danish is the language spoken in Denmark. 3) A danish (or Danish pastry) is a sweet, flaky pastry, often with fruit, custard or icing.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons Danish people live in Denmark in northern Europe; LEGO comes from Denmark. In history, Danish Vikings settled in England (the «Danelaw»). Everyday: a danish is a breakfast treat in bakeries and cafés.
examples from the lessons: LEGO is a Danish toy company. | My friend's mum speaks Danish. | The Danish flag is red with a white cross. | I had an apple danish for breakfast. | Danish Vikings once ruled part of England. | Hans Christian Andersen was a Danish writer of fairy tales. | Danish sounds a bit like Swedish and Norwegian.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital D for the people, country and language: Danish. The pastry is often written «danish» or «Danish pastry»; plural danishes. A person from Denmark is «a Dane».

meaning for a pupil: 1) To decode a secret message or code is to change it back into normal words so you can understand it. 2) In reading, to decode a word is to work it out by turning letters into their sounds and blending them. 3) To decode something is to understand a hidden meaning, like a strange look or difficult instructions. 4) In computing, to decode is to change data back into sound, pictures or text.
its sense in the lessons: In phonics lessons «decoding» is sounding out words: c-a-t → cat. In maths and coding puzzles, you decode messages with a key (A=1, B=2). In history, the code-breakers of Bletchley Park decoded enemy messages. In everyday talk, you decode a teacher's hint.
examples from the lessons: Use the key to decode the secret message. | Young readers decode words by sounding them out. | Alan Turing's team helped decode enemy messages. | If A = 1 and B = 2, decode 3-1-20. | I could not decode my brother's messy handwriting. | The TV decodes the signal into pictures. | Can you decode what Mum's look meant?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: decoded. Opposite: encode. «De-» means «undo». In the puzzle above, 3-1-20 decodes to CAT.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (grammar) A determiner is a word that comes before a noun and tells you which one, whose, or how many, such as «the», «a», «this», «my», «some», «every» and numbers like «three». 2) More generally, a determiner is something that decides or controls what happens.
its sense in the lessons: In English grammar lessons (and SATs tests in England), pupils find determiners: articles (a, an, the), demonstratives (this, that, these, those), possessives (my, your, their), quantifiers (some, many, every) and numbers. A determiner goes before any adjectives: «the big red bus».
examples from the lessons: In «the dog barked», «the» is a determiner. | «My», «your» and «their» are possessive determiners. | Underline the determiner in «Those apples are sour.» | «Some», «many» and «every» are determiners too. | Numbers like «two» can act as determiners: «two cats». | A determiner comes before the adjective: «a tall tree». | Use «an» before a vowel sound: «an elephant».
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: determiners. Trap: «this» is a determiner in «this book» but a pronoun in «I like this». «A» becomes «an» before a vowel sound: an apple, an hour, but a unicorn.

part of speech: adjective (domesticated); verb (domesticate, domesticates, domesticated, domesticating — past form)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A domesticated animal or plant has been tamed and bred by people over many generations to live with them or be useful, like dogs, cows, sheep and wheat. 2) Domesticated is the past of «domesticate»: tamed and bred for human use. 3) (humorous) A domesticated person likes or is good at housework and cooking.
its sense in the lessons: In history and science lessons, early farmers domesticated wolves into dogs and wild grasses into wheat, which allowed villages to grow. Domesticated animals differ from wild ones: one tame lion is tamed, not domesticated. In everyday jokes, «He's become very domesticated» means he now cooks and cleans.
examples from the lessons: Dogs were the first domesticated animals. | People domesticated sheep for wool and meat. | Wheat was domesticated thousands of years ago. | A cat is domesticated, but a fox is wild. | Horses were domesticated on the grasslands of Asia. | Dad's become very domesticated — he even irons now! | Domesticated pigs come from wild boar.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: «tame» means one animal is calm with people; «domesticated» means a whole species has been changed by breeding over many generations. Noun: domestication.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) Dorsal means on or to do with the back of an animal or the upper side of something. 2) The dorsal fin is the fin on the back of a fish, shark, dolphin or whale.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on fish and sea animals, the dorsal fin helps them balance and steer. In stories and films, a dorsal fin above the water is the classic sign of a shark (though dolphins have them too). In medicine and body science, «dorsal» means back-side; the opposite is «ventral» (belly side).
examples from the lessons: The shark's dorsal fin cut through the water. | Dolphins have a curved dorsal fin. | Label the dorsal fin on your fish diagram. | The dorsal side of a frog is green and spotty. | Some whales have a tiny dorsal fin. | The dorsal fin stops the fish from rolling over.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Science word, mostly in «dorsal fin». Opposite: ventral (the belly side). Trap: not every fin above the water is a shark — dolphins have dorsal fins too.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Ethylene is a colourless gas made of carbon and hydrogen; plants make it naturally, and it makes fruit ripen. 2) Ethylene is an important chemical used in factories to make plastics such as polythene (polyethylene).
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, ethylene explains why a banana put next to green fruit makes it ripen faster, and why one rotten apple spoils the bowl. In chemistry, it is the building block of polythene used for plastic bags and bottles. Scientists call it «ethene» in school chemistry.
examples from the lessons: Ripe bananas give off ethylene gas. | Put an avocado in a bag with a banana to help it ripen. | Ethylene makes fruit go soft and sweet. | Plastic bags are made from ethylene. | One rotten apple gives off ethylene and spoils the others. | Fruit is shipped cold to slow down ethylene.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Pronounced «ETH-uh-leen». School chemistry name: ethene. Polythene / polyethylene is made by joining many ethylene molecules in a chain.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Experimental means to do with experiments, tests done to find something out («experimental results»). 2) Experimental means new and still being tested, not yet proved to work («an experimental drug», «an experimental plane»). 3) Experimental art, music or writing tries new, unusual ways.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, «experimental» data comes from your own test; you compare it with your prediction, and keep a fair test by changing only one thing. In news, experimental medicines are being tested before doctors use them widely. In music and art, «experimental» means unusual or daring.
examples from the lessons: Write your experimental results in a table. | The experimental method helps us test ideas fairly. | The plane is experimental and has never carried passengers. | Doctors tried an experimental medicine. | The band plays strange, experimental music. | Our experimental group of plants got extra light. | The new timetable is only experimental for this term.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective from «experiment». In science, the «experimental group» gets the change, the «control group» does not. Stress: «ex-PERR-i-MEN-tul».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A fluke is a lucky chance, something good that happened by accident, not because of skill. 2) A fluke is a flat parasitic worm that can live inside animals or people. 3) The flukes are the two flat parts of a whale's tail. 4) A fluke is the flat pointed part of an anchor's arm.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and sport, «It was a fluke!» means a goal or win happened by luck. In maths and science, a fluke result is an odd one that probably happened by chance, so you repeat the test. In nature lessons, whale-watchers see the flukes when a whale dives.
examples from the lessons: That goal was a total fluke! | Was it skill or a fluke? | Repeat the experiment in case the result was a fluke. | The whale lifted its flukes and dived. | Liver flukes can make sheep ill. | Winning the raffle twice was a fluke. | He passed by fluke, not by revising.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: flukes. Adjective: «flukey» or «fluky» (informal). In science, one strange result can be a fluke; that is why scientists repeat tests and take averages.

part of speech: noun (gall — uncountable; a gall, galls); verb (gall, galls, galled, galling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Gall is rude, bold cheek: «He had the gall to ask for more after eating mine!» 2) A gall is a lump on a plant, such as an oak apple, made when an insect lays eggs in it. 3) (old) Gall is bile, a bitter liquid from the liver; the gall bladder stores it. 4) To gall someone is to annoy them a lot because it feels unfair.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday talk, «the gall of it!» shows outrage at rudeness. In science and nature lessons, oak galls are made by tiny wasps; long ago, oak galls were used to make ink. In body science, the gall bladder sits under the liver. In the Bible, «gall» means something very bitter.
examples from the lessons: She had the gall to push in front of me. | What gall! He took my seat and asked for my pencil. | We found round galls on the oak leaves. | Old ink was made from oak galls. | The gall bladder is near the liver. | It galls me that he got the prize for my idea. | Wasps cause galls to grow on plants.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable in the «cheek» sense: «have the gall to do something». Adjective «galling» = annoying. Pronounced «gawl». Not to be confused with «Gaul» (old name for France) or «gal» (informal for girl).

part of speech: noun (a gar, gars; also garfish, gar)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A gar is a long, thin fish with a narrow snout full of sharp teeth, such as the North American gar of rivers and lakes. 2) In the UK and Australia, «garfish» is a long thin sea fish with a beak-like jaw. 3) «gar» is also a short piece of words like «garden» or «cigar».
its sense in the lessons: In nature lessons, gars are old kinds of fish with hard, shiny scales, called «living fossils». Anglers in the USA catch alligator gar, which can be huge. On its own «gar» is rare in children's talk.
examples from the lessons: The alligator gar has a mouth like a crocodile. | A gar can breathe air at the surface. | Gars have tough, armour-like scales. | We saw a garfish in the harbour. | The gar waited still among the weeds. | Some gars grow longer than a grown-up.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; plural «gars» or «gar». Pronounced like «car» with a g. Mostly American and Australian in use.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Genocide is the deliberate killing of a large number of people because they belong to a particular nation, ethnic group, race or religion, with the aim of destroying that group. 2) (law) Genocide is an international crime; courts decide whether events count as genocide.
