its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, the Holocaust, when the Nazis murdered about six million Jews and others, is the best-known genocide; children also learn about Rwanda and the Holodomor famine in Ukraine, which Ukraine and many countries recognise as genocide. In news, some events are called genocide by some governments and disputed by others; it is a serious legal word, and people should say who is making the claim.
examples from the lessons: The Holocaust was a genocide. | Genocide is one of the worst crimes there is. | We remember victims of genocide on Holocaust Memorial Day. | The UN agreed a law against genocide after the Second World War. | Many countries recognise the Holodomor as a genocide. | A genocide took place in Rwanda. | Courts decide whether a crime is genocide.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Serious word: not for exaggeration or jokes. Mostly uncountable; «a genocide» for one event. From Greek «genos» (people, race) + Latin «-cide» (killing), as in «pesticide».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A goblin is an ugly, small, mischievous or wicked creature in fairy tales and fantasy stories, often green or grey, with pointy ears. 2) (informal, humorous) A goblin is a naughty child or someone acting greedily or sneakily.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, folk tales and games, goblins cause trouble, steal, live in caves or under hills, and guard treasure; in some books they run banks. Goblins are made-up creatures. In everyday jokes, «you little goblin» is a fond tease.
examples from the lessons: The goblin hid the gold under the bridge. | Goblins live in dark caves in the story. | The knight chased the goblins out of the village. | Ugh, a goblin mask for Halloween! | The goblin had long fingers and a crooked grin. | Stop being a goblin and share the sweets! | In the game, goblins drop coins when you beat them.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: goblins. Goblins are not real. Similar made-up creatures: imp, gremlin, troll, hobgoblin.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A goddess is a female god, a powerful being in some religions and myths, such as Athena, Greek goddess of wisdom, or Freya in Norse myths. 2) (informal) A goddess is a woman who is greatly admired, for her beauty or for being very good at something («a sports goddess»).
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons on Ancient Greece, Rome, Egypt and the Vikings, children learn about many gods and goddesses. Hindus today worship goddesses such as Lakshmi and Durga. Christians, Jews and Muslims believe in one God and do not speak of goddesses. In everyday talk «goddess» is high praise.
examples from the lessons: Athena was the Greek goddess of wisdom. | The Romans called the goddess of love Venus. | Isis was an important Egyptian goddess. | Hindus pray to the goddess Lakshmi at Diwali. | The temple was built for a goddess. | The fans called the tennis star a goddess. | Each Greek goddess had her own symbol.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: goddesses. Write «God» with a capital for the one God of Christians, Jews and Muslims; «a god» and «a goddess» with small letters for gods of myths. Be respectful about living religions.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Grim means very serious, stern and unsmiling («a grim face»). 2) Grim means unpleasant, worrying or sad («grim news»). 3) A grim place is dark, cold and gloomy. 4) (UK, informal) Grim means horrible or disgusting («The school toilets were grim»). 5) «Hold on like grim death» means to hold very tightly.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, grim faces and grim weather set a dark mood; the «Grim Reaper» is a picture of death in a hooded cloak with a scythe. In the news, «grim» describes bad news like disasters. In everyday UK talk, «that's grim» means yuck.
examples from the lessons: The teacher looked grim when she saw the mess. | The news about the flood was grim. | The castle was a grim, grey place. | The bins smelt grim in the heat. | He held on to the rope like grim death. | The weather forecast is grim for the weekend. | The Grim Reaper is a spooky picture of death.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparatives double the m: grimmer, grimmest. Not connected with the Brothers Grimm (a name, spelt with two m). Similar: stern, gloomy, bleak.

part of speech: noun (a grudge, grudges); verb (grudge, grudges, grudged, grudging)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A grudge is a feeling of anger or dislike you keep for a long time against someone who you think treated you badly. 2) To hold or bear a grudge is to keep that feeling and not forgive. 3) To grudge (or begrudge) something is to give it or let someone have it unwillingly.
its sense in the lessons: In lessons about feelings and friendship, holding a grudge is shown as hurting yourself more than the other person; forgiving lets go of a grudge. In stories, an old grudge explains why characters are enemies. A «grudge match» is a game between rivals.
examples from the lessons: He held a grudge against me for weeks. | Don't hold a grudge — say sorry and move on. | The two families had an old grudge. | She doesn't bear grudges; she forgives quickly. | It was a grudge match between the two teams. | I don't grudge him his win; he trained hard. | Holding a grudge made her feel bad inside.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: grudges. Phrases: «hold a grudge», «bear a grudge», «have a grudge against someone». Adjective «grudging» = unwilling («a grudging thank-you»).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Harmony is when people or things live, work or fit together peacefully and agree («live in harmony»). 2) In music, harmony is when different notes are played or sung together and sound pleasant. 3) A harmony is a second tune sung with the main one to make it sound richer.
its sense in the lessons: In music lessons, children sing rounds and harmonies, and chords are an example of harmony. In lessons about community and religion, «living in harmony» means getting along despite differences. In nature lessons, ecosystems are in harmony when plants and animals are in balance.
examples from the lessons: The choir sang in perfect harmony. | Our class lives in harmony most days. | She sang the harmony while I sang the tune. | The colours of the painting are in harmony. | People of different faiths live in harmony in our town. | Cats and dogs can live in harmony. | The band added a lovely harmony to the chorus.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly uncountable for peace and agreement; countable (harmonies) for musical parts. Adjective: harmonious. Opposite: discord, disagreement.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A headland is a high piece of land with steep cliffs that sticks out into the sea.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons about coasts, headlands form where hard rock wears away slowly while soft rock nearby is eaten away into bays. Waves attack headlands and make caves, arches and stacks. In stories, lighthouses often stand on headlands.
examples from the lessons: A lighthouse stands on the headland. | Waves crash against the rocky headland. | Headlands are made of hard rock. | The bay is sheltered between two headlands. | We walked along the cliff path to the headland. | Over time, a cave in a headland can become an arch. | From the headland we could see dolphins.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: headlands. Similar: cape, point, promontory (formal). Opposite coastal feature: a bay. Geography order: cave → arch → stack → stump.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The humerus is the long bone in the top part of your arm, between your shoulder and your elbow.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about the skeleton, children label the humerus, radius and ulna in the arm. The «funny bone» is not a bone at all but a nerve near the elbow end of the humerus — a pun on «humorous».
examples from the lessons: The humerus is the bone in your upper arm. | She broke her humerus falling off the swing. | Label the humerus on the skeleton diagram. | The humerus joins the shoulder at the top. | Below the elbow are the radius and ulna, not the humerus. | Your «funny bone» is a nerve near the humerus.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: humeri (rare). Sounds exactly like «humorous» (funny) — a homophone and a famous joke: «Why is the arm bone funny? Because it's the humerus!»

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To impede someone or something is to get in the way and slow it down or make it harder to happen or move.
its sense in the lessons: In formal writing and exams, «impede» means hinder: snow impedes traffic, noise impedes learning. In science, friction impedes movement, and in electricity, resistance impedes current. In everyday talk you would say «get in the way of» or «hold up».
examples from the lessons: Fallen trees impeded the rescue workers. | Heavy snow impeded traffic all morning. | Talking in class impedes learning. | Friction impedes the movement of the box. | Nothing should impede the fire exit. | Bad weather impeded the search for the boat.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal word; plain English: block, slow down, hold up. Noun: impediment («a speech impediment» = a stammer or difficulty speaking). Regular verb: impeded.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A jackal is a wild animal like a small, thin dog that lives in Africa and Asia and eats small animals and leftovers from other hunters. 2) (informal) A jackal can mean a sneaky person who takes advantage of others' work or misfortune.
its sense in the lessons: In nature lessons, jackals are hunters and scavengers that help clean up the savanna; they often live in pairs for life. In history lessons on Ancient Egypt, the god Anubis has a jackal's head. In stories and fables, the jackal is often a sly trickster.
examples from the lessons: A jackal crept towards the leftover meat. | Jackals howl at night on the savanna. | Anubis, the Egyptian god, had a jackal's head. | The jackal is a cousin of the dog and the wolf. | In the fable, the clever jackal tricks the lion. | Jackals live in pairs and raise their pups together. | We heard jackals calling in the dark.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: jackals. Pronounced «JACK-ul». A jackal is not a hyena, though both scavenge; hyenas are a different family.

part of speech: word (Japanese and Korean «ki» — not an English word); fragment
meaning for a pupil: 1) (Japanese, Korean) Ki is a word for life energy or inner strength, used in martial arts like aikido and karate; in Chinese it is «qi» or «chi». 2) «ki» is also a piece of longer words such as «kick», «kite» or «ski».
its sense in the lessons: In martial arts classes, teachers talk about breathing and «ki» (inner energy); this is a belief from East Asian traditions, not a measured thing in science. In Scrabble, «ki» is allowed in some word lists. On its own it is not an everyday English word.
examples from the lessons: In aikido, the teacher tells us to focus our ki. | «Ki» is the Japanese word for life energy. | The Chinese word «qi» means something similar. | Breathe slowly and feel your ki, the sensei said. | «Ki» is the first part of «kite». | Some Scrabble players use «ki» to get points.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Not an English word on its own: borrowed from Japanese/Korean or a fragment. Sounds like «key». Belief in ki belongs to traditions; science does not measure it as a kind of energy.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Legendary means from a legend, an old story that may or may not be true («the legendary King Arthur»). 2) Legendary means very famous and admired, talked about by many people («a legendary footballer»). 3) (informal) Legendary means brilliant or amazing («That party was legendary!»).
its sense in the lessons: In history and English lessons, legendary heroes like Robin Hood and King Arthur appear in stories, and pupils discuss which parts might be true. In sport and music, «legendary» praises famous people. In slang, «legend» or «legendary» means awesome.
examples from the lessons: King Arthur is a legendary king of Britain. | Robin Hood is a legendary outlaw. | The legendary striker scored over 300 goals. | Grandma's apple pie is legendary in our family. | The legendary dragon guarded the gold. | That sleepover was legendary! | Nobody knows if the legendary city really existed.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective from «legend». Trap: «legendary» can mean either «only in stories, maybe not true» or «really famous and real» — look at the context. Slang: «You're a legend!» = you're great.

part of speech: noun (a legion, legions); adjective (legion — formal, after a noun or verb)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A legion was a large army unit in ancient Rome, of about 5,000 soldiers. 2) A legion is a very large number of people or things («a legion of fans»). 3) (formal) «Legion» as an adjective means very many: «Her fans are legion.» 4) Some modern armed groups are called a legion, such as the French Foreign Legion, or veterans' clubs like the Royal British Legion.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons on the Romans, legions marched across Europe and built Hadrian's Wall in Britain. In the UK the Royal British Legion runs the poppy appeal for Remembrance Day. In the Bible, «My name is Legion, for we are many» comes from a story in the Gospels. Everyday: «legions of» = loads of.
examples from the lessons: A Roman legion had thousands of soldiers. | The legions built roads across Britain. | Legions of fans waited outside the stadium. | The Royal British Legion sells poppies in November. | Her mistakes were legion! | Each legion had its own eagle standard. | Legions of ants marched into the kitchen.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: legions. The adjective use «are legion» is formal and goes after the verb. Pronounced «LEE-jun».

part of speech: adjective (Lithuanian); noun (a Lithuanian, Lithuanians; Lithuanian — the language)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Lithuanian means from Lithuania, a country on the Baltic Sea in north-east Europe, or to do with its people. 2) Lithuanian is the language spoken in Lithuania. 3) A Lithuanian is a person from Lithuania.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons, Lithuania is one of the three Baltic states, with Latvia and Estonia; its capital is Vilnius. Lithuanian is famous as a very old-style language in the Indo-European family. Many Lithuanian families live in the UK and Ireland, so children meet classmates who speak it.
examples from the lessons: My classmate is Lithuanian. | Lithuanian is spoken in Vilnius. | She speaks Lithuanian at home and English at school. | The Lithuanian flag is yellow, green and red. | Lithuanians love basketball. | Lithuanian is one of the oldest-sounding languages in Europe. | We learnt to say «labas» — «hello» in Lithuanian.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always a capital L: Lithuanian, Lithuania. Pronounced «lith-yoo-AY-nee-un». It is not a Slavic language, though Lithuania is near Poland; it is a Baltic language, like Latvian.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Luminous means giving out light or glowing, especially in the dark («luminous paint», «a luminous watch»). 2) Luminous means very bright and shining («luminous eyes»). 3) (informal) Luminous colours are very bright, neon colours, like luminous yellow or green.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on light, luminous objects make their own light, like the Sun, stars, fire and torches; non-luminous objects, like the Moon and mirrors, only reflect light. In safety lessons, luminous (high-visibility) vests help drivers see you. In stories, «luminous» describes moonlit or magical scenes.
examples from the lessons: The Sun is a luminous object. | The Moon is not luminous; it reflects light. | My watch has luminous hands. | Wear a luminous jacket when cycling at night. | The stars were luminous in the clear sky. | Glow-worms are luminous insects. | She painted her nails luminous pink.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Science trap: the Moon looks bright but is not luminous — it reflects light from the Sun. Noun: luminosity. Similar: glowing, fluorescent (bright colour that shines under light).

part of speech: verb (master, masters, mastered, mastering — -ing form); noun (mastering — uncountable)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Mastering a skill or subject means learning it completely and becoming really good at it. 2) Mastering a feeling means getting control of it («mastering his fear»). 3) (music) Mastering is the last stage of making a recording, when the sound is balanced and made ready to sell or stream.
its sense in the lessons: In school, «mastering times tables» means knowing them quickly and without mistakes; many schools talk about «mastery». In stories, a character mastering fear shows courage. In music technology, mastering is a job in a studio.
examples from the lessons: She is mastering the 7 times table. | Mastering a new language takes years. | He is mastering his fear of heights. | Mastering the piano needs daily practice. | We are mastering long division this term. | The band's song is in the mastering stage. | Mastering a skateboard trick takes lots of falls.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «master» (no double r: mastered, mastering). «Master» as a verb is used for both girls and boys. «Mastery» is the noun for very good knowledge.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Metallic means made of metal or having the properties of metal. 2) Metallic means looking shiny like metal («metallic paint», «metallic blue»). 3) A metallic sound is hard and ringing; a metallic taste is like the taste of a coin.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on materials, metallic materials are usually shiny, hard, strong, and conduct heat and electricity; most are not magnetic except iron, nickel and cobalt. In art, metallic pens and paints are gold, silver and shiny colours. In stories, a metallic clang or taste adds detail.
examples from the lessons: Copper is a metallic element. | The car is painted metallic silver. | Metallic materials conduct electricity. | We heard a metallic clang in the shed. | The water had a metallic taste. | I used metallic gold pens for the card. | Metallic objects feel cold to touch because they conduct heat.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective from «metal»; spelt with double l. Trap: not all metallic things are magnetic — aluminium and copper are not. Do not confuse «metal» and «medal» (a prize).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Midwinter is the middle of winter, the coldest and darkest part. 2) Midwinter is the winter solstice, the shortest day of the year, in late December in the northern half of the world and in June in the southern half.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about the Earth and seasons, midwinter is when one half of the Earth tilts furthest away from the Sun, so days are shortest. In history, people at Stonehenge celebrated midwinter, and many festivals like Christmas, Yule and Hanukkah come near it in the north. In Australia and New Zealand, midwinter is in June, and some hold «Christmas in July» parties.
examples from the lessons: Midwinter is the shortest day of the year. | People gather at Stonehenge at midwinter. | In Australia, midwinter is in June. | The midwinter sun sets very early. | The carol «In the Bleak Midwinter» is a famous Christmas song. | It snowed heavily in midwinter. | Some towns hold midwinter festivals with lanterns.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable, no article: «at midwinter», «in midwinter». Opposite: midsummer. Seasons are opposite in the north and south of the world.

part of speech: noun (mince — uncountable) — UK, Ireland, Australia, NZ; verb (mince, minces, minced, mincing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Mince is meat cut into very small pieces in a machine, used for burgers, spaghetti bolognese and cottage pie; in the US and Canada it is called «ground beef» or «hamburger meat». 2) To mince food is to cut it into very small pieces. 3) To mince is to walk with small, quick, fussy steps. 4) «Not mince your words» means to say something directly, even if it is not polite.
its sense in the lessons: In cooking at home and school, mince is a cheap everyday meat; «mince and tatties» is a Scottish dish, and «mince pies» are a Christmas treat (now filled with fruit, not meat). In everyday talk, «she didn't mince her words» means she was very blunt. In Scotland, «talking mince» means talking nonsense (slang).
examples from the lessons: Mum bought beef mince for burgers. | Fry the mince with onions. | Mince the garlic very finely. | We eat mince pies at Christmas. | She didn't mince her words: «That's wrong.» | (Scotland) Stop talking mince! | In the US, mince is called ground beef. | The mince is browning in the pan.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable noun: «some mince», «500 grams of mince». Trap: «mince pies» in the UK are sweet fruit pies, not meat. «Mincemeat» is the sweet fruit filling; «make mincemeat of someone» = beat them easily.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A monarchy is a country ruled by a king, queen or emperor, whose position is usually passed on in the family. 2) The monarchy is the system of having a king or queen, or the royal family itself.
its sense in the lessons: In politics and history lessons, the UK is a constitutional monarchy: the King is head of state, but Parliament makes laws and the Prime Minister leads the government. Canada, Australia and New Zealand share the same monarch. The USA and Ireland are republics, with an elected president instead. Some people support the monarchy and some want a republic.
examples from the lessons: The United Kingdom is a monarchy. | In a monarchy, the crown passes from parent to child. | France stopped being a monarchy long ago. | Canada's head of state is the British monarch. | Some people want to keep the monarchy, others do not. | Saudi Arabia is an absolute monarchy. | The monarchy has existed in Britain for over a thousand years.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: monarchies. Ruler: monarch. Opposite system: republic. Pronounced «MON-ar-kee»; «ch» sounds like «k».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (a name) Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart was a famous Austrian composer of classical music who lived more than two hundred years ago; he wrote music from the age of five and died young, at 35. 2) «A Mozart» (informal) can mean a child who is very talented, especially at music.
its sense in the lessons: In music lessons, children listen to Mozart's pieces, such as «Eine kleine Nachtmusik» and «The Magic Flute», and learn he was a child prodigy who toured Europe playing for kings. The tune of «Twinkle Twinkle Little Star» is an old French tune that Mozart wrote variations on. The claim that playing Mozart to babies makes them cleverer (the «Mozart effect») is a myth that has not held up in studies.
examples from the lessons: Mozart wrote his first music when he was five. | We listened to Mozart in music class. | Mozart was born in Salzburg in Austria. | Mozart wrote operas, symphonies and piano pieces. | She plays piano like a young Mozart. | Mozart's father took him on tours across Europe. | «The Magic Flute» is an opera by Mozart.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A name: always a capital M. Pronounced «MOTE-sart». Myth: listening to Mozart does not make babies cleverer.

part of speech: noun (a nightingale, nightingales); proper noun (Nightingale — a name)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A nightingale is a small brown bird famous for its beautiful, loud, varied song, which it often sings at night as well as in the day. 2) (a name) Florence Nightingale was an English nurse in Victorian times who made hospitals cleaner and helped start modern nursing; she was called «the Lady with the Lamp».
its sense in the lessons: In nature lessons and poems, the nightingale's song is a symbol of beauty and spring nights. In history lessons, Florence Nightingale cared for soldiers in the Crimean War and used charts of numbers to show that clean hospitals saved lives. In stories, a «nightingale voice» means a lovely singing voice.
examples from the lessons: A nightingale sang in the bushes all night. | Nightingales are plain brown but sing beautifully. | Florence Nightingale carried a lamp on her night rounds. | Florence Nightingale used diagrams to show why soldiers were dying. | The poet wrote an ode to a nightingale. | Nightingales fly to Africa for the winter. | Her singing voice is like a nightingale's.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: nightingales. Capital N for Florence Nightingale. Despite the name, nightingales also sing in the daytime; the night song is what made them famous.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Nylon is a strong, light, man-made material made from chemicals (a plastic), used for clothes, ropes, toothbrush bristles, tents and fishing line. 2) (old-fashioned) Nylons are women's thin stockings or tights made of nylon.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on materials, nylon is a synthetic (man-made) fibre, not natural like cotton or wool; it is strong, stretchy, waterproof-ish and dries quickly. In history, nylon was invented in the USA less than a hundred years ago and used for parachutes in the Second World War. In environment lessons, nylon does not rot easily and old fishing nets pollute the sea.
examples from the lessons: My coat is made of nylon. | Nylon rope is strong and light. | Toothbrush bristles are usually nylon. | Nylon is a man-made material, not a natural one. | Parachutes were made of nylon in the war. | Nylon dries quickly after rain. | Old nylon fishing nets can trap sea animals.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable for the material: «made of nylon». Plural «nylons» only for stockings. Pronounced «NY-lon». Nylon melts if it gets too hot — keep it away from flames.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Opposition is strong disagreement with a plan or idea, often shown by speaking or acting against it. 2) The opposition is the team or player you are playing against. 3) (politics) The Opposition is the parties in parliament that are not in the government, especially the biggest one, which questions and challenges the government. 4) Opposition is being opposite or against something («in opposition to»).
its sense in the lessons: In politics lessons in the UK, Canada, Australia and New Zealand, the Leader of the Opposition and the Opposition party challenge the Prime Minister. In sport, «the opposition» are the other team. In everyday life, there is opposition to a new rule when many people disagree. In maths and science, opposition is rare as a technical word.
examples from the lessons: There was strong opposition to closing the library. | The opposition scored in the last minute. | The Leader of the Opposition asked the Prime Minister a question. | Parents voiced their opposition to the new uniform. | The Opposition voted against the law. | Our team beat the opposition easily. | She spoke in opposition to the plan.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly uncountable; capital O for the political Opposition in Westminster-style parliaments. Verb: oppose; adjective: opposite, opposed. «In opposition to» = against.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A pact is a serious agreement or promise between people, groups or countries to do something or to help each other. 2) A pact can be a secret promise between friends («We made a pact to never tell»).
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, pacts between countries (such as alliances and peace pacts) explain how wars started or ended; for example, NATO countries promise to defend each other. In stories, friends make a pact, sometimes with a handshake or pinkie promise. In old tales, a «pact with the devil» is a dangerous bargain.
examples from the lessons: We made a pact to stay friends forever. | The two countries signed a pact of peace. | The friends made a pact to keep the secret. | They broke their pact and told the teacher. | NATO countries have a pact to defend each other. | In the story, the wizard made a pact with a dragon. | Let's make a pact: no phones at dinner.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: pacts. Phrases: «make a pact», «sign a pact», «break a pact». Similar: agreement, deal, treaty (a formal written pact between countries).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A pandemic is an outbreak of an infectious disease that spreads across many countries or the whole world and makes very many people ill. 2) As an adjective, pandemic means spreading everywhere.
its sense in the lessons: In health and science lessons, the COVID-19 pandemic is a recent example: schools closed, people wore masks, and vaccines were made. In history, the Black Death and the great flu after the First World War were pandemics. An «epidemic» is a big outbreak in one area; a pandemic is worldwide.
examples from the lessons: The COVID-19 pandemic closed schools around the world. | During the pandemic we learnt at home. | The Black Death was a terrible pandemic. | Washing hands helps slow down a pandemic. | Scientists made vaccines during the pandemic. | A pandemic spreads to many countries. | Grandma remembers the pandemic lockdowns.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: pandemics. Trap: «pandemic» (worldwide) vs «epidemic» (one region) vs «endemic» (always present in a place). «Pan-» means «all», as in «panorama».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A perspective is a way of thinking about or seeing something, a point of view («from my perspective»). 2) In art, perspective is a way of drawing so that things look solid and far away, with far things smaller and lines meeting at a vanishing point. 3) To keep things in perspective is to understand how important or unimportant something really is.
its sense in the lessons: In English and history lessons, pupils look at events from different perspectives, such as a soldier's and a child's. In art lessons, children draw roads and railways with one-point perspective. In everyday life, «put it into perspective» means: it's not as bad as it seems. In stories, «first-person perspective» means told by «I».
examples from the lessons: From my perspective, the rule is unfair. | Write the story from the dog's perspective. | In art, we drew a road using perspective. | The lines meet at the vanishing point. | Losing a game is sad, but keep it in perspective. | Travelling gave her a new perspective on life. | Each witness had a different perspective on the accident.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable for points of view (different perspectives), uncountable for the drawing method. Trap: «perspective» (point of view) vs «prospective» (likely, future: «prospective students»).

part of speech: adjective (piscine — formal, rare); French noun «piscine» (not English)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal, science) Piscine means to do with fish or like a fish. 2) (French) «Une piscine» means a swimming pool; it sounds like «pee-SEEN» and is a French word, not English.
its sense in the lessons: In English, «piscine» is a rare scientific or jokey word: a «piscine smell» is fishy. In French lessons, «la piscine» is the swimming pool — a false friend for English learners. Related English word: «Pisces», the fish sign in star-sign lore.
examples from the lessons: The pond had a piscine smell. | The scientist studied piscine diseases. | «Je vais à la piscine» means «I'm going to the swimming pool» in French. | In French, «piscine» is the pool, not the fish. | Pisces is the star sign with two fish. | The aquarium is a piscine paradise.
note for the reader of a maths problem: English adjective is rare and formal, pronounced «PISS-ine» or «PIE-sine». False friend: French «piscine» = swimming pool. Everyday English for «piscine» is «fishy».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A piston is a short solid cylinder that moves up and down or in and out inside a tube, pushed by pressure; it is a key part of engines and pumps. 2) (informal) «Like pistons» describes something moving fast up and down, like legs running.
its sense in the lessons: In science and D&T (design and technology) lessons, pistons show how pressure and force make movement: in car engines, burning fuel pushes pistons, which turn the wheels; in syringes and bike pumps, a piston pushes air or liquid. Children make simple hydraulic models with syringes.
examples from the lessons: The piston moves up and down inside the engine. | A bike pump has a piston inside. | Pistons turn the crankshaft in a car. | We made a moving arm with syringes as pistons. | Steam pushed the pistons of the old train. | His legs went like pistons as he raced to the finish. | A syringe is a simple piston and cylinder.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: pistons. Not to be confused with «pistol» (a gun). Pronounced «PISS-tun».

part of speech: noun (a plateau, plateaus or plateaux); verb (plateau, plateaus, plateaued, plateauing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A plateau is a large, flat area of high land, higher than the land around it. 2) A plateau is a time when something stops going up or down and stays at the same level («Her progress reached a plateau»). 3) To plateau is to stop growing or improving and stay level.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons, plateaus such as the Tibetan Plateau or the Colorado Plateau are landforms, like mountains and valleys. In maths and science, on a line graph a plateau is the flat part where the value stays the same. In sport and learning, you «hit a plateau» when you stop improving for a while.
examples from the lessons: The Tibetan Plateau is the highest in the world. | The village stands on a flat plateau above the valley. | On the graph, the line reaches a plateau after ten minutes. | My reading scores have plateaued this term. | Athletes sometimes hit a plateau in training. | The temperature rose, then plateaued at 100 °C as the water boiled. | Cows grazed on the windy plateau.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: plateaus or plateaux (French spelling). Pronounced «PLAT-oh». On a graph, a flat line means «no change» in the amount.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The Pleiades is a bright cluster of stars in the night sky, in the constellation Taurus, also called the Seven Sisters; in Japan it is called Subaru, and in New Zealand Māori call it Matariki. 2) In Greek myths, the Pleiades were seven sisters, daughters of Atlas, who were turned into stars.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on space, the Pleiades is a star cluster you can see without a telescope in winter (in the north); people with good eyes count six or seven stars. In New Zealand, Matariki (the rising of the Pleiades in midwinter) marks the Māori New Year and is a public holiday. The cluster is mentioned in the Bible (Book of Job).
examples from the lessons: We saw the Pleiades on a clear winter night. | The Pleiades look like a tiny group of stars. | The Pleiades are also called the Seven Sisters. | In New Zealand, Matariki is the Māori name for the Pleiades. | The Subaru car logo shows the Pleiades. | In the Greek myth, the Pleiades were seven sisters. | With binoculars you can see dozens of stars in the Pleiades.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A proper name: capital P, with «the». Pronounced «PLY-uh-deez». It is a star cluster, not a planet or a constellation by itself.

part of speech: noun (a pong — UK, Australia, NZ, informal; Pong — a game); verb (pong, pongs, ponged, ponging)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (UK, Australia, informal) A pong is a strong, unpleasant smell. 2) (UK, informal) To pong is to smell bad. 3) Pong is one of the first video games, a simple tennis-like game from the early days of computers. 4) «Ping-pong» is table tennis.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday British and Australian talk, «What a pong!» or «Your trainers pong!» is a jokey way to say something stinks; adjective «pongy». In history-of-computers lessons, Pong was an early arcade game with two paddles and a ball. In PE, ping-pong is another name for table tennis.
examples from the lessons: What a pong! Who left the bin open? | Your football socks pong. | The fish market had a terrible pong. | The cheese ponged out the whole fridge. | Pong was one of the first video games. | We played ping-pong at the youth club. | The changing room is a bit pongy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal, not rude, mostly UK, Australia and NZ; Americans say «stink». Regular verb: ponged. Adjective: pongy.

part of speech: noun (a portrait, portraits); adjective (portrait — page layout)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A portrait is a painting, drawing or photograph of a person, especially of the face. 2) A portrait is a detailed description of someone or something in words or film («a portrait of village life»). 3) Portrait (layout) means a page or screen that is taller than it is wide; the opposite is landscape.
its sense in the lessons: In art lessons, children paint self-portraits and study famous portraits like the Mona Lisa. In history, portraits of kings and queens show how they wanted to be seen. In computing and printing, «portrait» and «landscape» are page settings. In English, a writer can give a portrait of a character.
examples from the lessons: She painted a portrait of her grandad. | The Mona Lisa is a famous portrait. | Draw a self-portrait using a mirror. | Old portraits of kings hang in the castle. | Turn the page to portrait, not landscape. | The book gives a portrait of life in a mining town. | A photographer took our class portrait.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: portraits. Pronounced «POR-trit» or «POR-trayt». «Self-portrait» = a picture of yourself by yourself. Page layout: portrait = tall, landscape = wide.

part of speech: noun (a potter, potters); verb (potter, potters, pottered, pottering — UK, Ireland, Australia; US «putter»); proper noun (Potter — a name)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A potter is a person who makes pots, bowls and other things from clay, often on a spinning wheel, and bakes them in a kiln. 2) (UK) To potter (about or around) is to do small, pleasant, unhurried jobs or move about slowly and happily («potter in the garden»). 3) (a name) Potter is a surname, as in Beatrix Potter, the author of Peter Rabbit, and the fictional Harry Potter.
its sense in the lessons: In art lessons, children try being potters with clay and learn that clay is soft but turns hard when fired. In history, potters made the pots archaeologists find today. In everyday British talk, grandparents «potter about» at the weekend. In the Bible, God is sometimes compared to a potter shaping clay.
examples from the lessons: The potter shaped a bowl on the spinning wheel. | Potters fire their pots in a hot kiln. | Grandad likes to potter about in his shed. | We spent Sunday pottering around the house. | Beatrix Potter wrote «The Tale of Peter Rabbit». | Harry Potter is a boy wizard in a book. | The potter's wheel spins very fast.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: potters. Verb is regular: pottered. US English says «putter» for the relaxed sense. Capital P for the names; the word «potter» for clay workers is lower case.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Presidential means to do with a president, the elected leader of a country such as the USA, France or Ireland, or the head of a club or company («a presidential election»). 2) Presidential can mean looking or acting serious and important, like a president should.
its sense in the lessons: In politics lessons, «presidential elections» in the USA happen every four years; the winner lives in the White House. In Ireland, the President is head of state and is chosen in a presidential election, but the Taoiseach leads the government. In the news, «presidential candidates» debate on TV.
examples from the lessons: The USA has a presidential election every four years. | The presidential candidates debated on TV. | The presidential palace is guarded day and night. | France has a presidential system. | Ireland held a presidential election. | He looked very presidential in his suit. | The presidential plane is called Air Force One.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective from «president»; spelt «-tial». Capital P only in names like «the Presidential Medal». Trap: in the UK, Canada and Australia there is a Prime Minister, not a president.

part of speech: noun (pulp — uncountable); verb (pulp, pulps, pulped, pulping); adjective (pulp — of cheap stories)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Pulp is a soft, wet, squashed mass, such as the soft inside of a fruit or vegetable. 2) Pulp is the mush of wood or old paper mixed with water that is used to make paper. 3) To pulp something is to crush it into a soft mass. 4) The pulp of a tooth is the soft living inside, with nerves and blood. 5) «Pulp» stories or magazines are cheap, exciting, not very serious ones.
its sense in the lessons: In science and D&T lessons, children make recycled paper from paper pulp, and learn that wood pulp makes new paper. In cooking, orange juice can be «with pulp» or «smooth». In health lessons, tooth decay that reaches the pulp hurts. «Beat someone to a pulp» is a violent phrase in stories.
examples from the lessons: I like orange juice with pulp. | We made new paper from paper pulp. | Wood is turned into pulp at the paper mill. | Mash the fruit into a pulp. | The unsold books were pulped and recycled. | The dentist said the pulp of the tooth was fine. | Grandpa reads old pulp adventure stories.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable noun: «some pulp». Regular verb: pulped. Adjective «pulpy». «Pulp fiction» = cheap, exciting stories.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The quagga was a kind of zebra from South Africa with stripes only on the front half of its body and a plain brown back; it became extinct more than a hundred years ago because of hunting.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about extinction, the quagga is an example of an animal wiped out by people; the last one died in a zoo in Amsterdam. Scientists studied its DNA and found it was a type of plains zebra, and a project in South Africa is breeding zebras that look like quaggas again.
examples from the lessons: The quagga was half zebra-striped and half brown. | The last quagga died in a zoo long ago. | Hunters killed the quaggas for meat and skins. | The quagga is now extinct. | Scientists found the quagga was a kind of zebra. | Only one quagga was ever photographed alive.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: quaggas. Pronounced «KWAG-uh». It was real, not a mythical creature. «Extinct» means no living ones are left anywhere.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Reddish means a little red, or nearly red, but not completely («reddish-brown hair»).
its sense in the lessons: In science and art lessons about colour, «-ish» words describe colours that are not pure: reddish, greenish, bluish. In science, Mars is called the Red Planet for its reddish soil. In stories, a reddish sky at sunset or a reddish glow sets the scene.
examples from the lessons: Mars looks reddish in the night sky. | The leaves turned reddish in autumn. | She has reddish-brown hair. | The sky was reddish at sunset. | Rust is a reddish-brown colour. | His face went reddish when he was embarrassed. | The rock had a reddish stripe.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double d: red → reddish. «-ish» means «a bit»: reddish = a bit red; it also makes «sevenish» (about seven o'clock). Often joined with another colour: reddish-brown.

part of speech: noun (REM — abbreviation; a rem, rems — old unit)
meaning for a pupil: 1) REM stands for «rapid eye movement», a stage of sleep when your eyes move quickly under your eyelids and you have most of your dreams. 2) A rem is an old unit for measuring how much radiation a body has taken in; scientists now use the sievert. 3) «rem» is also a piece of longer words like «remember».
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about sleep and health, REM sleep comes in cycles through the night and helps the brain; children need lots of sleep. In science about radiation, the rem (and now the sievert) measures possible harm to the body. On its own «rem» is not an everyday word.
examples from the lessons: We dream most during REM sleep. | During REM sleep, your eyes move quickly. | Babies spend a lot of time in REM sleep. | A night's sleep has several REM stages. | The rem is an old unit for radiation dose. | Scientists now measure radiation dose in sieverts.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Abbreviation: write REM in capitals for the sleep stage, say «R-E-M» or «rem». In computing, REM is a comment line in old BASIC programs. Not an English word on its own in ordinary talk.

part of speech: adjective (reticulate — science, formal); verb (reticulate, reticulates, reticulated, reticulating — rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) Reticulate means having a pattern of lines crossing each other like a net, as in the veins of a leaf («reticulate venation»). 2) (rare, formal) To reticulate is to divide or mark into a network. 3) A reticulated python is a huge snake with a net-like pattern on its skin.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on plants, leaves with net-like veins (like oak or rose leaves) have reticulate venation, while grass leaves have parallel veins — a way to sort flowering plants. In zoos, the reticulated python and the reticulated giraffe are named for their net patterns.
examples from the lessons: Rose leaves have reticulate veins. | Grass has parallel veins, not reticulate ones. | Hold the leaf up to the light to see its reticulate pattern. | The reticulated python is one of the longest snakes. | The reticulated giraffe has neat net-like patches. | A fishing net is a reticulate pattern.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal, scientific word; plain English: net-like. From Latin «reticulum», a little net. Pronounced «ri-TIK-yoo-lut» (adjective) or «ri-TIK-yoo-late» (verb).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Retrieval is getting something back, finding it and bringing it back from where it was («the retrieval of the lost boat»). 2) In learning, retrieval is bringing something back into your mind from memory, like remembering a fact for a quiz. 3) In computing, retrieval is finding and getting stored information, such as files or search results.
its sense in the lessons: In school, «retrieval practice» means short quizzes that make you remember what you learnt, which helps you remember it longer. In computing, information retrieval is what search engines do. Dogs called «retrievers» were bred to fetch shot birds; «retrieve» is the verb.
examples from the lessons: Retrieval of the sunken ship took weeks. | We do retrieval practice every Monday. | Quizzes help with retrieval of facts. | The search engine is good at information retrieval. | The divers worked on the retrieval of the lost diamonds. | Retrieval of old files can take a long time. | Golden retrievers love the retrieval of balls.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «retrieval of something». Verb: retrieve (i before e). Trap: spelt «-ieval», not «-eival».

part of speech: noun (a robocall, robocalls); verb (robocall, robocalls, robocalled, robocalling — informal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A robocall is an automatic phone call made by a computer, which plays a recorded message to many people at once, often to sell something, give information or trick people. 2) To robocall is to make such calls.
its sense in the lessons: In online and phone safety lessons, robocalls can be scams: if a recorded voice says you owe money, a parcel is waiting or your account is locked, hang up, do not press any number, and tell an adult. Some robocalls are useful, such as school closure messages or appointment reminders. The word is common in the USA and Canada.
examples from the lessons: We got another robocall about a car warranty. | The school sent a robocall saying it was closed for snow. | If a robocall asks for money, hang up. | Never press a number on a scam robocall. | Robocalls use a recorded voice, not a real person. | Politicians sometimes use robocalls before elections. | Grandma gets so many robocalls she stopped answering.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: robocalls. Informal, mostly US and Canada; in the UK people often say «automated call» or «nuisance call». Safety rule: never give personal details to a robocall.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A rudder is a flat, upright blade at the back of a boat or ship that is turned to steer it left or right. 2) On an aeroplane, the rudder is a movable flap on the upright part of the tail that helps turn the nose left or right. 3) (figurative) Something that guides or keeps a person or plan on course is sometimes called a rudder.
its sense in the lessons: In science and design lessons the rudder shows how a small surface pushing against water or air can change the direction of a big vehicle. In stories about sailing, pirates or storms, a broken rudder means the boat cannot be steered and is in danger. Phrases: «turn the rudder», «take the rudder», «without a rudder» (with no direction in life).
examples from the lessons: The sailor pushed the rudder to turn the boat towards the harbour. | A storm snapped the rudder, so the little ship drifted helplessly. | In our design challenge, we added a cardboard rudder to the paper boat. | The pilot used the pedals to move the plane's rudder. | Fish use their tails a bit like a rudder. | After his gran died, he felt like a boat without a rudder. | We tested whether a bigger rudder made the toy boat turn faster.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: one rudder, two rudders. Do not confuse with «udder» (the part of a cow that gives milk) or «ruder» (more rude). The rudder steers; the sail or engine moves the boat forward; oars row it.

part of speech: noun, proper (Sagittarius); adjective use (a Sagittarius child)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Sagittarius is a group of stars (a constellation) in the southern part of the night sky, often pictured as an archer who is half man and half horse. 2) In astrology, Sagittarius is one of the twelve star signs; people say someone born in late November to late December «is a Sagittarius». 3) Sagittarius A* is the name astronomers give to the giant black hole at the centre of our galaxy, which lies in the direction of this constellation.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons Sagittarius matters because the centre of the Milky Way lies in that direction, so the sky there is thick with stars. In everyday life the word mostly turns up in horoscopes in magazines. Scientists say star signs cannot predict anyone's personality or future; astronomy is science, astrology is not. Phrases: «the constellation Sagittarius», «a Sagittarius», «the Archer».
examples from the lessons: On a clear night far from the city, Dad pointed to Sagittarius low in the sky. | Sagittarius is drawn as an archer with a bow and arrow. | My cousin says she's a Sagittarius because her birthday is in December. | The middle of our galaxy lies in the direction of Sagittarius. | Astronomers photographed the black hole called Sagittarius A*. | In Australia and New Zealand, Sagittarius rides high overhead in winter. | Our teacher said horoscopes for Sagittarius are just for fun, not science.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always written with a capital S. Spelled with double «tt» and ending «-ius». The «g» sounds like «j» (sa-ji-TAIR-ee-us). Myth trap: star signs do not shape who you are; that is astrology, not astronomy. The Archer is a centaur, a creature from Greek myths.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Scarlet is a bright, strong red colour, a little bit orange. 2) Something scarlet is coloured this bright red, like a fire engine or a ripe strawberry. 3) If someone turns scarlet, their face goes very red because they are embarrassed, angry or out of breath. 4) In names of illnesses and creatures, «scarlet» describes a red rash or colour, as in «scarlet fever» or «scarlet macaw».
its sense in the lessons: In art lessons scarlet is one shade of red on the colour wheel. In stories it paints a strong picture: a scarlet cloak, scarlet cheeks of shame, scarlet poppies for remembrance. In health lessons «scarlet fever» is a bacterial illness that gives a rash and sore throat, treated with medicine. Phrases: «turn scarlet», «go scarlet», «scarlet fever», «scarlet with rage».
examples from the lessons: She wore a scarlet coat in the snow. | The robin has a scarlet-orange breast. | When the teacher read out his love poem, Jack went scarlet. | Poppies make the fields scarlet in summer. | Scarlet fever is treated with antibiotics from the doctor. | The scarlet macaw squawked from its perch. | Mix red with a tiny bit of yellow to get scarlet. | Her face was scarlet after running the cross-country race.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Scarlet is usually an adjective (a scarlet dress) but can be a noun for the colour (dressed in scarlet). It has no plural in normal use. «Scarlett» with two t's is a girl's name. Compare: crimson (deep red), scarlet (bright red), maroon (brownish red).

part of speech: verb (past participle of «shear»: shear, shears, sheared, shorn, shearing); adjective (shorn)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Shorn means having had the wool or hair cut off, usually with big scissors or electric clippers, as in «shorn sheep». 2) Shorn of something means having had it taken away, as in «shorn of his power». 3) (adjective) Shorn hair is cut very short.
its sense in the lessons: In farming and geography lessons about Australia, New Zealand and the UK, sheep are shorn each year so their wool can be used for clothes. In stories «shorn» can show a big change, like a hero with shorn hair or a king shorn of his crown. It is a slightly old or formal word; everyday talk often says «sheared» or «had their hair cut».
examples from the lessons: The sheep were shorn in spring, and the wool was piled high. | The freshly shorn lambs looked tiny without their fleece. | In New Zealand, the shearers had shorn hundreds of sheep by lunchtime. | His head was shorn for the charity challenge. | The castle, shorn of its walls, stood open to the wind. | Shorn wool is washed before it is spun. | Have the alpacas been shorn yet?
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Shorn» is the past participle: «they have shorn», «the sheep were shorn». The simple past is usually «sheared» (they sheared the sheep). Homophone trap: «shorn» sounds like «shawn» in many accents but is not related to «shore» or «shone».

part of speech: noun (a shuttle, shuttles); verb (shuttle, shuttles, shuttled, shuttling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A shuttle is a bus, train or plane that goes back and forth often between two places, like an airport and a car park. 2) A space shuttle was a spacecraft that could fly into space and land back on Earth like a plane, so it could be used again. 3) In badminton, a shuttle (shuttlecock) is the feathered object you hit over the net. 4) In weaving, a shuttle is the tool that carries the thread across the loom. 5) (verb) To shuttle means to go or carry people back and forth between places many times.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons «the space shuttle» comes up in the story of space travel. In PE, badminton uses a shuttle. In everyday life, families take shuttle buses at airports and theme parks. In stories, «shuttling between» shows someone rushing about, for example a child whose parents live apart. Phrases: «shuttle bus», «space shuttle», «shuttle between», «shuttle diplomacy».
examples from the lessons: We caught the shuttle bus from the car park to the airport. | The space shuttle landed on a long runway. | I hit the shuttle so high it touched the gym ceiling. | Mum shuttled us between football and swimming all Saturday. | The free shuttle runs every ten minutes. | On the loom, the shuttle flew from side to side. | My brother shuttles between Mum's house and Dad's house every weekend.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun; as a verb it is regular (shuttled, shuttling). «Shuttlecock» is the full name in badminton; «birdie» is common in North America. A shuttle goes back and forth on the same route, unlike a normal bus that has a long route.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A souslik is a small ground squirrel that lives in burrows on the grassy plains (steppes) of Eastern Europe and Central Asia, including Ukraine. 2) It is also spelled «suslik»; the word comes from Russian.
its sense in the lessons: In nature lessons about grasslands, the souslik shows how small animals survive by digging burrows, standing up on their back legs to look out for hawks and foxes, and sleeping through the cold winter (hibernating). In stories set on the steppe, a souslik popping up from its hole is a typical scene.
examples from the lessons: A souslik stood up on its back legs and whistled a warning. | Sousliks dig long tunnels under the grass. | In winter the souslik hibernates deep underground. | Eagles hunt sousliks on the open steppe. | The souslik stuffed seeds into its cheek pouches. | We saw a photo of a souslik in our book about Ukraine's wildlife.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: one souslik, two sousliks. Also spelled «suslik». It is a kind of ground squirrel, related to prairie dogs and chipmunks, not a rat or a mouse. A rare word in English; most English speakers say «ground squirrel».

part of speech: verb (splice, splices, spliced, splicing); noun (a splice, splices)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To splice two ropes or wires means to join their ends together firmly, often by weaving the strands into each other. 2) To splice film, tape or video means to join two pieces so they play one after the other. 3) In science, to splice genes means to cut and join pieces of DNA. 4) (noun) A splice is the place where two things have been joined. 5) (UK, informal) «Get spliced» means to get married.
its sense in the lessons: In science, «gene splicing» is part of how scientists change living things. In sailing and scouting, splicing rope is a useful skill. In film-making lessons, clips are spliced together to make a story. Phrases: «splice together», «splice in», «gene splicing», «get spliced» (old slang for marry).
examples from the lessons: The sailor spliced the two ropes so they would not slip apart. | We spliced our video clips together to make the class film. | The electrician spliced the broken wires. | Scientists can splice a gene from one plant into another. | You can hardly see the splice in the rope. | Grandad joked that he and Gran got spliced fifty years ago. | The editor spliced in a funny clip at the end.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: spliced, splicing (drop the «e» before «-ing»). «Splice» joins things; do not confuse it with «slice», which cuts them apart. «Get spliced» is jokey, old-fashioned talk.

part of speech: noun (a spotlight, spotlights; the spotlight); verb (spotlight, spotlights, spotlighted or spotlit, spotlighting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A spotlight is a strong lamp that shines a narrow, bright beam onto one person or area, especially on a stage. 2) «In the spotlight» means getting a lot of attention from people or the news. 3) (verb) To spotlight something means to shine a light on it or to draw special attention to it.
its sense in the lessons: In drama and the school play, the spotlight shows the audience where to look. In science, a spotlight is an example of light travelling in straight lines and making a bright circle. In everyday life and the news, someone «in the spotlight» is being watched and talked about, which can feel exciting or stressful. Phrases: «in the spotlight», «steal the spotlight», «shine the spotlight on», «out of the spotlight».
examples from the lessons: The spotlight followed Mia as she sang her solo. | The caretaker fixed the broken spotlight in the hall. | After winning the spelling bee, Sam was in the spotlight all week. | The dog ran onto the stage and stole the spotlight. | Our assembly spotlighted pupils who help others. | The famous singer wanted a quiet life out of the spotlight. | We used a torch as a spotlight for our shadow puppets.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: a spotlight, two spotlights; «the spotlight» for public attention. Past of the verb: «spotlighted» or «spotlit». It is one word, not «spot light».

part of speech: noun (Sucre, a city; a sucre, sucres — old money); word (French)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Sucre is the constitutional capital city of Bolivia, in South America. 2) The sucre was the money of Ecuador until it was replaced by the US dollar. 3) (French) «Sucre» is the French word for sugar; it sounds like «SOO-kruh» to an English ear and is not an English word.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons Sucre is useful because Bolivia has two capitals: Sucre is the official one, while the government mostly works in La Paz. In French lessons and on French food packets, «sucre» means sugar, as in «sans sucre» (without sugar). Phrases: «sans sucre», «sucre glace» (icing sugar).
examples from the lessons: Sucre is the official capital of Bolivia. | Many buildings in Sucre are painted white. | The government of Bolivia sits mostly in La Paz, not Sucre. | On the French yoghurt pot it said «sans sucre», which means no sugar. | In French class we learned that «sucre» means sugar. | Ecuador once used money called the sucre.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a city, always a capital S: Sucre. The French word «sucre» is masculine: «le sucre». Do not use it as an English word for sugar. Pronounced in French roughly «SOO-kruh»; the Spanish city name sounds like «SOO-kray».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A superfood is a food that people say is extra healthy because it has lots of vitamins, minerals or other good things in it, like blueberries, kale or salmon. 2) It is mostly a word used in adverts and magazines, not a scientific term.
its sense in the lessons: In health and food lessons, the word helps pupils learn that many fruits, vegetables, nuts and fish are very good for you, but no single food can keep you healthy on its own; a balanced diet matters most. In media lessons it is a good example of marketing words that make food sound magical so it sells for more. Phrases: «so-called superfood», «superfood smoothie».
examples from the lessons: Mum says blueberries are a superfood. | The café sells a green superfood smoothie. | Our teacher said there's no magic superfood; you need a mix of foods. | Kale was called a superfood in the magazine. | The advert claimed the seeds were a superfood that would make you clever. | Salmon is often called a superfood because of its healthy oils. | We made posters about real healthy eating, not just superfoods.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: one superfood, many superfoods. Myth trap: calling something a superfood does not prove it is better than ordinary vegetables; it is a selling word. Written as one word.

part of speech: noun (a tab, tabs); verb (tab, tabs, tabbed, tabbing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A tab is a small flap or strip sticking out of something, used for pulling, holding or labelling it, like the tab on a can or a folder. 2) On a computer, a tab is one of the pages open in a web browser, shown as a little label along the top. 3) The Tab key on a keyboard moves the cursor forward to the next space or box. 4) (informal) A tab is a bill for food or drinks that you pay later, as in «put it on my tab». 5) «Keep tabs on» someone means to watch them carefully to know what they are doing. 6) (UK, slang) A tab can mean a cigarette in some parts of England.
its sense in the lessons: In computing lessons, pupils open and close browser tabs and use the Tab key to move between boxes in a form. In everyday life, tabs are on drink cans, files and clothes labels. In stories, «keep tabs on» shows someone watching or checking on another person. Phrases: «open a new tab», «close the tab», «keep tabs on», «pick up the tab» (pay the bill), «ring-pull tab».
examples from the lessons: I had twelve tabs open, and the computer slowed down. | Press Tab to jump to the next box. | Pull the tab to open the can. | Our teacher keeps tabs on who has finished their reading. | Grandad picked up the tab for the whole family's dinner. | Each folder has a coloured tab with a name on it. | Close that tab and go back to the maths website. | The coat had a little tab for hanging it on a hook.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun. Verb forms double the b: tabbed, tabbing. «Pick up the tab» means pay for everyone, not lift a flap. «Tab» as a cigarette is regional British slang. In maths and data, «tab-separated» means split by tab spaces.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A tendril is a thin, curly, thread-like part of a climbing plant that wraps around things to help the plant climb, as on peas, grapes and cucumbers. 2) A tendril can be a thin curl of something that looks like that, such as a tendril of hair or a tendril of smoke.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about plants, tendrils show how climbing plants respond to touch and grow towards support so they can reach the light. In stories, «tendrils» of mist, smoke or hair paint a soft, curling picture, and «tendrils of fear» means fear slowly creeping in. Phrases: «tendrils of», «curling tendrils».
examples from the lessons: The pea plant's tendrils curled around the stick. | Grapevines climb using tendrils. | A tendril of hair escaped from her ponytail. | Tendrils of smoke rose from the campfire. | We watched a cucumber tendril wrap around the string over a week. | Tendrils of fog crept across the playing field. | In the spooky story, tendrils of ivy covered the old door.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: one tendril, many tendrils. A tendril is not the same as a root or a branch; it is a special thin part used for gripping. Spelled with one l at the end.

part of speech: noun (terracotta, uncountable; also terra cotta); adjective (terracotta)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Terracotta is a reddish-brown clay that has been baked hard, used for flowerpots, roof tiles and statues. 2) (adjective) Terracotta describes the orange-brown colour of this clay. 3) The Terracotta Army is a huge group of clay soldier statues buried with an ancient emperor in China.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons the Terracotta Army in China and Roman terracotta pots show how people long ago made things from baked clay. In art and DT, pupils may make terracotta models. In gardening, terracotta pots are common because they let air and water through. Phrases: «terracotta pot», «terracotta tiles», «the Terracotta Army».
examples from the lessons: We planted tomatoes in a terracotta pot. | The Terracotta Army has thousands of life-sized soldiers. | The roof was covered with terracotta tiles. | Her bedroom walls are painted terracotta. | Terracotta comes from Italian words meaning «baked earth». | In art we shaped a little terracotta owl. | Terracotta pots can crack if they freeze in winter.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable as a material (made of terracotta). Spelled as one word (terracotta) or two (terra cotta). It is a kind of pottery, not a kind of stone.

part of speech: noun (a triton, tritons; Triton, a name)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Triton is a sea god in the myths of ancient Greece, half man and half fish, who blows a conch shell like a trumpet. 2) Triton is the largest moon of the planet Neptune; it is icy and very cold. 3) A triton is also a large sea snail with a long, pointed shell (triton shell). 4) (Europe) In some books, «triton» is used for a kind of newt.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about the solar system, Triton is Neptune's big moon and is unusual because it goes round the planet backwards. In myths and stories, Triton is the son of Poseidon and calms or stirs the sea with his shell. In some cartoons, Triton is the name of a sea king. Phrases: «Triton, moon of Neptune», «triton shell».
examples from the lessons: Triton is the biggest moon of Neptune. | In the Greek myth, Triton blew his shell to calm the waves. | The space probe took photos of Triton's icy surface. | The museum had a huge triton shell. | Triton orbits Neptune in the opposite direction to the planet's spin. | Our fountain has a statue of Triton holding a conch. | Triton is so cold that nitrogen freezes on it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital T for the moon and the god; small t for the shell. Do not confuse with «titan» or Saturn's moon Titan. Pronounced «TRY-tun».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A tun is a very large barrel or cask, used in the past for wine, beer or water. 2) A tun was also an old unit for measuring how much liquid fits in such a barrel, a big amount. 3) It is a rare, old word; do not mix it up with «ton», «tonne» or «tune».
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons about ships and old trade, wine was carried in tuns, and the size of ships was once measured by how many tuns they could carry, which is where the word «tonnage» comes from. In stories set long ago, cellars and taverns may have tuns. It is not used in everyday modern speech.
examples from the lessons: The ship's cellar held a tun of wine. | A tun is much bigger than an ordinary barrel. | The old brewery had wooden tuns taller than a man. | Sailors filled a tun with fresh water before the voyage. | The word «ton» comes from the old word «tun». | In the story, the boy hid inside an empty tun.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: a tun, two tuns. Homophone traps: «ton» and «tonne» (weights) can sound the same; «tune» is music. Rare in modern English. In maths it is not a unit pupils use today.

part of speech: noun (ultrasound, uncountable; an ultrasound, ultrasounds — a scan)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Ultrasound is sound that is too high-pitched for humans to hear, but some animals like bats and dogs can hear it. 2) An ultrasound (scan) is a medical test that uses these sound waves to make a picture of the inside of the body, often used to look at a baby before it is born. 3) Ultrasound is also used in cleaning machines and in some medical treatments.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons ultrasound shows that sound is a vibration and that some sounds are beyond our hearing range; bats and dolphins use echoes of high sounds to find their way (echolocation). In everyday family life, a parent might show a grainy ultrasound picture of a new baby. It is safe and does not use X-rays. Phrases: «ultrasound scan», «have an ultrasound», «ultrasound picture».
examples from the lessons: Mum showed us the ultrasound of our baby sister. | Bats use ultrasound to find insects in the dark. | The doctor used ultrasound to look at Dad's sore knee. | We can't hear ultrasound, but a dog whistle shows dogs can. | The ultrasound picture looked like a fuzzy black-and-white blob. | Dolphins send out ultrasound clicks and listen for the echoes. | Ultrasound waves bounce back from things inside the body.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable for the sound itself; countable for a scan (an ultrasound, two ultrasounds). «Ultra-» means beyond: beyond the sounds we hear. Compare «infrasound», which is too low to hear. An ultrasound is not an X-ray.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unemployment is when people who want a job and can work cannot find one. 2) Unemployment is also the number or share of people in a country who have no job but are looking for one. 3) (US, Canada) «Unemployment» can mean money from the government for people who lost their job, as in «he's on unemployment».
its sense in the lessons: In citizenship, money and history lessons, unemployment shows how jobs affect families and countries; when many factories close, unemployment goes up. News reports give unemployment as a percentage. In family stories, a parent's unemployment can bring worry about money and changes at home, and children can help by being kind and patient. Phrases: «unemployment rate», «high unemployment», «unemployment benefit», «on unemployment».
examples from the lessons: Unemployment went up when the steelworks closed. | The unemployment rate fell to four per cent. | Dad was out of work for months, and unemployment made things tight at home. | The government helps people during unemployment with benefits. | In the old story, unemployment meant long queues for food. | Training new skills can help people out of unemployment. | The news said unemployment is lower in the south.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: say «unemployment is high», not «unemployments». «Unemployed» is the adjective (an unemployed worker). In maths, the unemployment rate = the number of unemployed people divided by everyone who could work, times 100, as a percentage. People who are retired or at school are not counted as unemployed.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An uprising is when a large group of people fight or protest together against the people in power, such as a government or ruler. 2) It is a kind of rebellion or revolt, often sudden and sometimes violent.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, uprisings show how ordinary people have pushed back against unfair rule, for example the Peasants' Revolt in England or uprisings against empires. In the news, an uprising may be described differently by each side: supporters call it a fight for freedom, rulers may call it a riot. Phrases: «an uprising against», «crush an uprising», «a popular uprising».
examples from the lessons: The peasants led an uprising against the unfair tax. | Soldiers were sent to crush the uprising. | The uprising began in the capital and spread across the country. | We read about the slaves' uprising in our history book. | Historians still argue about why the uprising failed. | A popular uprising forced the king to leave. | The film tells the story of an uprising in an occupied city.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: an uprising (starts with a vowel sound, so «an»). Similar words: rebellion, revolt, revolution (an uprising that succeeds in changing the government). Do not confuse with «up rising» (going up).

meaning for a pupil: 1) To widen something means to make it wider, like widening a road or a path. 2) To widen means to become wider, as in «the river widens near the sea». 3) To widen can mean to make something bigger in range, as in «widen your vocabulary» or «widen the search». 4) If eyes widen, they open more because of surprise or fear.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and DT, widening a shape changes its width, which changes its area. In geography, rivers widen as they get closer to the sea. In stories, «her eyes widened» shows surprise or fear. In everyday life, roads are widened to fit more cars. Phrases: «widen the gap», «widen the search», «eyes widened», «widen your horizons».
examples from the lessons: They are widening the road outside our school. | The river widens as it reaches the sea. | His eyes widened when he saw the birthday cake. | Reading lots of books widens your vocabulary. | The police widened the search for the lost dog. | The gap between the two teams widened in the second half. | If we widen the rectangle, its area gets bigger.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: widened, widening. «Widen» comes from «wide» + «-en», like «shorten», «brighten». Opposite: narrow. In maths, widening a rectangle while keeping its length increases the area.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A wiper (windscreen wiper, windshield wiper in the US) is a long arm with a rubber blade that moves back and forth to clear rain from a car's front window. 2) A wiper is anything used for wiping, like a cloth or wipe.
its sense in the lessons: In science and DT lessons, wipers are an example of a machine with simple back-and-forth motion. In everyday life and safety, working wipers help drivers see clearly in rain and snow. In stories, the swish of wipers sets a rainy, sleepy mood on a car journey. Phrases: «windscreen wipers», «turn on the wipers», «wiper blades».
examples from the lessons: Dad turned on the wipers when it started to pour. | The wipers squeaked across the glass. | The wiper blade was worn and left streaks. | In the US they say windshield wipers. | I fell asleep listening to the wipers go swish, swish. | The car failed its check because one wiper was broken. | Someone tucked a leaflet under the wiper.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun. UK, Ireland, Australia, New Zealand: «windscreen wiper»; US and Canada: «windshield wiper». A «wiper» is not a «wipe» (a single damp cloth).

meaning for a pupil: 1) To adhere means to stick firmly to something, like glue or a sticker on a surface. 2) (formal) To adhere to a rule, plan or belief means to follow it or keep to it carefully. 3) (formal) To adhere to a group or idea can mean to support it loyally.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, «adhere» describes how glue, tape and paint stick to materials, and «adhesive» is the name for sticky stuff. In the stiff exam or rules voice, «pupils must adhere to the uniform policy» means pupils must follow it. Phrases: «adhere to», «adhere strictly to».
examples from the lessons: The sticker would not adhere to the wet window. | Paint adheres better if the wall is clean. | All players must adhere to the rules of the game. | Our family adheres to a strict bedtime on school nights. | The glue helps the paper adhere to the card. | The school adheres to safety guidelines on trips. | Christians who adhere to the old ways keep Sunday as a day of rest.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: adhered, adhering. Usually followed by «to». It is a formal word; in everyday talk say «stick to» or «follow». Related words: adhesive (sticky stuff), adherent (a follower).

part of speech: adjective (alleged); verb (past of «allege»: allege, alleges, alleged, alleging)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Alleged means said to be true, or said to have happened, but not yet proven. 2) (law, news) An alleged crime or alleged thief is one that someone has accused, but a court has not yet decided. 3) (verb) If someone alleged something, they claimed it was true without proving it.
its sense in the lessons: In news and media lessons, «alleged» is an important word: reporters use it to be fair because a person is innocent until proven guilty. In stories and playground arguments, an «alleged» thing is just a claim. Phrases: «the alleged attack», «allegedly», «it is alleged that».
examples from the lessons: The newspaper wrote about the alleged robbery. | The alleged thief has not been found guilty yet. | My brother alleged that I ate his chocolate, but he had no proof. | The man denied the alleged crime in court. | It is alleged that the money went missing on Friday. | The so-called alleged monster in the lake has never been photographed clearly. | Reporters say «alleged» until a judge decides.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced «a-LEJD», two syllables. Spelled with «-ged», not «-dged». Adverb: «allegedly». Trap: «alleged» does not mean false; it means not yet proven either way.

part of speech: noun (an ambush, ambushes); verb (ambush, ambushes, ambushed, ambushing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) An ambush is a surprise attack by people or animals who have been hiding and waiting. 2) (verb) To ambush someone means to hide and then attack them by surprise. 3) (informal) To ambush someone can mean to surprise them with difficult questions or a sudden request.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, ambushes appear in stories of battles and wars. In nature lessons, ambush hunters like crocodiles and spiders wait still and then strike.
