In stories and games, an ambush makes a tense, exciting moment. In everyday talk, «Mum ambushed me with questions about homework» is a jokey use. Phrases: «lie in ambush», «walk into an ambush», «set an ambush».
examples from the lessons: The soldiers walked straight into an ambush. | The crocodile is an ambush hunter that waits in the water. | My little sisters ambushed me with water pistols. | The robbers lay in ambush beside the road. | The journalist ambushed the minister with a tricky question. | In the game, we set an ambush behind the castle wall. | The spider ambushed the fly from under a leaf.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural noun: ambushes. Regular verb: ambushed, ambushing. «An ambush» uses «an» because it starts with a vowel sound. An ambush is always a surprise; an open attack is not an ambush.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An architect is a person whose job is to design buildings and draw plans for how they should be built. 2) The architect of something is the person who planned it or made it happen, as in «the architect of the peace deal».
its sense in the lessons: In maths, art and DT lessons, architects use shapes, measuring, scale drawings and angles. In jobs lessons, being an architect needs creativity, maths and a lot of training. In history, famous buildings are linked to their architects. Phrases: «the architect of», «landscape architect», «trained architect».
examples from the lessons: The architect drew plans for our new school library. | An architect needs to be good at maths and drawing. | She wants to be an architect when she grows up. | The architect made a model of the bridge first. | He was the architect of the team's surprise win. | Landscape architects design parks and gardens. | We visited a museum designed by a famous architect.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: an architect (vowel sound, so «an»). Pronounced «AR-ki-tekt»; the «ch» sounds like «k». Related: architecture (the art of designing buildings), architectural. An architect designs; builders build.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Arid land or weather is very dry, with very little rain, so few plants can grow. 2) (figurative) Something arid can be dull and boring, with no life or interest in it.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and science lessons, arid areas like deserts get very little rain, and plants and animals there have special ways to save water, like cacti storing water and camels going long without drinking. Large parts of Australia are arid. Phrases: «arid region», «arid climate», «semi-arid».
examples from the lessons: The camel is well suited to arid deserts. | Much of central Australia is hot and arid. | Arid land is hard to farm without watering it. | Cactuses grow well in arid climates. | The arid soil cracked in the heat. | The lecture was so arid that half the class fell asleep. | A semi-arid area gets a little more rain than a desert.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective, usually «more arid». Noun: aridity. Opposite: wet, humid, damp. Pronounced «AR-id» (rhymes with «parrot» in many accents, roughly). «Arid» is about lack of water, not heat; a cold place can also be arid, like Antarctica.

part of speech: noun (asylum, uncountable — protection; an asylum, asylums — an old kind of hospital)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Asylum is safety and protection that a country gives to people who have run away from danger, war or unfair punishment in their own country. 2) Someone «seeking asylum» is asking another country to let them stay safely; they are called an asylum seeker. 3) (old-fashioned) An asylum was a large old hospital for people with serious mental illness; this word is not used for hospitals today.
its sense in the lessons: In citizenship and current-affairs lessons, asylum is about refugees and human rights: countries have agreed that people in real danger may ask for protection. In history lessons, old asylums show how badly mentally ill people were sometimes treated in the past. In stories, a spooky old asylum is a common but unkind cliché. Phrases: «seek asylum», «claim asylum», «grant asylum», «asylum seeker».
examples from the lessons: The family fled the war and asked for asylum in Canada. | The country granted her asylum because her life was in danger. | Asylum seekers wait for a decision on whether they can stay. | Our school welcomed a boy whose family had been given asylum. | In the past, people with mental illness were sometimes locked in asylums. | He sought asylum at an embassy. | Asking for asylum is a legal right under international law.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable for protection (give asylum, not «an asylum»). Countable for the old hospital. An asylum seeker is someone asking for protection; a refugee is someone recognised as needing it. Calling a hospital «an asylum» today is outdated and can be hurtful.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Austrian means from or connected with Austria, a country in central Europe with mountains called the Alps. 2) (noun) An Austrian is a person from Austria.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons, Austria is a landlocked country whose capital is Vienna and whose main language is German. In music lessons, Mozart is a famous Austrian composer. In stories and films, «The Sound of Music» is set in Austria. Phrases: «the Austrian Alps», «Austrian German», «an Austrian».
examples from the lessons: Mozart was an Austrian composer. | We went skiing in the Austrian Alps. | Austrians mostly speak German. | Vienna is the Austrian capital. | My friend's mum is Austrian and makes amazing apple strudel. | The Austrian flag is red, white and red. | An Austrian team won the ski race.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always capital A. Do not confuse Austrian (from Austria, in Europe) with Australian (from Australia). Austrian people speak German, not «Austrian» as a separate language.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An aviary is a large cage, building or enclosed space where birds are kept, big enough for them to fly about. 2) Zoos and bird parks often have walk-through aviaries where visitors can walk among the birds.
its sense in the lessons: In science and nature lessons about birds, an aviary is where people keep and care for birds, sometimes to help rare birds breed. In everyday life, some families or neighbours have a small aviary for budgies or finches. Phrases: «walk-through aviary», «garden aviary».
examples from the lessons: The zoo has a huge aviary full of parrots. | We walked through the aviary while birds flew over our heads. | Grandpa built an aviary for his budgies in the back garden. | The rare kakapo chicks were raised in an aviary. | The aviary netting stops the birds from escaping. | Feeding time at the aviary was noisy and colourful.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: aviaries (y changes to ies). Starts with a vowel sound, so «an aviary». Related: aviation (flying) comes from the same Latin word for bird, «avis». An aviary is for birds; an aquarium is for fish.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) Awesome means very good, great or cool, as in «That film was awesome!». 2) Awesome means so big, powerful or amazing that it fills you with wonder and a little fear, as in «the awesome power of the ocean». 3) (slang) «Awesome!» can be said on its own to mean «great!» or «OK, good».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday speech in the USA, Canada, Australia and the UK, children use «awesome» all the time to praise things. In stories and science writing, the older meaning, full of awe, is used for storms, mountains or space. In writing lessons teachers may ask pupils to choose a stronger, more exact word than «awesome». Phrases: «totally awesome», «awesome!», «that's awesome».
examples from the lessons: That roller coaster was awesome! | «I got the tickets.» «Awesome!» | Standing under the waterfall, we felt its awesome power. | My teacher is awesome at explaining fractions. | The view from the mountain top was awesome. | You did an awesome job on your project. | The awesome size of the blue whale left us speechless.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelled «awesome», with «e» after «aw». In formal writing, prefer «impressive» or «excellent». Related: awe (a feeling of wonder), awful (once meant full of awe, now means very bad). Comparison is usually «more awesome».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Belgian means from or connected with Belgium, a small country in western Europe. 2) (noun) A Belgian is a person from Belgium.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons, Belgium's capital is Brussels, and people there speak Dutch (Flemish), French or German. In food lessons, Belgian chocolate, waffles and chips are famous. In history, Belgium was a battleground in the World Wars. Phrases: «Belgian waffles», «Belgian chocolate», «the Belgian coast».
examples from the lessons: We bought a box of Belgian chocolates. | Belgian waffles are crispy with deep squares. | My penfriend is Belgian and speaks French and Dutch. | Tintin was created by a Belgian artist. | The Belgian team played well in the match. | Brussels, the Belgian capital, hosts many European offices.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always capital B. Pronounced «BEL-jun». There is no «Belgian language»; Belgians speak Dutch, French or German.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A bough is a large, main branch of a tree. 2) It is a slightly old-fashioned or poetic word; in everyday talk people usually say «branch».
its sense in the lessons: In stories, poems, songs and nursery rhymes, boughs appear often, as in «Rock-a-bye Baby» where «the bough breaks». In science lessons, boughs are the big branches growing out of the trunk. Phrases: «the bough breaks», «boughs of holly», «under the boughs».
examples from the lessons: The children sat in the shade under the boughs of the oak. | When the bough breaks, the cradle will fall. | Snow weighed down the boughs of the pine trees. | «Deck the halls with boughs of holly» is a Christmas carol. | A heavy bough fell in the storm and blocked the lane. | Birds built a nest on the highest bough.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: a bough, boughs. Pronounced «BOW» to rhyme with «cow» and «now». Homophone trap: «bow» (bend at the waist) sounds the same, but «bow» (for arrows, or a ribbon) rhymes with «go». Do not confuse with «bought» or «cough», which have the same letters «ough» but different sounds.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A bustard is a large, heavy bird with long legs that walks on grasslands and open plains; it can fly, but prefers to run. 2) The great bustard is one of the heaviest flying birds in the world.
its sense in the lessons: In nature lessons, bustards show birds that live on dry grasslands in Europe, Africa, Asia and Australia (the Australian bustard). In conservation lessons, the great bustard was wiped out in Britain and is being brought back on Salisbury Plain. Phrases: «great bustard», «Australian bustard».
examples from the lessons: The great bustard is one of the heaviest birds that can fly. | A bustard strutted across the dry grassland. | Scientists are bringing bustards back to England. | The Australian bustard can stand very still to hide. | The male bustard puffs out its feathers to show off. | We saw a bustard on our trip to the outback.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: one bustard, many bustards. Careful with spelling: it is «bustard», and it is a bird; do not mix it up with similar-sounding rude words.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A cataract is a cloudy patch in the lens of the eye that makes things look blurry; it is common in older people and can be fixed by an operation. 2) A cataract is also a large, powerful waterfall or a stretch of rough, rushing water in a river, like the cataracts of the River Nile.
its sense in the lessons: In science and health lessons, cataracts explain how the clear lens of the eye helps us see, and how doctors can replace a cloudy lens with a plastic one. In geography and history, the cataracts of the Nile were rocky rapids that boats in ancient Egypt could not easily pass. In family life, a grandparent may «have a cataract operation». Phrases: «cataract operation», «cataract surgery», «the Nile cataracts».
examples from the lessons: Grandma had a cataract operation and can see clearly again. | Cataracts make things look foggy. | The doctor said Grandad has a cataract in his left eye. | The boat could not sail past the cataract on the Nile. | The cataract roared as the river fell over the rocks. | Dogs can get cataracts too. | After the cataract was removed, colours looked brighter.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: a cataract, cataracts. It is not a skin on the eye; it is clouding inside the lens. Pronounced «KAT-a-rakt».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (medicine) Cervical means to do with the neck, as in «cervical vertebrae», the bones in your neck. 2) (medicine) Cervical also means to do with the cervix, the narrow opening of a woman's womb (uterus), as in a «cervical screening» test.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about the skeleton, the cervical vertebrae are the seven bones of the neck; almost all mammals, even giraffes, have seven. In health lessons and adult life, cervical screening is a check that women are invited to have to help stop cancer early, and there is a vaccine (HPV) that helps protect against cervical cancer. Phrases: «cervical spine», «cervical collar», «cervical screening».
examples from the lessons: The neck has seven cervical vertebrae. | A giraffe has the same number of cervical bones as a mouse. | After the car crash, he wore a cervical collar to protect his neck. | Mum went for her cervical screening test at the doctor's. | The HPV vaccine helps prevent cervical cancer. | The X-ray showed his cervical spine was fine.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective only. Pronounced «SER-vi-kul» (UK also «ser-VY-kul»). It is a medical word; in everyday talk say «neck». Do not confuse with «circle» or «surgical».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Cholera is a serious illness caused by germs (bacteria) in dirty water or food, which gives very bad diarrhoea and makes the body lose water quickly. 2) Without treatment cholera can kill, but drinking clean water with salts and sugar (rehydration) and medicine save most people.
its sense in the lessons: In history and science lessons, cholera is famous because a doctor named John Snow found that people caught it from a dirty water pump in London, which helped create clean water systems and sewers. In geography and current affairs, cholera still spreads where there is war, floods or no clean water. It teaches why washing hands and safe water matter. Phrases: «a cholera outbreak», «cholera epidemic».
examples from the lessons: Cholera spreads through dirty drinking water. | John Snow traced cholera to one water pump. | Clean water and toilets stopped cholera in many cities. | Aid workers rushed to stop a cholera outbreak after the flood. | People with cholera need lots of clean fluids. | There is a vaccine that helps protect against cholera. | In Victorian times, cholera killed thousands in crowded towns.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «cholera is», not «a cholera». Pronounced «KOL-er-a»; «ch» sounds like «k». Do not confuse with «choler» (old word for anger) or «collar».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Chronological means arranged in the order in which things happened, from earliest to latest. 2) «Chronological order» is putting events, dates or steps in time order.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, pupils put events in chronological order on a timeline. In English writing, a recount or biography is often written in chronological order using time words like «first, next, then, finally». In maths and data, sorting by time is a kind of ordering. Phrases: «chronological order», «in chronological order», «reverse chronological order».
examples from the lessons: Put these pictures in chronological order to tell the story. | Our history timeline is chronological, from the Stone Age to today. | A diary is written in chronological order. | The photos on my phone are arranged chronologically. | The teacher asked us to list the kings in chronological order. | Reverse chronological order puts the newest first. | A recount should be chronological so the reader can follow it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective. Spelled «chrono-» (Greek for time) + «logical». The «ch» sounds like «k»: «kron-o-LOJ-i-kul». Compare: alphabetical order (A to Z), numerical order (by number), chronological order (by time).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A cog is one of the teeth around the edge of a wheel in a machine; a whole wheel with teeth is also called a cog or cogwheel (gear). 2) (figurative) «A cog in the machine» is a person who has a small part in a big organisation and feels unimportant. 3) (UK, slang) In some places, «to cog» means to copy someone's homework.
its sense in the lessons: In science and DT lessons, cogs (gears) show how turning one wheel can turn another faster, slower or the other way; a small cog turning a big cog makes it turn more slowly but with more force. In stories, «the cogs were turning» means someone was thinking hard. Phrases: «a cog in the machine», «cogs turning», «cogwheel».
examples from the lessons: The clock's cogs turned slowly behind the glass. | When the big cog turns once, the small cog turns three times. | A missing tooth on the cog jammed the machine. | You could see the cogs turning in his head as he worked out the puzzle. | He felt like a tiny cog in a huge company. | We built a cog model from cardboard and pins. | The bike's chain runs over cogs at the back wheel.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: one cog, two cogs. In maths problems with gears, if a big cog has 30 teeth and a small one 10, the small cog turns 3 times for each turn of the big one (30 ÷ 10 = 3).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Colic is bad pain in the tummy, especially when a young baby cries for a long time for no clear reason, often in the evenings. 2) In horses, colic is a serious tummy pain that needs a vet quickly.
its sense in the lessons: In family life, parents of a new baby may talk about colic and long nights of crying; it usually gets better on its own after a few months. In stories about farms and ponies, colic is a worry because it can be dangerous for horses. Phrases: «a baby with colic», «colicky».
examples from the lessons: Our baby brother cried for hours with colic. | Mum walked up and down with the colicky baby. | The doctor said colic usually stops after a few months. | The vet came at night because the pony had colic. | Colic is not the parents' fault. | Rocking and quiet help some babies with colic.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «the baby has colic». Adjective: colicky. Pronounced «KOL-ik». Do not confuse with «colleague» or «comic».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A combination is two or more things joined or mixed together, like a combination of colours or flavours. 2) A combination is the set of numbers you need to open a combination lock or safe. 3) (maths) A combination is one way of choosing items from a group, where the order does not matter. 4) Combination is the act of combining things.
its sense in the lessons: In maths lessons, pupils list all the possible combinations, for example how many outfits can be made from 3 tops and 2 skirts (3 × 2 = 6). In science, chemicals in combination make new substances. In everyday life, padlocks, safes and lockers have combinations. Phrases: «in combination with», «a winning combination», «combination lock».
examples from the lessons: Red and yellow is a bright combination. | I forgot the combination for my bike lock. | How many combinations can you make with 3 shirts and 4 pairs of trousers? | Hard work and luck were a winning combination. | Salt and vinegar is my favourite crisp combination. | Exercise in combination with good food keeps you healthy. | There are 10 combinations of two different fruits from a bowl of five.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: a combination, combinations. Verb: combine. In maths, a combination ignores order (apple-pear is the same as pear-apple); a «permutation» cares about order. A «combination lock» really uses an order, so mathematically it is a permutation.

part of speech: noun (a contour, contours); adjective (contour lines); verb (contour, contours, contoured, contouring)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A contour is the outline or shape of something, especially its curves, like the contour of a face or a coastline. 2) On a map, a contour (contour line) is a line joining places that are the same height above sea level. 3) (verb) To contour means to shape something to fit a curve, or (make-up) to use darker and lighter make-up to shape the face.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons, contour lines on maps show hills and valleys: lines close together mean a steep slope, lines far apart mean gentle ground. In art lessons, contour drawing traces the outline of an object. Phrases: «contour lines», «contour map», «the contours of».
examples from the lessons: The contour lines are very close here, so the hill is steep. | Each contour on the map is 10 metres higher than the one below. | She traced the contour of the leaf with a pencil. | The car seat is contoured to fit your back. | We could see the contour of the mountains against the sunset. | A contour map shows the shape of the land. | In art we drew a contour drawing without lifting the pencil.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun. Pronounced «KON-toor». In maths and map work, contour intervals tell the height difference between lines; count the lines and multiply by the interval to find a height difference.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A conveyor (conveyor belt) is a long moving belt or line of rollers that carries things from one place to another, as in factories, airports and supermarket checkouts. 2) (formal) A conveyor is a person or thing that carries or passes something on, like a conveyor of news.
its sense in the lessons: In science and DT lessons, conveyor belts show machines that save work by moving objects automatically. In everyday life, children see them at supermarket tills, airport baggage claim and sushi restaurants. In stories, a conveyor belt can be a fun or scary place, like in chocolate-factory tales. Phrases: «conveyor belt», «on the conveyor», «a conveyor belt of» (an endless stream of).
examples from the lessons: Our suitcases came round on the conveyor belt. | Put your shopping on the conveyor at the checkout. | The factory's conveyor carries bottles to be filled. | Sushi plates go round on a conveyor in the restaurant. | The team seemed to have a conveyor belt of new young players. | In the film, the boy rode the conveyor belt into the sweet factory. | A conveyor carries coal out of the mine.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun. Spelled «conveyor» or sometimes «conveyer». Verb: convey (to carry or communicate).

part of speech: verb (-ing form of «creak»: creak, creaks, creaked, creaking); adjective (creaking); noun (creaking, uncountable)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Creaking is the long, squeaky, groaning sound that old wood, doors, floors or hinges make when they move or bear weight. 2) (adjective) A creaking thing makes this sound, like a creaking door. 3) (figurative) A creaking system or organisation is old and struggling to work well, as in «a creaking railway».
its sense in the lessons: In stories, especially spooky ones, creaking doors and floorboards build suspense and tell the reader someone may be coming. In science lessons about sound, creaking comes from vibrations when things rub or bend. In news, «creaking» hospitals or schools are old and under strain. Phrases: «creaking floorboards», «creaking door», «creak open».
examples from the lessons: The door opened with a long, creaking sound. | I heard the creaking floorboards as Dad came upstairs. | The old ship was creaking in the wind. | The creaking stairs gave away our midnight snack trip. | The tree was creaking under the weight of the snow. | People say the creaking bus service needs more money. | My grandad's knees make a creaking noise when he stands up.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Creak» (squeaky sound) is a homophone of «creek» (a small stream). Regular verb: creaked, creaking. «Creaky» is another adjective (a creaky chair).

part of speech: noun (the Cree, Cree — a people; Cree — a language); adjective (Cree)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The Cree are a group of First Nations (Indigenous) peoples of Canada, and some live in the northern United States. 2) Cree is the language, or group of related languages, spoken by Cree people. 3) It is a name of a people, written with a capital C.
its sense in the lessons: In history and geography lessons about Canada, the Cree are one of the largest First Nations groups, living across a huge area from the Rocky Mountains to Quebec. Learning about the Cree helps children understand Indigenous cultures, languages and rights. Some Cree is written in a special syllable script. Phrases: «the Cree Nation», «Cree language», «Cree syllabics».
examples from the lessons: The Cree are one of the largest First Nations in Canada. | My classmate's grandmother speaks Cree. | Cree is written with special symbols called syllabics. | Many Cree families live in northern Canada. | We learned some Cree words for animals. | Cree storytellers pass on stories from elders to children.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always capital C. The plural is also «Cree» (the Cree, many Cree). Use respectful terms like First Nations or Indigenous peoples.

part of speech: verb (-ing form of «decode»: decode, decodes, decoded, decoding); noun (decoding, uncountable)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Decoding means turning a secret code or message back into normal words so it can be read. 2) In reading, decoding is sounding out letters to work out what a written word says. 3) In computing, decoding means changing data from one form into one people or machines can use, like turning a file into a video.
its sense in the lessons: In phonics and English lessons, decoding is a key reading skill: blending letter sounds to read a word (c-a-t, cat). In maths and computing lessons, pupils enjoy decoding secret messages with ciphers. In history, decoding enemy messages at Bletchley Park helped in the Second World War. Phrases: «decoding words», «decoding a message».
examples from the lessons: Decoding new words gets easier with practice. | The spies were decoding the secret message all night. | Alan Turing's team worked on decoding enemy codes. | We used a key to decoding the pirate's map. | My little brother is good at decoding but slower at understanding. | The computer is decoding the video so it can play. | Decoding the number puzzle took us twenty minutes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Decode» = de- (undo) + code. Opposite: encoding. Regular verb, drop the «e» before «-ing». In reading, decoding (saying the word) is different from comprehension (understanding it).

part of speech: adjective (digestive); noun (a digestive, digestives — a biscuit, UK/Ireland)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Digestive means to do with digestion, the way the body breaks down food so it can use it. 2) The digestive system is the set of body parts, from mouth to stomach to intestines, that digests food. 3) (UK, Ireland, Australia) A digestive (digestive biscuit) is a plain, slightly sweet, round wholemeal biscuit, often dunked in tea.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, pupils learn the digestive system: mouth, oesophagus, stomach, small intestine, large intestine. In everyday British and Irish life, a digestive is a common biscuit; chocolate digestives are very popular. Phrases: «digestive system», «digestive juices», «chocolate digestive».
examples from the lessons: Food travels through the digestive system. | Your stomach is part of your digestive system. | Gran always has a digestive with her cup of tea. | Saliva starts the digestive process in your mouth. | I dunked my digestive and half of it fell in the tea. | Fibre is good for your digestive health. | Can I have a chocolate digestive?
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a biscuit name it is countable (two digestives). The name comes from an old belief that these biscuits help digestion; that is a myth, not proven. Related: digest (verb), digestion (noun).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Disinformation is false information that is spread on purpose to trick people, often to change what they think or how they vote. 2) It is different from misinformation, which is false information spread by mistake.
its sense in the lessons: In media literacy and citizenship lessons, disinformation is linked to propaganda, bots, fake accounts and deepfakes; pupils learn to check sources, look for other reports and ask «who made this and why?». In news, governments and groups are accused of disinformation campaigns, especially in wars and elections. Phrases: «spread disinformation», «a disinformation campaign», «fight disinformation».
examples from the lessons: The fake video was part of a disinformation campaign. | Disinformation spreads fast on social media. | Always check a story with trusted sources to avoid disinformation. | The website was shut down for spreading disinformation. | During the war, both sides were accused of disinformation. | Our teacher showed us how to spot disinformation. | Bots can share disinformation thousands of times.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «a lot of disinformation», not «disinformations». Key difference: disinformation is on purpose; misinformation can be an honest mistake. Both can be harmful.

part of speech: noun (exile, uncountable — the state; an exile, exiles — a person); verb (exile, exiles, exiled, exiling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Exile is being forced to live away from your own country, often as a punishment or for safety. 2) An exile is a person who lives in exile. 3) (verb) To exile someone means to send them away from their country and not let them return. 4) (Bible) The Exile is the time when many people of Judah were taken away to Babylon, as told in the Bible.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, kings, leaders and writers were often exiled, like Napoleon sent to an island. In Bible lessons, the Babylonian Exile is a key story in which the people longed for home, as in Psalm 137. In stories, an exiled prince or hero often returns. Today, some people live in exile because their own government would punish them. Phrases: «in exile», «go into exile», «government in exile», «self-imposed exile».
examples from the lessons: Napoleon was sent into exile on a small island. | The poet lived in exile for twenty years. | The king exiled his brother from the land. | The exiles dreamed of going home one day. | In the Bible, the people sang sad songs during the exile in Babylon. | The government in exile met in London during the war. | After the quarrel, the cat went into exile under the bed.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a state it is uncountable (in exile); as a person, countable (an exile, exiles). Regular verb: exiled, exiling. Pronounced «EG-zile» or «EK-sile». Exile is forced; emigration is usually a choice.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) Famished means very, very hungry. 2) (literary) Famished can mean starving from lack of food over a long time.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday talk, children say «I'm famished!» after school or sport; it is a strong, slightly funny way to say hungry. In stories, famished characters show hard times or a long journey. Phrases: «absolutely famished», «I'm famished».
examples from the lessons: I'm famished! What's for tea? | After the long hike, we were all famished. | The famished puppy gobbled its food in seconds. | He came home from rugby practice absolutely famished. | The famished travellers shared their last bread. | Don't go swimming famished; have a snack first.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective, not usually used before «very» in comparison; it already means «very hungry». Related: famine (a time when a whole area has too little food). Similar words: starving (informal), ravenous.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A federation is a country made of states or provinces that each run some of their own matters, but share one central government, like the USA, Canada, Australia or Germany. 2) A federation is also a group of clubs, unions or organisations that join together, like a football federation.
its sense in the lessons: In citizenship and geography lessons, pupils learn that Australia became a federation when its colonies joined, and that in a federation power is shared between national and state governments. In sport, federations make the rules, like FIFA, the world football federation. Phrases: «the Russian Federation», «a federation of», «football federation».
examples from the lessons: Australia is a federation of six states and two territories. | The USA is a federation with fifty states. | The national football federation chose a new coach. | The Russian Federation is the official name of Russia. | In a federation, states can make some of their own laws. | Several unions joined to form a federation.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun. Adjective: federal (the federal government). Do not confuse with «confederation» (a looser union) or «federal» with «feudal».

part of speech: word (French); noun (a fils, plural fils — money)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (French) «Fils» is the French word for son; it sounds like «feess» to an English ear and is not an English word. 2) In English, «fils» is sometimes put after a French name to mean «the son» or «junior», as in «Dumas fils», to tell a son apart from his father with the same name. 3) (money) A fils is a small coin, a fraction of the dinar or dirham, in some Arab countries like Kuwait, Bahrain and the UAE.
its sense in the lessons: In French lessons, «fils» comes up in family words: «mon fils» (my son), «père et fils» (father and son). Some shops are named «... et Fils» (and Son). In maths problems about world money, 1000 fils = 1 Kuwaiti dinar, or 100 fils = 1 UAE dirham. Phrases: «père et fils», «Dumas fils».
examples from the lessons: In French class we learned that «fils» means son. | The bakery sign said «Martin et Fils». | Alexandre Dumas fils wrote different books from his father. | The drink cost 500 fils in Kuwait. | «Mon fils» means «my son» in French. | The old coin was worth only a few fils.
note for the reader of a maths problem: French: the «l» and «s» spelling is tricky; it is said «feess». Plural in French is also «fils». As money, the plural is «fils». Not an English word for son.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Flamenco is a lively, passionate kind of music, singing and dance from southern Spain (Andalusia), with guitar playing, hand clapping and fast stamping feet. 2) (adjective use) Flamenco describes things to do with this style, like a flamenco dress or flamenco guitar.
its sense in the lessons: In music and dance lessons, flamenco is an example of folk art from Spain with strong rhythms, clapping (palmas) and dramatic movement. The Roma (Gitano) people of Spain helped create it. In everyday life, children may see flamenco dresses with frills and polka dots. Phrases: «flamenco dancer», «flamenco guitar», «dance flamenco».
examples from the lessons: The flamenco dancer stamped her heels in time to the guitar. | We clapped along to the flamenco rhythm in music class. | She wore a red flamenco dress with frills. | Flamenco comes from southern Spain. | My uncle plays flamenco guitar. | The flamenco show was loud, fast and exciting.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly uncountable (flamenco is), though «a flamenco» can mean one dance or song. Do not confuse with «flamingo», the pink bird.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Fleshy means thick, soft and juicy, especially describing fruit or plant parts, like a fleshy peach or fleshy cactus leaves. 2) Fleshy describes a body part that is plump or has a lot of flesh, like the fleshy part of your thumb. 3) Fleshy can mean having the pinkish colour of skin.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about plants, fleshy fruits (like plums and tomatoes) are eaten by animals that then spread the seeds; fleshy leaves store water in desert plants. In stories, «fleshy» can describe a creature's arms or face in a vivid, sometimes unpleasant way. Phrases: «fleshy fruit», «fleshy leaves», «the fleshy part of».
examples from the lessons: A peach is a fleshy fruit with a stone in the middle. | Cactuses have fleshy stems that store water. | The doctor gave the injection in the fleshy part of the arm. | Aloe vera has thick, fleshy leaves. | Mushrooms have a fleshy cap. | The troll had a big, fleshy nose.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative fleshier, superlative fleshiest. Do not confuse «fleshy» (soft and plump) with «fleshly» (to do with the body rather than the spirit, an old word) or «flesh-eating».

part of speech: verb (flex, flexes, flexed, flexing); noun (a flex, flexes — UK cable; a flex — slang showing off)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To flex means to bend a part of your body, like your arm or fingers. 2) To flex your muscles means to tighten them so they stand out, often to show strength. 3) (UK, Ireland, Australia) A flex is a bendy electric cable with a plug, for a lamp or kettle (in US English, a cord). 4) (slang) To flex means to show off something, like new trainers or money; «a flex» is a showing-off.
its sense in the lessons: In PE and science lessons, pupils flex and stretch joints and learn that muscles work in pairs. In safety lessons, worn flexes and trailing cables are dangers to report. In playground slang, «stop flexing» means «stop showing off», and «weird flex but OK» teases someone for bragging about something odd. Phrases: «flex your muscles», «flex your fingers», «weird flex».
examples from the lessons: Flex your arm and feel your biceps. | The gymnast flexed her feet before the jump. | Don't touch that kettle flex; it's frayed. | He was flexing his new phone all day. | «I've got two hundred cousins.» «Weird flex, but OK.» | The country flexed its muscles by showing off its army. | Gently flex your fingers after typing for a long time.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb is regular: flexed, flexing; noun plural: flexes. Related: flexible (bendy, or able to change). The slang sense is informal; avoid it in written work.

part of speech: verb (flounder, flounders, floundered, floundering); noun (a flounder, flounders or flounder — a fish)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A flounder is a flat sea fish that lies on the seabed, with both eyes on one side of its head. 2) (verb) To flounder means to struggle to move, splashing and stumbling, as in deep mud, snow or water. 3) (verb) To flounder can also mean to struggle and not know what to say or do, as in floundering in a test.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, the flounder is an example of camouflage: it changes colour to match the sand. In stories, floundering in water or mud shows a struggle; in school, «floundering» shows someone stuck and confused. Phrases: «flounder about», «flounder in», «begin to flounder».
examples from the lessons: The flounder lay hidden on the sandy seabed. | We floundered through the deep snow to the bus stop. | The horse floundered in the muddy field. | I floundered when the teacher asked me a question I hadn't heard. | A young flounder has eyes on both sides, but one eye moves as it grows. | The company floundered after it lost its biggest customer.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Fish plural: flounder or flounders. Verb is regular. Trap: «flounder» (struggle) and «founder» (sink or fail completely) are often confused; a floundering team is struggling, a foundering ship is sinking.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A frontier is a border between two countries, or the land near it. 2) (history, US/Canada/Australia) The frontier was the edge of land settled by newcomers, beyond which the land was wild or belonged to Indigenous peoples. 3) A frontier is the edge of what is known, as in «the frontiers of science», or «space, the final frontier».
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons about the American West, Canada and Australia, «the frontier» brings stories of settlers, pioneers, and also of Indigenous peoples losing their land. In science, «new frontiers» are areas where discoveries are still being made. Phrases: «the frontier», «frontier town», «push back the frontiers», «the final frontier».
examples from the lessons: Soldiers guarded the frontier between the two countries. | Pioneers moved west towards the frontier. | The frontier town had one dusty street. | Space exploration is the new frontier. | Scientists are pushing back the frontiers of medicine. | Many Indigenous people lost their land as the frontier moved. | We crossed the frontier by train.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun. Pronounced «FRUN-teer» (UK) or «frun-TEER» (US). Similar word: border. «Frontier» often has the feeling of an edge or limit, not just a line.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Genetic means to do with genes, the tiny instructions inside living cells that are passed from parents to children and decide things like eye colour. 2) A genetic illness or feature is one that is passed down in families through genes. 3) Genetic can describe science that studies or changes genes, as in «genetic engineering».
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on inheritance and evolution, pupils learn that offspring get a mix of genetic information from both parents, which explains why children look a bit like each parent. In news and ethics lessons, «genetically modified» (GM) food and genetic testing raise questions. Phrases: «genetic code», «genetic engineering», «genetically modified», «genetic disease».
examples from the lessons: Eye colour is partly genetic. | DNA carries the genetic code. | Some illnesses are genetic and run in families. | Scientists are studying the genetic differences between wolves and dogs. | The crops were genetically modified to resist pests. | Identical twins share the same genetic information. | Genetic tests can show where your ancestors came from.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective. Related: gene, genes, genetics (the science), genetically. Myth trap: not everything is genetic; what you eat, learn and do also shapes you.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Heritage is the history, traditions, buildings, art and language that a country or group has had for a long time and passes on. 2) Your heritage is the culture and background you get from your family and ancestors. 3) (adjective use) A heritage site, building or rail line is old and protected because it is important.
its sense in the lessons: In history and citizenship lessons, heritage covers castles, museums, World Heritage Sites and traditions to look after for the future. In everyday life, children may talk about their Irish, Polish, Chinese or Māori heritage with pride. Phrases: «cultural heritage», «World Heritage Site», «heritage railway», «of ... heritage».
examples from the lessons: Stonehenge is a World Heritage Site. | My mum is proud of her Jamaican heritage. | Old songs and stories are part of our heritage. | We rode a steam train on the heritage railway. | The town spent money protecting its heritage buildings. | Learning your grandparents' language keeps your heritage alive. | The museum shows the heritage of the local mining town.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable (our heritage). Related: inherit, inheritance. Heritage is what is passed on to a group; an inheritance is often money or things left to one person.

part of speech: noun (a hippopotamus, hippopotamuses or hippopotami); short form: hippo
meaning for a pupil: 1) A hippopotamus is a very large, heavy African animal with thick grey skin, a huge mouth and short legs, which spends most of the day in rivers and lakes. 2) People usually call it a hippo for short.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, the hippo shows how animals adapt: its eyes, ears and nostrils are on top of its head so it can see and breathe while almost under water. In safety and nature facts, hippos look slow and friendly but are among the most dangerous animals in Africa. In stories and songs, hippos are often funny characters. Phrases: «as big as a hippo», «hungry hippos».
examples from the lessons: The hippopotamus wallowed in the muddy river. | Hippos can't really swim; they walk along the river bottom. | A hippo's yawn shows its huge teeth. | The word «hippopotamus» means «river horse». | Hippos come out at night to eat grass. | Hippos are very dangerous if you get too close. | We saw a baby hippo at the zoo.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: hippopotamuses or hippopotami; short form plural: hippos. The name is from Greek «hippos» (horse) + «potamos» (river), but it is not related to horses; its closest living relatives are whales.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A hybrid is a plant or animal whose parents are two different kinds (species or varieties), like a mule, whose parents are a horse and a donkey. 2) A hybrid is anything that mixes two different things, like a hybrid car that uses both petrol and electricity. 3) (adjective) Hybrid means mixed, as in «hybrid learning» (some at school and some online) or «hybrid working».
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on living things, hybrids show how different species can sometimes breed, though the young (like mules) often cannot have babies of their own. In everyday life and environment lessons, hybrid cars use less fuel. Phrases: «a hybrid of», «hybrid car», «hybrid working», «hybrid vehicle».
examples from the lessons: A mule is a hybrid of a horse and a donkey. | Our new car is a hybrid, so it uses less petrol. | The gardener grew a hybrid rose with orange and pink petals. | Some lessons were hybrid, with half the class at home on video. | A liger is a hybrid of a lion and a tiger. | The film is a hybrid of comedy and horror. | Hybrid plants can be stronger than their parents.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun. Pronounced «HY-brid». Mules and most other hybrids between species cannot have young (are sterile).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Imperial means to do with an empire or an emperor, as in «the imperial palace». 2) Imperial units are the old British system of measures, such as inches, feet, miles, pints, pounds and stones. 3) (formal) Imperial can mean grand and commanding, like a powerful ruler.
its sense in the lessons: In maths lessons, pupils convert between imperial and metric units: 1 inch is about 2.5 cm, 1 mile is about 1.6 km, 1 pint is about 568 ml in the UK. In everyday UK life, road signs show miles and people give height in feet and weight in stones; the US also uses its own customary units much like imperial. In history, imperial means linked to empires like the Roman or British Empire. Phrases: «imperial units», «imperial system», «Imperial Rome», «imperial palace».
examples from the lessons: The British still use imperial miles on road signs. | Convert 6 feet from imperial to metric. | The emperor lived in the imperial palace. | Imperial Rome ruled a huge area. | A pint is an imperial unit. | My grandad measures everything in inches, the imperial way. | The imperial army marched across the desert.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective. Opposite in measures: metric. Maths note: 12 inches = 1 foot; 3 feet = 1 yard; 1760 yards = 1 mile; 16 ounces = 1 pound; 14 pounds = 1 stone; 8 pints = 1 gallon. A US pint (about 473 ml) is smaller than a UK imperial pint (about 568 ml). Do not confuse with «impartial» (fair, not taking sides).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Indeed is used to make something stronger, meaning «really» or «truly», as in «very good indeed». 2) Indeed is used to agree, meaning «yes, that is true», as in «"It's cold." "Indeed it is."». 3) (formal) Indeed adds a stronger point, meaning «in fact» or «even more than that». 4) (informal, ironic) «Indeed?» or «Why, indeed?» can show surprise or doubt.
its sense in the lessons: In writing lessons, «indeed» is a useful connective for persuasive writing: «Pets are good for us; indeed, they can help us feel calmer.» In everyday speech it sounds a bit formal or old-fashioned, but teachers and older people often say «Thank you very much indeed». In stories, a butler or a wise owl may say «Indeed». Phrases: «very ... indeed», «indeed it is», «a friend in need is a friend indeed».
examples from the lessons: Thank you very much indeed. | «Was the test hard?» «Indeed it was.» | It was a very long walk indeed. | Spiders are useful; indeed, they eat lots of pests. | «A friend in need is a friend indeed,» Gran said. | «You think you can beat me? Indeed?» laughed the knight. | That is indeed the right answer.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb. Often follows «very + adjective» (very kind indeed). It is one word, from «in deed». It can begin a sentence but sounds formal.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An intruder is a person who goes into a place where they are not allowed, especially a building, to steal or cause harm. 2) An intruder can be anyone or anything that comes in where it is not wanted, like an animal in a nest or a person in a private talk.
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons, children learn what to do if there is an intruder: tell an adult, stay safe, call the emergency number (999 in the UK and Ireland, 911 in the US and Canada, 000 in Australia, 111 in New Zealand). In stories, an intruder creates suspense. In computing, an intruder might be a hacker breaking into a system. Phrases: «intruder alarm», «an intruder in».
examples from the lessons: The intruder alarm went off in the middle of the night. | The dog barked at the intruder. | The police caught the intruder climbing out of a window. | The cuckoo chick is an intruder in another bird's nest. | Our school practises a lockdown drill in case of an intruder. | I felt like an intruder at their family party. | Hackers are intruders on computer networks.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun, starts with a vowel sound so «an intruder». Verb: intrude (to go in where not wanted). Related: intrusion, intrusive.

meaning for a pupil: 1) «Ir-» is a prefix meaning «not», used before words beginning with «r», as in irregular (not regular), irresponsible (not responsible) and irrelevant (not relevant). 2) «IR» is a short form for infrared, light just beyond red that we cannot see but feel as heat, used in TV remote controls. 3) «Ir» is the chemical symbol for the element iridium. 4) (Irish, Scots, slang) In some written dialect, «ir» may stand for «our» or «are».
its sense in the lessons: In spelling lessons, «ir-» explains the double r in words like «irregular» and «irresistible»: ir + regular. In science lessons, IR (infrared) cameras see heat and remote controls send IR signals. It is not a word on its own in standard English.
examples from the lessons: «Irregular» means «not regular»; the «ir-» means not. | The TV remote sends an IR signal to the television. | An IR camera can show warm animals at night. | Add «ir-» to «responsible» to make «irresponsible». | «Ir» is the symbol for iridium on the periodic table. | Irrelevant means not connected to the topic.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Not an English word on its own. As a prefix it doubles the «r»: ir + rational = irrational. Other «not» prefixes: un-, in-, im- (before m, p, b), il- (before l). «IR» in capitals is an abbreviation.

part of speech: adjective (junior); noun (a junior, juniors; Junior, a name)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Junior means younger, or for younger people, as in a junior school or junior football team. 2) Junior means lower in rank or less experienced in a job, as in a junior doctor. 3) (US, Canada) A junior is a student in the third year of a four-year high school or college. 4) (US) «Junior» (Jr.) is added after the name of a son who has the same name as his father, and «Junior» is sometimes used as his nickname. 5) (noun) You can be someone's junior, meaning younger than them, as in «three years my junior».
its sense in the lessons: In the UK, Ireland and Australia, «junior school» is the primary school for children about 7 to 11, and «the juniors» are pupils there. In sport, junior teams are for younger players. In jobs and hospitals, junior means newer or less senior. Phrases: «junior school», «junior league», «junior doctor», «three years my junior».
examples from the lessons: My sister moves up to junior school next year. | He plays in the junior rugby team. | She's a junior doctor working night shifts. | In the US, my cousin is a junior in high school. | Martin Luther King Jr. was named after his father. | My brother is two years my junior. | The juniors had their sports day on Friday.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: senior. «Junior to» (not «junior than»): «she is junior to him». In maths, «junior» on its own does not give a number; «three years my junior» means 3 years younger.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A learner is a person who is learning something, like a pupil at school or someone learning a new skill. 2) A learner driver is someone learning to drive a car who has not passed the driving test yet. 3) (UK, Ireland) An L-plate (a red L on white) shows that a car is driven by a learner.
its sense in the lessons: In school, teachers talk about «learners» and «good learning habits»; a «fast learner» picks things up quickly. In everyday life in the UK, Ireland, Australia and New Zealand, cars with L-plates show learners, so other drivers should be patient. Phrases: «a fast learner», «a slow learner», «learner driver», «English learners».
examples from the lessons: She's a fast learner and picked up chess in a week. | The car had L-plates because Mum is a learner driver. | Our school wants every learner to feel welcome. | English learners often find spelling tricky. | Be patient with learners; everyone starts somewhere. | Dad's a learner on the guitar, so it sounds a bit wobbly.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun. Made from «learn» + «-er» (the one who learns). Do not confuse «learner» with «teacher»; and in standard English we do not «learn» someone something; we teach them.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A macaque is a kind of monkey with a short tail or no tail, living mostly in Asia and one kind in North Africa. 2) Famous macaques include Japanese snow monkeys that bathe in hot springs, rhesus macaques, and the Barbary macaques of Gibraltar.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on primates, macaques show clever animal behaviour, like washing food and living in big groups. In travel and safety, macaques in tourist areas may grab food or bags, so it is unwise to feed or touch them. Phrases: «Japanese macaque», «Barbary macaque», «rhesus macaque».
examples from the lessons: Japanese macaques sit in hot springs to keep warm in winter. | A macaque snatched the banana from my hand in Gibraltar. | Macaques live in big family groups. | The scientist watched a macaque washing a sweet potato in the sea. | Don't feed the macaques; they can bite. | Rhesus macaques are found across much of Asia.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun. Pronounced «ma-KAK» or «ma-KAHK». The «-que» ending sounds like «k». A macaque is a monkey, not an ape.

part of speech: adjective (Malay); noun (a Malay, Malays; Malay — the language)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The Malays are a people living mostly in Malaysia, Indonesia, Brunei, Singapore and southern Thailand. 2) Malay is the language of the Malay people, an official language of Malaysia, Brunei and Singapore; Indonesian is a form of it. 3) (adjective) Malay describes things to do with this people, language or culture.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons on Southeast Asia, Malay is a widely spoken language written in the Latin alphabet, with words like «orang utan» meaning «person of the forest». In food and culture lessons, Malay dishes like nasi lemak and satay may come up. Phrases: «the Malay Peninsula», «Malay language», «Malay food».
examples from the lessons: Malay is spoken in Malaysia and Singapore. | The word «orangutan» comes from Malay. | We ate Malay satay with peanut sauce. | The Malay Peninsula stretches down to Singapore. | My friend's family is Malay and celebrates Hari Raya. | Malay uses the same alphabet as English.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always capital M. Do not confuse Malay (a people and language) with Malaysian (a citizen of Malaysia, who may be Malay, Chinese, Indian or other). Pronounced «ma-LAY».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A manifesto is a written public statement in which a political party or group says what it believes and what it promises to do if elected. 2) A manifesto can be any bold statement of ideas and aims by an artist, group or person.
its sense in the lessons: In citizenship lessons about elections, parties publish manifestos before voting so people can compare their promises. At school, pupils standing for class rep or school council may write their own manifesto (more playtime, better lunches). In history, some manifestos changed the world. Phrases: «election manifesto», «manifesto promise», «write a manifesto».
examples from the lessons: Each party published its manifesto before the election. | My school council manifesto promised a new bike shed. | The party broke its manifesto promise on taxes. | The artists wrote a manifesto about their new style. | We compared two manifestos in our politics lesson. | Read the manifesto before you decide how to vote.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun; plural manifestos (or manifestoes). From Italian. A manifesto is a statement of plans, not a law; promises in it are not always kept.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A marquis is a nobleman with a high title, ranking below a duke and above an earl or count. 2) In Britain the title is usually spelled «marquess»; «marquis» is used in France and other countries. 3) The wife of a marquis is a marchioness (UK) or a marquise (France).
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons about kings, queens and nobles, the marquis is one step on the ladder of titles: duke, marquess, earl, viscount, baron. In stories set in old France or Britain, a marquis is a rich, powerful aristocrat. Phrases: «the Marquis of ...», «the Marquis de ...».
examples from the lessons: The marquis lived in a grand castle in France. | A marquis ranks below a duke. | In the novel, the cruel marquis rode past the starving villagers. | The Marquess of Bath owns a safari park in England. | The marquis bowed to the queen. | His title passed from the old marquis to his son.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun; plural marquises. Pronounced «MAR-kwis» (English) or «mar-KEE» (French style). Do not confuse with «marquee» (a big tent), which sounds like the French way of saying it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A mathematician is a person who studies maths deeply or whose job is doing maths, finding new ideas, proving things or solving hard problems. 2) Someone who is very good at maths can be called a good mathematician.
its sense in the lessons: In maths lessons, teachers may say «think like a mathematician»: notice patterns, ask «what if?», explain and prove. In history of maths, famous mathematicians include Pythagoras, Hypatia, Ada Lovelace, Alan Turing, Katherine Johnson and Srinivasa Ramanujan. Phrases: «a great mathematician», «young mathematician».
examples from the lessons: Katherine Johnson was a mathematician who helped send astronauts into space. | A mathematician checks that a proof works for every number. | Our class has some keen young mathematicians. | Pythagoras was an ancient Greek mathematician. | Mathematicians use patterns to solve problems. | Ada Lovelace was a mathematician and the first computer programmer.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun. Spelled «mathematic-ian», with «-cian» said like «-shun»: «math-uh-muh-TISH-un». UK short form «maths», US «math», but the person is a mathematician everywhere.

part of speech: noun (a metro, metros; the Metro); adjective (metro, informal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A metro is an underground railway system in a city, also called a subway (US) or the Underground or Tube (London). 2) (US, Canada, Australia, informal) Metro means the whole city area including its suburbs, as in «the metro area». 3) Metro is part of the names of some newspapers, buses and shops.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons about cities, metros help millions of people travel quickly without cars, reducing traffic and pollution. In maths, metro maps are diagrams that show the order of stations and changes, not real distances. In everyday life, children may ride the Paris Métro, the Montreal Metro or the Tyne and Wear Metro. Phrases: «take the metro», «metro station», «metro map», «metro area».
examples from the lessons: We took the metro to the museum. | The metro station was crowded at rush hour. | In Paris, the Métro has stations with pretty old signs. | The metro map shows lines in different colours. | The storm stopped the metro trains for an hour. | The Toronto metro area has millions of people.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun. «Metro» comes from French «métropolitain». Names vary: Underground or Tube (London), subway (New York), Metro (Paris, Washington, Newcastle, Montreal). «Metric» is a different word (measurements).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A midge is a tiny flying insect, a bit like a very small fly or mosquito, that often flies in clouds near water. 2) Some midges bite, and in Scotland the Highland midge is famous for biting people on summer evenings.
its sense in the lessons: In nature lessons, midges are food for birds, bats and fish, and their young (larvae) live in water. In everyday life, camping in Scotland or Canada can mean clouds of midges, so people use midge spray and nets. In stories, «a midge» can mean something tiny. Phrases: «a cloud of midges», «midge bites», «midge repellent».
examples from the lessons: A cloud of midges hovered over the lake. | The midges in Scotland were biting us all evening. | Swallows swooped to catch midges. | Put on midge spray before we go camping. | I've got midge bites all over my arms. | Midges are so small they can get through some mosquito nets.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun; plural midges. Pronounced «mij». Not the same as «midget», a word that is now considered offensive.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A mutation is a change in the genes (DNA) of a living thing, which can cause a new feature; most mutations make no difference, some are harmful, a few are helpful. 2) A mutation is any change in form, a change from one shape or kind into another. 3) In some languages like Welsh and Irish, a mutation is a change to the first sound of a word.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on evolution and inheritance, mutations explain why living things vary and how new features, such as moths with darker wings, can spread over many generations. In comics and films, «mutations» give superheroes or monsters strange powers, which is fiction. In the news, virus mutations can create new variants. Phrases: «a genetic mutation», «a random mutation», «a new mutation».
examples from the lessons: A mutation in its genes gave the cat extra toes. | Mutations happen by chance when DNA is copied. | Most mutations are neither good nor bad. | The virus developed a mutation that helped it spread. | In the comic, a mutation gave the boy super strength. | A helpful mutation can spread through a population over time. | Welsh has mutations, so «cath» (cat) can become «gath».
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable (a mutation) or uncountable (the process). Verb: mutate. Related: mutant (a creature with a mutation). Myth trap: real mutations do not give superpowers.

part of speech: noun (Newfoundland, a place; a Newfoundland, Newfoundlands — a dog)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Newfoundland is a large island off the east coast of Canada; with Labrador it forms the Canadian province of Newfoundland and Labrador. 2) A Newfoundland (often called a Newfie) is a very large, strong, gentle dog with a thick coat, famous for rescuing people from water.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and history lessons on Canada, Newfoundland is known for fishing, icebergs, puffins, and as one of the first places in North America reached by Vikings (L'Anse aux Meadows). In stories about dogs, Nana in «Peter Pan» was a Newfoundland. Phrases: «Newfoundland and Labrador», «a Newfoundland dog».
examples from the lessons: Newfoundland is an island on the east coast of Canada. | We saw icebergs floating past Newfoundland. | The Vikings reached Newfoundland long ago. | A Newfoundland dog pulled the swimmer out of the lake. | Newfoundlands are huge but very gentle. | People from Newfoundland speak with a special accent. | Puffins nest on the cliffs of Newfoundland.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always capital N. Pronounced «NEW-fun-lund» or «new-fund-LAND»; locals say it to rhyme with «understand». «Newfie» can be a friendly nickname for the dog, but for people it can sound rude.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An olm is a pale, blind salamander (an amphibian) that lives in dark underground cave waters in southern Europe, especially Slovenia and Croatia. 2) Olms are pinkish-white, with tiny legs and red feathery gills, and can live for many decades without much food.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, the olm is an example of adaptation to darkness: it has no working eyes and finds food using smell, hearing and electricity sense. Local people once thought olms were baby dragons washed out of caves. Phrases: «the olm», «cave salamander».
examples from the lessons: The olm lives in dark caves and has no eyes. | Olms can survive for years without eating. | Its pink colour earned the olm the nickname «human fish». | People once believed olms were baby dragons. | We watched a video of an olm swimming in a cave pool. | The olm breathes using feathery red gills.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun; starts with a vowel so «an olm». Pronounced to rhyme with «holm» (ohlm). It is a rare word, also called «proteus». It is an amphibian, not a fish or a lizard.

part of speech: noun (par, uncountable); idioms (on a par with, up to par, below par, par for the course)
meaning for a pupil: 1) In golf, par is the number of strokes a good player is expected to need for a hole or a whole course. 2) «On a par with» means equal to or as good as. 3) «Up to par» means as good as it should be; «below par» or «under par» (not golf) means not as good or not as well as usual. 4) «Par for the course» means normal or expected, usually for something annoying. 5) (money) Par is the normal stated value of something like a share.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, «I'm feeling a bit below par» means «I'm a bit unwell or tired». In golf and maths, scores are counted against par: 2 under par means 2 strokes fewer. In stories, «par for the course» shows a character used to bad luck. Phrases: «under par», «over par», «on a par with», «up to par».
examples from the lessons: Par for this golf hole is three. | She finished the round two under par. | His homework wasn't up to par this week. | I'm feeling below par, so I'll stay home. | Rain on sports day is par for the course in Wales. | The new film is on a par with the first one. | Our team is now on a par with the best in the league.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. In golf maths, a score of 72 on a par-70 course is «2 over par» (72 − 70 = 2); a score of 68 is «2 under par». Careful: in golf «under par» is good, but in everyday talk «below par» is bad.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Photography is the art, hobby or job of taking photographs with a camera or phone. 2) Photography also means the photos in a book, film or magazine, and how they are done, as in «the film has beautiful photography».
its sense in the lessons: In art and computing lessons, pupils learn photography skills: framing, light, focus and editing. In science, cameras show how light makes an image. In everyday life, many children enjoy photography on phones; in online safety lessons, they learn to ask before taking or sharing photos of others. Phrases: «nature photography», «wildlife photography», «no flash photography», «take up photography».
examples from the lessons: My aunt does wildlife photography and waits hours for one shot. | Flash photography is not allowed in the museum. | We had a photography lesson on how to use light. | Photography was invented about two hundred years ago. | The film's photography made the mountains look magical. | He took up photography as a hobby.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «photography is fun», not «a photography». Stress: «fo-TOG-ra-fee». Related: photograph (a picture), photographer (the person), photographic. «Photo» is short for photograph, not photography.

part of speech: noun (a pickle, pickles; pickle, uncountable); verb (pickle, pickles, pickled, pickling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A pickle is a vegetable, especially a small cucumber (gherkin), kept in vinegar or salty water so it lasts a long time and tastes sour. 2) (UK) Pickle is a thick, chunky, sour-sweet sauce eaten with cheese or cold meat, as in a cheese and pickle sandwich. 3) (informal) To be «in a pickle» means to be in a difficult or awkward situation. 4) (verb) To pickle food means to preserve it in vinegar or salt water. 5) (UK, informal) «Little pickle» is a fond name for a cheeky child.
its sense in the lessons: In science and food lessons, pickling shows how vinegar and salt stop germs and keep food from going bad. In stories, characters «in a pickle» are in trouble and must find a way out. In everyday UK and Irish life, cheese and pickle sandwiches are common; in North America a pickle often comes with a burger. Phrases: «in a pickle», «cheese and pickle», «pickled onions», «little pickle».
examples from the lessons: Dad likes a pickle on the side of his burger. | Can I have a cheese and pickle sandwich? | We pickled onions in vinegar in science club. | I was in a real pickle when I forgot my PE kit. | Grandma calls my baby sister a little pickle. | Pickling helped people keep food through the winter. | The jar of pickles was too tight to open.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable for single pickles (two pickles); uncountable for the sauce (some pickle). «Pickled» as an adjective can be old slang for drunk. A gherkin is a kind of pickle.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A playlist is a list of songs or videos chosen to be played one after another, on a phone, music app or the radio. 2) (radio) A playlist is the list of songs a radio station has chosen to play often.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, children make playlists for parties, car journeys, exercise or sleep. In computing lessons, a playlist is an example of a list or sequence, where order matters and items can be added, removed or shuffled. In maths, you can work out how long a playlist lasts by adding song lengths. Phrases: «make a playlist», «add to the playlist», «shuffle the playlist».
examples from the lessons: I made a playlist for our road trip. | Add that song to my playlist! | The party playlist lasted three hours. | Shuffle the playlist so the songs come in a random order. | Our teacher has a calm playlist for writing time. | My playlist has twelve songs of about three minutes each, so it lasts about 36 minutes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun, written as one word. In maths problems, the total time of a playlist = the sum of the song lengths; remember 60 seconds = 1 minute when adding minutes and seconds.

part of speech: verb (past and past participle of «pluck»: pluck, plucks, plucked, plucking); adjective (plucked)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Plucked means pulled off or picked with the fingers, as in plucked flowers or fruit. 2) Plucked means having had the feathers pulled out, as in a plucked chicken. 3) Plucked means played by pulling and letting go of the strings, as on a guitar or harp. 4) Plucked can mean pulled quickly out of somewhere, as in «plucked from the sea» by a rescuer. 5) If someone plucked up courage, they made themselves brave.
its sense in the lessons: In music lessons, plucked string instruments (guitar, harp, ukulele) are compared with bowed ones (violin, cello). In stories, «plucked up the courage» shows a nervous character being brave. In news, a helicopter crew «plucked» people from a flood. Phrases: «plucked up courage», «plucked from obscurity», «plucked eyebrows», «plucked a string».
examples from the lessons: She plucked an apple from the tree. | Finally, Tom plucked up the courage to ask for help. | The harpist plucked the strings gently. | The farmer plucked the chicken before cooking it. | A lifeboat crew plucked the fisherman from the waves. | He plucked a number out of thin air as a guess. | The guitar's plucked notes echoed round the hall.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular past form of «pluck». «Pluck» as a noun also means courage (she showed pluck); «plucky» means brave. Do not confuse with «plugged».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A pollinator is an animal, usually an insect like a bee, butterfly or moth, that carries pollen from one flower to another so the plant can make seeds and fruit. 2) Some birds (like hummingbirds), bats and even the wind can act as pollinators.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on plants and life cycles, pollinators are vital: without them, many fruits and vegetables would not grow. In environment lessons, pollinators like bees are in danger from loss of wildflowers and pesticides, so schools plant bee-friendly gardens. Phrases: «pollinator garden», «important pollinators», «attract pollinators».
examples from the lessons: Bees are the best-known pollinators. | Hummingbirds are pollinators in the Americas. | We planted lavender to attract pollinators. | Without pollinators, there would be far fewer apples. | Moths are night-time pollinators. | Pesticides can harm pollinators. | Our school made a pollinator garden by the playground.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun. Related: pollen (the yellow powder), pollinate (verb), pollination (the process). The wind is sometimes called a pollinator, but usually the word means animals.

part of speech: word (French; also in English names); noun (the Porte — history)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (French) «Porte» is the French word for door or gate; it sounds like «port» to an English ear and is not an English word. 2) (French) «Porte» is also a form of the French verb «porter», meaning «carries» or «wears», as in «il porte un chapeau» (he wears a hat). 3) (history) «The Porte» or «the Sublime Porte» was the name used in Europe for the government of the Ottoman Empire.
its sense in the lessons: In French lessons, «porte» comes up in house words: «la porte» (the door), «ferme la porte» (close the door). In Paris, gates of the old city walls are named «Porte de ...». In history lessons on the Ottoman Empire, «the Porte» means its government. Related English words come from the same root: portal, porter, portable.
examples from the lessons: In French, «ferme la porte» means «close the door». | Our Métro stop was called «Porte de Clichy». | «Elle porte une robe rouge» means «she is wearing a red dress». | The English word «portal» is related to «porte». | Ambassadors sent letters to the Sublime Porte in Istanbul. | In French class we labelled the door «la porte».
note for the reader of a maths problem: Not an English word. In French it is feminine: «la porte». Pronounced «port», like English «port» (harbour), but the meaning is different. Do not confuse with «port» (a harbour, or a sweet wine).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Potassium is a soft, silvery chemical element, a metal, with the symbol K. 2) Potassium is also a mineral the body needs to keep the heart, muscles and nerves working, found in foods like bananas, potatoes and beans.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, potassium reacts very strongly with water, fizzing and catching fire with a lilac flame, so it is kept under oil; only teachers handle it. In health and food lessons, bananas are famous for potassium. In gardening, plants need potassium from fertiliser to flower and fruit. Phrases: «rich in potassium», «potassium chloride».
examples from the lessons: Bananas are a good source of potassium. | Potassium has the chemical symbol K. | The teacher dropped a tiny piece of potassium in water, and it burst into lilac flames. | Our bodies need potassium for healthy muscles. | Potassium is stored under oil because it reacts with air and water. | Tomato feed is rich in potassium.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. The symbol K comes from its Latin name «kalium», a trap in science tests. Pronounced «po-TASS-ee-um». Safety: never handle pure potassium yourself.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A projector is a machine that shines light through or from a picture or video so that a large image appears on a screen or wall. 2) In school, a projector is often fixed to the ceiling and connected to a computer or interactive whiteboard.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday school life, teachers use projectors to show slides and videos. In science lessons, a projector shows how a lens bends light to make an image bigger. In stories, an old film projector clicking in a dark room sets a mood. Phrases: «turn on the projector», «overhead projector», «film projector».
examples from the lessons: The teacher switched on the projector to show the video. | The projector bulb blew in the middle of the film. | We made a shoebox projector with a magnifying glass. | Old cinemas used huge film projectors. | Can someone turn the lights off so we can see the projector? | The projector made the picture as big as the wall.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun. Stress: «pro-JEK-tor». Related: project (verb: pro-JECT, to shine or throw forward) and project (noun: PRO-ject, a piece of work). Do not confuse with «protector».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A racehorse is a horse that is bred and trained to run in races. 2) Racehorses are usually fast, slim breeds such as Thoroughbreds.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, racehorses appear at famous races like the Grand National in the UK, the Melbourne Cup in Australia and the Kentucky Derby in the US. In maths, race results and odds can be used in number problems. In ethics lessons, pupils may discuss animal welfare in horse racing and the problems of gambling. Phrases: «a champion racehorse», «racehorse trainer».
examples from the lessons: The racehorse galloped across the finish line first. | Racehorses are trained every morning on the gallops. | My uncle works as a groom for racehorses. | The racehorse wore a numbered cloth and a jockey in bright colours. | Some people worry that racing is hard on racehorses. | Retired racehorses can find new homes as riding horses.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun, one word. A jockey rides the racehorse; a trainer trains it. «Race horse» as two words is also seen but less common.

part of speech: noun (a rally, rallies); verb (rally, rallies, rallied, rallying)
