meaning for a pupil: 1) A rally is a big public meeting where many people gather to support or protest about something. 2) A rally is a car race on ordinary or rough roads, often in stages. 3) In tennis, badminton or table tennis, a rally is a series of hits back and forth before a point is won. 4) (verb) To rally means to come together, or bring people together, to support someone or something. 5) (verb) To rally means to recover strength, as when a sick person or a losing team gets better.
its sense in the lessons: In citizenship lessons, rallies are a peaceful way for people to show what they believe. In PE, pupils try to keep a long rally going in badminton. In sport stories, a team that «rallied» came back from behind. In money news, prices «rally» when they go up after falling. Phrases: «hold a rally», «rally round», «rally driver», «rally support».
examples from the lessons: Thousands of people went to the climate rally. | The rally drivers raced through the forest. | We had a twenty-shot rally in table tennis. | Friends rallied round when Mum was in hospital. | Our team rallied in the second half and won. | Grandpa was very ill, but he has rallied. | The candidate gave a speech at the rally.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural noun: rallies. Verb: rallied, rallying (y to ie before -ed and -s). «Rally round» (UK) means to help someone in trouble together.

part of speech: noun (rap, uncountable — music; a rap, raps); verb (rap, raps, rapped, rapping)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Rap is a kind of music where words are spoken quickly in rhythm over a beat, instead of being sung. 2) (verb) To rap means to perform this kind of music. 3) A rap is a quick, sharp knock or hit, as in «a rap on the door». 4) (verb) To rap means to knock or hit quickly and sharply. 5) (informal) «A rap on the knuckles» is a mild telling-off; «take the rap» means to take the blame or punishment, often for someone else. 6) (US, informal) A rap sheet is a police record of crimes.
its sense in the lessons: In music and English lessons, rap shows rhyme, rhythm and wordplay; pupils may write their own raps about a topic. In stories, «a rap at the door» announces a visitor. In everyday talk, «he took the rap for his brother» means he got the blame. Phrases: «rap music», «a rap at the door», «take the rap», «a bad rap» (a bad reputation, often unfair).
examples from the lessons: We wrote a rap about the times tables. | There was a sharp rap at the window. | The teacher rapped on the desk for silence. | My brother loves rap music. | I took the rap for breaking the vase, but it was the dog. | Spiders get a bad rap, but most are harmless. | She can rap really fast without missing a word.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb doubles the p: rapped, rapping. Homophone trap: «wrap» (cover with paper) sounds the same as «rap» (knock or music). Rap music is uncountable; one song is «a rap».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A recommendation is advice about what someone should do, as in «the doctor's recommendation is rest». 2) A recommendation is a suggestion that something or someone is good, like a book, film or worker. 3) (formal) A letter of recommendation says good things about a person who is applying for a job or school.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, friends give recommendations for books, games and films; apps and websites also show recommendations based on what you have watched, made by computer programs. In science and report writing, a final section may give recommendations. In online safety, pupils learn that app recommendations are made to keep you watching. Phrases: «on someone's recommendation», «make a recommendation», «letter of recommendation».
examples from the lessons: Thanks for the book recommendation; I loved it! | The doctor's recommendation was to drink more water. | I tried the café on my friend's recommendation. | The report ends with three recommendations. | The video app's recommendations kept me watching too long. | The teacher wrote a letter of recommendation for the music school. | My recommendation is to start your homework early.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun. Spelling: one c, double m: re-co-mm-end-ation. Verb: recommend. Common mistake: «recommend me a book» is less standard than «recommend a book to me».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A rehearsal is a practice of a play, concert, dance or show before the real performance. 2) A dress rehearsal is the last full practice, done in costume as if it were real. 3) A rehearsal can be any practice for an important event, like a fire drill or practising a speech.
its sense in the lessons: In school, rehearsals happen before nativity plays, concerts, assemblies and school shows. In stories, rehearsals bring nerves, mistakes and funny moments. In everyday life, «a rehearsal» of a wedding or speech helps things run smoothly. Phrases: «dress rehearsal», «in rehearsal», «rehearsal time».
examples from the lessons: We have a rehearsal for the school play after lunch. | The dress rehearsal went wrong, but the real show was perfect. | The band needs more rehearsal before the concert. | I forgot my lines at rehearsal. | The fire drill is a rehearsal for a real emergency. | The choir stayed late for an extra rehearsal.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable (a rehearsal) or uncountable (more rehearsal). Verb: rehearse. Spelled «re-hear-sal», with «hear» inside, but it is not about hearing again.

part of speech: verb (rue, rues, rued, ruing); noun (rue — a plant; la rue — French)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal, literary) To rue something means to feel sorry about it and wish it had not happened, as in «you'll rue the day». 2) Rue is a strong-smelling herb with yellow flowers and bluish leaves, used in the past as a medicine. 3) (French) «Rue» is the French word for street, as in «rue de la Paix»; to an English ear it sounds a bit like «roo» with a tight, rounded mouth, and it is not an English word for street.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, a villain may threaten, «You'll rue the day you crossed me!», meaning you will regret it. In history and Shakespeare-style literature, rue was a symbol of sorrow. In French lessons and on French street signs, «rue» means street. Phrases: «rue the day», «la rue».
examples from the lessons: You'll rue the day you laughed at me! | He rued his decision not to bring a coat. | The team rued their missed chances. | Rue grew in the old herb garden. | The bakery is on the Rue de Rivoli in Paris. | In French, «la rue» means «the street».
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: rued, ruing (or rueing). It is formal and old-fashioned; everyday English says «regret». Related: rueful (sorry, regretful). Homophone: «roo» (Australian slang for kangaroo).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A sapphire is a precious stone, usually a clear, deep blue, used in jewellery. 2) (adjective) Sapphire describes a bright, deep blue colour, as in «sapphire eyes» or «a sapphire sea». 3) Sapphires can also be pink, yellow or other colours, except red, which is called a ruby.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on rocks and minerals, sapphire is a very hard gemstone, harder than most things except diamond. In stories, sapphires appear in crowns and treasure chests, and «sapphire» paints a rich blue sea or sky. A «sapphire wedding anniversary» is after 45 years of marriage. Phrases: «sapphire ring», «sapphire blue».
examples from the lessons: The queen's crown was set with sapphires. | The sea was a deep sapphire blue. | Sapphires are very hard, so they don't scratch easily. | Gran's ring has a small sapphire in the middle. | Rubies and sapphires are made of the same mineral. | Some phone screens and watch faces use man-made sapphire glass.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun. Spelled with double p and «ph»: s-a-p-p-h-i-r-e. Pronounced «SAF-fire». Ruby and sapphire are both forms of the mineral corundum.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A scarecrow is a figure made to look like a person, often stuffed with straw and dressed in old clothes, put in a field to scare birds away from crops. 2) (informal) Someone who looks thin and messy can be jokingly called a scarecrow.
its sense in the lessons: In farming and science lessons, scarecrows are an old, simple way to protect crops from birds like crows. In stories and festivals, scarecrows are characters, such as the Scarecrow in «The Wizard of Oz», who wanted a brain, and in village scarecrow festivals. Phrases: «scarecrow festival», «like a scarecrow».
examples from the lessons: The farmer put a scarecrow in the cornfield. | We made a scarecrow for the school garden. | The crows weren't scared of the scarecrow at all. | In «The Wizard of Oz», the Scarecrow wants a brain. | Our village holds a scarecrow competition every summer. | After the windy walk, my hair made me look like a scarecrow.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun; one word: scare + crow. Plural: scarecrows.

part of speech: word (Mandarin, pinyin: shàng; also Shang, a name in Chinese history)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (Mandarin, pinyin) «Shàng» means «up», «on» or «above», and also «to go up» or «to go to», as in «shàng xué» (go to school); to an English ear it sounds like «shahng», and it is not an English word. 2) (Mandarin) «Shàng» can mean «last» or «previous», as in «shàng ge yuè» (last month), and «Shànghǎi» is the city name meaning «on the sea». 3) (history) The Shang was an early dynasty (ruling family) of ancient China, famous for bronze work and writing on oracle bones. 4) (a name) Shang is also a Chinese surname and given name.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons on ancient China, the Shang dynasty is known for the earliest Chinese writing found on bones and shells, used to ask questions about the future. In Mandarin lessons, «shàng» is one of the first words learned, in phrases about going to school or going upstairs. Phrases: «the Shang dynasty», «shàng xué», «Shanghai».
examples from the lessons: The Shang dynasty ruled part of ancient China. | Shang kings asked questions by writing on oracle bones. | In Mandarin, «shàng» means up. | «Wǒ shàng xué» means «I go to school». | The city name Shanghai means «on the sea». | Our museum has a bronze pot from the Shang period.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Not an English word. In pinyin the mark on the «a» (shàng) shows a falling tone. Capital S for the dynasty and for names. Do not confuse with «shanghai» (old English slang: to trick someone onto a ship).

part of speech: noun (a silhouette, silhouettes); verb (silhouette, silhouettes, silhouetted, silhouetting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A silhouette is the dark shape or outline of someone or something seen against a brighter background, like a person standing in front of a sunset. 2) A silhouette is a picture of a person or thing cut out of black paper or painted all black, showing only the outline. 3) (verb) To be silhouetted means to appear as a dark shape against a light background. 4) In fashion, a silhouette is the overall shape of a piece of clothing.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about light and shadows, silhouettes show that light cannot pass through solid objects. In art, pupils make silhouette pictures against bright sunset backgrounds. In stories, «a silhouette in the doorway» adds mystery, since we cannot see the face. Phrases: «in silhouette», «silhouetted against».
examples from the lessons: The castle was silhouetted against the orange sky. | We painted sunset backgrounds and added black silhouettes of trees. | A tall silhouette appeared in the doorway. | Can you guess the animal from its silhouette? | The old portrait was a silhouette cut from black paper. | The birds made dark silhouettes on the telephone wire.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun. Tricky spelling: s-i-l-h-o-u-e-t-t-e (silent h, «ou», double t, final e). Pronounced «sil-oo-ET». A silhouette is the dark object itself; a shadow is the dark shape it casts on a surface.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Sincerely means honestly and truly, meaning what you say, as in «I sincerely hope you feel better». 2) «Yours sincerely» (UK, Ireland, Australia) or «Sincerely» (US, Canada) is a polite way to end a formal letter or email, before your name.
its sense in the lessons: In English writing lessons, pupils learn letter layout: in the UK, use «Yours sincerely» when you know the person's name (Dear Mrs Patel) and «Yours faithfully» when you do not (Dear Sir or Madam). In everyday life, «sincerely» makes thanks or apologies sound honest. Phrases: «Yours sincerely», «sincerely hope», «sincerely apologise».
examples from the lessons: I sincerely hope you enjoy the party. | Yours sincerely, Amy Brown. | He sincerely apologised for breaking the window. | We sincerely thank everyone who helped clear the park. | She said sorry sincerely, so I forgave her. | Sincerely, Jordan (at the end of a US letter).
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from «sincere» + «-ly»; keep the «e»: sincerely, not «sincerly». Noun: sincerity. UK rule: «Dear Mr Smith» → «Yours sincerely»; «Dear Sir or Madam» → «Yours faithfully».

part of speech: noun (a slur, slurs); verb (slur, slurs, slurred, slurring)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To slur means to speak words unclearly, so the sounds run together, for example when someone is very tired, ill or drunk. 2) A slur is an insult or unkind remark that damages someone's reputation, as in «a slur on his good name». 3) A slur is a nasty, hurtful word used against a group of people, such as because of their race, religion or disability; using slurs is bullying and can be against the law. 4) (music) A slur is a curved line over notes showing they should be played or sung smoothly together.
its sense in the lessons: In health and safety lessons, slurred speech can be a warning sign of a stroke, so you should get help fast (call emergency services). In PSHE lessons, pupils learn that slurs hurt people and should be reported. In music lessons, a slur is a smooth curve over notes. Phrases: «slurred speech», «a racial slur», «a slur on someone's character».
examples from the lessons: His speech was slurred because he had just woken from the operation. | Using slurs about someone's race is never OK. | The newspaper's story was a slur on her good name. | Slurred speech can be a sign of a stroke, so call for help quickly. | In music, play the notes under the slur smoothly. | The teacher told the class that slurs are a kind of bullying.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb doubles the r: slurred, slurring. Countable noun: a slur, slurs. Speaking unclearly from tiredness is not the same as using a slur (an insult); the meanings are very different.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Sonic means to do with sound or sound waves, as in «a sonic boom». 2) (science) Sonic speed is the speed of sound; «supersonic» means faster than sound and «subsonic» slower. 3) Sonic the Hedgehog is a famous fast blue character in video games.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, a «sonic boom» is the loud bang made when a plane flies faster than sound; sound travels at about 340 metres per second in air. In everyday life, sonic toothbrushes vibrate very fast. In games, Sonic is known for speed. Phrases: «sonic boom», «sonic toothbrush», «supersonic».
examples from the lessons: The jet broke the sound barrier with a loud sonic boom. | Bats use sonic signals to find their way. | My sonic toothbrush buzzes very fast. | Concorde was a supersonic passenger plane. | Sonic the Hedgehog collects gold rings. | Sound in air goes about 340 metres every second.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective. Related: supersonic, ultrasonic, subsonic. In maths problems about sound, distance = speed × time; at about 340 m/s, thunder heard 3 seconds after lightning is about 1 kilometre away.

part of speech: noun (the southeast, the South-East); adjective (southeast, southeastern); adverb (southeast); also south-east
meaning for a pupil: 1) Southeast is the direction halfway between south and east on a compass. 2) The southeast of a place is the part of it in that direction, as in «the southeast of England». 3) (adjective) Southeast describes things in or from that direction, like a southeast wind, which blows from the southeast. 4) Southeast Asia is the region including countries such as Thailand, Vietnam, Malaysia and Indonesia.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and maths lessons, pupils use the eight compass points (N, NE, E, SE, S, SW, W, NW); southeast is at 135 degrees clockwise from north, written SE. In weather reports, a «southeast wind» comes from the southeast. Phrases: «to the southeast», «south-east of», «Southeast Asia», «the South East».
examples from the lessons: The wind is blowing from the southeast. | Kent is in the southeast of England. | Turn to face southeast on your compass. | Our holiday was in Southeast Asia, in Thailand. | The town lies ten miles south-east of the city. | On the map, the beach is in the southeast corner. | Melbourne is in the southeast of Australia.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK style often writes «south-east» with a hyphen; US style «southeast». Abbreviation: SE. In maths, SE is 135° clockwise from north; turning from north to southeast clockwise is three-eighths of a full turn. A «southeast wind» blows from the southeast, not towards it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Spontaneously means doing something suddenly, without planning it first, because you feel like it, as in «the crowd spontaneously started clapping». 2) In science, something happens spontaneously when it happens by itself, without anything from outside causing it at that moment.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and stories, doing something spontaneously, like a surprise picnic, shows fun and freedom. In science lessons, some chemical reactions or changes happen spontaneously. In ethics lessons, a spontaneous act of kindness is one nobody asked for. Phrases: «spontaneously burst into», «act spontaneously».
examples from the lessons: The whole class spontaneously burst into song. | We spontaneously decided to go to the beach. | The fans stood up and cheered spontaneously. | Haystacks can sometimes catch fire spontaneously when they are damp and warm. | She spontaneously hugged the new girl. | The kittens spontaneously started chasing each other.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from «spontaneous» + «-ly». Spelling: s-p-o-n-t-a-n-e-o-u-s-l-y. Noun: spontaneity. Myth trap: humans cannot «spontaneously combust» (burst into flames by themselves); that is a myth.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A studbook is an official record book listing the parents, grandparents and births of animals of a particular breed, especially horses, but also dogs and cattle. 2) Zoos keep studbooks for rare animals so they can choose mates and keep the animals healthy and varied.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on inheritance and conservation, studbooks show how people track animal family trees to avoid breeding close relatives and to protect endangered species like snow leopards. In horse racing, a famous studbook records Thoroughbred racehorses. Phrases: «the General Stud Book», «in the studbook», «zoo studbook».
examples from the lessons: Every Thoroughbred foal is recorded in the studbook. | The zoo checked the studbook before pairing the snow leopards. | The pony's studbook shows its grandfather was a champion. | Studbooks help stop rare animals breeding with close relatives. | The dog's name was added to the breed's studbook. | Keepers around the world share one studbook for the red pandas.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun, usually one word (sometimes «stud book»). «Stud» here means a farm where animals are kept for breeding. It is like a family tree for animals.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A dark, cooler patch that appears for a while on the surface of the Sun. 2) (informal, UK) A sunny place where people go on holiday.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons sunspots show that the Sun is not a smooth, calm ball: its surface changes, and the number of sunspots rises and falls in a cycle of about eleven years. Scientists count them to study the Sun's activity, which can cause bright auroras on Earth. In travel talk «a holiday sunspot» means a warm, sunny resort. Phrases: «sunspot cycle», «solar flares and sunspots».
examples from the lessons: Sunspots look dark only because they are cooler than the gas around them. | You must never look straight at the Sun to find sunspots. | Astronomers project the Sun's image onto paper to see sunspots safely. | The number of sunspots goes up and down about every eleven years. | A big sunspot can be wider than the whole Earth. | Lots of sunspots can mean more northern lights. | Spain is a favourite sunspot for families from Ireland in summer.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: one sunspot, two sunspots. One word, not «sun spot». A sunspot is still extremely hot; it is only cooler than the rest of the Sun's surface. Safety: never look at the Sun directly or through binoculars to see one.

part of speech: adjective (superb; more superb, most superb — rare); adverb form: superbly
meaning for a pupil: 1) Extremely good; excellent. 2) Very grand and beautiful to look at.
its sense in the lessons: A strong word of praise: in stories and reports it tells the reader something was far better than ordinary. Teachers write «Superb work!» on a page; sports commentators say «a superb goal». It is stronger than «good» and «great» and a little more formal than «awesome». Phrases: «in superb condition», «a superb view», «superb!».
examples from the lessons: What a superb drawing of the dragon! | The goalkeeper made a superb save in the last minute. | From the top of the hill there was a superb view of the lake. | Your spelling test was superb — full marks. | The castle stands in superb grounds with gardens and a maze. | She sang superbly at the school concert. | The old bike is still in superb condition.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually not used with «very» because it already means «extremely good» (say «absolutely superb»). Stress on the second syllable: su-PERB. Do not confuse with «super» (informal, «really good») or «superior» (better than another).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (UK, Ireland) A large maple tree with five-pointed leaves and winged seeds that spin like helicopters as they fall. 2) (USA, Canada) A tall plane tree with bark that peels off in patches of white, green and brown. 3) (Bible) A kind of fig tree in the Middle East; in the story of Zacchaeus, a short man climbs a sycamore to see Jesus. 4) The pale wood of these trees, used for furniture and kitchen spoons.
its sense in the lessons: In nature lessons the sycamore is the tree whose «helicopter» seeds children throw in the air to watch them twirl; this shows how seeds are spread by the wind. In Bible lessons Zacchaeus climbs a sycamore (sycomore) fig tree. The same name means different trees in Britain and in North America, so the place matters. Phrases: «sycamore seeds», «sycamore helicopters».
examples from the lessons: We threw sycamore seeds from the bridge and watched them spin down. | The sycamore in the playground gives lots of shade in summer. | In autumn the sycamore leaves turn yellow and fall. | The sycamores along the river in Ohio have white, patchy bark. | Zacchaeus was too short to see over the crowd, so he climbed a sycamore tree. | My wooden spoon is made of sycamore. | Seeds with wings, like the sycamore's, can travel far from the parent tree.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable for trees (a sycamore, two sycamores), uncountable for the wood. In the Bible the old spelling «sycomore» is sometimes used for the fig tree. Do not mix up with «sick» or «more»: it is one word, SIK-uh-more.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A small monkey from the rainforests of Central and South America, with silky fur and a long tail; some, like the golden lion tamarin, have a bright mane.
its sense in the lessons: In science and nature lessons tamarins appear in topics about rainforests, food chains and endangered animals. The golden lion tamarin is a famous example of an animal saved by zoos and protected forests. They live in family groups and the fathers often carry the babies. Phrases: «golden lion tamarin», «cotton-top tamarin», «emperor tamarin».
examples from the lessons: A tamarin is small enough to sit in your hands. | The golden lion tamarin has orange fur like a little lion. | Tamarins eat fruit, insects and tree sap. | At the zoo we saw a family of tamarins jumping between branches. | The emperor tamarin has a long white moustache. | Tamarin fathers often carry the twin babies on their backs. | Cutting down the rainforest puts tamarins in danger.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one tamarin, two tamarins. Do not confuse with «tamarind», a fruit tree, or «tambourine», a musical instrument.

part of speech: noun (a Tatar, Tatars; Tatar — the language); adjective (Tatar)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A member of a Turkic people who live mainly in Tatarstan in Russia, and also in Crimea (Crimean Tatars) and other countries. 2) The language spoken by Tatars. 3) adjective Belonging to these people, their language or their culture.
its sense in the lessons: In history and geography lessons Tatars appear as a people with a long history in Eastern Europe and Central Asia. Crimean Tatars are the native people of Crimea in Ukraine; many were forced out of their homes in 1944 and many still suffer under Russian occupation. «Steak tartare» and «tartar sauce» come from an old spelling of the name. Usually written with a capital letter: Tatar.
examples from the lessons: Tatars have lived in Crimea for hundreds of years. | Kazan is the capital of Tatarstan, where many Tatars live. | She speaks Tatar with her grandmother. | Crimean Tatar food includes a pastry called chebureki. | The Tatar language is related to Turkish. | We read about Tatar horsemen in our history book.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spell it with a capital letter: Tatar, Tatars. The older spelling «Tartar» is now seen as wrong for the people. Do not confuse with «tartar», the hard stuff the dentist scrapes off teeth, or «tartar sauce».

part of speech: adjective (thrilled; more thrilled); also the past form of the verb thrill (thrill, thrills, thrilled, thrilling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Very happy and excited about something. 2) (verb, past) Gave someone a strong feeling of excitement: «The ride thrilled us».
its sense in the lessons: In stories «thrilled» tells the reader a character is delighted, often about good news, a present or a surprise. In everyday talk «I'm thrilled» is a strong way of saying «I'm very pleased». Said with a flat voice, «Oh, I'm thrilled» can be sarcastic and mean the opposite. Phrases: «thrilled to bits» (UK), «thrilled with», «thrilled about», «thrilled to hear».
examples from the lessons: I was thrilled when I got a puppy for my birthday. | Mum is thrilled with my school report. | The team were thrilled to win the cup. | Grandad was thrilled to bits with the card we made. | The fireworks thrilled the crowd. | We are thrilled that you can come to the party. | «Another maths test? I'm thrilled,» said Tom, rolling his eyes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Use with «with» for a thing (thrilled with the gift), «about» or «at» for news, «to» + verb (thrilled to see you). Stronger than «pleased» or «happy». Sarcasm trap: the tone of voice can turn it into its opposite.

part of speech: adjective (titanic; more titanic); proper noun (the Titanic)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Extremely big, strong or important; huge. 2) the Titanic: a giant British passenger ship that hit an iceberg and sank in the North Atlantic on its first voyage in 1912; more than 1,500 people died. 3) In Greek myths, to do with the Titans, a race of giant gods.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons the Titanic is a famous disaster that taught people about safety at sea: there were not enough lifeboats, and afterwards the rules changed. As an ordinary adjective «titanic» describes something enormous — «a titanic struggle», «a titanic effort». Phrases: «the sinking of the Titanic», «a titanic battle».
examples from the lessons: The Titanic sank after hitting an iceberg in 1912. | People said the Titanic was unsinkable, but they were wrong. | There were not enough lifeboats on the Titanic for everyone. | The final was a titanic battle between the two best teams. | It took a titanic effort to clear the snow from the whole street. | In the myth, the gods fought a titanic war against the Titans. | My little brother's tantrum was titanic.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital T and «the» for the ship: the Titanic. Small t for the adjective. Myth trap: the ship was never really «unsinkable»; that was a boast. «Titanic» is related to «titanium», a strong metal named after the Titans.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person whose job is to change writing from one language into another. 2) A computer program or app that changes words from one language into another. 3) (general) Someone who puts something difficult into easier words for others.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life translators help people read books, signs and documents written in other languages; in lessons about languages and jobs it is a career for people who know two or more languages well. A person who changes spoken words on the spot is usually called an interpreter. Phrases: «work as a translator», «a translator app», «online translator».
examples from the lessons: My aunt is a translator who turns German books into English. | The Harry Potter books were changed into many languages by translators. | We used a translator app to read the menu in Spain. | A good translator knows both languages very well. | Online translators sometimes make funny mistakes. | My big sister was my translator when the doctor used hard words.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a translator, translators. Translator = writing; interpreter = speech (but people often mix them). Do not spell «translater». Machine translators can be wrong, so check important words.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To open something that was folded so it lies flat or spreads out. 2) (of a story or events) To happen or become known little by little. 3) (of a leaf, flower or wing) To open out.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life you unfold a map, a letter or a towel. In stories and the news «events unfolded» means things happened one after another and we learnt about them slowly. In maths, unfolding a paper shape or a box shows its net. Phrases: «unfold a map», «as the story unfolds», «watch events unfold».
examples from the lessons: Unfold the map so we can find the beach. | She unfolded the letter and began to read. | As the story unfolds, we find out who the thief is. | We watched the race unfold on the big screen. | In spring the new leaves unfold on the trees. | The butterfly slowly unfolded its wings. | If you unfold the cereal box, you can see its net.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: unfolded, unfolding. The opposite of «fold». The prefix «un-» here means «undo», not «not». For a story it is often used without an object: «the plot unfolds».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Not held up by anything, so it might fall. 2) Not backed by facts or proof: an unsupported claim. 3) Without help from other people. 4) (computers) Not able to work with a certain device or program, or no longer looked after by the company that made it.
its sense in the lessons: In science and history lessons «unsupported» warns that a statement has no evidence, so we should not trust it yet. In building and safety it means something has nothing holding it up. On computers you may see «unsupported file type» or «this browser is unsupported». Phrases: «unsupported claims», «left unsupported», «unsupported file format».
examples from the lessons: The shelf was unsupported at one end and it crashed down. | The teacher said my answer was unsupported because I gave no evidence. | Don't believe unsupported rumours you see online. | The baby can now sit unsupported for a few seconds. | The game would not start on the old computer: «unsupported device». | Many single parents feel unsupported.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Made of un- + supported. Not used with «very». In science and reports it is a polite way to say «not proven». Do not confuse with «unsporting», which means not fair in sport.

part of speech: verb (weep, weeps, wept, weeping); noun (a weep — rare, informal: «a good weep»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To cry, letting tears fall, usually because you are sad. 2) (of a wound or surface) To let out a slow drip of liquid. 3) (Bible, literature) To cry in grief; «Jesus wept» is the shortest verse in many English Bibles.
its sense in the lessons: «Weep» is a more serious or old-fashioned word for «cry», used in stories, poems and the Bible; in everyday talk children say «cry». It tells the reader someone is deeply sad. «Weep for joy» means crying because you are happy. In the UK «Jesus wept!» is also said as a mild swear when annoyed, which some Christians find rude. Phrases: «weep for joy», «weep over», «it makes you weep».
examples from the lessons: The princess began to weep when she lost her ring. | She wept for joy when her dad came home from the army. | The old man wept at his wife's funeral. | In the Bible, Jesus wept when his friend Lazarus died. | The cut on my knee was weeping a little. | It's enough to make you weep — the whole homework got deleted!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular: weep → wept (not «weeped»). Weep is more formal or literary than cry. «Jesus wept!» as an exclamation is mild swearing (UK, Australia); avoid it in school.

part of speech: verb form (-ing of weep); adjective (weeping); noun (weeping — uncountable)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Crying with tears. 2) adjective Describes a tree whose branches hang down towards the ground, like a weeping willow. 3) adjective Describes a wound or sore that lets out liquid. 4) noun The sound or act of crying.
its sense in the lessons: In stories «weeping» shows deep sadness; in nature lessons «weeping willow» is a tree with long drooping branches beside rivers and ponds. Phrases: «weeping willow», «weeping and wailing», «a weeping wound».
examples from the lessons: The boy was weeping because his kite was lost. | A weeping willow hangs over the duck pond. | We heard weeping from the next room. | The nurse cleaned the weeping cut and put a plaster on. | The weeping cherry in our garden has pink flowers in spring. | In the Bible story there was weeping when the people heard the news.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From weep (past: wept). As an adjective it comes before the noun: a weeping willow. «Weeping» trees are not sad — the name is about the shape of their branches.

part of speech: noun (woodwind — the group, uncountable; a woodwind instrument, woodwinds); adjective (woodwind)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The family of musical instruments played by blowing, mostly with a reed or across a hole: flute, recorder, clarinet, oboe, bassoon and saxophone. 2) The players of these instruments in an orchestra or band.
its sense in the lessons: In music lessons the orchestra is split into families: strings, woodwind, brass and percussion. Woodwind instruments were first made of wood, but some, like the flute and the saxophone, are now metal and are still woodwind because of how the sound is made. The recorder is many children's first woodwind instrument. Phrases: «the woodwind section», «woodwind instruments».
examples from the lessons: The recorder is a woodwind instrument. | The clarinet and the oboe both belong to the woodwind family. | In the orchestra the woodwind sit behind the violins. | A flute is made of metal but it is still woodwind. | The woodwind played the bird song in «Peter and the Wolf». | My brother is learning the saxophone, which counts as woodwind.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable when it means the group (the woodwind is/are…). Trap: woodwind is not about material; brass instruments use buzzing lips, woodwind uses a reed or blowing across an edge. One word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) the ABC (or ABCs): the alphabet, the letters A to Z. 2) The ABC of something: the simplest basic facts about it. 3) (abbreviation) ABC is also the name of big TV and radio companies: the Australian Broadcasting Corporation and the American Broadcasting Company. 4) «Easy as ABC» means very easy.
its sense in the lessons: In early lessons children learn their ABC or ABCs and sing the alphabet song. In everyday talk «the ABC of cooking» means the basics. In Australia «the ABC» usually means the national TV and radio. Phrases: «learn your ABCs», «as easy as ABC», «ABC book».
examples from the lessons: My little sister is learning her ABC. | We sang the ABC song in nursery. | This book teaches the ABC of looking after a pet. | Fractions are as easy as ABC once you understand them. | We watched the news on the ABC in Sydney. | An ABC book has a picture for every letter.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually written in capitals: ABC. Say it as three letters: «ay-bee-see». In the USA «ABCs» is common, in the UK «ABC». Not a word in its own right but letters used as a name.

part of speech: noun (an acrostic, acrostics); adjective (an acrostic poem)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A poem or puzzle in which the first letters of each line, read downwards, spell a word, often the subject of the poem. 2) A word puzzle built in the same way.
its sense in the lessons: In English and literacy lessons children write acrostic poems: they write a word like SPRING down the side and start each line with one of its letters. It shows how to plan writing and to choose words. In the Bible some Psalms are acrostics in Hebrew, each verse starting with the next letter of the alphabet. Phrases: «write an acrostic poem», «acrostic for your name».
examples from the lessons: We wrote an acrostic poem using the letters of our names. | In my acrostic for CAT, the first line starts with C. | Read the first letters downwards to find the hidden word. | Psalm 119 is an acrostic in Hebrew. | Our class made acrostics for the word AUTUMN. | An acrostic doesn't have to rhyme.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Use «an»: an acrostic. Stress: a-CROS-tic. Each line usually starts with a capital letter so the hidden word stands out.

part of speech: adjective (alpine; Alpine); noun (an alpine — a mountain plant)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To do with high mountains, especially the Alps in Europe. 2) Alpine: belonging to the Alps themselves. 3) noun A small plant that grows high on mountains. 4) (sport) Alpine skiing: racing down slopes, as opposed to cross-country skiing.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons alpine describes high, cold mountain places above the trees, with snow, meadows and special plants and animals. In sport «alpine skiing» is downhill racing. Gardeners grow «alpines» in rock gardens. Phrases: «alpine meadow», «alpine village», «alpine plants», «alpine skiing».
examples from the lessons: We stayed in an alpine village in Switzerland. | Alpine meadows are full of flowers in summer. | Ibex and marmots are alpine animals. | Grandma grows little alpines in her rock garden. | Alpine skiers race down steep slopes. | The air is thin and cold in the alpine zone above the trees.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital A when it means the Alps (the Alpine region), small a for any high mountains. Use «an»: an alpine plant. Not «alpin».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A short, interesting or funny story about a real event or person. 2) (formal) A story from one person's experience used as evidence, which may not be true in general.
its sense in the lessons: In speaking and writing lessons pupils learn to start a talk with an anecdote to catch interest. In science, «anecdotal evidence» (one person's story) is weaker than a proper test with many cases. Phrases: «tell an anecdote», «a funny anecdote», «anecdotal evidence».
examples from the lessons: Grandad told us an anecdote about his first day at school. | The speaker began with a funny anecdote about her dog. | Write an anecdote about a time you were surprised. | One anecdote is not enough to prove that a medicine works. | His speech was full of anecdotes about the team. | That's just anecdotal — we need real data.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable, use «an»: an anecdote. Do not confuse with «antidote», a medicine that stops poison. Stress: AN-ec-dote.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A heavy iron block with a flat top on which a blacksmith hammers hot metal into shape. 2) A tiny bone in the middle ear, also called the incus. 3) (weather) The flat, spreading top of a big thundercloud.
its sense in the lessons: In history and stories the anvil belongs to blacksmiths, who hammer horseshoes and swords on it. In science lessons the ear has three tiny bones: hammer, anvil and stirrup. In cartoons an anvil often falls on a character's head. Phrases: «hammer and anvil», «anvil cloud».
examples from the lessons: The blacksmith hammered the red-hot horseshoe on the anvil. | Clang! went the hammer on the anvil. | The anvil is one of the three tiny bones in your ear. | A storm cloud with an anvil top can bring thunder and hail. | In the cartoon an anvil fell on the coyote. | An anvil is so heavy that it doesn't move when you hit it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable, use «an»: an anvil. Stress: AN-vil.

meaning for a pupil: 1) From Asia, used mostly in the names of animals and plants, such as the Asiatic lion or the Asiatic black bear. 2) (old-fashioned, can offend) Of people: Asian.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons «Asiatic» appears in names of animals, like the Asiatic lion that lives in India. For people, today we say «Asian»; «Asiatic» about people is old-fashioned and many find it offensive. Phrases: «Asiatic lion», «Asiatic black bear», «Asiatic cheetah».
examples from the lessons: The Asiatic lion lives only in one forest in India. | The Asiatic black bear has a white V on its chest. | Asiatic cheetahs are very rare. | Asiatic lions are a little smaller than African lions. | Old books sometimes call people «Asiatic», but we say «Asian» now.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital A. Use «Asian» for people. The word survives mainly in species names.

part of speech: noun (an audition, auditions); verb (audition, auditions, auditioned, auditioning)
meaning for a pupil: 1) noun A short performance to show whether you are good enough for a part in a play, a band, a choir or a show. 2) verb To do such a performance, or to watch and judge people doing it. 3) (science) The sense of hearing (formal).
its sense in the lessons: In school life auditions happen before the school play or the choir: children sing or act and the teachers choose. TV talent shows begin with auditions. Phrases: «go to an audition», «audition for a part», «pass the audition».
examples from the lessons: I have an audition for the school play on Friday. | She auditioned for the part of Dorothy. | Fifty children came to the choir auditions. | My hands were shaking at the audition. | The teachers auditioned everyone who wanted to sing a solo. | He didn't get the part, but he'll audition again next year.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Use «an»: an audition. You audition FOR a part. Regular verb: auditioned. Related to «audio» and «audience» — all about hearing.

part of speech: noun (autocorrect — uncountable); verb (autocorrect, autocorrects, autocorrected, autocorrecting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A tool in phones and computers that changes words it thinks are spelled wrong while you type. 2) verb To change a word in this way.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life autocorrect helps with spelling but also makes funny or embarrassing mistakes by putting the wrong word in. In lessons about computers, children learn to check their writing because autocorrect is not always right. Phrases: «turn off autocorrect», «autocorrect fail», «blame autocorrect».
examples from the lessons: Autocorrect changed «ducking» into something silly. | My phone autocorrected my friend's name into «Kitty». | Don't trust autocorrect — read your message before you send it. | I turned off autocorrect when I was writing in French. | Sorry, that was autocorrect, not me! | Autocorrect can't tell «their» from «there» very well.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable as a noun. Regular verb. Trap: autocorrect only checks if a word exists, not if it is the right word, so homophones like «their/there» slip through.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A piece of paper or plastic money printed by a country's bank, such as a £10 note or a $20 bill.
its sense in the lessons: In maths money problems banknotes stand for larger amounts than coins: a £5 note, a $10 bill. In the UK people say «note», in the USA and Canada «bill». Banknotes have special pictures, threads and holograms so they are hard to copy. Phrases: «a £20 banknote», «plastic banknotes», «fake banknotes».
examples from the lessons: She paid with a ten-pound banknote. | Australian banknotes are made of plastic. | The banknote has a hologram so it can't be copied easily. | How many £5 banknotes make £50? Ten. | Canadian banknotes come in different colours. | Grandad keeps an old banknote from Ireland before the euro.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word. Countable. In the UK usually just «a note», in the USA «a bill». In maths: count the value, not the number of notes.

part of speech: noun (a baron, barons; baroness for a woman)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A nobleman of the lowest rank in Britain and some other countries; in the Middle Ages a lord who held land from the king. 2) A very rich and powerful businessman in one industry: an oil baron, a media baron. 3) A powerful criminal boss: a drug baron.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons barons were powerful lords; in 1215 English barons made King John agree to Magna Carta. In the news the word means a powerful person who controls a big business, sometimes in a bad way. Phrases: «the barons and the king», «drug baron», «press baron».
examples from the lessons: The barons forced King John to sign Magna Carta. | A baron owned the castle and the lands around it. | He became a baron and sat in the House of Lords. | The newspaper baron owned ten papers. | The police caught a drug baron at the port. | The Red Baron was a famous German pilot in the First World War.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Woman: baroness. Do not confuse with «barren» (no plants or no fruit) — they sound the same. In the UK a baron is called «Lord Smith», not «Baron Smith», in speech.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Wet, soft and muddy like a bog, so your feet sink in.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and on walks «boggy» ground means you need wellies and must be careful; it is common on moors in Ireland, Scotland and northern England. In stories boggy land slows travellers down. Phrases: «boggy ground», «boggy field», «a boggy path».
examples from the lessons: The field was too boggy for football after the rain. | My boot got stuck in the boggy ground. | Ireland has lots of boggy land with peat. | Stay on the path — it's boggy over there. | The boggy bit by the stream is full of frogs. | This year's sports day was the boggiest ever.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative boggier, boggiest. From «bog». Do not confuse with «bogey» (snot, or a golf score) or «buggy» (a pushchair).

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a brave, confident way, not afraid of danger. 2) In a way that is easy to see: strong and clear. 3) (sometimes) In a cheeky, too confident way.
its sense in the lessons: In stories «boldly» tells the reader that a character acts bravely: «she stepped boldly into the cave». In art and writing «boldly coloured» means bright and strong. The famous line «to boldly go where no man has gone before» comes from Star Trek. Phrases: «boldly go», «boldly coloured», «speak boldly».
examples from the lessons: The knight walked boldly up to the dragon. | She spoke boldly in front of the whole school. | The poster was boldly painted in red and yellow. | The cat boldly stole a sausage from the table. | Write the title boldly so everyone can read it. | He boldly asked the queen a question.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from «bold». «To boldly go» splits the infinitive; it is fine in modern English. Do not confuse with «baldly» (said plainly, without softening).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A small sweet (candy), often with a soft or chocolate centre. 2) (Australia, NZ) A Christmas cracker.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and shops bonbons are little treats in a box. The word is French («bon» = good, said twice). In Australia and New Zealand a «bonbon» is the paper cracker pulled at Christmas dinner. Phrases: «a box of bonbons», «pull a bonbon».
examples from the lessons: Granny gave us a box of chocolate bonbons. | The bonbons were wrapped in shiny paper. | We pulled the bonbons at Christmas lunch in Melbourne and got paper hats. | In the story the witch's house was decorated with bonbons. | Don't eat all the bonbons before dinner!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Can be spelled «bon-bon». From French; the British «bonbons» (like toffee bonbons) are chewy sugar-coated sweets.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A large dark Arctic whale with a huge curved mouth and a very thick layer of blubber; it has no teeth and filters food with baleen.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons the bowhead whale is famous as perhaps the longest-living mammal: some have lived over 200 years. It lives in icy Arctic seas and can break ice with its head. Inuit communities hunt a small number of them in a controlled way. Phrases: «bowhead whale».
examples from the lessons: The bowhead whale can live for more than 200 years. | A bowhead breaks through thin ice to breathe. | Bowheads have baleen instead of teeth. | Its blubber is thicker than your arm is long. | Bowhead whales live in the cold Arctic Ocean. | The bowhead got its name from its curved, bow-shaped head.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Usually «bowhead whale». «Bow» here rhymes with «go» (like a bow for arrows), not with «cow».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (UK, Ireland, Canada, Australia, NZ) A printed paper form you write on to tell your bank to pay money from your account to someone. 2) (US spelling: check) The same thing.
its sense in the lessons: In money lessons a cheque is an older way of paying: you write the amount in figures and words and sign it. Many people now use cards and phone payments instead, but grandparents still post cheques for birthdays. Phrases: «write a cheque», «pay by cheque», «cash a cheque», «a blank cheque» (permission to spend anything).
examples from the lessons: Grandma sent me a cheque for my birthday. | You write the amount in words and numbers on a cheque. | Dad paid in the cheque at the bank. | Hardly any shops take cheques now. | The charity got a giant cheque for £1,000. | Don't sign a blank cheque — anyone could fill in the amount.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK spelling cheque, US spelling check; same sound as «check». In the USA «check» also means the bill in a restaurant. Countable.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A small rodent from the Andes mountains of South America, with very soft, thick grey fur and a bushy tail. 2) The fur of this animal.
its sense in the lessons: In nature lessons chinchillas are animals of the cold, high Andes; their fur is extremely thick to keep them warm. Some families keep them as pets; they clean their fur by rolling in dust, not by taking a bath. Phrases: «a pet chinchilla», «dust bath».
examples from the lessons: A chinchilla has the softest fur of any land animal. | Our pet chinchilla rolls in special dust to keep clean. | Chinchillas come from the Andes mountains. | Chinchillas must not get wet, because their fur takes too long to dry. | Wild chinchillas are now rare because they were hunted for fur. | The chinchilla nibbled a bit of hay.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Spelled with «ch» twice and «ll»; say chin-CHIL-uh. Not a hamster or a rabbit, though it looks a bit like both.

part of speech: verb (chuff, chuffs, chuffed, chuffing); noun (a chuff); adjective: chuffed (UK)
meaning for a pupil: 1) verb To make the puffing sound of a steam train: chuff-chuff. 2) chuffed (UK, informal): very pleased. 3) (UK, rude slang) Bottom; «chuffing» and «chuff me» are mild swear words like «flipping».
its sense in the lessons: In stories steam trains «chuff» along. In British everyday speech «I'm chuffed» or «chuffed to bits» means «I'm very pleased». «Chuffing» (as in «chuffing heck») is a mild, slightly rude word used when annoyed, mostly in northern England; not for school. Phrases: «chuffed to bits», «chuff along».
examples from the lessons: The little steam train chuffed up the hill. | Chuff, chuff, chuff went the engine. | I'm well chuffed with my new bike. (UK) | Mum was chuffed to bits with her present. | «Chuffing heck, it's raining again!» said Uncle Dave. (rude) | The kettle chuffed out steam.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Chuffed» is the common form and means pleased (UK, Ireland, Australia). Strange trap: «not chuffed» means displeased. «Chuffing» as a swear is mild but still rude.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A large, lemon-like citrus fruit with a very thick, bumpy rind, often candied and used in cakes. 2) (French) «citron» means «lemon» in French.
its sense in the lessons: In science and food lessons the citron is one of the oldest citrus fruits; lemons and limes come partly from it. In Jewish tradition a citron (etrog) is used at the festival of Sukkot. In French lessons «citron» is just «lemon», and «citron pressé» is fresh lemonade. Phrases: «candied citron peel».
examples from the lessons: A citron looks like a big, lumpy lemon. | Candied citron peel goes into fruit cake. | A citron has a very thick rind and little juice. | At Sukkot, Jewish families hold a citron called an etrog. | In Paris I ordered a «citron pressé», which is lemon juice with water. | The citron is one of the ancestors of the lemon.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. In French «citron» = lemon, so it is a false friend: an English citron is a different fruit. Say SIT-ron.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A sign at the start of a line of written music that shows how high or low the notes are: the treble clef for higher notes and the bass clef for lower ones.
its sense in the lessons: In music lessons the treble clef (curly, like a fancy G) is used for recorder, violin and right hand on the piano; the bass clef for low instruments and the left hand. Phrases: «treble clef», «bass clef», «G clef», «F clef».
examples from the lessons: Draw a treble clef at the start of the stave. | The bass clef is used for the cello and the tuba. | Piano music has a treble clef on top and a bass clef underneath. | The treble clef curls round the line for G. | In the bass clef, the notes have different names on the same lines.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: clefs. Say «clef» like «cleff». In French «clef» means «key». «Bass» clef sounds like «base», not like the fish «bass».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who takes part in a competition, quiz or game show and tries to win.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and on TV contestants answer questions or perform to win prizes. In school there are contestants in spelling bees, quizzes and talent shows. Phrases: «the next contestant», «game show contestant», «each contestant».
examples from the lessons: There were ten contestants in the spelling bee. | The contestant answered every question right and won a car. | Each contestant had two minutes to sing. | The youngest contestant was only eight. | The judges cheered for all the contestants. | She was a contestant on a cooking show for kids.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Ends in -ant, not -ent. Related verb: contest (to compete for, or to argue against).

part of speech: noun (a contrast, contrasts — also uncountable); verb (contrast, contrasts, contrasted, contrasting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) noun A clear difference between two things when you put them side by side. 2) verb To compare two things to show how they are different. 3) verb To be very different from something: «Her red coat contrasted with the white snow». 4) (art, screens) The difference between light and dark parts of a picture.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons «compare and contrast» means write about how things are alike and how they differ. Words like «however», «but» and «whereas» are words of contrast. In art and on screens «contrast» is how much light and dark stand apart. Phrases: «in contrast», «by contrast», «compare and contrast», «a sharp contrast».
examples from the lessons: There's a big contrast between the hot day and the cold night. | Compare and contrast life in a city and in the countryside. | In contrast to his brother, Ben is very quiet. | The black letters contrast well with the yellow paper. | Turn up the contrast so the picture is clearer. | «However» is a word that shows contrast.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stress changes: noun CON-trast, verb con-TRAST. Use «with»: contrast X with Y. «In contrast» and «by contrast» are both correct.

part of speech: noun (a creole, Creole — the people or language); adjective (Creole)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A language that grew from a mix of two or more languages and became the first language of a group of people, such as Haitian Creole or Jamaican Patois. 2) A person of mixed European and African or local descent in the Caribbean or Louisiana. 3) Creole cooking: spicy food from Louisiana in the USA, with rice, peppers and seafood.
its sense in the lessons: In language lessons creoles show how new languages are born when people speaking different languages live together, often after slavery and colonies. They are full, real languages with their own grammar, not «broken» English or French. Phrases: «Haitian Creole», «Creole food», «a French-based creole».
examples from the lessons: Haitian Creole is spoken by millions of people. | A creole is a real language with its own rules. | Jamaican Patois is an English-based creole. | We ate Creole jambalaya in New Orleans. | Many creoles grew up in the Caribbean. | Tok Pisin, a creole, is spoken in Papua New Guinea.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually capital C for names (Haitian Creole). Myth: creoles are not «bad» versions of other languages. Different from a pidgin, which is a simple trade language nobody speaks as a first language.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To do with the customs, beliefs, art, food and way of life of a group of people. 2) To do with art, music, theatre and books.
its sense in the lessons: In geography, history and PSHE lessons «cultural» describes festivals, food, clothes and traditions, and teaches respect for differences. «Cultural events» are concerts, plays and exhibitions. Phrases: «cultural differences», «cultural heritage», «cultural festival», «cultural centre».
examples from the lessons: Diwali is an important cultural festival for many families. | Our class learnt about cultural differences in greetings. | The city has a new cultural centre with a theatre. | Learning a language gives you cultural knowledge too. | The castle is part of our cultural heritage. | Some gestures are polite in one country and rude in another for cultural reasons.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective of «culture». Not «culturel» (that is French). Culturally = in a cultural way.

part of speech: noun (Dakota, the Dakotas; a Dakota — a person); adjective (Dakota)
meaning for a pupil: 1) North Dakota and South Dakota: two states in the middle north of the USA; together «the Dakotas». 2) The Dakota: a Native American people of the Great Plains, part of the Sioux nation; also their language. 3) (a name) Dakota is used as a first name.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons the Dakotas are US states with wide prairies and farms; Mount Rushmore is in South Dakota. In history lessons the Dakota people lived on the plains and hunted buffalo; their land was taken by settlers and the US army. Phrases: «North Dakota», «South Dakota», «the Dakota people».
examples from the lessons: Mount Rushmore is in South Dakota. | North Dakota has very cold winters. | The Dakota people are part of the Sioux nation. | The state is named after the Dakota people. | The word Dakota is often said to mean «friends» or «allies». | My cousin Dakota lives in Texas. (a name)
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always a capital D. «The Dakotas» = the two states. Related peoples: Lakota, Nakota.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A large dog with short white fur covered in black or brown spots. 2) Dalmatian: from Dalmatia, a coastal region of Croatia.
its sense in the lessons: In stories the most famous Dalmatians are in «101 Dalmatians». In history Dalmatians ran beside horse-drawn carriages and fire engines, so they are linked with firefighters in the USA. Puppies are born pure white and their spots appear later. Phrases: «a Dalmatian puppy», «101 Dalmatians».
examples from the lessons: A Dalmatian has black spots on white fur. | Dalmatian puppies are born without spots. | In the film, Cruella wanted the Dalmatians' fur for a coat. | Fire stations in America sometimes keep a Dalmatian. | Dalmatians need lots of exercise. | Split is a city on the Dalmatian coast of Croatia.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Often written with a capital D. Spelled -tian, not -shun or -sion. Dalmatians are not always friendly to strangers; they need training.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Broken pieces left after something has been destroyed or has fallen: bits of wood, stone, glass. 2) Rubbish or small pieces scattered about. 3) (science) Rock and dust, or pieces of old rockets and satellites in space (space debris).
its sense in the lessons: In news and safety lessons debris after a storm, earthquake or crash can be dangerous, so people stay away. In science «space debris» is junk orbiting the Earth. Phrases: «covered in debris», «flying debris», «space debris», «clear the debris».
examples from the lessons: After the storm the road was covered in debris. | Firefighters searched the debris for survivors. | Flying debris can be dangerous in a strong wind. | Space debris circles the Earth very fast. | The beach was full of debris from the shipwreck. | We cleared the debris from the garden.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «a lot of debris», not «debrises». Say DEB-ree (UK) or duh-BREE (US); the s is silent — it comes from French.

part of speech: noun (a defibrillator, defibrillators; informal: a defib)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A machine that gives an electric shock to the chest to make a heart that has stopped beating properly start a normal rhythm again.
its sense in the lessons: In first-aid and safety lessons children learn that public defibrillators (often in a green or yellow box on a wall) can save life when someone collapses with their heart stopped. They talk out loud and tell you exactly what to do, so anyone can use one; you also call 999, 911, 000 or 111 (NZ) and do CPR. Phrases: «public access defibrillator», «AED» (automated external defibrillator).
examples from the lessons: There is a defibrillator outside the leisure centre. | The defibrillator talks and tells you what to do. | Call an ambulance and send someone to get the defibrillator. | Doctors use a defibrillator to restart a heart's rhythm. | Our school has a defibrillator in the office. | You must not touch the person while the defibrillator gives a shock.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Long word: de-FIB-ril-ay-tor. Countable. Also called an AED. Myth from films: it does not restart a heart that is completely flat; it fixes a chaotic rhythm — but you still use it if told to.

part of speech: noun (deportation, deportations — countable and uncountable); verb: deport
meaning for a pupil: 1) Making a person leave a country by law, usually sending them back to the country they came from. 2) (history) Forcing a whole people or group to leave their homes and move far away.
its sense in the lessons: In news and law «deportation» is when a government removes someone who it says is not allowed to stay. In history lessons mass deportations were terrible events, such as the deportation of Crimean Tatars by Stalin in 1944 and the deportation of Jews by the Nazis. Today the news also reports Ukrainian children taken to Russia, which the UN and many countries call illegal deportation. Phrases: «face deportation», «deportation order».
examples from the lessons: The man faced deportation because his visa had run out. | The judge stopped the deportation of the family. | In 1944 the Crimean Tatars suffered mass deportation. | A deportation order says a person must leave the country. | Many people protested against the deportations. | Deportation can split families apart.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable and uncountable. Verb: deport (deported). Do not confuse with «departure» (leaving on your own) or «deportment» (how you stand and behave).

part of speech: noun (a detox, detoxes — also uncountable); verb (detox, detoxes, detoxed, detoxing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A time when a person stops taking a drug or alcohol so their body can get clean of it, often with doctors helping. 2) (informal) A time of eating only healthy food, which some people believe cleans the body. 3) (informal) A break from something: a digital detox is time away from phones and screens.
its sense in the lessons: In health lessons detox in hospital is real medical help for addiction. «Detox diets» and «detox teas» are mostly a marketing myth: your liver and kidneys already clean your blood. A «screen detox» means a break from devices, which can help sleep and mood. Phrases: «go into detox», «digital detox», «detox diet».
examples from the lessons: Dad is doing a digital detox — no phone all weekend. | The singer went into detox to stop drinking. | Doctors help people through detox safely. | Juice detoxes don't really clean your body. | We had a screen detox on our camping trip. | After the holidays Mum said she needed a chocolate detox.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Short for «detoxification». Stress: DEE-tox. Myth: detox drinks and foot pads do not remove «toxins»; your liver and kidneys do that.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Two letters that together make one sound, such as sh in «ship», ch in «chip», th in «thin», ee in «see» and ai in «rain».
its sense in the lessons: In phonics lessons children learn digraphs to read and spell: consonant digraphs (sh, ch, th, ph, wh, ck) and vowel digraphs (ee, oa, ai, oo). A trigraph is three letters making one sound (igh in «night»). «Split digraph» is a-e as in «cake». Phrases: «consonant digraph», «vowel digraph», «split digraph».
examples from the lessons: «Sh» is a digraph in the word «fish». | Find the digraph in «boat». It's «oa». | «Ph» in «phone» is a digraph that sounds like f. | The split digraph i-e makes «bike» say its name. | Underline every digraph in the sentence. | «Th» can sound different in «this» and «thin».
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Di- means two, -graph means writing. Not to be confused with «diagram» or «graph» in maths. A digraph is ONE sound, so «sh» is not s + h.

part of speech: verb (doodle, doodles, doodled, doodling); noun (a doodle, doodles)
meaning for a pupil: 1) verb To draw little pictures or patterns without thinking much, often while doing something else. 2) noun A little drawing made like this. 3) (Google Doodle) A special changing logo on the Google page. 4) A short form of «Labradoodle» or other «-doodle» dogs (informal).
its sense in the lessons: In everyday school life children doodle in the margins of exercise books; teachers may not like it, but some studies say doodling can help people listen. Phrases: «doodle on», «doodle in the margin».
examples from the lessons: I doodled stars all over my rough book. | Stop doodling and finish your sums! | Her doodle of a cat was really cute. | Grandpa doodles while he talks on the phone. | Today's Google Doodle is about a famous scientist. | Our neighbour has a fluffy doodle called Biscuit.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: doodled, doodling. Countable noun. «Yankee Doodle» is an old American song; «doodle» there is an old word for a fool.

part of speech: noun (an el, els); abbreviation (El, the El); (Spanish) el
meaning for a pupil: 1) The name of the letter L. 2) (USA) the El or el: an elevated railway, a train on a raised track above the street, especially in Chicago. 3) (Spanish) «el» means «the» before a masculine noun, as in El Paso or El Niño; it is not an English word. 4) El Niño: a change in the Pacific Ocean that makes the weather unusual around the world.
its sense in the lessons: You meet «El» mostly in names: El Paso, El Salvador, El Niño, Los Angeles. In geography lessons El Niño is a warming of the Pacific that brings floods to some places and droughts to others. In Chicago people ride «the El» to school and work. Sound: like «ell».
examples from the lessons: In Chicago we rode the El over the city streets. | El Paso is a city in Texas; the name is Spanish for «the pass». | El Niño can bring heavy rain to Peru and droughts to Australia. | «El» is the Spanish word for «the». | El Salvador is a small country in Central America. | Write a capital el at the start of «London».
note for the reader of a maths problem: As an English word it is rare. The letter's name is more often spelled «ell». In names it is Spanish and keeps its capital: El Salvador.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The name of the letter L. 2) An old measure of length, about the length of an arm, used for cloth (in England about 45 inches, a little over a metre). 3) (USA) An extension of a building at a right angle, making an L shape.
its sense in the lessons: In history and old stories the ell was a measure for cloth. The proverb «Give him an inch and he'll take an ell» means if you give someone a little, they will take a lot (today usually «a mile»). In lessons about letters, «ell» is how L is named. Phrases: «an ell of cloth».
examples from the lessons: The merchant sold three ells of cloth. | An ell was about the length of a man's arm. | «Give them an inch and they'll take an ell,» said Granny. | The farmhouse has an ell at the back. | Write a small ell and a capital ell.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Use «an»: an ell. Rare today. Do not confuse with «ill», «eel» or «hell».

meaning for a pupil: 1) The punctuation mark of three dots (…) that shows words are missing or that a sentence trails off. 2) (grammar) Leaving out words that are understood, as in «I can swim and so can Tom» (swim is left out).
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons the ellipsis builds suspense in stories («She opened the door slowly…») or shows a pause or unfinished thought. In quotes it marks words cut out. Phrases: «use an ellipsis», «end with an ellipsis».
examples from the lessons: She opened the box and saw… nothing! | Use an ellipsis to make the reader wait. | «Well… I'm not sure,» said Max. | The writer used an ellipsis to leave out part of the quote. | Don't put four dots — an ellipsis has three. | «Want some?» «Yes, please» is an example of ellipsis.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: ellipses (el-IP-seez). Always three dots, not two or five. Do not confuse with «ellipse», an oval shape in maths.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A round red felt hat with a flat top and a black tassel, with no brim, traditional in Turkey, North Africa and the Middle East. 2) Fez (or Fes): a famous old city in Morocco.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons the fez was worn in the Ottoman Empire until Turkey banned it in 1925. In stories and TV it is a fun costume hat; magicians sometimes wear one. Phrases: «wear a fez».
examples from the lessons: The magician wore a red fez with a black tassel. | My grandfather has an old fez from Morocco. | The fez is named after the city of Fez. | In Turkey the fez was banned about a hundred years ago. | Fezzes are cool! said the Doctor in Doctor Who. | The tassel on the fez swung as he danced.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: fezzes (double z). Capital F for the city.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The facts or results someone has discovered after studying, testing or investigating something. 2) (law) What a court or official inquiry decides is true.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons pupils write up their findings after an experiment: what they found out, often with a table or graph. In the news «the findings of a report» are its main results. Phrases: «report your findings», «the findings show», «key findings».
examples from the lessons: Write your findings in the table. | Our findings show that plants grow faster in light. | The scientists shared their findings with the world. | The findings of the report surprised everyone. | The inquiry's findings said the bridge was unsafe. | Present your findings to the class.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually plural: findings. «Findings show», not «shows». Different from «finding» as the verb form of «find».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Used to introduce the first point in a list of reasons or steps.
its sense in the lessons: In writing lessons «firstly» is a time-and-order connective, followed by «secondly», «thirdly» and «finally» or «lastly». It helps the reader follow an argument or instructions. Many writers prefer just «first». Phrases: «firstly … secondly … finally».
examples from the lessons: Firstly, wash your hands. | Firstly, dogs are loyal; secondly, they keep you fit. | Firstly, we will read the poem, then we will write our own. | I want a bike, firstly because it's fun and secondly because it's healthy. | Firstly, put the flour in the bowl.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually starts a sentence and is followed by a comma. Both «first» and «firstly» are correct (UK writers use «firstly» more).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Having a frill: a strip of cloth with folds or waves sewn on the edge. 2) (animals) Having a ruffled flap of skin, like the frilled lizard of Australia.
its sense in the lessons: In nature lessons the frilled lizard (or frill-necked lizard) of northern Australia opens a big umbrella-like collar around its neck to scare enemies. In clothes «frilled» means with a decorative wavy edge. Phrases: «frilled lizard», «frilled shark», «frilled collar».
examples from the lessons: The frilled lizard opened its collar and hissed. | She wore a white frilled blouse. | The frilled shark lives deep in the ocean. | The curtains had frilled edges. | When it's scared, the frilled lizard runs on its back legs.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Also «frilly» (more informal, for clothes). From «frill».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A small jumping insect whose young live inside a blob of froth on plants, called cuckoo spit; also called a spittlebug.
its sense in the lessons: In nature lessons the froghopper is one of the best jumpers on Earth for its size. The white foam seen on plants in spring is «cuckoo spit», made by froghopper young to hide and keep moist — not spit from cuckoos. Phrases: «cuckoo spit», «spittlebug».
examples from the lessons: A froghopper can jump much higher than its own body length. | The foam on the lavender is made by a froghopper nymph. | Froghoppers look a bit like tiny frogs. | Cuckoo spit has nothing to do with cuckoos — it's froghoppers. | We found a froghopper hiding in the bubbles.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable, one word. Myth: cuckoo spit is not bird spit.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Awkward and clumsy in how you behave with other people, saying or doing slightly wrong things. 2) (French) «gauche» means «left» in French: à gauche = to the left.
its sense in the lessons: In stories «gauche» describes a shy or socially clumsy person, often a teenager at a party. In French lessons «tournez à gauche» means «turn left». Sound: «gohsh». Phrases: «a bit gauche», «à gauche» (French).
examples from the lessons: He felt gauche and shy at his first dance. | It was a bit gauche to ask how much her dress cost. | In French, «gauche» means left and «droite» means right. | Tournez à gauche! — Turn left! | Her gauche manners made people smile kindly.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Borrowed from French. Pronounced «gohsh». Opposite in English: «graceful», «smooth». Do not confuse with «gouge» or «gaudy».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A list of hard or special words with their meanings, usually at the back of a book.
its sense in the lessons: In non-fiction reading and science lessons the glossary helps you understand words printed in bold. A glossary is like a small dictionary just for one book or topic. Phrases: «look it up in the glossary», «add to the glossary».
examples from the lessons: Look up «photosynthesis» in the glossary. | The words in bold are explained in the glossary. | Our class made a glossary of space words. | A glossary is in alphabetical order. | The glossary is on page 32. | Add «predator» to your science glossary.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: glossaries. Different from an index, which tells you which pages a word is on, not what it means.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Sad and quiet, looking unhappy and disappointed.
its sense in the lessons: In stories «glum» shows that a character is down, often after bad news, without crying. Phrases: «look glum», «a glum face», «feeling glum».
examples from the lessons: Why do you look so glum? | Tom was glum after losing the match. | The rain made everyone a bit glum. | She sat glumly by the window. | Cheer up, glum face! | The class went glum when break was cancelled.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative glummer, glummest (double m). Milder than «miserable».

part of speech: noun (a gorge, gorges); verb (gorge, gorges, gorged, gorging)
meaning for a pupil: 1) noun A deep, narrow valley with steep rocky sides, usually with a river at the bottom. 2) verb To eat a lot of food greedily until you are very full: «gorge yourself on cake». 3) (old) Your throat; «it makes my gorge rise» means it makes me feel sick.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons gorges are made by rivers cutting through rock over a very long time, like Cheddar Gorge in England or the Grand Canyon. In everyday talk «gorge on sweets» means eat too many. Phrases: «gorge on/oneself», «a river gorge».
examples from the lessons: The river runs through a deep gorge. | We walked along Cheddar Gorge. | Don't gorge yourself on chocolate before dinner. | The bears gorged on salmon before winter. | The gorge was so deep we could hardly see the bottom. | Water carved the gorge over thousands of years.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Rhymes with «George». Verb is regular: gorged. Do not confuse with «gorgeous» (beautiful).

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a very serious way, showing that something is important or worrying. 2) Very badly: gravely ill, gravely injured.
