its sense in the lessons: In stories «gravely» describes a serious voice or face: «the doctor nodded gravely». In news it means very badly hurt or very dangerously ill. Phrases: «gravely ill», «gravely concerned», «spoke gravely».
examples from the lessons: «This is very important,» said the headteacher gravely. | The soldier was gravely wounded. | Grandad was gravely ill but he got better. | She shook her head gravely. | The police are gravely concerned about the missing boy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «grave» (serious). Not related to graves in a churchyard in meaning, though spelled the same. Do not confuse with «gravelly» (rough, like gravel: a gravelly voice).

meaning for a pupil: 1) The Gregorian calendar: the calendar most of the world uses today, introduced by Pope Gregory XIII in 1582, with leap years. 2) Gregorian chant: an old, plain style of church singing without instruments, named after Pope Gregory I.
its sense in the lessons: In history and maths lessons the Gregorian calendar explains leap years: every 4 years, except century years not divisible by 400. In church music lessons Gregorian chant is sung by monks in Latin. Phrases: «Gregorian calendar», «Gregorian chant».
examples from the lessons: We use the Gregorian calendar. | The Gregorian calendar has a leap year every four years. | Britain changed to the Gregorian calendar in 1752 and lost eleven days. | The monks sang Gregorian chant in the abbey. | Some churches still use the older Julian calendar for Christmas.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always capital G. In maths: a year is a leap year if divisible by 4, but century years only if divisible by 400 (2000 was, 1900 was not).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A ring or circle of light drawn around the head of a holy person or angel in pictures. 2) A ring of light around the Sun or Moon, made by ice crystals in the sky. 3) (informal) Behaviour that makes someone seem perfectly good: «Her halo slipped» = she did something naughty.
its sense in the lessons: In church art and Bible pictures saints and angels have haloes. In science a halo round the Moon is caused by light bending in ice crystals in thin clouds. In everyday talk «his halo slipped» is a joke about a good child behaving badly. Phrases: «a halo around the Moon», «halo effect».
examples from the lessons: The angel in the painting has a golden halo. | There was a halo around the Moon last night. | Ice crystals high in the sky can make a halo around the Sun. | My little brother acts like he has a halo, but he ate the cake! | In nativity plays the angels wear tinsel haloes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: haloes or halos — both accepted. Say HAY-lo. Not «hallo» (hello).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Done very quickly, sometimes too quickly, without enough care or thought. 2) Of a person: acting too quickly.
its sense in the lessons: In stories «a hasty decision» or «a hasty retreat» tells the reader someone acted in a hurry. The lesson often is: think before you act. Phrases: «a hasty exit», «a hasty decision», «don't be hasty», «make haste».
examples from the lessons: We made a hasty exit when the dog barked. | Don't make a hasty decision — think it over. | He wrote a hasty note and ran out. | She hastily hid the present behind her back. | «Don't be hasty,» said the wise old owl. | My hasty work was full of mistakes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «haste». Comparative hastier, hastiest. Hastily = in a hurry.

part of speech: noun (a hazel, hazels — the tree); adjective (hazel — the colour)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A small tree or bush that grows hazelnuts. 2) adjective (of eyes) Greenish-brown or light brown. 3) (a name) Hazel is also a girl's name.
its sense in the lessons: In nature lessons hazel bushes grow in hedges and woods; their catkins hang like lambs' tails in late winter and the nuts feed squirrels and dormice. In descriptions, «hazel eyes» are a mixed green-brown. Phrases: «hazel eyes», «hazel catkins», «hazel stick».
examples from the lessons: Squirrels collect nuts from the hazel. | She has hazel eyes. | Hazel catkins appear in February. | He cut a hazel stick to use as a walking stick. | Dormice love hazel woods. | Hazel is my best friend's name.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable for trees. Not to be confused with «haze» (thin mist). The nut is a hazelnut (one word).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (football) Hitting the ball with your head. 2) Text at the top of every page of a document, such as the title or page number. 3) (computers) The first part of a file or email with information about it. 4) (UK, informal) A fall head first: «take a header».
its sense in the lessons: In PE and football a header is a key skill. In computing and in writing reports on a computer, the header is the top area where you put the title or date. Phrases: «score with a header», «header and footer».
examples from the lessons: She scored a brilliant header from the corner. | Put your name in the header of the page. | The header and footer appear on every page. | He took a header off his bike into the bushes. | The email header shows who sent it. | Practise headers with a soft ball.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Opposite of «footer» in documents. Safety: young children should be careful with heading heavy balls; some leagues limit heading for under-12s.

part of speech: noun (headquarters — singular or plural; abbreviation HQ)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The main office or place from which a company, army, police force or organisation is run.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and news the headquarters is where the bosses work. In games and stories «HQ» is the base. Phrases: «police headquarters», «company headquarters», «back to HQ».
examples from the lessons: The company's headquarters are in London. | The spies returned to headquarters. | Our den is the club's secret HQ. | The army set up its headquarters in the old castle. | Police headquarters received the call. | The United Nations headquarters is in New York.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Ends in -s even for one: «a headquarters». Can take a singular or plural verb. Short form: HQ.

part of speech: interjection (ho, ho ho); noun (a ho — rude slang)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A shout to get attention or to show surprise: «Land ho!» means «land ahead!». 2) «Ho ho ho!» is the laugh of Father Christmas (Santa). 3) (rude, slang) A very rude, insulting word for a woman, taken from «whore»; never use it.
its sense in the lessons: In stories sailors shout «Land ho!» when they see land, and Santa laughs «Ho ho ho!». «Westward ho!» means «go west!». The rude slang meaning is offensive and may be heard in songs or films; it is not acceptable at school. Phrases: «Land ho!», «Ho ho ho», «Westward ho!».
examples from the lessons: «Land ho!» shouted the sailor from the mast. | «Ho ho ho! Merry Christmas!» laughed Santa. | Westward Ho! is a village in Devon. | «Ho there!» called the guard. | That word in the song is a rude insult, so we don't say it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Not to be confused with «hoe» (a garden tool). The rude slang meaning is a slur; avoid it. Also not the Mandarin «hé».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A pot for keeping honey. 2) (informal) A place or thing that attracts lots of people, like bees to honey: a tourist honeypot. 3) (computers) A trap set up to catch hackers by pretending to be an easy target.
its sense in the lessons: In stories Winnie-the-Pooh keeps his honey in honeypots. In geography lessons a «honeypot site» is a popular place that gets crowded with visitors, which can cause traffic, litter and damage. Phrases: «honeypot site», «tourist honeypot».
examples from the lessons: Pooh had his head stuck in a honeypot. | The village is a honeypot for tourists in summer. | Honeypot sites need car parks and bins. | The bear licked the honeypot clean. | The company set up a honeypot to catch hackers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word (sometimes «honey pot»). In geography «honeypot» is a key term for tourism problems.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Very famous and seen as a symbol of something, so everyone recognises it. 2) (computers, art) To do with icons or pictures that stand for something.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday talk and the news «iconic» describes famous places, songs, outfits or people — the Eiffel Tower, the Sydney Opera House, a red London bus. It is overused in adverts. In church history, icons are holy pictures, especially in Orthodox churches. Phrases: «an iconic building», «an iconic moment».
examples from the lessons: The Sydney Opera House is an iconic building. | The red phone box is iconic of Britain. | That goal was an iconic moment in football history. | Her yellow raincoat became iconic. | The Statue of Liberty is iconic of New York. | Adverts call everything «iconic» these days.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Use «an»: an iconic... From «icon». Often overused; «famous» or «well-known» is plainer.

part of speech: verb (infer, infers, inferred, inferring); noun: inference
meaning for a pupil: 1) To work out something that is not said directly, using clues and what you already know. 2) (formal) To reach a conclusion from facts or reasoning.
its sense in the lessons: In reading lessons «infer» is a key skill: from clues in the text you work out a character's feelings («His fists were clenched» → he is angry). In science you infer from evidence. Phrases: «infer from», «what can you infer?».
examples from the lessons: From her red eyes, we can infer that she had been crying. | What can you infer about the weather from the picture? | Detectives infer who did it from clues. | I inferred that Mum was cross because she slammed the door. | Scientists infer what dinosaurs ate from their teeth.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double r: inferred, inferring. Common confusion: the writer or speaker IMPLIES (hints); the reader INFERS (works out).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A sudden good idea, or something that gives you ideas for writing, art or music. 2) A person or thing that makes you want to do well or be like them. 3) (Bible, church) Christians believe the Bible was written with the help of God's Spirit; this is called inspiration. 4) (science) Breathing in.
its sense in the lessons: In writing lessons pupils look for inspiration for stories in pictures, music or nature. In PSHE a role model is «an inspiration». Phrases: «a source of inspiration», «be an inspiration to», «draw inspiration from», «a flash of inspiration».
examples from the lessons: The sea gave me inspiration for my poem. | My nan is an inspiration — she ran a marathon at 70. | Suddenly I had a flash of inspiration. | Many artists drew inspiration from nature. | The coach was an inspiration to the whole team. | Christians believe the Bible is inspired by God.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Use «an» with the countable sense: an inspiration. Verb: inspire. Adjective: inspiring, inspirational.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A very hard, heavy, silvery metal, a chemical element (symbol Ir), which hardly rusts or wears away.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons iridium is famous because a thin layer rich in iridium around the world, laid down about 66 million years ago, helped scientists infer that a huge asteroid hit the Earth when the dinosaurs died out. It is used in spark plugs and pen nibs. Phrases: «iridium layer».
examples from the lessons: Iridium is one of the densest metals on Earth. | Scientists found a layer of iridium in rocks all over the world. | That iridium came from an asteroid. | Iridium hardly ever rusts. | The tip of the fountain pen is made with iridium.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Symbol Ir. Named from «iris» (rainbow) because its salts are many colours.

meaning for a pupil: 1) adjective From or belonging to the modern country of Israel. 2) noun A person from Israel.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and news lessons Israeli means of the state of Israel, founded in 1948. In conflicts the news uses «Israeli» and «Palestinian» for the two sides; good lessons show both peoples' suffering. Different from «Israelite», a person of ancient Israel in the Bible. Phrases: «Israeli food», «the Israeli government».
examples from the lessons: Hummus and falafel are popular in Israeli food. | An Israeli scientist won the prize. | Israelis speak Hebrew and many also speak Arabic or English. | The Israeli and Palestinian children both want peace. | The Israeli flag is blue and white with a star.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital I. Use «an»: an Israeli. Do not confuse with «Israelite» (Bible times) or «Jewish» (a religion and people, not all Israelis are Jewish and not all Jews are Israeli).

meaning for a pupil: 1) adjective From or belonging to Jamaica, an island country in the Caribbean. 2) noun A person from Jamaica.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and culture lessons Jamaica is known for reggae music, Bob Marley, sprinter Usain Bolt and food like jerk chicken and ackee and saltfish. Many families in the UK, the USA and Canada have Jamaican roots. Jamaican Patois is an English-based creole. Phrases: «Jamaican food», «Jamaican Patois».
examples from the lessons: Usain Bolt is a famous Jamaican runner. | We tried Jamaican jerk chicken. | Reggae is Jamaican music. | My grandparents are Jamaican and came to London in the 1960s. | The Jamaican flag is black, green and gold. | Jamaican Patois mixes English with African words.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital J. Spelled -aican.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (law) The official power to make decisions and judgments about something. 2) An area or group over which such power works: a state, a country or a court.
its sense in the lessons: In citizenship lessons and the news jurisdiction tells you which police force, court or country is in charge. For example a local school issue is not under the jurisdiction of the UN. Phrases: «under the jurisdiction of», «outside our jurisdiction».
examples from the lessons: That case is outside the jurisdiction of this court. | The park is under the jurisdiction of the city council. | Each state in the USA is a separate jurisdiction. | The International Court has jurisdiction over some disputes between countries. | «Sorry, it's not my jurisdiction,» said the sheriff.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal word. Stress: joor-is-DIK-shun. Related: jury, justice (from Latin «jus» = law).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A Native American people of the Great Plains, part of the Sioux nation, living mostly in North and South Dakota. 2) The language of the Lakota people.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons the Lakota are famous for leaders like Sitting Bull and Crazy Horse, for buffalo hunting on the plains and for the Battle of the Little Bighorn (1876). Their sacred Black Hills were taken by the USA. Many Lakota people today work to keep their language alive.
examples from the lessons: The Lakota lived on the Great Plains and hunted buffalo. | Sitting Bull was a Lakota leader. | The Black Hills are sacred to the Lakota people. | Some schools teach the Lakota language. | Lakota children learn the stories of their elders.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital L. Plural: Lakota or Lakotas. Related to Dakota and Nakota.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unable to walk normally because of a hurt leg or foot (used mostly about animals, especially horses). 2) (informal, slang) Boring, weak or not cool: «That joke is lame». 3) A lame excuse is a weak one that no one believes. 4) (Bible) Old word for people who cannot walk; Jesus healed the lame.
its sense in the lessons: In stories a lame horse cannot carry its rider. Children use «lame» as slang for «boring» or «uncool». Using «lame» about a disabled person is old-fashioned and can be hurtful; say «has a limp» or «cannot walk». Phrases: «lame excuse», «a lame duck» (a weak leader or business), «so lame».
examples from the lessons: The horse went lame after it hurt its hoof. | «The dog ate my homework» is a lame excuse. | That film was so lame! (slang) | In the Bible story, Jesus made the lame man walk. | The President was a lame duck in his last months. | His jokes are lame but we laugh anyway.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative lamer, lamest. The slang meaning can hurt people with disabilities; be careful. Do not confuse with «lamé» (shiny fabric).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Of a country or place: surrounded by land on all sides, with no coast on the sea.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons landlocked countries include Switzerland, Austria, Hungary, Nepal, Bolivia, Uganda and Mongolia. Being landlocked can make trade harder, because goods must pass through other countries to reach ports. Phrases: «a landlocked country».
examples from the lessons: Switzerland is a landlocked country. | Bolivia is landlocked, but it still has a navy on a big lake! | Landlocked countries depend on neighbours to reach the sea. | Look at the map: which African countries are landlocked? | Liechtenstein is surrounded by two landlocked countries. | The Caspian Sea is a landlocked sea.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word. A country with a coast even on a lake is still landlocked if it has no sea.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Usually part of «daddy longlegs»: a name for long-legged creatures. In the UK, Ireland and Australia it often means the crane fly; in the USA and Canada usually a harvestman (a spider-like creature) or a cellar spider. 2) (informal) A tall person with long legs, as a nickname.
its sense in the lessons: In nature lessons «daddy longlegs» shows how one common name can mean different animals in different countries. Myth: daddy longlegs are not deadly poisonous; they are harmless to people. Phrases: «daddy longlegs».
examples from the lessons: A daddy longlegs flew in through the window. | Crane flies are called daddy longlegs in Britain. | In America, a daddy longlegs is often a harvestman. | Daddy longlegs can't hurt you. | «Hey, Longlegs!» his friends called the tall boy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually written «daddy longlegs» or «daddy-long-legs». Myth trap: the story that they are the most venomous spiders is false.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A long, narrow wooden ship with oars and a square sail, used by the Vikings for raiding, trading and exploring.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons Viking longships could sail across the sea and also up shallow rivers, so Vikings could raid places like Lindisfarne in 793. They often had a carved dragon head at the front. Phrases: «Viking longship».
examples from the lessons: The Vikings sailed to Britain in longships. | A longship had a dragon's head carved at the front. | Rowers sat on chests along the sides of the longship. | Longships could sail up shallow rivers. | We made a model longship in class. | Some Vikings were buried in their longships.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word. Countable.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A large Australian bird that lives on the forest floor; the male has a long tail shaped like a lyre (an old harp) and is famous for copying almost any sound it hears.
its sense in the lessons: In nature lessons the lyrebird is a champion copycat: it can copy other birds, chainsaws, camera clicks and car alarms. It is on the Australian ten-cent coin. Phrases: «superb lyrebird».
examples from the lessons: The lyrebird copied the sound of a camera. | The male lyrebird spreads its tail to impress females. | You can see a lyrebird on the Australian ten-cent coin. | Lyrebirds live in the forests of south-east Australia. | A lyrebird can copy more than twenty other birds.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word. «Lyre» sounds like «liar» but is a musical instrument.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (French) A jersey or top worn by cyclists; in the Tour de France the leader wears the «maillot jaune» (yellow jersey). 2) A one-piece swimsuit, or tight clothes for dancers or gymnasts.
its sense in the lessons: It is a French word sometimes used in English, mostly in cycling and fashion. In French «maillot de bain» means swimsuit. Sound: «my-YO».
examples from the lessons: The race leader wore the maillot jaune. | In French, «maillot de bain» means swimming costume. | She wore a black maillot to the pool. | Each team has its own coloured maillot.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly French; in English it is rare and fancy. The final t is silent.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A big change to how a person looks, with new clothes, hair or make-up. 2) A big change to make a room, building or place look better. 3) (informal) Any change that makes something new and better: «The team needs a makeover».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and TV shows makeovers change bedrooms, gardens and people. In stories a makeover often shows a character changing on the outside, while the lesson is that what matters is inside. Phrases: «give something a makeover», «a bedroom makeover», «a complete makeover».
examples from the lessons: We gave my bedroom a makeover with new paint. | The old library got a makeover and now looks amazing. | On the show, a family got a garden makeover. | My sister did a makeover on Grandma's hair. | The website needs a makeover. | After the makeover, the classroom was bright and colourful.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word, countable. Verb phrase: «make over» (two words): «They made over the kitchen».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A large, slow, gentle plant-eating mammal that lives in warm coastal waters and rivers; it has flippers, a round paddle-shaped tail and is sometimes called a sea cow.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons manatees are mammals, not fish: they breathe air and feed their babies milk. They live in Florida, the Caribbean, West Africa and the Amazon. Boat propellers often injure them, so boats go slowly in «manatee zones». Sailors long ago may have mistaken them for mermaids. Phrases: «manatee zone», «sea cow».
examples from the lessons: A manatee eats sea grass all day. | Manatees come up to the surface to breathe. | Slow down — this is a manatee zone. | Baby manatees drink their mother's milk. | Many manatees have scars from boat propellers. | Old sailors thought manatees were mermaids.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Say MAN-uh-tee. Close relative: the dugong. Myth: they are not related to whales or seals; their closest land relatives are elephants.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Being grown-up and sensible in how you think and behave. 2) Being fully grown or developed (for animals, plants, fruit). 3) (money) The date when a loan or savings bond must be paid back.
its sense in the lessons: In PSHE and school reports maturity means acting responsibly and calmly, not just being older. In science, an animal reaches maturity when it is fully grown and can have young. Phrases: «show maturity», «reach maturity», «emotional maturity».
examples from the lessons: She showed great maturity when she said sorry first. | Salmon return to their river when they reach maturity. | The report said Sam has grown in maturity this year. | Some trees take fifty years to reach maturity. | Maturity is not about age but about how you behave. | The savings bond reaches maturity in five years.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Adjective: mature (opposite: immature). Do not confuse with «majority» (more than half).

meaning for a pupil: 1) The larva (young form) of a darkling beetle; it looks like a small yellow-brown worm and eats grain and flour. 2) Mealworms sold as food for birds, reptiles and pets.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons mealworms are used to watch life cycles: larva, pupa, beetle. Bird lovers put mealworms out for robins. Some people eat them as insect food rich in protein. They are not real worms. Phrases: «dried mealworms», «mealworm beetle».
examples from the lessons: We watched our mealworms turn into beetles. | Robins love mealworms in winter. | My lizard eats live mealworms. | A mealworm is a larva, not a worm. | Mealworms can live in old flour. | Some people cook mealworms as a snack.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word. Countable. Not a real worm — it is an insect.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A small rock or bit of metal travelling through space, smaller than an asteroid.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons pupils learn three linked words: a meteoroid is the rock in space, a meteor is the streak of light when it burns up in our air (a «shooting star»), and a meteorite is a piece that lands on the ground. Phrases: «meteoroid, meteor and meteorite».
examples from the lessons: A meteoroid travels very fast through space. | When a meteoroid enters the atmosphere, it becomes a meteor. | Most meteoroids are no bigger than a grain of sand. | If a bit survives and lands, it is a meteorite. | Meteoroids can damage satellites.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Common trap: meteoroid (space) vs meteor (light in the sky) vs meteorite (on the ground). Shooting stars are not stars.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A tree or shrub with fluffy yellow or pink flowers. 2) A small «sensitive plant» whose leaves fold up when you touch them. 3) A drink of orange juice and sparkling wine (in the UK called a Buck's Fizz).
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons the sensitive mimosa plant shows that plants can respond to touch. In France and Australia (where the yellow kind is called wattle) mimosa flowers mark early spring. The drink is for adults. Phrases: «sensitive plant».
examples from the lessons: When I touched the mimosa, its leaves folded up. | The mimosa tree was covered in fluffy yellow flowers. | Mimosa blossoms smell sweet. | In Australia, yellow mimosa is called wattle. | The grown-ups had mimosas at brunch.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Say mi-MOH-suh. The drink contains alcohol.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Wrong or false information, often spread by mistake. 2) (often confused with disinformation) False information spread on purpose to trick people.
its sense in the lessons: In media lessons pupils learn to check facts before sharing: look at the source, ask «who made this and why?», compare with trusted news. Misinformation spreads fast online, especially about health, wars and elections. Phrases: «spread misinformation», «tackle misinformation», «fact-check».
examples from the lessons: Don't share posts until you check they aren't misinformation. | There was lots of misinformation about the virus online. | The teacher showed us how to spot misinformation. | Misinformation can spread faster than the truth. | A fact-checker said the story was misinformation. | Bots spread misinformation during the election.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «a piece of misinformation». Strictly, misinformation is false by mistake; disinformation is false on purpose; propaganda is one-sided messages to change minds.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A tree with broad leaves and dark purple, red or white berries like long blackberries. 2) The fruit of this tree. 3) A dark purple-red colour.
its sense in the lessons: In history and science lessons silkworms eat only mulberry leaves, so mulberry trees were key for making silk in China. In songs «Here we go round the mulberry bush» is an old nursery rhyme. Phrases: «mulberry bush», «mulberry jam».
examples from the lessons: Silkworms eat mulberry leaves. | The mulberries stained my fingers purple. | We sang «Here we go round the mulberry bush». | Granny makes mulberry jam. | A mulberry tree can live for hundreds of years. | Her coat is a deep mulberry colour.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: mulberries. Countable.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A huge flock of starlings flying together and swirling in changing shapes in the sky, usually at dusk. 2) (literary) A soft, low murmuring sound.
its sense in the lessons: In nature lessons murmurations are an amazing example of animals moving together: each bird copies its nearest neighbours, and the whole flock moves like smoke. They help protect starlings from hawks. In the UK and Ireland they are watched in autumn and winter. Phrases: «a murmuration of starlings».
examples from the lessons: We watched a murmuration of starlings over the pier. | The murmuration swirled like a black cloud. | Thousands of starlings make a murmuration before they roost. | Each bird watches its neighbours in a murmuration. | A falcon dived into the murmuration but missed.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Collective noun for starlings: «a murmuration of starlings».

part of speech: noun (a nutcracker, nutcrackers; also a pair of nutcrackers)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A tool for cracking the hard shells of nuts. 2) A wooden doll shaped like a soldier whose jaw cracks nuts, popular at Christmas. 3) «The Nutcracker»: a famous Christmas ballet with music by Tchaikovsky. 4) A bird of the crow family that eats nuts and seeds.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life nutcrackers come out at Christmas with bowls of nuts. In music lessons «The Nutcracker» ballet and its «Dance of the Sugar Plum Fairy» are often studied. In science, a nutcracker is a simple machine — a lever. Phrases: «a pair of nutcrackers», «The Nutcracker Suite».
examples from the lessons: Pass me the nutcracker so I can open this walnut. | We went to see «The Nutcracker» ballet at Christmas. | A wooden nutcracker soldier stood on the shelf. | A nutcracker is a type of lever. | The Dance of the Sugar Plum Fairy comes from «The Nutcracker». | The nutcracker bird hides seeds for winter.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK often says «nutcrackers» or «a pair of nutcrackers» for the tool. One word. In maths and science it is a lever with the load between the pivot and the hand.

part of speech: verb (ooze, oozes, oozed, oozing); noun (ooze — uncountable)
meaning for a pupil: 1) verb (of a thick liquid) To flow out slowly: «Honey oozed from the jar». 2) verb To show a lot of a quality: «He oozes confidence». 3) noun Soft, wet mud, especially at the bottom of a sea, lake or river.
its sense in the lessons: In stories «ooze» describes slimy, gooey things — monsters, mud, melted cheese — and makes the reader picture it. In science the sea floor is covered with ooze made of tiny shells. Phrases: «ooze out», «ooze charm/confidence».
examples from the lessons: Jam oozed out of the doughnut. | Green slime oozed from the monster's mouth. | Mud oozed between my toes. | Blood oozed from the cut. | The singer oozed confidence on stage. | The sea floor is covered with soft ooze.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: oozed, oozing. A great word for descriptive writing (texture and sound).

meaning for a pupil: 1) To live longer than someone else. 2) To last longer than something, or to keep going after it has stopped being useful: «The rule has outlived its purpose».
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons «tortoises can outlive their owners» shows how long some animals live. In family life it is about which person lives longer. Phrases: «outlive its usefulness».
examples from the lessons: Some tortoises outlive their owners. | Women often outlive men. | Grandma outlived all her brothers. | This old law has outlived its usefulness. | Trees can outlive the people who plant them.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Prefix «out-» means «more than / longer than»: outlive, outrun, outgrow.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) A chemical made when another element joins with oxygen: rust is iron oxide; water is hydrogen oxide.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons oxides appear when things burn or rust: carbon dioxide (from burning and breathing), iron oxide (rust), zinc oxide (in sun cream). Phrases: «iron oxide», «carbon dioxide», «zinc oxide».
examples from the lessons: Rust is a kind of iron oxide. | Zinc oxide is in some sun creams. | When metals burn, they make oxides. | Carbon dioxide is an oxide of carbon. | Aluminium has a thin oxide layer that protects it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Use «an»: an oxide. Countable. «Di-» in dioxide means two oxygen atoms.

part of speech: noun (papyrus — uncountable; a papyrus, papyri or papyruses)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A tall water plant like a reed that grows by the River Nile. 2) A kind of paper made from this plant by the ancient Egyptians. 3) An ancient document written on this paper.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons about Ancient Egypt, scribes wrote hieroglyphs on papyrus scrolls. The word «paper» comes from «papyrus». Many old Bible texts were found on papyrus. Phrases: «papyrus scroll», «written on papyrus».
examples from the lessons: The Egyptians wrote on papyrus. | Papyrus grows along the River Nile. | We made our own papyrus in class from strips of paper. | The scroll was rolled-up papyrus. | The word «paper» comes from papyrus. | Old pieces of the Bible were found on papyri.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural for documents: papyri (pa-PIE-rye) or papyruses. Uncountable for the material.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The way an object seems to move against a far background when you look at it from two different places, such as with one eye and then the other.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons parallax explains why a nearby thing jumps when you close each eye in turn, and astronomers use it to measure how far away stars are. In maths and science it is also why you must read a ruler or measuring jug with your eye straight in front, to avoid «parallax error». Phrases: «parallax error».
examples from the lessons: Hold up your thumb and close one eye, then the other — that jump is parallax. | Read the measuring cylinder at eye level to avoid parallax error. | Astronomers use parallax to measure distances to stars. | Video games use parallax to make backgrounds look far away. | Parallax helps our two eyes judge depth.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Stress: PA-ra-lax. In measuring: look straight at the scale or your reading may be wrong.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (animals) Living by hunting and eating other animals. 2) (people) Trying to use or harm others for gain, especially weaker people: predatory lenders, predatory adults online.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons predatory animals (lions, owls, sharks) sit near the top of food chains. In safety lessons «predatory behaviour» warns about adults who try to trick children online: never share personal details, and tell a trusted adult. Phrases: «predatory birds», «predatory behaviour».
examples from the lessons: Owls are predatory birds that hunt at night. | Sharks are predatory fish. | A predatory adult may pretend to be a child online. | Tell a grown-up if anyone online asks you to keep secrets. | The predatory spider waits for flies in its web. | Some loan companies are predatory and charge huge interest.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «predator». Stress: PRED-a-tor-ee. Opposite of «prey» animals.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (maths) A straight line from the centre of a circle to its edge, or the length of that line. 2) A distance around a place in every direction: «within a 5-mile radius». 3) (body) One of the two bones in the forearm, on the thumb side.
its sense in the lessons: In maths the radius is half the diameter: diameter = 2 × radius. The area of a circle is π × r × r and the circumference is 2 × π × r. In everyday life «within a radius of» means within that distance all around. Phrases: «within a radius of», «radius and diameter».
examples from the lessons: The radius of this circle is 4 cm, so the diameter is 8 cm. | Draw a circle with a radius of 3 cm using a compass. | All pupils living within a two-mile radius can walk to school. | He broke his radius when he fell off the trampoline. | The radius goes from the centre to the edge. | A circle's area is π times the radius squared.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: radii (RAY-dee-eye) in maths, radiuses also accepted. Maths: radius = diameter ÷ 2; diameter = radius × 2.

part of speech: noun (a raven, ravens); adjective (raven — black and shiny)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A very large black bird of the crow family, with a deep croaking call and a thick beak. 2) adjective (of hair) Shiny black: raven hair.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and poems ravens are clever, mysterious birds; in Edgar Allan Poe's poem the raven says «Nevermore». In the Bible ravens fed the prophet Elijah, and Noah sent out a raven from the ark. At the Tower of London, legend says the kingdom will fall if the ravens leave. Phrases: «raven-haired», «as black as a raven».
examples from the lessons: A raven croaked from the top of the castle. | Ravens are among the cleverest birds. | Legend says six ravens must stay at the Tower of London. | In the Bible, ravens brought Elijah bread and meat. | The princess had long raven hair. | Noah sent out a raven to look for dry land.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Bigger than a crow, with a wedge-shaped tail. Do not confuse with «ravenous» (very hungry) or «ravine» (narrow valley).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Rh (rhesus) factor: a protein that may be on red blood cells; blood is Rh-positive or Rh-negative (as in A+ or O−). 2) RH: short for «right hand», as in music («RH» for the right hand on the piano). 3) RH or rh: short for «relative humidity», how much water vapour is in the air. 4) Rh: the chemical symbol for rhodium, a rare metal.
its sense in the lessons: In science and health lessons blood groups have a letter (A, B, AB, O) and a plus or minus sign for Rh. Doctors check Rh before blood transfusions and in pregnancy. In piano music RH and LH tell you which hand plays. Not a word you say; read the letters «R-H» or the full word.
examples from the lessons: My blood group is O, Rh positive. | Rh-negative blood is less common. | In piano music, RH means play with your right hand. | The weather station shows RH 80%. | Rh is the symbol for the metal rhodium.
note for the reader of a maths problem: An abbreviation, not a word. Say «R-H» or «rhesus». The meaning depends on the subject.

part of speech: adjective (Romanian); noun (a Romanian, Romanians; Romanian — the language)
meaning for a pupil: 1) adjective From or belonging to Romania, a country in south-eastern Europe. 2) noun A person from Romania. 3) noun The language of Romania, which comes from Latin like Italian, French and Spanish.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons Romania has the Carpathian mountains and the Danube delta; its capital is Bucharest. Many Romanian families live in the UK, Ireland and Canada. Romanian is a Romance language. The Dracula legend is set in Transylvania, a region of Romania. Phrases: «the Romanian language».
examples from the lessons: She speaks Romanian and English at home. | Romanian is a language that comes from Latin. | Bucharest is the Romanian capital. | Our new classmate is Romanian. | Romanian dishes include sarmale, cabbage rolls. | Transylvania is a region in Romania.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital R. Not the same as «Roman» (ancient Rome) or «Romani» (the Roma people, who live in many countries).

meaning for a pupil: 1) noun A person, often a child or teenager, who has run away from home or from somewhere. 2) adjective Out of control: a runaway train, a runaway horse. 3) adjective Happening very fast or very easily: a runaway success, a runaway winner.
its sense in the lessons: In stories runaways often set out on adventures, but in safety lessons pupils learn that running away is dangerous and that a trusted adult or a helpline (like Childline in the UK, Kids Helpline in Australia) can help with problems at home. A «runaway win» means an easy, big win. Phrases: «a runaway train», «a runaway success», «teenage runaways».
examples from the lessons: The runaway train sped down the hill. | The book was a runaway success. | Police found the runaway safe at the bus station. | The runaway horse galloped through the village. | She was the runaway winner of the race. | If you think about running away, talk to someone at Childline.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word as noun/adjective; the verb is two words: «run away» (ran away). Countable noun.

part of speech: adjective (Saharan, more Saharan — rare); noun (a Saharan, Saharans — rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Saharan means belonging to or coming from the Sahara, the huge hot desert in North Africa. 2) Saharan can describe weather or places that are very hot and dry, like the Sahara. 3) (rare) A Saharan is a person who lives in the Sahara.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons it tells you about the Sahara Desert: its sand dunes, camels, oases and dust storms; in science it comes up with dust, heat and dry climates; in everyday talk «Saharan heat» means an extremely hot day; phrases: Saharan dust, Saharan Africa, sub-Saharan Africa, Saharan heat.
examples from the lessons: Camels can walk for days across the Saharan sand. | Saharan dust sometimes blows all the way to Britain and makes cars dusty. | The Saharan sun is fierce at midday. | Many countries in sub-Saharan Africa lie south of the desert. | Our classroom felt Saharan after the heating broke and stayed on full. | We drew a map of the Saharan oases in geography. | Saharan nights can be surprisingly cold.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually written with a capital S because it comes from the name Sahara. «Sub-Saharan» means the parts of Africa south of the Sahara. The Sahara is not the biggest desert of all if you count cold deserts: Antarctica is bigger. Do not confuse with «Sahara» (the noun, the desert itself).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A sailfish is a big ocean fish with a tall fin on its back that looks like a sail and a long pointed bill like a sword. 2) It is one of the fastest fish in the sea and hunts smaller fish.
its sense in the lessons: In science and nature lessons it appears with ocean animals, speed records and food chains; in stories about fishing trips and the sea; the tall fin tells the reader about its shape and how it herds fish.
examples from the lessons: The sailfish raised its huge blue fin. | A sailfish can swim faster than a car on a town street. | Sailfish use their long bills to stun little fish. | We watched a video of sailfish hunting sardines. | The fisherman caught a sailfish and let it go again. | Sailfish live in warm oceans around the world.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The plural is usually the same: one sailfish, two sailfish («sailfishes» is used when talking about kinds). It is a fish, not a boat. Claims that it is «the fastest fish» are often repeated but hard to measure; say «one of the fastest».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Shale is a soft grey or dark rock made of hardened mud or clay that splits easily into thin flat layers. 2) Shale is also a source of oil and gas that companies drill for.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and science it is a sedimentary rock, made when mud settles and is pressed over millions of years; fossils are often found in it; in news it comes with «shale gas» and «fracking»; phrases: shale gas, shale oil, oil shale.
examples from the lessons: The cliff was made of crumbly grey shale. | Shale splits into thin flakes when you tap it. | We found a fossil fern in a piece of shale. | Shale is a sedimentary rock made from mud. | Some companies drill deep into shale to get gas. | The path was slippery with loose shale.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable: «some shale», «a piece of shale». Do not confuse with «slate», which is shale changed by heat and pressure into a harder rock; and with «shell».

part of speech: noun (a siege, sieges); verb (to siege — rare, usually «besiege»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A siege is when an army surrounds a town or castle and stops food and help getting in, so the people inside will give up. 2) A siege can also be when police surround a building where someone is hiding, often with hostages. 3) Under siege can mean being attacked or troubled from all sides by lots of problems or people.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons it comes with castles, walls, catapults and starving towns; in news, «a police siege»; in everyday talk «under siege» is a strong way to say very busy or attacked; phrases: lay siege to, under siege, siege of (a town), lift the siege.
examples from the lessons: The castle held out through a long siege. | The army laid siege to the city for six months. | During the siege the people ate rats to survive. | Police ended the siege after ten hours. | The siege was lifted when help arrived. | On sale day the shop was under siege from shoppers. | We built a model siege engine in history.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: «ie» — siege (not «seige»). The verb is usually «besiege». Countable: a siege, two sieges.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A silverfish is a small, shiny, silver-grey insect with no wings that wriggles like a fish and lives in damp corners of houses. 2) (rare) Silverfish is also a name for some small silvery fish.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons it comes up with insects and minibeasts and their habitats; in everyday life people find silverfish in bathrooms, under sinks or in old books; it tells the reader a place is damp or old.
examples from the lessons: A silverfish darted across the bathroom floor. | Silverfish like damp, dark places. | Silverfish nibble paper, glue and old books. | It is an insect even though it is called a fish. | We spotted three silverfish under the sink. | Silverfish are harmless to people but annoying.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural is the same: one silverfish, many silverfish. Trap: it is an insect, not a fish. It does not bite or sting people.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A skydiver is a person who jumps out of an aeroplane high up, falls through the air, and then opens a parachute to land safely.
its sense in the lessons: Used in stories about adventure, sport and bravery; in science lessons with gravity, air resistance and parachutes; related: skydiving (the sport), skydive (verb).
examples from the lessons: The skydiver leapt from the plane at four thousand metres. | Skydivers fall very fast before opening their parachutes. | My uncle is a skydiver and has done 200 jumps. | Air resistance slows the skydiver down. | The skydivers held hands in a circle in the sky. | A skydiver must check the parachute carefully before every jump.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a skydiver, skydivers. Science note: a skydiver speeds up only until air resistance balances gravity (terminal velocity); the parachute makes air resistance much bigger. Not the same as a «sky diver» in water (that is a «diver»).

part of speech: noun (slate, a slate, slates); verb (slate, slates, slated, slating)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Slate is a hard dark grey rock that splits into thin flat sheets. 2) A slate is a thin piece of this rock used to cover a roof, or in the past for children to write on with chalk. 3) A slate is a list of candidates or a plan of things, as in «a slate of films». 4) (UK, informal) To slate something means to criticise it very harshly. 5) (mostly US) To be slated for something means it is planned or expected. 6) A clean slate means a fresh start where past mistakes are forgotten.
its sense in the lessons: In science it is a metamorphic rock made from shale; in history, Victorian children wrote on slates; in Wales slate quarries are famous; in news and reviews, «slated» means badly criticised (UK) or scheduled (US); phrases: clean slate, wipe the slate clean, on the slate (old: on credit).
examples from the lessons: The old cottage has a slate roof. | Victorian children wrote sums on slates with chalk. | Slate is made when shale is squeezed and heated. | A slate fell off the roof in the storm. | Critics slated the new film. | The new library is slated to open next spring. | Let's wipe the slate clean and be friends again. | The coach picked a strong slate of players.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable when it means a roof tile or writing tablet («a slate»), uncountable as the rock («made of slate»). Watch the two different meanings of «slated»: UK «badly criticised», US «planned». Do not confuse with «shale» or «state».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A smartphone is a mobile phone that is also a small computer: it can go online, take photos, play games, use apps and make calls.
its sense in the lessons: Used in everyday life, online safety lessons and computing lessons (apps, screen time, passwords); in stories it shows modern life; phrases: on my smartphone, smartphone app, smartphone screen.
examples from the lessons: Mum checks the bus times on her smartphone. | A smartphone can take photos and videos. | My brother is not allowed a smartphone until he is twelve. | Never share your smartphone passcode with strangers. | The smartphone battery died halfway through the trip. | We used a smartphone app to identify birds. | Too much smartphone time before bed can spoil sleep.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a smartphone, two smartphones. Written as one word. People often just say «phone». Uses «a» (a smartphone).

part of speech: noun (a snowshoe, snowshoes); verb (snowshoe, snowshoes, snowshoed, snowshoeing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A snowshoe is a wide flat frame you tie under your boot so you can walk on deep snow without sinking. 2) To snowshoe means to walk on snow wearing snowshoes. 3) A snowshoe hare is a hare with big furry feet that turns white in winter.
its sense in the lessons: Comes up in stories and lessons about Canada, the Arctic, winter sports and First Nations inventions; in science, a snowshoe spreads your weight over a bigger area so the pressure is smaller; the snowshoe hare appears in food-chain lessons.
examples from the lessons: We strapped on snowshoes and crossed the meadow. | Snowshoes stop you sinking into deep snow. | Indigenous peoples of North America invented many kinds of snowshoe. | We went snowshoeing in the mountains in Canada. | The snowshoe hare turns white in winter. | Bigger snowshoes spread your weight over more snow.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually used in pairs: «a pair of snowshoes». Past form of the verb: snowshoed. Science link: same weight on a bigger area means less pressure.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A songwriter is a person who writes songs: the words, the tune, or both.
its sense in the lessons: Used in music lessons and everyday talk about pop stars and bands; related words: lyrics (the words), melody (the tune), singer-songwriter (someone who writes and sings their own songs).
examples from the lessons: Taylor Swift is a famous singer-songwriter. | The songwriter wrote the tune on her guitar. | Our class became songwriters for the school concert. | Many songs are written by teams of songwriters. | A songwriter needs ideas, rhyme and rhythm. | He dreams of being a songwriter one day.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. One word. A songwriter is not always the singer: many singers perform songs that other people wrote.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Spectacled means wearing glasses. 2) In animal names it means having rings or marks around the eyes that look like glasses, as in «spectacled bear» or «spectacled owl».
its sense in the lessons: Used in story descriptions of characters («a spectacled old man»), and in science/nature lessons in animal names; it is a slightly old-fashioned, bookish word.
examples from the lessons: A spectacled teacher peered over her desk. | The spectacled bear lives in South America. | The spectacled owl has white rings around its eyes. | A spectacled boy sat reading in the corner. | Spectacled flying foxes live in Australia.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comes from «spectacles» (an older word for glasses). Not connected with «spectacular». Mostly used before a noun: «a spectacled man».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A stalagmite is a pointed column of rock that grows upwards from the floor of a cave, made by drips of water full of dissolved minerals.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and science lessons about caves and limestone; it is usually taught with «stalactite», which hangs down from the ceiling; when the two join they make a column; it grows extremely slowly.
examples from the lessons: A huge stalagmite rose from the cave floor. | Stalagmites grow upwards as water drips onto them. | It took thousands of years for the stalagmite to form. | Please don't touch the stalagmites — oils from your hands harm them. | The stalactite and the stalagmite met to make a column. | We drew stalagmites in our cave diagram.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Memory trick: stalaGmites grow from the Ground; stalaCtites hang from the Ceiling (or «tites hold tight to the ceiling, mites might grow up»). Countable.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Stilts are a pair of long poles with footrests that you stand on to walk high above the ground. 2) Stilts are also tall posts that hold a house or building up above water or the ground. 3) A stilt is a wading bird with very long thin pink legs.
its sense in the lessons: Used in stories about circuses and fairs (stilt walkers), in geography about houses on stilts in flood areas, and in science about wading birds; phrases: on stilts, stilt walker, stilt house.
examples from the lessons: The clown walked on stilts at the fair. | Houses on stilts stay dry when the river floods. | I fell off my stilts twice before I got the hang of it. | The stilt waded through the shallow lake. | Stilt walkers led the carnival parade. | The beach hut stands on wooden stilts.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually plural: «a pair of stilts», «on stilts». Countable. «Stilted» (adjective) means stiff and unnatural, e.g. stilted speech.

part of speech: verb (stomp, stomps, stomped, stomping); noun (a stomp, stomps)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To stomp means to walk with heavy, loud steps, often because you are angry. 2) To stomp on something means to stamp on it hard with your foot. 3) A stomp is a heavy step, or a lively dance with heavy stamping steps. 4) (slang, sport) To stomp a team means to beat them easily.
its sense in the lessons: In stories it shows feelings: a character who stomps off is cross or sulking; in music and PE, stomping keeps a beat; phrases: stomp off, stomp out, stomp around, stomp on.
examples from the lessons: She stomped up the stairs and slammed her door. | The giant stomped through the forest. | Don't stomp on the flowers! | We stomped our feet in time to the music. | He stomped off in a huff after losing the game. | The dinosaur's stomp made the ground shake. | Our team got stomped 6–0 (slang).
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: stomped. Very close in meaning to «stamp»; «stomp» sounds more informal and often more cross or heavy.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A sultanate is a country or land ruled by a sultan, a Muslim king or ruler. 2) It can also mean the time when a sultan ruled, or the sultan's position.
its sense in the lessons: In history and geography lessons: the Ottoman Empire, the Delhi Sultanate, the Sultanate of Oman, Brunei; it tells the reader what kind of government a place has or had.
examples from the lessons: Oman is a sultanate on the Arabian Peninsula. | Brunei is a small sultanate on the island of Borneo. | The Delhi Sultanate ruled northern India for centuries. | The sultan's palace was the heart of the sultanate. | Trade made the sultanate rich.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Built from «sultan» + «-ate» (like «emirate» from «emir»). Do not confuse with «sultana» (a dried grape, or a sultan's wife).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (religion) A sutra is a holy teaching or text in Buddhism or Hinduism, often a sermon of the Buddha or short wise sayings. 2) In Hindu learning a sutra can also be a short rule or saying that is easy to remember.
its sense in the lessons: Used in religious education lessons about Buddhism and Hinduism: monks chant sutras; famous ones are the Lotus Sutra and the Heart Sutra; it tells the reader about sacred writings.
examples from the lessons: The monks chanted a sutra in the temple. | Buddhists believe the sutras record the Buddha's teachings. | The Heart Sutra is very short. | We learned that «sutra» comes from a Sanskrit word meaning thread. | Each sutra was copied by hand onto palm leaves.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comes from Sanskrit (an old language of India), meaning «thread». Countable: sutras. Say it «SOO-truh». Speak of beliefs respectfully: «Buddhists believe…».

part of speech: verb (sync, syncs, synced, syncing); noun (sync — mostly uncountable)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To sync means to make two things happen at exactly the same time, or to make devices share the same, up-to-date information. 2) In sync means happening together at the same time or speed; out of sync means not matching. 3) (informal) If people are in sync, they agree or get on well and think alike.
its sense in the lessons: In computing lessons: syncing photos or files between a phone and a computer; in music, dance and films, keeping sound and movement together; in everyday life, friends «in sync»; phrases: in sync, out of sync, sync up, lip-sync.
examples from the lessons: My tablet syncs my photos to the cloud. | The dancers moved perfectly in sync. | The sound in the video was out of sync with the lips. | We synced our watches before the race. | She and her best friend are always in sync. | Kids made a lip-sync video for the talent show.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Short for «synchronise» (UK) / «synchronize» (US). Past: synced (sometimes «synched»). Sounds like «sink» — homophone trap.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Tartar is a hard yellowish coating that builds up on teeth if they are not cleaned well. 2) Tartar sauce (also tartare) is a creamy sauce with pickles, often eaten with fish. 3) Cream of tartar is a white powder used in baking. 4) (history) A Tartar (more correctly Tatar) is a member of a Turkic people of Russia and Central Asia; Crimean Tatars are a people of Crimea in Ukraine. 5) (old-fashioned) A tartar is a fierce, bad-tempered person.
its sense in the lessons: In health lessons tartar comes with brushing, flossing and the dentist; in cooking, fish and chips with tartar sauce; in history and news about Crimea, the Tatars; in old stories, a strict, fierce person.
examples from the lessons: The dentist scraped the tartar off my teeth. | Brushing twice a day helps stop tartar building up. | I like tartar sauce with my fish fingers. | Add a pinch of cream of tartar to the egg whites. | Many Crimean Tatars were forced from their homes long ago. | The old housekeeper was a real tartar.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable for teeth and sauce. For the people, the modern, correct spelling is «Tatar»; «Tartar» is older and seen as less correct. Do not confuse with «tartan» (checked cloth) or «tart».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Taurus is a group of stars (a constellation) that looks like the shape of a bull. 2) In astrology, Taurus is a star sign for people born from about late April to late May. 3) (Latin) Taurus means «bull». 4) Taurus is also a name used for mountains in Turkey and for some products like cars.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons it appears with constellations and the night sky (the bright star Aldebaran and the Pleiades cluster are in Taurus); in everyday talk, horoscopes and star signs; science teaches that astrology is not a science.
examples from the lessons: Taurus looks like the head of a bull in the night sky. | The Pleiades star cluster is in Taurus. | My sister is a Taurus because her birthday is in May. | Aldebaran is the red eye of Taurus the bull. | The Taurus Mountains are in southern Turkey.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Written with a capital T. Myth trap: star signs (astrology) do not really decide your personality; astronomy (the science) studies constellations. Say it «TOR-us».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Tawny describes a warm orange-brown or yellowish-brown colour, like a lion's fur. 2) A tawny owl is a common brown owl in Britain and Europe. 3) Tawny port is a kind of brown wine (for adults).
its sense in the lessons: Used in stories and descriptions of animals, autumn leaves and hair; in science lessons about British wildlife, the tawny owl («twit-twoo» calls); it tells the reader about colour.
examples from the lessons: The lion shook its tawny mane. | A tawny owl hooted in the woods at night. | Her tawny hair glowed in the sunshine. | The hills were tawny with dry grass. | The tawny frogmouth is an Australian bird.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly used before a noun: «a tawny cat». Fun fact: the famous «twit-twoo» is often two tawny owls calling to each other, a female «twit» and a male «twoo».

part of speech: adjective (terrifying, more terrifying, most terrifying); verb form (present participle of terrify)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Terrifying means making you feel extremely frightened. 2) (informal) Terrifying can also mean very worrying or amazing in a scary way, as in «a terrifying amount of homework».
its sense in the lessons: In stories it builds suspense and fear: storms, monsters, cliff edges; in everyday talk people exaggerate («the test was terrifying»); it is stronger than «scary» or «frightening».
examples from the lessons: The roller coaster was terrifying! | A terrifying roar came from the cave. | Being lost in the crowd was terrifying for the little boy. | The storm made a terrifying noise. | It's terrifying how fast the summer goes. | The film had one terrifying scene with a shark. | Standing on the high diving board was terrifying.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Different from «terrified»: something is terrifying (it causes fear); a person is terrified (they feel fear). «Terrific» is a false friend: it usually means very good!

meaning for a pupil: 1) A tester is a person whose job is to test things, like games, apps, food or cars, to find problems. 2) A tester is a small sample of a product, such as perfume or paint, that you can try before you buy. 3) A tester can be a tool or device for testing, such as a battery tester.
its sense in the lessons: In computing lessons, testers find bugs in programs; in science, testing and fair tests; in shops, perfume or make-up testers; phrases: game tester, battery tester, paint tester.
examples from the lessons: The game tester found a bug in level three. | Mum tried a perfume tester in the shop. | We bought small paint testers to choose a colour. | The battery tester showed the battery was flat. | Testers check that toys are safe for children. | Software testers try to break programs on purpose.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Made from «test» + «-er» (a person or thing that does something). Do not confuse with «taster» (someone who tastes food).

part of speech: noun (texture, a texture, textures); verb (texture, textures, textured, texturing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Texture is how something feels when you touch it, such as rough, smooth, bumpy or soft. 2) Texture is also how food feels in your mouth, like crunchy, chewy or creamy. 3) In art and music, texture means the way different parts or layers are put together to make a surface or sound feel rich or simple. 4) To texture something means to give it a rough or patterned surface.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on materials and properties (rough, smooth); in art, rubbings and making textures with paint; in cooking, the texture of food; in music, thick or thin texture; phrases: rough texture, smooth texture, add texture.
examples from the lessons: Sandpaper has a rough texture. | The texture of a peach is soft and fuzzy. | I don't like the texture of mushrooms. | We made bark rubbings to show texture in art. | The cake had a light, fluffy texture. | The artist textured the wall with a sponge. | Silk has a smooth, slippery texture.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable or uncountable: «a smooth texture», «it has lots of texture». It is about feel (touch) more than colour. Past: textured.

part of speech: noun (a toll, tolls; the toll); verb (toll, tolls, tolled, tolling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A toll is money you must pay to use a road, bridge or tunnel. 2) The toll of a disaster is the number of people killed or hurt, as in «the death toll». 3) To take a toll (on) means to cause damage, harm or tiredness over time. 4) To toll means for a large bell to ring slowly again and again, often for a death. 5) A toll-free number is a phone number you can call without paying.
its sense in the lessons: In maths word problems, tolls are costs to add up; in geography, toll roads and bridges; in news, «the death toll rose»; in stories, church bells tolling for a funeral; phrases: toll road, toll booth, death toll, take its toll.
examples from the lessons: We paid a toll to cross the bridge. | The toll booth had a long queue. | The flood's death toll was sadly high. | Late nights took their toll on Dad. | The church bell tolled for the old king. | The toll road costs $4 each way. | Call the toll-free number for help.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a toll, tolls. Maths: «a $3 toll each way» means pay $3 going and $3 coming back = $6. Do not confuse with «tall» or «troll».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A trey is a card, dice face or domino with three spots. 2) (US, slang) In basketball, a trey is a shot scored from far away that is worth three points. 3) Trey is also a boy's name (a name), often used in the USA.
its sense in the lessons: In card games and dice games it names the three; in sports talk in the USA, «hit a trey» means score a three-pointer; it helps in maths games with cards and dice.
examples from the lessons: I need a trey to win this round of cards. | The dice showed a trey. | He hit a trey just before the buzzer (US, slang). | The trey of hearts was the last card in the pack. | My friend Trey lives next door (a name).
note for the reader of a maths problem: Old word coming from French «trois» (three). Rare in the UK except in card talk. Maths: a trey counts as 3.

part of speech: noun (a truss, trusses); verb (truss, trusses, trussed, trussing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A truss is a frame of beams joined in triangles that holds up a roof or a bridge. 2) To truss means to tie someone or something up tightly, for example the legs and wings of a chicken before cooking. 3) A truss is also a padded belt worn to support the body after an injury (medical, old-fashioned). 4) A truss is a bunch of flowers or fruit on one stalk, like truss tomatoes.
its sense in the lessons: In science and DT (design and technology) lessons, trusses show why triangles are strong shapes in bridges and roofs; in cooking, trussing a turkey; in stories, a villain trusses up the hero; phrases: truss up, roof truss, truss bridge.
examples from the lessons: The bridge is held up by steel trusses. | Triangles make a truss very strong. | Grandma trussed the turkey with string. | The robbers trussed up the guard with rope. | We built a truss bridge from straws in DT. | Mum bought a bag of truss tomatoes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Past: trussed. Maths/DT link: a triangle cannot change shape without bending its sides, which is why trusses use triangles. Do not confuse with «trust».

part of speech: noun (a verge, verges); verb (verge, verges, verged, verging)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A verge is the strip of grass beside a road or path. 2) On the verge of means very close to doing something or to something happening, as in «on the verge of tears». 3) To verge on something means to be almost that thing, as in «verging on rude».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and road safety: walk on the verge if there's no pavement; in stories it shows a character very close to an emotion or event; phrases: on the verge of, verge on, grass verge, roadside verge.
examples from the lessons: We walked along the grass verge to the farm. | Park on the verge, not on the road. | She was on the verge of tears when she lost her dog. | Scientists are on the verge of a big discovery. | His joke verged on being mean. | Wildflowers grow on the road verges in summer.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. «On the verge of» is followed by a noun or -ing form: «on the verge of crying». In the USA the grass strip is often called a «median» or «shoulder» or «parkway» instead.

part of speech: adjective (vertical); noun (the vertical, a vertical, verticals)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Vertical means going straight up and down, at a right angle to the flat ground, like a wall or a flagpole. 2) The vertical is a straight up-and-down line or direction. 3) In business (formal), a vertical is one kind of industry or market.
its sense in the lessons: In maths lessons, vertical lines, axes on graphs (the vertical axis is the y-axis), lines of symmetry and right angles; in science, objects falling vertically; in PE, a vertical jump; opposite of horizontal; phrases: vertical line, vertical axis, vertical jump.
examples from the lessons: Draw a vertical line down the middle of the page. | The flagpole is vertical. | The y-axis on the graph is vertical. | The climber went up a vertical cliff. | The letter T has one vertical line and one horizontal line. | My vertical jump is 40 centimetres.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite of «horizontal» (flat, like the horizon). Memory trick: vertical goes «v-up». In maths, a vertical and horizontal line meet at a right angle (90°). Adverb: vertically.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A vocalisation is a sound made with the voice, especially by an animal, like a bark, a howl, a song or a call. 2) Vocalisation is the act of making sounds with the voice or of singing. 3) (music) Vocalisation is singing a tune on vowel sounds without words.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on animal communication (whales, birds, monkeys); in music; it is a formal, scientific word for «a sound made by voice».
examples from the lessons: Wolves use many vocalisations, like howls and growls. | Scientists recorded the whale's vocalisations. | A baby's first vocalisations are coos and gurgles. | Birdsong is a kind of vocalisation. | The singer warmed up with vocalisation exercises.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK spelling «vocalisation»; US spelling «vocalization». Countable for single sounds, uncountable for the act. Verb: vocalise/vocalize.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In grammar, the vocative is the word or name used to speak directly to someone, as in «Tom, come here!». 2) In some languages (Latin, Ukrainian, Polish), the vocative is a special case: the name changes its ending when you call someone (Ukrainian «Ivan» becomes «Ivane»).
its sense in the lessons: In English grammar lessons, a vocative is set off with a comma («Thank you, Mum.»); in Latin and Ukrainian lessons, the vocative case has its own ending; the famous joke: «Let's eat, Grandma!» vs «Let's eat Grandma!» shows why the comma matters.
examples from the lessons: In «Hurry up, Sam», «Sam» is a vocative. | Use a comma before the vocative: «Thanks, Dad.» | «Let's eat, Grandma!» — the comma saves Grandma. | In Ukrainian, «mama» becomes «mamo» in the vocative. | «O Lord» is an old vocative used in prayers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: English has no special vocative ending, only commas: always separate the name you are calling from the rest of the sentence with a comma. Do not confuse with «vocabulary».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A wallaby is an Australian animal like a small kangaroo that hops and carries its baby (a joey) in a pouch. 2) (Australia, sport) The Wallabies are the national rugby union team of Australia.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about marsupials, Australian animals and habitats; in New Zealand some wallabies are pests; in sport news, the Wallabies play rugby; phrases: rock wallaby.
examples from the lessons: A wallaby hopped across the dusty track. | A wallaby is smaller than a kangaroo. | The baby wallaby peeped out of the pouch. | Rock wallabies live among cliffs and boulders. | The Wallabies beat the All Blacks on Saturday (Australia, sport). | Wallabies are marsupials.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: wallabies (y → ies). A marsupial: the mother carries the young in a pouch. Baby is called a «joey».

part of speech: noun (a walnut, walnuts; walnut — the wood, uncountable)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A walnut is a nut with a wrinkly brown shell and a wrinkly seed inside that looks a bit like a little brain. 2) A walnut is the tree that grows these nuts. 3) Walnut is the hard, dark brown wood of this tree, used to make furniture.
its sense in the lessons: In cooking (walnut cake, banana bread); in science (seeds, trees); in health and safety, nut allergies matter; in furniture and stories, a walnut table or desk.
examples from the lessons: I cracked the walnut with a nutcracker. | The inside of a walnut looks like a tiny brain. | Grandad has an old walnut tree in his garden. | Mum put walnuts in the banana bread. | The desk is made of polished walnut. | Some children are allergic to walnuts, so check the label.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable for nuts and trees, uncountable for the wood. Safety: nut allergies can be very dangerous; never share nut snacks at school without asking.

part of speech: verb (weld, welds, welded, welding); noun (a weld, welds)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To weld means to join pieces of metal together by heating them until they melt and stick. 2) A weld is the joint where two pieces of metal have been welded. 3) To weld people or things together means to unite them closely.
its sense in the lessons: In DT and science lessons, welding joins metals; in jobs and stories, welders wear masks to protect their eyes from the bright light; phrases: welded together, weld shut.
examples from the lessons: The worker welded the two steel beams together. | Welders wear masks to protect their eyes. | The weld on the gate has cracked. | Never look at welding without eye protection. | The team was welded together by hard training. | The old door had been welded shut.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: welded. A person who welds is a «welder». Safety: welding light can damage eyes, which is why special masks are used.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Whey is the watery liquid left over when milk is made into cheese or yoghurt; the solid lumps are called curds. 2) Whey protein is a powder made from whey that some athletes add to drinks.
its sense in the lessons: In nursery rhymes: «Little Miss Muffet sat on a tuffet, eating her curds and whey»; in science, separating solids from liquids; in food labels and allergies, whey comes from milk.
examples from the lessons: Little Miss Muffet ate her curds and whey. | When milk turns into cheese, the whey drains away. | The farmer fed the whey to the pigs. | This protein shake has whey in it. | Whey comes from milk, so check if you have a milk allergy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Homophone trap: «whey» sounds like «way» and «weigh». Sometimes spelt «whey» only — not «whay».

part of speech: adjective (winged); verb form (past of wing: winged)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Winged means having wings, as in «a winged horse». 2) (verb, past) Winged means flew, or hit someone in the wing or arm lightly, as in «The arrow winged the bird». 3) (informal) To have winged it means to have done something without preparing, making it up as you went along. 4) In compound words, -winged describes the type of wings, as in «long-winged», «red-winged blackbird».
its sense in the lessons: In stories and myths: winged horses (Pegasus), winged dragons, angels; in science, winged insects and seeds (sycamore seeds); in everyday talk, «I winged the speech» (I improvised); phrases: wing it, winged insect.
examples from the lessons: Pegasus is a winged horse in Greek myths. | Sycamore seeds are winged and spin as they fall. | A winged insect buzzed past my ear. | I forgot my notes so I winged my talk. | The stone winged the pigeon but did not hurt it badly. | The red-winged blackbird sings in the marsh.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As an adjective it is said in one syllable or two: «winged» (wingd) or «wing-ed» in poems. «Wing it» is informal. Past of «wing»: winged.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The afterlife is a life that many people believe comes after death, for example in heaven. 2) (rare, informal) The afterlife of something is what happens to it after it stops being used, like the afterlife of a plastic bottle.
its sense in the lessons: In religious education, Christians believe in heaven and resurrection; Muslims, Jews and others have their own teachings; ancient Egyptians buried pharaohs with things for the afterlife; in history and stories about mummies and ghosts; phrases: in the afterlife, belief in the afterlife.
examples from the lessons: Ancient Egyptians packed food and treasure for the afterlife. | Christians believe that people who trust God will live with him in the afterlife. | Different religions teach different things about the afterlife. | The pharaoh's tomb was filled with things for his afterlife. | Some people do not believe in an afterlife at all. | The lesson was about the afterlife of a recycled can.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually «the afterlife», singular. Say beliefs respectfully as beliefs: «Many people believe…», «Christians believe…». No one can prove the afterlife scientifically; it is a matter of faith.

part of speech: noun (an alloy, alloys); verb (alloy, alloys, alloyed, alloying)
meaning for a pupil: 1) An alloy is a metal made by mixing two or more metals, or a metal with another element, to make it stronger or better. 2) Alloy wheels are car wheels made of a light metal alloy. 3) To alloy means to mix metals together to make an alloy.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on materials and mixtures: steel (iron + carbon), brass (copper + zinc), bronze (copper + tin); history (the Bronze Age); in everyday life, coins, bikes and wheels are made of alloys.
examples from the lessons: Steel is an alloy of iron and carbon. | Bronze is an alloy of copper and tin. | Coins are usually made of alloys. | Dad's car has shiny alloy wheels. | Alloys can be harder than pure metals. | The Bronze Age began when people learned to make a new alloy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: an alloy, alloys. Uses «an» because it starts with a vowel sound. Science: an alloy is a mixture, not a new compound.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Antibacterial means killing bacteria or stopping them from growing. 2) (rare) An antibacterial is a substance that does this.
its sense in the lessons: In science and health lessons: hygiene, germs, soap and hand gel; antibacterial things do not kill viruses like colds and flu; phrases: antibacterial soap, antibacterial wipes, antibacterial spray.
examples from the lessons: Mum cleaned the kitchen with antibacterial spray. | Antibacterial wipes help keep the table clean. | Antibacterial gel is useful when you can't wash your hands. | Honey has some antibacterial power. | Ordinary soap and water work as well as antibacterial soap for handwashing.
