note for the reader of a maths problem: Prefix «anti-» means «against». Myth trap: antibacterial products do not kill viruses; and too much use can help bacteria become resistant. Antibiotics are medicines that fight bacteria inside the body.

part of speech: adjective (aquatic, more aquatic); noun (an aquatic, aquatics — rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Aquatic means living or growing in water, as in «aquatic plants». 2) Aquatic also means happening in or on water, as in «aquatic sports» like swimming and diving. 3) (rare) An aquatic is a plant or animal that lives in water.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on habitats, adaptations and food chains (aquatic animals, aquatic habitats); in PE and leisure, aquatic centres and sports; opposite: terrestrial (living on land).
examples from the lessons: Frogs lay their eggs in an aquatic habitat. | Water lilies are aquatic plants. | Fish have gills because they are aquatic. | We went to the aquatic centre for swimming lessons. | Diving and water polo are aquatic sports. | Otters are partly aquatic animals.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From Latin «aqua» (water), like aquarium. Opposite in science: «terrestrial» (land). «Marine» means living in the sea; «aquatic» means any water, fresh or salty.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An arena is a big building or space with seats all around, where people watch sports, concerts or shows. 2) In ancient Rome, the arena was the sandy area where gladiators fought. 3) An arena can also mean an area of activity where people compete, as in «the political arena».
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons on the Romans and the Colosseum; in everyday life, concerts and ice hockey at the arena; in news, «the political arena»; phrases: sports arena, enter the arena.
examples from the lessons: We saw a concert at the big arena. | Gladiators fought in the arena of the Colosseum. | The ice hockey arena was full of cheering fans. | Thousands of people filled the arena. | She entered the political arena when she became a mayor. | The horse show was held in an indoor arena.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Uses «an» (an arena). From Latin for «sand», because Roman arenas were covered with sand.

part of speech: noun (asphalt — uncountable); verb (asphalt, asphalts, asphalted, asphalting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Asphalt is a black sticky material mixed with stones and used to make road surfaces and playgrounds. 2) To asphalt means to cover a road or area with asphalt.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: roads, car parks and school playgrounds; in science, asphalt gets hot in the sun; in safety, falling on asphalt grazes knees; also called tarmac (UK), blacktop (US) and bitumen (Australia).
examples from the lessons: The new road was covered with fresh asphalt. | The asphalt felt hot under our bare feet. | I fell over and scraped my knee on the asphalt. | Workers asphalted the school car park. | Asphalt smells strong when it is being laid.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Spelling trap: «asphalt», not «ashphalt». In the UK people usually say «tarmac», in the US «blacktop», in Australia «bitumen».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Audio means sound, especially recorded or broadcast sound. 2) As an adjective, audio means to do with sound, as in «an audio book», «audio equipment». 3) In computing, audio is the sound part of a video or a file.
its sense in the lessons: In computing and media lessons (audio files, recording podcasts), in everyday life (audiobooks, audio guides in museums); phrases: audio file, audiobook, audio guide, audio description.
examples from the lessons: The audio on the video was too quiet. | I listen to audiobooks on long car trips. | We recorded an audio file of our poem. | The museum had an audio guide in five languages. | Check that the audio cable is plugged in. | The audio and the picture were out of sync.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «the audio», not «an audio». From Latin «I hear», like «audience» and «audition». Opposite in media: «video» (picture).

meaning for a pupil: 1) To avert something bad means to stop it from happening, as in «avert a disaster». 2) To avert your eyes means to look away, often because something is upsetting or embarrassing.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and news: a quick action averts a crash or a war; in stories, a character averts their gaze when shy, sad or ashamed; it is a slightly formal word; phrases: avert disaster, avert your eyes, avert a crisis.
examples from the lessons: The driver braked hard and averted a crash. | Quick thinking averted disaster. | She averted her eyes from the scary scene. | Talks between the leaders averted a war. | He averted his gaze when the teacher looked at him.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: averted. Do not confuse with «avoid» (keep away from) or «divert» (send another way); «avert» means prevent or turn away. Trap: «avert» vs «advert» (an advertisement).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Bacon is salty meat from the back or sides of a pig, cut in thin slices and usually fried or grilled. 2) (informal, idiom) To bring home the bacon means to earn money for your family. 3) (informal, idiom) To save someone's bacon means to rescue them from trouble.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: breakfast, BLT sandwiches, a full English breakfast; in religion lessons, Jews and Muslims usually do not eat pork, so not bacon; in idioms in stories and talk; also Francis Bacon, a famous English thinker (a name).
examples from the lessons: Dad fried bacon and eggs for breakfast. | I'd like a bacon sandwich, please. | Some people do not eat bacon because of their religion. | You saved my bacon by lending me a pen! | Grandad worked hard to bring home the bacon. | Crispy bacon smells delicious.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «some bacon», «a slice/rasher of bacon» (rasher is UK), not «a bacon». Halal and kosher food rules forbid pork.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Bacterial means caused by bacteria or to do with bacteria, the tiny living things too small to see.
its sense in the lessons: In science and health lessons: bacterial infections can sometimes be treated with antibiotics, viral ones cannot; microorganisms, hygiene and food safety; phrases: bacterial infection, bacterial growth, bacterial cells.
examples from the lessons: She had a bacterial infection and needed antibiotics. | Washing your hands reduces bacterial growth. | Leaving food out can lead to bacterial growth. | Scientists grew bacterial colonies on a dish. | Tooth decay is partly bacterial.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Made from «bacteria» (plural of bacterium). Trap: antibiotics work on bacterial infections, not viral ones like colds. Not all bacteria are harmful; many are helpful in our gut.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) A baddie is a bad person or villain in a story, film or game. 2) (informal) A baddie can be any person or thing seen as the cause of trouble.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, films and play: goodies and baddies; in talk about books and plays, the baddie is the villain or antagonist; it tells you who the reader should be against.
examples from the lessons: The baddie in the film had a secret lair. | We played goodies and baddies in the playground. | In fairy tales, the wolf is often the baddie. | The baddies got caught at the end. | Sugar is sometimes made the baddie of healthy eating.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal; in essays write «villain» or «antagonist». Also spelt «baddy». Plural: baddies. Opposite: goodie (goody).

meaning for a pupil: 1) The bagpipes are a musical instrument with a bag that the player fills with air and squeezes, and pipes that make a loud, buzzing sound.
its sense in the lessons: In music lessons and stories about Scotland and Ireland; played at weddings, parades and funerals; it shows Scottish tradition; phrases: play the bagpipes, a bagpipe player (piper).
examples from the lessons: The piper played the bagpipes at the wedding. | You can hear bagpipes from a long way away. | Bagpipes are famous in Scotland. | The bagpipe player wore a kilt. | Ireland and Spain have their own kinds of bagpipe.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually plural: «the bagpipes», «play the bagpipes». A player is a «piper». Myth: bagpipes are not only Scottish; many countries have them.

part of speech: name (Benjamin); noun (a benjamin, benjamins — US slang)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (a name) Benjamin is a boy's name; short forms are Ben and Benji. 2) (Bible) Benjamin was the youngest son of Jacob in the Bible and the brother of Joseph. 3) (US, slang) A benjamin is a 100-dollar bill, because it has Benjamin Franklin's face on it. 4) (a name) Benjamin Franklin was an American inventor and leader who did experiments with electricity and kites.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life it is a common name; in Bible stories, Joseph and his brothers; in history, Benjamin Franklin; in US slang, «benjamins» means money; it is not a common English word.
examples from the lessons: My cousin Benjamin is five. | In the Bible, Benjamin was Jacob's youngest son. | Benjamin Franklin flew a kite in a storm. | Joseph hid a cup in Benjamin's sack. | «It's all about the benjamins» means it's all about money (US, slang).
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a name it takes a capital B. The slang «benjamins» is US and very informal. Do not invent facts about people with this name.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Caesium is a soft, silvery-gold metal, a chemical element (symbol Cs) that reacts violently with water. 2) Caesium is used in atomic clocks, the most accurate clocks there are.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on elements and the periodic table (group 1 alkali metals with sodium and potassium); in maths and science, time: the second is defined using caesium atoms; in news about nuclear accidents, radioactive caesium.
examples from the lessons: Caesium explodes if you drop it into water. | Atomic clocks use caesium to keep perfect time. | Caesium's symbol is Cs. | Caesium melts on a very hot day. | Radioactive caesium spread after the nuclear accident.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK spelling «caesium»; US spelling «cesium». Uncountable. Say it «SEE-zee-um». Safety: alkali metals are dangerous and only handled by trained scientists.

part of speech: noun (a callus, calluses); verb (callus, callused — rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A callus is a patch of hard, thick skin on your hands or feet, made by rubbing or pressing again and again. 2) (science) A callus is also the hard lump that forms around a broken bone as it heals.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and health: gymnasts, guitar players and walkers get calluses; in science, how skin protects itself and how bones heal; it shows hard work or practice in stories.
examples from the lessons: Playing guitar gives you calluses on your fingertips. | The gymnast had calluses on her hands. | Walking barefoot can make calluses on your feet. | The farmer's hands were rough with calluses. | A callus forms around a broken bone as it heals.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: calluses. Homophone trap: «callous» (adjective) means unkind and uncaring, as in «a callous remark». Not the same as a blister (a bubble of fluid).

part of speech: noun (a cascade, cascades); verb (cascade, cascades, cascaded, cascading)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A cascade is a small waterfall, or a series of small waterfalls going down rocks. 2) A cascade is a large amount of something falling or hanging down, like a cascade of hair or flowers. 3) A cascade is a chain of events where one thing causes the next, and the next. 4) To cascade means to pour or fall down quickly in large amounts.
its sense in the lessons: In geography, waterfalls and rivers; in stories and descriptions, hair cascading down a back, water cascading over rocks; in science and computing, a chain reaction; phrases: cascade down, a cascade of.
examples from the lessons: Water tumbled down the cascade into a pool. | Her curly hair cascaded down her back. | A cascade of balloons fell from the ceiling. | One mistake set off a cascade of problems. | Flowers cascaded over the garden wall. | Rain cascaded off the roof.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable as a noun. Past: cascaded. In computing, CSS means «Cascading Style Sheets».

part of speech: noun (a catapult, catapults); verb (catapult, catapults, catapulted, catapulting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A catapult is an old war machine that throws heavy stones or objects a long way. 2) (UK) A catapult is a Y-shaped stick with a rubber band used to shoot small stones; in the USA it is called a slingshot. 3) To catapult means to throw or launch something hard and fast. 4) To be catapulted into something means to be moved suddenly into a new situation, as in «catapulted to fame».
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons (sieges and castles), in DT and science (making catapults to test forces and energy), in stories; phrases: catapult into, catapulted to fame.
examples from the lessons: The army used a catapult to throw stones at the castle walls. | We built a lolly-stick catapult in science. | He fired a pea from his catapult. | The crash catapulted him out of his seat. | The song catapulted the band to fame. | We measured how far the catapult could throw a marshmallow.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Past: catapulted. «Catapult» (UK) = «slingshot» (US). Safety: never aim a catapult at people or animals.

part of speech: noun (a catfish, catfish); verb (catfish, catfishes, catfished, catfishing — slang)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A catfish is a fish with long whiskers around its mouth, like a cat's. 2) (slang, online) To catfish someone means to pretend to be another person online, using a false name and photos, to trick them. 3) (slang) A catfish is a person who does this.
its sense in the lessons: In science, river animals and habitats; in online-safety lessons, catfishing is a danger: people online may not be who they say; tell a trusted adult if something feels wrong.
examples from the lessons: The catfish lives on the muddy river bottom. | A catfish has whiskers called barbels. | We caught a big catfish in the lake. | He was catfished by someone pretending to be a twelve-year-old (slang). | Catfishing is when someone lies about who they are online. | Never meet an online friend without a parent.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: catfish (same). Safety: catfishing is a serious online risk; never share personal details or photos with strangers online.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A cliffhanger is an exciting ending to a chapter or episode that leaves you not knowing what will happen next, so you want to read or watch more. 2) A cliffhanger is also any contest or situation where the result stays uncertain until the very end.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons on writing stories and suspense: end a chapter with a cliffhanger; in TV series and books; in sport, a close game; it tells the reader to keep going.
examples from the lessons: The chapter ended on a cliffhanger. | I couldn't stop reading because of the cliffhangers. | The match was a real cliffhanger until the final whistle. | Write a cliffhanger to end your story's middle part. | The TV series always ends with a cliffhanger.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. One word. The idea comes from old stories where the hero was left hanging from a cliff at the end of an episode.

part of speech: noun (a cluster, clusters); verb (cluster, clusters, clustered, clustering)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A cluster is a group of similar things close together, like a cluster of grapes or stars. 2) To cluster means to gather or stay close together in a group. 3) (language) A consonant cluster is a group of consonant letters together in a word, like «str» in «string».
its sense in the lessons: In science (star clusters, flowers, cells); in maths and statistics, clusters on a graph or chart where many data points group together; in phonics lessons, consonant clusters; in everyday life, people cluster round something.
examples from the lessons: A cluster of grapes hung from the vine. | The Pleiades is a famous star cluster. | Children clustered around the teacher's desk. | The dots on the graph form a cluster. | «Spl» in «splash» is a consonant cluster. | Mushrooms grew in clusters on the log.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Past: clustered. In maths, a cluster on a chart means many values are close together.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A coalition is a government made by two or more political parties working together, often because no one party won enough seats. 2) A coalition is any group of people, groups or countries who join together for a shared aim.
its sense in the lessons: In politics lessons (elections, parliaments, governments in the UK, Australia, Ireland, New Zealand); in Australia, «the Coalition» means the Liberal and National parties together; in history, countries formed coalitions in wars.
examples from the lessons: The two parties formed a coalition government. | A coalition of countries sent help after the earthquake. | Schools and charities formed a coalition to stop litter. | No party won enough seats, so they needed a coalition. | The Coalition won the election (Australia).
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Say it «koh-uh-LISH-un». It means joining forces, not becoming one.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Coloration is the pattern and colours on an animal or plant. 2) (formal) Coloration can mean the general colour of something, or the way something is coloured.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on adaptation and camouflage: warning coloration (bright colours on poisonous animals) and camouflage coloration; it tells the reader how an animal's colours help it survive.
examples from the lessons: The tiger's striped coloration hides it in long grass. | Bright warning coloration tells birds that the frog is poisonous. | The bird's coloration changes in winter. | Scientists studied the coloration of the butterfly wings. | Some animals use coloration to attract a mate.
note for the reader of a maths problem: US spelling «coloration»; UK sometimes «colouration». Formal, scientific word. Mostly uncountable.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) Comfy means comfortable: soft, cosy and pleasant to sit, lie or be in. 2) (informal) Comfy can also mean feeling relaxed and at ease.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday talk about clothes, beds, chairs and sofas; in stories it creates a warm, safe feeling; a short, friendly word.
examples from the lessons: This sofa is really comfy. | I put on my comfy pyjamas. | Are you comfy in that chair, Nan? | These trainers are comfier than my school shoes. | The cat found a comfy spot by the fire. | Make yourself comfy while I make some tea.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal: in writing for school, «comfortable» is often better. Comparatives: comfier, comfiest (y → i).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Comparatively means when compared with something else, or to some degree, as in «comparatively cheap».
its sense in the lessons: In maths and science, when comparing amounts; in history and geography, «comparatively small country»; it tells the reader that a judgement depends on what you compare it with; often before an adjective.
examples from the lessons: The test was comparatively easy this week. | Mice live a comparatively short time. | The flat is comparatively cheap for London. | Ireland is comparatively small. | Comparatively few people came to the meeting. | Our school is comparatively new.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal-ish. Means «relatively». It comes from «comparative», which in grammar also names the -er form (bigger, faster). Trap: «comparatively cheap» does not mean very cheap, only cheaper than others.

part of speech: adjective (complex, more complex, most complex); noun (a complex, complexes)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Complex means made of many connected parts and hard to understand or explain. 2) A complex is a group of buildings used for one purpose, as in «a sports complex». 3) A complex is a strong, worried feeling about something, as in «He has a complex about his height». 4) (science) A complex is a group of things that work together, like a complex of chemicals.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and science, complex problems and systems; in everyday life, sports complexes, apartment complexes; in English and psychology, a complex is a worry; phrases: sports complex, complex sentence (grammar: a sentence with a main clause and a subordinate clause).
examples from the lessons: This puzzle is quite complex. | The human brain is very complex. | We swim at the new leisure complex. | A complex sentence has a main clause and a subordinate clause. | She has a complex about her freckles. | The rules of the game were too complex for my little brother.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite of «simple». Do not confuse with «complicated» (usually more negative) — both are close. Grammar term: complex sentence. Stress: «COM-plex» or «com-PLEX» for the adjective.

part of speech: noun (conserves — plural of conserve); verb form (conserves — he/she conserves)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Conserves are jams made from whole fruit pieces cooked with sugar. 2) (verb) Someone or something conserves something when it saves it, protects it or uses it carefully so it is not wasted.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography: conserving energy, water and habitats; in physics, energy is conserved; in cooking, fruit conserves; phrases: conserves energy, conserves water.
examples from the lessons: Grandma makes strawberry conserves every summer. | A short shower conserves water. | The charity conserves rare forests. | Turning off lights conserves energy. | The jar of apricot conserves is nearly empty. | A camel conserves water in its body.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a noun usually plural (conserves); as a verb it is the third person form of «conserve» (past: conserved). Science: «energy is conserved» means it is not lost, only changed into other forms. Noun: conservation.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A continuation is something that continues or carries on from something before, like the next part of a story. 2) Continuation is the act of carrying on without stopping.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons, writing a continuation of a story; in maths, the continuation of a pattern or sequence; in history, continuation of traditions.
examples from the lessons: Write a continuation of the story where the dragon comes back. | The second book is a continuation of the first. | The next term is a continuation of this number pattern. | The rain was a continuation of last week's wet weather. | The festival is a continuation of an old tradition.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a continuation. Verb: continue. In maths, continuing a sequence means finding the rule and using it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (music, UK) A crotchet is a musical note that lasts for one beat in most music; in the USA it is called a quarter note. 2) (old-fashioned) A crotchet is a strange, fixed idea or habit.
its sense in the lessons: In music lessons: crotchets, minims (two beats) and quavers (half a beat); counting beats is like fractions in maths; it tells you how long to hold a note.
examples from the lessons: A crotchet lasts for one beat. | Two quavers fit into one crotchet. | Clap four crotchets in each bar. | A minim is as long as two crotchets. | The crotchet has a black head and a stem.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK = crotchet, US = quarter note. Maths: crotchet = 1 beat; minim = 2; semibreve = 4; quaver = 1/2. Do not confuse with «crochet» (making things with yarn and a hook) — a common spelling trap.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A curriculum is all the subjects and topics that are taught at a school, college or in a course. 2) A curriculum is also the plan of what is taught in one subject, like the maths curriculum.
its sense in the lessons: In school and education life: the national curriculum (England), the Australian Curriculum, the Curriculum for Excellence (Scotland); phrases: on the curriculum, national curriculum.
examples from the lessons: Coding is now on the school curriculum. | The national curriculum says what children learn in each year. | Our science curriculum includes space and plants. | Teachers plan lessons from the curriculum. | The new curriculum has more outdoor learning.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: curricula (from Latin) or curriculums. Not to be confused with «CV» (curriculum vitae), which is a list of your education and jobs.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Domestication is the long process by which people tamed wild animals and plants over many generations, so they live with or are farmed by people.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons (the Stone Age, the first farmers), science (evolution, selective breeding); dogs came from wolves through domestication; cows, sheep, wheat and rice too.
examples from the lessons: The domestication of the dog began thousands of years ago. | Domestication of wheat helped people settle in villages. | Horses changed life after their domestication. | Cats may have chosen domestication themselves, by living near farms. | Domestication made cows calmer than their wild ancestors.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly uncountable. Verb: domesticate; adjective: domesticated, domestic. Trap: taming one wild animal is not domestication; domestication takes many generations.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Drizzly describes weather with light, fine rain falling steadily.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and weather lessons, recording weather; in everyday life in the UK and Ireland, very common; in stories it sets a grey, gloomy mood.
examples from the lessons: It was a drizzly morning in Dublin. | We played outside even though it was drizzly. | The forecast says drizzly with sunny spells. | A drizzly day makes the windows misty. | It's been drizzly all week.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comes from «drizzle» (light rain). Drizzle is lighter than a shower or downpour.

part of speech: noun (a duet, duets); verb (duet, duets, duetted, duetting — rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A duet is a piece of music for two singers or two players. 2) A duet is a performance by two people together. 3) (rare) To duet means to perform a duet.
its sense in the lessons: In music lessons and concerts; in stories, two characters sing together; related: solo (one), trio (three), quartet (four).
examples from the lessons: My sister and I sang a duet at the concert. | The piano duet had four hands on one keyboard. | The birds seemed to sing a duet. | They duetted on a famous love song. | A duet needs two performers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Numbers: solo = 1, duet = 2, trio = 3, quartet = 4. Say it «dew-ET».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A dugong is a large, gentle sea mammal with a whale-like tail that grazes on seagrass in warm shallow seas, like a sea cow.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on marine animals, endangered species and Australian wildlife; related to the manatee; old sailors' stories of mermaids may come from dugongs.
examples from the lessons: The dugong munched seagrass in the shallow water. | Dugongs live in the seas around northern Australia. | A dugong is a mammal, so it breathes air. | Dugongs are protected because they are endangered. | Sailors may have mistaken dugongs for mermaids.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. It is a mammal, not a fish. Different from a manatee: a dugong has a fluked tail like a dolphin; a manatee has a round, paddle-like tail.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An edition is one version of a book, newspaper or magazine printed at one time, like a first edition. 2) An edition is one copy or issue of a regular newspaper, show or event, like «this week's edition». 3) A special or limited edition is a version made in small numbers or for a special reason.
its sense in the lessons: In English and library lessons: first editions, new editions with changes; in everyday life, special edition toys and games; phrases: first edition, latest edition, limited edition, special edition.
examples from the lessons: This is a first edition of the book. | The new edition has extra pictures. | Today's edition of the newspaper has a story about our school. | They made a limited edition of 500 teddy bears. | Grandad collects special edition coins.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Uses «an». Do not confuse with «addition» (adding, in maths) — they sound similar. The person who prepares texts is an «editor».

meaning for a pupil: 1) An embassy is the official building in a foreign country where an ambassador and their staff work to represent their own country. 2) An embassy is also the group of people who work there.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and politics lessons: countries keep embassies in each other's capitals; in everyday life, people go to embassies for visas and help abroad; phrases: the British Embassy, the American Embassy.
examples from the lessons: The Ukrainian Embassy is in London. | My aunt got her visa at the embassy. | If you lose your passport abroad, go to your embassy. | Guards stood outside the embassy gates. | The ambassador works in the embassy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: embassies (y → ies). An ambassador leads an embassy. A smaller office in other cities is a «consulate».

part of speech: noun (an emerald, emeralds; emerald — the colour); adjective (emerald)
meaning for a pupil: 1) An emerald is a bright green precious stone used in jewellery. 2) Emerald is a bright, rich green colour. 3) The Emerald Isle is a nickname for Ireland, because of its green fields.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, treasure, crowns and rings; in art and description, colours; in geography, Ireland's nickname; in science, gems and crystals; in The Wizard of Oz, the Emerald City.
examples from the lessons: The queen's ring had a huge emerald. | The sea was a sparkling emerald green. | Ireland is called the Emerald Isle. | Dorothy followed the road to the Emerald City. | Emeralds are mined in Colombia.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable as a stone, uncountable as a colour. Uses «an emerald». It is the birthstone for May.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (law) To enact a law means to make it officially into law. 2) To enact a story or scene means to act it out or perform it. 3) (formal) To enact something can also mean to carry out a plan.
its sense in the lessons: In politics and law lessons: Parliament enacts laws; in drama, children enact scenes from stories or history; in news, «enacted a new rule».
examples from the lessons: Parliament enacted a new law about plastic bags. | The class enacted the story of the Gunpowder Plot. | The plan was enacted after months of talks. | We enacted the story of Robin Hood in drama. | The law was enacted last year.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: enacted. Noun: enactment. Formal word; in drama, «act out» is more common for children.

part of speech: adjective (equipped, well-equipped, better equipped); verb form (past of equip: equipped)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Equipped means having the tools, machines or things you need for a job or activity. 2) Equipped (to do something) can also mean having the skills or knowledge you need.
its sense in the lessons: In science, labs are well equipped; in stories and adventures, explorers equipped with ropes and torches; in school, being equipped for lessons means having pencil, ruler and so on; phrases: well-equipped, equipped with, equipped for.
examples from the lessons: The lab is equipped with microscopes. | Come to school equipped with a pen and a ruler. | The climbers were well equipped for the snow. | Our new hall is equipped for drama shows. | After the course she felt equipped to help in an emergency. | The ambulance is equipped with oxygen.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: double p — equip → equipped, equipping. The noun «equipment» has one p and is uncountable.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An era is a long period of history with special features or events, like the Victorian era. 2) (science) In geology, an era is a very long period of Earth's history, like the Mesozoic Era when dinosaurs lived. 3) An era is any period marked by something new, as in «the era of smartphones».
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons (Victorian era, Tudor era), science (geological eras, dinosaurs), everyday talk («the end of an era»); phrases: a new era, end of an era, the modern era.
examples from the lessons: Queen Victoria gave her name to the Victorian era. | Dinosaurs lived in the Mesozoic Era. | The internet started a new era. | When our head teacher retired, it was the end of an era. | Steam trains were common in that era.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Uses «an era». Different words for time: an era is long; a decade is 10 years; a century is 100 years. CE and BCE are «Common Era» and «Before Common Era».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A fairground is an open area where a fair is held, with rides, games, stalls and food. 2) As an adjective-like word, fairground describes things from a fair, as in «fairground rides».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and stories: summer fairs, carousels, dodgems, candyfloss; in science, forces on rides; in safety, staying with adults and following ride rules; phrases: fairground ride, fairground games.
examples from the lessons: We went on the dodgems at the fairground. | The fairground lights glowed at night. | Hold Dad's hand so you don't get lost in the fairground. | The fairground was packed with families. | I won a teddy on a fairground game. | A big wheel stood in the middle of the fairground.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. One word. In the USA «fairgrounds» (plural) is often used for one place, as in «the county fairgrounds».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Finite means having an end or a limit; not going on forever. 2) (grammar) A finite verb is a verb that shows tense and agrees with its subject, as in «she runs».
its sense in the lessons: In maths, a finite set has a countable number of things; numbers themselves are infinite; in science and geography, finite resources like oil and coal will run out; in grammar, finite and non-finite verbs.
examples from the lessons: The Earth has finite supplies of oil. | Our time on the trip is finite, so let's hurry. | A finite set has an end, like the days of the week. | The counting numbers are infinite, not finite. | In «She sings», «sings» is a finite verb.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: «infinite» (no end). Say it «FY-nite»; but «infinite» is «IN-fin-it». Maths: finite = you could, in principle, finish counting.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Flexibility is the ability to bend easily without breaking. 2) Flexibility is being able to change or fit in with new situations or plans.
its sense in the lessons: In PE and health lessons, stretching improves flexibility; in science, materials' properties (rubber has flexibility); in everyday life, flexible plans or hours; phrases: show flexibility, improve flexibility.
examples from the lessons: Yoga helps improve flexibility. | Gymnasts need great flexibility. | Rubber's flexibility makes it good for tyres. | Teachers need flexibility when plans change. | The new timetable gives more flexibility.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «good flexibility», not «a flexibility». Adjective: flexible. Opposite: rigidity, stiffness.

part of speech: noun (froth — uncountable); verb (froth, froths, frothed, frothing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Froth is lots of small bubbles on top of a liquid, like foam on a milkshake. 2) To froth means to make or have froth. 3) Froth can mean something light and fun but not very important, like froth in a story or show. 4) (informal) To froth at the mouth means to be extremely angry.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: frothy coffee, milkshakes, bubble baths; in science, bubbles of gas trapped in liquid; in stories, an angry character frothing at the mouth; phrases: froth up, froth at the mouth.
examples from the lessons: The milkshake had a thick froth on top. | Waves left froth on the sand. | Mum frothed the milk for her coffee. | The angry man was frothing at the mouth. | That film is just froth, but it's fun.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Adjective: frothy. Similar: foam, bubbles.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A generalisation is a statement about all or most things of a kind, based on some examples. 2) A sweeping generalisation is one that is too broad and unfair, like «all boys hate reading». 3) (maths) A generalisation is a rule that works for all cases, like «the sum of two even numbers is always even».
its sense in the lessons: In maths, making generalisations from patterns («each term is 3 more than the last»); in science, conclusions from experiments; in English and PSHE, avoiding unfair generalisations and stereotypes.
examples from the lessons: It is a generalisation to say that all cats hate water. | From the pattern we made a generalisation: odd plus odd is even. | Be careful with generalisations about people. | Scientists test a generalisation with more experiments. | «Everyone loves pizza» is a generalisation.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK spelling «generalisation», US «generalization». Countable. Maths: a generalisation must be checked; one counterexample shows it is false.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Geographical means to do with geography: the places, land, seas, climate and people of the Earth. 2) Geographical also means connected with where something is.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons: geographical features (mountains, rivers, coasts), geographical location, geographical skills (maps, compass); phrases: geographical features, geographical area, geographical location.
examples from the lessons: Rivers and mountains are geographical features. | Our project is about the geographical location of Canada. | Maps show geographical information. | The geographical centre of Britain is in Lancashire. | The geographical spread of the disease was wide.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Also «geographic» (more US). Adverb: geographically. Noun: geography.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A geologist is a scientist who studies rocks, soil, minerals and how the Earth was formed and changes.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography lessons about rocks, volcanoes, earthquakes, fossils; in jobs; geologists find oil, water or metals; related: geology (the subject).
examples from the lessons: The geologist studied the layers in the cliff. | Geologists can tell how old a rock is. | My mum is a geologist who studies volcanoes. | A geologist found fossils in the shale. | Geologists help find water underground.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Not to be confused with a palaeontologist, who studies fossils of ancient life, or an archaeologist, who studies human history from objects.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Glacial means to do with glaciers or ice, as in «glacial valleys». 2) Glacial means extremely cold. 3) Glacial means very slow, as in «at a glacial pace». 4) (informal) Glacial can describe someone who is very unfriendly and cold.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons: glacial erosion, U-shaped glacial valleys, the Ice Age; in everyday talk and stories, a glacial wind or a glacial look; phrases: glacial valley, glacial period, glacial pace.
examples from the lessons: Glaciers carved this U-shaped glacial valley. | A glacial wind blew off the sea. | Traffic moved at a glacial pace. | She gave him a glacial stare. | The lake was formed in the last glacial period.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say it «GLAY-shul». The noun is «glacier» (river of ice). «Glacial pace» is an idiom meaning very slow.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Glassy means smooth, shiny and clear, like glass. 2) Glassy eyes look blank and without expression, often because of tiredness, illness or being upset.
its sense in the lessons: In descriptive writing: a glassy lake, a glassy stare; in science, glassy rocks like obsidian; in stories, a character's glassy eyes show shock or sleepiness.
examples from the lessons: The lake was glassy and still in the morning. | Obsidian is a glassy black rock. | His eyes went glassy with tiredness. | The sea was glassy calm. | She stared at us with a glassy look.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparatives: glassier, glassiest (y → i). Glassy water is calm with no waves.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (a name) Goldilocks is the girl in the fairy tale «Goldilocks and the Three Bears», who tries the bears' porridge, chairs and beds and likes the ones that are «just right». 2) (informal) Goldilocks describes something that is not too much and not too little but just right. 3) (science) The Goldilocks zone is the area around a star where a planet is neither too hot nor too cold for liquid water.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and literacy lessons, the fairy tale; in science, the Goldilocks zone in space lessons about planets and life; in everyday talk, «a Goldilocks amount».
examples from the lessons: Goldilocks ate the baby bear's porridge. | The porridge was too hot, then too cold, then just right. | Earth is in the Goldilocks zone of the Sun. | We need a Goldilocks amount of water for the seeds. | The three bears found Goldilocks asleep.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Written with a capital G. Not a real person. Her name means «golden hair» (locks = hair).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Haitian means from or to do with Haiti, a country in the Caribbean on the island of Hispaniola. 2) A Haitian is a person from Haiti. 3) Haitian Creole is the language most people speak in Haiti, together with French.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons about the Caribbean; in history, Haiti was the first country founded after enslaved people freed themselves; in news, earthquakes and aid; phrases: Haitian Creole, Haitian food, Haitian people.
examples from the lessons: My friend's family is Haitian. | Haitian Creole comes partly from French. | Haitian art is colourful and bright. | The Haitian Revolution ended slavery there. | Many Haitians live in Canada and the USA.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always a capital H. Say it «HAY-shun». Haiti shares its island with the Dominican Republic. Do not mix up with Tahitian (from Tahiti).

part of speech: noun (haze, a haze — mostly singular); verb (haze, hazes, hazed, hazing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A haze is a thin mist, smoke or dust in the air that makes it hard to see far. 2) A haze is a confused or dreamy state of mind, as in «in a haze». 3) (US) To haze someone means to make new members of a group do silly, embarrassing or dangerous things as a test; this is a kind of bullying.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and science, heat haze, smog and pollution; in stories, a dreamy or sleepy feeling; in safety and US news, hazing is harmful and against the rules; phrases: heat haze, in a haze.
examples from the lessons: A heat haze shimmered over the road. | The city was hidden in a haze of smoke. | I was in a haze after waking up. | Bushfire smoke left a brown haze over Sydney. | Hazing new team members is dangerous and banned.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: hazy. Usually «a haze» or «the haze». Hazing (US) is bullying, not a joke.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Headless means having no head, like a headless statue or ghost. 2) (informal) Running around like a headless chicken means rushing about in panic without thinking. 3) (computing) A headless computer or browser has no screen and is controlled by another computer.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, ghosts and legends (the Headless Horseman); in history, statues and executions (Anne Boleyn's ghost); in everyday talk, the idiom «like a headless chicken»; in computing, headless systems.
examples from the lessons: The Headless Horseman rode through the woods. | The museum had a headless Roman statue. | My dad ran around like a headless chicken looking for his keys. | The snowman was headless after the dog knocked it over. | The ghost story was about a headless knight.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Made from «head» + «-less» (without). Other -less words: careless, endless, homeless.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Healthcare is the work of looking after people's health: doctors, nurses, hospitals, medicine and the help people get when they are ill or hurt.
its sense in the lessons: In PSHE, citizenship and news: the NHS in the UK, Medicare in Australia and Canada; healthcare workers; phrases: healthcare worker, free healthcare, access to healthcare.
examples from the lessons: In the UK, healthcare is free through the NHS. | Nurses are important healthcare workers. | Everyone needs good healthcare. | Healthcare costs a lot of money in some countries. | My aunt works in healthcare as a midwife.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Written as one word or «health care» (two words, often in the US). Not «a healthcare».

part of speech: noun (a honeycomb, honeycombs); verb (honeycomb, honeycombed — usually passive)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A honeycomb is a wax structure made by bees with many six-sided cells where they store honey and raise their young. 2) Honeycomb is a sweet, crunchy, golden toffee full of bubbles. 3) A honeycomb pattern is a pattern of hexagons. 4) To be honeycombed with something means to be full of holes or tunnels, as in «a hill honeycombed with caves».
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on bees and pollination; in maths, the honeycomb shows hexagons tessellating (fitting together with no gaps); in food, honeycomb sweets and Crunchie bars.
examples from the lessons: Bees build a honeycomb from wax. | Each cell of a honeycomb is a hexagon. | Hexagons tessellate, just like a honeycomb. | I love honeycomb ice cream. | The hill is honeycombed with old mine tunnels. | The beekeeper lifted out a dripping honeycomb.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable as a bee structure; uncountable as a sweet. Maths: a hexagon has six sides; the honeycomb shape uses little wax for lots of space.

part of speech: noun (a husk, husks); verb (husk, husks, husked, husking)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A husk is the dry outer covering of some seeds or fruits, like corn, coconuts or rice. 2) A husk is the dry, empty shell of something when the inside has gone. 3) To husk means to remove the husk.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on seeds and plants; in cooking, husking corn; in the Bible, the prodigal son wanted to eat the pigs' husks; in stories, «a husk of his former self» means weak and empty; adjective «husky» can mean a rough, deep voice.
examples from the lessons: We pulled the husks off the corn cobs. | The coconut husk is hairy and tough. | In the Bible story, the lost son was so hungry he wished he could eat the pigs' husks. | After the illness he was a husk of his old self. | Rice husks are removed at the mill.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Past: husked. «Husky» can mean a sled dog, a hoarse voice, or full of husks — different senses.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An ibis is a wading bird with long legs and a long, thin, curved beak that lives near water. 2) (Australia, slang) The Australian white ibis is often called a «bin chicken» because it eats from rubbish bins.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on birds and habitats; in history, the ancient Egyptians thought the ibis was sacred to the god Thoth; in Australia, the bin chicken jokes.
examples from the lessons: An ibis poked its curved beak into the mud. | The ancient Egyptians mummified ibises. | A bin chicken stole my sandwich in the park (Australia, slang). | The scarlet ibis is bright red. | Ibises often nest in big groups.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: ibises (or ibis). Uses «an ibis». Say it «EYE-bis».

meaning for a pupil: 1) An impairment is a problem with part of the body or mind that makes it work less well, as in «hearing impairment» or «visual impairment». 2) Impairment is the state of being damaged or weakened.
its sense in the lessons: In PSHE and inclusion lessons: people with visual or hearing impairments; respectful talk about disability; in science and health, how the body works; phrases: hearing impairment, visual impairment, sight impairment.
examples from the lessons: My friend has a hearing impairment and uses hearing aids. | Braille helps people with a visual impairment to read. | Some impairments cannot be seen. | Ramps help people with mobility impairments. | Alcohol causes impairment of judgement (for adults).
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal word. Verb: impair; adjective: impaired. Use respectful language: «a person with a hearing impairment».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (grammar) The imperative is the form of a verb used to give orders, instructions or advice, like «Sit down!» or «Mix the flour». 2) Imperative means extremely important or urgent, as in «It is imperative that you arrive on time». 3) An imperative is something you must do, a duty or need.
its sense in the lessons: In English grammar lessons: imperative verbs in instructions, recipes and rules («Cut the paper. Fold it in half.»); in formal speech, «it is imperative» means it must happen; phrases: imperative verb, it is imperative that.
examples from the lessons: «Close the door» uses an imperative verb. | Recipes are full of imperatives like «stir» and «bake». | It is imperative that you wear a helmet. | Bossy verbs are imperatives. | Write instructions using imperative verbs. | Saving the forest is a moral imperative.
note for the reader of a maths problem: In grammar, the imperative has no subject: «(You) sit down». Teachers often call them «bossy verbs». Formal sense is in the stiff exam voice.

part of speech: noun (an implement, implements); verb (implement, implements, implemented, implementing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) An implement is a tool or instrument for doing a particular job, like a garden implement or a writing implement. 2) (formal) To implement a plan, rule or idea means to put it into action. 3) (computing) To implement means to write the code that makes something work.
its sense in the lessons: In history, Stone Age implements made of flint; in DT and farming, tools and implements; in news and formal writing, governments implement plans; phrases: farm implement, writing implement, implement a plan.
examples from the lessons: Stone Age people made implements from flint. | A pencil is a writing implement. | The school will implement a new uniform rule. | Farm implements were pulled by horses. | The coder implemented a new feature in the game.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun is said «IM-pli-ment»; verb is also «IM-pli-ment» with a different last syllable («-ment» like «ment», stronger). Formal word. Noun of the verb: implementation.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Innate means something you are born with, not something you learned, like an innate talent or instinct. 2) (formal) Innate means being a natural part of something.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about animal behaviour: instincts are innate (spiders spin webs without being taught); in PSHE and debates, nature vs nurture; phrases: innate ability, innate behaviour.
examples from the lessons: Babies have an innate ability to suck. | Spiders' web-building is innate. | She has an innate sense of rhythm. | Some scientists think a love of stories is innate in people. | Innate behaviour is not learned.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal. Opposite: learned (or acquired). Trap: most skills need practice even if some talent is innate.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Kin means your family and relatives. 2) Next of kin is your closest relative, often named on forms for emergencies. 3) (old-fashioned) Kin can mean people or animals of the same kind.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and history, kings and clans protected their kin; on forms, «next of kin»; in science, related animals; phrases: kith and kin (friends and family), next of kin.
examples from the lessons: The hospital called his next of kin. | They gathered all their kin for the wedding. | Kith and kin means friends and relatives. | Wolves protect their kin. | She is my kin; we share a great-grandmother.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Takes a plural verb: «My kin are coming». Not «a kin». Related: kinship, kinsfolk. Old-fashioned and formal words in many uses.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A kookaburra is a big Australian bird of the kingfisher family with a loud call that sounds like a person laughing.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about Australian animals, birds and habitats; in music, the old children's round «Kookaburra sits in the old gum tree»; in Australia, a familiar morning sound.
examples from the lessons: The kookaburra laughed loudly at dawn. | Kookaburras eat snakes, lizards and insects. | We sang «Kookaburra sits in the old gum tree». | A kookaburra snatched a sausage from the barbecue. | The laughing kookaburra is a kind of kingfisher.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Native to Australia (also introduced in New Zealand). Its laugh is actually a call to mark its territory.

part of speech: noun (a landing, landings); verb form (landing — present participle of land)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A landing is when an aircraft, spacecraft or bird comes down to the ground or water. 2) A landing is the flat area at the top of stairs or between two flights of stairs. 3) A landing is a place where boats stop to load and unload. 4) (verb form) Landing means coming down to the ground, or arriving, as in «landing on the Moon».
its sense in the lessons: In science and history: the first Moon landing, plane landings; in everyday homes, the landing upstairs; in stories, crash landings and safe landings; phrases: crash landing, Moon landing, landing gear, on the landing.
examples from the lessons: The plane made a smooth landing. | Astronauts first walked on the Moon after a Moon landing. | I left my shoes on the landing. | The crash landing scared the passengers. | The duck made a splashy landing on the pond. | Boats unload at the landing by the river.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. In homes, the landing is upstairs, not the hall at the bottom.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (Scotland, Northern England, informal) A lassie is a girl or young woman. 2) (a name) Lassie is a famous brave collie dog in books, films and TV.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and songs from Scotland; in everyday Scottish talk («a wee lassie»); in films, Lassie the dog rescues people; related: lass, laddie, lad.
examples from the lessons: The wee lassie was playing on the beach (Scotland). | «Come here, lassie!» called her granny. | Lassie the collie always saves the day. | The laddies and lassies danced at the ceilidh. | She's a fine lassie, that one.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal, Scottish. Masculine: «laddie» or «lad». Shorter form: «lass».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Leukaemia is a kind of cancer of the blood and bone marrow, where the body makes too many faulty white blood cells.
its sense in the lessons: In health and science lessons about blood cells; in stories and real life, children and adults can have leukaemia and many get better with treatment like chemotherapy; charities raise money for research; phrases: childhood leukaemia.
examples from the lessons: My cousin had leukaemia and got better after treatment. | Leukaemia affects the white blood cells. | Doctors treat leukaemia with medicines called chemotherapy. | Our school raised money for leukaemia research. | You cannot catch leukaemia from someone.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK spelling «leukaemia»; US «leukemia». Say it «loo-KEE-mee-uh». Uncountable. Myth trap: it is not contagious. Many children with leukaemia today are cured.

part of speech: noun (lidar — usually no plural; lidar scanners)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A way of measuring distance by sending out quick flashes of laser light and timing how long they take to bounce back. 2) The machine or sensor that does this, as on a self-driving car or a survey plane.
its sense in the lessons: In science and technology lessons lidar is an example of how machines "see": like a bat's echo, but with light instead of sound. It is used to map forests, find hidden ruins under trees, measure sea ice and help robots and driverless cars avoid things. In stories about the future it tells the reader a machine is scanning its surroundings. Phrases: lidar scan, lidar sensor, lidar map.
examples from the lessons: The self-driving car has a spinning lidar on its roof. | Scientists used lidar to find old Mayan cities hidden under the jungle. | A lidar sensor measures how far away the wall is. | The plane flew over the hills to make a lidar map. | Some new phones use lidar to measure a room. | Lidar works a bit like a bat's echo, but with light. | The robot vacuum uses lidar so it doesn't bump into the sofa.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced LY-dar. It comes from "light detection and ranging" (like radar, which uses radio waves). Usually uncountable: "lidar shows…"; "a lidar" means one sensor. Do not confuse with radar (radio waves) or sonar (sound). Light travels so fast that lidar measures tiny times; distance = speed × time ÷ 2, because the light goes there and back.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A piece of writing in which one letter of the alphabet is never used on purpose, for example a story with no letter "e".
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons and word puzzles a lipogram is a writing game and a challenge: you must find other words to say what you mean. It shows how common some letters are (e is the commonest in English). In olympiad puzzles you may be asked to spot which letter is missing. Phrases: write a lipogram, a lipogram without e.
examples from the lessons: Our teacher asked us to write a lipogram without the letter "a". | "I am big, I can run" is not a lipogram without "a", because "am" has an "a". | A whole French novel was written as a lipogram with no letter "e". | Writing a lipogram makes you think hard about words. | Can you spot which letter this lipogram leaves out? | My lipogram about a cat had no "t", so I called it a "kitty-cuddly animal"… oops, that has a "t"!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one lipogram, two lipograms. Pronounced LIP-oh-gram. From Greek "leaving out a letter". Not the same as a pangram, which uses every letter (The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog). Not to do with lips.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The international radio call for help used by ships and aircraft in great danger, said three times: "Mayday, mayday, mayday". 2) (informal) Any urgent call for help. 3) May Day (two words, capital letters) is a different thing: the first day of May, a spring festival and a workers' holiday.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and safety lessons "Mayday!" tells the reader that a pilot or captain is in life-or-death danger, such as an engine failure or a sinking boat. It is only for real emergencies; using it falsely is a crime. Phrases: send a mayday, a mayday call, put out a mayday. "Pan-pan" is the smaller urgent call when there is no immediate danger to life.
examples from the lessons: Mayday, mayday, mayday! Our engine is on fire! shouted the pilot. | The fishing boat sent a mayday when it began to sink. | The coastguard answered the mayday call within seconds. | Never say "mayday" on a radio as a joke. | My sister's text was a total mayday: "Help, I forgot my homework!" | In the film, the captain put out a mayday before the storm hit. | On May Day we danced round a maypole at school.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It comes from the French "m'aider" (help me), which sounds like "mayday". Written with a small letter or capital (Mayday!) when it is a call; written "May Day" for the spring holiday. It is said three times so it cannot be mistaken. Trap: do not mix up mayday (help!) with May Day (festival).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) A medicine: a substance used to treat an illness or injury, such as a tablet, cream or syrup.
its sense in the lessons: Medicament is a stiff, formal word; children, doctors and parents nearly always just say "medicine". You meet it on packets, in leaflets, in old books and in exam texts. It tells the reader the writing is official or old-fashioned. In other languages (French "médicament", Spanish "medicamento") it is the everyday word, so translators sometimes use it.
examples from the lessons: The nurse put the medicament on the cut. | Keep all medicaments out of the reach of children. | The leaflet explains how to store the medicament. | "Medicament" is a posh word for medicine. | In the old story, the doctor mixed a strange medicament in a jar. | Never take a medicament that was prescribed for someone else.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a medicament, medicaments. Formal; in everyday speech say "medicine" or "medication". False friend for French, Spanish and Ukrainian speakers, whose everyday word looks like it — in English it sounds stiff. Safety: only take medicines from a trusted adult or doctor.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A natural chemical (a hormone) your body makes when it gets dark, which helps you feel sleepy. 2) The same substance made in tablets or gummies, sometimes given by a doctor to help people sleep.
its sense in the lessons: In science and health lessons melatonin explains the body clock: darkness tells the brain to make melatonin, and bright light, especially screens at night, can stop it. That is why the lesson says to put phones away before bed. It also helps travellers with jet lag. Phrases: melatonin levels, take melatonin, melatonin and sleep.
examples from the lessons: Your body makes melatonin when the room gets dark. | Bright screens at bedtime can lower your melatonin. | Melatonin helps you feel sleepy at night. | The doctor said my brother could take a small dose of melatonin. | Jet lag happens partly because your melatonin is on the wrong time. | Animals make melatonin too, which helps them know the seasons.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: "melatonin is", not "a melatonin". Pronounced mel-a-TOH-nin. Not the same as melanin (the colouring in skin and hair). In some countries melatonin tablets need a prescription; children should only take them if a doctor says so. Myth: it is not a sleeping pill that knocks you out; it gently tells the body it is night.

part of speech: adjective (mighty, mightier, mightiest); adverb (mighty — informal, US)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Very strong or powerful. 2) Very big and impressive: a mighty river, a mighty oak. 3) (informal, mostly US) Very; really: "That's mighty kind of you." 4) (Bible) Strong, said of God or great heroes: "the mighty acts of God".
its sense in the lessons: In stories "mighty" makes something sound grand, strong or heroic: a mighty king, a mighty roar, a mighty wave. In poems and the Bible it gives a big, old-style feel. The saying "The pen is mightier than the sword" means words and ideas can be stronger than fighting. "High and mighty" means acting proud and bossy. In the US South and in cowboy films "mighty" is a friendly way to say "very".
examples from the lessons: The mighty lion roared across the plain. | A mighty oak grows from a tiny acorn. | The Amazon is a mighty river. | "That's mighty nice of you, partner," said the cowboy. | The pen is mightier than the sword. | Don't get all high and mighty with me just because you won! | Christians sing that God is mighty and kind. | With one mighty kick, she scored the winning goal.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Forms: mighty, mightier, mightiest. Comes from the noun "might" (strength), not from the verb "might" (maybe). Trap: "mighty" (strong) has nothing to do with "might" in "I might go". As an adverb "mighty" is informal: say "very" in school writing.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A small fish that lives on muddy shores and in mangrove swamps and can come out of the water, skipping and crawling on the mud with its strong front fins.
its sense in the lessons: In science and nature lessons the mudskipper is a famous example of an animal between water and land: it breathes partly through its skin and keeps water in its gill chambers. It helps pupils think about adaptation and how fish might once have moved onto land. It lives in warm places such as Africa, Asia and northern Australia.
examples from the lessons: The mudskipper hopped across the mud at low tide. | A mudskipper can stay out of water for a long time. | Mudskippers have eyes on top of their heads, like little periscopes. | We watched a nature show about mudskippers in the mangroves. | The male mudskipper jumps high to impress a female. | Is a mudskipper a fish or a frog? It is a fish!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a mudskipper, mudskippers. One word. It is a real fish, not an amphibian, even though it spends much time on land. Myth: it does not have lungs; it keeps damp to breathe.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The person or voice who tells the story in a book, poem, film or play. 2) A person who reads or speaks the words that explain what is happening, as in a documentary, audiobook or school play.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons you learn to find the narrator and ask who is telling the story: a first-person narrator says "I", a third-person narrator says "he", "she" or "they". A narrator can be honest or unreliable (not to be fully trusted). In school plays the narrator explains the scenes between the acting. Phrases: first-person narrator, third-person narrator, unreliable narrator, the narrator tells us.
examples from the lessons: The narrator of the story is a little dog. | In our class play I was the narrator. | "I opened the door," says the narrator, so it is a first-person story. | David Attenborough is the narrator of many nature programmes. | The narrator doesn't tell us the boy's name until the end. | Can we trust this narrator, or is he hiding something? | The audiobook narrator did funny voices for each character.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a narrator, narrators. Spelled with -or. Verb: narrate; noun: narration, narrative. The narrator is not always the author: a writer can invent a narrator who is a child, an animal or a villain.

part of speech: noun (the northwest); adjective (northwest wind); adverb (go northwest)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The direction halfway between north and west. 2) The part of a country or area that lies in that direction, as in "the Northwest of England". 3) (as adjective) In, from or facing the northwest: a northwest wind blows from the northwest.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and maps northwest is one of the eight compass points (NW), between north and west. It is used in map reading, directions and weather reports. The Northwest Passage is a sea route through the Arctic north of Canada. The Pacific Northwest is a region of the USA and Canada. Phrases: to the northwest, in the northwest, north-west of.
examples from the lessons: The wind is blowing from the northwest. | Manchester is in the northwest of England. | Walk northwest until you reach the river. | On the map, the castle is northwest of the village. | Explorers searched for the Northwest Passage for hundreds of years. | NW on a compass stands for northwest. | Seattle is in the Pacific Northwest.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Written northwest or north-west (UK often uses the hyphen). Short form NW. Capital letter when it names a region (the Northwest). A "northwest wind" comes FROM the northwest, not goes there — a common trap. Opposite direction: southeast. On a compass it is 315 degrees from north.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A very hard, painful or frightening experience that goes on for some time. 2) (history) In the Middle Ages, a cruel test, such as holding hot iron, used to "decide" if someone was guilty.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and news an ordeal tells the reader that a character went through something terrible and survived: being lost, trapped, ill or kidnapped. People say "after their ordeal" or "a terrible ordeal". In history lessons "trial by ordeal" was an old, unfair way of judging people. In everyday talk it can be used jokily for something boring or annoying: "The car journey was an ordeal."
examples from the lessons: The climbers were safe after a long ordeal on the mountain. | Being stuck in the lift for two hours was a real ordeal. | She told reporters about her ordeal at sea. | Trial by ordeal was used in medieval England. | The dentist visit was not the ordeal I expected. | After the ordeal, the lost hikers were given hot soup.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: an ordeal (use "an" — it begins with a vowel sound). Pronounced or-DEEL. Stronger than "difficulty" or "problem": an ordeal is long and upsetting.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Stretched out as far as possible, usually said of arms, hands, wings or legs.
its sense in the lessons: In stories "outstretched" paints a picture: outstretched arms can mean a welcome, a hug, begging, or reaching to save someone; outstretched wings mean a bird is flying or gliding. It often comes in the phrase "with arms outstretched" or "with an outstretched hand". In PE it describes body positions.
examples from the lessons: Grandma waited at the door with outstretched arms. | The eagle glided with its wings outstretched. | He reached for the rope with an outstretched hand. | Lie on the mat with your legs outstretched. | The little boy ran into his dad's outstretched arms. | The beggar held out an outstretched cup.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Only an adjective; it does not change form. It comes from the verb "stretch out" (stretched out). It can go before the noun (outstretched arms) or after it (arms outstretched).

part of speech: verb (overuse, overuses, overused, overusing); noun (overuse — uncountable)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (verb) To use something too much or too often. 2) (noun) Using something too much, so that it is wasted, worn out, harmful or boring.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons teachers warn about overusing words like "nice", "said" or "then": it makes writing dull. In science and health it comes up as overuse of water, antibiotics or screens, and overuse injuries in sport. Overused phrases are called clichés. Phrases: overuse of, overused word, overuse injury.
examples from the lessons: Try not to overuse the word "nice" in your story. | Overuse of antibiotics can make germs stronger. | My knee hurts from overuse after the football tournament. | "Awesome" is a bit overused, isn't it? | Overusing water in a drought is a bad idea. | The teacher circled every overused "then" in my writing.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb stress: o-ver-USE (z sound); noun stress: O-ver-use (s sound). Past: overused. The noun is uncountable: "the overuse of…". Do not confuse with "misuse" (using wrongly) or "abuse" (using badly or cruelly).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A small piece of bent wire used to hold sheets of paper together. 2) (computers) The small clip symbol that means "attach a file", for example in an email.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday school life paperclips hold worksheets together. In science lessons they are used in magnet tests (a paperclip is attracted to a magnet because it is made of steel) and in circuits as simple switches. In maths they are used for measuring ("the pencil is 4 paperclips long") and for spinners. Phrase: clip together with a paperclip.
examples from the lessons: Put a paperclip on your homework sheets. | The magnet picked up ten paperclips. | My pencil is five paperclips long. | She bent a paperclip into a heart shape. | Click the paperclip to attach a photo to the email. | We made a switch for our circuit with a paperclip.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Also written "paper clip" (two words). Countable: a paperclip, paperclips. Paperclips are attracted to magnets because they are steel (contains iron); plastic-coated ones still are. When measuring with paperclips, use the same size each time or the answer will not be fair.

part of speech: noun (the Paralympics; the Paralympic Games); adjective (Paralympic)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A big international sports competition for athletes with disabilities, such as athletes who are blind, use wheelchairs or have lost limbs, held after the Olympic Games every four years.
its sense in the lessons: In PE and citizenship lessons the Paralympics shows that disabled athletes are top sportspeople and teaches respect and inclusion. Sports include wheelchair basketball, blind football, boccia and para swimming. A Paralympian is an athlete who competes there. Phrases: the Summer Paralympics, the Winter Paralympics, a Paralympic champion, win a Paralympic medal.
examples from the lessons: The Paralympics take place in the same city as the Olympics. | She won a gold medal at the Paralympics in swimming. | Wheelchair rugby is one of the fastest Paralympic sports. | We watched the Paralympics on TV at school. | The Paralympics began from games for injured soldiers in England. | My hero is a Paralympian who runs with a blade.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always written with a capital P: the Paralympics, Paralympic. It takes "the". It can take a plural or singular verb (The Paralympics are/is on TV). "Para" here means "beside" (alongside the Olympics), not "paralysed". Say "disabled athletes" or "athletes with disabilities", not unkind words.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Made of a phrase, or to do with phrases. 2) In "phrasal verb": a verb made of a verb plus a small word like up, out, off or on, which together have a special meaning, like "give up" or "look after".
its sense in the lessons: In English grammar lessons "phrasal" almost always comes in "phrasal verb". Phrasal verbs are very common in everyday English: get up, put on, run out, find out. Their meaning is often not the sum of the parts: "give up" means stop trying, not give something upwards. Learners of English find them tricky.
examples from the lessons: Give up is a phrasal verb. | "Look after" is a phrasal verb meaning take care of. | Our teacher made a list of phrasal verbs with "get". | "Run out of milk" uses the phrasal verb "run out". | Can you replace "find out" with one formal word? Yes: "discover". | English has thousands of phrasal verbs.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced FRAY-zal. Only an adjective. Phrasal verbs often have a formal one-word partner: find out = discover, put off = postpone, give up = quit. Some can be split (turn the light off / turn off the light), some cannot (look after the baby).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A tiny piece in your blood that helps it clot (go thick and sticky) to stop bleeding when you are cut.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about the body, blood is made of plasma, red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets. Platelets rush to a cut and stick together to make a plug, which becomes a scab. In hospital stories a "platelet count" is checked; people can donate platelets.
examples from the lessons: Platelets help your blood clot when you cut your finger. | Blood is made of plasma, red cells, white cells and platelets. | The scab on your knee started with platelets sticking together. | The doctor checked her platelet count. | Platelets are much smaller than red blood cells. | Some people donate platelets to help patients in hospital.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a platelet, platelets; usually used in the plural. The word means "little plate" because of their flat shape. Platelets are not full cells; they are fragments of bigger cells.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To prevent something from happening, or make it impossible. 2) (formal) To stop someone from doing something: "His injury precluded him from playing."
its sense in the lessons: Preclude is a stiff exam and official word. It appears in rules, contracts, news and exam questions. In everyday life you would say "stop", "prevent" or "rule out". It tells the reader the text is formal. Phrase: preclude someone from doing something.
examples from the lessons: Bad weather precluded the school trip. | His broken arm precluded him from playing in the final. | Being young does not preclude you from having good ideas. | The rules preclude using a calculator in this test. | "Preclude" is a formal way to say "rule out". | Lack of money precluded any repairs to the hall.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal register. Past: precluded. Pattern: preclude something; preclude someone from doing something. Do not confuse with "prelude" (an opening piece of music) or "include" (the opposite idea).

part of speech: verb (past tense and past participle of proclaim: proclaim, proclaims, proclaimed, proclaiming); adjective (self-proclaimed)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Announced something officially and publicly: "The king proclaimed a holiday." 2) Said something loudly and proudly, as if to everyone: "'I won!' she proclaimed." 3) (Bible, church) Spoke God's message to people: "Jesus proclaimed the good news."
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons kings, queens and governments proclaimed laws, wars and new rulers. In stories "proclaimed" is a strong speaking verb instead of "said", showing the speaker is proud, loud or official. "Self-proclaimed" means someone calls themselves something without proof: "a self-proclaimed expert". In church readings preachers and prophets proclaim God's word.
examples from the lessons: The king proclaimed a day of celebration. | "I am the best footballer in the class!" Tom proclaimed. | Queen Victoria was proclaimed Empress of India. | The headteacher proclaimed Friday a non-uniform day. | Jesus proclaimed the good news in Galilee, the Bible says. | He is a self-proclaimed chess genius, but he lost to me. | Posters proclaimed the opening of the new library.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Base verb: proclaim; noun: proclamation (note the spelling change: proclaim → proclamation). Regular past -ed. Stronger and more official than "said" or "announced".

meaning for a pupil: 1) A deer-like animal of the grasslands of North America, with forked (pronged) horns, famous for being the fastest land animal in America.
its sense in the lessons: In science and nature lessons the pronghorn is an example of speed and adaptation: it can run about 90 km/h (55 mph) and keep going much longer than a cheetah. Pupils in the USA and Canada may see them in the Great Plains. It is often wrongly called an antelope.
examples from the lessons: A pronghorn can run faster than a racehorse. | We saw pronghorns grazing in Wyoming. | The pronghorn's horns have a little fork, or prong. | Pronghorns can run fast for a long time, not just in short bursts. | Wolves and coyotes chase pronghorn on the prairie. | The pronghorn is the fastest land animal in North America.
