note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: pronghorns, or pronghorn for a group. Often called "pronghorn antelope", but it is not a true antelope; its closest relatives are giraffes. It sheds the outer cover of its horns each year.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To read a piece of writing carefully to find and correct mistakes in spelling, punctuation and grammar before it is finished or printed.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons pupils are told to proofread their work before handing it in: check capital letters, full stops, spelling and missing words. Proofreading is the last step of the writing process (plan, draft, revise, edit, proofread). Phrases: proofread your work, a proofreader, proofreading marks.
examples from the lessons: Always proofread your story before you hand it in. | I proofread my email and found three spelling mistakes. | Can you proofread my letter, please? | Proofreading helps you catch missing full stops. | My mum's job is to proofread books before they are printed. | She proofreads by reading her work aloud. | The spellchecker didn't notice "there" for "their", so proofread too.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past tense: proofread (spelled the same, but said "proof-red"). Also written proof-read. Noun for the person: proofreader. Trap: a spellchecker cannot catch homophones (their/there, to/too), so you still need to proofread yourself.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A tiny, very heavy, spinning dead star (a neutron star) that sends out beams of radio waves or light, which reach Earth as very regular pulses, like a lighthouse.
its sense in the lessons: In science and space lessons pulsars come up when talking about what happens after a giant star explodes in a supernova. Their pulses are so regular that scientists use them like cosmic clocks. The first pulsar was discovered by Jocelyn Bell Burnell, a student from Northern Ireland.
examples from the lessons: A pulsar spins hundreds of times a second. | The pulsar's beam sweeps past Earth like a lighthouse. | Jocelyn Bell Burnell discovered the first pulsar. | At first scientists jokingly called the signal "little green men". | Pulsars are left over after a supernova. | Some pulsars keep time better than clocks on Earth.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a pulsar, pulsars. Comes from "pulsating star". Not the same as a quasar (a very bright centre of a faraway galaxy). A teaspoon of pulsar material would weigh millions of tonnes.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A rare, radioactive metal element (symbol Ra) that gives off dangerous radiation and glows faintly in the dark.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons radium is linked with Marie and Pierre Curie, who discovered it, and with learning about radioactivity. In history lessons it is a warning story: people once put radium in watch paint, toothpaste and drinks, not knowing it was harmful; the "Radium Girls" who painted glowing watch faces became very ill. It tells the reader about danger hidden in something that looks magical.
examples from the lessons: Marie Curie discovered radium with her husband Pierre. | Radium glows with a faint blue-green light. | Radium is radioactive, so it is very dangerous to touch. | Old watches had radium paint so you could read them in the dark. | The Radium Girls got ill from licking their paintbrushes. | Radium's symbol in the periodic table is Ra.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: "radium is", not "a radium". Chemical symbol Ra, atomic number 88. Myth from long ago: radium was sold as healthy; it is not. Do not confuse with "radius" (a line from the centre of a circle).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A part of the body, such as a nerve ending or a cell in the eye, nose or skin, that picks up a signal like light, smell, heat or touch and sends a message to the brain. 2) A tiny place on a cell where a particular chemical (like a hormone or a medicine) fits, like a key in a lock.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about the senses, receptors explain how we feel: taste receptors on the tongue, light receptors in the eye, pain receptors in the skin. In more advanced science, medicines work by fitting into receptors. It tells the reader how the body notices the world. Phrases: taste receptors, pain receptors, smell receptors.
examples from the lessons: Your tongue has thousands of taste receptors. | Receptors in your skin feel heat and cold. | Light receptors in your eyes are called rods and cones. | Dogs have many more smell receptors than people. | The medicine fits into receptors like a key in a lock. | Pain receptors warn you when you touch something hot.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a receptor, receptors. Related to "receive": a receptor receives signals. Do not confuse with "receptionist" (a person at a front desk) or "receiver".

part of speech: adjective (rechargeable); noun (a rechargeable, rechargeables — informal, a rechargeable battery)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Able to be filled up with electricity again after it runs out, so it can be used many times: a rechargeable battery.
its sense in the lessons: In science and everyday life rechargeable batteries are found in phones, tablets, toothbrushes and toys. In lessons about saving the planet they are better than single-use batteries because there is less waste. Safety lessons say only use the right charger and never charge damaged batteries. Phrases: rechargeable battery, rechargeable torch.
examples from the lessons: My game controller uses rechargeable batteries. | A rechargeable battery can be used hundreds of times. | Plug in the rechargeable torch overnight. | Rechargeable batteries make less rubbish than normal ones. | Never try to recharge a battery that is not rechargeable. | Electric cars have huge rechargeable batteries.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelled with -eable (recharge + able, keeping the e). Safety: never put ordinary (non-rechargeable) batteries in a charger; they can leak or burst. Do not throw batteries in the normal bin; recycle them.

part of speech: noun (rhubarb — uncountable as food; a rhubarb plant, rhubarbs); interjection (rhubarb rhubarb — UK, theatre)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A garden plant with long thick pink or red stalks that are cooked with sugar and eaten as a sweet food, as in rhubarb crumble. 2) (UK, informal) Nonsense or silly talk. 3) (theatre, UK) The word actors mutter, "rhubarb, rhubarb", to sound like a crowd talking in the background. 4) (US, old slang) A noisy argument or fight, especially in baseball.
its sense in the lessons: In cooking and gardening lessons rhubarb is a classic British and Irish pudding plant (rhubarb crumble, rhubarb and custard). In science and safety lessons it is a warning: the stalks are eaten but the big leaves are poisonous. In drama lessons extras say "rhubarb rhubarb" to make crowd noise.
examples from the lessons: Grandad grows rhubarb in his garden. | We had rhubarb crumble with custard for pudding. | Rhubarb is very sour, so you cook it with sugar. | Never eat rhubarb leaves; they are poisonous. | In the school play, the crowd muttered "rhubarb, rhubarb". | "That's a load of rhubarb!" said Nan, meaning nonsense. | Rhubarb and custard sweets are pink and yellow.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced ROO-barb; the "h" is silent. As food it is uncountable (some rhubarb). Rhubarb is a vegetable, though it is cooked like a fruit. Safety: only the stalks are eaten; the leaves contain poison (oxalic acid).

meaning for a pupil: 1) To do with robots, or done by a robot: a robotic arm. 2) Moving or speaking stiffly, without feeling, like a robot: a robotic voice.
its sense in the lessons: In science and technology lessons "robotic" describes machines that move by themselves: robotic arms in factories, robotic vacuum cleaners, robotic rovers on Mars. In stories and drama it can describe a person who is tired, bored or acting without feeling. Phrases: robotic arm, robotic voice, robotic surgery.
examples from the lessons: The factory uses robotic arms to build cars. | A robotic rover is exploring Mars. | We built a robotic hand from straws and string. | He answered in a flat, robotic voice. | After the long day, she moved in a robotic way. | Doctors can now do robotic surgery with tiny tools.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective from "robot". The study of robots is "robotics" (uncountable: robotics is fun). Comparison: more robotic, most robotic. The word "robot" comes from a Czech play and means forced work.

part of speech: noun (rosemary — uncountable as a herb; a rosemary bush, rosemaries — rare); name (Rosemary)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A small evergreen bush with needle-like leaves that smell strong and fresh, used as a herb in cooking. 2) (a name) Rosemary is also a girl's name.
its sense in the lessons: In cooking lessons rosemary flavours roast lamb, potatoes and bread. In gardens it is easy to grow and loved by bees. In Australia and New Zealand rosemary is worn on Anzac Day to remember soldiers who died, and in old stories and Shakespeare rosemary stands for remembrance.
examples from the lessons: Mum put rosemary on the roast potatoes. | Rosemary smells lovely when you rub its leaves. | Bees buzzed round the rosemary bush. | In Australia, people wear a sprig of rosemary on Anzac Day. | We planted rosemary in the school herb garden. | My aunt's name is Rosemary.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a herb it is uncountable: some rosemary, a sprig of rosemary. The name has a capital letter (Rosemary). It is not made of "rose" and "Mary"; the name comes from Latin for "dew of the sea".

part of speech: verb (sag, sags, sagged, sagging); noun (a sag — uncountable or countable)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To sink or hang down in the middle because of weight or because it is old or tired: the shelf sagged under the books. 2) To become weaker or lower: my spirits sagged; sales sagged. 3) (noun) A place where something sinks down, or a drop.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life old sofas, mattresses, tents and washing lines sag. In stories a character's shoulders sag when they are sad, tired or give up. In science and design lessons a bridge or shelf that sags shows the load is too heavy. Phrases: sag in the middle, shoulders sagged, a sagging roof.
examples from the lessons: The washing line sagged under the wet towels. | Our old sofa sags in the middle. | His shoulders sagged when he heard the bad news. | The tent sagged after the rain. | Put a support in the middle so the bridge doesn't sag. | Her energy sagged by the end of the race.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: sagged (double the g); -ing: sagging. "Saggy" is an informal adjective (saggy socks). Do not confuse with "saga" (a long story).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A safe place where animals are protected, such as a bird sanctuary or wildlife sanctuary. 2) A safe place for people who are in danger or being chased; safety itself: "They found sanctuary in the church." 3) (church) The holiest part of a church or temple, near the altar. 4) A calm, private place where someone feels peaceful: "My bedroom is my sanctuary."
its sense in the lessons: In nature lessons sanctuaries protect endangered or rescued animals: donkey sanctuaries, elephant sanctuaries, bird sanctuaries. In history, in the Middle Ages people fleeing could claim sanctuary in a church. In church life the sanctuary is the special area at the front. In stories it tells the reader a character has finally found safety. Phrases: seek sanctuary, find sanctuary, wildlife sanctuary, give sanctuary.
examples from the lessons: We visited a donkey sanctuary in the holidays. | The island is a sanctuary for seabirds. | In the past, a person could claim sanctuary in a church. | The refugees found sanctuary in a new country. | The priest stood in the sanctuary near the altar. | The library is my sanctuary on a noisy day. | The rescued koalas live in a sanctuary in Queensland.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: sanctuaries (y → ies). Comes from Latin "sanctus", holy. Countable when it is a place; uncountable when it means safety (seek sanctuary). Similar: refuge, haven, reserve.

part of speech: noun (a secretion, secretions; secretion — uncountable as a process)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A liquid that a living thing makes and lets out, such as saliva, sweat, tears, mucus or sap. 2) The process of making and releasing such a liquid.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about the body and animals, secretions do jobs: saliva starts digestion, sweat cools us, tears clean eyes, snail slime helps it move, spiders secrete silk. It tells the reader something is produced by glands. Phrases: the secretion of saliva, sticky secretions.
examples from the lessons: Saliva is a secretion from glands in your mouth. | Sweat is a secretion that helps cool your body. | The snail left a trail of sticky secretion. | Some frogs have poisonous skin secretions. | Bees make wax from a secretion of their bodies. | The secretion of tears keeps your eyes clean.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable for the liquid (secretions), uncountable for the process. Verb: secrete (to produce a liquid). Trap: "secrete" also can mean "hide", and "secretion" sounds like "secret" but has nothing to do with secrets here.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (music) The smallest step between two notes in Western music, such as from C to C sharp, or from E to F; half of a tone.
its sense in the lessons: In music lessons semitones are the steps between neighbouring keys on a piano, black or white. Two semitones make one tone (a whole step). Sharps raise a note by a semitone; flats lower it by a semitone. An octave has 12 semitones. In maths-and-music puzzles counting semitones is like counting on a number line.
examples from the lessons: From C to C sharp is one semitone. | E to F is a semitone, with no black key between. | Two semitones make a whole tone. | There are twelve semitones in an octave. | The singer went up a semitone for the last chorus. | A sharp raises a note by a semitone.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a semitone, semitones. US English often says "half step" (and "whole step" for a tone). "Semi" means half. Number fact: 12 semitones = 1 octave = 6 tones.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The title of the king of Iran (Persia) in the past. 2) A title used by some rulers in other lands such as Afghanistan and in old India. 3) (a name) Shah is also a common family name in South Asia.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons the shah was the monarch of Persia (now Iran); the last shah left in the Iranian revolution and Iran became an Islamic republic. In stories set in the old East a shah is like a king or emperor. In chess, the word "check" and "checkmate" come from Persian "shah" and "shah mat" (the king is helpless).
examples from the lessons: The Shah of Iran ruled from a palace in Tehran. | The last shah left Iran during a revolution. | In the old Persian story, the shah listened to a thousand tales. | "Checkmate" comes from Persian words meaning "the shah is helpless". | Our new classmate's surname is Shah. | The shah wore a jewelled crown.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a shah, shahs. Capital S as a title (the Shah). The queen or wife of a shah was called the shahbanu or empress. Do not confuse with "Shia" or "sharp"; as a surname it is a name, not a title.

part of speech: noun (shingles — uncountable illness; shingle — a pebble beach; a shingle, shingles — roof tiles)
meaning for a pupil: 1) An illness that causes a painful rash with blisters, usually on one side of the body; it is caused by the same virus as chickenpox waking up again years later. 2) (shingle, UK) Small smooth stones on a beach. 3) Small flat pieces of wood or other material that overlap to cover a roof or wall.
its sense in the lessons: In health lessons shingles shows that a virus (chickenpox) can hide in the body for years; it is mostly older people who get it, and there is a vaccine. In geography lessons on coasts, a shingle beach is a pebbly beach, common in Britain. In North America, roof shingles are what most house roofs are covered with.
examples from the lessons: Grandad has shingles and his side is very sore. | You can only get shingles if you have had chickenpox. | Shingles is not caught from someone's cough the way a cold is. | Brighton beach is covered in shingle, not sand. | The storm blew some shingles off our roof. | The shingle crunched under our feet as we walked to the sea. | Old people can have a vaccine against shingles.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The illness "shingles" looks plural but takes a singular verb: "Shingles is painful." The beach word is usually "shingle" (uncountable: a shingle beach). Roof shingles are countable. Health fact: a person with shingles can give chickenpox (not shingles) to someone who never had it, through the blisters.

part of speech: noun (a shovel, shovels); verb (shovel, shovels, shovelled/shoveled, shovelling/shoveling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (noun) A tool with a long handle and a wide, slightly curved blade for lifting and moving earth, snow, sand or coal. 2) (verb) To lift and move something with a shovel: shovel snow. 3) (verb, informal) To put a lot of something somewhere quickly and roughly: "He shovelled food into his mouth."
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life people shovel snow from paths (very common in Canada and the northern USA), dig gardens and fill wheelbarrows. In stories "shovelled food into his mouth" shows someone eating greedily or fast. In history, workers shovelled coal into steam trains. Phrases: shovel snow, a snow shovel, shovel it in.
examples from the lessons: Dad used a shovel to clear the snow from the drive. | We shovelled sand into the bucket. | The builder picked up a shovel and started digging. | He shovelled his dinner into his mouth and ran out to play. | In old steam trains, the fireman shovelled coal into the fire. | Bring a shovel and a bucket to the beach.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK spelling: shovelled, shovelling; US spelling: shoveled, shoveling. A shovel has a wider, scoop-shaped blade; a spade has a flatter blade for digging, but people often mix the two words up. In Australia "shovel" is the common word for both.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A farm tool with a short handle and a curved, C-shaped blade, used for cutting grass, grain or corn by hand. 2) Something shaped like this blade, such as a sickle moon (a thin crescent moon).
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons the sickle is an old harvest tool, used before machines. On the old Soviet flag the hammer and sickle stood for workers and farmers. In science lessons sickle cell disease is a blood illness in which red blood cells bend into a sickle shape. In stories and pictures, the Grim Reaper carries a scythe, which is a larger tool than a sickle.
examples from the lessons: The farmer cut the wheat with a sickle. | A thin sickle moon hung in the evening sky. | The old flag showed a hammer and sickle. | In sickle cell disease, red blood cells are curved. | Be careful: the blade of a sickle is very sharp. | People harvested crops with sickles long before tractors.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a sickle, sickles. Do not confuse with "scythe" (long handle, big blade, used standing up) or "tickle". Safety: real sickles are sharp tools for adults only.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Grass, maize or other green crops that are cut, packed tightly and kept without air so they ferment, to feed cows and sheep in winter.
its sense in the lessons: In farming and science lessons silage shows how food is stored: the crop is sealed in a clamp, pit, silo or in big black plastic-wrapped bales, and bacteria pickle it. Children in rural Ireland, the UK, New Zealand and Canada see silage bales in fields and smell it on farms. Phrases: silage bales, make silage, silage pit.
examples from the lessons: The cows eat silage all winter. | Big black bales of silage were stacked by the barn. | Farmers make silage in summer when the grass is long. | Silage has a strong, sour smell. | The tractor drove over the silage to squash out the air. | Silage is a bit like pickled grass.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: "some silage", "silage is". Pronounced SY-lij. Related to "silo" (a tall tower for storing grain or silage). Safety: silage pits and gases can be dangerous; children should not play near them.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A control on a screen or machine that you move along a line to change something, such as the volume or brightness. 2) (US) A small burger or sandwich. 3) A person or thing that slides, such as a type of turtle (red-eared slider). 4) (baseball, US) A type of pitch that curves sideways. 5) (UK, informal) A slide sandal or flip-flop-like shoe without a back (often "sliders").
its sense in the lessons: In computing lessons and on devices sliders let you set values smoothly; in maths apps a slider can change a number on a graph. In science or nature a red-eared slider is a common pet turtle. In everyday US life sliders are mini burgers at parties. In UK talk, sliders are casual sandals for the beach or swimming pool.
examples from the lessons: Drag the slider to turn up the volume. | Move the brightness slider to the left to make the screen darker. | We had cheese sliders at the barbecue. | My cousin has a red-eared slider turtle. | He wore his sliders to the swimming pool. | The pitcher threw a slider and the batter missed.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a slider, sliders. From the verb "slide". The burger and baseball meanings are mainly American; the sandal meaning is mainly British.

part of speech: adjective (slim, slimmer, slimmest); verb (slim, slims, slimmed, slimming — UK; slim down)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Thin in an attractive or healthy way: a slim girl, a slim phone. 2) Small in amount; not likely: a slim chance, a slim lead. 3) (verb, UK) To try to lose weight by eating less. 4) (verb) Slim down: to make smaller or reduce: "The school slimmed down the timetable."
its sense in the lessons: In descriptions "slim" is a kind word for thin (kinder than "skinny"). In sports and news "a slim chance" or "a slim lead" means only a little: a team winning by one goal has a slim lead. Health lessons teach that bodies come in all shapes and that being healthy matters more than being slim. Phrases: slim chance, slim chances, slim down, slim volume (a thin book).
examples from the lessons: The new tablet is very slim. | There is only a slim chance of snow tomorrow. | Our team had a slim lead of one point. | My aunt is tall and slim. | The company slimmed down to save money. | He read a slim book of poems. | Is there a slim hope they will find the lost cat? Yes, a slim one.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Forms: slim, slimmer, slimmest; verb: slimmed, slimming (double m). Slim is polite; skinny can sound rude. Trap: "slim chance" and "fat chance" both mean almost no chance! In maths stories, "a slim majority" means only a few more votes than the others.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Dirty, smoky, foggy air over a city, caused by pollution from cars, factories and fires, often mixed with fog.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography lessons smog is a key example of air pollution: it makes breathing hard, especially for people with asthma. The word was made from "smoke" + "fog". The Great Smog of London in the past killed thousands and led to clean air laws. Today many big cities issue smog warnings. Phrases: a smog warning, thick smog, photochemical smog.
examples from the lessons: The city was covered in thick brown smog. | On smog days, children with asthma should stay inside. | Smog comes from car fumes and factory smoke. | London once had a terrible smog that lasted for days. | We couldn't see the mountains through the smog. | Cleaner cars help reduce smog.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: "smog is", "some smog". A blend word: smoke + fog (like brunch = breakfast + lunch). Not the same as plain fog, which is just tiny water drops and is not polluted.

part of speech: noun (a smudge, smudges); verb (smudge, smudges, smudged, smudging)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (noun) A dirty or blurred mark, like a smear of ink, paint or chocolate. 2) (verb) To make something blurred or messy by rubbing it, or to become blurred: "My writing smudged." 3) (art) To blend chalk, charcoal or pastel on purpose with your finger to make soft shading.
its sense in the lessons: In school, left-handed writers often smudge their ink; teachers ask for neat work without smudges. In art lessons smudging charcoal makes shadows and soft clouds. In stories a smudge of dirt or flour on someone's face shows they have been working or playing. Phrases: a smudge of paint, smudge-proof, smudge the ink.
examples from the lessons: There's a smudge of chocolate on your cheek. | Let the ink dry or it will smudge. | My left hand smudged my handwriting. | Smudge the chalk with your finger to make a soft sky. | The window had smudges from little fingers. | Her mascara smudged when she cried.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: a smudge, smudges. Verb past: smudged. Adjective: smudgy. Similar words: smear, blot, stain; a smudge is usually small and blurred.

part of speech: noun (a speckle, speckles); verb (speckle, speckles, speckled, speckling); adjective (speckled)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (noun) A small spot or mark of colour, one of many: "speckles of paint". 2) (verb) To cover with lots of small spots. 3) (speckled, adjective) Covered with many small spots: a speckled egg.
its sense in the lessons: In nature lessons speckles help camouflage: speckled eggs, speckled trout and speckled birds blend into stones and leaves. In art lessons speckling (flicking paint off a toothbrush) makes stars or sand. In stories "speckled with" describes a surface dotted with something: a sky speckled with stars, a face speckled with freckles. Phrases: speckled with, speckled hen, speckled egg.
examples from the lessons: The thrush's egg was blue with dark speckles. | Her face was speckled with mud. | We speckled white paint on black paper to make stars. | The speckled frog sat on a log. | The trout has a speckled back. | The floor was speckled with sawdust.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Speckled (the adjective) is much more common than "speckle". Similar words: spot, dot, fleck, freckle. "Speckled with" + noun.

part of speech: verb (-ing form of spit: spit, spits, spat/spit, spitting); noun (spitting — uncountable); adjective (spitting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Forcing saliva (spit) or food out of your mouth. 2) (of rain, UK and Ireland) Raining very lightly: "It's only spitting." 3) Making small hot bursts or sparks, like fat in a pan or a fire. 4) (of an animal) Hissing angrily, like a cat. 5) In "spitting image": looking exactly like someone. 6) In "spitting distance": very close.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday and school rules spitting at people is rude and unhygienic, and spitting on the ground is often against the rules. Weather talk in the UK, Ireland and Australia uses "it's spitting" for a few drops. "Spitting mad" or "spitting feathers" means very angry. In stories a spitting fire or spitting cat sets an angry or lively mood.
examples from the lessons: Spitting at someone is very rude. | It's just spitting, so we can still go to the park. | The sausages were spitting in the hot pan. | The angry cat was spitting and hissing. | You're the spitting image of your mum! | The beach is within spitting distance of our hotel. | The coach was spitting mad after the match. | Brush your teeth, then finish by spitting into the sink.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double t: spit → spitting. Past: spat (UK) or spit (US). "Spitting image" is a fixed phrase meaning an exact look-alike. Spitting near others spreads germs; a cobra called the spitting cobra really does spray venom.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The strength and energy to keep doing something hard, especially physical activity, for a long time without getting tired.
its sense in the lessons: In PE and sport lessons stamina is built by running, swimming and cycling regularly; long-distance runners need lots of it. Health lessons connect stamina with a strong heart and lungs. It is also used for mental effort: "It takes stamina to finish a big project." Phrases: build up stamina, have the stamina to, lack stamina.
examples from the lessons: Running every day builds up your stamina. | Marathon runners need huge stamina. | I don't have the stamina to walk up that mountain. | Swimming is great for stamina. | Doing a hundred spellings in one go takes stamina! | The puppy has endless stamina for playing fetch. | The team lost because they ran out of stamina in the second half.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: "stamina", not "a stamina" or "staminas". Pronounced STAM-in-a. Similar: endurance. Strength means how much you can lift; stamina means how long you can keep going.

part of speech: noun (a steak, steaks; steak — uncountable as a food)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A thick, flat slice of good meat, usually beef, cooked by grilling or frying. 2) A thick slice of fish, such as a salmon or tuna steak. 3) (UK) Cheaper chopped beef used in pies and stews: steak and kidney pie.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life steak is a special meal, often at a barbecue or restaurant, cooked rare, medium or well done. In food and health lessons it is a source of protein and iron. In Australia and New Zealand steak is a barbecue favourite. Phrases: steak and chips, a steak dinner, rare steak, steak pie.
examples from the lessons: Dad grilled steaks on the barbecue. | I like my steak well done. | We had steak and chips for Dad's birthday. | A salmon steak is a thick slice of salmon. | Nan makes a delicious steak pie. | Vegetarians don't eat steak. | The cowboy ordered the biggest steak in the diner.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Homophone trap: steak (meat) and stake (a pointed stick; or money bet; or a share) sound the same. Countable for one piece (two steaks), uncountable as food in general (I don't eat steak). Food safety: rare steak is pink inside; minced beef (burgers) should be cooked through.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who pays regularly to receive something, such as a magazine, a streaming service or a phone plan. 2) A person who follows a channel online so they see new videos or posts, often for free. 3) (formal) A person who agrees with or supports an idea: "a subscriber to the view that…"
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life children hear about subscribers on YouTube channels and streaming services ("like and subscribe"). Money lessons explain that subscriptions cost money every month, and that free trials can turn into payments. In maths problems subscriber counts are used for big numbers and percentages. Phrases: subscriber count, paid subscriber, a million subscribers.
examples from the lessons: The channel just reached a million subscribers! | My uncle is a subscriber to a gardening magazine. | Subscribers get a new comic every month. | Only paying subscribers can watch the film. | Ask an adult before you click "subscribe" on anything that costs money. | The newspaper lost many subscribers last year.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a subscriber, subscribers. Verb: subscribe (to); noun: subscription. Pattern: a subscriber TO something. Safety and money: subscriptions repeat until you cancel them. In maths: if a channel goes from 2,000 to 3,000 subscribers, that is a gain of 1,000, or 50 percent.

part of speech: adjective (Swedish); noun (Swedish — the language, uncountable; the Swedish — the people)
meaning for a pupil: 1) From or to do with Sweden, a country in northern Europe: Swedish food, a Swedish girl. 2) The language spoken in Sweden (and partly in Finland).
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons Swedish is linked with Sweden, Scandinavia and the capital, Stockholm. In everyday life children meet Swedish meatballs, Swedish furniture shops and Swedish authors (Pippi Longstocking was created by a Swedish writer). In language lessons Swedish is a Germanic language related to English, Danish and Norwegian. "Swede" is a person from Sweden and also a vegetable (UK; called rutabaga in the US).
examples from the lessons: We ate Swedish meatballs with jam. | Swedish is spoken in Sweden and parts of Finland. | My pen pal is Swedish and lives in Stockholm. | The Swedish flag is blue with a yellow cross. | Pippi Longstocking is a famous Swedish book character. | "Tack" means "thank you" in Swedish.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always written with a capital S: Swedish. The person is "a Swede" (or a Swedish person); the people are "the Swedes". Trap: "swede" with a small s (UK) is a root vegetable; "Swiss" means from Switzerland, a different country.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (old-fashioned) A film with sound and spoken words, as opposed to a silent film; the first "talkies" were made a long time ago. 2) In "walkie-talkie": a small hand-held radio for talking to someone nearby.
its sense in the lessons: In history and media lessons "talkies" were a big change in cinema: before them films had no spoken sound and words appeared on cards. Many silent film stars lost their jobs when the talkies came. Children more often meet the word in "walkie-talkie", used in games, camping and by security guards.
examples from the lessons: The first talkies amazed cinema audiences. | Before talkies, films had music but no voices. | Grandpa's grandpa saw the very first talkies. | We used walkie-talkies to talk across the campsite. | "Over and out!" said Sam into the walkie-talkie. | Some silent film actors had funny voices and failed in the talkies.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a talkie, talkies. Old-fashioned word; today we just say "film" or "movie". Spelled -ie. "Walkie-talkie" has a hyphen.

part of speech: noun (the Taoiseach — a title; Taoisigh — Irish plural)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (Ireland) The title of the prime minister, the head of the government, of the Republic of Ireland. 2) (Irish language) The word means "chief" or "leader" in Irish.
its sense in the lessons: In citizenship and geography lessons in Ireland and the UK the Taoiseach is the leader of the Irish government, chosen by the Dáil (the Irish parliament). The President of Ireland is a different person and is the head of state. On the news you hear "the Taoiseach said…". The deputy is called the Tánaiste.
examples from the lessons: The Taoiseach spoke to the Dáil about schools. | The Taoiseach is the head of the Irish government. | The President of Ireland and the Taoiseach are two different people. | The Taoiseach visited the White House on Saint Patrick's Day. | "Taoiseach" is an Irish word meaning leader. | The new Taoiseach was elected by the Dáil.
note for the reader of a maths problem: An Irish (Gaelic) word used in English. Pronounced roughly TEE-shuck or TEE-shakh. Written with a capital T and usually "the Taoiseach". Irish plural: Taoisigh. The spelling looks very different from the sound, a trap for spelling.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A small mammal from Madagascar that often looks like a hedgehog or a shrew; some kinds have spines.
its sense in the lessons: In science and nature lessons tenrecs are an example of convergent evolution: they look like hedgehogs but are not closely related; they evolved spines separately on the island of Madagascar. Some tenrecs rattle their quills to talk to each other, and some have many babies at once. They come up in lessons on islands, adaptation and unusual animals.
examples from the lessons: The tenrec looks like a tiny hedgehog. | Tenrecs live only in Madagascar and a little of Africa. | The streaked tenrec rattles its spines to talk. | A tenrec is not a hedgehog, even though it looks like one. | Some tenrecs swim in streams like little otters. | The zoo has a lowland tenrec in the night house.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a tenrec, tenrecs. Pronounced TEN-rek. Not a hedgehog or porcupine; it belongs to a group of African mammals. Not to be mixed up with "tenner" (UK slang for ten pounds).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A stretch of land, especially as to what it is like: hilly, rocky, flat, muddy or rough. 2) (figurative) An area of knowledge or activity: "Algebra was new terrain for her."
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons terrain is described by its features: mountains, valleys, plains, deserts. In stories and adventure books rough terrain makes journeys hard. Vehicles and bikes are called "all-terrain" if they can travel over any kind of ground. In video games, terrain is the ground the player moves on. Phrases: rough terrain, rocky terrain, all-terrain vehicle, difficult terrain.
examples from the lessons: The hikers crossed rocky terrain. | Mountain bikes are made for rough terrain. | The terrain in the Outback is dry and flat. | An all-terrain vehicle can drive over sand and mud. | The soldiers knew the terrain well. | The map shows the terrain with contour lines. | Coding was new terrain for our class.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable (rough terrain, not a rough terrain), though "terrains" is possible. Stress on the second syllable: ter-RAIN. Do not confuse with "terrier" (a dog) or "territory" (an area owned or controlled by someone).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person from Texas, a big state in the south of the USA. 2) (adjective) From or to do with Texas: a Texan ranch, a Texan accent.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and US-themed stories Texans are linked with ranches, cowboys, oil, barbecue, rodeos and the city of Houston, where NASA's mission control is. A Texan accent has a famous drawl ("y'all"). In maths problems Texas is often used as an example of a very large state.
examples from the lessons: My cousin is a Texan and says "y'all". | Texans are proud of their huge state. | We ate Texan barbecue with brisket. | The rancher was a tall Texan in a cowboy hat. | "Howdy!" is a typical Texan greeting. | Many Texans speak both English and Spanish.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always written with a capital T: Texan, Texans. The state is Texas; the person is a Texan. "Tex-Mex" is food and culture mixing Texan and Mexican styles. Avoid stereotypes: not every Texan is a cowboy.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The strip of wood or stone on the floor at the bottom of a doorway; the point where you enter a room or house. 2) The level or amount at which something starts to happen or change: "a pain threshold", "the threshold for passing". 3) The start or beginning of something new: "on the threshold of a big discovery".
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life you cross the threshold when you step into a house; there is an old custom of a groom carrying the bride over the threshold. In science and maths a threshold is a cut-off number: water boils above a threshold temperature; you pass a test above a threshold mark. In stories "on the threshold of" tells the reader that something big is about to begin. Phrases: cross the threshold, pain threshold, above/below the threshold, on the threshold of.
examples from the lessons: She paused on the threshold before stepping inside. | The dog would not cross the threshold of the new house. | The pass threshold for the test is 60 marks. | He has a high pain threshold, so the jab didn't bother him. | Scientists were on the threshold of a great discovery. | If the noise goes above the threshold, the alarm sounds. | Wipe your feet at the threshold.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: only one "h" in the middle — thresh-old, not "threshhold". Countable. In maths: "above the threshold" means more than the number; check whether the threshold number itself counts (at least 60, or more than 60).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A stand with three legs used to hold a camera, telescope or other equipment steady. 2) (science) A three-legged metal stand for holding a beaker or dish over a Bunsen burner. 3) Any object or creature with three legs, such as the alien machines in "The War of the Worlds".
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons pupils put a gauze on a tripod above a Bunsen burner to heat water safely. In photography a tripod stops photos from being blurry. In maths and design lessons three legs make a stand stable even on bumpy ground, because three points always sit flat. Phrases: on a tripod, camera tripod.
examples from the lessons: Put the beaker on the tripod and gauze. | The photographer set her camera on a tripod. | A tripod doesn't wobble, even on uneven ground. | We watched the stars through a telescope on a tripod. | In the old story, giant alien tripods walked across England. | Be careful: the tripod gets hot over the Bunsen burner.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a tripod, tripods. "Tri" means three, "pod" means foot (as in tricycle, triangle). Maths fact: three points always lie on one flat plane, which is why a three-legged stool does not rock but a four-legged one can.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) To do with food and feeding, especially who eats whom in nature. 2) In "trophic level": the step or position a living thing has in a food chain, such as plant, plant-eater or meat-eater.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on food chains and food webs, trophic levels go from producers (plants) to primary consumers (herbivores) to secondary and tertiary consumers (predators). Energy is lost at each trophic level, so there are fewer animals at the top. A "trophic cascade" is when removing or adding a top predator, like wolves in Yellowstone, changes the whole ecosystem.
examples from the lessons: Plants are at the first trophic level. | Rabbits eat grass, so they are on the second trophic level. | Foxes are on a higher trophic level than rabbits. | Only about a tenth of the energy passes to the next trophic level. | Bringing wolves back to Yellowstone caused a trophic cascade. | Draw a pyramid to show the trophic levels.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Only an adjective, used in science. Pronounced TROF-ik or TROH-fik. From Greek "trophe", food. Maths in science: if each trophic level passes on about 10 percent of energy, then 1,000 units of plant energy give about 100 for herbivores and about 10 for carnivores.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A very large brass musical instrument with a wide bell, played by blowing into a mouthpiece; it makes the lowest notes in a brass band or orchestra.
its sense in the lessons: In music lessons the tuba is the biggest and lowest member of the brass family, along with the trumpet, trombone and French horn. It plays the "oom-pah" bass notes in marching bands. In stories a tuba often adds a funny or booming sound. Phrases: play the tuba, a tuba player.
examples from the lessons: The tuba plays the lowest notes in the brass band. | My brother plays the tuba in the school orchestra. | The tuba went "oom-pah, oom-pah". | A tuba has a lot of tubing coiled up inside. | The tuba player marched at the back of the parade. | It's hard to carry a tuba on the school bus!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a tuba, tubas. Say "play THE tuba" for instruments. Pronounced TYOO-ba (UK) or TOO-ba (US). A sousaphone is a kind of tuba that wraps round the player's body.

part of speech: verb (upload, uploads, uploaded, uploading); noun (an upload, uploads)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (verb) To send a file, photo or video from your device to the internet or to another computer. 2) (noun) A file that has been uploaded, or the act of uploading.
its sense in the lessons: In computing lessons upload is the opposite of download: download brings things to your device, upload sends them away. Online safety lessons teach to think before you upload: photos and posts can stay online for ever and strangers might see them. Teachers ask pupils to upload homework to a class website. Phrases: upload a photo, upload to the cloud, upload speed.
examples from the lessons: Upload your homework to the class page by Friday. | The video is still uploading. | Ask a parent before you upload a photo of yourself. | Once you upload something, it can be hard to delete. | My upload speed is much slower than my download speed. | She uploaded her drawing to the art competition website.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: uploaded. Opposite: download. Safety: never upload your address, school name or private photos; once online, copies may stay for ever. In maths: upload time = file size ÷ upload speed.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A group of connected underground holes and tunnels where rabbits live. 2) A building or area with many narrow, confusing passages or small rooms: "a warren of little streets". 3) (a name) Warren is also a boy's first name and a family name.
its sense in the lessons: In nature lessons a warren is a rabbit's home, with burrows linking many tunnels. In stories like "Watership Down" the rabbits leave their warren to find a new one. Describing a building as "a warren" tells the reader it is easy to get lost in. Phrases: rabbit warren, a warren of tunnels, a warren of streets.
examples from the lessons: The rabbits ran back into their warren. | A warren can have dozens of tunnels and exits. | The old school was a warren of corridors. | The town centre is a warren of narrow lanes. | In the book, the rabbits search for a safe new warren. | Our neighbour's name is Warren.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a warren, warrens. The name Warren has a capital letter. The holes are burrows; the whole system is the warren. Badgers live in a sett, not a warren; foxes in a den or earth.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) The unit used to measure power: how fast energy is used or produced. One watt is one joule of energy every second. 2) (a name) James Watt was a Scottish engineer who improved the steam engine; the unit is named after him.
its sense in the lessons: In science and energy lessons watts tell how powerful a device is: a light bulb might use 10 watts, a kettle 3,000 watts (3 kilowatts). Saving energy means choosing devices with fewer watts and switching them off. Electricity bills count kilowatt-hours. Phrases: a 60-watt bulb, kilowatt, megawatt, watts of power.
examples from the lessons: An LED bulb uses only about 10 watts. | The kettle uses 3,000 watts, or 3 kilowatts. | A watt is a unit of power. | The watt is named after James Watt. | Which uses more watts, the hairdryer or the phone charger? | The wind turbine makes two million watts, or two megawatts.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Symbol W; 1 kilowatt (kW) = 1,000 watts; 1 megawatt (MW) = 1,000,000 watts. Homophone trap: watt sounds like "what". Maths: energy = power × time, so a 100-watt lamp on for 10 hours uses 1,000 watt-hours = 1 kilowatt-hour. Watts measure power, volts measure electrical push, amps measure current.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A low wall or dam built across a river to control the flow of water or raise its level; water pours over the top.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons about rivers a weir is a human-made feature that controls water, helps mills and measures flow. Fish ladders help salmon get past weirs. Safety lessons warn that the water below a weir can trap swimmers and boats in a dangerous swirling current, so never swim near one. Phrases: over the weir, a weir pool.
examples from the lessons: The river rushes over the weir after heavy rain. | Salmon leap up the fish ladder beside the weir. | Never swim near a weir; the current can pull you under. | The old mill used water from the weir. | We watched the ducks above the weir. | The canoeists carried their boats around the weir.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a weir, weirs. Pronounced like "we're" or "wear" in some accents (UK: WEER). Homophone trap: weir (dam) vs we're (we are); not to be confused with "weird". Safety: weirs look calm but are among the most dangerous places on a river.

part of speech: adjective (wrinkly, wrinklier, wrinkliest); noun (a wrinkly, wrinklies — UK, slang, rude-ish)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Having many wrinkles or creases: wrinkly skin, a wrinkly shirt. 2) (UK, slang, rude) An old person; it can hurt feelings: "the wrinklies".
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life fingers go wrinkly after a long bath, and clothes go wrinkly in a suitcase. In stories wrinkly hands or faces show that a character is old, often in a warm way (Grandma's wrinkly smile). In science lessons wrinkly fingers in water are a fun puzzle: they may help grip wet things. The slang noun for old people is cheeky and can be unkind.
examples from the lessons: My fingers go wrinkly in the bath. | Grandad has a wrinkly, smiley face. | Your shirt is all wrinkly; hang it up. | Raisins are just wrinkly grapes. | The elephant has thick, wrinkly skin. | "Let the wrinklies have the comfy chairs," joked Uncle Pete, and Nan laughed but rolled her eyes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Forms: wrinkly, wrinklier, wrinkliest. Same idea as "wrinkled" (more formal). The noun "wrinkly" for an old person is UK slang and can be rude; don't use it about someone who might be hurt.

part of speech: adjective (abstract); noun (an abstract, abstracts); verb (abstract, abstracts, abstracted, abstracting — formal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (adjective) Being an idea or feeling rather than a thing you can touch or see: love, fairness and time are abstract. 2) (art) Not showing real things but using shapes, colours and lines: an abstract painting. 3) (noun) A short summary at the start of a science article or report. 4) (verb, formal) To take something out, or to pick out the main ideas.
its sense in the lessons: In English grammar lessons "abstract nouns" name ideas and feelings (happiness, bravery, freedom) as opposed to concrete nouns (table, dog). In art lessons abstract art uses shapes and colours, like works by Kandinsky. In maths, numbers are abstract: "three" is not a thing but an idea. In science, the abstract of a paper tells you quickly what was found. Phrases: abstract noun, abstract art, in the abstract.
examples from the lessons: Happiness is an abstract noun. | The painting was abstract: just red squares and blue lines. | Bravery is abstract; you can't hold it in your hand. | Read the abstract to see what the experiment found. | Fractions felt very abstract until we used pizza slices. | We made abstract art with splashes of paint. | "Chair" is concrete, but "comfort" is abstract.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stress: adjective and noun AB-stract; verb ab-STRACT. Opposite of abstract (adjective) is concrete. Trap: abstract nouns can be countable (an idea, ideas) or uncountable (happiness).

part of speech: adjective (accredited); verb (past of accredit: accredit, accredits, accredited, accrediting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Officially approved as being good enough or meeting the required standard: an accredited school, an accredited course. 2) (formal) Officially allowed to do a job or to be somewhere: an accredited journalist, an accredited diplomat. 3) (formal) Given credit for something: "The idea is accredited to her."
its sense in the lessons: Accredited is an official, formal word. Parents look for accredited schools, nurseries, coaches and courses, meaning an official body checked them. At big events like the Olympics, accredited reporters wear passes to get in. It tells the reader that something is checked and trusted. Phrases: fully accredited, accredited by, an accredited teacher.
examples from the lessons: The swimming coach is accredited by the national swimming club. | Only accredited journalists could enter the press room. | Is the course accredited, so it counts for a real qualification? | The new nursery became accredited after an inspection. | The ambassador was accredited to the United Nations. | Look for an accredited first-aid course.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal register; in everyday speech people say "approved" or "official". Double c, single d: a-cc-red-i-ted. Noun: accreditation. Do not confuse with "credited" (given credit) or "credit" (money owed or praise).

part of speech: noun (an Adélie penguin, Adélie penguins; an Adelie, Adelies); name (Adélie Land)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A kind of penguin of Antarctica, black and white with a white ring round each eye; one of the most common penguins. 2) (a name) Adélie Land is a part of the Antarctic coast, named after Adèle, the wife of the French explorer who found it; the penguin takes its name from it.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography lessons about Antarctica, Adélie penguins are a common example: they build nests of small stones, eat krill and are hurt by changes in sea ice, so scientists watch them to learn about climate change. Stories and cartoons often show them as small, busy, cheeky penguins.
examples from the lessons: Adélie penguins build their nests from pebbles. | An Adélie penguin has a white ring around each eye. | Adélies eat tiny shrimp-like animals called krill. | Some Adélie penguins steal stones from their neighbours' nests. | Scientists count Adélie penguins to learn how the ice is changing. | The Adélie is smaller than the emperor penguin.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually written with a capital A and often with an accent: Adélie (ah-DAY-lee). Usually "Adélie penguin"; "Adelie" alone is informal. It is named after a person (via a place), so it is a name-based word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Something added to something else and mixed in, especially a small amount: "water with an admixture of salt". 2) (formal) The act of mixing in. 3) (science) In the study of genes and people's ancestry, the mixing of different family lines (populations) over time.
its sense in the lessons: Admixture is a stiff, formal and scientific word. In science texts it describes small amounts of one thing in another (an admixture of sand in clay). In books about history and ancestry it means that people from different groups had children together. In everyday speech you would say "a bit of", "mix" or "mixture". It tells the reader the writing is formal or technical.
examples from the lessons: The paint has an admixture of sand to make it rough. | The builders added an admixture to the concrete so it set faster. | His story was truth with an admixture of fantasy. | Scientists study admixture to learn where people's ancestors came from. | The water had a small admixture of mud. | "Admixture" is a formal word for "something mixed in".
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal. Countable (an admixture of) or uncountable (genetic admixture). Similar to "mixture" but stresses an extra thing added in. Do not confuse with "admission" or "admiration".

part of speech: noun (plural of affair: an affair, affairs)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Matters or business, especially public or official ones: world affairs, foreign affairs, current affairs. 2) Personal business and money matters: "She put her affairs in order." 3) An event or situation, described in a certain way: "The party was a quiet affair." 4) (adult life) A secret romantic relationship between two people when at least one of them is married to someone else.
its sense in the lessons: In news and citizenship lessons "current affairs" means the important things happening in the world now; governments have a minister of foreign affairs. "State of affairs" means the situation. In adult life seen by a child, "put his affairs in order" means sorting out money and a will, often before an operation or death. "Having an affair" is when a married person secretly has a boyfriend or girlfriend, which often hurts a family deeply. Phrases: current affairs, foreign affairs, state of affairs, mind your own affairs.
examples from the lessons: We discuss current affairs every Friday in class. | The Minister for Foreign Affairs met the ambassador. | "This is a sorry state of affairs," sighed the teacher, looking at the messy room. | Before his operation, Grandad put his affairs in order. | My birthday was a small family affair. | Mind your own affairs! | In the story, the queen discovered the king was having an affair.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Affairs is the plural; "affair" is singular (an affair). Spelled with double f. Trap: "affair" (matter, event) is not "a fair" (a funfair). Plural "affairs" is used for public business (world affairs); singular "an affair" more often means one event or a secret relationship.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A mushroom with a cap and gills underneath, such as the common field mushroom. 2) In "fly agaric": the famous red mushroom with white spots, which is poisonous.
its sense in the lessons: In science and nature lessons, agarics are the typical mushroom shape with a stalk, a cap and gills under the cap that release spores. The fly agaric is the red-and-white toadstool from fairy tales and video games, and it is poisonous. Safety lessons teach never to pick or eat wild mushrooms without an expert.
examples from the lessons: The fly agaric has a red cap with white spots. | Fairies in picture books often sit on a fly agaric. | An agaric has gills under its cap. | Never eat a wild agaric unless an expert says it is safe. | We found agarics growing under the birch trees. | The field mushroom you buy in shops is an agaric.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: an agaric, agarics. Pronounced AG-a-rik or a-GAR-ik. Safety: the fly agaric is poisonous; touching is not usually dangerous, but wash your hands and never eat it. Not the same as "agar", a jelly used in science.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A large aeroplane that carries passengers on regular flights for an airline.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life airliners take families on holiday; in science and technology lessons they are used to talk about flight, jet engines and speed. In geography they connect cities around the world. In stories an airliner flight adds travel and sometimes danger. Phrases: jet airliner, passenger airliner, a jumbo jet (a big airliner).
examples from the lessons: The airliner carried three hundred passengers to Sydney. | A jumbo jet is a huge airliner. | We watched the airliners take off at the airport. | Airliners fly very high, above most clouds. | The pilot flew the airliner safely through the storm. | Modern airliners have two or four jet engines.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: an airliner (use "an"). Not the same as "airline", which is the company (an airline owns airliners). Also called a passenger jet or plane.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A colourless gas with a very strong, sharp smell, made of nitrogen and hydrogen. 2) A liquid solution of this gas in water, used in some cleaning products.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons ammonia is an example of a compound with a famous smell; it is made in nature when things rot and is in animal wee. Farmers use fertilisers made from ammonia to help crops grow. In safety lessons: never mix ammonia cleaners with bleach, because it makes poisonous gas. Phrases: smell of ammonia, ammonia cleaner.
examples from the lessons: Ammonia has a very strong smell. | The hamster cage smelled of ammonia. | Never mix bleach with ammonia; it makes a dangerous gas. | Ammonia is used to make fertilisers for farms. | Some glass cleaners contain ammonia. | Ammonia is made of nitrogen and hydrogen.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Chemical formula NH3 (one nitrogen atom, three hydrogen atoms). Safety: open windows when cleaning; never mix cleaning products. Not the same as "ammonium" (part of some salts).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (UK, Ireland, Australia, New Zealand) A doctor who gives patients medicine (anaesthetic) so they feel no pain or are fully asleep during an operation, and who watches over them until they wake up.
its sense in the lessons: In health lessons and hospital stories the anaesthetist is the doctor who says "count backwards from ten" before an operation and keeps the patient safe while asleep. It tells the reader an operation is about to happen. In the USA the word is "anesthesiologist", and a nurse who does this is a "nurse anesthetist".
examples from the lessons: The anaesthetist put me to sleep before my operation. | "Count back from ten," said the anaesthetist kindly. | An anaesthetist watches your breathing during surgery. | My mum is an anaesthetist at the children's hospital. | The anaesthetist checked that I hadn't eaten breakfast. | When I woke up, the anaesthetist asked how I felt.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK spelling: anaesthetist, anaesthetic; US spelling: anesthesiologist, anesthetic. Hard to spell: an-aes-the-tist. Countable, takes "an". "General anaesthetic" makes you fully asleep; "local anaesthetic" numbs just one part.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) An opening, hole or gap. 2) (photography, science) The hole in a camera or telescope that lets light in; its size can be changed to let in more or less light.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on light, the aperture of a camera works like the pupil of your eye: wider in the dark, smaller in bright light. In photography, a big aperture blurs the background. In formal writing "aperture" can mean any narrow opening, like a gap in a castle wall. Phrases: a wide aperture, a narrow aperture, adjust the aperture.
examples from the lessons: Light enters the camera through the aperture. | The pupil of your eye is like a camera's aperture. | Make the aperture smaller on a sunny day. | The cat squeezed through a narrow aperture in the fence. | Arrows were shot through apertures in the castle wall. | A telescope with a big aperture collects more light.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: an aperture (use "an"). Formal in the sense of "hole"; everyday speech says "hole" or "gap". Pronounced AP-er-cher.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The study of the human past by digging up and examining old things people left behind, such as tools, bones, pots, coins and buildings.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons archaeology is how we know about times before writing: the Stone Age, Romans, Vikings, ancient Egypt. Archaeologists dig carefully in layers (deeper is usually older) and record everything. In stories archaeology means adventure and mystery. Phrases: study archaeology, an archaeological dig, an archaeologist.
examples from the lessons: Archaeology tells us how Vikings lived. | Archaeologists found Roman coins under the car park. | We did an archaeology dig in the school sandpit. | Archaeology helps us learn about people who never wrote anything down. | The deeper layers in an archaeology dig are usually older. | Dinosaur bones are studied by palaeontologists, not by archaeology.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. UK spelling: archaeology; US often: archeology. Pronounced ar-kee-OL-o-jee. Person: archaeologist; adjective: archaeological. Myth: archaeologists do not dig up dinosaurs — that is palaeontology. Archaeology studies humans.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The science that studies the stars, planets, moons, comets, galaxies and everything else in space.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons astronomy covers the solar system, why we have day and night and seasons, the phases of the moon and the life of stars. Astronomers use telescopes and space probes. In history, astronomy helped sailors navigate and people make calendars. Phrases: study astronomy, an astronomy club, amateur astronomy.
examples from the lessons: Astronomy is the study of space. | I joined the astronomy club and saw Saturn's rings. | Galileo made important discoveries in astronomy. | Astronomy helped sailors find their way by the stars. | My big sister wants to study astronomy at university. | Astronomy uses lots of very big numbers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Person: astronomer; adjective: astronomical (which also means "enormously large", as in astronomical prices). Trap: astronomy is science; astrology (star signs predicting your life) is not science. In maths: distances in astronomy are so huge that light-years are used.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Being real or genuine, not fake or copied: the authenticity of a painting or a signature. 2) Being true to yourself; acting in a sincere, honest way rather than pretending.
its sense in the lessons: In history and art lessons experts check the authenticity of old documents, coins and paintings to spot forgeries. In online safety lessons pupils learn to check the authenticity of websites, emails and photos (is it really from the bank? is the picture real or edited?). In personal and ethics lessons authenticity means being yourself. Phrases: check the authenticity, certificate of authenticity, prove its authenticity.
examples from the lessons: Experts tested the authenticity of the old map. | The signed football came with a certificate of authenticity. | Always check the authenticity of a website before you type your password. | People admired the singer's authenticity; she never pretended. | The museum doubted the authenticity of the dinosaur egg. | Deepfake videos make authenticity hard to judge.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Adjective: authentic (real, genuine). Pronounced aw-then-TIS-i-tee. Opposite ideas: fake, forgery, counterfeit.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A computer system in an aircraft, ship or car that steers and controls it automatically, without a person doing it by hand. 2) (informal) In "on autopilot": doing something without thinking about it, out of habit.
its sense in the lessons: In technology lessons autopilots show how computers help pilots on long flights, though pilots still watch and take over for take-off and landing or in trouble. In everyday talk "on autopilot" describes doing things half-asleep, like walking to school without noticing the way. Phrases: on autopilot, switch on the autopilot.
examples from the lessons: The pilot switched on the autopilot over the ocean. | On long flights, the autopilot flies the plane for hours. | I was on autopilot and put the milk in the cupboard. | Some cars can steer themselves a little with autopilot. | He walked home on autopilot, thinking about the game. | Pilots must still watch carefully even on autopilot.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable for the device (an autopilot), uncountable in "on autopilot". "Auto" means self. Myth: autopilot does not mean the pilot sleeps or that the plane flies itself completely; people stay in charge.

part of speech: noun (Mandarin, pinyin: bái, bǎi, bài); name (Bai)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (Mandarin, pinyin) "bái" (白) means "white"; "bǎi" (百) means "hundred". It sounds like English "by" or "bye". It is not an English word. 2) (a name) Bai is a Chinese family name. 3) The Bai are an ethnic group of people in Yunnan, China.
its sense in the lessons: In Mandarin lessons and on the street children may hear "bái" in colour words and "bǎi" in counting: yī bǎi = one hundred. In Chinese, the tone changes the meaning, so the same sounds "bai" can mean different words. In stories it may appear as a person's surname, such as Li Bai (a famous old Chinese poet).
examples from the lessons: Bái means white in Mandarin. | "Yī bǎi" means one hundred in Chinese. | My friend's surname is Bai. | In Chinese, "bai" can mean different things depending on the tone. | Li Bai was a famous Chinese poet. | To an English ear, "bai" sounds just like "bye".
note for the reader of a maths problem: Not an English word: a Mandarin syllable written in pinyin (with tone marks bái, bǎi, bài) or a Chinese name (capital B). Do not confuse with English "by", "buy" or "bye", which sound the same. "Bái" + "tiān" (báitiān) means "daytime".

meaning for a pupil: 1) (history) A name the ancient Greeks and Romans gave to people from outside their world, whom they saw as wild and uncivilised. 2) A person who behaves in a very cruel, violent or rough way. 3) (informal, jokey) A person with bad manners or no taste: "You put ketchup on that? You barbarian!"
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons the "barbarians", such as Goths, Vandals and Huns, attacked the Roman Empire; pupils learn that the Romans used the word in a biased way about people with their own cultures. In stories barbarians are fierce warriors. In everyday talk the word is often a joke about bad manners. Phrases: barbarian tribes, at the gates (enemies close by).
examples from the lessons: The Romans built walls to keep out the barbarians. | The Greeks called foreigners barbarians because their speech sounded like "bar-bar". | Barbarian tribes attacked Rome. | "Who eats pizza with pineapple? Barbarians!" joked my uncle. | Only a barbarian would hurt an animal for fun. | The Vikings were seen as barbarians by the monks they raided.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a barbarian, barbarians. Related: barbaric (very cruel), barbarous, barbarism. Fairness note: the word was used by one side to look down on others; the so-called barbarians had their own laws, art and skills.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A large soft bag filled with small plastic balls, used as a comfy chair. 2) A small cloth bag filled with dried beans or rice, used for throwing and catching in games.
its sense in the lessons: In school, beanbags are in reading corners for comfy sitting, and small beanbags are used in PE for throwing, catching, balancing on your head and target games. In maths, beanbag-throwing games can count scores. Phrases: beanbag chair, beanbag toss.
examples from the lessons: I read my book on the big beanbag in the library. | In PE we balanced beanbags on our heads. | Throw the beanbag into the hoop to score five points. | The cat loves sleeping on the beanbag. | Our class got new beanbags for the reading corner. | He flopped down on the beanbag after school.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Also written "bean bag" (two words). Countable. Safety: small beanbag balls can be dangerous for babies if a bag splits.

part of speech: verb (bellow, bellows, bellowed, bellowing); noun (a bellow, bellows)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (verb) To shout something in a very loud, deep voice, often in anger. 2) (verb) Of a bull or large animal: to make a loud, deep roar. 3) (noun) A loud, deep shout or roar. 4) Bellows (always plural form): a tool that pumps air into a fire to make it burn hotter.
its sense in the lessons: In stories "bellowed" is a strong speaking verb used instead of "said" to show a big, loud, often angry character: "'Get out!' bellowed the giant." In nature writing bulls, stags and elephants bellow. Bellows are found by old fireplaces and in a blacksmith's forge.
examples from the lessons: Silence! bellowed the headmaster. | The bull bellowed across the field. | The coach bellowed instructions from the side of the pitch. | We heard a bellow of laughter from the kitchen. | The blacksmith pumped the bellows to heat the fire. | The giant bellowed so loudly the windows shook.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: bellowed. Pronounced BEL-oh. "Bellows" (the tool) is used like a plural even for one: "a pair of bellows". Do not confuse with "below" (under), which has one l.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A wild plant with nodding, bell-shaped blue or purple flowers that grows in woods in spring, especially in Britain and Ireland. 2) (Scotland) Another name for the harebell, a delicate blue summer flower. 3) In other places, other blue bell-shaped flowers, like Virginia bluebells in the USA.
its sense in the lessons: In nature lessons in the UK and Ireland, bluebell woods are a famous spring sight; they show that a wood is very old (ancient woodland). Bluebells are protected: it is illegal to dig them up from the wild. In fairy stories bluebells ring to call fairies. Phrases: bluebell wood, a carpet of bluebells.
examples from the lessons: In spring, the wood was carpeted with bluebells. | Bluebells grow best in old woods. | Don't pick or dig up wild bluebells; they are protected. | The bluebells smelled sweet in the sunshine. | We walked through a bluebell wood on our school trip. | Bees love bluebell flowers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a bluebell, bluebells. One word. Safety: all parts of bluebells are poisonous to eat, especially for pets. Its Latin name is Hyacinthoides.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A large snake that kills its prey by wrapping round it and squeezing, as the boa constrictor of Central and South America does. 2) A long, fluffy scarf made of feathers or fur, worn round the neck for dressing up: a feather boa.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons boas are an example of constrictors, which squeeze rather than use venom; they give birth to live young. In everyday life feather boas appear in dressing-up boxes, parties and shows. Phrases: boa constrictor, feather boa.
examples from the lessons: A boa constrictor squeezes its prey. | Boas are not venomous. | The zoo keeper let us touch a boa. | She wore a pink feather boa to the party. | Boas give birth to live baby snakes. | The boa wrapped itself around a branch.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a boa, boas. Pronounced BOH-a. Not the same as a python (which lays eggs) or an anaconda (a kind of boa). Myth: boas do not crush bones to kill; they squeeze so blood cannot flow.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The scientific study of plants: how they grow, what they are made of, how they are named and where they live.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons botany covers parts of a plant, photosynthesis, seeds and pollination. Botanists collect and name plants, and botanic gardens show plants from all over the world. In history, Joseph Banks collected plants on Captain Cook's voyage; Botany Bay in Australia is named after this. Phrases: study botany, botanical garden, a botanist.
examples from the lessons: Botany is the study of plants. | We learned about roots and leaves in our botany lesson. | A botanist collected seeds from the rainforest. | Botany Bay in Sydney was named for its many new plants. | The botanic garden has a giant water lily. | My aunt is a botanist who studies mosses.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Person: botanist; adjective: botanical or botanic. Pronounced BOT-a-nee. The study of animals is zoology; of living things in general, biology.

part of speech: verb (boycott, boycotts, boycotted, boycotting); noun (a boycott, boycotts)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (verb) To refuse to buy, use, take part in or deal with something or someone, as a protest. 2) (noun) An organised refusal of this kind.
its sense in the lessons: In history and citizenship lessons boycotts are a peaceful way to protest: the Montgomery bus boycott, led by Rosa Parks and Martin Luther King, helped end unfair bus rules in the USA. Countries sometimes boycott the Olympics. People boycott companies that harm workers or the planet. Phrases: boycott a shop, call for a boycott, a consumer boycott.
examples from the lessons: People boycotted the buses until the rules were changed. | The Montgomery bus boycott lasted over a year. | Some countries boycotted the Olympic Games. | We boycotted the café after it was rude to our friend. | A boycott is a peaceful way to protest. | The students called for a boycott of plastic straws.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: boycotted (double t). It comes from the name of Captain Charles Boycott, a land agent in Ireland whom local people refused to work for. Countable noun: a boycott. Not connected with "boy" or "cot".

meaning for a pupil: 1) A large, tough fern that grows thickly on hills, moors and in woods, green in summer and brown in autumn.
its sense in the lessons: In nature and geography lessons in the UK, Ireland, Australia and New Zealand, bracken covers hillsides and moors; walkers push through it, and it can hide ticks that may carry illness. In stories bracken is where animals hide and children make dens. Phrases: a patch of bracken, hide in the bracken.
examples from the lessons: The deer hid in the bracken. | The hillside was covered in brown bracken. | We made a den out of bracken and sticks. | Check your legs for ticks after walking through bracken. | In autumn, the bracken turns golden brown. | The path was hard to find under all the bracken.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: "some bracken", "bracken is". Not good to eat: bracken is poisonous to people and animals. Safety: ticks like bracken, so wear long trousers.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A huge plant-eating dinosaur with a very long neck, long tail and four thick legs; its name means "thunder lizard".
its sense in the lessons: In science and dinosaur lessons the brontosaurus is a famous long-necked sauropod. Its story is a lesson in how science changes: for many years scientists said it was really the same as Apatosaurus, so the name was dropped, but newer studies said it was different enough to be its own kind again. Phrases: a brontosaurus skeleton.
examples from the lessons: The brontosaurus had a very long neck. | Brontosaurus means "thunder lizard". | The brontosaurus ate plants, not meat. | We saw a brontosaurus skeleton at the museum. | Scientists argued for years about whether brontosaurus was a real separate dinosaur. | A brontosaurus was longer than a school bus.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: brontosauruses (common) or brontosauri. Name: Brontosaurus (capital B) in science writing. Myth: it did not live with humans; dinosaurs died out millions of years before people.

part of speech: noun (brunch, brunches); verb (brunch, brunches, brunched — informal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A meal eaten in the late morning instead of breakfast and lunch, often bigger than breakfast.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life brunch is a weekend treat with pancakes, eggs, bacon, avocado toast or waffles, often at a café. In English lessons "brunch" is a good example of a blend word, made from "breakfast" and "lunch" (like smog = smoke + fog). Phrases: have brunch, Sunday brunch, go out for brunch.
examples from the lessons: We had brunch at the café on Sunday. | Brunch is breakfast and lunch rolled into one. | For brunch we had pancakes and eggs. | "Brunch" is made by joining "breakfast" and "lunch". | Mum loves a lazy Sunday brunch. | We brunched at eleven and then went to the beach.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable or uncountable: "have brunch", "two brunches". A blend word (portmanteau). The verb is informal.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A small, long-tailed parrot from Australia, usually green and yellow in the wild, kept as a pet in many colours; usually called a budgie.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life budgies are popular pets that chirp, can learn to copy words and live in cages with mirrors and bells. In science lessons on Australian animals wild budgerigars fly in huge flocks over the dry inland. Pet-care lessons cover feeding them seeds and keeping them company. Phrases: pet budgie, budgie cage.
examples from the lessons: My nan has a blue budgerigar called Joey. | Our budgie can say "Hello, pretty bird!" | Wild budgerigars live in big flocks in Australia. | Budgies like to look at themselves in a mirror. | Clean the budgie's cage every week. | Budgerigars are a kind of small parrot.
