note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a budgerigar, budgerigars. Informal and much more common: budgie, budgies. The word comes from an Aboriginal Australian language. Pronounced BUJ-er-ee-gar.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Growing thickly, with lots of hair, fur or leaves: a bushy tail, bushy eyebrows, a bushy beard. 2) Covered with bushes: bushy land.
its sense in the lessons: In descriptions bushy shows thickness and fluffiness: a squirrel's bushy tail, a professor's bushy eyebrows, a bushy hedge. In nature lessons a fox or squirrel uses its bushy tail for balance and warmth. The phrase "bright-eyed and bushy-tailed" means lively and keen.
examples from the lessons: The squirrel waved its bushy tail. | Grandpa has big, bushy eyebrows. | The fox has a long, bushy tail. | The pirate had a bushy black beard. | Trim the bushy hedge before it covers the path. | You look bright-eyed and bushy-tailed this morning!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Forms: bushy, bushier, bushiest (y → i). From "bush". Opposite: thin, sparse. In Australia, "the bush" means wild country, but "bushy" still just means thick and fluffy.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who plays music, sings, juggles or performs in the street or another public place for money from people passing by.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life in towns in the UK, Ireland, Australia and elsewhere, buskers play guitars, violins or drums on high streets and in train stations, and people may drop coins into a hat or case. Some famous singers started as buskers. In some places buskers need a permit. Phrases: a street busker, busking pitch, go busking.
examples from the lessons: A busker was playing the guitar outside the station. | We gave the busker a pound for his song. | The busker juggled fire on the street corner. | Many famous musicians started as buskers. | My big brother went busking with his violin. | Buskers need a permit in some cities.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a busker, buskers. Verb: busk (busked, busking). Mostly a British, Irish and Australian word; Americans more often say "street performer". Rhymes with "husker".

meaning for a pupil: 1) The slightly sour liquid left after butter has been made from cream. 2) Milk made sour and thick on purpose, sold in shops and used in baking.
its sense in the lessons: In cooking lessons buttermilk makes pancakes, scones, soda bread and fried chicken soft and fluffy. In Ireland soda bread is traditionally made with buttermilk. In science lessons it shows how an acid (in buttermilk) reacts with bicarbonate of soda to make bubbles that help bread rise. Phrases: buttermilk pancakes, buttermilk scones.
examples from the lessons: We made buttermilk pancakes for breakfast. | Irish soda bread is made with buttermilk. | Buttermilk tastes a bit sour, like yoghurt. | The acid in buttermilk makes the dough rise with baking soda. | Southern fried chicken is often soaked in buttermilk. | There is no butter in buttermilk.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: "some buttermilk". One word. Trap: despite the name, buttermilk has very little fat and no butter in it.

part of speech: adjective (Cantonese); noun (Cantonese — the language, uncountable; the Cantonese — the people)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The Chinese language spoken in Guangzhou (once called Canton), Hong Kong, Macau and by many Chinese people abroad. 2) (adjective) From or to do with this area, its people or its food: Cantonese food.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and language lessons Cantonese is one of the main Chinese languages, different from Mandarin when spoken, though they share many written characters. Many Chinese communities in the UK, Canada, the USA and Australia speak Cantonese, so it may be heard on the street. Cantonese food includes dim sum, sweet and sour dishes and roast duck.
examples from the lessons: My friend's family speaks Cantonese at home. | Cantonese is spoken in Hong Kong. | We had Cantonese dim sum for lunch. | Cantonese and Mandarin sound very different. | "Nei hou" means hello in Cantonese. | Cantonese has more tones than Mandarin.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always written with a capital C. Pronounced kan-to-NEEZ. Cantonese is not the same as Mandarin, though both are Chinese; people who speak only one often cannot understand the other in speech.

part of speech: verb (-ing form of canvass: canvass, canvasses, canvassed, canvassing); noun (canvassing — uncountable)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Going from house to house or talking to people to ask for their votes or support for a person, party or cause, especially before an election. 2) Asking many people for their opinions: canvassing views. 3) (less common) Discussing an idea in detail.
its sense in the lessons: In citizenship and politics lessons canvassing is how candidates and helpers knock on doors, hand out leaflets and talk to voters before an election. Schools may canvass parents' opinions with a survey. In stories it shows someone working hard to win support. Phrases: go canvassing, canvassing for votes, canvassing opinions.
examples from the lessons: The candidate went canvassing on our street. | Volunteers were canvassing for votes before the election. | A woman knocked on our door canvassing for the Green Party. | The school is canvassing parents about a new uniform. | I helped my mum with canvassing for the class rep vote. | Canvassing means talking to lots of people to win support.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelled with double s (canvass); "canvas" with one s is the strong cloth used for tents and paintings — a common trap. Past: canvassed. Safety: children should never answer the door to strangers alone, even friendly canvassers.

part of speech: noun (a castor, castors; castor — uncountable in "castor oil"); name (Castor)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A small wheel fixed under a chair, bed, trolley or piece of furniture so it can be moved easily (also spelled "caster"). 2) In "castor oil": a thick, bad-tasting oil from the seeds of the castor oil plant, once given to children as a medicine. 3) In "castor sugar" (UK, also "caster sugar"): very fine white sugar used in baking. 4) (a name) Castor is a bright star in the Gemini constellation, named after one of the twins in Greek myths.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life office chairs and hospital beds roll on castors. In history and old stories castor oil was a nasty medicine children dreaded. In baking lessons caster or castor sugar dissolves quickly in cakes and meringues. In astronomy, Castor and Pollux are the twin stars of Gemini.
examples from the lessons: The office chair rolls on five castors. | One castor broke, so the trolley wobbles. | In old books, children were given a spoon of castor oil. | Use castor sugar to make meringues. | Castor and Pollux are the brightest stars in Gemini. | Castor oil comes from the seeds of the castor bean plant.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: both castor and caster are used for the wheel and the sugar. Safety: the seeds of the castor oil plant are very poisonous to eat, though the oil itself is processed safely. The star Castor has a capital C.

part of speech: noun (French: un chapeau, des chapeaux); exclamation (Chapeau! — informal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (French) "Chapeau" is the French word for "hat". It sounds like "sha-POH" to an English ear. It is not really an English word. 2) (informal, borrowed from French) "Chapeau!" is said to praise someone: "Hats off to you! Well done!" — used by some English speakers, especially in sport like cycling.
its sense in the lessons: In French lessons "chapeau" is a basic clothing word: "un chapeau rouge" (a red hat). English speakers sometimes use it jokingly for a fancy hat, and cycling fans say "Chapeau!" to show respect for a great ride. It tells the reader a speaker is using French for style or praise.
examples from the lessons: Chapeau means "hat" in French. | "J'ai un chapeau bleu" means "I have a blue hat". | The plural in French is "chapeaux", with an x. | She won the race all alone — chapeau! | The magician pulled a rabbit from his chapeau. | In English we would say "hats off" instead of "chapeau".
note for the reader of a maths problem: A French word, not an English one; the French plural is "chapeaux" (the x is silent). Pronounced sha-POH. "Chapeau!" as praise = "hats off!" (taking your hat off to someone to show respect).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (church) A minister, priest or religious leader who works not in a parish church but in a school, hospital, prison, army, university or sports team, caring for people there. 2) Today, some chaplains serve people of all faiths and none, offering a listening ear.
its sense in the lessons: In church life and school life a chaplain leads prayers or assemblies at a school, visits the sick in hospital and comforts soldiers or prisoners. Christians believe chaplains bring God's care into everyday places. In stories, a hospital or army chaplain often helps someone in a hard moment. Phrases: school chaplain, hospital chaplain, army chaplain.
examples from the lessons: The school chaplain led our assembly. | The hospital chaplain sat with Grandma and prayed with her. | Army chaplains go with soldiers to support them. | You can talk to the chaplain if you feel worried. | The college chaplain held a service in the chapel. | The prison chaplain visits people who are in jail.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a chaplain, chaplains. Pronounced CHAP-lin. Related word: chapel (a small church or prayer room). Not the same as Charlie Chaplin, the silent film comedian (a name, spelled differently).

part of speech: noun (cheddar — uncountable; a cheddar, cheddars — kinds)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A hard, yellow or orange-yellow cheese, mild or strong-tasting, first made in the village of Cheddar in Somerset, England. 2) (US, slang) Money: "He's got a lot of cheddar." 3) (a name) Cheddar is a village in England, famous for Cheddar Gorge and its caves.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life cheddar is the most popular cheese in the UK, Ireland, Australia, Canada and New Zealand, used in sandwiches, cheese on toast and macaroni cheese. In geography lessons Cheddar Gorge is a limestone gorge with caves where cheese was once stored. In US slang "cheddar" means money, like "dough".
examples from the lessons: I'd like a cheddar and pickle sandwich, please. | Mature cheddar has a strong taste. | We grated cheddar on top of the pasta. | Cheddar cheese is named after a village in England. | We visited the caves at Cheddar Gorge. | "That new bike must have cost some serious cheddar!" (slang)
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable (some cheddar). Small c for the cheese is common, capital C for the place. The slang meaning (money) is American and informal.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a way that involves chemistry or chemicals: chemically treated wood. 2) In terms of what something is made of at the level of atoms and molecules: "Chemically, water is H2O."
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons "chemically" helps describe chemical changes: when wood burns or iron rusts, it changes chemically into new substances, unlike melting ice, which is a physical change. In everyday life it appears on labels: chemically treated, chemically cleaned. Phrases: chemically identical, chemically different, react chemically.
examples from the lessons: Iron changes chemically when it rusts. | Diamond and coal are chemically very similar — both are carbon. | The wood has been chemically treated to stop it rotting. | Chemically, salt is sodium chloride. | Burning paper changes it chemically into ash and smoke. | Melting ice is not changed chemically; it is still water.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb of "chemical" (+ly → chemically, with -ally). Pronounced KEM-ik-lee; the "ch" sounds like k. Key science idea: a chemical change makes a new substance; a physical change does not.

part of speech: noun (a clamp, clamps); verb (clamp, clamps, clamped, clamping)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (noun) A tool that holds two things tightly together or holds something firmly in place, often by turning a screw. 2) (verb) To hold something tightly with a clamp, or to grip firmly: "He clamped his hand over his mouth." 3) (verb, UK) To fix a metal lock (a wheel clamp) on a car's wheel so it cannot be driven, as a punishment for bad parking. 4) (clamp down) To act strongly to stop something: "The school is clamping down on phones."
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons a clamp on a stand holds test tubes or burettes steady. In design and technology clamps hold wood while glue dries or while you saw. In stories, characters clamp their mouths shut, or clamp their hands over their ears. In news "clamp down on" means a strict new rule. Phrases: clamp down on, wheel clamp, clamp shut.
examples from the lessons: Use a clamp to hold the wood while the glue dries. | The test tube was held in a clamp on the stand. | She clamped her hands over her ears at the loud noise. | The car was clamped for parking in the wrong place. | The school is clamping down on bad language. | The crab clamped its claw onto my finger!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: clamped. "Clamp down on" (strict action) is a phrasal verb. Safety in technology lessons: always clamp your work before sawing or drilling, never hold it in your hand.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To do with ancient Greece and Rome, their languages, art and ideas: classical history, classical languages. 2) (music) Serious, traditional Western music by composers like Mozart and Beethoven, played by orchestras: classical music. 3) Traditional and accepted for a long time, the standard way: classical ballet, classical physics.
its sense in the lessons: In music lessons "classical music" means orchestral and concert music from the past (and new music in that style); strictly, the "Classical period" is the time of Mozart and Haydn. In history lessons classical Greece and Rome gave us columns, democracy, myths and the Olympics. In science "classical physics" is the older physics of Newton. Phrases: classical music, classical times, classical ballet, classical architecture.
examples from the lessons: We listened to classical music in our art lesson. | Mozart is a famous classical composer. | Classical Greek buildings have tall columns. | My sister does classical ballet. | Latin and Ancient Greek are classical languages. | The orchestra played a classical piece by Beethoven.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Do not confuse with "classic", which means excellent, typical or famous of its kind: "a classic film", "a classic mistake". "Classical" is about old Greece and Rome or serious music. Pronounced KLASS-ik-al.

part of speech: noun (cloning — uncountable); verb (-ing form of clone: clone, clones, cloned, cloning)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) Making an exact copy of a living thing, with the same genes, from one of its cells. 2) Making copies of plants from cuttings, which are clones of the parent plant. 3) (computers) Copying something exactly, such as a hard drive or a website. 4) (crime) Copying someone's bank card or phone details secretly to steal money.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons cloning is linked with Dolly the sheep, the first mammal cloned from an adult cell, and with identical twins, who are natural clones. Gardeners clone plants by taking cuttings. Ethics lessons discuss whether cloning animals or people is right. In computing, cloning copies a disk or project. In money safety lessons card cloning is a crime. Phrases: animal cloning, card cloning, cloning a plant.
examples from the lessons: Dolly the sheep was made by cloning. | Taking a cutting from a geranium is a kind of cloning. | Identical twins are natural clones of each other. | Scientists debate whether cloning animals is fair. | Card cloning is when criminals copy your bank card. | We are cloning the project so each of us has a copy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable as a noun. Verb: clone (cloned, cloning — drop the e). Myth: a clone is not a grown-up copy that appears at once; it starts as a baby and grows normally. A clone has the same genes but is still its own individual.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The front part of an aeroplane, where the pilot sits and flies it. 2) The small space where the driver sits in a racing car, or the steering area of a small boat or spaceship. 3) (old) A pit or ring where cockfights were held.
its sense in the lessons: In technology and transport lessons the cockpit is full of controls and screens; on airliners the pilot and co-pilot sit there and the door is locked for safety. In stories set in planes, racing cars or spaceships, the cockpit is where the action is. Phrases: in the cockpit, cockpit door, cockpit controls.
examples from the lessons: The pilot waved from the cockpit. | We were allowed to visit the cockpit after landing. | The racing driver climbed into the cockpit. | The cockpit had hundreds of buttons and switches. | The astronaut checked the controls in the cockpit. | The cockpit door is locked during the flight.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a cockpit, cockpits. One word. The word "cock" here is an old word for a rooster (from cockfighting pits); it is not rude. Similar: flight deck (on large airliners).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Commerce is the buying and selling of goods and services, especially in large amounts between companies and countries. 2) (formal) Commerce is the whole world of trade and business in a place, such as shops, banks and markets. 3) (old-fashioned) Commerce can mean dealings or contact between people.
its sense in the lessons: In history and geography lessons, commerce explains why towns grew near rivers, ports and roads: people met there to trade. In everyday life you see it in phrases like «chamber of commerce» (a club of local businesses) and «e-commerce» (buying and selling online). In stories it tells the reader that a place is busy with trade and money. Common phrases: «trade and commerce», «centre of commerce», «e-commerce», «chamber of commerce», «commerce between countries».
examples from the lessons: London became rich because it was a great centre of commerce. | The river carried commerce from the farms to the city. | Mum runs a small e-commerce shop that sells knitted hats online. | The chamber of commerce gave a prize to the best bakery in town. | Roads and railways helped commerce grow across Canada. | In the old port, commerce went on from dawn till dark. | Our class learned how commerce works by running a pretend market. | Sailors brought spices to Europe through commerce with Asia.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: say «commerce», not «a commerce» or «commerces». Stress on the first syllable: COM-merce. The adjective is «commercial» (a commercial is also a TV advert). Do not confuse with «commence» (to begin). «E-commerce» means online shopping and selling.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A consul is an official sent by a country to live in a foreign city to help its own citizens there and to look after trade. 2) (history) In ancient Rome, a consul was one of the two leaders chosen each year to run the republic. 3) (history) In France about two hundred years ago, Napoleon ruled with the title First Consul.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and safety, a traveller who loses a passport abroad goes to their country's consulate, where the consul or their staff can help. In history lessons about Rome, consuls were the top elected leaders. In stories a consul is often a calm, important person who helps travellers in trouble. Common phrases: «the British consul», «consul general», «honorary consul», «the consulate».
examples from the lessons: When Dad lost his passport in Spain, the consul helped him get a new one. | The Australian consul in Bali helps Australians who get into trouble there. | Ancient Rome chose two consuls every year. | Julius Caesar was a consul before he became a dictator. | The consul invited local business people to a dinner. | Her aunt works at the Canadian consulate in New York. | A consul is not quite the same as an ambassador.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: consuls. The office building is a «consulate». An ambassador works in the capital city and represents the whole country to the government; a consul works in other cities and mainly helps citizens and trade. Do not confuse «consul» with «council» (a group that runs a town) or «counsel» (advice, or a lawyer).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Continual means happening again and again, often in an annoying way, with short breaks in between. 2) Continual can also mean going on all the time without stopping, though «continuous» is the better word for that.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, continual tells the reader that something keeps happening and is often tiresome: «continual interruptions», «continual complaints». In science, careful writers use «continuous» for something that never stops, like a continuous line or a continuous flow, and «continual» for something that repeats. Common phrases: «continual noise», «continual interruptions», «continual rain», «a continual worry».
examples from the lessons: The teacher was tired of the continual chatter at the back of the class. | My little brother's continual questions drove me mad on the long car trip. | There was continual rain all week in Ireland. | The puppy needs continual attention while it is small. | Continual practice made her a good swimmer. | The old car had continual problems with its engine. | Their continual arguing spoiled the picnic.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The adverb is «continually». Trap: «continual» = again and again with breaks (the phone rang continually); «continuous» = without any break at all (a continuous line, continuous noise of a fridge). Many people mix them up, and in everyday talk this is accepted, but in tests choose «continuous» for no breaks.

part of speech: adjective (cooperative, more cooperative, most cooperative); noun (a cooperative, cooperatives — also «co-op»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) If you are cooperative, you are willing to help and work together with others and do what is asked. 2) Cooperative work or play is done by people working together for the same goal. 3) (noun) A cooperative is a business or farm owned and run by the people who work in it or use it, who share the profits.
its sense in the lessons: At school, cooperative learning means working in groups and helping each other; a cooperative game is one where everyone wins or loses together. In everyday life, a «co-op» can be a shop owned by its members, such as the Co-op in the UK. In stories, a cooperative character is helpful and easy to work with, while an uncooperative one is stubborn. Common phrases: «be cooperative», «cooperative game», «cooperative learning», «farmers' cooperative», «the Co-op».
examples from the lessons: The children were very cooperative and tidied up quickly. | We played a cooperative board game where we all had to stop the flood together. | The dentist said I was a cooperative patient. | The farmers formed a cooperative to sell their milk. | Nan buys her groceries at the Co-op. | The cat was not very cooperative when we tried to bath it. | A cooperative group shares the work fairly. | The police thanked the witness for being so cooperative.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Also spelled «co-operative» (UK) and shortened to «co-op». The opposite is «uncooperative». The verb is «cooperate» and the noun for the action is «cooperation». Say co-OP-er-a-tive. A cooperative (noun) is countable: a cooperative, two cooperatives.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A coprolite is fossilised poo (dung) from an animal that lived long ago, such as a dinosaur, that has slowly turned to stone.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about fossils and dinosaurs, coprolites are trace fossils: they show what ancient animals ate, because scientists can find bits of bone, fish scales or plants inside them. Children often find the word funny, and museums like to show them. Common phrases: «a dinosaur coprolite», «fossil coprolite», «trace fossil».
examples from the lessons: The museum had a coprolite from a Tyrannosaurus rex. | Scientists cut open the coprolite and found tiny pieces of bone inside. | A coprolite is a kind of trace fossil. | Mary Anning found coprolites on the beach at Lyme Regis. | The class giggled when they learned a coprolite is fossil poo. | Coprolites tell us what dinosaurs had for dinner. | The coprolite felt heavy and hard, just like a rock.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: coprolites. Say COP-ro-lite. It comes from Greek words meaning «dung» and «stone». A coprolite does not smell, because it has turned to rock. It is a polite, scientific word, not a rude one.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Correctness is the quality of being right or true, with no mistakes. 2) Correctness is also behaving in the proper, polite and accepted way. 3) «Political correctness» is the idea of avoiding words and actions that might be unfair or hurtful to groups of people; some people praise it and others mock it.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and spelling, the teacher checks the correctness of your answers. In computing, correctness means a program does exactly what it should. In stories, correctness of manners describes a very proper, careful character. Common phrases: «check the correctness», «the correctness of the answer», «political correctness», «grammatical correctness».
examples from the lessons: The teacher checked the correctness of each sum. | Please check the correctness of your spelling before you hand it in. | The computer tested the correctness of the program. | Grandad always dressed with great correctness. | We argued about the correctness of the answer to question five. | The judge doubted the correctness of the witness's story. | Some people say political correctness has gone too far, and others say it is just being kind.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: no plural. Built from «correct» + «-ness». Do not confuse correctness (being right) with accuracy (being exactly close to the true value) — in science a measurement can be precise but not accurate. In maths, correctness means the answer is right, not just that the method looks neat.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A cowrie is a small sea snail with a smooth, shiny, rounded shell. 2) A cowrie is also the shell of this snail, which was used as money in parts of Africa, Asia and the Pacific long ago and is still used in jewellery.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, cowrie shells are a famous example of early money: people traded goods for them. In art and design they decorate necklaces, bags and clothes. On beaches in Australia and New Zealand children sometimes find cowrie shells. Common phrases: «cowrie shell», «cowrie money», «a string of cowries».
examples from the lessons: She found a tiny cowrie shell on the beach in Queensland. | Long ago, people in West Africa used cowries as money. | The necklace was made of white cowrie shells. | A cowrie shell is smooth and shiny like glass. | Our teacher showed us a cowrie to explain early money. | The cowrie snail lives in warm, shallow seas. | He swapped a bag of cowries for a goat in the trading game.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: cowries. Also spelled «cowry». Say COW-ree (rhymes with «how-ree»). It has nothing to do with cows. In history, cowrie shells were a kind of money, so you could count prices in shells.

part of speech: noun (a craze, crazes); verb (craze, crazes, crazed, crazing — rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A craze is something that suddenly becomes very popular for a short time, like a toy, game or dance, and then fades. 2) (verb, rare) To craze means to make someone wild or mad, mostly seen as «crazed». 3) (verb) When glaze on pottery or glass crazes, it gets a pattern of tiny cracks.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, a craze is a fad in the playground: loom bands, fidget spinners, yo-yos, trading cards. In history lessons there were crazes like the hula hoop. In stories it shows something everyone suddenly wants. Common phrases: «the latest craze», «a craze for», «sweep the country», «craze took off», «crazed with fear».
examples from the lessons: Fidget spinners were a huge craze at our school. | The latest craze is a dance from a video app. | The hula hoop craze swept America long ago. | Every kid wanted the cards while the craze lasted. | Crazes come and go very quickly. | There was a craze for slime in Year 4. | The old teapot's glaze had crazed into a web of fine cracks. | The crazed bull charged at the fence.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: crazes. A craze is short-lived; if something stays popular for years, it is not just a craze. Related words: «crazy», «crazed» (wild with fear or anger). «Fad» means almost the same as «craze».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Something crumbly breaks easily into small pieces called crumbs. 2) Crumbly can also describe soil, rock or old walls that fall apart easily.
its sense in the lessons: In cooking, crumbly describes cakes, biscuits, scones and some cheeses. In science, crumbly rocks and soils are easy to break and weather fast. In stories, a crumbly old castle wall tells the reader it is very old and maybe unsafe. Common phrases: «crumbly biscuit», «crumbly cheese», «crumbly soil», «crumbly old wall», «nice and crumbly».
examples from the lessons: The shortbread was soft and crumbly. | Wensleydale is a crumbly white cheese. | The gardener said the soil should be dark and crumbly. | The crumbly old wall was not safe to climb. | Chalk is a soft, crumbly rock. | My cake was too crumbly to cut into neat slices. | Crumbly bits of biscuit fell all over the sofa.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative: crumblier, crumbliest. Built from «crumble» + «-y». «A crumble» is also a pudding (apple crumble). Crumbly is the opposite of «sticky», «chewy» or «firm».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A dachshund is a small dog with a very long body, short legs and long ears, first bred in Germany to hunt badgers.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life it is a popular pet, often nicknamed a «sausage dog» or «wiener dog». In stories and cartoons dachshunds are often funny and brave. Common phrases: «sausage dog», «miniature dachshund», «wiener dog» (USA).
examples from the lessons: Our neighbour has a dachshund called Frankie. | The dachshund's tummy nearly touched the ground. | Dachshunds were bred to dig into badger holes. | People call a dachshund a sausage dog because of its shape. | The miniature dachshund barked at the postman. | A dachshund must be careful with stairs because of its long back. | At the dog show, the dachshund wore a little jumper.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: dachshunds. It is a German word meaning «badger dog». Spelling trap: d-a-c-h-s-h-u-n-d. English speakers say DAK-sund or DASH-hund. Nicknames: «sausage dog» (UK, Australia), «wiener dog» (USA), «doxie».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Deafness is being unable to hear, or being able to hear only a little. 2) (figurative) Deafness can mean refusing to listen to something, as in «deafness to their pleas».
its sense in the lessons: In science and health lessons, deafness can be present from birth or come from illness, age or very loud noise, so we protect our ears. Many deaf people use sign language, such as British Sign Language or American Sign Language, and hearing aids or cochlear implants. In stories it may describe a character's challenge or how they communicate. Common phrases: «partial deafness», «total deafness», «deafness in one ear», «noise-induced deafness».
examples from the lessons: Beethoven kept writing music despite his deafness. | Loud music through headphones can cause deafness over time. | Her deafness meant she used sign language at home. | Grandpa has partial deafness and wears a hearing aid. | The doctor tested the baby for deafness. | Ear defenders protect workers from deafness. | The king's deafness to the people's complaints led to trouble.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Built from «deaf» + «-ness». Many Deaf people write «Deaf» with a capital D to mean a community with its own language and culture. Be respectful: say «deaf person» or «person who is deaf», not «deaf and dumb», which is old and hurtful. «Hard of hearing» means partly deaf.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Decorative means used to make something look pretty or attractive, rather than to be useful. 2) Decorative can also describe someone or something that looks nice but does little work.
its sense in the lessons: In art and design lessons, decorative patterns, borders and lettering make work look attractive. At home, decorative cushions, plates and lights are for looks. In stories, «purely decorative» can be a joke about a useless thing. Common phrases: «decorative border», «purely decorative», «decorative arts», «decorative lights».
examples from the lessons: We drew a decorative border around our poems. | The plates on Nan's wall are only decorative, not for eating off. | Christmas lights are decorative and cheerful. | The cake had decorative icing flowers on top. | The old fireplace is decorative and never used. | Celtic knots are a famous decorative pattern. | The sword on the wall was purely decorative and very blunt.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say DEC-or-a-tive. Related: «decorate» (verb), «decoration» (noun). Opposite in meaning: «useful», «practical», «functional».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Dehydration is when your body does not have enough water, which can make you thirsty, tired, dizzy and give you a headache. 2) In science and cooking, dehydration is removing water from something, such as drying fruit.
its sense in the lessons: In health and safety, children learn to drink water on hot days and during sport to prevent dehydration; dark yellow wee is a sign. In science, dehydration of food (like raisins from grapes) helps it keep longer. In stories, dehydration is a danger for people lost in a desert. Common phrases: «suffer from dehydration», «prevent dehydration», «signs of dehydration», «severe dehydration».
examples from the lessons: Drink plenty of water to avoid dehydration on hot days. | The runner was treated for dehydration after the race. | Headaches can be a sign of dehydration. | Raisins are made by the dehydration of grapes. | The lost hikers were suffering from dehydration. | Babies with tummy bugs can get dehydration quickly. | In the Australian outback, dehydration can be dangerous.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. The verb is «dehydrate» and the adjective «dehydrated». «De-» means «take away» and «hydr-» means «water». Myth: you do not have to wait until you are very thirsty — drinking regularly is the safe habit.

part of speech: noun (delight, delights); verb (delight, delights, delighted, delighting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Delight is a feeling of great happiness and pleasure. 2) A delight is something or someone that gives great pleasure. 3) (verb) To delight someone is to make them very happy. 4) (verb) To delight in something is to enjoy it very much, sometimes in a mean way.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, delight shows a character's joy: «squealed with delight», «to her delight». Teachers say «a delight to teach» on reports. Turkish delight is a sweet. Common phrases: «to my delight», «squeal with delight», «take delight in», «delight in», «a delight to», «Turkish delight».
examples from the lessons: The children screamed with delight on the roller coaster. | To my delight, the snow was still there in the morning. | Your daughter is a delight to have in class. | The magician delighted the audience with his tricks. | The puppy delights in chewing shoes. | The garden was full of summer delights. | Edmund ate the Turkish delight in the Narnia story. | We were delighted to win the cup.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a feeling, «delight» is uncountable (filled with delight); as a pleasing thing it is countable (the delights of the seaside). The adjective «delighted» means very pleased; «delightful» means very pleasant. Trap: «delighted at/with/by», and «delight in doing».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A depiction is a picture, description or performance that shows what someone or something is like. 2) Depiction is the act of showing something in art or words.
its sense in the lessons: In art and history lessons, we study depictions of kings, battles and everyday life in paintings, tapestries and books, and ask whether they are fair or true. In English lessons, a depiction of a character is how the author describes them. Common phrases: «a depiction of», «an accurate depiction», «a realistic depiction», «the depiction of women».
examples from the lessons: The Bayeux Tapestry is a depiction of the Battle of Hastings. | This painting is a depiction of a busy market. | The film's depiction of dinosaurs was very realistic. | Is this an accurate depiction of life in Victorian times? | The author's depiction of the giant is funny and kind. | Early depictions of the Earth show it with sea monsters. | We compared two depictions of the same queen.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: depictions. The verb is «depict» (to show or describe). A depiction is not always true — always ask who made it and why.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A derby is a sports match between two local teams from the same city or area, which is often very exciting. 2) A derby is a famous horse race; the Derby in England is run at Epsom, and the Kentucky Derby is in the USA. 3) (USA) A derby is a hard, round, black hat with a narrow brim, called a bowler hat in the UK. 4) A derby is any race or contest open to many people, such as a soapbox derby or roller derby. 5) Derby (with a capital D) is a city in England.
its sense in the lessons: In sport talk, a derby game means a big local rivalry, such as two football clubs from the same city. In the USA, children race homemade go-karts in a soapbox derby. In stories, a man in a derby hat looks old-fashioned. Common phrases: «local derby», «the Kentucky Derby», «soapbox derby», «roller derby», «derby day».
examples from the lessons: The Manchester derby is the biggest match of the year for our family. | Thousands watched the horses run in the Derby. | Grandpa wore a derby hat in the old photo. | Our class built a car for the soapbox derby. | My aunt plays roller derby on skates. | The derby ended in a draw, two all. | Derby is a city in the East Midlands of England.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: derbies. Pronunciation trap: in the UK, «derby» is said DAR-bee; in the USA it is said DUR-bee. The horse race is named after an Earl of Derby. «Bowler hat» (UK) = «derby» (USA).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Diabetic means having diabetes, an illness where the body cannot control the amount of sugar in the blood properly. 2) Diabetic also describes things connected with diabetes, such as diabetic food or diabetic care. 3) (noun) A diabetic is a person who has diabetes.
its sense in the lessons: In science and health lessons, children learn that the body uses a hormone called insulin to control blood sugar; in type 1 diabetes the body makes none, so people inject insulin or use a pump. In everyday safety, if a diabetic friend feels shaky or faint, they may need sugar quickly and an adult should be told. Common phrases: «diabetic coma», «diabetic friendly», «type 1 diabetic», «diabetic nurse».
examples from the lessons: My friend is diabetic and checks her blood sugar before lunch. | The diabetic nurse showed him how to use his insulin pump. | Diabetic people can still eat cake, but they plan for it. | Grandpa has diabetic socks that are gentle on his feet. | Our teacher keeps a snack box for diabetic pupils. | Many people with diabetes prefer «person with diabetes» to «a diabetic». | The shop sells diabetic chocolate.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural of the noun: diabetics. Some people prefer to be called «a person with diabetes» rather than «a diabetic». Myth: you do not catch diabetes from someone, and type 1 is not caused by eating sweets. «Hypo» is short for low blood sugar.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A dietitian is a trained health worker who gives expert advice about food and healthy eating, often in hospitals, to help people with illnesses or special needs.
its sense in the lessons: In health lessons, a dietitian helps plan meals for people with diabetes, allergies or other conditions, and schools may use dietitians to plan healthy lunches. In everyday life, a dietitian is a qualified expert, unlike some people online who give food advice. Common phrases: «see a dietitian», «hospital dietitian», «registered dietitian».
examples from the lessons: The dietitian helped my cousin plan meals without gluten. | A hospital dietitian checks what patients can eat. | The school asked a dietitian to plan healthier lunches. | My dad saw a dietitian after his heart operation. | Dietitians study science at university for years. | The dietitian said I should eat more vegetables and fewer crisps. | Athletes often work with a dietitian.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: dietitians. Both spellings «dietitian» and «dietician» are used; «dietitian» is more common. Say die-uh-TISH-un. In the UK, «dietitian» is a protected title for qualified people; a «nutritionist» may have less training.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Dire means very serious or terrible, often dangerous. 2) Dire needs or situations are extremely urgent. 3) (UK, informal) Dire means very bad or of low quality.
its sense in the lessons: In the news and in stories, dire describes disasters, warnings and danger: «dire warning», «in dire need», «dire straits» (a very difficult situation). In UK everyday talk, a film or a meal can be «dire» meaning awful. Common phrases: «in dire need of», «dire straits», «dire consequences», «dire warning», «absolutely dire».
examples from the lessons: The village was in dire need of clean water after the flood. | The scientists gave a dire warning about the melting ice. | If you break the rules, there will be dire consequences, the wizard said. | After losing his job, the family was in dire straits. | That film was absolutely dire — I fell asleep. | The weather was dire all weekend. | The lost sailors were in a dire situation.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative direr and superlative direst are rare; people say «more dire». Do not confuse with «dyer» (someone who dyes cloth). The informal «dire» meaning «rubbish» is mostly British.

part of speech: noun (disrespect — uncountable); verb (disrespect, disrespects, disrespected, disrespecting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Disrespect is rude behaviour that shows you do not value or care about someone or something. 2) (verb) To disrespect someone is to treat them rudely or without respect. 3) (slang) «Dis» or «diss» is a short form meaning to insult someone.
its sense in the lessons: In class rules and ethics lessons, disrespect means rude words, ignoring people or damaging their things, and it usually has consequences. In everyday talk, people say «no disrespect, but…» before saying something critical. In stories, disrespect often starts a quarrel. Common phrases: «show disrespect», «treat with disrespect», «no disrespect intended», «no disrespect to».
examples from the lessons: Talking while the teacher is talking shows disrespect. | He was sent out for disrespecting the referee. | No disrespect, but I think my answer is right. | Dropping litter shows disrespect for the countryside. | She felt disrespected when nobody listened to her idea. | Laughing at someone's accent is disrespect. | The rapper dissed his rival in a song.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a noun, uncountable: «a lot of disrespect», not «disrespects». The verb «disrespect» is newer and more informal; in formal writing say «show disrespect to». Adjective: «disrespectful». «Dis/diss» is slang.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The electorate is all the people in a country or area who are allowed to vote in an election. 2) (Australia, New Zealand) An electorate is an area that elects one member of parliament, called a constituency in the UK.
its sense in the lessons: In citizenship and politics lessons, the electorate is the voters; politicians try to win over the electorate. In Australia and New Zealand, people talk about «my electorate» meaning their voting district. Common phrases: «the British electorate», «a divided electorate», «appeal to the electorate», «young members of the electorate».
examples from the lessons: The electorate chose a new prime minister. | Politicians make promises to win the electorate's votes. | Children are not part of the electorate until they turn eighteen. | In Scotland, sixteen-year-olds are part of the electorate in some elections. | Our local member represents a big rural electorate in Queensland. | Half the electorate did not vote. | The electorate was split down the middle.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually used with «the». It is a group noun: «the electorate is» (in the UK also «are»). Related: «elect», «election», «elector» (one voter), «electoral». In maths problems, the electorate is the total number of voters, and turnout is the part that voted.

part of speech: noun (Esperanto — uncountable, a proper noun with a capital E)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Esperanto is a language invented more than a hundred years ago by L. L. Zamenhof, a doctor from Poland, so that people from different countries could talk easily in one simple shared language.
its sense in the lessons: In language lessons, Esperanto is an example of a made-up (constructed) language with very regular grammar: nouns end in -o and adjectives in -a. It is spoken by a small number of people worldwide. The name means «one who hopes». In stories it may show a character who loves languages or dreams of peace. Common phrases: «speak Esperanto», «in Esperanto», «Esperanto speakers».
examples from the lessons: Esperanto was invented to help people from different countries understand each other. | In Esperanto, «saluton» means hello. | My uncle learned Esperanto and wrote to friends in Japan. | Every noun in Esperanto ends in -o. | Esperanto is easier to learn than many natural languages. | There are Esperanto meetings in many big cities. | The inventor of Esperanto hoped it would bring peace.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Write it with a capital E: Esperanto. It is a real, living language, but nobody's country speaks it as its main language. Say es-per-AN-toe. It is not a dialect of Spanish, even though it looks a bit like Spanish and Italian.

meaning for a pupil: 1) «Eureka!» is a cry of joy when you suddenly discover or work out something. 2) (noun, as «eureka moment») A eureka moment is the instant when you suddenly understand something or have a great idea.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, the story goes that the Greek scientist Archimedes shouted «Eureka!» («I have found it!») in his bath when he realised how to measure the volume of a crown by the water it pushed out. In everyday life and stories, «eureka» marks a sudden discovery. Common phrases: «eureka moment», «shout eureka», «a eureka!».
examples from the lessons: «Eureka!» shouted Sam when he finally found the missing puzzle piece. | Archimedes is said to have cried «Eureka!» in his bath. | I had a eureka moment when the fractions finally made sense. | Scientists sometimes have eureka moments, but most discoveries take years of work. | California's state motto is «Eureka». | The detective's eureka moment came when she saw the muddy boots. | We all said «eureka» when the experiment worked.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say yoo-REE-kuh. It is a Greek word meaning «I have found it». Use «a eureka moment» (not «an»), because it starts with a «yoo» sound. The bath story about Archimedes may be a legend, but the science of displacement is real.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Expectancy is the feeling that something exciting or important is about to happen. 2) «Life expectancy» is the number of years a person or animal is likely to live, on average.
its sense in the lessons: In geography, science and maths, life expectancy compares how long people live in different countries or times; it has grown thanks to clean water, vaccines and better food. In stories, «an air of expectancy» tells the reader everyone is waiting for something. Common phrases: «life expectancy», «an air of expectancy», «a sense of expectancy», «full of expectancy».
examples from the lessons: Life expectancy in the UK is about eighty years. | There was an air of expectancy as the curtain rose. | Long ago, life expectancy was much lower because many babies died young. | The life expectancy of a pet hamster is about two years. | The children waited in silent expectancy for the results. | Clean water has raised life expectancy around the world. | A dog's life expectancy depends on its breed.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly uncountable; plural «expectancies» is rare. Trap in maths: life expectancy is an average — it does not mean everyone dies at that age. Low life expectancy long ago was mainly because many young children died, not because adults all died at forty.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An extractor (or extractor fan) is a machine that sucks out steam, smoke or smells from a room, such as a kitchen or bathroom. 2) An extractor is any tool or machine that pulls or takes something out, such as a juice extractor or a splinter extractor.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and safety, the extractor fan over the cooker removes steam and smoke, and the bathroom extractor stops damp and mould. In science, extractors separate substances, like honey from honeycomb. Common phrases: «extractor fan», «extractor hood», «juice extractor», «honey extractor».
examples from the lessons: Turn the extractor fan on when you fry the bacon. | The bathroom extractor stops mould growing on the ceiling. | Beekeepers spin the honeycombs in a honey extractor. | Mum made orange juice in the juice extractor. | The extractor hood above the cooker was greasy. | The noisy extractor hummed all night in the hotel. | The dentist used a small tool, a kind of extractor, on my tooth.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: extractors. Related: «extract» (verb: to take out; noun: a piece taken from a book or a substance taken from something). In the USA, a kitchen extractor is usually called a «range hood» or «exhaust fan».

part of speech: noun (fantasy, fantasies); adjective use (fantasy football, fantasy story)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Fantasy is a kind of story or film with magic, dragons, wizards or imaginary worlds. 2) A fantasy is something pleasant you imagine or daydream about, which is not likely to really happen. 3) Fantasy is imagination itself, or something that is not real. 4) Fantasy football (or another sport) is a game where you pick an imaginary team of real players and score points from their real results.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons, fantasy is a genre: The Hobbit, Harry Potter and Narnia are fantasy books. In everyday life, «it's just a fantasy» means it is only a dream. Many families play fantasy football or fantasy league. Common phrases: «fantasy world», «fantasy novel», «live in a fantasy world», «fantasy football», «a childhood fantasy», «fact or fantasy».
examples from the lessons: I love reading fantasy books full of dragons. | The Lord of the Rings is a famous fantasy story. | Winning the lottery is just a fantasy for most people. | My fantasy is to live in a treehouse. | He lives in a fantasy world and forgets his homework. | Dad is top of his fantasy football league. | Is the story fact or fantasy? | We wrote a fantasy tale about a talking fox.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: fantasies. The adjectives are «fantastic» (wonderful, or very strange) and «fantastical» (strange and imaginary). Fantasy is different from science fiction: fantasy uses magic, science fiction uses imagined science and technology.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Faux means fake or made to look like the real thing, used mostly for materials such as fur, leather or marble. 2) It is borrowed from French, where «faux» means «false».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and shopping, «faux fur» and «faux leather» are made without real animals. In design, a «faux finish» makes paint look like wood or stone. «Faux pas» (from French) means an embarrassing mistake in manners. Common phrases: «faux fur», «faux leather», «faux pas», «faux marble».
examples from the lessons: My winter coat has a faux fur hood. | The sofa is covered in faux leather. | The pillars look like stone, but they are faux marble. | Wearing a hat at the dinner table was a faux pas in Grandpa's house. | Faux fur is kinder to animals than real fur. | The shop sells faux flowers that never die. | Her bag is faux snakeskin.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say «foe» (the x is silent), so it sounds just like «foe» (enemy). It comes before the noun: «faux fur». In French it is an ordinary word for «false»; in English it is used mainly for fashion and decoration. «Faux pas» is said foe-PAH; plural is also «faux pas».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Fe is the chemical symbol for iron, a metal element; it comes from «ferrum», the Latin word for iron. 2) (Spanish, Portuguese) «Fe» is a Spanish word meaning «faith»; it is not an English word. 3) It may also be a fragment of a longer word, such as «fe» in «fee» or «female», or the start of «Fe» in a name.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, Fe stands for iron on the periodic table: iron is element number 26, rusts in water and air, and is attracted to magnets. The formula for rust contains Fe. Red blood cells need iron from food. Common forms: «Fe», «Fe2O3» (a kind of iron oxide, rust), «iron (Fe)».
examples from the lessons: The symbol Fe stands for iron. | Fe is element 26 on the periodic table. | The label on the cereal box lists iron (Fe). | Rust forms when Fe reacts with oxygen and water. | Our science teacher wrote Fe on the board next to «iron». | In Spanish, «fe» means faith. | Fe comes from the Latin word «ferrum».
note for the reader of a maths problem: Write the symbol with a capital F and small e: Fe. It does not look like «iron» because it comes from Latin. As a plain word «fe» is not English; in English «fee» means a payment. Related English words from «ferrum»: «ferrous», «ferric».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Fishy means smelling or tasting of fish. 2) (informal) Fishy means suspicious, as if something is wrong or someone is not telling the truth. 3) Fishy can also mean like a fish or full of fish.
its sense in the lessons: In cooking, a fishy smell can mean fish is not fresh. In stories, especially mysteries, «something fishy is going on» tells the reader to be suspicious. In safety talk, a «fishy» online message may be a scam. Common phrases: «something fishy», «smell fishy», «a bit fishy», «fishy business», «fishy smell».
examples from the lessons: The kitchen had a strong fishy smell after tea. | There's something fishy about that email asking for Mum's password. | His excuse sounded a bit fishy to the teacher. | The cat loved the fishy biscuits. | The detective thought the butler's story was fishy. | My hands smelled fishy after the beach. | This rock pool is very fishy — look at all those little fish!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative: fishier, fishiest. The «suspicious» meaning is informal and very common. A «fishy» message online is a warning sign — do not click links or share passwords; tell an adult.

part of speech: adjective (flaky, flakier, flakiest — also spelled flakey)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Flaky means breaking off easily into thin, flat pieces called flakes. 2) Flaky skin is dry and comes off in small bits. 3) (informal) A flaky person is unreliable: they forget things or cancel plans. 4) (informal) Something flaky, like a wifi connection or a computer program, works only some of the time.
its sense in the lessons: In cooking, flaky pastry is light with many thin layers, like in a sausage roll or croissant. In health, dry or flaky skin may need cream. In everyday talk and stories, a flaky friend is one you cannot count on. Common phrases: «flaky pastry», «flaky skin», «flaky paint», «a bit flaky», «flaky internet».
examples from the lessons: The sausage rolls were made with flaky pastry. | The old paint on the gate was flaky. | My lips get flaky in winter. | Don't rely on Jake — he's a bit flaky and always cancels. | The wifi is flaky in the garden. | Fish is cooked when it is white and flaky. | A Flake is a crumbly chocolate bar that goes in ice cream in the UK.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative: flakier, flakiest. Built from «flake» + «-y». The «unreliable» meaning is informal; it is a mild criticism, not a rude word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Flattery is praise that is too much or not sincere, often given to please someone or to get something from them.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and fables, flattery is a trick: in Aesop's fable the fox flatters the crow so it drops its cheese. In ethics lessons, flattery is different from honest praise. In everyday talk, «flattery will get you nowhere» is a joking reply to compliments. Common phrases: «flattery will get you nowhere», «empty flattery», «imitation is the sincerest form of flattery», «use flattery».
examples from the lessons: The fox used flattery to trick the crow into singing. | «Flattery will get you nowhere,» laughed Mum when I said she was the best cook in the world. | The courtiers covered the king in flattery. | Honest praise is better than flattery. | She saw through his flattery straight away. | Imitation is the sincerest form of flattery, people say. | He tried flattery to get an extra biscuit.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. The verb is «flatter» (to praise too much, or to make someone look better than real: that photo flatters you). «Flattering» clothes make you look nice. «I'm flattered» means «I'm pleased by your kind words». Do not confuse with «flatten» (make flat).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A forklift is a small, strong vehicle with two long metal prongs at the front that slide under heavy loads to lift and move them.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, forklifts are used in warehouses, factories, supermarkets and ports to move pallets of goods. In safety lessons, children learn to keep away from moving forklifts and that drivers need special training. Common phrases: «forklift truck», «forklift driver», «drive a forklift».
examples from the lessons: The forklift lifted the pallet of bottles onto the lorry. | Uncle Tom drives a forklift at the warehouse. | Stay away from the forklift area in the garden centre. | A forklift beeps when it reverses. | The forklift's two forks slid under the crate. | You need a licence to drive a forklift. | In the toy shop I got a little yellow forklift.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: forklifts. A compound of «fork» + «lift». In the UK people often say «forklift truck». Forklifts can tip over if a load is too high or too heavy, which is why drivers are trained.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A fortress is a large, strong building or town with thick walls, built to protect people from attack. 2) A fortress is any place that is very safe and hard to get into.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, fortresses include castles, walled towns and forts used in wars. In stories, a fortress is often the home of a king or a villain. In everyday talk, «a fortress» can describe a well-guarded house or a strong defence in sport. Common phrases: «an ancient fortress», «mountain fortress», «impregnable fortress», «turn into a fortress».
examples from the lessons: The soldiers hid inside the stone fortress. | The fortress stood on a hill above the river. | Edinburgh Castle was once a mighty fortress. | We built a pillow fortress in the living room. | The dragon guarded the gate of the dark fortress. | Their defence was like a fortress — no goals all season. | The fortress walls were three metres thick.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: fortresses. Related words: «fort» (usually smaller), «fortify» (make stronger), «fortification». A fortress is a kind of building, not a weapon.

part of speech: noun (fraise — French; fraise, fraises — rare English senses)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (French) «Fraise» is the French word for strawberry; it is said like «frez» to an English ear. 2) (history, rare English) A fraise is a stiff frilled collar like a ruff, or a fence of sharp stakes around a fort. 3) (rare English) A fraise is a tool for widening a hole.
its sense in the lessons: In French lessons, «une fraise» means a strawberry: «la glace à la fraise» is strawberry ice cream. In English, the word is rare and mostly appears in history books about forts and old clothes, or on menus with French names. Common phrases: «une fraise», «fraises des bois» (wild strawberries), «à la fraise».
examples from the lessons: In French, «fraise» means strawberry. | Je voudrais une glace à la fraise, said Emma in French class. | The menu offered «tarte aux fraises», a strawberry tart. | Fraises des bois are tiny wild strawberries. | The old fort had a fraise of sharp stakes round its wall. | Our teacher held up a strawberry and said, «une fraise!».
note for the reader of a maths problem: In everyday English this is not a common word; mostly it is French. French: feminine «une fraise», plural «des fraises» (the s is silent). Do not confuse with «phrase» (a group of words), which sounds a little similar.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Frothy means covered in or full of froth, a mass of tiny bubbles. 2) Frothy can describe something light and fun but not serious, like a frothy film or story.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: frothy milk on hot chocolate, frothy waves at the beach, frothy bubble bath. In science, froth forms when gas bubbles are trapped in a liquid, such as when mixing bicarbonate of soda and vinegar. In stories, a frothy mouth on an animal can be a sign of illness, so do not touch. Common phrases: «frothy milk», «frothy coffee», «frothy waves», «frothy bubbles».
examples from the lessons: I love a frothy hot chocolate with marshmallows. | The waves were white and frothy. | The volcano experiment made a frothy mess on the table. | Dad whisked the eggs until they were frothy. | The dog had a frothy mouth after running, so we gave it water. | It was a frothy, silly film, but we laughed a lot. | The bubble bath turned the water frothy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative: frothier, frothiest. Built from «froth» + «-y». Similar words: «foamy», «bubbly».

meaning for a pupil: 1) The gluteus is one of the three big muscles in each buttock (bottom) that help you stand up, walk, run and climb; the biggest is the gluteus maximus.
its sense in the lessons: In science and PE lessons, the gluteus maximus is often named as the biggest muscle in the human body, and «glutes» are worked by squats, running and climbing stairs. It is the polite medical word for bottom muscles. Common phrases: «gluteus maximus», «gluteus medius», «gluteus minimus», «glutes».
examples from the lessons: The gluteus maximus is the largest muscle in the body. | Squats make your gluteus muscles stronger. | The PE teacher said, «Squeeze your glutes!». | The gluteus helps you climb stairs. | Our science poster showed the gluteus muscles in red. | Runners need strong glutes. | The nurse gave the injection in the gluteus muscle.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: glutei (Latin), but everyday speech says «glutes». Say GLOO-tee-us. It is a polite, scientific word, not rude, though children often find «gluteus maximus» funny.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Gracefully means moving in a smooth, light and beautiful way. 2) Gracefully means behaving politely and kindly, especially in a hard moment such as losing.
its sense in the lessons: In PE, dance and gymnastics, you try to move gracefully. In stories, a swan or a dancer glides gracefully. In everyday life and ethics, losing gracefully means being a good sport. Common phrases: «move gracefully», «lose gracefully», «grow old gracefully», «bow out gracefully», «accept gracefully».
examples from the lessons: The swan glided gracefully across the lake. | The ballerina leapt gracefully across the stage. | Our team lost, but we shook hands gracefully. | The cat jumped gracefully onto the fence. | She gracefully accepted the second-place ribbon. | Grandma says she wants to grow old gracefully. | The gymnast landed gracefully on the mat.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Built from «graceful» + «-ly». The opposite is «clumsily» or «awkwardly». Related: «grace», «graceful», «disgrace» (shame — a different idea).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A greengrocer is a person who sells fresh fruit and vegetables in a shop. 2) A greengrocer's (or greengrocer) is the shop itself.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life in the UK, Ireland, Australia and New Zealand, the greengrocer's is a small shop or market stall for fruit and veg. In maths problems, greengrocers often sell apples by the kilo or by the bag. In grammar, «the greengrocer's apostrophe» is a joke name for wrong apostrophes such as «apple's 50p». Common phrases: «the greengrocer's», «local greengrocer», «greengrocer's apostrophe».
examples from the lessons: Mum buys carrots at the greengrocer's on the high street. | The greengrocer weighed the potatoes on his scales. | A greengrocer sells bananas for 20p each — how much do 6 cost? | The greengrocer's sign said «banana's», a classic greengrocer's apostrophe. | Our local greengrocer has the best strawberries. | In the USA, people usually buy produce at a grocery store or farmers' market. | The greengrocer gave me a free apple.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: greengrocers. «The greengrocer's» means the greengrocer's shop. Mostly British, Irish, Australian and New Zealand English; Americans say «produce store» or «fruit stand». A greengrocer is different from a grocer, who sells all kinds of food.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A guild is a group of people who do the same craft or job and join together to help each other and keep up good standards. 2) (history) In the Middle Ages, guilds of craftsmen such as bakers, weavers and builders controlled trade in towns and trained apprentices. 3) A guild can also be a club or society, or a team of players in an online game.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, medieval guilds set prices, checked quality and looked after members who were sick. Today there are writers' guilds and actors' guilds, and in online games players join guilds. In stories, a guild of thieves or wizards is a common idea. Common phrases: «a medieval guild», «guild hall» (guildhall), «join a guild», «writers' guild».
examples from the lessons: In the Middle Ages, the bakers' guild checked the weight of bread. | An apprentice had to train for years before joining the guild. | The town's guildhall is now a museum. | My brother's guild beat the dragon in the online game. | The Screen Actors Guild represents film actors. | The church flower guild meets on Saturdays. | Members of the guild helped each other when times were hard.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: guilds. Spelling trap: «guild» has a silent u and sounds exactly like «gild» (to cover with gold). Say GILD.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Hardship is a situation of suffering or difficulty, especially from not having enough money, food or other things you need. 2) A hardship is one particular difficulty that makes life hard.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, hardship describes war, famine and poverty, such as rationing in the Second World War. In everyday adult life seen by a child, families may face financial hardship if a parent loses a job, and schools sometimes have a hardship fund. In stories, characters overcome hardship. Common phrases: «financial hardship», «face hardship», «suffer hardship», «great hardship», «hardship fund».
examples from the lessons: The family faced great hardship during the war. | Many people suffered hardship when the factory closed. | Pioneers on the trail to Oregon endured many hardships. | The school has a hardship fund to help pay for trips. | Despite the hardship, they stayed cheerful. | Losing a job can bring financial hardship. | The explorers suffered hardships of cold and hunger.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable (much hardship); countable when you list them (the hardships of the journey). Built from «hard» + «-ship». It is a serious word, kinder than saying people are «poor».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Holey means full of holes, like old socks or a sieve.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, holey socks or jeans have holes worn in them. In stories it describes something old and worn out. Common phrases: «holey socks», «holey jumper», «old and holey».
examples from the lessons: My favourite socks are so holey that my toes poke out. | Grandad wears a holey old jumper in the garden. | The moths made the blanket holey. | Swiss cheese is famous for being holey. | A colander is holey so water can drain away. | His holey boots let the rain in.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Homophone trap: «holey» (full of holes), «holy» (connected with God or very sacred, as in the Holy Bible) and «wholly» (completely) all sound like HOLE-ee. A joke: «holey socks» are not «holy socks».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Hornless means having no horns.
its sense in the lessons: In science and farming, some cattle, goats and sheep are naturally hornless (often called «polled»), and some are bred that way for safety. In stories and myths, a hornless unicorn would be just a horse. Common phrases: «hornless cattle», «hornless goat», «a hornless breed».
examples from the lessons: Some breeds of cow are naturally hornless. | The farmer prefers hornless goats because they are safer. | A rhino whose horn has been cut off by rangers to protect it from poachers is left hornless for a while. | Female deer are usually hornless; we say they have no antlers. | The hornless sheep grazed quietly. | Polled cattle are hornless.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Built from «horn» + «-less» (without). Farmers often say «polled» for hornless. Strictly, deer have antlers, not horns, so «antlerless» is the exact word for them.

part of speech: adjective (Hungarian); noun (a Hungarian, Hungarians; Hungarian — the language, uncountable)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Hungarian means from or connected with Hungary, a country in central Europe. 2) (noun) A Hungarian is a person from Hungary. 3) (noun) Hungarian is the language spoken in Hungary, also called Magyar.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and language lessons, Hungarian is famous for being very different from its neighbours' languages: it is not Slavic or Germanic but belongs to the Uralic family, related distantly to Finnish. Hungarian foods like goulash and inventions such as the Rubik's Cube are well known. Common phrases: «Hungarian goulash», «speak Hungarian», «Hungarian music».
examples from the lessons: Budapest is the Hungarian capital. | Our new classmate is Hungarian. | The Rubik's Cube was invented by a Hungarian, Ernő Rubik. | Hungarian is a hard language for English speakers. | We ate Hungarian goulash for tea. | «Szia» means hi in Hungarian. | Many Hungarians love paprika.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always a capital H: Hungarian. Do not mix up «Hungary» (the country) and «hungry» (wanting food). The people call their language «magyar».

part of speech: noun (a hypo, hypos — informal, short form)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal, health) A hypo is a short word for hypoglycaemia: when the sugar in a person's blood, especially someone with diabetes, falls too low, making them shaky, sweaty, pale or confused. 2) (informal) Hypo can be short for a hypodermic needle (a syringe). 3) As a prefix, «hypo-» means «under» or «below», as in «hypothermia» (body too cold).
its sense in the lessons: In everyday safety, if a friend with diabetes says «I'm having a hypo», they need fast sugar such as juice or sweets straight away, and an adult should be told. In science, the prefix «hypo-» appears in words like hypothermia and hypothesis. Common phrases: «have a hypo», «hypo treatment», «hypo kit», «going hypo».
examples from the lessons: Lily felt shaky and said she was having a hypo. | Her hypo kit has jelly sweets and juice. | When someone has a hypo, give them sugar quickly and tell a teacher. | He keeps glucose tablets in his bag in case of a hypo. | Hypothermia means the body is too cold — «hypo» means under. | The nurse explained what a hypo feels like.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: hypos. Informal clipped word (UK, Australia, New Zealand especially). The full word is spelled «hypoglycaemia» (UK) or «hypoglycemia» (USA). The opposite, high blood sugar, is «hyperglycaemia» — «hyper-» means over. Trap: hypo = low, hyper = high.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An ibex is a wild mountain goat with long, curved, ridged horns that lives in steep rocky places in Europe, Asia and North Africa.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on habitats and adaptation, ibexes are amazing climbers with special hooves that grip rocks, and they can even climb nearly upright dam walls to lick salt. In stories and on nature programmes they show skill and balance. Common phrases: «Alpine ibex», «Nubian ibex», «a herd of ibex».
examples from the lessons: The ibex climbed the steep cliff with ease. | Male ibexes have huge curved horns. | We saw an Alpine ibex on holiday in Switzerland. | Ibex hooves grip the rocks like rubber. | A herd of ibex licked salt from the dam wall. | The ibex lives high in the mountains. | Ibex fight by clashing their horns.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: «ibexes» or «ibex» (both correct). Say EYE-bex. «An ibex» uses «an» because it starts with a vowel sound.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Ibuprofen is a common medicine that reduces pain, fever and swelling, sold as tablets or liquid under names like Nurofen or Advil.
its sense in the lessons: In health and safety lessons, children learn that medicines like ibuprofen must be given by an adult, at the right dose for age and weight, and never taken from someone else's packet. It is often used for headaches, toothache, sprains and fevers. Common phrases: «take ibuprofen», «children's ibuprofen», «a dose of ibuprofen».
examples from the lessons: Mum gave me some children's ibuprofen for my fever. | Ibuprofen helped the swelling in my sprained ankle go down. | Always ask an adult before taking ibuprofen. | The doctor said to take ibuprofen with food. | The pharmacist checked the right dose of ibuprofen. | Dad took ibuprofen for his toothache. | Read the label: the dose of ibuprofen depends on age.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable (some ibuprofen, not «an ibuprofen» — though people say «an ibuprofen tablet»). Say eye-byoo-PRO-fen. It is not the same as paracetamol (called acetaminophen in the USA). Safety: never take more than the label says.

meaning for a pupil: 1) III is the Roman numeral for 3, written with three I's. 2) After a name, III means «the third», as in Henry III or John Smith III. 3) It can number a part or chapter: Part III, Act III.
its sense in the lessons: In maths lessons, Roman numerals use letters: I = 1, V = 5, X = 10, so III = 3 and IV = 4. On clocks, III marks three o'clock. In history, kings and queens are numbered with Roman numerals: Richard III is said «Richard the Third». Common forms: «Part III», «Henry III», «Chapter III».
examples from the lessons: The clock shows III where the number 3 would be. | Richard III was king of England. | Read Chapter III for homework. | III + II = V in Roman numerals. | My cousin is called Robert Jones III, after his dad and grandad. | The film had a sequel called «Part III». | In Roman numerals, III means three ones added together.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually written in capitals: III. Read it aloud as «three», or «the third» after a name. It is not a word. Trap in maths: four is written IV (one before five), not IIII, though some clocks use IIII.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Imagery is the use of words to create pictures in the reader's mind, using descriptions of sights, sounds, smells, tastes and feelings, often through similes and metaphors. 2) Imagery is also pictures or images, such as satellite imagery or the images in a film or painting.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons, pupils look for imagery in poems and stories and explain its effect: «The sun was a golden coin» is imagery. In geography and science, satellite imagery shows the Earth from space. Common phrases: «vivid imagery», «use imagery», «satellite imagery», «powerful imagery», «religious imagery».
examples from the lessons: The poem uses imagery of the sea and storms. | Find two examples of imagery in the first paragraph. | The writer's vivid imagery made me feel I was in the forest. | Satellite imagery showed the size of the bushfire. | Church windows are full of religious imagery. | Similes and metaphors are kinds of imagery. | The film's imagery was dark and frightening.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «a lot of imagery», not «imageries». Say IM-ij-ree. Related: «image», «imagine», «imagination». In tests, when asked about imagery, name the picture it creates and how it makes you feel.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Impetigo is a common skin infection caused by bacteria, which gives red sores that burst and form golden-yellow crusts, often on the face and hands, mostly in young children.
its sense in the lessons: In health lessons, impetigo is very catching (contagious) by touching sores, towels or toys, so children with it may need to stay off school until it heals or after starting treatment. A doctor may give cream or medicine. Washing hands and not sharing towels helps stop it spreading. Common phrases: «have impetigo», «catch impetigo», «impetigo sores».
examples from the lessons: My little sister had impetigo round her mouth. | The doctor gave him cream for his impetigo. | Impetigo spreads easily, so don't share towels. | She stayed off school until the impetigo crusts dried. | Washing your hands helps stop impetigo. | Impetigo is caused by bacteria, not by being dirty. | The nurse said the golden crusts were a sign of impetigo.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Say im-puh-TIE-go. Myth: it is not caused by being dirty — anyone can catch it, usually through a small cut or scratch.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Inky means stained or covered with ink. 2) Inky means very dark, especially black or dark blue, like ink.
its sense in the lessons: In school life, children may have inky fingers after using fountain pens. In stories, «inky darkness» or an «inky sky» paints a very dark night. Common phrases: «inky fingers», «inky black», «inky darkness», «inky sky», «inky water».
