examples from the lessons: My fingers were inky after writing with a fountain pen. | The sky was inky black with no stars. | The octopus squirted an inky cloud. | We stepped into the inky darkness of the cave. | The inky water of the lake looked very deep. | Her school shirt had an inky blot on the pocket.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative: inkier, inkiest. Built from «ink» + «-y». In descriptive writing, «inky» is a strong word for darkness — a good example of imagery.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An investigator is a person whose job is to find out the facts about something, such as a crime or an accident, by asking questions and looking for evidence. 2) A private investigator is a detective who is paid by people, not by the police. 3) In science, an investigator is a researcher who carries out a study.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, pupils become investigators: they ask a question, plan a fair test, collect evidence and draw conclusions. In stories, investigators solve mysteries, and in the news, investigators look at the causes of accidents, such as air crash investigators. Common phrases: «private investigator», «crime scene investigator», «accident investigator», «lead investigator».
examples from the lessons: The investigator searched the room for clues. | A private investigator was hired to find the missing dog. | Accident investigators studied the train crash. | In science today, we will be investigators and test which paper towel is strongest. | The investigator asked each witness what they saw. | Crime scene investigators wear suits so they do not spoil the evidence. | The lead investigator held a press conference.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: investigators. Built from «investigate» + «-or». «Private investigator» is often shortened to «PI» or «private eye». A detective is a police investigator.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To irritate someone is to annoy them or make them a bit angry, often by doing something again and again. 2) To irritate part of the body, such as skin or eyes, is to make it sore, itchy or red.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and stories, «irritate» shows mild annoyance: a buzzing fly or a humming brother. In health and safety, some soaps, plants, smoke and chemicals irritate the skin or eyes, so we wear gloves or goggles. Common phrases: «irritate the skin», «irritate the eyes», «it irritates me when…», «get irritated», «irritating habit».
examples from the lessons: It really irritates me when people chew loudly. | My brother hummed just to irritate me. | Smoke from the bonfire irritated my eyes. | This wool jumper irritates my skin. | The teacher was irritated by the constant tapping. | Some cleaning sprays can irritate your lungs, so open a window. | Stinging nettles irritate your skin and make little bumps.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: irritated, irritating. «Irritated» = how you feel (I was irritated); «irritating» = what causes it (an irritating noise). Noun: «irritation». «Irritant» is a substance that irritates, a word seen on hazard labels. It is milder than «enrage» or «infuriate».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) A jiffy is a very short time, a moment. 2) (UK) A Jiffy bag is a padded envelope for posting things.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday talk, «I'll be back in a jiffy» means very soon. It is friendly, chatty language, more common with adults and in stories. Common phrases: «in a jiffy», «in half a jiffy», «just a jiffy», «Jiffy bag».
examples from the lessons: I'll be with you in a jiffy. | Dinner will be ready in a jiffy. | Just a jiffy — I need to find my shoes. | The cake was gone in a jiffy. | Mum posted the book in a Jiffy bag. | The puppy was out of the door in a jiffy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Used almost only in the phrase «in a jiffy». It is informal; in a formal essay write «very quickly» or «in a moment». «Jiffy bag» is a brand name, so it often has a capital J. Similar: «in a tick» (UK), «in a sec».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Lactose is the natural sugar found in milk and in foods made from milk, such as cheese, yoghurt and ice cream.
its sense in the lessons: In science and health lessons, some people are «lactose intolerant»: their bodies cannot break down lactose well, so milk gives them tummy aches, wind or diarrhoea. They may drink lactose-free milk or plant milks. Common phrases: «lactose intolerant», «lactose intolerance», «lactose-free milk», «milk sugar».
examples from the lessons: Lactose is the sugar in milk. | My friend is lactose intolerant, so she drinks lactose-free milk. | Hard cheeses contain very little lactose. | Lactose intolerance can cause tummy pains. | The yoghurt label says «contains lactose». | Babies get lactose from breast milk. | Many people around the world cannot digest lactose well as adults.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Say LAK-toes. Trap: lactose intolerance is not the same as a milk allergy — an allergy is a reaction to milk proteins and can be dangerous. Words ending in «-ose» are often sugars (glucose, fructose, sucrose).

part of speech: noun (a lance, lances); verb (lance, lances, lanced, lancing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A lance is a long spear with a pointed tip, carried by knights on horseback in battles and jousts. 2) (verb, medicine) To lance a boil or abscess is for a doctor to cut it open with a sharp tool so the pus can come out. 3) Lance is also a boy's name.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons about knights and the Middle Ages, two knights charged at each other with lances in a joust. In health, doctors lance boils with clean tools; you should not try it yourself. In stories, a knight's lance is a symbol of bravery. Common phrases: «couch a lance» (hold it ready), «break a lance», «lance a boil», «lance corporal» (a soldier's rank).
examples from the lessons: The knight lowered his lance and charged. | The lance broke against the shield in the joust. | The doctor lanced the boil on his neck. | Knights practised with lances at a target. | A lance is much longer than a sword. | His uncle is a lance corporal in the army. | Lance is the new boy in our class. (a name)
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: lances. A «lancet» is a small, sharp medical tool. Do not confuse «lance» with «launch» (send off). «Lance corporal» is the lowest rank of corporal in the British army.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A landmass is a very large, continuous area of land, such as a continent or a big island.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons, the seven continents are the main landmasses; Australia is the largest island landmass or the smallest continent. In science, the landmasses slowly move (plate tectonics), and long ago they were joined in a supercontinent called Pangaea. Common phrases: «a large landmass», «the Eurasian landmass», «the world's landmasses».
examples from the lessons: Africa is a huge landmass. | Pangaea was one giant landmass millions of years ago. | Greenland is the biggest island landmass that is not a continent. | The world's landmasses cover about 29 per cent of the Earth's surface. | The map showed the landmasses in green and the oceans in blue. | Europe and Asia form one landmass called Eurasia.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: landmasses. Can be written as one word or two. In maths and geography, «about 29 per cent» of Earth's surface is land; the rest (about 71 per cent) is water.

part of speech: noun (a lark, larks); verb (lark about/around, larks, larked, larking)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A lark is a small brown songbird that sings while flying high, such as the skylark. 2) (informal, UK) A lark is something done for fun or as a joke. 3) (verb, informal) To lark about or lark around is to play in a silly, noisy way. 4) (informal, UK) «This X lark» means a kind of activity, said in a slightly jokey or fed-up way.
its sense in the lessons: In science and nature, skylarks are famous for singing high in the sky. In everyday talk, «for a lark» means just for fun, and «stop larking about!» is what teachers say to silly pupils. In stories and poems, «up with the lark» means getting up very early. Common phrases: «for a lark», «lark about», «up with the lark», «a night owl or a lark», «what a lark!».
examples from the lessons: A skylark sang high above the field. | We dressed up as pirates just for a lark. | Stop larking about and line up! | Grandma is up with the lark every morning. | I'm a lark, not a night owl — I like mornings. | «This homework lark is hard work,» said Dad. | The boys were larking around in the pool.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: larks. The informal meanings are mostly British. A «lark» (morning person) is the opposite of a «night owl». Not rude.

part of speech: adjective (looney, looneyer — rare; also spelled «loony»); noun (a looney, looneys)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal, can be rude) Looney means crazy or very silly. 2) (informal, rude) A looney is a person who acts in a crazy way; calling someone this can be hurtful. 3) (Canada, informal, usually spelled «loonie») A loonie is the Canadian one-dollar coin, which has a loon bird on it.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday talk and cartoons (Looney Tunes), looney means wild and silly. In ethics and kindness lessons, children learn that words like «looney» can be hurtful to people with mental illness. In Canada, «loonie» is a normal word for the one-dollar coin, and «toonie» for two dollars. Common phrases: «looney idea», «go looney», «Looney Tunes», «the loonie» (Canada).
examples from the lessons: That's a looney idea, but it might just work! | Bugs Bunny is from Looney Tunes cartoons. | The dog went looney when it saw the snow. | Don't call people looney — it can hurt. | In Canada, a chocolate bar cost two loonies. | The loonie has a loon bird on one side.
note for the reader of a maths problem: More common spelling: «loony»; the Canadian coin is «loonie». It comes from «lunatic», an old word now seen as unkind. Playful use (a looney idea) is fine; using it about real people with illness is rude.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (Ukrainian) «Mamo» is how you call your mother in Ukrainian — «Mum!» or «Mom!» — the form used when speaking to her (from «mama», mother). 2) It is not an English word.
its sense in the lessons: In lessons about Ukrainian heard on the street, children hear «Mamo!» when a Ukrainian child calls their mum. To an English ear it sounds like MAH-mo. Ukrainian changes the end of a name or word when you call someone: «mama» becomes «mamo». Common phrases: «Mamo, dyvys!» (Mum, look!), «Mamo, ya tut» (Mum, I'm here).
examples from the lessons: «Mamo!» shouted the little boy at the playground. | In Ukrainian, a child calls «Mamo!» to their mum. | Our new classmate from Kyiv says «mamo» when she rings her mum. | «Mamo, dyvys!» means «Mum, look!» in Ukrainian. | Mamo sounds a bit like «Mama» in English. | «Mamo» is not an English word.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Ukrainian in Latin letters (in Ukrainian script: «мамо»). It is the vocative case — the form for calling someone — of «mama». Not used in English sentences except when quoting Ukrainian speakers. Do not write «a mamo».

part of speech: noun (Marmite — uncountable, a brand name); adjective use (informal, UK: «a Marmite thing»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Marmite is a dark brown, sticky, salty spread made from yeast, eaten on toast, especially in the UK; New Zealand has its own Marmite too. 2) (informal, UK) Something «Marmite» is something people either love or hate, with nobody in the middle. 3) (French) «Une marmite» is a large cooking pot, shown on the jar.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life in Britain and New Zealand, Marmite on toast is a common breakfast; its old advertising line «love it or hate it» led to the saying «it's a Marmite thing». Australians have a similar spread called Vegemite. In science, it is made from leftover yeast from brewing beer and contains B vitamins. Common phrases: «Marmite on toast», «a Marmite thing», «love it or hate it».
examples from the lessons: I have Marmite on toast every morning. | My brother hates Marmite and says it smells like old socks. | Pineapple on pizza is a Marmite thing — you love it or hate it. | Marmite is made from yeast. | You only need a thin layer of Marmite. | In Australia, people eat Vegemite instead of Marmite. | The singer is a bit Marmite: half my class loves her songs.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A brand name, so usually a capital M. Uncountable (some Marmite, not «a Marmite»). Say MAR-mite. New Zealand Marmite and British Marmite taste different. The «love it or hate it» meaning is informal British English.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A marmoset is a very small monkey with a long tail, soft fur and often tufts of hair on its ears, which lives in the rainforests of South America.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on habitats and food chains, marmosets live in trees, eat fruit, insects and tree gum, and live in family groups. They are seen in zoos; animal charities say they should not be kept as pets because they need special care and company. Common phrases: «common marmoset», «pygmy marmoset», «a family of marmosets».
examples from the lessons: A marmoset can fit in the palm of an adult's hand. | The pygmy marmoset is one of the smallest monkeys in the world. | Marmosets scratch tree bark to lick the gum. | At the zoo we saw marmosets with white ear tufts. | Marmosets usually have twins. | The marmoset leapt from branch to branch. | Marmosets live in the rainforests of Brazil.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: marmosets. Say MAR-mo-set. They are monkeys, not apes, and they have tails.

part of speech: noun (mayflower, mayflowers; the Mayflower — the ship)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The Mayflower was the ship that carried English settlers, now called the Pilgrims, across the Atlantic from Plymouth in England to America, where they started Plymouth Colony. 2) A mayflower is any of several plants that flower in spring, especially hawthorn in Britain and the trailing arbutus in North America. 3) The mayflower is the floral symbol of Nova Scotia in Canada and of Massachusetts in the USA.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons in the USA and UK, the Mayflower voyage is linked with the first Thanksgiving story, which is now taught alongside the history of the Wampanoag people who already lived there. In nature, «May flower» or hawthorn blossom is a sign of late spring. Common phrases: «the Mayflower», «the Mayflower Pilgrims», «the Mayflower Compact».
examples from the lessons: The Mayflower sailed from Plymouth, England. | About one hundred passengers crossed the ocean on the Mayflower. | The Pilgrims on the Mayflower landed in what is now Massachusetts. | The Wampanoag people helped the settlers after the Mayflower arrived. | The mayflower is the provincial flower of Nova Scotia. | The hedges were white with mayflower blossom. | We made a model of the Mayflower in class.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The ship's name has a capital M: the Mayflower. As a plant name it is usually lower case. Plural (plants): mayflowers.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Mayonnaise is a thick, creamy, pale yellow sauce made from egg yolks, oil and lemon juice or vinegar, eaten cold in sandwiches, on chips and in salads.
its sense in the lessons: In cooking and food science, mayonnaise is an emulsion: tiny drops of oil mixed into egg and vinegar so they do not separate. In food safety, homemade mayonnaise with raw eggs should be kept cold. Common phrases: «a dollop of mayonnaise», «egg mayonnaise», «chips and mayo», «a jar of mayonnaise».
examples from the lessons: Can I have mayonnaise in my chicken sandwich? | In the Netherlands, people eat chips with mayonnaise. | Egg mayonnaise is a classic picnic sandwich. | Keep the mayonnaise in the fridge. | Mayonnaise is made by slowly whisking oil into egg yolks. | Dad likes a big dollop of mayo on his burger. | Coleslaw has mayonnaise mixed through it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «some mayonnaise». Spelling trap: double n — m-a-y-o-n-n-a-i-s-e. It comes from French. Short form: «mayo» (informal). Say may-uh-NAZE.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A melody is a tune: a series of musical notes, one after another, that sounds pleasing and is easy to remember. 2) The melody is the main tune in a piece of music, often the part that is sung. 3) A melody is also any pleasant sound like music, such as birdsong.
its sense in the lessons: In music lessons, pupils learn the difference between melody (the tune), rhythm (the beat pattern) and harmony (notes played together); they may compose a simple melody on a glockenspiel or recorder. In stories, a melody drifts through the air to show calm or magic. Common phrases: «a catchy melody», «hum the melody», «play the melody», «a sweet melody».
examples from the lessons: She hummed a happy melody as she painted. | Can you play the melody of «Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star»? | The song has a catchy melody that sticks in your head. | The violins play the melody while the cellos play the harmony. | The blackbird's melody woke me up. | We composed a short melody using only five notes. | The melody goes up and then comes down.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: melodies. Adjectives: «melodic» (to do with melody) and «melodious» (pleasant to hear). Say MEL-o-dee.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Meltwater is water that comes from melting snow or ice, especially from glaciers and ice sheets.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and science lessons, meltwater feeds rivers in spring, carves valleys, and forms lakes at the edges of glaciers. With climate change, more meltwater from Greenland and Antarctica adds to rising sea levels. In safety, meltwater can cause sudden floods. Common phrases: «glacial meltwater», «spring meltwater», «meltwater streams», «meltwater lake».
examples from the lessons: Meltwater from the glacier made a milky blue lake. | In spring, meltwater fills the mountain rivers. | Meltwater from ice sheets is raising sea levels. | The meltwater stream was freezing cold. | Floods can happen when meltwater rushes down the valley. | Scientists measure meltwater on the Greenland ice sheet.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. A compound of «melt» + «water», written as one word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Metropolitan means belonging to a very big city, called a metropolis, and the towns around it. 2) (church) A metropolitan is a senior bishop in charge of an area, especially in the Orthodox churches. 3) Metropolitan France means the main part of France in Europe, not its overseas lands.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons, a metropolitan area is a big city plus its suburbs; for example, the Sydney metropolitan area. In the UK, London's police force is called the Metropolitan Police, or «the Met». In church life, Orthodox Christians have metropolitans as senior bishops. Common phrases: «metropolitan area», «the Metropolitan Police», «the Metropolitan Museum of Art», «metropolitan bishop».
examples from the lessons: More than five million people live in the Melbourne metropolitan area. | The Metropolitan Police look after London. | We visited the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York. | Metropolitan areas often have busy trains and buses. | The metropolitan led the Easter service in the cathedral. | Transport for London runs the Metropolitan line on the Underground. | Rural areas are quieter than metropolitan ones.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say met-ro-POL-i-tan. Short forms: «the Met» (police, or the New York museum or opera). The opposite of a metropolitan area is a «rural» area.

part of speech: noun (milligram, milligrams — also spelled milligramme in the UK; symbol mg)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A milligram is a very small unit of mass equal to one thousandth of a gram.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and science lessons, 1000 milligrams = 1 gram and 1000 grams = 1 kilogram; milligrams measure tiny amounts, like medicine doses or vitamins on food labels. In everyday safety, medicine labels give the dose in mg. Common phrases: «milligrams per day», «a 200 mg tablet», «mg of salt».
examples from the lessons: There are 1000 milligrams in one gram. | Each tablet contains 200 milligrams of ibuprofen. | A grain of salt weighs about a tenth of a milligram. | The label says 30 mg of vitamin C in each glass. | Convert 3 grams to milligrams: 3 × 1000 = 3000 mg. | A mosquito weighs about two milligrams. | The doctor checked the dose in milligrams.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: milligrams. Symbol: mg (no full stop, no s: 50 mg). «Milli-» means one thousandth. Trap: do not mix up mg (milligram) and ml (millilitre); mg measures mass, ml measures volume. To change grams to milligrams, multiply by 1000; milligrams to grams, divide by 1000.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Mortality is the fact that every living thing will one day die. 2) Mortality is also the number of deaths in a group or a place over a time, often called the mortality rate.
its sense in the lessons: In science, history and geography, «infant mortality» (babies dying young) fell a lot because of clean water and vaccines. In religion, ethics and stories, mortality means thinking about life being short. Common phrases: «infant mortality», «mortality rate», «human mortality», «face your own mortality».
examples from the lessons: Infant mortality was very high in Victorian times. | Vaccines lowered the mortality rate from measles. | Seeing the old tree fall made Grandpa think about his own mortality. | Mortality among the young birds was high in the cold spring. | Doctors study mortality to find which illnesses are most dangerous. | Christians believe that Jesus' resurrection gives hope beyond mortality.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly uncountable. The opposite is «immortality» (living for ever). Adjective: «mortal». In maths, a mortality rate is usually given as a number per 1000 people or as a percentage.

part of speech: adjective (mortified); verb past form of «mortify» (mortify, mortifies, mortified, mortifying)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Mortified means extremely embarrassed or ashamed. 2) (verb) To mortify someone is to make them feel very embarrassed. 3) (church, old) To mortify the body was to make it suffer on purpose as a religious practice, for example by fasting.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and stories, mortified is a strong feeling word, much stronger than «embarrassed»: falling over on stage, or when your dad dances at the school disco. In church history, some Christians practised «mortification» to grow in self-control. Common phrases: «absolutely mortified», «I was mortified», «mortifying moment».
examples from the lessons: I was mortified when my trousers split in assembly. | Mum was mortified that she had forgotten my birthday party. | He felt mortified after calling the teacher «Mum». | It was mortifying to trip up the stairs in front of everyone. | She was absolutely mortified when her phone rang during the play. | My sister was mortified by Dad's dancing.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Used mostly as an adjective after «be» or «feel». The «-ing» form «mortifying» describes the situation. It comes from Latin «mors» (death) — as if you could «die of embarrassment».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal, rare) Natation is the act or art of swimming. 2) (French) «La natation» is the ordinary French word for swimming as a sport or school subject; said «nah-tah-SYON» to an English ear.
its sense in the lessons: In English, natation is a very rare, old, formal word, so you will mostly meet it in French lessons and on signs in French-speaking places like France, Quebec or Belgium: «piscine» (pool), «cours de natation» (swimming lessons). In science, «natatorial» describes animals that swim. Common phrases: «la natation», «cours de natation», «natation synchronisée».
examples from the lessons: In French, «la natation» means swimming. | My cousin in Quebec has «cours de natation» every Saturday. | Natation is a fancy old English word for swimming. | The sign at the French campsite said «Natation interdite» — no swimming. | Our French teacher asked, «Tu aimes la natation?». | The old book described natation as a healthy exercise.
note for the reader of a maths problem: In everyday English, say «swimming», not «natation». In French it is feminine: «la natation». Related English words: «natatorium» (US: indoor swimming pool).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A naturalist is a person who studies plants, animals and nature, often by watching them carefully in the wild. 2) (rare, art and literature) A naturalist is a writer or artist who shows life exactly as it is.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, famous naturalists include Charles Darwin and David Attenborough, who observed living things closely. Children can be young naturalists by keeping nature diaries, pond dipping and bird watching. Common phrases: «a keen naturalist», «a young naturalist», «amateur naturalist», «field naturalist».
examples from the lessons: Charles Darwin was a naturalist who sailed around the world. | The park naturalist showed us how to find frogs. | She keeps a nature diary like a real naturalist. | David Attenborough is a famous naturalist and broadcaster. | The naturalist sketched every butterfly she saw. | Our class joined the Young Naturalists club. | A naturalist needs patience and sharp eyes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: naturalists. Do not confuse with «naturist» (a person who likes to go without clothes) — a funny but real trap. Related: «natural history» (the study of nature).

part of speech: adverb and interjection (nay — old or formal); noun (a nay, nays)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (old-fashioned) Nay means «no». 2) (formal) Nay is used to add a stronger word: «It was hard, nay, impossible», meaning «not only that, but even». 3) (noun) A nay is a «no» vote, as in «the ayes and the nays».
its sense in the lessons: In stories and the Bible (old translations), characters say «nay» for «no»: «Let your yea be yea; and your nay, nay.» In parliaments and meetings, votes are counted as yeas (or ayes) and nays. In formal writing, «nay» strengthens a point. Common phrases: «yea or nay», «the ayes and the nays», «nay, even», «say nay».
examples from the lessons: «Nay, my lord,» said the knight, «I will not go.» | The vote was ten yeas and four nays. | The task was difficult, nay, impossible. | In the King James Bible: «Let your yea be yea; and your nay, nay.» | The senators shouted «nay!». | Whether you say yea or nay, we must decide tonight.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Homophone trap: «nay» (no) sounds like «neigh» (the sound a horse makes). Say NAY. Opposite: «yea» or «aye» (yes). In everyday talk, use «no»; «nay» sounds old or jokey.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A Neanderthal was a kind of early human who lived in Europe and western Asia from about 400,000 to about 40,000 years ago and then died out. 2) (informal, rude) Calling someone a neanderthal means they are rough, rude or old-fashioned in their ideas.
its sense in the lessons: In history and science lessons about the Stone Age, Neanderthals made stone tools, used fire, wore clothes, buried their dead and maybe made art; many people today carry a little Neanderthal DNA. The old idea that they were stupid brutes is a myth. In stories and insults, «neanderthal» unfairly means boorish. Common phrases: «Neanderthal man», «Neanderthal tools», «Neanderthal DNA».
examples from the lessons: Neanderthals lived during the Ice Age. | Neanderthals made sharp stone tools. | Scientists found Neanderthal bones in a cave in Germany. | Some of our DNA comes from Neanderthals. | Neanderthals had big, strong bodies for the cold. | «Don't be such a neanderthal!» she said when he burped at the table. | Neanderthals and modern humans lived at the same time for thousands of years.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually written with a capital N for the early humans. Say nee-AN-der-tahl (also -thal). Named after the Neander Valley in Germany, where bones were found. Myth: Neanderthals were not simple cavemen who grunted — they were clever and skilled.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Nigerian means from or connected with Nigeria, a large country in West Africa. 2) (noun) A Nigerian is a person from Nigeria.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons, Nigeria has the largest population in Africa, many languages such as Yoruba, Igbo and Hausa, and English as its official language. In everyday life, Nigerian food like jollof rice, Nigerian music (Afrobeats) and Nigerian films (Nollywood) are popular worldwide. Common phrases: «Nigerian food», «Nigerian English», «Nigerian music».
examples from the lessons: My best friend's family is Nigerian. | Jollof rice is a famous Nigerian dish. | Lagos is the biggest Nigerian city. | Many Nigerian films are made in Nollywood. | The Nigerian football team are called the Super Eagles. | Nigerian English has its own special words. | Our class learned a Nigerian song.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always a capital N: Nigerian. Do not mix up Nigeria and Niger, a different country next to it; people from Niger are called «Nigerien». Say nye-JEER-ee-an.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A nugget is a small lump of gold or another precious metal found in the ground. 2) A nugget (chicken nugget) is a small piece of food, usually chicken, covered in breadcrumbs and fried or baked. 3) A nugget of information, wisdom or advice is a small but useful or interesting piece of it. 4) (Australia, informal) A nugget can be a short, strong, stocky person or animal.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, gold rushes in California, Australia and New Zealand began when people found gold nuggets. In everyday life, chicken nuggets are a common children's meal. In reading, «a nugget of information» is a useful fact. Common phrases: «gold nugget», «chicken nuggets», «a nugget of information», «a nugget of wisdom».
examples from the lessons: The miner found a gold nugget in the river. | Can I have chicken nuggets and chips? | Our teacher shared a nugget of wisdom: «Read the question twice.» | The museum has the biggest gold nugget ever found in Victoria. | Here's a nugget of information: octopuses have three hearts. | The little puppy is a solid nugget. | We dipped our nuggets in tomato sauce.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: nuggets. Countable. Say NUG-it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An oboe is a woodwind musical instrument shaped like a long thin tube, played by blowing through a double reed, which makes a clear, slightly sharp sound.
its sense in the lessons: In music lessons, the oboe belongs to the woodwind family of the orchestra, with the flute, clarinet and bassoon; the orchestra tunes to the oboe's note A. In «Peter and the Wolf», the oboe plays the duck. Common phrases: «play the oboe», «oboe solo», «oboe player» (oboist).
examples from the lessons: My sister plays the oboe in the school orchestra. | In «Peter and the Wolf», the oboe is the duck. | The oboe plays a note A so the whole orchestra can tune. | An oboe has a double reed made of cane. | The oboe solo sounded sad and beautiful. | Learning the oboe takes a lot of breath control. | An oboe player is called an oboist.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: oboes. Say OH-boh. Do not confuse with the clarinet, which has a single reed and a wider bell. «An oboe» (vowel sound).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Occasionally means sometimes, but not often or regularly.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, «we occasionally have pizza» means now and then. In maths and data lessons, occasionally sits on a scale of frequency: never, rarely, occasionally, sometimes, often, usually, always. In stories it shows something unusual. Common phrases: «only occasionally», «very occasionally», «occasionally visit».
examples from the lessons: We occasionally go to the cinema on Saturdays. | It occasionally snows in London. | I occasionally forget my PE kit. | The volcano still erupts occasionally. | Grandad visits us occasionally from Scotland. | Only very occasionally does the teacher shout. | Bears occasionally come into the campsite, so lock the bins.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: two c's and one s — o-c-c-a-s-i-o-n-a-l-l-y, with double l. From «occasion» + «-al» + «-ly». It is less often than «often» but more than «rarely».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Offshore means in the sea, away from the coast. 2) An offshore wind blows from the land out towards the sea. 3) (money) Offshore companies or bank accounts are kept in another country, often to pay less tax.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and science, offshore wind farms and oil rigs stand in the sea; offshore islands lie off the coast. In beach safety, an offshore wind can blow inflatables and swimmers out to sea, so be careful. In adult money news, «offshore accounts» are often linked to avoiding tax. Common phrases: «offshore wind farm», «offshore oil rig», «offshore wind», «offshore island», «offshore account».
examples from the lessons: There is a huge offshore wind farm near the coast. | Dad works on an offshore oil rig. | The boat anchored a mile offshore. | With an offshore wind, don't take your lilo into the sea. | The island lies just offshore. | The news said rich people hid money in offshore accounts. | Dolphins were swimming offshore.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: «onshore» (on the land, or blowing towards the land). Do not confuse with «inshore» (close to the coast). Not usually used with «the».

meaning for a pupil: 1) An oxbow (oxbow lake) is a curved lake that forms when a bend (meander) of a river is cut off from the main river. 2) An oxbow is also a big U-shaped bend in a river. 3) An oxbow is a U-shaped wooden collar that fits around an ox's neck to fix it to a yoke.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons, oxbow lakes are a classic feature of rivers in their lower course: erosion on the outside of meanders and deposition on the inside slowly cut off a loop, especially in floods. Pupils draw diagrams of how an oxbow lake forms. Common phrases: «oxbow lake», «form an oxbow», «meander and oxbow».
examples from the lessons: An oxbow lake forms when a meander is cut off. | We drew a diagram of how an oxbow lake forms. | The Mississippi River has many oxbow lakes. | Ducks swam on the quiet oxbow. | The flood cut through the neck of the meander and made an oxbow. | The farmer's old ox wore a wooden oxbow. | Oxbow lakes slowly fill with mud and plants.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: oxbows. A compound of «ox» + «bow» (bow rhymes with «go»). The lake gets its name because its curve looks like the U-shaped oxbow collar.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Palestinian means from or connected with the Palestinian people or the Palestinian territories, the West Bank and the Gaza Strip, in the Middle East. 2) (noun) A Palestinian is a person from this people, whether living there or elsewhere in the world.
its sense in the lessons: In current events lessons, Palestinians and Israelis have a long, painful conflict over land, safety and rights; both peoples have suffered, and many points are contested, so it is fair to give each side's view in its own words. In everyday life, Palestinian food such as hummus, falafel and maqluba is enjoyed around the world. In history and Bible lessons, the region was called Palestine in Roman and later times. Common phrases: «Palestinian people», «Palestinian territories», «Palestinian refugees», «Palestinian Authority».
examples from the lessons: Many Palestinian families live in Gaza and the West Bank. | Our neighbour is Palestinian and makes delicious maqluba. | The news showed Palestinian children in a camp for refugees. | Many countries recognise a State of Palestine, and some do not. | Palestinian embroidery has beautiful red patterns. | Leaders met to talk about peace between Israelis and Palestinians. | Palestinian Christians live in Bethlehem, where Christians believe Jesus was born.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always a capital P. Say pal-uh-STIN-ee-an. Most Palestinians are Muslim, and some are Christian. Talk about real people and conflicts with care: name what is reported, and say who says what when facts are disputed.

part of speech: noun (panto, pantos — informal, short for pantomime)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (UK, informal) A panto is a funny family musical play, usually shown around Christmas and New Year, based on a fairy tale such as Cinderella or Aladdin, with jokes, songs, a man dressed as a «dame», and lots of audience shouting. 2) (UK) Panto can describe anything silly and over-the-top, as in «a bit of a panto».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life in the UK and Ireland, going to the panto is a Christmas tradition; the audience shouts «He's behind you!» and «Oh no it isn't!» — «Oh yes it is!». In drama lessons, pupils learn panto characters: the dame, the principal boy, the villain who gets booed. In other countries «pantomime» often means mime, acting without words. Common phrases: «go to the panto», «panto season», «panto dame», «panto villain», «He's behind you!».
examples from the lessons: We go to the panto every Christmas. | The audience shouted «He's behind you!» at the panto. | Our teacher played the dame in the school panto. | This year's panto is Jack and the Beanstalk. | Everyone booed the panto villain. | Oh no it isn't! Oh yes it is! — that's panto for you. | The meeting turned into a bit of a panto.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: pantos. Short for «pantomime». Mostly British, Irish, and also known in Australia and Canada. In the USA, «pantomime» usually means mime (acting with no words), so Americans may not know British panto.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Papermaking is the craft or industry of making paper, usually from wood pulp, cotton, rags or recycled paper soaked in water, pressed into thin sheets and dried.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, papermaking was invented in China about two thousand years ago, traditionally credited to Cai Lun, and spread to the Arab world and Europe. In science and art lessons, children make recycled paper with a mould and deckle (a frame with a screen). In geography, papermaking uses lots of trees and water, so recycling helps. Common phrases: «the art of papermaking», «papermaking industry», «recycled papermaking».
examples from the lessons: Papermaking was invented in ancient China. | In art we tried papermaking with old newspapers and water. | The papermaking mill by the river used water power. | Papermaking uses a lot of trees, so we recycle. | The museum showed papermaking with cotton rags. | Wasps make their nests by a kind of papermaking from chewed wood. | We dried our papermaking sheets on the windowsill.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. A compound of «paper» + «making», written as one word. Related: «papermaker», «paper mill».

part of speech: noun (patois — same form for plural; uncountable as a language)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A patois is a form of a language spoken by ordinary people in a particular area, different from the standard language. 2) (Jamaica, UK) Patois (often spelled «Patwa») is the everyday language of Jamaica, based on English with West African influences, also heard among many Black British and Caribbean people. 3) A patois can also be the special talk or jargon of a group.
its sense in the lessons: In language lessons, patois shows that languages have many local forms; Jamaican Patois words like «wah gwaan» (what's going on) are heard in UK slang. It is a full way of speaking with its own rules, not «bad English». In stories, a character speaking patois shows where they are from. Common phrases: «Jamaican Patois», «speak patois», «local patois».
examples from the lessons: Grandma speaks Jamaican Patois with her sisters. | «Wah gwaan» is a greeting in Jamaican Patois. | The villagers spoke a patois the visitors could not understand. | Many words in London slang come from Patois. | The poem was written in Caribbean patois. | Every trade has its own patois of special words.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say PAT-wah (the s is silent). The plural is also spelled «patois» but said PAT-wahz. It comes from French. Respect: a patois is a real way of speaking, not broken or wrong language.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Phytoplankton are tiny living things, mostly too small to see, that float near the surface of seas and lakes and make their own food from sunlight, like plants do.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on food chains and the ocean, phytoplankton are producers: they are eaten by zooplankton, which are eaten by fish, and so on up to whales. They make a large part of the oxygen we breathe, perhaps about half. Satellites can see big green «blooms» of phytoplankton from space. Common phrases: «phytoplankton bloom», «marine phytoplankton», «phytoplankton and zooplankton».
examples from the lessons: Phytoplankton float near the surface of the sea. | Phytoplankton use sunlight to make food, just like plants. | Tiny animals called zooplankton eat phytoplankton. | Ocean phytoplankton make about half of the Earth's oxygen. | A phytoplankton bloom turned the sea green. | Krill feed on phytoplankton, and whales eat krill. | Without phytoplankton, ocean food chains would collapse.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually used like a plural or uncountable noun («phytoplankton are» or «phytoplankton is»). Say FIE-toe-PLANK-ton. «Phyto-» means plant; «zoo-» means animal; «plankton» means drifting. Trap: many phytoplankton are not true plants, but they live like plants.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Planetary means to do with planets. 2) Planetary can mean to do with the whole Earth, affecting the whole world.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on space, planetary orbits, planetary rings and planetary scientists are part of studying the Solar System. In geography and news, «planetary health» or «planetary crisis» means problems that affect the whole Earth. In stories, a planetary system is a star with planets around it. Common phrases: «planetary orbit», «planetary system», «planetary science», «planetary nebula», «on a planetary scale».
examples from the lessons: Saturn's planetary rings are made of ice and rock. | A planetary scientist studies Mars and other planets. | Our Solar System is one planetary system among many. | The planetary orbits are shaped like stretched circles called ellipses. | Climate change is a problem on a planetary scale. | We built a planetary model with balls and wire. | A planetary nebula is the glowing gas left by a dying star.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say PLAN-it-ree or PLAN-it-air-ee. From «planet» + «-ary». Trap: a «planetary nebula» has nothing to do with planets — the name came from how it looked in old telescopes.

part of speech: verb (pluck, plucks, plucked, plucking); noun (pluck — uncountable)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To pluck something is to pull it off or out quickly, such as a flower, a fruit or a hair. 2) To pluck a bird is to pull its feathers off before cooking. 3) To pluck the strings of a guitar or harp is to pull and let go with your fingers to make a note. 4) (noun) Pluck is courage and spirit in a difficult situation. 5) To pluck up courage is to make yourself brave enough to do something.
its sense in the lessons: In music lessons, you pluck the strings of a ukulele, harp or violin (pizzicato). In stories, a brave hero shows pluck, and a shy character «plucks up the courage» to speak. In everyday life, people pluck eyebrows or pluck apples from trees. Common phrases: «pluck up the courage», «pluck a string», «pluck out of the air», «plucked from the sea», «a lot of pluck».
examples from the lessons: She plucked an apple from the tree. | He finally plucked up the courage to ask a question. | Pluck the strings gently on your ukulele. | The lifeboat crew plucked the sailors from the stormy sea. | The farmer plucked the chicken for dinner. | The little girl showed real pluck when she spoke on stage. | He seemed to pluck the number out of thin air. | Mum plucks her eyebrows with tweezers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: plucked. Adjective: «plucky» (brave, especially when small or weak). The noun «pluck» (courage) is a bit old-fashioned and uncountable. Do not confuse «pluck» with «plug».

part of speech: verb (plunge, plunges, plunged, plunging); noun (a plunge, plunges)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To plunge is to jump or fall suddenly and steeply, especially into water. 2) To plunge something into something is to push it in quickly and hard. 3) To plunge (of prices, temperatures or numbers) is to fall suddenly by a lot. 4) To plunge into an activity is to start it eagerly and with energy. 5) (noun) A plunge is a sudden jump or fall, or a quick swim. 6) To be plunged into darkness is to lose all light suddenly.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, plunge makes action dramatic: «the car plunged off the cliff», «the room was plunged into darkness». In maths, science and news, temperatures or prices «plunge» means they drop fast, often shown on a graph. In everyday life, «take the plunge» means finally do something brave or new. Common phrases: «take the plunge», «plunge into», «plunged into darkness», «temperatures plunged», «plunge pool».
examples from the lessons: The diver plunged into the deep pool. | The lights went out and we were plunged into darkness. | Temperatures plunged to minus ten overnight. | She plunged her hands into the warm soapy water. | After weeks of thinking, Dad took the plunge and bought a dog. | The class plunged into the art project. | The price of the toy plunged after Christmas. | The graph shows a sharp plunge in sales in March.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: plunged, plunging. A «plunger» is a tool for unblocking sinks and toilets. «Plunging» can describe a steep drop (a plunging cliff). In maths, a «plunge» means a sharp decrease, much bigger than a small dip.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Polonium is a rare, extremely radioactive and poisonous chemical element, number 84, symbol Po, discovered by Marie and Pierre Curie.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on the periodic table and radioactivity, polonium is famous because Marie Curie discovered it and named it after her home country, Poland. In the news, it has been used in at least one notorious poisoning case. Safety: radioactive elements are handled only by experts with special equipment. Common phrases: «polonium-210», «radioactive polonium», «discovered polonium».
examples from the lessons: Marie Curie discovered polonium more than a hundred years ago. | Polonium was named after Poland. | Polonium is highly radioactive. | The symbol for polonium is Po. | Polonium is very rare in nature. | Scientists handle polonium with great care.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Say po-LOW-nee-um. Symbol Po (capital P, small o). Do not confuse with plutonium (Pu), another radioactive element.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A populous place has a lot of people living in it.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons, China and India are the most populous countries, and Lagos and Tokyo are among the most populous cities; maps of population density show populous areas darker. In maths, «the most populous» means the one with the biggest number of people. Common phrases: «the most populous country», «a populous city», «densely populous» (rare; «densely populated» is common).
examples from the lessons: India is now the most populous country in the world. | California is the most populous state in the USA. | New South Wales is Australia's most populous state. | London is a populous city. | The north of the island is less populous than the south. | Which is the most populous continent? Asia.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Homophone trap: «populous» (adjective: having many people) sounds exactly like «populace» (noun: the ordinary people of a country). Also common: «densely populated». In maths, «more populous» means a larger population number, not a larger area.

part of speech: adjective (possessive, more possessive, most possessive); noun (the possessive — grammar)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Possessive means wanting to keep something or someone all to yourself and not wanting to share. 2) (grammar) Possessive words show that something belongs to someone, such as «my», «your», «his», «hers», «its», «our», «their», or a noun with an apostrophe and s, like «Sam's». 3) (noun, grammar) The possessive is the form of a word that shows owning.
its sense in the lessons: In grammar lessons, pupils learn the possessive apostrophe: the dog's bone (one dog), the dogs' bones (many dogs), and possessive pronouns and determiners. In everyday life and stories, a possessive friend gets jealous if you play with others, and a possessive dog guards its toy. Common phrases: «possessive apostrophe», «possessive pronoun», «possessive determiner», «possessive of», «get possessive».
examples from the lessons: The possessive apostrophe in «Mia's coat» shows the coat belongs to Mia. | «Mine», «yours» and «theirs» are possessive pronouns. | My dog gets very possessive about his ball. | She was possessive of her new felt-tip pens. | Add an apostrophe to make the possessive: the children's toys. | A possessive friend may not like you having other friends. | «Its» is possessive, but «it's» means «it is».
note for the reader of a maths problem: Grammar trap: «its» (possessive, no apostrophe) vs «it's» (it is). Possessive pronouns like «hers», «ours», «yours» never take an apostrophe. Plural nouns ending in s take the apostrophe after the s: the girls' changing room.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A potlatch is a big traditional ceremony and feast of First Nations and Native American peoples of the Pacific Northwest coast of North America, such as the Kwakwaka'wakw and the Haida, where the host gives gifts to guests to mark important events like births, marriages, names and deaths.
its sense in the lessons: In history and social studies lessons in Canada and the USA, the potlatch shows how status and respect came from giving away wealth, not keeping it. The Canadian government banned potlatches for more than sixty years, which harmed these cultures; today potlatches are held again with pride. Common phrases: «hold a potlatch», «potlatch ceremony», «potlatch ban».
examples from the lessons: The family held a potlatch to celebrate a new chief. | At a potlatch, the host gives gifts to the guests. | Dancers wore carved masks at the potlatch. | The potlatch was banned in Canada for many years. | Today, potlatches are an important part of Northwest Coast culture again. | We learned about the potlatch in our First Nations unit.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: potlatches. Say POT-latch. The word comes from Chinook Jargon, a trade language of the region, meaning «to give». Speak about it respectfully as a living tradition.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Preferable means better or more suitable, so you would rather have or choose it.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and formal talk, «X is preferable to Y» means X is the better choice. In school, «it is preferable to show your working» means you should do it. In safety, «walking is preferable to running near the pool». Common phrases: «preferable to», «far preferable», «it is preferable to», «infinitely preferable».
examples from the lessons: A small, friendly school is preferable to a big one for my little brother. | Sleeping in a tent is preferable to sleeping outside in the rain. | It is preferable to use a pencil for maths. | Water is preferable to fizzy drinks when you're thirsty. | Short sentences are often preferable in instructions. | Any answer is preferable to a blank space in a test.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Use «preferable to», not «preferable than». Do not say «more preferable», because «preferable» already means «better». Adverb: «preferably». Say PREF-er-uh-bul (stress on the first syllable).

meaning for a pupil: 1) In maths, two amounts are proportional if they grow or shrink together at the same rate, so that one is always the same number times the other. 2) Proportional means having the right size or amount compared with something else, fair in size.
its sense in the lessons: In maths lessons, if 1 pencil costs 20p then 5 pencils cost 100p — cost is directly proportional to the number of pencils; the graph is a straight line through zero. Recipes and maps use proportion too. In ethics and law, a punishment should be proportional to the wrong done. In politics, «proportional representation» gives parties seats in proportion to their votes. Common phrases: «directly proportional», «inversely proportional», «proportional to», «proportional representation».
examples from the lessons: The cost is proportional to the number of tickets you buy. | If you double the recipe, keep the ingredients proportional. | The time taken is inversely proportional to the speed. | Her drawing of the face was nicely proportional. | The punishment should be proportional to what he did wrong. | On a graph, proportional amounts make a straight line through zero. | New Zealand uses a kind of proportional representation in elections.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Use «proportional to». In maths: «directly proportional» — when one doubles, the other doubles; «inversely proportional» — when one doubles, the other halves (more workers, fewer days). Trap: amounts that both increase are not always proportional — the ratio must stay the same (for example, a taxi with a starting fee is not proportional).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Prosperity is being successful and having plenty of money and good things, especially for a person, a town or a country.
its sense in the lessons: In history and geography lessons, prosperity grows with trade, jobs and good harvests, and falls in wars and recessions. In everyday life and festivals, people wish each other prosperity, for example at Chinese New Year and Diwali. In church life, Christians may pray for peace and prosperity. Common phrases: «peace and prosperity», «a time of prosperity», «economic prosperity», «wish you prosperity».
examples from the lessons: The town grew in prosperity after the railway came. | At Chinese New Year, people wish each other health and prosperity. | The country enjoyed years of peace and prosperity. | Trade brought prosperity to the port. | The war ended the town's prosperity. | Good harvests meant prosperity for the farmers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Verb: «prosper»; adjective: «prosperous». Say pros-PER-it-ee.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Psoriasis is a long-lasting skin condition that causes red, itchy, scaly patches, often on the elbows, knees and scalp.
its sense in the lessons: In health lessons, psoriasis happens when the body makes new skin cells too fast; it is not catching, so you cannot get it by touching someone. Doctors give creams and other treatments that help, but it can come and go. Being kind matters, because people with skin conditions may feel self-conscious. Common phrases: «have psoriasis», «psoriasis patches», «scalp psoriasis».
examples from the lessons: My uncle has psoriasis on his elbows. | Psoriasis is not contagious. | The cream helped calm her psoriasis. | Stress can make psoriasis flare up. | Psoriasis patches can be itchy and dry. | The doctor explained that psoriasis makes skin cells grow too fast.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Spelling and sound trap: the p is silent — say suh-RYE-uh-sis. Myth: you cannot catch psoriasis, and it is not caused by being dirty. It is different from eczema, though both make skin itchy.

part of speech: noun (pumice — uncountable; a pumice stone, pumice stones)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Pumice is a very light, rough grey rock full of tiny holes, made when frothy lava from a volcano cools quickly; it can float on water. 2) A pumice stone is a piece of this rock used to rub away hard skin, for example on your feet.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on rocks, pumice is an igneous rock formed from volcanic lava; because it is full of gas bubbles, it floats — a surprising fact for a rock. After some eruptions, rafts of floating pumice drift on the sea. In everyday life, pumice stones are in bathrooms. Common phrases: «pumice stone», «a raft of pumice», «floating pumice».
examples from the lessons: Pumice is the only rock that floats on water. | Pumice forms when bubbly lava cools very quickly. | Nan uses a pumice stone on her heels. | After the eruption, a raft of pumice floated across the Pacific. | We tested rocks in water, and the pumice floated. | Pumice is rough, light and full of holes. | Some toothpastes and cleaners contain powdered pumice.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable as a material; «a pumice stone» for one piece. Say PUM-iss. Strictly, not every pumice floats for ever — it sinks when its holes fill with water.

part of speech: noun (Mandarin, pinyin: qi; also spelled ch'i or chi)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (Mandarin, pinyin) In Chinese thought and traditional medicine, qi is the life energy that is believed to flow through the body and all living things; it is said like «chee» to an English ear. 2) (Mandarin, pinyin) As an ordinary Mandarin word, qì also means air, gas, breath or spirit, and other syllables spelled «qi» mean seven (qī), to ride (qí) and to rise (qǐ). 3) (games) «Qi» is a famous allowed word in Scrabble.
its sense in the lessons: In lessons about China and Mandarin heard on the street, qi appears in words like «tiānqì» (weather) and «qìgōng» and in tai chi, where people practise breathing and slow movements to balance their qi. Scientists have not found qi as a measurable energy; it is part of a tradition and belief. Common phrases: «tai chi», «qigong», «qi energy», «balance your qi».
examples from the lessons: In Chinese tradition, qi is the energy of life. | Tai chi exercises are said to help qi flow through the body. | «Qi» sounds like «chee» in English. | In Mandarin, «qī» means seven. | Grandpa scored lots of points playing «qi» in Scrabble. | «Tiānqì» means weather in Mandarin.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Not an English word, but borrowed into English for the life-energy idea. In pinyin, «q» is said like English «ch». Different tones change the meaning (qī seven, qí ride, qǐ rise, qì air). Say beliefs fairly: «In Chinese medicine, people believe qi…».

part of speech: noun (quarantine — uncountable; a quarantine, quarantines); verb (quarantine, quarantines, quarantined, quarantining)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Quarantine is a time when a person or animal who may have a catching disease is kept away from others so the disease does not spread. 2) (verb) To quarantine someone or something is to keep them apart for this reason. 3) In computing, to quarantine a file is to lock away a file that may have a virus.
its sense in the lessons: In science and health lessons, quarantine stops infections spreading, for example during the COVID-19 pandemic, when many people stayed home. In everyday life in Australia and New Zealand, strict quarantine (biosecurity) at airports stops pests and diseases arriving on food, plants and animals; pets coming from abroad may need quarantine. In history, ships with sick sailors were kept in quarantine. Common phrases: «in quarantine», «go into quarantine», «quarantine period», «under quarantine».
examples from the lessons: The new puppy had to stay in quarantine for ten days. | During the pandemic, our family went into quarantine. | Australian airports have strict quarantine rules for fruit and plants. | The ship was kept in quarantine until no one was sick. | The antivirus program quarantined the dangerous file. | Sick chickens were quarantined away from the flock. | The quarantine lasted two weeks.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say KWOR-an-teen. It comes from Italian «quaranta giorni», «forty days», the time ships waited long ago. Not the same as «isolation»: isolation is for people who are definitely sick; quarantine is for people who might be.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Racism is treating people unfairly, or thinking they are worse, because of their race, skin colour, nationality or ethnic group. 2) Racism is also unfair rules or systems in a society that disadvantage some groups because of race.
its sense in the lessons: In ethics and citizenship lessons, racism is wrong and hurtful, and in many countries racist acts are against the law; pupils learn to report it and stand up for others. In history lessons: slavery, segregation in the USA, apartheid in South Africa, and the work of people like Martin Luther King Jr and Nelson Mandela against racism. In sport, campaigns such as «Kick It Out» fight racism. Common phrases: «stand up to racism», «fight racism», «tackle racism», «racism in sport», «institutional racism».
examples from the lessons: Racism is never acceptable at our school. | Martin Luther King Jr spoke out against racism. | If you see racism, tell a trusted adult. | The footballers knelt to show they stand against racism. | Apartheid in South Africa was a system of racism. | Calling someone names because of their skin colour is racism. | The book helped us understand how racism hurts people.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Adjective and noun: «racist» (a racist joke; a person who is racist). Related: «prejudice» (judging before knowing), «discrimination» (unfair treatment). Myth: racism is not only open name-calling; it can be quiet or built into rules.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Randomness is the quality of happening by chance, with no pattern, plan or way to predict exactly what will happen. 2) (informal) Randomness is being strange, odd or unexpected, as in «the randomness of his jokes».
its sense in the lessons: In maths lessons on probability, a fair dice or coin shows randomness: each result is equally likely, but you cannot say which comes next. In science, random samples make fair tests. In computing, randomness is used in games so they do not repeat. In everyday slang, «random» means odd or unexpected: «that was so random!». Common phrases: «pure randomness», «element of randomness», «true randomness», «the randomness of».
examples from the lessons: Rolling a dice shows randomness — you can't predict the next number. | There is an element of randomness in which cards you get. | Computers find true randomness surprisingly hard. | The randomness of the weather makes holidays tricky to plan. | The randomness of my little brother's questions makes me laugh. | Scientists add randomness when choosing a sample to keep it fair. | The game uses randomness so every level is different.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Built from «random» + «-ness». Trap in maths: randomness does not mean results «even out» quickly — after five heads, the next coin toss is still 50/50 (the gambler's fallacy). Random does not mean equally likely in every case either.

part of speech: adjective (righteous, more righteous, most righteous); noun (the righteous — people who are good, formal or Bible)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Righteous means morally right and good, doing what is fair and honest. 2) (Bible, church) A righteous person is one who lives the way God wants; Christians and Jews believe God loves the righteous. 3) Righteous anger is anger you feel because something is truly unfair. 4) (slang, US, a bit old-fashioned) Righteous can mean really great or excellent.
its sense in the lessons: In stories it tells the reader a character is good and fair, or sometimes that a character only thinks they are good (self-righteous). In church and Bible lessons it describes people who obey God (the righteous, the path of the righteous). Phrases: righteous anger, righteous cause, self-righteous (thinking you are better than others).
examples from the lessons: The judge was a righteous man who treated everyone fairly. | Noah was called a righteous man in the Bible story. | She felt a righteous anger when the bully took the little boy's lunch. | The psalm says the righteous will flourish like a palm tree. | Fighting for clean water for the village is a righteous cause. | Don't be so self-righteous; you forget your homework too! | (slang, US) That skateboard jump was totally righteous, dude.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Sounds like RY-chus. Not used for maths. Self-righteous is not a compliment: it means smug about being good. The opposite is unrighteous or wicked. Say «a righteous person», not «a righteous».

part of speech: noun (French: le roi, les rois); (abbreviation in English) ROI
meaning for a pupil: 1) (French) Roi is the French word for king, as in «le roi» (the king); it is not an English word. To an English ear it sounds like «rwah». 2) (business, abbreviation) In English, ROI (written in capitals) stands for «return on investment»: how much money you get back compared with what you spent.
its sense in the lessons: In French lessons it comes in «le roi et la reine» (the king and the queen) and in the Epiphany cake «la galette des rois» (the kings' cake). In English it only appears as the business abbreviation ROI. The French word also hides inside English «Detroit» and «Leroy» (le roi).
examples from the lessons: (French) Le roi habite dans un grand château. — The king lives in a big castle. | (French) Vive le roi! means «Long live the king!» | In January French families share a galette des rois, and whoever finds the little toy becomes king for the day. | The name Leroy comes from French «le roi», the king. | Louis XIV of France was called le Roi Soleil, the Sun King. | (business) The shop worked out the ROI on its new sign. | (business) A good ROI means you earn back more than you spent.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Roi is French and masculine (le roi); the queen is la reine. The s in «rois» is silent. Do not confuse with «roy», an English name. In maths about money, ROI = (money gained − money spent) ÷ money spent, often given as a percentage.

part of speech: noun (a rook, rooks); verb (rook, rooks, rooked, rooking — informal, old-fashioned)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A rook is a large black bird of the crow family with a grey, bare patch of skin at the base of its beak; rooks live together in noisy groups. 2) A rook is a chess piece shaped like a castle tower that moves straight along rows and columns; it is also called a castle. 3) (informal, old-fashioned) To rook someone is to cheat them out of money.
its sense in the lessons: In nature lessons rooks are clever birds that nest in big groups called rookeries at the tops of trees, mostly in the UK and Europe. In chess lessons the rook is worth about five pawns and takes part in castling. Phrases: rook's nest, rookery, castling with the rook.
examples from the lessons: A rook landed on the field and pecked for worms. | Rooks build their nests together high in the elm trees. | The rookery was so noisy in spring that we heard it from the school. | My rook moved all the way across the board and captured her queen. | In chess each player starts with two rooks in the corners. | You can castle by moving your king two squares and jumping the rook over it. | (informal) The man at the fair rooked us out of five pounds.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural rooks. A rook is different from a crow: rooks have a pale face and live in groups; crows are usually alone or in pairs. In chess problems, a rook usually counts as 5 points, a pawn as 1. A rookie (a beginner) is a different word.

part of speech: noun (rosin, uncountable); verb (rosin, rosins, rosined, rosining)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Rosin is a hard, sticky, amber-coloured substance made from pine tree sap. 2) Violin, viola, cello and double bass players rub rosin on the bow so the hairs grip the strings and make a sound. 3) Athletes such as gymnasts, dancers, baseball pitchers and climbers use powdered rosin to stop their hands or shoes slipping. 4) To rosin something is to rub rosin on it.
its sense in the lessons: In music lessons rosin is the little block in the violin case; without it the bow makes almost no sound. In science it is an example of a natural resin from trees. In sport and safety it helps with grip. Phrases: rosin the bow, a block of rosin, rosin bag.
examples from the lessons: Before the concert, Mia rubbed rosin on her violin bow. | Without rosin, the bow just slides and the cello stays quiet. | Rosin is made from the sap of pine trees. | The ballet dancers dipped their shoes in rosin so they would not slip. | The baseball pitcher squeezed the rosin bag before throwing. | Rosin dust collected on the strings, so he wiped them with a cloth. | Remember to rosin your bow, but not too much!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «some rosin», «a block of rosin». Do not confuse with «resin» (the general word for sticky tree sap or plastic) or with «raisin» (a dried grape). Rosin is a kind of resin.

part of speech: noun (rye, uncountable; rye bread, rye whiskey)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Rye is a kind of cereal grass grown on farms; its grain is used for flour, bread and animal food. 2) Rye bread is a dark, heavy bread made with rye flour. 3) (US, Canada) Rye can mean rye whiskey, a strong alcoholic drink. 4) Rye is also the name of an old town in East Sussex, England.
its sense in the lessons: In science and farming lessons rye is a grain like wheat, oats and barley, which grows well in cold places with poor soil. In food lessons it is the grain in dark breads such as pumpernickel. Phrases: rye bread, rye flour, ryegrass, a field of rye.
examples from the lessons: Rye grows tall and golden in the summer fields. | Grandad likes a ham sandwich on rye bread. | Rye flour makes bread darker and heavier than wheat flour. | Farmers in cold northern countries often grow rye. | Wheat, barley, oats and rye are all cereal grains. | Ryegrass is used on football pitches. | We visited the old cobbled streets of Rye on our trip.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «some rye», not «a rye» (except «a rye» meaning a glass of whiskey in North America). Sounds exactly like «wry» (twisted, dryly funny) — a homophone. People with coeliac disease cannot eat rye because it contains gluten.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A saguaro is a giant cactus that grows in the Sonoran Desert of Arizona, USA, and Mexico; it can grow taller than a house and has arms that point upwards. 2) It is the cactus children often draw for a cowboy desert scene.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons the saguaro shows how desert plants survive: its pleated stem swells to store water after rain, its spines protect it, and birds such as woodpeckers and elf owls nest in holes in it. It grows very slowly and can live 150 to 200 years. Phrases: saguaro cactus, Saguaro National Park.
examples from the lessons: The saguaro stood tall against the orange desert sunset. | A saguaro may not grow its first arm until it is about 75 years old. | After a storm, the saguaro's stem swells as it stores water. | A little elf owl peeped out of a hole in the saguaro. | Saguaro flowers are white and bloom at night. | It is against the law to damage a saguaro in Arizona. | We saw hundreds of saguaros in Saguaro National Park.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced suh-WAH-roh (the g is silent). Plural saguaros. Its blossom is the state flower of Arizona. A saguaro can reach about 12 metres (40 feet) tall.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Salinity is how salty water or soil is: how much salt is dissolved in it. 2) (science) It is measured as the amount of salt in a certain amount of water, for example grams per litre or parts per thousand.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography lessons salinity explains why seawater is salty and rivers are fresh, why the Dead Sea lets you float, and why some fish live only in fresh water or only in the sea. In farming, high salinity in soil can stop crops growing. Phrases: high salinity, low salinity, ocean salinity, measure the salinity.
examples from the lessons: The salinity of the ocean is about 35 grams of salt in every litre. | The Dead Sea has such high salinity that people float easily. | Rivers have very low salinity, so their water is called fresh water. | We tested the salinity of three water samples in class. | Where rivers meet the sea, the salinity is in between. | High salinity in the soil made the wheat grow badly. | Some fish, like salmon, can cope with changes in salinity.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable in everyday use. Related words: saline (salty), salt. In maths problems salinity is a rate: if 1 litre holds 35 g of salt, 2 litres of the same water hold 70 g. Adding fresh water lowers the salinity; evaporating water raises it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A salon is a shop where people go to have their hair cut or styled, their nails done or their skin treated. 2) (old-fashioned, formal) A salon is an elegant sitting room in a big house where guests are received. 3) (history) A salon was a meeting of writers, artists and thinkers at a rich person's home, especially in France. 4) A salon can be an art exhibition, as in the famous Paris Salon.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life it is mostly a hair salon, beauty salon or nail salon. In history lessons it is the place where people talked about books and ideas in the 1700s and 1800s. Phrases: hair salon, beauty salon, nail salon, tanning salon.
examples from the lessons: Mum has an appointment at the hair salon on Saturday. | The salon smelled of shampoo and hair spray. | My big sister works in a nail salon. | The guests waited in the grand salon of the palace. | In old Paris, rich women held salons where writers shared ideas. | The painting was shown at the Paris Salon. | The salon was busy before the school dance.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural salons. Stress on the first syllable in UK English (SAL-on), often the second in US English (sa-LON). Do not confuse with «saloon» (an old-style bar in a Western, or a UK word for a car with a separate boot).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Sauerkraut is finely shredded cabbage that has been salted and left to ferment so that it turns sour. 2) It is a traditional food in Germany and central and eastern Europe, often eaten with sausages.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons sauerkraut is an example of fermentation: tiny bacteria turn the sugar in cabbage into acid, which preserves it. In history, sailors such as Captain Cook's crew ate it to help stop scurvy. In food lessons it is a German word for «sour cabbage». Phrases: hot dog with sauerkraut, a jar of sauerkraut.
examples from the lessons: Grandpa piled sauerkraut on his hot dog. | Sauerkraut tastes sour and a bit salty. | We made sauerkraut in class by packing cabbage and salt into a jar. | Bacteria help turn cabbage into sauerkraut. | Captain Cook took barrels of sauerkraut on his long voyages. | In Germany, sausages are often served with sauerkraut and mustard. | Ukrainian kitchens have kvashena kapusta, which is very like sauerkraut.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «some sauerkraut». It comes from German «sauer» (sour) and «Kraut» (cabbage). Pronounced SOW-er-krowt. Calling a German person «Kraut» is a rude old insult — do not use it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A sawfish is a large ray, a kind of flat fish related to sharks, with a long flat snout edged with sharp teeth like a saw. 2) It uses its saw to find, stun and slash small fish and to dig for food in mud.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons the sawfish is an example of an animal adapted to its habitat: its saw can sense the tiny electric signals of prey. It lives in warm coastal waters and rivers, for example in northern Australia. It is critically endangered, often caught by accident in fishing nets. Phrases: smalltooth sawfish, largetooth sawfish.
examples from the lessons: The sawfish swung its long saw through a shoal of little fish. | A sawfish can grow longer than a car. | The sawfish is a kind of ray, not a shark. | Sawfish live in warm seas and some even swim up rivers. | Sawfish are endangered because their saws get tangled in nets. | At the aquarium we watched a sawfish glide along the bottom. | The teeth on a sawfish's snout are really special scales.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural usually sawfish (like «fish»). Sawfish (a ray, gills underneath, saw with no whiskers) are different from sawsharks (smaller sharks with gills on the sides and whiskers on the saw).

part of speech: noun (a seam, seams); verb (seam, seams, seamed, seaming)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A seam is the line where two pieces of cloth, leather or other material are sewn or joined together. 2) A seam is a thin layer of coal, gold or another mineral in rock underground. 3) In cricket, the seam is the raised stitching round the ball. 4) To seam something is to join it with a seam.
its sense in the lessons: In sewing and design lessons seams hold clothes together. In geography and history a coal seam is what miners dug out. Phrases: come apart at the seams (break or fall apart, also about plans or people), bursting at the seams (very full), seamless (smooth, with no joins), seam bowler (cricket).
examples from the lessons: The seam on my jeans split when I bent down. | Grandma sewed a neat seam along the edge of the curtain. | The miners followed a thick seam of coal deep underground. | The football has stitched seams between its panels. | The cricket ball swung because the bowler held the seam upright. | The classroom was bursting at the seams with forty children. | Our plan for the party began to come apart at the seams.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural seams. Seam sounds exactly like «seem» (to appear) — a homophone: «It seems my seam is torn.» Seamless means smooth, with no breaks.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Secondly means «in the second place» and is used to give the second point in a list of reasons or steps, after «firstly» or «first». 2) It helps a reader or listener follow an argument step by step.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons it is a linking word (a connective) for writing explanations, arguments and instructions: firstly, secondly, thirdly, finally. In maths it helps explain methods: «Firstly, add the tens; secondly, add the ones.» Phrases: firstly … secondly … finally; and secondly.
examples from the lessons: Firstly, wash your hands; secondly, put on your apron. | I can't come, firstly because I'm ill and secondly because it's raining. | Secondly, multiply the answer by three. | Schools should have longer breaks: firstly, we need exercise; secondly, we learn better after playing. | Secondly, the knight rescued the dragon instead of fighting it. | In my persuasive letter, I wrote my second reason after «secondly». | Secondly, check your answer by doing the opposite operation.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Use «secondly» or «second» to start the second point; both are correct. Put a comma after it at the start of a sentence. It does not mean «in a second» (quickly). Do not mix «first» with «secondly» in careful writing; use «firstly … secondly» or «first … second».

part of speech: proper noun (Shetland, the Shetland Islands); adjective (Shetland pony, Shetland wool); noun (a Shetland — a Shetland pony)
