meaning for a pupil: 1) Shetland is a group of islands in the far north of Scotland, between mainland Scotland and Norway. 2) A Shetland pony (a Shetland) is a very small, strong, hairy pony first bred there. 3) Shetland wool is fine, soft wool from Shetland sheep, used to knit jumpers and shawls.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons Shetland is the most northern part of the UK, with Viking history, the Up Helly Aa fire festival and many seabirds such as puffins. In animal lessons the Shetland pony is a favourite small pony for children. It is a place name, so it has a capital letter. Phrases: the Shetland Islands, Shetland pony, Shetland jumper.
examples from the lessons: Shetland is so far north that summer nights hardly get dark. | My little cousin rode a Shetland pony at the farm. | Shetland ponies are small but very strong. | Grandma knitted me a Shetland wool jumper. | Puffins nest on the cliffs of Shetland. | Every winter Shetland holds a fire festival called Up Helly Aa. | The ferry from Aberdeen to Shetland takes all night.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always write Shetland with a capital S. Many local people say «in Shetland», not «on the Shetlands». Shetland is different from the Orkney Islands, which are nearer to mainland Scotland.

part of speech: proper noun (Shiva, Hindu god); noun (shiva, in «sit shiva» — Jewish mourning, also spelt shivah)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (religion) Shiva is one of the most important gods in Hinduism; Hindus believe he is both a destroyer and a renewer, and he is often shown dancing or meditating with a snake round his neck. 2) (Jewish life) Shiva is the seven days of mourning after a close relative dies, when the family stays at home and friends visit; people say they «sit shiva». 3) Shiva is also a name for people.
its sense in the lessons: In religious education lessons Shiva is one of the three main gods (with Brahma and Vishnu) and is worshipped at the festival of Maha Shivaratri. In lessons on Jewish life, sitting shiva shows how a community comforts a family after a death. It is not an English word in origin: the god comes from Sanskrit, the mourning word from Hebrew «seven».
examples from the lessons: Hindus believe Shiva destroys the old so that new things can be created. | The statue showed Shiva dancing inside a ring of fire. | Many Hindus visit Shiva's temples at Maha Shivaratri. | When Rachel's grandad died, her family sat shiva for seven days. | Neighbours brought food to the house during shiva. | People cover mirrors in the house while they sit shiva. | Shiva is a popular name in India.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The Hindu god is written with a capital S (Shiva). The Jewish mourning word is small (shiva or shivah). Speak about both respectfully: «Hindus believe…», «Jewish families…». Not used in maths.

part of speech: verb (signify, signifies, signified, signifying — past form); noun (the signified — in the study of language and signs)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Signified is the past form of signify: it means showed, meant or stood for. 2) It can mean made known by a sign or action: «She signified that she agreed by nodding.» 3) (formal, language study) The signified is the idea or meaning that a word or sign points to, as opposed to the sound or letters (the signifier).
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons it helps say what a symbol, colour or gesture means in a story: «The dark clouds signified danger.» In history it is used for events: «The fall of the wall signified the end of an era.» In language study the word and its idea are called the signifier and the signified. Phrases: signified that, signified the end of, signified agreement.
examples from the lessons: The red flag signified that swimming was not safe. | The bell signified the end of break. | She signified her agreement with a quick nod. | In the story, the white dove signified peace. | The teacher's raised hand signified that we should be quiet. | The ancient carving signified the sun god. | (formal) The word «dog» is the signifier; the idea of a dog is the signified.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Signify changes y to i: signify, signifies, signified, but signifying. It is a more formal word for «meant» or «showed». In maths, a symbol «signifies» something: the + sign signifies adding.

part of speech: noun (a sika, sika or sikas; sika deer)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A sika is a kind of deer that came from East Asia (Japan, China, Taiwan); it is small to medium-sized with a reddish-brown coat with white spots in summer. 2) Sika deer were brought to the UK, Ireland, New Zealand and the USA, where they now live in the wild.
its sense in the lessons: In nature lessons sika deer are an example of an animal brought from one country to another; in some places they harm young trees or mix with native red deer. In Nara, Japan, tame sika deer bow to visitors for biscuits. Phrases: sika deer, sika stag.
examples from the lessons: A sika deer stepped out of the forest and froze. | Sika deer have white spots on their coats in summer. | In Nara, sika deer wander through the park and bow for snacks. | Sika were brought to Ireland and Britain over a hundred years ago. | In New Zealand, hunters track sika in the hills. | The sika stag made a high whistling call. | Sika and red deer can have babies together, which worries scientists.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural sika or sikas. The name comes from Japanese «shika», meaning deer. Pronounced SEE-kuh.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To simplify something is to make it simpler or easier to understand or do. 2) (maths) To simplify a fraction is to write it with smaller numbers that mean the same amount, by dividing the top and bottom by the same number. 3) (maths) To simplify an expression is to write it in a shorter way, for example by collecting like terms.
its sense in the lessons: In maths lessons it is a common instruction: «Simplify 6/8» means write it as 3/4. In algebra «simplify 2a + 3a» means 5a. In everyday life and writing it means removing extra details so something is clearer. Phrases: simplify a fraction, simplify fully, simplify the rules, in its simplest form.
examples from the lessons: Can you simplify the instructions for the little ones? | Simplify 10/15 by dividing both numbers by 5 to get 2/3. | Simplify 3x + 4x to get 7x. | The new app simplifies homework by putting it all in one place. | We simplified the game so everyone could play. | Always simplify your answer fully. | The teacher simplified the story for the younger class.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: simplify, simplifies, simplified, simplifying (keep y before -ing). The noun is simplification. In maths, simplifying never changes the value: 4/8 and 1/2 are equal. «Simplify fully» means you cannot divide top and bottom by anything else (except 1).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A sitar is a musical instrument from India with a long wooden neck, a round body made from a gourd, and many strings, played by plucking. 2) It makes a bright, buzzing, ringing sound and is used in Indian classical music.
its sense in the lessons: In music lessons the sitar is a string instrument from India; besides the strings you play, it has extra strings underneath that ring along (sympathetic strings). Ravi Shankar was a famous sitar player, and the Beatles used a sitar in some songs. Phrases: play the sitar, sitar music.
examples from the lessons: The sitar has a long neck and curved metal frets. | Ravi Shankar played the sitar all over the world. | The sitar's strings buzzed and shimmered. | We listened to sitar music during our lesson on India. | You pluck a sitar with a wire pick worn on the finger. | George Harrison of the Beatles learned to play the sitar. | The sitar player sat on the floor with the instrument resting on his foot.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural sitars. Stress on the second syllable: si-TAR. Do not confuse with guitar, although both are plucked string instruments. A sitar often has about 18 to 21 strings.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A sixpence was a small British coin worth six old pennies, used until Britain changed to decimal money and kept for a while after. 2) (old-fashioned) Sixpence is the amount of six old pennies.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons it is part of old British money: 12 pennies made a shilling and 20 shillings a pound, so sixpence was half a shilling. In nursery rhymes and stories: «Sing a song of sixpence». At Christmas some families still hide a silver sixpence in the pudding for luck, and brides put one in a shoe. Phrases: a silver sixpence, turn on a sixpence (turn very quickly in a small space).
examples from the lessons: «Sing a song of sixpence, a pocket full of rye.» | Grandma found a sixpence in her Christmas pudding. | When Grandad was a boy, a comic cost sixpence. | Sixpence was worth half a shilling. | The bride had a sixpence in her shoe for good luck. | That little car can turn on a sixpence. | The old sixpence was also called a «tanner».
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural sixpences. Old money was written 6d (d for pennies). In maths: 2 sixpences = 1 shilling; 40 sixpences = 1 pound. Do not mix with modern pence: 1 old sixpence is not 6p today (it became 2½ new pence).

part of speech: verb (skid, skids, skidded, skidding); noun (a skid, skids)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To skid is to slide sideways or forwards out of control, especially on ice, water or a smooth surface. 2) A skid is a sliding movement like that. 3) (often skids) Skids are strips of wood or metal under a heavy load or helicopter, used to slide or rest it on. 4) (informal) On the skids means going badly, heading for failure.
its sense in the lessons: In science and safety lessons skidding happens when there is too little friction, so cars, bikes and people slide on ice or wet roads. That is why drivers slow down and why there are anti-skid road surfaces. Phrases: skid mark, skid to a halt, go into a skid, skid row (US, a poor rundown area).
examples from the lessons: The car skidded on the icy road. | I skidded on the wet floor and nearly fell. | The bike went into a skid on the gravel. | The cyclist skidded to a halt at the red light. | Tyres with deep treads help stop skids. | The helicopter landed on its metal skids. | (informal) His football team has been on the skids all season.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double the d: skidded, skidding. In science, a skid shows low friction: ice and water reduce friction; sand and grit increase it. «Skid marks» are the black lines tyres leave on a road.

part of speech: verb (slosh, sloshes, sloshed, sloshing); noun (a slosh, sloshes)
meaning for a pupil: 1) When liquid sloshes, it moves around noisily and splashes inside a container or over its edge. 2) To slosh liquid is to pour or splash it about carelessly. 3) To slosh through water or mud is to walk through it with splashing steps. 4) (UK informal) Sloshed means drunk.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life it describes water in buckets, baths, wellies and puddles. In science it shows that liquids move and take the shape of their container. In stories it is a sound word that helps the reader hear the scene. Phrases: slosh about, slosh around, slosh through the puddles.
examples from the lessons: The water sloshed in the bucket as I carried it. | We sloshed through the puddles in our wellies. | Don't slosh your juice all over the table! | The milk sloshed over the edge of the bowl. | The sea sloshed against the side of the boat. | Dad sloshed some paint on the old fence. | (UK informal) The man in the play came home sloshed.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb forms add -es: sloshes. «Sloshy» means wet and slushy. Do not confuse with «slush» (half-melted snow). «Sloshed» for drunk is informal; do not use it in school writing.

part of speech: verb (smirk, smirks, smirked, smirking); noun (a smirk, smirks)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To smirk is to smile in a smug, silly or unkind way, often because you think you are cleverer than someone or are pleased about their bad luck. 2) A smirk is a smile like that.
its sense in the lessons: In stories a smirk tells the reader that a character is pleased with themselves, sneaky or mean, not truly friendly. In everyday life adults may say «Wipe that smirk off your face!» when a child is being cheeky. Phrases: a smug smirk, wipe the smirk off someone's face.
examples from the lessons: The bully smirked when I dropped my books. | «I told you so,» she said with a smirk. | Wipe that smirk off your face and say sorry. | The villain smirked as he locked the door. | He tried not to smirk when the teacher got the answer wrong. | There was a little smirk on the cat's face after it stole the fish. | Her smirk showed she knew the secret.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A smirk is not the same as a smile or a grin: it is usually unkind or smug. Past form smirked. Countable noun: a smirk, two smirks.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Smug means too pleased with yourself and your own cleverness, luck or goodness, in a way that annoys other people. 2) (of a look or smile) showing that feeling.
its sense in the lessons: In stories smug describes a character who shows off or looks down on others; the reader usually does not like them. In everyday life children might say «Don't be so smug!» to a winner who boasts. Phrases: a smug smile, smug look, feel smug, smugly.
examples from the lessons: He looked smug after beating everyone at chess. | She gave a smug smile when the teacher praised her. | Don't be smug; next time you might lose. | The cat sat on the warm cushion looking very smug. | I felt a bit smug that I had remembered my umbrella. | The smug rabbit stopped to nap and lost the race to the tortoise. | He smugly told everyone his score.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb smugly, noun smugness. Comparative smugger, smuggest (double g). Smug is different from proud: being proud of good work is fine; being smug means showing off and looking down on others.

part of speech: adjective (sooty, sootier, sootiest); proper noun (Sooty — a famous UK puppet bear)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Sooty means covered with soot, the black powder left by smoke from burning coal, wood or oil. 2) Sooty means black or very dark, like soot. 3) Sooty is the name of a yellow glove-puppet bear with black ears on a long-running British children's TV show.
its sense in the lessons: In history and science lessons sooty chimneys and faces belong to the age of coal, when chimney sweeps (sometimes children) cleaned chimneys. In nature it names animals such as the sooty tern and sooty owl. Phrases: sooty chimney, sooty face, sooty black.
examples from the lessons: The chimney sweep had a sooty face and hands. | The old fireplace was sooty and dusty. | After the bonfire our clothes smelled smoky and looked sooty. | Sooty smoke poured from the factory chimney. | The cat had sooty paws after exploring the coal shed. | A sooty owl lives in the forests of Australia. | Granny remembers watching Sooty on TV.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Soot is uncountable; sooty is its adjective. Comparative sootier, sootiest (y becomes i). Sooty air is bad for lungs: that is why coal fires are now limited in cities.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Stainless means without stains or marks. 2) Stainless steel is a kind of steel mixed with chromium that does not rust or stain easily. 3) (formal, literary) Stainless can mean morally perfect, with no bad deeds.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons stainless steel is an example of an alloy, a mixture of metals, used for cutlery, sinks, pans and hospital tools because it is easy to clean and does not rust. In stories it can describe a person with a spotless, good reputation. Phrases: stainless steel, a stainless record.
examples from the lessons: Our kitchen sink is made of stainless steel. | Stainless steel spoons stay shiny for years. | Doctors use stainless steel tools because they are easy to keep clean. | Stainless steel has chromium in it to stop rust. | The water bottle is stainless steel, so it keeps my drink cold. | The knight had a stainless reputation. | The tablecloth was stainless after Mum washed it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stainless steel can still get fingermarks and can rust a little in salty water; it just resists rust much better. «-less» means «without»: stainless = without stains.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Starchy food contains a lot of starch, a kind of carbohydrate found in potatoes, bread, rice, pasta and corn. 2) Starchy clothes are stiff because they have been treated with starch. 3) (informal) A starchy person is stiff, formal and unfriendly.
its sense in the lessons: In science and health lessons starchy foods give the body energy and are a main food group on the healthy plate (the Eatwell Guide in the UK). In science, iodine turns blue-black when it touches starch, which is a classic experiment. Phrases: starchy foods, starchy vegetables, a starchy collar.
examples from the lessons: Potatoes, rice and pasta are starchy foods. | Starchy foods give us energy for running about. | The iodine turned blue-black, so the bread was starchy. | Sweetcorn is a starchy vegetable. | His shirt collar was so starchy it scratched his neck. | The starchy old butler never smiled. | Try to eat starchy foods with lots of vegetables.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative starchier, starchiest. Starch is a carbohydrate; when we chew it, saliva begins to turn it into sugar. Wholegrain starchy foods have more fibre than white ones.

part of speech: verb (steelman, steelmans, steelmanned, steelmanning); noun (a steelman, steelmen — rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To steelman someone's argument is to describe it in its strongest, fairest form before you answer it, even if you disagree. 2) A steelman is that strongest version of the other side's argument. 3) (rare, old) A steelman can also be a man who works making steel.
its sense in the lessons: In ethics, debate and philosophy lessons steelmanning is a fair way to argue: the opposite of a «straw man», where you twist the other side's view to make it easy to knock down. It shows respect and helps you think clearly. Phrases: steelman the argument, steelman the other side.
examples from the lessons: Before you disagree, try to steelman your friend's idea. | Let's steelman the argument for a longer school day. | She steelmanned the other team's point so well that they thanked her. | A straw man makes the other side look silly; a steelman makes it look its best. | In our debate club we must steelman before we argue back. | Can you steelman why some people want to ban phones in schools? | Steelmanning helps you find the truth instead of just winning.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It is a newer, informal word made as the opposite of «straw man». Spelling: steelmanned, steelmanning (double n is common). Not used in maths.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Stingless means having no sting or no working sting. 2) Stingless bees are small bees found in warm countries such as Australia, Brazil and Mexico that cannot sting; they make a small amount of honey.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons stingless bees show that not all bees sting; they protect their nests by biting or swarming instead. In Australia they are called native bees or sugarbag bees and help pollinate crops like macadamia nuts. Phrases: stingless bee, stingless nettle.
examples from the lessons: Stingless bees buzzed around the flowers in the school garden. | In Australia, stingless bees are called sugarbag bees. | Stingless bees cannot hurt you with a sting, but they might bite a little. | The Maya people kept stingless bees for honey. | Male bees are stingless; only females can sting. | Stingless bee honey is a bit sour and runny. | The teacher showed us a stingless bee hive in a wooden box.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «-less» means «without»: stingless = without a sting. Most stingless bees are tiny, smaller than a honeybee. Male honeybees (drones) also have no sting.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) Stinky means smelling very bad. 2) (informal, children's talk) Stinky can mean nasty or unfair, as in «a stinky trick».
its sense in the lessons: Children use it a lot in everyday talk: stinky socks, stinky cheese, stinky bin. In science lessons smelly things often contain sulphur compounds or are rotting because of bacteria. In stories it gives a funny, rude-but-not-swearing tone. Phrases: stinky feet, stinky socks, stinky cheese.
examples from the lessons: Take off those stinky trainers! | The bin was stinky after a hot weekend. | The stinky cheese made Dad hold his nose. | Skunks spray a stinky liquid when they are scared. | My little brother called me «stinky pants». | That was a stinky trick to play on your friend. | The stinkiest flower in the world smells like rotting meat.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal: in school writing use «smelly» or «foul-smelling». Comparative stinkier, stinkiest. Calling someone «stinky» can hurt their feelings.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) A stratum is one layer of rock or soil lying on top of another. 2) A stratum is a layer of anything, such as the air or the sea. 3) (formal) A stratum is a level or class of people in a society.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and science lessons strata are the layers you see in cliffs and canyons such as the Grand Canyon; lower strata are usually older, so they help scientists date fossils. In social studies it means a group at one level of wealth or power. Phrases: rock strata, social stratum, the upper strata.
examples from the lessons: Each stratum of rock in the cliff was a different colour. | The fossil was found in a stratum of limestone. | The Grand Canyon shows hundreds of strata. | The lowest stratum of rock is usually the oldest. | A thin stratum of ash came from an ancient volcano. | (formal) The book is about people from every stratum of society. | Clouds can form in a stratum of cold air.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural strata (Latin), not «stratums». People often use «strata» as if it were singular; in careful writing say «one stratum, many strata». Related: stratosphere, stratus clouds.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Stumpy means short and thick, like a tree stump. 2) A stumpy tail or leg is short and thick.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and everyday talk it describes animals, plants, people's legs or pencils in a slightly funny, friendly way. Phrases: stumpy tail, stumpy legs, a stumpy pencil.
examples from the lessons: The puppy had stumpy little legs. | Corgis are dogs with stumpy legs and long bodies. | I wrote with a stumpy pencil because I lost my good one. | The lizard has a fat, stumpy tail. | A stumpy candle burned on the table. | The old tree was cut down to a stumpy trunk. | The stumpy-tailed cat ran across the garden.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative stumpier, stumpiest. Calling a person stumpy can be rude. Related: stump (what is left of a tree after it is cut).

part of speech: adjective (submerged); verb (submerge, submerges, submerged, submerging — past form)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Submerged means under water or under the surface of a liquid. 2) Submerged is the past form of submerge: to go under water, or to push something under water. 3) (figurative) Submerged can mean hidden or buried by other things.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons submerged objects show floating and sinking and how water pushes up (upthrust); measuring water rise when an object is submerged gives its volume. Submerged plants live under water in ponds. In stories, floods submerge towns. Phrases: fully submerged, partly submerged, submerged rocks.
examples from the lessons: The rock was submerged at high tide. | We submerged the cube in water to find its volume. | The submarine submerged and disappeared. | Floods submerged the fields and roads. | Pondweed is a submerged plant. | The hippo stayed submerged with only its eyes showing. | Her quiet voice was submerged by the noise of the crowd.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The prefix «sub» means «under». In maths and science: when an object is fully submerged, the water level rises by the object's volume (if the container doesn't overflow). Spelling: submerging drops the e.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A substitution is putting one person or thing in the place of another. 2) (sport) A substitution is when a player is taken off and another player comes on. 3) (maths) Substitution means replacing a letter in an expression or formula with a number, to work out its value. 4) (cooking) A substitution is using a different ingredient instead of the one in the recipe.
its sense in the lessons: In maths lessons substitution is a key algebra skill: «If a = 3, find 2a + 1» — you substitute 3 for a to get 7. In science, a substitution reaction swaps atoms. In sport it is changing players. In codes, a substitution cipher swaps letters for other letters. Phrases: make a substitution, by substitution, substitution cipher.
examples from the lessons: The coach made a substitution at half-time. | By substitution, if x = 4, then 3x = 12. | Use substitution to check your answer to the equation. | We used honey as a substitution for sugar. | In a substitution cipher, A might become D and B might become E. | Two substitutions changed the whole match. | Substitution of the ingredients made the cake taste different.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb substitute: you substitute the new thing FOR the old one (substitute 5 for x). In maths, put brackets when substituting negatives: if a = −2, a² = (−2)² = 4. Countable for single changes (two substitutions).

part of speech: noun (a subtitle, subtitles); verb (subtitle, subtitles, subtitled, subtitling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Subtitles are words shown at the bottom of a film or TV screen to translate what people say or to write it down for people who cannot hear it. 2) A subtitle is a second, smaller title of a book or article that gives more detail. 3) To subtitle a film is to add subtitles to it.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life subtitles help deaf people and people learning languages, and let you watch foreign films. In English lessons a subtitle in a book or non-fiction text adds information under the main heading. Phrases: turn on the subtitles, with subtitles, English subtitles, closed captions (US).
examples from the lessons: We watched a Japanese cartoon with English subtitles. | Turn on the subtitles so Grandad can follow the film. | Reading subtitles helps me learn French. | The book's title is «Space» and its subtitle is «A Journey to the Stars». | The film was subtitled in twelve languages. | The subtitles were too fast for my little sister. | Write a title and a subtitle for your science report.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually plural for films: subtitles. In the US «closed captions» (CC) also show sounds like [door slams]. The prefix «sub» means «under»: subtitles sit under the picture.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) A sulphide is a chemical compound made of sulphur joined with another element, often a metal. 2) Hydrogen sulphide is a gas that smells of rotten eggs.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons sulphides are important ores: iron sulphide (fool's gold, pyrite), lead sulphide (galena) and zinc sulphide; metals are extracted from them. In safety lessons hydrogen sulphide from drains and volcanoes is smelly and poisonous in large amounts. Phrases: iron sulphide, hydrogen sulphide, copper sulphide.
examples from the lessons: Pyrite, or fool's gold, is iron sulphide. | The rotten-egg smell came from hydrogen sulphide. | When we heated iron and sulphur, they made iron sulphide. | Galena is a shiny grey lead sulphide ore. | Volcanoes give off hydrogen sulphide gas. | Silver turns black when it reacts with sulphides in the air. | Miners dug up copper sulphide to get copper.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK spelling sulphide, US and international science spelling sulfide; both are correct. Do not confuse with sulphate (sulphur and oxygen with another element). Names ending in «-ide» usually mean only two elements.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Talc is a very soft, white or grey mineral that feels soapy or greasy. 2) Talc (talcum powder) is a fine powder made from it, used on skin to keep it dry or to stop rubbing.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons talc is the softest mineral, number 1 on the Mohs scale of hardness (diamond is 10); you can scratch it with a fingernail. In everyday life it is in baby powder and used by gymnasts and climbers for grip. Phrases: talcum powder, as soft as talc.
examples from the lessons: Talc is so soft you can scratch it with your fingernail. | On the Mohs scale, talc is 1 and diamond is 10. | Mum put talc on the baby after the bath. | The gymnast clapped talc onto her hands. | Talcum powder smells of flowers. | We tested which rocks were harder than talc. | Talc feels smooth and soapy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «some talc». Talcum powder is often just called talc. Some people now use cornflour-based powder instead, because talc dust should not be breathed in. Do not confuse with chalk.

part of speech: noun (a tanner, tanners); proper noun (Tanner — a name)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A tanner is a person whose job is tanning animal skins to turn them into leather. 2) (UK slang, old-fashioned) A tanner was a sixpence coin. 3) (informal) A tanner can be a person or product that gives you a suntan. 4) Tanner is also a surname and a first name (a name).
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons tanners were important craftsmen, but tanneries smelled terrible, so they were often built outside towns near rivers. In Bible lessons Peter stayed with Simon the tanner. In old British money a tanner was half a shilling. Phrases: Simon the tanner, a tanner's yard.
examples from the lessons: The tanner soaked the cow hides in big pits. | Tanners' yards were smelly places near the river. | In the Bible, Peter stayed at the house of Simon the tanner. | (UK slang, old) «It only cost a tanner,» said Grandad. | Leather shoes were made from hides prepared by tanners. | My friend Tanner is the fastest runner in our class. | Self-tanner turned his legs orange!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural tanners. A tannery is the workshop. The word comes from «tan», from tannin, a substance in oak bark that was used to make leather. In money problems: 1 tanner = 6 old pennies.

part of speech: proper noun (Timothy — a name; Timothy in the Bible); noun (timothy, uncountable — timothy grass)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Timothy is a boy's or man's name (a name); short forms are Tim and Timmy. 2) (Bible) Timothy was a young friend and helper of the apostle Paul; two letters in the New Testament, 1 and 2 Timothy, were written to him. 3) Timothy (timothy grass) is a kind of grass grown for hay, fed to horses, rabbits and guinea pigs.
its sense in the lessons: In church and Bible lessons Timothy is known for being taught the faith by his mother Eunice and grandmother Lois. In pet care, timothy hay is the main food for rabbits and guinea pigs. Phrases: timothy hay, the letters to Timothy.
examples from the lessons: Timothy is in my class and he loves dinosaurs. | Paul wrote two letters to Timothy, which are in the New Testament. | Timothy learned about God from his mum and his grandma. | Our rabbit eats timothy hay every day. | Timothy grass grows tall in the farmer's fields. | Everyone calls him Tim, but his full name is Timothy. | Guinea pigs need lots of timothy hay to keep their teeth healthy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The name has a capital T; the grass is usually small (timothy). The grass is said to be named after Timothy Hanson, an American farmer. Not used in maths.

part of speech: adjective (tinned); verb (tin, tins, tinned, tinning — past form)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (UK, Australia, NZ) Tinned food is food sealed in a metal can to keep it fresh for a long time; in the US people say «canned». 2) Tinned means covered with a thin layer of tin, as tinned steel or tinned copper wire.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life tinned food (beans, tomatoes, tuna, peaches) is cheap, lasts long and is used in food banks and emergencies. In science and history lessons tinned food was invented to feed soldiers and sailors in the early 1800s. Phrases: tinned tomatoes, tinned fish, tinned fruit.
examples from the lessons: Mum opened a tin of beans, so we had tinned beans on toast. | We collected tinned food for the food bank. | Tinned peaches taste sweet and syrupy. | Explorers took tinned food to the Antarctic. | Tinned tuna is good in sandwiches. | Check the date on tinned food before eating it. | The electrician used tinned copper wire.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK «tinned» = US «canned»; both mean the same food. Cans are mostly steel with a tin coating, or aluminium. Throw away tins that are badly dented, swollen or rusty. Double n: tinned, tinning.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A tor is a small hill topped with a pile of bare, weathered rock, especially in south-west England on Dartmoor and Bodmin Moor. 2) A tor is also the rocky pile itself.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons tors are made of granite that has been weathered over millions of years by frost, rain and wind, leaving stacks of rounded blocks. Many Dartmoor place names include «Tor», such as Haytor and Hound Tor; the Ten Tors challenge is a famous hiking event for teenagers. Phrases: climb a tor, Ten Tors.
examples from the lessons: We climbed to the top of the tor and saw for miles. | Haytor is one of the most famous tors on Dartmoor. | The tor was a pile of granite blocks shaped by the weather. | Ten Tors is a long walk across Dartmoor for teenagers. | Ponies grazed below the tor. | Frost cracked the granite and slowly made the tor. | The wind howled around the rocky tor.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural tors. The word comes from an old Celtic word for a hill. Do not confuse with «Tor», the name of a privacy web browser, or with «tore» (past of tear), which sounds the same in many accents.

part of speech: verb (treble, trebles, trebled, trebling); adjective (treble); noun (a treble, trebles); determiner (treble the amount)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To treble is to become three times as big, or to make something three times as big. 2) Treble means three times as much or as many, or having three parts. 3) (music) The treble is the high part in music; a treble is a boy with a high singing voice, and the treble clef is the sign for high notes. 4) (sport) A treble is winning three trophies in one season, or (darts) the narrow ring that scores three times the number.
its sense in the lessons: In maths problems treble means multiply by 3, the same as triple. In music lessons the treble clef shows notes for the right hand on the piano, recorders and violins. In football a team that wins the league and two cups has won the treble. Phrases: treble clef, treble the price, the treble (sport), double or treble.
examples from the lessons: The price of the house has trebled in twenty years. | If you treble 5, you get 15. | My big brother sings treble in the cathedral choir. | Notes for the recorder are written on the treble clef. | The team won the treble: the league, the FA Cup and the European Cup. | He hit treble twenty, which scores 60 in darts. | We got treble the number of visitors this year.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Treble and triple mean the same in maths (×3); treble is more common in UK English. Do not confuse with «tremble» (shake) or «trouble». The low part in music is the bass. Verb spelling: trebled, trebling.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A trilobite was a sea animal with a hard, jointed shell and many legs that lived about 520 to 250 million years ago; trilobites are now extinct and known only from fossils. 2) A trilobite is also a fossil of one of these animals.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons trilobites are famous fossils: their bodies had three lobes (a middle and two sides), they were arthropods, related to insects, spiders and crabs, and some had some of the first complex eyes. Because each kind lived at a certain time, trilobite fossils help date rock layers. Phrases: trilobite fossil, extinct trilobites.
examples from the lessons: I found a trilobite fossil on the beach in Wales. | Trilobites crawled along the sea floor long before the dinosaurs. | A trilobite's body was split into three long parts. | Some trilobites could roll up into a ball like a woodlouse. | Trilobites had eyes made of crystal. | All trilobites died out about 250 million years ago. | The museum had a whole case of trilobites.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced TRY-luh-bite. Plural trilobites. The name means «three lobes». A woodlouse is NOT a living trilobite, even though it looks a bit like one.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A tyrant is a ruler who uses power cruelly and unfairly and does not let people choose or change their leaders. 2) (informal) A tyrant is anyone who bosses others about cruelly, such as a bossy boss, teacher or older sibling. 3) (history) In ancient Greece a tyrant was a ruler who took power by force, not always cruel.
its sense in the lessons: In history and politics lessons a tyrant is the opposite of a fair, chosen leader; people fight tyranny with laws, elections and courts. In stories tyrants are kings, queens or giants who frighten everyone until heroes stand up to them. Phrases: a cruel tyrant, overthrow a tyrant, petty tyrant, tyranny.
examples from the lessons: The people rose up against the cruel tyrant. | The tyrant threw anyone who disagreed into prison. | In the fairy tale, the tyrant king took all the farmers' food. | My big sister is a tyrant when it's her turn to choose the TV. | Ancient Athens was once ruled by tyrants. | Elections help stop a tyrant from taking power. | Tyrannosaurus rex means «tyrant lizard king».
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural tyrants. Related words: tyranny (cruel rule), tyrannical (cruel and bossy). Do not confuse tyrant with «tirade» (a long angry speech).

meaning for a pupil: 1) The ulna is one of the two long bones in the forearm, between the elbow and the wrist; it is on the little-finger side. 2) The other forearm bone is the radius, on the thumb side.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons the ulna is part of the skeleton; the bony tip of your elbow is the top of the ulna. The ulna and radius twist around each other when you turn your hand over. In first aid, a broken forearm may mean a fractured ulna or radius. Phrases: radius and ulna, broken ulna.
examples from the lessons: The ulna runs from your elbow to your wrist. | Feel the bony point of your elbow; that's the end of your ulna. | She broke her ulna falling off her scooter. | The ulna is on the same side as your little finger. | The radius and the ulna let you turn your palm up and down. | Birds have an ulna in their wings too. | The X-ray showed a crack in the ulna.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Use «an ulna» (it starts with a vowel sound). Plural ulnae (Latin) or ulnas. The «funny bone» is not a bone: it is a nerve near the end of the ulna and humerus that tingles when bumped.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unauthorised means done or used without permission from the person or group in charge. 2) An unauthorised person is someone who is not allowed to be somewhere or to do something.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday and safety life it appears on signs: «No unauthorised entry», «Unauthorised vehicles will be removed». In school, an unauthorised absence means missing school without a reason the school accepts. In online safety it means using an account or computer without permission, which can be against the law. Phrases: unauthorised access, unauthorised absence, unauthorised use.
examples from the lessons: The sign said «No unauthorised persons beyond this point.» | Missing school for a holiday is an unauthorised absence. | Unauthorised access to someone's account is against the law. | The guard stopped an unauthorised visitor at the gate. | Unauthorised parking will be fined. | The app sent a warning about an unauthorised login. | Using photos from the internet without permission can be unauthorised use.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK spelling unauthorised, US spelling unauthorized. «Un-» means «not». Opposite: authorised (allowed).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unfertilised describes an egg or egg cell that has not joined with a sperm cell, so it cannot grow into a baby animal. 2) Unfertilised describes a flower or ovule that has not received pollen, so it cannot make a seed. 3) Unfertilised soil or fields have had no fertiliser (plant food) added.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons it explains life cycles: the eggs we buy in shops are usually unfertilised, so they never become chicks. Unfertilised frogspawn does not hatch. In farming it is about fields that have not been fed with manure or fertiliser. Phrases: unfertilised egg, unfertilised flower.
examples from the lessons: Eggs from the supermarket are unfertilised, so no chick will grow. | Hens lay eggs even without a cockerel, but the eggs are unfertilised. | An unfertilised flower falls off without making fruit. | Unfertilised frogspawn turns white and does not hatch. | Queen bees lay unfertilised eggs that become male bees. | The unfertilised field grew smaller carrots. | Bees help flowers so they don't stay unfertilised.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK spelling unfertilised, US unfertilized. «Un-» means «not». Fertilised eggs need warmth to develop; an unfertilised egg cannot grow even if kept warm.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A vervet is a small African monkey with a grey-green or silvery coat, a black face fringed with white fur and a long tail. 2) Vervets live in groups in the savannas and woodlands of eastern and southern Africa.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons vervet monkeys are famous because they have different alarm calls for different dangers: one for leopards, one for eagles and one for snakes, and the troop reacts differently to each. They are often seen near safari camps, where they may snatch food. Phrases: vervet monkey, a troop of vervets.
examples from the lessons: A vervet monkey leapt onto the safari truck. | Vervets have black faces with white fur around them. | When a vervet sees an eagle, it gives a special call and everyone looks up. | A troop of vervets raided the campsite for bananas. | Baby vervets cling to their mothers' tummies. | Vervets eat fruit, leaves, seeds and insects. | Don't feed the vervets, or they will steal your lunch!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural vervets. Pronounced VER-vit. A group of monkeys is called a troop. Feeding wild monkeys is unsafe and makes them bold.

part of speech: noun (a visa, visas); proper noun (Visa — a card company)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A visa is an official stamp or document that lets you enter, stay in, study or work in a foreign country for a certain time. 2) Visa (with a capital V) is the name of a company whose logo appears on bank cards; people say «I'll pay by Visa».
its sense in the lessons: In geography and everyday life visas are needed to travel to some countries; you show your passport and visa at the border. In lessons on migration and adult life, families may need a work visa, student visa or tourist visa. Phrases: apply for a visa, tourist visa, work visa, student visa, visa-free.
examples from the lessons: Dad had to apply for a visa before his trip to China. | My cousin got a student visa to study in Canada. | Some countries let you visit visa-free for a short time. | The officer checked her passport and stamped her visa. | His visa runs out next month, so he must go home or renew it. | Mum paid for the shopping with her Visa card. | A work visa allows you to have a job in another country.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural visas. A visa is not the same as a passport: the passport shows who you are and where you come from; the visa is permission from the other country. Pronounced VEE-zuh.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Warty means covered with warts, small hard lumps on the skin. 2) Warty means having a lumpy, bumpy surface like warts.
its sense in the lessons: In nature lessons toads are often described as warty, and some animals and plants have warty skin to look less tasty or to hide. In stories witches and goblins are sometimes given warty noses. Phrases: warty skin, warty toad, warty nose.
examples from the lessons: The warty toad sat under a stone. | The witch in the story had a warty green nose. | Some pumpkins are warty and bumpy. | The warty newt has rough, dark skin. | Toads are warty, but frogs are usually smooth. | The old tree had a warty, knobbly trunk. | The goblin rubbed his warty hands together.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative wartier, wartiest. Myth: touching a toad does NOT give you warts; warts are caused by a virus spread between people. Calling a person warty is rude.

part of speech: verb (weave, weaves, wove, woven, weaving; also weaved for moving); noun (a weave, weaves)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To weave is to make cloth, a basket or a mat by crossing threads, strips or twigs over and under each other. 2) To weave can mean to move in and out between things, changing direction (past: weaved). 3) To weave a story is to make it up, especially by joining many parts. 4) A weave is the pattern or way that something is woven; a weave is also a style of hair extension.
its sense in the lessons: In design and history lessons weaving on a loom makes fabric; threads going one way are the warp, those going across are the weft. In art lessons children weave paper strips. In PE and safety, cyclists should not weave between cars. Spiders weave webs. Phrases: weave a basket, weave through the traffic, weave a tale, a tight weave.
examples from the lessons: We wove a mat from strips of coloured paper. | Grandma weaves rugs on her big wooden loom. | The spider wove a beautiful web. | The footballer weaved between the defenders and scored. | The cyclist weaved dangerously through the traffic. | The storyteller wove a tale of dragons and kings. | This fabric has a tight weave, so it keeps out the wind.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past forms: wove and woven for making cloth (She wove a basket; it was woven by hand); weaved for moving (He weaved through the crowd). Do not confuse with «wave» (move your hand).

part of speech: adjective (westward); adverb (westward, also westwards in UK English)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Westward means going towards the west. 2) Westward describes something that faces or lies towards the west.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons it is used with compass directions; the sun appears to move westward across the sky. In history lessons in the USA, the westward expansion is when settlers travelled west across North America in wagons, which also took land from Native American peoples. Phrases: head westward, the westward journey, westward expansion.
examples from the lessons: The ship sailed westward across the Atlantic. | The sun moves westward across the sky during the day. | Pioneers travelled westward in covered wagons. | The storm is moving westward towards the coast. | Our garden has a westward view, so we see the sunset. | Westward expansion forced many Native Americans off their land. | Turn westward at the old oak tree.
note for the reader of a maths problem: In UK English the adverb is often «westwards» (they walked westwards); the adjective is always westward (a westward journey). Same pattern: eastward, northward, southward. On a map, west is on the left.

part of speech: noun (yang, uncountable — Chinese idea); proper noun (Yang — a surname); (Mandarin, pinyin)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (Chinese philosophy) Yang is one half of yin and yang, the old Chinese idea that the world is made of two opposite forces that balance each other; yang is the bright, warm, active, «sunny» side. 2) (Mandarin, pinyin) Yáng is a Chinese word that can mean sun or sunshine (as in tàiyáng, the sun), or sheep or goat, depending on the tone and character; it is not an English word. To an English ear it sounds like «yahng». 3) Yang is a common Chinese surname (a name).
its sense in the lessons: In religion and culture lessons yin and yang is shown as a circle of a black and a white swirl, each with a dot of the other colour, meaning that opposites belong together. In Mandarin lessons yáng appears in words like tàiyáng (sun) and yáng (sheep) in the Chinese zodiac. Phrases: yin and yang.
examples from the lessons: Yin and yang are opposites that balance each other, like night and day. | The yin-yang symbol is a circle of black and white swirls. | In Chinese thought, yang is bright, warm and active. | (Mandarin) Tàiyáng means the sun. | (Mandarin) In the Chinese zodiac, the Year of the Goat is also called the Year of the Sheep, yáng. | Our new classmate's surname is Yang. | My brother is noisy and I am quiet; Mum says we are yin and yang.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always «yin and yang», in that order. Yang is not «good» and yin is not «bad»: they are equal halves. In pinyin the tone mark changes the meaning: yáng (sheep, sun) differs from yǎng (raise, look after).

part of speech: (not a standard English word — fragment or made-up word)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Zib is not an ordinary English word and is not in normal English dictionaries. 2) It may be a piece of a longer word, a sound or name invented for a story or game, or a word borrowed from another language.
its sense in the lessons: If you meet «zib» in a text, look at the context: it may be a made-up name for a creature or robot, a sound effect, or a typing mistake (for example for «zip»). In some languages it is a rude slang word, so it is best not to use it as a name for something.
examples from the lessons: The alien in the comic was called Zib. | «Zib, zib!» went the little robot as it beeped. | Did you mean «zip», not «zib»? | In the word game, Zib was a nonsense word. | The puzzle asked us to change «zib» into a real word by changing one letter: «zip». | We couldn't find «zib» in the dictionary. | The story's made-up planet was called Zib-Zob.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Honest note: «zib» has no standard English meaning. Do not confuse with «zip». In other languages it can be a rude word, so do not use it as a nickname.

part of speech: noun (zing, uncountable; a zing); verb (zing, zings, zinged, zinging)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) Zing is energy, excitement or liveliness. 2) (informal) Zing is a sharp, fresh, tangy taste, as from lemon or ginger. 3) A zing is a high, ringing or whistling sound, like something flying fast. 4) To zing is to move very fast with a high sound; (informal, US) to zing someone is to make a cheeky joke at them.
its sense in the lessons: In cooking and everyday talk zing describes lively flavours. In stories it is a sound word for fast movement, like arrows or bullets. In writing lessons, adding «zing» means making something more lively and interesting. Phrases: add some zing, full of zing.
examples from the lessons: A squeeze of lime adds zing to the salsa. | The new paint gave the classroom some zing. | The arrow zinged past the knight's ear. | Grandpa is still full of zing at eighty. | This lemonade has a real zing! | The ball zinged off the bat and over the fence. | Your story needs more zing at the start.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal word; in formal writing use «energy» or «flavour». Verb forms zinged, zinging. Related: zingy (tangy, lively). Do not confuse with «sing» or «zinc».

meaning for a pupil: 1) To affirm something is to say firmly and clearly that it is true. 2) To affirm a person is to support and encourage them, telling them they are valued. 3) (law, formal) To affirm is to make a solemn promise to tell the truth in court without swearing on a holy book. 4) (law) A higher court affirms a decision when it agrees that the decision was right.
its sense in the lessons: In ethics and PSHE lessons affirming someone means saying kind, true things that build them up. In law lessons people may «swear» on a Bible or «affirm» instead. In church, people affirm their faith by saying the creed. Phrases: affirm the truth, affirm your faith, an affirmation.
examples from the lessons: The witness affirmed that she had seen the car. | Our teacher affirmed that the answer was correct. | Saying «You worked so hard» affirms your friend's effort. | In court, he chose to affirm rather than swear on the Bible. | The church members affirmed their faith by saying the creed together. | The higher court affirmed the judge's decision. | Write three sentences that affirm what you are good at.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: affirmation; adjective: affirmative (an affirmative answer = yes). Do not confuse with «confirm» (check or prove that something is true or booked), though they are close. Opposite: deny.

part of speech: abbreviation (ag — agriculture; Ag — silver); interjection (ag — South Africa, informal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal, US, Canada, Australia) Ag is short for agriculture, the work of farming: «ag school», «ag science». 2) (science) Ag is the chemical symbol for silver, from its Latin name «argentum». 3) (South Africa, informal) Ag is an exclamation like «oh» or «ugh», showing annoyance, sympathy or giving up, said with a throaty sound like «ach».
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons the periodic table writes silver as Ag (capital A, small g), with atomic number 47. In North American and Australian schools, kids may join an «ag club» or study «ag» (farming). In stories from South Africa, characters say «Ag, man!» or «Ag shame». Phrases: ag science, ag college.
examples from the lessons: Silver's chemical symbol is Ag. | Ag comes from the Latin word argentum. | My cousin is studying ag science to become a farmer. | Our school's ag club keeps chickens and grows tomatoes. | (South Africa, informal) «Ag, man, I forgot my lunch again!» | (South Africa) «Ag shame, the poor puppy is lost.» | The ag show had prize cows and sheep.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Honest note: «ag» is an abbreviation or exclamation, not a full English word. Write the silver symbol as Ag, never AG or ag. Do not confuse with Au, the symbol for gold.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Airtight means sealed so tightly that no air can get in or out. 2) (figurative) An airtight argument, alibi or case has no weak points and cannot be proved wrong.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life airtight boxes and jars keep food fresh and stop it going stale or mouldy. In science lessons airtight containers show that things need air (oxygen) to burn or rot, and help in experiments with gases. In detective stories an airtight alibi proves a suspect could not have done the crime. Phrases: airtight container, airtight seal, airtight alibi.
examples from the lessons: Keep the biscuits in an airtight tin so they stay crunchy. | The jar has an airtight lid. | Without air, the candle in the airtight jar went out. | Astronauts' spacesuits must be airtight. | Never play inside an airtight box or old fridge — you could not breathe. | The detective could not arrest him because his alibi was airtight. | Her argument was airtight; nobody could find a flaw.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Written as one word: airtight. Similar: watertight (no water gets in). Safety: never close a person or pet inside an airtight space.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Algebra is the part of maths that uses letters and symbols, such as x or n, to stand for numbers that are unknown or that can change. 2) Algebra is also the rules for working with these letters in expressions, equations and formulas.
its sense in the lessons: In school maths algebra starts with missing number problems (□ + 3 = 7) and grows into equations (x + 3 = 7, so x = 4), formulas (area = length × width) and sequences (the nth term is 2n + 1). The word comes from Arabic «al-jabr», from a book by the Persian scholar al-Khwarizmi. Phrases: do algebra, algebra lesson, solve with algebra.
examples from the lessons: In algebra, we can use n to stand for any number. | Algebra helps us solve problems like «I think of a number, add 5 and get 12». | If 2x = 10, algebra tells us x = 5. | Our algebra homework was about simplifying expressions. | The formula for the perimeter of a square is P = 4s; that's algebra. | The word algebra comes from Arabic. | My big sister says algebra is like a puzzle with letters.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «some algebra», not «an algebra» (except in university maths). In algebra 3n means 3 × n, and n² means n × n. A letter in one problem keeps the same value throughout that problem. Adjective: algebraic.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Ambiguous means having more than one possible meaning, so it is unclear which one is meant. 2) Ambiguous can mean uncertain or not clearly decided.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons ambiguous sentences are a classic puzzle: «I saw the man with the telescope» (who had the telescope?). Clear writing avoids ambiguity with careful word order and commas. In maths, a question is ambiguous if it can be read in two ways, so mathematicians use brackets. Phrases: an ambiguous sentence, an ambiguous answer, ambiguous ending.
examples from the lessons: «Let's eat, Grandma» and «Let's eat Grandma» show how a comma removes ambiguous meaning. | The sign «Slow children» is ambiguous! | Her answer was ambiguous: I couldn't tell if it was yes or no. | The story has an ambiguous ending, so readers argue about what happened. | Is 6 − 2 + 1 ambiguous? Brackets make it clear. | «I saw her duck» is ambiguous: a bird or a movement? | The rules of the game were ambiguous, so we argued.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: ambiguity (plural ambiguities). Pronounced am-BIG-yoo-us. Do not confuse with «ambivalent» (having mixed feelings). In maths, 2 + 3 × 4 is NOT ambiguous because of the order of operations: it is 14.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Ancestral means belonging to, coming from or connected with your ancestors, the people in your family who lived long before you. 2) (science) Ancestral describes an early form of a living thing from which later kinds developed.
its sense in the lessons: In history and family lessons an ancestral home or land is where a family or people has lived for generations; Aboriginal Australians, Māori and Native American peoples talk about ancestral land. In science lessons on evolution, birds have ancestral links to dinosaurs. Phrases: ancestral home, ancestral land, ancestral language.
examples from the lessons: The castle was the duke's ancestral home. | The Māori people care deeply for their ancestral land. | Grandma took us to her ancestral village in Ireland. | Many families keep ancestral photos and letters. | Birds are thought to have dinosaurs as ancestral relatives. | The tribe performed an ancestral dance at the festival. | Our ancestral language was Ukrainian, though we now speak English.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Related: ancestor (a person), ancestry (your family line). Ancestors are earlier than grandparents usually; descendants are the people who come after you.

part of speech: noun (an antiseptic, antiseptics; antiseptic, uncountable); adjective (antiseptic)
meaning for a pupil: 1) An antiseptic is a substance you put on skin or a wound to kill germs and stop infection. 2) Antiseptic means able to kill germs. 3) (figurative) Antiseptic can mean very clean but cold and without feeling, like a hospital room.
its sense in the lessons: In first-aid and safety lessons you clean a cut, then may use antiseptic cream or wipes before a plaster. In science and history lessons Joseph Lister began using antiseptics in surgery in the 1860s, which saved many lives. Phrases: antiseptic cream, antiseptic wipe, antiseptic spray.
examples from the lessons: Mum dabbed antiseptic cream on my grazed knee. | The nurse cleaned the cut with an antiseptic wipe. | Antiseptics kill germs on skin. | Joseph Lister used antiseptic spray during operations. | The first-aid box has plasters, bandages and antiseptic. | The hospital corridor smelled antiseptic. | The new office looked antiseptic and unfriendly.
note for the reader of a maths problem: An antiseptic is used on living skin; a disinfectant cleans surfaces like tables and toilets. Antiseptics are not antibiotics (medicines that kill bacteria inside the body). «Anti-» means «against», «septic» means infected.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An aqueduct is a bridge that carries water, either a channel of water or a canal, across a valley or river. 2) An aqueduct is any man-made channel or pipe that carries water a long way, for example to a city.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons the ancient Romans built famous stone aqueducts with tall arches to bring fresh water to their cities, such as the Pont du Gard in France. In the UK, canal aqueducts like Pontcysyllte in Wales let boats cross valleys. In science they show water flowing gently downhill by gravity. Phrases: Roman aqueduct, canal aqueduct.
examples from the lessons: The Romans built an aqueduct to bring water to the city. | The aqueduct had rows of tall stone arches. | Water flowed slowly downhill along the aqueduct. | We crossed the Pontcysyllte Aqueduct on a narrowboat. | Some aqueducts were over 50 kilometres long. | The old aqueduct still stands in Segovia, Spain. | An aqueduct carries water; a viaduct carries a road or railway.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural aqueducts. Spelling trap: aquEduct, not «aquaduct». «Aqua» means water, «duct» means a pipe or channel. Use «an aqueduct».

meaning for a pupil: 1) An archerfish is a small fish of warm rivers and mangroves in Asia and northern Australia that shoots a jet of water from its mouth to knock insects off leaves above the water. 2) It then swims to eat the insect when it falls.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons the archerfish is an amazing hunter: it can aim even though light bends where water meets air (refraction), and it learns by watching other fish. It is an example of an animal adaptation. Phrases: archerfish jet, spit water.
examples from the lessons: The archerfish spat a jet of water and knocked a beetle into the river. | An archerfish can hit insects more than a metre away. | Archerfish live in mangrove swamps in Australia. | The archerfish corrects its aim for the bending of light. | Young archerfish learn by watching older ones. | At the aquarium, the archerfish shot water at a target. | The archerfish has stripes on its silvery sides.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural archerfish (like «fish»). Written as one word, sometimes «archer fish». It is not related to archery; it gets the name because it «shoots».

part of speech: adjective (articulated); verb (articulate, articulates, articulated, articulating — past form)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (UK) An articulated lorry, bus or vehicle has two or more parts joined by a bendy joint so it can turn corners. 2) Articulated means having joints, like a skeleton or a toy figure. 3) Articulated is the past form of articulate: to say something clearly, or to express ideas clearly in words.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life articulated lorries (artics, or semi-trucks in the US) and bendy buses need a lot of room to turn, which matters for road safety near them. In science, an articulated skeleton is one with its bones joined together. In English lessons, «she articulated her ideas well» means she explained clearly. Phrases: articulated lorry, articulated bus, articulated skeleton.
examples from the lessons: An articulated lorry swung slowly round the roundabout. | Never stand close to an articulated lorry when it turns. | The museum has an articulated skeleton of a whale. | The action figure has articulated arms and legs. | She articulated each word so the class could hear. | He articulated his reasons clearly in his speech. | The articulated bus bends in the middle.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The adjective «articulate» (said ar-TIK-yoo-lut) means good at speaking clearly; the verb (ar-TIK-yoo-late) means say clearly or join. UK «articulated lorry» = US «semi-truck» or «tractor-trailer».

meaning for a pupil: 1) An artwork is a piece of art, such as a painting, drawing, sculpture or collage. 2) Artwork (uncountable) is the pictures and designs in a book, magazine, game, album or poster.
its sense in the lessons: In art lessons pupils make and display their artwork and talk about the artworks of famous artists. In everyday life the artwork on a book cover or video game helps sell it. Phrases: display your artwork, original artwork, album artwork.
examples from the lessons: Our class artwork is on the wall in the corridor. | The museum has artworks from all over the world. | Leonardo's Mona Lisa is a famous artwork. | I love the artwork in this picture book. | She signed her artwork in the corner. | The game's artwork was drawn by hand. | Please take your artwork home at the end of term.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It can be countable (two artworks) or uncountable (the artwork in this book). One word: artwork.

part of speech: noun (an aurora, auroras or aurorae); proper noun (Aurora — a name; Roman goddess of dawn)
meaning for a pupil: 1) An aurora is a display of moving, coloured light (often green, pink or purple) in the night sky near the North or South Pole. 2) The aurora borealis (northern lights) is seen in the north; the aurora australis (southern lights) in the south. 3) Aurora is a girl's name (a name), the Roman goddess of the dawn, and the name of Sleeping Beauty in the Disney film.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons auroras happen when tiny charged particles from the Sun hit gases high in Earth's atmosphere and make them glow; Earth's magnetic field steers the particles towards the poles. People travel to Norway, Iceland, Canada, Scotland, Tasmania and New Zealand to see them. Phrases: aurora borealis, aurora australis, northern lights.
examples from the lessons: We watched the green aurora dance across the sky in Norway. | The aurora borealis is also called the northern lights. | In Tasmania you can sometimes see the aurora australis. | An aurora happens when particles from the Sun hit our atmosphere. | Last night the aurora was visible even in Scotland. | Aurora is the Roman goddess of the dawn. | Princess Aurora is the heroine of «Sleeping Beauty».
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural auroras or aurorae. Pronounced uh-ROAR-uh. Auroras are best seen on dark, clear nights, far from city lights.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Backstroke is a way of swimming on your back, moving your arms backwards one after the other over your head and kicking your legs. 2) A backstroke is one movement of the arm in this style.
its sense in the lessons: In PE and swimming lessons backstroke is one of the four main strokes (with front crawl, breaststroke and butterfly). It is the only race that starts in the water. Swimmers see flags above the pool before the wall so they know when to turn. Phrases: do backstroke, swim backstroke, 100 metres backstroke.
examples from the lessons: I swam two lengths of backstroke today. | In backstroke you float on your back and look at the ceiling. | Backstroke races start in the water, not from the blocks. | The flags warn backstroke swimmers that the wall is near. | She won the gold medal in the 200 metres backstroke. | Keep your tummy up when you do backstroke. | Each backstroke pulled him further down the pool.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable (do backstroke). One word. In swimming problems: a length is one way along the pool; a 25 m pool needs 4 lengths for 100 m.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A battlefield is a place where a battle is or was fought. 2) (figurative) A battlefield is any place or subject where people argue or compete fiercely.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons battlefields such as Hastings, the Somme and Gettysburg are places where many soldiers died; today some are memorials visited by school trips. In stories it is a place of danger and courage. Figuratively, a messy room or a heated argument can be called a battlefield. Phrases: on the battlefield, battlefield memorial.
examples from the lessons: Thousands of soldiers died on the battlefield at the Somme. | We visited the battlefield where the Battle of Hastings was fought. | Poppies grew on the battlefields of the First World War. | The knight rode bravely across the battlefield. | After the food fight, the dining hall looked like a battlefield. | The playground became a battlefield of snowballs. | Social media can become a battlefield of arguments.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word. Plural battlefields. Battlefields are often places of sadness and respect today; people visit quietly.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A billboard is a very large board beside a road or on a building for showing advertisements. 2) (US) Billboard is also the name of a magazine that publishes music charts, as in «the Billboard Hot 100».
its sense in the lessons: In media lessons billboards are a kind of advertising designed to be read quickly by drivers, using big pictures and few words. In UK English a billboard is also called a hoarding. In music, «number one on the Billboard charts» means the most popular song in the USA. Phrases: on a billboard, billboard advert, Billboard chart.
examples from the lessons: A huge billboard by the motorway showed a new phone. | The billboard said «Drink milk!» in giant letters. | Advertisers put billboards where many drivers will see them. | The song reached number one on the Billboard Hot 100. | In our media lesson we designed a billboard for a healthy snack. | The billboard lit up at night. | Some cities have banned billboards to make streets look nicer.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural billboards. UK also says «hoarding». Billboards are adverts, so ask: what are they trying to make me buy or believe?

part of speech: verb (birdwatch, birdwatches, birdwatched, birdwatching); noun (a birdwatch, birdwatches — an organised count)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To birdwatch is to watch wild birds in their natural surroundings as a hobby, often with binoculars and a bird book. 2) A birdwatch is an organised event where people watch and count birds.
its sense in the lessons: In science and nature lessons birdwatching helps children learn bird names, songs and habitats. The RSPB's Big Garden Birdwatch in the UK asks families to count birds for one hour, and the results help scientists. Similar counts happen in the USA, Canada, Australia and New Zealand. Phrases: go birdwatching, Big Garden Birdwatch, a keen birdwatcher.
examples from the lessons: We birdwatch from the kitchen window every Saturday. | Grandad took me birdwatching at the lake. | In the Big Garden Birdwatch we counted seven robins. | Bring binoculars when you go birdwatching. | Birdwatchers sit very quietly so they don't scare the birds. | The school held a birdwatch in the playground. | She birdwatched for hours and saw a kingfisher.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The activity is usually called «birdwatching» and the person a «birdwatcher» (or «birder», «twitcher» in the UK for very keen people). In maths, birdwatch data are tallies and bar charts.

part of speech: adjective (blackened); verb (blacken, blackens, blackened, blackening — past form)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Blackened means made black or dark, for example by fire, smoke or dirt. 2) (cooking) Blackened food has been cooked in a very hot pan with spices so the outside turns dark. 3) To blacken someone's name is to damage their reputation by saying bad things about them; blackened is its past form.
its sense in the lessons: In stories blackened walls or trees tell the reader there has been a fire. In history lessons, blackened buildings come from coal smoke in old cities. In cooking it is a style of Cajun food from Louisiana, USA. Phrases: blackened by smoke, blackened fish, blacken someone's name.
examples from the lessons: The fire left the walls blackened and burnt. | Blackened trees stood on the hillside after the bushfire. | The chimney sweep's face was blackened with soot. | Dad cooked blackened chicken with spicy seasoning. | Rotten bananas have blackened skins. | Lies blackened the poor man's good name. | The old church walls were blackened by years of coal smoke.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Blacken + -ed = blackened. A «blackened» name is figurative: it means a bad reputation, not black paint.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A bladderwort is a meat-eating water plant with tiny bladders (bags) on its underwater stems that suck in and trap very small animals. 2) It grows in ponds, bogs and wet places all over the world and has little yellow or purple flowers above the water.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons the bladderwort is a carnivorous plant like the Venus flytrap and sundew: it lives where the soil or water has few nutrients, so it gets extra food from tiny creatures such as water fleas. Its trap is one of the fastest movements in the plant world. Phrases: carnivorous plant, bladder trap.
examples from the lessons: The bladderwort has no roots and floats in the pond. | Tiny bladders on the bladderwort suck in water fleas. | A bladderwort's trap snaps shut in a split second. | Bladderworts have pretty yellow flowers. | Like the Venus flytrap, the bladderwort eats tiny animals. | We looked at a bladderwort under a magnifying glass. | Bladderworts grow in bogs where there are few nutrients.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural bladderworts. «-wort» is an old word for plant (as in St John's wort). It catches only very tiny animals, not insects like flies.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A blockage is something that blocks a pipe, tube, road or passage so things cannot get through. 2) (medicine) A blockage is something stopping blood, air or food from moving inside the body, such as in a blood vessel or the gut.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life blockages happen in sinks, drains and toilets (often from hair, fat or wet wipes). In science and health lessons a blockage in an artery can cause a heart attack, and choking is a blockage of the airway — an emergency. Phrases: clear a blockage, a blockage in the drain, cause a blockage.
examples from the lessons: A blockage in the sink stopped the water draining away. | The plumber cleared the blockage with a long rod. | Wet wipes cause blockages in drains, so don't flush them. | Fallen trees made a blockage on the road. | A blockage in an artery can cause a heart attack. | Choking happens when food makes a blockage in the airway. | The doctor found a blockage in the patient's gut.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a blockage, blockages. Verb: block. In first aid, if someone is choking and cannot breathe or speak, get an adult and call emergency services (999 UK, 911 US and Canada, 000 Australia, 111 NZ, 112/999 Ireland).

part of speech: noun (a blossom, blossoms; blossom, uncountable); verb (blossom, blossoms, blossomed, blossoming)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Blossom is the flowers on a fruit tree or bush, such as apple, cherry or plum, in spring. 2) A blossom is one of those flowers. 3) To blossom is to produce flowers. 4) (figurative) To blossom is to grow and develop well, becoming happier, more confident or more successful.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons blossom is the flower stage of a fruit tree's life cycle; after bees pollinate the blossom, fruit grows. In Japan, people celebrate cherry blossom (sakura) with picnics. In stories, a shy character «blossoms» into a confident one. Phrases: cherry blossom, apple blossom, in blossom, blossom into.
examples from the lessons: The cherry tree is covered in pink blossom. | Bees buzzed among the apple blossoms. | The orange trees blossom in spring. | Without blossom, there would be no fruit. | The new girl was shy at first but blossomed in Year 5. | Their friendship blossomed during the school trip. | In Japan, families picnic under the cherry blossom.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable for many flowers on a tree (lots of blossom), countable for single flowers (a blossom, three blossoms). Similar: bloom. Verb forms blossomed, blossoming (single m).

part of speech: noun (blubber, uncountable); verb (blubber, blubbers, blubbered, blubbering — informal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Blubber is the thick layer of fat under the skin of whales, seals and penguins that keeps them warm in cold water. 2) (informal) To blubber is to cry noisily, often with tears and sobs. 3) (informal, rude) Blubber is sometimes used unkindly about fat on a person.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons blubber is an adaptation for the cold: it insulates animals like the blue whale and walrus and stores energy. A classic experiment: put your hand in a glove of lard («blubber glove») and dip it in ice water. In history, whale blubber was boiled to make oil for lamps. Phrases: a layer of blubber, blubber glove.
examples from the lessons: Seals have thick blubber to keep warm in icy seas. | A whale's blubber can be 30 centimetres thick. | Our blubber glove experiment showed that fat keeps out the cold. | Long ago, whalers boiled blubber to make lamp oil. | Polar bears eat seal blubber for energy. | (informal) Stop blubbering — it's only a scratch! | The little boy blubbered when he lost his teddy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable as a noun: «a lot of blubber». Calling a person «blubber» is cruel name-calling — do not do it. Blubber is fat, not muscle.

part of speech: adjective (blurred); verb (blur, blurs, blurred, blurring — past form)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Blurred means not clear or sharp, so the edges or details are hard to see. 2) Blurred is the past form of blur: to become unclear or to make something unclear. 3) (figurative) Blurred lines or memories are not clearly separated or remembered.
its sense in the lessons: In science and health lessons blurred vision can mean you need glasses, or that you have hit your head (a warning sign to tell an adult). In photography and art, movement makes photos blurred. In stories, tears or speed blur things. Phrases: blurred vision, a blurred photo, blurred memories, the line has blurred.
examples from the lessons: The photo was blurred because I moved the camera. | Without his glasses, the board looked blurred. | Blurred vision after a bump on the head means you must see a doctor. | Tears blurred her eyes as she waved goodbye. | The fast car was just a blurred streak. | Grandma's memories of the war are blurred now. | The line between work and play blurred during the holiday.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double r: blurred, blurring. «Blurry» is the informal adjective (a blurry picture). Opposite: sharp, clear, in focus.

part of speech: noun (a bonsai, bonsai or bonsais; bonsai, uncountable — the art)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A bonsai is a tree or shrub kept very small by growing it in a shallow pot and carefully cutting its roots and branches, so it looks like a tiny old tree. 2) Bonsai is the art of growing such trees, which comes from Japan and, before that, China.
