its sense in the lessons: In art and culture lessons bonsai is a patient craft: a bonsai can live for hundreds of years and be passed down in families. In science lessons it shows that pruning and a small pot limit a plant's growth. The trees are normal kinds (maple, pine, juniper), not special tiny species. Phrases: bonsai tree, the art of bonsai.
examples from the lessons: Grandpa trims his bonsai with tiny scissors. | The bonsai looked like a big old pine tree, but it was only 30 cm tall. | Bonsai is a Japanese art. | Some bonsai trees are hundreds of years old. | A bonsai needs a shallow pot and careful watering. | We saw a bonsai maple with red leaves at the garden show. | Bonsai teaches you to be patient.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced BON-sye. Plural usually bonsai. The word means «tray planting» in Japanese. Myth: bonsai are NOT special dwarf trees; they are ordinary trees kept small.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Botanical means to do with plants or with botany, the science of plants. 2) Botanical means made from plants, as in botanical oils or medicines.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons a botanical garden (botanic garden) is a garden where plants from around the world are grown, labelled and studied, such as Kew Gardens in London. Botanical drawings are careful, detailed pictures of plants. Every plant has a botanical (scientific) name in Latin, such as Bellis perennis for the daisy. Phrases: botanical garden, botanical name, botanical illustration.
examples from the lessons: We visited the botanical garden and saw a giant water lily. | The botanical name for the sunflower is Helianthus annuus. | She made a botanical drawing of a dandelion. | The botanical gardens in Sydney are next to the harbour. | Scientists collect botanical samples from the rainforest. | This shampoo is made with botanical oils. | Kew Gardens is a famous botanical garden.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Related: botany (the science), botanist (a plant scientist). «Botanic garden» and «botanical garden» mean the same.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A breakthrough is an important discovery or development that suddenly solves a problem or makes great progress. 2) A breakthrough is a moment when someone finally succeeds after trying for a long time. 3) A breakthrough is breaking through a barrier, such as an army breaking through enemy lines.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons breakthroughs include the discovery of penicillin, vaccines and DNA. In everyday life it is a moment like finally understanding fractions. In sport, a breakthrough season or goal brings first success. Phrases: make a breakthrough, a major breakthrough, a medical breakthrough, breakthrough moment.
examples from the lessons: Penicillin was a breakthrough in medicine. | Scientists made a breakthrough in fighting the disease. | After weeks of practice, I had a breakthrough and could ride without stabilisers. | The detectives made a breakthrough when they found the fingerprint. | The first vaccine was a huge breakthrough. | Learning times tables was my maths breakthrough this year. | The soldiers made a breakthrough in the enemy's defences.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word as a noun: a breakthrough. As a verb it is two words: «break through» (The sun broke through the clouds).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Breaststroke is a way of swimming on your front where your arms push forward together and sweep round to the sides, while your legs kick like a frog. 2) A breaststroke is one stroke in this style.
its sense in the lessons: In PE and swimming lessons breaststroke is one of the four main strokes and is often learned early because you can keep your head up and see where you are going. It is the slowest of the four racing strokes. Phrases: swim breaststroke, breaststroke kick, frog kick, 100 metres breaststroke.
examples from the lessons: I can swim 50 metres of breaststroke. | In breaststroke, your legs kick like a frog. | Breaststroke lets you keep your head above the water. | Adam Peaty is a champion breaststroke swimmer. | Our teacher says to glide after each breaststroke. | Breaststroke is slower than front crawl. | She won the 100 metres breaststroke at the school gala.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word. Spelling trap: breast + stroke = breaststroke (double s in the middle, «st-st»). Usually uncountable (do breaststroke).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Brutal means very cruel and violent. 2) Brutal means very harsh, severe or unpleasant, as with weather or a test. 3) (informal) Brutal honesty or truth is said directly, even if it hurts. 4) (slang) Brutal can mean really bad or tough: «That maths test was brutal.»
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons brutal describes cruel rulers, wars and punishments. In everyday talk children and teenagers use it for anything hard or unfair, like a long run or a strict teacher. In stories it tells the reader that a character or event is cruel. Phrases: a brutal attack, brutal honesty, brutally cold, a brutal winter.
examples from the lessons: The brutal king punished anyone who disagreed. | The soldiers carried out a brutal attack on the village. | The winter in Canada was brutal, with temperatures of minus thirty. | (informal) That cross-country run was brutal! | With brutal honesty, my friend said my drawing looked like a potato. | The wolf's brutal teeth tore the meat. | It was a brutally hot day.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb brutally, noun brutality. Related: brute (a cruel or very strong person or animal). In formal writing use it for real cruelty; the «really hard» meaning is informal.

part of speech: noun (bryony, uncountable; a bryony, bryonies); proper noun (Bryony — a girl's name)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Bryony is a climbing plant found in hedges in Britain and Europe; there are two kinds, white bryony and black bryony, both with shiny red berries in autumn. 2) Bryony is also a girl's name (a name).
its sense in the lessons: In nature and safety lessons bryony is important because all parts of it, especially the red berries and the roots, are poisonous; children should never eat wild berries without an adult who knows plants. It climbs by curly tendrils (white bryony) or by twisting stems (black bryony). Phrases: white bryony, black bryony.
examples from the lessons: Bryony climbed all over the hedge by the lane. | The bright red berries of bryony are poisonous. | Never eat hedge berries like bryony. | White bryony holds on with curly tendrils. | In autumn the bryony berries hung like red beads. | Bryony is the name of the girl who sits next to me. | The teacher pointed out bryony on our nature walk and warned us not to touch it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced BRY-uh-nee. The plant is usually small b; the name has a capital B. The two bryonies are not closely related, despite their names.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Buoyant means able to float, or able to keep things floating. 2) Buoyant means cheerful and full of hope. 3) (money) A buoyant market or economy is doing well, with prices or sales rising.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons buoyant objects float because the water pushes up on them (upthrust or buoyancy) as much as their weight pushes down. Salt water is more buoyant than fresh water. Swimming aids like armbands are buoyant. In stories a buoyant mood is a happy one. Phrases: buoyant force, buoyant mood, buoyancy aid.
examples from the lessons: Cork is very buoyant, so it floats easily. | Armbands are buoyant and help children float. | Salt water is more buoyant than fresh water. | The empty bottle was buoyant and bobbed on the waves. | After the win, the team was in a buoyant mood. | Sales of ice cream were buoyant all summer. | Life jackets are made of buoyant material.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced BOY-unt (UK) or BOO-yunt (US). Spelling trap: «buoy» has u before o. Noun: buoyancy. An object floats if it is less dense than the liquid.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To busk is to play music, sing, juggle or perform in a public place, such as a street or station, for money from people passing by. 2) (informal) To busk it is to improvise, to do something without preparing.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life buskers perform in town centres and underground stations; people drop coins in a hat or guitar case, and some places need a permit. In music lessons busking is a way young musicians practise in public. Phrases: go busking, a busker, busk it.
examples from the lessons: A man was busking with his guitar outside the station. | People threw coins into the busker's hat. | My big brother busks at the market on Saturdays. | You may need a licence to busk in some cities. | The juggler busked for the crowd in Covent Garden. | I forgot my notes, so I had to busk it. | She started busking at fifteen and is now a famous singer.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The person is a busker; the activity is busking. Forms: busked, busking. Mostly UK, Irish and Australian English, but understood everywhere.

part of speech: noun (a buttress, buttresses); verb (buttress, buttresses, buttressed, buttressing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A buttress is a thick wall or support of stone or brick built against a wall to hold it up and stop it falling outwards. 2) A flying buttress is an arch that reaches from a separate pillar to support a tall wall, as in Gothic cathedrals. 3) To buttress something is to support or strengthen it, often an argument or idea. 4) A buttress root is a wide, flat root that holds up a tall rainforest tree.
its sense in the lessons: In history and design lessons buttresses let medieval builders make cathedrals with tall, thin walls and big stained-glass windows (Notre-Dame, Westminster Abbey). In science lessons rainforest trees have buttress roots. In English, «buttress your argument with evidence» means support it. Phrases: flying buttress, buttress roots, buttress an argument.
examples from the lessons: The old church wall is held up by stone buttresses. | Flying buttresses support the walls of Notre-Dame in Paris. | Rainforest trees have huge buttress roots. | Buttresses let builders make tall walls with big windows. | She buttressed her argument with lots of facts. | The castle wall had a buttress at each corner. | We crawled between the buttress roots of a giant fig tree.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural buttresses. The verb is formal; in everyday talk say «support». Do not confuse with «butter».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) A carpel is the female part of a flower, where seeds are made. 2) It has three parts: the stigma (sticky top that catches pollen), the style (stalk) and the ovary (bottom part with ovules that become seeds).
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on plant life cycles the carpel is labelled on flower diagrams, along with the stamen (the male part, with anther and filament). After pollination and fertilisation the ovary of the carpel grows into the fruit. Some flowers have one carpel, others many (as in a buttercup or strawberry). Phrases: stigma, style and ovary; female part of the flower.
examples from the lessons: The carpel is the female part of the flower. | Pollen lands on the stigma at the top of the carpel. | Label the carpel and the stamen on your flower diagram. | The ovary at the bottom of the carpel grows into the fruit. | A pea pod grows from a single carpel. | A buttercup has many little carpels in the middle. | Bees carry pollen from the stamens to the carpels.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural carpels. Sometimes called a pistil (one or more carpels joined together). Do not confuse with «carpal» (wrist bones) or «carpet».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Carrion is the dead and rotting flesh of animals. 2) (adjective use) Carrion animals, such as a carrion crow, eat dead animals.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons carrion is food for scavengers such as vultures, crows, hyenas, Tasmanian devils and burying beetles; they help clean up nature and recycle nutrients. Some flowers (carrion flowers) smell like carrion to attract flies. In stories it creates a grim, gloomy mood. Phrases: carrion crow, carrion flower, feed on carrion.
examples from the lessons: Vultures circled over the carrion in the desert. | Carrion crows eat dead animals by the roadside. | Hyenas feed on carrion as well as hunting. | The giant flower smelled like carrion and attracted flies. | Burying beetles bury carrion to feed their young. | Tasmanian devils clean up carrion in the bush. | The battlefield was full of carrion birds.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «some carrion». Pronounced KARR-ee-un. Animals that eat carrion are called scavengers. Do not confuse with «carry on».

part of speech: noun (a cauliflower, cauliflowers; cauliflower, uncountable as food)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A cauliflower is a vegetable with a large, firm white head made of tiny flower buds, surrounded by green leaves. 2) (as food) Cauliflower is the vegetable cooked or raw.
its sense in the lessons: In food and healthy eating lessons cauliflower is a vegetable in the cabbage family (with broccoli and Brussels sprouts), full of vitamin C and fibre. In the UK cauliflower cheese is a classic dish. In maths, a cauliflower (especially Romanesco) shows a fractal pattern where small parts look like the whole. Phrases: cauliflower cheese, cauliflower rice, cauliflower ear.
examples from the lessons: Dad made cauliflower cheese for tea. | A cauliflower is really a bunch of tiny flower buds. | Cauliflower can be white, orange, green or purple. | Romanesco cauliflower makes spiral fractal shapes. | We grew a cauliflower in the school garden. | Cauliflower rice is made by chopping it very finely. | A rugby player can get «cauliflower ear» from bumps to the ear.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable for the whole vegetable (two cauliflowers), uncountable as food (some cauliflower). Spelling: cauli-flower. «Cauliflower ear» is a swollen ear from injuries.

part of speech: noun (censure, uncountable; a censure); verb (censure, censures, censured, censuring)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Censure is strong, official criticism or disapproval. 2) (formal) To censure someone is to criticise them strongly and officially, especially for something they did wrong. 3) A vote of censure is when a parliament or group officially says it disapproves of a leader or member.
its sense in the lessons: In politics and law lessons censure is a formal punishment, for example when a parliament or the US Congress censures a member who has broken rules. In exam texts it is the stiff, formal word for «telling off». Phrases: vote of censure, face censure, public censure.
examples from the lessons: (formal) The council faced public censure for closing the library. | Parliament voted to censure the minister. | The referee was censured for unfair decisions. | The report censured the company for polluting the river. | Cheating at the competition brought censure from the judges. | The senator was formally censured by Congress. | (formal) The headteacher's censure was severe but fair.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal word; in everyday talk say «criticise» or «tell off». Trap: censure (to criticise) is NOT the same as censor (to remove or ban parts of books, films or news), though they sound alike.

part of speech: noun (a chainsaw, chainsaws); verb (chainsaw, chainsaws, chainsawed, chainsawing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A chainsaw is a powerful handheld saw with a motor that drives a loop of sharp teeth (a chain) round a metal bar, used to cut down trees and cut logs. 2) To chainsaw something is to cut it with a chainsaw.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday and safety life chainsaws are used by tree surgeons, foresters and farmers. They are very dangerous, so users wear helmets, goggles, ear defenders, gloves and special trousers; children must stay well away. In art, people make chainsaw sculptures from tree trunks. Phrases: chainsaw safety, chainsaw carving.
examples from the lessons: The tree surgeon cut the fallen branch with a chainsaw. | We could hear a chainsaw buzzing in the woods. | Chainsaws are very dangerous, so stay far away. | He wore ear defenders because chainsaws are so loud. | The artist used a chainsaw to carve a bear from a log. | After the storm, neighbours chainsawed the fallen tree. | Dad sharpens the chainsaw's chain before cutting firewood.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word: chainsaw. In horror films chainsaws are used to scare people; in real life they are a tool for wood.

part of speech: adjective (chapped); verb (chap, chaps, chapped, chapping — past form)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Chapped skin or lips are dry, rough, cracked and sore, usually because of cold wind or dry air. 2) Chapped is the past form of chap: to make skin crack in this way.
its sense in the lessons: In health and everyday life chapped lips and hands are common in winter; lip balm, gloves and hand cream help. In science, cold wind removes moisture from the skin. In stories it shows a cold, harsh setting or a hard-working person. Phrases: chapped lips, chapped hands.
examples from the lessons: My lips get chapped in winter. | Put on some lip balm for your chapped lips. | The farmer's hands were red and chapped from the cold. | Wear gloves so your hands don't get chapped. | Licking your lips makes them more chapped. | The icy wind chapped our cheeks. | Her chapped knuckles stung when she washed her hands.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double p: chapped. Tip: licking dry lips makes them worse, not better. «Chap» also means a man (UK informal), which is a different word.

part of speech: noun (a chauffeur, chauffeurs); verb (chauffeur, chauffeurs, chauffeured, chauffeuring)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A chauffeur is a person whose job is driving someone else's car, often for a rich or important person. 2) To chauffeur someone is to drive them around, often as a job or a favour.
its sense in the lessons: In stories chauffeurs drive rich families and royals and open the car door for them. In everyday life parents joke that they are their children's «chauffeur» because they drive them to clubs and parties. Phrases: a uniformed chauffeur, chauffeur-driven car, chauffeur someone around.
examples from the lessons: The chauffeur opened the car door for the queen. | A chauffeur-driven car took the actors to the film premiere. | Mum says she's our chauffeur because she drives us everywhere. | Dad chauffeured us to football, then to swimming, then to Grandma's. | The chauffeur wore a cap and white gloves. | In old films, rich families had a chauffeur and a butler. | My uncle works as a chauffeur for a hotel.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A French word: pronounced SHOW-fur (UK) or show-FUR (US). Spelling trap: ch-au-ff-eur, double f. A taxi driver is not usually called a chauffeur.

part of speech: noun (a chokepoint, chokepoints; also choke point)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A chokepoint is a narrow place, such as a strait, mountain pass or narrow road, where movement is squeezed together and can easily be blocked. 2) (figurative) A chokepoint is any point in a system where things slow down or get stuck.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and history lessons famous sea chokepoints include the Strait of Hormuz, the Suez Canal, the Panama Canal and the Strait of Gibraltar; if one is blocked, world trade slows, as when a giant ship got stuck in the Suez Canal a few years ago. In battles, armies defend chokepoints like the pass at Thermopylae. In safety lessons, crowded doors and stairs are chokepoints. Phrases: a strategic chokepoint, traffic chokepoint.
examples from the lessons: The Suez Canal is a chokepoint for ships between Europe and Asia. | When a huge ship blocked the canal, the chokepoint stopped trade for days. | The Spartans held the narrow chokepoint at Thermopylae. | The school gate becomes a chokepoint at home time. | Oil tankers pass through the Strait of Hormuz chokepoint. | The narrow bridge was a chokepoint for traffic. | Fire exits should never become chokepoints.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Written as one word or two (chokepoint, choke point). Mostly used in geography, news and military talk. Related: bottleneck, which means much the same.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Chromium is a hard, shiny, silvery-grey metal; it is a chemical element with the symbol Cr and atomic number 24. 2) (informal) Chrome is a shiny coating of chromium put on other metals.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons chromium is mixed with iron to make stainless steel, which does not rust. It is used to plate car parts, taps and bicycle handlebars so they shine. Chromium compounds give colour to rubies (red) and emeralds (green). Our bodies need a very tiny amount of chromium. Phrases: chromium-plated, chrome.
examples from the lessons: The bike's handlebars are coated with chromium. | Stainless steel contains chromium so it does not rust. | The chemical symbol for chromium is Cr. | A little chromium makes rubies red. | The old car had shiny chromium bumpers. | Chromium is a hard, silvery metal. | The taps in the bathroom are chromium-plated.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Informally called chrome. The name comes from Greek «chroma» meaning colour, because its compounds are so colourful. Some chromium compounds are poisonous.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A cicada is a large insect with clear wings and big eyes that lives in warm places; male cicadas make a very loud buzzing or clicking song in summer. 2) Young cicadas (nymphs) live underground for years, then climb out, shed their skin and become adults.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons cicadas show life cycles and metamorphosis: they leave empty skins on trees. Some North American cicadas (periodical cicadas) come out all together every 13 or 17 years — both prime numbers. In Australia, children collect cicadas with names like Green Grocer and Black Prince. Phrases: cicada song, cicada shell, periodical cicadas.
examples from the lessons: The cicadas sang loudly all through the hot afternoon. | We found an empty cicada shell stuck to the tree. | Periodical cicadas come out every 17 years in some parts of the USA. | Male cicadas make sound with drum-like parts on their bodies. | In Australia, the Green Grocer cicada is bright green. | Cicadas suck sap from trees. | The cicada nymph lived underground for years.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced si-KAH-duh (UK) or si-KAY-duh (US). Plural cicadas. Myth: cicadas are not locusts (locusts are a kind of grasshopper). In maths, 13 and 17 are prime numbers, which helps the cicadas avoid predators with shorter cycles.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A cinchona is a tree or shrub from the Andes mountains of South America whose bark contains quinine. 2) Cinchona bark is the dried bark of this tree, used for centuries to treat malaria.
its sense in the lessons: In science and history lessons cinchona bark was used by Indigenous peoples of Peru and Bolivia and later brought to Europe; quinine from it was the first effective medicine against malaria. Quinine gives tonic water its bitter taste. The cinchona tree appears on Peru's coat of arms. Phrases: cinchona bark, quinine.
examples from the lessons: Quinine, a medicine for malaria, comes from cinchona bark. | The cinchona tree grows in the Andes mountains. | People in Peru used cinchona bark long before Europeans arrived. | Tonic water tastes bitter because of quinine from cinchona. | The cinchona tree is shown on Peru's coat of arms. | Explorers smuggled cinchona seeds to grow the tree in Asia. | Cinchona bark helped save many lives from malaria.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced sin-KOH-nuh. Today malaria is treated with newer medicines, but quinine is still used sometimes. Do not take bark or plants as medicine yourself.

part of speech: proper noun (Cinderella — a story character); noun (a Cinderella — something or someone ignored, figurative)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Cinderella is the girl in a famous fairy tale who is treated badly by her stepmother and stepsisters, goes to the prince's ball with help from her fairy godmother, loses a glass slipper and marries the prince. 2) (figurative) A Cinderella is a person or thing that is ignored or treated as less important but deserves more attention. 3) (sport) A Cinderella story is when a small, unexpected team or person does very well.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons Cinderella is a classic fairy tale told in many countries (versions by Charles Perrault and the Brothers Grimm, and very old ones from China and Egypt). At Christmas it is a favourite UK pantomime. Figuratively, news writers say a subject is «the Cinderella of the school curriculum». Phrases: Cinderella story, be home by midnight like Cinderella.
examples from the lessons: Cinderella's fairy godmother turned a pumpkin into a coach. | At midnight Cinderella ran away and lost her glass slipper. | We saw Cinderella as a pantomime at Christmas. | The little village team had a Cinderella run to the final. | Music is often the Cinderella subject at some schools. | «Be home by midnight, Cinderella!» joked Dad. | There are hundreds of versions of the Cinderella story around the world.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital C for the character. The name means «little cinder girl», because she slept in the ashes by the fire. Not used in maths.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Clinically means in a medical way, as judged by doctors examining patients: «clinically tested», «clinically proven». 2) Clinically can mean in a cold, calm, unemotional way, like a hospital. 3) (sport, informal) Clinically means very efficiently and accurately: «He finished clinically.»
its sense in the lessons: In health and science lessons «clinically tested» means a product or medicine was tried on people in a careful study; adverts use «clinically proven» to sound trustworthy, so it is wise to ask what was tested. «Clinically obese» or «clinically depressed» are medical terms. In football reports a striker who scores calmly «finished clinically». Phrases: clinically proven, clinically tested, clinically dead.
examples from the lessons: The cream has been clinically tested on sensitive skin. | Doctors said the boy was clinically well and could go home. | The advert said the toothpaste was «clinically proven», but we wanted to see the evidence. | The room was clinically clean and white. | She explained the facts clinically, without any emotion. | The striker finished clinically into the corner of the net. | Clinically depressed means a doctor has diagnosed depression.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From clinic and clinical (+ -ly). Do not confuse with «cynically». In media literacy: «clinically proven» in an advert does not always mean a big, fair study.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Coca is a bush that grows in the Andes mountains of South America; its leaves are chewed or made into tea by local people to help with tiredness and mountain sickness. 2) Coca leaves are also used to make the illegal and very dangerous drug cocaine.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and history lessons coca has been part of Andean culture for thousands of years, especially in Bolivia and Peru, where coca tea is legal and common. In health and safety lessons cocaine is a harmful, illegal drug. In history, early Coca-Cola contained a little coca extract, which was later removed. Phrases: coca leaves, coca tea.
examples from the lessons: Farmers in Bolivia grow coca on the mountainsides. | Visitors to the Andes may drink coca tea for altitude sickness. | Coca leaves have been chewed in the Andes for thousands of years. | Cocaine, an illegal drug, is made from coca leaves. | The name Coca-Cola comes from coca leaves and kola nuts. | The coca bush has small oval leaves. | Growing coca is controlled by law in many countries.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Coca is not the same as cocoa (from cacao beans, used for chocolate) or coconut — a common confusion. Uncountable. Safety: cocaine is illegal and harmful.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The cochlea is a small, spiral-shaped tube in the inner ear, shaped like a snail shell and filled with liquid. 2) It turns sound vibrations into nerve signals that travel to the brain so we can hear.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on hearing the ear has three parts: the outer ear, the middle ear (eardrum and tiny bones) and the inner ear (cochlea). Tiny hair cells inside the cochlea can be damaged by very loud noise, which causes hearing loss, so ear protection matters. A cochlear implant helps some deaf people hear. Phrases: inner ear, cochlear implant, hair cells.
examples from the lessons: The cochlea is shaped like a snail shell. | Sound makes the liquid in the cochlea move. | Hair cells in the cochlea send signals to the brain. | Very loud music can damage the cochlea. | My cousin has a cochlear implant that helps him hear. | The cochlea is in the inner ear, deep inside the skull. | Wear ear defenders at loud events to protect your cochlea.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced KOK-lee-uh. Plural cochleae or cochleas. Adjective: cochlear (a cochlear implant). The name comes from Greek for snail.

part of speech: proper noun (Collins — a surname; Collins Dictionary); noun (a collins, collinses — a tall iced drink, rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (a name) Collins is a common surname in Ireland, the UK, the USA and Australia, from the old Irish and English family names. 2) Collins is also the name of a well-known British publisher of dictionaries and school books (Collins Dictionary). 3) (rare) A collins, like a Tom Collins, is a tall cold mixed drink for adults made with lemon juice, sugar and fizzy water.
its sense in the lessons: In lessons you meet Collins as a person's surname in a story or as the name on a dictionary cover; it tells the reader who someone is or which book is used. Famous people named Collins include the Irish leader Michael Collins and the astronaut Michael Collins, who flew to the Moon on Apollo 11 but stayed in orbit. Phrases: «Mr Collins», «Mrs Collins», «the Collins Dictionary».
examples from the lessons: Mrs Collins is our new class teacher. | Look the word up in the Collins Dictionary. | Michael Collins flew round the Moon while the others walked on it. | The Collins family live next door to us. | Is your surname spelled Collins with two l's? | Dad ordered a Tom Collins at the wedding, and I had lemonade.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A name, so it starts with a capital letter: Collins. Spelled with double l. The possessive is «Collins's» or «Collins'» (both are used). Not a general English word; do not invent facts about a person called Collins.

part of speech: verb (colonise, colonises, colonised, colonising); US spelling colonize
meaning for a pupil: 1) To colonise a place means a country sends people to settle there and takes control of the land, often from the people already living there. 2) (science) When plants, animals or germs colonise a place, they spread into it and start living and growing there.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons it tells how empires such as Britain, Spain and France took over lands in America, Africa, Asia and Australia, and how this often harmed the people who already lived there. In science it is used for living things moving into a new place: moss colonises bare rock, bacteria colonise a wound. Related words: colony, colonist, colonial, colonisation, decolonise.
examples from the lessons: Britain began to colonise Australia in 1788. | Settlers from Europe colonised large parts of North America. | The First Nations people did not invite anyone to colonise their land. | Weeds quickly colonised the empty car park. | Bacteria can colonise a cut if you do not clean it. | Some scientists dream of colonising Mars one day. | Lichens are often the first living things to colonise bare rock.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK, Australian, NZ and Irish spelling: colonise; US and usually Canadian: colonize. Past: colonised. Noun: colonisation; a person: colonist; the place: colony. Not the same as «colon» (the punctuation mark or part of the gut). Colonising is seen very differently by the settlers and by the people whose land was taken; good history tells both sides.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A communist is a person who believes in communism: the idea that land, factories and wealth should be owned by everyone together, not by private people, so that people are more equal. 2) (adjective) Communist describes a country, party or government that follows these ideas, usually run by one party, like the old Soviet Union or China today. 3) (often written with a capital) A Communist is a member of a Communist Party.
its sense in the lessons: In history and politics lessons it comes up with the Russian Revolution, the Soviet Union, the Cold War, China, Cuba and North Korea. It tells the reader about a political idea and system. Phrases: «the Communist Party», «a communist country», «communist rule», «the Cold War between communist and capitalist countries». People argue a lot about communism: supporters praise its aim of equality; critics point to one-party rule, lack of freedom and famines under some communist governments.
examples from the lessons: Karl Marx wrote about communist ideas in the 1800s. | The Soviet Union was a communist country. | China is ruled by the Communist Party. | My grandad grew up in Ukraine when it was under communist rule. | During the Cold War, communist and capitalist countries were rivals. | In a communist system, the state owns the factories. | Some people called him a communist as an insult.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: a communist, two communists. Capital C when it means a member of a named party (the Communist Party). Related: communism (the idea), capitalism (its rival idea), socialist (a related, milder idea). Not the same as «community», though both come from the Latin for «shared». Using «communist» as an insult is common in arguments; say who is calling whom that.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A confederacy is a group of states, tribes or people who join together for a shared purpose, like defence, while keeping much of their own power. 2) (history, USA) The Confederacy was the group of eleven southern US states that broke away in 1861 to keep slavery and fought the North in the American Civil War. 3) (formal) A secret group that plans something together, especially something wrong.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons it appears with the American Civil War (the Confederacy versus the Union), and with alliances such as the Iroquois Confederacy of Native American nations. It tells the reader that several groups are allied but loosely. Phrases: «the Confederate States», «Confederate flag», «join the confederacy». The Confederacy lost the war in 1865 and slavery was ended.
examples from the lessons: The Iroquois Confederacy joined six Native American nations. | The Confederacy fought the Union in the Civil War. | Abraham Lincoln led the North against the Confederacy. | The Confederacy wanted to keep slavery. | Several tribes formed a confederacy to protect their lands. | Today many people see the Confederate flag as a symbol of racism. | The pirates had a confederacy to share the treasure.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a confederacy, confederacies. «The Confederacy» with a capital means the southern US states of 1861–1865. Related: confederate (a member or ally; also an adjective), confederation (a similar union, e.g. Canada became a confederation in 1867). Not the same as «federation», where the central government is stronger.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Continually means again and again, very often, with short breaks in between. 2) Sometimes it is used to mean all the time, without stopping.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and stories it often shows something is annoying or tiring: «He continually interrupts». In science it can describe something that keeps happening: the Earth is continually moving. It tells the reader that an action repeats a lot. Often confused with «continuously».
examples from the lessons: My little brother continually asks «Why?». | The teacher had to remind them continually to stay in their seats. | The phone rang continually all afternoon. | The coastline is continually changing because of the waves. | She was continually late for football practice. | Scientists are continually finding new species in the rainforest. | Prices in the shop seem to go up continually.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from the adjective «continual». Spelled with double l: continually. Trap: «continually» usually means repeated with gaps (the dog barked continually all night, in bursts), while «continuously» means without any break at all (the river flows continuously). Many people mix them up, and in casual talk they are often used the same way.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Conventionally means in the usual, normal, accepted way that most people do things. 2) (science, maths) Done by a usual agreed rule, a convention, such as writing numbers in a certain way. 3) (farming) Conventionally grown food is grown with the usual modern methods, often with chemicals, not organically.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life it describes ordinary behaviour or dress: «conventionally dressed». In maths and science it shows an agreed custom: conventionally, the x-axis is horizontal; current is conventionally said to flow from + to −. In stories it can show that a character is ordinary or follows the rules. Phrases: «conventionally attractive», «conventionally grown».
examples from the lessons: He was dressed conventionally in a suit and tie. | Conventionally, we write the x-axis across the page. | Conventionally, a story has a beginning, a middle and an end. | These apples were grown conventionally, not organically. | She chose not to live conventionally and travelled the world in a van. | Electric current is conventionally shown flowing from positive to negative. | In maths, angles are conventionally measured anticlockwise.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from «conventional» (usual) and «convention» (an agreed custom, or a big meeting). Spelled with double l: conventionally. Opposite: unconventionally. In science, a «conventional» direction can be different from what really happens (electrons actually move from − to +), so conventionally does not always mean «truly».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Convergence is when lines, roads, paths or things come together and meet at one point. 2) Convergence is when ideas, opinions or groups become more and more alike. 3) (maths) Convergence is when a list of numbers gets closer and closer to one fixed number. 4) (science) In geography, a convergence is where two plates of the Earth's crust or two ocean currents push towards each other.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and geometry it means lines meeting or a sequence approaching a limit (1/2, 3/4, 7/8 … gets close to 1). In geography, plate convergence makes mountains and volcanoes. In everyday talk it means people or things coming together. Opposite: divergence. Phrases: «point of convergence», «convergence of ideas».
examples from the lessons: The convergence of the two rivers makes one big river. | Follow the paths to their point of convergence. | Mountains like the Himalayas formed at a convergence of two plates. | There was a convergence of opinions after the long debate. | The sum 1/2 + 1/4 + 1/8 + … shows convergence towards 1. | In the drawing, railway tracks show convergence in the distance. | The convergence of phones and cameras means one device now does both.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly uncountable: convergence, though «a convergence» is used for one meeting point. Verb: converge (the roads converge); adjective: convergent. Opposite: divergence, diverge. In maths, a sequence that converges gets as close as you like to its limit but may never actually reach it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A couplet is a pair of lines of poetry that go together, usually rhyming and with the same rhythm. 2) (rare) A couplet can mean a pair of anything.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons pupils write and spot couplets in poems and songs. A rhyming couplet often ends a poem or a sonnet with a strong, neat point. It tells the reader where two lines form one small unit. Phrases: «rhyming couplet», «a closing couplet», «heroic couplet» (lines of ten syllables).
examples from the lessons: «Twinkle, twinkle, little star, / How I wonder what you are» is a couplet. | Write a rhyming couplet about your pet. | The poem is made of six couplets. | A sonnet by Shakespeare ends with a couplet. | The last couplet made everyone laugh. | Can you find the couplet that does not rhyme? | My birthday card had a funny couplet inside.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a couplet, couplets. A couplet = 2 lines; a tercet = 3; a quatrain = 4; a stanza or verse is a group of lines. Pronounced «CUP-let». Do not confuse with «couple» (two people or two things) — a couplet is about lines of poetry.

meaning for a pupil: 1) CPR stands for cardiopulmonary resuscitation: first aid for someone whose heart has stopped and who is not breathing, done by pushing hard and fast on the middle of their chest, sometimes with rescue breaths. 2) It is said as three letters: «C-P-R».
its sense in the lessons: In safety and health lessons pupils learn that CPR can keep blood moving to the brain until an ambulance arrives. Children learn: check for danger, call for help (999 in the UK and Ireland, 911 in the USA and Canada, 000 in Australia, 111 in New Zealand), then start chest compressions if trained. Phrases: «do CPR», «give CPR», «perform CPR», «learn CPR», «CPR training». A defibrillator (AED) is often used with CPR.
examples from the lessons: The lifeguard gave him CPR until the ambulance came. | We learned CPR on a dummy at school. | Push hard and fast in the middle of the chest when you do CPR. | Call for help before you start CPR. | Dad took a CPR course at work. | CPR helped save the footballer's life. | The song «Stayin' Alive» has about the right beat for CPR.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always written in capitals: CPR (here in lower case only as a dictionary headword). Uncountable: «give CPR», not «a CPR». Myth from films: CPR does not usually wake someone up straight away; it keeps them alive until doctors and a defibrillator can help. Pupils should get proper training; in an emergency, calling for adult help comes first. About 100–120 compressions a minute is the advised speed.

part of speech: verb (crop, crops, cropped, cropping — past and -ed form); adjective (cropped)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Cropped is the past form of crop: to cut something short, like hair or grass, or to cut off the edges of a picture. 2) (adjective) Cropped clothes are cut short on purpose, such as a cropped top or cropped trousers. 3) (adjective) Cropped hair is cut very short. 4) (verb) If something cropped up, it appeared or happened suddenly, without being expected.
its sense in the lessons: In computing and art lessons pupils crop photos to cut off the parts they do not want. In everyday life it describes fashion and haircuts. In farming, a field that has been cropped has had crops grown or cut on it. The phrase «crop up» means a problem or chance that turns up suddenly.
examples from the lessons: I cropped the photo so only my face showed. | She wore a cropped denim jacket. | His hair was cropped short for summer. | The sheep cropped the grass very close. | A problem cropped up, so we were late. | The field was cropped with wheat last year. | Your name cropped up when we were talking about the play.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double the p: crop → cropped, cropping. «Crop up» is a phrasal verb: «Something cropped up». A crop (noun) is also a plant grown for food, like wheat; and a crop top is a short top. In computing, «crop» and «resize» are different: cropping cuts parts away, resizing makes the whole picture bigger or smaller.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Cuneiform is one of the oldest kinds of writing in the world, made of small wedge-shaped marks pressed into wet clay with a reed, first used in ancient Mesopotamia (now Iraq) over 5,000 years ago. 2) (adjective) Cuneiform describes something shaped like a wedge, or written in this script.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons it comes with the Sumerians, Babylonians, Assyrians and the first cities. It tells the reader about how writing began: for counting grain, animals and taxes, then for laws, letters and stories like the Epic of Gilgamesh. Clay tablets with cuneiform are kept in museums such as the British Museum.
examples from the lessons: The Sumerians wrote in cuneiform on clay tablets. | Cuneiform marks look like tiny triangles and lines. | Scribes pressed a reed into wet clay to write cuneiform. | Some cuneiform tablets are lists of sheep and barley. | We tried writing our names in cuneiform with lollipop sticks and clay. | The British Museum has thousands of cuneiform tablets. | Experts can now read cuneiform.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «written in cuneiform». Pronounced «KYOO-nee-i-form» (UK also «kyoo-NAY-i-form»). From Latin «cuneus», a wedge. It is a writing system, not a language: it was used for several languages, such as Sumerian and Akkadian. Not to be confused with Egyptian hieroglyphs, which are pictures.

part of speech: adjective (curt, curter, curtest — comparatives rare; usually more curt)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Curt means rudely short: a curt reply uses very few words and sounds cold or unfriendly. 2) (rare) Curt can mean simply brief or short.
its sense in the lessons: In stories it shows a character's mood: a curt answer tells the reader that someone is cross, busy or does not want to talk. In everyday life it helps describe how people speak. Phrases: «a curt reply», «a curt nod», «curt tone». Related adverb: curtly.
examples from the lessons: «No,» she said in a curt voice. | His curt reply made me feel silly for asking. | The shopkeeper gave us a curt nod. | Try not to be curt with your little sister. | The email was curt: «Not today.» | The coach was curt after the team lost. | I'm sorry I was so curt with you this morning.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective; adverb: curtly; noun: curtness. Do not confuse with «Kurt» or «Curt» (boys' names) or with «curtain». A curt answer is short in a rude way; a «brief» answer is just short, not necessarily rude.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Cyan is a bright greenish-blue colour, like a clear tropical sea. 2) (science, printing) Cyan is one of the main colours of printer ink, together with magenta, yellow and black (CMYK).
its sense in the lessons: In art and computing lessons cyan appears in colour mixing: in light, green + blue light make cyan; in printing, cyan ink absorbs red light. Printers often need a new cyan cartridge. It tells the reader an exact shade of blue-green. Related colours: turquoise, aqua, teal.
examples from the lessons: The printer has run out of cyan ink. | Cyan is a mix of blue and green light. | She painted the sky cyan in her picture. | The swimming pool water looked cyan in the sun. | CMYK stands for cyan, magenta, yellow and black. | On the screen, cyan and red together make white light. | The cyan text was hard to read on the white page.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced «SY-an». Uncountable when it is a colour name. Cyan is very close to «aqua» and «turquoise»; in screen colours, cyan and aqua are the same. In printing, CMY are the subtractive primary colours; in light, RGB (red, green, blue) are the additive primary colours, and cyan is the opposite of red.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A dashboard is the panel at the front of a car, under the windscreen, with the speedometer, dials, lights and controls. 2) (computing) A dashboard is a screen on a computer or app that shows the most important information at a glance, often with charts and numbers. 3) (history) On an old horse-drawn carriage, a dashboard was a board at the front to stop mud splashing the driver.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life it is the front of the car; children may be told not to put feet on the dashboard. In computing and maths lessons, a dashboard shows data like scores, weather or website visits in graphs. It tells the reader where information is shown. Phrases: «on the dashboard», «a warning light on the dashboard».
examples from the lessons: Mum checked the speed on the dashboard. | A red light came on on the dashboard. | Don't put your feet on the dashboard! | The satnav is stuck to the dashboard. | Our class dashboard shows how many books we have read. | The weather app has a dashboard with temperature and wind speed. | The teacher's dashboard shows who has finished the quiz.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a dashboard, dashboards. Also called «dash» informally: «on the dash». In the UK people also say «fascia» for the car part. In safety: never sit with feet on the dashboard, because the airbag comes out of it in a crash.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To deflect something means to make it change direction, especially by hitting it, like a ball bouncing off a player. 2) To deflect attention, blame or a question means to turn it away from yourself or onto something else. 3) (science) Light, a ray or a magnet's needle is deflected when it is turned to a new direction.
its sense in the lessons: In sport it describes a ball hitting a player and changing direction (a deflected shot). In science lessons, mirrors deflect light and magnets deflect a compass needle. In stories and everyday life it shows a character avoiding blame or a hard question. Phrases: «deflect the blame», «deflect criticism», «deflect attention».
examples from the lessons: The goalkeeper deflected the ball over the bar. | The shot was deflected off a defender and went in. | A mirror can deflect a beam of light. | The shield deflected the arrow. | He tried to deflect the blame onto his sister. | She deflected the question by talking about the weather. | The magnet deflected the compass needle.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: deflected. Noun: deflection. In football, a goal that is deflected may count as an own goal if it was heading wide. Not the same as «reflect»: reflect means bounce back (a mirror reflects); deflect means turn aside. Deflecting blame is often seen as unfair.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To delude someone means to trick them into believing something that is not true. 2) To delude yourself means to believe something untrue because you want it to be true.
its sense in the lessons: In stories it shows a character who is fooled, or who fools himself: «Don't delude yourself». In everyday life it is often used when someone has false hopes. Related words: deluded (adjective: believing false things), delusion (a false belief). Phrases: «delude yourself», «deluded into thinking».
examples from the lessons: Don't delude yourself — you can't learn the whole song in five minutes. | The fox deluded the crow into dropping the cheese. | He was deluded into thinking he would win easily. | She deluded herself that nobody had noticed. | Advertisements can delude people into buying things they don't need. | The king was deluded by flattering advisers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: deluded. Noun: delusion; adjective: deluded («a deluded man»). Do not confuse with «dilute» (to make weaker with water) or «elude» (to escape from). «Deluded» is fairly strong; calling someone deluded can be rude. In medicine, a «delusion» is a fixed false belief that can be a sign of illness.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The derivation of a word is where it comes from and how it was made, for example from Latin or from another English word. 2) (maths) A derivation is a step-by-step working that shows how a formula or answer is reached. 3) (formal) Derivation is getting something from a source, like getting a product from a plant.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons it is about word origins (etymology) and making new words with prefixes and suffixes: «happiness» is derived from «happy». In maths and science, a derivation shows how a rule is worked out from other rules. It tells the reader where something comes from. Phrases: «of Latin derivation», «the derivation of a formula».
examples from the lessons: The derivation of «tele» is a Greek word meaning «far». | «Unkind» is a derivation from «kind». | The word «sandwich» has an interesting derivation. | Show the derivation of the area formula. | The teacher wrote the derivation on the board step by step. | Many English words are of French derivation. | The derivation of rubber from trees takes a lot of work.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a derivation, derivations. Verb: derive (derive from); adjective: derivative, derived. In grammar, derivation (making new words: kind → kindness) is different from inflection (changing the form of the same word: kind → kinder). «Etymology» is the study of word origins.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To deteriorate means to become worse, more and more, over time. 2) (things) Buildings, food, roads or materials deteriorate when they wear out, rot or break down.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life it is used for weather, health, behaviour or things getting worse: «the weather deteriorated». In science it describes food going off, metal rusting or old paper falling apart. In stories it builds tension: «Her health deteriorated». Opposite: improve. Phrases: «deteriorate rapidly», «a deteriorating situation».
examples from the lessons: The weather deteriorated, so the match was called off. | Grandpa's eyesight has deteriorated with age. | Without a roof, the old castle deteriorated quickly. | Fruit deteriorates fast in hot weather. | His behaviour deteriorated after lunch. | The road surface has deteriorated badly over the winter. | The patient's condition deteriorated overnight.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: deteriorated. Noun: deterioration. Pronounced «di-TEER-ee-uh-rate» (five syllables); a common mistake is to say or write «deteriate». It is a formal word for «get worse». It is intransitive: something deteriorates by itself; you do not «deteriorate something».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A disappearance is when someone or something goes out of sight or cannot be found any more. 2) The disappearance of something, such as a species or a habit, is when it stops existing.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and mysteries it starts the plot: «the disappearance of the cat». In science and geography it is used for animals dying out, ice melting or forests being cut down. In the news it may describe a missing person. Phrases: «a mysterious disappearance», «since her disappearance».
examples from the lessons: The disappearance of my homework is a mystery. | Police are looking into the disappearance of a boat. | The sudden disappearance of the magician amazed us. | Scientists worry about the disappearance of bees. | The disappearance of the dinosaurs happened about 66 million years ago. | After the disappearance of the sun, it got cold. | Nobody noticed the cake's disappearance until teatime.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a disappearance, disappearances. Spelling: dis + appear + ance — one s, double p. Verb: disappear; opposite: appearance. A common spelling mistake is «dissappearance».

part of speech: verb (diss, disses, dissed, dissing) — slang; noun (a diss, disses — slang)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (slang) To diss someone means to show them disrespect, by insulting them or saying unkind things about them. 2) (slang, noun) A diss is an insult, especially in a rap song (a diss track).
its sense in the lessons: In everyday talk among teenagers it means being rude or unkind: «Don't diss my football team». It comes from hip hop slang in the USA in the 1980s and is a clipped form of «disrespect». In lessons about kindness online, dissing people is a form of being mean. Phrases: «diss someone», «a diss track».
examples from the lessons: Don't diss my trainers, they're new! | He dissed the other team after the match. | That rapper released a diss track about his rival. | Stop dissing your little brother. | She felt dissed when nobody said hello. | Was that a diss or a joke? | It's not cool to diss people online.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Slang, informal; do not use in a school essay. Also spelled «dis». Double s in the past form: dissed, dissing. Short for «disrespect». Not related to the prefix «dis-» in words like «disagree», though it comes from the same part of «disrespect».

part of speech: noun (a doge, doges; the Doge); noun (Doge — slang, internet meme)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (history) The Doge was the elected ruler of the old city states of Venice and Genoa in Italy, for about a thousand years until 1797. 2) (slang, internet) Doge is a joke internet meme of a Shiba Inu dog with funny broken English like «much wow, very amaze». 3) Dogecoin is an online money that started as a joke based on this meme.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons it comes with Venice, its canals, trade and the Doge's Palace. Online, children see «doge» memes and Dogecoin in the news. It tells the reader a ruler of Venice, or the dog meme, depending on the context.
examples from the lessons: The Doge of Venice lived in a grand palace. | The Doge was chosen for life. | We visited the Doge's Palace on holiday in Venice. | Venice was ruled by doges for centuries. | My cousin sent me a doge meme: «such homework, very wow». | Dogecoin started as a joke. | The doge meme uses a Shiba Inu dog.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced «dohzh» or «dohj» for the Venice ruler (Italian), and usually «dohj» or «dohg» for the meme. Countable: a doge, doges. The meme is slang and not for formal writing. Dogecoin and other online coins can go up and down very fast; they are risky, not safe savings.

part of speech: adjective (dominant; more dominant, most dominant); noun (a dominant — music, rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Dominant means the strongest, most important or most powerful in a group. 2) Dominant can mean the most noticeable, the thing you see most, like a dominant colour. 3) (science) A dominant gene is one whose feature shows up even if you got it from only one parent. 4) (music) The dominant is the fifth note of a scale.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and sport it means stronger than the rest: «a dominant team». In science (genetics), brown eyes are often given as an example of a dominant feature (simplified), while blue are recessive. With animals, the dominant one leads the pack. Most people have a dominant hand, the one they write with. Phrases: «dominant hand», «dominant species», «dominant player».
examples from the lessons: Lions are the dominant animals on the savannah. | My dominant hand is my left hand. | Red is the dominant colour in the painting. | The dominant wolf eats first. | Our team was dominant in the second half. | The gene for brown eyes is usually dominant. | English is the dominant language on the internet.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective; noun: dominance; verb: dominate. Spelled with -ant (not -ent). Opposite in genetics: recessive. Myth: eye colour is controlled by several genes, so the simple «brown beats blue» rule is only an approximation.

part of speech: verb (drool, drools, drooled, drooling); noun (drool, uncountable)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To drool means to let spit (saliva) run out of your mouth, like a baby or a hungry dog. 2) (informal) To drool over something means to want it very much or to admire it in a silly way. 3) (noun) Drool is the spit that runs from someone's mouth.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life babies drool when their teeth come through and dogs drool when they see food. In science, saliva helps you digest food; Pavlov's dogs drooled at a bell. In stories and jokes, «drooling over» a cake or a new game shows great wanting. Phrases: «drool over», «drool on».
examples from the lessons: The baby drooled all over my shirt. | Our dog drools when he smells sausages. | I woke up and there was drool on my pillow. | My brother drools over every new video game. | The cakes in the window made me drool. | Babies drool a lot when they are teething. | Wipe the drool off your chin!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: drooled, drooling — one l in both UK and US spelling. Noun drool is uncountable. Informal; a more formal word is «salivate». «Drool over» is used in a jokey way.

part of speech: verb (-ing form of drum: drum, drums, drummed, drumming); noun (drumming, uncountable)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Drumming is playing a drum or drums. 2) Drumming is a repeated beating or tapping sound, like rain on a roof or fingers on a table. 3) (noun) Drumming is the music or skill of playing drums.
its sense in the lessons: In music lessons it is about rhythm and beat; drumming is used in many cultures, such as African, Japanese taiko and Irish bodhrán drumming. In stories it describes sounds: «the drumming of rain». In everyday life, drumming your fingers shows impatience. Phrases: «drumming your fingers», «drum up support», «drum something into someone».
examples from the lessons: She is learning drumming at school. | The drumming of the rain kept me awake. | He was drumming his fingers on the desk. | Taiko drumming comes from Japan. | The woodpecker was drumming on the tree. | We heard drumming from the parade. | They are drumming up support for the school fair.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double the m: drum → drummed, drumming, drummer. «Drum up» means to get people to help or buy. «Drum something into someone» means to teach it by repeating it many times. Woodpeckers drum on trees to make a noise, not only to find food.

part of speech: verb (dub, dubs, dubbed, dubbing); noun (dub, uncountable — music)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To dub a film or TV show means to replace the voices with voices in another language, or to add sounds to it. 2) To dub someone means to give them a nickname or a name: «They dubbed him the Wizard». 3) (history) To dub a knight means to make someone a knight by touching his shoulders with a sword. 4) (music) Dub is a kind of reggae music from Jamaica with lots of echo and bass.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life children watch cartoons that are dubbed into English from Japanese or other languages. In stories and the news, people or things are «dubbed» with nicknames. In history lessons, a king dubbed knights. It tells the reader something was named or given new voices.
examples from the lessons: The film was dubbed into French. | Newspapers dubbed her «the Queen of the Court». | The king dubbed him Sir Lancelot. | Do you prefer anime dubbed or with subtitles? | The actor dubbed the voice of the lion. | The class dubbed our hamster «Mr Fluff». | Dub music has a deep, booming bass.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double the b: dubbed, dubbing. Dubbing (new voices) is different from subtitles (written words on screen). «Dubbed» often goes with a name in quotation marks. In slang, «dub» (USA) can mean a win (from «W»), as in «We got the dub».

part of speech: verb (-ing form of dub: dub, dubs, dubbed, dubbing); noun (dubbing, uncountable)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Dubbing is replacing the spoken words of a film or show with words in another language, said by new voice actors. 2) Dubbing is giving someone or something a nickname. 3) (history) Dubbing is the ceremony of making someone a knight. 4) (old) Dubbing (also «dubbin») is a grease for making leather boots soft and waterproof.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, dubbing decides whether a foreign cartoon is heard in English or read with subtitles. In media lessons pupils talk about dubbing versus subtitles. In history lessons dubbing is part of becoming a knight. Phrases: «English dubbing», «the dubbing is bad».
examples from the lessons: The dubbing in this cartoon is really good. | Dubbing actors must match the mouth movements. | My dad hates dubbing and prefers subtitles. | They are dubbing the film into Spanish. | The dubbing of a knight was a special ceremony. | Fans were dubbing him «the Flash». | Rub some dubbing on your football boots to keep them soft.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double b. As a noun it is uncountable: «the dubbing». Do not confuse with «doubling». The boot grease is usually spelled «dubbin» (UK). Bad dubbing, where lips and words don't match, is a common joke.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A duchy is an area of land ruled by a duke or a duchess. 2) (UK) The Duchy of Cornwall and the Duchy of Lancaster are special estates of land owned by the British royal family.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons it appears with kings, dukes and medieval Europe: many countries were once split into duchies, like the Duchy of Normandy. Luxembourg is still a Grand Duchy today. It tells the reader a land ruled by a duke. Related: duke, duchess, kingdom, principality.
examples from the lessons: William was the Duke of Normandy and ruled the duchy. | Luxembourg is a Grand Duchy. | The prince gets money from the Duchy of Cornwall. | The duchy was smaller than a kingdom. | Germany was once made of many duchies and kingdoms. | The duke protected the people of his duchy. | Duchy Originals sells biscuits from royal land.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: plural duchies (y → ies). Pronounced «DUTCH-ee». Related: duke (man), duchess (woman or a duke's wife). A duchy is smaller than a kingdom; a county was ruled by a count or earl. Not to be confused with «Dutch».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A dumpling is a small ball of dough that is boiled, steamed or fried, sometimes filled with meat or vegetables. 2) A dumpling is a pudding of fruit wrapped in pastry, like an apple dumpling. 3) (informal) Dumpling is a fond name for a small, chubby child or pet.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life dumplings come from many food cultures: British dumplings in stew, Chinese jiaozi, Polish pierogi, Ukrainian varenyky, Japanese gyoza. They are popular at Chinese New Year. In maths, sharing dumplings is a common problem. Phrases: «stew and dumplings», «steamed dumplings».
examples from the lessons: Grandma makes stew with fluffy dumplings. | We ate pork dumplings at the Chinese restaurant. | My mum and I fold dumplings for Lunar New Year. | Ukrainian varenyky are dumplings filled with potato or cherries. | There are 24 dumplings shared among 4 people, so each gets 6. | An apple dumpling is wrapped in pastry and baked. | «Come here, my little dumpling!» said Gran.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a dumpling, dumplings. The pet name is affectionate, but calling someone a dumpling can sound like teasing about weight. In maths problems, «each», «share equally» and «in all» show whether to divide or multiply the dumplings.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An ecosystem is all the living things in one place — plants, animals, fungi and tiny germs — together with the non-living things around them, like water, soil, air and sunlight, all affecting each other. 2) (figurative) An ecosystem is a group of things or companies that work closely together, like apps, phones and computers made to work together.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons pupils study ecosystems such as ponds, forests, coral reefs, deserts and the Australian bush; they learn about food chains, producers, consumers and decomposers, and how one change (pollution, a new species) affects the whole system. In everyday talk «tech ecosystem» means products that work together. Phrases: «a balanced ecosystem», «damage the ecosystem», «marine ecosystem».
examples from the lessons: A pond is a small ecosystem. | The Great Barrier Reef is a huge ecosystem. | Rabbits harmed the Australian ecosystem when they spread. | Every living thing in an ecosystem depends on others. | Pollution can damage the whole ecosystem. | We built a mini ecosystem in a jar. | Removing wolves changed the ecosystem of Yellowstone. | My phone and tablet are part of the same ecosystem.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: an ecosystem (use «an» because it starts with a vowel sound). Pronounced «EE-koh-sis-tem». An ecosystem includes non-living parts; a «habitat» is just the home of one kind of living thing; a «community» is only the living things.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An elf is a small magical creature in stories and folk tales, often with pointed ears, who can be helpful or tricky. 2) In Christmas stories, elves are Santa's helpers who make toys at the North Pole. 3) In fantasy books and games, like «The Lord of the Rings», elves are tall, wise, beautiful people who live very long.
its sense in the lessons: In stories it tells the reader there is magic: elves help the shoemaker, play tricks or fight in fantasy battles. At Christmas, «Elf on the Shelf» is a toy elf families move around. It is a made-up creature, not real. Phrases: «Santa's elves», «elf on the shelf», «elf ears».
examples from the lessons: The elves made shoes for the poor shoemaker. | Santa's elves wrap presents in the workshop. | Our Elf on the Shelf moves every night. | Legolas is an elf in «The Lord of the Rings». | She dressed up as an elf for the school play. | The elf had pointy ears and a green hat. | In Iceland some people tell stories about hidden elves.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular plural: one elf, two elves (f → ves, like shelf → shelves). Adjective: elfin or elvish. Elves are imaginary. Not the same as a «pixie» or «fairy», though stories often mix them up. «Elf» is also the name of a Christmas film.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Emergent means starting to appear, grow or become known. 2) (science) An emergent plant grows in water but its top sticks up out of the water, like a reed. 3) (science, rainforest) The emergent layer is the very top of a rainforest, where the tallest trees poke above the canopy. 4) (formal) An emergent property is something a whole group has that its single parts do not have.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and science lessons pupils learn rainforest layers: forest floor, understorey, canopy, emergent layer. In pond studies, emergent plants grow at the edge. In everyday or formal talk, emergent means new and growing: «emergent readers» are children just starting to read. Phrases: «emergent layer», «emergent writing», «emergent technology».
examples from the lessons: The emergent layer is home to eagles and monkeys. | The tallest trees in the rainforest are emergent trees. | Reeds are emergent plants at the edge of the pond. | Teachers help emergent readers with simple books. | An ant colony is clever even though each ant is simple — that is an emergent property. | Emergent countries are growing quickly.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective only. Related: emerge (verb), emergence (noun). Do not confuse with «emergency» (a sudden dangerous event) — they share a root but mean different things. «Emerging» is the more common everyday word: «emerging markets».

meaning for a pupil: 1) An empress is a woman who rules an empire. 2) An empress is the wife of an emperor.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons it appears with famous rulers like Empress Catherine the Great of Russia, Empress Maria Theresa of Austria, Empress Wu of China and Queen Victoria, who was Empress of India. In fairy tales an empress is like a very powerful queen. Phrases: «Empress of India», «empress dowager» (the mother or widow of an emperor).
examples from the lessons: Catherine the Great was Empress of Russia. | Queen Victoria was also called Empress of India. | Wu Zetian was the only woman to rule China as empress. | The empress wore a gold crown. | The emperor and the empress greeted the visitors. | In the story, the empress loved nightingales.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: an empress, empresses (add -es after s). Male form: emperor. With a name it has a capital: Empress Matilda. An empress rules an empire; a queen rules a kingdom. Starts with a vowel sound, so «an empress».

part of speech: noun (an encyclopedia, encyclopedias); UK also encyclopaedia
meaning for a pupil: 1) An encyclopedia is a book or a set of books, or a website, with information about many subjects, usually in alphabetical order. 2) (figurative) A person who knows a lot is sometimes called a walking encyclopedia.
its sense in the lessons: In school and the library pupils use encyclopedias for research projects; online encyclopedias like Wikipedia are written by volunteers. Teachers remind children to check facts in more than one source. Phrases: «look it up in an encyclopedia», «an online encyclopedia», «a walking encyclopedia».
examples from the lessons: Look up «volcanoes» in the encyclopedia. | Our library has a children's encyclopedia of animals. | Wikipedia is an online encyclopedia. | My grandad had a whole shelf of encyclopedias. | She knows everything about dinosaurs — she's a walking encyclopedia! | The encyclopedia has a picture of every planet. | Check the encyclopedia and one other source.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: an encyclopedia (use «an»). US spelling: encyclopedia; UK sometimes: encyclopaedia (both correct in the UK). Pronounced «en-SY-kloh-PEE-dee-uh». Adjective: encyclopedic (knowing a lot). Not the same as a dictionary, which explains words, not topics.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To enlist means to join the army, navy or air force. 2) To enlist someone's help means to ask them to help you and get them to agree.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons it is used for soldiers joining up, for example in the First World War when many young men enlisted, some lying about their age. In everyday life it means getting people to help: «We enlisted Dad to carry the boxes». Phrases: «enlist in the army», «enlist the help of».
examples from the lessons: My great-grandad enlisted in the navy when he was eighteen. | Thousands of men enlisted in 1914. | She enlisted in the air force after school. | We enlisted our neighbour to help find the cat. | The teacher enlisted parents to run the bake sale. | Some boys lied about their age to enlist.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: enlisted. Noun: enlistment. An «enlisted» soldier in the USA is one who is not an officer. Opposite in the army: discharge, leave. Not to be confused with «list» or «listen».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Environmental means about the natural world — air, water, land, plants and animals — and how people affect it. 2) Environmental can mean about the surroundings or conditions around someone, like noise or light.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography lessons it goes with pollution, climate change, recycling and protecting wildlife: «environmental problems», «environmental group». In everyday life children hear about environmental campaigns and eco-clubs. Phrases: «environmental damage», «environmental issues», «environmentally friendly».
examples from the lessons: Plastic in the sea is a big environmental problem. | Our school has an environmental club. | Cutting down forests causes environmental damage. | Environmental scientists study rivers and soil. | Is this packaging environmentally friendly? | The new road had an environmental report. | Greta Thunberg is an environmental campaigner.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective; adverb: environmentally. Spelling trap: «environment» has an n before the m — environ-ment-al. Noun: environment; person: environmentalist. Starts with a vowel sound: «an environmental problem».

meaning for a pupil: 1) An envoy is a person sent by a government or a ruler to take a message to another country or to talk for them. 2) A special envoy is someone sent to deal with one problem, such as peace talks.
its sense in the lessons: In history and news lessons envoys carry messages between kings, presidents or the United Nations to make deals or stop wars. In stories an envoy brings news from a far kingdom. Phrases: «special envoy», «peace envoy», «UN envoy».
examples from the lessons: The king sent an envoy to the queen of the next kingdom. | A UN envoy is trying to arrange peace talks. | The envoy brought a letter from the emperor. | The president's special envoy visited the region. | Envoys travelled for weeks on horseback in the old days. | The envoy was treated as an honoured guest.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: an envoy, envoys (y → s, because there is a vowel before the y). Pronounced «EN-voy». Similar: ambassador, diplomat, messenger. An ambassador lives in the other country; an envoy is often sent for a particular job.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To eradicate something bad means to get rid of it completely, so that it no longer exists. 2) (science, health) To eradicate a disease means to destroy it everywhere in the world.
its sense in the lessons: In science and history lessons pupils learn that smallpox was eradicated in 1980 thanks to vaccines, and that people are trying to eradicate polio and malaria. In geography and nature lessons, people try to eradicate pests like rats or invasive weeds. In everyday life it is a strong word for «get rid of»: «eradicate poverty». Phrases: «eradicate a disease», «eradicate poverty».
examples from the lessons: Smallpox has been eradicated. | Doctors hope to eradicate polio soon. | The island eradicated all its rats to save the birds. | We want to eradicate bullying from our school. | It is hard to eradicate weeds completely. | Charities work to eradicate poverty and hunger.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: eradicated. Noun: eradication. Formal word; everyday words are «wipe out», «get rid of». «Eradicate» means completely — so only smallpox counts as truly eradicated among human diseases; others are «controlled» or «reduced».

part of speech: verb (past and -ed form of erode: erode, erodes, eroded, eroding); adjective (eroded)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Eroded means worn away slowly by wind, water, ice or waves. 2) (figurative) Eroded means made weaker little by little, like trust or confidence.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons pupils learn how rivers, sea, rain and wind erode rocks and soil, making cliffs, caves, arches and canyons. In everyday life and the news it means something has slowly weakened: «Her confidence was eroded». Related: erosion, weathering, deposition.
examples from the lessons: The cliffs have been eroded by the sea. | The river eroded the rock and made a deep canyon. | Strong winds eroded the soil on the farm. | The old statue's face was eroded by rain. | Houses fell when the coast eroded. | His trust in his friend was eroded by lies. | The Grand Canyon was eroded by the Colorado River over millions of years.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past form of the regular verb erode. Noun: erosion. In geography, erosion (wearing away and carrying off) is slightly different from weathering (breaking down rocks in place). Pronounced «ih-ROH-did».
