meaning for a pupil: 1) Eurasian means about Eurasia — Europe and Asia together, the biggest piece of land on Earth. 2) (science) Many animals have Eurasian in their names because they live across Europe and Asia, like the Eurasian otter or Eurasian jay. 3) (dated) A Eurasian was a person with one European and one Asian parent.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons Europe and Asia are often treated as one continent called Eurasia; the Eurasian plate is a huge piece of the Earth's crust. In science, species names like «Eurasian blue tit» tell where an animal lives. Phrases: «Eurasian plate», «Eurasian otter».
examples from the lessons: The Eurasian plate is one of the biggest tectonic plates. | Europe and Asia together form the Eurasian landmass. | We saw a Eurasian jay in the woods. | The Eurasian otter lives in rivers. | The Eurasian steppe is a huge grassland. | The Himalayas formed where the Indian and Eurasian plates meet.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Written with a capital: Eurasian. Starts with a «you» sound, so «a Eurasian», not «an». Using it for a person is old-fashioned; today people usually say «of mixed European and Asian heritage».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Extraction is taking or pulling something out, like a tooth from a mouth or oil from the ground. 2) (science) Extraction is getting a substance out of a mixture, like getting juice out of fruit or salt from sea water. 3) (formal) A person's extraction is the country or family they come from: «of Irish extraction».
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons pupils learn extraction of metals from ores, of salt by evaporation, of colour from plants. In geography, extraction means mining and drilling. At the dentist, an extraction is taking out a tooth. Phrases: «tooth extraction», «oil extraction», «of … extraction».
examples from the lessons: The dentist did an extraction of my wobbly tooth. | Oil extraction can harm the environment. | We did an extraction of colour from beetroot in science. | Salt extraction from sea water uses evaporation. | She is of Italian extraction. | Coal extraction used to be the town's main job. | The extraction of iron from rock needs a furnace.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable when it is one event (two extractions), uncountable for the process. Verb: extract. Adjective: extractive. «Of Irish extraction» is formal and means Irish family background.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An eyespot is a round patch of colour that looks like an eye, on the wings of a butterfly or moth, or on the body of a fish, to scare or fool predators. 2) (science) An eyespot is a tiny light-sensitive spot on very simple living things, such as Euglena, that helps them find light.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons it explains camouflage and defence: birds may attack the false eye instead of the head, or be frightened by big eyespots. In microscopy, pupils see the red eyespot of single-celled Euglena. Phrases: «false eyespots», «eyespot on the wing».
examples from the lessons: The peacock butterfly has four big eyespots. | Birds may peck the eyespot instead of the butterfly's head. | Some fish have an eyespot near their tail. | Under the microscope we saw the red eyespot of a Euglena. | The moth opened its wings and flashed its eyespots. | Eyespots make small creatures look bigger and scarier.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: an eyespot, eyespots. One word. Also called «eye spot» or «ocellus» (plural ocelli) by scientists. An eyespot on a wing cannot see; it is only a pattern.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To facilitate something means to make it easier or help it happen. 2) To facilitate a meeting or discussion means to guide it so everyone can take part.
its sense in the lessons: It is a formal word used by teachers, reports and exam questions: «The new ramp facilitates access for wheelchairs». In everyday talk people usually say «help» or «make easier». In science, things like enzymes facilitate reactions. Phrases: «facilitate learning», «facilitate a discussion».
examples from the lessons: The new bridge will facilitate travel between the towns. | Ramps facilitate access for wheelchair users. | The teacher facilitated our class discussion. | Computers can facilitate learning. | Enzymes facilitate digestion. | Clear rules facilitate fair play.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: facilitated. Noun: facilitation; person: facilitator. Formal register. You facilitate something (a process), not usually a person: «facilitate the move», not «facilitate me». Pronounced «fuh-SIL-ih-tate».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A fatality is a death caused by an accident, war, disaster or violence. 2) (formal) Fatality is the quality of causing death: «the fatality of the disease».
its sense in the lessons: In the news and safety lessons it is used to count deaths: «There were no fatalities in the crash». It is a serious, formal word used in reports. In geography it comes with earthquakes, floods and storms. Phrases: «no fatalities», «road fatalities».
examples from the lessons: Luckily, there were no fatalities in the fire. | Wearing seat belts reduces road fatalities. | The storm caused three fatalities. | Fatalities from the disease have fallen thanks to vaccines. | The report gave the number of fatalities. | The crossing was made safer after a fatality last year.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a fatality, fatalities (y → ies). Adjective: fatal (causing death). Formal word, used in the news; everyday word: death. A «fatal» mistake in a game or story may just mean a very bad one, not a death.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Fearful means afraid or worried that something bad will happen. 2) (old-fashioned) Fearful means frightening or terrible. 3) (informal, old) Fearful can mean very great or very bad: «a fearful mess».
its sense in the lessons: In stories it describes a character's feeling: «a fearful look». In older books and the Bible it can describe frightening things. In everyday life people say «afraid» or «scared» more often. Phrases: «fearful of», «fearful that».
examples from the lessons: The fearful puppy hid under the bed. | She was fearful of the dark. | They were fearful that the bridge would break. | The children gave a fearful glance at the old house. | There was a fearful storm that night. | Don't be fearful — I'm here. | «Fear not,» said the angel to the fearful shepherds.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective; adverb: fearfully; noun: fearfulness. One l at the end: fearful (the suffix «-ful» has one l). «Fearful of» something. Opposite: fearless, brave. Note the two opposite senses: a fearful person feels fear, but a fearful sight causes fear.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (medicine) Febrile means having a fever, a high body temperature. 2) (formal) Febrile means nervous, excited and restless, often in a busy or tense way: «a febrile mood».
its sense in the lessons: In medicine and health lessons it is a doctor's word: «a febrile child» is one with a fever; febrile convulsions are fits some young children have during a high fever. In formal writing and the news it describes a tense, excited atmosphere. It is a rare, formal word.
examples from the lessons: The doctor said the baby was febrile. | Febrile convulsions can happen with a high temperature. | The atmosphere in the crowd was febrile before the final. | The election campaign had a febrile mood. | A febrile patient needs fluids and rest. | The city was febrile with rumours.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective; formal or medical. Pronounced «FEE-bryle» (UK) or «FEB-ril» (US). Everyday words: «feverish», «having a temperature». Opposite in medicine: afebrile (no fever). A normal body temperature is about 37 °C; a fever is usually 38 °C or more.

part of speech: verb (ferment, ferments, fermented, fermenting); noun (ferment, uncountable)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) To ferment means to change chemically because of yeast or bacteria, which break down sugar and make gas, acid or alcohol. 2) To ferment trouble means to cause it or stir it up (more often «foment»). 3) (noun, formal) A ferment is a state of excitement, unrest or trouble in a group of people.
its sense in the lessons: In science and cooking lessons pupils learn that bread rises because yeast ferments sugar and makes carbon dioxide; yoghurt, cheese, sauerkraut, kimchi and soy sauce are made by fermentation. In history and formal writing, «in a ferment» means people are restless. Phrases: «leave to ferment», «in a state of ferment».
examples from the lessons: Yeast makes the dough ferment and rise. | Milk ferments into yoghurt. | Cabbage is fermented to make sauerkraut. | The grape juice fermented in big barrels. | We watched a balloon fill with gas from fermenting sugar water. | The city was in a ferment after the news. | Kimchi is fermented cabbage from Korea.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: fermented. Noun: fermentation. Stress: verb «fer-MENT», noun «FER-ment». Trap: «ferment» is often confused with «foment» (to stir up trouble); «foment» is the correct word for that sense. Fermentation needs living microbes; it is not the same as rotting, though both use microbes.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) Fibrin is a stringy protein in the blood that forms a net of threads to make a clot and stop bleeding when you cut yourself.
its sense in the lessons: In science and health lessons pupils learn how blood clots: platelets stick to the cut, and fibrin threads form a mesh that traps blood cells to make a scab. It is a scientific word. Related: fibrinogen, platelets, clotting.
examples from the lessons: Fibrin forms a net over a cut. | Platelets and fibrin help blood to clot. | The scab on my knee is made with the help of fibrin. | Fibrin threads trap red blood cells. | Without fibrin, a small cut could keep bleeding. | Under the microscope, fibrin looks like a tangle of thread.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable, scientific. Pronounced «FY-brin». Not the same as «fibre» (fiber in US), which is in food or cloth, though both come from the Latin for «thread». Fibrin is made from fibrinogen, a protein dissolved in blood.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A filmmaker is a person who makes films, especially a director or producer who has the main ideas.
its sense in the lessons: In media and art lessons pupils learn about filmmakers and how films are planned, shot and edited; they can be young filmmakers with phones. It tells the reader someone's job or hobby. Phrases: «a young filmmaker», «an award-winning filmmaker».
examples from the lessons: Steven Spielberg is a famous filmmaker. | Our class became filmmakers for a day. | The filmmaker filmed whales in the ocean. | She wants to be a wildlife filmmaker. | The filmmaker edited the video on a laptop. | Young filmmakers entered the school film festival.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a filmmaker, filmmakers. Spelled as one word (filmmaker) or with a hyphen (film-maker, more British); both are correct. Double m in the one-word spelling. In the USA people often say «moviemaker» too. A filmmaker is not always the actor.

part of speech: noun (a flashcard, flashcards); also flash card
meaning for a pupil: 1) A flashcard is a small card with a word, picture, question or sum on one side and the answer on the other, used to learn and remember things quickly. 2) (computing) A digital flashcard is the same thing on an app or computer.
its sense in the lessons: In school pupils use flashcards to learn spellings, times tables, foreign words and facts for tests. Teachers «flash» the card quickly and children answer. Phrases: «make flashcards», «test me with flashcards», «revision flashcards».
examples from the lessons: I made flashcards for my spelling test. | Mum tested me with times-table flashcards. | Our French teacher held up a flashcard of a cat. | Flashcards help you remember new words. | Shuffle the flashcards before you start. | My app has flashcards for Spanish. | Write the question on one side and the answer on the other side of the flashcard.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a flashcard, flashcards. Spelled as one word or two (flash card). Learning with flashcards works best if you test yourself and come back to them over several days, rather than just reading them.

part of speech: noun (a fleck, flecks); verb (fleck, flecks, flecked, flecking)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A fleck is a tiny spot or mark of colour, or a small piece of something, like a fleck of paint or dust. 2) (verb) To be flecked with something means to have small spots of it scattered over it.
its sense in the lessons: In art and descriptive writing it helps paint a precise picture: «green eyes with flecks of gold». In everyday life it describes small bits: «a fleck of mud». Phrases: «flecks of», «flecked with».
examples from the lessons: There was a fleck of paint on her nose. | His eyes were blue with flecks of grey. | The bird's feathers were flecked with white. | I found a fleck of gold in the stream. | Flecks of snow drifted past the window. | The wall was flecked with mud after the football game.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a fleck, flecks. Past form: flecked (used as an adjective too: «a flecked egg»). Similar words: speck, spot, dot. «Fleck» is used more for colour; «speck» for dust and dirt.

part of speech: verb (-ing form of forage: forage, forages, foraged, foraging); noun (foraging, uncountable)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Foraging means searching for food, especially wild food, like animals looking for something to eat. 2) Foraging is the hobby of collecting wild food like berries, nuts, mushrooms and herbs. 3) (informal) Foraging means searching around for something: «foraging in the cupboard for biscuits».
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons it describes animal behaviour: bees foraging for nectar, squirrels foraging for nuts, ants foraging for food. In everyday life people go foraging for blackberries. Safety lessons warn never to eat wild plants or mushrooms unless an expert adult says they are safe. Phrases: «foraging for food», «go foraging».
examples from the lessons: Bees spend the day foraging for nectar. | The bears were foraging for berries. | We went foraging for blackberries in the lane. | Never eat a mushroom you found foraging without asking an expert. | My brother was foraging in the fridge for a snack. | Ants leave trails while foraging. | Deer were foraging at the edge of the woods.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb form of forage; spelled with one r and one g before -ing (the e is dropped: forage → foraging). Noun: forager. Foraging can be dangerous: some wild mushrooms and berries are deadly poisonous. In many places it is not allowed to pick plants in nature reserves.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Forcibly means by using force, so that someone or something is made to do it against their will. 2) Forcibly can mean strongly and clearly: «He argued forcibly».
its sense in the lessons: In history and news lessons it is used for people being moved or taken against their will: «forcibly removed», «forcibly deported». In stories it shows violence or great strength. It tells the reader that someone had no choice. Phrases: «forcibly removed», «forcibly entered».
examples from the lessons: The police forcibly removed the man from the stadium. | The door was forcibly opened. | Many people were forcibly moved from their homes. | He was forcibly held back by his friends. | She argued forcibly for a longer break. | Children were forcibly taken from their families in the past, which is now seen as a great wrong.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from «forcible» (done with force). Spelled -ibly, not -ably. Do not confuse with «forcefully» (with a lot of energy or confidence), although they overlap. Forcibly usually means against someone's will.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Frankly means honestly and openly, saying what you really think. 2) (sentence adverb) Frankly is used at the start of a sentence to show you are going to say something honest, often a bit rude or surprising.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday talk it often starts a sentence: «Frankly, I don't care». In stories it shows a character speaking openly. It can sound blunt. Phrases: «frankly speaking», «to put it frankly», «quite frankly».
examples from the lessons: Frankly, that film was boring. | She spoke frankly about her worries. | Quite frankly, I've had enough of the rain. | Can I speak frankly? I don't like the new rule. | He frankly admitted he had broken the window. | Frankly, my dear, I don't give a damn — a famous film line.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from «frank» (honest and direct). Not related to the name Frank. «Frankly» often signals a strong or unwelcome opinion; using it a lot can sound rude.

part of speech: noun (freight, uncountable); verb (freight, freights, freighted, freighting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Freight is goods carried by trains, ships, trucks or planes. 2) Freight is the system of carrying goods, or the money paid for it. 3) (verb) To freight goods means to send them by transport.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons it comes with trade, ports, railways and container ships. In everyday life, freight trains and lorries carry food and parcels. In maths problems, freight is weighed in tonnes. Phrases: «freight train», «air freight», «by freight».
examples from the lessons: A long freight train rattled past. | The ship carried freight from China to Australia. | Air freight is fast but expensive. | The freight was loaded into containers. | The company freighted the cars by sea. | The lorry carried 20 tonnes of freight.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «a lot of freight», not «freights» (except as the verb). Pronounced «frate» — the «gh» is silent, like «eight» and «weight». Related: freighter (a cargo ship), cargo. In the USA, «freight» is common; in the UK people also say «goods» (a goods train).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A galley is the kitchen on a ship, boat or plane. 2) (history) A galley was a long ship moved mainly by many oars, often rowed by slaves or prisoners, used by ancient Greeks, Romans and in the Mediterranean. 3) (printing) A galley (or galley proof) is a long first printing of a text, used to check for mistakes.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons galleys appear with the Romans, Vikings (longships are similar) and sea battles. In stories about ships, the cook works in the galley. On a plane, the flight attendants prepare food in the galley. Phrases: «galley slave», «ship's galley».
examples from the lessons: The cook made soup in the ship's galley. | Roman galleys had rows of oars. | Galley slaves rowed in chains. | The flight attendant went to the galley to get drinks. | The narrow galley on our boat had a tiny stove. | Pirates attacked the galley near the coast.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a galley, galleys (y → s after a vowel). Do not confuse with «gallery» (a place for art) or «gully» (a small valley). A galley kitchen in a house is a narrow kitchen like a ship's.

part of speech: verb (gargle, gargles, gargled, gargling); noun (a gargle, gargles)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To gargle means to hold liquid in the back of your throat and blow air through it to make it bubble, to clean or soothe your throat. 2) (noun) A gargle is the act of gargling, or a liquid used for it, like salt water. 3) (noun, Irish/UK slang) A gargle is an alcoholic drink.
its sense in the lessons: In health lessons it is a home remedy for a sore throat: gargle with warm salt water. In everyday life, people gargle mouthwash after brushing their teeth. It also describes a bubbling sound. Phrases: «gargle with salt water».
examples from the lessons: Gargle with warm salt water to soothe your sore throat. | Dad gargles mouthwash every morning. | Don't swallow the mouthwash — just gargle and spit. | The baby made a funny gargling sound. | The water gargled down the drain. | I can gargle the tune of «Happy Birthday»! | (Ireland, slang) «Fancy a gargle after work?»
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: gargled. Gargling liquid is spat out, not swallowed. It can soothe a sore throat but is not a cure for an infection. The Irish slang sense means a drink of alcohol and is for adults.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Gelatine is a clear substance with no taste, made by boiling animal bones and skin, which makes liquids set into a wobbly solid when they cool. 2) (science) Gelatine is used to make jelly, sweets, glue, capsules for medicine and photographic film.
its sense in the lessons: In cooking and science lessons pupils make jelly with gelatine and learn how a liquid sets into a gel. Many gummy sweets contain gelatine, so they are not suitable for vegetarians, and some religions avoid it unless it comes from an allowed animal (halal or kosher gelatine). Vegetarian versions use agar from seaweed. Phrases: «a sheet of gelatine», «gelatine-free».
examples from the lessons: Jelly sets because of the gelatine. | Gummy bears are made with gelatine. | These sweets are gelatine-free, so they are vegetarian. | Soak the gelatine sheets in cold water first. | Medicine capsules are often made of gelatine. | Agar is a plant-based swap for gelatine. | The gelatine made the dessert wobble.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. UK, Ireland, Australia, NZ: gelatine; USA and Canada: gelatin. Pronounced «JEL-uh-teen». In the USA, «Jell-O» is a brand of jelly; in the USA «jelly» means jam. Gelatine comes from animals, which matters for vegetarians, vegans and some faiths.

part of speech: proper noun (Gemini); noun (a Gemini, Geminis — astrology)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Gemini is a group of stars (a constellation) in the night sky, named after the twins Castor and Pollux from Greek myths. 2) (astrology) Gemini is one of the twelve star signs; people born roughly late May to late June are called Geminis. 3) (space) Gemini was a NASA space programme in the 1960s that flew two astronauts at a time, before the Apollo Moon landings.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons Gemini is a constellation with the bright stars Castor and Pollux. In everyday life children see it in horoscopes; scientists say star signs do not predict personality or the future. In history of space, Project Gemini tested spacewalks and docking. The word is Latin for «twins». It is also the name of an AI system made by a technology company.
examples from the lessons: Gemini is the constellation of the twins. | You can see Gemini in the winter sky in the north. | My birthday is in June, so my star sign is Gemini. | Castor and Pollux are the two brightest stars in Gemini. | Project Gemini taught astronauts how to do spacewalks. | Horoscopes say Geminis are chatty, but there is no scientific evidence for that.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Written with a capital: Gemini. Pronounced «JEM-in-eye» or «JEM-in-ee». Latin for «twins». Astronomy (the science of space) is not astrology (star signs, which science does not support). The dates of star signs no longer match where the Sun really is among the stars.

part of speech: proper noun (Gemma — a girl's name); noun (a gemma, gemmae — science, rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (a name) Gemma is a girl's name, popular in the UK, Ireland and Australia; it comes from Italian and Latin for «gem» or «jewel». 2) (science) A gemma is a tiny bud or group of cells on mosses and liverworts that breaks off and grows into a new plant.
its sense in the lessons: In stories Gemma is a person's first name and tells the reader who someone is. In science lessons, liverworts have little cups full of gemmae, washed out by raindrops to start new plants — a way of reproducing without seeds or spores. It is also the name of an AI model made by a technology company.
examples from the lessons: Gemma is my best friend's big sister. | Ask Gemma to pass the scissors. | The liverwort had tiny cups full of gemmae. | Raindrops splash the gemmae out of their cups. | Each gemma can grow into a new plant. | Gemma scored the winning goal in netball.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a name it has a capital and nothing else should be invented about the person. Pronounced «JEM-uh». The science plural is «gemmae» (Latin, «JEM-ee»). Not the same as «gem» (a precious stone), though the name comes from it.

part of speech: noun (a glaze, glazes); verb (glaze, glazes, glazed, glazing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A glaze is a shiny coating painted on pottery before it is baked in a kiln, which makes it smooth, coloured and waterproof. 2) A glaze in cooking is a shiny coating of egg, sugar, syrup or juice brushed onto food. 3) (verb) To glaze a window means to fit glass into it. 4) (verb) If your eyes glaze over, they go dull and blank because you are bored or tired.
its sense in the lessons: In art lessons pupils glaze clay pots and tiles. In cooking, pastry is glazed with beaten egg and doughnuts with sugar. In building, «double glazing» means windows with two layers of glass. In stories, eyes that «glaze over» show boredom. Phrases: «glaze over», «double glazing», «egg glaze».
examples from the lessons: We painted a blue glaze on our clay bowls. | Brush the pastry with an egg glaze. | The doughnuts have a chocolate glaze. | The builder glazed the new windows. | Our house has double glazing to keep it warm. | His eyes glazed over when Dad talked about taxes. | The glaze turned shiny in the kiln.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: glazed (adjective too: «glazed doughnut», «a glazed look»). A glazier is a person who fits glass. In pottery, a glaze must be fired in a kiln to become glassy; before that it is a powdery paint.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Graphics are pictures, drawings, charts and diagrams, especially ones made on a computer. 2) Graphics is the art or skill of making designs and pictures, like posters and logos (graphic design). 3) (computing) In video games, graphics are how the game's pictures look.
its sense in the lessons: In computing and art lessons pupils make graphics for posters and slides. In maths, graphs and charts are a kind of graphics showing data. In everyday life, gamers say a game has «great graphics». Phrases: «computer graphics», «graphics card», «good graphics».
examples from the lessons: This game has amazing graphics. | We made graphics for our science poster. | My dad works in graphics and designs logos. | The news used graphics to show the storm's path. | A new graphics card makes games run smoothly. | Graphics help readers understand numbers quickly.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually used with a plural verb when it means pictures («the graphics are good») and singular when it means the art («graphics is fun»). Adjective: graphic — which can also mean very detailed and shocking: «graphic violence», a warning on some films. Related: graph, graphic novel.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (slang, dated) Groovy means cool, fashionable, exciting or very nice; it was popular in the 1960s and 1970s and now often sounds funny or old-fashioned. 2) (rare) Groovy means having grooves (lines cut into a surface).
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life children hear it from grandparents, in old films or as a joke: «Groovy, man!». In stories it shows a character from the hippie era or someone trying to sound cool. It tells the reader approval in a playful way.
examples from the lessons: That's a groovy shirt, Grandad! | «Groovy!» said the hippie in the cartoon. | We danced to some groovy 70s music. | Your new bike is pretty groovy. | The party had groovy lights and a disco ball. | Dad still says «groovy», and we all laugh.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Slang, dated — not for formal writing. Comparative: groovier, grooviest. From «in the groove», meaning playing music well. Today «cool» is the usual word; «groovy» is often used ironically.

part of speech: verb (gurgle, gurgles, gurgled, gurgling); noun (a gurgle, gurgles)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To gurgle means for water or liquid to make a bubbling sound as it flows, like water going down a drain. 2) A baby gurgles when it makes happy bubbling sounds in its throat. 3) (noun) A gurgle is such a bubbling sound.
its sense in the lessons: In stories it is a sound word (onomatopoeia) that helps the reader hear the scene: a gurgling stream, a gurgling baby, a gurgling tummy. In English lessons it is used for describing sounds. Phrases: «gurgle with laughter», «the gurgle of the stream».
examples from the lessons: The stream gurgled over the stones. | The baby gurgled and smiled at me. | Water gurgled down the plughole. | My tummy gurgled before lunch. | We heard the gurgle of a little brook. | She gurgled with laughter.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: gurgled. It is an onomatopoeic word — it sounds like what it means. Similar: burble, babble, bubble. Do not confuse with «gargle» (bubbling liquid in your throat on purpose).

part of speech: noun (a gyre, gyres); verb (gyre, gyres, gyred, gyring — poetic)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) A gyre is a huge circle of ocean currents that moves round and round across a large part of an ocean. 2) (poetic) A gyre is a spiral or whirling movement; to gyre means to spin or whirl round.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and science lessons pupils learn there are five big ocean gyres; plastic rubbish collects in them, such as the Great Pacific Garbage Patch. In poetry, Lewis Carroll's «Jabberwocky» says «did gyre and gimble in the wabe», and W. B. Yeats wrote of «the widening gyre». Phrases: «ocean gyre», «North Pacific Gyre».
examples from the lessons: The North Pacific Gyre carries rubbish into a huge patch. | There are five major ocean gyres. | Ocean gyres move warm and cold water around the world. | Plastic bottles can drift in a gyre for years. | «'Twas brillig, and the slithy toves did gyre and gimble in the wabe.» | The leaves gyred in the wind.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a gyre, gyres. Pronounced «JY-er» (rhymes with «fire»), sometimes «GY-er». Rare word outside science and poetry. The verb sense is poetic or old. Related: gyroscope.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A hamburger is a flat round cake of minced beef, fried or grilled and served in a bread bun, often with salad, cheese and sauce. 2) (USA) Hamburger can also mean the minced beef itself, before it is cooked.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life it is a popular fast food; children see it at barbecues and fast food restaurants. In health lessons it is discussed as food to eat sometimes, not every day. In maths problems, hamburgers are used for costs and counting. Phrases: «hamburger bun», «a hamburger and chips», «veggie burger».
examples from the lessons: Can I have a hamburger with cheese, please? | Dad grilled hamburgers at the barbecue. | A hamburger costs £3, so three cost £9. | My vegetarian friend had a veggie burger instead of a hamburger. | The hamburger came with chips and ketchup. | (USA) Mom bought two pounds of hamburger at the store.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a hamburger, hamburgers. Usually shortened to «burger». Trap: it contains no ham; the name comes from the German city of Hamburg. In the UK «chips» = US «fries». In the USA, «hamburger» also means minced beef (UK: «mince»).

part of speech: noun (handwash, uncountable; a handwash); verb (handwash, handwashes, handwashed, handwashing); also hand wash
meaning for a pupil: 1) Handwash is liquid soap for washing your hands. 2) To handwash clothes means to wash them by hand in water, not in a washing machine. 3) (noun) Handwashing is washing your hands with soap and water.
its sense in the lessons: In health and science lessons pupils learn that handwashing with soap for about 20 seconds removes germs and stops illness spreading. On clothes labels, a symbol of a hand in water means «handwash only». In everyday life, handwash is the soap by the sink. Phrases: «handwash only», «a bottle of handwash».
examples from the lessons: There's handwash by the sink. | Wash your hands with handwash for 20 seconds. | This jumper says «handwash only». | Mum handwashed my woolly hat. | We're out of handwash — can you buy some? | Handwashing stops germs from spreading. | Sing «Happy Birthday» twice while you handwash.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelled as one word (handwash), two words (hand wash) or with a hyphen; all are seen. Uncountable for the soap. Handwashing with soap is better than water alone; hand gel helps when there is no sink but does not work well on very dirty hands.

part of speech: verb (haul, hauls, hauled, hauling); noun (a haul, hauls)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To haul something means to pull or drag it with effort, because it is heavy. 2) (noun) A haul is an amount of something gained or caught, like fish in a net, stolen goods, or sweets at Halloween. 3) (noun) A haul is a distance travelled: «a long haul». 4) (verb, informal) To be hauled up or hauled in front of someone means to be made to go there to be told off.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life children talk about their «Halloween haul» of sweets; in sport, a player has a «haul» of goals or medals. In stories it shows effort: «They hauled the boat onto the beach». In transport, lorries haul goods. Phrases: «long haul», «haul up», «for the long haul», «haul of medals».
examples from the lessons: We hauled the heavy bags up the stairs. | The fishermen hauled in their nets. | My Halloween haul was 40 sweets! | Police found a big haul of stolen phones. | Australia won a haul of gold medals. | It's a long haul flight to New Zealand. | He was hauled in front of the head teacher.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: hauled. Homophone: «hall» (a big room or corridor) in many accents — haul and hall sound the same in UK English. «Long-haul» (with a hyphen before a noun) means a very long trip. «For the long haul» means for a long time.

part of speech: verb (haunt, haunts, haunted, haunting); noun (a haunt, haunts)
meaning for a pupil: 1) In stories, a ghost haunts a place or person when it appears there again and again. 2) If a memory or worry haunts you, you keep thinking about it and it upsets you. 3) To haunt a place means to go there very often. 4) (noun) A haunt is a place someone visits often, like a favourite café.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and Halloween, haunted houses and castles are full of ghosts. In everyday life and stories, a bad mistake can «come back to haunt you». A «favourite haunt» is a place you love to go. Ghosts are not proven to be real; haunted-house tales are for fun and spooky stories. Phrases: «haunted house», «come back to haunt», «favourite haunt».
examples from the lessons: They say a ghost haunts the old castle. | We went to a haunted house at the fair. | The sad song haunted me for days. | That silly mistake came back to haunt him. | The park is our favourite haunt after school. | Pirates once haunted these seas. | The memory of the storm still haunts her.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: haunted (also an adjective: «a haunted house»). Pronounced «hawnt». Adjective: haunting (beautiful and sad, staying in your mind: «a haunting tune»). Science has found no evidence that ghosts exist; creaks and cold spots usually have ordinary causes.

part of speech: noun (a haw, haws); verb (haw — in «hum and haw»); interjection (haw)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A haw is the small red berry of the hawthorn tree. 2) (verb) To hum and haw (US: hem and haw) means to take a long time to decide, making noises like «um» and «er». 3) (interjection) «Haw» is the sound of a loud laugh, often written «haw haw». 4) (farming, USA) «Haw!» is a call to a horse or ox to turn left (and «gee» means turn right).
its sense in the lessons: In nature walks and science lessons, hawthorn haws are winter food for birds such as blackbirds and thrushes. In everyday life «humming and hawing» describes someone who can't decide. In comics, «haw haw» is a laugh. Phrases: «hum and haw», «hem and haw».
examples from the lessons: Birds were eating the red haws on the hawthorn. | The haws ripen in autumn. | Stop humming and hawing and choose a flavour! | He hemmed and hawed before answering. | «Haw haw!» laughed the pirate. | The farmer shouted «Haw!» and the horse turned left.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a haw, haws. In many UK accents haw sounds like «hoar» (as in hoar frost). «Hum and haw» is British; «hem and haw» is American. Haws are not good to eat raw for people; leave them for birds, and the seeds can be harmful.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A hazelnut is the small, round, brown nut of the hazel tree, with a hard shell. 2) (adjective use) Hazelnut is the flavour of this nut, used in chocolate spreads, ice cream and coffee.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life children find hazelnuts in chocolate, spreads and cereals. In science and nature lessons, hazel trees, squirrels and dormice that eat hazelnuts are studied. In health and safety lessons, nut allergies are serious: some people get very ill from nuts, so schools often ban them. Phrases: «chocolate hazelnut spread», «hazelnut tree».
examples from the lessons: The squirrel buried a hazelnut. | I love chocolate hazelnut spread on toast. | Hazelnuts grow on hazel trees. | Our school is nut-free because of allergies, so no hazelnut snacks. | Dormice eat hazelnuts before they hibernate. | Crack the hazelnut with a nutcracker. | A bag holds 50 hazelnuts; how many in 4 bags?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a hazelnut, hazelnuts. One word. Also called a «cobnut» or «filbert». «Hazel» also describes a light brown-green eye colour. Nut allergies can be life-threatening; always check labels and never share nut foods with someone who has an allergy.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (history) A helot was one of the people in ancient Sparta who were made to work the land for the Spartans, almost like slaves, and could not leave. 2) (formal, rare) A helot is anyone treated like a slave or a serf.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons about ancient Greece it explains how Sparta worked: the helots farmed so that Spartan citizens could train as soldiers; Spartans feared helot rebellions and treated them harshly. It tells the reader about unfree people. Related: serf, slave.
examples from the lessons: The helots farmed the land for the Spartans. | There were many more helots than Spartan citizens. | Spartans feared that the helots would rebel. | Helots could not leave the farms they worked on. | The helots rose up against Sparta several times. | Spartan boys trained as soldiers while helots grew the food.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a helot, helots. Pronounced «HEL-ot». Rare word, mostly in history about Sparta. Helots were not exactly the same as slaves: they belonged to the state and were tied to the land, more like serfs.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Hemp is a tall plant whose strong stem fibres are used to make rope, cloth, paper and other things. 2) Hemp also means the fibre, seeds or oil from this plant, used in food, clothes and building. 3) Hemp is a kind of cannabis plant, but the hemp used for rope and food is grown so that it has very little of the drug in it.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, hemp rope and canvas were used for sailing ships. In science and design lessons it is a fast-growing, eco-friendly material. In everyday life, hemp seeds and hemp milk are sold as food. Phrases: «hemp rope», «hemp seeds», «hemp fabric».
examples from the lessons: The sailors used hemp rope to tie the sails. | Hemp grows very fast and tall. | Mum puts hemp seeds on her salad. | The bag is made of hemp fabric. | Paper can be made from hemp. | Hemp needs less water than cotton.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Industrial hemp and marijuana come from the same plant species (cannabis), but industrial hemp is grown to have very little THC, the substance that makes people high. Laws on growing hemp differ from country to country.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) Hereditary describes a feature or illness that is passed from parents to children through genes. 2) Hereditary describes a title, job or right that is passed down in a family from parent to child, like a crown.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons it goes with inheritance and genes: eye colour, freckles and some illnesses are hereditary. In history and politics, kings, queens and some lords hold hereditary titles; the UK House of Lords used to have many hereditary peers. Phrases: «hereditary disease», «hereditary title», «hereditary monarchy».
examples from the lessons: Freckles are often hereditary. | The doctor asked if the illness was hereditary. | The UK has a hereditary monarchy. | His grandfather had a hereditary title as a lord. | Being left-handed is partly hereditary. | Some hereditary diseases can be tested for before birth.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective. Pronounced «huh-RED-ih-tree» or «huh-RED-ih-tair-ee». Related: heredity (noun), heritage, inherit, heir. Trap: not everything that runs in a family is hereditary — habits and language are learned, not passed by genes.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Historically means in the past, or over a long period of history. 2) Historically means connected with history, or in a way that is true to history.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons it helps compare the past with today: «Historically, girls were not allowed to go to school». In stories and films, «historically accurate» means the details are true to the time. It tells the reader that something was true in the past or for a long time. Phrases: «historically accurate», «historically important».
examples from the lessons: Historically, children worked in mills and mines. | The castle is historically important. | Is the film historically accurate? | Historically, our town was famous for making boots. | Women were historically paid less than men. | Historically, the Vikings travelled as far as Canada.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from «historical» (about history). Spelled with -ally: historically (five syllables). Related: «historic» means very important in history («a historic day»), while «historical» means about history («historical novel»). Use «a historical», though «an historical» is also seen in old British writing.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Hollywood is an area of Los Angeles in California, USA, where many famous film studios are. 2) Hollywood also means the American film industry as a whole.
its sense in the lessons: In media lessons and everyday life, Hollywood stands for big, expensive American films and film stars. The Hollywood sign on a hill and the Walk of Fame are well-known sights. It tells the reader about films and celebrities. Phrases: «Hollywood star», «a Hollywood film», «Hollywood ending» (a happy ending). Other film industries have similar names, like Bollywood (India) and Nollywood (Nigeria).
examples from the lessons: She dreams of becoming a Hollywood star. | The Hollywood sign stands on a hill. | Hollywood makes hundreds of films every year. | We saw stars' handprints in Hollywood. | The story had a Hollywood ending — everyone was happy. | Bollywood films come from Mumbai, not Hollywood.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A place name, so it has a capital: Hollywood. Bollywood (Hindi films, from Bombay + Hollywood) and Nollywood (Nigeria) are named after it. «Hollywood» used as an adjective can mean glamorous or unrealistic.

part of speech: noun (horseback, uncountable — in «on horseback»); adjective (horseback); adverb (horseback, US)
meaning for a pupil: 1) On horseback means riding on a horse. 2) (adjective) Horseback describes something done while riding a horse, like horseback riding.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons knights, cowboys, messengers and the Mongols travelled on horseback. In everyday life, «horseback riding» (US) is the same as «horse riding» (UK). In stories it shows travel in older times. Phrases: «on horseback», «horseback riding».
examples from the lessons: The knights rode into battle on horseback. | The police patrol the park on horseback. | We went horseback riding on our holiday. | Messengers on horseback carried the news. | Cowboys herded cattle on horseback. | It took three days to cross the hills on horseback.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly in the phrase «on horseback». One word. Americans say «horseback riding»; British, Irish and Australian people usually say «horse riding». Safety: always wear a riding hat when on horseback.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Hourly means happening every hour, once an hour. 2) Hourly means counted or paid by the hour: an hourly wage. 3) (adverb) Hourly can mean very often, any time now: «expected hourly».
its sense in the lessons: In maths problems it means «per hour»: an hourly rate of £10 means 10 pounds for each hour; to find the total, multiply the hourly rate by the number of hours. In everyday life, buses run hourly and the news is updated hourly. Phrases: «hourly rate», «hourly pay», «on the hour, every hour».
examples from the lessons: The bus to town runs hourly. | Her hourly pay is £12. | She earns £12 an hour, so for 5 hours she earns £60. | The weather app shows an hourly forecast. | The nurse checked his temperature hourly. | The news is on hourly. | They expect the baby to arrive hourly!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Both an adjective (an hourly bus) and an adverb (the bus runs hourly). The h is silent: «OUR-lee», so use «an»: «an hourly bus». Maths: hourly rate × hours = total; total ÷ hours = hourly rate. Do not confuse with «hour by hour» (gradually) or «every half hour».

part of speech: noun (a hyperlink, hyperlinks); verb (hyperlink, hyperlinks, hyperlinked, hyperlinking)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A hyperlink is a word, picture or button on a web page or document that you click to go to another page, website or file. 2) (verb) To hyperlink something means to make it into a link.
its sense in the lessons: In computing lessons pupils learn that hyperlinks join web pages together to make the World Wide Web; they add hyperlinks to their own documents and slides. Safety lessons teach children to check a link before clicking, because some hyperlinks in emails or messages lead to scams. Phrases: «click the hyperlink», «insert a hyperlink».
examples from the lessons: Click the hyperlink to watch the video. | Hyperlinks are usually blue and underlined. | I added a hyperlink to our class website. | Don't click hyperlinks in strange emails. | Hover over a hyperlink to see where it goes. | She hyperlinked the title to the source.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a hyperlink, hyperlinks. Often shortened to «link». The address a hyperlink goes to is a URL. Safety: the words shown for a link can differ from the real address, so hover to check, and ask an adult if unsure.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Immature means behaving in a silly, childish way, not as sensible as you should be for your age. 2) (science) Immature means not fully grown or developed yet, like an immature bird or fruit.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life it is often a criticism: «Stop being so immature!». In science lessons it describes young animals, plants or cells that are not yet adult or ripe. In stories it shows a character who needs to grow up. Opposite: mature. Phrases: «immature behaviour», «emotionally immature».
examples from the lessons: It's immature to laugh when someone falls over. | Stop being so immature and say sorry. | Immature gulls have brown feathers. | Immature fruit is hard and sour. | The tadpoles are immature frogs. | He was too immature to look after a puppy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective; noun: immaturity. Prefix «im-» (not) + «mature», so double m. Calling someone immature is a criticism. For children, being playful is normal — immature means acting younger than expected in a situation.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An indri is the largest kind of lemur, a black-and-white tree-living animal found only in the rainforests of Madagascar, famous for its loud singing calls.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography lessons about Madagascar and endangered animals, the indri shows how special the island's wildlife is. Indris live in family groups, eat leaves and leap between trees. They are critically endangered because their forest is being cut down. Phrases: «the indri's song».
examples from the lessons: The indri lives only in Madagascar. | Indris sing loud songs that echo through the forest. | The indri is the biggest living lemur. | Indris leap from tree to tree. | Indris are critically endangered. | An indri has a very short tail, unlike other lemurs.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: an indri, indris. Pronounced «IN-dree». Rare word, used in nature topics. Trap: a well-known story says «indri» means «there it is» in Malagasy, because a French explorer misheard his guide; this tale may be true or partly myth.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Infinite means without any end or limit; so big it can never be measured or counted. 2) (informal) Infinite means extremely great: «infinite patience». 3) (maths) An infinite set or line goes on for ever, like the counting numbers 1, 2, 3, ….
its sense in the lessons: In maths lessons pupils learn there are infinitely many numbers: you can always add 1. A line goes on infinitely in both directions; a line segment does not. In science, people wonder whether space is infinite. In everyday life it is used to exaggerate: «infinite homework». Symbol: ∞ (infinity). Phrases: «infinite number», «infinite patience».
examples from the lessons: There is an infinite number of counting numbers. | The teacher has infinite patience. | Is the universe infinite? | A line is infinite, but a line segment has two ends. | You can't count to infinity because numbers are infinite. | The sky looked infinite from the mountain top. | The choices in the game seemed infinite.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced «IN-fin-it», not «in-FINE-ite» (even though «finite» is «FY-nite»). Opposite: finite. Noun: infinity; adverb: infinitely. Infinity is not a number you can reach; «infinity plus one» is still infinity. Some infinities are bigger than others, a surprising fact from maths.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To inspire someone means to give them the wish and the energy to do something good or creative. 2) To inspire a feeling means to make people feel it: «inspire confidence», «inspire fear». 3) If something inspired a story, picture or invention, it gave the idea for it. 4) (science, rare) To inspire means to breathe in.
its sense in the lessons: In school it is used for role models, books and trips: «Her talk inspired us to recycle». In art and writing lessons pupils say what inspired their work. In stories heroes inspire others. Related: inspiration, inspiring, inspired. Phrases: «inspire someone to do something», «inspired by».
examples from the lessons: The astronaut's visit inspired me to study science. | Her bravery inspires us all. | The story was inspired by a real shipwreck. | Good teachers inspire their pupils. | The music inspired her to dance. | The captain's calm voice inspired confidence. | What inspired you to write this poem?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: inspired. Noun: inspiration; adjectives: inspiring (gives inspiration), inspired (very clever or creative: «an inspired idea»). Pattern: «inspire someone to do something». Opposite of the breathing sense: expire (breathe out), though «expire» usually means to end.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Intake is the amount of something you take into your body, like food, water or air. 2) An intake is the group of new people who join a school, college, job or the army at one time. 3) An intake is a place or opening where water, air or fuel goes into a pipe or machine. 4) An intake of breath is a quick breath in, from surprise or shock.
its sense in the lessons: In health lessons it is about daily intake of food, sugar, salt and water: «Reduce your sugar intake». In school life, the year's intake is the new pupils starting. In maths problems, intake can be measured in grams or litres per day. Phrases: «daily intake», «intake of breath», «this year's intake».
examples from the lessons: Try to cut down your sugar intake. | Your water intake should go up when it's hot. | This year's intake at our school is 60 children. | There was a sharp intake of breath when the vase fell. | The engine's air intake was blocked. | The recommended daily intake of salt is less than 6 grams for adults.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: an intake, intakes (often used with «of»). Stress on the first syllable: «IN-take». The verb is «take in», not «intake». In maths problems, total intake = amount per meal × number of meals.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An interpreter is a person whose job is to change what someone says from one language into another, out loud, as they speak. 2) (computing) An interpreter is a computer program that reads and runs code line by line. 3) An interpreter is someone who explains the meaning of something, like a performer of music or a person who explains a dream or a text.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life interpreters help at hospitals, courts, schools and international meetings; sign language interpreters help deaf people. In computing lessons, Python uses an interpreter. In the Bible, Joseph was an interpreter of dreams. Phrases: «through an interpreter», «sign language interpreter».
examples from the lessons: The doctor spoke to the family through an interpreter. | A sign language interpreter stood next to the speaker. | Interpreters at the UN listen and speak at the same time. | My aunt works as a Ukrainian interpreter. | Joseph was the interpreter of Pharaoh's dreams. | Python code runs in an interpreter.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: an interpreter (starts with a vowel, so «an»). Verb: interpret; noun: interpretation. Trap: an interpreter works with speech, a translator works with writing — people often mix them up. Spelled -er.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Invariable means never changing; always the same. 2) (grammar) An invariable word does not change its form, for example «sheep» has the same singular and plural. 3) (maths, rare) An invariable or invariant is a value that stays the same when other things change.
its sense in the lessons: In formal writing and stories it means «always the same»: «his invariable breakfast of toast». In grammar lessons, invariable nouns like «sheep», «deer» and «fish» have the same plural. Related adverb: invariably (always). Phrases: «an invariable rule», «invariable habit».
examples from the lessons: Her invariable answer was «Maybe later». | Grandpa had an invariable habit of reading the paper after lunch. | The rule is invariable: no phones in class. | «Sheep» is an invariable noun: one sheep, two sheep. | His invariable smile cheered everyone up. | Nothing in nature is truly invariable.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective, formal. Adverb: invariably (more common: «It invariably rains on sports day»). In- (not) + variable (able to change). Opposite: variable. In maths, «variable» is also a letter that stands for a number, and «constant» is the usual word for a value that does not change.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The iris is the coloured ring in your eye around the black pupil; it gets bigger or smaller to control how much light goes into the eye. 2) An iris is a tall garden flower with sword-shaped leaves and flowers often purple, blue, yellow or white. 3) (a name) Iris is a girl's name; in Greek myths Iris was the goddess of the rainbow.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about the eye, the iris and the pupil let in more light in the dark and less in bright light; eye colour is the colour of the iris. In nature and art, irises are flowers painted by Van Gogh. It also appears as a name. Phrases: «the iris of the eye», «blue irises».
examples from the lessons: The iris is the coloured part of your eye. | In bright light, the iris makes the pupil smaller. | Her irises are green. | Purple irises grew by the pond. | Van Gogh painted a field of irises. | My great-aunt is called Iris. | The rainbow goddess Iris carried messages for the gods.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: plural irises (sometimes «irides» in science). Pronounced «EYE-ris». The pupil is the black hole in the middle; the iris is around it — a common mix-up. The fleur-de-lis symbol is based on an iris.

part of speech: noun (jasper, uncountable; a jasper); proper noun (Jasper — a boy's name)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Jasper is a hard stone, usually red, yellow, brown or green, often with patterns, polished to make jewellery and ornaments. 2) (a name) Jasper is a boy's name; Jasper is also a town and national park in the Rocky Mountains of Canada. 3) Jasperware is a kind of pottery, usually pale blue with white raised pictures, made by the Wedgwood company.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about rocks and minerals, jasper is a kind of quartz (chalcedony). In the Bible, jasper is one of the precious stones in the high priest's breastplate and the walls of the heavenly city. In stories, Jasper may be a character's name. Phrases: «red jasper», «Jasper National Park».
examples from the lessons: This necklace is made of red jasper. | We found a piece of jasper on the beach. | Jasper is a kind of quartz with lots of colour. | Jasper is my brother's friend. | We saw elk in Jasper National Park. | In the Bible, the wall of the holy city is described as jasper.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The stone is usually uncountable (made of jasper), but «a jasper» for one piece. With a capital as a name. Do not invent facts about a person called Jasper. Jasper is not a gemstone like a diamond; it is opaque (you cannot see through it).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A journal is a book in which you write about what happens each day, your thoughts and feelings; a kind of diary. 2) A journal is a serious magazine about a subject, like science or medicine, where experts publish their work. 3) A journal is a newspaper (used in some newspaper names, like «The Wall Street Journal»). 4) (money) In bookkeeping, a journal is a record of money in and out.
its sense in the lessons: In school pupils keep reading journals, science journals and nature journals to record observations. In science, «published in a journal» means checked by other experts (peer-reviewed). In stories, a hidden journal reveals secrets. Phrases: «keep a journal», «scientific journal», «journal entry».
examples from the lessons: I write in my journal every night. | Keep a science journal of how your bean plant grows. | Anne Frank's diary is a famous journal. | The discovery was published in a science journal. | Dad reads a medical journal for his job. | Today's journal entry is about the school trip.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a journal, journals. Related: journalist (a person who writes news), journalism, journey (all from the French «jour», day). Journal vs diary: very similar; a diary may also be a calendar of appointments, while a journal is more for thoughts and records.

part of speech: noun (a kip — slang; kip, kips — money); verb (kip, kips, kipped, kipping — slang)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (slang, UK, Ireland, Australia) A kip is a sleep or a nap; to kip means to sleep, especially somewhere other than your own bed. 2) (slang, Ireland) A kip is a dirty, messy, horrible place. 3) The kip is the money of Laos, a country in Asia.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday British, Irish and Australian talk it is a relaxed word for sleep: «I'm going for a kip». «Kip down» means to sleep somewhere for the night, like on a sofa. In geography lessons, the kip is Laos's currency. Phrases: «have a kip», «grab a kip», «kip down».
examples from the lessons: I'm knackered — I need a kip. | Grandad has a kip after Sunday lunch. | Can I kip on your sofa tonight? | We kipped in the car on the way to the beach. | (Ireland) This room's an absolute kip — tidy it! | The price was 10,000 kip in Laos.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Slang, informal; do not use in essays — say «sleep» or «nap». Double p: kipped, kipping. «Kip down» = sleep somewhere for the night. The money sense is a different word from the Lao language.

part of speech: noun (a knockout, knockouts); adjective (knockout); also knock-out
meaning for a pupil: 1) In boxing, a knockout is a punch or a win when a fighter is knocked down and cannot get up in time. 2) A knockout competition is one where the loser of each game leaves, until one winner is left. 3) (informal) A knockout is something or someone extremely good or beautiful: «The show was a knockout».
its sense in the lessons: In sport lessons and the news it describes tournaments: «the knockout stage of the World Cup». In maths, pupils count the games in a knockout tournament: with 16 teams, there are 8 + 4 + 2 + 1 = 15 games. In everyday talk, «a knockout» is high praise. Phrases: «knockout round», «knockout punch», «knock-out blow».
examples from the lessons: The boxer won by a knockout in round three. | England reached the knockout stage. | In a knockout cup, if you lose you go home. | With 32 teams in a knockout, there are 31 matches. | Her singing was an absolute knockout. | That was a knockout idea! | The dodgeball game was a knockout: hit players are out.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelled as one word, or with a hyphen (knock-out, UK). The verb is two words: «knock out». Maths trick: in a knockout with n teams, there are always n − 1 games, because every game knocks out exactly one team. Being «knocked out» in real life (losing consciousness) is a serious injury; see a doctor.

part of speech: noun (a lifespan, lifespans); also life span
meaning for a pupil: 1) A lifespan is how long a person, animal or plant lives, or usually lives. 2) A lifespan is how long a thing lasts or works, like a battery or a machine.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons pupils compare lifespans: a mayfly lives a day, a mouse about 2 years, a dog about 12, a human about 80, a Greenland shark hundreds of years. In maths, lifespans are used for subtraction and comparison problems. In everyday life, the lifespan of a phone or light bulb tells how long it lasts. Phrases: «average lifespan», «short lifespan», «expected lifespan».
examples from the lessons: The average lifespan of a dog is about 12 years. | A mayfly has a very short lifespan. | Tortoises can have a lifespan of over 100 years. | Human lifespans have grown longer thanks to medicine. | This light bulb has a lifespan of 10,000 hours. | If a cat lives 15 years and a hamster 2 years, the cat's lifespan is 13 years longer.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a lifespan, lifespans. One word or two (life span). «Average lifespan» or «life expectancy» is an average: many live shorter or longer. Myth: people in the past did not all die at 30; the average was low mainly because many babies died.

part of speech: noun (a ling, ling or lings — fish; ling, uncountable — plant); (Mandarin, pinyin) líng / lǐng / lìng
meaning for a pupil: 1) A ling is a long sea fish of the cod family, caught for food in the North Atlantic and around Australia and New Zealand. 2) Ling is a kind of heather, a low shrub with small purple flowers that grows on moors. 3) (Mandarin, pinyin) «Ling» is a Chinese syllable: líng means «zero» (零), and it is part of many names; it is not an English word. 4) (a name) Ling is a Chinese given name or surname.
its sense in the lessons: In nature lessons, ling heather covers moors in Scotland, Ireland and northern England. In Australia and NZ, ling is a fish sold at the fish shop. When Mandarin is heard on the street or in maths, «líng» (zero) sounds like English «ling». As a name it tells the reader who someone is. Phrases: «ling heather», «ling fillet».
examples from the lessons: The moor was purple with ling. | We had ling and chips at the beach. | Ling is caught in deep water. | In Mandarin, «líng» means zero. | Ling is new in our class; she is from Shanghai. | Bees make honey from ling heather.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Fish plural: ling or lings. In pinyin, the tone marks change the meaning (líng = zero; lǐng = collar or to lead; lìng = another, or to order). The Mandarin word sounds like English «ling». As a name, do not invent details. Also a suffix in English (duckling, seedling), meaning «small or young».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) The lithosphere is the hard, rocky outer layer of the Earth: the crust plus the very top part of the mantle, about 100 km thick, broken into tectonic plates.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and science lessons pupils learn the Earth's layers (crust, mantle, outer core, inner core) and the «spheres»: lithosphere (rock), hydrosphere (water), atmosphere (air) and biosphere (living things). The lithosphere's plates move slowly, causing earthquakes, volcanoes and mountains. Phrases: «the Earth's lithosphere», «oceanic lithosphere».
examples from the lessons: The lithosphere is broken into tectonic plates. | The lithosphere includes the crust and the top of the mantle. | Earthquakes happen when parts of the lithosphere move. | The lithosphere floats on a softer layer called the asthenosphere. | Rocks, mountains and soil are part of the lithosphere. | The lithosphere is thinner under the oceans than under continents.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable, used with «the». Pronounced «LITH-oh-sfeer». From Greek «lithos» = stone. Not quite the same as «the crust»: the lithosphere is the crust plus the stiff upper mantle. Myth: the mantle is not a sea of liquid lava; it is mostly solid rock that flows very slowly.

part of speech: noun (litmus, uncountable); adjective (litmus — in litmus test, litmus paper)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) Litmus is a dye made from lichens that turns red in acid and blue in alkali, used to test liquids. 2) A litmus test is a test with litmus paper; (figurative) it is also a simple test that clearly shows what someone thinks or what something is really like.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons pupils dip litmus paper into lemon juice (turns red, acid), soap water (turns blue, alkali) and pure water (no change, neutral). In everyday and political talk, «a litmus test» means one key question that shows the truth. Phrases: «litmus paper», «red litmus», «blue litmus», «litmus test».
examples from the lessons: Lemon juice turned the blue litmus paper red. | Soap turned the red litmus paper blue. | Use litmus to find out if the liquid is an acid. | Water does not change the colour of litmus. | The vote was a litmus test for the new leader. | How people treat waiters is a litmus test of their kindness.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «some litmus», «litmus paper». Rule to remember: acids turn blue litmus red; alkalis turn red litmus blue. Litmus shows acid or alkali but not how strong; universal indicator gives a range of colours (pH 1–14).

meaning for a pupil: 1) An earlobe (lobe) is the soft round part at the bottom of your ear. 2) (science) A lobe is a round part of an organ, like the lobes of the brain, the lungs or the liver. 3) A lobe is a rounded part of a leaf or another shape that sticks out.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons pupils learn the brain has lobes (frontal, parietal, temporal, occipital), each doing different jobs, and the right lung has three lobes, the left two. In nature study, oak leaves have rounded lobes. In everyday life, ear piercings are often in the lobe. Phrases: «ear lobe», «frontal lobe».
examples from the lessons: She has her ear lobes pierced. | The frontal lobe of the brain helps us plan. | The right lung has three lobes. | Oak leaves have wavy lobes. | The occipital lobe helps us see. | My earlobes get cold in winter.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a lobe, lobes. «Earlobe» is usually one word. Myth: attached versus free earlobes is not a simple one-gene trait, though textbooks often say so. Do not confuse with «globe» or «lob» (a high throw).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Locomotion is the ability to move from one place to another, or the way an animal or person moves. 2) (history) Locomotion is also the name of one of the first steam railway engines (Locomotion No. 1, 1825).
its sense in the lessons: In science and PE lessons it covers how animals move — walking, running, hopping, slithering, swimming, flying — and the body parts used (muscles, bones, fins, wings). In history lessons, steam locomotion changed travel. Related: locomotive (train engine). Phrases: «means of locomotion», «animal locomotion».
examples from the lessons: Fish use their fins for locomotion. | Snakes have a special kind of locomotion without legs. | Walking on two legs is human locomotion. | Muscles and bones work together for locomotion. | In PE we practised different locomotion skills, like skipping and hopping. | Locomotion No. 1 pulled the first public steam train.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable, formal or scientific word for moving. Adjective and noun: locomotive (a railway engine). From Latin «loco» (from a place) + «motion». Plants are not capable of locomotion, though they move in other ways (turning to light).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A lorikeet is a small, very brightly coloured parrot from Australia, New Guinea and nearby islands, which feeds on nectar and pollen from flowers with a brush-tipped tongue.
its sense in the lessons: In Australian and NZ life, rainbow lorikeets are common in gardens and parks, noisy and colourful (blue head, green back, orange chest). In science lessons they show how birds pollinate flowers and adapt to eat nectar. In New Zealand and Western Australia they can be pests because they were brought in and compete with local birds. Phrases: «rainbow lorikeet», «a flock of lorikeets».
examples from the lessons: A rainbow lorikeet landed on our balcony. | Lorikeets drink nectar from gum tree flowers. | The lorikeets screeched in the trees at sunset. | Lorikeets have tongues like little brushes. | Feeding bread and honey to lorikeets can make them sick. | We counted twelve lorikeets in the park.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a lorikeet, lorikeets. Pronounced «LOR-ih-keet». Related: lory (a bigger parrot). Wildlife experts say not to feed wild lorikeets honey or bread, as it is bad for their health.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Magenta is a bright purplish-red or pinkish-purple colour. 2) (science, printing) Magenta is one of the main colours of printer ink, with cyan, yellow and black (CMYK).
its sense in the lessons: In art and computing lessons it is used in colour mixing: in light, red + blue light make magenta; in printing, magenta ink is a primary colour. It is named after the town of Magenta in Italy, where a battle took place in 1859, the year the dye was discovered. Phrases: «magenta ink», «bright magenta».
examples from the lessons: She painted the flowers bright magenta. | The printer needs a new magenta cartridge. | Red and blue light together make magenta. | My new scarf is magenta. | Mixing magenta and yellow ink makes red. | The sunset sky was streaked with magenta.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable when it is the colour name. Pronounced «muh-JEN-tuh». Interesting fact: there is no single wavelength of light for magenta; our brains make it when we see red and blue light together. Similar: fuchsia, pink, purple.

part of speech: noun (makeup, uncountable; a make-up — UK); also make-up
meaning for a pupil: 1) Makeup is coloured creams and powders, like lipstick, mascara and foundation, put on the face to change how it looks. 2) The makeup of something is what it is made of, or the different parts or people in it: «the makeup of the class». 3) A person's makeup is their character. 4) (US, school) A makeup test or class is one you take later because you missed the first one.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life makeup is used by many adults and by actors on stage; face paint at fairs is a kind of makeup. In science and maths, «the makeup» means the parts of something: «the makeup of the air is about 78% nitrogen». In US schools, a «makeup exam» is a test taken later. Phrases: «put on makeup», «stage makeup», «the makeup of».
examples from the lessons: Mum puts on makeup before work. | The actors wore stage makeup. | The clown's makeup made him look happy. | The makeup of the team is five girls and six boys. | What is the makeup of the Earth's atmosphere? | Being kind is part of his makeup. | (US) I missed the test, so I have a makeup on Friday.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelled «makeup» (more US), «make-up» (more UK) or «make up» as a verb. The verb is two words: «make up» (to invent, to become friends again, or to put on makeup). Uncountable: «a lot of makeup», not «makeups».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A mallard is the most common wild duck; the male (drake) has a shiny green head, a white ring round the neck and a grey body, and the female is speckled brown.
its sense in the lessons: In science and nature lessons it is the duck children see on ponds and rivers in Britain, Ireland, North America, Australia and NZ; most farm ducks come from mallards. In history, «Mallard» is also the name of a famous British steam train that set the world speed record for steam in 1938 (126 mph). Phrases: «a pair of mallards», «mallard ducklings».
examples from the lessons: A mallard swam across the pond. | The male mallard has a bright green head. | The female mallard is brown so she is hidden on the nest. | Mallard ducklings followed their mother in a line. | Don't feed the mallards bread — give them peas or oats instead. | The steam engine Mallard is the fastest steam locomotive.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: mallards, or mallard for a group (like «fish»). Pronounced «MAL-ard». The male is a drake, the female a duck, the young are ducklings. Bread is not good for ducks; it can make them ill and pollute the water.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal, Ireland, UK north, Scotland) A child's word for mother, like «mum» or «mammy» said by Irish children. 2) (old-fashioned, offensive, US history) A racist stereotype name once used for a Black woman who looked after a white family's children; it is not used today except when talking about history.
its sense in the lessons: In stories set in Ireland or the north of England, a child calling «Mammy!» shows a warm, homely family voice. In everyday Irish speech adults may still say «my mammy» about their own mother. In history lessons about slavery and the American South, the word appears as an example of an unfair stereotype. Phrases: «my mammy», «go ask your mammy», «mammy and daddy».
examples from the lessons: Mammy, can I have a biscuit? | Siobhan ran home to tell her mammy about the prize. | In Dublin lots of kids still say mammy instead of mum. | «Wait till your mammy hears about this!» said Granda. | My mammy makes the best brown bread in Cork. | The old film used a hurtful «mammy» character, and our teacher explained why it is racist. | Mammy and Daddy are coming to the school play.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «mammies». Informal and family-only: in writing at school use «mother» or «mum». The Irish/UK sense is warm and normal; the US history sense is a racist stereotype, so do not call anyone «a mammy». Do not confuse with «mummy» (UK mum, or an Egyptian wrapped body) or «mammal».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Connected with the sea, ships and sailing. 2) Near the sea or living by the sea: a maritime country or climate. 3) (Canada) «the Maritimes» are the three east-coast provinces: Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island.
its sense in the lessons: In geography, a maritime climate is mild and wet because the sea keeps the land from getting very hot or very cold — like Ireland or New Zealand. In history, maritime trade and maritime empires were built with ships. A maritime museum shows boats, maps and sailors' tools. Phrases: «maritime climate», «maritime museum», «maritime law», «maritime nation», «the Maritimes».
examples from the lessons: We visited the maritime museum and saw an old ship's wheel. | Britain has a maritime climate with cool summers and mild winters. | Portugal was a great maritime nation that sent explorers across the oceans. | Maritime law decides who owns a shipwreck. | My cousin lives in the Maritimes, in Halifax, Nova Scotia. | The maritime police check boats in the harbour. | Lighthouses are part of maritime safety.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective only; it goes before a noun («maritime history»). Formal-sounding word; in everyday speech people say «sea» or «seaside». Spelling: mari-time (from Latin «mare», sea). Do not confuse with «marine» (living in the sea: marine animals) — maritime is more about ships, trade and coasts.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To do with the Maya, the people of Central America (Mexico, Guatemala, Belize, Honduras) whose ancient civilisation built stone cities and pyramids. 2) A Maya person; also the Mayan languages, which millions of people still speak today.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons «the ancient Maya» or «Mayan civilisation» (about 2000 BC to AD 1500 and later) is a common topic: pyramids such as Chichén Itzá, a writing system of glyphs, a calendar, maths with zero, and chocolate drinks made from cacao. In maths the Mayan number system uses dots (1), bars (5) and a shell for zero, and counts in twenties. Phrases: «Mayan calendar», «Mayan pyramid», «Mayan numbers», «Mayan gods».
examples from the lessons: The Mayan pyramid had steep steps up to a temple. | We wrote our ages in Mayan numbers using dots and bars. | Mayan people still live in Guatemala and speak Mayan languages. | The Mayan calendar was very accurate. | Ancient Mayan farmers grew maize, beans and squash. | A shell stood for zero in Mayan maths. | Some people claimed the Mayan calendar said the world would end, but it did not say that.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital letter: Mayan, Maya. Experts often say «Maya» for the people and the ancient civilisation and «Mayan» for the languages, but both are common. Myth: the Mayan calendar did not predict the end of the world; a long cycle simply started again. Do not confuse with «Aztec» or «Inca», other American civilisations. In Mayan numbers a bar = 5, a dot = 1, and place values go up in twenties.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) A very thin layer, like a skin, that covers or lines a part of a living thing or a cell. 2) A thin sheet of material, natural or man-made, that lets some things pass through and stops others. 3) The cell membrane: the thin outer layer around every living cell that controls what goes in and out.
its sense in the lessons: In science, the cell membrane is part of every cell (plant and animal); it lets water, food and oxygen in and waste out. The eardrum is a membrane that vibrates with sound. Inside an eggshell there is a thin membrane. Builders use waterproof membranes under floors and roofs. Phrases: «cell membrane», «thin membrane», «waterproof membrane», «mucous membrane».
