examples from the lessons: The cell membrane controls what goes in and out of the cell. | Peel the egg carefully and you will see a thin membrane under the shell. | The eardrum is a membrane that shakes when sound hits it. | A frog has a membrane that covers its eyes underwater. | Bats' wings are made of a stretchy membrane of skin. | The builder put a plastic membrane under the concrete to keep out damp. | Your nose is lined with a wet membrane that traps dust.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: a membrane, membranes. Mostly a science word. Do not confuse «cell membrane» with «cell wall»: plant cells have both, animal cells have only a membrane. Spelling: mem-brane (not «membraine»).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A unit of mass equal to one millionth of a gram; its symbol is µg (sometimes mcg on medicine labels).
its sense in the lessons: In science and on vitamin or medicine labels, micrograms measure very tiny amounts, such as vitamin D or vitamin B12. In maths, conversions: 1 gram = 1000 milligrams = 1 000 000 micrograms; 1 milligram = 1000 micrograms. Phrases: «micrograms of vitamin D», «per microgram», «µg».
examples from the lessons: The vitamin tablet has 10 micrograms of vitamin D. | One milligram equals one thousand micrograms. | A grain of sand weighs much more than a microgram. | The label says «400 µg of folic acid». | Scientists measure tiny amounts of poison in micrograms. | How many micrograms are in half a milligram? Five hundred. | Medicine doses in micrograms must be measured very carefully.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «micrograms». Symbol µg (µ is the Greek letter mu) or «mcg». Maths: micro = one millionth; to change grams to micrograms multiply by 1 000 000; milligrams to micrograms multiply by 1000. Trap: do not mix up mg (milligram) and µg (microgram) — a microgram is 1000 times smaller. Safety: only adults should give medicines.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A living thing so tiny that you can only see it with a microscope, such as a bacterium, a virus (usually counted with them), some fungi like yeast, or algae.
its sense in the lessons: In science, microorganisms (microbes) can be helpful — making bread rise, yogurt, cheese and compost, and living in your gut — or harmful, causing illness and making food go off. Hygiene lessons explain washing hands to remove harmful microorganisms. Phrases: «harmful microorganisms», «useful microorganisms», «under a microscope», «germs».
examples from the lessons: Yeast is a microorganism that makes bread dough rise. | Some microorganisms cause food to go mouldy. | Washing your hands with soap removes many harmful microorganisms. | We looked at pond water and saw microorganisms swimming under the microscope. | Bacteria in yogurt are helpful microorganisms. | Microorganisms in the compost heap break down leaves and peel. | Fridges slow down the growth of microorganisms.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a microorganism, microorganisms. Also spelled «micro-organism» (common in the UK). Everyday words: «microbe», «germ» (germ usually means a harmful one). Myth: not all microorganisms are bad — most are harmless or helpful. Viruses are often grouped with microorganisms although scientists argue whether they are truly alive.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A box or device that connects a computer or home network to the internet through a phone line, cable or fibre. 2) Often, at home, the same box as the router that makes the Wi-Fi.
its sense in the lessons: In computing lessons the modem is the link between your home and the internet provider: data goes from the computer to the router, to the modem, and out along the line. Old modems made screeching noises when they dialled up. Everyday: «turn the modem off and on again» is a common fix when the internet is down. Phrases: «reset the modem», «the modem lights», «modem and router».
examples from the lessons: The internet stopped, so Dad switched the modem off and on again. | The modem has blinking green lights. | Our modem is plugged into the phone socket. | In the old days modems made a squealing sound when they connected. | The modem and router are in one box in our hallway. | A modem turns computer signals into signals that can travel along a cable. | The engineer came to fit a new fibre modem.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a modem, modems. The name comes from «modulator–demodulator». Common confusion: a modem connects to the internet, while a router shares the connection between devices (Wi-Fi); many homes have one box doing both. Stress on the first syllable: MO-dem.

part of speech: adjective (moderate, more moderate, most moderate); verb (moderate, moderates, moderated, moderating); noun (a moderate, moderates)
meaning for a pupil: 1) adjective: Not too much and not too little; medium in size, amount or strength. 2) adjective: Not extreme in opinions, especially in politics. 3) verb: To make or become less strong or extreme. 4) verb: To be in charge of a discussion, debate or online chat and keep it fair and safe. 5) verb (UK, school): To check that teachers' marks on exams are fair. 6) noun: A person with moderate (not extreme) political views.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday health talk «moderate exercise» means activity that makes you warm and a bit out of breath; «in moderation» means not too much (sweets, screen time). In weather reports «moderate rain» or «moderate winds» are in the middle. In politics a moderate is in the middle, not extreme. Online, moderators remove unkind or unsafe posts. Phrases: «moderate exercise», «in moderation», «moderate heat», «moderate a debate».
examples from the lessons: Cook the soup over a moderate heat. | Eat sweets in moderation, not every day. | There will be moderate winds and showers this afternoon. | Thirty minutes of moderate exercise is good for your heart. | Our teacher moderated the class debate so everyone had a turn. | The forum moderator deleted the rude comment. | She was a moderate who wanted both parties to agree. | He moderated his voice when the baby fell asleep.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronunciation differs: adjective/noun MOD-er-ut, verb MOD-er-ate. Adverb «moderately» (moderately difficult). Noun for the person: «moderator». «Moderation» means keeping to a sensible amount. In maths problems «moderate» is not a number word, but «moderately» can mean «fairly».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A small pile of earth pushed up by a mole digging its tunnels underground. 2) In the saying «make a mountain out of a molehill»: to treat a small problem as if it were a huge one.
its sense in the lessons: In nature lessons molehills on a lawn or field show that a mole lives underground. In everyday speech and stories, the idiom tells the reader that someone is overreacting. Phrases: «make a mountain out of a molehill», «a field full of molehills».
examples from the lessons: The football pitch was covered in molehills. | A mole digs tunnels and pushes the soil up into molehills. | You've only lost a pencil — don't make a mountain out of a molehill! | Grandad grumbled about the molehills on his lawn. | We never saw the mole, only fresh molehills each morning. | Mum said the argument was a molehill, not a mountain. | Gardeners sometimes use the fine soil from molehills for seed pots.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a molehill, molehills. One word. The idiom is common and means «overreacting». The animal is a mole; do not confuse with «mole» the dark spot on skin or «mole» in chemistry.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A building or group of buildings where monks live, pray and work together under religious rules. 2) (history) Such a place as a centre of learning, farming and copying books in the Middle Ages.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, monasteries such as Lindisfarne and Iona were places where monks copied books by hand and were attacked by Vikings; Henry VIII closed many English monasteries. In religious education, monasteries exist in Christianity and in Buddhism. Phrases: «live in a monastery», «a ruined monastery», «monastery garden», «dissolution of the monasteries».
examples from the lessons: The monks in the monastery get up early to pray. | We visited the ruins of an old monastery on the island. | Vikings attacked the monastery at Lindisfarne. | In the Middle Ages monks in the monastery copied books by hand. | There is a Buddhist monastery in the mountains of Tibet. | The monastery garden grew herbs for medicine. | Henry VIII closed the monasteries and took their land.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «monasteries» (y → ies). A place for monks; a place for nuns is usually a «convent» or «nunnery». «Abbey» and «priory» are kinds of monastery. Adjective: «monastic». Spelling: monast-ery (ends in -ery, not -ary).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Meat from an adult sheep, older than lamb, with a stronger taste. 2) In the saying «mutton dressed as lamb» (UK, informal, unkind): an older person dressed in clothes made for much younger people.
its sense in the lessons: In food lessons and stories, mutton is used in stews, curries (mutton curry is common in South Asian cooking) and in old recipes like Irish stew and Scotch broth. In history, mutton was a cheap everyday meat. Phrases: «mutton stew», «mutton curry», «leg of mutton», «mutton chop», «mutton dressed as lamb».
examples from the lessons: Grandma made a mutton stew with potatoes and carrots. | Mutton comes from older sheep and lamb from young ones. | The restaurant sells spicy mutton curry. | In the old story the farmer ate bread and cold mutton. | Mutton takes a long time to cook so it gets tender. | «Mutton chops» are also long sideburns on a man's face. | It is rude to say someone looks like mutton dressed as lamb.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «some mutton», not «a mutton». Lamb = young sheep's meat; mutton = adult sheep's meat; hogget = in between. In some countries (India, Pakistan) «mutton» can also mean goat meat. «Mutton chops» = a cut of meat or a style of whiskers.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The money of Nigeria; one naira is divided into 100 kobo. Its sign is ₦.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and money lessons naira may appear in word problems about Nigeria or currency exchange. In stories set in Nigeria, prices in naira tell the reader the setting. Phrases: «a hundred naira», «the naira fell», «naira notes».
examples from the lessons: The book cost five hundred naira at the market in Lagos. | One naira is made of a hundred kobo. | The sign for naira is ₦. | Ada saved her naira notes in a tin. | The news said the naira had lost value against the dollar. | If one mango costs 200 naira, how much do three cost? Six hundred naira.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural is usually «naira» (200 naira), sometimes «nairas». Not capitalised in English. Maths: 100 kobo = 1 naira, so 250 kobo = 2.5 naira. Pronounced NYE-ra.

meaning for a pupil: 1) noun: A person who strongly believes their nation should rule itself, or who thinks their own country is more important than others. 2) adjective: To do with such beliefs or groups: a nationalist party. 3) (Ireland, Northern Ireland) A person who wants Northern Ireland to join the rest of Ireland.
its sense in the lessons: In history and politics lessons, nationalists led independence movements (for example, ending empires) but nationalism has also been used to stir up hatred of other nations, as in wars of the 20th century. In news about Scotland, Wales, Catalonia or Northern Ireland, «nationalist» names parties that want self-rule. Phrases: «a nationalist party», «nationalist movement», «Irish nationalists», «Scottish nationalists».
examples from the lessons: The nationalists wanted their country to be free from the empire. | The Scottish National Party is a nationalist party. | In Northern Ireland, nationalists hope for a united Ireland. | Some nationalist leaders started wars against their neighbours. | The history book explained how nationalist feelings grew in Europe. | Loving your country is patriotism; thinking other countries are worse can be extreme nationalism.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun and adjective. Related: «nation», «nationalism». Usage trap: the word can be neutral (wanting self-rule) or negative (thinking your nation is better than others); look at the context. Do not confuse with «national» (belonging to a nation: national anthem) or «nationality» (the country you belong to).

part of speech: verb (neigh, neighs, neighed, neighing); noun (a neigh, neighs)
meaning for a pupil: 1) verb: When a horse neighs, it makes its long, high, loud call. 2) noun: The sound a horse makes.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, a horse neighing tells the reader it is excited, frightened or calling to other horses. In early reading, animal sounds: cows moo, sheep baa, horses neigh. Phrases: «neigh loudly», «a loud neigh», «gave a neigh».
examples from the lessons: The horse neighed when it saw the farmer with the hay. | We heard a loud neigh from the stable. | The pony neighed and tossed its head. | Cows moo and horses neigh. | The frightened horse gave a high neigh and galloped away. | Can you neigh like a horse?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past «neighed». Pronounced «nay», the same sound as «nay» (old word for no). Spelling has silent «gh» like in «weigh» and «eight». Homophone: nay. Other horse sounds: whinny, snort, nicker.

part of speech: noun (a nerd, nerds); adjective (nerdy, nerdier, nerdiest)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal, slang) A person who is very interested and clever in one subject, such as computers, science or maths, and knows a lot about it. 2) (slang, can be unkind) A person thought of as boring or not cool because they study a lot or like unusual hobbies. 3) (informal, friendly) Used proudly about yourself: «I'm a book nerd».
its sense in the lessons: In school life, «nerd» can be a teasing name, but today many people say it proudly: «science nerd», «maths nerd», «Lego nerd». In stories, the nerd character is often clever and saves the day. Phrases: «computer nerd», «total nerd», «nerd out about», «nerdy glasses».
examples from the lessons: Sam is a total science nerd and knows every planet's moons. | I'm a bit of a book nerd — I read every night. | Don't call him a nerd; it's unkind. | She nerded out about dinosaurs for an hour. | The computer nerds in the film saved the spaceship. | That joke about prime numbers is so nerdy. | Being a nerd just means you really care about something.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a nerd, nerds. Adjective «nerdy». Register: informal/slang; it can hurt when used to mock someone, so tone matters. Similar words: geek (very similar), boffin (UK, a clever scientist), swot (UK, someone who studies a lot).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) A chemical reaction in which an acid and an alkali (or base) react and cancel each other out, making a salt and water. 2) The act of making something have no effect, or stopping a danger.
its sense in the lessons: In science, neutralisation is used to treat indigestion (an antacid neutralises stomach acid), bee and wasp stings, acid soil (farmers add lime), and in toothpaste. Indicator paper turns green at neutral (pH 7). The general formula: acid + alkali → salt + water. Phrases: «neutralisation reaction», «acid and alkali», «pH 7».
examples from the lessons: Neutralisation happens when an acid reacts with an alkali. | Indigestion tablets work by neutralisation of stomach acid. | Acid + alkali → salt + water is a neutralisation reaction. | After neutralisation, the universal indicator turned green. | Farmers spread lime on acid soil for neutralisation. | The bomb squad worked on the neutralisation of the old bomb.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK spelling «neutralisation»; US spelling «neutralization». Verb: neutralise/neutralize; adjective: neutral. Neutral means pH 7 — not acid and not alkali. Myth: «vinegar for wasp stings and baking soda for bee stings» is a popular tip, but the evidence is weak; safety: a bad sting reaction needs an adult and a doctor.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A secret fighter or spy in old Japan, trained in fighting, sneaking and disguises. 2) (informal) A person who is very skilled at something: «a spelling ninja».
its sense in the lessons: In stories, cartoons and games, ninjas wear black, move silently and do clever tricks; real ninjas in history were spies and scouts in Japan in the 1400s–1600s. In everyday kid talk, «ninja» praises skill or stealth. Phrases: «ninja warrior», «like a ninja», «ninja moves», «maths ninja».
examples from the lessons: The ninja crept silently across the rooftop. | I sneaked downstairs like a ninja to get a snack. | Ninjas were real spies in old Japan. | You solved that puzzle so fast — you're a maths ninja! | The cartoon about ninja turtles is very old but still popular. | My brother does ninja moves on the trampoline.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «ninjas» (sometimes «ninja» as in Japanese). Myth: real ninjas did not always wear black suits — they often disguised themselves as farmers or travellers. Do not confuse with «samurai», the warrior class who served lords openly.

part of speech: adjective (Norman); noun (a Norman, Normans; Norman — a name)
meaning for a pupil: 1) noun (history): The Normans were people from Normandy in northern France; in 1066 William the Conqueror led them to conquer England. 2) adjective: To do with the Normans: Norman castles, Norman French. 3) (a name) Norman is a man's first name, and also a surname.
its sense in the lessons: In UK history lessons, the Norman Conquest of 1066, the Battle of Hastings, the Bayeux Tapestry, the Domesday Book and Norman motte-and-bailey castles are key topics. Norman French added many words to English (beef, pork, judge, castle). Phrases: «the Norman Conquest», «Norman castle», «Norman French», «Norman invasion».
examples from the lessons: The Normans invaded England in 1066. | William the Conqueror was a Norman duke. | We visited a Norman castle with thick stone walls. | Norman French gave English words like «beef» and «court». | The Bayeux Tapestry shows the Norman invasion. | My grandad's name is Norman. | Norman churches have round arches.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital letter: Norman. Plural «Normans». Related: Normandy (the region in France). The Normans were descended from Vikings (Norsemen). Trap: a lower-case «norman» is not a normal English word; it is a name or the people/style. In history, Norman architecture = Romanesque, with round arches.

part of speech: noun (nu — the Greek letter); interjection (nu — Yiddish, informal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The 13th letter of the Greek alphabet, written Ν (capital) and ν (small); it sounds like English «n». 2) (Yiddish, informal) A word meaning «well?», «so?» or «come on», heard in some Jewish families' English. 3) Sometimes a playful spelling of «new» in brand names («nu-look»).
its sense in the lessons: In maths and science, the small letter ν (nu) is used for frequency in physics or for numbers in some formulas; it looks like a small v, so pupils often mix them up. In the Greek alphabet lessons: alpha, beta, … mu, nu, xi. In stories, a Yiddish-speaking grandparent saying «Nu?» means «Well? Go on!». Not a common English word on its own.
examples from the lessons: Nu is the Greek letter that comes after mu. | The small letter nu looks like a v. | In physics, nu can stand for frequency. | «Nu? Are you going to eat your soup or not?» asked Bubbe. | The alphabet song in Greek goes «…lambda, mu, nu, xi…». | The shop sign said «Nu Look Hair» instead of «New Look».
note for the reader of a maths problem: Not an ordinary English word: it is a Greek letter name, a Yiddish interjection, or a playful spelling of «new». Pronounced «new» or «noo». Trap: in printed formulas ν (nu) and v (vee) look almost the same.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To do with numbers or shown in numbers. 2) In order of numbers: «in numerical order» means 1, 2, 3 and so on.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, «numerical order» means arranging by number value; «numerical answer» means an answer as a number; «numerical data» are numbers you can measure or count (as opposed to words or categories). In science, results in tables are numerical. Phrases: «numerical order», «numerical value», «numerical data», «numerical answer».
examples from the lessons: Put the cards in numerical order, from smallest to biggest. | The answer must be numerical, not a word. | Height and weight are numerical data, but eye colour is not. | The houses on our street are not in numerical order! | Each letter in the code has a numerical value. | The test had numerical questions and word questions.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective only. Related: number, numeral, numerous (means «many» — a different meaning!). Trap: «numerical order» means by number value, not alphabetical order. In statistics, numerical data can be counted or measured; categorical data are names or groups.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To do with nutrition: the food a body needs to grow, have energy and stay healthy. 2) To do with how much good a food gives the body: its nutritional value.
its sense in the lessons: In food and health lessons, the «nutritional information» label on packets shows energy (calories or kilojoules), fat, sugar, salt, protein and fibre per 100 g or per serving. Pupils compare labels and read traffic-light colours (UK). Phrases: «nutritional value», «nutritional information», «nutritional needs», «nutritional label».
examples from the lessons: Read the nutritional information on the back of the cereal box. | Fruit and vegetables have high nutritional value. | Babies have different nutritional needs from adults. | The nutritional label says there are 5 grams of sugar per 100 grams. | Crisps are tasty but have little nutritional value. | Athletes plan their meals for nutritional balance.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective; formal word. Related: nutrition, nutrient, nutritious (= good for you: «a nutritious meal»). Trap: «nutritional» describes things about food value; «nutritious» means healthy. In maths on labels, «per 100 g» lets you compare foods fairly.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To do with the ocean or living in the ocean. 2) Like an ocean: very big and wide. 3) (geography) To do with Oceania, the region of Australia, New Zealand and the Pacific islands.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and science: «oceanic climate» (mild, wet, like Ireland and New Zealand), «oceanic crust» (the rock under the oceans), «oceanic trench» (very deep cracks such as the Mariana Trench), oceanic animals like whales and albatrosses. Phrases: «oceanic crust», «oceanic trench», «oceanic islands», «oceanic climate».
examples from the lessons: Whales and albatrosses are oceanic animals. | The oceanic crust is thinner than the continental crust. | Hawaii is a group of oceanic islands made by volcanoes. | The Mariana Trench is the deepest oceanic trench. | New Zealand has an oceanic climate. | Oceanic winds carried the boat far from land.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective; pronounced oh-shee-AN-ik. Related: ocean, oceanography, Oceania. Similar: marine (living in the sea), maritime (ships and the sea). Trap: «ocean» vs «sea» — oceans are the five biggest bodies of salt water.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To do with seeing and the eyes. 2) To do with light and how it travels, or with instruments that use light, such as lenses, microscopes and telescopes.
its sense in the lessons: In science, «optical illusion» is a picture that tricks your eyes and brain; «optical fibre» carries light (and internet data) along thin glass threads. Opticians sell glasses. Phrases: «optical illusion», «optical fibre», «optical instrument», «optical mouse».
examples from the lessons: The picture is an optical illusion: the two lines look different but are the same length. | Optical fibres carry internet signals as flashes of light. | A telescope is an optical instrument. | The optical mouse uses a tiny light to see movement. | Optical shops sell glasses and contact lenses. | The magician used optical tricks with mirrors.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective. Related: optician (a person who tests eyes and sells glasses), optics (the science of light). UK spelling «optical fibre», US «optical fiber». Trap: «optical» is about sight and light, not «optional» (you can choose).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A group of people who work together for a purpose, such as a charity, a club, a company or a school. 2) The planning and arranging of things so they work well. 3) The way something is arranged or put together.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, organizations include charities (Red Cross, UNICEF), sports clubs and companies. In school, «organization» is a skill: having your bag packed, homework planned and notes in order. In writing lessons, the organization of a text means paragraphs and order of ideas. Phrases: «a charity organization», «good organization», «lack of organization», «the World Health Organization».
examples from the lessons: The Red Cross is an organization that helps people in disasters. | Good organization helps you finish your homework on time. | Our teacher praised the organization of my story into clear paragraphs. | The United Nations is an international organization. | The school trip failed because of poor organization. | She works for an organization that protects wildlife.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable (an organization) and uncountable (good organization). UK spelling «organisation» is also common; US and Canada use «-ization». Verb: organize/organise; person: organizer. Adjective: organized (tidy, planned). Trap: in names, keep the official spelling (World Health Organization).

meaning for a pupil: 1) The direction something faces or points: north, south, up, sideways. 2) (school) A short welcome time or tour that helps new pupils or workers learn their way around. 3) (maps, maths) Finding your way using a map and compass; or how a shape is turned. 4) (formal) A person's basic beliefs, interests or who they are attracted to (as in «sexual orientation»).
its sense in the lessons: In maths, the orientation of a shape changes when you rotate or reflect it; a page can be portrait or landscape orientation. In geography and outdoor education, orienteering is a sport of finding your way with a map. In school, «orientation day» welcomes new students. Phrases: «portrait/landscape orientation», «orientation day», «sense of orientation», «sexual orientation».
examples from the lessons: Turn the page to landscape orientation for your graph. | The new pupils had an orientation tour of the school. | After the shape is rotated, its orientation changes but its size stays the same. | Use the compass to check the orientation of the map. | The house has a south-facing orientation, so it gets lots of sun. | Freshers' week at university begins with orientation.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable and uncountable. Verb: orient (US) / orientate (UK). Related: orienteering. Maths: rotations and reflections change orientation; translations do not. «Sexual orientation» is a respectful formal phrase used in law and health.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The Japanese art of folding paper into shapes like birds, animals and boxes, usually without cutting or glue.
its sense in the lessons: In art and maths lessons, origami teaches following steps, symmetry, fractions (folding in half, quarters) and shapes (squares, triangles). A famous model is the paper crane; in Japan, folding 1000 cranes is linked to wishes and peace. Phrases: «origami crane», «origami paper», «fold an origami frog».
examples from the lessons: We made an origami frog that can jump. | Origami usually starts with a square piece of paper. | Folding the paper in half makes two equal rectangles. | Sadako folded origami cranes while she was in hospital. | Origami helped us learn about lines of symmetry. | My nan taught me origami on a rainy day.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «some origami», «an origami model» (not «an origami» in careful speech). Japanese word: «ori» = fold, «kami» = paper. Pronounced or-i-GAH-mee. Similar art: kirigami (folding and cutting).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A sea animal with a soft body inside a rough, hinged shell; some are eaten as food. 2) A pearl oyster: a kind of oyster that can make a pearl inside its shell. 3) In the saying «the world is your oyster»: you can go anywhere and do anything you choose.
its sense in the lessons: In science, oysters are molluscs that filter water to feed; oyster reefs clean the sea. In history and food, oysters were once a cheap food in London. The idiom «the world is your oyster» is often said to young people leaving school. Phrases: «oyster shell», «pearl oyster», «oyster bed», «the world is your oyster».
examples from the lessons: An oyster has a hard rough shell. | A pearl grows inside an oyster when sand or grit gets in. | Oysters clean the water by filtering it. | Grandad loves eating oysters at the seaside. | You're young and clever — the world is your oyster! | Fishermen collected oysters from the oyster beds. | London's «Oyster card» is used to pay for buses and the Tube.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: an oyster, oysters (use «an»). Myth: not every oyster makes pearls, and pearls usually form around a tiny parasite or bit of tissue, not just a grain of sand. Safety: raw oysters can make people ill; only eat them fresh from a safe source.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To cut away the thin outer skin or edge of something, such as fruit or nails, with a knife. 2) To make something smaller bit by bit: «pare down», «pare back» costs or a list.
its sense in the lessons: In cooking, you pare an apple or a potato with a paring knife. In everyday and business talk, «pare down» means cut down to the important parts: pare down a story, pare back spending. Phrases: «pare an apple», «paring knife», «pare down», «pare back».
examples from the lessons: Mum pared the apple in one long curly strip. | Use a paring knife to pare the potatoes. | We had to pare down our list of party guests. | The school pared back spending on trips this year. | She pared her story down to 300 words. | Grandpa pared his fingernails on the porch.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past «pared». Homophones: pair (two), pear (the fruit) — all sound the same! Trap: «pare» (cut thinly) vs «peel» (more common for fruit). Safety: knives need adult help.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (punctuation) A word, phrase or sentence put into another sentence as extra information, marked by brackets, commas or dashes. 2) (US) One of the round brackets ( ). 3) (maths) Round brackets that show which part of a calculation to do first.
its sense in the lessons: In grammar lessons (UK Key Stage 2), pupils learn parenthesis: extra information marked by brackets, dashes or commas, as in «My dog (who is very old) sleeps a lot». In maths, operations inside parentheses are done first (BIDMAS, BODMAS, PEMDAS). Phrases: «in parentheses», «use parenthesis», «brackets for parenthesis».
examples from the lessons: My cat, who is very lazy, sleeps all day — this is parenthesis with commas. | Put extra information in parentheses (like this). | In maths, work out the parentheses first: (3 + 4) × 2 = 14. | Use dashes for parenthesis — they make it stand out. | The teacher asked us to add a parenthesis to our sentence. | In the US, ( ) are called parentheses; in the UK they are usually «brackets».
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «parentheses» (-is → -es, like crisis/crises). Adjective «parenthetical». Maths: (2 + 3) × 4 = 20 but 2 + 3 × 4 = 14 — brackets change the answer. Trap: in UK school grammar «parenthesis» means the extra phrase itself; in US use it often means the bracket marks.

part of speech: noun (a pasty, pasties — PAST-ee); adjective (pasty, pastier, pastiest — PAYST-ee)
meaning for a pupil: 1) noun (UK): A pastry case folded around a filling of meat and vegetables, baked; the Cornish pasty is famous. 2) adjective: (of a face or skin) Pale and unhealthy-looking, like dough. 3) adjective: Like paste: thick and sticky.
its sense in the lessons: In UK and Cornish life, pasties are a lunch food; Cornish miners took them underground and held the thick crust edge. In stories, «a pasty face» shows someone is ill, tired or has not been outside. Phrases: «Cornish pasty», «a meat pasty», «pasty-faced», «pale and pasty».
examples from the lessons: We bought a hot Cornish pasty at the beach. | The pasty was filled with beef, potato and onion. | Tin miners used to eat pasties down the mines. | After being ill all week he looked pasty and tired. | The paint looked thick and pasty. | Gran bakes cheese and onion pasties on Saturdays.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Two pronunciations: the food is PASS-tee (short a); the pale adjective is PAYS-tee (like «paste»). Plural noun: pasties. In the US, the food is less known except in Michigan; «pasties» there can also mean something else, so be careful. Comparatives: pastier, pastiest.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A soldier or police officer, often sent by the United Nations, whose job is to stop fighting and keep peace between groups after a war. 2) A person who calms arguments and helps others make friends again.
its sense in the lessons: In news and history lessons, UN peacekeepers wear blue helmets and work in places like Cyprus, Lebanon, South Sudan and the Congo; Ireland, Canada, Fiji and New Zealand often send them. In school life, a peacekeeper is the friend who stops quarrels in the playground. Phrases: «UN peacekeepers», «blue helmets», «peacekeeping force», «peacekeeping mission».
examples from the lessons: UN peacekeepers wear blue helmets. | Irish soldiers have served as peacekeepers in Lebanon for many years. | The peacekeepers patrolled the border to stop the fighting. | My sister is the peacekeeper in our family when we argue. | Canada was proud of its peacekeepers. | A peacekeeper helps both sides talk instead of fight. | Peacekeepers protected the camp where refugees lived.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a peacekeeper, peacekeepers. Related: peacekeeping (noun and adjective), peacemaker (someone who makes peace happen). Trap: peacekeepers keep a peace that has been agreed; they are not sent to win a war. One word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A small hole, or one of a line of small holes, made in paper so it can be torn off neatly. 2) A hole made through something. 3) (medicine) A hole in a part of the body that should not have one, such as a perforated eardrum.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, perforations are on stamps, tickets, toilet roll and tear-off forms: «tear along the perforation». In medicine, a perforated eardrum is a small hole in the eardrum that usually heals. Phrases: «tear along the perforations», «perforated line», «perforated eardrum».
examples from the lessons: Tear the coupon along the perforation. | Stamps have tiny perforations around their edges. | Toilet paper has perforations so you can tear one sheet. | The doctor said he had a small perforation in his eardrum. | Draw a dotted line to show where the perforation goes. | The metal sheet was full of perforations to let air through.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Verb «perforate»; adjective «perforated». Spelling: per-for-a-tion. Trap: do not confuse with «performance».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who picks fruit, vegetables, flowers or cotton, often as a job. 2) A person or tool that picks or chooses something: a litter picker, a nose picker (rude, joking). 3) (work) A person in a warehouse who collects items for orders.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and social studies, fruit pickers do seasonal farm work (strawberry picking in the UK, fruit picking in Australia and New Zealand for backpackers). At school, a «litter picker» is a grabbing tool for collecting rubbish safely. In history, cotton pickers in the US South were often enslaved people. Phrases: «fruit picker», «litter picker», «cotton picker», «grape picker».
examples from the lessons: Strawberry pickers start work very early in summer. | We used litter pickers to clean the playground. | My cousin worked as a fruit picker in Queensland. | The machine is a cotton picker that harvests whole fields. | Grape pickers fill baskets in the vineyard. | «Stop it, you nose picker!» laughed my little brother. | Warehouse pickers collect the things people order online.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a picker, pickers. From the verb «pick» + -er (a person or tool that does it). Related: «picky» (fussy about food). «Nose picker» is a cheeky, mildly rude joke.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A fruit like a big banana that is usually cooked before eating, often fried, boiled or baked; popular in Africa, the Caribbean and Latin America. 2) A common wild plant (weed) with flat leaves close to the ground and thin spikes of tiny flowers; it grows on lawns and paths.
its sense in the lessons: In food lessons about the Caribbean and West Africa, fried plantain is a favourite side dish. In nature lessons in the UK and Ireland, plantain is a weed on school fields; ribwort plantain stems can be used for a «soldiers» conker-like game. Phrases: «fried plantain», «ripe plantain», «green plantain», «ribwort plantain».
examples from the lessons: Fried plantain is sweet and soft when it is ripe. | Plantains look like bananas but are usually cooked. | My Nigerian friend's mum makes plantain with rice. | Green plantain is hard and starchy. | There is plantain growing all over our lawn. | We played a game knocking the heads off ribwort plantain.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Pronounced PLAN-tin or plan-TAYN. Two very different meanings: a cooking banana and a weed. Trap: do not eat wild plants unless an adult knows they are safe.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) The pale yellow liquid part of blood that carries blood cells, food and waste around the body. 2) (science) A fourth state of matter: a very hot gas in which particles have an electric charge, as in the Sun, lightning and neon signs. 3) A kind of flat-screen television (a plasma TV or «a plasma»).
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about blood, plasma is about 55% of blood; people can donate plasma. In physics, after solid, liquid and gas, plasma is called the fourth state of matter; stars are made mostly of plasma. Phrases: «blood plasma», «plasma TV», «plasma ball», «states of matter».
examples from the lessons: Plasma is the liquid part of blood. | Red cells float in the plasma. | The Sun is a giant ball of plasma. | Lightning makes plasma for a split second. | Touch the plasma ball and the purple sparks follow your finger. | Grandma still has an old plasma TV. | Some people donate plasma to help patients.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable in the science senses. Pronounced PLAZ-ma. Trap: in science «plasma» (state of matter) has nothing to do with blood plasma — same word, different meanings. Do not confuse with «plaster».

part of speech: noun (a plume, plumes); verb (plume, plumes, plumed, pluming — rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A large, soft, beautiful feather, or a bunch of feathers worn as decoration. 2) A long cloud of smoke, steam, dust or water that rises and spreads out. 3) verb (rare): To rise in a plume, or for a bird to tidy its feathers.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, knights and soldiers wear plumes on their helmets; peacocks show off plumes. In geography and science, a volcano sends up a plume of ash; a factory sends plumes of smoke; a whale's breath makes a plume of spray. Phrases: «a plume of smoke», «a plume of ash», «feathered plume», «plume of steam».
examples from the lessons: A plume of smoke rose from the chimney. | The volcano sent a huge plume of ash into the sky. | The knight wore a red plume on his helmet. | The peacock shook its plumes. | The whale blew a plume of spray. | Planes could not fly through the ash plume.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a plume, plumes. Related: plumage (all of a bird's feathers). Pronounced «ploom». Trap: do not confuse with «plum» (a fruit) or «plumber».

part of speech: noun (a pollock, pollock or pollocks; Pollock — a name)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A sea fish of the North Atlantic, related to the cod, often eaten as fish fingers or fish and chips. 2) (a name) Pollock is a surname; Jackson Pollock was an American painter famous for dripping and splashing paint on large canvases.
its sense in the lessons: In food lessons, pollock is a cheaper fish used in fish fingers and frozen fish; it is more plentiful than cod. In art lessons, Jackson Pollock's «drip paintings» are a style called action painting; pupils copy it with splashes of paint. Phrases: «Alaska pollock», «pollock fillets», «Jackson Pollock painting».
examples from the lessons: These fish fingers are made from pollock. | Pollock is a white fish like cod. | Fishermen caught pollock off the coast of Ireland. | We made splashy pictures like Jackson Pollock. | Pollock's paintings look messy but he planned them carefully. | Mum grilled pollock with lemon for tea.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural usually «pollock» (like «fish»), sometimes «pollocks». Also spelled «pollack» for the fish. Trap: do not confuse with «bollocks», a rude UK swear word that sounds similar; «pollock» is a polite, normal word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A plant that grows in ponds and slow rivers, often under or on the water, with green leaves or stems.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, pondweed (often Canadian pondweed, Elodea) is used in experiments on photosynthesis: put it in water under a lamp and count the oxygen bubbles. Pondweed gives food, shelter and oxygen to pond animals like tadpoles and snails. In stories, pondweed is slimy and tangly. Phrases: «count the bubbles», «pondweed experiment», «covered in pondweed».
examples from the lessons: We counted the oxygen bubbles coming from the pondweed. | When the lamp was closer, the pondweed made more bubbles. | Tadpoles hide in the pondweed. | The frog jumped out covered in green pondweed. | Too much pondweed can choke a pond. | Our class pond has lots of pondweed.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable («some pondweed»); «pondweeds» for kinds. One word. In the experiment, more light means more bubbles (more photosynthesis) up to a point — a fair test changes only the distance of the lamp.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Covered in sharp points or prickles, like a hedgehog, cactus or holly. 2) Giving a stinging or tingling feeling: a prickly jumper. 3) (of a person) Easily annoyed or upset; grumpy. 4) (of a problem) Hard to deal with and likely to cause arguments.
its sense in the lessons: In science, prickly plants (cactus, gorse, holly, thistles) use prickles to protect themselves from being eaten; hedgehogs and porcupines have spines. In stories, a prickly character is touchy and grumpy. Health: «prickly heat» is an itchy rash in hot weather. Phrases: «prickly heat», «prickly pear», «prickly as a hedgehog», «a prickly subject».
examples from the lessons: The hedgehog is prickly so foxes leave it alone. | Be careful, the cactus is very prickly. | This wool jumper feels prickly on my neck. | Grandad gets prickly when he is tired. | Money can be a prickly subject. | Holly leaves are prickly. | She got prickly heat on holiday in Spain.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparatives: pricklier, prickliest. Noun «prickle» (a sharp point); «prickliness». Related: «prick» (to make a tiny hole). Trap: «prickly» describes the thing or person, «prickle» is the spine itself.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A country or area ruled by a prince or princess, such as Monaco or Liechtenstein. 2) (UK) «The Principality» is sometimes used to mean Wales. 3) (Bible) «Principalities» are a kind of spiritual power or angelic order mentioned by St Paul.
its sense in the lessons: In geography, small European principalities include Monaco, Liechtenstein and Andorra (a co-principality). In UK news and sport, «the Principality» means Wales (the Prince of Wales title). In church and Bible readings, Ephesians speaks of «principalities and powers». Phrases: «the Principality of Monaco», «the Principality» (Wales).
examples from the lessons: Monaco is a tiny principality on the coast of France. | Liechtenstein is a principality between Switzerland and Austria. | The rugby match was held in the Principality Stadium in Cardiff. | A principality is ruled by a prince. | The Bible reading talked about «principalities and powers». | Andorra is ruled by two co-princes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «principalities». Capital «P» when it is a name. Trap: Wales is part of the UK and has its own parliament (the Senedd); calling it «the Principality» is traditional but some Welsh people dislike it. Do not confuse with «principal» (head teacher, main) or «principle» (a rule or belief).

part of speech: verb (pronk, pronks, pronked, pronking); noun (a pronk, pronks)
meaning for a pupil: 1) verb: When an animal like a springbok, gazelle or deer pronks, it leaps high into the air with all four legs stiff, often several times. 2) noun: Such a leap.
its sense in the lessons: In nature lessons about Africa, springboks pronk (also called «stotting») to show predators like cheetahs that they are fit and fast, so not worth chasing. Lambs and goats sometimes pronk when playful. Phrases: «springboks pronk», «pronking gazelles».
examples from the lessons: The springbok pronked high into the air. | Gazelles pronk to show lions they are strong. | Pronking is also called stotting. | The lambs were pronking around the field in spring. | We watched a video of antelopes pronking. | Our puppy did a funny little pronk when it saw the ball.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past «pronked». From Afrikaans «pronk» (to show off). Not a common word; mainly in nature books. Same idea: «stot», «stotting».

meaning for a pupil: 1) To grow new plants from a parent plant, for example from cuttings, seeds or runners. 2) (of plants and animals) To breed or reproduce. 3) (formal) To spread an idea, news or belief to many people. 4) (science) For sound, light or waves to travel through something.
its sense in the lessons: In science and gardening, pupils propagate spider plants, strawberries or geraniums from cuttings or runners. In history and citizenship, propaganda (from the same root) propagates ideas. In physics, sound propagates through air, water and solids but not through space. Phrases: «propagate from cuttings», «propagate a rumour», «waves propagate».
examples from the lessons: We propagated new spider plants from the babies on the runners. | Gardeners propagate roses from cuttings. | Strawberries propagate by sending out runners. | Sound cannot propagate through empty space. | The newspaper propagated a false story. | Some trees propagate by seeds carried on the wind.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past «propagated». Noun «propagation». Formal word; everyday words are «grow», «spread». Related: «propaganda». Trap: do not confuse with «propel» (push forward).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A small plant-eating dinosaur from Mongolia and China, about the size of a sheep, with a parrot-like beak and a bony frill at the back of its head; it lived about 75 million years ago.
its sense in the lessons: In dinosaur lessons, Protoceratops is an early relative of Triceratops but had no big horns. A famous fossil shows a Protoceratops and a Velociraptor locked in a fight. Some think Protoceratops skulls found by ancient travellers helped start the legend of the griffin. Phrases: «Protoceratops fossil», «fighting dinosaurs», «Gobi Desert».
examples from the lessons: Protoceratops had a beak like a parrot. | A Protoceratops was about as big as a sheep. | The famous fossil shows a Protoceratops fighting a Velociraptor. | Protoceratops lived in the Gobi Desert. | Protoceratops ate plants. | Scientists found Protoceratops nests and eggs.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually written with a capital P as a scientific name; plural the same. Pronounced pro-toe-SERR-a-tops; means «first horned face». Trap: the griffin link is an idea some historians suggest, not a proven fact. Do not confuse with Triceratops (bigger, three horns).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) A tiny particle with a positive electric charge, found in the nucleus (centre) of every atom.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about atoms, an atom has protons and neutrons in the nucleus and electrons around it. The number of protons decides which element it is: hydrogen has 1, carbon has 6, oxygen has 8, gold has 79. Phrases: «protons, neutrons and electrons», «proton number», «atomic number».
examples from the lessons: A hydrogen atom has just one proton. | Protons have a positive charge. | The number of protons tells you which element it is. | Carbon has six protons in its nucleus. | Protons and neutrons are in the nucleus. | Scientists smash protons together in the Large Hadron Collider.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Charges: proton +, electron −, neutron 0. Maths in science: atomic number = number of protons; in a neutral atom, protons = electrons. Protons are much heavier than electrons (about 1836 times).

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a way that shows you are pleased and happy about something you or someone close to you did or has. 2) In a way that shows you think you are better than others (arrogantly). 3) In a grand, impressive way: a castle standing proudly on a hill.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, «said proudly» or «smiled proudly» tells the reader a character feels pride — at winning, finishing something hard, or a family member's success. In writing lessons it is an example adverb for dialogue tags. Phrases: «smiled proudly», «proudly showed», «proudly presents», «stood proudly».
examples from the lessons: Mia proudly showed her certificate to her nan. | «I did it all by myself!» he said proudly. | The flag flew proudly over the town hall. | Dad proudly watched me score my first goal. | The castle stood proudly on the hill. | Our school proudly presents the summer concert. | She walked proudly past the others without saying hello.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from «proud» + -ly. Noun «pride». Good pride (pleased with effort) vs bad pride (thinking you are better than others) — the story tells you which. Spelling: proud-ly.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A round fungus (mushroom) without a cap or stalk, white or brown, that bursts and puffs out a cloud of spores like dust when it is old. 2) Anything round, soft and fluffy, like a dandelion clock or a fluffy chick (informal).
its sense in the lessons: In nature lessons, puffballs show how fungi spread spores. Giant puffballs can grow as big as a football. In stories, a puffball can be a fluffy pet or a cloud. Safety: only experts should pick fungi to eat. Phrases: «giant puffball», «puff of spores».
examples from the lessons: When I stepped on the puffball, a brown cloud of spores came out. | We found a giant puffball in the field. | Puffballs spread their spores in the wind. | The kitten was a tiny white puffball. | Never eat a wild puffball unless an expert checks it. | Puffballs have no gills like other mushrooms.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; one word. Safety: some young poisonous mushrooms look like puffballs, so do not touch or eat wild fungi without an adult expert. The «smoke» is millions of spores, not smoke.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A small black-and-white seabird with a large, brightly coloured orange and blue beak and orange feet; it lives on cliffs and islands in the North Atlantic.
its sense in the lessons: In nature lessons, puffins nest in burrows on islands (Skellig Michael in Ireland, the Farne Islands in England, Iceland, Newfoundland), dive for fish like sand eels, and carry many fish crosswise in their beaks. Their nickname is «sea parrot» or «clown of the sea». Phrases: «puffin colony», «puffin burrow», «Puffin Books».
examples from the lessons: The puffin had six little fish in its beak. | Puffins nest in burrows on cliff tops. | We took a boat trip to see the puffins. | Puffins flap their wings very fast when they fly. | A puffin's beak is bright orange in spring. | Puffin chicks are called pufflings. | My favourite paperback has a puffin on the spine.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a puffin, puffins. Baby: puffling. Fact: puffins spend winter far out at sea and come to land only to breed. «Puffin Books» is a children's publisher.

part of speech: noun (a pussy, pussies) — several unrelated meanings
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal, childish) A cat or kitten, especially in nursery rhymes and baby talk: «pussy cat». 2) (rude, slang) A vulgar word for a woman's private parts; it is offensive and not for school. 3) (rude, slang) An insulting word for someone thought to be weak or cowardly. 4) «Pussy willow»: a willow tree with soft, furry grey buds in spring.
its sense in the lessons: In nursery rhymes such as «Pussycat, pussycat, where have you been?» and «Ding dong bell, pussy's in the well», and in «The Owl and the Pussy-cat», it simply means a cat. In older children's speech, the rude senses may be heard as swearing or insults; teachers treat them as bad language. Phrases: «pussy cat», «pussy willow», «Puss in Boots» (a related word).
examples from the lessons: Pussycat, pussycat, where have you been? | The Owl and the Pussy-cat went to sea in a beautiful pea-green boat. | Grandma calls her kitten «little pussy». | The pussy willow by the stream has soft grey buds. | Puss in Boots is a clever cat in a fairy tale. | Calling someone «a pussy» is rude and unkind, so we don't say it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «pussies». Register trap: the cat sense is old-fashioned and childish; many people now avoid the word because the rude senses are well known. Say «cat», «kitten», «kitty» instead. The rude senses are vulgar or insulting — do not use them at school. «Puss» = a cat (as in Puss in Boots).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (history) A set of knotted coloured strings used by the Inca people of South America to record numbers and information, such as how many people, animals or goods there were.
its sense in the lessons: In history and maths lessons about the Incas, the quipu shows that a writing-free civilisation could keep records: the type and position of knots stand for units, tens, hundreds (a base-10 system), and the colours for different things. Officials called quipucamayocs read them. Phrases: «Inca quipu», «knotted strings», «record numbers».
examples from the lessons: The Incas used a quipu to count llamas. | Each knot on the quipu stood for a number. | A knot near the end of the string showed units; higher up meant tens and hundreds. | We made our own quipu from coloured wool. | Experts are still trying to work out if quipus recorded words too. | The quipu helped officials keep track of taxes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Also spelled «khipu». Plural «quipus». Pronounced KEE-poo. Maths: the quipu uses place value in base 10, like our numbers, with an empty space for zero. Not an English word in origin — it comes from Quechua, the Inca language.

part of speech: adjective (radiant, more radiant, most radiant); noun (a radiant — science, rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Shining brightly; giving off light or warmth. 2) (of a person) Looking very happy, healthy or beautiful, as if glowing. 3) (science) Sent out as rays: radiant heat, radiant energy.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, «a radiant smile» or «a radiant bride» means joy shines from someone. In science, the Sun gives radiant energy (light and heat) that travels through space; radiant heaters warm you directly. Phrases: «a radiant smile», «radiant with joy», «radiant heat», «radiant energy».
examples from the lessons: The bride looked radiant in her white dress. | She gave me a radiant smile. | The radiant sun warmed the beach. | The fire gave off radiant heat. | Radiant energy from the Sun reaches the Earth in about eight minutes. | Her face was radiant with happiness when she won.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective. Noun: radiance. Related: radiate, radiation, radiator. Pronounced RAY-dee-ant. Trap: radiant (glowing, very happy) is positive; radiation is the scientific word for energy sent out as waves or particles.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To change the order or position of things. 2) To change the time or date of a meeting or event. 3) (maths) To change the order of numbers or letters, or to change a formula so a different letter is on its own.
its sense in the lessons: In school, «rearrange the letters to make a word» (anagrams), «rearrange the furniture», and in maths «rearrange the numbers» or «rearrange the equation». Everyday: «we'll rearrange the dentist appointment». Phrases: «rearrange the room», «rearrange the meeting», «rearrange the letters», «rearrange the formula».
examples from the lessons: Rearrange the letters of «listen» to make «silent». | We rearranged the desks into groups. | The match was rearranged for next Saturday. | Can you rearrange 3, 1, 2 to make the biggest number? 321. | Mum rearranged the furniture in the living room. | Rearrange the formula so that x is on its own. | The doctor's appointment had to be rearranged.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past «rearranged». Noun «rearrangement». Prefix re- (again) + arrange. Maths: adding and multiplying can be rearranged in any order (3 + 5 = 5 + 3), but subtracting and dividing cannot (8 − 3 ≠ 3 − 8). With digits, rearranging changes the value.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Connected with what is being talked about or done, and useful or important for it. 2) Still important and meaningful to people now: an old story that is still relevant.
its sense in the lessons: In school, «only include relevant information», «underline the relevant facts in the question» and «is this relevant to your answer?» In maths word problems, some numbers are not relevant and you must ignore them. In reading, a relevant example supports your point. Phrases: «relevant to», «relevant information», «not relevant», «still relevant today».
examples from the lessons: Only write down the information relevant to the question. | Is that relevant to our project on volcanoes? | The colour of the bus is not relevant to the maths problem. | Highlight the relevant parts of the text. | His joke wasn't relevant, so the teacher ignored it. | Aesop's fables are still relevant today. | Bring any relevant documents to the meeting.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Followed by «to»: relevant to the topic. Opposite: irrelevant. Noun: relevance. Spelling trap: relev-ANT (not «revelant» or «relevent»). Maths tip: in word problems, cross out numbers that are not relevant before calculating.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A substance, traditionally from a calf's stomach, used to make milk curdle (go thick and lumpy) when making cheese. 2) Vegetable or microbial rennet: a similar substance made from plants or microbes, used for vegetarian cheese.
its sense in the lessons: In science and food lessons, rennet contains an enzyme that makes milk proteins clump into curds, separating them from the liquid whey; curds become cheese. «Little Miss Muffet» ate curds and whey. Vegetarians check cheese labels for animal rennet. Phrases: «animal rennet», «vegetarian rennet», «curds and whey».
examples from the lessons: Cheesemakers add rennet to milk to make curds. | Rennet makes the milk go thick and lumpy. | This cheese is made with vegetarian rennet. | Traditional rennet comes from a calf's stomach. | The curds are pressed into cheese and the whey drains away. | Junket is a soft pudding made with milk and rennet.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «some rennet». The key chemical is an enzyme called chymosin. Food trap: not all cheese is vegetarian, because animal rennet is used in some.

part of speech: noun (a republican, republicans; a Republican, Republicans); adjective (republican; Republican)
meaning for a pupil: 1) noun and adjective: A person who wants their country to be a republic, ruled by elected leaders with no king or queen. 2) (US politics) A Republican is a member or supporter of the Republican Party, one of the two main parties; its symbol is an elephant and its colour red. 3) (Ireland, Northern Ireland) A person who wants a united, independent Ireland; sometimes linked to the IRA in history.
its sense in the lessons: In US politics and news lessons, Republicans and Democrats are the two big parties. In the UK and Australia, republicans want to replace the monarch with an elected head of state. In Irish history, republicans fought for independence. Phrases: «Republican Party», «Republican candidate», «republican movement», «Irish republican».
examples from the lessons: The Republican candidate won the election in that state. | The elephant is the symbol of the Republican Party. | Some Australians are republicans and want their own president instead of the King. | Republicans and Democrats argued about the new law. | Irish republicans wanted Ireland to be free from British rule. | A republican government has no king or queen.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital R for the US party and its members; small r for the general idea. Related: republic. Trap: «republican» (US party) and «Republican» in Northern Ireland mean very different things; also the US party name says nothing about being for or against kings. Opposites: monarchist (general), Democrat (US politics), unionist/loyalist (Northern Ireland).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Able to be changed back to how it was before. 2) (clothes) Able to be worn either side out: a reversible jacket. 3) (science) A reversible change is one where you can get the original materials back, like melting ice or dissolving salt.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, pupils sort changes into reversible (melting, freezing, dissolving, evaporating) and irreversible (burning, cooking an egg, rusting). In maths, some operations can be reversed: adding is reversed by subtracting. In everyday life, «reversible» clothes have two looks. Phrases: «reversible change», «reversible reaction», «reversible jacket».
examples from the lessons: Melting chocolate is a reversible change, because it can set again. | Burning paper is not reversible. | My coat is reversible: blue on one side and red on the other. | Dissolving salt is reversible — evaporate the water and the salt is left. | The doctor said the damage was reversible with rest. | Is cooking an egg a reversible change? No!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: irreversible. Verb: reverse. Spelling: -ible (not «-able»). Maths link: inverse operations reverse each other (× and ÷, + and −).

part of speech: noun (a rhea, rheas; Rhea — a name)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A large flightless bird from South America, like a small ostrich or emu, with grey-brown feathers and long legs, which runs fast. 2) (myth, a name) Rhea was a Titan in Greek myths, the mother of Zeus. 3) Rhea is also a moon of Saturn, and a girl's name.
its sense in the lessons: In nature lessons, rheas live on the grasslands (pampas) of Argentina, Brazil and Uruguay; the father sits on the eggs and cares for the chicks. In Greek myths and space lessons, Rhea is a Titan and the second-largest moon of Saturn. Phrases: «greater rhea», «lesser rhea», «flightless birds».
examples from the lessons: The rhea is a big bird that cannot fly. | Rheas live on the pampas in South America. | The male rhea looks after the eggs. | Rheas, ostriches and emus are all flightless birds. | In Greek myths, Rhea was the mother of Zeus. | Rhea is one of Saturn's many moons.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «rheas». Pronounced REE-a. Capital R for the Titan and the moon. Trap: rhea vs emu (Australia) vs ostrich (Africa) — similar birds on different continents.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Like rubber: soft and bendy, or bouncy. 2) (food) Tough and chewy in an unpleasant way, often because it was cooked too long. 3) (legs, informal) Weak and wobbly, from fear or tiredness.
its sense in the lessons: In science, describing materials: a rubbery material is flexible and springs back. In cooking, overcooked eggs or squid go rubbery. In stories, «my legs felt rubbery» shows fear or exhaustion. Phrases: «rubbery texture», «rubbery legs», «rubbery eggs».
examples from the lessons: The jelly felt rubbery and wobbly. | The squid was overcooked and rubbery. | After the long race my legs felt rubbery. | The new trainers have rubbery soles that grip the floor. | The octopus has rubbery arms. | The scrambled eggs went rubbery in the microwave.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparatives: rubberier, rubberiest (rare; «more rubbery» is common). From «rubber» + -y. Related words: elastic, flexible, bouncy, chewy.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Broken pieces of stone, brick and concrete left when a building falls down or is knocked down. 2) Rough broken stones used to fill gaps or make a base for a path or wall.
its sense in the lessons: In news and history (earthquakes, wars, bombing in the Blitz), rubble shows destruction; rescuers search the rubble for survivors. In building, rubble is used as hardcore under paths. Phrases: «reduced to rubble», «pile of rubble», «search the rubble», «buried under rubble».
examples from the lessons: After the earthquake, houses were reduced to rubble. | Rescuers dug through the rubble to find survivors. | The old factory is now just a pile of rubble. | During the war, many cities were full of rubble. | Builders used rubble to fill the hole. | The dog sniffed the rubble for people trapped inside.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «a pile of rubble», not «a rubble». Safety: never play on building sites or in rubble; it can collapse. Similar: debris, wreckage, ruins.

meaning for a pupil: 1) adjective: From or to do with Scandinavia — Norway, Sweden and Denmark (often also Finland and Iceland). 2) noun: A person from Scandinavia.
its sense in the lessons: In geography, Scandinavia is in northern Europe, with fjords, long winter nights and the midnight sun. In history, the Vikings were Scandinavian. In everyday life, «Scandinavian design» (simple, light furniture) and Scandinavian food (meatballs, smoked fish) are well known. Phrases: «Scandinavian countries», «Scandinavian design», «Scandinavian languages».
examples from the lessons: Norway, Sweden and Denmark are Scandinavian countries. | The Vikings came from Scandinavia. | Our kitchen has a simple Scandinavian style. | Scandinavian winters are long and dark. | Swedish, Norwegian and Danish are Scandinavian languages that are quite similar. | Many Scandinavians speak very good English.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always a capital S. Trap: strictly, Scandinavia = Norway, Sweden and Denmark; «Nordic countries» adds Finland, Iceland, the Faroe Islands and Greenland. Finnish is not a Scandinavian language (it is related to Estonian).

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a way that uses science or follows the methods of science: careful observing, testing and measuring. 2) According to science, as science shows.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, «work scientifically» means asking questions, predicting, doing fair tests, measuring, recording and drawing conclusions (UK curriculum term). In everyday talk, «scientifically proven» is used — and sometimes misused — in adverts. Phrases: «work scientifically», «scientifically proven», «scientifically speaking», «scientifically accurate».
examples from the lessons: We worked scientifically by changing only one thing in our test. | Is it scientifically true that goldfish have short memories? No, they can remember for months. | Scientifically speaking, a tomato is a fruit. | The advert said the cream was «scientifically proven», but showed no evidence. | The film was exciting but not scientifically accurate. | Scientists check results scientifically by repeating experiments.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from «scientific» + -ally (not «scientificly»). Spelling: sci-en-tif-ic-al-ly. Trap: «scientifically proven» in adverts may be exaggeration — ask for the evidence. Myth example: the «three-second memory» of goldfish is false.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Untidy and a bit dirty or worn out, about a person, clothes or a place. 2) (of an animal) With messy, rough fur.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, a scruffy character might be poor, lazy, busy or simply relaxed — a scruffy dog is often lovable. In school, teachers may say «your uniform looks scruffy» (tuck your shirt in). Phrases: «scruffy clothes», «scruffy hair», «a scruffy little dog», «look scruffy».
examples from the lessons: His jumper was scruffy with holes in the elbows. | A scruffy little dog followed us home. | Tuck your shirt in — you look scruffy. | The garden looked scruffy after the winter. | Her handwriting was scruffy because she rushed. | The scruffy old teddy was still his favourite.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparatives: scruffier, scruffiest. Informal but polite. Opposites: smart, neat, tidy. Similar: messy, shabby, untidy.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The hard empty shell of a sea animal, such as a snail, clam, mussel or scallop, often found on the beach.
its sense in the lessons: In science, seashells are the outer skeletons of molluscs; they are made mostly of calcium carbonate. On beach days children collect, sort and count shells. In literacy, the tongue twister «She sells seashells by the seashore». Phrases: «collect seashells», «hold a seashell to your ear».
examples from the lessons: We collected seashells on the beach. | She sells seashells by the seashore. | Hold a seashell to your ear and you seem to hear the sea. | Hermit crabs live in old seashells. | We sorted the seashells by size and colour. | The seashell was spiral like a snail's.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; one word (also «sea shell»). Myth: the «sea sound» in a shell is not the ocean — it is the noise around you echoing inside the shell. Kindness to nature: in some places taking shells from beaches is not allowed.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (a name) Seb is a short form of the boy's name Sebastian. 2) Not an ordinary English word in lower case; as letters it can be an abbreviation used by organisations.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and school lists, «Seb» is a friendly nickname for Sebastian. Nothing else common.
examples from the lessons: Seb is my best friend in Year 5. | Sebastian likes to be called Seb. | «Pass the ball, Seb!» shouted the coach. | Seb's birthday party is on Saturday.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A name: write it with a capital S. Pronounced like the start of «Sebastian». It is not an English word on its own.

meaning for a pupil: 1) prefix «semi-»: half, or partly: semicircle (half a circle), semi-final, semi-detached, semicolon. 2) noun (UK, Ireland, Australia, informal): A semi-detached house — a house joined to one other house on one side. 3) noun (informal, sport): A semi-final. 4) noun (US, Canada, Australia, informal): A semi-trailer truck, a very large lorry.
its sense in the lessons: In maths: semicircle = half a circle. In sport, «we're through to the semis» means the semi-finals (the round before the final). In UK house talk, people live in «a semi» or «a detached» or «a terrace». In grammar: the semicolon (;). Phrases: «semi-final», «semicircle», «semi-detached», «semi-skimmed milk».
examples from the lessons: We live in a semi on the edge of town. | Our team reached the semis! | A semicircle is half of a circle. | The semi-final is next week. | A big semi rumbled down the highway. | Semi-skimmed milk has some of the fat taken out. | Use a semicolon to join two linked sentences.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a word on its own, «semi» is informal and its meaning depends on the country (house in the UK, truck in North America). Pronounced SEM-ee (UK), also SEM-eye (US). Maths: semi- = ½; a semicircle's area is half the circle's area. Words with semi- are written with or without a hyphen: semicircle, semi-final.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A woody plant smaller than a tree, with several stems growing from near the ground; a bush.
its sense in the lessons: In science and gardening, shrubs (lavender, rosemary, holly, hydrangea, gorse) are a plant group between small plants and trees. Gardens and parks have shrub borders; birds nest in shrubs. Phrases: «plant a shrub», «flowering shrub», «shrub border», «trees and shrubs».
examples from the lessons: Lavender is a shrub with purple flowers. | Birds built a nest in the shrub by the fence. | We planted shrubs along the school path. | A shrub has many woody stems, but a tree usually has one trunk. | The gardener trimmed the shrubs into round shapes. | Rosemary is a shrub that smells lovely.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Similar word: bush (more everyday). A group of shrubs: shrubbery. Trap: «shrub» vs «tree» — a tree usually has one main trunk and grows tall.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A small rattlesnake from the deserts of the south-western USA and Mexico that moves sideways by throwing its body in loops across the sand. 2) Any snake that moves this way (some vipers in African deserts do too).
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about deserts and animal movement, sidewinding lets a snake move on loose, hot sand with only small parts of its body touching the ground, leaving J-shaped tracks. The sidewinder has little horns above its eyes. Phrases: «sidewinder rattlesnake», «sidewinding».
examples from the lessons: The sidewinder moved sideways across the hot sand. | Sidewinders leave J-shaped tracks in the desert. | Only a little of the sidewinder's body touches the sand at once. | The sidewinder is a small rattlesnake. | Sidewinders hunt lizards and mice at night. | Never go near a rattlesnake, even a small one.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Related: «sidewind» (verb, rare), «sidewinding». Safety: the sidewinder is venomous — keep away and tell an adult. Also the name of a missile, but children rarely need that.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A machine or computer program that copies real conditions so people can practise or test something safely, for example a flight simulator. 2) A computer game that copies a real activity: a farm simulator, a driving simulator.
its sense in the lessons: In technology lessons, pilots and astronauts train on simulators; science museums have earthquake or driving simulators. Kids play simulator games (farming, cooking, building). Phrases: «flight simulator», «driving simulator», «simulator game», «train on a simulator».
examples from the lessons: Pilots practise emergencies in a flight simulator. | The science museum has an earthquake simulator. | My brother plays a farming simulator on his tablet. | Learner drivers can use a driving simulator. | Astronauts trained in a simulator before going into space. | The simulator shook and tilted like a real plane.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Verb: simulate; noun: simulation. Spelling: -ator (not «-er»). A simulator copies reality; it is not real, so mistakes in it are safe.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A long, thin, flat strip of wood, metal or plastic, usually one of a row with gaps between, as in a fence, bed, bench or blind.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, beds have slats under the mattress, Venetian blinds have slats you can tilt, and park benches have wooden slats. In design and technology, pupils build things using slats. Phrases: «wooden slats», «bed slats», «slats of the blind», «between the slats».
examples from the lessons: Sunlight shone through the slats of the blind. | One of the bed slats broke when we jumped on the bed. | The park bench has green wooden slats. | The cat peeped through the slats of the fence. | Tilt the slats to let in more light. | We made a bird table from old slats.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Adjective «slatted» (a slatted fence). Do not confuse with «slate» (a grey stone used on roofs) or «slant» (a slope).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (UK, Ireland, Australia, informal) A person who walks, works or does things too slowly; said in a teasing, friendly way.
its sense in the lessons: In family and school life, adults and children say «Come on, slowcoach!» to someone who is lagging behind. In the US the word is «slowpoke». Phrases: «come on, slowcoach», «don't be such a slowcoach».
examples from the lessons: Come on, slowcoach, we'll miss the bus! | I'm always the slowcoach when we walk up the hill. | Grandad called me a slowcoach because I took ages to tie my shoes. | Don't be a slowcoach — it's nearly time to go. | The tortoise was a slowcoach, but it still won the race. | «Hurry up, slowcoaches!» shouted the teacher.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «slowcoaches». Informal, friendly teasing; not very rude. US/Canada word: slowpoke. One word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The fact or quality of being slow: moving, happening or working without much speed. 2) Being slow to understand or react.
its sense in the lessons: In science, the slowness of a process (erosion, growth of a tree) explains why we do not notice it. In stories, a character's slowness can be funny or worrying. Phrases: «the slowness of», «frustrated by the slowness».
examples from the lessons: The slowness of the queue made everyone grumpy. | Snails are famous for their slowness. | We were annoyed by the slowness of the internet. | The slowness of erosion means canyons take millions of years to form. | Despite his slowness, the tortoise kept going. | The doctor worried about the slowness of her heartbeat.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. From «slow» + -ness. Opposites: speed, quickness. Formal-ish; in everyday speech people say «how slow it is».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who secretly and illegally takes goods or people into or out of a country, to avoid taxes or because the goods are banned.
its sense in the lessons: In history (Cornwall, Devon, Yorkshire coasts in the 1700s), smugglers brought brandy, tea and tobacco to avoid tax, hiding goods in caves; many adventure stories (Enid Blyton's, «Moonfleet») feature smugglers. In today's news, smugglers move drugs, weapons and sometimes people, which is very dangerous and cruel. Phrases: «smugglers' cove», «drug smugglers», «people smugglers».
examples from the lessons: The smugglers hid barrels of brandy in the cave. | In the story, the children discovered a smugglers' tunnel. | Customs officers caught the smugglers at the airport. | People smugglers put migrants in dangerous small boats. | Cornwall is famous for smugglers' coves. | The smuggler was sent to prison.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Verb: smuggle; noun: smuggling. Smuggling is a crime. Spelling: double g — smuggler. Trap: in old stories smugglers can seem exciting, but real smuggling hurts people.

part of speech: verb (sniffle, sniffles, sniffled, sniffling); noun (a sniffle, sniffles; the sniffles)
