meaning for a pupil: 1) verb: To sniff again and again, because you have a cold or because you are crying quietly. 2) noun «the sniffles» (informal): A mild cold with a runny nose. 3) noun: The sound of sniffling.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, «he's got the sniffles» means a mild cold — usually he can still go to school. In stories, a character sniffling shows they are sad or trying not to cry. Health: use a tissue, catch it, bin it, kill it. Phrases: «the sniffles», «sniffle into a tissue».
examples from the lessons: I've got the sniffles, but I can still go to school. | She sniffled quietly after the sad film. | Use a tissue instead of sniffling. | We heard a little sniffle from behind the door. | The puppy sniffled around the garden. | Winter brings coughs and sniffles.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past «sniffled». Related: sniff, snuffle. «The sniffles» is always plural in this sense. Health tip: wash hands to stop colds spreading.

part of speech: verb (snooze, snoozes, snoozed, snoozing); noun (a snooze, snoozes)
meaning for a pupil: 1) verb (informal): To have a short, light sleep, especially in the daytime. 2) noun: A short sleep; a nap. 3) The snooze button on an alarm clock or phone, which stops the alarm for a few minutes.
its sense in the lessons: In family life, Grandad snoozes in his armchair after lunch; cats snooze in the sun. The snooze button is a classic morning habit. The saying «you snooze, you lose» means if you are slow you miss your chance. Phrases: «have a snooze», «hit the snooze button», «you snooze, you lose».
examples from the lessons: Grandad had a snooze on the sofa. | The cat is snoozing in the sun. | I pressed the snooze button three times this morning. | You snooze, you lose — the last cake has gone! | Dad snoozed through the whole film. | The baby needs a snooze after lunch.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past «snoozed». Informal word; formal: sleep, nap, doze. Related: doze, nap, kip (UK slang). Trap: «snooze» rhymes with «news», «lose».

part of speech: verb (sob, sobs, sobbed, sobbing); noun (a sob, sobs); abbreviation (SOB — rude, US)
meaning for a pupil: 1) verb: To cry noisily, with short sharp breaths. 2) noun: The sound of loud crying. 3) «sob story» (informal): a sad story told to make people feel sorry for you, maybe to get something. 4) SOB (rude, US slang): short for a swear insult; not for school.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, sobbing shows deep sadness, fear or relief (more than crying quietly). «Sob your heart out» means cry a lot. «Sob story» shows suspicion that someone is exaggerating. Phrases: «sob loudly», «sob your heart out», «between sobs», «sob story».
examples from the lessons: The little boy sobbed when he lost his balloon. | She sobbed her heart out when her hamster died. | «I can't find my mum,» he said between sobs. | We heard sobs from the next room. | He told the teacher a sob story about why his homework was late. | The audience sobbed at the sad ending.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past «sobbed», «sobbing» (double b). Similar: cry, weep (formal), wail (loud), whimper (quiet). Capital «SOB» is a rude US abbreviation — avoid.

part of speech: adjective (Somali); noun (a Somali, Somalis; Somali — the language)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To do with Somalia, a country in the Horn of East Africa, or its people. 2) A Somali person. 3) The Somali language, spoken by about 20 million people in Somalia, Djibouti, Ethiopia, Kenya and by Somalis around the world.
its sense in the lessons: In geography, Somalia has the longest coastline in mainland Africa; most people are Muslim; many Somali families live in UK cities (London, Bristol, Birmingham), Canada (Toronto) and the US (Minneapolis). In news, Somalia has faced drought and conflict. Phrases: «Somali people», «Somali language», «Somali food».
examples from the lessons: My friend Hodan is Somali and speaks Somali at home. | Somali is written with Latin letters. | The Somali community celebrated Eid at the park. | Somalia is on the Horn of Africa. | Somali families often drink spiced tea. | Many Somalis live in Minneapolis.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital S. Plural «Somalis». Country: Somalia; people/language: Somali. Pronounced so-MAH-lee. Trap: Somaliland is a region in the north that says it is independent, but most countries do not recognise it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (history) A Spartan was a person from Sparta, a city in ancient Greece famous for its tough soldiers and strict training. 2) adjective (lower case): Very simple and plain, without comfort or decoration: a spartan room. 3) adjective: Strict, tough and self-disciplined.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons about ancient Greece, Sparta and Athens are compared: Spartan boys trained as soldiers from age 7; the Battle of Thermopylae (300 Spartans). In everyday life, «spartan» describes a very plain room, meal or lifestyle. Sports teams often call themselves «the Spartans». Phrases: «a spartan room», «spartan lifestyle», «Spartan warriors», «Spartan race».
examples from the lessons: Spartan boys left home at seven to train as soldiers. | The Spartans fought bravely at Thermopylae. | The hostel room was spartan, with just a bed and a chair. | Grandad lives a spartan life — no TV and cold showers. | Athens and Sparta were rivals in ancient Greece. | Our school team is called the Spartans.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital S for the people of Sparta; small s for the «plain, simple» meaning. Myth: films show Spartans as heroes, but Sparta also kept most people in its land as slaves (helots).

part of speech: noun (a squire, squires); verb (squire — old-fashioned, rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (history) A young man training to be a knight, who served a knight and carried his shield and armour. 2) (UK, old-fashioned) The main landowner in a village or country area. 3) (UK, informal, old-fashioned) A friendly way a man may address another man: «All right, squire?».
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons on the Middle Ages, the path to knighthood was page (age 7), squire (about 14), then knight (about 21). In old English novels, the squire is the important gentleman of the village. In comic UK speech, a market trader might say «What can I get you, squire?». Phrases: «page, squire, knight», «the village squire», «the squire's manor».
examples from the lessons: The squire polished his knight's armour. | At fourteen, a page could become a squire. | The squire lived in the big house at the end of the village. | «Cheers, squire!» said the man at the market stall. | A squire helped the knight get on his horse. | In the story, the squire and his dog went hunting.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Old-fashioned word in all senses. Related: «esquire», «Esq.» (a polite title after a man's name in old letters). Order to knighthood: page → squire → knight.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Full of stars; lit by stars. 2) Shining like stars; sparkling. 3) «starry-eyed»: hopeful and dreamy, not seeing problems. 4) (informal) To do with famous people: a starry cast.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and poems, «a starry night» sets a calm, magical or lonely mood. In art lessons, Van Gogh's «The Starry Night» is a famous swirly painting. In science, a starry sky is best away from city lights. Phrases: «a starry night», «starry sky», «starry-eyed», «starry cast».
examples from the lessons: We lay on the grass and looked at the starry sky. | Van Gogh painted «The Starry Night». | The starry night was cold and clear. | Her eyes were starry with excitement. | He was starry-eyed about becoming a famous footballer. | The film has a starry cast of famous actors.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparatives: starrier, starriest. From «star» + -ry (double r). Trap: «starry» vs «stary» (not a word) vs «staring».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A fish of warm shallow seas (Indian and Pacific Oceans, including northern Australia) that looks exactly like a rock or lump of coral and has very venomous spines on its back; it is one of the most venomous fish in the world.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about camouflage and dangerous animals, the stonefish hides on the seabed, waiting for small fish; if a person steps on it, the spines inject painful venom. In Australia, beach safety signs warn swimmers to wear reef shoes. Phrases: «stonefish sting», «step on a stonefish», «reef shoes».
examples from the lessons: The stonefish looks just like a rock. | Wear reef shoes in case you step on a stonefish. | A stonefish sting is very painful. | Stonefish hide on the seabed and catch passing fish. | The stonefish is one of the most venomous fish in the world. | Hot water helps ease the pain of a stonefish sting until you reach a hospital.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural usually «stonefish». Safety: a stonefish sting is an emergency — get an adult and medical help (in Australia, call 000). Camouflage word: blends in.

part of speech: verb form (stripping — the -ing form of strip); noun (stripping — uncountable)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Taking off a covering or layer: stripping wallpaper, stripping paint, stripping a bed. 2) Taking off clothes; undressing (for a doctor, a swim). 3) Taking something away from someone officially: stripping a winner of a medal. 4) (adult) Taking off clothes slowly as a show for money; not a topic for school.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, «stripping the beds» means taking off the sheets to wash them; «stripping wallpaper» is part of decorating. In sport news, a cheating athlete may be stripped of their medal. In science, «strip» can mean to remove layers (wind stripping leaves from trees). Phrases: «strip the bed», «strip off», «stripped of a title», «strip away».
examples from the lessons: Mum is stripping the beds to wash the sheets. | We spent Saturday stripping old wallpaper. | The wind was stripping leaves from the trees. | The runner was stripped of his medal for cheating. | The boys were stripping off to jump in the lake. | Stripping old paint needs gloves and fresh air.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «strip» (verb): strip, strips, stripped, stripping — double p. Noun «strip» is also a long thin piece (a strip of paper) and a football kit (UK: «the team's new strip»). Trap: «striping» (with one p) means adding stripes. Safety: paint strippers are chemicals — adults only.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To give the main points of something in a few words, leaving out the details.
its sense in the lessons: In school, «summarise the story in three sentences», «summarise the paragraph», «summarise your results» are common tasks in reading, history and science. A good summary keeps the key ideas and uses your own words. Phrases: «summarise the main points», «to summarise», «summarise in one sentence».
examples from the lessons: Summarise the story in three sentences. | To summarise, plants need light, water and air. | Can you summarise what happened in the chapter? | The scientist summarised her results in a table. | The news reader summarised the day's main stories. | Summarise the paragraph in your own words.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK spelling «summarise»; US and Canada «summarize». Noun «summary» (plural summaries). Tip: a summary leaves out details, examples and opinions; it is much shorter than the original. Trap: not «summerise» (no summer!).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Added to something to make it bigger, better or complete; extra. 2) (maths) Supplementary angles are two angles that add up to 180 degrees.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, «supplementary angles» make a straight line (180°); compare «complementary angles», which make a right angle (90°). In school, «supplementary materials» or «supplementary questions» are extra ones. In formal English, a «supplementary question» is an extra question after the first answer. Phrases: «supplementary angles», «supplementary information», «supplementary benefit» (UK, old).
examples from the lessons: Angles of 120° and 60° are supplementary because they add up to 180°. | If one angle is 110°, its supplementary angle is 70°. | The teacher gave us a supplementary worksheet for practice. | The museum offers supplementary guides for children. | She asked a supplementary question after his answer. | Vitamins can be supplementary to a healthy diet, not a replacement.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective. Noun «supplement» (an extra thing, e.g. a vitamin supplement or a newspaper supplement). Maths trap: Supplementary = 180° (think «S» for «straight»); Complementary = 90° (think «C» for «corner»).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Stopping something by force or power, such as a protest, a rebellion or news. 2) Holding back or hiding a feeling, a cough, a sneeze or a thought. 3) Stopping something from growing or working: fire suppression.
its sense in the lessons: In history and citizenship lessons, the suppression of protests, newspapers or rights shows unfair power. In science and health, medicines can cause «suppression» of a cough or of the immune system. In buildings, «fire suppression systems» (sprinklers) stop fires. Phrases: «suppression of the rebellion», «suppression of free speech», «fire suppression».
examples from the lessons: The king ordered the suppression of the rebellion. | The suppression of newspapers meant people did not know the truth. | Sprinklers are part of the fire suppression system. | Constant suppression of your feelings can make you unhappy. | The medicine helps with the suppression of coughing at night. | Suppression of free speech is a sign of a cruel government.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable (usually). Verb: suppress. Formal word. Spelling: double p, double s — sup-pres-sion.

part of speech: noun (a taipan, taipans); noun (taipan — history, a business boss)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A large, very venomous snake from Australia and New Guinea; the inland taipan has the strongest venom of any land snake. 2) (history, Hong Kong and China) A powerful head of a foreign business company in the 1800s and early 1900s.
its sense in the lessons: In nature and safety lessons in Australia, the coastal taipan and inland taipan (fierce snake) are well known; the inland taipan is shy and lives in remote areas, so bites are very rare. Safety: if you see a snake, stay still and back away; call 000 for a bite. Phrases: «inland taipan», «coastal taipan», «fierce snake».
examples from the lessons: The inland taipan has the strongest venom of any land snake. | Taipans live in Australia. | The ranger said the taipan is shy and avoids people. | A taipan bite needs urgent medical help. | The coastal taipan hunts rats in sugar cane fields. | In old Hong Kong, a taipan ran a big trading company.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Pronounced TY-pan. Safety: never touch any snake; in Australia, keep still, use a pressure bandage and call 000 after a bite. Myth: taipans are not aggressive hunters of people; they bite in self-defence.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A heavy piece of cloth with a picture or pattern made by weaving or sewing coloured threads, hung on a wall. 2) (literary) A rich mixture of many different things: «a tapestry of cultures».
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, the Bayeux Tapestry (actually an embroidery) tells the story of the Norman Conquest and the Battle of Hastings in 1066; castles had tapestries to keep rooms warm and colourful. In writing, «a rich tapestry» describes variety. Phrases: «the Bayeux Tapestry», «woven tapestry», «a rich tapestry of».
examples from the lessons: The Bayeux Tapestry shows the Battle of Hastings. | The castle walls were covered with old tapestries. | Tapestries helped keep cold stone rooms warm. | Our class made a tapestry from scraps of wool. | London is a rich tapestry of cultures and languages. | The tapestry shows hunters, dogs and a deer.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «tapestries» (y → ies). Fact trap: the Bayeux Tapestry is about 70 metres long and is really embroidery (sewn on linen), not woven tapestry. Spelling: tap-es-try.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (a name) The River Tay is the longest river in Scotland (about 190 km), flowing past Perth and into the sea at Dundee; also Loch Tay and the Firth of Tay. 2) (Irish English, dialect) An old Irish country way of saying and spelling «tea» — «a cup of tay».
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons about the UK, the Tay is the longest river in Scotland and carries the most water of any British river. In history, the Tay Bridge disaster of 1879 (a railway bridge fell in a storm) is famous, and so is William McGonagall's poem about it. In stories set in rural Ireland, «tay» shows a strong Irish accent. Phrases: «the River Tay», «Tay Bridge», «Firth of Tay», «a cup of tay».
examples from the lessons: The River Tay flows into the sea at Dundee. | The Tay is the longest river in Scotland. | The Tay Bridge fell down in a storm in 1879. | Salmon swim up the River Tay. | «Will you have a cup of tay?» asked the old farmer. | We drove along the banks of Loch Tay.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a name, write «Tay» with a capital T. The lower-case «tay» is dialect spelling of «tea», used in Irish-set stories and jokes; in normal writing use «tea». It is not a standard English word on its own.

meaning for a pupil: 1) If you have a tendency to do something, you often do it or are likely to do it. 2) A general direction in which something is changing or moving; a trend. 3) (maths) «Central tendency»: the middle or typical value of a set of data (mean, median, mode).
its sense in the lessons: In everyday speech: «He has a tendency to forget his PE kit.» In science, «metals have a tendency to rust». In maths and statistics, measures of central tendency are the mean, median and mode. Phrases: «a tendency to», «natural tendency», «central tendency».
examples from the lessons: He has a tendency to talk too fast when he is nervous. | Cats have a tendency to sleep a lot. | Prices have a tendency to rise every year. | The mean, median and mode are measures of central tendency. | Iron has a tendency to rust when it gets wet. | There is a tendency for children to eat more sweets at Halloween.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «tendencies». Verb «tend» (to tend to = to usually do). Followed by «to» + verb: a tendency to forget. Maths: central tendency = average-type values.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Living on land or growing on land, not in water or the air. 2) To do with the planet Earth, not space. 3) (TV, UK) Terrestrial TV is broadcast from transmitters on the ground, not by satellite or cable.
its sense in the lessons: In science, terrestrial animals (lions, ants) live on land; aquatic ones live in water. In space science, terrestrial planets (Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars) are rocky; «extra-terrestrial» means from beyond Earth (an alien, ET). Phrases: «terrestrial animals», «terrestrial planets», «extra-terrestrial», «terrestrial television».
examples from the lessons: Elephants are terrestrial animals. | Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars are the terrestrial planets. | Frogs live on land and in water, so they are not only terrestrial. | ET is an extra-terrestrial from another planet. | Grandma only watches terrestrial TV channels. | Most snails are terrestrial, but some live in ponds.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective. Opposites: aquatic (water), marine (sea), celestial (sky/space). Related: extra-terrestrial (from outside Earth). Spelling: ter-res-tri-al (double r).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Coming last in a line of a thousand, number 1000 in order (1000th). 2) One of a thousand equal parts of something: 1/1000 or 0.001.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, decimal place value: the third digit after the decimal point is the thousandths place (in 4.256, the 6 means six thousandths). A millimetre is a thousandth of a metre; a millilitre is a thousandth of a litre. Everyday: «for the thousandth time» means «again and again». Phrases: «a thousandth of a second», «thousandths place», «for the thousandth time».
examples from the lessons: A millimetre is one thousandth of a metre. | In 3.125, the digit 5 is in the thousandths place. | She won the race by a thousandth of a second. | Tidy your room — I'm telling you for the thousandth time! | The shop gave a prize to its thousandth customer. | Write three thousandths as a decimal: 0.003.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: thousand + th (thousandth). Maths: 1/1000 = 0.001; tenths (0.1), hundredths (0.01), thousandths (0.001). Trap: «thousandths» (parts) vs «thousands» (place value to the left). «For the thousandth time» is an exaggeration, not an exact count.

part of speech: adjective (tiptop — informal, old-fashioned); noun (the tiptop — rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal, old-fashioned) Excellent; in the very best condition: «in tiptop shape». 2) (rare) The very top or highest point.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday speech, grandparents say «I'm feeling tiptop» or «the bike is in tiptop condition». In stories, it gives a cheerful, old-fashioned voice. In New Zealand, Tip Top is a famous ice-cream brand. Phrases: «in tiptop condition», «tiptop shape», «feeling tiptop».
examples from the lessons: Grandpa's old car is still in tiptop condition. | «How are you?» «Tiptop, thank you!» | Keep your bike in tiptop shape by oiling the chain. | The squirrel climbed to the tiptop of the tree. | The garden looks tiptop for the summer fair. | We had a tiptop time at the beach.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Also written «tip-top». Informal and a bit old-fashioned. Similar: excellent, first-class, top-notch.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Accepting and respecting other people's beliefs, ways of life or opinions, even when they are different from yours. 2) Patient with things that might annoy you. 3) (science) Able to survive or grow in difficult conditions: a drought-tolerant plant; also able to take a medicine or food without harm.
its sense in the lessons: In citizenship and school values lessons (British values: mutual respect and tolerance), being tolerant means respecting people of other faiths, cultures and opinions. In science and gardening, «salt-tolerant» or «drought-tolerant» plants survive harsh places. In health, «lactose intolerant» people get ill from milk. Phrases: «tolerant of», «drought-tolerant», «lactose intolerant».
examples from the lessons: Our school wants everyone to be tolerant of different beliefs. | Be tolerant when your little brother asks lots of questions. | Cacti are drought-tolerant plants. | He is lactose intolerant, so he drinks oat milk. | A tolerant community welcomes newcomers. | The teacher was tolerant of our noise before the holiday.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Followed by «of»: tolerant of others. Noun: tolerance; verb: tolerate. Opposite: intolerant. Trap: being tolerant does not mean accepting bullying or unkindness.

meaning for a pupil: 1) One of two small soft lumps at the back of your throat, one on each side, which help fight germs.
its sense in the lessons: In health and science lessons, tonsils are part of the immune system. When they get infected and swollen (tonsillitis), your throat hurts; some children have them taken out in an operation (a tonsillectomy). Phrases: «swollen tonsils», «have your tonsils out», «tonsillitis».
examples from the lessons: The doctor shone a light to look at my tonsils. | My tonsils are swollen and my throat hurts. | My cousin had her tonsils out and ate lots of ice cream afterwards. | Tonsillitis is an infection of the tonsils. | You have two tonsils at the back of your throat. | Say «aah» so I can see your tonsils.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually plural «tonsils» (there are two). Related: tonsillitis (double l). Myth: the dangly thing in the middle of your throat is the uvula, not a tonsil.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The people who live in a town, especially when thought of all together.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and fairy tales (like «The Pied Piper of Hamelin»), the townspeople react together: they cheer, panic or refuse to pay. In history, townspeople were merchants and craftspeople, different from farmers or lords. Phrases: «the townspeople gathered», «the townspeople of Hamelin».
examples from the lessons: The townspeople gathered in the square to hear the news. | The townspeople of Hamelin would not pay the Piper. | All the townspeople came out to watch the parade. | The flood forced the townspeople to leave their homes. | In the Middle Ages, townspeople paid taxes to the lord. | The townspeople cheered when the hero returned.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural noun: «the townspeople are…», never «a townspeople». Also: townsfolk (similar, a bit old-fashioned), townsperson (one, rare). One word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who follows the tracks or signs of animals or people to find them. 2) A device or app that shows where something or someone is, or records information: a GPS tracker, a fitness tracker. 3) A chart or list for following progress: a reading tracker, a habit tracker. 4) (internet) A hidden piece of code on a website that records what you do online.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and nature lessons, Aboriginal Australian and Native American trackers were famous for reading footprints and signs. In everyday life, fitness trackers count steps; parcel trackers show where your delivery is. In online safety lessons, websites use trackers and cookies to collect data. Phrases: «fitness tracker», «GPS tracker», «parcel tracker», «reading tracker».
examples from the lessons: The tracker followed the bear's footprints in the snow. | Dad's fitness tracker says he walked 10,000 steps today. | We put a GPS tracker on the dog's collar. | Fill in your reading tracker every night. | The parcel tracker says our delivery will arrive this afternoon. | Some websites use trackers to see what you click.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. From «track» + -er. Online safety: trackers collect data about you; ask an adult before accepting cookies or sharing location.

part of speech: noun (a transplant, transplants); verb (transplant, transplants, transplanted, transplanting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) noun (medicine): An operation in which a damaged organ (heart, kidney, liver) is replaced with a healthy one from a donor. 2) verb (medicine): To move an organ or tissue from one person to another. 3) verb (gardening): To dig up a plant and plant it somewhere else. 4) verb: To move people or things to a new place to live.
its sense in the lessons: In science and health lessons, organ transplants save lives; organ donation (giving organs after death, or a kidney while alive) is a kind act; a blood type match is needed. In gardening, seedlings are transplanted from pots into the garden. Phrases: «heart transplant», «kidney transplant», «organ donor», «transplant seedlings».
examples from the lessons: She had a kidney transplant and is healthy now. | The first heart transplant was in 1967. | We transplanted the tomato seedlings into bigger pots. | Organ donors help transplant patients. | Water the plants after you transplant them. | The family was transplanted from the city to a small farm.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stress: noun TRANS-plant; verb trans-PLANT. Past «transplanted». Related: implant, organ donation. Trap: in UK and Wales the organ donor system is «opt-out», but families are still asked.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (church) A Trappist is a Catholic monk or nun of a strict order (the Cistercians of the Strict Observance), known for prayer, hard work and long periods of silence. 2) adjective: To do with this order: a Trappist monastery. 3) Trappist beer or cheese: made in or under the control of Trappist monasteries.
its sense in the lessons: In religious education, Trappist monks live in monasteries such as Mount Melleray and Roscrea in Ireland, Mount Saint Bernard in England and Gethsemani in the USA; they pray several times a day and support themselves by farming, baking or brewing. «Trappist silence» is a phrase for keeping very quiet. Phrases: «Trappist monk», «Trappist monastery», «Trappist silence».
examples from the lessons: Trappist monks spend much of the day in silence and prayer. | The Trappist monastery sells honey and bread. | The order got its name from La Trappe Abbey in France. | Thomas Merton was a famous Trappist writer. | Trappist nuns also live in silent communities. | The class was as quiet as Trappist monks during the test.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital T. Plural «Trappists». Myth: Trappist monks do not take a total «vow of silence»; they speak when needed but keep silence much of the time. Christians believe this way of life brings them close to God.

part of speech: noun (a trek, treks); verb (trek, treks, trekked, trekking)
meaning for a pupil: 1) noun: A long, hard journey, especially on foot through mountains, forests or wild country. 2) verb: To go on such a journey. 3) (informal) A long tiring walk to an ordinary place: «It's a trek to the shops».
its sense in the lessons: In geography and adventure stories, people go trekking in the Himalayas or the Andes; in history, the Great Trek was a migration of Boers in South Africa. In everyday speech, «trek» exaggerates a long walk. Phrases: «go trekking», «a long trek», «trek across», «pony trekking» (UK).
examples from the lessons: We went on a three-day trek through the mountains. | It's a real trek from the car park to the beach. | Explorers trekked across the frozen Arctic. | Pony trekking in Wales was the best part of our holiday. | The refugees trekked for weeks to reach safety. | Make sure you take water on a long trek.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past «trekked», «trekking» (double k). Comes from Afrikaans/Dutch «trekken» (to travel, pull). «Star Trek» is a famous TV series. Safety: tell someone your route before a trek.

part of speech: interjection (tut, tut-tut); verb (tut, tuts, tutted, tutting); noun (a tut)
meaning for a pupil: 1) interjection: A small clicking sound made with the tongue, written «tut» or «tut-tut», showing that you disapprove or are annoyed. 2) verb: To make this sound: «She tutted at the noisy boys». 3) (Tut, informal) Short for Tutankhamun, the famous young pharaoh of ancient Egypt — «King Tut».
its sense in the lessons: In stories, «tutted» shows a grown-up is annoyed or disapproving, but quietly — often a British habit in queues. In history lessons about Egypt, «King Tut» is Tutankhamun, whose tomb was found in 1922. Phrases: «tut-tut», «tutted loudly», «King Tut».
examples from the lessons: «Tut-tut, what a mess!» said Grandma. | The lady in the queue tutted when someone pushed in. | Mum tutted at the muddy footprints. | He gave a loud tut and rolled his eyes. | King Tut was only a boy when he became pharaoh. | Stop tutting at me, I'm going as fast as I can!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past «tutted», «tutting» (double t). The written «tut» stands for a click, not a real word sound. Similar: «tsk». «Tut» for Tutankhamun is a nickname; his tomb's treasures are in Cairo.

part of speech: noun (a twit, twits); verb (twit — old-fashioned, rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal, UK, Ireland, Australia, mildly rude) A silly or foolish person. 2) (old-fashioned, rare) verb: to tease someone.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and everyday British talk, «you twit!» is a mild, often jokey insult — stronger than «silly», much milder than swear words. Roald Dahl's book «The Twits» is about Mr and Mrs Twit, a nasty, dirty couple who play tricks on each other. Phrases: «you silly twit», «what a twit», «The Twits».
examples from the lessons: «You twit, you've put your jumper on inside out!» laughed my sister. | Don't be a twit — wear your helmet. | Mr and Mrs Twit are horrible people in a Roald Dahl book. | I felt like a twit when I forgot my lines. | He's a bit of a twit, but he means well. | Calling someone a twit in class might still get you told off.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a twit, twits. Mild insult (rude, but not a swear word); between friends it can be friendly. Similar: idiot, nitwit, prat (UK), plonker (UK), drongo (Australia). Do not confuse with «tweet» or «twitch».

meaning for a pupil: 1) The feeling or state of not being sure about something. 2) Something that you do not know or cannot be sure about. 3) (science, maths) How much a measurement might be wrong; the range of possible values.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and news, «uncertainty» about the weather, the future or exam results can make people worried. In science, every measurement has some uncertainty (a ruler measures to the nearest millimetre). In maths, probability describes uncertainty: an event may be certain, likely, unlikely or impossible. Phrases: «a time of uncertainty», «uncertainty about», «measurement uncertainty».
examples from the lessons: There is a lot of uncertainty about tomorrow's weather. | Moving to a new school brought months of uncertainty. | Every measurement has some uncertainty. | Probability helps us talk about uncertainty. | She felt uncertainty about which club to join. | Life is full of uncertainties.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable (the feeling) and countable (uncertainties = things not known). From «un-» + «certain» + «-ty». Opposite: certainty. Maths: on the probability scale, 0 = impossible, 1 = certain; values in between show uncertainty.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Dirty; not washed or not clean. 2) (Bible, church) In old religious laws, not pure, so a person or thing had to be kept apart or washed in a special way before taking part in worship. 3) Morally bad or wicked, in old or religious writing.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life it is a stiff word for «dirty», often about water, hands or places where germs could spread. In Bible lessons it describes animals people were told not to eat, or people who had touched something forbidden, and Jesus touching an «unclean» person shows kindness breaking rules. Phrases: unclean water, unclean hands, unclean spirit.
examples from the lessons: Do not drink unclean water from the pond. | The nurse said unclean hands spread germs. | In the old law, pigs were called unclean animals. | The story tells of a man with an unclean spirit. | The kitchen was left unclean after the party. | People with skin disease were called unclean and had to live apart. | Unclean tools can make a cut infected.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It is formal or old-fashioned; in everyday talk say «dirty». It is the opposite of «clean» with the prefix «un-» meaning «not». The religious sense is about rules of purity, not just dirt.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To take a door or lid off its hinges. 2) To upset someone so much that they stop thinking clearly or calmly. 3) (informal) «Unhinged» means acting in a wild, strange or crazy way.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, «unhinged» tells the reader a character has lost control or is acting madly, like a villain. In everyday and online talk, people say a joke or video is «unhinged» when it is wildly silly. In DIY, you unhinge a door to fix or paint it.
examples from the lessons: Dad had to unhinge the door to fit the new carpet. | The cupboard door was unhinged and lay on the floor. | The shock of the news seemed to unhinge him. | The villain gave an unhinged laugh. | That comedy sketch was completely unhinged. | Don't let one bad mark unhinge you before the test. | We unhinged the gate and carried it to the shed.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly used as the adjective «unhinged». Calling a real person «unhinged» can be unkind, because it suggests they are mentally ill; be careful using it about people.

meaning for a pupil: 1) With no people living there. 2) With no animals or living things living there (less common).
its sense in the lessons: In geography and stories it describes islands, deserts, planets or houses where nobody lives. It tells the reader a place is empty, lonely or wild. Phrases: an uninhabited island, an uninhabited house.
examples from the lessons: The sailors were shipwrecked on an uninhabited island. | Much of Antarctica is uninhabited. | The old farmhouse has been uninhabited for years. | Scientists think the Moon is uninhabited. | They explored an uninhabited valley. | The rocket landed on an uninhabited planet in the story.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: «inhabited» means people live there, and «uninhabited» means nobody does; but «inhabitable» (can be lived in) and «uninhabitable» (cannot be lived in) are different words. Not countable; it is an adjective.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A language spoken mainly in Pakistan and India, written with an Arabic-style script from right to left. 2) As an adjective, to do with that language, such as Urdu poetry.
its sense in the lessons: In lessons about languages and the world, Urdu is the national language of Pakistan and is spoken by many families in the UK, the USA and Canada. It is very close to Hindi when spoken, but written in a different script. Phrases: speak Urdu, in Urdu, Urdu poetry.
examples from the lessons: My friend speaks Urdu with her grandmother. | Urdu is the national language of Pakistan. | The sign was written in English and Urdu. | Urdu is written from right to left. | We learned to say hello in Urdu. | Urdu poetry is famous for its love songs called ghazals.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always written with a capital U in English. Not countable: «speaks Urdu», not «an Urdu». Spoken Urdu and Hindi are very similar, but the writing systems differ.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A large meat-eating dinosaur with a big curved claw on each foot, which lived about 125 million years ago in what is now Utah, USA.
its sense in the lessons: In dinosaur and science lessons it is one of the biggest raptors, about 6 to 7 metres long, much bigger than the real velociraptor. Fossils show it was related to birds and probably had feathers.
examples from the lessons: Utahraptor was named after the state of Utah. | A utahraptor had a huge claw on each foot. | Scientists think utahraptors had feathers. | The utahraptor was much bigger than a velociraptor. | We saw a utahraptor skeleton at the museum. | Utahraptor lived in the Early Cretaceous period.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a scientific name it is written Utahraptor with a capital letter; in everyday writing «a utahraptor» is fine. Use «a», not «an», because it starts with a «you» sound. Myth: films show velociraptors as big as people, but it was utahraptor that was that big.

part of speech: verb (vaccinate, vaccinates, vaccinated, vaccinating); noun (vaccination, vaccine)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To give a person or animal a vaccine, usually by injection, so that their body learns to fight a disease before catching it.
its sense in the lessons: In science and health lessons, vaccinating helps the immune system make defences, so people are protected from illnesses like measles, polio or flu. Pets are vaccinated at the vet too. Phrases: get vaccinated, be vaccinated against something.
examples from the lessons: The nurse vaccinated the children against measles. | Our puppy was vaccinated at the vet. | Have you been vaccinated against flu this year? | Doctors vaccinate babies to protect them. | Vaccinating many people stops a disease spreading. | Farmers vaccinate their cows too.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say «vaccinated against» a disease. The thing given is a «vaccine»; the act is a «vaccination». It is spelled with double c. A vaccine prevents illness; it is not a cure for an illness you already have.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A very small porpoise that lives only in the northern Gulf of California, in Mexico, and is the most endangered sea mammal in the world.
its sense in the lessons: In science and nature lessons the vaquita is an example of an animal close to extinction, with only about ten left, because it gets caught in fishing nets. Its name is Spanish for «little cow». It has dark rings around its eyes like a panda.
examples from the lessons: The vaquita is the smallest porpoise in the world. | Only a few vaquitas are left in the wild. | Vaquitas get trapped in fishing nets by mistake. | A vaquita has dark rings around its eyes. | Scientists are trying to save the vaquita. | Vaquitas live only in one small part of the sea.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say it «va-KEE-ta». It comes from Spanish. It is a porpoise, not a dolphin or a whale, though they are related.

part of speech: adjective (Venetian); noun (a Venetian, Venetians); noun (venetian blind, venetian blinds)
meaning for a pupil: 1) From or to do with Venice, a city in Italy built on water with canals instead of streets. 2) A person who comes from Venice. 3) A venetian blind is a window blind made of many thin flat strips that tilt to let light in or keep it out.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, Venetian merchants traded across the Mediterranean, and Marco Polo was Venetian. In art, Venetian glass and Venetian masks are famous. At home, a venetian blind is a common kind of blind.
examples from the lessons: Marco Polo was a famous Venetian traveller. | We bought a Venetian mask for the carnival. | Venetian boats are called gondolas. | Pull the cord to open the venetian blind. | The Venetians built their city on islands. | Venetian glass is beautiful and colourful.
note for the reader of a maths problem: With a capital V when it means Venice; the blind is often written with a small v. Do not confuse with «Venusian» (from the planet Venus).

part of speech: numeral (Roman numeral VI); abbreviation (vi, Vi); noun (vi, a computer program)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The Roman numeral for 6. 2) A short name for a text-editing program used by computer programmers. 3) Sometimes a short form of the name Violet or Vienna, or a part of a word in other languages (a name or fragment).
its sense in the lessons: In maths and history, Roman numerals appear on clocks, in kings' names (Henry VI) and for chapter numbers; VI means 5 + 1 = 6. In computing lessons, vi is an old text editor. Otherwise it is usually a fragment, not an English word.
examples from the lessons: King Henry VI became king when he was a baby. | Chapter VI is the exciting part. | On the clock, VI stands where the 6 would be. | VI means five plus one. | My uncle writes code in vi. | Write the number 6 in Roman numerals: VI.
note for the reader of a maths problem: In Roman numerals, a smaller numeral after a bigger one is added: V (5) + I (1) = 6. Compare IV, where I comes first and is taken away: 4. Usually written in capitals: VI.

meaning for a pupil: 1) From the time when Queen Victoria ruled Britain, from 1837 to 1901. 2) A person who lived in that time. 3) Old-fashioned, very strict or prim, like people imagined the Victorians to be. 4) (Australia) From or to do with the state of Victoria in Australia.
its sense in the lessons: In UK history lessons, the Victorians are a big topic: factories and the Industrial Revolution, railways, children working in mines and as chimney sweeps, strict schools, and inventions. Victorian houses and buildings are common in British towns. Calling rules «Victorian» means they are old-fashioned and strict.
examples from the lessons: The Victorians built many railways. | Our school is in an old Victorian building. | Victorian children often worked in factories. | We dressed up as Victorians for history day. | Grandad has very Victorian ideas about manners. | Charles Dickens was a Victorian writer. | Melbourne is the capital of the Victorian state in Australia.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always a capital V. The Victorian era is the 1800s, roughly the 19th century. Victorian schools used slates, chalk and harsh punishments, which many lessons compare with schools today.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The Roman numeral for 8.
its sense in the lessons: In history it appears in kings' names, most famously Henry VIII, the English king who had six wives. In maths lessons on Roman numerals, VIII means 5 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 8. It also numbers chapters and clock hours.
examples from the lessons: Henry VIII had six wives. | The clock showed VIII for eight o'clock. | Turn to chapter VIII. | VIII is five plus three. | Pope Urban VIII lived long ago. | Write 8 in Roman numerals: VIII.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Read «Henry VIII» as «Henry the Eighth». Roman numerals add the smaller numbers after V: V + III = VIII. It is not an English word, just a number.

part of speech: verb (wallow, wallows, wallowed, wallowing); noun (a wallow, wallows)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To roll about in mud or water, as pigs, hippos and buffalo do to cool down. 2) To let yourself stay sad or upset for a long time and enjoy feeling sorry for yourself. 3) To enjoy something a lot, like wallowing in a hot bath. 4) A muddy place where animals roll about.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, animals wallow in mud to keep cool and keep insects off. In stories and everyday life, «wallowing in self-pity» means staying miserable instead of trying to feel better. Phrases: wallow in mud, wallow in self-pity.
examples from the lessons: The pigs wallowed happily in the mud. | Hippos wallow in rivers on hot days. | Stop wallowing and come and play. | She wallowed in a warm bubble bath. | He wallowed in self-pity after losing the match. | The buffalo found a muddy wallow.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Often followed by «in». Do not confuse with «swallow» (to take food down your throat) or «hollow» (empty inside).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A Native American people of what is now Massachusetts and Rhode Island in the USA. 2) Their language, also called Wôpanâak.
its sense in the lessons: In US history lessons, the Wampanoag met the Pilgrims who arrived on the Mayflower in 1620, helped them survive, and shared the harvest feast remembered as the first Thanksgiving. Lessons today also tell how they later lost land and lives in wars and disease, and that the Wampanoag still live there today.
examples from the lessons: The Wampanoag lived in New England long before the Pilgrims came. | Tisquantum, also called Squanto, was a Wampanoag man. | The Wampanoag showed the settlers how to grow corn. | Many Wampanoag people still live in Massachusetts. | The Wampanoag language is being taught again. | Massasoit was a leader of the Wampanoag.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say it «WAM-pa-NO-ag». Always a capital W. Use it as a people's name, respectfully; the people are not only in the past, they live today.

part of speech: adjective (warring); verb (form of war: war, wars, warred, warring)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Fighting a war against each other. 2) Quarrelling or arguing strongly, like two sides who will not agree.
its sense in the lessons: In history and stories, «warring kingdoms» or «warring tribes» are groups fighting each other. In everyday life, «warring neighbours» or «warring brothers» are people who keep arguing. Phrases: warring sides, warring factions.
examples from the lessons: The two warring kingdoms finally made peace. | The warring sides agreed to stop fighting. | Our warring neighbours shout over the fence. | Ancient China had a time called the Warring States. | The teacher sat the warring twins at different tables. | Peace talks brought the warring groups together.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelled with double r. It is mostly used before a noun: warring sides. Do not confuse with «wearing» (having clothes on).

part of speech: verb (whack, whacks, whacked, whacking); noun (a whack, whacks); adjective (whacked, informal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To hit something or someone hard, often with a stick or hand. 2) A hard hit, or the sound of it. 3) (informal) A share or amount of something, as in «pay your whack». 4) (informal) «Have a whack at it» means have a try. 5) (slang) «Whacked» or «whacked out» means very tired. 6) (slang, US) «Out of whack» means not working properly.
its sense in the lessons: In stories it gives a loud, comic hitting action. In everyday talk, «out of whack» means something is broken or wrong, and «I'm whacked» means very tired. Hitting people is not okay; you whack a ball, a nail or a piñata.
examples from the lessons: He whacked the ball over the fence. | The piñata burst open with one big whack. | Give it a whack, it might start working. | I'll have a whack at the puzzle. | My sleep is all out of whack after the holiday. | I'm completely whacked after the swimming race. | Everyone paid their whack for the pizza.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal word. The «h» is silent for most speakers: «wack». «Wack» (slang, US) without h means bad or silly, a different word. Hitting people or animals hurts; say «whack» for things.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A strong alcoholic drink made from grain such as barley, corn or rye, for adults only.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and stories it is a grown-up drink; a cowboy in a western might order whiskey. Children should not drink it; alcohol is harmful for young bodies. In geography, whisky is famous from Scotland and Ireland.
examples from the lessons: Grandad keeps a bottle of whiskey for special visitors. | Whiskey is an alcoholic drink for adults. | Scotland is famous for its whisky. | The cowboy ordered a whiskey at the saloon. | Whiskey is made from barley or corn. | Children must never drink whiskey.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: Irish and American usually spell it «whiskey»; Scottish and Canadian usually «whisky». Plurals: whiskeys, whiskies. Alcohol is illegal for children to buy.

part of speech: verb (whoop, whoops, whooped, whooping); noun (a whoop, whoops); interjection (whoop)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To shout loudly with joy or excitement. 2) A loud shout of happiness. 3) The noisy breath-in sound of whooping cough, an illness. 4) (slang, US) To beat someone easily, as in «whoop them».
its sense in the lessons: In stories it shows people cheering, like «whooped with joy». In health lessons, whooping cough is a disease babies are vaccinated against. «Whoops» (with s) is a different little word said after a small mistake. Phrases: whoop with joy, whoop it up (party noisily).
examples from the lessons: The children whooped when the bell rang for the holidays. | We heard a whoop from the winning team. | She gave a whoop of delight. | Whooping cough makes a loud whoop sound. | The fans whooped and cheered. | We're going to whoop them in the final!
note for the reader of a maths problem: The «wh» can be said «w» or «h»: «woop» or «hoop». «Whoops!» means oops and is a separate word. «Whoop-de-doo» is said sarcastically to mean «so what».

meaning for a pupil: 1) The distance from the tip of one wing to the tip of the other wing when they are stretched out, of a bird, bat, insect or aeroplane. 2) (informal) The distance between someone's fingertips when their arms are stretched out sideways.
its sense in the lessons: In science and maths lessons, wingspan is measured in centimetres or metres to compare animals; the wandering albatross has a wingspan of about 3 metres. In sport, a basketball player's wingspan helps them reach. It is a length.
examples from the lessons: An albatross has the biggest wingspan of any bird. | The plane's wingspan is 60 metres. | Measure the butterfly's wingspan with a ruler. | Pterosaurs had huge wingspans. | My arm wingspan is about the same as my height. | The eagle spread its wings to show its wingspan.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word. In maths problems it is a length, so it is measured in cm or m; to compare, subtract the smaller from the larger. Your arm span is usually close to your height.

part of speech: verb (woo, woos, wooed, wooing); interjection (woo, woo-hoo); noun (woo, informal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (old-fashioned) To try to make someone love you so they will be your boyfriend, girlfriend or partner. 2) To try hard to get someone's support, such as voters or customers. 3) (informal) «Woo!» or «woo-hoo!» is a cry of excitement. 4) (slang) «Woo» or «woo-woo» means ideas that are mystical and not backed by science.
its sense in the lessons: In fairy tales and old stories, a prince woos a princess. In news, politicians woo voters and shops woo customers. In everyday life, children shout «woo-hoo!» when happy. In science talk, «woo» is a dismissive word for unscientific claims.
examples from the lessons: The prince wooed the princess with songs. | The shop is trying to woo new customers with discounts. | Both parties are wooing young voters. | Woo-hoo, it's snowing! | Woo, we won! | She thinks crystal healing is a lot of woo.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past form «wooed», said «wood». Say «woo» like «too». The «woo-woo» sense is informal and can be rude about someone's beliefs.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A small clock you wear on a strap or band around your wrist.
its sense in the lessons: In maths lessons, children read the time on a wristwatch, in analogue (with hands) or digital (with numbers). In history, wristwatches became common about a hundred years ago; before that people carried pocket watches. Today smartwatches are a kind of wristwatch.
examples from the lessons: Grandpa gave me his old wristwatch. | Check your wristwatch to see if it's playtime. | My wristwatch has hands and numbers. | A digital wristwatch shows the time as numbers. | She wears her wristwatch on her left wrist. | Soldiers used wristwatches in the First World War.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word. Plural adds -es: wristwatches. Usually people just say «watch». The «w» in «wrist» is silent: «rist».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (slang, mildly rude) A person who is seen as weak, scared or not brave.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday talk among children or in stories, calling someone a «wuss» teases them for being scared. It is mildly insulting and can be unkind; being careful or scared of danger is often sensible, not weak.
examples from the lessons: Don't be a wuss, the water's not that cold! | He called me a wuss for not going on the big ride. | I'm a total wuss about spiders. | Stop calling your brother a wuss. | Only a wuss would quit now, said the bully. | It's not wussy to wear a helmet, it's smart.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Slang, mainly US. Plural: wusses. It is a teasing insult; avoid it in school writing. Saying it about yourself («I'm a wuss about needles») is friendly.

part of speech: numeral (Roman numeral XI); noun (xi, the Greek letter Ξ ξ); noun (Xi, a name)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The Roman numeral for 11. 2) The 14th letter of the Greek alphabet, written Ξ or ξ. 3) (Mandarin, pinyin) A Chinese syllable or family name, as in Xi Jinping, the leader of China (a name); in Chinese it sounds like «shee».
its sense in the lessons: In maths, XI means 10 + 1 = 11. In sport, a cricket or football «XI» is a team of eleven players, as in «the England XI». In news, Xi is the family name of China's leader.
examples from the lessons: The football team is called the first XI. | Chapter XI is the last chapter. | XI means ten plus one. | Pope Pius XI lived about a hundred years ago. | Xi is a letter in the Greek alphabet. | The news showed President Xi meeting other leaders.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Read «the first XI» as «the first eleven». In Chinese names «Xi» is said «shee», not «zy». It is not an English word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The Roman numeral for 12.
its sense in the lessons: On clock faces with Roman numerals, XII is at the top, where 12 o'clock is. In maths lessons, XII means 10 + 1 + 1 = 12. It also numbers chapters, kings and popes.
examples from the lessons: The clock's hands both pointed to XII at midday. | Pope Pius XII lived in the 1900s. | Chapter XII tells the end of the story. | XII means ten plus two. | Write 12 in Roman numerals: XII. | Louis XII was a king of France.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Read kings' and popes' names as «the Twelfth». X is 10 and each I adds 1. It is not an English word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A large, hairy, ape-like creature that some people say lives in the Himalaya mountains; it is a legend, and no one has ever proved it is real. 2) Another name for the Abominable Snowman.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and myths, the yeti is a mystery creature of the snowy mountains of Nepal and Tibet. In science lessons it is an example of a claim without good evidence: footprints and hairs said to be from a yeti turned out to be from bears and other animals.
examples from the lessons: Climbers said they saw yeti footprints in the snow. | The yeti is a legend from the Himalayas. | Scientists tested «yeti hair» and found it came from bears. | In the film, the yeti was friendly. | The yeti is also called the Abominable Snowman. | Do you believe in the yeti?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: yetis. Myth trap: there is no scientific proof that yetis exist. Bigfoot or Sasquatch is a similar legend from North America.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (UK, Canada, Australia, Ireland, New Zealand) The name of the last letter of the alphabet, Z. 2) (informal) «Catch some zeds» means get some sleep, because cartoon sleepers show «zzz».
its sense in the lessons: In spelling and alphabet lessons, British, Canadian, Australian, Irish and New Zealand children say «zed», while American children say «zee». In maths, z is often a letter standing for a number or for the third axis.
examples from the lessons: The alphabet goes from A to zed. | «Zebra» starts with a zed. | Americans say «zee» but we say «zed». | Spell «zoo»: zed, oh, oh. | I'm off to catch some zeds. | Write a capital zed at the end.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Only the name of the letter; you write the letter as Z. In the USA it is «zee». It is not a word you write in a sentence on its own often.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (French) Means «sharp» or «high»; in English it is used in «accent aigu», the acute accent, the little mark sloping up to the right on the letter é. It is not an English word.
its sense in the lessons: In French lessons, the accent aigu is put on e (é) to show it sounds like «ay», as in «café» and «été». To an English ear it sounds like «ay-GOO» (the French u is said with rounded lips). Other French accents are grave (è) and circonflexe (ê).
examples from the lessons: The word «café» has an accent aigu on the e. | Put an accent aigu on the e in «école». | An accent aigu slopes up to the right. | «Été» has two accents aigus. | The teacher drew an é with an accent aigu. | Accent aigu makes the e sound like «ay».
note for the reader of a maths problem: French word, not English. In English the mark is called the «acute accent». The French plural is «aigus». Do not confuse it with the grave accent, which slopes the other way (è).

part of speech: interjection (Arabic phrase, alhamdulillah; also al-hamdu lillah)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (Arabic, Islam) A phrase meaning «praise be to God» or «thanks be to God», said by Muslims to thank God, for good news and in everyday life. It is not an English word.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life with Muslim friends and families, people say «alhamdulillah» when asked «How are you?», after eating, or when something good happens. In religious education lessons it is a key phrase of Islam. To an English ear it sounds like «al-HAM-doo-li-LAH».
examples from the lessons: «How are you?» «Alhamdulillah, I'm fine.» | Alhamdulillah, the baby arrived safely. | My friend says alhamdulillah after every meal. | Alhamdulillah, we passed the test! | Muslims believe in thanking God in good and hard times. | Grandma smiled and said, «Alhamdulillah».
note for the reader of a maths problem: Arabic, used in English by Muslims of all backgrounds. Respectful to use; spellings vary. It is said in both good times and hard times, to show thanks to God.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A large meat-eating dinosaur that walked on two legs and lived about 150 million years ago, in the Jurassic period, in what is now North America and Europe.
its sense in the lessons: In dinosaur lessons, allosaurus was the top hunter of its time, about 8 to 10 metres long, with sharp teeth and three-fingered hands. It lived long before Tyrannosaurus rex. Its name means «different lizard».
examples from the lessons: Allosaurus was a fierce Jurassic hunter. | An allosaurus walked on two strong legs. | Allosaurus may have hunted stegosaurus. | We saw an allosaurus skeleton at the museum. | Allosaurus lived millions of years before T. rex. | The allosaurus had three claws on each hand.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Scientific name Allosaurus with a capital A. Use «an allosaurus». Trap: dinosaurs did not live at the same time as people, and allosaurus and T. rex never met.

part of speech: adjective (ambient); noun (ambient, as in ambient music)
meaning for a pupil: 1) In the surroundings; around you, such as ambient temperature or ambient light. 2) Ambient music is quiet, gentle music made to create a calm mood, not to be listened to closely.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, «ambient temperature» means the temperature of the air around, often room temperature. In everyday life, ambient light or noise is the light or sound already there. Phrases: ambient temperature, ambient noise, ambient light.
examples from the lessons: Keep the medicine at ambient temperature. | The ambient noise in the canteen was very loud. | Ambient light from the window lit the room. | The spa played soft ambient music. | Measure the ambient temperature before the experiment. | The ice melted faster in the warm ambient air.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A formal or science word. Usually used before a noun. Say «AM-bee-ent».

part of speech: noun (amp, amps); verb (amp up, amps up, amped up, amping up); adjective (amped, slang)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Short for «ampere», the unit used to measure electric current. 2) Short for «amplifier», a machine that makes sound from a guitar or microphone louder. 3) (slang) «Amp up» means make something stronger or more exciting. 4) (slang) «Amped» means very excited.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on electricity, current is measured in amps (A) with an ammeter. In music, a guitarist plugs into an amp. In slang, people get «amped» for a match or a concert.
examples from the lessons: The current in the circuit was two amps. | The guitar was plugged into a huge amp. | Turn the amp down, it's too loud! | This fuse is rated at 13 amps. | The coach amped up the training before the final. | I'm so amped for the school trip!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Symbol for the unit is A. In maths and science problems, amps measure current; volts measure push; watts measure power (watts = volts × amps). The full word «ampere» is named after André-Marie Ampère.

part of speech: noun (anagram, anagrams — this is the plural)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Words or phrases made by changing the order of the letters of another word or phrase, using every letter once, like «listen» and «silent».
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons and puzzles, anagrams are a word game and appear in crosswords and spelling bees. In olympiad puzzles you may find anagrams of names or hidden words. Phrases: solve anagrams, an anagram of.
examples from the lessons: «Listen» and «silent» are anagrams. | «Dormitory» is an anagram of «dirty room». | We solved anagrams in the puzzle club. | Make anagrams of the word «stop»: pots, tops, spot, opts. | Crosswords often use anagrams as clues. | My name has funny anagrams.
note for the reader of a maths problem: This form is the plural of «anagram». An anagram must use exactly the same letters, the same number of times. Spaces and capital letters are usually ignored.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Again, once more. 2) In a new and different way, starting fresh.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and the stiff written voice, «begin anew» means start again from the beginning. In everyday life people more often say «again» or «start over». Phrases: begin anew, start anew.
examples from the lessons: After the storm, they built their house anew. | Each spring the garden comes alive anew. | Let's start anew tomorrow. | She read the poem anew and saw new meanings. | After moving schools, he felt he could begin anew. | The war started anew after the peace failed.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal or literary. One word. Say «a-NEW». Do not confuse with «a new» (two words), as in «a new bike».

part of speech: noun (Angus, Angus cattle); proper noun (Angus, a name and a place)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A breed of black or red cattle with no horns, first from Scotland, famous for beef. 2) (a name) A Scottish boy's name. 3) Angus is also an area in eastern Scotland.
its sense in the lessons: In farming and food, Angus beef is a well-known kind of beef in burgers. In stories, Angus is a common Scottish name. In geography, Angus is a council area in Scotland.
examples from the lessons: The farmer keeps Angus cattle. | This burger is made with Angus beef. | Angus cows are usually black. | My cousin's name is Angus. | Angus is a region of Scotland. | Angus cattle have no horns.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always a capital A. Plural for cattle is still «Angus». As a name, it is a person's first name.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A style of cartoon film or TV series from Japan, with bright colours, big eyes and exciting stories.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, many children watch anime and read manga, which are Japanese comics. In art lessons, children may draw characters in an anime style. Phrases: watch anime, an anime series.
examples from the lessons: My favourite anime is about a boy who wants to be a hero. | She draws people in anime style. | Many anime are based on manga comics. | We watched an anime film at the sleepover. | Anime is very popular in Japan. | He collects anime posters.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say «AN-ee-may». Usually uncountable: «I watch anime». Some anime are made for adults, so check the age rating.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal, law) To officially say that something such as a marriage, contract or election never counted and is cancelled. 2) (church) In the Catholic Church, an annulment declares that a marriage was never valid.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, Henry VIII wanted the Pope to annul his marriage to Catherine of Aragon; when the Pope said no, England broke away from the Catholic Church. In law and news, courts annul results or agreements.
examples from the lessons: Henry VIII asked the Pope to annul his first marriage. | The court annulled the election result. | The contract was annulled because it was unfair. | Their marriage was annulled after a few months. | The judge annulled the agreement. | Catholics believe an annulment means a marriage was never valid.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal word. Double l in «annulled» and «annulling», but one l in «annuls». It is different from divorce: divorce ends a marriage; annulment says it was never valid.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a way that is right or suitable for the situation. 2) Fittingly; in a way that matches nicely, sometimes in a funny way.
its sense in the lessons: In school, teachers ask pupils to dress appropriately, behave appropriately and use words appropriately. In stories it can show a neat match, like a dog «appropriately named Barky». Phrases: dress appropriately, behave appropriately, respond appropriately.
examples from the lessons: Please dress appropriately for the cold weather. | He behaved appropriately at the funeral. | Answer the question appropriately with full sentences. | The fish shop is appropriately called The Plaice. | Use the tools appropriately in the science lab. | She spoke appropriately to the head teacher.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: double p, double r is wrong: a-pp-r-o-p-r-i-a-t-e-l-y. The opposite is «inappropriately». Do not mix up with the verb «appropriate» (to take for yourself), which is said differently.

part of speech: noun (archduke, archdukes; archduchess for a woman)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A very important prince in the old royal family of Austria.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, Archduke Franz Ferdinand of Austria was shot in Sarajevo in 1914, and this event led to the start of the First World War. The word shows a rank higher than a duke.
examples from the lessons: Archduke Franz Ferdinand was killed in 1914. | His death helped start the First World War. | An archduke is higher than a duke. | The archduke rode in an open car. | The archduke's wife was also killed. | Austria was ruled by archdukes and emperors.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Arch-» means chief or highest, as in archbishop. Say «arch-DYOOK» or «arch-DOOK». A woman of this rank is an archduchess.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An agreement between enemies in a war to stop fighting, usually while they talk about peace.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, the armistice that ended the fighting of the First World War began at 11 o'clock on the 11th day of the 11th month. Armistice Day, now Remembrance Day or Veterans Day, is marked with two minutes' silence and poppies.
examples from the lessons: The armistice ended the fighting in the First World War. | We hold a two-minute silence on Armistice Day. | Both sides signed an armistice. | The armistice began at eleven o'clock. | Poppies remind us of the soldiers who died before the armistice. | The Korean War ended with an armistice, not a peace treaty.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say «AR-mis-tis». An armistice stops fighting; a peace treaty is the final agreement. Remembrance Day (UK, Canada, Australia), Veterans Day (USA).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To say that something was caused by something, as in «ascribe her success to hard work». 2) (formal) To say that a piece of writing, art or saying was made by a certain person.
its sense in the lessons: In the stiff exam and history voice, «ascribed to» means «said to come from». A poem ascribed to someone may not be proved to be theirs. Phrases: ascribe something to something.
examples from the lessons: He ascribed his win to lots of practice. | This poem is ascribed to an unknown monk. | The doctor ascribed the cough to the cold weather. | Many sayings are wrongly ascribed to famous people. | Scientists ascribe the change to pollution. | The painting is ascribed to a student of the master.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal word; in everyday talk say «put it down to» or «say it was by». Always used with «to». Do not mix up with «describe» or «subscribe».

meaning for a pupil: 1) To do with astronomy, the science of stars, planets and space. 2) (informal) Extremely large, especially about prices or numbers.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, an astronomical unit is the distance from Earth to the Sun, about 150 million kilometres; astronomical events include eclipses. In everyday talk, «astronomical prices» means very, very expensive. In maths, astronomical numbers are huge numbers.
examples from the lessons: The price of the concert tickets was astronomical. | An eclipse is an astronomical event. | The distances in space are astronomical. | The astronomical society meets to look at stars. | Our phone bill was astronomical this month. | An astronomical unit is the distance from Earth to the Sun.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Do not confuse with «astrological» (about horoscopes, which is not science). In maths problems, an «astronomical» number is an informal way to say very large; it gives no exact value.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A huge wild ox with long horns that lived in Europe, Asia and North Africa and became extinct in 1627; it is the ancestor of today's cattle.
its sense in the lessons: In history and science lessons, aurochs were painted in cave paintings like those at Lascaux, and they show how animals can go extinct because of hunting and loss of land. Farm cows are their tamed descendants.
examples from the lessons: The last aurochs died in Poland in 1627. | Cave paintings show aurochs with long horns. | Aurochs were much bigger than cows today. | Our farm cattle came from the aurochs. | Julius Caesar wrote about the wild aurochs. | Scientists are breeding cattle to look like aurochs.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The word ends in -s but can be singular: «an aurochs». Plural is the same, «aurochs». Say «OR-ocks».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Real and true, not a copy or a fake. 2) Done in the traditional or original way, like authentic Italian pizza. 3) Honest and sincere, true to yourself.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, an authentic object is a real one from the past, not a copy. In everyday life, food or clothes can be called authentic. In being honest, an authentic person is true to who they are. Phrases: authentic copy (trap), authentic recipe.
examples from the lessons: This is an authentic Roman coin. | The restaurant serves authentic Mexican food. | The expert said the painting was authentic. | She was authentic and never pretended. | The museum has authentic Victorian toys. | Is that signature authentic or fake?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: fake, forged, inauthentic. Say «aw-THEN-tik». Use «an authentic», because it starts with a vowel sound.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A strong dislike of something. 2) A feeling of wanting to avoid something.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and the formal voice, a character might have «an aversion to cats» or «an aversion to hard work». In science, animals learn an aversion to bad-tasting food. Phrases: an aversion to, risk aversion.
examples from the lessons: He has a strong aversion to spiders. | My cat has an aversion to water. | She developed an aversion to fish after being sick. | I have an aversion to getting up early. | Birds learn an aversion to bitter caterpillars. | His aversion to crowds kept him home.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually «an aversion to» something. It is a formal word; in everyday talk say «hates» or «can't stand». Do not confuse with «version».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A large formal meal for many people, usually to celebrate something, with speeches.
its sense in the lessons: In history and stories, kings held banquets in great halls with roast meat. Today schools and clubs hold banquets for awards. In Bible lessons, Jesus told stories of a great banquet to show that God invites everyone. Phrases: hold a banquet, a wedding banquet, banquet hall.
examples from the lessons: The king held a banquet for his knights. | We went to the sports banquet for the awards. | The banquet had five courses. | The wedding banquet lasted all evening. | In the story, a great banquet was ready but the guests made excuses. | The banquet hall was full of long tables.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say «BANG-kwit». Bigger and fancier than a dinner or a feast. Countable: a banquet, two banquets.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A tropical fig tree from India whose branches drop roots down to the ground, which grow into new trunks so one tree can look like a whole forest.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography lessons, the banyan is the national tree of India and an example of aerial roots. In stories and religion, people rest and meet under banyan trees; Hindus and Buddhists see it as special.
examples from the lessons: The banyan tree spread across the whole village square. | Banyan roots hang down from the branches. | One banyan can cover a huge area. | The banyan is India's national tree. | Children played under the shady banyan. | A banyan starts life growing on another tree.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say «BAN-yan». Countable. It is a kind of fig tree.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A soft, silvery chemical element, a metal, with the symbol Ba and atomic number 56. 2) A white drink with a barium compound that patients swallow so their stomach shows up on an X-ray (a barium meal).
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, barium is in the periodic table and is used in fireworks to make green colours. In hospitals, doctors use a barium meal or swallow to see the gut on X-rays.
examples from the lessons: Barium makes fireworks glow green. | The symbol for barium is Ba. | My granddad had to drink barium before his X-ray. | Barium is a metal in the periodic table. | Pure barium reacts with water. | Barium shows up white on an X-ray.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Symbol Ba (capital B, small a). Many barium compounds are poisonous, but the one used in hospitals is safe because it does not dissolve.

part of speech: noun (Batman, a name); noun (batman, batmen, old military)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (a name) Batman is a famous comic-book and film superhero who fights crime in Gotham City wearing a bat costume; his real name in the stories is Bruce Wayne. 2) (old, UK military) A soldier who worked as a personal servant to an officer.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and play, children know Batman from comics, cartoons, films and toys; he has no superpowers but uses gadgets and training. In history books about the British Army, a batman looked after an officer's uniform and kit.
examples from the lessons: My brother dressed as Batman for the party. | Batman lives in Gotham City. | Batman's sidekick is Robin. | Batman uses gadgets instead of superpowers. | The officer's batman polished his boots. | We watched a Batman cartoon.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a superhero, it is a name with a capital B. The old military word is a different meaning and is said «BAT-man» too. Plural of the soldier: batmen.

part of speech: verb (behead, beheads, beheaded, beheading — this is the past form); adjective (beheaded)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Killed by having the head cut off. 2) Having had the head or top part removed, as with a flower or statue.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, kings and queens were beheaded, such as Anne Boleyn and Charles I in England, and many people in the French Revolution by the guillotine. It is a serious and violent word; history tells it to show how harsh punishments were.
examples from the lessons: Anne Boleyn was beheaded in 1536. | King Charles I was beheaded in London. | Many nobles were beheaded during the French Revolution. | The statue was beheaded by vandals. | The rhyme says: divorced, beheaded, died. | In the past, beheading was used as a punishment.
note for the reader of a maths problem: This is the past form of «behead». Henry VIII's wives rhyme: divorced, beheaded, died, divorced, beheaded, survived. A grim history word.

part of speech: noun (beryl, beryls); proper noun (Beryl, a name)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A hard mineral that forms crystals, found in many colours; green beryl is emerald and blue-green beryl is aquamarine. 2) (a name) Beryl is an old-fashioned girl's name.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on rocks and gems, beryl is an example of a crystal mineral. In stories, Beryl might be a grandmother's name. In the Bible, beryl is one of the precious stones listed in the city of heaven.
