examples from the lessons: Emerald is a green kind of beryl. | The museum had a large beryl crystal. | Aquamarine is a blue beryl. | Great-aunt Beryl knitted me a scarf. | Beryl contains the element beryllium. | The jeweller polished the beryl.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say «BERR-il». As a name, capital B. Countable for crystals, uncountable for the mineral in general.

part of speech: noun (Beth, a name); noun (beth, the Hebrew letter ב)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (a name) Beth is a girl's name, a short form of Elizabeth or Bethany. 2) The second letter of the Hebrew alphabet, also spelled bet. 3) In Welsh and Hebrew place names, a part meaning «house», as in Bethlehem («house of bread»).
its sense in the lessons: In stories, Beth is a common character name, like Beth March in «Little Women». In Bible lessons, Beth- in place names such as Bethlehem and Bethel means «house». It is a name or fragment, not an everyday English word.
examples from the lessons: My best friend is called Beth. | Beth March is one of the sisters in «Little Women». | Bethlehem means «house of bread». | Beth is short for Elizabeth. | Beth is the second letter of the Hebrew alphabet. | Ask Beth if she wants to play.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a name, capital B. Short for Elizabeth or Bethany. Not an English word on its own.

part of speech: noun (blah, informal); interjection (blah, blah blah); adjective (blah, informal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) Words used to stand for boring or empty talk, usually «blah blah blah». 2) (informal) Used instead of saying the rest of something that is obvious or boring. 3) (informal, US) Dull or not interesting; feeling a bit low.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday talk, children say «blah blah blah» to show someone is talking too long or saying something boring. «The blahs» is a feeling of being dull and fed up. It is never used in formal writing.
examples from the lessons: He kept going on about football, blah blah blah. | She said sorry, it won't happen again, blah blah. | The film was a bit blah. | I've got the blahs today. | Don't just say blah blah, explain properly! | The rules are: be kind, tidy up, blah blah blah.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Very informal; never use it in school essays. Saying «blah blah» while someone is talking can be rude.

part of speech: noun (bobby, bobbies); proper noun (Bobby, a name)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (UK, old-fashioned informal) A police officer. 2) (a name) Bobby is a boy's or girl's name, short for Robert or Roberta. 3) A bobby pin is a small hair grip (US, Canada).
its sense in the lessons: In British history and stories, police officers are called bobbies, after Sir Robert Peel, who set up the London police in 1829. People say «a bobby on the beat» for a police officer walking the streets. «Bobby pin» is an American word for a hair clip.
examples from the lessons: The bobby helped the lost child find her mum. | In Victorian London, bobbies walked the streets. | Police officers are called bobbies after Robert Peel. | Bobby is my grandad's name. | She held her fringe back with a bobby pin. | We need more bobbies on the beat.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: bobbies. Friendly British slang; «copper» is another. As a name it has a capital B.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Having no bones, or with the bones taken out, especially of meat or fish. 2) (informal) Weak and floppy, as if without bones.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and cooking, boneless chicken or fish fillets are easy to eat. In science lessons, animals without backbones are invertebrates, and some, like jellyfish and worms, have no bones at all. In playful talk, a child going floppy to avoid being picked up is «boneless».
examples from the lessons: I'd like boneless chicken, please. | A jellyfish is completely boneless. | Check the fish is boneless before giving it to the baby. | The toddler went boneless and wouldn't move. | Octopuses are boneless so they can squeeze through tiny holes. | Boneless wings are just chicken pieces.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «-less» means «without». Trap: «boneless wings» are not wings at all, just chicken pieces.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) A baby boomer, a person born in the years just after the Second World War, roughly 1946 to 1964, when many babies were born. 2) (slang) «OK boomer» is a teasing way to brush off an older person's opinion as old-fashioned. 3) (Australia) A large male kangaroo.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday and online talk, «boomer» is often used about grandparents' generation. «OK boomer» is a cheeky put-down and can be rude. In Australia, a boomer is a big kangaroo.
examples from the lessons: My grandparents are baby boomers. | Lots of boomers grew up without the internet. | He said «OK boomer» to his uncle and got told off. | A huge boomer hopped across the road. | Boomers remember the first Moon landing. | Not every older person is a boomer.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «OK boomer» can be rude and disrespectful; avoid it with adults. In Australia, the kangaroo sense is common and friendly.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To do with plants and the study of plants (botany).
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons and on trips, a botanic garden is a garden where many kinds of plants are grown for study and for people to see, like Kew Gardens in London. Botanists study plants.
examples from the lessons: We visited the botanic gardens on our school trip. | The botanic garden has plants from every continent. | She drew botanic pictures of leaves. | A botanist works at the botanic garden. | The botanic greenhouse was hot and steamy. | Botanic gardens help save rare plants.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Botanic» and «botanical» mean the same; «botanical» is more common in the USA. Mostly used in «botanic garden».

part of speech: noun (bran, uncountable); proper noun (Bran, a name)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The brown outer layer of grains like wheat and oats, which comes off when flour is made; it is full of fibre. 2) (a name) Bran is a name in Welsh and Irish legends.
its sense in the lessons: In health lessons, bran is part of whole grain foods and has fibre which helps digestion. At home, bran flakes and bran muffins are breakfast foods. In old fairs, a «bran tub» was a tub of bran with hidden prizes.
examples from the lessons: I eat bran flakes for breakfast. | Bran has lots of fibre. | Brown bread contains bran. | We dipped into the bran tub at the fair. | Horses sometimes eat bran mash. | Bran comes from the outside of the wheat grain.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «some bran», not «a bran». Do not confuse with «brand» or «brain».

part of speech: noun (brine, uncountable); verb (brine, brines, brined, brining)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Very salty water. 2) Salty water used to keep food fresh or add flavour, such as for pickles or olives. 3) (literary) The sea.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, brine is a salt solution, and children evaporate brine to get salt crystals. In cooking, food is soaked in brine. In stories, «the briny» or «the brine» can mean the sea.
examples from the lessons: The olives are kept in brine. | Leave the brine in the sun and salt crystals form. | Gherkins are pickled in brine. | Dad brined the turkey overnight. | Brine shrimp live in very salty lakes. | The old sailor smelled of brine.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. In maths and science problems, brine is salt dissolved in water; more salt means a stronger solution.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A company that sends out radio or TV programmes, such as the BBC. 2) A person who speaks on radio or TV, presenting news or programmes.
its sense in the lessons: In media lessons, broadcasters like the BBC, CBC, ABC, RTÉ and PBS share news and shows. Pupils learn that broadcasters should report fairly. Sir David Attenborough is a famous broadcaster.
examples from the lessons: The BBC is a British broadcaster. | David Attenborough is a famous nature broadcaster. | The broadcaster showed the match live. | She wants to be a sports broadcaster. | Public broadcasters are paid for by the public. | The broadcaster apologised for the mistake.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From the verb «broadcast» (broadcast, broadcasts, broadcast, broadcasting). Countable.

part of speech: noun (brood, broods); verb (brood, broods, brooded, brooding)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A family of baby birds or other young animals born at the same time. 2) (humorous) A large family of children. 3) To sit on eggs to keep them warm until they hatch. 4) To keep thinking about something that makes you unhappy or angry, in a gloomy way.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, a hen broods her eggs and raises a brood of chicks. In stories, a brooding character is quiet and gloomy. A «broody» hen wants to sit on eggs; a broody person (UK informal) wants a baby.
examples from the lessons: The hen had a brood of ten chicks. | The bird broods her eggs for two weeks. | Stop brooding over that argument. | He sat brooding in his room. | Mrs Weasley looked after her large brood. | The ducks led their brood to the pond.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Do not confuse with «brewed». Brooding is like sulking and worrying together; talking to someone often helps.

part of speech: adjective (Burmese); noun (Burmese, the language; a Burmese, Burmese people); noun (a Burmese cat)
meaning for a pupil: 1) From or to do with Burma, now called Myanmar, a country in Southeast Asia. 2) The main language of Myanmar. 3) A person from Myanmar. 4) A breed of cat with short glossy brown fur.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons, Burmese people live in Myanmar, a country with many Buddhist temples. Burmese pythons are large snakes from that region. At home, a Burmese is a friendly breed of cat.
examples from the lessons: Burmese is the main language of Myanmar. | We visited a Burmese restaurant. | A Burmese python is a very big snake. | Our Burmese cat follows us everywhere. | Burma is now called Myanmar. | The Burmese alphabet has round letters.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always a capital B. Say «bur-MEEZ». The plural for people is also Burmese.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A large bowl-shaped hollow formed when the top of a volcano collapses after a huge eruption.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and science lessons, calderas are shown as giant craters, sometimes filled with lakes, like Crater Lake in the USA or the Yellowstone caldera. Lake Taupō in New Zealand fills a caldera.
examples from the lessons: Yellowstone sits on top of a huge caldera. | The caldera filled with water and became a lake. | A caldera forms when a volcano collapses. | Lake Taupō in New Zealand is in a caldera. | Scientists measured the size of the caldera. | The island of Santorini is a broken caldera.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say «kal-DAIR-a». It comes from Spanish, meaning «cauldron». A caldera is much bigger than an ordinary crater.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A glass jug with a narrow neck and no lid, used for serving water or wine at the table.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and restaurants, water is served in a carafe. In maths problems, a carafe may hold, say, 1 litre, and pupils work out how many glasses it fills.
examples from the lessons: The waiter brought a carafe of water. | The carafe holds one litre. | Pour the juice from the carafe. | Mum put a carafe of water on the table. | How many 250 ml glasses can a 1 litre carafe fill? | The glass carafe broke on the floor.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say «ka-RAFF». Countable. In maths problems, use its capacity: a 1 litre carafe fills four 250 ml glasses.

part of speech: noun (carbonate, carbonates); verb (carbonate, carbonates, carbonated, carbonating)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) A chemical compound containing carbon and oxygen, like calcium carbonate in chalk and limestone. 2) To add carbon dioxide gas to a drink to make it fizzy.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, carbonates fizz when acids like vinegar are added, giving off carbon dioxide; chalk, limestone and eggshells are calcium carbonate. In everyday life, carbonated drinks are fizzy drinks.
examples from the lessons: Chalk is made of calcium carbonate. | Vinegar makes the carbonate fizz. | Carbonated water has bubbles in it. | The factory carbonates the lemonade. | Limestone is a carbonate rock. | Bicarbonate of soda is used in baking.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Carbonated» means fizzy. Baking soda is sodium bicarbonate. Say «CAR-bo-nate».

meaning for a pupil: 1) The Carboniferous was a time in Earth's history, about 359 to 299 million years ago, when huge swamp forests grew and later turned into coal. 2) Containing or producing coal.
its sense in the lessons: In science and history-of-Earth lessons, the Carboniferous had giant insects, like dragonflies as big as seagulls, and forests of giant ferns. Coal mined in Britain and elsewhere formed from Carboniferous plants.
examples from the lessons: Coal formed from plants in the Carboniferous. | Giant dragonflies lived in the Carboniferous period. | The Carboniferous was before the dinosaurs. | These carboniferous rocks contain coal. | Forests of tree ferns grew in the Carboniferous. | Amphibians were common in the Carboniferous.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As the name of a period, use a capital C. «Carbon-iferous» means «coal-bearing». It was long before the dinosaurs.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To do with the heart.
its sense in the lessons: In science and health lessons, cardiac muscle is the heart muscle. In everyday life and safety, a cardiac arrest is when the heart suddenly stops; people can help by calling an ambulance, doing CPR and using a defibrillator. Phrases: cardiac arrest, cardiac surgeon, cardiac muscle.
examples from the lessons: A cardiac surgeon operates on hearts. | Cardiac muscle never gets tired. | He had a cardiac arrest, and a stranger did CPR. | The hospital has a cardiac ward. | Cardiac means to do with the heart. | Learn where the defibrillator is in case of cardiac arrest.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal medical word. A cardiac arrest (heart stops) is different from a heart attack (blood to the heart is blocked), though people mix them up. Say «KAR-dee-ak».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A long, thin, soft hanging cluster of tiny flowers on trees such as willow, hazel and birch.
its sense in the lessons: In science and nature lessons in spring, children find catkins on hazel and willow trees; they spread pollen on the wind. Pussy willow catkins are soft and furry like a cat's paw.
examples from the lessons: The hazel tree is covered in yellow catkins. | Catkins release pollen in the wind. | Pussy willow catkins feel soft and furry. | We collected catkins on our spring walk. | Catkins are a sign that spring is coming. | Birch catkins hang like little tails.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Catkins are flowers, though they do not look like usual flowers. They can cause hay fever because of the pollen.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person from very long ago, in the Stone Age, who is imagined as living in caves. 2) (informal) A rough or old-fashioned man with rude manners.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, early humans in the Stone Age sometimes sheltered in caves and made cave paintings, but many lived in huts and tents too. In cartoons, cavemen often wrongly live with dinosaurs. Calling someone a caveman teases them for being rough.
examples from the lessons: Cavemen painted animals on the walls. | The caveman made a spear from flint. | In the cartoon, a caveman rode a dinosaur. | Stone Age people did not all live in caves. | Stop eating like a caveman! | We built a caveman shelter in the woods.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: cavemen. Myth trap: people and dinosaurs never lived at the same time. Many historians prefer «Stone Age people».

part of speech: verb (caw, caws, cawed, cawing); noun (a caw, caws)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The loud harsh cry of a crow, rook or raven. 2) To make this sound.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and nature lessons, crows caw from trees. Writers use «caw» as a sound word to set a spooky or wild scene.
examples from the lessons: The crow cawed from the rooftop. | We heard the caw of a raven. | Rooks caw loudly in the evening. | «Caw! Caw!» went the crow. | The birds cawed when the cat came near. | A single caw broke the silence.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It is an onomatopoeia: the word sounds like the noise. Do not confuse with «core» or «cor» (UK slang for surprise), which sound similar in some accents.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person or animal who chases someone or something. 2) A drink taken straight after another, especially a weaker drink after a strong alcoholic one, or a strong one after beer (adults). 3) (sport) A horse that races over fences (steeplechaser), or a player in the Harry Potter game Quidditch. 4) Storm chaser: a person who follows storms to study or film them.
its sense in the lessons: In playground games like tag, the chaser tries to catch the others. In science, storm chasers follow tornadoes. In everyday adult life, a chaser is a drink. In stories, a dream chaser is someone who follows their dreams.
examples from the lessons: In tag, the chaser has to catch everyone. | The storm chasers filmed the tornado. | My grandad drank water as a chaser. | The chaser horse jumped every fence. | You be the chaser this time! | Ambulance chasers are lawyers who look for accident victims.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «chase» plus «-er» (a person who does). Countable.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A loose, simple dress or a woman's undergarment like a long shirt, worn in the past under other clothes. 2) (French) «Chemise» means «shirt» in French.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, Victorian and Tudor women wore a chemise under their dresses. In French lessons, «une chemise» is a shirt, a false friend for English learners.
examples from the lessons: In Tudor times, women wore a linen chemise under their dress. | The chemise kept the outer clothes clean. | In French, «chemise» means shirt. | The museum showed a white chemise from 1800. | She wore a simple chemise dress. | Washing the chemise was easier than washing the gown.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say «she-MEEZ». In English it is an old-fashioned garment; in French it is an ordinary shirt.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A group of fruit trees, and their juicy fruits with thick peel, such as oranges, lemons, limes and grapefruit.
its sense in the lessons: In science and health lessons, citrus fruits are full of vitamin C; sailors once ate limes to prevent scurvy. In cooking, citrus flavour is sharp and fresh. In science experiments, lemon juice is an acid.
examples from the lessons: Oranges and lemons are citrus fruits. | Citrus fruits are full of vitamin C. | I love the smell of citrus. | Sailors ate citrus fruit to stop scurvy. | Lemon juice is acidic because it's a citrus. | Citrus trees grow in warm places.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Often used as an adjective: citrus fruit. Spelling: citrus (not «citrous» for the noun).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person or thing that sorts things into groups. 2) (computing) A computer program that decides which group or label something belongs to, like spam or not spam. 3) (language) In some languages like Mandarin, a word used between a number and a noun, like «a piece of» in English.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, scientists classify animals, and a classifier is a tool or key for sorting. In computing and AI lessons, a classifier learns from examples to label new things. In Mandarin, «ge» is a common classifier.
examples from the lessons: The classifier sorted the emails into spam and not spam. | A classification key is a kind of classifier for animals. | In Mandarin, you need a classifier between the number and the noun. | The AI classifier recognised the cat in the photo. | «A loaf of bread» works like a classifier in English. | We trained a classifier on pictures of fruit.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «classify». Countable. A classifier can be wrong; it makes guesses based on what it learned.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person from the East End of London, traditionally someone born within the sound of the Bow Bells church. 2) The accent and dialect of London's East End, which drops some h sounds and uses «rhyming slang».
its sense in the lessons: In English and history lessons, Cockney is an example of a dialect. Cockney rhyming slang says a rhyme instead of the word, like «apples and pears» for stairs. In films, characters like Mary Poppins' Bert speak Cockney.
examples from the lessons: He was born in the East End, a true Cockney. | «Apples and pears» means stairs in Cockney rhyming slang. | She speaks with a Cockney accent. | Cockneys often drop the h: «'ello». | «Use your loaf» is Cockney for «use your head». | Bert in «Mary Poppins» has a Cockney accent.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Often capital C. Cockney is a dialect, not wrong English; Standard English is used in school writing. Rhyming slang: «loaf of bread» = head, so «loaf» means head.

part of speech: adjective (coeliac; US celiac); noun (a coeliac, coeliacs)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Coeliac disease is an illness in which eating gluten, found in wheat, barley and rye, damages the gut. 2) A person who has coeliac disease.
its sense in the lessons: In health and everyday life, children with coeliac disease must eat gluten-free food, so they cannot eat ordinary bread, pasta or cake. Schools and parties need to check food labels. It is not an allergy or a choice; it is an autoimmune disease.
examples from the lessons: My friend is coeliac, so she eats gluten-free bread. | Coeliac disease damages the gut. | The café has a coeliac-friendly menu. | Check the label for gluten if a coeliac is coming to the party. | He was diagnosed with coeliac disease last year. | Coeliacs must avoid wheat, barley and rye.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK spelling «coeliac», US spelling «celiac». Say «SEE-lee-ak». It is not the same as just disliking bread.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To live or exist together at the same time and in the same place. 2) To live together peacefully even though you are different.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, different animals coexist in a habitat. In ethics and citizenship, people of different religions and cultures can coexist peacefully. Phrases: coexist peacefully, coexist with.
examples from the lessons: Lions and zebras coexist on the savannah. | People of many faiths coexist in our town. | Can cats and dogs coexist in one house? | Two ideas can coexist in your mind. | The old and new buildings coexist in the city. | Countries must learn to coexist peacefully.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Co-» means together. Usually «coexist with». No hyphen is needed, though «co-exist» is also seen.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A high-ranking officer in the army, air force or marines, above a major and below a general.
its sense in the lessons: In history and stories, colonels lead large groups of soldiers. In everyday life, Colonel Sanders is the face of a fried chicken brand. Phrases: Colonel Mustard (in the game Cluedo or Clue).
examples from the lessons: The colonel gave the order to march. | A colonel is higher than a major. | Colonel Mustard did it in the library with the rope! | The colonel's uniform had shiny badges. | Her grandfather was a colonel in the army. | The soldiers saluted the colonel.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling and sound trap: it is spelled «colonel» but said «KER-nel», like «kernel» (the seed of corn). Capital C before a name: Colonel Smith.

meaning for a pupil: 1) When one country takes control of another land and sends people to live there, often taking power from the people already living there. 2) (science) When plants or animals move into a new place and start living there.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, the colonisation of America, Australia, Africa and India by European powers is studied, including the harm done to Indigenous peoples. In science, plants colonise bare ground after a fire. Phrases: the colonisation of, space colonisation.
examples from the lessons: The colonisation of Australia began in 1788. | Colonisation took land from Indigenous peoples. | Moss is often the first plant in the colonisation of bare rock. | Some people dream of the colonisation of Mars. | India gained independence after years of British colonisation. | Lessons discuss both what colonisers built and the harm they did.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK -isation, US -ization. Verb: colonise/colonize. People see it from different sides; Indigenous peoples often describe it as invasion.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A group of people chosen to make decisions or plan something for a bigger group.
its sense in the lessons: In school, a school council or eco committee plans projects. In everyday life, clubs, churches and governments have committees. Phrases: on a committee, committee meeting.
examples from the lessons: She was chosen for the school eco committee. | The committee met to plan the summer fair. | The church committee raised money for the roof. | Parliament has many committees. | Our class has a party committee. | The committee voted on the new rules.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: double m, double t, double e: c-o-m-m-i-t-t-e-e. It can take a singular or plural verb in UK English («the committee is/are»).

meaning for a pupil: 1) To collect information or things and put them together, such as a list, book or report. 2) (computing) To turn the code a programmer writes into a program the computer can run.
its sense in the lessons: In school, pupils compile a list, a scrapbook or a class report. In computing lessons, a compiler translates code like Rust into machine code. Phrases: compile a list, compile the code.
examples from the lessons: We compiled a list of all the birds we saw. | The teacher compiled our stories into a book. | The code won't compile because of a mistake. | He compiled a playlist for the party. | Scientists compiled the data from many tests. | A dictionary is compiled by many writers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Said «com-PILE». A «compilation» is a collection, like a compilation album. In computing, «it doesn't compile» means the code has errors.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Going well together and making each other better or complete. 2) (maths) Complementary angles add up to 90 degrees. 3) (art) Complementary colours are opposite each other on the colour wheel, like red and green. 4) Complementary medicine is treatment used alongside normal medicine.
its sense in the lessons: In maths lessons, if one angle is 30°, its complementary angle is 60°. In art, complementary colours make each other stand out. In everyday life, two friends with complementary skills make a good team.
examples from the lessons: Angles of 40° and 50° are complementary. | Blue and orange are complementary colours. | Their skills are complementary: one draws, one writes. | Find the complementary angle to 25°. | Complementary colours look bright side by side. | Salt and pepper are complementary flavours.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: «complementary» (completing) is different from «complimentary» (praising, or free of charge). In maths, complementary angles add to 90°; supplementary angles add to 180°.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Made dirty, impure or harmful by something mixed in, such as germs, poison or chemicals.
its sense in the lessons: In science and safety lessons, contaminated water or food can make people ill, and scientists keep experiments from being contaminated. In everyday life, raw meat can contaminate other food, so wash hands and boards. Phrases: contaminated water, contaminated with.
examples from the lessons: Don't drink the water; it's contaminated. | The food was contaminated with bacteria. | Oil spills leave beaches contaminated. | Wash the board so it isn't contaminated by raw chicken. | The sample got contaminated and the test failed. | Radiation contaminated the land near Chernobyl.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually «contaminated with» or «by». Opposite: clean, pure, uncontaminated.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To do with conversation, or like ordinary friendly talk. 2) Good enough to have simple conversations in a language, as in «conversational French».
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons, a conversational tone is relaxed and friendly, like talking to a friend, not formal. In language lessons, conversational skills mean you can chat simply. In computing, a conversational program, like a chatbot, talks with you.
examples from the lessons: The book is written in a conversational style. | She speaks conversational French. | He said it in a conversational tone. | The chatbot is a conversational program. | Letters to friends can be conversational. | I'm working on my conversational Spanish.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal register is the opposite of conversational. Adverb: conversationally.

part of speech: adjective (coordinated; also co-ordinated); verb (coordinate, coordinates, coordinated, coordinating)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Able to move different parts of your body together well and smoothly. 2) Organised so that people or things work well together. 3) Matching, such as clothes in colours that go together.
its sense in the lessons: In PE lessons, coordinated movement helps with catching, skipping and dancing. In everyday life, a coordinated plan means everyone knows their job. In fashion, a coordinated outfit matches. In maths, «coordinates» are the numbers that show a point on a grid (a related word).
examples from the lessons: Gymnasts are very coordinated. | The rescue teams carried out a coordinated search. | Her hat and scarf are coordinated. | I'm not very coordinated at skipping. | The teachers coordinated the sports day. | The dancers made perfectly coordinated moves.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: uncoordinated or clumsy. Spelling with or without a hyphen: coordinated, co-ordinated.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A large dark sea bird with a long neck and hooked beak that dives underwater to catch fish.
its sense in the lessons: In nature lessons, cormorants are seen on rocks by the sea or rivers, holding their wings out to dry because their feathers are not fully waterproof. In China and Japan, people traditionally fished with trained cormorants.
examples from the lessons: A cormorant dived and came up with a fish. | The cormorants stood on the rocks drying their wings. | Cormorants can swim fast underwater. | We saw a cormorant at the harbour. | Cormorants have hooked beaks. | Fishermen in China once used cormorants to catch fish.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say «COR-mor-ant». Countable. In New Zealand cormorants are often called shags.

meaning for a pupil: 1) From or to do with Cornwall, a county in the far south-west of England. 2) The old Celtic language of Cornwall, which is being learned again.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and food, Cornish pasties, Cornish cream teas and Cornish beaches are famous. In history, Cornish tin mines were important. In language lessons, Cornish is a revived Celtic language related to Welsh and Breton.
examples from the lessons: We ate Cornish pasties on the beach. | Cornish tin mines are now museums. | A few people speak Cornish today. | The Cornish coast has beautiful cliffs. | In Cornwall, you put jam first on a cream tea. | «Kernow» is the Cornish name for Cornwall.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always capital C. A «Cornish pasty» is a pastry with meat and vegetables folded inside.

part of speech: noun (corona, coronas or coronae); noun (Corona, short for coronavirus)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The hot outer layer of gas around the Sun, seen as a glowing ring during a total solar eclipse. 2) (informal) Short for coronavirus, especially COVID-19. 3) A ring of light around something.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, the Sun's corona can be seen only during a total eclipse. In recent history, «corona» was everyday talk for the COVID-19 pandemic, with lockdowns and home learning. The word is Latin for «crown».
examples from the lessons: During the eclipse we saw the Sun's corona. | The corona is hotter than the Sun's surface. | Schools closed during the corona pandemic. | Coronaviruses look like they have a crown of spikes. | A corona of light shone around the moon. | Corona means crown in Latin.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Never look straight at the Sun, even near an eclipse, without proper eclipse glasses. Corona is also a brand name of beer.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A very strong poison that can kill quickly.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, especially old murder mysteries, cyanide is a poison said to smell of bitter almonds. In science, tiny amounts are found naturally in apple seeds and cherry stones, but too little to harm you if you swallow a few by accident. It is used in some industries like gold mining.
examples from the lessons: In the detective story, the victim was poisoned with cyanide. | Cyanide is a deadly poison. | Apple seeds contain a tiny bit of cyanide. | Factories must store cyanide safely. | Cyanide is used in gold mining. | The detective noticed a smell of bitter almonds.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say «SY-a-nide». Safety: never taste unknown chemicals. Not everyone can smell cyanide.

part of speech: verb (dazzle, dazzles, dazzled, dazzling); noun (dazzle); adjective (dazzling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) When a bright light shines in your eyes so that you cannot see for a moment. 2) To amaze and impress someone very much with beauty, skill or cleverness.
its sense in the lessons: In science and safety lessons, car headlights can dazzle drivers. In stories and everyday life, a performer dazzles the audience. «Razzle-dazzle» is a showy display. Phrases: dazzled by, a dazzling smile.
examples from the lessons: The bright headlights dazzled the driver. | She dazzled everyone with her dancing. | The snow was dazzling in the sunshine. | The magician dazzled the crowd. | He gave a dazzling smile. | Don't dazzle people with your torch.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double z. Dazzling can mean very bright or very impressive.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To slow down; to go less fast.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on forces and motion, friction and air resistance make objects decelerate. In maths, deceleration means speed is getting smaller over time. In everyday life, cars decelerate when the driver brakes.
examples from the lessons: The car decelerated as it reached the corner. | Friction makes the sledge decelerate. | The rocket decelerated before landing. | A parachute helps a skydiver decelerate. | The train decelerated into the station. | The ball decelerated as it rolled up the hill.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: accelerate. In maths, if speed goes from 20 m/s to 10 m/s in 5 seconds, it decelerates by 2 m/s every second. «De-» means down or away.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (UK) A person whose job is painting and wallpapering rooms and houses. 2) Someone who decorates things, like a cake decorator or interior decorator. 3) (computing) A special code feature that adds behaviour to a function (in languages like Python).
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, a painter and decorator paints walls. In art and cooking, a cake decorator makes cakes beautiful. In computing lessons, decorators appear in Python code.
examples from the lessons: We hired a decorator to paint the living room. | The painter and decorator wallpapered my bedroom. | She works as a cake decorator. | Interior decorators choose furniture and colours. | The decorator covered the floor with sheets. | Christmas decorators hung lights everywhere.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «decorate» plus «-or». Spelled -or, not -er.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To force someone to leave a country, usually because they are not allowed to live there or have broken the law. 2) (old-fashioned) To behave in a certain way (deport yourself).
its sense in the lessons: In news and citizenship lessons, people may be deported if they do not have permission to stay. In history, people were deported to prison camps, such as in the Holocaust or when Stalin deported whole peoples like the Crimean Tatars. It is a serious word.
examples from the lessons: He was deported back to his home country. | The government deported people without visas. | In the war, families were deported to camps. | The Crimean Tatars were deported in 1944. | She feared her family would be deported. | Courts decide who can be deported.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: deportation. Opposite in a way: admit or allow in. People argue about deportation; reports state each side's view.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Separated or taken off from something. 2) A detached house stands on its own, not joined to another house. 3) Not feeling or showing much emotion; not involved.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life (UK), houses are described as detached, semi-detached (joined on one side) or terraced (in a row). In science, a detached retina is a serious eye problem. In stories, a detached character seems cold or far away. In maths and school, you detach the tear-off slip.
examples from the lessons: They live in a big detached house. | Our house is semi-detached. | The trailer became detached from the car. | Detach the slip and return it to school. | He seemed detached and didn't join in. | A detached retina needs urgent treatment.
note for the reader of a maths problem: In UK estate agent talk, detached is usually more expensive than semi-detached. Opposite: attached.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To hate something or someone very much.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and the more formal voice, characters detest things like cruelty, cabbage or rude people. In everyday talk children usually say «hate» or «can't stand». It is a strong word.
examples from the lessons: I detest getting up early. | She detests unkindness. | He detests broccoli. | The villain detested the hero. | My cat detests baths. | They detest the cold, wet winters.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stronger and more formal than «dislike». Not usually used in «-ing» form: «I detest it», not «I am detesting it».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A straight line going from one side of a circle to the other, passing through the centre. 2) The length of that line; how wide a circle or round thing is.
its sense in the lessons: In maths lessons, the diameter is twice the radius, and the circumference is about 3.14 (pi) times the diameter. In science and everyday life, the diameter of a pipe, a wheel or a planet tells its width. Phrases: in diameter.
examples from the lessons: The diameter of the circle is 10 cm. | The radius is half the diameter. | The Earth's diameter is about 12,700 km. | Measure the diameter of the pizza. | The pipe is 5 cm in diameter. | The circumference is pi times the diameter.
note for the reader of a maths problem: In maths problems: diameter = 2 × radius; radius = diameter ÷ 2; circumference = π × diameter (about 3.14 × d). Do not confuse with «perimeter».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (a name) Dick is an old short form of the name Richard, as in Dick Whittington. 2) (rude, slang) A rude word for a man's private part, the penis. 3) (rude, slang) A rude insult for a mean or annoying person. 4) (old US slang) A detective («private dick»).
its sense in the lessons: In stories and pantomimes, Dick Whittington is a famous character who becomes Lord Mayor of London with his cat. In older books, Dick is a normal name. In today's talk, the slang meanings are rude and should not be used at school. «Moby-Dick» is a famous novel about a whale.
examples from the lessons: Dick Whittington went to London with his cat. | We watched the pantomime of Dick Whittington. | «Moby-Dick» is a story about a white whale. | In the old book, Dick and Jane go shopping. | The detective was called a private dick in old films. | Calling someone a dick is rude and not allowed in class.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Because of the rude meanings, many children laugh at old names like Dick; it was a normal name. Do not use the slang senses at school; it is swearing.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal, UK) To cheat someone, especially out of money, in a sneaky way. 2) (informal) To waste time or fiddle about with something. 3) In the nursery rhyme «Hey diddle diddle», it is a nonsense sound.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday talk, «I've been diddled» means «I've been cheated» or overcharged. In nursery rhymes, «Hey diddle diddle, the cat and the fiddle» is nonsense fun. Children should know that people who diddle others are being dishonest.
examples from the lessons: The shop diddled us out of ten pounds. | Hey diddle diddle, the cat and the fiddle. | Stop diddling about and get ready! | I think I've been diddled; this toy is broken. | The con man diddled lots of old people. | He diddled with the radio knobs.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal; mostly British. Some slang senses in the USA can be rude, so avoid it in formal writing.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A large animal with a tall sail on its back that lived about 295 to 272 million years ago, before the dinosaurs.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, dimetrodon is often sold in dinosaur toy sets, but it was not a dinosaur; it was a synapsid, more closely related to mammals than to dinosaurs. Its sail may have helped it warm up or show off.
examples from the lessons: Dimetrodon had a big sail on its back. | Dimetrodon lived before the dinosaurs. | It was not a dinosaur, though it is often called one. | Dimetrodon was a meat eater. | The sail may have helped dimetrodon stay warm. | We saw a dimetrodon fossil in the museum.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Myth trap: dimetrodon is not a dinosaur. Say «dy-MET-ro-don». Scientific name with a capital D.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The feeling of not believing that something is true or real, often because it is surprising or shocking. 2) Lack of belief, for example in God.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, characters stare «in disbelief» when something amazing or terrible happens. In reading, «suspend disbelief» means to accept a story's magic while you read. Phrases: in disbelief, shake your head in disbelief.
examples from the lessons: She stared in disbelief at her test score. | He shook his head in disbelief. | The crowd gasped in disbelief. | To enjoy fantasy books, you suspend disbelief. | There was disbelief when the old tree fell. | Thomas showed disbelief until he saw Jesus, the Bible says.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. «Dis-» means not. Different from «unbelief», which is used more for religious lack of faith.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Not active or growing for a time, but able to become active again, like a sleeping volcano. 2) Resting, as plants and seeds do in winter or animals in hibernation.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons, a dormant volcano has not erupted for a long time but could erupt again; an extinct one will not. In science, seeds and bulbs stay dormant until spring. Phrases: lie dormant, a dormant volcano.
examples from the lessons: Mount Fuji is a dormant volcano. | The seeds lay dormant all winter. | The tree is dormant in the cold months. | A dormant volcano could erupt again. | Bears are not fully dormant when they hibernate. | His talent lay dormant until he tried painting.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Volcano words: active (erupting now or recently), dormant (sleeping), extinct (dead). Say «DOR-mant».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Twice as much; in two ways. 2) Even more, or especially.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, «doubly sure» means very sure, checked twice. In maths, «doubly» relates to double, meaning ×2. Phrases: doubly important, doubly careful, make doubly sure.
examples from the lessons: Make doubly sure the door is locked. | It is doubly important to wear a helmet on a busy road. | She was doubly happy: she won and her friend won too. | Check your work doubly carefully. | The cake was doubly sweet with icing and jam. | It's doubly hard when it's cold and wet.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: doubly, not «doublely». In maths problems, «doubly» suggests multiplying by 2, but often just means «very».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A drey is the nest of a squirrel, built high in a tree from twigs, leaves and moss. 2) It is round like a ball, with a soft lining inside where the squirrel sleeps and keeps its babies warm.
its sense in the lessons: A nature word used in science lessons about animal homes and in stories set in woods and parks, especially in the UK. It tells the reader that a squirrel lives nearby. Phrases: «a squirrel's drey», «build a drey», «a drey in the oak».
examples from the lessons: We spotted a drey high up in the oak tree. | Grey squirrels build their dreys from twigs and leaves. | In winter the drey is easy to see because the branches are bare. | Baby squirrels are born in the drey. | A drey looks like a messy ball of sticks. | The squirrel ran up the trunk and disappeared into its drey. | Our class drew a map of all the dreys in the park. | A bird's nest is open on top, but a drey usually has a roof.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: one drey, two dreys. Rhymes with «day». Not the same as a bird's nest; a rabbit has a burrow, a fox has a den, a squirrel has a drey. Rare word that many adults do not know.

part of speech: adjective (drowsy, drowsier, drowsiest); adverb drowsily; noun drowsiness
meaning for a pupil: 1) Drowsy means sleepy, when your eyes feel heavy and you could easily fall asleep. 2) A drowsy place or time is quiet and slow, making people feel sleepy, like a warm summer afternoon. 3) (medicine) Some medicines can make you drowsy; the label warns you not to drive or use machines.
its sense in the lessons: In stories it shows a character is tired or about to fall asleep; in health lessons and safety it appears on medicine labels («may cause drowsiness»). Phrases: «feel drowsy», «a drowsy afternoon», «drowsy driving».
examples from the lessons: After the big lunch I felt drowsy. | The drowsy cat curled up by the fire. | This medicine may make you drowsy. | It was a drowsy Sunday, and nobody wanted to do anything. | Mum said drowsy drivers should stop and rest. | The baby gave a drowsy yawn. | The warm classroom made everyone drowsy. | He answered drowsily from under the blanket.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Drowsy is softer than «asleep»: you are nearly asleep but still awake. Spelling: drowsy, drowsier, drowsiest (y changes to i). Do not mix up with «dozy», which can also mean slow-witted (UK).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A dynamo is a machine that turns movement into electricity, like the small one on an old bicycle that lights the lamp when the wheel turns. 2) A person who is a dynamo is full of energy and gets lots done. 3) Dynamo is part of the name of several football and sports clubs, such as Dynamo Kyiv.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons it shows how electricity can be made from motion (generators, wind turbines). In everyday talk it praises a very busy, lively person. Phrases: «a bike dynamo», «a human dynamo», «a dynamo of energy».
examples from the lessons: My grandad's bike has a dynamo that powers the front light. | When you pedal faster, the dynamo makes the lamp brighter. | A dynamo uses magnets and coils of wire to make electricity. | Our new coach is a real dynamo. | She is a dynamo in the classroom, always helping someone. | We built a tiny dynamo in science club. | Dynamo Kyiv is a famous football club in Ukraine. | A wind-up torch has a little dynamo inside.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: dynamos (not dynamoes). A dynamo makes electricity; a motor does the opposite and uses electricity to make movement. Modern big machines are usually called generators.

part of speech: noun (Emmental, uncountable; a piece of Emmental); also spelled Emmentaler, Emmenthal
meaning for a pupil: 1) Emmental is a yellow Swiss cheese with big round holes in it. 2) It has a mild, nutty taste and melts well, so it is used in sandwiches and fondue.
its sense in the lessons: A food word met in cooking lessons, shops and stories; it is the cheese cartoons show with holes. The holes are made by gas bubbles from tiny bacteria while the cheese ripens, which makes it a nice science example. Phrases: «a slice of Emmental», «Swiss cheese».
examples from the lessons: Emmental is the cheese with the big holes. | I had a ham and Emmental sandwich for lunch. | The holes in Emmental come from bubbles of gas. | Mice in cartoons always eat cheese that looks like Emmental. | We melted Emmental on toast. | Dad bought Emmental for the fondue. | Emmental comes from Switzerland. | Americans often just call it Swiss cheese.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually written with a capital E because it is named after the Emme valley in Switzerland. Uncountable: «some Emmental», «a piece of Emmental». Myth: mice do not especially love cheese with holes; that is only cartoons.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An emollient is a cream or lotion that makes dry skin soft and smooth. 2) (formal) Emollient words or behaviour are calming and gentle, meant to stop people getting angry.
its sense in the lessons: In health lessons and on chemist labels it means moisturiser for dry skin or eczema. In formal writing and news it describes soothing speeches. Phrases: «emollient cream», «an emollient tone».
examples from the lessons: The doctor gave me an emollient for my eczema. | Rub the emollient cream into dry patches of skin. | Emollients help skin keep its water in. | Use an emollient after a bath. | The head teacher spoke in an emollient tone to calm the angry parents. | (formal) The minister gave an emollient reply to the protesters. | Grandma uses an emollient on her hands in winter. | Emollient creams can make the bath slippery, so be careful.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say it «ee-MOL-ee-ent». Countable as a noun: an emollient, emollients. Safety: emollient creams can soak into clothes and bedding and make them burn more easily, so keep away from flames.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An enclave is a small piece of land belonging to one country that is completely surrounded by another country. 2) An enclave is also a part of a town where a particular group of people live together, apart from others, such as a neighbourhood where many people share one language. 3) It can mean any small area that is different from everything around it.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons it explains strange borders, such as Vatican City and San Marino inside Italy, or Lesotho inside South Africa. In social studies it describes communities. Phrases: «a tiny enclave», «a cultural enclave», «enclave and exclave».
examples from the lessons: Vatican City is an enclave inside the city of Rome. | Lesotho is a whole country that is an enclave in South Africa. | San Marino is surrounded by Italy, so it is an enclave. | The old quarter is a quiet enclave in the busy city. | There is an Italian enclave in our city with lots of pizza shops. | The garden was a green enclave among the grey buildings. | On the map, the enclave looked like an island on land. | We looked for enclaves on the world map in geography.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: an enclave, enclaves. Starts with a vowel sound, so use «an». An exclave is the same land seen from the country it belongs to; one place can be both. Say it «EN-klave» or «ON-klave».

part of speech: noun (an epaulette, epaulettes); US spelling epaulet
meaning for a pupil: 1) An epaulette is a decoration on the shoulder of a uniform, often with gold fringe or stripes showing a person's rank. 2) A strap on the shoulder of a coat or shirt, used for style.
its sense in the lessons: Seen in history lessons and stories about soldiers, sailors, pilots and marching bands; it tells the reader that someone wears a smart or important uniform. Phrases: «gold epaulettes», «shoulder epaulettes».
examples from the lessons: The captain's jacket had gold epaulettes. | Epaulettes show how important an officer is. | The band leader wore red epaulettes with tassels. | Pilots have stripes on their epaulettes. | My raincoat has little epaulettes on the shoulders. | In the old painting the admiral's epaulettes shone. | The toy soldier had painted epaulettes. | Count the stripes on the epaulette to find the rank.
note for the reader of a maths problem: British spelling epaulette, American epaulet. Say «EP-uh-let». Comes from French «épaule», shoulder. Countable noun.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The epiglottis is a small flap at the back of your throat that closes when you swallow, so food goes down to your stomach and not into your lungs. 2) It opens again when you breathe so air can reach your windpipe.
its sense in the lessons: A body word in science and health lessons about swallowing, breathing and choking. If food goes «down the wrong way», the epiglottis did not close in time and you cough. Phrases: «the epiglottis closes», «flap of the epiglottis».
examples from the lessons: The epiglottis stops food going into your lungs. | When you swallow, the epiglottis covers your windpipe. | If you laugh while eating, the epiglottis may not close in time. | Coughing helps clear food that went down the wrong way past the epiglottis. | We labelled the epiglottis on a diagram of the throat. | The epiglottis is made of soft cartilage. | Don't talk with your mouth full, because your epiglottis has to choose air or food. | The doctor explained the epiglottis with a model.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say «ep-ih-GLOT-is». Usually «the epiglottis», since each person has one. Do not confuse with the uvula, the dangly bit you see at the back of your mouth.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (a name) Erie is one of the five Great Lakes of North America, between the USA and Canada; its full name is Lake Erie. 2) (a name) Erie is a city in Pennsylvania, USA, on the shore of Lake Erie. 3) (a name) The Erie were a Native American people who lived near the lake, and the Erie Canal is a famous old canal in New York State.
its sense in the lessons: A geography name used in lessons about the Great Lakes (Superior, Michigan, Huron, Erie, Ontario). It is the shallowest of them, so it warms up quickly in summer and freezes over in winter. Phrases: «Lake Erie», «the Erie Canal».
examples from the lessons: Lake Erie is one of the Great Lakes. | Erie lies between Canada and the USA. | We remembered the Great Lakes with the word HOMES: Huron, Ontario, Michigan, Erie, Superior. | Lake Erie is the shallowest Great Lake. | The Erie Canal joined the Great Lakes to the Hudson River. | Niagara Falls is on the river that flows from Lake Erie to Lake Ontario. | My cousin lives in Erie, Pennsylvania. | Lake Erie sometimes freezes over in a cold winter.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always written with a capital E. Sounds exactly like «eerie» (strange and spooky): «The eerie fog lay over Lake Erie». Not a common English word by itself.

part of speech: verb (erode, erodes, eroded, eroding); noun erosion
meaning for a pupil: 1) To erode means to wear away slowly, as wind, water or ice rub away rock and soil. 2) To erode can mean to make something slowly weaker or smaller, like trust or confidence being eroded.
its sense in the lessons: A key geography and science word: rivers erode valleys, waves erode cliffs, rain erodes soil. In everyday talk and news it means something is getting slowly weaker. Phrases: «erode away», «be eroded by the sea», «erode trust».
examples from the lessons: The waves erode the cliffs a little every year. | Rivers erode rock and carry it downstream. | Wind can erode sand dunes. | Trees help stop the soil from eroding. | The old statue's face had eroded in the rain. | Telling lies can erode your friends' trust. | Over thousands of years the river eroded a deep canyon. | Soil erosion happens when plants are cut down.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: eroded, eroding. Noun: erosion. Erosion is moving bits away; weathering is breaking rock where it stands; the two often happen together. Erosion is slow, so «erode» usually suggests a long time.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An estuary is the wide part of a river where it meets the sea, so fresh water and salty sea water mix. 2) (UK) Estuary English is a way of speaking common around London and the Thames estuary.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and science lessons estuaries are habitats with mud flats, tides and many birds. Phrases: «the Thames estuary», «at the estuary», «tidal estuary», «Estuary English».
examples from the lessons: The river widens into an estuary before it reaches the sea. | Lots of wading birds feed on the mud in the estuary. | Estuary water is a mix of fresh water and salt water. | At low tide the estuary turns into mud flats. | We went on a field trip to the estuary to look for crabs. | The Thames estuary is in the south-east of England. | Ships sail up the estuary to the port. | My uncle speaks Estuary English and drops his t's.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: estuaries (y changes to ies). Say «ES-tyoo-ree». Countable. A delta is different: a delta is where a river splits into many channels and builds new land.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Ethane is a gas with no colour or smell, made of carbon and hydrogen, found in natural gas. 2) It burns easily and is used in factories to make plastics.
its sense in the lessons: A chemistry word for older pupils, met when learning about fuels and the alkanes methane, ethane, propane and butane. Its formula is C2H6: two carbon atoms and six hydrogen atoms. Phrases: «ethane gas», «methane and ethane».
examples from the lessons: Ethane is found in natural gas. | Ethane has two carbon atoms and six hydrogen atoms. | Methane, ethane and propane are all gases that burn. | Factories turn ethane into the plastic used in bags. | Ethane has no smell at all. | We built a model of ethane with balls and sticks. | Saturn's moon Titan has lakes containing ethane and methane. | Never play near gas pipes, because gases like ethane can catch fire.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Say «EE-thane». Do not confuse with ethanol (an alcohol) or methane (one carbon). The smell of gas at home is added on purpose so people notice leaks.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (church) The examen is a short daily prayer in which a person looks back over the day, thanks God for good things and asks forgiveness for wrong ones; it comes from Saint Ignatius of Loyola. 2) (French) «Examen» is the French word for an exam or test; it is not an ordinary English word in that sense. 3) (old, formal) An examination or careful study.
its sense in the lessons: In church and religion lessons it describes a quiet habit of reflecting on the day, often at bedtime. In French lessons it means an exam. Phrases: «the daily examen», «pray the examen».
examples from the lessons: Every night before bed she prays the examen. | In the examen you think about the best moment of your day. | Christians who pray the examen ask God to help them do better tomorrow. | Our teacher led a short examen at the end of the school day. | The examen was taught by Saint Ignatius. | (French) «J'ai un examen demain» means «I have an exam tomorrow». | The examen has steps: thanks, review, sorry and hope. | We wrote our own examen in our reflection journals.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say «ex-AH-men» in the church sense. In French it sounds like «eg-za-MAN» (nasal end). Do not confuse with «amen». In English an exam is «exam» or «examination», not «examen».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Fallow land is a field that is ploughed but left without crops for a season so the soil can rest and get healthy again. 2) A fallow time is a quiet period when nothing much is happening or being produced. 3) A fallow deer is a smallish deer, light brown with white spots in summer.
its sense in the lessons: In history and farming lessons it explains crop rotation, where fields take turns to rest. In stories it describes empty fields or quiet times. Phrases: «lie fallow», «leave a field fallow», «a fallow period», «fallow deer».
examples from the lessons: The farmer left the field fallow this year. | In the Middle Ages one field in three lay fallow. | Letting land lie fallow helps the soil recover. | The team had a fallow season and won nothing. | We saw fallow deer in the park. | Fallow deer have white spots on their backs. | My art ideas went through a fallow patch, then came back. | Weeds grew in the fallow field.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually an adjective after «lie», «leave» or «be». Fallow deer is a fixed name; the plural is also «deer». Do not confuse with «follow» or «hollow».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A federal country is made of several states or provinces that run some things themselves but share one national government; the USA, Canada, Australia and Germany are federal. 2) Federal means belonging to that national government, as in federal laws, federal taxes or the federal police (the FBI in the USA). 3) (US, informal) «Make a federal case out of it» means make a big fuss about something small.
its sense in the lessons: In social studies it explains how countries are organised: in the USA the federal government is in Washington, while each state has its own government too. In news it shows something is national, not local. Phrases: «federal government», «federal law», «federal holiday», «federal election».
examples from the lessons: The USA has a federal government and fifty state governments. | Australia holds a federal election every few years. | Canada is a federal country with ten provinces. | Stealing mail is a federal crime in the USA. | A federal holiday means government offices are closed. | The federal capital of Australia is Canberra. | The FBI is the Federal Bureau of Investigation. | (US, informal) It was just a spilled drink, don't make a federal case out of it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective only; no plural. Say «FED-er-ul». The UK is not a federal country in the usual sense. A federation is the whole group of states joined together.

part of speech: verb form of ferment (ferment, ferments, fermented, fermenting); adjective (fermenting); noun fermentation
meaning for a pupil: 1) Fermenting is when tiny living things such as yeast or bacteria slowly change sugar into gas, acids or alcohol, as when bread dough rises or milk becomes yogurt. 2) Fermenting food is food that is going through this change on purpose, like sauerkraut or kimchi. 3) Something fermenting can be trouble or anger slowly building up in a group of people.
its sense in the lessons: In science and cooking lessons it explains bubbles in bread, yogurt, cheese and pickles; carbon dioxide gas is made. In stories it can describe bad feelings growing. Phrases: «fermenting dough», «fermenting fruit», «trouble was fermenting».
examples from the lessons: The yeast is fermenting the sugar and making bubbles. | Fermenting cabbage turns into sauerkraut. | The dough rose because the yeast was fermenting. | Old fruit left in the sun starts fermenting and smells sour. | Yogurt is made by bacteria fermenting milk. | We watched a balloon fill with gas from fermenting yeast. | Anger was fermenting in the crowd. | Fermenting foods have a sharp, sour taste.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From the verb ferment, which is regular: fermented, fermenting. Do not confuse with «foment» (to stir up trouble, formal). Fermenting is done by living things; it is not the same as going rotten, though spoiled food can ferment too.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A fiddler is a person who plays the fiddle, which is a violin, especially in folk, country or Irish music. 2) A fiddler crab is a small crab where the male has one huge claw that he waves. 3) (UK, informal) A fiddler is someone who cheats a little, for example by changing numbers on forms to get money.
its sense in the lessons: In music lessons and stories it is a folk musician playing at a dance or ceilidh. In nursery rhymes Old King Cole called for his fiddlers three. Phrases: «a folk fiddler», «fiddler crab», «Fiddler on the Roof».
examples from the lessons: The fiddler played a fast Irish jig. | Old King Cole called for his fiddlers three. | Everyone danced when the fiddler started playing. | The fiddler crab waved its giant claw. | My grandad was a fiddler in a country band. | A fiddler and a piper played at the wedding. | (UK, informal) The boss found out he was a fiddler who changed his work hours. | The street fiddler had a hat for coins.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. A fiddle and a violin are the same instrument; «fiddle» is used for folk music. «Fiddle» also means to play with something nervously («stop fiddling with your pen»), but a «fiddler» usually means the musician.

part of speech: noun (fingerspelling, uncountable); verb fingerspell (fingerspell, fingerspells, fingerspelled/fingerspelt, fingerspelling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Fingerspelling is spelling out words letter by letter with hand shapes, as part of a sign language. 2) It is used for names, places and words that have no sign of their own.
its sense in the lessons: In lessons about deaf people, sign language and inclusion, pupils learn to fingerspell their names. British Sign Language uses two hands for fingerspelling; American Sign Language uses one hand. Phrases: «fingerspell your name», «the fingerspelling alphabet».
examples from the lessons: We learned fingerspelling in assembly. | I can fingerspell my name in British Sign Language. | Fingerspelling is used for names that have no sign. | In American Sign Language, fingerspelling uses one hand. | British fingerspelling uses both hands. | She fingerspelled the word «cat» slowly so I could follow. | A poster of the fingerspelling alphabet hangs in our classroom. | Fingerspelling fast takes lots of practice.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Often written as one word, sometimes «finger spelling». Fingerspelling is only one part of sign language; most words have their own whole signs. Sign languages differ between countries, so BSL and ASL are not the same.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A fissure is a long, narrow crack, especially in rock or the ground. 2) In the body a fissure is a natural groove, such as a fold in the brain, or a small painful crack in the skin. 3) A fissure can also mean a split or disagreement between people in a group.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and science lessons it is a crack where lava comes out of a volcano (a fissure eruption) or where earthquakes split the ground. Phrases: «a fissure in the rock», «volcanic fissure», «fissure eruption».
examples from the lessons: Lava poured out of a long fissure in the ground. | The climber put her hand into a fissure in the rock. | After the earthquake a fissure opened across the road. | In Iceland some volcanoes erupt from fissures. | Water seeped through the fissures in the cave. | The brain has deep fissures and folds. | A fissure grew between the two friends after the argument. | Never go near fissures on a volcano; hot gas can come out.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Say «FISH-er». A fissure is longer and deeper than a little crack. Not to be confused with «fission», the splitting of atoms.

part of speech: noun (a flier, fliers); also spelled flyer
meaning for a pupil: 1) A flier is a person or thing that flies, such as a pilot, a bird or a passenger on planes. 2) A flier is also a sheet of paper advertising something, handed out or put through letterboxes; this is more often spelled flyer. 3) (informal) A fast runner or a very quick start, as in «get off to a flier».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life fliers advertise school fairs, pizza shops and lost pets. In stories about planes it means pilot or traveller. Phrases: «frequent flier», «hand out fliers», «a high flier» (someone very successful), «get off to a flier».
examples from the lessons: We handed out fliers for the school fair. | A flier for a new pizza place came through the door. | My dad is a frequent flier because he travels for work. | The early fliers built planes out of wood and cloth. | Swifts are amazing fliers that hardly ever land. | She is a high flier and got top marks. | Our team got off to a flier and scored in the first minute. | We made a flier about the missing cat.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Both «flier» and «flyer» are correct; «flyer» is more common for the paper and in the UK. Plural fliers or flyers. A «high flier» is a person who succeeds, not a bird.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) Folks means people, especially ordinary people: «Folks round here are friendly». 2) (informal) Your folks are your parents or family: «I'll ask my folks». 3) (informal) Folks is a friendly word to talk to a group: «That's all, folks!» 4) Folk (adjective) describes traditional music, stories and dances of ordinary people, as in folk songs and folk tales.
its sense in the lessons: Used in friendly speech, US and Canadian talk especially, in cartoons, by teachers and presenters addressing a group. Phrases: «my folks», «hi, folks», «old folks», «folk tale», «folk music».
examples from the lessons: Hi, folks, welcome to the show! | I'll ask my folks if I can come to the sleepover. | That's all, folks! | Old folks love it when we sing at the care home. | The folks next door have a new puppy. | Okay, folks, line up quietly. | We read folk tales from Ireland and Ghana. | My grandma's folks came from Scotland.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal; in formal writing use «people» or «parents». «Folk» and «folks» both mean people; «folks» is more common in American English. The l is silent: say «fokes».

part of speech: adjective (fortified); verb form of fortify (fortify, fortifies, fortified, fortifying)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A fortified place has strong walls, towers or other defences to protect it from attack, like a castle or a walled town. 2) Fortified food has extra vitamins or minerals added to make it healthier, like cereal fortified with iron. 3) Fortified wine has strong alcohol added, like port or sherry. 4) To be fortified is to feel stronger or braver, often after food or encouragement.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons it describes castles, forts and city walls; on food labels in science and health lessons it shows added nutrients. Phrases: «a fortified town», «fortified with vitamins», «fortified by a good breakfast».
examples from the lessons: The fortified town had thick stone walls. | Soldiers fortified the hill with ditches and fences. | This cereal is fortified with iron and vitamin D. | Fortified milk has extra vitamins added. | York is an old fortified city. | Fortified by hot soup, the explorers set off again. | The castle was so well fortified that nobody could get in. | Port is a fortified wine, which is only for adults.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Fortify changes y to i: fortifies, fortified. Fortified food is still ordinary food; the label tells you what was added. A fort is a fortified building.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Freshness is being newly made, picked or caught, so food is not old or stale. 2) Freshness is also clean, cool, pleasant air or a smell like clean washing or mint. 3) Freshness can mean newness and originality, like the freshness of a new idea. 4) It can mean feeling lively and rested, not tired.
its sense in the lessons: In cooking, shopping and science lessons it helps judge food (check the date and smell); in adverts it describes soaps and toothpastes. Phrases: «keep freshness», «the freshness of the morning», «sealed for freshness».
examples from the lessons: The bread lost its freshness after two days. | The bag is sealed to keep in the freshness. | I love the freshness of the air after rain. | You can test an egg's freshness by putting it in water. | The freshness of the strawberries made them taste sweet. | Mint gives the toothpaste a feeling of freshness. | The judges liked the freshness of her story. | Morning freshness filled the garden.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «freshness», not «a freshness» usually, and no plural. Made from fresh + ness. Do not confuse with «fresh» in UK slang (cheeky) or US slang (cool).

part of speech: verb (fret, frets, fretted, fretting); noun (a fret, frets)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To fret means to worry and be upset about something, often again and again. 2) A fret is one of the thin metal ridges across the neck of a guitar or similar instrument; you press strings behind them to make different notes. 3) (UK, dialect) A sea fret is a cold mist or fog that comes in from the sea. 4) (old) To fret means to rub or wear something away.
its sense in the lessons: In stories it shows a worried character («don't fret»); in music lessons it is part of a guitar; on the coast of England a sea fret makes the day grey. Phrases: «don't fret», «fret about», «fret over», «sea fret».
examples from the lessons: Don't fret, we'll find your lost shoe. | Mum fretted about the long drive in the snow. | He fretted over his spelling test all evening. | Press the string just behind the third fret. | A guitar has about twenty frets. | A sea fret rolled in and hid the beach. | Stop fretting and go to sleep. | The puppy fretted when we left it alone.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Fret doubles the t: fretted, fretting. «Don't fret» is a kind, informal thing to say. Fret and worry mean nearly the same, but fretting sounds restless and nervous.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Fri is the short form of Friday, the day after Thursday and before Saturday. 2) It is used in calendars, timetables, shop opening hours and diaries where there is little space.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life it appears on school timetables, bus times and calendars, such as «Mon–Fri» meaning Monday to Friday, the school or work week. Phrases: «Mon–Fri», «Fri night», «open Mon to Fri».
examples from the lessons: The shop is open Mon–Fri. | Swimming club is on Fri after school. | Our timetable says Fri: PE and art. | See you Fri! | The library is closed on Fri afternoon. | The bus runs every hour Mon–Fri. | Fri is spelling test day. | Write «Fri» in the box for Friday.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually written with a capital F and sometimes a full stop: Fri or Fri. Read it aloud as «Friday», not «fry». Not a word by itself. Other day short forms: Mon, Tue, Wed, Thu, Sat, Sun.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A galleon was a large sailing ship with several masts and decks, used long ago by Spain, England and other countries for war and trade. 2) Galleons carried gold, silver and goods across the oceans, so pirates often attacked them.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons about explorers, the Spanish Armada and pirates; in stories about treasure and sea battles. Phrases: «a Spanish galleon», «treasure galleon», «a sunken galleon».
examples from the lessons: The Spanish galleon was full of gold and silver. | Pirates chased the slow galleon across the sea. | A galleon had tall masts and many sails. | Divers found the wreck of a sunken galleon. | We built a model galleon out of cardboard. | Galleons had cannons on their lower decks. | The galleon sailed from Mexico to Spain. | In the story, the treasure was hidden on a galleon.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Say «GAL-ee-un». Do not confuse with «gallon», a measure of liquid; the extra e makes it a ship. Galleons belong to the age of sail, centuries ago.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Gamma is the third letter of the Greek alphabet, written γ (small) and Γ (capital), after alpha and beta. 2) (science) Gamma rays are very powerful, invisible rays given off by radioactive materials and by explosions in space; they can harm living things. 3) Gamma is used as a label for the third thing in a list, after alpha and beta.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and science it can stand for an angle or a value; in science lessons about light and radiation gamma rays come at the high-energy end of the electromagnetic spectrum. Phrases: «gamma rays», «alpha, beta and gamma».
examples from the lessons: Gamma is the third letter of the Greek alphabet. | Alpha, beta, gamma, delta. | Gamma rays are stronger than X-rays. | Hospitals use gamma rays to kill germs on equipment. | In the comic, the hero was hit by gamma rays. | We labelled the third angle gamma. | Thick lead blocks stop gamma rays. | Gamma rays come from exploding stars.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say «GAM-uh». The word «alphabet» comes from alpha and beta. Comic stories about gamma rays giving superpowers are fiction; real gamma rays are dangerous.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (a name) Gaul was the old name for a large area of western Europe in Roman times, mostly where France and Belgium are today. 2) A Gaul was a person from Gaul, one of the Celtic peoples who lived there.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons about the Romans: Julius Caesar conquered Gaul. Children know it from the Asterix comics about a little Gaulish village. Phrases: «Roman Gaul», «the Gauls», «Gaulish».
examples from the lessons: Julius Caesar conquered Gaul. | The Gauls were Celtic people. | In the Asterix stories, one village of Gauls holds out against Rome. | Gaul was divided into three parts, Caesar wrote. | France was once part of Gaul. | The Gauls fought bravely against the Roman army. | We drew a map of Roman Gaul. | A Gaulish warrior wore a helmet and a cloak.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always written with a capital G. Sounds like «gall» and «Gaul» in some accents. Adjective: Gaulish or Gallic. Not the same as «goal».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A Glaswegian is a person who comes from Glasgow, the biggest city in Scotland. 2) Glaswegian means belonging to Glasgow, such as its people, buildings or way of speaking. 3) Glaswegian is also the strong local accent and dialect of Glasgow, with words like «wean» (child) and «messages» (shopping).
its sense in the lessons: In geography and in lessons about accents and dialects it shows how English sounds in different places. In stories it tells the reader where a character comes from. Phrases: «a Glaswegian accent», «a proud Glaswegian».
examples from the lessons: My uncle is a Glaswegian. | She speaks with a strong Glaswegian accent. | Glaswegian people are known for being friendly and funny. | «Wean» is a Glaswegian word for a child. | The Glaswegian comedian made everyone laugh. | We listened to a Glaswegian storyteller. | A Glaswegian might say «Gonnae no dae that» for «Please don't do that». | Lots of famous bands are Glaswegian.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always capital G. Say «glaz-WEE-jun». Glaswegian is a dialect of Scots and English, not a separate language; it is not wrong, just local.

part of speech: verb form of gloat (gloat, gloats, gloated, gloating); noun (gloating, uncountable); adjective (gloating)
