meaning for a pupil: 1) Gloating is showing that you are pleased about your own success or about someone else's bad luck, in a smug, unkind way. 2) A gloating look or voice shows this nasty pleasure.
its sense in the lessons: In stories villains gloat when they think they have won; in PE and games lessons pupils learn that gloating is bad sportsmanship. Phrases: «gloat over», «gloat about», «stop gloating», «no gloating».
examples from the lessons: Stop gloating, it was only a game. | The villain was gloating over his stolen treasure. | Good winners don't go round gloating. | He gave a gloating smile when I lost. | She was gloating about her new phone all day. | Gloating makes the other team feel worse. | The fox sat gloating at the trapped hen. | Our coach says: win nicely, no gloating.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: gloat, gloated, gloating. Gloating is different from being proud: pride can be quiet and kind, gloating rubs it in. Usually followed by «over» or «about».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A glowworm is a kind of beetle whose females, which look like soft grubs without wings, give off a green light from their tails at night. 2) In New Zealand and Australia, glowworms are the tiny larvae of a gnat that hang in caves and glow blue, like stars.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about animals that make light (bioluminescence) and in night-time stories. Waitomo caves in New Zealand are famous for them. Phrases: «glowworm caves», «glowing like a glowworm».
examples from the lessons: The glowworm shone in the grass at night. | In New Zealand we saw glowworms in a cave. | Glowworms make light inside their bodies. | The cave roof looked like a sky full of stars because of the glowworms. | Female glowworms glow to attract males. | We walked quietly so we didn't disturb the glowworms. | A glowworm is not really a worm. | Fireflies and glowworms are related beetles.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word or with a hyphen: glowworm, glow-worm. Trap: a glowworm is not a worm but an insect larva or beetle. Their light makes almost no heat.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Glucose is a kind of sugar that your body uses for energy; your blood carries it to all your cells. 2) Plants make glucose from sunlight, water and carbon dioxide. 3) Glucose is also sold as sweets, drinks or tablets, used by athletes and by people with diabetes when their blood sugar is low.
its sense in the lessons: A science word in lessons about food, digestion, plants (photosynthesis) and health. People with diabetes check their «blood glucose». Phrases: «blood glucose», «glucose tablets», «glucose level».
examples from the lessons: Your body turns food into glucose for energy. | Plants make glucose in their leaves. | My friend has diabetes and checks his glucose level. | The runner ate glucose tablets during the race. | Glucose travels round the body in your blood. | Bread and pasta are broken down into glucose. | Too much sugar can raise your blood glucose. | We tested the drink for glucose in science.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Say «GLOO-kose». Glucose is one type of sugar; table sugar (sucrose) is another. Not every sweet thing is glucose.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Gory means full of blood and violence, often in a film, game or story. 2) (informal) The gory details are the unpleasant or embarrassing details of something, told fully: «Tell me all the gory details!»
its sense in the lessons: Used about horror stories, history lessons about battles and Horrible Histories, and film age ratings. In everyday chat «the gory details» is a joke way to ask for every bit of a story. Phrases: «gory details», «a gory film».
examples from the lessons: That film is too gory for children. | The history book had a gory picture of a battle. | I covered my eyes at the gory part. | Tell me all the gory details of your camping trip! | My brother loves gory zombie stories. | The age rating warns that the game is gory. | Horrible Histories tells the gory side of the past. | The fox left a gory mess in the chicken run.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative gorier, superlative goriest. Gore means blood from a wound. Do not confuse with «gaudy» or with «Gorey», a place name.

part of speech: verb form of graft (graft, grafts, grafted, grafting); noun (grafting, uncountable)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Grafting is joining a piece cut from one plant onto another plant so that they grow together, as gardeners do with apple trees. 2) (medicine) Grafting is moving healthy skin or other tissue from one part of the body to another to repair it, for example after a bad burn. 3) (UK, informal) Grafting means working very hard, especially at tiring work: «He's been grafting all day». 4) (US) Graft is also using power dishonestly to get money, a kind of corruption.
its sense in the lessons: In science and gardening lessons it explains how fruit trees are grown; in health lessons it explains skin grafts. In British everyday talk a «grafter» is a hard worker. Phrases: «skin grafting», «grafting a tree», «hard graft».
examples from the lessons: The gardener is grafting a branch onto the apple tree. | Grafting lets one tree grow two kinds of apples. | After the fire she needed skin grafting on her arm. | (UK) Dad's been grafting on the building site all week. | (UK) Our team won because everyone was grafting. | (UK) Learning to play the piano takes hard graft. | (US) The mayor was accused of graft. | We tried grafting cactus plants in science club.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Graft is regular: grafted, grafting. In the UK, «graft» as hard work is informal and a compliment; in the US, «graft» as corruption is very negative. A «grafter» (UK) is a hard worker.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Gravitation is the force by which everything with mass pulls on everything else; it keeps us on the ground and the Moon going round the Earth. 2) (formal) Gravitation can mean moving towards something or being drawn to it, like a gravitation of people towards cities.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons it is the scientific name for gravity; Isaac Newton described the law of gravitation. Phrases: «the law of gravitation», «universal gravitation», «gravitational pull».
examples from the lessons: Gravitation keeps the planets moving round the Sun. | Newton wrote about the law of gravitation. | Gravitation pulls the apple down to the ground. | The Moon's gravitation causes the tides. | Everything has gravitation, even you and me, but it is tiny. | Bigger objects have stronger gravitation. | There was a gravitation of families towards the new park. | Astronauts float because they are falling around the Earth, not because gravitation stops.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Gravitation and gravity mean almost the same; «gravity» is the everyday word. Myth: there is gravity in space; astronauts float because they are in free fall.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Gritty means full of tiny hard bits like sand or small stones. 2) A gritty person is brave and determined and does not give up when things are hard. 3) A gritty story or film shows life in a hard, realistic way, including poverty, crime or difficult times.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons it describes textures of soils and rocks; in PE and life lessons «grit» means perseverance. Phrases: «gritty sand», «a gritty performance», «a gritty drama», «true grit».
examples from the lessons: The spinach was gritty because it wasn't washed. | The path was gritty with sand. | The team gave a gritty performance and won in the end. | She is gritty and never gives up. | The film is a gritty story about life in a poor town. | My shoes felt gritty after the beach. | Gritty determination helped him finish the race. | Rub the gritty paper on the wood to make it smooth.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative grittier, superlative grittiest. Grit also means sand put on icy roads in the UK (a gritter lorry spreads it). «Grit your teeth» means hold on through something hard.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A groundhog is a North American animal, a large brown rodent that lives in burrows and sleeps through the winter; it is also called a woodchuck. 2) Groundhog Day is a custom in the USA and Canada where people watch a groundhog come out of its burrow: if it sees its shadow, there will be six more weeks of winter. 3) (informal) «Groundhog Day» means a situation that keeps repeating in the same boring way, from a famous film.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about hibernation and in American and Canadian culture. The weather custom is folklore, not science. Phrases: «Groundhog Day», «like Groundhog Day».
examples from the lessons: The groundhog dug a burrow under the shed. | Groundhogs hibernate all winter. | On Groundhog Day everyone waits to see the groundhog's shadow. | The groundhog saw its shadow, so the story says winter will last longer. | A groundhog is also called a woodchuck. | How much wood would a woodchuck chuck? | Every day at the bus stop is like Groundhog Day. | Groundhogs eat plants and can whistle when scared.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Myth: groundhogs cannot really predict the weather; the custom is for fun. Groundhog and woodchuck are the same animal.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A grower is a person or company that grows plants, fruit or vegetables to sell, such as a fruit grower or a flower grower. 2) A grower is a plant that grows in a certain way: «a fast grower», «a slow grower». 3) (informal) Something that is «a grower» is a song, show or thing you do not like at first but come to like more and more.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and farming lessons growers produce food; in gardening it describes how plants grow. In everyday talk about music: «That song's a grower». Phrases: «fruit grower», «a fast grower», «tomato grower».
examples from the lessons: My uncle is a strawberry grower. | Coffee growers in Kenya pick the berries by hand. | Bamboo is a very fast grower. | The grower sells his apples at the market. | Oak trees are slow growers. | I didn't like the song at first, but it's a grower. | Flower growers in the Netherlands grow millions of tulips. | We visited a tomato grower's greenhouse.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Made from grow + er, like «farmer». Grow is irregular (grow, grew, grown), but grower is simply «someone who grows».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Guano is the droppings of seabirds or bats, which pile up in huge amounts on rocks and in caves. 2) Guano is used as a strong fertiliser to help plants grow because it is full of nitrogen and phosphorus.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and history lessons it explains why some islands near Peru were once very valuable; in science lessons it shows how nutrients cycle in nature. Phrases: «bat guano», «bird guano», «guano islands».
examples from the lessons: Guano is bird or bat poo. | The rocks were white with seabird guano. | Farmers used guano to help crops grow. | The bat cave floor was covered in guano. | Islands near Peru were mined for guano long ago. | Guano is full of nutrients for plants. | Wear a mask in bat caves because guano dust can make you ill. | Penguins make burrows in old guano.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Say «GWAH-no». The word comes from Spanish, which took it from the Quechua language of Peru. Safety: guano dust can carry germs, so do not touch or breathe it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A hallucination is seeing, hearing, feeling or smelling something that is not really there, as if it were real. 2) It can be caused by high fever, some illnesses, lack of sleep, some medicines or drugs. 3) (computers) An AI hallucination is when a computer program confidently says something false or made up.
its sense in the lessons: In health lessons it explains why very ill or very tired people may see strange things; in computing lessons it is a warning that AI answers must be checked. Phrases: «have hallucinations», «see a hallucination», «AI hallucination».
examples from the lessons: With a high fever, he had hallucinations of spiders on the wall. | A hallucination feels real to the person having it. | Lack of sleep can cause hallucinations. | The explorer in the desert saw a hallucination of a lake. | Some drugs cause dangerous hallucinations. | The chatbot gave a hallucination: it invented a book that does not exist. | Always check facts, because AI can produce hallucinations. | The doctor asked if she had any hallucinations.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Say «huh-loo-sih-NAY-shun». A mirage (a fake lake on a hot road) is different: it is a real trick of light that cameras can photograph, while a hallucination is only in the mind. Hallucinations are a health matter; tell an adult.

part of speech: adjective (handsome, handsomer, handsomest; also more handsome, most handsome); adverb handsomely
meaning for a pupil: 1) Handsome means good-looking, usually said about a man or boy. 2) A handsome animal, building or object is fine and attractive to look at, like a handsome horse or a handsome old house. 3) A handsome amount is large and generous, like a handsome reward or a handsome win.
its sense in the lessons: In fairy tales the handsome prince is a common character; in everyday life it is a compliment. In news and sport «a handsome win» means winning by a lot. Phrases: «tall, dark and handsome», «a handsome reward», «a handsome profit».
examples from the lessons: The handsome prince rode a white horse. | Grandpa looks very handsome in his suit. | What a handsome dog! | They offered a handsome reward for the lost cat. | The team won by a handsome margin of five goals. | It is a handsome old building made of stone. | She made a handsome profit selling lemonade. | Handsome is as handsome does, says the old proverb.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Silent d: say «HAN-sum». For women and girls people usually say «beautiful» or «pretty», though «handsome woman» exists too. The proverb «handsome is as handsome does» means good actions matter more than looks.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Heartburn is a burning, painful feeling in the chest or throat, caused when acid from the stomach comes back up. 2) It often happens after eating too much, eating spicy or fatty food, or lying down right after a meal.
its sense in the lessons: In health lessons it explains digestion: the problem is in the food pipe, not the heart. Adverts for indigestion tablets mention it. Phrases: «get heartburn», «suffer from heartburn», «heartburn tablets».
examples from the lessons: Dad got heartburn after the spicy curry. | Heartburn has nothing to do with your heart. | Don't lie down straight after a big meal or you may get heartburn. | Grandma takes a tablet for her heartburn. | Heartburn feels like burning behind your chest bone. | Eating slowly can help stop heartburn. | The acid in your stomach causes heartburn. | Pregnant women often get heartburn.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «I have heartburn», not «a heartburn». Trap: despite the name, heartburn does not come from the heart. Chest pain in an adult can be serious, so always tell a grown-up.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (church) Heavenly means belonging to heaven or to God, as in «heavenly Father» or «the heavenly host» of angels. 2) Heavenly means about the sky and space, as in «heavenly bodies» for the Sun, Moon, planets and stars. 3) (informal) Heavenly means wonderful and very pleasant: «This chocolate cake is heavenly!»
its sense in the lessons: In religion lessons and church songs it describes God and heaven; in science, «heavenly bodies» are objects in space; in everyday talk it is strong praise for food, smells or weather. Phrases: «heavenly Father», «heavenly bodies», «absolutely heavenly».
examples from the lessons: Christians pray to their heavenly Father. | The angels sang a heavenly song in the Christmas story. | Stars and planets are heavenly bodies. | This hot bath is heavenly! | The bakery smelled heavenly. | The choir sounded heavenly. | Mum said the cake was absolutely heavenly. | Ancient people studied the movements of heavenly bodies.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Ends in -ly but is an adjective, not an adverb. Heaven is spelled with ea. Christians believe heaven is where God is and where people go to be with God after death.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A herder is a person who looks after a group of animals, such as cattle, sheep, goats or reindeer, moving them to fresh grass and keeping them safe. 2) It is also part of names like «cattle herder» or «reindeer herder».
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons about how people live in mountains, deserts and the Arctic; in Bible stories, shepherds are herders of sheep. Phrases: «goat herder», «reindeer herder», «a nomadic herder».
examples from the lessons: The herder led his goats up the mountain. | Reindeer herders in Lapland follow their animals across the snow. | A shepherd is a herder of sheep. | The cattle herder used a dog to help him. | Herders in Mongolia live in round tents called gers. | The herder counted his sheep at sunset. | In dry years herders must walk far to find water. | Our story was about a young yak herder.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. A herd is the group of animals; a herder is the person. Similar words: shepherd (sheep), cowboy or stockman (cattle), drover (Australia).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Hooray is a word you shout when you are very happy or excited, or to cheer for someone. 2) (UK, informal) A «Hooray Henry» is a loud, rich young man who shows off, said in a mocking way.
its sense in the lessons: Used in stories, birthday parties, sports and celebrations. «Hip hip hooray!» is a group cheer. Phrases: «hip hip hooray», «shout hooray», «hooray for …».
examples from the lessons: Hooray, it's snowing! | Hip hip hooray! | Hooray for the winning team! | We shouted hooray when the bell rang for the holidays. | Hooray, I found my lost key! | The crowd cheered hooray as the runners finished. | Hooray, no homework tonight! | (UK, informal) A bunch of Hooray Henrys were shouting outside.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Hooray, hurray and hurrah all mean the same. Usually followed by an exclamation mark. It is not used in formal writing except in quoted speech.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A horsefly is a large fly whose females bite people and animals and drink their blood. 2) Its bite is painful and can swell and itch.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about insects and in summer safety talks near farms, rivers and woods. Phrases: «a horsefly bite», «bitten by a horsefly».
examples from the lessons: A horsefly bit me by the river. | Horsefly bites really hurt. | Only female horseflies bite. | The horse swished its tail to keep the horseflies away. | Horseflies have huge, colourful eyes. | Put a cold cloth on a horsefly bite. | We saw a big horsefly buzzing round the picnic. | Horseflies like warm, damp summer days.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural horseflies (y to ies). Also written horse-fly or horse fly. Tell an adult if a bite gets very swollen, hot or red, since it can get infected. In Australia a similar insect is called a march fly.

part of speech: noun (humiliation, uncountable; a humiliation, humiliations); verb humiliate; adjective humiliating
meaning for a pupil: 1) Humiliation is the very bad, hot feeling of shame you get when someone makes you look stupid or weak in front of others. 2) A humiliation is an event that makes someone feel like this, such as losing badly in public.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, bullying lessons and PSHE it names a strong painful feeling; teachers explain that laughing at others' mistakes causes humiliation. In sport news a «humiliation» is a heavy defeat. Phrases: «feel humiliation», «public humiliation», «a humiliating defeat».
examples from the lessons: Bullies sometimes try to cause humiliation. | She felt the humiliation of falling over on stage. | Losing ten–nil was a humiliation for the team. | Never laugh at someone to cause them humiliation. | His face went red with humiliation. | Public humiliation can hurt as much as a punch. | The story is about a girl who overcomes humiliation and becomes brave. | Being kind after a mistake helps someone recover from humiliation.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say «hyoo-mil-ee-AY-shun». Humiliation is stronger than embarrassment. Not the same as «humility», which is a good quality of not boasting.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Ideally means in the best possible way or the way you would most like, if everything were perfect: «Ideally, I'd like a puppy». 2) Ideally means perfectly or exactly right for something: «The house is ideally placed near the school».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday speech it introduces a wish that may not happen. In maths and science it can mean «in a perfect model», ignoring small real-world problems. Phrases: «ideally suited», «ideally located», «ideally, we would…».
examples from the lessons: Ideally, we should go to bed by nine. | Ideally, you'd water the plants every day. | The cottage is ideally placed near the beach. | She is ideally suited to be team captain. | Ideally, a recipe should be easy to follow. | Ideally the experiment would be repeated three times. | We'd ideally like sunny weather for sports day. | Ideally, wash your hands for twenty seconds.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelled with two l's: ideal + ly. Often starts a sentence and is followed by a comma. It shows a hope or best case, not a fact.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Impartial means fair to everyone and not taking sides, so you do not favour one person or team. 2) (law) An impartial judge or jury decides only on the facts, without friendship or dislike affecting the decision.
its sense in the lessons: In citizenship lessons it describes referees, judges and the news, which should report both sides. Phrases: «an impartial referee», «impartial advice», «stay impartial».
examples from the lessons: A referee must be impartial. | The judge listened to both sides and stayed impartial. | We need someone impartial to decide who won. | The teacher was impartial and gave everyone a turn. | News should give impartial reports. | It's hard to be impartial when your best friend is playing. | (law) Every person has the right to an impartial trial. | Mum stayed impartial when my sister and I argued.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Im + partial: «partial» can mean favouring one side, so «impartial» means not favouring. Trap: «partial» also means «not complete», but «impartial» never means «complete». Same as «unbiased».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Inborn means present in a person or animal from birth, not learned later, like an inborn talent or an inborn fear. 2) (medicine) An inborn condition is one a baby is born with.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons it describes natural instincts and traits; in stories and talk about talent it suggests a gift. Phrases: «an inborn talent», «an inborn ability», «inborn instinct».
examples from the lessons: She has an inborn talent for music. | Babies have an inborn ability to suck. | Some people think kindness is inborn, but it can be learned too. | Ducklings have an inborn instinct to follow their mother. | His love of animals seemed inborn. | Fear of loud noises is inborn in babies. | Practice can beat inborn talent. | The doctor said the heart problem was inborn.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Used before a noun: an inborn talent. Means about the same as «innate» or «natural». Not «inborned». A skill can start inborn and still need practice to grow.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Incredibly means extremely or very, very: «It was incredibly cold». 2) Incredibly can mean in a way that is hard to believe: «Incredibly, the cat survived the fall».
its sense in the lessons: Very common in everyday speech, stories and TV to make a describing word stronger. Phrases: «incredibly hard», «incredibly lucky», «incredibly, …».
examples from the lessons: The test was incredibly hard. | She is incredibly good at chess. | It was incredibly hot at the beach. | Incredibly, the little team won the cup. | That roller coaster is incredibly fast. | We were incredibly lucky with the weather. | The puppy is incredibly cute. | Incredibly, nobody was hurt in the storm.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelled with -ibly: incredible becomes incredibly. Often overused in speech; in writing try other words like «extremely», «remarkably». At the start of a sentence it means «hard to believe».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Indestructible means impossible to break or destroy. 2) (informal) Indestructible can mean very strong and long-lasting, even if not truly unbreakable, like an indestructible old phone.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and superhero comics it describes heroes, armour and magic objects; in everyday life it praises tough toys and tools. Phrases: «almost indestructible», «seemingly indestructible».
examples from the lessons: The superhero's shield was indestructible. | My old phone seems indestructible; I've dropped it a hundred times. | These toys are almost indestructible. | Plastic is nearly indestructible, which is why it pollutes the sea. | Diamonds are very hard, but not indestructible. | The castle walls seemed indestructible. | Our friendship felt indestructible. | Tardigrades are tiny animals that are nearly indestructible.
note for the reader of a maths problem: In + destructible: «destructible» means can be destroyed. Ends in -ible, not -able. Real objects are rarely truly indestructible; people often exaggerate.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) If something is indicative of something else, it shows or suggests it: «A high temperature is indicative of an infection». 2) (grammar) The indicative is the ordinary form of a verb used for facts and questions, like «She runs» or «Did it rain?», as opposed to commands or wishes.
its sense in the lessons: In formal writing, exam questions and science reports it means «a sign of». In grammar and foreign-language lessons (French, Spanish) it names a verb mood. Phrases: «indicative of», «the indicative mood», «present indicative».
examples from the lessons: Dark clouds are often indicative of rain. | (formal) His smile was indicative of his good mood. | Yellow leaves can be indicative of a thirsty plant. | (formal) The results are indicative of a pattern. | In French we learned the present indicative. | «I walk» is in the indicative mood. | The indicative is used to state facts. | Missing homework is indicative of a busy week, the teacher joked.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say «in-DIK-uh-tiv». Usually followed by «of». Formal word; in speech use «a sign of». In the UK, a car's «indicator» flashes to show which way it will turn.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Indispensable means so important or useful that you cannot manage without it. 2) An indispensable person is someone a team or group really needs.
its sense in the lessons: In formal writing, adverts and everyday talk it shows that something is necessary. Phrases: «indispensable to», «indispensable for», «an indispensable tool».
examples from the lessons: Water is indispensable to life. | A map is indispensable on a long walk. | Our goalkeeper is indispensable to the team. | Glasses are indispensable for reading if you need them. | A good dictionary is indispensable for learning a language. | The nurse was indispensable during the emergency. | Sunscreen is indispensable on a sunny beach. | Teamwork is indispensable for winning.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Ends in -able, not -ible. In + dispensable: «dispensable» means you can do without it. Similar to «essential»; the opposite is «unnecessary».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Infrared is a kind of light that our eyes cannot see, just beyond red light; we feel it as heat. 2) Infrared things use or show this light, like infrared cameras that see warm bodies in the dark, or TV remote controls.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on light, heat and the electromagnetic spectrum; in everyday life remote controls, motion sensors and thermal cameras use it. Phrases: «infrared light», «infrared camera», «infrared sensor».
examples from the lessons: Your TV remote sends infrared light. | Infrared cameras can see animals at night by their warmth. | We can't see infrared, but we can feel it as heat. | Snakes called pit vipers can sense infrared. | The burglar alarm uses an infrared sensor. | The Sun gives off infrared as well as visible light. | Infrared photos show warm things as bright colours. | Firefighters use infrared cameras to find people in smoke.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Sometimes written infra-red. «Infra» means below: its energy is below red light. Ultraviolet is on the other side, beyond violet. Infrared is not dangerous like ultraviolet in ordinary amounts.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Ingenuity is being clever and inventive, so you find new and smart ways to solve problems. 2) (a name) Ingenuity was also the name of a small helicopter flown on Mars.
its sense in the lessons: In science, design and technology lessons it praises clever solutions; in stories it shows a resourceful hero. Phrases: «human ingenuity», «show ingenuity», «use your ingenuity».
examples from the lessons: The team showed great ingenuity in building a bridge out of paper. | With a bit of ingenuity, we fixed the bike with string. | Robinson Crusoe survived by ingenuity. | Engineers use ingenuity to solve problems. | Human ingenuity put people on the Moon. | Her ingenuity amazed the judges. | The Ingenuity helicopter flew on Mars. | Use your ingenuity to escape the puzzle room.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Say «in-juh-NYOO-ih-tee». Trap: ingenuity goes with «ingenious» (clever), not with «ingenuous» (innocent and trusting).

part of speech: verb form of intensify (intensify, intensifies, intensified, intensifying); adjective (intensified)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Intensified means became stronger, bigger or more extreme: «The storm intensified overnight». 2) Intensified means made stronger on purpose: «The police intensified their search».
its sense in the lessons: In weather reports, geography lessons about storms, and news about searches, efforts or conflicts. Phrases: «the storm intensified», «intensified efforts», «the fighting intensified».
examples from the lessons: The rain intensified and we ran inside. | The hurricane intensified over the warm sea. | The search for the missing dog intensified. | The smell intensified as we got closer to the bin. | The team intensified their training before the final. | As the music intensified, everyone started dancing. | The heat intensified during the afternoon. | Worry intensified when the bus was late.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Intensify changes y to i: intensifies, intensified. Similar to «increased» or «got stronger». In English grammar, an «intensifier» is a word like «very» or «really».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Intensive means using a lot of effort or work in a short time: «an intensive course». 2) (medicine) Intensive care is a part of a hospital for very ill people who need constant care and special machines. 3) Intensive farming uses lots of machines, chemicals or animals in a small space to produce more food.
its sense in the lessons: In health lessons and news «intensive care» (ICU) is a serious hospital ward. In geography lessons intensive farming is compared with extensive farming. Phrases: «intensive care», «intensive course», «intensive farming».
examples from the lessons: She took an intensive swimming course in the holidays. | Grandpa was in intensive care after his operation. | Intensive farming produces lots of food from small fields. | The team had an intensive week of training. | Doctors in intensive care watch patients day and night. | Learning French in two weeks was intensive. | Intensive chicken farms keep many birds indoors. | The search was intensive but quick.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Do not confuse with «intense», which means very strong or extreme (intense heat). «Intensive» describes lots of concentrated work. Intensive care is also called ICU or ITU (UK).

part of speech: verb (interact, interacts, interacted, interacting); noun interaction; adjective interactive
meaning for a pupil: 1) To interact means to talk, play or work with other people and respond to them. 2) In science, things interact when they affect each other, like chemicals reacting or animals in a food web. 3) To interact with a computer, game or display means to use it by clicking, touching or speaking.
its sense in the lessons: In PSHE, people interact with friends; in science, living things interact in ecosystems; in computing, users interact with apps. Phrases: «interact with», «interact online», «interactive whiteboard».
examples from the lessons: Our puppy loves to interact with other dogs. | The new pupil was shy but soon began to interact with the class. | Plants and animals interact in a habitat. | Some medicines interact with each other badly. | You can interact with the museum displays by pressing buttons. | We interact online, but be careful who you talk to. | Bees and flowers interact: bees get food, flowers get pollen moved. | The game lets players interact with characters.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Usually followed by «with». An interactive whiteboard lets you touch the screen. Safety: only interact online with people you know in real life.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An isogram is a word in which no letter appears more than once, such as «dog», «planet» or «uncopyrightable». 2) (geography) An isogram is also a line on a map joining places that have the same value, such as the same temperature or height; isotherms and contour lines are kinds of isograms.
its sense in the lessons: In word puzzles, spelling games and olympiad problems pupils check whether a word repeats a letter; in geography it names lines on weather and height maps. Phrases: «is it an isogram?», «the longest isogram».
examples from the lessons: «Lamp» is an isogram because no letter repeats. | «Letter» is not an isogram, because it has two t's and two e's. | Can you find a ten-letter isogram? | «Background» is an isogram. | We played a game to write the longest isogram. | On the weather map, an isogram joined places with the same temperature. | Contour lines are a kind of isogram. | «Isogram» itself is an isogram!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Say «EYE-so-gram». «Iso» means equal and «gram» means something written or drawn. Check carefully: capital letters count the same as small ones.

part of speech: verb (joust, jousts, jousted, jousting); noun (a joust, jousts)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To joust was to fight on horseback with long wooden poles called lances, as knights did in the Middle Ages, often as a sport at tournaments. 2) A joust is one such contest between two knights. 3) To joust can also mean to argue or compete, as people do in a debate.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons about castles, knights and the Middle Ages, and in stories and fairs where jousting is shown. In news, politicians «joust» in debates. Phrases: «a jousting tournament», «joust with», «verbal jousting».
examples from the lessons: The knights jousted in front of the king. | Each knight tried to knock the other off his horse in the joust. | We watched a jousting show at the castle. | Jousting was a dangerous sport. | The knight's lance broke during the joust. | The two candidates jousted on television. | In the story, the young squire won his first joust. | Jousting knights wore heavy armour.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Say «jowst» (rhymes with «doused») or «just». A tournament was a big event with many jousts.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Jr is short for «Junior», added after a man's name when he has the same name as his father, such as Martin Luther King Jr. 2) It can also mean junior in other short forms, such as on sports teams or school forms, meaning younger or lower level.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons it appears in names like Martin Luther King Jr.; in American families it shows a son is named after his father. Phrases: «Sr. and Jr.», «John Smith Jr.».
examples from the lessons: Martin Luther King Jr. was a great leader. | Mr Smith Jr. is the son of Mr Smith Sr. | His name is Robert Brown Jr., named after his dad. | We read a speech by Martin Luther King Jr. | Jr is short for Junior. | The jr team plays on Saturday mornings. | On the form, write Jr after your name if you have one. | Sammy Davis Jr. was a famous singer.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually written with a capital J, with or without a full stop: Jr or Jr. Read aloud as «Junior». It is common in the USA, less so in the UK. The opposite is Sr (Senior). Not a word by itself.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Karaoke is singing along to recorded music while the words of the song appear on a screen, for fun. 2) A karaoke machine or karaoke night is the equipment or event for this.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life it is a fun party, birthday or holiday activity; in music lessons it helps practise singing. It comes from Japan. Phrases: «sing karaoke», «karaoke night», «karaoke machine».
examples from the lessons: We sang karaoke at my birthday party. | Grandma loves karaoke nights. | The karaoke machine shows the words on the TV. | My dad sang a funny song at karaoke. | Karaoke comes from Japan. | Let's do karaoke after dinner! | She was shy, but she sang at karaoke anyway. | The words turned yellow on the karaoke screen as we sang.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «karaoke», not «a karaoke» (but «a karaoke night»). English speakers say «karry-OH-kee»; in Japanese it is «kah-rah-oh-keh» and means «empty orchestra».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A Kenyan is a person who comes from Kenya, a country in East Africa. 2) Kenyan means belonging to Kenya or its people, such as Kenyan food, Kenyan runners or Kenyan wildlife.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons about Africa and in sport: Kenyan runners often win long-distance races. Kenya has safari parks, Mount Kenya and the Great Rift Valley; its capital is Nairobi. Phrases: «a Kenyan runner», «Kenyan tea».
examples from the lessons: A Kenyan runner won the marathon. | Our class has a pen pal who is Kenyan. | Kenyan tea is grown in the highlands. | Many Kenyans speak Swahili and English. | We read a Kenyan folk tale about a clever hare. | Kenyan safari parks have lions, elephants and giraffes. | The Kenyan flag is black, red and green with white lines and a shield. | My uncle visited a Kenyan school.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always capital K. Say «KEN-yun». Kenya's main languages are Swahili and English. Not all Kenyans are runners; it is one famous strength.

part of speech: noun (a killing, killings); verb form of kill (kill, kills, killed, killing); adjective (killing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Killing is causing someone or something to die. 2) A killing is a murder or a death caused on purpose, as reported in the news. 3) (informal) To make a killing means to make a lot of money quickly. 4) (slang) «You're killing me!» means «You're so funny» or «You're annoying me»; «My feet are killing me» means they hurt a lot.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons it is used for germs (soap is killing bacteria) and food chains; in news it is a serious crime word. In everyday slang it is about laughter, pain or money. Phrases: «make a killing», «killing time», «killing me».
examples from the lessons: The lion is killing a zebra for food. | Soap helps by killing germs. | The police are investigating a killing. | Killing animals for fun is cruel. | They made a killing selling ice creams on the hot day. | We were killing time before the film started. | (slang) Stop, you're killing me! That joke is so funny. | (informal) These new shoes are killing my feet.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Kill is regular: killed, killing. «Killing time» means doing something just to fill time while waiting. Serious killing words are not for jokes about real people.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A landline is a telephone connected by a wire to the phone network, usually fixed in a house or office, not a mobile phone. 2) It also means the phone number of that fixed phone.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and safety lessons children learn their home number; many homes now have only mobiles. Phrases: «call the landline», «landline number», «on the landline».
examples from the lessons: Grandma still has a landline in her hall. | Call me on the landline if my mobile is off. | We don't have a landline any more. | Learn your home landline number in case of an emergency. | The landline rang during dinner. | A landline works even when the mobile signal is weak. | Our school office has several landlines. | The landline number starts with the area code.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. One word: landline. The opposite is a mobile (UK) or cell phone (US). In an emergency you can call 999 (UK, Ireland), 911 (USA, Canada), 000 (Australia) or 111 (New Zealand) from any phone.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A lanternfish is a small deep-sea fish with spots on its body that glow with light. 2) Lanternfish are among the most common fish in the world; they swim up near the surface at night to feed and go deep down in the day.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about the deep ocean, food chains and animals that make light (bioluminescence). Phrases: «glowing lanternfish», «deep-sea lanternfish».
examples from the lessons: The lanternfish has glowing spots along its body. | Lanternfish live deep in the ocean. | At night, lanternfish swim up to eat tiny animals. | Whales and seabirds eat lanternfish. | There may be more lanternfish than any other kind of fish. | We saw a lanternfish in a deep-sea documentary. | The glowing spots help lanternfish recognise each other. | A lanternfish is only about as long as your finger.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural lanternfish or lanternfishes. Their light is made by chemicals in their bodies, not by a real lantern. Do not confuse with the anglerfish, which has a glowing lure on its head.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (French) «Lapin» is the French word for rabbit; it sounds like «la-PAN» with a nasal end to an English ear. 2) In English, lapin is rabbit fur used for clothes, often dyed to look like more expensive fur. 3) In cooking, lapin can appear on menus meaning rabbit meat.
its sense in the lessons: In French lessons it is an animal word («J'ai un lapin»: I have a rabbit). In English it is rare and mostly about fur or old-style menus. It is not an ordinary English word for the animal; say «rabbit».
examples from the lessons: (French) «Le lapin» means «the rabbit». | (French) «J'ai un lapin blanc» means «I have a white rabbit». | In French class we learned «lapin», «chat» and «chien». | Grandma's old coat has a lapin collar. | The French restaurant served lapin with mustard. | (French) «Le lapin mange une carotte»: the rabbit eats a carrot. | A lapin is not a different animal; it is just rabbit. | Lapin fur is often dyed.
note for the reader of a maths problem: In French it is a masculine noun: le lapin, plural les lapins (the s is silent). In English it is uncountable when it means fur. Say «rabbit» for the animal in English.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A larder is a cool room or large cupboard in a house where food is kept, especially in older homes. 2) It can mean the store of food a person or family has. 3) Some animals have a larder: squirrels and shrikes store food to eat later.
its sense in the lessons: In stories set in older or country houses, and in British homes; in science lessons about animals storing food for winter. Phrases: «a well-stocked larder», «raid the larder».
examples from the lessons: Mum keeps the jam in the larder. | The old cottage had a cold stone larder. | The mice found their way into the larder. | Our larder is empty, we need to go shopping. | Squirrels make a larder of nuts for the winter. | The shrike stores insects on thorns as a larder. | I raided the larder for a midnight snack. | In the story, the larder was full of pies.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Similar to «pantry»; both are rooms or cupboards for food, and many people use them for the same thing. Mainly British; Americans more often say «pantry».

part of speech: noun (a lei, leis); also plural of leu (lei)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A lei is a Hawaiian garland or necklace made of flowers, leaves, shells or feathers, given as a sign of welcome, love or celebration. 2) Lei is also the plural of «leu», the money of Romania and Moldova: one leu, ten lei.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and culture lessons about Hawaii and the Pacific; in maths money problems about Romania, «lei» is the currency. Phrases: «a flower lei», «give someone a lei».
examples from the lessons: They put a flower lei round our necks when we arrived in Hawaii. | We made paper leis for the Hawaiian party. | Giving a lei is a sign of welcome. | The lei smelled of fresh flowers. | Hawaiian people celebrate Lei Day with flowers. | Some leis are made of shells or feathers. | In Romania a sandwich costs about ten lei. | One leu, two lei: that is Romanian money.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say «lay». Plural in Hawaiian sense: leis. As money, lei is already the plural of leu. Show respect: in Hawaii a lei is a meaningful gift, and it is polite not to take it off in front of the giver.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To lengthen something means to make it longer: «lengthen a skirt», «lengthen a sentence». 2) To lengthen means to become longer: «The days lengthen in spring».
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography lessons about seasons (days lengthen in spring, shorten in autumn); in writing lessons pupils lengthen sentences with adjectives and clauses; in maths it means increasing a length. Phrases: «lengthen the days», «lengthen a stride».
examples from the lessons: The days lengthen after midwinter. | Mum lengthened my trousers because I grew. | Can you lengthen this sentence with an adjective? | The shadows lengthened as the sun went down. | Runners lengthen their stride to go faster. | The teacher lengthened break time because of the sunshine. | We lengthened the rope by tying two together. | The queue lengthened as more people came.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Made from length + en, like strengthen and widen. In maths, if a 10 cm line is lengthened by 3 cm, it becomes 13 cm long: «lengthen by» means add.

part of speech: adjective (licensed); verb form of license (license, licenses, licensed, licensing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Licensed means having official permission to do something, such as a licensed driver, a licensed taxi or a licensed doctor. 2) A licensed shop, café or restaurant is allowed to sell alcohol. 3) A licensed product, like a toy or T-shirt, uses a famous name or character with the owner's permission.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and safety: only licensed drivers may drive, and it is safer to take a licensed taxi. In shops licensed toys show characters from films. Phrases: «licensed to drive», «fully licensed», «a licensed premises».
examples from the lessons: My big sister is now a licensed driver. | Only take a licensed taxi. | The doctor is licensed to work in hospitals. | This café is licensed, so adults can have wine with dinner. | The toy is officially licensed by the film company. | A licensed electrician fixed our wiring. | Pilots must be licensed to fly planes. | You need to be licensed to sell fireworks.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: in British English the noun is «licence» and the verb «license»; in American English both are «license». The past form is always «licensed». Say «LIE-sunst».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A liger is the baby of a male lion and a female tiger; it is a hybrid, a mix of two kinds of animal. 2) Ligers are huge, often bigger than both parents, with faint stripes and a lion-like face.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about animals, hybrids and inheritance. Ligers almost never happen in the wild, because lions and tigers live in different places; they are bred in zoos or animal parks. Phrases: «a lion and tiger hybrid».
examples from the lessons: A liger has a lion dad and a tiger mum. | Ligers are the biggest cats in the world. | A tigon has a tiger dad and a lion mum. | Ligers are not found in the wild. | The liger had faint stripes on its back. | Mules and ligers are both hybrids. | We read about a liger that weighed more than a lion and a tiger. | Many scientists say breeding ligers is not good for the animals.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Say «LIE-ger». It is a blend of «lion» and «tiger». A tigon is the opposite mix. Ligers are real but rare.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A limitation is something that limits what a person or thing can do: «The robot has some limitations». 2) Limitation is the act of keeping something under control or within limits: «the limitation of noise». 3) (science) The limitations of an experiment are its weaknesses, things that could make the results less accurate.
its sense in the lessons: In science reports pupils write the limitations of their experiment; in everyday life people know their limitations. Phrases: «know your limitations», «limitations of the study», «time limitations».
examples from the lessons: Every experiment has limitations. | One limitation was that we only tested three plants. | I know my limitations: I can't sing high notes. | The old computer has many limitations. | Despite his limitations, he never gave up. | Time limitations meant we finished early. | A wheelchair user may face limitations from badly designed buildings. | Write the limitations of your test at the end.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable when meaning a weakness: «a limitation», «limitations». From the verb «limit». In science, naming limitations is good, honest work, not a failure.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (Latin) «Lingua» is the Latin word for tongue and language. 2) In English it appears mainly in the phrase «lingua franca», a language used by people who speak different languages so they can understand each other. 3) (medicine) The lingua is a rare medical word for the tongue.
its sense in the lessons: In language lessons it explains words like «linguist», «bilingual» and «language», which come from it. Today English is a lingua franca in many parts of the world. Phrases: «lingua franca».
examples from the lessons: «Lingua» is Latin for tongue. | English is a lingua franca for many travellers. | Swahili is a lingua franca in East Africa. | Long ago, Latin was the lingua franca of Europe. | «Bilingual» comes from «bi» (two) and «lingua» (tongue). | A linguist studies languages, from «lingua». | In the market, they spoke a lingua franca to trade. | (Italian) «Lingua» also means tongue and language in Italian.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Not an ordinary English word alone; use «lingua franca» as a whole phrase. Say «LING-gwuh». Plural of lingua franca: lingua francas or linguae francae.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Longevity means living a long life: «Tortoises are famous for their longevity». 2) Longevity can also mean lasting for a long time, like the longevity of a building or a TV show.
its sense in the lessons: In science and health lessons about animals, healthy habits and old age; in news and sport it praises a long career. Phrases: «the secret of longevity», «known for its longevity».
examples from the lessons: Giant tortoises are known for their longevity. | Exercise and good food can help longevity. | The longevity of the old bridge surprised the engineers. | Some trees have amazing longevity and live thousands of years. | Japan is famous for the longevity of its people. | The singer's longevity is impressive; she has performed for decades. | What is the secret of longevity? Grandma says porridge. | Greenland sharks hold a record for longevity.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Say «lon-JEV-ih-tee». Formal word; in speech say «living a long time». Myth: no single food guarantees longevity.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Lye is a very strong chemical, an alkali, used to make soap and to clean drains. 2) Lye can burn skin and eyes badly, so it is dangerous.
its sense in the lessons: In science and history lessons about how soap was made from fat and lye; in safety lessons it is a household danger that must be locked away. Phrases: «lye soap», «caustic lye».
examples from the lessons: People once made soap from animal fat and lye. | Lye is so strong it can burn your skin. | Drain cleaners often contain lye. | Never touch lye without gloves and goggles. | Lye is used to make pretzels shiny and brown. | Pioneers made lye from wood ash and water. | Keep lye locked away from children. | Lye is an alkali, the opposite of an acid.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Homophone: «lye» sounds the same as «lie» (to say something untrue, or to rest flat). Safety: if lye touches skin, rinse with lots of water and tell an adult straight away.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (French) «Mademoiselle» is the French word for «Miss», used for a girl or young unmarried woman; it sounds like «mad-mwa-ZELL» to an English ear. 2) In English it is used in stories and jokes to sound French, or for a French governess or teacher.
its sense in the lessons: In French lessons it is a polite title: «Bonjour, mademoiselle». In France it is used less now; many people say «madame» to all women. Phrases: «Bonjour, mademoiselle», «Mademoiselle Dupont».
examples from the lessons: (French) «Bonjour, mademoiselle!» means «Hello, miss!» | Our French teacher is called Mademoiselle Martin. | In the story, the little girl was called Mademoiselle by the waiter. | (French) «Merci, mademoiselle» means «Thank you, miss». | Mademoiselle is like Miss in English. | Madame is like Mrs or Ms. | The French nanny in the book was known as Mademoiselle. | Short form: Mlle.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Not an English word, though English speakers know it. Plural: mesdemoiselles. Short form Mlle. Spelled with one d and «moiselle». Many people in France now prefer «madame» for every woman.

part of speech: noun (manure, uncountable); verb (manure, manures, manured, manuring)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Manure is animal poo, often mixed with straw, used to make soil richer so plants grow better. 2) To manure a field or garden means to spread manure on it.
its sense in the lessons: In science and farming lessons it shows how nutrients are recycled; in country stories the smell of manure tells you you are near a farm. Phrases: «horse manure», «cow manure», «spread manure», «green manure» (plants dug in to feed soil).
examples from the lessons: The farmer spread manure on the field. | Roses grow well with horse manure. | The smell of manure means we are near a farm. | Manure is full of nutrients for plants. | We put manure on the school vegetable patch. | Wash your hands after touching manure. | Some people sell bags of manure by the road. | Green manure is a plant crop dug back into the soil.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «some manure», «a pile of manure». Say «muh-NYOOR». Similar to «dung»; «compost» is rotted plants and food. Hygiene: manure has germs, so always wash your hands.

part of speech: adjective (maroon); noun (maroon, a maroon, maroons); verb (maroon, maroons, marooned, marooning)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Maroon is a dark brownish-red colour, like the colour of some school uniforms. 2) To maroon someone means to leave them alone in a place they cannot escape from, like a desert island; if you are marooned, you are stuck. 3) The Maroons were people in Jamaica and other places who escaped slavery and built free communities in the mountains. 4) (UK) A maroon is a loud firework rocket used as a signal, once used to call lifeboat crews. 5) (Australia) The Maroons is the nickname of the Queensland rugby league team.
its sense in the lessons: In art lessons it is a colour name; in pirate stories sailors are marooned on islands; in history lessons the Maroons resisted slavery. Phrases: «maroon jumper», «marooned on an island», «marooned by the floods».
examples from the lessons: Our school jumpers are maroon. | The pirates marooned the captain on a tiny island. | We were marooned at home because of the snow. | Maroon is darker than red. | The Maroons of Jamaica fought for their freedom. | Robinson Crusoe was marooned for many years. | (Australia) The Maroons won the State of Origin match. | The flood marooned the village for a week.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a colour it does not change: «maroon socks». Marooned is often passive: «They were marooned». In cartoons «maroon» is sometimes said as a joke for «moron», which is an insult.

part of speech: noun (a massacre, massacres); verb (massacre, massacres, massacred, massacring)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A massacre is the cruel killing of many people who cannot defend themselves. 2) To massacre people is to kill many of them in this way. 3) (informal) In sport and games a massacre is a very heavy defeat: «It was a massacre: ten–nil!» 4) (informal) To massacre a song or a language means to perform it very badly.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons and news it is a very serious word for terrible events that people remember and mourn. In everyday sport talk it is an exaggeration. Phrases: «a terrible massacre», «remember the massacre», «it was a massacre».
examples from the lessons: The massacre is remembered every year with a minute of silence. | History books tell of massacres in many wars. | Soldiers massacred the people of the village. | Our team lost twelve–nil; it was a massacre. | (informal) Dad massacred that song at karaoke. | We learned how survivors told the story of the massacre. | Memorials help people remember victims of massacres. | (informal) Sorry, I massacred the French pronunciation.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say «MASS-uh-ker». Spelling: -cre, like «acre». Past: massacred. Be careful: the joking sport sense should not be used near people who have lost family in real massacres.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) A meanie is a person who is unkind, selfish or not generous, said in a childish or playful way. 2) It is often used by young children or as a joke: «Don't be a meanie, share your sweets!»
its sense in the lessons: In playground talk, picture books and family jokes. It is gentle and not a serious insult. Phrases: «don't be a meanie», «big meanie», «you meanie!»
examples from the lessons: Don't be a meanie, let me have a turn! | My brother is a big meanie; he ate all the cake. | You meanie, you hid my shoes! | The meanie in the story stole the toys. | Dad pretended to be a meanie and said no more biscuits. | She called me a meanie, then laughed. | Nobody likes a meanie. | Stop being a meanie and invite her to play.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal and childish; not for formal writing. Plural meanies. Sometimes spelled «meany». It comes from «mean», which here means unkind (not the maths «mean»).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (a name; US) Medicare is the US government health insurance for people aged 65 and over and some disabled people. 2) (a name; Australia) Medicare is Australia's public health system, which pays for doctors and hospital care for citizens and residents. 3) (Canada) Medicare is an informal name for Canada's public health insurance.
its sense in the lessons: In social studies and news about health care, taxes and older people. Phrases: «on Medicare», «Medicare card», «covered by Medicare».
examples from the lessons: Grandpa is on Medicare now that he is over 65. | In Australia, Mum showed her Medicare card at the doctor's. | Medicare helps pay for hospital visits. | (Australia) The visit was free with Medicare. | (US) Medicare is for older Americans. | In the UK, the NHS does a similar job. | Medicare is paid for by taxes. | Canadians call their health system medicare.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually capital M. Say «MED-ih-care». Do not confuse with «Medicaid» in the USA, which helps people with low income. Different countries use the name for different systems.

part of speech: noun (a memorandum, memoranda or memorandums); short form memo
meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) A memorandum is a short written message sent inside an office, school or company, telling people about something. 2) (formal) A memorandum is a note to help you remember something. 3) (law) A memorandum of understanding is a written agreement between two groups or countries.
its sense in the lessons: In formal and office writing, history lessons about governments, and in writing lessons about formats. In everyday talk people say «memo». Phrases: «send a memorandum», «a memorandum of understanding».
examples from the lessons: The head teacher sent a memorandum to all staff. | (formal) Please read the memorandum about the new rules. | Dad got a memo at work about the holiday party. | The two countries signed a memorandum of understanding. | A memorandum should be short and clear. | Write a memorandum to remind the class about the trip. | The memo said «No parking near the gates». | The secret memorandum was found in the archive.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: memoranda (Latin) or memorandums. Short form «memo», plural «memos». Formal word. From Latin «something to be remembered».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Micro means very small: «a micro farm», «micro plastics». 2) As a prefix, micro- makes words about tiny things: microscope, microchip, microphone, microwave. 3) (science) In measurement, micro- means one millionth, as in micrometre or microgram. 4) (informal) A micro is a short name for a small computer, a microwave oven, or the BBC micro:bit used in schools.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons micro- names tiny things (micro-organisms); in computing, children program the micro:bit. In everyday talk «micro» means tiny. Phrases: «micro:bit», «micro scooter», «micro-organism».
examples from the lessons: We programmed the micro:bit to show a heart. | A microscope helps you see micro-organisms. | My little brother has a micro scooter. | Micro means very small. | Microplastics are tiny bits of plastic in the sea. | A micrometre is one millionth of a metre. | (informal) Put the soup in the micro for two minutes. | The micro-chip in the dog's neck has its owner's details.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a prefix it often joins the word: microscope, microphone. In maths and science micro means one millionth: 1 micrometre is 0.000001 m. The opposite size prefix is «macro» (large) or «mega» (a million).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (a name) The Minotaur is a monster in Greek myths with the body of a man and the head of a bull. 2) It lived in a maze called the Labyrinth on the island of Crete, and the hero Theseus killed it with help from Ariadne's thread.
its sense in the lessons: In history and literature lessons on Ancient Greece and myths; in maze puzzles. It tells the reader of danger hidden in a maze. Phrases: «Theseus and the Minotaur», «the Labyrinth».
examples from the lessons: Theseus fought the Minotaur in the Labyrinth. | The Minotaur had a bull's head and a man's body. | Ariadne gave Theseus a ball of thread to find his way out. | King Minos kept the Minotaur on Crete. | We drew a maze with the Minotaur in the middle. | The Minotaur is a myth, not a real animal. | In the story, young people were sent to the Minotaur. | Our class acted out Theseus and the Minotaur.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually «the Minotaur», with a capital M. Say «MY-nuh-tor». «Mino» comes from King Minos, «taur» means bull. It is a myth; there is no evidence such a creature lived.

part of speech: verb (misrepresent, misrepresents, misrepresented, misrepresenting); noun misrepresentation
meaning for a pupil: 1) To misrepresent someone or something means to describe them in a false or unfair way, so others get the wrong idea. 2) To misrepresent yourself means to pretend to be something you are not, such as lying about your age online.
its sense in the lessons: In citizenship and media lessons about news, adverts and quoting people fairly; in online safety, people may misrepresent who they are. Phrases: «misrepresent the facts», «be misrepresented», «misrepresent someone's words».
examples from the lessons: The advert misrepresented how big the toy was. | Don't misrepresent what your friend said. | The newspaper misrepresented the facts. | People online sometimes misrepresent themselves. | She felt misrepresented by the story about her. | Leaving out the bad parts can misrepresent the truth. | The graph misrepresented the numbers by starting at fifty. | Checking sources helps us spot when news misrepresents events.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Mis + represent: «mis» means wrongly. In maths, a graph can misrepresent data if the axis does not start at zero or the scale is uneven.

part of speech: verb (modify, modifies, modified, modifying); noun modification
meaning for a pupil: 1) To modify something means to change it a little, usually to improve it or make it fit a purpose. 2) (grammar) A word modifies another when it describes it or changes its meaning, like an adjective modifying a noun. 3) (science) Genetically modified (GM) plants have had their genes changed by scientists.
its sense in the lessons: In design and technology, pupils modify their designs after testing; in grammar lessons adjectives and adverbs modify; in science GM crops are discussed. Phrases: «modify a design», «modified version», «genetically modified».
examples from the lessons: We modified our paper plane so it flew further. | Dad modified the recipe to use less sugar. | The game has been modified for younger players. | In «a red car», «red» modifies «car». | Scientists modify plants to resist pests. | Can you modify your sentence to make it clearer? | The bike was modified with a basket. | After testing, modify your model and test again.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Modify changes y to i: modifies, modified. Means about the same as «change» or «adjust» but sounds more formal. Modifying is changing a little, not completely.

part of speech: noun (a moray, morays); also moray eel
meaning for a pupil: 1) A moray, or moray eel, is a long, snake-like fish with sharp teeth that lives in holes in coral reefs and rocks in warm seas. 2) (a name) Moray is also an area in the north-east of Scotland, and the Moray Firth is a sea inlet there famous for dolphins.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about oceans, coral reefs and predators; in Scottish geography. Morays open and close their mouths to breathe, which makes them look scary. Phrases: «moray eel», «Moray Firth».
examples from the lessons: A moray eel peeked out of its hole in the reef. | Moray eels have two sets of jaws. | Divers keep their hands away from moray eels. | The moray looked fierce but stayed in its hole. | We saw dolphins in the Moray Firth. | Moray is in the north of Scotland. | Morays hunt fish and octopus at night. | Cleaner shrimps clean the moray eel's teeth.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say «MOR-ay» or «muh-RAY». Countable. The place name Moray has a capital M and is said «MURR-ee» by Scots. Do not confuse with «Murray» or «morel».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (French) «Mouton» is the French word for sheep, and also for mutton (sheep meat); to an English ear it sounds like «moo-TON» with a nasal end. 2) In English, mouton is sheepskin that has been treated to look like beaver or seal fur, used for coats.
its sense in the lessons: In French lessons it is a farm animal word («un mouton»: a sheep). Also the source of English «mutton». It is not an ordinary English word for the animal; say «sheep». Phrases: «(French) un mouton», «revenons à nos moutons» (let's get back to the point).
examples from the lessons: (French) «Un mouton» means «a sheep». | (French) «Les moutons sont dans le champ»: the sheep are in the field. | The English word «mutton» comes from French «mouton». | Grandma's old coat has a mouton collar. | (French) Le Petit Prince asks the pilot to draw him a mouton. | In French class we counted moutons. | (French) «Revenons à nos moutons» means «let's get back to the subject». | A mouton is just a sheep, not a special animal.
note for the reader of a maths problem: In French it is masculine: le mouton, les moutons (the final s is silent). In English it is rare and uncountable. Note: English has two words, sheep (animal) and mutton (meat), while French uses mouton for both.

part of speech: noun (a muddle, muddles); verb (muddle, muddles, muddled, muddling); adjective muddled
meaning for a pupil: 1) A muddle is an untidy mess, or a state of confusion: «My drawer is in a muddle». 2) To muddle things means to mix them up or put them in the wrong order. 3) To be muddled or get in a muddle means to feel confused or make mistakes because you cannot think clearly. 4) (UK) To muddle through means to manage somehow, without a good plan.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life it describes untidy rooms and mixed-up facts; in maths lessons pupils get «in a muddle» with steps. Phrases: «in a muddle», «muddle up», «muddle through», «get muddled».
examples from the lessons: My socks are in a muddle. | I always muddle up «their» and «there». | Grandpa gets muddled when he's tired. | Don't muddle the numbers in your answer. | We had no map but muddled through. | The twins are easy to muddle. | The instructions were a total muddle. | Slow down so you don't get in a muddle with the sums.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: muddled, muddling (drop the e). «Muddle» is softer and gentler than «mess». It is common in British English.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A multivitamin is a tablet, gummy or liquid that contains many different vitamins and often minerals together. 2) It is taken to help people get vitamins they might not get enough of from food.
its sense in the lessons: In health and science lessons about food, nutrients and a balanced diet. Doctors say most vitamins should come from healthy food; supplements are an extra. Phrases: «take a multivitamin», «children's multivitamin».
examples from the lessons: I take a multivitamin with breakfast. | Multivitamins come as tablets, gummies or drops. | A multivitamin has vitamins A, C, D and more. | Eating fruit and vegetables is better than relying on multivitamins. | Don't eat multivitamin gummies like sweets. | Mum checked the label to see the right dose of multivitamin. | Some multivitamins also contain iron. | The doctor said I could take a children's multivitamin in winter.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Multi + vitamin: «multi» means many. Safety: vitamins and iron can be harmful if a child eats too many, so only take them as an adult says. Myth: multivitamins do not replace healthy eating.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A mutant is a living thing whose genes have changed, so it is different from its parents in some way, like a white tiger or a plant with odd leaves. 2) In science fiction and comics, mutants are characters with strange bodies or superpowers, like the X-Men or the Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles. 3) (informal) «Mutant» can be a joking word for anything odd-looking: «a mutant carrot».
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about genes, variation and evolution; in stories and cartoons for superheroes and monsters. Phrases: «mutant gene», «mutant strain», «Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles».
examples from the lessons: A white tiger is a mutant with a changed colour gene. | Scientists studied mutant fruit flies. | The X-Men are a team of mutants. | We grew a mutant carrot with three legs! | Some mutants are healthy and some are not. | A mutant virus can spread differently. | The Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles love pizza. | In the comic, mutant powers appeared when the hero turned thirteen.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Related words: mutate (change), mutation (the change). Myth: real mutations do not give superpowers; most are small or have no effect. Mutation is a normal part of how living things vary.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Mutualism is a relationship between two different kinds of living things in which both of them benefit. 2) Examples are bees and flowers, or clownfish and sea anemones.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about ecosystems, food chains and how animals and plants live together. It is one kind of symbiosis; others include parasitism (one is harmed) and commensalism (one benefits, the other is not affected). Phrases: «an example of mutualism».
examples from the lessons: Bees and flowers show mutualism: bees get nectar and flowers get pollinated. | Clownfish and sea anemones live in mutualism. | Oxpecker birds eat ticks off zebras; that is mutualism. | Mutualism means both sides win. | We drew a poster of mutualism in the rainforest. | Fungi and tree roots help each other in mutualism. | The bacteria in your gut and you share a kind of mutualism. | Is a flea on a dog mutualism? No, the dog is harmed.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Say «MYOO-choo-uh-liz-um». From «mutual», meaning shared by both sides. Do not confuse with parasitism, where one side is harmed.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (a name) Nara is a city in Japan that was once the capital; it is famous for its old temples and the tame deer that walk freely in Nara Park and bow to visitors. 2) (a name) NARA is short for the National Archives and Records Administration of the USA, which keeps important government papers. 3) The nara is also a spiky melon plant that grows in the deserts of Namibia.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons about Japan and in culture stories about temples and deer. Not an ordinary English word. Phrases: «Nara Park», «Nara deer».
examples from the lessons: In Nara, deer walk around the park. | The deer in Nara bow for special crackers. | Nara has a giant bronze Buddha. | Nara was the capital of Japan long ago. | We watched a video of the Nara deer. | NARA keeps the Declaration of Independence in Washington. | The nara melon grows in the Namib desert. | Our pen pal visited Nara on a school trip.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually capital N as a place name; NARA in capitals for the US archives. Say «NAH-rah». Not an English word by itself.

part of speech: noun (a negotiation, negotiations; negotiation, uncountable); verb negotiate
meaning for a pupil: 1) Negotiation is talking with others to reach an agreement when you want different things, like deciding bedtime with your parents. 2) Negotiations are formal talks between countries, companies or groups, for example to end a war or agree a price. 3) (informal) Negotiation can mean finding a way through or past something difficult.
its sense in the lessons: In PSHE and citizenship lessons pupils learn to negotiate fairly instead of fighting; in news, peace negotiations and pay negotiations. Phrases: «open to negotiation», «peace negotiations», «after long negotiation».
examples from the lessons: After some negotiation, we agreed to share the swing. | The price is open to negotiation. | Peace negotiations can take many months. | Good negotiation means both sides get something. | My bedtime is not up for negotiation, says Mum. | The teachers' union is in negotiations about pay. | Negotiation is better than shouting. | The countries began negotiations to end the war.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable for formal talks (negotiations), uncountable for the skill. Say «nuh-go-shee-AY-shun». The verb is «negotiate». In maths money problems, negotiation can lower a price.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A nelson is a hold in wrestling where you put your arm under your opponent's arm and push on the back of their neck; a full nelson uses both arms, a half nelson one. 2) (a name) Nelson is a man's first name or surname, as in Nelson Mandela, the South African leader. 3) (a name) Admiral Horatio Nelson was a famous British naval hero; Nelson's Column stands in Trafalgar Square, London. 4) (a name) Nelson is a city in New Zealand. 5) (cricket) A «Nelson» is a score of 111, which some cricket fans think is unlucky.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons about Nelson Mandela and Admiral Nelson; in sport (wrestling and cricket). Phrases: «full nelson», «half nelson», «Nelson's Column».
examples from the lessons: Nelson Mandela fought against apartheid. | Nelson's Column is in Trafalgar Square in London. | Admiral Nelson won the Battle of Trafalgar. | The wrestler put his opponent in a full nelson. | A half nelson uses only one arm. | Nelson is a sunny city in New Zealand. | (cricket) When the score reached 111, the umpire stood on one leg for Nelson. | My cousin's name is Nelson.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a name, always capital N. The wrestling hold is written with a small n. Safety: wrestling holds can hurt the neck; do not try them in the playground. The cricket «unlucky 111» is only a superstition.

part of speech: adverb (nigh); adjective (nigh, old: nigher, nighest); preposition (nigh)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (old) Nigh means near, either in place or in time: «The end is nigh». 2) Nigh on or well nigh means almost or nearly: «It took nigh on an hour». 3) (UK, dialect) Some people in parts of England still use «nigh» in everyday speech for near.
its sense in the lessons: Mostly in old stories, poems, the Bible and fairy tales, or in jokey speech. Phrases: «the end is nigh», «well nigh impossible», «nigh on», «draw nigh».
examples from the lessons: The end is nigh! shouted the man with the sign. | Winter is drawing nigh. | It was well nigh impossible to see in the fog. | We waited nigh on two hours for the bus. | (Bible) «The kingdom of God is nigh at hand.» | The knight rode nigh to the castle. | Bedtime is nigh, so brush your teeth. | Grandad says it's nigh on ten miles to the coast.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say «nye», rhymes with «sky». The gh is silent, as in «night» and «high». Old-fashioned; in normal writing use «near» or «nearly». In maths problems, «nigh on 50» means almost 50, a bit less.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A nipple is the small raised point in the middle of each breast or on a man's or boy's chest; mothers feed babies milk through their nipples. 2) (US) A nipple is the rubber or plastic teat on a baby's bottle that the baby sucks; in the UK this is called a teat. 3) A nipple is a small nozzle on a machine, such as a grease nipple or a pipe fitting.
its sense in the lessons: In science and health lessons about the human body and mammals: all mammals feed their young with milk, and nipples show this. Said plainly in biology. Phrases: «baby bottle nipple», «grease nipple».
