examples from the lessons: All mammals have nipples. | A mother pig has many nipples to feed her piglets. | Babies drink milk from their mother's nipples or a bottle. | Boys have nipples too, even though they do not make milk. | (US) Put a clean nipple on the baby's bottle. | (UK) The bottle teat was too small. | The mechanic pumped grease into the nipple on the bike. | We labelled the parts of a cow in science, including the udder and teats.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A plain body word, fine in science lessons. Countable. Some children giggle at it, but it is not rude. Do not confuse with «nibble».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (religion) In Buddhism, nirvana is the state of perfect peace a person reaches when they are free from all desire and suffering and are no longer reborn; Buddhists believe the Buddha reached it. 2) (informal) Nirvana means a place or state of perfect happiness: «This chocolate shop is nirvana!» 3) (a name) Nirvana was a famous American rock band.
its sense in the lessons: In religion lessons about Buddhism alongside Hinduism, where the idea is related; in everyday talk it is a joke word for bliss. Phrases: «reach nirvana», «pure nirvana».
examples from the lessons: Buddhists believe the Buddha reached nirvana. | Nirvana means freedom from suffering in Buddhism. | Following the Eightfold Path leads towards nirvana, Buddhists teach. | (informal) Lying in the hammock in the sun was nirvana. | For my brother, a pizza buffet is nirvana. | Nirvana was a famous rock band from Seattle. | We learned about nirvana in our lesson on Buddhism. | «Nirvana» is a word from Sanskrit.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say «nur-VAH-nuh». Small n for the religious and informal meanings, capital for the band. It is not the same as the Christian idea of heaven; it is a state of peace, not a place.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Nomadic people move from place to place instead of living in one fixed home, often following food, water or grass for their animals. 2) Nomadic animals wander over a large area and do not stay in one territory. 3) (informal) A nomadic life is one where a person keeps moving house, school or job.
its sense in the lessons: In history and geography lessons it describes herders and hunters who travel with the seasons, such as Bedouin, Mongolian herders and some Sámi reindeer herders; it is the opposite of «settled». In stories it tells the reader a character has no fixed home and is used to travelling. Phrases: «a nomadic tribe», «a nomadic way of life», «nomadic herders».
examples from the lessons: Nomadic herders in Mongolia move their tents, called gers, several times a year. | Long ago many people were nomadic and followed the animals they hunted. | When farming began, some nomadic groups settled in villages. | Wildebeest are nomadic and travel huge distances to find fresh grass. | Dad's job in the army gave us a nomadic childhood; I went to five schools. | The class compared a nomadic life with life in a farming village. | Camels help nomadic people cross the desert.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective only; the noun is «nomad» (a nomad, nomads). It is not «a nomadic» on its own. Do not confuse with «monadic» (a maths word). Nomadic does not mean homeless or poor: nomads have homes they carry with them.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Nonstop means without stopping or pausing. 2) A nonstop flight, train or bus goes straight to the end without stopping at any station or airport on the way. 3) (informal) Happening all the time, so much that it feels like it never ends.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life it is used for travel («a nonstop flight to London») and for things that seem endless («nonstop rain», «she talks nonstop»). In maths problems «drove nonstop for 3 hours» means the time counts with no breaks. Phrases: «nonstop flight», «work nonstop», «nonstop fun», «talk nonstop».
examples from the lessons: We took a nonstop flight from Sydney to Perth. | It rained nonstop for the whole camping trip. | My little brother talked nonstop all the way to Nan's house. | The train ran nonstop from London to Edinburgh. | A cyclist rode nonstop for 2 hours at 15 km an hour, so she went 30 km. | The party was nonstop fun from start to finish. | The phone rang nonstop after the news came out.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Both an adjective (a nonstop flight) and an adverb (it rained nonstop). Spelled «nonstop» (more US) or «non-stop» (more UK); both are correct. In maths, nonstop means no rest stops, so total time equals moving time.

part of speech: noun (the northeast); adjective (northeast, northeastern); adverb (northeast); also «north-east»
meaning for a pupil: 1) Northeast is the direction halfway between north and east on a compass. 2) The northeast of a country or area is the part in that direction, for example the Northeast of England or the northeastern United States. 3) A northeast wind blows from the northeast.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and maps it is one of the eight main compass points (N, NE, E, SE, S, SW, W, NW); on a map with north at the top it is the top-right corner. In maths it is halfway between north and east, 45 degrees from each. Phrases: «in the northeast», «to the northeast of», «head northeast», «a northeast wind».
examples from the lessons: The treasure is buried to the northeast of the old oak tree. | Newcastle is in the northeast of England. | Turn the compass so the needle points north, then look halfway towards east: that is northeast. | A cold northeast wind blew across the field. | Maine and Vermont are in the northeastern United States. | The ship sailed northeast for two days. | Northeast is written NE on a map.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Short form NE. US spelling usually «northeast», UK often «north-east». Wind names say where the wind comes FROM: a northeast wind blows from the northeast towards the southwest. Northeast is 45 degrees clockwise from north.

part of speech: noun (a novice, novices); adjective (novice, as in «a novice skier»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A novice is a beginner: someone who is new to an activity and has little skill or experience yet. 2) (church) A novice is a person who has joined a religious community, such as monks or nuns, and is training before making their final promises. 3) In sport and competitions, a novice event or class is for beginners.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and stories it shows that someone is just starting and may make mistakes, the opposite of an expert. Children meet it in swimming, chess, riding and coding clubs («novice level»). In church life it names a trainee monk or nun. Phrases: «a complete novice», «novice level», «novice class».
examples from the lessons: I am a complete novice at chess, so please explain the rules. | The novice skiers practised on the gentle slope. | Even experts were novices once. | She entered the novice class at the pony show. | The novice nun learned the prayers and daily work of the convent. | This coding website has puzzles for novices and for experts. | As a novice cook, Dad burnt the toast twice.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a novice, two novices. Opposite: expert, veteran. Similar words: beginner, learner, newcomer. Do not confuse with «novel» (a book or something new).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Obsolete means no longer used because something newer or better has replaced it. 2) An obsolete word, rule or law is out of date and not used any more. 3) In biology, an obsolete body part is one that has become very small or no longer works.
its sense in the lessons: In technology and history lessons it describes old machines and methods, such as floppy disks, typewriters and fax machines. In everyday life it tells you something is out of date. Phrases: «become obsolete», «make something obsolete», «obsolete technology».
examples from the lessons: Floppy disks are obsolete; nobody uses them for homework now. | Smartphones made many old gadgets obsolete. | That word is obsolete, so you will only find it in very old books. | Will paper money become obsolete one day? | Grandad still has an obsolete video player in the loft. | Old maps can become obsolete when new roads are built. | The rule was obsolete, so the school removed it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective; «become obsolete», not «get obsoleted». The noun is «obsolescence». Obsolete means not used any more, not simply old: an old thing that still works and is used is not obsolete.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An obstruction is something that blocks a road, path, pipe or passage so that things cannot get through. 2) Obstruction is the act of stopping or delaying something on purpose. 3) (sport) In football, hockey and other games, obstruction is illegally blocking an opponent with your body. 4) (law) Obstruction of justice means trying to stop the police or a court from doing their job.
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons it reminds children to keep fire exits and stairs clear of obstructions. In science and the body it can mean a blocked tube, such as something stuck in the throat. In sport it names a foul. Phrases: «cause an obstruction», «clear an obstruction», «obstruction of justice».
examples from the lessons: A fallen tree caused an obstruction on the road. | Keep the fire exit free from any obstruction. | The plumber cleared an obstruction from the drain. | The referee gave a free kick for obstruction. | Bags in the corridor are an obstruction and someone could trip. | The doctor checked whether there was an obstruction in the dog's throat. | Lying to the police can be obstruction of justice.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable when it is a thing (an obstruction, two obstructions); uncountable when it is the action. Verb: obstruct. Related: obstacle (something in your way). In sport it is a foul even if no one falls.

part of speech: noun (an opal, opals; opal as a material)
meaning for a pupil: 1) An opal is a precious stone that shows flashing rainbow colours when you move it in the light. 2) Opal is the material itself, a kind of hardened silica that contains water. 3) Opal is also a milky, pale colour.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on rocks and minerals it is an example of a gemstone; Australia produces most of the world's opal, and Coober Pedy is a famous opal-mining town where people live underground. In stories an opal is a treasure. Phrases: «an opal ring», «black opal», «opal mine».
examples from the lessons: Nan has an opal ring that sparkles blue and green. | Most of the world's opals come from Australia. | In Coober Pedy, miners dig for opal and some families live in underground houses. | The black opal is Australia's national gemstone. | When I tilted the opal, colours flashed like a tiny rainbow. | Opals contain water, so they can crack if they dry out. | The bathroom glass had a milky opal colour.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable for a stone (an opal, opals), uncountable for the material (made of opal). Use «an» because it starts with a vowel sound. Opal is the birthstone of October in many lists.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An opener is a tool for opening something, such as a tin opener, can opener or bottle opener. 2) The opener is the first thing in a series: the first game of a season, the first song of a show, or the first words of a talk. 3) (sport) In cricket, an opener is one of the two batters who bat first. 4) An eye-opener is something that surprises you and teaches you something new.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and kitchen safety it names tools («use the tin opener carefully, the edges are sharp»). In sport it names the first match or the first batters. In writing lessons a good opener is the first sentence that grabs the reader. Phrases: «tin opener», «can opener», «bottle opener», «season opener», «an eye-opener», «sentence opener».
examples from the lessons: Pass me the tin opener so I can open the beans. | Be careful: a can opener leaves sharp edges. | Our team won the season opener 3–1. | The openers scored fifty runs before the first wicket fell. | Start your story with a strong opener to hook the reader. | The school trip to the farm was a real eye-opener. | The band played their best song as the opener.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: an opener, openers. Use «an» before it. UK says «tin opener», US says «can opener». In writing lessons, «sentence openers» are words like «Suddenly», «Meanwhile», «After that».

part of speech: adjective (oral); noun (an oral, orals — an oral exam, UK)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Oral means spoken, not written: an oral test or an oral report is done by talking. 2) Oral means to do with the mouth: oral hygiene is keeping your mouth and teeth clean. 3) Oral medicine is taken by mouth, swallowed, not injected. 4) (UK, noun) An oral is a speaking exam, especially in a foreign language.
its sense in the lessons: At school it names speaking tasks («oral presentation», «oral French exam»). In health lessons «oral health» means teeth and gums. In history, «oral history» is history told by people speaking about their memories. Phrases: «oral exam», «oral report», «oral history», «oral hygiene», «oral tradition», «by mouth (orally)».
examples from the lessons: We have an oral exam in French next week, so I am practising speaking. | Brushing twice a day is good oral hygiene. | Take this oral medicine with a glass of water. | My oral presentation was about volcanoes. | Many old stories were passed down in an oral tradition before they were written. | We recorded Grandma's oral history of growing up on a farm. | The dentist checks your oral health.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb: orally (take orally = swallow it). Do not confuse with «aural», which means to do with hearing; they sound almost the same. «Verbal» is often used to mean spoken too.

part of speech: adjective (overcast); noun (the overcast — rare, weather talk)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Overcast describes a sky completely covered with grey clouds, so you cannot see the sun. 2) (weather report) An overcast day is dull and grey but not necessarily rainy.
its sense in the lessons: In science weather lessons it is one of the words for cloud cover: clear, partly cloudy, cloudy, overcast. In stories a grey overcast sky often sets a gloomy or sad mood. Phrases: «an overcast sky», «overcast and cool», «a grey, overcast day».
examples from the lessons: The sky was overcast, so we could not see the eclipse. | It was overcast all day but it never rained. | On overcast days you can still get sunburnt. | Write in your weather diary: Monday, overcast and cold. | The beach looked grey and gloomy under the overcast sky. | The forecast says overcast in the morning, sunny later. | Pilots fly above the overcast into bright sunshine.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective; not used with «very» much because it already means completely cloudy. Overcast does not mean raining. It looks like a verb «over + cast», but in weather talk it is an adjective.

part of speech: noun (a padlock, padlocks); verb (padlock, padlocks, padlocked, padlocking)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A padlock is a lock you can take off and move, with a curved metal bar (a shackle) that clicks into the body, opened with a key or a combination. 2) To padlock something is to lock it with a padlock. 3) A small padlock picture on a website means the connection is secure.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life padlocks lock bike chains, school lockers, gates and sheds. In online safety lessons the padlock in the browser's address bar shows a secure site, though it does not prove the site is honest. In maths puzzles, combination padlocks give counting problems. Phrases: «a combination padlock», «padlock the gate», «the padlock icon».
examples from the lessons: I put a padlock on my locker at school. | Dad padlocked the shed so nobody could take the bikes. | My padlock has a three-number code. | A three-digit combination padlock has 1000 possible codes, from 000 to 999. | The rusty padlock would not open. | Look for the padlock in the address bar before typing a password. | The farmer padlocked the gate to keep the cows in.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a padlock, padlocks. Past: padlocked. A padlock icon means the data is encrypted, not that the website is safe or trustworthy. Counting codes: digits 0–9 on each wheel, so 10 × 10 × 10 = 1000 for three wheels.

part of speech: verb (pant, pants, panted, panting); noun (a pant, pants — a quick breath); adjective (pant, in «pant leg», US)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To pant is to breathe fast and loudly with your mouth open, because you are hot, tired or excited. 2) A pant is one quick, short breath. 3) (old or literary) To pant for something is to want it very much. 4) (US) «Pant» is used before another noun to mean trousers, as in «pant leg»; see also «pants».
its sense in the lessons: In science and PE it describes what happens after running: the body needs more oxygen, so you pant. Dogs pant to cool down because they cannot sweat much. In stories panting shows a character has been running or is scared. Phrases: «pant for breath», «huffing and panting», «panting dog».
examples from the lessons: After the race I was panting and red in the face. | The dog lay in the shade, panting with its tongue out. | Dogs pant to cool down on hot days. | She ran up the stairs and arrived panting. | We could hear the wolf panting outside the door. | In PE we counted our breaths while we panted after sprinting. | He rolled up his pant leg to show the scratch.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: panted. Do not mix up with «pants»: in the UK pants are underwear; in the US and Canada pants are trousers. «Pant» as one breath is less common. A panting dog on a very hot day may need water and shade quickly.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A participle is a form of a verb used to make tenses or used like an adjective. 2) The present participle ends in «-ing»: running, eating, singing. 3) The past participle often ends in «-ed», «-en» or has a special form: walked, eaten, sung, gone.
its sense in the lessons: In English grammar lessons participles help make tenses: «I am running» (present participle), «I have eaten» (past participle), «The window was broken» (passive). They also act like adjectives: «a crying baby», «a broken toy». In SATs grammar tests pupils are asked to find or use them. Phrases: «present participle», «past participle», «participle phrase».
examples from the lessons: In «She is singing», singing is the present participle. | In «I have finished my homework», finished is the past participle. | The past participle of «go» is «gone». | «A broken window» uses the past participle as an adjective. | Write the past participle of «write»: written. | Some verbs have odd participles, such as swim, swam, swum. | «Running late, we jumped in the car» starts with a participle phrase.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Irregular verbs have past participles you must learn (see, saw, seen; take, took, taken). Trap: «I have went» is wrong in Standard English; it is «I have gone». Another trap: «I seen it» uses the participle without «have»; Standard English is «I saw it» or «I have seen it».

part of speech: noun (pasteurisation, uncountable); US and international spelling «pasteurization»; verb: pasteurise / pasteurize
meaning for a pupil: 1) Pasteurisation is heating milk, juice or other food to a set temperature for a short time to kill harmful germs, then cooling it quickly. 2) It is named after the French scientist Louis Pasteur, who showed that tiny microbes make food go bad and cause disease.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons it is an example of how microbes can be killed by heat and how science made food safer; pasteurised milk lasts longer in the fridge and is much less likely to make you ill. It is not the same as boiling: the milk is heated less, so it still tastes like milk. Phrases: «pasteurised milk», «unpasteurised cheese», «the process of pasteurisation».
examples from the lessons: Pasteurisation kills harmful bacteria in milk. | Most milk in shops has gone through pasteurisation. | Louis Pasteur discovered the idea behind pasteurisation. | Pasteurised juice keeps longer than freshly squeezed juice. | Pregnant women are often told to avoid unpasteurised cheese. | In one common method, milk is heated to about 72 °C for 15 seconds. | Our science poster showed the steps of pasteurisation.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. UK spelling with «s», US with «z»; both are correct. Pasteurisation does not kill every microbe, so milk still needs a fridge. It is not sterilisation, which kills everything.

part of speech: verb form (present participle of «peel»: peel, peels, peeled, peeling); adjective (peeling); noun (peelings, usually plural)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Peeling is the -ing form of «peel»: taking the skin off fruit or vegetables, or a covering coming off. 2) Peeling describes paint, wallpaper or skin that is coming off in thin strips or flakes. 3) Peelings are the bits of skin you have peeled off fruit or vegetables.
its sense in the lessons: In the kitchen it is about preparing food («peeling potatoes») and kitchen safety with a peeler. In health it describes skin after sunburn. In stories peeling paint shows an old, uncared-for house. Phrases: «peeling potatoes», «peeling paint», «my skin is peeling», «potato peelings», «peeling off».
examples from the lessons: I am peeling an orange for my lunch. | The old house had peeling paint and a broken gate. | After the sunburn my shoulders started peeling. | Put the potato peelings in the compost bin. | Peel away from your hand when you use a peeler. | The sticker kept peeling off my water bottle. | Mum and I were peeling carrots for the soup.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Peeling» as a noun for the bits is usually plural: peelings. Do not confuse «peel» with «peal» (the ringing of bells). Peeling skin after sunburn means the skin was damaged; wear sunscreen.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A pheromone is a chemical that an animal gives off to send a message to others of its own kind, such as «follow me», «danger» or «I am looking for a mate». 2) Pheromones are smelled or tasted by the other animals, not seen or heard.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on insects and communication: ants leave pheromone trails to food, bees release alarm pheromones, moths find mates by pheromones from far away. Farmers use pheromone traps to catch pests without spraying. Phrases: «pheromone trail», «alarm pheromone», «pheromone trap».
examples from the lessons: Ants follow a pheromone trail from the nest to the crumbs. | When a bee stings, it releases an alarm pheromone that warns other bees. | A male moth can smell a female's pheromone from a long way away. | Farmers hang pheromone traps to catch pests. | Wipe the ants' path with soapy water and the pheromone trail is broken. | Scientists study pheromones to learn how animals talk without words. | Queen bees use pheromones to keep the hive working together.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a pheromone, pheromones. Spelled with «ph» at the start, said «FAIR-uh-mone». Myth: perfumes sold as «human pheromones» to make people fall in love have no good scientific proof.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Pied means having patches of two or more colours, especially black and white, like a magpie or a pied wagtail. 2) The Pied Piper of Hamelin is a character in an old German legend, a piper in colourful clothes who leads away the rats and then the children. 3) (French) «Pied» means «foot» in French; «à pied» means «on foot». It is said roughly «pee-AY» and is not an English word in this sense.
its sense in the lessons: In nature lessons it appears in bird names (pied wagtail, pied kingfisher, pied currawong in Australia). In literature it is the Pied Piper story, about keeping promises. In French lessons it is the word for foot. Phrases: «the Pied Piper», «pied wagtail», «à pied» (French).
examples from the lessons: A pied wagtail hopped across the playground. | The Pied Piper played his pipe and the rats followed him. | The town did not pay the Pied Piper, so he led the children away. | The pied horse had big black and white patches. | In French, «Je vais à l'école à pied» means «I go to school on foot». | A pied currawong was calling from the gum tree. | Magpies have pied feathers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: In English it is an old-fashioned adjective used mostly in names. A «pied-à-terre» is a small second flat in a city (from French, «foot on the ground»). In French, «pied» is said «pee-AY», with no «d» sound at the end.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A placebo is a fake medicine, such as a sugar pill, that has no medicine in it. 2) The placebo effect is when someone feels better just because they believe they have been treated. 3) In a science test of a medicine, one group gets the real medicine and another group gets a placebo, so scientists can compare.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons it teaches fair testing: to know if a medicine really works, you compare it with a placebo, and often neither the patients nor the doctors know who got which (a «blind» test). In everyday talk it means something that makes you feel better without really doing anything. Phrases: «the placebo effect», «given a placebo», «placebo group».
examples from the lessons: Half the volunteers got the new medicine and half got a placebo. | The placebo was just a sugar pill. | Some people felt better because of the placebo effect. | The scientists compared the medicine group with the placebo group. | If the medicine works no better than a placebo, it does not really work. | The lift's «close door» button might be a placebo that does nothing. | Our class did a taste test where some drinks were a placebo.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a placebo, placebos. Said «pluh-SEE-boh». It comes from Latin «I shall please». The placebo effect is real but small, mostly on feelings like pain or tiredness; it does not cure serious diseases.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Plumbing is the system of pipes, taps, toilets and drains that bring clean water into a building and take dirty water away. 2) Plumbing is the job of putting in and fixing these pipes, done by a plumber. 3) (informal, joking) Someone's plumbing can mean the inside of their body, especially the bladder or bowels.
its sense in the lessons: In science and history lessons it shows how clean water and sewers stop disease; the Romans had lead pipes, and «plumbing» comes from the Latin word for lead, «plumbum». In everyday life, leaks and blocked drains are plumbing problems. Phrases: «indoor plumbing», «the plumbing is blocked», «fix the plumbing».
examples from the lessons: The old cottage had no indoor plumbing, so they used a well. | Water was dripping because the plumbing leaked. | My uncle does plumbing and fixes boilers. | Don't flush wipes; they block the plumbing. | Roman towns had surprisingly good plumbing. | Plumbing helped stop diseases like cholera spreading in cities. | When the plumbing froze in winter, we had no water.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: no «a plumbing», no «plumbings». The «b» is silent: «PLUM-ing». Same in «plumber». The chemical symbol for lead, Pb, comes from the same Latin word.

part of speech: noun (a podcast, podcasts); verb (podcast, podcasts, podcasted or podcast, podcasting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A podcast is a series of audio (sometimes video) shows on the internet that you can download or stream and listen to whenever you like. 2) One episode of such a show is also called a podcast. 3) To podcast is to make and publish these shows.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life children listen to podcasts about stories, science, history or sport; in school they may make their own podcast as a speaking project. In media lessons pupils learn that podcasts can share opinions, so they should check facts. Phrases: «listen to a podcast», «a new episode of the podcast», «start a podcast», «host a podcast».
examples from the lessons: We listened to a science podcast in the car. | Our class made a podcast about the Romans. | The podcast comes out every Friday. | My favourite podcast tells spooky stories for kids. | She hosts a podcast about football. | You can subscribe so new podcasts download automatically. | Not everything said on a podcast is true, so check other sources.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a podcast, podcasts. The name comes from iPod + broadcast. A podcast is usually recorded, not live like radio.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (French) «Porc» is the French word for pig, and also for pork, the meat from a pig. It is said roughly «por», with no «c» sound. 2) It is not an English word; in English the meat is «pork» and the animal is «pig».
its sense in the lessons: In French lessons it appears in food topics and on menus: «du porc» means some pork, «une côtelette de porc» is a pork chop. Learners spot that English «pork» came from French after the Norman Conquest, when Norman nobles ate meat with French names (pork, beef, mutton) while English farmers kept the animals with English names (pig, cow, sheep). Phrases: «le porc», «du porc», «rôti de porc» (roast pork).
examples from the lessons: On the French menu, «rôti de porc» means roast pork. | «Je ne mange pas de porc» means «I don't eat pork». | In French, porc sounds like «por». | English «pork» comes from French «porc». | The farmer's pig is «un porc» or «un cochon» in French. | Some people do not eat pork for religious reasons, so the canteen labels dishes with porc. | Our French worksheet matched «le porc» to a picture of ham.
note for the reader of a maths problem: French noun, masculine: le porc. Not English: do not write «porc» in English sentences; write «pork». The final «c» is silent in French. A live pig is more often «un cochon» in everyday French.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A presenter is a person who introduces and hosts a TV or radio programme, or talks to the audience on a show. 2) A presenter is anyone who gives a talk or presentation to a group. 3) (awards) The presenter of a prize is the person who hands it over.
its sense in the lessons: In media lessons it names the person on screen who talks to viewers, such as a news presenter or a children's TV presenter. In school, the pupil giving a talk is the presenter, and good presenters speak clearly and look at the audience. Phrases: «TV presenter», «news presenter», «weather presenter», «guest presenter».
examples from the lessons: The TV presenter smiled and said, «Welcome back!» | The weather presenter warned us about snow. | Each group chose a presenter to speak to the class. | A good presenter looks at the audience, not the floor. | The presenter of the award shook my hand. | She wants to be a nature presenter like David Attenborough. | The radio presenter played my song request.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a presenter, presenters. In the US a TV presenter is often called a «host» or «anchor» (for news). Verb: present (stress on «-SENT»); noun «a present» (a gift) has stress on «PRES-».

part of speech: noun (a preview, previews); verb (preview, previews, previewed, previewing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A preview is a chance to see something before it is shown to everyone, such as a film or a show. 2) A preview is a short look at something coming later, like a trailer or a summary of what a lesson will cover. 3) On a computer, a preview shows how a file, photo or page will look before you print, send or open it. 4) To preview something is to look at it, or show it, in advance.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: film previews and trailers, phone message previews, print preview. In reading lessons, «previewing» a book (looking at the cover, title and headings first) helps you predict and understand. Phrases: «a sneak preview», «print preview», «preview the chapter».
examples from the lessons: We got a sneak preview of the school play at the dress rehearsal. | Click print preview to check the page before you print. | The teacher previewed tomorrow's lesson on fractions. | Before reading, preview the headings and pictures. | My phone shows a preview of each message. | The film preview made it look really scary. | Preview your email before you send it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun; verb is regular (previewed). «Pre-» means before, so preview = view before. Message previews can show private messages on a locked screen, so you can turn them off.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A pug is a small dog with a flat, wrinkly face, a curly tail and short fur, usually pale brown with a black face, or all black. 2) (old slang) «Pug» was once a short word for a boxer (from «pugilist»).
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life pugs are popular pets. In science and animal-welfare talk, pugs are an example of how breeding for flat faces can cause breathing problems, so owners must keep them cool and not let them get too tired. Phrases: «a pug dog», «a pug nose» (a short, turned-up nose).
examples from the lessons: Our neighbour's pug snores very loudly. | The pug wagged its curly tail. | Pugs can overheat on hot days, so walk them in the cool morning. | He has a pug nose, short and turned up. | Flat-faced dogs like pugs can find it hard to breathe. | The pug wore a little coat in the snow. | My friend named her pug Biscuit.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a pug, pugs. «Pug nose» means a short, turned-up nose. Pugs originally came from China and were later loved in Europe.

part of speech: noun (Quechua — the language and the people); adjective (Quechua)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Quechua is a family of languages spoken by millions of Indigenous people in the Andes mountains of South America, mostly in Peru, Bolivia and Ecuador. 2) The Quechua are the peoples who speak these languages. 3) Quechua was the main language of the Inca Empire.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and history lessons about South America and the Incas. Some English words came from Quechua, such as llama, condor, puma, jerky and quinine. Phrases: «speak Quechua», «Quechua people», «Quechua words».
examples from the lessons: Quechua is spoken by millions of people in Peru and Bolivia. | The Incas spoke Quechua. | The word «llama» comes from Quechua. | Many children in the Andes learn Quechua at home and Spanish at school. | Quechua is an official language of Peru and Bolivia. | Quechua farmers grow potatoes high in the mountains. | Our class learned to say hello in Quechua: «Allillanchu?»
note for the reader of a maths problem: Proper noun: write it with a capital Q (Quechua). Said «KETCH-wa». It is not one single language but a group of closely related languages.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Quinine is a bitter medicine made from the bark of the cinchona tree from South America, used for a long time to treat malaria. 2) Quinine gives tonic water its bitter taste.
its sense in the lessons: In science and history lessons it shows medicine coming from plants: Quechua healers in the Andes knew about cinchona bark, and later quinine helped people fight malaria in hot countries. Today doctors use newer drugs for malaria. A fun fact: tonic water glows blue under ultraviolet light because of the quinine. Phrases: «quinine tablets», «tonic water with quinine».
examples from the lessons: Quinine comes from the bark of the cinchona tree. | For hundreds of years quinine was used to treat malaria. | Tonic water tastes bitter because it contains quinine. | Under a UV lamp, tonic water glows blue because of the quinine. | Explorers carried quinine to protect themselves from malaria. | Doctors now use newer medicines for malaria. | Quinine is very bitter, so it was mixed into drinks.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. UK says «KWIN-een», US often «KWY-nine». Medicine should only be taken as a doctor says: tonic water does not prevent malaria.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Radioactivity is the giving off of invisible energy, called radiation, by the centres (nuclei) of some unstable atoms as they break down. 2) Radioactivity is also a measure of how much of this radiation something gives off.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons it is introduced with Marie Curie, who studied it and won two Nobel Prizes, with uranium and radium, nuclear power stations, X-rays and safety signs (the yellow trefoil). In everyday life small amounts of radioactivity are all around us naturally, even in bananas and rocks; large amounts are dangerous. Phrases: «levels of radioactivity», «measure radioactivity», «natural radioactivity».
examples from the lessons: Marie Curie studied radioactivity and discovered radium and polonium. | A Geiger counter clicks when it detects radioactivity. | High levels of radioactivity can damage living cells. | Bananas have a tiny, harmless amount of radioactivity. | After the Chernobyl accident, radioactivity spread over a wide area. | Scientists use radioactivity to date very old objects. | The yellow warning sign means radioactivity is present.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Adjective: radioactive. Radioactivity is not the same as radio waves; radios use a harmless kind of wave. Myth: radioactive things do not glow green like in cartoons.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A raider is a person who makes a sudden attack on a place, especially to steal things or cause damage, for example Viking raiders. 2) A raider is a robber who breaks into a shop or bank suddenly. 3) In sport, games and stories, raiders are attackers who make quick surprise attacks.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons it names Vikings who attacked monasteries and towns by boat, and border raiders. In news it is used for robbers («ram raiders» crash a car into a shop). In stories it means a bandit or attacker. Phrases: «Viking raiders», «ram raiders», «raiders of the lost ark», «fridge raider» (joking: someone who sneaks snacks).
examples from the lessons: Viking raiders attacked the monastery at Lindisfarne. | The raiders sailed away with gold and slaves. | Police caught the bank raiders. | Ram raiders smashed a car through the shop window. | The castle walls kept the raiders out. | My brother is a fridge raider at midnight. | In the game, raiders try to steal your treasure.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a raider, raiders. Verb: raid. Noun: a raid. Do not confuse with «rider» (someone riding a horse or bike).

part of speech: noun (a rand, rand or rands); also the Rand (a region)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The rand is the money of South Africa; one rand is made of 100 cents. Its symbol is R, and its code is ZAR. 2) The Rand (short for the Witwatersrand) is an area of ridges around Johannesburg, famous for gold mines. 3) (rare) A rand is a strip of leather in a shoe.
its sense in the lessons: In maths lessons on money and exchange rates the rand appears with other currencies. In geography it links South Africa with its gold mines. Phrases: «ten rand», «the South African rand», «R50».
examples from the lessons: In South Africa, a loaf of bread costs a few rand. | The rand is divided into 100 cents. | Prices in Cape Town are written with R, as in R25. | Gold was found on the Rand long ago, and Johannesburg grew up around the mines. | If 1 pound buys 20 rand, then 5 pounds buy 100 rand. | She changed her dollars into rand at the airport. | The coin had a springbok on it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural is often «rand» (ten rand), though «rands» is also used. Currency name: lower case «rand»; the region: capital «Rand». Do not confuse with «random» or «Rand» as a surname. In money problems, convert using the rate given: multiply or divide as the problem says.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A rarity is a thing or event that is rare, which means it is not often seen or found. 2) Rarity is the quality of being rare. 3) (collecting, games) Rarity is how rare an item, card or stamp is, which often makes it more valuable.
its sense in the lessons: In nature lessons rare animals or plants are rarities. In everyday life children meet it in trading cards and games, where items have rarity levels like common, rare and legendary. In maths, rare events have low probability. Phrases: «a real rarity», «because of its rarity», «rarity level».
examples from the lessons: Snow in Perth is a rarity. | Because of its rarity, the stamp is worth a lot of money. | That card's rarity makes everyone want it. | A sunny day on our camping trip was a rarity. | The museum shows rarities like a dodo skeleton. | In the game, items come in four rarity levels. | A white kangaroo is a rarity.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable for things (a rarity, rarities), uncountable for the quality. Adjective: rare. Rare things are not always valuable; it depends on whether people want them. In probability, a rare event is unlikely but still possible.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Repetitive means doing or saying the same thing again and again. 2) A repetitive task or job is boring because it is the same every time. 3) In writing, repetitive means using the same words or sentence starts too many times.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons teachers warn against repetitive writing («then … then … then») and suggest varied sentence openers; but repetition can also be used on purpose in poems and songs. In maths and computing, repetitive steps can be done with a loop. In health, repetitive movement can strain muscles. Phrases: «a repetitive job», «repetitive strain injury», «repetitive pattern».
examples from the lessons: Copying lines is repetitive and boring. | Your story is a bit repetitive, so try new sentence openers. | The song has a repetitive chorus that is easy to remember. | A computer is good at repetitive jobs, so we use a loop. | The wallpaper had a repetitive pattern of stars. | Typing all day can cause repetitive strain injury. | The robot does the same repetitive movement thousands of times.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective. Noun: repetition; verb: repeat. Spelling trap: «repetitive», with «-pet-», not «repeatitive». Repetitive is usually a criticism; «rhythmic» or «patterned» can sound kinder.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Replete with something means full of it or well supplied with it. 2) (formal) Replete can also mean very full after eating.
its sense in the lessons: In the stiff exam or book voice it says something has lots of something: «a story replete with adventure». Children meet it in classic books and reading tests; in everyday talk people say «full of» instead. Phrases: «replete with», «feeling replete».
examples from the lessons: The museum is replete with dinosaur bones. | After the huge Christmas dinner, we all sat back, replete. | The garden was replete with flowers. | His essay was replete with spelling mistakes. | The old castle is replete with secret passages. | In plain words, replete with means full of.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal word; normally used with «with». In everyday speech «full of» is better. Do not confuse with «deplete» (to use up), which is almost the opposite.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To restate something is to say it again, often in different, clearer words. 2) (formal) To restate a rule, view or promise is to say it again firmly.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, pupils restate a word problem in their own words to understand it; in writing, a conclusion often restates the main idea. In reading tests, «restate the question in your answer» is a common tip. Phrases: «restate the question», «restate the main idea», «restate in your own words».
examples from the lessons: Start your answer by restating the question. | Can you restate the problem in your own words? | The conclusion restates the main point of the essay. | The head teacher restated the rule about phones. | When I restated the problem, I saw it was a subtraction. | She restated her promise to help. | Restate the fact more simply for younger children.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: restated. «Re-» means again. Similar: rephrase, repeat, paraphrase. Restating is not copying word for word; usually the words change but the meaning stays.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A retriever is a kind of dog bred to fetch and bring back birds that hunters have shot, for example the golden retriever and the Labrador retriever. 2) A retriever is anyone or anything that fetches and brings things back.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life golden retrievers and Labradors are popular, friendly family dogs, and often guide dogs and assistance dogs. In computing, a retriever is a program that fetches information. Phrases: «golden retriever», «Labrador retriever», «a ball retriever».
examples from the lessons: Our golden retriever loves swimming in the lake. | The retriever brought the stick back and dropped it at my feet. | Labrador retrievers are often trained as guide dogs. | A retriever has a soft mouth, so it carries things gently. | The tennis club has a ball retriever on a stick. | Retrievers need lots of exercise. | My cousin's retriever has golden fur.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a retriever, retrievers. Verb: retrieve (fetch back). Spelling: «ie», as in «retrieve».

part of speech: noun (a ripper, rippers); adjective (ripper — Australia, NZ slang)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A ripper is a person or tool that rips or tears things. 2) (Australia, NZ, slang) «Ripper!» means great or excellent; «a ripper» is something really good. 3) «Jack the Ripper» is the name given to an unknown murderer in London long ago; this is a grim, adult part of history.
its sense in the lessons: In Australian and New Zealand speech it is cheerful praise («You little ripper!»). In history it may come up with Victorian London. As a tool word, a «seam ripper» unpicks stitches in sewing. Phrases: «You little ripper!», «a ripper of a day», «seam ripper».
examples from the lessons: That was a ripper of a game, mate! | «You little ripper!» Grandpa shouted when we won. | Mum used a seam ripper to undo the wrong stitches. | It was a ripper day at the beach. | Bluey's dad might call a good cake a ripper. | The police never caught Jack the Ripper.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The slang sense is informal and friendly, mainly Australian and New Zealand. Countable noun: rippers. The name «Jack the Ripper» is about real murders and is not a joke word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A rodeo is a show and competition where cowboys and cowgirls ride bucking horses and bulls, rope calves and race horses round barrels. 2) (informal) A rodeo can mean any noisy, chaotic event. 3) «This isn't my first rodeo» (US, informal) means «I have done this before, I have experience».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and geography it belongs to ranching areas of the USA, Canada (the Calgary Stampede), Australia and Mexico. Some people argue rodeos can be cruel to animals, while others say they are a tradition; both views are discussed. Phrases: «go to the rodeo», «rodeo rider», «not my first rodeo».
examples from the lessons: We watched barrel racing at the rodeo. | The cowboy stayed on the bull for eight seconds. | The Calgary Stampede has one of the biggest rodeos in the world. | Some animal charities say rodeos are cruel to the animals. | Don't worry about me, this isn't my first rodeo. | Rodeo clowns help protect riders who fall off. | The town holds a rodeo every summer.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a rodeo, rodeos (no «e» before the s). Said «ROH-dee-oh» or «roh-DAY-oh». It comes from Spanish «rodear», to go round, because cattle were rounded up.

meaning for a pupil: 1) SA is a short form of South Australia, a state of Australia whose capital is Adelaide. 2) SA is also a short form of South Africa. 3) (French) «Sa» is a French word meaning «his» or «her» before a feminine noun, as in «sa mère» (his or her mother); said like «sah». It is not an English word. 4) (business) After a company name, S.A. is like «Ltd» or «Inc.» in some countries.
its sense in the lessons: In Australian geography SA is used on maps and addresses. In French lessons «sa» is one of the words for his/her (mon, ma, mes; ton, ta, tes; son, sa, ses). As a lower-case «sa» it is usually a fragment of a longer word. Phrases: «Adelaide, SA», «sa sœur» (French: his or her sister).
examples from the lessons: Adelaide is the capital of SA. | Grandma lives in Port Lincoln, SA. | The rugby match was SA against New Zealand. | In French, «sa maison» means his house or her house. | «Elle aime sa chatte» means «She loves her cat». | Write SA in capitals when you mean South Australia.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Write the abbreviation in capitals: SA. In French, «sa» goes with feminine nouns and does not show whether the owner is a boy or a girl: «sa mère» can be his mother or her mother. Not an English word on its own.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Saline means containing salt or salty. 2) Saline (noun), or saline solution, is clean salty water used in medicine, for example to wash wounds, rinse eyes or contact lenses, or in a drip in hospital.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons it comes up with solutions and with the sea: seawater is saline, river water is fresh. In health it is the salt water nurses use. Phrases: «saline solution», «saline drip», «saline water», «a saline lake».
examples from the lessons: Seawater is saline, so you cannot drink it. | The nurse cleaned the cut with saline. | He rinses his contact lenses in saline solution. | In hospital she was given a saline drip. | The Dead Sea is a very saline lake. | We made a saline solution by dissolving salt in water. | Saline nose spray helps clear a blocked nose.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Said «SAY-line». Adjective and uncountable noun. Similar words: salty, briny. Saline solution in medicine is made sterile; homemade salt water is not the same for eyes.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Salsa is a sauce, often spicy, made from chopped tomatoes, onions, chillies and herbs, eaten with tortilla chips and Mexican food. 2) Salsa is a lively dance and a kind of music from Latin America and the Caribbean, especially Cuba and Puerto Rico. 3) In Spanish and Italian, «salsa» simply means sauce.
its sense in the lessons: In cooking lessons it is an easy no-cook recipe that practises knife safety and measuring. In music and PE it is a lively partner dance. Phrases: «tomato salsa», «chips and salsa», «salsa dancing», «salsa class».
examples from the lessons: We dipped tortilla chips in tomato salsa. | This mango salsa is sweet and spicy. | Mum goes to salsa classes on Thursdays. | Salsa music has a fast, bouncy beat. | Chop the tomatoes carefully when making salsa. | Add a little lime juice to the salsa. | They danced salsa at the wedding.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable (some salsa); «a salsa» can mean one kind of sauce or dance. Do not confuse with «salsa verde» (a green herb sauce) or «sauce» in general. Wash hands after chopping chillies and do not touch your eyes.

part of speech: adjective (saturated); verb form (past of «saturate»: saturate, saturates, saturated, saturating)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Saturated means completely soaked with water or another liquid. 2) (science) A saturated solution has so much dissolved in it that no more can dissolve. 3) (food) Saturated fat is a kind of fat found mostly in butter, cheese and fatty meat; eating too much is not good for the heart. 4) A saturated market or place is so full of something that there is no room for more. 5) A saturated colour is strong and bright.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on dissolving: stir salt into water until no more dissolves and the solution is saturated. In health lessons it appears on food labels («saturates»). In everyday life a saturated pitch means a waterlogged field. Phrases: «saturated solution», «saturated fat», «saturated with», «completely saturated».
examples from the lessons: After the storm, the ground was saturated and the match was cancelled. | Keep adding sugar until the water is saturated and crystals stay at the bottom. | Warm water can dissolve more salt before it is saturated. | Butter is high in saturated fat. | My socks were saturated after I stepped in the puddle. | The photo looks better with more saturated colours. | The town is saturated with coffee shops.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective and past form of the verb «saturate». Food labels in the UK call it «saturates». In science: a saturated solution is a fixed limit; heating the water usually raises the limit for solids.

part of speech: adjective (savage; more savage, most savage); noun (a savage, savages — offensive when used about people); verb (savage, savages, savaged, savaging)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Savage means very fierce, violent and cruel, like a savage attack by a wild animal. 2) Savage can mean very severe or harsh, such as savage cuts to spending or savage criticism. 3) To savage someone or something is to attack it fiercely, with teeth or with words. 4) (slang) Savage means boldly harsh, rude in a funny way, or super cool: «That comeback was savage!» 5) (offensive, old) In the past Europeans called other peoples «savages»; this was unfair and racist, and we do not use it about people today.
its sense in the lessons: In stories it describes fierce animals and storms. In history lessons pupils learn that calling Indigenous peoples «savages» was a way of looking down on them. In young people's slang «savage» praises a brutal joke or a bold move. Phrases: «a savage attack», «savage storm», «be savaged by a dog», «that's savage» (slang).
examples from the lessons: The farmer's sheep were savaged by a dog. | A savage storm destroyed the pier. | Critics savaged the new film. | «Your jokes are like your football: weak.» «Oof, savage!» | Old explorers called local people «savages», which was cruel and wrong. | The lion gave a savage roar. | The school faced savage cuts to its budget.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective, verb and noun. Calling people «savages» is offensive. Slang «savage» is a compliment among friends but can hurt if used to be mean. Adverb: savagely.

part of speech: noun (a scallop, scallops); verb (scallop, scallops, scalloped, scalloping)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A scallop is a sea creature with two fan-shaped, ridged shells; it swims by clapping its shells together. 2) Scallop is the meat of this animal eaten as seafood. 3) A scallop is one of a row of curves along an edge, like on a pie crust or lace; to scallop an edge is to cut it into such curves. 4) (Australia, regional) In Victoria and Tasmania a «potato scallop» is a slice of potato fried in batter (elsewhere called a potato cake).
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on sea life, scallops have many tiny eyes along the edge of their shell. In art and sewing, scalloped edges are a decorative pattern. In history, the scallop shell is the badge of pilgrims to Santiago de Compostela. Phrases: «scallop shell», «fried scallops», «scalloped edge», «potato scallop».
examples from the lessons: A scallop can swim by snapping its shells shut. | Scallops have dozens of tiny blue eyes. | We had pan-fried scallops at the seaside restaurant. | Cut the paper with scalloped edges to make a pretty border. | Pilgrims to Santiago carry a scallop shell. | At the fish and chip shop in Melbourne I ordered two potato scallops. | The petrol company Shell uses a scallop shell as its logo.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a scallop, scallops. Said «SKOL-up» or «SKAL-up». Some people are allergic to shellfish like scallops. «Scalloped potatoes» (US) are sliced potatoes baked in sauce.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Scant means very little, hardly enough. 2) Scant can mean a bit less than a stated amount, as in «a scant teaspoon» (not quite a full one).
its sense in the lessons: In books and the formal exam voice it shows that there is not enough of something: «scant evidence», «paid scant attention». In cooking recipes «a scant cup» means slightly less than a full cup. Phrases: «scant attention», «scant regard», «scant evidence», «a scant cup».
examples from the lessons: There was scant food left after the party. | He paid scant attention to the warning signs. | The scientist said there was scant evidence for the claim. | Add a scant teaspoon of salt. | The desert gets scant rain each year. | The explorers had scant hope of rescue.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal word; everyday words are «little», «hardly any», «not much». Used before uncountable nouns (scant attention, scant rain). Not «scanty» exactly: «scanty» often describes clothes that cover little. In recipes, «scant» means a little under the measure.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Scarcely means hardly, almost not at all: «I could scarcely see» means I could only just see. 2) Scarcely … when means that one thing happened almost straight after another. 3) Scarcely can mean surely not: «You can scarcely blame him».
its sense in the lessons: In stories and the formal voice it shows something only just happened or almost did not happen. In reading tests pupils must notice it is a negative word: «scarcely any» means almost none. Phrases: «scarcely any», «scarcely ever», «could scarcely believe», «had scarcely … when».
examples from the lessons: It was so foggy that we could scarcely see the road. | There was scarcely any milk left. | I could scarcely believe my eyes. | We had scarcely sat down when the fire alarm rang. | She scarcely ever watches TV. | The baby is scarcely a week old. | You can scarcely blame him for being tired.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from «scarce». It already has a negative meaning, so do not add «not»: «I could scarcely hear», not «I couldn't scarcely hear». In word problems «scarcely any» means almost zero. Formal inverted order: «Scarcely had we arrived when …».

meaning for a pupil: 1) To scavenge is to search through rubbish or leftovers for something useful, such as food or materials. 2) In nature, animals scavenge when they eat dead animals or scraps they did not kill themselves.
its sense in the lessons: In science food chain lessons, scavengers like vultures, hyenas, crows and foxes clean up dead animals. In everyday life, a «scavenger hunt» is a game of finding a list of things. In stories, characters scavenge for food when they are lost or poor. Phrases: «scavenge for food», «scavenger hunt», «scavenging birds».
examples from the lessons: Seagulls scavenge for chips on the beach. | Vultures scavenge on dead animals. | Foxes scavenge through bins at night. | The castaways scavenged the wreck for tools. | We did a scavenger hunt in the park. | Raccoons scavenge in city rubbish in North America. | Scavenging animals help recycle nutrients in nature.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: scavenged. Noun: scavenger. A scavenger is different from a predator, which hunts and kills its food; some animals do both.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A Scotsman is a man from Scotland. 2) «The Scotsman» is the name of a newspaper in Edinburgh. 3) «The Flying Scotsman» is a famous steam train that ran between London and Edinburgh.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and history lessons it names people of Scotland: a Scotswoman is a woman, and «Scots» or «Scottish people» covers everyone. Phrases: «a proud Scotsman», «the Flying Scotsman».
examples from the lessons: The Scotsman wore a kilt at the wedding. | My grandad is a Scotsman from Glasgow. | The Flying Scotsman is a famous steam engine. | A Scotsman, an Englishman and an Irishman walked into a joke. | Alexander Graham Bell, who worked on the telephone, was a Scotsman. | We saw the Flying Scotsman at the railway museum in York.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Write it with a capital S: Scotsman. Plural: Scotsmen. People from Scotland are «Scottish» or «Scots», not «Scotch»; «Scotch» is used for whisky and some foods (Scotch egg). For a woman: Scotswoman.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Seagrass is a flowering plant that grows underwater in shallow seas, forming green meadows on the sea floor. 2) Seagrass is also a strong grass-like material used to weave mats and baskets.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on habitats it is a home and food for animals such as dugongs, manatees, turtles, seahorses and baby fish; seagrass meadows also store a lot of carbon and calm the waves. Unlike seaweed, seagrass has roots, leaves and flowers. Phrases: «seagrass meadow», «seagrass bed», «protect the seagrass».
examples from the lessons: Dugongs graze on seagrass like cows on grass. | Seagrass meadows are nurseries for baby fish. | Seagrass has roots, stems and even flowers. | Boat anchors can tear up seagrass beds. | Shark Bay in Western Australia has huge seagrass meadows. | Our kitchen has a seagrass mat. | Seagrass helps store carbon from the air.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable (seagrass), sometimes «seagrasses» for different kinds. Trap: seagrass is not seaweed; seaweeds are algae with no true roots or flowers. Also written «sea grass».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Sep or Sep. is a short form of September, the ninth month. 2) Sep. can be a short form of «separate» in notes. 3) As a lower-case «sep», it is usually a fragment of a longer word, not a word on its own.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life short month names appear on calendars, tickets, receipts and food labels. Some writers use «Sept» instead. Phrases: «Sep» on a calendar.
examples from the lessons: On the calendar, Sep is short for September. | The school year in England starts in Sep. | Some people write Sept instead of Sep. | Jan, Feb, Mar … Aug, Sep, Oct, Nov, Dec. | «Sep» on the label shows the month the jam is best before. | Write the full word, September, in your story.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Write with a capital S when it means September: Sep or Sept. It is not a word to use in sentences; write «September» in full in schoolwork. September is the 9th month and has 30 days.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Severity is how serious, strong or bad something is, such as the severity of an illness, an injury, a storm or a punishment. 2) Severity can mean strictness or harshness, as in a teacher's severity.
its sense in the lessons: In science and safety it is used to rank dangers: storms, earthquakes and allergies are graded by severity. In first aid, you judge the severity of an injury to know whether to call for help. In stories it describes a stern, strict manner. Phrases: «the severity of», «depending on the severity», «reduce the severity».
examples from the lessons: Doctors decide treatment by the severity of the injury. | The severity of the storm surprised everyone. | Earthquakes are measured to show their severity. | Her allergy varies in severity from a rash to trouble breathing. | The punishment was too harsh for the severity of the crime. | He spoke with such severity that the room went silent. | Wearing a helmet reduces the severity of head injuries.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Adjective: severe. Spelling: «severity», not «severety». Similar words: seriousness, strength; for people: strictness, sternness.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A shearer is a person whose job is to cut the wool off sheep. 2) A shearer can be any person or machine that shears or cuts.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and history lessons about Australia and New Zealand, shearers travel from farm to farm in shearing season, working in a woolshed; fast shearers can shear hundreds of sheep in a day. It is hard physical work. Phrases: «a sheep shearer», «gun shearer» (Australia, NZ slang: a very fast, skilled shearer), «shearers' cook».
examples from the lessons: The shearer clipped the fleece off in one piece. | Shearers travel from station to station in the spring. | A gun shearer can shear over 200 sheep a day. | The shearer's back aches after a long day in the woolshed. | My uncle is a shearer in New Zealand. | Shearing doesn't hurt the sheep, like a haircut. | If one shearer takes 4 minutes per sheep, how many can she shear in an hour? 15.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a shearer, shearers. Verb: shear (sheared, shorn). Do not confuse «shear» (cut) with «sheer» (steep or see-through).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (UK) A shire is an old word for a county, a large area of a country; many English counties end in «-shire», such as Yorkshire and Lancashire. 2) (Australia) A shire is a country local council area with its own council. 3) The Shire is the peaceful home of the hobbits in Tolkien's books. 4) A Shire horse is a very large, strong farm horse from England.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons it explains county names (Yorkshire, Hampshire); «the shires» means the countryside of England. In Australia, kids see «Shire of …» on signs. Phrases: «the shires», «Shire horse», «shire council».
examples from the lessons: Yorkshire and Lancashire are counties ending in -shire. | In Australia, the local shire council collects the rubbish. | Shire horses once pulled ploughs on farms. | Frodo and Bilbo lived in the Shire. | A Shire horse can weigh as much as a small car. | The road sign said «Welcome to the Shire of Broome».
note for the reader of a maths problem: In county names «-shire» is usually said «-sher», like «YORK-sher», not «-shy-er». On its own «shire» rhymes with «fire». Capital letter for names: the Shire, Shire horse.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A siphonophore is a strange sea animal, related to jellyfish, that is really a colony of many tiny animal parts joined together and working as one body. 2) Each part has its own job: some swim, some catch food, some digest it, some make young.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on ocean life it is an amazing example of teamwork in nature. The Portuguese man o' war is a famous siphonophore with stinging tentacles; some deep-sea siphonophores are longer than a blue whale, though very thin. Phrases: «a giant siphonophore», «colony of zooids».
examples from the lessons: A siphonophore looks like one animal but is made of many tiny parts. | The Portuguese man o' war is a siphonophore, not a true jellyfish. | Scientists filmed a giant siphonophore deep under the sea off Australia. | Some siphonophores are longer than a blue whale. | Do not touch a man o' war on the beach; it can still sting. | In a siphonophore, some parts swim and some parts catch food. | Many siphonophores glow in the dark.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Said «SY-fon-oh-for» or «sy-FON-oh-for». The tiny parts are called zooids. Not every sea jelly is a siphonophore.

part of speech: verb form (past and past participle of «smuggle»: smuggle, smuggles, smuggled, smuggling); adjective (smuggled)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Smuggled means secretly taken into or out of a country against the law, such as smuggled goods, drugs or animals. 2) Smuggled can mean secretly brought somewhere it is not allowed, like sweets smuggled into class. 3) As an adjective, smuggled describes goods brought in this way.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons: smugglers on the coasts of Cornwall and other places brought in tea, brandy and lace to avoid taxes. In news and law: smuggling is a crime; endangered animals and their parts are sometimes smuggled. In everyday life it can be playful («I smuggled a biscuit»). Phrases: «smuggled in», «smuggled out», «smuggled goods».
examples from the lessons: Long ago, tea and brandy were smuggled into Cornwall at night. | Border police found smuggled parrots in a suitcase. | She smuggled a torch into her bedroom to read after lights out. | The prisoners smuggled out a secret letter. | Smuggled ivory hurts elephants. | He smuggled a chocolate bar into the cinema. | The pirates hid the smuggled goods in a cave.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past and participle of «smuggle»; double «g». Noun: smuggler, smuggling. Smuggling things across borders is a crime; the joking sense (sweets into class) is just breaking a small rule.

part of speech: noun (a snag, snags); verb (snag, snags, snagged, snagging)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A snag is a small hidden problem or difficulty: «The only snag is that it's raining». 2) A snag is a sharp or rough bit that catches on things, or a pull or tear in cloth caused by catching on it. 3) To snag something is to catch or tear it on something sharp. 4) (informal) To snag something is to get it quickly, like snagging the last seat. 5) (Australia, informal) A snag is a sausage, especially on a barbecue: a «sausage sizzle» sells snags in bread.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life it names small problems in plans and pulls in jumpers or tights. In Australia snags are the classic barbecue sausage, often sold at school fetes and outside shops at elections. Phrases: «hit a snag», «the only snag», «snag a jumper», «snag in bread».
examples from the lessons: Our plan hit a snag when the bus was late. | The only snag is that we have no glue. | My jumper snagged on the fence. | There's a snag in your tights. | I snagged the last cupcake! | We bought snags at the school sausage sizzle. | Throw a few snags on the barbie, mate.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun; verb doubles the «g»: snagged, snagging. In Australia and New Zealand «snag» = sausage (informal). «Hit a snag» means meet a problem, not hit something.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A snailfish is a small, soft, tadpole-shaped fish with smooth, jelly-like skin and no scales. 2) Some snailfish live deeper in the ocean than almost any other fish, in deep trenches thousands of metres down.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on the deep sea it shows how animals adapt to huge pressure, cold and darkness: a snailfish was filmed in a deep ocean trench at over 8,000 metres, one of the deepest fish ever seen. Phrases: «deep-sea snailfish», «hadal snailfish».
examples from the lessons: A snailfish has soft, jelly-like skin and no scales. | Scientists filmed a snailfish more than 8,000 metres down. | Snailfish can live under huge water pressure. | The snailfish looked like a pale, wiggly tadpole. | Some snailfish live in cold shallow seas, others in deep trenches. | No fish has been found much deeper than the deepest snailfish.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural usually «snailfish» (like «fish»), sometimes «snailfishes» for kinds. It is a fish, not a snail; the name is about its soft body.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The SNP is the Scottish National Party, a political party in Scotland that wants Scotland to become an independent country, separate from the United Kingdom. 2) (science) An SNP, said «snip», is a single-nucleotide polymorphism: a place where one letter of DNA differs between people.
its sense in the lessons: In politics lessons about the UK, the SNP is a major party in the Scottish Parliament at Holyrood and sends MPs to Westminster; supporters and opponents of independence disagree, and both views are held by many Scots. In science, SNPs help explain why people's DNA is slightly different. Phrases: «SNP leader», «SNP MPs», «vote SNP».
examples from the lessons: The SNP wants Scotland to be independent. | Some people in Scotland vote SNP and some vote for other parties. | The SNP sits in the Scottish Parliament in Edinburgh. | In a vote, Scotland chose to stay in the UK, but the debate goes on. | Scientists compare SNPs to study families and illnesses. | An SNP is a one-letter difference in DNA.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always written in capitals: SNP. «The SNP» for the party; «an SNP» for the DNA term (said «snip»). Not a word on its own.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To solidify is to become solid, or to make something become solid, usually when a liquid cools or freezes. 2) To solidify a plan, friendship or idea is to make it firmer and more certain.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on states of matter it is the change from liquid to solid (freezing): water solidifies into ice at 0 °C, lava solidifies into rock, melted chocolate solidifies in the fridge. It is the opposite of melting. Phrases: «solidify into», «allow to solidify», «solidify a friendship».
examples from the lessons: Water solidifies into ice at 0 °C. | When lava cools, it solidifies into rock. | Put the jelly in the fridge to solidify. | The melted wax solidified into a candle. | Candle wax melts when hot and solidifies when it cools. | Working on the project together solidified their friendship. | Melted chocolate solidifies as it cools.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: solidifies, solidified (y changes to i). Noun: solidification. Opposite: melt. Freezing is solidifying, even for hot things like metal or lava, which «freeze» at high temperatures.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Somerset is a county in the south-west of England, famous for farms, apples and cider, Cheddar cheese, the Somerset Levels and the city of Bath. 2) «Somerset» is also used in place names in other countries, such as towns in Australia and the USA, and as a name. 3) It is sometimes confused with «somersault», a forward roll in the air, which sounds similar.
its sense in the lessons: In UK geography lessons it is a county with Glastonbury, Wells, Cheddar Gorge and the Somerset Levels, which flood in winter. Phrases: «in Somerset», «Somerset cider».
examples from the lessons: Cheddar cheese first came from the village of Cheddar in Somerset. | Glastonbury is in Somerset. | The Somerset Levels often flood in winter. | We went camping in Somerset and saw apple orchards. | Somerset is in the south-west of England. | Somerset House is a big building in London.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Proper noun: always a capital S. Said «SUM-er-set». Not the same as «somersault» (a roll in the air), although they sound alike.

part of speech: noun (sourdough, uncountable; a sourdough, sourdoughs for loaves)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Sourdough is bread made with a starter, a mix of flour and water full of wild yeast and bacteria, instead of packet yeast; it tastes slightly sour. 2) A sourdough starter is the bubbly mixture kept alive and «fed» with flour and water to make this bread. 3) (US, old) A sourdough was an old-timer in Alaska or the Yukon, especially a gold prospector.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons it shows microbes at work: the yeast makes carbon dioxide gas, which makes bread rise, and the bacteria make acid, which gives the sour taste. In everyday life many families bake sourdough at home. Phrases: «a sourdough loaf», «sourdough starter», «feed the starter».
examples from the lessons: We had sourdough toast for breakfast. | Our sourdough starter bubbles because of the wild yeast. | Feed the starter with flour and water every day. | Sourdough tastes a bit sour because of the bacteria. | The bakery sells a crusty sourdough loaf. | Gas bubbles from the yeast make holes in sourdough. | San Francisco is famous for its sourdough.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable as bread (some sourdough), countable as loaves (two sourdoughs). It is one word. The sour taste is from lactic acid, the same acid as in yogurt.

part of speech: noun (a sphinx, sphinxes or sphinges; the Sphinx)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The Great Sphinx is a huge ancient stone statue in Egypt with a lion's body and a human head, near the pyramids of Giza. 2) A sphinx is any statue or creature in myths with a lion's body and a human (or other animal's) head. 3) In Greek myths, the Sphinx was a monster who asked travellers a riddle and ate those who got it wrong. 4) A sphinx is a person who is mysterious and hard to read. 5) A Sphynx is a hairless breed of cat (spelled with a «y»).
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons on Ancient Egypt and Greece. The Greek Sphinx's riddle is a famous puzzle: «What walks on four legs in the morning, two at noon and three in the evening?» The answer: a human (crawling baby, adult, old person with a stick). Phrases: «the Great Sphinx», «the riddle of the Sphinx», «sphinx-like smile».
examples from the lessons: The Great Sphinx guards the pyramids at Giza. | The Sphinx has a lion's body and a human head. | Oedipus solved the riddle of the Sphinx. | The Sphinx's nose has been missing for hundreds of years. | She gave a sphinx-like smile and said nothing. | A Sphynx cat has no fur and feels warm like a peach. | We built a model sphinx from clay.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital S for the famous statue or the Greek monster: the Sphinx. Plural: sphinxes. The cat breed is spelled «Sphynx». Myth: the story that Napoleon's soldiers shot off the nose is not supported by evidence; it was damaged earlier.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A spoiler is information that tells you what happens in a story, film or game, especially the ending, before you have seen it. 2) A spoiler on a car or plane is a flat part that changes the air flow to keep it steady or slow it down. 3) (politics) A spoiler is a candidate who cannot win but takes votes away from another candidate. 4) A spoiler is someone who spoils things for others.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and online, people write «spoiler alert!» before giving away an ending, so others can stop reading. In science and design, spoilers on race cars push them down onto the road. Phrases: «spoiler alert», «no spoilers», «spoiler-free review», «rear spoiler».
examples from the lessons: No spoilers, please, I haven't finished the book! | Spoiler alert: the wolf does not get the pigs. | My brother told me the ending, what a spoiler. | The racing car has a big spoiler at the back. | Planes raise spoilers on the wings to slow down after landing. | This review is spoiler-free. | Don't be a spoiler, let her guess the answer.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a spoiler, spoilers. From the verb «spoil». Be kind online: mark spoilers so you don't ruin a story for others.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A spoonerism is a slip of the tongue where you swap the first sounds of two words, often by accident and with a funny result: «a well-boiled icicle» instead of «a well-oiled bicycle». 2) It is named after William Spooner, an Oxford teacher who was said to make this mistake often.
its sense in the lessons: In English and language lessons it is a fun wordplay puzzle, often used in jokes and olympiad word games; it shows how we plan sounds before we speak. Phrases: «make a spoonerism», «a famous spoonerism».
examples from the lessons: «Tease my ears» for «ease my tears» is a spoonerism. | Saying «fighting a liar» instead of «lighting a fire» is a spoonerism. | Our teacher made a spoonerism and said «bunny phone» for «funny bone». | Write three spoonerisms of your own. | Many famous spoonerisms were probably invented by Spooner's students. | A spoonerism swaps sounds, not letters: «chew the dores» for «do the chores».
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Spoonerisms swap sounds, so spelling may change. Most famous examples credited to Spooner were made up by others.

part of speech: noun (stealth, uncountable); adjective (stealth, used before a noun: a stealth plane)
