meaning for a pupil: 1) Stealth is moving or acting quietly and secretly so that no one notices you. 2) Stealth technology makes planes, ships or other machines hard to detect by radar. 3) (games) Stealth is a style of video game or play where you sneak past enemies instead of fighting.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, cats, spies and ninjas move with stealth. In science and nature lessons, predators use stealth to catch prey. In gaming talk «stealth mode» means sneaking. Phrases: «by stealth», «with stealth», «stealth mode», «stealth bomber».
examples from the lessons: The cat crept towards the bird with great stealth. | The spies entered the castle by stealth. | A stealth plane is hard to see on radar. | Owls hunt with stealth because their feathers make almost no sound. | I used stealth to get a biscuit without Mum noticing. | In the game, stealth mode lets you sneak past guards. | Tigers rely on stealth, not speed, to get close.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: no «a stealth» (but «a stealth plane» is fine). Adjective: stealthy; adverb: stealthily. Said with «ea» as in «health».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A stickleback is a small fish with sharp spines on its back, found in ponds, streams and coastal waters of the Northern Hemisphere. 2) The male three-spined stickleback builds a nest of plants and turns red underneath in the breeding season.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on ponds, food chains and animal behaviour, sticklebacks are easy to watch: the male builds a nest, guards the eggs and fans water over them. Children in the UK, Ireland and Canada may catch them in a net at a pond (and should put them back). Phrases: «three-spined stickleback», «pond dipping».
examples from the lessons: We caught a stickleback while pond dipping and then let it go. | The stickleback has spiky spines on its back. | The male stickleback builds a nest and guards the eggs. | In spring the male stickleback's belly turns red. | Herons and kingfishers eat sticklebacks. | Sticklebacks raise their spines so bigger fish can't swallow them. | Scientists study sticklebacks to learn how animals change over time.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a stickleback, sticklebacks. Compound of «stickle» (spine, prickle) + «back». Handle gently with wet hands and return to the water.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A stimulus is something that causes a living thing to react, such as light, sound, heat or touch. 2) A stimulus is something that encourages activity or growth, such as a reward or extra money. 3) (money) A stimulus is money a government spends to help the economy grow, such as stimulus payments.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on senses and the nervous system, a stimulus is detected by a sense organ and causes a response: touching something hot (stimulus) makes you pull your hand away (response). Plants respond to stimuli too: shoots grow towards light. Phrases: «stimulus and response», «respond to a stimulus», «a stimulus package».
examples from the lessons: A bright light is a stimulus that makes your pupils shrink. | The bell was a stimulus that made the dogs expect food. | Plants grow towards the stimulus of light. | Touching a hot pan is a stimulus; pulling your hand away is the response. | The prize was a stimulus to work harder. | The government gave a stimulus payment to families. | Different stimuli make us react in different ways.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: stimuli (said «STIM-you-lie»), not «stimuluses». Verb: stimulate. Do not confuse with «stimulant», which is a substance like caffeine that makes the body more active.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A stoat is a small, fierce, meat-eating animal with a long thin body, short legs, brown fur and a black tip on its tail. 2) In cold places a stoat's fur turns white in winter, except for the black tail tip; it is then called ermine.
its sense in the lessons: In nature lessons on British and Irish wildlife, stoats hunt rabbits much larger than themselves. In New Zealand stoats were brought in and became pests that kill native birds like kiwi, so they are trapped. In stories (Wind in the Willows) stoats and weasels are the baddies. Phrases: «stoat and weasel», «ermine fur».
examples from the lessons: A stoat can kill a rabbit bigger than itself. | The stoat's fur turned white in winter, but its tail tip stayed black. | In New Zealand, stoats are pests that eat kiwi chicks. | Rangers set traps to protect native birds from stoats. | How to tell a stoat from a weasel: the stoat is bigger and has a black tail tip. | The stoat danced to confuse the rabbit. | In The Wind in the Willows, stoats and weasels take over Toad Hall.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a stoat, stoats. Similar: weasel (smaller, no black tail tip). «Ermine» is the white winter fur, once used on royal robes. Ireland has stoats but no weasels.

part of speech: noun (a stocking, stockings); verb form (-ing of «stock»: stock, stocks, stocked, stocking)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A stocking is a long, thin covering for the foot and leg, usually worn by women, often in pairs. 2) A Christmas stocking is a big sock hung up on Christmas Eve to be filled with small presents. 3) Stocking is the -ing form of «stock»: putting goods on shelves, or filling something with supplies, like stocking a pond with fish. 4) A «stocking filler» (UK) or «stocking stuffer» (US) is a small, cheap present.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and Christmas stories it names the stocking for Santa's presents. In shops «stocking the shelves» is a job. In farming «stocking rate» is how many animals per area of land, a maths idea. Phrases: «Christmas stocking», «stocking filler», «in stockinged feet», «stocking up on».
examples from the lessons: I hung my stocking by the fireplace on Christmas Eve. | In the morning my stocking was full of sweets and a tangerine. | The shop worker was stocking the shelves with milk. | Gran wore thick stockings in winter. | A pencil is a good stocking filler. | We are stocking up on food before the snowstorm. | The farmer is stocking the field with ten sheep per hectare.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a stocking, stockings (often a pair). «In stockinged feet» means wearing socks or stockings but no shoes. «Stocking up» means buying lots of supplies.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Strontium is a soft, silvery metal, a chemical element with the symbol Sr and atomic number 38. 2) Strontium compounds give fireworks and flares a bright red colour.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on elements and the periodic table it is in the same group as calcium and magnesium. Fireworks are a fun example: strontium makes red, copper makes blue, barium makes green, sodium makes yellow. It is named after Strontian, a village in Scotland where it was found. A radioactive kind, strontium-90, is dangerous and was released by nuclear tests and accidents. Phrases: «strontium salts», «strontium-90».
examples from the lessons: Strontium makes fireworks burn bright red. | The symbol for strontium is Sr. | Strontium was named after a village in Scotland. | Strontium is a metal in the same group as calcium. | Red emergency flares contain strontium. | Strontium-90 is a dangerous radioactive form.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Said «STRON-tee-um» or «STRON-shum». Chemical symbol Sr with a small r. Ordinary strontium is not radioactive; only some kinds (isotopes) are.

part of speech: adjective (stunted); verb form (past of «stunt»: stunt, stunts, stunted, stunting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Stunted means smaller or shorter than normal because growth has been stopped or slowed, often by poor food, illness or a hard place to live. 2) Stunted can describe something that has not developed properly, like stunted progress.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on plants it is a result of too little light, water or nutrients, which pupils test in fair-test experiments. In geography and health, stunted growth in children is caused by not having enough good food over a long time, an important world problem. Phrases: «stunted growth», «stunted trees», «stunt the growth of».
examples from the lessons: The plant kept in the dark was pale and stunted. | High on the mountain only stunted trees could grow. | Children without enough food can have stunted growth. | Wind and salt left the trees stunted and bent. | Our results showed that plants with no water were stunted. | The war stunted the town's growth for many years.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past form of «stunt» used as an adjective. «Stunt» also means a daring trick (a stunt), which is a different word. Myth: coffee does not stunt children's growth, but it is still not good for children.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A sunbeam is a ray or narrow beam of sunlight, especially one you can see shining through a gap, a window or clouds. 2) (informal, UK) «Ray of sunshine» or «sunbeam» can be a fond name for a cheerful child.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons sunbeams show that light travels in straight lines; you can see the beam because dust or water droplets scatter the light. In stories sunbeams make scenes warm and hopeful. Phrases: «a sunbeam through the window», «dust dancing in a sunbeam».
examples from the lessons: The cat lay asleep in a warm sunbeam. | Dust danced in the sunbeam from the window. | Sunbeams broke through the clouds after the storm. | A sunbeam shows that light travels in straight lines. | We could see sunbeams shining down through the forest trees. | «Morning, sunbeam!» said Nan when I came down to breakfast.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a sunbeam, sunbeams. One word. You see a beam only when tiny bits in the air, like dust or mist, scatter the light into your eyes. Never look straight at the sun.

part of speech: verb form (past participle of «swear»: swear, swears, swore, sworn, swearing); adjective (sworn)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Sworn is the past participle of «swear»: «I have sworn to keep the secret». 2) Sworn means made with a serious promise: a sworn statement or sworn evidence is given after promising to tell the truth. 3) Sworn enemies or sworn friends are completely and permanently enemies or friends. 4) Sworn can also come from «swear» meaning to use rude words: «He has sworn at the referee».
its sense in the lessons: In law, witnesses in court are «sworn in»: they promise to tell the truth, sometimes on the Bible or by another promise. In stories «sworn enemies» are bitter rivals and «sworn to secrecy» means promised not to tell. Phrases: «sworn to secrecy», «sworn enemies», «sworn in», «sworn statement».
examples from the lessons: The knights had sworn to protect the queen. | I was sworn to secrecy about the surprise party. | Cats and dogs in cartoons are often sworn enemies. | The new president was sworn in. | The witness gave sworn evidence in court. | He has sworn never to eat sprouts again. | The player was sent off after he had sworn at the referee.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Forms: swear, swore (past), sworn (with have/had/be). Wrong: «I have swore». «Sworn in» means officially started a job by taking an oath. Swearing as using bad words is rude and breaks school rules.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The taka is the money of Bangladesh; one taka is made of 100 poisha. Its symbol is ৳ and its code is BDT. 2) (Bengali) «Taka» in Bengali also simply means money or a rupee-like coin; it is not an English word in that sense.
its sense in the lessons: In maths lessons on world currencies and exchange rates, and in geography lessons about Bangladesh, the taka appears in shopping problems. Phrases: «fifty taka», «Bangladeshi taka».
examples from the lessons: In Dhaka, a cup of tea costs only a few taka. | The taka is the money of Bangladesh. | A taka is divided into 100 poisha. | If one pound is worth 140 taka, then 3 pounds are worth 420 taka. | The banknote showed the Bangladeshi flag and said taka. | Our worksheet compared prices in taka, rupees and dollars.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural usually «taka» (ten taka). Said «TAH-kah». In money problems, use the rate given and multiply or divide.

part of speech: noun (a tam, tams); abbreviation or fragment (tam)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A tam (short for tam-o'-shanter) is a soft, round, flat woollen cap, often with a bobble (pom-pom) on top, traditionally worn in Scotland. 2) (Ukrainian, in Latin letters) «Tam» means «there» in Ukrainian (там), said like «tum»; it is not an English word in that sense. 3) Tam is also a short form of the name Tamsin or Thomas (a name).
its sense in the lessons: In geography and history it is part of traditional Scottish dress. «Tam o' Shanter» is a poem by Robert Burns about a farmer chased by witches. In Ukrainian lessons «tut i tam» means «here and there». Phrases: «a tartan tam», «tam-o'-shanter», «tut i tam» (Ukrainian).
examples from the lessons: The piper wore a tartan tam with a red bobble. | In winter Nan knits me a woolly tam. | «Tam o' Shanter» is a poem by Robert Burns. | In Ukrainian, «Vin tam» means «He is there». | My friend Tam plays the bagpipes. | A tam is softer and flatter than a beanie.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a tam, tams. Not to be confused with a «tam-tam», a large gong. In Ukrainian the word is written там in Cyrillic.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A tamale is a Mexican and Central American food made of corn dough (masa) filled with meat, cheese, beans or vegetables, wrapped in a corn husk or banana leaf and steamed. 2) You unwrap and throw away the husk before eating.
its sense in the lessons: In food and culture lessons, tamales are made by families together, especially for festivals and Christmas in Mexico and in Mexican-American homes in the USA; making tamales together is called a «tamalada». Phrases: «chicken tamales», «a dozen tamales», «sweet tamales».
examples from the lessons: We steamed tamales wrapped in corn husks. | Grandma makes tamales every Christmas. | Don't eat the corn husk, just the tamale inside. | Some tamales are sweet and filled with fruit. | The whole family helped fold the tamales. | A Mexican food truck sold chicken tamales. | In Central America, tamales are often wrapped in banana leaves.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a tamale, tamales. Said «tuh-MAH-lee». In Spanish one is «un tamal», plural «tamales»; English made «tamale» from the plural.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A taproot is a large main root that grows straight down into the ground, with smaller roots growing off it. 2) Carrots, parsnips, radishes and dandelions have taproots.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on plants it is compared with fibrous roots (many thin roots, like grass). A taproot anchors the plant and reaches water deep down; in carrots and beetroot it also stores food, which is why we eat it. Phrases: «a long taproot», «taproot and fibrous roots».
examples from the lessons: A carrot is a taproot that stores food. | Dandelions are hard to pull up because of their long taproot. | Grass has fibrous roots, but a carrot has a taproot. | The oak tree's taproot grows deep to find water. | Draw a taproot and label the side roots. | Parsnips and radishes are taproots too.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; one word (sometimes «tap root»). Opposite type: fibrous roots. A taproot is still a root, not a stem, even when we eat it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A tarsier is a tiny primate from islands in South-East Asia, such as the Philippines and Borneo, with huge round eyes, long back legs and a long thin tail. 2) Each tarsier eye is about as big as its brain.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on adaptations, the tarsier is nocturnal: its huge eyes help it see at night, and it can turn its head almost all the way round like an owl. It eats insects and leaps between branches. Some kinds are endangered because their forests are cut down. Phrases: «Philippine tarsier», «tarsier's eyes».
examples from the lessons: The tarsier has eyes as big as its brain. | Tarsiers hunt insects at night. | A tarsier can turn its head almost right round. | The tarsier leaps from tree to tree on its long legs. | Tarsiers live on islands in South-East Asia. | Loud noise and camera flashes can stress tarsiers, so visitors must be quiet.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a tarsier, tarsiers. Said «TAR-see-er». Its name comes from its long ankle bones (tarsus). A tarsier is a primate, related to monkeys and apes, not a rodent.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A teapot is a pot with a handle, a lid and a spout, used for making and pouring tea. 2) «I'm a Little Teapot» is a children's song with actions.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life in the UK, Ireland, Australia, New Zealand and Canada, tea is made in a teapot or with a teabag in a mug. In kitchen safety, a hot teapot can scald, so children should be careful. In maths and science, a teapot holds a capacity (for example 1 litre) and teaches pouring and measuring. Phrases: «put the kettle on», «a pot of tea», «a storm in a teapot» (US: a big fuss about nothing; UK says «a storm in a teacup»).
examples from the lessons: Nan poured the tea from a flowery teapot. | Warm the teapot before you make the tea. | Be careful, the teapot is full of hot tea. | We sang «I'm a Little Teapot» and did the actions. | The teapot holds 1 litre, so it fills four 250 ml cups. | The spout of the teapot dripped on the tablecloth. | In Alice in Wonderland the Dormouse is pushed into a teapot.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a teapot, teapots. One word. UK idiom: «a storm in a teacup» means a lot of fuss about something small.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A theropod is a member of a large group of dinosaurs that walked on two legs, mostly meat-eaters, such as Tyrannosaurus rex, Velociraptor and Allosaurus. 2) Birds are living theropods: scientists say birds evolved from small feathered theropod dinosaurs.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on dinosaurs and fossils, theropods had hollow bones, three main toes and sharp teeth or beaks; many had feathers. It is a key example of evolution: a robin is a living relative of T. rex. Phrases: «theropod dinosaurs», «a large theropod», «theropod footprints».
examples from the lessons: T. rex was a huge theropod. | Theropods walked on two legs. | Many theropods had feathers. | Scientists say birds are living theropod dinosaurs. | The fossil footprints had three toes, so they were made by a theropod. | Velociraptor was a theropod about the size of a turkey.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Said «THEER-oh-pod». Means «beast foot» in Greek. Myth: Velociraptor was not as big as in films; it was small and feathered.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A thesaurus is a book or website that lists words grouped with others of similar meaning (synonyms), and sometimes opposite meaning (antonyms). 2) You use it to find a better or more exact word.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons a thesaurus helps make writing more interesting: instead of «said», you might find «whispered», «shouted» or «muttered». Pupils learn to check the meaning in a dictionary, because synonyms are not always exact matches. Phrases: «look it up in a thesaurus», «use a thesaurus», «online thesaurus».
examples from the lessons: I used a thesaurus to find another word for «big». | The thesaurus gave «enormous», «huge» and «gigantic». | Check the meaning in a dictionary before using a word from the thesaurus. | My thesaurus lists antonyms too. | Instead of «nice», the thesaurus suggested «kind», «pleasant» and «lovely». | The class shared one thesaurus per table. | A dinosaur called «Thesaurus» is a common classroom joke.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Plural: thesauruses or thesauri. Said «thi-SOR-us». A dictionary explains meanings; a thesaurus gives similar words. Trap: a word from a thesaurus may not fit your sentence, for example «colossal» for a «big» mistake is fine, but not for a «big sister».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A thriller is an exciting book, film or TV show full of suspense and danger, often about crime, spies or chases, that keeps you wanting to know what happens next. 2) (informal) A thriller is any very exciting event, like a match that is close until the end.
its sense in the lessons: In reading lessons it is a genre, with features like cliffhangers, a ticking clock, twists and a hero in danger. In sport talk, «a thriller» is a close, exciting game. Phrases: «a spy thriller», «a crime thriller», «a real thriller», «edge of your seat».
examples from the lessons: The spy thriller kept me reading late into the night. | The match was a thriller that ended 4–3. | A good thriller ends chapters with a cliffhanger. | Mum likes crime thrillers on TV. | That film is a thriller, so it may be too scary for little kids. | Our class wrote a short thriller about a stolen painting. | «Thriller» is also the name of a famous Michael Jackson song.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a thriller, thrillers. From «thrill» (a strong feeling of excitement). A thriller is not exactly a horror story; it is about suspense more than fright, though they can overlap.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Titanium is a strong, light, silver-grey metal, a chemical element with the symbol Ti and atomic number 22. 2) It does not rust easily, so it is used in planes, spacecraft, bicycles, glasses frames and medical implants.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on materials, titanium is a good example of choosing a material for its properties: strong but light, does not corrode, and the body accepts it, so it is used for artificial hips, dental implants and pins in broken bones. Titanium dioxide is a white powder in paint, toothpaste and sunscreen. Phrases: «titanium alloy», «titanium frame», «titanium dioxide».
examples from the lessons: Titanium is strong but light. | Grandad's new hip is made of titanium. | Some bike frames are made of titanium. | Titanium does not rust in seawater. | Its chemical symbol is Ti. | White paint often contains titanium dioxide. | Titanium is used in planes and rockets.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Named after the Titans of Greek myths. Symbol Ti (capital T, small i).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A tombstone is a large flat stone over or at the end of a grave, with the name of the person buried there and often words about them. 2) In films and games, tombstones are often used for spooky graveyard scenes.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, old tombstones in churchyards are sources about people from the past: names, ages, families. In church life a tombstone (also called a gravestone or headstone) marks where someone is buried, and visiting is a way to remember them; visitors should be respectful and quiet. Phrases: «carved on the tombstone», «an old tombstone», «tombstone inscription».
examples from the lessons: The tombstone was covered in moss. | We read the names on old tombstones in the churchyard. | The tombstone said «Beloved mother and grandmother». | In history we used tombstones to find out how long people lived. | Please don't climb on the tombstones; it is disrespectful. | At Halloween the house had pretend tombstones in the garden.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Similar words: gravestone, headstone. The «b» in «tomb» is silent: «TOOM-stone». A tomb is the burial place; the tombstone is the stone that marks it.

part of speech: noun (tongs, plural; a pair of tongs)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Tongs are a tool with two long arms joined at one end, used to pick up and hold things, such as food on a barbecue, salad, ice cubes or hot coals. 2) Science tongs (crucible tongs) hold hot things in the lab. 3) (UK) Curling tongs are a hot tool for curling hair.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life tongs keep hands away from hot food and germs. In science safety, tongs are used to hold hot crucibles or test tubes. In maths/science, tongs are a lever. Phrases: «a pair of tongs», «barbecue tongs», «salad tongs», «hammer and tongs» (with great energy, often noisily arguing).
examples from the lessons: Use the tongs to turn the sausages. | Pass me the salad tongs, please. | In science we held the hot crucible with tongs. | She picked up the ice cubes with tongs. | Mum curls her hair with curling tongs. | They were arguing hammer and tongs. | Tongs are a kind of lever.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural noun: «the tongs are», «a pair of tongs». Do not say «a tong». Not to be confused with «tongues». Check tongs are not too hot before touching the ends.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (law) A tort is a wrong done to someone, such as hurting them through carelessness or damaging their property, for which they can sue in a civil court for money (damages), even though it may not be a crime. 2) It is not the same as «torte», a rich cake, or «taut», which means tight.
its sense in the lessons: In lessons about adult life and the law, it explains that if someone's carelessness hurts you (for example a shop leaves a wet floor with no sign and you fall), you may claim compensation; this is called negligence, a kind of tort. Phrases: «tort law», «the law of torts», «sue for a tort».
examples from the lessons: Negligence is a tort, like when a careless driver hits a parked car. | Tort law decides who must pay when someone is harmed. | Trespassing on land can be a tort. | A lawyer explained that the tort case was about a dog bite. | In a tort case, the winner usually gets money, not a prison sentence for the other side. | Spreading lies that harm someone's name can be a tort called defamation.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a tort, torts. Formal legal word. A crime is punished by the state; a tort is a wrong for which the hurt person sues. Some acts can be both. Do not confuse with «torte» (a cake, from German) or «taught».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Treeless means with no trees, or almost no trees.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons it describes landscapes like the Arctic tundra, deserts, grasslands, high mountains and some windswept islands; trees cannot grow because of cold, little rain, strong wind or people cutting them down. Phrases: «a treeless plain», «treeless tundra», «bleak and treeless».
examples from the lessons: The tundra is a cold, treeless land. | Above the tree line, the mountain is treeless. | The Nullarbor Plain in Australia is flat and treeless. | Sheep grazed on the treeless hills of the island. | After the trees were cut down, the hillside was left treeless. | It was hard to find shade on the treeless plain.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective. «-less» means without, so treeless = without trees. Like «homeless», «endless», «careless».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A trident is a spear with three sharp points, like a fork with three prongs. 2) In myths, Neptune (Roman) and Poseidon (Greek), the gods of the sea, carry a trident. 3) The trident is the coat of arms of Ukraine (the «tryzub»). 4) Trident is the name of the UK's nuclear missile system.
its sense in the lessons: In history and myths lessons, Poseidon strikes the ground with his trident to make earthquakes. Britannia, the symbol of Britain, holds a trident. In Ukrainian studies the gold trident on blue is the national symbol. Fishermen once used tridents to spear fish. Phrases: «Poseidon's trident», «a three-pronged trident».
examples from the lessons: Poseidon raised his trident and the sea grew wild. | A trident has three sharp points. | Britannia holds a trident and a shield. | The trident, called the tryzub, is Ukraine's national symbol. | Fishermen used tridents to spear fish. | In the cartoon, King Triton waves a golden trident. | Debates about Trident, Britain's nuclear weapons, are part of UK politics.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. «Tri-» means three, as in triangle and tricycle. «-dent» means tooth, as in dentist.

part of speech: verb form (past and past participle of «trim»: trim, trims, trimmed, trimming); adjective (trimmed)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Trimmed means cut a little to make it neat or tidy, such as trimmed hair, hedges or nails. 2) Trimmed means made smaller by cutting away extra parts, such as fat from meat or words from an essay. 3) Trimmed with something means decorated along the edges: a coat trimmed with fur. 4) (maths, statistics) A trimmed mean is an average worked out after removing the highest and lowest values.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: hair, hedges, nails and Christmas trees are trimmed. In writing lessons a long story can be trimmed. In maths, a trimmed mean ignores the extremes. Phrases: «neatly trimmed», «trimmed with lace», «trim the tree», «trimmed down».
examples from the lessons: Dad trimmed the hedge with big shears. | I got my fringe trimmed at the hairdresser's. | The dress was trimmed with blue ribbon. | We trimmed the Christmas tree with tinsel and lights. | The butcher trimmed the fat off the meat. | My essay was too long, so I trimmed it down to 300 words. | The judges used a trimmed mean, removing the top and bottom scores.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past of «trim»: double «m» in trimmed and trimming. «Trim» can also be an adjective meaning slim and neat («a trim figure»).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A truffle is a soft, round chocolate sweet, often covered in cocoa powder. 2) A truffle is a rare, strong-smelling fungus that grows underground near tree roots and is very expensive to eat.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life truffles are chocolates in gift boxes. In science lessons on fungi, truffles grow underground; pigs and specially trained dogs sniff them out. They are among the most expensive foods in the world. Phrases: «chocolate truffle», «truffle oil», «truffle hunting», «truffle dog».
examples from the lessons: Gran gave me a box of chocolate truffles. | We rolled chocolate truffles in cocoa powder. | Truffles grow underground near oak trees. | Trained dogs sniff out truffles in the forest. | Some truffles cost more than gold by weight. | Truffle oil smells very strong. | A truffle is a fungus, like a mushroom, but it grows under the soil.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a truffle, truffles. A chocolate truffle is named after the fungus because of its round, dark shape. Never eat wild fungi you find: some are deadly.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A typist is a person who types, especially someone whose job is typing letters and documents. 2) Anyone who types can be called a typist, such as «a fast typist».
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons about offices, typists worked on typewriters, often in big typing pools, before computers. Today the word mostly describes how fast or accurately someone types; children practise touch typing in computing lessons. In maths problems, typing speed is given in words per minute. Phrases: «a fast typist», «touch typist», «a two-finger typist».
examples from the lessons: The typist typed 60 words a minute. | Grandma worked as a typist in an office. | I'm a slow typist because I use two fingers. | Touch typists don't look at the keyboard. | A typist who types 40 words a minute types 400 words in 10 minutes. | In old films, rows of typists clatter away on typewriters.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a typist, typists. Verb: type; the machine is a typewriter. «Typo» is a typing mistake.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To unblock something is to clear it so that things can pass through again, such as a drain, a sink, a road or a nose. 2) On a phone, app or website, to unblock someone is to let them contact you or see you again after you blocked them.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life it is about clearing blocked sinks and drains. In online safety lessons, children learn they can block people who are unkind and only unblock them if they feel safe; a trusted adult can help. Phrases: «unblock the sink», «unblock a number», «unblock someone».
examples from the lessons: Dad used a plunger to unblock the toilet. | We need a plumber to unblock the drain. | A steamy shower can help unblock a stuffy nose. | She decided to unblock her cousin after they made up. | Only unblock someone if you feel safe talking to them again. | The council sent a truck to unblock the road after the snow.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: unblocked. «Un-» means undo, so unblock = undo a block.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To unbox something is to take it out of its box or packaging. 2) An unboxing (video) is a film of someone opening a new product and showing it, popular online.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life children watch unboxing videos of toys and gadgets. In media lessons they learn that many unboxing videos are paid adverts, even when they look like a friend sharing, so they should look for «ad» or «sponsored». In computing, «unboxing» also means taking a value out of a wrapper, a programming idea. Phrases: «unbox a new phone», «unboxing video».
examples from the lessons: We unboxed the new laptop and set it up. | Unboxing videos show people opening toys. | Some unboxing videos are paid adverts. | Recycle the cardboard after you unbox your present. | I couldn't wait to unbox my birthday parcel. | The YouTuber unboxed a new games console.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb; third person «unboxes». The noun «unboxing» is countable (an unboxing, unboxings). Look for words like «ad», «sponsored» or «gifted» to spot paid videos.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unrealistic means not sensible or likely to happen, especially about plans or hopes: an unrealistic goal. 2) Unrealistic means not looking or seeming real or true to life, as in an unrealistic drawing or film scene.
its sense in the lessons: In maths problems, checking whether an answer is realistic is an important step: if a child's height comes out as 15 metres, that is unrealistic, so check the working. In writing, unrealistic dialogue sounds unnatural. In PSHE it is used about goals and about body images in adverts that are edited to look perfect. Phrases: «unrealistic expectations», «an unrealistic goal», «totally unrealistic».
examples from the lessons: An answer of 300 kg for a cat is unrealistic, so check your sum. | Getting 100 % in every test is an unrealistic goal. | The film's car chase was so unrealistic it was funny. | Photos in adverts can be edited and give unrealistic ideas of how people look. | Setting smaller goals is better than setting unrealistic ones. | His drawing of the horse was unrealistic because it had five legs.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective. Opposite: realistic. Adverb: unrealistically. In maths, always ask «Is my answer realistic?» — sensible size, sensible units.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Your upbringing is the way your parents or carers raised you as a child: how they cared for you, taught you and what they believed was right. 2) Upbringing can also mean the place and conditions you grew up in.
its sense in the lessons: In PSHE and ethics lessons it explains why people have different manners, beliefs and habits: a strict upbringing, a religious upbringing, a farm upbringing. In stories it tells the reader about a character's past. It also appears with foster care and adoption in lessons about families. Phrases: «a strict upbringing», «a happy upbringing», «a religious upbringing», «because of his upbringing».
examples from the lessons: She had a happy upbringing on a farm in Ireland. | His strict upbringing taught him to be on time. | Children in foster care can still have a loving upbringing. | Her upbringing in a big family made her good at sharing. | They gave their children a religious upbringing. | Your upbringing shapes you, but you can still make your own choices.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually singular: «an upbringing», «her upbringing»; plural is rare. One word. Verb: «bring up» (to bring up a child). Not the same as «education», which is more about school learning.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Upstream means towards the source of a river or stream, against the way the water flows. 2) An upstream place is further up the river, nearer its source. 3) (informal) Swimming upstream can mean doing something hard, against what most people do or want.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons on rivers: the source is upstream and the mouth is downstream; salmon swim upstream to lay eggs. In science, pollution upstream can flow down and affect places downstream. In maths, problems with boats going upstream mean the boat's speed minus the river's speed. Phrases: «swim upstream», «travel upstream», «upstream of the bridge».
examples from the lessons: Salmon swim upstream to lay their eggs. | We paddled the canoe upstream, which was hard work. | The village upstream has cleaner water. | Pollution upstream can harm fish downstream. | A boat goes 10 km/h in still water and the river flows at 2 km/h, so upstream it goes 8 km/h. | The source of the river is upstream from here.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb and adjective. Opposite: downstream. Maths rule: upstream speed = boat speed − current speed; downstream speed = boat speed + current speed.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A urinal is a kind of toilet on a wall, used by men and boys for weeing (urinating) while standing up, found in public and school toilets. 2) A urinal can also be a bottle used in hospital for a patient to wee into.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life urinals are in boys' and men's toilets. In health and hygiene lessons children learn to flush and wash hands afterwards. Phrases: «use the urinal», «public urinals».
examples from the lessons: The boys' toilets have three urinals and two cubicles. | Remember to wash your hands after using the urinal. | Some urinals flush automatically. | In hospital, the nurse gave Grandad a urinal so he didn't have to get up. | Waterless urinals save water.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a urinal, urinals. Use «a», not «an», because it starts with a «you» sound: «a urinal». Said «you-RYE-nul» (UK) or «YOOR-in-ul» (US). Related: urine, urinate (formal words for wee).

part of speech: noun (Velcro, uncountable — a brand name; velcro in general use); verb (velcro, velcros, velcroed — informal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Velcro is a fastener made of two strips: one with tiny hooks and one with tiny loops, which stick together when pressed and pull apart with a ripping sound. 2) (informal) To velcro something is to fasten it with Velcro.
its sense in the lessons: In science and design lessons it is a famous example of biomimicry: the Swiss engineer George de Mestral invented it after studying burrs (seeds with hooks) stuck in his dog's fur. In everyday life it is on children's shoes, coats and bags. Phrases: «Velcro shoes», «Velcro strap», «hook and loop».
examples from the lessons: My little brother has Velcro shoes because he can't tie laces yet. | Velcro was inspired by burrs stuck on a dog's fur. | One side of Velcro has hooks and the other has loops. | The Velcro strap on my bag makes a loud ripping sound. | Astronauts use Velcro to stop things floating away. | Look at Velcro under a magnifying glass to see the hooks.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It is a brand name, so it often has a capital V; the general name is «hook-and-loop fastener». Uncountable: some Velcro, a strip of Velcro. Myth: NASA did not invent Velcro, though astronauts used it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Verbatim means in exactly the same words as were used originally, word for word.
its sense in the lessons: In school it appears with copying and quoting: copying a website verbatim into your project without saying where it came from is plagiarism; if you quote verbatim, use quotation marks and name the source. In law and news, a verbatim record is an exact copy of what was said. Phrases: «quote verbatim», «a verbatim copy», «repeat verbatim».
examples from the lessons: She repeated the instructions verbatim. | Don't copy the website verbatim; use your own words. | If you quote verbatim, put the words in quotation marks. | The court keeps a verbatim record of what was said. | He learned the poem verbatim. | The newspaper printed the speech verbatim.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal, from Latin «verbum» (word). Adverb and adjective; no plural. Similar: word for word, exactly. Not to be confused with «verbal».

part of speech: noun (vibes, plural; a vibe, singular) — informal, slang
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal, slang) Vibes are the feelings or mood that a place, person, song or situation gives you: good vibes, bad vibes, cosy vibes. 2) (slang) «Vibes» on its own or «it's a vibe» means something feels good or cool. 3) (slang) «Vibing» means relaxing and enjoying the mood. 4) (music) Vibes is a short name for the vibraphone, a metal xylophone-like instrument.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday young people's talk it describes atmosphere; in English lessons pupils learn that «vibes» is informal, and in formal writing they would say «atmosphere», «mood» or «impression». Phrases: «good vibes», «bad vibes», «weird vibes», «give off vibes», «it's a vibe», «vibe check».
examples from the lessons: This café has really cosy vibes. | I got bad vibes from that dark alley, so we went another way. | Fairy lights and music? It's a vibe! | We were just vibing to music in my room. | The new teacher gives off friendly vibes. | «Vibe check: how's everyone feeling?» | In a story, write «the house felt creepy» rather than «the house had creepy vibes».
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal; plural «vibes», singular «a vibe». Short for «vibrations». Trust bad vibes when you feel unsafe and tell an adult. Use «atmosphere» or «mood» in formal writing.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A viola is a string instrument like a violin but a little bigger, with a deeper, warmer sound; it is played with a bow and held under the chin. 2) A viola is also a small garden flower, like a little pansy. 3) Viola is a girl's name, as in Shakespeare's «Twelfth Night» (a name).
its sense in the lessons: In music lessons it is part of the string family: violin, viola, cello, double bass, from highest to lowest. Viola music is written in a special alto clef. In gardening and science, violas are easy plants for school gardens. Phrases: «play the viola», «viola section», «viola and violin».
examples from the lessons: I play the viola in the school orchestra. | The viola is a bit bigger than the violin and sounds deeper. | Viola players read music in the alto clef. | We planted purple violas in the school garden. | In the string family, the viola sits between the violin and the cello. | Viola is the heroine of a play by Shakespeare.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. The instrument is usually said «vee-OH-la»; the flower is often «VY-oh-la». Do not confuse with «violin» or «viol» (an older instrument).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A VIP is a «very important person»: someone famous or important who gets special treatment, such as a celebrity, a leader or an honoured guest. 2) «VIP» describes special areas, tickets or treatment for such people: VIP seats, VIP lounge, VIP pass.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life it appears at concerts, sports events and parties; at school, a «VIP» might be a visiting guest or a pupil of the week. In maths, ticket problems may have VIP and standard prices. Phrases: «VIP treatment», «VIP area», «VIP tickets», «VIP pass».
examples from the lessons: The VIPs sat in the front row at the concert. | We got VIP treatment at Grandma's birthday. | The mayor was a VIP guest at sports day. | VIP tickets cost £50 and standard tickets cost £20. | Only people with a VIP pass could go backstage. | I was class VIP this week and fed the fish.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always in capitals: VIP; plural VIPs. Said as letters «vee-eye-pee». Use «a VIP» (a vee sound). Not a word on its own in lower case.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Almost; very nearly but not quite: «virtually empty» means almost completely empty. 2) In a computer or online world rather than in real life: «we met virtually» means we met on a video call or online. 3) (formal) In effect, as good as: «it is virtually impossible» means it can hardly ever happen.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday talk it softens a big word like «all», «every», «nothing» or «impossible». In science and computing it means «done by computer, not in person»: a virtual tour, virtual lessons, virtual reality. In maths word problems «virtually all» does not give an exact number. Phrases: «virtually impossible», «virtually nothing», «virtually everyone», «meet virtually».
examples from the lessons: The bus was virtually empty after the last stop. | Virtually everyone in our class has a library card. | It is virtually impossible to lick your own elbow. | During the snow days we had lessons virtually, on the laptop. | The two pictures are virtually the same, but one has a missing button. | My nan visits us virtually every Sunday by video call. | There was virtually no rain all summer, so the grass went brown. | You can now visit the museum virtually from home.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from «virtual». «Virtually» means almost, NOT exactly: «virtually all the cake» means a tiny bit is left. Do not confuse with «actually» (really, in fact). In maths it gives no number; never treat «virtually all» as «all». Online sense: «virtual» means made by computer.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Small beads made from white and purple shells, strung together or woven into belts by Native American peoples of eastern North America. 2) Wampum belts were used to record agreements, tell histories and mark important promises between nations. 3) Later, European settlers also used wampum as a kind of money, so the word sometimes means shell money. 4) (old slang, US) Money in general — now rare and can sound disrespectful.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons about Native Americans (for example the Haudenosaunee, also called Iroquois, and the Wampanoag) wampum shows that these peoples kept records and treaties without paper. In stories it marks a peace treaty or a solemn promise. Phrases: «wampum belt», «strings of wampum».
examples from the lessons: The museum showed a wampum belt made of purple and white shell beads. | Wampum belts were used to remember a treaty between two nations. | The beads were made from quahog clam shells. | Our teacher said wampum was much more than money. | A speaker held up a string of wampum before giving an important message. | The pattern on the belt showed two paths side by side.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «some wampum», «a wampum belt», not «a wampum». It is a word from Algonquian languages. Treat it respectfully: wampum is still important to Native nations today, so do not call it «just beads» or «Indian money».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Careful and a little worried because something might be dangerous or tricky. 2) Not quick to trust someone or something: «wary of strangers». 3) Watchful, keeping an eye out for trouble.
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons, being wary is good: be wary of strangers online, of deep water, of emails that ask for passwords. In stories a wary character watches, waits and does not trust easily; a wary animal stays alert to danger. Phrases: «be wary of», «keep a wary eye on», «wary look».
examples from the lessons: The cat was wary of the new dog and stayed on the shelf. | Be wary of emails that ask for your password. | The deer gave us a wary look and ran into the trees. | Mum is wary of buying things from pop-up adverts. | I was a bit wary of the big slide at first. | The lifeguard kept a wary eye on the swimmers near the rocks. | Pupils should be wary of websites that promise free prizes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Do not confuse «wary» (careful, suspicious) with «weary» (very tired) or «wear». «Wary of» something, not «wary from». Opposites: trusting, careless. Noun: wariness; adverb: warily.

part of speech: noun (welding — uncountable); verb form (weld, welds, welded, welding)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Joining two pieces of metal (or plastic) by heating them until they melt a little and flow together, then letting them cool into one piece. 2) «Welding» is also the -ing form of «weld»: «He is welding the gate». 3) The job or trade of a welder.
its sense in the lessons: In science and technology lessons welding shows how heat can melt metal and how melted metal hardens when it cools. In everyday life you see welding on bridges, cars, ships and playground frames. Safety: welding makes very bright light and sparks, so welders wear a dark mask, gloves and thick clothes; never look at the flash. Phrases: «welding torch», «welding mask», «weld together».
examples from the lessons: My uncle does welding at the shipyard. | The welder wore a dark mask to protect her eyes from the bright light. | They are welding the broken gate back together. | Sparks flew from the welding torch. | Never stare at welding light, because it can hurt your eyes. | The steel beams of the bridge were joined by welding. | At the school fair a robot showed how car welding works.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable as a noun: «some welding», «a lot of welding». A person who welds is a «welder». Welding is different from gluing (sticky stuff) and soldering (joining with a softer metal at a lower heat, used in electronics).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A very strange desert plant from Namibia and Angola in south-west Africa that has only two long, leathery leaves. 2) The leaves keep growing from the base for its whole life, getting torn and curled into a messy heap. 3) Some welwitschias are thought to be well over a thousand years old.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons it is an example of how plants adapt to deserts: it gets water from fog and has deep roots. In nature books it is called a «living fossil» because it is very old and unusual. It appears on the coat of arms of Namibia.
examples from the lessons: The welwitschia has only two leaves, but they never stop growing. | Our teacher showed us a picture of a welwitschia in the Namib Desert. | The welwitschia drinks water from the morning fog. | Some welwitschias may be over a thousand years old. | The leaves of the welwitschia look like a tangled pile of ribbons. | Kew Gardens in London grows a welwitschia in a glasshouse.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say «wel-WITCH-ee-uh». It is named after Friedrich Welwitsch, the botanist who described it. Myth: it looks like many leaves, but it really has just two that split into strips. Plural: welwitschias.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (old-fashioned) From where: «Whence did he come?» means «Where did he come from?». 2) (formal) From which place or reason: «the town whence she came». 3) (formal) Which is why: «He was late, whence the trouble.»
its sense in the lessons: You mostly meet «whence» in old stories, poems, the Bible and fairy tales, where it gives an old, grand feel. In modern speech people use «where … from» instead. In the Bible: «I will lift up mine eyes unto the hills, from whence cometh my help» (Psalm 121, King James Version). Related old words: «hence» (from here), «thence» (from there), «whither» (to where).
examples from the lessons: «Whence came you, stranger?» asked the old king. | The river flows back to the mountains whence it came. | In the old poem the knight returned to the land whence he had set out. | «From whence cometh my help?» we read in the psalm. | Nobody knew whence the strange noise came. | Today we would say «Where did you come from?» instead of «Whence came you?»
note for the reader of a maths problem: Strictly «whence» already means «from where», so «from whence» repeats «from» — but it is very common in old texts and the Bible, so it is not wrong there. Do not confuse with «when» (time) or «hence» (so, from here). Do not use it in normal writing; it sounds very old.

part of speech: verb form (wilt, wilts, wilted, wilting); adjective (wilting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Drooping and going soft because of not enough water, too much heat, or being picked: a wilting flower bends and its leaves hang down. 2) (of a person) Getting tired, weak or less lively, especially in heat: «The children were wilting in the sun.» 3) Losing confidence or energy: «Her smile was wilting.»
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons wilting shows that plants need water: water pushes against plant cells and keeps them stiff; without it the plant goes floppy. If watered in time, a wilting plant can perk up again. In stories a wilting flower can stand for sadness or something ending. Phrases: «wilting in the heat», «wilting flowers».
examples from the lessons: The sunflowers were wilting because we forgot to water them. | After an hour in the heat, the football team was wilting. | The lettuce in the fridge drawer was wilting. | We watered the wilting basil and it stood up again by evening. | The bunch of roses had been wilting for days. | In our experiment, the plant without water started wilting first. | By the last lap I was wilting like an old daisy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Base verb «wilt»; past «wilted». «Wilt» is also an old Bible form of «will» with «thou» («thou wilt»), a different word. Wilting is not dying yet: a wilted plant can often recover. Opposite: perk up, revive.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To keep something back and refuse to give it: «withhold information» means not telling something you know. 2) To hold back a payment or reward: «The shop withheld his pay until the work was finished.» 3) (money) To take part of someone's pay for tax before they get it.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and stories, withholding the truth or help is often a sign of a secret or of punishment. In safety: an adult should never ask a child to withhold (keep secret) something that makes them feel unsafe. In money and law: tax is withheld from wages. Phrases: «withhold information», «withhold payment», «withhold your name», «withheld number».
examples from the lessons: The detective thought the butler was withholding something. | Please do not withhold information that could help find the lost dog. | The phone screen said «number withheld». | The teacher withheld the prize until everyone had tidied up. | The company withheld part of his wages for tax. | She withheld her smile until the judges had finished. | If someone asks you to keep a secret that worries you, do not withhold it from a trusted adult.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular: withhold, withheld, withheld (like «hold, held»). Spelled with two h's: with + hold. Formal-ish word; everyday words are «keep back», «hold back», «not tell». Noun: withholding.

part of speech: noun (Wolof — a people and their language); adjective (Wolof)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The Wolof are a people of West Africa, living mostly in Senegal, The Gambia and Mauritania. 2) Wolof is also their language, widely spoken in Senegal by many people, including those who are not Wolof. 3) As an adjective it describes things of this people or language: «Wolof music».
its sense in the lessons: In geography and language lessons Wolof is an example of an African language used every day in markets, music and radio, alongside French in Senegal. English has borrowed a few words that may come from Wolof, perhaps «banana» and «jive», though experts are not sure. Usually written with a capital W.
examples from the lessons: Wolof is spoken by millions of people in Senegal. | My friend from Dakar taught me to say hello in Wolof. | Many Senegalese people speak Wolof and French. | The Wolof people have a long tradition of griots, who sing family histories. | «Jërëjëf» means «thank you» in Wolof. | The radio played a song in Wolof.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Proper noun: write «Wolof» with a capital letter. Say «WOH-lof». Do not call Wolof a «dialect»; it is a full language. Names of peoples and languages are not plural with -s here: «the Wolof», «speak Wolof».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A plant with silvery-grey leaves and a very bitter taste, used long ago in medicine and in some strong drinks. 2) Something very bitter or painful to bear: «The defeat was wormwood to him.» 3) (Bible) In the Bible wormwood stands for bitterness and sorrow, and in the Book of Revelation «Wormwood» is the name of a star that falls and makes waters bitter.
its sense in the lessons: In science and history lessons it is a herb of old medicine; its name comes from an old belief that it drove out worms. In stories and poems «gall and wormwood» means great bitterness. In the Bible (Lamentations, Revelation) it is a sign of grief. Phrases: «gall and wormwood», «as bitter as wormwood».
examples from the lessons: Wormwood has soft grey leaves and smells strong. | The old herbalist hung bunches of wormwood to dry. | Wormwood tastes so bitter that nobody wanted a second sip. | In the story, losing the race was wormwood to the proud prince. | In Revelation, a star called Wormwood falls from the sky. | Gardeners sometimes plant wormwood to keep some insects away.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable. It is not a worm and not wood. Some wormwood is poisonous in large amounts, so never eat wild plants. In Ukrainian, a kind of wormwood is called «chornobyl», which people sometimes link to the Chernobyl story.

part of speech: word (Mandarin, pinyin «wǔ», «wù», «wú»); proper noun (Wu — a Chinese surname and dialect group)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (Mandarin, pinyin) «Wǔ» means «five»: «wǔ» 五. It sounds like «woo» to an English ear. 2) (Mandarin, pinyin) «Wǔ» can also mean «dance» or «noon» (wǔfàn, lunch), and «wú» can mean «not have, none». 3) (a name) Wu is a common Chinese family name. 4) Wu Chinese is a group of Chinese varieties spoken around Shanghai. It is not an English word.
its sense in the lessons: In Mandarin lessons it is learnt early because of counting: yī, èr, sān, sì, wǔ (one to five). Pinyin uses tone marks, so one written «wu» can be several different words. In English you meet it in names and in the martial art «wushu».
examples from the lessons: In Mandarin, «wǔ» means five. | We counted «yī, èr, sān, sì, wǔ» in our Chinese club. | «Wǔfàn» means lunch in Mandarin. | My classmate's surname is Wu. | In Shanghai some people speak Wu Chinese at home. | Wu sounds like «woo», but the tone matters.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Not English. Without tone marks «wu» is ambiguous in pinyin: wǔ (five, dance), wú (none), wù (thing, fog, mistake). Do not invent meanings for a person called Wu: it is a name.

part of speech: verb (yap, yaps, yapped, yapping); noun (a yap, yaps)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (of a small dog) To give short, high, sharp barks: «The puppy yapped at the postman.» 2) (informal) To talk a lot, loudly or in a silly way: «Stop yapping!» 3) (slang, rude) Your mouth: «Shut your yap!» 4) A short, sharp bark.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, a small dog that yaps is usually noisy and annoying, but often brave. «Yapping» about someone is chatter that can turn into gossip. «Shut your yap» is rude; do not say it to teachers. Related: «yappy» (a yappy dog).
examples from the lessons: The little dog next door yaps every time the doorbell rings. | Stop yapping and finish your homework! | The terrier gave a yap and ran after the ball. | «Shut your yap!» shouted the pirate. | They were yapping on the phone for an hour. | Our neighbour's yappy dog woke the whole street.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double the p: yapped, yapping. «Yap» is for small dogs; big dogs «bark» or «woof». The «your yap» sense is rude slang, like «gob» or «trap». Do not confuse with «yep» (yes, informal).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A very large ancient tower built in steps, getting smaller towards the top, with a temple on the highest level. 2) Ziggurats were built in ancient Mesopotamia (now mostly Iraq) by peoples such as the Sumerians and Babylonians. 3) Any building that rises in flat steps like this.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons about ancient Mesopotamia, the ziggurat shows how cities honoured their gods and how people built with mud bricks. Some people think the story of the Tower of Babel in the Bible may be linked to a ziggurat in Babylon. In maths it is like a stack of cuboids, each smaller than the one below.
examples from the lessons: The Great Ziggurat of Ur was built of mud bricks. | A ziggurat had a temple at the very top. | We built a ziggurat out of Lego blocks, each layer smaller. | Ziggurats are not the same as Egyptian pyramids. | Priests climbed the steps of the ziggurat. | The hotel was shaped like a ziggurat, with gardens on each step.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say «ZIG-oo-rat». Not a pyramid: a ziggurat has flat steps and a flat top with a temple, and it was not a tomb; Egyptian pyramids were tombs with smooth or stepped sides to a point. Plural: ziggurats.

part of speech: noun (a Zulu, Zulus; Zulu — the language); adjective (Zulu)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The Zulu are a large people of southern Africa, living mostly in South Africa, especially KwaZulu-Natal. 2) Zulu (isiZulu) is their language, the most widely spoken home language in South Africa. 3) «Zulu» is the word for the letter Z in the international spelling alphabet (Alpha, Bravo … Yankee, Zulu). 4) (military, aviation) «Zulu time» means world standard time (UTC).
its sense in the lessons: In history and geography lessons you meet the Zulu kingdom and King Shaka, and South Africa's many languages. On the radio, pilots and police spell letters with words: «Z for Zulu». Usually written with a capital Z.
examples from the lessons: Zulu is one of South Africa's official languages. | «Sawubona» means «hello» in Zulu. | The Zulu kingdom was powerful under King Shaka. | My cousin spelled her postcode on the phone: «Bravo, Zulu, one, four». | The pilot gave the time in Zulu time. | We watched a Zulu dance with drums and shields.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Write with a capital Z. In Zulu itself the people are «amaZulu» and the language «isiZulu». Avoid old pictures that show Zulu people only as warriors; they are a modern nation of millions. Plural: Zulus or the Zulu.

part of speech: noun (aa — a kind of lava; also written «ʻaʻā»); abbreviation (AA)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) Aa (from Hawaiian «ʻaʻā») is a kind of lava that cools into rough, sharp, jagged lumps. 2) (abbreviation) AA is a battery size: a small cylinder battery used in remote controls and toys («AA batteries»). 3) (UK) The AA is the Automobile Association, which helps drivers whose cars break down. 4) (abbreviation) AA also means Alcoholics Anonymous, a group that helps people stop drinking alcohol.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about volcanoes, aa lava is contrasted with pahoehoe, which is smooth and ropy. In everyday life «AA» is most often a battery size: AA is bigger than AAA. On road signs in the UK, yellow AA signs show detours. Say «ah-ah» for the lava.
examples from the lessons: Aa lava is rough and sharp, so you must never walk on it. | The remote needs two AA batteries. | AAA batteries are thinner than AA ones. | Our car broke down, so Dad called the AA. | On Hawaii we saw fields of black aa lava. | The scientist explained the difference between aa and pahoehoe.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The lava word is Hawaiian and sounds like «ah-ah». Capital «AA» is an abbreviation: for batteries, the Automobile Association, or Alcoholics Anonymous — which one depends on context. Not a normal English word on its own.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An African mammal with a long snout, long ears, a thick tail and strong claws, which digs into ant and termite nests at night and eats the insects with its long sticky tongue. 2) It lives in burrows and comes out mostly at night.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons it is an example of an animal adapted to its food: claws for digging, a long tongue for catching termites, good hearing and smell for night life. In dictionaries it is often one of the first words. Its name comes from Afrikaans and means «earth pig», though it is not a pig.
examples from the lessons: The aardvark dug into the termite mound with its claws. | An aardvark can eat thousands of ants in one night. | Aardvarks sleep in burrows during the day. | «Aardvark» is one of the first words in the dictionary. | The aardvark's long ears help it hear insects. | At the zoo we only saw the aardvark in the nocturnal house.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Use «an aardvark» (starts with a vowel sound). Spelled with double a. It is not an anteater; anteaters live in South and Central America and are a different animal. Not a pig, despite the name.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Using rude, insulting or cruel words: «abusive language». 2) Treating someone cruelly or violently, hurting them again and again: «an abusive relationship». 3) Using something wrongly or unfairly, especially power.
its sense in the lessons: In safety and PSHE lessons «abusive» describes behaviour that is never okay: being hit, threatened, insulted or hurt by anyone, including adults or people online. If someone is abusive to you, tell a trusted adult. Online, abusive messages can be reported and blocked. Phrases: «abusive language», «abusive messages», «abusive behaviour».
examples from the lessons: Abusive messages should be reported and blocked. | The referee sent off the player for abusive language. | No one deserves to be in an abusive home. | If an adult is abusive to you, tell a teacher you trust. | The website removes abusive comments. | The shop sign said staff will not accept abusive behaviour.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From the noun and verb «abuse». Strong word: it is more serious than «mean» or «rude». Spelling: abusive (drop the e of «abuse», add -ive). Say «uh-BYOO-siv». Abuse is never the fault of the child who is hurt.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Coming to the throne or to an important position: «the king's accession» is when he became king. 2) (formal) Joining an organisation or agreement: «accession to the European Union». 3) A new item added to a collection, such as a book added to a library or an object to a museum.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons it is used for kings and queens: «after his accession to the throne». In news about countries it means joining a group of countries. In libraries and museums an «accession number» is the number given to a new item. Phrases: «accession to the throne», «Accession Day».
examples from the lessons: After her accession to the throne, the queen gave a speech. | The country celebrated the new king's accession. | Ukraine has asked for accession to the European Union. | The museum's newest accession is a Roman coin. | Every library book has an accession number. | The history book lists each monarch's accession and death.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal word. Do not confuse with «access» (a way in) or «succession» (one after another; who comes next to the throne). Countable: «accessions» for new items. Verb: accede (formal).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Sharpness of a sense, especially of eyesight or hearing: «visual acuity» means how clearly you can see small details. 2) (formal) Sharpness of the mind: being quick to notice and understand things.
its sense in the lessons: In science and health lessons, eye tests measure visual acuity with a chart of letters getting smaller. Doctors say «20/20» (US) or «6/6» (UK) for normal acuity. In stories it describes a detective's sharp mind. Phrases: «visual acuity», «mental acuity».
examples from the lessons: The eye test measured my visual acuity. | Eagles have amazing visual acuity and can spot a mouse from high up. | The detective's acuity helped her solve the case. | Older dogs can lose some hearing acuity. | The optician said my acuity is better with glasses. | Owls have great acuity in the dark.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal word; everyday words are «sharpness», «how well you see». Say «uh-KYOO-it-ee». Related: «acute» (sharp; also an acute angle, less than 90 degrees). Not «accuracy», though they are related in meaning.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The person a letter, parcel, email or message is sent to. 2) (language) The person someone is speaking to.
its sense in the lessons: In writing lessons, when you write a letter, the addressee's name and address go on the envelope; you are the sender. In emails the addressee is in the «To» line. Phrases: «the addressee's address», «return to sender if addressee unknown».
examples from the lessons: The postman could not find the addressee, so the letter was returned. | Write the addressee's name in the middle of the envelope. | The sender's address goes on the back, and the addressee's on the front. | Only the addressee should open this letter. | Check you have the right addressee before you click «Send». | The parcel said «Addressee unknown».
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelled with double d, double s and double e. The ending -ee means the person something is done to (employee, trainee); the opposite is «sender». Do not confuse with «address» (where someone lives) or «addresser» (the sender, rare).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Very sweet, cute and lovely, so that you want to cuddle or look after it: «an adorable puppy». 2) Charming and easy to love.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday talk people use «adorable» for babies, small animals and cute things, and sometimes for a funny thing someone says. In stories it shows that a character finds someone sweet. Stronger than «cute». Phrases: «absolutely adorable», «so adorable».
examples from the lessons: The puppy with the floppy ears is adorable! | My baby cousin looks adorable in his little hat. | Grandma thought my drawing was adorable. | The kittens were curled up in an adorable heap. | «You're adorable,» said the girl to her hamster. | The lamb's wobbly first steps were adorable.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: adore + able, drop the «e» of adore: adorable. Noun: adorableness (rare). Can sound babyish if said about an older child; some people don't like being called adorable.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A very hard or unlucky time, full of problems and troubles: illness, being poor, losing someone, or facing danger. 2) A particular difficult event or misfortune (plural adversities).
its sense in the lessons: In stories and history lessons heroes often «overcome adversity», showing courage and patience. In PSHE and ethics it is linked to resilience: getting through hard times. Phrases: «in the face of adversity», «overcome adversity», «triumph over adversity».
examples from the lessons: She showed great courage in the face of adversity. | The team overcame adversity to win the final. | The family faced many adversities after the flood. | Adversity can make friends grow closer. | The story is about a boy who triumphs over adversity. | Helen Keller's life is an example of courage in adversity.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal word; everyday words are «hard times», «trouble». Mostly uncountable: «in adversity». Related: «adverse» (harmful, unfavourable: «adverse weather»). Do not confuse with «adversary» (an enemy or opponent).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) A long sleep-like rest that some animals go into during very hot, dry weather, to save water and energy — like hibernation, but in summer. 2) (botany) The way the parts of a flower bud are folded before it opens.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about animal adaptations, aestivation is compared with hibernation (winter sleep). Snails, lungfish, some frogs, tortoises and crocodiles can aestivate: they hide in mud or burrows and slow down until the rain comes. Verb: aestivate.
examples from the lessons: Some frogs in Australia survive drought by aestivation underground. | The African lungfish wraps itself in mucus during aestivation. | Snails seal their shells with a dry layer during aestivation. | Hibernation is for winter, and aestivation is for hot, dry summers. | After weeks of aestivation, the frogs woke when the rain fell. | The desert tortoise uses aestivation to escape the heat.
note for the reader of a maths problem: British spelling «aestivation», American «estivation». Comes from Latin «aestas», summer. Say «ee-stiv-AY-shun». Uncountable. Do not mix up with «hibernation» (winter).

part of speech: adjective (afflicted); verb form (afflict, afflicts, afflicted, afflicting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Suffering from an illness, pain or trouble: «afflicted with a cough». 2) Past form of «afflict»: to cause someone pain or trouble: «The village was afflicted by floods.» 3) (formal) «The afflicted» means people who suffer.
its sense in the lessons: In history, health and Bible lessons «afflicted» describes people struck by disease, famine or disaster; the Bible speaks of comforting the afflicted. In news it is used for places hit by drought or war. Phrases: «afflicted with», «afflicted by», «comfort the afflicted».
examples from the lessons: The town was afflicted by a terrible drought. | He was afflicted with a bad cough all winter. | Nurses cared for the afflicted during the plague. | Many crops were afflicted by disease that year. | Jesus healed many who were afflicted, Christians believe. | The old dog was afflicted with stiff legs.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal word; everyday words: «suffering from», «hit by». Noun: affliction (an illness or trouble). Do not confuse with «inflicted» (caused to someone else: «inflict pain»). Use «afflicted with/by».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Able to move quickly, easily and lightly: «an agile monkey». 2) Able to think quickly and cleverly: «an agile mind». 3) (computing, work) «Agile» is a way of working in teams in short steps, changing plans often.
its sense in the lessons: In PE and nature lessons agile describes gymnasts, goalkeepers, cats and monkeys that move and turn fast. In stories an agile hero leaps, climbs and dodges. Phrases: «quick and agile», «an agile mind», «agility training».
examples from the lessons: The cat was agile enough to jump onto the fence. | Monkeys are agile climbers. | The goalkeeper was quick and agile. | Gymnasts must be strong and agile. | Grandpa is still agile for his age. | She has an agile mind and solves puzzles fast.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say «AJ-ile» (UK) or «AJ-ul» (US). Noun: agility. Opposites: clumsy, stiff, slow. Agile is about ease and speed of movement, not about strength.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Moving or carried through the air: «airborne seeds», «airborne germs». 2) (of a plane, bird or person) Off the ground and flying: «The plane is airborne.» 3) (military) Soldiers trained to arrive by parachute or aircraft: «airborne troops».
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons «airborne» explains how seeds spread on the wind (dandelions, sycamore), and how some germs travel in tiny drops in the air, so covering coughs helps. In sport, a jumper or footballer can be «airborne» for a moment. Phrases: «become airborne», «airborne disease».
examples from the lessons: The dandelion seeds were airborne in seconds. | The plane became airborne at the end of the runway. | Colds can be airborne, so catch your sneeze in a tissue. | The skateboarder was airborne over the ramp. | Pollen is airborne in spring. | The kite stayed airborne for an hour.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word: air + borne (carried). Not «air-born» (born in the air). Adjective only. Related: waterborne (carried by water).

meaning for a pupil: 1) With no fresh air moving; stuffy and hard to breathe in: «an airless room». 2) With no air at all: «the airless surface of the Moon». 3) (of weather) Very still, with no wind.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, the Moon is airless, so there is no wind, no sound and no breathing without a spacesuit. In everyday life an airless room needs a window opened. In stories an airless place feels hot, heavy or scary.
examples from the lessons: The classroom was hot and airless, so we opened the windows. | The Moon is airless, so astronauts carry oxygen. | It was an airless summer night. | The cellar was dark and airless. | Sound cannot travel in airless space. | We felt sleepy in the airless bus.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The suffix -less means «without»: airless = without air. Do not confuse with «airtight» (no air can get in or out). Opposite: airy, breezy.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Arrangement in a straight line or in the right position: «the alignment of the wheels». 2) (science) When planets or stars appear in a line in the sky. 3) Agreement or being on the same side: «in alignment with the rules». 4) (computing, writing) How text is lined up: left, centre, right.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and design, alignment means lining things up neatly along a straight edge. In computing, «text alignment» buttons line text to the left, centre or right. In space science, «planetary alignment» is when planets look lined up from Earth. Phrases: «in alignment», «out of alignment», «align with».
examples from the lessons: The mechanic checked the alignment of the car's wheels. | Use a ruler to keep the alignment of your columns straight. | Set the title's alignment to centre. | The planets were in alignment in the evening sky. | My front teeth are out of alignment, so I have a brace. | The teams are in alignment about the plan.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From the verb «align» (line up). Spelling: keep the silent g: alignment. Do not write «allignment». Countable and uncountable.

part of speech: noun (an amoeba, amoebas or amoebae; US also ameba)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A tiny living thing made of just one cell, which you can only see with a microscope. 2) It has no fixed shape: it moves by pushing out parts of itself like fingers (called pseudopods) and eats by wrapping round its food.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons the amoeba is a classic example of a single-celled organism that lives in ponds, soil and water. Some kinds cause illness if dirty water is drunk, which is why we boil or clean water. In everyday talk «amoeba-like» means shapeless.
examples from the lessons: Under the microscope the amoeba changed its shape. | An amoeba is made of just one cell. | The amoeba wrapped around a tiny bit of food. | Amoebae live in pond water. | We drew the amoeba with its little pseudopods. | Some amoebas can make people ill if they drink dirty water.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say «uh-MEE-buh». Two plurals: amoebas (everyday) and amoebae («uh-MEE-bee», science). US spelling ameba. It is not a bacterium and not an animal in the usual sense.

part of speech: noun (an amplifier, amplifiers; informal an amp)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A machine that makes sounds louder, especially from guitars, microphones and music players. 2) (science) Any device that makes an electric signal stronger. 3) Something that makes a feeling or effect stronger.
its sense in the lessons: In music and science lessons the amplifier shows how sound is turned into electric signals, made stronger and turned back into louder sound by a speaker. In bands, guitarists plug into an «amp». Phrases: «plug into the amplifier», «turn up the amp».
