examples from the lessons: The guitarist plugged into the amplifier. | Turn the amplifier down, it's too loud! | A microphone, an amplifier and a speaker work together. | The school hall has a big amplifier for assemblies. | A hearing aid is a tiny amplifier. | Our band's amp crackled during the concert.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Short form: «amp» (informal; also «amp» means ampere, a unit of current). Verb: amplify (make louder or stronger). Spelling: -ifier, like «magnifier».

meaning for a pupil: 1) The study of the parts of the body and how they are arranged: bones, muscles, organs. 2) The body structure of a person, animal or plant: «the anatomy of a frog». 3) (informal, humorous) A part of the body: «He hurt a delicate part of his anatomy.» 4) A close, careful study of something: «the anatomy of a crime».
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons «human anatomy» covers the skeleton, heart, lungs and other organs. Doctors and artists study anatomy. In books «The Anatomy of …» means a detailed study. Related words: anatomical, anatomist.
examples from the lessons: We learned about the anatomy of the heart. | Doctors must study anatomy for years. | The poster shows the anatomy of a fish. | Leonardo da Vinci drew careful pictures of human anatomy. | The anatomy of a flower includes petals, stamens and a pistil. | The ball hit him in a painful part of his anatomy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say «uh-NAT-uh-mee». Anatomy is about structure (what parts there are); physiology is about how the parts work. Usually uncountable.

part of speech: noun (an annex, annexes; UK often annexe); verb (annex, annexes, annexed, annexing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (noun) An extra building joined to or near a main building: «the school annexe». 2) (noun) An extra part added to a document. 3) (verb) To take control of land or a country and make it part of your own, usually by force and without agreement: «Russia annexed Crimea». 4) (verb) To add something as an extra part.
its sense in the lessons: In history and news lessons «annex» describes one country seizing land from another; most countries in the UN called Russia's annexation of Crimea illegal. In school life, the «annexe» is often an extra classroom block. Noun: annexation.
examples from the lessons: Our art lessons are in the annexe behind the main building. | The hotel has a new annexe with ten rooms. | Russia annexed Crimea from Ukraine, and most UN members voted that this was not valid. | The empire annexed the small kingdom. | See the annex at the end of the report for the tables. | The library annexe is open on Saturdays.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stress: noun «AN-eks», verb «uh-NEKS». UK spelling for the building: «annexe»; US: «annex». Annexing land by force is against international law. Do not confuse with «attach» (simply join).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A medicine that makes stomach acid weaker, used for heartburn and indigestion. 2) (adjective) Working against acid: «antacid tablets».
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons antacids show neutralisation: a base (alkali) reacts with acid and makes it less acidic. Many antacids contain calcium carbonate or magnesium hydroxide. In everyday life adults take them after spicy or big meals. Safety: only take medicine with an adult's permission.
examples from the lessons: Grandpa took an antacid after the spicy curry. | Antacids neutralise stomach acid. | In science we dropped an antacid tablet into vinegar and watched it fizz. | The doctor said to take antacids for heartburn. | Some antacids taste like chalk. | Medicines like antacids must be kept away from small children.
note for the reader of a maths problem: anti + acid = against acid; spelled «antacid» with one i. Say «ant-ASS-id». Not a medicine for a «stomach bug» or germs. Countable: an antacid, two antacids.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A medicine that calms allergic reactions such as sneezing, itchy eyes, rashes and hay fever. 2) (science) It works by blocking histamine, a chemical the body releases when it reacts to things like pollen, pet hair or insect bites.
its sense in the lessons: In health lessons, antihistamines help with hay fever and mild allergies. Some make you sleepy. For a severe allergy (anaphylaxis) an antihistamine is not enough: people need an adrenaline pen and an ambulance. Phrases: «take an antihistamine», «antihistamine cream».
examples from the lessons: I take an antihistamine in summer for my hay fever. | The nurse put antihistamine cream on the bee sting. | Some antihistamines make you drowsy. | My dog allergy is better when I take antihistamines. | For a serious allergy, call an ambulance; an antihistamine is not enough. | The pharmacist gave Mum an antihistamine syrup for me.
note for the reader of a maths problem: anti + histamine. Say «an-tee-HISS-tuh-meen». Countable. Only take medicines with a trusted adult or a doctor's advice.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (heraldry) The colour silver or white on a coat of arms or shield. 2) (old-fashioned, poetic) Silver, or silvery in colour: «the argent moon». 3) (French) «Argent» in French means «silver» and also «money»; it is pronounced differently («ar-ZHAHN»).
its sense in the lessons: You meet «argent» in history lessons about knights and coats of arms, where colours have special names (gules = red, azure = blue, or = gold, argent = silver). In chemistry, silver's symbol Ag comes from Latin «argentum». Argentina's name also comes from this word.
examples from the lessons: The knight's shield was argent with a red cross. | In heraldry, argent means silver. | The poet wrote of the argent light of the stars. | Silver's symbol is Ag, from Latin argentum. | Argentina was named after the Latin word for silver. | In French, «argent» also means money.
note for the reader of a maths problem: In English say «AR-jent». In French it means both «silver» and «money» — a false friend: in English it never means money. Mostly found in heraldry and poems.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The belief that the positions of the Sun, Moon, planets and stars at the time someone is born, or on a certain day, affect people's character and what will happen to them. 2) The practice of making horoscopes based on star signs (such as Aries, Leo, Capricorn).
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons astrology is contrasted with astronomy: astronomy is the science of space, while astrology is a belief with no scientific evidence that it works. In everyday life people read horoscopes in magazines for fun. Many Christians and scientists do not accept astrology. Phrases: «star sign», «horoscope», «zodiac».
examples from the lessons: Astrology says your star sign depends on your birthday. | Scientists have found no evidence that astrology predicts the future. | My aunt reads the astrology page for fun. | Astronomy is a science, but astrology is not. | Long ago, astrology and astronomy were studied together. | In astrology there are twelve signs of the zodiac.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Do not confuse with «astronomy» (the real science of stars and planets) — a very common trap. Uncountable. Person: astrologer; adjective: astrological. «Astro-» means star.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A legendary island city that, in an old story by the Greek writer Plato, sank under the sea in one day and night. 2) In stories and films, Atlantis means a lost, wonderful underwater city. 3) (a name) Also the name of a NASA space shuttle and of some hotels and games.
its sense in the lessons: In history and reading lessons Atlantis is an example of a myth: there is no evidence it really existed, though people still search for it. Plato probably made it up to teach a lesson about pride. Written with a capital A.
examples from the lessons: Plato wrote about an island called Atlantis that sank into the sea. | Many films show Atlantis as an underwater city. | Nobody has ever found Atlantis. | The space shuttle Atlantis flew many missions. | In our story, the divers discovered a lost Atlantis. | Is Atlantis real, or just a legend?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Proper noun, capital A. A legend, not history: there is no proof it existed. Related adjective «Atlantean». Not the same as the Atlantic Ocean, though the names are linked.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Possible to reach or achieve: «an attainable goal». 2) Possible to get: «Tickets are still attainable.»
its sense in the lessons: In school and PSHE lessons, teachers talk about setting goals that are challenging but attainable (SMART goals: specific, measurable, achievable). In maths, an attainable value is one a number can actually reach. Opposite: unattainable.
examples from the lessons: Set yourself an attainable goal, like reading ten pages a day. | A gold star is attainable if you try hard. | The summit is attainable in one day. | Is a perfect score attainable on this test? | The coach set goals that were hard but attainable. | For a beginner, swimming a length is attainable.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «attain» (reach, achieve) + -able. Formal; everyday words: «achievable», «possible». Opposite: unattainable.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A picture or character that stands for you in a game, app or online chat. 2) (Hinduism) In Hindu belief, a god appearing on Earth in a human or animal form, like Krishna as an avatar of Vishnu. 3) (formal) A person who perfectly shows an idea: «an avatar of kindness».
its sense in the lessons: In computing lessons and online safety, your avatar can be a cartoon instead of a real photo, which is safer. In games you design and dress your avatar. In religious education it is a Hindu word from Sanskrit. Also the name of films and a cartoon.
examples from the lessons: I made a dragon avatar for my game. | Use a cartoon avatar instead of your real photo online. | My avatar has blue hair and a cape. | In Hindu stories, Rama is an avatar of the god Vishnu. | She changed her avatar to a picture of her cat. | The avatar walked across the virtual world.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say «AV-uh-tar». Countable. The Hindu meaning is the original one; the computing meaning is newer. Online safety: an avatar should not show your face, school or address.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To do with birds: «avian flu» is bird flu. 2) (science) Belonging to birds as a group: «avian dinosaurs» means birds, which scientists count as living dinosaurs.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons «avian» is the scientific word for bird-related: avian biology, avian eggs, avian flu. Vets who treat birds are avian vets. Latin «avis» means bird; «aviation» (flying) comes from the same root.
examples from the lessons: Avian flu is a disease that spreads among birds. | Scientists say birds are avian dinosaurs. | The vet specialises in avian medicine. | Feathers are an avian feature. | The zoo has a new avian house full of parrots. | Avian eggs come in many colours.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say «AY-vee-un». A formal or scientific word; in everyday talk say «bird». Related: aviary (a big cage for birds), aviation (flying aircraft).

meaning for a pupil: 1) To talk quickly in a way that is hard to understand or silly: «She babbled about her holiday.» 2) (of a baby) To make speech-like sounds before real words: «ba-ba-ba». 3) (of water) To make a soft, bubbling sound: «a babbling brook». 4) (noun) A noise of many voices at once, or silly talk.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on growing up, babbling is a stage when babies practise sounds before talking. In stories and poems a «babbling brook» is a gentle stream. In the Bible the Tower of Babel story is often linked (by sound) to «babble». Phrases: «babble on», «a babble of voices», «babbling brook».
examples from the lessons: The baby babbled happily in her cot. | Stop babbling and tell me what happened! | We sat by a babbling brook. | A babble of voices filled the canteen. | He babbled on about his new game for ages. | Babies babble before they say their first word.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double b in the middle, one l: babble, babbled, babbling. Do not confuse with «bubble». Babbling is not rude for babies, but saying someone «babbles» can sound unkind.

part of speech: verb form (bag, bags, bagged, bagging); noun (bagging — uncountable)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Putting things into bags: «bagging groceries». 2) (informal) Catching, getting or winning something: «bagging a goal», «bagging the best seat». 3) (slang, US) «Bagging on someone» means making fun of or criticising them. 4) (noun) Rough cloth used for making sacks. 5) (UK, hiking) Climbing a list of hills: «Munro bagging».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life bagging happens at supermarket tills and in the garden (bagging leaves). In sports reports «bagging a goal» means scoring. Children say «Bags I go first!» (UK) to claim something. Phrases: «bag up», «bag a seat», «bags first».
examples from the lessons: He's been bagging groceries at the supermarket after school. | We spent Saturday bagging up autumn leaves. | She ended up bagging two goals in the match. | I'm bagging the front seat! | They were bagging on my new haircut. | Uncle Rory is bagging all the Munros in Scotland.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double the g: bag, bagged, bagging. «Bags I» or «bagsy» (UK, children's slang) means «I claim it». The slang «bag on» is US and can be unkind.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A pen with a tiny metal ball at its tip that rolls and spreads ink as you write; also called a ballpoint pen. 2) (adjective) Of this kind of pen: «ballpoint ink».
its sense in the lessons: In school, pupils often move from pencils to ink pens; some schools prefer fountain or handwriting pens, others allow ballpoints. In the UK a ballpoint is often called a «biro», after its inventor László Bíró. Ballpoint ink cannot be rubbed out like pencil.
examples from the lessons: Can I borrow a blue ballpoint? | The ballpoint pen ran out of ink in the middle of my test. | Ballpoint ink dries quickly. | Write your answer in ballpoint, not pencil. | The tiny ball in a ballpoint rolls as you write. | My ballpoint leaked in my pencil case.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word: ballpoint. UK informal word: biro; US: pen. Countable. A felt-tip and a fountain pen are different kinds.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (idiom) Something that suddenly becomes popular, which many people join just because others do: «jump on the bandwagon». 2) A large cart that carried a band playing music in a parade.
its sense in the lessons: In lessons about persuasion, adverts and politics, the «bandwagon effect» is a trick: «everyone is buying it, so you should too». Thinking for yourself means not just jumping on the bandwagon. Phrases: «jump on the bandwagon», «climb on the bandwagon».
examples from the lessons: When the toy became popular, everyone jumped on the bandwagon. | The advert used the bandwagon trick: «Everyone has one!» | Don't just join the bandwagon; decide what you think. | In old parades the band rode on a bandwagon. | Lots of fans jumped on the bandwagon once the team started winning. | The fidget spinner bandwagon didn't last long.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word. Almost always used in the idiom «jump/climb on the bandwagon», which can sound a bit critical: joining for popularity, not because you believe in it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A building with baths for public use, where people go to wash, bathe and relax. 2) Ancient Roman baths, Turkish baths (hammams), Japanese bathhouses (sento, onsen) and Finnish saunas are all kinds of bathhouses. 3) (old) A building at a beach where swimmers change.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons Roman bathhouses had hot, warm and cold rooms (caldarium, tepidarium, frigidarium) and were places to meet friends. In many cultures public bathhouses were needed when homes had no baths. In stories and films they appear as warm, steamy places.
examples from the lessons: The Romans built a bathhouse in Bath. | The bathhouse had a hot room and a cold pool. | Romans met friends at the bathhouse. | In Japan some people visit a public bathhouse. | We saw the ruins of a Roman bathhouse on our school trip. | Steam filled the old bathhouse.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word, double h: bath + house. Plural: bathhouses. Not the same as a «bathroom» in a home.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A very poisonous plant, also called deadly nightshade, with purple flowers and shiny black berries. 2) A drug made from this plant, used carefully in medicine (for example to widen the pupils of the eyes).
its sense in the lessons: In science and safety lessons belladonna is an example of a poisonous wild plant: never eat berries you do not know. Its name means «beautiful lady» in Italian, because long ago women used drops of it to make their eyes look bigger, which was dangerous. In stories it is a poison used by villains.
examples from the lessons: Belladonna berries are shiny, black and very poisonous. | Never eat wild berries; they might be belladonna. | Belladonna is also called deadly nightshade. | In the mystery story, the poison was belladonna. | Long ago, ladies used belladonna drops to make their pupils big. | Doctors make a medicine from belladonna, used in tiny doses.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say «bell-uh-DON-uh». Italian «bella donna» = beautiful lady. Deadly nightshade is very dangerous: even a few berries can kill a child. Do not confuse with the harmless-ish tomato and potato, which are in the same plant family.

part of speech: noun (bellows — plural in form; a pair of bellows); verb form (bellow, bellows, bellowed, bellowing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A tool with handles and a soft folding middle that pushes out a strong stream of air when you squeeze it, used to make a fire burn hotter. 2) The folding air part of an accordion, organ or old camera. 3) «Bellows» is also the -s form of the verb «bellow»: to shout or roar loudly. «He bellows at the dog.»
its sense in the lessons: In history and science lessons blacksmiths used bellows to blow air into fires to make them hot enough to melt metal: more oxygen makes a fire burn hotter. Our lungs work a bit like bellows. In stories a giant or angry man «bellows» orders.
examples from the lessons: The blacksmith pumped the bellows to make the fire glow. | Grandpa uses a pair of bellows to start the fire. | The accordion's bellows squeezed in and out. | Our lungs work a bit like bellows. | The coach bellows at us from the side of the pitch. | The bull bellows in the field.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Bellows» the tool is singular or plural: «the bellows is» or «the bellows are»; «a pair of bellows». Say «BELL-ohz». The verb «bellow» means shout loudly — a different meaning.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Able to speak two languages well: «a bilingual child». 2) Written or spoken in two languages: «a bilingual dictionary», «bilingual signs».
its sense in the lessons: In language lessons and everyday life, many children are bilingual: they speak one language at home and another at school. In Canada signs are bilingual (English and French), in Wales (English and Welsh), in Ireland (English and Irish). Being bilingual is a skill, not a problem. Related: monolingual (one), trilingual (three), multilingual (many).
examples from the lessons: My friend is bilingual in English and Polish. | Road signs in Wales are bilingual. | Canada has a bilingual government. | I used a bilingual dictionary in French class. | Bilingual children often switch languages in one sentence. | Our school newsletter is bilingual.
note for the reader of a maths problem: bi- means two (bicycle, biannual). Say «by-LING-gwul». Myth: learning two languages does not confuse children; most become fluent in both. Noun: bilingualism.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A furry, dark animal from the rainforests of South-East Asia, also called a bearcat, though it is neither a bear nor a cat. 2) It lives mostly in trees, can hold on with its long tail, eats fruit and small animals, and is famous for smelling like buttered popcorn.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons it is an example of a prehensile (gripping) tail and of rainforest animals threatened by forest loss. In zoos people notice its popcorn smell, which comes from a chemical in its scent. Phrases: «bearcat».
examples from the lessons: The binturong curled its tail around a branch. | A binturong smells like buttered popcorn! | Binturongs are also called bearcats. | The binturong at the zoo was asleep high in a tree. | Binturongs help spread seeds of strangler figs. | Cutting down rainforests puts binturongs in danger.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say «bin-TOO-rong». It is related to civets, not to bears or cats. Plural: binturongs. Its tail can grip, like a monkey's.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) Light made by living things, such as fireflies, glow-worms, some fungi and many deep-sea animals. 2) The glowing itself, for example blue sparkles in the sea at night caused by tiny plankton.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons bioluminescence is a chemical reaction in an animal's body (luciferin and an enzyme) that gives off light with little heat. Animals use it to attract mates, lure prey, scare predators or hide. In the deep sea most animals make some light. Adjective: bioluminescent.
examples from the lessons: Fireflies flash by bioluminescence. | The anglerfish uses bioluminescence to lure prey. | We saw blue bioluminescence in the waves at night. | Bioluminescence happens because of a chemical reaction. | Glow-worms in New Zealand caves light up the ceiling with bioluminescence. | Some mushrooms glow in the dark with bioluminescence.
note for the reader of a maths problem: bio (life) + luminescence (giving off light). Uncountable. Not the same as fluorescence (glowing when another light shines on it) or reflection. Spelling trap: -scence.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (history) A member of the group of Russian communists, led by Lenin, who took power in Russia in a revolution and later created the Soviet Union. 2) (adjective) To do with the Bolsheviks: «the Bolshevik Revolution». 3) (old slang, UK) «Bolshie» or «bolshy» means stubborn and rebellious, from this word.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons about the Russian Revolution, the Bolsheviks overthrew the government, killed the royal family and set up a one-party state; a civil war and much suffering followed, including in Ukraine. The name comes from Russian «bolshinstvo», majority. Written with a capital B.
examples from the lessons: The Bolsheviks were led by Lenin. | The Bolshevik Revolution changed Russia forever. | The Bolsheviks took control of the government in Petrograd. | Many people suffered under Bolshevik rule. | Our history book has a poster from the Bolshevik era. | Stop being so bolshie and do your chores!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital B. Plural: Bolsheviks. Their rivals were the Mensheviks. «Bolshie» (UK, informal) is a separate word meaning difficult or stubborn.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person whose job is to keep careful records of the money a business earns and spends. 2) (old) Someone who looks after books.
its sense in the lessons: In money and maths lessons, a bookkeeper records every sale and every bill so a business knows if it is making a profit. Bookkeeping uses adding, subtracting and checking that totals match. Related: accountant (who checks and plans the money, usually more qualified).
examples from the lessons: The bookkeeper wrote down every sale in the ledger. | Our corner shop has a bookkeeper who comes on Fridays. | A good bookkeeper checks that the numbers add up. | Mum works as a bookkeeper for a building company. | The bookkeeper found a mistake in the bill. | «Bookkeeper» has three double letters in a row!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Famous spelling: oo, kk, ee — three double letters in a row. One word. Noun for the job: bookkeeping. Not a «librarian» (who looks after library books).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) Very clever and good at thinking and learning. 2) (informal) Smart in a bookish way.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday talk «brainy» is a friendly or teasing way to say clever; a «brainbox» (UK) or «brainiac» (US) is a very brainy person. In stories the brainy friend often solves the puzzle. Some children feel teased when called brainy, so use it kindly.
examples from the lessons: My sister is really brainy at maths. | The brainy kid in the film builds a robot. | You don't have to be brainy to be kind. | She's the brainiest girl in our class. | Owls are thought of as brainy birds in stories. | Ask Tom, he's brainy about dinosaurs.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal. Comparisons: brainier, brainiest (y changes to i). Myth: owls are not actually cleverer than other birds. Synonyms: clever, smart, bright.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A word shouted to praise someone for doing something very well, especially at the end of a performance: «Bravo!» 2) «Bravo» is the word for the letter B in the international spelling alphabet (Alpha, Bravo, Charlie …). 3) (noun, old) A hired thug or killer, in old stories.
its sense in the lessons: In music and theatre, the audience shouts «Bravo!» and claps. The word comes from Italian. On radios, phones and in the army, letters are spelled with code words: «B for Bravo». Phrases: «Bravo!», «a chorus of bravos».
examples from the lessons: «Bravo!» shouted the audience when the song ended. | The teacher said «Bravo!» when I finished my piano piece. | My postcode starts with «Bravo Sierra». | The pilot spelled out «Bravo, Alpha». | Bravo, you've tidied your room at last! | Cries of «bravo» filled the theatre.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Italian word. Strictly «brava» for a woman and «bravi» for a group in Italian, but in English «bravo» is used for everyone. Sometimes said sarcastically: «Oh, bravo,» meaning «well done (not)».

meaning for a pupil: 1) From or to do with Brazil, the largest country in South America: «Brazilian football». 2) A person from Brazil. 3) «Brazilian Portuguese» is the kind of Portuguese spoken in Brazil.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons Brazil has the Amazon rainforest and many people speak Portuguese, not Spanish. Brazilian football, carnival and food (feijoada, brigadeiros) are famous. Written with a capital B.
examples from the lessons: She is Brazilian and speaks Portuguese. | The Brazilian team won the match. | We tasted Brazilian food at the festival. | The Amazon rainforest is mostly in Brazilian land. | Many Brazilians celebrate Carnival with music and dancing. | A Brazilian nut is a big seed from the Amazon.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital B. People in Brazil speak Portuguese, not Spanish — a common mistake. The nut is usually called «Brazil nut». Plural: Brazilians.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Being short of breath and finding it hard to breathe, for example after running or because of illness. 2) A feeling of great excitement or surprise, as if you cannot breathe.
its sense in the lessons: In health and PE lessons breathlessness after exercise is normal; it shows the body needs more oxygen. But sudden breathlessness when resting, or with asthma, needs help from an adult or doctor. In stories it shows fear, excitement or tiredness. Adjective: breathless.
examples from the lessons: After the race I felt a bit of breathlessness. | Breathlessness can be a sign of an asthma attack. | The doctor asked about Grandma's breathlessness. | The climbers felt breathlessness high on the mountain. | In the story her breathlessness came from excitement. | Tell an adult if breathlessness doesn't go away.
note for the reader of a maths problem: breath + less + ness. Spelling: «breath» is the noun (say «breth»), «breathe» is the verb. Uncountable. Adjective «breathless», adverb «breathlessly».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A soft, creamy French cheese with a white, soft rind, originally from the Brie region near Paris. 2) (a name) Brie is also a region of France.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life brie is eaten with bread or crackers; it is served at parties and picnics. In French lessons it is one of many famous cheeses (camembert, roquefort). Safety: pregnant women are often told to avoid soft cheeses like brie.
examples from the lessons: We had brie and grapes at the picnic. | Brie has a soft white rind. | Dad cut a slice of brie for his sandwich. | Brie comes from France. | The brie was so ripe it was runny. | My little brother doesn't like the smell of brie.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say «bree». Can be written with a capital B because it comes from a place name. Uncountable: «some brie», «a piece of brie». You can eat the white rind.

part of speech: verb (browse, browses, browsed, browsing); noun (a browse)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To look through things in a relaxed way, without looking for something particular: «browse in a bookshop». 2) (computing) To look at web pages on the internet: «browse the web». 3) (of animals) To feed on leaves and twigs of bushes and trees: «Giraffes browse on acacia trees.» 4) (noun) A relaxed look: «have a browse».
its sense in the lessons: In computing and online safety lessons a «browser» is the program for looking at websites, and «safe browsing» means visiting trusted sites. In science, «browsers» are animals that eat leaves (giraffes), while «grazers» eat grass (cows). Phrases: «browse the shelves», «browse online», «just browsing».
examples from the lessons: I like to browse in the library on Saturdays. | We browsed the web for facts about volcanoes. | «Can I help you?» «No thanks, I'm just browsing.» | Giraffes browse on the top leaves of trees. | Have a browse through this catalogue. | Only browse websites your teacher says are safe.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Rhymes with «cows». Noun for the program: browser (Chrome, Safari, Firefox). «Just browsing» in shops means you are only looking.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The amount that one bucket can hold: «a bucketful of water». 2) (informal) A large amount: «bucketfuls of rain».
its sense in the lessons: In maths and science problems «bucketful» is a unit of measure: if a bucket holds 10 litres, 3 bucketfuls hold 30 litres. In everyday talk, «it rained buckets» or «bucketfuls» means very heavy rain. Phrases: «by the bucketful».
examples from the lessons: We carried a bucketful of sand to make the castle. | It took six bucketfuls to fill the paddling pool. | The bucket holds 8 litres, so 4 bucketfuls are 32 litres. | She poured a bucketful of water over the campfire. | They earned money by the bucketful. | The farmer gave the pigs a bucketful of scraps.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: bucketfuls (standard) or bucketsful (rarer). Same pattern: spoonful, cupful, handful. In maths: number of bucketfuls × capacity of one bucket = total.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who takes part in a bullfight, a public show in which people tease and fight a bull, usually ending with the bull being killed. 2) The main bullfighter is called a matador.
its sense in the lessons: In culture and ethics lessons bullfighting is a tradition in Spain, Portugal, southern France and parts of Latin America, but many people think it is cruel to animals and some places have banned it. In stories a bullfighter waves a red cape. Myth: bulls are not angered by the colour red; they react to the cape moving.
examples from the lessons: The bullfighter waved a red cape. | Many people protest that bullfighting is cruel. | The matador is the most famous bullfighter. | Some cities in Spain have banned bullfights. | In the painting a bullfighter stands in the ring. | Bulls are colour-blind to red; they charge at the moving cape.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word: bull + fighter. Spanish words: torero, matador. Myth trap: bulls do not hate red; the movement matters. A sensitive topic: treat both the tradition and the animal-welfare view fairly.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) The upward push that water (or air) gives to an object, which makes things float or feel lighter. 2) The ability of something to float: «Cork has great buoyancy.» 3) Cheerfulness and the ability to recover quickly from bad times: «her buoyancy of spirit». 4) (money) When prices or business stay high and strong.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons buoyancy explains why boats float and stones sink: an object floats if the upthrust of the water is as big as its weight. Salty water gives more buoyancy, so floating in the sea is easier than in a pool. Swimmers use buoyancy aids (armbands, floats). Related: upthrust, float, sink, density.
examples from the lessons: Buoyancy keeps the boat afloat. | A life jacket gives you buoyancy in the water. | It is easier to float in the sea because salt water gives more buoyancy. | We tested the buoyancy of different fruits: the orange floated. | Submarines change their buoyancy to dive and rise. | Despite losing the match, the team's buoyancy returned quickly.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say «BOY-un-see» (UK) or «BOO-yun-see» (US). Spelling trap: «buoy» comes first (u before o). Adjective: buoyant. Myth: heavy things can float if their shape pushes away enough water — a steel ship floats.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A dark purplish-red colour, like red wine. 2) (a name) Burgundy is a region in eastern France, famous for its wine. 3) Wine from Burgundy, red or white.
its sense in the lessons: In art and everyday life «burgundy» is a colour name for clothes, school uniforms and cars. In history, the Dukes of Burgundy were powerful in the Middle Ages. In French the region is «Bourgogne».
examples from the lessons: My school blazer is burgundy. | She painted her door a deep burgundy. | Burgundy is a region in France. | The Duke of Burgundy was a rich and powerful ruler. | The velvet curtains were burgundy. | Burgundy is darker than red and a bit purple.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Use a capital B for the region and the wine from it; small b for the colour. Synonym colours: maroon (brownish), wine red, crimson (brighter).

part of speech: adjective (calculated); verb form (calculate, calculates, calculated, calculating)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Past form of «calculate»: worked out using numbers: «We calculated the area.» 2) Carefully planned to get a result, often in a sneaky way: «a calculated lie». 3) Meant or likely to do something: «a joke calculated to make him laugh». 4) «A calculated risk» is a risk you take after thinking about the chances.
its sense in the lessons: In maths lessons, «calculated» is what you did when you worked out an answer; «show how you calculated it». In stories, a «calculated move» is a clever, planned action by a hero or villain. Phrases: «calculated risk», «carefully calculated».
examples from the lessons: We calculated the perimeter of the playground. | She calculated that the trip would take two hours. | His friendliness was calculated; he wanted something. | The firefighter took a calculated risk to save the cat. | The cost was calculated at £50. | The advert was calculated to make children want the toy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past form of calculate: drop -e, add -ed. «Calculated» about a person's action can sound cold or sneaky; «calculated risk» is neutral. In maths it just means worked out.

part of speech: adjective (calculating); verb form (calculate, calculates, calculated, calculating)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The -ing form of «calculate»: working something out with numbers: «I'm calculating the total.» 2) (of a person) Cold and sneaky, always planning how to get what they want, often by tricking others: «a calculating villain».
its sense in the lessons: In maths lessons «calculating» is doing the sums: calculating area, calculating change. In stories «calculating» describes a sly, scheming character, often a villain or a fox. Phrases: «calculating machine», «a cold, calculating look».
examples from the lessons: I'm calculating how much pocket money I'll have by summer. | The calculating fox tricked the crow out of her cheese. | Calculating the area of a rectangle is easy: length times width. | She gave him a cold, calculating look. | Early calculating machines were huge. | Use a calculator when calculating big numbers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a verb form it is neutral; as an adjective for people it is negative (sly, scheming). Noun: calculation; tool: calculator.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A bush with shiny dark green leaves and large flowers like roses, usually pink, red or white, that bloom in late winter or spring. 2) The tea plant is a kind of camellia (Camellia sinensis).
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, camellias show evergreen plants; tea leaves come from one kind. In gardens in the UK, Ireland, Australia and New Zealand camellias flower early, when little else is blooming. In stories «The Lady of the Camellias» is a famous old French novel.
examples from the lessons: The camellia bush is covered in pink flowers. | Tea is made from the leaves of a camellia plant. | Camellias bloom in late winter. | Grandma's camellia has white flowers. | Frost turned the camellia petals brown. | The camellia's leaves are shiny and dark green.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say «kuh-MEE-lee-uh» (UK) or «kuh-MEEL-yuh» (US). Spelling: one m, double l. Plural: camellias.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (medicine) A thin tube put into a vein or into the body by a doctor or nurse, so that medicine or fluid can go in, or fluid can come out. 2) A small tube under the nose that gives oxygen (a nasal cannula).
its sense in the lessons: In hospital, a patient may have a cannula in the back of the hand for a drip. It is put in with a needle, but the needle comes out and a soft plastic tube stays. In stories about hospital it helps children understand what they see.
examples from the lessons: The nurse put a cannula in my hand for the drip. | It stung a bit, but then the cannula didn't hurt. | Grandpa had a nasal cannula for oxygen. | The cannula was taped down so it wouldn't move. | Doctors use a cannula to give medicine straight into a vein. | The nurse took the cannula out before I went home.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say «KAN-yoo-luh». Plural: cannulas (everyday) or cannulae. Verb: cannulate (medical). Not the same as a «canal» or «cannon».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A constellation (group of stars) whose name means «goat-horned», pictured as a sea-goat. 2) In astrology, one of the twelve star signs, for people born roughly between late December and mid-January; such a person is called «a Capricorn». 3) (geography) The Tropic of Capricorn is an imaginary line around the Earth south of the equator.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons the Tropic of Capricorn marks the most southern place where the Sun can be straight overhead at midday; it crosses Australia, Brazil and southern Africa. In science, Capricornus is a real constellation. In astrology the star sign is a belief, not science.
examples from the lessons: The Tropic of Capricorn passes through Australia. | Capricorn is pictured as a goat with a fish's tail. | My uncle says he is a Capricorn because his birthday is in January. | We found the constellation Capricorn in the star chart. | Rockhampton in Queensland is near the Tropic of Capricorn. | Astrology says Capricorns are hard-working, but there is no science behind it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital C. The constellation's Latin name is Capricornus. The northern line is the Tropic of Cancer. Star signs are part of astrology, not astronomy.

part of speech: adjective (carbonated); verb form (carbonate, carbonates, carbonated, carbonating)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (of a drink) With bubbles of carbon dioxide gas in it; fizzy: «carbonated water». 2) Past form of «carbonate»: to add carbon dioxide to a liquid.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons carbonated drinks show a gas dissolved in a liquid: when you open the bottle the pressure drops and bubbles escape. In health lessons many carbonated drinks have lots of sugar, which is bad for teeth. Everyday words: fizzy (UK), sparkling, soda or pop (US), soft drink.
examples from the lessons: Carbonated water has tiny bubbles. | Shake a carbonated drink and it will spray when opened. | Fizzy drinks are carbonated with carbon dioxide. | The doctor said to drink fewer sugary carbonated drinks. | We tested how fast carbonated water goes flat. | Lemonade in the UK is usually carbonated.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal or scientific word; children usually say «fizzy». Opposite: still (still water), flat (lost its fizz). Carbon dioxide is a gas, not «carbon» itself.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A deep, bright red colour. 2) A red dye or paint made from cochineal insects, used in food, make-up and art.
its sense in the lessons: In art lessons carmine is one of the reds in a paint box. In science and food labels, carmine (also «E120» or «cochineal extract») is a natural red colouring made from crushed insects, so it is not vegetarian. Related: crimson, scarlet, cochineal.
examples from the lessons: She painted the rose petals carmine. | Carmine is a deep, rich red. | The strawberry yoghurt was coloured with carmine. | Carmine is made from tiny insects called cochineal. | The artist mixed carmine with white to make pink. | The label said «colour: carmine (E120)».
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say «KAR-mine» or «KAR-min». Uncountable. Vegetarians and vegans often avoid carmine because it comes from insects.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) An orange-yellow substance found in carrots, sweet potatoes, pumpkins and many green leaves, which gives them their colour. 2) The body turns it into vitamin A, which helps eyes, skin and the immune system.
its sense in the lessons: In science and food lessons carotene explains why carrots are orange and why autumn leaves show yellow and orange when the green chlorophyll fades. Myth: eating carrots will not let you see in the dark, though vitamin A does help eyes. Related: beta-carotene, vitamin A.
examples from the lessons: Carrots are orange because of carotene. | Carotene turns into vitamin A in your body. | Sweet potatoes and mangoes are full of carotene. | In autumn, when the green fades, the carotene in leaves shows up. | Eating huge amounts of carrots can turn your skin a bit orange because of carotene. | Flamingos are not pink from carotene but from similar colourings in their food.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say «KARR-uh-teen». Uncountable. Named after the carrot. Myth trap: carrots help healthy eyes but do not give night vision; that story was spread in wartime as a cover story.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who draws cartoons: funny or simple drawings, comic strips, or animated films. 2) Someone who draws cartoons for newspapers that make a point about news or politics.
its sense in the lessons: In art lessons pupils learn how cartoonists use simple lines, speech bubbles and exaggeration. In history and media lessons, political cartoons by cartoonists comment on events and leaders; they can be funny and also make serious points. Charles Schulz (Peanuts) and Hergé (Tintin) were famous cartoonists.
examples from the lessons: I want to be a cartoonist when I grow up. | The cartoonist drew the prime minister with a giant nose. | Charles Schulz was the cartoonist who drew Snoopy. | A cartoonist visited our school and taught us to draw faces. | The newspaper cartoonist made a joke about the weather. | Cartoonists often work with a pencil first and then ink.
note for the reader of a maths problem: cartoon + -ist (a person who does something). Plural: cartoonists. Similar: animator (makes moving cartoons), illustrator (draws pictures for books).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A CD (compact disc) is a thin, shiny, round plastic disc that stores music or computer data, read by a laser. 2) (computing) «cd» is a command for «change directory»: it moves you to another folder in a terminal. 3) (science) «cd» is the symbol for the candela, the unit of light brightness. 4) Other meanings in context: CD can mean «certificate of deposit» (money) or «corps diplomatique» (diplomat's car sign).
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life CDs were used for music and games before streaming; many families still have them. In computing and coding lessons, «cd» is one of the first terminal commands. In history of technology, the CD followed records and cassettes. Phrases: «burn a CD», «CD player».
examples from the lessons: Grandad still listens to music on CDs. | Put the CD in the player and press play. | The CD was scratched, so it kept skipping. | Type «cd Documents» to go into the Documents folder. | Our class made a CD of our songs. | A CD is read by a laser beam.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually capitals: CD; plural CDs (no apostrophe). Say each letter: «see-dee». In computing it is small letters: cd. «Disc» with a c is used for CDs and DVDs.

part of speech: noun (a cedar, cedars; cedar — the wood, uncountable)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A tall evergreen tree with needle-like leaves and cones, such as the cedar of Lebanon. 2) The pleasant-smelling, reddish wood of cedar trees, used for chests, fences and pencils. 3) Some other trees with sweet-smelling wood are also called cedars (for example western red cedar in Canada).
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons cedars are conifers. In the Bible the cedars of Lebanon are symbols of strength and grandeur; Solomon's temple was built with cedar wood. Cedar appears on the flag of Lebanon. In everyday life cedar wood keeps moths away from clothes.
examples from the lessons: A huge cedar stands in the middle of the park. | The cedar of Lebanon is on Lebanon's flag. | Grandma keeps her blankets in a cedar chest. | Cedar wood smells lovely. | King Solomon built the temple with cedar, the Bible says. | The fence is made of red cedar.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say «SEE-dur». Do not confuse with «cider» (an apple drink) or «seeder». Countable for trees, uncountable for the wood.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (money) A small coin and unit of money worth one hundredth of a franc, used in France before the euro, and still used in Switzerland (one hundredth of a Swiss franc) and some African countries. 2) (French) In France people still say «centime» for a euro cent.
its sense in the lessons: In French lessons centimes are like pennies or cents: 100 centimes make one franc (or one euro, in everyday French speech). In maths, money problems with centimes work like cents: 50 centimes = half a franc.
examples from the lessons: In Switzerland, one franc is a hundred centimes. | The bread cost two euros and fifty centimes. | A centime is like a cent or a penny. | Grandpa has old French centime coins from his trip. | In maths: 250 centimes make 2.50 francs. | «Ça coûte cinquante centimes» means «It costs fifty cents.»
note for the reader of a maths problem: French word used in English: say «SON-teem». 1 centime = 1/100 of a franc. In the eurozone the official word is «cent», but French people say «centime». Do not confuse with «centimetre» (a length).

meaning for a pupil: 1) To say officially, often in writing, that something is true or correct: «The doctor certified that he was ill.» 2) To give someone an official paper showing they have trained and passed: «She was certified as a lifeguard.» 3) To officially say that something meets a standard: «certified organic».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday and adult life, certificates are official papers: birth certificates, swimming certificates, exam results. A «certified» teacher, nurse or electrician has proven training. In law, a doctor can certify a death or illness. Noun: certification, certificate.
examples from the lessons: The swimming coach will certify that you can swim 25 metres. | The eggs are certified free-range. | My aunt is a certified first-aid trainer. | The doctor certified that I needed a week off school. | The judges certified the new world record. | A teacher must certify that this is your own work.
note for the reader of a maths problem: y changes to i: certifies, certified. Formal word. Related: certain, certificate. Do not confuse with «certificate» (the paper) and «certify» (the action).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A competition to find the best player or team in a sport or game: «the world championship». 2) The title or position of being the champion: «She won the championship.» 3) (formal) Strong support for a cause: «his championship of animal rights».
its sense in the lessons: In PE and sports news, championships are big tournaments: the World Championships, the Six Nations championship (rugby), the Championship (the second English football league). In everyday life there are school chess or spelling championships. Phrases: «win the championship», «championship title».
examples from the lessons: Our team won the county championship. | The swimming championship lasts three days. | She is training for the world championship. | The school chess championship is on Friday. | They lost in the final of the championship. | Leeds played in the Championship last season.
note for the reader of a maths problem: champion + -ship. Countable. «The Championship» with a capital C is the name of an English football league. Related: champion (the winner), champ (informal).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (Greek myth) Charon is the ferryman in ancient Greek stories who rowed the souls of the dead across the river Styx (or Acheron) into the underworld, in return for a coin. 2) (science) Charon is the largest moon of the dwarf planet Pluto, about half Pluto's size.
its sense in the lessons: In history and myths lessons Charon explains why ancient Greeks sometimes put a coin with the dead. In space science, Pluto and Charon are so close in size that they circle around a point between them. Written with a capital C.
examples from the lessons: Charon rowed the dead across the river Styx. | The Greeks put a coin with the dead to pay Charon. | Charon is Pluto's biggest moon. | The New Horizons spacecraft took photos of Charon. | Pluto and Charon spin around each other like dancers. | In the story the hero had no coin for Charon.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital C. Say «KAIR-on» or «SHAR-on» (the moon is often said «SHAR-on»). A name from myth and a moon, not an ordinary word. Not the name «Sharon».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) A person, often a child, who talks a lot and seems never to stop. 2) (UK) A folded paper game, also called a fortune teller or cootie catcher, that you open and close with your fingers.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life it is a friendly, teasing word for someone talkative; a teacher might say «You're a real chatterbox today!» In stories a chatterbox character can be funny or give away secrets. In the playground pupils make paper chatterboxes to tell silly fortunes.
examples from the lessons: My little sister is a real chatterbox. | «Quiet please, chatterboxes!» said the teacher. | We made paper chatterboxes at break time. | The parrot was a chatterbox and copied every word. | Grandma calls me a chatterbox on long car journeys. | The chatterbox couldn't keep a secret.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word. Plural: chatterboxes. Mostly friendly, but can be a mild telling-off. Related: chatter, chatty.

part of speech: verb form (chatter, chatters, chattered, chattering); noun (chattering — uncountable); adjective (chattering)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Talking quickly and a lot about small, unimportant things: «The girls were chattering in the corridor.» 2) (of teeth) Knocking together quickly because you are cold or scared: «My teeth were chattering.» 3) (of birds, monkeys, squirrels) Making quick, high, repeated sounds. 4) (of machines) Making quick rattling noises.
its sense in the lessons: In science and health lessons, teeth chattering is a sign of being cold: the body shivers to make heat. In stories chattering children, birds or monkeys fill a scene with noise. «The chattering classes» (UK, informal) means educated people who like to discuss news and politics.
examples from the lessons: We were chattering when the teacher walked in. | My teeth were chattering after the swim in the cold sea. | Monkeys were chattering in the trees. | Stop chattering and listen, please. | The magpies kept chattering on the roof. | The old engine was chattering loudly.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double t: chatter. Chattering teeth = cold or fear, not talking. Synonyms: chatting, nattering (UK), gabbing.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A hamburger with a slice of melted cheese on top of the meat patty, served in a bun.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life cheeseburgers are fast food in many countries. In health lessons they are an example of food high in fat and salt, fine as a treat but not every day. In maths problems they often appear in shop prices. Related: burger, hamburger, veggie burger.
examples from the lessons: I ordered a cheeseburger and chips. | A cheeseburger costs £3, so two cost £6. | The cheese melted over the burger. | Dad made cheeseburgers on the barbecue. | Fast food like cheeseburgers is a treat, not an every-day meal. | Do you want pickles on your cheeseburger?
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word. Plural: cheeseburgers. Myth trap: «hamburger» has no ham in it; it is named after Hamburg in Germany.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A machine or cabinet that keeps food or drink very cold, like a fridge in a shop or kitchen. 2) (informal) A frightening story or film that gives you a shiver: «a spine-chiller». 3) (UK, informal) «A chiller» can also mean a relaxed, calm person or time.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life supermarkets keep milk and meat in chillers. In science and food safety, cold slows the growth of germs. In reading lessons a «chiller» or «spine-chiller» is a scary story. Related: chill, chilly, chilling.
examples from the lessons: The milk is in the chiller at the back of the shop. | The café has a drinks chiller by the door. | That ghost story was a real chiller. | Keep raw meat in the chiller to stop germs growing. | The film is a spine-chiller, so don't watch it before bed. | Fish are packed in ice and kept in a chiller.
note for the reader of a maths problem: chill + -er. Countable. A chiller is colder than a room but usually not as cold as a freezer.

part of speech: noun (a chisel, chisels); verb (chisel, chisels, chiselled, chiselling; US chiseled, chiseling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A tool with a flat, sharp metal end, used with a hammer or mallet to cut or shape wood, stone or metal. 2) (verb) To cut or carve with a chisel: «He chiselled his name into the stone.» 3) (adjective form) «Chiselled» features means a face with sharp, clear lines. 4) (old slang, US) To cheat someone.
its sense in the lessons: In design and technology and history lessons, sculptors and stonemasons use chisels to carve statues and letters. Safety: always cut away from your body and keep hands behind the blade. In stories «chiselled» faces are handsome and strong.
examples from the lessons: The carpenter used a chisel to make a groove. | Michelangelo carved marble with a chisel. | Always cut away from your body with a chisel. | They chiselled the names into the war memorial. | The stonemason tapped the chisel with a mallet. | The hero had a chiselled jaw.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: chisel (one l). UK: chiselled, chiselling (double l); US: chiseled, chiseling. Say «CHIZ-ul».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (of the sea or a lake) Full of small, rough waves, because of wind: «choppy water». 2) (of writing, speech or music) Broken into short, jerky parts that do not flow well. 3) (of hair) Cut in uneven layers on purpose.
its sense in the lessons: In geography, travel and safety, choppy water makes boat trips bumpy and can make people seasick; swimmers and kayakers must take care. In writing lessons, teachers say «Your sentences are choppy — try joining some with «and» or «because»».
examples from the lessons: The sea was too choppy for the ferry to sail. | We felt seasick on the choppy water. | The lake got choppy when the wind picked up. | Your paragraph is a bit choppy; join some sentences together. | The video was choppy because the internet was slow. | She has a short, choppy haircut.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparatives: choppier, choppiest. Opposites: calm, smooth, flat. Not to do with chopping food, though it comes from «chop».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) A way of separating a mixture into the different substances in it, by letting a liquid or gas carry them along paper or another material at different speeds. 2) Paper chromatography is a simple school experiment that shows the different colours hidden in an ink.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons you draw a felt-tip dot on filter paper, dip the edge in water, and the water carries the colours up at different speeds, splitting black ink into blue, yellow and pink. Scientists and police labs use chromatography to test food, medicines and crime evidence. The result is a «chromatogram».
examples from the lessons: In chromatography, we saw black ink split into blue and orange. | The water climbed up the paper and carried the colours with it. | Police labs use chromatography to test evidence. | Chromatography shows that one ink can contain many colours. | Our chromatography experiment used coffee filter paper. | Draw the line in pencil, because pencil does not run in chromatography.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say «kroh-muh-TOG-ruh-fee». chroma (colour) + graphy (writing). Uncountable. Use a pencil line for the start, because pencil (graphite) does not dissolve.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (abbreviation) CI often means «Chief Inspector», a senior police officer in the UK. 2) (abbreviation, science and maths) CI means «confidence interval», a range of numbers that probably contains the true value. 3) (abbreviation) The Channel Islands (Jersey, Guernsey and others) are sometimes written CI; CI is also the code for Côte d'Ivoire. 4) (Mandarin, pinyin) «Cì» means «time» as in «once, twice» (yí cì = once), and «cí» means «word»; it sounds like «tsuh». 5) (Italian) «Ci» means «us» or «there». It is not an English word.
its sense in the lessons: You meet CI in police dramas («DCI» = Detective Chief Inspector), in science reports about results, and in Mandarin lessons when counting how many times something happens. In computing, CI also means «continuous integration», automatically testing code.
examples from the lessons: The CI arrived at the crime scene. | DCI Smith led the detectives. | The scientists gave a 95% CI for the average height. | In Mandarin, «yí cì» means «once». | We went on holiday to the Channel Islands, written CI on the map. | «Ci vediamo» means «see you» in Italian.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Not an English word on its own. What it means depends on context: police rank, statistics, a place code, Mandarin pinyin («cì», sounds like «tsuh») or Italian. Do not guess; look at the sentence around it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) To do with or coming from citrus fruits such as lemons, limes and oranges. 2) Citric acid is a weak acid found in citrus fruits, which gives them their sour taste.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons citric acid is a safe, everyday acid: lemon juice turns blue litmus red; mixed with baking soda it fizzes, as in bath bombs and sherbet. In food, citric acid (E330) is added to sweets and drinks for a sour taste and to keep food fresh.
examples from the lessons: Lemons taste sour because of citric acid. | Bath bombs fizz because citric acid reacts with baking soda. | Citric acid is added to sour sweets. | Our class tested citric acid with litmus paper. | Limes contain a lot of citric acid. | The label says «acid: citric acid».
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say «SIT-rik». Mostly used in «citric acid». From «citrus». Citric acid is a weak acid, but it can still sting eyes and cuts.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A large, organised society with cities, government, laws, writing, art and trade: «the ancient Egyptian civilization». 2) Human society in general, especially its achievements: «the history of civilization». 3) (informal, humorous) Comfortable modern life with shops, toilets and internet: «After camping we were glad to be back in civilization.»
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons pupils study early civilizations: Sumer, Egypt, the Indus Valley, China, Greece, Rome, the Maya, the Aztecs and the Benin Kingdom. These had farming, cities, writing and rulers. Be careful: calling some peoples «civilized» and others «uncivilized» was used in the past to justify unfair treatment.
examples from the lessons: The ancient Egyptian civilization built the pyramids. | Writing is one sign of a civilization. | The Maya civilization had its own calendar. | After a week of camping we were happy to be back in civilization. | The Indus Valley civilization had drains and toilets. | Rivers helped early civilizations grow food.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: UK often «civilisation», US «civilization»; both are correct (Oxford spelling uses -ization). Adjective: civilized/civilised (polite, well-ordered). Countable for different civilizations.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A board with a hinged stick on top that is clapped shut in front of the camera at the start of each shot of a film, showing the scene and take number. 2) (North America, building) Clapboard: long, thin, overlapping boards on the outside of wooden houses.
its sense in the lessons: In media and film lessons, the clapperboard helps editors match up the picture and the sound, because the clap makes a clear sound at the exact moment the sticks meet. Someone shouts «Scene four, take two!» and claps. In US and Canadian houses «clapboard» siding is common.
examples from the lessons: «Action!» called the director after the clapperboard snapped shut. | The clapperboard showed «Scene 3, Take 2». | We made a clapperboard for our class film. | The clap helps match the sound to the picture. | The old house in Maine had white clapboard walls. | I held the clapperboard in our school play video.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word. Also called a «slate» or «clapper». In building, the North American word is usually «clapboard».

meaning for a pupil: 1) To clean something thoroughly, especially skin or a wound: «Cleanse the cut with water.» 2) To make someone or something pure, free from sin or guilt (church, Bible): «Cleanse me from my sin.» 3) To remove harmful or unwanted things: «cleanse the air». 4) (history) «Ethnic cleansing» means driving out or killing a whole group of people because of who they are — a terrible crime.
its sense in the lessons: In health and first aid, you cleanse a wound to stop germs. In adverts «cleanser» is soap for the face. In church and the Bible, Christians believe God can cleanse people from sin; Psalm 51 asks «cleanse me from my sin». In history lessons «ethnic cleansing» is a grave crime against humanity.
examples from the lessons: Cleanse the scratch with clean water before putting on a plaster. | Mum uses a face cleanser every night. | «Wash me and cleanse me from my sin,» says the psalm. | The rain seemed to cleanse the dusty city. | The nurse cleansed the wound carefully. | Christians believe that God's forgiveness cleanses the heart.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say «klenz»: the «ea» sounds like the «e» in «bed», not like «clean». Formal or medical; everyday word: clean, wash. Noun: cleanser.

part of speech: noun (a clew, clews); verb (clew, clews, clewed, clewing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (sailing) The lower back corner of a sail, where a rope is attached. 2) (old-fashioned) A ball of thread or yarn. 3) (old spelling) An old way of writing «clue». 4) (verb, sailing) «Clew up» means to pull up a sail by its corners.
its sense in the lessons: In stories from Greek myth, Theseus used a clew (ball of thread) to find his way out of the Minotaur's labyrinth, and that is how «clue» got its meaning: something that leads you to an answer. In sailing lessons, the clew is one of the three corners of a triangle sail (head, tack, clew).
examples from the lessons: The sailor tied the rope to the clew of the sail. | Ariadne gave Theseus a clew of thread to find his way out. | The word «clue» comes from «clew», a ball of thread. | Pull the clew tight to trim the sail. | The three corners of a sail are the head, the tack and the clew. | The old book spelled «clue» as «clew».
note for the reader of a maths problem: Sounds exactly like «clue» (homophone). Today «clew» is only used in sailing or old stories; for detective hints, write «clue».

part of speech: noun (a cloak, cloaks); verb (cloak, cloaks, cloaked, cloaking)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A loose coat without sleeves that hangs from the shoulders and is fastened at the neck. 2) Something that covers or hides: «under a cloak of darkness». 3) (verb) To cover or hide something: «The hills were cloaked in mist.»
its sense in the lessons: In stories cloaks are worn by wizards, knights, heroes and villains; an invisibility cloak hides you. In history lessons Romans and medieval people wore cloaks. «Cloak-and-dagger» means secret spy business. A «cloakroom» is where you leave coats. Phrases: «under the cloak of», «cloaked in mystery».
examples from the lessons: The wizard swirled his long black cloak. | The thieves escaped under cloak of darkness. | The mountains were cloaked in fog. | Little Red Riding Hood wore a red cloak with a hood. | Hang your coats in the cloakroom. | It was a cloak-and-dagger mission.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Rhymes with «oak». Not a «clock». A cape is similar but usually shorter. Countable.

part of speech: noun (a clove, cloves); verb form (cleave — old past tense «clove»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A small, dried, nail-shaped flower bud used as a strong-smelling spice, for example in cooking, mulled drinks and Christmas oranges. 2) One small section of a bulb of garlic: «a clove of garlic». 3) (old) Past tense of «cleave» (to split): «He clove the log in two.»
its sense in the lessons: In cooking and science, cloves come from a tree grown in Indonesia and Zanzibar; clove oil was used to numb toothache. In history lessons cloves were part of the spice trade. In recipes «two cloves of garlic» means two small segments, not two bulbs.
examples from the lessons: Add two cloves of garlic to the sauce. | We pushed cloves into an orange to make a pomander. | Cloves smell warm and spicy. | Grandma rubbed clove oil on her sore tooth. | Ships sailed far to buy cloves and nutmeg. | One bulb of garlic has about ten cloves.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one clove, two cloves. A clove of garlic is not the whole garlic bulb — a common recipe trap. The old verb form «clove» (from cleave) is only in old stories and the Bible.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A deep red dye made from tiny scale insects that live on prickly pear cacti, used to colour food, drinks, make-up and cloth. 2) The insect itself.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons cochineal was prized by the Aztecs and later shipped to Europe by the Spanish; it coloured British soldiers' red coats. In science and food labels, cochineal (carmine, E120) shows that natural colours can come from animals, so it is not vegetarian.
examples from the lessons: Cochineal makes a bright red colour. | The pink icing was coloured with cochineal. | Cochineal comes from tiny insects that live on cacti. | The Aztecs used cochineal to dye cloth. | Vegetarians check labels for cochineal. | It takes thousands of insects to make a little cochineal.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say «koch-ih-NEEL». Uncountable as a dye. Also called carmine or E120.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To pay someone or give them something because they have lost something, been hurt or done work: «The company compensated the family for the damage.» 2) To make up for something bad or missing with something good: «His speed compensated for his size.» 3) (formal) To pay for work.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, if a train is very late you may be compensated with money back. In law and adult life, people who are hurt by someone else's mistake can get compensation. In maths, «compensating» is a mental trick: to add 39, add 40 and then take away 1. Phrases: «compensate for», «be compensated».
examples from the lessons: The airline compensated us for the lost suitcase. | My glasses compensate for my poor eyesight. | To add 99, add 100 and compensate by taking away 1. | He worked extra hard to compensate for missing a week of school. | The shop compensated her with a free cake. | Nothing can compensate for losing a friend.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say «KOM-pen-sate». «Compensate for» something. Noun: compensation. In maths, compensation means changing a number to make it easier and then fixing the answer.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A machine that squeezes air or gas into a smaller space, making its pressure higher, used to pump tyres, power tools and fridges. 2) (music) A sound device that evens out loud and quiet parts. 3) (medicine) A muscle or tool that presses something.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, compressors show that gases can be squashed (compressed) but liquids hardly can. Fridges and air conditioners use a compressor to move heat. At garages, an air compressor fills car and bike tyres. Related: compress, compression.
examples from the lessons: The garage used an air compressor to pump up the tyres. | A fridge hums when its compressor is running. | Divers' tanks are filled with a compressor. | The compressor squashes air into the tank. | The builders' compressor powered the drill. | Gases can be compressed, but liquids are hard to squash.
note for the reader of a maths problem: compress + -or. Countable. Safety: compressed air is powerful; never point an air hose at a person.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A small meat-eating dinosaur about the size of a chicken or turkey, which ran on two legs and lived about 150 million years ago in what is now Germany and France. 2) Its name means «pretty jaw».
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about dinosaurs and fossils, Compsognathus is famous for being one of the smallest dinosaurs known for a long time; one fossil had a lizard in its stomach, showing what it ate. It is related to the ancestors of birds. Often shortened to «compy» in films.
examples from the lessons: Compsognathus was only about the size of a turkey. | Scientists found a lizard inside a Compsognathus fossil. | Compsognathus ran fast on two thin legs. | Its name means «pretty jaw». | Compsognathus lived in the Jurassic period. | In the film, a pack of compies chased the boy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say «komp-sog-NAY-thus». Dinosaur names are usually written with a capital letter and in italics in science. Plural is often the same word. Not all dinosaurs were huge.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A sweet food such as a cake, sweet, chocolate or pudding, especially a fancy one. 2) Something elaborate and decorated, like a fancy dress or building: «a confection of lace and ribbons». 3) (formal) The making of something by mixing.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life «confectionery» means sweets and chocolates; a «confectioner» makes or sells them. In stories a wedding cake or a fancy hat may be called «a confection». Health lessons say sweet confections are a treat, not a meal.
examples from the lessons: The bakery window was full of sugary confections. | The wedding cake was a tall white confection. | Her hat was a confection of feathers and flowers. | Sweets and chocolate are called confectionery. | The chef made a confection of meringue and cream. | Too many confections are bad for your teeth.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Related: confectionery (sweets in general, uncountable), confectioner (person). Do not confuse with «confession».

part of speech: noun (a conglomerate, conglomerates); adjective (conglomerate); verb (conglomerate — rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (money, business) A big company made up of many different businesses that sell different things. 2) (science, geology) A kind of rock made of rounded pebbles and stones stuck together by finer material, like natural concrete. 3) A mass of different things gathered together.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about rocks, conglomerate is a sedimentary rock: the rounded pebbles show they were once rolled by rivers or the sea. In money and business lessons, conglomerates own many brands. Related: agglomerate (with sharp pieces), breccia.
examples from the lessons: Conglomerate rock looks like pebbles glued together. | The conglomerate owns a TV channel, a bank and a cereal brand. | We found a piece of conglomerate on the beach. | Rounded pebbles in conglomerate were shaped by water. | The big conglomerate bought the toy company. | The cliffs are made of conglomerate and sandstone.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun and adjective: «kon-GLOM-er-it»; rare verb: «kon-GLOM-er-ate». In geology: conglomerate has rounded pieces; breccia has sharp, broken pieces.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person, army or country that takes control of a land or people by force, or wins a war. 2) Someone who overcomes a difficulty: «the conqueror of Everest».
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons William the Conqueror invaded England and won at the Battle of Hastings; Alexander the Great and the Romans were conquerors. Stories show conquerors as heroes or as cruel invaders, depending on who tells them. In the Bible, Romans 8 says Christians are «more than conquerors» through God's love.
examples from the lessons: William the Conqueror won the Battle of Hastings. | The conquerors forced the people to pay taxes. | Alexander the Great was a famous conqueror. | Hillary and Tenzing were the first conquerors of Everest. | For the people who were conquered, the conqueror was an invader. | «We are more than conquerors,» says the Bible.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: «conqu-» then «-eror», not «-orer». Say «KONK-er-er». Verb: conquer; noun: conquest. History looks different from the side of the conquered.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A Spanish (or Portuguese) soldier and explorer who invaded and conquered lands in the Americas after Columbus, such as Hernán Cortés (who conquered the Aztec Empire) and Francisco Pizarro (the Inca Empire).
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons conquistadors are studied with the Aztecs, Maya and Incas. They had guns, horses and steel, and brought diseases like smallpox that killed millions of Native people. They searched for gold (stories of El Dorado). Today many historians stress the suffering they caused, as well as their journeys. The word is Spanish for «conqueror».
examples from the lessons: The conquistador Hernán Cortés reached the Aztec capital. | Conquistadors searched for gold in South America. | Diseases brought by the conquistadors killed many Native people. | Pizarro was the conquistador who conquered the Incas. | The conquistadors wore metal helmets and armour. | The museum shows the Aztec side of the story, not only the conquistadors'.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spanish word; say «kon-KEES-tuh-dor». Plural: conquistadors (English) or conquistadores (Spanish). Usually refers to the Spanish in the Americas.

part of speech: adjective (conscientious; more conscientious, most conscientious); adverb conscientiously; noun conscientiousness
meaning for a pupil: 1) Careful to do your work well and thoroughly, because you want to do the right thing. 2) Guided by what you believe is right and wrong, as in a «conscientious objector», a person who refuses to fight in a war because they believe it is wrong.
its sense in the lessons: In school reports a «conscientious pupil» is one who checks their work, hands in homework on time and tries hard; it is high praise. In stories it tells the reader a character is reliable and dutiful. In history lessons «conscientious objector» comes up in the World Wars. Phrases: «a conscientious worker», «conscientious about (something)».
examples from the lessons: Maya is a conscientious pupil who always checks her sums twice. | The teacher wrote «conscientious and hard-working» on my report. | Be conscientious about washing your hands before you cook. | He was a conscientious objector and refused to carry a gun in the war. | A conscientious dog owner always picks up after the dog. | Our conscientious librarian puts every book back in the right place. | She conscientiously recorded the temperature every hour for her science project.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective, used before a noun or after «be». Spelling trap: «consci-» like «conscience», then «-entious»; say «con-shee-EN-shus». Do not confuse with «conscious» (awake and aware) or «conscience» (the inner sense of right and wrong).

part of speech: verb (conserve, conserves, conserved, conserving); noun (a conserve, conserves — formal or old-fashioned for jam)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To save something so it is not wasted or used up, such as water, energy or money. 2) To protect something, such as nature, wildlife or old buildings, so that it stays in good condition. 3) (science) In physics, energy is «conserved»: it is never made or destroyed, only changed from one form to another. 4) (noun, formal) Jam made with large pieces of fruit, as in «strawberry conserve».
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography it is about saving energy, water and habitats; «conservation» is the noun for protecting nature. In everyday life adults say «conserve energy» about switching off lights. In PE or a long race you «conserve your energy» by not running too fast at the start. Phrases: «conserve water», «conserve energy», «conserve resources».
examples from the lessons: Turn off the tap while you brush your teeth to conserve water. | We conserve electricity by switching off lights when we leave a room. | The runner conserved her energy for the last lap. | Rangers work to conserve the rainforest and its animals. | In a closed system, energy is conserved. | Gran spread apricot conserve on her scones. | The town is trying to conserve its old castle walls.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: conserved, conserving. Nouns: «conservation» (protecting things), «conservationist» (a person who does it). Not the same as «conservative» (wanting to keep old ways; also a political party) or «conservatory» (a glass room on a house).

part of speech: adjective (constitutional); adverb constitutionally; noun (a constitutional — old-fashioned, a walk for your health)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To do with a country's constitution, the main set of laws that says how the country is governed and what rights people have. 2) Allowed by the constitution; a law that is «constitutional» follows those rules, and an «unconstitutional» one breaks them. 3) To do with a person's body or nature, as in a «constitutional weakness». 4) (noun, old-fashioned) A walk taken for your health, as in «a morning constitutional».
its sense in the lessons: In citizenship and history lessons: the USA has a written Constitution; the UK has a «constitutional monarchy», where the king or queen reigns but Parliament makes the laws.
