Australia and Canada are also constitutional monarchies. In the news: «a constitutional crisis», «a constitutional right», «constitutional court».
examples from the lessons: The UK is a constitutional monarchy, so the king does not make the laws. | Free speech is a constitutional right in the United States. | The judges decided the new law was not constitutional. | Changing the constitution needs a constitutional amendment. | Grandpa takes his morning constitutional around the park. | The class learned about constitutional government in Canada. | Some people say the vote was unconstitutional.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: «unconstitutional». The word comes from «constitution», which also means a person's general health («a strong constitution»). The capital C «Constitution» usually means the US Constitution.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A snake that kills its prey by wrapping its body around it and squeezing until the animal cannot breathe, such as a boa constrictor or a python. 2) (science) A muscle that tightens or narrows a part of the body. 3) Anything that squeezes or narrows something.
its sense in the lessons: In science and nature lessons constrictors are an example of how predators hunt; boas and pythons are not venomous. In zoo visits and animal books the «boa constrictor» is a famous example. In body lessons a constrictor muscle squeezes, for example in the throat.
examples from the lessons: A boa constrictor wraps around its prey and squeezes. | Pythons are constrictors, not venomous snakes. | The zookeeper let us touch a small constrictor. | The constrictor swallowed the rat whole. | Constrictor muscles in your throat help you swallow. | In the story, the jungle explorer met a huge constrictor hanging from a tree.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «constrictors». From the verb «constrict», to squeeze or make narrower. Myth: constrictors do not usually crush bones; they stop the prey's blood flow and breathing. Spelling: «-or» not «-er».

meaning for a pupil: 1) One of a family of viruses that can cause illnesses in people and animals, from a common cold to serious illnesses. Under a microscope they have spikes that look like a crown. 2) (everyday) The virus that caused the COVID-19 pandemic that spread around the world from 2020, and the illness it caused.
its sense in the lessons: In science and health lessons it is an example of a virus and how germs spread through coughs, sneezes and touch; it is why we learned handwashing, masks and staying home when ill. In history it names the pandemic years with lockdowns and online school. People often say «Covid» for short.
examples from the lessons: The coronavirus spread around the world in 2020. | Coronaviruses are named after the crown-like spikes on their surface. | During the coronavirus lockdown we had school on the computer. | Some colds are caused by a coronavirus. | Wash your hands to stop viruses like the coronavirus spreading. | Scientists made vaccines against the coronavirus. | My nan stayed home a lot while the coronavirus was spreading.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Corona» is Latin for «crown». Plural «coronaviruses». COVID-19 is the illness; SARS-CoV-2 is the virus's scientific name. Antibiotics do not kill viruses; that is a common myth.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The dead body of a person, and sometimes of an animal. 2) (UK, slang, theatre) To «corpse» is to burst out laughing by accident while acting, when you should be serious.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, especially mysteries, ghost stories and history (wars, plagues), «corpse» tells the reader someone has died; it is a stark, grim word. Gentler words are «body» or «remains». In science it may come up with decomposers and fossils. Phrase: «as pale as a corpse».
examples from the lessons: The detective found a corpse in the library. | The old story tells of a corpse that walked at night. | Flies laid their eggs on the bird's corpse. | Egyptians wrapped a corpse in cloth to make a mummy. | He looked as pale as a corpse after the roller coaster. | The actor corpsed and couldn't stop giggling on stage.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one corpse, two corpses. Do not confuse with «corps» (said «core», a group of soldiers or workers, as in «Marine Corps»). «Corpse» is a strong word; for a family member people say «body» or «passed away».

part of speech: noun (corruption — usually uncountable; a corruption of something)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Dishonest or illegal behaviour by people with power, such as taking bribes or using public money for themselves. 2) Making something bad or rotten, or changing something so it is spoiled, such as «corruption of a computer file». 3) A word or name that has changed from its older or proper form over time, as in «"Ta" is a corruption of "thank you"».
its sense in the lessons: In citizenship, history and news: corrupt leaders, police or officials who take bribes break the trust of the people; courts and a free press help fight it. In computing a file «corruption» means the data is damaged and won't open. In stories it shows a good character turning bad. Phrases: «fight corruption», «accused of corruption».
examples from the lessons: The mayor was arrested for corruption. | A free newspaper helps people find out about corruption. | Giving a referee money to cheat is a kind of corruption. | File corruption meant my homework would not open. | In the story, the king's power led to corruption. | «Hello» may be a corruption of an older greeting. | Many countries pass laws to stop corruption.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable: «a lot of corruption», not «corruptions». Adjective «corrupt», verb «to corrupt». A «bribe» is money given to make someone act dishonestly.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A small flower that grows from a bulb-like corm and comes up early in spring, often purple, yellow or white, shaped like a cup. 2) A kind of crocus that flowers in autumn gives saffron, a spice made from its red threads.
its sense in the lessons: In science and nature lessons crocuses are a sign of spring and come up even through snow; they show how plants store food underground. In art and poems they stand for new beginnings. Bees visit them early in the year.
examples from the lessons: The first crocuses were peeping through the snow. | We planted crocus bulbs in the school garden in autumn. | A bee buzzed into a purple crocus. | Saffron comes from a special crocus. | The park lawn was covered in yellow and white crocuses. | Crocuses close their petals when it is cloudy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «crocuses» is usual; «croci» is also correct but rare. Strictly they grow from «corms», not true bulbs. Saffron is very expensive because each flower has only three threads.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (art) A style of painting and sculpture begun around 1907–1908 by Pablo Picasso and Georges Braque, in which people and objects are shown as flat geometric shapes like cubes and angles, often seen from several sides at once.
its sense in the lessons: In art lessons pupils learn about Cubism and make pictures by cutting faces or still lifes into shapes and showing them from different angles. It is linked to maths shapes. A «Cubist» is an artist who works in this style.
examples from the lessons: Picasso is famous for Cubism. | In art class we made a Cubist portrait out of triangles and squares. | Cubism shows a face from the front and the side at the same time. | The guitar in the painting is broken into shapes, which is typical of Cubism. | Our teacher showed us how Cubism changed modern art.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable; often written with a capital C. Adjective «Cubist». The name came from a critic saying the paintings looked like little cubes. Not connected with «cubic» units in maths except by the shape idea.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (medicine) To do with a cyst, a small sac or bubble in the body filled with fluid. 2) (medicine) To do with the bladder or gall bladder. 3) Mostly heard in «cystic fibrosis», an illness people are born with that makes thick, sticky mucus in the lungs and gut.
its sense in the lessons: Children meet this word mainly in «cystic fibrosis» (CF), an inherited illness; children with CF take medicines, do physio to clear their lungs, and must avoid passing germs to each other. In health lessons it is a reminder that some illnesses come from genes and cannot be caught.
examples from the lessons: My cousin has cystic fibrosis and does breathing exercises every day. | Cystic fibrosis is not catching; you are born with it. | The doctor said the lump was a cystic swelling, full of fluid. | Children with cystic fibrosis often need extra salt and food. | Charities raise money to research cystic fibrosis.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Said «SIS-tik». Adjective only, almost never used alone in everyday talk. «Cyst» is the noun. «Fibrosis» means the growth of too much tough tissue.

part of speech: verb (dabble, dabbles, dabbled, dabbling); noun dabbler
meaning for a pupil: 1) To try an activity a little, as a hobby, without being very serious about it, as in «dabble in painting». 2) To move your hands or feet gently in water, splashing a bit. 3) (of ducks) To feed by tipping forward to reach food in shallow water.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life «dabble in» means having a go at a hobby. In nature lessons, «dabbling ducks» like mallards tip up to eat. In stories, a character dabbling their toes in a stream shows a calm, lazy moment. Phrases: «dabble in», «dabble with», «dabble your feet».
examples from the lessons: My dad dabbles in photography at weekends. | We dabbled our toes in the cool stream. | Mallards are dabbling ducks that tip upside down to feed. | She dabbled with the guitar before choosing the drums. | The wizard had dabbled in magic he did not understand. | I only dabble in cooking, but I can make pancakes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb, double b: dabbled, dabbling. «A dabbler» is someone who tries many things lightly. Not the same as «dribble» or «babble».

part of speech: adjective (dazed); verb form (daze, dazes, dazed, dazing); noun (in a daze)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Unable to think clearly for a short time, because of a hit on the head, a shock, tiredness or great surprise. 2) (past form of the verb «daze») Made confused or stunned, as in «the bright light dazed him».
its sense in the lessons: In safety and first aid: if someone is dazed after a fall or bump to the head, tell an adult; it can be a sign of concussion. In stories, «dazed» shows a character is shocked or confused after something big happens. Phrases: «in a daze», «dazed and confused», «look dazed».
examples from the lessons: After he fell off his bike, Tom looked dazed. | She walked around in a daze after hearing the amazing news. | The bird was dazed after flying into the window. | The boxer was dazed by the punch. | We came out of the cinema dazed by the bright sunshine. | If a player seems dazed after a knock, they must stop playing.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Dazed» is said like «days» + d. Do not confuse with «dazzled» (blinded by bright light or very impressed), though they are close. «Daze» as a noun: «in a daze».

part of speech: noun (a democrat, democrats; a Democrat, Democrats)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who believes in democracy, where people choose their leaders by voting and everyone has equal rights. 2) (USA, with a capital D) A member or supporter of the Democratic Party, one of the two biggest political parties in the United States; the other is the Republican Party.
its sense in the lessons: In citizenship and politics lessons: in the USA, elections are mostly between Democrats and Republicans; on maps Democrats are shown in blue and Republicans in red. With a small d it means anyone who supports democracy, in any country. In the UK there are the «Liberal Democrats» (Lib Dems).
examples from the lessons: My aunt in Ohio votes for the Democrats. | The Democrat and the Republican argued on television. | A true democrat accepts the result of a fair vote. | Some states usually vote Democrat and others Republican. | Barack Obama was a Democrat. | In Britain, the Liberal Democrats are a political party.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital D for the US party, small d for the general idea. Adjective «democratic» / «Democratic». Do not confuse with «democracy» (the system). Say «DEM-uh-krat».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) The thick inner layer of the skin, under the epidermis, which holds blood vessels, nerves, hair roots and sweat glands.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about the body and skin: skin has layers — the epidermis on the outside, the dermis below it, and fat beneath. The dermis helps you feel touch, heat and pain and helps keep you at the right temperature. A tattoo's ink sits in the dermis, which is why it stays.
examples from the lessons: The dermis lies under the epidermis. | Nerves in the dermis let you feel the heat of a cup. | Sweat glands in the dermis help cool your body. | A deep cut goes through to the dermis and may bleed. | Hair grows from roots in the dermis. | We labelled the epidermis and dermis on a skin diagram.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable, usually «the dermis». From Greek «derma», skin; related to «dermatologist», a skin doctor. «Epi-» means «on top of», so the epidermis is on top of the dermis.

part of speech: verb (detach, detaches, detached, detaching); adjective detached; noun detachment
meaning for a pupil: 1) To separate one thing from another thing it is fixed to, as in «detach the coupon». 2) To come off by itself, as in «the handle detached». 3) To stop feeling involved; a «detached» person stays calm and not emotional. 4) (army) To send a group of soldiers away for a special job.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life you «detach» a form along a dotted line or a part of a toy. In science, a retina or a leaf can detach. In UK housing, a «detached house» stands alone; a «semi-detached» house is joined to one other. In stories, a «detached» character seems cold or far away in feeling.
examples from the lessons: Detach the slip along the dotted line and give it to your teacher. | The trailer detached from the car on the hill. | You can detach the hood from this coat. | We live in a semi-detached house. | She felt strangely detached, as if she were watching a film. | The captain detached ten soldiers to guard the bridge.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: «detach» has no t before ch (not «detatch»). Opposite: «attach». Regular verb: detached, detaching.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Something that decides or strongly affects what happens, as in «Sleep is a big determinant of how well you learn». 2) (maths) A special number worked out from a square table of numbers (a matrix), used in higher maths; it is not usually taught at primary school.
its sense in the lessons: In science and health it means a factor: «Diet and exercise are determinants of health». In geography: «Climate is a determinant of where people live». In secondary or university maths, the determinant of a matrix tells, for example, whether a set of equations has one answer. It is a formal, exam-style word.
examples from the lessons: Weather is a key determinant of how many people visit the beach. | Practice is the main determinant of how well you play. | Scientists studied the determinants of good health. | Rainfall is a determinant of which plants can grow. | In older maths classes you learn to find the determinant of a matrix. | Price is often a determinant of what people buy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal word; in everyday talk say «factor» or «what decides». Do not confuse with «determined» (having made up your mind) or «deterrent» (something that stops people doing a thing).

part of speech: noun (a detour, detours); verb (detour, detours, detoured, detouring)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A longer or different way you take to avoid something, such as a closed road or traffic. 2) A trip off your main route to visit somewhere, as in «make a detour to see the waterfall». 3) (verb) To go a different way, or to send traffic a different way.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: road signs say «Detour» (US) or «Diversion» (UK). In maths problems about journeys, a detour adds extra distance: if the normal route is 10 km and the detour adds 3 km, the trip is 13 km. In stories, a detour often leads to an adventure. Phrases: «take a detour», «make a detour».
examples from the lessons: The bridge was closed, so we took a detour. | We made a detour to see the lighthouse. | The detour added 5 miles to our journey. | Traffic was detoured around the parade. | The story goes off on a detour about the hero's childhood. | Follow the detour signs to get to school.
note for the reader of a maths problem: In UK English the road sign usually says «Diversion»; «detour» is common in the USA, Canada and Australia. Said «DEE-toor». From French «détour», a turning aside.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Very wicked or cruel, as if done by the Devil, as in «a diabolical plan». 2) (UK, informal) Extremely bad or of very poor quality, as in «The traffic was diabolical».
its sense in the lessons: In stories villains have «diabolical plots» and «diabolical laughs»; the word shows evil cleverness. In everyday British talk, adults use it to complain: «That refereeing was diabolical». It comes from «diabolos», Greek for devil.
examples from the lessons: The villain revealed his diabolical plan to flood the city. | The weather on our holiday was diabolical. | That's a diabolical penalty decision! | The witch gave a diabolical cackle. | My handwriting was diabolical when I was in a hurry. | The trap was diabolically clever.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Said «dye-uh-BOL-ik-ul». The informal «very bad» sense is mainly British. Related: «devil», «diabolic».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A medicine made from the foxglove plant, used by doctors to make a weak heart beat more strongly and steadily. 2) The foxglove plant itself, a tall plant with purple or white bell-shaped flowers.
its sense in the lessons: In science and history lessons foxglove is an example of a plant that gives a medicine: in 1785 a doctor, William Withering, wrote about using foxglove for heart and swelling problems. Safety: foxgloves are poisonous; never eat any part of the plant. Medicine is only safe in the right dose given by a doctor.
examples from the lessons: Digitalis comes from the foxglove plant. | Doctors used digitalis to help patients with weak hearts. | Foxgloves are also called digitalis in gardening books. | Every part of the digitalis plant is poisonous. | The scientist measured the right dose of digitalis carefully.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. From Latin «digitus», finger, because a finger fits into the flower. A good example that «natural» does not mean «safe».

part of speech: adjective (disagreeable; more disagreeable, most disagreeable); adverb disagreeably
meaning for a pupil: 1) Unpleasant, not nice to experience, as in «a disagreeable smell». 2) Unfriendly, bad-tempered and hard to get on with, as in «a disagreeable old man».
its sense in the lessons: In stories, especially classic children's books, a «disagreeable» character is grumpy and rude, like Mary in «The Secret Garden» at the start. In everyday life it is a slightly formal or old-fashioned way to say «nasty» or «grumpy».
examples from the lessons: The cheese had a disagreeable smell. | Mary was a disagreeable child who scowled at everyone. | It was a disagreeable job to clean out the drains. | The weather turned cold and disagreeable. | He was disagreeably rude to the waiter. | Being tired can make anyone a bit disagreeable.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: «agreeable» (pleasant). It does not mean «disagreeing»; a person who often disagrees is not necessarily disagreeable. Spelling: «dis» + «agree» + «able».

part of speech: verb (disprove, disproves, disproved, disproving; past participle disproved or disproven)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To show that an idea or statement is false by giving facts or evidence. 2) (maths and science) To show a rule does not always work, often by finding one counterexample.
its sense in the lessons: In science, experiments can disprove an idea (a hypothesis); a good scientist changes their mind when the evidence disproves them. In maths, one counterexample disproves a rule: «All odd numbers are prime» is disproved by 9. In arguments and debates, you try to disprove the other side's claims with evidence.
examples from the lessons: The experiment disproved the idea that heavy things fall faster. | One example can disprove a rule in maths. | The number 9 disproves the claim that all odd numbers are prime. | No one could disprove his story. | Galileo helped disprove old ideas about the sky. | The detective used the CCTV to disprove the alibi.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: «prove». «Disproved» and «disproven» are both fine as past participles. Proving something is true usually needs much more than disproving it.

part of speech: verb (dissipate, dissipates, dissipated, dissipating); noun dissipation
meaning for a pupil: 1) To slowly disappear or spread out until gone, as in «The fog dissipated». 2) To make something disappear or fade, as in «The wind dissipated the smoke». 3) (science) To lose energy, usually as heat, as in «Energy is dissipated as heat». 4) To waste money or energy foolishly.
its sense in the lessons: In science: energy is often «dissipated» as heat or sound, which is why machines are never 100% efficient. In geography and weather, fog, clouds and storms dissipate. In stories, anger or fear «dissipates» when a character calms down. It is a formal word.
examples from the lessons: By noon the fog had dissipated. | The crowd slowly dissipated after the match. | Her anger dissipated when she heard the truth. | Some of the energy is dissipated as heat. | The storm dissipated before it reached the coast. | The laptop has a fan to dissipate heat.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; in everyday talk say «clear», «fade» or «spread out». Spelling: double s, one p: «dis-si-pate». A «dissipated» person (adjective) is one who has wasted their life on bad habits — old-fashioned.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Clearly and easily heard, seen or remembered, as in «speak distinctly». 2) Very definitely, without doubt, as in «I distinctly remember locking the door». 3) Noticeably, quite, as in «It was distinctly cold».
its sense in the lessons: In speaking and drama lessons, teachers ask you to «speak clearly and distinctly». In stories and arguments, «I distinctly remember» shows a character is sure. «Distinctly» can also make a word stronger: «distinctly unhappy».
examples from the lessons: Please speak distinctly so everyone can hear. | I distinctly remember putting my keys on the table. | The bell rang distinctly across the playground. | It was distinctly colder after the sun went down. | The two twins have distinctly different voices. | She looked distinctly annoyed.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «distinct» (clear, separate). Do not confuse with «distinctively» (in a special way that makes something stand out).

part of speech: verb (distort, distorts, distorted, distorting); noun distortion; adjective distorted
meaning for a pupil: 1) To change the shape of something so it looks twisted or wrong, as in a fun-house mirror that distorts your face. 2) To change facts or words so they give a false idea, as in «distort the truth». 3) To change a sound so it is unclear or crackly.
its sense in the lessons: In science, lenses and water can distort light so things look bent, like a straw in a glass. In media and news lessons, «distorting facts» is a warning about propaganda and fake news. In music, guitars use «distortion» on purpose. In maths, map projections distort the size of countries near the poles.
examples from the lessons: The curved mirror distorted my face. | The newspaper distorted what the mayor said. | Water distorts the look of a pencil in a glass. | The speaker was too loud and distorted the music. | Maps distort the size of Greenland. | Don't distort the facts to win an argument.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Noun «distortion». Related idea: «exaggerate» makes something bigger; «distort» bends it into a wrong shape.

part of speech: adjective (diverse; more diverse, most diverse); noun diversity
meaning for a pupil: 1) Made up of many different kinds of people or things, as in «a diverse class». 2) Very different from each other, varied, as in «diverse interests».
its sense in the lessons: In citizenship lessons, schools and countries like the UK, USA, Canada and Australia are called «diverse» because people come from many backgrounds, cultures and faiths. In science, a rainforest is a diverse habitat with many species («biodiversity»). Phrases: «culturally diverse», «a diverse range of».
examples from the lessons: Our school is very diverse, with children from twenty countries. | Coral reefs are home to a diverse range of fish. | The library has a diverse collection of books. | My friends have diverse hobbies, from chess to surfing. | London is one of the most diverse cities in the world. | A diverse team can solve problems in different ways.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Said «dye-VERS» or «DYE-vers». Noun «diversity». Do not confuse with «divers» (people who dive) or «diverse» with «divorce».

part of speech: noun (the doldrums — plural in form, used with «the»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A feeling of being sad, bored or stuck, with no energy, as in «in the doldrums». 2) A time when nothing is happening or growing, as in «the economy is in the doldrums». 3) (geography) An area of sea near the equator where there is often very little wind, so sailing ships could be stuck for days.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons about winds and oceans, the doldrums are near the equator where the trade winds meet. In everyday life, «in the doldrums» means fed up or not doing well. In «The Phantom Tollbooth» the hero gets stuck in the Doldrums, a place where thinking is not allowed.
examples from the lessons: I was in the doldrums all week after my best friend moved away. | Sailing ships were stuck in the doldrums for days with no wind. | The team was in the doldrums after losing five matches. | The doldrums lie close to the equator. | Shops are in the doldrums in January after Christmas. | A sunny walk got me out of the doldrums.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always with «the». Used like a place: «in the doldrums», «out of the doldrums». Not usually counted.

part of speech: verb form (past of dominate: dominate, dominates, dominated, dominating); adjective (dominated, as in «male-dominated»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Controlled or ruled by someone more powerful, as in «The country was dominated by its neighbour». 2) Was the strongest or best in something, as in «Our team dominated the match». 3) Was the biggest or most noticeable thing, as in «The castle dominated the skyline». 4) (adjective) Mostly made of or run by one group, as in «a male-dominated job».
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, empires dominated other lands. In sport reports, a team that «dominated» had the ball most of the time. In science, a «dominated» habitat has one species that takes over. In social studies, «male-dominated» or «dominated by» shows unfairness or imbalance. In stories, a bully dominates others.
examples from the lessons: The Romans dominated much of Europe. | Our team dominated the second half. | The news was dominated by the storm. | A tall church dominated the little village. | Engineering used to be a male-dominated job. | One loud boy dominated the group discussion. | Weeds dominated the old garden.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Dominated» is the past tense and past participle of «dominate». Noun «domination»; adjective «dominant». «Dominate» (verb, -ate) is different from «dominant» (adjective, -ant).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (architecture) The oldest and plainest style of ancient Greek columns, thick and strong with a simple round top, as on the Parthenon in Athens. 2) (Scotland) Doric is the name of the Scots dialect spoken in the north-east of Scotland, around Aberdeen. 3) (history) To do with the Dorians, one of the ancient Greek peoples, and their dialect of Greek.
its sense in the lessons: In history and art lessons on Ancient Greece, pupils learn the three column styles: Doric (plain), Ionic (with scrolls) and Corinthian (with leaves). In Scotland, children may hear Doric words like «loon» (boy) and «quine» (girl). Usually written with a capital D.
examples from the lessons: The Parthenon has Doric columns. | Doric columns have a plain, round top. | We drew Doric, Ionic and Corinthian columns in history. | My granny in Aberdeen speaks Doric. | In Doric, a boy is a «loon» and a girl is a «quine». | The museum front has six Doric columns.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually a capital D. Order of fanciness: Doric (plainest), Ionic, Corinthian (most decorated). The Scottish Doric is a dialect of Scots, not of standard English.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A bridge that can be pulled up or lifted, especially over a castle moat, to stop enemies getting in. 2) A modern bridge over a river that lifts to let tall ships pass, like Tower Bridge in London.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons on castles, the drawbridge, moat, portcullis and battlements are the main defences. In stories about knights and sieges, «Raise the drawbridge!» means the castle is closing to attackers. Tower Bridge in London is a famous bridge that lifts (a bascule bridge).
examples from the lessons: The guards raised the drawbridge as the army came near. | The drawbridge crossed the moat to the castle gate. | We built a cardboard castle with a drawbridge on string. | Tower Bridge opens like a drawbridge to let ships through. | The knight rode over the drawbridge. | Pull up the drawbridge! shouted the king.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; one word. «Draw» here means «pull», as in «draw the curtains». Opposite actions: «raise / pull up the drawbridge» and «lower / let down the drawbridge».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A camel with one hump, found in North Africa, the Middle East and India, and also living wild in central Australia. 2) (old use) A fast camel bred for riding.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography: dromedaries are adapted to the desert — their hump stores fat (not water), they have wide feet for sand and can go days without drinking. The Bactrian camel has two humps. Memory trick: a capital D lies on its side with one hump; a capital B has two.
examples from the lessons: A dromedary has one hump on its back. | Dromedaries can walk for days without water. | Australia has many wild dromedaries in the outback. | We rode a dromedary at the desert camp. | The Bactrian camel has two humps, but the dromedary has only one. | The dromedary's hump is full of fat.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «dromedaries» (y → ies). Myth: the hump does not hold water; it stores fat. Said «DROM-uh-dair-ee» (UK «DROM-uh-dree»).

part of speech: verb (droop, droops, drooped, drooping); noun (a droop)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To hang or bend down because of being weak, tired or without water, as in «The flowers drooped in the heat». 2) To become sad or lose energy, as in «His spirits drooped». 3) (noun) A downward bend or slope.
its sense in the lessons: In science, a plant without water droops because its cells lose water and it cannot stay stiff (a wilting plant). In stories, drooping eyelids show tiredness, a drooping head shows sadness. In art, it describes shapes that sag.
examples from the lessons: The sunflowers drooped in the hot sun. | Water the plant before it droops. | My eyelids drooped during the long film. | The puppy's ears droop when it is sad. | His shoulders drooped when he heard the bad news. | The tent drooped after the rain.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Close words: «wilt» (for plants), «sag», «flop». Do not confuse with «drop» (fall down) or «drool» (spit coming from the mouth).

part of speech: verb form (present participle of droop: droop, droops, drooped, drooping); adjective (drooping)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Hanging or bending down, especially because of weakness, tiredness or lack of water, as in «drooping flowers». 2) Becoming sad or losing energy, as in «drooping spirits».
its sense in the lessons: In science, drooping leaves are a sign a plant needs water or is too hot. In stories, «drooping eyelids», «a drooping moustache» and «drooping shoulders» paint a picture of tiredness, age or sadness. It is a common describing word in creative writing.
examples from the lessons: The drooping roses needed water. | She had drooping eyelids after the sleepover. | The old dog walked with a drooping tail. | His drooping shoulders told us he had lost. | The willow tree has long, drooping branches. | The balloons were drooping by the end of the party.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Drooping» is the -ing form of «droop»; it keeps both o's. As an adjective it goes before a noun: «a drooping flower». See also «droopy» (informal).

part of speech: noun (dynamite, uncountable); verb (dynamite, dynamites, dynamited, dynamiting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A powerful explosive made in sticks, used to blast rock in mines and building work. 2) (verb) To blow something up with dynamite. 3) (informal) Something or someone very exciting, powerful or likely to cause big trouble, as in «That news is dynamite».
its sense in the lessons: In history and science: Alfred Nobel invented dynamite in 1867 and later left his money to start the Nobel Prizes. Safety: explosives are dangerous and only trained experts handle them. In cartoons, a red stick of dynamite with a fizzing fuse is a classic joke. In slang, «dynamite» means amazing.
examples from the lessons: Miners used dynamite to blast the rock. | Alfred Nobel invented dynamite. | The old bridge was dynamited to make way for a new one. | That singer's voice is dynamite! | In the cartoon, the coyote's dynamite blew up in his face. | The secret was political dynamite.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «some dynamite», «a stick of dynamite». From Greek «dynamis», power — like «dynamic» and «dynamo».

part of speech: noun (an earwig, earwigs); verb (UK, informal: earwig, earwigs, earwigged, earwigging)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A small brown insect with a long body and a pair of pincers at its tail end. 2) (UK, informal) To listen secretly to other people's conversations, as in «Stop earwigging!»
its sense in the lessons: In science and garden lessons earwigs are minibeasts found under stones, bark and flowerpots; they eat plants and small insects. Myth: they do not crawl into people's ears to lay eggs. In UK homes, a nosy child might be told off for «earwigging».
examples from the lessons: We found earwigs under the flowerpot. | An earwig has pincers on its tail. | Earwigs come out at night to eat. | Earwigs do not really crawl into your ears. | Stop earwigging on our conversation! | Mum said I was earwigging when I listened at the door.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Takes «an»: «an earwig». The verb sense is British and informal. The pincers are called «cerci»; they can give a pinch but are harmless.

part of speech: adjective (efficient; more efficient, most efficient); adverb efficiently; noun efficiency
meaning for a pupil: 1) Working well without wasting time, energy, money or materials, as in «an efficient way to tidy up». 2) (of a person) Good at organising work and getting it done quickly and well. 3) (science) Turning most of the energy put in into useful energy, as in «an energy-efficient light bulb».
its sense in the lessons: In science, an efficient machine wastes little energy as heat or sound; LED bulbs are more efficient than old bulbs. In maths, an «efficient method» gets the answer in fewer steps, like using times tables instead of counting. In everyday life, adults praise an «efficient» person who gets jobs done. Phrases: «energy-efficient», «fuel-efficient».
examples from the lessons: LED bulbs are more efficient than old bulbs. | Chunking is an efficient way to divide big numbers. | Our new school secretary is very efficient. | An efficient car uses less fuel. | We worked efficiently and finished the poster early. | Recycling is an efficient use of materials.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: «effi-cient», with «-cient» like «ancient». Opposite: «inefficient». Do not confuse with «effective» (it works) — something can work well but slowly, so it is effective but not efficient. In science, efficiency = useful energy out ÷ total energy in, never more than 100%.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Allowed to do or get something because you meet the rules, as in «eligible to vote» or «eligible for free school meals». 2) (old-fashioned) A good person to marry, usually rich and single, as in «an eligible bachelor».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and school: you might be eligible for a team, a prize or a competition if you are the right age. In citizenship, people in the UK, USA, Canada and Australia are eligible to vote at 18. In old novels like «Pride and Prejudice», characters talk about eligible young men. Phrases: «eligible for», «eligible to».
examples from the lessons: Children aged 9 to 11 are eligible for the chess competition. | You are eligible to vote at 18. | Only Year 6 pupils are eligible to be prefects. | She was not eligible because she had already won. | Some families are eligible for free school meals. | In the novel, he was the most eligible bachelor in town.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: «ineligible». Spelling: «eli-gible», with «-gible» like «legible». Not the same as «legible» (easy to read).

part of speech: adjective (elliptical); adverb elliptically; noun (an elliptical — US, an exercise machine)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (maths) Shaped like an ellipse, a stretched circle or oval, as in «an elliptical orbit». 2) (language) Leaving out words that the listener can guess, as in «Coming?» instead of «Are you coming?». 3) Said in a way that is hard to understand because it is not direct. 4) (US, noun) An exercise machine where you move your legs in an oval path.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, planets move around the Sun in elliptical (oval) orbits, not perfect circles. In maths, an ellipse is a curved closed shape like a squashed circle. In English grammar, «ellipsis» is leaving words out, and «…» is also called an ellipsis.
examples from the lessons: Earth travels around the Sun in an elliptical orbit. | The running track is elliptical. | We drew an elliptical shape using two pins and a loop of string. | «Ready?» is an elliptical way of saying «Are you ready?» | His answer was so elliptical that no one understood it. | Mum uses the elliptical at the gym.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Also «elliptic» in higher maths. Noun «ellipse» (the shape) and «ellipsis» (missing words, or «…»). Earth's orbit is only slightly elliptical, so it is very close to a circle; seasons are caused by Earth's tilt, not its distance from the Sun.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) The thin outer layer of the skin that you can see and touch; it protects the body from germs, water and sunlight. 2) (plants) The outer layer of cells on a leaf, stem or root.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on the body: the epidermis is on top of the dermis; it is constantly making new cells and shedding old dead ones as dust. In plant lessons, students look at leaf epidermis under a microscope to see the tiny holes (stomata). Sunburn damages the epidermis.
examples from the lessons: The epidermis is the outer layer of your skin. | Dead cells from the epidermis flake off every day. | Sunburn damages the epidermis. | We peeled a thin layer of onion epidermis to look at under the microscope. | The epidermis has no blood vessels, so a tiny scrape may not bleed. | A plant's epidermis is covered in a waxy layer.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. «Epi-» means «on top of» + «dermis» (skin). Said «ep-ih-DER-mis».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A describing word or phrase added to a name, like «the Great» in «Alfred the Great» or «Lionheart» in «Richard the Lionheart». 2) A word used to describe someone, often an insult or nasty name. 3) (stories, poems) A short describing phrase used again and again, like «rosy-fingered dawn» in old Greek poems.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, kings and queens have epithets: «William the Conqueror», «Ivan the Terrible», «Ethelred the Unready». In English lessons, epithets are describing phrases in poems and myths. In everyday news, an «epithet» can mean an insulting name, which is unkind.
examples from the lessons: «The Great» is an epithet given to Alfred. | Richard I had the epithet «Lionheart». | Homer gives Athena the epithet «grey-eyed». | The bully shouted nasty epithets in the playground. | Mum's epithet for my bedroom is «the swamp». | Can you think of a fun epithet for your pet?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Said «EP-ih-thet». Countable. Close words: «nickname», «title», «label». An epithet is not an «epitaph» (words on a gravestone).

part of speech: verb (escalate, escalates, escalated, escalating); noun escalation
meaning for a pupil: 1) To become bigger, worse or more serious, as in «The argument escalated into a fight». 2) To make something bigger or more serious. 3) To pass a problem to a more senior person, as in «escalate a complaint».
its sense in the lessons: In citizenship, news and conflict lessons: wars and quarrels can escalate; good friends «de-escalate» by calming things down, listening and walking away. In everyday life prices «escalate» (rise fast). In safety lessons, if a problem escalates, tell a trusted adult. Phrase: «escalate into».
examples from the lessons: The small argument escalated into a shouting match. | Prices escalated during the winter. | The teacher stepped in before things escalated. | The fighting between the two countries escalated. | If the problem escalates, tell an adult. | Let's calm down so this doesn't escalate.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Opposite: «de-escalate». Related to «escalator», the moving stairs that take you up.

part of speech: noun (an escargot, escargots) — a French word used in English
meaning for a pupil: 1) (French food) A snail cooked to be eaten, usually with garlic butter, a famous dish in France. 2) (French) In French, «escargot» is simply the everyday word for «snail»; it sounds like «ess-car-GO» with a silent t.
its sense in the lessons: In French lessons and lessons about food around the world, escargots are a classic example of French cuisine. In stories, a character who tries escargots is being brave about new foods. On menus in English-speaking countries the French word is used.
examples from the lessons: Have you ever tried escargots? | The restaurant served escargots in garlic butter. | In French class we learned that «escargot» means snail. | My brother said escargots tasted like chewy mushrooms. | Escargots are eaten with special tongs and a little fork. | «Un escargot» is a garden snail in French.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Borrowed French word: the final t is silent. Plural «escargots». In English it means only the dish, while in French it is any snail.

meaning for a pupil: 1) From or to do with Ethiopia, a country in East Africa, or its people, languages and culture. 2) (noun) A person from Ethiopia.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons: Ethiopia is in the Horn of Africa, its capital is Addis Ababa, and it has high mountains and an ancient history. Ethiopian food includes injera, a spongy flatbread. Many Ethiopian runners have won Olympic medals. In history, Ethiopia was one of very few African countries never colonised for long. Coffee probably first came from Ethiopia. The Ethiopian Orthodox Church is one of the oldest Christian churches.
examples from the lessons: My friend's family is Ethiopian. | Ethiopian runners often win long-distance races. | We tried Ethiopian injera with spicy stew. | Coffee was first grown in the Ethiopian highlands. | The Ethiopian calendar is about seven years behind ours. | The Ethiopian flag is green, yellow and red.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always a capital E. The main language is Amharic, but many languages are spoken there. Ethiopia is a country, not a city.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who sets or marks an exam or test, as in «The examiner marked our papers». 2) A person who checks something carefully, as in a «driving examiner» or a «medical examiner». 3) (in a newspaper name) Several newspapers are called «The Examiner».
its sense in the lessons: In school, especially the UK, examiners mark SATs, GCSEs and music exams; teachers say «Show your working for the examiner». In everyday life, a driving test examiner decides if you pass. In crime stories, a «medical examiner» finds out how someone died.
examples from the lessons: The examiner said to start writing. | Write neatly so the examiner can read your answer. | Mum passed her driving test first time — the examiner was impressed. | The piano examiner asked me to play a scale. | The medical examiner looked at the evidence. | Examiners give marks for showing your working.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Takes «an». The person who takes the exam is the «candidate» or «examinee». Verb: «examine».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Solid waste that comes out of the body of a person or animal; poo.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on digestion and animals it is the formal word for poo; scientists study animal excrement (droppings, scat) to learn what animals eat. Safety: never touch excrement; wash hands after cleaning a pet's litter. In everyday talk people say «poo», «droppings» or «mess».
examples from the lessons: The park sign said to clean up dog excrement. | Owls cough up pellets, which are not excrement. | Scientists studied bat excrement in the cave. | Bird excrement covered the statue. | Animal excrement can spread germs, so wash your hands. | Dung beetles roll balls of excrement.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «some excrement», not «an excrement». Formal or scientific. Everyday words: «poo» (UK), «poop» (US), «droppings» (for small animals and birds). Related verb: «excrete».

part of speech: verb (excrete, excretes, excreted, excreting); noun excretion
meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) To get rid of waste from the body, such as poo, urine (wee), sweat or carbon dioxide.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons excretion is one of the life processes of all living things (in «MRS GREN»: Movement, Respiration, Sensitivity, Growth, Reproduction, Excretion, Nutrition). The kidneys excrete urine, the lungs excrete carbon dioxide, and the skin excretes sweat. Plants excrete waste gases through their leaves.
examples from the lessons: All living things excrete waste. | The kidneys excrete waste in urine. | We excrete carbon dioxide when we breathe out. | Plants excrete oxygen as a waste product of photosynthesis. | Sweat helps the body excrete some salt. | Excretion is one of the seven life processes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Scientific word. Noun «excretion». Do not confuse with «secrete» (to make and release a useful liquid, like saliva) or with «excrement» (the solid waste itself).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Special skill or knowledge in a subject that comes from study, training or experience, as in «medical expertise».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, adults hire someone with «expertise» — a plumber, doctor or lawyer. In school, pupils can share their expertise, such as a child who knows a lot about dinosaurs. In science and the news, «scientific expertise» means trustworthy knowledge from experts. Phrases: «expertise in», «lack the expertise».
examples from the lessons: The vet has expertise in treating horses. | Gran's baking expertise is legendary. | We needed someone with computer expertise to fix the problem. | Her expertise in maths helped the team win the quiz. | Building a bridge takes a lot of expertise. | Ask the coach — football is his area of expertise.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «a lot of expertise», not «an expertise». Said «ek-sper-TEEZ». Related: «expert» (a person, or adjective).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Said clearly and fully, so nobody can be confused, as in «explicit instructions». 2) Showing or describing things very openly, especially violence or sex, which is not suitable for children, as in «explicit content».
its sense in the lessons: In school, teachers give «explicit instructions» and children may be asked for «explicit» answers. In online safety, a label «explicit» on songs, films or websites warns that the content is for adults; children should not watch it and should tell an adult if they see it. In maths, an «explicit formula» gives the answer directly.
examples from the lessons: The teacher gave explicit instructions not to run in the corridor. | Make it explicit what each number stands for. | The song had an «explicit» label, so my mum skipped it. | The rules were explicit: no phones in class. | If you see explicit pictures online, close them and tell an adult. | His meaning was explicit.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: «implicit» (suggested but not said directly). On music apps «E» means explicit language. Said «ik-SPLIS-it».

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a clear and direct way, saying exactly what you mean so there is no doubt, as in «She explicitly told us not to touch it». 2) Openly showing or describing adult content.
its sense in the lessons: In school and rules, a thing «explicitly» forbidden is clearly written or spoken, so «I didn't know» is no excuse. In reading comprehension, questions ask whether something is «explicitly stated» in the text or only suggested (implied). In maths, «explicitly» show your working means write every step.
examples from the lessons: Mum explicitly said no sweets before dinner. | The rules explicitly ban phones in exams. | The text explicitly states that the boy was scared. | Please explain explicitly how you got your answer. | He never explicitly said yes, but he smiled. | The sign explicitly said «No swimming».
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb of «explicit». Opposite: «implicitly». Reading-test tip: «explicit» information is written in the text; «implicit» information you must infer.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a sudden, loud and violent way, like an explosion, as in «The balloon burst explosively». 2) Very fast and with great energy, as in «The sprinter started explosively». 3) In a sudden angry way, as in «He reacted explosively».
its sense in the lessons: In science, gases or chemicals that react explosively are dangerous and only experts handle them. In PE and sport, coaches say «push off explosively» for a strong start. In stories, a character who reacts explosively loses their temper. In maths and science, «grow explosively» means grow extremely fast.
examples from the lessons: The volcano erupted explosively. | The sprinter pushed off explosively from the blocks. | The cola fizzed explosively when we added the mints. | Dad laughed explosively at the joke. | The town's population grew explosively. | She reacted explosively when her brother broke her model.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from «explosive» and «explode». Spelling: «explo-sive-ly», keep the e before -ly.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A metal container, usually red, filled with water, foam, powder or gas, used to put out a fire; full name «fire extinguisher». 2) Anything that puts out a fire or a light, such as a candle snuffer.
its sense in the lessons: In fire safety lessons: children should not use an extinguisher themselves; they should get out, stay out and call 999 (UK), 911 (USA and Canada), 000 (Australia), 111 (New Zealand) or 112/999 (Ireland). Different extinguishers are for different fires; water must never be used on oil or electrical fires.
examples from the lessons: There is a fire extinguisher by every classroom door. | The firefighter showed us how an extinguisher works. | Never use a water extinguisher on an electrical fire. | The chef used a fire extinguisher on the burning pan. | The extinguisher is checked every year. | Children should leave the building, not grab the extinguisher.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Takes «an». Spelling: «ex-tin-guish-er». Verb: «extinguish», to put out a fire.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Coming from or existing outside the Earth, in space, as in «extraterrestrial rocks». 2) (noun) A living being from another planet, an alien; often shortened to «ET».
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about space, meteorites are extraterrestrial rocks, and scientists search for extraterrestrial life, such as microbes on Mars, but none has been found yet. In stories and films like «E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial», extraterrestrials visit Earth. It is good to say clearly: aliens are imagined; no one has proved they exist.
examples from the lessons: The meteorite in the museum is extraterrestrial. | Scientists are looking for signs of extraterrestrial life. | In the film, a friendly extraterrestrial wants to go home. | No one has ever found proof of extraterrestrials. | We wrote stories about an extraterrestrial visiting our school. | Telescopes listen for extraterrestrial radio signals.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Extra-» means «outside» + «terrestrial» (of the Earth). Opposite: «terrestrial». Can be written with or without a hyphen. Takes «an»: «an extraterrestrial».

part of speech: noun (fa, fah — a music note); also an abbreviation (FA)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (music) The fourth note of the musical scale in the sol-fa system: do, re, mi, fa, so, la, ti, do. Also spelt «fah». 2) (UK, sport) «The FA» is the Football Association, which runs football in England, including the FA Cup. 3) (slang, as «sweet FA») Nothing at all — a rude-ish British phrase, as in «He did sweet FA all day».
its sense in the lessons: In music lessons, children sing «do, re, mi, fa, so, la, ti, do», as in the song «Do-Re-Mi» from «The Sound of Music» («Fa, a long long way to run»). In sport, the FA Cup is a famous English football competition. «Sweet FA» is a cheeky, slightly rude phrase best avoided at school.
examples from the lessons: Do, re, mi, fa, so, la, ti, do! | «Fa» is the fourth note of the scale. | We sang «Fa, a long, long way to run» in music. | My team won a match in the FA Cup. | The FA makes the rules for English football. | (rude, UK) He did sweet FA to help tidy up.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Not an ordinary English word on its own. «Fa» rhymes with «car». In the music sense it is lower case; FA for the football body is capital letters. «Sweet FA» is a rude euphemism, so use «nothing at all» at school.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Joking at the wrong time, about something serious, so it seems silly or rude, as in «a facetious remark».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and school, a teacher might say «Don't be facetious» when a pupil makes a cheeky joke instead of answering seriously. In stories, a facetious character uses jokes to avoid dealing with a problem. It is a formal, grown-up word.
examples from the lessons: When the teacher asked why he was late, he gave a facetious answer: «My bed wouldn't let me go.» | Don't be facetious — this is important. | Her facetious comment upset her friend, who was sad. | He was only being facetious when he said he'd eat his homework. | A facetious answer will not get you marks in an exam.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Said «fuh-SEE-shus». Fun fact: «facetious» has all five vowels, a, e, i, o, u, in order. Close words: «flippant», «cheeky».

part of speech: noun (a farewell, farewells); exclamation (farewell!); adjective (farewell, as in «a farewell party»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (old-fashioned or formal) Goodbye, as in «Farewell, my friend!» 2) (noun) The act of saying goodbye, especially when someone leaves for a long time, as in «We said our farewells». 3) (adjective) Done to say goodbye, as in «a farewell party».
its sense in the lessons: In stories, poems and old books, characters say «Farewell!» when parting, often for ever. In school, a «farewell assembly» is held when Year 6 leaves or a teacher retires. In everyday life, «bid farewell» means say goodbye. Phrases: «say farewell», «bid farewell», «a fond farewell».
examples from the lessons: We had a farewell party for our teacher. | «Farewell!» said the knight, riding away. | They said their farewells at the airport. | The class sang a farewell song in the last assembly. | We bid farewell to summer as the leaves fell. | She waved a fond farewell from the train.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word: «farewell», not «fare well» (though it comes from «fare well», meaning «travel well»). More formal than «bye».

part of speech: verb (fatten, fattens, fattened, fattening); adjective fattening
meaning for a pupil: 1) To make an animal or person fatter, especially farm animals before they are sold for meat, as in «fatten the pigs». 2) To become fatter. 3) (informal) To make something bigger, as in «fatten your wallet».
its sense in the lessons: In farming lessons, farmers fatten cattle, pigs or turkeys. In stories, like «Hansel and Gretel», the witch tries to fatten Hansel up to eat him. In everyday life, adults call rich foods «fattening». Phrase: «fatten up».
examples from the lessons: The witch tried to fatten Hansel up. | Farmers fatten turkeys before Christmas. | Bears fatten up in autumn before they sleep for the winter. | Cream cakes are fattening. | The geese were fattening on grain. | Saving pocket money will fatten your piggy bank.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double t: fatten, fattened, fattening. Be kind: talking about people's weight can hurt feelings. «Fattening» describes foods with lots of energy (calories).

meaning for a pupil: 1) To do with cats or the cat family, which includes house cats, lions, tigers, leopards and cheetahs. 2) Like a cat, graceful, quiet and smooth in the way you move, as in «feline grace». 3) (noun) A cat or any animal of the cat family.
its sense in the lessons: In science, «felines» (the family Felidae) are meat-eating mammals with sharp claws and whiskers. Vets talk about «feline health». In stories, «feline» describes someone who moves quietly and gracefully, or has catlike eyes. Related word for dogs: «canine».
examples from the lessons: Lions, tigers and house cats are all felines. | The vet specialises in feline illnesses. | She moved with feline grace across the stage. | The cheetah is the fastest feline. | My cat has a very feline way of ignoring me. | The feline eyes glowed in the dark.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Said «FEE-line». Compare: «canine» (dogs), «equine» (horses), «bovine» (cows).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (medicine) A condition where too much tough, thick tissue (like scar tissue) grows in a part of the body, such as the lungs, making it stiff and not work as well.
its sense in the lessons: Children mostly hear it in «cystic fibrosis», an inherited illness that makes thick mucus in the lungs and gut, and in «pulmonary fibrosis» (scarring of the lungs) in grown-ups. In health lessons it shows how scar tissue can stop organs working. It is a doctor's word.
examples from the lessons: My classmate has cystic fibrosis, so she takes medicine before lunch. | Fibrosis makes the lungs stiff. | The doctor explained that fibrosis is like scarring inside the body. | People with cystic fibrosis do physio to clear their lungs. | Smoking can damage the lungs and may lead to fibrosis.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Said «fy-BROH-sis». Uncountable. From «fibre» (thread) + «-osis» (a condition). Cystic fibrosis cannot be caught from someone.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Invented, made up, not real, as in «a fictional character». 2) To do with fiction, stories that are imagined rather than true.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons, pupils sort books into fiction (made-up stories) and non-fiction (facts). Harry Potter and Paddington Bear are fictional characters. In reading tests you may be asked whether a text is fictional or factual. In media lessons, fictional TV shows are not the news.
examples from the lessons: Sherlock Holmes is a fictional detective. | The village in the book is fictional, but it is based on a real place. | Dragons are fictional creatures. | We wrote a fictional diary of a Roman soldier. | The film is fictional, even though it feels real. | Is this a fictional story or a true one?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: «real», «factual», «non-fiction». Do not confuse «fictional» with «fictitious» (made up in order to trick, like a fictitious name) — though they are close.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (computing, maths) «First in, first out»: a rule where the first thing to come in is the first thing to go out, like a queue. 2) (Australia, informal) «Fly-in fly-out»: a worker, often in a mine, who flies to work far away for some weeks and then flies home, as in «Dad is a FIFO worker».
its sense in the lessons: In computing and maths lessons, FIFO describes a queue, like children lining up for lunch: the first child in the line is served first. Its opposite is LIFO (last in, first out), like a stack of plates. In Australia, many children in Western Australia and Queensland have FIFO parents working in mines.
examples from the lessons: A lunch queue works on FIFO: first in, first out. | The printer prints pages in FIFO order. | My dad is a FIFO worker on a mine in the Pilbara. | FIFO families often use video calls to keep in touch. | A stack of plates is LIFO, not FIFO. | Shops use FIFO so older milk is sold first.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Said «FYE-foh». An abbreviation, not an ordinary word; usually written in capitals. The Australian sense is everyday talk there.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A very hard grey or black stone that makes sparks when struck against steel, and breaks into sharp edges. 2) A piece of flint used to light a fire or, long ago, as a tool or arrowhead. 3) A small piece of metal in a lighter that makes the spark.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons on the Stone Age, people made axes, knives and arrowheads from flint, and lit fires with flint and steel. In science (rocks), flint is found in chalk, for example on beaches and cliffs in southern England. In stories, a «heart of flint» means a very hard, unkind heart.
examples from the lessons: Stone Age people made tools from flint. | We found a flint on the chalk beach. | He struck flint and steel to make a spark. | The arrowhead was made of sharp flint. | The museum showed a flint hand axe. | She had a heart of flint and never forgave anyone.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable for the material («made of flint»), countable for pieces («two flints»). Adjective «flinty» (hard, like flint).

part of speech: adjective (fluent; more fluent); adverb fluently; noun fluency
meaning for a pupil: 1) Able to speak, read or write a language easily and well, as in «fluent in French». 2) Done smoothly and easily without stopping, as in «a fluent reader». 3) Smooth and graceful, as in «fluent movements».
its sense in the lessons: In school, «fluent readers» read aloud smoothly with expression, and reading fluency is assessed in KS1 and KS2. In maths, «fluency» means knowing facts like times tables quickly and accurately. In language lessons, being fluent is the goal; many children are fluent in two or more languages.
examples from the lessons: My friend is fluent in English and Polish. | She is a fluent reader who uses lots of expression. | Practise your times tables until you are fluent. | He spoke fluently about his project. | After living in Quebec, Mum became fluent in French. | The dancer's moves were fluent and smooth.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually «fluent in» + a language. Noun «fluency». Being fluent does not mean you never make mistakes.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The way a person moves their feet, especially in sports and dancing, as in «good footwork». 2) (informal) Clever, quick actions to get out of a difficult situation, as in «some fancy footwork».
its sense in the lessons: In PE and sport, coaches train footwork for football, tennis, boxing, netball and dancing; quick footwork helps you dodge and balance. In stories and the news, «nifty footwork» can mean clever ways of avoiding trouble or difficult questions.
examples from the lessons: The striker's quick footwork fooled the defender. | In netball, footwork rules say you can't run with the ball. | Our dance teacher made us practise the footwork slowly. | Boxers skip rope to improve their footwork. | With some fancy footwork, he got out of doing the washing up. | Good footwork helps you keep your balance.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «good footwork», not «a footwork». One word. In netball, «footwork» is also the name of a rule about stepping with the ball.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) One of the front legs of an animal with four legs, or the wing or arm that is in the same place, such as a bird's wing or a person's arm.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about skeletons and evolution, the forelimbs of a human, a bat, a whale and a cat all have the same kinds of bones (one upper bone, two lower bones, many small hand bones), which shows they are related. In nature books, forelimbs are used for running, digging, swimming or flying.
examples from the lessons: A bat's wing is its forelimb. | A mole uses its strong forelimbs to dig. | The kangaroo's forelimbs are short. | Whales have flippers instead of forelimbs with fingers. | T. rex had tiny forelimbs. | Human arms are forelimbs.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Scientific word. Opposite: «hind limb» (back leg). «Fore-» means «front», as in «forehead».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A front foot (paw) of an animal that has paws, such as a dog, cat, bear or squirrel.
its sense in the lessons: In nature writing and science, forepaws are used for holding food (squirrels), digging (badgers), grooming or catching. In stories, a pet lifting a forepaw might be asking for something or be hurt.
examples from the lessons: The squirrel held the nut in its forepaws. | The dog raised one forepaw to shake hands. | Badgers dig with their strong forepaws. | The kitten licked its forepaw clean. | The bear's forepaw left a big print in the mud.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word. Opposite: «hind paw» (back paw). Only used for animals with paws, not hooves.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) To do with ants. 2) (chemistry) «Formic acid» is a stinging acid made by ants and stinging nettles; it causes the itchy, burning feeling of an ant bite or nettle sting.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about acids and alkalis: nettle and ant stings contain formic acid; some people rub on a mild alkali (like soap) to ease them, and a dock leaf is a traditional remedy. Some birds sit on ant nests so the ants spray formic acid that cleans their feathers («anting»).
examples from the lessons: Ants spray formic acid to defend themselves. | Nettle stings contain formic acid. | The burning feeling of an ant bite comes from formic acid. | Formic acid got its name from the Latin word for ant. | Birds sometimes use formic acid from ants to clean their feathers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Used almost only in «formic acid». From Latin «formica», ant. Not related to «form» or «formal».

part of speech: verb (fossilise, fossilises, fossilised, fossilising); US spelling fossilize
meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) To slowly turn into a fossil, where a dead plant or animal is preserved in rock over millions of years. 2) (of ideas or habits) To become fixed and unable to change, as in «Their ideas had fossilised».
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on rocks and evolution: when a creature dies and is buried quickly in mud, its hard parts can fossilise as minerals replace them. Mary Anning found famous fossils on the Jurassic Coast in England. In everyday talk, «fossilised» can mean very old-fashioned.
examples from the lessons: The dinosaur bones fossilised over millions of years. | Footprints can fossilise in mud that turns to rock. | Soft parts like skin rarely fossilise. | We made a fossilised leaf print from plaster. | Mary Anning found a fossilised ichthyosaur. | Grandpa jokes that his old car is a fossilised wreck.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK spelling «fossilise» or «fossilize»; US, Canada «fossilize». Noun «fossil», «fossilisation». Most living things never fossilise, because they rot away first.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (French) In French, «framboise» means «raspberry»; it sounds like «from-BWAHZ». 2) In English it is used on menus and labels for raspberry flavour, raspberry liqueur (an alcoholic drink for adults) or a raspberry beer.
its sense in the lessons: In French lessons it is a fruit word, like «fraise» (strawberry) and «pomme» (apple). In shops and cafés you may see «framboise» on cakes, jams or sorbets. It is not an English word; it is French.
examples from the lessons: «Framboise» is French for raspberry. | The café sold a framboise tart. | In French class we learned «une framboise» and «une fraise». | The sorbet was framboise flavour, bright pink and sweet. | Mum bought a jar of framboise jam in Paris.
note for the reader of a maths problem: French word, feminine: «une framboise», plural «des framboises». The «-se» sounds like «z». Do not confuse with «fraise» (strawberry).

part of speech: noun (a franchise, franchises); verb (franchise, franchises, franchised, franchising)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (business) Permission from a company to sell its products or run a shop using its name, as in «a burger franchise». 2) A shop or business run in this way. 3) A series of films, games, books and toys based on the same characters, as in «the Star Wars franchise». 4) (formal) The right to vote in elections, as in «women won the franchise». 5) (US, sport) A professional sports team.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, «the franchise» was extended so more people could vote; the Suffragettes fought for women's franchise. In business and everyday life, many fast-food shops are franchises. In films and games, a big «franchise» has many sequels and toys. In US sport, team owners own the franchise.
examples from the lessons: That pizza shop is a franchise of a big chain. | The Marvel franchise has dozens of films. | Women gained the franchise in the UK in 1918 and 1928. | Uncle Tom bought a coffee franchise. | The company franchises its name to shops around the world. | The football franchise moved to a new city.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Said «FRAN-chyze». The voting sense is formal; «suffrage» is a close word. «Disenfranchise» means to take away someone's right to vote.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A man who comes from France or is French. 2) (history, informal) Sometimes used to mean a French person or soldier in general.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, famous Frenchmen include Napoleon and Louis Braille. In geography, French people live in France and many other places. «Frenchwoman» is used for a woman, and «French people» or «the French» for everyone. In stories, a stereotype of a Frenchman with a striped shirt and beret should be seen as a joke, not the truth.
examples from the lessons: Louis Braille was a Frenchman who invented writing for blind people. | The Frenchman spoke to us in French. | Napoleon was a famous Frenchman. | The Frenchman's café sold croissants. | Our new neighbour is a Frenchman from Lyon.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always a capital F. Plural «Frenchmen» (like «man/men»). For women use «Frenchwoman», and for a mixed group «French people».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Decorated with frills, wavy strips of cloth or lace gathered into folds, as on a dress, curtain or sock. 2) (informal) Fancy and with too much decoration, as in «a frilly speech».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life it describes clothes such as frilly dresses, frilly socks or a frilly blouse, and fancy things like frilly lettuce or paper cases. In nature lessons, the «frilled lizard» of Australia spreads a frilly neck to scare enemies. In stories, frilly clothes can show a character is fancy or old-fashioned.
examples from the lessons: She wore a frilly pink dress to the party. | The baby has frilly white socks. | The curtains had a frilly edge. | The frilled lizard opens its frilly collar to look scary. | I like plain cupcakes, not frilly ones. | Lettuce leaves have frilly edges.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative «frillier», superlative «frilliest». Noun «frill». «No frills» means plain and simple, with no extras.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (medicine) FSH stands for «follicle-stimulating hormone», a chemical messenger in the body that helps grown-ups' bodies develop and have babies. 2) A spelling of a soft hissing sound, like air or a fizzy drink, as in «Fsh! went the can».
its sense in the lessons: Not an English word on its own. In biology for older pupils, FSH is one of the hormones involved in puberty. In comics and stories, sound spellings like «fsh» or «pssh» show a hiss. In phonics, «fsh» is not a real word; children might be tested on blending «f» and «sh».
examples from the lessons: FSH is a hormone made in the brain. | The doctor checked her FSH level. | «Fsh!» went the bottle when Dad opened it. | The snake made a soft «fsh» sound. | In the comic, the rocket said «FSHHH».
note for the reader of a maths problem: An honest note: «fsh» is an abbreviation or a sound, not a normal word. In medicine it is written in capitals: FSH.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) In addition, also, used to add another, often stronger, point, as in «It's raining. Furthermore, it's freezing».
its sense in the lessons: In English writing lessons «furthermore» is a connective (conjunctive adverb) used in persuasive and discussion texts to add points: «Firstly…, Furthermore…, In conclusion…». In speeches and debates it makes an argument sound strong. In everyday speech people more often say «also», «and» or «what's more».
examples from the lessons: Homework helps you practise. Furthermore, it teaches you to plan. | The trip is too expensive; furthermore, the bus is full. | Dogs are loyal. Furthermore, they keep you active. | The bridge is old and, furthermore, it is unsafe. | Use «furthermore» in your persuasive letter to add a point. | I'm tired; furthermore, I've got a headache.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word. Usually at the start of a sentence followed by a comma. Close words: «moreover», «in addition», «also», «what's more». Do not overuse it in one piece of writing.

part of speech: abbreviation and fragment (GA, Ga, ga — with several uses)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (US) GA is the short form for Georgia, a state in the south-eastern United States, used in addresses. 2) (science) Ga is the chemical symbol for gallium, a soft silver metal that melts in your hand. 3) (slang, as «ga-ga») To «go ga-ga» means to become very excited and silly about something, or (old-fashioned and unkind) to become confused in old age. 4) Baby talk, as in «goo goo ga ga».
its sense in the lessons: Not a normal English word on its own. In geography, «Atlanta, GA» is a US address. In science, gallium is in the periodic table. In stories, a baby babbling says «ga ga». «Go ga-ga over» is informal for liking something very much.
examples from the lessons: My pen pal lives in Savannah, GA. | Ga is the symbol for gallium. | Gallium melts in your hand. | The baby said «ga ga» and laughed. | My sister goes ga-ga over puppies. | Atlanta, GA is a big city in the USA.
note for the reader of a maths problem: An honest note: «ga» alone is an abbreviation, a symbol or a baby sound. Calling an old person «gaga» is unkind.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (medicine) An illness where the stomach and intestines (gut) become sore and swollen, usually caused by a virus or bacteria, giving sickness, diarrhoea and tummy pain; often called a «tummy bug» or «stomach flu».
its sense in the lessons: In health lessons, gastroenteritis spreads easily, so wash hands with soap after the toilet and before eating; stay off school for 48 hours after the last sickness or diarrhoea (UK school rule). Drink small sips of water to avoid dehydration. Norovirus is a common cause.
examples from the lessons: Half the class was off with gastroenteritis. | Gastroenteritis is often called a tummy bug. | Wash your hands to stop gastroenteritis spreading. | After gastroenteritis, drink plenty of water. | The doctor said it was gastroenteritis, not food allergy. | You must stay home for two days after gastroenteritis.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Said «gas-troh-en-tuh-RYE-tis». Uncountable. «Gastro» = stomach, «entero» = intestines, «-itis» = swelling. In Australia people say «gastro» for short. «Stomach flu» is not really flu.

part of speech: noun (geology, uncountable); adjective geological; noun geologist
meaning for a pupil: 1) The science of the Earth's rocks, soil, minerals, volcanoes, earthquakes and how the Earth has changed over time. 2) The rocks and land features of a particular place, as in «the geology of Scotland».
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography lessons pupils study geology: igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic rocks, fossils, volcanoes and the rock cycle. Geologists help find water, oil and safe ground for buildings. Mary Anning was a famous early fossil hunter.
examples from the lessons: Geology is the study of rocks. | A geologist showed us her rock collection. | The geology of the Lake District includes old volcanoes. | We learned about the rock cycle in geology club. | My uncle studied geology at university. | Geology helps us understand earthquakes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. «Geo-» = Earth, «-logy» = study of. Do not confuse with «geography» (study of places and people) or «genealogy» (study of family history).

part of speech: noun (gingerbread, uncountable; a gingerbread man, gingerbread men)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A sweet, spicy cake or biscuit flavoured with ginger, often with treacle or golden syrup. 2) A biscuit cut into a shape, especially a person (a gingerbread man), often decorated with icing. 3) (old use) Fancy carved decoration on a building, as in a «gingerbread house» style.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, «The Gingerbread Man» runs away shouting «Run, run, as fast as you can!» and in «Hansel and Gretel» the witch lives in a gingerbread house. At Christmas, families bake gingerbread houses. In maths, gingerbread biscuits can be used for sharing and counting problems.
