examples from the lessons: We baked gingerbread men for the class party. | «Run, run, as fast as you can, you can't catch me, I'm the Gingerbread Man!» | The witch's house was made of gingerbread. | The kitchen smelled of warm gingerbread. | We decorated a gingerbread house at Christmas. | If 12 gingerbread men are shared between 4 children, each gets 3.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable as the cake («a slice of gingerbread»); countable with «man/men/biscuits». One word. In the US, gingerbread is often a soft cake; in the UK it is more often a biscuit.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) A sticky, wet, soft substance, like slime, glue or melted cheese. 2) (informal) Too much soppy, sentimental feeling, as in «romantic goo». 3) Baby talk, as in «goo goo ga ga».
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, children make «goo» (oobleck) from cornflour and water, which acts like a solid when pressed and a liquid when poured. In everyday life, goo is the sticky mess from slime, glue or sweets. In stories, monsters leave a trail of green goo.
examples from the lessons: My hands were covered in sticky goo from the slime. | The alien left a trail of green goo. | Cornflour and water make a strange goo. | The cake had chocolate goo in the middle. | The baby gurgled «goo goo». | The film was full of soppy goo.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «some goo», not «a goo». Adjective «gooey», as in «a gooey brownie».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A thick, prickly bush with sharp spines and bright yellow flowers that smell a little like coconut, growing on heaths, hillsides and cliffs; also called «furze» or «whin».
its sense in the lessons: In nature lessons in the UK and Ireland, gorse grows on moors, heaths and coastal paths and gives food and shelter for birds and insects. There is a saying: «When gorse is out of bloom, kissing's out of fashion», because some gorse is flowering nearly all year. In New Zealand gorse is a big weed problem brought from Britain. Safety: gorse is very prickly and burns easily.
examples from the lessons: The hillside was covered in yellow gorse. | Gorse flowers smell like coconut. | I scratched my legs on the gorse bushes. | Small birds nest safely in the prickly gorse. | Gorse fires can spread fast in dry weather. | In New Zealand, gorse is a weed that farmers try to remove.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «a gorse bush», «some gorse». Close names: «furze», «whin». Not the same as «horse».

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a way that follows the rules of grammar, as in «grammatically correct». 2) To do with grammar, as in «The two sentences are grammatically different».
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons and SATs, sentences must be «grammatically correct», with the right verb forms, agreement, and punctuation. Teachers mark writing for grammar. A sentence can be grammatically correct but still make no sense, as in «Colourless green ideas sleep furiously».
examples from the lessons: Make sure your sentence is grammatically correct. | «We was» is not grammatically correct in Standard English. | Her story was exciting and grammatically perfect. | The sentence is grammatically fine but does not make sense. | Grammatically, «I» is the subject of the sentence. | Read your work aloud to check it sounds grammatically right.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from «grammatical»; spelling «gram-mat-i-cal-ly», with -ally. Note: dialect forms like «we was» are not «wrong» in that dialect, but they are not Standard English, which exams use.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (chess) The highest title a chess player can win, given by the World Chess Federation (FIDE) to the very best players. 2) A great expert in a game or skill, as in «a grandmaster of magic». 3) The head of some clubs, orders of knights or martial arts schools.
its sense in the lessons: In chess clubs and the olympiad, children learn about grandmasters like Magnus Carlsen; some players become grandmasters as teenagers. In everyday life it means a true master. In martial arts and knightly orders, a Grandmaster is the leader. Short form: «GM».
examples from the lessons: She dreams of becoming a chess grandmaster. | The grandmaster played twenty children at once. | Magnus Carlsen is a famous grandmaster. | He is a grandmaster of card tricks. | The Grandmaster led the order of knights. | The youngest grandmasters earned the title at about 12 years old.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word (sometimes «grand master»). Countable. Not the same as «grandmother» or «grandfather».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Good enough for people or animals to live in, as in «a habitable house». 2) (science) Able to support life, as in «a habitable planet» or «the habitable zone».
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about space, the «habitable zone» (Goldilocks zone) is the area around a star where a planet is not too hot or too cold for liquid water. In geography, some places like deserts and ice caps are hardly habitable. In everyday life, a house must be habitable (safe, with water and heating) before a family moves in.
examples from the lessons: Earth is the only habitable planet we know of. | The old cottage is not habitable until the roof is fixed. | Scientists look for planets in the habitable zone. | Antarctica is not very habitable for people. | After the flood, the houses were not habitable. | Mars might once have been habitable for tiny microbes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: «uninhabitable». Trap: «inhabitable» also means «able to be lived in» — it does NOT mean «not habitable». Related: «habitat», «inhabit».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A ball of hair that forms in the stomach of an animal, especially a cat, after it licks its fur, and is then coughed up. 2) (informal) A tangle of hair, for example in a hairbrush or plughole.
its sense in the lessons: In pet care, cats swallow fur when they wash; brushing them helps prevent hairballs. Vets give advice if a cat has too many. In stories and cartoons, a cat coughing up a hairball is a common funny or gross moment.
examples from the lessons: The cat coughed up a hairball on the rug. | Brushing your cat helps stop hairballs. | Long-haired cats get more hairballs. | Dad pulled a huge hairball out of the shower drain. | The vet gave us food that reduces hairballs.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word. Countable. Not dangerous usually, but if a cat cannot bring one up, see a vet.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Having no hair or very little hair, as in «a hairless cat» or «a hairless baby mouse».
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on mammals, most mammals have hair, but some are almost hairless, like naked mole rats and dolphins; the Sphynx is a hairless breed of cat. Newborn mice and many baby birds are born hairless or featherless. In stories, a hairless character might be old, a baby, or an alien.
examples from the lessons: Sphynx cats are hairless. | Baby mice are born pink and hairless. | Naked mole rats are almost hairless. | Dolphins are mammals but they are nearly hairless. | The newborn puppy's tummy was hairless. | The alien in the comic had a hairless green head.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «-less» means «without». Close word: «bald» (usually for a person's head). «Hairless» is more for animals and body parts.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) The mineral name for natural rock salt, the same chemical as table salt (sodium chloride), often found as clear or white cube-shaped crystals.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geology lessons, halite is an example of a mineral and of crystals; it forms when salty seas or lakes dry up. People mine halite for salt for food and to grit icy roads. Its crystals are cubes, which links to 3D shapes in maths.
examples from the lessons: Halite is the mineral name for rock salt. | Halite crystals are shaped like little cubes. | Halite forms when salty water evaporates. | The council spread crushed halite on icy roads. | We tasted a tiny piece of halite in science (with the teacher's permission). | There are old halite mines in Cheshire.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Said «HAL-ite» or «HAY-lite». Uncountable. Do not taste unknown rocks — only when a teacher says it is safe. From Greek «hals», salt.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A bed made of cloth or net hung between two trees or posts, which you lie in and can swing. 2) (old use, ships) A bed hung between beams on a ship, used by sailors.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, hammocks are used in gardens, on camping trips and on holiday. In history lessons, sailors on ships like HMS Victory slept in hammocks. In stories, a character lazing in a hammock shows a relaxed, sunny moment. The word came from the Taíno people of the Caribbean.
examples from the lessons: Dad fell asleep in the hammock in the garden. | Sailors slept in hammocks below deck. | We hung a hammock between two trees at the campsite. | The cat curled up in the swinging hammock. | Getting out of a hammock is harder than it looks! | Some sloths look like they are in a hammock when they hang from branches.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Spelling: double m, «-ock». Safety: never put a baby to sleep in a hammock without an adult and don't swing too high.

part of speech: noun (a handicap, handicaps); verb (handicap, handicaps, handicapped, handicapping)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Something that makes it harder for you to do well, a disadvantage, as in «Being small was a handicap in basketball». 2) (sport) In golf, horse racing and some games, a handicap is a score or weight that makes the contest fair between stronger and weaker players. 3) (old-fashioned, now often hurtful) A disability; today people usually say «disability» instead. 4) (verb) To make it harder for someone to do something.
its sense in the lessons: In sport, a golfer's handicap shows how good they are: the lower the number, the better. In maths problems about races, a «handicap» start gives some runners a head start. In citizenship lessons, children learn that «handicapped» is old-fashioned and many find it hurtful; say «disabled person» or «person with a disability».
examples from the lessons: Not having a map was a big handicap. | Grandpa's golf handicap is 12. | The racehorse carried extra weight as a handicap. | Being new to the school was a handicap at first. | The bad weather handicapped the rescue team. | People now say «disabled» rather than «handicapped».
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double p in «handicapped», «handicapping». In golf, a lower handicap means a better player. «Handicap» meaning disability is old and may cause offence.

part of speech: noun (a hank, hanks); also a name (Hank)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A loop or coil of wool, yarn, thread, rope or hair, loosely wound and tied, as in «a hank of wool». 2) (a name) Hank is a man's first name, mostly in the USA, a short form of Henry; for example the singer Hank Williams.
its sense in the lessons: In craft lessons and knitting, wool is often sold in hanks that need winding into balls. In stories, a «hank of hair» is a thick lock of hair. As a name it is common in American stories and films.
examples from the lessons: Gran bought three hanks of blue wool. | We wound the hank of yarn into a ball. | A hank of hair fell over her eyes. | The sailor coiled a hank of rope. | My uncle Hank lives in Texas.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. As a name it needs a capital H. Close words: «skein», «coil», «lock» (of hair).

part of speech: adjective (hardy, hardier, hardiest); noun hardiness; also a name (Hardy)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Strong and able to live through hard conditions such as cold, wind or little food, as in «hardy sheep». 2) (plants) Able to survive winter frost outdoors, as in «a hardy plant». 3) Brave and tough, as in «a few hardy swimmers went into the icy sea». 4) (a name) Hardy is a surname, as in the writer Thomas Hardy.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about adaptation, hardy animals and plants survive in tough habitats such as mountains and tundra. In gardening, «hardy» plants stay outside in winter. In stories and on the news, «hardy» people swim on Christmas Day or camp in the snow.
examples from the lessons: Highland cattle are hardy animals that live outside all winter. | Pansies are hardy flowers. | A few hardy fans stayed despite the rain. | The hardiest plants grow high up on mountains. | Only hardy souls go swimming in the sea in January. | Thomas Hardy wrote novels about the countryside.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative «hardier», superlative «hardiest». Not the same as «hard» (solid, difficult) or «hearty» (warm, big, as in «a hearty meal»).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A small creature with a round body and eight very long, thin legs, related to spiders but not a true spider; also called «daddy longlegs» in North America.
its sense in the lessons: In science and minibeast lessons, harvestmen are arachnids, like spiders and scorpions, but their body is one round blob and they cannot spin silk or make venom. They are common in autumn around harvest time, which gave them their name. Myth: «daddy longlegs are the most venomous creature but their fangs are too short» — this is false. In the UK, «daddy longlegs» usually means a crane fly instead.
examples from the lessons: We found a harvestman under a log. | A harvestman has eight long legs but no silk. | Harvestmen are related to spiders. | The harvestman walked slowly across the garden wall. | In Canada, people call a harvestman a daddy longlegs. | Harvestmen are harmless to people.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «harvestmen». «Daddy longlegs» means different creatures in different countries: a harvestman (USA, Canada), a crane fly (UK, Ireland), or a cellar spider (sometimes Australia).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who will receive someone's money, house or other property when that person dies, as in «She is heir to the farm». 2) The person who will become king, queen or ruler next, as in «the heir to the throne». 3) Someone who carries on another person's work or ideas.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, kings and queens worried about having an heir; Henry VIII's search for a son is a famous example. In the news, the heir to the British throne is the next in line. In law and family life, an heir inherits property. In stories, a lost heir often finds out who they are.
examples from the lessons: Prince William is the heir to the throne. | Henry VIII wanted a son as his heir. | She was the only heir to her uncle's fortune. | In the story, the orphan turned out to be the lost heir of the kingdom. | The farm passed to the oldest heir. | He saw himself as the heir to his grandad's woodworking skills.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The h is silent: say «air», so it takes «an»: «an heir». Homophones: «air» and «ere». An «heirloom» is a treasure passed down a family. «Heiress» is an old word for a woman heir.

part of speech: adjective (heroic; more heroic, most heroic); adverb heroically; noun (heroics)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Very brave, like a hero, as in «a heroic rescue». 2) To do with heroes in old stories and poems, as in «heroic legends». 3) Very great or large in effort, as in «a heroic effort to finish». 4) (noun, «heroics») Showing off brave actions, sometimes foolishly.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, myths and history, heroic acts include saving lives and standing up to danger; Greek heroes like Hercules are «heroic» characters. In the news, firefighters and lifeboat crews make heroic rescues. In school, a «heroic effort» is very hard work. Safety: being heroic does not mean taking silly risks — get help first.
examples from the lessons: The firefighter made a heroic rescue. | Odysseus had many heroic adventures. | It was a heroic effort to finish the marathon. | The dog heroically barked until help came. | No heroics — call an adult if someone is in danger. | The poem tells of a heroic battle.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Said «hih-ROH-ik», with an «a» before it: «a heroic act» (the h is sounded). Noun «hero» (plural «heroes»), «heroine» (a female hero), «heroism».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Having a lot of hills, as in «hilly countryside».
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons about landscapes, hilly areas include the Pennines, the Lake District, Wales and much of Ireland and New Zealand. In maths and PE, a hilly route takes longer to run or cycle. In stories, a hilly road might make a journey tiring.
examples from the lessons: Wales is a very hilly country. | Cycling home was hard because the road is hilly. | The hilly fields were full of sheep. | San Francisco is a famous hilly city. | The cross-country course was the hilliest we had run. | We walked through hilly woodland on the school trip.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative «hillier», superlative «hilliest». Opposite: «flat». Related: «mountainous» (with mountains).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) A chemical made by the body that causes allergy symptoms such as sneezing, itching, swelling and a runny nose when the body reacts to things like pollen, dust or insect bites.
its sense in the lessons: In health and science lessons on allergies and hay fever: when pollen gets in your nose, the body releases histamine. «Antihistamine» medicines block it and help with hay fever, rashes and itchy bites. Safety: only take medicine given by an adult; serious allergies need an EpiPen and an ambulance.
examples from the lessons: Histamine makes your eyes itch when you have hay fever. | An antihistamine tablet stopped my sneezing. | A mosquito bite swells because of histamine. | The body releases histamine when it meets an allergen. | Nettle stings contain some histamine.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Said «HIS-tuh-meen». «Antihistamine» means a medicine against histamine.

part of speech: noun (a hitch, hitches); verb (hitch, hitches, hitched, hitching)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (noun) A small problem that delays something, as in «a technical hitch». 2) (verb) To fasten something to something else, as in «hitch the horse to the cart» or «hitch a trailer to the car». 3) (verb) To pull something up quickly, as in «He hitched up his trousers». 4) (informal) To hitchhike: to get a free ride by asking drivers, as in «hitch a ride». 5) (noun) A kind of knot used to tie a rope to a post or ring. 6) (informal) «Get hitched» means get married.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, «without a hitch» means everything went smoothly. In scouts and guides, children learn knots such as the clove hitch. In stories of the Wild West, cowboys hitch horses outside the saloon. Safety: children must never hitch rides with strangers.
examples from the lessons: The school play went off without a hitch. | There was a technical hitch, so the film started late. | Dad hitched the caravan to the car. | He hitched up his socks before the race. | We practised tying a clove hitch at scouts. | Never hitch a ride with a stranger. | My aunt and uncle got hitched in Dublin.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb; «hitches» with -es. «Without a hitch» = perfectly. «Hitchhike» / «hitchhiker» is the full word. «Get hitched» is informal.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A sound people make when they are thinking, not sure, or doubting something, as in «Hm, let me think». 2) A sound that shows you are not convinced or a bit suspicious, as in «Hmm, are you sure?»
its sense in the lessons: In stories and comics, «Hm» or «Hmm» shows a character is thinking, puzzled or doubtful. In speech, it gives you time to think before answering. Teachers may say «Hmm» when they want you to check your answer again. In texting, «hm» or «hmm» can sound doubtful or unimpressed.
examples from the lessons: Hm, I'm not sure which answer is right. | «Hmm,» said the detective, looking at the footprints. | Hm, that's a good question. | «I did my homework.» «Hmm, did you really?» | Hmm, maybe we should try a different way. | She looked at the sum and said, «Hm, let me check.»
note for the reader of a maths problem: An honest note: «hm» is a sound, not a full word. It is spelled «hm», «hmm» or «hmmm» — more m's mean a longer think. Tone of voice changes its meaning.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (Scotland) The Scottish name for New Year's Eve, 31 December, and the parties and customs that celebrate the start of the new year.
its sense in the lessons: In lessons about festivals and the UK, Hogmanay is a big celebration in Scotland with fireworks, street parties in Edinburgh, and singing «Auld Lang Syne» at midnight. A custom called «first-footing» says the first visitor to a home after midnight brings luck, ideally a tall, dark-haired person carrying coal, shortbread or a gift.
examples from the lessons: We went to Edinburgh for Hogmanay. | At Hogmanay, everyone sang «Auld Lang Syne». | Gran sets out shortbread for first-footers at Hogmanay. | The fireworks at Hogmanay lit up the castle. | In Scotland, Hogmanay is sometimes bigger than Christmas. | We stayed up until midnight on Hogmanay.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always a capital H. Said «hog-muh-NAY». Mostly Scottish; elsewhere people say «New Year's Eve». The origin of the word is not certain.

part of speech: verb (hoist, hoists, hoisted, hoisting); noun (a hoist, hoists)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To lift or pull something heavy up, often with ropes or a machine, as in «hoist the sails». 2) To raise a flag up a pole. 3) (noun) A machine for lifting heavy things or people, as in «a hospital hoist». 4) (informal) To lift yourself or someone else up, as in «Dad hoisted me onto his shoulders».
its sense in the lessons: In history and stories of pirates and sailors: «Hoist the sails!» and «Hoist the Jolly Roger!». In science lessons, pulleys help hoist heavy loads with less effort. In everyday life, care homes and hospitals use a hoist to lift people safely. In a phrase: «hoist with his own petard» means caught by your own trick.
examples from the lessons: The sailors hoisted the sails. | They hoisted the flag on the school's sports day. | A crane hoisted the steel beams onto the roof. | Dad hoisted me onto his shoulders to watch the parade. | The nurse used a hoist to lift the patient. | A pulley makes it easier to hoist a heavy bucket.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: hoisted. «Hoist» (not «hoisted») is also an old past form in the phrase «hoist with his own petard». Close words: «lift», «raise», «haul».

part of speech: adjective (homeopathic; UK also homoeopathic); noun homeopathy
meaning for a pupil: 1) To do with homeopathy, a kind of alternative treatment invented about 200 years ago, using tiny sugar pills or drops made from substances diluted so much in water that usually none of the original substance is left. 2) (informal) A very, very tiny amount, as in «a homeopathic amount of chocolate».
its sense in the lessons: In science and health lessons, homeopathy is a good example for checking claims: careful scientific tests have found that homeopathic remedies work no better than a dummy pill (placebo). Some people still use them and believe they help. For real illness, ask a doctor or pharmacist. Shops sell homeopathic remedies next to real medicines, so read labels.
examples from the lessons: The shop sold homeopathic pills for colds. | Scientists have tested homeopathic remedies and found they work no better than sugar pills. | Some people believe homeopathic treatments help them. | There was only a homeopathic amount of jam in that sandwich! | Always ask a doctor before trying any treatment.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Said «hoh-mee-oh-PATH-ik». UK spelling can be «homoeopathic». Do not confuse with «homeopath» (a person who gives it) or «osteopath» (a different therapist).

part of speech: noun (a homer, homers); verb (US, informal: homer, homers, homered); also a name (Homer)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (US, baseball, informal) A home run: a hit that lets the batter run all the way round the bases and score. 2) (a name) Homer was an ancient Greek poet who is said to have composed the «Iliad» and the «Odyssey». 3) (a name) Homer Simpson is the dad in the cartoon «The Simpsons». 4) A homing pigeon. 5) (sport, informal) A referee or decision that seems to favour the home team.
its sense in the lessons: In history and English lessons, Homer's «Odyssey» tells of the hero Odysseus's long journey home; no one is sure Homer was one real person. In sport talk in the USA and Canada, «hit a homer» means hit a home run. In everyday culture, Homer Simpson says «D'oh!».
examples from the lessons: She hit a homer in the last inning! | Homer told the story of the Trojan War. | The «Odyssey» is an epic poem by Homer. | Homer Simpson loves doughnuts. | That ref is a real homer — every call goes to the home team. | The homer pigeon flew back to its loft.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital H for the names. The baseball sense is informal American. Adjective «Homeric» means to do with Homer or very great and heroic.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Towards home, as in «We walked homeward». 2) (adjective) Going towards home, as in «the homeward journey».
its sense in the lessons: In stories and poems, characters turn «homeward» at the end of an adventure; Odysseus is «homeward bound». In everyday life it is a slightly formal way to say «going home». In maths problems, «the homeward journey» is the trip back, often on the same distance: 12 km out and 12 km homeward is 24 km in all.
examples from the lessons: After the match, we started our homeward journey. | The tired walkers turned homeward as it got dark. | Birds fly homeward in spring. | The ship was homeward bound. | The homeward trip took longer because of traffic. | We walked homewards across the fields.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Homeward» and «homewards» mean the same; «homewards» is more British as an adverb, while the adjective is always «homeward». «-ward» means «in the direction of», as in «forward», «backward».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Homophonous words sound exactly the same but have different meanings, and often different spellings, like «pair» and «pear». 2) (music, rare) Homophonous music has one main tune with the other parts moving along with it as chords.
its sense in the lessons: In English and spelling lessons it describes word pairs that trick writers: «there, their, they're», «to, too, two», «knight, night». Teachers use it when explaining why a spell checker will not catch every mistake. Phrases: «homophonous words», «homophonous pairs», «homophonous with».
examples from the lessons: «Pair» and «pear» are homophonous. | «Knight» is homophonous with «night», so the joke works when you say it aloud. | Our spelling list this week is full of homophonous words. | Many jokes and puns depend on homophonous words. | «Their», «there» and «they're» are homophonous, so check which one you mean. | A spell checker cannot spot a homophonous slip like «I one the race». | In some accents «caught» and «court» are homophonous, in others they are not.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective only; the noun is «homophone» (a homophone, homophones). Do not confuse with «homonym» (same spelling and sound, different meaning, like «bat») or «homograph» (same spelling, maybe different sound, like «lead» the metal and «lead» the dog). Whether two words are homophonous can depend on accent (UK, USA, Australia differ).

part of speech: noun (a horseman, horsemen); feminine: horsewoman, horsewomen
meaning for a pupil: 1) A horseman is a man who rides a horse, especially one who rides well. 2) A horseman is a soldier or traveller on horseback in history and stories. 3) (Bible) The Four Horsemen of the Apocalypse are four riders in the Book of Revelation who stand for war, famine, disease and death.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons horsemen are cavalry, knights, messengers and nomad riders such as the Mongols. In stories a horseman galloping in often brings news or danger; «the Headless Horseman» is the ghost in «The Legend of Sleepy Hollow». In everyday life it means a good rider. Phrases: «a skilled horseman», «a lone horseman», «the Four Horsemen».
examples from the lessons: A lone horseman rode across the hills at sunset. | Grandad was a fine horseman when he was young. | The Mongol horsemen could ride for days without stopping. | A horseman brought the news of the battle to the king. | My cousin wants to be a horsewoman and enter show jumping. | The Headless Horseman chases Ichabod Crane in the old American story. | In the Bible the Four Horsemen appear in the Book of Revelation. | Ten horsemen trotted past the farm.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «horsemen», not «horsemans». A woman rider is a «horsewoman»; a neutral word is «rider» or «equestrian». «Horsemanship» is the skill of riding and caring for horses. In maths problems count horsemen as people: 6 horsemen means 6 people and 6 horses unless told otherwise (so 24 horse legs and 12 human legs).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) A howler is a silly, obvious mistake, especially a funny one in writing or an exam. 2) A howler is an animal or person that howls, such as a howler monkey. 3) A howler monkey is a large South and Central American monkey with a very loud call. 4) (UK, old-fashioned) A howler was a letter that shouted at its reader; in the Harry Potter books a Howler is a magic red letter that yells.
its sense in the lessons: In school it means a big, laughable error: writing «the Pacific Ocean is in Paris» is a howler. In science lessons howler monkeys are known as among the loudest land animals, heard kilometres away. In stories a howler can be a ghostly wind or a wolf. Phrases: «make a howler», «a real howler», «howler monkey».
examples from the lessons: Writing that Shakespeare invented the telephone was a real howler. | The goalkeeper made a howler and let the ball roll between his legs. | Howler monkeys shout to each other across the rainforest at dawn. | Our teacher collects the funniest howlers from exam papers. | The wind was a howler that night, rattling every window. | Ron got a Howler from his mum, and it screamed at him in the Great Hall. | Check your answer twice so you don't make a howler.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one howler, two howlers. Comes from the verb «howl» (a long loud cry). «Howler» for a mistake is informal but not rude. A howler monkey is a real animal, not a made-up one.

meaning for a pupil: 1) «Humourous» is a common misspelling of «humorous», which means funny or meant to make people laugh. 2) Some writers use «humourous» by mistake because the UK noun is «humour» with a «u».
its sense in the lessons: In spelling lessons it is a classic trap: in the UK, Canada, Australia, New Zealand and Ireland the noun is «humour», but the adjective drops the «u» and is «humorous» everywhere, also in the USA. The meaning, when used, is just «funny». Phrases you will see are really «a humorous story», «humorous poem».
examples from the lessons: The correct spelling is «humorous», not «humourous». | She wrote a humorous poem about her cat. | My teacher circled «humourous» in red and wrote «humorous». | British English has «humour», but still «humorous». | The film was humorous and kind. | A humorous speech makes the audience laugh.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Not standard English: use «humorous» (UK, USA, Canada, Australia all agree). Same pattern: «vigour» but «vigorous», «glamour» but «glamorous», «labour» but «laborious». A spell checker will mark «humourous» as wrong.

part of speech: noun (a Hun, the Huns — the people); noun (hun — slang, a term of address)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (history) The Huns were a nomadic people from Central Asia who rode into Europe in the 300s and 400s AD; their most famous leader was Attila. 2) (slang, UK and Australia) «Hun» is a short form of «honey», used as a friendly or loving way to call someone, like «love» or «dear». 3) (offensive, historical) In the First and Second World Wars «the Hun» was an insulting name British people used for German soldiers; it is not used for people today.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons the Huns appear with the fall of the Roman Empire and Attila the Hun. In everyday chat, especially in messages, «hun» is a warm word: «You OK, hun?». In old war stories and posters «the Hun» shows wartime hatred, so readers should notice it as name-calling. Phrases: «Attila the Hun», «thanks hun», «you alright hun?».
examples from the lessons: Attila the Hun led his army across Europe. | The Huns fought on horseback and moved from place to place. | «Thanks for the cake, hun!» said Mum's friend. | «Don't cry, hun, it's only a scratch,» said the nurse. | Old wartime posters called German soldiers «the Hun». | The Romans feared the Huns more than almost any other enemy. | «Love you, hun x,» she wrote at the end of the text.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital «Hun» for the people; small «hun» for the friendly slang. The slang is informal: fine among friends and family, odd in a school essay. The war insult is offensive and only appears in history. Not the same as «Hungarian», although the name «Hungary» is sometimes wrongly linked to the Huns.

part of speech: verb (hush, hushes, hushed, hushing); noun (a hush); interjection (hush!)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To hush someone is to make them be quiet or calm. 2) As a command, «Hush!» means «Be quiet!». 3) A hush is a sudden quiet, when everyone stops talking. 4) To hush something up is to keep it secret so people do not find out, often something bad.
its sense in the lessons: In stories a hush often comes just before something important happens: «A hush fell over the room». Parents hush babies with lullabies («Hush, little baby»). In news and history «hush it up» means hiding a scandal. Phrases: «a hush fell», «hush up», «hush-hush» (informal, secret), «hush money».
examples from the lessons: «Hush now, the baby's asleep,» whispered Dad. | A hush fell over the hall when the head teacher walked in. | Mum hushed us when the phone rang. | The company tried to hush up the accident. | «Hush, little baby, don't say a word» is an old lullaby. | The plan is all very hush-hush, so don't tell anyone. | In the hush of the forest we heard a woodpecker.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past form «hushed». «A hushed voice» means a very quiet voice. «Hush-hush» is informal for «secret». «Hush money» is money paid to keep someone from telling a secret, which is often wrong or illegal. Countable as a noun only in «a hush».

part of speech: noun (a hyacinth, hyacinths); adjective (hyacinth — a colour, rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A hyacinth is a spring plant that grows from a bulb and has a thick spike of small, sweet-smelling, bell-shaped flowers, often blue, purple, pink or white. 2) Hyacinth is a purplish-blue colour. 3) (myth) In Greek stories Hyacinthus was a young man loved by the god Apollo; after he died a flower grew from his blood. 4) A water hyacinth is a floating plant that can cover rivers and lakes.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons hyacinths are used to show how bulbs store food and grow roots, sometimes in a glass of water on the classroom windowsill. In gardens they are a sign of spring. Water hyacinth appears in lessons about invasive plants. Phrases: «a pot of hyacinths», «hyacinth bulbs», «blue hyacinths».
examples from the lessons: We planted hyacinth bulbs in autumn and they flowered in March. | The hyacinths on the windowsill made the whole room smell sweet. | Our teacher grew a hyacinth in a jar so we could watch its roots. | Water hyacinth can block rivers so boats cannot pass. | Gran's favourite flowers are pink hyacinths. | The bridesmaids wore hyacinth-blue dresses. | Wear gloves when handling hyacinth bulbs, because they can make your skin itchy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one hyacinth, two hyacinths. Spelled with «y» then «i»: hy-a-cinth, said «HY-uh-sinth». Bulbs are poisonous to eat for people and pets. Not the same as a «hyena».

part of speech: noun (hydraulics — uncountable, takes a singular verb); adjective: hydraulic
meaning for a pupil: 1) Hydraulics is the science and use of liquids, usually oil or water, pushed through pipes to move or lift things. 2) The hydraulics of a machine are its parts that work by liquid pressure.
its sense in the lessons: In science and design-and-technology lessons hydraulics explains how a small push on a liquid in one syringe can lift a heavy load at the other end, because liquids cannot be squashed. Diggers, car brakes, lifts, dentist chairs and aeroplane flaps use hydraulics. Phrases: «hydraulic lift», «hydraulic brakes», «the hydraulics failed».
examples from the lessons: Hydraulics lets a small digger lift huge rocks. | We built a hydraulic arm from syringes, tubes and water. | The pilot said there was a problem with the hydraulics. | Car brakes use hydraulics to press the pads on the wheels. | The engineer studied hydraulics at university. | When the hydraulics failed, the drawbridge would not rise. | A hydraulic jack can lift a car with one person pumping the handle.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Looks plural but takes a singular verb: «Hydraulics is useful». The adjective is «hydraulic» (no «s»). From Greek «hydro» (water). Related: «pneumatics» works the same way but with air. In maths and science problems, liquid pressure is the same everywhere in a closed system, so a piston with a bigger area pushes with a bigger force.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Hydroelectric means making electricity from moving water, usually water rushing down from a dam through turbines. 2) A hydroelectric power station or dam is a place where this happens.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography lessons it is a kind of renewable energy: water held behind a dam falls and spins turbines, which turn generators. Famous examples are the Hoover Dam in the USA, the Three Gorges Dam in China and many stations in Norway, New Zealand, Canada and Tasmania. Lessons weigh pros (clean, steady) and cons (flooded valleys, harm to fish). Phrases: «hydroelectric power», «hydroelectric dam», «hydroelectric scheme».
examples from the lessons: Hydroelectric power uses falling water to make electricity. | Much of New Zealand's electricity is hydroelectric. | The hydroelectric dam flooded the valley behind it. | Water spins the turbines inside a hydroelectric power station. | Hydroelectric energy is renewable because rain refills the rivers. | Building the hydroelectric scheme meant moving a whole village. | Norway gets most of its electricity from hydroelectric stations.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective; the short informal noun is «hydro» («powered by hydro»). One word, sometimes with a hyphen. Renewable does not mean harmless: dams can harm fish and flood land. In energy problems, the higher the water falls and the more water flows, the more electricity it can make.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Ignition is the moment something catches fire or starts burning. 2) The ignition in a car is the switch, often turned with a key or a button, that starts the engine. 3) (science) Ignition is the start of burning in an engine or rocket when fuel is lit.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on fire, ignition needs the three parts of the fire triangle: fuel, heat and oxygen. In everyday life Dad «turns the key in the ignition». In rocket launches the countdown ends with «ignition» and «lift-off». Phrases: «turn the key in the ignition», «point of ignition», «ignition key», «ignition!».
examples from the lessons: Mum turned the key in the ignition and the car started. | «Three, two, one, ignition, lift-off!» | Never leave the keys in the ignition. | A spark caused the ignition of the gas. | Ignition needs heat, fuel and oxygen. | The firefighters found the point of ignition in the kitchen. | The rocket's engines roared at ignition.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun from the verb «ignite» (to set on fire). Spelled with «-tion». Usually uncountable for the act; countable for the car switch («the ignition»). Safety: sources of ignition (matches, sparks, flames) must be kept away from petrol and gas.

part of speech: adjective (illogical, more illogical, most illogical); adverb: illogically
meaning for a pupil: 1) Illogical means not making sense, or not following the rules of good reasoning. 2) Illogical describes a feeling or action that has no good reason behind it.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and logic lessons an illogical step is one where the conclusion does not follow from the facts. In everyday life people call fears or rules illogical when they cannot see a reason. In stories a character such as Mr Spock in Star Trek says «Illogical» to point out muddled thinking. Phrases: «totally illogical», «it is illogical to», «an illogical fear».
examples from the lessons: It is illogical to wear sunglasses to read in the dark. | His argument was illogical because it contradicted itself. | I know my fear of spiders is illogical, but I still scream. | Saying «all cats are pets, so all pets are cats» is illogical. | The rule seemed illogical until the teacher explained it. | Mr Spock raised an eyebrow and said, «Illogical.» | Changing the answer without checking was an illogical move.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Prefix «il-» before «l» means «not»: illegal, illegible, illogical. Not the same as «untrue»: a sentence can be logical but untrue. In maths reasoning, «if A then B» does not mean «if B then A»; mixing them up is illogical.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Impermeable means not letting water, air or other liquids and gases pass through. 2) (figurative) Impermeable can describe a person who is not affected by something, like criticism.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on materials, students test which materials are permeable (let water through) and which are impermeable, for example plastic, glass and rubber. In geography, clay and granite are impermeable rocks, so rain runs off them and causes floods. A raincoat must be impermeable. Phrases: «impermeable to water», «impermeable rock», «impermeable layer».
examples from the lessons: A raincoat is made of impermeable material. | Clay is impermeable, so water collects on top of it. | We tested paper, foil and cotton to see which was impermeable. | The pond liner is impermeable to water. | Glass is impermeable, but a sponge is not. | Water ran off the impermeable concrete into the drains. | She seemed impermeable to the teasing and just smiled.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: «permeable» (lets liquids through). Similar words: «waterproof», «watertight». Prefix «im-» means «not». Followed by «to»: «impermeable to water».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Impossibly means in a way that cannot happen or be done. 2) Impossibly also means extremely or unbelievably, so much that it seems impossible: «impossibly tall».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday talk and stories it exaggerates: «impossibly hard», «impossibly beautiful». In maths it can point to a real impossibility, but usually it just means «very, very». Phrases: «impossibly difficult», «impossibly tall», «impossibly fast».
examples from the lessons: The giraffe's neck looked impossibly long. | The puzzle was impossibly hard, so we asked for a hint. | The skyscraper rose impossibly high into the clouds. | Her handwriting was impossibly small. | The magician seemed to float impossibly above the stage. | The queue for the ride was impossibly long. | The cake was impossibly delicious.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from «impossible». Usually goes before an adjective. Often an exaggeration, so in a story it does not mean the thing truly cannot happen. Not the same as «impossible»: «It is impossible» (adjective), «impossibly hard» (adverb).

part of speech: noun (an imprint, imprints); verb (imprint, imprints, imprinted, imprinting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) An imprint is a mark or shape pressed into a surface, like a footprint in mud. 2) An imprint is a lasting effect that something leaves on a person or a place. 3) To imprint something is to press or print a mark onto it. 4) To imprint something on your mind is to fix it firmly in your memory. 5) (books) A publisher's imprint is the brand name it puts on a book.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons fossils are often imprints of leaves, shells or footprints in rock. In stories an experience «leaves its imprint» on someone. In everyday life a coin or a stamp can be imprinted with a design. In biology, a young animal can imprint on its mother (see «imprinting»). Phrases: «leave an imprint», «imprinted on my memory», «an imprint of».
examples from the lessons: The dinosaur left an imprint of its foot in the mud. | The fossil is the imprint of a fern. | The face of the queen is imprinted on the coin. | That holiday left a happy imprint on all of us. | The phone number is imprinted on my mind. | Her hand left an imprint in the wet clay. | This book is published under a children's imprint.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stress differs: noun «IM-print», verb «im-PRINT». Past form «imprinted». Countable noun. Similar to «print» and «impression».

part of speech: noun (imprinting — uncountable); verb form (imprinting — present participle of imprint)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (biology) Imprinting is the way some baby animals, like ducklings and goslings, learn to follow and trust the first moving thing they see after hatching, usually their mother. 2) Imprinting is the act of pressing or printing a mark or design onto something.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons imprinting explains why ducklings line up behind their mother, and why a gosling that first sees a person may follow that person; the scientist Konrad Lorenz studied this with geese. In design lessons imprinting means printing a logo onto T-shirts or mugs. Phrases: «imprinting on», «the imprinting period».
examples from the lessons: Ducklings follow their mother because of imprinting. | The goslings imprinted on the farmer and followed him everywhere. | Konrad Lorenz studied imprinting in geese. | Imprinting happens in the first hours after a chick hatches. | The factory is imprinting the school logo on our new sweatshirts. | Zookeepers wear puppets so the chicks do not start imprinting on people.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a verb form: «The chick is imprinting on its mother». As a noun it is uncountable. Imprinting mostly happens soon after birth; it is not ordinary learning by practice.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Improperly means in a wrong or incorrect way, not as it should be done. 2) Improperly means in a way that is not polite, honest or allowed.
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons it warns about things done the wrong way: «improperly stored chemicals», «improperly fitted car seat». In news and law it means breaking rules: «He acted improperly». Phrases: «improperly dressed», «improperly used», «behave improperly».
examples from the lessons: The car seat was fitted improperly, so it was not safe. | Food stored improperly can make you ill. | The ladder was used improperly and it slipped. | The judge said the officer had acted improperly. | If you wash wool improperly, it shrinks. | The bin was closed improperly and the foxes got in. | He was improperly dressed for a wedding, in muddy football kit.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from «improper». Opposite: «properly». Spelled with two «p»s in the middle: im-prop-er-ly. «Improperly» is a bit formal; in everyday speech people say «the wrong way».

meaning for a pupil: 1) The incidence of something, like an illness or a crime, is how often it happens. 2) (science) The angle of incidence is the angle at which a ray of light hits a surface, measured from the normal line.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on light and mirrors, the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection. In health and news, «the incidence of flu» means how many people catch it. In maths it is linked to rates and statistics. Phrases: «angle of incidence», «a high incidence of», «the incidence of disease».
examples from the lessons: The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection. | We measured the angle of incidence with a protractor. | There is a high incidence of colds in winter. | Washing hands lowers the incidence of tummy bugs. | The report shows the incidence of road accidents has fallen. | Draw the normal before you mark the angle of incidence.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Not the same as «incidents» (events), though they sound alike. «Incidence» is usually uncountable and means a rate. In maths and science problems, the angle of incidence is measured from the normal (the line at right angles to the mirror), not from the mirror surface; if a ray hits at 30° to the normal, it bounces off at 30° to the normal.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An incision is a careful cut made into something, especially a cut a surgeon makes into the body during an operation. 2) An incision is a neat cut or notch made with a sharp tool.
its sense in the lessons: In health lessons and hospital stories a surgeon makes an incision, then closes it with stitches. In science, «incisors» (front teeth) come from the same Latin word for cutting. In crafts and cooking an incision is a small precise cut. Phrases: «make an incision», «a small incision», «surgical incision».
examples from the lessons: The surgeon made a small incision to take out the appendix. | After the operation the incision was closed with stitches. | Keep the incision clean and dry. | The vet made an incision in the dog's paw to remove the thorn. | The chef made an incision in each sausage. | The scar from the incision faded over time.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one incision, two incisions. Formal or medical word; in everyday talk people say «cut». Related: «incisor» (a front tooth), «incisive» (sharp and clear, of a comment). Sounds like «in-SIZH-un».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Incubation is keeping eggs warm so they can develop and hatch. 2) (medicine) The incubation period is the time between catching an illness and showing the first signs of it. 3) Incubation is keeping something, like bacteria or a new business idea, in the right conditions so it can grow.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons classes watch chick eggs in an incubator during incubation, about 21 days for chickens. In health lessons, chickenpox has an incubation period of about two weeks, so you can spread it before you feel ill. Phrases: «incubation period», «during incubation», «the incubation of eggs».
examples from the lessons: Chicken eggs need about 21 days of incubation. | During incubation the hen turns her eggs. | Chickenpox has an incubation period of 10 to 21 days. | The bacteria were kept at body temperature for incubation. | We checked the eggs every morning during incubation. | Penguin fathers do the incubation in some species.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun from «incubate». Uncountable in most uses. In maths problems: if incubation takes 21 days and starts on 1 March, the chicks hatch around 22 March (count the days carefully).

meaning for a pupil: 1) An incubator is a machine that keeps eggs warm so they can hatch. 2) An incubator is a special clear cot in hospital that keeps a baby born too early or ill warm and safe. 3) An incubator is a warm box used in labs for growing bacteria or cells. 4) (business) An incubator is a place or program that helps new small companies grow.
its sense in the lessons: In school science classes often hatch chicks or ducklings in an incubator. In hospital stories a premature baby stays in an incubator until strong enough. In business news, start-up incubators help new ideas. Phrases: «in an incubator», «egg incubator», «hospital incubator».
examples from the lessons: Our class hatched six chicks in an incubator. | The incubator keeps the eggs at 37.5 degrees. | My baby brother was born early and spent two weeks in an incubator. | The scientist put the dish of bacteria in the incubator. | Don't open the incubator lid too often or the eggs will cool. | The new app company started in a business incubator.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one incubator, two incubators. From «incubate». In maths problems: if 12 eggs go in and 9 hatch, 3 did not hatch, and the hatch rate is 9/12 = 75%.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Inferior means not as good as something else, or of poor quality. 2) Inferior means lower in rank or position. 3) An inferior is a person of lower rank than someone, such as a junior worker. 4) (science, anatomy) Inferior means lower down in the body: the inferior vena cava carries blood from the lower body.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life it is used for cheap or badly made things: «inferior goods». In stories and history it shows unfairness when people are treated as inferior because of who they are, which is wrong. In science it appears in body names. Phrases: «inferior to», «feel inferior», «inferiority complex», «of inferior quality».
examples from the lessons: This plastic toy is inferior to the wooden one. | Nobody should be treated as inferior because of their skin colour. | The shop sold inferior shoes that fell apart in a week. | He felt inferior next to his clever older sister. | In the army an officer gives orders to inferiors. | The copy was of inferior quality to the original painting.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Use «inferior to», not «inferior than». Opposite: «superior». It is already a comparison, so do not say «more inferior». The noun «inferiority» means the state of being inferior. Calling a person inferior is hurtful.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Inflammation is when part of the body becomes red, swollen, hot and painful, usually because it is hurt or fighting an infection. 2) Inflammation is the body's own defence reaction that brings extra blood and helper cells to a damaged place.
its sense in the lessons: In health and science lessons inflammation is explained as the immune system at work: a sprained ankle or an infected cut swells. Many illness names ending in «-itis» mean inflammation: tonsillitis, appendicitis, conjunctivitis. Phrases: «inflammation of», «reduce inflammation», «signs of inflammation».
examples from the lessons: My sprained ankle showed inflammation, so I put ice on it. | Tonsillitis is an inflammation of the tonsils. | Redness and swelling are signs of inflammation. | The doctor gave her medicine to reduce the inflammation. | Inflammation is the body's way of protecting itself. | A bee sting causes inflammation around the spot.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelled «inflammation» with two «m»s, but the adjective is «inflammatory» and the verb «inflame». Not the same as «inflammable» (catches fire easily). The ending «-itis» in medicine means inflammation.

part of speech: noun (an institute, institutes); verb (institute, institutes, instituted, instituting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) An institute is an organisation set up for a special purpose, such as research, teaching or science, and also the building it uses. 2) (formal) To institute something is to start or set it up, like a rule or system.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life you see names like «the Women's Institute» (UK), «the Smithsonian Institution» or a «research institute». In history and civics, kings and governments «institute» new laws or taxes. Phrases: «research institute», «institute of technology», «institute a rule».
examples from the lessons: She works at a science institute that studies the ocean. | The Massachusetts Institute of Technology is a famous university. | Gran goes to the Women's Institute every Thursday. | The school instituted a new rule about phones. | The king instituted a tax on salt. | The institute opened a new museum for children.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun. The verb is formal; in speech people say «start» or «set up». Related: «institution» (a big organisation, or a custom), «instituted» (past form). Do not confuse with «substitute».

meaning for a pupil: 1) To intensify means to become stronger, greater or more extreme. 2) To intensify something means to make it stronger or more extreme.
its sense in the lessons: In weather reports storms intensify into hurricanes. In stories tension intensifies before the climax. In science lessons heat or light can intensify. In news, fighting or efforts can intensify. Phrases: «the storm intensified», «intensify efforts», «the pain intensified».
examples from the lessons: The storm intensified overnight. | The smell of smoke intensified as we got closer. | The police intensified their search for the missing dog. | The music intensified as the hero reached the door. | Adding salt can intensify the flavour of chocolate. | His fear intensified when the lights went out.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: «intensifies», «intensified» (y changes to i). Related: «intense» (adjective), «intensity» (noun). An «intensifier» in grammar is a word like «very» or «really» that makes another word stronger.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To interleave things is to put them between each other in turn, like mixing two piles of cards one by one. 2) To interleave a book is to put blank or extra pages between its pages.
its sense in the lessons: In study skills, interleaving means mixing different kinds of practice problems together instead of doing one kind at a time, which research suggests helps learning. In computing it means mixing two streams of data. Phrases: «interleave A with B», «interleaved practice».
examples from the lessons: Interleave the red and black cards so they alternate. | The teacher interleaved addition and subtraction questions on the sheet. | Interleaved practice helps you remember better than doing one type at once. | She interleaved the photos with tissue paper to protect them. | The old diary was interleaved with pressed flowers. | The computer interleaves the two sounds so they play together.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past form «interleaved». Mostly used in study, printing and computing; not an everyday word. Pattern: A, B, A, B, like a zip.

part of speech: verb form (past tense and past participle of «inter»: inter, inters, interred, interring)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Interred means buried; a person who is interred has been placed in a grave or tomb after death. 2) Interred can also mean placed in a tomb, vault or urn (burial place).
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons and on old gravestones and church plaques, «here lies interred» or «his remains were interred» means buried. In church life, ashes may be interred in a churchyard. It is a respectful, formal word. Phrases: «interred in», «buried and interred», «was interred at».
examples from the lessons: The king was interred in Westminster Abbey. | Grandpa's ashes were interred in the churchyard. | The soldiers are interred in a war cemetery in France. | The poet was interred beside his wife. | The plaque says that a famous scientist is interred here. | The ancient Egyptians interred their pharaohs in great tombs.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double «r» in «interred» and «interring». Do not confuse with «interned» (held in a camp, as in wartime) or «interrupt». The noun is «interment» (burial), not «internment» (being held prisoner). Formal; in everyday talk «buried».

meaning for a pupil: 1) An invader is a person, army or country that enters another place by force to take it over. 2) (science) An invader is a plant, animal or germ that spreads into a place where it does not belong and causes harm. 3) An invader is anyone who comes in where they are not wanted.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons Britain had many invaders: Romans, Anglo-Saxons, Vikings and Normans. In science, invasive species like cane toads in Australia or grey squirrels in the UK are called invaders, and the immune system fights invaders such as germs. In games like Space Invaders aliens attack. Phrases: «foreign invaders», «Viking invaders», «fight off the invaders».
examples from the lessons: The Vikings were invaders who sailed from Scandinavia. | The castle walls kept out the invaders. | Cane toads are invaders that harm Australian wildlife. | White blood cells attack invaders such as bacteria. | In the game you shoot down alien invaders. | The cat chased the invader out of its garden. | In 1066 the Norman invaders won the Battle of Hastings.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. From the verb «invade»; related «invasion», «invasive». An invader comes from outside; a defender protects. In history, describe invasions fairly: from each side's point of view.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (money) To invest is to put money into something, like a business, shares or a bank account, hoping to get more money back later. 2) To invest time or effort in something is to spend it because you think it will be worth it. 3) To invest in something can mean to buy something useful that will last. 4) (formal) To invest someone with power is to give them official power or a title.
its sense in the lessons: In money lessons children learn that investing can grow money but can also lose it, unlike keeping it safe in a piggy bank. In everyday life people «invest in a good coat» or «invest time in practice». Phrases: «invest in», «invest money», «invest time», «a good investment».
examples from the lessons: Grandma invested her savings in a small bakery. | If you invest your money, it might grow, but it might also shrink. | I invested a lot of time in this model rocket. | It's worth investing in good football boots. | The town invested in a new playground. | The company invests in solar panels. | Practising every day is investing in yourself.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Followed by «in»: «invest in a business». Nouns: «investment», «investor». In maths problems: if you invest £100 and it grows by 10% in a year, you have £110; a loss of 10% leaves £90. Investing is not the same as saving: saving keeps money safe, investing takes a risk.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Ironclad means covered or protected with iron plates. 2) An ironclad was a 19th-century warship covered with iron armour. 3) (figurative) Ironclad means so strong it cannot be broken or doubted: «an ironclad promise».
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons ironclads appear in the American Civil War, where the USS Monitor and CSS Virginia fought in 1862, the first battle between ironclad ships. In everyday and news language «ironclad» means very sure: an ironclad excuse, alibi or guarantee. Phrases: «ironclad guarantee», «ironclad alibi», «ironclad ship».
examples from the lessons: The ironclad ship could not be sunk by wooden cannonballs. | The USS Monitor was a famous ironclad. | The detective found that the butler had an ironclad alibi. | The company gave an ironclad guarantee that the toy was safe. | Ironclads replaced wooden warships in the 1800s. | Her excuse was ironclad: she was at the dentist.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word, no hyphen. «Clad» means clothed or covered (as in «snow-clad hills»). The figurative sense is common in news and law.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Iroquoian is a family of languages spoken by Native American and First Nations peoples of north-eastern North America, including Mohawk, Seneca, Oneida, Onondaga, Cayuga, Tuscarora and Cherokee. 2) Iroquoian describes these peoples, their languages and their culture.
its sense in the lessons: In history and geography lessons about the USA and Canada, Iroquoian peoples lived around the Great Lakes and St Lawrence River, often in longhouses, growing the «Three Sisters» (corn, beans and squash). The Haudenosaunee (Iroquois) Confederacy joined several Iroquoian nations. Phrases: «Iroquoian languages», «Iroquoian peoples».
examples from the lessons: Mohawk is an Iroquoian language. | Cherokee is also part of the Iroquoian family, though spoken further south. | Iroquoian villages had long wooden longhouses. | Iroquoian farmers grew corn, beans and squash together. | Some schools in Canada teach Iroquoian languages to keep them alive. | Many place names in New York State come from Iroquoian words.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Written with a capital «I». «Iroquois» names the confederacy; many of its people call themselves Haudenosaunee. «Iroquoian» is the wider language family. Say «IR-uh-KWOY-un».

part of speech: adjective (irresponsible, more irresponsible, most irresponsible); adverb: irresponsibly
meaning for a pupil: 1) Irresponsible means not thinking about the results of what you do, or not taking care of things you should look after. 2) An irresponsible action is careless and may put people or things in danger.
its sense in the lessons: In safety and PSHE lessons it describes risky choices: leaving a toddler near a pool, playing with matches, sharing passwords. In stories a character's irresponsible act often causes the problem the plot must fix. Phrases: «it was irresponsible of you to», «totally irresponsible», «irresponsible behaviour».
examples from the lessons: It was irresponsible to leave the gate open, because the dog ran out. | Riding a bike without a helmet on a busy road is irresponsible. | The irresponsible campers left their fire burning. | «That was very irresponsible of you,» said Mum. | It is irresponsible to share your password with strangers. | The pet owner was irresponsible and forgot to feed the fish. | Driving too fast near a school is irresponsible.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Prefix «ir-» before «r» means «not»: irregular, irrelevant, irresponsible (double «r»). Ends in «-ible», not «-able». Opposite: «responsible». The noun is «irresponsibility».

part of speech: adjective (irritating, more irritating, most irritating); verb form (irritating — present participle of irritate)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Irritating means annoying, making you feel cross or impatient. 2) (body) Irritating means making a part of the body sore, itchy or red: an irritating rash, irritating smoke.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life it describes a dripping tap, a buzzing fly or a sibling who keeps humming. In science and safety lessons chemicals labelled «irritant» can be irritating to skin and eyes. In stories it helps describe a character's mood. Phrases: «really irritating», «an irritating habit», «irritating to the skin».
examples from the lessons: My brother has an irritating habit of clicking his pen. | The buzzing fly was so irritating. | Smoke is irritating to the eyes. | This wool jumper is irritating my neck. | It is irritating when the bus is late again. | Stop irritating the cat, or it will scratch you. | The advert has an irritating little song.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Compare «irritating» (causing annoyance) and «irritated» (feeling annoyed): «The noise is irritating; I am irritated». Same pattern as boring/bored, annoying/annoyed. Double «r».

part of speech: adjective (isolated, more isolated); verb form (isolated — past of isolate)
meaning for a pupil: 1) An isolated place is far away from other places, towns or people. 2) An isolated person feels alone or has little contact with others. 3) An isolated event happens only once or rarely, not as part of a pattern. 4) Isolated means kept apart from others, for example to stop an illness spreading.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons isolated islands, farms and villages are remote, like the island of Tristan da Cunha or outback stations in Australia. In health lessons sick people may be isolated. In news «an isolated incident» means it happened only once. In science an isolated substance has been separated out. Phrases: «isolated village», «feel isolated», «an isolated case», «isolated from».
examples from the lessons: The farm is very isolated, an hour from the nearest shop. | After moving to a new town she felt isolated. | Patients with the illness were isolated in a special ward. | It was an isolated shower; the rest of the day was sunny. | The island was isolated by the storm, with no boats for a week. | Scientists isolated the chemical from the plant. | If a friend seems isolated, ask them to join in.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past form of «isolate»; the noun is «isolation». Isolated is different from «alone»: you can be isolated in a crowd if nobody talks to you. Feeling isolated is common and it helps to tell a trusted adult.

part of speech: noun (a jackrabbit, jackrabbits); verb (jackrabbit, jackrabbits, jackrabbited — informal, US)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A jackrabbit is a large hare of western North America with very long ears and strong back legs. 2) (informal, US) To jackrabbit is to start or move suddenly and fast, like a car shooting off from traffic lights.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about deserts, jackrabbits use their huge ears to lose heat and can run up to about 60 km per hour. Despite the name, a jackrabbit is a hare, not a rabbit: hares are born with fur and open eyes. Phrases: «jackrabbit start», «black-tailed jackrabbit».
examples from the lessons: A jackrabbit leapt out from behind the cactus. | Jackrabbits have long ears that help them stay cool. | The black-tailed jackrabbit lives in the deserts of the USA and Mexico. | A jackrabbit can run faster than most dogs. | The car made a jackrabbit start when the lights turned green. | Coyotes and eagles hunt jackrabbits.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word. A jackrabbit is a hare, not a true rabbit. Plural «jackrabbits». Mostly American; in the UK you would say «hare».

part of speech: noun (a judgment, judgments; also spelled judgement, judgements)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Judgment is the ability to make good, sensible decisions. 2) A judgment is an opinion you form after thinking about something. 3) (law) A judgment is a decision made by a judge or a court. 4) (Bible, church) Judgment Day or the Last Judgment is when, Christians believe, God will judge all people at the end of time.
its sense in the lessons: In PSHE lessons «use your judgment» means think it through before acting, for example about online safety. In law and news, a court «gives its judgment». In church and art lessons the Last Judgment is painted in many churches, such as Michelangelo's in the Sistine Chapel. Phrases: «good judgment», «pass judgment on», «use your judgment», «a judgment call», «against my better judgment».
examples from the lessons: Use your judgment and stay away from the riverbank in a flood. | She showed good judgment when she told a teacher. | The judge gave her judgment in the afternoon. | Don't pass judgment on him before you know the facts. | It's a judgment call whether to play in the rain. | Against my better judgment, I ate the whole bag of sweets. | Christians believe in a final Judgment Day.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Two spellings: «judgment» is usual in the USA and in law; «judgement» is common in the UK, Australia and New Zealand outside law. Both are correct; keep one style. From the verb «judge». Countable for a decision, uncountable for the ability.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Kale is a leafy green vegetable in the cabbage family, with curly or flat dark leaves. 2) (Scotland, old) Kail or kale was an old word for cabbage soup or for food in general.
its sense in the lessons: In healthy eating lessons kale is given as an example of a vegetable full of vitamins and fibre. In everyday life people put it in salads, smoothies, soups or bake it into crisps. It grows well in cold weather. Phrases: «kale chips», «curly kale», «a bunch of kale».
examples from the lessons: Mum put kale in the green smoothie. | Curly kale grows well even in frost. | We baked kale chips with a little oil and salt. | Kale is in the same family as broccoli and cabbage. | Dad bought a bunch of kale at the market. | Caterpillars love munching our kale.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «some kale», not «a kale» (but «a bunch of kale»). Rhymes with «sale». Kale chips (US) are called kale crisps in the UK.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Kerosene is a thin, clear oil made from petroleum that is burned as fuel in lamps, heaters, stoves and jet engines. 2) (Australia, USA, Canada) Kerosene is the usual name for paraffin oil; in the UK it is often called paraffin.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons kerosene lamps lit homes before electricity. In science it is a fossil fuel, a flammable liquid. Planes run on jet fuel, which is mostly kerosene. In safety lessons it must be kept away from children and flames. Phrases: «kerosene lamp», «kerosene heater».
examples from the lessons: Before electricity, people read by kerosene lamps. | Jet planes burn a fuel made mainly of kerosene. | The cabin was heated by a kerosene stove. | Kerosene is flammable, so keep it away from flames. | Never drink kerosene; call for help at once if a child swallows some. | In the UK, kerosene is often called paraffin.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Also spelled «kerosine» in some technical texts. UK «paraffin» = US/Australian «kerosene»; in the USA «paraffin» usually means paraffin wax. Swallowing it is very dangerous: get emergency help, do not make the person sick.

part of speech: noun (a keystone, keystones); adjective (keystone — as in «keystone species»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A keystone is the central wedge-shaped stone at the top of an arch that holds all the other stones in place. 2) A keystone is the most important part of a plan, idea or system, which everything else depends on. 3) (science) A keystone species is an animal or plant that its whole ecosystem depends on, like sea otters or beavers.
its sense in the lessons: In history and design lessons, Roman bridges and church arches stand because of the keystone. In science lessons about food webs, removing a keystone species makes the ecosystem change greatly. Pennsylvania is called «the Keystone State». Phrases: «keystone species», «the keystone of».
examples from the lessons: The keystone at the top holds the whole arch together. | When the builders put in the keystone, they could remove the wooden frame. | Sea otters are a keystone species because they eat sea urchins that destroy kelp forests. | Reading is the keystone of learning. | Beavers are a keystone species that build dams and make ponds. | Pennsylvania is known as the Keystone State.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. In an arch, the keystone is pushed from both sides, which locks it in; this is why arches carry heavy loads. «Keystone» is not the same as «cornerstone» (a stone at the corner of a building), though both can mean «the most important part».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Knobbly means covered with small round lumps or bumps. 2) Knobbly knees are bony knees that stick out.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and stories it describes old trees, tree roots, potatoes, walking sticks or a knobbly old man's hands. In science lessons on materials or plants it describes bumpy textures. Phrases: «knobbly knees», «a knobbly stick», «knobbly tyres».
examples from the lessons: The old oak tree had a knobbly trunk. | He laughed at his own knobbly knees in his shorts. | The mountain bike has knobbly tyres for mud. | Gran's knobbly walking stick is made from a branch. | Ginger is a knobbly root. | The toad's back was knobbly and brown.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mainly UK, Australia and New Zealand; the USA usually says «knobby». The «k» is silent: «NOB-lee». Comes from «knob» (a round lump or handle).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Kwa is a large family of languages spoken in West Africa, in countries such as Ghana, Togo, Benin, Côte d'Ivoire and Nigeria; Akan (Twi), Ewe and Fon are Kwa languages. 2) (Swahili) «Kwa» is a common little word meaning «for», «to», «with» or «by», as in «kwa heri» (goodbye). 3) As a fragment, «kwa» may be part of a longer word or a sound effect, like a duck's or frog's call; it is not an English word.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and language lessons Kwa languages show how many languages are spoken in West Africa. Children may meet Swahili «kwa heri» in songs and lessons about East Africa. In English texts it is never a normal word on its own. Phrases: «the Kwa languages», «kwa heri» (Swahili, goodbye).
examples from the lessons: Twi and Ewe belong to the Kwa languages of West Africa. | Millions of people in Ghana speak a Kwa language. | «Kwa heri!» means «Goodbye!» in Swahili. | Linguists group Ewe and Fon in the Kwa family. | The comic showed a frog going «kwa kwa». | Kwa is not an English word; it is a name for a language group.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital «Kwa» for the language family. Said «kwah». Not English: a name from African linguistics, or a Swahili word.

part of speech: verb form (lagging — present participle of lag: lag, lags, lagged, lagging); noun (lagging — uncountable)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Lagging means falling behind, moving more slowly than others. 2) Lagging is material wrapped around pipes, tanks or boilers to keep heat in and stop them freezing. 3) (computing, informal) A lagging game or video call is slow and jerky because the connection or computer cannot keep up.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life «lagging behind» is said about a runner at the back of a race or a pupil behind with homework. In science lessons about heat and insulation, lagging on a hot water tank saves energy. Gamers complain the game is lagging. Phrases: «lagging behind», «pipe lagging», «the game keeps lagging».
examples from the lessons: My little brother was lagging behind on the walk. | Put lagging on the pipes so they don't freeze in winter. | The game is lagging because the Wi-Fi is slow. | Our team is lagging in the league this season. | The lagging around the hot water tank keeps the heat in. | Stop lagging and hurry up! | The video call was lagging, so her face froze.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double «g»: lag → lagging, lagged. «Lag» as a noun is a delay: «jet lag», «time lag». In science problems lagging is a kind of insulation that slows heat loss; it does not make heat.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A lagomorph is a member of the group of mammals that includes rabbits, hares and pikas.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on classification, lagomorphs look like rodents but are a separate order: they have two pairs of upper front teeth (a small pair behind the big ones), while rodents have one pair. Lagomorphs eat plants and often eat some of their droppings to digest food twice. Phrases: «lagomorphs and rodents».
examples from the lessons: A rabbit is a lagomorph, not a rodent. | Hares, rabbits and pikas are all lagomorphs. | Lagomorphs have a tiny second pair of upper front teeth. | The pika is a small lagomorph that lives on rocky mountains. | Scientists sorted the animals into rodents and lagomorphs. | Lagomorphs eat grass, leaves and bark.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Said «LAG-uh-morf». From Greek «hare-shaped». A common myth is that rabbits are rodents; they are lagomorphs.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A lander is a spacecraft built to land on the surface of a planet, moon, comet or asteroid. 2) (rare) A lander is someone who lands, or a person from a particular land (as in «Highlander»).
