its sense in the lessons: In science and space lessons landers such as the Apollo Lunar Module, Viking on Mars, Philae on a comet and Chandrayaan-3's Vikram on the Moon are compared with orbiters (which circle) and rovers (which drive around). Phrases: «Mars lander», «lunar lander», «the lander touched down».
examples from the lessons: The lander touched down safely on the Moon. | A lander stays where it lands, but a rover can drive around. | The Philae lander bounced on the comet. | The Mars lander measured quakes inside the planet. | We built a paper lander to protect an egg when dropped. | The Apollo lunar lander carried two astronauts to the surface.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. From the verb «land». Compare: orbiter (goes around), lander (lands), rover (moves on the surface), probe (any uncrewed spacecraft). In egg-drop maths/science tasks, a good lander slows the fall and spreads the impact.

part of speech: noun (a larch, larches; larch — the wood)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A larch is a tall cone-bearing tree with soft needles that turn yellow and fall off in autumn. 2) Larch is the strong wood of this tree, used for fences, boats and buildings.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons the larch is a surprise: it is a conifer, but it is deciduous, losing its needles in winter, unlike most conifers which are evergreen. It grows in cold northern forests, in Siberia, Canada and the Alps, and in UK plantations. Phrases: «larch trees», «larch wood», «larch cones».
examples from the lessons: The larch turns golden yellow in autumn. | Unlike a pine, a larch drops its needles in winter. | The garden shed is built of larch. | We found small round larch cones on the path. | Larch forests cover huge areas of Siberia. | The larch needles grow in little bunches.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «larches». Not every conifer is evergreen: larch is the classic exception. Countable for trees, uncountable for the wood.

part of speech: noun (a latch, latches); verb (latch, latches, latched, latching)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A latch is a simple metal bar or catch that keeps a door or gate shut. 2) To latch a door or gate is to close it with a latch. 3) To latch on to something is to grab and hold it tightly, or to start following or understanding an idea. 4) When a baby latches on, it attaches its mouth to the breast to feed.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and safety: «latch the gate so the dog can't get out», «pool gates must self-latch» (an important safety rule in Australia and elsewhere). «Latchkey kid» means a child who lets themselves into an empty home after school. In stories a lifted latch creaks before someone enters. Phrases: «on the latch» (UK: shut but not locked), «latch on to», «latchkey».
examples from the lessons: Please close the gate and lift the latch to check it's shut. | The door was on the latch, so we walked straight in. | The pool gate must latch by itself to keep toddlers safe. | The puppy latched on to my sleeve and wouldn't let go. | She quickly latched on to the new game. | The latch on the old shed is rusty. | Grandad latched the barn door for the night.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «latches», «latches» for the verb too. «Latch on to» (UK) or «latch onto» (US). A latch keeps a door shut but is not always a lock: you may not need a key.

part of speech: noun (a lazybones; plural lazybones — same form)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) A lazybones is a lazy person, someone who does not want to get up or do any work; it is usually a playful, joking word.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday family life a parent might call «Get up, lazybones!» on a school morning. In stories it is a friendly tease, not a serious insult. Phrases: «come on, lazybones», «you lazybones».
examples from the lessons: «Wake up, lazybones, it's nearly nine!» called Mum. | The cat is a real lazybones; it sleeps all day. | Don't be a lazybones; help me carry the shopping. | Grandad called us lazybones when we stayed in bed. | Our dog is a lazybones on hot afternoons. | «Who's the lazybones who left the dishes?»
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal and playful. Singular and plural are both «lazybones» («he is a lazybones», «they are lazybones»). One word. Calling someone lazy for real can hurt, so it depends on tone.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Leaky describes something with a hole or crack that lets liquid or gas escape or get in: a leaky tap, a leaky roof. 2) (informal) Leaky can describe a person or group that lets secrets out.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life a leaky tap drips, a leaky boot lets water in, a leaky tent gets everyone wet. In science and maths problems a leaky tank or bucket loses water over time. In news a «leaky» government lets secrets reach the press. Phrases: «a leaky tap», «a leaky roof», «leaky boat».
examples from the lessons: The leaky tap dripped all night. | Put a bucket under the leaky roof. | My wellies are leaky, so my socks are soaked. | They rowed across the lake in a leaky old boat. | A leaky pen left ink all over my pencil case. | The team was so leaky that the coach's plan reached the other side.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «leak» (noun and verb). Do not confuse «leak» with «leek» (the vegetable). In maths problems: if a leaky tank loses 2 litres an hour, after 5 hours it has lost 10 litres; if it is also being filled, subtract the leak from the filling rate.

part of speech: verb form (past tense and past participle of «lengthen»: lengthen, lengthens, lengthened, lengthening); adjective (lengthened)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Lengthened means made longer, or became longer. 2) Lengthened can describe time: days lengthen in spring, a lesson can be lengthened.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons days lengthen in spring and summer as the Earth's tilt points our hemisphere towards the Sun. In everyday life a tailor lengthens trousers, and a school can lengthen its break. In maths a lengthened side changes the perimeter and area. Phrases: «lengthened shadows», «the days lengthened».
examples from the lessons: Gran lengthened my school skirt because I had grown. | The days lengthened as spring came. | The shadows lengthened in the evening sun. | The playtime was lengthened by ten minutes. | The bridge was lengthened to cross the wider river. | When each side of the square was lengthened by 2 cm, its perimeter grew by 8 cm.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «length» + «-en» (to make). Spelled «lengthened» with «-ened». Opposite: «shortened». In maths problems: lengthening each side of a square by 2 cm adds 8 cm to the perimeter (4 sides × 2 cm), but the area grows more than you might guess.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A lentil is a small round flat seed, brown, green, red or yellow, that grows in pods and is cooked and eaten, often in soups and stews. 2) Lentils are a pulse, part of the bean and pea family.
its sense in the lessons: In healthy eating lessons lentils are a cheap source of protein and fibre, important in vegetarian food. They are used in Indian dal, lentil soup and Middle Eastern dishes. In science lessons dried lentils are counted, weighed or sprouted. In the Bible Esau sells his birthright to Jacob for a bowl of red lentil stew. Phrases: «lentil soup», «red lentils», «a handful of lentils».
examples from the lessons: Dad made lentil soup for lunch. | Red lentils turn soft and yellow when cooked. | Dal is an Indian dish made with lentils. | We sprouted lentils on wet cotton wool in science. | Lentils are full of protein. | In the Bible, Esau traded his birthright for a bowl of lentil stew. | Rinse the lentils before you cook them.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually plural: «lentils». Lentils are seeds, pulses, not grains. Said «LEN-til». In maths problems with weights, dried lentils roughly double or more in weight when cooked because they soak up water.

part of speech: noun (the Levant — a region); verb (levant — old UK slang, rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The Levant is an old name for the lands on the eastern shore of the Mediterranean Sea, today mainly Lebanon, Syria, Israel, Palestine and Jordan, and sometimes Cyprus and parts of Turkey. 2) (old slang, UK, rare) To levant was to run away without paying your debts.
its sense in the lessons: In history and geography lessons the Levant appears with ancient Phoenicians, Bible lands, the Crusades and trade routes; the name comes from French «lever» (to rise), because the sun rises in the east. Its food, like hummus and falafel, is called Levantine. Phrases: «the Levant», «Levantine food», «the countries of the Levant».
examples from the lessons: The Phoenicians were sailors from the Levant. | Crusader castles still stand in the Levant. | Hummus is popular all over the Levant. | Merchants brought spices through the ports of the Levant. | Lebanon and Syria are countries of the Levant. | The Levant lies on the eastern edge of the Mediterranean.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Written with a capital and «the»: «the Levant». Adjective «Levantine». The verb sense is very old slang; you will hardly ever see it. Said «luh-VANT».

part of speech: noun (a lilac, lilacs; lilac — the colour); adjective (lilac)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A lilac is a bush or small tree with large bunches of small, sweet-smelling purple, pink or white flowers in spring. 2) Lilac is a pale purple colour.
its sense in the lessons: In gardens and science lessons lilac is a spring-flowering shrub. In art and fashion lilac is a soft colour name. In poems and stories the smell of lilac often brings memories of spring. Phrases: «a lilac bush», «lilac blossom», «pale lilac».
examples from the lessons: The lilac by the gate is in flower. | Her bedroom walls are painted lilac. | The scent of lilac drifted through the window. | She wore a lilac dress to the wedding. | White lilac grows in Gran's garden. | Bees buzzed around the lilac blossom.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable for the bush (two lilacs), uncountable for the colour. Said «LY-lak». Lilac is lighter than violet or purple; mauve and lavender are similar colours.

part of speech: verb (lob, lobs, lobbed, lobbing); noun (a lob, lobs)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To lob something is to throw or hit it high in the air, in a slow curve. 2) In tennis, football and other games, a lob is a high shot over an opponent's head. 3) (informal, UK and Australia) To lob something is to throw it carelessly: «Lob it in the bin». 4) (informal, Australia and New Zealand) To lob or lob in is to arrive, often unexpectedly: «He lobbed in at midnight».
its sense in the lessons: In PE and sport a lob goes over a defender or goalkeeper. In science lessons the curve of a lobbed ball is a parabola. In everyday talk «lob it here» means «throw it to me». Phrases: «lob the ball», «lob over», «lob in».
examples from the lessons: She lobbed the ball over the goalkeeper's head. | His lob landed just inside the line. | «Lob us the keys, would you?» | He lobbed his bag onto the bed. | The cousins lobbed in for lunch without warning. | The snowball was lobbed high over the fence. | A lob is hard to return if you are close to the net.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double «b»: lobbed, lobbing. Informal senses are friendly, not rude. In maths and science, a lobbed ball goes up, slows, stops for an instant at the top and comes down along a curved path.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Loin is a cut of meat from the back of an animal, between the ribs and the hips: pork loin, lamb loin. 2) (old, Bible) The loins are the part of the body around the hips and lower belly; «gird up your loins» meant get ready for hard work or a fight.
its sense in the lessons: In cooking and shops: pork loin, loin chops, sirloin steak. In the Bible and old stories, people «gird up their loins» (tuck in long robes to run or work) and children are said to come «from the loins» of a father. Phrases: «loin of pork», «loin chops», «gird up your loins», «loincloth».
examples from the lessons: We had roast pork loin for Sunday dinner. | The butcher cut four lamb loin chops. | Sirloin is a cut of beef from near the loin. | «Gird up your loins,» says an old Bible verse. | In hot lands some people wore only a loincloth. | Grandad joked, «Gird your loins, we're cleaning the garage!»
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually plural «loins» for the body part; that use is old-fashioned. «Sirloin» and «tenderloin» are related meat words. «Loincloth» is a cloth worn round the hips.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A lullaby is a soft, gentle song sung to help a baby or small child fall asleep. 2) A lullaby is any soft, calming sound: the lullaby of the waves.
its sense in the lessons: In music lessons lullabies have slow, rocking rhythms; famous ones are «Hush, Little Baby», «Rock-a-bye Baby», «Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star» and Brahms's Lullaby. Every culture has its own lullabies. In stories a lullaby shows comfort and love. Phrases: «sing a lullaby», «hum a lullaby».
examples from the lessons: Mum sang a lullaby until the baby fell asleep. | «Rock-a-bye Baby» is an old English lullaby. | The waves were a lullaby that sent me to sleep. | Gran hums a Ukrainian lullaby. | We learned a lullaby from Ghana in music. | Brahms wrote a famous lullaby for piano.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «lullabies» (y → ies). Said «LULL-uh-by». From «lull» (to calm). Countable.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Lustre is a soft, shining glow on a surface, like the shine on pearls, silk, metal or healthy hair. 2) Lustre is the special quality or fame that makes something seem bright and admired. 3) (science) Lustre is how a mineral reflects light: metallic, glassy, pearly, dull.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on rocks and metals, lustre is one way to identify minerals: gold has a metallic lustre, quartz a glassy one. In everyday life polishing brings back lustre. In stories «the event lost its lustre» means it became less exciting. Phrases: «metallic lustre», «lose its lustre», «add lustre to».
examples from the lessons: The pearl had a beautiful soft lustre. | Gold keeps its lustre for thousands of years. | Polishing the old spoon brought back its lustre. | We sorted the minerals by lustre: metallic or non-metallic. | Her hair had a healthy lustre. | After a week, the new game lost its lustre.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK, Australia, Canada, New Zealand: «lustre»; USA: «luster». Adjective «lustrous» (shiny). Uncountable.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A lute is an old stringed musical instrument with a pear-shaped body and a bent-back neck, played by plucking the strings with the fingers. 2) (rare) Lute is a sticky paste used to seal joints.
its sense in the lessons: In music and history lessons the lute was very popular in Europe in the Middle Ages and Renaissance; minstrels and courtiers played it. It came from the Arabic «oud». In stories a bard with a lute sings at the castle. Phrases: «play the lute», «lute music».
examples from the lessons: The minstrel played his lute at the banquet. | A lute has a round back like half a pear. | Queen Elizabeth I could play the lute. | We heard lute music on the museum tour. | The lute came to Europe from the Arabic oud. | The bard tuned his lute before the song.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Homophone: «loot» (stolen goods) sounds the same in most accents. A person who plays it is a «lutenist» or «lutanist»; a person who makes stringed instruments is a «luthier».

part of speech: adjective (magnificent, more magnificent, most magnificent); adverb: magnificently
meaning for a pupil: 1) Magnificent means very beautiful, grand and impressive. 2) (informal) Magnificent means extremely good or excellent.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and history it describes palaces, cathedrals, views and costumes; Suleiman the Magnificent was a great Ottoman sultan. In everyday talk people say «You were magnificent!» after a performance or a match. Phrases: «a magnificent view», «look magnificent», «simply magnificent».
examples from the lessons: The view from the top of the mountain was magnificent. | The peacock spread its magnificent tail. | «You were magnificent in the play!» said Dad. | The castle had a magnificent hall with a painted ceiling. | The goalkeeper made a magnificent save. | The cathedral is a magnificent building from the 1300s. | Suleiman the Magnificent ruled a huge empire.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: mag-ni-fi-cent, ending «-cent» not «-sent». Noun «magnificence». It is already very strong, so «very magnificent» sounds odd.

part of speech: noun (Marathi — a language and people); adjective (Marathi)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Marathi is a language spoken by about 80 to 100 million people, mainly in the state of Maharashtra in western India, including the city of Mumbai. 2) Marathi describes the people, culture or things of Maharashtra.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and language lessons Marathi is one of India's official languages, written in the Devanagari script, the same script as Hindi. Marathi speakers live around the world, including in the UK, the USA and Australia. Phrases: «speak Marathi», «Marathi film», «Marathi food».
examples from the lessons: Marathi is spoken in Mumbai and across Maharashtra. | My friend's grandma tells stories in Marathi. | Marathi is written in the Devanagari script. | We watched a Marathi film with English subtitles. | «Namaskar» is a Marathi greeting. | Over 80 million people speak Marathi.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always a capital «M». Said «muh-RAH-tee». It is not an English word but a language name. Do not confuse with «Maratha» (a people and empire in Indian history) or «Mahratta» (old spelling).

part of speech: noun (Marseille — a city; also English spelling Marseilles)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Marseille is a large port city on the Mediterranean coast in southern France, the second-largest city in France. 2) (French) The name is French; in older English it is often spelled «Marseilles».
its sense in the lessons: In geography and history lessons Marseille was founded by Greek sailors about 600 BC; it is one of the oldest cities in France. The French national anthem, «La Marseillaise», is named after soldiers from Marseille who sang it in 1792. In French lessons it is said «mar-SAY». Phrases: «the port of Marseille», «La Marseillaise».
examples from the lessons: Marseille is a busy port in the south of France. | Greek sailors founded Marseille long ago. | The French national anthem is called «La Marseillaise». | We took a ferry from Marseille to Corsica. | Marseille has a famous football club. | Fish soup called bouillabaisse comes from Marseille.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A place name (French), capital «M». Said «mar-SAY» (French) or «mar-SAYZ» for «Marseilles». Not an English word. Adjective «Marseillais».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal, science) To masticate is to chew food so it is broken into small pieces before swallowing. 2) (technical) To masticate rubber is to soften it by crushing and kneading it.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on digestion, mastication by the teeth is the first step: molars grind, incisors cut, saliva softens. In everyday talk it is a big, funny word for «chew». Phrases: «masticate your food», «mastication».
examples from the lessons: Digestion starts when you masticate your food. | The cow lay in the field slowly masticating grass. | Molars help you masticate tough food. | «Masticate thoroughly,» the doctor said, meaning «chew well». | Cows masticate their food twice by chewing the cud. | Mastication mixes food with saliva.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal word; everyday word «chew». Noun «mastication». In everyday writing «chew» is clearer. Past form «masticated».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Meaningless means having no meaning or no sense: a meaningless string of letters. 2) Meaningless means having no purpose or importance.
its sense in the lessons: In language lessons a meaningless word or sentence makes no sense, like «green ideas sleep furiously» which is grammatical but meaningless. In maths an answer can be meaningless if it does not fit the question, like 2.5 buses. In everyday life it describes pointless rules or empty promises. Phrases: «completely meaningless», «a meaningless gesture».
examples from the lessons: «Xqvzt» is a meaningless jumble of letters. | The score was meaningless because the match was only practice. | Without units, the answer 12 is meaningless. | He made a meaningless promise he never kept. | The old code looked meaningless until we found the key. | A long list of facts can feel meaningless without a story.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Suffix «-less» means «without». Opposite: «meaningful». In maths problems, check the answer is meaningful: you cannot have half a person or a negative number of apples, so round sensibly or recheck.

part of speech: noun (a medina, medinas; Medina — a city)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Medina is a city in Saudi Arabia, the second holiest city in Islam, where the Prophet Muhammad lived after moving from Mecca and where he is buried. 2) A medina is the old walled part of a city in North Africa, such as in Marrakesh or Fez, with narrow streets and markets. 3) Medina is also a girls' name (a name).
its sense in the lessons: In religious education lessons Medina is linked with the Hijra (the Prophet Muhammad's journey from Mecca to Medina in 622 AD), which marks the start of the Islamic calendar. In geography and travel the medina of Fez or Marrakesh is a maze of alleys and souks. Phrases: «Mecca and Medina», «the old medina».
examples from the lessons: Muslims believe the Prophet Muhammad moved from Mecca to Medina in 622. | Medina is a holy city for Muslims. | We got lost in the narrow streets of the medina in Marrakesh. | The medina sells spices, lamps and carpets. | The Prophet's Mosque is in Medina. | The Islamic calendar starts with the journey to Medina.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital «Medina» for the city and the name; small «medina» for an old town quarter. Said «meh-DEE-nuh». From Arabic «madina» (city). Not an English word in origin.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Melodious means having a pleasant tune, sweet and pleasing to hear.
its sense in the lessons: In music and English lessons it describes songs, birdsong and voices. Poets describe nightingales and blackbirds as melodious. Phrases: «a melodious voice», «melodious song».
examples from the lessons: The blackbird's melodious song woke me. | She has a melodious voice. | The harp played a melodious tune. | The stream made a melodious sound over the stones. | The nightingale is famous for its melodious singing. | The choir sang melodiously in the old church.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «melody». Spelled «mel-o-di-ous». Similar: «tuneful», «musical». Opposite: «harsh», «tuneless».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Milkweed is a North American plant with a milky white sap, pinkish flower clusters and pods full of fluffy seeds. 2) Milkweed is the only food monarch butterfly caterpillars eat.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about life cycles and food chains, monarch butterflies lay eggs on milkweed; the caterpillars eat its leaves and the plant's poison makes them taste bad to birds. Schools in the USA and Canada plant milkweed gardens to help monarchs. Phrases: «milkweed pods», «plant milkweed».
examples from the lessons: Monarch caterpillars eat only milkweed. | We planted milkweed in the school garden to help butterflies. | The milkweed pod burst and fluffy seeds floated away. | Milkweed sap is white and sticky like milk. | The poison in milkweed protects monarchs from birds. | We found a monarch egg on a milkweed leaf.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word. Mostly North American; in the UK «milkweed» may also mean other plants with milky sap. The sap can irritate the eyes, so wash your hands after touching it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (church) A missionary is a person sent by a church or religion to another place to spread their faith, and often to run schools, hospitals or help people in need. 2) Missionary describes this work: missionary work, a missionary school. 3) (figurative) With missionary zeal means with very strong, eager belief in an idea.
its sense in the lessons: In history and religious education lessons missionaries such as St Patrick, St Augustine of Canterbury, David Livingstone and many others travelled to share Christianity. Lessons note that missionaries built schools and hospitals, and that some missionary work was linked with empire and hurt local cultures. Phrases: «missionary work», «a missionary to», «missionary zeal».
examples from the lessons: St Patrick was a missionary in Ireland. | David Livingstone was a Scottish missionary and explorer in Africa. | Her aunt does missionary work at a hospital in Uganda. | The missionaries started a school in the village. | Christians believe Jesus sent his followers out as missionaries. | He talked about recycling with missionary zeal.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «missionaries». Related: «mission» (a task or a church base). Missionaries exist in several religions, though the word is most often about Christians. Describe history fairly: good and harmful effects were both real.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A mnemonic is a trick that helps you remember something, like a rhyme, a saying or a word made from first letters. 2) Mnemonic means helping the memory.
its sense in the lessons: In school mnemonics are everywhere: «Richard Of York Gave Battle In Vain» for rainbow colours (red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet), «Never Eat Shredded Wheat» for compass points, «BIDMAS/PEMDAS» for order of operations in maths, «Big Elephants Can Always Understand Small Elephants» to spell «because». Phrases: «a mnemonic for», «use a mnemonic».
examples from the lessons: «Richard Of York Gave Battle In Vain» is a mnemonic for the rainbow. | BIDMAS is a mnemonic for the order of operations. | «Never Eat Shredded Wheat» helps you remember North, East, South, West. | I made up a mnemonic to remember the planets. | «Thirty days hath September» is a mnemonic rhyme. | A mnemonic helped me spell «necessary»: one collar, two sleeves.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The first «m» is silent: said «nih-MON-ik». Countable. From Greek «mnēmē» (memory). In maths: BIDMAS (UK), BODMAS, PEMDAS (US) all mean brackets/parentheses first, then powers, then × and ÷ left to right, then + and − left to right.

part of speech: noun (Mohawk — a people and language; a mohawk — a hairstyle, mohawks); also mohican (UK, hairstyle)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The Mohawk are a First Nations and Native American people of the Haudenosaunee (Iroquois) Confederacy, living in what is now New York State, Quebec and Ontario. 2) Mohawk is the Iroquoian language of the Mohawk people. 3) A mohawk is a hairstyle with the sides shaved and a strip of hair standing up down the middle; in the UK it is often called a «mohican».
its sense in the lessons: In history and geography lessons about North America the Mohawk were one of the Six Nations; Mohawk ironworkers later helped build New York skyscrapers. In everyday life the punk hairstyle is a «mohawk». Phrases: «the Mohawk people», «the Mohawk language», «a mohawk haircut».
examples from the lessons: The Mohawk are one of the Six Nations of the Haudenosaunee. | Some children in Quebec learn Mohawk at school. | Mohawk ironworkers helped build tall bridges and skyscrapers. | The punk rocker had a bright green mohawk. | My cousin wants a mohawk, but his mum said no. | The Mohawk River flows through New York State.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital «Mohawk» for the people and language; small «mohawk» often for the haircut. The Mohawk call themselves «Kanien'kehá:ka». The UK word «mohican» for the haircut comes from a different people in a famous novel.

part of speech: noun (a mollie, mollies — the fish; also molly); name (Mollie — a name)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A mollie, or molly, is a small, lively freshwater fish often kept in home aquariums; the females give birth to live babies instead of laying eggs. 2) Mollie is a girls' name (a name), a pet form of Mary.
its sense in the lessons: In science and pet care lessons mollies, like guppies, are livebearers, which makes them interesting for learning about life cycles. In stories Mollie is a girl's name; in «Animal Farm» Mollie is a vain horse. Phrases: «black mollies», «a mollie fish».
examples from the lessons: We have three black mollies in our fish tank. | Mollies give birth to live baby fish. | The mollie hid behind the plant. | Mollie is my best friend's name. | In «Animal Farm», Mollie is a horse who loves ribbons and sugar. | Sailfin mollies have a tall fin on their backs.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelled «molly» or «mollie» for the fish; plural «mollies». Capital «Mollie» for the name. As a name, it says nothing about a real person.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A mollusc is an animal with a soft body and no backbone, which often has a hard shell; snails, slugs, clams, mussels, oysters, octopuses and squid are molluscs.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on classification, molluscs are invertebrates, a huge group living on land, in fresh water and in the sea. Octopuses and squid are clever molluscs without outer shells. Phrases: «a sea mollusc», «molluscs and crustaceans».
examples from the lessons: A snail is a mollusc with a coiled shell. | Slugs are molluscs that have no shell. | Octopuses are very clever molluscs. | We found mollusc shells on the beach. | Mussels and oysters are molluscs that live in the sea. | A mollusc has no backbone.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK, Australia and New Zealand: «mollusc»; USA: «mollusk»; Canada uses both. Plural «molluscs». Crabs and prawns are not molluscs; they are crustaceans.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A monotreme is a mammal that lays eggs instead of giving birth to live young; the platypus and the echidnas are the only living monotremes.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on classification monotremes are a surprise: they are mammals (they have fur and feed babies milk) but lay eggs. They live only in Australia and New Guinea. Phrases: «egg-laying mammals», «the platypus is a monotreme».
examples from the lessons: The platypus is a monotreme, a mammal that lays eggs. | Echidnas are spiny monotremes. | Monotremes feed their babies milk but have no nipples; the milk comes through the skin. | Only five kinds of monotreme are alive today. | Monotremes live in Australia and New Guinea. | The baby echidna is called a puggle.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Said «MON-oh-treem». Other mammal groups: marsupials (pouch, like kangaroos) and placental mammals (like humans). Myth: «all mammals give birth to live young» is false because of monotremes.

part of speech: verb (moo, moos, mooed, mooing); noun (a moo, moos); interjection (moo!)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A moo is the long, low sound a cow makes. 2) To moo is to make this sound. 3) (UK, informal, rude) «Silly moo» or «old moo» is a cheeky or rude name for a woman, meaning a silly person.
its sense in the lessons: In early lessons and stories it is the cow's sound in «Old MacDonald Had a Farm»: «with a moo-moo here». In everyday UK talk «you silly moo» is a mild, sometimes affectionate, sometimes rude insult. Phrases: «moo-moo», «the cows mooed», «silly moo».
examples from the lessons: The cow said «Moo!» | The cows mooed loudly at milking time. | With a moo-moo here and a moo-moo there! | We heard a sad moo from the barn. | My little sister moos every time she sees a cow. | «You silly moo, you've locked us out!» laughed Gran.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past form «mooed». As an insult it can be rude, so be careful. Homophones: none common, though «moo» rhymes with «zoo». «Moot» is a different word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A mouser is a cat (or sometimes another animal) that is good at catching mice. 2) (UK) The Chief Mouser to the Cabinet Office is the official cat at 10 Downing Street, the home of the British Prime Minister.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday and farm life a good mouser keeps a barn or shop free of mice. In UK news Larry the cat has been the Chief Mouser at Downing Street since 2011. In stories and history, ships and bakeries kept mousers. Phrases: «a good mouser», «Chief Mouser».
examples from the lessons: Our farm cat is an excellent mouser. | The bakery kept a mouser to protect the flour. | Larry is the Chief Mouser at 10 Downing Street. | Ships once carried mousers to catch rats and mice. | That lazy cat is no mouser; the mice walk past it. | A mouser can catch several mice a night.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Said «MOW-zer» (rhymes with «trouser»). From «mouse» + «-er».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A moustache is hair that grows on a man's upper lip, between the nose and the mouth. 2) (informal) A milk moustache is a white line of milk left on the upper lip after drinking.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and stories a moustache helps describe a character: a curly moustache for a villain, a walrus moustache for a grandad. In history, many famous men had moustaches. «Movember» is a November charity event where men grow moustaches for men's health. Phrases: «grow a moustache», «a bushy moustache», «a milk moustache».
examples from the lessons: Grandad has a big grey moustache. | The villain twirled his curly moustache. | You've got a milk moustache! | Dad grew a moustache for Movember. | Hercule Poirot is famous for his neat moustache. | The walrus has a moustache of stiff whiskers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK, Australia, Canada, New Zealand, Ireland: «moustache»; USA: «mustache». Said «muh-STAHSH» (UK) or «MUS-tash» (US). A beard grows on the chin and cheeks; a moustache only above the lip.

part of speech: abbreviation (MRI — magnetic resonance imaging); noun (an MRI, MRIs)
meaning for a pupil: 1) MRI stands for magnetic resonance imaging, a hospital machine that uses strong magnets and radio waves to make detailed pictures of the inside of the body. 2) An MRI or MRI scan is one such picture or test.
its sense in the lessons: In health and science lessons MRI is compared with X-rays: it uses no harmful radiation and shows soft parts like the brain, muscles and ligaments clearly. Patients lie still inside a noisy tube. Metal must be removed because of the powerful magnet. Phrases: «an MRI scan», «have an MRI», «MRI machine».
examples from the lessons: The doctor sent her for an MRI to check her knee. | An MRI scan uses magnets, not X-rays. | You have to lie very still during an MRI. | The MRI machine bangs and buzzes loudly. | Take off anything metal before an MRI. | The MRI showed a small tear in the ligament.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Written in capitals: MRI. Use «an MRI» (because it is said «em-ar-eye»). Not an English word but an abbreviation. Safety: no metal near the magnet; people with some implants cannot have one.

part of speech: verb (muffle, muffles, muffled, muffling); noun (a muffle — rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To muffle a sound is to make it quieter and less clear, for example by covering it. 2) To muffle someone or something up is to wrap them in warm clothes or cloth.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on sound, materials like foam, cloth and egg boxes muffle sound by absorbing vibrations. In stories muffled voices come through a wall or muffled footsteps in snow make a scene mysterious. Phrases: «muffled voices», «muffle the sound», «muffled up against the cold».
examples from the lessons: The thick snow muffled our footsteps. | We heard muffled voices through the wall. | She muffled her giggles with a pillow. | We tested which material muffles sound best. | The children were muffled up in scarves and hats. | Car mufflers (US) make engines quieter.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past form «muffled». Related: «muffler» (a scarf, UK old-fashioned; a car exhaust silencer, US). Muffling does not stop sound completely; it reduces it.

part of speech: noun (mumps — uncountable, usually with a singular verb)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Mumps is an infectious illness caused by a virus that makes the glands under the ears swell, so the cheeks and jaw puff up and hurt.
its sense in the lessons: In health and science lessons mumps is one of the illnesses prevented by the MMR vaccine (measles, mumps and rubella), which most children in the UK, USA, Australia and elsewhere are offered. It spreads through coughs, sneezes and saliva. Phrases: «have mumps», «catch mumps», «the MMR jab».
examples from the lessons: My dad had mumps when he was a boy. | Mumps makes your cheeks swell like a hamster's. | The MMR vaccine protects against measles, mumps and rubella. | She caught mumps and missed two weeks of school. | Mumps spreads through coughs and sneezes. | Mumps is rare now because of vaccines.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Looks plural but takes a singular verb: «Mumps is catching». Often used without «the»: «He has mumps». The «M» in MMR stands for measles, the second «M» for mumps.

part of speech: noun (Muscat — a city; muscat — a grape)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Muscat is the capital city of Oman, a country on the Arabian Peninsula, on the Gulf of Oman. 2) A muscat is a kind of sweet grape with a musky, flowery flavour, used for eating, raisins and sweet wine.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons Muscat is a historic port city and capital of Oman, once important for sea trade with India and East Africa. In food and farming muscat grapes are among the oldest grape varieties. Phrases: «Muscat, Oman», «muscat grapes».
examples from the lessons: Muscat is the capital of Oman. | The old forts of Muscat guard the harbour. | Muscat grapes taste sweet and flowery. | Dried muscat grapes make big juicy raisins. | Ships from Muscat sailed to India and Zanzibar. | We flew to Muscat on holiday.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital «Muscat» for the city (a place name); small «muscat» for the grape. Said «MUS-kat». Do not confuse with «musket» (an old gun) or «muskrat».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Mushy means soft and squashy, like mashed food or over-ripe fruit. 2) (informal) Mushy means too sentimental, full of soppy love feelings: a mushy film.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life «mushy peas» are a British dish served with fish and chips, and over-cooked vegetables go mushy. Children often call romantic films or kissing scenes «mushy». In science, fruit going mushy is a sign of decay. Phrases: «mushy peas», «go mushy», «all mushy».
examples from the lessons: The banana went mushy in my lunchbox. | We had fish and chips with mushy peas. | The cereal turns mushy if you leave it in the milk too long. | Ugh, this film is too mushy! | Cook the carrots longer if you like them mushy. | The card was full of mushy poems.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparatives: mushier, mushiest. From «mush» (a soft wet mass). The sentimental sense is informal and slightly mocking, not rude.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Nationwide means happening or existing in every part of a country. 2) As an adverb, nationwide means across the whole country.
its sense in the lessons: In news and everyday life: a nationwide search, a nationwide strike, a nationwide competition, shops «nationwide». In civics lessons a nationwide vote or survey includes the whole country. Phrases: «nationwide campaign», «available nationwide», «a nationwide search».
examples from the lessons: The school took part in a nationwide reading challenge. | There was a nationwide celebration after the team won. | The new toy is sold in shops nationwide. | Police began a nationwide search for the missing painting. | A nationwide survey asked children about their screen time. | The storm caused power cuts nationwide.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word. Works both as adjective («a nationwide event») and adverb («sold nationwide»). Similar: «countrywide», «national». «Worldwide» means across the whole world.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Naval means to do with a navy, warships or sailors in the armed forces: a naval officer, a naval battle.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons naval battles include Trafalgar (1805), where Admiral Nelson's British fleet won, and Midway (1942). Naval bases, naval ships and naval history appear in lessons about empires and wars. Phrases: «naval battle», «naval base», «naval officer», «naval history».
examples from the lessons: Nelson won the naval battle of Trafalgar. | Grandpa was a naval officer in the Royal Navy. | Portsmouth has a famous naval museum. | The naval base is full of grey warships. | Britain was a great naval power for centuries. | The naval band played on the dock.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Homophone trap: «naval» (navy) and «navel» (belly button) sound the same; a «navel orange» has a small belly-button shape. Adjective only; the noun is «navy».

part of speech: noun (a neap, neaps; neap tide); adjective (neap)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A neap tide is a tide with the smallest difference between high and low water, which happens twice a month when the Sun and Moon pull at right angles to each other.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography lessons tides are caused mainly by the Moon's pull; neap tides happen around the first and last quarter Moons, while spring tides (the biggest) happen at new and full Moon. Sailors and fishermen check neap and spring tides. Phrases: «neap tide», «at neaps».
examples from the lessons: At neap tide the sea does not go out very far. | Neap tides happen about twice a month. | Spring tides are bigger than neap tides. | The fishermen waited for the neap tide to launch the boat. | During neaps, the rock pools stay covered. | The Moon at half full means a neap tide is near.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually in «neap tide». Rhymes with «deep». Trap: «spring tide» has nothing to do with the season spring. In science problems: spring tides at new and full Moon (Sun, Earth, Moon in a line); neap tides at quarter Moons (at right angles).

part of speech: noun (Negro, Negroes — outdated and now offensive); adjective (Negro — historical names only); Spanish/Portuguese word (negro — black)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (outdated, now offensive) «Negro» was a word once used in English for a Black person, especially a person of African descent; today it is considered offensive and is not used to describe people. 2) (historical) It appears in old names and documents, for example the «Negro Leagues» in American baseball, «Negro spirituals», and in speeches by Dr Martin Luther King Jr, who used the word because it was normal in his time. 3) (Spanish, Portuguese) «Negro» means «black» in Spanish and Portuguese; it is in place names such as the Rio Negro («Black River») in South America.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons about slavery, the Civil Rights Movement and segregation in the USA, pupils meet the word in old sources, signs and speeches; teachers explain why it is no longer used and why respectful words today are «Black» or «African American» (USA), «Black British» (UK). In geography the Rio Negro is a great river joining the Amazon. Phrases met in history: «Negro Leagues», «Negro spirituals».
examples from the lessons: In old American documents the word «Negro» was used for Black people; today we say «Black». | Jackie Robinson played in the Negro Leagues before joining Major League Baseball. | «Swing Low, Sweet Chariot» is one of the old songs once called Negro spirituals. | Martin Luther King Jr used words of his time in his speeches. | The Rio Negro is a huge black-water river in the Amazon. | In Spanish, «negro» simply means the colour black.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Do not use it to describe people: it is outdated and offensive. You may read it in history quotes; when quoting, keep it inside quotation marks. Respectful terms today: «Black» (often with a capital), «African American», «Black British». The Spanish word «negro» (black) is a colour word with a different use. Plural of the old English noun was «Negroes».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A niche is a small hollow or alcove built into a wall, often to hold a statue or ornament. 2) A niche is a job, place or activity that suits someone perfectly: «She found her niche in drama». 3) (science) An ecological niche is the role and place a living thing has in its habitat: what it eats, where it lives, how it survives. 4) (informal, business) Niche describes something that only a small group of people like or buy: a niche hobby.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons different species avoid competing because they fill different niches. In church and history lessons statues of saints stand in niches. In everyday talk a niche interest is something unusual, like collecting train tickets. Phrases: «find your niche», «a niche market», «ecological niche».
examples from the lessons: A small statue stood in a niche in the church wall. | After trying many sports, he found his niche in swimming. | Owls and hawks hunt at different times, so they fill different niches. | Collecting bottle caps is a niche hobby. | The shop sells niche toys you can't find anywhere else. | Every animal in the pond has its own niche.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Said «neesh» (UK, most common) or «nitch» (US, also common). Plural «niches». As an adjective («a niche hobby») it is informal.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal, UK and Australia) Nippy means cold, especially with a sharp, biting chill: a nippy morning. 2) (informal) Nippy means quick and lively, able to move fast: a nippy little car. 3) (rare) Nippy describes a dog likely to nip or bite.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday British and Australian talk «It's a bit nippy out» means it is cold, so take a coat. In sport a nippy winger is fast and hard to catch. Phrases: «a bit nippy», «nippy little car», «nippy winger».
examples from the lessons: Wrap up warm, it's a bit nippy this morning. | The wind was nippy on the beach. | Our new car is small and nippy in traffic. | She's a nippy little player who dodges every tackle. | That terrier can be nippy with strangers. | It gets nippy at night in the desert.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal, friendly word. Comparatives «nippier», «nippiest». From «nip» (a small bite, or a sharp chill). «Nippy» means fairly cold, not freezing.

part of speech: verb (nudge, nudges, nudged, nudging); noun (a nudge, nudges)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To nudge someone is to push them gently, usually with your elbow, to get their attention. 2) To nudge something is to move it a little by pushing gently. 3) To nudge someone towards something is to gently encourage them to do it. 4) A nudge is a small push or a gentle reminder. 5) To nudge a number is to come close to it: «Prices are nudging ten pounds».
its sense in the lessons: In class a friend nudges you when the teacher asks a question. In everyday life apps «nudge» you with reminders. In news, numbers «nudge up». In stories a nudge can be a secret signal. Phrases: «a gentle nudge», «nudge nudge, wink wink» (UK, joking), «nudge up», «nudge someone in the ribs».
examples from the lessons: My friend nudged me when my name was called. | She nudged the ball into the goal. | Mum nudged me to say thank you. | Could you nudge the chair a bit closer to the table? | The temperature is nudging 30 degrees. | Give me a nudge if I fall asleep. | The app nudges you to drink water.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past form «nudged». A nudge is gentle; a shove is hard. In maths and news «nudging 100» means close to 100 but not yet over it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An observatory is a building with big telescopes and instruments for watching and studying stars, planets and space. 2) An observatory is a place for watching and recording weather, earthquakes, birds or other natural things.
its sense in the lessons: In science and space lessons famous observatories include the Royal Observatory at Greenwich (where the Prime Meridian, 0° longitude, runs), Mauna Kea in Hawaii and the observatories in the Chilean desert. They are built on high, dry, dark places away from city lights. Phrases: «the Royal Observatory», «weather observatory», «at the observatory».
examples from the lessons: We visited the observatory and looked at Saturn's rings. | The Royal Observatory in Greenwich marks the Prime Meridian. | Observatories are built on mountains, away from city lights. | The observatory's dome slid open at night. | Scientists at the observatory discovered a new comet. | The weather observatory records rain every day.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «observatories». Spelled with «-ory» like «laboratory». From «observe». Said «ob-ZUR-vuh-tree» (UK) or «ob-ZUR-vuh-tor-ee» (US).

part of speech: adjective (olden — used before a noun, mostly in «olden days» and «olden times»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Olden means belonging to the long-ago past; «in the olden days» means a long time ago.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday talk children and grandparents say «in the olden days» about life before phones, cars or electricity. In history lessons it is a friendly, informal way to say «in the past». Phrases: «in the olden days», «olden times».
examples from the lessons: In the olden days, people washed clothes by hand. | Grandad says in the olden days there were only three TV channels. | Children in olden times walked miles to school. | We dressed up as children from the olden days. | In olden days candles lit every house. | «Was that in the olden days, Gran?»
note for the reader of a maths problem: Almost only used in «olden days» or «olden times». Old-fashioned, informal and a bit playful; in a history essay say «in the past» or give the date. «Olden days» can be vague: be clear which time you mean.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Orthography is the system of spelling and writing a language: which letters stand for which sounds, and rules for capital letters, hyphens and punctuation. 2) Orthography is correct spelling.
its sense in the lessons: In English and language lessons, English orthography is famous for being tricky: «though, through, tough, cough» are spelled alike but sound different. Other languages, like Finnish, Spanish or Ukrainian, have more regular orthographies. UK and US orthography differ («colour/color»). Phrases: «English orthography», «spelling and orthography».
examples from the lessons: English orthography has many silent letters, like the «k» in «knee». | Spanish orthography is more regular than English. | The orthography of Ukrainian uses the Cyrillic alphabet. | Noah Webster changed American orthography, writing «color» instead of «colour». | Learning orthography means learning the spelling rules. | Old books show a different orthography, like «olde shoppe».
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable in general use; «orthographies» for different systems. Adjective «orthographic». From Greek «ortho» (correct) + «graph» (writing). Not the same as «orthodontist» (a teeth-straightening dentist).

meaning for a pupil: 1) An otoscope is a small medical tool with a light and a magnifying lens that a doctor uses to look inside your ear.
its sense in the lessons: In health lessons and doctor visits the doctor uses an otoscope to check the ear canal and eardrum for wax, infection or damage. Some kids' doctor play sets include a toy otoscope. Phrases: «look in your ear with an otoscope».
examples from the lessons: The doctor looked in my ear with an otoscope. | The otoscope has a little light on the end. | Through the otoscope she could see my eardrum. | The nurse put a clean tip on the otoscope. | My toy doctor's kit has a plastic otoscope. | The otoscope showed an ear infection.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Said «OH-tuh-skope». From Greek «oto» (ear) + «scope» (look). Compare stethoscope (listening to the chest) and microscope (seeing tiny things).

part of speech: verb (outshine, outshines, outshone, outshining; US also outshined)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To outshine someone or something is to be much better or more impressive than them. 2) To outshine is to shine more brightly than something else.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and sport a new player may outshine the team captain, or a younger sister may outshine her older brother. In science, Venus outshines every star in the night sky. Phrases: «outshine the rest», «outshone everyone».
examples from the lessons: The new pupil outshone everyone in the spelling bee. | Venus outshines all the stars at dusk. | Cinderella outshone her stepsisters at the ball. | The goalkeeper outshone the strikers in the final. | Don't try to outshine your friends; enjoy their success too. | The full Moon outshone the faint stars.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past form usually «outshone» (UK) and also «outshined» (US). Prefix «out-» means «more than»: outrun, outsmart, outshine.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The outskirts of a town or city are the parts at its edge, furthest from the centre.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons on settlements, the outskirts often have newer housing estates, retail parks, factories and farmland, while the centre has old buildings and shops. In stories a lonely house «on the outskirts of the village» sets the scene. Phrases: «on the outskirts of», «the outskirts of town».
examples from the lessons: We live on the outskirts of Manchester. | The big supermarket is on the outskirts of town. | A spooky old house stood on the outskirts of the village. | The airport is on the outskirts of the city. | Farms begin where the outskirts end. | The army camped on the outskirts of Rome.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always plural: «the outskirts», with «on the outskirts of». No singular «outskirt» in normal use. Similar: «edge», «suburbs» (suburbs are areas of houses around a city).

meaning for a pupil: 1) To outsmart someone is to beat them by being cleverer or trickier.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and fairy tales clever small characters outsmart bigger ones: the Gruffalo's mouse, Brer Rabbit, the three little pigs. In everyday life and games you outsmart an opponent at chess. In safety lessons scammers try to outsmart people, so we learn their tricks. Phrases: «outsmart the fox», «be outsmarted by».
examples from the lessons: The little mouse outsmarted the fox in the deep dark wood. | She outsmarted me at chess with a clever move. | The squirrel outsmarted our bird feeder. | Scammers try to outsmart people, so never share your password. | The detective outsmarted the thief. | Brer Rabbit outsmarted Brer Fox again.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past form «outsmarted». Prefix «out-» means «do better than». Similar: «outwit», «outfox». Informal but fine in writing.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (history) A pagan was a person who followed an old religion with many gods and goddesses, before Christianity or Islam spread, such as the old religions of the Romans, Anglo-Saxons and Vikings. 2) (today) A Pagan is a follower of a modern nature-based religion, such as Wicca or Druidry. 3) (old, often unkind) Christians in the past used «pagan» for anyone who was not Christian, Jewish or Muslim.
its sense in the lessons: In history and religious education lessons Anglo-Saxons and Vikings were pagans who worshipped gods like Woden (Odin) and Thor; many days of the week come from pagan gods (Wednesday = Woden's day, Thursday = Thor's day). Some Christian festivals took over pagan customs, such as Yule and Easter eggs. Phrases: «pagan gods», «pagan festivals», «pagan times».
examples from the lessons: The Anglo-Saxons were pagans before they became Christian. | Thursday is named after the pagan god Thor. | Stonehenge was built long before Christianity, in pagan times. | Some Christmas customs, like holly and the Yule log, have pagan roots. | Modern Pagans celebrate the summer solstice. | The missionaries tried to turn the pagans to Christianity.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital «Pagan» often for modern Pagans as a religion; small «pagan» for history. In the past it was sometimes used as an insult, so use it carefully and respectfully. Said «PAY-gun».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Painfully means in a way that hurts or causes pain. 2) Painfully means very, so much that it is uncomfortable: painfully slow, painfully shy.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and everyday talk it intensifies: «painfully obvious» means extremely obvious, often embarrassingly. In health: «he walked painfully» shows an injury. Phrases: «painfully slow», «painfully shy», «painfully obvious», «painfully aware».
examples from the lessons: He limped painfully off the pitch. | The queue moved painfully slowly. | She was painfully shy on her first day. | It was painfully obvious that he had not done his homework. | My sunburn felt painfully hot. | The old dog climbed the stairs painfully.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «painful» + «-ly»: two «l»s in «painfully». Often goes before an adjective to mean «very» in an unpleasant way.

part of speech: noun (a pairing, pairings); verb form (pairing — present participle of «pair»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A pairing is two people or things put together, as a pair or a team. 2) Pairing is the act of putting things into pairs. 3) (technology) Pairing is connecting two devices, such as headphones and a phone, by Bluetooth.
its sense in the lessons: In school, pairing pupils is how teachers make pair-work partners. In maths, pairing numbers helps add quickly (1+9, 2+8) and pairing objects shows if a number is odd or even. In sport a pairing is a doubles team. In cooking, food pairings like cheese and apple go well together. Phrases: «a good pairing», «pairing up», «Bluetooth pairing».
examples from the lessons: The teacher announced the pairings for the science project. | Pairing the socks takes ages after washing. | My headphones are pairing with my tablet. | Cheese and apple is a tasty pairing. | The tennis pairing won the doubles final. | Pairing 1 with 9 and 2 with 8 makes adding quick.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «pair» (two). Homophones of «pair»: «pear» (fruit), «pare» (to peel). In maths problems: if you can pair every object with no one left over, the number is even; if one is left over, it is odd. Pairing the numbers 1 to 10 into (1,10), (2,9) … gives 5 pairs of 11, so the sum is 55.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The pancreas is an organ in the belly, behind the stomach, that makes digestive juices and the hormone insulin, which controls the amount of sugar in the blood.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on the body and digestion, the pancreas sends juices into the small intestine to break down food. In health lessons it is linked with diabetes: in type 1 diabetes the pancreas does not make enough insulin, so people take insulin by injection or pump. Phrases: «the pancreas makes insulin».
examples from the lessons: The pancreas sits behind the stomach. | The pancreas makes insulin to control blood sugar. | My friend has type 1 diabetes because her pancreas doesn't make insulin. | Juices from the pancreas help digest fat. | The pancreas is about as long as a banana. | In science we labelled the pancreas on a body diagram.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Said «PAN-kree-us». Usually «the pancreas» (everyone has one). Adjective «pancreatic». Not the same as the liver or the spleen, which are nearby organs.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Parthenogenesis is a way some animals and plants have babies from an egg that has not been fertilised, so no father is needed.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on reproduction it is a surprising fact: aphids, some lizards (like whiptail lizards), some sharks and Komodo dragons in zoos, water fleas and bees (male drones) can reproduce this way. Offspring are often almost copies of the mother. Phrases: «reproduce by parthenogenesis».
examples from the lessons: Some aphids reproduce by parthenogenesis in summer. | A Komodo dragon in a zoo had babies by parthenogenesis. | Whiptail lizards are all female and use parthenogenesis. | Parthenogenesis means a baby grows from an unfertilised egg. | Male honeybees come from unfertilised eggs, a kind of parthenogenesis. | Scientists were surprised to find parthenogenesis in a shark.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Said «PAR-thuh-noh-JEN-uh-sis». From Greek «parthenos» (maiden) + «genesis» (birth). It is natural in some animals; it does not happen naturally in mammals.

part of speech: noun (a pasture, pastures; pasture — grassland); verb (pasture, pastures, pastured, pasturing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A pasture is a field of grass where cows, sheep, horses or other animals graze. 2) To pasture animals is to put them in a field to eat the grass. 3) (figurative) «Pastures new» or «greener pastures» means a new place or job that might be better. 4) (Bible) In Psalm 23, «He maketh me to lie down in green pastures» is a picture of God caring for people like a shepherd.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and farming lessons pastures are grazing land. In the Bible and church, «green pastures» in the 23rd Psalm stands for peace and care. In everyday talk «moving on to pastures new» means starting something new. Phrases: «green pastures», «put out to pasture» (retired), «pastures new».
examples from the lessons: The cows are grazing in the pasture. | The farmer moved the sheep to a fresh pasture. | «He makes me lie down in green pastures,» says Psalm 23. | After ten years at the school, our teacher left for pastures new. | The old horse was put out to pasture. | Pasture land covers much of New Zealand.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable for fields, uncountable for grassland in general. «Pastures new» (UK, from Milton's poem) and «greener pastures» (US) mean the same. Do not confuse with «pastor» (a minister of a church) or «posture» (how you stand).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A patina is a thin green or brown layer that forms on copper, bronze and some other metals over time, like on the Statue of Liberty. 2) A patina is the soft shine or worn look that old wood, leather or stone gets from age and use. 3) (figurative) A patina is a thin outer look: «a patina of calm».
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons the green patina on copper shows a chemical reaction with air and water (copper corrodes to form copper carbonate and other compounds). The Statue of Liberty was brown copper and turned green in about 30 years. In art and antiques patina makes old things valued. Phrases: «green patina», «a patina of age».
examples from the lessons: The Statue of Liberty is green because of its copper patina. | The old church roof has a green patina. | The wooden handrail had a shiny patina from many hands. | The bronze statue developed a patina over the years. | Polishing would remove the coin's patina. | Beneath a patina of calm, she was very nervous.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Said «PAT-in-uh» (UK) or «puh-TEE-nuh» (US). Patina is not dirt; on bronze and copper it can protect the metal underneath.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Peafowl are large birds of the pheasant family; the male is a peacock, the female is a peahen, and the babies are peachicks.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons peafowl are a classic example of the difference between males and females: the peacock has a long, colourful tail with «eye» spots that he fans out to attract peahens, while the peahen is brown and plain. The Indian peafowl is India's national bird. Phrases: «a flock of peafowl», «Indian peafowl».
examples from the lessons: Peafowl wandered across the castle lawn. | A peacock is a male peafowl, and a peahen is a female. | Baby peafowl are called peachicks. | The Indian peafowl is India's national bird. | Peafowl screech loudly at dawn. | Green peafowl live in South-East Asia.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural can be «peafowl» or «peafowls». In everyday talk people often call all of them «peacocks», but strictly the peacock is only the male. In counting problems: 3 peacocks and 4 peahens make 7 peafowl.

part of speech: noun (a phoebe, phoebes); proper noun (Phoebe — a name)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (a name) Phoebe is a girl's name, from an old Greek word meaning bright or shining. 2) A phoebe is a small grey-brown bird of North America that catches flies in the air and wags its tail. 3) (space) Phoebe is one of the moons of Saturn, a dark, small moon that goes round the planet backwards. 4) (myths) In Greek myths Phoebe was a Titan, a goddess linked with the Moon and light.
its sense in the lessons: In stories Phoebe is most often just a character's first name, so it tells you who is speaking or acting. In nature lessons about North American birds the phoebe is a common backyard bird named after its call, which sounds like "fee-bee". In space lessons Phoebe appears in lists of Saturn's many moons.
examples from the lessons: Phoebe sat next to me in maths today. | My best friend Phoebe has a dog called Biscuit. | A phoebe built its nest under our porch roof. | The phoebe called "fee-bee, fee-bee" from the fence. | Phoebe is one of more than a hundred moons of Saturn. | Phoebe orbits Saturn in the opposite direction to most of its moons. | In the Greek myth, Phoebe was the grandmother of Apollo and Artemis.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say it "FEE-bee": the final e is spoken, like in "Chloe". As a name it takes a capital letter; the bird (a phoebe, two phoebes) does not. Do not invent facts about a person called Phoebe — it is just a name. Not the same as "Phobos", a moon of Mars.

part of speech: noun (phosphorus — uncountable); adjective forms: phosphorous, phosphoric
meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) Phosphorus is a chemical element, a non-metal with the symbol P and atomic number 15. 2) It is needed by all living things: it is in our bones, teeth and DNA, and plants need it to grow. 3) Pure white phosphorus glows in the dark and catches fire by itself in air, so it is very dangerous; red phosphorus is safer and is used on matchboxes.
its sense in the lessons: In science it appears in the periodic table, in lessons on bones and healthy food (milk, fish, nuts) and in plant fertiliser (N-P-K: nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium). In history and safety, white phosphorus is a dangerous chemical used in some weapons. The word comes from Greek for "light-bringer" because it glows.
examples from the lessons: Phosphorus is element number 15 in the periodic table. | Our bones and teeth contain calcium and phosphorus. | Farmers add phosphorus to the soil so crops grow well. | The strip on the side of a matchbox has red phosphorus in it. | White phosphorus glows faintly in the dark. | Never touch white phosphorus; it can burn your skin. | Milk, eggs and fish give us phosphorus.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: say "some phosphorus", not "a phosphorus". Spelling trap: the noun ends -us (phosphorus); "phosphorous" with -ous is an adjective. Glow-in-the-dark toys usually do not contain phosphorus — they use other materials called phosphors. Symbol P, not Ph.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A pinhead is the tiny round top of a pin. 2) Something "the size of a pinhead" is very, very small. 3) (slang, rude) Calling someone a pinhead means you think they are stupid; it is an insult.
its sense in the lessons: In science and maths it is used for comparing sizes: a dot the size of a pinhead is about 1–2 millimetres. In stories it shows something is tiny (a pinhead of light far away). As an insult it is unkind and should not be used about people.
examples from the lessons: The seed was no bigger than a pinhead. | Push the pin in until only the pinhead shows. | A tiny spider, the size of a pinhead, ran across the page. | Far away we saw a pinhead of light from the lighthouse. | Ladybird eggs are about the size of a pinhead. | (rude) "Watch where you're going, you pinhead!" he shouted. | Calling someone a pinhead is rude, so Mum told him to say sorry.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word, no hyphen. Countable: a pinhead, pinheads. "The size of a pinhead" is a size comparison, not an exact measurement. The insult sense is rude.

part of speech: noun (pinyin — uncountable); used before nouns (pinyin spelling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Pinyin is the official way of writing Chinese (Mandarin) words with the Latin letters we use for English. 2) It also shows the tones of Mandarin with little marks over the vowels, such as mā, má, mǎ, mà.
its sense in the lessons: In language lessons pinyin helps learners read and say Mandarin before they know Chinese characters. Children in China learn pinyin at school, and it is used for typing Chinese on phones. Place names like Beijing are written in pinyin. A word in pinyin (ming, mei, ni hao) is Chinese, not English.
examples from the lessons: Nǐ hǎo is "hello" written in pinyin. | We learnt the pinyin for numbers one to ten. | The card had the Chinese character and the pinyin underneath. | In pinyin, "Beijing" replaced the old spelling "Peking". | My cousin types Chinese messages using pinyin. | The little marks in pinyin show the four tones. | Pinyin letters do not always sound like English letters: "x" sounds a bit like "sh".
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pinyin is not a language; it is a way of spelling Mandarin. Its letters have their own sounds: q is like "ch", x like "sh", zh like "j". Usually written without a capital, though some books write Pinyin. Uncountable.

part of speech: noun, plural (pirozhki; singular pirozhok); Ukrainian: pyrizhky (singular pyrizhok)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Pirozhki are small baked or fried buns filled with things like potato, cabbage, meat, mushrooms, cheese or fruit, eaten in Russia, Ukraine and nearby countries. 2) It is a borrowed word (from Russian), not an English word; in Ukrainian they are called pyrizhky.
its sense in the lessons: In lessons on food around the world and on Ukrainian life, pirozhki are an everyday snack or picnic food, often made by grandmothers. In stories they show a warm, homely kitchen. Do not confuse them with pierogi (Polish dumplings) or Ukrainian varenyky, which are boiled.
examples from the lessons: Gran made pirozhki filled with potato and onion. | We bought hot pirozhki at the market stall. | Some pirozhki are sweet, with apple or cherry inside. | My friend's mum brought pirozhki to the class food fair. | Pirozhki can be baked in the oven or fried in a pan. | In Ukrainian they are called pyrizhky. | One little bun is a pirozhok; lots are pirozhki.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Already plural: say "some pirozhki", not "pirozhkis". Spellings vary (piroshki, pirozhky). Stress near the end: "pi-rozh-KEE". Not the same as pierogi or varenyky (boiled dumplings).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A pistol is a small gun that you hold and fire with one hand. 2) A starting pistol is a toy-like pistol that only makes a loud bang, used to start races. 3) A water pistol is a toy that squirts water.
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons the message is: a real pistol is dangerous; if you find a gun, do not touch it, leave the place and tell an adult. On sports day a starting pistol starts a race. In history stories pistols appear in duels and in police and army life; in police news the word tells the reader a weapon was involved.
examples from the lessons: The race began with a bang from the starting pistol. | We had a water pistol fight in the garden. | If you ever see a pistol lying around, don't touch it and tell an adult. | The police officer carried a pistol on her belt. | In the old story two men fought a duel with pistols. | Pirates in films often carry a pistol and a sword. | My water pistol holds half a litre of water.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a pistol, two pistols. "Pistol" is a handgun; a rifle is long and held with two hands. Do not confuse with "pistil", the female part of a flower, which sounds the same. Toy and starting pistols are not real weapons, but treat anything that looks like a real gun with care.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A pitcher is a large jug with a handle and a lip for pouring drinks such as water, milk or juice (US: any jug; UK: often a big pottery jug). 2) (sport) In baseball and softball, the pitcher is the player who throws the ball to the batter. 3) A pitcher plant is a plant with jug-shaped leaves that trap and digest insects.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, a pitcher holds a capacity (a 2-litre pitcher) in measuring problems. In US school life and sport, the pitcher is the key player in a baseball game. In science, pitcher plants are meat-eating plants. Old saying: "Little pitchers have big ears" means children hear more than adults think.
examples from the lessons: Please fill the pitcher with cold water. | A pitcher of lemonade stood on the picnic table. | The pitcher holds 2 litres; how many 250 ml cups can you fill? | Our team's pitcher threw three strikes in a row. | She wants to be the pitcher in the softball team. | A pitcher plant traps flies inside its slippery leaves. | Dad poured milk from the pitcher into our glasses.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: pitchers. In British English "jug" is more common for drinks; "pitcher" sounds American. In baseball the pitcher throws, the batter hits, the catcher catches. Do not confuse with "picture".

meaning for a pupil: 1) A plaza is an open public square in a town or city, often with paved ground, benches and sometimes a fountain. 2) (US) A plaza can also mean a shopping centre or a group of shops and offices, as in "a shopping plaza".
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons about towns, a plaza is a meeting place at the heart of a city, especially in Spanish-speaking countries (the word is Spanish). In everyday life in the USA and Canada, "plaza" often appears in names of malls and buildings. In stories it is where crowds gather, markets happen or people meet.
examples from the lessons: We ate ice cream by the fountain in the plaza. | The town plaza was full of market stalls on Saturday. | There is a big Christmas tree in the plaza every December. | Mum parked at the shopping plaza near our school. | Pigeons gathered all over the plaza. | The parade ended in the main plaza. | In Spain and Mexico most towns have a central plaza.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: plazas. Say "PLAH-za" (also "PLAZ-a" in the US). In the UK "square" is more usual for an open town space; "plaza" is borrowed from Spanish.

part of speech: verb form (present participle of plead: plead, pleads, pleaded/pled, pleading); adjective (pleading eyes); noun (pleading, pleadings — law)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Pleading means begging or asking for something very strongly and emotionally. 2) As an adjective, a pleading look or voice asks for help or kindness without words. 3) (law) In court, pleading guilty or not guilty means saying officially whether you did the crime; pleadings are the written statements of each side.
its sense in the lessons: In stories "pleading" shows a character desperate for something, so readers feel how much they want it (a dog's pleading eyes). In citizenship lessons about courts, "pleading guilty" and "pleading not guilty" are key phrases. Phrases: pleading with someone, pleading for mercy, pleading eyes.
examples from the lessons: The puppy gave me a pleading look when I ate my sandwich. | "Please, just five more minutes," she said, pleading with Mum. | He was pleading for one more go on the trampoline. | The prisoner was pleading for mercy. | (law) The man is pleading not guilty to the charge. | Her pleading voice made the teacher listen. | After a lot of pleading, Dad let us stay up for the fireworks.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past of plead is "pleaded" in the UK; "pled" is also common in the US. You plead WITH a person FOR a thing. "Pleading guilty" means admitting the crime in court; "not guilty" means denying it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A podium is a small raised platform that a person stands on to speak, conduct an orchestra or receive a prize. 2) In sport, the podium is the three-step stand where the first, second and third winners stand; "to get on the podium" means to finish in the top three. 3) (US) A podium can also mean a lectern, the stand that holds a speaker's notes.
its sense in the lessons: In sports lessons and the Olympics, the podium shows gold, silver and bronze places: first in the middle (highest), second on one side, third on the other. In school assemblies a speaker may stand at a podium. In maths problems "made the podium" means finished 1st, 2nd or 3rd.
examples from the lessons: The three winners stood on the podium to get their medals. | She finished second and stood on the podium with a silver medal. | Our team just missed the podium by coming fourth. | The head teacher spoke from the podium in the hall. | The conductor stepped onto the podium and raised his baton. | The gold medal winner stands on the highest step of the podium. | Making the podium at the swimming gala was her dream.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: podiums (usual) or podia (formal). "Podium" is something you stand ON; a "lectern" is a stand for notes, though Americans often call that a podium too. In maths and sport, the podium = top 3 places only.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A pogrom is a violent attack by a mob on a group of people because of their religion or people, in which homes and shops are destroyed and people are hurt or killed. 2) The word was first used for attacks on Jewish people in the Russian Empire, including in towns that are now in Ukraine, in the 1800s and early 1900s.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons a pogrom is a terrible event of hatred and persecution; the word tells the reader that innocent people were attacked for who they were, often while the authorities did nothing or helped. Kristallnacht in Germany in 1938 was a pogrom against Jews. Lessons use it to teach why prejudice is dangerous.
examples from the lessons: A pogrom is an attack on people just because of their religion or background. | Many Jewish families left the Russian Empire after pogroms destroyed their homes. | Kristallnacht in 1938 was a pogrom against Jewish people in Germany. | During the pogrom, shops were smashed and families were hurt. | My great-grandparents moved to America to escape the pogroms. | The museum taught us how hatred can grow into a pogrom. | Remembering the pogroms helps people stand up against prejudice.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a pogrom, pogroms. It is a Russian word meaning "destruction", "to wreak havoc". Use it carefully and only for real mob attacks on a group; it is not a word for an ordinary fight or riot.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) A polymer is a substance made of very long chain-like molecules, built from many small units (called monomers) joined together. 2) Plastics are polymers, but so are many natural things such as rubber, wool, silk, starch and the DNA in our cells.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons polymers explain why plastic bags stretch, why slime is gooey and why rubber bounces. "Poly" means "many" and "mer" means "part".
