In everyday life polymer banknotes (in Australia, Canada, the UK and New Zealand) are made of a plastic polymer, not paper. Environment lessons talk about polymers that do not rot.
examples from the lessons: Plastic is a polymer made from many small molecules joined in a chain. | We made slime in class, and it is a kind of polymer. | Rubber is a natural polymer that comes from trees. | Australian and British banknotes are made of polymer, not paper. | Silk and wool are natural polymers made by animals. | Some polymers take hundreds of years to break down. | A polymer chain is like a long string of beads.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: polymers. "Poly-" means many (as in polygon). Not every polymer is a plastic: starch, DNA and rubber are natural polymers. Myth: "polymer" does not mean "dangerous chemical".

meaning for a pupil: 1) Popularly means by most ordinary people, or in the way many people say it: "popularly called" means the everyday name. 2) It can also mean by the votes or choice of the people, as in "popularly elected".
its sense in the lessons: In history and science texts "popularly known as" introduces a nickname or common name (Sirius is popularly called the Dog Star). In citizenship lessons "popularly elected" means chosen by voters. The word warns that the common belief may differ from the exact truth: "popularly believed" can mean a myth.
examples from the lessons: The plant is popularly known as the sunflower. | Elizabeth I was popularly called "Good Queen Bess". | It is popularly believed that goldfish forget everything in three seconds, but that is not true. | The mayor is popularly elected by the people of the city. | The game is popularly called "tag" in the USA and "tig" in parts of the UK. | The planet Venus is popularly called the Morning Star. | Big Ben is popularly used as the name of the whole clock tower.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: popular + ly = popularly (just add -ly). "Popularly believed" does not mean true — check the facts. Formal-sounding; in speech people say "most people call it".

part of speech: adjective (posterior — formal/science); noun (a posterior, posteriors — humorous)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal, science) Posterior means at the back or behind; it is the opposite of anterior (at the front). 2) (formal) Posterior can also mean later in time. 3) (humorous) Someone's posterior is their bottom.
its sense in the lessons: In science and medicine lessons it names the back part of an animal or body (the posterior legs of a frog, the posterior part of the brain). In stories it is a jokey, polite-sounding word for a person's bottom, used to be funny. In maths and statistics for older pupils, "posterior" names a probability updated after new evidence.
examples from the lessons: The posterior legs of a frog are longer than the front legs. | The doctor checked the posterior part of the knee. | A fish's tail is at its posterior end. | (humorous) He slipped on the ice and landed on his posterior. | (humorous) "Get your posterior off the sofa and help!" said Gran. | The ear's posterior side is the side facing the back of your head. | In science we label anterior (front) and posterior (back) on the diagram.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pair to learn: anterior = front, posterior = back. Formal or scientific; in daily talk say "back" or "bottom". Not the same as "poster". The humorous sense is mild, not rude.

part of speech: adjective (potent, more potent, most potent); noun potency
meaning for a pupil: 1) Potent means very strong and powerful in its effect: a potent medicine, poison or drink works strongly. 2) Potent can describe an idea, symbol or argument that has a strong effect on people's minds.
its sense in the lessons: In science and health lessons, a potent medicine or poison works even in tiny amounts, so it must be used with great care; this is a safety signal. In history and English, "a potent symbol" moves people deeply (a flag, a poppy). In stories a potent potion is a strong magic drink.
examples from the lessons: Some snake venom is so potent that a tiny drop can be deadly. | This medicine is potent, so only take the dose on the label. | The witch brewed a potent potion. | The poppy is a potent symbol of remembrance. | Garlic has a potent smell. | Her speech was a potent reminder to be kind. | Strong coffee is too potent for children.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: impotent or weak (but "impotent" also has an adult medical meaning, so "weak" or "powerless" is better for pupils). Noun: potency. Say "POH-tent". Do not confuse with "patent" (a legal right to an invention).

part of speech: noun (precision — uncountable); adjective (precision tools, precision engineering)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Precision means being very exact and careful, getting every small detail right. 2) (maths, science) Precision is how exact a measurement is, for example to the nearest millimetre rather than to the nearest metre. 3) As an adjective before a noun, precision means made to be very exact (precision tools).
its sense in the lessons: In maths and science, precision is about the number of decimal places or how small the units are (3.14159 is more precise than 3.14). Precision differs from accuracy: accurate means close to the true value, precise means exact and repeatable. In stories and sport it shows skill (a goal kicked with precision).
examples from the lessons: She cut the paper with great precision. | Measure to the nearest millimetre for more precision. | Surgeons work with precision. | The arrow hit the target with amazing precision. | Giving π as 3.14159 shows more precision than 3.14. | The watch was made with precision tools. | Gymnasts need precision and balance.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: "with precision", not "a precision". Adjective: precise; adverb: precisely. Trap: precision is not accuracy — you can be very precise and still wrong (5.287 m when the real length is 6 m). Spelling: -sion, not -tion.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) Prehensile means able to grip, hold or wrap around things, used about a body part such as a tail, foot, trunk or lip.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about animal adaptations, a prehensile tail lets monkeys, possums, chameleons and seahorses hang on to branches or plants. An elephant's trunk and a giraffe's tongue are prehensile too. Human hands, with their thumbs, are said to be prehensile.
examples from the lessons: Spider monkeys have prehensile tails that can hold branches. | A seahorse wraps its prehensile tail around seaweed. | A chameleon uses its prehensile tail like an extra hand. | An elephant's trunk is prehensile; it can pick up a single peanut. | The possum hung from the tree by its prehensile tail. | A giraffe's long prehensile tongue pulls leaves off branches. | Our thumbs make our hands prehensile.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say "pree-HEN-sile". From Latin "prehendere", to grasp (like "comprehend"). Myth trap: not all monkeys have prehensile tails — most monkeys from Africa and Asia do not; many from South and Central America do.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Prehistoric means from the very long time before people wrote things down, so before written history began. 2) (informal, humorous) Prehistoric can also mean very old-fashioned or out of date.
its sense in the lessons: In history and science lessons, prehistoric times include the Stone Age, Bronze Age and Iron Age, and prehistoric animals include dinosaurs and woolly mammoths. We learn about prehistoric people from cave paintings, bones and tools, not from books. As a joke, children call an old phone or computer "prehistoric".
examples from the lessons: Stonehenge was built in prehistoric times. | Prehistoric people painted animals on cave walls. | Dinosaurs were prehistoric reptiles. | We found a prehistoric flint tool in the museum. | Woolly mammoths were prehistoric animals that lived in the Ice Age. | (humorous) Dad's phone is prehistoric — it can't even take photos! | Archaeologists dig up prehistoric bones to learn how people lived.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pre- means before, so prehistoric = before history (writing). Myth trap: cavemen and dinosaurs did NOT live at the same time; dinosaurs died out about 66 million years before the first humans. Prehistory ended at different times in different places.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (money) A prepayment is money you pay before you get something, instead of afterwards. 2) It can also mean paying back part of a loan early, before it is due.
its sense in the lessons: In money lessons, prepayment explains pay-as-you-go phones, prepayment gas and electricity meters (topped up with a card or key in the UK) and deposits for holidays. In maths, a prepayment is subtracted from the total cost to find what is left to pay. Phrases: "prepayment meter", "prepayment required".
examples from the lessons: Prepayment is required, so you must pay when you book. | Our flat has a prepayment meter for the electricity. | Mum topped up the prepayment card at the shop. | The trip costs £60; after a £20 prepayment we still owe £40. | Some restaurants ask for a prepayment for big parties. | Prepayment means you pay first and get the item later. | My phone works on prepayment, so I buy credit before I use it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable or uncountable: "a prepayment of £20", "prepayment is required". Verb: prepay (prepaid). In maths, prepayment reduces the amount still owed: remaining = total − prepayment. A deposit is a kind of prepayment.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Pretence is acting as if something is true when it is not, for example pretending to be asleep or happy. 2) A pretence can be a false reason given to hide the real one, as in "under the pretence of helping". 3) "Make no pretence" means not even trying to look as if you are something.
its sense in the lessons: In stories pretence shows that a character is hiding their real feelings or plans; readers should look for the truth behind it. In honesty and safety lessons, "under false pretences" means tricking people, as scammers do. Play pretence (make-believe) is a normal, healthy part of children's games.
examples from the lessons: Her smile was just a pretence; inside she was sad. | He kept up the pretence of being ill to miss the test. | The scammer got into the house under the pretence of checking the meter. | Let's drop the pretence and tell the truth. | Their game of pretence turned the sofa into a pirate ship. | He made no pretence of liking broccoli. | Getting money under false pretences is a crime.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK, Australia, NZ, Ireland: pretence; USA: pretense; Canada uses both. Verb: pretend. Phrase: "under false pretences" (plural). Pretending in a game is fine; pretence to trick people is dishonest.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A primrose is a small wild plant with pale yellow flowers that bloom early in spring, common in Britain and Europe. 2) Primrose, or primrose yellow, is a soft, pale yellow colour. 3) (a name) Primrose can be a girl's name.
its sense in the lessons: In nature lessons primroses are a sign that spring has come; they grow in woods, hedges and banks. The name comes from Latin "prima rosa", the first rose, because it flowers so early. The old phrase "the primrose path" means an easy, pleasant way that leads to trouble.
examples from the lessons: Primroses were flowering along the hedge in March. | The woods were full of pale yellow primroses. | We painted the bedroom primrose yellow. | Please don't pick wild primroses; leave them for the bees. | Primrose is one of the first flowers of spring. | My aunt's cat is called Primrose. | The primrose has a ring of five soft petals.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: primroses. It is not a rose. Evening primrose is a different plant. In some places it is illegal to dig up wild primroses, so look but do not uproot them.

part of speech: noun (procrastination — uncountable); verb procrastinate; person procrastinator
meaning for a pupil: 1) Procrastination is putting off something you should do, especially something boring or hard, and doing it later or at the last minute.
its sense in the lessons: In school life, procrastination is leaving homework or revision until the night before. Lessons on habits and self-reflection explain why we procrastinate (fear, boredom) and how to stop: break the task into small steps, start with five minutes, remove distractions. Saying: "Procrastination is the thief of time."
examples from the lessons: My procrastination meant I did my project the night before it was due. | Procrastination is when you tidy your desk instead of doing your homework. | Mum says playing games before chores is pure procrastination. | To beat procrastination, start with just five minutes. | Procrastination made the job feel even bigger. | "Procrastination is the thief of time," says the old proverb. | Breaking the essay into small parts helped me stop procrastination.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Long word: pro-cras-ti-na-tion ("pro" forward + "cras" tomorrow, in Latin). Verb: procrastinate. It is not the same as laziness; people often procrastinate because a task feels hard or worrying.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Prone to something means likely to have it or do it, often something bad: prone to colds, prone to flooding. 2) Lying prone means lying flat on your front, face down.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and safety lessons, "flood-prone" or "earthquake-prone" areas are places where these disasters often happen. In health, "accident-prone" describes someone who often has accidents. In first aid and PE, prone (face down) is the opposite of supine (face up). Phrases: prone to, accident-prone, injury-prone.
examples from the lessons: My little brother is prone to nosebleeds. | This road is prone to flooding after heavy rain. | Japan is an earthquake-prone country. | I'm accident-prone; I tripped twice today. | The soldier lay prone in the grass. | Lie prone on the mat with your arms stretched out. | Some dogs are prone to getting fat.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Followed by "to" + noun or verb: prone to colds, prone to forget. Compound adjectives with a hyphen: accident-prone, flood-prone. Prone = face down; supine = face up — a common mix-up.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Your psyche is your mind and soul — your thoughts, feelings and the deep part of who you are. 2) (myths) In Greek myths Psyche was a beautiful young woman who fell in love with Cupid (Eros) and became a goddess of the soul. 3) (slang, "psych") Different word: to psych someone out or get psyched up.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and lessons on feelings, the psyche is the inner self; a frightening event can "leave a mark on her psyche". Psychology, the study of the mind, comes from the same Greek word. In space news, Psyche is also a metal-rich asteroid and the NASA mission to it.
examples from the lessons: The scary film stayed in my psyche for days. | Bullying can hurt a person's psyche, not just their body. | Writers try to show the psyche of their characters. | In the myth, Psyche had to complete hard tasks to win back Cupid. | Psychology is the study of the human psyche. | NASA sent a spacecraft to the asteroid Psyche. | Winning the game was good for the team's psyche.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say "SY-kee" — two syllables, the final e is spoken; the p is silent. Do not confuse with "psych" (one syllable, "syke"): "I'm psyched" (slang) means excited. Countable but usually singular.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To qualify for something is to earn a place in it or the right to it, often by meeting the rules or doing well enough: to qualify for the final. 2) To qualify as something is to pass the training or exams to do a job: she qualified as a nurse. 3) To qualify can mean to count as something: does a tomato qualify as a fruit? 4) To qualify a statement is to add something that makes it less strong or limits it ("It's good — but only for little kids").
its sense in the lessons: In sport, teams qualify for the next round or the World Cup. In money lessons, people qualify for help or discounts by meeting rules (age, income). In maths, a number qualifies if it meets a condition (does 15 qualify as a multiple of 5?). In writing, words like "usually" and "some" qualify a claim. In grammar, an adjective qualifies a noun.
examples from the lessons: Our team qualified for the cup final! | You must be over 12 to qualify for the bigger rides. | She qualified as a doctor after many years of study. | Does a tomato qualify as a fruit? Yes, in science it does. | Children under 5 qualify for free entry. | He won his heat and qualified for the 100 m final. | Which of these numbers qualify as even: 3, 8, 12? | I'd like to qualify what I said: most dogs are friendly, not all.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: qualify → qualifies, qualified (y changes to i). Qualify FOR a competition or prize; qualify AS a job title. In maths, "qualify" means "meet the condition". A qualification is a certificate or exam you have passed.

part of speech: verb form (present participle of qualify); adjective (a qualifying round, qualifying exam); noun (qualifying — the stage of a sport)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Qualifying is the -ing form of qualify: trying to earn a place, pass the rules or count as something. 2) As an adjective, a qualifying round, race or match decides who goes through to the next stage. 3) (sport) "Qualifying" can be a noun for the practice races that decide starting places, as in motor racing.
its sense in the lessons: In sport the qualifying stage comes before the main event: only teams that do well in qualifying go to the finals. In money, a "qualifying purchase" or "qualifying age" is one that meets the rules. In maths word problems, the qualifying numbers are the ones that meet the condition. In grammar, a qualifying word limits another word.
examples from the lessons: She ran fast in the qualifying race and made the final. | Our school is in the qualifying round of the chess cup. | He crashed during qualifying, so he started the race last. | The qualifying age for the junior team is under 11. | Ireland are still qualifying for the World Cup. | Only qualifying entries will be judged. | Circle the qualifying numbers: those bigger than 20.
note for the reader of a maths problem: No e before -ing: qualify → qualifying (keep the y). "Qualifying" (the round) comes before "the finals". In everyday talk "qualifiers" means qualifying matches.

part of speech: proper noun (Ra — Egyptian god); abbreviation (RA, Ra); interjection (rah)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (myths) Ra (also Re) was the sun god of ancient Egypt, often shown with a falcon's head and the sun disc on top. 2) (science) Ra is the chemical symbol for radium, a radioactive element. 3) (abbreviation) RA can stand for the Royal Academy of Arts in London, a resident assistant in US college dorms, or rheumatoid arthritis, a joint illness. 4) "Rah" or "ra" is a cheering shout, as in "rah-rah".
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons on ancient Egypt, Ra was the most important god; Egyptians believed he sailed across the sky in a boat each day and through the underworld each night. Pharaohs were called "son of Ra". In chemistry tables Ra is radium. On its own, "ra" is not an everyday English word.
examples from the lessons: The ancient Egyptians worshipped Ra, the sun god. | Ra was painted with the head of a falcon and a sun above it. | Egyptians believed Ra crossed the sky in a golden boat. | Ra is the symbol for radium in the periodic table. | We visited an exhibition at the RA in London. | The cheerleaders shouted, "Rah, rah, go team!" | Pharaohs called themselves sons of Ra.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital R for the god and the symbol (Ra), capitals for abbreviations (RA). Ra rhymes with "car". Egyptians believed in Ra; it is a myth, not a fact about the Sun. Not an ordinary English word on its own.

part of speech: verb form (present participle of raid: raid, raids, raided, raiding); noun (raiding — uncountable)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Raiding is making a sudden attack on a place, usually to steal things or catch people. 2) (police) Police raiding a building means going in suddenly to search it or arrest people. 3) (informal, humorous) Raiding the fridge or the biscuit tin means taking food from it, often secretly.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, Vikings were raiding monasteries and towns along the coasts of Britain and Ireland; "raiding parties" were groups sent to attack. In the news, police are raiding a house when they search it suddenly. At home, kids joke about raiding the fridge at night. In games, raiding means attacking an enemy base.
examples from the lessons: The Vikings were raiding villages along the coast. | Police were raiding the house at dawn. | My brother was caught raiding the biscuit tin. | Foxes keep raiding our bins at night. | The raiding party came by boat. | We went raiding the dressing-up box for costumes. | Squirrels were raiding the bird feeder again.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Raid + ing = raiding (no change). The thing you raid comes straight after: raiding the fridge (no "on"). A "raider" is a person who raids. The fridge sense is joking and not a crime.

part of speech: noun (a ransom, ransoms); verb (ransom, ransoms, ransomed, ransoming)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A ransom is money demanded by criminals to set free a person they have kidnapped or to give back something they have taken. 2) To ransom someone is to pay to free them, or to hold them until money is paid. 3) "Hold to ransom" means forcing people to do something by threatening them; "a king's ransom" means a huge amount of money.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and history, kings and knights were captured and ransomed, such as King Richard the Lionheart in 1192–1194. In the news and online safety, "ransomware" is a computer virus that locks files until money is paid. In maths, ransom amounts can appear in old-story problems. The phrase "a king's ransom" is used for something very expensive.
examples from the lessons: The kidnappers asked for a ransom of a million dollars. | The pirates held the captain for ransom. | King Richard was freed after England paid a huge ransom. | Those trainers cost a king's ransom! | The ransom note was made of letters cut from newspapers. | Ransomware locked the company's computers and asked for money. | Never pay strangers online who threaten your files; tell an adult.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a ransom, ransoms. Phrases: "hold someone to ransom" (UK) / "hold someone for ransom" (US). Not related to "random". "Ransomware" is the computer crime version.

part of speech: noun (rapeseed — uncountable); also called rape, oilseed rape, canola
meaning for a pupil: 1) Rapeseed is a plant with bright yellow flowers, grown in fields for its seeds. 2) The oil pressed from these seeds is rapeseed oil, a common cooking oil (called canola oil in Canada, the USA and Australia).
its sense in the lessons: In geography and farming lessons, spring fields of bright yellow rapeseed are a common sight in the UK and Europe; the crop gives cooking oil, animal feed and biofuel. "Canola" is a type of rapeseed bred in Canada. The name comes from Latin "rapum", meaning turnip, as the plant is related to turnips and cabbages.
examples from the lessons: The hills were covered in bright yellow rapeseed. | Mum fries potatoes in rapeseed oil. | Bees love the flowers of rapeseed. | Rapeseed belongs to the cabbage family. | In Canada rapeseed oil is called canola oil. | The farmer will harvest the rapeseed in summer. | Rapeseed fields can make some people sneeze.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. The "rape" in rapeseed comes from a Latin word for turnip; it has nothing to do with the crime. Farmers often say "oilseed rape" or just "rape" for the crop; "canola" is the North American and Australian name.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A recitation is saying a poem, speech or piece of writing aloud from memory, often in front of an audience. 2) A recitation can also be a long spoken list of facts or events, said one after another. 3) (church) Recitation of a prayer or psalm means saying it aloud, often together.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons and school assemblies, poetry recitation helps pupils learn rhythm and speak clearly; there are recitation competitions. In church, the congregation joins in the recitation of the Lord's Prayer. In older stories children did recitations for visitors. In religious life, recitation of the Quran is also a skilled art.
examples from the lessons: She won a prize for her recitation of a poem by Christina Rossetti. | Every pupil did a short recitation at the assembly. | The recitation of the Lord's Prayer ended the service. | His recitation of the times tables was fast and perfect. | Grandpa gave a long recitation of all his old football results. | We practised the recitation until we knew every word. | Poetry recitation helps you speak with expression.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a recitation, recitations. Verb: recite. A "recital" is usually a music or dance performance; a recitation is spoken words.

part of speech: verb form (past tense and past participle of reconstruct: reconstruct, reconstructs, reconstructed, reconstructing); adjective (a reconstructed village)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Reconstructed means built again after being damaged or destroyed. 2) Reconstructed can mean worked out or pieced together from clues, like a reconstructed event or crime. 3) As an adjective, it describes a copy built to show how something used to look, such as a reconstructed Iron Age house.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, museums have reconstructed Viking ships, Roman forts and Stone Age houses so we can see past life; a reconstructed object is not the original. In science, scientists reconstructed what dinosaurs looked like from fossils. In news, police reconstructed what happened from cameras and witnesses. After wars or earthquakes, cities are reconstructed.
examples from the lessons: The old bridge was reconstructed after the flood. | We visited a reconstructed Iron Age roundhouse. | Scientists reconstructed the dinosaur from its bones. | The police reconstructed the accident to see what went wrong. | After the war, the city centre was reconstructed stone by stone. | Shakespeare's Globe in London is a reconstructed theatre. | The face of the ancient king was reconstructed using computer models.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Re- + construct + -ed. A reconstructed building is a new copy, not the original — historians say how much is guesswork. Noun: reconstruction.

part of speech: verb (redesign, redesigns, redesigned, redesigning); noun (a redesign, redesigns)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To redesign something is to design it again, changing its look, shape or the way it works to make it better. 2) A redesign is the new design or the act of changing it.
its sense in the lessons: In design and technology lessons, pupils test a model, find problems and redesign it: test, improve, test again. In everyday life, apps, websites, logos, playgrounds and coins get redesigns. Scientists and engineers redesign machines after a failure.
examples from the lessons: Our paper bridge broke, so we redesigned it with more triangles. | The school is going to redesign the playground. | The app had a redesign and now the buttons are bigger. | She redesigned her poster to make the title clearer. | The car was redesigned to be safer. | After testing, we redesigned the boat so it would float. | The website's redesign made it easier to use.
note for the reader of a maths problem: No hyphen: redesign. Say "ree-di-ZINE"; the g is silent. Re- means again. Both a verb and a countable noun.

part of speech: verb (refract, refracts, refracted, refracting); noun refraction
meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) To refract light is to bend it as it passes from one material into another, such as from air into water or glass. 2) Sound and other waves can also refract when they change speed.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on light, refraction explains why a straw looks bent in a glass of water, why a swimming pool looks shallower than it is, how lenses in glasses and magnifying glasses work, and how a prism or raindrops refract and split white light into a rainbow. Safety: pools are deeper than they look because of refraction.
examples from the lessons: Water refracts light, so the straw looks bent. | A prism refracts white light into a rainbow of colours. | Glasses lenses refract light to help people see clearly. | Raindrops refract and reflect sunlight to make rainbows. | The pool looks shallow because water refracts the light. | Light refracts when it goes from air into glass. | Draw how the light ray refracts at the surface.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Do not confuse refract (bend light passing through) with reflect (bounce light back, as a mirror does). Noun: refraction. The light changes direction because it changes speed.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Refrigeration is keeping things cold, especially food and medicine, using a fridge, freezer or other cooling machine. 2) It also means the technology and machines that make things cold.
its sense in the lessons: In science and food safety lessons, refrigeration slows down the growth of bacteria so food stays fresh longer; fridges should be below about 5 °C (41 °F). In history, before refrigeration people used ice houses, salt and smoking to keep food. Labels say "keep refrigerated" or "requires refrigeration after opening".
examples from the lessons: Milk needs refrigeration or it goes sour. | Before refrigeration, people kept food cold with ice from lakes. | The vaccine must be kept under refrigeration. | Refrigeration slows down the growth of germs. | The ketchup bottle says "refrigeration after opening". | Lorries with refrigeration carry frozen food to shops. | Refrigeration changed how people shop and eat.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Verb: refrigerate; adjective: refrigerated. "Fridge" is short for refrigerator — note fridge has a d, refrigerator does not. Cold slows germs but does not kill them.

part of speech: verb (regurgitate, regurgitates, regurgitated, regurgitating); noun regurgitation
meaning for a pupil: 1) To regurgitate food is to bring swallowed food back up into the mouth. 2) (science) Some animals regurgitate food on purpose to feed their babies, like birds and wolves. 3) (informal, school) To regurgitate facts is to repeat what you learnt word for word without really understanding it.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on animals, birds regurgitate food for chicks, cows bring up cud to chew again, and owls regurgitate pellets of bones and fur that pupils dissect. In school, teachers warn against just regurgitating facts in an exam; explain in your own words instead.
examples from the lessons: The mother bird regurgitates worms into her chicks' mouths. | Owls regurgitate pellets full of tiny bones. | The baby regurgitated a bit of milk on Dad's shirt. | Cows regurgitate their food and chew it again. | Don't just regurgitate the textbook — explain it in your own words. | Penguins regurgitate fish to feed their young. | We dissected an owl pellet that the owl had regurgitated.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A polite or scientific word for bringing food back up; "be sick" or "vomit" are more common for people. Spelling: re-gurg-i-tate. The school sense means copying facts without understanding.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Rejection is refusing to accept, use or agree to something: the rejection of a plan or an offer. 2) Rejection is also the feeling of being unwanted or not chosen by someone. 3) (medicine) Rejection is when the body attacks a new organ after a transplant.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and lessons on feelings, rejection hurts — not being picked for a team or invited to a party — and lessons teach how to cope and how to include others. In science, the body's rejection of a transplanted organ is fought with medicines. Authors and inventors often face many rejections before success.
examples from the lessons: Not being picked for the team felt like rejection. | J. K. Rowling had many rejections before her first book was published. | His plan met with rejection from the whole class. | Fear of rejection stopped her from asking to join the game. | Doctors give medicine to stop the rejection of a new kidney. | The letter was a polite rejection. | Learning to deal with rejection makes you stronger.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable (a rejection, rejections) or uncountable (fear of rejection). Verb: reject. Rejection of an idea is not rejection of you as a person.

part of speech: verb form (present participle of repel: repel, repels, repelled, repelling); adjective (a repelling force)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Repelling means pushing something away or keeping it away. 2) (science) Magnets are repelling when like poles (north and north, or south and south) push away from each other. 3) Repelling an attack means fighting it off. 4) (rarer) Something repelling can make you feel disgust (more often "repellent" or "repulsive").
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on magnets, like poles repel and unlike poles attract; you can feel the repelling force. Waterproof coats are good at repelling water. Insect spray works by repelling mosquitoes. In history, castles were built for repelling attackers.
examples from the lessons: The two north poles are repelling each other. | Feel how the magnets push apart — they're repelling. | This coat is great at repelling rain. | Citronella candles help with repelling mosquitoes. | The soldiers succeeded in repelling the attack. | Oil and water are repelling each other in the jar. | Ducks' feathers are good at repelling water.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double l: repel → repelled, repelling. Opposite: attract. Noun: repulsion; "repellent" is a spray or an adjective. Remember: like poles repel, unlike (opposite) poles attract.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Reunification is joining together again something that had been split, especially a country that was divided into two. 2) It can also mean bringing a family back together after being separated.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, German reunification in 1990 joined East and West Germany after the Berlin Wall fell in 1989. Lessons may mention debates about the reunification of Ireland, Korea, Cyprus or China and Taiwan, with each side's view. In family and law contexts, "family reunification" lets refugees bring relatives to join them.
examples from the lessons: German reunification happened in 1990. | After the Berlin Wall fell, people celebrated the coming reunification. | Some people in Korea hope for reunification of North and South. | Family reunification brought the refugee children back to their parents. | The Irish debate about reunification has strong views on both sides. | The reunification of the two school sites took a year. | The film showed the joy of the family's reunification.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Re- + unification (unify = make one). Usually uncountable. A smaller event, like friends meeting again, is a "reunion", not a reunification.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To rewire a building, machine or circuit is to put new electrical wires in it, or connect them in a new way. 2) (informal, science) To rewire the brain or your habits means to change how you think or act by practice.
its sense in the lessons: In science and DT, pupils rewire a simple circuit to add a switch or bulb. In everyday life, old houses need rewiring for safety; this job is for a qualified electrician, never for children — mains electricity can kill. In talk about learning, people say practice "rewires your brain".
examples from the lessons: The electrician had to rewire the whole house. | We rewired the circuit so both bulbs lit up. | Never try to rewire a plug at home; ask an adult. | They are rewiring the old school hall. | Learning to play the piano can rewire your brain. | He rewired his toy robot to make it move faster. | The flat was rewired before we moved in.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: rewire, rewired, rewiring (drop the e before -ing). Safety: mains rewiring is only for trained adults. Battery circuits in class are safe.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A Rottweiler is a large, strong breed of dog, black with brown markings, first bred in Germany to herd cattle and guard. 2) (informal) Calling someone a rottweiler means they are fierce and aggressive in arguing or defending something.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life Rottweilers are kept as guard dogs and family pets; they are loyal and protective but powerful, so children should ask the owner before stroking any dog. In news and politics, a tough, attacking person may be called a "rottweiler". The breed is named after the German town of Rottweil.
examples from the lessons: Our neighbours have a friendly Rottweiler called Bruno. | A Rottweiler is black with brown patches on its face and legs. | Always ask the owner before you stroke a Rottweiler. | Rottweilers were once used to herd cattle to market. | The guard dog was a huge Rottweiler. | (informal) The new manager is a rottweiler in meetings. | Rottweilers need lots of exercise and training.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Breed names usually take a capital: Rottweiler. Spelling: two t's, "ei". Nickname: Rottie. Myth: not every Rottweiler is dangerous — behaviour depends on training — but any big dog should be treated with care.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (cooking) A roux is a mixture of melted butter (or fat) and flour cooked together, used to thicken sauces, soups and gravy. 2) Roux is also a French word meaning reddish-brown; it is a French surname too.
its sense in the lessons: In cooking lessons, a roux is the first step of white sauce for macaroni cheese or lasagne: melt butter, stir in flour, then slowly add milk. In Cajun and Creole cooking from Louisiana, a dark roux gives flavour to gumbo. The word is French.
examples from the lessons: Melt the butter, add the flour, and stir to make a roux. | Slowly whisk milk into the roux for a smooth white sauce. | A roux thickens the gravy. | Cook the roux for a minute so it doesn't taste of flour. | Gumbo in Louisiana starts with a dark brown roux. | Our cheese sauce was lumpy because the roux was too hot. | Use the same amount of butter and flour for a roux.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say "roo"; the x is silent (French). Plural is the same (roux) or sometimes rouxs. Safety: hot fat burns, so an adult should help at the cooker.

part of speech: noun (a ruby, rubies); adjective (ruby-red, ruby); proper noun (Ruby — a name; Ruby — a programming language)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A ruby is a precious stone with a deep red colour, used in rings and necklaces. 2) Ruby, or ruby-red, is a deep, rich red colour. 3) (a name) Ruby is a girl's name. 4) (computers) Ruby is a programming language. 5) A ruby wedding anniversary is the 40th one.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography, rubies are a form of the mineral corundum, very hard, mined in places like Myanmar. In stories, rubies are treasure and jewels in crowns. In fairy tales, Dorothy's ruby slippers come from the film of The Wizard of Oz. Many girls in schools in the UK, Australia and NZ are called Ruby.
examples from the lessons: The queen's crown sparkled with rubies and diamonds. | Mum's ring has a small ruby in the middle. | Her lips were painted ruby red. | Dorothy clicked the heels of her ruby slippers. | Rubies are very hard; only diamonds are much harder. | My friend Ruby lives next door. | Grandma and Grandpa celebrated their ruby wedding — 40 years! | Rubies are dug out of the ground and then cut and polished.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: rubies (y → ies). The name Ruby has a capital. Fact check: diamond is the hardest gem; ruby and sapphire (both corundum) are next, equally hard. Ruby is red; sapphire is the same mineral in other colours, mostly blue.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Saffron is a spice made from the dried red-orange threads (stigmas) of a crocus flower; it gives food a golden colour and a special taste. 2) Saffron is also a deep orange-yellow colour.
its sense in the lessons: In food and geography lessons, saffron is famous as the most expensive spice in the world by weight, because each flower gives only three tiny threads that are picked by hand; it is used in paella, risotto, Indian and Persian rice dishes and Cornish saffron buns. In religion lessons, saffron robes are worn by many Buddhist monks.
examples from the lessons: A pinch of saffron turned the rice golden yellow. | Saffron comes from the crocus flower. | It takes about 150 flowers to make one gram of saffron. | Saffron is the most expensive spice in the world. | The Buddhist monks wore saffron robes. | Gran baked saffron buns from Cornwall. | Spanish paella often has saffron in it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: "some saffron", "a pinch of saffron". Saffron is not the same as turmeric, a cheaper yellow spice. Spelling: double f.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Saltiness is how salty something tastes or is. 2) It can also mean how much salt is in water, like the saltiness of the sea.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on taste, saltiness is one of the basic tastes, along with sweet, sour, bitter and umami. In geography, the saltiness (salinity) of seas differs: the Dead Sea is so salty you float easily. In health lessons, too much salt is bad for the heart, so food labels show salt.
examples from the lessons: The chef tasted the soup to check its saltiness. | I could taste the saltiness of the sea on my lips. | Crisps have a lot of saltiness. | The saltiness of the Dead Sea makes people float. | Saltiness is one of the five basic tastes. | Add lemon to balance the saltiness. | Scientists measure the saltiness of ocean water.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Built from salt → salty → saltiness (y changes to i). The science word for the saltiness of water is "salinity".

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) A salutation is a greeting, a word or action that says hello, such as "Good morning" or a wave. 2) In a letter or email, the salutation is the greeting at the start, like "Dear Sam,". 3) (formal) "Salutations!" can be said as a jokey, old-fashioned "hello".
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons on letter writing, pupils learn the parts of a letter: address, date, salutation ("Dear Sir or Madam"), body, and sign-off ("Yours faithfully"). In stories, knights and courtiers bow in salutation. In Charlotte's Web, the spider Charlotte greets Wilbur with "Salutations!".
examples from the lessons: Start your letter with a salutation such as "Dear Aunt Jo,". | He raised his hat in salutation. | "Salutations!" said Charlotte the spider to Wilbur. | The salutation in a formal letter is often "Dear Sir or Madam". | Underline the salutation in this letter. | A wave is a friendly salutation. | The knights bowed to the king in salutation.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: salutations. Formal word; in daily talk say "greeting". In a letter, if the salutation is "Dear Sir or Madam", the sign-off is "Yours faithfully" (UK); if a name, "Yours sincerely". Related: salute.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Sarcastically means saying something in a mocking way, where you say the opposite of what you mean in order to tease or hurt, like saying "Oh, great!" when something bad happens.
its sense in the lessons: In English reading, "she said sarcastically" tells the reader not to take the words literally; the speaker means the opposite. Sarcasm is a kind of irony, often shown by tone of voice. In lessons on kindness, sarcasm can hurt feelings, and it is easy to misunderstand in texts and messages.
examples from the lessons: Oh, brilliant, he said sarcastically, as the rain started. | "Thanks a lot," she said sarcastically when her brother ate the last biscuit. | He clapped sarcastically when I dropped the ball. | "What a lovely surprise," Mum said sarcastically, looking at the muddy floor. | Don't speak sarcastically to your teacher. | She rolled her eyes and answered sarcastically. | Read the line sarcastically and the meaning changes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: sarcastic + -ally (not -ly): sarcastically. Noun: sarcasm. Sarcastic words mean the opposite of what they say, so look at the tone and the situation. Sarcasm is hard to spot in writing, which causes arguments online.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (abbreviation) SARS stands for Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome, a serious lung illness caused by a coronavirus that spread to several countries in 2002–2003. 2) (science) SARS-CoV-2 is the name of the virus that causes COVID-19. 3) (abbreviation) In some places SAR or SARs can mean other things, such as Hong Kong and Macau's status as Special Administrative Regions of China.
its sense in the lessons: In science and health lessons, SARS is an example of how new viruses can jump from animals to people and how hand-washing, masks and quarantine help stop spread. The virus that caused the COVID-19 pandemic was named SARS-CoV-2 because it is related. "Sars" written in lower case is just the abbreviation.
examples from the lessons: SARS was a dangerous illness that spread in 2003. | The SARS virus attacked people's lungs. | The virus that causes COVID-19 is called SARS-CoV-2. | Doctors stopped SARS spreading with careful hygiene and quarantine. | SARS is short for Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome. | Scientists think SARS came from animals. | Hand-washing helps protect against viruses like SARS.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually written in capitals: SARS. Say "sarz". It is an abbreviation, not an ordinary English word. SARS (2003) and COVID-19 are different illnesses caused by related viruses.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To satisfy someone is to make them pleased or content because they got what they wanted or needed. 2) To satisfy hunger or thirst is to make it go away. 3) To satisfy a rule, need or condition is to meet it. 4) (maths) A number satisfies an equation if it makes the equation true. 5) (formal) To satisfy yourself that something is true is to make sure of it.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, "find the value of x that satisfies x + 3 = 7" means find the number that makes it true (x = 4). In everyday life, a good meal satisfies hunger; a good answer satisfies a curious friend. In stories, "curiosity was satisfied" means the character finally found out. Phrases: satisfy your curiosity, satisfy the rules.
examples from the lessons: This sandwich will satisfy your hunger until tea. | Nothing seemed to satisfy the grumpy king. | The number 4 satisfies the equation x + 3 = 7. | Your project must satisfy all the rules on the sheet. | She opened the box to satisfy her curiosity. | A cold drink satisfied my thirst. | The teacher was satisfied with our work. | Which numbers satisfy "greater than 5 and less than 9"?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: satisfies, satisfied (y → i). Adjectives: satisfied (how you feel), satisfying (what makes you feel that). In maths, "satisfies" = "makes true" or "meets the condition".

part of speech: noun (a saxophone, saxophones); short form sax
meaning for a pupil: 1) A saxophone is a musical instrument made of brass, shaped like a curved J, played by blowing into a mouthpiece with a reed and pressing keys.
its sense in the lessons: In music lessons the saxophone is in the woodwind family, even though it is made of metal, because the sound is made by a wooden reed. It was invented by Adolphe Sax in Belgium in the 1840s. It is famous in jazz, pop and school bands. Kinds: soprano, alto, tenor and baritone saxophone.
examples from the lessons: My sister plays the saxophone in the school band. | The saxophone was invented by Adolphe Sax. | A jazz player played a cool tune on his sax. | The saxophone is part of the woodwind family. | The alto saxophone is a good size for children to learn. | You need a reed in the mouthpiece to play the saxophone. | The baritone saxophone makes a deep, low sound.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: saxophones. Short form: sax. A player is a saxophonist. Trap: it is metal but counts as woodwind because of the reed. Spelling: -phone, like telephone (phone = sound).

part of speech: noun (a scaffold, scaffolds); verb (scaffold, scaffolds, scaffolded, scaffolding)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A scaffold is a framework of metal poles and planks put up around a building so workers can stand on it while building or repairing; the whole structure is usually called scaffolding. 2) (history) A scaffold was a raised wooden platform where criminals were executed in public. 3) (school) To scaffold learning is to give support step by step, then take it away as the learner gets better.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and safety, scaffolding on buildings is dangerous to climb — keep away. In history lessons, people like Anne Boleyn and Charles I died on the scaffold. In school, teachers "scaffold" tasks with hints, word banks and examples; the support is removed once you can do it alone.
examples from the lessons: Builders put up a scaffold around the church tower. | Never climb on scaffolding; it is very dangerous. | King Charles I was executed on a scaffold in 1649. | The teacher scaffolded the story-writing task with a planning sheet. | Workers stood on the scaffold to paint the windows. | The scaffold was taken down when the roof was finished. | Watch out for poles sticking out from the scaffolding.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: double f. "Scaffolding" (uncountable) is the usual word for the poles and planks; "a scaffold" can mean the same or the execution platform. Do not confuse with "scaffold" in learning, which means support.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A scimitar is a sword with a curved blade that gets wider towards the end, used in the past in the Middle East, Persia, North Africa and Central Asia.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons and stories about the Crusades, Ottoman Turks or tales like the Arabian Nights, scimitars are the curved swords of warriors. It tells the reader about a setting in the past. Curved blades were good for slashing from horseback.
examples from the lessons: The warrior raised his shining scimitar. | A scimitar has a curved blade. | Pictures in the old book showed guards with scimitars. | The museum had a scimitar with a jewelled handle. | Riders on horseback used scimitars to slash. | In the story, the genie held a golden scimitar. | Swords and scimitars must never be played with; real blades are dangerous.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say "SIM-i-tar" — the c is silent. Countable: scimitars. Myth trap: stories often show scimitars as huge and wide, but real ones were usually slim and light.

part of speech: noun (a Scot, Scots); related: Scots, Scottish, Scotch; phrase: scot-free
meaning for a pupil: 1) A Scot is a person from Scotland. 2) (history) The Scots were a people from Ireland who settled in western Scotland about 1,500 years ago and gave Scotland its name. 3) "Scot-free" means without being punished or harmed; the old word "scot" meant a tax or payment.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and history lessons on the UK, a Scot is someone from Scotland, one of the four nations of the UK. Famous Scots include Robert the Bruce and Alexander Graham Bell. The everyday phrase "get off scot-free" has nothing to do with Scotland; it comes from not paying the "scot" tax.
examples from the lessons: My uncle is a Scot from Glasgow. | The Scots won the battle of Bannockburn in 1314. | Mary Queen of Scots was a famous ruler. | The thief got off scot-free because nobody saw him. | A Scot invented the telephone: Alexander Graham Bell. | Many Scots wear a kilt at weddings. | The Scots were a people who came from Ireland long ago.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital S for the person: a Scot, the Scots. Adjective for things from Scotland: Scottish. "Scotch" is used for whisky and some foods (Scotch egg); many Scots dislike being called "Scotch". "Scots" is also the name of a language spoken in Scotland. "Scot-free" is not about Scotland.

part of speech: verb (secrete, secretes, secreted, secreting); noun secretion
meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) To secrete is to make and give out a liquid or substance from a part of a plant or animal body: glands secrete sweat, tears and saliva. 2) (formal) To secrete something can also mean to hide it secretly.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, the stomach secretes acid, the salivary glands secrete saliva, the skin secretes sweat, bees secrete wax and some frogs secrete poison from their skin. In old stories, a character may secrete a letter in a drawer, meaning hide it.
examples from the lessons: Your mouth secretes saliva when you smell food. | Bees secrete wax to build their honeycomb. | Some frogs secrete poison through their skin. | The stomach secretes acid to digest food. | Sweat glands secrete sweat to cool you down. | Snails secrete slime so they can slide along. | (formal) She secreted the key inside her shoe.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say "si-KREET". Related to "secret" (the hiding sense) but the science sense means give out. Noun: secretion. Do not confuse with "excrete" (get rid of waste).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Sensory means to do with the senses — sight, hearing, touch, taste and smell. 2) A sensory room, toy or garden is made to let people enjoy or calm themselves through the senses.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, sensory organs (eyes, ears, nose, tongue, skin) collect information and sensory nerves carry it to the brain. In school life, sensory play (sand, water, slime) helps young children learn, and sensory rooms help some pupils, including autistic children, feel calm. "Sensory overload" means too much noise, light or touch at once.
examples from the lessons: Our eyes and ears are sensory organs. | The school has a sensory garden full of smelly herbs. | Little children love sensory play with sand and water. | Loud music can cause sensory overload. | Sensory nerves send messages to the brain. | The sensory room has soft lights and calm music. | Writers use sensory details so readers can see, hear and smell the scene.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Only an adjective: sensory organs (not "a sensory"). Related: sense, sensor. Not the same as "sensitive". In writing lessons, "sensory language" means words for the five senses.

part of speech: noun (a sett, setts); also spelt set
meaning for a pupil: 1) A sett is the home of a badger: a set of underground tunnels and rooms dug into the earth. 2) A sett is also a rectangular stone block used to pave old streets (often wrongly called cobbles).
its sense in the lessons: In nature lessons in the UK and Ireland, badger setts are found in woods and hedges, with several entrances and big piles of dug earth; badgers and their setts are protected by law, so you must not disturb them. In old towns, roads made of setts are bumpy to ride a bike on.
examples from the lessons: Badgers live in an underground sett. | We saw a badger come out of its sett at dusk. | The sett had five holes and big piles of earth. | It is against the law to damage a badger sett. | The old high street is paved with granite setts. | Bikes rattle over the stone setts. | Some setts are used by badgers for hundreds of years.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelt with double t to tell it apart from "set". It sounds the same as "set". Countable: setts. A fox's home is an earth or den; a rabbit's is a burrow or warren.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Shaggy means having long, thick, untidy hair or fur. 2) Shaggy can describe a carpet, rug or plant with long, rough threads or leaves. 3) "A shaggy dog story" is a long joke or story with a silly or pointless ending.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, a shaggy dog, pony or monster is described as hairy and scruffy, often friendly. Shaggy is also the name of a character in Scooby-Doo. In science, shaggy coats keep animals like yaks and musk oxen warm in cold places.
examples from the lessons: A big shaggy dog bounded up to us. | The Highland cow has a shaggy coat. | His hair was long and shaggy after the summer. | We lay on the shaggy rug by the fire. | Yaks have shaggy fur to keep warm in the mountains. | The shaggy monster turned out to be a friendly giant. | Grandpa told a shaggy dog story with a silly ending.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative: shaggier, shaggiest (y → i). Spelling: double g. Opposite: smooth, sleek.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (religion) Shinto is the traditional religion of Japan, in which people honour spirits called kami that are believed to live in nature (mountains, trees, rivers), in places and in ancestors.
its sense in the lessons: In religion lessons, Shinto is studied alongside Buddhism, as many Japanese people follow both. Followers visit Shinto shrines, marked by a red gate called a torii, to pray and ask for luck, washing their hands and mouth first. Festivals (matsuri) and New Year visits are important. Shinto followers believe the kami should be respected.
examples from the lessons: Shinto is the oldest religion of Japan. | A red torii gate marks the entrance to a Shinto shrine. | Shinto followers believe in spirits called kami. | People wash their hands before praying at a Shinto shrine. | Many Japanese families celebrate both Shinto and Buddhist festivals. | Mount Fuji is a sacred place in Shinto. | We learnt about Shinto in our world religions topic.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital S: Shinto. Means "the way of the gods" in Japanese. Not a person's word: someone who follows it is a Shinto follower or practitioner. Say beliefs as "followers believe".

part of speech: verb form (past tense and past participle of shred: shred, shreds, shredded, shredding); adjective (shredded cheese)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Shredded means torn or cut into thin strips or small pieces. 2) As an adjective in cooking: shredded cheese, lettuce, carrot or chicken is cut or grated into thin strips. 3) Paper that is shredded has been cut up by a machine so no one can read it. 4) (slang) "Shredded" can mean having very visible muscles; in skateboarding or guitar "shredded" means played or rode brilliantly.
its sense in the lessons: In cooking lessons, recipes use shredded vegetables and cheese. In online safety, shredding old letters with names and bank details stops identity theft. In stories, a coat or a sail is shredded by a storm or an animal's claws. "Shredded Wheat" is a cereal.
examples from the lessons: Sprinkle the shredded cheese on the pizza. | The puppy shredded my homework! | Mum shredded old bank letters so no one could steal her details. | The storm shredded the tent. | Add shredded carrot to the salad. | The cat shredded the arm of the sofa with its claws. | (slang) After a year at the gym, he's totally shredded.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double d: shred → shredded, shredding. "Shredded" (thin strips) differs from "grated" (rubbed on a grater), though they often mean the same in recipes. The muscle sense is slang.

part of speech: verb form (present participle of shut: shut, shuts, shut, shutting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Shutting is closing something, like a door, window, lid or your eyes. 2) Shutting can mean a shop, school or business closing for the day or for ever. 3) Phrases: shutting down (switching off a computer or closing a factory), shutting up (rude: telling someone to stop talking), shutting out (keeping someone or something out).
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, shops are shutting at 5 o'clock; computers need shutting down properly. In safety, shutting doors can slow a fire from spreading. In stories, "shutting someone out" shows a character excluding others or hiding feelings. "Shut up" is rude; "please be quiet" is polite.
examples from the lessons: Please stop shutting the door so loudly. | The shop is shutting in ten minutes. | She was shutting her eyes tight during the scary bit. | Our library is shutting down for repairs. | Remember shutting the gate so the dog can't get out. | He kept shutting his friends out when he was sad. | Shutting doors at night helps stop fire spreading.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double t: shut → shutting. Past tense and past participle are both "shut" (not "shutted"). "Shut up" is rude; say "please be quiet". In the UK "shut" for shops is common; "closed" is more formal.

part of speech: adjective (skilful, more skilful, most skilful; US spelling skillful); adverb skilfully
meaning for a pupil: 1) Skilful means very good at doing something because of practice and ability. 2) Something done in a skilful way is done with great skill.
its sense in the lessons: In sport, art, music and DT, a skilful player, painter or builder does things well and neatly. School reports may praise skilful work. In stories, a skilful thief or sailor is one with great ability. Being skilful usually comes from practice, not just talent.
examples from the lessons: She is a skilful footballer who can dribble past anyone. | The skilful potter made a perfect bowl. | It took skilful hands to fix the old clock. | He was a skilful liar, but he got caught in the end. | The skilful pilot landed the plane in the storm. | With practice you can become a skilful juggler. | She made a skilful drawing of a horse.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK, Ireland, Australia, NZ: skilful (one l in the middle); USA: skillful (two l's); Canada often uses skillful. Noun: skill. Adverb: skilfully (UK) / skillfully (US).

part of speech: adjective (slack, slacker, slackest); noun (slack — uncountable); verb (slack, slacks, slacked, slacking; slack off); plural noun slacks (trousers)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Slack means loose, not pulled tight: a slack rope. 2) Slack means not busy: business is slack in winter. 3) (informal) Slack means lazy or careless: slack work. 4) To slack or slack off is to work less hard than you should. 5) (informal) "Cut someone some slack" means be less strict and more forgiving with them. 6) (UK slang) "That's slack" can mean unfair or mean. 7) Slacks are casual trousers.
its sense in the lessons: In science and PE, a rope or string that is slack hangs loose, while a taut one is tight; a slack tightrope wobbles. In school, a teacher may say "Don't slack off before the test." In everyday talk, "Give him some slack, he's new" asks for patience. Slack is also the name of a messaging app.
examples from the lessons: The rope went slack when he let go. | Pull the washing line tight so it isn't slack. | Business at the ice-cream van is slack in winter. | Stop slacking and finish your homework! | Cut her some slack — she's had a hard week. | (UK slang) "You ate all the sweets? That's slack!" | Dad wore smart slacks to the party. | The coach told us not to slack off in training.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite of slack (loose) is taut or tight. Person who slacks: a slacker. "Slacks" (trousers) is always plural. "Slack" for unfair is mild slang in the UK and Ireland.

part of speech: verb (slouch, slouches, slouched, slouching); noun (a slouch, slouches)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To slouch is to sit, stand or walk with your shoulders rounded and your head hanging forward, in a lazy, droopy way. 2) A slouch is that droopy way of sitting or standing. 3) (informal) "No slouch" means very good at something: she's no slouch at maths.
its sense in the lessons: In health and PE lessons, slouching at a desk or over a phone is bad posture and can make your back ache; sit up straight with your back supported. In stories, a slouching character may be bored, tired, sad or sulky. A slouch hat is a soft hat with a wide brim, famous in Australian army uniform.
examples from the lessons: Don't slouch at your desk; sit up straight. | He slouched off to his room in a huff. | The teenager slouched on the sofa looking at his phone. | Slouching over a screen can give you a sore neck. | She's no slouch on the football pitch. | The tired boy walked with a slouch. | Australian soldiers wore slouch hats.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural noun and verb: slouches. "No slouch" is a compliment, not an insult. Rhymes with "couch".

part of speech: verb form (past tense and past participle of slur: slur, slurs, slurred, slurring); adjective (slurred speech)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Slurred speech is speech where the words run into each other and are hard to understand. 2) (music) Slurred notes are played smoothly joined together, shown by a curved line called a slur. 3) To have slurred someone can mean to have insulted them unfairly (a slur is an insult).
its sense in the lessons: In health and safety lessons, suddenly slurred speech can be a warning sign of a stroke (with a drooping face and a weak arm — call the emergency number at once), or of being very tired, drunk or ill. In music lessons, slurred notes are played legato. In stories, slurred words show a character is sleepy, ill or drunk.
examples from the lessons: His speech was slurred because he was so sleepy. | Slurred speech can be a sign of a stroke, so call an ambulance. | The drunk man slurred his words. | Play these two notes slurred, without a gap. | She slurred "goodnight" as she fell asleep. | The curved line means the notes are slurred. | After the dentist's injection, my words were slurred for an hour.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double r: slur → slurred, slurring. Emergency numbers: 999 (UK, Ireland also 112), 911 (USA, Canada), 000 (Australia), 111 (New Zealand). A "slur" (noun) can also be a nasty insult about a group of people.

part of speech: noun (slush — uncountable); adjective slushy; noun (a slushie / slushy — a drink)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Slush is snow that has partly melted and turned into wet, dirty, half-frozen mush on the ground. 2) A slush or slushie is a drink of flavoured crushed ice. 3) (informal) Slush can also mean silly, over-sweet, soppy talk or writing about love.
its sense in the lessons: In weather and science lessons, slush forms when snow starts to melt, showing change of state from solid to liquid; it is slippery and splashes. In everyday life, children buy fruit slushies in summer. A "slush fund" (money) is a hidden pot of money, often for dishonest use.
examples from the lessons: The snow turned to grey slush by lunchtime. | The bus splashed slush all over my coat. | Walk carefully — the slush is slippery. | I had a blue raspberry slush at the cinema. | The film was full of romantic slush. | Melting snow becomes slush before it becomes water. | Our boots got soaked in the slush.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: some slush, not a slush (except the drink: a slush, a slushie). Adjective: slushy. Slush is a mix of solid ice and liquid water.

part of speech: noun (a snipe, snipe or snipes); verb (snipe, snipes, sniped, sniping)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A snipe is a wading bird with a very long straight beak that lives in marshes and wet fields. 2) To snipe is to shoot at people from a hidden place far away. 3) (informal) To snipe at someone is to make nasty, sly little criticisms of them. 4) (informal) To snipe in an online auction or game is to win at the last second.
its sense in the lessons: In nature lessons, snipe probe mud with their long beaks for worms and are hard to spot. The word "sniper" comes from hunting snipe, which were so quick that only good shooters could hit them. In stories and news, "sniping" between people means unkind remarks. A "snipe hunt" is a joke in North American camps where someone is sent looking for an imaginary animal.
examples from the lessons: A snipe pushed its long beak into the mud. | Snipe are well camouflaged in the marsh grass. | The two brothers kept sniping at each other all through dinner. | Soldiers were sniped at from the rooftops. | She sniped the last item in the online auction. | The older campers sent us on a snipe hunt as a joke. | Stop sniping and say what you really think.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The bird's plural is often the same: snipe. Person who shoots: a sniper. The "sly comment" sense is informal and is usually "snipe at someone".

part of speech: noun (Sol — the Sun; sol — music note; a sol — a Mars day; sol — chemistry; sol — money of Peru); also French and Spanish word
meaning for a pupil: 1) (space) Sol is a name for our Sun, from Latin. 2) (space) A sol is one day on Mars, about 24 hours 40 minutes. 3) (music) Sol (or so, soh) is the fifth note of the do-re-mi scale. 4) (science) A sol is a liquid with tiny solid bits spread through it (a kind of colloid). 5) The sol is the money of Peru. 6) (French) "Sol" means floor or ground; (Spanish, Portuguese) "sol" means sun — not English words.
its sense in the lessons: In space lessons, scientists number Mars rover days in sols ("on sol 100 the rover found a rock"); science fiction calls our Sun "Sol". In music, do-re-mi-fa-sol-la-ti-do is sung in The Sound of Music ("so, a needle pulling thread"). In French lessons, "par terre" or "sur le sol" means on the ground.
examples from the lessons: The Mars rover took a photo on its 200th sol. | A sol on Mars is about 40 minutes longer than an Earth day. | Sol is the Latin name for the Sun. | Sing do, re, mi, fa, sol, la, ti, do. | In science fiction, Earth's sun is called Sol. | The price was ten soles in a market in Lima. | (French) "Le sol" means the ground or the floor. | (Spanish) "Hace sol" means "it is sunny".
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital S for the Sun's name (Sol). The music note is also spelt "so" or "soh". Plural of the Peruvian money: soles. In French "sol" is not the sun (that is "soleil"). Do not confuse with "soul" or "sole".

meaning for a pupil: 1) A sortie is a sudden attack made by soldiers rushing out from a place that is surrounded by enemies. 2) A sortie is also one flight by a military aircraft on a mission. 3) (informal, humorous) A sortie can mean a short trip out somewhere, like a sortie to the shops.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, defenders of a castle under siege made sorties to attack the besiegers. In news and stories about the Battle of Britain or air forces, pilots flew many sorties a day. In everyday humorous talk, a sortie is a quick outing. The word is French for "going out" (sortie = exit in French).
examples from the lessons: The defenders made a sortie from the castle at night. | The Spitfire pilots flew three sorties that day. | Each sortie lasted about an hour. | Mum made a quick sortie to the corner shop for milk. | The knights' sortie surprised the enemy camp. | (French) In France, "Sortie" on a sign means "Exit". | The plane returned safely from its sortie.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say "SOR-tee". Countable: sorties. It comes from French "sortir", to go out; in French, "sortie" on signs means exit — a false friend for English speakers who know only the military sense.

part of speech: noun (a soufflé, soufflés; also written souffle)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (cooking) A soufflé is a light, fluffy baked dish made with beaten egg whites, which puffs up high in the oven; it can be savoury (cheese) or sweet (chocolate, lemon). 2) The word is French and means "puffed up" or "breathed".
its sense in the lessons: In cooking lessons, soufflés teach how air beaten into egg whites expands when heated, so the dish rises — a bit of science. Soufflés are famous for being tricky: they collapse quickly if you open the oven or wait too long. In stories and TV cookery shows, a sinking soufflé is a classic disaster.
examples from the lessons: The cheese soufflé rose high above the dish. | Don't open the oven door or the soufflé will sink! | We had a chocolate soufflé for pudding. | A soufflé is made with whipped egg whites. | Serve the soufflé straight away before it falls. | The chef's soufflé was as light as a cloud. | Hot air in the egg bubbles makes a soufflé puff up.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Written with an accent in French and in careful English: soufflé; "souffle" without the accent is common in plain text. Say "SOO-flay". Countable: soufflés. A different medical word "souffle" (a soft heart sound) exists but is rare.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A speller is a person who spells words, described as good or bad at it: she's a good speller. 2) (US, Canada) A speller is also a school book of spelling lists and exercises. 3) A spell-checker on a computer is sometimes called a speller.
its sense in the lessons: In school life, spelling tests and spelling bees show who is a strong speller; contestants in a spelling bee are called spellers. In US schools pupils may have a speller workbook. Being a poor speller has nothing to do with being clever — many smart people find spelling hard, including some with dyslexia.
examples from the lessons: My sister is a brilliant speller. | I'm a terrible speller, so I check my work carefully. | Fifty spellers took part in the spelling bee. | Open your spellers to page 12. | The best speller in the class won a dictionary. | The speller on my laptop missed my mistake. | Good spellers read a lot.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: spellers. "Speller" is the person; "spelling" is the activity. Being a weak speller is not the same as being unintelligent.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Spiny means covered with spines — sharp, stiff points like thorns or prickles.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on adaptations, spiny animals (hedgehogs, porcupines, echidnas, sea urchins, spiny lobsters) and spiny plants (cactuses, holly) use spines for protection from predators. The spiny anteater is another name for the echidna of Australia and New Guinea. Safety: do not touch spiny sea creatures on the beach.
examples from the lessons: A hedgehog has a spiny back. | The echidna, or spiny anteater, lives in Australia. | Cactuses have spiny stems to stop animals eating them. | Don't step on that spiny sea urchin. | The spiny fish puffed itself up. | Holly leaves are spiny at the edges. | Spiny lobsters have no big claws, just spiky shells.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spine (sharp point) + -y = spiny (drop the e). Comparative: spinier. Do not confuse with "spine" meaning backbone; spiny means prickly, not having a backbone.

part of speech: verb form (present participle of spiral: spiral, spirals, spiralled, spiralling; US spiraled, spiraling); adjective (spiralling costs)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Spiralling means moving in a spiral, going round and round in a curve that gets wider or narrower, often while going up or down. 2) Spiralling prices or problems are rising quickly and getting out of control. 3) Spiralling down (or into something) means getting worse and worse.
its sense in the lessons: In science and nature, a sycamore seed comes spiralling down, and water goes spiralling down the plughole. In money and news, "spiralling costs" or "spiralling prices" mean prices are going up fast. In lessons on feelings, worries can be spiralling, getting bigger the more you think about them; talking to someone helps stop them.
examples from the lessons: The leaf came spiralling down from the tree. | The eagle was spiralling high above the hills. | Water went spiralling down the drain. | Spiralling food prices make life hard for families. | His worries were spiralling out of control. | The plane was spiralling towards the ground. | The staircase went spiralling up the lighthouse.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK, Ireland, Australia, NZ: spiralling (double l); USA: spiraling (one l); Canada uses both. A spiral is a curve going round a centre, like a snail shell or a spring.

part of speech: noun (a spook, spooks); verb (spook, spooks, spooked, spooking); adjective spooky
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) A spook is a ghost. 2) To spook someone or an animal is to frighten or startle them suddenly. 3) (informal, US) A spook is a spy. 4) (offensive) "Spook" has also been used as a nasty insult for Black people; it should not be used about people.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and at Halloween, spooks and spooky houses are fun scary things. In nature and farm life, a sudden noise can spook a horse, which may bolt; that is a safety point around horses. In spy stories, spooks are secret agents.
examples from the lessons: The old house was said to be full of spooks. | The loud bang spooked the horse and it ran off. | Don't creep up behind me — you spooked me! | We dressed up as spooks for Halloween. | The film was about spooks working for the secret service. | The cat was spooked by its own reflection. | Walk calmly near horses so you don't spook them.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: spooky ("a spooky story"). Usually informal. The insult sense is offensive and must never be used. "Spooked" means suddenly frightened.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A spork is a plastic or metal eating tool that is a spoon and a fork in one: a spoon shape with short prongs at the tip.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, sporks come with take-away food, lunch boxes and camping kits. The word is a blend (portmanteau) of "spoon" and "fork", like "brunch" from breakfast and lunch — useful for English lessons on how words are made. In the Toy Story 4 film, the character Forky is made from a spork.
examples from the lessons: I ate my salad with a plastic spork. | Camping kits often include a spork. | A spork is a spoon and a fork joined together. | "Spork" is made by blending the words "spoon" and "fork". | The spork wasn't good for soup — the soup ran through the gaps. | Forky in Toy Story 4 is made from a spork. | Bring a reusable spork instead of a plastic one.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: sporks. A blend word (spoon + fork), like smog (smoke + fog) and brunch. There is also a "splayd" in Australia: a spoon, fork and knife in one.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A spotter is a person who watches out for something, especially as a hobby: a train spotter, a bird spotter, a plane spotter. 2) (sport) In gym and weightlifting, a spotter stands by to catch you or help if you lose control. 3) A spotter is someone who watches for danger or for an enemy and reports it, like a fire spotter or an aircraft spotter in wartime.
its sense in the lessons: In PE, gymnastics and trampolining, spotters keep others safe; that is a safety rule. Train spotters in the UK note down train numbers as a hobby. In history lessons, wartime spotters watched the sky for enemy planes. In storm chasing, weather spotters report tornadoes and storms.
examples from the lessons: Grandpa has been a train spotter since he was a boy. | A spotter stood beside the trampoline. | Never lift heavy weights without a spotter. | Bird spotters waited quietly in the hide. | In the war, spotters on rooftops watched for enemy planes. | Weather spotters reported the tornado. | The talent spotter asked the girl to join the football academy.
