note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: spotters. "Trainspotter" is sometimes used in the UK as a mild joke for someone who loves collecting small facts. Related verb: spot (to notice).

part of speech: verb (squabble, squabbles, squabbled, squabbling); noun (a squabble, squabbles)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To squabble is to argue noisily about something small and unimportant. 2) A squabble is a small, silly argument.
its sense in the lessons: In family life and stories, siblings squabble over the TV remote, the front seat or the last biscuit. Lessons on friends and families teach how to stop squabbling: take turns, share, listen. In the news, politicians' squabbles are minor quarrels. Birds such as seagulls squabble over food.
examples from the lessons: My brother and I squabbled over the last slice of pizza. | Stop squabbling and take turns! | The twins had a squabble about whose turn it was. | Seagulls squabbled over a chip on the beach. | The kids squabbled all the way to the seaside. | It was just a little squabble; they were friends again by lunchtime. | The politicians squabbled about the new road.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double b: squabble. Drop the e before -ing: squabbling. A squabble is smaller and sillier than a fight or a quarrel.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Squashy means soft and easy to press or squeeze out of shape. 2) Fruit that is squashy is too soft and a bit squashed or overripe.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on materials, squashy materials (sponge, marshmallow, foam) change shape when you press them and may spring back. In everyday life, squashy sofas and cushions are comfy; squashy tomatoes and bananas may be past their best. It is an informal, mainly British word.
examples from the lessons: She sank into the big squashy sofa. | The banana at the bottom of my bag was squashy. | Marshmallows are soft and squashy. | A squashy ball is good for squeezing when you're stressed. | Sort the materials into hard and squashy. | These tomatoes are too squashy to slice. | The puppy loves its squashy toy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal, more common in the UK, Australia and NZ; Americans often say "squishy". Squashy (soft) is different from "squash" the drink (UK) or the vegetable or the sport.

meaning for a pupil: 1) "Sss" is the hissing sound of a snake, written down. 2) It can be the sound of air or steam escaping, or of something sizzling. 3) In phonics, /s/ or "sss" is how teachers say the sound of the letter s.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and comics, "Sss!" shows a snake hissing, which tells the reader it may be angry or warning. In phonics lessons, children learn to say "sss" for s, not "ess". It is also similar to "shh" or "psst", used to get attention quietly. It is a sound, not a real word.
examples from the lessons: Sssss! hissed the snake from behind the rock. | The tyre went "sss" as the air came out. | Sausages went "sss" in the hot pan. | In phonics, the letter s says "sss", like a snake. | "Sss — keep your voice down!" whispered my friend. | The kettle went "sssss" before it boiled. | Draw a snake and write "sss" in a speech bubble.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Not a dictionary word but a written sound (onomatopoeia). You can add more s's to make the sound longer. Different from "shh" (be quiet) and "psst" (to catch someone's attention).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A stanza is a group of lines in a poem, set apart from the other groups by a space, like a paragraph in a story; it is often called a verse.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons on poetry, pupils count stanzas, find the rhyme scheme of each stanza and describe its pattern: a couplet (2 lines), tercet (3), quatrain (4). Answering questions like "In the second stanza, how does the poet feel?" is common in reading tests. In songs, a stanza is a verse, and the repeated part is the chorus.
examples from the lessons: This poem has four stanzas. | Each stanza has four lines that rhyme. | Read the first stanza aloud. | In the last stanza, the poet feels hopeful. | Write a stanza about your favourite season. | A stanza is like a paragraph in a poem. | The second stanza describes the sea at night.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: stanzas. "Verse" can mean stanza, but "verse" also means poetry in general, and in hymns and the Bible a verse is a numbered line. From Italian, meaning "room" or "stopping place".

part of speech: noun (a stencil, stencils); verb (stencil, stencils, stencilled, stencilling; US stenciled, stenciling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A stencil is a thin sheet of card, plastic or metal with shapes or letters cut out of it; you paint or colour through the holes to copy the shapes onto a surface underneath. 2) To stencil is to make a pattern or letters this way. 3) A stencil can also be the picture made using it.
its sense in the lessons: In art lessons, pupils use stencils to print patterns, letters and shapes neatly; street artists like Banksy are famous for stencil art. In history, cave people made hand stencils by blowing paint around their hands on cave walls, some of the oldest art we know. In maths, shape stencils help draw neat polygons and circles.
examples from the lessons: I used a star stencil to decorate my card. | Hold the stencil still and dab paint over it. | We stencilled our names on our school bags. | Banksy is famous for stencil graffiti. | Ancient hand stencils were found on cave walls. | The road workers stencilled "SLOW" on the road. | Use a shape stencil to draw a perfect hexagon.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK, Ireland, Australia, NZ: stencilled, stencilling (double l); USA: stenciled, stenciling. Countable noun: stencils. Not "stencel".

part of speech: noun (a strangler, stranglers); related: strangle, strangulation
meaning for a pupil: 1) A strangler is a person who kills or hurts someone by squeezing their throat so they cannot breathe; it is a word from crime news and stories. 2) (science) A strangler fig is a tropical plant that grows around a tree, wraps it in roots and can slowly kill it. 3) Weeds that wrap around and choke other plants are sometimes called stranglers.
its sense in the lessons: In nature lessons on rainforests, the strangler fig starts as a seed high in a tree, sends roots down to the ground and slowly surrounds its host. In crime news and detective stories, "the strangler" is a nickname for a violent criminal; that tells the reader the story is about serious crime. Safety: never put anything around anyone's neck, even in play.
examples from the lessons: The strangler fig wrapped its roots around the old tree. | In the rainforest, strangler figs can grow taller than their host trees. | The detective story was about the hunt for a strangler. | Bindweed is a strangler that chokes garden plants. | The police finally caught the strangler. | A strangler fig can leave a hollow tower of roots after the host tree dies. | Gardeners pull out stranglers like ivy and bindweed.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: stranglers. Verb: strangle. Do not mix up "strangler" with "stranger" (a person you do not know). Safety: games that squeeze the neck are very dangerous.

part of speech: noun (a strawman or straw man, strawmen / straw men); verb (strawman, strawmanning — informal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (logic) A strawman is an unfair trick in an argument: you change the other person's idea into a weaker or sillier version and then attack that instead of what they really said. 2) A straw man is also a figure made of straw, like a scarecrow or a dummy for practice. 3) (informal) A straw man can be a person used to hide who is really behind something.
its sense in the lessons: In lessons on logic, debating and checking the news, the strawman is a common "fallacy" (a mistake in reasoning) — to argue fairly, repeat the other person's real point first. Example: "I think we should have less homework." "So you think children shouldn't learn anything!" That reply is a strawman.
examples from the lessons: Saying I hate all vegetables because I don't like peas is a strawman. | "You want less homework, so you don't care about learning!" — that's a strawman argument. | Politicians sometimes attack a strawman instead of the real idea. | The scarecrow was a straw man stuffed with hay. | Don't strawman my point; listen to what I actually said. | Our debate coach taught us to spot strawman arguments. | Knights practised with their lances on a straw man.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Written as one word (strawman) or two (straw man); both are used. It is a fallacy, not just a disagreement: it means misrepresenting someone's view. The fair opposite is called "steelmanning" — stating the other person's view in its strongest form.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) Subduction is when one of the Earth's tectonic plates slides down underneath another plate and sinks into the hot mantle. 2) A subduction zone is the place where this happens.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and science lessons on plate tectonics, subduction explains volcanoes, deep ocean trenches and big earthquakes and tsunamis: the Pacific "Ring of Fire" around Japan, Chile, Alaska, New Zealand and the west coast of North America is full of subduction zones. The Mariana Trench, the deepest place in the ocean, formed by subduction.
examples from the lessons: Subduction happens when one plate sinks under another. | Japan has many earthquakes because of subduction. | The Mariana Trench was made by subduction. | Volcanoes often form above subduction zones. | The 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami was caused by an earthquake in a subduction zone. | Ocean plates are heavier, so they sink in subduction. | Draw a diagram of a subduction zone with arrows.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Verb: to subduct ("the plate is subducted"). "Sub-" means under. Usually the heavier ocean plate sinks under a lighter continental plate.

part of speech: verb (submerge, submerges, submerged, submerging); adjective submerged
meaning for a pupil: 1) To submerge is to go under water, or to put something completely under water or another liquid. 2) Submerged means covered by water. 3) To be submerged in work or noise means to be completely surrounded or overwhelmed by it.
its sense in the lessons: In science, submarines submerge by filling tanks with water and surface by blowing it out — a lesson on floating and sinking. In geography, floods submerge roads and fields. In safety lessons: never drive or walk through submerged roads — water can be deeper and faster than it looks. In maths and science, you find the volume of an object by submerging it and measuring the rise in water.
examples from the lessons: The submarine began to submerge. | Submerge the egg in water to see if it floats. | Heavy rain submerged the football pitch. | The car was stuck on a submerged road. | Never walk through floodwater that has submerged the path. | Drop the stone in and measure how much the water rises when it is submerged. | She was submerged in homework all weekend.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: drop the e before -ing (submerging). "Sub-" means under. Opposite: surface, emerge. Volume trick: the rise in water = the volume of the submerged object.

part of speech: verb form (present participle of subordinate: subordinate, subordinates, subordinated, subordinating); adjective (subordinating conjunction)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (grammar) A subordinating conjunction is a joining word such as because, when, if, although, while, since, before or until that starts a subordinate clause — a part of a sentence that cannot stand alone. 2) (formal) Subordinating something means treating it as less important than something else.
its sense in the lessons: In English grammar lessons (and UK SATs), pupils learn subordinating conjunctions to write complex sentences: "I stayed inside because it was raining." The memory trick "I SAW A WABUB" (if, since, as, when, although, while, after, before, until, because) helps. Coordinating conjunctions (and, but, or) join equal parts instead.
examples from the lessons: Because is a subordinating conjunction. | Underline the subordinating conjunction: "We went home when the bell rang." | "Although" is a subordinating conjunction that shows contrast. | Use a subordinating conjunction to join the two sentences. | Subordinating conjunctions start subordinate clauses. | (formal) She was subordinating her own wishes to the needs of the team. | Start your sentence with a subordinating conjunction, like "If it snows, ...".
note for the reader of a maths problem: Subordinating ≠ coordinating: coordinating conjunctions (FANBOYS: for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so) join equal parts; subordinating ones make one part depend on another. A comma goes after the subordinate clause when it comes first: "When it rains, we stay in."

meaning for a pupil: 1) Subterranean means underground, below the surface of the earth. 2) (formal) It can also mean hidden or secret.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography lessons, subterranean rivers, caves, tunnels and animals (moles, some insects, blind cave fish) live or flow underground. In stories, subterranean worlds and passages add mystery. "Sub-" means under and "terra" means earth, like in "terrain" and "territory".
examples from the lessons: Moles live in subterranean tunnels. | The cave had a subterranean river. | Explorers found a subterranean city in Turkey. | Some ants build huge subterranean nests. | The London Underground is a subterranean railway. | Blind fish swim in subterranean lakes. | The story was set in a subterranean kingdom.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; in everyday talk say "underground". Say "sub-ter-RAY-nee-an". Latin roots: sub (under) + terra (earth).

part of speech: noun (a suffragist, suffragists); related: suffrage, suffragette
meaning for a pupil: 1) (history) A suffragist was a person who campaigned for the right to vote (suffrage), especially for women, using peaceful and lawful methods such as petitions, meetings and marches.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons in the UK, suffragists (led by Millicent Fawcett, NUWSS) used peaceful methods, while suffragettes (led by Emmeline Pankhurst, WSPU) also used direct action such as breaking windows. In the USA, suffragists like Susan B. Anthony and Elizabeth Cady Stanton campaigned for women's votes, won in 1920. New Zealand was the first self-governing country to give women the vote in national elections in 1893, after suffragist Kate Sheppard's petition.
examples from the lessons: Millicent Fawcett was a famous British suffragist. | The suffragists held peaceful marches and wrote petitions. | Kate Sheppard was a suffragist in New Zealand. | Women in the USA won the vote in 1920 after years of work by suffragists. | Suffragists believed women should be able to vote like men. | Some men were suffragists too. | Explain the difference between a suffragist and a suffragette.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: suffragist (peaceful campaigner, man or woman) vs suffragette (a word mainly for the British women of the WSPU who used more militant action). "Suffrage" means the right to vote; it has nothing to do with "suffer".

part of speech: noun (sulfur — uncountable; UK also sulphur); adjective sulfurous/sulphurous, sulfuric/sulphuric
meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) Sulfur is a chemical element, a yellow non-metal with the symbol S and atomic number 16. 2) When it burns or forms some compounds, it makes a smell like rotten eggs.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, sulfur is found near volcanoes and hot springs as yellow crystals; it is used to make sulfuric acid, matches, rubber and fertilisers. In the Bible, "fire and brimstone" — brimstone is an old word for sulfur — is used for God's punishment. The rotten-egg smell is actually from a sulfur compound, hydrogen sulfide.
examples from the lessons: Sulfur is a bright yellow element. | Yellow sulfur crystals form around volcanoes. | The hot spring smelt of sulfur, like rotten eggs. | Sulfur's chemical symbol is S. | Matches contain sulfur. | (Bible) "Brimstone" is an old name for sulfur. | Our bodies need a little sulfur, found in eggs and onions.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: "sulfur" is the scientific standard (IUPAC) and the US spelling; "sulphur" is the traditional British, Irish, Australian and NZ spelling, still common. Both are correct. Pure sulfur does not smell much; its compounds do.

part of speech: adjective (sulphuric; US and science standard: sulfuric)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) Sulphuric means containing or made from sulphur. 2) Sulphuric acid is a very strong, dangerous acid (H2SO4) used in car batteries, fertiliser making and industry.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, sulphuric acid is a classic example of a strong acid on the pH scale (pH about 1); it is corrosive and burns skin, so the hazard symbol must be respected and only teachers handle it. In geography, sulphuric acid in clouds causes acid rain; Venus has clouds of sulphuric acid.
examples from the lessons: Sulphuric acid can burn through cloth and skin. | Car batteries contain sulphuric acid. | Venus is covered in clouds of sulphuric acid. | Acid rain can contain sulphuric acid from factory smoke. | The bottle of sulphuric acid had a "corrosive" warning sign. | Only the teacher may handle sulphuric acid in the lab. | Sulphuric acid has the formula H2SO4.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: UK, Ireland, Australia, NZ: sulphuric; USA and international science: sulfuric. Say "sul-FURE-ic". Safety: never touch or mix acids without an adult; add acid to water, never water to acid.

part of speech: noun (a sultana, sultanas); proper noun use (Sultana — a title)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A sultana is a dried, light-golden seedless grape, like a raisin but paler and sweeter. 2) A sultana is the wife, mother or daughter of a sultan (a Muslim ruler), or a woman who is a sultan herself.
its sense in the lessons: In food lessons and baking, sultanas go into scones, flapjacks, fruit cake and cereal; a small box of sultanas is a common lunchbox snack in the UK, Australia and NZ. In the USA, sultanas are usually called "golden raisins". In history, sultanas lived in the courts of the Ottoman Empire and other sultanates.
examples from the lessons: I put sultanas in my porridge. | Gran's fruit scones are full of sultanas. | A small box of sultanas is a healthy snack. | In the USA, sultanas are called golden raisins. | The sultana lived in a beautiful palace. | Count the sultanas in each muffin. | Sultanas are dried grapes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: sultanas. Raisins are usually darker; currants are tiny dried grapes. Sultanas and raisins are bad for dogs — never feed them to pets.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To supersede something is to take its place because it is newer or better, so the old thing is no longer used.
its sense in the lessons: In history and science lessons, new inventions supersede old ones (cars superseded horses and carts; e-books are not superseding paper books entirely). In law and rules, a new rule supersedes the old one. In science, a new theory may supersede an old one when evidence changes.
examples from the lessons: Cars superseded horse-drawn carts. | The new timetable supersedes the old one. | Smartphones have superseded many cameras. | Electric lights superseded gas lamps. | Einstein's ideas did not throw out Newton's laws, but in some cases they superseded them. | The new rules supersede everything in last year's handbook. | Streaming has superseded DVDs for many families.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Famous spelling trap: supersede ends in -sede (not -cede like precede). Formal word; in everyday speech say "replace" or "take the place of".

meaning for a pupil: 1) Supplementation is adding something extra to make something complete or to make up for what is missing, especially adding vitamins or minerals to a diet.
its sense in the lessons: In health and science lessons, vitamin D supplementation is often advised in winter in the UK, Ireland and Canada when there is little sunshine; iron supplementation may be needed for some people. Doctors decide on supplementation; too much of some vitamins can harm you. In money or school, "supplementation" can mean extra funding or extra lessons.
examples from the lessons: Doctors recommend vitamin D supplementation in winter. | Iron supplementation helped her feel less tired. | Farmers use supplementation to feed their animals extra minerals. | Babies sometimes need vitamin supplementation. | Supplementation should only be done with a doctor's advice. | The school got some supplementation of its budget. | A balanced diet usually needs little supplementation.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Noun: a supplement (the thing added); verb: supplement; adjective: supplementary. Safety: never take vitamin pills or supplements without an adult; some, like iron, are dangerous in large amounts.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A supplier is a person or company that provides goods or services to other people or businesses, often regularly.
its sense in the lessons: In money and business lessons, a shop buys goods from a supplier and sells them to customers for more, which is how it makes a profit. In maths problems, a supplier's price per item is used to work out costs. Energy suppliers provide gas and electricity to homes.
examples from the lessons: The bakery gets its flour from a local supplier. | Our energy supplier sends a bill every month. | The shop changed suppliers to get cheaper prices. | A supplier sells 100 pencils for £5; how much is each pencil? | The school's food supplier delivers every morning. | Farmers are suppliers to supermarkets. | Good suppliers deliver on time.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: suppliers. Spelling: supply → supplier (y → i). Verb: supply. In maths, the shop's profit = selling price − the supplier's price.

part of speech: noun (a suture, sutures); verb (suture, sutures, sutured, suturing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (medicine) A suture is a stitch, or a row of stitches, that a doctor uses to close a cut or wound. 2) To suture a wound is to sew it closed. 3) (science) A suture is also a fixed, wiggly joint between bones, like the lines where the bones of the skull meet.
its sense in the lessons: In science and health lessons, doctors and nurses use sutures (stitches) for deep cuts; some sutures dissolve on their own, others must be removed after about a week. Babies have soft gaps between skull bones that later join at the sutures. In history, ancient doctors used thread, hair or even ant jaws to close wounds.
examples from the lessons: The doctor put five sutures in my cut. | The sutures will dissolve in a week. | The nurse took out the sutures from his knee. | The vet sutured the dog's leg. | Your skull has wiggly lines called sutures. | Some sutures are made of special thread. | Keep the sutures clean and dry.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: sutures. Everyday word: stitches. Say "SOO-cher". Do not confuse with "suitor" (someone who wants to marry a person) or "future".

part of speech: adjective; noun sycophant (a sycophant, sycophants); noun sycophancy
meaning for a pupil: 1) Sycophantic means praising and agreeing with a powerful or important person too much, in a fake way, to get something from them.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, a sycophantic courtier flatters the king; this tells the reader the character is not honest. In school life, the informal words are "teacher's pet", "suck-up" (US), "crawler" (UK, Australia) or "brown-noser" (rude). In honesty lessons, sycophancy is a kind of dishonesty: real kindness tells the truth politely.
examples from the lessons: The sycophantic servants told the king every idea he had was brilliant. | His sycophantic praise of the boss made everyone cringe. | Don't be sycophantic; give your honest opinion. | In the fable, the fox's sycophantic words tricked the crow into dropping the cheese. | The emperor's sycophantic advisers praised his invisible clothes. | A good friend tells you the truth, not sycophantic flattery. | The film's villain was surrounded by sycophantic followers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say "sik-oh-FAN-tik". Formal word. Person: a sycophant. Being polite or thanking someone is not sycophantic; it is sycophantic when the praise is fake and meant to gain favour.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A synthesis is a mix or combination of different ideas, parts or things into one new whole. 2) (science) Synthesis is making a substance by joining simpler substances, in nature or in a lab. 3) (science) Photosynthesis is how plants make their own food from light, water and carbon dioxide. 4) (music, computers) Sound synthesis is making sounds electronically, and speech synthesis is a computer speaking.
its sense in the lessons: In science, plants carry out photosynthesis, and chemists synthesise medicines. In English and history, a synthesis brings together ideas from several sources into your own summary. In music, a synthesiser makes sounds. "Syn-" means together and "thesis" means putting.
examples from the lessons: Photosynthesis is how plants make food from sunlight. | The report was a synthesis of ideas from many books. | Scientists made the medicine by chemical synthesis. | Our project was a synthesis of art and science. | Speech synthesis lets the computer read stories aloud. | The synthesis of proteins happens inside our cells. | Your essay should be a synthesis, not a copy of one source.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: syntheses ("SIN-thuh-seez"). Verb: synthesise (UK) / synthesize (US). Opposite: analysis (breaking something into parts). A "synthetic" material is man-made, like nylon.

part of speech: noun (a tack, tacks); verb (tack, tacks, tacked, tacking); noun (tack — uncountable, for horses)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A tack is a small nail with a flat head; a drawing pin or thumbtack holds paper on a board. 2) To tack something is to fix it with tacks, or to sew it loosely with big temporary stitches. 3) (sailing) To tack is to change a sailing boat's direction by turning its front through the wind, so it can zigzag against the wind. 4) A tack is a way or plan of doing something: try a different tack. 5) Tack is the saddle, bridle and other equipment for riding a horse. 6) To tack something on is to add it at the end, often as an afterthought.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday school life, notices are tacked to the noticeboard with thumbtacks (US) or drawing pins (UK). In sailing lessons and stories, a boat tacks to sail upwind. In horse riding, cleaning the tack is a chore at the stables. In problem-solving, "try a different tack" means try another method.
examples from the lessons: Pin the poster up with a tack. | Mum tacked the hem before sewing it properly. | The sailors had to tack back and forth against the wind. | That didn't work, so let's try a different tack. | She cleaned the saddle and the rest of the tack. | He tacked a joke on to the end of his speech. | Ouch, I stepped on a tack! | Use a thumbtack to hold the map on the wall.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Safety: tacks are sharp; keep them away from small children. "Thumbtack" (US, Canada), "drawing pin" (UK, Ireland, Australia, NZ). "Blu Tack" (UK, Australia) is a sticky putty. "Tacky" can mean sticky or, informally, cheap-looking and tasteless.

part of speech: proper noun (Tai — peoples and languages); part of "tai chi"; Mandarin pinyin (tài, tāi, tái); also a name
meaning for a pupil: 1) Tai chi (or t'ai chi) is a Chinese system of slow, flowing exercise movements, practised for health and calm. 2) The Tai peoples and Tai languages include Thai and Lao and related languages of South-East Asia and southern China. 3) (Mandarin, pinyin) "Tài" means "too" or "very", as in "tài hǎo le!" (great! — sounds like "tie how luh"); "tài" is also in "tàiyáng", the sun. 4) (a name) Tai is a first name, for example a Welsh or Chinese name. It is not an English word on its own.
its sense in the lessons: In PE and health lessons, tai chi is a calm exercise done in parks across China and the world, good for balance, especially for older people. In geography, Tai languages are spoken in Thailand, Laos and southern China. In Mandarin heard on the street, "tài" comes before adjectives: tài lěng le (too cold).
examples from the lessons: Grandma does tai chi in the park every morning. | Tai chi moves are slow and gentle. | Thai and Lao are Tai languages. | (Mandarin, pinyin) "Tài hǎo le!" means "That's great!" | (Mandarin, pinyin) "Tài guì le" means "too expensive". | We tried tai chi in PE and it was surprisingly hard. | (a name) Tai is new in our class.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Tai sounds like "tie" to an English ear. On its own it is not an English word: it appears in "tai chi", names, and Chinese words written in pinyin. Do not confuse with "Thai" (from Thailand), which sounds the same, or with the word "tie".

part of speech: noun (takeout, takeouts — US, Canada); adjective (takeout food); UK, Ireland: takeaway; Australia, NZ: takeaway
meaning for a pupil: 1) Takeout is food cooked and bought at a restaurant or shop to eat somewhere else, usually at home. 2) A takeout is the place that sells it or one meal bought this way. 3) (sport) In curling, a takeout is a shot that knocks an opponent's stone out of play.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life in the USA and Canada, families "order takeout" (pizza, Chinese food) on busy nights; in the UK, Ireland, Australia and NZ the same thing is called a "takeaway". In health lessons, takeout is fine sometimes but often has more salt, fat and sugar. In maths, takeout menus give prices for money problems.
examples from the lessons: We ordered Chinese takeout on Friday night. | Mum was too tired to cook, so we got takeout. | The takeout came in little paper boxes. | A large takeout pizza costs $15; how much for three? | (UK) In Britain, people say "takeaway" instead of "takeout". | Is this to eat in or takeout? | Too much takeout isn't good for you.
note for the reader of a maths problem: North American word; also written "take-out". The UK, Irish, Australian and NZ word is "takeaway". Watch out: "take out" as two words is a verb ("take out the rubbish", "take someone out to dinner").

part of speech: noun (Ukrainian: тату, vocative "Tatu!"); also other languages
meaning for a pupil: 1) (Ukrainian) "Tatu" is the Ukrainian word for Dad when you call him or speak to him directly: "Tatu!" means "Dad!". The ordinary form is "tato" (тато) — dad. It sounds like "TAH-too" to an English ear. It is not an English word. 2) (Swahili) "Tatu" means the number three. 3) (Portuguese) "Tatu" means armadillo. 4) t.A.T.u. was the name of a Russian pop duo.
its sense in the lessons: In lessons on Ukrainian heard on the street and at home, a child calls "Tatu!" to their father, just as an English child calls "Dad!"; "Mamo!" is "Mum!". Ukrainian changes the ending of a name or noun when you call someone (the vocative case), something English does not do. In Swahili counting: moja, mbili, tatu (one, two, three).
examples from the lessons: (Ukrainian) "Tatu, look at my drawing!" Olenka shouted. | (Ukrainian) "Tatu" means "Dad!" when you call him. | (Ukrainian) When talking about him, Ukrainian children say "tato" — dad. | (Ukrainian) "Dobranich, tatu!" means "Good night, Dad!" | (Swahili) Moja, mbili, tatu — one, two, three. | (Portuguese) In Brazil, "tatu" is an armadillo. | Ukrainian has a special calling form, so "tato" becomes "tatu".
note for the reader of a maths problem: Not an English word. In Ukrainian it is the calling (vocative) form of "tato" (dad), written тату in Cyrillic letters; stress on the first syllable, "TAH-too". Do not confuse with "tattoo" (a picture on the skin), which sounds a bit like it.

part of speech: adjective (taxonomic; more taxonomic is not used)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Taxonomic means to do with sorting living things into named groups, such as kingdom, family, genus and species. 2) More broadly, it means to do with any careful system of naming and grouping things.
its sense in the lessons: In science it comes up when pupils learn how living things are classified: a taxonomic group, a taxonomic key, taxonomic rank. It tells the reader that things are being sorted into groups by shared features. Phrases: taxonomic group, taxonomic key, taxonomic name, taxonomic rank.
examples from the lessons: Lions and tigers are in the same taxonomic family, the cat family. | Our class made a taxonomic key to sort the minibeasts we found. | Species is the smallest main taxonomic rank. | Scientists argued about the taxonomic place of the giant panda for years. | A taxonomic name is usually written in Latin, like Homo sapiens. | The museum labels show each fossil's taxonomic group. | The library uses a kind of taxonomic system to sort books by subject.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal science word; adjective only. Related: taxonomy (the system or science of classifying), taxonomist (a scientist who classifies). Stress: tax-o-NOM-ic. Do not confuse with taxidermy (stuffing dead animals) or taxes (money paid to the government).

part of speech: noun (teal, teals — the duck; plural often teal); noun (teal — the colour, uncountable); adjective (teal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Teal is a blue-green colour, darker than turquoise. 2) A teal is a small wild duck; the males often have a green stripe on the head and wing.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life it is mostly a colour word for clothes, paint, school uniforms and art. In nature studies it names a small freshwater duck seen on ponds and marshes. Phrases: teal blue, dark teal, a flock of teal.
examples from the lessons: She wore a teal jumper to the party. | Teal is a mix of blue and green. | We painted the sea teal in our art lesson. | A pair of teal landed on the pond. | The teal is one of the smallest ducks in Britain. | My new pencil case is teal with silver stars. | Dark teal looks good on the classroom wall display.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a colour it is uncountable (a nice teal, but not usually teals). For the duck the plural is often the same: a flock of teal. Not to be confused with teel or with steal/steel.

part of speech: noun (a teardrop, teardrops); adjective-like before a noun (a teardrop shape)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A teardrop is a single tear falling from the eye. 2) A teardrop shape is round at the bottom and pointed at the top, like a falling drop of water.
its sense in the lessons: In stories a teardrop shows that someone is very sad, moved or happy enough to cry. In art and maths it names a shape. Phrases: a single teardrop, teardrop shape, teardrop earrings.
examples from the lessons: A teardrop rolled down her cheek when the puppy left. | Raindrops are not really teardrop shaped; small ones are almost round. | Grandma gave me teardrop earrings. | Draw a teardrop shape for each leaf. | Not a single teardrop fell, but he felt sad inside. | The pendant was a blue glass teardrop. | The leaf of the lime tree has a teardrop outline.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one teardrop, two teardrops. It is one word. Myth: real falling raindrops are not teardrop shaped; small ones are round and big ones flatten like a bun.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Telegraphic means to do with the telegraph, the old machine that sent messages along wires as electric signals. 2) Telegraphic speech or writing is very short and leaves out little words, like an old telegram: "Arrive Monday stop."
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons it describes old telegraph messages. In English lessons and in talk about how babies learn to speak, telegraphic speech means short sentences without little words ("Daddy go car"). Phrases: telegraphic message, telegraphic style, telegraphic speech.
examples from the lessons: In the 1800s, telegraphic messages crossed oceans along cables under the sea. | His notes were telegraphic: "Lunch. Park. Rain. Home." | Toddlers use telegraphic speech, like "Me want juice." | The old station still has a telegraphic office. | Text messages can sound telegraphic because people leave out words. | The teacher said my story summary was too telegraphic and needed full sentences.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Fairly formal. Related: telegraph (the machine and the system), telegram (one message sent by telegraph). Telegraphic style is fine for notes but not for a written answer in a test.

part of speech: verb (teleport, teleports, teleported, teleporting); noun (a teleport — a place or device for teleporting, in games and stories)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To teleport is to move from one place to another instantly, without travelling through the space between; it happens only in science fiction, games and stories. 2) A teleport (in games) is a pad or doorway that sends a player to another place.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, films and video games it tells the reader that a character jumps across space by magic or super-technology. In real science, "quantum teleportation" moves information about tiny particles, not people. Phrases: teleport to, teleport back, teleport pad.
examples from the lessons: In the game, you can teleport back to your base. | I wish I could teleport to school instead of walking in the rain. | The wizard teleported out of the tower. | Step on the glowing teleport to reach the next level. | No real machine can teleport a person. | "Beam me up" is how characters teleport in an old space show.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: teleported, teleporting. Noun for the act: teleportation. Trap: people cannot really teleport; quantum teleportation in science is something different and very small.

part of speech: noun (a tetra, tetras); also a prefix tetra- meaning four
meaning for a pupil: 1) A tetra is a small, often brightly coloured freshwater fish from South America or Africa, popular in home aquariums, such as the neon tetra. 2) Tetra- at the start of a word means four, as in tetrahedron (a solid with four faces) and tetrapod (an animal with four limbs).
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life tetras are pet fish kept in tanks. In maths and science the prefix tetra- signals the number four. Phrases: neon tetra, a shoal of tetras, tetrahedron.
examples from the lessons: We have six neon tetras in our fish tank. | Tetras like to swim together in a shoal. | A tetrahedron is a pyramid with four triangle faces. | The neon tetra has a shiny blue stripe. | Frogs, lizards, birds and people are all tetrapods. | Feed the tetras a small pinch of flakes. | The pet shop sells tetras, guppies and goldfish.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one tetra, two tetras. In maths, tetra- = 4 (tri- = 3, penta- = 5). Tetra Pak is a brand name for drink cartons, not a fish.

part of speech: noun (a textile, textiles); adjective-like before a noun (textile factory)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A textile is any cloth or fabric that is woven, knitted or made from threads, such as cotton, wool or silk. 2) Textiles is also a school subject or craft where you design and make things from fabric.
its sense in the lessons: In design and technology lessons pupils study textiles: natural and man-made fibres, weaving, sewing. In history it names the textile mills of the Industrial Revolution. Phrases: textile industry, textile mill, textile design, natural textiles.
examples from the lessons: Cotton and wool are natural textiles. | In textiles class we sewed a cushion. | The town grew around a big textile mill in the 1800s. | Polyester is a man-made textile. | Many children worked in textile factories long ago. | This museum shows textiles from all over the world. | Recycling old textiles keeps clothes out of landfill.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; often plural textiles for the subject or the industry. Stress: TEX-tile. Related: texture (how something feels), text (originally from the same Latin word for weaving).

part of speech: noun (a thatcher, thatchers); proper noun (Thatcher — a surname, a name)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A thatcher is a person whose job is to make roofs from straw, reeds or similar dry plants. 2) (a name) Thatcher is an English surname; Margaret Thatcher was Prime Minister of the United Kingdom from 1979 to 1990, the first woman in that job.
its sense in the lessons: In history and country life it names an old craft still used on cottages in England and Ireland. As a name it appears in UK history lessons about modern Britain. Phrases: master thatcher, a thatched roof.
examples from the lessons: The thatcher climbed onto the cottage roof with bundles of reed. | A good thatcher can make a roof that lasts thirty years. | Thatchers use long wooden pegs called spars. | Margaret Thatcher was the first woman Prime Minister of the UK. | Our village still has a thatcher who learned the craft from his father. | The thatcher's ladder leaned against the wall.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one thatcher, two thatchers. Related: thatch (the roof material, and the verb), thatched. As a surname it takes a capital letter. People still argue strongly about Margaret Thatcher's politics; history lessons give different views.

part of speech: noun (a thrill, thrills); verb (thrill, thrills, thrilled, thrilling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A thrill is a sudden strong feeling of excitement and pleasure. 2) To thrill someone is to make them very excited and happy. 3) Thrilled (adjective) means very pleased.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and stories it describes excitement: rides, sports, surprises, adventures. Phrases: the thrill of, a thrill ride, thrills and spills, thrilled to bits (UK), thrill seeker.
examples from the lessons: The roller coaster gave me a real thrill. | I was thrilled when I won the spelling bee. | The goal thrilled the crowd. | Feel the thrill of your first ride on a horse! | Mum was thrilled to bits with her birthday card. | Some people love the thrill of danger, but safety comes first. | It was a thrill to meet a real author at school.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: thrilled, thrilling. Thrilling (adjective) = very exciting; thriller = an exciting story or film, often about crime. Thrilled is stronger than pleased.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A throaty voice or sound is low and rough, as if it comes from deep in the throat. 2) It can describe the deep roar of an engine, like a throaty motorbike.
its sense in the lessons: In stories it describes how a character sounds, for example when they have a cold, are emotional, or have a deep voice. Phrases: a throaty laugh, a throaty voice, a throaty roar.
examples from the lessons: She gave a throaty laugh. | With a cold, my voice sounded throaty. | The old car started with a throaty rumble. | The lion let out a throaty growl. | The singer had a warm, throaty voice. | "Come in," said a throaty voice from behind the door.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comes from throat + -y. Comparative throatier, superlative throatiest. Similar: husky, hoarse, gravelly.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Tinsel is long strings of thin, shiny, glittering material used as decoration, especially at Christmas. 2) Tinsel can also mean something that looks bright and exciting but has little real value.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life it is a Christmas decoration on trees, in classrooms and at school plays. In stories it can stand for showy glamour, as in "Tinseltown" (a nickname for Hollywood). Phrases: a strand of tinsel, gold tinsel, tinsel and baubles.
examples from the lessons: We wrapped silver tinsel around the Christmas tree. | The angel in the nativity play wore tinsel as a halo. | Tinsel sparkled in the classroom window. | The cat kept pulling the tinsel off the tree. | In Australia, people hang tinsel even though Christmas is in summer. | The film star's life was all tinsel and no real happiness.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: some tinsel, a strand of tinsel (not a tinsel). Safety: keep tinsel away from pets and very small children, who may swallow it.

part of speech: noun (a tipi, tipis); also spelled tepee or teepee
meaning for a pupil: 1) A tipi is a cone-shaped tent made of animal skins or cloth over long wooden poles, traditionally used by some Native American peoples of the Great Plains.
its sense in the lessons: In history and geography it is taught when learning about the Plains peoples such as the Lakota, who moved with the buffalo herds. Today tipis are also used at festivals and camps. Phrases: put up a tipi, inside the tipi.
examples from the lessons: The Lakota lived in tipis that could be taken down quickly. | A tipi has a smoke hole at the top. | We slept in a tipi at the summer camp. | The tipi poles were tied together at the top. | Not all Native American peoples lived in tipis; many lived in wooden or earth houses. | Buffalo hide was used to cover the tipi.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one tipi, two tipis. Spellings tipi, tepee and teepee are all correct. Trap: it is a myth that all Native Americans lived in tipis; homes differed by people and region.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Tonal means to do with tone: the sound, pitch or quality of something. 2) A tonal language uses the rise and fall of the voice to change the meaning of a word, like Mandarin Chinese. 3) In art, tonal means to do with light and dark shades of a colour.
its sense in the lessons: In music lessons it is about pitch and keys; in art lessons about shading from light to dark; in languages it explains why in Mandarin "ma" can mean mother or horse depending on the tone. Phrases: tonal language, tonal range, tonal shading.
examples from the lessons: Mandarin is a tonal language with four main tones. | In art we did tonal shading with a pencil, from dark to light. | The piano has a warm tonal quality. | English is not a tonal language, though our voice rises in questions. | Make a tonal scale with five boxes. | The singer's tonal range is wide.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective only; noun: tone, tonality. Trap: tonal (about tone) is not the same as total (all added together).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Torchlight is the light from a torch. In the UK, Ireland, Australia and New Zealand a torch is a battery light you hold (a flashlight in the USA). 2) In history and stories, torchlight is the light of burning sticks or flaming torches.
its sense in the lessons: In stories it sets a scene: in a cave, at night, at a castle or a procession. Phrases: by torchlight, in the torchlight, a torchlight procession.
examples from the lessons: We read comics under the covers by torchlight. | The castle hall flickered in the torchlight. | The cave walls glittered in the torchlight. | The villagers held a torchlight procession. | By torchlight, we found the path back to the tent. | In the torchlight, the shadows looked like monsters.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: no plural. UK torch = US flashlight; a flaming torch is a stick with fire at the end. American readers may picture flames rather than a battery light.

part of speech: noun (a torpedo, torpedoes); verb (torpedo, torpedoes, torpedoed, torpedoing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A torpedo is a long, cigar-shaped weapon that moves underwater by itself and explodes when it hits a ship. 2) To torpedo a ship is to hit it with a torpedo. 3) To torpedo a plan (informal) is to ruin it completely. 4) A torpedo ray is a fish that can give an electric shock.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons it comes up in both World Wars, with submarines and ships such as the Lusitania. In everyday talk, torpedoing a plan means wrecking it. Phrases: fire a torpedo, torpedo boat, torpedo a plan.
examples from the lessons: The submarine fired a torpedo at the warship. | The ship was torpedoed in 1915. | The rain torpedoed our picnic plans. | Torpedoes travel just under the water's surface. | The dolphin shot through the water like a torpedo. | The torpedo ray stuns small fish with electricity.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: torpedoes (with -es). Past: torpedoed. The informal sense (to ruin) is common in news.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A tortilla is a thin, flat, round bread made from maize (corn) or wheat flour, from Mexico, used for tacos, wraps and burritos. 2) In Spain, a tortilla is a thick omelette made with eggs and potatoes.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life it is a common food in school lunches, wraps and Mexican-style meals. In geography and food lessons it shows how food words travel and change between countries. Phrases: tortilla wrap, tortilla chips, corn tortilla, Spanish tortilla.
examples from the lessons: I had a chicken wrap in a tortilla for lunch. | Tortilla chips are cut from tortillas and fried. | Warm the tortillas in a dry pan. | In Spain, my aunt made a tortilla with eggs and potatoes. | A taco is a folded tortilla with filling. | Corn tortillas have been eaten in Mexico for thousands of years.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one tortilla, two tortillas. Said tor-TEE-ya; the double l sounds like y. Trap: a Spanish tortilla is not the same as a Mexican tortilla.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Tourism is the business of people travelling to places for holidays and of providing them with hotels, trips and things to see. 2) It also means the activity of visiting places as a tourist.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons it is studied as an industry: how it brings money and jobs but can also cause crowding, litter and pollution. Phrases: the tourism industry, mass tourism, eco-tourism, sustainable tourism.
examples from the lessons: Tourism brings a lot of money to seaside towns. | New Zealand is famous for adventure tourism like bungee jumping. | Too much tourism can damage beaches and coral reefs. | Eco-tourism tries to protect nature while people visit. | The pandemic hit tourism very hard. | My uncle works in tourism as a tour guide.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: no plural. Person: tourist; adjective: touristy (informal, often negative). Spelling: tour + ism.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Toxicity is how poisonous or harmful a substance is. 2) (informal) Toxicity also means nasty, unkind or harmful behaviour between people, for example online.
its sense in the lessons: In science and safety it is about chemicals, plants and medicines and how much harm they can do. In everyday talk it describes bullying, unkind comments or harmful friendships. Phrases: high toxicity, low toxicity, the toxicity of, online toxicity.
examples from the lessons: Some mushrooms have very high toxicity. | Scientists test the toxicity of new medicines. | The dose matters: almost anything has toxicity in a large amount. | Lead paint was banned because of its toxicity. | The chat game was spoiled by toxicity and name-calling. | Chocolate has toxicity for dogs, even though it is safe for people.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly uncountable. Adjective: toxic. Key science idea: "the dose makes the poison" — even water is harmful in huge amounts. Safety: never taste unknown plants, berries or chemicals.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A tract is a large area of land or water. 2) In the body, a tract is a long system of connected parts, like the digestive tract or the respiratory tract. 3) A tract is also a short booklet or leaflet that tries to persuade people, often about religion or politics.
its sense in the lessons: In science it comes up in the body: the digestive tract (food pipe, stomach, intestines) and the respiratory tract (nose, windpipe, lungs). In geography it describes big pieces of land. In history and church life a tract was a booklet handed out to spread an idea. Phrases: a vast tract of, digestive tract, respiratory tract, a religious tract.
examples from the lessons: Huge tracts of rainforest have been cut down. | Food passes through the digestive tract. | A cold is an infection of the upper respiratory tract. | The settlers bought a tract of land near the river. | A man at the station was handing out religious tracts. | Vast tracts of Australia are desert.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Trap: tract is not track (a path or rail) and not traction. Related words: attract, extract, subtract all share the Latin root for "pull".

meaning for a pupil: 1) Tragic means very sad, usually because someone has died or suffered something terrible. 2) In literature, tragic means to do with a tragedy, a serious play or story that ends in disaster for the main character. 3) (informal, slang) Tragic can mean embarrassingly bad: "His dancing is tragic."
its sense in the lessons: In news and history it describes accidents, wars and disasters. In English lessons it names a kind of story or hero. In playground talk it can be a jokey insult. Phrases: a tragic accident, tragic news, tragic hero, a tragic ending.
examples from the lessons: The ship sank in a tragic accident. | It is tragic that so many animals lose their homes in fires. | The story has a tragic ending. | The tragic hero makes one big mistake that ruins him. | (slang) "That haircut is tragic," my brother joked. | We heard the tragic news on the radio.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb: tragically. Noun: tragedy. The slang sense is jokey and can sound unkind. Do not use "tragic" for small problems in formal writing.

part of speech: noun (a trainee, trainees); adjective-like before a noun (a trainee teacher)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A trainee is a person who is being taught how to do a job.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life you meet trainee teachers in school, trainee nurses in hospital and trainee drivers. It tells the reader that the person is still learning. Phrases: trainee teacher, trainee nurse, trainee pilot, trainee chef.
examples from the lessons: Our class has a trainee teacher this term. | The trainee chef chopped the onions. | Every trainee pilot practises in a simulator first. | The trainee wore a badge that said "In training". | Be patient with trainees; they are still learning. | She started as a trainee and is now the manager.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. The -ee ending means the person something is done to (trainee = the one trained; trainer = the one who trains), like employee/employer. Trap: trainers in the UK are also sports shoes.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A transformer is a device that changes the voltage of electricity, making it higher or lower. 2) Anything that changes something else can be called a transformer. 3) Transformers is a famous toy and film series about robots that change into cars and trucks. 4) In computing, a transformer is a type of computer program used in many modern AI language models.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons it explains how power stations send electricity long distances at high voltage and transformers lower it for homes. In everyday life children know the robot toys. Phrases: step-up transformer, step-down transformer, power transformer.
examples from the lessons: A transformer near our street lowers the voltage for houses. | Phone chargers contain a small transformer. | Never climb fences around electricity transformers — it is very dangerous. | My brother collects Transformers toys. | A step-up transformer raises the voltage. | Many chatbots are built on a kind of program called a transformer.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Verb: transform. Safety: substations and transformers carry deadly voltages; stay out and never fetch a ball from inside the fence.

part of speech: verb (trudge, trudges, trudged, trudging); noun (a trudge — a long tiring walk)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To trudge is to walk slowly and heavily because you are tired, or because the ground is hard to walk on. 2) A trudge is a long, tiring walk.
its sense in the lessons: In stories it shows a character is tired, sad or walking through snow, mud or sand. Phrases: trudge home, trudge through the snow, trudge up the hill, a long trudge.
examples from the lessons: We trudged home through the snow. | The soldiers trudged along the muddy road. | After the match, the team trudged back to the changing room. | It was a long trudge up the hill. | She trudged to school with her heavy bag. | The explorers trudged across the ice for days.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: trudged, trudging. Stronger than walk; shows effort and tiredness. Similar: plod, tramp, slog.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A tuatara is a lizard-like reptile found only in New Zealand; it is the last living member of a very old group of reptiles that lived alongside the dinosaurs.
its sense in the lessons: In science and New Zealand studies it is a famous "living fossil" example. It shows how islands can keep very old kinds of animals. The name comes from Maori and means "peaks on the back". Phrases: a living fossil, tuatara sanctuary.
examples from the lessons: The tuatara lives only in New Zealand. | A tuatara is not a true lizard, even though it looks like one. | Some tuatara live for more than a hundred years. | The tuatara has spines along its back. | Rats nearly wiped out the tuatara on many islands. | We saw a tuatara at the wildlife sanctuary.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: tuatara (as in Maori) or tuataras. Said too-a-TAH-ra. Trap: it looks like a lizard but belongs to a different group. Young tuatara have a "third eye" spot on the top of the head that senses light.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Turbid water or liquid is cloudy or muddy because it has mud, sand or other bits stirred up in it. 2) (formal) Turbid can also describe confused or unclear thoughts or writing.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography it is used when testing water quality: turbid water lets less light through. Phrases: turbid water, a turbid river.
examples from the lessons: After the storm the river was turbid and brown. | We tested whether the pond water was clear or turbid. | Fish find it hard to see in turbid water. | The turbid water slowly cleared as the mud settled. | Filtering made the turbid sample clear. | The essay was turbid and hard to follow.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal or science word; everyday words: cloudy, muddy, murky. Noun: turbidity. Do not confuse with turgid (swollen, or pompous) or torpid (sluggish).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Turkic describes a family of related languages, including Turkish, Azerbaijani, Kazakh, Uzbek, Kyrgyz, Turkmen, Uyghur and Tatar. 2) It also describes the peoples who speak these languages and their cultures.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and history lessons it names a large group of peoples across Central Asia, Turkey and parts of Russia and China. Phrases: Turkic languages, Turkic peoples.
examples from the lessons: Turkish and Kazakh are both Turkic languages. | Turkic peoples live from Turkey to Siberia. | Many Turkic languages are written in Latin or Cyrillic letters. | The Crimean Tatars speak a Turkic language. | Words in Turkic languages are built by adding many endings. | Uzbek is the Turkic language with the most speakers after Turkish.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Written with a capital T. Trap: Turkic is the whole family; Turkish is just one language in it, spoken in Turkey. Not the same as turkey the bird.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Turnout is the number of people who come to an event, or who vote in an election. 2) (UK, old-fashioned) A turnout can also mean the way someone is dressed. 3) A turnout is a place at the side of a road where cars can pull over (USA).
its sense in the lessons: In news and politics, turnout tells how many voters took part, often as a percentage. In school life it tells how many came to a concert, match or meeting. Phrases: a good turnout, a low turnout, voter turnout, turnout was high.
examples from the lessons: There was a great turnout for the school fair. | Voter turnout was 67 per cent. | Despite the rain, the turnout at the match was good. | Low turnout means many people did not vote. | We were pleased with the turnout at the bake sale. | The truck stopped at a turnout on the mountain road.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word as a noun (turnout); the verb is two words: turn out ("Lots of people turned out"). In maths problems turnout is often a percentage: if 300 of 500 voted, turnout = 300 ÷ 500 = 60%.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Twisty means full of twists and bends, like a twisty road or path. 2) A twisty story or plot has many surprising turns.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life it describes roads, paths, slides and hair. In stories it describes plots full of surprises. Phrases: a twisty road, twisty plot, twisty and turny.
examples from the lessons: The road up the mountain is very twisty. | Our water slide was long and twisty. | The book had a twisty plot with a surprise ending. | Twisty paths wound through the woods. | She has twisty curls. | The twisty lane made me feel car-sick.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal. Comparative twistier, superlative twistiest. Similar: winding, bendy, windy (said WINE-dee for roads).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) A tyke is a small child, especially a cheeky or naughty one, said in a friendly way. 2) (UK, informal) A Tyke is a nickname for a person from Yorkshire. 3) (old, mostly UK) A tyke is a dog of no special breed, a mongrel.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday talk adults call a little child a tyke with affection. In northern England, Yorkshire people are sometimes called Tykes. Phrases: little tyke, cheeky tyke.
examples from the lessons: Come here, you little tyke! | The cheeky tyke hid Grandad's glasses. | Even as a tyke, she loved football. | (UK) He's a proper Yorkshire tyke. | The old farmer's tyke barked at the gate. | Those tykes have muddy footprints all over the floor.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal and friendly, not rude for a child. Spelling: tyke (sometimes tike). Can be a slight insult for an adult.

part of speech: noun (a ukulele, ukuleles); also spelled ukelele
meaning for a pupil: 1) A ukulele is a small guitar-like instrument with four strings, first made popular in Hawaii.
its sense in the lessons: In music lessons the ukulele is a favourite first instrument in schools because it is small, cheap and easy to learn chords on. Phrases: play the ukulele, strum a ukulele, ukulele chords.
examples from the lessons: Our whole class is learning the ukulele. | She strummed a happy song on her ukulele. | A ukulele has four nylon strings. | The ukulele came to Hawaii from a Portuguese instrument in the 1800s. | Tune your ukulele before you play. | I can play three chords on the ukulele.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a ukulele (with "a", because it starts with a "you" sound). Said you-ka-LAY-lee; in Hawaiian, oo-koo-LEH-leh. Informal short form: uke.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unheard means not heard by anyone, or not listened to. 2) Unheard of (phrase) means never known or done before, very unusual.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and life it describes voices or feelings that nobody pays attention to. "Unheard of" is common in news and everyday talk. Phrases: go unheard, unheard of, voices unheard.
examples from the lessons: Her cry for help went unheard in the storm. | Snow in July is almost unheard of here. | Children's ideas often go unheard, so the school started a pupil council. | My knock was unheard because the music was so loud. | It was unheard of for a nine-year-old to win the chess cup. | Let the unheard voices speak.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective from un- + heard. "Unheard of" is a fixed phrase; before a noun write "an unheard-of idea" with hyphens. Do not confuse with unhurt (not injured).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unification is the act of joining separate things, groups or countries into one whole.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons it names events such as the unification of Germany (1871), of Italy, or of England's kingdoms. In science it can mean joining ideas into one theory. Phrases: the unification of, German unification, Italian unification.
examples from the lessons: The unification of Germany happened in 1871. | Italian unification joined many small states into one country. | The unification of the two schools made one big school. | Scientists hope for the unification of all forces in one theory. | After unification, the country used one money. | The treaty led to the unification of the kingdoms.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly uncountable. Verb: unify; adjective: unified. Prefix uni- means one (unicorn, uniform, unit).

part of speech: adjective (unified); past form of the verb unify (unify, unifies, unified, unifying)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Unified means joined together into one whole. 2) It also means made the same or consistent everywhere, as in a unified system.
its sense in the lessons: In history it describes countries made from smaller parts. In everyday life it describes teams that work as one, or systems that are the same everywhere. Phrases: a unified country, a unified team, unified rules.
examples from the lessons: Germany became a unified country in 1871. | The team was unified behind its captain. | The school wants a unified set of rules for all classes. | The king unified the kingdoms. | Scientists want a unified theory. | After the argument, the class felt unified again.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb unify: unifies, unified, unifying (y changes to i). Similar: united, joined, combined.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An unprovoked attack or action happens without any reason, when the other person did nothing to cause it.
its sense in the lessons: In news, history and safety it describes violence or attacks that came out of nowhere. In school it can describe hitting or unkindness with no cause. Phrases: an unprovoked attack, completely unprovoked.
examples from the lessons: The dog's bite was unprovoked; the boy had not touched it. | Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 was widely described as unprovoked. | The teacher said the push was unprovoked and unfair. | Shark attacks on people are rare, and unprovoked ones are rarer still. | It was an unprovoked insult. | The court heard it was an unprovoked assault.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Made from un- + provoked (provoke = to cause someone to react, often angrily). Used mostly about attacks and insults.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unsuited means not right or not suitable for a person, job, place or purpose.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life it describes something that does not fit its use, like shoes unsuited to hiking, or a pet unsuited to a small flat. Phrases: unsuited to, unsuited for, ill-suited.
examples from the lessons: These sandals are unsuited to a muddy walk. | A husky is unsuited to a hot climate. | He felt unsuited to the job of goalkeeper. | The old hall is unsuited for big concerts. | Some plants are unsuited to shady gardens. | They were a couple unsuited to each other.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually followed by "to" or "for": unsuited to the job. Do not confuse with unsuitable (more common before a noun: an unsuitable film).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Untrustworthy means not able to be trusted: a person who may lie or break promises, or information that may be false.
its sense in the lessons: In ethics and stories it describes liars, cheats and villains. In online safety it describes websites or messages that may be fake or scams. Phrases: an untrustworthy person, an untrustworthy source, look untrustworthy.
examples from the lessons: He told so many lies that everyone found him untrustworthy. | That website looks untrustworthy, so don't type your password. | An untrustworthy friend shares your secrets. | The fox in the story is clever but untrustworthy. | Check facts from untrustworthy sources against good ones. | Breaking promises makes you seem untrustworthy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Made from un- + trust + worthy. Opposite: trustworthy, reliable. Spelled with -worthy (deserving), not -worthly.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Upwind means in the direction the wind is coming from, against the wind. 2) If you are upwind of something, the wind blows from you towards it.
its sense in the lessons: In science, sailing and safety it matters for smells, smoke and gas: stand upwind of a bonfire so smoke blows away from you. Hunters and animal watchers stay downwind so animals cannot smell them. Phrases: upwind of, sail upwind.
examples from the lessons: Stand upwind of the barbecue so the smoke does not blow in your face. | The deer smelled us because we were upwind. | It is harder to sail upwind than downwind. | The factory is upwind of the town, so the smell reaches the houses. | Keep upwind of any chemical spill. | We cycled upwind and it was hard work.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: downwind (the direction the wind blows to). Safety rule: in a fire or gas leak, move upwind, away from the smoke.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Validity is how true, fair or correct something is, for example an argument or a test. 2) (law) Validity is whether a document, ticket or rule is official and still accepted, for example a passport's validity.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and logic it means an argument follows correctly from its premises. In science it means a test really measures what it should (a fair test). In everyday life it is about tickets, passports and cards that have not expired. Phrases: the validity of, check the validity, period of validity.
examples from the lessons: The scientist questioned the validity of the results. | Check the validity of your passport before you travel. | A fair test makes your experiment more valid; that is its validity. | The ticket's validity ends at midnight. | The judge looked at the validity of the will. | The teacher asked us to judge the validity of each argument.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly uncountable. Adjective: valid; opposite: invalid. Trap in logic: an argument can be valid (the steps follow) even if a premise is false.

part of speech: verb form (venting — from vent, vents, vented, venting); noun (venting — uncountable)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Venting is letting out strong feelings, especially anger or frustration, by talking or shouting about them. 2) Venting is letting air, gas, smoke or steam escape through an opening.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and wellbeing lessons it is about letting feelings out safely, for example by talking to a friend. In science and safety it is about letting fumes or steam out of a room or machine. Phrases: venting about, venting anger, venting steam.
examples from the lessons: Sorry for venting — I'm just so annoyed about the test. | She was venting to her best friend about her brother. | The kitchen fan is venting the steam outside. | Venting your feelings can help, but don't be unkind. | The volcano was venting gas and ash. | He spent an hour venting about the referee.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From the verb vent; "vent your anger" and "vent about something". A vent is also a small opening for air. Venting feelings is fine; taking anger out on others is not.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A vocalist is a singer, especially one who sings with a band or group.
its sense in the lessons: In music it names the singer in a band, choir or concert. Phrases: lead vocalist, backing vocalist, guest vocalist.
examples from the lessons: She is the lead vocalist in the school band. | The backing vocalists sang "ooh" behind him. | Our guest vocalist sang a song in Welsh. | Every band needs a strong vocalist. | The vocalist warmed up her voice before the show. | He started as a drummer but became a vocalist.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Related: vocal (to do with the voice), vocals (the singing part of a song). Similar: singer.

part of speech: noun (a void, voids); adjective (void); verb (void, voids, voided, voiding)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A void is a completely empty space. 2) A void is also a feeling that something important is missing, for example after losing someone. 3) (law) Void means no longer valid or legal: "The ticket is void." 4) To void something is to cancel it officially. 5) Void of (formal) means completely without something.
its sense in the lessons: In science and space stories it describes empty space. In everyday life and law it means cancelled, as in "null and void". In maths and computing, void can mean empty or nothing. Phrases: the void, null and void, void of, fill the void.
examples from the lessons: The spaceship drifted into the dark void. | After Grandad died, there was a void in our family. | The contract was declared null and void. | The shop voided the sale and gave me a refund. | His face was void of expression. | Getting a puppy filled the void after our old dog passed away.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable as a noun. "Null and void" is a fixed legal phrase. Similar: empty, vacuum, gap. Do not confuse with avoid (to keep away from).

part of speech: verb (wail, wails, wailed, wailing); noun (a wail, wails)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To wail is to cry out with a long, loud, high sound because of pain, sadness or anger. 2) A wail is such a long cry. 3) Things like sirens or the wind can also wail.
its sense in the lessons: In stories it shows deep sadness or a baby's crying, or creates spooky sounds (the wind wailing). Phrases: let out a wail, wail with grief, the wail of a siren.
examples from the lessons: The baby began to wail when her toy fell. | The siren wailed as the ambulance raced past. | The wind wailed around the old house. | "It's not fair!" he wailed. | A long wail came from the forest. | The mourners wailed at the funeral.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: wailed, wailing. Homophone: whale (the sea animal). Similar: howl, moan, sob.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (Australia) A walkabout is a traditional journey on foot through the bush made by some Aboriginal Australians, linked to culture, country and learning. 2) (UK) A walkabout is when a king, queen or famous person walks among a crowd, shaking hands and talking. 3) (informal) To go walkabout means to wander off or go missing.
its sense in the lessons: In Australian history and culture it is about Aboriginal connection to land; it should be spoken of with respect. In UK news it describes royal visits. Informally, things or people "go walkabout" when lost. Phrases: go walkabout, a royal walkabout.
examples from the lessons: The King went on a walkabout to meet the crowd. | My PE kit has gone walkabout again! | Walkabout is a traditional journey linked to Aboriginal culture. | The prime minister did a walkabout in the town centre. | The dog went walkabout and came home at tea time. | Crowds waited for hours for the royal walkabout.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable as a noun; "go walkabout" has no "a". Some Aboriginal people find the jokey "go walkabout" (meaning to disappear) disrespectful, so use it with care.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Wan means pale and looking ill or tired. 2) A wan smile is a weak, tired or sad smile. 3) (old, poetic) Wan light is faint and weak. 4) (Mandarin, pinyin) wǎn can mean evening or late, and wàn means ten thousand; these are not English words.
its sense in the lessons: In stories it shows a character is unwell, worried or exhausted. Phrases: a wan face, a wan smile, look wan.
examples from the lessons: She looked wan after a week with flu. | He gave a wan smile and said he was fine. | The wan winter sun barely warmed the garden. | Your face is so wan — sit down and have some water. | The patient's cheeks were wan and thin. | In Mandarin, "wǎn shàng hǎo" means good evening.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Literary word; everyday words are pale, pasty. Rhymes with "con". Do not confuse with want or won.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A warlord is a military leader who controls an area by force with his own army, usually when there is no strong government.
its sense in the lessons: In history and news it is used for leaders in civil wars, in ancient China's Warring States period, or in places without a working government. It tells the reader that power comes from weapons, not elections. Phrases: local warlord, rival warlords.
examples from the lessons: Rival warlords fought for control of the region. | In the 1920s, warlords ruled many parts of China. | The warlord's soldiers stole food from the villages. | Without a government, warlords took over. | The game's villain is a cruel warlord. | Peace talks brought the warlords to one table.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Made from war + lord. Usually negative. Similar: chieftain (older, more neutral), strongman.

part of speech: verb (warp, warps, warped, warping); noun (warp — the threads; a warp — a bend)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To warp is to bend or twist out of shape, often because of heat or water. 2) To warp someone's mind or ideas is to change them in a bad, unfair way. 3) In weaving, the warp is the long threads that run lengthwise on a loom; the weft goes across them. 4) In science fiction, warp speed is faster-than-light travel.
its sense in the lessons: In science and design it describes wood or plastic bending with damp or heat. In textiles lessons it names the long threads. In stories it appears in "time warp" and "warp speed". Phrases: warp and weft, time warp, warp speed, a warped sense of humour.
examples from the lessons: The wooden door warped in the damp weather. | Don't leave the plastic ruler on the radiator or it will warp. | In weaving, the warp threads go up and down the loom. | The ship jumped to warp speed. | Hatred can warp a person's mind. | That village feels like it is stuck in a time warp.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: warped, warping. Warped (adjective) can mean twisted in shape or strange in a nasty way. Warp = lengthwise threads, weft = crosswise threads.

part of speech: proper noun (Waterloo — a name of a place); noun (a waterloo — a final defeat, as in "meet your Waterloo")
meaning for a pupil: 1) (a name) Waterloo is a town in Belgium where Napoleon was finally defeated in 1815 by British, Dutch, Belgian and Prussian armies. 2) Waterloo is a big railway station and area in London. 3) To meet your Waterloo means to suffer a final defeat after a long run of success. 4) "Waterloo" is also a famous 1974 song by the Swedish band ABBA.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons it ends the Napoleonic Wars. In the UK it is a station and many places named after the battle. In everyday speech "meet your Waterloo" means final defeat. Phrases: the Battle of Waterloo, Waterloo Station, meet your Waterloo.
examples from the lessons: Napoleon lost the Battle of Waterloo in 1815. | We took the train to London Waterloo. | The champion finally met his Waterloo in the final. | The Duke of Wellington led the British army at Waterloo. | ABBA won Eurovision with "Waterloo". | Waterloo is also a city in Ontario, Canada.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Written with a capital W. "Meet your Waterloo" is an idiom; the place itself is a small town south of Brussels.
