part of speech: noun (a weasel, weasels); verb (weasel, weasels, weaselled/weaseled, weaselling/weaseling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A weasel is a small, thin, fast wild animal with brown fur and a long body that hunts mice and voles. 2) (informal, rude) A weasel is a sneaky person who cannot be trusted. 3) To weasel out of something (informal) is to avoid doing it in a sneaky way. 4) Weasel words are vague words used to avoid saying something clearly.
its sense in the lessons: In nature studies it is a small hunter of the British countryside. In stories, weasels are often sly villains (as in "The Wind in the Willows"). In English lessons, "weasel words" are a trick in adverts and speeches. Phrases: weasel out of, weasel words, sly as a weasel.
examples from the lessons: A weasel slipped into the hole after a mouse. | Don't trust him — he's a real weasel. | He tried to weasel out of washing up. | "Up to 50% off" uses weasel words. | The weasels took over Toad Hall in the story. | Weasels are the smallest meat-eating mammals in Britain.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. UK spelling weaselled, US weaseled. Calling a person a weasel is an insult. Pop Goes the Weasel is a nursery rhyme. Stoats look similar but are bigger with a black tail tip.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Webbing is strong, flat woven material in narrow strips, used for straps, belts, seat belts and bags. 2) Webbing is also the skin between the toes of animals like ducks and frogs.
its sense in the lessons: In design and technology it is a material for straps and harnesses. In science it describes webbed feet that help animals swim. Phrases: nylon webbing, webbing strap, the webbing between its toes.
examples from the lessons: The rucksack straps are made of nylon webbing. | Seat belts are made of very strong webbing. | Ducks have webbing between their toes to help them swim. | The climbing harness has thick webbing loops. | We used webbing to make a dog lead in DT. | Frogs' webbing pushes against the water.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: some webbing, a piece of webbing. Related: web, webbed (webbed feet).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Weirdly means in a strange or unusual way. 2) Weirdly (at the start of a sentence) means "strangely enough", to show that something is surprising.
its sense in the lessons: Common in everyday talk and stories to show surprise. Phrases: weirdly enough, weirdly quiet, acting weirdly.
examples from the lessons: The house was weirdly quiet when we got home. | Weirdly, the cat likes cucumbers. | He was acting weirdly all morning. | Weirdly enough, I passed the test without studying. | The sky looked weirdly green before the storm. | The clock stopped, weirdly, at midnight.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from weird + -ly. Spelling trap: "weird" breaks the "i before e" rule. Mostly informal; formal writing prefers strangely or unusually.

part of speech: adverb (westwards — mainly UK); also westward (mainly US, and as adjective)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Westwards means towards the west, the direction where the sun sets.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons it is used for directions, maps, winds and journeys, such as settlers moving westwards across North America. Phrases: head westwards, move westwards, travel westwards.
examples from the lessons: The ship sailed westwards across the Atlantic. | The storm is moving westwards. | Settlers travelled westwards in wagons. | The sun moves westwards across the sky during the day. | Walk westwards along the beach to find the cave. | The river flows westwards to the sea.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK usually westwards (adverb), US westward; westward is also the adjective: a westward journey. Opposite: eastwards. The sun seems to move west because Earth spins towards the east.

part of speech: noun (a whipping, whippings); verb form (whipping — from whip, whips, whipped, whipping); adjective (whipping cream)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A whipping is a punishment of being hit with a whip; it is cruel and now banned in most places. 2) (informal) A whipping is a heavy defeat in a game. 3) Whipping is beating cream or eggs fast to make them thick and fluffy. 4) Whipping (verb form) can mean moving fast and suddenly, like wind whipping.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons it describes cruel punishments of the past, including on enslaved people and sailors. In cooking it is about cream and egg whites. In sport talk it means a big win or loss. Phrases: whipping cream, a good whipping, whipping boy, the wind whipping.
examples from the lessons: In the past, sailors could get a whipping as punishment. | Whipping cream makes it thick and fluffy. | Our team got a whipping, 6–0. | The wind was whipping my hair across my face. | Buy whipping cream for the trifle. | A whipping boy is someone blamed for other people's mistakes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From whip (whipped, whipping; double p). Whipping cream is a type of cream; whipped cream is cream after whipping. Hitting people as punishment is wrong and illegal in many countries.

part of speech: noun (a whirlwind, whirlwinds); adjective-like before a noun (a whirlwind tour)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A whirlwind is a column of air that spins very fast, like a small tornado. 2) A whirlwind of activity is a lot of things happening very fast. 3) A whirlwind trip or romance is one that is very quick.
its sense in the lessons: In science it is a weather word; in stories and everyday life it describes busy, rushed or exciting times. Phrases: a whirlwind of, whirlwind tour, like a whirlwind.
examples from the lessons: A whirlwind picked up the leaves and spun them round. | The day was a whirlwind of parties and presents. | She came into the room like a whirlwind. | We had a whirlwind tour of London in one day. | Dust whirlwinds called dust devils form on hot days. | The last week of term is always a whirlwind.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Made from whirl (spin) + wind. Similar weather words: tornado, cyclone, dust devil (smaller whirlwind).

part of speech: verb (whizz, whizzes, whizzed, whizzing); noun (a whizz, whizzes); also spelled whiz (mainly US)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To whizz is to move very fast, often with a buzzing or whistling sound. 2) A whizz (informal) is a person who is very good at something: a maths whizz. 3) To whizz through something is to do it very quickly.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday talk it describes fast bikes, cars and arrows. In school, a "maths whizz" or "computer whizz" is someone very skilled. Phrases: whizz past, whizz by, whizz through, a whizz at, whizz-kid.
examples from the lessons: A bike whizzed past us on the path. | She is a whizz at mental maths. | I whizzed through my homework. | Arrows whizzed over the castle wall. | The fireworks whizzed into the sky. | My little brother is a computer whizz.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK spelling whizz, US whiz. Forms: whizzes, whizzed, whizzing. A "whizz-kid" is a young person who is very clever or successful. (UK slang, adults) whizz can also be a name for a drug — avoid.

part of speech: noun (widening — the act of making wider); verb form (widening — from widen, widens, widened, widening); adjective (widening)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Widening means becoming or making something wider. 2) A widening gap or problem is one that is getting bigger.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life it describes roads, rivers and eyes ("her eyes widening"). In news it describes growing gaps, like a widening gap between rich and poor. Phrases: road widening, widening gap, eyes widening.
examples from the lessons: The council is widening the road. | Her eyes were widening with surprise. | There is a widening gap between the two teams. | The river is widening as it nears the sea. | The road widening caused traffic jams. | The crack in the wall is widening.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From widen (wide + -en); drop the e: widening. Similar -en verbs: lengthen, shorten, deepen, brighten.

part of speech: noun (a wildcat, wildcats); adjective (wildcat — sudden and not officially allowed)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A wildcat is a wild cat that looks like a big tabby, living in Europe, Africa and Asia; the Scottish wildcat is very rare. 2) In America, wildcat can mean any wild member of the cat family, like a bobcat. 3) A wildcat strike is a sudden strike by workers without the union's official approval. 4) (informal) A wildcat is a fierce, wild person.
its sense in the lessons: In nature studies it is a rare, protected British animal. In news, a "wildcat strike" is a sudden, unofficial strike. Phrases: Scottish wildcat, wildcat strike.
examples from the lessons: The Scottish wildcat is one of Britain's rarest animals. | A wildcat looks like a tabby cat with a thick, ringed tail. | Workers walked out in a wildcat strike. | Wildcats hide in forests and hunt at night. | She fought like a wildcat. | Wildcats should not be kept as pets.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; one word (wildcat), though "wild cat" in two words is fine for any wild cat. Trap: a feral cat is a pet cat gone wild, not a true wildcat.

part of speech: noun (a wile, wiles — usually plural); verb (wile away — rare, usually "while away")
meaning for a pupil: 1) Wiles are clever tricks or charming ways used to persuade or fool someone.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and fairy tales it describes clever tricksters like foxes, witches or charming villains. Phrases: use all your wiles, feminine wiles (old-fashioned).
examples from the lessons: The fox used all his wiles to trick the crow. | Despite her wiles, the guard did not let her in. | The cat used its wiles to get an extra treat. | Odysseus was famous for his wiles. | He fell for the trickster's wiles.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually plural: wiles. Adjective: wily (clever and tricky, like a wily fox). Homophone: while (time). "While away the hours" is the usual spelling, though "wile away" is also seen.

part of speech: adjective (windward); adverb (windward); noun (the windward — the side facing the wind)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Windward means on the side facing the wind, the side the wind blows onto.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons it explains rain: the windward side of mountains gets more rain, while the leeward side is drier (a rain shadow). In sailing it names the side facing the wind. Phrases: the windward side, to windward, Windward Islands.
examples from the lessons: The windward side of the mountain is green and wet. | The leeward side is in a rain shadow and is drier. | The sailors steered to windward. | Waves are bigger on the windward shore. | The Windward Islands are in the Caribbean. | Trees on the windward side grow bent.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: leeward (said LOO-ard by sailors). Similar to upwind. Key geography idea: relief rainfall falls on the windward side.

part of speech: adjective (wireless); noun (a wireless, wirelesses — old-fashioned UK: a radio; wireless — wireless technology)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Wireless means working without wires, using radio waves, like wireless internet (Wi-Fi), wireless headphones or wireless charging. 2) (old-fashioned UK) A wireless is a radio set.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life it describes Wi-Fi, Bluetooth and phones. In history lessons, families in the 1930s and 1940s listened to news on the wireless during the war. Phrases: wireless network, wireless headphones, on the wireless.
examples from the lessons: Our school has a wireless network in every classroom. | My wireless headphones need charging. | In the war, Grandad's family heard the news on the wireless. | A wireless mouse uses a tiny radio signal. | Wireless charging works by putting the phone on a pad. | Turn off the wireless if you don't need it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective usually. The old noun "wireless" (radio) is still heard from grandparents. Safety: don't join unknown public wireless networks for anything private.

part of speech: numeral (XIII — Roman numeral, usually written in capitals)
meaning for a pupil: 1) XIII is the Roman numeral for thirteen: X = 10, I + I + I = 3, so XIII = 13. 2) It is used in names of kings, queens and popes (Louis XIII) and in some titles and clock faces.
its sense in the lessons: In maths lessons pupils read and write Roman numerals. In history it appears in rulers' names. Phrases: Louis XIII, chapter XIII, Pope Leo XIII.
examples from the lessons: XIII means thirteen. | King Louis XIII of France lived in the 1600s. | Chapter XIII is the last chapter of the book. | XIII = X + III = 10 + 3. | Pope Leo XIII was pope for 25 years. | Write the number 13 in Roman numerals: XIII.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Not a word but a number. Read "the thirteenth" after a name: Louis XIII = Louis the Thirteenth. Roman numerals have no zero. 14 is XIV (not XIIII), because 4 is written IV.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A xylophone is a musical instrument made of a row of wooden bars of different lengths that you hit with small hammers called beaters or mallets; each bar plays a different note.
its sense in the lessons: In music lessons it is a common classroom percussion instrument. In science lessons it shows that shorter bars make higher notes and longer bars make lower notes. It is also the classic "X" word in alphabet books. Phrases: play the xylophone, xylophone beaters.
examples from the lessons: I played a tune on the xylophone in music. | The shortest bar on the xylophone makes the highest note. | X is for xylophone. | Hit the bars gently with the beaters. | The orchestra's xylophone player sat with the drummers. | A glockenspiel looks like a xylophone but has metal bars.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Said ZY-lo-fone: the x sounds like z. From Greek xylon (wood) + phone (sound). Trap: a toy with metal bars is really a glockenspiel or metallophone, not a xylophone.

part of speech: noun/proper noun (Yi — a people, a language, a surname, a name); (Mandarin, pinyin) yī
meaning for a pupil: 1) (Mandarin, pinyin) yī means "one" in Mandarin Chinese; it sounds like English "ee". It is not an English word. 2) (a name) The Yi are an ethnic group in south-west China, with their own Yi language and script. 3) (a name) Yi is a common Korean and Chinese surname (also written Lee or Li), as in Admiral Yi Sun-sin of Korea.
its sense in the lessons: In language lessons it is one of the first Mandarin numbers: yī, èr, sān (1, 2, 3). In geography it names a people of China. Phrases: yī, èr, sān; the Yi people.
examples from the lessons: In Mandarin, yī, èr, sān means one, two, three. | "Yi" sounds like "ee" to an English ear. | The Yi people live in the mountains of south-west China. | Admiral Yi Sun-sin is a hero in Korean history. | Yī gè píngguǒ means "one apple" in Mandarin. | The Yi language has its own script.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Not an English word. In pinyin the mark on yī shows a high, flat tone. As a name it takes a capital letter.

part of speech: noun (yore — only in the phrase "of yore")
meaning for a pupil: 1) Yore means long ago; "days of yore" means the old days, times long past.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, poems and fairy tales it gives an old-fashioned feel, like "Once upon a time". Phrases: of yore, days of yore, in days of yore.
examples from the lessons: In days of yore, knights rode out to fight dragons. | Castles of yore had thick stone walls. | Grandpa likes to tell stories of yore. | The town still holds a fair, just as in days of yore. | Heroes of yore were remembered in songs. | It sounds like something from the days of yore.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Old-fashioned and literary; used almost only in "of yore". Homophones: your, you're (in many accents), yaw. Spelling: y-o-r-e.

part of speech: proper noun (Zhou — a name); (Mandarin, pinyin) zhōu
meaning for a pupil: 1) (a name) The Zhou dynasty ruled China for about 800 years, from about 1046 BC to 256 BC, longer than any other Chinese dynasty. 2) (a name) Zhou is a common Chinese surname, as in Zhou Enlai, a Chinese premier. 3) (Mandarin, pinyin) zhōu can mean "week" (xīngqī and zhōu both mean week), "state" or "province", or "porridge/congee" (粥 zhōu). It sounds like "joe" to an English ear. It is not an English word.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons the Zhou dynasty is the time of Confucius and the idea of the "Mandate of Heaven". In everyday Chinese, zhōu is part of words for week and for rice porridge. Phrases: the Zhou dynasty, zhōumò (weekend).
examples from the lessons: The Zhou dynasty lasted about 800 years. | Confucius lived near the end of the Zhou dynasty. | Zhōumò means "weekend" in Mandarin. | Zhou is a common family name in China. | Many Chinese people eat zhōu, rice porridge, for breakfast. | "Zhou" sounds a bit like "joe".
note for the reader of a maths problem: Not an English word. Pinyin zh sounds like English j. As a name it takes a capital letter. BC dates count down, so 1046 BC is earlier than 256 BC.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) A zinger is a quick, clever and funny remark, often a sharp joke at someone. 2) (informal) A zinger can also be something surprising or striking, like a zinger of a question.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday talk and comedy it names a witty one-liner. In stories it shows a sharp, funny character. Phrases: deliver a zinger, a real zinger.
examples from the lessons: Grandma came back with a real zinger that made everyone laugh. | The comedian had a zinger for every heckler. | The quiz ended with a zinger of a question. | He thought of the perfect zinger an hour too late. | A good zinger is funny without being cruel. | Her speech ended with a zinger.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal, mainly American but understood everywhere. Countable. A zinger at someone can hurt; be kind.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An abattoir is a building where animals such as cows, pigs and sheep are killed for meat. Another word is slaughterhouse.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and food lessons it explains where meat comes from. It is used in news about farming, food safety and animal welfare. Phrases: sent to the abattoir, abattoir worker.
examples from the lessons: The cattle were taken to the abattoir. | Abattoirs must follow strict rules about hygiene. | Many people become vegetarian after learning about abattoirs. | Vets check animals at the abattoir. | The local abattoir closed down. | Animal welfare laws say animals must not suffer in abattoirs.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: an abattoir (an before a vowel sound). Said AB-a-twar; from French. Spelling: one b, double t. Similar: slaughterhouse.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To abdicate is to give up being king or queen. 2) (formal) To abdicate a responsibility is to fail to do something you should.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons it is used for monarchs who stepped down, such as King Edward VIII in 1936. In formal writing it means not taking responsibility. Phrases: abdicate the throne, abdicate responsibility.
examples from the lessons: King Edward VIII abdicated in 1936 so he could marry. | Queen Margrethe of Denmark abdicated in 2024. | The emperor was forced to abdicate. | Parents cannot abdicate their responsibility to keep children safe. | After the king abdicated, his brother became king. | She refused to abdicate.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: abdicated. Noun: abdication. Not the same as resign (for jobs) or retire, though the meaning is similar.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) Abs are the stomach muscles; it is short for abdominal muscles. 2) ABS (in capitals) stands for anti-lock braking system, which stops a car's wheels locking when the driver brakes hard. 3) ABS is also a hard plastic used for things like LEGO bricks.
its sense in the lessons: In PE and health it names the core muscles at the front of the tummy. In cars and design lessons ABS is a safety system or a material. Phrases: work your abs, six-pack abs, ABS brakes.
examples from the lessons: Sit-ups help to strengthen your abs. | The coach said, "Tighten your abs and keep your back straight." | The car has ABS, so it can steer while braking hard. | LEGO bricks are made of ABS plastic. | Strong abs help you keep good posture. | He showed off his abs at the beach.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Abs is a clipped form of abdominals and is always plural. ABS is an abbreviation, said A-B-S. Myth: doing only sit-ups does not remove tummy fat from one spot.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Acetic means to do with vinegar or acetic acid. 2) Acetic acid is the weak acid that gives vinegar its sour taste and sharp smell.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons it appears in experiments with acids, such as vinegar and bicarbonate of soda fizzing. Phrases: acetic acid.
examples from the lessons: Vinegar is mostly water with some acetic acid. | Acetic acid gives vinegar its sour smell. | When vinegar meets baking soda, the acetic acid reacts and makes bubbles. | Strong acetic acid can burn your skin, so scientists wear gloves. | The pickles tasted sharp because of the acetic acid. | Acetic acid is a weak acid.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Said a-SEE-tic. Do not confuse with ascetic (living a very simple life without comforts) or aesthetic (about beauty). Safety: concentrated acids are dangerous even if vinegar is safe.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An acrobat is a performer who does difficult and exciting movements like flips, balancing and jumps, especially in a circus.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and stories it is about circus performers, gymnasts and very agile animals. Phrases: circus acrobat, trapeze acrobat, a natural acrobat.
examples from the lessons: The acrobat did a backflip on the tightrope. | Chinese acrobats can balance on each other's shoulders. | Monkeys are acrobats of the forest. | She wants to be an acrobat when she grows up. | The acrobats flew from one trapeze to another. | Our cat is a real acrobat on the fence.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: an acrobat. Adjective: acrobatic; noun for the skill: acrobatics. Safety: practise flips only with a trained coach and mats.

part of speech: noun (an acropolis, acropolises); proper noun (the Acropolis — a name of a place in Athens)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (a name) The Acropolis is a rocky hill in Athens, Greece, with ancient temples on top, including the Parthenon. 2) An acropolis is the high, fortified part of any ancient Greek city.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons about Ancient Greece it is a key place, linked with the goddess Athena and Greek architecture. Phrases: the Acropolis of Athens, on the Acropolis.
examples from the lessons: The Parthenon stands on the Acropolis in Athens. | The Acropolis was built to honour the goddess Athena. | Many Greek cities had an acropolis on a hill for defence. | We saw the Acropolis lit up at night. | The Acropolis is about 2,500 years old. | Tourists climb the hill to visit the Acropolis.
note for the reader of a maths problem: With a capital A for the one in Athens. From Greek akro (high) + polis (city). Plural acropolises (rare). Said a-KROP-o-lis.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An activator is something that starts something working or makes it more active. 2) In science, an activator is a substance that starts or speeds up a chemical change, like the hardener in some glues.
its sense in the lessons: In science and technology it is a word for whatever switches something on. In everyday life it appears on glue, paint and cleaning products. Phrases: glue activator, activator solution.
examples from the lessons: Add the activator to the slime glue to make it thicken. | The alarm's activator is a small sensor by the door. | Some glue needs an activator to set hard. | The coach was the team's activator, always getting them moving. | Read the safety label before using the activator. | Sunlight acts as an activator for some reactions.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. From activate (to make active) + -or. Related: active, activity, activation. Safety: activators in craft kits can irritate skin — follow instructions.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An activist is a person who works hard to bring about political or social change, for example by campaigning, protesting or writing letters.
its sense in the lessons: In history and citizenship lessons it describes people like Rosa Parks, Malala Yousafzai or Greta Thunberg. In news it is used for campaigners on any side. Phrases: climate activist, civil rights activist, human rights activist.
examples from the lessons: Rosa Parks was a civil rights activist. | Malala became an activist for girls' education. | Climate activists marched through the city. | Activists collected signatures for a petition. | You can be an activist by writing to your local council. | The activists held up signs outside parliament.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: an activist. Related: active, activism. "Activist" itself is neutral; people may disagree about a particular activist's cause or methods. Peaceful protest is legal in many countries; violence and damage are not.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Adaptable means able to change to suit new situations or places. 2) An adaptable thing can be changed for different uses.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons it describes animals and plants that survive in many habitats, like foxes and rats. In everyday life it praises people who cope well with change, like moving school. Phrases: highly adaptable, adaptable to.
examples from the lessons: Foxes are adaptable and live in both cities and forests. | Be adaptable when plans change. | This adaptable table can be made bigger. | Humans are very adaptable animals. | Good teachers are adaptable to every pupil. | The adaptable plant grows in sun or shade.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From adapt + -able. Noun: adaptability; adaptation (science: a feature that helps a living thing survive). Do not confuse adapt with adopt (to take as your own).

meaning for a pupil: 1) An adder is a small poisonous snake, the only venomous snake native to Britain, with a dark zig-zag pattern down its back. Another name is common European viper. 2) An adder is a person or thing that adds numbers, such as a part of a computer that adds.
its sense in the lessons: In nature and safety it is a snake of heathland and moors; bites are rare but need medical help. In computing it is a simple circuit. In Australia, the death adder is a different, very dangerous snake. Phrases: adder bite, death adder.
examples from the lessons: An adder was sunbathing on the heath path. | The adder has a black zig-zag stripe. | If an adder bites you, keep still and get medical help. | Adders are shy and usually slip away from people. | A computer has an adder circuit that adds numbers. | The death adder lives in Australia.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: an adder. Fun fact: "a nadder" became "an adder" long ago. Safety: never touch a snake; walk away calmly, and keep dogs on leads on heaths.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Adherence is sticking closely to a rule, plan, belief or agreement and following it. 2) Adherence is also the act of sticking physically to something.
its sense in the lessons: In formal writing, news and health it means following rules or treatment, like adherence to the school code or to a doctor's medicine plan. Phrases: adherence to, strict adherence.
examples from the lessons: The school expects adherence to its uniform rules. | Strict adherence to safety rules keeps the lab safe. | Adherence to medicine is important for getting better. | The team's adherence to the plan won the match. | Their adherence to tradition is strong. | The glue's adherence to plastic is poor.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; everyday words: following, sticking to. Verb: adhere (to); adhesive = glue. An adherent is a follower of a belief.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Admirable means deserving praise and respect; very good.
its sense in the lessons: In ethics and stories it describes good qualities and actions such as honesty, courage and kindness. In school reports it praises effort. Phrases: an admirable effort, admirable courage, quite admirable.
examples from the lessons: It was admirable that she told the truth. | Firefighters show admirable courage. | The team made an admirable effort despite losing. | His patience with his little brother is admirable. | Admirable qualities include kindness and honesty. | The speech was admirable.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb: admirably. Verb: admire. Stress: AD-mir-a-ble (not ad-MIRE-able). Spelling: -able.

part of speech: noun (an advocate, advocates); verb (advocate, advocates, advocated, advocating)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To advocate something is to publicly support it or speak in favour of it. 2) An advocate is a person who speaks up for an idea or for other people. 3) (law) An advocate is a lawyer who speaks for someone in court, especially in Scotland.
its sense in the lessons: In citizenship and news it is about people who argue for change, like advocates for animal rights. In law it names a type of lawyer. Phrases: advocate for, an advocate of, devil's advocate.
examples from the lessons: She advocates healthy school meals. | He is an advocate for children's rights. | The advocate spoke for the accused in court. | Many doctors advocate more exercise. | Playing devil's advocate means arguing the other side to test an idea. | Be your own advocate and ask for help.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronunciation differs: the noun ends "-kit" (AD-vo-kit), the verb ends "-kate" (AD-vo-kate). Noun: advocacy. In Scotland, advocates are like barristers in England.

part of speech: proper noun (the Aegean — a name of a sea); adjective (Aegean)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (a name) The Aegean Sea is the part of the Mediterranean Sea between Greece and Turkey, with many islands. 2) Aegean describes the islands and ancient peoples of that area.
its sense in the lessons: In history and geography lessons about Ancient Greece it is the sea of Greek islands, trade and myths. Phrases: the Aegean Sea, Aegean islands.
examples from the lessons: The Aegean Sea lies between Greece and Turkey. | Crete is the largest island in the Aegean. | Greek sailors traded across the Aegean. | The water of the Aegean is clear and blue. | In the myth, King Aegeus threw himself into the sea, and it was named the Aegean. | Ferries hop between the Aegean islands.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Written with a capital A. Said ee-JEE-an. Spelling: Ae at the start.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (UK, Ireland, Australia, NZ) An aerial is a wire or rod that sends or picks up radio or TV signals; in the US it is called an antenna. 2) Aerial means from the air or in the air, like an aerial photograph taken from a plane or drone. 3) An aerial in sport (skiing, snowboarding) is a jump with a flip in the air.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons, aerial photos and maps show a place from above. In everyday life the TV aerial is on the roof. Phrases: aerial view, aerial photograph, TV aerial, aerial ropeway.
examples from the lessons: The TV aerial blew off the roof in the storm. | This aerial photo shows our school from above. | Drones take aerial pictures. | An aerial view helps you draw a map. | The snowboarder did an aerial with two flips. | Bats are aerial hunters.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable as a noun. UK aerial = US antenna. Said AIR-ee-al. Related: aeroplane, aero- = air.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Affirmative means saying "yes" or agreeing. 2) In grammar, an affirmative sentence is a positive statement, not a negative one ("I like cats" not "I don't like cats"). 3) "Affirmative!" (informal) is a way of saying yes, as in films with soldiers or pilots. 4) Affirmative action (USA) means policies to help groups who have been treated unfairly.
its sense in the lessons: In English grammar lessons it contrasts with negative sentences. In debates, the affirmative side argues for the motion. Phrases: in the affirmative, affirmative sentence, affirmative answer.
examples from the lessons: I can swim is an affirmative sentence. | She answered in the affirmative: yes. | "Affirmative, captain!" | The affirmative team spoke first in the debate. | Change the negative sentence into the affirmative. | He nodded, an affirmative sign.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: negative. Formal; everyday word: yes, positive. Verb: affirm.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Affordable means cheap enough for people to be able to buy or pay for.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and money lessons it is about prices of food, homes and toys. In news it appears in "affordable housing". Phrases: affordable housing, affordable prices, more affordable.
examples from the lessons: This bike is more affordable than that one. | The town needs more affordable homes. | Fresh fruit should be affordable for every family. | We looked for an affordable holiday. | Second-hand books are very affordable. | Prices became less affordable this year.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From afford + -able. Opposite: unaffordable, expensive. In maths problems, "affordable" means the price is not more than the money you have: with £20, a £15 toy is affordable, a £25 one is not.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An aftershock is a smaller earthquake that comes after a big earthquake in the same area. 2) Aftershocks can also mean the effects or upsets that follow a big shocking event.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and safety lessons it explains why people stay careful after an earthquake. In news it describes after-effects of a big event. Phrases: strong aftershock, aftershocks continued.
examples from the lessons: Aftershocks shook the city for days after the earthquake. | Stay out of damaged buildings because of aftershocks. | The aftershock was smaller than the main quake. | New Zealand had many aftershocks after the Christchurch earthquake. | The aftershocks of the news were felt across the school. | Drop, cover and hold on during an aftershock too.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; one word. Safety: aftershocks can knock down buildings weakened by the main earthquake.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An agave is a plant with thick, spiky, sword-shaped leaves that grows in hot, dry places, mainly Mexico and the south-west USA. 2) Agave syrup (agave nectar) is a sweet syrup made from it.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons it is an example of a plant adapted to the desert, storing water in its thick leaves. In food it is a sweetener. Phrases: agave syrup, blue agave, century plant.
examples from the lessons: The agave stores water in its fat, spiky leaves. | Some agaves flower only once after many years and then die. | Mum uses agave syrup instead of sugar. | Be careful — agave leaves have sharp tips. | The agave is sometimes called the century plant. | Agaves grow in dry, sunny gardens.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Said a-GAH-vee. Myth: the "century plant" does not take a hundred years to flower — usually 10 to 30. Agave is not a cactus.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Alertness is being awake, watchful and ready to notice and react quickly.
its sense in the lessons: In safety and health it matters for crossing roads, driving and learning; sleep and breakfast help alertness. In science it is linked to the brain and caffeine. Phrases: mental alertness, stay alert, increase alertness.
examples from the lessons: Sleep helps your alertness in class. | The guard's alertness stopped the thief. | Drivers need full alertness. | Too much screen time at night lowers alertness the next day. | Dogs show alertness when they prick up their ears. | Coffee can increase alertness in adults.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. From alert + -ness. Related: alert (adjective, noun, verb). Children should not use energy drinks to boost alertness.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (law) An alibi is proof that a person was somewhere else when a crime happened, so they could not have done it. 2) (informal) An alibi is an excuse.
its sense in the lessons: In detective stories it is a key idea: the detective checks each suspect's alibi. In everyday talk it means any excuse. Phrases: a strong alibi, a cast-iron alibi, check an alibi.
examples from the lessons: The butler had an alibi: he was at the shop. | The detective checked every suspect's alibi. | Her alibi was proved false by the CCTV. | "I was with my gran" was his alibi. | My alibi for being late was the bus. | A cast-iron alibi cannot be broken.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: alibis. From Latin for "elsewhere". Said AL-i-bye.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An allergen is a substance that causes an allergic reaction in some people, such as pollen, peanuts, dust mites, pet fur or bee stings.
its sense in the lessons: In science, health and safety lessons it explains allergies, food labels and why some schools are nut-free. Phrases: common allergen, food allergen, allergen-free.
examples from the lessons: Peanuts are a common allergen. | Food labels show allergens in bold. | Pollen is the allergen that causes hay fever. | The school kitchen keeps a list of allergens. | Cat fur is an allergen for my cousin. | An allergen can cause sneezing, rash or swelling.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Related: allergy, allergic. Safety: a severe reaction (anaphylaxis) is an emergency — use the adrenaline pen and call for help. Allergen is said AL-er-jen.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Ambergris is a waxy, grey substance made in the gut of sperm whales; it is sometimes found floating in the sea or washed up on beaches and was used in perfumes.
its sense in the lessons: In science and nature stories it is a strange and valuable natural material. In history it was traded like treasure. Phrases: a lump of ambergris.
examples from the lessons: Ambergris comes from sperm whales. | People who find ambergris on the beach can sometimes sell it for lots of money. | Ambergris was used in perfume to make the smell last. | It has a sweet, earthy smell when old. | Most perfumes now use man-made substitutes for ambergris. | A lump of ambergris washed up on the shore.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Said AM-ber-grees. Not the same as amber (fossil tree resin). In some countries trading ambergris is restricted to protect whales.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An amphipod is a small shrimp-like animal with no shell on its back, such as the sand hopper found on beaches.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on minibeasts, rock pools and food chains it is a common invertebrate. Phrases: freshwater amphipod, sand hoppers.
examples from the lessons: Sand hoppers are amphipods that jump on the beach. | Amphipods are food for fish and birds. | We found amphipods under stones in the stream. | Amphipods are crustaceans, like crabs and shrimps. | Some amphipods live in the deepest ocean trenches. | Our pond dip found tiny amphipods.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. From Greek amphi (both kinds) + pod (foot). Related groups: isopods (woodlice), decapods (crabs).

meaning for a pupil: 1) To amplify a sound is to make it louder, often with electronic equipment. 2) To amplify something is to make it bigger, stronger or more important. 3) To amplify a statement is to add more detail to explain it.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons it is about sound and electricity: amplifiers make sound louder. In everyday life and news it is about making voices or problems bigger. Phrases: amplify sound, amplify a message, amplify a problem.
examples from the lessons: The speakers amplify the singer's voice. | A megaphone amplifies your voice. | Shouting amplified the argument. | Social media can amplify rumours. | Could you amplify your answer with an example? | Cupping your hands round your mouth amplifies your call.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: amplifies, amplified (y changes to i). Noun: amplifier (amp), amplification. Similar: boost, increase.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The amygdala is a small almond-shaped part deep inside the brain that helps us feel and react to emotions, especially fear.
its sense in the lessons: In science and wellbeing lessons it helps explain feelings: the amygdala sounds the alarm in danger ("fight, flight or freeze"). Phrases: the amygdala, brain's alarm.
examples from the lessons: The amygdala helps you feel scared when you see danger. | Your amygdala reacts before you even think. | Deep breathing helps calm the amygdala. | The amygdala is shaped like an almond. | Each brain has two amygdalae, one on each side. | Scientists study the amygdala to understand fear.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually "the amygdala". Plural amygdalae or amygdalas. Said a-MIG-da-la. From Greek for almond. Simplified idea: the brain is much more complex than "alarm" parts.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Anatomically means in a way that is to do with the structure of the body.
its sense in the lessons: In science it describes models and drawings of the body and how body parts are shaped. Phrases: anatomically correct, anatomically similar.
examples from the lessons: The model skeleton is anatomically correct. | Anatomically, a whale's flipper is like a human hand. | Humans and chimpanzees are anatomically similar. | The artist drew the horse anatomically accurately. | Anatomically, the heart is slightly to the left. | Anatomically modern humans appeared about 300,000 years ago.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal science word. From anatomy (the structure of the body, and the science of it). Myth: the heart is near the middle of the chest, only tipped slightly left.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Your ancestry is all the people in your family who lived long before you, such as great-grandparents, and the places and groups they came from.
its sense in the lessons: In history and family-history projects it is about family trees and where families came from. Phrases: of Irish ancestry, trace your ancestry, ancestry test.
examples from the lessons: She is of Irish and Polish ancestry. | We drew a family tree to trace our ancestry. | Many Americans have European, African or Asian ancestry. | His ancestry goes back to Viking times. | DNA tests can tell you some things about your ancestry. | Ancestry is about the past; who you are is also about your choices.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Related: ancestor (one person), ancestral. Ancestors are people before you; descendants come after you.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An angelfish is a brightly coloured tropical fish with a flat body and long fins, living on coral reefs or kept in aquariums.
its sense in the lessons: In science and nature lessons it is an example of a coral reef or freshwater tropical fish. Phrases: freshwater angelfish, marine angelfish.
examples from the lessons: The angelfish swam gracefully in the tank. | Angelfish live on coral reefs. | Its fins look like wings, so it was named angelfish. | Freshwater angelfish come from the Amazon. | Angelfish have flat, tall bodies. | We saw blue and yellow angelfish when snorkelling.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural usually angelfish. One word.

part of speech: noun (an ante, antes); verb (ante, antes, anted, anteing — ante up); prefix (ante- meaning before)
meaning for a pupil: 1) An ante is a stake put into the pot before a card game starts. 2) To up the ante means to increase what is at stake or make a situation more serious or demanding. 3) Ante- at the start of a word means "before", as in antenatal (before birth) or anteroom.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday talk "up the ante" is common in news and sport. In words, ante- means before. Phrases: up the ante, raise the ante, ante up.
examples from the lessons: The team upped the ante by training twice a day. | The players put in their ante. | Antenatal classes help parents before a baby is born. | The bully upped the ante, so the teacher stepped in. | An anteroom is a small room before a bigger one. | Ante up — everyone puts in a coin!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: ante- (before) is different from anti- (against): antenatal vs antibiotic. Said AN-tee.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To apprehend someone is to catch and arrest them. 2) (formal) To apprehend something is to understand it.
its sense in the lessons: In news and detective stories police "apprehend a suspect". In formal writing it can mean understand. Phrases: apprehend a suspect, apprehended by police.
examples from the lessons: The police apprehended the thief at the station. | The suspect was apprehended after a chase. | It took time to apprehend the full danger. | Officers apprehended two people. | Security guards cannot always apprehend shoplifters. | She quickly apprehended what was happening.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; everyday words: catch, arrest, understand. Noun: apprehension. Regular verb: apprehended.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Apprehension is worry or fear that something bad might happen. 2) (formal) Apprehension is the arrest of someone. 3) (formal) Apprehension can also mean understanding.
its sense in the lessons: In stories it shows a character's nervous feeling before something, like a test or a scary place. In news it means arrest. Phrases: feel apprehension, with apprehension, a sense of apprehension.
examples from the lessons: She felt apprehension before her first day at a new school. | With apprehension, he opened the door. | The apprehension of the robber took weeks. | There was apprehension in his voice. | Talking to someone can ease apprehension. | They waited for the results with apprehension.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly uncountable for the feeling. Adjective: apprehensive (worried). Similar: anxiety, unease, dread.

part of speech: noun (an apricot, apricots); adjective (apricot — the colour)
meaning for a pupil: 1) An apricot is a small, round, soft fruit with orange-yellow skin and a large stone inside. 2) Apricot is a pale orange-yellow colour.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life it is a fruit for snacks, jam and dried fruit. In art it is a colour name. Phrases: dried apricots, apricot jam, apricot tree.
examples from the lessons: I had dried apricots in my lunchbox. | Apricot jam is my favourite. | The apricot tree is full of fruit. | She painted her room apricot. | Apricots have a large stone in the middle. | Apricot kernels should not be eaten — they can be poisonous.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable for the fruit. Said AY-pri-cot (UK) or AP-ri-cot (US). Safety: the seed (kernel) inside the stone contains a poison.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Arsenic is a chemical element (symbol As); many of its compounds are very poisonous. 2) In history and crime stories, arsenic was a famous poison.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons it is an element in the periodic table. In history it was used in wallpaper, medicines and pest killers, and in old mystery stories as poison. Phrases: arsenic poisoning, traces of arsenic.
examples from the lessons: Arsenic is a poisonous element. | The Victorians used arsenic in green wallpaper. | Water in some countries has dangerous arsenic in it. | Arsenic's chemical symbol is As. | The detective suspected arsenic poisoning. | Rice can contain tiny amounts of arsenic from soil.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Said AR-se-nik. Safety: never touch or taste unknown chemicals.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Artistic means good at art or creative things like drawing, painting, music or design. 2) Artistic means to do with art or artists. 3) Artistic also means attractive and done with skill and imagination.
its sense in the lessons: In school it praises creative pupils and describes art subjects and choices. Phrases: artistic talent, artistic skills, artistic flair, artistic licence.
examples from the lessons: She is very artistic and loves painting. | The display was really artistic. | Artistic licence lets writers change facts for a story. | He shows great artistic talent. | The town has an artistic community. | The cake was decorated in an artistic way.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb: artistically. Related: art, artist, artwork. "Artistic licence" (UK spelling licence, US license).

meaning for a pupil: 1) One part or side of a situation, problem or idea that you can think about. 2) The way something looks or seems from a certain point of view. 3) The direction a building, room or garden faces, such as a south aspect. 4) (grammar) A way a verb shows whether an action is finished, ongoing or repeated, as in "I am reading" versus "I read".
its sense in the lessons: In school it appears in essays and science ("consider every aspect of the problem"), in geography (a slope's aspect affects sunlight), and in grammar lessons about verb forms. It tells the reader that something has several parts and one of them is being looked at. Common phrases: "every aspect of", "in all aspects", "one aspect of", "the most important aspect".
examples from the lessons: Safety is the most important aspect of the trip. | We looked at every aspect of the problem before deciding. | The house has a sunny southern aspect, so the garden is warm. | One aspect of being a good friend is listening. | Money was only one aspect of the argument. | The teacher asked us to write about a different aspect of life in Roman Britain. | Plants on the north aspect of the hill grow more slowly. | "I was running" shows the continuous aspect of the verb.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: an aspect, two aspects; starts with a vowel sound, so "an aspect". Do not confuse with "respect" or "expect". Often followed by "of": "an aspect of the job". In grammar, aspect (finished or ongoing) is different from tense (past, present, future).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Belonging to or coming from Athens, the capital city of Greece, especially ancient Athens. 2) A person who lived in ancient Athens or lives in Athens today.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons about ancient Greece it describes the people, buildings, government and ideas of Athens, the city famous for early democracy, the Parthenon and thinkers like Socrates and Plato. Stories often compare Athenians with Spartans. Common phrases: "Athenian democracy", "the Athenian army", "an Athenian citizen".
examples from the lessons: The Athenians built the Parthenon on a hill called the Acropolis. | Athenian democracy let some citizens vote on laws. | Women and slaves could not vote in the Athenian assembly. | Socrates was a famous Athenian thinker. | The Athenian navy fought the Persians at Salamis. | We compared Athenian and Spartan children in class. | An Athenian boy went to school to learn reading, music and sport.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Written with a capital A because it comes from a place name. Plural: Athenians. Remember that Athenian democracy was not for everyone: only free adult men who were citizens could vote. Do not confuse Athens (Greece) with Athens, a town in the USA.

part of speech: adjective (attentive, more attentive, most attentive); adverb attentively; noun attentiveness
meaning for a pupil: 1) Listening or watching carefully and paying close attention. 2) Kind and helpful, noticing what other people need.
its sense in the lessons: At school a teacher may praise an attentive class or pupil who listens well. In stories it describes a careful listener or a caring host, nurse or friend. It tells the reader that someone is focused or thoughtful. Common phrases: "attentive to", "an attentive listener", "listen attentively".
examples from the lessons: The class was very attentive during the science demonstration. | Be attentive when the lifeguard gives the rules. | She is an attentive listener and remembers what you say. | The waiter was attentive and refilled our water. | The nurse was attentive to every patient. | Attentive readers will spot the clue in chapter two. | The dog sat attentively, waiting for the ball.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It is an adjective; the noun is "attention" (pay attention) and the adverb is "attentively". Use "attentive to" someone or something. Do not confuse with "attractive" (nice to look at) or "attendant" (a helper).

meaning for a pupil: 1) The fact of being the person who wrote a book, article, song or other piece of work. 2) The question of who wrote something, when it is not certain.
its sense in the lessons: In English and history lessons it appears when we ask who wrote a text, and in discussions about copying and giving credit. It tells the reader who made a piece of writing. Common phrases: "the authorship of", "claim authorship", "disputed authorship", "joint authorship".
examples from the lessons: The authorship of the old poem is unknown. | Nobody is sure about the authorship of some fairy tales. | The two friends shared authorship of the comic. | You must not claim authorship of work you copied. | Experts argued about the authorship of the letter. | Putting your name on a project shows your authorship.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable: "authorship", not "an authorship". It comes from "author" plus "-ship" (like friendship). Copying someone's work and saying it is yours is called plagiarism and is cheating.

part of speech: noun (automation, uncountable); verb automate (automate, automates, automated, automating)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Using machines and computers to do work by themselves, without people doing each step. 2) The system or machines that do this work.
its sense in the lessons: In science, computing and design lessons it describes robots in factories, self-service tills, automatic doors and programs that repeat tasks. In everyday talk and the news it often comes up with jobs, because automation can replace some jobs and create others. Common phrases: "factory automation", "home automation", "due to automation".
examples from the lessons: Automation means robots can build cars in a factory. | The car wash uses automation, so nobody scrubs the cars by hand. | Some jobs disappeared because of automation. | Home automation can switch the lights on when you come in. | Our coding club learned about automation with a simple program. | Automation makes the work faster but needs people to fix the machines. | Dad says automation at the supermarket means fewer cashiers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: "automation", not "an automation". The verb is "automate", the adjective is "automatic". Automation is not the same as artificial intelligence: many automatic machines just follow fixed steps.

part of speech: noun (a backup, backups); adjective (backup plan); verb phrase back up (back up, backs up, backed up, backing up)
meaning for a pupil: 1) An extra copy of computer files kept safe in case the first copy is lost. 2) Extra help or support, such as more police or players who can join when needed. 3) Something kept ready in case the first plan fails, like a backup plan. 4) (US) A traffic jam or a blockage, such as a sink backup.
its sense in the lessons: In computing lessons pupils learn to make a backup of their work. In everyday life and safety it means having a second plan or extra help. In stories police "call for backup". Phrases: "make a backup", "backup plan", "call for backup", "back up your files", "back someone up" (support them).
examples from the lessons: Always make a backup of your homework on a memory stick. | My laptop broke, but I had a backup in the cloud. | If it rains, our backup plan is the cinema. | The officer called for backup. | The backup goalkeeper came on in the second half. | Please back up your files before the update. | My friend backed me up when I told the truth. | There was a backup of cars on the motorway.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Written as one word "backup" for the noun and adjective, but as two words "back up" for the verb: "I back up my files" and "I have a backup". Countable: a backup, two backups.

part of speech: adjective (baffled); verb past form of baffle (baffle, baffles, baffled, baffling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Completely confused, not able to understand or explain something. 2) (past form of baffle) Made someone confused.
its sense in the lessons: In stories it shows a character who cannot work something out, often a detective or a teacher with a puzzle. In maths and science it describes a pupil stuck on a hard problem. Phrases: "completely baffled", "baffled by", "left baffled".
examples from the lessons: I was baffled by the last maths question. | The detective was baffled by the missing key. | Scientists were baffled by the strange light in the sky. | The magic trick left everyone baffled. | Grandad looked baffled when I explained the video game. | Her answer baffled the whole class. | The puzzle baffled us for an hour.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelled with double f. Use "baffled by" something. The related adjective "baffling" describes the puzzle itself: "a baffling puzzle" makes you "baffled". Similar words: puzzled, confused, bewildered.

part of speech: noun (ballast, uncountable); verb (ballast, ballasts, ballasted, ballasting — rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Heavy material, such as stones, sand or water, put low in a ship or balloon to keep it steady. 2) The stones laid under railway tracks to hold them in place. 3) Something that gives steadiness or balance to a person or plan.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about floating and balance, ballast shows how weight low down keeps a boat upright and how submarines take in water to sink. Hot-air balloons drop sandbags of ballast to rise. Railway workers lay ballast under tracks. Phrases: "ballast tanks", "drop ballast", "take on ballast".
examples from the lessons: The ship carried rocks as ballast to stop it rolling over. | The submarine filled its ballast tanks with water to dive. | The balloonist threw out a bag of sand ballast and the balloon rose. | Grey ballast stones lie under the railway sleepers. | We added coins to the bottom of our model boat as ballast. | Weight low down acts as ballast and keeps the boat steady.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable: "some ballast". Throwing out ballast makes a balloon lighter so it rises; taking on ballast makes a ship or submarine heavier so it sits lower. Do not confuse with "ballet" or "balance".

meaning for a pupil: 1) A female ballet dancer, especially a leading one in a ballet company. 2) A ballerina shoe or flat: a flat, soft shoe that looks like a ballet slipper.
its sense in the lessons: It appears in stories, music and dance lessons and when talking about shows like The Nutcracker or Swan Lake. It tells the reader a girl or woman dances ballet, often with skill and grace. Phrases: "prima ballerina", "ballerina shoes", "a music box ballerina".
examples from the lessons: The ballerina spun on the tips of her toes. | My sister wants to be a ballerina when she grows up. | The prima ballerina danced the lead in Swan Lake. | A tiny ballerina turned in the music box. | Ballerinas train for many hours every day. | She wore ballerina flats to the party. | Boys and men who dance ballet are called ballet dancers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: ballerinas. A male ballet dancer is usually just called a ballet dancer (sometimes "danseur"), not a ballerina. "Prima ballerina" means the most important female dancer in a company.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A small sea animal with a hard shell that sticks itself to rocks, ships and whales and stays there. 2) (informal) A person who sticks to someone and will not go away.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about rock pools and sea life, barnacles are crustaceans (related to crabs) that feed by waving feathery legs to catch food. On a beach trip children see them on rocks and piers. Phrases: "covered in barnacles", "barnacle geese".
examples from the lessons: The rocks at the beach were covered in barnacles. | Barnacles stick to the bottom of boats and slow them down. | A barnacle catches food with its feathery legs. | Be careful, barnacles are sharp on bare feet. | The old whale had barnacles on its skin. | Barnacles are related to crabs and lobsters, not to snails. | My little brother clung to me like a barnacle all day.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a barnacle, barnacles. Many people think barnacles are shellfish like mussels, but they are crustaceans. The barnacle goose is a bird; old stories wrongly said it grew from barnacles.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The yard or area around a barn on a farm, where animals walk and feed. 2) (as an adjective) To do with farm animals, or rough and rude, like "barnyard humour".
its sense in the lessons: It appears in farm stories, songs and picture books about cows, pigs, hens and ducks, and in science lessons about farm animals. It sets a farm scene for the reader. Phrases: "barnyard animals", "in the barnyard", "barnyard noises".
examples from the lessons: The hens pecked at grain in the barnyard. | We made barnyard animal noises in music class. | The pig rolled in the mud of the barnyard. | The story is set in a noisy barnyard. | A rooster crowed from the barnyard fence. | Children fed the goats in the barnyard at the farm park. | The comedian told silly barnyard jokes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a barnyard, barnyards. Mainly used in American English; British speakers often say "farmyard". Made of "barn" plus "yard".

part of speech: adjective (barred); verb past form of bar (bar, bars, barred, barring)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Not allowed to go in or to do something: banned. 2) Having bars across it, like a barred window or gate. 3) Having stripes of colour, like a barred owl's feathers. 4) (past form of bar) Blocked a way, or stopped someone.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life it means banned from a place or activity ("barred from the club"). In stories it describes locked or blocked windows, gates and roads, often in castles or prisons. In nature it describes striped feathers or fur. Phrases: "barred from", "barred the way", "no holds barred" (with no rules).
examples from the lessons: He was barred from the game for cheating. | The prison had barred windows. | A fallen tree barred the road. | Dogs are barred from the playground. | The barred owl has striped feathers on its chest. | The guards barred the castle gate at night. | The debate was no holds barred.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past form of "bar" doubles the r: bar, barred, barring. Do not confuse "barred" with "bard" (a poet), which sounds the same. "Barred from" means not allowed.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A shiny ball or decoration hung on a Christmas tree. 2) A small, cheap piece of jewellery or a pretty object of little value.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, especially in the UK, Ireland, Australia and New Zealand, baubles are Christmas tree decorations. In stories it can describe cheap trinkets, sometimes to show that someone values worthless things. Phrases: "Christmas baubles", "glass baubles", "a mere bauble".
examples from the lessons: We hung red and gold baubles on the Christmas tree. | The cat knocked a glass bauble off the branch. | In art we painted our own baubles. | The queen's crown was real gold, not a cheap bauble. | She bought a little bauble at the market stall. | Be careful: broken baubles can cut your fingers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a bauble, baubles. In American English people often say "ornament" for a Christmas bauble. Sounds like "BAW-bul".

meaning for a pupil: 1) A market, especially in the Middle East or South Asia, with many small shops and stalls in a street or covered area. 2) A sale held to raise money for a school, church or charity, also called a fete or fair.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and history lessons it describes busy markets in places such as Istanbul, Cairo or Delhi. In school and church life, a bazaar or Christmas bazaar is a fundraising sale with cakes, toys and crafts. Phrases: "Christmas bazaar", "the Grand Bazaar", "a church bazaar".
examples from the lessons: The bazaar was full of spices, carpets and lamps. | The Grand Bazaar in Istanbul has thousands of shops. | Our school holds a Christmas bazaar every December. | Mum baked cupcakes for the church bazaar. | We bargained for a bag at the bazaar. | The bazaar raised enough money for new library books.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelled with double z and double a: b-a-z-a-a-r. Do not confuse with "bizarre" (very strange), which sounds similar. Countable: a bazaar, bazaars.

part of speech: adjective (biased, more biased, most biased); verb past form of bias (bias, biases, biased, biasing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Unfairly favouring one person, side or idea over another, often without good reasons. 2) (maths and science) Not fair or not random, like a biased coin or dice that lands one way more often. 3) (past form of bias) Made someone or something unfair.
its sense in the lessons: In lessons on news and history pupils learn to spot biased reports that show only one side. In maths, a biased dice changes probabilities, and in science a biased test is not fair. In everyday life a biased referee favours one team. Phrases: "biased against", "biased towards", "biased opinion", "a biased coin".
examples from the lessons: The referee was biased towards the home team. | This article is biased because it only gives one side. | A biased dice landed on six far too often. | Try not to be biased when you judge the drawings. | The survey was biased because they only asked their friends. | Everyone can be a little biased without noticing. | Our science test was unfair and biased, so we did it again.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelled with one s (biased) in most dictionaries; "biassed" is a rare British spelling. In maths, for a fair coin each side has probability 1/2; for a biased coin the probabilities are different, so you need to test it many times to find them. The noun is "bias".

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who offers money for something at an auction. 2) A company or person who offers to do a job for a certain price.
its sense in the lessons: It appears in stories and real life about auctions, online sales and building contracts. It tells the reader someone is competing to buy or to get work. Phrases: "the highest bidder", "the lowest bidder", "sold to the highest bidder".
examples from the lessons: The painting was sold to the highest bidder. | There were ten bidders at the farm auction. | The bidder in the green hat raised her paddle. | Online, the last bidder won the toy at the final second. | The council chose the bidder with the best plan. | Only one bidder offered more than the starting price.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comes from "bid" (bid, bids, bid, bidding) with double d. "The highest bidder" wins an auction. In maths problems about auctions, each new bid must be bigger than the one before.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A true book or story about a real person's life, written by someone else. 2) A short description of a person's life, such as on a website or book cover.
its sense in the lessons: In English and history lessons pupils read and write biographies of famous people like Mary Seacole or Martin Luther King. A biography is non-fiction, so it should use facts, dates and order of events. Phrases: "write a biography", "a biography of", "a short biography".
examples from the lessons: We wrote a biography of Florence Nightingale. | A biography tells a real person's life story. | The library has a whole shelf of sports biographies. | My biography of Grandma includes her move to Canada. | A good biography uses facts and dates in order. | The author's short biography is on the back cover.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: biographies (y changes to ies). A story you write about your own life is an "autobiography", not a biography. Writers of biographies are "biographers".

part of speech: noun (the bise — wind); (French) noun (une bise, des bises)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A cold, dry wind that blows from the north or north-east over Switzerland and parts of France. 2) (French) A light kiss on the cheek used as a greeting, as in "faire la bise". It sounds like "beez" and is not an everyday English word.
its sense in the lessons: In geography it names a local wind, like the mistral. In French lessons and on the street in France or Quebec, "la bise" is the cheek-kiss greeting between friends and family. Phrases: "faire la bise" (French), "grosses bises" (French, "big kisses", at the end of a letter).
examples from the lessons: The bise blew cold across Lake Geneva. | In winter the bise makes Geneva feel freezing. | In France, friends greet each other with la bise. | Grosses bises means "big kisses" at the end of a French note. | My French penfriend gave me la bise on both cheeks. | How many kisses in la bise depends on the region.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced "beez". In English it is only used for the wind and when talking about the French greeting; it is not a common English word. Do not confuse with "bees" or "bis".

meaning for a pupil: 1) In an angry, hurt and unhappy way. 2) Very, extremely, when talking about cold weather: bitterly cold. 3) Very strongly, in phrases like bitterly disappointed or bitterly opposed.
its sense in the lessons: In stories it shows strong unhappy feelings ("she wept bitterly") or very harsh weather. In the news and history it describes fierce arguments and fights. Phrases: "bitterly cold", "bitterly disappointed", "bitterly complained", "bitterly fought".
examples from the lessons: It was bitterly cold, so we wore two jumpers. | He cried bitterly when his dog ran away. | We were bitterly disappointed when the trip was cancelled. | The two teams fought bitterly for the cup. | "That's not fair," she said bitterly. | The wind blew bitterly across the field.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from the adjective "bitter" (sour taste, or angry and hurt). "Bitterly cold" just means very cold, not angry.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A black, sticky, tar-like substance made from oil, used to make road surfaces and waterproof roofs. 2) (Australia, New Zealand) The tarred surface of a road; also called "the bitumen".
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about materials and oil it is a material that is waterproof and sticky when hot and hard when cool. In Australia and New Zealand people say "the bitumen" for a sealed road compared with a dirt road. In history, bitumen was used to waterproof boats and in ancient building. Phrases: "on the bitumen" (Australia), "bitumen roof".
examples from the lessons: The workers spread hot bitumen on the road. | Bitumen keeps the roof dry. | In Australia we drove off the bitumen onto a dusty track. | Bitumen gets soft and sticky on very hot days. | Ancient people used bitumen to seal their boats. | Do not touch hot bitumen; it can burn your skin.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: "some bitumen". Pronounced "BITCH-oo-men" or "BIT-yoo-men". Americans usually say "asphalt" or "blacktop"; British people often say "tarmac" for the road surface. Hot bitumen is dangerous.

part of speech: verb (blab, blabs, blabbed, blabbing); noun (a blab, blabbermouth — informal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) To tell a secret, often by talking carelessly. 2) (informal) To talk too much about silly things.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday talk and stories it describes someone who cannot keep a secret, like a friend who tells about a surprise party. Phrases: "blab to", "blab about", "don't blab", "a blabbermouth" (someone who blabs).
examples from the lessons: Don't blab about the surprise party! | Who blabbed to the teacher? | My brother blabbed my secret to the whole class. | He blabbed on about football for an hour. | She promised not to blab, and she didn't. | You can't tell him anything, he's such a blabbermouth.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal word. Past form doubles the b: blabbed, blabbing. Telling an adult when someone is in danger is not "blabbing"; it is the right thing to do.

part of speech: adjective (blond, blonder, blondest; blonde often used for women); noun (a blond, a blonde)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Having pale yellow or golden hair. 2) Pale yellow or golden in colour, like blond hair or blond wood. 3) A person with blond hair.
its sense in the lessons: It appears in descriptions of people in stories, character writing and everyday talk. It tells the reader hair colour. Phrases: "blond hair", "dyed blonde", "strawberry blonde" (reddish blond), "platinum blonde" (very pale).
examples from the lessons: My cousin has curly blond hair. | Her hair goes blonder in the summer sun. | The baby was born with fluffy blond hair. | The table is made of light blond wood. | He dyed his hair blond for the concert. | The girl with the blonde plait is my sister.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Two spellings: "blond" for men and things and often in American English for everyone; "blonde" often for women and girls, especially in British English, and as the noun "a blonde". Calling someone "a blonde" can sound rude; it is kinder to say "she has blonde hair". Jokes that say blond people are not clever are a false stereotype.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A path made of wooden boards, often built over sand, mud or wet ground. 2) (US) A wooden walkway along a beach with shops, food stands and rides.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and nature it describes paths through wetlands, beaches and forests that protect plants and keep feet dry. In American everyday life, a boardwalk is a seaside promenade, like Atlantic City. Phrases: "along the boardwalk", "on the boardwalk".
examples from the lessons: We walked along the boardwalk through the swamp. | The boardwalk stops people trampling the sand dunes. | We ate ice cream on the boardwalk by the beach. | The wooden boardwalk was slippery after the rain. | A turtle crossed under the boardwalk. | Stay on the boardwalk to protect the plants.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a boardwalk, boardwalks. Made of "board" plus "walk". In the UK, a seaside walkway is more often called a "promenade" or "prom".

part of speech: noun (a bola, bolas; also bolas as singular)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A throwing weapon made of two or three heavy balls joined by cords, thrown to wrap around an animal's legs and catch it. 2) (Bola) The name of a spider called the bolas spider, which catches moths with a sticky ball on a thread.
its sense in the lessons: In history and geography lessons it is linked with the gauchos (cowboys) of Argentina and with the native peoples of South America, who used bolas for hunting. In science it appears with the bolas spider. Phrases: "throw a bola", "bolas spider".
examples from the lessons: The gaucho swung the bola around his head. | A bola wrapped around the running animal's legs. | Native hunters in South America used bolas to catch rheas. | The museum had a bola made of stones and leather. | The bolas spider swings a sticky ball to catch moths.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Both "bola" and "bolas" are used for one weapon; the plural can be "bolas" or "bolases". Not a toy: bolas can hurt people and animals.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A large tropical seabird with bright blue or red feet that dives into the sea to catch fish. 2) (old-fashioned) A silly or stupid person. 3) (rude, slang) a rude word for a part of the body; not for school. 4) A booby trap: a hidden trap, often a hidden bomb, set off when someone touches something harmless-looking.
its sense in the lessons: In science and nature it is a seabird, like the blue-footed booby of the Galapagos. In stories and history "booby trap" means a hidden trap. The slang breast sense is rude and children may hear it as a giggle word. Phrases: "blue-footed booby", "booby trap", "booby prize" (a joke prize for coming last).
examples from the lessons: The blue-footed booby dances to show off its feet. | Boobies dive from high up to catch fish. | Don't open the box, it might be a booby trap! | The soldiers checked the road for booby traps. | I came last and won the booby prize, a wooden spoon. | (rude) The older boys giggled and said "boobies".
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: boobies. The breast meaning is rude slang; do not use it at school. "Booby prize" is a joke prize for the worst result. The bird's name may come from a Spanish word for "fool", because it was easy to catch.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A small, thin book with a paper cover, often giving information or instructions.
its sense in the lessons: At school pupils get exam booklets, reading booklets and maths booklets; in everyday life there are instruction booklets, travel booklets and safety booklets. Phrases: "answer booklet", "instruction booklet", "information booklet".
examples from the lessons: Write your answers in the answer booklet. | The toy came with an instruction booklet. | We made a booklet about our class trip. | Read the safety booklet before using the bike. | The teacher handed out a maths booklet for homework. | The museum gave us a free booklet about the dinosaurs.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a booklet, booklets. "-let" means small, as in "piglet" and "droplet", so a booklet is a small book.

part of speech: noun (brachiation, uncountable); verb brachiate (brachiate, brachiates, brachiated, brachiating)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A way of moving through trees by swinging from branch to branch using the arms, as gibbons and some monkeys do.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about animals and movement it describes how gibbons, orangutans and spider monkeys travel. Children on monkey bars are doing a kind of brachiation. Phrases: "move by brachiation".
examples from the lessons: Gibbons move through the forest by brachiation. | Brachiation lets apes swing fast from tree to tree. | On the monkey bars we copied brachiation. | A gibbon's long arms are perfect for brachiation. | Spider monkeys also use their tails during brachiation.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable science word. Pronounced "bray-kee-AY-shun". It comes from a Latin word for "arm", like "brachial".

meaning for a pupil: 1) Slightly salty, a mix of fresh water and sea water, like water where a river meets the sea. 2) (of water) Not nice to drink, a bit salty or dirty.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and science lessons it describes estuaries, mangroves, marshes and lagoons, where special plants and animals live. Phrases: "brackish water", "brackish lagoon".
examples from the lessons: Brackish water is found where rivers meet the sea. | Mangroves grow well in brackish water. | The well water tasted brackish. | Some fish can live in fresh, salty and brackish water. | The Baltic Sea is brackish, less salty than the ocean. | Never drink brackish water when camping; it can make you ill.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective only. Brackish water is in between fresh water (almost no salt) and sea water (about 35 grams of salt per litre).
