part of speech: noun (bragging, uncountable); verb -ing form of brag (brag, brags, bragged, bragging)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Talking proudly about yourself and what you have or can do, in a way that annoys others: boasting. 2) (as in "bragging rights") The right to boast because you won.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and lessons on kindness it shows a character who is a show-off. In everyday life it comes up after games and tests. Phrases: "stop bragging", "bragging about", "bragging rights".
examples from the lessons: Stop bragging about your new trainers. | He was bragging that he scored three goals. | Nobody likes bragging. | The winners get bragging rights until next year. | She kept bragging about her test score. | In the fable, the hare was bragging about his speed.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The g doubles: brag, bragged, bragging. Similar word: boasting. Telling people good news is fine; bragging means doing it to look better than others.

part of speech: noun (Braille or braille, uncountable); adjective (braille letters)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A system of raised dots that blind and partly sighted people read by touching them with their fingers. Each letter is a pattern of up to six dots.
its sense in the lessons: In lessons on disability, history and communication pupils learn that Louis Braille, a blind French boy, invented it in the 1820s. In everyday life braille appears on lift buttons, medicine boxes and signs. Phrases: "in braille", "read braille", "braille signs".
examples from the lessons: My aunt reads books in braille. | The lift buttons have braille on them. | Louis Braille invented braille when he was a teenager. | Each braille letter is made of up to six raised dots. | We wrote our names in braille using glue dots. | The medicine box has the name in braille.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Often written with a capital B because it is named after Louis Braille, but lower case "braille" is also common. Uncountable: "some braille", "in braille". Braille is not a language; it is a way of writing many languages.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A tropical tree from the coast of Brazil with hard red wood. 2) The red wood of this tree, used to make red dye and the best bows for violins.
its sense in the lessons: In history and geography lessons, brazilwood gave the country Brazil its name, because Portuguese traders came for its red dye. In music it is the wood of fine violin bows. It is now endangered. Phrases: "brazilwood tree", "brazilwood bow".
examples from the lessons: Brazil was named after the brazilwood tree. | Traders used brazilwood to make red dye for cloth. | Good violin bows are made of brazilwood. | Brazilwood trees are now rare and protected. | The heartwood of brazilwood is a deep orange-red.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word, usually lower case. Also called "pau-brasil" in Portuguese. Do not confuse with the brazil nut, which comes from a different tree.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A soft, sweet French bread made with eggs and butter, often shaped like a bun with a little top knot.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life it is breakfast bread or a burger bun; in French lessons it is a French word kept in English. In history the line "Let them eat cake" is really "qu'ils mangent de la brioche" in French. Phrases: "brioche bun", "a slice of brioche".
examples from the lessons: I had a brioche with jam for breakfast. | The burger came in a shiny brioche bun. | Brioche is softer and sweeter than normal bread. | We baked brioche in French class. | The baker brushed the brioche with egg so it would shine.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced "BREE-osh". Can be countable (a brioche, two brioches) or uncountable (some brioche). It contains eggs, milk and butter, so it is not suitable for people with egg or milk allergies.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Meat cut from the chest of a cow, cooked slowly until it is soft.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and cooking it is a barbecue favourite in the USA (especially Texas), a Jewish holiday dish, and a slow roast in the UK, Ireland and Australia. Phrases: "smoked brisket", "beef brisket", "salt beef brisket".
examples from the lessons: Dad smoked a beef brisket for eight hours. | Brisket is tough unless you cook it slowly. | Grandma makes brisket for family holidays. | The barbecue restaurant is famous for its brisket. | We had brisket sandwiches at the fair.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable for the meat: "some brisket"; "a brisket" means a whole piece. Pronounced "BRIS-kit".

part of speech: adjective (brooding); verb -ing form of brood (brood, broods, brooded, brooding); noun (brooding)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Thinking for a long time about something that makes you sad, worried or angry. 2) Looking dark, gloomy or threatening, like brooding clouds. 3) (of birds) Sitting on eggs to keep them warm until they hatch.
its sense in the lessons: In stories it describes moody characters or a gloomy setting; in science it describes hens and other birds sitting on eggs. Phrases: "brooding over", "a brooding silence", "brooding hen".
examples from the lessons: He sat brooding over the lost match. | Dark, brooding clouds hung over the mountains. | The brooding hen would not leave her eggs. | Stop brooding and talk to someone about it. | The hero was quiet and brooding. | The castle looked brooding in the mist.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From the verb "brood". A "brood" is also a noun for a group of baby birds. If you keep brooding about a worry, it helps to tell a trusted adult.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Friendship and loyalty between people, like the feeling between brothers. 2) A group or society of people with the same aims or job, such as a religious brotherhood. 3) The relationship of being brothers.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, history and church life it appears in ideas of fairness and peace ("the brotherhood of all people") and in names of groups like monks or trade unions. Phrases: "brotherhood of man", "a sense of brotherhood", "a religious brotherhood".
examples from the lessons: The team felt a strong sense of brotherhood. | Martin Luther King dreamed of brotherhood between all people. | The monks lived together as a brotherhood. | Songs about peace often talk about brotherhood. | War broke the brotherhood between the two towns. | Their brotherhood lasted all their lives.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Can be uncountable (a feeling) or countable (a group). Although it says "brother", it often includes everyone; the word "sisterhood" is used for women.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A bush with long, cone-shaped clusters of purple, white or pink flowers that attract many butterflies; also called the butterfly bush.
its sense in the lessons: In science and nature lessons it appears in gardens and wild places, especially in the UK, where it grows on railway sides and old walls. It is loved by butterflies but can spread too much. Phrases: "butterfly bush", "a purple buddleia".
examples from the lessons: Butterflies crowded on the buddleia. | A buddleia was growing out of the old wall. | We planted a buddleia to attract butterflies. | The buddleia flowers smell of honey. | Buddleia can spread fast and push out wild plants.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelled buddleia or buddleja. Pronounced "BUD-lee-uh". It is named after a man called Adam Buddle.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Strong enough to stop bullets from going through, like a bulletproof vest or glass. 2) (informal) Not able to fail or be harmed; very safe or certain.
its sense in the lessons: In news and stories it appears with police, soldiers and important people. In everyday talk it means very strong or reliable ("a bulletproof plan"). Phrases: "bulletproof vest", "bulletproof glass", "bulletproof car".
examples from the lessons: Police officers wear bulletproof vests. | The president's car has bulletproof glass. | The bank counter is protected by bulletproof screens. | His excuse wasn't bulletproof, and the teacher saw through it. | Nobody is bulletproof, so ride your bike carefully.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word. "-proof" means protected against, like waterproof and soundproof. Many "bulletproof" vests are really bullet-resistant and cannot stop every bullet.

part of speech: noun (a bypass, bypasses); verb (bypass, bypasses, bypassed, bypassing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A road that goes around a town instead of through it. 2) (medicine) An operation that makes a new path for blood to flow around a blocked part of the heart's blood vessels. 3) (verb) To go around something or someone to avoid it. 4) (verb) To ignore a rule or system or avoid using it.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and everyday life a bypass helps traffic avoid a busy town. In health lessons and news, heart bypass surgery is common. In computing, "bypass security" means getting around protection, which can be illegal. Phrases: "heart bypass", "take the bypass", "bypass the rules".
examples from the lessons: We took the bypass to avoid the town traffic. | Grandad had a heart bypass operation. | The new road will bypass the village. | You cannot bypass the queue just because you're in a hurry. | Hackers tried to bypass the password. | The river bypassed the old mill.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word for both noun and verb. Past form: bypassed. Bypassing a safety lock or password without permission is wrong and may be illegal.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (UK, informal) A small, simple, cheap café, often serving fried breakfasts, tea and sandwiches. It is a short form of "café".
its sense in the lessons: In British everyday talk and stories it describes a "greasy spoon" café where workers eat. Phrases: "the local caff", "greasy caff".
examples from the lessons: We had egg and chips at the local caff. | The builders always stop at the caff for a cuppa. | Meet you at the caff on the corner. | The caff opens at six for breakfast. | The old caff by the station has steamed-up windows.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal British word, rhymes with "laugh" in some accents and with "gaff" in others. Spelled with double f. It means the same as café but sounds casual.

part of speech: verb (calculate, calculates, calculated, calculating); noun calculation; adjective calculated, calculating
meaning for a pupil: 1) To work out an amount or answer using numbers, in your head, on paper or with a calculator. 2) To judge or estimate something by thinking carefully. 3) (calculated) Planned on purpose, like "a calculated risk". 4) (calculating) Clever in a cold, selfish way, planning to get what you want.
its sense in the lessons: In maths it is the main instruction word: "Calculate the area", "Calculate the total". In science it means finding values like speed. In stories "calculating" describes a cunning villain. Phrases: "calculate the total", "calculate how many", "a calculated risk".
examples from the lessons: Calculate 24 × 3. | We calculated the area of the playground. | Calculate how much change you get from £5. | Scientists calculate how fast the planet moves. | She calculated that she could finish before dark. | It was a calculated risk to go for the goal. | The calculating fox tricked the crow.
note for the reader of a maths problem: In a maths question "calculate" means show working and give an exact number. Not the same as "estimate" (a rough answer). Spelled with one l: calculate, calculator.

part of speech: adjective (canned); verb past form of can (can, cans, canned, canning — to put into tins)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Kept in a sealed metal can or tin, like canned beans. 2) (of laughter, music) Recorded earlier and played again, not live, like canned laughter on TV. 3) (US, informal) Fired from a job. 4) (informal) Stopped or cancelled, like a canned TV show.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and cooking it means tinned food. In media lessons, canned laughter is recorded laughter added to comedy shows. Phrases: "canned food", "canned laughter", "got canned" (lost a job).
examples from the lessons: We collected canned food for the food bank. | Canned peaches last a long time. | That show has canned laughter. | The factory canned tomatoes all summer. | He got canned from his job at the cinema. | The TV series was canned after one season.
note for the reader of a maths problem: In British English people often say "tinned" food. The verb "can" (to put in cans) doubles the n: canned, canning. This is different from the helping verb "can" (be able), which has no past "canned". Throw away cans that bulge or leak: the food may be unsafe.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A very large wild bird of the grouse family that lives in pine forests in Scotland, Scandinavia and other cold parts of Europe and Asia. The males are black and puff out their tails in spring.
its sense in the lessons: In science and nature lessons, especially in Scotland, it is an endangered bird that people work to protect. In spring the males gather and make clicking and popping sounds to attract females. Phrases: "capercaillie display".
examples from the lessons: The capercaillie is the biggest grouse in the world. | Capercaillies live in old Scottish pine forests. | The male capercaillie fanned out his tail. | Only a few capercaillies are left in Scotland. | Keep dogs on a lead so they don't disturb capercaillies.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced "kap-er-KAY-lee". Its name comes from Scottish Gaelic and means "horse of the woods".

meaning for a pupil: 1) (US) The Capitol: the building in Washington, D.C. where the US Congress meets to make laws. 2) (US) The building where a state's lawmakers meet, a state capitol. 3) (history) The temple of Jupiter on the Capitoline Hill in ancient Rome.
its sense in the lessons: In lessons about the USA and politics it is the building with the big white dome. It is easily confused with "capital". Phrases: "the Capitol building", "Capitol Hill", "the state capitol".
examples from the lessons: The US Congress meets in the Capitol. | The Capitol has a huge white dome. | We visited the state capitol in Austin. | Capitol Hill is often used to mean the US Congress. | In ancient Rome, the Capitol was a temple on a hill.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: "capitol" with -ol means a building; "capital" with -al means a main city (Washington is the capital), money, or a big letter. Memory trick: the Capitol has a dOme, so it has an O.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (church) A senior leader in the Roman Catholic Church who wears red and helps choose the Pope. 2) A bright red songbird of North America; the male is red with a crest. 3) (adjective) Most important or basic, as in "a cardinal rule". 4) (maths) A cardinal number is a counting number like one, two, three, as opposed to first, second, third. 5) A deep red colour.
its sense in the lessons: In church and history lessons cardinals elect the Pope. In nature lessons in the USA and Canada the cardinal is a common garden bird. In maths, cardinal numbers count how many and ordinal numbers show order. Geography uses "cardinal points" for north, south, east and west. Phrases: "cardinal points", "cardinal numbers", "cardinal rule", "cardinal sin".
examples from the lessons: The cardinals met in Rome to choose a new Pope. | A red cardinal sat on our bird feeder. | The cardinal points are north, east, south and west. | Three is a cardinal number; third is an ordinal number. | The cardinal rule of the pool is no running. | The cardinal wore a red robe and hat.
note for the reader of a maths problem: In maths: cardinal numbers = 1, 2, 3 (how many); ordinal numbers = 1st, 2nd, 3rd (which position). "Cardinal sins" in church teaching are the seven deadly sins. Plural: cardinals.

part of speech: noun (a caricature, caricatures); verb (caricature, caricatures, caricatured, caricaturing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A funny drawing of a person that makes some features, like a big nose or ears, look much bigger than they are. 2) A description of a person or thing that makes them seem silly by exaggerating them. 3) (verb) To draw or describe someone in this exaggerated way.
its sense in the lessons: In art lessons pupils draw caricatures; in history and media lessons political cartoons use caricature to make a point. In stories it can mean a character who is too simple, like a cartoon. Phrases: "a caricature of", "draw a caricature".
examples from the lessons: An artist at the fair drew a caricature of me with huge teeth. | The newspaper cartoon was a caricature of the prime minister. | In the film, the villain is a caricature, not a real person. | We caricatured our teacher's big smile, kindly. | The caricature made the king's crown enormous.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced "KARR-ik-a-chur". A caricature exaggerates on purpose; it should not be used to bully people about their looks.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A small plastic box with magnetic tape inside, used to record and play music or sound, popular from the 1970s to the 1990s. 2) A small sealed case that holds film, ink or other things for a machine. 3) (bikes) The set of gear cogs on a bike's back wheel.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons about technology it shows how people listened to music before CDs and streaming. Grandparents may talk about cassette players and mixtapes. Phrases: "cassette tape", "cassette player", "on cassette".
examples from the lessons: Mum still has her old cassette tapes. | You needed a pencil to rewind a tangled cassette. | Grandad played a cassette in the car. | We recorded our band on a cassette. | Cassettes came before CDs and streaming. | The mechanic changed the cassette on my bike.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced "ka-SET". Spelled with double s and double t. Plural: cassettes. Often shortened to "tape".

meaning for a pupil: 1) Speeding up a chemical reaction without being used up; working as a catalyst. 2) Causing important changes to happen.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons it describes catalysts that make reactions faster, like enzymes in the body. In everyday life, cars have a "catalytic converter" that turns harmful exhaust gases into less harmful ones. Phrases: "catalytic converter", "catalytic role".
examples from the lessons: A catalytic converter cleans a car's exhaust gases. | Enzymes are catalytic and speed up digestion. | Thieves sometimes steal catalytic converters from cars. | The teacher showed a catalytic reaction that made foam. | Her speech played a catalytic role in changing the rules.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective of "catalyst". Pronounced "kat-a-LIT-ik". A catalyst is not used up in the reaction, so it can work again and again.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A sudden terrible event that causes great damage or suffering, like an earthquake or flood. 2) (informal) Something that goes very badly wrong.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and history lessons it describes natural disasters and wars; in everyday talk it can be a joking exaggeration ("the cake was a catastrophe"). Phrases: "a natural catastrophe", "end in catastrophe", "avert a catastrophe".
examples from the lessons: The flood was a catastrophe for the town. | Scientists warn that the dam could fail and cause a catastrophe. | The volcano eruption was a catastrophe for Pompeii. | Our science fair project was a total catastrophe. | Quick action prevented a catastrophe. | Forgetting the tickets would be a catastrophe!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced "ka-TAS-truh-fee" with four syllables; the final e is said. Plural: catastrophes. Adjective: catastrophic.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person or thing that catches something. 2) (baseball, softball) The player who crouches behind the batter and catches the balls the pitcher throws. 3) A tool or device for catching, like a rat catcher or a dream catcher.
its sense in the lessons: In sports lessons in the USA and Canada the catcher is a key baseball position. In everyday life and stories there are dream catchers, fly catchers and rat catchers. Phrases: "the catcher's mitt", "dream catcher", "fly catcher".
examples from the lessons: The catcher signalled to the pitcher. | Our catcher wears a mask and padding. | I made a dream catcher in art class. | The rat catcher came to the old barn. | The flycatcher is a bird that catches insects in the air. | He is a good catcher of a ball.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a catcher, catchers. "-er" means a person or thing that does the action, like "teacher" or "runner".

meaning for a pupil: 1) The process of one thing making another thing happen; cause and effect. 2) (formal) The link showing that one event was really caused by another.
its sense in the lessons: In science, maths and history lessons pupils learn that two things happening together (correlation) does not always mean one causes the other (causation). Phrases: "correlation is not causation", "cause and causation", "prove causation".
examples from the lessons: Scientists did tests to prove causation. | Ice cream sales and sunburn rise together, but that is not causation; the sun causes both. | Historians study the causation of wars. | Correlation does not mean causation. | We looked at causation in our science experiment.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable, formal word. Do not confuse with "correlation" (two things going up or down together). To show causation in science you usually need a fair test where you change only one thing.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A large cave, often deep under the ground. 2) Any large, dark, empty space that feels like a cave.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and science lessons caverns form when water dissolves limestone over thousands of years. In stories and fantasy, caverns are full of dragons, treasure and danger. Phrases: "underground cavern", "a vast cavern", "cavern system".
examples from the lessons: The explorers found a huge cavern under the hill. | Stalactites hung from the cavern ceiling. | The dragon slept in a dark cavern. | Water carved out the cavern over thousands of years. | Never explore caverns without an adult and a guide. | The empty hall felt like a cavern.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a cavern, caverns. A cavern is usually bigger than a cave. Adjective: "cavernous" (huge and empty).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who is 100 years old or older.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and science lessons it links with "cent" meaning 100 (century, centimetre). In news and everyday life, people celebrate when a grandparent becomes a centenarian. Phrases: "become a centenarian".
examples from the lessons: My great-grandma is a centenarian; she is 101. | The centenarian got a birthday card from the King. | Japan has many centenarians. | A centenarian has lived for at least a century. | The village threw a party for its first centenarian.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced "sen-ten-AIR-ee-an". "Cent-" means 100: a century is 100 years. If someone was born in 1925, they become a centenarian in 2025 (2025 − 1925 = 100). In the UK, people turning 100 get a card from the King.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The soft, waxy, often brightly coloured patch of skin at the top of a bird's beak, around the nostrils, found in birds such as parrots, budgies, hawks and pigeons.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons and pet care, the colour of a budgie's cere can show whether it is male (often blue) or female (often brown or pale). Phrases: "the cere of a budgie".
examples from the lessons: The budgie's blue cere shows it is a male. | Hawks have a yellow cere above the beak. | The vet checked the parrot's cere. | A female budgie's cere is often brown. | The cere has the bird's nostrils in it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced like "seer". Do not confuse with "sear" (to burn) or "Ceres" (a dwarf planet and a Roman goddess). Countable: ceres.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To do with the brain, especially the main part of it called the cerebrum. 2) Thinking a lot in a clever, serious way, using the mind more than feelings.
its sense in the lessons: In science and health lessons it appears in "cerebral palsy" (a condition affecting movement, from birth) and in descriptions of the brain. In stories it describes a thoughtful, clever character or film. Phrases: "cerebral palsy", "cerebral cortex", "a cerebral film".
examples from the lessons: The cerebral cortex is the wrinkly outer layer of the brain. | My classmate has cerebral palsy and uses a walker. | Chess is a very cerebral game. | The film was too cerebral for my little brother. | A cerebral detective solves crimes by thinking hard.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced "SER-uh-bral" or "suh-REE-bral". Cerebral palsy is not an illness you can catch, and people with it can be just as clever as anyone.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal, history, law) The act of giving up land or rights to another country or person, often after a war or by a treaty.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons it describes land handed over by treaties, such as the Mexican Cession of 1848 to the United States, or Hong Kong's cession to Britain. Phrases: "the cession of", "land cession", "the Mexican Cession".
examples from the lessons: The treaty forced the cession of the island. | The Mexican Cession gave the USA land including California. | Cession of land often happened after a war. | Hong Kong was given to Britain by cession in 1842. | Native nations were pushed into the cession of their lands.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal word. It sounds exactly like "session" (a meeting or period of time), which is a homophone; do not mix them up. The verb is "cede".

meaning for a pupil: 1) Likely to change often, not staying the same, like changeable weather. 2) Able to be changed.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and science it describes weather, especially in the UK and Ireland, where sun and rain can come in one day. In stories it describes moody characters. Phrases: "changeable weather", "changeable mood".
examples from the lessons: The weather is changeable, so take a raincoat. | April weather in Ireland is very changeable. | His mood was changeable, happy one minute and cross the next. | The phone has a changeable cover. | Weather forecasts say "changeable" when sun and showers mix.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: keep the e: change + able = changeable (the e keeps the g soft, like "j"). Not "changable".

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a very messy, confused and disorganised way, with no order.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and everyday life it describes busy, out-of-control scenes like a party or a classroom. In science, chaos theory studies systems that seem to change chaotically. Phrases: "run around chaotically", "chaotically organised".
examples from the lessons: The puppies ran chaotically around the kitchen. | Toys were scattered chaotically across the floor. | The game ended chaotically when the ball went over the fence. | Traffic moved chaotically after the lights failed. | The crowd pushed chaotically towards the exit, which was dangerous.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced "kay-OT-ik-lee", with a hard k sound at the start. Adverbs from "-ic" adjectives end in "-ically": chaotic, chaotically. In an emergency it is safer to move calmly, not chaotically.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (UK, Australia, informal) Having a lot of mucus in the chest from a cold, with a deep, wet cough, as in "a chesty cough". 2) (rude, slang) a rude word about a woman's body; not for school. 3) (informal) Having a big, broad chest; proud and showy.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life in the UK, Ireland and Australia, cough medicine boxes say "for chesty coughs" and "for dry coughs". The breast sense is rude slang. Phrases: "a chesty cough", "chesty cold".
examples from the lessons: I've got a chesty cough and I can't stop coughing. | Mum bought medicine for chesty coughs. | Grandad sounds chesty this morning. | The doctor said my chesty cold should clear in a week. | If a chesty cough lasts for weeks, see a doctor.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal. The commonest sense is about coughs. The body-shape sense is rude and should not be used about people. Comparative: chestier, chestiest.

part of speech: noun (chi — the Greek letter; chi or qi — Chinese idea); (Mandarin, pinyin) chī, "to eat"
meaning for a pupil: 1) The 22nd letter of the Greek alphabet, written χ, said "kye" (rhymes with "sky"). 2) (Chinese tradition) Also spelled qi: in Chinese belief, a life energy said to flow through the body and nature, used in tai chi, kung fu and traditional medicine. 3) (Mandarin, pinyin) chī means "to eat", as in chī fàn, "eat a meal". It sounds like "chir" to an English ear and is not an English word.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and science the Greek letter χ appears in statistics (the chi-squared test). In PE and culture lessons, tai chi is a slow exercise from China. In Mandarin on the street, "chī fàn le ma?" means "Have you eaten?", a friendly greeting. Phrases: "tai chi", "chi-squared".
examples from the lessons: Grandma does tai chi in the park every morning. | Chi is the Greek letter that looks like an x. | Some people believe chi flows through the body. | In Mandarin, chī means "to eat". | My friend said "chī fàn le ma?" to his grandad. | Scientists say there is no proof that chi exists as a real energy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced "kye" for the Greek letter and "chee" for the Chinese energy (qi). "Qi" is the official pinyin spelling of the energy word. Saying "chi" is a belief in Chinese tradition, not a scientific fact. The Greek χ is not the English letter x.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A small striped squirrel of North America (and one kind in Asia) that lives in burrows and carries food in its cheek pouches.
its sense in the lessons: In science and nature lessons in the USA and Canada it is a common woodland animal that stores nuts for winter. In stories and cartoons (like Alvin and the Chipmunks) chipmunks are cheeky and fast. Phrases: "chipmunk cheeks" (puffed-out cheeks).
examples from the lessons: A chipmunk stuffed acorns into its cheeks. | Chipmunks have stripes down their backs. | We saw a chipmunk at the campsite in Canada. | The chipmunk ran into its burrow. | With his mouth full of marshmallows he had chipmunk cheeks. | Chipmunks sleep a lot in winter and wake to eat stored food.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a chipmunk, chipmunks. Chipmunks do not live wild in the UK, Ireland, Australia or New Zealand. Do not feed wild chipmunks; they can bite.

part of speech: verb (chomp, chomps, chomped, chomping); noun (a chomp)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To bite and chew food noisily and with big mouthfuls. 2) (noun) A big, noisy bite.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and everyday talk it describes hungry people and animals, like a crocodile chomping. Phrases: "chomp on", "chomp through", "chomping at the bit" (very eager to start).
examples from the lessons: The horse chomped on an apple. | He chomped through three sandwiches. | The crocodile's jaws went chomp! | Don't chomp with your mouth open. | We were chomping at the bit to start the race. | The dog chomped the biscuit in one bite.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal word. It is a bit like "chew" plus "champ". "Chomping at the bit" comes from horses chewing the metal bit in their mouths when they are eager to go.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A thick roll of dried tobacco leaves that people light and smoke.
its sense in the lessons: In health lessons pupils learn that cigars, like cigarettes, contain tobacco and harm health, causing cancers and heart disease. In stories and old films they are linked with rich businessmen or gangsters. Phrases: "cigar smoke", "light a cigar", "close but no cigar" (nearly right, but not quite).
examples from the lessons: The man in the film smoked a fat cigar. | Cigar smoke smells strong and is bad for your lungs. | Smoking cigars can cause mouth cancer. | Close, but no cigar: the answer is 48, not 46. | Winston Churchill was famous for his cigars.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: cigars. A cigar is bigger than a cigarette and wrapped in tobacco leaf, not paper. Children cannot legally buy tobacco. "Close but no cigar" is an idiom meaning almost right.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To do with films and the cinema. 2) Looking or feeling like a film, exciting and grand, with big scenes and music.
its sense in the lessons: In media and art lessons it describes camera shots and storytelling; in gaming and everyday talk "cinematic" means very dramatic and beautiful. Phrases: "cinematic experience", "cinematic effects", "a cinematic view".
examples from the lessons: The game has cinematic cut scenes. | The sunset over the sea looked cinematic. | The book has cinematic action scenes. | We learned about cinematic camera angles. | Watching on a big screen is a real cinematic experience.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced "sin-uh-MAT-ik". From "cinema". Used as an adjective only.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To do with the body's natural daily clock, a cycle of about 24 hours that controls when we sleep, wake and feel hungry.
its sense in the lessons: In science and health lessons, circadian rhythms explain why we feel sleepy at night, why jet lag happens, and why screens before bed can keep us awake. Plants and animals have them too. Phrases: "circadian rhythm", "circadian clock".
examples from the lessons: Your circadian rhythm tells you when to sleep. | Jet lag happens when your circadian clock is out of step with local time. | Bright screens at night can confuse your circadian rhythm. | Flowers that open in the morning follow a circadian rhythm. | Teenagers' circadian rhythms make them sleepy later at night.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced "sur-KAY-dee-un". From Latin "circa" (about) and "dies" (day): about one day, roughly 24 hours.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To sail, fly or travel all the way around something, especially the world or an island. 2) To find a way around a problem or obstacle.
its sense in the lessons: In history and geography lessons it is linked with explorers like Ferdinand Magellan's crew, who first sailed around the world (1519–1522). In everyday talk it can mean getting around an obstacle. Phrases: "circumnavigate the globe", "circumnavigate the island".
examples from the lessons: Magellan's crew were the first to circumnavigate the globe. | We circumnavigated the lake on our bikes. | She plans to circumnavigate the world in a small boat. | We circumnavigated the puddle to keep our shoes dry. | Pilots have circumnavigated the Earth in balloons.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Long word: circum (around) + navigate. Magellan himself died on the voyage; his crew finished it, so it is a trap to say Magellan himself sailed all the way around.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A journey all the way around something, especially around the world by sea or air.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons it describes the voyages of Magellan and Elcano (1519–1522) and Francis Drake (1577–1580). In geography and maths, the distance of a circumnavigation of the Earth around the equator is about 40,000 km. Phrases: "the first circumnavigation", "circumnavigation of the globe".
examples from the lessons: The first circumnavigation of the globe took three years. | Francis Drake completed a circumnavigation in 1580. | Her solo circumnavigation took 72 days. | A circumnavigation of the island takes a day by boat. | Only 18 of Magellan's sailors survived the circumnavigation.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun of "circumnavigate". In maths, the length of a circumnavigation of the Earth at the equator is about 40,000 km, its circumference.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Found around the North Pole or South Pole, or living in the regions near them. 2) (astronomy) Describing a star or group of stars that never sets below the horizon from a certain place, but circles around the pole star.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and science it describes Arctic and Antarctic peoples, animals and currents (the Antarctic Circumpolar Current). In astronomy the Plough (Big Dipper) is circumpolar from the UK and Canada. Phrases: "circumpolar stars", "circumpolar current", "circumpolar peoples".
examples from the lessons: From Scotland, the Plough is a circumpolar constellation. | Circumpolar stars never set; they circle the pole star all night. | The Antarctic Circumpolar Current flows all around Antarctica. | Inuit and Sami are circumpolar peoples. | Polar bears are circumpolar animals.
note for the reader of a maths problem: circum (around) + polar (of the poles). Which stars are circumpolar depends on where you are: the further north you live, the more stars are circumpolar.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The act of clearing something away, like clearing land or rubbish. 2) Official permission to do something, such as security clearance or clearance for a plane to land. 3) The amount of space between two things, like the height under a bridge. 4) A clearance sale: a sale with low prices to sell old stock. 5) (football, rugby) Kicking or heading the ball away from your goal.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and everyday safety, clearance signs show how high a vehicle can be to pass under a bridge. In shops, the clearance rack has cheap items. In history, the Highland Clearances were when people in Scotland were forced off their land in the 1700s and 1800s. Phrases: "clearance sale", "security clearance", "height clearance".
examples from the lessons: The bridge has a clearance of 3.5 metres, so the lorry can't fit. | I bought shoes in the clearance sale. | The pilot waited for clearance to land. | The defender made a great clearance off the line. | The Highland Clearances forced families from their homes. | The council did a clearance of the old rubbish.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable or uncountable. In maths problems with clearance: a vehicle can pass only if its height is less than the clearance: 3.4 m < 3.5 m fits, 3.6 m does not.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A small, sweet orange fruit that is easy to peel and usually has no seeds. 2) (a name) Clementine is a girl's name, as in the old song "Oh My Darling, Clementine".
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life clementines are a popular lunchbox and Christmas fruit, especially in the UK. In maths they appear in sharing and counting problems. Phrases: "a bag of clementines", "peel a clementine".
examples from the lessons: I put a clementine in my lunchbox. | Clementines are easy to peel. | We got clementines in our Christmas stockings. | A bag has 12 clementines; share them between 4 people, that's 3 each. | "Oh My Darling, Clementine" is an old American song. | The clementine segments were sweet and juicy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: clementines. Similar fruits are tangerines, mandarins and satsumas; they are related but not quite the same. Usually lower case for the fruit and capital C for the name.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A water clock: an ancient device that measures time by how much water drips into or out of a container.
its sense in the lessons: In history and science lessons about time it shows how people in ancient Egypt, Greece and China measured time before mechanical clocks. Ancient Athenian courts used one to time speeches. Phrases: "a water clock (clepsydra)".
examples from the lessons: A clepsydra measures time with dripping water. | Ancient Egyptians used a clepsydra at night when sundials didn't work. | We built a clepsydra from a plastic cup with a hole. | In Athens, a clepsydra timed each speaker in court. | Marks on the clepsydra showed how many hours had passed.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced "KLEP-sid-ra". From Greek for "water thief". In maths: if water drips at a steady rate, the time is in proportion to the amount of water, so double the water means double the time.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Big, heavy and awkward, not smooth or neat to use, like clunky old shoes or a clunky machine. 2) (of writing, computer programs) Awkward and not well put together.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life it describes old phones, computers and furniture; in English lessons a teacher may call a sentence clunky if it reads badly. Phrases: "a clunky sentence", "clunky old computer".
examples from the lessons: Grandad's old phone is clunky and heavy. | She wore clunky boots to the party. | This sentence is clunky; try making it shorter. | The website is clunky and hard to use. | The robot moved in a clunky way. | The clunky old lift rattled up the shaft.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal. Comparative: clunkier, clunkiest. From the sound "clunk".

part of speech: noun plural (clutches); verb form of clutch (clutch, clutches, clutched, clutching); noun (a clutch, clutches)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (the clutches of) The power or control of someone dangerous, as in "in the clutches of the villain". 2) (verb) Holds something tightly, often because of fear or pain. 3) (plural of clutch) The pedals or devices in cars that connect and disconnect the engine from the wheels. 4) (plural of clutch) Sets of eggs laid at one time, or small groups of people or things. 5) Small handbags with no handles, called clutch bags.
its sense in the lessons: In stories it shows danger ("escaped from the clutches of the witch") or fear ("she clutches her teddy"). In science, a bird or turtle lays clutches of eggs. In cars, the driver presses the clutch to change gear. Phrases: "in the clutches of", "clutches at straws" (tries anything, even if hopeless).
examples from the lessons: The princess escaped from the clutches of the dragon. | She clutches her bag tightly on the bus. | The turtle laid two clutches of eggs this year. | Manual cars have clutches; most automatic cars don't. | He clutches his tummy because it hurts. | When he can't answer, he clutches at straws.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Clutches can be the plural noun or the he/she/it form of the verb "clutch". Past form: clutched. "Clutches at straws" means trying desperately.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The small bone at the very bottom of the spine, made of tiny bones joined together; also called the tailbone.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about the skeleton it is often called a leftover of a tail from long-ago ancestors. In everyday life people hurt it when they fall on their bottom. Phrases: "bruise your coccyx", "tailbone".
examples from the lessons: The coccyx is at the bottom of your spine. | I fell on the ice and hurt my coccyx. | Another name for the coccyx is the tailbone. | Scientists think the coccyx is a leftover from a tail. | The coccyx helps hold muscles in place when you sit.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced "KOK-six". Plural: coccyges ("kok-SY-jeez") or coccyxes. It still has a job (holding muscles), so it is not completely useless.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) Crooked, not straight or level, like a cockeyed picture. 2) (informal) Silly or not sensible, like a cockeyed plan. 3) (old-fashioned, can be unkind) Having eyes that look in different directions; cross-eyed.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday talk and stories it describes crooked hats and pictures or foolish ideas. Phrases: "a cockeyed idea", "knocked cockeyed".
examples from the lessons: The picture on the wall is cockeyed. | His hat sat cockeyed on his head. | That's a cockeyed idea; it'll never work. | The fence leans at a cockeyed angle. | The cartoon cat looked cockeyed after the bump.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal. Using it about someone's eyes can be hurtful; say "has a squint" or "has a lazy eye" instead. Sometimes spelled "cock-eyed".

meaning for a pupil: 1) An old book written by hand, with pages bound together, especially an ancient or medieval book. 2) A book of laws or rules (old use).
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons it appears with ancient Mayan and Aztec books (like the Dresden Codex), early Bibles (Codex Sinaiticus) and Leonardo da Vinci's notebooks. A codex replaced the scroll because it was easier to use. Phrases: "an ancient codex", "Codex Sinaiticus".
examples from the lessons: The codex was written by monks on animal skin. | The Maya painted their codices on bark paper. | Leonardo da Vinci's notebooks are called codices. | A codex has pages you turn, but a scroll is rolled up. | Codex Sinaiticus is one of the oldest Bibles.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: codices ("KOH-di-seez"), less often codexes. A codex is a book with pages, unlike a scroll.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In an unfriendly way, without warmth or kindness.
its sense in the lessons: In stories it shows a character who is unkind, angry or distant ("she looked at him coldly"). It tells the reader about feelings, not temperature. Phrases: "replied coldly", "stared coldly", "coldly polite".
examples from the lessons: I don't need your help, she said coldly. | The guard stared coldly at the visitors. | He coldly ignored my wave. | The queen smiled coldly. | The shopkeeper answered coldly and turned away.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from "cold". It almost always describes behaviour, not the weather; to talk about weather say "it was very cold".

part of speech: noun (a coloniser, colonisers); US spelling colonizer
meaning for a pupil: 1) A country or person that takes control of another land, settles there and rules the people who already live there.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons it is used when studying empires, for example British, French, Spanish and Portuguese colonisers in Africa, Asia, Australia and the Americas, and how this affected the Indigenous peoples. It is often used to show the side of the people who were colonised. Phrases: "European colonisers", "colonisers and colonised".
examples from the lessons: The colonisers took land from the Aboriginal people. | Spanish colonisers came to South America in the 1500s. | Many colonisers forced local people to work for them. | The museum shows the story from the point of view of the colonised, not just the colonisers. | Some colonisers built railways, but mainly to take away goods. | Ireland had English colonisers in the plantation times.
note for the reader of a maths problem: British spelling: coloniser; American: colonizer. From "colony" and "colonise". History is complicated, and historians use evidence from both colonisers and colonised peoples.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) A combination of things that go together, like a meal deal of burger, chips and drink. 2) (games) A series of moves or hits done quickly one after another for extra points. 3) A small band of musicians, often playing jazz. 4) (informal) The code of a combination lock.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life it appears in fast-food menus and video games. In music lessons a jazz combo is a small group. Phrases: "meal combo", "combo move", "a winning combo".
examples from the lessons: I'll have the burger combo with a milkshake. | He pulled off a ten-hit combo in the game. | Strawberries and cream are a classic combo. | A jazz combo played at the school fair. | What's the combo for your bike lock? | Sun and wind are a good combo for drying washing.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal short form of "combination". Plural: combos. In a maths problem, a "combo" price is often cheaper than buying each item separately: compare the total of the parts with the combo price.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A separate part or section inside a container, bag, car or box. 2) A separate section of a railway carriage with its own seats and door.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life lunchboxes, pencil cases, bags and cars have compartments. On trains in the UK and Europe, older carriages have compartments. In science, cells and ships have compartments too. Phrases: "glove compartment", "freezer compartment", "secret compartment", "overhead compartment".
examples from the lessons: My pencil case has three compartments. | Put the map in the glove compartment. | The treasure was hidden in a secret compartment. | We had a train compartment all to ourselves. | Ice cream goes in the freezer compartment. | Put your bag in the overhead compartment on the plane.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a compartment, compartments. Spelled with "-ment" at the end. Ships have watertight compartments so that one leak does not sink the whole ship.

part of speech: verb (concuss, concusses, concussed, concussing); noun concussion
meaning for a pupil: 1) To hurt someone's brain by a hard knock to the head, so that they may feel dizzy, sick, confused or even pass out for a short time.
its sense in the lessons: In PE, sport and safety lessons, pupils learn that a head bump can concuss you and that you must stop playing and tell an adult. Rugby, football and cycling have rules about concussion. Phrases: "be concussed", "concussion protocol".
examples from the lessons: He was concussed when he fell off his bike. | A hard tackle can concuss a player. | If you might be concussed, stop playing straight away. | Wearing a helmet makes it less likely you'll be concussed. | The doctor checked whether she was concussed.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Most often used in the passive: "be concussed". Noun: concussion. Safety: after a head knock, signs like headache, sickness, sleepiness or confusion mean get medical help; never "play on".

meaning for a pupil: 1) A group of states, countries, organisations or people who join together for a shared purpose, while keeping much of their own power. 2) (Canada) Confederation: the joining of Canadian provinces into one country in 1867.
its sense in the lessons: In history and civics lessons it appears in the Confederate States (the southern US states that broke away in the Civil War), the Swiss Confederation, and Canadian Confederation in 1867. In sport, football confederations group countries by continent. Phrases: "Canadian Confederation", "Swiss Confederation", "a confederation of".
examples from the lessons: Canada was formed by Confederation in 1867. | Switzerland's official name is the Swiss Confederation. | The tribes formed a confederation to defend their land. | UEFA is the football confederation for Europe. | The Iroquois Confederation was a union of several nations.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Related words: "confederacy" and "confederate". In a confederation, the members keep a lot of power, unlike in one strong central state.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Too many cars or people in one place, so movement is slow, like traffic congestion. 2) A blocked feeling in the nose or chest from a cold, with too much mucus.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and citizenship lessons it comes up with traffic, pollution and city planning (London's "congestion charge"). In health, a cold can cause nasal congestion. Phrases: "traffic congestion", "congestion charge", "nasal congestion".
examples from the lessons: There was heavy congestion on the motorway. | London has a congestion charge to cut traffic. | Bikes and buses can help reduce congestion. | I have a cold with nasal congestion. | The steam helped clear my congestion. | Congestion at the school gate makes it unsafe.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: "a lot of congestion", not "a congestion". Adjective: congested ("congested roads", "a congested nose").

part of speech: noun (a conscript, conscripts); verb (conscript, conscripts, conscripted, conscripting); noun conscription
meaning for a pupil: 1) (noun) A person who is made by law to join the army or armed forces. 2) (verb) To make someone join the armed forces by law.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, many young men were conscripted in both World Wars; in news, some countries still conscript young people today, including Ukraine during the war. Phrases: "be conscripted", "conscript army", "military conscription".
examples from the lessons: My great-grandad was conscripted in 1940. | Conscripts trained for only a few weeks. | Some countries still conscript young men. | Conscription was introduced in Britain in 1916. | He didn't volunteer; he was a conscript.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stress changes: noun "CON-script", verb "con-SCRIPT". A conscript is forced to join; a volunteer chooses to join. Noun: conscription.

part of speech: adjective (conserved); verb past form of conserve (conserve, conserves, conserved, conserving)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Protected and kept safe from damage or being wasted, like conserved forests or conserved water. 2) (science) Staying the same in total, not being made or destroyed, as in "energy is conserved". 3) (biology) Kept almost the same over a very long time in many living things, like a conserved gene.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, "mass is conserved" in a chemical reaction and "energy is conserved". In geography and everyday life it means saved or protected. Phrases: "energy is conserved", "conserved area", "conserved for future".
examples from the lessons: In a reaction, mass is conserved: nothing is lost. | Energy is conserved; it just changes form. | The old painting was carefully conserved. | We conserved water by taking shorter showers. | The wetland is conserved for birds. | Some genes are conserved in humans and fish.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past form of "conserve" (one r, ends in -ed). In science, "conserved" means the total amount stays the same: if you start with 100 g of reactants, you end with 100 g of products. Noun: conservation.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In the same way every time, again and again, without changing. 2) In a way that agrees and does not contradict itself.
its sense in the lessons: In school reports teachers write "works consistently hard". In science, results that are consistently the same are reliable. In sport, a player who scores consistently is dependable. Phrases: "consistently good", "consistently late", "consistently high".
examples from the lessons: She consistently gets full marks in spelling. | He is consistently late for school. | The results were consistently the same, so the test was reliable. | Our team played consistently well all season. | Water boils consistently at 100 °C at sea level. | Practise consistently and you will improve.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: consist-ent-ly, with "-ent", not "-ant". In maths, data that are consistently close together have a small range.

part of speech: adjective (conspicuous, more conspicuous, most conspicuous); adverb conspicuously
meaning for a pupil: 1) Very easy to see or notice; standing out. 2) (in phrases) Attracting attention, as in "conspicuous by its absence" (noticeable because it is missing).
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons, bright clothing makes you conspicuous to drivers. In stories, a conspicuous detail can be an important clue. Phrases: "make yourself conspicuous", "conspicuous by its absence", "conspicuous spending".
examples from the lessons: Wear a conspicuous yellow vest when cycling. | The red door was conspicuous in the grey street. | His name was conspicuous by its absence from the list. | The bird's bright feathers made it conspicuous. | She felt conspicuous in her costume. | Put the sign in a conspicuous place.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced "kon-SPIK-yoo-us". The opposite is "inconspicuous" (hard to notice). Being conspicuous is good for safety on roads.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (politics, UK, Canada, Ireland, Australia) An area of a country whose voters elect one or more members to parliament. 2) The people who live and vote in such an area. 3) A group of people who support someone or whose interests someone represents.
its sense in the lessons: In citizenship and politics lessons it explains how MPs are elected in the UK: each constituency elects one MP. In news at election time it is used a lot. Phrases: "my constituency", "a marginal constituency", "constituency MP".
examples from the lessons: There are 650 constituencies in the UK. | Our constituency elected a new MP. | The MP held a meeting for people in her constituency. | Ireland's constituencies elect several members each. | He visits his constituency every weekend.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: constituencies. In the USA, the area is usually called a "district". Also related: "constituent" (a voter in a constituency).

part of speech: adjective (convenient, more convenient, most convenient); adverb conveniently; noun convenience
meaning for a pupil: 1) Easy to use, reach or do; saving time and trouble. 2) Suitable for someone's plans or time. 3) Near and easy to get to.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life it describes shops, times and food ("convenience food"). In stories, a "convenient excuse" may be a lie. Phrases: "at a convenient time", "convenient for", "convenience store", "conveniently forgot".
examples from the lessons: The shop is convenient because it's next to school. | Is Saturday convenient for you? | Microwave meals are convenient but not always healthy. | He conveniently forgot to do the washing-up. | It's convenient to have a bus stop outside our house. | A convenience store is open late.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: con-ven-ient. Opposite: inconvenient. "Convenient for" a person, place or time.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal, often used by children) A person who copies what someone else does, says or wears. 2) (adjective) Copying something that happened before, like a copycat crime.
its sense in the lessons: In school and playground talk, "copycat!" is a teasing word. In news, a copycat crime is done in the same way as an earlier, well-known crime. Phrases: "don't be a copycat", "copycat crime", "copycat product".
examples from the lessons: Copycat! she shouted when her brother copied her drawing. | My little sister is a copycat; she copies everything I do. | Police worried about copycat attacks. | That shop sells copycat versions of famous trainers. | Copying in a test isn't just being a copycat; it's cheating.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal. One word. Calling someone a copycat can be teasing; younger children often copy because they admire someone.

part of speech: noun (a corps, corps — same spelling for plural)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A part of an army with a special job, like the medical corps or the Marine Corps. 2) A group of people who work together on a special task, like the press corps or a dance corps. 3) (ballet) The corps de ballet: the group of dancers who dance together, not the soloists.
its sense in the lessons: In history and the news it names military units, such as the US Marine Corps or the Royal Army Medical Corps, and groups like the Peace Corps. In dance it means the main group of dancers. Phrases: "Marine Corps", "Peace Corps", "diplomatic corps", "corps de ballet".
examples from the lessons: He joined the Army Medical Corps as a nurse. | The US Marine Corps is part of the American armed forces. | The Peace Corps sends volunteers to help other countries. | The press corps waited outside for the prime minister. | She dances in the corps de ballet.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced "core" (the p and s are silent); the plural is spelled the same but said "cores". Do not confuse with "corpse" (a dead body, said "korps").

meaning for a pupil: 1) A connection or relationship between two things, where they change together. 2) (maths, science) A measure of how closely two sets of numbers go up or down together, as shown on a scatter graph.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and science lessons pupils draw scatter graphs and describe positive correlation (both go up), negative correlation (one goes up, the other down) or no correlation. A key idea: correlation does not prove causation. Phrases: "positive correlation", "negative correlation", "no correlation", "a strong correlation".
examples from the lessons: There is a positive correlation between height and shoe size. | The graph shows a negative correlation: as temperature rises, coat sales fall. | There was no correlation between hair colour and test scores. | Correlation does not mean one thing causes the other. | Scientists found a correlation between exercise and sleep.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: double r. In maths, positive correlation = points slope upward; negative = points slope downward; no correlation = points scattered. A correlation alone does not prove one thing causes the other.

part of speech: noun (counselling, uncountable); US spelling counseling; verb counsel
meaning for a pupil: 1) Help and advice from a trained person who listens to someone with problems or worries and helps them think things through. 2) Advice in general (formal).
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and school, children may get counselling after a hard time like a family break-up, bullying or the death of someone close. Many schools have a counsellor. Phrases: "go to counselling", "school counselling", "grief counselling", "marriage counselling".
examples from the lessons: After Grandad died, I had some counselling at school. | Counselling helped her feel less worried. | The school counsellor listens and keeps things private. | Mum and Dad went to counselling to talk things through. | There is free counselling for children on helplines. | Counselling is a safe place to talk about feelings.
note for the reader of a maths problem: British spelling: counselling (double l); American: counseling. Uncountable. Do not confuse with "council" (a group that runs a town) or "councillor". Going to counselling is normal and brave, not a sign of being weak.

part of speech: adjective (counterfeit); noun (a counterfeit, counterfeits); verb (counterfeit, counterfeits, counterfeited, counterfeiting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Made to look exactly like something real in order to trick people; fake, like counterfeit money. 2) (noun) A fake copy. 3) (verb) To make fake money or goods illegally.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and money lessons, banknotes have special features (holograms, watermarks) to stop counterfeit notes. In news, counterfeit goods like fake trainers or medicines can be dangerous. Phrases: "counterfeit money", "counterfeit goods", "counterfeit notes".
examples from the lessons: The shop checks for counterfeit £20 notes. | Counterfeit toys may not be safety tested. | Making counterfeit money is a serious crime. | The watermark showed the note was counterfeit. | Police seized thousands of counterfeit watches. | The forger counterfeited old coins.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced "KOWN-ter-fit". Spelling trap: "-feit" (ei), not "-fiet". Counterfeit medicine is dangerous; only buy medicine from proper pharmacies.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A sudden, often violent, illegal taking of power in a country, usually by the army; also called a coup d'état. 2) A clever, successful action that wins something hard to get.
its sense in the lessons: In history and news lessons it appears when soldiers or leaders take over a government without an election. In everyday talk it can mean a great success ("getting that star player was a coup"). Phrases: "military coup", "failed coup", "a coup d'état", "a real coup".
examples from the lessons: The army took power in a coup. | The coup failed, and the president stayed in power. | Getting the famous author to visit our school was a real coup. | After the coup, there were protests in the streets. | A coup d'état is French for "a blow against the state".
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced "koo"; the p is silent. Plural: coups (also "koos"). From French "coup" meaning a blow or hit. Do not confuse with "coop" (a hen house) or "coupe".

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who spends time at the court of a king or queen, as an adviser, friend or attendant.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons about the Tudors, Versailles and other royal courts, courtiers tried to please the monarch to win favour. In stories and fairy tales (like The Emperor's New Clothes) courtiers flatter the ruler. Phrases: "the king's courtiers", "a royal courtier".
examples from the lessons: The courtiers bowed as the queen entered. | Henry VIII's courtiers had to be careful what they said. | In the fairy tale, the courtiers pretended to see the emperor's clothes. | Sir Walter Raleigh was a courtier of Elizabeth I. | The courtiers whispered about the new king.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced "KOR-tee-er". From "court" in the sense of a royal household, not a law court or a tennis court.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A small, sheltered bay on a coastline, with land curving around it. 2) (old slang, UK, Australia) A man or fellow, as in "a strange cove".
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons it is a coastal landform made where waves wear away soft rock behind harder rock, like Lulworth Cove in England. In adventure stories coves are hiding places for smugglers and pirates. Phrases: "a sheltered cove", "a hidden cove".
examples from the lessons: We swam in a quiet little cove. | Lulworth Cove is shaped like a horseshoe. | Smugglers hid their boats in the cove. | The cove was sheltered from the wind. | Check the tide times before exploring a cove so you don't get cut off. | "He's a funny old cove," said the farmer.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a cove, coves. A cove is smaller than a bay. The "fellow" sense is old-fashioned slang from Britain and Australia.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A steep, rough, rocky cliff or high rock sticking out from a hill or mountain.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons, glaciers left "crag and tail" landforms, like Edinburgh Castle Rock. In stories, eagles nest on crags and heroes climb them. Phrases: "a rocky crag", "a craggy face" (lined and rugged).
examples from the lessons: An eagle perched on the crag. | Edinburgh Castle stands on a volcanic crag. | Climbers scaled the steep crag. | Mist hid the crags above the valley. | The old sailor had a craggy face. | Don't climb crags without proper gear and an instructor.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a crag, crags. Adjective "craggy" describes rough rocks or a rugged face.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Thick, smooth and rich, like cream, or containing a lot of cream. 2) Pale yellowish-white in colour, like cream.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday cooking and food descriptions it describes soups, yoghurt, ice cream and sauces. In art it describes a pale colour. In science, mixing can make liquids creamy. Phrases: "creamy texture", "creamy white", "smooth and creamy".
examples from the lessons: This tomato soup is lovely and creamy. | Stir the butter and sugar until creamy. | The cat has creamy fur. | Creamy ice cream melted on my cone. | The paint was a creamy white colour. | The creamiest milkshake had banana in it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative: creamier, creamiest (y changes to i). Not always made with real cream; "creamy" can just describe the texture.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A weapon made of a small bow fixed across a wooden stock, which shoots short arrows called bolts when you pull a trigger.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons about the Middle Ages, crossbows were powerful and easy to learn compared with longbows. In stories and games, characters hunt or fight with crossbows. Phrases: "fire a crossbow", "crossbow bolt".
examples from the lessons: Medieval soldiers fired crossbows at the castle walls. | A crossbow bolt is shorter than an arrow. | Crossbows were slower to reload than longbows. | The museum had a crossbow from the 1400s. | Crossbows are dangerous weapons, not toys. | In ancient China, people also used crossbows.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word. Plural: crossbows. Its arrows are called bolts or quarrels. In many places it is illegal for children to own or use a crossbow.

part of speech: noun (a cryptocurrency, cryptocurrencies; cryptocurrency, uncountable); informal crypto
meaning for a pupil: 1) (money) A kind of digital money that exists only on computers, uses special codes to keep it secure, and is not issued by a government or bank, such as Bitcoin.
its sense in the lessons: In money and computing lessons it is explained as a new kind of money with prices that go up and down very fast. In the news it appears with scams, investments and energy use. Phrases: "buy cryptocurrency", "crypto wallet", "the price of cryptocurrency".
examples from the lessons: Bitcoin was the first cryptocurrency. | The price of cryptocurrency can rise or fall a lot in one day. | My uncle lost money when his cryptocurrency crashed. | Cryptocurrency is kept in a digital wallet. | Scammers often ask for payment in cryptocurrency. | Some cryptocurrencies use a lot of electricity.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: cryptocurrencies. Often shortened to "crypto". It is risky: values change fast and money can be lost or stolen, and there is usually no bank to get it back. Online, never send crypto to someone who promises to "double your money"; that is a scam.

part of speech: verb, past form of crystallise (crystallise, crystallises, crystallised, crystallising); adjective (crystallised fruit, crystallised ginger)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Turned into crystals: a liquid or a solution formed solid pieces with flat, regular faces. 2) Became clear and fixed: an idea, a plan or a feeling took a definite shape. 3) (adjective, food) Coated or preserved in sugar, so it sparkles, like crystallised ginger.
its sense in the lessons: In science, salt or sugar crystallises when water evaporates from a solution or when a hot solution cools; children grow crystals on a string. In stories and history it tells the reader that a vague idea suddenly became clear and firm. In cooking, crystallised fruit or ginger is sweet and sugary. Phrases: «the salt crystallised out», «the plan crystallised», «crystallised honey».
examples from the lessons: The salt crystallised on the saucer after the water dried up. | Our sugar solution crystallised into tiny cubes overnight. | Old honey in the jar had crystallised and gone grainy. | Her idea for the science fair crystallised after the trip to the beach. | Slowly the plan crystallised in his mind. | Nan put crystallised ginger on top of the cake. | The water crystallised into frost on the window. | In the cave, minerals had crystallised into shining points.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK and Australian spelling; US spelling is «crystallized». Double «l». Regular verb: crystallise, crystallised. Not the same as «frozen», though ice is also a crystal. Crystallised honey is not spoiled; it can be warmed to turn runny again.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To prepare and use land for growing crops: to dig, plant and look after it. 2) To grow plants or crops on purpose. 3) To build up or develop something slowly with care, such as a skill, a habit or a friendship. 4) (science) To grow bacteria or cells in a lab.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and history it is about farming: early people began to cultivate wheat and rice, which let them settle in villages. In science, scientists cultivate bacteria in dishes. In everyday life and stories it means working patiently on something: to cultivate good habits, a garden or a friendship. Phrases: «cultivate the land», «cultivate a friendship», «cultivated fields».
examples from the lessons: Farmers cultivate wheat on the wide plains. | The first farmers learned to cultivate rice along rivers. | Grandad cultivates tomatoes in his greenhouse. | Our class cultivated a vegetable patch behind the school. | Try to cultivate the habit of reading every night. | She cultivated a friendship with the new girl next door. | Scientists cultivate bacteria in small round dishes. | This land is too rocky to cultivate.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Noun: cultivation. «Cultivated» can also be an adjective: cultivated land (farmed land) or a cultivated person (well educated and polite). Formal-sounding; in everyday talk people say «grow» or «farm».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Tiny living things, a kind of bacteria, that make their own food from sunlight like plants do. 2) Sometimes called blue-green algae, they live in water and can turn ponds and lakes green.
its sense in the lessons: In science, cyanobacteria matter because they were among the first living things to make oxygen by photosynthesis, which helped make Earth's air breathable for animals. In safety, a lake with a «blue-green algae» warning may contain cyanobacteria that can be poisonous to people and dogs, so you should not swim there. Phrases: «blue-green algae», «algal bloom».
examples from the lessons: Cyanobacteria make food from sunlight just like plants. | Billions of years ago, cyanobacteria filled the air with oxygen. | The sign said the lake had cyanobacteria, so no swimming. | Keep your dog out of the green, scummy water. | Under the microscope the cyanobacteria looked like tiny green threads. | Stromatolites are rocky mounds built by cyanobacteria. | A warm summer can make cyanobacteria grow fast in ponds.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually used in the plural. Pronounced «sigh-AN-oh-bac-TEER-ee-a». «Cyano» means blue. They are often called algae, but they are really bacteria, not true algae. Safety: blue-green algae can make you ill; do not drink or swim in water with a warning sign.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who takes part in a debate: a formal argument where speakers give reasons for and against an idea. 2) Anyone who is good at arguing a point clearly with reasons.
its sense in the lessons: In school, debaters join a debate club or team and speak for or against a motion, such as «Homework should be banned»; a judge decides who argued better. In stories, a «good debater» is someone quick and clever with words. Phrases: «a skilled debater», «the debating team», «for and against».
examples from the lessons: Maya is the best debater in our class. | Each debater had three minutes to speak. | The debaters on our team argued that school should start later. | A good debater listens to the other side carefully. | The judge praised both debaters for their politeness. | He is a fierce debater at the dinner table. | Our school's debaters won the regional final.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: one debater, two debaters. Comes from «debate» + «-er» (drop the final «e» before «-er»). A debater does not always believe the side they argue; in contests the side is often given to them.

part of speech: noun (a debut, debuts); verb (debut, debuts, debuted, debuting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The first time someone performs or appears in public, such as a singer's first concert or a player's first game. 2) The first time a new product, show or film is shown to the public. 3) (verb) To appear or be shown for the first time.
its sense in the lessons: In sport and music news, a «debut» tells the reader it is someone's first big appearance: «made his debut for England». In stories it marks a nervous, exciting first time. Phrases: «make your debut», «debut album», «debut match», «a stunning debut».
examples from the lessons: She made her debut in the school play last night. | The young striker scored on his debut. | The band's debut album came out in spring. | The new game debuts next week. | It was the dog's debut at the agility show. | His debut for the national team was a great success. | The film debuted in cinemas on Friday.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced «DAY-byoo»; the «t» is silent, because the word comes from French. Can be written «début». As a verb it is newer and some people prefer «make a debut». Countable noun.

part of speech: verb, past form of decipher (decipher, deciphers, deciphered, deciphering); adjective (a deciphered message)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Worked out the meaning of a secret code and turned it into plain words. 2) Managed to read writing that is very hard to read, like messy handwriting or an old script. 3) Understood something puzzling.
its sense in the lessons: In history, people deciphered Egyptian hieroglyphs with help from the Rosetta Stone, and code-breakers deciphered secret wartime messages. In maths and puzzles, deciphering a code means finding the rule, such as each letter moved three places. In stories it shows a mystery being solved. Phrases: «deciphered the code», «could hardly be deciphered».
examples from the lessons: The detectives deciphered the secret message. | Champollion deciphered Egyptian hieroglyphs in 1822. | I finally deciphered my brother's messy handwriting. | We deciphered the code by shifting each letter back by one. | The old map had faded and could barely be deciphered. | She deciphered the meaning of his strange look. | Code-breakers deciphered enemy messages during the war.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: decipher, deciphered. Opposite: encipher or encode. Very close to «decode»; «decipher» is also used for hard handwriting. Spelled with «ph», which sounds like «f».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Polite respect shown to someone by accepting their opinion or wishes, often because they are older, wiser or more important. 2) (phrase) «In deference to» means out of respect for someone or something.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and history, deference shows who has power or respect: servants showed deference to lords, and pupils may show deference to a head teacher. In everyday life it is about politeness, such as letting an elder speak first. Phrases: «out of deference to», «in deference to her wishes», «treat with deference».
examples from the lessons: The children spoke to the old chief with great deference. | In deference to Gran, we turned the music down. | He nodded with deference when the judge spoke. | The flags were lowered in deference to those who had died. | She treats her coach with deference. | Out of deference to the teacher, the class stood up when she came in.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: no «a» and no plural. Verb: defer (to defer to someone means to accept their view). Trap: not the same as «difference», though they sound a little alike. Formal word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An amount by which something is too small: how much is missing compared with what is needed. 2) (money) The amount by which money spent is more than money coming in. 3) (sport) The number of points or goals a team is behind.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and money problems, a deficit is a shortfall: if you need 50 and have 35, the deficit is 15. In news, a government «budget deficit» means it spends more than it collects in taxes. In sport, a team «came back from a two-goal deficit». Phrases: «a deficit of», «budget deficit», «sleep deficit», «make up the deficit».
examples from the lessons: We needed 30 chairs but had only 24, a deficit of six. | The club has a deficit, so it must raise money. | The government's budget deficit grew this year. | Our team overcame a three-goal deficit to win. | After the late night I had a sleep deficit. | The school fair helped make up the deficit. | There is a deficit of rain this summer.
