note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun. Pronounced «DEF-i-sit». Opposite: surplus (more than needed). In maths: deficit = amount needed minus amount you have, so it is a subtraction. «Attention deficit» is part of the name of the condition ADHD.

part of speech: noun (a deinonychus, deinonychuses; often written Deinonychus as the name of the animal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A meat-eating dinosaur about 3 metres long that ran on two legs and had a large curved claw on each foot. The name means «terrible claw».
its sense in the lessons: In science and dinosaur lessons, Deinonychus showed scientists that some dinosaurs were fast, active hunters, closely related to birds; it probably had feathers. It lived in North America about 115 million years ago. In stories and films it inspired the fast, clever «raptors».
examples from the lessons: Deinonychus had a big curved claw on each foot. | Its name means «terrible claw». | Scientists think Deinonychus had feathers. | Deinonychus lived in North America long before people. | The museum has a Deinonychus skeleton in a running pose. | The raptors in films are partly based on Deinonychus. | Deinonychus was about as long as a car.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced «die-NON-i-kus». As a scientific name it is written with a capital and often in italics: Deinonychus. It is a dinosaur name from Greek, not an everyday word. Myth: film raptors are much bigger than the real animal.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A scientist who studies populations: how many people live in a place, how old they are, how many are born, die or move.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and social studies, demographers use the census and other numbers to show how populations grow or shrink and how they change; governments use their work to plan schools, hospitals and homes. Phrases: «demographers predict», «population trends», «birth rate».
examples from the lessons: A demographer studies how many people are born each year. | Demographers say the town's population will double. | The demographer used census numbers to make a chart. | Demographers noticed that families are getting smaller. | Planners asked a demographer how many school places would be needed. | My aunt is a demographer who studies where people move.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun. Related words: demography (the study), demographic (about population, or a group of people). Pronounced «de-MOG-ra-fer». «Demo» comes from Greek for people, as in democracy.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a way that can be clearly shown or proved: you can point to facts that show it is true.
its sense in the lessons: In science and arguments it tells the reader a claim is backed by evidence, not just opinion: «demonstrably false». In the exam voice it is a strong, formal word. Phrases: «demonstrably true», «demonstrably false», «demonstrably better».
examples from the lessons: That claim is demonstrably false: look at the results. | The new bridge is demonstrably safer than the old one. | Practice has made her demonstrably faster at times tables. | The medicine works, as the tests demonstrably show. | His story was demonstrably untrue, because the shop was closed. | Recycling demonstrably reduces rubbish in our bins.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from «demonstrable» (able to be shown) and the verb «demonstrate». Stress on «MON»: «de-MON-stra-bly» (some say «DEM-on-stra-bly»). Formal; in everyday talk people say «clearly» or «provably».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Sending soldiers, ships or equipment to a place so they are ready to act. 2) Putting something into use, for example opening a parachute, inflating an airbag, or releasing new software. 3) A time when a soldier is sent away to serve.
its sense in the lessons: In news and military history, a deployment means troops sent somewhere; children of service families talk about a parent being «on deployment». In technology, deployment is when an airbag or parachute opens, or a new app version is released. Phrases: «on deployment», «troop deployment», «airbag deployment».
examples from the lessons: Dad is away on deployment for six months. | The deployment of troops was on the evening news. | The airbag's deployment saved the driver from injury. | The rover's parachute deployment went perfectly. | The deployment of the new app is planned for Monday. | The fire service ordered the deployment of more engines. | Families wrote letters during the long deployment.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun from the verb «deploy» (to send out or put into use). Can be countable (a long deployment) or uncountable. Often used in formal and military language.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who puts money into a bank account. 2) Someone who puts something down or leaves something somewhere for safe keeping.
its sense in the lessons: In money lessons, a depositor puts money in the bank; the bank keeps it safe and may pay interest. In news, when a bank is in trouble, «depositors» may rush to take their money out. Phrases: «bank depositors», «protect depositors».
examples from the lessons: Every depositor gets a statement each month. | As a depositor, Sam earns a little interest on his savings. | The bank promised that depositors' money was safe. | When rumours spread, worried depositors queued outside the bank. | Young depositors can open a children's savings account. | The law protects depositors if a bank fails.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun from «deposit» + «-or». Note the spelling ends in «-or», not «-er». In money problems: deposits add to the balance, withdrawals subtract.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (money) The loss of value of something as it gets older or is used, like a car being worth less each year. 2) (money) A fall in the value of a country's money compared with other currencies. 3) (formal) Saying that something is of little worth.
its sense in the lessons: In money maths, depreciation is often a percentage taken off each year: a bike worth 200 that loses 10% a year is worth 180 after one year. In business and news it explains why second-hand things cost less and why a currency buys less abroad. Phrases: «depreciation of the pound», «the car's depreciation».
examples from the lessons: New cars suffer fast depreciation in the first year. | Because of depreciation, Dad's old phone is worth very little. | The depreciation of the dollar made holidays abroad dearer. | We worked out the depreciation of the laptop in maths. | Toys usually lose value, but some rare ones avoid depreciation. | The company counts depreciation on its machines every year.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: appreciation (going up in value). Verb: depreciate. In maths problems: depreciation means the value goes down; with a percentage each year, work it out on the new value each time (like compound interest in reverse).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who comes later in the same family line: a child, grandchild, great-grandchild and so on. 2) An animal or plant that has developed from an earlier kind. 3) Something that has grown out of an earlier thing.
its sense in the lessons: In history and family-tree lessons, descendants are the people who come after an ancestor. In science, birds are thought to be descendants of dinosaurs. In stories, «a descendant of the king» tells the reader someone has royal blood. Phrases: «a direct descendant», «descendants of», «ancestors and descendants».
examples from the lessons: She is a descendant of Irish farmers. | Birds are descendants of dinosaurs. | The old queen had dozens of descendants. | We drew a family tree with Great-Gran at the top and her descendants below. | Modern dogs are descendants of wolves. | He claims to be a descendant of a famous pirate. | Today's computers are descendants of huge early machines.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: ancestor (someone who came before). Spelling trap: the noun is usually «descendant» (with «-ant»); «descendent» is a rarer adjective. Do not confuse with «descent» (going down, or family origin). Countable.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The process of drying something out completely, or the state of being very dry. 2) The removal of water from food, soil or living things.
its sense in the lessons: In science, desiccation is drying: food is dried to keep it longer, and desert plants and animals have tricks to survive desiccation. In geography, desiccation of land can lead to drought and cracked soil. In labs, a desiccator is a jar that keeps things dry. Phrases: «protect from desiccation», «desiccation cracks».
examples from the lessons: Cacti have thick skin to avoid desiccation. | The pond's desiccation left fish stranded in the mud. | Desiccation is used to preserve fruit like raisins. | Mud cracks form during the desiccation of a lake bed. | Frogs must keep moist to avoid desiccation. | Raisins are grapes dried by desiccation in the sun.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Spelling trap: one «s», double «c»: desiccation (from the verb «desiccate»). The little «silica gel» packets in new shoes are desiccants: they soak up moisture to keep things dry. Formal or scientific word; everyday word is «drying out».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Stopping people from doing something by making them afraid of what would happen to them if they did it. 2) (politics) The idea that a country can stop attacks by having strong weapons that would hit back.
its sense in the lessons: In citizenship and history lessons, deterrence explains why there are punishments and fines: to stop people breaking rules. In news and the Cold War topic, «nuclear deterrence» means countries keep weapons hoping never to use them. In everyday safety, CCTV signs are a deterrent to thieves. Phrases: «nuclear deterrence», «as a deterrence», «deterrent».
examples from the lessons: Fines for littering are a form of deterrence. | The bright lights act as deterrence against burglars. | During the Cold War, both sides relied on nuclear deterrence. | Some people argue that deterrence works better than punishment after a crime. | The guard dog provides deterrence. | Deterrence only works if people believe the threat.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Related: deter (verb: to put someone off), deterrent (noun: the thing that deters). Spelled with double «r». People argue about how well deterrence works; it is a debated idea, not a proven fact.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The writing system (script) used for Hindi, Marathi, Nepali, Sanskrit and several other languages of India and Nepal.
its sense in the lessons: In language and geography lessons, Devanagari is recognised by the straight line along the top that letters hang from. It is written left to right. It shows how different languages use different scripts, like Latin letters for English or Cyrillic for Ukrainian. Phrases: «written in Devanagari», «the Devanagari script».
examples from the lessons: Hindi is written in the Devanagari script. | In Devanagari, letters hang from a line across the top. | Our classmate wrote her name in Devanagari for us. | Sanskrit, an ancient language, also uses Devanagari. | Devanagari is read from left to right, like English. | The shop sign was in both English and Devanagari.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A proper name, usually written with a capital D. Pronounced «day-va-NAH-ga-ree». It is not a language but a script: Hindi is the language, Devanagari is how it is written. It has about 47 main letters.

part of speech: noun, plural only (slang: dibs; «dibs on»); interjection «Dibs!»
meaning for a pupil: 1) (slang) A claim to have or do something first: if you say «Dibs on the front seat!», you mean you get it. 2) (slang, UK, old) Money.
its sense in the lessons: In children's everyday life, «dibs» is said to claim a seat, the last biscuit or the first go; it works like «bagsy» in the UK and «shotgun» for the front car seat. In stories it shows children's playful arguing. Phrases: «dibs on», «I call dibs», «have dibs on».
examples from the lessons: Dibs on the window seat! | I called dibs on the last slice of pizza. | You can't have it, Ellie already has dibs. | Dibs on going first! | Who's got dibs on the top bunk? | He shouted «dibs!» before anyone else could.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Slang, mostly US, Canada, Australia; in the UK children often say «bagsy» instead. Always plural in form: «dibs», not «a dib». It is a game rule, not a real right, so it can cause arguments. Not used in formal writing.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A trained health expert who gives advice about food and eating, to help people stay healthy or manage an illness.
its sense in the lessons: In health lessons and everyday life, a dietician helps plan meals, for example for someone with diabetes, allergies or who needs to gain or lose weight. Hospitals and schools sometimes have dieticians. Phrases: «see a dietician», «a hospital dietician».
examples from the lessons: The dietician helped Tom plan meals for his allergy. | My aunt is a dietician at the hospital. | The dietician said to eat more fruit and vegetables. | After his illness, Grandad saw a dietician. | A dietician knows which foods give you energy. | The school asked a dietician to check the lunch menu.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Also spelled «dietitian» (more official in many countries). Countable. Trap: a dietician is a qualified professional; anyone can call themselves a «nutritionist» in some places. «Diet» here means what you usually eat, not only eating less.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who represents their country in another country and helps the two governments talk and agree. 2) Someone who is tactful: good at dealing with people without upsetting them.
its sense in the lessons: In history and citizenship, diplomats work in embassies, make treaties and try to solve problems between countries peacefully. In everyday life, calling a friend «a real diplomat» means they are good at calming arguments. Phrases: «a foreign diplomat», «a born diplomat», «diplomatic».
examples from the lessons: The diplomat worked at the embassy in Paris. | Diplomats met to try to stop the war. | Her mum is a diplomat, so they have lived in four countries. | Jack is a diplomat; he always stops fights in the playground. | The diplomats signed a peace treaty. | Be a diplomat and tell her kindly that her song was too long.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Related words: diplomacy (the work), diplomatic (adjective). Stress on the first syllable: «DIP-lo-mat». Diplomats often have «diplomatic immunity», a special protection in the country where they work.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A small bird that lives by fast streams and walks or dives under water to catch insects. 2) A ladle or cup with a long handle for scooping water. 3) (the Big Dipper, the Little Dipper) Groups of stars shaped like a ladle; in the UK the Big Dipper is called the Plough. 4) (UK) A roller-coaster ride at a fair; a «big dipper».
its sense in the lessons: In science and nature, the dipper is a bird famous for walking underwater in rivers. In astronomy, the Big Dipper helps you find the North Star. At the seaside, a «big dipper» is a fairground ride. Phrases: «the Big Dipper», «a water dipper».
examples from the lessons: A dipper bobbed on a rock in the stream. | We watched the dipper walk right under the water. | Use the dipper to scoop water from the barrel. | On a clear night we found the Big Dipper. | In the UK, the Big Dipper is called the Plough. | We rode the big dipper at the fair and screamed. | The pointer stars of the Big Dipper lead to the North Star.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. From the verb «dip». The Big Dipper is part of the larger constellation Ursa Major (Great Bear), not a full constellation itself. Capital letters for the star group: the Big Dipper.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To officially refuse to accept something, especially a goal, point or claim, because it broke a rule. 2) To not permit something.
its sense in the lessons: In sport, a referee may disallow a goal for offside or a foul. In school and law, a claim or answer can be disallowed if it breaks the rules. In computing, settings can disallow certain apps. Phrases: «disallow a goal», «the goal was disallowed».
examples from the lessons: The referee disallowed the goal for offside. | Phones are disallowed during the exam. | The judge disallowed the late entry. | Our answer was disallowed because we used a calculator. | The app disallows chat for children under 13. | Fans groaned when the try was disallowed.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. «Dis-» means not, so disallow means not allow. Most common in the passive: «the goal was disallowed». More formal than «not allow» or «ban».

meaning for a pupil: 1) To see, hear or notice something that is hard to see or hear. 2) To understand or recognise something, often a difference, by thinking carefully. 3) (formal) To tell apart, such as right from wrong.
its sense in the lessons: In reading lessons, pupils discern the author's meaning or a character's feelings from clues. In science, you may discern a pattern in data. In fog or dark, you can barely discern shapes. In church and ethics, Christians speak of discerning what is right or what God wants. Phrases: «hard to discern», «discern between», «discern a pattern».
examples from the lessons: Through the fog we could just discern the lighthouse. | Can you discern a pattern in these numbers? | It was hard to discern what she meant. | Babies soon learn to discern their mother's voice. | Good readers discern clues the writer has hidden. | He could not discern any difference between the two cakes. | The judge must discern truth from lies.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal word; pronounced «di-SURN» (the «s» sounds like «s», sometimes «z»). Adjective: discerning (good at judging quality). Noun: discernment. In everyday talk people say «make out» or «spot».

meaning for a pupil: 1) To send people away or let them leave: «Class dismissed!» 2) To decide that an idea or feeling is not worth thinking about. 3) To remove someone from their job. 4) (law) To end a court case without a trial. 5) (cricket) To get a batter out.
its sense in the lessons: In school, a teacher dismisses the class at the end of a lesson. In stories and arguments, dismissing an idea tells you a character thinks it is silly. In adult life, an employer may dismiss a worker. In cricket, a bowler dismisses a batter. Phrases: «class dismissed», «dismiss an idea», «dismiss out of hand», «dismissed from his job».
examples from the lessons: The teacher dismissed the class at three o'clock. | Class dismissed! | She dismissed my idea as too silly. | Don't dismiss your worries; talk to someone. | The manager dismissed the worker for stealing. | The judge dismissed the case. | The bowler dismissed three batters in one over. | He dismissed the rumour with a laugh.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb; double «s» at the end: dismisses, dismissed. Noun: dismissal. «Dismiss» someone from a job is formal; everyday is «sack» or «fire». Adjective: dismissive.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Showing that you think something or someone is not important or not worth your attention. 2) Rude in a way that ignores what another person says or feels.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, a dismissive tone, wave or shrug shows a character does not care or looks down on someone. In PSHE and kindness lessons, being dismissive of someone's feelings («just get over it») is unkind. Phrases: «dismissive of», «a dismissive wave», «dismissive attitude».
examples from the lessons: He gave a dismissive wave and walked off. | She was dismissive of my plan before hearing it all. | Don't be dismissive when a friend says they're sad. | The coach's dismissive reply upset the team. | «Whatever,» she said in a dismissive voice. | Being dismissive can make people stop sharing their ideas.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective from «dismiss». Adverb: dismissively. Followed by «of»: dismissive of something. Opposite: attentive, respectful.

part of speech: noun (uncountable: distrust); verb (distrust, distrusts, distrusted, distrusting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (noun) A feeling that you cannot trust someone or something; you think they may lie or let you down. 2) (verb) To not trust someone or something.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, distrust between characters builds tension: «the villagers eyed the stranger with distrust». In history, distrust between countries can lead to conflict. In online safety, a healthy distrust of strangers and too-good-to-be-true offers keeps you safe. Phrases: «with distrust», «a deep distrust of», «mutual distrust».
examples from the lessons: The cat looked at the new dog with distrust. | After he broke his promise, she began to distrust him. | There was distrust between the two teams after the argument. | Distrust strangers online who ask for your address. | The villagers distrusted the travelling salesman. | Years of war left deep distrust between the countries.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Both a noun and a verb. Very close to «mistrust»; «distrust» is a bit stronger and based on reasons. Adjective: distrustful. Opposite: trust.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Moving or spreading apart in different directions from one point. 2) Different from each other or from what is usual, such as divergent opinions. 3) (maths) Describes a series or sequence that does not settle down to one value.
its sense in the lessons: In science, divergent rays of light spread out from a lens; at divergent plate boundaries Earth's plates move apart. In discussions, «divergent views» means people disagree. In thinking lessons, «divergent thinking» means coming up with many different ideas. Phrases: «divergent views», «divergent thinking», «divergent boundary».
examples from the lessons: The two paths were divergent, one going up the hill and one to the sea. | At a divergent boundary, two plates move apart. | The class had divergent opinions about the school uniform. | Divergent thinking helps you invent many uses for a paperclip. | The light rays become divergent after the lens. | Their lives took divergent paths after school.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective from the verb «diverge». Noun: divergence. Opposite: convergent (coming together). Formal word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A different route that traffic must take when a road is closed. 2) Something that takes attention away from what is really happening, often on purpose. 3) The act of turning something, such as a river or money, to another direction or use. 4) Something fun that passes time; an amusement.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life in the UK, Ireland and Australia, yellow «Diversion» signs show drivers a way round roadworks (Americans say «detour»). In stories, a character «creates a diversion» to distract guards. In geography, a river diversion channels water elsewhere. Phrases: «create a diversion», «follow the diversion», «a welcome diversion».
examples from the lessons: The road was closed, so we followed the diversion signs. | Tom made a diversion while his sister grabbed the ball. | The puppy's barking was a diversion from the real thief. | Engineers built a diversion to stop the town flooding. | Board games are a pleasant diversion on rainy days. | The bus took a long diversion because of the parade.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Verb: divert. In US English a road diversion is usually called a «detour». In money or law, «diversion of funds» means using money for something it was not meant for, often wrongly.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (maths) The number being divided in a division sum: in 12 ÷ 3 = 4, the dividend is 12. 2) (money) A share of a company's profit paid to people who own shares in it. 3) A benefit or reward that comes later from something you did, as in «pay dividends».
its sense in the lessons: In school maths, dividend ÷ divisor = quotient: the dividend is the number you start with. In money lessons, shareholders receive dividends. In everyday talk, «hard work will pay dividends» means it will bring good results later. Phrases: «pay dividends», «dividend ÷ divisor = quotient».
examples from the lessons: In 20 ÷ 5 = 4, the dividend is 20. | Write the dividend inside the bus-stop division box. | The company paid a dividend to its shareholders. | Grandma gets a small dividend every year from her shares. | Practising spelling will pay dividends in the test. | If the dividend is 0, the answer is 0.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. In maths: dividend = divisor × quotient + remainder. Trap: do not mix up dividend (the number divided) and divisor (the number you divide by). «Pay dividends» is an idiom meaning bring benefits.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Trying to find out about the future or hidden things by special or magical means, such as reading cards, stars or tea leaves. 2) A clever guess or insight.
its sense in the lessons: In history and religion lessons, many ancient peoples practised divination, such as the oracle at Delphi or Chinese oracle bones. In fantasy stories, divination is a kind of magic. In science lessons, it is an example of a claim that has no scientific evidence. The Bible forbids divination for believers. Phrases: «a form of divination», «practise divination».
examples from the lessons: The ancient Greeks visited the oracle for divination. | Reading tea leaves is a kind of divination. | In the story, the witch taught divination with a crystal ball. | Chinese kings used oracle bones for divination. | There is no scientific evidence that divination can predict the future. | The Bible tells believers not to practise divination.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly uncountable. Related: divine (to guess by magic, or relating to God), diviner (a person who does it). «Water divining» or dowsing is searching for water with a stick; tests have not shown it works.

part of speech: noun (Italian; a donna, donne); a name (Donna)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (a name) Donna is a woman's first name. 2) (Italian) The Italian word for «woman» or «lady», and an old title of respect for a lady, like «Madam». 3) In the phrase «prima donna»: the main woman singer in an opera, and (informal) a person who is vain and expects special treatment.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday English «donna» is mostly met as a name or in «prima donna», which tells the reader someone is behaving like a fussy star. In music lessons, the prima donna is the leading opera singer. Phrases: «prima donna», «Madonna» (my lady, a title of Mary, the mother of Jesus).
examples from the lessons: Donna is my mum's best friend. | Stop acting like a prima donna and help tidy up! | The prima donna sang the final song beautifully. | In Italian, «donna» means woman. | Madonna, which means «my lady», is a name for Mary in Christian art. | He threw a prima-donna tantrum when he lost the game.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Not an ordinary English word on its own: it is Italian, or a name (written with a capital: Donna). Pronounced «DON-a». «Prima donna» can be written with or without a hyphen; it is a mild insult when used about ordinary people.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A time when a living thing is alive but not active or growing, as in seeds waiting to sprout or animals hibernating. 2) A time when a volcano or other thing is quiet but could become active again.
its sense in the lessons: In science, seeds stay in dormancy until there is water and warmth; trees are dormant in winter; some animals hibernate. In geography, a volcano in dormancy has not erupted for a long time but may erupt again. Phrases: «period of dormancy», «break dormancy».
examples from the lessons: The seeds stayed in dormancy until the spring rain. | Trees lose their leaves and enter dormancy in winter. | The volcano woke up after centuries of dormancy. | Bears are in a kind of dormancy during winter. | Cold weather helps some bulbs break their dormancy. | After years of dormancy, the old club started meeting again.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Adjective: dormant. Comes from French «dormir», to sleep. A dormant volcano is not the same as an extinct one: extinct means it is not expected to erupt again.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A large bedroom with many beds, such as in a boarding school, camp or hostel. 2) (US) A college or university building where students live; often shortened to «dorm». 3) (UK, also «dormitory town») A town where people live but travel elsewhere to work.
its sense in the lessons: In school stories, especially boarding-school ones, the dormitory is where children sleep and have midnight feasts. On school trips and camps, pupils share dormitories. In geography, a dormitory town or suburb shows commuting patterns. Phrases: «in the dormitory», «dormitory town», «lights out».
examples from the lessons: We slept in a dormitory with twelve bunk beds on camp. | The girls had a midnight feast in the dormitory. | My cousin lives in a university dormitory. | Lights out in the dormitory is at nine. | The boarding school has a dormitory for each year group. | Many commuters live in the dormitory town and work in the city.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: dormitories (change «y» to «ies»). Informal short form: dorm. From Latin «dormire», to sleep (as in dormant).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A widow who has a title or property from her dead husband, such as a «dowager duchess» or «dowager queen». 2) (informal) A grand, dignified old lady.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons and classic novels, a dowager is a noble widow, often the mother of the new duke or king. In stories it suggests an important, sometimes strict, older woman. Phrases: «dowager duchess», «Empress Dowager», «Queen Dowager».
examples from the lessons: The dowager duchess still lived in the old castle. | The Empress Dowager ruled China for many years. | After the king died, his widow became the queen dowager. | A stern dowager sat in the front row of the concert. | The young duke's mother was now called the dowager. | The dowager wore pearls and a feathered hat.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Pronounced «DOW-a-jer» (DOW rhymes with cow). Old-fashioned and formal; mostly in history and novels. Comes from «dower», property given to a widow.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Very much and often suddenly: a big change. 2) In a way that is like acting in a play, showing feelings in a big, showy way. 3) Relating to drama or plays.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, science and geography, «dramatically» describes a big rise or fall: «the temperature dropped dramatically», which tells the reader to expect a large difference in the numbers. In stories, a character who sighs dramatically is showing off feelings. Phrases: «rise dramatically», «fall dramatically», «sigh dramatically».
examples from the lessons: The temperature fell dramatically overnight. | Prices rose dramatically last year. | Her reading improved dramatically after the summer. | He sighed dramatically when told to tidy his room. | She threw her arms up dramatically, like an actress. | The coastline has changed dramatically in a hundred years. | The story ends dramatically with a storm.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from «dramatic»; spelled with «-ally», not «-ly»: dramatically. In maths or graph questions it means a large change, but it does not give a number; check the data. Informal overuse: «you're being dramatic» means overreacting.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Hanging down loosely or tiredly, like wilting flowers, floppy ears or a sagging tent. 2) (informal) Tired, sad or without energy.
its sense in the lessons: In science, a droopy plant is a sign it needs water or light. In everyday life, droopy ears, eyelids or socks describe how something looks. In stories, a droopy character seems tired or fed up. Phrases: «droopy ears», «droopy eyelids», «feeling droopy».
examples from the lessons: The sunflowers were droopy because we forgot to water them. | The basset hound has long droopy ears. | My socks are droopy and keep falling down. | After the long walk I felt a bit droopy. | His droopy eyelids showed he needed sleep. | The tent was droopy in the rain.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal adjective from the verb «droop». Comparative: droopier, droopiest («y» becomes «i»). Similar: saggy, floppy, wilted.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Making an exact copy of something, or the copy itself. 2) Doing the same work twice when once would be enough; unnecessary repeating. 3) (science) A part of a chromosome or gene that is copied twice.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, duplication can mean doubling; in computing, data duplication means the same file stored twice. At work and in school projects, «avoid duplication» means do not do the same job twice. In science, gene duplication is one way living things change over time. Phrases: «avoid duplication», «duplication of effort», «gene duplication».
examples from the lessons: We split the tasks to avoid duplication. | The duplication of keys was done at the hardware shop. | Duplication of the photo made two identical copies. | There was some duplication: two groups wrote the same poster. | Gene duplication can lead to new features in living things. | Copying and pasting caused a duplication in my list.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun from the verb «duplicate». Can be countable or uncountable. Related: duplicate (an exact copy), «in duplicate» means in two copies. In maths, duplicating a number means multiplying it by 2.

part of speech: adjective (dyslexic); noun (a dyslexic, dyslexics — less preferred)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Having dyslexia: a difference in how the brain handles words, which makes reading, spelling and sometimes writing harder, but has nothing to do with how clever someone is.
its sense in the lessons: In school life, dyslexic pupils may get extra time, coloured overlays, audiobooks or special help with phonics. In stories and real life, many dyslexic people are creative and successful. It teaches kindness: struggling to read is not being lazy or slow. Phrases: «she is dyslexic», «dyslexic-friendly font», «a person with dyslexia».
examples from the lessons: My brother is dyslexic, so he uses audiobooks. | Dyslexic pupils can get extra time in tests. | The teacher printed the worksheet in a dyslexic-friendly font. | Being dyslexic doesn't mean you're not clever. | Many famous inventors and artists were dyslexic. | Coloured paper helps some dyslexic readers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mainly used as an adjective: «He is dyslexic». Many people prefer «a dyslexic person» or «a person with dyslexia» rather than «a dyslexic». Noun for the condition: dyslexia. Myth: dyslexia is not just seeing letters backwards and is not caused by poor teaching or low intelligence.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The part of a phone, headphones or other device that you hold to or put in your ear to hear sound. 2) A tiny speaker worn in the ear, used by security guards, TV presenters or with hearing aids. 3) One of the arms of a pair of glasses that rest over the ears.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, people use earpieces for phone calls or music; security guards and TV presenters wear earpieces to hear instructions. In science, the earpiece of a stethoscope goes in the doctor's ears. Phrases: «a wireless earpiece», «speak into the earpiece».
examples from the lessons: The security guard listened to his earpiece. | The newsreader heard the producer through her earpiece. | My earpiece fell out when I was running. | The doctor put the stethoscope earpieces in her ears. | One earpiece of my glasses is bent. | Dad uses an earpiece to talk on the phone while driving.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable compound noun: ear + piece. Uses «an» before it: an earpiece. Safety: keep the volume low to protect hearing, and do not wear both ears covered when crossing roads.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A small white woolly-looking flower that grows high in the Alps and other mountains of Europe; it is a famous symbol of Switzerland and Austria.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and nature lessons, edelweiss shows how mountain plants survive cold and strong sunlight with fluffy hairs. In music, it is the name of a famous song from the film «The Sound of Music». Phrases: «a sprig of edelweiss», «the Alps».
examples from the lessons: Edelweiss grows high up in the Alps. | Its petals look as if they are made of white felt. | We sang «Edelweiss» in the school concert. | Edelweiss is a symbol of Austria and Switzerland. | Picking wild edelweiss is not allowed in many places. | The fluffy hairs help edelweiss stay warm.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A German word meaning «noble white». Pronounced «AY-del-vice». The plural is usually the same: edelweiss. The song «Edelweiss» was written for a musical; it is not an old Austrian anthem, a common myth.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To teach someone over a long time, especially at school, college or university. 2) To give people information so they understand something better, such as about health or safety. 3) (passive) «Be educated at» a school means you went to school there.
its sense in the lessons: In school and everyday life, parents and teachers educate children; campaigns educate people about road safety or recycling. In stories and history, being educated could change someone's life, and in the past many children, especially girls, were not educated. Phrases: «educate people about», «well educated», «educated guess».
examples from the lessons: Teachers educate children to read and write. | The poster educates people about recycling. | She was educated at a small village school. | In the past, many girls were not educated at all. | We want to educate our friends about online safety. | Make an educated guess if you are not sure.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Noun: education; adjective: educational. «An educated guess» means a guess based on what you know. Pronounced «ED-yoo-kate» or «EJ-oo-kate».

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a way that gets a job done well without wasting time, energy, money or materials.
its sense in the lessons: In science, efficiently means using energy well: LED bulbs turn electricity into light efficiently. In maths, working efficiently means using a quick method, like the column method instead of counting. In everyday life, a team that works efficiently finishes fast without fuss. Phrases: «work efficiently», «use energy efficiently», «run efficiently».
examples from the lessons: She tidied her room quickly and efficiently. | LED bulbs use electricity more efficiently than old bulbs. | Use the column method to add the numbers efficiently. | The team worked efficiently and finished early. | The new boiler heats the house more efficiently. | Bees collect nectar very efficiently.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from «efficient»; noun: efficiency. Trap: «efficiently» (no waste) is not the same as «effectively» (it works). Spelling: «-cie-», like «sufficient».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Done or seeming to be done without trying hard; looking easy. 2) Natural and smooth, without strain.
its sense in the lessons: In sport and music, an effortless performance looks easy because of lots of practice. In stories it shows skill or grace: «she glided across the ice with effortless ease». Phrases: «effortless ease», «made it look effortless».
examples from the lessons: The skater's jump looked effortless. | She made the hard sum look effortless. | His effortless swimming came from years of practice. | The eagle soared in effortless circles. | Riding a bike becomes effortless once you learn. | Her effortless smile put everyone at ease.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: effort + «-less» (without). Adverb: effortlessly. Myth to notice: things that look effortless usually took lots of effort to learn.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To push or throw something out with force. 2) To make someone leave a place, often by force. 3) To take a disc, cartridge or memory stick out of a machine, or to tell a computer you are removing it. 4) (of a pilot) To escape from a plane by being shot out in a special seat.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday technology, you press «eject» before removing a USB stick or disc. In science, a volcano ejects ash and lava. In sport and stories, a player or rowdy fan may be ejected. Pilots eject in emergencies. Phrases: «eject button», «be ejected from», «ejector seat».
examples from the lessons: Press the button to eject the disc. | Always eject the memory stick before pulling it out. | The volcano ejected hot rocks and ash. | The pilot ejected just before the plane crashed. | Security ejected the rowdy fan from the stadium. | The toaster ejected the bread with a pop. | The referee ejected the player for fighting.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Noun: ejection. Stress on «JECT»: «ee-JECT». Similar but less formal: «throw out», «kick out». In US sport, «ejected» means sent off.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The ability of a material to stretch or bend and then go back to its original shape. 2) (money) How much the amount people buy changes when the price changes.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, rubber bands, springs and balloons show elasticity; pupils test materials by stretching them and measuring. Skin and muscles also have elasticity. In economics, it describes how people react to prices. Phrases: «lose its elasticity», «elastic limit».
examples from the lessons: Rubber bands have great elasticity. | The old elastic in my trousers has lost its elasticity. | We tested the elasticity of different materials. | Skin loses some elasticity as people get older. | A trampoline works because of the elasticity of its mat. | Springs have elasticity until you stretch them too far.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Adjective: elastic. Pronounced «ee-las-TIS-i-tee». In science, if you stretch something past its «elastic limit», it will not return to its shape.

meaning for a pupil: 1) By using electronic devices such as computers, phones or the internet. 2) Using electricity and electronic parts, not by hand or by moving parts.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, homework, money and letters are often sent electronically. In safety, money taken or sent electronically needs care with passwords. In science, devices controlled electronically use circuits and chips. Phrases: «sent electronically», «paid electronically», «electronically controlled».
examples from the lessons: Please hand your homework in electronically. | Mum paid the bill electronically. | The tickets were sent to us electronically. | The doors are locked electronically at night. | Votes were counted electronically. | Library books can be borrowed electronically as e-books.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from «electronic». Spelled with «-ally». Not the same as «electrically» (powered by electricity in general); «electronically» suggests computers, chips and digital systems.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To get a reaction, answer or information from someone, often by asking questions or doing something.
its sense in the lessons: In school, teachers ask questions to elicit ideas from the class. In stories, a joke may elicit a laugh, and a sad scene may elicit tears. In science, a stimulus elicits a response. Phrases: «elicit a response», «elicit information», «elicit a smile».
examples from the lessons: The clown's trick elicited laughter from the children. | The teacher's question elicited many good answers. | The police tried to elicit information from the witness. | His sad story elicited sympathy. | A loud noise elicits a jump from most people. | Her joke failed to elicit even a smile.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal word. Trap: «elicit» (to draw out) sounds like «illicit» (illegal, not allowed). Regular verb: elicit, elicited. Pronounced «ee-LIS-it».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Having the right to do or get something because you meet the rules, such as the right age, address or qualifications.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday and school life, eligibility rules decide who can join a team, enter a competition, get free school meals or vote. In forms, «check your eligibility» means see if you qualify. Phrases: «eligibility for», «eligibility rules», «check eligibility».
examples from the lessons: Check the eligibility rules before you enter the competition. | Age is one condition for eligibility to vote. | Your eligibility for free school meals depends on family income. | The coach checked each player's eligibility for the under-11 team. | Living in the town is needed for eligibility for the library card. | Eligibility for the prize was limited to pupils under 12.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Adjective: eligible (allowed or qualified). Spelling: «-ibility». In maths word problems, eligibility rules are conditions: check each person against every rule (for example age ≤ 11 and lives in the town).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A living thing at a very early stage of growing, before it is born or hatches: inside an egg, a seed or its mother's womb. 2) The tiny part inside a seed that will grow into a new plant. 3) (in embryo) Something at a very early stage that may develop later, like an idea.
its sense in the lessons: In science, pupils learn that a chick embryo grows inside an egg, a human embryo grows in the womb, and a bean seed contains an embryo that grows into a plant. In everyday talk, «a plan in embryo» means it has only just started. Phrases: «in embryo», «a chick embryo», «embryo plant».
examples from the lessons: A chick embryo grows inside the egg for three weeks. | Inside the bean seed is a tiny embryo. | A human embryo is smaller than a grain of rice at first. | We saw a picture of a frog embryo in the jelly. | The idea for our club was only an embryo then. | The embryo gets food from the yolk.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; plural: embryos (no «e»). Pronounced «EM-bree-oh». Adjective: embryonic. In humans, after about eight weeks it is called a foetus (US: fetus). This is a topic where people hold different moral and religious views.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Coming out from somewhere and becoming visible, like an insect from a cocoon. 2) Starting to exist or becoming known or important, like a new idea or country.
its sense in the lessons: In science, the emergence of a butterfly from its chrysalis or of seedlings from soil is a stage in a life cycle. In history, «the emergence of» farming, cities or new nations tells when something began. Phrases: «the emergence of», «emergence from».
examples from the lessons: We watched the emergence of a butterfly from its chrysalis. | The emergence of the first shoots shows spring is here. | The emergence of the internet changed how people talk. | History tells of the emergence of the first cities. | The mayfly's emergence happens in early summer. | Scientists studied the emergence of a new island from the sea.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun from the verb «emerge». Trap: not the same as «emergency» (a sudden dangerous situation), though both come from «emerge». Formal word.

part of speech: verb (emote, emotes, emoted, emoting); noun (an emote, emotes — gaming)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To show feelings in a strong, often over-the-top way, especially when acting. 2) (gaming, slang) An «emote» is an animation or small picture that a character in a video game does to show a feeling, like a dance or a wave.
its sense in the lessons: In drama, an actor who emotes too much is overacting. In children's online life, emotes are dances and gestures in games or symbols in chat. Phrases: «emote on stage», «buy an emote», «use an emote».
examples from the lessons: The actor emoted wildly, waving his arms about. | In drama class we practised how to emote without shouting. | She did a victory dance emote after winning the game. | He spent his pocket money on a new emote. | The singer emoted every word of the sad song. | Chat filled with laughing emotes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb, often a bit mocking: it suggests too much feeling. The gaming noun is newer slang. Related: emotion, emoji (not the same thing as an emote, though similar).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A mixture of two liquids that do not usually mix, such as oil and water, where tiny drops of one are spread through the other. 2) (UK) Emulsion paint: a water-based paint for walls and ceilings. 3) The light-sensitive coating on old photographic film.
its sense in the lessons: In science, emulsions show mixtures: mayonnaise, milk and salad dressing are emulsions; shaking oil and vinegar makes a short-lived one, and egg yolk helps hold it together. In everyday British life, people paint walls with «white emulsion». Phrases: «oil and water emulsion», «matt emulsion».
examples from the lessons: Mayonnaise is an emulsion of oil and egg yolk. | Shake the dressing to make an emulsion. | Milk is an emulsion of fat in water. | The oil and vinegar separated when the emulsion settled. | Dad painted the ceiling with white emulsion. | Old cameras used film with a light-sensitive emulsion.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable or uncountable. Pronounced «ee-MUL-shun». Verb: emulsify; an emulsifier helps the two liquids stay mixed. In science, an emulsion is a type of mixture, not a solution: the liquids do not dissolve in each other.

part of speech: verb, past form of encircle (encircle, encircles, encircled, encircling); adjective
meaning for a pupil: 1) Formed a circle around something or someone; surrounded. 2) (in war) Surrounded an army or city so it could not escape.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, «the wolves encircled the camp» creates danger; in history, armies encircled cities in sieges. In maths or art, a shape may be encircled by a ring. In everyday life, a garden encircled by a hedge. Phrases: «encircled by», «encircled the town».
examples from the lessons: Tall trees encircled the quiet lake. | The children encircled the birthday girl and sang. | The castle was encircled by a deep moat. | The army encircled the city. | Circle the answer: put a ring round it so it is encircled. | A ring of light encircled the moon. | Sharks encircled the small boat.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: encircle, encircled. «En-» means put into or make: encircle = put in a circle. Often passive: «encircled by». Similar: surround, ring.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A disease that spreads quickly to many people in one area at the same time. 2) A sudden fast spread of something bad, like bullying or a craze. 3) (adjective) Happening widely and fast.
its sense in the lessons: In science and history, epidemics like cholera, plague and flu show how germs spread and why hygiene, clean water and vaccines matter. In maths, epidemic numbers can double quickly. In news, «an epidemic of» is used for any fast-spreading problem. Phrases: «a flu epidemic», «an epidemic of», «epidemic proportions».
examples from the lessons: A cholera epidemic hit the city long ago. | Washing hands helps stop an epidemic. | There was a flu epidemic at school, and half the class was off. | Scientists study how an epidemic spreads. | The town faced an epidemic of bike thefts. | Vaccines helped end the epidemic.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Compare: an outbreak is small and local; an epidemic spreads widely in a region; a pandemic spreads across many countries or the whole world. In maths, epidemic growth is often modelled by doubling: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Near the equator, the imaginary line around the middle of the Earth. 2) Typical of places near the equator: hot and often wet all year.
its sense in the lessons: In geography, equatorial regions have rainforests and almost the same temperature and day length all year. Countries like Ecuador, Kenya and Indonesia have equatorial areas. In science, an equatorial orbit goes around the planet's middle. Phrases: «equatorial rainforest», «equatorial climate», «Equatorial Guinea».
examples from the lessons: The Amazon has an equatorial climate. | Equatorial rainforests get rain almost every day. | It is hot all year in equatorial countries. | Equatorial Guinea is a country in Africa. | The satellite has an equatorial orbit. | Day and night are about twelve hours each in equatorial places.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective from «equator». Pronounced «ek-wa-TOR-ee-al». Myth: not every equatorial place is low and hot; mountains near the equator, like Kilimanjaro, can have snow.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Using unclear words or answers on purpose so you do not have to give a straight answer or tell the full truth. 2) (logic) A mistake in an argument where one word is used with two different meanings.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and politics, equivocation shows a character dodging the question. In thinking and ethics lessons, it is a trick to spot: «a feather is light; what is light cannot be dark; so a feather cannot be dark» uses «light» in two senses. Phrases: «without equivocation», «answer without equivocation».
examples from the lessons: The minister's answer was pure equivocation. | «Did you eat the cake?» «Well, cakes get eaten...» That is equivocation. | Please answer without equivocation: yes or no? | The argument fails because of equivocation on the word «bank». | His equivocation made us think he was hiding something. | Spot the equivocation in the riddle.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal word. Verb: equivocate. Adjective: equivocal (unclear, open to two meanings). Opposite: «unequivocal» (completely clear). Pronounced «ee-kwiv-o-KAY-shun».

part of speech: verb, present participle of erode (erode, erodes, eroded, eroding); adjective (an eroding cliff)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Slowly wearing away rock, soil or land by wind, water or ice. 2) Being slowly worn away. 3) Slowly making something weaker or smaller, such as trust or savings.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and science, waves are eroding cliffs, rivers are eroding valleys, and wind is eroding rocks into strange shapes. In everyday and money talk, «eroding trust» or «rising prices eroding savings» shows something getting weaker little by little. Phrases: «eroding the coast», «eroding away», «eroding confidence».
examples from the lessons: The sea is eroding the cliffs every winter. | The river is slowly eroding its banks. | Houses near the eroding coast may fall into the sea. | Wind is eroding the soft sandstone. | His lies are eroding her trust in him. | Rising prices are eroding the value of our pocket money.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Form of «erode»; drop the «e» before «-ing». Noun: erosion. Trap: erosion (wearing away and carrying off) is different from weathering (breaking rock where it is).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Not regular or steady; changing suddenly in a way you cannot predict. 2) (geology, noun: an erratic) A large boulder carried far by a glacier and left in a place where that type of rock is not normally found.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and stories, erratic behaviour, driving or a heartbeat tells the reader something is wrong or worrying. In science and data, erratic results jump around and are hard to trust. In geography, glacial erratics show where ice once moved. Phrases: «erratic behaviour», «erratic driving», «glacial erratic».
examples from the lessons: The car moved in an erratic way across the lanes. | Our results were erratic, so we repeated the test. | The puppy's erratic running made us laugh. | The Wi-Fi is erratic: it keeps cutting out. | His erratic moods confused his friends. | A huge erratic boulder sits alone in the field, left by a glacier.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective (also a noun in geology). Adverb: erratically. Pronounced «i-RAT-ik». Not the same as «error», though related in origin (both from Latin «errare», to wander).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) A colourless liquid with a strong smell that evaporates easily; it was used long ago to put patients to sleep for operations. 2) (old science) An invisible substance that people once thought filled space and carried light; experiments showed it does not exist. 3) (poetic) The clear sky or upper air. 4) (informal) «Into the ether»: lost or disappeared, especially online or on the radio.
its sense in the lessons: In history of medicine, ether was one of the first anaesthetics, used from the 1840s. In science history, the idea of the ether is an example of a theory that was tested and dropped. In everyday talk, a message «vanished into the ether» means it was lost. Phrases: «into the ether», «over the ether».
examples from the lessons: Doctors once used ether to put patients to sleep. | Ether evaporates very quickly. | Scientists once believed light travelled through the ether. | Experiments showed there was no ether. | My email just vanished into the ether. | Birds flew high in the blue ether.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Pronounced «EE-ther». Can also be spelled «aether» for the old idea of space. Safety: ether is very flammable. Not the same as «either».

meaning for a pupil: 1) To escape from or keep away from someone or something, like a chaser. 2) To avoid answering a question or doing something you should do, often by being clever or dishonest.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and games, a character evades capture or guards. In sport, a player evades a tackle. In law and money, «evading tax» means not paying tax you owe, which is a crime. In discussions, «evading the question» means not answering. Phrases: «evade capture», «evade the question», «tax evasion».
examples from the lessons: The fox evaded the hounds by running into the river. | The winger evaded two defenders and scored. | He evaded my question by changing the subject. | The thief evaded the police for weeks. | Some animals evade predators by hiding. | Evading tax is against the law.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Noun: evasion; adjective: evasive (not giving clear answers). Trap: «tax evasion» is illegal, while «tax avoidance» uses legal tricks.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Careful judging of how good, useful or valuable something is. 2) A written or spoken report that gives that judgement. 3) (maths) Working out the value of an expression.
its sense in the lessons: In school science, the «evaluation» section of an experiment asks what went well, what went wrong and how to improve. In design and technology, pupils evaluate their products. Teachers give evaluations of work. In maths, evaluation means calculating: evaluate 3 × (2 + 4) = 18. Phrases: «self-evaluation», «write an evaluation», «evaluation of».
examples from the lessons: Write an evaluation of your experiment. | In our evaluation, we said the test was not fair. | The teacher's evaluation of my story was very kind. | Self-evaluation helps you see how to improve. | The evaluation of 5 + 3 × 2 gives 11. | The school had an evaluation by inspectors.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun from the verb «evaluate». In maths: «evaluate» means find the value; follow the order of operations. In science write-ups, the evaluation comes after the conclusion.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Happening at the end of a long time or after a series of events; final.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and sport, «the eventual winner» tells the reader who won in the end, after many rounds. In history, «the eventual result» shows what finally happened. Phrases: «the eventual winner», «eventual success», «eventual outcome».
examples from the lessons: Spain were the eventual champions. | After many tries, his eventual success made him proud. | The eventual cost of the bridge was double the plan. | We didn't know the eventual result until the last day. | The eventual outcome of the war changed the map of Europe. | Practice led to her eventual win.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective; adverb: eventually (in the end). False friend: in some languages a similar word means «possible», but in English «eventual» means final, not possible. Used before a noun: «the eventual winner».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Breathing out: pushing air out of your lungs. 2) The air, steam or smell that is breathed out or given off.
its sense in the lessons: In science and PE, breathing has two parts: inhalation (in) and exhalation (out); during exhalation the diaphragm relaxes and the chest gets smaller, and we breathe out more carbon dioxide. In calm and mindfulness lessons, a slow exhalation helps you relax. Phrases: «slow exhalation», «on the exhalation».
examples from the lessons: During exhalation, air leaves the lungs. | Take a deep breath in, then a slow exhalation. | We see our exhalation as mist on cold days. | The singer used a long exhalation to hold the note. | Exhalation removes carbon dioxide from the body. | Count to four on each exhalation.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun from the verb «exhale». Opposite: inhalation. Pronounced «ex-ha-LAY-shun». Can be countable (one exhalation) or uncountable.

part of speech: verb (exploit, exploits, exploited, exploiting); noun (an exploit, exploits)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (verb) To use someone unfairly for your own gain, like paying workers too little or tricking children. 2) (verb) To make full use of something, such as resources or a chance. 3) (noun) A brave, exciting or daring deed, an adventure. 4) (computing) A trick or piece of code that uses a weakness in a program.
its sense in the lessons: In history and citizenship, factory owners exploited child workers; in online safety, bad people may try to exploit children, so tell a trusted adult. In geography, countries exploit oil or coal. In stories, «the hero's exploits» are adventures. In games, an exploit is a glitch players use to cheat. Phrases: «exploit a weakness», «exploit workers», «daring exploits».
examples from the lessons: Factory owners once exploited children by making them work long hours. | The team exploited the gap in the defence. | The country exploits its forests for wood. | We read about Robin Hood's exploits. | Never let anyone online exploit you; tell an adult. | Hackers used an exploit to break into the game. | She exploited every chance to practise.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb stressed «ex-PLOIT»; noun stressed «EX-ploit». Noun: exploitation (unfair use). Using an exploit in an online game may break its rules and get you banned.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person, company or country that sells goods to other countries.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and economics, exporters send goods abroad: Australia is a big exporter of iron ore, New Zealand of milk products, Canada of wood. It shows how countries trade and depend on each other. Phrases: «a major exporter of», «the world's biggest exporter».
examples from the lessons: New Zealand is a big exporter of butter and milk powder. | The company is an exporter of toys to Europe. | Brazil is the world's largest exporter of coffee. | Exporters sell goods to other countries. | The exporter shipped the cars across the ocean. | Ukraine is a major exporter of wheat and sunflower oil.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; from «export» + «-er». Opposite: importer. In maths problems about trade, exports bring money in; imports send money out.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (mainly US) Glasses: two lenses in a frame that you wear in front of your eyes to help you see better.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, many children and adults wear eyeglasses for short or long sight; an optician tests eyes. In science, the lenses bend light to focus it. Phrases: «a pair of eyeglasses», «wear eyeglasses».
examples from the lessons: Grandpa can't read without his eyeglasses. | I got my first pair of eyeglasses this year. | My eyeglasses steam up when I come inside. | The optician checked if I needed eyeglasses. | Eyeglasses have curved lenses that bend light. | She keeps her eyeglasses in a red case.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always plural: «my eyeglasses are...», «a pair of eyeglasses». Mostly US; in the UK, Ireland and Australia people usually say «glasses» or «spectacles» («specs», informal).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A visor: a band with a stiff brim at the front that shades the eyes from light, worn without a top. 2) A soft mask worn over the eyes to block light while sleeping.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and sport, tennis players and golfers wear eyeshades in the sun; on planes, travellers use eyeshades to sleep. In old stories and films, newspaper editors and accountants wear green eyeshades. Phrases: «a green eyeshade», «sleep with an eyeshade».
examples from the lessons: She wore an eyeshade to play tennis in the sun. | I sleep better with an eyeshade on the plane. | The old editor wore a green eyeshade. | Put on your eyeshade so the light doesn't wake you. | An eyeshade keeps the sun off your face but not your head. | The golfer pulled down his eyeshade.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable compound: eye + shade. Uses «an»: an eyeshade. Similar: visor, sleep mask. A visor does not protect the top of your head from sunburn, so use sun cream too.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Too simple; said or done without careful thought, so it ignores the real problem. 2) (old or literary) Done easily, smooth and effortless.
its sense in the lessons: In debates and essays, a «facile answer» or «facile argument» is one that is too easy and shallow; teachers may write it as criticism. In stories, an old-style sense means smooth and skilful. Phrases: «a facile answer», «facile solution», «facile comparison».
examples from the lessons: Saying «just be happy» is a facile answer to sadness. | The critic called the film's ending facile. | Don't give a facile reply; think it through. | There is no facile solution to traffic jams. | His facile excuses annoyed the teacher. | It is facile to blame one person for the whole problem.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal and usually critical. Pronounced «FASS-ile» (UK, «-ile» as in «mile») or «FASS-ul» (US). False friend: French «facile» simply means «easy», but in English it usually means too simple, in a bad way.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Making something easier to do or helping it happen. 2) Leading a group discussion or meeting so that everyone can take part and work well.
its sense in the lessons: In school and work, a facilitator leads a group activity, and «facilitation» is that guiding role. In science, «facilitation» can mean one living thing helping another to grow. In the formal exam voice it replaces «help». Phrases: «facilitation of», «trade facilitation».
examples from the lessons: The teacher's facilitation helped every group share ideas. | Ramps provide the facilitation of access for wheelchair users. | Good facilitation keeps a meeting on time. | The new bridge led to the facilitation of trade between towns. | Some plants grow better because of facilitation by nearby shrubs. | With careful facilitation, even shy pupils spoke up.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal. Verb: facilitate; person: facilitator. In everyday talk people say «help» or «making it easier». Uncountable.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who keeps, trains and flies falcons, hawks or other birds of prey, especially to hunt or for displays.
its sense in the lessons: In history, kings and nobles kept falconers to hunt with trained birds; falconry was a sign of high status. Today, falconers give displays at shows and use birds to scare pigeons from airports and buildings. In stories it suggests patience and skill. Phrases: «a falconer's glove», «a falconry display».
examples from the lessons: The falconer wore a thick leather glove. | At the show, a falconer flew an owl over our heads. | The falconer called the hawk back with a whistle. | Medieval kings kept falconers at their castles. | Some airports hire a falconer to scare birds away. | The falconer fed the falcon a piece of meat as a reward.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Pronounced «FAL-kon-er» or «FAWL-kon-er». The sport is called falconry. A falconer uses many birds, not just falcons: hawks, eagles and owls too.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A small bird with a tail that spreads out like a fan; in New Zealand the fantail (pīwakawaka) is a common, friendly bird that follows walkers to catch insects. 2) A kind of fancy pigeon or goldfish with a fan-shaped tail. 3) A tail or end shaped like a fan.
its sense in the lessons: In nature lessons in New Zealand and Australia, fantails are familiar birds; in Māori stories the pīwakawaka has a special role, linked with the hero Māui. Fantail pigeons and fantail goldfish are bred as pets. Phrases: «a fantail pigeon», «fantail goldfish».
examples from the lessons: A fantail flitted along the bush track beside us. | The fantail spread its tail like a little fan. | In New Zealand the fantail is called pīwakawaka. | Grandad keeps white fantail pigeons. | Our fantail goldfish has a long, flowing tail. | The fantail snapped up insects that our feet disturbed.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable compound: fan + tail. In Australia there are several kinds called fantails or willie wagtails (a close relative). Names of breeds and birds are not always written with capitals.

part of speech: adjective (fattening food); verb, present participle of fatten (fatten, fattens, fattened, fattening)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (adjective) Likely to make you put on weight, usually because it has lots of fat or sugar. 2) (verb) Making an animal or person fatter, especially farm animals before they are sold.
its sense in the lessons: In health lessons, fattening foods such as chips, sweets and fizzy drinks are fine sometimes but should not be eaten every day. On farms, farmers fatten cattle, pigs or geese. In fairy tales, the witch in «Hansel and Gretel» was fattening Hansel. Phrases: «fattening food», «fattening up».
examples from the lessons: Cakes are tasty but fattening. | Fizzy drinks are fattening because of the sugar. | The farmer is fattening the lambs on fresh grass. | The witch was fattening Hansel up in a cage. | Nan says I need fattening up after being ill. | Fried snacks are more fattening than fruit.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double «t»: fatten, fattening. No food is «fattening» by itself in small amounts; it is about how much and how often. Be careful: comments about other people's weight can be hurtful.

part of speech: noun (a fay, fays — old or poetic); a name (Fay, Faye)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (old, poetic) A fairy: a small magical being in old stories and poems. 2) (a name) Fay or Faye is a woman's first name. 3) (Morgan le Fay) The name of a magical woman, an enchantress, in the stories of King Arthur.
its sense in the lessons: In fairy tales, old poems and fantasy books, a fay is a fairy; it gives the writing an old-fashioned, magical feel. In King Arthur stories, Morgan le Fay is Arthur's half-sister and a sorceress. Otherwise it is mostly met as a name. Phrases: «Morgan le Fay», «the fays of the forest».
examples from the lessons: In the old poem, a fay danced in the moonlight. | Morgan le Fay was a powerful enchantress in the Arthur stories. | My aunt's name is Fay. | The children pretended to be fays in the woods. | The story told of a fay who granted three wishes. | Faye is spelled with an «e» in some families.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Old-fashioned word; in everyday English people say «fairy». As a name it takes a capital: Fay or Faye. Pronounced like «day» with an «f». Not to be confused with «fey», which means strange and dreamy.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Belonging to the feudal system: the way society was organised in medieval Europe, where kings gave land to lords in return for loyalty and soldiers, and peasants worked the land for the lords. 2) (informal) Old-fashioned and unfair, where a few powerful people control many others.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, the feudal system is often drawn as a pyramid: king at the top, then barons and lords, then knights, then peasants or serfs at the bottom. It explains castles, manors and why peasants had few rights. Phrases: «the feudal system», «feudal lord», «feudal society».
examples from the lessons: In the feudal system, the king owned all the land. | The feudal lord let peasants farm his land. | Knights served their lords in feudal times. | We drew a feudal pyramid in history. | Serfs in feudal England could not leave the manor. | The boss runs the company like a feudal lord.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective. Noun: feudalism. Pronounced «FYOO-dal». The pyramid picture is a simplification; the real system varied from place to place and changed over time.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Made of or containing fibres: long, thin threads. 2) (food) Tough and stringy, like celery or old beans; full of fibre.
its sense in the lessons: In science, fibrous materials include wood, cotton, muscle and some rocks; fibrous roots are many thin roots spreading out, unlike a single tap root such as a carrot. In health, fibrous foods help digestion. Phrases: «fibrous roots», «fibrous tissue», «fibrous plants».
examples from the lessons: Grass has fibrous roots that spread in every direction. | Celery is crunchy and fibrous. | Muscles are made of fibrous tissue. | The coconut husk is very fibrous. | A carrot has a tap root, but grass has fibrous roots. | Fibrous foods like oats help keep your tummy healthy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective from «fibre» (UK) or «fiber» (US); spelled «fibrous» in both. Pronounced «FY-brus».

meaning for a pupil: 1) In very small or thin pieces: «finely chopped onion». 2) Very carefully and exactly, with small details: «finely balanced», «finely tuned». 3) (old or formal) In a fine, beautiful way.
its sense in the lessons: In cooking, recipes tell you to chop or grate something finely. In science and engineering, instruments are finely tuned or finely adjusted. In arguments and sport, «finely balanced» means very close. Phrases: «finely chopped», «finely balanced», «finely tuned», «finely ground».
examples from the lessons: Chop the onion finely. | Grate the cheese finely over the pasta. | The match was finely balanced until the last minute. | The violin was finely tuned before the concert. | Coffee beans are finely ground into powder. | The model ship was finely made, with tiny ropes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from «fine». Not used to mean «okay» («I'm fine» does not become «finely»). Opposite in cooking: coarsely or roughly.

part of speech: noun (a fir, firs; also fir tree)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A tall evergreen tree with flat needles and upright cones; many are used as Christmas trees. 2) The wood of this tree.
its sense in the lessons: In science and nature lessons, firs are conifers: they keep their needles in winter and have cones. In everyday life, fir trees are popular Christmas trees and their wood is used for building. Phrases: «fir tree», «fir cone», «Douglas fir».
examples from the lessons: We decorated a fir tree for Christmas. | Fir trees stay green all winter. | The forest smelled of fir and pine. | Squirrels nibbled seeds from the fir cones. | The cabin was built from fir wood. | A fir's needles are soft and flat.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Homophone trap: «fir» (tree) sounds the same as «fur» (animal hair). Many trees called «pine» or «spruce» look like firs; fir cones stand upright on branches and fall apart there.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A gun that a person can carry, such as a pistol, rifle or shotgun.
its sense in the lessons: In news, law and safety, «firearms» is the formal word for guns. Laws on firearms are very strict in the UK, Australia and New Zealand, and different in the USA and Canada. Safety rule for children: if you find a gun, do not touch it, leave the area and tell an adult. Phrases: «firearms licence», «firearms officer», «a loaded firearm».
examples from the lessons: Police said the man was carrying a firearm. | You need a licence to own a firearm. | Firearms officers are specially trained police. | If you ever see a firearm, don't touch it; tell an adult. | Australia changed its firearms laws after a terrible shooting in 1996. | Farmers may keep a firearm to protect animals.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal word, used in news and law; everyday word is «gun». Usually countable; «firearms» in the plural is common. Toy and real guns can look alike; treat any gun as real and dangerous.

part of speech: noun (a flank, flanks); verb (flank, flanks, flanked, flanking)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The side of an animal's or person's body between the ribs and the hip. 2) The side of an army, a team formation or a building. 3) (verb) To be at the side of someone or something: «flanked by guards». 4) (verb) To go round the side of an enemy to attack.
its sense in the lessons: In history and battles, generals attack an enemy's flank, its weak side. In sport, players run down the flank (the wing). In stories, «the president, flanked by bodyguards» tells you who stood beside him. In farming, a horse's or cow's flank is its side. Phrases: «flanked by», «on the left flank», «attack the flank».
examples from the lessons: The horse had a scratch on its flank. | The army attacked the enemy's left flank. | The winger ran down the right flank and crossed the ball. | The headteacher walked in, flanked by two teachers. | Tall trees flanked the path. | The soldiers tried to flank the castle from the hill.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun and regular verb. Often passive: «flanked by». In sport, «flank» means wing.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A simple soft worm with a flat body and no legs; many live in water or damp places, and some are parasites that live inside other animals.
its sense in the lessons: In science, flatworms are among the simplest animals with a head and tail; planarian flatworms can regrow lost parts. Some flatworms, like tapeworms, live in animals' guts, which is why pets get worming tablets. In New Zealand and the UK, garden flatworms can harm earthworms. Phrases: «planarian flatworm», «parasitic flatworm».
examples from the lessons: A flatworm glided across the bottom of the pond. | Flatworms have soft, flat bodies. | Some flatworms can regrow if cut in half. | The tapeworm is a kind of flatworm that lives inside animals. | We found a flatworm under a damp rock. | Bright sea flatworms look like tiny ribbons.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable compound: flat + worm. Not all flatworms look like earthworms; earthworms are round and have segments, flatworms do not.

part of speech: noun (a floe, floes; also ice floe)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A large flat sheet of floating ice on the sea.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and science about polar regions, floes break off the sea ice; polar bears hunt seals from them, and seals rest on them. As the climate warms, there is less sea ice and fewer floes in summer. In stories, explorers drift on floes. Phrases: «ice floe», «drifting floes».
