examples from the lessons: A polar bear stood on the ice floe. | Seals rested on the floating floe. | The ship pushed slowly between the floes. | The explorers drifted for months on an ice floe. | Warmer seas mean fewer ice floes in summer. | The floe cracked and split in two.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Homophone trap: «floe» (ice) sounds like «flow» (to move like a liquid). Pronounced «flo». An iceberg is different: it comes from a glacier and sits deep in the water; a floe is flatter sea ice.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (adjective) From or about Florence, a famous city in Italy known for art and the Renaissance. 2) (noun, food) A thin, crisp biscuit made of nuts and candied fruit, often with chocolate on one side. 3) (cooking, «florentine» after a dish name) Served with spinach, as in «eggs florentine».
its sense in the lessons: In history and art lessons, Florentine painters and sculptors like Michelangelo and Leonardo were part of the Renaissance. In everyday life and cafés, florentines are biscuits and «eggs florentine» is a breakfast with spinach. Phrases: «Florentine art», «eggs florentine», «a chocolate florentine».
examples from the lessons: Florentine artists painted famous pictures in the Renaissance. | Mum bought a box of chocolate florentines. | Dad ordered eggs florentine with spinach. | Michelangelo was a Florentine sculptor. | The Florentine palace had huge painted ceilings. | We baked florentines with almonds and cherries.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As an adjective about Florence it takes a capital: Florentine. In cooking it is often lower case. Pronounced «FLOR-en-teen» or «FLOR-en-tine».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Being able to speak, read or write a language easily, quickly and well. 2) Being able to do something smoothly and confidently, like reading aloud or doing maths facts.
its sense in the lessons: In school, reading fluency means reading at a good speed with expression; in maths, fluency means knowing number facts and methods quickly and accurately. In language lessons, fluency in French or Mandarin takes practice. Phrases: «reading fluency», «fluency in French», «gain fluency».
examples from the lessons: Her reading fluency improved with practice. | He speaks with fluency in English and Ukrainian. | Times-table practice builds maths fluency. | Fluency in a new language takes years. | The teacher listened to each child read to check fluency. | Reading aloud every night helps fluency.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Adjective: fluent (speaks fluent French); adverb: fluently. Fluency is not the same as accuracy: you can speak quickly but with mistakes, or slowly but correctly.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Film or video recordings of an event. 2) (old, measuring) A length measured in feet.
its sense in the lessons: In news and everyday life, «CCTV footage» or «footage of the storm» means video. In media lessons, pupils learn that footage can be edited or even faked, so check where it came from. Phrases: «video footage», «CCTV footage», «news footage», «behind-the-scenes footage».
examples from the lessons: The news showed footage of the floods. | Police checked the CCTV footage. | We watched old footage of the moon landing. | The footage was shaky because it was filmed on a phone. | Behind-the-scenes footage showed how the film was made. | Footage can be edited, so always ask where it came from.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «some footage», not «a footage». Comes from film being measured in feet. Media literacy: a clip can be cut, slowed or taken out of context to mislead.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A narrow bridge only for people walking, not for cars.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, footbridges cross railways, busy roads, rivers and streams; they keep walkers safe from traffic. In design and technology lessons, pupils build model footbridges to test strength. Phrases: «cross the footbridge», «a wooden footbridge».
examples from the lessons: We crossed the stream on a wooden footbridge. | Use the footbridge to get over the railway. | The footbridge over the motorway keeps walkers safe. | In D&T we built a footbridge out of straws. | The old footbridge wobbled in the wind. | Bikes must be walked across the footbridge.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable compound: foot + bridge. Safety: always use the footbridge or crossing instead of running across railway lines or busy roads.

part of speech: verb (forage, forages, foraged, foraging); noun (uncountable: forage)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (verb) To search for food, especially as animals do in the wild. 2) (verb) To search around for something: «foraged in his bag for a pen». 3) (verb) To gather wild food like berries, mushrooms and herbs. 4) (noun) Food for horses and cattle, such as grass and hay.
its sense in the lessons: In science, animals forage for food: bees forage for nectar, squirrels for nuts. In everyday life, families may forage for blackberries. Safety: never eat wild berries or mushrooms unless an expert adult says they are safe. On farms, forage is animal feed. Phrases: «forage for food», «forage around in», «foraging trip».
examples from the lessons: Bees forage for nectar among the flowers. | The fox foraged in the bins at night. | We foraged for blackberries along the hedge. | She foraged in her pocket for a coin. | Never eat wild mushrooms you've foraged without asking an expert. | The farmer stored forage for the winter.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Pronounced «FOR-ij». Person: forager. Usually followed by «for»: forage for food.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Strong and confident in what you say or do, making people listen. 2) Using strength or force; powerful.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, a forceful character is bossy or determined; a forceful argument is strong and convincing. In sport, a forceful kick or tackle uses lots of power. In PSHE, being forceful is different from being assertive in a polite way. Phrases: «a forceful argument», «a forceful personality», «a forceful push».
examples from the lessons: She made a forceful speech about saving the park. | The captain has a forceful personality. | His forceful kick sent the ball flying. | The waves gave a forceful push against the rocks. | «Stop that now,» he said in a forceful voice. | Her forceful argument changed our minds.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: force + «-ful». Adverb: forcefully. Not the same as «forcible» (done by physical force, like a forcible entry).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A wall, tower, ditch or other structure built to defend a place from attack. 2) The act of making a place stronger against attack. 3) (food) Adding vitamins or minerals to food, such as vitamins added to cereal.
its sense in the lessons: In history, castles, city walls, hill forts and Hadrian's Wall are fortifications. In geography, coastal fortifications defended harbours. In health, «fortified» cereals and flour have added vitamins, iron or folic acid. Phrases: «stone fortifications», «coastal fortifications», «food fortification».
examples from the lessons: The castle's fortifications included a moat and high walls. | Romans built fortifications along the border. | We visited the old harbour fortifications. | The fortification of the town took ten years. | Iron fortification of cereal helps children's health. | Soldiers dug trenches as fortifications.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun from the verb «fortify». Countable for the structures, uncountable for the process. Related: fort, fortress.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A bird kept for its eggs or meat, such as a chicken, duck, goose or turkey. 2) (old or in phrases) Any bird, as in «wildfowl» or «the fowl of the air» in the Bible.
its sense in the lessons: On farms, fowl are kept for eggs and meat. In the Bible and old texts, «fowl» means birds in general. In hunting and nature, «wildfowl» are ducks and geese. Phrases: «neither fish nor fowl» (not clearly one thing or another), «wildfowl», «waterfowl».
examples from the lessons: The farmer keeps fowl for their eggs. | Ducks and geese are waterfowl. | In the Bible, God made «the fowl of the air». | The market sold fresh fowl at Christmas. | Wildfowl gathered on the frozen lake. | The idea was neither fish nor fowl.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural is often the same, «fowl», especially for a group. Homophone trap: «fowl» (bird) sounds like «foul» (dirty, smelly, or against the rules in sport).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (church) A man who belongs to a Christian religious order, such as the Franciscans or Dominicans, who has promised to live simply and travels among people to preach and help the poor. 2) Used as a title before a name: Friar Tuck.
its sense in the lessons: In history and church lessons, friars appeared in medieval Europe; unlike monks, who mostly stay in a monastery, friars went out into towns to preach, teach and help the poor. In stories, Friar Tuck is the jolly friar in Robin Hood. Phrases: «Franciscan friar», «Friar Tuck».
examples from the lessons: Friar Tuck was a jolly friend of Robin Hood. | The friar walked from town to town, preaching. | Franciscan friars wear brown robes. | Friars promised to live simply and own very little. | The old friary was where friars once lived. | A friar gave bread to the poor at the gate.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Pronounced «FRY-er», the same as «fryer» (a pan or machine for frying): a homophone. A friar is not quite the same as a monk: monks mainly live in a monastery, friars work out among people.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (Japanese) A pufferfish, or a Japanese dish made from it. The fish contains a deadly poison, so only specially trained and licensed chefs may prepare it.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and food lessons about Japan, fugu is a famous, risky delicacy. In science, it shows that some animals make strong toxins to protect themselves: the poison is in parts like the liver and ovaries. Safety: it can kill, so it must only be prepared by experts. Phrases: «fugu chef», «poisonous pufferfish».
examples from the lessons: Fugu is a pufferfish eaten in Japan. | Only licensed chefs are allowed to prepare fugu. | Parts of the fugu contain a deadly poison. | A pufferfish blows itself up like a ball when scared. | The fugu restaurant had a special licence. | Eating badly prepared fugu can be fatal.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A Japanese word, not an English one; pronounced «FOO-goo». The poison (tetrodotoxin) has no known antidote; there is no easy cure, which is why the rules are strict.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Having no chance of success; useless, because it cannot change anything.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, a futile attempt or struggle shows hopelessness: «it was futile to run». In arguments and ethics, people debate whether something is futile or worth trying. Phrases: «a futile attempt», «it is futile to», «futile effort».
examples from the lessons: It was futile to argue with the referee. | The fly made futile attempts to get through the window. | Trying to stay dry in that storm was futile. | Their search for the lost ring seemed futile until the dog found it. | Don't think practice is futile; it does help. | He made a futile effort to catch the bus.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective. Pronounced «FYOO-tile» (UK) or «FYOO-tl» (US). Noun: futility. Stronger and more formal than «useless» or «pointless».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (UK, informal) The boss: a manager, foreman or the person in charge, especially of a football team or a group of workers. 2) (film and TV) The chief electrician who looks after the lights on a film set. 3) (UK, old, informal) An old man, especially in the countryside.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday British, Irish and Australian talk and sports news, «the gaffer» is the boss or football manager. In film credits, the gaffer is in charge of lighting. In old stories, «old gaffer» is a country old man. Phrases: «the gaffer said», «ask the gaffer», «gaffer tape».
examples from the lessons: The gaffer wants us at work by eight. | The team's gaffer was angry at half-time. | Ask the gaffer if we can leave early. | The gaffer set up the lights for the film. | Old Gaffer Jones sat on the bench by the pub. | Gaffer tape is strong, sticky cloth tape.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal, mostly UK. «Gaffer tape» is strong tape used on film sets (in the US often called duct tape, though they differ). Not the same as «gaffe» (an embarrassing mistake).

meaning for a pupil: 1) The way a person or animal walks or runs: the pattern and style of their steps. 2) (horses) One of the ways a horse moves: walk, trot, canter or gallop.
its sense in the lessons: In science and PE, scientists and physiotherapists study gait to understand movement and injuries. In stories, a character's gait (limping, swaggering, shuffling) tells the reader about them. In horse riding, gaits are the different speeds. Phrases: «an uneven gait», «a slow gait», «gait analysis».
examples from the lessons: The old man walked with a slow, shuffling gait. | You could tell it was Grandad by his gait. | A horse has four main gaits. | The injured dog had an uneven gait. | Her confident gait showed she wasn't scared. | The trainer filmed my gait to check my running shoes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Homophone trap: «gait» (way of walking) sounds the same as «gate» (a door in a fence).

part of speech: adjective (Galician); noun (a Galician, Galicians; Galician — the language)
meaning for a pupil: 1) From Galicia, a region in the north-west of Spain, or about its people. 2) (language) Galician, a language spoken in Galicia, close to Portuguese. 3) From Galicia, a historic region now split between western Ukraine and south-east Poland, around Lviv and Kraków.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and language lessons, Galician shows that Spain has several languages (Spanish, Catalan, Basque, Galician). In history, Galician in the Ukrainian–Polish sense is used for people and places of the old Kingdom of Galicia, part of Austria-Hungary until 1918. Which Galicia is meant comes from the context. Phrases: «Galician coast», «speak Galician», «Galician bagpipes».
examples from the lessons: Santiago de Compostela is a Galician city. | Many people in Galicia speak Galician and Spanish. | The Galician coast is rocky and green. | Galician is close to Portuguese. | Lviv was the chief city of Galicia in Austria-Hungary. | Her great-grandparents were Galician farmers from near Lviv. | Galician bagpipes are called gaitas.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always with a capital G: Galician. Pronounced «ga-LISH-un». Two different places share the name Galicia: one in Spain, one in Ukraine and Poland; they are not linked.

meaning for a pupil: 1) About the stomach.
its sense in the lessons: In science and health, gastric juice in the stomach contains acid that helps break down food; a «gastric bug» or «gastric flu» is an illness of the stomach and gut, often with sickness and diarrhoea. In medicine, «gastric» appears in words like gastric ulcer. Phrases: «gastric juice», «gastric bug», «gastric pain».
examples from the lessons: Gastric juice helps break down food in the stomach. | Half the class was off with a gastric bug. | The doctor asked about his gastric pain. | Gastric acid is strong enough to kill many germs. | Wash your hands to stop gastric illnesses spreading. | A gastric ulcer is a sore in the stomach lining.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal or medical; everyday word is «stomach» or «tummy». From Greek «gaster», stomach. «Gastric flu» is not real flu; it is a stomach bug caused by other germs.

part of speech: verb (gaze, gazes, gazed, gazing); noun (a gaze, gazes)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (verb) To look at something steadily for a long time, often because you are thinking, amazed or in love. 2) (noun) A long, steady look. 3) (noun) The direction someone is looking.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and poems, characters gaze at the stars, the sea or each other; it tells the reader they are dreamy, curious or deeply interested. In science, children gaze at the night sky. Phrases: «gaze at», «gaze out of the window», «stargazing», «avert your gaze», «hold someone's gaze».
examples from the lessons: We lay on the grass and gazed at the stars. | She gazed out of the window during the lesson. | The baby gazed at her mum. | His gaze moved slowly across the room. | Never gaze straight at the sun; it can hurt your eyes. | He couldn't hold the teacher's gaze and looked down. | Stargazing is fun on clear nights.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb; usually followed by «at», «into» or «out of». Different from «stare»: «stare» can be rude or surprised; «gaze» is usually calm or dreamy. Safety: never gaze at the sun, even with sunglasses.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A precious or beautiful stone that is cut and polished to be used in jewellery, such as a diamond, ruby, sapphire or emerald.
its sense in the lessons: In science, most gemstones are minerals that formed as crystals deep in the Earth; their colour comes from tiny amounts of other elements. In everyday life, gemstones are used in rings, necklaces and crowns. In history and stories, kings' crowns and pirates' treasure sparkle with gemstones. Phrases: «precious gemstones», «a birthstone».
examples from the lessons: A ruby is a red gemstone. | The crown was covered in gemstones. | Diamonds are the hardest gemstones. | We found tiny gemstones when panning at the museum. | Each month has its own birthstone gemstone. | Gemstones are cut so they sparkle in the light. | Amber is a gemstone made from old tree resin.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable compound: gem + stone. Also simply called «gems» or «jewels». Not all gemstones are minerals: pearls come from oysters and amber from tree resin.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a kind way that gives more money, time or help than expected. 2) In a large amount; plentifully: «generously sized», «spread generously». 3) In a fair and kind way when judging others.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and stories, someone who gives generously shares freely; this is praised in moral and church lessons. In cooking, «spread the butter generously» means use plenty. In news, people «gave generously» to a charity appeal. Phrases: «give generously», «generously donated», «generously sized».
examples from the lessons: People gave generously to the food bank. | Gran generously paid for our trip to the zoo. | Spread the jam generously on the toast. | She generously shared her sweets with everyone. | The teacher marked my work generously. | The portions were generously sized.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from «generous»; noun: generosity. In maths word problems, «generously» does not give a number; the numbers must come from the problem.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To do with the natural heat inside the Earth. 2) Geothermal energy or power is electricity or heating made from that underground heat, for example from hot water and steam deep in the ground.
its sense in the lessons: In science it comes up in lessons on energy sources and volcanoes: geothermal energy is renewable and clean, used a lot in Iceland and New Zealand. In everyday life you meet it in hot springs, geysers and heat pumps. Phrases: geothermal energy, geothermal power station, geothermal heating, geothermal spring.
examples from the lessons: Iceland gets much of its heating from geothermal energy. | The geysers at Rotorua in New Zealand are a sign of geothermal activity. | A geothermal power station uses steam from deep underground to turn turbines. | We swam in a warm geothermal pool on holiday. | Geothermal energy is renewable because the Earth keeps making heat. | Our science project compared solar, wind and geothermal power. | Some houses use geothermal heat pumps to stay warm in winter.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Built from geo (earth) + thermal (heat). An adjective, so it has no plural; it goes before a noun: geothermal energy. Say jee-oh-THER-mal. Do not mix up with geothermal and solar: solar heat comes from the Sun, geothermal heat comes from inside the Earth.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (medicine) A rare condition in which a child grows far taller than usual, usually because a gland in the brain makes too much growth hormone. 2) Being very large in size, for example animals or plants that are much bigger than their relatives (island gigantism).
its sense in the lessons: Used in science and health lessons about hormones and growth, and in nature lessons about island animals such as giant tortoises or the giant weta. It tells the reader that something is unusually, abnormally big. Phrases: island gigantism, a case of gigantism.
examples from the lessons: Robert Wadlow, the tallest man ever recorded, had gigantism. | Gigantism is caused by too much growth hormone in childhood. | Doctors can treat gigantism if they find it early. | The giant tortoises of the Galapagos are an example of island gigantism. | Some dinosaurs show a kind of gigantism. | The giant weta of New Zealand is a famous case of gigantism in insects.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: say gigantism, not a gigantism (but a case of gigantism). From giant. Be kind: people with gigantism are not monsters or fairy-tale giants; it is a medical condition. Related word: acromegaly, when the same problem starts in adults.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) A natural substance found in many foods such as tomatoes, cheese and mushrooms; it gives the savoury taste called umami. 2) Monosodium glutamate (MSG), a salt of it added to food to make it taste more savoury. 3) (biology) A chemical messenger that nerve cells in the brain use to pass signals.
its sense in the lessons: Comes up in science lessons about taste (the five tastes: sweet, sour, salty, bitter, umami) and on food labels. Phrases: monosodium glutamate, MSG, flavour enhancer.
examples from the lessons: Parmesan cheese is rich in natural glutamate. | Monosodium glutamate is often written as MSG on packets. | Glutamate gives food the savoury taste called umami. | Ripe tomatoes contain more glutamate than green ones. | Some crisps have glutamate added as a flavour enhancer. | Your brain uses glutamate to send messages between nerve cells.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say GLOO-ta-mate. Countable in science (glutamates) but usually uncountable for food. Myth: many people think MSG is harmful; scientific reviews have found it safe for most people in normal amounts. Related: glutamic acid.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A thick, clear, sweet-tasting liquid with no colour or smell, used in soap, medicines, cosmetics and food. 2) (science) The everyday name of glycerol, a chemical made from fats and oils.
its sense in the lessons: In science and craft lessons glycerine is used to make bubble mixture stronger and in soap-making; on labels it appears as E422. Phrases: bubble mixture with glycerine, glycerine soap, a drop of glycerine.
examples from the lessons: Add a spoonful of glycerine to make bubbles that last longer. | Glycerine soap is clear like glass. | Mum puts glycerine on the icing so it stays soft. | Some cough syrups contain glycerine. | Glycerine keeps skin from drying out. | In chemistry, glycerine is called glycerol.
note for the reader of a maths problem: British spelling glycerine, American glycerin; both are right. Uncountable: some glycerine, not a glycerine. Say GLISS-er-in. Do not confuse with nitroglycerine, a dangerous explosive made from it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The part of a sundial that sticks up and casts the shadow that shows the time. 2) (maths) In geometry, the L-shaped piece left when a smaller shape is cut out of the corner of a larger similar shape, such as a square.
its sense in the lessons: Used in science and history lessons on telling time by the Sun, and in maths puzzles about shapes and patterns. It tells the reader which part throws the shadow. Phrases: the gnomon of a sundial, the shadow of the gnomon.
examples from the lessons: The gnomon casts a shadow on the sundial. | We made a sundial with a pencil as the gnomon. | At noon the shadow of the gnomon is shortest. | The gnomon must point north in the UK. | In Australia the gnomon of a sundial points south. | In maths, a gnomon is the L-shape left when you take a small square out of a big one.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Silent g: say NO-mon. Plural gnomons. Do not confuse with gnome (a little garden figure). The gnomon is tilted at the same angle as your latitude so the sundial works all year.

part of speech: noun (a gob, gobs); verb (gob, gobs, gobbed, gobbing — slang, rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (UK, slang, rude) Your mouth: Shut your gob! 2) (slang) A lump or blob of something soft and wet, like a gob of spit or a gob of glue. 3) (US, informal) Gobs of something means a lot of it: gobs of money. 4) (UK, slang) To gob means to spit.
its sense in the lessons: Heard in everyday British, Irish and Australian talk and in stories with rough characters; not polite. Phrases: shut your gob, gobsmacked (amazed), gobstopper (a very big hard sweet), a gob of spit.
examples from the lessons: Shut your gob, you're giving the game away! | There was a gob of chewing gum under the desk. | He's got a big gob, he tells everyone everything. | I was gobsmacked when I won the prize. | Grandad bought me a gobstopper at the seaside. | They've got gobs of money, they live in a mansion. | Don't gob on the pavement, it's disgusting.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Rude and informal: do not say Shut your gob to a teacher. Gobsmacked (very surprised) is friendly slang and fine with friends. Gobstopper is a sweet, not rude at all. Gob is not a short form of goblin.

part of speech: noun (gore — uncountable; a gore, gores — cloth); verb (gore, gores, gored, goring)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Thick blood from a wound, especially lots of it, as in violent films. 2) To gore means to wound someone with a horn or tusk: the bull gored the farmer. 3) (sewing) A gore is a triangular piece of cloth sewn into a skirt, sail or umbrella to make it wider.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and film ratings it tells the reader there is lots of blood and violence; in farm and nature stories, an animal attack with horns. Phrases: blood and gore, gored by a bull, too much gore.
examples from the lessons: The film was too scary, full of blood and gore. | The farmer was gored by an angry bull. | The rhino can gore a lion with its horn. | Horror films are full of gore. | The skirt has six gores, so it swirls when you spin. | That video game is rated 18 because of the gore.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Gore (blood) is uncountable: too much gore. Past of the verb: gored. Do not confuse gory (full of blood) with glory. Al Gore is a name of an American politician.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A baby goose. 2) (rare) A young, silly or inexperienced person.
its sense in the lessons: In nature and farm stories and lessons on animal babies (duckling, cygnet, gosling). Phrases: fluffy goslings, a goose and her goslings.
examples from the lessons: The goose led her goslings down to the pond. | Goslings are covered in soft yellow fluff. | We saw six goslings at the park in spring. | A baby duck is a duckling and a baby goose is a gosling. | The goslings followed the farmer as if he were their mother. | The gosling hid under its mother's wing.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural goslings. Baby birds: duck - duckling, goose - gosling, swan - cygnet, owl - owlet. Goslings imprint: they follow the first moving thing they see.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A large fruit with a hard skin, related to pumpkins and melons, often dried and hollowed out. 2) A container, bottle or bowl made from a dried gourd, used for water or as a musical rattle. 3) (US, slang) Out of your gourd means crazy or silly.
its sense in the lessons: In history and geography lessons gourds are early water bottles and instruments (maracas); at Halloween and harvest festivals, decorative gourds. Phrases: a water gourd, a gourd rattle, out of your gourd.
examples from the lessons: The traveller drank water from a gourd. | We painted gourds for the harvest festival. | Maracas were first made from dried gourds. | Pumpkins, squashes and gourds belong to the same family. | In Argentina people drink mate tea from a gourd. | Are you out of your gourd? It's snowing and you're in shorts!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say GORD or GOORD. Plural gourds. Most decorative gourds are not good to eat. Out of your gourd is informal US slang.

part of speech: adjective (gracious, more gracious, most gracious); exclamation (gracious!, goodness gracious!)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Kind, polite and generous, especially to people who have less power. 2) Graceful, comfortable and elegant: gracious living. 3) (exclamation, old-fashioned) Gracious! or Goodness gracious! shows surprise. 4) (church) Full of mercy and kindness, as when Christians say God is gracious.
its sense in the lessons: In stories it describes a polite host, a kind queen or a good loser; in church language it describes God's mercy. Phrases: a gracious host, gracious in defeat, goodness gracious, good gracious me.
examples from the lessons: The queen was gracious to everyone she met. | Be gracious in defeat and shake hands with the winners. | Goodness gracious, look at the mess in here! | Our host was gracious and made us feel at home. | Christians believe God is gracious and forgiving. | They lived in a gracious old house with big gardens. | Thank you, that's very gracious of you.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: ungracious or rude. Noun: grace; adverb: graciously. Goodness gracious! is an old-fashioned, polite way to show surprise, often used by grandparents. Do not confuse with graceful (moving beautifully).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person whose job is to dig graves in a cemetery for burying the dead. 2) Someone or something that brings about the end of something (figurative).
its sense in the lessons: In stories, history and churchyards; in adult life it is a real, respectful job. Phrases: the old gravedigger, the gravedigger's spade.
examples from the lessons: The gravedigger worked quietly in the churchyard. | Nowadays most gravediggers use small diggers. | In the story the gravedigger found a strange box. | The gravedigger tidied the flowers after the funeral. | Being a gravedigger is hard but important work. | The village gravedigger also looked after the church garden.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word, sometimes written grave-digger. Plural gravediggers. Related: grave, cemetery, churchyard, funeral.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a greedy way, wanting or taking more than you need, especially food or money. 2) Very eagerly, wanting something very much: reading greedily.
its sense in the lessons: In stories it shows a character is selfish or very hungry; in everyday life it describes gobbling food. Phrases: eat greedily, look greedily at, grab greedily.
examples from the lessons: The dog ate its dinner greedily. | He greedily grabbed all the sweets for himself. | The dragon looked greedily at the gold. | She read the book greedily, page after page. | The baby birds opened their beaks greedily. | Don't eat so greedily, you'll get a stomach ache.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from greedy: change y to i and add -ly. Spelling trap: greedily, not greedyly. Greed is the noun.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A real or imagined unfair thing that makes someone feel upset and want to complain. 2) (work, law) An official complaint by a worker about unfair treatment.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and history it explains why people feel wronged and why conflicts start; in adult life workers can raise a grievance. Phrases: have a grievance against, air a grievance, a sense of grievance, a list of grievances.
examples from the lessons: He had a grievance against his neighbour about the noisy dog. | The workers took their grievances to the manager. | Write down your grievance and we will look at it fairly. | The colonists sent a long list of grievances to the king. | She nursed a grievance for years. | The school council listened to pupils' grievances about lunch.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a grievance, grievances. Say GREE-vance. Related: grieve (feel very sad), but grievance is about unfairness, not grief. Spelling: -ance.

part of speech: noun (a griffin, griffins); also spelled gryphon, griffon
meaning for a pupil: 1) (myth) An imaginary creature with the head, wings and claws of an eagle and the body of a lion. 2) Griffin is also a surname (a name).
its sense in the lessons: In stories, legends, coats of arms and fantasy books. It tells the reader of something strong, proud and watchful, guarding treasure. Phrases: a griffin guarding gold.
examples from the lessons: The griffin spread its eagle wings and roared like a lion. | A griffin guarded the dragon's treasure. | There is a stone griffin on the old bank. | In the story the hero rode on a griffin. | Griffins appear on many coats of arms. | Gryphon is another way to spell griffin.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Not real: a creature of myth. Spellings griffin, griffon and gryphon all exist. A griffon is also a breed of dog and a kind of vulture.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A machine or tool that crushes something into small bits or powder: a coffee grinder, a pepper grinder. 2) A power tool with a spinning disc that smooths or cuts metal or stone. 3) (informal) A back tooth (molar). 4) (US) A long sandwich, also called a sub.
its sense in the lessons: In kitchens, workshops and science lessons about changing materials. Phrases: coffee grinder, pepper grinder, angle grinder, meat grinder.
examples from the lessons: Dad turns the pepper grinder over his pasta. | The coffee grinder is very noisy in the morning. | The builder used an angle grinder to cut the metal pipe. | Sparks flew from the grinder. | Wear goggles when someone uses a grinder. | Your back teeth are grinders that crush your food.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From the verb grind (grind, ground, ground). Safety: angle grinders are dangerous and only for adults with goggles and gloves.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A small group of trees, or a small wood. 2) An orchard of fruit trees, such as an orange grove or olive grove. 3) Used in street names: Elm Grove.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and poems a grove is a quiet, shady, sometimes magical place; in geography, farming of olives and oranges. Phrases: olive grove, orange grove, a shady grove.
examples from the lessons: We had a picnic in a shady grove of oak trees. | Olive groves cover the hills in Greece. | They picked oranges in the orange grove. | The elves lived in a secret grove. | My cousin lives on Maple Grove. | Birds sang in the grove all morning.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural groves. A grove is smaller than a wood or a forest. Do not confuse with groove (a long cut) or with grovel.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Gu on its own is not an English word. 2) (Mandarin, pinyin) gu is a syllable with many meanings by tone: gǔ means old or ancient, bone, or drum; gū means aunt (father's sister); gù means reason or so. It sounds like goo. 3) Gu can be part of a name (a surname, Gu). 4) It may be a fragment cut from a longer word such as gum or guide.
its sense in the lessons: In lessons on Mandarin heard on the street it appears in words like gǔdài (ancient times) and gūgu (aunt). In English texts it is usually a fragment or a name.
examples from the lessons: Gu is not an English word. | In Mandarin, gǔ can mean drum. | Gūgu is how a Chinese child says auntie on her father's side. | Gu sounds like goo to an English ear. | Mr Gu is our new maths teacher. | The word got cut and only gu was left on the page.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Not English. In Mandarin the tone changes the meaning: gū, gú, gǔ, gù are different words. As a surname it is a name; nothing more is known.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A green dip or sauce from Mexico made of mashed avocado, usually with lime, onion, tomato, chilli and salt.
its sense in the lessons: In food, cooking lessons and parties; in geography, Mexican food. Phrases: tortilla chips and guacamole, a bowl of guacamole, guac (informal).
examples from the lessons: We dipped tortilla chips into the guacamole. | Guacamole is made from mashed avocados. | Add lime juice so the guacamole doesn't go brown. | Can I have extra guac on my burrito? | We made guacamole in our food technology lesson. | Guacamole comes from Mexico and the Aztecs made it long ago.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say gwah-ka-MOH-lee. Uncountable: some guacamole. Informal short form: guac. Lime or lemon juice slows it turning brown because air reacts with the avocado.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Guernsey is one of the Channel Islands, between England and France (a place name). 2) A guernsey is a thick, warm, tightly knitted woollen jumper, first worn by fishermen. 3) (Australia) A sleeveless jersey worn by Australian rules football players; to get a guernsey means to be picked for a team or to get recognition. 4) A Guernsey is a breed of brown-and-white dairy cow.
its sense in the lessons: In geography, the Channel Islands; in Australian sport talk, footy jumpers; on farms, a cattle breed. Phrases: get a guernsey (Australia), a Guernsey cow.
examples from the lessons: Guernsey is a small island near France. | Grandad still wears his old navy guernsey when he goes fishing. | He finally got a guernsey in the first team. (Australia) | The footy players pulled on their guernseys. | Guernsey cows give rich, creamy milk. | We took a ferry to Guernsey in the summer holidays.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital G for the island and the cow; small g for the jumper. Guernsey is not part of the UK but belongs to the British Crown. Australians say footy guernsey; others say jersey or shirt.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who plays the guitar.
its sense in the lessons: In music lessons and talk about bands. Phrases: lead guitarist, bass guitarist, a famous guitarist.
examples from the lessons: My brother wants to be a guitarist in a rock band. | The guitarist played a long solo. | Our school band needs a bass guitarist. | Jimi Hendrix was a famous guitarist. | The guitarist tuned her strings before the show. | She is the best guitarist in our class.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stress on the second syllable: gi-TAR-ist. Plural guitarists. Same pattern: pianist, violinist, cellist.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) Any thick, sticky, dirty or slimy stuff that you do not want, such as grease in a drain or goo on a shoe.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and funny stories about cleaning and mess. Phrases: full of gunk, clean the gunk out, gunk up (to block with gunk).
examples from the lessons: The plughole was full of gunk. | What's this green gunk on my shoe? | Dad cleaned the gunk out of the bike chain. | The pond was covered in slimy gunk. | Old food gunked up the sink. | Wipe the gunk off the keyboard.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal and uncountable: some gunk, not a gunk. Adjective: gunky. Similar informal words: goo, gloop, muck.

part of speech: verb (gush, gushes, gushed, gushing); noun (a gush, gushes)
meaning for a pupil: 1) For a liquid to flow out suddenly and fast in large amounts. 2) A gush is a sudden fast flow: a gush of water. 3) To talk with too much praise or excitement about something, in a way that can sound silly.
its sense in the lessons: In science (water, volcanoes, pipes) and stories (blood, tears, rivers); about people who praise too much. Phrases: gush out, gush from, a gush of water, gush about.
examples from the lessons: Water gushed out of the broken pipe. | Oil gushed from the well. | A gush of cold air came in when the door opened. | She gushed about how wonderful the film was. | Tears gushed down his cheeks. | The river gushes over the rocks after rain.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: gushed. Gush is stronger and faster than flow or trickle. Gushing praise can be a bit too much or not quite sincere.

part of speech: proper noun (the Habsburgs; Habsburg) — a name
meaning for a pupil: 1) (a name) The Habsburgs were a royal family of Europe who ruled Austria, the Holy Roman Empire, Spain and other lands for hundreds of years, from the Middle Ages until 1918. 2) Habsburg is used as an adjective: the Habsburg Empire.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons on European kings and empires, Austria-Hungary and the First World War. Phrases: the Habsburg Empire, the Habsburg family, the Habsburg jaw.
examples from the lessons: The Habsburgs ruled Austria for more than six hundred years. | Maria Theresa was a famous Habsburg empress. | The Habsburg Empire ended after the First World War in 1918. | Many Habsburgs married their cousins. | Vienna was the capital of the Habsburg lands. | Archduke Franz Ferdinand was a Habsburg.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A name, always with a capital H. Also spelled Hapsburg. Say HAPS-burg. The family is called the House of Habsburg.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The hairs or feathers along the back of the neck of a dog, cat or bird that stand up when it is angry or frightened. 2) To raise someone's hackles (or make their hackles rise) means to make them angry.
its sense in the lessons: In nature lessons about animal body language; in stories and everyday talk about people getting annoyed. Phrases: raise someone's hackles, her hackles rose, put someone's hackles up.
examples from the lessons: The dog's hackles rose when it saw the fox. | Rude comments really raise my hackles. | The cat arched its back and its hackles stood up. | His bossy tone put my hackles up. | A cockerel's hackles are long shiny neck feathers. | Her hackles rose when someone called her a cheat.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Almost always plural: hackles. Used as an idiom about people: the hairs do not really rise. Related: get your back up.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A thin net worn over the hair to keep it in place or to stop hairs falling into food.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life you see hairnets on dinner ladies, cooks and factory workers for hygiene; also in old-fashioned stories about grannies with curlers. Phrases: wear a hairnet.
examples from the lessons: The dinner lady wears a hairnet in the kitchen. | Workers in the cake factory must wear hairnets. | Gran put on her hairnet before bed. | A hairnet stops hairs getting in the food. | We had to wear hairnets on the school trip to the bakery. | The ballet dancer's bun was held by a hairnet.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word. Plural hairnets. Hygiene rule: in kitchens, long hair must be tied back or covered.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (a name) George Frideric Handel (1685–1759) was a German-born composer who lived and worked in London; he wrote Messiah, Water Music and Music for the Royal Fireworks. 2) Handel can also be a surname. 3) handel is not an English common word; do not confuse with handle.
its sense in the lessons: In music lessons about Baroque composers and in church music: the Hallelujah Chorus from Messiah is sung at Christmas and Easter.
examples from the lessons: Handel wrote Messiah in just a few weeks. | The choir sang the Hallelujah Chorus by Handel. | Handel's Water Music was played on a boat on the River Thames for King George I. | Handel was born in Germany but became British. | We listened to Handel in our music lesson. | The audience stands up for Handel's Hallelujah Chorus.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A name with a capital H. Spelling trap: the composer is Handel; a door has a handle. In German his name is Händel.

part of speech: noun (a harbor, harbors); verb (harbor, harbors, harbored, harboring) — US spelling of harbour
meaning for a pupil: 1) A sheltered area of water by the coast where ships and boats can stay safely. 2) To harbor someone means to hide or shelter them, often someone wanted by the police. 3) To harbor a feeling means to keep it in your mind for a long time: harbor a grudge. 4) To harbor germs or pests means to let them live and grow there.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and stories of the sea; in history (Pearl Harbor, Sydney Harbour); in science, places that harbor germs. Phrases: in the harbor, safe harbor, harbor a grudge, harbor doubts.
examples from the lessons: The fishing boats came back into the harbor. | Sydney Harbour Bridge is famous around the world. | The attack on Pearl Harbor brought the USA into the war in 1941. | It is a crime to harbor a criminal. | She still harbors a grudge against her old friend. | Dirty sponges can harbor germs. | We watched the ferries leave the harbor.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Harbor is the American spelling; harbour is British, Canadian, Australian, NZ and Irish. Names keep their own spelling: Pearl Harbor, Sydney Harbour. Harbor and port are close; a harbor is the sheltered water, a port is the town and docks for trade.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a cruel, unkind or too strict way: treated harshly. 2) In a rough, unpleasant way to the senses: a light shining harshly, a voice sounding harshly.
its sense in the lessons: In stories about strict teachers, cruel rulers or unfair punishment; in everyday life when someone is judged too strictly. Phrases: speak harshly, treat harshly, judge harshly, punish harshly.
examples from the lessons: The cruel king treated his servants harshly. | Don't judge yourself too harshly, everyone makes mistakes. | The coach spoke harshly to the team after the loss. | The light shone harshly in my eyes. | The thief was punished harshly. | The wind blew harshly across the moor.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from harsh + -ly. Noun: harshness. Opposite: gently, kindly.

part of speech: noun (a hashtag, hashtags); verb (hashtag, hashtags, hashtagged, hashtagging — informal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A word or phrase with the # sign in front, used on social media so that posts on the same topic can be found together: #worldbookday. 2) (UK) The # symbol itself is sometimes called a hashtag; it is also called hash, pound sign (US) or number sign. 3) (informal, joke) Said out loud before a phrase to sound trendy: hashtag winning.
its sense in the lessons: In computing and online-safety lessons and in everyday life on social media. Phrases: use a hashtag, trending hashtag, hashtag campaign.
examples from the lessons: The school posted photos with the hashtag #sportsday. | That hashtag is trending all over the world. | Type a hashtag to find posts about the match. | Hashtags have no spaces between the words. | My sister said hashtag best day ever as a joke. | Press the hashtag key at the end of the phone number.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural hashtags. In the USA the # key on a phone is often called the pound key; in the UK it is the hash key. Online safety: hashtags make your post public and easy to find.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who hates someone or something. 2) (slang) Someone who is always negative, jealous or rude about other people, especially online: Haters gonna hate.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday and online talk among young people; in lessons on kindness online and bullying. Phrases: haters gonna hate (slang), ignore the haters, a hater of.
examples from the lessons: Don't listen to the haters, your video is great. | Haters gonna hate, just keep dancing. (slang) | He is a hater of Mondays. | Online haters often hide behind fake names. | Being a hater won't make you feel better. | She's no hater, she just didn't like the film.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural haters. Haters gonna hate is slang (gonna = going to); not for formal writing. Ignoring and reporting hateful comments is a safe choice online.

part of speech: verb, -ing form of haul (haul, hauls, hauled, hauling); noun (hauling — uncountable)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Pulling or dragging something heavy with effort. 2) Carrying goods by lorry or truck from place to place; hauling as a noun is this job. 3) (informal) Taking someone somewhere they do not want to go: hauling them off to the dentist.
its sense in the lessons: In science (forces, pulling) and in stories of fishermen, sailors and builders; in adult life, trucking jobs. Phrases: hauling in the nets, hauling up, long-distance hauling.
examples from the lessons: The fishermen were hauling in their nets. | We were hauling the heavy box up the stairs. | The truck is hauling logs to the sawmill. | Horses were used for hauling carts long ago. | Mum is hauling us off to see Aunt Jean. | Hauling a sledge uphill is hard work.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Base verb haul; past hauled. Homophone trap: haul sounds like hall. Haul as a noun also means a lot of stolen or caught things: a big haul of fish.

part of speech: verb, -ing form of haunt (haunt, haunts, haunted, haunting); adjective (haunting, more haunting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Of a ghost: visiting a place again and again (in stories). 2) Of a memory or worry: staying in your mind and troubling you. 3) (adjective) Beautiful, sad or strange in a way you cannot forget: a haunting tune.
its sense in the lessons: In spooky stories and at Halloween; in music and poetry reviews describing a sad, beautiful sound. Phrases: a haunting melody, a haunting memory, haunting the castle.
examples from the lessons: A ghost is said to be haunting the old castle. | The song has a haunting melody. | The haunting cry of the owl echoed through the woods. | That mistake kept haunting him for weeks. | The film's last scene is haunting. | People say a grey lady is haunting the library.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective use is about feelings, not ghosts: a haunting tune is just very moving. Related: haunted (a haunted house). Ghosts are not proven to be real; haunting is used in stories and legends.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A hawksbill (hawksbill turtle) is a sea turtle with a narrow beak curved like a hawk's, living on coral reefs in warm seas; it is critically endangered.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography lessons on oceans, coral reefs and endangered animals (Great Barrier Reef, Caribbean). Phrases: hawksbill turtle, hawksbill sea turtle.
examples from the lessons: The hawksbill turtle eats sponges on the coral reef. | Hawksbills are critically endangered. | People used to make tortoiseshell combs from hawksbill shells. | We saw a hawksbill while snorkelling on the Great Barrier Reef. | The hawksbill gets its name from its pointed beak. | It is illegal to buy products made from hawksbill shell.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word. Plural hawksbills. Real tortoiseshell came from hawksbill turtles; now it is banned in international trade.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Cutting grass, drying it in the sun and gathering it as hay to feed animals in winter. 2) (sport, informal) A haymaker is a big wild punch; haymaking can mean throwing such punches.
its sense in the lessons: In farm stories, history and harvest lessons; the saying make hay while the sun shines (use a good chance while it lasts). Phrases: haymaking season, make hay while the sun shines.
examples from the lessons: Haymaking starts in early summer. | The whole village helped with the haymaking. | Haymaking needs a few dry sunny days. | In the old days, haymaking was done with scythes. | Make hay while the sun shines, and do your homework while you have time! | The farmer is busy with haymaking this week.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Hay is dried grass for animals; straw is the dry stalks left after grain is harvested. Do not mix them up.

part of speech: verb (headbutt, headbutts, headbutted, headbutting); noun (a headbutt, headbutts)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To hit someone or something hard with the top or front of your head. 2) A headbutt is a hit like this.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and news about fights and football fouls; animals like goats and rams headbutt. Safety: headbutting can cause serious head injuries. Phrases: give someone a headbutt, headbutt the ball.
examples from the lessons: The goat headbutted the gate. | Rams headbutt each other to show who is strongest. | The player was sent off for a headbutt. | Never headbutt anyone, it can badly hurt you both. | The puppy headbutted my hand to be stroked. | Cats sometimes headbutt you gently to show they like you.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Also written head-butt. Past: headbutted (double t). It is violence when done to a person; a cat's gentle headbutt (bunting) is friendly.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Anything worn on the head, such as hats, helmets and caps. 2) (sport) Protective head covering, for example in boxing or rugby. 3) A brace worn on the head to help straighten teeth.
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons (helmets for cycling and sport) and history lessons (crowns, headdresses). Phrases: protective headgear, wear headgear.
examples from the lessons: Protective headgear is required in boxing. | Crowns and helmets are kinds of headgear. | The museum showed headgear from many cultures. | Some rugby players wear soft headgear called scrum caps. | Bike helmets are the most important headgear you'll ever wear. | He has to wear dental headgear at night.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: some headgear, not a headgear (say a piece of headgear). Similar: headwear.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Things you have heard from other people but do not know are true; rumour. 2) (law) Evidence in court about what someone else said, not what the witness saw themselves; it is often not allowed.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life it warns that a story is gossip; in law and history lessons it is weak evidence. Phrases: it's just hearsay, based on hearsay, hearsay evidence.
examples from the lessons: That's just hearsay, nobody actually saw it. | You shouldn't believe hearsay about people. | The judge said the statement was hearsay. | The story spread round school by hearsay. | Is this a fact or just hearsay? | Good journalists check facts instead of printing hearsay.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. From hear + say. Checking sources is the way to tell fact from hearsay.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (maths) A metric unit of area equal to 10,000 square metres, the size of a square 100 metres by 100 metres; symbol ha.
its sense in the lessons: In maths problems on area and measures, and in geography for farms, forests and parks. A hectare is a bit larger than a football pitch. Phrases: per hectare, hectares of land.
examples from the lessons: A hectare is a square 100 metres on each side. | The farm covers 50 hectares. | A football pitch is about three quarters of a hectare. | The forest fire burned 2,000 hectares. | How many square metres are in 3 hectares? 30,000. | The farmer grows 8 tonnes of wheat per hectare.
note for the reader of a maths problem: For the numbers: 1 hectare = 10,000 m²; 100 hectares = 1 km²; 1 hectare is about 2.47 acres. Symbol ha. Plural hectares. Say HEK-tair.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To stop or pause before doing or saying something because you are unsure, nervous or worried. 2) Don't hesitate to means feel free to do it at once: Don't hesitate to ask.
its sense in the lessons: In stories it shows a character is unsure or afraid; in everyday and formal letters, don't hesitate to contact us. Phrases: hesitate to, without hesitating, he who hesitates is lost.
examples from the lessons: She hesitated before jumping into the cold water. | Don't hesitate to ask if you need help. | He answered without hesitating. | I hesitated because I wasn't sure of the answer. | The cat hesitated at the edge of the wall. | If you see a fire, don't hesitate, call 999.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: hesitated. Noun: hesitation. Adjective: hesitant. Followed by to + verb: hesitate to say. In an emergency: 999 (UK, Ireland also 112), 911 (USA, Canada), 000 (Australia), 111 (NZ).

part of speech: adjective (Himalayan); noun (a Himalayan, Himalayans — the cat)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To do with the Himalayas, the highest mountain range in the world, in Asia, which includes Mount Everest. 2) A Himalayan is a breed of long-haired cat with markings like a Siamese. 3) Himalayan salt is pinkish rock salt mined in Pakistan.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons on mountains and countries (Nepal, Bhutan, India, China, Pakistan). Phrases: Himalayan mountains, Himalayan expedition, Himalayan balsam (a weed), Himalayan salt.
examples from the lessons: Mount Everest is the highest Himalayan peak. | The climbers set off on a Himalayan expedition. | Snow leopards live in the Himalayan mountains. | Himalayan balsam is a pink flower that spreads along British rivers. | Our neighbour has a fluffy Himalayan cat. | Himalayan salt lamps glow pink.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital H because it comes from a name. Say him-a-LAY-an. Myths: pink salt lamps do not clean the air.

part of speech: noun (a hog, hogs); verb (hog, hogs, hogged, hogging)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A pig, especially a large one kept for meat (US) or a male pig (UK). 2) (informal) A greedy or selfish person: a road hog. 3) To hog something means to keep it all to yourself and not share: hog the remote. 4) Go the whole hog means do something completely.
its sense in the lessons: In farm stories; in everyday and school talk about sharing. Phrases: hog the ball, road hog, go the whole hog, hedgehog, groundhog.
examples from the lessons: The farmer fed the hogs. | Stop hogging the computer, it's my turn! | He hogged the ball and never passed. | A road hog drives in the middle of the road. | We went the whole hog and had a three-course meal. | Groundhog Day is in February in the USA and Canada.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: hogged (double g). Calling someone a hog is rude. Hedgehog and groundhog are not pigs.

part of speech: noun (an hombre, hombres) — Spanish word used in US slang
meaning for a pupil: 1) (Spanish) Hombre means man in Spanish; it is not really an English word. 2) (US slang) A man, a guy, especially a tough one in cowboy films: a tough hombre.
its sense in the lessons: Heard in westerns and US slang, and when people speak Spanish. Phrases: tough hombre, bad hombre.
examples from the lessons: Hombre means man in Spanish. | The sheriff said he was one tough hombre. | In Spanish class we learnt hombre and mujer. | Hey hombre, how's it going? (slang) | The cowboy film had a mysterious hombre riding into town. | Hombre sounds like OM-bray; the h is silent.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spanish word: the h is silent, say OM-bray. Slang and informal in English. Plural hombres.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A bird of Africa, Europe and Asia with pinkish-brown feathers, black-and-white striped wings, a long thin beak and a big crest like a fan on its head; its call sounds like oop-oop-oop.
its sense in the lessons: In nature lessons on birds, and in stories and old tales; the hoopoe is the national bird of Israel. Phrases: a hoopoe's crest.
examples from the lessons: The hoopoe raised its crest like a fan. | We saw a hoopoe in Spain on holiday. | A hoopoe digs for insects with its long beak. | The hoopoe's call sounds like oop-oop-oop. | Hoopoes are rare visitors to Britain. | In an old tale, a hoopoe leads the birds on a long journey.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say HOO-poo. Plural hoopoes. Its name copies its call.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Flat and level, going straight from side to side, parallel to the ground or the horizon. 2) (maths) A horizontal line goes across the page, from left to right, like the x-axis. 3) The horizontal is a horizontal line or position.
its sense in the lessons: In maths (lines, graphs, axes, symmetry), science (levels, spirit levels) and art. It tells the reader which way something lies. Phrases: horizontal line, horizontal axis, horizontal and vertical.
examples from the lessons: Draw a horizontal line across the page. | The x-axis on a graph is horizontal. | The water in a glass stays horizontal even when you tip it. | A shelf must be horizontal or things will roll off. | Vertical lines go up and down, horizontal lines go across. | The gymnast held her body horizontal on the bar.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: vertical (up and down). Adverb: horizontally. Memory trick: horizontal is like the horizon, flat across. Maths: a horizontal line of symmetry splits a shape into top and bottom halves.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Hard, rough and tough like horn: horny skin, a horny beak. 2) Having horns: horny-headed. 3) (rude, adult slang) a rude word grown-ups use; not for school or for children to use.
its sense in the lessons: In science and nature lessons: a turtle's horny beak, horny plates on reptiles, horny skin on feet. The slang sense is adult and rude, so in a school text it usually means hard like horn. Phrases: a horny beak, horny scales.
examples from the lessons: Turtles have no teeth, only a horny beak. | The gardener's hands were horny from years of work. | Rhino horn is made of a horny material like fingernails. | Reptiles are covered in horny scales. | Horny skin on your heel can be softened with cream. | The beetle has a horny shell.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: in modern everyday English the slang (adult) meaning is common, so people may giggle; in science the word means hard like horn. Safer school words: hard, tough, keratin.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A common small grey fly that lives near people and buzzes around houses, food and rubbish.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on insects, life cycles (egg, larva or maggot, pupa, adult) and hygiene: houseflies can spread germs onto food. Phrases: swat a housefly, cover the food.
examples from the lessons: A housefly landed on my sandwich. | Houseflies spread germs, so cover your food. | A housefly has two wings and six legs. | Maggots grow into houseflies. | The housefly buzzed against the window. | A housefly tastes with its feet.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural houseflies (y to ies). Also written house fly. Like all insects it has six legs and three body parts.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A back with a big hump or curve, from a medical condition (kyphosis). 2) (old-fashioned, often hurtful) A person with such a back; today it is kinder to say a person with a curved spine. 3) The Hunchback of Notre-Dame is a famous novel by Victor Hugo about Quasimodo.
its sense in the lessons: In classic stories and films; in health lessons about the spine and good posture. Phrases: The Hunchback of Notre-Dame, hunchback whale (a mistake: it is humpback).
examples from the lessons: Quasimodo, the hunchback of Notre-Dame, rang the cathedral bells. | Sitting badly for years can give you a slightly hunched back. | In old stories, a hunchback was often wrongly shown as wicked. | The doctor checked his spine for a hunchback. | Don't call people names about their bodies. | The novel The Hunchback of Notre-Dame was written by Victor Hugo.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Calling a person a hunchback is now seen as rude; describe the condition kindly. Do not confuse with humpback (humpback whale). Adjective: hunchbacked; hunched means bent forward.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (a name, astronomy) The Hyades are a cluster of stars in the constellation Taurus, shaped like a V, the closest star cluster to Earth (about 150 light years away). 2) (myth) In Greek myths, the Hyades were nymphs, daughters of Atlas, linked with rain.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on stars and constellations: near the bright red star Aldebaran and the Pleiades. Phrases: the Hyades cluster.
examples from the lessons: The Hyades form the V-shaped face of Taurus the Bull. | You can see the Hyades with your eyes on a dark winter night. | The Hyades are close to the Pleiades in the sky. | Aldebaran looks as if it is in the Hyades but it is much nearer to us. | In Greek myths the Hyades were rain nymphs. | Through binoculars the Hyades look like a scatter of jewels.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A name: capital H and always the Hyades. Say HY-a-deez. Aldebaran is not truly part of the cluster.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A garden bush with large round heads of small flowers in blue, pink, purple or white.
its sense in the lessons: In gardens and science lessons: the flower colour depends on the soil; acid soil makes blue flowers, chalky (alkaline) soil makes pink ones. Phrases: a hydrangea bush, blue hydrangeas.
examples from the lessons: Gran's hydrangeas are bright blue this year. | Hydrangeas like shade and lots of water. | In acid soil, hydrangeas turn blue; in chalky soil, they turn pink. | We picked a big pink hydrangea for the table. | The hydrangea flowers are dry and papery in autumn. | Hydrangea leaves are poisonous if eaten.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say hy-DRAIN-ja. Plural hydrangeas. A real-life pH indicator, like red cabbage. Not for pets or people to eat.

part of speech: verb (hydrate, hydrates, hydrated, hydrating); noun (a hydrate, hydrates — chemistry)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To give water to your body or skin so it has enough: drink water to hydrate. 2) (science) To add water to something, or for a substance to combine with water. 3) (chemistry) A hydrate is a substance that has water joined into its crystals, such as blue copper sulfate.
its sense in the lessons: In PE, health and sport (stay hydrated on hot days); in chemistry lessons on crystals and reactions. Phrases: stay hydrated, hydrate your skin, rehydrate, dehydrated.
examples from the lessons: Remember to hydrate during the football match. | Drink plenty of water to stay hydrated in the heat. | This cream hydrates dry skin. | Blue copper sulfate is a hydrate; heating it drives out the water. | Plants need to hydrate their cells to stand upright. | After being sick, sip water slowly to rehydrate.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: hydrated. Opposite: dehydrate (lose water). Noun: hydration. Signs of dehydration: thirst, headache, dark wee. Say HY-drate.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (biology) The hyoid bone is a small U-shaped bone in the front of the neck, under the tongue; it is the only bone in the body not joined to another bone.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on the skeleton and on speech: it holds up the tongue and helps us swallow and speak. Phrases: the hyoid bone.
examples from the lessons: The hyoid bone sits in your neck below your jaw. | The hyoid is the only bone not joined to any other bone. | Muscles of the tongue are attached to the hyoid. | The hyoid helps you swallow and talk. | Scientists study the hyoid of Neanderthals to learn whether they could speak. | You can feel your hyoid move when you swallow.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say HY-oid. From the Greek letter upsilon, which it looks like. Usually used with bone: the hyoid bone.

part of speech: verb, past form of hypnotise (hypnotise, hypnotises, hypnotised, hypnotising); adjective (hypnotised)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Put into a sleep-like state in which a person is very relaxed and open to suggestions (hypnosis). 2) So fascinated by something that you cannot stop watching it: hypnotised by the screen.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, stage shows and cartoons (swinging watch, spiral eyes); in everyday talk about being glued to a screen. Phrases: hypnotised by, as if hypnotised.
examples from the lessons: The magician said he had hypnotised a man from the audience. | The cat was hypnotised by the fish in the tank. | We sat hypnotised by the fireworks. | In the cartoon, the snake hypnotised the boy with its eyes. | She stared at the screen as if hypnotised. | Some doctors use hypnosis to help people stop smoking.
note for the reader of a maths problem: British spelling hypnotised; American hypnotized. Noun: hypnosis. Myth: a hypnotised person cannot be made to do something they really believe is wrong, and real hypnosis is not like cartoons.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) An idea or guess that explains something and that you can test with an experiment or observation. 2) (formal) Any idea suggested as a starting point for thinking, which may or may not be true.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons it is a key step of a fair test: question, hypothesis (prediction with reasons), experiment, results, conclusion. It tells the reader that something is not yet proven. Phrases: test a hypothesis, form a hypothesis, the hypothesis was supported.
examples from the lessons: My hypothesis is that plants grow faster in sunlight. | We tested our hypothesis with a fair test. | The results did not support the hypothesis. | A good hypothesis can be proved wrong by an experiment. | Scientists made a new hypothesis after the surprise result. | Write your hypothesis before you start the experiment.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural hypotheses (say hy-POTH-uh-seez). Adjective: hypothetical. Trap: a hypothesis is not the same as a fact or a theory; a scientific theory is a well-tested explanation, not a guess.

meaning for a pupil: 1) -ic is a suffix (word ending) that makes adjectives: magic, heroic, metallic, athletic; it means of or like. 2) (abbreviation) IC stands for integrated circuit, a tiny electronic chip. 3) (abbreviation) In some places I/C means in charge. 4) On its own, ic is not an English word.
its sense in the lessons: In spelling and grammar lessons on suffixes (hero to heroic, atom to atomic); in computing, IC chips.
examples from the lessons: Ic on its own is not a word. | Add -ic to hero to make heroic. | Words ending in -ic often add -ally to make adverbs: magic, magically. | A phone is full of IC chips. | The -ic ending in Arctic is easy to forget when you say it. | Volcano becomes volcanic with -ic.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Honest entry: a fragment and an abbreviation. Spelling trap: adverbs from -ic words end in -ically (basically, not basicly); public is the exception: publicly.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Too messy, faded or unclear to be read.
its sense in the lessons: In school about handwriting; in everyday life about faded signs and smudged notes. It tells the reader that words cannot be read. Phrases: illegible handwriting, almost illegible.
examples from the lessons: The doctor's handwriting was illegible. | Rain made the note illegible. | Please write neatly, this answer is illegible. | The old gravestone was worn and illegible. | My signature looks illegible but it's my name. | The smudged ink left the last line illegible.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: legible (clear enough to read). Noun: illegibility. Do not confuse with illegal (against the law) or ineligible (not allowed to take part).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who draws or paints the pictures for books, magazines, posters or websites.
its sense in the lessons: In reading and art lessons: the author writes the words and the illustrator draws the pictures. Phrases: author and illustrator, children's book illustrator.
examples from the lessons: Quentin Blake was the illustrator of many Roald Dahl books. | The illustrator drew a funny dragon on every page. | Who is the illustrator of this picture book? | She wants to be an illustrator when she grows up. | Some authors are also their own illustrators. | The illustrator used watercolours for the pictures.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Use an, not a: an illustrator. Verb: illustrate; noun: illustration. The title page often says Illustrated by.

meaning for a pupil: 1) ILO stands for the International Labour Organization, a part of the United Nations that sets fair rules for work, such as fighting child labour. 2) On its own ilo is not an English word; it may be part of a name or a cut piece of a word (kilo, silo).
its sense in the lessons: In lessons on work, rights and the UN: the ILO says children should be at school, not working. Phrases: ILO conventions, the ILO in Geneva.
examples from the lessons: The ILO is part of the United Nations. | The ILO works to end child labour. | The ILO has its headquarters in Geneva, Switzerland. | ILO rules say workers should be safe at work. | The ILO was set up in 1919, after the First World War. | Ilo on its own isn't an English word.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Written in capitals: ILO. Say each letter: I-L-O. Labour is spelt Labour in its name.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To give or pass on information, knowledge or wisdom to someone: impart knowledge. 2) (formal) To give a quality, taste or feeling to something: herbs impart flavour.
its sense in the lessons: In formal and exam writing and in cooking; teachers impart knowledge. Phrases: impart knowledge, impart wisdom, impart flavour, impart news.
examples from the lessons: Teachers impart knowledge to their pupils. | The old man imparted his wisdom to the children. | Lemon imparts a fresh taste to the cake. | She had important news to impart. | Smoke imparts a special flavour to the fish. | Grandma imparted her secret recipe only to me.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal: in everyday talk say give, tell, pass on, add. Past: imparted. Followed by to: impart something to someone.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (art) A way of painting with very thick paint, so that the brush or knife marks stand up from the surface.
its sense in the lessons: In art lessons on painters and techniques: Van Gogh used impasto in The Starry Night and Sunflowers. Phrases: impasto technique, thick impasto.
examples from the lessons: Van Gogh used impasto, so his paintings look bumpy. | We tried impasto with a palette knife in art class. | The impasto makes the sunflowers look 3D. | Impasto takes a long time to dry. | You can see the brushstrokes in the impasto. | Add flour to poster paint for a pretend impasto.
note for the reader of a maths problem: An Italian word, say im-PAS-toe. Uncountable. Opposite style: smooth, flat glazing.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Not able to wait calmly; easily annoyed when things take time. 2) Very eager to do something soon: impatient to start. 3) Impatient with someone means easily annoyed by them.
its sense in the lessons: In stories it shows a character's feelings; in everyday life queues, waiting for presents, slow computers. Phrases: impatient to, impatient with, grow impatient.
examples from the lessons: The children were impatient for the holidays to start. | Don't be impatient, your turn will come. | The driver grew impatient in the traffic jam. | He was impatient with his little brother. | I'm impatient to open my presents! | The impatient customer tapped her foot.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: patient. Noun: impatience. Adverb: impatiently. Trap: patient is also a noun (someone seen by a doctor), but impatient is only an adjective.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Not allowed; not permitted by the rules or the law.
its sense in the lessons: In formal writing, rules, law and ethics lessons. It tells the reader something is forbidden. Phrases: morally impermissible, impermissible behaviour.
examples from the lessons: Cheating in exams is impermissible. | The judge ruled the evidence impermissible. | Bullying is impermissible at our school. | It is impermissible to park here at any time. | Some philosophers argue that lying is always impermissible. | Phones are impermissible in the exam hall.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal: in everyday English say not allowed or forbidden. Opposite: permissible. Prefix im- means not.

part of speech: verb, past form of implant (implant, implants, implanted, implanting); adjective (implanted)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (medicine) Put into the body by surgery: an implanted pacemaker, implanted teeth. 2) Fixed firmly in someone's mind: an idea implanted by a story. 3) (biology) Fixed into place, such as a fertilised egg attaching in the womb.
its sense in the lessons: In science and health lessons about medicine and technology (cochlear implants, pacemakers, microchips in pets); in stories about ideas planted in minds. Phrases: implanted under the skin, deeply implanted.
examples from the lessons: The vet implanted a microchip in our puppy. | A pacemaker is implanted to help the heart beat steadily. | The doctor implanted a cochlear implant so she could hear. | The fear of spiders was implanted when he was small. | Dentists can fix implanted teeth into the jaw. | The idea was implanted in my head by an advert.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb implant: stress on -plant; noun an implant: stress on IM-. Past: implanted.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To suggest something without saying it directly: Are you implying I'm lazy? 2) (logic, maths) For one thing to mean that another must be true: being a square implies having four sides.
its sense in the lessons: In reading lessons (inference: what the writer implies, the reader infers); in maths and logic, if-then statements. Phrases: imply that, what are you implying, is implied by.
examples from the lessons: Are you implying that I took your pen? | His smile implied he knew the secret. | The writer implies the house is haunted without saying it. | Being a square implies having four equal sides. | Her silence implied she was upset. | A dark sky often implies rain is coming.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: implied; he implies. Noun: implication. Common confusion: the speaker implies, the listener infers. In logic, A implies B does not mean B implies A.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (law) Being kept in prison as a punishment. 2) Being shut in or not free to leave a place.
its sense in the lessons: In history (prisoners, castles, Nelson Mandela) and law (sentences in court). Phrases: life imprisonment, sentenced to imprisonment, years of imprisonment.
examples from the lessons: Nelson Mandela survived 27 years of imprisonment. | The robber was sentenced to five years' imprisonment. | Life imprisonment is the most serious sentence in the UK. | The princess escaped from her imprisonment in the tower. | Imprisonment without trial is unfair. | Animals in tiny cages suffer a kind of imprisonment.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable. Verb: imprison; person: prisoner. Spelling: imprison + -ment.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Not enough, or not good enough for what is needed: inadequate food. 2) (feeling) Feeling not good or able enough: feel inadequate.
its sense in the lessons: In reports and science (inadequate data), in history (inadequate food in a famine), and in feelings about yourself. Phrases: inadequate for, feel inadequate, totally inadequate.
examples from the lessons: The old bridge was inadequate for heavy lorries. | The refugees had inadequate shelter. | The answer was inadequate: it needed more detail. | Everyone feels inadequate sometimes, it's normal. | The lighting was inadequate for reading. | Inadequate sleep makes it hard to concentrate.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: adequate (enough). Adverb: inadequately. Say in-AD-i-kwit. Formal; in everyday talk say not enough.
