meaning for a pupil: 1) Including something or someone as part of a bigger whole: the incorporation of new ideas. 2) (business, law) Making a business into an official company, a corporation (Inc. in the USA). 3) Joining a town or area into another one.
its sense in the lessons: In formal and exam writing, history (a land joined into a country) and business. Phrases: incorporation of, articles of incorporation.
examples from the lessons: The incorporation of fruit into school meals made them healthier. | The incorporation of the village into the city happened in 1900. | Inc. after a company name means it is incorporated. | The teacher praised the incorporation of quotes in my essay. | Incorporation of new players into the team took time. | The incorporation of Crimea by Russia in 2014 was not accepted by most UN countries.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal. Verb: incorporate. The abbreviation Inc. means incorporated (USA); in the UK, Ltd or plc.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Food that is hard or impossible for the stomach to break down. 2) Hard to understand or accept: an indigestible textbook.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on digestion (fibre is mostly indigestible but good for you); in everyday talk about heavy food or boring books. Phrases: indigestible fibre.
examples from the lessons: Plastic is indigestible, so animals that eat it get ill. | Fibre is indigestible but helps food move through your gut. | The stew was heavy and indigestible. | That long report was indigestible. | Cows can digest grass that is indigestible to humans. | Cherry stones are indigestible.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: digestible. Related: indigestion (a sore, uncomfortable tummy after eating).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Not going straight: an indirect route. 2) Not said openly or plainly: an indirect answer. 3) Happening as a side result rather than directly: an indirect cause. 4) (grammar) Indirect speech reports what someone said without their exact words; an indirect object receives the thing given (She gave me a book: me).
its sense in the lessons: In grammar (indirect speech, indirect object), science (indirect evidence), maths (indirect proportion), and everyday life (indirect hints). Phrases: indirect speech, indirect object, indirect route, indirect sunlight.
examples from the lessons: We took an indirect route through the park. | He gave an indirect answer and didn't say yes or no. | Direct speech: Tom said, I am hungry. Indirect speech: Tom said he was hungry. | In She gave me a pen, me is the indirect object. | Some plants like indirect sunlight. | Smoking is an indirect cause of many illnesses.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: direct. Adverb: indirectly. Indirect speech: no speech marks and often the tense moves back (am to was). Also called reported speech.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Something that persuades or encourages someone to do something, such as a reward or a bribe.
its sense in the lessons: In formal writing, law and business; an inducement may be fair (a bonus) or wrong (a bribe). Phrases: an inducement to, offer an inducement, financial inducement.
examples from the lessons: Free pizza was an inducement to come to the meeting. | The shop offered a discount as an inducement to buy. | Offering an inducement to a referee is against the rules. | There was little inducement to stay in the rain. | Prizes are an inducement to read more books. | He refused all inducements to change his vote.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; in everyday talk say reason, reward, incentive. Verb: induce.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The work of making goods in factories: heavy industry. 2) An industry is all the businesses that make or do one kind of thing: the car industry, the tourist industry. 3) (formal) Hard work: a person of great industry.
its sense in the lessons: In history (the Industrial Revolution), geography (primary, secondary, tertiary industry) and everyday life (jobs). Phrases: the film industry, heavy industry, light industry, the Industrial Revolution.
examples from the lessons: The car industry employs thousands of people. | Tourism is a big industry in Ireland. | The Industrial Revolution started in Britain in the 1700s. | Many towns grew up around coal and steel industry. | The bees work with great industry. | My aunt works in the music industry.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural industries. Adjective industrial (factories); industrious means hard-working. Say IN-dus-tree, stress on the first syllable.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) The way an object stays still or keeps moving at the same speed in a straight line until a force changes it. 2) Lack of energy or wish to move or change: laziness.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on forces and Newton's first law, and road safety (seatbelts stop your body flying forward). In everyday life, feeling too sluggish to start. Phrases: law of inertia, overcome inertia.
examples from the lessons: When the bus stops suddenly, inertia keeps you moving forward. | Seatbelts protect you against inertia in a crash. | A heavy trolley has more inertia than a light one. | Pull the tablecloth fast and inertia keeps the plates in place. | After the holiday, inertia kept me on the sofa. | Newton's first law is called the law of inertia.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Say in-ER-sha. Myth: things do not stop because they run out of force; friction and other forces stop them. More mass means more inertia.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a way that cannot be avoided or stopped; as you would expect.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, history and essays it tells the reader that the result was certain to come: inevitably, it rained. Phrases: inevitably leads to.
examples from the lessons: Inevitably, it rained on sports day. | The ice cream inevitably melted in the sun. | Leaving homework till late inevitably leads to stress. | We all grow older, inevitably. | Inevitably, my little brother wanted the same toy. | War inevitably brings suffering.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: inevitable. Say in-EV-i-ta-blee. Often at the start of a sentence with a comma.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (grammar) The basic form of a verb, often with to in front: to run, to be, to eat; the bare infinitive has no to: run, be, eat.
its sense in the lessons: In grammar lessons in English and French (manger, aller); dictionaries list verbs by the infinitive. Phrases: to-infinitive, split infinitive, bare infinitive.
examples from the lessons: To swim is an infinitive. | I want to go home: to go is an infinitive. | In French, aller is the infinitive meaning to go. | A split infinitive puts a word between to and the verb: to boldly go. | Can and must are followed by the bare infinitive: I can swim. | Look up a verb in the dictionary by its infinitive.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural infinitives. Split infinitives are now accepted by most writers; old rules said avoid them. Say in-FIN-i-tiv.

part of speech: verb, past form of inflate (inflate, inflates, inflated, inflating); adjective (inflated)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Filled with air or gas, so that it gets bigger: an inflated balloon. 2) Made bigger, higher or more important than is true or fair: inflated prices, an inflated ego. 3) (money) Inflated prices have gone up because of inflation.
its sense in the lessons: In science (air takes up space), in everyday life (tyres, bouncy castles), money and adult life (prices rising), and in stories about boastful people. Phrases: inflated prices, fully inflated, an inflated opinion of himself.
examples from the lessons: We inflated the paddling pool with a pump. | The tyres must be properly inflated. | Tickets were sold at inflated prices. | He has an inflated idea of how good he is. | The lifejacket inflated when it touched the water. | Prices are inflated near the beach in summer.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: deflated (also means disappointed). Noun: inflation. Past: inflated.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Having a lot of influence: able to change what other people think or do, or how things happen.
its sense in the lessons: In history, science and news about important people, books and ideas. Phrases: an influential person, highly influential, influential in.
examples from the lessons: Darwin's book was very influential in science. | She is an influential leader in her town. | The Beatles were one of the most influential bands ever. | Advertising can be influential on what children want. | Our class rep was influential in getting new benches. | An influential teacher can change your life.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: influence; verb: influence. Say in-floo-EN-shul. Influencer (online) is a newer, related word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) The act of going in, or the right to go in: a way in. 2) (technical) The getting in of water, dust or air where it should not be: water ingress.
its sense in the lessons: In formal, legal and technical writing, building and gadgets (IP ratings say how well a phone stops dust and water ingress). Phrases: ingress and egress, water ingress, means of ingress.
examples from the lessons: The door is the only point of ingress. | The phone is protected against water ingress. | Ingress and egress mean entry and exit. | Damp walls are often caused by water ingress. | The castle had a narrow ingress guarded by soldiers. | The rules allow ingress only with a pass.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal and technical; everyday words: entry, way in. Opposite: egress (way out). Say IN-gress.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To slow down, block or stop something from happening or growing: salt inhibits bacteria. 2) To make someone feel shy or unable to act freely: being watched inhibits him.
its sense in the lessons: In science (substances that inhibit growth or reactions, enzymes) and in feelings and behaviour (shyness). Phrases: inhibit growth, feel inhibited.
examples from the lessons: Salt inhibits the growth of bacteria. | Cold weather inhibits plant growth. | Fear of mistakes can inhibit learning. | Some medicines inhibit pain signals. | Being filmed inhibited her dancing. | Shade inhibits weeds from growing.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: inhibited. Noun: inhibition (can mean shyness). Adjective inhibited means shy and holding back. Formal; everyday words: stop, slow down, hold back.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (law) An official inquiry by a court, led by a coroner, to find out why and how a person died, when the death was sudden or unexplained. 2) (informal) A long discussion after something has gone wrong to find out why: a post-match inquest.
its sense in the lessons: In news and adult life seen by a child (UK, Ireland, Australia, NZ); in sports talk about losing. Phrases: hold an inquest, the coroner's inquest, an inquest into.
examples from the lessons: An inquest will be held into the accident. | The coroner leads the inquest. | The inquest found that the death was an accident. | After the defeat, the team held an inquest. | An inquest helps families understand what happened. | The inquest was opened and adjourned.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: an inquest. Inquest does not mean someone is on trial; it seeks facts, not blame. Similar word: inquiry (or enquiry).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Unconscious; not awake or aware: knocked insensible. 2) (formal) Not aware of something or not caring about it: insensible to the danger. 3) Not able to feel something: insensible to cold. 4) (old) Too small or slow to notice: by insensible degrees.
its sense in the lessons: In old novels and formal writing. It is a false friend: insensible does not mean the opposite of sensible (that is silly). Phrases: insensible to, knocked insensible.
examples from the lessons: The fall knocked him insensible. | She seemed insensible to the cold wind. | He lay insensible on the floor until the doctor came. | The king was insensible to the suffering of the poor. | Frozen fingers become insensible to pain. | In the old story, the hero drank the potion and fell insensible.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: the opposite of sensible (wise) is silly or foolish, not insensible. Close words: unconscious, unaware, insensitive (unkind about feelings).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Putting a machine, system or program in place so it is ready to use: the installation of a new boiler, software installation. 2) (art) An installation is a large work of art built in a room or space that people walk around or into. 3) A military or industrial base or building: a military installation.
its sense in the lessons: In computing (install an app), everyday life (workers fitting things), art lessons and news. Phrases: software installation, art installation, installation wizard.
examples from the lessons: The installation of the new heating took two days. | Wait for the installation to finish before you open the app. | The museum has an art installation made of a thousand paper birds. | The army has an installation near the coast. | The installation of solar panels saves money. | Follow the installation instructions carefully.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: install (UK also instal). Say in-sta-LAY-shun. Uncountable for the process, countable for things and artworks.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who teaches a practical skill or sport, such as driving, swimming, skiing or climbing.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life (swimming lessons, driving lessons, gym) and stories. Phrases: driving instructor, swimming instructor, ski instructor, fitness instructor.
examples from the lessons: My swimming instructor taught me to dive. | The ski instructor showed us how to stop. | Mum's driving instructor was very patient. | Listen to the instructor at the climbing wall. | The fitness instructor led the class. | A first-aid instructor came to school.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Use an: an instructor. Verb: instruct; noun: instruction. Instructor is for skills; teacher is the general word for school.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (biology) A tough outer layer or covering of an animal or plant, such as skin, a shell, a husk or the coat of a seed.
its sense in the lessons: In science (biology) texts and formal writing. The integumentary system is skin, hair and nails. Phrases: the integumentary system.
examples from the lessons: Skin is the integument of the human body. | A seed's integument protects the baby plant inside. | The beetle's integument is hard and shiny. | Snakes shed their integument as they grow. | The integumentary system includes skin, hair and nails. | The bark is the integument of the tree.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Technical word; everyday words: skin, covering, coat, shell. Say in-TEG-yu-ment.

part of speech: verb (intercept, intercepts, intercepted, intercepting); noun (an intercept, intercepts)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To stop someone or something on the way and catch or block it before it gets where it was going: intercept a pass. 2) To secretly catch messages meant for someone else: intercept a letter. 3) (maths) An intercept is the point where a line or graph crosses an axis: the y-intercept.
its sense in the lessons: In sport (football, netball), history (codebreakers at Bletchley Park intercepted enemy messages), and maths graphs. Phrases: intercept a pass, intercepted messages, y-intercept.
examples from the lessons: The defender intercepted the pass. | Codebreakers intercepted secret messages in the war. | The police intercepted the stolen car. | The line y = 2x + 3 has a y-intercept of 3. | Find where the graph intercepts the x-axis. | The goalkeeper intercepted the cross.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb stress: in-ter-SEPT; noun stress: IN-ter-sept. Noun: interception. Maths: in y = mx + c, c is the y-intercept.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a way where two or more things can be swapped for each other without changing the result or meaning.
its sense in the lessons: In language lessons (words used interchangeably: sofa and couch), science, maths and parts that fit each other. Phrases: used interchangeably.
examples from the lessons: People use sofa and couch interchangeably. | These batteries can be used interchangeably. | The words big and large are often used interchangeably. | In this game, red and blue cards work interchangeably. | Mum and Mom are used interchangeably in some families. | Speed and velocity are not quite interchangeable in science.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: interchangeable. Trap: words used interchangeably can still have small differences (speed and velocity). Long word: in-ter-CHANGE-a-bly.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Getting involved in someone else's business when you are not wanted: interference in their affairs. 2) (science, radio) Noise or crackle that spoils a radio, TV or phone signal. 3) (sport) A foul when a player wrongly blocks another. 4) (science) The way waves combine and add up or cancel out.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and history (outside interference in elections), science lessons on waves and signals, and sport. Phrases: interference in, without interference, radio interference.
examples from the lessons: The radio crackled with interference. | She resented her brother's interference in her plans. | The referee called interference. | Countries should hold elections without foreign interference. | Mobile phones can cause interference on speakers. | Light waves show interference patterns.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Verb: interfere. Spelling: interference has -ence. Say in-ter-FEER-ence.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Stopping and starting again and again; not continuous.
its sense in the lessons: In weather forecasts (intermittent rain), science, and everyday life (an intermittent fault). Phrases: intermittent rain, intermittent showers, intermittent signal.
examples from the lessons: The forecast is for intermittent rain. | We had an intermittent Wi-Fi signal in the caravan. | There was an intermittent beeping from the smoke alarm, so we changed the battery. | Intermittent showers stopped the cricket match several times. | His cough was intermittent. | The streetlight has an intermittent fault.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb: intermittently. Opposite: continuous, constant. Smoke alarm beeping every so often usually means the battery is low.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (biology) Between the bones of the spine (vertebrae). Intervertebral discs are soft cushions between the vertebrae.
its sense in the lessons: In science and health lessons on the skeleton and back care. Phrases: intervertebral disc.
examples from the lessons: Intervertebral discs cushion the bones in your back. | The intervertebral discs act like shock absorbers. | A slipped disc is a damaged intervertebral disc. | Lift heavy bags with bent knees to protect your intervertebral discs. | You are slightly taller in the morning because your intervertebral discs have rested. | Each intervertebral disc has a soft middle.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Technical word: inter (between) + vertebral (of vertebrae). Fun fact: you are about 1 cm taller in the morning than in the evening.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The rise and fall of your voice when you speak, which can change the meaning: a question often goes up at the end. 2) (music) Singing or playing exactly in tune.
its sense in the lessons: In English and language lessons (reading aloud with expression, questions, sarcasm), French and Mandarin lessons, and music. Phrases: rising intonation, falling intonation, good intonation.
examples from the lessons: Use rising intonation when you ask a yes-no question. | Her intonation showed she was joking. | Reading aloud with good intonation makes a story come alive. | The violinist worked on her intonation. | In some Australian and New Zealand speech, statements end with a rising intonation. | Intonation can turn Really. into Really?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Not the same as tone in Mandarin: tones change the meaning of single words; intonation is the tune of a whole sentence. Uncountable usually.

part of speech: adjective (intoxicated); verb, past form of intoxicate (intoxicate, intoxicates, intoxicated, intoxicating)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal, law) Drunk, or affected by drugs, so that you cannot think or act normally. 2) Very excited and happy, as if drunk: intoxicated by success.
its sense in the lessons: In law, news and health (driving while intoxicated is a crime and dangerous); in stories about excitement. Phrases: driving while intoxicated, intoxicated with joy.
examples from the lessons: It is illegal to drive while intoxicated. | The police said the man was intoxicated. | The team was intoxicated by their win. | Alcohol is not safe for children's growing bodies. | She felt intoxicated by the smell of roses. | Intoxicated people may fall and hurt themselves.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal word for drunk. Noun: intoxication. Adjective intoxicating: very exciting. Safety: driving after drinking is dangerous and illegal.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Belonging to the real nature of something itself, not coming from outside: intrinsic value.
its sense in the lessons: In formal writing, maths (intrinsic properties), science and ethics; intrinsic motivation means doing something because you enjoy it, not for a reward. Phrases: intrinsic value, intrinsic motivation, intrinsic to.
examples from the lessons: Gold has intrinsic value, but paper money has value because people agree it does. | Kindness is intrinsic to her character. | Reading for fun gives intrinsic motivation. | Every person has intrinsic worth. | Risk is intrinsic to mountain climbing. | The coin's intrinsic value is less than its face value.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal. Opposite: extrinsic (coming from outside). Adverb: intrinsically.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) A flood; when water covers land that is usually dry. 2) A very large amount of things arriving at once: an inundation of letters.
its sense in the lessons: In geography (floods, the Nile's yearly inundation in ancient Egypt) and formal writing. Phrases: an inundation of, the annual inundation.
examples from the lessons: The yearly inundation of the Nile made the soil rich. | Coastal towns face inundation as sea levels rise. | The inundation destroyed many farms. | There was an inundation of emails after the announcement. | The levee protected the town from inundation. | Ancient Egyptians had a season called Inundation.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; everyday word: flood. Verb: inundate (often passive: we were inundated with entries).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Not able to be changed back to how it was before.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on changes of materials: burning, cooking an egg and rusting are irreversible changes; melting ice is reversible. Also in health and environment (irreversible damage). Phrases: irreversible change, irreversible damage.
examples from the lessons: Baking a cake is an irreversible change. | Burning paper is irreversible. | Melting chocolate is reversible but burning it is irreversible. | Extinction is irreversible: the dodo is gone forever. | Some hearing damage is irreversible, so turn the music down. | The decision was irreversible.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: reversible. Science: an irreversible change usually makes a new material; a reversible change (melting, freezing, dissolving) does not.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A substance that makes your skin, eyes, nose or throat sore, red or itchy. 2) Something or someone that annoys you.
its sense in the lessons: In science and safety: warning signs on cleaning products say irritant; pollen and dust are irritants. Phrases: skin irritant, eye irritant.
examples from the lessons: Bleach is an irritant, so wear gloves. | Pollen is an irritant for people with hay fever. | The label had a warning symbol for irritants. | Smoke is an irritant to the eyes. | The buzzing fly was a constant irritant. | If an irritant gets in your eye, rinse it with clean water.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: irritate; noun: irritation. Safety: if a chemical gets in your eyes, rinse with water and tell an adult.

meaning for a pupil: 1) With rough, sharp, uneven points or edges: jagged rocks.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and descriptions (jagged mountains, jagged glass, jagged lightning); in safety (broken glass). Phrases: a jagged edge, jagged rocks, jagged peaks.
examples from the lessons: Be careful, the broken glass has jagged edges. | Jagged rocks stuck out of the sea. | A jagged line of lightning lit the sky. | The mountains had jagged peaks. | The tin was opened and left a jagged lid. | The graph showed a jagged line going up and down.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say JAG-id (two syllables). Opposite: smooth. Safety: do not pick up broken glass with bare hands.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal, old-fashioned) A person who is in prison or has often been in prison.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, cartoons and old films about criminals. It is a joking or rude label. Phrases: an old jailbird.
examples from the lessons: The jailbird escaped through a tunnel. | In the cartoon the jailbird wore a striped suit. | Grandad called the villain an old jailbird. | The story is about a jailbird who turns his life around. | The jailbird was back behind bars. | Calling someone a jailbird is not kind.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal. Also gaolbird (old British spelling: gaol = jail). Plural jailbirds.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (French) Jambon means ham in French; it is not an English word. It sounds like zhom-BON to an English ear, with a nasal ending. 2) Used on English menus in names like jambon-beurre (a ham and butter baguette).
its sense in the lessons: In French lessons and cafés, menus. Phrases: un sandwich au jambon, jambon-beurre.
examples from the lessons: Jambon is the French word for ham. | I ordered a jambon-beurre in Paris. | Un sandwich au jambon, s'il vous plaît. | In French, le jambon is masculine. | The menu said jambon et fromage: ham and cheese. | My little sister giggles every time she hears jambon.
note for the reader of a maths problem: French, not English: masculine noun (le jambon). Do not mix with jamboree (a big gathering) or jam.

part of speech: noun (a jeep, jeeps; Jeep — a brand name)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A small, strong motor vehicle with four-wheel drive for rough ground, first made for the US Army in the Second World War. 2) Jeep is also a brand name of such cars.
its sense in the lessons: In history (WWII), stories of safaris and outback trips, everyday life. Phrases: in a jeep, a safari jeep.
examples from the lessons: We went on safari in an open jeep. | Soldiers drove jeeps in the Second World War. | The jeep bumped along the dirt road. | My uncle has a Jeep for the farm. | The jeep could drive through mud and rivers. | Philippine jeepneys were made from old army jeeps.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital J for the brand. Plural jeeps. Say JEEP.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) A feeling of being very nervous and shaky, especially before something important.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and stories (first-night jitters, exam jitters). Phrases: get the jitters, have the jitters, pre-match jitters.
examples from the lessons: I always get the jitters before a test. | She had the jitters on the first day at a new school. | The actors had first-night jitters. | A deep breath helps calm the jitters. | The goalkeeper's jitters made him drop the ball. | Spooky noises gave us the jitters.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always plural with the: the jitters. Adjective: jittery. Similar: butterflies in your tummy, nerves.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (history) In the Second World War, Japanese pilots who flew planes full of explosives into enemy ships on purpose, dying in the attack; also their planes. 2) (informal) Kamikaze describes something wildly reckless, as if you did not care about getting hurt: a kamikaze run down the hill.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons about the Second World War in the Pacific; in everyday talk about crazy, dangerous moves. The Japanese word means divine wind. Phrases: kamikaze pilot, kamikaze attack.
examples from the lessons: Kamikaze pilots attacked American ships near the end of the war. | The word kamikaze means divine wind in Japanese. | The cat made a kamikaze leap off the fridge. | That was a kamikaze tackle, you could have got hurt. | Many young kamikaze pilots were barely adults. | The fly made kamikaze dives at the lamp.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say ka-mi-KAH-zee. Japanese word. Be respectful: real kamikaze attacks killed many people on both sides. The informal sense is about recklessness.

part of speech: noun (a Kazakh, Kazakhs; Kazakh — the language); adjective (Kazakh)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A person from Kazakhstan, or a member of the Kazakh people. 2) Kazakh is the main language of Kazakhstan, a Turkic language now changing from Cyrillic to Latin letters. 3) (adjective) To do with Kazakhstan or the Kazakh people: Kazakh food.
its sense in the lessons: In geography: Kazakhstan is the largest country in Central Asia and the ninth largest in the world, with steppes, mountains and the Baikonur space launch site. Phrases: Kazakh language, Kazakh culture, Kazakh eagle hunters.
examples from the lessons: Kazakh eagle hunters train golden eagles. | Kazakh is spoken in Kazakhstan. | My friend's family is Kazakh. | Kazakhstan is the biggest country with no coast to the open sea. | Yuri Gagarin's rocket was launched from Baikonur on the Kazakh steppe. | We tried a Kazakh dish called beshbarmak.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital K. Say ka-ZAKH. Country: Kazakhstan; capital city: Astana. Plural: Kazakhs.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A khanate is a land or state ruled by a khan, a ruler of Mongol or Turkic peoples. 2) It also means the power or rule of a khan.
its sense in the lessons: Met in history lessons about Genghis Khan, the Mongol Empire, the Golden Horde and the Crimean Khanate; it tells the reader the place was a kingdom ruled by a khan. Phrases: the Crimean Khanate, the Khanate of Kazan, a powerful khanate.
examples from the lessons: The Mongol Empire split into several khanates. | The Crimean Khanate lasted for more than three hundred years. | Each khanate had its own khan. | Our history book shows a map of the Golden Horde khanate. | The khanate collected taxes from the towns it ruled. | Moscow was once forced to pay tribute to a khanate. | Kazan was the capital of a khanate.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: one khanate, two khanates. It is built from «khan» + «-ate», like «sultanate» or «emirate». Say «a khanate» (the k sounds hard). Do not confuse «khan» (a ruler) with the ordinary word «can».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (a name) Khufu was a king (pharaoh) of ancient Egypt, about 4,500 years ago. 2) The Great Pyramid of Giza was built as his tomb, so it is often called the Pyramid of Khufu.
its sense in the lessons: Met in history lessons on ancient Egypt, pyramids and the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World. The Greeks called him Cheops.
examples from the lessons: Khufu was a pharaoh of ancient Egypt. | The Great Pyramid was built for Khufu. | The Greeks called Khufu «Cheops». | Khufu's pyramid is the oldest of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World. | Thousands of workers built Khufu's tomb. | Only one small statue of Khufu has ever been found.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A name, so it takes a capital letter: Khufu. Say it «KOO-foo». The same king is also called Cheops; they are not two people. Myth: the pyramids were not built by slaves in chains, as old films show; most workers were paid labourers.

part of speech: noun (Kodiak; a Kodiak bear, Kodiak bears)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Kodiak is a large island off the south coast of Alaska, USA. 2) A Kodiak bear is a very large kind of brown bear that lives on Kodiak and nearby islands.
its sense in the lessons: Met in science and nature lessons about bears and the biggest land meat-eaters, and in geography about Alaska. Phrases: Kodiak bear, Kodiak Island.
examples from the lessons: The Kodiak bear is one of the largest bears in the world. | Kodiak Island is in Alaska. | A Kodiak bear can stand taller than a door on its back legs. | Kodiak bears catch salmon in the rivers. | We watched a film about the bears of Kodiak. | Kodiak bears eat berries, grass and fish. | The town of Kodiak has a big fishing harbour.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital K for the island and usually for the bear too. Plural: Kodiak bears (or Kodiaks). Trap: «Kodiak» is not the same as «Kodak», the camera company. A Kodiak bear and a polar bear are both huge, but they are different species.

part of speech: noun (kola, kola nuts); also a place name (the Kola Peninsula)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Kola (or cola) is a tree from West Africa whose nuts contain caffeine. 2) A kola nut is the seed of this tree; people chew it, and it was once used to flavour cola drinks. 3) (a name) The Kola Peninsula is a large piece of land in the far north-west of Russia, near Finland and Norway.
its sense in the lessons: Met in science about plants and caffeine, in food lessons about where cola drinks got their name, and in geography about the Arctic. In parts of West Africa kola nuts are shared as a sign of welcome and friendship.
examples from the lessons: The kola nut tastes bitter. | Kola nuts contain caffeine, like coffee. | In Nigeria, guests may be offered kola nuts as a welcome. | Cola drinks were named after the kola nut. | The Kola Peninsula is inside the Arctic Circle. | The deepest hole ever drilled is on the Kola Peninsula. | The kola tree grows in hot, wet forests.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelled «kola» or «cola»; both are right for the tree and nut. Do not mix up «kola» with «koala» (the Australian animal). Kola nuts contain caffeine, so they are not good for small children in large amounts.

part of speech: noun (Kongo; the Kongo people, the Kingdom of Kongo); adjective (Kongo art)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The Kongo are a people of Central Africa who live in Angola, the Republic of the Congo and the Democratic Republic of the Congo. 2) The Kingdom of Kongo was a large African kingdom on the Atlantic coast from about 1390 to the 1800s. 3) Kongo (Kikongo) is the language of the Kongo people.
its sense in the lessons: Met in history lessons about African kingdoms and the Atlantic slave trade, and in geography; the Congo River and the countries named Congo take their name from the Kongo.
examples from the lessons: The Kingdom of Kongo traded with Portugal. | Many Kongo people speak Kikongo. | Kongo artists carved beautiful wooden figures. | The Congo River is named after the Kongo people. | The king of Kongo wrote letters to the king of Portugal. | We read a folk tale told by the Kongo people.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A name, so capital K. Historians often spell the old kingdom «Kongo» with a K to keep it apart from today's countries spelled «Congo». The Kongo are a people, not a country.

part of speech: verb (kowtow, kowtows, kowtowed, kowtowing); noun (a kowtow)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To kowtow is to kneel and touch the ground with your forehead to show deep respect, as people once did before the Emperor of China. 2) (informal) To kowtow to someone is to obey them too much and try too hard to please them. 3) A kowtow is this deep kneeling bow.
its sense in the lessons: In history about imperial China it is a real bow; in everyday talk it is a criticism: someone «kowtows to» the boss, the bully or the rich, so the reader learns that person is not standing up for themselves. Phrase: kowtow to someone.
examples from the lessons: Visitors had to kowtow before the emperor. | A British ambassador refused to kowtow in 1793. | He kowtows to the team captain all the time. | Don't kowtow to bullies; tell a teacher. | The servant made a low kowtow. | I won't kowtow just because she is popular. | The king expected everyone to kowtow to him.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comes from Chinese «kētóu», meaning «knock head». Past: kowtowed. In the second sense it is negative and a little rude about the person who kowtows. Usually followed by «to».

part of speech: noun (on the lam); verb (lam, lams, lammed, lamming)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (slang, US) To be «on the lam» is to be running away and hiding, usually from the police. 2) (informal, UK) To lam someone is to hit them hard. 3) (a name) Lam is also a family name, for example in Chinese and Vietnamese families.
its sense in the lessons: Met in crime stories, old films and detective books: «on the lam» tells the reader a character has escaped and is hiding. The hitting sense is old-fashioned and rare.
examples from the lessons: The robber has been on the lam for three weeks. | The detective found the thief who was on the lam. | The escaped prisoners went on the lam in the hills. | «Lam into him!» shouted the pirate in the old story. | Mr Lam is our new maths teacher. | After the jewel heist, the gang went on the lam.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly used in the fixed phrase «on the lam». Past form: lammed. Do not confuse with «lamb» (a young sheep), which sounds the same but has a silent b.

part of speech: noun (a landscape, landscapes); verb (landscape, landscapes, landscaped, landscaping); adjective (landscape format)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A landscape is everything you can see when you look across a wide area of land: hills, fields, rivers, trees and buildings. 2) A landscape is also a painting or photo of such a view. 3) Landscape (format) means a page or screen that is wider than it is tall. 4) To landscape a garden or park is to change its shape and plant things to make it look nicer. 5) The landscape of something is its general situation, for example «the political landscape».
its sense in the lessons: In geography: the shape of the land and how people and rivers change it (a rural or urban landscape); in art lessons: painting landscapes; on computers and printers: choosing landscape or portrait. In stories, describing the landscape sets the scene. Phrases: a beautiful landscape, landscape mode, the landscape of.
examples from the lessons: The landscape around the lake was green and hilly. | Glaciers shaped the landscape of Scotland. | We painted a landscape with a red sky. | Turn the paper to landscape for your poster. | Hold the tablet in landscape to watch the video. | They landscaped the school garden with ponds and paths. | Factories changed the landscape of the town. | The desert landscape looked empty and dry.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: a landscape, landscapes. In art and computing the opposite of «landscape» is «portrait» (taller than wide). A landscape is about land; a view of the sea is called a «seascape».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Larval means to do with a larva, the young stage of an insect, frog or other animal before it changes into its adult form.
its sense in the lessons: Met in science lessons about life cycles: a caterpillar is the larval stage of a butterfly, a tadpole is the larval stage of a frog. It tells the reader we are talking about the young, not-yet-changed form. Phrase: the larval stage.
examples from the lessons: A caterpillar is the larval stage of a butterfly. | The larval stage of a frog is called a tadpole. | Mosquito larvae live in water during their larval stage. | Larval beetles are often called grubs. | Some insects spend years in their larval form. | We drew the egg, larval, pupal and adult stages.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comes from «larva» (one), «larvae» (more than one). «Larval» is only an adjective: say «the larval stage», not «a larval». Do not mix up «larva» (young insect) with «lava» (melted rock from a volcano).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Laterally means sideways, or to the side. 2) To think laterally is to solve a problem in an unusual, creative way instead of the obvious one.
its sense in the lessons: In science and sport it describes movement to the side (crabs walk laterally); in puzzles and olympiad questions «lateral thinking» means looking for a clever, unexpected answer.
examples from the lessons: Crabs move laterally across the sand. | The pass went laterally across the pitch. | The bridge can move laterally a little in strong wind. | Try to think laterally about this riddle. | The fish has eyes placed laterally, on the sides of its head. | Lateral thinking puzzles need you to think laterally.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from the adjective «lateral» (to the side). Spelled with «-ally». «Lateral thinking» was named by Edward de Bono. In maths, a «lateral face» is a side face of a prism or pyramid, not the top or bottom.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A layout is the way the parts of something are arranged, such as the rooms in a house, the streets in a town or the shops in a mall. 2) A layout is also the way words and pictures are arranged on a page or screen. 3) A keyboard layout is the order of the letters on the keys.
its sense in the lessons: In school it is used for planning posters, newspapers and web pages, for maps and floor plans in maths, and in design and technology. Phrases: page layout, floor layout, keyboard layout.
examples from the lessons: The layout of the new school is easy to follow. | I changed the layout of my poster so the title is bigger. | The museum map shows the layout of every room. | Most English keyboards use the QWERTY layout. | The layout of the town is like a grid. | The magazine has a bright, clear layout. | We drew a layout of our dream bedroom on squared paper.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: a layout, layouts. It is one word. The verb is two words: «lay out» («Lay out the cards on the table»). Do not write «lay-out».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Leakage is liquid, gas or light escaping through a hole or crack. 2) Leakage is also the amount that escapes. 3) Leakage of information is when secret or private facts get out to people who should not have them.
its sense in the lessons: In science it is about pipes, batteries and gas safety; in everyday life about leaking roofs and taps; in news about secret information getting out. A gas leakage is dangerous: leave the place and tell an adult.
examples from the lessons: Water leakage made a stain on the ceiling. | The plumber found the cause of the leakage. | Old batteries can have leakage of acid. | A gas leakage can cause a fire, so open the windows and get out. | The tank lost ten litres through leakage. | The company worried about the leakage of secret plans.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable: «some leakage». The verb is «leak», and «a leak» is the more common everyday noun. In a maths problem, leakage is an amount lost, so you subtract it.

part of speech: adjective (the leeward side); adverb (sail leeward); noun (to leeward)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Leeward means on the side away from the wind, the sheltered side. 2) To leeward means in the direction the wind is blowing towards.
its sense in the lessons: In geography it explains rain: the windward side of a mountain gets rain, the leeward side is dry (a rain shadow). In sailing and pirate stories, sailors talk about leeward and windward.
examples from the lessons: The leeward side of the island is dry and sunny. | We sheltered on the leeward side of the boat. | The ship drifted to leeward. | The Leeward Islands are in the Caribbean. | Rain falls on the windward side, and the leeward side stays dry. | Pitch your tent on the leeward side of the hill.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: windward. Sailors often say it «LOO-erd». «Lee» means shelter from the wind. Do not mix up with «lee» as a name.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A legionary was a soldier in a legion, a large unit of the ancient Roman army. 2) Legionary as an adjective means to do with a legion.
its sense in the lessons: Met in history lessons about the Romans and Roman Britain: legionaries built roads, forts and Hadrian's Wall. Stories show them with a shield, helmet and short sword.
examples from the lessons: A Roman legionary carried a heavy pack. | Legionaries built Hadrian's Wall. | Each legionary had a shield called a scutum. | The legionaries marched about 30 kilometres a day. | We dressed up as Roman legionaries for history day. | A legionary served in the army for about 25 years.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: legionaries (y changes to ies). A legion had about 5,000 legionaries. Do not mix up «legionary» with «legendary» (very famous).

meaning for a pupil: 1) «Ler» is not a usual English word on its own; it is most often a piece of a longer word, for example the end of «butler», «sprinkler» or «tumbler». 2) (a name) Ler (Lir) is a sea god in old Irish stories; the tale of «The Children of Lir» is about his children turned into swans.
its sense in the lessons: In text it usually appears because a word was split; in Irish myths it is the name of the sea god, father of the swan children.
examples from the lessons: The story «The Children of Lir» is an old Irish legend. | Lir's children were turned into swans. | In «butler», the last three letters are l-e-r. | Some old books spell the sea god's name Ler. | Words like «sprinkler» end in -ler.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Not a full English word; check whether it is part of a longer word. As a name it takes a capital letter: Ler or Lir.

part of speech: noun (a levy, levies); verb (levy, levies, levied, levying)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A levy is a tax or charge that people or companies must pay. 2) To levy a tax or fine is to make people pay it. 3) (history) A levy was also a group of soldiers called up to fight.
its sense in the lessons: Used in news, adult life and money lessons: a sugar levy on fizzy drinks, a plastic bag levy. In history: a king levied taxes or levied troops. Phrases: levy a tax, impose a levy.
examples from the lessons: The government put a levy on sugary drinks. | Shops charge a small levy for plastic bags. | The king levied a tax on wool. | The council levied a fine on the builder. | A levy of soldiers was raised for the war. | Part of the price goes to the levy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: levies. Past: levied. It is a formal word; in everyday talk people say «tax» or «charge». In a maths problem, a levy is an extra amount added to the price, so you add it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Liaison is the way people or groups talk to each other and work together. 2) A liaison (officer) is the person whose job is to keep two groups in touch. 3) (formal, adult) A liaison can also mean a secret romantic relationship.
its sense in the lessons: Used in school offices (a parent liaison), the police, the army and companies. It tells the reader someone links two groups. Phrases: liaison officer, in liaison with.
examples from the lessons: The school has a parent liaison who helps families. | The police liaison officer visited our class. | There is close liaison between the hospital and the school. | She is the liaison between the two teams. | The council works in liaison with local clubs. | Good liaison stops mistakes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Tricky spelling: l-i-a-i-s-o-n (two i's). Comes from French. The verb is «liaise». It is a formal word; in everyday talk people say «link» or «contact».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Lifeless means dead, or never having had life. 2) Lifeless means with no living things, like a lifeless planet. 3) Lifeless can mean dull, without energy or excitement.
its sense in the lessons: In science: the Moon is lifeless; in stories: a lifeless body is a sad or scary detail; in English lessons: a lifeless voice or story is boring.
examples from the lessons: The bird lay lifeless on the grass. | Mars seems to be a lifeless planet. | The desert looked lifeless, but many animals hid under the sand. | Her voice was flat and lifeless. | The doll's lifeless eyes stared at me. | Add more detail so your story isn't lifeless.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Made from «life» + «-less» (without). Opposite: lively, alive, full of life. No comparative is usually needed. It is gentler to say «not alive» to small children.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Likeable means easy to like; pleasant and friendly.
its sense in the lessons: Used about people and characters in stories: a likeable hero, a likeable new pupil. In writing, authors make a character likeable so readers care about them.
examples from the lessons: Our new neighbour is very likeable. | The hero of the book is brave and likeable. | Ben is likeable because he is always kind. | Even the villain is a bit likeable in this film. | She has a likeable smile. | He tried hard to be likeable at his new school.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelled «likeable» (UK, common everywhere) or «likable» (US); both are correct. Opposite: unlikeable, unpleasant.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A limpet is a small sea animal with a cone-shaped shell that clings very tightly to rocks. 2) (informal) Someone who sticks to you like a limpet will not leave you alone.
its sense in the lessons: Met in science on the seashore and rock pools; in everyday talk «cling like a limpet» means hold on very tightly.
examples from the lessons: We found limpets on the rocks at low tide. | A limpet clings to the rock so the waves can't move it. | Limpets eat tiny plants called algae. | My little brother clung to Mum like a limpet. | You can't pull a limpet off a rock easily. | Limpet teeth are one of the strongest natural materials.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: a limpet, limpets. A limpet is a snail-like animal (a mollusc), not a plant. Be gentle with rock-pool animals and put them back.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Literary means to do with literature: books, poems, plays and stories, and the people who write them. 2) Literary language is the special, fancy kind used in books, not in everyday talk.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons: literary devices (simile, metaphor), a literary prize, literary characters. It tells the reader something belongs to the world of books. Phrases: literary device, literary festival, literary language.
examples from the lessons: A simile is a literary device. | She won a literary prize for her poems. | Our town has a literary festival every summer. | «Steed» is a literary word for horse. | Sherlock Holmes is a famous literary detective. | He likes literary magazines.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Do not confuse «literary» (about books) with «literally» (really, exactly) or «literacy» (being able to read and write).

meaning for a pupil: 1) To be «at loggerheads» with someone is to disagree strongly and argue with them. 2) A loggerhead turtle is a large sea turtle with a big head. 3) (old) A loggerhead was an old word for a stupid person.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday talk and news: two people or groups are «at loggerheads» over something. In science: loggerhead turtles lay eggs on beaches and are protected.
examples from the lessons: The two neighbours are at loggerheads over the fence. | My brother and I were at loggerheads about the TV. | Loggerhead turtles nest on warm beaches. | A loggerhead turtle can live for over 50 years. | The councils have been at loggerheads for months. | Plastic in the sea harms loggerhead turtles.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The phrase is always plural: «at loggerheads». In nature, «loggerhead» is short for loggerhead turtle (also a loggerhead shrike, a bird).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Lopsided means leaning to one side, with one side bigger, lower or heavier than the other. 2) A lopsided result or game is very unequal.
its sense in the lessons: Used about drawings, cakes, smiles and buildings in everyday life; in sport about very one-sided scores. In maths it is the opposite of symmetrical or balanced.
examples from the lessons: My cake came out lopsided. | He gave me a lopsided smile. | The picture on the wall is lopsided. | The snowman looked lopsided. | It was a lopsided game: 10–0. | The shelf is lopsided because one bracket is loose.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word. Similar words: crooked, uneven, wonky (UK, informal). Opposite: even, balanced, symmetrical.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (Ireland) A lough is a lake or a long, narrow arm of the sea in Ireland, like a Scottish loch.
its sense in the lessons: Met in geography of Ireland and Northern Ireland: Lough Neagh is the largest lake in the UK and Ireland. Place names often start with «Lough».
examples from the lessons: Lough Neagh is the biggest lake in the British Isles. | We went fishing on the lough. | Lough Erne has many small islands. | The lough was calm and grey in the morning. | Swans swam across the lough. | Lough Foyle opens into the sea.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Said like «lock» but with a soft throaty «ch» at the end, like Scottish «loch»; never like «laugh» or «tough». Plural: loughs. Used as part of names with a capital L.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Luminescence is light given off by something that is not hot, for example glow-in-the-dark stickers, fireflies or some deep-sea fish.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on light: bioluminescence is light made by living things; it is different from the light of a hot bulb or fire.
examples from the lessons: The jellyfish glowed with a blue luminescence. | Glow-in-the-dark stars show luminescence after you switch off the light. | Fireflies make their own luminescence. | The waves sparkled with luminescence at night. | Scientists study luminescence in deep-sea animals. | The watch hands shine by luminescence.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: no plural normally. Adjective: luminescent. «Bioluminescence» means light from living things. Hard spelling: l-u-m-i-n-e-s-c-e-n-c-e.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Lycopene is a natural red colouring found in tomatoes, watermelon and pink grapefruit. 2) It is an antioxidant, a substance that may help protect the body's cells.
its sense in the lessons: Met in science and healthy-eating lessons about what makes fruit red and why tomatoes are good for you. It tells the reader about chemistry inside food.
examples from the lessons: Lycopene makes tomatoes red. | Watermelon also contains lycopene. | Cooked tomatoes give your body more lycopene than raw ones. | Lycopene is a kind of antioxidant. | Ketchup has lycopene in it, but also a lot of sugar. | Scientists study whether lycopene helps keep hearts healthy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Say «LIE-ko-peen». Health claims about lycopene are still studied; it is not a medicine and does not cure illness on its own.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Lymph is a clear, watery fluid that moves around the body in thin tubes and carries white blood cells that fight germs.
its sense in the lessons: Met in science lessons about the body and in doctors' talk: lymph nodes (often called glands) can swell when you have an infection. Phrases: lymph node, lymphatic system.
examples from the lessons: Lymph helps the body fight infection. | The doctor felt the lymph nodes in my neck. | Lymph nodes can swell when you have a cold. | Lymph flows through the lymphatic system. | White blood cells travel in the lymph. | Lymph is almost colourless.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Say «limf». Adjective: lymphatic. Swollen «glands» in the neck are really lymph nodes.

part of speech: noun (a mac, macs; a Mac, Macs)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (UK) A mac is a raincoat (short for mackintosh). 2) A Mac is an Apple Macintosh computer. 3) (informal, US) «Mac» is a way of speaking to a man whose name you don't know, like «buddy». 4) Mac (or Mc) at the start of a name means «son of» in Scottish and Irish names, like MacDonald. 5) Mac and cheese is a dish of macaroni pasta in cheese sauce.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday UK life: «Take your mac, it's raining». In computing lessons: using a Mac or a PC. In names and stories: Scottish clans.
examples from the lessons: Put your mac on; it's pouring. | Our school computer room has Macs. | «Hey, Mac, you dropped your wallet!» | MacGregor is a Scottish name. | We had mac and cheese for tea. | Her yellow mac kept her dry. | Is this program for Mac or Windows?
note for the reader of a maths problem: The computer is written with a capital M: Mac. The raincoat is lower case: mac (also «mackintosh», named after Charles Macintosh). Plural: macs. «Mac» as a way to address a man is old-fashioned US slang.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A macadamia is a round, creamy nut with a very hard shell. 2) It is also the tree it grows on, which comes from Australia.
its sense in the lessons: Met in food lessons, recipes and geography of Australia; macadamia cookies are popular. Allergies matter in school.
examples from the lessons: Macadamia nuts come from Australia. | Mum baked white chocolate and macadamia cookies. | The macadamia has a very hard shell. | Macadamia trees grow in warm places like Queensland and Hawaii. | Some children are allergic to macadamias. | Macadamias are rich in oil.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: macadamias. Say «mak-a-DAY-mee-a». Nuts can cause serious allergies; check before sharing food. Macadamias are poisonous to dogs.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Magically means by magic. 2) Magically also means in a wonderful, surprising way, as if by magic.
its sense in the lessons: In fairy tales, things change magically; in everyday talk, people say something «magically» appeared when they don't know how. Also used jokingly.
examples from the lessons: The pumpkin magically turned into a coach. | The snow made the garden look magically white. | My homework didn't magically do itself! | The door opened magically by itself. | The lights twinkled magically. | My lost sock magically appeared under the bed.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from «magic»/«magical»; spelled with «-ally». Real magic tricks are skill and illusion, not real magic.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A maglev is a train that floats just above its track using powerful magnets, so it does not touch the rails. 2) It is short for «magnetic levitation».
its sense in the lessons: Met in science lessons on magnets (like poles push apart) and in technology about fast transport; maglevs run in China and Japan.
examples from the lessons: A maglev train floats above the track. | Maglevs can go faster than 400 kilometres an hour. | Shanghai has a maglev line to the airport. | Magnets push the maglev forward. | Because it doesn't touch the rails, a maglev is quiet. | We built a model maglev with fridge magnets.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Short for «magnetic levitation»; one word, lower case. Plural: maglevs. The train does not float by magic; it uses magnets that repel each other.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (old, literary) A maiden is a girl or young woman who is not married. 2) Maiden as an adjective means first, for example a ship's maiden voyage. 3) A maiden name is the family name a woman had before she married. 4) (cricket) A maiden (over) is an over in which no runs are scored.
its sense in the lessons: In fairy tales: a fair maiden in a tower. In history and news: the Titanic sank on its maiden voyage. In sport: a maiden over in cricket. On forms: «mother's maiden name».
examples from the lessons: The knight rescued the maiden from the dragon. | The Titanic sank on its maiden voyage in 1912. | My mum's maiden name was Murphy. | The bowler sent down a maiden over. | The pilot made his maiden flight. | She gave her maiden speech in Parliament.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The «young girl» meaning is old-fashioned and found in stories. «Maiden» as «first» comes before the noun: maiden voyage, maiden flight. Not to be confused with «made».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A mako is a large, very fast shark that lives in warm and mild seas.
its sense in the lessons: Met in science about ocean animals and fastest swimmers; makos can leap out of the water.
examples from the lessons: The mako is the fastest shark in the sea. | A mako shark can jump high out of the water. | Makos have long, pointed teeth. | The mako is shiny dark blue on top. | Mako sharks are now endangered because of overfishing. | The mako swims across whole oceans.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: makos. Say «MAY-ko» or «MAH-ko». The word comes from the Māori language of New Zealand.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Malice is the wish to hurt someone or make bad things happen to them. 2) (law) Malice is the intention to do harm when breaking the law.
its sense in the lessons: In stories malice marks a villain; in ethics lessons, it separates a mistake from a cruel act done on purpose. Phrases: with malice, out of malice, without malice.
examples from the lessons: The witch looked at the princess with malice. | He broke the toy by accident, not out of malice. | There was no malice in her joke. | The bully acted with malice. | «Malice aforethought» is an old legal phrase. | Gossip can be full of malice.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Adjective: malicious. In ethics, what someone meant (malice or an accident) matters a lot when judging what they did.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The Manchu are a people from Manchuria in north-east China. 2) Manchu is also their language. 3) The Manchu ruled China as the Qing dynasty from 1644 to 1912.
its sense in the lessons: Met in history lessons on imperial China, the last emperors and the Qing dynasty.
examples from the lessons: The Manchu ruled China for almost 300 years. | The last emperor of China was Manchu. | Manchu is written in a script that runs from top to bottom. | Very few people speak Manchu today. | Manchu soldiers rode horses and shot arrows. | The Qing dynasty was founded by the Manchu.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A name of a people and language, so capital M. Plural: the Manchu or Manchus. Do not confuse with «Manchester».

meaning for a pupil: 1) The mandible is the lower jawbone. 2) Mandibles are the biting mouthparts of insects such as ants and beetles. 3) In birds, the mandibles are the two parts of the beak.
its sense in the lessons: Met in science lessons on skeletons, teeth and insects. It is the scientific word for jaw.
examples from the lessons: The mandible is the only bone in the skull that moves. | Ants carry leaves in their mandibles. | The stag beetle has huge mandibles. | The dentist looked at an X-ray of my mandible. | A parrot's lower mandible fits inside its upper one. | The fossil had a strong mandible with sharp teeth.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: mandibles. «Mandible» is the scientific word; in everyday talk, say «jaw». Upper jaw: maxilla.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A mango is a sweet, juicy tropical fruit with orange flesh, a smooth skin and a large flat stone inside. 2) It is also the tree it grows on.
its sense in the lessons: Met in food lessons, recipes and geography (mangoes grow in India, Pakistan, the Caribbean and northern Australia). In maths problems, mangoes are counted and shared.
examples from the lessons: I had a mango for breakfast. | Mangoes grow on tall trees in hot countries. | The mango is the national fruit of India. | Mango juice is my favourite. | Sam bought 6 mangoes and gave 2 away; he has 4 left. | A ripe mango smells sweet.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: mangoes or mangos; both are correct. Say «a mango». The stone is big; don't try to bite through it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A mara is a South American animal that looks like a small deer or long-legged hare but is a rodent, a relative of the guinea pig. 2) (a name) The Mara is a river and area in Kenya and Tanzania; the Masai Mara is a famous wildlife reserve. 3) (a name) Mara is also a girl's name.
its sense in the lessons: Met in science lessons about animals of Patagonia and in zoos; in geography and nature films about the great migration in the Masai Mara.
examples from the lessons: The mara hops like a rabbit and runs like a deer. | Maras live in Argentina. | Maras are big rodents. | Wildebeest cross the Mara River every year. | We saw maras at the zoo. | Mara is my best friend's name.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: maras. Also called the Patagonian hare, but it is not a hare. As a name, it takes a capital M.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Marshy means soft and wet, like a marsh, so water lies on or just under the ground.
its sense in the lessons: Met in geography and nature lessons about wetlands, and in stories where heroes cross dangerous marshy land.
examples from the lessons: The field by the river is marshy. | Our boots sank into the marshy ground. | Frogs love marshy places. | The path got marshy after the rain. | Ducks nest in the marshy reeds. | Be careful: marshy ground can be deeper than it looks.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Made from «marsh» + «-y». Similar: boggy, swampy, soggy. Safety: marshy land can be dangerous; keep to paths.

part of speech: verb (marvel, marvels, marvelled/marveled, marvelling/marveling); noun (a marvel, marvels)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A marvel is a wonderful, amazing thing or person. 2) To marvel at something is to feel great surprise and admiration.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and science: the marvels of nature, the marvels of technology. In everyday talk: «It's a marvel you didn't fall.» Phrases: marvel at, a marvel of.
examples from the lessons: The pyramids are one of the marvels of the ancient world. | We marvelled at the stars. | The new bridge is a marvel of engineering. | It's a marvel that nobody was hurt. | Grandma marvels at how fast I type. | The museum is full of marvels.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK spelling: marvelled, marvelling; US spelling: marveled, marveling. Adjective: marvellous (UK), marvelous (US). Marvel is also the name of a comic company; that use has a capital M.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The Maasai (Masai) are a people of Kenya and Tanzania, famous for cattle herding and their bright red cloth. 2) (a name) The Masai Mara is a wildlife reserve in Kenya.
its sense in the lessons: Met in geography and culture lessons about East Africa and in nature films of the Masai Mara. It should be said with respect: they are a living people, not a story.
examples from the lessons: The Maasai keep large herds of cattle. | Many Maasai wear red cloth called shuka. | Maasai warriors are known for their high jumping dance. | We watched lions in the Masai Mara. | The Maasai speak a language called Maa. | Maasai beadwork is very colourful.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Today «Maasai» is the preferred spelling; «Masai» is older but still used, especially in «Masai Mara». A people's name, so capital M.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The Matabele (Ndebele) are a people of south-western Zimbabwe, around the city of Bulawayo. 2) Matabeleland is the region where they live.
its sense in the lessons: Met in history lessons about southern Africa and colonial wars. Today the people are usually called Ndebele.
examples from the lessons: The Matabele kingdom was founded by Mzilikazi. | Bulawayo is the main city of Matabeleland. | The Matabele are also called the Ndebele. | British settlers fought wars against the Matabele in the 1890s. | Matabeleland has wide, dry grasslands.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Matabele» is an older name; «Ndebele» is the people's own name and is preferred today. Capital M.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A matinee is a performance of a play, show or film in the afternoon.
its sense in the lessons: Used in everyday life about theatre and cinema trips, especially family outings.
examples from the lessons: We went to the Saturday matinee of the pantomime. | Matinee tickets are often cheaper. | The matinee starts at 2 o'clock. | Grandad took us to a matinee of «The Lion King». | There is no matinee on Mondays. | The cinema shows a kids' matinee every Sunday.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From French «matin» (morning), but it means afternoon in English. Also spelled «matinée». Plural: matinees.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Measurable means able to be measured. 2) Measurable also means big enough to be noticed, like a measurable difference.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and science: length, mass, time and temperature are measurable; in goals and school reports, «measurable progress» means you can show how much better.
examples from the lessons: Height is measurable with a tape measure. | Is happiness measurable? | There was a measurable rise in temperature. | Set a measurable goal, like reading 20 pages a day. | The plant showed measurable growth in a week. | Kindness isn't easily measurable.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: drop the final e of «measure» and add «-able»: measurable. Opposite: immeasurable (too big to measure).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Meatless means without meat.
its sense in the lessons: Used in food and healthy-eating lessons: meatless meals, Meatless Monday. Also in church life: some Christians eat meatless meals on Fridays or in Lent.
examples from the lessons: We have a meatless dinner on Mondays. | This pizza is meatless; it has only cheese and vegetables. | In Lent some Christians eat meatless meals. | Meatless burgers are made from beans or soy. | The café has a meatless menu. | During the war, families had meatless days to save food.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Made from «meat» + «-less» (without). Do not confuse «meat» (food) with «meet» (to come together). Meatless meals can still include fish in some traditions, which is why words like «vegetarian» are clearer.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Mechanically means by a machine or using machinery. 2) Mechanically also means doing something without thinking, like a robot. 3) Mechanically can mean about how machines work, as in «mechanically minded».
its sense in the lessons: In design and technology: a gate is opened mechanically; in stories: a sad character answers mechanically, showing they are numb or bored.
examples from the lessons: The doors are opened mechanically. | She answered mechanically, without looking up. | The car is mechanically sound. | He is mechanically minded and loves fixing bikes. | The crops are harvested mechanically now. | I read the words mechanically and didn't understand them.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from «mechanical»; spelled «-ally». In maths, doing sums «mechanically» means following steps without understanding them.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In maths, the median is the middle number when a list of numbers is put in order. 2) (UK, Australia) The median strip is the strip of land between the two sides of a road. 3) In geometry, a median is a line from a corner of a triangle to the middle of the opposite side.
its sense in the lessons: In school maths with mean, mode and range. In news: «median income» or «median age». On roads: the median (US: median strip).
examples from the lessons: The median of 2, 5 and 9 is 5. | Put the numbers in order before you find the median. | For 3, 4, 8 and 10 the median is 6, halfway between 4 and 8. | The median age of the class is 10. | The car hit the median of the highway. | The median of a triangle goes to the middle of a side.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Maths: put the numbers in order; with an odd count, the median is the middle one; with an even count, it is halfway between the two middle ones. Do not confuse with the mean (average), mode (most common) or range.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Megalosaurus was a large meat-eating dinosaur that lived in what is now England about 166 million years ago. 2) It was the first dinosaur ever given a scientific name, in 1824.
its sense in the lessons: Met in science and history lessons about fossils and the first dinosaur discoveries in Oxford.
examples from the lessons: Megalosaurus walked on two legs. | Megalosaurus was the first dinosaur to be named. | Its bones were found near Oxford. | Megalosaurus means «great lizard». | Charles Dickens mentioned a Megalosaurus in one of his books. | Megalosaurus had sharp, curved teeth.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Name of a kind of dinosaur, often written with a capital M. Plural is rare: megalosauruses. Old pictures showed it on four legs; we now know it walked on two.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Menthol is a substance from mint oil that gives a cool, fresh feeling and smell.
its sense in the lessons: Used in everyday life and health: menthol is in cough sweets, chest rubs, toothpaste and chewing gum.
examples from the lessons: Menthol makes my throat feel cool. | Cough sweets often contain menthol. | The chest rub smells strongly of menthol. | Menthol comes from mint plants. | This toothpaste has menthol in it. | Menthol tricks your skin into feeling cold.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Menthol does not really make you colder; it tricks the nerves. Medicines with menthol should only be used as the label says.

part of speech: verb (merge, merges, merged, merging); noun (a merge)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To merge is to join together to become one. 2) When traffic merges, two lanes join into one. 3) On a computer, to merge files or cells is to put them together.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: roads, rivers, companies and schools merge. In computing: merge cells in a table. In maths, merging groups means adding them. Phrases: merge into, merge with.
examples from the lessons: The two rivers merge to form a bigger one. | The schools will merge next year. | Cars must merge into one lane. | Merge these two cells in the table. | The colours merged together in the rain. | Two clubs merged to make one big team.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: merged. Noun: a merger (for companies). In a maths problem, if a class of 12 merges with a class of 15, there are 12 + 15 = 27 pupils.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Merged is the past form of «merge»: joined together into one. 2) As an adjective, merged means already joined, like a merged class.
its sense in the lessons: Used in stories, news and maths problems about things that have joined.
examples from the lessons: The two roads merged near the bridge. | Our class merged with Year 5 for the trip. | The merged company is very big. | The colours merged into a muddy brown. | The two streams merged and flowed to the sea. | We used merged cells for the title of the table.
note for the reader of a maths problem: See «merge». Spelling: merge + d (the e is already there). In a maths problem, merged groups are added together.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Merging is the -ing form of «merge»: joining together into one. 2) As a noun, merging is the act of joining.
its sense in the lessons: Seen on road signs («Merging traffic») and in computing and news.
examples from the lessons: The cars are merging into one lane. | Watch out for merging traffic. | The two schools are merging next year. | Merging the files took a minute. | The clouds were merging into one dark mass. | Merging two teams can make it stronger.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: drop the e of «merge» and add «-ing»: merging. Road safety: at a merge, drivers take turns.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Mestizo is a Spanish word for a person with both Spanish (European) and Native American ancestors, used especially in Latin America.
its sense in the lessons: Met in history lessons about Spanish colonies in the Americas and in geography of Mexico and South America. It describes family origins, and today many Latin Americans call themselves mestizo.
examples from the lessons: Many people in Mexico are mestizo. | In colonial times, Spanish rulers sorted people into groups such as mestizo. | Mestizo culture mixes Spanish and native traditions. | The word mestizo comes from Spanish. | The country's population is largely mestizo.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From Spanish; plural: mestizos. A woman may be called «mestiza». Words about people's ancestry can be sensitive; use them only as people use them about themselves.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To metabolise food is for the body to break it down and use it for energy and growth. 2) To metabolise a medicine or substance is for the body to process and change it.
its sense in the lessons: Met in science and health lessons on digestion and energy; doctors talk about how fast the body metabolises medicine.
examples from the lessons: Your body metabolises food to make energy. | Some people metabolise sugar faster than others. | The liver metabolises many medicines. | Plants metabolise sunlight into food. | Babies metabolise caffeine very slowly. | Exercise helps you metabolise fat.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK spelling «metabolise»; US spelling «metabolize». Noun: metabolism. Past: metabolised.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (Bible) Methuselah is a man in the Book of Genesis who is said to have lived 969 years, the oldest person in the Bible. 2) (informal) A methuselah is a very old person or thing. 3) A methuselah is also a very large wine bottle holding six litres.
its sense in the lessons: Met in Bible lessons and in sayings: «as old as Methuselah» means extremely old. Also the name of a very old bristlecone pine tree in California.
examples from the lessons: The Bible says Methuselah lived to be 969 years old. | Grandad jokes that he is as old as Methuselah. | Methuselah was the grandfather of Noah. | A pine tree called Methuselah is nearly 5,000 years old. | That old car is a real methuselah. | A methuselah holds as much as eight normal bottles.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a Bible name, capital M. Christians and Jews read the long ages in Genesis in different ways; some take them literally, many see them as symbolic. No real person today lives anywhere near that long.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A metronome is a device that ticks or clicks at a steady speed to help musicians keep time.
its sense in the lessons: Met in music lessons; also used to describe something very regular («ticking like a metronome»).
examples from the lessons: My piano teacher sets the metronome to 80 beats a minute. | The metronome clicked steadily. | Practise with a metronome to keep a steady beat. | The old metronome has a swinging arm. | There is a metronome app on my phone. | His running steps were as regular as a metronome.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: metronomes. Its speed is measured in beats per minute (bpm). In a maths problem, at 60 bpm the metronome clicks once each second.

part of speech: verb (miaow, miaows, miaowed, miaowing); noun (a miaow); interjection (miaow!)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A miaow is the sound a cat makes. 2) To miaow is to make that sound.
its sense in the lessons: Used in stories, poems and everyday talk about pets; in English lessons, it is an example of onomatopoeia (a word that sounds like its meaning).
examples from the lessons: The kitten gave a little miaow. | «Miaow!» said the cat at the door. | Our cat miaows when she is hungry. | The cat miaowed all night. | «Miaow» is an onomatopoeia. | I heard a sad miaow from the tree.
