note for the reader of a maths problem: UK spelling «miaow»; also «meow» (US and common everywhere) and «mew». Past: miaowed.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A millstone is one of a pair of large, round, flat stones used in a mill to grind grain into flour. 2) A millstone (round your neck) is a heavy problem or responsibility you can't get rid of.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons on old mills and bread; in sayings and the Bible; in news: debt can be «a millstone round someone's neck».
examples from the lessons: The millstone turned slowly and ground the wheat. | Old millstones are sometimes used in gardens. | The river turned the wheel that turned the millstone. | The debt was a millstone round his neck. | A millstone is very heavy. | Jesus spoke of a millstone in one of his warnings in the Gospels.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: millstones. The phrase is «a millstone round/around your neck». A «milestone» (an important stage) is a different word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A Mississippian is a person from the US state of Mississippi. 2) The Mississippian culture was a Native American civilisation that built great earth mounds along the Mississippi valley, about 800 to 1600. 3) (science) The Mississippian is a period of Earth's history about 359–323 million years ago, used in the USA.
its sense in the lessons: Met in US geography, Native American history (the city of Cahokia) and geology about rock layers and coal.
examples from the lessons: My cousin is a Mississippian. | The Mississippian people built huge earth mounds. | Cahokia was the largest Mississippian city. | Coal formed in the Mississippian period. | Mississippian farmers grew corn and beans. | A famous Mississippian writer is William Faulkner.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital M because it comes from a name. Spelling: double s, double s, double p: Mi-ss-i-ss-i-pp-ian.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (a name) Missouri is a state in the middle of the USA. 2) (a name) The Missouri River is the longest river in North America; it flows into the Mississippi. 3) The Missouri are also a Native American people the state is named after.
its sense in the lessons: Met in US geography lessons and in history about explorers Lewis and Clark. «Show-Me State» is its nickname.
examples from the lessons: Missouri is in the middle of the United States. | The Missouri River joins the Mississippi near St Louis. | Lewis and Clark travelled up the Missouri. | Kansas City is partly in Missouri. | Mark Twain grew up in Missouri. | The Missouri is longer than the Mississippi.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A name, so capital M. Say «mi-ZOOR-ee» or «mi-ZOOR-uh». Many people think the Mississippi is longest, but the Missouri is slightly longer.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Mnemonics are tricks that help you remember things, like a rhyme, a sentence or a pattern. 2) Mnemonics is also the study and use of such memory tricks.
its sense in the lessons: Very useful in school: «Never Eat Shredded Wheat» for North, East, South, West; «Richard Of York Gave Battle In Vain» for the colours of the rainbow; «i before e except after c».
examples from the lessons: Mnemonics help me remember spelling. | «My Very Easy Method Just Speeds Up Naming» is a mnemonic for the planets. | Our teacher taught us mnemonics for the rainbow. | «BIG ELEPHANTS CAN'T ALWAYS UNDERSTAND SMALL ELEPHANTS» is a mnemonic for «because». | Make up your own mnemonics for times tables. | Mnemonics make hard lists easier.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The first m is silent: say «ni-MON-iks». One trick is «a mnemonic»; several are «mnemonics». Spelling trap: it starts m-n.

part of speech: adjective (Mongolian); noun (a Mongolian, Mongolians; Mongolian, the language)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Mongolian means from or to do with Mongolia, a country between Russia and China. 2) A Mongolian is a person from Mongolia. 3) Mongolian is the language spoken there.
its sense in the lessons: Met in geography and history lessons about the Mongol Empire, Genghis Khan, yurts (gers) and nomads on the steppe.
examples from the lessons: Mongolian herders live in round tents called gers. | Mongolian is written in the Cyrillic alphabet today. | The Mongolian steppe is huge and grassy. | Many Mongolians ride horses from a young age. | Mongolian throat singing sounds amazing. | Ulaanbaatar is the Mongolian capital.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital M. Do not use it as an old, rude word about people with Down syndrome; that use is offensive and out of date.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Moonlit means lit by the light of the Moon.
its sense in the lessons: Used in stories and poems to describe night scenes; it gives a calm, magical or sometimes spooky feeling.
examples from the lessons: We walked along the moonlit beach. | The moonlit garden looked silver. | An owl flew across the moonlit sky. | The castle stood dark on a moonlit hill. | A moonlit night is good for spotting badgers. | The lake shone in the moonlit darkness.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word: moon + lit. Only an adjective before a noun. Science fact: moonlight is really sunlight reflected by the Moon.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Mortar is a mixture of sand, cement or lime and water used to stick bricks or stones together. 2) A mortar is a strong bowl in which you crush things with a pestle. 3) A mortar is also a short gun that fires shells high into the air, used in war. 4) A mortarboard is a flat square hat worn at graduations.
its sense in the lessons: In design and technology and building; in cooking and science (mortar and pestle); in news about war. Phrases: bricks and mortar, mortar and pestle.
examples from the lessons: The builder spread mortar between the bricks. | Grind the spices with a mortar and pestle. | Mortar holds the old wall together. | The news reported mortar fire in the city. | The mortar dried hard overnight. | Graduates threw their mortarboards in the air.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Building mortar is uncountable («some mortar»); a bowl or gun is countable («a mortar, two mortars»). «Bricks and mortar» means real buildings, as opposed to online.

part of speech: adjective (motivated, more motivated); verb, past form of «motivate» (motivated)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Motivated means keen and wanting to work hard to do something. 2) Motivated also means caused or made to happen by a reason, as in «a racially motivated attack». 3) Past form of «motivate»: gave someone a reason to act.
its sense in the lessons: In school reports and sport: a motivated pupil works hard. In news: what something was motivated by tells the reader why it happened.
examples from the lessons: She is very motivated to learn the piano. | The coach motivated the team at half-time. | I feel motivated after the holidays. | His kindness was motivated by love. | The crime was motivated by money. | Motivated pupils often ask lots of questions.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: motivation. Opposite: unmotivated. It is often followed by «to» + verb («motivated to win») or «by» + reason.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A mountaineer is a person who climbs mountains as a sport or hobby. 2) Mountaineering is the sport of climbing mountains.
its sense in the lessons: Met in geography and history lessons about Everest (Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay) and in adventure stories. Safety: mountaineers use ropes, helmets and maps.
examples from the lessons: The mountaineer reached the top of Everest. | Tenzing Norgay was a famous mountaineer. | Mountaineers carry ropes and ice axes. | My uncle is a keen mountaineer. | The mountaineers set up camp below the summit. | Mountaineering can be dangerous in bad weather.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: mountaineers. The verb «to mountaineer» is rare; people say «go mountaineering» or «climb».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Mouthparts are the parts around an insect's or other small animal's mouth that it uses to bite, suck or chew food.
its sense in the lessons: Met in science lessons about insects: butterflies have a long sucking mouthpart, beetles have biting mouthparts, mosquitoes have piercing ones.
examples from the lessons: A butterfly's mouthpart is like a long straw. | Mosquitoes have sharp mouthparts for piercing skin. | Ants use their mouthparts to carry food. | Scientists study insect mouthparts under a microscope. | A grasshopper has strong chewing mouthparts. | The bee uses its mouthparts to drink nectar.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually plural: mouthparts. One word. Used mostly for insects and other small animals, not people.

part of speech: noun (a mugging, muggings); verb, -ing form of «mug» (mugging)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A mugging is an attack in a public place where someone is robbed, often with threats or violence. 2) Mugging is the -ing form of «mug» (to rob). 3) (informal) Mugging (for the camera) means pulling silly faces. 4) (informal, UK) Mugging up means studying hard quickly, cramming.
its sense in the lessons: In news and safety lessons: stay in groups, stay in lit places, give up your phone rather than fight, and tell an adult or the police. In everyday talk: mugging for photos, mugging up for a test.
examples from the lessons: There was a mugging near the station last night. | The police are looking for the people behind the mugging. | If someone tries mugging you, let them take your things and get away safely. | He was mugging for the camera. | I'm mugging up on my spellings. | Muggings are less common in busy, well-lit streets.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: a mugging, muggings. The person who does it is a mugger. Spelling: double g. Your safety matters more than your phone.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Mycelium is the mass of thin white threads of a fungus that grows underground or inside rotting wood; mushrooms grow out of it.
its sense in the lessons: Met in science lessons on fungi, decomposers and soil. Mycelium links tree roots and helps plants share food, sometimes called the «wood wide web».
examples from the lessons: Mushrooms grow from mycelium under the ground. | The mycelium spread through the rotting log. | Mycelium looks like white cotton threads. | Fungi break down dead leaves with their mycelium. | Some trees swap food through mycelium in the soil. | A single mycelium can be huge.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: mycelia. Say «my-SEE-lee-um». The mushroom is only a small part of the fungus; most of it is the mycelium.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Myoglobin is a protein in muscles that holds oxygen until the muscle needs it.
its sense in the lessons: Met in science lessons on muscles and blood; it makes red meat red and lets whales and seals hold their breath for a long time.
examples from the lessons: Myoglobin stores oxygen in muscles. | Whale muscles have a lot of myoglobin. | Red meat is red because of myoglobin. | Myoglobin is like haemoglobin, but it stays in the muscle. | Diving seals depend on myoglobin. | Chicken breast has little myoglobin, so it is pale.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Say «my-o-GLOW-bin». Do not confuse with haemoglobin, which carries oxygen in the blood.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Nahuatl is the language of the Aztecs, still spoken today by over a million people in Mexico.
its sense in the lessons: Met in history lessons about the Aztecs and in word lessons: English words like chocolate, tomato, avocado and chilli come from Nahuatl.
examples from the lessons: The Aztecs spoke Nahuatl. | «Chocolate» comes from a Nahuatl word. | About 1.5 million people in Mexico speak Nahuatl. | «Tomatl» is the Nahuatl word for tomato. | Nahuatl was written in pictures before the Spanish came. | Some Mexican place names come from Nahuatl.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A name of a language, so capital N. Say «NAH-wah-tl». It is not an English word, but it gave English several words.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Neatness is being tidy, clean and well arranged.
its sense in the lessons: Used at school about handwriting, presentation and tidy desks; in reports: «Work on the neatness of your writing».
examples from the lessons: Our teacher gives a sticker for neatness. | Neatness counts in your science book. | I admired the neatness of her drawing. | His room is famous for its neatness. | Take care with the neatness of your answers. | Neatness helps others read your work.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. From «neat» + «-ness». In maths, neatness matters: tidy columns help you avoid adding mistakes.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The Nenets are a people of the Arctic in northern Russia who traditionally herd reindeer. 2) Nenets is also their language.
its sense in the lessons: Met in geography lessons about the Arctic, tundra and nomadic peoples who move with their reindeer.
examples from the lessons: The Nenets herd reindeer across the tundra. | Nenets families live in tents called chums. | The Nenets travel hundreds of kilometres each year. | Nenets children wear warm reindeer-skin coats. | The Nenets language is related to Finnish and Hungarian. | Gas drilling has changed the Nenets' land.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital N. «Nenets» is both singular and plural. Their language is distantly related to Finnish and Hungarian.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To neuter a pet animal is to have a vet do an operation so it can't have babies. 2) (grammar) Neuter means neither masculine nor feminine; some languages, like German, have neuter nouns. 3) Neuter can mean having no sex organs, like worker bees.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life about pets (neutering cats and dogs). In language lessons about grammatical gender in German, Latin and Ukrainian.
examples from the lessons: We had our cat neutered at the vet. | Neutering helps stop too many stray kittens. | In German, «das Kind» is neuter. | English nouns don't have neuter gender in grammar. | Worker ants are neuter. | The vet neuters dogs on Tuesdays.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: neutered. Do not confuse with «neutral» (not taking sides). «Neutered» animals are often called «spayed» (females) or «castrated» (males).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (slang) A newbie is someone who is new to something, like a game, club, job or website, and doesn't know much yet.
its sense in the lessons: Used in gaming, online forums and everyday chat. Can be friendly or a bit teasing. Phrases: a total newbie, help the newbies.
examples from the lessons: I'm a newbie at chess, so go easy on me. | The newbies on our team are learning fast. | Everyone was a newbie once. | He's a newbie in the game, so he keeps falling off. | Be kind to newbies in the forum. | As a newbie, I asked lots of questions.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Slang, informal. Plural: newbies. Similar: beginner, rookie, novice. «Noob» is a ruder version used in gaming; calling someone a noob can be unkind.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The nobility are the people of the highest social class, such as dukes, earls and lords, who have titles passed down in their families. 2) Nobility is also the quality of being noble: good, honest and brave.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons about kings, castles, the feudal system and the French Revolution; in ethics and stories, nobility of character.
examples from the lessons: In the Middle Ages, the nobility owned most of the land. | The king invited the nobility to the feast. | Many of the nobility lost power in the French Revolution. | He showed great nobility by forgiving his enemy. | Members of the nobility had titles like duke and earl. | The nobility sat in the House of Lords.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «The nobility» is used with a plural or singular verb. One member is «a noble» or «a nobleman/noblewoman». Adjective: noble.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A nomad is a person who belongs to a group that moves from place to place with their animals instead of living in one place. 2) (informal) A nomad is anyone who moves a lot and has no fixed home.
its sense in the lessons: Met in geography and history about Mongols, Bedouin, Maasai, Sami and early humans; in everyday talk, a digital nomad works online while travelling.
examples from the lessons: Nomads move to find fresh grass for their animals. | Bedouin nomads live in the desert. | Early humans were nomads before farming began. | The family lived like nomads, moving every year. | Mongolian nomads carry their homes on horses and camels. | A digital nomad works from different countries.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: nomads. Adjective: nomadic. Not the same as homeless; nomads move by choice and tradition.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Nowruz is the Persian New Year, a spring festival on the spring equinox, around 20–21 March. 2) It is celebrated in Iran, Afghanistan, Central Asia, Azerbaijan, by Kurds and others.
its sense in the lessons: Met in lessons about festivals around the world: families clean the house, jump over small fires, set a special table (haft-sin) and visit relatives.
examples from the lessons: Nowruz means «new day». | We celebrate Nowruz on the first day of spring. | At Nowruz, families set a table with seven things beginning with «s». | Children get gifts and new clothes at Nowruz. | Nowruz is over 3,000 years old. | My friend's family visits relatives at Nowruz.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A name of a festival, so capital N. Also spelled Norouz, Navruz or Nauryz. Say «no-ROOZ». It is not a religious holiday for one faith only; people of many faiths keep it.

part of speech: noun (a nuke, nukes); verb (nuke, nukes, nuked, nuking)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) A nuke is a nuclear weapon, a bomb of enormous power. 2) (informal) To nuke a place is to attack it with nuclear weapons. 3) (slang) To nuke food is to heat it in a microwave. 4) (slang) To nuke something can mean to destroy or delete it completely, for example in a game or on a computer.
its sense in the lessons: In news and history (the Cold War, Hiroshima) it is a serious word; in everyday slang it is jokey: «nuke the pizza».
examples from the lessons: Some countries have nukes. | Nukes were used only twice in war, in 1945. | Just nuke the leftovers for two minutes. | I accidentally nuked all my saved files. | The Cold War was a time of fear about nukes. | In the game, he nuked the whole base.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal; in formal writing say «nuclear weapon». Past: nuked. The microwave sense is a joke: microwaves are not nuclear and do not make food radioactive.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A nutritionist is a person who knows a lot about food and how it affects health, and gives advice on healthy eating.
its sense in the lessons: Met in healthy-eating and science lessons, at hospitals and in sport; it is also a job children may hear about.
examples from the lessons: The nutritionist said we should eat more vegetables. | Our football club has a nutritionist. | A nutritionist helped plan the school menu. | She wants to become a nutritionist. | The nutritionist explained why breakfast matters. | Ask a doctor or nutritionist before changing your diet a lot.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: nutritionists. In the UK, a «dietitian» is a protected title with special training; anyone can call themselves a nutritionist in some countries, so check who gives advice.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Obscene means very rude and shocking, especially about sex or the body, and not acceptable in public. 2) Obscene also means shockingly unfair or too much, as in «an obscene amount of money».
its sense in the lessons: In school rules and online safety: obscene words and pictures are not allowed; tell an adult if you see them. In news: «obscene profits» or «obscene waste» shows strong disapproval.
examples from the lessons: Obscene language is not allowed at school. | If you see obscene pictures online, tell a trusted adult. | He made an obscene gesture and got a red card. | They spent an obscene amount on a car. | It's obscene that food is thrown away while people go hungry. | The film was cut for obscene scenes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: obscenity. Strong word; it says the speaker thinks something is very wrong. Do not confuse with «obscure» (hard to find or understand).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Observable means able to be seen or noticed. 2) (science) An observable fact is one you can check by looking, measuring or testing.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons: observable changes in an experiment (colour, bubbles, temperature). In astronomy: the observable universe.
examples from the lessons: The change in colour was easily observable. | Write down every observable change. | The observable universe is the part we can see from Earth. | There was no observable difference between the two plants. | Melting ice is an observable change of state. | Bacteria are not observable without a microscope.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «observe» + «-able»; drop the e. In science, an observation is what you notice; a conclusion is what you work out from it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An ocelot is a wild cat about twice the size of a pet cat, with spotted and striped fur, living in the forests of Central and South America.
its sense in the lessons: Met in science lessons about rainforest animals and endangered species. Ocelots hunt at night.
examples from the lessons: The ocelot has beautiful spotted fur. | Ocelots live in South American rainforests. | An ocelot hunts small animals at night. | Ocelots are good at climbing and swimming. | People once hunted ocelots for their fur. | The ocelot is about twice as big as a house cat.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say «an ocelot» (starts with a vowel). Plural: ocelots. Say «OSS-uh-lot». It is a wild animal, not a pet.

part of speech: noun (an oink, oinks); verb (oink, oinks, oinked, oinking); interjection (oink!)
meaning for a pupil: 1) An oink is the grunting sound a pig makes. 2) To oink is to make that sound.
its sense in the lessons: Used in farm stories, nursery rhymes and lessons on onomatopoeia.
examples from the lessons: The pig went «oink, oink». | «Oink!» said the piglet. | We heard the pigs oinking in the barn. | «Old MacDonald had a farm… with an oink oink here». | My little sister oinks when she laughs. | The piglets oinked for their food.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say «an oink». It is an onomatopoeia. Calling a person «oink» or «pig» is unkind.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Omega is the last letter of the Greek alphabet, written Ω or ω. 2) «The alpha and the omega» means the beginning and the end; (Bible) in the Book of Revelation, God says «I am the Alpha and the Omega». 3) Omega-3 is a kind of healthy fat found in oily fish. 4) (science) Ω is the symbol for ohms, the unit of electrical resistance.
its sense in the lessons: Met in maths, science, the Bible and healthy eating (omega-3 in salmon).
examples from the lessons: Omega is the last letter of the Greek alphabet. | Ω is the sign for ohms on a resistor. | Salmon is rich in omega-3. | In the Bible God says, «I am the Alpha and the Omega.» | The capital omega looks like a horseshoe. | Alpha comes first and omega comes last.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say «OH-meg-uh». Capital Ω, small ω. Ω stands for the unit «ohm»; the letter itself is called omega.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In football, rugby and hockey, onside means in a position where you are allowed to play the ball; it is the opposite of offside. 2) (informal, UK) To get someone onside is to get them to agree with you and support you.
its sense in the lessons: In PE and sport lessons; in everyday and news talk about winning people's support.
examples from the lessons: The striker was onside when she scored. | The referee checked and said he was onside. | Stay onside until the ball is passed. | We need to get Mum onside before we ask Dad for a puppy. | The coach got the parents onside. | The goal counted because the winger was onside.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: offside. Also written «on side» in the second meaning.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An optometrist is a person trained to test people's eyesight, check eye health and prescribe glasses or contact lenses.
its sense in the lessons: Met in everyday life and science lessons on the eye; children visit for eye tests. Phrases: go to the optometrist, eye test.
examples from the lessons: The optometrist tested my eyes. | I read letters on a chart at the optometrist's. | The optometrist said I need glasses for reading. | An optometrist looks at the back of your eye with a light. | Mum is an optometrist. | Children should see an optometrist regularly.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say «an optometrist». In the UK, people often say «optician». An ophthalmologist is a doctor who does eye surgery; an optometrist is not a surgeon.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Orbital means to do with an orbit, the path of something going round a planet, star or moon. 2) (UK) An orbital road goes round a city, like London's M25. 3) The orbital bone is the bony cup around the eye. 4) (science) An orbital is a region in an atom where electrons are found.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on space (orbital period, orbital speed) and in geography and road maps.
examples from the lessons: The Moon's orbital period is about 27 days. | The space station has an orbital speed of about 28,000 km an hour. | The M25 is an orbital motorway round London. | He hurt his orbital bone playing rugby. | Earth's orbital path is almost a circle. | Satellites are placed in orbital paths around Earth.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «orbit» + «-al». In a maths or science problem, the orbital period is the time for one full trip round; Earth's is about 365 days.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Overconfident means too sure of yourself, so you take risks or don't prepare enough.
its sense in the lessons: Used in sport, exams and stories: the hare in «The Tortoise and the Hare» was overconfident. It warns the reader that the character may fail.
examples from the lessons: The hare was overconfident and lost the race. | Don't be overconfident; check your answers. | The team was overconfident and didn't train. | He felt overconfident and skipped revision. | Being overconfident on ice can be dangerous. | She was a little overconfident about the spelling test.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word. Noun: overconfidence. «Over-» means too much. Opposite: underconfident, unsure.

part of speech: noun (an overdose, overdoses); verb (overdose, overdoses, overdosed, overdosing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) An overdose is too much of a medicine or drug taken at once, which can make someone very ill or kill them. 2) To overdose is to take such a dangerous amount. 3) (informal) An overdose of something is too much of it, like an overdose of sugar or TV.
its sense in the lessons: In health and safety lessons: only take medicine an adult gives you, as the label says; an overdose is an emergency (call 999, 911, 000 or 111, 112). In jokes: «an overdose of homework».
examples from the lessons: Taking too many tablets can cause an overdose. | If someone takes an overdose, call an ambulance at once. | Keep medicines away from small children to prevent an overdose. | The label shows the right dose so you don't overdose. | I had an overdose of chocolate at the party. | Even vitamins can be dangerous in an overdose.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: overdoses. Short form: OD (informal). Safety: never take medicine on your own; follow the dose. In maths, the dose is an amount; an overdose is more than the safe amount.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Overlordship is the power or position of an overlord, a ruler who has power over other lords or kings.
its sense in the lessons: Met in history lessons on the Middle Ages and empires: the Vikings or Normans claimed overlordship of lands; a king might accept another king's overlordship.
examples from the lessons: The Normans claimed overlordship of England. | Welsh princes had to accept the overlordship of the English king. | The emperor's overlordship covered many small kingdoms. | Overlordship meant lesser lords paid tribute. | The Mongols held overlordship over Russia for 200 years.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. From «over» + «lord» + «-ship». The person is an «overlord».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Overly means too much, more than needed.
its sense in the lessons: Used in everyday and school talk, often with «not»: «not overly keen» means not very keen (a polite, understated way of speaking).
examples from the lessons: Don't be overly worried about the test. | The film was overly long. | I'm not overly fond of broccoli. | She was overly polite to the visitors. | The rules seemed overly strict. | He was overly careful with the eggs.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Used before an adjective: overly long, overly careful. «Not overly» is a gentle way of saying «not very». More common in US English; in the UK people also say «too» or «over-».

part of speech: verb (override, overrides, overrode, overriding, overridden); noun (an override)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To override a decision or order is to cancel it using greater power. 2) To override is to be more important than something else. 3) To override a machine is to stop it working automatically and control it yourself. 4) An override is a switch or way to do this.
its sense in the lessons: In school: the head can override a teacher's decision; in technology: a manual override; in ethics: safety overrides other rules.
examples from the lessons: The head teacher overrode the decision. | Safety overrides everything else. | The pilot used the manual override. | Parents can override the tablet's settings. | His fear was overridden by his curiosity. | Press the override button to stop the alarm.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular: override, overrode, overridden. Do not confuse with «overrun» or «overrate».

meaning for a pupil: 1) To overstate something is to make it sound bigger, better or more important than it really is; to exaggerate.
its sense in the lessons: In English and news lessons: a writer who overstates loses trust. Phrases: «It's hard to overstate…» means it is extremely important.
examples from the lessons: Don't overstate how good your project is. | It is hard to overstate how important water is. | The advert overstated what the toy could do. | The danger was overstated in the news. | He overstated his score to impress us. | Writers should not overstate their evidence.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: overstated. Noun: overstatement. Opposite: understate. In maths, if you overstate a number, it is bigger than the real one.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To overstretch a muscle is to stretch it too far and hurt it. 2) To overstretch yourself, a budget or people is to make them do more than they can manage.
its sense in the lessons: In PE and health: warm up and don't overstretch. In news and adult life: overstretched hospitals, schools or budgets.
examples from the lessons: Don't overstretch when you warm up. | She overstretched her leg in gymnastics. | The nurses are overstretched this winter. | Buying a big house would overstretch their budget. | The army was overstretched. | I overstretched myself by joining five clubs.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: overstretched. Adjective: overstretched (too busy). Healthy stretching should never hurt.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To overwhelm someone is to give them so much of a feeling or so much to do that they can't cope. 2) To overwhelm an enemy or team is to beat them completely with greater force. 3) To overwhelm can mean to cover completely, like a flood.
its sense in the lessons: In feelings and well-being lessons: feeling overwhelmed is normal; break the task into small steps and talk to someone. In history and sport: an army overwhelms its enemy.
examples from the lessons: The noise of the party overwhelmed me. | I was overwhelmed by all the kind messages. | When homework overwhelms you, do one task at a time. | The bigger army overwhelmed the castle. | The wave overwhelmed the small boat. | She felt overwhelmed on her first day at school.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: overwhelmed. Adjective: overwhelming (an overwhelming win = a very large win). The h after w is silent for many speakers.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Overworking is working too hard or too long. 2) Overworking someone or something is making them work too much.
its sense in the lessons: In health and adult life: overworking can make people tired and ill; in stories: a cruel master overworking his horses.
examples from the lessons: Dad has been overworking and needs a rest. | Overworking can make you ill. | Stop overworking your brain; take a break. | The farmer was accused of overworking his horses. | Overworking the dough makes the bread tough. | Many nurses are overworking this winter.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «overwork». Past: overworked. Adjective: overworked (very tired from too much work).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Pachycephalosaurus was a plant-eating dinosaur with a very thick, dome-shaped skull, which lived in North America about 66 million years ago.
its sense in the lessons: Met in science and dinosaur books; its name means «thick-headed lizard». Scientists argue about whether it head-butted others.
examples from the lessons: Pachycephalosaurus had a skull 25 centimetres thick. | Its name means «thick-headed lizard». | Pachycephalosaurus walked on two legs. | It lived at the same time as T. rex. | Some scientists think Pachycephalosaurus butted heads like goats. | Its dome was ringed with bony knobs.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say «PAK-ee-SEF-uh-low-SAW-rus». Name of a dinosaur, often written with a capital P. Whether it head-butted is still argued; do not state it as fact.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A packer is a person or machine that packs goods into boxes or containers. 2) (informal) In the phrase «Green Bay Packers» it is the name of an American football team.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday adult life: warehouse jobs, food factories and removal companies; in maths problems about boxes and items packed.
examples from the lessons: The packer filled each box with 12 eggs. | My cousin works as a packer in a warehouse. | The machine is a fast packer. | The packers loaded our furniture into the van. | A packer can pack 60 boxes an hour; in 3 hours that is 180. | Fruit packers work hard in the summer.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: packers. From «pack» + «-er» (a person or thing that does). In maths, a packer's rate × time = how many items are packed.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A paddlefish is a large freshwater fish with a long, flat, paddle-shaped snout, found in the rivers of the USA.
its sense in the lessons: Met in science lessons about river animals and endangered species; very old fish families.
examples from the lessons: The paddlefish has a long snout like a paddle. | Paddlefish live in the Mississippi River. | Paddlefish eat tiny animals called plankton. | The paddlefish is an ancient kind of fish. | Its snout helps the paddlefish sense food. | The Chinese paddlefish is now extinct.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: paddlefish (the same) or paddlefishes. One word. The snout is called a «rostrum».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A paediatrician is a doctor who looks after babies, children and teenagers and treats their illnesses. 2) It is also a doctor who checks that a child is growing and developing well, even when the child is not ill.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life a family may take a sick or newborn child to a paediatrician, often after the family doctor (GP) sends them there. In stories and health lessons the word tells the reader the patient is a child. Phrases: see a paediatrician, a children's hospital paediatrician, referred to a paediatrician.
examples from the lessons: The paediatrician listened to the baby's chest. | My little brother sees a paediatrician every few months. | Our GP sent me to a paediatrician about my asthma. | The paediatrician measured how tall I had grown. | A paediatrician works on the children's ward. | Mum asked the paediatrician whether my rash was serious. | She trained for many years to become a paediatrician. | The paediatrician gave Ellie a sticker after her injection.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one paediatrician, two paediatricians; use «a» (a paediatrician). UK, Ireland, Australia and New Zealand spelling is «paediatrician»; the USA and often Canada write «pediatrician». The field is «paediatrics». Do not confuse with «podiatrist», a foot doctor, or with «paedophile», which is a completely different and bad word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (medicine) Palliative care is care that keeps a very ill person comfortable and free from pain when their illness cannot be cured. 2) (formal) Palliative means making a problem feel less bad for now without fixing its cause. 3) (noun, formal) A palliative is something that eases pain or a problem for a while.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life children may hear the word when a grandparent is very ill and goes into palliative care or a hospice; it tells the reader that doctors are now caring for comfort, not cure. In the formal exam voice it describes a quick fix that hides a problem. Phrases: palliative care, a palliative care nurse, only a palliative.
examples from the lessons: Grandad is now in palliative care at the hospice. | The palliative care nurses made sure Nan was not in pain. | Palliative care helps people stay comfortable and calm. | The family could visit every day during his palliative care. | (formal) Painting over the crack was only a palliative measure. | (formal) Extra homework club is a palliative, not a cure, for the reading problem. | A palliative doctor talks gently with the patient and the family.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say PAL-ee-uh-tiv. Mostly used as an adjective before a noun (palliative care, palliative treatment). Palliative care does not mean doctors have stopped caring; it means the care is about comfort, dignity and family time. A sensitive word: use it kindly.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Panamanian means coming from or belonging to Panama, a country in Central America that joins North and South America. 2) A Panamanian is a person from Panama.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons it describes things from Panama, famous for the Panama Canal, which lets ships pass between the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans. Phrases: Panamanian people, the Panamanian flag, Panamanian food, a Panamanian city.
examples from the lessons: The Panamanian flag is red, white and blue with two stars. | Many Panamanian people speak Spanish. | A Panamanian boy joined our class this term. | Panamanian workers run the locks on the canal. | We tasted a Panamanian soup called sancocho. | Panama City is the Panamanian capital. | The ship sailed past the Panamanian coast.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always written with a capital P because it comes from a country's name. Countable as a noun: a Panamanian, two Panamanians. Note the spelling with «-anian». A «Panama hat» is actually made in Ecuador, a famous trap.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Papua is the name of a large area in the western half of the island of New Guinea, now part of Indonesia. 2) It is part of the name of the country Papua New Guinea, which is on the eastern half of the same island, north of Australia.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons it appears in maps of the Pacific and in «Papua New Guinea», a country with more than 800 languages, rainforests, mountains and birds of paradise. It is a name, not an ordinary word. Phrases: Papua New Guinea, the island of New Guinea, Papua province.
examples from the lessons: Papua New Guinea is just north of Australia. | More than 800 languages are spoken in Papua New Guinea. | Birds of paradise live in the forests of Papua. | We found Papua on the map of Indonesia. | Port Moresby is the capital of Papua New Guinea. | Our class read about the mountains of Papua. | Papua New Guinea gained independence from Australia in 1975.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A place name, so always with a capital P. Say PAP-oo-uh. The people of Papua New Guinea are called Papua New Guineans. Do not mix up Papua (Indonesian part) with the separate country Papua New Guinea on the same island.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A parakeet is a small, often brightly coloured parrot with a long tail. 2) (USA) In the USA a budgerigar (budgie), kept as a pet in a cage, is often called a parakeet.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons parakeets are birds that eat seeds and fruit and live in flocks; in some cities, like London, wild green ring-necked parakeets now live in parks. In everyday life it is a common pet. Phrases: a pet parakeet, a flock of parakeets, a parakeet cage.
examples from the lessons: Our parakeet can say «hello». | A flock of green parakeets flew over the park. | The parakeet cracked a seed with its beak. | My cousin in Ohio has a blue parakeet. | Parakeets need clean water and fresh food every day. | Wild parakeets now live in some British cities. | The parakeet's long tail feathers were bright yellow.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one parakeet, two parakeets; use «a». In the UK and Australia a small pet parrot is usually called a budgie, in the USA a parakeet. All parakeets are parrots, but not all parrots are parakeets.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A paramecium is a tiny living thing made of just one cell, shaped like a slipper, that lives in ponds and fresh water. 2) It moves by beating thousands of tiny hairs called cilia and can only be seen with a microscope.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons it is a classic example of a single-celled organism (a protist) that pupils look at under a microscope; it eats bacteria and moves, so it shows that one cell can do everything needed to live. Phrases: look at a paramecium, a drop of pond water, single-celled organism.
examples from the lessons: We saw a paramecium in a drop of pond water. | A paramecium is made of just one cell. | The paramecium swam fast using its tiny hairs. | You need a microscope to see a paramecium. | The teacher drew a paramecium shaped like a slipper. | A paramecium eats bacteria. | Many paramecia were moving on the slide.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; scientific plural «paramecia», everyday plural «parameciums» is also seen. Say par-uh-MEE-see-um. It is not an animal or a plant; it is a protist. The tiny hairs are «cilia».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Your parentage is who your parents are. 2) It can also mean the family or country your parents come from, your origin.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and stories it is a slightly formal word for where someone comes from; old stories may make a mystery of a hero's parentage. In science, a plant or animal's parentage is which parents it was bred from. Phrases: of mixed parentage, of Irish parentage, unknown parentage.
examples from the lessons: The orphan in the story did not know his parentage. | She is of Irish and Jamaican parentage. | The puppy's parentage was written on its papers. | The prince's true parentage was a secret. | Scientists checked the parentage of the new apple tree. | Nobody should be judged by their parentage.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable: no «a», no plural. Formal; in everyday talk people say «who your parents are» or «family background». Do not confuse with «parenting», which means looking after and raising children.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A parr is a young salmon or trout in its first year or two of life in a river, before it swims to the sea. 2) It has dark marks on its sides called parr marks that help it hide.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on life cycles, the salmon goes from egg to alevin to fry to parr to smolt to adult; the word tells the reader which stage the fish is at. It is common in UK, Irish and Canadian river studies. Phrases: salmon parr, parr marks.
examples from the lessons: A parr is a young salmon living in the river. | The parr have dark stripes on their sides. | In the life cycle, the fry grows into a parr. | We counted twenty parr in the stream. | The parr will turn into a smolt before going to sea. | Kingfishers sometimes catch parr.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; the plural is often the same, «parr», like «fish». Say PAR. Also a surname (Parr), for example Catherine Parr, the last wife of Henry VIII — that use is a name.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Patchwork is sewing in which many small pieces of different cloth are stitched together to make a quilt, cushion or bag. 2) A patchwork of things is a mixture of many different parts, like fields of different colours seen from above. 3) As an adjective it means made of patches or of mixed parts.
its sense in the lessons: In art and craft lessons it is a sewing and design activity with shapes and patterns, linked to maths (squares, triangles, tessellation). In geography and stories it describes a landscape or a mix of ideas. Phrases: a patchwork quilt, a patchwork of fields, a patchwork of rules.
examples from the lessons: Gran made a patchwork quilt from old shirts. | From the plane, the fields looked like a patchwork. | Our class made a patchwork from felt squares. | The patchwork cushion had red and blue triangles. | The town is a patchwork of old and new houses. | We used hexagons to plan a patchwork pattern. | The rules were a patchwork that nobody understood.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly uncountable (do patchwork), but «a patchwork of» is used for a mixture. In maths, patchwork shapes that fit with no gaps are a tessellation.

part of speech: noun (the Paternoster, paternosters); noun (a paternoster lift — UK)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (church) The Paternoster is the Lord's Prayer, the prayer Jesus taught, named from its first words in Latin, «Pater noster», meaning «Our Father». 2) (church) A paternoster can also be one bead in a rosary, or a whole string of prayer beads. 3) (UK) A paternoster lift is an old kind of lift made of open cabins that keep moving slowly in a loop.
its sense in the lessons: In church life lessons it tells the reader about Catholic and old English worship; in history it appears in place names like Paternoster Square in London, where rosary makers worked. Phrases: say the Paternoster, a paternoster lift.
examples from the lessons: The monks said the Paternoster every morning. | «Paternoster» is Latin for «Our Father». | Christians believe Jesus taught this prayer to his disciples. | She moved a bead of her paternoster with each prayer. | Paternoster Square is next to St Paul's Cathedral. | The old office had a paternoster lift that never stopped. | You must step quickly into a paternoster lift.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say pat-er-NOS-ter. With a capital P when it means the prayer. In English the same prayer is usually called the Lord's Prayer. Comes from Latin, not French.

part of speech: noun (pax — uncountable); interjection (pax! — old UK school slang)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (Latin) Pax is the Latin word for peace. 2) (history) Pax followed by a name, like Pax Romana, means a long time of peace kept by one powerful country. 3) (old UK slang) In old British school stories, children shouted «Pax!» to mean «Truce! Stop fighting!» 4) (church) In some churches the pax is the sign or kiss of peace.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons it appears in «Pax Romana», the peace across the Roman Empire. In old school stories it is a call to stop a game or fight. In church life it is linked to sharing the peace. Phrases: Pax Romana, cry pax, the pax.
examples from the lessons: «Pax» means peace in Latin. | The Pax Romana lasted about two hundred years. | «Pax!» shouted Jennings, holding up his hands. | (old slang) The boys called pax and shook hands. | Some coins have the word PAX on them. | In church the people shared the pax with a handshake.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Not a common everyday English word now; mostly Latin or old-fashioned. No plural. Sounds like «packs», so do not mix them up.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Peculiar means strange or unusual, sometimes in a slightly worrying way. 2) Peculiar to someone or something means belonging only to that person, place or thing. 3) (UK, informal) Feeling peculiar means feeling a bit ill or dizzy.
its sense in the lessons: In stories it signals that something odd is happening and the reader should notice: «a peculiar smell», «a peculiar man». In science and geography «peculiar to» means found only in one place. Phrases: peculiar to, a peculiar feeling, feel a bit peculiar.
examples from the lessons: There was a peculiar smell in the kitchen. | The cat was acting in a peculiar way. | Kangaroos are peculiar to Australia. | What a peculiar hat! | I feel a bit peculiar after that ride. | The old house made peculiar noises at night. | This custom is peculiar to our village. | It's peculiar that the door was open.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: p-e-c-u-l-i-a-r, ending «-iar». «Peculiar to» means «only found in», not «strange to». Use «a» (a peculiar idea). Similar words: odd, strange, weird, unusual.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Peppermint is a mint plant with a strong, fresh, cool taste and smell. 2) Peppermint is the flavour or oil from this plant, used in sweets, toothpaste and tea. 3) A peppermint is a sweet with this flavour.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life it is a flavour in sweets, gum, toothpaste and tea; in science, its oil makes the mouth feel cold because a chemical called menthol tricks the nerves. Phrases: peppermint tea, a peppermint cream, peppermint oil, a packet of peppermints.
examples from the lessons: Gran always has peppermints in her bag. | Peppermint tea helps settle your tummy. | This toothpaste tastes of peppermint. | We grew peppermint in the school garden. | Can I have a peppermint, please? | Peppermint makes your mouth feel cool. | The candy cane was striped red and white with peppermint flavour.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable for the plant or flavour; countable for the sweets (two peppermints). Peppermint does not contain pepper. American spelling «flavor» but the word itself is the same everywhere.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Periodically means happening again and again, from time to time. 2) It can mean happening at regular times, like every week or every year.
its sense in the lessons: In science it describes things that repeat, like checking a plant or the Moon's phases; in everyday life and safety it says how often to check things, like smoke alarms. In maths it hints at a pattern that repeats. Phrases: checked periodically, update periodically.
examples from the lessons: Check the smoke alarm periodically. | We measured the plant periodically to see it grow. | The comet returns periodically. | Dad periodically clears out the garage. | The teacher periodically reminded us to save our work. | Water the seeds periodically, not every minute. | The computer updates itself periodically.
note for the reader of a maths problem: An adverb from «periodic» and «period». Note «-ically» (periodically, not «periodicly»). It does not always say exactly how often; if a problem says «every 3 days», use that number.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Perishable food goes bad or rotten quickly, like milk, meat and fruit. 2) (noun, plural) Perishables are foods or goods that go off quickly.
its sense in the lessons: In science and food safety lessons it tells pupils to keep such food in the fridge and check the use-by date. In everyday life shops and lunch boxes keep perishables cool. Phrases: perishable food, perishable goods, keep perishables chilled.
examples from the lessons: Milk is perishable, so keep it in the fridge. | Perishable food needs a cool place. | Tinned beans are not perishable. | The lorry carried perishable goods. | Put the perishables in the cool bag. | Strawberries are very perishable. | Throw away perishable food after its use-by date.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From the verb «perish» (to die or rot). Spelling ends in «-able». Opposite: non-perishable (rice, tins, dried pasta). As a noun it is nearly always plural: perishables.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A periwinkle is a small sea snail with a spiral shell, found on rocks at the seashore. 2) A periwinkle is also a low garden plant with blue or purple flowers. 3) Periwinkle is a soft blue-purple colour.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on the seashore and rock pools the periwinkle is a common small snail; in gardens it is a ground-cover flower; in art it names a colour. Phrases: rock pool periwinkles, periwinkle blue.
examples from the lessons: We found periwinkles in the rock pool. | A periwinkle clings to the rock when the tide goes out. | The periwinkle flowers were blue. | My new jumper is periwinkle blue. | Seagulls sometimes eat periwinkles. | Periwinkles eat tiny plants on the rocks. | Some people cook and eat periwinkles, called winkles.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable for the snail or plant. The snail is often shortened to «winkle». The same word names two unrelated things (snail and flower) — read the context.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (law) Perjury is the crime of telling a lie in court after promising to tell the truth. 2) It can also mean breaking a solemn promise.
its sense in the lessons: In lessons on law and honesty it shows that lying under oath is a serious crime because courts need the truth to be fair. In stories and news it tells the reader a witness lied. Phrases: commit perjury, charged with perjury, guilty of perjury.
examples from the lessons: Lying in court is called perjury. | The witness was charged with perjury. | Perjury can be punished with prison. | Before speaking, witnesses swear to tell the truth. | If you commit perjury, the trial may be unfair. | The judge warned him about perjury.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: no «a», no plural. Verb phrase: «commit perjury»; a person is «a perjurer». An ordinary lie is not perjury; it must be under oath in court or a legal statement.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Personalised means made specially for one person, often with their name or initials on it. 2) Personalised also means changed to suit one person's needs or likes. 3) (verb) To personalise something is to make it your own or suited to you.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life it appears with gifts (a personalised mug), learning (a personalised reading plan) and apps (personalised adverts). In online safety lessons, personalised adverts and feeds show that websites collect your data. Phrases: a personalised gift, personalised learning, personalised number plate.
examples from the lessons: I got a personalised pencil case with my name on it. | The teacher made a personalised plan for each reader. | You can personalise your phone's background. | The app shows personalised adverts. | Mum ordered a personalised birthday cake. | Personalised number plates cost a lot of money. | We personalised our lockers with stickers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK, Australia and NZ spelling «personalised»; USA and Canada «personalized». Do not confuse with «personal» (private, about you) or «personnel» (staff). Personalised ads use your data.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Philippine means belonging to or coming from the Philippines, a country in Southeast Asia made of more than 7,000 islands. 2) The Philippines is the name of the country itself.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons it describes the islands, seas and things of the Philippines; the people are called Filipinos. Phrases: the Philippine Islands, the Philippine Sea, the Philippine flag, Philippine eagle.
examples from the lessons: The Philippine eagle is one of the biggest eagles in the world. | Manila is the capital of the Philippines. | The Philippines has more than 7,000 islands. | Typhoons often cross the Philippine Sea. | My friend's family is from the Philippines. | The Philippine flag has a sun and three stars.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always a capital P. Spelling trap: Philippines has one l and two p's (Ph-i-l-i-pp-i-n-e-s). The people are Filipinos (with F), and «Filipino» is also an adjective. The country is «the Philippines», with «the».

meaning for a pupil: 1) The photosphere is the bright outer surface of the Sun (or another star) that we see, from which most of its light shines out. 2) It is a layer of very hot gas, about 5,500 degrees Celsius, not a solid surface.
its sense in the lessons: In science and space lessons it names the visible layer of the Sun, where sunspots appear; above it lie the chromosphere and the corona, seen during a total eclipse. Phrases: the Sun's photosphere, sunspots on the photosphere.
examples from the lessons: The photosphere is the part of the Sun we can see. | Sunspots are darker patches on the photosphere. | The photosphere is about 5,500 degrees Celsius. | Never look at the photosphere without special glasses. | Light from the photosphere takes about eight minutes to reach Earth. | Above the photosphere is the corona.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually «the photosphere», no plural in school use. «Photo» means light, «sphere» means ball. The Sun has no solid ground; the photosphere is gas. Safety: never look straight at the Sun.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A physiotherapist is a health worker who helps people move better and get stronger after an injury, illness or operation, using exercises, massage and stretches.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and sport, a physiotherapist (often «physio») helps a footballer back from injury or a grandparent walk after a hip operation. In stories it shows someone is recovering. Phrases: see a physiotherapist, the team physio.
examples from the lessons: The physiotherapist gave me exercises for my knee. | After the accident, Dad saw a physiotherapist every week. | The football team's physio ran onto the pitch. | Our physiotherapist showed Nan how to use a walking frame. | A physiotherapist helps you get stronger. | I do my stretches every night, like the physiotherapist said.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; «a physiotherapist». Often shortened to «physio» in the UK, Ireland, Australia and NZ; in the USA and Canada it is usually «physical therapist». Spelling: physio + therapist.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Physiotherapy is treatment that helps people heal and move better using exercises, stretching, massage and sometimes heat or cold, not medicine.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life people have physiotherapy after a broken bone, a sports injury or an operation; in science and health lessons it shows how muscles and joints get stronger with practice. Phrases: have physiotherapy, physiotherapy sessions, a course of physiotherapy.
examples from the lessons: After breaking her leg, Mia had physiotherapy. | Physiotherapy helped Grandad walk again. | I go to physiotherapy on Thursdays. | Physiotherapy exercises can be hard work. | The swimmer needed physiotherapy for her shoulder. | Her physiotherapy took six weeks.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: no «a», no plural («a physiotherapy session» is fine). Short form «physio». In the USA: «physical therapy».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A pickaxe is a heavy tool with a long wooden handle and a curved metal head with a point on one or both ends, used for breaking hard ground, rock or ice.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons miners, gold rush diggers and road builders use pickaxes; in stories and video games a pickaxe is a digging tool. In safety, heavy tools are for adults. Phrases: swing a pickaxe, a miner's pickaxe.
examples from the lessons: The miner swung his pickaxe at the rock. | Gold rush diggers carried pickaxes and shovels. | Workers broke up the road with a pickaxe. | In the game you need a pickaxe to dig for diamonds. | A pickaxe is too heavy for small children to use. | The climbers used an ice axe, a kind of small pickaxe.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: plural «pickaxes». US spelling is often «pickax». Often shortened to «pick». Not the same as an axe, which has a flat blade for chopping wood.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Pickled food has been kept in vinegar or salty water so it lasts a long time and tastes sour. 2) (verb) To pickle food is to keep it in vinegar or salt water. 3) (slang, old-fashioned) Pickled can mean drunk.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and food lessons it describes onions, cucumbers (gherkins), beetroot and eggs; in science and history it shows how people kept food before fridges, because vinegar and salt stop germs growing. Phrases: pickled onions, pickled herring, pickled in vinegar.
examples from the lessons: I love pickled onions with cheese. | Gran pickled the beetroot from her garden. | Pickled cucumbers are called gherkins. | Vinegar stops pickled food going bad. | The museum kept animals pickled in jars. | (slang) Uncle Pete was a bit pickled after the party. | We pickled red cabbage in class.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past form of «pickle»; one «l» before «-ed» (pickled). «In a pickle» is a different idiom meaning in trouble. «Pickled» for drunk is joking, not polite.

part of speech: noun (a pickup, pickups); verb phrase (pick up, picks up, picked up, picking up)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A pickup (pickup truck) is a vehicle with a cabin in front and an open back for carrying things. 2) A pickup is the act of collecting someone or something: «school pickup». 3) A pickup is a rise or improvement, for example in sales. 4) (music) A pickup is the part on an electric guitar that turns string sounds into electric signals. 5) (verb phrase, two words) To pick up is to lift something, to collect someone, or to learn something easily.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life «school pickup» is when parents collect children; in stories a pickup truck shows a farm or country setting, especially in the USA, Canada and Australia (where it is also a «ute»). Phrases: pickup time, pickup truck, pick up the phone, pick up a language.
examples from the lessons: Grandpa drives a red pickup truck. | Pickup time is half past three. | Can you pick me up after football? | Please pick up your coat from the floor. | The pickup on the guitar was broken. | She picked up French quickly on holiday. | We loaded the hay into the back of the pickup. | Safety: wait inside the school until pickup.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The noun is one word (a pickup) or hyphenated (pick-up); the verb is two words (pick up). Past form: picked up. In Australia and NZ a pickup truck is often called a «ute».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A pigsty is a pen or small building on a farm where pigs are kept. 2) (informal) A pigsty is a very dirty or untidy room or place.
its sense in the lessons: On the farm in stories and science it is where pigs live; in everyday life parents say «Your room is a pigsty!» to mean it is a mess. Phrases: muck out the pigsty, like a pigsty.
examples from the lessons: The pigs rolled in the mud in their pigsty. | The farmer cleaned out the pigsty. | «Your bedroom is a pigsty!» said Mum. | We visited the pigsty at the city farm. | After the party, the kitchen looked like a pigsty. | The piglets slept in a corner of the pigsty.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: pigsties (y changes to ies). Also called a «sty» or «pigpen» (USA). Saying someone's room is a pigsty is rude-ish but common family talk. Pigs actually like to keep their sleeping place clean.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A pika is a small, round furry mammal with short ears and no tail, related to rabbits, that lives among rocks on cold mountains in Asia and North America.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons pikas are an example of animals affected by climate change, because they need cool mountain air; they collect grass into «haypiles» for winter. Phrases: an American pika, a pika's haypile.
examples from the lessons: A pika looks like a tiny hamster but is related to rabbits. | The pika squeaked from the rocks. | Pikas gather grass to eat in winter. | We saw a pika on our trip to the Rocky Mountains. | Pikas cannot survive in very hot weather. | The pika hid between two big stones.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one pika, two pikas. Say PIE-kuh or PEE-kuh. Not the same as the cartoon character Pikachu, though that name may come from it. Not a rodent; it is a lagomorph, like rabbits.

part of speech: noun (a pirouette, pirouettes); verb (pirouette, pirouettes, pirouetted, pirouetting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A pirouette is a fast spin on one foot, especially in ballet, often on the toes. 2) (verb) To pirouette is to spin round on one foot.
its sense in the lessons: In dance and PE lessons it names a turn; in stories it shows someone spinning gracefully or happily. Phrases: do a pirouette, a double pirouette.
examples from the lessons: The ballerina did a perfect pirouette. | Sophie practised her pirouettes in the hall. | He pirouetted across the kitchen with joy. | A double pirouette means spinning twice. | Keep your eyes on one spot when you do a pirouette. | The ice skater pirouetted on the rink.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From French, meaning «spinning top». Say pir-oo-ET. Countable noun. Past form: pirouetted (double t).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A planetarium is a building with a round domed ceiling where pictures of the stars, planets and night sky are shown, so people can learn about space. 2) It can also be the machine that projects the sky onto the dome.
its sense in the lessons: In science and on school trips, the planetarium shows the night sky, constellations and planets; it tells the reader that the scene is about space learning. Phrases: a trip to the planetarium, the planetarium show.
examples from the lessons: Our class went on a trip to the planetarium. | At the planetarium we lay back and looked at the stars. | The planetarium show was about black holes. | The dome of the planetarium went dark. | We saw how the sky changes through the year in the planetarium. | The planetarium is next to the science museum.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; plural «planetariums» (common) or «planetaria» (formal). Say plan-uh-TAIR-ee-um. A planetarium shows a picture of the sky; an observatory has real telescopes.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A planetesimal is a small solid lump of rock, dust or ice, from a few metres to a few kilometres across, that moved around a young star; scientists think many of them crashed and stuck together to build planets.
its sense in the lessons: In space science lessons it explains how the planets of our Solar System formed about 4.6 billion years ago; asteroids and comets are thought to be leftover planetesimals. Phrases: dust grows into planetesimals.
examples from the lessons: Planets formed from millions of planetesimals. | A planetesimal is like a building block of a planet. | Some asteroids may be leftover planetesimals. | The planetesimals bumped and stuck together. | Scientists study planetesimals to learn how Earth formed. | Earth may have grown from planetesimals crashing together.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Say plan-uh-TES-im-ul. Built from «planet» and «infinitesimal» (very tiny). An advanced science word; «building blocks of planets» is a simple way to explain it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A playwright is a person who writes plays for the theatre.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons a playwright writes scripts with characters, dialogue and stage directions; famous playwrights include Shakespeare, Oscar Wilde and Arthur Miller. Phrases: a famous playwright, the playwright's notes.
examples from the lessons: Shakespeare is the most famous English playwright. | Our class became playwrights and wrote short plays. | The playwright watched the first show from the back. | A playwright writes what actors say. | The young playwright won a prize. | Oscar Wilde was an Irish playwright.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: «wright», not «write». «Wright» is an old word for a maker or builder (as in wheelwright, shipwright), so a playwright is a «play maker». Countable: playwrights.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (history) In ancient Rome, a plebeian was an ordinary citizen, not one of the rich noble families called patricians. 2) (formal, often rude) Plebeian means common, ordinary or not refined; snobs use it to look down on people or things. 3) (UK slang, rude) The short form «pleb» is an insult for someone thought to be common or low class.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons on Rome, plebeians and patricians struggled over rights; in everyday life the short insult «pleb» is used, especially in UK schools, and is unkind. Phrases: plebeians and patricians, plebeian tastes.
examples from the lessons: In Rome, most people were plebeians. | Plebeians could not at first marry patricians. | The plebeians fought for their own leaders, the tribunes. | (formal) The snobby lady called the funfair plebeian. | (rude) «Don't be a pleb,» he sneered. | Calling someone a pleb is unkind.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say pleh-BEE-un. Spelling: «-beian». The short form «pleb» is rude in the UK. Look down on nobody: in history plebeians were the ordinary working people.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Plentiful means there is a lot of something, more than enough.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography it describes food, water or animals that are easy to find; in stories it shows good times (a plentiful harvest). Phrases: plentiful supply, plentiful food.
examples from the lessons: Apples were plentiful in the autumn. | Fish are plentiful in this river. | There was a plentiful supply of water. | In a good year, food is plentiful. | Rabbits are plentiful in the fields. | Sunshine is plentiful in Australia.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: plenty → plentiful (y changes to i, and one l at the end). Opposite: scarce. «Plentiful» means «a lot» but no exact number; maths problems will give the number.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A pneumatophore is a special root of a mangrove tree that sticks up out of the mud or water like a pencil, so the tree can take in air.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography lessons on mangrove swamps and adaptation, pneumatophores show how plants survive in salty mud with little oxygen, for example in Australia and Southeast Asia. Phrases: mangrove pneumatophores, breathing roots.
examples from the lessons: Pneumatophores poke up from the mud like pencils. | Mangrove trees breathe through their pneumatophores. | At low tide we saw hundreds of pneumatophores. | Pneumatophores are an adaptation to wet, salty mud. | Crabs hid among the pneumatophores. | Without pneumatophores, mangrove roots could not get air in the mud.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say new-MAT-oh-for; the p is silent. «Pneuma» is Greek for air or breath. Often called «breathing roots» or «aerial roots». Advanced science word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Pneumonia is a serious illness in which the lungs become swollen and fill with fluid, often caused by germs, making it hard to breathe.
its sense in the lessons: In health and science lessons it shows how germs can infect the lungs; it is treated by doctors and can be dangerous for babies and old people. Vaccines help prevent some kinds. Phrases: catch pneumonia, have pneumonia, treated for pneumonia.
examples from the lessons: Grandad was in hospital with pneumonia. | Pneumonia makes it hard to breathe. | The doctor said she had pneumonia and gave her medicine. | Some vaccines help protect against pneumonia. | Pneumonia can follow a bad cold or flu. | He coughed a lot when he had pneumonia.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: no «a» (have pneumonia). Say new-MOH-nee-uh; the p is silent. Myth: you do not catch pneumonia just from being cold or having wet hair; it is caused by germs.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) Polarisation of light is when light waves are made to vibrate in only one direction, as in polarised sunglasses that cut glare. 2) Polarisation of people is when a group splits into two sides with opposite views that move further apart. 3) (science) It can also mean something gaining two opposite poles or charges, like a magnet or battery.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons it explains polarised sunglasses and how light waves travel; in news and citizenship lessons it describes politics where people stop listening to each other. Phrases: political polarisation, polarisation of light.
examples from the lessons: Polarised sunglasses use the polarisation of light to cut glare. | The class argued, and there was real polarisation. | News reports talk about polarisation in politics. | Polarisation means people end up on two opposite sides. | Fishermen wear polarised glasses to see into water. | Polarisation in the group meant nobody would agree.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK, Australia, NZ spelling: polarisation; USA and Canada: polarization. From «polar» and «pole». Usually uncountable.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A polecat is a wild animal of the weasel family, with dark brown fur and a pale face mask, that gives off a strong smell when frightened. 2) (USA) In the USA, «polecat» is an old country word for a skunk. 3) (old, insult) Calling someone a polecat once meant they were nasty.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons it is a carnivore of Europe; the pet ferret comes from it. In US stories, a «polecat» may be a skunk. Phrases: European polecat.
examples from the lessons: The polecat hunted rabbits at night. | Pet ferrets are related to polecats. | Polecats live in Britain and Europe. | The polecat has a dark mask on its face. | (USA) Grandpa called the skunk a polecat. | A frightened polecat gives off a nasty smell.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: polecats. It is not a cat and has nothing to do with poles; the name may come from old French for chicken, because it ate hens.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Polystyrene is a light plastic. The common white kind is full of air bubbles and is used for packaging, cups and food boxes. 2) Hard clear polystyrene is used for things like plastic cutlery and CD cases.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons it is an insulator that keeps heat in or out and floats; in environment lessons it is hard to recycle and pollutes seas. Phrases: polystyrene cup, polystyrene packaging, polystyrene balls.
examples from the lessons: The TV came packed in polystyrene. | A polystyrene cup keeps the tea hot. | Polystyrene is very light and floats on water. | We used polystyrene balls to make model planets. | Polystyrene is hard to recycle. | Bits of polystyrene were washed up on the beach.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. In the USA the foam is often called «Styrofoam», which is a brand name. Say pol-ee-STY-reen. A good thermal insulator but bad for the environment.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A postponement is when an event is moved to a later time instead of happening when planned.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life sports matches, trips and parties have a postponement because of rain or illness; in stories it shows waiting or disappointment. Phrases: a postponement due to rain, announce a postponement.
examples from the lessons: The match had a postponement because of snow. | We were sad about the postponement of sports day. | The postponement was only for one week. | Rain caused another postponement. | The school announced a postponement of the trip. | The postponement of the concert gave us more time to practise.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From the verb «postpone» (postpone, postpones, postponed). A postponement is not a cancellation: the event still happens, later. Countable.

part of speech: noun (a prawn, prawns); verb (prawn — rare, to fish for prawns)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A prawn is a small sea animal with a thin shell, long feelers and ten legs, which turns pink when cooked and is eaten as food. 2) (Australia, slang) «Don't come the raw prawn» means «don't try to fool me».
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons prawns are crustaceans that live in the sea; in everyday life they are food (prawn cocktail, prawn crackers, prawns on the barbie). Some people are allergic to them. Phrases: prawn sandwich, king prawns.
examples from the lessons: We had prawn sandwiches at the beach. | Prawns turn pink when you cook them. | A prawn has ten legs. | My sister is allergic to prawns. | In Australia, people throw prawns on the barbie. | (Australia, slang) «Don't come the raw prawn with me, mate!» | We saw prawns in the rock pool.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. In the USA most of these are called «shrimp»; in the UK and Australia «prawn» is usual. Allergy warning: shellfish can cause serious reactions.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Preferential means giving one person or group better treatment than others.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life it is used when someone gets special treatment, which may feel unfair; in maths and economics, preferential prices or rates are lower or better. Phrases: preferential treatment, preferential rates.
examples from the lessons: The teacher's son should not get preferential treatment. | Members got preferential prices for tickets. | It is unfair to give preferential treatment to friends. | Older people get preferential seats on the bus. | The club had preferential booking for families. | Should the captain get preferential treatment? No, everyone should be treated fairly.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «prefer» and «preference». Often with «treatment». It can be fair (for those in need) or unfair (favouritism).

part of speech: noun (a preform, preforms); verb (preform, preforms, preformed, preforming — rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (technical) A preform is an object that has been partly shaped before its final shape, such as the small plastic tube that is blown up into a drinks bottle. 2) (verb, rare) To preform is to shape something beforehand.
its sense in the lessons: In design and technology lessons, plastic bottles start as preforms that are heated and blown into moulds. In ordinary spelling it is often a mistake for «perform». Phrases: a bottle preform.
examples from the lessons: Plastic bottles start as small preforms. | The machine heats the preform and blows it into a bottle. | We looked at a preform in technology class. | The preform looks like a thick test tube. | Glass fibre is pulled from a preform. | A preform is heated until it is soft.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A trap: «preform» (shape beforehand) is NOT «perform» (act, sing, do). Most of the time you want «perform». Pre- means «before».

part of speech: noun (a premise, premises; premises — a building)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A premise is an idea or fact that an argument or plan is based on. 2) The premise of a story or film is its basic idea. 3) Premises (plural) means a building and the land around it, such as a shop or school.
