its sense in the lessons: In logic and thinking lessons, a premise leads to a conclusion; in English lessons, a story's premise is its main idea; in everyday safety signs «on the premises» means inside the building. Phrases: on the premises, the premise of the story, a false premise.
examples from the lessons: The premise of the story is a boy who can fly. | No dogs are allowed on the premises. | If the premise is wrong, the conclusion may be wrong too. | The shop moved to new premises. | «All cats have tails» is a premise in the argument. | Smoking is not allowed on school premises.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Premises» meaning a building is always plural (the premises). Also spelt «premiss» in old logic books. Do not confuse with «promise».

meaning for a pupil: 1) The presidency is the job of being president. 2) A presidency is the time during which a person is president.
its sense in the lessons: In politics and citizenship lessons, the presidency is the top job in countries like the USA, France and Ireland; it can also be the top job in a club or company. Phrases: during his presidency, run for the presidency, win the presidency.
examples from the lessons: She won the presidency of the school council. | Lincoln's presidency was during the American Civil War. | He ran for the presidency in the election. | The presidency lasts four years in the USA. | During her presidency, many laws changed. | The presidency of the club passed to Mrs Ahmed.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; plural «presidencies» (y → ies). The USA, Ireland and many others have a presidency; the UK and Australia do not have a president.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Priceless means worth so much that no price could be put on it. 2) (informal) Priceless means very funny or amusing.
its sense in the lessons: In history and museum lessons, priceless treasures are irreplaceable; in everyday talk «That's priceless!» means very funny. Phrases: a priceless painting, priceless memories.
examples from the lessons: The museum has a priceless gold crown. | Her face when she saw the cake was priceless! | Friendship is priceless. | The robbers stole a priceless painting. | That joke was priceless. | Old family photos are priceless to Nan.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A trap: priceless does NOT mean worthless or free; it means extremely valuable. Opposite: worthless. Not used with «more» or «very» normally.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) Pricey means expensive, costing a lot of money.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday talk and shopping problems it means something costs more than usual; it is a casual word. Phrases: a bit pricey, too pricey.
examples from the lessons: That toy is a bit pricey. | Cinema snacks are really pricey. | The pricier trainers are not always better. | London is a pricey place to live. | It was the priciest ice cream in the shop. | Mum said the hotel was too pricey.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal. Also spelt «pricy». Comparatives: pricier, priciest. In maths problems «pricier» means costs more.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Profound means very great or very strong, like a profound effect or profound sadness. 2) Profound means showing deep thinking and understanding. 3) (medicine) Profound deafness means being almost completely deaf.
its sense in the lessons: In English and philosophy lessons a profound idea is deep and thoughtful; in news and science a profound change is very big. Phrases: profound effect, profound silence, a profound question.
examples from the lessons: The book had a profound effect on me. | There was a profound silence in the hall. | «Why are we here?» is a profound question. | The war caused profound changes. | Grandma said something profound about kindness. | My cousin has profound hearing loss.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say pruh-FOUND. Do not confuse with «profane» (rude about holy things). Noun: profundity.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A prolongation is when something is made longer in time, such as a meeting or a stay. 2) It can also be when something is made longer in space, like a line extended.
its sense in the lessons: In formal speech and maths (extending a line) it is used; in everyday talk «extension» is more common. Phrases: prolongation of a life, prolongation of a line.
examples from the lessons: The rain led to a prolongation of the match. | Medicine can bring a prolongation of life. | The prolongation of the meeting annoyed everyone. | In maths, draw the prolongation of line AB. | The prolongation of the holiday was a surprise. | A prolongation of the dry weather harmed the crops.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal. From the verb «prolong». Countable and uncountable. In football, «extra time» is the usual phrase.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Prose is ordinary written or spoken language in sentences and paragraphs, not in the lines and rhythm of poetry. 2) A writer's prose is their writing style.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons pupils compare prose (stories, articles, letters) with poetry; novels are prose. Phrases: in prose, prose fiction, a prose passage.
examples from the lessons: Novels are written in prose. | Rewrite the poem in prose. | Her prose is clear and lively. | A newspaper article is prose. | We compared a poem with a prose passage. | Most of our reading books are prose.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: no «a prose». Sounds like «pros» (plural of pro), a homophone. Opposite: poetry, verse.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Provisional means for now, not final, and likely to change later. 2) (UK) A provisional driving licence is the first licence a learner driver gets.
its sense in the lessons: In school life, provisional dates, results or plans may change; in maths and science a provisional answer is a first estimate to check. In UK everyday life learners have a provisional licence and L plates. Phrases: provisional date, provisional results, provisional licence.
examples from the lessons: The trip is on a provisional date of 5 May. | These results are provisional and may change. | My sister got her provisional licence. | The team list is provisional until Friday. | The provisional government ran the country after the revolution. | This is a provisional plan, so check again later.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: final, definite. From «provision» (arranging for the future). A provisional number in a problem may be updated later.

part of speech: noun (a prune, prunes); verb (prune, prunes, pruned, pruning)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A prune is a dried plum, dark and wrinkly, eaten as a snack or cooked. 2) (verb) To prune a tree or bush is to cut off some branches so it grows better. 3) (verb) To prune something is to cut out parts you do not need, such as words in a story.
its sense in the lessons: In gardening and science lessons pruning helps plants grow healthy; in everyday life prunes are a food said to help digestion; in English lessons pupils prune long sentences. Phrases: prune the roses, prune juice, fingers like prunes.
examples from the lessons: Grandpa likes prunes with his breakfast. | We pruned the apple tree in winter. | Prunes are dried plums. | After the bath my fingers looked like prunes. | Prune your story so it is not too long. | Dad pruned the hedge with shears.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable for the fruit (prunes). Verb past form: pruned. In some languages «prune» means a fresh plum (French «prune»); in English it is a dried one — a false friend.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Psychology is the science that studies the mind, feelings and how people (and animals) think and behave. 2) Someone's psychology is the way they think and feel.
its sense in the lessons: In lessons on feelings and the body, psychology explains learning, memory and emotions; in everyday life a psychologist helps people. Phrases: study psychology, child psychology, the psychology of colour.
examples from the lessons: My aunt studied psychology at university. | Psychology helps us understand why people feel sad. | Child psychology is about how children think. | Shops use psychology to make you buy more. | The coach understood the team's psychology. | We learned some psychology about memory.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Say sy-KOL-uh-jee; the p is silent. A psychologist studies the mind; a psychiatrist is a medical doctor for mental illness.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A ptarmigan is a plump bird of the grouse family that lives in cold mountains and the Arctic; its feathers turn white in winter for camouflage and brown in summer.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons it is a classic example of camouflage and adaptation; it lives in Scotland, Canada, Alaska and Scandinavia. Phrases: rock ptarmigan, willow ptarmigan.
examples from the lessons: The ptarmigan turns white in winter. | We spotted a ptarmigan in the Scottish mountains. | A ptarmigan's feathery feet work like snowshoes. | Ptarmigan hide from foxes by staying very still. | In summer the ptarmigan has brown speckled feathers. | The ptarmigan nests on the ground.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say TAR-mi-gun; the p is silent (it was added by mistake long ago). Plural often the same, «ptarmigan».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A pterodactyl is a flying reptile that lived at the time of the dinosaurs, with wings made of skin stretched from a long finger. 2) In everyday talk, any flying reptile from that time (a pterosaur) is often called a pterodactyl.
its sense in the lessons: In science and history lessons it appears with dinosaurs and fossils; strictly it was not a dinosaur and not a bird. Phrases: a pterodactyl fossil, flying reptiles.
examples from the lessons: The pterodactyl soared over the sea. | A pterodactyl was not a dinosaur, but it lived with them. | We saw a pterodactyl skeleton at the museum. | Pterodactyls had wings of skin. | My little brother screeched like a pterodactyl. | Pterodactyls died out about 66 million years ago.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say ter-uh-DAK-til; the p is silent. «Ptero» means wing, «dactyl» means finger. Myth: pterodactyls were not dinosaurs and are not ancestors of birds.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (a name) Ptolemy was a Greek scientist who lived in Alexandria in Egypt about 1,900 years ago (around 100–170 AD); he wrote that the Earth was at the centre of the universe and made famous maps. 2) (a name) Ptolemy was also the name of several kings of ancient Egypt after Alexander the Great, including the family of Cleopatra.
its sense in the lessons: In science history lessons Ptolemy's Earth-centred model was later replaced by Copernicus's Sun-centred model; in history lessons the Ptolemies ruled Egypt. Phrases: Ptolemy's model, the Ptolemaic kings.
examples from the lessons: Ptolemy thought the Sun went round the Earth. | Ptolemy drew maps of the known world. | Copernicus showed Ptolemy's model was wrong. | Cleopatra came from the family of Ptolemy. | Ptolemy lived in Alexandria. | The Ptolemy kings built the great library of Alexandria.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A name: capital P. Say TOL-uh-mee; the p is silent. Adjective: Ptolemaic.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A pundit is an expert who often gives opinions on TV, radio or in newspapers, for example about football or politics. 2) (Hinduism) A pundit (pandit) is a learned teacher or priest.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, football pundits on TV explain the game; in news lessons, pundits give opinions, which pupils should check against facts. Phrases: a football pundit, political pundits.
examples from the lessons: The football pundit said the referee was wrong. | Pundits argued about who would win the election. | My uncle shouts at TV pundits. | A pundit's opinion is not always a fact. | The cricket pundit explained the rules. | The pundit predicted the wrong winner.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Comes from Hindi/Sanskrit «pandit», learned man. A pundit gives opinions; check whether they are facts.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A quadrillion is the number 1,000,000,000,000,000: a thousand trillion, a 1 followed by 15 zeros. 2) (informal) It can mean a huge number.
its sense in the lessons: In maths lessons on place value and big numbers: million (6 zeros), billion (9), trillion (12), quadrillion (15). In science it describes huge counts, like ants on Earth. Phrases: a quadrillion dollars.
examples from the lessons: A quadrillion has fifteen zeros. | There may be about twenty quadrillion ants on Earth. | A quadrillion is a thousand trillions. | I've told you a quadrillion times! | Computers can do a quadrillion sums a second. | Write one quadrillion in digits: 1,000,000,000,000,000.
note for the reader of a maths problem: In maths: 1 quadrillion = 10^15 = 1,000 trillion. In the old British system it meant 10^24, but today almost everyone uses 10^15. After a number, no -s: «two quadrillion».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A radish is a small crunchy root vegetable, often red outside and white inside, with a hot peppery taste, usually eaten raw in salads.
its sense in the lessons: In science and gardening lessons radishes are quick to grow from seed (about four weeks), so they are good for class gardens. Phrases: a bunch of radishes, radish seeds.
examples from the lessons: We grew radishes in the school garden. | The radish tasted hot and peppery. | Radishes grow quickly. | Mum sliced radishes into the salad. | A radish is a root you can eat. | Our radish seeds sprouted in three days.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: plural «radishes». «Horseradish» is a different plant used for a hot sauce.

part of speech: noun (a rasp, rasps); verb (rasp, rasps, rasped, rasping)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A rasp is a rough harsh sound, like a scraping voice. 2) A rasp is a coarse file, a tool for shaping wood or metal. 3) (verb) To rasp is to say something in a rough, harsh voice, or to scrape with a rough tool.
its sense in the lessons: In stories it describes a rough voice or sound («a rasping voice»); in design and technology lessons it is a tool. Phrases: a rasping voice, rasp the wood.
examples from the lessons: «Who's there?» rasped the old man. | We used a rasp to smooth the wooden edge. | His cough had a rasp to it. | The door rasped on the stone floor. | The cat's tongue feels rough like a rasp. | Her voice was a dry rasp after the cold.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Rhymes with «grasp». Past: rasped. Do not confuse with «raspberry».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (law, formal) To ratify a treaty, agreement or law is to make it official by voting or signing to approve it. 2) Ratified describes something that has been approved in this way.
its sense in the lessons: In history and citizenship lessons, countries ratify treaties like the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child; parliaments ratify agreements. Phrases: ratified the treaty, ratified by parliament.
examples from the lessons: The treaty was ratified by both countries. | Almost every country has ratified the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child. | The school council ratified the new rules. | The changes must be ratified before they count. | Parliament ratified the agreement. | Once ratified, the treaty became law.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal. Past form: ratified (y → ied). Signing an agreement and ratifying it can be different steps.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Readable means easy and pleasant to read. 2) Readable means clear enough to be read, for example handwriting.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons a readable story or handwriting is clear; in computing, readable code is easy for people to understand. Phrases: easy to read, readable handwriting.
examples from the lessons: Please make your handwriting readable. | The book was very readable. | The sign was faded but still readable. | Good code is readable. | Bigger letters made the poster more readable. | Large print makes books readable for Grandma.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Legible» is used for handwriting; «readable» for both clear writing and enjoyable text.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Realistically means thinking about what can really happen, not wishing. 2) Realistically means in a way that looks real or true to life.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday talk it starts a sensible thought («Realistically, we won't finish today»); in art and stories it describes true-to-life work. Phrases: realistically speaking.
examples from the lessons: Realistically, we can't visit every museum in one day. | The painting shows the dog realistically. | Realistically, how much can we save each week? | The film shows life in the war realistically. | Realistically, it will take two hours. | Realistically, we need more players to win.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: realistic + ally (realistically). In maths word problems «realistically» asks for a sensible estimate.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To reappear is to appear again or come back into view after being gone.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, a character or object reappears; in science, the Moon reappears after an eclipse. Phrases: reappear from behind, disappear and reappear.
examples from the lessons: The Sun reappeared after the clouds. | The cat disappeared and reappeared an hour later. | The magician made the coin reappear. | The rash reappeared after a week. | Old toys sometimes reappear in the attic. | The stars reappeared when the clouds moved away.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Re- means again. Past: reappeared. Opposite: disappear.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A receiver is the part of a phone you hold to your ear and speak into. 2) A receiver is a device that picks up radio or TV signals. 3) (sport) A receiver is a player who catches or receives the ball, such as in American football or tennis. 4) (law, money) A receiver is a person put in charge of a company that cannot pay its debts.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on sound and electricity, a receiver takes in signals; in everyday life it is a phone part; in sport, a receiver catches. Phrases: pick up the receiver, a radio receiver.
examples from the lessons: She picked up the receiver and said hello. | The radio receiver picked up a signal. | The receiver caught the ball. | A satellite dish is a kind of receiver. | Put the receiver back after the call. | In tennis, the receiver returns the serve.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: «ei» after «c» (receive, receiver). Opposite: sender, transmitter.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) Redshift is when light from a star or galaxy moving away from us is stretched so it looks redder, shifting towards the red end of the rainbow. 2) It is evidence that the universe is expanding.
its sense in the lessons: In space science lessons redshift shows that distant galaxies are moving away from us, supporting the Big Bang theory. Phrases: the redshift of galaxies.
examples from the lessons: Redshift tells us galaxies are moving away. | The further away a galaxy, the bigger its redshift. | Scientists measured the redshift of the light. | Redshift is like the change in a passing siren's sound, but for light. | Redshift helped scientists discover that the universe is getting bigger. | Red light has longer waves, so redshift means stretched waves.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Sometimes written «red shift». The opposite, light from something coming nearer, is «blueshift».

meaning for a pupil: 1) To refute an idea or claim is to prove that it is wrong. 2) (formal) To refute can also mean to say firmly that something is not true, even without proof.
its sense in the lessons: In science, debate and news lessons it is about proving claims wrong with evidence. Phrases: refute a claim, refute the argument.
examples from the lessons: She refuted his claim with photos. | The scientist refuted the old idea. | Can you refute this argument? | The evidence refuted the rumour. | He refuted the story, saying it was false. | Use evidence to refute a false claim.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal. «Refute» means prove wrong; «deny» just says it is not true. Past: refuted.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) Regeneration is when a living thing grows back a lost part, such as a lizard's tail or a starfish's arm. 2) Regeneration of a town or area is when it is improved and rebuilt. 3) Regeneration of a forest is when it grows back.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons it shows how some animals regrow body parts and how forests grow back; in geography it means making old areas better. Phrases: urban regeneration, regeneration of the forest.
examples from the lessons: A starfish can grow a new arm by regeneration. | Lizards use regeneration to regrow tails. | The town centre was improved by regeneration. | The forest showed regeneration after the fire. | Human skin has some regeneration. | Planting trees helps the regeneration of the land.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Verb: regenerate. Re- means again; «generate» means make.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A regulator is a device that controls something, like the pressure of gas or water or the speed of a clock. 2) A regulator is an official organisation that makes sure companies follow rules, such as for energy, water or TV.
its sense in the lessons: In science and technology it controls flow; in news and citizenship lessons, regulators watch over businesses. Phrases: pressure regulator, energy regulator.
examples from the lessons: Divers use a regulator to breathe from their tank. | The regulator keeps the gas pressure steady. | The energy regulator decides price caps. | The TV regulator checked complaints. | A clock's regulator keeps the time correct. | The heating has a regulator to keep the room warm.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Verb: regulate. In diving, the regulator is the mouthpiece.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To reintroduce an animal or plant is to bring it back to a place where it used to live. 2) To reintroduce something, like a rule, is to bring it back into use.
its sense in the lessons: In science and nature lessons, beavers and wolves are reintroduced; in school life, rules may be reintroduced. Phrases: reintroduce into the wild.
examples from the lessons: Beavers were reintroduced to Scotland. | Wolves were reintroduced to Yellowstone Park. | The school reintroduced the no phones rule. | The zoo plans to reintroduce rare frogs. | They reintroduced school milk. | Scientists want to reintroduce the lynx.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Re- = again. Past: reintroduced. Noun: reintroduction.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A reintroduction is when an animal or plant is brought back to a place it used to live. 2) It can mean bringing back a rule or product.
its sense in the lessons: In conservation lessons reintroduction projects help endangered species; in news, reintroduction of laws. Phrases: reintroduction programme, the reintroduction of wolves.
examples from the lessons: The reintroduction of beavers helped the river. | The reintroduction of wolves changed the park. | A reintroduction programme needs careful planning. | The reintroduction of school uniform was argued about. | The reintroduction of red kites was a success in England. | Reintroduction means bringing back, not bringing something new.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable and uncountable. From the verb reintroduce.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To rejoin a group, club or person is to join or meet them again. 2) (formal) To rejoin can mean to reply, often quickly or sharply.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday and school life you rejoin a team or class after illness; in stories «he rejoined» can mean he answered back. Phrases: rejoin the group, rejoin the road.
examples from the lessons: I rejoined the football team after my injury. | The path rejoins the main road. | After the trip, she rejoined her class. | «Not likely!» he rejoined. | They rejoined the club last year. | Rejoin your group after the toilet break.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Re- = again. Past: rejoined. Noun (formal reply): rejoinder.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Relinquishment is the act of giving up something, such as power, a right, a claim or control, often unwillingly. 2) (law) Relinquishment can mean a parent formally giving up their rights to a child, or someone giving up citizenship.
its sense in the lessons: In history and citizenship lessons it describes kings giving up a throne or countries giving up land; it is a stiff, formal exam word. Everyday words: giving up, handing over. Phrases: relinquishment of power, relinquishment of control.
examples from the lessons: The king's relinquishment of the throne surprised everyone. | The treaty required the relinquishment of the land. | Relinquishment of power is hard for many leaders. | (law) The form was for the relinquishment of citizenship. | The captain's relinquishment of the armband came after the match. | Her relinquishment of the prize was a kind act.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal. From the verb «relinquish» (relinquish, relinquishes, relinquished). Say ri-LING-kwish-ment. Plain English: «giving up».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A remora is a fish with a flat sucker on top of its head that it uses to stick to sharks, whales, turtles and boats and ride along with them.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons it is an example of animals living together (symbiosis, commensalism): the remora gets a free ride and scraps of food. Phrases: a remora on a shark, suckerfish.
examples from the lessons: A remora clung to the shark's belly. | Remoras eat scraps left by the shark. | The remora has a sucker on its head. | Divers saw remoras stuck to a turtle. | A remora is also called a suckerfish. | The shark does not seem to mind the remora.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: remoras. Say REM-or-uh. Myth: sailors once believed remoras could stop ships; they cannot.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A remover is a substance used to take something off, like nail varnish remover, stain remover or paint remover. 2) (UK) Removers are people or a company that move your furniture to a new house.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and safety lessons, removers are chemicals that must be kept away from small children and used with fresh air. Phrases: nail polish remover, stain remover, a removal company.
examples from the lessons: Mum used nail varnish remover on her nails. | Stain remover got the juice out of my shirt. | The removers carried our sofa to the new house. | Keep paint remover away from little children. | This remover smells very strong. | Make-up remover wipes are in the bathroom.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. From «remove». In the UK, «removal men» or «removers»; in the USA and Canada «movers».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A replica is a very exact copy of something, such as a famous ship, statue, building or shirt.
its sense in the lessons: In history and museum lessons, replicas let people see what precious or lost objects looked like; in sport, replica shirts copy the team kit. Phrases: a replica of, replica kit, a full-size replica.
examples from the lessons: We visited a replica of the Golden Hind. | The museum shows a replica of the crown. | I have a replica football shirt. | The model is a replica of the Eiffel Tower. | A replica dinosaur skeleton stood in the hall. | The real painting is safe; this is a replica.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. A replica is a copy made openly, not to cheat; a fake is meant to trick people.

part of speech: interjection/noun (requiescat; Requiescat in pace, RIP) — Latin
meaning for a pupil: 1) (Latin, church) Requiescat means «may he or she rest». It comes from the prayer «Requiescat in pace», «May he or she rest in peace», said for a person who has died. 2) The short form RIP, now read as «rest in peace», comes from it.
its sense in the lessons: In church life and on old gravestones, requiescat or RIP is written for the dead; Christians believe it is a prayer that the person be at peace with God. It is Latin, not ordinary English. Phrases: requiescat in pace, RIP.
examples from the lessons: «Requiescat in pace» was carved on the old grave. | RIP stands for «requiescat in pace». | The priest said «requiescat in pace» at the funeral. | Requiescat is Latin for «may he rest». | On the gravestone it said: RIP. | People write RIP when someone dies.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Latin, not an English word. Say rek-wee-ES-kat. Used respectfully. «RIP» is used in English today, sometimes jokingly, but on real deaths it should be respectful.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To resell something is to sell it again after buying it, often for a higher price.
its sense in the lessons: In maths money problems, buying and reselling gives profit or loss; in everyday life people resell clothes or tickets. Phrases: resell for a profit.
examples from the lessons: He bought the bike for £50 and resold it for £70. | Some people resell concert tickets. | You can resell old toys online. | The shop resells second-hand books. | Reselling tickets for too much money is sometimes illegal. | She resold the dress she never wore.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular past: resold (not «reselled»). In maths: profit = resale price minus buying price.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A reservation is an arrangement to keep a table, seat, room or ticket for you, a booking. 2) A reservation is a doubt you have about something. 3) A reservation (in the USA and Canada) is land kept for Native American peoples. 4) (UK) The central reservation is the strip in the middle of a motorway.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life you make a reservation at a restaurant or hotel; in history lessons reservations were land given to Native Americans; in opinion writing «reservations» means doubts. Phrases: make a reservation, without reservation, have reservations about.
examples from the lessons: Dad made a reservation for dinner. | We have a reservation for four at seven o'clock. | I have reservations about this plan. | Many Native Americans live on reservations. | The car hit the central reservation. | She agreed without reservation.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. From «reserve». In the USA and Canada «reservation» is also called «reserve» (Canada). «Without reservation» means completely.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A resilient person can recover quickly from hard times or disappointments and keep going. 2) A resilient material can bend or stretch and spring back into shape without breaking.
its sense in the lessons: In wellbeing and PSHE lessons resilience is bouncing back after mistakes; in science, resilient materials like rubber spring back. Phrases: resilient children, a resilient material.
examples from the lessons: She was resilient and tried again after failing. | Rubber is a resilient material. | Children can be very resilient. | Resilient people learn from mistakes. | The town was resilient after the flood. | The team showed it was resilient and won the next game.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: resilience. Being resilient does not mean you never feel sad; it means you recover and carry on.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A restorer is a person whose job is to repair old paintings, furniture, buildings or objects so they look as they used to. 2) A restorer can be a product that restores something, like hair restorer.
its sense in the lessons: In history and art lessons, restorers carefully clean and repair treasures in museums. Phrases: furniture restorer, art restorer.
examples from the lessons: The restorer cleaned the old painting. | A furniture restorer fixed Gran's chair. | The art restorer used tiny brushes. | Restorers worked on the cathedral roof. | The restorer found a hidden picture under the paint. | Hair restorer did not work for Grandad.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. From «restore». Noun for the work: restoration.

part of speech: proper noun (Reuben) — a name; noun (a Reuben — USA, a sandwich)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (a name) Reuben is a boy's name. 2) (Bible) Reuben was the eldest son of Jacob in the Bible and gave his name to one of the twelve tribes of Israel. 3) (USA) A Reuben is a hot sandwich of corned beef, Swiss cheese and sauerkraut on rye bread.
its sense in the lessons: In Bible lessons, Reuben is Joseph's eldest brother who tried to save him from the other brothers. As a name it is common in the UK and elsewhere. Phrases: the tribe of Reuben, a Reuben sandwich.
examples from the lessons: Reuben is in my class. | In the Bible, Reuben was Jacob's first son. | Reuben tried to save Joseph from his brothers. | Dad ordered a Reuben in New York. | The tribe of Reuben was one of twelve. | Reuben scored the winning goal.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A name: capital R. Say ROO-bun. In the Bible spelt Reuben. The sandwich is mainly American.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To revere someone or something is to respect and admire them very deeply. 2) (a name) Paul Revere was an American who rode at night in 1775 to warn that British soldiers were coming.
its sense in the lessons: In history and religion lessons people revere saints, leaders or holy places; Christians revere God and the saints. Phrases: deeply revered, revered as a hero.
examples from the lessons: Many people revere Nelson Mandela. | The monks revered their teacher. | She is revered as a great scientist. | Christians revere Jesus as the Son of God. | Paul Revere's ride is a famous story. | The old tree was revered by the village.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal. Past: revered. Noun: reverence. Adjective: reverent.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Rhythmic means having a regular repeated pattern of sounds or movements, like a beat.
its sense in the lessons: In music lessons rhythm is the pattern of beats; in PE, rhythmic gymnastics uses ribbons and balls; in poetry, rhythmic lines have a beat; in science, the heart beats rhythmically. Phrases: rhythmic clapping, rhythmic gymnastics.
examples from the lessons: The drum made a rhythmic sound. | We clapped in a rhythmic pattern. | The waves made a rhythmic noise on the beach. | Rhythmic gymnastics uses hoops and ribbons. | The poem has a rhythmic beat. | His breathing was slow and rhythmic.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: r-h-y-t-h-m-i-c (no vowels except y and i). Also «rhythmical». Adverb: rhythmically.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Rico is usually part of the name Puerto Rico, an island in the Caribbean that belongs to the USA. 2) (a name) Rico is a boy's name, often short for Ricardo or Enrico. 3) (Spanish) In Spanish «rico» means rich or tasty; it is not an English word.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons it appears in «Puerto Rico» (Spanish for «rich port»). Otherwise it is a name. Phrases: Puerto Rico, Puerto Rican.
examples from the lessons: Puerto Rico is an island in the Caribbean. | My friend Rico plays the guitar. | «Puerto Rico» means «rich port» in Spanish. | People from Puerto Rico are Puerto Ricans. | (Spanish) «¡Qué rico!» means «How tasty!». | Hurricanes sometimes hit Puerto Rico.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Not an ordinary English word. As a name, capital R. Say REE-koh.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Rigorous means very careful, thorough and exact. 2) Rigorous means strict or hard, like rigorous training.
its sense in the lessons: In science and maths lessons rigorous testing or proof is careful and checks everything; in sport, rigorous training is tough. Phrases: rigorous testing, a rigorous check.
examples from the lessons: Scientists do rigorous tests. | The training was rigorous. | We need a rigorous proof in maths. | The new medicine had rigorous checks. | Their rules are rigorous. | Her rigorous notes helped everyone.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: rigor + ous (rigorous), even in UK English, where the noun is «rigour». Similar: thorough, strict.

part of speech: noun (a rowan, rowans); proper noun (Rowan) — a name
meaning for a pupil: 1) A rowan is a small tree with feathery leaves and bunches of bright red-orange berries in autumn, also called a mountain ash. 2) (a name) Rowan is a first name for boys and girls.
its sense in the lessons: In science and nature lessons, birds eat rowan berries in autumn; in folklore in Scotland and Ireland, a rowan near a house was said to keep away witches. Phrases: rowan berries, rowan tree.
examples from the lessons: Birds ate the rowan berries. | A rowan tree grows by our gate. | The rowan's berries are bright red. | Rowan is in Year 5. | Old stories say rowan keeps witches away. | Rowan leaves look like feathers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say ROH-un (Scotland also ROW-un). As a name, capital R. Rowan berries are not for eating raw.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Royalty means kings, queens, princes, princesses and their families. 2) Royalty is the state of being royal. 3) (money) Royalties are payments made to writers, musicians or inventors each time their work is sold or used.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons it is about the royal family; in everyday life and money, authors get royalties from book sales. Phrases: treated like royalty, royalty payments, pay royalties.
examples from the lessons: The guests were treated like royalty. | Royalty lived in the castle. | The author gets royalties from every book sold. | Kings and queens are royalty. | The singer earns royalties when songs are played. | Many people love watching royalty at events.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable for royal people; countable for payments (royalties). In maths problems a royalty is often a percentage of the price.

meaning for a pupil: 1) .ru is the internet ending (domain) for websites from Russia. 2) RU or ru is the short code for Russia or the Russian language. 3) It is a fragment, not a word on its own.
its sense in the lessons: In computing and online safety lessons, domain endings like .ru, .uk and .com tell where a site is from; check unknown links before clicking. Phrases: a .ru website.
examples from the lessons: The website ended in .ru. | RU is the code for Russia. | «ru» is the code for the Russian language. | Check unknown websites before you open them. | .uk is for the United Kingdom and .ru for Russia. | On the language menu, RU means Russian.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Not an English word; an abbreviation. Usually read out as letters «R U» or «dot R U». «R u» in texting also means «are you» (slang).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Rubella, also called German measles, is an illness caused by a virus that gives a red spotty rash and fever; it is usually mild in children but dangerous for unborn babies.
its sense in the lessons: In health and science lessons, the MMR vaccine protects against measles, mumps and rubella. Phrases: MMR vaccine, catch rubella, German measles.
examples from the lessons: Rubella is also called German measles. | The MMR jab protects against rubella. | Rubella causes a pink spotty rash. | Rubella can harm unborn babies. | Few children catch rubella because of vaccines. | The doctor checked whether it was rubella.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Say roo-BEL-uh. Not the same illness as measles, despite the name.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The rupee is the money used in India, Pakistan, Sri Lanka, Nepal, Mauritius and other countries.
its sense in the lessons: In maths money problems and geography lessons it is a currency, like pounds or dollars; its symbol in India is ₹. Phrases: a hundred rupees, Indian rupee.
examples from the lessons: The book cost 200 rupees. | India's money is called the rupee. | We changed pounds into rupees. | A rupee is divided into 100 paise. | The note was 500 rupees. | Sri Lanka also uses the rupee.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one rupee, two rupees. Use the exchange rate in problems. Indian symbol ₹; written Rs too.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Rural means to do with the countryside, not towns or cities.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons rural areas have farms, villages and fewer people; urban areas are towns and cities. In everyday life rural schools may be small. Phrases: rural area, rural life, rural school.
examples from the lessons: We live in a rural area with lots of farms. | Rural schools are often small. | Rural buses do not come often. | Many people moved from rural areas to cities. | Rural life can be quiet. | The map shows rural and urban areas.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: urban. Say ROOR-ul. Hard to say, so speak slowly.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Salami is a kind of large sausage made of dried, spiced meat (often pork), eaten in thin slices, cold.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life it is a pizza topping or sandwich filling from Italy; in food safety, it is a cured meat. Phrases: salami slices, salami pizza.
examples from the lessons: I had salami on my pizza. | Dad cut thin slices of salami. | Salami comes from Italy. | Salami is often eaten cold. | We bought salami at the market. | Some salami is very spicy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable for the food (some salami); countable for whole sausages (two salamis). Plural in Italian is «salami»; English uses it as singular.

part of speech: noun (a sally, sallies); verb (sally, sallies, sallied, sallying); proper noun (Sally) — a name
meaning for a pupil: 1) (a name) Sally is a girl's name. 2) (old, war) A sally is a sudden attack by soldiers rushing out from a castle or town that is under siege. 3) (literary) A sally is a quick, witty remark. 4) (verb) To sally forth is to set out boldly, often jokingly.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons a sally is a castle attack; in stories, characters «sally forth» on adventures; «Aunt Sally» is an old fairground game. Phrases: sally forth, sally port.
examples from the lessons: Sally is my best friend. | The knights made a sally from the castle. | We sallied forth to the shops. | His sally made everyone laugh. | The sally port was a small castle door. | Sally walked her dog in the park.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a name, capital S. Past: sallied. «Sally forth» is old-fashioned and often jokey.

part of speech: adjective (Samoan); noun (a Samoan, Samoans; Samoan — the language)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Samoan means from or belonging to Samoa, islands in the Pacific Ocean. 2) A Samoan is a person from Samoa. 3) Samoan is the language spoken there.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons Samoa is in Polynesia; many Samoans live in New Zealand and Australia, and Samoan is widely spoken in Auckland. Phrases: Samoan language, Samoan culture.
examples from the lessons: She speaks Samoan with her grandmother. | The Samoan rugby team did a war dance. | Samoan people live on the islands of the Pacific. | My friend's family is Samoan. | Many Samoans live in New Zealand. | «Talofa» means hello in Samoan.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital S. American Samoa is a separate US territory near Samoa.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Sanskrit is an ancient language of India, used for Hindu holy texts and old poems and stories. 2) It is related to English, Latin and Greek through the Indo-European family.
its sense in the lessons: In religion and history lessons it is the language of Hindu scriptures like the Vedas; English words like «yoga», «karma» and «avatar» come from it. Phrases: Sanskrit text, in Sanskrit.
examples from the lessons: Sanskrit is an old language of India. | Hindu holy books were written in Sanskrit. | The word «yoga» comes from Sanskrit. | Sanskrit is related to English. | Some people still learn Sanskrit today. | The scroll was in Sanskrit.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital S. No plural. Not a living everyday language for most people, but still studied and used in worship.

part of speech: noun (a savannah, savannahs); also savanna; proper noun (Savannah) — a name and a city
meaning for a pupil: 1) A savannah is a large flat grassy land with few trees, in hot places like Africa, where zebras and lions live. 2) (a name) Savannah is a girl's name and a city in Georgia, USA.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and science lessons it is a biome with wet and dry seasons; food chains include grass, zebra, lion. Phrases: the African savannah.
examples from the lessons: Lions hunt on the savannah. | The savannah has dry seasons. | Zebras graze on the savannah. | Savannah is my sister's name. | We learned about the savannah biome. | Elephants walk across the savannah.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Two spellings: savannah and savanna. Countable. As a name or city, capital S.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) A sax is a saxophone, a curved metal wind instrument played with a reed, used in jazz and pop.
its sense in the lessons: In music lessons and bands, the sax is a woodwind instrument, even though made of brass. Phrases: play the sax.
examples from the lessons: He plays the sax in the school band. | The sax solo was great. | My sax is in the case. | Jazz bands often have a sax. | I want to learn the sax. | The sax player blew a long note.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Short for saxophone. Plural: saxes. Sounds like «sacks» and «Saxe», homophones.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (history) The Saxons were a Germanic people who settled in England from about AD 450, with the Angles and Jutes; together they are called the Anglo-Saxons. 2) Saxon means about these people or their times. 3) Saxony is a region of Germany; Saxon also means from there.
its sense in the lessons: In UK history lessons, the Anglo-Saxons founded England, its early kingdoms and Old English; Saxon villages and kings are common topics. Phrases: Anglo-Saxon, Saxon king, Saxon village.
examples from the lessons: The Saxons came to England by boat. | We built a Saxon village in class. | Saxon kings ruled parts of England. | Old English was spoken by the Anglo-Saxons. | Sutton Hoo is a famous Saxon burial. | Saxon houses had thatched roofs.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital S. Countable as a noun. Many English place names come from Saxon words (-ton, -ham).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Scalloped means having an edge cut into a row of curves, like the edge of a scallop shell. 2) (cooking, USA) Scalloped potatoes are sliced and baked in a creamy sauce.
its sense in the lessons: In art, sewing and design lessons, scalloped edges are a decorative pattern; in cooking, scalloped dishes. Phrases: scalloped edge.
examples from the lessons: The tablecloth had a scalloped edge. | Cut a scalloped edge on your card. | Mum made scalloped potatoes. | The skirt has a scalloped hem. | Use pinking shears or scissors for scalloped paper. | The plate had a scalloped rim.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «scallop», a shellfish with a fan-shaped shell. Spelling: «scalloped» has a double l and one p.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The scapula is the shoulder blade, a flat triangle-shaped bone at the top of your back.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about the skeleton, the scapula joins the arm bone (humerus) to the collarbone (clavicle). Phrases: shoulder blade.
examples from the lessons: The scapula is also called the shoulder blade. | Your scapula moves when you lift your arm. | We found the scapula on the skeleton model. | He broke his scapula falling off his bike. | The scapula is flat and triangle-shaped. | Muscles attach to the scapula.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: scapulae (Latin) or scapulas. Say SKAP-yoo-luh.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Scholarly describes a person who studies a lot and knows a great deal about a subject. 2) A scholarly book or article is serious, careful writing by experts, with facts checked and sources given. 3) Scholarly can describe a quiet, bookish way of looking or behaving, like someone who loves learning.
its sense in the lessons: In school it often describes serious sources for a project: a scholarly article is written by experts and is more trustworthy than a random web page. In stories a scholarly character is usually a professor, librarian or wise old person with glasses and books. Phrases: «scholarly work», «scholarly article», «scholarly journal», «a scholarly man».
examples from the lessons: My grandad is a scholarly man who reads history books every night. | The museum guide gave a scholarly talk about the Romans. | For our project, Miss Patel wants at least one scholarly source. | A scholarly journal is read mostly by experts. | The old wizard had a scholarly look, with ink on his fingers. | She wrote a scholarly book about the birds of New Zealand. | His glasses and pile of books made him look very scholarly.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It is an adjective even though it ends in -ly; it is not an adverb (you cannot say «he spoke scholarly»; say «he spoke in a scholarly way»). Comes from «scholar» (a person who studies). Do not confuse with «scholarship» (money given to help a student study, or careful learning).

part of speech: noun (a schoolboy, schoolboys); adjective use (a schoolboy joke, schoolboy error)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A schoolboy is a boy who goes to school. 2) Used before another noun, schoolboy means the kind of thing a schoolboy would do or have, often silly or simple: a schoolboy joke, a schoolboy error. 3) (UK, sport) A schoolboy player is a boy who plays a sport for his school or at under-18 level.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and old books schoolboys wear caps and blazers and have adventures. In everyday talk, especially in the UK, «a schoolboy error» means a very basic mistake that even a beginner should avoid, and «schoolboy humour» means rude or silly jokes. The girl's word is «schoolgirl»; a neutral word is «pupil» or «student».
examples from the lessons: The schoolboy ran to catch the bus with his bag flapping. | In the old photo, the schoolboys wear shorts and caps. | Forgetting to carry the one was a schoolboy error. | My uncle still laughs at schoolboy jokes about burps. | He played schoolboy rugby in Ireland. | Every schoolboy in the story wanted to find the treasure. | The schoolboys lined up in the yard.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one schoolboy, two schoolboys. One word, no space or hyphen. «Schoolboy error» is a fixed phrase meaning a basic mistake; it can be said about anyone, even adults. Plural is regular: schoolboys (not schoolboies).

part of speech: verb form (scrape, scrapes, scraped, scraping); noun (a scraping, scrapings)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Scraping means pulling something hard or sharp across a surface, often to remove something: scraping mud off your boots. 2) Scraping is also the rough, harsh sound this makes. 3) Scraping means hurting your skin by rubbing it on something rough: scraping your knee. 4) Scrapings are the small bits that come off when you scrape something. 5) Scraping (by, through) means only just managing: scraping through a test, scraping by on little money.
its sense in the lessons: Everyday life: scraping ice off a car window, scraping plates into the bin, scraping a knee in the playground. In science, scraping can collect a sample, like scraping cells from inside your cheek to look at under a microscope. In stories, the scraping of a chair or a door makes things tense. Phrases: «scraping by», «scrape through», «scraping the barrel» (using the last, worst things left), «bowing and scraping» (being too polite to someone important).
examples from the lessons: Dad is scraping the ice off the windscreen. | I heard a scraping sound under the floorboards. | She fell off her scooter, scraping both knees. | We are scraping the last bits of cake mix from the bowl. | The scientist looked at the scrapings under a microscope. | He is only just scraping through in maths this term. | Stop scraping your chair on the floor! | The family is scraping by on one small wage.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: scrape loses its e before -ing: scraping (not scrapeing). Past: scraped. Do not confuse with «scrapping» (double p, from scrap = to throw away or fight). «Scraped knee» is a minor injury: clean it and cover it.

part of speech: adjective (searing); verb form (sear, sears, seared, searing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Searing means extremely hot, hot enough to burn: searing heat. 2) Searing pain is sudden, sharp and very strong. 3) Searing words or criticism are very harsh and strong. 4) As a verb, searing means cooking the outside of meat quickly at a very high heat, or burning a surface.
its sense in the lessons: Weather and geography: «searing heat» in a desert or an Australian summer. Cooking: chefs sear meat in a very hot pan to brown it. In stories, «a searing pain» shows an injury is serious, and «a searing look» shows anger. Safety: searing heat can cause burns and heatstroke, so stay in the shade and drink water.
examples from the lessons: The desert sun was searing at midday. | She felt a searing pain when she touched the hot pan. | The chef is searing the steak on both sides. | Bushfires bring searing winds in Australia. | The coach gave a searing speech after the loss. | Searing temperatures closed the beach. | The metal was searing hot after hours in the sun.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: sear + ing, from «sear» (to burn the surface). Do not confuse with «seeing» or «sharing». Homophone trap: «sear» sounds like «seer» (a person who sees the future) and «sere» (dry). Mostly used for strong things; «searing cold» is rare.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Seasick means feeling sick, dizzy or wanting to vomit because a boat or ship is moving up and down on the water.
its sense in the lessons: Everyday life and travel: on ferries, fishing boats or cruise ships. Science: seasickness happens because your eyes and your inner ear send your brain different messages about movement. Tips: look at the horizon, get fresh air, avoid reading. In stories, a seasick pirate or explorer is often funny. Phrase: «get seasick», «feel seasick».
examples from the lessons: I always get seasick on the ferry to Ireland. | The seasick passengers stood by the rail. | Look at the horizon if you feel seasick. | Even the captain was seasick in the storm. | My sister took a tablet so she would not be seasick. | The rocking boat made Tom feel seasick. | Some people are never seasick at all.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word. Similar words: carsick, airsick, travel sick (UK), motion sickness. It is an adjective; the noun is «seasickness». You can be seasick on a big lake too, not only the sea.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Seasickness is the sick, dizzy feeling some people get when a boat moves on the water. It can make you vomit, feel tired and look pale.
its sense in the lessons: Science: a kind of motion sickness caused by your eyes and your balance organs (in the inner ear) disagreeing about how you are moving. Everyday life: people take tablets, wristbands or ginger to help. In history and stories, sailors and explorers often suffered from seasickness on long voyages.
examples from the lessons: Seasickness ruined the first day of our boat trip. | Ginger biscuits may help with seasickness. | Many sailors get over seasickness after a few days. | The doctor gave Mum a patch for seasickness. | Seasickness is a kind of motion sickness. | Fresh air on deck eased his seasickness. | Lord Nelson, a famous admiral, is said to have suffered from seasickness.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: say «seasickness», not «a seasickness» or «seasicknesses». Adjective: seasick. Spelling: sea + sick + ness, one word, no hyphen.

part of speech: verb (seel, seels, seeled, seeling) — old, rare
meaning for a pupil: 1) (old, falconry) To seel a hawk or falcon was to sew its eyelids shut for a while to tame it. This is not done today and is thought cruel. 2) (old, poetry) Seel can mean to close someone's eyes, to blind them.
its sense in the lessons: Very rare: you will only meet it in old books, poems or history of falconry. Much more often you will hear its sound-alikes: «seal» (an animal; to close tightly) and «ceiling». If you see «seel» in a modern text, check whether it is a spelling mistake for «seal».
examples from the lessons: In medieval times, falconers would seel a young hawk. | The old poem talks of night coming to seel the eyes of day. | The book explained that seeling hawks is no longer allowed. | Is «seel» a typo for «seal» in this sentence? | Hunters once seeled falcons to calm them. | «Seel» is one of the rarest words in our dictionary.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Homophones: seel, seal, ceil (rare) all sound like /seel/. In almost every modern sentence the right word is «seal». It is also a surname. Not the same as German «Seele» (soul).

part of speech: noun (a seine, seines; the Seine); verb (seine, seines, seined, seining)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A seine is a large fishing net that hangs straight down in the water, with floats on top and weights at the bottom; the ends are pulled together to trap fish. 2) To seine is to catch fish with this kind of net. 3) The Seine (with a capital S) is the river that flows through Paris in France.
its sense in the lessons: Geography: the River Seine runs through Paris to the English Channel, and famous bridges and the Eiffel Tower stand near it. Science and nature: scientists use seine nets to count fish in rivers and the sea. The French word «Seine» sounds like «sen».
examples from the lessons: The fishermen pulled the seine onto the beach. | We took a boat trip on the Seine in Paris. | Scientists used a seine to count the small fish. | They were seining for sardines at dawn. | The Seine flows past Notre-Dame. | A seine has floats on top and weights below. | Paris grew up on both banks of the Seine.
note for the reader of a maths problem: English «seine» (the net) is said like «sane» or «seen»; the river name is said the French way, «sen». The river needs a capital letter and «the». Do not confuse with «sign», «sane», «scene».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Seismic means to do with earthquakes or the shaking of the earth: seismic waves, seismic activity. 2) Seismic can also mean very big and important, like a huge change that shakes everything: a seismic shift.
its sense in the lessons: Science and geography: seismic waves travel through the Earth after an earthquake; a seismometer (seismograph) records them; New Zealand, Japan and California have a lot of seismic activity because they sit on plate edges. Everyday news: «a seismic shift in opinion» means a big change. Safety: in seismic zones buildings are made to sway without falling.
examples from the lessons: Seismic waves spread out from the centre of an earthquake. | New Zealand has a lot of seismic activity. | The seismic station recorded a small tremor last night. | Schools in Japan practise for seismic events. | Winning the cup caused a seismic change in the town's mood. | Engineers build bridges to resist seismic shaking. | We drew a seismic wave on graph paper in science.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Said «SIZE-mik». From a Greek word for shaking. Related words: seismology (study of earthquakes), seismologist, seismograph. Not the same as «cosmic» (to do with space). The «big change» sense is figurative.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Selective means choosing carefully, only taking some things and not others. 2) A selective school only takes pupils who pass a test or meet certain standards. 3) Selective can mean affecting only some things: a selective weedkiller kills weeds but not grass. 4) «Selective hearing» or «a selective memory» jokingly means only hearing or remembering what you want to.
its sense in the lessons: School: in the UK, grammar schools are selective schools that take pupils after the 11-plus test. Science: selective breeding means choosing which animals or plants have young so good features are passed on (like dog breeds or bigger crops). Everyday: being selective about what you eat or watch. Phrases: «selective breeding», «selective school», «selective hearing».
examples from the lessons: Farmers used selective breeding to make cows give more milk. | She is very selective about which books she reads. | My brother has selective hearing when it is time to tidy up. | It is a selective school, so you have to sit an exam. | The gardener used a selective weedkiller on the lawn. | Be selective with your photos and only share the best ones. | Cats can be selective eaters.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective; adverb is «selectively», noun «selection», verb «select». In science, selective breeding (done by people) is different from natural selection (done by nature, without anyone choosing).

part of speech: adjective (semantic); noun «semantics» (uncountable, takes a singular verb)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Semantic means to do with the meanings of words and sentences. 2) Semantics is the study of meaning in language. 3) (informal) «Just semantics» means an argument only about which word to use, not about the real facts.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons, a semantic field is a group of words about one topic (e.g. war: battle, soldier, attack). In computing, «semantic search» finds results by meaning rather than exact words. Everyday arguments: «That is just semantics» means «we are arguing about words, not facts».
examples from the lessons: Big, huge and giant are in the same semantic field. | The poem uses a semantic field of cold: ice, frost, shiver. | There is a semantic difference between borrow and steal. | Semantics is the study of meaning. | Whether you call it a bun or a roll is just semantics. | The computer uses semantic search to understand the question. | Our teacher showed us a semantic map of words about the sea.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Said «si-MAN-tik». «Semantics» ends in -s but is usually treated as singular: «semantics is interesting». Compare: grammar (how words are put together), semantics (what they mean), phonics (sounds).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Sensitivity is being kind and careful about other people's feelings. 2) Sensitivity is how easily something reacts or is hurt: skin sensitivity, sensitivity to light. 3) A sensitivity can be a mild allergy or bad reaction to something, like a food. 4) In science and tools, sensitivity is how well an instrument can notice very small changes. 5) The sensitivity of a topic is how likely it is to upset people.
its sense in the lessons: Everyday life and feelings: showing sensitivity when a friend is sad. Health: «gluten sensitivity», «tooth sensitivity» to cold drinks. Science: a sensitive thermometer or microphone notices tiny changes; you can change the sensitivity of a computer mouse. In stories, a character's sensitivity shows they notice how others feel.
examples from the lessons: She handled the news with great sensitivity. | My teeth have sensitivity to ice cream. | Some people have a sensitivity to milk. | Turn up the sensitivity of the microphone. | Dogs have amazing sensitivity to smells. | The teacher talked about the war with sensitivity. | Light sensitivity can come with a headache.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable in the «allergy» sense (sensitivities), otherwise mostly uncountable. Adjective: sensitive. Trap: «sensitive» (easily hurt, aware of feelings) is not the same as «sensible» (showing good sense). False friend for some learners: French «sensible» means sensitive.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A sequel is a book, film or game that continues the story of an earlier one. 2) A sequel can also be something that happens after and because of an earlier event.
its sense in the lessons: Everyday life: film and book series have sequels (the second Harry Potter book is a sequel to the first). In English lessons, pupils sometimes write a sequel to a story they have read, keeping the same characters. Opposite idea: a prequel tells what happened before. Phrases: «a sequel to», «the long-awaited sequel».
examples from the lessons: The sequel was even better than the first film. | We are writing a sequel to «The Gruffalo» in class. | Fans waited three years for the sequel. | The game's sequel has new levels and characters. | Is there a sequel to this book? | As a sequel to the storm, the river flooded. | Most sequels keep the same hero.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a sequel, two sequels. Use «a sequel to» something. Do not confuse with «sequence» (things in order) or «equal». Prequel = story set before; sequel = story set after; series = the whole set.

part of speech: noun (a setup, setups; also set-up); verb as two words «set up» (set up, sets up, set up, setting up)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A setup is the way things are arranged or organised: a gaming setup, the classroom setup. 2) Setup is the process of getting something ready to use, like a new computer or phone. 3) (informal) A setup is a trick planned to make someone look guilty or foolish: «It was a setup!» 4) In a story or joke, the setup is the first part that prepares for what comes next.
its sense in the lessons: Everyday life: «setup» on a new tablet, a camping setup, a desk setup. In stories and detective films, a character who has been framed shouts «It's a setup!». In writing lessons, the setup is the beginning that introduces characters and setting before the problem. Computers: «setup file», «setup wizard».
examples from the lessons: Dad has a cool gaming setup in the spare room. | The setup of the new laptop took ages. | We need to set up the tables before the party. | The detective realised the whole thing was a setup. | The joke's setup was long but the punchline was great. | I like the new classroom setup with groups of tables. | Follow the setup steps on the screen.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun is one word (setup) or hyphenated (set-up, common in the UK); the verb is always two words: «set up the tent», not «setup the tent». Past of the verb «set up» is also «set up».

part of speech: ordinal number / adjective (seventieth); noun (a seventieth, seventieths)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Seventieth means number 70 in order, coming after the sixty-ninth: her seventieth birthday. 2) A seventieth is one of 70 equal parts of something (1/70).
its sense in the lessons: Maths: ordinal numbers tell position (first, second ... seventieth); 70th is the short form. A seventieth as a fraction is 1/70, a very small part. Everyday life: a seventieth birthday is a big celebration for grandparents. Phrases: «seventieth birthday», «seventieth anniversary».
examples from the lessons: Grandma is having a party for her seventieth birthday. | He finished in seventieth place out of a hundred runners. | The school celebrated its seventieth anniversary. | One seventieth of 140 is 2. | This is the seventieth page of my book. | The queen's seventieth year on the throne was called the Platinum Jubilee.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Short form: 70th. Spelling: seventy changes y to ie: seventieth (not seventyth). In maths, «a seventieth» = 1/70; «seventy times» means ×70. Do not confuse with «seventeenth» (17th).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Sharpness is how sharp something is, how well its edge or point can cut or pierce. 2) Sharpness of a picture or image is how clear and detailed it is. 3) Sharpness of mind is being quick and clever. 4) Sharpness in someone's voice means it is a bit harsh or cross. 5) Sharpness can be a sour or strong taste, like lemon or strong cheese.
its sense in the lessons: Safety: knives and scissors must be handled carefully because of their sharpness. Technology: you can adjust the sharpness of a photo. In stories, «sharpness in her voice» shows a character is annoyed. Food: the sharpness of a lemon or vinegar.
examples from the lessons: Test the sharpness of a pencil before the exam. | The camera lets you change the sharpness of the photo. | There was a sharpness in Mum's voice when I was late. | Her sharpness of mind helped her solve the puzzle first. | I love the sharpness of cheddar cheese. | Be careful, the sharpness of that blade can cut you. | The sharpness of the frost made our fingers sting.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: say «the sharpness», not «a sharpness» (except «a sharpness in her voice»). From sharp + ness. Opposite: bluntness, dullness, blurriness.

part of speech: verb (shear, shears, sheared, shorn or sheared, shearing); noun (shears = big scissors; shear in science)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To shear a sheep is to cut off its wool. 2) To shear can mean to cut or break something off, often by a strong sideways force: the bolt sheared off. 3) Shears (plural) are large scissors for cutting hedges, grass or wool. 4) (science) Shear is a force that pushes parts of something sideways in opposite directions, like rubbing your hands together.
its sense in the lessons: Farming and everyday life: sheep shearing happens in spring in New Zealand, Australia, the UK and Ireland; shearers can shear hundreds of sheep a day. Gardening: hedge shears. Science and engineering: shear forces can snap bolts or make rocks slide in an earthquake; «wind shear» is dangerous for planes.
examples from the lessons: The farmer will shear the sheep in spring. | The sheep looked tiny after it was shorn. | Grandpa trims the hedge with garden shears. | The strong wind sheared a branch off the tree. | Sheep shearing is a big sport in New Zealand. | In science we learned how shear forces break things. | The shearers worked fast all day.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Homophone trap: «shear» (cut) sounds like «sheer» (very steep; complete; see-through, as in sheer curtains). Past participle: shorn (for sheep or hair) or sheared (for metal). «Shears» is plural like «scissors»: «a pair of shears».

part of speech: noun (Shia; a Shia, Shias); adjective (Shia); also spelled Shi'a, Shiite
meaning for a pupil: 1) (religion) Shia is one of the two main branches of Islam; the other, larger one is Sunni. 2) A Shia (or Shia Muslim) is a person who belongs to this branch.
its sense in the lessons: Religious education: Shia Muslims believe that, after the Prophet Muhammad, the leader of Muslims should have been his cousin and son-in-law Ali and his descendants; Sunni Muslims followed other leaders chosen by the community. Both share the Qur'an and the main practices of Islam. Most people in Iran and Iraq are Shia. In the news, Shia and Sunni groups are sometimes mentioned in conflicts; people of both branches mostly live peacefully side by side.
examples from the lessons: Shia and Sunni Muslims both pray and fast in Ramadan. | Most people in Iran are Shia. | Our RE lesson compared Shia and Sunni Islam. | Shia Muslims remember the death of Husayn, Ali's son, at Ashura. | A Shia mosque was opened in the city. | The word Shia comes from Arabic for «the party of Ali».
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always a capital S. Said «SHEE-uh». Other spellings: Shi'a, Shi'ite or Shiite (the person). Be respectful: it is a faith group, not an insult. Not to be confused with the English word «she» or «shea» (shea butter, from a tree).

part of speech: verb (shimmer, shimmers, shimmered, shimmering); noun (a shimmer)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To shimmer is to shine with a soft light that seems to move or shake a little, like light on water. 2) A shimmer is a soft, wavering shine. 3) In very hot weather, the air above a road can seem to shimmer.
its sense in the lessons: Stories and poetry: writers use «shimmer» to make a scene look magical or calm (shimmering lake, shimmering dress). Science: hot air bends light, so a road seems to shimmer or show a mirage. Phrases: «shimmer of hope» (a small bit of hope).
examples from the lessons: The lake shimmered in the moonlight. | Her dress shimmered when she danced. | The road shimmered in the summer heat. | A shimmer of gold caught my eye in the sand. | Fish scales shimmer under water. | There was a shimmer of hope in his eyes. | The fairy's wings shimmered like glass.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: double m: shimmer, shimmered, shimmering. Similar words: glimmer (faint light), glitter (sparkle in small flashes), gleam. Shimmer is softer and wavier than sparkle.

part of speech: noun (a shredder, shredders); (slang) a shredder = a very good guitar player or snowboarder
meaning for a pupil: 1) A shredder is a machine that cuts paper into thin strips so it cannot be read. 2) A shredder can be a kitchen tool or machine part that cuts food or other things into thin pieces. 3) (slang) A shredder is someone who plays very fast, skilled guitar, or who surfs or snowboards brilliantly.
its sense in the lessons: Everyday life and safety: grown-ups shred letters with names, addresses and bank details to protect against identity theft. Safety: keep fingers away from a paper shredder and never feed it when it is jammed. Recycling: shredded paper can be used as bedding for hamsters. Slang: «he's a total shredder on the guitar».
examples from the lessons: Mum put the old bank letters in the shredder. | Keep your fingers away from the shredder. | The shredder jammed because I put too much paper in. | We used shredded paper for the hamster's bed. | The office has a big shredder by the printer. | My cousin is a real shredder on the electric guitar. (slang) | The vegetable shredder made thin strips of carrot.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. From «shred» (to tear into thin strips); the verb doubles the d: shred, shredded, shredding. In the slang sense «shred» means to play or ride amazingly well.

part of speech: adjective (shrill, shriller, shrillest); verb (shrill, shrills, shrilled — rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A shrill sound is very high, loud and sharp, often unpleasant: a shrill whistle, a shrill scream. 2) Shrill can describe someone who complains or argues in a loud, annoying way. 3) (rare, verb) To shrill is to make a shrill sound.
its sense in the lessons: Science (sound): shrill sounds have a high pitch because the vibrations are very fast. Everyday life: a referee's shrill whistle, a smoke alarm's shrill beeping (which tells you to get out). Stories: «a shrill voice» often shows fear, panic or a bossy character.
examples from the lessons: The referee blew a shrill whistle. | A shrill scream came from the playground. | The smoke alarm gave a shrill beep. | The bird's shrill call woke me up. | Her voice became shrill when she was scared. | The kettle let out a shrill whistle. | The shrill cries of seagulls filled the harbour.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective; adverb «shrilly», noun «shrillness». Opposite: deep, low, soft. In science, «high-pitched» is the neutral word; «shrill» adds that it hurts the ears.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A signer is a person who signs their name on something, like a letter, card or important document. 2) A signer is also a person who uses sign language, especially one who interprets speech into sign language for deaf people.
its sense in the lessons: History: the signers of the Declaration of Independence (USA, 1776) put their names on it. Everyday life: a signer stands next to a speaker on TV or at an event, translating into British Sign Language (BSL), American Sign Language (ASL) or Auslan. Law: the signer of a form agrees to what it says.
examples from the lessons: A signer stood beside the Prime Minister on TV. | The card had twenty signers from our class. | John Hancock was a famous signer of the Declaration of Independence. | Every signer must print their name too. | Our school play had a signer for deaf families. | She is learning to be a BSL signer. | The petition needs one hundred signers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. The g is silent: said «SINE-er». Do not confuse with «singer» (sing-er), which has the letters swapped. A signatory is the formal word for a person or country that signs an agreement.

part of speech: noun (a siphon, siphons; also syphon); verb (siphon, siphons, siphoned, siphoning)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A siphon is a bent tube that moves liquid from a higher container to a lower one, over an edge, without a pump, once the tube is full. 2) To siphon is to move liquid this way. 3) To siphon off money or resources is to take them away bit by bit, often secretly or wrongly. 4) In animals like squids and clams, a siphon is a tube used to suck in or squirt out water.
its sense in the lessons: Science: a siphon works because the liquid flowing down the longer side pulls the rest along; air pressure helps push the liquid up the short side. Everyday life: emptying a fish tank or a paddling pool with a hose. Safety: never siphon petrol by mouth, it is poisonous. News: «siphoning off money» is a kind of stealing.
examples from the lessons: We used a siphon to empty the fish tank. | Dad siphoned the water out of the paddling pool. | The squid shoots water out of its siphon. | In science we made a siphon with a tube and two jugs. | The thief siphoned off money from the club. | The siphon only works if the end is lower than the water. | Never siphon petrol with your mouth.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Said «SY-fun». Spelling: siphon (more common) or syphon (also used in the UK). The ph sounds like f. A siphon needs the outlet to be lower than the surface of the liquid; it cannot lift water higher than it started.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Skeletal means to do with the skeleton, the frame of bones inside a body: the skeletal system. 2) Skeletal can describe a person or animal that is very, very thin, so their bones show. 3) Skeletal can mean only the most basic parts, with little else: a skeletal plan, a skeletal staff.
its sense in the lessons: Science: the skeletal system (206 bones in an adult human) supports the body, protects organs like the brain and heart, and works with muscles to move. Skeletal muscles are the ones we control, like arm and leg muscles. In stories and Halloween, skeletal hands and figures are spooky. Health: a skeletal look can be a sign of illness or hunger. Phrases: «skeletal system», «skeletal remains», «a skeletal crew».
examples from the lessons: The skeletal system protects our heart and lungs. | Skeletal muscles help us run and jump. | Scientists found the skeletal remains of a dinosaur. | A skeletal hand reached out of the grave in the spooky story. | The rescued dog was skeletal and needed food. | Over the holidays the school had only a skeletal staff. | Our first plan was just a skeletal outline.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Said «SKEL-uh-tul». Adjective from «skeleton». The «very thin» sense describes illness or hunger; it is unkind to use it about someone's body as an insult.

part of speech: verb form (skim, skims, skimmed, skimming); noun (skimming)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Skimming means reading something quickly to get the main idea, without reading every word. 2) Skimming means removing something from the top of a liquid, like cream from milk or leaves from a pond. 3) Skimming means moving quickly just above or across a surface: a bird skimming the water. 4) Skimming stones is throwing flat stones so they bounce across water. 5) (crime) Skimming is secretly copying bank card details with a hidden device, or secretly taking small amounts of money.
its sense in the lessons: Reading lessons: skimming (for the main idea) and scanning (for one fact) are two quick-reading skills. Cooking: skimming fat off soup.
