Outdoors: skimming stones on a lake (in the USA often called «skipping stones»). Safety: card skimming devices can be hidden on cash machines, so grown-ups cover the keypad and check the slot.
examples from the lessons: I am skimming the article to see what it is about. | Skimming is useful before you answer questions on a text. | Grandma was skimming the cream off the milk. | Swallows were skimming low over the river. | We spent the afternoon skimming stones at the beach. | My stone skimmed five times! | Police warned shoppers about card skimming at cash machines.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: skim doubles the m: skimmed, skimming. «Skimmed milk» (UK) = «skim milk» (US), milk with most fat removed. Skimming is not the same as scanning: skim = main idea, scan = find one detail.

part of speech: verb form (skin, skins, skinned, skinning); adjective (-skinned in compounds)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Skinned is the past of «to skin»: to take the skin off an animal or fruit. 2) If you have skinned your knee, you have scraped some skin off it. 3) As part of a word, -skinned describes the kind of skin something has: thick-skinned, dark-skinned, smooth-skinned. 4) Thick-skinned means not easily upset by criticism; thin-skinned means easily upset.
its sense in the lessons: Everyday life and safety: a skinned knee from falling off a bike needs washing and a plaster. Cooking: skinned chicken or skinned tomatoes. Feelings: «You need to be thick-skinned to be a referee». Phrases: «keep your eyes skinned» (watch very carefully), «more than one way to skin a cat» (more than one way to do something).
examples from the lessons: I skinned my knee on the gravel. | The cook skinned the potatoes. | Keep your eyes skinned for the bus. | She is thick-skinned and laughs off teasing. | He is thin-skinned and gets upset easily. | The recipe uses skinned tomatoes. | The hunter skinned the rabbit for its fur.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: skin doubles the n: skinned, skinning. Be careful with words for people's skin colour: describe kindly and only when it matters. «There's more than one way to skin a cat» is an old saying and does not mean hurting cats.

part of speech: noun (a slob, slobs); verb phrase (slob out / slob about — UK informal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal, rude) A slob is a person who is lazy, messy and does not care about being tidy or clean. 2) (UK informal) To slob out or slob about means to relax lazily, doing nothing much.
its sense in the lessons: Everyday talk at home: «Don't be such a slob — pick up your socks!» It is an insult, though often said jokingly in families. «Slobbing out on the sofa» means lazing around. In stories, a slob character leaves pizza boxes and dirty clothes everywhere.
examples from the lessons: My brother is a slob; his room is full of crisp packets. | Stop being a slob and make your bed. | On Sunday we just slobbed out in front of the telly. (UK) | The cartoon slob never washed his dishes. | I felt like a slob after lying in bed all morning. | Don't call people slobs, it is unkind. | Dad slobbed about in his pyjamas all day.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal and a bit rude; do not use it in formal writing or to hurt someone. Verb: slob, slobbed, slobbing. Adjective: slobby. Do not confuse with «slobber» (to let spit dribble from the mouth).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A snapshot is a photo taken quickly and casually, not posed carefully. 2) A snapshot is a quick look or short piece of information that shows what something is like at one moment: a snapshot of life in Victorian times. 3) In computing, a snapshot is a saved copy of how a system or files looked at one moment.
its sense in the lessons: History and geography lessons: a diary or photo gives «a snapshot» of the past. Maths and science: a survey on one day is a snapshot, not the full picture, so results can change on other days. Everyday life: holiday snapshots. Computers: snapshots let you go back if something goes wrong.
examples from the lessons: Mum took a snapshot of us at the beach. | The old diary gives a snapshot of life in the war. | This survey is just a snapshot of what pupils think today. | The album is full of family snapshots. | The computer saved a snapshot before the update. | The report is a snapshot of the town in 1900. | He keeps a snapshot of his dog in his wallet.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a snapshot, snapshots. One word. Informal short form: «a snap» (UK: «holiday snaps»). A snapshot shows one moment only, so it can be misleading if things change.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A snowdrop is a small plant with a white flower that hangs down like a drop; it is one of the first flowers to bloom at the end of winter, sometimes while snow is still on the ground.
its sense in the lessons: Nature and science: snowdrops grow from bulbs and flower in January to March in the UK and Ireland, a sign that spring is coming. Each flower has three outer white petals and a small inner cup with green marks. In stories and poems, snowdrops stand for hope and new beginnings. Safety: snowdrop bulbs are poisonous if eaten.
examples from the lessons: The first snowdrops appeared under the hedge in February. | Snowdrops hang their white heads like little lamps. | We counted snowdrops on our nature walk. | Don't eat snowdrop bulbs; they are poisonous. | Grandma planted snowdrops under the old apple tree. | The snowdrops pushed up through the frost. | In the poem, the snowdrop is a sign of hope.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable, one word. Name comes from the flower looking like a drop (an earring) in the snow. Not the same as a snowflake. Its scientific name is Galanthus.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To soar is to fly high in the air, often gliding without flapping much: eagles soar. 2) To soar is to rise very quickly to a high level: prices soared. 3) To soar can mean to rise up tall: mountains soaring above the valley. 4) If your spirits or hopes soar, you suddenly feel very happy and hopeful.
its sense in the lessons: Nature: eagles, hawks and gliders soar on rising warm air. Maths and the news: «temperatures soared to 40°C», «sales soared» means numbers went up a lot and fast. Stories: «her heart soared» shows great joy. Phrases: «soar to», «soaring prices».
examples from the lessons: The eagle soared above the hills. | Temperatures soared during the heatwave. | The kite soared into the sky. | Food prices have soared this year. | My heart soared when I saw my name on the team list. | The cliffs soared above the beach. | The ball soared over the goalkeeper's head.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Homophone trap: «soar» (fly high) sounds like «sore» (painful) and, for many people, «saw». In maths problems, «soared» means increased by a large amount, but it does not tell you the exact number.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Sober means not drunk, not affected by alcohol. 2) Sober means serious, calm and sensible: a sober mood. 3) Sober colours or clothes are plain and dull, not bright. 4) To sober up is to stop being drunk; to sober (someone) is to make them serious. 5) Sober also describes someone who has stopped drinking alcohol for good.
its sense in the lessons: Safety and health: drivers must be sober; drinking alcohol and driving is dangerous and against the law. Everyday life: «stone-cold sober». In stories and news, «a sober reminder» is something that makes people think seriously. Phrases: «sober up», «sobering thought».
examples from the lessons: The bus driver must be sober. | After the accident, the town was in a sober mood. | He wore a sober grey suit to the funeral. | Uncle Pete has been sober for five years. | That was a sobering thought. | The news sobered everyone up quickly. | She gave a sober account of what happened.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite of «drunk». Noun: sobriety. «Sobering» means making you feel serious. Do not confuse with «sombre» (sad and dark).

part of speech: noun (a softie, softies; also softy) — informal
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) A softie is a kind, gentle person who is easily moved, often showing feelings openly. 2) (informal, teasing) A softie can be someone who is not tough or brave, or who gives in easily.
its sense in the lessons: Everyday family talk: «Dad's a big softie — he cried at the film.» It is usually friendly and loving, but can tease someone for being weak. In stories, a tough-looking character who turns out to be a softie is a common surprise.
examples from the lessons: My grandad looks grumpy but he is a big softie. | Don't be such a softie; it is only a little rain! | Our teacher is a softie when it comes to animals. | The giant was a softie who loved flowers. | Mum is a softie and always lets us stay up late. | He cries at every film; he is a real softie.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal. Two spellings: softie or softy; plural softies. Usually affectionate. Opposite: tough nut, hard case.

part of speech: verb form (solidify, solidifies, solidified, solidifying); adjective (solidified)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Solidified means turned from a liquid or gas into a solid, often by cooling: solidified lava. 2) Solidified means made stronger, firmer or more certain: their friendship solidified.
its sense in the lessons: Science: a liquid solidifies when it cools to its freezing point; water solidifies into ice at 0°C, melted chocolate solidifies in the fridge, lava solidifies into rock (igneous rock). This is the opposite of melting. Everyday: wax solidified on the table. In stories and news, a plan or a team's lead «solidified».
examples from the lessons: The lava cooled and solidified into black rock. | The melted chocolate solidified in the fridge. | Candle wax solidified on the tablecloth. | Water solidified into ice overnight. | Their friendship solidified during the camping trip. | The win solidified our place at the top of the league. | The jelly had solidified by teatime.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: solidify changes y to ie: solidifies, solidified; but solidifying keeps the y. Noun: solidification. In science, «freezing» and «solidifying» mean the same change (liquid to solid).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A solstice is one of the two days each year when the Sun is at its highest or lowest point in the sky at noon. The summer solstice has the longest daylight; the winter solstice has the shortest.
its sense in the lessons: Science and geography: solstices happen because the Earth's axis is tilted. In the Northern Hemisphere (UK, Ireland, USA, Canada) the summer solstice is around 21 June and the winter solstice around 21 December; in Australia and New Zealand it is the other way round. History: Stonehenge and Newgrange in Ireland line up with the solstice sun. Compare «equinox» (day and night about equal).
examples from the lessons: The summer solstice is the longest day of the year. | People gather at Stonehenge for the solstice sunrise. | In Australia, the winter solstice is in June. | At Newgrange, sunlight fills the passage at the winter solstice. | After the winter solstice, days slowly get longer. | We measured our shadow on the solstice. | There are two solstices and two equinoxes each year.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Said «SOL-stiss». Countable. Comes from Latin for «sun stands still». Trap: the solstice is not always on the 21st; it can be the 20th to 22nd. Solstice (longest/shortest day) is not the same as equinox (equal day and night).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) A solvent is a liquid that dissolves another substance; water is the most common solvent. 2) Solvent can mean a strong chemical liquid that dissolves paint, glue or grease, like white spirit or nail-varnish remover. 3) (money) A person or company that is solvent has enough money to pay all its debts.
its sense in the lessons: Science: in a solution, the solvent does the dissolving and the solute is dissolved (salt is the solute, water is the solvent). Safety: many chemical solvents have strong fumes that are harmful to breathe; use them in fresh air, keep them away from flames, and never sniff them. Money and news: a business that is no longer solvent may go bust.
examples from the lessons: Water is a solvent for sugar and salt. | In a solution, the solvent dissolves the solute. | Dad cleaned the brushes with a solvent. | Solvent fumes can make you dizzy, so open a window. | Nail-varnish remover is a solvent. | The shop is still solvent, though times are hard. | Sugar dissolves faster in a warm solvent.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun. Opposite of solvent (money) is «insolvent». Do not confuse «solvent» with «solution» (the mixture) or «soluble» (able to dissolve). Water is sometimes called the «universal solvent» because it dissolves so many things, though not everything (not oil).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A solver is a person who solves something, like a problem, puzzle or crime: a problem solver. 2) In computing and maths, a solver is a program that finds answers to equations or puzzles.
its sense in the lessons: School: «a good problem solver» tries different ways, checks answers and does not give up; teachers praise this in maths. Puzzles: crossword and Sudoku solvers. Computing: an online solver can work out an equation, but you still need to understand the steps.
examples from the lessons: She is a brilliant problem solver. | Crossword solvers enjoy tricky clues. | The fastest solver of the Rubik's cube won a prize. | Our class practised being good maths solvers. | The computer solver found the answer in one second. | A good solver checks their answer at the end. | The detective was a famous solver of mysteries.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. From «solve» + r (solve drops nothing, just adds -r). Common phrase: «problem solver», «problem-solving» (with hyphen when used before a noun: problem-solving skills).

part of speech: noun (a sop, sops); verb (sop, sops, sopped, sopping — rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A sop is something small given to someone to calm them down or keep them quiet, without really fixing the problem: a sop to the angry fans. 2) (old) A sop is a piece of bread soaked in milk, soup or gravy. 3) (rare verb) To sop up is to soak up liquid with bread or a cloth.
its sense in the lessons: Mostly used in news and adult talk: «a sop to voters» means a small gift meant to please them. The related word «sopping wet» means soaking wet (very common in the UK and Ireland). Phrases: «a sop to», «sop up the gravy», «sopping wet».
examples from the lessons: The free badge was just a sop to the angry customers. | He sopped up the gravy with his bread. | I came home from the rain sopping wet. | The small pay rise was a sop to the workers. | In the old story, the boy fed sops of bread to the dog. | The extra playtime was a sop to stop us complaining.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: sop, sopped, sopping (double p). Do not confuse with «soap», «sob» or «stop». Also an abbreviation SOP (standard operating procedure, the usual set of steps at work).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Southward means towards the south: a southward journey, birds flying southward.
its sense in the lessons: Geography: on a map, south is usually at the bottom; southward means moving down the map. Science and nature: many birds migrate southward in autumn in the Northern Hemisphere to find warmer weather and food. Stories and history: explorers sailing southward towards Antarctica.
examples from the lessons: The geese flew southward for the winter. | The ship turned southward towards Africa. | We walked southwards along the coast. | The river flows southward to the sea. | The storm is moving southward. | Scott led his team southward to the South Pole. | Head southward until you reach the bridge.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Southward» and «southwards» are both fine as adverbs; «southwards» is more common in the UK, «southward» in the USA. As an adjective, use «southward» (a southward wind). Compare: northward, eastward, westward. Do not confuse «southward» (towards the south) with «southern» (in the south).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Sovereignty is the full right and power of a country to govern itself without being controlled by another country. 2) Sovereignty is the supreme power of a king, queen or government over a land.
its sense in the lessons: History and citizenship: countries fight to keep their sovereignty; for example, Ukraine defends its sovereignty against Russia's invasion. The UN Charter says countries should respect each other's sovereignty and borders. In the UK, «parliamentary sovereignty» means Parliament makes the final laws. Phrases: «national sovereignty», «respect sovereignty».
examples from the lessons: Ukraine is fighting to protect its sovereignty. | Ireland won its sovereignty after a long struggle. | The UN says every country's sovereignty should be respected. | The treaty recognised the island's sovereignty. | In old times, sovereignty belonged to the king. | People argued about sovereignty in the news.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Said «SOV-rin-tee». Uncountable. Spelling trap: there is a «g» you do not hear: sovereign-ty. Related: sovereign (a king or queen; also an old gold coin worth one pound).

part of speech: verb (specialise, specialises, specialised, specialising; US: specialize)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To specialise is to study or work mainly on one subject or skill and become an expert in it: she specialises in heart surgery. 2) A shop or business that specialises in something mainly sells or does that one thing.
its sense in the lessons: Everyday life and jobs: doctors specialise (a vet might specialise in horses); shops specialise in shoes or comics. Science: cells specialise, which means they become a special type (nerve cells, muscle cells) to do one job. Phrase: «specialise in».
examples from the lessons: My aunt is a doctor who specialises in children's illnesses. | This shop specialises in Lego. | Later at university you can specialise in maths. | Some cells specialise to carry oxygen. | The team specialises in rescues on mountains. | He wants to specialise in dinosaur bones.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK, Australia, NZ, Ireland: specialise; USA and often Canada: specialize. Always «specialise in», not «specialise on». Noun: specialist, specialism; specialisation.

part of speech: adjective (specialised; US: specialized); verb form (past of specialise)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Specialised means made or trained for one particular job or purpose: specialised equipment, a specialised doctor. 2) Past of «specialise»: she specialised in history.
its sense in the lessons: Science: specialised cells have a special shape for their job, like red blood cells (carry oxygen), nerve cells (carry messages) and root hair cells (take in water). This is a key idea in primary and secondary science. Everyday life: specialised tools, specialised schools, specialised knowledge.
examples from the lessons: Red blood cells are specialised to carry oxygen. | Firefighters wear specialised clothing. | The hospital has a specialised unit for burns. | Divers need specialised equipment. | Nerve cells are long and specialised to send messages. | Grandpa specialised in fixing old clocks. | This job needs specialised training.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK spelling specialised; US specialized. Do not confuse with «special» (unusual, important). «Specialised» means designed for one job.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A spiracle is a tiny breathing hole in the side of an insect's or spider's body. 2) In some fish, like sharks and rays, and in whales, a spiracle is a breathing opening on the head (a whale's blowhole is sometimes called this).
its sense in the lessons: Science: insects do not have lungs; air goes in through spiracles along their body into tiny tubes called tracheae, which carry oxygen to the cells. Caterpillars have a row of spiracles you can see on their sides. Rays use spiracles behind their eyes to take in water while lying on the sea floor.
examples from the lessons: Insects breathe through spiracles. | We saw the spiracles on the caterpillar's side with a magnifying glass. | Air enters through the spiracles and travels down tubes. | A stingray has spiracles behind its eyes. | Spiracles can close to keep water out. | Insects have no lungs, only spiracles and air tubes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Said «SPY-ruh-kul» or «SPEER-uh-kul». Countable, usually plural. From Latin for «breath». Trap: insects do not breathe through their mouths.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A spire is a tall, pointed, cone-shaped structure on top of a building, usually on a church tower. 2) A spire can be anything tall, thin and pointed, like a rock spire or the tip of a tree.
its sense in the lessons: Church life and buildings: many towns in the UK and Ireland have a church spire you can see from far away; it points upward to heaven. Maths: a spire is often shaped like a cone or a pyramid. Geography: Oxford is called «the city of dreaming spires». Salisbury Cathedral has the tallest church spire in the UK.
examples from the lessons: The church spire rose above the village. | Salisbury Cathedral has a very tall spire. | We could see the spire from the motorway. | Oxford is famous for its spires. | Lightning struck the spire during the storm. | Rocky spires stood up from the sea. | A spire is shaped like a tall cone.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Do not confuse with «spiral», «steeple» (the tower and spire together) or «inspire». A spire sits on top of a tower; a steeple usually means the whole tower plus spire.

part of speech: noun (spite; uncountable); verb (spite, spites, spited, spiting); preposition phrase (in spite of)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Spite is a wish to hurt, annoy or upset someone on purpose: he broke it out of spite. 2) To spite someone is to do something just to annoy or upset them. 3) In spite of means «even though» or «without being stopped by»: we played in spite of the rain.
its sense in the lessons: Stories and feelings: a character who acts «out of spite» is being mean on purpose; it shows a nasty side. Everyday life: «cut off your nose to spite your face» means hurting yourself while trying to hurt someone else. Grammar: «in spite of» and «despite» join two ideas that seem opposite.
examples from the lessons: She hid my pencil case out of spite. | In spite of the rain, we went to the beach. | He refused to help just to spite his brother. | Don't let spite ruin your friendship. | We won in spite of having only ten players. | Don't cut off your nose to spite your face. | The witch laughed with spite.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable noun. «In spite of» is three words; «despite» is one word and has no «of» (despite the rain, not despite of). Adjective: spiteful (mean on purpose).

part of speech: noun (a splat, splats); verb (splat, splats, splatted, splatting); interjection (splat!)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Splat is the wet slapping sound something soft makes when it hits a surface hard: splat! 2) A splat is a messy mark made this way. 3) To splat is to hit something with this sound, or to squash flat.
its sense in the lessons: Stories and comics: splat is an onomatopoeia (a word that sounds like what it means), like bang, pop and splash, used in poetry and English lessons. Everyday life: an egg or tomato going splat on the floor.
examples from the lessons: The egg fell on the floor — splat! | The tomato hit the wall with a splat. | Splat! The snowball hit his back. | There was a big paint splat on the carpet. | The mud pie went splat on the ground. | The cartoon cat went splat against the window. | Onomatopoeia words include splat, crash and buzz.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal. Verb doubles the t: splatted, splatting. Similar words: splash (water), splodge (UK, a messy mark), splatter (spray of drops).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A spokesperson is someone whose job is to speak for a group, company, government or organisation, giving its news and answering questions.
its sense in the lessons: News and citizenship: «a police spokesperson said ...», «a government spokesperson» — what they say is the official view of the group, not just their own opinion. Reading the news: knowing who the spokesperson works for helps you think about whose side they are giving. Older words: spokesman, spokeswoman.
examples from the lessons: A police spokesperson said nobody was hurt. | The school's spokesperson answered questions from parents. | The team picked her as their spokesperson. | A spokesperson for the zoo said the panda was healthy. | The company's spokesperson would not comment. | Our class spokesperson read our ideas to the head teacher.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: spokespeople (more common) or spokespersons. Gender-neutral form of spokesman/spokeswoman. A spokesperson tells the group's official view, which may favour that group.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (old-fashioned) Sportive means playful and full of fun: a sportive puppy. 2) Sportive can mean to do with sport, or sporty in look (a sportive car — more common in other languages). 3) (cycling) A «sportive» (noun) is a long organised bike ride that is not a race.
its sense in the lessons: Rare in everyday English: you meet it in old books and poems for playful animals or children. In cycling (UK, Ireland), a sportive is a popular long ride with timing, open to amateurs. Learners from other languages may say «sportive» when English speakers would say «sporty».
examples from the lessons: The sportive lambs jumped about the field. | The poem describes sportive dolphins in the waves. | Dad entered a 100-kilometre cycling sportive. | She was in a sportive mood and played tricks all day. | In English we usually say «sporty», not «sportive», for someone who likes sport. | The kittens were sportive and chased the string.
note for the reader of a maths problem: False friend: French «sportif» and some other languages' words mean «sporty» or «athletic»; in English, «sporty» is the normal word. «Sportive» is old-fashioned, except as the cycling noun.

part of speech: verb (sprawl, sprawls, sprawled, sprawling); noun (sprawl; urban sprawl)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To sprawl is to sit or lie with your arms and legs spread out in a relaxed or careless way. 2) To sprawl can mean to fall so that you land spread out. 3) A town or city that sprawls spreads out over a large area in an untidy way. 4) Sprawl (urban sprawl) is the spreading of houses, shops and roads into the countryside around a city.
its sense in the lessons: Everyday life: sprawling on the sofa, sending someone sprawling in football. Geography: urban sprawl around big cities like Los Angeles or Sydney means people need cars, and countryside is lost; planners try to control it with green belts (UK). Stories: «sprawled on the floor» can show someone exhausted or knocked down.
examples from the lessons: He sprawled on the sofa after football. | The tackle sent her sprawling onto the grass. | The city sprawls for miles. | Urban sprawl is eating up farmland. | The cat lay sprawled in the sun. | A sprawling old house stood on the hill. | Green belts stop sprawl around London.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective «sprawling» = spreading widely. Noun «sprawl» is usually uncountable (urban sprawl). Do not confuse with «crawl» or «brawl» (a rough fight).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal, UK, Ireland, Australia, NZ) A spud is a potato. 2) (old, tool) A spud is a small digging tool with a narrow blade, for weeding.
its sense in the lessons: Everyday life and cooking: «Pass the spuds» at Sunday dinner. Ireland is famous for spuds in history (the Great Famine of 1845–1852 happened when potato blight destroyed the crop). Phrases: «couch potato», «jacket spud» (UK, a baked potato), «Spud» as a nickname.
examples from the lessons: Can you peel the spuds for dinner? | We had jacket spuds with beans. | Grandad grows spuds in the garden. | Mashed spuds are my favourite. | In 1845 a disease destroyed Ireland's spuds. | There's a bag of spuds in the cupboard. | My friend's nickname is Spud.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal; in formal writing say «potato». Countable: spuds. Plural of potato is potatoes (with e), but spud is just spuds.

part of speech: verb (squat, squats, squatted, squatting); noun (a squat, squats); adjective (squat, squatter, squattest); (slang, US) squat = nothing
meaning for a pupil: 1) To squat is to bend your knees and lower your body so you sit on your heels or just above the ground. 2) A squat is an exercise where you bend your knees and stand up again, keeping your back straight. 3) To squat is to live in an empty building or on land without permission or paying rent; the building is then called a squat. 4) Squat (adjective) means short and wide: a squat little teapot. 5) (US slang) Squat or «diddly-squat» means nothing at all: «you know squat».
its sense in the lessons: PE and health: squats make leg muscles strong; keep your knees over your toes. Everyday life: squatting down to look at a bug. Law and news: squatting in empty buildings is a crime in some places, like homes in England. Stories: a squat house or a squat toad is short and fat.
examples from the lessons: We did twenty squats in PE. | She squatted down to look at the snail. | The toad was squat and brown. | People were squatting in the empty building. | Keep your back straight when you squat. | He knows squat about football. (US slang) | The old lighthouse looked squat next to the hotel.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: squatted, squatting (double t). A person who squats in a building is a «squatter». The slang sense «squat» = nothing is informal, mostly American.

part of speech: verb (squawk, squawks, squawked, squawking); noun (a squawk, squawks)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To squawk is to make a loud, harsh cry like a parrot or a scared chicken. 2) A squawk is that loud, harsh cry. 3) (informal) To squawk is to complain loudly.
its sense in the lessons: Nature: parrots, cockatoos (very loud in Australia), seagulls and hens squawk. Stories: squawk is an onomatopoeia that brings birds to life; a character who squawks is upset or complaining. Aviation: a «squawk code» is a number a pilot sets so air traffic control can identify the plane.
examples from the lessons: The parrot squawked «Hello!» | A cockatoo squawked from the gum tree. | The hens squawked when the fox came near. | With a squawk, the seagull grabbed my chip. | My sister squawked when I took her chair. | The radio gave a squawk and went quiet. | Stop squawking about bedtime!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: squawk has «aw»; do not write «squalk». Similar words: squeal (high), screech (high and harsh), cluck (hen's normal sound).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Sterling is the money of the United Kingdom; its main unit is the pound (£). «Pound sterling» is its full name. 2) Sterling silver is silver that is 92.5% pure. 3) Sterling (adjective) means excellent and reliable: sterling work, a sterling effort.
its sense in the lessons: Money and maths: in the UK, prices are in pounds sterling: £1 = 100 pence. Exchange rates show how many dollars or euros you get for one pound. Everyday praise (UK): «You've done sterling work» means very good work. Jewellery: sterling silver often has a little stamp, 925.
examples from the lessons: The price is given in pounds sterling. | £1 sterling is worth 100 pence. | Grandma's necklace is sterling silver. | The volunteers did sterling work at the fair. | We changed our sterling into euros for the trip to Ireland. | The goalkeeper made a sterling save. | Sterling is one of the oldest currencies still used.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The money name is not capitalised: sterling, pound sterling. The symbol £ goes before the number: £5, not 5£. Note: in Ireland (the Republic), the money is the euro; Northern Ireland uses sterling.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A stirrup is a metal loop that hangs on each side of a horse's saddle, for the rider to put their foot in. 2) The stirrup (or stapes) is also a tiny bone in the middle ear, shaped like a stirrup; it is the smallest bone in the human body.
its sense in the lessons: Everyday life and sport: horse riders keep their feet in the stirrups for balance. History: stirrups helped riders stay on horses in battle and changed how wars were fought. Science: the ear has three tiny bones: hammer, anvil and stirrup, which pass sounds to the inner ear.
examples from the lessons: Put your feet in the stirrups before you ride. | She shortened the stirrups for the pony. | The knight stood up in his stirrups. | The stirrup is the smallest bone in your body. | Hammer, anvil and stirrup are the ear bones. | His foot slipped out of the stirrup. | A stirrup cup is a drink before a ride (old custom).
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable, usually in pairs. Spelling: double r and a single p: s-t-i-r-r-u-p. Said «STIR-up».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A stocky person or animal is short, broad and strong-looking, with a solid body.
its sense in the lessons: Stories: describing a character as stocky gives a picture of a short, sturdy, strong build, like a rugby player or a dwarf in fantasy books. Nature: some horse and dog breeds are stocky (Shetland ponies, bulldogs). It is a fairly neutral, polite word, not an insult.
examples from the lessons: The farmer was a stocky man with big hands. | The stocky pony carried the bags up the hill. | Bulldogs are stocky dogs. | Our goalkeeper is short and stocky. | A stocky dwarf guarded the door. | He grew stocky and strong from working on the farm.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative: stockier, stockiest (y changes to i). Similar: sturdy, thickset, chunky. Opposite: slim, lanky, slender. Not the same as «stock» (things kept in a shop).

part of speech: verb (stoop, stoops, stooped, stooping); noun (a stoop, stoops)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To stoop is to bend your body forwards and down: he stooped to pick up the coin. 2) A stoop is a habit of standing with your shoulders and head bent forward. 3) To stoop to something is to do something bad or mean that is below your usual standards: I would never stoop to cheating. 4) (US, Canada) A stoop is a small set of steps and a platform in front of a house door.
its sense in the lessons: Everyday life and health: stoop to tie your shoelaces; bend your knees when lifting heavy things, not just stoop with your back. Stories: an old man with a stoop; a villain who «stoops to lies». US: kids sitting on the front stoop in city streets.
examples from the lessons: She stooped to pick up the shell. | Grandad walks with a slight stoop. | He stooped under the low doorway. | I would never stoop to stealing. | They sat on the stoop eating ice lollies. (US) | Don't stoop when you lift the heavy box; bend your knees. | The giant had to stoop to enter the house.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Homophone: «stoop» sounds like «stoup» (a holy-water basin in a church; rare). Do not confuse with «stop» or «swoop». «Stoop to» = lower yourself morally.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Strenuous means needing a lot of effort, energy or strength: a strenuous climb. 2) Strenuous can describe very determined effort: strenuous efforts to save the forest.
its sense in the lessons: PE and health: strenuous exercise makes your heart beat fast and your breathing heavy; warm up first and drink water. Doctors may tell someone ill to avoid strenuous activity. News: «made strenuous efforts» means tried very hard. Formal register, common in reports and exam texts.
examples from the lessons: The climb up the mountain was strenuous. | Avoid strenuous exercise after a big meal. | After the strenuous match, we were exhausted. | Volunteers made strenuous efforts to clean the beach. | Moving house is strenuous work. | The doctor said no strenuous activity for a week.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Said «STREN-yoo-us». Adverb: strenuously (he strenuously denied it = denied it very strongly). Similar: tiring, demanding, exhausting. Opposite: easy, effortless, gentle.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science, medicine) Streptococcus is a type of round bacteria that grow in chains. Some kinds live harmlessly in us; others cause illnesses such as strep throat, scarlet fever and some skin and ear infections.
its sense in the lessons: Science and health: doctors can test for «strep» with a throat swab; infections are usually treated with antibiotics, and you must finish the course. Washing hands and covering coughs helps stop the spread. Under a microscope streptococci look like strings of beads. Short everyday word: «strep» (strep throat, US).
examples from the lessons: Streptococcus bacteria look like chains of beads. | The doctor tested for streptococcus with a throat swab. | Strep throat is caused by streptococcus. | Scarlet fever is caused by a kind of streptococcus. | Streptococci are passed on by coughs and sneezes. | Antibiotics can kill streptococcus bacteria.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Said «strep-tuh-KOK-us». Plural: streptococci («strep-tuh-KOK-sye» or «-KOK-ee»). Often shortened to «strep». Antibiotics work on bacteria like these, not on viruses like colds.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Structural means to do with the structure of something: how its parts are built, joined or organised. 2) Structural damage is damage to the main frame of a building or object, which can make it unsafe.
its sense in the lessons: Science and design and technology: structural parts (beams, frames, triangles) hold a bridge or building up; triangles are strong structural shapes. Safety: after a fire, earthquake or flood, engineers check for structural damage before people go back in. English: structural features of a text are headings, paragraphs and order.
examples from the lessons: The earthquake caused structural damage to the school. | Triangles are strong structural shapes. | A structural engineer checked the old bridge. | We looked at the structural features of a newspaper article. | The tower had a structural weakness. | Steel beams give the building structural strength.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective from «structure»; adverb «structurally» (structurally safe). Said «STRUK-chuh-rul».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A subdivision is a smaller part made when something already divided is divided again. 2) Subdivision is the act of dividing something into smaller parts. 3) (US, Canada, Australia, NZ) A subdivision is an area of land divided into plots where new houses are built, a housing estate.
its sense in the lessons: Maths: on a ruler, centimetres are subdivided into millimetres; scales and number lines have subdivisions, so you count each small mark carefully. Geography: a county or district is a subdivision of a country or state. Everyday life (North America, Australia, NZ): «They live in a new subdivision».
examples from the lessons: Each centimetre has ten subdivisions called millimetres. | A county is a subdivision of a country. | They bought a house in a new subdivision. | Count the subdivisions between 0 and 1 on the scale. | The farm was sold for subdivision. | Chapters have subdivisions called sections.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Verb: subdivide. Maths tip: if there are 5 spaces (subdivisions) between 0 and 10, each space is worth 2, not 1 — count spaces, not lines.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A subheading is a smaller heading under the main heading of a text, telling you what one section is about.
its sense in the lessons: English and reading lessons: non-fiction texts, reports and leaflets use subheadings to organise information; they help you skim and find facts quickly. When writing a report, pupils add subheadings like «Habitat», «Diet», «Life cycle». Subheadings are a structural (organisational) feature of a text.
examples from the lessons: Add subheadings to your report on penguins. | The subheading «Diet» tells you what the animal eats. | Use the subheadings to find the answer quickly. | Our leaflet had a title and four subheadings. | Each subheading starts a new section. | Subheadings are usually in bold.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable, one word (also «sub-heading»). Also called a subtitle or subhead. A heading is the main title; a subheading is under it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Submersion is being completely under water or another liquid. 2) Submersion is the act of putting something or someone fully under water.
its sense in the lessons: Science: floating and sinking; submarines control submersion by filling tanks with water. Safety: water submersion is dangerous; drowning can happen quickly and quietly, so swim where there are lifeguards and never swim alone. Everyday life: some watches and phones are tested for submersion. Church life: some Christians are baptised by full submersion (immersion) in water.
examples from the lessons: The phone survived thirty minutes of submersion. | Submarines can stay in submersion for weeks. | The plants died after long submersion in the flood. | Lifeguards train for rescues from submersion. | Some churches baptise by full submersion. | The field was in danger of submersion when the river rose.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Verb: submerge. Similar: immersion (often used for baptism and language learning). Do not confuse with «submission» (giving in, or handing in work).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A suburb is an area where people live on the edge of a city or town, mostly with houses, schools and shops rather than big offices or factories. 2) The suburbs means all such areas around a city.
its sense in the lessons: Geography: settlements include cities, towns, villages and suburbs; suburbs grew when trains and cars let people live further from work. Everyday life: in Australia and New Zealand people often name their suburb (e.g. Bondi is a suburb of Sydney). In stories and films, the suburbs are quiet streets with gardens and driveways.
examples from the lessons: We live in a suburb of Dublin. | Many people commute from the suburbs to the city. | Bondi is a suburb of Sydney. | The suburbs have more gardens than the city centre. | Our new school is in a leafy suburb. | Trains helped suburbs grow in Victorian times.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Adjective: suburban. Said «SUB-urb». Compare: city centre (UK) / downtown (US); countryside / rural area.

part of speech: adjective (Sumerian); noun (a Sumerian, Sumerians; Sumerian, the language)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Sumerian means from or to do with Sumer, one of the world's first civilisations, in southern Mesopotamia (now southern Iraq), about 5,000 years ago. 2) A Sumerian was a person from Sumer. 3) Sumerian is the language they spoke, written in cuneiform, one of the oldest written languages.
its sense in the lessons: History lessons: the Sumerians built some of the first cities (like Ur and Uruk), invented an early form of writing (cuneiform, pressed into clay tablets with a reed), and used a number system based on 60, which is why we have 60 minutes in an hour and 360 degrees in a circle. They built ziggurats (stepped temples) and told the story of Gilgamesh.
examples from the lessons: The Sumerians wrote on clay tablets. | Sumerian cities were built between two rivers. | We made Sumerian cuneiform with lolly sticks and clay. | Our 60 minutes in an hour comes from the Sumerian way of counting. | Ur was a great Sumerian city. | The Sumerian king Gilgamesh is the hero of a very old story. | Sumerian is not related to any language spoken today.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always capital S. Said «soo-MAIR-ee-un» or «soo-MEER-ee-un». Sumer is not the same as «summer». Sumerian is a language isolate: no known living relatives.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A superficial wound or damage is only on the surface and not deep or serious: a superficial cut. 2) Superficial means only looking at the outside or the obvious parts, not thinking deeply: a superficial reading of the text. 3) A superficial person cares mostly about looks and unimportant things, not deep feelings or ideas. 4) A superficial likeness is one that seems the same at first but is different underneath.
its sense in the lessons: Health and first aid: a superficial graze only needs cleaning and a plaster. Reading lessons: a superficial answer just copies words; a deeper answer explains why. Stories: a superficial character judges others by their clothes. Science: two animals may have a superficial likeness (a dolphin and a shark look alike, but one is a mammal and one is a fish).
examples from the lessons: It was only a superficial cut. | The car had superficial damage to its paint. | Your answer is a bit superficial; explain your reasons. | Don't be superficial and judge people by their trainers. | Dolphins and sharks have a superficial likeness. | The storm caused only superficial damage. | He had a superficial knowledge of football.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Said «soo-per-FISH-ul». Adverb: superficially. Opposite: deep, thorough, profound. Not the same as «artificial» (made by people, not natural).

meaning for a pupil: 1) To suspend something is to hang it from above: a lamp suspended from the ceiling. 2) To suspend something is to stop it for a while: matches were suspended because of snow. 3) To suspend a pupil, worker or player is to stop them from coming to school, work or playing for a time as a punishment. 4) (science) If tiny bits are suspended in a liquid or gas, they float in it without sinking or dissolving.
its sense in the lessons: School life: a pupil can be suspended (UK: «excluded» for a fixed time) for serious bad behaviour. Science: in a suspension (like muddy water) bits float and slowly settle; this is different from a solution. Everyday news: trains suspended, services suspended. Stories: «suspend disbelief» means pretending for a while that a magic story is real. Phrases: «suspended sentence» (law), «suspended animation».
examples from the lessons: A big chandelier was suspended from the ceiling. | All flights were suspended because of the storm. | He was suspended from school for fighting. | The player was suspended for two matches. | Mud particles were suspended in the water. | The bridge is suspended from strong cables. | The club suspended training during the holidays.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun forms: suspension (the act or a mixture), suspense (the tense feeling in a story). «Suspension bridge» = a bridge hung from cables. Do not confuse «suspend» with «expel» (to remove permanently).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A swallowtail is a large, brightly coloured butterfly with long points on its back wings that look like the forked tail of a swallow (a bird). 2) Swallowtail can describe any shape with a deep forked end, like a swallowtail flag or swallowtail coat.
its sense in the lessons: Science and nature: swallowtails are a big family of butterflies found around the world; the UK's swallowtail lives only in the Norfolk Broads. Their caterpillars can push out a smelly orange «horn» to scare off birds. Life cycle: egg, caterpillar, chrysalis, butterfly.
examples from the lessons: A yellow swallowtail landed on the flower. | The swallowtail butterfly has long tails on its wings. | In the UK, swallowtails live in the Norfolk Broads. | The swallowtail caterpillar was green with black stripes. | The ship flew a swallowtail flag. | We drew a swallowtail for our minibeast project.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable, one word. Named after the bird, the swallow, which has a forked tail. Not to be confused with «swallow» (to gulp down food).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Swampy land is wet, soft and muddy, like a swamp, with water lying on it and plants growing in the water.
its sense in the lessons: Geography and science: swamps and marshes are wetlands; they are homes for frogs, birds, alligators (USA) and many insects, and they store water and stop floods. Stories: swampy places are often spooky, misty or home to monsters like Shrek. Everyday: a swampy football pitch after rain.
examples from the lessons: The path became swampy after the rain. | Alligators live in swampy parts of Florida. | The football pitch was swampy and we got covered in mud. | Mosquitoes breed in swampy ground. | The ogre lived in a swampy forest. | Swampy land is good for frogs and herons.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative: swampier, swampiest. Related: swamp (noun; also verb «to swamp» = to flood or overwhelm: I'm swamped with homework). Similar: marshy, boggy (UK and Ireland: bog).

part of speech: verb (swipe, swipes, swiped, swiping); noun (a swipe, swipes)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To swipe a screen is to move your finger across it to change what is shown: swipe left. 2) To swipe a card is to pass it through or over a reader to pay or open a door. 3) To swipe at someone or something is to hit or try to hit with a big swinging movement. 4) (informal) To swipe something is to steal it quickly: someone swiped my pen. 5) A swipe is an unkind comment that criticises someone: he took a swipe at his rival.
its sense in the lessons: Everyday technology: swiping on phones and tablets; «swipe card» for school gates or buses. Online safety: think before you swipe to share or accept anything. Stories: a bear swiped at the fish; a cat took a swipe at the dog. News: politicians «take a swipe» at each other.
examples from the lessons: Swipe left to see the next photo. | Mum swiped her card to pay. | The cat swiped at the string. | Someone swiped my rubber! (informal) | The bear took a swipe at the beehive. | The coach took a swipe at the referee in his interview. | You need a swipe card to get into the building.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: swipe drops e before -ing: swiping; past: swiped. The «steal» sense is informal; in formal writing say «stole». Similar: swish, swat (hit), nick (UK slang for steal).

part of speech: noun (a swot, swots); verb (swot, swots, swotted, swotting; swot up) — UK, Ireland, Australia, NZ informal; SWOT (abbreviation)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (UK informal, teasing) A swot is a pupil who studies very hard, sometimes said in a mocking way. 2) (UK informal) To swot or swot up is to study hard, especially before a test. 3) SWOT (capitals) is short for Strengths, Weaknesses, Opportunities, Threats, a way to plan or judge an idea in business or school projects.
its sense in the lessons: School talk in the UK, Ireland, Australia and NZ: «Stop being such a swot!» can be teasing, but working hard is a good thing. «Swot up on your spellings before Friday». In the USA a similar word is «nerd» or «grind». In business studies, a SWOT analysis is a four-box table.
examples from the lessons: She's a swot and always does extra homework. | I need to swot up on my times tables. | He spent the weekend swotting for his test. | Don't call people swots for working hard. | We did a SWOT analysis of our school fair plan. | Being a swot paid off when she won the quiz.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal, mostly British-English countries. Verb doubles the t: swotted, swotting. Do not confuse with «swat» (to hit a fly). Teasing someone for studying hard is unkind.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Sympathetic means showing that you understand and care about someone's sadness or problems: a sympathetic friend. 2) Sympathetic to an idea or group means agreeing with it or supporting it. 3) A sympathetic character in a story is one readers like and care about.
its sense in the lessons: Feelings and PSHE: being sympathetic means listening, saying kind words, and helping when a friend is upset. English lessons: authors make a character sympathetic by showing their struggles and kindness. Science (older pupils): the sympathetic nervous system prepares the body for «fight or flight».
examples from the lessons: The nurse was very sympathetic when I hurt my arm. | My friends were sympathetic when my cat died. | The head teacher is sympathetic to our idea for a garden. | The hero is a sympathetic character because he is brave and kind. | She gave me a sympathetic smile. | Not everyone was sympathetic to his complaints.
note for the reader of a maths problem: False friend: in many European languages (French sympathique, Spanish simpático, Ukrainian «симпатичний») the word means «nice, likeable» or «good-looking», but English «sympathetic» means «understanding and caring about someone's troubles». Noun: sympathy. Compare: empathy (feeling what another person feels).

part of speech: noun (a tablespoon, tablespoons; short forms tbsp, T)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A tablespoon is a large spoon used for serving food or for measuring in cooking. 2) A tablespoon (tablespoonful) is the amount it holds, used as a measure in recipes.
its sense in the lessons: Maths and cooking: in the UK, Ireland, the USA and NZ a tablespoon is about 15 ml; in Australia it is 20 ml. 1 tablespoon = 3 teaspoons (UK/US). Recipes write «tbsp» (tablespoon) and «tsp» (teaspoon) — mixing them up can ruin a cake. Measures are usually level, not heaped, unless the recipe says so. Health: medicine should be measured with the special spoon or syringe it comes with, not a kitchen spoon.
examples from the lessons: Add two tablespoons of sugar. | One tablespoon is the same as three teaspoons. | Mum served the peas with a tablespoon. | The recipe says 1 tbsp of oil. | Use a level tablespoon of flour, not a heaped one. | How many millilitres are in 4 tablespoons? (60 ml in the UK) | Don't confuse tbsp with tsp!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable, one word. Short forms: tbsp, Tbsp, T; teaspoon is tsp or t. Maths: 1 tbsp ≈ 15 ml (20 ml in Australia), so 2 tbsp ≈ 30 ml. Plural: tablespoons (or tablespoonfuls).

part of speech: noun (a tally, tallies); verb (tally, tallies, tallied, tallying)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A tally is a record of a count, often made by drawing small lines: a tally chart. 2) A tally is the total number counted so far: his goal tally this season. 3) To tally (up) is to count or add up. 4) If two things tally, they match or agree: the stories tally.
its sense in the lessons: Maths and data handling: tally charts record data quickly; you draw four lines and then a fifth line across them to make a gate of 5 (卌 shape), then count in fives. Science: tally the number of birds you see in a survey. Sport: a player's goal tally. Everyday: making sure the money tallies with the receipt.
examples from the lessons: We made a tally chart of our favourite fruits. | Draw a line across four tally marks to make five. | What is his goal tally this season? | Let's tally up the votes. | The two witnesses' stories did not tally. | Count the tally marks in fives. | Her tally of points was the highest in the class.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: tallies; verb: tallies, tallied (y to i), but tallying. Maths: one gate of tally marks = 5, so three gates and two lines = 17. «Tally» does not mean the same as «tall».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Tangy describes a sharp, strong, pleasant taste or smell, often a bit sour, like lemon, lime or orange.
its sense in the lessons: Food and science: taste words — sweet, salty, sour, bitter, umami; tangy is a sharp, fresh mix often from sour fruit. Stories and descriptive writing: «the tangy smell of the sea». Advertisements: «tangy orange flavour».
examples from the lessons: This lemonade is lovely and tangy. | I like tangy cheese and onion crisps. | The orange juice tasted tangy. | The salty, tangy air of the seaside. | Add lime for a tangy flavour. | Rhubarb is tangy, so we add sugar.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative: tangier, tangiest. Noun: tang (a sharp taste or smell). Similar: zesty, sharp, sour. Tangy is usually a pleasant word; sour may be unpleasant.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Tanzanian means from or to do with Tanzania, a country in East Africa. 2) A Tanzanian is a person from Tanzania.
its sense in the lessons: Geography: Tanzania has Mount Kilimanjaro (Africa's highest mountain), the Serengeti plains with the great wildebeest migration, the island of Zanzibar, and shores on Lake Victoria and the Indian Ocean. Its capital is Dodoma; its biggest city is Dar es Salaam. People speak Swahili (Kiswahili) and English. Its money is the Tanzanian shilling.
examples from the lessons: Kilimanjaro is a Tanzanian mountain. | Our pen pal is Tanzanian and speaks Swahili. | Tanzanian children learn in Swahili at primary school. | The Serengeti is a famous Tanzanian national park. | We cooked a Tanzanian dish of rice and beans. | Many Tanzanians live by the coast.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always capital T. Said «tan-zuh-NEE-un». Tanzania was formed in 1964 by joining Tanganyika and Zanzibar, which is where the name comes from.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Tapioca is a starch made from the root of the cassava plant; it comes as flour, flakes or small white balls (pearls). 2) Tapioca (pudding) is a sweet milky pudding made with tapioca pearls.
its sense in the lessons: Food and science: cassava grows in hot countries in South America, Africa and Asia; tapioca pearls swell and go see-through when cooked. Bubble tea uses big chewy tapioca pearls. In old UK school dinners, tapioca pudding was famous (some children called it «frogspawn»). Tapioca flour is gluten-free.
examples from the lessons: Grandma made tapioca pudding with milk. | Bubble tea has tapioca pearls at the bottom. | Tapioca comes from the cassava root. | Some children used to call tapioca «frogspawn». | The tapioca balls turned clear as they cooked. | Tapioca flour is used in gluten-free bread.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Said «tap-ee-OH-kuh». Raw cassava root is poisonous unless prepared properly, but tapioca from shops is safe.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A tassel is a bunch of threads or strings tied together at the top and hanging loose at the bottom, used for decoration on cushions, curtains, hats or bookmarks. 2) A tassel is also the tuft of flowers at the top of a maize (corn) plant.
its sense in the lessons: Everyday life: tassels on graduation caps (moved from one side to the other at the ceremony in the USA), on scarves, school bags and cushions. Art and crafts: making tassels from wool. Science: the maize tassel makes pollen that falls on the silks below.
examples from the lessons: Her scarf has tassels at each end. | We made tassels from wool in craft club. | At graduation he moved his tassel to the left. | The curtains were tied back with gold tassels. | The bookmark has a red tassel. | The tassels on top of the corn shed pollen.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Spelling: double s, single l: tassel. Said «TASS-ul». Do not confuse with «tussle» (a rough struggle) or «hassle».

part of speech: noun (tectonics; plate tectonics) — uncountable, takes a singular verb
meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) Tectonics, or plate tectonics, is the idea that the Earth's outer shell is broken into huge pieces called plates that move very slowly, and the study of how they move. 2) Tectonics can also mean big shifts or changes in politics or society (formal, figurative).
its sense in the lessons: Geography and science: tectonic plates move a few centimetres a year (about as fast as fingernails grow); where they meet there are earthquakes, volcanoes and mountains (the Himalayas, the Andes). New Zealand and Iceland sit on plate boundaries. The idea grew from Alfred Wegener's «continental drift» (1912). Phrases: «plate tectonics», «tectonic plates», «tectonic shift».
examples from the lessons: Plate tectonics explains why earthquakes happen. | The Himalayas formed because of plate tectonics. | Iceland is splitting apart because of tectonics. | We learned about tectonics in geography. | Tectonic plates move about as fast as your fingernails grow. | New Zealand lies where two tectonic plates meet.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Ends in -s but usually singular: «plate tectonics is ...». Adjective: tectonic (tectonic plates). Myth: plates do not float on liquid lava; they slide on hot, slowly-flowing solid rock in the mantle.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To televise something is to show it on television, often live as it happens: the match will be televised.
its sense in the lessons: Everyday life and news: big football matches, royal events, elections and the Olympics are televised. Citizenship: parliaments' debates are televised so people can see what their representatives do. Sport: televised games may change times to suit TV.
examples from the lessons: The cup final will be televised live. | The king's coronation was televised around the world. | Is the school concert being televised? No, just filmed! | Parliament's debates are televised. | The 1969 Moon landing was televised to millions. | Not every match is televised.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: televise with «s» in all countries (not -ize). Past: televised. Related: television, telly (UK informal), TV.

part of speech: adjective (telltale; also tell-tale); noun (a telltale, telltales)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A telltale sign is a small clue that shows something is true or has happened: telltale crumbs on his face. 2) (UK, Ireland, Australia, NZ; children's word) A telltale (or tell-tale) is a child who tells adults about other children's naughty behaviour, a tattletale (US).
its sense in the lessons: Stories and detective work: telltale signs and clues help solve a mystery. Science: «telltale signs» of a disease, or of rain. Playground: «Telltale tit!» is a rhyme children use to tease. Safety: telling a grown-up when someone is hurt, in danger or bullied is not being a telltale — it is the right thing to do.
examples from the lessons: The chocolate on his chin was a telltale sign. | Muddy paw prints were the telltale clues. | Don't be a telltale! | Telling a teacher about bullying is not being a telltale. | Yawning is a telltale sign you need sleep. | The telltale smoke showed where the fire was.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: telltale or tell-tale (UK often hyphenated). US word for the person: tattletale. «Tell tales» (two words) = to tell on someone, or to tell lies. Getting help in danger is never «telling tales».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A terrorist is a person who uses violence or threats against ordinary people, often by bombing or attacking, to frighten people and force a government or society to do what they want, usually for political or religious aims.
its sense in the lessons: Citizenship and news: terrorism is a serious crime in every country; police and security services work to stop it. History: terrorist attacks such as 11 September 2001 in the USA changed airport security. Safety (UK «Run, Hide, Tell»): if something dangerous happens, run away if you can, hide if you cannot, and tell the police (999 in the UK, 911 in the USA and Canada, 000 in Australia, 111 in NZ, 112 or 999 in Ireland). If news scares you, talk to a grown-up. Different sides sometimes call the same group terrorists or freedom fighters, so the news may say who calls them that.
examples from the lessons: The police arrested a terrorist before he could attack. | A terrorist attack hurts innocent people. | Airport checks help stop terrorists. | The news said the group was listed as terrorist by several countries. | Terrorists want people to feel afraid. | Remember: run, hide, tell. | If the news about terrorists worries you, talk to an adult.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Related: terror (great fear), terrorism (the crime), terrorise/terrorize (to frighten badly — in everyday talk a bully can «terrorise» a playground, which is not terrorism). Not every attacker is a terrorist; the word means violence used to scare people for a political or religious aim.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) Testosterone is a hormone, a chemical messenger in the body. Men and boys have much more of it, but women and girls have some too. It helps the body grow muscles and bones and causes many changes in boys during puberty, like a deeper voice and facial hair.
its sense in the lessons: Science and PSHE (growing up): during puberty, hormones such as testosterone (mostly in boys) and oestrogen (mostly in girls) make the body change. In sport news, testosterone is mentioned in doping rules, because extra testosterone taken as a drug is banned. Myth: people sometimes blame all anger or showing off on «testosterone», but behaviour depends on many things and every person is responsible for their choices.
examples from the lessons: Testosterone is a hormone. | During puberty, testosterone makes boys' voices deeper. | Girls have some testosterone too, just less. | Athletes are not allowed to take extra testosterone. | Hormones like testosterone travel in the blood. | Testosterone helps build muscle and bone.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Said «tes-TOS-tuh-rone». Hormones are chemical messengers carried in the blood. Not something you take yourself unless a doctor says so.

part of speech: noun (a testudo, testudos or testudines); (science) Testudo — a genus of tortoises
meaning for a pupil: 1) (history) A testudo was a Roman army formation: soldiers stood close together and held their shields in front of them and over their heads, like a tortoise's shell, to protect themselves from arrows and stones. 2) (science) Testudo is the scientific name of a group of tortoises, such as the Greek tortoise and Hermann's tortoise.
its sense in the lessons: History lessons on the Romans: the testudo («tortoise» in Latin) let legionaries move up to enemy walls safely; pupils sometimes act it out with cardboard shields. Science: many pet tortoises in the UK are from the genus Testudo.
examples from the lessons: The legionaries formed a testudo to protect themselves. | In the testudo, the soldiers' shields made a roof. | Testudo is Latin for tortoise. | Our class made a testudo with cardboard shields. | The arrows bounced off the testudo. | Hermann's tortoise belongs to the genus Testudo.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Said «tes-TOO-doh». Latin word. Plural: testudos (or the Latin testudines). The science name is written with a capital T and in italics: Testudo.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A threadworm (also pinworm) is a tiny white worm, like a piece of thread, that can live in people's intestines (gut) for a while and causes itching around the bottom, especially at night.
its sense in the lessons: Health and hygiene: threadworms are very common in children and are not a sign of being dirty; they spread when tiny eggs get on fingers and then into mouths. Washing hands, scrubbing under nails, not biting nails, and washing bedding stop them. A chemist sells medicine, and usually the whole family takes it. Science: threadworms are parasites (they live on another living thing).
examples from the lessons: Threadworms are very common in children. | Threadworms can make your bottom itch at night. | Wash your hands to stop threadworms spreading. | The whole family took medicine for threadworms. | A threadworm is as thin as a piece of cotton. | Threadworms are parasites.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable, one word. US name: pinworm. Not the same as an earthworm (lives in soil, harmless) or a tapeworm. Nothing to be ashamed of; tell a grown-up if you itch.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (old-fashioned) Thrice means three times: he knocked thrice.
its sense in the lessons: Old stories, fairy tales, poems and the Bible use «thrice»; in modern talk people say «three times». Maths: thrice a number means the number multiplied by 3. Bible: Jesus told Peter he would deny him thrice before the cock crowed. Compare: once, twice, thrice, then «four times».
examples from the lessons: The knight knocked thrice on the castle door. | Thrice the witch stirred the pot. | Thrice 4 is 12. | Peter denied knowing Jesus thrice. | He was thrice champion. | In modern English we usually say «three times», not «thrice».
note for the reader of a maths problem: Old-fashioned; in school maths write «three times» or «×3». There is no «fource»: after thrice, say «four times», «five times». Maths: thrice 7 = 21.

part of speech: noun (a thud, thuds); verb (thud, thuds, thudded, thudding)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A thud is a dull, heavy sound made when something heavy falls or hits something soft: the bag hit the floor with a thud. 2) To thud is to fall or hit with such a sound, or to beat heavily: my heart was thudding.
its sense in the lessons: Stories and poetry: thud is an onomatopoeia that shows weight and impact; «my heart thudded» shows fear or excitement. Everyday life: a book thuds onto the floor; footsteps thud upstairs. Compare sounds: a thud is dull and low, a clang is metal, a crash is loud and breaking.
examples from the lessons: The heavy book fell with a thud. | We heard a thud from upstairs. | My heart was thudding before the race. | The apple thudded onto the grass. | His boots thudded down the stairs. | The ball hit the door with a loud thud.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb doubles the d: thudded, thudding. Similar: thump, bump. A thud is lower and duller than a bang.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A thumbnail is the nail on your thumb. 2) A thumbnail is a small picture on a screen that stands for a bigger picture or video; you click it to see the full one. 3) A thumbnail sketch or description is very short and gives only the main points.
its sense in the lessons: Computers and online safety: video sites show thumbnails, and some are made to look exciting to trick you into clicking («clickbait»). Art: artists do thumbnail sketches to plan a picture. Writing: «a thumbnail biography» gives just the key facts.
examples from the lessons: I broke my thumbnail on the door. | Click the thumbnail to see the full photo. | The video's thumbnail looked exciting, but it was clickbait. | The artist drew quick thumbnail sketches first. | Give a thumbnail description of the main character. | The thumbnails are too small to see clearly.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable, one word. The b in «thumb» is silent: said «THUM-nail». Thumbnails can be misleading — the real video may be different.

part of speech: adjective (Tibetan); noun (a Tibetan, Tibetans; Tibetan, the language)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Tibetan means from or to do with Tibet, a high region in the Himalayas, now part of China. 2) A Tibetan is a person from Tibet. 3) Tibetan is the language of Tibet, written in its own script.
its sense in the lessons: Geography: Tibet is called «the roof of the world» because it is a very high plateau; great rivers like the Yangtze and the Brahmaputra start there. Religion: most Tibetans are Buddhists; the Dalai Lama is their best-known religious leader and has lived in India since 1959. News: China rules Tibet; many Tibetans and others say their freedom and culture are not respected, and China disagrees. Animals: the yak; dog breeds such as the Tibetan mastiff and Tibetan terrier.
examples from the lessons: Tibetan monks chant prayers. | The Tibetan plateau is very high. | Tibetan prayer flags flapped in the wind. | Yaks carry loads for Tibetan farmers. | Tibetan is written in its own alphabet. | We read a Tibetan folk tale in class. | The Tibetan terrier has long, shaggy fur.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always capital T. Said «ti-BET-un». Do not confuse with «Tibet» (the place) — Tibetan is the people, language and adjective.

part of speech: noun (a tier, tiers); verb (tier, tiers, tiered — less common)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A tier is one of several layers or levels placed one above another: a three-tier wedding cake, tiers of seats. 2) A tier is a level in a system or ranking: the top tier of football, a tier of government.
its sense in the lessons: Everyday life: tiered cakes at weddings, tiers of seats in a stadium or theatre. Maths: counting objects in tiers (e.g. a stack of cups with 1, 2, 3, 4 per tier) leads to number patterns like triangular numbers. School: some exams have tiers (foundation and higher). Business: price tiers (basic, premium).
examples from the lessons: The wedding cake had three tiers. | We sat in the top tier of the stadium. | The Premier League is the top tier of English football. | Each tier of the pyramid had fewer blocks. | The exam has two tiers: foundation and higher. | Town councils are one tier of government.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Said like «tear» (as in crying): «teer». Homophone trap: «tier» (a level) sounds like «tear» (a drop from the eye), not like «tire/tyre». Maths: a tower of 4 tiers with 1, 2, 3, 4 blocks has 10 blocks in all.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A tigress is a female tiger. 2) (figurative) A tigress can describe a woman who is fierce and brave, especially when protecting her children.
its sense in the lessons: Science and nature: a tigress raises her cubs alone for about two years and teaches them to hunt. Tigers are endangered; they live in parts of Asia. Stories: «she fought like a tigress» shows fierce courage.
examples from the lessons: The tigress carried her cub in her mouth. | A tigress hunts alone at night. | The zoo's tigress had three cubs. | Mum defended us like a tigress. | Wild tigresses live in India and Russia. | The tigress licked her cubs clean.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: tigresses. Male: tiger; young: cub. The -ess ending marks a female (lioness, tigress, princess).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A toadstool is a fungus with a round cap on a stalk, like a mushroom; the word is often used for kinds that are poisonous or not eaten, like the red one with white spots (fly agaric).
its sense in the lessons: Science and nature: toadstools are the fruiting parts of fungi, which grow in damp woods, especially in autumn, and help rot down dead leaves and wood. Safety: never pick or eat wild mushrooms or toadstools — some are deadly, and they are hard to tell apart; wash hands after touching. Stories and fairy tales: fairies, gnomes and pixies sit on red-and-white toadstools.
examples from the lessons: A red toadstool with white spots grew under the birch tree. | Never eat a toadstool you find in the woods. | In the story, a fairy lived under a toadstool. | Toadstools pop up after autumn rain. | We drew toadstools on our nature walk but didn't touch them. | Fungi like toadstools help break down dead leaves.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable, one word. There is no scientific difference between a mushroom and a toadstool; «toadstool» usually suggests not safe to eat. Toads do not really sit on them.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A toolbox is a box for keeping and carrying tools such as a hammer, screwdrivers and a tape measure. 2) A toolbox can mean a set of skills, methods or ideas you can use for a job: a maths toolbox of strategies.
its sense in the lessons: Everyday life and DT: a toolbox in the shed or the car. School: teachers talk about a «toolbox» of strategies (number lines, drawing a picture, times tables) for solving problems, or a «calm-down toolbox» for feelings. Computing: a toolbox (or toolbar) holds the tools in a program.
examples from the lessons: Dad keeps a hammer in his toolbox. | Fetch the screwdriver from the toolbox. | Drawing a diagram is a good strategy in your maths toolbox. | The plumber carried a heavy toolbox. | My calm-down toolbox includes deep breathing. | The art program has a toolbox with brushes and pens.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable, one word. Plural: toolboxes. Similar: toolkit, tool chest.

part of speech: verb (transform, transforms, transformed, transforming); noun (a transform — maths, rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To transform something is to change it completely, often making it better: the garden was transformed. 2) To transform is to change from one form or shape into another: a caterpillar transforms into a butterfly. 3) (maths) To transform a shape is to move or change it by a translation, reflection, rotation or enlargement. 4) (science) To transform energy is to change it from one type into another.
its sense in the lessons: Science: metamorphosis — tadpoles transform into frogs; energy is transformed (e.g. a battery's chemical energy into light in a torch). Maths: transformations of shapes on a grid. Stories: magical transformations (a frog into a prince, Cinderella's pumpkin into a coach). Everyday: «The new playground transformed our school».
examples from the lessons: The caterpillar transformed into a butterfly. | The new paint transformed my bedroom. | Reflect the triangle to transform it. | A solar panel transforms light into electricity. | In the story, the frog transformed into a prince. | Learning to read transformed her life. | Rotation and translation are ways to transform a shape.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: transformation; person or thing that transforms: transformer (also a device that changes voltage). In maths, translation and rotation keep the same shape and size; enlargement changes the size.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A treadmill is an exercise machine with a moving belt that you walk or run on without going anywhere. 2) (figurative) A treadmill is a boring routine of work that goes on and on and never seems to get anywhere. 3) (history) A treadmill was a large wheel turned by people or animals walking on it, used to grind grain or pump water, and in Victorian prisons as a punishment.
its sense in the lessons: Health and PE: treadmills at gyms let people run indoors; you can set speed and slope. Safety: children should not use treadmills without an adult — fingers and clothes can get caught. History: Victorian prisoners were made to walk the treadmill for hours. Everyday talk: «I'm stuck on the treadmill» means my life feels like the same tiring work every day.
examples from the lessons: Mum runs on the treadmill when it is raining. | The treadmill was set to a slow walk. | Victorian prisoners had to walk on the treadmill. | He felt his job was a never-ending treadmill. | Keep fingers away from a moving treadmill. | Vets use underwater treadmills to help dogs recover.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable, one word. From «tread» (to step) + «mill». Similar: running machine (UK).

part of speech: noun (a trill, trills); verb (trill, trills, trilled, trilling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A trill is a quick, high, repeated sound, like a bird singing. 2) (music) A trill is when two notes next to each other are played or sung very quickly one after the other many times. 3) (language) A trill is a sound made by letting the tongue flutter, like the rolled «r» in Spanish or Scottish English. 4) To trill is to make such a sound, or to say something in a high, happy voice.
its sense in the lessons: Nature: robins and canaries trill. Music lessons: a trill is marked «tr» above a note. Languages: rolling your r's in Spanish, Italian or Ukrainian is a trill. Stories: a character who «trilled» speaks in a high, cheerful (sometimes fake-sweet) voice.
examples from the lessons: A blackbird's trill came from the hedge. | The flute player added a trill at the end. | In Spanish, «perro» has a trilled r. | «Good morning, darlings!» she trilled. | The phone trilled on the table. | Can you roll your r's into a trill?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: trilled, trilling. Do not confuse with «thrill» (an exciting feeling), «drill», or «trail».
