part of speech: verb form (trim, trims, trimmed, trimming); noun (trimming, trimmings)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Trimming means cutting a little off something to make it tidy: trimming a hedge, trimming hair. 2) Trimming (noun) is decoration added to the edge of something, like lace or ribbon on a dress. 3) The trimmings are the extra foods served with a main dish, especially at Christmas dinner: turkey with all the trimmings. 4) Trimmings are the small bits cut off. 5) Trimming can mean reducing something a little: trimming costs.
its sense in the lessons: Everyday life: a haircut «just a trim», trimming the hedge, trimming your nails. Christmas in the UK, Ireland, Australia and NZ: «roast turkey with all the trimmings» (stuffing, roast potatoes, sprouts, pigs in blankets, gravy). Sewing and crafts: lace trimming. News: trimming a budget.
examples from the lessons: Dad is trimming the hedge. | I need my fringe trimming. | We had turkey with all the trimmings. | The dress had gold trimming on the hem. | Put the grass trimmings in the compost. | The school is trimming its spending this year. | She is trimming the crusts off the sandwiches.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: trim doubles the m: trimmed, trimming. «All the trimmings» is a fixed phrase. «Trimmings» (plural) is the usual form for food extras and cut-off bits.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A trio is a group of three people or things. 2) (music) A trio is a group of three musicians or singers, or a piece of music for three players.
its sense in the lessons: Music lessons: a piano trio is piano, violin and cello. Stories and everyday talk: «the famous trio» — three friends such as Harry, Ron and Hermione. Maths: a trio is a set of 3; e.g. how many trios can you make from 6 children? (2 trios, if each child is in one).
examples from the lessons: The three friends made a trio of detectives. | A jazz trio played at the wedding. | We sang a song as a trio. | Harry, Ron and Hermione are a famous trio. | Arrange the 12 pupils into trios — that makes 4 trios. | The shop sells a trio of cakes for £3.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; plural trios. Said «TREE-oh». Number words: solo (1), duet or duo (2), trio (3), quartet (4), quintet (5). Maths: number of trios = number of people ÷ 3.

part of speech: noun (a triumph, triumphs; triumph — uncountable); verb (triumph, triumphs, triumphed, triumphing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A triumph is a great victory or success: the concert was a triumph. 2) Triumph is the great joy or pride you feel when you win or succeed. 3) To triumph is to win, succeed or beat something difficult: good triumphs over evil. 4) (history) In ancient Rome, a triumph was a grand parade through the city to honour a winning general.
its sense in the lessons: Stories: a story often ends with the hero's triumph; «good triumphs over evil» is a common theme. History: Roman triumphs; the Arc de Triomphe in Paris. Everyday: «a triumph of teamwork». Phrases: «in triumph», «triumph over», «a shout of triumph».
examples from the lessons: The school play was a triumph. | She raised the cup in triumph. | Good triumphed over evil in the end. | Climbing the mountain was a personal triumph. | He gave a shout of triumph. | The Roman general rode through the city in a triumph. | They triumphed against the odds.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Said «TRY-umf». Adjectives: triumphant (feeling or showing triumph), triumphal (to celebrate a triumph: a triumphal arch). Spelling: ph sounds like f.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Turmeric is a bright yellow-orange spice made from the dried and ground root of a plant in the ginger family. It is used in curries and to colour food.
its sense in the lessons: Food and geography: turmeric is used a lot in Indian, South Asian and other cooking and gives curry its yellow colour; India grows most of the world's turmeric. Science: it stains clothes and fingers yellow, and its colour changes to red-brown in alkaline solutions, so it can be used as an indicator in experiments. Myth: turmeric is sometimes sold as a cure for many illnesses, but scientists have not shown strong proof that it cures diseases.
examples from the lessons: Turmeric makes the rice yellow. | Mum added a spoon of turmeric to the curry. | Turmeric stained my fingers orange. | Turmeric comes from a root, like ginger. | In science, turmeric paper turned red with soap. | Be careful, turmeric stains are hard to wash out.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Spelling trap: tur-mer-ic (people often say «TOO-mer-ik» and forget the first r). Said «TUR-muh-rik».

part of speech: verb (twirl, twirls, twirled, twirling); noun (a twirl, twirls)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To twirl is to spin round and round quickly, or to make something spin: she twirled in her new dress. 2) To twirl something is to twist it round your finger: he twirled his hair. 3) A twirl is a quick spin or turn. 4) A twirl is a curly shape or mark, like a loop of icing.
its sense in the lessons: Dance and PE: twirling in ballet or gymnastics with ribbons. Everyday: twirling spaghetti on a fork, twirling a baton in a parade. Stories: a character who twirls a moustache is often shown as a sneaky villain. Phrase: «give us a twirl» (UK: show off your outfit by spinning).
examples from the lessons: She twirled around in her party dress. | He twirled spaghetti on his fork. | The majorette twirled her baton. | Give us a twirl so we can see your costume! | The villain twirled his moustache. | The cake had twirls of chocolate on top. | The dancer did three twirls on one foot.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: twirled, twirling. Similar: spin, whirl, swirl (swirl is usually liquid or air moving round). Do not confuse with «twirly» (informal for curly).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A UFO is short for «unidentified flying object»: something seen in the sky that people cannot explain or name. 2) In everyday talk and films, a UFO often means a flying saucer, an alien spaceship.
its sense in the lessons: Science and critical thinking: most UFO sightings turn out to be planes, satellites, weather balloons, drones, planets like Venus, or tricks of light; «unidentified» only means not yet explained, not «alien». Governments now often use the term UAP (unidentified anomalous phenomena). Scientists say there is no confirmed evidence that aliens have visited Earth. Stories and films: UFOs bring aliens to Earth.
examples from the lessons: Grandad says he saw a UFO over the lake. | The «UFO» turned out to be a weather balloon. | In the film, a UFO landed in the park. | UFO stands for unidentified flying object. | Scientists check UFO reports carefully. | My little brother drew a UFO with green aliens. | That bright «UFO» was actually the planet Venus.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually written in capitals: UFO, plural UFOs. Said «you-ef-OH» or «YOO-foh». «Unidentified» does not mean «from space» — it means nobody knows yet what it is. Note: the input is lower case «ufo», but the normal spelling is UFO.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A unanimous decision or vote is one that everyone in the group agrees with, with nobody against. 2) If people are unanimous, they all agree about something.
its sense in the lessons: Used about votes in class, councils, juries, courts and clubs; it tells the reader there was no disagreement at all. Phrases: «a unanimous vote», «a unanimous decision», «unanimous agreement», «unanimous in their praise». In maths problems about votes it means every voter chose the same option.
examples from the lessons: The class vote for the trip to the zoo was unanimous. | The jury reached a unanimous verdict. | All twelve judges were unanimous that the rule was unfair. | The teachers were unanimous in their praise of the play. | The council gave unanimous approval to the new skate park. | Not one hand went up against it, so the decision was unanimous. | The team made a unanimous choice for captain.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective only; adverb «unanimously». Pronounced yoo-NAN-i-mus. From Latin «one mind». Unanimous means ALL agree, not just most: if 29 of 30 vote yes, it is not unanimous. In vote problems: unanimous = votes for = total voters, votes against = 0.

meaning for a pupil: 1) If something is done unanimously, everyone in the group agrees to it and nobody is against it.
its sense in the lessons: Used in reports of votes and decisions at school councils, in parliaments, courts and clubs: «voted unanimously», «agreed unanimously», «unanimously elected». It tells the reader the whole group was on one side.
examples from the lessons: The school council voted unanimously to plant more trees. | Maya was unanimously chosen as team captain. | The judges unanimously agreed that the cake was the best. | The motion was passed unanimously. | The players unanimously decided to share the prize. | The new rule was adopted unanimously by the club. | The United Nations Security Council voted unanimously on the resolution.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from «unanimous». «Unanimously» means every single person; «by a large majority» means most but not all. In maths: if a class of 28 voted unanimously, 28 voted yes and 0 voted no.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Uncleanliness is the state of being dirty or not clean. 2) Uncleanliness is also the habit of not keeping yourself or your things clean. 3) (Bible) In older Bible translations, uncleanliness or uncleanness can mean being not pure in God's eyes or by religious rules.
its sense in the lessons: Used in health and hygiene lessons, in inspections of kitchens and hospitals, in stories about poor living conditions, and in old religious texts. It tells the reader that dirt may cause germs and illness.
examples from the lessons: The inspector closed the café because of its uncleanliness. | Uncleanliness can spread germs and make people ill. | The old ship was famous for its uncleanliness. | Washing your hands helps prevent the dangers of uncleanliness. | The report blamed the outbreak on the uncleanliness of the water supply. | In the story, the giant's cave smelled of uncleanliness and old bones. | Victorian cities suffered from great uncleanliness before proper sewers were built.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: no plural. A rather formal word; everyday speech says «dirt», «dirtiness» or «mess». Opposite: «cleanliness». The Bible usually says «uncleanness», which means much the same.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To uncover something is to take a cover or lid off it so it can be seen. 2) To uncover something is to find something that was hidden, buried or secret. 3) To uncover a crime, plot or truth is to find out about it.
its sense in the lessons: Used in cooking («uncover the pan»), archaeology and science («uncover fossils, ruins»), detective stories and news («uncover the truth, a plot, a secret»). It tells the reader that something hidden is now seen or known.
examples from the lessons: Uncover the dish and let it cool. | The archaeologists uncovered an old Roman coin. | The wind uncovered the footprints in the sand. | The detective uncovered the thief's secret plan. | Reporters uncovered the truth about the company. | We uncovered a box of old photos in the attic. | Scientists uncovered the bones of a dinosaur. | Please keep the paint uncovered for only a minute.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. «Uncover» (find hidden things) is close to «discover», but discover can also mean finding something new that was never covered. Opposite: «cover», «hide».

part of speech: noun (an undercoat, undercoats); verb (undercoat, undercoats, undercoated, undercoating — rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) An undercoat is a first layer of paint put on before the top layer, to help the top coat stick and look smooth. 2) An undercoat is the soft, thick layer of fur close to an animal's skin, under the longer outer hairs. 3) (verb, rare) To undercoat something is to give it a first layer of paint.
its sense in the lessons: Used in DIY and art («put on an undercoat, then the topcoat»), and in pet care and science about animals keeping warm (dogs, cats, sheep, arctic animals).
examples from the lessons: Dad painted an undercoat on the fence before the green paint. | The white undercoat helps the bright colour show up. | Leave the undercoat to dry overnight. | Huskies have a thick undercoat that keeps them warm in the snow. | Our dog sheds its undercoat in spring. | Brush the cat often to remove the loose undercoat. | Arctic foxes grow a dense undercoat in winter.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun. Not to be confused with «overcoat», which is a long warm coat people wear. In painting, the undercoat is also called a primer or base coat; the last one is the topcoat.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Undisclosed means not told or not made public; kept secret.
its sense in the lessons: Mostly used in news and business: «an undisclosed sum», «an undisclosed location», «for undisclosed reasons». It tells the reader that a fact exists but people were not told it. In maths it means the number is unknown.
examples from the lessons: The footballer joined the club for an undisclosed fee. | The prize was sold for an undisclosed amount. | The witness was moved to an undisclosed location for safety. | She left the job for undisclosed reasons. | The company paid an undisclosed sum to settle the case. | The name of the winner remains undisclosed until Friday.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal word, used in news. From «disclose» (to tell or reveal). «Undisclosed» does not mean «unknown to everyone»: someone knows, but it has not been shared. In a maths problem an undisclosed amount cannot be used unless other clues let you work it out.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Undivided attention or support is complete and given to only one thing. 2) Something undivided is whole and not split into parts.
its sense in the lessons: Used most in the phrase «undivided attention», often by teachers and parents: «I need your undivided attention». Also «undivided loyalty», «an undivided country», «one nation, indivisible» in civics.
examples from the lessons: Please give me your undivided attention. | The baby needed her mother's undivided attention. | The coach had the team's undivided attention. | The farm was passed down undivided to the eldest son. | The fans gave the team their undivided support. | Put your phone away so the speaker gets your undivided attention.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective only. Opposite: «divided» (split, or partly elsewhere). Common phrase: «undivided attention» means listening to one thing only, with no phone or chatting.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unhurt means not injured or harmed, especially after an accident or danger.
its sense in the lessons: Used in news and stories after accidents, falls, crashes and fires: «escaped unhurt», «was found unhurt». It tells the reader that someone was in danger but is safe.
examples from the lessons: The driver escaped unhurt from the crash. | Luckily the cat was unhurt after its fall. | All the children were unhurt when the fire alarm went off. | The climber was found cold but unhurt. | He fell off his bike but got up unhurt. | Everyone on the boat was brought ashore unhurt.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually used after verbs like «be», «escape», «come out»: «She was unhurt». We rarely say «an unhurt boy»; we say «an uninjured boy». Same meaning as «uninjured», «unharmed».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unintelligible speech or writing cannot be understood because it is unclear, mumbled, too messy, or in a code or language you do not know.
its sense in the lessons: Used about mumbling, bad phone lines, messy handwriting, noisy announcements, and foreign languages. It tells the reader that the words could not be understood, not that they were wrong.
examples from the lessons: The message on the radio was unintelligible because of the noise. | His handwriting was almost unintelligible. | She muttered something unintelligible and went to bed. | The station announcement was unintelligible over the trains. | The baby's babble is still unintelligible to visitors. | The code looked like unintelligible nonsense until we found the key.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal word. Opposite: «intelligible» (can be understood). Not about intelligence: an unintelligible person is not stupid; their words just cannot be understood. Similar: «incomprehensible».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Uninterrupted means going on without being stopped or broken. 2) An uninterrupted view is one that nothing blocks.
its sense in the lessons: Used about sleep, time, work, views and journeys: «uninterrupted sleep», «an uninterrupted view of the sea», «uninterrupted power supply». It tells the reader that nothing stopped or blocked it.
examples from the lessons: I want an hour of uninterrupted reading. | The baby had six hours of uninterrupted sleep. | Our room had an uninterrupted view of the mountains. | The rain fell for three uninterrupted days. | The speech went on uninterrupted for twenty minutes. | Hospitals need an uninterrupted supply of electricity.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «interrupt» (to stop someone or something for a moment). In maths, «uninterrupted» time means one continuous stretch: «3 uninterrupted hours» is one block, not three hours spread over a day.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unlawfully means in a way that is against the law.
its sense in the lessons: Used in news, law and history: «unlawfully killed», «unlawfully detained», «entered the country unlawfully». It tells the reader that an action broke the law.
examples from the lessons: The man was arrested for unlawfully entering the building. | The court said the workers had been unlawfully dismissed. | Taking someone's bike without asking is acting unlawfully. | The prisoner claimed he was held unlawfully. | The land had been taken unlawfully many years ago. | The company unlawfully dumped waste in the river.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; everyday speech says «illegally». Opposite: «lawfully», «legally». «Unlawfully» means against the law; «unfairly» means not fair but may still be legal.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An unlikeable person or character is hard to like because they are unkind, rude, selfish or unpleasant.
its sense in the lessons: Used in book reviews and stories about characters: «an unlikeable hero», «an unlikeable villain». It tells the reader how we feel about a character.
examples from the lessons: The main character was so selfish that he was unlikeable. | Mr Twit is an unlikeable man who plays nasty tricks. | Some readers found the princess unlikeable at first. | She was rude and bossy, which made her unlikeable. | A good writer can make an unlikeable character interesting. | By the end of the book, the unlikeable boy had changed.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Two spellings: «unlikeable» (more British) and «unlikable» (more American). Opposite: «likeable». Being unlikeable is not the same as being evil; a character can be annoying but still good.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unmarked means having no sign, label or name on it. 2) Unmarked work has not yet been checked and scored by a teacher. 3) Unmarked means without scratches, stains or damage. 4) (sport) An unmarked player has no one from the other team guarding them.
its sense in the lessons: Used about police cars, graves, roads, homework and sport: «an unmarked police car», «an unmarked grave», «left unmarked», «a player unmarked in the box».
examples from the lessons: The police arrived in an unmarked car. | The road was unmarked, so we nearly missed the turning. | The teacher still has a pile of unmarked tests. | The table came out of the move unmarked. | The striker was unmarked and scored easily. | The soldier was buried in an unmarked grave. | Leave the unmarked boxes by the door.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective from «mark». In schools in the UK, «marking» means checking and scoring work; in the US people say «grading», so unmarked work is «ungraded». An unmarked grave is a respectful but sad phrase: nobody put a name on it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unreadable writing is so messy, faded or small that you cannot read it. 2) An unreadable book or text is so boring or badly written that it is hard to keep reading. 3) An unreadable face shows no feeling, so you cannot tell what the person thinks. 4) (computers) An unreadable file or disk cannot be opened by the computer.
its sense in the lessons: Used about handwriting, old letters, books, faces in stories and broken files. Phrases: «almost unreadable», «an unreadable expression».
examples from the lessons: The rain made the note unreadable. | The doctor's handwriting was unreadable. | The old gravestone was worn and unreadable. | The book was so dull it was unreadable. | Her face was unreadable as she opened the letter. | The memory stick was damaged and the files were unreadable.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: «readable». Similar to «illegible», which is only about handwriting or print. An unreadable face is a calm, blank face: it does not mean the person is angry.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An untreated illness or injury has not been given medical care. 2) Untreated water, sewage or materials have not been cleaned or processed with chemicals. 3) Untreated wood has not been painted or protected.
its sense in the lessons: Used in health («left untreated»), science and environment («untreated sewage flowed into the river»), and DIY. It warns the reader of danger or harm.
examples from the lessons: Left untreated, the cut became infected. | The cough got worse because it went untreated. | Untreated water can carry germs. | Untreated sewage was pumped into the sea. | Untreated wood will rot in the rain. | Tooth decay can cause pain if it is untreated.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Common phrase: «if left untreated» (if nobody gives care). Not the same as «mistreated» (treated badly or cruelly).

meaning for a pupil: 1) To untwist something is to turn it the other way so it is no longer twisted.
its sense in the lessons: Used about wires, ropes, lids, bags, threads and DNA models in science; in crafts and everyday life.
examples from the lessons: Untwist the wire to open the bag of bread. | She untwisted the lid of the jar. | The rope slowly untwisted as it hung. | Untwist the cable before you plug it in. | He untwisted the paper clip to make a hook. | In the model, the two strands of DNA untwist.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Opposite: «twist». Similar: «unscrew» (for lids), «unwind» (for string or thread).

meaning for a pupil: 1) To unzip something is to open its zip (US: zipper). 2) (computers) To unzip a file is to open a compressed (zipped) file so you can use what is inside.
its sense in the lessons: Used about coats, bags, tents and pencil cases; in computing lessons about files.
examples from the lessons: Unzip your coat when you come inside. | She unzipped her pencil case and took out a pen. | The tent was unzipped and the cold came in. | He unzipped his backpack to find his lunch. | Download the folder and unzip it. | The game files must be unzipped before you can play.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double «p» in «unzipped», «unzipping». British English «zip»; American «zipper», but both say «unzip». Opposite: «zip up». A zipped file is smaller; unzipping makes it full size again.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Uric means to do with urine (wee). It is used mainly in «uric acid», a waste chemical made in the body and taken out in urine.
its sense in the lessons: Used in science and medicine: «uric acid». Too much uric acid can cause gout, a painful joint illness; bird droppings are white because of uric acid.
examples from the lessons: Uric acid is a waste product made by the body. | Bird droppings are white because they contain uric acid. | The doctor tested the man's blood for uric acid. | Too much uric acid can cause gout in the toes. | Reptiles get rid of waste as uric acid to save water. | The kidneys help remove uric acid from the blood.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced YOOR-ik. A science word, almost only in «uric acid». Related: «urine», «urinary».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Usable means able to be used, or in a good enough state to be used.
its sense in the lessons: Used about tools, rooms, space, objects and data: «still usable», «usable space», «usable water». In maths problems it tells you how much can actually be used.
examples from the lessons: The old bike is rusty but still usable. | Only half of the paper was usable after the spill. | We cleared the shed to make it usable again. | The garden has 20 square metres of usable space. | Is this pencil usable, or is it too short? | After the storm, the road was not usable for cars.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Usable» is the usual spelling; «useable» is also seen. Not the same as «useful»: something can be usable but not useful for your task. In maths, «usable» parts are often total minus broken parts: 30 tiles, 4 cracked, 26 usable.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Variegated leaves or flowers have patches, stripes or edges of different colours, often green and white or yellow. 2) Variegated means having many different colours or kinds.
its sense in the lessons: Used in gardening and science about plants («variegated ivy», «variegated leaves»), and sometimes about yarn, stones or animals.
examples from the lessons: The variegated ivy has green and cream leaves. | Grandma grows a variegated holly with yellow edges. | Variegated plants need lots of light. | The shop sold variegated wool in many colours. | We drew a variegated leaf in science. | The snake had variegated scales of brown and gold.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced VAIR-ee-uh-gay-tid. A rather technical word; everyday speech says «striped», «patchy» or «multicoloured». In science: white patches have less chlorophyll, so they cannot make food from light.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Verifiable means able to be checked and shown to be true or false.
its sense in the lessons: Used in science, news and research lessons: «verifiable facts», «a verifiable source». It teaches pupils to tell checked facts from rumours and opinions.
examples from the lessons: Use verifiable facts in your report. | Is that claim verifiable, or is it just a rumour? | A good scientist makes verifiable predictions. | The website gives no verifiable source for its story. | Your age is verifiable from your birth certificate. | A fact is verifiable; an opinion is not.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «verify» (to check that something is true). Verifiable does not mean already proved true: it means it CAN be checked. A verifiable claim may turn out to be false.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A veterinarian is a doctor who looks after sick and injured animals and helps keep them healthy.
its sense in the lessons: Used about pets, farms and zoos; in stories and jobs lessons. Mostly American and Canadian; in the UK, Ireland, Australia and New Zealand people usually say «vet». Phrases: «take the dog to the veterinarian».
examples from the lessons: The veterinarian gave our puppy its first injections. | My aunt is a veterinarian who works with horses. | The farmer called the veterinarian when the cow was ill. | Zoo veterinarians look after lions and elephants. | To become a veterinarian you study for many years. | The veterinarian checked the cat's teeth and ears. | We took the injured bird to a veterinarian.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Long word: vet-er-ih-NAIR-ee-un. Short form «vet» is used everywhere and is the usual word in the UK and Australia; the formal British word is «veterinary surgeon». Do not confuse «vet» (animal doctor) with «vet» short for «veteran» (a former soldier, US).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A viceroy is a person sent by a king or queen to rule a country or colony in their name. 2) The viceroy is also the name of an orange North American butterfly that looks like the monarch.
its sense in the lessons: Used in history lessons about empires: the Viceroy of India under British rule, Spanish viceroys in Mexico and Peru. It tells the reader that the real ruler was far away.
examples from the lessons: The Viceroy of India lived in a huge palace in Delhi. | The king sent a viceroy to govern the colony. | Spanish viceroys ruled Mexico for nearly three hundred years. | Lord Mountbatten was the last Viceroy of India in 1947. | The people had to obey the viceroy's orders. | A viceroy butterfly looks a lot like a monarch butterfly.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced VICE-roy. «Vice» here means «in place of», as in «vice-captain»; «roy» comes from French «roi», king. Not to be confused with «vice» meaning a bad habit.

meaning for a pupil: 1) VII is the Roman numeral for 7 (V = 5, plus I + I = 2). 2) It is used in names of kings, queens and popes, like Henry VII, said «Henry the Seventh».
its sense in the lessons: Used in maths lessons on Roman numerals, on clock faces, in chapter and book numbers, film sequels and in history (Henry VII, Edward VII).
examples from the lessons: VII means seven. | Henry VII was the first Tudor king of England. | The clock shows VII instead of 7. | Chapter VII begins with a storm. | V plus II makes VII. | Edward VII was king after Queen Victoria. | Write 7 in Roman numerals: VII.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Not an English word but a number in Roman letters; usually written in capitals (VII), sometimes small (vii) for page numbers in the front of a book. Rule: a smaller numeral after a bigger one is added: V + I + I = 7. Do not read it as a word «vee». In names it is said «the Seventh».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Virgo is a large constellation (a group of stars) whose name is Latin for «the virgin» or «young woman». 2) Virgo is one of the twelve signs of the zodiac used in astrology, for people born from about 23 August to 22 September. 3) (informal) A Virgo is a person born under that sign.
its sense in the lessons: Used in science and space lessons (constellations, the bright star Spica) and in horoscopes in magazines. Astronomy is science; astrology (star signs telling your future) is not science.
examples from the lessons: Virgo is one of the biggest constellations in the sky. | The bright star Spica is in Virgo. | My birthday is in September, so my star sign is Virgo. | My sister is a Virgo and loves things tidy. | The Virgo cluster contains thousands of galaxies. | The horoscope for Virgo said I would have a lucky day.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Written with a capital V. Pronounced VUR-go. Star signs are fun but not science: there is no evidence they decide anyone's character or future. Plural for people: «Virgos».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Vulnerability is being easy to hurt, harm or attack, in body or feelings. 2) A vulnerability is a weak point that could let something bad happen. 3) (computers) A vulnerability is a weakness in a program that hackers could use. 4) Vulnerability can also mean being open and honest about your feelings, even when it is hard.
its sense in the lessons: Used in safety and wellbeing lessons (showing your feelings is brave), in computing (security vulnerabilities), in science (vulnerability of species), and in stories (a hero's weak spot).
examples from the lessons: The castle's vulnerability was its weak back gate. | Babies and old people have a greater vulnerability to cold. | Achilles' heel was his only vulnerability. | The update fixed a vulnerability in the app. | Talking about your worries shows vulnerability, and that takes courage. | Islands have a vulnerability to rising seas. | The team found the vulnerability in the other side's defence.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: «vulnerable». Plural «vulnerabilities» for several weak points. Vulnerability is not the same as weakness of character: showing feelings can be a strength.

part of speech: noun (a waffle, waffles; waffle — uncountable for talk); verb (waffle, waffles, waffled, waffling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A waffle is a crisp flat cake made of batter, cooked in a hot iron that gives it a grid of little squares. 2) (UK, informal) Waffle is long talk or writing that says very little. 3) (UK, informal) To waffle is to talk or write too much without saying anything useful. 4) (US, informal) To waffle is to keep changing your mind and not decide.
its sense in the lessons: Used for breakfast food (with syrup, berries, ice cream), and by teachers about essays: «Don't waffle — get to the point».
examples from the lessons: We had waffles with maple syrup for breakfast. | Belgian waffles are thick and soft inside. | My teacher said my essay was full of waffle. | Stop waffling and answer the question! | He waffled on for ages about his holiday. | The mayor waffled about whether to close the park. | The waffle iron leaves a pattern of squares.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Two meanings in one spelling: food, and empty talk. The UK sense «waffle on» means talking too long; the US sense means being unsure. Food plural: «waffles». The talk sense is uncountable: «a lot of waffle», not «waffles».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A waterway is a river, canal or other stretch of water that boats can travel along.
its sense in the lessons: Used in geography and history: canals in Britain, the Mississippi, the St Lawrence Seaway, Venice; trade and transport before railways.
examples from the lessons: The canal was an important waterway for carrying coal. | Boats carry goods along the waterways of Europe. | The Mississippi is a busy American waterway. | Rubbish in waterways harms fish and birds. | Venice has many narrow waterways instead of streets. | The town grew up beside a great waterway.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Compound of «water» + «way». Countable. Not every river is a waterway in this sense: it must be usable by boats.

part of speech: noun (weaving; uncountable; a weaving — a woven piece); verb form (-ing form of weave: weave, weaves, wove/weaved, woven/weaved, weaving)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Weaving is making cloth by crossing threads over and under each other on a loom. 2) A weaving is a piece of cloth or art made this way. 3) Weaving means moving in and out between things, like a car or runner going around others.
its sense in the lessons: Used in art and history lessons (looms, the Industrial Revolution, Aboriginal and Māori weaving with flax), in science (birds weaving nests), and in action descriptions (weaving through traffic).
examples from the lessons: We did paper weaving in art class. | Weaving was done by hand before the factories came. | Māori weaving uses flax from New Zealand. | The weaver bird is weaving a nest of grass. | The cyclist was weaving through the traffic. | She hung her weaving on the classroom wall. | The footballer went weaving past three defenders.
note for the reader of a maths problem: For cloth the past is «wove», «woven»; for moving in and out it is usually «weaved»: «He weaved through the crowd». Do not confuse with «waving» (moving your hand).

meaning for a pupil: 1) To wend your way is to travel slowly, often following a winding path.
its sense in the lessons: Literary; used almost only in «wend your way». It gives a story an old-fashioned, gentle feeling.
examples from the lessons: The travellers wended their way through the forest. | We wended our way home after the fair. | The river wends its way to the sea. | The children wended their way up the hill. | Slowly the parade wended its way down the street. | The old man wended his way to the village shop.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Old and literary. The old past tense of «wend» was «went», which became the past tense of «go». Today the past is «wended». Do not confuse with «wind» (rhymes with «find») meaning to twist and turn, though the ideas are close.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Wetness is the state of being wet, covered in or full of water or another liquid.
its sense in the lessons: Used in science (absorbency tests, weather), in baby care, in describing weather and places.
examples from the lessons: The wetness of the grass soaked our shoes. | We tested which paper towel took away the most wetness. | The nappy has a line that changes colour to show wetness. | The wetness of the cave made the walls shine. | Sponges hold wetness inside their holes. | She could feel the wetness of the rain through her coat.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: no plural. Usually we just say «wet»: «The grass is wet». Opposite: «dryness».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A whim is a sudden wish or idea to do something, often without a good reason.
its sense in the lessons: Used in stories and everyday talk: «on a whim», «at the whim of», «a passing whim». It tells the reader that a choice was sudden and not planned.
examples from the lessons: On a whim, we went to the beach after school. | She bought the hat on a whim. | The king changed the laws at his every whim. | Sailors were at the whim of the weather. | It was just a whim, and he forgot about it the next day. | Don't spend all your money on a whim.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Adjective: «whimsical» (playful, odd). «At the whim of» means controlled by someone's sudden wishes.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A whorl is a pattern of curved lines that go round and round, like a spiral. 2) In fingerprints, a whorl is a circle or spiral pattern in the middle of the print. 3) In plants, a whorl is a ring of leaves or petals growing around a stem at the same point. 4) A whorl is one turn of a shell's spiral.
its sense in the lessons: Used in science (fingerprints in forensic investigation, plant structure, shells) and art. Fingerprint types: arches, loops and whorls.
examples from the lessons: My thumbprint has a whorl in the middle. | Fingerprints have loops, arches and whorls. | The snail shell has five whorls. | The leaves grow in a whorl around the stem. | The wood showed whorls where the branches had been. | She painted a whorl of blue and white in the sky.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced «whurl» or «wawl», rhymes with «world» without the d in many accents. Do not confuse with «whirl» (to spin fast) or «world».

part of speech: noun (a wildflower, wildflowers; also written wild flower)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A wildflower is a flower that grows naturally without being planted by people.
its sense in the lessons: Used in nature, science and environment lessons: wildflower meadows help bees and butterflies; in the countryside code (do not pick protected wildflowers).
examples from the lessons: The field was full of poppies and other wildflowers. | We planted a wildflower patch for the bees. | Bluebells are wildflowers that grow in woods. | Please don't pick wildflowers in the national park. | We drew wildflowers in our nature journals. | Australia has many wildflowers that grow nowhere else.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Written as one word or two: «wildflower», «wild flower». Countable. «Wild» means not grown or kept by people.

part of speech: noun (a windmill, windmills); verb (windmill, windmills, windmilled — rare, to swing arms round)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A windmill is a building with large sails that the wind turns to grind grain or pump water. 2) A windmill is also a modern tall tower with blades that makes electricity (more exactly a wind turbine). 3) A windmill is a toy on a stick with paper or plastic blades that spin in the wind (UK: a pinwheel or windmill).
its sense in the lessons: Used in science and energy lessons (renewable energy, wind power), history (flour mills, the Netherlands), and stories («Don Quixote tilting at windmills»).
examples from the lessons: The old windmill ground wheat into flour. | The Netherlands is famous for its windmills. | Windmills on the farm pump water for the cattle. | The hills are covered with modern windmills making electricity. | We made a paper windmill in science. | The sails of the windmill turned slowly. | Wind power is a clean source of energy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Compound: wind + mill. Strictly, machines that make electricity are «wind turbines», but people often call them windmills. In America a toy windmill is a «pinwheel».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A windsock is a cloth tube on a pole that fills with wind and shows which way and how strongly the wind is blowing.
its sense in the lessons: Used at airports, airfields and on boats; in weather and science lessons about measuring wind.
examples from the lessons: The windsock shows the pilot which way the wind blows. | When the windsock stands straight out, the wind is strong. | We made a windsock for our school weather station. | The windsock hung limp because there was no wind. | Airports have bright orange windsocks. | A windsock points away from where the wind comes from.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Compound: wind + sock. Trap: the windsock points in the direction the wind is going TO; a «north wind» blows FROM the north, so the windsock points south.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Wordplay is a clever or funny use of words, such as puns, rhymes or words with two meanings.
its sense in the lessons: Used in English lessons and jokes: puns, riddles, tongue twisters, spoonerisms, crossword clues; writers like Roald Dahl and Lewis Carroll use a lot of wordplay.
examples from the lessons: The joke «Why was six afraid of seven? Because seven eight nine» uses wordplay. | Roald Dahl loved wordplay and invented new words. | The riddle depended on wordplay. | Crossword clues often use wordplay. | Our class wrote poems full of wordplay. | The comedian's wordplay made everyone groan and laugh.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «a lot of wordplay», not «wordplays». A single example is «a pun» or «a play on words».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Yellowish means a little yellow, or partly yellow.
its sense in the lessons: Used in describing colours in art, science (yellowish liquid in experiments, yellowish leaves when a plant lacks water or light) and health (yellowish skin can be a sign of illness).
examples from the lessons: The old paper had turned yellowish. | The leaves went yellowish without enough sunlight. | The sky had a yellowish glow before the storm. | The liquid in the test tube was yellowish. | The bruise turned yellowish as it healed. | A yellowish-green frog sat on the leaf.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The ending «-ish» means «a bit»: reddish, greenish, yellowish. No double «l» problem: yellow + ish.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Yiddish is a language spoken by many Jewish people, especially those whose families came from Central and Eastern Europe. It grew from German with words from Hebrew and Slavic languages and is written in Hebrew letters.
its sense in the lessons: Used in history, culture and language lessons; English has borrowed many Yiddish words, such as «glitch», «schmooze», «klutz», «chutzpah», «bagel».
examples from the lessons: My great-grandmother spoke Yiddish at home. | «Klutz» comes from Yiddish and means a clumsy person. | Yiddish is written with Hebrew letters. | Many Yiddish speakers lived in Poland before the Second World War. | There are Yiddish newspapers in New York. | The song was sung in Yiddish.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Written with a capital Y. It is a language, not a religion. Yiddish and Hebrew are different languages, though both use Hebrew letters.

part of speech: noun (yin; uncountable; usually in «yin and yang»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (Chinese philosophy) Yin is the dark, cool, quiet, soft side in the old Chinese idea of yin and yang: two opposite forces that balance each other in everything. 2) (Mandarin, pinyin) «yīn» is a Chinese syllable with several meanings, for example «shady, cloudy» or «sound».
its sense in the lessons: Used in lessons on world beliefs and Chinese culture, and in everyday talk: «they are the yin and yang of the team» means they are opposites that fit together. The yin-yang symbol is a circle of black and white parts.
examples from the lessons: Yin and yang show how opposites balance each other. | In the symbol, yin is the dark part and yang is the light part. | Night is linked with yin, and day with yang. | The twins are the yin and yang of our class: one quiet, one loud. | Each half of the yin-yang symbol has a small dot of the other colour. | The teacher explained yin and yang in our lesson about China.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A loanword from Mandarin Chinese, pronounced like English «yin» (rhymes with «tin»). Almost always paired: «yin and yang». In Scotland «yin» can also be dialect for «one» («that wee yin»).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A yogi is a person who practises yoga a lot, especially as a teacher or a religious or spiritual person in Hinduism. 2) (informal) A yogi is someone who loves doing yoga. 3) Yogi Bear is a cartoon bear, and Yogi Berra was a famous American baseball player (a name).
its sense in the lessons: Used in lessons on religions of India and on health and exercise.
examples from the lessons: The yogi sat cross-legged and meditated for hours. | In India, some yogis live simple lives in the mountains. | My aunt is a real yogi; she does yoga every morning. | The yogi taught us how to breathe slowly. | Yogi Bear loves stealing picnic baskets. | The yogi could hold the pose for a long time.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From Sanskrit. Pronounced YOH-gee. Plural «yogis». A woman yogi is sometimes called a «yogini».

meaning for a pupil: 1) «Aah» is a sound you make when you feel relief, pleasure or calm. 2) «Aah» shows that you suddenly understand something. 3) «Aah» is the sound people make at something sweet, like a baby or a kitten. 4) «Aah» is the sound a doctor asks you to make so they can see your throat.
its sense in the lessons: Used in speech, comics and stories to show feelings: «Aah, that's better», «Aah, now I see!». The written number of a's shows how long the sound is.
examples from the lessons: «Aah, a nice cold drink!» said Dad. | Aah, now I understand the sum. | Everyone went «aah» when they saw the puppy. | «Open wide and say aah,» said the dentist. | She sank into the warm bath. «Aah.» | Aah, there you are! I've been looking for you.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling of a sound, not a fixed word; also written «ah» or «ahh». Not to be confused with «argh» or «aargh» (a cry of pain or annoyance).

meaning for a pupil: 1) An aardwolf is a small striped animal of southern and eastern Africa, related to the hyena, that eats mainly termites.
its sense in the lessons: Used in science lessons about animals, food chains and adaptation; it licks up thousands of termites each night with its long sticky tongue.
examples from the lessons: The aardwolf eats termites, not big animals. | An aardwolf can eat over 200,000 termites in one night. | The aardwolf looks like a small striped hyena. | Aardwolves sleep in burrows during the day. | The aardwolf has very small teeth. | We read about the aardwolf in our book of African animals.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced ARD-wolf. Name means «earth wolf» in Afrikaans, but it is not a wolf. Plural «aardwolves» (like wolf, wolves). Not the same as the «aardvark», a different termite-eating animal.

part of speech: noun (an ab, abs — informal); abbreviation (ab, AB)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) An ab is one of the stomach muscles; people usually say «abs», short for «abdominal muscles». 2) AB is a blood group (type AB). 3) (abbreviation) Ab can stand for other things, such as Alberta in Canadian addresses (AB) or «able seaman» (AB) on ships. 4) (Latin) «ab» means «from», as in «ab initio» (from the beginning).
its sense in the lessons: Used in PE and health lessons («ab exercises», «work your abs»), in science about blood groups, and in addresses.
examples from the lessons: Sit-ups make your abs stronger. | The PE teacher showed us an ab stretch. | The superhero had big muscles and six-pack abs. | My blood group is AB. | People with type AB blood can receive blood from any group. | The parcel was sent to Calgary, AB.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly a clipped form of «abdominal»; usually plural «abs». «Six-pack» is slang for clearly visible stomach muscles. As a blood group it is written in capitals: AB. Not a full English word on its own in normal writing.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An abuser is a person who hurts, frightens or treats another person or an animal badly, often again and again. 2) An abuser is also someone who uses something in a harmful or wrong way, for example drugs or alcohol, or their power.
its sense in the lessons: Used in safety and wellbeing lessons, news and law. It tells the reader that someone is causing harm; safety lessons teach that harm is never the child's fault and that you should tell a trusted adult.
examples from the lessons: The animal shelter rescued the dog from its abuser. | No one has the right to hurt you; tell a trusted adult about any abuser. | The abuser was sent to prison. | Some people who were hurt are afraid to speak about their abuser. | A drug abuser needs help and treatment. | The law protects children from abusers. | The king was an abuser of his power.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «abuse» (verb: a-BYOOZ; noun: a-BYOOSS). Countable. A serious word: in safety lessons, if anyone hurts you or makes you feel unsafe, tell a trusted adult, teacher or call a helpline such as Childline (UK) or Kids Helpline (Australia).

meaning for a pupil: 1) «acc.» is a short form of «account», as in a bank account. 2) «acc.» is short for «accusative», a grammar case in languages like German, Latin and Ukrainian. 3) «acc» can be short for «according (to)», «accompanied» or «accommodation» in notes and ads. 4) (informal, online) «acc» is short for «account» (an online account) or «actually» in texting: «I acc love this song».
its sense in the lessons: Seen in bank statements, grammar books, notes, ads and text messages. It is not a word you say aloud.
examples from the lessons: Acc. no. 12345 is printed on the bank card. | In German, «den» is the acc. form of «der». | Ads say «acc. for 4 people» for a holiday cottage. | Log in to your acc to play the game. | «I acc finished my homework,» she texted. | In the music, «acc.» can mark the accompaniment.
note for the reader of a maths problem: An abbreviation, not a full word. Write the full word in schoolwork. «acct» is another short form of «account».

part of speech: noun (acceleration; uncountable; an acceleration — one case)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Acceleration is getting faster: the speed going up. 2) (science) Acceleration is how quickly speed (or velocity) changes; slowing down is a negative acceleration (deceleration). 3) Acceleration is how quickly a car can speed up. 4) Acceleration is also any speeding up of a process: the acceleration of climate change.
its sense in the lessons: Used in science lessons on forces and motion (Newton's laws, gravity makes falling objects accelerate), cars and sport (sprinters), and in maths (change of speed per second).
examples from the lessons: The rocket's acceleration pushed the astronauts into their seats. | Gravity gives falling objects an acceleration. | This sports car has amazing acceleration. | The sprinter's acceleration out of the blocks won the race. | A bigger force gives a bigger acceleration. | On the graph, a steeper line shows greater acceleration. | Scientists worry about the acceleration of ice melting.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: «accelerate». Double «c», one «l»: acceleration. In maths and science: acceleration = change in speed ÷ time. A car going from 0 to 20 metres per second in 4 seconds has an acceleration of 5 metres per second every second. Near Earth, falling objects accelerate at about 9.8 m/s². Constant speed means zero acceleration.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Accordingly means in a way that fits what has just been said or what is needed. 2) (formal) Accordingly means «so» or «therefore»; it links a reason to a result.
its sense in the lessons: Used in instructions («Read the rules and act accordingly»), formal writing, reports and exam texts. It tells the reader that an action follows from something already mentioned.
examples from the lessons: The weather will be cold, so dress accordingly. | You know the rules, so behave accordingly. | The bus was late; accordingly, we missed the start of the film. | Prices went up, and we changed our shopping list accordingly. | The recipe is for four people; if there are eight of you, double it accordingly. | He was the oldest, and he was treated accordingly.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal word. «According to» is different: it means «as said by» («According to the map, the park is near»). In maths, «adjust accordingly» means change the numbers in the same way, e.g. double all amounts.

part of speech: noun (an accordion, accordions); adjective use (accordion, as in accordion folds)
meaning for a pupil: 1) An accordion is a musical instrument you hold in your hands and squeeze in and out; the folding middle part pushes air through reeds while you press keys or buttons. 2) Accordion (before a noun) means folding in zigzags like an accordion: an accordion file, accordion pleats.
its sense in the lessons: Used in music lessons, folk music (Irish, French, German, Ukrainian, Cajun), and in crafts (accordion-fold paper books).
examples from the lessons: Grandad plays the accordion at parties. | The accordion has keys like a piano on one side. | A street musician was playing the accordion in Paris. | We made an accordion book by folding paper in zigzags. | The music of the accordion filled the dance hall. | She squeezed the accordion and a jolly tune came out.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: «accordion» ends in «-ion», not «-ian», though the player is an «accordionist». Double «c». A smaller similar instrument with buttons is a «concertina».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Acidity is how acidic something is: how strong an acid it is. 2) Acidity is the sour taste of acidic food like lemons. 3) (informal) Acidity can mean heartburn or too much acid in the stomach. 4) Acidity of words or a manner means sharpness or unkindness (literary).
its sense in the lessons: Used in science (the pH scale: below 7 is acidic; testing with litmus or red cabbage indicator), in gardening (soil acidity), environment (acid rain, ocean acidity), cooking and health.
examples from the lessons: We tested the acidity of lemon juice with indicator paper. | Vinegar has a high acidity. | The pH scale measures acidity. | Some plants need soil with high acidity. | The acidity of the oceans is rising as they absorb carbon dioxide. | The acidity of the orange made my mouth tingle. | Too much fizzy drink can cause acidity in the stomach.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Adjective: «acidic» or «acid». On the pH scale, a LOWER number means HIGHER acidity: pH 2 is more acidic than pH 5. Opposite: «alkalinity».

part of speech: adjective (acoustic); noun (acoustics, plural — the sound qualities of a room; an acoustic — informal, an acoustic guitar)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Acoustic means to do with sound or hearing. 2) An acoustic musical instrument makes sound without electric power, like an ordinary guitar or piano. 3) Acoustic music is played on such instruments, not electric ones. 4) (plural noun) Acoustics are how well sound carries in a room or hall.
its sense in the lessons: Used in science (sound waves, echoes), music (acoustic guitar, an acoustic version of a song), and buildings (concert hall acoustics).
examples from the lessons: She plays an acoustic guitar, not an electric one. | The band did an acoustic version of their hit song. | The hall has great acoustics, so everyone can hear. | Bats use acoustic signals to find food. | Acoustic panels on the wall stop echoes. | We learned about acoustic waves in science.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced a-KOO-stik. «Acoustics» (the qualities of a room) usually takes a plural verb: «The acoustics are good». As a science subject, «acoustics» is singular: «Acoustics is the study of sound».

meaning for a pupil: 1) To activate something is to make it start working, like a machine, alarm or account. 2) (science) To activate a process or chemical is to make it start or become active.
its sense in the lessons: Used about alarms, cards, accounts, apps, buttons, games and science (yeast is activated by warm water). In instructions: «Press to activate».
examples from the lessons: The smoke activated the fire alarm. | Press the red button to activate the robot. | You need to activate your new library card. | Warm water activates the yeast in bread. | The trap is activated when someone steps on it. | Sunlight activates the solar lamp. | The hero activated the shield just in time.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Noun: «activation». Opposite: «deactivate», «switch off». More formal than «turn on» or «start».

part of speech: noun (activation; uncountable; an activation — one case)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Activation is making something start working or become active.
its sense in the lessons: Used about cards, accounts, alarms and software («activation code»), and in science (activation of yeast, enzymes, the immune system).
examples from the lessons: The activation code is printed on the back of the card. | Activation of the alarm takes ten seconds. | The new phone needs activation before you can use it. | Heat starts the activation of the yeast. | The game key worked and activation was quick. | Activation of the airbag happens in a split second.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun from «activate». Mostly uncountable. Formal or technical word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Adhesion is the sticking of one thing to another. 2) (science) Adhesion is the force that makes different substances cling together, like water droplets on glass. 3) (medicine, an adhesion, adhesions) An adhesion is tissue inside the body that sticks parts together after an operation or injury.
its sense in the lessons: Used in science (water climbing up a paper towel, glue), engineering (tyre adhesion to a road) and medicine. Compare «cohesion» (water sticking to water).
examples from the lessons: Glue works by adhesion. | Water drops stay on the window because of adhesion. | Wet roads reduce the adhesion of tyres. | Sticky notes have weak adhesion so you can peel them off. | Adhesion helps water move up plant stems. | The tape lost its adhesion in the rain.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable in the science sense. Verb: «adhere» (to stick). Adjective/noun: «adhesive» (glue). Trap: adhesion is different things sticking together; cohesion is the same thing sticking to itself.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An advertiser is a person or company that pays to show adverts (ads) to tell people about something they want to sell. 2) «The Advertiser» is a name used by some newspapers (a name).
its sense in the lessons: Used in media literacy lessons: advertisers try to persuade you to buy; they pay websites, TV channels and YouTubers. It teaches pupils to ask who is trying to sell what.
examples from the lessons: Advertisers pay a lot to show ads during big football matches. | The advertiser wants children to want the new toy. | Some videos are paid for by advertisers. | Advertisers use bright colours and catchy songs. | The magazine lost an advertiser after the complaint. | Ask yourself what the advertiser wants you to believe.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «advertise». Not the same as an «advert» or «advertisement» (the ad itself). In maths problems, the advertiser usually pays a cost per advert or per day.

part of speech: noun (an adze, adzes; also spelled adz in the US)
meaning for a pupil: 1) An adze is an old cutting tool like an axe, but with its blade set across the handle, used for shaping wood.
its sense in the lessons: Used in history lessons (Stone Age tools, Māori and Pacific canoe makers, shipbuilders), and woodwork.
examples from the lessons: The Stone Age people made an adze from stone. | Māori carvers used a toki, a kind of adze. | The shipbuilder shaped the beam with an adze. | An adze blade is turned sideways, unlike an axe. | The museum has a polished stone adze. | He swung the adze to smooth the log.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced like «adds». US spelling «adz». Not the same as an axe: an axe's blade is in line with the handle; an adze's blade is across it, like a hoe.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Afrikaans is a language spoken in South Africa and Namibia. It grew from Dutch brought by settlers in the 1600s, with words from Malay, Portuguese, Khoekhoe and other languages.
its sense in the lessons: Used in geography and language lessons about South Africa (one of its official languages). English took some words from it: «aardvark», «trek», «meerkat».
examples from the lessons: Afrikaans is one of South Africa's official languages. | «Dankie» means «thank you» in Afrikaans. | The word «aardvark» comes from Afrikaans and means «earth pig». | My friend from Cape Town speaks English and Afrikaans. | Afrikaans is closely related to Dutch. | We listened to a song in Afrikaans.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Written with a capital A. Pronounced af-ri-KAHNS. A person who speaks it as their family language may be called an Afrikaner (mainly for white Afrikaans speakers), but many people of colour also speak Afrikaans.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Aggregation is bringing many things together into one group or total. 2) An aggregation is a group or mass of things, animals or people gathered together. 3) (formal, data) Aggregation is combining many numbers into one, such as a total or an average.
its sense in the lessons: Used in science (an aggregation of ladybirds, fish shoals), maths and data (aggregation of scores), and websites that collect news from many sources (news aggregation).
examples from the lessons: An aggregation of ladybirds spent the winter under the bark. | The website is an aggregation of news from many papers. | Aggregation of the test scores gave the class average. | A huge aggregation of jellyfish washed up on the beach. | The report used aggregation, so no single pupil's mark is shown. | Cities are an aggregation of many small communities.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal word. Verb: «aggregate». In maths, aggregation often means adding up (a total) or finding an average; check which one the problem means.

part of speech: noun (agitation; uncountable; an agitation — a campaign)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Agitation is a worried, nervous or upset feeling that makes you restless. 2) Agitation is shaking or stirring something, such as a liquid. 3) Agitation is public campaigning or protest to make people demand change.
its sense in the lessons: Used in stories to show feelings («in great agitation, she paced the room»), in science (agitation of a mixture helps it dissolve), and in history (agitation for votes for women).
examples from the lessons: He paced up and down in agitation. | Her agitation grew as the clock ticked. | The dog showed signs of agitation during the fireworks. | Agitation helps the sugar dissolve faster. | The washing machine cleans clothes by agitation. | There was agitation in the streets for fairer laws.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: «agitate». Adjective: «agitated» (worried and restless). In science, agitation = stirring or shaking, which speeds up dissolving.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An agouti is a rodent of Central and South America, with long legs, like a large guinea pig, that eats fruit and nuts. 2) Agouti is also a fur colour pattern where each hair has bands of light and dark, common in wild rabbits and mice.
its sense in the lessons: Used in science lessons about rainforests, seed dispersal (agoutis bury Brazil nuts that later grow into trees), and genetics of animal colours.
examples from the lessons: The agouti buried a Brazil nut in the forest floor. | Agoutis can crack very hard nuts with their sharp teeth. | Some buried nuts are forgotten and grow into new trees. | The agouti ran into the bushes when it heard us. | Our pet rabbit has agouti fur, like a wild rabbit. | Agoutis live in the rainforests of South America.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced a-GOO-tee. Plural «agoutis». It is a real animal, not a made-up one.

meaning for a pupil: 1) If a ship runs aground or goes aground, it gets stuck on sand, rocks or the sea bottom in shallow water.
its sense in the lessons: Used in stories, news and history about ships and boats: «ran aground», «was aground», «went aground on a sandbank». It tells the reader a ship is stuck and maybe in danger.
examples from the lessons: The ship ran aground on a sandbank. | The huge container ship went aground in the canal. | At low tide the little boat was left aground. | Rescuers helped the sailors when their boat ran aground. | The pirates' ship was aground on the rocks. | They waited for the high tide to float the ship that had gone aground.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Used with «run», «go», «be». Not used before a noun. Not the same as «on the ground». Opposite: «afloat».

meaning for a pupil: 1) An ailment is an illness, usually a minor one, like a cold, cough or rash.
its sense in the lessons: Used in health and history lessons (old remedies for common ailments), in pharmacies, and in stories. It is softer and more formal than «illness» or «disease».
examples from the lessons: Colds and coughs are common winter ailments. | Grandma had a herbal remedy for every ailment. | The pharmacist can help with minor ailments. | The puppy's ailment turned out to be a sore paw. | In the old days, people used honey to treat many ailments. | Tummy aches are a common ailment among children.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Verb «ail» (old: to make ill): «What ails you?». An ailment is usually not serious; a «disease» can be serious.

part of speech: noun (an airdrop, airdrops); verb (airdrop, airdrops, airdropped, airdropping)
meaning for a pupil: 1) An airdrop is sending food, medicine or other supplies by dropping them from an aircraft, often by parachute. 2) To airdrop something is to drop it from a plane to people on the ground. 3) (computers, AirDrop) AirDrop is an Apple feature for sending photos or files to a nearby device; people say «airdrop it to me».
its sense in the lessons: Used in news about disasters and wars (aid airdropped to people cut off), in history (the Berlin airlift), in video games, and in everyday tech talk.
examples from the lessons: The army made an airdrop of food to the flooded villages. | Medicine was airdropped to the cut-off town. | Parachutes slowed the boxes in the airdrop. | In the game, an airdrop brings new supplies. | Can you airdrop me that photo? | Airdrops can help when roads are blocked by snow.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double «p» in «airdropped», «airdropping». As the Apple brand it is written «AirDrop». Safety: only accept AirDrop files from people you know.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To allege something is to say it is true, especially that someone did something wrong, without proving it yet.
its sense in the lessons: Used in news and law: «police allege», «it is alleged that». The adjective «alleged» shows that a claim has not been proved: «the alleged thief». It teaches pupils that an accusation is not proof.
examples from the lessons: The newspaper alleges that the mayor broke the rules. | The boy alleged that his sister had taken his sweets. | Police allege the man stole a car. | It is alleged that the money went missing. | The alleged thief said he was innocent. | She alleged she had seen a ghost, but nobody believed her.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced a-LEDGE. Spelling trap: no «d» before the «g» — «allege», not «alledge». A person is innocent until proved guilty; «alleged» reminds us of that. Noun: «allegation».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Alternately means first one thing, then the other, again and again, taking turns.
its sense in the lessons: Used in maths patterns (red and blue beads placed alternately), instructions in cooking and crafts, PE and stories («she was alternately laughing and crying»).
examples from the lessons: Thread red and blue beads alternately. | The light flashed red and green alternately. | We took turns alternately to read a page. | She was alternately happy and sad all day. | Plant the tulips and daffodils alternately. | Hop alternately on your left and right foot.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Confusing pair: «alternately» means taking turns (A, B, A, B); «alternatively» means «as another choice» («We could walk; alternatively, we could take the bus»). In maths: in a pattern placed alternately, items 1, 3, 5... are one kind and items 2, 4, 6... are the other; with 10 beads, 5 of each.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Amblyopia is an eye problem, often called «lazy eye», where one eye does not see clearly because the brain uses the other eye more.
its sense in the lessons: Used in health and science lessons about eyes and vision; children may wear an eye patch over the stronger eye to make the weaker one work harder.
examples from the lessons: Amblyopia is often called lazy eye. | She wore an eye patch to treat her amblyopia. | Amblyopia is best treated when a child is young. | Eye tests at school can find amblyopia early. | Glasses can help some children with amblyopia. | With amblyopia, the brain ignores the blurry eye.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced am-blee-OH-pee-uh. Medical word; everyday name «lazy eye». It is not laziness: the eye and brain have not learned to work together. Not the same as a squint (strabismus), though they can go together.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal, medical) To ambulate is to walk or move about.
its sense in the lessons: Used in hospitals and medical reports («The patient can ambulate with a frame»). In everyday life people say «walk».
examples from the lessons: After the operation, the patient began to ambulate with help. | The nurse helped Grandpa ambulate down the corridor. | He can now ambulate without crutches. | Patients are encouraged to ambulate soon after surgery. | The robot could ambulate on two legs. | The doctor checked how well she could ambulate.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal, medical word. Related: «ambulance» (originally a moving hospital), «ambulatory» (able to walk). Use «walk» in ordinary writing.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An ambusher is a person or animal that hides and waits to attack someone by surprise.
its sense in the lessons: Used in stories, history and nature lessons about predators (crocodiles and some spiders are ambushers that wait for prey).
examples from the lessons: The ambushers hid behind the rocks. | A crocodile is an ambusher that waits in the water. | The knights were attacked by ambushers in the forest. | Trapdoor spiders are clever ambushers. | The ambusher leapt out from behind the tree. | In the game, watch out for ambushers in the long grass.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «ambush». Countable. In science, an «ambush predator» waits for prey instead of chasing it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Amelioration is making something bad better, or the process of it getting better.
its sense in the lessons: Used in formal writing, history, science and exam texts: «amelioration of living conditions», «amelioration of the soil».
examples from the lessons: The new laws led to the amelioration of factory conditions. | Adding compost brings an amelioration of poor soil. | The doctors hoped for an amelioration of her symptoms. | The charity works for the amelioration of poverty. | There was a slow amelioration in the weather. | Better lighting was an amelioration for the old school.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Very formal; everyday speech says «improvement». Verb: «ameliorate». Pronounced a-meel-yuh-RAY-shun.

part of speech: verb (amend, amends, amended, amending); noun (amends — only in «make amends»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To amend something written, like a law, rule or document, is to change it a little to correct or improve it. 2) To make amends is to do something good to show you are sorry for a wrong you did.
its sense in the lessons: Used in law and civics (amending a constitution, the Amendments to the US Constitution), in schoolwork (amend your draft), and in stories about saying sorry.
examples from the lessons: The council voted to amend the rules for the park. | Please amend your story to add more detail. | The law was amended to protect wild birds. | The teacher amended my mark after checking again. | He made amends by fixing the broken fence. | She wanted to make amends for being unkind.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Noun «amendment» (a change to a law). «Amends» is always plural in «make amends». Not the same as «emend» (to correct a text, very formal).

meaning for a pupil: 1) To amuse someone is to make them laugh or smile. 2) To amuse someone is to keep them busy and interested so they do not get bored.
its sense in the lessons: Used in everyday life and stories: «amuse yourself», «keep the baby amused», «not amused» (annoyed). Adjective «amusing» (funny), noun «amusement» (amusement park, arcade).
examples from the lessons: The clown amused the children with silly tricks. | Her joke amused the whole class. | We amused ourselves with card games on the train. | The toys kept the baby amused for an hour. | The teacher was not amused when the frog jumped out. | Dad's funny voices always amuse me.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. «Amused» = feeling something is funny; «amusing» = causing laughter. «Not amused» is a polite way to say «annoyed».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) Anabolic means building up bigger molecules from smaller ones in the body, like building muscle and growing. 2) Anabolic steroids are drugs that build muscle; using them in sport is cheating and can harm health.
its sense in the lessons: Used in biology (anabolism, the opposite of catabolism), health and sport news about doping and banned drugs.
examples from the lessons: Growth is an anabolic process. | Anabolic reactions use energy to build new tissue. | The athlete was banned for taking anabolic steroids. | Anabolic steroids can damage the heart and liver. | Sleep helps the body's anabolic work of repair. | Building proteins from amino acids is anabolic.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Science word. Opposite: «catabolic» (breaking down). Anabolic steroids are not the same as steroid medicines like asthma inhalers or creams, which doctors give safely.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Anaemia is an illness where the blood does not have enough healthy red blood cells or iron, so the person feels very tired, weak and pale.
its sense in the lessons: Used in health, science and food lessons: iron in foods like spinach, beans, red meat and fortified cereals helps prevent anaemia.
examples from the lessons: The doctor said her tiredness was caused by anaemia. | Eating iron-rich foods helps prevent anaemia. | Anaemia can make your skin look pale. | Red blood cells carry oxygen, so anaemia makes you breathless. | Some people with anaemia take iron tablets. | A blood test showed he had anaemia.
note for the reader of a maths problem: British spelling «anaemia», American «anemia»; adjective «anaemic» / «anemic». Pronounced a-NEE-mee-uh. «Anaemic» is also used informally for something weak or pale: «an anaemic performance».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Analysis is studying something carefully by looking at its parts, to understand it or find out what it is made of. 2) An analysis is a report or piece of work that explains such careful study. 3) (science) Analysis is testing a substance to find out what is in it. 4) (maths) Analysis of data means looking for patterns, totals and averages.
its sense in the lessons: Used in science (analysing results), English (analysis of a poem or character), maths and data, sport (match analysis on TV), news. Phrases: «in the final analysis» (when everything is considered).
examples from the lessons: We did an analysis of our science results. | The detective's careful analysis solved the mystery. | Write an analysis of the main character. | Analysis of the water showed it was safe to drink. | The pundits gave their analysis after the match. | Data analysis showed most pupils walk to school. | In the final analysis, honesty mattered most.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «analyses» (an-AL-uh-seez). Verb: «analyse» (UK) / «analyze» (US). Person: «analyst». Adjective: «analytical». Analysis breaks into parts; «synthesis» puts parts together.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (old science) An animalcule is a tiny living thing that can only be seen with a microscope, such as a single-celled creature.
its sense in the lessons: Used in history of science: Antonie van Leeuwenhoek in the 1670s called the microbes he saw in his microscope «animalcules». Today scientists say «microorganisms» or «microbes».
examples from the lessons: Leeuwenhoek saw animalcules swimming in a drop of pond water. | The old book describes animalcules in rainwater. | Today we call animalcules microorganisms. | The scientist was amazed by the tiny animalcules. | Animalcules were the first microbes ever seen. | Under the lens, the animalcules wriggled about.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Old-fashioned word. Pronounced an-ih-MAL-kyool. It means «little animal», though many such creatures are not animals at all (e.g. bacteria).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Animosity is a strong feeling of dislike or anger towards someone, often lasting a long time.
its sense in the lessons: Used in stories, history and news about enemies, rivals and quarrels: «animosity between», «feel no animosity». It tells the reader that people strongly dislike each other.
examples from the lessons: There was animosity between the two rival teams. | The old animosity between the families lasted for years. | I feel no animosity towards you; let's be friends. | The argument left a lot of animosity in the class. | Peace talks tried to end the animosity between the countries. | The two cats watched each other with open animosity.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal word; everyday words: «hatred», «dislike», «hostility». Usually uncountable. Pronounced an-ih-MOS-ih-tee.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Annexation is when one country takes control of land that belonged to another country and makes it part of itself, often by force. 2) Annexation is also when a town or city joins nearby land to itself by law.
its sense in the lessons: Used in history and current affairs lessons: Russia's annexation of Crimea in 2014 was condemned by most countries at the United Nations as illegal; history has many annexations by empires.
examples from the lessons: Russia's annexation of Crimea in 2014 was not recognised by most countries. | The United Nations General Assembly voted that the vote used to justify the annexation was not valid. | The empire grew through the annexation of smaller kingdoms. | The city's annexation of the village made it bigger. | Many people protested against the annexation. | Annexation by force breaks international law.
