note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: «annex» (an-NEX); noun «an annex» or «annexe» (UK) also means an extra building joined to a main one. Annexation usually means one side took land without the other side's free agreement.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An antecedent is something that came before something else and led to it. 2) (grammar) An antecedent is the noun or phrase that a pronoun refers back to: in «Sam lost his hat», «Sam» is the antecedent of «his». 3) (plural, formal) Your antecedents are your ancestors or family background. 4) (formal adjective) Antecedent means coming before.
its sense in the lessons: Used in English grammar lessons (pronouns and their antecedents), history (antecedents of a war) and formal writing.
examples from the lessons: In «The dog wagged its tail», «dog» is the antecedent of «its». | Make sure every pronoun has a clear antecedent. | The bicycle's antecedent was a wooden walking machine. | The causes antecedent to the war were complicated. | His antecedents came from Ireland. | The penny-farthing was an antecedent of the modern bike.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal word. Pronounced an-tih-SEE-dent. Opposite idea: «consequence» or «successor». In grammar, an unclear antecedent confuses readers: «Tom told Ben he was late» — who was late?

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) Anterior means at or near the front, especially of the body. 2) (formal) Anterior means earlier in time.
its sense in the lessons: Used in biology and medicine (anterior and posterior: front and back; the anterior cruciate ligament, ACL, in the knee, often injured in sport), and very formal writing.
examples from the lessons: The head is at the anterior end of a worm. | The footballer hurt his anterior cruciate ligament. | Fish have anterior fins near the head. | The anterior part of the brain helps us plan. | The front legs are the anterior limbs. | The event was anterior to the war (formal).
note for the reader of a maths problem: Science word. Opposite: «posterior» (at the back). Do not confuse with «interior» (inside).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Antifungal means killing or stopping the growth of fungi, such as mould or the fungus that causes athlete's foot. 2) An antifungal is a medicine or cream that does this.
its sense in the lessons: Used in health (athlete's foot cream, treating ringworm and thrush), science (fungi, mould) and gardening.
examples from the lessons: The doctor gave him an antifungal cream for athlete's foot. | Antifungal medicine treats ringworm. | Some plants make antifungal chemicals to protect themselves. | The bathroom paint is antifungal to stop mould. | Antifungals do not work on bacteria. | Keep your feet dry and use an antifungal powder.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Anti-» means «against». Also written «anti-fungal». Antibiotics fight bacteria, antifungals fight fungi, antivirals fight viruses — they are not the same.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Apartheid was a system of laws in South Africa from 1948 to the early 1990s that kept people apart by race and gave white people power and rights that Black and other people of colour were denied. 2) Apartheid is also used for any system that separates and treats groups of people unequally by law.
its sense in the lessons: Used in history and citizenship lessons about racism, human rights and Nelson Mandela, who was in prison for 27 years for fighting apartheid and became president in 1994 after it ended.
examples from the lessons: Under apartheid, Black and white children went to separate schools. | Nelson Mandela fought against apartheid. | Apartheid ended in the early 1990s, and free elections were held in 1994. | Many countries refused to trade with South Africa because of apartheid. | Signs under apartheid said «Whites only». | People around the world protested against apartheid. | We learned how apartheid was unfair and cruel.
note for the reader of a maths problem: An Afrikaans word meaning «apartness»; pronounced a-PAR-tide or a-PAR-tate. Uncountable. Written with a small «a». When people today call another system «apartheid», it is often a disputed political claim, so lessons say who is saying it.

part of speech: noun (an apatosaurus, apatosauruses or apatosauri; as a genus name Apatosaurus)
meaning for a pupil: 1) An apatosaurus was a huge plant-eating dinosaur with a very long neck and long tail, which lived in North America about 150 million years ago.
its sense in the lessons: Used in science and dinosaur lessons, museums and story books. It was for a long time known as «brontosaurus»; scientists now treat Brontosaurus as a separate but close relative.
examples from the lessons: The apatosaurus was as long as two buses. | Apatosaurus ate leaves from tall trees and low plants. | We saw an apatosaurus skeleton at the museum. | Apatosaurus lived in the Jurassic period. | Its long tail may have cracked like a whip. | An apatosaurus weighed as much as several elephants.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced a-PAT-oh-SOR-us. Name means «deceptive lizard». As a scientific genus name it starts with a capital and is often in italics: Apatosaurus. Myth: the old idea that it lived in water to hold up its weight is wrong; it lived on land. Dinosaurs died out long before humans lived.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To appease someone is to calm them or stop them being angry by giving them what they want. 2) (history) To appease an aggressive country is to give in to its demands to avoid war. 3) To appease hunger or thirst is to satisfy it (formal).
its sense in the lessons: Used in history (appeasement of Hitler before the Second World War, the Munich Agreement 1938), stories and everyday life (appeasing a crying toddler). It often suggests giving in too easily.
examples from the lessons: Mum gave the toddler a biscuit to appease him. | The king tried to appease the angry crowd with gifts. | Britain and France tried to appease Hitler in 1938. | Giving in to a bully rarely appeases them for long. | The dragon could not be appeased with gold. | A sandwich appeased his hunger.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Noun: «appeasement». Often has a negative feel: it can mean giving in to bad behaviour.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An appendage is a part that sticks out from the main body, such as an arm, leg, tail, antenna or fin. 2) An appendage is something added to a bigger, more important thing.
its sense in the lessons: Used in science (insects have jointed appendages; crabs, lobsters, octopus arms), and sometimes in writing about less important attachments.
examples from the lessons: Insects have six legs and two antennae as appendages. | A lobster uses its front appendages to grab food. | The octopus has eight appendages called arms. | Fins are appendages that help fish swim. | The small shed was an appendage to the big house. | Some insects can regrow a lost appendage.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Not the same as the «appendix», a small tube in the body, though the words are related (both from «append», to attach).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Apt means suitable or just right for the situation. 2) If someone is apt to do something, they often tend to do it. 3) (old-fashioned) An apt pupil learns quickly.
its sense in the lessons: Used in English lessons («an apt word», «an apt description») and everyday speech («He is apt to forget»).
examples from the lessons: «Busy as a bee» is an apt description of my mum. | That was an apt name for such a fast dog. | The old door is apt to stick in wet weather. | Little brothers are apt to copy everything you do. | She was an apt pupil and learned to read quickly. | It is apt that the gardening club meets in spring.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Short and a bit formal. Noun «aptness», «aptitude» (natural talent). «Apt to» means «likely to» and usually is about a habit, often a bad one.

part of speech: verb (aquaplane, aquaplanes, aquaplaned, aquaplaning); noun (an aquaplane — old, a board pulled by a boat)
meaning for a pupil: 1) If a car aquaplanes, its tyres slide on a layer of water on a wet road and lose grip, so the driver cannot steer or brake well. 2) (old) An aquaplane was a board towed by a motorboat that a person stood on, like early water-skiing.
its sense in the lessons: Used in road safety and science about friction (water reduces grip). US English often says «hydroplane». Drivers slow down in heavy rain to avoid aquaplaning.
examples from the lessons: The car aquaplaned on the flooded road. | Slow down in heavy rain, or your car may aquaplane. | Worn tyres make aquaplaning more likely. | The lorry aquaplaned and slid into the hedge. | Water between the tyre and road reduces friction. | Road signs warn drivers about aquaplaning.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. «Aqua» means water. American English: «hydroplane». In science: less friction means less grip and longer stopping distances.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Architecture is the art and work of designing buildings. 2) Architecture is the style of buildings in a place or time, such as Gothic or Roman architecture. 3) (computers) The architecture of a computer or program is the way its parts are planned and put together.
its sense in the lessons: Used in art, history and design lessons (Roman arches, Gothic cathedrals, Victorian houses, skyscrapers), in computing, and in jobs (an architect designs buildings).
examples from the lessons: She wants to study architecture and design houses. | Gothic architecture has tall pointed windows. | We looked at the architecture of our town on a walk. | Sydney Opera House is famous modern architecture. | Ancient Roman architecture used arches and domes. | The computer's architecture lets it do many tasks at once. | The architecture of the castle made it hard to attack.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced AR-ki-tek-cher; «ch» sounds like «k». Uncountable. Person: «architect». Adjective: «architectural».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Arduous means very hard and tiring, needing a lot of effort for a long time.
its sense in the lessons: Used in stories, history and news about long journeys, climbs, work and training: «an arduous journey», «an arduous task».
examples from the lessons: The explorers made an arduous journey across the ice. | Climbing the mountain was long and arduous. | Building the railway was arduous work. | After an arduous day, the farmer fell asleep at once. | The pioneers' trek west was arduous and dangerous. | Learning a new instrument can be arduous at first.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; everyday words: «hard», «tough», «exhausting». Pronounced AR-joo-us or ARD-yoo-us.

part of speech: adjective (Argentine; also Argentinian, Argentinean); noun (an Argentine, Argentines — a person)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Argentine means from or to do with Argentina, a country in South America. 2) An Argentine is a person from Argentina. 3) (rare) argentine with a small «a» means silvery, like silver. 4) (an argentine) An argentine is also a small silvery sea fish.
its sense in the lessons: Used in geography (the Argentine pampas, Buenos Aires), sport (Argentine footballers like Lionel Messi, the World Cup) and food (Argentine beef).
examples from the lessons: Lionel Messi is an Argentine footballer. | The Argentine flag is light blue and white with a sun. | Argentine cowboys are called gauchos. | Many Argentines speak Spanish. | We tasted Argentine empanadas at the food fair. | The tango comes from Argentine dance halls.
note for the reader of a maths problem: For the nationality, write a capital A. Pronounced AR-jen-tine or AR-jen-teen. «Argentinian» is also common and correct. The country was once called «the Argentine» in old British English, but today it is «Argentina». From Latin «argentum», silver.

part of speech: noun (an armchair, armchairs); adjective (armchair — before a noun)
meaning for a pupil: 1) An armchair is a comfortable chair with side parts to rest your arms on. 2) (informal, before a noun) Armchair describes someone who talks about or follows something without doing it themselves: an armchair fan, an armchair traveller, an armchair expert.
its sense in the lessons: Used in describing homes and stories («Grandpa dozed in his armchair»), and in everyday talk about people who only watch or talk.
examples from the lessons: Grandpa fell asleep in his armchair. | The cat curled up on the armchair. | We bought a big red armchair for the living room. | He's an armchair football fan who never plays. | She is an armchair traveller who loves reading about far-off places. | Armchair experts on TV always know what the coach should have done.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Compound: arm + chair. «Armchair» as an adjective is often a little mocking: an «armchair critic» judges without real experience.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Arousal is the state of being awake, alert or excited, when the body and mind are ready for action. 2) (science) Arousal is when the brain and body become active, for example when the heart beats faster with fear or excitement. 3) (adult) Grown-ups also use it in a sense that is not for school.
its sense in the lessons: Used in science and psychology (sleep and arousal, fight-or-flight), sport (players need the right level of arousal, not too nervous, not too sleepy). Because of the adult sense, everyday speech often says «excitement» or «being alert» instead.
examples from the lessons: Fear causes arousal: your heart beats faster and you breathe quickly. | Loud noise woke the sleeper into arousal. | Athletes try to control their arousal before a race. | Too much arousal can make a player nervous and clumsy. | Coffee increases arousal and keeps people awake. | Scientists measured the animals' arousal by their heart rate.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. From «arouse». Because grown-ups also use it in an adult sense, it is best used in clear science contexts; for everyday feelings say «excitement», «alertness».

meaning for a pupil: 1) To arouse a feeling is to cause it, like interest, curiosity, anger or suspicion. 2) (literary) To arouse someone is to wake them up. 3) (adult) Grown-ups also use it in a sense that is not for school.
its sense in the lessons: Used in stories and formal writing: «arouse suspicion», «arouse curiosity», «arouse interest». It tells the reader that something started a feeling.
examples from the lessons: The strange noise aroused our curiosity. | His nervous face aroused the detective's suspicion. | The new library aroused a lot of interest. | The unfair rule aroused anger among the pupils. | She was aroused from sleep by the barking dog. | The trailer aroused excitement for the film.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Usually used with feelings: «arouse suspicion». Not the same as «rouse» (to wake someone or stir them to act), though close. Because of the adult sense, use with feelings («arouse curiosity») rather than about people.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Artemisia is a group of plants with strong-smelling, often silvery leaves, including wormwood, mugwort, sagebrush and tarragon. 2) Sweet wormwood (Artemisia annua) is the plant from which the malaria medicine artemisinin is made. 3) (a name) Artemisia is a woman's name, for example Artemisia Gentileschi, an Italian painter of the 1600s, and Artemisia, an ancient queen of Caria.
its sense in the lessons: Used in science (plants and medicine; Tu Youyou won a Nobel Prize in 2015 for discovering artemisinin), gardening and art history.
examples from the lessons: Artemisia plants have silvery, scented leaves. | Tarragon is a kind of artemisia used in cooking. | A medicine against malaria comes from sweet wormwood, an artemisia. | Sagebrush covers the dry hills of the American West. | Artemisia Gentileschi was a famous Italian painter. | The garden had a border of grey artemisia.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced ar-tih-MEE-zee-uh or ar-tih-MIZ-ee-uh. Named after the Greek goddess Artemis. As a genus name it is capitalised: Artemisia. Do not take herbal plants as medicine without a doctor.

part of speech: adjective (articulate, more articulate, most articulate); verb (articulate, articulates, articulated, articulating)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (adjective) An articulate person can express ideas clearly and well in words. 2) (verb) To articulate ideas or feelings is to express them clearly in words. 3) (verb) To articulate sounds is to say them clearly. 4) (verb, science) To articulate is to join with a joint so parts can move, like bones.
its sense in the lessons: Used in English and speaking lessons («articulate your ideas»), school reports, science (joints, articulated skeletons), and transport (an articulated lorry, a long lorry that bends in the middle).
examples from the lessons: She is a very articulate speaker. | Try to articulate your feelings instead of shouting. | Articulate each word so the audience can hear you. | The museum has an articulated dinosaur skeleton. | An articulated lorry bends in the middle when it turns. | The upper arm bone articulates with the shoulder. | He was too upset to articulate what had happened.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Two pronunciations: adjective ar-TIK-yoo-lut; verb ar-TIK-yoo-late. Noun: «articulation». In the UK «articulated lorry» is often shortened to «artic»; in the US people say «semi» or «tractor-trailer».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Artificially means made or done by people, not by nature. 2) Artificially can mean in a way that is not real or natural, or that is forced.
its sense in the lessons: Used in food labels («artificially coloured», «artificially sweetened»), science (artificially grown crystals), and economics and news («prices kept artificially low»).
examples from the lessons: The sweets are artificially coloured. | This drink is artificially sweetened. | The lake was made artificially by building a dam. | The diamonds were grown artificially in a lab. | The flowers are lit artificially in the greenhouse. | Prices were kept artificially low by the government. | Her smile looked artificially bright.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «artificial». Opposite: «naturally». «Artificial» does not always mean bad or harmful; it just means made by people. AI stands for «artificial intelligence».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (history) Aryan was an old name for the ancient people who spoke early Indo-Iranian languages in Iran and northern India; «arya» meant «noble» in Sanskrit. 2) (history, Nazi) The Nazis in Germany misused «Aryan» to mean a made-up «master race» of white, often blond, people; this idea was false and cruel and was used to justify the Holocaust. 3) (a name) Aryan (also spelled Aarya or Arian) is also a boy's name in India and elsewhere.
its sense in the lessons: Used in history lessons on ancient India and Iran and on Nazi Germany and the Second World War; it teaches how racist ideas are false and dangerous. Scientists today say «Indo-European» or «Indo-Iranian» for the languages.
examples from the lessons: The Nazis falsely claimed that «Aryans» were better than other people. | There is no such thing as a master race. | The name Iran comes from an old word linked to «Aryan». | In ancient Sanskrit, «arya» meant «noble». | Hitler's ideas about an «Aryan race» led to terrible crimes. | My classmate's name is Aryan.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Written with a capital A. Pronounced AIR-ee-un. Because of its Nazi misuse, the word is avoided in science today; there is no «Aryan race». As a name in India it is common and respectful.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (handwriting, printing) An ascender is the part of a lowercase letter that goes up above the middle of the line, as in b, d, f, h, k, l and t. 2) An ascender is a climbing tool that grips a rope so a climber can go up it. 3) An ascender is a person or thing that goes up.
its sense in the lessons: Used in handwriting lessons («tall letters with ascenders»), typography and design, and in climbing and caving. Compare «descender» (the tail going down in g, j, p, q, y).
examples from the lessons: The letters b, d and h have ascenders. | Make your ascenders tall and straight. | The letter «g» has a descender, not an ascender. | The climber clipped an ascender onto the rope. | Cavers use ascenders to climb out of deep holes. | In joined-up writing, loop your ascenders neatly.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «ascend» (to go up). Opposite: «descender». Capital letters do not usually count as having ascenders.

part of speech: verb (aspirate, aspirates, aspirated, aspirating); noun (an aspirate, aspirates)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (speech) To aspirate a sound is to say it with a puff of breath, like the «h» in «hat» or the «p» in «pin». 2) (noun, phonetics) An aspirate is an «h» sound or a sound said with a puff of air. 3) (medicine) To aspirate something is to suck it out with a tube or needle, such as fluid from the body. 4) (medicine) To aspirate food or liquid is to breathe it into the lungs by accident.
its sense in the lessons: Used in phonics and languages (dropping your aitches in some English accents, aspirated «p» in «pin» but not in «spin»; Mandarin pinyin «p» vs «b»), and in medicine and first aid.
examples from the lessons: In «pin», the «p» is aspirated; hold your hand in front of your mouth to feel the puff. | Some London speakers do not aspirate the «h» in «house». | In Mandarin, «p» is aspirated and «b» is not. | The doctor aspirated fluid from the swollen knee. | Babies can aspirate milk if they are fed lying flat. | Old grammar books call «h» an aspirate.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: AS-pi-rate; noun: AS-pi-rut. Noun «aspiration» can mean this breathing sound, but more often means a hope or ambition. Related: «respirate», «inspire» (all from Latin «breathe»).

meaning for a pupil: 1) An asset is a person or thing that is useful or valuable, that helps you. 2) (money) Assets are things a person or company owns that are worth money, such as houses, land, savings or machines.
its sense in the lessons: Used in everyday life and school («She is an asset to the team»), in money and business lessons (assets and debts), and in games (game assets, the pictures and sounds).
examples from the lessons: Tom is a real asset to the school choir. | Her kindness is her greatest asset. | A good memory is an asset in exams. | The company's assets include three shops and a lorry. | The family's main asset is their house. | The game designer made new assets for the level. | A calm head is an asset in an emergency.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Opposite in money: «liability» or «debt». In maths and money problems: net worth = assets − debts; if a shop has assets of £50,000 and debts of £20,000, it is worth £30,000.

part of speech: adjective (Assyrian); noun (an Assyrian, Assyrians; Assyrian — the language)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (history) Assyrian means to do with ancient Assyria, a powerful empire in Mesopotamia (today mostly northern Iraq), with cities like Nineveh and Assur, strongest about 900–600 BC. 2) An Assyrian is a person of ancient Assyria. 3) Assyrians today are a people of the Middle East and around the world, mostly Christians, who speak Neo-Aramaic (also called Assyrian or Syriac). 4) (Bible) In the Bible the Assyrians conquered the northern Kingdom of Israel, and Jonah was sent to preach in their city Nineveh.
its sense in the lessons: Used in history (Mesopotamia, cuneiform writing, winged bull statues, King Ashurbanipal's library), Bible lessons (Jonah and Nineveh, Isaiah), and in learning about Middle Eastern peoples today.
examples from the lessons: The Assyrian king lived in a palace at Nineveh. | The British Museum has huge Assyrian stone carvings. | Assyrian soldiers had iron weapons and chariots. | In the Bible, Jonah was sent to the great Assyrian city of Nineveh. | Assyrian scribes wrote in cuneiform on clay tablets. | My neighbour's family are Assyrians from Iraq. | Many Assyrian Christians celebrate Easter with special bread.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Written with a capital A. Do not confuse with «Syrian» (from modern Syria), though the names may be related. BC dates count backwards: 700 BC is earlier than 600 BC.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An old instrument made of brass discs and a pointer, used to measure how high the Sun or a star is above the horizon. 2) With it, sailors and astronomers could work out the time and where they were on Earth.
its sense in the lessons: In history and science lessons it appears in stories of early astronomers and Islamic and medieval scholars, and in lessons on how people found their way before GPS. It tells the reader the scene is long ago and about stars, time or navigation. Phrases: «a brass astrolabe», «use an astrolabe».
examples from the lessons: The museum had a shiny brass astrolabe in a glass case. | Sailors once used an astrolabe to find how far north they were. | The astronomer held up the astrolabe to the night sky. | Our class made a paper astrolabe in science. | An astrolabe measures the height of a star above the horizon. | Scholars in Baghdad improved the astrolabe long ago. | She turned the ring of the astrolabe to line it up with the Sun.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: an astrolabe, two astrolabes. Stress on the first syllable: AS-tro-labe. Not a telescope: it does not make things look bigger, it measures angles. Later sailors used the sextant instead.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person whose job is to look after people or a place, such as a flight attendant, a car park attendant or a pool attendant. 2) (formal, adjective) Coming along with something or caused by it, as in «the attendant risks».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life children meet attendants at swimming pools, museums, petrol stations and on planes; in safety lessons the attendant is a grown-up helper you can ask. In stories, «attendants» may serve a king or queen. In the formal exam voice «attendant problems» means the problems that come with something.
examples from the lessons: The flight attendant showed us how to fasten our seat belts. | Ask the pool attendant if you lose your goggles. | The museum attendant told us not to touch the paintings. | The car park attendant waved us into a space. | The queen walked in with her attendants. | The petrol station attendant filled up the tank. | Moving house brought all the attendant stress of packing. (formal) | A toilet attendant kept the washrooms clean.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: an attendant (with «an»). Flight attendant is the modern word for air hostess or steward. Spelling ends in -ant, not -ent. «Attendance» is a different word: how many people came or whether you were present.

part of speech: adjective (auspicious; more auspicious, most auspicious) — formal
meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Showing signs that something will go well; a lucky or promising start. 2) (formal) Special and important, as in «on this auspicious occasion».
its sense in the lessons: It is a formal, rather grand word used in speeches, stories and exam writing; it tells the reader things look hopeful. In lessons on festivals, people choose an «auspicious day» for weddings or new starts (for example in Chinese and Hindu traditions). Phrases: «an auspicious start», «an auspicious day», «hardly auspicious».
examples from the lessons: Winning the first match was an auspicious start to the season. | The head teacher began, «On this auspicious occasion, we open our new library.» | Many families pick an auspicious day for a wedding. | Rain on sports day was not an auspicious beginning. | The rainbow seemed an auspicious sign to the travellers. | It was hardly an auspicious moment to ask for more pocket money. | Red is seen as an auspicious colour at Chinese New Year.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective only, formal register; in everyday talk say «a good sign» or «promising». Opposite: inauspicious (an unlucky or poor start). Spelling: au-spi-cious, ends in -cious. Use «an» before it: an auspicious start.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Checking that someone really is who they say they are, for example with a password, a code or a fingerprint. 2) Checking that a thing, such as a painting or a signature, is real and not a fake.
its sense in the lessons: In computing and online safety lessons, authentication is how a website or app makes sure it is really you logging in. «Two-factor authentication» means two checks, like a password plus a code sent to a phone. In art and history it means proving that something is genuine.
examples from the lessons: The app asks for authentication before you can see your messages. | Two-factor authentication sends a code to Mum's phone. | Face authentication unlocked the tablet. | Never share an authentication code with anyone, even a friend. | The museum sent the old letter for authentication. | Experts did an authentication of the painting and found it was real. | Your password is one kind of authentication.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable: «authentication», not «an authentication» (though experts may say «an authentication» of one item). Verb: authenticate. Adjective: authentic (real, genuine). Safety trap: a message asking for your authentication code is almost always a scam.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A book or story of a person's life written by that person. 2) The kind of writing (genre) where people tell their own life story.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons pupils read and write autobiographies, using «I», the past tense and events in time order. It tells the reader the facts come from the person's own memory and point of view. Compare it with a biography, written by someone else. Phrases: «write your autobiography», «in her autobiography».
examples from the lessons: The footballer wrote an autobiography about growing up in Manchester. | In his autobiography, he describes his first day at school. | Our homework is to write a short autobiography. | An autobiography is written in the first person, using «I». | Grandad says his autobiography would fill ten books. | The library has a shelf of autobiographies by famous scientists. | Her autobiography tells how she learned to swim at forty.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: an autobiography (with «an»), plural autobiographies (y → ies). auto = self, bio = life, graphy = writing. Trap: a biography is about someone else; a memoir is a story of part of your own life. Adjective: autobiographical.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Whether something can be got, bought or used right now. 2) Whether a person is free to do something or meet someone at a certain time.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life it is used in shops, booking holidays and websites: «check availability». At school a teacher may ask about «your availability» for a match or club. It is a rather formal word; in plain talk people ask «Is it free?» or «Is it in stock?».
examples from the lessons: The website shows the availability of seats on the train. | Please check the availability of the swimming pool on Saturday. | Mum asked about the coach's availability for an extra practice. | The availability of fresh water is important for every town. | Toy availability is low just before Christmas. | Subject to availability, you can choose your own room. (formal) | The doctor has no availability until next week.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly uncountable: «availability», no «an». From the adjective «available» (able to be got or used). «Subject to availability» means only if there are some left. Spelling: avail-ab-il-ity, with -ility.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a clumsy way that is not smooth or easy, as in «he fell awkwardly». 2) In an embarrassed or uncomfortable way, as when nobody knows what to say. 3) In a way that is hard to handle or badly placed, as in «an awkwardly shaped box».
its sense in the lessons: In stories it tells the reader that a character feels shy, embarrassed or clumsy, or that a moment is uncomfortable. In PE and safety talk, «landed awkwardly» means landed badly and could get hurt. Phrases: «laughed awkwardly», «stood awkwardly», «fell awkwardly».
examples from the lessons: She landed awkwardly and twisted her ankle. | He smiled awkwardly when everyone sang to him. | The two new boys stood awkwardly by the door. | The sofa was awkwardly shaped and would not fit through the door. | I awkwardly tried to hold three bags and an umbrella. | They laughed awkwardly after the joke fell flat. | The bus stop is awkwardly placed on a busy corner.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from the adjective «awkward»; it describes how something is done. Spelling trap: awk-ward-ly has a w twice (awkward). Comparative: more awkwardly. Opposites: smoothly, gracefully, comfortably.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A pile of work or jobs that should have been done already and are still waiting. 2) A list of things still to be done in order, such as orders, emails or tasks.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday and adult life, a backlog builds up when there is too much work and too little time, for example at the post office or a hospital. At school a pupil can have a backlog of homework after being ill. In computing, a «backlog» is the team's list of jobs to do. Phrases: «a backlog of», «clear the backlog».
examples from the lessons: After a week off sick, I had a backlog of homework. | The post office has a huge backlog of parcels before Christmas. | The plumbers are busy clearing a backlog of jobs. | Dad spent Sunday working through his backlog of emails. | There is a long backlog of patients waiting at the hospital. | Our game-making team keeps a backlog of ideas. | Snow caused a backlog of trains at the station.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a backlog, backlogs; usually «a backlog of» something. Not about logs of wood or the back of anything. In maths problems a backlog is the amount still left over: if 40 orders came and 25 were done, the backlog is 15.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The bags and suitcases you take when you travel. 2) Worries, bad memories or old problems that a person carries with them from the past (said as a picture).
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life it is used at airports: «baggage reclaim», «check in your baggage». In stories, «emotional baggage» tells the reader a character is carrying old hurts. In safety, never leave baggage unattended and never carry a bag for a stranger.
examples from the lessons: We collected our baggage from the moving belt. | Each passenger may bring one piece of baggage. | Do not leave your baggage alone at the station. | The baggage was too heavy, so we paid extra. | Go to baggage reclaim after you land. | He carried a lot of baggage from his old school, like worry about being teased. | Our baggage arrived on the wrong plane!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «some baggage», «a piece of baggage», never «a baggage» or «baggages». Similar to luggage (more common in the UK); Americans often say baggage. «Hand baggage» or «carry-on» goes into the plane cabin with you.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To do with the Balkans, a mountainous region in south-east Europe. 2) The Balkans: the countries of that region, such as Greece, Albania, Bulgaria, North Macedonia, Serbia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Montenegro, Croatia and Kosovo.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and history lessons it names a region and its peoples, foods, music and mountains (the Balkan Mountains in Bulgaria). In history it appears in lessons on the First World War and the wars of the 1990s. It tells the reader the place is south-east Europe.
examples from the lessons: The Balkan countries lie in south-east Europe. | We tasted Balkan food like burek and stuffed peppers. | The Balkan Mountains run across Bulgaria. | Many Balkan towns have old stone bridges. | She went on holiday to the Balkans last summer. | Balkan music often uses fast, lively rhythms. | Our history class learned about the Balkan wars.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A proper adjective, so it is written with a capital letter: Balkan, the Balkans (always with «the»). The input is lower case only because of the word list. Not a single country. The name comes from a Turkish word for a chain of wooded mountains.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Made of basalt, a dark, heavy rock that forms when lava from a volcano cools quickly. 2) Like basalt or containing a lot of it.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography lessons it describes rocks, lava and the sea floor: «basaltic lava» is runny and flows far, as in Hawaii and Iceland. It tells the reader we are talking about volcanoes and igneous rock. Phrases: «basaltic rock», «basaltic lava», «basaltic columns».
examples from the lessons: The Giant's Causeway in Northern Ireland is made of basaltic columns. | Basaltic lava is runny and flows a long way. | Most of the ocean floor is basaltic rock. | The island has black basaltic beaches. | Our rock kit has a basaltic sample that feels heavy. | The Moon's dark patches are basaltic plains. | Volcanoes in Hawaii pour out basaltic lava.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective from the noun basalt (BASS-alt, stress on the first syllable in the UK, often on the second in the US). Basaltic is said bass-AWL-tic. Basalt is an igneous rock, made from cooled lava; granite is another igneous rock but cooled slowly underground.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A starting measurement that you use to compare later results with. 2) In tennis and some other sports, the line at the back of each end of the court. 3) A basic line or level, such as the lowest acceptable standard.
its sense in the lessons: In science experiments, the baseline is what you measure before you change anything, so you can see how much changed. In school tests, a «baseline test» shows what a pupil knows at the start of the year. In tennis lessons, players serve from behind the baseline.
examples from the lessons: We measured the plant's height as a baseline before adding fertiliser. | The baseline test showed what we knew in September. | My resting heart rate is my baseline before running. | She hit the ball right on the baseline. | Stand behind the baseline to serve. | Compared with the baseline, the temperature rose by 5 degrees. | A baseline helps you see if your spelling has improved.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a baseline, baselines; sometimes spelt «base line». In maths and science problems, the change = new value − baseline: if the baseline is 20 and the new value is 26, the increase is 6. Do not confuse with «bassline» (the low notes in music).

part of speech: verb form (bawl, bawls, bawled, bawling); noun (bawling — uncountable)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Crying very loudly, like a baby or an upset child. 2) Shouting loudly and roughly at someone. 3) (informal) «Bawl someone out» means to tell them off angrily (mainly US).
its sense in the lessons: In stories, «bawling» tells the reader that someone is crying noisily and without holding back, or shouting rudely. It is a strong, slightly informal word. Phrases: «bawling your eyes out», «bawling at someone», «bawling baby».
examples from the lessons: The baby was bawling in the back of the car. | I was bawling my eyes out at the end of the film. | The coach was bawling orders across the field. | Stop bawling, you will wake up Grandma! | We heard the toddler bawling in the supermarket. | The bawling went on for an hour until he fell asleep. | The coach bawled him out for being late. (US, informal)
note for the reader of a maths problem: -ing form of the verb «bawl» (past: bawled). Homophone trap: «bawl» (cry loudly) sounds like «ball» (a round toy) and «bawling» like «balling». Meaning is stronger than «crying» or «sobbing»; «wailing» is similar.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The tall stem of a bean plant that climbs up a pole or string. 2) The magic giant beanstalk in the fairy tale «Jack and the Beanstalk» that grows up into the clouds.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons children grow bean plants to see how stems grow towards the light and how climbing plants twist around supports. In stories and pantomime it brings to mind Jack, the magic beans, the giant and «Fee-fi-fo-fum». Phrases: «climb the beanstalk», «Jack and the Beanstalk».
examples from the lessons: Jack climbed the beanstalk up into the clouds. | Our beanstalk grew ten centimetres in a week. | The beanstalk curled around the bamboo cane. | In the play, I was the giant at the top of the beanstalk. | We measured the beanstalk every Monday and drew a graph. | The magic beans grew into an enormous beanstalk overnight. | Grandad's runner beans have very long beanstalks.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable compound noun: bean + stalk, written as one word. Plural: beanstalks. «Stalk» here means stem (not «to stalk», which means to follow someone secretly). In maths lessons, beanstalk growth is often used for measuring and drawing line graphs.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To become a friend to someone, especially someone who is new, lonely or needs help. 2) To make friends with an animal so it trusts you.
its sense in the lessons: In stories it tells the reader a character is kind and reaching out to someone. In PSHE and online safety, a warning: strangers online may try to befriend children to trick them — tell a trusted adult. Phrases: «befriend a new pupil», «was befriended by».
examples from the lessons: Maya befriended the new girl on her first day. | The lonely old man was befriended by a little dog. | We befriended a robin that came to our window every morning. | Be careful if a stranger online tries to befriend you. | He befriended a boy who sat alone at lunch. | The children befriended the shy horse with carrots. | In the story, the mouse befriends the lion.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: befriended, befriending. It takes an object: you befriend someone (not «befriend with»). More formal and storybook-like than «make friends with». Opposite idea: to shun or ignore someone.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A pale, light brown colour, like sand or milky tea. 2) (informal) Dull or boring, with nothing exciting about it, as in «a very beige outfit».
its sense in the lessons: In art lessons it is a neutral colour, made by mixing white with a little brown or yellow. In everyday life, many walls, carpets, coats and school uniforms are beige. As slang among young people, «beige» can mean boring or plain (a «beige flag» is a small odd habit of a partner, said jokingly).
examples from the lessons: She wore a beige coat and red boots. | Mix white paint with a little brown to make beige. | The walls of the waiting room were all beige. | Sand on this beach is a pale beige. | Our school jumpers used to be beige. | That party was so beige, nothing happened at all. (informal) | Beige goes well with navy blue.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Said «bayzh», rhyming roughly with «stage» but with a soft zh sound at the end. Spelling trap: b-e-i-g-e, «ei» not «ie». It is a French word that came into English. As a colour noun it is uncountable: «I like beige».

part of speech: noun (a bel, bels); name (Bel — a name)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A unit for measuring how loud a sound is or comparing power levels; one bel is ten decibels. 2) (a name) Bel, a short form of names like Isabel or Belinda. 3) In old stories, Bel is the name of an ancient Babylonian god (Bible: «Bel and the Dragon»).
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on sound, you nearly always meet the decibel (dB), which is one tenth of a bel; the bel itself is rarely used. It was named after Alexander Graham Bell, who worked on the telephone. In everyday life «Bel» is usually a nickname.
examples from the lessons: One bel equals ten decibels. | Sound levels are usually measured in decibels, not bels. | The bel was named after Alexander Graham Bell. | My friend Isabel likes to be called Bel. | A whisper is about two bels, or twenty decibels. | In the Bible story, Daniel showed that the idol Bel did not really eat food.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a bel, bels; symbol B. Usually lower case as a unit, capital as a name. Homophone trap: «bel» sounds like «bell» (which rings). In maths: to change bels to decibels, multiply by 10 (3 bels = 30 dB). Each extra bel means ten times more sound power.

part of speech: adjective (Belarusian); noun (a Belarusian, Belarusians; Belarusian — the language)
meaning for a pupil: 1) From or to do with Belarus, a country in eastern Europe between Poland, Lithuania, Latvia, Russia and Ukraine. 2) A person from Belarus. 3) The Belarusian language, a Slavic language close to Ukrainian and Russian.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and current events lessons it names the people, language and things of Belarus, whose capital is Minsk. In news, Belarus is often mentioned as an ally of Russia; its people are described in their own right. It tells the reader where someone or something comes from.
examples from the lessons: Minsk is the Belarusian capital. | Our new classmate is Belarusian and speaks three languages. | Belarusian is written in the Cyrillic alphabet. | Many Belarusians love potato pancakes called draniki. | We learned a Belarusian folk song in music. | The Belarusian forests are home to European bison. | Belarusian sounds a bit like Ukrainian and Polish.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Proper adjective and noun, so write it with a capital B: Belarusian, a Belarusian, Belarusians. The input is lower case only because of the word list. Older spellings «Byelorussian» and «White Russian» are out of date. Not the same as Russian.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A round, soft, flat hat without a brim, often made of wool or felt. 2) A beret worn as part of a uniform, especially by soldiers (for example «the Green Berets»).
its sense in the lessons: In French lessons and pictures the beret is a famous symbol of France, often shown with a striped top and a baguette (a cliché, not what most French people wear today). In history and uniforms, soldiers and Scouts wear berets. In art, painters are often drawn wearing one.
examples from the lessons: She wore a red beret to school on a cold day. | The artist in the picture had a black beret. | Soldiers in the parade wore green berets. | My nan knitted me a beret. | In our French play, Tom wore a beret and a stripy top. | The beret sat on the side of his head. | The Scouts wear blue berets.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a beret, berets. Said «BEH-ray» in the UK and «buh-RAY» in the US; the t is silent because the word is French. Not the same as «berry». A cap has a peak; a beret does not.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An illness caused by not having enough vitamin B1 (thiamine) in food; it can weaken the muscles, nerves and heart.
its sense in the lessons: In science and health lessons about a balanced diet, beriberi is an example of a deficiency disease, like scurvy (from too little vitamin C). It was common long ago where people ate mostly white polished rice, and was cured by eating brown rice, beans, meat and whole grains. History of science: it helped scientists discover vitamins.
examples from the lessons: Beriberi is caused by too little vitamin B1. | Sailors who ate only white rice sometimes got beriberi. | Eating whole grains helps prevent beriberi. | Our science sheet listed scurvy, rickets and beriberi. | A doctor found that brown rice cured beriberi in chickens. | Beriberi is rare today in countries with varied food.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «beriberi», not «a beriberi». Said «berry-berry». It is not catching: you cannot get it from another person. The name comes from a Sinhala word meaning «weak, weak».

meaning for a pupil: 1) To surround a castle, town or city with an army so that nobody can get in or out, to make it give up. 2) To crowd around someone or something, as in «fans besieged the singer». 3) To send someone very many questions, letters or requests.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons it is used for sieges of castles and walled towns, with soldiers, catapults and hunger inside the walls. In stories and news, «besieged by reporters» tells the reader someone is surrounded by a crowd. Phrases: «besieged by», «besiege a castle».
examples from the lessons: The army besieged the castle for six months. | The town was besieged and food ran out. | Fans besieged the footballer outside the stadium. | The teacher was besieged with questions about the trip. | Reporters besieged the house after the news broke. | The Vikings besieged Paris in 885. | Our shop was besieged by shoppers on sale day.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: besieged, besieging. Spelling trap: «ie» in besiege, like siege (i before e). Noun: siege, as in «the siege lasted a year». Often used in the passive: «was besieged by».

part of speech: verb (beware — used only as «beware» and «to beware»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Be careful of something or someone because it could be dangerous or harmful. 2) A warning word on signs and in stories, as in «Beware of the dog».
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons and on signs it is a strong warning: «Beware of falling rocks», «Beware of scams». In stories and fairy tales it adds drama and danger. Phrases: «beware of», «buyer beware».
examples from the lessons: Beware of the dog! | The sign said, «Beware of falling rocks». | Beware of emails that ask for your password. | «Beware the dark forest,» said the old woman. | Swimmers should beware of strong currents. | Beware of strangers who offer you sweets. | Beware, the floor is wet and slippery.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Unusual verb: it is used only in its base form, in commands («Beware!») and after «must», «should» or «to». There is no «bewares», «bewared» or «bewaring». Followed by «of» or directly by a noun: «beware of the dog» or «beware the dog».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A very rich person who owns money and things worth at least one billion dollars, pounds or euros.
its sense in the lessons: In money lessons and the news it describes the richest people, often owners of big companies. It helps children understand how huge a billion is. In stories, a billionaire character tells the reader about great wealth and power. Phrases: «a tech billionaire», «become a billionaire».
examples from the lessons: A billionaire owns at least a thousand million pounds. | The billionaire paid for a new hospital. | He went from selling lemonade to being a billionaire. | Some billionaires build rockets to go to space. | Being a billionaire does not always make you happy. | The story was about a billionaire who lost everything. | There are more millionaires than billionaires in the world.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a billionaire, billionaires. Spelling: billion + -aire, with one n before -aire (billionaire, like millionaire). In maths: one billion = 1,000,000,000 = a thousand million (in the USA, UK, Canada, Australia today). A billionaire is a thousand times richer than someone with one million.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A way of writing numbers using only the digits 0 and 1, which computers use. 2) Made of two parts, or having only two choices, like yes or no, on or off. 3) A binary star is a pair of stars that go round each other.
its sense in the lessons: In computing lessons, binary is how computers store everything as ones and zeros (bits). In maths, it is base 2 instead of our usual base 10. In science, binary stars orbit each other. In talk about people, «non-binary» describes someone who does not feel only male or only female.
examples from the lessons: Computers store pictures and songs in binary. | In binary, the number 5 is written 101. | We made bracelets with beads in binary code. | A light switch is binary: it is on or off. | Each 0 or 1 in binary is called a bit. | Sirius is a binary star. | The question was binary: you could only answer yes or no.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Said «BYE-nuh-ree». In maths, binary place values go 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 (doubling) instead of 1, 10, 100: so binary 1010 = 8 + 2 = 10. Trap: «10» in binary means two, not ten. Not to be confused with «binocular» (two eyes).

part of speech: verb (binge, binges, binged, bingeing or binging); noun (a binge, binges)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To do too much of something in a short time, especially eating, drinking alcohol or watching TV. 2) A short time of doing too much, as in «a chocolate binge». 3) (informal) «Binge-watch» means to watch many episodes of a show one after another.
its sense in the lessons: In health lessons, binge eating or binge drinking is described as unhealthy and something to talk to a trusted adult or doctor about. In everyday talk children use «binge-watch» about series and cartoons. It tells the reader there was too much, all at once.
examples from the lessons: We binged on popcorn during the film. | I binge-watched the whole series at the weekend. | After the party, he went on a sweet binge. | Doctors warn that binge drinking is dangerous. | Mum said no more binge-watching on school nights. | She binges on biscuits when she is worried. | A shopping binge left them with no money.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: binged; the -ing form is «bingeing» or «binging» (both are used). Countable noun: a binge. Said «binj». The words «binge-watch» and «binge-eat» are written with a hyphen.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A scientist who studies living things such as plants, animals, people and tiny living things like bacteria.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons it names a job: biologists observe, experiment and record how living things grow, feed, move and survive. In careers talk it shows how science leads to work in hospitals, labs, zoos, oceans and forests. Kinds include marine biologists (sea life) and wildlife biologists.
examples from the lessons: A biologist studies how frogs grow from tadpoles. | My aunt is a marine biologist who studies whales. | The biologist looked at the cells under a microscope. | Charles Darwin was a famous biologist. | Biologists count the birds in the forest every spring. | When I grow up, I want to be a biologist. | The biologist explained how bees help flowers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a biologist, biologists. bio = life, -logist = someone who studies. Subject: biology; adjective: biological. Stress: bye-OL-o-jist.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The musical sounds that birds make, especially in the early morning and in spring.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons birdsong helps identify birds and shows how birds mark their territory and attract a mate. In poetry and stories it creates a calm, peaceful mood or tells the reader it is morning. Phrases: «the dawn chorus» (lots of birdsong at sunrise).
examples from the lessons: We woke to birdsong outside the tent. | The dawn chorus is full of birdsong in May. | We recorded birdsong in the school garden. | A blackbird's birdsong is loud and sweet. | The poem was about birdsong after rain. | You can identify birds by their birdsong. | The quiet woods were filled with birdsong.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable: «birdsong», «some birdsong», not «a birdsong». Written as one word. Scientists separate «songs» (long, musical) from «calls» (short sounds, like alarms).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) Short for «business», especially a trade or industry, as in «show biz». 2) (slang) «The biz» means the entertainment or music industry. 3) (slang, UK) «The biz» can also mean the very best, as in «that's the biz».
its sense in the lessons: It is a clipped, chatty word seen in magazines, adverts and casual talk. «Show biz» or «showbiz» means the world of films, TV and theatre. It tells the reader the style is informal or journalistic. It is not used in school writing.
examples from the lessons: She wants to be a star in show biz. | He has been in the music biz for years. | My uncle runs a small cake biz from home. (informal) | That new trainer is the biz! (UK slang) | Showbiz news is all about celebrities. | «How's the biz going?» Dad asked his friend.
note for the reader of a maths problem: An abbreviation of «business», said «biz» (rhymes with «his»). Informal: in written work use «business». «Showbiz» is usually written as one word. Uncountable when it means an industry.

part of speech: verb (bleat, bleats, bleated, bleating); noun (a bleat, bleats)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The shaky «baa» sound a sheep, lamb or goat makes. 2) To make that sound. 3) (informal) To complain in a weak, whining way, as in «stop bleating about it».
its sense in the lessons: In science and farm lessons it is the name of the sheep's and goat's call (like a dog barks and a cow moos). In stories it tells the reader there are sheep nearby or that a character is moaning in a feeble way. Phrases: «bleat on about».
examples from the lessons: The lambs bleated for their mothers. | We heard the bleat of a goat in the field. | A sheep bleats, a dog barks and a cow moos. | The little lamb gave a sad bleat. | Stop bleating about your homework and just do it! (informal) | The goats bleated when the farmer brought hay. | He bleated that it was not fair.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: bleated, bleating. Countable noun: a bleat. Rhymes with «sheet». Animal sounds: sheep and goats bleat, horses neigh, pigs oink or grunt, ducks quack.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (slang) Shiny, expensive-looking jewellery such as big gold chains and sparkly rings. 2) (slang) A flashy show of wealth, or something covered in glitter or sparkles.
its sense in the lessons: It is an informal, fun word from hip-hop slang. In everyday life children use it for sparkly things: «bling» on a phone case or dance costume. In stories it tells the reader someone is showing off wealth. Phrase: «bling-bling».
examples from the lessons: The rapper wore loads of bling. | My little sister covered her pencil case in bling. | Her party dress had lots of bling on it. | That watch is so bling! (slang) | The dance costumes were full of sparkly bling. | He likes clothes with no bling at all. | The car had gold bling on the wheels.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Slang and uncountable: «lots of bling», not «a bling». It imitates the sound of light flashing off jewels. Not used in formal writing; say «jewellery» or «sparkly decorations» instead.

part of speech: noun (a blitz, blitzes; the Blitz); verb (blitz, blitzes, blitzed, blitzing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The Blitz: the heavy German bombing of British cities, especially London, in 1940–1941 during the Second World War. 2) A sudden, strong attack. 3) (informal) A big, fast effort to get something done, as in «a cleaning blitz». 4) (informal) To do something very quickly or to blend food fast.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons the Blitz is studied with air-raid shelters, blackouts, sirens and evacuated children. In everyday life, «have a blitz» means tidying or working hard fast. In cooking, «blitz it» means whizz it in a blender. In sport, a blitz is a rush attack.
examples from the lessons: Many children were evacuated during the Blitz. | People slept in Underground stations during the Blitz. | We had a quick blitz on our bedroom before Grandma came. | Blitz the strawberries in the blender. | The team made a blitz on goal in the last minute. | The shop ran an advertising blitz before Christmas. | I blitzed my spelling homework in ten minutes. (informal)
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital B for the historical event: the Blitz. It comes from the German word «Blitzkrieg» (lightning war). Plural: blitzes. Verb is regular: blitzed, blitzing.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Made of block shapes, with square edges and corners. 2) Looking chunky and not smooth or detailed, like the pictures in some video games.
its sense in the lessons: In art and computing lessons it describes pictures made of big squares or pixels, like in Minecraft-style games. In design and technology it describes models made of building blocks. It tells the reader a shape is square and chunky.
examples from the lessons: The game has blocky trees and square clouds. | My drawing looked blocky because I used a ruler. | The old computer made blocky pictures. | We built a blocky castle out of building bricks. | The robot had a blocky head and arms. | When you zoom in too far, the photo gets blocky. | Her handwriting is blocky and upright.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective made from «block» + -y. Comparatives: blockier, blockiest (y → i). Informal-ish, but fine in description. Similar words: chunky, pixelated, square.

part of speech: adjective (blonde or blond); noun (a blonde, blondes)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Having pale yellow or golden hair. 2) Pale yellow or golden in colour, like light hair, wood or beer. 3) A person with blonde hair (said mostly of women; it can sound rude).
its sense in the lessons: In stories it describes what a character looks like. In everyday life it is used for hair colours and hair dye. Trap: «blonde jokes» that say blonde people are not clever are an unkind stereotype and not true.
examples from the lessons: She has long blonde hair. | His hair is blond and curly. | The baby's hair turned blonder in the summer sun. | Mum dyed her hair blonde. | The table is made of pale blonde wood. | Hair colour does not show how clever someone is. | My cousin has blond eyebrows.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Two spellings: «blonde» (often for women and girls, and usual in the UK) and «blond» (often for boys and men, and usual in the US). Both are said the same. Saying «a blonde» about a person can sound rude; «a girl with blonde hair» is kinder.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The blood that flows round and round the body through the blood vessels (arteries, veins and capillaries).
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on the body, the heart pumps blood into the bloodstream, which carries oxygen and food to every part and takes waste away. In health lessons, medicines and also harmful things like alcohol or drugs can get «into the bloodstream». Phrases: «enter the bloodstream», «in the bloodstream».
examples from the lessons: Oxygen travels around the body in the bloodstream. | The heart pumps blood into the bloodstream. | Medicine from a drip goes straight into the bloodstream. | Food is broken down and carried by the bloodstream. | Germs can get into the bloodstream through a cut. | Doctors take a little blood to test what is in the bloodstream. | Your bloodstream carries water to your muscles.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually «the bloodstream», uncountable, written as one word. It is not a separate river inside you; it means the blood moving through all the blood vessels.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A long, thin tube used as a weapon or for hunting: a person blows hard into one end to shoot a small dart out of the other.
its sense in the lessons: In history and geography lessons it is linked with hunting traditions of peoples in the Amazon rainforest and South-East Asia (such as Borneo). In stories it adds adventure and jungle danger. Safety: real blowguns are weapons, not toys.
examples from the lessons: Hunters in the rainforest used a blowgun to catch birds. | The blowgun was made from a long hollow cane. | He blew into the blowgun and the dart flew silently. | The museum showed a blowgun from Borneo. | In the adventure story, an arrow from a blowgun stuck in the tree. | Some darts for a blowgun were dipped in poison.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a blowgun, blowguns; also called «blowpipe» (UK) or «blow gun». It uses breath, not gunpowder, so it is not a gun in the usual sense.

part of speech: noun (a bludger, bludgers — Australia, New Zealand, slang); noun (Bludger — Harry Potter)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (Australia, NZ, slang) A lazy person who avoids work or lets others do it, or someone who lives on other people's money. 2) In the Harry Potter books, a Bludger is a heavy ball in the game of Quidditch that flies around trying to knock players off their brooms.
its sense in the lessons: In Australian and New Zealand everyday talk, «bludger» is a mildly insulting slang word; «dole bludger» is a rude name for someone on unemployment money. Verb «bludge»: to slack off, and «a bludge» is an easy task. For many children it is first known from Harry Potter.
examples from the lessons: Get up and help, you bludger! (Australia, slang) | He's a bit of a bludger, he never washes up. | P.E. today was a total bludge. (Australia, slang) | The Bludger nearly knocked Harry off his broom. | Beaters hit the Bludgers away from their team. | Don't be a bludger, do your share of the project.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a bludger, bludgers. Slang and rude-ish, mostly Australia and NZ; not used in formal writing. Calling someone a «dole bludger» is unkind and unfair to people who need help. In Harry Potter it is written with a capital B.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The quality of being blue, or how blue something is. 2) (rare, old-fashioned) A feeling of sadness, from «feeling blue».
its sense in the lessons: In poems and descriptive writing it describes the colour of the sky, the sea or eyes: «the blueness of the sky». In science it can come up when explaining why the sky looks blue. It is a descriptive, slightly literary word.
examples from the lessons: The blueness of the sea surprised us. | She painted the sky with deep blueness. | The blueness of his lips showed he was very cold. | We noticed the blueness of the glacier ice. | The poem talks about the blueness of the evening. | Sunlight scattering in air gives the sky its blueness.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable noun made from «blue» + -ness. Keep the final e of blue: blue-ness. Health note: blueness of the lips or skin can be a sign that someone needs help quickly.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A man whose job is to row, sail or look after boats, or to carry people across water in a boat. 2) A person who hires out boats.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and myths a boatman often ferries travellers across a river (in Greek myths, Charon the boatman carries the dead across the River Styx). In history and geography lessons, boatmen worked on rivers and canals carrying goods and people.
examples from the lessons: The boatman rowed us across the lake. | We paid the boatman two coins for the ride. | In Venice, a boatman steers a gondola. | The old boatman knew every bend in the river. | In the Greek myth, the boatman Charon carried souls across the river. | The boatman hired out rowing boats for the afternoon. | A boatman shouted a warning about the rocks.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular plural: boatmen (not boatmans). A woman may be called a boatwoman, or people say «boat operator» or «ferry worker». Similar words: ferryman, gondolier, oarsman.

part of speech: noun (a bobtail, bobtails); adjective (bobtail or bobtailed)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A short tail, or a tail that has been cut short. 2) An animal with a short tail, such as a bobtail cat or a rabbit. 3) The Old English Sheepdog, a big shaggy dog, is often called a «bobtail».
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on animals, a short tail can be natural (rabbits, Manx cats, bobtail squid). In stories it describes animals. In everyday British talk, «bobtail» is a nickname for the Old English Sheepdog. Old phrase: «ragtag and bobtail» meant a ragged crowd.
examples from the lessons: The rabbit's white bobtail bounced as it ran. | Our neighbour has a fluffy bobtail sheepdog. | A Manx cat has a bobtail or no tail at all. | The bobtail squid glows in the dark sea. | The horse had a bobtail. | The bobtail dog shook water all over us. | Deer flash their bobtails as a warning.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a bobtail, bobtails. «Bob» here means cut short, like a bob haircut. As an adjective you can say «bobtail» or «bobtailed».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Fake or not real, pretending to be something it is not. 2) (slang) Unfair or bad, as in «That's so bogus!».
its sense in the lessons: In online safety and money lessons, «bogus» warns about fake websites, bogus callers and scams: a bogus caller pretends to be from the bank or the gas company. In everyday slang (especially American) it means unfair or rubbish.
examples from the lessons: That website is bogus; it is not the real shop. | A bogus caller pretended to be from the water company. | The email had a bogus link, so we deleted it. | He gave a bogus excuse for missing practice. | The prize message was bogus, a trick to get your details. | «No dessert? That's so bogus!» (slang) | Police warned about bogus charity collectors.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective only; no comparative forms used often. Said «BOH-gus». Safety rule: if something seems bogus, do not click, do not share details, tell a trusted adult. Similar words: fake, phony, sham.

part of speech: noun (Bohemia — a region; bohemia — a lifestyle)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Bohemia: a historic region in the west of the Czech Republic, with Prague as its main city. 2) (bohemia, lower case) A free, artistic way of life led by artists, writers and musicians who do not follow ordinary rules.
its sense in the lessons: In history and geography lessons Bohemia is a former kingdom in central Europe, famous for glass and castles; King Wenceslas of the Christmas carol was a duke of Bohemia. In arts and stories, «bohemian» describes free-living artists.
examples from the lessons: Prague is the capital of Bohemia. | Good King Wenceslas was a duke of Bohemia. | Bohemia is famous for its beautiful glass. | The kingdom of Bohemia was once part of the Holy Roman Empire. | The painter lived a life of bohemia in a messy attic. | The story is set in the hills of Bohemia.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital B for the region: Bohemia. The input is lower case only because of the word list. Adjective: Bohemian (from the region) or bohemian (artistic and unconventional), as in the song «Bohemian Rhapsody». Today Bohemia is part of the Czech Republic (Czechia), not a country itself.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The round seed pod of the cotton plant (or flax plant) that opens to show the fluffy cotton fibres inside.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography lessons, it explains where cotton comes from: the boll bursts open and the white fibres are picked and spun into thread. In history, cotton picking links to the story of slavery in the American South. The «boll weevil» is a beetle that eats cotton bolls.
examples from the lessons: The cotton boll split open, showing white fluff. | Workers picked the cotton from the bolls. | The boll weevil damaged the cotton crop. | Each boll holds seeds wrapped in soft fibres. | We looked at a dried cotton boll in class. | The field was full of bursting bolls.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a boll, bolls. Homophone trap: «boll» sounds like «bowl» (a dish) and «bole» (a tree trunk). Not the same as «ball».

part of speech: noun (Bologna — a city; bologna — a sausage)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Bologna: a city in northern Italy, famous for its old university and its food. 2) (bologna, especially US and Canada) A large smoked sausage of pork and beef, sliced thinly for sandwiches; also called «baloney» or «boloney».
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons Bologna is an Italian city; spaghetti bolognese (pasta with meat sauce) is named after it. In everyday American and Canadian life, a bologna sandwich is a common packed lunch. In slang, «baloney» also means nonsense.
examples from the lessons: Bologna has one of the oldest universities in the world. | I had a bologna sandwich for lunch. (US) | Spaghetti bolognese is named after Bologna. | The deli sliced the bologna very thin. | We visited Bologna and ate delicious pasta. | Fried bologna is a favourite in some US homes. | «That's a load of baloney!» meaning nonsense. (slang)
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital B for the city: Bologna, said «buh-LOHN-ya». The sausage is often said «buh-LOH-nee» and spelt «baloney» or «boloney». The input is lower case only because of the word list. Uncountable for the meat: «some bologna».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person or company that takes bets on horse races, football matches and other events and pays out if people win. Also called a «bookie». 2) (rare) A person who makes or prints books.
its sense in the lessons: In money and adult-life lessons, a bookmaker is part of gambling, which is only for adults (18+ in the UK, Ireland, Australia and New Zealand; it varies in the USA and Canada) and can lead to losing money. «Betting shop» or «the bookies» is where adults place bets. In maths, the odds a bookmaker gives link to probability.
examples from the lessons: The bookmaker offered odds of 5 to 1 on the horse. | Gambling with a bookmaker is only for adults. | Grandad says the bookmaker always wins in the end. | There is a bookmaker's shop on the high street. | The bookmaker took bets on the cup final. | My uncle lost money at the bookmaker's. | Long ago, a bookmaker could also mean someone who bound books.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a bookmaker, bookmakers. Informal: bookie. «The bookmaker's» means the shop. Maths note: odds of 5 to 1 mean if you bet 1 pound and win, you get 5 pounds plus your 1 pound back; bookmakers set odds so that, overall, they make money.

part of speech: verb (bore, bores, bored, boring); noun (a bore, bores); verb form (bore — past of bear)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To make someone feel tired and uninterested because something is dull. 2) A person or thing that is dull and tiresome, as in «He's such a bore». 3) (informal, UK) A nuisance, as in «What a bore, the bus is late». 4) To make a deep round hole with a drill. 5) The width of the inside of a pipe or gun barrel, or a hole drilled for water (a borehole). 6) The past tense of «bear», as in «she bore the pain» or «the tree bore fruit». 7) A tidal bore: a big wave that rushes up some rivers, like the Severn Bore.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life «bored» and «boring» are very common: «I'm bored» means I have nothing interesting to do. In design and technology, to bore means to drill a hole. In geography, the Severn Bore in England is a famous tidal wave up a river. In stories, «bore» as the past of «bear» appears in phrases like «bore a child» or «bore the weight».
examples from the lessons: Long speeches bore me. | Uncle Bill can be a bit of a bore at parties. | Workers bored a hole through the rock. | Surfers ride the Severn Bore up the river. | She bore the pain bravely. | The apple tree bore lots of fruit this year. | The farmers drink water from a deep bore. (Australia) | What a bore, we have to wait another hour!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap 1: «I am bored» (how you feel) vs «It is boring» (what makes you feel that way). Trap 2: homophone «boar» (a wild pig) sounds the same as «bore». Trap 3: «bore» can be the past of «bear»: bear, bore, born/borne. Nouns: boredom, borehole.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Of the far north, near the Arctic. 2) Belonging to the cold northern forest belt of conifer trees (the boreal forest or taiga) that stretches across Canada, Alaska, Scandinavia and Russia.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and science lessons about biomes, the boreal forest is the world's largest land biome, with long, cold winters, short summers and evergreen trees like spruce, pine and fir. Animals include moose, lynx, wolves and bears. It tells the reader we are in the cold north.
examples from the lessons: Canada has huge boreal forests. | The boreal forest is also called the taiga. | Moose and lynx live in the boreal forest. | Boreal winters are long and very cold. | Spruce and pine trees grow well in the boreal zone. | The northern lights are also called the aurora borealis. | Boreal forests store a lot of carbon.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective only. Said «BOR-ee-ul». It comes from Boreas, the Greek god of the north wind; «aurora borealis» means the northern dawn (the northern lights). Opposite region: austral (southern).

meaning for a pupil: 1) From or to do with Borneo, the third-largest island in the world, in South-East Asia, shared by Malaysia, Indonesia and Brunei. 2) A person from Borneo.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and science lessons it describes the rainforest animals and peoples of Borneo: the Bornean orangutan, the Bornean pygmy elephant and the Dayak peoples. It tells the reader the place is the tropical island of Borneo. Conservation lessons talk about protecting Bornean rainforests from logging and palm oil plantations.
examples from the lessons: The Bornean orangutan lives only on Borneo. | Bornean rainforests are among the oldest in the world. | We read about the Bornean pygmy elephant. | Many Bornean animals are endangered. | The Bornean jungle is hot and wet all year. | Our class adopted a Bornean orangutan through a charity. | Some Bornean peoples live in longhouses.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Proper adjective and noun, so write it with a capital B: Bornean. The input is lower case only because of the word list. Said «BOR-nee-un». Borneo is an island, not a country.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Belonging to the middle class, people who have comfortable jobs, homes and money. 2) (informal, often unkind) Too interested in owning things, being respectable and following ordinary middle-class tastes. 3) In history (especially Karl Marx's ideas), the bourgeoisie are the people who own factories and businesses.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons it appears in the French Revolution and in ideas about social class. In everyday adult talk it can be a mocking word for things seen as posh or fussy, often said jokingly («a bit bourgeois, isn't it?»). It tells the reader about class and lifestyle.
examples from the lessons: The bourgeois family lived in a big house in Paris. | In the story, the bourgeois merchant cared only about money. | Dad joked that eating olives was very bourgeois. | The bourgeoisie gained power after the French Revolution. | Karl Marx wrote about workers and the bourgeoisie. | She said the fancy coffee shop was too bourgeois for her.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A French word. Said «BOOR-zhwah» (the s is silent). Spelling trap: b-o-u-r-g-e-o-i-s. The group noun is «the bourgeoisie» (boor-zhwah-ZEE). Can sound like an insult, so use it carefully.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A piece of underwear worn by women and older girls to support and cover their breasts. Short for «brassiere».
its sense in the lessons: In health and growing-up lessons (puberty), girls learn that wearing a bra is a normal, personal choice as the body changes; a «first bra» or «training bra» is common for older girls. In PE, a sports bra gives extra support. It is a private, everyday word, not rude.
examples from the lessons: She bought a sports bra for netball. | Mum took my sister to buy her first bra. | Bras come in many sizes. | The bra is hanging on the washing line. | A sports bra helps when running and jumping. | You can ask the school nurse questions about puberty and bras.
