note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a bra, bras. Short for «brassiere» (a French-looking word; in French «bras» means arm). It is a normal word, not a swear word; joking about someone's underwear can be unkind teasing.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The bottom part of the brain that joins it to the spinal cord and controls automatic actions like breathing, heartbeat, swallowing and sleeping.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on the nervous system, the brain has three main parts: the cerebrum (thinking), the cerebellum (balance) and the brainstem (life-keeping automatic jobs). It tells the reader about things the body does without us thinking. In safety lessons, it shows why helmets protect the head and neck.
examples from the lessons: The brainstem controls your breathing even when you sleep. | Messages travel through the brainstem to the spinal cord. | The brainstem keeps your heart beating. | Our model brain had a brainstem at the bottom. | You do not have to think to breathe; your brainstem does it. | The brainstem connects the brain to the rest of the body.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually «the brainstem»; also spelt «brain stem». Countable but mostly used in the singular. It is not a separate brain; it is part of the brain.

part of speech: adjective (braised); verb form (braise, braises, braised, braising)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Cooked slowly in a covered pot with a little liquid, after first being browned in hot fat. 2) The past tense and past participle of «braise», as in «she braised the beef».
its sense in the lessons: In cooking lessons and on menus it tells you how food was cooked: «braised beef», «braised red cabbage», «braised lamb shanks». Slow braising makes tough meat soft and tender. Phrases: «slow-braised», «braised in».
examples from the lessons: We had braised beef with mashed potatoes. | Gran braised the carrots in orange juice. | Braised red cabbage is lovely at Christmas. | The menu offered braised lamb with peas. | The meat was braised for three hours until soft. | Braised leeks taste sweet and buttery. | Chinese braised pork is cooked in soy sauce.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: braise, braised, braising. Homophone trap: «braise» sounds like «brays» (a donkey brays), and «braised» like «brayed». Different from boiled (lots of water), roasted (dry oven) and stewed (lots of liquid, small pieces), although braising and stewing are close.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Out of breath, breathing hard after running or effort. 2) Very excited, amazed or eager, so that you almost stop breathing. 3) (of air or weather) Still, with no wind.
its sense in the lessons: In PE and science lessons, exercise makes you breathless because your muscles need more oxygen. In health, feeling breathless for no reason can be a sign of illness or asthma, so tell an adult. In stories it shows excitement or fear: «breathless with excitement», «a breathless hush».
examples from the lessons: I was breathless after running up the hill. | We watched the final in breathless silence. | She was breathless with excitement on her birthday. | The race left everyone breathless. | If you feel breathless at rest, tell an adult. | It was a breathless, hot afternoon with no breeze. | He arrived breathless, saying, «The bus has gone!»
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: breath + -less (without breath). Adverb: breathlessly. Spelling: «breath» (noun) has no e at the end, «breathe» (verb) has one. Say «out of breath» in plain talk.

meaning for a pupil: 1) So beautiful, amazing or exciting that it almost makes you stop breathing. 2) Shockingly big or surprising, as in «breathtaking rudeness».
its sense in the lessons: In writing lessons it is a strong describing word for views, sights, music and sport, but teachers warn not to overuse it. In stories it tells the reader something is spectacular. Phrases: «a breathtaking view», «breathtaking speed».
examples from the lessons: The view from the mountain was breathtaking. | The fireworks were breathtaking. | She ran at breathtaking speed. | The Grand Canyon is a breathtaking sight. | We saw breathtaking northern lights in Canada. | His rudeness was breathtaking! | The dancers gave a breathtaking show.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective, written as one word. Adverb: breathtakingly. Similar: stunning, amazing, spectacular. It does not mean you really stop breathing.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Using few words; being short and to the point when speaking or writing. 2) (formal) The shortness of time something lasts, as in «the brevity of life».
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons it is praised in writing: say what you mean clearly without extra words. A famous saying from Shakespeare's Hamlet: «Brevity is the soul of wit». In exams and formal writing, «for brevity» means «to keep it short».
examples from the lessons: The teacher praised the brevity of my answer. | For brevity, I will only list the main points. | Brevity is the soul of wit. | The brevity of the summer made us sad. | Text messages need brevity. | The speech was famous for its brevity: only two minutes. | Haiku poems show the beauty of brevity.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable formal noun; in everyday talk say «shortness» or «keeping it short». Related adjective: brief. Spelling: brev-i-ty, not «brief-ity».

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a general way, without all the details, as in «broadly speaking». 2) Widely and openly, as in «she smiled broadly» (a big, wide smile). 3) Mostly or on the whole, as in «I broadly agree».
its sense in the lessons: In school writing and exams it helps you summarise: «broadly speaking», «broadly similar». In science and maths reports it means roughly or in general. In stories, «grinned broadly» tells the reader someone is very happy.
examples from the lessons: Broadly speaking, our class enjoyed the trip. | He smiled broadly when he got his medal. | The two results were broadly the same. | I broadly agree with your idea. | The plan was broadly accepted by the council. | Broadly, plants need light, water and air. | She grinned broadly at the joke.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from «broad» (wide). «Broadly speaking» is a fixed phrase meaning «in general». In maths results, «broadly the same» means close, but not exactly equal.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (of a hen) Wanting to sit on her eggs to keep them warm until they hatch. 2) (informal, UK) Wanting to have a baby. 3) Quiet, moody and thinking gloomy thoughts.
its sense in the lessons: In farm and science lessons, a broody hen sits on eggs and stops laying. In stories, a broody character is quiet and serious, thinking about worries. In grown-up talk, «feeling broody» means wanting a baby.
examples from the lessons: The broody hen would not leave her nest. | Our broody chicken sat on the eggs for three weeks. | He has been broody and silent all afternoon. | Seeing her baby cousin made Aunt Sue feel broody. (informal, UK) | The broody boy stared out of the window. | A broody hen puffs up her feathers if you come near.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective; comparatives broodier, broodiest. Related: brood (a group of baby birds; or to think gloomily). Not the same as «bloody» or «brutal».

part of speech: verb form (browse, browses, browsed, browsing); noun (browsing — uncountable)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Looking through things in a relaxed way without searching for anything special, as in shops or books. 2) Looking at pages on the internet. 3) (of animals) Eating leaves and twigs from bushes and trees.
its sense in the lessons: In computing lessons, browsing the web uses a web browser like Chrome, Safari or Firefox; online safety says browse safe sites and tell an adult if you see something upsetting. In the library, «just browsing» means looking at shelves. In science, giraffes and deer are browsers, while cows graze on grass.
examples from the lessons: I am just browsing, thank you. | We spent an hour browsing in the bookshop. | Browsing the internet can be fun but stay safe. | Your browsing history shows which sites you visited. | The giraffe was browsing on the treetops. | Dad was browsing the menu for vegetarian food. | Private browsing does not make you invisible online.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The -ing form of «browse» (drop the e: browse → browsing). Noun: a browse, a browser (the program). Trap: «private browsing» only stops your own device saving history; your school or internet provider may still see it.

part of speech: noun (a Brummie, Brummies — informal, UK); adjective (Brummie — informal, UK)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal, UK) A person from Birmingham, the big city in the middle of England. 2) (informal, UK) The accent and way of speaking of people from Birmingham. 3) (informal, UK) From or to do with Birmingham.
its sense in the lessons: In lessons on accents and dialects, Brummie is one of the best-known English accents, with its own sounds and words (like «bab» for a friendly «dear»). It is a friendly, proud nickname, though some people unfairly make fun of the accent. The name comes from «Brummagem», an old local name for Birmingham.
examples from the lessons: My nan is a proud Brummie. (UK) | He speaks with a strong Brummie accent. | The Brummie comedian made everyone laugh. | «Ta-ra-a-bit, bab» is a Brummie way to say goodbye. | Peaky Blinders is set among Brummies a hundred years ago. | No accent is better than another, Brummie included. | She moved to London but kept her Brummie voice.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually written with a capital B: Brummie, Brummies. Informal, UK. Accents are not mistakes: Brummie, Scouse (Liverpool) and Geordie (Newcastle) are regional ways of speaking English, and Standard English can be spoken in any accent.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The way a painter uses a paintbrush, and the marks the brush leaves on a painting.
its sense in the lessons: In art lessons pupils look at brushwork to talk about a painting: thick, swirly brushwork (Van Gogh), tiny dots, smooth blending or quick dabs (Monet and the Impressionists). It tells the reader about the artist's style and skill. Phrases: «loose brushwork», «bold brushwork».
examples from the lessons: Van Gogh's brushwork is thick and swirly. | Our teacher praised my careful brushwork. | You can see the brushwork up close on the canvas. | Monet used quick, loose brushwork to paint water. | Chinese brushwork uses ink and a soft brush. | The brushwork made the sky look windy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «brushwork», not «a brushwork». Written as one word: brush + work. It is about how the paint is put on, not about cleaning brushes.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A plant grown for its small, triangle-shaped seeds, which are cooked like grain or ground into flour. 2) The seeds or flour of this plant, used for porridge, pancakes and noodles.
its sense in the lessons: In food and science lessons, buckwheat is surprising: despite its name it is not a kind of wheat and has no gluten, so people with coeliac disease can eat it. In world-food lessons it appears in Japanese soba noodles, French galettes (Brittany crêpes) and Ukrainian, Russian and Polish «kasha» (hrechka in Ukrainian).
examples from the lessons: Buckwheat is not related to wheat. | Grandma cooks buckwheat porridge for breakfast. | Soba noodles are made from buckwheat flour. | Buckwheat pancakes are popular in Brittany. | My friend eats buckwheat because it has no gluten. | Bees love buckwheat flowers. | Ukrainian families often eat buckwheat with mushrooms.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «some buckwheat». Trap: the name contains «wheat», but buckwheat is gluten-free and is a seed related to rhubarb, not a grass. Written as one word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A young male cow that has been castrated (had its parts removed so it cannot father calves), usually raised for beef. 2) (US) A young bull.
its sense in the lessons: In farm and geography lessons, bullocks are raised for meat or, in some countries (such as India), used to pull carts and ploughs. In stories, a bullock cart is an old or rural way to travel. It tells the reader we are on a farm.
examples from the lessons: The farmer moved the bullocks to the top field. | A pair of bullocks pulled the heavy cart. | The bullock grazed quietly by the river. | In India, bullock carts carry crops to market. | The bullocks crowded round the water trough. | Grandad sold three bullocks at the market.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a bullock, bullocks. Farm words: a bull is an adult male that can father calves; a steer (US) or bullock (UK) is a castrated male; a cow is a female that has had a calf; a heifer is a young female. Do not confuse with «bollocks», a rude UK swear word.

part of speech: adjective (burdensome; more burdensome, most burdensome) — formal
meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Heavy or hard to carry. 2) (formal) Causing a lot of work, worry or difficulty, as in «burdensome rules».
its sense in the lessons: It is a rather formal word used in exam writing, news and adult talk: «burdensome taxes», «burdensome paperwork». It tells the reader something is a weight on someone. In plain talk say «a pain», «hard» or «heavy».
examples from the lessons: The heavy pack became burdensome on the long hike. | Carers can find their duties burdensome. | The new rules were burdensome for small shops. | He did not want to be burdensome to his family. | Too much homework can feel burdensome. | The king's taxes were burdensome to the poor.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective from «burden» (a heavy load) + -some. Formal register. Opposite: light, easy.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An office or government department that does a special job, such as the FBI (Federal Bureau of Investigation) or a tourist information bureau. 2) (UK) A writing desk with drawers and a lid that folds down. 3) (US) A chest of drawers for clothes.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life you meet bureaus as offices: a «travel bureau», a «weather bureau» (the Bureau of Meteorology in Australia), a «bureau de change» (where you swap money for travel). In homes, Grandma's old bureau may hold letters and pens.
examples from the lessons: The Bureau of Meteorology says it will rain tomorrow. (Australia) | We changed our money at a bureau de change. | The FBI is the Federal Bureau of Investigation. | Grandma keeps her letters in an old wooden bureau. | My socks are in the top drawer of the bureau. (US) | Ask at the tourist bureau for a map.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Two plurals: bureaus (common, US) and bureaux (UK, French style). Said «BYOOR-oh». Spelling trap: b-u-r-e-a-u, from French. Related: bureaucracy (lots of offices and rules), bureaucrat.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A small African animal with huge round eyes, big ears and a long tail that lives in trees and comes out at night. Also called a galago.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about animals and habitats, the bushbaby is a primate (a relative of monkeys and lemurs) that is nocturnal: its big eyes help it see in the dark, and it leaps from branch to branch eating insects and gum. Its name comes from its cry, which sounds like a crying baby.
examples from the lessons: The bushbaby leapt from tree to tree in the dark. | A bushbaby has huge eyes for seeing at night. | We heard a bushbaby crying in the African night. | Bushbabies eat insects and tree gum. | The zoo's nocturnal house has bushbabies. | A bushbaby can jump much further than its own body length.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a bushbaby, bushbabies (y → ies); also «bush baby». It is a nocturnal primate, not a baby of anything. Its other name is galago. It should not be kept as a pet.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A man who works in business, for example running a company, buying and selling, or working in an office in trade. 2) A man who is good at making deals and money.
its sense in the lessons: In money and careers lessons, businesspeople start and run companies, sell products and hire workers. In stories, a businessman may wear a suit and carry a briefcase, but business people come in all kinds. Phrases: «a successful businessman», «a local businessman».
examples from the lessons: The businessman opened three new shops. | My dad is a businessman who sells bikes. | A local businessman paid for the new playground. | The businessman flew to Tokyo for a meeting. | He became a businessman after starting a lemonade stand. | Businessmen and businesswomen met at the conference.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular plural: businessmen. For a woman: businesswoman; neutral: businessperson or business people. Spelling trap: «business» has no letter between «s» and «i»: b-u-s-i-n-e-s-s.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A unit of computer memory or data made of 8 bits (8 ones and zeros); one byte can store one letter like «A».
its sense in the lessons: In computing lessons, bytes measure file sizes and memory: kilobytes (KB), megabytes (MB), gigabytes (GB), terabytes (TB). It tells you how much space a photo, song or game takes up. Phrase: «a byte of data».
examples from the lessons: One byte is made of eight bits. | A single letter takes up about one byte. | This photo is about 3 megabytes. | My tablet has 64 gigabytes of storage. | A kilobyte is about a thousand bytes. | The game needs a lot of bytes of memory. | We counted the bytes in our secret binary message.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a byte, bytes. Homophone trap: «byte» sounds like «bite» (with teeth) and «bight» (a curve in a coast). In maths: 1 byte = 8 bits; 1 kilobyte = 1,000 bytes (or 1,024 in older computer counting); 1 megabyte = 1,000 kilobytes; 1 gigabyte = 1,000 megabytes.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A branch of advanced maths that studies how things change and how to add up endless tiny pieces, used for speed, curves, areas and motion. 2) (medicine) A hard stone that forms in the body, such as a kidney stone; also hard tartar on teeth (dental calculus).
its sense in the lessons: In school maths, calculus is for older students (high school and university), but children may hear of it as the maths of rockets, planets and engineering. In history of science, Isaac Newton and Gottfried Leibniz invented calculus in the 1600s. At the dentist, «calculus» means hard plaque on teeth.
examples from the lessons: My big sister is learning calculus at college. | Calculus helps engineers design bridges and rockets. | Newton and Leibniz both worked out calculus. | Calculus can tell you how fast a ball is moving at each moment. | The dentist cleaned the calculus off my teeth. | You need algebra before you can learn calculus.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable for the maths: «calculus», no «a». Plural «calculi» only for stones. It comes from the Latin word for a small pebble, because counting was once done with stones. Related: calculate, calculator.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (UK) A plain, cheap cotton cloth, usually cream or white and not dyed. 2) (US) A cotton cloth printed with small bright patterns, often flowers. 3) (US) A calico cat: a cat with patches of white, black and orange fur.
its sense in the lessons: In design and technology lessons, calico is used for practice sewing, bags and printing. In history, calico came from Calicut in India and was traded around the world. In American stories and pioneer life, girls wore calico dresses. In science, nearly all calico cats are female because of how fur colour genes work.
examples from the lessons: We printed our designs on calico bags. | The pioneer girl wore a calico dress. | Our calico cat has orange, black and white patches. (US) | The teacher gave each of us a square of calico to sew. | Calico was once shipped from India to England. | Calico is a cheap, plain cotton fabric. (UK)
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable for the cloth: «some calico», «a piece of calico». Plural «calicoes» or «calicos» for kinds or cats. Said «KAL-ih-koh». In the UK a calico cat is usually called a «tortoiseshell and white» cat.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (of a cow, whale, elephant and some other animals) To give birth to a calf. 2) (of a glacier or iceberg) To have a big piece of ice break off and fall into the sea.
its sense in the lessons: In farm and science lessons, cows calve in spring on many farms. In geography and climate lessons, glaciers calve when chunks break off and become icebergs, a sight shown in films about Antarctica, Greenland and Alaska.
examples from the lessons: The cow is due to calve next week. | Most of the cows calved in March. | The glacier calved a huge iceberg into the sea. | We watched a video of ice calving into the ocean. | Elephants calve about every four or five years. | The farmer stayed up all night while the cow calved.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: calved, calving. Trap: «calves» is both the verb («the cow calves») and the plural of «calf» (baby cows, or the backs of your lower legs). Said «kahv» (UK) or «kav» (US); the l is silent.

part of speech: noun (calving — uncountable); verb form (calve, calves, calved, calving)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The birth of a calf, especially on a farm. 2) The breaking off of ice from the edge of a glacier or ice sheet into the sea, making icebergs.
its sense in the lessons: In farm life, «calving season» is the busy time when many calves are born, and farmers help if there is trouble. In geography and climate science, calving makes icebergs; more calving can show glaciers are melting faster. Phrases: «calving season», «calving glacier».
examples from the lessons: It is calving season on the dairy farm. | The vet came to help with a difficult calving. | Calving at the glacier made a huge splash. | Scientists measure calving to see how fast ice sheets shrink. | During calving, the farmer checks the cows at night. | The noise of calving ice sounded like thunder.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The -ing form of «calve», also used as a noun. Drop the e: calve → calving. The l is silent: «KAHV-ing».

part of speech: noun (a canton, cantons); noun (Canton — old name)
meaning for a pupil: 1) One of the states into which Switzerland is divided (26 cantons), each with its own government. 2) A small district of some other countries, such as France or Luxembourg. 3) Canton: the old English name for Guangzhou, a big city in southern China; Cantonese food and language come from there. 4) The top corner of a flag next to the pole (in heraldry and flag design).
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons it is used for Switzerland: Zurich, Geneva and Bern are cantons. In lessons on China, «Cantonese» is the language spoken in Guangzhou and Hong Kong. In flag lessons, the US flag has its stars in the canton.
examples from the lessons: Switzerland is made up of 26 cantons. | Geneva is a canton and also a city. | Each canton has its own laws about schools. | Canton is the old name for Guangzhou. | Cantonese is spoken in Hong Kong. | The Union Jack is in the canton of the Australian flag.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a canton, cantons. Capital C for the old Chinese city name, Canton. Said «KAN-ton». Not to be confused with «cantor» (a singer in a synagogue or church).

part of speech: verb form (capsize, capsizes, capsized, capsizing); noun (capsizing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Turning over in the water, so that the bottom of a boat is on top. 2) Making a boat turn over.
its sense in the lessons: In water safety lessons, capsizing is a danger in boats, canoes and kayaks: wear a life jacket, stay with the boat and keep calm. In sailing clubs, children practise capsizing on purpose to learn how to right the boat. In news, it describes boat accidents.
examples from the lessons: The canoe was capsizing in the big wave. | Wear a life jacket in case of capsizing. | We practised capsizing and righting the dinghy. | Too many people on one side can cause capsizing. | The ferry was capsizing in the storm. | After capsizing, hold on to the boat and wait for help.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The -ing form of «capsize» (drop the e). Past: capsized. Spelling: c-a-p-s-i-z-e; American and British spelling are the same with z. Similar: overturn, keel over. Opposite: right the boat.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An inn with a big courtyard on old trade routes in Asia, the Middle East and North Africa, where travellers and their camels or horses could rest for the night. 2) A group of people travelling together (rare, literary).
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons on the Silk Road, merchants with camel caravans stopped at caravanserais to sleep, trade, water animals and stay safe from robbers. It tells the reader the story is set long ago on desert trade routes. Phrases: «stop at a caravanserai».
examples from the lessons: The merchants rested at a caravanserai on the Silk Road. | Camels drank water in the caravanserai courtyard. | We saw the ruins of a caravanserai in Turkey. | A caravanserai had rooms around a big square yard. | Traders swapped silk and spices at the caravanserai. | The storyteller described a busy caravanserai at night.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a caravanserai, caravanserais (also spelt caravansary). Said «kara-VAN-suh-rye». It comes from Persian: caravan (a group of travellers) + sarai (palace or inn). Not related to the British meaning of «caravan» (a home on wheels).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A doctor who is an expert in the heart and blood vessels and treats heart problems.
its sense in the lessons: In science and health lessons, a cardiologist checks the heart with tools like a stethoscope, an ECG (heart tracing) and an ultrasound scan. In careers talk, it is a hospital specialist. It tells the reader the problem is with the heart.
examples from the lessons: The cardiologist listened to Grandad's heart. | A cardiologist is a heart doctor. | The cardiologist did a scan of my heart. | My aunt trained for many years to become a cardiologist. | The cardiologist said exercise keeps your heart strong. | Children's cardiologists treat babies born with heart problems.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a cardiologist, cardiologists. cardio = heart, -logist = expert. Subject: cardiology. Said «kar-dee-OL-o-jist». Related: cardiac (to do with the heart), cardio (exercise that works the heart).

meaning for a pupil: 1) As many people or things as a car can hold, as in «a carful of children».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life it is used for trips and shopping: «a carful of kids», «a carful of shopping». In maths word problems it can be a unit: if one carful is 5 children, how many cars for 23 children? It is not very common and some say «a carload».
examples from the lessons: A carful of cousins arrived for Sunday lunch. | We took a carful of old toys to the charity shop. | Each carful can hold five people. | Two carfuls of football fans drove to the match. | Mum came back with a carful of shopping. | The team needed four carfuls to get to the game.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a carful, carfuls. Like spoonful, cupful, handful: -ful with one l. Trap: do not confuse with «careful» (taking care). Maths: if a carful is 5 people, 23 people need 5 cars (round up, because 4 cars hold only 20).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Made of cartilage, the tough, bendy tissue found in your ears, nose and the ends of bones. 2) (of fish) Having a skeleton made of cartilage instead of bone, like sharks and rays.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on animals, «cartilaginous fish» (sharks, rays, skates) are one big group of fish; «bony fish» (like salmon and goldfish) are the other. In lessons on the body, cartilage cushions joints. It tells the reader about a bendy, rubbery material.
examples from the lessons: Sharks are cartilaginous fish. | Your ears are cartilaginous, so they bend. | Rays and skates have cartilaginous skeletons. | The tip of your nose is cartilaginous. | Cartilaginous fish have no swim bladder. | We compared cartilaginous fish with bony fish in class.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective from «cartilage». Said «kar-ti-LAJ-i-nus». Long, scientific word; in plain talk say «made of cartilage» or «gristly». Sharks do not have bones at all, apart from teeth, which are not bone either.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A raised road or path across wet ground, marshes or shallow water. 2) The Giant's Causeway: a famous place in Northern Ireland with about 40,000 six-sided rock columns.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons, some islands are joined to the mainland by a causeway that floods at high tide, like Holy Island (Lindisfarne) in England. In safety lessons, check the tide times before crossing a tidal causeway. In science, the Giant's Causeway was made by cooling lava.
examples from the lessons: We walked across the causeway to the island. | Check the tide times before driving over the causeway. | The causeway disappears under the sea at high tide. | The Giant's Causeway has hexagonal columns. | Legend says the giant Finn McCool built the causeway. | A long causeway crosses the marsh.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a causeway, causeways. Not about «cause» (a reason); the word comes from an old word for a raised path. Safety: cars get stuck on tidal causeways every year when drivers ignore the tide.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Able to burn or eat away skin and other materials by a chemical action, as in «caustic soda». 2) Cruel and sharp in a clever, sarcastic way, as in «a caustic remark».
its sense in the lessons: In science and safety lessons, caustic chemicals such as drain cleaner, oven cleaner and caustic soda (sodium hydroxide) are strong alkalis that burn skin and eyes: never touch them, keep them locked away, and read hazard labels. In stories, a caustic comment tells the reader that a character is being bitingly unkind.
examples from the lessons: Caustic soda can burn your skin. | The drain cleaner bottle had a caustic warning sign. | Wear gloves and goggles with caustic chemicals. | She made a caustic remark about his drawing. | The critic wrote a caustic review of the film. | Keep caustic cleaners out of children's reach. | His caustic jokes hurt people's feelings.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective. Said «KAWS-tik». Science note: caustic usually means a strong alkali (base), not an acid, but both can burn. If a caustic chemical gets on skin, rinse with lots of water and get an adult or call for help.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Careful to avoid danger, risks or mistakes. 2) Slow to decide or to trust, as in «cautious about strangers».
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons it describes good behaviour: be cautious near roads, water, fire and online. In stories it tells the reader a character is careful, maybe nervous. In maths and science, a cautious estimate is a careful one that does not overclaim. Phrases: «be cautious about», «cautious optimism».
examples from the lessons: Be cautious when crossing a busy road. | The cat was cautious around the new puppy. | She is cautious about talking to strangers online. | He took a cautious step onto the ice. | The cautious driver slowed down in the fog. | Scientists were cautious about the early results. | My cautious guess is about 50 sweets in the jar.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective. Adverb: cautiously; noun: caution. Spelling: c-a-u-t-i-o-u-s, with «au» and «-tious». Opposites: careless, reckless, bold.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, Canada's public radio and TV broadcaster (in French: Radio-Canada). 2) (medicine) A complete blood count, a common blood test that counts the different kinds of cells in your blood.
its sense in the lessons: In Canada, children know CBC for news, radio and kids' shows (CBC Kids); it is like the BBC in the UK or the ABC in Australia. In health, a doctor may order a CBC to check for illness. It is an abbreviation, not a word.
examples from the lessons: We watched the news on CBC. (Canada) | CBC Kids has lots of cartoons. | The doctor ordered a CBC blood test. | CBC is Canada's public broadcaster, like the BBC. | My aunt works for CBC radio in Toronto. | A CBC counts red cells, white cells and platelets.
note for the reader of a maths problem: An abbreviation, written in capital letters: CBC, said letter by letter «see-bee-see». The input is lower case only because of the word list. Not to be confused with the BBC (UK) or the ABC (Australia).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To give up land, power or rights to someone else, often because you have to, for example after a war or a deal. 2) (formal, sport) To give away a point or advantage, as in «cede possession».
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, countries ceded land in treaties: Spain ceded Florida, and China ceded Hong Kong to Britain in 1842. In news and politics it is the formal word for handing over control. It tells the reader power or land is changing hands.
examples from the lessons: The country had to cede land after the war. | In 1842, China ceded Hong Kong Island to Britain. | The king would not cede any power to the nobles. | The team ceded the ball too easily. | The landowner ceded part of his field for a road. | Spain ceded Florida to the United States in 1819.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: ceded, ceding. Formal: in plain talk say «give up» or «hand over». Homophone trap: «cede» sounds like «seed». Related nouns: cession (not «session»). Spelling family: cede, concede, precede, recede.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To do with the sky or outer space, as in «celestial bodies» like stars, planets and moons. 2) To do with heaven, or heavenly and very beautiful, as in «celestial music».
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, «celestial bodies» means objects in space, and the «celestial sphere» is the imaginary dome of the sky used in astronomy. In stories and church language, «celestial» describes heaven and angels. It tells the reader of something high, starry or heavenly.
examples from the lessons: The Sun, the Moon and the planets are celestial bodies. | Ancient sailors used celestial navigation by the stars. | The choir sounded celestial. | A celestial map shows the constellations. | In the poem, angels sang in the celestial city. | The comet was a rare celestial event. | Christians believe in a celestial heaven with God.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective. Said «suh-LES-tee-ul» or «suh-LES-chul». Opposite: terrestrial (to do with Earth). Spelling: c-e-l-e-s-t-i-a-l.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An officer in the army of ancient Rome, in charge of about 80 to 100 soldiers (a century). 2) (Bible) Centurions appear in the New Testament, such as the centurion at Capernaum whose servant Jesus healed, and the centurion at the cross.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons on the Romans, the centurion had a helmet with a sideways crest and carried a vine stick; he trained and led his soldiers. In Bible lessons, the centurion's faith is a well-known story («Lord, I am not worthy…»). In cricket and sport slang, a «centurion» is a player who scores a hundred.
examples from the lessons: The centurion shouted orders to his soldiers. | A centurion led about eighty legionaries. | Our class built a model of a centurion's helmet. | In the Bible, a centurion asked Jesus to heal his servant. | The centurion's helmet had a crest from side to side. | Roman centurions guarded Hadrian's Wall.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a centurion, centurions. From Latin «centum» (a hundred), like century and cent. Maths link: a century of soldiers was named for 100, but in practice it was often 80 men.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Chief Executive Officer: the most important manager of a company or organisation, who makes the big decisions and leads the other managers.
its sense in the lessons: In money and careers lessons, the CEO is the boss of a business, answering to a board of directors. In news, CEOs of big tech or car companies are often in the headlines. Children sometimes joke «I'm the CEO of snacks» meaning in charge of something.
examples from the lessons: The CEO announced a new phone. | My mum is the CEO of a small charity. | The CEO reports to the board of directors. | She started the company and became its CEO. | The CEO visited the factory workers. | He joked he was CEO of the family's TV remote. (informal)
note for the reader of a maths problem: An abbreviation, written in capitals: CEO, plural CEOs; said letter by letter «see-ee-oh». The input is lower case only because of the word list. Use «a CEO» (because it starts with a consonant sound «see»). Similar titles: managing director (UK), president.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Containing chalk or made of chalk, as in «chalky soil» or «chalky cliffs». 2) White and pale like chalk, as in «a chalky face». 3) Dry and powdery, as in «chalky tablets».
its sense in the lessons: In geography and science lessons, chalky land (like the White Cliffs of Dover and the South Downs) is made of a soft white rock formed from tiny sea creatures. In stories, a «chalky» face means very pale, often from fear or illness. On the playground, chalk drawings leave chalky hands.
examples from the lessons: The White Cliffs of Dover are chalky. | After drawing on the pavement, my hands were chalky. | His face went chalky white when he saw the spider. | Some plants grow well in chalky soil. | The medicine tasted dry and chalky. | Chalky water leaves white marks on the kettle.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: chalk + -y. Comparatives: chalkier, chalkiest. Science note: chalk is a kind of limestone (calcium carbonate). Chalky soil drains water quickly.

part of speech: noun (charades — a game, used with a singular verb)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A party game where one player acts out a word, film, book or song title without speaking, and the others try to guess it. 2) (charade, a charade, charades) A silly pretence that everyone can see through, as in «the meeting was a charade».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday family life and drama lessons, charades is a fun game, especially at Christmas, with signs like holding up fingers for the number of words and tugging an ear for «sounds like». In stories, «a charade» tells the reader something is fake or just for show.
examples from the lessons: We played charades after Christmas dinner. | In charades, you must not speak. | I acted out «Frozen» in charades. | Charades is my favourite party game. | His kindness was just a charade to get our sweets. | Hold up two fingers in charades to show two words.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The game name «charades» looks plural but takes a singular verb: «Charades is fun». Said «shuh-RAHDZ» (UK) or «shuh-RAYDZ» (US). For a pretence use the singular: «a charade».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A special charm and confidence that makes people like, notice and follow someone. 2) (church) In some churches, a spiritual gift (charism) that Christians believe is given by the Holy Spirit.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and news it describes leaders, actors and singers who draw people in. In stories it tells the reader a character is magnetic and persuasive. Children use «rizz» in slang for a similar idea about charm. In church talk, «charismatic» churches stress spiritual gifts like lively praise.
examples from the lessons: The new class captain has lots of charisma. | Good leaders often have charisma. | The singer's charisma filled the whole stadium. | He was not handsome, but he had charisma. | Charisma helped her win the election. | Some people mistake charisma for being kind.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «charisma», not «a charisma». Adjective: charismatic. Said «kuh-RIZ-muh» (the ch sounds like k). Trap: charisma does not mean someone is good or honest; persuasive people can mislead too.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A visit to a doctor, dentist or vet to check that you are healthy, even when you feel fine. 2) A check of a machine or car to make sure it works properly.
its sense in the lessons: In health lessons, regular checkups at the dentist and the doctor help find problems early. In everyday life, a car or boiler can also have a checkup. Phrases: «go for a checkup», «a dental checkup».
examples from the lessons: I have a dental checkup next week. | The doctor gave the baby a checkup. | The dentist said my teeth were fine at my checkup. | Our dog went to the vet for a checkup. | Dad took the car in for a checkup before the trip. | Regular checkups help catch problems early.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a checkup, checkups. Also spelt «check-up» (common in the UK) or «checkup» (US). The verb is two words: «The doctor will check up on you».

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a happy, bright and friendly way. 2) Willingly, without complaining, as in «she cheerfully helped». 3) Without caring or noticing a problem, as in «he cheerfully ignored the rules».
its sense in the lessons: In stories it tells the reader that a character is in a good mood or happy to help. In PSHE lessons, doing jobs cheerfully is shown as a kind attitude. Phrases: «cheerfully agreed», «whistled cheerfully».
examples from the lessons: She cheerfully said good morning to everyone. | He whistled cheerfully as he walked to school. | The children cheerfully tidied the classroom. | Grandpa waved cheerfully from the window. | The sun shone cheerfully on the garden. | He cheerfully ignored the «Keep Off the Grass» sign.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from «cheerful» + -ly: two l's (cheer-ful-ly). Opposites: gloomily, grumpily, sadly.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Tasting or smelling of cheese, or full of cheese. 2) (informal) Silly, cheap or too sentimental in an embarrassing way, as in «a cheesy joke» or «a cheesy song». 3) (informal) A «cheesy grin» is a very big, wide smile, often a bit fake, like when you say «cheese» for a photo.
its sense in the lessons: In food talk, cheesy pasta or cheesy chips have lots of cheese. In everyday and school talk, «cheesy» is a common informal word for corny jokes, films and pop songs. In writing lessons, teachers may say an ending is «cheesy» if it is too sweet or predictable.
examples from the lessons: We had cheesy pasta bake for tea. | Dad tells really cheesy jokes. | The film had a cheesy happy ending. | He gave a big cheesy grin for the photo. | These crisps are extra cheesy. | That song is so cheesy, but I love it. | Cheesy feet smell is caused by bacteria!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: cheese + -y (drop the e). Comparatives: cheesier, cheesiest. Informal for meanings 2 and 3. Similar: corny (jokes), naff (UK).

part of speech: adjective (chewy, chewier, chewiest); noun (chewy — Australia, informal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Needing a lot of chewing because it is soft but tough or sticky, as in «chewy sweets» or «chewy meat». 2) (Australia, NZ, informal) «Chewy» is slang for chewing gum.
its sense in the lessons: In food lessons it describes texture: chewy cookies, chewy toffee, chewy bread crusts. In dental health lessons, sticky chewy sweets can harm teeth. In Australian everyday talk, «Got any chewy?» means «Have you got any gum?».
examples from the lessons: These toffees are very chewy. | The steak was too chewy to eat. | I like chewy cookies more than crunchy ones. | Got any chewy? (Australia, informal) | Chewy sweets can stick to your teeth. | The bagel was warm and chewy. | Gummy bears are soft and chewy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: chew + -y. Comparatives: chewier, chewiest. Opposite textures: crunchy, crispy, tender. In Australia, «chewy» as a noun is uncountable: «some chewy».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A natural gum made from the milky sap of the sapodilla tree of Central America, used in the past to make chewing gum.
its sense in the lessons: In history and geography lessons, the Maya and Aztec peoples chewed chicle long ago, and chewing gum companies in the USA later used it. Most modern gum is made from plastics-like synthetic gum instead. It links science (plant sap) to everyday life (gum).
examples from the lessons: Chicle comes from the sap of the sapodilla tree. | The ancient Maya chewed chicle. | Workers called chicleros collected chicle in the forest. | Early chewing gum was made from chicle. | Most gum today is not made from chicle. | We saw a photo of chicle being tapped from a tree.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «some chicle». Said «CHIK-ul». It comes from a Nahuatl (Aztec) word. Do not confuse with «chuckle» or «tickle». The brand name «Chiclets» comes from it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) Cheerful and lively, full of energy, as in «you're very chipper this morning». 2) (Ireland, Scotland, informal) A chip shop, a takeaway selling fish and chips. 3) A machine that chops wood or branches into small chips (a wood chipper).
its sense in the lessons: In everyday talk it describes a happy, bouncy mood. In Ireland and Scotland, «going to the chipper» means getting chips from the takeaway. In gardening and safety, a wood chipper is a dangerous machine only adults should use.
examples from the lessons: Grandma was feeling chipper after her walk. | You're very chipper for a Monday morning! (informal) | We got fish and chips from the chipper. (Ireland) | The gardeners fed branches into the chipper. | Stay well away from the wood chipper. | He sounded chipper on the phone.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal adjective; it does not usually take «more» or «-er». Similar: cheerful, perky, upbeat. Countable as a noun: a chipper, chippers. In the UK, a chip shop is also called a «chippy».

meaning for a pupil: 1) The rules and ideals that medieval knights were supposed to follow: being brave, loyal, honest, protecting the weak and serving God and their lord. 2) Polite, kind and generous behaviour, especially old-fashioned courtesy shown by men to women, like holding a door.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons about the Middle Ages, chivalry is the knights' code, linked with castles, tournaments and stories of King Arthur. In everyday life, «chivalry is not dead» is said when someone is gallant or courteous. Today kindness and good manners are for everyone, not just men to women.
examples from the lessons: Knights were expected to follow the rules of chivalry. | King Arthur's knights were famous for their chivalry. | Holding the door for someone is a small act of chivalry. | «Chivalry isn't dead!» said Gran when the boy carried her bags. | The story is full of chivalry, quests and dragons. | Chivalry asked knights to protect the weak.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «chivalry», not «a chivalry». Adjective: chivalrous. Said «SHIV-ul-ree» (the ch sounds like sh, from French). Myth: real medieval knights did not always live up to chivalry.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A chemical made from chlorine and ammonia, used to kill germs in tap water. 2) The smelly chemicals that form in swimming pools when chlorine mixes with sweat and wee; they cause the «pool smell» and sore eyes.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on clean water, some water companies use chloramine to keep tap water safe. In swimming and health lessons, the strong «chlorine smell» at pools is actually mostly chloramines, which is why you should shower before swimming. Safety: never mix bleach and ammonia cleaners; that makes chloramine gas, which is harmful to breathe.
examples from the lessons: Some cities add chloramine to tap water to kill germs. | The strong pool smell comes from chloramines. | Shower before swimming to reduce chloramines. | Never mix bleach and ammonia cleaners; they make chloramine gas. | Chloramine in tap water can harm pet fish, so it must be removed first. | Chloramines can make your eyes red and itchy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable in science (chloramines are a group of chemicals); uncountable for the substance. Said «KLOR-uh-meen». Myth: a strong pool smell does not mean too much chlorine; it often means the water needs more cleaning.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To add chlorine to water to kill germs and make it safe for drinking or swimming. 2) (chemistry) To combine a substance with chlorine.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography lessons on clean water, towns chlorinate drinking water, which has saved millions of lives by stopping diseases like cholera. At swimming pools, the water is chlorinated to keep it clean. It tells the reader about keeping water germ-free.
examples from the lessons: They chlorinate the pool water every day. | Our tap water is chlorinated to kill germs. | Chlorinating drinking water stops cholera. | The lifeguard tested how chlorinated the pool was. | Engineers chlorinate the water at the treatment works. | Chlorinated water can make your hair feel dry.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: chlorinated, chlorinating. Noun: chlorination. Said «KLOR-in-ate». Safety: the chlorine chemicals used to treat pools are dangerous on their own and are handled only by trained adults.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A tiny green part inside plant cells where photosynthesis happens: it uses sunlight to make food (sugar) from water and carbon dioxide, giving off oxygen.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on cells, chloroplasts are found in plant cells but not animal cells; they contain chlorophyll, the green pigment that makes leaves green. Pupils label them on cell diagrams, together with the nucleus, cell wall and vacuole.
examples from the lessons: Chloroplasts make food for the plant using sunlight. | Plant cells have chloroplasts, but animal cells do not. | Chloroplasts contain green chlorophyll. | Under the microscope, we saw green chloroplasts in the leaf cells. | Photosynthesis happens inside the chloroplasts. | Label the chloroplast on your cell diagram.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a chloroplast, chloroplasts. chloro = green, plast = formed thing. Trap: chlorophyll is the green chemical; the chloroplast is the tiny part of the cell that holds it. Nothing to do with chlorine except the Greek word for green.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) Very careful about what you choose, and hard to please, especially about food, clothes or friends.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life it describes picky eaters and shoppers. Phrases: «Beggars can't be choosers», meaning if you need help you must accept what you are given. In nature lessons, some animals are «choosy» about mates or food. It can be a fair or a slightly critical word.
examples from the lessons: My little brother is choosy about his food. | Cats can be very choosy eaters. | She is choosy about which books she reads. | Don't be so choosy, just pick a sweet! | The female bird is choosy about her mate. | You can't be choosy when you are starving.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal adjective: choose + -y (drop the e). Comparatives: choosier, choosiest. Similar: picky, fussy. Spelling trap: choosy, not «choosey» (that spelling is sometimes seen but less common).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Slightly fat and round in a soft, often cute way, as in «chubby cheeks» or «a chubby baby».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, people often say «chubby» about babies, puppies and cheeks in a fond way. In PSHE lessons, children learn that commenting on someone's body or weight can hurt, so it is kinder not to call people chubby. In stories it describes how a character looks.
examples from the lessons: The baby had chubby little hands. | Our puppy is round and chubby. | Grandma pinched my chubby cheeks. | The chubby hamster stuffed seeds into its cheeks. | It is unkind to tease someone for being chubby. | The cartoon bear had a chubby tummy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective. Comparatives: chubbier, chubbiest (double b, y → i). Softer than «fat» and often affectionate, but can still hurt about older children or adults. Similar: plump, podgy (UK), roly-poly.

part of speech: verb (chuckle, chuckles, chuckled, chuckling); noun (a chuckle, chuckles)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To laugh quietly, often with your mouth closed, because something is amusing. 2) A soft, quiet laugh.
its sense in the lessons: In stories it tells the reader a character is gently amused, not roaring with laughter; it often fits a kind grandparent or a sly villain. In writing lessons, it is one of many laughing verbs: giggle, chuckle, chortle, snigger, cackle, guffaw. Phrase: «have a chuckle».
examples from the lessons: Grandpa chuckled at his own joke. | She gave a little chuckle as she read the comic. | The audience chuckled at the funny line. | «Very clever,» he chuckled. | We had a good chuckle about the muddy football match. | The sly fox chuckled to himself.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: chuckled, chuckling (drop the e). Countable noun: a chuckle. Laughing words from soft to loud: chuckle, giggle, laugh, guffaw, roar. A «snigger» is an unkind laugh.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (UK, Ireland, Australia, NZ) An alcoholic drink made from the juice of crushed apples, a bit like beer in strength. 2) (USA, Canada) Cloudy apple juice that has not been filtered, often drunk hot in autumn; it has no alcohol unless called «hard cider». 3) A glass or bottle of this drink: «two ciders».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life children meet cider at autumn fairs, apple orchards, harvest festivals and Halloween in North America (hot apple cider with cinnamon), and as an adult drink in pubs in the UK and Ireland. In science lessons it shows fermentation: yeast turns the sugar in apple juice into alcohol and gas. Phrases: «hot cider», «hard cider», «apple cider vinegar», «cider press», «a pint of cider». In stories it often sets a cosy autumn or country scene (Somerset farms, orchards).
examples from the lessons: We drank hot apple cider at the pumpkin patch. | In Canada, cider at the farm stand is just thick apple juice. | My uncle ordered a pint of cider at the pub. | Cider is for grown-ups in England because it contains alcohol. | The farmer put the apples into the cider press. | Yeast turns the sugar in apple juice into alcohol, and that is how cider is made. | Mum puts a splash of apple cider vinegar in the salad dressing. | The orchard smelt of apples and cider.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelled with a C, not «sider». Usually uncountable («some cider»), but «a cider» means a glass or bottle of it. The big trap is the meaning: in the USA and Canada «cider» is usually non-alcoholic juice, while in the UK, Ireland, Australia and NZ it is an alcoholic drink, so a recipe or story may mean different things. «Hard cider» (US) is the alcoholic one. Apple cider vinegar is not a drink.

part of speech: noun (cipher, ciphers; also spelled cypher, UK); verb (cipher, ciphers, ciphered, ciphering — rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A secret code in which letters are swapped or mixed up by a rule so that only people who know the rule can read the message. 2) A message written in such a code. 3) A person who has no power or importance and just does what others say: «The king was a mere cipher». 4) (old or formal) The figure zero, 0; in old books also any number digit. 5) (verb, old) To do sums or to write in code.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and computing lessons ciphers teach patterns and shifting: a Caesar cipher moves every letter a fixed number of places along the alphabet (A becomes D with a shift of 3). In history it links to Alan Turing and the code-breakers of Bletchley Park who broke the German Enigma cipher in the Second World War. In stories a cipher is a puzzle the heroes must crack. Phrases: «Caesar cipher», «break a cipher», «crack the cipher», «written in cipher», «a cipher key».
examples from the lessons: We wrote secret notes to each other in a Caesar cipher. | With a shift of three, the word CAT becomes FDW in the cipher. | The spies sent the plans in cipher. | It took the code-breakers months to crack the cipher. | Without the key the cipher looked like nonsense. | In the story, the map was covered in a strange cipher. | The new prime minister was just a cipher for the party bosses. | Our maths teacher turned the times tables into a cipher puzzle.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelled cipher (US and most UK) or cypher (older UK). Strictly, a code swaps whole words, while a cipher changes single letters, but in everyday talk people use both for secret writing. To «encipher» or «encrypt» is to put a message into a cipher; to «decipher» or «decrypt» is to get it back out. «Decipher» also means to read messy handwriting. In a maths puzzle, a shift cipher wraps around: after Z comes A again.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The tank above or behind a toilet that holds water for flushing. 2) A tank, often in the loft or under the ground, that stores water for a house or building. 3) In old times and dry places, a large underground pool or tank for collecting rainwater.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life the cistern is the part of the toilet that fills after you flush; plumbers fix «a leaking cistern». In science and geography it connects to water storage and saving rainwater in dry countries. In history, ancient cities such as Istanbul had huge underground cisterns. Phrases: «toilet cistern», «cold-water cistern», «the cistern is refilling».
examples from the lessons: The toilet will not flush until the cistern fills up again. | Dad lifted the lid of the cistern to fix the chain. | The cold-water cistern is up in the loft. | The ancient city kept rainwater in a great stone cistern. | We visited a huge underground cistern with hundreds of columns. | Water dripped from the cistern all night. | On the farm, a cistern collects rain from the roof.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one cistern, two cisterns. Do not confuse with «sister» or «system». A cistern stores water; a «tank» is a more general word. In maths problems a cistern is often the container being filled or emptied: if a pipe fills it at 5 litres a minute, a 60-litre cistern takes 12 minutes.

part of speech: verb (clasp, clasps, clasped, clasping); noun (a clasp, clasps)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (verb) To hold something tightly in your hand or arms: «She clasped her teddy». 2) (verb) To put your hands together with the fingers locked: «clasp your hands». 3) (noun) A small metal fastener that holds two parts together, for example on a necklace, bag or belt. 4) (noun) A tight hold or grip: «a firm clasp».
its sense in the lessons: In stories «clasped» shows strong feeling: a frightened child clasps a parent's hand, a happy friend clasps someone in a hug, someone prays with clasped hands. In everyday life clasps fasten jewellery, purses and old books. In PE or drama teachers might say «clasp your hands behind your back». Phrases: «clasp hands», «hands clasped», «clasp to your chest», «necklace clasp».
examples from the lessons: She clasped her little brother's hand as they crossed the road. | He sat with his hands clasped in his lap. | Grandma could not open the tiny clasp on her necklace. | The old diary had a brass clasp and a lock. | The winner clasped the trophy to her chest. | My bag's clasp snapped open and my pencils fell out. | They clasped each other in a big hug at the airport. | Clasp your hands behind your head and lie back.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past form: clasped (one syllable, said «claspt»). «Clasp» is stronger and more careful than «hold» and often shows emotion. A «grasp» is a firm hold, often to take something; a «clasp» is holding close or fastening. «Clasp» as a fastener is countable: a clasp, two clasps.

part of speech: noun (clout; also a clout, clouts); verb (clout, clouts, clouted, clouting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (noun) Power and influence over what happens: «The big companies have a lot of clout». 2) (noun, informal, UK) A hard hit, especially with the hand: «a clout round the ear». 3) (verb, informal) To hit someone or something hard. 4) (noun, sport) In baseball or cricket, a hard hit of the ball. 5) (noun, old, UK dialect) A piece of cloth or a rag, as in the saying «Ne'er cast a clout till May be out».
its sense in the lessons: In news and politics «clout» means power to get your way: rich countries, big firms or famous people «have clout». In stories set in the past, an angry adult might give a naughty child «a clout», which today we know is hitting and is not okay. In sport commentary a batter «clouts» the ball for a home run or a six. Phrases: «political clout», «financial clout», «have clout», «a clout round the ear», «don't cast a clout till May be out» (do not take off warm clothes too early in spring).
examples from the lessons: The school council does not have much clout, but the head teacher listens to it. | Big supermarkets use their clout to get low prices from farmers. | In the old story, the farmer gave the boy a clout round the ear. | The batter clouted the ball over the fence. | Hitting people is wrong, so nobody should get a clout for a mistake. | Grandma says, «Ne'er cast a clout till May be out», so I kept my coat on. | The star footballer's clout helped raise money for the hospital. | That country has a lot of clout at the United Nations.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Clout» meaning power is uncountable (much clout, a lot of clout). «A clout» meaning a hit is countable. The «hit» sense is informal and mostly British; hitting a person is never a safe or kind thing to do. Do not confuse with «cloud» (sky) or «clot» (a lump of blood; also UK slang for a silly person).

part of speech: verb (cluck, clucks, clucked, clucking); noun (a cluck, clucks)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (verb) When a hen clucks, she makes her short, low, repeated sound. 2) (noun) That sound a hen makes. 3) (verb) To make a clicking sound with your tongue to show you disapprove, are sorry or are worried: «Mum clucked her tongue». 4) (verb) To fuss over someone in a worried, caring way, like a mother hen: «cluck over the baby». 5) (noun, slang, US, old) A silly or stupid person: «You dumb cluck!»
its sense in the lessons: In farm topics and animal sounds in early reading: cows moo, hens cluck. In stories «clucked her tongue» shows an adult who is unhappy, worried or sympathetic; «clucked over» shows someone fussing. Phrases: «cluck your tongue», «cluck over», «cluck and fuss», «cluck-cluck».
examples from the lessons: The hens clucked happily in the farmyard. | We heard a cluck from inside the henhouse. | Gran clucked her tongue when she saw my muddy shoes. | The aunties clucked over the new baby all afternoon. | Cluck, cluck, went the chicken as it pecked the corn. | The teacher clucked sympathetically when I told her about my lost dog. | In the old cartoon, the sailor called his friend a dumb cluck.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The word copies the sound itself (onomatopoeia), like «moo» and «quack». A hen clucks; a rooster crows; chicks cheep. «Cluck» (sound) and «clock» (time) sound different. «Dumb cluck» is old-fashioned and a bit unkind.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A large, fluffy breed of chicken with feathers growing down over its legs and feet, first brought to Britain from Asia in the 1800s. 2) (a place name) Cochin, the old English name of Kochi, a port city in the state of Kerala in south-west India, famous for spices and fishing nets. 3) (a place name) Cochin China, an old French name for the southern part of Vietnam.
its sense in the lessons: It appears in farm, pet-chicken and history texts. Cochin chickens are gentle, round birds that children keep as pets; the place Cochin appears in stories of the spice trade and of explorers like Vasco da Gama. Phrases: «a Cochin hen», «bantam Cochin», «Cochin (now Kochi)».
examples from the lessons: Our neighbour keeps a fluffy Cochin hen in her garden. | Cochin chickens have feathers right down to their toes. | The Cochin was so calm that the little ones could stroke it. | Ships sailed to Cochin to buy pepper and spices. | Cochin is now called Kochi. | We saw the big Chinese fishing nets of Kochi in a geography video.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually written with a capital C because it comes from a place name. Said «KO-chin» or «KOH-chin». The city's official name today is Kochi; Cochin is the older English spelling. It is not connected to «coach».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A large brown European beetle, also called a May bug or doodlebug, that flies clumsily on spring evenings and buzzes loudly. 2) Its young, a fat white grub that lives in the soil and eats plant roots.
its sense in the lessons: In science (minibeasts, life cycles) the cockchafer shows complete metamorphosis: egg, larva (grub), pupa, adult beetle; the grubs can live underground for three or four years. In the UK and Europe children see them bumping into lit windows in May. Phrases: «May bug», «cockchafer grub», «cockchafer larvae».
examples from the lessons: A cockchafer bumped against our window in the evening. | The cockchafer has fan-shaped feelers. | Its grubs live underground for years eating roots. | People also call the cockchafer a May bug. | The cockchafer buzzed loudly and flew in a wobbly line. | Farmers once thought cockchafers were a pest because the grubs ate crops. | We drew the life cycle of the cockchafer in science.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Said «COCK-chay-fer». «Chafer» is an old word for beetle; «cock» here just means big or male and is not rude. Plural: cockchafers. Although noisy and big, cockchafers do not sting or bite people.

part of speech: noun (coco, cocos); proper noun (Coco, a name)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The coconut palm, the tall tropical tree that grows coconuts; also short for coconut in words like «coco fibre» and «coco husk». 2) (a name) Coco is a first name or pet name for people and animals, for example the fashion designer Coco Chanel or a pet dog called Coco. 3) Part of brand and film names, such as the breakfast cereal Coco Pops and the Disney film «Coco» about the Mexican Day of the Dead.
its sense in the lessons: It is a short honest entry: in everyday life the word mostly appears as part of «coconut», in plant-pot fibre («coco coir»), and as a name. In geography it links to tropical beaches where coconut palms grow. Phrases: «coco palm», «coco fibre», «coco coir».
examples from the lessons: The coco palm grows along tropical beaches. | Mum lined the hanging basket with coco fibre. | Our neighbour's poodle is called Coco. | We watched the film «Coco» about a boy and his family's music. | Coco Chanel was a famous French fashion designer. | I had a bowl of Coco Pops before school.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Do not confuse «coco» (the coconut palm) with «cocoa» (powder from cacao beans used for chocolate drinks); they sound the same but are different plants. As a name it is written with a capital C.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal, UK, Australia, NZ) Nonsense; something that is silly and untrue: «That's a load of codswallop!»
its sense in the lessons: It is a fun, cheeky word adults use when they think a story, excuse or claim is rubbish. It is not rude, so you might hear it from grandparents, teachers or on TV. In critical-thinking lessons it is a word for claims without evidence. Phrases: «a load of codswallop», «utter codswallop», «complete codswallop».
examples from the lessons: «The dog ate my homework? What a load of codswallop!» | Grandad said the advert's promises were utter codswallop. | That story about a monster in the school basement is complete codswallop. | «Codswallop!» shouted the old man at the telly. | Don't believe that codswallop about chocolate making you fly. | The scientist showed that the claim was codswallop by doing a fair test.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «a load of codswallop», never «a codswallop» or «codswallops». It is informal but not a swear word. A popular story says it came from a man called Hiram Codd who made fizzy-drink bottles, but nobody really knows; that tale is probably a myth. Similar words: rubbish, nonsense, poppycock, balderdash, (US) baloney.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To work together with other people to make something or reach a shared goal: «We collaborated on the poster». 2) (history, negative) To help an enemy who has taken over your country, especially in a war: «Some people collaborated with the invaders».
its sense in the lessons: In school, teachers ask pupils to collaborate in group work, science projects and team problem-solving; it is a key skill for scientists, artists and engineers. In history lessons the second, negative sense describes people who helped occupying armies, as in the Second World War. Phrases: «collaborate with someone», «collaborate on a project», «collaborate closely».
examples from the lessons: Our class collaborated with another school to make a newspaper. | The two authors collaborated on a book about dinosaurs. | Scientists from many countries collaborated to build the space station. | In maths we collaborated to solve the puzzle in pairs. | Musicians collaborate when they write a song together. | In the war, some people were punished for collaborating with the enemy. | Let's collaborate instead of arguing about whose idea is best.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelled with double l: col-LAB-or-ate. You collaborate WITH a person ON a thing. The noun is «collaboration» and a person who collaborates is a «collaborator» (in history this can be an insult meaning a traitor). Do not confuse with «corroborate», which means to support or confirm a story with evidence.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Done by people working together, not alone: «a collaborative project». 2) Good at working with others or liking to share work: «a collaborative team».
its sense in the lessons: In school reports and lesson plans it describes group work: «collaborative learning», «collaborative writing», «a collaborative art piece». In science and business it describes shared research and teamwork. Phrases: «collaborative project», «collaborative learning», «collaborative effort», «in a collaborative way».
examples from the lessons: The mural was a collaborative project by the whole school. | Our class story was collaborative: everybody wrote one page. | Scientists say that most big discoveries are collaborative. | The coach praised the team for its collaborative spirit. | We use a collaborative document so we can all type at the same time. | Building the robot was a collaborative effort.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It comes from the verb «collaborate» with the ending -ive. Spelled with double l. The adverb is «collaboratively» (we worked collaboratively). Similar: cooperative, joint, shared. The opposite is individual or solo.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (history) The forcing of farmers to give up their own land and animals and join big farms run by the state, as in the Soviet Union in the late 1920s and 1930s. 2) More generally, putting things that belonged to separate people under shared or state ownership.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons it is part of the story of the Soviet Union under Stalin: private farms were taken and joined into collective farms (kolkhozes); farmers who resisted were punished, and grain was seized. In Ukraine this led to the man-made famine of 1932–1933 called the Holodomor, in which millions of people died; Ukraine and many countries recognise it as a genocide. China also collectivised farms in the 1950s. Phrases: «forced collectivisation», «the collectivisation of agriculture».
examples from the lessons: Collectivisation took land away from millions of farmers. | During collectivisation, families had to give their cows to the collective farm. | Forced collectivisation helped cause the Holodomor famine in Ukraine. | Our history book has a chapter on collectivisation in the Soviet Union. | Many farmers who refused collectivisation were sent far away. | Collectivisation was meant to grow more food, but harvests fell.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK spelling with -s- (collectivisation), US spelling with -z- (collectivization). Uncountable. The verb is «collectivise» (collectivize). Do not confuse it with friendly sharing such as a co-op that people choose to join: collectivisation in history usually means it was forced.

part of speech: noun (a colobus, colobuses; also colobus monkey)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A slender African monkey with long silky fur, a long tail and only a stump instead of a thumb; the best-known kind is black and white. 2) The group of these monkeys, which live high in forest trees and eat mostly leaves.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography lessons on rainforests and animal adaptations, the colobus shows how animals fit their habitat: it has a special stomach with many parts to digest tough leaves, and it leaps between branches without needing a thumb. Phrases: «black-and-white colobus», «red colobus», «colobus monkey».
examples from the lessons: The colobus leapt from tree to tree high above us. | A black-and-white colobus has a long, white, bushy tail. | Colobus monkeys eat leaves, not bananas. | The word «colobus» comes from a Greek word meaning «cut short», because of its missing thumb. | We saw colobus monkeys at the zoo in their tall tree house. | Cutting down forests puts some kinds of colobus in danger.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Said «KOL-uh-bus». Plural: colobuses or colobus monkeys. A trap: many people think all monkeys need thumbs to climb, but the colobus manages with just hooked fingers.

part of speech: noun (colouring, colourings; US spelling coloring); verb form (present participle of colour: colouring)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (noun) The colour or colours of something, especially of a person's skin, hair and eyes or an animal's fur or feathers: «a fox's red colouring». 2) (noun) A substance added to food or drink to give it colour: «food colouring». 3) (noun) The activity of filling in pictures with crayons, pencils or pens: «a colouring book». 4) (verb form) Giving colour to something now: «I am colouring the sky blue». 5) (noun, formal) The way something is presented that changes how people feel about it: «political colouring».
its sense in the lessons: In art and early school, colouring in is a common activity («colouring-in sheet», «stay inside the lines»). In science, animal colouring helps camouflage or warns predators (a wasp's warning colouring). In cooking, a few drops of food colouring change icing or play dough. Phrases: «colouring in», «colouring book», «colouring pencils», «food colouring», «natural colouring», «warning colouring».
examples from the lessons: My little sister loves her dinosaur colouring book. | We added green food colouring to the icing for St Patrick's Day. | The tiger's striped colouring helps it hide in long grass. | I am colouring the sea in two shades of blue. | She has her dad's colouring: red hair and freckles. | Some sweets use colouring made from beetroot. | Bright warning colouring tells birds that the frog is poisonous. | Finish your colouring in and then put the pencils away.
note for the reader of a maths problem: British, Irish, Canadian, Australian and NZ spelling: colouring; American spelling: coloring. Countable for kinds of food dye (artificial colourings), uncountable for the activity. «Colouring in» means filling in an outline. Using «colouring» about a person usually means hair, skin and eyes, not just skin.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a way that feels relaxed and free from pain or worry: «sitting comfortably». 2) Easily, with plenty to spare: «They won comfortably». 3) With enough money to live well: «They live comfortably».
its sense in the lessons: In stories and storytime «Are you sitting comfortably? Then I'll begin» is a famous British opening. In sport reports «won comfortably» means by a big margin. In maths word problems «comfortably fits» means there is room left over. In everyday talk about money «comfortably off» means not rich but with no money worries. Phrases: «sit comfortably», «comfortably off», «win comfortably», «fit comfortably».
examples from the lessons: Are you sitting comfortably? Then I'll begin. | The cat curled up comfortably on the sofa. | Our team won comfortably, five goals to one. | Twenty children fit comfortably in the minibus. | My grandparents are comfortably off since they retired. | The patient was resting comfortably after the operation. | The box comfortably holds all our books with room to spare.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually said in three syllables: «KUMF-ta-blee». Spelled with «-ably», not «-ibly». Comes from the adjective «comfortable». In maths, «comfortably more than» means clearly and easily more, not only just.

part of speech: noun (a commander, commanders; Commander as a title)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who is in charge of a group of soldiers, a ship, an aircraft, a mission or a police operation. 2) (title) A rank in some navies (between lieutenant commander and captain) and in the London police. 3) Anyone who leads or gives orders, like the commander of a space mission.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons commanders lead armies and fleets (for example Admiral Nelson at Trafalgar). In science and space topics, the commander leads a space mission: Neil Armstrong was the commander of Apollo 11. In games and stories children play «commander» and give orders. Phrases: «commander in chief», «army commander», «mission commander», «Commander Smith».
examples from the lessons: The commander told the soldiers to wait for the signal. | Neil Armstrong was the commander of Apollo 11. | The commander of the ship stayed on deck during the storm. | In the US, the President is the Commander in Chief of the armed forces. | My brother wants to be a space station commander one day. | The police commander spoke to the news reporters. | In our game, Sam was the commander and gave us all secret missions.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelled with double m. When used as a title before a name it takes a capital: Commander Hadfield. «Command» is the verb (to give orders) and also a noun (an order). «Commander in chief» (or commander-in-chief) is the highest commander of all forces.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A collection of things, such as songs, videos, facts or stories, put together in one album, book or list: «a compilation of funny animal clips». 2) The act of collecting and arranging such things: «The compilation of the dictionary took years». 3) (computing) The process in which a program called a compiler turns code written by people into code the computer runs.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life there are compilation albums («Now That's What I Call Music»), compilation videos and «best of» collections. In school, a class might make a compilation of poems or recipes. In computing lessons with languages like Rust or C, the code must go through compilation before it can run. Phrases: «a compilation album», «a compilation video», «a compilation of», «compilation error».
