examples from the lessons: Dad bought a compilation of the greatest songs of the 1980s. | We watched a compilation of the funniest football fails. | Our class made a compilation of favourite family recipes. | The compilation of the report took the whole weekend. | The program would not run because of a compilation error. | This book is a compilation of fairy tales from around the world. | The yearbook is a compilation of photos from the whole school year.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comes from the verb «compile» (to collect and put together). Countable when it means a collection (two compilations), uncountable when it means the process. Said «kom-pi-LAY-shun». Do not confuse with «complication» (a difficulty).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Fruit cooked slowly with sugar and a little water until soft, served cold or warm as a dessert or with yoghurt, porridge or pancakes. 2) (Ukraine, Russia, Poland) A sweet drink made by boiling fruit or berries in water with sugar, often kept in big jars for winter. 3) (rare) A bowl on a stem for serving fruit or sweets, also called a compotier.
its sense in the lessons: In cooking lessons and at home compote is an easy recipe: chop fruit, add sugar, simmer. In families from Ukraine and Eastern Europe «compote» (kompot) is a common homemade drink children have with dinner. In science it shows how heat softens fruit. Phrases: «apple compote», «berry compote», «rhubarb compote», «a jar of compote».
examples from the lessons: We had pancakes with warm berry compote. | Grandma made apple compote with cinnamon. | Simmer the plums with sugar to make a compote. | My Ukrainian friend's mum gave us a glass of cherry compote to drink. | Compote is nice on top of porridge or yoghurt. | The shelves in the cellar were full of jars of compote for winter.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Said «KOM-poht» (the final e is silent). It comes from French. Countable (two compotes) for kinds or servings, uncountable for the food in general. Not the same as «compost» (rotting garden waste); be careful, the words look alike. Jam is thicker and has more sugar than compote.

part of speech: adjective (comprehensive; more comprehensive, most comprehensive); noun (UK: a comprehensive, comprehensives)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Including everything or almost everything that is needed; complete and thorough: «a comprehensive guide to birds». 2) (UK) A comprehensive school is a state secondary school that takes children of all abilities without an entrance test; people often just say «a comprehensive». 3) (sport) A comprehensive win is a very big, clear win. 4) (insurance) Comprehensive car insurance covers damage to your own car as well as to other people's.
its sense in the lessons: In school it describes complete revision notes, a thorough test or a full report. In the UK most secondary pupils go to a comprehensive, unlike grammar schools that need an exam (the 11-plus). In news and sport: «a comprehensive victory». Phrases: «a comprehensive list», «comprehensive school», «comprehensive review», «comprehensive coverage».
examples from the lessons: This book is a comprehensive guide to the planets. | My big sister goes to the local comprehensive. | The teacher gave us a comprehensive list of spellings to learn. | City won a comprehensive victory, six–nil. | The museum has a comprehensive collection of fossils. | Dad needs comprehensive insurance for his new car. | Our science report must be comprehensive and include every result.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Do not confuse with «comprehensible» (easy to understand) or «comprehension» (understanding what you read, as in a reading comprehension test). Comprehensive means complete, not easy. Spelled with -sive, not -sife.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Something you agree to give up or allow in order to end an argument or reach a deal: «Both sides made concessions». 2) Admitting that someone else is right or that you have lost: «a concession speech». 3) (UK, Australia) A cheaper price for certain people, such as children, students or older people: «concession tickets». 4) (US, Canada) A stall or small shop selling food and drinks at a cinema, stadium or fair: «the concession stand». 5) (business, law) A right given by a government or owner to do business or use land, such as to drill for oil.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life children see «concessions» on ticket prices at cinemas, buses and zoos in the UK and Australia, and «concession stands» selling popcorn in the USA. In history and news, peace talks and strikes end when each side makes concessions. In elections, the loser gives a «concession speech». Phrases: «make a concession», «as a concession to», «concession ticket», «concession stand», «concession speech».
examples from the lessons: Children and pensioners pay the concession price at the pool. | We bought hot dogs at the concession stand during the game. | After hours of talks, both sides made concessions. | The loser gave a polite concession speech after the election. | As a concession, Mum let us stay up for ten more minutes. | Can I get a concession fare with my student card? | The company won a concession to run the railway.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one concession, many concessions. The verb is «concede» (to admit or give up). In maths problems, a concession price is the lower price: if adults pay £12 and concessions pay £8, a family of 2 adults and 2 children pays 24 + 16 = £40. In the US people say «discount» rather than «concession» for cheaper tickets.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A creamy liquid you put on your hair after shampoo to make it soft, smooth and easier to comb. 2) Fabric conditioner (UK) or fabric softener (US): a liquid added in the washing machine to make clothes soft and smell nice. 3) Any substance that improves something, such as soil conditioner for gardens or leather conditioner. 4) Short for air conditioner: a machine that cools the air in a room.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and personal care, children learn «shampoo, then conditioner». In science lessons on materials, conditioners change how surfaces feel. In hot countries like Australia and the southern USA, «the air conditioner» or «the air con» cools houses and cars. Phrases: «hair conditioner», «leave-in conditioner», «fabric conditioner», «air conditioner».
examples from the lessons: Rinse out the shampoo and then put on some conditioner. | Conditioner helps get the knots out of my long hair. | Mum added fabric conditioner to the washing. | The air conditioner was humming all night during the heatwave. | We have run out of conditioner, so my hair is all frizzy. | Gardeners mix conditioner into the soil to help plants grow.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable (some conditioner), but countable for kinds or bottles (two conditioners). Spelled with -er at the end. «Air conditioner» is the machine; «air conditioning» or «air con» is the system or the cool air.

part of speech: verb (confine, confines, confined, confining); noun (confines — see the separate entry)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To keep someone or something inside a small or closed space: «The dog was confined to the kitchen». 2) To keep something within a limit and not let it spread or go beyond: «Please confine your answer to 100 words». 3) Be confined to bed, a wheelchair or the house: to have to stay there because of illness or injury. 4) (old) To be confined: to be in bed to give birth to a baby.
its sense in the lessons: In science and safety texts: a fire was «confined to one room», a virus «confined to one area». In school instructions: «confine your answer to the question». In stories, prisoners or animals are confined in cells or cages. Phrases: «confined to», «confine yourself to», «confined space», «confined to bed».
examples from the lessons: The fire was confined to the kitchen and did not spread. | Grandad was confined to bed with flu for a week. | Please confine your talk to five minutes. | The tiger paced in its confined enclosure. | Cats hate being confined in a box. | Firefighters train for rescues in confined spaces. | The flooding was confined to the low part of town.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually used in the passive: «be confined to». Stress on the second syllable: con-FINE. The noun «confinement» means being kept somewhere (solitary confinement in prison). «Confine» is formal; in everyday talk people say «keep in», «shut in» or «limit to».

meaning for a pupil: 1) The edges or limits of a place: «within the confines of the school grounds». 2) The limits of an idea, rule or activity: «within the confines of the law».
its sense in the lessons: In school rules and safety talks: «Pupils must stay within the confines of the playground». In stories, characters long to escape «the confines» of a small room, a prison or a dull life. Phrases: «within the confines of», «beyond the confines of», «the narrow confines of».
examples from the lessons: Pupils must stay within the confines of the school grounds at lunch. | The puppy was happy to escape the confines of its crate. | In the narrow confines of the cave, we had to crawl. | Artists like to work beyond the confines of the usual rules. | Everything must be done within the confines of the law. | The fox lived within the confines of the city park.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always plural and usually with «the»: «the confines», never «a confine». Stress on the first syllable: CON-fines (unlike the verb con-FINE). It is a formal or written word; in speech people say «inside» or «the limits of».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Behaving the same way as most other people or as the rules expect, instead of being different: «pressure towards conformity». 2) Being in agreement with a rule, law or standard: «in conformity with the safety rules».
its sense in the lessons: In PSHE, ethics and citizenship lessons, conformity is linked to peer pressure: wearing what everyone wears, saying what everyone says; we learn to think for ourselves while still keeping good rules. In science and technology, products must be «in conformity with» safety standards (the CE or UKCA mark). In history, some groups were forced into religious conformity. Phrases: «in conformity with», «pressure to conform», «social conformity».
examples from the lessons: School uniforms are partly about conformity. | Some teenagers dye their hair to rebel against conformity. | The toy was tested for conformity with safety rules. | Conformity is not always bad: we all drive on the same side of the road. | The story is about a girl who refuses to give in to conformity. | Scientists ran a famous experiment showing how strong the pressure to conformity can be.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. The verb is «conform» (to follow the rules or do what others do) and a person who always conforms is a «conformist»; one who does not is a «nonconformist». In UK history, «Nonconformist» with a capital N means Protestant Christians outside the Church of England, such as Methodists and Baptists.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A way of thinking and living based on the teachings of Confucius, a Chinese teacher who lived about 2,500 years ago; it stresses kindness, honesty, good manners, education and respect for parents, elders and rulers. 2) The tradition of schools, rituals and books that grew from these teachings in China, Korea, Japan and Vietnam.
its sense in the lessons: In religious education and history lessons about China, Confucianism is studied alongside Daoism and Buddhism. Key ideas pupils meet: «filial piety» (respect and care for your parents), «ren» (kindness to others) and the Golden Rule: «Do not do to others what you would not want done to yourself». Many people see it more as a philosophy of good behaviour than as a religion with a god. Phrases: «the teachings of Confucius», «Confucian values», «the Analects».
examples from the lessons: Confucianism teaches that children should respect and care for their parents. | Confucius said, «Do not do to others what you would not want them to do to you». | For centuries, Confucianism shaped schools and government in China. | Our RE class compared Confucianism and Daoism. | Confucianism values learning, so exams were very important in old China. | Many families in East Asia still follow Confucian customs at New Year.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always written with a capital C because it comes from the name Confucius (in Chinese, Kong Fuzi, «Master Kong»). Said «kon-FYOO-shun-iz-um». Uncountable. The adjective is «Confucian». A common myth is that Confucius wrote all the jokes and sayings that begin «Confucius say…»; most of those are modern made-up jokes.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A thick, soft rice porridge made by cooking rice in lots of water for a long time, eaten across China and East and South-East Asia, often for breakfast or when someone is ill.
its sense in the lessons: In food and culture lessons about China and Asia, congee is a common breakfast, sometimes with fish, pork, egg, ginger or spring onion on top, or plain for an upset tummy. In Chinese it is called «zhou» or «jook». Phrases: «a bowl of congee», «chicken congee», «plain congee».
examples from the lessons: Grandma made me a bowl of congee when I had a cold. | In Hong Kong, many people eat congee for breakfast. | We topped the congee with spring onions and soy sauce. | Congee is rice cooked with lots of water until it is very soft. | My friend's family eats congee with pickles and a salted egg. | The café sells chicken and ginger congee.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Said «KON-jee». Usually uncountable (some congee), but «a bowl of congee». It is a word English borrowed from Tamil in India. Do not confuse with «conjee» (the same word, older spelling) or with «congeal» (to turn thick as it cools).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Describing trees, such as pine, fir, spruce and larch, that have cones and needle-like or scaly leaves; most stay green all year. 2) Describing a forest or woodland made mainly of these trees: «coniferous forest».
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography, pupils compare coniferous trees (cones, needles, mostly evergreen) with deciduous trees (broad leaves that fall in autumn). The huge coniferous forest of the far north is called the taiga or boreal forest (Canada, Scandinavia, Russia). Christmas trees are conifers. Phrases: «coniferous tree», «coniferous forest», «coniferous woodland», «coniferous and deciduous».
examples from the lessons: Pine and spruce are coniferous trees. | Coniferous trees have needles instead of flat leaves. | Much of Canada is covered in coniferous forest. | Most coniferous trees keep their needles all winter. | The larch is a coniferous tree that loses its needles in autumn. | We collected pine cones in the coniferous woodland. | Deciduous trees lose their leaves, but coniferous ones mostly stay green.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The noun is «conifer» (a coniferous tree). Trap: «coniferous» is not exactly the same as «evergreen». Most conifers are evergreen, but a few (larch) drop their needles, and some evergreens (holly) are not conifers. The opposite group in school is «deciduous». Said «kuh-NIF-er-us».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Based on a guess or an idea that has not been proved, not on firm facts: «The date of the old map is conjectural».
its sense in the lessons: In history, science and maths texts, «conjectural» warns the reader that something is a guess: the colour of dinosaurs or the look of an ancient building may be conjectural. In maths, a conjecture is a statement that people think is true but nobody has proved yet (like the famous Goldbach conjecture). Phrases: «purely conjectural», «highly conjectural».
examples from the lessons: The colours of the dinosaur in the picture are conjectural. | Any answer about life on other planets is still conjectural. | The museum said the drawing of the castle was partly conjectural. | His story about the treasure was purely conjectural. | Scientists test conjectural ideas with experiments. | The age of the cave paintings was once conjectural, but now it has been measured.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal word. It comes from «conjecture» (a guess; to guess). Said «kun-JEK-cher-ul». In maths, «conjectural» means «not proved yet», which is different from «false»: a conjecture may turn out true or false. Similar words: speculative, hypothetical, unproven.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To join or combine two or more things together into one: «two ideas conjoined». 2) Conjoined twins: twins who are born with their bodies joined together at some part.
its sense in the lessons: It is a rare, formal word. Pupils mostly meet it in science or news as «conjoined twins», who sometimes have operations to separate them. In grammar, words that join ideas are called «conjunctions» (and, but, because), which comes from the same root. Phrases: «conjoined twins», «conjoined with».
examples from the lessons: The two rivers conjoin just below the bridge. | Conjoined twins share part of their body. | Surgeons spent hours separating the conjoined twins. | In the poem, joy and sadness are conjoined. | The two villages conjoined to make one town. | The ancient symbol shows two circles conjoined.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal and rare; in everyday speech say «join» or «combine». Past form: conjoined. The older term «Siamese twins» is now replaced by «conjoined twins» because it is considered outdated. Related grammar word: «conjunction».

meaning for a pupil: 1) As a result; because of that: «It rained all day; consequently, the match was cancelled».
its sense in the lessons: In writing, maths and science reasoning, «consequently» links a cause with its result, like «so» or «therefore»; teachers count it as a good «connective» or «conjunctive adverb» in written work. It is formal and common in exam and report language. Phrases: «and consequently», «; consequently,».
examples from the lessons: I forgot my homework; consequently, I had to stay in at lunch. | The ice melted and, consequently, the water level rose. | The shop ran out of bread and consequently closed early. | Plants need light, and consequently they grow towards the window. | She practised every day and consequently won the spelling bee. | The road was blocked; consequently, the bus was late.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; in speech people usually say «so». It often comes after a semicolon or a full stop and is followed by a comma. Do not confuse with «subsequently», which means «later, after that» (about time, not cause). The noun is «consequence» (a result). In maths reasoning, «consequently» marks the step that follows from the one before.

part of speech: adjective (conservative; more conservative, most conservative); noun (a conservative, conservatives; a Conservative)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Not liking sudden change and preferring traditional ways, values and styles: «My grandad has conservative taste in music». 2) (estimates) Careful and on the low side, so the real number is probably bigger: «a conservative estimate». 3) (politics) Supporting traditional values, gradual change, lower taxes and free business; in the UK and Canada, a Conservative is a member or supporter of the Conservative Party (also called the Tories). 4) (clothes, style) Plain and not showy: «a conservative suit». 5) (noun) A person who has conservative views.
its sense in the lessons: In citizenship and politics lessons, pupils learn the main UK parties (Conservative, Labour, Liberal Democrats and others) and that in the USA the Republican Party is usually called conservative. In maths and science, a «conservative estimate» means one chosen low on purpose to be safe. In everyday life it describes cautious people, plain clothes, or careful choices. Phrases: «a conservative estimate», «the Conservative Party», «at a conservative guess», «socially conservative».
examples from the lessons: At a conservative estimate, two thousand people came to the fair. | My grandma is quite conservative and doesn't like loud colours. | The Conservatives won the most seats in the election. | Dad wore a conservative grey suit to the interview. | Some people are conservative about money and save carefully. | Each side has good ideas, and people can be conservative or progressive and still be kind to each other. | The doctor took a conservative approach and waited before operating.
note for the reader of a maths problem: With a capital C it means the political party (UK, Canada); with a small c it means traditional or cautious in general. In maths, a conservative estimate is a deliberately low (safe) guess, so the true number is likely higher. The opposite in politics is often called «liberal» or «progressive». In science, «conservation» (saving nature or energy) is a different word from «conservative», though they share a root.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A secret plan made by a group of people to do something harmful or illegal: «a conspiracy to rob the bank». 2) The act of planning such a thing: «They were found guilty of conspiracy». 3) A conspiracy theory: a belief that a secret group is behind events, often without good evidence.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, the Gunpowder Plot of 1605 (Guy Fawkes, remembered on Bonfire Night in the UK) was a conspiracy to blow up Parliament. In media literacy and online-safety lessons, pupils learn to check conspiracy theories (for example, that the Moon landings were faked) against reliable evidence. In mystery stories, the detective uncovers a conspiracy. Phrases: «a conspiracy theory», «a conspiracy to», «a conspiracy of silence», «uncover a conspiracy».
examples from the lessons: The Gunpowder Plot was a conspiracy to blow up Parliament in 1605. | The detective uncovered a conspiracy to steal the crown jewels. | My cousin believes a conspiracy theory that the Moon landings were faked, but there is strong evidence they were real. | The men were jailed for conspiracy to commit fraud. | There was a conspiracy of silence about the missing money. | Always check a conspiracy theory with trusted sources. | The kids joked that there was a conspiracy to give them extra homework.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: conspiracies (y changes to ies). The verb is «conspire» and a person who does it is a «conspirator». Trap: calling something a «conspiracy theory» does not make it automatically false or true; the question is the evidence. Some real conspiracies have happened, but most popular conspiracy theories have no good evidence.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To make something narrower or tighter by squeezing it: «The snake constricted its prey». 2) (body) When blood vessels, pupils of the eye or airways get narrower: «Cold makes blood vessels constrict». 3) To limit what someone can do: «Tight rules constricted the players».
its sense in the lessons: In science, a boa constrictor or python kills by constricting (squeezing) its prey; in the body, blood vessels constrict in cold weather to keep heat in, and airways constrict during an asthma attack (an inhaler helps them open). In stories, a «constricted throat» or «tight, constricting clothes» show fear or discomfort. Phrases: «constrict blood vessels», «a constricted throat», «constricting clothes».
examples from the lessons: The python constricts its prey until it stops breathing. | In the cold, the blood vessels in your fingers constrict. | During an asthma attack, the airways constrict, so it is hard to breathe. | His throat constricted with fear. | The tight collar constricted her neck. | Bright light makes the pupils of your eyes constrict. | Too many rules can constrict creativity.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The noun is «constriction» and a snake that does this is a «constrictor». The opposite in the body is «dilate» (to get wider). Do not confuse with «restrict» (to limit by rules) or «construct» (to build).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Existing or happening at the same time as something else: «contemporaneous accounts of the battle». 2) Contemporaneous notes or records: written down at the time something happened, not later.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, «contemporaneous sources» (also called primary sources or contemporary sources) are records written at the time of an event, such as diaries, letters and newspapers; historians trust them more about details than later retellings. In law, police make contemporaneous notes. Phrases: «contemporaneous with», «contemporaneous accounts», «contemporaneous records».
examples from the lessons: Samuel Pepys wrote a contemporaneous account of the Great Fire of London. | The dinosaurs were not contemporaneous with humans. | Historians compared two contemporaneous reports of the battle. | The police officer made contemporaneous notes. | The building of the two castles was roughly contemporaneous. | Diaries are useful because they are contemporaneous with the events.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Very formal. Said «kon-tem-puh-RAY-nee-us». It is close to «contemporary», but «contemporary» can also mean «modern, of today» (contemporary art), while «contemporaneous» only means «of the same time as something else». A common myth in cartoons is that dinosaurs and cave people lived together; they were not contemporaneous: the last big dinosaurs died about 66 million years before humans.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Contend with: to have to deal with a problem or difficulty: «Farmers have to contend with drought». 2) To compete with others to win something: «Five teams are contending for the cup». 3) (formal) To say firmly that something is true, especially in an argument: «She contends that the plan will fail».
its sense in the lessons: In sport, a «contender» is a team or person with a real chance to win. In news and history: people contend with floods, wars or poverty. In debates and essays, «X contends that…» introduces someone's argument or claim, which is useful for reporting views fairly. Phrases: «contend with», «contend for», «contend that», «a contender for the title».
examples from the lessons: Explorers in Antarctica had to contend with freezing winds. | Three schools are contending for the trophy. | The scientist contends that the bones belong to a new species. | Our team is a strong contender for the championship. | Teachers contend with noisy classrooms every day. | Some people contend that school should start later.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past form: contended. Do not confuse «contended» with «contented» (happy and satisfied). The noun is «contention» (an argument; also «in contention» = with a chance to win) and a competitor is a «contender». In essays, «contend» shows a claim, not a proven fact.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A situation in which two statements or facts cannot both be true: «There is a contradiction between his two stories». 2) Saying the opposite of what someone else has said: «She spoke without contradiction». 3) A contradiction in terms: a phrase whose parts seem to oppose each other, like «a quiet shout».
its sense in the lessons: In maths and logic, a contradiction is a statement that can never be true, like «this number is both odd and even»; «proof by contradiction» shows something is true by showing its opposite leads to nonsense. In stories and detective work, contradictions in a suspect's account give them away. In reading lessons, pupils spot contradictions between texts. Phrases: «a contradiction in terms», «in contradiction to», «proof by contradiction», «without contradiction».
examples from the lessons: There is a contradiction in your story: first you said Monday, then Tuesday. | «Freezing hot» is a contradiction in terms. | The detective noticed a contradiction in the butler's alibi. | In maths we used proof by contradiction to show there is no biggest number. | His actions were in contradiction to his promises. | Saying that all rules must be broken is a contradiction, because that is itself a rule. | The two websites gave answers in direct contradiction.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable (a contradiction, two contradictions). The verb is «contradict» (to say the opposite) and the adjective «contradictory». «Contra» means «against» and «dict» means «say». In maths, if you reach a contradiction, the assumption you began with must be false.

part of speech: adjective (contrived; more contrived); verb form (past of contrive: contrived)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (adjective) Seeming false and planned, not natural or believable: «The ending of the film felt contrived». 2) (verb, past of contrive) Managed to do something by being clever or tricky: «She contrived to escape». 3) (verb, past of contrive) Made or invented something cleverly: «They contrived a raft from old barrels».
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons and book reviews, «contrived» is a criticism of a plot that relies on unlikely coincidences, or of dialogue that sounds forced. In stories, a clever character «contrives» a plan or a way out. Phrases: «a contrived plot», «a contrived smile», «contrived to», «feel contrived».
examples from the lessons: The story's happy ending felt contrived. | His contrived smile showed he was not really pleased. | The prisoners contrived a rope from their bedsheets. | She somehow contrived to finish her homework during breakfast. | The film's coincidences were so contrived that we laughed. | Write dialogue that sounds natural, not contrived.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As an adjective it is negative: «contrived» = forced, too obviously planned. The verb «contrive» is formal. The noun «contrivance» means a clever device or a trick. Opposite of the adjective: natural, believable, genuine.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A strong belief or opinion: «She has a deep conviction that animals should be treated kindly». 2) The feeling of being sure, shown in how you speak or act: «He spoke with conviction». 3) (law) The decision of a court that someone is guilty of a crime: «a conviction for theft». 4) (law) A record that someone has been found guilty before: «He had no previous convictions».
its sense in the lessons: In speaking and drama, teachers praise pupils who speak «with conviction» (sounding sure). In citizenship and law topics, a «conviction» is the end of a trial when the jury or judge finds someone guilty; the opposite is an «acquittal». In religious education, people act from their «religious convictions». Phrases: «with conviction», «strong convictions», «a criminal conviction», «previous convictions», «have the courage of your convictions».
examples from the lessons: She read her poem aloud with real conviction. | It is my conviction that everyone deserves a second chance. | The thief's conviction was announced in court. | The man had no previous convictions. | He has the courage of his convictions and speaks up for what is right. | Without evidence, there can be no conviction. | The team played with conviction and won.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Two very different senses: a belief (everyday) and a guilty verdict (law). The verb «convict» (con-VICT) means to find guilty; the noun «a convict» (CON-vict) is a person in prison. Being «convinced» (sure) is related to the belief sense. A conviction in court needs proof «beyond reasonable doubt» in the UK, USA and similar countries.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In large amounts; more than enough: «copious notes», «copious amounts of food».
its sense in the lessons: In school, teachers may praise «copious notes» (a lot of notes). In science and weather: «copious rain». In stories, it shows plenty: «copious tears», «copious amounts of cake». It is a slightly formal word that makes writing richer than «lots of». Phrases: «copious notes», «copious amounts of», «copious tears».
examples from the lessons: She took copious notes during the science talk. | The party had copious amounts of cake and jelly. | Copious rain made the river burst its banks. | He drank copious amounts of water after the race. | The baby shed copious tears when the balloon popped. | Plants need copious watering in a heatwave.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually goes before a noun (copious notes) and with uncountable or plural nouns. Said «KOH-pee-us». The adverb is «copiously» (bleeding copiously). Similar: plentiful, abundant, ample. Do not confuse with «copy», though they come from different meanings.

part of speech: noun (cornbread, cornbreads; usually uncountable; also corn bread)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A sweet or savoury bread made from cornmeal (ground maize), often baked in a pan or skillet; it is a traditional food of the southern United States.
its sense in the lessons: In food and culture lessons about the USA, cornbread is eaten with chilli, barbecue, beans and at Thanksgiving. In history, it comes from Native American ways of cooking maize, which European settlers learned. Phrases: «a slice of cornbread», «skillet cornbread», «cornbread muffins».
examples from the lessons: We had chilli with a big square of cornbread. | Grandma in Texas bakes cornbread in a black iron skillet. | Cornbread is made from yellow cornmeal. | Native Americans cooked bread from maize long before cornbread recipes were written down. | The cornbread was a bit crumbly but delicious with butter. | At Thanksgiving, my aunt makes cornbread stuffing.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable (some cornbread, a piece of cornbread). In American English «corn» means maize; in British English «corn» can mean any grain (like wheat), which is a common confusion. Sometimes written as two words, «corn bread».

meaning for a pupil: 1) The clear, curved, dome-shaped layer at the front of the eye that covers the iris and pupil and helps focus light.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on the eye and seeing, pupils label the parts: cornea, iris, pupil, lens, retina, optic nerve. The cornea bends light first, then the lens finishes focusing it on the retina. In health and safety, goggles protect the cornea from chemicals and flying bits; a scratch on the cornea hurts a lot. Some people receive a donated cornea in a transplant. Phrases: «a scratched cornea», «corneal transplant».
examples from the lessons: Light passes through the cornea before it reaches the lens. | We labelled the cornea on our diagram of the eye. | Wear goggles to protect your cornea in the lab. | The doctor said I had a tiny scratch on my cornea. | The cornea has no blood vessels, so it is clear. | A cornea transplant can help some people see again.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Said «KOR-nee-uh». Plural: corneas. The adjective is «corneal». Do not confuse the cornea (clear front window) with the iris (the coloured part) or the retina (at the back, where light is sensed).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) Old-fashioned, silly or used too many times to be funny or moving, but often in a sweet way: «a corny joke». 2) Too sentimental, sweet or soppy: «a corny love song». 3) (rare) Of or full of corn.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday talk and stories, «corny jokes» are the groan-worthy ones dads tell and Christmas cracker jokes (What do you call a deer with no eyes? No idea!). In reviews of films and songs, «corny» means cheesy. Phrases: «corny joke», «a bit corny», «corny but sweet».
examples from the lessons: Dad's jokes are so corny that we all groan. | The cracker joke was corny, but we laughed anyway. | The ending of the film was a bit corny. | That corny love song makes my sister cry. | I know it sounds corny, but you're my best friend. | Why did the scarecrow win a prize? He was outstanding in his field. — That's so corny!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative: cornier, corniest. Informal. Similar: cheesy (informal), soppy (UK), sappy (US). «Corny» is gentle teasing, not a strong insult.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (space) Of the corona, the outer layer of the Sun's atmosphere: «a coronal mass ejection» is a huge burst of hot gas and magnetism thrown out from the Sun. 2) (body, science) A coronal plane is an imaginary flat slice that divides the body into front and back halves; a coronal suture is a joint across the top of the skull. 3) (speech) A coronal sound is made with the front part of the tongue, like t, d, n and s. 4) (rare, noun) A crown or wreath worn on the head.
its sense in the lessons: In space science, coronal mass ejections from the Sun cause space weather that can make the northern and southern lights (auroras) brighter and can disturb satellites. The Sun's corona can be seen during a total solar eclipse. In anatomy and medical scans, doctors look at «coronal» views. Phrases: «coronal mass ejection» (CME), «coronal plane», «coronal hole».
examples from the lessons: A coronal mass ejection can cause beautiful auroras on Earth. | Scientists watch the Sun for coronal storms. | During the eclipse we saw the Sun's glowing corona. | The scan showed a coronal view of the knee. | The coronal suture runs across the top of the skull. | In phonics we learned that t and d are made with the tip of the tongue.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Said «kuh-ROH-nul» or «KOR-uh-nul». It comes from «corona», Latin for crown. It is not linked in meaning to the coronavirus except through the same Latin word (the virus looks like it wears a crown).

part of speech: adjective (correlated); verb form (past of correlate: correlated)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (adjective) When two things are correlated, they tend to change together: when one goes up, the other usually goes up (or down) too: «Height and shoe size are correlated». 2) (verb, past) Compared or connected two things to see how they match: «The scientist correlated the temperature with ice-cream sales».
its sense in the lessons: In maths and science lessons on data and graphs, pupils learn that points on a scatter graph can show a positive correlation (both rise), a negative correlation (one rises as the other falls) or no correlation. A key lesson is «correlation does not mean causation»: two things changing together does not prove one causes the other. Phrases: «positively correlated», «negatively correlated», «correlated with», «strongly correlated».
examples from the lessons: Hours of practice and test scores were correlated. | Ice-cream sales and sunny days are positively correlated. | Temperature and the number of people wearing coats are negatively correlated. | The researchers correlated the children's sleep with their marks. | Just because two things are correlated does not mean one causes the other. | Our scatter graph showed that arm span and height are strongly correlated.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The verb is «correlate» (correlates, correlated, correlating); the noun is «correlation». Spelled with double r. Trap: ice-cream sales and sunburn are correlated, but ice cream does not cause sunburn; both are caused by sunny weather. In maths, «positively correlated» means both numbers grow together; «negatively correlated» means one grows as the other shrinks.

meaning for a pupil: 1) When metal corrodes, or something corrodes it, it is slowly damaged and eaten away by chemical action, such as rust from water and air or damage from acid: «Salt water corrodes the car». 2) To slowly weaken or destroy something good, such as trust or friendship: «Lies corrode trust».
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on materials and chemical change, pupils test which conditions make iron nails rust (corrode) — water and air together — and how paint, oil or galvanising (zinc coating) protect them. In everyday life, salty roads in winter and sea air corrode cars and bikes. Phrases: «corrode away», «corroded pipes», «corroded battery».
examples from the lessons: Iron corrodes when it gets wet and is exposed to air. | The sea air had corroded the old bike. | Acid can corrode metal. | Old batteries can leak and corrode, so do not touch the white crust. | Paint stops the gate from corroding. | Telling lies can corrode a friendship. | Gold does not corrode, which is why old gold coins still shine.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The noun is «corrosion» and the adjective «corrosive» (a corrosive liquid can burn skin — the safety sign shows a hand being damaged). «Rust» is the name for corrosion of iron and steel; other metals corrode in other ways (copper turns green). Spelled with double r.

part of speech: noun (a Cortina, Cortinas; a cortina, cortinas); proper noun (Cortina)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (a name) The Ford Cortina, a very popular family car in Britain, Ireland, Australia and New Zealand from 1962 to 1982. 2) (a place name) Cortina d'Ampezzo, a ski town in the Dolomite mountains of northern Italy that hosted Winter Olympics in 1956 and, with Milan, in 2026. 3) (science, rare) A cobweb-like veil under the cap of some young mushrooms. 4) (Spanish) In Spanish, «cortina» means a curtain; it is not an English word in that sense.
its sense in the lessons: It is a short honest entry: in English texts it is almost always a name — of an old car seen in stories set in 1970s Britain, or of the Italian ski town in sports news. Phrases: «a Ford Cortina», «Cortina d'Ampezzo».
examples from the lessons: Grandad's first car was a blue Ford Cortina. | The skiers raced down the slopes at Cortina. | The 2026 Winter Olympics were held in Milan and Cortina. | In the old photo, the family stands next to their Cortina. | Some mushrooms have a cortina, a web-like veil under the cap.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually written with a capital C as a name. Said «kor-TEE-nuh». In Spanish and Italian it means «curtain», which can confuse learners.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Of or from the universe or outer space beyond the Earth: «cosmic rays», «cosmic dust». 2) Very great in size or importance: «a disaster of cosmic proportions». 3) (informal, slang, old-fashioned) Amazing, mind-blowing or dreamy: «That's cosmic, man».
its sense in the lessons: In space science, pupils meet «cosmic rays» (high-energy particles from space), «cosmic dust» and the «cosmic microwave background» (faint heat left over from the Big Bang). In stories and comics, «cosmic» powers are huge and come from space. In everyday talk, «cosmic joke» means fate playing a trick. Phrases: «cosmic rays», «cosmic dust», «cosmic scale», «of cosmic proportions», «cosmic joke».
examples from the lessons: Cosmic rays come from far out in space. | Astronauts are exposed to more cosmic radiation than people on Earth. | The comet left a trail of cosmic dust. | Losing my homework on the bus felt like a cosmic joke. | In the comic, the hero got cosmic powers from a meteor. | The mess in my room was of cosmic proportions! | The Big Bang left a faint cosmic glow we can still measure.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It comes from «cosmos», the universe. The adverb is «cosmically». Do not confuse with «cosmetic» (to do with make-up or only on the surface). «Cosmic» in science is a real description; in casual talk it is exaggeration.

part of speech: noun (Costa; a name); noun (costa, costae — science, rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (a name) Costa Coffee, a big chain of coffee shops in the UK and Ireland; people say «Let's go to Costa». 2) (a place name) Part of names of coasts and countries: Costa Rica (a country in Central America), Costa del Sol and Costa Brava (holiday coasts in Spain). 3) (Spanish, Portuguese, Italian) «Costa» means «coast» in these languages; it is not an English common word. 4) (a name) A surname, as in the footballer Diego Costa. 5) (science, rare) A rib, or a rib-like ridge, for example the strong front vein of an insect's wing.
its sense in the lessons: It is a short honest entry: in English texts it is almost always a name — of a coffee shop, a holiday coast or a country. In geography, Costa Rica is famous for rainforests, volcanoes and wildlife such as sloths and toucans. Phrases: «Costa Rica», «Costa del Sol», «Costa Coffee».
examples from the lessons: Mum bought a hot chocolate for me at Costa. | Costa Rica is home to sloths and toucans. | We went on holiday to the Costa del Sol in Spain. | «Costa» means coast in Spanish. | The footballer Costa scored in the final. | Costa Rica has no army.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually written with a capital C as a name. Said «KOSS-tuh». The science sense is rare; its plural is «costae». Do not confuse with «cost» (price).

part of speech: noun (a counselor, counselors; UK spelling counsellor)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A trained person whose job is to listen to people and help them with personal problems, worries or feelings: «a school counselor». 2) (US, Canada) A camp counselor: a young adult who looks after children at a summer camp. 3) (US, law) A lawyer, especially in court: «Counselor, please approach the bench». 4) (formal, old) An adviser to a king, queen or leader.
its sense in the lessons: In school and wellbeing lessons, children learn that a school counselor is a safe, trusted adult to talk to about worries, bullying or sadness, and that such talks are private unless someone is at risk. In American summer-camp stories, counselors run activities. In American TV courtroom dramas, judges call lawyers «counselor». In the Bible, God is called «Wonderful Counselor» in Isaiah. Phrases: «school counselor», «guidance counselor», «camp counselor», «marriage counselor».
examples from the lessons: I talked to the school counselor when my parents split up. | Our camp counselor taught us to paddle a canoe. | The guidance counselor helped my sister choose her classes. | «Objection, counselor!» said the judge. | The king's counselors advised him not to go to war. | The counselor listened without judging me. | If something worries you, a counselor is a good person to tell.
note for the reader of a maths problem: American spelling: counselor (one l); British, Irish, Australian and NZ: counsellor (double l); Canada uses both. Homophone trap: «councillor» (UK) or «councilor» (US) is a member of a town council, a different job. «Counsel» means advice or to advise; «council» is a group that runs a town.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (grammar) A countable noun is a noun that can have a number in front of it and a plural form, like «one apple, two apples»; also called a «count noun». 2) (maths, general) Able to be counted: «a countable number of sweets». 3) (maths, advanced) A countable set is one whose members can be listed one by one (1st, 2nd, 3rd…), even if the list never ends, like the whole numbers.
its sense in the lessons: In grammar lessons pupils sort nouns into countable (chair, dog, idea) and uncountable (water, rice, information) and learn the rules: «a/an» and «many», «fewer» go with countable nouns; «much», «less» go with uncountable ones. In maths, counting objects is the first step to number; older pupils and olympiad puzzles meet the idea that some infinite sets are countable and some are not. Phrases: «countable noun», «countable and uncountable».
examples from the lessons: «Apple» is a countable noun, but «water» is not. | We say «many books» because «book» is countable. | Some nouns are both countable and uncountable, like «cake» and «a cake». | «Information» is uncountable, so you cannot say «two informations». | The marbles in the jar are countable, but it would take a long time. | Mathematicians say the whole numbers are a countable set. | Use «fewer» with countable nouns: fewer sweets, fewer children.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: uncountable (also «mass noun»). Trap: some words are countable in one language and uncountable in another (furniture, advice, homework and information are uncountable in English). Words like «hair», «paper», «coffee» and «chicken» can be both, with different meanings (a paper = a newspaper or essay). In maths, «countable» does not mean small: the whole numbers go on forever but are still countable.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To act against something so that it has less effect or no effect: «Exercise helps counteract sitting all day».
its sense in the lessons: In science and health, medicines counteract poisons or pain; an alkali counteracts (neutralises) an acid, as when toothpaste counteracts acids that harm teeth or bicarbonate soothes a bee sting. In everyday talk, people counteract bad habits with good ones. Phrases: «counteract the effects of», «counteract a poison».
examples from the lessons: The doctor gave him a medicine to counteract the poison. | Toothpaste helps counteract the acids that damage your teeth. | Drinking water counteracts the hot weather's drying effect. | Planting trees can help counteract air pollution. | A short walk can counteract hours of sitting at a screen. | An alkali counteracts an acid.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelled as one word: counteract (counter + act). Stress on the last part: coun-ter-ACT. Noun: counteraction (rare). Similar: offset, neutralise, cancel out. «Counter» means «against», as in «counterattack».

meaning for a pupil: 1) The room in a law court where trials and hearings take place, with places for the judge, the jury, the lawyers, the person accused and the public.
its sense in the lessons: In citizenship and law lessons, pupils learn who sits where in a courtroom: the judge (sometimes in a wig in the UK), the jury of twelve ordinary people, the defence and prosecution lawyers, witnesses giving evidence, and the defendant. Classes may hold mock trials in a pretend courtroom. TV and stories use «courtroom drama». In adult life children may hear about family courts deciding custody, which are usually private. Phrases: «in the courtroom», «courtroom drama», «a packed courtroom».
examples from the lessons: The courtroom fell silent as the judge came in. | Our class turned the hall into a courtroom for a mock trial. | Everyone in the courtroom must stand when the judge enters. | The witness sat nervously at the front of the courtroom. | My uncle loves courtroom dramas on TV. | Phones are not allowed in the courtroom. | The jury left the courtroom to decide on their verdict.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word: courtroom (court + room). Countable. «Court» alone often means the same thing («in court»). Do not confuse a law court with a tennis or basketball court, or with a royal court.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) Special behaviour that animals use to attract a mate, such as dancing, singing, showing off bright feathers or bringing gifts: «the courtship dance of the peacock». 2) (old-fashioned) The time when two people are getting to know each other romantically before getting married. 3) (formal) Trying hard to win someone's support or favour: «the company's courtship of new customers».
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on animal behaviour and life cycles, courtship comes before mating: male peacocks spread their tails, bowerbirds decorate nests, birds sing, and penguins give pebbles. In older novels and history, couples have a «courtship» with walks and visits before marriage. Phrases: «courtship display», «courtship dance», «courtship ritual».
examples from the lessons: The peacock spreads its tail in a courtship display. | Male birds sing in spring as part of courtship. | Some penguins give a pebble as a courtship gift. | In the old novel, their courtship lasted three years. | Bowerbirds decorate their bowers with blue things during courtship. | Great crested grebes do a famous courtship dance on the water. | Scientists filmed the frogs' courtship calls at night.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable in general (animal courtship), countable for one relationship (a long courtship). The old-fashioned verb «court» means to try to win someone's love («He courted her for a year»). Not connected to the meaning «law court».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (a place name) Coventry, a city in the West Midlands of England. 2) (UK, idiom) Send someone to Coventry: to refuse to speak to someone on purpose, as a group, to punish or leave them out.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, Coventry is known for the legend of Lady Godiva, its medieval cathedral bombed in the Blitz in 1940, and the new cathedral built beside the ruins as a symbol of peace and reconciliation; Coventry is twinned with Stalingrad (now Volgograd) and Dresden. In PSHE lessons, «sending someone to Coventry» is a form of bullying by leaving someone out, which is unkind. Phrases: «send someone to Coventry», «Coventry Cathedral».
examples from the lessons: Coventry is a city in the middle of England. | The old Coventry Cathedral was bombed in 1940. | The ruins of Coventry Cathedral now stand for peace and forgiveness. | The other girls sent her to Coventry and wouldn't speak to her. | Sending someone to Coventry is a kind of bullying. | Coventry once made bicycles and cars.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always a capital C. Said «KOV-en-tree» (UK). The idiom is British; nobody is sure where it came from, so stories about its origin may not be true. Ignoring someone on purpose as a group is hurtful; tell a trusted adult if it happens to you.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The reporting of news or events on TV, radio, in newspapers or online: «live coverage of the match». 2) How much of an area or surface is covered by something: «mobile phone coverage», «paint coverage». 3) (money) What an insurance policy will pay for: «The insurance gives coverage for theft». 4) How fully a topic or set of things is included: «The book has good coverage of the planets».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, children hear «no coverage» or «no signal» on phones in the countryside, and «live coverage» of the World Cup or Olympics. In media lessons, they compare news coverage from different sources. In maths and science, «coverage» can mean how much area paint or a map covers: one tin covers 10 square metres. Phrases: «live coverage», «news coverage», «media coverage», «phone coverage», «full coverage».
examples from the lessons: The BBC had live coverage of the royal wedding. | There's no phone coverage in the mountains. | The match got lots of coverage in the newspapers. | One tin of paint gives coverage of about ten square metres. | The insurance coverage paid for the broken window. | The story didn't get much media coverage. | Our textbook has good coverage of the water cycle.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «much coverage», «a lot of coverage», never «a coverage». Said «KUV-er-ij». In maths problems about painting, coverage tells you area per tin: if one tin covers 12 square metres, a 36-square-metre wall needs 36 ÷ 12 = 3 tins.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person, traditionally a man, who is skilled at making things by hand, such as furniture, pots, jewellery or stone carvings: «a skilled craftsman». 2) Anyone who does their work with great care and skill.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, craftsmen in medieval towns belonged to guilds and trained apprentices: blacksmiths, carpenters, potters, weavers, stonemasons who built cathedrals. In design and technology and art, pupils learn about craftsmanship (the skill and care in making things). In the Bible, Jesus is described as the son of a carpenter, a craftsman. Phrases: «a skilled craftsman», «master craftsman», «craftsman-built».
examples from the lessons: The craftsman carved the wooden chair by hand. | Medieval craftsmen built the great cathedrals. | A master craftsman trained young apprentices. | The clock was made by a Swiss craftsman. | Look at the craftsmanship in this old table! | Joseph, in the Bible, was a craftsman who worked with wood. | The stained glass was made by a local craftsman.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: craftsmen (-men, said the same as «-man» in quick speech). Gender-neutral words: craftsperson, craftspeople, artisan, maker; for a woman, also craftswoman. The noun «craftsmanship» means the skill shown in the work.

part of speech: noun (a crank, cranks); verb (crank, cranks, cranked, cranking)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (noun) A handle or bar bent at a right angle that you turn round and round to make a machine work, like on an old car engine, a pencil sharpener or a jack-in-the-box. 2) (noun, informal) A person with strange, fixed ideas who will not listen to evidence: «a crank who thinks the Earth is flat». 3) (noun, US, informal) A grumpy, bad-tempered person. 4) (verb) To turn a crank to start or move something: «crank the handle». 5) (verb, informal) Crank up: to turn up the volume, heat or power: «crank up the music». 6) (slang, US) Crank: a slang name for an illegal drug (methamphetamine) — dangerous and against the law.
its sense in the lessons: In science and D&T lessons about simple machines, a crank turns rotation into back-and-forth motion (and the other way), as in bicycle pedals (the cranks) or a wind-up toy. In stories and comedy, a «crank call» is a prank phone call. Phrases: «crank the handle», «crank up», «crank out» (produce lots quickly), «crank call», «a bit of a crank».
examples from the lessons: In the old days, drivers had to crank the engine by hand. | The pedals of a bike are attached to cranks. | Turn the crank and the music box plays. | Can you crank up the heating? It's freezing. | Some cranks still claim the Earth is flat. | Grandpa is a bit of a crank before his morning coffee. | The factory cranks out thousands of toys a day. | Don't make crank calls; it is mean and can be illegal.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: a crank, cranks. «Cranky» (adjective) means grumpy or irritable. Calling a person a «crank» is unkind. The drug sense is US slang; illegal drugs are dangerous. Related: «crankshaft», the part of an engine that turns.

part of speech: noun (a crayfish; plural crayfish or crayfishes)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A small freshwater animal like a tiny lobster, with claws, a hard shell and ten legs, living in rivers, streams and lakes. 2) (UK, Australia, NZ) A name also used for the spiny lobster (rock lobster), a sea animal without big claws; in NZ it is also called «crayfish» or «koura». 3) The meat of these animals eaten as food: «crayfish sandwich».
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on rivers and habitats, crayfish are crustaceans (like crabs and shrimps) and their presence can show clean water. In the UK, the native white-clawed crayfish is endangered because the larger American signal crayfish spreads a disease; people must not move crayfish between rivers. In the southern USA, «crawfish boils» are a Louisiana tradition. Phrases: «freshwater crayfish», «signal crayfish», «crayfish boil».
examples from the lessons: We found a crayfish hiding under a stone in the stream. | Crayfish have ten legs and two big claws. | The white-clawed crayfish is the UK's only native crayfish. | In Louisiana, people call them crawfish and boil them with corn. | In New Zealand, we ate crayfish caught off the coast. | Crayfish shed their hard shells as they grow. | Herons eat crayfish from the river.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural usually «crayfish» (the same), sometimes «crayfishes». In the USA, also «crawfish» or «crawdad». It is not a fish; the name comes from an old French word for crab that English speakers changed to sound like «fish». It is a crustacean, not an insect.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Making a long, high, squeaking sound when moved or stepped on: «a creaky door», «creaky stairs». 2) Old and not working as well as before: «creaky knees», «a creaky old computer». 3) (of plans or systems) Weak, out of date or not well put together: «a creaky plan».
its sense in the lessons: In stories, especially spooky ones, creaky doors, floorboards and stairs build suspense. In everyday life, older people joke about their creaky joints. In science, creaking is a sound made by friction between wood or metal parts; oil reduces it. Phrases: «creaky floorboards», «creaky door», «creaky joints», «creaky old».
examples from the lessons: The creaky stairs gave us away when we sneaked down at night. | The old house was full of creaky floorboards. | Grandad says his knees are getting creaky. | Dad oiled the creaky gate. | We heard a creaky door open in the dark. | Our creaky old laptop takes ages to start. | The plan was a bit creaky, but it worked.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative: creakier, creakiest. The verb and noun «creak» (the sound) is a homophone of «creek» (a small stream; in the US and Australia, any small river). Similar: squeaky. The word copies the sound.

part of speech: noun (plural: credentials; rarely singular: a credential)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Qualifications, training and experience that show someone is suitable or trustworthy for a job or role: «Her credentials as a doctor are excellent». 2) Documents that prove who you are or what you are allowed to do, like an ID badge or press pass: «The guard checked his credentials». 3) (computing) Your username and password used to log in: «Never share your login credentials».
its sense in the lessons: In online-safety lessons, credentials are your username and password; you must never give them to anyone, and real companies never ask for them by email or message (that is a scam called «phishing»). In everyday life and news, people «show their credentials» to prove they are real officials, and we check the credentials of experts before trusting them. Phrases: «login credentials», «check credentials», «impressive credentials», «green credentials» (how environmentally friendly something is).
examples from the lessons: Never share your login credentials with anyone online. | The police officer showed her credentials before coming in. | The new coach has great credentials: he played for England. | The company boasts about its green credentials. | Check the author's credentials before you trust a website. | Reporters wear their press credentials around their necks. | A scam email may ask for your credentials, so don't reply.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Almost always plural: credentials. Related to «credible» (believable) and «credit», from Latin «credere», to believe. In computing, credentials can also be keys or tokens, not only passwords. A strong password plus two-step verification keeps credentials safe.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) Active mainly at twilight, at dawn and dusk, rather than in the day or night: «Rabbits and deer are crepuscular». 2) (formal, literary) Of or like twilight; dim and half-dark: «the crepuscular light». 3) (science) Crepuscular rays: beams of sunlight shining through gaps in clouds, often seen at sunrise or sunset.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, animals are grouped by when they are active: diurnal (day), nocturnal (night) and crepuscular (dawn and dusk) — such as rabbits, deer, hedgehogs at dusk, many cats and fireflies. In nature writing and stories, «crepuscular» sets a dim, mysterious mood. Pupils may photograph crepuscular rays («sunbeams» or «God rays»). Phrases: «crepuscular animals», «crepuscular rays», «crepuscular light».
examples from the lessons: Rabbits are crepuscular, so you often see them at dusk. | Deer come out at dawn and dusk because they are crepuscular. | Crepuscular rays streamed through the clouds at sunset. | My cat is most playful at dawn: it's crepuscular. | Bats are nocturnal, but many moths are crepuscular. | The forest was full of crepuscular light.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Said «kri-PUS-kyuh-lur». A long scientific word from Latin «crepusculum», twilight. The three activity words to remember: diurnal (day), nocturnal (night), crepuscular (twilight). Trap: crepuscular is not the same as nocturnal.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A town crier: in olden times, a person who walked through the streets ringing a bell and shouting out news and announcements, often starting «Oyez! Oyez!» Some towns still have one for ceremonies. 2) A person, especially a baby or child, who cries a lot: «The baby is a real crier». 3) (law, old) An officer in a law court who makes announcements.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons about life before newspapers and the internet, the town crier spread news; today some UK, Canadian and Australian towns keep a crier for festivals. In family life, parents describe babies as «good sleepers» or «criers». Phrases: «town crier», «a big crier», «Oyez, oyez!»
examples from the lessons: The town crier rang his bell and shouted the news. | In the Middle Ages, most people learned the news from the town crier. | Our town crier wears a red coat and a three-cornered hat. | «Oyez! Oyez!» called the crier. | My baby cousin is a real crier at bedtime. | I'm a bit of a crier at sad films. | The town crier announced the birth of the prince.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelled «crier», not «cryer» (though «cryer» appears sometimes as a name). Formed from «cry»: the y changes to i before -er. «Oyez» is an old French word meaning «hear ye!» (listen!), said «oh-YAY».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Saying what is bad or wrong about someone or something; finding fault: «She was critical of my drawing». 2) Very important, because what happens next depends on it: «a critical moment», «critical information». 3) (health) Very ill or badly hurt and in danger of dying: «in a critical condition». 4) Thinking carefully and judging fairly using evidence: «critical thinking». 5) Giving expert judgement about books, films or art: «The film got critical praise». 6) (science) At the exact point where something changes: «critical temperature», «critical mass».
its sense in the lessons: In school, «critical thinking» means questioning claims, checking evidence and not believing everything you read online. In news and hospital stories, «critical condition» means very serious. In science, a «critical point» is where a big change happens. In everyday talk, being «too critical» of friends can hurt feelings, so feedback should be kind and helpful. Phrases: «critical of», «critical thinking», «critical condition», «critical moment», «critically important», «critical acclaim».
examples from the lessons: Don't be so critical of your little brother; he's trying his best. | Good critical thinking means checking where information comes from. | The man was taken to hospital in a critical condition. | The next five minutes of the match are critical. | Water is critical for life on Earth. | The book received critical acclaim. | In science we learned that a dam has a critical water level. | It is critical that you wash your hands before cooking.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Two different families of meaning: «finding fault» and «extremely important». Context tells you which. The noun «critic» is a person who judges (a film critic); «criticism» is the act of criticising; the verb is «criticise» (UK) or «criticize» (US). «Critical» and «crucial» both mean very important. Constructive criticism is helpful and kind; it does not just say «it's bad».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Extremely important, because something else depends on it: «Sleep is crucial for growing children». 2) (UK, slang, old) Brilliant, excellent: «That tune is crucial!»
its sense in the lessons: In science and maths explanations, «crucial» marks the key step, ingredient or fact. In sport reports, «a crucial goal» decides the match. In everyday safety advice, «it is crucial to wear a helmet». Phrases: «crucial to», «crucial for», «crucial role», «crucial moment», «absolutely crucial».
examples from the lessons: Sleep is crucial for your brain and body. | Her crucial goal won the cup final. | It is crucial to look both ways before you cross the road. | Bees play a crucial role in pollinating crops. | Reading the question carefully is crucial in a maths test. | The crucial clue was a muddy footprint. | Water is crucial to all living things.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Said «KROO-shul». You say «crucial to» or «crucial for» something. Similar: vital, essential, key, critical. «Crux» (the most important point) and «crucial» come from the Latin word for «cross» — a crossroads where you must choose. The slang «crucial = brilliant» is old 1980s–90s UK youth talk.

part of speech: noun (the crux; plural cruxes or cruces, rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The most important or difficult part of a problem, question or argument: «The crux of the matter is that we don't have enough money». 2) (climbing) The hardest move or section on a climbing route. 3) (astronomy) Crux, the Southern Cross: a small, bright group of stars seen in the southern sky, shown on the flags of Australia and New Zealand.
its sense in the lessons: In essays, debates and maths problems, the crux is the key point you must sort out first. In geography and science for children in Australia and NZ, the Southern Cross (Crux) helps find south at night. Phrases: «the crux of the matter», «the crux of the problem», «the crux of the argument».
examples from the lessons: The crux of the problem is that the bridge is too short. | Let's get to the crux of the argument. | The crux of the story is whether the dragon will forgive the knight. | The crux of the climb was a tricky overhang. | On the flags of Australia and New Zealand you can see the Southern Cross, called Crux. | Working out what the question asks is the crux of most maths problems.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually «the crux of» + something. Plural rare: cruxes (normal) or cruces (Latin). Comes from Latin «crux», meaning «cross». A slightly formal word; in speech, say «the main point» or «the key thing».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) Made of crystals or having the regular, repeating structure of a crystal: «Salt is a crystalline solid». 2) (literary) Very clear, bright and sparkling, like crystal: «crystalline water». 3) (of sound or speech) Very clear and pure: «a crystalline voice».
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on solids and materials, crystalline substances (salt, sugar, quartz, ice, snowflakes) have particles arranged in a neat repeating pattern, giving flat faces and sharp edges; when you grow crystals from salt or sugar water you make crystalline solids. In stories and poems, «crystalline» describes clear lakes, icy air or bright voices. Phrases: «crystalline solid», «crystalline structure», «crystalline waters».
examples from the lessons: Salt and sugar are crystalline solids. | Under the microscope, the snowflake showed a crystalline pattern. | Quartz has a crystalline structure. | We swam in the crystalline waters of the bay. | Her crystalline voice filled the church. | Glass looks like crystal but is not crystalline inside. | Diamonds are crystalline forms of carbon.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Said «KRIS-tuh-line» or «KRIS-tuh-leen». Trap: «crystal glass» in kitchens is not crystalline in the scientific sense; glass has a jumbled, non-crystalline structure. The opposite in science is «amorphous» (without a regular shape inside).

part of speech: verb (crystallise, crystallises, crystallised, crystallising; US crystallize)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) When a substance crystallises, it forms crystals, usually as a liquid cools or water evaporates: «Salt crystallises as the water dries». 2) When an idea, feeling or plan crystallises, it becomes clear and definite: «Her plan crystallised in her mind». 3) (cooking) To coat fruit or flowers with sugar so they become sweet and hard: «crystallised ginger».
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, pupils dissolve salt, sugar or copper sulfate in water and leave it to evaporate so that crystals form; this shows separating a solid from a solution. In cooking, honey sometimes crystallises (gets grainy) in the jar; crystallised fruit decorates cakes. In stories, a vague idea «crystallises» into a plan. Phrases: «crystallise out», «crystallised fruit», «crystallised ginger».
examples from the lessons: As the water evaporated, the salt crystallised on the saucer. | Our sugar solution crystallised on the string overnight. | Honey can crystallise if you keep it in the cold. | Gran decorated the cake with crystallised violets. | Slowly, my idea for the story crystallised. | The talk helped crystallise what I wanted to be when I grow up.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK, Irish, Australian and NZ spelling: crystallise; US and Canadian: crystallize. Spelled with double l. The noun is «crystallisation» (crystallization). In chemistry, cooling a hot saturated solution slowly gives bigger crystals.

meaning for a pupil: 1) ct: short for «carat», the unit for the weight of diamonds and gems (1 carat = 0.2 grams), and also for «karat» (in the US), the measure of how pure gold is (24 ct = pure gold). 2) ct: short for «cent» or «cents» in prices, as in «50 ct». 3) Ct: short for «Court» in addresses: «12 Oak Ct». 4) CT: short for «computed tomography»: a CT scan is an X-ray scan that makes pictures of slices of the inside of the body. 5) CT: the postal code for Connecticut, a state in the USA. 6) (sport, other) ct also stands for «caught» in some cricket scorecards and «count» in some lists.
its sense in the lessons: It is an honest entry for an abbreviation, not a word. Children see «ct» on jewellery («18 ct gold»), on addresses, in hospital talk («a CT scan») and on maps and letters in the USA. In maths, «ct» on a price label means cents. Phrases: «18 ct gold», «a CT scan».
examples from the lessons: Mum's ring is 18 ct gold. | The diamond weighs 2 ct. | We live at 4 Maple Ct. | The doctor sent Grandad for a CT scan of his head. | My penpal lives in Hartford, CT. | The sticker said 99 ct.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Not a word you say aloud: read it as «carat», «cent», «court», «C-T scan» or «Connecticut» depending on the place. Trap: «carat» (gem weight), «karat» (gold purity, US spelling) and «carrot» (vegetable) sound the same. In maths, 24-carat gold is pure; 18-carat gold is 18/24 = three quarters gold.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal, law) Deserving blame for something wrong or bad: «He was culpable for the accident».
its sense in the lessons: In law and ethics lessons, being culpable means being responsible for harm and deserving blame; courts decide how culpable someone is, and a person who did not mean harm may be less culpable. In stories and history, characters argue about who is culpable. Phrases: «held culpable», «morally culpable», «culpable negligence», «culpable homicide» (Scotland, law: killing without meaning to murder).
examples from the lessons: The driver was found culpable for the crash. | Everyone who knew about the bullying and did nothing felt a little culpable. | Is a child as culpable as an adult for breaking a rule? | The judge said the company was culpable for the pollution. | In ethics we discussed when someone is morally culpable. | She was not culpable, because she did not know the bridge was unsafe.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; in speech say «to blame» or «guilty». Said «KUL-puh-bul». The noun is «culpability». It comes from Latin «culpa», fault, as in «mea culpa» (my fault). The opposite is «blameless» or «innocent».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal, from Latin) Combined with; also being used as: «a kitchen-cum-dining room» is one room that is both a kitchen and a dining room; «a shed-cum-workshop». 2) (Latin, school and university) In Latin, «cum» means «with», as in the university honours «cum laude» (with praise) and «magna cum laude» (with great praise). 3) (rude, adult slang) A rude word grown-ups use; not for school.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday British English and in house adverts, «X-cum-Y» means one thing doing two jobs. In American school and college life, students graduate «cum laude». In names of English places, «cum» joins villages, as in «Chorlton-cum-Hardy» in Manchester. Phrases: «X-cum-Y», «cum laude», «magna cum laude», «summa cum laude».
examples from the lessons: Our kitchen-cum-dining room is where we do homework. | Dad uses the garage as a gym-cum-workshop. | My aunt graduated magna cum laude from college. | The spare room is a study-cum-guest room. | Chorlton-cum-Hardy is part of Manchester.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Said «kum» (rhymes with «sum»). Usually written with hyphens between the two things: bedroom-cum-office. «Summa cum laude» is the highest honour, «magna cum laude» next, «cum laude» third. Because of the rude slang sense, careful writers often use «combined with» or «and» instead.

part of speech: noun (cupping; uncountable); verb form (present participle of cup: cupping)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (verb form) Holding your hands in a curved shape like a cup: «cupping water in her hands», «cupping his ear to hear». 2) (noun) Cupping therapy: an old treatment in which cups are placed on the skin and the air in them is reduced so the skin is sucked up, leaving round marks; some people believe it helps aches, but there is little good scientific evidence for it. 3) (noun) In the coffee and tea trade, cupping is a careful tasting of coffee by smelling and slurping it to judge its quality.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and stories, people cup their hands to drink from a stream, carry a baby bird, warm their hands or call out loudly. Swimmers at the Olympics have shown round cupping marks, which led to news stories; in science lessons this is a good example to ask «what is the evidence?». Phrases: «cupping your hands», «cupping your ear», «cupping therapy», «coffee cupping».
examples from the lessons: She was cupping a tiny frog in her hands. | He shouted with his hands cupped around his mouth. | Grandad was cupping his ear because he couldn't hear me. | The swimmer had round red marks on his back from cupping. | Scientists say there is not much evidence that cupping therapy works. | We drank from the stream by cupping the water in our hands. | At the coffee shop, the staff were cupping new beans to taste them.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comes from the verb «cup» (cup, cups, cupped, cupping) with double p. «Cupping» is not about cups of tea in the everyday sense. When a health treatment is popular with famous people, that is not proof it works; look for fair tests.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The quality of being curly, having curls or twists: «the curliness of her hair». 2) How much something bends or curls, such as a pig's tail, a fern or ribbon.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and descriptive writing, it describes hair, fur or leaves. In science lessons on inheritance, curliness of hair is a trait that can run in families; hair is curly partly because of the shape of the hair follicle (oval follicles make curlier hair). Phrases: «the curliness of», «natural curliness».
examples from the lessons: The curliness of her hair grew in the rainy weather. | My dog's curliness means he doesn't shed much fur. | Damp air increases the curliness of my hair. | The curliness of the pig's tail made us laugh. | Hair curliness can run in families. | The ribbon kept its curliness after we pulled it with the scissors.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Made from «curly» + -ness; the y changes to i: curly → curliness. Similar: waviness, frizziness. The opposite is straightness.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (noun) Joined-up handwriting, in which the letters of a word are connected by flowing strokes: «We are learning cursive». 2) (adjective) Written with joined, flowing letters: «cursive writing», «a cursive font».
