its sense in the lessons: In primary school in the UK, Ireland, Australia and NZ, children learn «joined-up writing» around ages 6–8; in the USA and Canada it is called «cursive», though some schools teach it less now that people type. Handwriting lessons practise entry and exit strokes. Old letters, birthday cards and historical documents (like the US Declaration of Independence) are often in cursive. Phrases: «write in cursive», «cursive handwriting», «cursive script».
examples from the lessons: We practise cursive every morning in Year 3. | Grandma's letters are in beautiful cursive. | Some children find cursive faster than printing. | Can you read the cursive on this old postcard? | The invitation was printed in a curly cursive font. | Joining the letters is the trick to cursive writing. | My teacher says neat cursive helps spelling.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable as a noun: «write in cursive», not «a cursive». UK schools usually say «joined-up writing»; «cursive» is the usual US word. The opposite is «print» or «printing» (separate letters). Said «KUR-siv».

part of speech: noun (a Cyclops, Cyclopes or Cyclopses; also cyclops, cyclopes)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (myth) A Cyclops is a giant with only one eye in the middle of its forehead, from ancient Greek myths; the most famous is Polyphemus, who trapped Odysseus (Ulysses) in his cave. 2) (science) Cyclops: a tiny freshwater animal (a copepod, a kind of crustacean) with one eye spot, found in ponds. 3) (a name) A character name in comics and films, such as the X-Men hero who shoots beams from his eyes.
its sense in the lessons: In classic myths and stories, Odysseus escapes the Cyclops by blinding him and telling him his name is «Nobody», so when the Cyclops shouts «Nobody is hurting me!», no one comes to help. In pond-dipping in science, pupils may spot a cyclops under a microscope or magnifying glass. Phrases: «the Cyclops Polyphemus», «one-eyed Cyclops».
examples from the lessons: The Cyclops had one huge eye in the middle of his forehead. | Odysseus tricked the Cyclops by saying his name was «Nobody». | In Greek myths, the Cyclopes made thunderbolts for Zeus. | We saw a tiny cyclops wriggling in the pond water under the microscope. | My little brother dressed up as a Cyclops for Halloween. | The Cyclops rolled a giant stone across the cave door.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Said «SY-klops». Plural: Cyclopes (Greek, said «sy-KLOH-peez») or Cyclopses; in everyday English people sometimes wrongly use «cyclops» as plural. Usually a capital C for the myth. The name means «round eye» in Greek. It is a creature of myth, not a real animal; a myth (not proved) says fossils of dwarf elephant skulls, with one big nasal hole, made the Greeks imagine Cyclopes.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (ballet, from French) A male ballet dancer; «premier danseur» means a leading male dancer in a ballet company. 2) (French) In French, «danseur» simply means «dancer» (a man who dances); English uses it only in ballet.
its sense in the lessons: It is a ballet word. In arts and music lessons, children learn that ballet's words come from French (plié, pirouette, pas de deux). A danseur partners the ballerina, lifting and supporting her and dancing solos with big jumps. Phrases: «premier danseur», «danseur noble» (a dancer of princely, classical roles).
examples from the lessons: The danseur lifted the ballerina high above his head. | He became a premier danseur at the Royal Ballet. | The danseur leapt across the stage. | In French, a danseur is just a male dancer. | Our ballet teacher showed us a famous danseur on video.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Said «dahn-SUR» (the n is soft, from the nose). It is a French word used in English ballet talk; in ordinary English just say «dancer» or «ballet dancer». The female form is «danseuse». Many people wrongly think ballet is only for girls; boys and men dance it too.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (ballet, from French) A female ballet dancer; «première danseuse» means a leading female dancer. 2) (French) In French, «danseuse» simply means «dancer» (a woman who dances); English uses it mainly in ballet.
its sense in the lessons: It is a ballet word, used mainly in old-fashioned or formal writing; today English speakers usually say «ballerina» or «dancer». In arts lessons pupils meet ballet's French words. Phrases: «première danseuse», «a danseuse of the Paris Opera».
examples from the lessons: The danseuse spun on the tips of her toes. | She was the première danseuse of the company. | In French, a danseuse is a woman who dances. | The danseuse wore a white tutu in «Swan Lake». | The old poster showed a danseuse in mid-leap.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Said «dahn-SURZ». A French word used in English; the male form is «danseur». «Ballerina» (from Italian) is the more common English word, and strictly means a principal female dancer. Avoid «danseuse» in everyday talk; it sounds old-fashioned.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A Chinese tradition of thought and religion based on the «Dao» (or «Tao»), «the Way» — the natural flow of the universe; it teaches living simply, calmly and in harmony with nature. 2) The religion that grew from these ideas, with temples, priests, festivals and many gods and immortals.
its sense in the lessons: In religious education and lessons about China, pupils learn that Daoism is linked to the teacher Laozi (Lao Tzu) and the book «Dao De Jing» (Tao Te Ching), and to the yin-yang symbol showing how opposites (dark and light, quiet and active) balance each other. It is often compared with Confucianism, which focuses on rules and duties; Daoism focuses on nature and going with the flow. Tai chi and some Chinese medicine have Daoist roots. Phrases: «the Dao», «the Way», «yin and yang», «Daoist temple».
examples from the lessons: Daoism teaches people to live in harmony with nature. | The yin-yang symbol is linked with Daoism. | Laozi is said to have written the Dao De Jing. | Daoism and Confucianism both began in ancient China. | My grandad does tai chi, which has roots in Daoism. | In RE we compared Daoism with Buddhism. | Daoists believe water shows the Way: soft, yet able to wear down stone.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Written with a capital D. The spellings «Daoism» (newer pinyin) and «Taoism» (older) are the same word; both are said «DOW-ism» (rhymes with «how»). Uncountable. The adjective is «Daoist» (Taoist).

part of speech: noun (Darjeeling; also darjeeling, the tea); proper noun (Darjeeling, a place)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (a place name) Darjeeling, a town in the Himalayan hills of West Bengal in north-east India, famous for its tea gardens and its little «toy train». 2) A light, fragrant black tea grown in the Darjeeling hills, sometimes called «the champagne of teas»: «a cup of Darjeeling».
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons on India and mountains, Darjeeling shows how tea is grown on steep, misty slopes and picked by hand; you can see Kangchenjunga, the third highest mountain in the world, from the town. In everyday British life, Darjeeling is a tea name on boxes in the kitchen. The Darjeeling Himalayan Railway is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Phrases: «Darjeeling tea», «a pot of Darjeeling», «the Darjeeling toy train».
examples from the lessons: Darjeeling is a hill town in India famous for tea. | Grandma only drinks Darjeeling with breakfast. | The tea pickers in Darjeeling pick only the top leaves. | The little steam train climbs up to Darjeeling. | From Darjeeling you can see snowy Kangchenjunga. | Darjeeling tea is lighter than English breakfast tea.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually written with a capital D. Said «dar-JEE-ling». Uncountable as tea (some Darjeeling), but «a Darjeeling» can mean a cup of it. Only tea grown in the Darjeeling area may legally be sold as Darjeeling tea.

part of speech: adjective (dazzled); verb form (past of dazzle: dazzled)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Unable to see clearly for a moment because of a very bright light: «I was dazzled by the car's headlights». 2) Very impressed by something amazing, beautiful or clever: «The audience was dazzled by the acrobats». 3) (verb, past) Made someone unable to see, or amazed them: «The sun dazzled the drivers».
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons, drivers and cyclists can be dazzled by low sun or headlights, which causes accidents; never shine lasers or torches into people's eyes. In stories, characters are dazzled by treasure, fireworks, palaces or a famous person. In science, dazzle camouflage on old warships used bold stripes to confuse enemies. Phrases: «dazzled by», «dazzled with», «dazzle camouflage».
examples from the lessons: I was dazzled by the bright sunlight when I came out of the cinema. | The crowd was dazzled by the fireworks. | The driver was dazzled by the low sun and slowed down. | We were dazzled by the jewels in the Tower of London. | The magician dazzled the children with his tricks. | Don't shine your torch at me; I'm dazzled! | The judges were dazzled by her singing.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: dazzle, dazzles, dazzled, dazzling. «Dazzling» means very bright or amazing (a dazzling smile). «Dazzled» describes the person who is affected; «dazzling» describes the thing that causes it. Do not confuse «dazzled» with «dizzy» (feeling the room spin).

meaning for a pupil: 1) DC, d.c.: short for «direct current», electricity that flows in one direction only, as from a battery. 2) D.C.: short for «District of Columbia», as in Washington, D.C., the capital city of the United States. 3) DC: DC Comics, an American comic company known for Superman, Batman and Wonder Woman. 4) (UK) DC: Detective Constable, a police rank. 5) (music) D.C.: short for Italian «da capo», meaning «go back to the beginning» in sheet music.
its sense in the lessons: It is an honest entry for an abbreviation, not a word. In science lessons on electricity, batteries give DC, while the mains sockets at home give AC (alternating current). In geography and politics, Washington, D.C. is where the President lives in the White House and Congress meets. Children meet DC on comic books and films. In music, «D.C. al fine» means go back to the start and play until «Fine» (the end).
examples from the lessons: A battery gives DC, which flows one way only. | We visited the White House in Washington, D.C. | The plug for the laptop changes AC into DC. | My brother collects DC comics about Batman. | DC Patel from the police came to our school. | At D.C. in the music, go back to the beginning.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Read aloud as letters: «D-C». Washington, D.C. is not in any state; it is a special federal district. Trap: Washington state, in the north-west of the USA, is a different place. AC and DC are both electricity; AC changes direction many times each second.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To make so much noise that people cannot hear anything else, or can hardly hear for a while: «The music deafened us». 2) To damage someone's hearing or make them deaf: «The explosion deafened him in one ear».
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on sound, very loud noises (measured in decibels) can damage the tiny hair cells in the inner ear; ear defenders and earplugs protect hearing at concerts, fireworks and in noisy jobs. In stories, «deafening» noise and «deafening silence» add drama. Phrases: «a deafening roar», «deafening noise», «a deafening silence» (a silence that is very noticeable, often after something awkward).
examples from the lessons: The cheers of the crowd deafened us. | The fireworks were so loud they nearly deafened the dog. | Wear ear defenders so the drills don't deafen you. | The explosion deafened him in one ear. | There was a deafening roar as the rocket took off. | When the teacher asked who broke the window, there was a deafening silence.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Said «DEF-un» (the «deaf» part rhymes with «chef»). The adjective «deafening» (very loud) is used more than the verb. Respectful language: «deaf» is a normal word, and many Deaf people use sign language (BSL in the UK, ASL in the USA and Canada, Auslan in Australia).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (noun, maths) A decimal (or decimal number) is a number written with a decimal point, such as 3.5 or 0.25, to show parts smaller than one. 2) (adjective) Decimal system: counting in tens, using the ten digits 0 to 9, where each place is worth ten times the place to its right. 3) (adjective) Decimal money: money in which 100 small coins make one big unit, like 100 pence = £1 or 100 cents = $1. 4) Decimal place: one digit after the decimal point.
its sense in the lessons: In maths lessons, pupils learn tenths, hundredths and thousandths, place value columns, rounding to one or two decimal places, adding and multiplying decimals, and converting between fractions, decimals and percentages (½ = 0.5 = 50%). In everyday life decimals appear in prices (£2.99), measurements (1.5 metres), sports times (9.58 seconds) and temperatures. In history, Britain and Ireland switched to decimal money on «Decimal Day», 15 February 1971; Australia did in 1966 and New Zealand in 1967. Phrases: «decimal point», «decimal place», «to two decimal places», «recurring decimal», «decimal fraction».
examples from the lessons: 0.5 is the decimal for one half. | Round 3.476 to two decimal places: it's 3.48. | Put the decimal point in the right place! | Our money is decimal: 100 pence make one pound. | The sprinter ran 100 metres in 9.58 seconds, a decimal number. | One third as a decimal is 0.333…, a recurring decimal. | We counted in tens because the decimal system uses ten digits. | Gran remembers when Britain went decimal in 1971.
note for the reader of a maths problem: In the UK, USA, Australia and similar countries the decimal point is a dot (3.5); in many European countries it is a comma (3,5). Trap: more digits does not mean bigger: 0.5 is bigger than 0.45, because 5 tenths is more than 4 tenths. Say «three point one four», not «three point fourteen». Multiplying by 10 moves the digits one place to the left: 0.35 × 10 = 3.5.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Showing great respect and politeness to someone, often by agreeing with them or letting them decide: «a deferential bow».
its sense in the lessons: In history and stories, servants, courtiers and citizens are deferential to kings, lords and important people; they bow, curtsey and speak politely. In everyday life, being deferential to elders and teachers is polite, but being too deferential (always agreeing) can stop people speaking up when something is wrong. In ethics lessons, pupils discuss when respect turns into fear. Phrases: «deferential to», «deferential tone», «overly deferential».
examples from the lessons: The butler was deferential to everyone in the house. | She spoke in a deferential tone to the head teacher. | The knights gave a deferential bow to the queen. | The young doctor was too deferential to question the surgeon's mistake. | In some cultures, children are expected to be deferential to older relatives. | His deferential manner made the visitors feel important.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Said «def-uh-REN-shul». Comes from «defer to» (to let someone else decide, out of respect) and «deference» (respect). Different from «different» and «differential». Similar: respectful, polite, humble; the opposite: disrespectful, rude, cheeky.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To say exactly what a word or idea means: «Can you define 'habitat'?» 2) To state or show clearly what something is, its limits or its nature: «The rules define who can enter». 3) To make the edges or shape of something clear and sharp: «a well-defined outline». 4) To be the most important feature of someone or something: «Kindness defines her».
its sense in the lessons: In every subject, teachers ask pupils to «define» key words (define a prime number, define photosynthesis), and a glossary or dictionary gives definitions. In maths, we define shapes by their properties (a square is defined as a shape with four equal sides and four right angles). In computing, programmers «define» functions and variables. In PSHE: «Don't let one mistake define you». Phrases: «define a word», «clearly defined», «well-defined», «define yourself».
examples from the lessons: Can you define the word «evaporate»? | A triangle is defined as a shape with three straight sides. | The river defines the border between the two countries. | The photo was sharp, with every leaf clearly defined. | In the program, we define a function called «jump». | Her courage defines her. | Don't let one bad test define you.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: «definition». Adjective: «definite» (sure, fixed) and «definitive» (final, most complete) — easy to mix up. A good definition does not use the word itself inside it. In maths, definitions are exact; in everyday talk words can be looser.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Final and settled, so that nobody can argue with or change it: «a definitive answer». 2) The best, most complete or most trusted version of something: «the definitive guide to sharks». 3) (stamps) Definitive stamps are the ordinary, long-running stamps, not special issues.
its sense in the lessons: In school and science, a «definitive answer» or «definitive proof» is one that settles a question beyond doubt; scientists are often careful to say results are «not yet definitive». In book and film reviews, «the definitive version» is the best one. Phrases: «a definitive answer», «definitive proof», «the definitive guide», «definitive list».
examples from the lessons: We still have no definitive answer to how big the universe is. | This is the definitive guide to British birds. | The test gave definitive proof that the water was safe. | Mum's answer was a definitive «No». | Is this the definitive list of winners? | The scientists said the result was exciting but not definitive.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Do not confuse with «definite» (clear and sure: «a definite yes»). «Definitive» is stronger: final and authoritative. Adverb: «definitively». Said «dih-FIN-uh-tiv».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Letting the air or gas out of something, so it gets smaller and softer: «the deflation of a tyre». 2) (economics, money) A general fall in prices in a country over time, the opposite of inflation. 3) A sudden feeling of disappointment or loss of confidence: «a sense of deflation after the match». 4) (sport) A cheating scandal in which footballs were said to be under-inflated («Deflategate», USA).
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on air and pressure, deflating balloons, balls and bouncy castles shows that air takes up space. In money and economics lessons, pupils learn that inflation (prices rising) is more common, while deflation (prices falling) can sound good but may mean businesses earn less and people lose jobs. In stories, characters feel deflated after bad news. Phrases: «tyre deflation», «a period of deflation», «a sense of deflation».
examples from the lessons: The slow deflation of the bouncy castle meant the party was over. | Deflation means prices go down across a whole country. | Japan had years of deflation in the 1990s and 2000s. | After losing the final, the team felt a great deflation. | The bike tyre's deflation was caused by a tiny nail. | Economists worry about deflation as much as about inflation.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Verb: «deflate» (deflate, deflated, deflating); adjective: «deflated» (let down or disappointed). Opposite: inflation. Trap: in maths, if deflation is 2% a year, a £100 basket of shopping costs about £98 a year later; under inflation of 2% it would cost £102.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A change in direction when something bounces off or is pushed sideways: «The ball went in off a deflection». 2) (science) The amount something bends or moves aside under a force, such as a beam under a load or a needle on a meter: «the deflection of the compass needle». 3) Turning attention, blame or a question away from yourself onto something else: «His joke was just a deflection».
its sense in the lessons: In football and other sports, a goal scored «off a deflection» changed direction when it hit another player. In science lessons on forces, magnets deflect a compass needle, and light can be deflected (bent) by mirrors and lenses. In PSHE and media literacy, «deflection» is avoiding a hard question by changing the subject or blaming others. Phrases: «a deflection off», «deflection of the needle», «a lucky deflection».
examples from the lessons: The goal came from a lucky deflection off a defender. | The magnet caused a deflection of the compass needle. | We measured the deflection of the ruler when we hung weights on it. | When asked about the broken vase, his answer was a clear deflection. | Without that deflection the shot would have missed. | The deflection of light by a prism splits it into colours.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelled «deflection» (UK sometimes «deflexion», old). Verb: «deflect». In science, «deflection» is often measured in millimetres or degrees. In sport commentary, «a wicked deflection» means a big, unlucky change of direction.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To change the normal shape of something, often by bending, squashing or stretching it: «Heat deformed the plastic». 2) (of a body part) To grow or be made into an unusual shape, for example by illness or injury.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on forces and materials, pupils test how springs and modelling clay deform when pushed or pulled; elastic materials go back to their shape, plastic ones stay deformed. In geography, rock layers deform into folds when continents push together, forming mountains. Phrases: «deform under pressure», «permanently deformed», «deformed by heat».
examples from the lessons: The plastic bottle deformed in the hot car. | Squeezing the ball deforms it, but it springs back. | The bridge was built not to deform under heavy lorries. | Rocks deform into folds when plates push together. | The clay deforms easily when you press it. | Too much weight will deform the shelf.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: «deformation» (in science) and «deformity» (an unusual body shape). Calling a person «deformed» is hurtful; say they have a disability or a particular condition. In science, «elastic deformation» goes back; «plastic deformation» stays.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (law) To trick someone out of money, property or rights by lying or cheating: «He defrauded old people of their savings».
its sense in the lessons: In money and law topics, defrauding is a crime called fraud: fake emails, scam calls and bogus sellers try to defraud people. In online-safety lessons, pupils learn not to share bank details or passwords and to tell an adult about strange messages. In news, companies or people are charged with «conspiracy to defraud». Phrases: «defraud someone of something», «attempt to defraud», «conspiracy to defraud».
examples from the lessons: The fake charity defrauded people of thousands of pounds. | Scammers try to defraud people with fake prize emails. | The banker was jailed for defrauding his customers. | Never give your card details to strangers who might try to defraud you. | The company was accused of defrauding the government. | He defrauded his grandmother of her savings, which made the whole family sad.
note for the reader of a maths problem: You defraud a person «of» money. Noun: «fraud» (the crime) and «fraudster» (the criminal). Formal and legal; in everyday speech say «cheat», «con» or «scam». The «de-» here means «away from»: defraud = take away by fraud.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To let frozen food become unfrozen before cooking or eating: «Defrost the chicken in the fridge». 2) To remove ice from a freezer, fridge or car windscreen: «We need to defrost the freezer». 3) To become unfrozen: «The peas will defrost in an hour».
its sense in the lessons: In cooking and food-safety lessons, frozen meat should be defrosted in the fridge or microwave, not left on the counter, and not refrozen once thawed, to stop harmful bacteria growing. In winter, drivers defrost their windscreens before driving. In science, defrosting shows melting: ice changing from solid to liquid as it warms. Phrases: «defrost in the fridge», «defrost setting», «defrost the windscreen».
examples from the lessons: Mum took the fish out of the freezer to defrost. | Always defrost meat in the fridge, not on the worktop. | Dad turned the car heater on to defrost the windscreen. | We had to defrost the old freezer because it was full of ice. | Use the defrost setting on the microwave. | Leave the bread to defrost for an hour.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Similar: thaw. US also «unthaw» (informal and illogical, but used). In science, defrosting is melting, a reversible change. Food safety rule: cook defrosted meat soon and do not refreeze it raw.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Gently and carefully, so as not to break or hurt something: «She held the eggshell delicately». 2) In a fine, light and graceful way: «delicately painted flowers». 3) Tactfully, with care not to upset anyone: «He delicately asked about her illness». 4) (food) With a light, gentle flavour: «delicately spiced».
its sense in the lessons: In science and practical work, pupils handle fragile things such as glassware, insects or seedlings delicately. In art, delicately drawn lines are thin and light. In stories and PSHE, people speak delicately about sad or private topics. Phrases: «handle delicately», «delicately balanced», «put it delicately».
examples from the lessons: She delicately lifted the butterfly onto a leaf. | The vase was delicately painted with tiny birds. | Handle the test tubes delicately. | The teacher delicately asked if everything was all right at home. | The soup was delicately flavoured with herbs. | How can I put this delicately? Your shoes smell! | The rock was delicately balanced on the cliff edge.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From the adjective «delicate» + -ly (no extra e dropped: delicate → delicately). Said «DEL-ih-kut-lee». «To put it delicately» is a polite way to start saying something awkward.

part of speech: adjective (delineated); verb form (past of delineate: delineated)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Described or explained clearly and in detail: «The rules are clearly delineated in the handbook». 2) Marked out with lines or edges, so the limits are clear: «The pitch is delineated by white lines». 3) (art) Drawn or outlined: «a delineated shape».
its sense in the lessons: In geography and maps, borders, fields and areas are delineated (marked out). In school instructions and reports, responsibilities or steps are «clearly delineated». In science diagrams, parts are delineated with labels and lines. Phrases: «clearly delineated», «sharply delineated», «well delineated».
examples from the lessons: The car park spaces are delineated with yellow paint. | Each person's job was clearly delineated on the poster. | On the map, the national park is delineated in green. | The mountains were sharply delineated against the sunset. | The rules of the game are delineated in the booklet. | The artist delineated the face with a few quick strokes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal. Verb: delineate, delineates, delineated, delineating; said «dih-LIN-ee-ate». Noun: «delineation». It comes from Latin «linea», a line. In everyday speech, say «marked out», «set out» or «described».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A strong cotton cloth, usually blue, used to make jeans, jackets, skirts and overalls. 2) (plural, informal) Denims: clothes, especially jeans, made of this cloth.
its sense in the lessons: In design and technology and textiles lessons, denim is a twill weave (diagonal lines) dyed with indigo, which is why jeans fade. In history, jeans were made strong for miners and workers in the American West by Levi Strauss and Jacob Davis in 1873. In everyday life, denim is the classic casual fabric. Phrases: «denim jacket», «denim shorts», «double denim», «blue denim».
examples from the lessons: My favourite jacket is made of denim. | Jeans are made of strong cotton denim. | Denim was first used for workers' trousers because it is tough. | She wore denim shorts on the beach. | Wearing a denim jacket with jeans is called «double denim». | Denim fades each time you wash it. | Indigo dye gives denim its blue colour.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «some denim», «a denim jacket» (as an adjective). The word may come from French «serge de Nîmes» (cloth from the town of Nîmes), though experts are not completely sure. «Jeans» are the trousers; «denim» is the cloth.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) One of the tiny tooth-like scales that cover the skin of sharks and rays, making it feel rough like sandpaper; also called «dermal denticles». 2) Any small tooth or tooth-shaped bump, for example on a leaf edge, insect leg or shell.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on sea animals and adaptation, shark skin is covered in denticles that point backwards; they reduce drag, help sharks swim fast and quietly, and stop barnacles and algae sticking. Engineers copied them (biomimicry) for swimsuits, boat hulls and hospital surfaces. Phrases: «dermal denticles», «shark denticles».
examples from the lessons: Shark skin is covered in tiny denticles. | Stroke a shark from tail to head and the denticles feel like sandpaper. | Denticles help sharks glide through the water. | Scientists copied shark denticles to make faster swimsuits. | Each denticle is built like a tiny tooth. | Under the microscope, the denticles looked like little ridged shields.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Said «DEN-tih-kul». Plural: denticles. It comes from Latin «dens», tooth (as in «dentist»). Fun fact: a shark's denticles are made of the same materials as teeth (enamel-like outer layer and dentine), not the same as fish scales.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The hard, yellowish layer that makes up most of a tooth, under the white enamel and around the soft pulp in the middle.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on teeth, pupils label a tooth: enamel (hardest outer layer), dentine (underneath), pulp (nerves and blood vessels), root and gum. When enamel wears away from sugary or acid drinks, the dentine is exposed and teeth can feel sensitive to cold. Elephant tusks are mostly dentine (ivory). Phrases: «exposed dentine», «enamel and dentine».
examples from the lessons: Dentine lies under the hard white enamel of the tooth. | If enamel wears away, the dentine underneath can feel sensitive. | We labelled enamel, dentine and pulp on our tooth diagram. | Ivory from elephant tusks is a kind of dentine. | Dentine is softer than enamel but harder than bone. | The dentist said acid drinks were wearing my enamel down towards the dentine.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK spelling: dentine (said «DEN-teen»); US spelling: dentin (said «DEN-tin»). Uncountable. Trap: enamel, not dentine, is the hardest substance in the human body.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Relying on someone or something to survive, cope or work: «the baby's dependency on its parents». 2) A state of needing a drug, alcohol or a habit and finding it very hard to stop; addiction: «nicotine dependency». 3) (politics, geography) A territory ruled by another country but not fully part of it: «The Isle of Man is a Crown Dependency». 4) (computing) A piece of code or a program that another program needs in order to work.
its sense in the lessons: In science and PSHE, pupils learn about food chains and how living things depend on each other, and about the dangers of drug, alcohol and screen dependency. In geography, the Crown Dependencies (Jersey, Guernsey, the Isle of Man) belong to the British Crown but are not part of the UK. In computing, a project lists its dependencies. Phrases: «dependency on», «drug dependency», «Crown Dependency», «a culture of dependency».
examples from the lessons: A newborn baby has total dependency on its parents. | The country tried to reduce its dependency on oil. | Nicotine dependency makes it hard for smokers to quit. | Jersey is a Crown Dependency, not part of the UK. | Our game would not run because a dependency was missing. | Too much dependency on calculators can make mental maths harder.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: dependencies (y → ies). Close to «dependence»; «dependence» is more often used for the general idea of relying, «dependency» for addiction, territories and computing. Adjective: «dependent» (relying); noun «dependant» (UK) or «dependent» (US) means a person who depends on someone, like a child.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To use up a large amount of something so that there is much less left: «Overfishing has depleted fish stocks».
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography lessons on the environment, people deplete natural resources (oil, coal, forests, fish, fresh water); the ozone layer was depleted by chemicals called CFCs, which were banned in 1987 (the Montreal Protocol), and it is slowly recovering. In health, exercise depletes energy stores and you need to eat and drink to refill them. In stories, an army's supplies are «depleted». Phrases: «depleted stocks», «deplete resources», «ozone depletion», «severely depleted».
examples from the lessons: Overfishing has depleted the cod in the North Sea. | The long winter depleted our firewood. | Running a marathon depletes your body's energy. | Chemicals called CFCs depleted the ozone layer. | The team was depleted by injuries. | We must not deplete the Earth's water faster than rain can refill it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: «depletion». Adjective: «depleted» (a depleted team = one with fewer players). Formal; in everyday speech say «use up» or «run down». In maths problems, «deplete by 20%» means 80% is left: a store of 500 litres depleted by 20% has 400 litres.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (writing, typing) The part of a lower-case letter that goes below the line, as in g, j, p, q and y; also a letter that has such a part. 2) A person or thing that goes down: «a fast descender» (cyclist or skier). 3) (climbing, abseiling) A metal device that controls the speed of going down a rope.
its sense in the lessons: In handwriting lessons, children learn letters with ascenders (b, d, h, k, l, t — going up) and descenders (g, j, p, q, y — going down), and that descenders should dip below the line. In design and fonts, descenders help readers recognise word shapes. In sport, cyclists who are fast downhill are good descenders. Phrases: «ascenders and descenders», «a good descender».
examples from the lessons: The letters g, j, p, q and y all have descenders. | Make sure your descenders go below the line. | In our handwriting book, ascenders go up and descenders go down. | The cyclist was a brilliant descender on the mountain roads. | The climber clipped the descender onto the rope. | In this font, the descenders are very long and curly.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: «ascender» (letters that go up, like b, d, h). Spelled -er, not -or. Related verb «descend» (go down) and noun «descendant» (a child, grandchild or later relative).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (politics) Handing some powers from a central government to smaller regional governments or parliaments: «Devolution gave Scotland its own Parliament». 2) (science, old) Change of a living thing into a simpler form; this idea is not used much in modern biology. 3) (formal) Passing a job, duty or property on to someone else.
its sense in the lessons: In UK citizenship and history lessons, devolution in 1999 created the Scottish Parliament, the Welsh Assembly (now called the Senedd) and the Northern Ireland Assembly, which make laws on things like schools and health, while the UK Parliament in Westminster keeps other powers such as defence. Pupils compare this with federal systems such as the USA, Canada and Australia, where states or provinces have their own powers. Phrases: «Scottish devolution», «devolution of power», «devolved government».
examples from the lessons: Devolution gave Wales its own parliament, the Senedd. | Because of devolution, Scotland decides its own school system. | The Northern Ireland Assembly was set up through devolution. | Some people want more devolution to English cities. | Devolution means power moves from the centre to the regions. | In history we learned that devolution came in 1999.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Verb: «devolve» (to pass power down); adjective «devolved» (devolved government). Trap: devolution is not independence; Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland are still part of the UK. Do not confuse with «evolution» (how living things change over time) or «revolution» (sudden overthrow or turning).

part of speech: verb (devote, devotes, devoted, devoting); devote yourself to; adjective devoted
meaning for a pupil: 1) To devote time, effort or money to something is to give a lot of it to that one thing. 2) To devote yourself to someone or something is to care for it or work for it with your whole heart. 3) (formal) To set a place or a part of something aside for one use, as in a page devoted to sport.
its sense in the lessons: Tells the reader how much someone cares: a person who devotes years to a task is patient and loyal. In school: «devote ten minutes to checking your work». In stories, devoted pets, parents and friends stay by someone's side. Phrases: devote time to, devote yourself to, devoted to, a devoted fan, devoted parents.
examples from the lessons: She devotes every Saturday morning to swimming practice. | The scientist devoted her whole life to studying bees. | Devote the last five minutes of the test to checking your answers. | Our class devoted a whole wall to the history project. | Grandad is devoted to his garden. | The dog was devoted to the little boy and followed him everywhere. | The magazine devotes two pages to puzzles. | He devoted his pocket money to saving for a bike.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pattern: devote something TO something (devote time to reading), not «devote for». Devoted is also an adjective meaning very loving and loyal (a devoted friend). Noun: devotion. Do not mix up with «divide» or «vote». In maths problems «devotes 20 minutes a day» is a rate you multiply by the number of days.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Wet with dew, the tiny drops of water that form on grass and leaves on cool nights. 2) Fresh, soft and slightly shiny, as in dewy skin. 3) Dewy-eyed means with eyes wet with tears, or too hopeful and innocent.
its sense in the lessons: In science it shows that water vapour in the air has cooled and turned to liquid (condensation) on cold surfaces at night. In stories a dewy morning sets a calm, fresh, early scene. Phrases: dewy grass, dewy morning, dewy-eyed.
examples from the lessons: Our shoes got soaked running across the dewy grass. | The spider web sparkled on the dewy morning. | The dewy leaves were cold to touch. | By noon the sun had dried the dewy field. | Mum's face cream promises dewy skin. | Gran got dewy-eyed watching the school play. | We saw the dewy windows of the car before school.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comes from dew (not «due» or «do» — homophones in many accents). Dew is not rain: it forms from the air itself when the ground cools. Dewier, dewiest for comparisons.

part of speech: noun (a diagram, diagrams); verb (diagram, diagrams, diagrammed, diagramming — less common)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A diagram is a simple drawing with lines, shapes and labels that shows how something works, what its parts are, or how things are connected. 2) In maths a diagram is a drawing that helps you solve or show a problem, like a Venn diagram, a tree diagram or a bar model. 3) (verb, mainly US) To diagram something is to show it as a diagram, as in diagramming a sentence.
its sense in the lessons: Used in every subject: science (a labelled diagram of a plant or the water cycle), maths (Venn, Carroll, tree and number-line diagrams), geography (a diagram of a volcano), and instructions for building things. «Label the diagram» and «draw a diagram» are common task words. Phrases: labelled diagram, Venn diagram, tree diagram, flow diagram, draw a diagram.
examples from the lessons: Label the diagram of the flower with petal, stem and leaf. | Draw a diagram to show how you solved the problem. | The Venn diagram shows children who like cats, dogs or both. | The instructions had a diagram of every step. | Our teacher drew a diagram of the heart on the board. | A tree diagram helps us list all the outcomes of tossing two coins. | The diagram shows that the water goes up as vapour and comes down as rain.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a diagram, two diagrams. A diagram is simpler than a picture: it leaves out details and adds labels. In maths a diagram is «not drawn to scale» if the note says so — then you must not measure it, only use the numbers given. UK «labelled», US «labeled». Adjective: diagrammatic.

part of speech: noun (diligence — uncountable); adjective diligent; adverb diligently
meaning for a pupil: 1) Diligence is careful, steady, hard work that keeps going until the job is done properly. 2) (law, business) Due diligence is checking something carefully before making a big decision, such as buying a company or a house. 3) (history) A diligence was also a stagecoach in France and nearby countries long ago.
its sense in the lessons: A school value word on reports and posters: it praises effort, care and not giving up. In stories it describes a hard-working character. Phrases: with diligence, due diligence, hard work and diligence.
examples from the lessons: Her diligence paid off when she finally learned her times tables. | The teacher praised Sam's diligence in checking every sum. | Ants are famous for their diligence. | With diligence, the team finished the model in time. | The bank did its due diligence before lending the money. | He showed great diligence in practising the piano every day. | The travellers rode a diligence across France in the old story.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «a lot of diligence», not «diligences» (except for old coaches). Diligent is the adjective (a diligent pupil). Diligence is about steady care, not about being clever; a slow worker can be very diligent.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A diode is a small electronic part that lets electric current flow in only one direction, like a one-way door. 2) A light-emitting diode (LED) is a diode that gives out light when current passes through it.
its sense in the lessons: Used in science and technology lessons about circuits: a diode in the wrong way round stops the circuit working. LEDs are in torches, screens, traffic lights and Christmas lights because they use little energy. Phrases: light-emitting diode (LED), a diode in a circuit, forward and reverse.
examples from the lessons: A diode lets the current go only one way. | We put the LED in the circuit backwards, so it did not light up. | Our torch uses tiny diodes instead of an old bulb. | The circuit diagram shows a diode as a triangle with a line. | LED stands for light-emitting diode. | The robot's eyes are two red diodes. | If the diode is turned round, the buzzer stops.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Say «DY-ode». LED is said letter by letter (L-E-D) or sometimes «led». A diode is not a battery: it does not make electricity, it only controls which way it flows. Its long leg is usually the positive one.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Discontinuation is stopping something that used to go on, such as a product, a service, a bus route or a medicine. 2) (formal) It is the word used in official letters and on labels for ending something on purpose.
its sense in the lessons: A formal, adult word: shops, companies, doctors and councils use it. In everyday talk people say «they stopped making it» or «they cut the bus». In a story or news it tells the reader something familiar is ending. Phrases: discontinuation of a product, discontinuation of a service.
examples from the lessons: The discontinuation of my favourite cereal made me sad. | The council announced the discontinuation of the late bus. | The doctor explained the discontinuation of the medicine had to be slow. | After the discontinuation of the toy, collectors paid more for it. | The letter told parents about the discontinuation of the after-school club. | Fans complained about the discontinuation of the game.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Long formal noun; the verb is discontinue and the adjective discontinued (a discontinued line). Simpler words: stopping, ending, cancellation. Do not confuse with «discontent» (unhappiness).

part of speech: noun (dismay — uncountable); verb (dismay, dismays, dismayed, dismaying); adjective dismayed
meaning for a pupil: 1) Dismay is a sudden sad, worried feeling when something bad or disappointing happens. 2) To dismay someone is to make them feel shocked and upset. 3) (formal) To someone's dismay means «and they were upset that».
its sense in the lessons: A feelings word in stories: it tells the reader a character has just had bad news or a nasty surprise, often with a falling heart. In news and formal writing «to the dismay of fans». Phrases: in dismay, to my dismay, filled with dismay, dismayed by.
examples from the lessons: To my dismay, the ice cream van had gone. | She stared in dismay at the broken vase. | The rain dismayed everyone at the sports day. | He was dismayed to find his homework was missing. | The fans groaned in dismay as the ball hit the post. | Much to our dismay, the trip was cancelled. | The teacher was dismayed by the mess in the classroom.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Dismay is uncountable (no «a dismay»). Dismayed is used with «by», «at» or «to + verb». It is stronger than disappointment but weaker than horror. Not a «dis-» opposite of «may».

part of speech: adjective (dissatisfied, more dissatisfied); verb dissatisfy; noun dissatisfaction
meaning for a pupil: 1) Dissatisfied means not pleased or not happy because something was not as good as you hoped or expected. 2) A dissatisfied customer is one who complains or wants their money back.
its sense in the lessons: Used in everyday life about shops and services, in surveys (very satisfied ... very dissatisfied), and in stories to show a character wants more or something better. Phrases: dissatisfied with, dissatisfied customer, feel dissatisfied.
examples from the lessons: She was dissatisfied with her drawing and started again. | Dissatisfied customers can ask for a refund. | The coach was dissatisfied with how we defended. | He felt dissatisfied after the short, boring film. | In the survey, five children said they were dissatisfied with lunch. | The king was dissatisfied with every cake the baker made.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Use «dissatisfied with» something. Double s: dis + satisfied. Close to «unsatisfied» but dissatisfied usually means unhappy and complaining, while unsatisfied often means a need is not yet met (unsatisfied hunger). In a survey chart, count the dissatisfied group as its own category.

part of speech: adjective (distended); verb distend (distend, distends, distended, distending)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Distended means swollen and stretched out from inside, often by gas, liquid or food. 2) (medicine) A distended belly or stomach is swollen, which can be a sign of illness or hunger.
its sense in the lessons: A medical and science word; doctors and nature books use it. In stories and news it can describe sick or starving people or animals, so it is a serious word. Phrases: distended belly, distended stomach, distended veins.
examples from the lessons: After the huge feast the snake's body was distended. | The vet checked the cow's distended stomach. | The balloon was distended until it nearly popped. | The doctor said a distended tummy can mean trapped wind. | The photo showed hungry children with distended bellies. | The frog's throat was distended as it croaked.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; everyday words are swollen, puffed up, bloated. Do not mix up with «distant» or «extended». The verb distend is rarer than the adjective.

part of speech: noun (a distortion, distortions; uncountable too); verb distort
meaning for a pupil: 1) Distortion is when the shape, sound or picture of something is twisted or stretched so it looks or sounds wrong. 2) A distortion of the truth or facts is a version that changes them so they give a false idea. 3) In music, distortion is a rough, buzzing sound effect used on electric guitars.
its sense in the lessons: In science: lenses, curved mirrors and water cause distortion of light (a funhouse mirror, a straw looking bent). In media and politics lessons: a distortion of facts is a warning sign of propaganda or misleading charts. Phrases: a distortion of the truth, sound distortion, image distortion.
examples from the lessons: The funhouse mirror caused a funny distortion of our faces. | The water made a distortion so the pencil looked bent. | The loud speaker gave the music a crackly distortion. | Saying I broke it on purpose is a distortion of what happened. | A graph that does not start at zero can create a distortion. | The guitarist turned on the distortion pedal. | Heat over the road made a wobbly distortion in the air.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable for single cases (a distortion of the facts) and uncountable for the effect (too much distortion). A distortion is not the same as a lie: it can bend true facts. In maths charts, a stretched or cut axis is a classic distortion — read the numbers, not the bar heights.

part of speech: noun (divergence, divergences); verb diverge; adjective divergent
meaning for a pupil: 1) Divergence is when two or more things go further apart, like paths that split and go different ways. 2) A divergence of opinion is when people disagree or think differently. 3) (maths, science) Divergence is a growing difference between numbers, lines or results.
its sense in the lessons: A formal word: used in science, maths and debates. In stories, the divergence of two roads or two friends' lives is a turning point. Phrases: divergence of opinion, point of divergence, divergence between.
examples from the lessons: At the divergence of the two paths we chose the left one. | There was a divergence of opinion about where to go on holiday. | The two lines on the graph show a growing divergence. | The divergence between the twins' handwriting grew each year. | Scientists study the divergence of species from a common ancestor. | The map shows the river's divergence into two streams.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: convergence (coming together). Formal; simpler words are difference, split, disagreement. In a maths problem, divergence means the gap between values gets bigger — find it by subtracting.

part of speech: verb (divvy up, divvies, divvied, divvying — informal); noun (a divvy, divvies — UK slang); noun (divvy — informal, share)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) To divvy up something is to share it out between people. 2) (UK slang) A divvy is a silly or foolish person; it is a mild insult. 3) (informal, older) A divvy is a share or dividend, a part of the money that people get.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday talk and stories about sharing sweets, money or jobs; in maths it is the idea of division and fair shares. As an insult it is playground language in the UK, mild but not kind. Phrases: divvy up, divvy out, you divvy.
examples from the lessons: Let's divvy up the sweets so everyone gets five. | We divvied the chores between the three of us. | (UK slang) Don't be a divvy, you've got your shoes on the wrong feet! | They divvied out the pizza slices. | The pirates divvied up the treasure. | (UK slang) My brother called me a divvy for forgetting my bag.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal; in school writing use «share out» or «divide». Comes from divide/dividend. «Divvy up 12 sweets between 4» means 12 ÷ 4 = 3 each. Calling someone a divvy can hurt feelings even if it sounds funny.

part of speech: noun (a DJ, DJs); verb (DJ, DJs, DJ'd or DJed, DJing — informal); abbreviation
meaning for a pupil: 1) (abbreviation) A DJ, short for disc jockey, is a person who plays recorded music for people at a party, club or on the radio. 2) (informal verb) To DJ is to be the DJ at an event. 3) (UK, informal, older) DJ can also stand for dinner jacket, a smart black jacket worn at formal events.
its sense in the lessons: Everyday word for parties, school discos, weddings and radio. Tells the reader there is music and dancing. Phrases: radio DJ, the DJ at the disco, DJ set, guest DJ.
examples from the lessons: The DJ played my favourite song at the school disco. | My uncle is a radio DJ in the mornings. | She wants to DJ at her cousin's wedding. | The DJ asked everyone to put their hands up. | He DJed for the class party with a laptop. | (UK) Dad wore a DJ and bow tie to the ball.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Written DJ in capitals; said «dee-jay». Plural DJs (no apostrophe). The second meaning (dinner jacket) is British and rarer; in the US it is a tuxedo. Not a real word on its own, only letters.

part of speech: noun (a dolly, dollies); adjective (UK slang — dolly bird, old)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A dolly is a child's word for a doll. 2) A dolly is a small low platform with wheels for moving heavy things or for moving a film camera smoothly. 3) (UK, cricket) A dolly or dolly catch is a very easy catch. 4) (old UK slang, sexist) A «dolly bird» was a rude-ish old word for a pretty young woman; it is not polite now.
its sense in the lessons: In little children's play; in film-making and moving house; in cricket commentary. Tells the reader of play, or of moving something heavy carefully. Phrases: rag dolly, dolly catch, camera dolly, dolly mixtures (a UK sweet).
examples from the lessons: My little sister carries her rag dolly everywhere. | The movers used a dolly to wheel the fridge out. | The camera moved on a dolly along the track. | (UK, cricket) He dropped a dolly and the crowd groaned. | We bought a bag of dolly mixtures at the shop. | She tucked her dolly into the toy pram.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural dollies (y becomes ies). «Dolly» is cosier and more babyish than «doll». Dolly the sheep (1996) was the first mammal cloned from an adult cell — a name. Avoid «dolly bird»: it treats women as decorations.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A domain is an area of land that a king, lord or person owns or rules. 2) A domain is an area of knowledge, work or activity, as in «maths is her domain». 3) (internet) A domain or domain name is the address of a website, like example.com. 4) (maths) The domain of a function is the set of numbers you are allowed to put into it.
its sense in the lessons: In history (a king's domain), in computing lessons (website names and safety: checking the domain before clicking), and in older maths. In stories a character's domain is their own place: «the kitchen was Gran's domain». Phrases: domain name, public domain, in the domain of.
examples from the lessons: The castle and forest were the king's domain. | The kitchen is Dad's domain on Sundays. | Check the domain name before you type your password. | The website's domain ends in .org. | Space science is her domain. | Old stories in the public domain are free to share. | The lion guarded his domain on the savanna.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. «Public domain» means no one owns the copyright any more, so anyone may use it. A fake website can use a domain that looks almost like the real one (amaz0n) — a safety trap. Do not confuse with «domino».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Domineering describes someone who tries to control other people all the time and tells them what to do without listening. 2) It means bossy in a strong, unpleasant way.
its sense in the lessons: Used in stories and in lessons about friendships and families to describe a bossy, controlling character. Tells the reader that person does not respect others' choices. Phrases: domineering parent, domineering boss, domineering manner.
examples from the lessons: The domineering captain never let anyone else choose the game. | Her domineering older cousin decided everything. | In the story the domineering queen ruled with fear. | Nobody liked working with the domineering boy. | He realised he was being domineering and asked what others thought. | A domineering friend can make you feel small.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stronger and more negative than «bossy». Pronounced «dom-i-NEER-ing». Related: dominate, dominant. Being a leader is not the same as being domineering: good leaders listen.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Doomsday is the end of the world, or a day of terrible disaster. 2) (Bible, church) Doomsday is an old name for the Day of Judgement, when Christians believe God will judge all people. 3) (history) The Domesday Book (1086) was William the Conqueror's survey of England; the name is linked to «doomsday». 4) Till doomsday means for an extremely long time.
its sense in the lessons: In films, stories and news it tells the reader of fear of a huge disaster. In history lessons the Domesday Book shows how the Normans counted land and animals. Phrases: doomsday scenario, doomsday clock, until doomsday, doomsday warnings.
examples from the lessons: The film was about a comet heading for Earth on doomsday. | You could wait till doomsday and he still wouldn't say sorry. | Christians believe in a day of judgement, once called Doomsday. | The Domesday Book listed pigs, cows and mills in every village. | The news gave a doomsday warning about the storm, but it was only windy. | The doomsday clock is a symbol of how close the world might be to disaster.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: doomsday (end of world) vs Domesday Book (history), said the same. Many doomsday predictions have been made and none came true — a good example to check claims. Not a real date.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Dotted means marked with small dots or made of dots, like a dotted line. 2) Dotted with means having small things spread here and there, as in a field dotted with sheep. 3) (music) A dotted note lasts half as long again as the plain note. 4) Sign on the dotted line means agree to and sign an official paper.
its sense in the lessons: In school: «cut along the dotted line», «trace the dotted letters», dotted lines in maths for lines of symmetry or hidden edges, and graphs. In stories it paints a scene with things spread out. Phrases: dotted line, dotted with, dotted around, sign on the dotted line.
examples from the lessons: Cut along the dotted line. | Trace the dotted letters to practise writing. | The hillside was dotted with sheep. | Draw a dotted line to show the line of symmetry. | Islands are dotted around the coast. | A dotted crotchet lasts one and a half beats. | Mum signed on the dotted line to join the gym.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double t in dotted, dotting. In geometry a dotted line often shows a line you cannot see (a hidden edge) or a fold. In music a dot after a note adds half its value: a dotted minim = 2 + 1 = 3 beats.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A downpour is a very heavy fall of rain that comes down suddenly. 2) (figurative) A downpour of something is a lot of it coming at once.
its sense in the lessons: Weather and geography lessons (rainfall, floods); everyday safety (shelter, flash floods, slippery roads); in stories a downpour soaks characters or changes the mood. Phrases: sudden downpour, heavy downpour, caught in a downpour.
examples from the lessons: We were caught in a downpour on the way home. | The sudden downpour flooded the playground. | Sports day stopped because of a downpour. | During the downpour we sheltered under a tree, but not in a thunderstorm. | The downpour lasted only ten minutes. | After the downpour the air smelled fresh.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a downpour. Stronger than shower or drizzle. Safety: in a thunderstorm do not shelter under a lone tree. In a maths problem rainfall in a downpour is often measured in millimetres per hour.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A downside is the bad part or disadvantage of something that is mostly good. 2) The downside of a plan is what could go wrong or what it costs you.
its sense in the lessons: Used in debates, persuasive writing and decision-making: listing upsides and downsides (pros and cons). Tells the reader there is a catch. Phrases: the downside is, on the downside, upside and downside.
examples from the lessons: The downside of having a dog is walking it in the rain. | Living near school is great; the only downside is no bus ride with friends. | Every plan has a downside. | One downside of screens at night is poor sleep. | On the downside, the trip costs a lot. | List the upsides and downsides before you choose.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: upside. Informal-neutral; formal word: disadvantage. Do not mix up with «downside up» (a joke) or «upside down». In a decision problem, weigh downsides against upsides.

part of speech: noun (drafting — uncountable); verb form of draft (draft, drafts, drafted, drafting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Drafting is writing a first, rough version of a story, letter or plan that you will improve later. 2) Drafting is making careful technical drawings, such as plans for buildings or machines. 3) Drafting is choosing people for a team or, in some countries, calling people into the army. 4) (sport) Drafting is riding or running close behind someone so the air pushes against them, not you.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons the writing process is planning, drafting, editing and publishing. In design and technology drafting means drawing plans. In news, drafting players into teams. Phrases: drafting a letter, the drafting stage, drafting in.
examples from the lessons: We are drafting our stories today and will edit them tomorrow. | Drafting is messy, and that is fine. | Mum is drafting an email to the school. | The architect spent weeks drafting the plans. | The coach is drafting in two new players. | The cyclists saved energy by drafting behind each other.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK spelling «draught» is used for a cold wind and for the game draughts, but writing drafts are spelled «draft» in the UK too. A first draft is not the final copy; mistakes are expected.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Dreary means dull, grey and making you feel sad or bored, like a wet, cloudy day. 2) A dreary job, book or talk is boring and has nothing exciting in it.
its sense in the lessons: Describes weather and settings in stories to set a gloomy mood; also boring tasks. Phrases: dreary day, dreary weather, dreary work.
examples from the lessons: It was a dreary, drizzly Monday morning. | The dreary grey sky made everyone sleepy. | Copying out spellings felt like a dreary job. | The house looked dreary until we painted it yellow. | The speech was long and dreary. | We cheered up a dreary afternoon with a board game.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Drearier, dreariest. Similar: dull, gloomy, bleak. Not spelled «dreery». Do not mix up with «dream» or «weary» (tired), though dreary days can make you weary.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Dryness is being dry, having little or no water or wetness. 2) Dryness of skin, eyes or mouth is when they feel dry and uncomfortable. 3) Dryness of humour is a quiet, serious-faced way of being funny.
its sense in the lessons: Science and geography: dryness of deserts and soil, drought. Health: dry skin, eyes and lips, drinking water. In writing, dry humour. Phrases: dryness of the soil, skin dryness, dryness of the air.
examples from the lessons: The dryness of the desert means few plants can grow. | The dryness of the soil showed we needed to water the beans. | Lip balm helps with dryness in winter. | The dryness of the air made my eyes itch. | Cacti survive dryness by storing water. | I liked the dryness of his jokes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Spelling keeps the y: dry + ness (not «driness»), although dried and drier change it. Opposite: wetness, moisture, damp.

part of speech: adjective (dun); noun (dun — a colour, a horse); verb (dun, duns, dunned, dunning — old)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Dun is a dull greyish-brown colour. 2) A dun is a horse of this colour, usually with a darker mane and tail. 3) (old) To dun someone is to keep asking them firmly to pay money they owe. 4) In some dialects «dun» is just a spelling of «done» in very casual writing.
its sense in the lessons: Rare in children's books except for horses and old-fashioned descriptions of plain clothes and land. Tells the reader something looks plain and earthy. Phrases: dun-coloured, a dun pony.
examples from the lessons: The farmer rode a dun pony with a black mane. | The moor was dun and brown in winter. | She wore a plain dun coat. | (old) The landlord dunned him for the rent. | The sparrow's feathers are dun and grey. | In the old book, a dun cow grazed in the field.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Sounds like «done» and «Dunn» (a surname). «I'm dun» for «I'm done» is a texting misspelling, not standard. Dunned has double n.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Durability is how long something lasts and how well it stands up to use, wear and damage. 2) In science and design it is a property of a material, like strength or flexibility.
its sense in the lessons: Design and technology and science lessons: choosing materials for durability (a school bag, shoes, bridges). Shopping: durable goods last longer. Phrases: durability test, for durability, built for durability.
examples from the lessons: We tested the durability of three fabrics by rubbing them with sandpaper. | Plastic is chosen for lunch boxes because of its durability. | These boots are famous for their durability. | Stone gives the castle walls great durability. | The durability of the toy was poor; it broke in a day. | Engineers check the durability of a bridge.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Durable = lasting long; durability is the noun. Not the same as hardness: glass is hard but not very durable when dropped. In a fair test, keep everything the same except the material.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A durian is a big, spiky tropical fruit from Southeast Asia with soft, creamy flesh inside. 2) It is famous for its very strong smell, which some people love and many find awful.
its sense in the lessons: Geography and food lessons about Southeast Asia (Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia, Singapore). In stories it is a funny or exotic detail. Some hotels and trains ban it because of the smell. Phrases: durian fruit, king of fruits.
examples from the lessons: A durian is covered in sharp spikes. | The durian smelled so strong we opened the windows. | In Singapore some trains have signs saying no durians. | People call the durian the king of fruits. | My friend from Malaysia loves durian ice cream. | Carry a durian carefully, the spikes can hurt.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Say «DOOR-ee-an». It is a real fruit, not invented. The smell is real but harmless; tastes are personal. It grows on tall trees, and falling durians can hurt people.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Ecological means to do with ecology, the study of how living things live together and depend on each other and on their surroundings. 2) Ecological also means caring for nature and the environment, as in ecological farming.
its sense in the lessons: Science and geography lessons: food chains, habitats, ecosystems, pollution. In news, ecological damage or an ecological disaster means harm to nature. Phrases: ecological balance, ecological damage, ecological footprint, ecological disaster.
examples from the lessons: Cutting down the forest caused ecological damage. | Bees play a big ecological role by pollinating flowers. | The oil spill was an ecological disaster for the birds. | An ecological footprint shows how much of the Earth's resources we use. | The pond is a small ecological system with frogs, snails and plants. | Our school garden uses ecological ways to stop pests, like ladybirds.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say «ee-ko-LOJ-ik-al» or «ek-o-». Ecology is the science; ecological describes it; eco- is a short prefix (eco-friendly). Similar to «environmental» but more about how living things connect.

part of speech: verb (economise, economises, economised, economising); US economize
meaning for a pupil: 1) To economise is to spend less money or use less of something so that you save. 2) To economise on something is to cut back on that one thing.
its sense in the lessons: Everyday life and money lessons: families economise when money is short; saving energy and water at school. In stories a poor family economises. Phrases: economise on, need to economise.
examples from the lessons: We economise by turning off lights we are not using. | Mum is economising on snacks this month. | The school economised on paper by printing on both sides. | To save for the trip, I economised by not buying sweets. | The family had to economise after Dad lost his job. | Campers economise on water in the desert.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK spelling economise, US and often Canada economize. Pattern: economise ON something. Related: economy, economic, economical (good at saving). In a maths problem, if you economise by £2 a week, multiply by the number of weeks to find the saving.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) An edifice is a large, grand or impressive building. 2) (formal, figurative) An edifice is a big system or set of ideas built up over time, which could fall apart.
its sense in the lessons: A fancy word in older books, guidebooks and formal writing for a cathedral, palace or tower. In stories it makes a building sound huge and important. Phrases: a grand edifice, a stone edifice, the whole edifice.
examples from the lessons: The cathedral is a magnificent stone edifice. | Tourists stared up at the huge edifice. | The old bank was an edifice of marble and glass. | In the story, the wizard's tower was a dark edifice on the hill. | One lie and the whole edifice of his excuses fell apart. | The town hall is the oldest edifice on the square.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; plain word is building. Say «ED-i-fis». «An edifice» (starts with a vowel sound). Do not mix up with «edify» (to teach someone to be better), though they share a Latin root meaning to build.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An editorial is an article in a newspaper or magazine that gives the opinion of the editors, not just the news. 2) Editorial (adjective) means to do with editing or with the people who choose and check what is published, as in editorial team.
its sense in the lessons: In media literacy lessons pupils learn to tell news reports (facts) from editorials and opinion pieces (views). Phrases: newspaper editorial, editorial team, editorial decision, editorial staff.
examples from the lessons: The editorial said the town needs a new park. | Remember, an editorial gives an opinion, not only facts. | The class wrote an editorial for the school newspaper about longer playtimes. | The editorial team chose which photos to print. | That was an editorial decision by the magazine. | We compared a news report and an editorial on the same story.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable as a noun. An editorial is persuasive writing; it can use facts but its aim is to convince. Do not confuse with an «edition» (one version or printing of a book or paper).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Eerie means strange and frightening in a quiet, mysterious way, making you feel uneasy. 2) Eerily means strangely, as in eerily quiet or eerily similar.
its sense in the lessons: A favourite word in ghost stories and spooky settings: empty houses, fog, silence, owls at night. It builds suspense for the reader. Phrases: eerie silence, eerie feeling, eerie glow, eerily quiet.
examples from the lessons: An eerie silence filled the old house. | The fog gave the graveyard an eerie look. | We heard an eerie howl in the night. | The empty school felt eerie in the holidays. | The moon cast an eerie glow over the lake. | The two drawings were eerily similar. | There was something eerie about the abandoned fairground.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: eerie (not «eery» in standard use; and not Lake Erie, which sounds the same). Eerie is quiet-scary, not loud-scary. Eerier, eeriest.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Effectiveness is how well something works or does the job it is meant to do. 2) In science tests, effectiveness is measured by comparing results, for example how well a soap removes dirt.
its sense in the lessons: Science and fair tests (effectiveness of insulators, sun cream, magnets), health (effectiveness of a vaccine or medicine), and in reviewing your own work. Phrases: the effectiveness of, test the effectiveness, improve effectiveness.
examples from the lessons: We tested the effectiveness of three materials at keeping ice cold. | The effectiveness of the plan surprised everyone. | Doctors check the effectiveness of medicines in careful trials. | The coach judged the effectiveness of our new tactic. | Washing hands with soap has great effectiveness against germs. | The survey measured the effectiveness of the new reading club.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Effective (works well) vs efficient (works without waste) — different. Affect/effect confusion: effect is the noun, so effectiveness has e. In maths, effectiveness can be shown as a percentage, like «90% effective».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Ejection is pushing or throwing something out with force. 2) Ejection is making someone leave a place, such as a sports player sent off. 3) An ejection seat lets a pilot be shot out of a plane in an emergency.
its sense in the lessons: Science: ejection of lava and ash from a volcano. Sport: a player's ejection from a game (US). Technology: ejecting a disc or memory stick. Phrases: ejection seat, ejection from, ejection of.
examples from the lessons: The ejection of ash from the volcano darkened the sky. | The player's ejection from the game upset the fans. | The pilot escaped using the ejection seat. | Press the button for ejection of the disc. | The bouncer's ejection of the rude man was quick. | The ejection of the cork from the bottle made a pop.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal noun; the verb eject is more common in everyday talk (eject the USB stick). Countable for single events. «Sent off» (UK football) and «ejected» (US sports) mean the same idea.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The elite is a small group of people who are the best at something, or who have the most power, money or importance. 2) Elite (adjective) means the very best or of the highest level, as in elite athletes. 3) Sometimes «the elite» is used as a complaint about rich, powerful people who seem out of touch.
its sense in the lessons: Sport (elite athletes, elite teams), the army (elite soldiers), and politics lessons, where «elites» is a word in arguments. Phrases: the elite, elite athletes, elite squad, elite schools.
examples from the lessons: Only elite athletes can run that fast. | The elite squad trained every day. | She joined the elite group of chess players at the club. | Some people say the elite do not understand ordinary families. | The country's elite went to the same old schools. | Elite gymnasts start training very young.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say «ay-LEET» or «ih-LEET». «The elite» takes a plural or singular verb. In arguments, notice that calling someone «elite» can be praise or an insult — check the tone. Elitism means favouring a small top group.

part of speech: noun (elongation, elongations); verb elongate; adjective elongated
meaning for a pupil: 1) Elongation is making something longer or becoming longer, by stretching or growing. 2) (science) Elongation is how much a material stretches before it breaks.
its sense in the lessons: Science: plants show elongation as their stems grow toward light; materials stretch under force; springs and elastic bands. Maths: an elongated shape is long and thin. Phrases: elongation of, stem elongation.
examples from the lessons: The elongation of the elastic band showed how heavy the weight was. | Plant stems show elongation as they reach for light. | We measured the elongation of the spring in centimetres. | The giraffe's neck is an example of elongation of bones. | Heat can cause elongation of metal rails. | Each extra weight caused more elongation.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Scientific word; plain phrase is stretching or getting longer. In an experiment, elongation = new length minus original length (for example 15 cm − 10 cm = 5 cm). Elongated is the adjective (an elongated oval).

part of speech: verb (embalm, embalms, embalmed, embalming); noun embalming, embalmer
meaning for a pupil: 1) To embalm a dead body is to treat it with special chemicals or salts so it does not rot quickly. 2) In ancient Egypt, embalming was part of making a mummy.
its sense in the lessons: History lessons on ancient Egypt (mummies, canopic jars, natron salt). In modern life, funeral directors may embalm a body before a funeral. A serious, respectful word. Phrases: embalm the body, embalming fluid.
examples from the lessons: The ancient Egyptians embalmed their kings and queens. | Embalming a pharaoh took about seventy days. | They used natron salt to dry out the body before embalming it. | The museum showed tools used to embalm mummies. | Some families choose to have a loved one embalmed before the funeral. | The embalmers wrapped the body in linen.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The l is silent in most accents: «em-BAHM» (like palm, calm). A respectful topic: speak about it calmly. Do not mix up with «embark» or «balm» (a soothing cream), though they share a root.

part of speech: adjective (embedded); verb form of embed (embed, embeds, embedded, embedding)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Embedded means fixed firmly inside something else, like a stone stuck in mud. 2) (grammar) An embedded clause is a part of a sentence put inside the main sentence, usually between commas. 3) (computers) An embedded video or picture is placed inside a web page. 4) An embedded journalist travels with soldiers to report.
its sense in the lessons: English grammar lessons (embedded relative clauses: «The dog, which was muddy, ran in»). Science (fossils embedded in rock). Computing (embedded videos). Phrases: embedded in, embedded clause, deeply embedded.
examples from the lessons: The fossil was embedded in the rock. | A splinter was embedded in my finger. | Add an embedded clause to your sentence: The cat, who was hungry, meowed. | The teacher embedded a video in the slides. | The ring was embedded with tiny diamonds. | Kindness is embedded in our school rules.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double d: embed, embedded, embedding. Commas around an embedded clause are like brackets: the sentence still makes sense without them. Also spelled «imbed», rarely.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Emphatic means said or done strongly and clearly, to show you really mean it. 2) An emphatic win is a very clear win by a lot.
