its sense in the lessons: In writing and speech: an emphatic «No!», emphatic body language. In sport news: an emphatic victory. Exclamation marks and bold letters can make writing emphatic. Phrases: emphatic no, emphatic victory, emphatically deny.
examples from the lessons: Her answer was an emphatic «No!» | He nodded in an emphatic way. | The team had an emphatic 6–0 win. | She emphatically denied eating the last biscuit. | Use an exclamation mark for an emphatic sentence. | The teacher was emphatic that phones stay in bags.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Related: emphasis (noun), emphasise (verb). Being emphatic does not make you right; it only shows you feel strongly. In sport, an emphatic win means a big score difference.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An enchanter is a person in stories who uses magic spells, especially to charm or control people. 2) (figurative) An enchanter is someone who charms and delights people.
its sense in the lessons: Fairy tales, legends and fantasy books (Merlin is often called an enchanter). Tells the reader there is magic and maybe a trick. Phrases: a wicked enchanter, the enchanter's spell.
examples from the lessons: The enchanter turned the prince into a frog. | In the legend, Merlin the enchanter helped King Arthur. | The wicked enchanter cast a sleeping spell on the castle. | The children broke the enchanter's spell with kindness. | The storyteller was a real enchanter; nobody moved while she spoke. | An enchantress lived in the tower.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Enchantress is the old female form; today «enchanter» can be anyone. Related: enchant, enchanted, enchanting. Enchanters are not real; magic in stories is make-believe.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To encircle something is to form a circle round it or surround it on all sides. 2) To encircle a place in war is to surround it so nobody can get in or out.
its sense in the lessons: Geography and maps (mountains encircle a valley), history (armies encircled a city), and descriptions in stories. Phrases: encircled by, encircle with.
examples from the lessons: A ring of trees encircled the pond. | Mountains encircle the little village. | The children encircled the teacher to hear the story. | Draw a line to encircle the correct answer. | The army encircled the city. | A wall encircles the old town of York.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Similar: surround, ring. «Circle the answer» is more usual in instructions than «encircle». Not to be mixed up with «encyclopedia».

meaning for a pupil: 1) An endearment is a loving word or name you call someone, like «love», «sweetheart», «darling» or «pet». 2) Endearment is the act of showing love or affection.
its sense in the lessons: Everyday family life and stories: what grandparents, parents and couples call each other. Regional: «love» (northern England), «pet» (north-east England), «hen» (Scotland), «darl» (Australia). Phrases: term of endearment, words of endearment.
examples from the lessons: «Sweetheart» is a term of endearment. | Nan calls me «duck», which is an endearment in her part of England. | In Scotland you might hear «hen» as an endearment. | The bus driver said «Thanks, love» — just a friendly endearment. | The letter was full of endearments. | Pet names like «sunshine» are endearments.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Endearments from strangers can be friendly in some regions, but if they make you uncomfortable it is fine to say so. Related: endearing (sweet and lovable).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Enormously means very much or to a very great amount. 2) Enormously big means hugely, extremely big.
its sense in the lessons: Used to make adjectives and verbs stronger in speech and writing: enormously helpful, enjoyed it enormously, enormously popular. Phrases: enormously important, enormously grateful.
examples from the lessons: I enjoyed the trip enormously. | The new library is enormously popular. | Thank you, you've been enormously helpful. | The whale was enormously long. | Prices have risen enormously. | Practice helped her enormously.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb of enormous. Overusing intensifiers weakens writing; choose one strong word. Not a maths term: «enormously more» tells you a big amount but not how much — check the numbers.

part of speech: noun (an enquirer, enquirers); US usually inquirer
meaning for a pupil: 1) An enquirer is a person who asks for information about something. 2) (formal) An enquirer may also be someone who investigates or looks into a question.
its sense in the lessons: In formal letters, offices and shops («all enquirers will receive a reply»). In science, a curious enquirer asks questions. Newspapers called The Enquirer or The Inquirer are names. Phrases: curious enquirer, each enquirer.
examples from the lessons: The receptionist answered every enquirer politely. | The museum sends leaflets to each enquirer. | A good scientist is a curious enquirer. | Several enquirers phoned about the lost dog poster. | The enquirer wanted to know when the pool opens. | Our class became young enquirers about space.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK: enquire/enquirer for asking; inquire/inquiry often for formal investigations. US: inquire/inquirer for both. Formal; everyday words are «someone asking» or «caller».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To enrobe someone is to dress them in a robe or special clothes. 2) (cooking) To enrobe food is to coat it all over, especially in chocolate.
its sense in the lessons: Rare. Seen on sweet packets («enrobed in milk chocolate») and in old or ceremonial writing (a judge or bishop enrobed). Phrases: enrobed in chocolate.
examples from the lessons: The biscuits are enrobed in milk chocolate. | The factory machine enrobes each sweet in chocolate. | The new judge was enrobed in red. | The king was enrobed for the ceremony. | The packet said «wafers enrobed in caramel». | The choir was enrobed in white gowns.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A fancy word; plain words are «coated» or «dressed». Mainly used by food companies to sound posh. Not «unrobe» (which is the opposite: disrobe).

meaning for a pupil: 1) An ensemble is a small group of musicians, singers, dancers or actors who perform together. 2) An ensemble is a set of clothes that are worn together as an outfit. 3) Ensemble means a group of things seen as a whole.
its sense in the lessons: Music lessons (a wind ensemble, string ensemble), drama (the ensemble cast, chorus), fashion. Comes from French meaning «together». Phrases: music ensemble, ensemble cast, in ensemble.
examples from the lessons: She plays flute in the school wind ensemble. | The ensemble sang without a conductor. | The play had an ensemble cast with no single star. | Her party ensemble had a sparkly top and matching shoes. | Our brass ensemble played at the fair. | The dancers moved as one ensemble.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say «on-SOM-bul». A French borrowing, now English. Countable. A duet (2) and trio (3) are small ensembles; an orchestra is a large one.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To ensnare an animal is to catch it in a snare or trap. 2) To ensnare a person is to trick them into a bad situation they cannot easily get out of.
its sense in the lessons: Stories and nature books (spiders ensnare flies, hunters ensnare rabbits); online safety (scammers try to ensnare people). Phrases: ensnared in, ensnared by.
examples from the lessons: The spider's web ensnared a fly. | The rabbit was ensnared by a wire trap. | Scammers try to ensnare people with fake prizes. | The hero was ensnared by the villain's lies. | The net ensnared the fish. | The sticky plant ensnares insects.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Similar: trap, catch, entrap. Snare is a wire noose trap; also a snare drum (different meaning). Formal-literary word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An entanglement is when things are twisted and caught together, like string, nets or wire. 2) An entanglement is a difficult or confusing situation or relationship you are caught up in. 3) (science) Quantum entanglement is a strange link between tiny particles studied by physicists.
its sense in the lessons: Nature and conservation lessons: entanglement of whales, turtles and birds in fishing nets and plastic. In stories, emotional or political entanglements. Phrases: entanglement in nets, barbed-wire entanglements, romantic entanglement.
examples from the lessons: Plastic rings can cause entanglement of seabirds. | The diver freed the turtle from its entanglement in the net. | Our kite strings ended up in a big entanglement. | The soldiers crawled under barbed-wire entanglements. | He wanted no entanglement in their argument. | Quantum entanglement puzzles even scientists.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable and uncountable. Verb: entangle (entangled in). Cutting plastic loops before recycling helps prevent animal entanglement.

part of speech: verb (entrap, entraps, entrapped, entrapping); noun entrapment
meaning for a pupil: 1) To entrap someone or something is to catch them in a trap. 2) To entrap someone is to trick them into doing something wrong, especially so they can be caught. 3) (law) Entrapment is when police unfairly trick someone into committing a crime.
its sense in the lessons: Stories, nature, crime and law. Tells the reader there is a trick or trap. Phrases: entrapped by, police entrapment.
examples from the lessons: The hunters tried to entrap the wolf. | Bubbles of air were entrapped in the ice. | The villain's plan was to entrap the detective. | The judge said the police had used entrapment. | Flies get entrapped in the sticky paper. | He felt entrapped by his promise.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double p: entrapped, entrapping. Formal; everyday word is trap. Entrapment has a special legal meaning in some countries.

part of speech: verb (envision, envisions, envisioned, envisioning); UK also envisage
meaning for a pupil: 1) To envision something is to imagine it or picture it in your mind, especially something in the future. 2) To envision a plan is to expect or hope that it will happen in a certain way.
its sense in the lessons: Used in planning, art, design and goals («envision your perfect playground»). Common in US English; UK English often uses envisage. Phrases: envision a future, envision how.
examples from the lessons: Close your eyes and envision your dream bedroom. | The architect envisioned a building made of glass. | I never envisioned winning the race. | Envision what the town might look like in 100 years. | She envisions becoming a vet. | The team envisioned a garden on the roof.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Similar: imagine, picture, foresee. Envision and envisage mean nearly the same. Do not mix up with «envy».

part of speech: noun (an eon, eons); UK also aeon
meaning for a pupil: 1) An eon is an extremely long period of time, too long to count easily. 2) (science) In geology an eon is the biggest division of Earth's history, lasting hundreds of millions of years or more. 3) (informal) Eons means a very long time, as in «I waited for eons».
its sense in the lessons: Science (Earth's history, rocks, fossils) and everyday exaggeration. Phrases: for eons, eons ago, the Phanerozoic eon.
examples from the lessons: Rocks form over eons. | Dinosaurs lived eons before people. | I've been waiting for eons! | The Earth's history is split into eons, eras and periods. | The canyon was carved by the river over eons. | It feels like eons since summer.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK spelling often aeon; US eon. Said «EE-on». In geology an eon is longer than an era, which is longer than a period. «Eons» in speech is an exaggeration, not a real count.

part of speech: adjective (epileptic); noun (an epileptic — older, now often avoided); noun epilepsy
meaning for a pupil: 1) Epileptic means to do with epilepsy, a brain condition that can cause seizures (fits), when a person may shake, stare blankly or fall. 2) An epileptic seizure is one of these episodes. 3) Many people now prefer «a person with epilepsy» to calling someone «an epileptic».
its sense in the lessons: Health and safety lessons: what to do if someone has a seizure — keep calm, move hard things away, cushion the head, do not hold them down or put anything in their mouth, time it, call an adult or 999/911/000/111 if it lasts long. Flashing light warnings on games and TV. Phrases: epileptic seizure, epileptic fit, epilepsy medication.
examples from the lessons: My friend has epilepsy and takes medicine every day. | If someone has an epileptic seizure, move sharp things away. | Never put anything in their mouth during a seizure. | The game has a warning about flashing lights for people with epilepsy. | The teacher timed the seizure and called the nurse. | Most people with epilepsy live full, normal lives.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Kind language: say «person with epilepsy» rather than «an epileptic». «Fit» is common in the UK but «seizure» is the medical word. Myth: you cannot swallow your tongue — so never push anything into the mouth.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Essentially means basically, in the most important way, when you leave out small details. 2) (formal) Essentially can mean necessarily, as something that must be there.
its sense in the lessons: Used in explanations and summaries: «essentially, a bat is a flying mammal». In arguments it introduces the main point. Phrases: essentially the same, is essentially, essentially means.
examples from the lessons: A tadpole is essentially a baby frog. | The two games are essentially the same, just with different colours. | Essentially, we need more chairs. | The story is essentially about friendship. | Multiplication is essentially repeated addition. | The plan is essentially finished.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comes from essential and essence. Note double l: essentially. Spoken English sometimes overuses it as a filler. In maths «essentially the same» does not mean exactly equal — check the numbers.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Estrangement is when people who used to be close, especially family members, stop speaking or seeing each other. 2) It is a feeling of being distant or cut off from someone or something.
its sense in the lessons: Adult life seen by a child: an estranged parent, grandparent or sibling; also in stories and news about families and countries. A sad, serious word. Phrases: estrangement from, years of estrangement, estranged father.
examples from the lessons: After years of estrangement, the brothers finally met again. | Her estrangement from her aunt began with an argument. | The novel is about a girl and her estranged father. | Estrangement can make holidays hard for some families. | The two countries ended their estrangement with a peace deal. | He felt a strange estrangement from his old friends after moving away.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal. Estranged is the common adjective («her estranged husband» means they are separated). It is nobody's fault to talk about in class; family situations are private and often complicated.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (abbreviation) EV stands for electric vehicle, a car, bus or bike that runs on electricity from a battery instead of petrol or diesel. 2) (science) eV stands for electronvolt, a tiny unit of energy used in physics. 3) In some contexts «ev» is a fragment of «every» or «even» in casual typing.
its sense in the lessons: Everyday life and science lessons about energy, pollution and climate: charging an EV at home or at a charging point. Phrases: EV charger, EV charging point, buy an EV.
examples from the lessons: Our neighbour bought an EV and charges it overnight. | The car park has six EV charging points. | EVs are quiet, so be careful crossing the road. | An EV does not give off exhaust fumes from the car itself. | The school minibus is now an EV. | How far can the EV go on a full charge?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Not a real word on its own, only letters: say «ee-vee». Write EV in capitals; plural EVs. Electricity can still be made by burning fuel at power stations, so EVs are cleaner on the street but not always fully clean. In maths problems EV range is in miles or km per charge.

part of speech: noun (an evacuee, evacuees); verb evacuate; noun evacuation
meaning for a pupil: 1) An evacuee is a person who has been moved away from a dangerous place to somewhere safer. 2) (history, UK) In the Second World War, evacuees were children sent from cities to the countryside to escape bombing.
its sense in the lessons: History lessons on the Second World War (Operation Pied Piper, 1939: labels, gas masks, suitcases, host families). News: evacuees from floods, fires, wars and hurricanes. Phrases: child evacuees, wartime evacuee.
examples from the lessons: The evacuee arrived at the station with a label on her coat. | Thousands of evacuees left London in 1939. | The farmer's family took in two evacuees. | Evacuees from the wildfire stayed in the school hall. | In the story, the evacuee missed his mum terribly. | The town welcomed evacuees from the flood.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say «ih-vak-yoo-EE». Countable. Evacuate (verb) is what is done; evacuation is the event; the evacuee is the person. Different from refugee, who has fled to another country; an evacuee is often moved within their own country.

part of speech: noun (evasion, evasions); verb evade; adjective evasive
meaning for a pupil: 1) Evasion is avoiding something you should do or face, like a question, a rule or a duty. 2) (law, money) Tax evasion is illegally not paying the tax you owe. 3) Evasion is also escaping or dodging someone who is chasing you.
its sense in the lessons: Stories (a criminal's evasion of the police), money lessons (tax evasion is a crime; tax avoidance uses legal loopholes), and politics (a politician's evasion of a question). Phrases: tax evasion, evasion of, an evasion.
examples from the lessons: His answer was an evasion; he did not really say yes or no. | Tax evasion is against the law. | The fox's evasion of the hounds was clever. | The thief's evasion of the police ended at the bridge. | Fare evasion means riding a bus without paying. | The reporter would not accept another evasion.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable and uncountable. Evasive (adjective) describes someone who avoids answering. Tax evasion (illegal) and tax avoidance (legal but sometimes unfair) are different.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Evidential means to do with evidence or serving as evidence, the facts that show whether something is true. 2) (law) Evidential value is how much a fact or object helps prove something in court.
its sense in the lessons: A formal word in law, science and history (how strong is the evidence). Pupils will meet «evidence» much more. Phrases: evidential value, evidential weight, evidential basis.
examples from the lessons: The footprint had real evidential value. | The judge asked about the evidential weight of the photo. | Scientists need an evidential basis for a claim. | Diaries are evidential sources for historians. | Without the video, there was little evidential support. | The museum records the evidential details of each find.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; plain words: «as evidence». Say «ev-i-DEN-shul». Not the same as «evidently» (clearly).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Evidently means clearly or obviously, because you can see it from the signs. 2) Evidently can also mean apparently, «it seems that», when you have heard or worked something out.
its sense in the lessons: Used in stories and reports to show a conclusion from clues: «Evidently, someone had been in the kitchen.» Good for detective writing and inference in reading. Phrases: was evidently, evidently not.
examples from the lessons: There were crumbs everywhere; evidently, someone had eaten the cake. | She was evidently tired after the match. | Evidently the bus is late again. | The dog was evidently happy to see us. | Evidently, nobody had read the instructions. | He had evidently been crying.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comes from evident (clear). Slightly formal; in speech people say «obviously» or «clearly». Do not mix up with «evidential». A good reading skill: notice the clue that makes something evident.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Evolutionary means to do with evolution, the very slow change of living things over many generations, as scientists explain it. 2) Evolutionary also means changing slowly and step by step, not suddenly, as in an evolutionary change in design.
its sense in the lessons: Science lessons on evolution and inheritance, fossils, adaptation, Charles Darwin and Mary Anning. Technology: evolutionary improvements. Phrases: evolutionary tree, evolutionary history, evolutionary change.
examples from the lessons: Birds and dinosaurs share an evolutionary history. | The evolutionary tree shows how animals are related. | Darwin's work helped explain evolutionary change. | Fossils give clues about evolutionary steps. | The new phone is an evolutionary change, not a revolution. | Camouflage gives animals an evolutionary advantage.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Evolution happens to populations over very long times, not to one animal in its life. Evolutionary (slow, step by step) vs revolutionary (sudden, huge change). Some people hold religious views on how life began; in science lessons evolution is the accepted scientific explanation.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An excavator is a big machine with an arm and a bucket for digging up earth and rocks. 2) An excavator is also a person who digs carefully at a site to find old objects, like an archaeologist.
its sense in the lessons: Everyday life (building sites, roadworks), children's books about diggers, and history lessons about archaeology. Safety: stay away from working machines. Phrases: hydraulic excavator, mini excavator.
examples from the lessons: The excavator dug a deep hole for the new pool. | My little brother loves watching excavators. | The excavator's bucket scooped up the soil. | Archaeologists worked as careful excavators at the Roman site. | Stay far away from a working excavator. | A mini excavator fitted through the garden gate.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Everyday name: digger (UK, Australia) or backhoe (a type, US). Say «EX-ka-vay-ter».

meaning for a pupil: 1) An excerpt is a short part taken from a longer book, film, speech or piece of music. 2) (formal verb) To excerpt is to take out such a part to show or use it.
its sense in the lessons: Reading lessons and tests use excerpts («Read the excerpt and answer the questions»). Music and film too. Phrases: an excerpt from, short excerpt, read the excerpt.
examples from the lessons: Read the excerpt from «The Secret Garden». | The test had an excerpt about whales. | We watched an excerpt from the film. | The choir sang an excerpt from the musical. | This excerpt shows how the character feels. | The newspaper printed an excerpt of the speech.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say «EK-surpt». Similar: extract, passage, clip. An excerpt is only part of the story, so you may not know what happened before or after.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Excitable describes a person or animal that gets excited, nervous or upset very easily. 2) An excitable puppy or child gets wound up quickly and finds it hard to calm down.
its sense in the lessons: Describing characters and pets in stories and everyday life. Phrases: an excitable puppy, easily excitable, get excitable.
examples from the lessons: Our excitable puppy jumps on everyone. | My little cousin gets excitable before birthdays. | The excitable crowd cheered loudly. | Sugar does not really make children excitable, but parties do. | The excitable parrot squawked at every noise. | Take a deep breath if you feel too excitable.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Not the same as exciting: an exciting film is fun; an excitable person gets excited easily. Myth: sugar makes children hyper — studies mostly find the excitement comes from the party setting.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Excretion is how living things get rid of waste that their bodies have made, such as urine, sweat and carbon dioxide. 2) An excretion is a waste substance that is passed out of a living thing.
its sense in the lessons: Science lessons: one of the life processes (MRS GREN: movement, respiration, sensitivity, growth, reproduction, excretion, nutrition). Kidneys, lungs and skin take part. Phrases: excretion of waste, organs of excretion.
examples from the lessons: Excretion is one of the seven life processes. | The kidneys help with excretion by making urine. | We breathe out carbon dioxide as part of excretion. | Plants also do excretion through their leaves. | Sweating is a kind of excretion. | Animals need excretion to stay healthy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Science word. Excretion (getting rid of waste made by the body) is different from egestion (getting rid of undigested food as faeces), though at primary school they are often taught together. Not to be confused with «secretion» (making useful substances like saliva).

meaning for a pupil: 1) An expanse is a very wide, open area of land, sea, sky or something else. 2) It suggests something large and empty or smooth stretching out far.
its sense in the lessons: Descriptive writing about landscapes: deserts, oceans, snow, sky. Geography lessons. Phrases: a vast expanse, an expanse of water, wide expanse.
examples from the lessons: A vast expanse of sand stretched in front of us. | We looked out over the blue expanse of the ocean. | The plane flew over a white expanse of snow. | An expanse of green fields surrounded the farm. | Stars filled the dark expanse of the sky. | The prairie was a huge, flat expanse.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Not the same as expense (cost) — a common confusion. Related to expand.

part of speech: noun (exploration, explorations); verb explore; noun explorer
meaning for a pupil: 1) Exploration is travelling to and looking around a place to find out what is there, especially a place nobody knows well. 2) Exploration is also looking closely at an idea or question to learn more. 3) (medicine) An exploration can be a doctor examining part of the body.
its sense in the lessons: History lessons (Age of Exploration, polar exploration, space exploration), science investigations, and stories of adventure. Phrases: space exploration, voyage of exploration, ocean exploration.
examples from the lessons: Space exploration has taken people to the Moon. | The children went on an exploration of the woods. | The class did an exploration of how magnets work. | Ocean exploration finds new creatures every year. | The Age of Exploration changed maps of the world. | Polar exploration was cold and dangerous.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable and uncountable. Explorers of the past often met people who already lived in the places «discovered», so «discovered» can be one-sided. Spelling: explore drops the e: exploration.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Extravagant means spending much more money than is sensible or needed. 2) Extravagant means far too much, fancy or showy, like an extravagant party or costume. 3) Extravagant claims or praise go far beyond what is true or reasonable.
its sense in the lessons: Money lessons (needs vs wants, budgets), stories (a greedy king's extravagant palace), and media (extravagant claims in adverts). Phrases: extravagant gift, extravagant lifestyle, extravagant claims.
examples from the lessons: Buying a new phone every month is extravagant. | The queen threw an extravagant party with fountains of chocolate. | Her costume was extravagant, with feathers and sparkles. | The advert made extravagant claims that the cream stops ageing. | Dad said a limousine was too extravagant for my birthday. | His extravagant spending left him with no savings.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: extrav-A-gant. Opposite: thrifty, sensible, economical. In a money problem, an extravagant choice often costs much more than a budget allows — compare totals.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An eyelet is a small round hole in cloth, leather or paper that a lace, string or hook goes through. 2) It is also the small metal ring that strengthens such a hole.
its sense in the lessons: Everyday life: shoes, trainers, tents, banners and curtains. Design and technology lessons. Phrases: lace through the eyelets, metal eyelets.
examples from the lessons: Thread the lace through each eyelet. | My trainers have eight eyelets on each side. | The tent pegs go through the eyelets. | The banner hung by its metal eyelets. | One eyelet tore out of my school bag. | Use a hole punch to make eyelets in the card.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Say «EYE-let». Sounds like «islet» (a small island) — a homophone. Count eyelets in pairs on shoes.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An eyewitness is a person who saw something happen with their own eyes, like an accident or crime. 2) An eyewitness account is a report by someone who was there.
its sense in the lessons: History lessons (eyewitness accounts as primary sources), news reports, crime stories, and science of memory (eyewitnesses can remember wrongly). Phrases: eyewitness account, according to eyewitnesses.
examples from the lessons: An eyewitness saw the car go through the red light. | We read an eyewitness account of the Great Fire of London. | Eyewitnesses said the dog ran into the shop. | The police asked for eyewitnesses to come forward. | Samuel Pepys wrote as an eyewitness to the fire. | Even honest eyewitnesses can make mistakes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural eyewitnesses. Eyewitness evidence is a primary source but not always reliable: memory changes, and people see from one angle. Compare several accounts.

part of speech: noun (the fae, fae — fantasy); preposition (fae — Scots)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (fantasy) The fae are fairies or fairy folk in stories and legends, especially in Celtic tales; fae can also describe things belonging to them. 2) (Scots) Fae means «from», as in «I'm fae Glasgow». 3) (name/pronoun) Fae is sometimes used as a personal pronoun by a few people; it is rare.
its sense in the lessons: Fantasy books and games (the fae courts, fae magic); Scottish speech heard in films and in Scotland. Phrases: the fae folk, fae magic, (Scots) fae here.
examples from the lessons: In the story, the fae lived under the hill. | Never eat the food of the fae, the old tale warned. | (Scots) Ma pal's fae Aberdeen. | The book was about a girl who made a deal with the fae. | (Scots) Ah got a letter fae ma gran. | Fae magic glittered in the moonlight.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say «fay». Fae (fairies) is an old spelling of fay. The Scots «fae» is dialect for «from»; in school English write «from». Fairies are not real; they are folklore.

part of speech: adjective (fallible, more fallible); noun fallibility; opposite infallible
meaning for a pupil: 1) Fallible means able to make mistakes or be wrong. 2) Fallible things, like memory or tests, are not always reliable.
its sense in the lessons: Ethics, science and growth-mindset lessons: everyone is fallible, so we check our work and accept others' mistakes. In science: even experts and machines are fallible. Phrases: all humans are fallible, fallible memory.
examples from the lessons: All people are fallible, even teachers. | Our memory is fallible, so we write things down. | Computers are fallible too when the data is wrong. | Being fallible is why we check our answers. | The detective knew eyewitnesses are fallible. | Admitting you are fallible is a sign of good sense.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite infallible (never wrong). Spelling: fall-I-ble. In some churches, Catholics believe the Pope is infallible only in special formal teachings — not in everything.

part of speech: adjective (comparative of fancy: fancy, fancier, fanciest); noun (a fancier, fanciers)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Fancier means more decorated, elaborate or posh than something else. 2) A fancier is a person who keeps or breeds a certain kind of animal or plant as a hobby, like a pigeon fancier or a dog fancier.
its sense in the lessons: Comparisons in everyday talk (a fancier restaurant). The hobby meaning is common in UK and older writing (pigeon fanciers in the north of England). Phrases: fancier than, pigeon fancier, rose fancier.
examples from the lessons: This cake is fancier than the one we made. | We went to a fancier restaurant for Gran's birthday. | My great-uncle was a pigeon fancier with fifty birds. | Her party dress is fancier than mine. | A dog fancier showed his poodles at the show. | Do you want the fancier pencil case or the plain one?
note for the reader of a maths problem: As an adjective: fancy, fancier, fanciest (y becomes ie). As a noun: «a fancier» of something. Say «FAN-see-er».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (music) A fantasia is a piece of music written freely, following the composer's imagination rather than a strict pattern. 2) A fantasia is also a mixture of well-known tunes played together. 3) Fantasia is also the name of a 1940 Disney film set to classical music (a name).
its sense in the lessons: Music lessons (Vaughan Williams' Fantasia on Greensleeves, Fantasia on British Sea Songs at the Proms). Can also mean any dreamlike, imaginative mix. Phrases: fantasia on, a musical fantasia.
examples from the lessons: The orchestra played a fantasia on old sea songs. | A fantasia does not follow strict rules. | We listened to Fantasia on Greensleeves in music class. | The Proms end with a fantasia of British songs. | Disney's «Fantasia» sets cartoons to classical music. | The garden show was a fantasia of colour.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say «fan-TAY-zee-a» or «fan-ta-ZEE-a». Related to fantasy. Plural fantasias.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Fatherless means without a father, because he has died, left or is not known. 2) In old writing, «the fatherless» means children without fathers, often named with widows as people to care for.
its sense in the lessons: Stories and family lessons; the Bible often asks people to care for «the widow and the fatherless». Families come in many shapes, and children without a father at home can have very happy lives. Phrases: fatherless child, the fatherless.
examples from the lessons: In the story, the fatherless boy was raised by his grandmother. | The charity helps fatherless children with school costs. | (Bible) The psalm says God defends the fatherless. | Being fatherless did not stop her becoming a great scientist. | Many famous people grew up fatherless. | The village looked after the fatherless family.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A sensitive word; in class use kindly. Similar: motherless, parentless, orphan (without both parents, usually). The suffix -less means without.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) A felid is any member of the cat family, Felidae: from pet cats to lions, tigers, lynxes and cheetahs. 2) Felid is a scientific word; everyday English says «cat» or «wild cat».
its sense in the lessons: Science and nature books about classification. Felids are meat-eaters with sharp claws, keen eyes and whiskers. Phrases: big felids, small felids, the felid family.
examples from the lessons: A cheetah is the fastest felid. | Lions, tigers and house cats are all felids. | Most felids hunt alone, but lions live in groups. | Scientists study how felids use their whiskers. | The snow leopard is a rare felid of the mountains. | The zoo has five kinds of felid.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say «FEE-lid». Rare, scientific. Feline is the usual adjective (feline grace). Do not mix up with «canid» (dog family).

part of speech: noun (a fen, fens; the Fens — a region in England)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A fen is low, flat, wet land, like a marsh, often with reeds and peat. 2) The Fens are a large flat area of eastern England, much of it drained for farming. 3) (Mandarin, pinyin) fēn is a Chinese money unit (one hundredth of a yuan) and a word for «minute» or «points»; it is not an English word in that sense.
its sense in the lessons: Geography and nature lessons about wetlands; history (Hereward the Wake, draining the Fens). Stories set in eerie marshes. Phrases: the Fens, fen land, fenland.
examples from the lessons: The fen was full of reeds and birds. | Much of the Fens was drained to grow crops. | Mist rose over the fen at dawn. | Peat forms in a fen over thousands of years. | Ely Cathedral stands like a ship above the Fens. | (Mandarin, pinyin) In China, ten fen make one jiao.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Fenland is the land of fens. A fen is fed by groundwater and less acid than a bog. Names: the Fens (capital F) is a place.

part of speech: verb (fend, fends, fended, fending); phrasal verbs fend for, fend off
meaning for a pupil: 1) To fend for yourself is to look after yourself without help. 2) To fend off someone or something is to push it away or defend yourself against it. 3) (rugby) A fend or hand-off is pushing away a tackler with your arm.
its sense in the lessons: Everyday life and stories: young animals learning to fend for themselves, fending off an attack, fending off questions. Phrases: fend for yourself, fend off.
examples from the lessons: Baby turtles must fend for themselves from the start. | When Mum was ill, we had to fend for ourselves at dinner time. | The knight fended off the dragon with his shield. | She fended off the reporters' questions. | The goalkeeper fended off a hard shot. | Fox cubs learn to fend for themselves by autumn.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Almost always used as «fend for» or «fend off». Related: defend, fender (car bumper in the US; fireguard in the UK).

part of speech: noun (fermentation — uncountable); verb ferment; adjective fermented
meaning for a pupil: 1) Fermentation is a natural change in which tiny living things like yeast or bacteria break down sugars, often making gas, acid or alcohol. 2) It is how bread rises, how yoghurt, cheese, sauerkraut and kimchi are made, and how wine and beer are made. 3) (figurative, formal) Fermentation can mean excitement or unrest among people.
its sense in the lessons: Science lessons on microorganisms (yeast blowing up a balloon), cooking and food lessons. Phrases: yeast fermentation, fermented foods, during fermentation.
examples from the lessons: Yeast fermentation makes bread dough rise. | We watched fermentation blow up a balloon on a bottle. | Yoghurt is made by fermentation of milk. | Kimchi is a fermented cabbage dish from Korea. | Fermentation gives off carbon dioxide gas. | Warmth speeds up fermentation.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Fermentation needs living microbes, food (sugar) and warmth; too hot kills yeast. Not the same as rotting, though both use microbes. Do not mix up with «fomentation».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Fertility is how well soil or land can grow plants and crops. 2) Fertility is a living thing's ability to have babies or young. 3) Fertility of mind means being full of ideas.
its sense in the lessons: Geography and farming (fertile soil near rivers like the Nile), science (reproduction), history (ancient fertility goddesses). Health and adult life: fertility treatment. Phrases: soil fertility, fertility of the land, fertility treatment.
examples from the lessons: The Nile floods brought fertility to the fields. | Farmers add compost to improve soil fertility. | Volcanic soil is famous for its fertility. | The zoo studies the fertility of its rare tigers. | Some couples have help from fertility doctors to have a baby. | Ancient people prayed to gods for the fertility of their crops.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Opposite: infertility. Fertile (adjective) vs fertiliser (what you add). Be sensitive: fertility is a private topic for families.

part of speech: noun (fertilizer, fertilizers); UK also fertiliser; verb fertilize/fertilise
meaning for a pupil: 1) Fertilizer is a substance added to soil to give plants the food (nutrients) they need to grow better. 2) It can be natural, like manure and compost, or made in factories.
its sense in the lessons: Science and farming lessons: plant nutrients (nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium), fair tests on plant growth, and pollution when fertilizer runs into rivers. Safety: keep away from children and pets. Phrases: natural fertilizer, chemical fertilizer, liquid fertilizer.
examples from the lessons: We added fertilizer to half the bean plants for our test. | Manure is a natural fertilizer. | Too much fertilizer can wash into rivers and harm fish. | The tomatoes grew bigger with fertilizer. | Wash your hands after touching fertilizer. | Farmers spread fertilizer in spring.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: US and Canada fertilizer; UK, Australia and NZ often fertiliser (both accepted in UK). Uncountable usually (some fertilizer), countable for types. Plants make their own food by photosynthesis; fertilizer gives minerals, not energy.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Feverish means having a fever, with a high body temperature, feeling hot, shivery and unwell. 2) Feverish also means very fast, excited and nervous, as in feverish activity.
its sense in the lessons: Health lessons and everyday illness (rest, drink water, tell an adult; normal temperature is about 37 °C). In stories: feverish dreams, or working feverishly before a deadline. Phrases: feel feverish, feverish dreams, work feverishly, feverish excitement.
examples from the lessons: I felt feverish and Mum took my temperature. | The feverish child slept all afternoon. | He had strange feverish dreams. | The builders worked feverishly to finish before the storm. | There was feverish excitement before the final. | She searched feverishly for her lost ticket.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A fever is usually 38 °C or above. Feverishly (adverb) is mostly the second meaning: in a rush. Do not take medicine without an adult.

part of speech: verb form (fib, fibs, fibbed, fibbing); noun fibber
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) Fibbing is telling small lies, usually about unimportant things. 2) A fibber is someone who tells fibs.
its sense in the lessons: Everyday and playground talk; honesty lessons. «Fib» sounds softer than «lie» but it is still not telling the truth. Phrases: stop fibbing, are you fibbing?, a little fib.
examples from the lessons: Are you fibbing about eating your vegetables? | He was fibbing when he said the dog ate his homework. | Stop fibbing and tell me what happened. | I caught my brother fibbing about brushing his teeth. | She admitted she had been fibbing. | Fibbing gets you into more trouble in the end.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double b: fibbed, fibbing. Informal; in formal writing use «lying». A fib is still a lie, even if small. Not related to «fibre».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Fibreglass is a light, strong material made of very thin glass threads, often set in plastic. 2) It is used to make boats, car bodies, helmets, slides and surfboards, and to keep houses warm as insulation in lofts.
its sense in the lessons: Science and design lessons about materials and their properties (light, strong, waterproof, insulating). Safety: loft insulation can make skin itch; use gloves. Phrases: fibreglass boat, fibreglass insulation.
examples from the lessons: The boat is made of fibreglass. | Fibreglass insulation keeps the loft warm. | Wear gloves when touching fibreglass, it makes skin itchy. | The playground slide is fibreglass. | Fibreglass is light but strong. | The surfboard has a fibreglass coat.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK, Australia and NZ: fibreglass; US: fiberglass; Canada uses both. Uncountable. Fibreglass is made from glass but it bends and does not shatter like a window.

part of speech: adjective (fidgety, fidgetier, fidgetiest); verb fidget; noun a fidget
meaning for a pupil: 1) Fidgety means unable to keep still, moving your hands, feet or body a lot because you are bored, nervous or restless. 2) A fidget toy is a small toy for busy hands.
its sense in the lessons: Classroom and everyday life (long assemblies, car journeys). In stories it shows a character is nervous, bored or excited. Phrases: feel fidgety, get fidgety, fidget toy, stop fidgeting.
examples from the lessons: I get fidgety in long assemblies. | The fidgety puppy would not sit still. | He was fidgety before his turn on stage. | A short run helps fidgety children focus. | The fidgety girl kept twisting her hair. | Long car journeys make my brother fidgety.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Fidget (verb or noun), fidgety (adjective). Being fidgety is normal; some children concentrate better with something to hold.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Filth is very bad, disgusting dirt. 2) (informal) Filth is rude, offensive words, pictures or talk. 3) (UK slang, rude, offensive) «The filth» is a rude word for the police; it is insulting.
its sense in the lessons: In stories it shows poverty or neglect (filth in the streets of Victorian London); in science and health, dirt and germs. In speech, adults may call rude jokes or magazines «filth». Phrases: covered in filth, live in filth, (slang) the filth.
examples from the lessons: The pigsty was full of filth. | Victorian streets were covered in filth and smoke. | Wash the filth off your boots. | Germs grow in filth, so we keep the kitchen clean. | Grandad called the rude song «filth» and turned it off. | (UK slang, rude) In the TV drama the robber shouted, «Run, it's the filth!»
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Adjective: filthy (very dirty). «Filthy rich» (informal) means very rich. The police meaning is offensive slang; do not use it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A fishery is a place where fish are caught or bred, like a part of the sea or a fish farm. 2) A fishery is the business or industry of catching fish.
its sense in the lessons: Geography and environment lessons (overfishing, fishing quotas, sustainable fisheries), and coastal life in Canada, Ireland, Iceland and New Zealand. Phrases: sustainable fishery, cod fishery, fisheries minister.
examples from the lessons: The cod fishery off Canada closed after overfishing. | The village depends on the fishery for jobs. | A trout fishery breeds fish in ponds. | Sustainable fisheries leave enough fish to breed. | The government sets rules for fisheries. | We visited a salmon fishery in Scotland.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural fisheries. Look for the blue «sustainable» fish label. In maths, quotas are fixed amounts of fish allowed each year.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A flashback is a part of a story, film or play that goes back to show something that happened earlier. 2) A flashback is a sudden, very clear memory of a past event, often a frightening one, that feels like it is happening again.
its sense in the lessons: English lessons on narrative structure (flashbacks to give backstory), films and TV. Health: some people who lived through scary events have flashbacks and can get help. Phrases: in a flashback, flashback scene, have flashbacks.
examples from the lessons: The film opens with a flashback to the hero's childhood. | Write a flashback to show why the character is afraid of dogs. | In the flashback we learn the grandfather was a sailor. | The soldier had flashbacks of the war. | Use the past perfect tense to start a flashback: «She had once lived by the sea.» | The wavy picture told us it was a flashback.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. A flashback breaks time order, so use clues (tense, «years before») for the reader. Opposite: flash-forward.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A flatfish is a fish with a flat body that lies on one side on the sea floor, such as a plaice, sole, flounder, halibut or turbot. 2) Both its eyes end up on the upper side of its head as it grows.
its sense in the lessons: Science and nature lessons (adaptation, camouflage on the sea bed). Food: fish and chips can be plaice. Phrases: flatfish such as plaice.
examples from the lessons: A flatfish hides by lying flat on the sand. | Plaice is a flatfish with orange spots. | Young flatfish swim upright until one eye moves over. | The flatfish changed colour to match the gravel. | Halibut is the largest flatfish. | We saw a flatfish in the rock pool.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural usually flatfish (like fish, sheep). A flatfish lies on its side, not its belly — unlike rays, which are flat from top to bottom.

part of speech: adjective (Flemish); noun (Flemish — the language; the Flemish — the people)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Flemish means to do with Flanders, the northern Dutch-speaking part of Belgium, or its people. 2) Flemish is the name for the Dutch spoken in Belgium. 3) Flemish art means paintings by artists from Flanders, like Bruegel and Van Eyck.
its sense in the lessons: Geography (Belgium has Flemish-, French- and German-speaking areas), history and art lessons (Flemish painters, Flemish weavers who came to England). Phrases: Flemish painters, Flemish speakers.
examples from the lessons: In Belgium, Flemish is spoken in the north. | Bruegel was a Flemish painter. | The museum has Flemish paintings of village life. | Flemish weavers came to England in the Middle Ages. | Flemish is very close to the Dutch of the Netherlands. | Brussels has signs in French and Flemish.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always written with a capital F (it is a name for a people and place). Flemish and Dutch are essentially the same language with local differences. Not to be confused with «phlegm» or «flamingo».

part of speech: noun (flotation, flotations); UK also floatation; verb float
meaning for a pupil: 1) Flotation is floating, or the ability of something to stay on top of water. 2) A flotation device is something that helps you float, like a life jacket or armbands. 3) (money) A flotation is when a company first sells shares to the public on the stock market.
its sense in the lessons: Science (floating and sinking, upthrust), water safety (life jackets, flotation aids, «float to live»), and money news. Phrases: flotation device, flotation aid, flotation tank.
examples from the lessons: Wear a flotation device on the boat. | Armbands are a flotation aid for beginners. | Air pockets give the raft its flotation. | We tested the flotation of different materials in a tank. | If you fall in cold water, float on your back to stay safe. | The company's flotation made its founders rich.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usual spelling: flotation (one a). Safety: a flotation aid is not a replacement for adult supervision. In science, things float when upthrust is equal to their weight.

part of speech: verb (flourish, flourishes, flourished, flourishing); noun (a flourish, flourishes)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To flourish is to grow well and be healthy and strong, like plants in good soil. 2) To flourish is to do very well and be successful, like a business or a person. 3) To flourish something is to wave it around to show it off. 4) A flourish is a fancy curl in handwriting, or a showy movement or bit of music.
its sense in the lessons: Science (plants flourish with light and water), history (civilizations flourished), and wellbeing (children flourish with care). In stories, with a flourish = showily. Phrases: with a flourish, flourish in, flourishing business.
examples from the lessons: The sunflowers flourished in the sunny corner. | Ancient Egypt flourished along the Nile. | She has flourished at her new school. | The magician bowed with a flourish. | He signed his name with a flourish. | The knight flourished his sword. | Small shops flourish when people buy locally.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: flour-ish (not «flurish»). Say «FLUR-ish». Similar: thrive. Not related to flour for baking.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A flowerpot is a container, usually of clay or plastic, for growing a plant in, with a hole in the bottom for water to drain out. 2) (UK TV) «Bill and Ben, the Flowerpot Men» were puppets in an old children's programme (a name).
its sense in the lessons: Science (growing plants, fair tests with identical pots), gardening at school and home, art and DIY. Phrases: clay flowerpot, plant in a flowerpot.
examples from the lessons: Plant three seeds in each flowerpot. | The flowerpot has a hole so water can drain. | We painted terracotta flowerpots for Mother's Day. | The cat knocked the flowerpot off the windowsill. | Put the flowerpots in a sunny place. | For a fair test, use the same size flowerpot for every plant.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. One word (also «flower pot»). In maths, flowerpot problems often ask how many seeds per pot: total seeds ÷ seeds per pot = pots.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Flustered means nervous, confused and a bit embarrassed, especially because you are rushed or things are going wrong. 2) To fluster someone is to make them feel like this.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and everyday life to show a character in a muddle (red faced, dropping things, late). Phrases: get flustered, look flustered, all flustered.
examples from the lessons: Mum got flustered when she couldn't find the car keys. | The new teacher looked flustered when the projector broke. | I got flustered and forgot my lines. | Don't get flustered, take a deep breath. | The flustered waiter dropped the tray. | The questions flustered him.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Flustered is milder than panicked. Not «flusted». Calm-down tips: breathe, slow down, do one thing at a time.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (UK, Australia) A flyover is a bridge that carries one road over another road or railway. 2) (US) A flyover, also flypast (UK), is a planned flight of aircraft low over a place for a show or ceremony. 3) (US informal) «Flyover country» is a joking name for the middle states of the USA that people fly over between the coasts.
its sense in the lessons: Everyday travel and geography (roads and junctions); ceremonies (the Red Arrows flypast). Phrases: go over the flyover, under the flyover, military flyover.
examples from the lessons: The bus went over the flyover into town. | The skateboarders met under the flyover. | (US) Jets did a flyover at the football game. | The new flyover stops traffic jams at the junction. | In the UK, the Red Arrows do a flypast, which Americans call a flyover. | We could see the river from the top of the flyover.
note for the reader of a maths problem: US English often says overpass for the road bridge. Countable. One word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A forester is a person whose job is to look after a forest: planting and cutting trees, protecting wildlife and preventing fires. 2) In old stories a forester guarded the king's forest from poachers.
its sense in the lessons: Jobs and environment lessons, geography of woodlands, fairy tales and Robin Hood stories. Phrases: forest ranger, the king's forester.
examples from the lessons: The forester planted a hundred new oak trees. | A forester showed us how to tell the age of a tree. | Foresters watch for forest fires in dry weather. | In the tale, the forester saved the girl from the wolf. | The king's foresters chased Robin Hood. | Being a forester means working outdoors in all weather.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Related: forest, forestry (the work). Not to be confused with «forecaster» (weather).

meaning for a pupil: 1) To foretell something is to say what will happen in the future, often by magic, prophecy or special knowledge. 2) To foretell can also mean to be a sign of something to come.
its sense in the lessons: Stories, myths and the Bible (prophets, fortune-tellers, witches foretelling a king's fate). In real life, nobody can truly foretell the future; science predicts using evidence. Phrases: foretell the future, as foretold.
examples from the lessons: The old woman claimed to foretell the future. | In the myth, the oracle foretold the hero's journey. | (Bible) Christians believe the prophets foretold the birth of Jesus. | Dark clouds foretell rain. | Nobody can foretell exactly who will win. | The legend foretold that a child would pull the sword from the stone.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular past: foretold (not «foretelled»). Similar: predict, forecast, prophesy. Predict is the science word (based on evidence); foretell sounds magical. Be careful of people who claim to foretell the future for money.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A forewing is one of the two front wings of an insect that has four wings, like a butterfly, moth, bee or beetle. 2) In beetles the forewings are hard cases that cover and protect the back wings.
its sense in the lessons: Science lessons on insects and minibeasts, butterfly patterns and classification. Phrases: forewing and hindwing, front wing.
examples from the lessons: The butterfly's forewings have orange spots. | A ladybird's red forewings protect the wings underneath. | Count the forewings and hindwings: four in all. | The moth's forewings are bigger than its hindwings. | Bees hook their forewings and hindwings together to fly. | We drew the pattern on the forewing in science.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; opposite hindwing (back wing). «Fore-» means front. Insects have six legs and many have two pairs of wings: 2 forewings + 2 hindwings = 4.

part of speech: noun (a format, formats); verb (format, formats, formatted, formatting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A format is the way something is arranged, set out or organised, like the layout of a letter or the shape of a book. 2) A format is the type of a computer file or recording, such as a picture or video type. 3) A format is the plan or rules of a game show, contest or event. 4) To format something is to arrange how it looks, or (computers) to prepare a memory card or drive, which wipes it.
its sense in the lessons: English lessons (the format of a letter, newspaper report, poem); computing (file formats, formatting text with bold or headings); sport (tournament format). Phrases: in the right format, file format, the format of.
examples from the lessons: Use the correct format for a formal letter: address, date, greeting. | Save your picture in a format the printer can read. | The quiz has a new format this year. | Format the title in bold. | Don't format the memory stick, it will delete everything. | The tournament format is groups, then knockouts. | The book comes in a large-print format.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double t: formatted, formatting. Careful: formatting a drive erases data. Related: formal, form.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A fragrance is a pleasant, sweet smell, like flowers or fresh bread. 2) A fragrance is also perfume or a scent that people wear or that is added to soap and shampoo.
its sense in the lessons: Descriptive writing (senses), science (smells and the nose), shopping. Some people are allergic to fragrances. Phrases: sweet fragrance, the fragrance of, fragrance-free.
examples from the lessons: The fragrance of roses filled the garden. | Mum's new fragrance smells of vanilla. | This soap is fragrance-free for sensitive skin. | The bakery's fragrance drifted down the street. | Lavender has a calming fragrance. | Bees are attracted by the fragrance of flowers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pleasant smells only; a bad smell is a stink or odour. Adjective: fragrant. Countable for different perfumes, uncountable for smell in general.

part of speech: noun (a fritter, fritters); verb (fritter away, fritters, frittered, frittering)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A fritter is a piece of fruit, vegetable or meat dipped in batter and fried, like an apple fritter or corn fritter. 2) To fritter away time or money is to waste it little by little on unimportant things.
its sense in the lessons: Food and cooking (UK chip shops sell spam and pineapple fritters; NZ whitebait fritters; Australian potato fritters called scallops in some states). Money lessons: frittering away pocket money. Phrases: fritter away, apple fritter, corn fritters.
examples from the lessons: We had sweetcorn fritters for lunch. | The apple fritter was warm and sugary. | Don't fritter away your pocket money on sweets. | He frittered away the whole afternoon on his phone. | In New Zealand, whitebait fritters are a treat. | She saved instead of frittering her money away.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double t: frittered, frittering. «Fritter away» is always about wasting slowly. In a money problem, small amounts frittered away add up: 50p a day for 7 days = £3.50.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A frogfish is a small, lumpy sea fish that lives in warm oceans, often on coral reefs; it is a kind of anglerfish. 2) It walks on the sea floor using fins like legs and uses a lure on its head to catch prey.
its sense in the lessons: Nature and science lessons on adaptations, camouflage and coral reefs. Frogfish can swallow prey as big as themselves. Phrases: hairy frogfish, frogfish camouflage.
examples from the lessons: The frogfish looked just like a sponge on the reef. | A frogfish walks along the sea floor on its fins. | The frogfish wiggled its lure to attract a small fish. | Frogfish can change colour to hide. | The hairy frogfish is covered in skin spines that look like hair. | Divers struggled to spot the frogfish.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural frogfish or frogfishes. It is a fish, not a frog: it breathes with gills and lives only in water.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Frontal means at the front or facing the front of something. 2) In the body, frontal means to do with the forehead, as in the frontal bone or the frontal lobe of the brain. 3) A frontal attack or approach comes straight at something from the front, openly and directly. 4) (weather) A frontal system is a line where warm air and cold air meet, often bringing rain. 5) (church) A frontal is a decorated cloth hung over the front of an altar.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons the frontal lobe is the front part of the brain that helps us plan, choose and control ourselves; the frontal bone is the forehead bone. In weather maps a frontal system means rain or a change is coming. In stories a frontal attack is bold and direct, not sneaky. Phrases: frontal lobe, frontal bone, head-on frontal collision, full-frontal (UK: very open or blunt).
examples from the lessons: The frontal lobe sits just behind your forehead. | The doctor pointed to the frontal bone on the skeleton. | The knights made a frontal attack on the castle gate. | A frontal system will bring showers this afternoon. | The car crash was a frontal collision. | The photo shows a frontal view of the house. | The vicar put the green frontal on the altar for the new season. | Instead of a frontal approach, the fox crept round the side.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually an adjective that comes before a noun: frontal lobe, frontal view. Not the same as «front» (a noun) — we say «the front of the bus» but «a frontal view». A weather front is a noun; frontal is its adjective. The altar cloth sense is a countable noun: one frontal, two frontals.

part of speech: verb form (froth, froths, frothed, frothing); adjective (frothing); noun (froth, uncountable)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Frothing means making or having lots of tiny bubbles on top, like foam on a milkshake or soap. 2) An animal or person frothing at the mouth has foamy spit coming out, which can be a sign of illness. 3) (informal) Frothing (at the mouth) can mean being extremely angry or excited.
its sense in the lessons: In science, frothing happens when air is trapped in a liquid, for example when you shake a fizzy drink or whisk egg whites. In everyday life coffee machines froth milk. In safety, a dog frothing at the mouth may be ill and you should not touch it. In stories, «frothing with rage» tells the reader someone is furious. Phrases: frothing at the mouth, frothing milk, frothy coffee.
examples from the lessons: The milk was frothing in the jug. | The waves were frothing white against the rocks. | When we mixed vinegar and baking soda, the bottle started frothing. | Never touch a strange dog that is frothing at the mouth. | Dad was frothing about the parking ticket. | The coach was frothing at the mouth when the ref gave a penalty. | Mum likes a frothy cappuccino. | The bubble bath was frothing over the side of the tub.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Frothing» is the -ing form of the verb «froth». Froth is uncountable: some froth, not «a froths». Froth and foam mean almost the same thing. «Frothing at the mouth» about anger is an exaggeration, not real foam.

part of speech: proper noun (Fuji, Mount Fuji); noun (a Fuji apple, Fuji apples)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (a name) Fuji, or Mount Fuji, is the tallest mountain in Japan, a volcano with a snowy top near Tokyo. 2) A Fuji is a kind of sweet, crunchy apple first grown in Japan. 3) (a name) Fuji is also part of the name of some Japanese companies, such as makers of cameras and film.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons Mount Fuji is an example of a volcano and a famous landmark of Japan; it is about 3,776 metres high and it last erupted in 1707. In art, Japanese prints show the mountain many times. In the shop, Fuji apples are a common type. It is a name, so it starts with a capital letter.
examples from the lessons: Mount Fuji is the highest mountain in Japan. | From Tokyo on a clear day you can see Fuji. | Mount Fuji is a volcano, but it is quiet at the moment. | Many people climb Fuji in the summer. | I packed a Fuji apple for lunch. | Fuji apples are sweet and crunchy. | The famous print shows a big wave with Fuji in the background.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It is a proper noun and should be written with a capital F: Fuji. People often say «Mount Fuji» or «Fujisan» in Japanese; «Fujiyama» is an older name used outside Japan. Do not mix it up with Fiji, an island country in the Pacific.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The furcula is the wishbone of a bird: a forked bone in its chest made of two collarbones joined together. 2) In some tiny insects called springtails, the furcula is a forked tail-like part that flicks down to make them jump.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons the furcula helps show how birds are built for flying: it works like a spring when the wings flap. Scientists also found furculas in some dinosaurs, which is one clue that birds came from dinosaurs. In everyday life it is the wishbone people pull at a roast chicken dinner and make a wish.
examples from the lessons: The furcula is also called the wishbone. | After the roast chicken, my brother and I pulled the furcula and made a wish. | A bird's furcula bends like a spring as it flaps. | Some dinosaurs had a furcula, just like birds. | The springtail jumped by snapping its furcula against the ground. | Find the furcula on the diagram of the bird skeleton.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A science word from Latin meaning «little fork». Plural: furculas or furculae. Countable. The everyday word is «wishbone».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Fury is very strong, wild anger. 2) Fury can also mean great force or violence, as in the fury of a storm. 3) (myth) The Furies were three goddesses of revenge in ancient Greek and Roman stories.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, fury tells the reader a character is so angry they may lose control. In geography or science, the fury of a storm, the sea or a volcano means its great power and danger. Phrases: in a fury, full of fury, with fury, «hell hath no fury» (an old saying). The adjective is furious.
examples from the lessons: Mum's face was red with fury when she saw the broken window. | He slammed the door in a fury. | The fury of the storm knocked down trees. | The sailors were afraid of the fury of the sea. | She ran with fury to catch the ball. | In the Greek myth, the Furies chased the wrongdoer. | Take a deep breath when you feel fury rising. | The team played with fury after going a goal down.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable (fury), but «a fury» is used in «in a fury». Plural «furies» is rare except for the Furies of myth. The adjective is «furious», the adverb «furiously». Fury is stronger than anger or annoyance.

part of speech: noun (Gallus — a name of a genus); adjective (gallus — Scotland); noun (gallus, galluses — dialect: braces)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) Gallus is the Latin scientific name for the group (genus) of jungle fowl that includes the chicken: the chicken is Gallus gallus domesticus. 2) (Scotland, slang) Gallus means bold, cheeky and full of confidence, often in a fun, likeable way. 3) (dialect, old) Galluses are braces, the straps that hold up trousers. 4) (a name) Gallus was the name of some Romans and of an early saint, Saint Gall.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons Gallus appears in the scientific names of the chicken and the red junglefowl, its wild ancestor. In Scotland, especially Glasgow, people say «gallus» to praise or tease someone daring. It is mostly not used in other English-speaking countries.
examples from the lessons: The chicken's scientific name is Gallus gallus domesticus. | The red junglefowl, Gallus gallus, lives in the forests of Asia. | (Scotland) That wee lad is pure gallus, he sang in front of the whole school. | (Scotland) She gave the teacher a gallus grin. | (dialect) Grandpa hitched up his galluses. | Scientific names like Gallus are written in italics.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a scientific name it starts with a capital letter and is written in italics. The Scottish word «gallus» is slang and can mean both «admirably bold» and «too cheeky». «Galluses» for braces is old American and British dialect.

part of speech: verb (galvanise, galvanises, galvanised, galvanising); US spelling galvanize
meaning for a pupil: 1) To galvanise people means to shock or excite them into acting quickly. 2) To galvanise iron or steel means to coat it with zinc so that it does not rust. 3) (science, old) To galvanise once meant to give something an electric shock, from the scientist Luigi Galvani.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, galvanising is a way to stop rusting: a zinc layer protects the iron underneath, as on buckets, fences and nails. In stories and news, a speech or event that galvanises people makes them suddenly work together. Phrases: galvanise into action, galvanised steel, galvanised bucket.
examples from the lessons: The fence posts are made of galvanised steel so they will not rust. | Galvanising coats iron with a layer of zinc. | The captain's speech galvanised the team. | The flood galvanised the whole town into action. | We tested whether a galvanised nail rusts in salty water. | The coach hoped to galvanise the players at half-time. | The farmer filled a galvanised bucket with water.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK and Australian spelling: galvanise; US and Canadian spelling: galvanize. Past: galvanised. It comes from the name Galvani, an Italian scientist. Galvanised metal is not rust-proof forever; the zinc slowly wears away.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (money) GDP stands for gross domestic product: the total value of all the goods and services a country makes in one year. 2) GDP is often used to compare how big or rich countries' economies are.
its sense in the lessons: In money and economics lessons, GDP is a number that shows the size of a country's economy. GDP per person (per capita) is the GDP divided by the number of people, which gives a rough idea of how well-off people are on average. In the news, «GDP grew by 2%» means the economy made 2% more than the year before. Phrases: GDP growth, GDP per capita, a fall in GDP.
examples from the lessons: The USA has the largest GDP in the world. | GDP measures everything a country makes and sells in a year. | If GDP goes down for six months, people talk about a recession. | To find GDP per person, divide the GDP by the population. | The news said GDP grew by 1 percent this year. | A country with a small GDP can still have happy people. | Tourism adds a lot to New Zealand's GDP.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It is an abbreviation, so it is written in capital letters: GDP. Say each letter: «G-D-P». In maths problems, GDP per person = total GDP ÷ number of people. GDP does not measure happiness, fairness or unpaid work like caring at home.

part of speech: noun (genetics, uncountable; takes a singular verb); adjective (genetic)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Genetics is the science of how features, like eye colour, are passed from parents to children through genes. 2) Someone's genetics are the genes they were born with, which affect how they grow and look.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons genetics explains why children look a bit like their parents, why brothers and sisters are different, and how farmers breed plants and animals. Gregor Mendel studied pea plants in the 1860s and is called the father of genetics. DNA carries genes. Phrases: good genetics, genetic disease, genetic code.
examples from the lessons: Genetics is the study of how living things inherit features. | Mendel discovered rules of genetics by growing peas. | My red hair comes from genetics; both my grandads had it. | Genetics helps doctors understand some illnesses. | Farmers use genetics to breed cows that give more milk. | Scientists who study genetics are called geneticists. | Tall parents often have tall children because of genetics.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Ends in -s but is one subject, like maths: «Genetics is interesting», not «are». The adjective is «genetic», as in «a genetic disease». Do not confuse with «generic», which means general. Features you learn, like speaking French, are not passed on by genetics.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) A genus is a group of closely related kinds (species) of living things; it is a step in how scientists sort life. 2) (formal) A genus can mean any kind or class of things.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons living things are sorted in steps: kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species. The scientific name of a living thing has two parts: the genus first, then the species, like Homo sapiens for humans or Panthera leo for lions. The genus name starts with a capital letter and is written in italics.
examples from the lessons: Lions and tigers belong to the same genus, Panthera. | Humans are the only living species in the genus Homo. | The genus name always comes first in a scientific name. | Write the genus with a capital letter: Canis lupus. | Scientists found a new genus of frog in the rainforest. | One genus can include many species.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: genera (not «genuses» in science). Countable: one genus, two genera. Genus is bigger than species but smaller than family. Do not confuse with «genius», a very clever person.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A geyser is a hot spring in the ground that shoots hot water and steam high into the air from time to time. 2) (UK, old) A geyser is a gas water heater in a kitchen or bathroom. 3) A geyser can mean any sudden jet of liquid shooting up.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and science lessons geysers happen in volcanic places where underground water is heated by hot rock until it bursts out. Famous geysers are Old Faithful in Yellowstone, USA, and Strokkur in Iceland; New Zealand has geysers near Rotorua. For safety, the water is boiling hot and the ground near geysers can be thin, so people must stay on paths.
examples from the lessons: Old Faithful is a geyser that erupts about every hour and a half. | We watched the geyser shoot steam into the sky in Iceland. | Geysers form where hot rocks heat underground water. | Stay on the boardwalk because the water near a geyser is boiling. | The word geyser comes from Geysir, a hot spring in Iceland. | When the pipe burst, a geyser of water sprayed across the street. | Rotorua in New Zealand has bubbling mud and geysers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a geyser, geysers. Usual pronunciation: «GUY-zer» (US) or «GEE-zer» (UK). It sounds like the UK slang word «geezer» (a man), but they are different words.

part of speech: noun (gin, gins); verb (gin, gins, ginned, ginning — rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Gin is a strong, clear alcoholic drink flavoured with juniper berries; it is for adults only. 2) A cotton gin is a machine that separates cotton fibres from the seeds. 3) (old) A gin is a trap or snare for catching animals. 4) Gin, or gin rummy, is a card game.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons the cotton gin, made by Eli Whitney in 1793, made cotton farming faster and, sadly, led to more enslaved people being forced to work on cotton plantations in the USA. In everyday life gin is an adult drink, like wine or beer; children should never drink it. Families may play gin rummy. Phrases: gin and tonic, cotton gin, gin rummy.
examples from the lessons: Gin is an alcoholic drink for grown-ups. | Grandma had a gin and tonic at the party. | Eli Whitney's cotton gin cleaned cotton much faster than people could by hand. | The cotton gin changed farming in the American South. | We played gin rummy on the rainy holiday. | In the old story, the rabbit was caught in a gin. | Alcohol like gin is not safe for children.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Gin the drink is usually uncountable (some gin), but «a gin» means a glass of it. The cotton gin and trap are countable. «Gin» (machine) is short for «engine». The drink's name comes from the Dutch word for juniper.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Glacé (often written glace) describes fruit, such as cherries, that has been cooked in sugar syrup so it is shiny and sweet. 2) Glacé icing is a simple runny icing made from icing sugar and water. 3) Glacé leather is very shiny smooth leather. 4) (French) «Glace» is the French word for ice or ice cream, said «glass».
its sense in the lessons: In cooking and in the kitchen, glacé cherries are bright red sweet cherries put in fruit cakes and on top of buns. Glacé icing is spread on cupcakes and biscuits. In French lessons, «une glace» means an ice cream. Phrases: glacé cherries, glacé icing, glacé ginger.
examples from the lessons: Grandma put glacé cherries on top of the cake. | We made glacé icing with icing sugar and a little water. | The fruit cake was full of glacé cherries and raisins. | The glacé ginger tasted sweet and spicy. | (French) «Je voudrais une glace» means «I would like an ice cream». | Her shoes were made of shiny glacé leather.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The proper English spelling has an accent: glacé, said «GLASS-ay». Written without the accent, «glace» is also the French word for ice or ice cream, said «glass». Do not confuse with «glance» (a quick look) or «glacier».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Glamorous means very attractive and exciting, often in a rich, stylish, showy way. 2) A glamorous job or life seems exciting and special to other people, even if it is not always so in real life.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and everyday life, glamorous describes film stars, red-carpet events, fancy clothes and exciting places.
