It often tells the reader that something looks better from outside than it really is. Phrases: a glamorous life, a glamorous dress, not very glamorous (meaning ordinary or messy work).
examples from the lessons: The actress wore a glamorous gold dress. | Being a pilot sounds glamorous, but it is hard work. | The party at the hotel was very glamorous. | Cleaning out the rabbit hutch is not glamorous. | Aunt Rosie looked glamorous with her red lipstick. | Hollywood is famous for glamorous film premieres. | Mum said a glamorous life on social media is often just a show.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: glamorous drops the «u» of glamour (UK) — it is glamorous in every country, never «glamourous» in careful writing. Comparative: more glamorous.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Glamour is the special exciting attraction of something that seems rich, stylish or beautiful. 2) (old, stories) A glamour was a magic spell that made things look different from what they are.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life glamour belongs to film stars, fashion, and big shows. In stories, a glamour spell can trick people into seeing a beggar as a prince. Writers use the word to show that something shiny may hide something ordinary. Phrases: the glamour of Hollywood, add a touch of glamour, glamour and fame.
examples from the lessons: The film star loved the glamour of the red carpet. | Gold balloons added a touch of glamour to the party. | The glamour of being famous soon wore off. | Behind the glamour, actors work long hours. | In the fairy tale, the witch cast a glamour so the old hut looked like a palace. | The city has the glamour of bright lights and big shops.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK, Australian and Canadian spelling: glamour; US spelling: glamor (glamour is also used in the US). The adjective is glamorous, with no «u» after the m. Uncountable: «some glamour», not «a glamour», except in the old magic sense.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A glassblower is a person who makes glass objects, like vases and bottles, by blowing air through a long tube into a blob of hot, melted glass.
its sense in the lessons: In history and science lessons glassblowing shows how glass becomes soft and runny when very hot and hard when it cools. It is an old craft, used since Roman times. For safety, glassblowers work near a furnace over 1,000 °C and wear protection. Children may watch at museums or craft fairs.
examples from the lessons: The glassblower turned the hot glass on the end of a long pipe. | We watched a glassblower make a blue vase at the museum. | Glassblowers have to work fast before the glass cools. | The Romans had skilled glassblowers. | The glassblower blew gently and the glass grew into a bubble. | Being a glassblower takes years of practice.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a glassblower, glassblowers. Often written as one word; «glass blower» is also seen. The craft is «glassblowing».

meaning for a pupil: 1) To glisten means to shine with a soft, sparkly light because something is wet or oily. 2) Eyes glisten when they are full of tears.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and descriptive writing, glisten is a lovely word for wet things shining: dew on grass, a seal's skin, a road after rain. It helps the reader see and feel the scene. Phrases: glisten with sweat, glistening with tears, glistening snow.
examples from the lessons: Dew glistened on the grass in the morning. | The seal's wet fur glistened in the sun. | Her eyes glistened with tears at the end of the film. | The road glistened after the rain. | His forehead glistened with sweat after the race. | The fresh snow glistened under the street lights. | The cherries glistened in the bowl.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The «t» is silent: say «GLISS-en». Glisten is used mostly for wet or oily shine; glitter is for tiny flashing sparkles, and glint for a quick flash of light.

part of speech: verb (gloat, gloats, gloated, gloating); noun (a gloat — rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To gloat means to show you are very pleased about your own success or about someone else's bad luck, in a smug and unkind way.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and sport, gloating is seen as bad manners: being a good winner means not gloating. In stories, a villain who gloats tells the reader they are cruel and proud. Phrases: gloat over, gloat about, no gloating.
examples from the lessons: Do not gloat when you win a game; shake hands instead. | My brother gloated about beating me at chess all week. | The villain gloated over the trapped hero. | She tried not to gloat when her prediction came true. | It is unkind to gloat when someone gets told off. | «No gloating!» said the teacher after the quiz. | The fans gloated after their team won the derby.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually followed by «over» or «about». Gloating is always negative; being happy and proud of a win is fine, gloating is rubbing it in.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Globalisation is the way countries around the world are becoming more and more connected through trade, travel, the internet, money and ideas. 2) It also means big companies selling the same things in many countries.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and money lessons, globalisation explains why your trainers may be made in Vietnam, your phone in China and your banana in Ecuador. It brings jobs, cheaper goods and sharing of cultures, but it can also mean factories closing in one place, pollution from shipping, and local shops or traditions disappearing. People argue about whether its good sides outweigh its bad sides.
examples from the lessons: Globalisation means a shirt can be designed in London and made in Bangladesh. | Because of globalisation you can buy the same burger in Sydney and Dublin. | The internet has sped up globalisation. | Some people say globalisation helps poor countries get jobs. | Others worry that globalisation closes factories at home. | Our geography project was about globalisation and food miles.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK and Australian spelling: globalisation; US and Canadian spelling: globalization. Uncountable: no «a» and no plural. It comes from «global», meaning to do with the whole world.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A glyph is a picture or symbol used as a sign for a word, a sound or an idea, like an Egyptian hieroglyph or a Maya sign. 2) In computers, a glyph is the shape drawn for a letter, number or symbol in a particular font.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons glyphs are carved on stones by ancient Egyptians and the Maya. In computing, the letter A looks different in each font: each look is a glyph. Emojis are glyphs too. Phrases: Maya glyphs, a carved glyph.
examples from the lessons: The Maya carved glyphs on stone to record dates and kings. | Each Egyptian hieroglyph is a glyph. | The archaeologist tried to read the glyph on the pot. | This font has a funny glyph for the letter g. | A smiley face emoji is a kind of glyph. | We drew our own glyphs to write a secret message.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Rhymes with «cliff». Countable: one glyph, two glyphs. «Hieroglyph» is a special kind of glyph from ancient Egypt.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A gnat is a tiny flying insect, a bit like a very small fly, often seen in clouds near water; some kinds bite.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons gnats are insects with six legs and two wings; many are food for birds, bats and fish. In everyday life gnats buzz around faces on summer evenings. In stories, something annoying but small may be compared to a gnat. Phrases: a cloud of gnats, «strain at a gnat» (Bible: fuss over tiny things).
examples from the lessons: A cloud of gnats hovered over the pond. | I got bitten by gnats on the camping trip. | Swallows swoop to catch gnats in the air. | The gnat was so small it got through the window net. | In the Bible, Jesus speaks of people who strain out a gnat but swallow a camel. | The little gnat kept buzzing round my ear.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The «g» is silent: say «nat». Countable. In the US, «gnat» covers many small flies; in the UK, «midge» is often used for biting ones.

part of speech: noun (a golconda — old, rare); proper noun (Golconda)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (a name) Golconda is an old fort and city ruin near Hyderabad in India, once famous for its diamond mines and diamond trade. 2) (old, literary) A golconda is a source of great wealth, like a very rich mine.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons Golconda is famous because some of the world's best-known diamonds, such as the Koh-i-Noor and the Hope Diamond, are believed to come from its mines. In old books, calling something «a golconda» means it is a treasure chest of riches. It is also the name of a famous painting by René Magritte with men in bowler hats falling like rain.
examples from the lessons: Golconda Fort stands on a hill near Hyderabad in India. | The diamonds of Golconda were famous all over the world. | The Koh-i-Noor diamond is believed to come from the Golconda mines. | (old) To the explorers, the gold field was a real golconda. | Magritte's painting Golconda shows men in bowler hats floating in the sky.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a place name it has a capital G. The common-noun sense («a golconda») is old-fashioned and very rare today; «a gold mine» is the everyday phrase.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (old-fashioned) A goodly amount means quite a large amount. 2) (old, Bible) Goodly means good-looking, fine or pleasant.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life today, people mostly use it in the phrase «a goodly number» or «a goodly sum», often with a smile because it sounds old. In the Bible and old stories, a goodly land or goodly person means a fine, beautiful one. It tells the reader the writing has an old-fashioned voice.
examples from the lessons: A goodly crowd turned up for the school fair. | Grandpa saved a goodly sum for his holiday. | We waited a goodly while for the bus. | (Bible) «I have a goodly heritage.» | In the old tale, the prince rode to a goodly castle. | The cake was a goodly size.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It looks like an adverb because of -ly, but it is an adjective: «a goodly amount». Not used much in everyday speech; «a good amount» or «quite a lot» is more usual.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) Grabby means wanting to grab or take things for yourself, often greedily. 2) (informal) A grabby person touches or grabs others too much. 3) (informal) A grabby headline or idea catches attention quickly.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life a toddler or a pet can be grabby with toys or food. Calling a person grabby is a mild criticism about greed or about not respecting other people's things or bodies. In safety lessons, if someone is grabby with you when you do not want it, you can say no and tell a trusted adult.
examples from the lessons: The baby is very grabby with my hair. | Don't be grabby; wait your turn for a biscuit. | The seagulls got grabby when we opened the chips. | My little cousin is grabby with everyone's toys. | That newspaper headline is a bit grabby. | If someone is grabby and it makes you uncomfortable, tell a teacher.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal; not for formal writing. Comparative: grabbier, grabbiest (change y to i). From the verb «grab».

part of speech: noun (graft, grafts — for plants and skin; graft, uncountable — work, corruption); verb (graft, grafts, grafted, grafting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A graft is a piece of skin, bone or other body tissue moved by a surgeon to repair another part of the body. 2) A graft is also a cut piece of a plant joined onto another plant so they grow together. 3) (UK, Australia, informal) Graft is hard work. 4) (US) Graft is dishonest use of power to get money, like a bribe. 5) As a verb, to graft means to join a plant or tissue onto another, or (UK informal) to work hard.
its sense in the lessons: In science, grafting lets gardeners grow a tasty apple branch on a strong root; most fruit trees are grafted. In medicine, a skin graft helps burns heal. In UK and Australian everyday talk, «hard graft» praises someone's effort. In US news, graft means corruption by officials.
examples from the lessons: The surgeon used a skin graft to cover the burn. | Grandad grafted a pear branch onto the old tree. | Most apple trees are grown by grafting. | (UK) It took a lot of hard graft to build the shed. | (UK) He's a real grafter; he never stops working. | (US) The mayor went to prison for graft. | (Australia) Winning the cup took years of graft. | The bone graft helped her broken leg heal.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Be careful: in British and Australian English «graft» is a good thing (hard work), but in American English it is a bad thing (corruption). A person who works hard is a «grafter» (UK).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Grainy means having a rough texture with small bits or grains in it, like sand, or food that is not smooth. 2) A grainy photo or video is not clear and looks spotty, made of tiny dots. 3) Grainy bread or wood has a visible grain pattern.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, grainy describes the texture of materials like sand or sugar. In everyday life, old or zoomed-in photos and security videos can be grainy, so it is hard to see faces. In stories, a grainy picture can be a clue that is hard to read.
examples from the lessons: The old photo of Great-Grandma is grainy and faded. | The custard went grainy because it got too hot. | The video of the UFO was too grainy to prove anything. | This bread has a nice grainy texture. | The beach sand felt grainy between my toes. | When you zoom right in, the picture becomes grainy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative: grainier, grainiest (change y to i). Opposite for photos: sharp or clear; for food: smooth.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A grapheme is a letter or group of letters that stands for one sound (phoneme) in writing, like «sh» in ship or «igh» in night.
its sense in the lessons: In English and phonics lessons in UK, Australian and New Zealand schools, children learn graphemes and the sounds they make. One sound can be written with different graphemes: the sound «ee» can be ee (see), ea (sea), e (me) or y (happy). Phrases: grapheme–phoneme correspondence (GPC), split grapheme (a_e in cake), digraph (two-letter grapheme), trigraph (three letters).
examples from the lessons: The word «ship» has three graphemes: sh, i, p. | «igh» in «light» is a three-letter grapheme. | The split grapheme a_e makes «cap» into «cape». | Our teacher put the new grapheme on the phonics wall. | How many graphemes are in the word «boat»? | The sound «f» can be spelled with the grapheme ph, as in phone.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. A phoneme is a sound; a grapheme is how it is written. A grapheme is not always one letter: «ch» is one grapheme of two letters. Counting graphemes is not the same as counting letters.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A graphic is a picture, diagram, chart or design, especially one made on a computer. 2) Graphics are the pictures and images in a computer game, film or book. 3) A graphic description shows something in very clear, detailed and sometimes upsetting ways. 4) Graphic also means to do with drawing or design, as in graphic design.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and computing lessons, graphics include charts, graphs and diagrams that show data. In games, «good graphics» means the pictures look real and smooth. Films and news may warn of «graphic images» or «graphic violence», meaning very realistic and possibly upsetting things; it is fine to look away. Phrases: graphic novel (a comic-style book), graphic design, graphics card, graphic organiser.
examples from the lessons: The game has amazing graphics. | We made a graphic to show how many pets each class has. | A graphic novel tells a story in comic pictures. | The news warned that the report contained graphic images. | My aunt works in graphic design and makes logos. | He gave a graphic description of his sprained ankle. | Use a graphic organiser to plan your story.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Graphics» (plural) usually means images in general. «Graphic» as an adjective about violence or details is a warning word. Do not confuse with «graph», a maths diagram with axes; a graph is one kind of graphic. Graphically is the adverb.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Gratefulness is the feeling of being thankful and glad for something someone did for you or for good things in your life.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and wellbeing lessons, gratefulness means noticing good things and saying thank you. Some families or classes keep a gratitude journal. In church, Christians give thanks to God in prayer as a sign of gratefulness. In stories, a character's gratefulness shows kindness and good manners.
examples from the lessons: She felt deep gratefulness to the firefighters who saved her cat. | Writing thank-you cards shows gratefulness. | Our class shared moments of gratefulness every Friday. | His gratefulness made the old lady smile. | Gratefulness can help you feel happier. | The family prayed with gratefulness before the meal.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. «Gratitude» means the same and is more common; gratefulness is correct but used less. Adjective: grateful (only one «l» at the end, not «greatful»).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A grommet is a metal or plastic ring put in a hole in cloth, leather or paper to make the hole strong, like the holes for laces or for a tent rope. 2) (medicine, UK, Australia) A grommet is a tiny tube a doctor puts in a child's eardrum to let fluid drain out and help hearing. 3) (Australia, NZ, slang) A grommet (or grom) is a young surfer or skateboarder.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life you see grommets on shoes, curtains, banners and tents. Many children have grommets in their ears for «glue ear»; it is a small, common operation. In Australian and New Zealand beach life, groms are kids learning to surf. In design and technology lessons, grommets protect cables going through holes.
examples from the lessons: The tent rope goes through the metal grommet. | The banner has a grommet in each corner. | I had grommets put in my ears when I was five. | After the grommets, Lily could hear much better. | (Australia) The grommets were out surfing at dawn. | (Australia) That little grom can already ride big waves. | Put a rubber grommet where the wire passes through the box.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. The surfing sense is slang from Australia and New Zealand; «grom» is the short form. The ear tube is also called a «tympanostomy tube» by doctors (US: «ear tubes»).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A grouper is a big, heavy sea fish with a wide mouth that lives in warm seas, often near coral reefs and rocks.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons groupers are reef fish; some, like the giant grouper, can grow longer than a person. Some groupers can change from female to male as they grow older. People catch and eat them, and some kinds are endangered from overfishing. In Australia some kinds are called «groper».
examples from the lessons: A huge grouper swam slowly past the divers. | The giant grouper can weigh as much as a small car. | Groupers hide in caves on the coral reef. | Dad ordered grilled grouper at the seafood restaurant. | Some groupers change from female to male. | Overfishing has made some grouper rare.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: groupers, or grouper when talking about many as food or a catch. Not related to the word «group». In Australia and New Zealand, «groper» is used for some kinds.

part of speech: noun (a grouse, grouse — bird; a grouse, grouses — complaint); verb (grouse, grouses, groused, grousing); adjective (grouse — Australia, slang)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A grouse is a plump, brown wild bird with feathered legs that lives on moors and in forests. 2) (informal) To grouse means to complain or grumble, and a grouse is a complaint. 3) (Australia, NZ, slang) Grouse means really good or excellent.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography lessons, red grouse live on heather moors in Scotland and northern England; in North America there are ruffed grouse and sage grouse. Grouse shooting is a sport in the UK, which some people oppose. In everyday talk, a person who grouses is always moaning. In Australia, «that's grouse!» means «that's great!» (a bit old-fashioned now).
examples from the lessons: A grouse flew up from the heather. | Red grouse live on the moors of Scotland. | The male sage grouse puffs up its chest to show off. | Stop grousing about the rain and put your coat on. | My only grouse is that the film was too long. | (Australia) That pie was grouse, mate! | Grouse are hard to see because their feathers match the moor.
note for the reader of a maths problem: For the bird, the plural is usually also «grouse»: «three grouse». For the complaint, the plural is «grouses». The Australian slang «grouse» (good) is the opposite of the complaining sense, so listen to context.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (a name) Guinness is a famous dark Irish beer (a stout) made in Dublin since 1759; it is an alcoholic drink for adults. 2) (a name) Guinness World Records is a book and organisation that checks and lists world records, like the tallest person or the fastest runner. 3) (a name) Guinness is also an Irish family name, such as Arthur Guinness, who started the brewery.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life children know Guinness mostly from the Guinness World Records book, which is full of amazing facts and records. In Ireland and the UK, a pint of Guinness is a well-known adult drink; children should not drink alcohol. Phrases: a Guinness world record, break a Guinness world record.
examples from the lessons: I got the Guinness World Records book for my birthday. | She wants to set a Guinness world record for the longest hula-hoop spin. | The Guinness book lists the tallest man who ever lived. | Guinness is a dark beer from Dublin. | Grandad drinks a pint of Guinness on Sundays. | Arthur Guinness opened his brewery in Dublin in 1759.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It is a name, so it is written with a capital G and double n and double s: Guinness. It is not an ordinary English word. Do not confuse with «guineas» (old British coins) or «Guinea» (a country).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Gypsum is a soft white or grey mineral found in rocks, used to make plaster, chalk-like boards for walls, and some fertilisers.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons gypsum is a soft mineral: on the Mohs hardness scale it is 2, so you can scratch it with your fingernail. It forms when salty water dries up. Plasterboard (drywall) and plaster of Paris for casts are made from gypsum. White Sands in New Mexico, USA, is made of gypsum sand.
examples from the lessons: Gypsum is soft enough to scratch with a fingernail. | Plaster of Paris is made by heating gypsum. | The walls of our house are made of gypsum plasterboard. | White Sands in New Mexico has dunes of gypsum. | Farmers sometimes spread gypsum on clay soil. | We tested the hardness of gypsum and quartz in science.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: no «a», no plural. Say «JIP-sum». Do not confuse gypsum with chalk, which is a different mineral (calcium carbonate), although both are soft and white.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To habituate someone means to make them used to something by doing or meeting it again and again. 2) (science) An animal becomes habituated when it stops reacting to something harmless that happens often, like birds ignoring a scarecrow.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, habituation is a simple kind of learning: animals stop responding to a sound or sight that keeps happening and never harms them. In wildlife safety, wild animals like bears or foxes that get habituated to people can become dangerous, so you should not feed them. In everyday life we habituate to a ticking clock and stop hearing it. Phrases: habituated to, habituate yourself to.
examples from the lessons: The birds soon habituated to the scarecrow and ate the seeds anyway. | Don't feed the bears, or they will become habituated to people. | We habituated to the noise of the trains after a week. | The puppy was slowly habituated to the vacuum cleaner. | Astronauts must habituate themselves to floating. | Snails habituate to being touched and stop pulling in.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal or scientific; in everyday speech people say «get used to». Usually followed by «to». The noun is «habituation». Related to «habit».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A hacker is a person who uses computer skills to get into computers or systems, often without permission, which is a crime. 2) A hacker can also be a very skilled programmer who enjoys solving computer problems in clever ways. 3) An ethical hacker («white hat») is paid to find weak spots so they can be fixed. 4) (informal) A hacker in sport is a poor player, especially in golf.
its sense in the lessons: In computing and online safety lessons, hackers are a reason to use strong passwords and never share them. Breaking into someone's account is illegal even for a joke. Some hackers work for companies to keep systems safe. In news, «hackers stole data» means criminals got into a system. Phrases: ethical hacker, white-hat hacker, black-hat hacker.
examples from the lessons: A hacker tried to get into the school website. | Use a strong password to protect your account from hackers. | Ethical hackers help banks find weak spots. | Hackers stole thousands of email addresses. | My cousin is a hacker who builds robots in his garage. | Logging into someone else's account without permission is a crime. | The hackers at the competition fixed the bug in an hour.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. The word itself can be good (a clever programmer) or bad (a criminal); the news nearly always uses the bad sense. The verb is «hack».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A haddock is a sea fish of the North Atlantic, related to cod, with a black line along its side and a dark spot near its fins; it is a popular food fish.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life in the UK and Ireland, haddock is often eaten as fish and chips, or smoked for breakfast and in fish pie. In Scotland smoked haddock is called «finnan haddie». In science, haddock live near the sea floor and eat small animals. Overfishing has made fishing limits necessary.
examples from the lessons: I had haddock and chips at the seaside. | Mum made a fish pie with smoked haddock. | Haddock have a dark spot just behind the head. | The trawler caught cod and haddock. | In Scotland we have smoked haddock for breakfast. | Haddock lives in cold waters of the North Atlantic.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: often the same, «haddock», especially for food or catch; «haddocks» is also fine. Uncountable when it means the food: «some haddock».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A hadrosaur is a duck-billed dinosaur: a large plant-eating dinosaur with a wide, flat mouth like a duck's beak.
its sense in the lessons: In science and history lessons hadrosaurs lived in the Late Cretaceous, about 100 to 66 million years ago, in North America, Asia and Europe. Some, like Parasaurolophus, had a hollow crest on their head that may have made honking sounds. They had hundreds of teeth for grinding plants and lived in herds. Scientists found nests and babies of the hadrosaur Maiasaura in Montana, USA.
examples from the lessons: A hadrosaur is a duck-billed dinosaur. | Parasaurolophus was a hadrosaur with a long crest on its head. | Hadrosaurs had hundreds of teeth for chewing plants. | The museum has a complete hadrosaur skeleton. | Maiasaura hadrosaurs looked after their babies in nests. | Hadrosaurs walked on two or four legs.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Say «HAD-ro-sore». «-saur» means lizard in Greek, as in dinosaur. Hadrosaurs were plant-eaters, not meat-eaters.

part of speech: adjective (hale, haler, halest); verb (hale, hales, haled, haling — old)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Hale means strong and healthy, usually said about an older person. 2) (old) To hale someone means to pull or drag them, especially to court.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life the phrase «hale and hearty» means fit and well, often about grandparents. The verb is old-fashioned and appears in old books or the Bible: «haled into court». It tells the reader a person is in good health despite age.
examples from the lessons: Grandpa is still hale and hearty at ninety. | The old farmer looked hale and strong. | After the holiday, everyone came back hale and well. | (old) The thief was haled before the judge. | My nan is hale enough to walk five miles a day.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly used in «hale and hearty». It sounds the same as «hail» (ice from the sky, or to call out to), but they are different words: homophones.

part of speech: noun (a hamper, hampers); verb (hamper, hampers, hampered, hampering)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A hamper is a large basket with a lid, used to carry food for a picnic or as a gift full of treats. 2) (US) A hamper is a basket for dirty clothes (laundry hamper). 3) To hamper means to get in the way of something and make it slower or harder.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life in the UK, Ireland and Australia, a Christmas hamper is a gift basket of food. In the US, the hamper is where dirty laundry goes. In stories and news, «the rescue was hampered by bad weather» means it was made harder. Phrases: picnic hamper, Christmas hamper, laundry hamper.
examples from the lessons: We packed sandwiches into the picnic hamper. | Granny got a Christmas hamper full of cheese and chutney. | Put your dirty socks in the hamper. | Heavy snow hampered the rescue team. | The broken wheel hampered our progress. | A sore ankle hampered her running. | The hamper had a little drawer for the knives and forks.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Two different words: the basket (noun) and «to hamper» (verb, to hinder). The verb is a bit formal; everyday words are «slow down» or «get in the way of».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A handbook is a small book that gives useful facts and instructions about a subject, or rules about a place, such as a school or a club.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life schools give families a school handbook with rules, times and uniform lists. Scouts, Guides and many clubs have handbooks. Workers get a staff handbook. In science, a field handbook helps you identify birds or plants. It tells the reader where to find the rules or the facts.
examples from the lessons: Read the school handbook to find the uniform rules. | The bird handbook helped us name the robin. | Every new Cub Scout gets a handbook. | The staff handbook explains what to do in a fire drill. | Check the handbook before you set up the tent. | The teacher's handbook lists all the science experiments.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. One word. Similar to «manual» (instructions for a machine) and «guide»; a handbook is usually a reference you keep looking things up in.

part of speech: word (hǎo — Mandarin, pinyin; not an English word)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (Mandarin, pinyin) Hǎo means «good», «well» or «fine»; it is one of the most common Chinese words. 2) (Mandarin, pinyin) «Nǐ hǎo» (you good) means «hello». 3) (Mandarin, pinyin) Hào, said with a different tone, can mean a number or a date in the month, as in «sān hào» (the 3rd).
its sense in the lessons: In Mandarin lessons and on the street, children hear «nǐ hǎo» as a greeting and «hǎo» as «OK, good». To an English ear «hao» sounds like «how», with the tone going down and then up. The Chinese character for hǎo (好) is made of «woman» and «child» side by side. It is not an English word.
examples from the lessons: (Mandarin) «Nǐ hǎo!» means «Hello!» | (Mandarin) «Hǎo» means «good» or «OK». | (Mandarin) «Nǐ hǎo ma?» means «How are you?» | (Mandarin) «Hěn hǎo» means «very good». | The character 好 is said «hǎo». | Our teacher said «hǎo» sounds a bit like the English word «how».
note for the reader of a maths problem: Not an English word. In pinyin the tone mark matters: hǎo (third tone) = good; hào (fourth tone) = number, date or to like. Without tone marks, «hao» is ambiguous. Pinyin «h» is breathier than English «h».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A haricot (haricot bean) is a small white bean, the kind used to make baked beans. 2) (French) «Haricot» is the French word for bean, as in «haricots verts» (green beans).
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life in the UK, Ireland and Australia, tinned baked beans are haricot beans in tomato sauce; in the US they are called navy beans. In science and food lessons, beans are seeds and a good source of protein and fibre. In cooking, French recipes use «haricots verts» for thin green beans. Say «HA-ri-koh»: the t is silent.
examples from the lessons: Baked beans are made from haricot beans. | Soak the haricot beans in water overnight. | Haricot beans are full of protein. | In America, haricot beans are called navy beans. | Mum added haricots to the stew. | (French) «Haricots verts» are thin green beans.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The «t» is silent, as in French: «HA-ri-koh». Countable: haricots. It is a borrowed French word, used in English mostly as «haricot bean».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A haystack is a large pile or stack of dried grass (hay) kept outside on a farm to feed animals in winter.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and on farms, hay is now often rolled into round bales, but old stories and paintings show haystacks. The phrase «like looking for a needle in a haystack» means something is almost impossible to find. In safety, haystacks and hay bales can catch fire and should not be played on without permission. Famous paintings of haystacks were made by Claude Monet.
examples from the lessons: The farmer built a big haystack next to the barn. | Finding my earring on the beach was like looking for a needle in a haystack. | The children hid behind the haystack. | Monet painted haystacks in different light. | The horses eat the hay from the haystack in winter. | Searching the internet without good words is like searching a haystack.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. One word. Hay is dried grass for animals; straw is the dry stalks left after grain is harvested — they are not the same.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A headdress is a special covering or decoration worn on the head, often for ceremonies, celebrations or as part of traditional dress.
its sense in the lessons: In history and religion lessons, headdresses include the feathered war bonnets of some Plains Indian nations, the crowns and nemes of Egyptian pharaohs, and religious head coverings. In everyday life, carnival dancers and brides may wear headdresses. Respect matters: some headdresses are sacred and are not costumes. Phrases: a feathered headdress, a ceremonial headdress.
examples from the lessons: The pharaoh wore a striped headdress. | The carnival dancer had a huge headdress of feathers. | For some First Nations peoples, a feathered headdress is sacred and must be earned. | The bride wore a headdress of flowers. | Our class made paper headdresses for the play. | The museum showed a beaded headdress from Kenya.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word with a double d and double s: headdress. Plural: headdresses. It is more special than a hat; everyday hats are not usually called headdresses.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Heartfelt means deeply and sincerely felt, coming truly from the heart.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life we give heartfelt thanks, heartfelt apologies or heartfelt wishes when we really mean them. In stories, a heartfelt speech or letter tells the reader the character is honest and moved. Phrases: heartfelt thanks, heartfelt apology, heartfelt message, heartfelt condolences (said when someone has died).
examples from the lessons: Please accept our heartfelt thanks for your help. | He wrote a heartfelt apology to his friend. | The class sent heartfelt get-well cards to Mr Patel. | Her speech at Grandad's funeral was heartfelt. | We offer our heartfelt condolences to the family. | The song was simple but heartfelt.
note for the reader of a maths problem: An adjective, usually before a noun. It is always positive about sincerity. Spelled as one word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A hearth is the floor of a fireplace and the area just in front of it, where the fire burns. 2) (literary) Hearth can mean home and family life, as in «hearth and home».
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, the hearth was the centre of the home in the past: people cooked, kept warm and gathered there. In safety, keep toys, paper and clothes away from the hearth. In stories, sitting by the hearth means a cosy, safe, homely scene. Phrases: hearth and home, by the hearth, hearth rug.
examples from the lessons: The cat slept on the warm hearth. | Grandma swept the ashes from the hearth. | In Viking houses the hearth was in the middle of the room. | Keep the fireguard in front of the hearth. | The soldiers longed to return to hearth and home. | We hung our stockings above the hearth on Christmas Eve.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say «harth»; in the UK it rhymes with «path», not with «earth». Do not confuse with «heart» or «earth», which look similar. Countable.

part of speech: verb (heckle, heckles, heckled, heckling); noun (a heckle, heckles)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To heckle means to shout rude or annoying comments at someone who is speaking or performing in public, to interrupt them. 2) A heckle is one of those shouted comments.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life hecklers can be heard at comedy shows, football matches and political speeches. Heckling is usually seen as rude, though in Parliament some loud comments are a tradition. In stories, a heckler shows a crowd is against the speaker. A good performer may reply to a heckle with a joke. The person is a heckler.
examples from the lessons: Someone in the crowd heckled the politician. | The comedian had a funny answer for every heckle. | It is rude to heckle a speaker at assembly. | The fans heckled the referee all game. | Hecklers kept shouting during the speech. | She kept calm even when they heckled her.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: heckled, heckling. A person who heckles is a heckler. Heckling is shouting at a speaker; it is different from asking a question politely.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Herpes is a common infection caused by a virus; one kind causes cold sores, small painful blisters around the mouth. 2) Some kinds of herpes viruses also cause chickenpox and shingles.
its sense in the lessons: In health lessons, cold sores are caused by the herpes simplex virus; they spread by touching or kissing, so do not share cups or lip balm when someone has one. Chickenpox, which many children catch, is caused by another herpes virus. Herpes is very common and is not a sign of being dirty. A doctor or pharmacist can give cream to help.
examples from the lessons: A cold sore is caused by a herpes virus. | Don't share your water bottle when you have a cold sore, because herpes spreads easily. | Chickenpox comes from a kind of herpes virus. | Shingles is caused by the same virus as chickenpox. | Many people carry the herpes virus without knowing. | The pharmacist gave Mum a cream for her herpes cold sore.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Ends in -s but is singular and uncountable: «Herpes is…». Say «HER-peez». The name of the illness and the virus family; there is no plural «herpeses».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Hexagonal means shaped like a hexagon: having six straight sides and six corners.
its sense in the lessons: In maths lessons a regular hexagon has six equal sides and six equal angles of 120°; hexagons fit together with no gaps, which is called tessellation. In science, honeycomb cells in a beehive are hexagonal, and snowflakes have hexagonal (six-fold) shapes. The Giant's Causeway in Northern Ireland has hexagonal stone columns. Many nuts (for bolts) and pencils are hexagonal.
examples from the lessons: Bees build hexagonal cells in their honeycomb. | This pencil is hexagonal so it does not roll off the desk. | The Giant's Causeway is made of hexagonal rock columns. | A hexagonal shape has six sides. | The snowflake had a hexagonal pattern. | Hexagonal tiles fit together without gaps. | A hexagonal prism has two hexagonal faces and six rectangle faces.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective from «hexagon». «Hex-» means six (Greek). In maths, a hexagon has 6 sides, 6 vertices, and its interior angles add up to 720°. Do not confuse with pentagon (5) or octagon (8).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Hideous means extremely ugly or horrible to look at. 2) Hideous also means very unpleasant or shocking, like a hideous crime or a hideous noise.
its sense in the lessons: In stories hideous describes monsters, trolls and nasty faces, helping the reader picture something frightening. In everyday talk, children may joke that a jumper or wallpaper is hideous, which is an exaggeration. Be kind: calling a person hideous is very hurtful. Phrases: a hideous monster, hideous noise.
examples from the lessons: The troll had a hideous face covered in warts. | Aunt Jo knitted me a hideous orange jumper. | The machine made a hideous screech. | The witch let out a hideous laugh. | That was a hideous crime. | I think the new car colour is hideous, but Dad loves it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say «HID-ee-us». Stronger than ugly. The adverb is «hideously». It is not related to «hide», although it looks similar.

part of speech: noun (highland, highlands); adjective (highland); proper noun (the Highlands)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Highland is land that is high up, with hills and mountains. 2) (a name) The Highlands are the mountainous north and west part of Scotland. 3) As an adjective, highland means from or to do with high land, especially the Scottish Highlands.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons, highlands are areas of high ground, opposite to lowlands; they are often colder, wetter and less crowded. In Scotland the Highlands are famous for mountains, lochs, castles, Highland cattle, Highland dancing and bagpipes. Highland games include tossing the caber. Many countries have highlands, such as the Ethiopian Highlands.
examples from the lessons: We went on holiday to the Scottish Highlands. | Highland cows have long shaggy hair and big horns. | At the Highland games, a man tossed a huge log called a caber. | Highland dancing is done to bagpipe music. | Few people live in the highland areas. | The highlands of Kenya are good for growing tea.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «The Highlands» (capital H) means the Scottish region. As a general word, usually plural: highlands. Opposite: lowland, lowlands.

part of speech: noun (a hinny, hinnies); noun (hinny — dialect, term of endearment)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A hinny is the young of a male horse and a female donkey; it looks a bit like a mule. 2) (dialect, northern England and Scotland) «Hinny» is a loving word for someone, like «honey» or «pet», especially in the North East (Geordie).
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, a hinny and a mule are both crosses between a horse and a donkey: a mule has a donkey dad and a horse mum; a hinny has a horse dad and a donkey mum. Hinnies are rarer than mules and usually cannot have babies. In Newcastle and Northumberland, «hinny» or «hinney» is a friendly name, and «singin' hinnies» are griddle cakes.
examples from the lessons: A hinny has a horse father and a donkey mother. | Hinnies are rarer than mules. | Like mules, hinnies usually cannot have foals. | (dialect) «Come here, hinny, and give us a hug,» said Nana. | (dialect) «Ta, hinny,» said the lady at the shop in Newcastle. | Singin' hinnies are cakes that sizzle on the griddle.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: hinnies (change y to ie). The trap: hinny and mule are opposite crosses; remember «mule = mum is a horse». Also «hinny» can mean the sound of a horse (whinny) in old dialect, but «whinny» is the usual word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Historic means important in history, or likely to be remembered in the future as important. 2) Historic also describes old buildings, places or things from the past that are worth keeping, like a historic castle.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons historic events are big turning points, like the moon landing in 1969 or the fall of the Berlin Wall in 1989. In everyday life, a «historic town centre» means an old part of a town. In news and sport, a «historic win» is a very special first. Phrases: historic moment, historic building, historic site, historic day.
examples from the lessons: The moon landing was a historic moment. | We visited a historic castle in Wales. | The team had a historic win in the cup final. | York has a historic city centre. | The signing of the peace treaty was historic. | The National Trust looks after many historic houses.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Historic means «important in history»; historical means «about history or from the past» (a historical novel). Many people mix them up. You can write «a historic» or (UK, old-fashioned) «an historic»; «a historic» is more common now.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A hitter is a person who hits, especially a batter in baseball or softball whose job is to hit the ball. 2) (informal) A heavy hitter is a powerful or important person or organisation. 3) In cricket and other sports, a hitter is someone who hits the ball hard.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday sport in the US and Canada, hitters are batters: a «good hitter» hits the ball often, a «power hitter» hits it far. In cricket, a «big hitter» scores lots of sixes. In maths problems about baseball, a hitter's batting average = hits ÷ times at bat. In news, «heavy hitters» are big important people.
examples from the lessons: She is the best hitter on our softball team. | The hitter swung and sent the ball over the fence. | He is a big hitter who scores lots of sixes. | A power hitter can hit home runs. | The heavy hitters of tech came to the meeting. | The coach moved the left-handed hitter up the order.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. In baseball, «batter» is the usual word for the person batting; hitter is used too. Batting average in maths: hits ÷ at-bats, written like .300 (3 hits in 10).

meaning for a pupil: 1) The hoatzin is a strange bird of the Amazon rainforest in South America, with a spiky crest, blue face and red eyes; it eats leaves and smells bad, so it is also called the stinkbird.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons the hoatzin is famous because its chicks have claws on their wings to climb back into trees after dropping into water to escape danger. It digests leaves by fermenting them, like a cow, which gives it a smell like manure. It is the national bird of Guyana. It is a good example of adaptation.
examples from the lessons: The hoatzin lives along rivers in the Amazon rainforest. | Baby hoatzins have claws on their wings. | The hoatzin is nicknamed the stinkbird. | Hoatzin chicks drop into the water to escape snakes. | The hoatzin eats leaves and digests them like a cow. | The hoatzin is the national bird of Guyana.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say «wat-SEEN» or «ho-AT-sin». Countable. The name comes from a Native Mexican (Nahuatl) word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Homogeneous means the same all the way through, with every part alike. 2) A homogeneous group is made of people or things that are all of the same kind.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, a homogeneous mixture looks the same everywhere, like salt fully dissolved in water or air; a heterogeneous mixture has parts you can see, like sand in water. In maths and data, a homogeneous group has very similar members. In everyday life and society, people may say a town is less homogeneous as people from many places move there. Opposite: heterogeneous.
examples from the lessons: Salt water is a homogeneous mixture. | Stir the paint until it is homogeneous. | A fruit salad is not homogeneous; you can see the pieces. | The class was not homogeneous: there were children from twelve countries. | Air is a homogeneous mixture of gases. | Mix the batter until it is smooth and homogeneous.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say «hom-uh-JEE-nee-us». «Homo-» means same, «-gen-» means kind. «Homogenous» (without the second e) is a common variant, but in science «homogeneous» is the standard spelling. Opposite: heterogeneous.

part of speech: adjective (homogenised); verb form (homogenise, homogenises, homogenised, homogenising); US spelling homogenized
meaning for a pupil: 1) Homogenised milk has been treated so the cream is broken into tiny drops and mixed through, so it does not rise to the top. 2) Homogenised means made all the same or mixed evenly. 3) (disapproving) Homogenised can mean dull, with all the interesting differences taken away.
its sense in the lessons: In science and food lessons, homogenising milk pushes it through tiny holes at high pressure so the fat droplets become very small and stay mixed. Most shop milk is homogenised and pasteurised. In talk about culture, people complain that high streets have become homogenised, with the same shops everywhere.
examples from the lessons: Most milk in the supermarket is homogenised. | Homogenised milk has no layer of cream on top. | The machine homogenised the mixture. | Some people say pop music has become homogenised. | Every town centre looks homogenised with the same chain shops. | Grandma remembers milk before it was homogenised, with cream on top.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK, Australian spelling: homogenised; US, Canadian spelling: homogenized. Homogenised is not the same as pasteurised (heated to kill germs); milk is usually both.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A honeycreeper is a small, often brightly coloured bird that feeds on nectar and insects; there are Hawaiian honeycreepers and tropical American honeycreepers.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons the Hawaiian honeycreepers are a famous example of adaptive radiation: from one ancestor many kinds evolved with different beaks for different foods, like Darwin's finches. Many are now endangered or extinct because of introduced mosquitoes, rats and lost forest. In Central and South America, honeycreepers like the red-legged honeycreeper are bright blue.
examples from the lessons: The red-legged honeycreeper has bright blue feathers. | Hawaiian honeycreepers have beaks of many different shapes. | The curved beak helps the honeycreeper drink nectar. | Many honeycreepers in Hawaii are endangered. | Mosquitoes brought malaria that harmed the honeycreepers. | We saw a honeycreeper in the rainforest canopy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. One word. It is a name for several bird groups that are not all closely related; they share the habit of drinking nectar.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Horsehair is the hair from a horse's mane or tail, used to make things such as violin bows, brushes and stuffing for old furniture.
its sense in the lessons: In music lessons, violin, viola and cello bows are strung with horsehair, which is rubbed with rosin so it grips the strings. In history, horsehair was used to stuff mattresses and sofas and to make judges' and barristers' wigs in the UK. Horsehair plaster was used in old houses.
examples from the lessons: A violin bow is strung with horsehair. | The old sofa was stuffed with horsehair. | British judges' wigs are made of horsehair. | Rub rosin on the horsehair before you play. | The paintbrush was made of horsehair. | The scratchy horsehair mattress was uncomfortable.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «some horsehair». One word. Taking hair from a horse's mane or tail does not hurt the horse when done properly.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Humanitarian means caring about people's lives and suffering, and trying to help them, especially in disasters and wars. 2) A humanitarian is a person who works to help people who suffer.
its sense in the lessons: In news and citizenship lessons, humanitarian aid means food, water, medicine and shelter given to people after earthquakes, floods, famines or wars. Groups like the Red Cross, Red Crescent and UN agencies do humanitarian work. A «humanitarian crisis» means many people urgently need help. International humanitarian law sets rules to protect civilians in war.
examples from the lessons: The charity sent humanitarian aid after the earthquake. | Trucks carried food and medicine as humanitarian help. | The war has caused a humanitarian crisis. | Florence Nightingale was a great humanitarian. | Doctors Without Borders does humanitarian work. | Humanitarian law protects people who are not fighting. | The school raised money for humanitarian relief.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Can be an adjective (humanitarian aid) or a noun (a humanitarian). Not the same as «human» or «humane», though related: humane means kind and gentle; humanitarian is about helping people who suffer, often on a big scale.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A hundredfold means a hundred times as much or as many. 2) (Bible, literary) Hundredfold means greatly or many times over.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, if something grows a hundredfold, you multiply it by 100: 5 becomes 500. In the news, «prices rose a hundredfold» means they became 100 times higher. In the Bible, Jesus's parable of the sower says some seed fell on good soil and produced «a hundredfold», meaning a huge harvest.
examples from the lessons: The number of visitors grew a hundredfold. | If you invest wisely, your work may be repaid a hundredfold. | The cost of the stamp increased a hundredfold since Grandad was a boy. | (Bible) Some seed fell on good ground and gave fruit a hundredfold. | The bacteria multiplied a hundredfold overnight. | A hundredfold increase means ×100.
note for the reader of a maths problem: In maths, «a hundredfold» means multiply by 100, not «add 100». Also: twofold (×2), tenfold (×10), thousandfold (×1000). Usually written as one word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Hyperactivity means being much more active, restless and full of energy than usual, finding it very hard to sit still. 2) (medicine) Hyperactivity is part of ADHD (attention deficit hyperactivity disorder), a condition that affects attention and activity.
its sense in the lessons: In health and everyday life, everyone can be very active sometimes, but hyperactivity is when it happens a lot and makes school or home harder. ADHD is a real condition, not bad behaviour; children with it can get help and often have great strengths. In science, «hyperactivity» can also describe an organ or gland working too much. Myth: sugar causes hyperactivity — studies have mostly not found this.
examples from the lessons: ADHD stands for attention deficit hyperactivity disorder. | His hyperactivity made it hard to sit through long lessons. | The teacher gave her movement breaks to help with hyperactivity. | Many people believe sugar causes hyperactivity, but studies show little effect. | Hyperactivity is only one part of ADHD. | Some children with hyperactivity are brilliant at sport.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. «Hyper-» means over or too much. The adjective is «hyperactive». Trap: «hyper» in everyday slang («I'm so hyper!») just means very excited, not a medical condition.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Hyperbole is a huge exaggeration that is not meant to be taken literally, used to make a point or be funny, like «I've told you a million times».
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons, hyperbole is a figure of speech, along with simile and metaphor. Writers use it for humour, drama or strong feeling. In everyday speech it is everywhere: «I'm starving», «this bag weighs a ton». In adverts and politics, hyperbole can make things sound better than they are, so readers should check facts.
examples from the lessons: «I'm so hungry I could eat a horse» is hyperbole. | «I've told you a million times» is an example of hyperbole. | The poet used hyperbole to show how much she loved him. | Find the hyperbole in the paragraph. | The advert's claim to be «the best in the universe» is hyperbole. | «This bag weighs a ton!» she said, using hyperbole.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say «hy-PER-bo-lee», four syllables — not «hyper-bowl». Often uncountable; «a hyperbole» for one example. Adjective: hyperbolic. In maths, «hyperbola» is a different word: a type of curve.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Icelandic means from or to do with Iceland, an island country in the North Atlantic. 2) Icelandic is the language spoken in Iceland.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons, Iceland has volcanoes, glaciers, hot springs and geysers, so Icelandic landscapes are a favourite example. The Icelandic language is close to Old Norse, the language of the Vikings, so Icelanders can still read their old sagas. Icelandic horses are small and sturdy. Icelandic names use the father's or mother's name plus -son or -dóttir.
examples from the lessons: Icelandic horses have a special smooth walk. | The Icelandic sagas tell stories of Viking families. | Icelandic is spoken by about 350,000 people. | My Icelandic friend's surname is Jónsdóttir. | We read about Icelandic volcanoes in geography. | Icelandic has letters like þ and ð that English lost long ago.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always with a capital I: Icelandic. Iceland the country, Icelander a person, Icelandic the language and adjective. Despite its name, Iceland is greener than Greenland in summer.

part of speech: noun (an iceman, icemen); proper noun (the Iceman)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (old, US) An iceman was a man who delivered blocks of ice to homes for iceboxes before fridges. 2) (a name) The Iceman, called Ötzi, is a 5,300-year-old mummy of a man found frozen in the Alps between Italy and Austria in 1991. 3) (informal) An «iceman» is a nickname for someone who stays very calm under pressure.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, Ötzi the Iceman tells us how people lived in the Copper Age: his clothes, copper axe, bow and arrows and even his last meals survived in the ice. He was probably killed by an arrow. In everyday history, before electric fridges, the iceman brought ice by cart. In sport, a calm player may be nicknamed «the Iceman».
examples from the lessons: Ötzi the Iceman was found in the Alps in 1991. | The Iceman had tattoos and a copper axe. | Scientists found out what the Iceman ate for his last meal. | Before fridges, the iceman delivered ice to houses. | The goalkeeper was called «the Iceman» because he never panicked. | You can see the Iceman in a museum in Bolzano, Italy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: icemen. «The Iceman» with capitals means Ötzi. One word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (slang, abbreviation) IG is short for Instagram, a social media app for photos and videos. 2) (texting) «ig» can be short for «I guess». 3) (abbreviation) IG can stand for Inspector General, a person who checks that an organisation follows the rules. 4) (fragment) «ig» is also a word part, as in «igloo» or «pig», and «Ig» is in «Ig Nobel Prize», a joke prize for funny real science. 5) (biology) Ig is short for immunoglobulin, an antibody.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life teens say «Are you on IG?» meaning Instagram. In online safety lessons, social media like IG has age limits (usually 13+), and you should keep accounts private and not share personal details. In texting, «ig» shows an unsure answer. The Ig Nobel Prizes celebrate science that makes people laugh, then think.
examples from the lessons: My big sister posted a photo on IG. | «Are you coming to the park?» — «ig» (I guess). | You must be 13 to have an IG account. | The Ig Nobel Prize once went to a study of why woodpeckers don't get headaches. | The IG report checked how the money was spent. | The doctor tested her Ig levels.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Not an ordinary English word but an abbreviation or fragment, so context tells which. IG for Instagram is usually written in capitals; «ig» for «I guess» is texting slang, not for school writing.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Immaterial means not important or not relevant to what is being talked about. 2) (formal) Immaterial also means not made of matter, with no physical body, like a spirit.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and in arguments, «that's immaterial» means «that doesn't matter here». In maths problems, some numbers are immaterial: they are given but you don't need them. In law, immaterial facts don't change the result. In religion and philosophy, the soul is described as immaterial.
examples from the lessons: Whether the car is red or blue is immaterial; it needs fixing. | The cost is immaterial if it saves a life. | In this problem, the colour of the bags is immaterial. | Christians believe the soul is immaterial. | Whether he meant to break it is immaterial; it is broken. | Ghosts in stories are often immaterial and walk through walls.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; everyday words are «not important» or «doesn't matter». «Im-» means not. Opposite: material (meaning relevant or physical).

part of speech: verb form (impede, impedes, impeded, impeding); adjective (impeding)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Impeding means getting in the way of something and slowing it down or making it harder. 2) (sport, UK) Impeding is a rule-break in football or hockey where a player blocks an opponent without playing the ball.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, «impeding traffic» means blocking the road. In science and safety, a blocked exit impedes escape in a fire, so keep fire exits clear. In sport, a referee may give a free kick for impeding. In news, «impeding the investigation» means making a police search harder. It is formal; everyday words are «blocking» or «holding up».
examples from the lessons: A fallen tree was impeding the traffic. | Do not leave bags in the corridor impeding the fire exit. | The referee gave a free kick for impeding. | The mud was impeding our progress up the hill. | He was arrested for impeding a police officer. | Fear can stop you, impeding your learning.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The -ing form of «impede». Formal. Not the same as «impending», which means about to happen (an impending storm) — a common confusion.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Impenetrable means impossible to get through, into or see through, like a thick forest or a strong wall. 2) Impenetrable also means impossible to understand, like a very difficult text.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, an impenetrable forest, fog or fortress makes the hero's journey hard. In science, a material that water or light cannot pass through can be called impenetrable. In everyday life, a book full of jargon may be called impenetrable. Phrases: impenetrable jungle, impenetrable darkness, impenetrable defence.
examples from the lessons: The castle walls were impenetrable. | They hacked a path through the impenetrable jungle. | The fog was so thick it was impenetrable. | The instructions were impenetrable; nobody understood them. | Our team's defence was impenetrable all season. | The darkness of the cave was impenetrable.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Im-» means not; «penetrate» means go into or through. Say «im-PEN-i-tra-bul». The opposite «penetrable» is rarely used.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Impossibility is the state of being impossible: something that cannot happen or cannot be done. 2) An impossibility is a thing that cannot happen.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, probability lessons say an impossible event has a probability of 0, such as rolling a 7 on a normal six-sided dice. In logic, an impossibility is something that contradicts itself, like a square circle. In stories, heroes face near-impossibilities. Phrases: a near impossibility, a physical impossibility, a logical impossibility.
examples from the lessons: Rolling a 7 on one normal dice is an impossibility. | Winning without practice is close to an impossibility. | A square circle is a logical impossibility. | Being in two places at once is a physical impossibility. | Getting a ticket was almost an impossibility. | The impossibility of the task made them want to try harder.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable and uncountable. In maths, impossible = probability 0; very unlikely is not the same as impossible (probability above 0). Adjective: impossible.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (law) To impound means for the police or officials to take something away and keep it until rules are followed, such as a car, a dog or goods. 2) To impound water means to hold it back behind a dam or wall, making a reservoir.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, a car parked illegally may be impounded and taken to a pound; the owner pays a fine to get it back. Stray animals can be impounded by the council. In geography, a dam impounds a river to make a lake. Phrases: car impound, impounded vehicle, impound lot (US).
examples from the lessons: The police impounded the car because it had no insurance. | The stray dog was impounded until its owner came. | Customs officers impounded the fake trainers. | The dam impounds the river to make a reservoir. | Dad had to pay a fine to get the car back from the impound. | The ship was impounded at the port.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Related to «pound», a place where stray animals or towed cars are kept. Formal or legal; everyday words are «take away» or «seize».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Inaccessible means impossible or very hard to reach or get into. 2) Inaccessible also means hard to understand. 3) A place or website that is inaccessible cannot be used easily by disabled people, for example with no ramp for wheelchairs.
its sense in the lessons: In geography, an inaccessible place like a mountain top or remote island is hard to reach. In everyday life and citizenship, buildings must be made accessible with ramps, lifts and wide doors; an inaccessible building leaves people out. In safety, keep medicines inaccessible to small children. In computing, a website is inaccessible if screen readers cannot use it.
examples from the lessons: The village is inaccessible in winter because of snow. | Keep medicines inaccessible to toddlers. | The old library was inaccessible to wheelchair users until they built a ramp. | The treasure was hidden in an inaccessible cave. | The website was inaccessible during the storm. | His writing is so complicated it is inaccessible to most readers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «In-» means not. Spelling: double c and double s — inaccessible. Opposite: accessible.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Inaction means not doing anything, especially when something should be done.
its sense in the lessons: In news and citizenship lessons, people criticise «inaction on climate change» when governments do not act. In ethics, choosing inaction is still a choice with consequences: if you see bullying and do nothing, your inaction matters. In stories, a character's inaction can lead to disaster. Phrases: a period of inaction, inaction on, criticised for inaction.
examples from the lessons: The council was criticised for its inaction over the potholes. | Inaction on pollution harms the planet. | His inaction let the problem grow worse. | After weeks of inaction, the team finally made a plan. | Sometimes inaction is the safest choice, like waiting for help. | Doing nothing when a friend is bullied is a kind of inaction.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Formal. «In-» means not; inaction is the opposite of action. Not the same as «inactive» (an adjective).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Inadvertently means by accident, without meaning to.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life you can inadvertently hurt someone's feelings or share a secret. In online safety, people can inadvertently share their location in a photo. In science, a discovery made inadvertently is found by chance, like penicillin by Alexander Fleming in 1928. It tells the reader the action was not on purpose. Phrases: inadvertently left, inadvertently deleted.
examples from the lessons: I inadvertently deleted my homework. | She inadvertently stepped on the cat's tail. | He inadvertently told her about the surprise party. | Fleming inadvertently discovered penicillin. | Be careful not to inadvertently share where you live online. | The tap was inadvertently left running all night.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; everyday words are «by accident» or «accidentally». Adjective: inadvertent. Long word: in-ad-VER-tent-ly.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An inauguration is a formal ceremony to bring a new leader into office, like a president. 2) An inauguration is also the official opening or start of something new, like a building or a festival.
its sense in the lessons: In citizenship and history lessons, the US president's inauguration happens on 20 January after an election; the president takes an oath of office. In everyday life, a new bridge or school may have an inauguration ceremony with a ribbon cutting. Phrases: inauguration day, inaugural speech, inauguration ceremony.
examples from the lessons: The president gave a speech at his inauguration. | Inauguration Day in the USA is 20 January. | Thousands of people watched the inauguration on TV. | The mayor cut the ribbon at the inauguration of the new library. | At the inauguration, the new leader swore an oath. | The inauguration of the Olympic Games began with fireworks.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Verb: inaugurate; adjective: inaugural (an inaugural speech). Long word: in-aw-gew-RAY-shun.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Inauspicious means showing signs that things will go badly; unlucky or not a good start.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and news, an inauspicious start means things began badly, though they may get better. Writers use it to hint that trouble is coming. In history, some people believed in omens, so they thought certain days or signs were inauspicious. Phrases: an inauspicious start, inauspicious beginnings.
examples from the lessons: The trip had an inauspicious start: the bus broke down. | It was an inauspicious beginning for the new team, losing 5–0. | Rain on the first day of the fair seemed inauspicious. | The Romans thought some bird signs were inauspicious. | Despite inauspicious beginnings, she became a great scientist. | Falling over at the start of the race was inauspicious.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal. «In-» means not; «auspicious» means a good sign. Say «in-aw-SPISH-us».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Inbred describes animals or people whose parents are closely related, such as brother and sister or cousins; this can cause health problems. 2) Inbred also means natural and present since birth, like an inbred sense of fairness. 3) (rude) «Inbred» is used as an insult meaning stupid or narrow-minded; it is unkind.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, inbreeding reduces the variety of genes, so inbred animals, like some pedigree dogs, may get more illnesses. Zoos and farms avoid inbreeding. Most countries have laws against marrying very close relatives. As an insult it is hurtful and should not be used.
examples from the lessons: Inbred dogs may have breathing or hip problems. | The tiny island population of wolves became inbred. | Zoos swap animals to stop them becoming inbred. | She has an inbred love of music. | Calling people inbred is rude and unkind. | Some royal families in the past were inbred.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past form of «inbreed». The noun is inbreeding. The opposite in biology is outbred. Avoid using it as an insult.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Incompatible means not able to work together or exist together, like a game that does not work on your console. 2) People who are incompatible are too different to get along well. 3) (medicine) Incompatible blood types cannot be safely mixed in a transfusion.
its sense in the lessons: In computing, a charger or app can be incompatible with your device. In science, some blood groups are incompatible, so doctors test before a transfusion. In ethics or rules, two ideas are incompatible if both cannot be true at once. In everyday life, friends or flatmates may be incompatible. Phrases: incompatible with, completely incompatible.
examples from the lessons: This game is incompatible with my old tablet. | The charger is incompatible with the new phone. | Cats and mice are usually incompatible pets! | The two plans were incompatible; we had to choose one. | Some blood types are incompatible, so doctors check first. | Bullying is incompatible with our school values.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually followed by «with». Opposite: compatible. Spelling ends in -ible.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Incompletely means not fully or not totally; with some parts missing or not finished.
its sense in the lessons: In science and maths, a problem incompletely solved is missing steps; a substance incompletely burned produces smoke and harmful gases like carbon monoxide, which is a safety point. In everyday life, homework done incompletely means some parts are missing. It is formal.
examples from the lessons: The form was incompletely filled in. | The wood burned incompletely and gave off smoke. | The answer was incompletely explained, so she lost a mark. | The map was incompletely drawn. | The dinosaur skeleton was found incompletely; some bones were missing. | Food cooked incompletely may make you ill.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb of «incomplete». Formal; everyday is «not fully». «In-» means not.

part of speech: verb form (incorporate, incorporates, incorporated, incorporating); adjective (incorporated); abbreviation (Inc.)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Incorporated means included as part of something bigger. 2) (money, law) An incorporated company has been officially set up as a corporation, a legal business; «Inc.» after a company name stands for incorporated. 3) An incorporated town or city has its own official local government.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life you see «Inc.» after US company names, like «Apple Inc.». In school, a teacher may say «your ideas were well incorporated into your essay». In cooking, «incorporate the eggs» means mix them in well. In UK English, «Ltd» or «plc» are used instead of Inc.
examples from the lessons: She incorporated her friends' ideas into the poster. | The flour was incorporated into the mixture. | The company was incorporated in 1998. | «Inc.» stands for incorporated. | The village was incorporated as a city. | Our project incorporated drawings, facts and a quiz.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past form of «incorporate». Abbreviation: Inc. (US); in the UK, Ltd (limited) is similar. Say «in-KOR-por-ay-tid».

part of speech: verb (indent, indents, indented, indenting); noun (an indent, indents)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To indent means to start a line of writing a little way in from the margin, as at the start of a new paragraph. 2) An indent (or indentation) is that space at the start of a line. 3) An indent can also be a small dent or notch in something. 4) (UK, business) An indent is an official order for goods.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons, indenting shows the start of a new paragraph in handwriting. In computing and coding, indenting lines with spaces or tabs shows how code is grouped; in Python indentation is part of the rules. In design, an indented coastline has many bays and inlets.
examples from the lessons: Indent the first line of each new paragraph. | The teacher reminded us to indent our paragraphs. | In Python, you must indent the code inside a loop. | Press Tab to make an indent. | The coastline of Norway is deeply indented with fjords. | There was an indent in the car door where the trolley hit it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun stress: IN-dent; verb stress: in-DENT. The longer noun «indentation» is also common. Do not confuse with «dent», a hollow made by a hit.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Indeterminable means impossible to find out, measure or decide exactly.
its sense in the lessons: In science, some things are indeterminable with our tools, such as the exact age of a very damaged fossil. In maths, if a problem does not give enough information, the answer is indeterminable. In history, the exact birth date of some ancient people is indeterminable. It is a stiff, formal word.
examples from the lessons: The age of the old bone was indeterminable. | Without the price of one apple, the total is indeterminable. | The cause of the fire was indeterminable. | The colour of the faded flag is now indeterminable. | Her accent was of an indeterminable origin. | How many sweets are in the jar is indeterminable without counting.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal. Means «cannot be determined». Close to «indeterminate» but stronger: indeterminable means you cannot find it out at all, indeterminate means not fixed or not clear.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Indeterminate means not exactly known, fixed or clear; vague. 2) (maths) An indeterminate answer or form is one that cannot be worked out as a single value from the information given. 3) (law) An indeterminate sentence is a prison sentence with no fixed end date.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life «a man of indeterminate age» means you cannot tell how old he is. In maths, a problem is indeterminate when there are many possible answers, for example x + y = 10 with no other clue. In science, an indeterminate colour or shape is hard to name. In stories it adds mystery.
examples from the lessons: He was a man of indeterminate age, maybe forty or sixty. | The dog was a brown of indeterminate shade. | The meeting will last an indeterminate time. | With one equation and two unknowns, the answer is indeterminate. | The judge gave an indeterminate sentence. | A creature of indeterminate shape moved in the fog.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal. In maths, «indeterminate» means more than one answer is possible or the value cannot be fixed. Compare indeterminable (cannot be found out).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Inevitability is the fact that something is certain to happen and cannot be avoided. 2) An inevitability is something that will surely happen.
its sense in the lessons: In science, the inevitability of seasons and tides follows from how the Earth moves. In life, ageing and death are inevitabilities; in religion and ethics people think about how to live with them. In stories, a sense of inevitability builds when readers feel a disaster is coming. In maths, an event with probability 1 is certain.
examples from the lessons: There was an inevitability about the result after the first goal. | Growing older is an inevitability. | The inevitability of winter means we must store food. | The story built a sense of inevitability towards the shipwreck. | Change is an inevitability in every school. | Some people accept the inevitability of mistakes and learn from them.
