note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun from «inevitable». Usually uncountable; «an inevitability» for one sure thing. In maths, certainty = probability 1.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Inexperienced means not having much knowledge or skill in something because you have not done it much.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life a new driver, new player or new teacher can be inexperienced; that is normal and everyone starts that way. In safety, inexperienced swimmers or climbers should stay with adults or instructors. In stories, an inexperienced hero learns as the story goes on. Phrases: inexperienced at, inexperienced in, young and inexperienced.
examples from the lessons: The team was young and inexperienced. | An inexperienced sailor should not go out in a storm. | She was inexperienced at cooking but keen to learn. | Inexperienced swimmers should stay in the shallow end. | The inexperienced goalkeeper let in three goals. | Everyone is inexperienced at first.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «In-» means not. Opposite: experienced. Noun: inexperience. Followed by «at» or «in».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Infancy is the time when someone is a baby or very young child. 2) Infancy also means the very early stage of something new, like an idea or invention.
its sense in the lessons: In science and health lessons, infancy is the first stage of human life, roughly the first year or two, when babies grow very fast. In history, «died in infancy» means died as a baby, which was common in the past. In technology and news, «space travel is still in its infancy» means it has only just begun.
examples from the lessons: Many children died in infancy in the 1800s. | During infancy, babies learn to smile, sit and crawl. | The internet was in its infancy when Mum was a child. | His love of drawing started in infancy. | The project is still in its infancy. | Vaccines protect babies during infancy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Related to «infant» (a baby). In law, «infancy» can mean being under 18 in some countries, but in everyday English it means babyhood.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Infinity is the idea of something that has no end and goes on for ever, bigger than any number. 2) (maths) Infinity is shown by the symbol ∞; counting numbers go on to infinity. 3) An infinity of something is an extremely large or endless amount.
its sense in the lessons: In maths lessons, there is no biggest number: whatever number you say, you can add 1, so numbers go on to infinity. Infinity is not a normal number, so you cannot really do sums like infinity minus infinity. In space science, people wonder if the universe goes on to infinity. In stories, «to infinity and beyond» is a famous line from Toy Story. In religion, Christians believe God is infinite.
examples from the lessons: The symbol for infinity is ∞, like a sideways eight. | Numbers go on to infinity. | There is no largest number because counting goes on to infinity. | «To infinity and beyond!» shouted Buzz Lightyear. | Two mirrors facing each other seem to show reflections going to infinity. | The universe may stretch to infinity. | There are an infinity of possible stories.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable. Adjective: infinite. Trap: infinity is not a number you can reach; infinity + 1 is still infinity. Some infinities are bigger than others (a mathematician called Cantor showed this).

meaning for a pupil: 1) To inflame feelings means to make people angrier or more excited. 2) (medicine) When a body part is inflamed, it becomes red, swollen, hot and painful, often from infection or injury. 3) (old) To inflame can mean to set on fire.
its sense in the lessons: In science and health, inflammation is the body's response to injury or germs: a cut that is red and swollen is inflamed. In news, a rude comment can inflame a situation and make an argument worse. In stories, a speech that inflames the crowd starts a riot. Phrases: inflame tensions, inflamed throat.
examples from the lessons: His rude words inflamed the argument. | The splinter made my finger inflamed and sore. | Her throat was inflamed with tonsillitis. | The news inflamed the angry crowd. | Scratching the bite will only inflame it. | The referee's decision inflamed the fans.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Noun: inflammation. Trap: «inflammable» means easily set on fire, the same as «flammable», not the opposite.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Informative means giving useful facts and knowledge.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons, informative writing (non-chronological reports, leaflets, articles) gives facts to the reader, not a story or opinion. A good informative text has headings, facts and clear explanations. In everyday life, a trip to a museum or a documentary can be informative. Phrases: very informative, an informative talk.
examples from the lessons: The museum guide gave an informative talk. | Write an informative leaflet about recycling. | The documentary about sharks was very informative. | An informative text uses facts, not opinions. | Thanks for the informative email. | The poster was colourful and informative.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective from «inform». Informative writing is different from persuasive writing (which tries to change your mind) and narrative writing (stories).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Innocence is the state of not being guilty of a crime or wrongdoing. 2) Innocence also means not knowing about bad or unpleasant things in life, especially as a young child. 3) Innocence can mean being simple and trusting, sometimes too trusting.
its sense in the lessons: In law and citizenship lessons, people are presumed innocent until proven guilty: the court must prove guilt, the person does not have to prove innocence. In stories, a child's innocence can be lost when they see something sad or cruel. In church, Christians speak of innocence before sin in the story of Adam and Eve. Phrases: prove your innocence, loss of innocence, in all innocence.
examples from the lessons: The man proved his innocence in court. | In the UK, you are innocent until proven guilty. | The puppy looked up with innocence after chewing the shoe. | The war took away the children's innocence. | She asked the question in all innocence. | The lawyer fought to show his client's innocence.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Adjective: innocent. Spelling: double n, -ence (not -ance).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Innovation is making new ideas, methods or inventions, or making changes to how things are done. 2) An innovation is a new idea, invention or way of doing something.
its sense in the lessons: In science and technology lessons, innovations like the printing press, the steam engine, vaccines and the internet changed the world. In business and design, innovation means finding better ways to solve problems. In everyday life, schools may have an innovation day or a design-and-make challenge. Phrases: technological innovation, a major innovation.
examples from the lessons: The smartphone was a great innovation. | The printing press was an innovation that spread books. | Our school held an innovation fair for inventions. | Innovation helps us find cleaner energy. | Velcro was an innovation inspired by burrs on a dog. | The company is known for innovation.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable and uncountable. Verb: innovate; adjective: innovative; person: innovator. Double n at the start.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Insectivorous means eating insects as the main food.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, insectivorous animals include bats, swallows, frogs, hedgehogs, anteaters and many lizards. Insectivorous plants, like the Venus flytrap and sundews, catch insects to get nutrients from poor soil. In food chains, insectivores are consumers. The noun is insectivore. Compare herbivorous (plants), carnivorous (meat), omnivorous (both).
examples from the lessons: Bats are insectivorous and eat thousands of insects a night. | The Venus flytrap is an insectivorous plant. | Hedgehogs are insectivorous animals. | Many birds are insectivorous in summer. | Sundews are insectivorous plants that trap flies with sticky hairs. | Insectivorous animals help control pests.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say «in-sek-TIV-or-us». «-vorous» means eating. Noun: insectivore. Spiders are not insects but are often eaten by insectivorous animals too.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Insertion is the act of putting something into something else. 2) An insertion is a thing put in, such as extra words added to a text or an advert in a newspaper.
its sense in the lessons: In computing, an insertion point is where the cursor is when you type. In English, an insertion mark (a caret, ^) shows where to add a missing word. In science and medicine, the insertion of a tube or needle is done carefully by doctors. In maths and computing, insertion sort is a simple way to put a list in order.
examples from the lessons: The doctor explained the insertion of the drip. | Use a caret mark for the insertion of a missing word. | Click to place the insertion point. | Insertion sort puts cards in order one at a time. | The insertion of the key opened the old box. | The editor made an insertion in the second paragraph.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable and uncountable. Verb: insert. Say «in-SUR-shun».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Insufficiency means not having enough of something. 2) (medicine) Insufficiency is when a body part does not work well enough, like heart insufficiency.
its sense in the lessons: In maths problems, an insufficiency of information means you cannot get the answer. In medicine, doctors use it for organs not working enough. In everyday life it is a formal word for a shortage. Phrases: an insufficiency of, kidney insufficiency.
examples from the lessons: The plan failed because of an insufficiency of money. | The doctor said he had a heart valve insufficiency. | There is an insufficiency of data to prove it. | An insufficiency of water made the plants wilt. | The judge noted the insufficiency of the evidence. | Insufficiency of vitamin D can weaken bones.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; everyday words are «lack» or «shortage». Adjective: insufficient. In maths, «insufficient information» means the problem cannot be solved as given.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An insurgent is a person who fights against the government or ruling power of their country, often with weapons. 2) Insurgent as an adjective means rebelling or rising up against those in power. 3) Insurgent can also describe a new challenger rising against an old leader, like an insurgent party in politics.
its sense in the lessons: In news and history lessons, insurgents fight in civil wars or against occupying forces. Whether someone is called an insurgent, a rebel or a freedom fighter can depend on who is telling the story, so careful readers notice the words chosen. In politics, an insurgent campaign challenges the established leaders.
examples from the lessons: Insurgents attacked the army base. | The government said the insurgents had been defeated. | The insurgent groups controlled the hills. | Some called them insurgents; others called them freedom fighters. | The insurgent candidate surprised everyone by winning. | History is full of insurgent movements.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Noun: insurgency (the uprising). Similar to «rebel». The word chosen often shows the speaker's view of the fighters.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Integral means necessary and important as a part of a whole: you cannot have the whole without it. 2) Integral also means built in, made as one piece with something. 3) (maths, advanced) An integral is a calculation in calculus that finds things like the area under a curve.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life «an integral part of the team» means a key member. In design, an integral handle is part of the object, not stuck on. In secondary-school and university maths, integrals are part of calculus, invented by Newton and Leibniz. In younger maths, «integer» (a whole number) is a different but related word.
examples from the lessons: Practice is an integral part of learning music. | She is an integral member of the choir. | The bike has an integral lock. | Water is integral to life. | In calculus, an integral finds the area under a curve. | Kindness is integral to our school values.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say «IN-tuh-grul» (also «in-TEG-rul»). Do not confuse with «integer» (a whole number) or «integrity» (honesty). The calculus sense is advanced maths.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Intensely means very strongly, deeply or extremely.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, «she stared intensely» shows deep concentration or strong feeling. In everyday life, things can be intensely hot, bright, boring or annoying. In science, light or heat can be intensely strong. It adds force to describing words.
examples from the lessons: The sun was intensely hot at noon. | He stared intensely at the chessboard. | She trained intensely for the race. | The cheese smelled intensely of garlic. | They argued intensely about the rules. | The film was intensely scary.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from «intense». Do not confuse with «intensively» (in a very concentrated, organised way, like intensive farming) or «intently» (with full attention).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Intentional means done on purpose, deliberately, not by accident.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and school, the difference between intentional and accidental matters: an intentional push is a choice, an accidental bump is not. In sport, an intentional foul gets a bigger punishment. In law and ethics, intention changes how wrong an act is. Being intentional can also be positive, like intentional kindness.
examples from the lessons: Was the trip intentional or an accident? | The referee gave a red card for an intentional handball. | The spelling mistake was intentional, to make the joke work. | Intentional kindness can make someone's day. | The teacher asked if the damage was intentional. | The fire was intentional, said the police.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb: intentionally. Opposite: unintentional or accidental. Noun: intention.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To interbreed means for animals or plants of different kinds, breeds or groups to mate and have young together.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, members of the same species can interbreed and have fertile young; that is one way scientists define a species. Different species usually cannot, or their young are infertile, like a mule from a horse and a donkey. Scientists found that early modern humans and Neanderthals interbred, so many people today carry a little Neanderthal DNA.
examples from the lessons: Lions and tigers can interbreed in zoos, but not in the wild. | Horses and donkeys interbreed to produce mules. | Wolves and dogs can interbreed. | Neanderthals and modern humans interbred long ago. | Farmers interbred cattle to get better milk. | Two species that cannot interbreed are kept apart by nature.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular past: interbred (not «interbreeded»). «Inter-» means between. Noun: interbreeding.

part of speech: verb (interlock, interlocks, interlocked, interlocking); noun (an interlock, interlocks — rarer)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To fit or lock firmly together, with parts of one thing going into gaps in another. 2) To be closely joined so that one thing depends on another. 3) (noun) A device or knitted fabric whose parts are linked together, such as a safety lock on a machine or interlock cotton.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and craft lessons, jigsaw pieces, gears, cogs and building bricks interlock; in science, puzzle-like shapes show how parts fit together; in design and technology, interlocking joints hold wood without nails. In stories, interlocking fingers or arms show closeness or holding tight; interlocking plans or events show things that depend on each other. Phrases: interlocking pieces, interlocking rings, interlock fingers.
examples from the lessons: The jigsaw pieces interlock perfectly. | The Olympic flag has five interlocking rings. | She interlocked her fingers and stretched her arms. | Lego bricks interlock so the tower does not fall. | The teeth of the two gears interlock and turn together. | The stories in the book interlock, so you meet the same people again. | The washing machine has a door interlock, so it will not open while it spins. | My granny's cardigan is made of soft interlock cotton.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: interlocked, interlocking. Usually without an object («the pieces interlock») or with «with» («one piece interlocks with the next»). Do not confuse with «interlocutor» (a person you talk with). Stress: in-ter-LOCK for the verb, IN-ter-lock for the noun.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) A person you are talking with in a conversation. 2) (formal) A person or group that talks on behalf of others, especially in official talks between countries or groups. 3) (old use) The person in the middle of an old-style stage show who asked the questions and led the jokes.
its sense in the lessons: A stiff, formal word met in exam passages, news and history books about talks and peace deals; in everyday life people say «the person I was talking to». In stories it tells the reader there is a two-way talk, often serious or polite. Phrases: my interlocutor, a reliable interlocutor, a trusted interlocutor.
examples from the lessons: My interlocutor nodded but said nothing. | In a good conversation, you listen to your interlocutor. | The government wanted a trusted interlocutor to speak with the rebels. | The writer describes her interlocutor as calm and patient. | Be polite to your interlocutor, even when you disagree. | In the debate, each pupil faced an interlocutor from the other team. | The old stage show had an interlocutor who asked silly questions.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: an interlocutor, interlocutors. Formal; in speech say «the person you're talking to». Stress: in-ter-LOK-yoo-tor. Not the same as «interlock» or «interpreter» (an interpreter translates between languages).

meaning for a pupil: 1) The person who is asked questions in an interview, for example for a job, a school place, a newspaper or a TV programme. 2) A person who answers the questions in a survey or research study.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons pupils write interview questions and act as interviewer and interviewee; in history and science projects they interview grandparents or experts; in news reports the interviewee is the person speaking. Phrases: the interviewee said, put the interviewee at ease, job interviewee.
examples from the lessons: The interviewee sat down and smiled nervously. | Our interviewee for the school magazine was the head teacher. | Each interviewee answered the same five questions. | The reporter thanked the interviewee at the end. | In the role play, Sam was the interviewer and I was the interviewee. | The interviewee told us what school was like in 1960. | A good interviewer lets the interviewee finish speaking.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: an interviewee, interviewees. The ending «-ee» means the person something is done to (employee, trainee), while «-er» means the person who does it: the interviewer asks, the interviewee answers. Stress on the last syllable: in-ter-view-EE.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The person who asks the questions in an interview, for example on TV, radio, in a newspaper or for a job. 2) A person who asks people questions for a survey or a study.
its sense in the lessons: In English and media lessons pupils play the interviewer, plan open questions and take notes; in history projects they interview older relatives. In news and stories the interviewer leads the conversation and can be friendly or tough. Phrases: a TV interviewer, the interviewer asked, a tough interviewer.
examples from the lessons: The interviewer asked me why I wanted to join the club. | A famous interviewer spoke to the prime minister on the radio. | As the interviewer, you should ask open questions. | The interviewer wrote down every answer. | Our class interviewer asked the firefighter about his job. | The interviewer was kind, so I stopped feeling nervous. | A survey interviewer knocked on our door and asked about recycling.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: an interviewer, interviewers. «-er» = the one who asks; «-ee» = the one who answers (interviewee). Spelling: «interview» + «-er», with «ie» as in «view».

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a very close, detailed way; very well, from long experience. 2) In a very close and personal way, as between close family, best friends or partners. 3) Very closely connected, so that one thing affects the other.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography texts it means «very closely» («intimately connected»); in stories it shows how well someone knows a place or a person. Phrases: know something intimately, intimately connected, intimately linked.
examples from the lessons: The old fisherman knew the river intimately. | Weather and farming are intimately linked. | She knew every corner of the castle intimately. | The two friends talked intimately by the fire. | Plants and bees are intimately connected. | The guide knew the mountain paths intimately after forty years. | Our health is intimately tied to what we eat and how we sleep.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from «intimate» + «-ly». It is neutral in «know something intimately» (very well), but used about two people it can mean a romantic relationship, so in school writing «closely» is often safer. Stress: IN-ti-mate-ly.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Not being willing to accept people whose ideas, beliefs, habits or ways of life are different from yours. 2) (health) When your body cannot deal well with a certain food or medicine and it makes you feel unwell. 3) Not being able to bear something, such as heat, cold or pain.
its sense in the lessons: In citizenship and religious education it is the opposite of tolerance and respect: lessons explain religious and racial intolerance and why it hurts people. In health and science, food intolerances (lactose intolerance, gluten intolerance) are discussed, and school kitchens check them. Phrases: religious intolerance, lactose intolerance, intolerance of, zero intolerance (wrong; the phrase is «zero tolerance»).
examples from the lessons: Intolerance can lead to bullying and unfairness. | The school stands against racism and intolerance. | My brother has lactose intolerance, so he drinks oat milk. | A food intolerance is not the same as an allergy. | History shows how religious intolerance drove many families from their homes. | Grandad has an intolerance to heat and stays inside at midday. | We learned that kindness is the answer to intolerance.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable for the attitude; countable for a body's reaction («an intolerance to wheat»). Opposite: tolerance. Trap: a food intolerance usually causes discomfort like tummy ache, while an allergy involves the immune system and can be dangerous; they are different. Adjective: intolerant.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To say something slowly in a steady, flat voice, almost like singing on one note. 2) (church) To sing or chant words of a prayer or service on one note, as a priest or choir does.
its sense in the lessons: In stories it shows a serious, slow, sometimes boring or spooky voice: a wizard intones a spell, a teacher intones the rules. In church life, priests and choirs intone prayers and psalms. Phrases: intone a prayer, intone the words, intoned solemnly.
examples from the lessons: The priest intoned the opening prayer. | «Silence in the library,» the librarian intoned. | The wizard raised his staff and intoned a spell. | The monks intoned the psalm in a low voice. | The robot intoned, «Please enter the password.» | Mr Shaw intoned the list of names without looking up. | The choir intoned the same note again and again.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: intoned, intoning. It describes the way of speaking, not just speaking: use it for slow, steady, solemn voices. Related noun: intonation (the rise and fall of the voice), which in language lessons means something wider than «intone».

part of speech: adjective (inundated); past form of the verb inundate (inundate, inundates, inundated, inundating)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Getting so many things, like letters, calls or jobs, that it is hard to deal with them all. 2) Flooded; covered with a large amount of water.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and science lessons it means flooded (fields inundated by the river); in everyday life and news it means overwhelmed by too much of something (inundated with requests). Phrases: inundated with, inundated by.
examples from the lessons: The school office was inundated with phone calls after the snow day. | After the heavy rain, the fields were inundated. | The vet was inundated with sick puppies. | Our class was inundated with entries for the poetry prize. | The town was inundated when the river burst its banks. | Santa is inundated with letters every December. | The shop was inundated with customers on the first day of the sale.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually passive: «be inundated with/by». More formal than «flooded» or «swamped». Pronounced IN-un-day-tid. Not connected with «in a date».

part of speech: verb form (present participle of invade: invade, invades, invaded, invading); adjective (invading)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Entering a country or place by force, with an army, to take control of it. 2) Coming into a place in large numbers, often in an unwanted way, like insects or weeds. 3) Getting into the body and causing harm, as germs do. 4) Going into someone's private space or life without being wanted.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons: Romans, Vikings and Normans invading Britain; in science: germs invading the body and plants invading habitats (invasive species); in everyday life: «you're invading my space». In stories, an invading army brings danger and fear. Phrases: invading army, invading forces, invading my privacy, invading germs.
examples from the lessons: The Vikings were invading the coast of England. | The invading army crossed the river at dawn. | White blood cells fight invading germs. | Ants are invading our kitchen again. | Stop reading my diary, you're invading my privacy! | Russia's army invading Ukraine in 2022 was condemned by most countries at the UN. | Cane toads are invading new parts of Australia. | The weeds are invading the vegetable patch.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: drop the «e» of «invade» before «-ing»: invading. Person: invader; noun: invasion. «Invading» often goes with an army, a country or germs as the subject; it is a strong, negative word.

part of speech: noun (an inventory, inventories); verb (inventory, inventories, inventoried, inventorying — mostly US)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A complete list of all the things in a place, such as goods in a shop or items in a house. 2) All the goods a shop or company has in store, ready to sell (stock). 3) (games) The list or box of things a player carries in a video game. 4) (verb) To make a full list of things.
its sense in the lessons: In maths it appears in shop and stock problems (counting, adding and taking away items); in business and everyday life shops «take inventory»; in video games your inventory holds your tools and treasure. In stories, a character may make an inventory of what they have when lost or shipwrecked. Phrases: take (an) inventory, inventory list, in the inventory.
examples from the lessons: The shop takes an inventory of everything on the shelves each January. | Robinson made an inventory of the things he saved from the wreck. | My inventory is full, so I can't pick up the sword. | The library inventory shows 3,000 books. | Before we moved, Mum made an inventory of the furniture. | The toy shop's inventory ran low before Christmas. | If the inventory had 120 pens and 45 were sold, 75 are left.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: an inventory, inventories (y → ies). UK English often uses «stock» for goods; «inventory» is more US. Stress: IN-ven-tor-y (UK often IN-ven-tree). Do not confuse with «invention». In maths problems it is the starting amount of items, usually changed by sales (subtract) and deliveries (add).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Turning something upside down or the other way round. 2) (maths) Changing to the opposite or reverse, such as swapping the top and bottom of a fraction, or using the inverse operation. 3) (grammar) Changing the usual order of words, like putting the verb before the subject in a question («Are you…?»). 4) (weather) A temperature inversion: a layer of warm air over cold air near the ground that traps fog and smoke. 5) (music) Changing the order of the notes in a chord.
its sense in the lessons: In maths it links to inverse operations (addition and subtraction undo each other) and to flipping fractions when dividing. In English grammar, questions and phrases like «Never have I seen…» use inversion. In science and geography, temperature inversions cause smog. On roller coasters, an inversion is a loop that turns riders upside down. Phrases: temperature inversion, word order inversion.
examples from the lessons: The roller coaster has three inversions. | To divide by a fraction, we use inversion: 1/2 becomes 2/1. | «Are you ready?» uses inversion of the subject and the verb. | A temperature inversion trapped the smoke over the city. | The poem uses inversion to make the rhyme fit. | The pianist played the chord in its first inversion. | Inversion of colours turns black into white on the screen.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable or uncountable. Verb: invert; related adjective and noun: inverse. Trap: in maths «inverse» is the usual word for the opposite operation; «inversion» is the act of turning it over. Do not mix up with «invasion».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) A chemical element (symbol I, number 53) that forms dark purple-black crystals and a violet gas when heated. 2) A brown liquid made with iodine that is put on cuts to kill germs. 3) (health) A mineral the body needs in tiny amounts to make hormones, found in fish, seaweed, milk and iodised salt.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons it appears in the periodic table and in the starch test: iodine solution turns from orange-brown to blue-black when starch is present. In health it is a nutrient (iodised salt); in first aid an antiseptic. Phrases: iodine solution, iodine test, iodised salt.
examples from the lessons: We dropped iodine on the bread and it turned blue-black, so it has starch. | The nurse dabbed iodine on my grazed knee. | Iodine is element number 53 on the periodic table. | Seaweed contains a lot of iodine. | Our salt says «iodised» on the packet. | When heated, iodine gives off a purple vapour. | Iodine stains are hard to wash out of clothes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Pronounced EYE-oh-deen or EYE-oh-dyne. Its symbol is a capital I (one letter). Safety: iodine solution is for use on skin or in experiments, never to drink. Adjective: iodised (UK) / iodized (US).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) An atom or a small group of atoms that has an electric charge because it has gained or lost one or more electrons. 2) A positive ion has lost electrons; a negative ion has gained electrons.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons ions explain how salt dissolves in water, how batteries work and why salty water conducts electricity. In everyday adverts you hear about «lithium-ion batteries» in phones and laptops. Phrases: positive ion, negative ion, lithium-ion battery, sodium ion.
examples from the lessons: Salt is made of sodium ions and chloride ions. | A lithium-ion battery powers my tablet. | An ion has an electric charge. | When an atom loses an electron, it becomes a positive ion. | Salty water conducts electricity because it contains ions. | Our science teacher drew the ions as little circles with plus and minus signs. | Some air purifiers claim to release negative ions.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: an ion, ions; «an», because it begins with a vowel sound. Pronounced EYE-on (two syllables). The word is also a suffix in many words (-ion: action, creation), but alone it is the science word. Claims that «negative ions» make you healthier are mostly advertising, not proven science.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A short written note that says you owe someone money; it stands for «I owe you» because the letters sound like those words. 2) (informal) A promise to do something or pay back later.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and money lessons IOUs show debt: the note means someone must pay later. In everyday life children write IOUs for pocket money or favours, and in stories an IOU can be a clue to a debt. Phrases: write an IOU, an IOU for £5, give someone an IOU.
examples from the lessons: I didn't have any money, so I gave my sister an IOU for £2. | Dad found an old IOU in his wallet. | The pirate's map came with an IOU for ten gold coins. | My birthday card had an IOU for a trip to the cinema. | If you write an IOU, you must pay it back. | Tom has three IOUs from his brother for chores. | An IOU for $10 means the writer owes $10.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually written in capitals: IOU, plural IOUs. «An IOU», because the first sound is «eye». It is a pun: I-O-U sounds like «I owe you». In maths problems, an IOU counts as money owed, so it is taken away from what the writer has.

part of speech: verb (isolate, isolates, isolated, isolating); noun (an isolate, isolates — science, rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To keep a person or thing apart from others, especially to stop a disease spreading. 2) To separate one thing from a mixture or group so you can study it. 3) To make someone feel alone and left out. 4) (maths) To get one letter or number on its own on one side of an equation.
its sense in the lessons: In health lessons and during illness people isolate at home; in science pupils isolate a variable to make a fair test, or scientists isolate a germ; in maths, «isolate x» means get x by itself. In stories and PSHE, being isolated means lonely, and isolating someone on purpose is a kind of bullying. Phrases: self-isolate, isolate the problem, feel isolated, isolated village.
examples from the lessons: The doctor told him to isolate at home until his fever went away. | Scientists isolated the germ that caused the illness. | To find x, isolate it on one side of the equation. | In a fair test we isolate one variable and keep the others the same. | Leaving a classmate out of every game can isolate them. | The snowstorm isolated the village for three days. | The farm is isolated, ten miles from the nearest shop.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: isolated, isolating. Pronounced EYE-so-late. Adjective: isolated (alone, far away); noun: isolation. «Self-isolate» became a common word during the COVID-19 pandemic.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (geography) A narrow strip of land with sea on both sides that joins two larger pieces of land. 2) (science) A narrow part joining two bigger parts in the body or in a plant.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons pupils learn the Isthmus of Panama (joining North and South America, cut by the Panama Canal), the Isthmus of Suez and the Isthmus of Corinth; New Zealand's Auckland stands on an isthmus. It is the opposite idea of a strait (narrow sea joining two seas). Phrases: the Isthmus of Panama, a narrow isthmus.
examples from the lessons: The Isthmus of Panama joins North America and South America. | Auckland is built on a narrow isthmus. | A canal was dug across the isthmus so ships could pass. | On the map, the isthmus looks like a thin bridge of land. | The castle stood at the end of a rocky isthmus. | At high tide the isthmus almost disappears under the waves. | An isthmus joins two lands; a strait joins two seas.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: an isthmus, isthmuses (rarely isthmi). Pronounced IS-mus — the «th» is silent in most accents. Trap: do not confuse with «peninsula» (land almost surrounded by water) or «strait» (narrow strip of water).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Printed letters that slope to the right, like handwriting, used to show titles or to make a word stand out. 2) (Italic) To do with ancient Italy and its peoples and languages.
its sense in the lessons: In English and computing lessons pupils use italics for book titles, foreign words and emphasis, and press Ctrl+I (Cmd+I) to make text italic. In stories, italics often show thoughts, dreams or a word said with stress. Phrases: in italics, italic font, italic handwriting.
examples from the lessons: The title of the book is printed in italics. | Press Ctrl+I to make your word italic. | In the story, the girl's thoughts are in italics. | My teacher writes in a neat italic hand. | Use italics for the names of ships, like the Titanic. | The word «really» was in italics to show it was said loudly. | Italic letters lean to the right.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «In italics» uses the plural. Opposite: roman (upright) type; also compare bold. When writing by hand, underline what would be in italics in print. Comes from «Italy», where this type was invented around 1500.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (maths) The Roman numeral for 9: I (1) before X (10) means 10 minus 1. 2) Used in names of kings, popes, chapters and events, like Charles IX or Super Bowl IX, read as «the ninth» or «nine». 3) It is not an English word on its own; as small letters «ix» it is just two letters.
its sense in the lessons: In maths lessons Roman numerals teach place and subtraction: putting a smaller numeral before a bigger one means subtract. On clocks, in book chapters and in history (King Louis IX of France) you meet IX. Phrases: Chapter IX, Louis IX.
examples from the lessons: IX means 9 in Roman numerals. | Chapter IX is the scariest part of the book. | King Louis IX of France lived in the 1200s. | On our old clock, the 9 is written as IX. | X minus I gives IX, which is 9. | Can you write 19 in Roman numerals? It is XIX. | Pope Pius IX is read «Pope Pius the Ninth».
note for the reader of a maths problem: Written in capitals: IX. Trap: some old clocks and puzzles show 9 as VIIII, but the usual form is IX; never IIX for 8 (8 is VIII). In maths, IX = 9, XI = 11: the order changes the value. Read «Henry IX» as «Henry the Ninth».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (religion) An ancient religion from India that teaches non-violence to all living things, honesty, and freeing the soul by living simply. 2) Jains follow the teachings of Mahavira and earlier great teachers called Tirthankaras.
its sense in the lessons: In religious education lessons Jainism is studied with Hinduism, Buddhism and Sikhism. Jains believe in ahimsa (never harming any living being), so many are strict vegetarians and some monks sweep the path so as not to step on insects. The festival of Diwali is also important to Jains. Phrases: follower of Jainism, Jain temple.
examples from the lessons: Jainism began in India over 2,500 years ago. | Jainism teaches respect for every living thing. | Many people who follow Jainism do not eat meat, fish or eggs. | Jains believe that the soul can be freed from the cycle of rebirth. | There is a beautiful Jain temple in Leicester. | In RE we compared Jainism and Buddhism. | Ahimsa, or non-violence, is the heart of Jainism.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Written with a capital J: Jainism. A follower is a Jain; the adjective is also Jain. Pronounced JINE-iz-um (rhymes with «mine»). Uncountable. Say «Jains believe…», as the beliefs belong to the faith.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (history) A soldier in the elite foot army of the Ottoman (Turkish) sultans, from about the 1300s to 1826. 2) (rare) A loyal follower or guard who does whatever a powerful leader wants.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons about the Ottoman Empire, the janissaries were the sultan's trained soldiers; boys from Christian families in the Balkans were taken and trained for this army, which is a sad and important part of the story. They also had famous military bands. Phrases: the Janissary corps, a janissary band.
examples from the lessons: The janissaries guarded the Ottoman sultan. | Janissary bands played loud drums and cymbals. | Many janissaries were taken from their families as boys. | The sultan closed down the janissaries in 1826. | Our history book shows a janissary with a tall white hat. | The janissaries were famous for their discipline. | Some dictators surround themselves with janissaries who never question them.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a janissary, janissaries (y → ies). Often with a capital J. Also spelled «janizary». Pronounced JAN-i-ser-ee. A historical word; in modern talk it is used only as a strong image.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (Java) A large island of Indonesia, where the capital Jakarta is. 2) (US, slang) Coffee. 3) (Java) A computer programming language used to make apps and programs. 4) A kind of coffee grown on the island of Java.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons Java is a crowded volcanic island in Indonesia. In computing, Java is a well-known programming language (different from JavaScript). In American everyday talk, «a cup of java» means coffee. Phrases: a cup of java, Java programming, the island of Java.
examples from the lessons: Java is one of the most crowded islands in the world. | Jakarta is on the island of Java. | «Grab me a cup of java,» said the detective. | My cousin writes games in Java. | Java has many active volcanoes. | Java and JavaScript are two different programming languages. | Mum likes strong java in the morning.
note for the reader of a maths problem: With a capital J for the island and the language; lowercase «java» for coffee (US slang). Trap: Java and JavaScript are not the same language, despite the names. Pronounced JAH-vuh.

part of speech: adjective (jobless); noun (the jobless — people without jobs)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Without a paid job; unemployed. 2) (the jobless) People who do not have jobs.
its sense in the lessons: In news and economics lessons «jobless» appears in headlines (jobless figures, jobless rate). In stories about families it shows money worries and hard times; children learn that losing a job is not a person's fault and that help exists. Phrases: jobless rate, jobless figures, left jobless.
examples from the lessons: Many people were left jobless when the factory closed. | The jobless rate went down this year. | Dad was jobless for three months, then found new work. | The charity helps the jobless find training. | The news said the number of jobless people had risen. | Being jobless can be very stressful for a family. | She was jobless but used the time to learn new skills.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Jobless» is a news word; in everyday talk people say «out of work» or «unemployed». «The jobless» takes a plural verb: «The jobless need help». Related: unemployment.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (US, slang) A young person, especially a boy, who loves sport and is part of the sporty, popular group at school, sometimes shown as not interested in study. 2) (UK, slang, can be offensive) A Scottish person, especially a Scottish man; often «Jock». 3) (informal) Short for a disc jockey (DJ) or a jockey who rides racehorses. 4) (informal) Short for a jockstrap, a support worn by boys and men in sport.
its sense in the lessons: In American school stories and films, jocks, nerds and other groups are stereotypes; stories often show that people are more than their label. In the UK «Jock» as a nickname for Scots can be friendly between friends but rude from strangers. Phrases: a dumb jock (rude stereotype), radio jock, shock jock.
examples from the lessons: In the film, the jocks sat at their own table in the cafeteria. | He's a jock, but he also loves poetry. | The radio jock played my favourite song. | Calling someone a «dumb jock» is unkind and untrue. | The football jocks were training on the field. | «Hey, Jock!» shouted his English cousin, and he didn't like it. | A shock jock says rude things on the radio to get attention.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a jock, jocks. Slang. «Jock» for a Scot is capitalised and can be offensive. The sporty-student meaning is mostly US and Canadian. Trap: a «jockey» (rider of a racehorse) is a different full word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (law) To do with judges, law courts and the way the law is applied. 2) (law) Done by a court or a judge, as in a judicial decision. 3) (law) The judicial branch of government is the part made up of courts, separate from the lawmakers and the government.
its sense in the lessons: In citizenship lessons about how a country works: the three branches of government are the legislative (makes laws), the executive (runs the country) and the judicial (courts that judge cases). In the news: judicial review, judicial system. Phrases: judicial system, judicial review, judicial branch, judicial decision.
examples from the lessons: The judicial system makes sure trials are fair. | In the USA, the Supreme Court leads the judicial branch. | The judge made a judicial decision. | A judicial review checks if the government followed the law. | Judges must be free from pressure, so the judicial system is independent. | We drew a poster of the three branches: legislative, executive and judicial. | The case went through a long judicial process.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective only; used before a noun. Pronounced joo-DISH-ul. Trap: «judicious» means wise and sensible, not about courts. Related: judge, judiciary (all the judges together).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) A particular moment or point in time, especially an important one in a series of events. 2) (formal) A place where two things join; a joint or junction.
its sense in the lessons: A stiff exam and news word: «at this juncture» means «at this point». In history writing it marks a turning point; in stories it signals that a decision must be made. Phrases: at this juncture, at a critical juncture, at that juncture.
examples from the lessons: At this juncture, we should stop and think. | The war had reached a critical juncture. | At that juncture, the captain decided to turn the ship around. | The bone broke at the juncture with the knee. | It is too early, at this juncture, to say who will win. | The story reaches a key juncture when the map is stolen. | The two roads meet at a busy juncture.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a juncture, junctures. Formal: in normal speech say «at this point» or «now». Do not confuse with «junction» (a place where roads or railways meet), though they share a root. Pronounced JUNK-chur.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (history) The title of the emperor of Germany from 1871 to 1918, and earlier of the emperors of Austria and the Holy Roman Empire. 2) (the Kaiser) Usually means Kaiser Wilhelm II, the German emperor during the First World War. 3) (US) A kaiser roll: a round, crusty bread roll.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons about the First World War, the Kaiser was the ruler of Germany who fought against Britain, France and their allies; posters and cartoons of the time often made fun of him. The word comes from the Roman name «Caesar», like the Russian «tsar». Phrases: the Kaiser, Kaiser Wilhelm, a kaiser roll.
examples from the lessons: The Kaiser ruled Germany during the First World War. | Kaiser Wilhelm II had a famous curled moustache. | After the war ended in 1918, the Kaiser gave up his throne. | The word «kaiser» comes from «Caesar». | British soldiers sang songs mocking the Kaiser. | In New York, Grandpa ate a kaiser roll with cheese. | The tsar of Russia and the Kaiser of Germany were cousins.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital K when it is a title for one person: the Kaiser, Kaiser Wilhelm. Pronounced KY-zer (rhymes with «wiser»). Related titles: Caesar (Roman), tsar or czar (Russian).

part of speech: verb (kidnap, kidnaps, kidnapped, kidnapping — US also kidnaped, kidnaping); noun (a kidnap, kidnaps — UK)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (law) To take a person away by force or by tricking them, and keep them against their will, often to demand money. 2) (noun, UK) The crime of kidnapping.
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons children learn to stay with trusted adults, never go off with strangers, and tell someone if anyone tries to take them; in stories and news, kidnapping is a serious crime and often the start of an adventure or mystery. In law, kidnapping is punished with long prison sentences. Phrases: kidnap someone, a kidnap attempt, held for ransom.
examples from the lessons: The villain planned to kidnap the princess. | Never get into a stranger's car, even if they say your mum sent them. | The police rescued the kidnapped boy within a day. | The kidnappers asked for a ransom of one million dollars. | In the book, pirates kidnap the hero and take him to sea. | The news reported a failed kidnap attempt. | My little brother «kidnapped» my teddy, but I got it back!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: double «p» in kidnapped, kidnapping, kidnapper in UK English (US sometimes single «p»). A kidnapper is the criminal; the money demanded is a ransom. Joking use about toys or pets is common among children. Not related to «kid» meaning a goat in its use today, though «kid» = child.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A powder made from the tiny hairs on the flowers of the cannabis plant, which is a drug and is illegal in many countries. 2) (old, North Africa and Middle East) A dreamy, lazy, peaceful feeling, as if half asleep.
its sense in the lessons: A rare word that children may meet in news or drug-safety lessons; drug education teaches that cannabis can harm a young person's growing brain and is illegal for children everywhere. In old travel books «kef» meant a pleasant dreamy rest. Phrases: smoke kief (drugs).
examples from the lessons: Kief is made from the cannabis plant. | The police found kief and other drugs in the car. | Cannabis and kief can harm young people's brains. | In an old travel book, the writer lay in the sun in a state of kef. | Our drug-safety lesson explained why cannabis products are illegal for children. | Kief is not something to try or touch.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Spellings: kief, kif, keef, kef. Pronounced KEEF. It is linked to illegal drugs, so it is a word to understand, not to use. From Arabic «kayf» (pleasure).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) A unit of power equal to 1,000 watts, written kW. 2) It measures how fast an electrical machine uses or makes energy.
its sense in the lessons: In science and maths lessons pupils convert units (1 kW = 1,000 W) and work out energy use; electricity bills charge for kilowatt-hours (kWh): using 1 kilowatt for 1 hour. Kettles, heaters and car engines are rated in kilowatts. Phrases: kilowatt-hour (kWh), a 2-kilowatt heater.
examples from the lessons: A kilowatt is 1,000 watts. | Our kettle uses 3 kilowatts of power. | Electricity is sold in kilowatt-hours. | The solar panels on our roof make about 4 kilowatts on a sunny day. | 2.5 kilowatts is the same as 2,500 watts. | The electric car's motor is rated at 150 kilowatts. | A 1-kilowatt heater on for 3 hours uses 3 kilowatt-hours.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Symbol: kW (small k, capital W). Trap: a kilowatt (kW) is power (how fast); a kilowatt-hour (kWh) is energy (how much). In maths problems: multiply kW by hours to get kWh; multiply by 1,000 to get watts.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A special skill or clever way of doing something, often one that is hard to explain. 2) A habit or tendency to do something, often by accident, like «a knack for getting into trouble».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and stories it describes a natural talent (a knack for drawing, a knack for making friends). In school, teachers say «you'll get the knack of it» when learning long division or skipping rope. Phrases: have a knack for, get the knack of, there's a knack to it.
examples from the lessons: She has a knack for solving puzzles. | Opening this jar is easy once you get the knack. | There's a knack to riding a unicycle. | My dog has a knack for finding mud. | Tom has a knack for making people laugh. | I finally got the knack of long division. | Grandma has a knack with plants; everything she grows is huge.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable, but nearly always «a knack» or «the knack». The «k» at the start is silent: say NAK. Followed by «for» + noun/-ing, or «of» + -ing in «get the knack of».

part of speech: noun (a KO, KOs); verb (KO, KO's, KO'd, KO'ing — informal) — abbreviation
meaning for a pupil: 1) (sport) Short for «knockout»: in boxing, hitting the other fighter so hard they cannot get up and the fight ends. 2) (informal) To knock someone out; also to make someone fall asleep or very tired. 3) In games and video games, «KO» means a character has been beaten. 4) (Ko) A surname, for example in Korea and China (a name).
its sense in the lessons: Children meet KO in video games and cartoons about fighting games («K.O.!» on the screen), and in sports news about boxing. In everyday slang, «I was totally KO'd» means very tired. Phrases: a KO punch, win by KO, TKO (technical knockout).
examples from the lessons: The boxer won by KO in the third round. | «K.O.!» flashed on the game screen. | That long walk totally KO'd me. | A TKO means the referee stopped the fight. | The champion's KO punch was famous. | My little sister was KO'd on the sofa by eight o'clock. | In the cartoon, the robot got KO'd by a giant rubber duck.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually written in capitals: KO or K.O.; plural KOs. Pronounced «kay-oh». It is a shortened form, not a full English word. Safety note: real knockouts in boxing can hurt the brain; it is not a playground game.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (South Africa) A small hill, usually rocky, standing alone on flat open land (the veld). 2) It comes from Afrikaans and Dutch, meaning «little head».
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons about southern Africa, kopjes are small rocky hills on the grasslands, where lions and other animals rest; in history lessons about the Boer War, soldiers fought around kopjes. A similar word is «tor» on Dartmoor. Phrases: a rocky kopje.
examples from the lessons: The lions lay on top of the kopje, watching the plain. | A kopje is a small rocky hill in South Africa. | From the kopje, we could see the whole valley. | The soldiers hid behind a kopje. | Baboons climbed over the rocks of the kopje. | The safari truck stopped near a kopje at sunset.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a kopje, kopjes. Pronounced KOP-ee. The «j» is silent, as in Dutch and Afrikaans. Also spelled «koppie». A South African English word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (the Kremlin) The old walled fortress in the centre of Moscow, where the President of Russia has his offices. 2) (the Kremlin) Used in the news to mean the Russian government itself. 3) (a kremlin) Any old Russian walled fortress in the middle of a city.
its sense in the lessons: In history and current-events lessons: the Kremlin with its red walls and towers is beside Red Square; news reports say «the Kremlin said…» to mean the Russian government, for example about Russia's invasion of Ukraine. Phrases: the Kremlin said, Kremlin walls, inside the Kremlin.
examples from the lessons: The Kremlin stands next to Red Square in Moscow. | «The Kremlin denied the report,» said the newsreader. | The Kremlin's walls are made of red brick. | Many old Russian towns have their own kremlin. | The President of Russia works in the Kremlin. | The Kremlin has many churches with golden domes. | Most countries at the UN criticised the Kremlin for invading Ukraine.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital K for the Moscow one: the Kremlin. Like «Downing Street» or «the White House», the place stands for the government. Pronounced KREM-lin.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A large African antelope with grey-brown fur and thin white stripes; the males have long, spiral, twisted horns. 2) There are two kinds: the greater kudu and the lesser kudu.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography lessons about African animals and food chains: kudu eat leaves and are hunted by lions and leopards. Their horns are used as musical horns in some places. Phrases: greater kudu, lesser kudu, kudu horn.
examples from the lessons: The kudu has amazing spiral horns. | We saw three kudu drinking at the waterhole. | Kudu eat leaves from bushes and trees. | A lion was stalking a kudu in the long grass. | Female kudu do not have horns. | The kudu jumped over a two-metre fence. | In the food chain, kudu are herbivores.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: plural «kudus» or «kudu». Pronounced KOO-doo. Comes from a southern African language via Afrikaans.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A complicated network of paths or passages where it is easy to get lost; a maze. 2) Something very complicated and confusing, like a labyrinth of rules. 3) (Greek myth) The maze on the island of Crete where the Minotaur lived. 4) (science) The inner part of the ear, which helps with hearing and balance. 5) A single winding path used for walking and thinking or prayer, found in some churches and gardens.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and myths, Theseus went into the Labyrinth to fight the Minotaur and used a thread to find his way out. In maths puzzles pupils solve mazes; in science, the inner ear's labyrinth controls balance. In church life, some cathedrals have prayer labyrinths. Phrases: a labyrinth of streets, lost in a labyrinth.
examples from the lessons: Theseus entered the labyrinth to fight the Minotaur. | The old town is a labyrinth of narrow streets. | We got lost in the hedge labyrinth at the castle. | The tax forms were a labyrinth of rules. | The inner ear's labyrinth helps you keep your balance. | Ariadne gave Theseus a ball of thread to escape the labyrinth. | Chartres Cathedral has a famous labyrinth set in its floor.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a labyrinth, labyrinths. Spelling: «y» after «b», «-inth» at the end. Pronounced LAB-uh-rinth. Adjective: labyrinthine (very complicated). A maze may have dead ends; strictly, an old-style labyrinth is one winding path, but in everyday English they mean the same.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Made of lace, or decorated with lace (a fine fabric with patterns of holes). 2) Looking like lace: with a delicate pattern of holes or thin lines.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life it describes clothes, curtains and tablecloths; in science and nature writing, frost, leaves eaten by caterpillars and snowflakes can look lacy. In stories it gives a delicate, pretty or old-fashioned picture. Phrases: lacy collar, lacy pattern, lacy frost.
examples from the lessons: She wore a white dress with a lacy collar. | Frost made lacy patterns on the window. | The caterpillars left the cabbage leaves lacy and full of holes. | Grandma's lacy curtains let in the sunlight. | The fern had lacy green leaves. | Snowflakes look lacy under a magnifying glass.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparison: lacier, laciest (y → i). From «lace» (drop the «e», add «-y»). Pronounced LAY-see.

part of speech: adjective (laden); old past participle of lade
meaning for a pupil: 1) Carrying a heavy load; full of something. 2) Weighed down with a lot of something, often a worry or feeling.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and history: ships and carts laden with goods; in nature writing, trees laden with fruit or snow. In news and health, «sugar-laden» or «fat-laden» food means food with a lot of sugar or fat. Phrases: laden with, heavily laden, sugar-laden, guilt-laden.
examples from the lessons: The ship was laden with gold and spices. | The apple tree was laden with fruit. | We came home laden with shopping bags. | Snow-laden branches bent towards the ground. | Sugar-laden drinks are bad for your teeth. | The camels walked slowly, heavily laden. | He came back laden with guilt after the lie.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually after a verb or with «with»: «laden with apples». Pronounced LAY-den. A little old-fashioned or literary; everyday words are «loaded», «full of». As a suffix: sugar-laden, debt-laden.

part of speech: noun and numeral (a lakh, lakhs or lakh) — South Asian English
meaning for a pupil: 1) (numbers) In India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Nepal and Sri Lanka, a lakh is one hundred thousand (100,000). 2) Ten lakh make one million; a hundred lakh make one crore (10,000,000).
its sense in the lessons: In maths lessons about number systems around the world, pupils learn that in India 100,000 is written 1,00,000 and called «one lakh». In news from South Asia, prices and populations are given in lakhs and crores. Phrases: one lakh rupees, lakhs of people.
examples from the lessons: One lakh is the same as one hundred thousand. | The car cost five lakh rupees. | Lakhs of people came to the festival. | In India, 100,000 is written 1,00,000. | Ten lakh is one million. | My aunt in Delhi says prices are «in lakhs». | A crore is a hundred lakh.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Not used in UK or US English except when speaking about South Asia. Pronounced LAKH or LACK. Plural «lakhs» or «lakh» after a number («five lakh»). In maths problems: 1 lakh = 100,000; 1 crore = 10,000,000; commas go after groups of two digits after the first three (1,00,000).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) The voice box: the part at the top of the windpipe in the throat, which holds the vocal cords that vibrate to make sounds. 2) It also helps stop food going into the lungs when you swallow.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about the body, breathing and sound, the larynx is where voice comes from; when boys' voices «break» at puberty, the larynx grows and sticks out as the Adam's apple. Laryngitis is an illness that makes you lose your voice. Phrases: voice box, laryngitis.
examples from the lessons: The larynx is also called the voice box. | Your vocal cords are inside your larynx. | When you speak, air from your lungs makes the vocal cords in your larynx vibrate. | The Adam's apple is the front of the larynx. | She had laryngitis and could only whisper. | Put your fingers on your throat and feel your larynx buzz when you hum. | The larynx sits on top of the windpipe.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: plural larynges (formal) or larynxes. Pronounced LA-rinks. Common spelling trap: it is «larynx», not «larnyx». Related: laryngitis (lar-in-JY-tis).

part of speech: adjective and noun (a lateen, lateens; lateen sail)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A lateen sail is a triangular sail tied to a long pole that hangs at an angle on a short mast. 2) A boat with such a sail.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons about exploration and trade, lateen sails helped Arab dhows, and later Portuguese caravels, sail closer to the wind, making long sea journeys possible. In science, they show how sails use wind from the side. Phrases: lateen sail, lateen-rigged.
examples from the lessons: The dhow has a large lateen sail. | A lateen sail is shaped like a triangle. | Portuguese explorers used ships with lateen sails. | The lateen sail let the boat sail against the wind. | On the Nile, feluccas still use lateen sails. | We drew a caravel with three lateen sails.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually used before «sail». Pronounced luh-TEEN. The name comes from French «latine», meaning Latin (Mediterranean).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A white milky liquid that comes from some plants, especially the rubber tree, and is used to make rubber. 2) A rubbery material made from this liquid or made artificially, used for gloves, balloons and paint.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography lessons, latex is tapped from rubber trees in places like Malaysia and Brazil. In health and safety, latex gloves are used by doctors and dentists, and some people have a latex allergy, so schools may avoid latex balloons. Phrases: latex gloves, latex allergy, latex paint.
examples from the lessons: Rubber is made from latex. | Workers cut the bark of the rubber tree to collect latex. | The dentist wore latex gloves. | My friend is allergic to latex, so we use foil balloons at her party. | Latex paint is easy to wash off brushes. | Dandelion stems also give out a white latex.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Pronounced LAY-tex. A latex allergy can be serious; people with it should avoid latex gloves and balloons.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A long vegetable with a white stem and green leaves that tastes like a mild onion. 2) The leek is a national symbol of Wales.
its sense in the lessons: In food and healthy-eating lessons, leeks are used in soups and pies (leek and potato soup). In Wales, people wear a leek or a daffodil on St David's Day, 1 March. In gardening, leeks grow in rows in the vegetable patch. Phrases: leek and potato soup, chicken and leek pie.
examples from the lessons: Mum made leek and potato soup. | We wore leeks on St David's Day. | The leek is a symbol of Wales. | You have to wash leeks well, as soil gets between the leaves. | Grandad grows giant leeks for the village show. | A leek looks like a very big spring onion.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a leek, leeks. Homophone trap: «leak» (water escaping, or a secret getting out) sounds exactly the same. Leek = vegetable; leak = hole that lets liquid out.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person or organisation that lends something, especially money, which must be paid back. 2) (money) A bank or company that gives loans or mortgages and charges interest.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and money lessons about borrowing and interest, the lender gives money and the borrower pays it back with extra (interest). In everyday life, the bank is a mortgage lender. In stories, a lender can be kind or greedy. Phrases: money lender, mortgage lender, lender of last resort.
examples from the lessons: The bank is the lender, and Dad is the borrower. | A lender charges interest on a loan. | «Neither a borrower nor a lender be» is a famous old line. | The mortgage lender agreed to lend money for the house. | In the old story, the money lender was very greedy. | If the lender charges 10% interest on £100, you pay back £110. | My friend was the lender of the pencil, so I gave it back.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Opposite: borrower. Trap: «lend» = give for a while; «borrow» = take for a while. Not «Can you borrow me a pen?» but «Can you lend me a pen?» In maths problems, the lender receives the loan back plus interest.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Not strict; gentle in punishing people or in making them follow rules. 2) (law) Giving a lighter punishment than expected.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday school life it describes teachers or parents who allow more, or rules that are soft; in law and news, a lenient sentence is a light punishment. In stories it can show kindness or weakness. Phrases: a lenient teacher, lenient with, lenient sentence.
examples from the lessons: Our supply teacher was very lenient and let us talk. | Mum is lenient with my little brother. | The judge gave a lenient sentence because it was his first crime. | The referee was too lenient and didn't give a yellow card. | Some people think the new rules are too lenient. | Grandma is more lenient about bedtime than Dad.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually «lenient with someone» or «lenient on something». Opposite: strict, harsh. Noun: leniency. Pronounced LEE-nee-ent.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (Irish folklore) A small, mischievous fairy, usually shown as a little man with a red or ginger beard, a green coat and hat, who makes shoes and hides a pot of gold. 2) It is a figure from stories, not a real creature.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and St Patrick's Day crafts (17 March), children build leprechaun traps and look for the pot of gold at the end of the rainbow. In Irish folklore, if you catch a leprechaun he must grant wishes or show his gold, but he is very tricky. Phrases: pot of gold, leprechaun trap.
examples from the lessons: The leprechaun hid his pot of gold at the end of the rainbow. | We made a leprechaun trap for St Patrick's Day. | In the story, the leprechaun tricked the farmer. | Leprechauns are said to be shoemakers. | My little cousin believes a leprechaun messed up his room. | The leprechaun wore a green hat with a gold buckle.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Spelling is tricky: l-e-p-r-e-c-h-a-u-n. Pronounced LEP-ruh-kawn. Myth: leprechauns are characters of Irish folklore, not real. In older stories they wore red, not green.

part of speech: noun (a lev, leva) — Bulgarian money; Ukrainian and Russian word in Latin letters
meaning for a pupil: 1) (money) The money of Bulgaria; one lev is divided into 100 stotinki. Plural: leva. 2) (Ukrainian, Russian «лев») The word for «lion»; it sounds like «lev» to an English ear. It is not an English word. 3) (a name) Lev is a man's first name, as in the Russian writer Lev (Leo) Tolstoy, and a Hebrew name meaning «heart».
its sense in the lessons: In maths and geography lessons about money around the world, the Bulgarian lev appears in exchange-rate problems. In stories from Eastern Europe, Lev is a common name. Phrases: Bulgarian lev.
examples from the lessons: The lev is the money of Bulgaria. | The ice cream cost three leva. | One lev is 100 stotinki. | Lev Tolstoy wrote very long novels. | «Lev» means «lion» in Ukrainian. | In our maths problem, we changed pounds into Bulgarian leva.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural of the money: leva. Pronounced LEV. «Lev» as a word for lion is Ukrainian/Russian, not English. Do not confuse with «level» or «leave». Bulgaria decided to replace the lev with the euro.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (Bible) A huge sea monster described in the Bible, in books such as Job, Psalms and Isaiah. 2) Anything very large and powerful, such as a huge ship, whale or company. 3) (history) «Leviathan» is the title of a famous 1651 book by Thomas Hobbes about the power of government.
its sense in the lessons: In Bible lessons, Leviathan is a mighty creature showing God's power; in stories and adventure books, a leviathan is a giant sea beast or a gigantic ship. In news, a big company can be called a «corporate leviathan». Phrases: a leviathan of the deep, a leviathan of a ship.
examples from the lessons: In the Bible, Leviathan is a great sea monster. | The blue whale is the leviathan of the oceans. | The cruise ship was a leviathan, taller than any building in the port. | Sailors told tales of a leviathan that swallowed ships. | Christians read about Leviathan in the Book of Job. | The new supermarket is a leviathan that has put small shops out of business.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Pronounced luh-VY-uh-thun. Capital L when it means the Bible monster or Hobbes's book. A literary, dramatic word; in everyday talk say «giant» or «monster».

part of speech: adjective (liberal, more liberal, most liberal); noun (a liberal, liberals; a Liberal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Respecting people's freedom and willing to accept ideas and ways of life different from your own. 2) (politics) Believing in individual freedom, equal rights and gradual change; in the USA «liberal» often means left of centre. 3) (politics, Canada and Australia) The Liberal Party is a big party: in Canada it is centre or centre-left, in Australia it is centre-right. 4) Generous; given or used in large amounts. 5) Not exact or strict, as in a liberal translation.
its sense in the lessons: In citizenship and news lessons, liberal and conservative are words for political views, explained with each side in its own words. In everyday life, «a liberal amount of butter» means a lot. In school, «liberal arts» means subjects like history, languages and literature. Phrases: liberal with, liberal democracy, Liberal Democrats (UK party), liberal amount.
examples from the lessons: She put a liberal amount of jam on her toast. | The Liberal Party won the election in Canada. | In Australia, the Liberal Party is on the centre-right. | My aunt has liberal views about how children should dress. | A liberal democracy protects free speech and free elections. | Dad is liberal with his praise. | That's a very liberal translation; it changes some words. | In the USA, people often argue about liberal and conservative ideas.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective and noun. Capital L for a party name (Liberal Party, Liberal Democrats). Trap: the meaning changes by country; in Australia a «Liberal» politician is centre-right, while an American «liberal» is centre-left. Noun: liberty, liberalism; verb: liberate (set free).

meaning for a pupil: 1) An officer in the army, navy or air force, of a junior to middle rank. 2) A person who helps and acts for a leader; a deputy. 3) (US) A police or fire officer of middle rank.
its sense in the lessons: In history and war stories, lieutenants lead small groups of soldiers; in the navy a lieutenant ranks above a sub-lieutenant. In crime stories, the boss's lieutenant is his chief helper. Phrases: second lieutenant, lieutenant colonel, Lieutenant Governor (Canada, US).
examples from the lessons: The lieutenant led his soldiers across the river. | My great-grandad was a lieutenant in the navy. | The gang leader sent his lieutenant to do the dirty work. | Lieutenant Smith gave the order to march. | In the US, a police lieutenant is above a sergeant. | The captain's chief lieutenant took over the ship. | In Canada, each province has a Lieutenant Governor.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Pronunciation differs: UK «lef-TEN-ant», US «loo-TEN-ant». Spelling trap: l-i-e-u-tenant. Short form: Lt. or Lieut. Comes from French «lieu tenant» = place-holder.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To say that one thing is like another; to compare them. 2) Used with «to»: «liken A to B» means say A is similar to B.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons about figurative language, writers liken things to other things (similes and metaphors): a poet likens the moon to a silver coin. In history and science, people liken the heart to a pump or the brain to a computer. Phrases: liken something to something, often likened to.
examples from the lessons: The poet likens the sea to a hungry dog. | Scientists liken the heart to a pump. | Many people liken the city to a giant ant nest. | He was often likened to his famous grandfather. | Our teacher likened the brain to a busy library. | The story likens growing up to climbing a mountain. | I wouldn't liken a cat to a dog; they are so different.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: likened, likening. Always «liken X to Y», not «with». A bit formal; in speech say «compare to» or «say it's like». Do not confuse with «like» (enjoy) or «likely».

part of speech: noun (a limousine, limousines; informal: limo, limos)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A large, expensive, comfortable car, often with a long body and a driver (chauffeur), sometimes with a glass wall between driver and passengers. 2) (US, Canada) A van or bus that carries passengers to and from an airport.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and stories, limousines are for weddings, proms, film stars and presidents; children may imagine arriving at a party in a stretch limo. In news, the president's limousine is armoured for safety. Phrases: stretch limousine, ride in a limo, airport limousine.
examples from the lessons: The bride arrived at the church in a white limousine. | The film star stepped out of a long black limousine. | For her birthday treat, they rode in a stretch limo. | The president's limousine is bulletproof. | A chauffeur drove the limousine. | The airport limousine took us to the hotel. | The limo was so long it couldn't turn the corner.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Short form: limo (informal), plural limos. Pronounced LIM-uh-zeen. Spelling: l-i-m-o-u-s-i-n-e.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (sport) An official who helps the referee or umpire by watching the lines of the pitch or court and showing with a flag when the ball goes out or a player is offside. 2) A worker who puts up and repairs telephone or electricity lines, or railway lines.
its sense in the lessons: In PE and sport, in football the linesmen are now officially called «assistant referees»; in tennis, line judges call «Out!». In everyday news, linesmen repair power lines after storms. Phrases: the linesman's flag, raise the flag.
examples from the lessons: The linesman raised his flag for offside. | The ball went out, and the linesman pointed for a throw-in. | The players argued with the linesman. | After the storm, linesmen worked all night to fix the power lines. | In tennis, the linesman shouted «Out!». | The referee checked with the linesman before giving the goal. | Linesmen climbed the poles to repair the broken cable.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: linesmen. Officially in football: assistant referee; in tennis: line judge. A woman doing the job is often called «lineswoman» or «assistant referee». Pronounced LINES-mun.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To do with language or languages. 2) To do with linguistics, the science that studies how languages work.
its sense in the lessons: In English and language lessons: linguistic skills (reading, writing, speaking), linguistic features of a text (word choice, sentence types). In schools with many home languages, teachers talk of linguistic diversity. Phrases: linguistic skills, linguistic features, linguistic diversity, linguistic puzzle (as in olympiad language puzzles).
examples from the lessons: She has great linguistic skills and speaks four languages. | Our class has a lot of linguistic diversity. | We listed the linguistic features of a persuasive letter. | The olympiad had a linguistic puzzle about an unknown language. | Babies learn language through linguistic games like rhymes. | The museum shows the linguistic history of English. | A linguistic expert studied how the children in the town spoke.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective only. Noun: linguistics (the science), linguist (a person who studies or speaks many languages). Pronounced ling-GWIS-tik. Spelling: «-guis-», not «-gis-».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Colour for the lips, usually in a small stick that comes out of a tube. 2) A stick or tube of this colour.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, adults and teens wear lipstick; in science, it can be tested for colours by chromatography. In stories, lipstick marks or a lipstick message on a mirror can be clues in mysteries. The phrase «lipstick on a pig» means making something bad look better on the outside only. Phrases: wear lipstick, put on lipstick, red lipstick.
