examples from the lessons: Mum put on red lipstick before the party. | My little sister drew on the wall with a lipstick. | There was a lipstick mark on the cup. | Lipstick comes in many colours. | The detective found a message written in lipstick. | Granny never goes out without her lipstick. | «That's just lipstick on a pig,» said Dad about the new paint on the old car.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable for the substance («some lipstick»); countable for a stick («two lipsticks»). One word: lipstick. Related: lip gloss, lip balm (for dry lips).

part of speech: noun (a locomotive, locomotives); adjective (locomotive — formal, science)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A railway engine that pulls a train. 2) (science, formal) To do with movement from place to place; «locomotion» is how animals move.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons about the Industrial Revolution, George Stephenson's «Rocket» (1829) was a famous steam locomotive. In science, animals' locomotion (walking, swimming, flying) is studied. In everyday life, children see diesel and electric locomotives. Phrases: steam locomotive, diesel locomotive, Locomotion No. 1.
examples from the lessons: The steam locomotive puffed out clouds of smoke. | Stephenson's Rocket was an early locomotive. | The locomotive pulled twenty wagons of coal. | An electric locomotive takes power from wires above the track. | We visited a museum full of old locomotives. | Birds and fish have different kinds of locomotion. | The locomotive's driver blew the whistle.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Pronounced loh-kuh-MOH-tiv. In everyday speech «engine» or «train engine» is more common. Related: locomotion (movement). Trap: the «train» is the whole line of carriages; the locomotive is the engine.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (geography) A very fine, yellowish-brown soil made of dust blown by the wind, often after the Ice Age. 2) It makes very fertile farmland but wears away easily.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and science lessons about soils and rocks, loess is wind-blown sediment; the Loess Plateau in China is famous, and the Yellow River gets its colour from loess. Phrases: the Loess Plateau, loess soil.
examples from the lessons: Loess is soil carried by the wind. | The Yellow River is yellow because of loess. | Farmers grow good crops on loess. | The Loess Plateau in China is covered with deep loess. | Loess can be washed away quickly by heavy rain. | Our geography teacher showed us a jar of fine loess.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Pronounced LOH-es, LURSS or LESS. Comes from German. A specialist word in geography.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Sad because you are alone and have no friends or company; lonely. 2) Far from other people; empty and quiet, as in a lonesome road.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, songs and cowboy tales («lonesome cowboy»), it shows sadness and loneliness. In everyday American and Canadian talk, «I'm lonesome» means «I'm lonely». Phrases: feel lonesome, on your lonesome (UK, informal: all alone), lonesome road.
examples from the lessons: The puppy felt lonesome without its brothers and sisters. | The cowboy sang a lonesome song by the fire. | A lonesome road led across the desert. | Grandpa gets lonesome since Grandma died. | «What are you doing here on your lonesome?» asked Nan. | The lonesome wolf howled at the moon. | If a friend seems lonesome, ask them to play.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly US and Canadian; in British English «lonely» is usual. «On your lonesome» (UK, informal) = alone. Compare: alone (no one with you, can be happy) and lonely/lonesome (sad about it).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A large bow, about as tall as a man, made of one piece of wood (often yew), used for shooting arrows. 2) (history) The famous weapon of English and Welsh archers in the Middle Ages.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons about medieval battles, longbowmen helped the English win at Crécy (1346) and Agincourt (1415). In stories about Robin Hood, he shoots a longbow. In PE or clubs, archery may use modern bows. Phrases: longbowman, draw a longbow.
examples from the lessons: Robin Hood was a great shot with the longbow. | English longbows were made from yew wood. | The archers drew their longbows and fired. | At Agincourt, longbowmen helped win the battle. | A longbow can shoot an arrow over 200 metres. | Medieval boys had to practise with the longbow every Sunday. | The longbow is taller than most people.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one word. Compare: crossbow (a bow fixed on a stock and fired with a trigger), shortbow. «To draw the longbow» is also an old idiom meaning «to tell exaggerated stories».

part of speech: noun (a loom, looms); verb (loom, looms, loomed, looming)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (noun) A machine or frame for weaving thread into cloth. 2) (verb) To appear as a large, dark, unclear shape, often in a frightening way. 3) (verb) To seem about to happen, especially something worrying or important, like tests or a storm. 4) (loom large) To seem very important or worrying.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons about the Industrial Revolution, power looms in mills changed how cloth was made; in crafts, children weave on small looms. In stories, castles and mountains loom out of the fog; in everyday life, exams loom. Phrases: loom large, loom over, looming deadline, weaving loom.
examples from the lessons: Grandma weaves rugs on a wooden loom. | A dark castle loomed out of the mist. | The SATs are looming, so we are revising. | Huge power looms filled the cotton mill. | A big storm loomed on the horizon. | The giant loomed over the tiny village. | The problem of money loomed large for the family.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: loomed, looming. As a verb it usually describes something big, unclear or threatening. Noun and verb are the same spelling but different meanings. Rhymes with «room».

part of speech: noun (a louse, lice; a louse, louses — slang meaning); verb (louse up — informal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A tiny insect without wings that lives on the skin or hair of people or animals and feeds on blood; plural «lice». 2) (slang, rude) A nasty, mean person; plural «louses». 3) (louse up, informal) To spoil or mess something up.
its sense in the lessons: In health and school life, head lice spread easily between children; parents comb hair with a special nit comb and use treatment, and it is not a sign of being dirty. In science, lice are parasites. In old stories and slang, calling someone a louse is an insult. Phrases: head lice, nit comb, louse up.
examples from the lessons: There's a note from school saying a child in our class has head lice. | A louse is a tiny insect that lives in hair. | Mum combed my hair to get rid of the lice. | Lice are parasites that feed on blood. | «You louse! You stole my sweets!» | Don't louse up the plan by being late. | In history, soldiers in the trenches suffered from lice.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular plural: one louse, two lice (like mouse/mice). For the insult, the plural is «louses». Nits are lice eggs. Myth: head lice like clean hair as much as dirty hair; anyone can get them. Adjective: lousy (very bad, informal).

part of speech: fragment / pinyin (Mandarin) — not an English word
meaning for a pupil: 1) (Mandarin, pinyin) «Lù» means road or way (路), as in «yi lu ping an» (have a safe journey); «lǜ» means green (绿); «Lu» is also a common Chinese surname. 2) It sounds like «loo» to an English ear. 3) (informal, rare) A short form of the name Lucy or Louise (a name).
its sense in the lessons: It is not an English word. Children may hear it in Mandarin lessons and on the street (lǜ sè = green colour; mǎ lù = road). In English, «loo» (UK, informal) means toilet and sounds the same — a trap. Phrases (Mandarin): yi lu ping an (have a safe trip), lǜ sè (green).
examples from the lessons: In Mandarin, «lù» means road. | «Yi lu ping an!» my Chinese teacher said before the trip. | «Lǜ» means green in Chinese. | Mr Lu is our new neighbour from Shanghai. | «Lu» sounds just like «loo», but it is not the same word. | My cousin Lucy's nickname is Lu.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Not an English word: a Mandarin syllable written in pinyin (tone marks show the meaning: lù, lǜ). Pronounced «loo». Homophone trap: «loo» is British slang for toilet.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) The white half-moon shape at the bottom of a fingernail or toenail. 2) (history) A flat gold neck ornament shaped like a crescent moon, made in Ireland and Britain in the Bronze Age.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about the body, the lunula is part of the nail, usually biggest on the thumb. In history lessons about the Bronze Age, gold lunulae are shown in museums like the National Museum of Ireland. Phrases: nail lunula, gold lunula.
examples from the lessons: The lunula is the white half-moon on your nail. | Your thumbnail has the biggest lunula. | The museum has a shiny gold lunula from the Bronze Age. | «Lunula» comes from the Latin word for «little moon». | Some people's lunulae are hard to see. | The Bronze Age lunula was worn around the neck.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: lunulae (LOO-nyoo-lee). Pronounced LOO-nyoo-luh. Latin «luna» = moon (like lunar). A specialist word.

part of speech: adjective (Macedonian); noun (a Macedonian, Macedonians; Macedonian, the language)
meaning for a pupil: 1) From or to do with North Macedonia, a country in the Balkans, its people or its language. 2) The Macedonian language: a Slavic language written in Cyrillic letters, spoken in North Macedonia. 3) (history) From ancient Macedonia, the kingdom of Philip II and Alexander the Great. 4) From Macedonia, a region of northern Greece.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, Alexander the Great was a Macedonian king who built a huge empire. In geography, North Macedonia changed its name in 2019 after a long disagreement with Greece about the word «Macedonia», and people on each side feel strongly about it. Phrases: Macedonian army, Macedonian language.
examples from the lessons: Alexander the Great was a Macedonian king. | The Macedonian army crossed into Asia. | Skopje is the capital of North Macedonia. | Macedonian is written in the Cyrillic alphabet. | My friend's family is Macedonian and speaks Macedonian at home. | Thessaloniki is the main city of the Greek region of Macedonia. | The ancient Macedonians spoke a form of Greek.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital M: Macedonian. Pronounced mass-uh-DOH-nee-un. Trap: modern Macedonian (a Slavic language) is different from the ancient Macedonian of Alexander's time; the name is a sensitive topic between Greece and North Macedonia.

part of speech: adjective (magnified); past form of the verb magnify (magnify, magnifies, magnified, magnifying)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Made to look bigger than it really is, using a lens, microscope or magnifying glass. 2) Made louder, stronger or more serious than before. 3) Made to seem more important than it really is; exaggerated. 4) (church, Bible) Praised; «magnify the Lord» means praise God.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, pupils look at magnified cells, insects and crystals, and learn that «× 10» means magnified ten times. In everyday life, worries and noises can be magnified. In church, the Magnificat, Mary's song, begins «My soul magnifies the Lord». Phrases: magnified × 100, magnified image, greatly magnified.
examples from the lessons: Under the microscope, the onion cells were magnified 100 times. | The magnified picture of a fly's eye was amazing. | The ant looked huge when magnified. | In the empty hall, every sound was magnified. | The problem got magnified because everyone was shouting. | The magnifying glass magnified the tiny letters. | «My soul magnifies the Lord,» sang the choir.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: magnify → magnified, magnifies (y → i). Noun: magnification. In maths and science, «magnified × 20» means 20 times bigger in length; to find the real size, divide the image size by the magnification.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A wine or champagne bottle that holds twice as much as a normal bottle (1.5 litres). 2) A powerful gun or bullet (from «Magnum» as a trade name). 3) (Magnum) A brand name of ice cream on a stick, coated with chocolate. 4) (magnum opus) A person's greatest work.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life children may know Magnum ice creams; in stories and films, a detective's magnum is a powerful handgun; at celebrations, adults open a magnum of champagne. In English and art lessons, «magnum opus» means an artist's greatest work. Phrases: a magnum of champagne, magnum opus.
examples from the lessons: Dad bought a magnum of champagne for the wedding. | A magnum holds as much as two bottles. | I'd love a Magnum ice cream on a hot day. | The cowboy in the film carried a magnum. | The painter called the huge picture her magnum opus. | That novel is the writer's magnum opus. | The racing driver sprayed a magnum of champagne from the podium.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a magnum, magnums. Latin «magnum» = great. «Magnum opus» (plural magna opera) is a fixed phrase. Capital M for the ice-cream brand. In maths problems, a magnum = 1.5 litres = 2 standard 75 cl bottles.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To do with Malaya, the old name for the land on the Malay Peninsula that later became part of Malaysia. 2) (animals) Found in the Malay Peninsula region, as in the Malayan tiger, Malayan tapir or Malayan sun bear. 3) (old use) A person from Malaya.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons about the British Empire and the Second World War, Malaya was a British colony that became independent in 1957 and joined Malaysia in 1963. In science and nature lessons, Malayan tigers and tapirs are endangered animals. Phrases: Malayan tiger, Malayan tapir, Malayan Emergency.
examples from the lessons: The Malayan tiger is endangered. | The Malayan tapir is black with a white middle. | Malaya became independent in 1957. | Grandad served in the Malayan Emergency. | The Malayan sun bear is the smallest bear in the world. | Malayan rubber was shipped all over the world.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital M. «Malayan» is about the place Malaya; «Malay» is the people and language; «Malaysian» is about the modern country Malaysia. These three are easy to mix up. Pronounced muh-LAY-un.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A breed of Belgian Shepherd dog with short fawn fur and a dark face, very clever and full of energy. 2) It is often trained as a police, army or search-and-rescue dog.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and news, Malinois dogs work with police and soldiers, sniffing out drugs, explosives and missing people; in stories about brave dogs they are heroes. Owners need lots of time to train and exercise them. Phrases: Belgian Malinois, police Malinois.
examples from the lessons: The police dog was a Belgian Malinois. | A Malinois needs a lot of exercise every day. | The Malinois found the lost hiker in the woods. | Malinois look a bit like small German Shepherds. | Army Malinois are trained to parachute with soldiers. | Our neighbour's Malinois can jump very high.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital M (breed name). Same form for singular and plural. Pronounced MAL-in-wah (French, from the Belgian town of Malines/Mechelen). The final «s» is silent.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who comes from or lives in Manchester, a big city in north-west England. 2) (adjective) To do with Manchester, its people or its way of speaking.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and everyday talk, Mancunians are known for football (Manchester United and Manchester City), music and a strong local accent. Children may meet the word in news and sport. Phrases: a proud Mancunian, Mancunian accent.
examples from the lessons: My uncle is a proud Mancunian. | She speaks with a strong Mancunian accent. | Mancunians love their football. | The band was made up of four young Mancunians. | The Mancunian rain is famous. | «Our kid» is a phrase many Mancunians use for a brother or sister.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital M. Pronounced man-KYOO-nee-un. It comes from «Mancunium», an old Latin name for Manchester, which is why it does not look like «Manchester». Similar: Liverpudlian (Liverpool), Glaswegian (Glasgow).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Required by a law or a rule; something you must do; compulsory. 2) (law) A mandatory sentence is a punishment the law says must be given.
its sense in the lessons: In school life, «attendance is mandatory» and safety gear is mandatory on trips; in exam papers and forms it marks questions you must answer; in law and news, mandatory rules and sentences appear. Phrases: mandatory for, it is mandatory to, mandatory field (on forms).
examples from the lessons: Wearing a helmet is mandatory on the bike trip. | School uniform is mandatory at our school. | It is mandatory to wear a seat belt in a car. | The fields marked with a star are mandatory. | Swimming lessons are mandatory in Year 4. | The new law made recycling mandatory. | A mandatory fire drill takes place every term.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective. Formal word; everyday words are «compulsory» or «you have to». Opposite: optional, voluntary. Pronounced MAN-duh-tree (UK) or MAN-duh-tor-ee (US).

meaning for a pupil: 1) All people in the world, considered together; the human race; humankind. 2) (older use) Men, as opposed to women — this use is rare now.
its sense in the lessons: In history, science and RE lessons, writers talk about the history of mankind and inventions that helped mankind. Neil Armstrong said on the Moon in 1969: «That's one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind». Today many people prefer «humankind» or «humanity» so that women are clearly included. Phrases: the history of mankind, for the good of mankind.
examples from the lessons: The invention of writing changed mankind forever. | «One giant leap for mankind,» said Neil Armstrong. | Christians believe Jesus came to save mankind. | Medicine is one of the greatest gifts to mankind. | Pollution is a danger to all mankind. | The wheel was one of mankind's greatest inventions.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable; no «the» or «a». Many style guides suggest «humankind» or «humanity» instead, to include everyone. Stress: man-KIND.

part of speech: noun (a marcel, marcels); verb (marcel, marcels, marcelled, marcelling); name (Marcel)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (a name) Marcel is a man's first name, especially in France, as in the French mime artist Marcel Marceau. 2) (old use) A marcel or marcel wave is a hairstyle with deep, regular waves made with hot curling irons, popular in the 1920s. 3) (verb, old use) To make such waves in hair.
its sense in the lessons: Most children meet Marcel as a name in French lessons and stories. In history lessons about the 1920s, photographs show women with marcelled hair. Phrases: marcel wave.
examples from the lessons: Marcel is a popular French boy's name. | Marcel Marceau was a famous French mime artist. | In the 1920s, many women had a marcel wave. | Great-Granny's photo shows her hair marcelled in neat waves. | The hairdresser used hot irons to make a marcel. | In our French book, Marcel lives in Paris with his dog.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital M for the name. The hairstyle is named after the French hairdresser Marcel Grateau. Pronounced mar-SEL. Spelling of the verb: marcelled, marcelling (UK).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A garden plant with bright orange or yellow flowers. 2) There are different kinds: pot marigolds (calendula) and French or African marigolds.
its sense in the lessons: In science and gardening lessons, children grow marigolds from seed and learn how flowers attract insects; gardeners plant them to keep pests away. In India, marigold garlands are used at festivals like Diwali and at weddings. In Mexico, they decorate the Day of the Dead. Phrases: marigold garland, Marigold gloves (UK, a brand of rubber kitchen gloves).
examples from the lessons: We planted marigold seeds in yoghurt pots. | The marigolds are bright orange. | Marigold garlands hung everywhere for Diwali. | Gardeners plant marigolds next to tomatoes to keep pests away. | Bees love the marigolds in our school garden. | Mum puts on her Marigolds to wash the dishes. | In Mexico, marigolds decorate the Day of the Dead.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a marigold, marigolds. Capital M for the glove brand. Pot marigold petals can be eaten, but children should never eat plants without asking an adult.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (old or literary) A sailor; a person who works on a ship. 2) (Mariner) The name of some space probes and sports teams, such as NASA's Mariner probes or the Seattle Mariners baseball team.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and poems, mariners sail the seas; the famous poem «The Rime of the Ancient Mariner» (1798) by Samuel Taylor Coleridge tells of a sailor who shot an albatross. In history lessons, mariners used compasses and the stars to navigate. Phrases: the Ancient Mariner, master mariner, mariner's compass.
examples from the lessons: The old mariner told stories of storms at sea. | «The Rime of the Ancient Mariner» is a long poem. | Mariners used the North Star to find their way. | A master mariner can captain a big ship. | The mariner's compass was a great invention. | NASA's Mariner 4 sent the first close pictures of Mars. | The mariners sang as they pulled the ropes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Old-fashioned or poetic; in everyday speech say «sailor». Pronounced MA-rin-er. Related: marine (to do with the sea), maritime.

part of speech: noun (plural of marshal: a marshal, marshals); verb form (marshals, from marshal: marshal, marshals, marshalled, marshalling — US marshaled, marshaling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (noun) Officials who organise people at a big event, such as a race, parade or festival, and keep them safe. 2) (noun, US) Law officers who catch criminals and help the courts, like the US Marshals; in old Western stories, a town marshal is like a sheriff. 3) (noun) Very high-ranking army or air-force officers, such as a field marshal. 4) (verb) «Marshals» = he or she gathers and organises people or things, such as ideas or soldiers.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, marshals in high-vis jackets guide runners, cars and crowds at fun runs, car races and festivals. In history and Western stories, marshals keep law and order. In English lessons, a writer marshals arguments in an essay. Phrases: race marshals, US Marshals, field marshal, marshal your thoughts.
examples from the lessons: The marshals waved flags to guide the runners. | Marshals in yellow jackets showed us where to park. | The US Marshals caught the escaped prisoner. | In the Western, the marshal faced the outlaws alone. | Before the debate, she marshals her ideas on a card. | The teacher marshals the children into lines for the fire drill. | Field marshals led huge armies in the war.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: «marshal» has one «l» at the end; «martial» (as in martial arts) is different; «Marshall» with double «l» is usually a name. UK verb forms: marshalled, marshalling; US: marshaled, marshaling.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person, animal or object that a team, school or club keeps because it is believed to bring good luck. 2) A character, often a person in a big furry costume, that stands for a team, event, company or product and entertains people. 3) A small toy or figure kept for luck, for example in a car or a pencil case.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and sport, football and school teams have mascots who dance on the pitch, and the Olympics and World Cup have official mascots. In schools, a class mascot (often a soft toy) goes home with a different child each weekend, who then writes about its adventures. In stories, a mascot can be a brave dog or a lucky cat on a ship. Phrases: team mascot, school mascot, class mascot, lucky mascot.
examples from the lessons: Our team mascot is a giant bear. | The school mascot is a lion called Leo. | This weekend I took the class mascot home and wrote in its diary. | The mascot waved to the crowd before the match. | Every Olympic Games has its own mascot. | The ship's cat was the sailors' lucky mascot. | She kept a little mascot in her pencil case for the test.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a mascot, mascots. Pronounced MASS-kot. Myth: a mascot does not really bring luck; it is a fun tradition and a team symbol.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A state in the north-east of the USA, in the region called New England; its capital and biggest city is Boston. 2) (history) The Massachusett were a Native American people of the area, and the state is named after them; the name is often explained as «near the great hill».
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, the Pilgrims landed at Plymouth, Massachusetts, in 1620 on the Mayflower, and the Boston Tea Party (1773) helped start the American Revolution. In everyday life, Massachusetts is home to famous universities such as Harvard and MIT. Phrases: Boston, Massachusetts; the Commonwealth of Massachusetts.
examples from the lessons: Boston is the capital of Massachusetts. | The Pilgrims landed in Massachusetts in 1620. | The Boston Tea Party happened in Massachusetts. | Harvard University is in Massachusetts. | Massachusetts is one of the six New England states. | My pen pal lives in Massachusetts and loves snow. | Massachusetts is named after a Native American people.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A name, so always with a capital M. Spelling trap: M-a-s-s-a-c-h-u-s-e-t-t-s (double s, double s, double t). Pronounced mass-uh-CHOO-sits. Short form: MA or Mass. Officially called a «Commonwealth».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) The strong muscle in each cheek that pulls the lower jaw up, so you can close your mouth and chew. 2) For its size, it is one of the strongest muscles in the body.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about muscles and the body, the masseter is the chewing muscle; you can feel it bulge in your cheek when you clench your teeth. Phrases: masseter muscle.
examples from the lessons: The masseter helps you chew your food. | Clench your teeth and feel your masseter at the side of your face. | The masseter is a very strong muscle for its size. | Animals that chew a lot, like cows, have big masseters. | Grinding your teeth at night can make the masseter sore. | The dentist pressed on my masseter to check it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Pronounced muh-SEE-ter. A science and medical word. Do not confuse with «master» or «masseur» (a person who gives massages).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A work of art, book, music or other creation of great skill; one of the best of its kind. 2) The best work a particular person has ever made. 3) Anything done extremely well, like a goal or a cake.
its sense in the lessons: In art, music and English lessons, pupils study masterpieces such as the Mona Lisa or famous novels. In everyday life, people joke that their sandwich or Lego tower is a masterpiece. In history, a craftsman made a «masterpiece» to prove he was skilled enough to be a master. Phrases: a true masterpiece, a masterpiece of, a culinary masterpiece.
examples from the lessons: The Mona Lisa is a famous masterpiece by Leonardo da Vinci. | My little brother's drawing is his masterpiece. | That goal was a masterpiece! | The museum is full of masterpieces. | The cake Grandma baked was a masterpiece. | Many people think «Charlotte's Web» is a masterpiece. | In the Middle Ages, an apprentice had to make a masterpiece to become a master.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. One word. Praise word; it is strong, so for small things it is often used jokingly.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A small box that holds matches, with a rough side for striking them. 2) Something very small, like a «matchbox car» (a tiny toy car) or a very small room or house.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and safety lessons: matches and matchboxes are for adults, children should give any they find to an adult. Matchboxes are used in craft (matchbox drawers, tiny dioramas) and maths (measuring volume of a small box). In stories, a «matchbox flat» means a tiny home. Phrases: matchbox car, matchbox label.
examples from the lessons: Grandad keeps a matchbox by the fireplace. | We made a tiny bed for the doll from a matchbox. | My brother collects matchbox cars. | The flat was the size of a matchbox. | If you find a matchbox, give it to a grown-up. | The matchbox is 5 cm long, 3 cm wide and 1 cm high, so its volume is 15 cubic centimetres. | Some people collect old matchbox labels.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: plural matchboxes (add «-es» after «x»). One word. Safety: matches can cause fires and burns; children should not play with them.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To do with mathematics. 2) Done carefully, exactly and logically, like a calculation. 3) (mathematical certainty / chance) Exact, as sure or as small as numbers can show.
its sense in the lessons: In maths lessons, pupils solve mathematical problems, use mathematical symbols (+, −, ×, ÷, =) and mathematical language (sum, product, difference). In everyday life, someone with a «mathematical mind» thinks logically. Phrases: mathematical problem, mathematical symbol, mathematical vocabulary, mathematical certainty.
examples from the lessons: We use mathematical symbols like + and =. | Our homework is a mathematical puzzle. | She has a very mathematical mind. | The tiles were laid with mathematical precision. | Ada Lovelace was a great mathematical thinker. | Explain your answer using mathematical words like «sum» and «difference». | It is a mathematical certainty that 2 + 2 = 4.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective; adverb: mathematically. Spelling: math-e-mat-i-cal (there is an «e» after «math»). Pronounced math-uh-MAT-i-kul.

part of speech: noun (mathematics, uncountable; short forms: maths in the UK, Australia, NZ, Ireland; math in the USA and Canada)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The study of numbers, quantities, shapes, patterns and measurements, and the logic connecting them. 2) The school subject that teaches this. 3) The calculations or reasoning involved in something, as in «the mathematics of the problem».
its sense in the lessons: At school, mathematics includes arithmetic (adding, subtracting, multiplying, dividing), fractions, geometry, measures, statistics and algebra. In everyday life it is used for money, time, cooking and sport. In olympiads, it includes logic puzzles. Phrases: do mathematics, mathematics lesson, pure and applied mathematics.
examples from the lessons: Mathematics is my favourite subject. | We have mathematics every morning. | Mathematics helps us understand patterns in nature. | My sister wants to study mathematics at university. | The mathematics behind the game is quite simple. | Builders use mathematics to measure and plan. | Mathematics is the same in every language: 3 × 4 is always 12.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Ends in «s» but is singular and uncountable: «Mathematics is fun», not «are». Short forms: «maths» (UK and Commonwealth), «math» (US, Canada). Spelling trap: math-E-matics.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (computing) MB = megabyte: a unit of computer memory or file size, about one million bytes. 2) (computing) Mb = megabit, used for internet speed (Mbps, megabits per second); 8 megabits make 1 megabyte. 3) (science, weather) mb = millibar, a unit of air pressure on weather maps. 4) (MB) Short for Manitoba, a province of Canada. 5) MB is also used for «Bachelor of Medicine» after a doctor's name.
its sense in the lessons: In computing lessons pupils compare file sizes (KB, MB, GB): a photo is about 3 MB. In science and weather, air pressure is shown in millibars. On Canadian addresses, MB = Manitoba. Phrases: 5 MB file, 50 Mbps broadband.
examples from the lessons: This photo is 3 MB. | The file is too big to email; it is 40 MB. | Our broadband speed is 70 Mbps. | 1,000 MB is about 1 GB. | The weather map shows 1,000 mb of pressure. | Winnipeg, MB, is in Canada. | A song is usually about 4 MB.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Not a word, only an abbreviation. Capital B = byte, small b = bit: MB (megabyte) is 8 times bigger than Mb (megabit). In maths and computing problems, 1 GB ≈ 1,000 MB; 1 MB ≈ 1,000 KB (some computers use 1,024).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science, health) The first poo of a newborn baby: dark green, thick and sticky, made from what the baby swallowed in the womb.
its sense in the lessons: In science and health lessons about babies and growing up, meconium is mentioned as a baby's first poo in the first day or two after birth. Midwives and doctors check for it to make sure the baby's gut is working. Phrases: pass meconium.
examples from the lessons: A newborn baby's first poo is called meconium. | Meconium is dark green and sticky. | The midwife checked that the baby had passed meconium. | After a few days, a baby's poo changes from meconium to yellow. | My aunt, who is a nurse, told us about meconium. | Meconium is made of things the baby swallowed before it was born.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Pronounced mi-KOH-nee-um. A medical word. Comes from Greek «mekon», poppy (from the dark colour).

part of speech: noun (a med, meds — informal); adjective (med, informal); abbreviation (Med, med.)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) Short for «medicine» or «medication», usually in the plural: «meds». 2) (informal) Short for «medical», as in «med school» (medical school) or «med student». 3) (the Med, UK informal) The Mediterranean Sea, or the countries around it. 4) (abbreviation) Short for «medium», as on clothes or menus.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, «Did you take your meds?» means medicine; families go on holiday «to the Med». In hospital stories, med students learn to be doctors. Safety: only take meds a trusted adult gives you. Phrases: take your meds, med school, holiday in the Med.
examples from the lessons: Grandma takes her meds every morning. | My cousin is at med school to be a doctor. | We went on holiday to the Med, to Spain. | The T-shirt says «Med» on the label, for medium. | Don't take any meds unless an adult gives them to you. | The med student shadowed the doctor all day. | Cruise ships sail around the Med in summer.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal clipped form. «Meds» (plural) is the usual form for medicines. «The Med» = Mediterranean (capital M). Not an English full word; in formal writing say «medicine», «medical» or «Mediterranean».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (history) From or to do with the Middle Ages, the time in Europe from about 500 to 1500 AD. 2) (informal, negative) Very old-fashioned or cruel, as in «mediaeval punishments».
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, mediaeval castles, knights, monasteries, the Black Death and the Magna Carta (1215) are studied. In everyday talk, people complain that something old or harsh is «positively mediaeval». Phrases: mediaeval castle, mediaeval times, mediaeval village.
examples from the lessons: We visited a mediaeval castle in Wales. | Mediaeval knights wore heavy armour. | In mediaeval times, most people worked on farms. | The Black Death killed many people in mediaeval Europe. | The town still has its mediaeval walls. | Monks copied books by hand in mediaeval monasteries. | «Sending kids to bed with no phone? That's mediaeval!» joked my brother.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Mediaeval» is an older British spelling; «medieval» is the usual spelling today in all countries. Pronounced med-ee-EE-vul or mid-EE-vul. Comes from Latin «medium aevum», the middle age. The period is also called the Middle Ages.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Worth remembering, or easy to remember, because it is special, unusual, very good or very bad. 2) Easy to remember, as a short phrase or tune.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons, pupils write about memorable days and try to make story openings and adverts memorable; in everyday life, birthdays, trips and holidays can be memorable. Phrases: a memorable day, memorable moment, make it memorable.
examples from the lessons: Our trip to the zoo was memorable. | Write about a memorable day in your life. | The play had a very memorable ending. | Choose a password that is memorable to you but hard for others to guess. | The song has a memorable tune. | Winning the cup was the most memorable moment of the year. | The storm made it a memorable camping trip.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective; adverb: memorably. Spelling: «memor» + «able» (drop nothing; there is no «y»). Stress: MEM-or-uh-bul. Opposite: forgettable.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The act of learning something so you can remember it exactly, such as a poem, times tables or spellings. 2) Learning by heart.
its sense in the lessons: In school, memorisation is used for times tables, spelling lists, poems, number bonds and lines for a play. Teachers explain that memorisation is useful, but understanding why something is true matters too. Phrases: rote memorisation, memorisation techniques.
examples from the lessons: Memorisation of times tables helps you do mental maths quickly. | Learning a poem by heart takes memorisation. | Repeating aloud helps memorisation. | Rote memorisation without understanding is not enough. | The actor used memorisation tricks to learn her lines. | Flashcards are good for memorisation of spellings.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. UK, Australia, NZ, Ireland: memorisation (with «s»); US, Canada: memorization (with «z»). Verb: memorise / memorize. Pronounced mem-or-eye-ZAY-shun.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Deserving praise or reward because it is very good or brave. 2) (formal, school and army) Used in names of awards, like «Meritorious Service Medal».
its sense in the lessons: A formal word used in the army, police, award ceremonies and stiff exam passages. In school, merit badges and certificates reward meritorious work or behaviour. Phrases: meritorious service, meritorious conduct.
examples from the lessons: The firefighter received an award for meritorious service. | Her science project was judged meritorious. | The soldier's meritorious conduct was praised. | The head teacher read out the names of pupils with meritorious work. | The medal is given for meritorious acts of courage. | It was a meritorious effort, even though they lost.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective. Formal; in everyday speech say «excellent», «praiseworthy» or «deserving». Pronounced meh-ri-TOR-ee-us. From «merit» (worth, value).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) The change of rocks by great heat and pressure deep in the Earth, without melting them, so they become new kinds of rock (metamorphic rocks).
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography lessons about the rock cycle, metamorphism turns limestone into marble, shale into slate, and sandstone into quartzite. It is one of the three ways rocks form, with igneous (from melted rock) and sedimentary (from layers). Phrases: contact metamorphism, regional metamorphism.
examples from the lessons: Metamorphism turns limestone into marble. | Slate forms from shale by metamorphism. | Heat and pressure cause metamorphism deep underground. | Metamorphism is part of the rock cycle. | Rocks near hot magma can change by contact metamorphism. | Our teacher showed us rocks changed by metamorphism.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Adjective: metamorphic (metamorphic rock). Trap: «metamorphosis» means an animal changing its body shape, such as a caterpillar becoming a butterfly; «metamorphism» is about rocks. Pronounced met-uh-MOR-fiz-um.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (maths, science) Using the metric system of measurement, based on the metre, the kilogram and the litre, with units that go up in tens (10, 100, 1,000). 2) (noun, formal) A measure used to judge or compare how well something is doing, such as test scores or sales. 3) (poetry, rare) To do with the rhythm or metre of a poem.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and science lessons pupils use metric units (millimetres, centimetres, metres, kilometres, grams, kilograms, millilitres, litres) and convert between them by multiplying or dividing by 10, 100 or 1,000. They compare them with imperial units (inches, feet, pounds, pints), still used in the USA and partly in the UK. Phrases: metric system, metric units, metric ton/tonne, go metric.
examples from the lessons: Most countries use the metric system. | Centimetres and kilograms are metric units. | In the UK, road signs show miles, but food is weighed in metric. | A metric tonne is 1,000 kilograms. | Convert 3 metres into centimetres using metric rules: 300 cm. | The USA still mostly uses imperial, not metric. | The company uses customer happiness as a key metric.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective in measurement; noun «a metric» (business) is formal. In maths problems: kilo- = 1,000; centi- = 1/100; milli- = 1/1,000; to change metres to centimetres multiply by 100. Related: metre/meter, imperial.

part of speech: verb (mew, mews, mewed, mewing); noun (a mew, mews)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The soft, high crying sound a cat or kitten makes; to make this sound. 2) The cry of a gull or other bird, especially the mew gull (a kind of seagull). 3) (mews, UK) A row of old stables in a city, now turned into houses, or a small street with such houses.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and everyday life, kittens mew when they are hungry; «miaow» or «meow» is the usual word for the sound. In the UK, a «mews» is a pretty, narrow street of small houses in cities like London. Phrases: mew softly, a mews house.
examples from the lessons: The kitten mewed for its mother. | We heard a tiny mew from under the shed. | Gulls mewed over the harbour. | My aunt lives in a mews in London. | The cat gave a sad little mew at the door. | A mew gull is smaller than a herring gull.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: mewed, mewing. Compare: meow / miaow (louder, the usual word), purr (happy rumble), hiss (angry). «Mews» (street) is singular with an «s»: «a mews». Pronounced MYOO, like «mule» without the «l».

part of speech: adverb and adjective (midway); noun (a midway — US)
meaning for a pupil: 1) In the middle, halfway between two places or two points in time. 2) (US, Canada) The area at a fair with rides, games and food stalls. 3) (Midway) The Midway Atoll in the Pacific Ocean, site of a famous 1942 sea battle.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, «midway» means the midpoint: midway between 4 and 10 is 7 (add and halve). In everyday life and stories, something happens «midway through» a film, lesson or race. In history, the Battle of Midway was a turning point in the Second World War in the Pacific. Phrases: midway through, midway between, midway point.
examples from the lessons: The town is midway between London and Manchester. | Midway through the film, the power went off. | The number midway between 10 and 20 is 15. | We stopped for lunch midway along the path. | We won a teddy at a game on the midway. | The Battle of Midway was fought in 1942. | She fell asleep midway through the story.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb or adjective; one word. In maths problems: to find the number midway between two numbers, add them and divide by 2 ((4 + 10) ÷ 2 = 7). Same meaning as «halfway».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (old use) A girl or woman who milks cows by hand or works in a dairy. 2) (stories) A common character in old tales, nursery rhymes and pictures of country life.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons about farms before machines, milkmaids milked cows by hand. In science history, the doctor Edward Jenner noticed in the 1790s that milkmaids who caught cowpox did not catch smallpox, which led to the first vaccine. In stories and fables, «The Milkmaid and Her Pail» teaches not to count your chickens before they hatch. Phrases: The Milkmaid and Her Pail.
examples from the lessons: The milkmaid carried two buckets of milk. | Edward Jenner studied a milkmaid called Sarah Nelmes. | In the fable, the milkmaid dreamed of riches and spilled her milk. | Milkmaids got up very early to milk the cows. | The painting shows a milkmaid pouring milk. | Today, milking machines do the work of the old milkmaids.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; one word. Old-fashioned: today people say «dairy worker» or «dairy farmer». Related: milkman (who delivers milk).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) A wrong or bad action, especially a crime or a breaking of rules. 2) Something naughty or wicked that a person has done.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, history and RE lessons, characters confess their misdeeds and say sorry; villains are punished for their misdeeds. In church life, confession is a time to admit misdeeds and ask for forgiveness. Phrases: past misdeeds, punished for his misdeeds, own up to a misdeed.
examples from the lessons: The king was punished for his misdeeds. | The pirate confessed his misdeeds before he died. | Everyone has small misdeeds they regret. | In the story, the boy owns up to his misdeed and says sorry. | The newspaper reported the company's misdeeds. | Christians believe God forgives misdeeds when people are truly sorry.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; usually plural «misdeeds». A bit formal or old-fashioned; in speech say «wrong», «bad thing», «crime». «Mis-» means badly or wrongly; «deed» means an action.

part of speech: verb (misdo, misdoes, misdid, misdone, misdoing — rare, old-fashioned)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (rare, old use) To do something wrongly or badly. 2) (rare, old use) To do wrong; to behave badly.
its sense in the lessons: Very rarely used today; you may meet it in old books. The noun «misdoing» (a wrong action, usually «misdoings») is more common. In everyday English say «do something wrong» or «make a mistake». Phrases: misdoings (wrong actions).
examples from the lessons: To misdo a task is to do it wrongly. | The old book said he would never misdo again. | The villain's misdoings were found out at last. | «I have misdone,» confessed the knight. | If you misdo the steps, the cake will not rise. | Her misdoings were forgiven by the village.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular, like «do»: misdid, misdone. Rare and old-fashioned; better to say «do it wrong». «Mis-» means wrongly (misspell, misunderstand). Pronounced mis-DOO.

part of speech: noun (missy — informal, usually as a form of address)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) A way of speaking to a young girl, often in a playful, teasing or slightly cross way: «Listen, missy!» 2) (old use) A young lady; a miss.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and everyday life, a parent, grandparent or teacher might say «Now then, missy» when a girl is being cheeky. It can sound bossy or old-fashioned. Phrases: young missy, little missy.
examples from the lessons: «Don't you talk back to me, missy!» said Grandma. | «Come along, little missy, time for bed.» | The shopkeeper winked: «What can I get for you, missy?» | «Listen here, young missy, homework first.» | Missy is also a nickname for girls named Melissa. | My uncle calls my sister «missy» when she bosses him around.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal; usually used to talk TO a girl, not about her. It can sound cross or patronising, so it is not polite to use with grown women. «Missy» can also be a name (a nickname for Melissa).

meaning for a pupil: 1) To translate words from one language into another wrongly, so the meaning changes.
its sense in the lessons: In language lessons, pupils see how a word can be mistranslated if you translate word by word, and how false friends trick people (French «librairie» is a bookshop, not a library). In news and history, mistranslated messages have caused confusion. Phrases: mistranslated sign, badly mistranslated.
examples from the lessons: The sign was mistranslated and said «Please slip carefully». | If you mistranslate one word, the whole sentence can change. | The online tool mistranslated my French homework. | The menu was so mistranslated that «chicken» became «kitchen». | Translators check their work so they don't mistranslate anything. | Some famous mistakes came from mistranslated words. | Be careful: French «actuellement» means «currently», and it is often mistranslated as «actually».
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: mistranslated, mistranslating. Noun: mistranslation. «Mis-» = wrongly. Translation is from one language to another; interpreting is spoken translation.

part of speech: adjective (mistreated); past form of the verb mistreat (mistreat, mistreats, mistreated, mistreating)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Treated badly, cruelly or unfairly. 2) Harmed or neglected, as with animals or children who are not cared for properly.
its sense in the lessons: In PSHE and safety lessons, children learn that no child or animal should be mistreated, and if someone is being hurt or neglected, they should tell a trusted adult or call a helpline (such as Childline in the UK). In stories, mistreated characters (Cinderella, Harry Potter at the Dursleys') find kindness at last. In law, mistreating animals is a crime. Phrases: mistreated animals, felt mistreated, badly mistreated.
examples from the lessons: The dog had been mistreated, so it was scared of people. | Cinderella was mistreated by her stepsisters. | If you feel mistreated, tell a teacher or an adult you trust. | The prisoners were mistreated by the guards. | The rescue centre looks after mistreated horses. | It is against the law to mistreat animals. | The workers said they were mistreated and paid too little.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: mistreat → mistreated. Noun: mistreatment. Similar words: abuse (stronger), neglect (not caring for). «Mis-» = badly.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A machine or tool for mixing things, such as a food mixer in a kitchen or a cement mixer on a building site. 2) A drink, such as lemonade, tonic or juice, mixed with another drink. 3) (music, TV) A machine for mixing sounds, or a person who does this. 4) (informal) A party or event where people meet and get to know each other. 5) (good mixer) A person who makes friends easily.
its sense in the lessons: In cooking lessons, an electric mixer beats eggs and cake mixture; on building sites, a cement mixer turns slowly. In music, a sound mixer balances voices and instruments. In everyday life, a «good mixer» is friendly in groups. Phrases: food mixer, cement mixer, sound mixer, a good mixer.
examples from the lessons: Mum used the mixer to beat the cake batter. | The cement mixer turned round and round. | The DJ moved the sliders on the mixer. | He's a good mixer and makes friends easily. | At the parents' mixer, the teachers met the new families. | The lemonade was used as a mixer for the adults' drinks. | Turn off the mixer before you lick the beaters!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Safety: always switch off and unplug a mixer before touching the beaters or blades. Verb: mix; noun: mixture (the stuff mixed), mixer (the machine or person).

part of speech: noun (mocha, uncountable; a mocha, mochas); adjective (mocha)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A coffee drink made with chocolate, hot milk and espresso. 2) A kind of strong coffee, first traded from the port of Mocha in Yemen. 3) A mid-brown colour like milky coffee. 4) A flavour mixing coffee and chocolate, as in mocha cake.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, adults order mochas in cafés; mocha cakes and ice cream are popular. In history and geography, Mocha (also al-Mukha) in Yemen was once the world's most famous coffee port. In art and clothes, mocha is a soft brown colour. Phrases: a mocha latte, mocha brown, mocha cake.
examples from the lessons: Mum ordered a mocha with whipped cream. | A mocha has coffee and chocolate in it. | The sofa is a mocha brown colour. | Mocha in Yemen was a famous coffee port long ago. | Grandad baked a mocha cake for his birthday. | My hot chocolate is for me; the mocha is for Dad. | Coffee drinks like mochas have caffeine, so they are not good for children.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable when it is a cup («two mochas»), uncountable for the flavour or colour. Pronounced MOK-uh (UK) or MOH-kuh (US). Note: a mocha contains caffeine. Capital M for the port in Yemen.

part of speech: verb (moisturise, moisturises, moisturised, moisturising); US spelling moisturize
meaning for a pupil: 1) To put cream or lotion on your skin so that it stays soft and does not get dry. 2) To make something less dry by adding a little water or oil to it.
its sense in the lessons: An everyday and health word: people moisturise dry hands in winter, after swimming, or when they have eczema. In science lessons it links to skin as an organ that can lose water. Common phrases: «moisturise your skin», «moisturise your hands», «moisturising cream».
examples from the lessons: Mum told me to moisturise my hands after washing up. | In winter my skin gets so dry that I have to moisturise every night. | The nurse said to moisturise the eczema patches twice a day. | Dad never moisturises, and his lips get cracked. | This shampoo claims to moisturise your hair. | After swimming in chlorine, Grandma always moisturises her face. | Moisturising cream feels cold when you first put it on.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: moisturised, moisturising. UK, Ireland, Australia and New Zealand often write -ise (moisturise); the USA and Canada write -ize (moisturize). Related words: moisture (noun, uncountable), moisturiser (the cream). Do not confuse with «moisten», which means to make a little wet, not to put cream on.

meaning for a pupil: 1) For a very short time, only a moment. 2) (mainly US) Very soon, in a moment.
its sense in the lessons: Used in stories to show something lasting only a second or two: «she was momentarily blinded by the flash». In the USA it is also heard in announcements meaning «very soon»: «we will be landing momentarily». It tells the reader that the event was short, or that it will happen shortly.
examples from the lessons: The lights flickered and the room went momentarily dark. | I was momentarily confused, then I remembered the answer. | The dog stopped momentarily to sniff the lamppost. | The pilot said, «We will be landing momentarily.» | Ella was momentarily lost for words when she won the prize. | The sun came out momentarily before the rain started again. | Your teacher will be with you momentarily.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It comes from «moment». A trap: in British English it usually means «for a moment», while in American English it often means «in a moment» (soon), so «the train will stop momentarily» can sound odd to a British listener. It is an adverb, so it describes a verb or adjective.

part of speech: noun (a moonwalk, moonwalks); verb (moonwalk, moonwalks, moonwalked, moonwalking)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A walk on the surface of the Moon by an astronaut. 2) A dance move where you seem to walk forwards but actually slide backwards, made famous by the singer Michael Jackson. 3) To do this dance move, or to walk on the Moon.
its sense in the lessons: In science and history lessons, moonwalks are the trips astronauts made outside their spacecraft on the Moon, starting with Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin in 1969 (Apollo 11). In everyday life and at school discos, it is the famous backwards-sliding dance step.
examples from the lessons: Neil Armstrong's moonwalk was watched by millions of people on television. | The astronauts collected rocks during their moonwalk. | Leo can moonwalk across the kitchen floor in his socks. | At the school disco everyone tried to moonwalk. | On a moonwalk, astronauts bounce because the Moon's gravity is weak. | Michael Jackson made the moonwalk famous in 1983. | We read a book about the first moonwalk.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: one moonwalk, two moonwalks. Usually written as one word. Twelve people walked on the Moon between 1969 and 1972. The dance move does not involve the Moon at all; it is named that because it looks floaty, like walking with low gravity.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A soft, white, mild Italian cheese that becomes stretchy and stringy when it is melted, often used on pizza.
its sense in the lessons: An everyday food word: pizza, lasagne, salads and sandwiches. Traditional mozzarella is made from the milk of water buffalo or cows. Phrases: «a ball of mozzarella», «mozzarella sticks», «tomato and mozzarella salad».
examples from the lessons: I like extra mozzarella on my pizza. | The melted mozzarella stretched when I pulled the slice away. | We bought a ball of mozzarella for the salad. | Mozzarella sticks are cheese fried in breadcrumbs. | Grandma puts mozzarella on top of her lasagne. | Fresh mozzarella is kept in a little bag of water. | Mozzarella tastes milder than cheddar.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable (some mozzarella), but «a mozzarella» can mean one ball. Spelling trap: double z and double l: m-o-z-z-a-r-e-l-l-a. It is an Italian word; English speakers often say «mots-a-REL-a».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A tall wild plant with grey-green, deeply cut leaves that are silvery underneath, found on roadsides and waste ground; it has a strong smell.
its sense in the lessons: A nature and science word: a common weed of roadsides in Britain, Ireland and North America. In the past people used it in herbal medicine and to flavour beer, and in folk tales it was thought to protect travellers. Its pollen can cause hay fever.
examples from the lessons: We found mugwort growing by the railway line. | Mugwort leaves are silvery on the underside. | Our nature guide said mugwort was once used to flavour beer. | In old stories, travellers put mugwort in their shoes to stop them getting tired. | Mugwort pollen makes some people sneeze in late summer. | The field was full of nettles, docks and mugwort.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable. It is a herb related to wormwood. A safety point: do not eat wild plants unless an adult who knows plants says it is safe; mugwort is not for children to eat or drink. The «wort» in the name is an old word meaning «plant».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Short-sightedness: being able to see things close to you clearly but things far away look blurry. 2) (formal) Not thinking about the future or about what will happen later; only thinking about now.
its sense in the lessons: In science and health lessons, myopia is explained with the eye and lenses: the eye focuses light in front of the retina instead of on it, so glasses with concave (curved-in) lenses help. In news and formal writing it can mean a lack of foresight, e.g. «political myopia».
examples from the lessons: The optician said I have myopia, so I need glasses for the board. | Myopia means you can read a book but not a sign across the road. | More children have myopia today, and doctors say playing outside may help. | Glasses for myopia have lenses that are thinner in the middle. | My brother's myopia got worse, so he got contact lenses. | The newspaper blamed the council's myopia for not planning ahead.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. The adjective is «myopic» (a myopic child; a myopic decision). The opposite is hypermetropia or long-sightedness (US: nearsighted = myopic, farsighted = long-sighted). Pronounced «my-OH-pee-a».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Found in myths and legends, not real: a mythical creature like a dragon or unicorn. 2) Imagined or made up, believed in but not true: a mythical «perfect day».
its sense in the lessons: In stories and English lessons, mythical creatures are dragons, unicorns, the phoenix, mermaids and the kraken. In history and religious education, it describes stories from Greek, Norse and other myths. In everyday talk people use it jokingly for something that seems never to exist: «the mythical tidy bedroom».
examples from the lessons: The dragon is a mythical creature that breathes fire. | We made a poster of mythical beasts from Greek stories. | The unicorn is Scotland's national animal, even though it is mythical. | Pegasus is a mythical horse with wings. | My dad talks about the mythical day when he will clean the garage. | The kraken is a mythical sea monster. | Is the Loch Ness monster real or mythical?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comes from «myth». Similar words: legendary, imaginary, fictional. A trap: «legendary» can also mean very famous (a legendary footballer), but «mythical» usually means not real. Do not confuse with «mystical», which is about spiritual or magical mystery.

part of speech: noun (a narc, narcs); verb (narc, narcs, narced, narcing) — slang
meaning for a pupil: 1) (slang, US) A police officer who works to stop illegal drugs. 2) (slang) A person who tells on others to a teacher, parent or the police; a snitch or tell-tale. 3) (slang) To tell on someone. 4) (slang) Short for «narcissist», a very selfish, vain person.
its sense in the lessons: This word is street and playground slang, not used in school writing. Children may hear «don't be a narc» meaning «don't tell the teacher». In US crime films a «narc» is a drug police officer. It tells the reader the speaker sees someone as disloyal or a spy.
examples from the lessons: «Don't be a narc and tell Miss,» said Jayden. | In the film, the narc pretended to be a student. | He narced on us about the broken window. | Nobody likes a narc, but telling an adult about danger is the right thing to do. | She called her ex a narc because he only cared about himself. | The older boys thought the new kid was a narc.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Slang; also spelled «nark» in the UK (an old word for a police informer, and «narky» in the UK means grumpy). Safety point: telling a trusted adult when someone is hurt or in danger is not «being a narc»; it is being responsible. Comes from «narcotics».

meaning for a pupil: 1) To tell a story, describing what happens in order. 2) To speak the words that go with a film, TV programme or audiobook, explaining what we see.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons, the narrator is the person or voice that narrates the story: first person (I, we) or third person (he, she, they). Pupils narrate events in a recount or a story. In everyday life, famous people narrate nature documentaries and audiobooks.
examples from the lessons: David Attenborough narrates many nature programmes. | The story is narrated by a talking cat. | Can you narrate what happened on the school trip, in order? | Grandpa narrated the tale of how he met Grandma. | The audiobook was narrated by a famous actor. | In this book, the events are narrated by two different children. | She narrated her own video for the science fair.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Related: narrator (the one who tells), narrative (the story or the telling, also an adjective). In story writing, «first-person narrator» uses «I». A trap: the narrator is not always the author; an author can invent a narrator.

part of speech: adjective; Natal (a name of a place)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal, science) To do with being born or with the time of birth: «natal day», «natal home». 2) Natal: the old name of a province of South Africa (now KwaZulu-Natal), and a city in Brazil (a name).
its sense in the lessons: Mostly a science and formal word. In biology, «natal stream» is the river where a salmon hatched and returns to lay eggs; «natal» also appears in longer words: prenatal (before birth), postnatal (after birth), neonatal (newborn). It tells the reader the topic is birth.
examples from the lessons: Salmon swim back to their natal river to lay their eggs. | Turtles return to their natal beach years later. | A neonatal unit looks after newborn babies in hospital. | Mum went to prenatal classes before my sister was born. | Natal Day is a holiday in some places, celebrating the founding of the town. | Durban is a city in KwaZulu-Natal.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Rare on its own; much more common inside prenatal, postnatal, neonatal and antenatal (UK: antenatal classes). Do not confuse with «nasal» (to do with the nose) or «naval» (to do with the navy).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A small toad of Europe, including Britain and Ireland, with a yellow stripe down its back, that runs rather than hops and has a very loud croak.
its sense in the lessons: A nature and science word: the natterjack toad lives in sand dunes, heaths and salt marshes, is protected in the UK and Ireland, and is Ireland's only native toad. Male natterjacks call loudly on spring nights; their croak can be heard far away. Useful in lessons on habitats and endangered animals.
examples from the lessons: The natterjack toad has a yellow line down its back. | Natterjacks run along the sand instead of hopping. | We heard natterjacks croaking at the nature reserve. | Natterjack toads are protected because their homes are disappearing. | In Ireland, natterjacks live in a few places in County Kerry. | A natterjack's call can be heard over a kilometre away.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun. The name probably comes from «natter» (to chat noisily) because of its loud call. Do not handle wild toads: they are protected and their skin can make you ill.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A sea animal related to the octopus and squid, which lives inside a coiled, striped shell divided into chambers. 2) Nautilus: the name of famous submarines, including Captain Nemo's in Jules Verne's novel and the first nuclear submarine (a name).
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons the nautilus is an example of a mollusc and a «living fossil», as its relatives lived over 400 million years ago. Its shell is a spiral, used in maths to show spirals in nature. It floats by changing the gas in its shell chambers, like a submarine.
examples from the lessons: A nautilus has up to ninety small tentacles. | The nautilus shell is a beautiful spiral. | The nautilus moves up and down by filling its chambers with gas or water. | In «Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea», the submarine is called the Nautilus. | We saw a nautilus at the aquarium. | Ammonites were ancient animals like the nautilus.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: nautiluses or nautili. Pronounced «NAW-ti-lus». A myth: the nautilus shell is often said to follow the «golden ratio» exactly, but real measurements show it does not.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Saying «no» or «not»; making a sentence mean the opposite by adding a word like not, never or no. 2) (maths, logic) The opposite of a statement: the negation of «it is raining» is «it is not raining». 3) (formal) The complete opposite or cancelling out of something.
its sense in the lessons: In grammar lessons, negation is making negative sentences with «not», «don't», «never», «no», «nobody». In maths and logic puzzles, the negation of a statement is true when the statement is false. In formal writing: «cheating is the negation of fair play».
examples from the lessons: «I do not like it» is a negation of «I like it». | Add «not» to make a negation. | The negation of «all cats are black» is «not all cats are black». | Double negation, like «I didn't do nothing», is a dialect form. | In maths, the negation of «x is bigger than 5» is «x is not bigger than 5». | Bullying is the negation of kindness.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «negate» and «negative». Trap: the negation of «all» is «not all» (some are not), not «none». In maths, negating a number (making it negative) means changing its sign: the negation of 5 is -5. Double negatives in Standard English cancel out, but in many dialects they just add emphasis.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A short printed sheet or email sent regularly to a group of people, with news about a school, club, company or place.
its sense in the lessons: An everyday school word: the school newsletter tells parents about trips, events, holidays and achievements. Children may make a class newsletter in English lessons, using headlines, short reports and pictures. Phrases: «weekly newsletter», «sign up for the newsletter».
examples from the lessons: The school newsletter comes home every Friday. | Our class wrote a newsletter about the science week. | Mum read in the newsletter that the trip is on Tuesday. | The football club sends a monthly newsletter by email. | My poem was printed in the newsletter! | You can unsubscribe from a newsletter if you do not want it any more.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one newsletter, two newsletters. One word. Online safety: only sign up for newsletters with a parent's permission, as they ask for your email address.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Interesting or important enough to be reported in the news.
its sense in the lessons: Used in media and English lessons about journalism: reporters decide what is newsworthy, often something new, unusual, local, or important to many people. It helps pupils understand why some events make the news and others do not.
examples from the lessons: A dog that can surf is newsworthy. | The editor said the story was not newsworthy enough. | Winning the national competition was newsworthy, so the local paper came to school. | Why do you think this event is newsworthy? | Celebrities often do things that are not very important but are seen as newsworthy. | The opening of the new library was newsworthy in our town.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective, one word. A point for media lessons: being newsworthy does not mean being the most important; news often picks rare and dramatic events, which can make them seem more common than they are.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (phonics) The letter pair «ng» that makes one sound, as at the end of sing, ring and long. 2) (abbreviation, informal) «no good», as in «that plan is NG». 3) (abbreviation) A short code for Nigeria (NG) or for «National Guard» or «nanogram» (ng) in science.
its sense in the lessons: In phonics lessons «ng» is a digraph: two letters, one sound, heard in king, song, thing, sing. It is not a word on its own. In text messages and some jobs «NG» means «no good». In science, «ng» is a nanogram, a billionth of a gram.
examples from the lessons: The words sing, ring and bang all end in «ng». | Can you think of five words with «ng» at the end? | In «finger» you can hear «ng» followed by a «g» sound. | The engineer wrote «NG» on the broken part, meaning no good. | NG is the country code for Nigeria. | A nanogram, written ng, is a billionth of a gram.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Not an English word on its own. In phonics: «singer» has just the «ng» sound, but «finger» has «ng» plus a hard «g». Some names from other languages begin with Ng (for example Ng, a Chinese surname, or Ngozi, an Igbo name) — these are names.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) The belief that nothing really matters or has meaning, and that life has no purpose. 2) (formal, history) The idea that all rules, laws and traditions should be rejected or destroyed.
its sense in the lessons: A philosophy and ethics word, mainly for older pupils and adults. In philosophy lessons children may meet the question «Does anything matter?», and nihilism is the answer «no». Many thinkers and religions disagree and say life has meaning through love, kindness, God, or what we choose to do.
examples from the lessons: Nihilism is the idea that life has no meaning. | The villain in the story shows nihilism: he thinks nothing matters. | Our philosophy club talked about nihilism and whether kindness matters. | Christians believe life has meaning because God made people, so they disagree with nihilism. | Some teenagers joke about nihilism when they are bored. | The writer Nietzsche wrote a lot about nihilism.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. A nihilist is a person who believes it; the adjective is nihilistic. Pronounced «NY-ill-ism» or «NEE-ill-ism». From Latin «nihil» meaning «nothing». A trap: being sad or bored is not nihilism; nihilism is a belief.

meaning for a pupil: 1) At night; in a way that happens during the night, especially about animals that are active at night.
its sense in the lessons: A science word linked to «nocturnal» animals: owls, bats, hedgehogs, foxes and badgers are active nocturnally and sleep in the day. The opposite is «diurnally» (in the day). Used in lessons on habitats and animal behaviour.
examples from the lessons: Hedgehogs feed nocturnally, so you rarely see them in the day. | Bats hunt nocturnally for insects. | Many desert animals live nocturnally to avoid the heat. | Our hamster is active nocturnally and keeps us awake. | Owls see well because they hunt nocturnally. | The flowers open nocturnally and are visited by moths.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from the adjective «nocturnal» (more common). Opposites: diurnal, diurnally. Crepuscular animals are active at dawn and dusk. From Latin «nox, noctis», night.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A point where lines, branches or paths meet or join. 2) (science) A lump or swelling, such as a lymph node in the body. 3) (plants) The place on a stem where a leaf or bud grows. 4) (computing) One device or point in a network, like a computer connected to others.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, a node is a point on a graph or network diagram where lines meet. In science, lymph nodes are small glands that help fight infection (they can swell when you are ill). In plant lessons, cuttings are made just below a node. In computing, each computer in a network is a node.
examples from the lessons: The nurse felt the lymph nodes in my neck. | Cut the stem just below a node to grow a new plant. | In the network diagram, each circle is a node. | Every node on the map is a station where train lines meet. | The leaves grow from the nodes on the stem. | If one node in the network breaks, messages can go another way.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Do not confuse with «nod» (moving your head). In maths networks, nodes are also called vertices (one vertex), and lines are called edges or arcs. In physics, a node on a vibrating string is a point that does not move.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A small round lump, especially on the body, a plant root or in a rock.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, root nodules on peas, beans and clover hold bacteria that take nitrogen from the air and feed the plant. In medicine, a nodule is a small lump that a doctor checks. In geology, flint and other minerals form nodules in rocks like chalk.
examples from the lessons: Clover has little nodules on its roots. | The bacteria in the nodules help the plant get nitrogen. | We found flint nodules in the chalk cliff. | The doctor checked a small nodule on Grandad's neck. | Nodules on bean roots look like tiny pink beads. | Most nodules are harmless, but a doctor should look at any new lump.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. It means a small node or lump. Related: node. Safety: if you find a new lump on your body, tell a parent, who may ask a doctor; most are harmless.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In name only, but not really or not in practice: «He is nominally in charge, but his deputy does the work.» 2) (money, formal) Officially, as a written amount, before other things are counted: «nominally worth £1».
its sense in the lessons: A formal word used in history, politics and money. It tells the reader that what something is called and what it really is are different: a nominally independent country is really controlled by another. In money and maths, a nominal value is the number printed on something, not what it can actually buy.
examples from the lessons: The king was nominally the ruler, but the generals made the decisions. | The club is nominally free, but you have to buy the kit. | Granddad is nominally retired, but he still works three days a week. | The rent rose by only a little, nominally. | Our class has a captain nominally, but everyone decides together. | The coin is nominally worth one pound.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from «nominal» (in name). From Latin «nomen», name. A trap: «nominal» in money can also mean «very small» (a nominal fee = a tiny fee). Do not confuse with «nominate» (to suggest someone for a job or prize).

meaning for a pupil: 1) To write something down using a system of signs or symbols, especially music, dance steps or chess moves.
its sense in the lessons: Used in music lessons: you notate a tune with notes on a stave. Also used for chess (writing moves like e4), maths (writing with symbols) and dance. It tells the reader that something heard or done is being put into a written code.
examples from the lessons: The composer notated the melody on the stave. | Can you notate this rhythm using crotchets and quavers? | Chess players notate every move in a game. | She hummed the tune and her teacher notated it. | Dances can be notated with special symbols. | In maths we notate «less than» with the sign <.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. More common: the noun «notation» (music notation, maths notation). Do not confuse with «note» (to write a quick reminder) or «annotate» (to add notes to a text or picture).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Oct. — short for October, the tenth month. 2) Short for octave in music, or octal (base 8) in computing and maths.
its sense in the lessons: Used on calendars, dates and forms: «12 Oct 2025». In music, an octave is the gap from one note to the next note with the same name (8 notes). In computing, «oct» can mean octal numbers. Prefix «oct-» means eight: octopus, octagon.
examples from the lessons: The school trip is on 14 Oct. | Write the date as 3 Oct or 3 October. | Half-term starts at the end of Oct. | The calendar showed Sep, Oct, Nov. | Oct- means eight, as in octagon. | The piano piece jumps up an oct here.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Not a word on its own; it is an abbreviation, often with a full stop (Oct.). Trap: October is the tenth month, even though «oct» means eight; in the old Roman calendar it was the eighth month, before January and February were added.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) A person who behaves in a strange or unusual way. 2) (informal, adjective) Strange or unusual: an oddball idea.
its sense in the lessons: An informal everyday word. It can be friendly (someone fun and different) or unkind (someone left out). In stories, an «oddball» character is often quirky and later becomes a hero. Kindness lessons may talk about not leaving out people who seem different.
examples from the lessons: My uncle is a bit of an oddball, but he is great fun. | She had an oddball idea to paint the shed purple. | The film is about a group of oddballs who become friends. | Don't call him an oddball; everyone is different. | It's an oddball little shop full of old toys. | The class oddball turned out to be brilliant at chess.
