note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal. Countable noun: an oddball, oddballs. Uses «an» because it starts with a vowel sound. Can hurt if used to mock someone. Similar: weirdo (ruder), eccentric (more formal, often kinder).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who has broken the law or done a crime. 2) A person or thing that causes a problem or does something wrong: «The worst offender for noise was the dog.»
its sense in the lessons: In law, news and citizenship lessons: «young offenders», «first-time offender», «repeat offender». In everyday talk, people joke about the «worst offender» for leaving dishes or being late. It tells the reader someone has done wrong.
examples from the lessons: The police caught the offender near the station. | Young offenders may be given community work instead of prison. | He was a first-time offender, so the judge gave him a warning. | In our house, the worst offender for leaving lights on is my brother. | Repeat offenders are people who keep breaking the law. | Fizzy drinks are the main offender for bad teeth.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. From the verb «offend» (to break a law, or to upset someone). Related: offence (UK, Ireland, Australia) / offense (US). Use «an» before it. Trap: «offended» means upset, not the same as being an offender.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A brown, night-flying bird of South America and Trinidad that lives in caves, eats fruit and finds its way in the dark by clicking, a bit like a bat.
its sense in the lessons: A science word in lessons on echolocation and adaptations: oilbirds are among the few birds that echolocate. They are called oilbirds because the chicks get very fat, and long ago people boiled them to make oil for lamps and cooking.
examples from the lessons: The oilbird lives in dark caves in South America. | Oilbirds make clicking sounds to find their way, like bats. | Oilbirds eat fruit, not insects. | Thousands of oilbirds come out of the cave at night. | Oilbird chicks are very fat, which is how they got their name. | We learnt that oilbirds and swiftlets can both echolocate.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; one word. Use «an» (an oilbird). It is the only bird of its family. Oilbirds are protected; people no longer use them for oil.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (Ireland) The national parliament of Ireland, made of the President, the Dáil (lower house) and the Seanad (Senate). 2) (Ireland) Also the name of a large Irish-language arts festival (Oireachtas na Gaeilge) and an Irish-dancing championship.
its sense in the lessons: In Irish citizenship and politics lessons: the Oireachtas makes the laws of Ireland and meets in Leinster House in Dublin. TDs (members of the Dáil) and senators are its members. It is an Irish (Gaelic) word, and is not an English word, but is used in Irish English.
examples from the lessons: The Oireachtas makes the laws for Ireland. | Our class visited the Oireachtas in Dublin. | The Dáil and the Seanad are the two houses of the Oireachtas. | A new law has to be passed by the Oireachtas and signed by the President. | My cousin danced at the Oireachtas championships. | TDs are elected to the Dáil, part of the Oireachtas.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irish (Gaelic) word, written with a capital O. Pronounced roughly «ER-uck-tas» or «ERR-akh-tus». Compare: Parliament (UK), Congress (USA), Parliament (Canada, Australia, New Zealand).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Working, in action: «The new system is now operative.» 2) (noun) A worker, especially one who works machines in a factory. 3) (noun) A secret agent or spy. 4) To do with a medical operation: «post-operative care».
its sense in the lessons: Formal and news word. «The operative word» means the most important word in a sentence. In hospitals: pre-operative (before surgery) and post-operative (after). In spy stories, an operative is an agent on a mission.
examples from the lessons: The new lift will be operative from Monday. | The factory hired ten more operatives. | The spy film followed a secret operative in Paris. | «Free» was the operative word in the advert. | After his operation Grandad needed post-operative care. | The rules became operative at the start of term.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective and countable noun. Related: operate, operation, operator. Phrase: «the operative word» = the key word. Use «an» before it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Able to be placed opposite and pressed against the other fingers, like a human thumb, so that the hand can grip and pick things up.
its sense in the lessons: A science word in lessons on humans, apes and adaptations: «opposable thumbs» let humans, apes and many monkeys hold tools, write and climb. Some animals, like koalas and opossums, have opposable digits on their feet or hands.
examples from the lessons: Humans have opposable thumbs, so we can hold a pencil. | Try picking up a coin without using your opposable thumb. | Chimpanzees have opposable thumbs and big toes. | Opposable thumbs helped early humans to make tools. | Koalas have two opposable digits for gripping branches. | Pandas have a special bone that works like an opposable thumb.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective, used almost always in «opposable thumb(s)». From «oppose» (to place against). Nothing to do with being against someone.

part of speech: noun (an orang, orangs); also a word in Malay
meaning for a pupil: 1) Short for orangutan, the large red-haired ape of Borneo and Sumatra. 2) (Malay, Indonesian) «Orang» means «person» or «people»; orangutan means «person of the forest».
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography lessons on rainforests and endangered animals: orangutans are great apes that live in trees, and are in danger from forests being cut down for palm oil. «Orang» on its own is a short, less common form. It is not related to the colour orange.
examples from the lessons: The orang swung from branch to branch. | Orangs build a new nest of leaves every night. | «Orangutan» comes from Malay words meaning «person of the forest». | In Malay, «orang» means person. | The zoo has two orangs and a baby. | Orangs are in danger because their forests are being cut down.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Spelling trap: «orangutan» (also orang-utan), not «orangutang». Not the same as «orange». Use «an» before it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Military weapons, especially large guns, bombs, shells and ammunition. 2) Ordnance Survey: the government map-making organisation of Great Britain (Ordnance Survey Ireland in Ireland) (a name).
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons about wars: «unexploded ordnance» means old bombs or shells that have not gone off, which can still be found on beaches and building sites. In geography lessons in the UK, OS (Ordnance Survey) maps are the detailed maps with grid references.
examples from the lessons: We used an Ordnance Survey map to find the path. | Find the church on the OS map using a four-figure grid reference. | Unexploded ordnance from the war was found on the beach. | The army stored its ordnance in a guarded building. | The Ordnance Survey began by mapping Britain for the army. | Ordnance experts made the old bomb safe.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Spelling trap: «ordnance» (weapons, no i) and «ordinance» (a law or rule, with an i) are different words. Safety: if you find something that looks like an old bomb or shell, do not touch it; move away and tell an adult, who calls the police.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A dentist who specialises in straightening teeth and fixing the way teeth and jaws fit together, often by fitting braces.
its sense in the lessons: An everyday and health word: many children go to the orthodontist at about 10–14 years old for braces or retainers. In science lessons about teeth, it shows that teeth can be slowly moved with gentle pressure.
examples from the lessons: I'm going to the orthodontist to get my braces tightened. | The orthodontist said my teeth are too crowded. | My sister wears a retainer from the orthodontist at night. | The orthodontist took a mould of my teeth. | You can't eat sticky toffee when you have braces, says the orthodontist. | After two years, the orthodontist took my brace off.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; use «an». Related: orthodontics (the science), orthodontic (adjective). An orthodontist is a kind of dentist. «Ortho» means straight, «dont» means tooth. UK often says «a brace», US «braces».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Leaving someone out on purpose, so they are not included by a group. 2) (history) In ancient Athens, a vote to send a powerful citizen away from the city for ten years.
its sense in the lessons: In lessons about friendship and bullying, ostracism means deliberately excluding someone, which can hurt as much as words. In history lessons on ancient Greece, Athenians wrote a name on a broken piece of pottery (an ostrakon) to vote someone out.
examples from the lessons: Leaving someone out on purpose is a form of bullying called ostracism. | The new girl suffered ostracism because she was different. | In Athens, ostracism sent a man away for ten years. | Voters scratched names on pieces of pottery for an ostracism. | Ostracism can make people feel lonely and unwanted. | Our class talked about how to stop ostracism in the playground.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Verb: ostracise (UK) / ostracize (US). Pronounced «OS-tra-sizm». It comes from the Greek «ostrakon», a broken pot. Not related to «ostrich».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A part of rock that sticks out of the ground or a hillside. 2) A small group of something appearing in an unexpected place.
its sense in the lessons: A geography and science word: geologists study rock outcrops to see layers and fossils. On walks, outcrops are good places to look at kinds of rock (granite, limestone). In a city, an «outcrop» of shops can mean a small cluster.
examples from the lessons: We sat on a rocky outcrop to eat our lunch. | The outcrop of limestone was full of fossils. | Climbers practised on the granite outcrop. | From the outcrop we could see the whole valley. | Be careful near outcrops; the edges can be crumbly. | The Australian outback has red rock outcrops.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; one word. Use «an». Related: «crop out» (verb, rarer). Safety: keep away from the edges of outcrops and cliffs.

part of speech: verb (overestimate, overestimates, overestimated, overestimating); noun (an overestimate, overestimates)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To guess or think that an amount is bigger than it really is. 2) To think someone or something is better, stronger or more important than they really are. 3) (noun) A guess that is too large.
its sense in the lessons: In maths lessons, estimating means making a sensible guess; an overestimate is higher than the true answer, and rounding up gives an overestimate. In everyday life, people overestimate how much they can do in a day. Phrases: «don't overestimate», «a slight overestimate».
examples from the lessons: I overestimated how many sweets were in the jar. | Rounding 48 up to 50 gives an overestimate. | We overestimated how far we could walk and got very tired. | Don't overestimate your strength when lifting boxes. | My guess of 300 was an overestimate; the answer was 271. | The team overestimated the other side and were surprised to win.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: underestimate. In maths: overestimate = estimate bigger than the real answer; e.g. estimating 6.8 × 3 as 7 × 3 = 21 is an overestimate of 20.4. Regular verb. «Over-» means too much.

part of speech: adjective; verb form (present participle of overlie)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Lying on top of something else; covering it. 2) (formal) Being more noticeable or on the surface, over a deeper thing.
its sense in the lessons: A science and geography word: rock layers lie one on another, and the overlying layer is usually younger than the one below it. In medicine, the overlying skin is the skin on top of a lump or bone.
examples from the lessons: The overlying rock is younger than the rock beneath it. | The overlying layer of soil was full of worms. | Snow formed an overlying blanket on the ice. | The doctor looked at the overlying skin. | Fossils in the overlying layers are more recent. | The overlying clay keeps the water trapped underground.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «overlie» (overlie, overlies, overlay, overlain, overlying) — a rare verb. Trap: «overlay» is both the past of overlie and a different verb meaning to cover with a layer. Mostly used as an adjective before a noun.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To make someone, or yourself, far too tired, so that they become grumpy or unwell.
its sense in the lessons: An everyday family word, especially about babies and young children: an overtired child often cries and finds it harder to fall asleep. In health and PE lessons, it links to the importance of rest. The adjective «overtired» is much more common than the verb.
examples from the lessons: Don't overtire yourself before the race. | The baby is overtired and won't stop crying. | Long journeys overtire my little brother. | Grandma was ill, so we did not stay too long and overtire her. | When I'm overtired I get grumpy. | The coach did not want to overtire the players before the final.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. «Overtired» (adjective) is the most common form: «He's overtired». Odd fact: being overtired can make it harder to fall asleep.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Oxalic acid: a poisonous acid found in small amounts in plants like rhubarb leaves, sorrel and spinach, also used for cleaning and bleaching.
its sense in the lessons: A science word: in lessons on safety and plants, children learn that rhubarb stalks are eaten but the leaves are poisonous because they contain a lot of oxalic acid. In chemistry it is used to remove rust and stains.
examples from the lessons: Rhubarb leaves are poisonous because they have oxalic acid in them. | Spinach contains a little oxalic acid. | Oxalic acid can remove rust stains from wood. | Never eat rhubarb leaves, only the stalks. | The chemist warned that oxalic acid is harmful if swallowed. | Some kidney stones are made with oxalic acid.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Almost always in «oxalic acid». Pronounced «ox-AL-ik». Salts are called oxalates. Safety: rhubarb stalks are safe to cook, but never eat the leaves; keep cleaning chemicals away from food.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (US, politics) PAC: political action committee, a group that collects money to help elect politicians or support causes. 2) Part of names, such as Pac-Man (a famous video game) and the Pac-12 (a group of US university sports teams). 3) (informal) Short for package or pack in some names and shops.
its sense in the lessons: In US news and politics, PACs and «super PACs» raise and spend money in elections. Children most often meet «Pac» in Pac-Man, the yellow circle that eats dots in a maze game from 1980. On its own it is not an everyday English word.
examples from the lessons: Pac-Man eats dots and runs from ghosts. | The PAC spent money on adverts before the election. | A super PAC can spend huge amounts on political adverts. | Dad played Pac-Man when he was a boy. | The news said many PACs gave money to both parties. | Pac-Man was made in Japan in 1980.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Not a full English word on its own; an abbreviation or part of a name. Usually written in capitals (PAC) for the politics meaning. Do not confuse with «pack» (a group or a bag) or «pact» (an agreement).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who paddles a canoe, kayak or paddleboard. 2) (UK, Ireland) A person, often a child, walking in shallow water at the seaside or in a paddling pool.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday and PE contexts: kayak and canoe paddlers on a river or lake, and stand-up paddleboarders. At the beach, paddlers wade with bare feet in shallow water. Water safety lessons tell paddlers to wear life jackets and to watch for tides.
examples from the lessons: The paddlers raced their canoes down the river. | Paddlers must wear life jackets. | Little paddlers splashed in the shallow pool. | The lifeguard warned the paddlers that the tide was coming in. | She is a strong paddler and won the kayak race. | Two paddlers pushed off from the jetty at sunrise.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. From «paddle» (verb and noun). UK «paddle» = walk in shallow water; US uses «wade». Safety: even shallow water can be dangerous with currents and tides; always paddle with an adult nearby.

part of speech: noun (paisley, uncountable); adjective (a paisley tie); Paisley (a name)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A pattern of curved, teardrop shapes with patterns inside them, used on fabric, ties and scarves. 2) Paisley: a town in Scotland near Glasgow, which gave the pattern its name (a name).
its sense in the lessons: In art and design lessons, paisley is a pattern to copy or design. The shape came from Persia and India and was copied by weavers in Paisley, Scotland, in the 1800s. In fashion, paisley shirts, ties and bandanas are common.
examples from the lessons: Dad wore a paisley tie to the wedding. | We drew paisley patterns in art. | The paisley shape looks a bit like a teardrop or a comma. | Grandma has a red paisley scarf. | Paisley in Scotland was famous for weaving shawls. | My bandana has a black and white paisley pattern.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable as a pattern; can be used as an adjective (a paisley shirt). Write Paisley with a capital when it is the town. Pronounced «PAYZ-lee».

part of speech: noun (a pantheon, pantheons); the Pantheon (a name)
meaning for a pupil: 1) All the gods of a people or religion, taken together: the Greek pantheon. 2) A group of the most famous or important people in an area: the pantheon of great footballers. 3) The Pantheon: a famous ancient temple in Rome with a huge dome, and a building in Paris where famous French people are buried (a name).
its sense in the lessons: In history and religious education lessons on Greek, Roman, Norse and Egyptian myths: the pantheon is the full set of gods, such as Zeus, Hera and Athena. In everyday talk, sports fans say a player has joined the «pantheon» of greats.
examples from the lessons: Zeus was the king of the Greek pantheon. | The Norse pantheon includes Odin, Thor and Loki. | The Pantheon in Rome has a hole in the top of its dome. | She has joined the pantheon of great tennis players. | We made a family tree of the Egyptian pantheon. | Many famous French writers are buried in the Panthéon in Paris.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Pronounced «PAN-thee-on». From Greek «pan» (all) and «theos» (god). Capital P for the buildings. Christianity, Judaism and Islam believe in one God, so they do not have a pantheon.

part of speech: noun (a pantomime, pantomimes; panto informal UK); verb (pantomime, pantomimed — rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (UK, Ireland, Australia) A funny family play, usually at Christmas, based on a fairy tale, with songs, jokes, a man dressed as a woman (the Dame), and the audience shouting back. 2) Telling a story with movements and faces but no words; mime. 3) (informal) A silly, over-the-top situation: «The meeting was a pantomime.»
its sense in the lessons: A big part of children's winter life in the UK and Ireland: going to «the panto» to see Cinderella, Aladdin, Jack and the Beanstalk or Dick Whittington. The audience shouts «He's behind you!» and «Oh no it isn't!» «Oh yes it is!» In drama lessons, pantomime also means acting without words.
examples from the lessons: We went to the pantomime at Christmas and shouted «He's behind you!» | The Dame in the panto wore a huge pink wig. | This year's pantomime is Cinderella. | In drama we did a pantomime of making a sandwich, without speaking. | «Oh no it isn't!» «Oh yes it is!» shouted the audience. | Dad called the traffic jam a complete pantomime. | My school puts on a panto every December.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Informal UK short form: panto. In the USA, «pantomime» usually just means mime; the Christmas panto is a British tradition. Pantomime villains are booed, heroes cheered.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (old-fashioned or family word) Father, dad. 2) (in some families) Grandfather, grandad. 3) In the NATO phonetic alphabet, the word for the letter P. 4) (other languages) «Papa» also means dad in French, Italian, Spanish (papá) and many more; in Ukrainian the usual word for dad is «tato».
its sense in the lessons: In older English books and stories, children call their father «Papa». Today in English it is more common in some families, cultures, and for grandfathers (especially in the USA, Canada, Australia). On radios, police and pilots spell P as «Papa». Phrases: «Papa Bear» in Goldilocks.
examples from the lessons: «Goodnight, Papa,» said the girl in the old story. | Papa Bear's porridge was too hot. | We call Grandad «Papa». | P for Papa, Q for Quebec. | In French, «papa» means dad. | My friend's papa picks her up from school. | Papa Smurf is the leader of the Smurfs.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Stress is usually on the second syllable in old British use (pa-PAH), and on the first in the USA (PAH-pa). Similar: pa, pop, dad, daddy. «Papal» and «Pope» come from a related word for father, used for the Pope.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Living on or inside another living thing (the host) and taking food from it, often harming it. 2) Caused by parasites: a parasitic disease. 3) (about people, disapproving) Taking from others without giving anything back.
its sense in the lessons: A science word: in lessons on food chains and living things, parasitic animals and plants include fleas, ticks, head lice, tapeworms and mistletoe. In health lessons, children learn about parasitic worms and how washing hands helps. In stories it can describe a greedy, lazy character.
examples from the lessons: Head lice are parasitic insects that live in hair. | Mistletoe is a parasitic plant that grows on trees. | Some wasps are parasitic and lay eggs inside caterpillars. | Washing your hands helps stop parasitic worms spreading. | The vet gave the dog a tablet for parasitic worms. | The story's villain lived a parasitic life, spending other people's money.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «parasite». Pronounced «pa-ra-SIT-ik». Opposite ideas: mutualism (both gain). A parasite usually does not kill its host quickly, because it needs the host to stay alive.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To do with a parliament: parliamentary elections, a parliamentary debate. 2) Done by a parliament or having a parliament: a parliamentary democracy.
its sense in the lessons: In citizenship and history lessons: the UK, Ireland, Canada, Australia and New Zealand have parliamentary systems, where the government is led by the party with most seats in parliament. Phrases: «parliamentary democracy», «parliamentary seat», «parliamentary candidate».
examples from the lessons: The UK is a parliamentary democracy. | There will be a parliamentary election next year. | Our school council copied parliamentary rules for debates. | She won the parliamentary seat by 200 votes. | Canada has a parliamentary system and a king as head of state. | The bill had to pass a parliamentary vote.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective. Spelling trap: parliament and parliamentary keep the silent «a» after «li»: p-a-r-l-i-a-m-e-n-t. The USA has Congress, not a parliament, and a presidential system.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) A unit for measuring huge distances in space, equal to about 3.26 light years, or about 31 million million kilometres.
its sense in the lessons: In space and science lessons, astronomers use parsecs and light years because kilometres are far too small. The nearest star to the Sun, Proxima Centauri, is about 1.3 parsecs away. Fans of Star Wars know the line about the Kessel Run «in less than twelve parsecs».
examples from the lessons: A parsec is about 3.26 light years. | The nearest star is a little over one parsec away. | Astronomers measure the distance to galaxies in millions of parsecs. | In Star Wars, Han Solo boasts about doing the Kessel Run in twelve parsecs. | A parsec is a measure of distance, not time. | The galaxy is about 30,000 parsecs across.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. A common trap (even in films): a parsec measures distance, not time. Maths: 1 parsec ≈ 3.26 light years ≈ 31 trillion km (31,000,000,000,000 km); a kiloparsec = 1,000 parsecs, a megaparsec = 1,000,000 parsecs. The name comes from «parallax second».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (adjective) Strongly supporting one political party or side, often without being fair to the other side. 2) (noun) A strong supporter of a party, person or idea. 3) (noun, history) A fighter in a secret army who fights against soldiers who have taken over their country, especially in the Second World War.
its sense in the lessons: In citizenship, news and media lessons: partisan news shows only one side, so pupils learn to check several sources. «Non-partisan» or «bipartisan» means not taking sides or supported by both sides. In history lessons, partisans in Europe fought the Nazi occupiers from forests and mountains.
examples from the lessons: The newspaper's report was very partisan. | A good referee is not partisan. | The partisans hid in the forest and blew up railway lines. | Bipartisan laws are supported by both main parties. | The crowd was partisan and cheered only for the home team. | The judge must be non-partisan.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective and countable noun. Pronounced «PAR-ti-zan» or «par-ti-ZAN». Related: partisanship (taking sides). Opposites: impartial, neutral, non-partisan. «Partisan» comes from «party».

part of speech: noun (passion, uncountable; a passion, passions); the Passion (church)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A very strong feeling, such as love, anger or excitement. 2) A strong love or enthusiasm for an activity or subject: a passion for football. 3) (church) The Passion: the suffering and death of Jesus on the cross, remembered by Christians especially at Easter.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and school, people talk about their passions: hobbies and subjects they love. In stories, passion shows strong feeling: «she spoke with passion». In religious education and church life, the Passion is the story told on Palm Sunday and Good Friday, and in musical «Passions» by Bach.
examples from the lessons: Her passion is horse riding. | He spoke with passion about saving the rainforest. | Find your passion and practise it every day. | Christians remember the Passion of Jesus on Good Friday. | Our choir sang music from Bach's St Matthew Passion. | Dad has a passion for old cars. | The football fans sang with passion.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable for the feeling, countable for a hobby or love (my passions). Adjective: passionate. Related: passion fruit (a fruit named after the Passion of Jesus because of its flower). The word comes from Latin «pati», to suffer.

part of speech: verb (pasteurise, pasteurises, pasteurised, pasteurising); US spelling pasteurize
meaning for a pupil: 1) To heat a drink or food, like milk or juice, to a set temperature for a short time to kill harmful germs, then cool it.
its sense in the lessons: A science and food word: named after the French scientist Louis Pasteur. In lessons on microbes and food safety, pupils learn that milk is pasteurised (about 72°C for 15 seconds) so that it is safer and lasts longer. Labels say «pasteurised» or «unpasteurised».
examples from the lessons: Milk is pasteurised to kill harmful bacteria. | Louis Pasteur showed how heating could stop germs. | The factory pasteurises the apple juice before bottling it. | Pregnant women are told to avoid some unpasteurised cheeses. | Pasteurising does not boil the milk. | We learnt how farmers pasteurise milk in science.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. -ise in UK/Ireland/Australia/NZ, -ize in US/Canada. A myth: pasteurising does not kill every single microbe (that is sterilising); it kills the harmful ones, which is why milk still goes off in the end. Capital P only for the name Pasteur.

part of speech: adjective; verb form (past of pasteurise); US spelling pasteurized
meaning for a pupil: 1) (of milk, juice, cheese or eggs) Heated for a short time to kill harmful germs, then cooled. 2) Past tense of pasteurise.
its sense in the lessons: Seen on food labels: «pasteurised milk», «made with pasteurised eggs». In science lessons on microbes and food safety, it tells the buyer the food is safer from germs like salmonella and listeria. Opposite: unpasteurised or raw.
examples from the lessons: This carton says «pasteurised whole milk». | The cheese is made with pasteurised milk. | Pasteurised eggs are safer in homemade mayonnaise. | The juice was pasteurised to make it last longer. | Raw milk is milk that has not been pasteurised. | Most milk in shops is pasteurised.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective and past form of the verb. UK/Ireland/Australia/NZ spell it -ised; US/Canada -ized. Trap: pasteurised food can still go off; keep it in the fridge and check the date.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A name made from the name of your father or a male ancestor, like Johnson (son of John) or Ukrainian Ivanovych (son of Ivan). 2) (adjective) Made from a father's name.
its sense in the lessons: In history, English and languages lessons on names: surnames like Robertson, Williams, O'Brien (Irish «Ó» = descendant), MacDonald (Scottish «Mac» = son), Jones (son of John) began as patronymics. In Ukrainian and Russian, people have a patronymic as a middle name, e.g. Ivanovych or Ivanivna. In Iceland, Björk Guðmundsdóttir means daughter of Guðmundur.
examples from the lessons: Johnson is a patronymic surname meaning son of John. | In Ukrainian, a patronymic is used in polite address, like Taras Hryhorovych. | Icelandic people often use patronymics instead of family names. | «Mac» in MacDonald works like a patronymic. | Our teacher explained that Fitzgerald means son of Gerald. | A name from your mother is a matronymic, not a patronymic.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Pronounced «pa-truh-NIM-ik». From Greek «pater» (father) and «onoma» (name). The female form often has a different ending (Ukrainian -ivna for daughters, -ovych/-yovych for sons).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A flat round cake of minced meat or other food, especially the meat in a burger. 2) A small pie or pastry, e.g. a Jamaican patty with a spicy filling. 3) (US) A small flat sweet, as in a peppermint patty.
its sense in the lessons: An everyday food word: burger patties (beef, chicken, veggie, bean). In the UK and Canada, Jamaican patties are a popular snack. Kitchen safety: cook meat patties right through so they are not pink in the middle.
examples from the lessons: Dad grilled the burger patties on the barbecue. | My veggie patty is made of beans and sweetcorn. | We bought Jamaican patties for lunch. | Shape the mince into four flat patties. | Make sure the patty is cooked through. | A peppermint patty is a mint sweet covered in chocolate.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; plural patties (y → ies). Patty is also a girl's name (short for Patricia) — a name. Do not confuse with «paddy» (a rice field) or «pâté» (a meat spread).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) A little bit hungry.
its sense in the lessons: An everyday British word: «I'm feeling a bit peckish» means you'd like a snack, not a big meal. It comes from birds pecking at food. In stories it gives a friendly, casual tone.
examples from the lessons: I'm a bit peckish; can I have a biscuit? | Are you peckish? There's fruit in the bowl. | By eleven o'clock I always feel peckish. | The cat looks peckish. | Grandad gets peckish before bed and eats toast. | If you're peckish after school, have an apple.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal adjective, mostly British, Irish and Australian English; less common in the USA. It means only a little hungry; «starving» or «ravenous» means very hungry.

part of speech: noun (a pedigree, pedigrees); adjective (a pedigree dog)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The list of an animal's parents, grandparents and earlier ancestors, showing it is of one pure breed. 2) (adjective) A pedigree animal comes from parents of the same breed, with records. 3) A person's family background or ancestry. 4) The past record of something, showing it is good: «the team's winning pedigree».
its sense in the lessons: Used about dogs, cats, horses and cattle at shows and on farms. In science lessons on inheritance, a pedigree chart shows how features like eye colour pass through a family. In sport and business it means a record of success.
examples from the lessons: Our dog is a pedigree Labrador. | The breeder showed us the puppy's pedigree. | Pedigree cats can be very expensive. | The horse had a famous pedigree. | We drew a pedigree chart of our family's eye colours. | The coach has a strong pedigree in winning cups. | Mixed-breed dogs are often healthier than some pedigrees.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Opposite of pedigree animal: mixed breed, crossbreed or mongrel. Pedigree is also a brand name of dog food (a name). Pronounced «PED-i-gree».

part of speech: noun (a peen, peens); verb (peen, peens, peened, peening)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The rounded or wedge-shaped end of a hammer head, opposite the flat striking face (as in ball-peen hammer). 2) (verb) To hit metal with a hammer to shape or harden it.
its sense in the lessons: A design-and-technology and workshop word: a ball-peen hammer is used for metalwork and shaping rivets. Metalworkers «peen» metal to bend or harden it. Rare in everyday talk.
examples from the lessons: A ball-peen hammer has a round end for shaping metal. | Use the peen of the hammer to round off the rivet. | The blacksmith peened the edge of the blade. | Dad keeps a ball-peen hammer in his toolbox. | In DT we watched a teacher peen a copper bowl. | The peen is on the opposite side to the flat face.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun and regular verb. Also spelled «pein» or «pane» in older British use. Safety: wear goggles when hammering metal.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science, formal) The fur, hair or wool covering a mammal's body.
its sense in the lessons: A scientific word used by zoologists and in nature books: an Arctic fox's pelage turns white in winter and brown in summer. In lessons on adaptations, pelage helps animals keep warm and hide.
examples from the lessons: The Arctic fox changes its pelage with the seasons. | A seal's thick pelage keeps it warm in icy water. | The scientist described the colour of the bat's pelage. | Polar bears have a dense pelage over black skin. | The pelage of a stoat turns white in winter, and it is then called ermine. | The new species has a reddish pelage.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Pronounced «PEL-ij». A formal science word; in everyday English we say fur or coat. Only mammals have pelage; birds have plumage.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Able to be seen, heard, felt or noticed, even if only just.
its sense in the lessons: A formal word used in science and descriptions: «a barely perceptible sound», «a perceptible change in temperature». In science experiments pupils note whether changes are perceptible to the senses or need instruments to measure them.
examples from the lessons: There was a barely perceptible smile on her face. | The change in temperature was hardly perceptible. | The sound was too quiet to be perceptible to humans, but the dog heard it. | There has been a perceptible improvement in your handwriting. | The earthquake was perceptible as a faint shake. | Without a microscope, the cells were not perceptible.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective. Opposite: imperceptible (too small to notice). Related: perceive, perception. Spelling: -ible, not -able. Often with «barely» or «just».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A simple language made up when people who speak different languages need to talk, often for trade, mixing words from both. 2) (informal) Broken or very simple speech in a language you do not know well: «pidgin French».
its sense in the lessons: In language and history lessons: pidgins grew up in ports and plantations. When children grow up speaking a pidgin as their first language, it becomes a full language called a creole. Tok Pisin in Papua New Guinea and Nigerian Pidgin are well-known examples spoken by millions.
examples from the lessons: A pidgin has a small vocabulary and simple grammar. | Nigerian Pidgin is spoken by millions of people. | Tok Pisin began as a pidgin and is now an official language of Papua New Guinea. | On holiday, Dad got by with pidgin Spanish. | Traders made a pidgin so they could buy and sell. | When a pidgin becomes a first language, it is called a creole.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Homophone trap: «pidgin» (language) and «pigeon» (bird) sound the same. Countable for a particular language; uncountable for the kind of speech. Calling someone's speech «pidgin» can sound rude; pidgins and creoles are real languages with their own rules.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An arcade game in which you shoot a metal ball up a sloping table and use flippers to keep it bouncing off targets to score points. 2) (verb, informal) To bounce quickly from one place to another: «The ball pinballed around the box.»
its sense in the lessons: Everyday games word: pinball machines are found in arcades, cafes and on computers. In science lessons it can illustrate forces, slopes and bouncing (collisions). Sports commentators say a ball «pinballed» around the penalty area.
examples from the lessons: We played pinball at the arcade on the pier. | Press the buttons to move the flippers in pinball. | I got a high score on the pinball machine. | The ball went pinballing between the defenders. | Pinball machines use springs, slopes and magnets. | Gravity pulls the pinball down the table.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable as a game (play pinball); countable as a machine (two pinball machines). One word. The verb «pinball» is informal.

meaning for a pupil: 1) One of the two claws of a crab, lobster or scorpion, used for gripping. 2) Pincers: a tool with two handles and two curved jaws for gripping things or pulling out nails. 3) A pincer movement: an attack in which two groups come at an enemy from both sides.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on minibeasts and sea creatures: crabs, lobsters, earwigs and scorpions have pincers. In DT, pincers pull nails. In history lessons about battles, a pincer movement traps an army between two forces.
examples from the lessons: The crab nipped my finger with its pincer. | Earwigs have pincers at the end of their bodies. | Dad pulled the nail out with a pair of pincers. | The scorpion grabbed the beetle with its pincers. | The army attacked in a pincer movement from the north and south. | A lobster's pincers are very strong.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; often plural. The tool is «a pair of pincers», like «a pair of scissors». Do not confuse with «pliers» (a tool for gripping and bending) though they are similar. Safety: be gentle with crabs on the beach and put them back where you found them.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Slightly pink; a colour with a little pink in it.
its sense in the lessons: Used in art and science descriptions: a pinkish sky at sunset, pinkish flowers, pinkish skin. The ending «-ish» means «a bit» or «roughly», as in reddish, tallish, sevenish.
examples from the lessons: The sky turned pinkish at sunset. | The prawn turned pinkish when it was cooked. | Litmus paper can go pinkish in weak acid. | Her cheeks were pinkish from the cold. | The flowers are white with pinkish edges. | Cook the chicken until it is no longer pinkish inside.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective, not graded (we say «more pinkish» rarely). The suffix «-ish» softens a word: «sevenish» means about seven o'clock. Food safety: chicken should not be pinkish in the middle.

part of speech: noun (a pinwheel, pinwheels); verb (pinwheel, pinwheeled — rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (US, Canada) A toy made of paper or plastic blades on a stick that spin round in the wind; in the UK called a windmill. 2) A firework that spins round, also called a Catherine wheel. 3) A round spiral shape, such as pinwheel sandwiches or biscuits.
its sense in the lessons: Children make pinwheels in science and DT lessons to learn about wind and energy. In art and cooking, a pinwheel is a spiral design, like rolled sandwiches cut into slices. On Bonfire Night, spinning fireworks are called Catherine wheels or pinwheels.
examples from the lessons: We made paper pinwheels to see which way the wind blows. | My pinwheel spun faster when I ran. | The Catherine wheel firework spun like a pinwheel. | Mum made pinwheel sandwiches for the party. | The galaxy looks like a giant pinwheel. | Blow on the pinwheel and watch it turn.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. One word. UK English often says «windmill» for the toy. Firework safety: only adults should light fireworks.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Being able to be shaped or moulded easily and keep the new shape, like clay. 2) (science) The ability of the brain or a living thing to change and adapt, e.g. when learning something new.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on materials, plasticity is a property of clay, putty and some metals. In lessons about the brain and learning, «brain plasticity» (neuroplasticity) means the brain makes new connections when we practise, which is why practice helps.
examples from the lessons: Clay has great plasticity, so we can make pots from it. | Brain plasticity means you can get better with practice. | The plasticity of warm wax makes it easy to model. | Children's brains have a lot of plasticity. | Metals like gold have plasticity and can be hammered thin. | The plasticity of the dough let us shape it into animals.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. It is not about plastic material; plastic got its name because it can be shaped, from Greek «plastikos», able to be moulded. Opposite properties: brittleness, rigidity, elasticity (springs back to its shape).

meaning for a pupil: 1) How believable or likely to be true something seems.
its sense in the lessons: In English and science lessons: pupils judge the plausibility of an explanation, a story ending, or an answer. In maths, checking the plausibility of an answer (is it about the right size?) catches mistakes. In media literacy, a plausible-sounding claim can still be false, so check sources.
examples from the lessons: The detective doubted the plausibility of the thief's excuse. | Check the plausibility of your answer by estimating. | The plausibility of the story made people believe the fake news. | Scientists test an idea, not just its plausibility. | His excuse had some plausibility, but it wasn't true. | The plot lost its plausibility when the dog started flying a plane.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Adjective: plausible; opposite: implausibility, implausible. Trap: plausible means it sounds true, not that it is true. In maths problems, a plausible answer is one of a sensible size (a child cannot be 300 cm tall).

part of speech: noun (a pleat, pleats); verb (pleat, pleats, pleated, pleating)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A fold made in cloth by doubling it over and pressing or sewing it in place. 2) (verb) To make folds like this in cloth or paper.
its sense in the lessons: Used in clothes, school uniforms and art and DT: pleated skirts and kilts have many pleats; children fold paper into pleats to make fans and concertina books.
examples from the lessons: My school skirt has pleats all round. | A kilt has neat pleats at the back. | We pleated paper to make a fan. | Iron the pleats so they stay sharp. | The curtains were pleated at the top. | Fold the paper into pleats like an accordion.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun and regular verb. Adjective: pleated. Do not confuse with «plead» (to beg) or «plait» (UK: to braid hair, pronounced «plat»).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Easily bent without breaking; flexible. 2) (about people) Easily persuaded or controlled by others.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on materials: pliable materials include clay, wire, rubber and willow; brittle ones like glass break instead. In stories and safety talks, a pliable person might be easily talked into doing something wrong.
examples from the lessons: Willow twigs are pliable, so we can weave baskets. | Warm the clay in your hands to make it more pliable. | Copper wire is pliable and easy to bend. | The leather became pliable after oiling. | The bully picked a pliable boy to do his dirty work. | Pliable plastic is used for lunchboxes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective. Similar: flexible, bendy, supple. Opposite: rigid, stiff, brittle. Spelling: -able. Related: pliant.

part of speech: noun (plural: pliers; a pair of pliers)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A hand tool with two handles and two jaws, used for gripping, bending, twisting or cutting wire.
its sense in the lessons: Used in DT and everyday home repairs: pliers grip small things, bend wire and cut it. In science, pliers are a lever, showing how a small force on the handles makes a bigger force at the jaws.
examples from the lessons: Pass me the pliers so I can bend this wire. | Dad used a pair of pliers to pull out the nail. | Pliers are a kind of lever. | The electrician cut the cable with pliers. | Long-nose pliers can reach into small spaces. | We used pliers to make jewellery from wire.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural noun: «the pliers are», «a pair of pliers», like scissors and trousers. Do not say «a plier». Different from pincers (for pulling nails), though similar. Safety: never use pliers on electric wires that are plugged in.

part of speech: noun (poaching, uncountable); verb form (present participle of poach)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Illegally hunting or catching animals, birds or fish, especially on someone else's land or protected animals like elephants and rhinos. 2) Cooking food, such as eggs or fish, gently in water or milk that is just below boiling. 3) Taking or tempting away someone else's workers, players or ideas: «poaching players».
its sense in the lessons: In geography and science lessons on endangered animals, poaching for ivory and horns is a big threat to elephants, rhinos and tigers; rangers try to stop poachers. In cooking lessons and at breakfast, poaching eggs is a healthy way to cook them. In sport news, clubs accuse others of poaching players.
examples from the lessons: Poaching has made black rhinos very rare. | Rangers patrol the park to stop poaching. | Dad is poaching eggs for breakfast. | Poaching fish in milk keeps it soft. | The big club was accused of poaching young players. | Poaching deer on the lord's land was once punished harshly.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «poach» (poach, poaches, poached, poaching). A poacher is a person who poaches animals. In football, a «poacher» is a striker who scores close to the goal. Poached egg = egg cooked without its shell in simmering water.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To do with poetry or written in the form of poems. 2) Beautiful, expressive or imaginative, like a poem: a poetic description. 3) Poetic justice: when someone who has done wrong gets a fitting, almost funny punishment.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons: poetic devices include rhyme, rhythm, alliteration, simile and metaphor. «Poetic licence» means a poet is allowed to break rules of grammar or truth for effect. In everyday talk, a beautiful sunset can be «poetic».
examples from the lessons: Her description of the sea was very poetic. | Alliteration is a poetic device. | It was poetic justice when the bully slipped on his own banana skin. | The poet used poetic licence and changed the word order. | The song has poetic lyrics. | Write a poetic sentence about the moon.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective. Related: poem, poet, poetry, poetically. «Poetic licence» (UK) / «poetic license» (US). Pronounced «poh-ET-ik».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A plant from Mexico with large bright red (or pink or white) leaves around small yellow flowers, popular at Christmas.
its sense in the lessons: An everyday and festive word: poinsettias decorate homes, churches and shops at Christmas. In science lessons, the red parts are not petals but special leaves called bracts. Named after Joel Poinsett, a US ambassador to Mexico.
examples from the lessons: We bought a poinsettia for the Christmas table. | The red parts of a poinsettia are leaves, not petals. | Poinsettias come from Mexico. | The church was decorated with red poinsettias. | Keep a poinsettia warm and away from draughts. | In Mexico the poinsettia is called the Christmas Eve flower.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Spelling trap: p-o-i-n-s-e-t-t-i-a; many people say «poin-SET-a». A myth: poinsettias are often said to be deadly to children and pets; they can cause an upset stomach or skin rash but are not deadly. Still, do not eat them.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A serious illness caused by a virus that can damage the nerves and cause paralysis, so people cannot move parts of their body. Its full name is poliomyelitis.
its sense in the lessons: In history and health lessons: polio was once common around the world, especially among children. Vaccines developed by Jonas Salk and Albert Sabin in the 1950s and 60s made it rare; today it remains in very few places, and worldwide vaccination aims to wipe it out. Former US President Franklin D. Roosevelt had polio.
examples from the lessons: Polio vaccines have saved millions of children from paralysis. | Grandma remembers getting the polio vaccine on a sugar lump. | Polio is caused by a virus. | Jonas Salk made one of the first polio vaccines. | Today polio has almost disappeared from the world. | Some people who had polio needed leg braces to walk.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable; short for poliomyelitis. Pronounced «POH-lee-oh». It cannot be cured once someone has it, but it can be prevented by vaccination.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A substance that makes air, water or soil dirty and harmful to living things.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography lessons: pollutants include car exhaust gases, smoke, plastic, oil, sewage and pesticides. Pupils learn how pollutants harm health, rivers and wildlife, and how to reduce them (walking to school, recycling).
examples from the lessons: Car exhaust contains pollutants that are bad for our lungs. | Plastic is a pollutant in the oceans. | The factory let pollutants into the river. | Trees can trap some air pollutants. | Fertiliser running off fields can be a pollutant. | Scientists measured the pollutants near the school gate.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. From «pollute» (verb) and «pollution» (uncountable noun). Spelling: -ant, not -ent. Use «a pollutant» but «pollution» without «a».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) All the ordinary people who live in a country or area; the general public.
its sense in the lessons: A formal word used in history, news and exam writing: «The king ignored the needs of the populace.» In everyday life people say «the public» or «the people». It tells the reader the writer is talking about everyone, not the rulers.
examples from the lessons: The king taxed the populace heavily. | The new law was popular with the populace. | The whole populace was asked to vote. | During the war, the populace had to use ration books. | The emperor gave bread and games to keep the populace happy. | The town's populace gathered in the square.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; usually «the populace». Homophone trap: «populace» (the people) and «populous» (an adjective meaning having many people: a populous city) sound the same. Related: population.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A large, grand doorway or entrance to a building. 2) (stories, games) A magic doorway that takes you to another world or place. 3) (computing) A website that is the starting point for using a service, such as a school login page.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and games, portals take characters to other worlds (as in Narnia's wardrobe, or Minecraft's Nether portal). At school, children use a parent portal or learning portal to log in. In history and art, cathedral portals have carved stone arches.
examples from the lessons: The cathedral's portal was carved with saints. | In the game, we built a portal to another world. | The wardrobe was like a portal to Narnia. | Mum checked my homework on the school portal. | Log in to the portal with your username and password. | The stone portal was covered in ivy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Online safety: only type your password into the real school portal, and never share your login.

meaning for a pupil: 1) How strong or powerful something is, especially a medicine, drug, poison or chemical. 2) (formal) Power or influence: the potency of an idea.
its sense in the lessons: In science and health lessons: the potency of a medicine tells how strong its effect is, which is why doses must be measured carefully. In history or English, the «potency» of a speech or symbol means its power to move people.
examples from the lessons: The potency of the medicine means you only need a small dose. | Some medicines lose their potency after their expiry date. | The snake's venom has great potency. | The speech showed the potency of words. | Scientists tested the potency of the new vaccine. | Strong sunlight can reduce the potency of vitamins.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Adjective: potent. Safety: never take more of a medicine than the label or doctor says; a potent medicine can be dangerous in large amounts.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Birds kept on farms for their meat or eggs, such as chickens, ducks, geese and turkeys. 2) The meat from these birds.
its sense in the lessons: In geography, science and food lessons: poultry farms, free-range poultry, and kitchen hygiene (wash hands after touching raw poultry; cook it thoroughly). Phrases: «poultry farm», «raw poultry», «poultry and fish».
examples from the lessons: The farmer keeps poultry and sheep. | Chickens, ducks and turkeys are all poultry. | Wash your hands after touching raw poultry. | The shop sells meat, poultry and fish. | Free-range poultry can walk outside. | Bird flu can spread among poultry.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «poultry is» (meat) or «poultry are» (the birds, used as a plural). No «poultries». Food safety: raw poultry can carry salmonella, so use a separate chopping board and cook it until no pink remains.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Able to be done or put into practice successfully; possible in real life.
its sense in the lessons: A formal word in official and exam English: «as soon as practicable» means as soon as it can be done. It tells the reader a plan is realistic. Teachers or rules may say «where practicable» (when possible).
examples from the lessons: Building a bridge here is not practicable. | Please reply as soon as practicable. | Is it practicable to walk to school every day? | The plan was clever but not practicable. | Fire exits must be kept clear wherever practicable. | The engineer looked for a practicable route over the mountain.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Common confusion: «practicable» means can be done; «practical» means useful, sensible or hands-on (a practical person, practical work in science). Opposite: impracticable.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An action or decision from the past that is used as an example or rule for what to do later. 2) (law) An earlier judgement in court that judges follow in similar cases.
its sense in the lessons: Used in law, history and politics: «set a precedent», «without precedent» (never happened before), «break with precedent». In everyday life, parents might worry that letting one child stay up late sets a precedent for the others.
examples from the lessons: If I let you stay up late, it will set a precedent. | The judge followed a precedent from an earlier case. | The flood was without precedent in the town's history. | Her election as the first woman leader set a precedent. | There is no precedent for a dog joining the school choir. | Courts in England follow precedent.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Pronounced «PRESS-i-dent». Homophone-ish trap: «precedent» (an example) vs «president» (a leader). Related: unprecedented (never happened before), precede (to come before).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Something that must be true or must happen before something else can happen.
its sense in the lessons: Used in formal talk, science and maths: «Water is a precondition for life.» In negotiations and rules: «There are no preconditions for joining the club.» In computing, a precondition is what must be true before a program step runs.
examples from the lessons: Finishing your homework is a precondition for going out to play. | Oxygen is a precondition for fire. | The talks began without any preconditions. | A precondition for joining the team is coming to training. | Trust is a precondition for friendship. | Light is a precondition for photosynthesis.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Similar: requirement, condition, prerequisite. «Pre-» means before. Usually followed by «for» or «of».

meaning for a pupil: 1) The very long time in the past before people wrote things down, so we learn about it from things they left behind, like tools, bones and cave paintings. 2) The early beginnings of something: the prehistory of computers.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons (especially the UK primary curriculum): the Stone Age, Bronze Age and Iron Age are prehistory. Archaeologists study prehistory through Stonehenge, Skara Brae, flint tools and cave art. Dinosaurs lived long before any humans, in the much older past of the Earth.
examples from the lessons: Stonehenge was built in prehistory. | We are learning about British prehistory, from the Stone Age to the Iron Age. | Archaeologists dig up tools to learn about prehistory. | Cave paintings tell us about life in prehistory. | Prehistory ended at different times in different places. | The museum has a gallery on prehistory.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Adjective: prehistoric. Prehistory ends when writing begins, which happened at different times around the world (about 5,000 years ago in Mesopotamia, much later in Britain). Myth: cavemen and dinosaurs did not live at the same time; dinosaurs died out about 66 million years before humans.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Happening or done too early, before the right time. 2) (of a baby) Born too early, before 37 weeks of pregnancy.
its sense in the lessons: In health and family life: premature babies are often cared for in an incubator in a special hospital unit. In everyday talk: «It's premature to celebrate before the match ends.» In science, premature conclusions are drawn before enough evidence.
examples from the lessons: My cousin was born premature and spent weeks in hospital. | It's premature to say who will win; the game isn't over. | Premature babies are often very small. | The celebration was premature; the other team scored. | Smoking can cause premature ageing of the skin. | The scientist warned against premature conclusions.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective. Informal: «prem» or «preemie» (premature baby). Adverb: prematurely. Opposite: overdue (late), timely. Pronounced «PREM-a-cher» or «pree-ma-TURE».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Planned or thought about carefully beforehand, especially a crime or a bad act.
its sense in the lessons: Used in law and crime stories: a premeditated crime is planned, not done in a sudden moment, and courts usually treat it as more serious. In ethics lessons it helps compare doing harm on purpose and by accident.
examples from the lessons: The judge said the attack was premeditated. | It wasn't an accident; it was premeditated. | The burglary was premeditated; they had studied the house for weeks. | A premeditated lie is worse than a mistake. | In the detective story, the murder was carefully premeditated. | The prank was premeditated, not spur-of-the-moment.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective (from the verb premeditate). Opposite: spontaneous, unplanned, spur-of-the-moment. «Pre-» = before, «meditate» = think.

part of speech: verb (pressurise, pressurises, pressurised, pressurising); US spelling pressurize
meaning for a pupil: 1) (UK, Ireland, Australia) To try to make someone do something by pushing or persuading them hard; to pressure. 2) To keep the air pressure inside an aeroplane, spacesuit or container at a set level, usually higher than outside.
its sense in the lessons: In PSHE and safety lessons: friends may pressurise you to do something you don't want to; it is fine to say no. In science lessons: aeroplane cabins and spacesuits are pressurised so people can breathe high up; aerosol cans are pressurised.
examples from the lessons: Don't let anyone pressurise you into doing something unsafe. | The older kids pressurised him to skip school. | Aeroplane cabins are pressurised. | The can is pressurised, so never put it in a fire. | Astronauts' suits are pressurised. | I felt pressurised to agree with everyone.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb; -ise in UK spelling. In US English, «pressure» is more common as the verb for people (they pressured him), and «pressurize» for air. Safety: pressurised cans can explode if heated.

meaning for a pupil: 1) How common or widespread something is in a place or group at a given time.
its sense in the lessons: Used in science, health and news: «the prevalence of asthma in children», «the prevalence of mobile phones». In maths and statistics, prevalence is often given as a percentage or a fraction of a group.
examples from the lessons: The prevalence of head lice goes up when school starts. | The survey studied the prevalence of short-sightedness. | The prevalence of smartphones has changed how people talk. | Scientists measured the prevalence of the disease. | The prevalence of plastic on beaches is shocking. | Allergies have a higher prevalence than they used to.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Adjective: prevalent. In maths: if 20 out of 100 children have glasses, the prevalence is 20%, or 1 in 5. Not the same as «incidence», which counts new cases in a time period.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A country or land ruled by a prince; a principality. 2) The rank or position of a prince.
its sense in the lessons: A rare, old-fashioned word in history and fairy tales. Real principalities today include Monaco and Liechtenstein; Wales is often called a principality. Stories use «princedom» for small kingdoms ruled by princes.
examples from the lessons: The tiny princedom lay between two great kingdoms. | Monaco is a small princedom by the sea. | He inherited the princedom from his father. | In the fairy tale, the princedom was cursed by a witch. | The princedom had its own coins and flag. | Old maps of Europe show many small princedoms.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. The more common word is «principality». Rare and old-fashioned.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An artist who makes pictures by printing, such as woodcuts, lino prints, etchings or screen prints.
its sense in the lessons: An art word: in art lessons children are printmakers when they make lino or polystyrene prints, using ink and rollers. Famous printmakers include Albrecht Dürer and Katsushika Hokusai (The Great Wave).
examples from the lessons: Hokusai was a famous Japanese printmaker. | The printmaker carved a design into the wood. | Today we are printmakers, using polystyrene tiles. | A printmaker can make many copies of one picture. | The printmaker rolled ink onto the lino. | We visited a printmaker's studio.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; one word. Related: printmaking (uncountable), print (noun and verb).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A bush with small, dark green, shiny leaves that is often grown as a garden hedge.
its sense in the lessons: An everyday British, Irish and Australian garden word: privet hedges line front gardens. In nature lessons, privet flowers attract bees and its berries are eaten by birds but are poisonous to people. Harry Potter fans know the Dursleys live at Privet Drive.
examples from the lessons: Our front garden has a privet hedge. | Dad trims the privet every summer. | Privet berries are poisonous, so don't eat them. | Bees love the white privet flowers. | Birds nest in the thick privet. | The Dursleys lived at number four, Privet Drive.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable (a hedge of privet). Do not confuse with «private». Safety: privet berries and leaves are poisonous to people and pets.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An official public announcement, especially from a king, queen, president or government. 2) A clear, strong public statement of a belief or idea.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons: royal proclamations, the Emancipation Proclamation (1863) by Abraham Lincoln, and the Proclamation of the Irish Republic (1916). In stories, a herald reads out the king's proclamation in the town square.
examples from the lessons: The king's proclamation was read in the market square. | Lincoln's Emancipation Proclamation aimed to free enslaved people. | The 1916 Proclamation of the Irish Republic was read outside the GPO in Dublin. | A proclamation announced the new queen. | The town crier shouted the proclamation. | Her speech was a proclamation of hope.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. From the verb «proclaim». Spelling trap: proclaim has «ai», but proclamation has just «a».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (law) The person who makes a promise in a contract or agreement. The person who receives the promise is the promisee.
its sense in the lessons: A legal word for contracts, rarely heard in everyday life. In lessons about adult life and law, a contract is a set of promises: the promisor promises to do something (pay money, deliver goods) for the promisee.
examples from the lessons: In the contract, the promisor agrees to pay £100. | The promisee can go to court if the promisor breaks the promise. | The bank was the promisor in the agreement. | Lawyers call the person who promises the promisor. | If the promisor delivers the bike, the promisee must pay. | A promisor must keep the terms of the contract.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; legal and formal. Spelled -or in law, though «promiser» is used in ordinary English. Pair: promisor (gives the promise) and promisee (gets it), like employer/employee.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (law) To officially accuse someone of a crime in a court of law and try to prove they are guilty. 2) (formal) To carry on or continue something, such as a war or a plan, until it is finished.
its sense in the lessons: In law and citizenship lessons: the police or state (the prosecution) prosecute a person accused of a crime; the defence argues for them; the judge or jury decides. Signs warn: «Trespassers will be prosecuted». History books say a country «prosecuted the war».
examples from the lessons: Shoplifters will be prosecuted. | The police decided to prosecute the driver for speeding. | He was prosecuted for stealing a car. | The lawyer who prosecutes is called the prosecutor. | The sign said trespassers would be prosecuted. | The general prosecuted the war for five years.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Related: prosecution, prosecutor. Common trap: «prosecute» (take to court) and «persecute» (treat cruelly, especially for beliefs) sound alike but mean very different things.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To be successful, especially to grow rich or do well over time. 2) To grow strongly and be healthy, like plants or animals.
its sense in the lessons: In history, geography and RE lessons: towns prospered from trade, farms prosper with good harvests. In Bible and blessing language: «May you prosper». Common in stories: «The village prospered after the bridge was built».
examples from the lessons: The town prospered when the railway came. | Her business prospered and she opened another shop. | The plants prospered in the warm greenhouse. | «Live long and prosper» is a famous line from Star Trek. | The Romans prospered by trading across their empire. | The Bible often speaks of people who prosper because they trust God.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb, no object (the town prospers). Related: prosperous (adjective), prosperity (noun). Opposite: struggle, fail, decline.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The main character in a story, play, film or game. 2) A leading person in a real event, or a strong supporter of an idea or cause.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons, pupils identify the protagonist (main character) and the antagonist (the character or force against them) when analysing stories. In news and history, the protagonists of a debate or conflict are the main people involved.
examples from the lessons: Harry Potter is the protagonist of the books. | The protagonist has to overcome a problem by the end. | Who is the antagonist working against the protagonist? | In «Matilda», the protagonist is a clever girl who loves books. | Describe how the protagonist changes in the story. | She was a protagonist in the campaign for clean air.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Opposite: antagonist. Trap: the protagonist is not always good or a hero; sometimes the main character is a villain. From Greek: «first actor».

meaning for a pupil: 1) To stick out from a surface or edge.
its sense in the lessons: Used in science, safety and description: «a nail protruding from the wood», «protruding teeth». In science lessons, animals may have protruding eyes (frogs). In stories it adds clear visual detail.
examples from the lessons: A rusty nail protruded from the fence. | The frog's eyes protrude from the top of its head. | Be careful of the branch protruding over the path. | His tongue protruded as he concentrated. | Rocks protrude from the sand at low tide. | The pencil protruded from her bag.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Adjective: protruding. Noun: protrusion. Safety: tell an adult about protruding nails or sharp edges at school or in the playground.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (prefix) «pseudo-» means false or pretend, looking like something it is not: pseudoscience, pseudonym. 2) (informal adjective) Fake, not genuine, or pretending to be clever: «His pseudo-intellectual talk annoyed everyone.»
its sense in the lessons: Mostly met as a prefix in school words: a pseudonym is a pen name (Mark Twain was a pseudonym), pseudoscience is a claim that looks like science but does not use proper evidence (like horoscopes). In maths and computing, «pseudocode» is a plan for a program written in simple words.
examples from the lessons: Mark Twain is the pseudonym of Samuel Clemens. | Astrology is a pseudoscience, not a real science. | Write your program in pseudocode first. | His pseudo-friendliness didn't fool anyone. | Some authors use a pseudonym to stay private. | The advert used pseudo-scientific words to sound clever.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly a prefix; on its own it is informal. The «p» is silent: «SOO-doh» or «SYOO-doh». From Greek «pseudes», false.

part of speech: verb (publicise, publicises, publicised, publicising); US spelling publicize
meaning for a pupil: 1) To make information about something known to many people, especially by advertising or reporting it.
its sense in the lessons: Used in school and everyday life: pupils publicise a bake sale with posters, assemblies and the newsletter. In media lessons, companies publicise products and news publicises events. Phrase: «widely publicised».
examples from the lessons: We made posters to publicise the school fair. | The charity publicised its fun run on social media. | The case was widely publicised in the news. | Don't publicise your address online. | The band publicised their new song on the radio. | The council publicised the new bus times.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb; -ise in UK, Ireland, Australia, NZ; -ize in US and Canada. Related: public, publicity. Online safety: never publicise personal details like your address or school.

part of speech: noun (a pueblo, pueblos); Pueblo (a name of peoples)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A village of flat-roofed houses made of adobe (mud brick) or stone, built by Native American peoples in the south-west of the USA. 2) Pueblo peoples: Native American nations such as the Hopi, Zuni and Taos, who live in these villages (a name). 3) (Spanish) «Pueblo» means town, village or people.
its sense in the lessons: In history and geography lessons on Native Americans: Taos Pueblo in New Mexico has been lived in for about 1,000 years. Pueblo houses have thick walls that keep them cool in the desert. The word came into English from Spanish.
examples from the lessons: Pueblo houses are made of adobe, a kind of mud brick. | Taos Pueblo is one of the oldest lived-in places in the USA. | The Hopi are one of the Pueblo peoples. | People climbed ladders to get into the upper rooms of the pueblo. | Thick walls keep the pueblo cool in summer. | In Spanish, «pueblo» means village.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Capital P when naming the peoples or a particular place (Taos Pueblo). Pronounced «PWEB-loh». Spanish word used in English.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A regular beat or throb, like a heartbeat. 2) (science) A regular swelling and shrinking, such as a star that grows bigger and smaller, or a wave of pressure.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on the heart and blood, the pulse is the pulsation of the arteries with each heartbeat. In space science, some stars (pulsating stars) get brighter and dimmer as they swell and shrink. In music, a pulsation is a strong regular beat.
examples from the lessons: You can feel the pulsation of blood in your wrist. | The pulsation of the music filled the hall. | The star's pulsation makes it brighter and dimmer. | The doctor felt for a pulsation in his neck. | Jellyfish move by pulsation of their bells. | Count the pulsations in fifteen seconds and multiply by four.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable or uncountable. Related: pulse, pulsate. In maths: to find beats per minute, count pulses in 15 seconds and multiply by 4 (e.g. 20 × 4 = 80 beats per minute).

part of speech: noun (a punt, punts); verb (punt, punts, punted, punting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A long, flat-bottomed boat with square ends, pushed along a river with a long pole. 2) (verb) To travel in a punt by pushing a pole against the river bed. 3) (sport) A kick in which the ball is dropped from the hands and kicked before it hits the ground, used in rugby, American football and Australian rules. 4) (informal, UK, Ireland, Australia) A bet or a guess: «take a punt on it». 5) (history, Ireland) The Irish pound, Ireland's money before the euro in 2002.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday British life, people go punting on the rivers in Oxford and Cambridge. In sport, punts kick the ball long down the field. In informal speech, «I'll take a punt» means «I'll have a go» or guess. In Irish history, the punt was the currency.
examples from the lessons: We went punting on the river in Cambridge. | Push the pole down to the river bed to punt. | The kicker punted the ball down the field. | I don't know the answer, but I'll take a punt: is it twelve? | Grandad still talks about prices in punts. | The punt drifted slowly under the bridge.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun and regular verb. «Take a punt» is informal. A punter (UK) means a customer or someone who bets; in Australia also any ordinary person. Water safety: sit still in a punt and wear a life jacket if you can't swim.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) According to what is said or claimed, though it may not be true.
its sense in the lessons: A formal and news word: «The letter was purportedly written by the queen.» It tells the reader that something is claimed but not proved. In media literacy lessons, it is a signal to check the facts.
examples from the lessons: The photo purportedly shows the Loch Ness monster. | The video was purportedly filmed in space, but it was fake. | The painting is purportedly by a famous artist. | The email was purportedly from the bank, but it was a scam. | The treasure was purportedly buried on the island. | The note was purportedly signed by the headteacher.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal adverb. Related: purport (to claim), purported (adjective). Similar: allegedly, supposedly, reportedly. Online safety: an email «purportedly» from a bank or school might be a scam; check with an adult.

part of speech: noun (putty — usually uncountable); verb (putty, putties, puttied, puttying — rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A soft grey or white paste that is pressed into gaps, for example to hold glass in a window frame, and that goes hard as it dries. 2) Any soft stuff that can be pressed and shaped easily, like the stretchy toy "silly putty". 3) (idiom) "Putty in someone's hands" means a person who is easily persuaded or controlled by someone else. 4) (verb, rare) To fill or fix something with putty.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and DIY, putty seals windows and fills holes in wood or walls before painting. In science, putty is a good example of a material that can change shape (it is "malleable") and then set hard. In stories, "he was putty in her hands" tells the reader that a character is easily won over, often by charm. Phrases: window putty, wood putty, silly putty, putty knife, putty in someone's hands.
examples from the lessons: Dad pressed fresh putty around the new pane of glass. | Fill the nail holes with putty before you paint the shelf. | My little brother stretched his silly putty across the table. | The putty takes a day to go hard. | The puppy looked up with big eyes, and Gran was putty in his hands. | We used a putty knife to scrape away the old putty. | In art club we shaped putty into tiny animals.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable: "some putty", not "a putty" (but "a putty" can mean a kind of putty). The colour "putty" means a pale greyish-brown. "Putty in your hands" is a fixed phrase, not about real putty. Do not mix up with "puddle" or "pudding".

meaning for a pupil: 1) The state of making little or no noise; silence or near silence. 2) A calm, peaceful feeling in a place or a person. 3) Being a quiet, shy or gentle kind of person who does not talk much.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, quietness is what we need in a library, during a test, or when a baby sleeps.
