In stories, the quietness of a place can feel peaceful (a snowy morning) or creepy (a house where something is wrong) — it sets the mood. Describing a character's quietness tells us they are shy, thoughtful or keeping something to themselves. Phrases: the quietness of the night, a sudden quietness, her quietness.
examples from the lessons: I love the quietness of the house early in the morning. | The teacher asked for quietness during the spelling test. | A strange quietness fell over the playground when the head teacher walked in. | His quietness made some kids think he was unfriendly, but he was just shy. | We enjoyed the quietness of the forest after the busy city. | In the quietness, we could hear an owl hooting. | The quietness of the empty school felt spooky at night.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: "the quietness", not "a quietness" (though "a sudden quietness" is fine with an adjective). "Quiet" itself is also a noun and is more common: "peace and quiet". Do not confuse "quiet" (no noise) with "quite" (fairly) or "quit" (stop).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A fixed amount or number of something that a person, group or country is allowed to have, or must reach. 2) A limit on how many things can come in or be sold, for example a quota on fish that can be caught. 3) (work) A target number of jobs or sales a worker must do in a set time.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, quotas set limits (fishing quotas protect fish so they do not run out) or targets (a salesperson's monthly quota). In school maths, a quota is a share or fixed number: if each class has a quota of 5 tickets, 6 classes get 30 tickets. In the news, quotas appear in talk about trade, fishing and immigration. Phrases: meet the quota, fill a quota, a fishing quota, over quota, a daily quota.
examples from the lessons: Each class has a quota of five tickets for the school play. | Fishing boats must not catch more than their quota of cod. | I have reached my screen-time quota for today. | The factory had to meet its quota of 500 bikes a week. | Mum jokes that she has used up her quota of patience. | Some countries set a quota on how many cars can be imported. | If each of 8 teams has a quota of 12 players, there are 96 players in all.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one quota, two quotas. In maths problems, a quota is usually a fixed number per person or group: multiply the quota by the number of groups to get the total, and anything over the quota is the extra. Do not confuse with "quote" (words someone said).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A track, usually an oval or loop, where horses, cars, bikes or runners race. 2) A place where horse races are held, with stands for the crowd (also called a racecourse).
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, racetracks are places for car racing (like Formula 1), horse racing and running races. In maths, a racetrack loop is a good example for distance problems: if one lap is 400 metres, 5 laps are 2,000 metres. In stories, a racetrack brings speed, noise and excitement. Phrases: round the racetrack, at the racetrack, a lap of the racetrack.
examples from the lessons: The cars zoomed round the racetrack. | We went to the racetrack to watch the horses. | One lap of the school racetrack is 400 metres. | My toy racetrack has a loop-the-loop. | The crowd at the racetrack cheered as the winner crossed the line. | She ran four laps of the racetrack, which is 1,600 metres.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a racetrack, racetracks. One word (sometimes "race track"). In the UK, a place for horse races is often called a "racecourse". In maths, distance = laps × length of one lap.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a way that is connected with race — the groups people are sometimes divided into because of skin colour, family background or where their families came from. 2) In phrases like "racially abused", in a way that treats someone badly because of their race, which is wrong and often against the law.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and school, the word appears in talk about fairness: a "racially mixed" class has children from many backgrounds, and "racially motivated" means something bad was done because of someone's race. Schools teach that treating people unfairly because of race (racism) is wrong. In history lessons, it appears in topics like the US civil rights movement, where some places were racially segregated (kept apart). Phrases: racially mixed, racially diverse, racially abused, racially motivated, racially segregated.
examples from the lessons: Our school is racially diverse, with families from all over the world. | In the past, some American schools were racially segregated. | Calling someone names because of their skin colour is racially abusive and wrong. | The police said the attack was racially motivated. | Rosa Parks stood up against racially unfair laws on buses. | The football club banned a fan for racially insulting a player.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from "racial" (adjective) and "race" (noun). Spelling: racially has double l. Note "race" also means a running contest — "racially" is never about running. Scientists today say all humans are one species; "race" is an idea people made up, but racism is still very real and hurts people.

part of speech: adjective (radical, more radical, most radical); noun (a radical, radicals)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Very big and basic, changing the most important parts of something: a radical change. 2) Having very strong or extreme ideas about how society or politics should change. 3) (noun) A person with extreme political ideas. 4) (maths) To do with roots, such as the square root sign √, which is called the radical sign. 5) (science) A free radical is an atom or group of atoms with an unpaired electron, which reacts easily. 6) (slang, US, dated) Really cool or amazing — "Radical, dude!"
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, a radical change is a huge one, like moving to a new country. In politics and history lessons, radicals were people who wanted big changes fast, sometimes peaceful, sometimes violent. In maths, the radical sign √ shows a square root: √16 = 4. In stories, a "radical" character challenges how things are. Phrases: radical change, radical idea, radical sign, free radical.
examples from the lessons: The new head teacher made radical changes to the timetable. | Moving from the city to a farm was a radical change for our family. | Some radicals wanted to get rid of the king. | In maths, the radical sign √ means "square root of". | √25 is called a radical expression, and it equals 5. | "That skateboard trick was radical!" shouted the surfer dude. | Her idea to have no homework at all seemed radical to the teachers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Radical comes from Latin "radix", meaning root — so a radical change goes right to the roots. In maths, √ is the radical sign: √9 = 3 because 3 × 3 = 9. The slang meaning "cool" is old-fashioned 1980s surfer talk, now mostly a joke. Adverb: radically.

part of speech: verb (rant, rants, ranted, ranting); noun (a rant, rants)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (verb) To talk or shout for a long time in an angry, excited way, often without listening to others. 2) (noun) A long, angry speech or piece of writing. 3) (informal, online) A post or video where someone complains loudly about something.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, people rant about things that annoy them, like traffic, homework or a game update. Online, a "rant" is a long complaining post. In stories, a character who rants is angry and losing control, and others may roll their eyes. Phrases: rant about, rant and rave, go on a rant, have a rant.
examples from the lessons: Grandad ranted about the price of bread. | My sister went on a rant about her phone being taken away. | Sorry for the rant, I'm just really annoyed! | The coach ranted and raved at the referee. | He posted a long rant about the new game update. | Stop ranting and listen to me for a second.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past form: ranted. Countable noun: a rant, two rants. "Rant and rave" is a fixed phrase meaning to shout angrily. Ranting is usually seen as not very calm or fair, so calling someone's words a "rant" can sound rude.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A French vegetable stew made by slowly cooking tomatoes, courgettes (zucchini), aubergines (eggplants), peppers, onions and garlic in olive oil. 2) (a name) "Ratatouille" is also a 2007 Pixar film about a rat called Remy who wants to be a chef in Paris.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, ratatouille is a healthy dish from Provence in the south of France, eaten hot or cold. In cooking and science lessons, it is a good example of a vegetable dish full of vitamins. Children often know the word from the Pixar film. Say it "rat-a-TOO-ee".
examples from the lessons: We made ratatouille in cooking class with courgettes and tomatoes. | Ratatouille comes from the south of France. | Mum serves ratatouille with rice and grilled chicken. | In the film Ratatouille, a rat cooks in a Paris restaurant. | The ratatouille smelt of garlic and herbs. | Ratatouille is a great way to eat lots of vegetables.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced "rat-a-TOO-ee"; the final "-lle" is not said like "lil". It is a French word used in English. Uncountable: "some ratatouille". Courgette (UK) = zucchini (US, Australia); aubergine (UK) = eggplant (US, Australia).

meaning for a pupil: 1) To take something back in again after it has come out or been given off, like a sponge soaking up water again. 2) (science) For the body to take a substance back into the blood, as the kidneys reabsorb water and sugar. 3) To bring people or things back into a group or system they left.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, the kidneys filter the blood and then reabsorb useful things like water and glucose, so only waste leaves as urine. Plants and soil can reabsorb water too. In everyday talk, a company or team may reabsorb workers who left. Phrases: reabsorb water, reabsorbed into the blood, reabsorbed into the team.
examples from the lessons: The kidneys reabsorb most of the water back into the blood. | The sponge dried out, but it reabsorbed the water when I dunked it again. | A bruise fades as the body reabsorbs the blood under the skin. | After the flood, the soil slowly reabsorbed the water. | The workers were reabsorbed into the main factory. | Some of the heat is reabsorbed by the ground.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Made of re- (again) + absorb (soak up). Spelling: absorb with a "b", but the noun is "reabsorption" with a "p". Past form: reabsorbed.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) Likely to change quickly when it meets another substance; a reactive metal like sodium reacts strongly with water. 2) Acting only after something has happened, instead of planning ahead (the opposite of "proactive"). 3) Easily upset or quick to respond strongly to things, like a reactive dog that barks at everything.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, the reactivity series lists metals from most reactive (potassium, sodium) to least reactive (gold, platinum) — gold stays shiny because it is not reactive. In everyday life, a reactive person or team waits for problems and then fixes them, while a proactive one prevents them. Phrases: highly reactive, reactive metal, reactive to light, reactive rather than proactive.
examples from the lessons: Sodium is so reactive that it fizzes and bursts into flame in water. | Gold is not very reactive, so it does not rust. | Our dog is reactive and barks at every bike. | Don't just be reactive — plan ahead before problems happen. | Some sunglasses are reactive to light and darken in the sun. | Potassium is more reactive than iron.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite in science: unreactive or inert. Opposite in behaviour: proactive. Noun: reactivity (science) or reaction. Do not confuse "reactive" (likely to react) with "radioactive" (giving off radiation).

part of speech: noun (reassurance — usually uncountable; a reassurance, reassurances)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Words or actions that make someone feel less worried or afraid. 2) A promise or statement that something is true or safe, given to calm someone.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, children often need reassurance before tests, visits to the doctor or the first day at a new school; a hug or kind words give reassurance. In safety lessons, it is fine to ask a trusted adult for reassurance when something online is scary. In stories, a character looking for reassurance is nervous, and the one giving it is kind and steady. Phrases: give reassurance, need reassurance, look for reassurance, words of reassurance.
examples from the lessons: I needed some reassurance before my swimming test. | Dad squeezed my hand for reassurance. | The nurse gave us reassurance that the injection would be quick. | She looked at her teacher for reassurance. | The pilot's calm voice was a reassurance to the passengers. | A few words of reassurance helped him stop crying. | We got reassurance that the bridge was safe.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly uncountable: "some reassurance", but "a reassurance" is possible. From the verb "reassure" (make someone feel less worried). Spelling: re-assur-ance, double s.

part of speech: verb (rebuke, rebukes, rebuked, rebuking); noun (a rebuke, rebukes)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (verb, formal) To tell someone sharply that they have done something wrong. 2) (noun) Sharp words of blame or criticism. 3) (Bible) In Bible stories, Jesus rebukes the wind and the waves, meaning he commands them firmly to stop.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, "rebuke" is a more formal word for "tell off" or "scold"; it is common in books, the news and the Bible. In stories, a rebuke shows someone in charge correcting someone, and the rebuked character may feel ashamed. Phrases: a sharp rebuke, a gentle rebuke, rebuke someone for something.
examples from the lessons: The teacher rebuked him for talking during the assembly. | Mum gave my brother a sharp rebuke for being rude. | The captain rebuked the sailors for falling asleep on watch. | In the Bible, Jesus rebuked the wind, and the storm became calm. | Her quiet rebuke made me feel ashamed. | The judge rebuked the lawyer for shouting.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal word: in everyday speech people say "tell off" (UK) or "scold". Rebuke someone FOR something. Past form: rebuked. Countable noun: a rebuke, rebukes.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A performance of music, dance or poetry, often by one person or by pupils, for an audience. 2) A spoken list or account of many things, one after another: a recital of complaints. 3) The act of saying a poem or text aloud from memory (recitation).
its sense in the lessons: In everyday and school life, a piano recital or dance recital is a show where pupils perform what they have learned for parents. In stories, a recital can be a nervous, exciting moment. "A recital of facts" means a long telling of them. Phrases: piano recital, dance recital, give a recital, end-of-year recital.
examples from the lessons: My piano recital is on Saturday. | Everyone clapped at the end of the dance recital. | She practised her violin every day before the recital. | Our class gave a poetry recital in assembly. | Grandma listened to my long recital of everything that went wrong at school. | I was nervous before the recital, but I played well.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a recital, recitals. From the verb "recite" (say aloud from memory). A recital is a performance; a "rehearsal" is the practice before it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Doing dangerous things without caring or thinking about what could go wrong. 2) Done in a careless, risky way: reckless driving, reckless spending.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and safety lessons, reckless behaviour — like riding a bike in traffic without a helmet, or running across a road — can hurt you or others. In law, "reckless driving" is a crime. In stories, a reckless character is brave but foolish and often gets into trouble. Phrases: reckless driving, reckless behaviour, reckless with money, reckless disregard.
examples from the lessons: It was reckless to climb the cliff without a rope. | The driver was fined for reckless driving. | Don't be reckless — look both ways before you cross. | He was reckless with his pocket money and spent it all in one day. | The reckless knight charged at the dragon without a plan. | Swimming alone in the sea at night is reckless.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb: recklessly. Noun: recklessness. The "reck" part is an old word meaning "care", so reckless = without care. Reckless is stronger than careless: careless means not paying attention; reckless means ignoring a danger.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To begin again after a stop or break. 2) To start doing something again.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, people usually say "start again" or "resume"; "recommence" is used in formal notices, the news and exam papers: "Lessons will recommence after the holiday." In stories it sounds stiff and official. Phrases: work recommenced, recommence play, recommence lessons.
examples from the lessons: Lessons will recommence on Monday. | After the rain stopped, the match recommenced. | The builders recommenced work on the bridge. | The music stopped, then recommenced a minute later. | Please recommence your test when the bell rings. | Trains will recommence running at six o'clock.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal: in normal speech say "start again". Spelling: re + commence, double m. Past form: recommenced. Do not confuse with "recommend" (say something is good).

meaning for a pupil: 1) To make dried food or powder into its original form again by adding water: reconstituted milk or orange juice. 2) (formal) To form a group, organisation or system again, often in a new way.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and cooking, you reconstitute powdered milk, dried soup or dried mushrooms by adding water. Juice labels may say "from concentrate", meaning it was reconstituted. In history or the news, a government or team can be reconstituted after breaking up. Phrases: reconstituted juice, reconstitute with water, reconstituted the committee.
examples from the lessons: Add hot water to reconstitute the dried soup. | This orange juice is reconstituted from concentrate. | Astronauts reconstitute their dried food with water. | The club was reconstituted with new members. | The powder is reconstituted into milk for the baby. | After the war, the army was reconstituted.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal word. Noun: reconstitution. Past form: reconstituted. In maths-style recipes, follow the ratio: "1 scoop of powder to 200 ml water".

part of speech: verb (reek, reeks, reeked, reeking); noun (a reek — singular)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (verb) To have a very strong, unpleasant smell. 2) (noun) A strong, bad smell. 3) (figurative) To strongly suggest something bad: "This plan reeks of trouble." 4) (Scotland, Northern England) Smoke.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, smelly things reek: old socks, rotten fish, bins in summer. In stories, "reek" helps the reader smell the scene and feel disgust. Figuratively, something that "reeks of" cheating or fear seems clearly that way. Phrases: reek of, reeking of, the reek of.
examples from the lessons: The bin reeked after a week in the sun. | His football boots reek! | The kitchen reeked of burnt toast. | We held our noses at the reek of the rotten eggs. | The whole story reeked of lies. | The pirate's cabin reeked of fish and old rum. | My clothes reek of smoke after the bonfire.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Do not confuse with the homophone "wreak" (cause damage: "wreak havoc"), which sounds the same. Past form: reeked. "Reek of something" is the common pattern. A reek is always a bad smell, never a nice one.

part of speech: noun (a reel, reels); verb (reel, reels, reeled, reeling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (noun) A round thing that thread, film, fishing line or wire is wound on. 2) (noun) A fast lively folk dance from Scotland or Ireland, and its music. 3) (verb) To pull something towards you by winding a line: reel in a fish. 4) (verb) To walk unsteadily, as if about to fall; to stagger. 5) (verb) To feel shocked or confused: "My head is reeling." 6) (noun, social media) A short video on an app like Instagram.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, a fishing rod has a reel, and old films were on reels. In Scotland and Ireland, children learn reels at ceilidhs and Irish dancing. In stories, a character reels from a punch or from shocking news. Phrases: reel in, reel off (say a long list quickly), reeling from the news, a cotton reel, highlights reel.
examples from the lessons: Grandad reeled in a huge fish. | Pass me the reel of cotton, please. | At the ceilidh we danced a Scottish reel. | He reeled back after bumping his head. | I was still reeling from the news that we were moving. | She reeled off the names of all the planets. | My cousin posted a funny reel of her dog.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Homophone: "real" (true, not fake) sounds almost the same — do not mix them up. Past form: reeled. "Reel off" means say quickly from memory; "reel in" means pull in. A cotton reel (UK) = a spool of thread (US).

part of speech: verb (refocus, refocuses or refocusses, refocused or refocussed, refocusing or refocussing); noun (a refocus)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To bring your attention or effort back to something, or onto something new. 2) To adjust a camera, telescope or your eyes again so that the picture becomes sharp.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday school life, a teacher may say "Let's refocus" when the class gets distracted. Sports coaches tell players to refocus after a mistake. In science, you refocus a microscope when you change the lens. Phrases: refocus on, refocus your attention, refocus the lens.
examples from the lessons: After the fire drill, the class took a minute to refocus. | Take a deep breath and refocus on your work. | The coach told us to refocus after we lost the first goal. | Turn the knob to refocus the microscope. | My eyes needed to refocus after staring at the screen. | The company decided to refocus on making toys.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Both "refocused" (common in the US and now in the UK) and "refocussed" are correct. Made of re- (again) + focus.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A kind of popular music from Jamaica, with a strong off-beat rhythm, often with words about love, peace, faith and fairness. 2) (adjective use) Of or like this music: reggae band, reggae beat.
its sense in the lessons: In music lessons, reggae is taught as a style from Jamaica that grew in the late 1960s; Bob Marley is its most famous singer. Children in the UK, Canada and elsewhere hear it at carnivals, like the Notting Hill Carnival in London. Reggae songs often carry messages about peace and justice. Phrases: reggae music, reggae beat, reggae band.
examples from the lessons: Bob Marley is the most famous reggae singer. | We danced to reggae music at the carnival. | Reggae comes from Jamaica. | In music class we clapped along to a reggae beat. | My uncle plays guitar in a reggae band. | "Three Little Birds" is a cheerful reggae song.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: double g and "ae" — reggae. Pronounced "REG-ay". Uncountable: "reggae music", not "a reggae". Usually written with a small letter.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The quality of happening at the same times or in the same way again and again. 2) Being even, neat and following a pattern: the regularity of a shape. 3) How often something happens: "Accidents happen there with worrying regularity."
its sense in the lessons: In maths, regularity means a pattern repeats: a regular polygon has equal sides and angles, and regularity helps you spot number patterns. In science, scientists look for regularities (patterns) in their results. In everyday life, the regularity of a timetable or a heartbeat is something we count on. Phrases: with regularity, with clockwork regularity, regularity of meals.
examples from the lessons: The buses come with great regularity, every ten minutes. | The regularity of her heartbeat showed she was calm. | We noticed the regularity of the pattern: 2, 4, 6, 8. | The bells rang with clockwork regularity. | Doctors say regularity of sleep helps children learn. | The regularity of the square's sides makes it a regular shape.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun from "regular". Spelling: regular + ity. In maths, a regular shape has all sides and all angles equal; a pattern with regularity repeats by the same rule.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Sending or bringing someone back to their own country. 2) Returning things, like money or museum objects, to the country they came from. 3) (euphemism-like, formal) Bringing home the body of someone who died abroad, for a funeral.
its sense in the lessons: In history and the news, repatriation is about refugees, prisoners of war or citizens being brought home, and about museums returning objects taken long ago (like the Benin Bronzes). It can be kind (bringing someone home) or hard (sending people back who do not want to go). Phrases: repatriation of refugees, repatriation flight, repatriation of artefacts.
examples from the lessons: After the war, there was a repatriation of prisoners. | The museum agreed to the repatriation of the ancient statue. | Many families waited for the repatriation of their loved ones. | A repatriation flight brought the stranded tourists home. | Some refugees were afraid of repatriation to a dangerous country. | The insurance covers repatriation if you fall ill abroad.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: repatriate. "Patria" is Latin for "homeland", so repatriation = back to the homeland. The opposite idea is "expatriate" (someone living abroad). Formal word used in news and law.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (money) That must be paid back, usually by a certain time. 2) That can be paid back.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and money lessons, a loan is repayable: you borrow money and must give it back, often with interest (extra money). A gift or grant is not repayable. In maths problems, "a loan of £100 repayable in 5 equal parts" means each payment is £100 ÷ 5 = £20. Phrases: repayable loan, repayable in instalments, repayable on demand, non-repayable.
examples from the lessons: The loan is repayable over two years. | Mum said the money for my bike was repayable from my pocket money. | A £60 loan repayable in 6 weeks means £10 a week. | Grants are not repayable, but loans are. | The deposit is repayable when you return the keys. | The money is repayable on demand, which means at any time it is asked for.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From "repay" + -able. In maths: repayable in N equal parts means total ÷ N each time; if interest is added, total to repay = amount borrowed + interest. "Non-repayable" means you never have to give it back.

part of speech: noun (repose — uncountable); verb (repose, reposes, reposed, reposing — formal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Rest, sleep or calm. 2) (verb, formal) To lie down or rest. 3) (verb, formal) To be kept or placed somewhere. 4) (church) "The repose of the soul" means the peaceful rest of someone who has died; Christians pray for the repose of the souls of the dead.
its sense in the lessons: Repose is an old-fashioned, formal word found in poetry, classic books and church prayers. In stories, a face "in repose" is calm and still. In science, the "angle of repose" is the steepest slope a pile of sand or gravel can have before it slides. Phrases: in repose, angle of repose, repose of the soul.
examples from the lessons: The cat lay in repose by the fire. | Her face was peaceful in repose. | The jewels repose in a velvet box. | The priest prayed for the repose of Grandad's soul. | After the long walk, the travellers sought repose under a tree. | In science we measured the angle of repose of a pile of sand.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal or poetic; everyday words are "rest" and "lie". Do not confuse with "reposition" or "repost" (post again online). Uncountable noun.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who has a normal job but has trained as a soldier, sailor or airman and can be called up to serve in the armed forces when needed. 2) A member of a reserve force.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, reservists work as teachers, builders or nurses, then train some weekends; in an emergency they may be called up. In the news and history lessons, reservists are called up in wartime or after floods and disasters. Phrases: army reservist, call up reservists, a reservist soldier.
examples from the lessons: My aunt is a nurse and an army reservist. | The government called up thousands of reservists. | Reservists train on some weekends and in the summer. | Ukraine called up reservists to defend the country. | The reservists helped with sandbags during the floods. | Dad became a navy reservist after leaving the full-time navy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a reservist, reservists. From "reserve" (kept ready for later). In the UK the Army Reserve used to be called the Territorial Army.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To change the shape of something. 2) To change the way something is organised or how it works, often in a big way.
its sense in the lessons: In art and design lessons, you reshape clay or a model. In maths, you can reshape a shape by cutting and moving parts: the area stays the same even if the shape changes. In history and the news, inventions or wars "reshape the world". Phrases: reshape the future, reshape a city, reshaped by.
examples from the lessons: She reshaped the clay into a bowl. | The internet has reshaped how we learn. | If you reshape a rectangle into a triangle by cutting it, the area stays the same. | The storm reshaped the beach. | The new coach reshaped the team. | The river has reshaped the valley over thousands of years.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past form: reshaped. re- + shape. In maths: cutting and rearranging pieces reshapes a figure but keeps the same area (perimeter may change).

meaning for a pupil: 1) The ability to recover and keep going after something hard, sad or frightening; bouncing back. 2) The ability of a material to spring back into shape after being bent, squashed or stretched. 3) The ability of a place, system or community to cope with problems like floods or power cuts.
its sense in the lessons: In school wellbeing lessons, resilience means not giving up when things go wrong — learning from mistakes and asking for help. In science, rubber has resilience. In geography and the news, towns build resilience against floods. In stories, a resilient hero gets knocked down and gets up again. Phrases: build resilience, show resilience, emotional resilience.
examples from the lessons: Learning to ride a bike takes resilience — you fall, then try again. | The team showed real resilience after losing the first match. | Our class talked about how to build resilience. | Rubber has great resilience; it springs back into shape. | The village's resilience after the flood amazed everyone. | Resilience doesn't mean never feeling sad; it means you keep going.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Adjective: resilient. Spelling: resilience (ends -ience, not -iance). A myth is that resilient people never feel upset — they do, but they recover.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To do with breathing and the parts of the body we breathe with: the nose, windpipe and lungs. 2) (medicine) Affecting the breathing system, like a respiratory infection.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, the respiratory system is made of the nose, mouth, trachea (windpipe), bronchi and lungs; it takes in oxygen and gives out carbon dioxide. In health and the news, respiratory illnesses include colds, flu, asthma and Covid. Phrases: respiratory system, respiratory infection, respiratory problems, respiratory rate.
examples from the lessons: The lungs are the main organs of the respiratory system. | A cold is a respiratory infection. | Smoking damages the respiratory system. | Asthma is a respiratory condition. | The doctor counted her respiratory rate — how many breaths a minute. | Fish have gills instead of lungs in their respiratory system.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced "RES-pi-ra-tree" (UK) or "RES-pruh-tor-ee" (US). From "respiration" (breathing; in science also the process cells use to release energy). Do not confuse respiration (in cells) with just breathing.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Starting something again after it has stopped. 2) The return of something that had paused: the resumption of lessons, of talks, of play.
its sense in the lessons: In news and formal notices, "resumption" is used for restarting things: "the resumption of train services", "the resumption of peace talks". In sport, it is the restart after a break. Everyday words are "restart" or "start again". Phrases: the resumption of play, resumption of talks, resumption of school.
examples from the lessons: After the rain, there was a quick resumption of play. | Everyone was happy about the resumption of school after lockdown. | The resumption of train services was delayed. | Leaders agreed to the resumption of peace talks. | We waited for the resumption of the film after the advert. | The resumption of power came after three hours in the dark.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal noun from the verb "resume" (start again). Spelling: resumption has a "p" though resume does not. Do not confuse with "résumé" (a CV in the US) or "assumption" (something you think is true).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Done to hit back or pay someone back for something bad they did. 2) (news, war) Describing an attack or action that answers an earlier attack.
its sense in the lessons: In the news, "retaliatory strikes" or "retaliatory tariffs" are actions one side takes after the other side did something first. In school and everyday life, hitting back is retaliating — teachers explain that it often makes things worse and that telling an adult is better. In stories, a retaliatory act can start a cycle of revenge. Phrases: retaliatory attack, retaliatory strike, retaliatory measures.
examples from the lessons: The country launched a retaliatory attack after being bombed. | The new taxes were a retaliatory move against the other country. | His retaliatory push got him sent off too. | Retaliatory insults only made the argument worse. | The teacher said, "No retaliatory hitting — come and tell me." | Both sides took retaliatory measures.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal word. Verb: retaliate (hit back). Noun: retaliation. Pronounced "ri-TAL-ee-uh-tree".

meaning for a pupil: 1) Able to be pulled back in or folded away when not in use. 2) Describing something that can slide or roll back into a case or body.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: retractable pens, retractable dog leads, retractable roofs on stadiums, retractable aeroplane landing gear. In science and nature lessons: cats have retractable claws — they can pull them in. Phrases: retractable claws, retractable roof, retractable pen, retractable lead.
examples from the lessons: Cats have retractable claws. | The stadium has a retractable roof for rainy days. | Click the retractable pen to make the tip come out. | Our dog's lead is retractable. | The plane's wheels are retractable and fold up after take-off. | A tape measure has a retractable metal tape.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: retractable (ends -able). From the verb "retract". Dogs' claws are mostly not retractable, unlike cats'.

part of speech: adjective (retracted); verb, past form of «retract» (retract, retracts, retracted, retracting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Pulled back in: a cat with retracted claws. 2) (verb, past) Took back something said or written, admitting it was wrong: "He retracted his statement." 3) (science) Withdrawn or taken back, like a scientific paper that is retracted because it had mistakes.
its sense in the lessons: In nature lessons, a tortoise's retracted head is inside its shell. In news and science, a retracted story or study has been officially taken back. In stories, a character who retracts a promise breaks trust. Phrases: retracted claws, retracted a claim, a retracted paper, retracted the wheels.
examples from the lessons: The cat walked with its claws retracted. | The newspaper retracted the false story and said sorry. | The snail retracted its horns when I touched them. | He retracted what he said about cheating. | The scientist's paper was retracted because the data was wrong. | The pilot retracted the landing gear.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Retract is regular: retract, retracted. Taking back words = retract (formal) or "take back" (everyday). A retracted study should not be trusted.

part of speech: verb (revert, reverts, reverted, reverting); noun (a revert — rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To go back to an earlier state, habit or way of doing things. 2) (computing) To undo changes and go back to an earlier version of a file or page. 3) (law) For property to go back to its first owner. 4) (business English) "Revert to you" is sometimes used to mean "reply to you" — this is common in India, but many speakers think it is wrong.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, people revert to old habits. In computing and online, editors revert changes to a Wikipedia page or a document. In science, something may revert to its natural state, like a garden reverting to wild. Phrases: revert to, revert back (common but repeats itself), revert changes.
examples from the lessons: After the holiday, I reverted to going to bed late. | The field reverted to wild meadow. | The teacher reverted the document to yesterday's version. | Wikipedia editors reverted the silly changes. | When he is nervous, he reverts to biting his nails. | The land reverted to the original owner.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Revert to is the pattern. "Revert back" says "back" twice, so careful writers avoid it. Past form: reverted. Noun: reversion. In much English, "revert" does not mean "reply".

part of speech: verb (rewatch, rewatches, rewatched, rewatching); noun (a rewatch, rewatches)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To watch a film, show or video again. 2) (noun) The act of watching something again.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, children rewatch favourite films and series. In school, rewatching a video helps you notice details you missed. Phrases: rewatch a film, on a rewatch, worth a rewatch.
examples from the lessons: I have rewatched Frozen ten times. | On a rewatch, I noticed clues I missed the first time. | Let's rewatch the goal in slow motion. | The teacher let us rewatch the science video. | That film is worth a rewatch. | We rewatched the whole series over the holidays.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal but common. Past form: rewatched. Plural noun: rewatches. re- + watch.

part of speech: verb (rewind, rewinds, rewound, rewinding); noun (a rewind)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To make a video, song or tape go back to an earlier point. 2) To wind something, like a thread or a clock spring, again. 3) (informal) To go back in a story or conversation: "Let's rewind — what happened before?" 4) (noun) The button or act of going back.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, we rewind videos to see something again. Old cassette tapes and videotapes had to be rewound. In stories, "Let's rewind to last Tuesday" means the writer jumps back in time (a flashback). Phrases: rewind the video, hit rewind, rewind to.
examples from the lessons: Can you rewind the video? I missed the goal. | Press rewind to hear the song again. | Let's rewind — who started the fight? | Grandma used to rewind cassette tapes with a pencil. | I wish I could rewind the day and start again. | The story rewinds to when the twins were babies.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular past: rewound (rhymes with "found"), not "rewinded". Pronounced "ree-WINED" like wind a clock, not "wind" (moving air).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science, medicine) A kind of very small germ (a virus) that is the most common cause of the common cold. 2) Any of the many types of these cold viruses.
its sense in the lessons: In science and health lessons, rhinoviruses spread through coughs, sneezes and touching hands, then infect the nose — "rhino" is Greek for nose. Washing hands and catching sneezes in a tissue help stop them. Antibiotics do not work on viruses. Phrases: rhinovirus infection, catch a rhinovirus.
examples from the lessons: Most colds are caused by a rhinovirus. | "Rhino" means nose, so a rhinovirus is a nose virus. | Rhinoviruses spread when people sneeze. | Washing your hands helps stop rhinoviruses spreading. | Antibiotics can't kill a rhinovirus. | There are over 100 types of rhinovirus, which is why we catch so many colds.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Nothing to do with rhinoceroses — both words use Greek "rhino" (nose). Plural: rhinoviruses. Myth: going out with wet hair or getting cold does not by itself give you a cold; a virus does.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The state of fruit, vegetables or grain being fully grown and ready to eat or pick. 2) Being fully developed or ready: "the ripeness of time".
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and science lessons, ripeness is checked by colour, smell and softness: a ripe banana is yellow, an unripe one green. Ripening is a chemical change; some fruits ripen faster near bananas because of a gas called ethylene. Phrases: at the peak of ripeness, check for ripeness.
examples from the lessons: Check the ripeness of an avocado by gently pressing it. | The strawberries were picked at full ripeness. | You can tell the ripeness of a banana by its colour. | The farmer waited for the wheat to reach ripeness. | The sweet smell showed the melon's ripeness. | In science we recorded the ripeness of pears each day.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. From "ripe" + -ness. Opposite: unripeness. "Overripe" means too ripe.

part of speech: noun (a rivet, rivets); verb (rivet, rivets, riveted, riveting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (noun) A short metal pin used to join pieces of metal or leather; its end is hammered flat to hold it. 2) (verb) To fasten something with rivets. 3) (verb) To hold someone's attention completely: "The film riveted us." 4) "Riveted to the spot" means unable to move, from fear or surprise.
its sense in the lessons: In design and technology, rivets join metal sheets; ships, bridges and planes have thousands. Jeans have small copper rivets on the pockets. In stories, a riveting book is so exciting you cannot stop reading, and a character "riveted to the spot" is frozen in fear. Phrases: riveted to the screen, riveted to the spot, a riveting story.
examples from the lessons: The old ship was held together by thousands of rivets. | Look at the little metal rivets on your jeans. | The workers riveted the steel beams together. | The whole class was riveted by the story. | She stood riveted to the spot when she saw the bear. | It was a riveting match right to the last second.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past form: riveted (one t, in UK and US). Adjective: riveting (very exciting). Do not confuse with "rivet" and "ribbit" (frog noise).

meaning for a pupil: 1) The part of a road that cars and other vehicles drive on, not the pavement (sidewalk). 2) A road in general, especially a main road.
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons, pupils learn to stay on the pavement (sidewalk) and only cross the roadway at safe places like zebra crossings. In the news, a "roadway closed" sign means cars cannot pass. Phrases: on the roadway, blocking the roadway, the roadway was flooded.
examples from the lessons: Never play on the roadway. | A fallen tree blocked the roadway. | The roadway was flooded after the storm. | Stay on the pavement, not the roadway. | Workers painted new lines on the roadway. | The bridge has a roadway for cars and a path for bikes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a roadway, roadways. Pavement (UK) = sidewalk (US); in the US "pavement" can mean the road surface itself, which can confuse.

part of speech: noun (the Roma, Roma; a Rom, Roma — plural); proper noun (Roma — a name); noun (a roma tomato)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The Roma are a people who have lived in Europe for about a thousand years; their ancestors came from northern India and many have travelled and kept their own language, Romani. 2) (a name) Roma is the Italian name for Rome, the capital of Italy; also the name of the football club AS Roma. 3) A roma (plum) tomato is a long, egg-shaped tomato good for sauces.
its sense in the lessons: In history and citizenship lessons, the Roma are taught as Europe's largest minority people, who have faced much unfair treatment, including being murdered in the Holocaust. The word "Gypsy" is used by some but can be hurtful; "Roma" or "Romani" is respectful. In everyday life and cooking, roma tomatoes are common in shops. Phrases: Roma people, Roma community, Roma culture, AS Roma.
examples from the lessons: The Roma have their own language called Romani. | Many Roma families live in Romania and Hungary. | In history, we learned that Roma people were persecuted in the Holocaust. | In Italy, Rome is called Roma. | AS Roma is a football team from Rome. | Mum chopped roma tomatoes for the pasta sauce.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Use a capital R for the people and the city. Not connected to Romania, though the names look alike. "Gypsy" can be offensive; prefer Roma or Romani. In shops "roma tomato" is often written with a small r.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) A tiny water animal, usually too small to see without a microscope, with a ring of little hairs at its head that wave and look like spinning wheels.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, rotifers are seen under a microscope in pond water. They are animals, not bacteria, and some can dry out for years and come back to life when wet. The name means "wheel-bearer" in Latin. Phrases: pond rotifers, rotifers under the microscope.
examples from the lessons: We saw rotifers in pond water under the microscope. | A rotifer's hairs look like spinning wheels. | Rotifers are animals, even though they are tiny. | Some rotifers can survive drying out for years. | Fish eat rotifers. | Our teacher showed us a video of rotifers feeding.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a rotifer, rotifers. Pronounced "ROH-tuh-fer". Its "wheels" do not really spin; the hairs wave in a pattern that looks like spinning.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The quality of being round or curved like a circle or ball. 2) A full, smooth quality, for example of a sound or a taste.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, roundness is about circles, spheres and curves; a circle is perfectly round. In science and geography, the roundness of the Earth (it is close to a sphere) explains why ships seem to disappear over the horizon. In art, roundness makes a drawing look solid. Phrases: the roundness of the Earth, the roundness of her face.
examples from the lessons: The roundness of the ball helps it roll. | The Earth's roundness was known to the ancient Greeks. | Pebbles get their roundness from being rolled by water. | The artist shaded the apple to show its roundness. | The roundness of the cello's sound was lovely. | We measured the roundness of each orange.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. From "round" + -ness. The Earth is not perfectly round — it bulges a little at the equator. Myth: people in the Middle Ages did not all think the Earth was flat; educated people knew it was round.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To wake someone up. 2) To make someone feel a strong emotion like anger or excitement, or make them act: rouse a crowd. 3) (Australia, informal) "Rouse on" someone means to tell them off.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, a sleeper is roused by a noise, and a leader rouses people with a speech. A "rousing" song or cheer is loud and exciting. In Australia, a teacher may "rouse on" a pupil. Phrases: rouse from sleep, rouse suspicion, rousing speech, rouse on (Australia).
examples from the lessons: The alarm roused me at six o'clock. | The barking dog roused the whole street. | The captain's speech roused the team to win. | His strange behaviour roused suspicion. | We sang a rousing song at the end of assembly. | (Australia) Mum roused on me for leaving the gate open.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past form: roused. Rhymes with "cows". Similar: arouse (to cause a feeling), but "arouse" can sound adult, so "rouse" or "wake" is safer for waking someone. Do not confuse "rouse" with "rose" or "ruse" (a trick).

meaning for a pupil: 1) As a normal, regular part of what happens; usually. 2) Often, as a habit, without special reason.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, doctors routinely check children's height, and teachers routinely take the register. In the news, "routinely" means something happens all the time, sometimes something bad that should not ("cyclists are routinely ignored"). Phrases: routinely checked, routinely used.
examples from the lessons: The nurse routinely checks our height and weight. | Planes are routinely inspected before flights. | Our teacher routinely takes the register at nine. | He routinely forgets his PE kit. | Seat belts are now routinely worn by everyone. | Scientists routinely repeat their experiments.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from "routine" (a regular way of doing things). Spelling: routine + ly. Pronounced "roo-TEEN-lee".

part of speech: verb (ruffle, ruffles, ruffled, ruffling); noun (a ruffle, ruffles)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (verb) To make something uneven or messy, like hair, feathers or a smooth surface. 2) (verb) To annoy or upset someone a little: "ruffle someone's feathers". 3) (noun) A strip of gathered cloth used as decoration on a dress or shirt; a frill. 4) (noun) A soft drum roll.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, grown-ups ruffle children's hair as a friendly gesture. In nature, birds ruffle their feathers to keep warm or look bigger. In stories, the wind ruffles water or leaves; "ruffle feathers" means upset people. Phrases: ruffle someone's hair, ruffle feathers, unruffled (calm), a dress with ruffles.
examples from the lessons: Grandad ruffled my hair and smiled. | A breeze ruffled the surface of the lake. | The bird ruffled its feathers in the cold. | Her rude comment ruffled a few feathers. | The princess wore a dress with lots of ruffles. | He stayed calm and unruffled during the test.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past form: ruffled. "Unruffled" means calm. Do not confuse with "rumple" (crease) or "raffle" (prize draw).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A letter of an old alphabet used by Vikings and other Germanic peoples, carved on wood, stone or bone. 2) A mark or symbol that is believed to have magic or secret meaning, as in fantasy stories and games.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, runes are the Viking alphabet (called the futhark) carved on rune stones. In fantasy books and games, runes are magical symbols. Phrases: rune stone, carved runes, ancient runes, to read the runes (UK idiom: to guess what will happen).
examples from the lessons: The Vikings carved runes on stones. | We wrote our names in runes in history class. | The runes on the old sword glowed in the story. | Rune stones can still be seen in Sweden. | The wizard read the runes in his spell book. | Some runes look like straight lines and arrows because they were easy to carve.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a rune, runes. Adjective: runic. There is no proof runes ever had real magic; old people sometimes believed they did.

part of speech: noun (a rut, ruts); verb (rut, ruts, rutted, rutting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A deep line in soft ground made by wheels. 2) (idiom) A boring way of life or habit that is hard to change: "stuck in a rut". 3) (animals) The season when male deer and some other animals fight and look for mates; (verb) to be in this season.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, a muddy track has ruts from tractor wheels. "Stuck in a rut" is a very common phrase meaning life feels boring and the same every day. In nature lessons, in autumn male red deer roar and fight in the rut. Phrases: stuck in a rut, get out of a rut, deep ruts, the rutting season.
examples from the lessons: The tractor left deep ruts in the muddy field. | My bike wheel got stuck in a rut. | Dad felt stuck in a rut, so he took up drumming. | Let's try something new to get out of this rut. | In the autumn rut, stags roar and lock antlers. | The path was full of ruts and puddles.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past form: rutted (double t). "In a rut" and "stuck in a rut" are the common patterns. Adjective: rutted (a rutted track).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A small sealed plastic or paper packet holding a small amount of something, like sugar, ketchup, shampoo or medicine. 2) A small cloth bag of nice-smelling dried flowers or herbs, put in drawers.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, sachets come with takeaways (ketchup), in cafés (sugar) and with medicine (powders to mix with water). In maths problems, sachets are counted: "Each box has 12 sachets; how many in 5 boxes?" 12 × 5 = 60. Phrases: a sachet of sugar, sachet of ketchup, lavender sachet.
examples from the lessons: Can I have a sachet of ketchup, please? | Mix one sachet of powder in a glass of water. | Gran puts lavender sachets in her drawers. | The hotel gave us little sachets of shampoo. | A box holds 20 sachets of hot chocolate. | Don't leave empty sachets on the table.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced "SASH-ay" — a French word in English. Countable: a sachet, sachets. In maths, total = sachets per box × boxes.

part of speech: noun (sage — herb, uncountable; a sage, sages — person); adjective (sage, sager, sagest — formal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A herb with soft grey-green leaves that is used in cooking, for example in stuffing. 2) A very wise person, often an old and respected teacher. 3) (adjective, formal) Wise: sage advice. 4) Sage green is a soft grey-green colour.
its sense in the lessons: In cooking, sage and onion stuffing is eaten with roast chicken or turkey in the UK and the US. In history and stories, sages are wise people whom others come to for advice. Phrases: sage advice, sage and onion, a wise old sage, sage green.
examples from the lessons: Mum added sage to the stuffing. | Sage leaves feel soft and fuzzy. | The village sage gave the boy advice. | "Be patient," was Grandma's sage advice. | Confucius is often called a Chinese sage. | Our bedroom is painted sage green.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Herb sense is uncountable ("some sage"); person sense is countable ("a sage"). Do not confuse with "saga" (a long story) or "sag" (droop).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A bird of dry, sandy places in Africa and Asia, related to pigeons, with sandy-coloured feathers that hide it on the ground.
its sense in the lessons: In nature lessons, sandgrouse are famous because the males soak their belly feathers in water at a pool and fly many kilometres back to carry water to their chicks in the desert. They are an example of an animal adapted to dry habitats. Phrases: a flock of sandgrouse, desert sandgrouse.
examples from the lessons: Sandgrouse live in deserts and dry grasslands. | A male sandgrouse carries water to its chicks in its belly feathers. | The sandgrouse's colours match the sand. | We watched a video of sandgrouse flying to a waterhole. | Sandgrouse are related to pigeons, not to grouse. | A flock of sandgrouse landed by the pool at dawn.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural usually "sandgrouse" (same as singular). Despite the name, sandgrouse are not true grouse. One word.

part of speech: noun (sargasso, sargassos — rare); proper noun (the Sargasso Sea — a name)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (a name) The Sargasso Sea is a part of the North Atlantic Ocean with no coast around it, famous for floating brown seaweed. 2) Sargasso (also sargassum) is the kind of brown seaweed that floats there in large mats.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and science lessons, the Sargasso Sea is the only sea with no land borders; it is bounded by ocean currents. Eels from Europe and North America swim there to lay eggs, and baby turtles shelter in the seaweed. Huge mats of sargassum sometimes wash onto Caribbean beaches. Phrases: the Sargasso Sea, sargasso weed.
examples from the lessons: The Sargasso Sea is in the middle of the Atlantic Ocean. | European eels travel thousands of kilometres to the Sargasso Sea. | Sargasso seaweed floats in huge golden mats. | Baby sea turtles hide in the sargasso weed. | The Sargasso Sea has no coastline at all. | Sailors once feared their ships would get stuck in the Sargasso.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital S for the sea. The seaweed is usually called "sargassum" by scientists. Myth: ships do not really get trapped in the seaweed; old stories exaggerated.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To do with Satan, who Christians believe is the devil, the chief spirit of evil. 2) Very evil or cruel. 3) (literature) "Dark satanic mills" is a famous phrase from William Blake's poem "Jerusalem", often taken to mean the grim factories of the Industrial Revolution.
its sense in the lessons: In religion lessons, Christians believe Satan is a fallen angel who tempts people to do wrong; "satanic" describes anything linked to him. In history and English lessons, Blake's "dark satanic mills" are discussed when learning about factories. In stories, "satanic" is a strong word for something wicked. Phrases: satanic forces, dark satanic mills, satanic laugh.
examples from the lessons: Christians believe Satan is the devil, so "satanic" means "of the devil". | We sang "Jerusalem", which mentions "dark satanic mills". | The villain gave a satanic laugh. | The old film was about a satanic cult. | Blake may have meant the factories when he wrote "satanic mills". | Some people called the cruel king satanic.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Often written with a capital S when it refers to Satan directly ("Satanic"). Strong word; in everyday speech "evil" or "wicked" is gentler. Pronounced "suh-TAN-ik".

meaning for a pupil: 1) A smooth, shiny cloth, often made of silk or polyester, used for dresses, ribbons and pyjamas. 2) (adjective) Smooth and shiny like satin; a "satin" paint finish is a soft shine, between matt and gloss.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, satin is used for ribbons, ballet shoes, wedding dresses and pillowcases. In design and technology lessons, satin is an example of a woven fabric with a shiny side and a dull side. In DIY, satin paint has a soft sheen. Phrases: satin ribbon, satin dress, satin finish.
examples from the lessons: The ballerina wore pink satin shoes. | She tied the present with a satin ribbon. | The satin dress shone under the lights. | Satin feels smooth and cool. | Dad painted the door with satin paint. | The kitten's fur was soft as satin.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: "some satin", "a piece of satin". Do not confuse with "Satan" (the devil) — different spelling and sound ("SAT-in" vs "SAY-tun"). Adjective: satiny.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal, old-fashioned, playful) A child or person who behaves badly but in a cheeky, likeable way; a rascal. 2) (US history) After the American Civil War, "scalawag" was an insult for white Southerners who supported the Union government.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, grandparents might call a cheeky child "you little scallywag" with a smile. In stories, scallywags are mischievous characters, like pirates or naughty children. The US history sense is spelt "scalawag". Phrases: you little scallywag, a bunch of scallywags.
examples from the lessons: Come here, you little scallywag! laughed Grandad. | The puppy is a scallywag — he stole my sock. | A gang of scallywags knocked on doors and ran away. | The pirate captain was a lovable scallywag. | My little brother is a real scallywag at bedtime. | Those scallywags ate all the biscuits!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually affectionate, not a strong insult. Also spelt "scalawag" (US). Similar words: rascal, rogue, rapscallion, scamp.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (geography) A steep slope or cliff, often a long line of steep ground where land has been worn away or moved along a fault. 2) (castles) The inner steep wall of a ditch in a fortress.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons, a scarp (or escarpment) is the steep side of a ridge; the gentle side is the dip slope. Earthquakes can make fault scarps. In history, castle scarps made attacks hard. Phrases: a steep scarp, scarp slope, fault scarp.
examples from the lessons: The path climbs a steep scarp to the top of the hill. | In geography we drew the scarp slope and the dip slope. | The earthquake left a scarp across the field. | Soldiers could not climb the castle's scarp. | From the top of the scarp we could see the whole valley. | Chalk hills often have a scarp on one side.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Short for "escarpment". Countable: a scarp, scarps. Do not confuse with "scrap" or "scarf".

meaning for a pupil: 1) The natural features of a place, like hills, rivers, trees and sky, especially when beautiful. 2) (theatre) The painted backgrounds and objects on a stage that show where the play is happening. 3) (idiom) "A change of scenery" means going somewhere different for a rest or new start.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and geography, people travel to enjoy scenery — mountains, lakes and coasts. In drama, pupils paint scenery for the school play. In stories, describing the scenery helps the reader picture the setting. Phrases: beautiful scenery, stunning scenery, a change of scenery, part of the scenery.
examples from the lessons: The scenery in Scotland is amazing. | We painted the scenery for the school play. | Look out of the window and enjoy the scenery. | Dad needed a change of scenery after a hard week. | The stage scenery fell over in the middle of the show! | The mountain scenery was covered in snow.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: "the scenery", "beautiful scenery" — never "a scenery" or "sceneries". For one view, say "a view" or "a scene". Spelling: scenery (not "scenary").

meaning for a pupil: 1) Money given to a pupil or student, usually because they are very good at something or need help, to pay for their school or university. 2) (uncountable) Serious study and learning, the work of scholars.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, a pupil might win a scholarship to a private school, or a sports scholarship to a university, especially in the US. In history lessons, "scholarship" means careful study, like the scholarship of monks who copied books. Phrases: win a scholarship, get a scholarship, a full scholarship, sports scholarship, on a scholarship.
examples from the lessons: My cousin won a scholarship to study music. | She went to university on a football scholarship. | A full scholarship pays for everything. | The school offers scholarships to children who cannot afford the fees. | His book shows great scholarship. | Monks in the Middle Ages kept scholarship alive.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable for the money (a scholarship); uncountable for learning. Similar: bursary (UK, often based on need), grant. A scholarship usually does not have to be paid back, unlike a loan.

part of speech: verb (scissor, scissors, scissored, scissoring); noun (scissor — used before another noun; the full tool is «scissors»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) "Scissor" is used before another noun for things linked to scissors or shaped like them: scissor blade, scissor kick, scissor lift. 2) (verb) To cut with scissors. 3) (verb) To open and close like scissors, as legs do in a scissor kick.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life the tool is always "scissors" (a pair of scissors). "Scissor" alone appears in words like "scissor kick" (football or swimming) and "scissor lift" (a lifting platform). In school, children learn to carry scissors safely, points down. Phrases: scissor kick, scissor lift, scissor jump, scissor blade.
examples from the lessons: He scored with a brilliant scissor kick. | In PE we did scissor jumps. | One scissor blade was blunt. | The workers stood on a scissor lift to fix the ceiling. | Her legs scissored as she swam. | Walk with scissors pointing down.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The tool is plural: "these scissors are sharp", "a pair of scissors". "A scissor" for the tool is a common mistake. Spelling: sc-iss-or, silent c.

part of speech: noun (scope — uncountable; a scope, scopes); verb (scope, scopes, scoped, scoping — informal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The range of things that a subject, job or plan deals with. 2) The chance or opportunity to do something: "There is scope for improvement." 3) (informal) Short for telescope, microscope or the sight on a rifle. 4) (verb, informal) "Scope out" means to look at something carefully to check it.
its sense in the lessons: In school and everyday life, "scope for improvement" is common teacher talk meaning you can do better. "Beyond the scope" means outside what is covered. In science, "scope" can be short for microscope. Phrases: scope for, within the scope of, beyond the scope, scope out.
examples from the lessons: There is plenty of scope for improvement in your handwriting. | This question is beyond the scope of our lesson. | The project is huge in scope. | Look through the scope to see the cells. | Let's scope out the new playground first. | The new park gives children more scope to play.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Scope (range, chance) is uncountable. Many words end in -scope (telescope, microscope, periscope, kaleidoscope); "-scope" comes from Greek for "look". "Scope out" is informal.

part of speech: noun (Scotch — whisky, uncountable); adjective (Scotch — in fixed names); verb (scotch, scotches, scotched, scotching)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (noun) Scotch is whisky made in Scotland (an alcoholic drink for adults). 2) (verb) To stop a rumour, idea or plan, often by showing it is false: "scotch a rumour". 3) (adjective) Used in some fixed names: Scotch egg (a boiled egg wrapped in sausage meat and breadcrumbs), Scotch pancake, Scotch mist. 4) (a name) Scotch tape is a US brand of clear sticky tape (UK: Sellotape).
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, children meet Scotch eggs at picnics and Scotch tape in the US. Adults may drink Scotch. In news and formal talk, people "scotch rumours". Note: for people from Scotland, say "Scottish" or "Scots", not "Scotch", which many Scottish people find old-fashioned or wrong. Phrases: scotch a rumour, Scotch egg, Scotch tape, Scotch whisky, Scotch mist.
examples from the lessons: We had Scotch eggs at the picnic. | The head teacher scotched the rumour that school would close. | Can you pass the Scotch tape? (US) | Grandad likes a glass of Scotch after dinner. | The rain scotched our plans for a barbecue. | She is Scottish, not "Scotch"!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital S for the whisky and in Scotch egg; small s for the verb. Use "Scottish" for people and most things from Scotland. Alcohol is for adults only.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (UK, informal) A person from Liverpool, a city in north-west England. 2) "Scouse" is also the Liverpool accent and dialect, and a beef or lamb stew eaten there.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday British life, "Scouser" is a common, usually friendly word; many Liverpudlians use it proudly. The Beatles were famous Scousers. In stories and TV, a Scouser character might say "boss" for great or "our kid" for a brother or sister. Phrases: a proud Scouser, a Scouse accent, a bowl of scouse.
examples from the lessons: My uncle is a Scouser and supports Liverpool. | She has a strong Scouse accent. | The Beatles were four Scousers. | We ate scouse, a hot stew, in Liverpool. | Scousers are known for their sense of humour. | "That's boss!" said the Scouser, meaning "That's great!"
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually written with a capital S. Formal word: Liverpudlian. Can be friendly or, from some people, a jokey insult — tone matters. The name comes from "lobscouse", a sailors' stew.

part of speech: verb (scramble, scrambles, scrambled, scrambling); noun (a scramble, scrambles)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (verb) To climb or move quickly and awkwardly, using your hands and feet. 2) (verb) To hurry or push against others to get something: "scramble for seats". 3) (verb) To mix up eggs and cook them, stirring them in a pan. 4) (verb) To mix something up so it cannot be understood, like a secret code or letters. 5) (verb) For fighter planes to take off quickly in an emergency. 6) (noun) A rush or struggle; a hurried climb; a motorbike race over rough ground.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, children scramble over rocks at the beach, and people scramble for bargains. In cooking, you scramble eggs. In puzzles, scrambled words (anagrams) have mixed-up letters: "tca" unscrambles to "cat". In history, the "Scramble for Africa" was when European countries rushed to take over African land in the late 1800s. Phrases: scramble up, scramble for, a mad scramble, scramble eggs, unscramble.
examples from the lessons: We scrambled up the rocks to see the sea. | There was a mad scramble for the last cake. | Can you scramble some eggs for breakfast? | Unscramble these letters to make a word: "dbir". | The fighter jets scrambled to meet the unknown plane. | In history we learned about the Scramble for Africa. | Everyone scrambled to find their coats when the bell rang.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past form: scrambled. Opposite of scramble (mix up) is "unscramble". "Scramble for" means rush to get. Scrambled eggs are cooked eggs, not raw.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (of eggs) Beaten and cooked in a pan while being stirred, so they become soft lumps. 2) Mixed up so it makes no sense or cannot be read: scrambled letters, a scrambled signal. 3) (verb, past) Climbed or moved quickly and awkwardly: "We scrambled up the hill." 4) (informal) Confused: "My brain is scrambled."
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, scrambled eggs on toast is a common breakfast. In word puzzles, scrambled words are anagrams to unscramble. In science and technology, scrambled signals are coded so outsiders cannot read them. In stories, "scrambled" shows a hurried, messy escape. Phrases: scrambled eggs, scrambled letters, scrambled to safety.
examples from the lessons: I had scrambled eggs on toast for breakfast. | Unscramble these scrambled words: "olohcs" = "school". | The TV picture was scrambled. | We scrambled to safety as the wave came in. | After the long test, my brain felt scrambled. | The spy sent a scrambled message.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Scrambled is the past form and an adjective. Scrambled eggs are not the same as fried or boiled eggs. In puzzles, the letters stay the same, just in a new order.

part of speech: adjective (screeching); verb, present participle of «screech» (screech, screeches, screeched, screeching); noun (screeching — uncountable)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Making a loud, high, harsh sound, like a scream: a screeching owl. 2) (of wheels or brakes) Making a high, rough noise when stopping suddenly: screeching tyres. 3) (noun) A loud, harsh, high noise. 4) (idiom) "Come to a screeching halt" means stop very suddenly.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, we hear screeching brakes, screeching seagulls and screeching chalk on a board. In stories, screeching sounds create tension or fear — a screeching car means danger. In science, a screech is a high-pitched sound with fast vibrations. Phrases: screeching brakes, screeching tyres, a screeching halt, screeching owl.
examples from the lessons: The car stopped with screeching tyres. | Screeching seagulls stole our chips. | The screeching of chalk on the board made us shiver. | The bus came to a screeching halt. | A barn owl makes a screeching call at night. | My little sister ran round the garden screeching with laughter.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From "screech". Similar: shriek, squeal, scream. In science, a high sound has a high pitch (fast vibrations). Spelling: double e, then "ch".

part of speech: noun (a scrooge, scrooges); proper noun (Scrooge — a name)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (a name) Ebenezer Scrooge is the mean old man in Charles Dickens's story "A Christmas Carol" (1843), who learns to be kind and generous after visits from three ghosts. 2) (informal) A mean person who hates spending money or does not enjoy Christmas.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons, "A Christmas Carol" is a famous classic; Scrooge says "Bah! Humbug!" about Christmas but changes his ways. In everyday life, calling someone "a scrooge" means they are stingy. Phrases: don't be a scrooge, a real Scrooge, Scrooge-like.
examples from the lessons: Ebenezer Scrooge is visited by three ghosts. | "Bah! Humbug!" says Scrooge. | Don't be such a scrooge — share your sweets! | At the end of the story, Scrooge becomes generous. | Dad is a bit of a scrooge about turning the heating on. | The Muppets made a film of Scrooge's story.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital S for the character; small s is common when calling someone mean. Opposite: generous. Scrooge McDuck, Donald Duck's rich uncle, is named after him.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal, UK) A person who often gets things from others without paying or working for them. 2) (insulting) A person who is said to live off other people or the government instead of working — this is often an unfair, hurtful label.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, a scrounger asks for your sweets, pens or money all the time. In the news, "benefit scroungers" is a harsh phrase some newspapers use; many people say it unfairly blames poor or sick people. In stories, a scrounger can be a funny, cheeky character. Phrases: a bit of a scrounger, benefit scrounger.
examples from the lessons: My brother is a scrounger — he always eats my crisps. | The seagull is a scrounger, waiting for chips. | "Stop being a scrounger and buy your own!" | Some newspapers call poor people scroungers, which is unkind. | The cat is a real scrounger at dinnertime. | He's a scrounger; he never brings his own pencil.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal, often insulting. Verb: scrounge (scrounge, scrounged). Be careful: calling people "scroungers" can be cruel; many who get help cannot work.

part of speech: noun (sculling — uncountable); verb, present participle of «scull» (scull, sculls, sculled, sculling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Rowing a boat with two oars, one in each hand, or a single oar at the back of the boat. 2) (swimming) Moving your hands back and forth in the water to stay still or move gently. 3) (Australia, slang) Drinking a whole drink very fast in one go (adults, often beer).
its sense in the lessons: In sport, sculling is a kind of rowing at clubs and the Olympics (single sculls, double sculls). In swimming lessons, children learn sculling to float and tread water. Phrases: single sculls, sculling boat, sculling with your hands.
examples from the lessons: She won a medal in single sculling. | In swimming we practised sculling to stay afloat. | The sculling boat glided along the river. | He was sculling with both hands to keep still. | My aunt goes sculling on the Thames every Sunday. | Sculling uses two oars, one in each hand.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced "SKUL-ing", like "skull" — homophone of "skull" (the bone). A "scull" is also the oar itself. In rowing (sweep), each person holds one oar with both hands; in sculling, each holds two.

part of speech: verb (scurry, scurries, scurried, scurrying); noun (a scurry — singular)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To run or move quickly with short, fast steps, like a mouse. 2) To hurry because you are in a rush or afraid. 3) (noun) A hurried movement or the sound of it.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and nature lessons, mice, crabs, beetles and squirrels scurry. People scurry to get out of the rain. In writing, "scurry" is a vivid verb to use instead of "run". Phrases: scurry away, scurry about, scurry off, a scurry of feet.
examples from the lessons: A mouse scurried across the kitchen floor. | Crabs scurried sideways into the rocks. | We scurried inside when it began to pour. | I heard the scurry of little feet in the attic. | The squirrel scurried up the tree. | Children scurried to their seats when the teacher came in.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past form: scurried (y → ied). Third person: scurries. Similar: scamper, scuttle, dash.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The land along the edge of the sea, such as a beach, rocks or sand. 2) The area between high tide and low tide.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography lessons, the seashore is a habitat for crabs, limpets, seaweed and seabirds; rock pools form there. In everyday life, families walk and collect shells on the seashore. In safety lessons, children learn about tides and keeping away from cliff edges. Phrases: along the seashore, on the seashore, seashore creatures.
examples from the lessons: We collected shells on the seashore. | Crabs and starfish live on the seashore. | We walked along the seashore at sunset. | Rock pools are found on the rocky seashore. | "She sells seashells on the seashore" is a tongue-twister. | The tide covers the seashore twice a day.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually "the seashore". One word. Similar: beach, coast, shore, seaside. "The seaside" is a place for holidays; "the seashore" is the actual edge of the sea.

part of speech: adjective (sedate, more sedate, most sedate); verb (sedate, sedates, sedated, sedating)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (adjective) Calm, slow and quiet, without excitement. 2) (verb, medicine) To give a person or animal a drug that makes them calm or sleepy, for example before an operation.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, a "sedate pace" is a slow, calm speed. In medicine, vets sedate animals so they can treat them, and doctors may sedate patients. In stories, a sedate character is calm and proper. Phrases: a sedate pace, sedate life, sedated for the operation.
examples from the lessons: We walked at a sedate pace through the park. | Grandma lives a sedate life in the countryside. | The vet sedated the dog before cleaning its teeth. | The zoo keepers sedated the tiger to move it. | The old horse trotted along at a sedate speed. | He was sedated during the operation.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced "si-DATE". Noun: sedation; a drug that sedates is a sedative. Sedate (calm) is not the same as "sedentary" (sitting a lot).
