meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who is believed to be able to see what will happen in the future; a prophet. 2) (Bible, history) In the Bible, "seer" is an old word for a prophet, like Samuel. 3) Literally, someone who sees.
its sense in the lessons: In myths, history and fantasy stories, seers foretell the future, like the Oracle of Delphi in ancient Greece. In the Bible, Samuel is called a seer. Today scientists say no one can truly see the future; forecasts use evidence instead. Phrases: a seer foretold, an ancient seer.
examples from the lessons: The seer warned the king about the battle. | In Greek myths, the seer Tiresias was blind but could see the future. | Samuel was called a seer in the Bible. | The fortune-teller claimed to be a seer. | The village seer looked into the fire and spoke. | "I am no seer," said Dad, "but I think it will rain."
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced "SEE-er" or "seer" (rhymes with "beer"). Do not confuse with "sear" (burn) or "sheer" (complete, steep). Myth vs fact: there is no evidence that anyone can see the future.

part of speech: proper noun (Seneca — a name); noun (the Seneca — a people; a Seneca, Seneca)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (a name) Seneca was a Roman thinker and writer (about 4 BC – AD 65), a Stoic philosopher who wrote letters about living wisely and calmly, and was a teacher of the emperor Nero. 2) The Seneca are a Native American (First Nations) people of the Haudenosaunee (Iroquois) Confederacy in New York State and Ontario; also their language. 3) (a name) Seneca Falls, a town in New York, where a famous women's rights meeting took place in 1848.
its sense in the lessons: In history and philosophy lessons, Seneca's sayings are quoted, like "We suffer more often in imagination than in reality." In Canadian and US history, the Seneca are one of the Six Nations. Phrases: Seneca the Younger, the Seneca Nation, Seneca Falls.
examples from the lessons: Seneca was a Roman philosopher. | Seneca wrote letters to his friend Lucilius about living well. | The Seneca people live in New York State. | The Seneca are one of the Six Nations of the Haudenosaunee. | The Seneca Falls meeting called for women's right to vote. | Seneca was a teacher of the emperor Nero.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A name, always with a capital S. Many quotes said to be by Seneca were not really his, so check sources. Not an English common word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A soldier or guard whose job is to watch for danger; a sentry. 2) Something that stands like a guard or watches over a place: a tree standing sentinel on a hill. 3) (science, medicine) Something used to give early warning: a sentinel species (like canaries in coal mines) or a sentinel node.
its sense in the lessons: In history and stories, sentinels guard castle walls and gates. "Stand sentinel" means stand still and watch. In science, scientists use sentinel animals or plants to warn of pollution. Phrases: stand sentinel, keep sentinel, a lone sentinel.
examples from the lessons: A sentinel stood on the castle wall. | The old oak stood sentinel over the village. | The sentinel shouted a warning when he saw the enemy. | Canaries were once sentinels for gas in coal mines. | The lighthouse is a lonely sentinel by the sea. | Robots act as sentinels in the sci-fi film.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a sentinel, sentinels. Similar: sentry, guard, lookout. "Sentinel" sounds more formal or poetic than "sentry".

meaning for a pupil: 1) A soldier who stands guard at a gate, building or camp to check who comes and to watch for danger. 2) (also sentry duty) The job of guarding.
its sense in the lessons: In history and everyday life, sentries guard palaces and army camps; the guards outside Buckingham Palace stand in sentry boxes. In stories, sneaking past a sentry is a classic moment of tension. Phrases: on sentry duty, sentry box, post a sentry, sentry go.
examples from the lessons: A sentry stood at the palace gates. | The soldier was on sentry duty all night. | The guards in London stand in sentry boxes. | The spies crept past the sleeping sentry. | The captain posted a sentry at the camp. | "Halt! Who goes there?" called the sentry.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: sentries (y → ies). Similar: sentinel, guard. Do not confuse with "century" (100 years) or "sentence".

part of speech: adjective (Serbian); noun (a Serbian, Serbians; Serbian — the language, uncountable)
meaning for a pupil: 1) From or to do with Serbia, a country in south-east Europe in the Balkans, whose capital is Belgrade. 2) (noun) A person from Serbia (also called a Serb). 3) (noun) The language of Serbia, a Slavic language that can be written in both Cyrillic and Latin letters.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons, Serbia is a landlocked country on the River Danube. In sport, Novak Djokovic is a famous Serbian tennis player. In language lessons, Serbian is interesting because it uses two alphabets. In history, Serbia is linked to the start of World War One (1914) and the wars in the former Yugoslavia in the 1990s. Phrases: Serbian food, Serbian language, Serbian flag.
examples from the lessons: Novak Djokovic is a Serbian tennis star. | Serbian can be written in two alphabets. | Belgrade is the Serbian capital. | My friend's grandparents are Serbian. | We tried Serbian food: grilled meat and peppers. | The Serbian flag is red, blue and white.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always a capital S. "Serb" is also used for a person of Serbian background. Serbian is close to Croatian and Bosnian; speakers usually understand each other. Siberian (from Siberia, Russia) is a different word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Good enough to be used; working well, even if not new or beautiful. 2) Strong and practical, made to last: serviceable shoes. 3) Able to be repaired or serviced.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, an old but serviceable bike still works fine. In stories and reviews, "serviceable" can be faint praise — good enough, but not special: "a serviceable performance". Phrases: in serviceable condition, perfectly serviceable.
examples from the lessons: My old coat is still perfectly serviceable. | The tent was old but serviceable. | She wore serviceable boots for the farm. | His Spanish is serviceable — good enough to order food. | The car is in serviceable condition. | The film had a serviceable plot, but nothing exciting.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: keep the e — service + able = serviceable. It can sound slightly negative ("just about OK"), so it is not strong praise.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Having no clear or definite shape. 2) (clothes) Loose and baggy, not fitting the body. 3) Not well organised: a shapeless story.
its sense in the lessons: In art and science, shapeless things like clouds, jelly or blobs of clay have no fixed shape; liquids and gases take the shape of their container. In stories, a "shapeless figure in the fog" is mysterious and scary. Phrases: a shapeless jumper, a shapeless mass, a shapeless lump.
examples from the lessons: The clay was a shapeless lump until she made a pot. | He wore a big, shapeless jumper. | A shapeless figure moved in the mist. | Water is shapeless; it takes the shape of the glass. | The essay was long and shapeless. | The melted snowman became a shapeless heap.
note for the reader of a maths problem: shape + -less (without). Noun: shapelessness. Opposite: shapely (having a nice shape) or well-shaped.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (money) A person or organisation that owns shares (small parts) in a company, and so owns a small part of it. 2) Someone who may get a share of the company's profits, called dividends.
its sense in the lessons: In money and economics lessons, a company can split its ownership into shares; shareholders buy them and hope the company does well so the shares grow in value. In the news, shareholders vote at meetings. In maths, if a profit of £1,000 is shared among 4 equal shareholders, each gets £250. Phrases: major shareholder, shareholders' meeting, shareholder vote.
examples from the lessons: Grandma is a shareholder in a big supermarket company. | The shareholders voted for a new boss. | Each shareholder got a dividend from the profits. | The biggest shareholder owns half the company. | If 5 shareholders share £500 equally, each gets £100. | Shareholders can lose money if the company does badly.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Also called "stockholder" (US). In maths, each shareholder's part = profit ÷ shares × shares they own. Owning shares can make or lose money; it is not a sure thing.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A woman or girl who looks after sheep. 2) (stories, art) A figure of a pretty shepherdess in old paintings, poems and china ornaments.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, nursery rhymes and old art, shepherdesses tend sheep in the fields, like Little Bo-Peep who lost her sheep. Today the word "shepherd" is often used for both men and women. In the Bible, Rachel looked after her father's sheep. Phrases: a china shepherdess, little shepherdess.
examples from the lessons: Little Bo-Peep was a shepherdess who lost her sheep. | The shepherdess led the flock up the hill. | Gran has a china shepherdess on her shelf. | In the Bible, Rachel was a shepherdess. | The shepherdess whistled to her dog. | The story is about a shepherdess and a chimney sweep.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: shepherdesses. Today many people say "shepherd" for any person who looks after sheep. Spelling: shep-herd-ess, silent h in "shepherd" (said "SHEP-erd").

part of speech: proper noun (Sherlock — a name); noun (a Sherlock, Sherlocks — informal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (a name) Sherlock Holmes is a famous fictional detective in stories by Arthur Conan Doyle, who solves crimes by careful noticing and logical thinking. 2) (informal) A person who is good at finding things out: "Well done, Sherlock!" 3) (informal, sarcastic) Said to someone who has just stated something obvious: "No kidding, Sherlock!" (a ruder version uses a swear word).
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons, Sherlock Holmes stories are classic mysteries; he lives at 221B Baker Street in London with his friend Dr Watson. In everyday life, "Sherlock" is a jokey name for anyone acting like a detective, often sarcastically. In logic puzzles, thinking "like Sherlock" means using clues step by step. Phrases: Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock and Watson, no kidding Sherlock.
examples from the lessons: Sherlock Holmes lived at 221B Baker Street. | "It's raining." "Well spotted, Sherlock!" | My sister played Sherlock and found my hidden chocolate. | Sherlock solves crimes by noticing small clues. | Dr Watson helps Sherlock on his cases. | Let's be Sherlocks and work out who took the cake.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A name, so capital S. Holmes's famous line "Elementary, my dear Watson" does not actually appear in the original books. The sarcastic "Sherlock" can sound rude.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (history, UK) An old British coin worth 12 old pennies; 20 shillings made one pound. It was used until 1971, when British money became decimal. 2) The money used today in some countries, such as Kenya, Uganda, Tanzania and Somalia. 3) (Ireland, Australia, New Zealand, history) An old coin in those places too.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, old British money is "pounds, shillings and pence" (£sd); a shilling was written "1s" or "1/-". In maths problems from old books: 1 pound = 20 shillings, 1 shilling = 12 pence, so 1 pound = 240 old pence. After 1971 a shilling became 5 new pence. In the news, the Kenyan shilling is Kenya's money. Phrases: a shilling, two shillings, the Kenyan shilling, take the King's shilling (join the army).
examples from the lessons: Before 1971, a shilling was worth 12 pennies. | There were 20 shillings in a pound. | The milk cost one shilling. | Kenya uses the Kenyan shilling. | Grandad remembers buying sweets for a shilling. | In old maths books, sums are in pounds, shillings and pence.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a shilling, shillings. Old written forms: 2s, 2/-. In maths: 1 pound = 20 shillings; 1 shilling = 12 old pence; after decimal money, 1 shilling = 5p.

part of speech: noun (shingle — beach stones, uncountable; a shingle, shingles — roof tile); noun (shingles — illness, uncountable)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Small round stones on a beach, larger than sand. 2) A thin flat piece of wood or other material laid in overlapping rows on roofs or walls. 3) (US) A small sign outside a doctor's or lawyer's office: "hang out your shingle" means start your own business. 4) "Shingles" (always plural form) is an illness causing a painful rash, caused by the same virus as chickenpox.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons, shingle beaches like Chesil Beach in England are made of pebbles; waves shape them. In building, wooden or slate shingles cover roofs in North America and elsewhere. In health, shingles is a painful illness older people can get. Phrases: shingle beach, roof shingles, a bank of shingle, hang out a shingle.
examples from the lessons: The shingle beach crunched under our feet. | Waves rolled the shingle up and down the shore. | Some shingles blew off the roof in the storm. | The cabin has a wooden shingle roof. | Grandpa had shingles and needed rest. | Brighton has a shingle beach, not a sandy one.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Beach shingle is uncountable ("lots of shingle"). Roof shingles are countable. The illness "shingles" takes a singular verb: "Shingles is painful." Shingles is not the same as chickenpox, though the same virus causes both.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A place by the water where ships are built and repaired.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, shipyards in Belfast (where the Titanic was built), Glasgow and Newcastle were famous industries. In everyday life and the news, shipyard workers build ships for navies and companies. Phrases: work in a shipyard, shipyard workers, naval shipyard.
examples from the lessons: The Titanic was built in a shipyard in Belfast. | My great-grandad worked in a shipyard in Glasgow. | Huge cranes stood over the shipyard. | The navy's new ship left the shipyard. | Many shipyards closed in the 1980s. | We could hear hammering from the shipyard.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a shipyard, shipyards. One word. Similar: dockyard (often for repairs and navy ships).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person whose job is making or repairing shoes and boots. 2) (stories) A character in fairy tales, like "The Elves and the Shoemaker".
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, shoemaking was a common trade before factories; shoemakers worked by hand with leather. In stories, "The Elves and the Shoemaker" by the Brothers Grimm tells of elves secretly making shoes at night. Today a person who repairs shoes is often called a cobbler. Phrases: the shoemaker's shop, the Elves and the Shoemaker.
examples from the lessons: The shoemaker cut the leather carefully. | In "The Elves and the Shoemaker", elves make shoes at night. | Long ago, every village had a shoemaker. | The shoemaker fixed the hole in my boot. | A shoemaker uses a hammer, nails and thread. | My great-grandmother's father was a shoemaker.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. One word. "Cobbler" usually means someone who repairs shoes (and is also a fruit pudding). The surname Schumacher means shoemaker in German.

part of speech: noun (a shred, shreds); verb (shred, shreds, shredded, shredding)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (noun) A small, thin piece torn or cut from something. 2) (noun) A very small amount: "not a shred of evidence". 3) (verb) To tear or cut something into small thin pieces. 4) (verb) To destroy papers with a shredding machine. 5) (slang) To play guitar very fast and well, or to skate or surf very well; "shredded" also means very muscly.
its sense in the lessons: In cooking, you shred cheese, lettuce or cabbage. In offices and safety, people shred papers with private details so others cannot read them. In stories and the news, "not a shred of evidence" means none at all. Phrases: in shreds, tear to shreds, a shred of truth, shredded cheese.
examples from the lessons: Mum shredded the cheese for the pizza. | The dog tore my homework to shreds! | There is not a shred of evidence that he did it. | Dad shredded the old bank letters. | Her dress was in shreds after the storm. | That guitarist can really shred! (slang)
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past form: shredded (double d). "Tear someone to shreds" (figurative) means to criticise them harshly. "Shredded wheat" is a cereal.

part of speech: adjective (shrieking); verb, present participle of «shriek» (shriek, shrieks, shrieked, shrieking); noun (shrieking — uncountable)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Making a loud, high, sharp cry, from fear, pain, excitement or laughter. 2) (noun) The sound of loud high cries.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, children shriek on roller coasters, in water fights or when they see a spider. In stories, a shrieking sound signals fear or wild fun. Phrases: shrieking with laughter, shrieking in terror, shrieking wind.
examples from the lessons: The children were shrieking with laughter on the slide. | We heard shrieking from the haunted house. | The shrieking wind rattled the windows. | She ran away shrieking when she saw the mouse. | The monkeys were shrieking in the trees. | Stop shrieking — the baby's asleep!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling rule: i before e — shriek. Similar: screech, scream, squeal. "Shriek" is often of surprise or delight; "screech" is harsher.

part of speech: verb (shrivel, shrivels, shrivelled (UK) / shriveled (US), shrivelling (UK) / shriveling (US))
meaning for a pupil: 1) To become smaller, dry and wrinkled, often because of heat, cold or lack of water. 2) To make something do this. 3) (figurative) To feel very small or ashamed: "I shrivelled with embarrassment."
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, plants shrivel without water, and grapes shrivel into raisins when dried. In cooking, things shrivel in a hot pan. In stories, a character might shrivel under a fierce look. Phrases: shrivel up, shrivelled leaves, shrivel in the heat.
examples from the lessons: The flowers shrivelled in the heat. | Grapes shrivel into raisins when they dry. | My fingers shrivel in the bath. | The leaves shrivelled up and fell off. | The slug shrivelled when salt touched it. | I shrivelled with embarrassment when I fell over on stage.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK spelling doubles the l (shrivelled, shrivelling); US uses one l (shriveled). Adjective: shrivelled. Fingers wrinkle in water because of nerves controlling blood vessels, not just water soaking in.

part of speech: noun (a shroud, shrouds); verb (shroud, shrouds, shrouded, shrouding)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (noun) A cloth that a dead body is wrapped in before burial. 2) (noun) Something that covers or hides: "a shroud of mist", "a shroud of secrecy". 3) (verb) To cover or hide something: "Fog shrouded the town." 4) (noun, sailing) One of the ropes that hold a ship's mast steady.
its sense in the lessons: In history and religion lessons, bodies were wrapped in shrouds; the Turin Shroud is a famous cloth that some Christians believe wrapped Jesus's body, though its age is disputed. In stories, "shrouded in mystery" means hidden and secret. Phrases: shrouded in mist, shrouded in mystery, a shroud of secrecy, burial shroud.
examples from the lessons: The castle was shrouded in fog. | The old house was shrouded in mystery. | The body was wrapped in a white shroud. | A shroud of smoke hung over the city. | The plan was kept under a shroud of secrecy. | The sailor climbed the shrouds to the top of the mast.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Shrouded in is the common pattern. Rhymes with "cloud". Scientists who tested the Turin Shroud dated it to the Middle Ages; others still argue.

part of speech: verb (shuck, shucks, shucked, shucking); noun (a shuck, shucks); interjection (shucks — US, informal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (verb, mainly US) To remove the outer covering of corn, peas, beans or oysters: shuck corn. 2) (noun) An outer covering, like a husk or pod. 3) (verb, informal) To take off clothes or get rid of something: "He shucked off his coat." 4) (interjection, US, old-fashioned) "Shucks!" or "Aw, shucks" shows mild disappointment or shyness at praise.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life in North America, people shuck corn (remove the husks) before cooking it, and chefs shuck oysters. "Aw, shucks" is a shy, folksy thing to say when someone praises you, often in old films or cartoons. Phrases: shuck corn, shuck oysters, shuck off, aw shucks.
examples from the lessons: We shucked the corn before putting it in the pot. | The chef shucked a dozen oysters. | He shucked off his wet jacket. | "Aw, shucks, it was nothing," said the cowboy. | Peel the shucks off the corn cobs. | Shucks! I missed the bus again.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly American English. Past form: shucked. "Shucks" as an interjection is gentle, not rude.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a shy way — nervously and quietly, because you feel uncomfortable with other people or new things.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, a new pupil might smile shyly on the first day. In stories, "shyly" shows a character's feelings: they are nervous, gentle or embarrassed. Phrases: smiled shyly, said shyly, looked away shyly.
examples from the lessons: The new girl smiled shyly at the class. | He shyly asked if he could join the game. | The puppy peeked out shyly from behind the sofa. | She shyly handed the teacher a card. | The little boy looked shyly at his feet. | "Thank you," she said shyly.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: shy + ly = shyly (keep the y). Also seen as "shily" in old books, but "shyly" is standard. Noun: shyness.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A large black gibbon (a kind of small ape) that lives in the rainforests of Malaysia, Thailand and Sumatra in Indonesia, famous for its loud calls made with a big throat sac.
its sense in the lessons: In nature and science lessons, siamangs are apes (not monkeys) — they have no tails. They swing through trees with long arms and sing loud duets with their partners each morning. They are endangered because of forest loss, including for palm oil. Phrases: siamang gibbon, siamang call.
examples from the lessons: The siamang is the biggest gibbon. | A siamang's throat swells up like a balloon when it calls. | Siamangs swing from branch to branch with their long arms. | Siamang pairs sing together every morning. | Siamangs live in the rainforests of Sumatra. | Siamangs are apes, so they have no tail.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced "SEE-uh-mang" or "SY-uh-mang". Apes (gibbons, orangutans, gorillas, chimps) have no tails; most monkeys do.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A way of swimming while lying on your side, pushing with a scissor kick and moving your arms alternately under the water.
its sense in the lessons: In swimming lessons and lifesaving, sidestroke is useful because you can keep your face out of the water and pull a person along. It is calm and saves energy. Phrases: swim sidestroke, do the sidestroke.
examples from the lessons: Lifeguards learn sidestroke to tow people to safety. | I swam a length of sidestroke. | Sidestroke uses a scissor kick. | Grandma swims sidestroke so her hair stays dry. | Sidestroke is slow but restful. | Our teacher showed us sidestroke after backstroke.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word, like backstroke and breaststroke. Usually uncountable: "swim sidestroke". Not an Olympic racing stroke (those are freestyle, backstroke, breaststroke and butterfly).

meaning for a pupil: 1) The eighteenth letter of the Greek alphabet, written Σ (capital) and σ or ς (small). 2) (maths) The capital Σ means "add up all of these" (the sum); small σ is used in statistics for standard deviation (how spread out numbers are). 3) (slang, internet) Used by some young people to mean "cool", "independent" or "the best", as in "sigma male"; often a joke or meme.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, Σ appears in sums: Σ of 1 to 4 means 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10. In science, Greek letters name many things. In playground and internet slang, "sigma" is a meme word for someone who goes their own way; teachers and parents often find it silly. Phrases: sigma notation, sigma male (slang), "that's so sigma" (slang).
examples from the lessons: Σ is the Greek capital letter sigma. | In maths, Σ means "add them all up". | The sum Σ from 1 to 5 equals 15. | "He didn't care what anyone thought — so sigma," joked my brother. | Small sigma σ is used to show spread in statistics. | In Greek, sigma makes an "s" sound.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Sounds like "SIG-muh". Greek sigma = English "s". The slang meaning comes from online videos; using it seriously can sound silly, and "sigma male" ideas are not science.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Smooth, soft and shiny, like silk. 2) (voice, movement) Smooth and gentle: a silky voice, silky skills (in sport).
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, silky describes hair, fur, cloth and smooth sauces. In sport commentary, "silky skills" means smooth, clever moves with the ball. In stories, a "silky voice" can be gentle or, for a villain, falsely sweet. Phrases: silky hair, silky smooth, silky skills, silky fur.
examples from the lessons: The kitten had silky fur. | Her hair was long and silky. | The chocolate sauce was silky smooth. | The footballer showed silky skills. | The fox spoke in a silky voice to trick the hen. | Satin feels silky to touch.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative: silkier, silkiest (y → i). From "silk", made by silkworms. Similar: smooth, glossy, sleek.

part of speech: verb (simmer, simmers, simmered, simmering); noun (a simmer — singular)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To cook something gently in liquid just below boiling, with small bubbles. 2) (of a feeling) To stay strong under the surface without bursting out: anger simmering. 3) "Simmer down" (informal) means calm down. 4) (noun) The state of gently bubbling: "Bring to a simmer."
its sense in the lessons: In cooking, recipes say "bring to the boil, then simmer for 10 minutes". In science, simmering is gentler than boiling; water boils at 100 °C at sea level, and simmering is a bit below. In stories, simmering anger warns the reader that trouble is coming. Phrases: bring to a simmer, simmer gently, simmer down, simmering tension.
examples from the lessons: Let the soup simmer for twenty minutes. | Bring the water to a simmer, then add the pasta. | The tension between the two teams simmered all match. | "Simmer down, everyone!" said the teacher. | Her anger simmered as she waited. | The sauce simmered on the stove.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past form: simmered. Simmer is gentler than boil: in a simmer, small bubbles; in a boil, big rolling bubbles. Kitchen safety: keep handles turned in and ask an adult.

part of speech: adjective (simplex); noun (a simplex, simplexes or simplices)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (technical) Simple, made of one part; not compound. 2) (communication) A simplex link sends messages in only one direction, like a radio broadcast (unlike duplex, which goes both ways). 3) (maths) A simplex is the simplest shape in any number of dimensions: a point, a line segment, a triangle, a tetrahedron. 4) (medicine) In "herpes simplex", the name of the virus that causes cold sores.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, a triangle is a 2-dimensional simplex and a tetrahedron (a triangle-based pyramid) is a 3-dimensional one. In computing and science, "simplex" describes one-way communication. In health, herpes simplex causes cold sores. Most pupils will meet the word only in these technical uses. Phrases: simplex method (a maths way to solve problems), herpes simplex, simplex communication.
examples from the lessons: A triangle is a simplex in two dimensions. | A TV broadcast is simplex: it only goes one way. | Cold sores are caused by herpes simplex virus. | A tetrahedron is a three-dimensional simplex. | Walkie-talkies are half-duplex, not simplex. | The simplex method helps factories plan their work.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A technical word, not used in everyday speech. Plural: simplexes or simplices. Opposite in communication: duplex (two-way). "Simplex" is Latin for simple.

part of speech: noun (skittles — uncountable game; a skittle, skittles — pins); proper noun (Skittles — a name)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A game in which you roll a ball to knock down wooden pins; like bowling. 2) (plural of skittle) The wooden or plastic pins used in this game. 3) (a name) Skittles is a brand of small, fruity, colourful chewy sweets (candies).
its sense in the lessons: In PE and at parties, children play skittles with plastic pins and a ball. In pubs in England, skittles is a traditional game. In maths, skittles are good for counting problems: "10 skittles, 7 knocked down — how many standing?" 10 − 7 = 3. The sweets are popular in the US, UK and elsewhere. Phrases: play skittles, a skittle alley, knock down the skittles, a bag of Skittles.
examples from the lessons: We played skittles in the garden. | I knocked down eight skittles with one ball. | If you knock down 6 of 9 skittles, 3 are still standing. | My friend shared her bag of Skittles. | The skittles fell over with a clatter. | Grandad plays skittles at the pub on Fridays.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The game takes a singular verb: "Skittles is fun." The pins are countable: "a skittle, skittles". The sweets are a brand name with a capital S. In maths: standing = total − knocked down.

part of speech: verb, past participle of «slay» (slay, slays, slew, slain, slaying); adjective (slain)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal, old-fashioned) Killed violently, especially in battle or in stories: "The dragon was slain." 2) (adjective) Killed: "the slain soldiers". 3) (slang, from «slay») Overwhelmed with laughter or amazement — "I'm slain" (rare); "slay" in slang means do something brilliantly: "You slayed!"
its sense in the lessons: In stories, myths and the Bible, heroes slay dragons and giants: David slew Goliath. In the news, "slain" is used in headlines for people who have been killed. Modern slang uses "slay" to mean look amazing or do brilliantly. Phrases: slain in battle, the slain, dragon-slayer.
examples from the lessons: The knight has slain the dragon! | Many soldiers were slain in the battle. | In the Bible, Goliath was slain by David. | The newspaper headline said "Police officer slain". | St George is said to have slain a dragon. | "You totally slayed that dance!" (slang)
note for the reader of a maths problem: Forms: slay — slew — slain (for killing). In slang, the past is "slayed": "She slayed it." Formal and story word; everyday speech uses "killed".

meaning for a pupil: 1) Without sleep, or with very little: a sleepless night. 2) Not able to sleep, because of worry, excitement or pain.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, people have sleepless nights before exciting days, during storms, or when a baby cries. In health lessons, children learn that sleep helps memory and mood, so too many sleepless nights is bad. In stories, a sleepless character is worried or haunted by something. Phrases: a sleepless night, sleepless with worry, Sleepless in Seattle.
examples from the lessons: I had a sleepless night before the school trip. | The new baby gave Mum and Dad many sleepless nights. | She lay sleepless, listening to the thunder. | He was sleepless with worry about the test. | The storm kept the whole town sleepless. | After three sleepless nights, the sailors were exhausted.
note for the reader of a maths problem: sleep + -less (without). Noun: sleeplessness. Usually used before a noun ("a sleepless night") or after "lie", "spend". Similar: wakeful; long-term trouble sleeping is called insomnia.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Thick, soft, wet mud or a mix of mud and dirty liquid. 2) Thick, dirty stuff left after cleaning water or from machines: sewage sludge, oil sludge. 3) (informal) Any thick, unpleasant mess, like soggy food or slushy snow.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, sludge collects at the bottom of ponds, gutters and drains. In science and geography, water treatment plants separate sludge from water, and some sludge becomes fertiliser or energy. In stories, sludge gives a gross, squelchy feel. Phrases: green sludge, a layer of sludge, sewage sludge.
examples from the lessons: Our wellies sank into the sludge. | Green sludge covered the bottom of the pond. | The drain was blocked with sludge. | At the water works, sludge is taken out of the dirty water. | The porridge turned into a cold grey sludge. | Car engines can fill with oil sludge if they are not serviced.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: "some sludge", "a layer of sludge". Adjective: sludgy. Similar: slime, mud, gunge (UK), goo, slush (melting snow).

part of speech: noun (a slum, slums); verb (slum, slums, slummed, slumming — informal: slum it)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A slum is a very poor, crowded part of a city where houses are badly built and people often lack clean water, toilets and safe electricity. 2) (informal, UK) A very messy, dirty room or house: "Your bedroom is a slum!" 3) (verb, informal) To slum it means to live or stay somewhere much cheaper or less comfortable than you are used to, often just for a short time.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and history lessons slums appear when cities grow fast: in Victorian London, in big cities of India, Brazil, Kenya and elsewhere today. The word tells the reader about poverty, overcrowding and danger from disease or fire. In stories it sets a hard, gritty scene. Phrases: "slum housing", "slum clearance", "live in a slum", "slum it", "slum landlord" (a landlord who rents out bad, unsafe homes).
examples from the lessons: Many families in the slum shared one water tap. | In Victorian times, slums near the factories were full of smoke and disease. | The city cleared the old slums and built new flats. | Mum looked into my room and said it was a total slum. | We had to slum it in a tiny tent when the hotel was full. | Charities help children in slums go to school. | A slum landlord was fined for leaving the flats damp and cold. | Our geography teacher showed photos of a huge slum in Mumbai.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one slum, two slums. Calling someone's home a slum is hurtful unless it is a joke about your own mess. Many people now say "informal settlement" or "shanty town" in geography. "Slum it" is informal; past: slummed it. Not the same as "slump" (a sudden fall).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Slurry is a thick, runny mixture of water and something solid, such as mud, cement or crushed rock. 2) (farming) On farms, slurry is liquid animal manure (dung and urine mixed with water) kept in tanks or pits and spread on fields as fertiliser.
its sense in the lessons: In science it is a good example of a mixture that is not a solution: the solid bits are suspended in the liquid and settle if left. In everyday country life children hear about slurry tanks, slurry spreading and the smell. Safety: slurry pits and tanks are very dangerous; they give off poisonous gases and people and animals can drown in them, so children must keep away. Phrases: "slurry pit", "slurry tank", "spread slurry", "cement slurry".
examples from the lessons: The farmer sprayed slurry on the field, and the whole village smelled it. | Never go near a slurry pit on a farm. | The builders poured a slurry of cement into the hole. | When the river flooded, a brown slurry of mud covered the road. | Our science teacher mixed clay and water to make a slurry. | If you leave the slurry still, the solid bits sink to the bottom. | Farm safety posters warn that slurry gas can kill in seconds.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable: "some slurry", "a lot of slurry"; "slurries" is used only by scientists for different kinds. Do not confuse with "slurred" (speech that is not clear) or "slur" (an insult). In science, a slurry is a suspension, not a solution.

part of speech: noun (a snakebite, snakebites; also written snake bite)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A snakebite is a bite from a snake, or the wound it leaves; some snakebites are venomous (poisonous) and need a hospital fast. 2) (UK, adults) Snakebite is also an alcoholic drink of lager mixed with cider, sold in pubs; it is for adults only.
its sense in the lessons: In science and nature lessons snakebites come up with venomous snakes such as adders in the UK, rattlesnakes in the USA and brown snakes and taipans in Australia. First aid: keep still and calm, call emergency services, keep the bitten limb still (in Australia a firm pressure bandage is used); do not cut the wound or suck out venom. Antivenom is the medicine that treats it. Phrases: "treat a snakebite", "snakebite kit", "die of snakebite".
examples from the lessons: He was taken to hospital with a snakebite on his ankle. | Snakebites are rare in the UK, but adders can bite if trodden on. | The ranger explained what to do in case of a snakebite. | Antivenom saves many people after a snakebite. | In Australia, bushwalkers carry a bandage for snakebites. | Dad's friend ordered a snakebite at the pub, which is lager and cider. | Wear boots in long grass to avoid a snakebite.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a snakebite, snakebites. Myth: sucking out venom or using a tourniquet is wrong and can make things worse. Most snakes are not venomous, but you should treat every bite as serious until a doctor checks. The drink sense is UK pub talk and only for adults.

part of speech: noun (a snare, snares); verb (snare, snares, snared, snaring)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A snare is a trap for catching animals, usually a loop of wire or string that tightens around the animal. 2) A snare is also something that tricks or traps a person, like a clever trap of words. 3) (music) A snare, or snare drum, is a small drum with wires underneath that make a sharp rattling sound. 4) (verb) To snare means to catch an animal in a trap, or to catch or win something by skill or a trick: "She snared the last ticket."
its sense in the lessons: In history and stories, hunters and poachers set snares for rabbits and birds. In music lessons the snare drum is part of the drum kit and the marching band. In everyday news it can mean catching a prize or a criminal ("police snared the thief"). The word tells the reader about trapping, sometimes sneakily. Phrases: "set a snare", "caught in a snare", "snare drum", "a snare and a delusion" (old: a trap that only looks good).
examples from the lessons: The rabbit was caught in a wire snare. | Poachers set snares in the woods at night. | The drummer hit the snare hard at the end of the song. | In the marching band, I play the snare drum. | The police snared the robber with a hidden camera. | Our team snared a last-minute goal to win. | The question was a snare to see if we were listening. | Snares can hurt pets, so many places ban them.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a snare, snares. Verb past: snared. Spelling: one r, final e. Do not confuse with "sneer" (a mean smile) or "share". "Snare" for drum is short for "snare drum".

part of speech: verb (snarl, snarls, snarled, snarling); noun (a snarl, snarls)
meaning for a pupil: 1) When an animal such as a dog snarls, it shows its teeth and makes a deep, angry growl. 2) When a person snarls, they say something in an angry, nasty voice. 3) (noun) A snarl is that angry growl or angry look. 4) A snarl is also a tangle, a knot of hair, string or wool; and things such as traffic can snarl, become stuck and tangled up. 5) (UK) A snarl-up is a traffic jam.
its sense in the lessons: In stories "snarled" is a strong speech verb that shows anger instead of "said". In nature lessons it describes warning signs of dogs, wolves and big cats: back away slowly. In everyday life, hair snarls and traffic snarl-ups. Phrases: "snarl at someone", "snarl up", "a snarl of wires", "traffic snarl".
examples from the lessons: The guard dog snarled at the stranger at the gate. | "Get out of my room!" my sister snarled. | The wolf gave a low snarl and showed its teeth. | Mum combed the snarls out of my hair. | The fishing line got snarled around the reel. | There was a huge snarl-up on the motorway this morning. | If a dog snarls, stand still and do not stare at it. | The villain snarled his answer.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: snarled, snarling. "Snarl" (growl) and "snarl" (tangle) look the same but come from different old words. "Snarl-up" is mostly British. Do not confuse with "snail" or "sneer".

meaning for a pupil: 1) A sniper is a soldier or gunman who shoots at people from a hidden place, often from far away with a special rifle. 2) (games, informal) In video games, a sniper is a player or character who shoots from far away; "sniper" can also mean the long-range rifle itself.
its sense in the lessons: In history and news it comes up in wars, for example the Second World War and the war in Ukraine, and the word tells the reader about hidden danger. Children also meet it in video games. Phrases: "sniper fire", "sniper rifle", "shot by a sniper", "sniper's nest". Related verb: "snipe" (to shoot from hiding; or to make sneaky mean comments).
examples from the lessons: The soldiers stayed low because of sniper fire. | A sniper was hiding in the old tower. | In the news, they said a sniper had shot at the town. | In the game, my brother always picks the sniper. | The sniper used a telescope sight on his rifle. | During the war, snipers made the streets very dangerous. | "Stop sniping at your sister," said Dad, meaning stop making mean little comments.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a sniper, snipers. From "snipe", a bird that is hard to shoot, so good shooters were called snipers. This is a serious war word; in real life guns are never a game.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A snob is a person who thinks they are better than others because of money, family, school or class, and looks down on people they think are lower. 2) A snob is also someone who thinks their taste is better and looks down on other people's choices: a food snob, a music snob, a book snob.
its sense in the lessons: In stories snobs are often comic or unpleasant characters who learn a lesson; the word tells the reader the person is proud and unkind. In PSHE lessons it links to respect and not judging people by money or accent. Phrases: "a food snob", "a coffee snob", "snob value", "inverted snob" (someone who looks down on rich or posh things).
examples from the lessons: The snob at the party would not talk to anyone without a big house. | Don't be a snob about cheap trainers. | My uncle is a coffee snob and only drinks special beans. | She is a book snob who thinks comics are silly. | The new girl seemed like a snob, but she was just shy. | In the story, the snobby duchess learns that kindness matters more than money. | Calling someone a snob is not a compliment.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a snob, snobs. Adjectives: snobbish, snobby; noun: snobbery. It is an insult, so use it carefully. Being shy or quiet is not the same as being a snob.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Snobby means acting like a snob: thinking you are better than others because of money, class or taste, and looking down on them. 2) (informal) A snobby place or thing seems posh and unfriendly to ordinary people: a snobby restaurant.
its sense in the lessons: Mostly everyday and story talk; it describes characters' attitudes and places. It is a bit informal; the more standard word is "snobbish". Phrases: "a snobby attitude", "snobby about food", "snobby school".
examples from the lessons: The snobby girl laughed at my old coat. | Don't be snobby about other people's lunches. | That shop is too snobby for me. | He got a bit snobby after he won the prize. | My cousin is snobby about music and only likes old bands. | The snobby customer complained about everything. | In the book, the snobby family learns to share.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative: snobbier, snobbiest (y changes to i). Informal; in writing, "snobbish" sounds more standard. It is an unkind word for a person, so be careful using it about someone.

part of speech: verb (snuffle, snuffles, snuffled, snuffling); noun (a snuffle, the snuffles)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To snuffle means to breathe noisily through your nose, for example when you have a cold or are crying. 2) When an animal snuffles, it sniffs noisily along the ground, looking for food or a smell, like a dog, pig or hedgehog. 3) (noun) A snuffle is that noisy breathing sound; "the snuffles" (informal) is a light cold with a runny nose.
its sense in the lessons: In stories it describes small sounds of animals and of children who are sad or ill; it makes a scene feel close and real. In nature lessons hedgehogs and badgers snuffle for worms and beetles. Phrases: "snuffle around", "snuffle about", "have the snuffles".
examples from the lessons: The puppy snuffled around the garden for its ball. | A hedgehog snuffled through the leaves at night. | My little brother snuffled into his pillow after the bad dream. | I have the snuffles, so I need tissues. | The pig snuffled in the mud for food. | We heard a snuffle under the bed and found the cat. | She stopped crying and gave a last snuffle.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: snuffled, snuffling. Close to "sniffle" (sniffing because of a cold or tears) and "sniff". "The snuffles" is informal.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Socialisation is the way a child learns how to behave with other people and fit into their family, school and society: sharing, manners, language, rules and customs. 2) For animals, socialisation is getting a puppy or kitten used to people, other animals, sounds and places, so it is calm and friendly. 3) (formal, money/politics) Putting a business or service under the control of the state or the community.
its sense in the lessons: In PSHE, citizenship and sociology it explains how we learn what is normal and polite from family, friends, school, TV and the internet. Pet owners use it often ("puppy socialisation classes"). The word tells the reader about learning by living with others, not by lessons. Phrases: "early socialisation", "puppy socialisation", "lack of socialisation".
examples from the lessons: School helps with children's socialisation, not just learning facts. | Socialisation teaches us to say please and thank you. | Our puppy goes to socialisation classes on Saturdays. | Without good socialisation, a dog may be scared of strangers. | Playing team games is part of socialisation. | Different countries have different socialisation, so manners differ. | Grandma says too much screen time can slow socialisation.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. UK spelling with s, US with z; both are right. Verb: socialise/socialize (also means to go out and meet friends). Do not confuse with "socialism" (a political idea).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Softness is being soft to touch: easy to press, smooth and gentle, like a pillow or a kitten's fur. 2) Softness is being quiet or gentle in sound or light: the softness of her voice, the softness of candlelight. 3) Softness is also gentleness and kindness in a person; sometimes it means being too weak or not strict enough.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons softness is a property of materials, compared with hardness (a material is soft if it is easily scratched or squashed). In stories it describes feelings, fabrics, voices and light. Phrases: "the softness of", "softness of heart".
examples from the lessons: I love the softness of my new blanket. | We tested the softness of different materials by pressing them. | The softness of her voice calmed the baby. | Talc is famous for its softness; you can scratch it with a fingernail. | The softness of the morning light woke me gently. | The coach said his softness with the team made them lazy. | The kitten's fur has an amazing softness.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: no plural. Formed from soft + -ness. Opposite: hardness, roughness. In science, "soft" means easily scratched or shaped, not just nice to touch.

part of speech: noun (solder — uncountable); verb (solder, solders, soldered, soldering)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Solder is a soft metal mixture that melts at a low temperature and is used to join pieces of metal or wires together. 2) (verb) To solder means to join metal parts or wires using melted solder and a hot tool called a soldering iron.
its sense in the lessons: In design and technology and science lessons pupils solder components onto circuit boards; it makes a strong electrical connection. Safety: the soldering iron is extremely hot (over 300 °C), wear goggles, work in air that moves and wash hands after. Phrases: "soldering iron", "solder a joint", "solder wires together", "lead-free solder".
examples from the lessons: We soldered an LED onto the circuit board in D and T. | Hold the soldering iron by the handle only. | The wire came loose, so Dad soldered it back on. | Modern solder is usually lead-free. | Melt a little solder on the joint and let it cool. | The plumber soldered the copper pipes. | A good solder joint looks shiny and smooth.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced "SOL-der" or "SOD-der" (US often "SOD-er"); the l is often silent in US speech. Do not confuse with "soldier". Solder is uncountable: "some solder". Welding is different: it melts the metal parts themselves.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Someday means at some time in the future that is not known yet: "Someday I'll go to Japan." It often expresses a hope or dream.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and songs it shows wishes and dreams about the future. In everyday talk parents use it for "not now, maybe later". Phrases: "someday soon", "someday I'll …", "one day" (a common British way to say the same).
examples from the lessons: Someday I want to be an astronaut. | "Can we get a dog?" "Someday, maybe." | Someday we will laugh about this. | She hopes to visit her grandparents in Ireland someday. | Someday soon the new park will open. | I'll learn to play the guitar someday. | Someday the little seed will be a tall tree.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Written as one word mostly in American English; British English often writes "some day" or says "one day". Do not confuse with "Sunday". "Some day" as two words can also mean "a certain day": "Let's meet some day next week."

part of speech: noun (a soprano, sopranos or soprani); adjective (soprano)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A soprano is the highest singing voice, usually of women and girls, and also of boys before their voices break. 2) A soprano is a singer with that voice. 3) (adjective) Soprano describes an instrument in the highest range of its family: soprano recorder, soprano saxophone.
its sense in the lessons: In music lessons voices are grouped as soprano, alto, tenor and bass (SATB) in a choir. Children's school recorders are usually soprano (descant) recorders. Phrases: "sing soprano", "soprano part", "soprano line", "boy soprano".
examples from the lessons: My sister sings soprano in the school choir. | The soprano hit a very high note. | Boys can sing soprano before their voices break. | I play the soprano recorder. | The soprano part has the tune in this song. | A famous soprano sang at the opera house. | In SATB, S stands for soprano.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: sopranos (common) or soprani (old, Italian). It is an Italian word meaning "above". "Treble" is used for a boy soprano in the UK. Alto is the lower women's voice.

part of speech: noun (a soviet, soviets; the Soviets); plural form of soviet; adjective Soviet
meaning for a pupil: 1) (history) The Soviets were the people, government or army of the Soviet Union (USSR), a large country that existed from 1922 to 1991, led from Moscow. 2) (history) A soviet (small s) was a council of workers or soldiers in Russia around 1917; "soviet" is the Russian word for "council".
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons it appears with the Russian Revolution, the Second World War, the Cold War, the Space Race (the Soviets sent the first satellite, Sputnik, in 1957 and the first person, Yuri Gagarin, into space in 1961) and the fall of the Berlin Wall. The USSR included Russia, Ukraine, Belarus, the Baltic countries and others, many of which did not choose to join. Phrases: "the Soviets", "the Soviet Union", "Soviet times".
examples from the lessons: The Soviets launched the first satellite in 1957. | The Soviets and the Americans raced to reach space. | In 1917, workers formed soviets in Russian cities. | Ukraine was ruled by the Soviets until 1991. | The Cold War was a long rivalry between the USA and the Soviets. | My grandad remembers Soviet times. | The Soviets lost millions of people in the Second World War.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Soviets with a capital S means the people or government of the USSR; with small s it is the councils. The Soviet Union is not the same as Russia: it was 15 republics, and Ukraine and others became independent countries in 1991.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Sparkly means shining with lots of tiny flashes of light, like glitter, sequins, frost or diamonds. 2) (informal) Sparkly can also mean lively, bright and full of fun: a sparkly personality. 3) (informal) Sparkly drinks are fizzy ones.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life children use it for clothes, shoes, decorations and craft materials. In stories it makes descriptions bright and magical. Phrases: "sparkly dress", "sparkly shoes", "sparkly eyes".
examples from the lessons: She wore a sparkly dress to the party. | We made sparkly Christmas cards with glitter. | The snow was sparkly in the sun. | My little sister loves sparkly shoes. | The fairy had a sparkly wand. | He has sparkly eyes when he laughs. | The frost made the grass look sparkly.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal word; more formal: sparkling, glittering. Comparative: sparklier, sparkliest. Glitter is bad for the environment because it is tiny plastic; some schools now use eco-glitter.

part of speech: noun (sparring — uncountable); verb form (spar, spars, sparred, sparring); adjective (sparring partner)
meaning for a pupil: 1) In boxing and martial arts, sparring is practice fighting with a partner, using light hits and safety gear, to train, not to hurt. 2) Sparring is also arguing in a friendly or not very serious way, trading quick clever remarks. 3) (verb) To spar means to do that practice fighting, or to argue with someone.
its sense in the lessons: In PE and clubs such as karate or taekwondo, sparring has rules, gloves and head guards. In stories and news, politicians or friends "spar" with words. Phrases: "sparring partner" (someone you train or argue with often), "sparring session", "spar with".
examples from the lessons: We have sparring practice at karate on Fridays. | You must wear a head guard for sparring. | The boxer's sparring partner helped him get ready. | The two friends enjoy sparring about football. | The leaders sparred on TV about taxes. | In taekwondo sparring, you score points for kicks. | Sparring is not real fighting; we stop when the coach says.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spar doubles the r: sparred, sparring. A "spar" is also a pole on a ship's mast (a different word). Sparring partner can mean a friend you often argue with for fun.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Specifically means exactly, clearly and in detail: "I specifically asked for no onions." 2) Specifically means for one particular purpose or person only: "This book was written specifically for children." 3) We use it to give a more exact detail: "I like animals, specifically cats."
its sense in the lessons: In school, teachers use it to make instructions exact ("specifically, find three adjectives"). In science and maths it narrows things down to an exact case. In writing it helps explain clearly. Phrases: "more specifically", "specifically designed for", "specifically asked".
examples from the lessons: I specifically told you to bring your PE kit. | The playground was built specifically for little children. | I like fruit, specifically mangoes. | The teacher specifically said no calculators. | This glue is made specifically for paper. | Which bird, specifically, did you see? | The test is about plants, more specifically about leaves.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: specific + ally (specifically, with -ically), not "specificly". Many people mispronounce it as "pacifically" or "specifically" with missing syllables; say "spuh-SIF-ik-lee". Do not confuse with "Pacific" (the ocean).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Speedy means fast, moving or happening quickly: a speedy car, a speedy runner. 2) Speedy also means happening soon, without delay: "Get well soon and have a speedy recovery."
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life it is a friendly, informal word for fast. Cards often say "wishing you a speedy recovery". In stories it describes animals or characters. Phrases: "speedy recovery", "speedy service", "speedy delivery", "speedy reply".
examples from the lessons: The cheetah is the speediest land animal. | Thanks for your speedy reply! | We wish Grandpa a speedy recovery. | The shop promised speedy delivery. | My speedy little dog always wins the race. | We had a speedy lunch before the match. | A speedy decision is not always a good one.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative: speedier, speediest (y to i). Noun: speed; adverb: speedily. In maths, "speed" is distance divided by time; "speedy" is just a describing word.

part of speech: noun (a spoof, spoofs); verb (spoof, spoofs, spoofed, spoofing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A spoof is a funny copy of something, such as a film, song or advert, that makes fun of it by exaggerating it. 2) (verb) To spoof something is to make that kind of funny copy. 3) (computers) Spoofing is pretending to be someone else online, for example sending an email that looks as if it comes from your bank or school, to trick people. 4) (informal) A spoof can also be a trick or hoax.
its sense in the lessons: In English and media lessons spoofs are a kind of parody, and the word tells the reader something is meant as a joke. In online safety lessons spoofed emails, websites and phone numbers are a warning sign of scams: check the sender and never give passwords. Phrases: "a spoof of", "spoof video", "spoof email", "spoofed number".
examples from the lessons: The film is a spoof of old superhero movies. | Our class made a spoof news report for fun. | Comedians love to spoof politicians. | That email is a spoof; it isn't really from the bank. | Scammers spoofed the school's phone number. | It was only a spoof, but some people believed it. | The song spoofs famous pop stars.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a spoof, spoofs; verb regular: spoofed. Close words: parody, send-up, hoax. A spoof is meant to be funny; a spoofed email is meant to trick, which is dangerous.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A springbok is a small, fast antelope (a deer-like animal) of southern Africa, brown and white, famous for jumping high into the air. 2) The Springboks are the national rugby union team of South Africa, named after the animal.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography lessons springboks appear in African savannah food chains and animal adaptations: they leap straight up, "pronking", maybe to show predators they are strong. In sport talk the Springboks are a famous rugby team who won the Rugby World Cup several times. The springbok is a national symbol of South Africa.
examples from the lessons: A springbok can jump higher than a grown-up's head. | Cheetahs and lions hunt springboks. | Springboks live on dry grasslands in southern Africa. | The Springboks beat New Zealand in the final. | We saw a herd of springboks on the safari video. | The springbok is South Africa's national animal. | When scared, springboks leap with stiff legs; this is called pronking.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: springboks (sometimes springbok). From Afrikaans/Dutch: "spring" (jump) + "bok" (antelope or goat). With a capital S, it means the rugby team.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A sprocket is a wheel with teeth around its edge that fit into the links of a chain or the holes in a film or tape, so that it can turn it or be turned by it. On a bicycle, the toothed wheels the chain goes round are sprockets.
its sense in the lessons: In design and technology and science lessons sprockets and chains are a way to pass turning force from one wheel to another (like gears). On a bike, a big front sprocket and a small back sprocket make the back wheel turn faster. Old cinema film and camera film had sprocket holes. Phrases: "chain and sprocket", "sprocket holes", "rear sprocket".
examples from the lessons: The bike chain slipped off the sprocket. | The front sprocket has more teeth than the back one. | Sprockets and chains are used in bicycles and motorbikes. | Old film had little sprocket holes along its edges. | We built a model with plastic sprockets in D and T. | Oil the chain so it runs smoothly over the sprockets. | If the front sprocket has 40 teeth and the back has 20, the back wheel turns twice for each turn of the pedals.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. In maths problems, the number of teeth matters: turns of the small sprocket = teeth of big ÷ teeth of small × turns of the big one. A sprocket differs from a gear because a sprocket works with a chain, while gears touch each other.

part of speech: noun (a squiggle, squiggles); verb (squiggle, squiggles, squiggled, squiggling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A squiggle is a short wavy or curly line, especially one drawn quickly or messily. 2) (verb) To squiggle means to draw such lines, or to wriggle or twist about.
its sense in the lessons: In art and handwriting lessons squiggles are scribbles; in maths a squiggle "~" (tilde) can mean "about" or "approximately" in notes. In stories it describes messy writing or wriggling worms. Phrases: "draw a squiggle", "squiggly line", "a squiggle of icing".
examples from the lessons: The baby drew squiggles all over the paper. | Can you turn this squiggle into a picture? | The teacher couldn't read my squiggles. | She put a squiggle of icing on each cupcake. | The worm squiggled across the path. | A red squiggly line under a word on the computer means it may be spelled wrongly. | His signature is just a squiggle.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Adjective: squiggly. Informal and fun word. "The squiggle game" is a drawing game where you turn a random line into a picture.

part of speech: verb (squirm, squirms, squirmed, squirming); noun (a squirm)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To squirm means to twist and wriggle your body because you are uncomfortable, bored or trying to get free: "The puppy squirmed out of my arms." 2) To squirm also means to feel very embarrassed or ashamed: "His joke made me squirm."
its sense in the lessons: In stories it shows a character's discomfort or guilt without saying it directly. In everyday school life, children squirm on the carpet or squirm when asked a hard question. Phrases: "squirm in your seat", "squirm out of" (escape from something wriggling), "make someone squirm".
examples from the lessons: The little boy squirmed in his chair during the long assembly. | The fish squirmed in the net. | I squirmed when Mum showed my baby photos. | The puppy squirmed out of my arms. | He squirmed with embarrassment when he forgot his lines. | Worms squirmed in the wet soil. | The tricky question made the minister squirm.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: squirmed. Close words: wriggle, writhe, fidget. "Squirm" often hints at embarrassment or guilt; "wriggle" is just movement.

part of speech: adjective (squishy, squishier, squishiest); noun (a squishy, squishies — informal toy)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Squishy means soft and wet or soft and easy to squeeze, so it changes shape when pressed: squishy mud, a squishy tomato. 2) (informal) A squishy is a soft squeezy toy that slowly goes back to its shape. 3) (informal) Squishy can also mean soft-hearted or a bit unclear and not firm.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons it is an everyday word for materials that are soft and flexible. Children use it for toys, food and mud. Phrases: "squishy toy", "squishy mud", "nice and squishy".
examples from the lessons: I stepped in squishy mud at the park. | That banana is too squishy to eat. | My squishy toy looks like a strawberry. | The jelly felt squishy and cold. | Kids at school collect squishies. | The sofa cushions are really squishy. | Squeeze the sponge; feel how squishy it is when wet.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal word. Comparative: squishier. It comes from "squish", a sound word (onomatopoeia). In science writing, say "soft" or "flexible" instead.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (UK) Stabilisers are the two small extra wheels on the back of a child's bicycle that stop it falling over while you learn to ride (US: training wheels). 2) A stabiliser is any part or device that keeps something steady, such as the fins on a ship or the small horizontal wings at the back of an aeroplane. 3) (food, science) A stabiliser is a substance added to food or chemicals to keep them mixed and stop them changing.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life children learn to ride a bike "without stabilisers". In science and D and T lessons stabilisers keep boats, planes and structures balanced. On food labels, stabilisers are listed among ingredients (for example in ice cream). Phrases: "take off the stabilisers", "ride without stabilisers".
examples from the lessons: I learned to ride without stabilisers when I was five. | Dad took the stabilisers off my bike. | In America they call stabilisers training wheels. | Big ships have stabilisers to stop them rolling in waves. | The ice cream has a stabiliser to keep it smooth. | The plane's stabiliser helps it fly straight. | She still needs stabilisers on her bike.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK spelling with s (stabiliser); US with z (stabilizer). Verb: stabilise. Countable: a stabiliser, stabilisers. "Training wheels" is the US and Canadian word for bike stabilisers.

part of speech: noun (a stake, stakes); verb (stake, stakes, staked, staking)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A stake is a strong pointed stick or post pushed into the ground, for example to hold up a plant, a tent or a fence. 2) A stake is money or something valuable that you risk in a bet or game. 3) A stake in something is a share or interest in it, so you gain or lose if it does well or badly: "She has a stake in the company." 4) "At stake" means at risk, able to be won or lost: "The championship is at stake." 5) (verb) To stake means to fix with stakes, to bet or risk something, or to claim: "stake a claim". 6) (history) In the past some people were cruelly killed by burning while tied to a stake.
its sense in the lessons: In gardening and science, stakes hold up tomato and bean plants. In maths and money lessons, a stake in a bet is the amount risked; the winnings depend on the odds. In stories and news, "high stakes" and "at stake" tell the reader something important can be lost. In history, people were "burned at the stake", for example during religious persecutions. Phrases: "at stake", "high stakes", "stake a claim", "stake out" (watch a place secretly), "pull up stakes" (move away).
examples from the lessons: We tied the tomato plant to a wooden stake. | Hammer the tent stakes into the ground. | His job was at stake if the project failed. | It was a high-stakes final, so everyone was nervous. | Miners staked their claims during the gold rush. | Workers who own shares have a stake in the company. | The police staked out the house all night. | Joan of Arc was burned at the stake in 1431.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Homophone trap: stake (post, bet, share) and steak (a thick slice of meat) sound the same. Countable: a stake, stakes. In money problems, if you lose a bet you lose your stake; if you win, you usually get your stake back plus winnings.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Statistical means about statistics: the collecting, counting and studying of numbers and data to find patterns and facts. 2) Statistical describes something shown by numbers rather than by single stories: a statistical link, statistical evidence.
its sense in the lessons: In maths lessons it appears with tables, charts, averages (mean, median, mode) and surveys; in science with results of experiments; in the news with reports about health, weather and money. It tells the reader a claim rests on data. Phrases: "statistical evidence", "statistical analysis", "statistical chart", "statistical survey".
examples from the lessons: We did a statistical survey of favourite fruits in our class. | The report gives statistical evidence that the river is cleaner. | A statistical chart showed how many children walk to school. | Scientists used statistical tests to check their results. | There is a statistical link between sleep and good marks. | The statistical summary showed the mean height was 135 cm. | Is the difference real or just a statistical accident?
note for the reader of a maths problem: No comparative forms. Related: statistics (noun), statistically (adverb), statistician (person). A statistical link (correlation) does not prove that one thing causes the other.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Statistically means according to statistics, judging by numbers and data: "Statistically, flying is safer than driving." 2) "Statistically significant" (formal, science) means a result is very unlikely to have happened just by chance.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, science and news it introduces a fact based on data. It helps children see that numbers about many people tell us what is likely, not what will happen to one person. Phrases: "statistically speaking", "statistically significant", "statistically more likely".
examples from the lessons: Statistically, more babies are born in summer here. | Statistically speaking, you are safer on a train than in a car. | Girls and boys did statistically the same in the test. | The new medicine worked statistically better than the old one. | Statistically, it rains on half the days in our town. | The result was statistically significant, so it was not just luck. | Statistically, you are very unlikely to win the lottery.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: statistic + ally. "Statistically likely" does not mean certain for every person. Pronounce "stuh-TIS-tik-lee".

part of speech: noun (a stave, staves); verb (stave, staves, staved or stove, staving; stave off, staved off)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (music, UK) A stave is the set of five lines on which music notes are written (US: staff). 2) A stave is one of the curved wooden strips that make the sides of a barrel or a wooden bucket. 3) A stave is also a strong stick or pole. 4) (verb) To stave off something means to stop it happening for a while: "We ate apples to stave off hunger." 5) (verb) To stave in means to break a hole in something by hitting it.
its sense in the lessons: In music lessons pupils write notes on the stave with the treble clef. In history lessons coopers made barrels from staves. In stories and everyday speech, "stave off" is used for hunger, boredom, illness or danger. Phrases: "stave off", "treble stave", "bass stave", "stave in".
examples from the lessons: Draw a treble clef at the start of the stave. | The note sits on the second line of the stave. | The cooper bent the wooden staves to make a barrel. | We ate a snack to stave off hunger before the match. | The team staved off defeat with a late goal. | The waves staved in the side of the boat. | The old shepherd leaned on his stave.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: staves (also the plural of "staff" in the old sense of stick). "Stave off" past: staved off. "Staff" is the US word for the music stave. "Stove in" is an old past form used for ships.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Stellar means about stars in space: stellar light, stellar systems. 2) (informal) Stellar means excellent, brilliant, outstanding: a stellar performance.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons it appears with stars, the Sun, galaxies and the life cycle of stars ("stellar evolution"). In everyday talk, sport and news it is praise. Phrases: "stellar performance", "stellar career", "stellar wind", "stellar nursery" (a cloud where new stars form).
examples from the lessons: Our Sun is a stellar object, just one star among billions. | Astronomers study stellar explosions called supernovae. | The Orion Nebula is a stellar nursery. | She gave a stellar performance in the school play. | The goalkeeper had a stellar season. | Your homework is stellar; well done! | Stellar winds blow particles out from stars.
note for the reader of a maths problem: No comparative. From Latin "stella" (star). "Interstellar" means between the stars. In praise, "stellar" is informal but polite.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Sterile means completely clean and free from germs (bacteria and viruses): sterile bandages, a sterile operating room. 2) Sterile means unable to have babies or young, or (of plants) unable to make seeds or fruit. 3) Sterile land cannot grow crops. 4) Sterile also means dull, lifeless, without ideas or warmth: a sterile argument, a sterile room.
its sense in the lessons: In science and health lessons it appears with hygiene, first aid, hospitals and microbes: sterile means no living germs at all. In biology it appears with reproduction in animals and plants. In stories a sterile place feels cold and empty. Phrases: "sterile dressing", "sterile water", "keep sterile", "sterile environment".
examples from the lessons: Doctors use sterile gloves during operations. | The nurse opened a sterile bandage. | Boiling water can make baby bottles sterile. | A mule is usually sterile, so it cannot have foals. | The desert soil was sterile and nothing grew. | The new office felt sterile, with white walls and no plants. | In the lab, keep the dish sterile so no germs grow.
note for the reader of a maths problem: British pronunciation "STER-ile" (rhymes with "mile"), American "STER-ul". Verb: sterilise (UK) / sterilize (US); noun: sterility. "Sterile" in science means not even one living germ, which is more than just "clean".

meaning for a pupil: 1) To stimulate means to make something more active or make it grow or work more: "Exercise stimulates your heart." 2) To stimulate a person means to make them interested, excited or full of ideas: "The trip stimulated my interest in rocks." 3) (science) In biology, to stimulate a nerve or sense is to make it react, for example light stimulates the eye.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons it appears with senses, nerves, muscles and plant growth. In money and news it is used for the economy ("stimulate spending"). In school, teachers want to stimulate curiosity and discussion. Phrases: "stimulate interest", "stimulate growth", "stimulate the brain", "stimulating conversation".
examples from the lessons: Puzzles stimulate your brain. | Sunlight stimulates plants to grow. | The museum visit stimulated our curiosity about Egypt. | Coffee stimulates adults and keeps them awake. | Bright colours stimulate babies' eyes. | The government cut taxes to stimulate the economy. | The teacher asked questions to stimulate a discussion.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Adjective: stimulating (interesting, exciting). Noun: stimulation, stimulus (plural stimuli). Something that stimulates is a "stimulant".

meaning for a pupil: 1) Stimulation is making something more active, or the thing that does it: the stimulation of a muscle, of growth. 2) Stimulation is something that makes the mind busy and interested: "Children need play and stimulation." 3) (science) In biology, stimulation is when a nerve, sense or cell is made to react, for example by light, sound, touch or electricity.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons it appears with the nervous system and senses. In everyday life parents and teachers talk about "mental stimulation" and babies needing stimulation to learn. Too much stimulation (noise, screens, lights) can make people tired or upset: "overstimulation". Phrases: "mental stimulation", "lack of stimulation", "electrical stimulation".
examples from the lessons: Babies need lots of stimulation from talking and play. | Reading gives the brain good stimulation. | Bored pets need more stimulation, like toys and walks. | Electrical stimulation can help weak muscles. | The noisy party was too much stimulation for the toddler. | Puzzles provide mental stimulation for older people. | The eye reacts to stimulation by light.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable. Verb: stimulate; related: stimulus, stimuli. "Overstimulation" means too much at once.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A stomatopod is a mantis shrimp, a sea animal related to crabs and shrimps (a crustacean) that hunts by striking or stabbing prey with super-fast front claws.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons stomatopods are famous for amazing facts: their punch is one of the fastest movements of any animal and can crack shells and even aquarium glass, and their eyes see colours and kinds of light that humans cannot. They live in warm shallow seas, often in burrows. The word is a scientific name used for the whole group.
examples from the lessons: A stomatopod can punch faster than a bullet leaves some guns. | Stomatopods are also called mantis shrimps. | The stomatopod smashed the crab's shell with its claw. | Scientists study stomatopod eyes, which see polarised light. | Stomatopods live in burrows on coral reefs. | Divers saw a colourful stomatopod peeping out of the sand. | Some aquariums keep stomatopods in very thick tanks.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced "STOM-uh-toh-pod" or "stoh-MAT-uh-pod". Plural: stomatopods. It is not a true shrimp and not a praying mantis; the name "mantis shrimp" just describes its shape. Scientific, not an everyday word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Streaky means having streaks: long thin lines or marks of a different colour, often uneven: streaky windows, streaky hair dye. 2) (UK, Ireland, Australia) Streaky bacon is bacon with stripes of fat and meat, cut from the belly. 3) (informal, sport) Streaky means not steady, sometimes very good and sometimes bad; in cricket, a streaky shot is a lucky edge.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life it describes cleaning, painting, hair and food. In art lessons streaky paint shows uneven strokes. In sport commentary, a "streaky" player has winning and losing streaks. Phrases: "streaky bacon", "streaky windows", "a streaky shot".
