examples from the lessons: I cleaned the window, but it's still streaky. | The paint dried streaky because I used too little. | Dad made sandwiches with streaky bacon. | Her fake tan went a bit streaky. | The sky was streaky with pink clouds. | His batting is streaky: one week great, the next week awful. | That was a streaky four off the edge of the bat.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative: streakier, streakiest. "Streaky bacon" is a UK/Irish/Australian name; Americans just say "bacon". From "streak", a line or a run of wins or losses.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Stringy food is full of tough fibres like strings and is hard to chew: stringy meat, stringy celery. 2) Stringy hair is thin, hangs in long straight strands and often looks greasy or untidy. 3) A stringy person is thin with lean, wiry muscles. 4) Stringy also describes anything that stretches into thin strings, like melted cheese.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life it describes food and hair; in stories it helps paint a character's looks. In science, fibres in plants like celery make them stringy. Phrases: "stringy cheese", "stringy hair", "stringy beans".
examples from the lessons: This beef is stringy and hard to chew. | Pull the stringy bits off the celery. | The melted cheese on the pizza was all stringy. | After swimming, my hair was wet and stringy. | The old farmer was stringy and strong. | Runner beans get stringy if you pick them late. | Her stringy fringe hung over her eyes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative: stringier, stringiest. Saying someone's hair is stringy is not polite. "String cheese" is a snack made to peel into strings.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A stronghold is a strong, well-defended place such as a castle or fort that is hard to attack. 2) A stronghold is also a place where a group, idea, animal or plant is still strong and common: "The Highlands are a stronghold of the red squirrel." 3) In politics, a stronghold is an area where most people support one party.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons castles, hill forts and mountain hideouts are strongholds. In science and conservation, a stronghold is where a rare species survives in good numbers. In news, "a party's stronghold". In stories it is where the hero or villain hides. Phrases: "last stronghold", "rebel stronghold", "stronghold of".
examples from the lessons: The knights retreated to their stronghold on the hill. | The castle was a stronghold that no army could take. | Scotland is a stronghold for red squirrels. | The rebels held a stronghold in the mountains. | This town is a stronghold of the Labour Party. | The villain's stronghold was hidden under the sea. | The island is the last stronghold of the rare bird.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a stronghold, strongholds. Compound of strong + hold. Close words: fortress, castle, fort, bastion.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Stubbornness is refusing to change your mind or do what others want, even when there are good reasons. 2) Stubbornness can also be a good thing, meaning determination: not giving up when things are hard. 3) Stubbornness of a thing means it is hard to move, remove or fix: the stubbornness of a stain.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and PSHE it is a character trait, sometimes a fault and sometimes a strength. In everyday talk parents describe toddlers' stubbornness. Phrases: "out of stubbornness", "sheer stubbornness", "stubbornness of a mule" (mules are thought of as stubborn).
examples from the lessons: His stubbornness stopped him from saying sorry. | Out of stubbornness, she would not wear a coat. | Her stubbornness helped her finish the marathon. | The toddler's stubbornness made bedtime hard. | Mules are famous for their stubbornness. | Sheer stubbornness kept the team going in the rain. | The stubbornness of the stain meant we had to scrub it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: two n's in the middle (stubborn + ness). Uncountable. Adjective: stubborn; adverb: stubbornly. Close words: obstinacy (formal), pigheadedness (informal), determination (positive).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A subcontinent is a very large piece of land that is part of a continent but is separate in some way, by mountains, sea or history. 2) "The Indian subcontinent" or just "the subcontinent" usually means South Asia: India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Nepal, Bhutan, Sri Lanka and often the Maldives.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons it appears when learning continents and plates: the Indian subcontinent sits on its own tectonic plate that crashed into Asia and pushed up the Himalayas. In history it comes with the British Raj and the partition of India in 1947. Phrases: "the Indian subcontinent", "across the subcontinent".
examples from the lessons: The Indian subcontinent is separated from the rest of Asia by the Himalayas. | Many languages are spoken across the subcontinent. | Cricket is very popular on the subcontinent. | Monsoon rains fall over the subcontinent each summer. | The subcontinent moved north and crashed into Asia millions of years ago. | My grandparents came to Britain from the subcontinent. | The map showed the subcontinent in orange.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: one word, sub + continent. When someone says "the subcontinent" in the UK, they almost always mean South Asia. It is not a continent itself: it is part of Asia.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Subjective means based on someone's own feelings, tastes or opinions rather than on facts that everyone can check: "Which song is best is subjective." 2) (grammar) The subjective case is the form of a pronoun used as the subject of a sentence: I, he, she, we, they (not me, him, her, us, them).
its sense in the lessons: In English and science lessons pupils learn the difference between subjective (opinion) and objective (fact you can measure or check). In reviews and persuasive writing, opinions are subjective. In science, measuring with instruments reduces subjective judgement. Phrases: "purely subjective", "a subjective opinion", "subjective judgement".
examples from the lessons: Whether pizza is better than pasta is subjective. | Art marks can be a bit subjective. | "This film is boring" is a subjective statement. | Scientists use rulers instead of subjective guesses. | Taste is subjective: my sister loves olives, I hate them. | His report was subjective, full of his own feelings. | Is beauty subjective or objective? We debated it in class.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: objective. Adverb: subjectively. A subjective opinion is not wrong; it is just yours, and others may disagree. Facts can be checked; opinions cannot be proved true or false.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A submersible is a small underwater vehicle used to explore the deep sea, often with a crew of one to three people or controlled by remote control. 2) (adjective) Submersible means able to work or be used underwater: a submersible pump, a submersible watch.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography lessons submersibles explore the ocean floor, shipwrecks such as the Titanic and deep trenches like the Mariana Trench. They are different from submarines, which are bigger and travel on their own for long trips. Phrases: "deep-sea submersible", "manned submersible", "submersible pump".
examples from the lessons: The submersible dived to the bottom of the ocean. | Scientists in a submersible found new kinds of fish. | A submersible explored the wreck of the Titanic. | The submersible had bright lights and robotic arms. | This pump is submersible, so you can put it in the pond. | A remote-controlled submersible filmed the deep trench. | Only a few submersibles can go deeper than 10,000 metres.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. A submersible usually needs a support ship; a submarine can travel alone. From "submerge" (go under water). Spelling ends in -ible.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Suffrage is the right to vote in elections. 2) "Women's suffrage" means women's right to vote, and "universal suffrage" means all adult citizens can vote.
its sense in the lessons: In history and citizenship lessons it comes with the suffragists and suffragettes, who campaigned for women's votes: women in New Zealand won the vote in 1893, in the UK some women in 1918 and all women at 21 in 1928, in the USA in 1920 (19th Amendment). Black Americans and many others also fought long for equal suffrage. Phrases: "women's suffrage", "universal suffrage", "suffrage movement".
examples from the lessons: New Zealand was the first country where women won national suffrage, in 1893. | The suffrage movement held big marches in London. | Universal suffrage means every adult citizen can vote. | Suffragettes fought for women's suffrage. | In 1920, American women gained suffrage. | We made posters about suffrage in history. | The right to vote is called suffrage.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Not related to "suffer", even though it looks similar. Suffragists campaigned peacefully; suffragettes (a UK name) sometimes used direct action. Spelling: double f, "-rage".

part of speech: noun (a sulfide, sulfides; UK spelling also sulphide)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) A sulfide is a chemical compound made of sulfur joined with another element, often a metal, such as iron sulfide or hydrogen sulfide. 2) Many sulfides are minerals and metal ores, such as pyrite (fool's gold), which is iron sulfide.
its sense in the lessons: In chemistry and science lessons sulfides appear when iron and sulfur are heated together to make iron sulfide (a compound, not a mixture: a magnet no longer separates them). Hydrogen sulfide is the gas that smells of rotten eggs, made by rotting things and volcanoes, and it is poisonous in large amounts. Phrases: "iron sulfide", "hydrogen sulfide", "sulfide ore".
examples from the lessons: When we heated iron and sulfur, we made iron sulfide. | Fool's gold is iron sulfide, not real gold. | Hydrogen sulfide smells of rotten eggs. | Copper is often mined from sulfide ores. | Black smokers on the sea floor pour out sulfides. | Iron sulfide is a compound, so a magnet cannot pull the iron out. | The bad smell near the swamp came from sulfides.
note for the reader of a maths problem: US and international science spelling: sulfide, sulfur; traditional UK spelling: sulphide, sulphur; both are correct. Do not confuse with sulfate (sulfur plus oxygen and another element).

part of speech: adjective (sunken); old past participle of sink
meaning for a pupil: 1) Sunken means lying at the bottom of the sea, a lake or a river after sinking: a sunken ship, sunken treasure. 2) Sunken means lower than the area around it: a sunken garden, a sunken bath. 3) Sunken eyes or cheeks look hollow and fallen in, often because a person is ill, hungry or very tired.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and history it appears with shipwrecks, pirates and treasure. In everyday life and design it describes gardens and rooms built lower. In health, sunken eyes can be a sign of dehydration. Phrases: "sunken ship", "sunken treasure", "sunken eyes", "sunken garden".
examples from the lessons: Divers explored the sunken ship. | Pirates dreamed of sunken treasure. | The sunken garden was three steps below the lawn. | After the long illness, his cheeks were sunken. | Sunken eyes can be a sign that you need to drink water. | A sunken road ran between the high banks. | The Mary Rose was a sunken Tudor warship raised in 1982.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Grammar: today the past participle of "sink" is usually "sunk" ("The ship has sunk"), but before a noun we use "sunken" ("a sunken ship"). Past simple is "sank". Do not say "the ship has sunken".

meaning for a pupil: 1) Superfluous means more than is needed, extra and not necessary: "Cut the superfluous words from your sentence." 2) (formal) Superfluous can mean not wanted or useful, so a person may feel superfluous when they are not needed.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons, editing writing means removing superfluous words and repetition. In formal exam language it means unnecessary. In maths word problems, some information may be superfluous: you do not need it to solve the problem. Phrases: "superfluous detail", "superfluous information", "feel superfluous".
examples from the lessons: Delete any superfluous words from your story. | The extra decorations were superfluous. | The problem had superfluous information about the colour of the bus. | Packing three umbrellas seems superfluous. | With two helpers already, I felt superfluous. | His long speech had a lot of superfluous detail. | Shoes inside a swimming pool are superfluous.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced "soo-PER-floo-us" (stress on PER). Formal word; simpler: unnecessary, extra. In maths, spotting superfluous numbers is a skill: not every number in a problem must be used.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) A supergiant is one of the biggest and brightest kinds of star, many times larger and heavier than our Sun. 2) (adjective, informal) Supergiant can mean enormous: a supergiant shark in a film.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons supergiants appear in the life cycle of stars: very massive stars swell into red supergiants and later may explode as supernovae, leaving neutron stars or black holes. Famous examples: Betelgeuse (red supergiant in Orion) and Rigel (blue supergiant). Phrases: "red supergiant", "blue supergiant".
examples from the lessons: Betelgeuse is a red supergiant in the constellation Orion. | A supergiant can be hundreds of times wider than the Sun. | When a supergiant dies, it can explode as a supernova. | Rigel is a blue supergiant, very hot and bright. | Our Sun will never become a supergiant; it is too small. | If a red supergiant replaced the Sun, it would swallow the inner planets. | Supergiants live much shorter lives than small stars.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Supergiants burn fuel very fast, so they live only millions of years, not billions like the Sun. Size order: dwarf stars, giants, supergiants, hypergiants.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (grammar) A superlative is the form of an adjective or adverb that shows the most or least: biggest, fastest, most beautiful, best, worst. 2) (formal) Superlative means extremely good, of the highest quality: a superlative performance. 3) (noun) Superlatives can also be words of very high praise: "The review was full of superlatives."
its sense in the lessons: In English grammar lessons (and SATs), pupils learn comparatives (bigger, more) and superlatives (biggest, most): short words take -est, long words take "most", and some are irregular (good, better, best; bad, worse, worst). In maths, superlatives in word problems ("the tallest", "the fewest") tell you to find the maximum or minimum. Phrases: "superlative form", "run out of superlatives".
examples from the lessons: Tallest is the superlative of "tall". | The superlative of "good" is "best". | Use "the" before a superlative: the fastest runner. | The chef cooked a superlative meal. | The critics ran out of superlatives to describe the show. | Find the superlative: "Mount Everest is the highest mountain on Earth." | "Most exciting" is a superlative made with "most".
note for the reader of a maths problem: Rules: one syllable: add -est (big, biggest — double the final consonant after a short vowel); ending in y: change to -iest (happy, happiest); long words: "most" + adjective. Do not use both: not "most biggest". In maths problems, superlatives mean largest (maximum) or smallest (minimum).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Sustenance is food and drink that keeps a person, animal or plant alive and strong: "The travellers had no sustenance for days." 2) Sustenance also means anything that supports or strengthens someone, like comfort, hope or faith: "Her letters gave him sustenance."
its sense in the lessons: In formal or old-fashioned writing, history and the Bible, it means nourishment. In science, it links to food chains and nutrients that living things need. In church language, believers may speak of prayer or faith as spiritual sustenance. Phrases: "means of sustenance", "spiritual sustenance", "for sustenance".
examples from the lessons: The explorers needed sustenance after the long walk. | Bread was the main sustenance of poor families in the past. | Plants get sustenance from sunlight, water and soil. | Many Christians say prayer gives them spiritual sustenance. | The squirrels stored nuts for sustenance in winter. | A cup of tea and a biscuit gave Grandma some sustenance. | Hope was their only sustenance during the war.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable and formal; simpler words: food, nourishment. Related verb: sustain. Spelling: "sustenance", not "sustainance".

part of speech: noun (a swab, swabs); verb (swab, swabs, swabbed, swabbing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A swab is a small piece of cotton wool, often on a stick, used to clean a wound or put on medicine. 2) A swab is also a sample taken with such a stick from someone's nose, throat or mouth, so it can be tested for germs: a Covid swab. 3) (verb) To swab means to clean or wipe with a swab, or to take such a sample. 4) (verb) To swab the deck means to clean the floor of a ship with a mop.
its sense in the lessons: In health and science lessons swabs are used in testing for infections and in first aid. In history and pirate stories sailors "swab the decks". In science experiments pupils may swab surfaces to grow bacteria on a plate. Phrases: "cotton swab", "throat swab", "nose swab", "take a swab", "swab the deck".
examples from the lessons: The nurse cleaned the cut with a swab. | The doctor took a swab from my throat. | We did a swab test at home when I had a cough. | The pirates were made to swab the decks. | We swabbed the door handle and grew bacteria in a dish. | Use a cotton swab to dab on the cream. | Police can swab the inside of the cheek for DNA.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb doubles the b: swabbed, swabbing. Countable noun. In the USA cotton swabs are often called by the brand name Q-tips; in the UK "cotton buds". Never put cotton buds deep into ears.

part of speech: noun (swag — uncountable; Australia: a swag, swags); verb (swag, swags, swagged — rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (slang) Swag means cool style and confidence in how you look or act: "He walked in with loads of swag." 2) (informal) Swag is free stuff given away at events, such as badges, pens, stickers and T-shirts with a company's name. 3) (old slang) Swag is stolen goods, especially what a burglar carries away in a bag. 4) (Australia, New Zealand) A swag is a bedroll: a waterproof canvas bag with a mattress for sleeping outdoors; a swagman was a traveller who carried one. 5) A swag is also a piece of cloth or a decoration hanging in a curve, as above a window.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday young people's talk "swag" is praise for style (a bit dated slang now). In stories, cartoon robbers carry a bag marked "SWAG". In Australian history and the song "Waltzing Matilda", the swagman camps by a billabong. At conventions and fairs, people collect swag. Phrases: "got swag", "conference swag", "roll out the swag", "swag bag".
examples from the lessons: The burglar ran off with a bag of swag. | We got lots of swag at the science fair: pens, stickers and a cap. | My cousin thinks his new trainers give him swag. | In the outback we slept in swags under the stars. | Once a jolly swagman camped by a billabong. | The curtains had a swag of red silk across the top. | That dance move has serious swag! (slang)
note for the reader of a maths problem: The style sense is slang; the stolen-goods sense is old slang from robber stories. In Australia "a swag" is countable (two swags); the other senses are uncountable. "Swagger" means a proud, confident walk.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Sycophancy is flattering and agreeing with an important or powerful person too much, to please them and get something for yourself. 2) For computers and AI, sycophancy means a chatbot telling people what they want to hear instead of what is true.
its sense in the lessons: In English and history lessons it describes courtiers and advisers around kings who praised them falsely, and characters in stories who "suck up" to the boss. In computing lessons about AI it is a known problem: a good helper should be honest, even when the answer is not welcome. Close informal words: sucking up, brown-nosing (rude), crawling (UK), teacher's pet behaviour.
examples from the lessons: The king's advisers were full of sycophancy and never told him bad news. | His sycophancy towards the head teacher annoyed the class. | Sycophancy is not real friendship. | The AI's sycophancy meant it agreed with every wrong answer. | In the play, the servant's sycophancy hides his plan to steal. | Honest feedback is better than sycophancy. | She rejected the sycophancy of people who only liked her money.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable, formal. Person: sycophant; adjective: sycophantic. Pronounced "SIK-uh-fun-see". Do not confuse with "psychology" or "symphony". Being kind and polite is not sycophancy; sycophancy is false praise for your own gain.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Syllabic means about syllables, the beats or sound parts that words are divided into: "hap-py" has two syllables. 2) A syllabic writing system (a syllabary) uses one symbol for each syllable, like Japanese kana or the Cherokee syllabary. 3) (phonetics) A syllabic sound, like the "n" in "button" or "l" in "bottle", makes a syllable on its own without a vowel.
its sense in the lessons: In English and phonics lessons pupils clap syllables to read and spell longer words; in poetry, syllable counts matter for haiku (5-7-5) and for rhythm. In language lessons, children learn that some scripts are syllabic, some alphabetic (one letter per sound), and Chinese is mostly logographic. Phrases: "syllabic script", "syllabic structure", "syllabic verse".
examples from the lessons: Japanese hiragana is a syllabic script. | We clapped the syllabic beats of our names. | A haiku has a strict syllabic pattern: 5, 7, 5. | The Cherokee leader Sequoyah invented a syllabic writing system. | In "bottle", the final l is syllabic. | Syllabic poems count syllables, not stresses. | Breaking a long word into syllabic parts helps you spell it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced "si-LAB-ik". Noun: syllable; plural syllables. An alphabet (like English) is not syllabic: each letter stands for a sound, not a whole syllable.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) Symbiotic describes a close relationship between two different kinds of living things that live together, especially one where both are helped: bees and flowers, clownfish and sea anemones. 2) Symbiotic also describes any relationship between people, groups or things that help each other: "The farm and the village had a symbiotic relationship."
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons it appears with habitats and food webs: in mutualism both partners gain, in commensalism one gains and the other is not harmed, in parasitism one gains and the other is harmed. Examples: lichens (fungus and alga), the bacteria in our gut, oxpeckers on buffalo, cleaner fish. Phrases: "symbiotic relationship", "symbiotic bacteria".
examples from the lessons: Clownfish and sea anemones have a symbiotic relationship. | Our gut has symbiotic bacteria that help digest food. | A lichen is a symbiotic partnership of a fungus and an alga. | Bees and flowers are symbiotic: bees get food, flowers get pollinated. | The shop and the café next door have a symbiotic relationship. | Cleaner fish eat parasites from bigger fish in a symbiotic deal. | Coral lives in a symbiotic relationship with tiny algae.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: symbiosis (plural symbioses). Pronounced "sim-bye-OT-ik". In everyday use, "symbiotic" means both sides benefit; in strict science, it can include parasitism too.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A symphony is a long piece of music for a full orchestra, usually in three or four parts called movements. 2) A symphony is also an orchestra that plays such music: "the London Symphony Orchestra" or just "the symphony" (US). 3) A symphony of something is a rich mixture of things that go well together: "a symphony of colours".
its sense in the lessons: In music lessons pupils listen to famous symphonies by Haydn, Mozart and Beethoven (Beethoven's Fifth with its "da-da-da-DUM" and his Ninth with "Ode to Joy") and learn the sections of the orchestra. In stories it is a fancy way to describe many sounds, smells or colours together. Phrases: "symphony orchestra", "a symphony of sounds", "go to the symphony".
examples from the lessons: We listened to Beethoven's Fifth Symphony in music class. | Haydn wrote more than a hundred symphonies. | The symphony orchestra has strings, woodwind, brass and percussion. | The first movement of the symphony was fast and loud. | The forest at dawn was a symphony of birdsong. | My aunt took me to the symphony for my birthday. | The kitchen smelled like a symphony of spices.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: symphonies. Adjective: symphonic. Spelled with "ph" (sounds like f). Composers number their symphonies, so "Symphony No. 9" is the ninth.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Synthetic means made by people from chemicals or in a factory, not naturally grown or found: synthetic materials such as nylon, polyester and plastic. 2) Synthetic also means fake or artificial: synthetic flavours, synthetic diamonds. 3) (noun) Synthetics are synthetic materials or fabrics. 4) (formal, science) Synthetic can mean made by combining parts into a whole (synthesis).
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons materials are sorted into natural (wool, cotton, wood) and synthetic (nylon, polyester, acrylic, plastics); pupils compare their properties, such as strength and waterproofing, and discuss pollution from microplastics. On food labels, synthetic colourings may be listed. Phrases: "synthetic fibre", "synthetic rubber", "synthetic grass", "synthetic drug".
examples from the lessons: Nylon is a synthetic fibre. | My raincoat is made of a synthetic material that keeps water out. | Wool is natural, but polyester is synthetic. | The pitch has synthetic grass, so it never needs mowing. | Synthetic rubber is made from oil. | Synthetic diamonds are made in labs. | Washing synthetics can release tiny plastic bits into the sea.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: natural. Related: synthesis, synthesise. Synthetic does not always mean worse; many synthetic materials are very useful, such as medicines and safety gear.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Tactile means about the sense of touch, or able to be felt by touching: tactile paving, a tactile map. 2) A tactile thing is nice to touch: "The soft clay is very tactile." 3) A tactile person likes to touch others a lot, for example hugging or patting people.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons it links to the five senses (touch, sight, hearing, taste, smell). In everyday life, tactile paving (bumpy pavement at crossings) and Braille help blind and partially sighted people. In art and early years, tactile materials and sensory boxes help learning. Phrases: "tactile paving", "tactile learner", "tactile display".
examples from the lessons: Braille is a tactile way of reading. | The bumpy tactile paving shows blind people where the crossing is. | Babies explore the world in a very tactile way. | This book has tactile pages with fur and sandpaper. | Grandma is very tactile and always hugs everyone. | The museum has a tactile display you are allowed to touch. | Some children are tactile learners who learn best by handling things.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced "TAK-tile" (UK) or "TAK-tul" (US). Formal-ish word; simple word: touchy-feely (informal, about people). Do not confuse with "tactic" (a plan).

part of speech: noun (taekwondo — uncountable; also tae kwon do)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Taekwondo is a martial art and sport from Korea, famous for high, fast kicks and jumping and spinning kicks. It is an Olympic sport.
its sense in the lessons: In PE and after-school clubs children learn taekwondo for fitness, self-control and respect; they wear a white uniform called a dobok and coloured belts that show their level, up to black belt. Lessons include patterns (forms), sparring with protective gear and breaking boards. Phrases: "do taekwondo", "taekwondo class", "black belt in taekwondo".
examples from the lessons: I go to taekwondo on Tuesdays. | My sister got her yellow belt in taekwondo. | Taekwondo is famous for its spinning kicks. | In taekwondo we bow to show respect. | Taekwondo became an Olympic sport in 2000. | We wear head guards when we spar in taekwondo. | The taekwondo master broke a board with one kick.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: "do taekwondo", not "a taekwondo". Korean word, roughly "the way of the foot and the fist", pronounced "TIE-kwon-DOH". Spelled as one word or "tae kwon do".

meaning for a pupil: 1) A tagger is a person who sprays or writes their nickname or sign (a tag) on walls, trains or buildings, often without permission, which is illegal vandalism. 2) In the playground game of tag (UK: tig, it), the tagger is the player who chases and touches the others. 3) (computing) A tagger is a computer program that labels things automatically, for example labelling each word in a sentence as noun, verb or adjective (a part-of-speech tagger). 4) A tagger is also a person or tool that attaches tags or labels, as on clothes or animals.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and citizenship lessons, taggers and graffiti raise questions about property and art. In the playground, the tagger is "it". In computing and language science, taggers help computers understand text. Phrases: "graffiti tagger", "part-of-speech tagger".
examples from the lessons: Taggers had sprayed their names on the bus shelter. | The council paid to clean up the taggers' graffiti. | In the game, Mia was the tagger and chased us round the field. | If the tagger touches you, you become the tagger. | A part-of-speech tagger marks "run" as a verb or a noun. | The scientist used a tagger to put tracking tags on the birds. | Graffiti by taggers is against the law without permission.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. In the UK the chase game is often called "tig" or "it", in the USA "tag". A graffiti tag is a quick signature; a "piece" is a large, artistic graffiti picture.

part of speech: adjective (Tahitian); noun (a Tahitian, Tahitians; Tahitian — the language)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Tahitian means from or about Tahiti, the largest island of French Polynesia in the South Pacific Ocean. 2) A Tahitian is a person from Tahiti. 3) Tahitian is also the Polynesian language spoken there, related to Māori and Hawaiian.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons Tahiti is an example of a volcanic tropical island with coral reefs; its capital is Papeete and French is also an official language there. In art lessons, the French painter Paul Gauguin painted Tahitian people and landscapes. In history, Captain James Cook visited Tahiti in 1769. Phrases: "Tahitian dance", "Tahitian pearl", "Tahitian vanilla".
examples from the lessons: Tahitian dancers move their hips very fast to drum music. | Tahitian black pearls come from oysters in lagoons. | Gauguin painted many Tahitian women. | Tahitian is a Polynesian language close to Māori. | A Tahitian fisherman paddled his outrigger canoe. | Tahitian vanilla smells sweet and flowery. | Captain Cook watched the stars from a Tahitian beach.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always written with a capital T (input lower case is only for the list). Pronounced "tuh-HEE-shun". Tahiti belongs to France, so Tahitians are French citizens.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A tailorbird is a small bird of tropical Asia, such as India and Southeast Asia, that makes its nest by sewing leaves together with plant fibres or spider silk, using its sharp beak like a needle.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons tailorbirds are a famous example of animal behaviour and adaptation: they pierce holes in the edges of large leaves and pull threads through to make a cup, then build the nest inside. They are small, often green with a reddish cap and an upright tail. They also appear in Rudyard Kipling's story "Rikki-Tikki-Tavi" (Darzee the tailorbird).
examples from the lessons: A tailorbird sews leaves together to hide its nest. | The tailorbird uses its beak like a needle. | Tailorbirds live in gardens and forests in India. | The tailorbird's nest is hidden inside a leafy cup. | In "Rikki-Tikki-Tavi", Darzee is a tailorbird. | Tailorbirds use spider silk as thread. | We watched a video of a tailorbird stitching a nest.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word: tailorbird. Plural: tailorbirds. Named after a tailor, a person who sews clothes.

part of speech: noun (Tamil — the language; a Tamil, Tamils — the people); adjective (Tamil)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Tamil is a language spoken by more than 70 million people, mainly in the state of Tamil Nadu in south India and in Sri Lanka, and also in Singapore, Malaysia and by communities in the UK, Canada and elsewhere. It is one of the oldest languages still spoken, with poems over 2,000 years old. 2) A Tamil is a person whose people and language are Tamil. 3) (adjective) Tamil describes the language, people or culture: Tamil food, Tamil script.
its sense in the lessons: In geography, RE and culture lessons, children meet Tamil festivals such as Pongal (harvest festival) and Hindu temples with tall towers. Tamil has its own script with rounded letters. Some English words come from Tamil, such as "curry" and "mango" (via Portuguese). Phrases: "speak Tamil", "Tamil script", "Tamil New Year".
examples from the lessons: My friend speaks Tamil at home and English at school. | Tamil is an official language in Sri Lanka and Singapore. | The word "curry" probably comes from a Tamil word. | Tamil families celebrate Pongal by cooking sweet rice. | The Tamil script looks curly and round. | Chennai is the biggest Tamil-speaking city in India. | Tamil poems have been written for more than 2,000 years.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always written with a capital T. Pronounced "TAM-il" (UK) or "TAH-mil". Tamil belongs to the Dravidian language family, not the same family as Hindi.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A tankful is the amount a tank can hold when full: a tankful of petrol, a tankful of water.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life it is used for fuel in cars and water in fish tanks. In maths word problems, a tankful is a measure: "A tankful of petrol is 50 litres; the car goes 600 km on a tankful." Phrases: "a tankful of", "on one tankful", "fill a tankful".
examples from the lessons: The car can go 500 miles on a tankful of petrol. | We emptied a tankful of dirty water from the fish tank. | A tankful costs a lot of money now. | How many buckets make a tankful? | The farmer used a tankful of water for the cows each day. | If a tankful is 40 litres and you use 8 litres a day, it lasts 5 days. | The firefighters sprayed a whole tankful on the fire.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: tankfuls (not "tanksful"). The ending -ful makes a measuring noun, like cupful, spoonful, handful. In maths problems, a tankful is the tank's full capacity; half a tankful is half of that.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The tarpan was a wild horse that lived in Europe and western Asia, including the steppes of Ukraine and Russia; it is now extinct. The last known tarpan died in a zoo in Russia in 1909.
its sense in the lessons: In science and history lessons the tarpan is an example of extinction caused by humans: hunting, farming and mixing with farm horses. Grey-brown, with a dark stripe down its back, it was small and sturdy. Today some breeds, such as the Polish Konik, are said to look like it, and some people have bred "tarpan-like" horses, but the real tarpan is gone. Phrases: "the extinct tarpan", "wild tarpan".
examples from the lessons: The tarpan was a wild horse of Europe. | Tarpans once ran across the steppes of southern Ukraine. | The last tarpan died in 1909. | Hunting and farming helped make the tarpan extinct. | Konik ponies look a bit like the tarpan. | The tarpan had a dark stripe down its back. | We read about the tarpan in our lesson on extinct animals.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a tarpan, tarpans. Probably from a Turkic language word. Do not confuse with "tarpaulin" (a waterproof sheet) or Przewalski's horse, a different wild horse that still lives in Mongolia.

part of speech: noun (Tarzan — a name; a Tarzan — informal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (a name) Tarzan is a made-up character created by the American writer Edgar Rice Burroughs in the novel "Tarzan of the Apes" (1912): a boy raised by apes in the African jungle who grows up very strong and swings through the trees on vines. Disney made a cartoon film of him in 1999. 2) (informal) A Tarzan is a very strong, muscly man, often said as a joke.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and films Tarzan is famous for his loud yell and swinging on vines; his friend is Jane. In everyday talk people jokingly call someone "Tarzan" when they show off their strength or swing on a rope. Today some people point out that the old books show Africa and Africans in an unfair way. Phrases: "Tarzan yell", "Tarzan swing", "Me Tarzan, you Jane" (a famous film joke, not in the book).
examples from the lessons: Tarzan swung through the jungle on long vines. | My brother did a Tarzan yell from the climbing frame. | In the story, Tarzan is raised by apes. | Disney's "Tarzan" has songs by Phil Collins. | "Okay, Tarzan, put the sofa down," laughed Mum. | We tied a Tarzan swing to the big oak tree. | Tarzan and Jane meet in the jungle.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A name, so it is written with a capital T. It is a fictional character, not a real person. A "Tarzan swing" or "rope swing" is a rope tied to a branch.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Teary means full of tears or close to crying: teary eyes, a teary goodbye. 2) Teary also describes something that makes people cry: a teary film. 3) (informal) Teary-eyed means with tears in your eyes, often because you are moved, happy or sad.
its sense in the lessons: In stories it shows feelings gently: the character is moved but not sobbing. In everyday life it is used for goodbyes, weddings, school leavers' assemblies and sad films. Phrases: "teary-eyed", "get teary", "a teary farewell".
examples from the lessons: Grandma got teary when we sang for her birthday. | It was a teary goodbye at the airport. | My eyes went teary when I chopped the onions. | The ending of the film made the whole class teary. | Mum was teary-eyed at my sister's graduation. | He gave a teary speech at his last assembly. | Don't get teary; we'll see each other soon.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative: tearier, teariest. Rhymes with "dreary": the "tear" here is the drop from your eye (rhymes with "here"), not "tear" meaning to rip (rhymes with "bear"). Close words: tearful (more formal), weepy.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Tempura is a Japanese dish of pieces of seafood (like prawns) or vegetables dipped in a light batter and deep-fried until crispy.
its sense in the lessons: In food technology and geography lessons it appears when learning about Japanese food alongside sushi and ramen. It is usually eaten with a dipping sauce. Safety: deep-frying uses very hot oil, so only adults should do it. Phrases: "prawn tempura", "vegetable tempura", "tempura batter".
examples from the lessons: We had prawn tempura at the Japanese restaurant. | Tempura batter is made with very cold water. | The sweet potato tempura was crunchy and light. | Tempura is often eaten with soy-based dipping sauce. | My dad tried to make tempura, but the batter was soggy. | Portuguese visitors may have brought the idea of tempura to Japan in the 1500s. | Vegetable tempura is good for people who don't eat meat.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: "some tempura". Japanese word, pronounced "TEM-puh-ruh" (or "tem-POOR-uh"). Do not confuse with "tempera" (a type of paint).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Tenure is the length of time someone holds an important job or position: "During her tenure as head teacher, the school grew." 2) (education, especially USA) Tenure is a permanent job given to some teachers or professors after a trial period, so they cannot easily be sacked. 3) (law, money) Tenure is the right to live in or use a house or land, and the terms of it, for example owning (freehold) or renting.
its sense in the lessons: In history and news it is used for the time of a ruler, president or official in office. In adult life seen by a child, it comes with housing, jobs and job security. Phrases: "during his tenure", "tenure of office", "get tenure", "security of tenure" (the right not to be thrown out of your home or job easily).
examples from the lessons: During his tenure as captain, the team won three cups. | The president's tenure lasted eight years. | Professors in the USA hope to get tenure. | Tenants with security of tenure cannot be evicted without good reason. | Land tenure was very unfair in the Middle Ages: lords owned most land. | Her tenure as mayor ended last year. | Our coach's tenure was short but successful.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal word. Pronounced "TEN-yer". Not related to "tender". In maths problems, if a tenure "lasted from 2010 to 2018", it was 8 years.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Terminally ill means having an illness that cannot be cured and will lead to death. 2) (informal, joking) Terminally means extremely or hopelessly: "He's terminally lazy." "terminally boring".
its sense in the lessons: In health and life lessons, and sometimes in family life, children may hear that a relative is terminally ill; hospices care for such people and help them be comfortable. The word is serious and should be used gently. The joking sense is used in everyday talk and reviews. Phrases: "terminally ill", "terminally boring", "terminally uncool".
examples from the lessons: Grandad was terminally ill, so he stayed in a hospice. | Nurses help terminally ill patients feel calm and free from pain. | The charity raises money for terminally ill children. | The film was terminally boring. (informal) | My uncle is terminally late for everything. (joking) | When she was terminally ill, her family visited every day. | Doctors told the family gently that he was terminally ill.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From "terminal" (the end). Be careful: the joking sense can sound unkind near people who are really ill. "Terminal" also means a station or airport building, or a computer screen and keyboard.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To terrify someone means to make them extremely frightened: "Thunder terrifies my dog." 2) "Terrified" (adjective) means very, very scared; "terrifying" means causing great fear.
its sense in the lessons: In stories the word makes fear strong and dramatic; it is a powerful choice instead of "scare". In everyday talk, children say they are "terrified of spiders" or "terrified of heights". In PSHE, it links to fears, phobias and how to cope. Phrases: "terrified of", "terrified to", "scared the life out of" (informal close phrase).
examples from the lessons: Thunder terrifies our puppy. | I'm terrified of spiders. | The roller coaster was terrifying but fun. | The ghost story terrified my little brother. | She was terrified to speak in front of the whole school. | The loud bang terrified the horses. | Don't let the dark terrify you; it's the same room with the lights off.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: y changes to i: terrifies, terrified; but keeps y in "terrifying". Order of strength: scared, frightened, terrified. "Terrific" looks similar but now means "great".

part of speech: adjective (Thai); noun (a Thai, Thais; Thai — the language)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Thai means from or about Thailand, a country in Southeast Asia whose capital is Bangkok. 2) A Thai is a person from Thailand. 3) Thai is the main language of Thailand, with its own alphabet and five tones that change the meaning of words.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons Thailand appears with monsoons, rice farming, Buddhist temples and elephants (its national animal). In food lessons Thai food is famous for green curry, pad thai noodles and the mix of sweet, sour, salty and spicy. Thailand was once called Siam. Phrases: "Thai food", "Thai boxing" (Muay Thai), "Thai New Year" (Songkran water festival).
examples from the lessons: We had Thai green curry for dinner. | Thai is a tonal language, like Chinese. | At Songkran, Thai people throw water at each other for New Year. | Muay Thai is also called Thai boxing. | Many Thai people are Buddhists. | The Thai alphabet has 44 consonants. | Our class learned to say hello in Thai: "sawasdee".
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced "TIE" (like "tie"); the h is silent. Always capital T. Homophones: Thai, tie, Tye. Thailand is in Southeast Asia, not to be confused with Taiwan.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Theatrical means about the theatre, plays and acting: a theatrical company, theatrical costumes. 2) Theatrical also means exaggerated and showy, as if acting for an audience: "He gave a theatrical sigh." 3) (noun) Amateur theatricals are plays put on by ordinary people, not professional actors.
its sense in the lessons: In drama lessons it appears with stage, costumes, lighting and props. In stories and everyday life it describes someone who makes a big show of their feelings ("Don't be so theatrical!"). Phrases: "theatrical performance", "theatrical gesture", "theatrical makeup".
examples from the lessons: The school put on a theatrical show at Christmas. | She bowed in a very theatrical way. | My brother gave a theatrical groan when Mum said "homework". | The theatrical costumes were stored in the hall. | Don't be so theatrical; it's only a small scratch. | The theatrical company toured the country with their play. | Theatrical makeup has to be bright so the audience can see it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb: theatrically. Spelling: theatre (UK) / theater (US), but "theatrical" is the same in both. The exaggerated sense is a bit critical.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A thimble is a small metal or plastic cap worn on the tip of your finger to protect it when you push a needle through cloth while sewing. 2) A thimble is also a tiny amount, as in "a thimbleful".
its sense in the lessons: In D and T and textiles lessons pupils use thimbles when hand-sewing. In stories and games, a thimble is a small treasure; in Monopoly it was a classic playing piece. In "Peter Pan", Wendy gives Peter a "thimble" when she means a kiss. Phrases: "a thimbleful of", "hunt the thimble" (an old party game).
examples from the lessons: Wear a thimble so the needle doesn't hurt your finger. | Grandma's silver thimble is very old. | I played as the thimble in Monopoly. | In Peter Pan, a kiss is called a thimble. | We played hunt the thimble at the party. | The doll drank from a cup no bigger than a thimble. | Add just a thimbleful of milk.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Ending -ble like "bubble", "tumble". A thimbleful is a very small measure, not an exact unit.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (old-fashioned, formal) Thither means "to that place" or "there": "He went thither on foot." 2) "Hither and thither" means here and there, in many directions: "The leaves blew hither and thither."
its sense in the lessons: It appears in old books, the Bible (King James Version), poems and fairy tales; it tells the reader the language is old or grand. In modern speech it survives mainly in "hither and thither". Paired old words: hither (to here), thither (to there), whither (to where?), hence, thence, whence (from here, there, where).
examples from the lessons: They journeyed thither by boat. (old style) | The children ran hither and thither across the field. | Ants scurried hither and thither. | "Go thither and bring me water," said the king. | In the old story, the knight rode thither to save the town. | The wind blew the paper hither and thither. | Whither goest thou? Thither, to the sea. (old poem style)
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced "THITH-er" with the soft "th" of "the". Do not use it in normal modern writing except in "hither and thither". It means "to there", not "at there".

meaning for a pupil: 1) Thrilling means very exciting and making you feel a strong, happy rush of excitement: a thrilling ride, a thrilling match. 2) (verb form) Thrilling is also the -ing form of "thrill": "The magician was thrilling the crowd."
its sense in the lessons: In stories, reviews and book blurbs it tells the reader the action is full of excitement and suspense. In everyday life it is used for rides, sports and adventures. Phrases: "a thrilling finish", "thrilling adventure", "thrilling to watch".
examples from the lessons: The match had a thrilling finish in the last minute. | The roller coaster was thrilling. | This thrilling adventure story kept me reading all night. | It was thrilling to see a real whale. | The magician was thrilling the crowd with his tricks. | Scoring my first goal was thrilling. | The film has a thrilling chase through the city.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Related: thrill (noun and verb), thrilled (feeling very pleased: "I'm thrilled with my present"), thriller (an exciting crime or spy story). Thrilling describes the thing; thrilled describes the person.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Throwaway things are made to be used once or for a short time and then thrown away: throwaway cups, throwaway razors. 2) A throwaway remark or line is said quickly and casually, without much thought, though it may matter. 3) "Throwaway culture" or "throwaway society" means people buying cheap things and throwing them away too fast, which wastes resources and makes pollution. 4) (noun) A throwaway is something thrown away or treated as unimportant.
its sense in the lessons: In science, geography and citizenship lessons it appears with waste, plastics, recycling and climate change: reduce, reuse, recycle. In English lessons a throwaway line in a story might be a clue. Phrases: "throwaway plastic", "throwaway comment", "throwaway society", "throwaway fashion".
examples from the lessons: Throwaway plastic cups fill up rubbish dumps. | Our school is trying to stop using throwaway bottles. | It was just a throwaway comment, but it hurt her feelings. | The detective noticed a throwaway line that was actually a clue. | We live in a throwaway society. | Throwaway fashion means clothes are worn a few times and binned. | Bring a reusable bag instead of a throwaway one.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word when it comes before a noun (a throwaway cup); two words as a verb: "throw away the rubbish". Close words: disposable, single-use.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The tibia is the shinbone, the bigger and stronger of the two bones in your lower leg, between your knee and your ankle. 2) In insects, the tibia is one of the sections of the leg.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about the human skeleton, the tibia is named with the femur (thigh bone), fibula (thin bone beside the tibia) and patella (kneecap). It carries most of the body's weight in the lower leg. Football players wear shin pads to protect it. Phrases: "broken tibia", "tibia and fibula".
examples from the lessons: The tibia is the second longest bone in the body. | He broke his tibia playing rugby. | Shin pads protect your tibia during football. | The fibula is thinner than the tibia. | You can feel your tibia at the front of your leg. | The tibia joins the femur at the knee. | Grasshoppers have long, strong tibias for jumping.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: tibias (common) or tibiae (scientific Latin). Pronounced "TIB-ee-uh". Everyday word: shinbone. The longest bone is the femur, not the tibia.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A tickler is a person or thing that tickles. 2) (informal) A brain tickler or brain-teaser is a fun puzzle that makes you think. 3) (informal) A tickler can also be something that makes you laugh or a little problem that bothers you, like a "tickle" in your throat. 4) (old, US) A tickler file is a reminder system of notes about things to do on certain days.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and puzzle books, "brain ticklers" are riddles and logic problems. In family play, the "tickle monster" chases children. Phrases: "brain tickler", "rib tickler" (a very funny joke), "tickler file".
examples from the lessons: Grandpa is the best tickler in the family. | Here's a brain tickler: what has keys but can't open locks? | That joke was a real rib tickler. | The feather was a perfect tickler. | Our maths teacher gives us a tickler at the start of each lesson. | The baby giggled at the tickler. | Write it in your tickler file so you don't forget. (old)
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Informal word. "Rib-tickler" is usually written with a hyphen.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Tidily means in a neat and orderly way, with everything in its proper place: "Fold your clothes tidily." 2) (informal, UK) Tidily can also mean nicely and well enough: "The plan worked out tidily."
its sense in the lessons: In school, teachers ask pupils to write tidily, set out maths working tidily and put equipment away tidily. In everyday life it is about rooms, drawers and clothes. Neat setting-out in maths helps avoid mistakes. Phrases: "tidily arranged", "tidily dressed", "put away tidily".
examples from the lessons: Please write tidily so I can read it. | The books were tidily arranged on the shelf. | He folded his PE kit tidily. | Set out your sums tidily in columns. | The cat sat tidily with its tail around its paws. | The shoes were lined up tidily by the door. | Everything fitted tidily into the box.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: tidy + ly, y changes to i: tidily. Opposite: messily, untidily. Adjective: tidy; noun: tidiness.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Tightness is being tight: fitting very closely, being firmly fixed, or being pulled hard: the tightness of my shoes, the tightness of a rope. 2) Tightness in your body is a feeling of being squeezed or stiff: tightness in the chest, in the muscles. 3) Tightness can also mean being close and loyal, as a group: the tightness of a team. 4) Tightness of money means there is very little to spare.
its sense in the lessons: In PE and health lessons, stretching helps muscle tightness. Safety: sudden chest tightness, especially with pain or trouble breathing, needs an adult and maybe emergency help; in asthma, chest tightness is a warning sign to use an inhaler. In stories it describes worry: "a tightness in her throat". Phrases: "chest tightness", "muscle tightness", "tightness of money".
examples from the lessons: The tightness of my new shoes gave me blisters. | Stretching before the race helped the tightness in my legs. | Tell an adult if you feel tightness in your chest. | My asthma makes my chest feel tight; the tightness goes after my inhaler. | Check the tightness of the bike's bolts before you ride. | She felt a tightness in her throat before she cried. | The team's tightness helped them win.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Formed from tight + ness. Adverb: tightly. "Tight" can also be informal UK slang for mean with money (stingy).

part of speech: noun (timpani — plural; one drum is a timpano, rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Timpani are large, round, bowl-shaped drums made of copper with skin or plastic stretched over the top, played with soft-headed sticks in an orchestra; they are also called kettledrums. Unlike most drums, each one can be tuned to play a particular note.
its sense in the lessons: In music lessons pupils learn timpani are in the percussion section at the back of the orchestra; the player (timpanist) uses pedals to change the pitch. They make rolls like thunder and dramatic booming beats, for example in "Also sprach Zarathustra" and many symphonies. Phrases: "timpani roll", "play the timpani".
examples from the lessons: The timpani boomed like thunder at the end of the piece. | The timpanist tuned the drums with foot pedals. | Timpani are also called kettledrums. | An orchestra usually has two to five timpani. | The timpani roll made the music feel scary. | Each timpano can play a different note. | We saw the timpani at the back of the orchestra.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural word from Italian; it takes a plural verb: "The timpani are loud." One drum: "a timpano" (rare) or "one of the timpani". Sometimes spelled "tympani". Pronounced "TIM-puh-nee".

meaning for a pupil: 1) A tine is one of the pointed prongs of a fork, rake or garden fork. 2) A tine is also one of the pointed branches of a deer's antler.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life it is the "spike" part of a fork. In nature lessons, the number of tines on a stag's antlers can show its age and health roughly. In D and T, a tine is a sharp point on a tool. Phrases: "the tines of a fork", "antler tines".
examples from the lessons: One tine of my fork is bent. | A garden fork has four strong tines. | The stag's antlers had twelve tines. | Push the tines of the rake through the leaves. | Be careful: the tines of a pitchfork are sharp. | The fork's tines left lines in the mashed potato. | Count the tines to see how many points the antlers have.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a tine, tines. Do not confuse with "tin" or "tine" in "tinny". In maths problems, if a fork has 4 tines, 6 forks have 24 tines.

part of speech: noun (a toboggan, toboggans); verb (toboggan, toboggans, tobogganed, tobogganing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A toboggan is a long, narrow sledge without runners, with a curled-up front, used for sliding down snowy hills; in everyday use it is often any sledge or sled. 2) (verb) To toboggan means to slide down a snowy hill on a toboggan. 3) (Canada, some US areas, informal) A toboggan can also mean a knitted woolly hat (a tuque or beanie) in parts of the southern USA.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday winter life in Canada, the USA, the UK and Ireland, children toboggan on snow days. The toboggan came from the Indigenous peoples of Canada, and the word comes from the Mi'kmaq/Algonquian languages. Safety: go feet first, choose a slope away from roads, trees and ponds, and wear a helmet if you can. Phrases: "toboggan run", "toboggan hill", "go tobogganing".
examples from the lessons: We took the toboggan to the big hill. | Four of us fitted on the long toboggan. | They tobogganed down the slope screaming with joy. | The toboggan run was icy and fast. | Indigenous peoples in Canada used toboggans to carry loads over snow. | Stay away from the road with your toboggan. | In Tennessee, my cousin calls his woolly hat a toboggan.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun; verb is regular: tobogganed. Spelling: one b, two g's, double n in "tobogganing". In the UK people mostly say "sledge", in the USA "sled", in Canada "toboggan".

part of speech: noun (tobogganing — uncountable); verb form (-ing of toboggan)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Tobogganing is the activity of sliding down snowy hills on a toboggan or sledge. 2) (sport) Tobogganing is also a winter sport of racing down icy tracks, related to luge and bobsleigh.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday winter life children "go tobogganing" on snow days. In PE and the Winter Olympics, luge, skeleton and bobsleigh are racing kinds of tobogganing. Safety rules: feet first, one person at a time on small hills, avoid roads, trees, fences and frozen ponds, wear warm clothes and a helmet. Phrases: "go tobogganing", "tobogganing hill", "tobogganing accident".
examples from the lessons: We went tobogganing after school when it snowed. | Tobogganing is my favourite winter activity. | The park banned tobogganing on the steep hill near the road. | After tobogganing, we drank hot chocolate. | Luge is a fast kind of tobogganing. | Wear a helmet when you go tobogganing. | We were tobogganing until it got dark.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Spelling: tobogganing (one b, two g's, two n's). UK people often say "sledging", US "sledding".

part of speech: noun (a toggle, toggles); verb (toggle, toggles, toggled, toggling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A toggle is a short piece of wood, plastic or metal used like a button: it is pushed through a loop to fasten a coat or bag, as on a duffel coat. 2) (computing) A toggle is a switch or button that turns something on or off, one press changing it each time. 3) (verb) To toggle means to switch between two states or options, like on and off: "Toggle between the two windows." 4) A toggle is also the sliding stopper on a drawstring.
its sense in the lessons: In computing lessons, toggles switch settings (Wi-Fi, dark mode, caps lock). In everyday life, duffel coats and Scout neckerchiefs (woggles) use toggles. In science and D and T, a toggle switch is a lever switch in circuits. Phrases: "toggle switch", "toggle on", "toggle off", "toggle between".
examples from the lessons: My duffel coat has wooden toggles instead of buttons. | Tap the toggle to turn on dark mode. | Press the key to toggle between capital and small letters. | The toggle switch on the lamp clicked on. | Pull the toggle to tighten the hood. | You can toggle the sound on and off. | We used a toggle switch in our circuit project.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: toggled, toggling. A toggle always has two states; pressing it again undoes it. A Scout's "woggle" is a different word.

part of speech: noun (a ton, tons; tons of); plural of ton; adverb (informal: tons better)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) Tons, or "tons of", means a lot, a great amount: "I've got tons of homework." 2) Tons is the plural of ton, a unit of weight: in the USA a (short) ton is 2,000 pounds (about 907 kg); in the UK an old (long) ton is 2,240 pounds (about 1,016 kg). 3) A metric ton, usually spelled "tonne", is 1,000 kilograms. 4) (informal) "Tons" can mean much: "She's tons better at chess than me." 5) (UK, informal) "A ton" is also 100: "doing a ton" means 100 miles per hour, and in cricket a ton is a century (100 runs).
its sense in the lessons: In maths and science lessons tons and tonnes measure very heavy things: lorries, ships, whales and elephants. In everyday talk children say "tons of" all the time. Safety signs on bridges show maximum weight in tons/tonnes (with "t" as the symbol). Phrases: "tons of", "weigh a ton", "like a ton of bricks" (very hard).
examples from the lessons: I've got tons of homework tonight. | An elephant can weigh about 6 tons. | The bridge sign says lorries over 7.5 tonnes cannot cross. | My bag weighs a ton! (informal) | There were tons of people at the fair. | A blue whale weighs over 100 tons. | I feel tons better after a sleep. | He scored a ton in the cricket match, 100 runs.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: ton (US 2,000 lb, UK 2,240 lb) and tonne (1,000 kg) are different; in maths problems use the unit given, and "metric ton" means tonne. 1 tonne = 1,000 kg, so 3 tonnes = 3,000 kg. "Tons of" with uncountable or plural nouns is informal: in exam writing use "a lot of" or "many". Do not confuse ton with "tun" (a large barrel).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Toothless means having no teeth, or having lost teeth: a toothless baby, a toothless grin. 2) Toothless also means having no real power to make people obey: a toothless law, a toothless rule that no one enforces.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life babies and some old people are toothless, and children have gappy, toothless grins when baby teeth fall out. In news and citizenship lessons, a "toothless" rule, watchdog or body has no power to punish. In "How to Train Your Dragon", Toothless is the name of the dragon (he can pull in his teeth). Phrases: "toothless grin", "toothless law", "toothless watchdog".
examples from the lessons: The baby gave us a big toothless smile. | After losing two front teeth, my brother had a toothless grin. | Grandpa takes out his false teeth and looks toothless. | Without fines, the new rule is toothless. | Critics called the committee a toothless watchdog. | In the film, Toothless is a black Night Fury dragon. | Some whales are toothless and filter food instead.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formed from tooth + less ("without"). A law with "teeth" is one that can punish; a toothless law cannot. As a name (Toothless the dragon) it has a capital T.

part of speech: noun (a topping, toppings); adjective (topping — old UK slang); verb form (-ing of top)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A topping is food put on top of another food: pizza toppings, an ice-cream topping, a crumble topping. 2) (old-fashioned UK slang) Topping means excellent, splendid: "What a topping idea!" (now mostly used jokingly, like in old school stories). 3) (verb form) Topping is the -ing form of "top", as in "topping up" (filling up again) or "topping the charts" (being number one). 4) (old UK slang) "Topping" someone meant killing them; it is old crime-story language.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and food lessons, children choose toppings for pizza, pancakes and desserts. In maths, toppings are used in counting and combination problems ("How many pizzas with 2 of 5 toppings?"). In old children's books, posh schoolchildren say "topping!". Phrases: "pizza topping", "top up" (topping up a phone or a drink), "topping the league".
examples from the lessons: My favourite pizza topping is pineapple. | We had pancakes with chocolate topping. | The crumble topping was golden and crunchy. | "What a topping day!" said the boy in the old story. | Mum is topping up my phone credit. | Our team is topping the league this year. | If a pizza can have 3 toppings from 6 choices, there are 20 different pizzas.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a topping, toppings. The "excellent" sense is old-fashioned UK slang, like "spiffing". In maths problems, toppings are classic for counting combinations: order does not matter when choosing toppings.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Torpor is a state of being very sleepy, slow and inactive, without energy: "The heat filled us with torpor." 2) (science) In animals, torpor is a short sleep-like state when body temperature and heartbeat drop to save energy, for example in hummingbirds at night, bats and some mice; long-lasting torpor in winter is called hibernation.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons it comes with adaptations and survival in cold or lack of food. In stories and formal writing, torpor describes a lazy, heavy mood on a hot afternoon or after a big meal. Phrases: "fall into torpor", "summer torpor", "a state of torpor".
examples from the lessons: Hummingbirds go into torpor at night to save energy. | After the huge Christmas lunch, the whole family sank into torpor. | Bats can enter torpor on cold days. | The heat of the afternoon filled the classroom with torpor. | Hibernation is a long kind of torpor. | The dog lay in a happy torpor by the fire. | The sudden noise shook him out of his torpor.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable, formal. Adjective: torpid. Pronounced "TOR-per". Torpor lasts hours or days; hibernation lasts weeks or months.

part of speech: noun (tortoiseshell — uncountable; a tortoiseshell, tortoiseshells); adjective (tortoiseshell)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Tortoiseshell is the hard, brown-and-yellow mottled shell material that comes from the hawksbill sea turtle (not from tortoises), once used for combs, glasses frames and jewellery; trading it is now banned to protect the turtles. 2) Tortoiseshell also means a pattern or plastic copying that mottled brown and amber look: tortoiseshell glasses. 3) A tortoiseshell is a cat with a coat patterned in black and orange (ginger) patches; almost all of them are female. 4) A tortoiseshell is also a butterfly, the small tortoiseshell, with orange, black and yellow wings.
its sense in the lessons: In science and citizenship lessons it comes up with endangered animals and the CITES ban on trading hawksbill shell. In nature lessons the small tortoiseshell butterfly is a common British garden butterfly. In everyday life, "tortie" cats and tortoiseshell-style glasses. Phrases: "tortoiseshell cat", "tortoiseshell frames", "small tortoiseshell".
examples from the lessons: My cat is a tortoiseshell with black and ginger patches. | Almost all tortoiseshell cats are female. | Dad's glasses have tortoiseshell frames, but they are plastic. | Real tortoiseshell came from hawksbill turtles, which are now endangered. | A small tortoiseshell butterfly landed on the buddleia. | The old hairbrush in the museum was made of tortoiseshell. | Selling real tortoiseshell is banned in most countries.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word. Despite the name, it comes from sea turtles, not land tortoises. Informal name for the cat: "tortie". The cat being nearly always female is due to genes on the X chromosome.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Townsfolk are the people who live in a particular town, or town people in general as opposed to country people.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, fairy tales and history, "the townsfolk" are the ordinary people of a town who gather, gossip, celebrate or are afraid, as in "The Pied Piper of Hamelin". It sounds a little old-fashioned and storybook-like; in news, "townspeople" or "residents" are more common. Phrases: "the local townsfolk", "the townsfolk gathered".
examples from the lessons: The townsfolk gathered in the square to hear the news. | The Pied Piper led the rats away, but the townsfolk did not pay him. | The townsfolk cheered when the knight returned. | All the townsfolk came to the summer fair. | The townsfolk were afraid of the dragon on the hill. | The mayor asked the townsfolk to help clean the river. | In the past, townsfolk and country folk lived very different lives.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural noun with a plural verb: "The townsfolk were happy." There is no "a townsfolk"; for one person say "a townsperson" or "someone from the town". Also "townspeople". "Folk" means people.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A transaction is an act of buying or selling something, or of moving money, such as paying in a shop, withdrawing cash or sending money online. 2) (formal) A transaction is any piece of business or exchange between people or organisations. 3) (computing) A transaction is a set of computer actions that must all happen together or not at all, as in banking systems.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and money lessons, transactions appear in problems with prices, change, bank statements, credits and debits. In everyday life, card payments, receipts and bank apps show transactions. In online safety, check your transactions and never share bank details. Phrases: "make a transaction", "cash transaction", "online transaction", "transaction fee".
examples from the lessons: Every transaction is printed on the receipt. | The bank statement lists all our transactions for the month. | The shop charges a small transaction fee for card payments. | Buying a house is a big transaction. | The transaction was declined because there wasn't enough money. | If you start with £20 and make transactions of −£5, +£12 and −£8, you end with £19. | Online transactions must be kept safe and secret.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Verb: transact (formal); adjective: transactional. In maths, a transaction usually changes a balance: money in is added (credit), money out is subtracted (debit).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Transmissible means able to be passed from one person, animal or thing to another, especially a disease: "Measles is very transmissible." 2) (formal) Transmissible can also describe other things that can be passed on, such as traits from parents to children or signals.
its sense in the lessons: In science and health lessons it comes up with germs, infections, vaccines and hygiene: washing hands, covering coughs and vaccinations reduce how many people catch a transmissible disease. In news it was used a lot during Covid-19 about new variants. Phrases: "highly transmissible", "more transmissible", "transmissible disease".
examples from the lessons: Chickenpox is highly transmissible among children. | The new variant was more transmissible than the old one. | Colds are transmissible through coughs and sneezes. | Washing your hands helps stop transmissible germs. | Not all diseases are transmissible; diabetes cannot be caught. | Some plant diseases are transmissible by insects. | Doctors want to know how transmissible a virus is.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling ends in -ible. Close words: infectious, contagious, catching. "Transmissible" is a more scientific word. Related noun: transmission; verb: transmit.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To transmute means to change something completely into something different, in form or nature: "The caterpillar is transmuted into a butterfly." 2) (history, science) In alchemy, to transmute meant to turn one metal into another, especially lead into gold; in modern science, nuclear reactions can really change one element into another (transmutation).
its sense in the lessons: In history and science lessons alchemists in the Middle Ages tried to transmute base metals into gold, and their experiments helped start chemistry. In physics, radioactive decay transmutes elements. In stories and formal writing, feelings or situations "are transmuted". Phrases: "transmute into", "transmute lead into gold".
examples from the lessons: Alchemists tried to transmute lead into gold. | Radioactive uranium slowly transmutes into lead. | The artist transmuted her sadness into a beautiful song. | In the myth, the king's touch transmuted everything to gold. | Scientists can transmute one element into another in a nuclear reactor. | Hard work transmuted the empty field into a garden. | The witch transmuted the frog into a prince.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal word; simpler: transform, change. Regular verb: transmuted. Noun: transmutation. Ordinary chemical reactions do not transmute elements; only nuclear reactions do.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Transparency is being see-through, letting light pass so you can see clearly through, like glass or clean water. 2) Transparency means being open and honest so that people can see what is happening and why: transparency in government or in a company. 3) (old) A transparency is a clear plastic sheet with words or pictures on it, shown with an overhead projector, or a photographic slide.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons pupils sort materials as transparent (glass), translucent (tracing paper) and opaque (wood). In citizenship and news, transparency means leaders explain decisions and spending openly, which helps trust. In computing and AI, transparency means you can see how a decision was made. Phrases: "transparency of glass", "lack of transparency", "for transparency".
examples from the lessons: We tested the transparency of different materials with a torch. | Clean water has great transparency. | Voters want transparency about how taxes are spent. | The club showed transparency by sharing its accounts. | The teacher put a transparency on the old overhead projector. | Transparency means people can check a decision is fair. | Ice loses its transparency when it has lots of air bubbles.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: transparencies (for the plastic sheets). Adjective: transparent; adverb: transparently. Transparent (clear) is different from translucent (light passes but you cannot see clearly).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Transversely means across, lying or moving from side to side, at a right angle to the length of something: "Cut the carrot transversely into rounds."
its sense in the lessons: In science and maths it describes cutting or placing something crosswise, for example a transverse section (cross-section) of a stem in biology, or transverse waves in physics (light and water waves, which wiggle up and down at right angles to the direction they travel). In cooking, slicing across. Phrases: "cut transversely", "placed transversely", "transverse wave".
examples from the lessons: Cut the stem transversely to see the tubes inside. | The beams were laid transversely across the bridge. | In a transverse wave, the particles move transversely to the wave's direction. | Slice the cucumber transversely into circles. | The engine is mounted transversely in many small cars. | The scientist cut the bone transversely and looked at it under the microscope. | The stripes run transversely across the flag.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal or technical; simpler: across, crosswise. Opposite: longitudinally (along the length). Adjective: transverse. In maths, "at right angles" means 90 degrees.

part of speech: noun (travail, travails); verb (travail, travails, travailed, travailing — old)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal, old) Travail is very hard, tiring work or effort. 2) Travails (plural) are difficulties and troubles someone goes through: "the travails of moving house". 3) (old, Bible) Travail can mean the pain and effort of giving birth: "a woman in travail".
its sense in the lessons: It appears in formal writing, old books and the King James Bible, and sometimes in news or humour about troubles ("the travails of the England team"). In French, "travail" is the ordinary word for "work", which is a false-friend trap. Phrases: "the travails of", "years of travail", "in travail" (old, giving birth).
examples from the lessons: After years of travail, they finished the cathedral. | The book describes the travails of a family crossing the ocean. | The team's travails continued with another defeat. | In the Bible, the woman was in travail before her child was born. | The farmers travailed in the fields from dawn to dusk. (old) | We laughed about the travails of our camping trip. | The travails of the journey made them tired but proud.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal and old-fashioned. Pronounced "TRAV-ail" (rhymes with "gravel" plus "ale", stress on first syllable, often "truh-VAIL"). False friend: French "travail" just means "work" or "job". Do not confuse with "travel", though both come from the same old word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A trebuchet is a huge medieval siege machine like a giant catapult that throws heavy stones over castle walls, powered by a heavy counterweight that falls and swings a long arm with a sling.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons trebuchets appear with castles and sieges in the Middle Ages, for example Edward I's huge trebuchet "Warwolf" at Stirling Castle in 1304. In science and D and T lessons pupils build small model trebuchets to learn about levers, forces, energy (gravitational potential energy turning into movement) and projectiles. Phrases: "build a trebuchet", "counterweight trebuchet", "model trebuchet".
