examples from the lessons: The trebuchet hurled a huge stone at the castle wall. | We built a model trebuchet out of lolly sticks in D and T. | A trebuchet uses a heavy counterweight, not a twisted rope. | Edward I used a giant trebuchet called Warwolf. | The trebuchet's long arm acts like a lever. | Our trebuchet threw a marshmallow three metres. | Trebuchets could throw stones weighing as much as a person.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced "TREB-yoo-shet" (UK) or "treb-uh-SHAY" (from French). Spelling: trebuchet. It is not the same as a catapult or mangonel, which use twisted ropes or tension; a trebuchet uses a falling weight. In maths and science, a heavier counterweight or longer arm throws further.

part of speech: noun (triage — uncountable); verb (triage, triages, triaged, triaging)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Triage is deciding the order in which sick or injured people are treated, based on who needs help most urgently, as in a hospital emergency department or after a disaster. 2) (general) Triage means sorting any problems or jobs into order of importance so the most urgent are dealt with first. 3) (verb) To triage means to sort patients or jobs in this way.
its sense in the lessons: In health and first-aid lessons, triage explains why, in A and E, a badly hurt person is seen before someone who arrived earlier with a small cut: it is fair because it is about need. In everyday and work life, teachers, IT helpers and parents also "triage" jobs. Phrases: "triage nurse", "in triage", "triage system".
examples from the lessons: At A and E, a triage nurse checked how ill I was. | Triage means the most urgent patients are seen first. | After the earthquake, doctors set up triage tents. | Someone with a broken leg may wait while a heart attack patient is treated; that's triage. | The help desk triaged all the computer problems. | Mum triaged the chores: dinner first, washing later. | The paramedics did triage at the scene of the crash.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable noun; verb is regular: triaged. From French "trier" (to sort). Pronounced "TREE-ahzh". Being seen later in triage does not mean you are not important; it means others are in more danger.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Trickery is using tricks to deceive or cheat people, making them believe something false: "He won the game by trickery." 2) Trickery can also mean clever illusions, as in magic shows or special effects, that fool the eye on purpose for fun.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and fables, sly characters like the fox or Anansi use trickery; the word often tells the reader someone is dishonest. In online safety lessons, scammers use trickery such as fake messages and spoofed websites. In magic and film, "camera trickery" and "visual trickery" are fun illusions. Phrases: "by trickery", "camera trickery", "a bit of trickery", "trickery and deceit".
examples from the lessons: The fox got the cheese by trickery. | Scammers use trickery to get people's passwords. | The magician's trickery amazed the audience. | The film used clever camera trickery to make the giant look huge. | Winning by trickery is not really winning. | Anansi the spider is famous for trickery in West African stories. | The ref spotted the player's trickery and gave a yellow card.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: no plural. Related: trick (noun/verb), tricky (hard or sly), trickster (a person who tricks). Close words: deceit, deception, cunning.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A trireme was a long, fast wooden warship of ancient Greece, Phoenicia and Rome, rowed by about 170 men sitting in three rows, one above another. 2) It had a bronze ram at the front for smashing into enemy ships, and a sail for when the wind was good.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons on ancient Greece and Rome, the trireme comes up with the Battle of Salamis (480 BC), when Athenian triremes beat the much bigger Persian fleet; it tells the reader about sea power, teamwork and rowing. «Tri-» means three (as in triangle, tricycle) and «-reme» comes from the Latin for oar, so the word itself says «three rows of oars». Phrases: «a fleet of triremes», «rowers in a trireme», «ramming speed».
examples from the lessons: The Athenians built two hundred triremes to fight the Persians. | A trireme needed about 170 rowers working together. | The trireme's bronze ram could punch a hole in an enemy ship. | In our history book there is a drawing of a trireme with three rows of oars. | The rowers in a trireme had to keep time to the beat of a flute. | A model trireme stands in the museum near the Greek vases. | We made a trireme out of cardboard and lollipop sticks for our project.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: triremes. Countable. It is a history word: there are no triremes today, except a modern copy called the Olympias, built in Greece in the 1980s. Myth: rowers were usually paid free citizens in Athens, not chained slaves as in films. Do not confuse «trireme» with «bireme» (two rows of oars). In maths problems, «three rows» and about 170 rowers are the useful numbers.

part of speech: adjective (Trojan); noun (a Trojan, Trojans; a trojan, trojans — computer)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Trojan means from Troy, the ancient city in what is now Turkey; a Trojan is a person from Troy. 2) The Trojan Horse is the story of a huge wooden horse the Greeks left outside Troy; soldiers were hiding inside it, and at night they came out and took the city. 3) (computers) A trojan is a harmful program that pretends to be something useful, like a game or a free app, so that you let it into your computer. 4) (UK, old-fashioned) «To work like a Trojan» means to work very hard.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and history lessons (Greek myths, the Iliad, the Trojan War) the word tells the reader about Troy and its war with the Greeks. In computing and online safety lessons, a «trojan» or «Trojan horse» warns pupils not to download unknown files: something that looks like a gift may hide danger. Phrases: «the Trojan War», «the Trojan Horse», «a Trojan horse» (any trick that gets an enemy inside), «work like a Trojan».
examples from the lessons: The Trojans pulled the giant wooden horse into their city. | The Trojan War lasted ten years, says the old story. | Hector was the bravest of the Trojans. | My brother's laptop got a trojan from a fake game download. | The free app was really a trojan that stole passwords. | Never open a file from a stranger — it could be a trojan. | The new rule was a Trojan horse: it looked kind but hid a nasty surprise. | Mum worked like a Trojan to get the garden ready.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Write «Trojan» with a capital letter when it means Troy or its people; the computer word is often written in small letters, «a trojan». Countable: a Trojan, Trojans. The Trojan Horse is a story from Greek myth and poems; historians are not sure it really happened. «Beware of Greeks bearing gifts» comes from this story. A trojan is not exactly a virus: a virus copies itself, a trojan tricks you into letting it in.

part of speech: noun (a trumpetfish; plural trumpetfish or trumpetfishes)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A trumpetfish is a long, thin fish with a tube-shaped snout like a trumpet, which lives on warm coral reefs. 2) It often hangs head-down among sea plants or hides behind bigger fish to sneak up on small fish and shrimps, which it sucks into its snout.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on oceans, coral reefs and animal adaptations, the trumpetfish shows camouflage and hunting by hiding. In nature books and documentaries it tells the reader about a clever, sneaky reef hunter. Phrases: «a trumpetfish hiding», «head-down among the corals», «shadowing a bigger fish».
examples from the lessons: A trumpetfish floated upright among the sea fans, looking just like one of them. | The trumpetfish sucked up a tiny fish in a flash. | Divers in the Caribbean often see trumpetfish on the reef. | The trumpetfish hid behind a big parrotfish to get close to its prey. | Its snout is shaped like the end of a trumpet. | We drew a trumpetfish for our coral reef poster. | Some trumpetfish are yellow, others brown or blue.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word: trumpetfish. Plural: usually «trumpetfish» for many fish (like «fish»), «trumpetfishes» for different kinds. Countable. It does not make any trumpet sound; the name comes from its shape. Do not confuse it with a cornetfish or a pipefish, which are relatives with similar long bodies.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Tubular means shaped like a tube: long, round and hollow, like a pipe or a drinking straw. 2) Tubular also means made of tubes, like a tubular steel chair frame. 3) (slang, old-fashioned, US) Tubular meant great or cool, in surfer talk of the 1980s.
its sense in the lessons: In science and technology lessons, «tubular» describes shapes and structures: tubular bones, tubular flowers, tubular steel in bikes and bridges; hollow tubes are strong but light. In music, «tubular bells» are long metal tubes you hit. In stories it is a describing word for shape. Phrases: «tubular steel», «tubular bells», «tubular frame».
examples from the lessons: Bike frames are often made of tubular steel or aluminium. | The flower has tubular petals, so only bees with long tongues can reach the nectar. | The school chairs have tubular metal legs. | The orchestra played the tubular bells at the end of the piece. | A drinking straw is a tubular shape. | Worms have long tubular bodies. | (slang) «That wave was totally tubular, dude!» said the surfer in the old film.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective only. Stress on «TU»: TOO-byoo-lur. It comes from «tube». The slang meaning is old and jokey; today most people say «cool» or «awesome». A tubular thing is hollow; a solid round bar is a rod or cylinder, not a tube.

part of speech: noun (tuff — uncountable); adjective (slang, tuff — spelling of «tough»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Tuff is a light, rough rock made from volcanic ash that has been pressed and stuck together over time. 2) (slang) «Tuff» is a playful spelling of «tough», used online and by young people to mean cool, impressive or hard: «that's tuff».
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography lessons on rocks and volcanoes, tuff is a kind of igneous rock made from ash; it tells the reader that a volcano once erupted nearby. Ancient Romans and the people of Easter Island carved and built with tuff because it is soft enough to cut. In slang, «tuff» appears in chats and on social media.
examples from the lessons: Tuff forms when volcanic ash settles and hardens into rock. | The famous Easter Island statues are carved from tuff. | Our rock kit has a piece of pale, crumbly tuff. | Some old houses in Italy are built of tuff blocks. | The guide said the cliff was made of tuff from an eruption long ago. | (slang) «Your new trainers are tuff!» | (slang) «That level was tuff, I nearly gave up.»
note for the reader of a maths problem: Rock sense: uncountable, «some tuff», «a block of tuff». Sounds exactly like «tough» (homophones) — in a science text, «tuff» is rock; in an ordinary text, the hard-or-strong word is spelt «tough». Do not confuse tuff with «tufa», a different soft rock made in water. The slang spelling is not used in school writing.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Tusked means having tusks: long, pointed teeth that stick out of the mouth, like those of an elephant, walrus, wild boar or narwhal.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons and nature books, «tusked» describes animals; tusks are used for digging, fighting, lifting and showing off. In stories and fantasy, tusked monsters and beasts sound fierce. Phrases: «a tusked boar», «tusked mammals», «long-tusked».
examples from the lessons: The tusked walrus pulled itself onto the ice. | A tusked wild boar burst out of the bushes. | Mammoths were huge tusked animals of the Ice Age. | The narwhal is a tusked whale with one long spiral tooth. | In the story, the tusked troll guarded the bridge. | Elephants are the best-known tusked animals.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective made from the noun «tusk» + «-ed». One syllable: «tuskt». Not all elephants are tusked: many female Asian elephants have no tusks. Tusks are teeth, not horns.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A tutu is a short, stiff, frilly skirt that sticks out, worn by ballet dancers. 2) A tutu is also any light, puffy, net skirt that children wear for dressing up.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, PE and dance lessons, the tutu shows ballet: girls and sometimes boys dancing «Swan Lake» or «The Nutcracker». In everyday life it appears at dance shows, fancy-dress parties and fun runs, where people wear tutus as a joke. Phrases: «a pink tutu», «ballet shoes and a tutu», «in a tutu».
examples from the lessons: She wore a white tutu for the ballet show. | My little sister put on her sparkly tutu and twirled round the kitchen. | The dancers' tutus stuck out like plates. | For the charity fun run, Dad wore a pink tutu. | The tutu is made of many layers of stiff net. | In «Swan Lake» the swans dance in white tutus.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: tutus. Countable. The word is French. Say «TOO-too». Do not confuse with «Tutu» as a surname, as in Archbishop Desmond Tutu of South Africa (a name).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A typeface is a design for a set of letters, numbers and signs, used in printing and on computers, such as Times New Roman, Arial or Comic Sans. 2) It is the style or look of the letters: plain or fancy, thick or thin, with little feet (serifs) or without.
its sense in the lessons: In computing lessons and when making posters or slides, pupils choose a typeface; a clear typeface makes text easy to read. In history lessons on printing it links to Gutenberg's movable type. In everyday life, typefaces are on signs, books, sweets packets and road signs. Phrases: «choose a typeface», «a bold typeface», «a serif typeface», «a sans-serif typeface».
examples from the lessons: Our teacher asked us to use a clear typeface for the poster. | Arial is a typeface without serifs. | The old book was printed in a beautiful typeface. | Road signs in Britain use a special typeface called Transport. | I changed the typeface on my story to make the title look spooky. | Some typefaces are easier to read for people with dyslexia. | Comic Sans is a typeface many people love and many people dislike.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a typeface, typefaces. People often say «font» for typeface; strictly, a typeface is the design (Arial) and a font is one size and style of it (Arial bold 12), but in everyday talk they mean the same. One word: typeface.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A typewriter is a machine for writing: you press keys and small metal letters hit an inked ribbon, printing letters straight onto paper. 2) It was used in offices and homes before computers became common.
its sense in the lessons: In history and computing lessons, the typewriter shows how writing machines led to the computer keyboard; the QWERTY layout comes from typewriters. In stories, a typewriter suggests an old-fashioned writer or office, with clacking keys and a bell at the end of a line. Phrases: «type on a typewriter», «an old typewriter», «typewriter ribbon».
examples from the lessons: Grandad wrote his letters on a typewriter. | The typewriter went clack-clack-clack and then ding! | Our computer keyboard has the same QWERTY letters as an old typewriter. | You could not delete a mistake on a typewriter, so people used white correction fluid. | The museum lets children try typing on a real typewriter. | The writer in the film sat at a typewriter all night.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a typewriter, typewriters. One word. The verb is «type» (typed, typing); a person who types is a «typist». «Typewriter» is a long English word you can type using only the top row of letters on the keyboard — a fun fact.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Typically means usually; in the way that something normally happens: «It typically rains in April.» 2) Typically means in a way that is very like a certain person or thing: «a typically British breakfast». 3) It can also mean «as you would expect» about something annoying: «Typically, the bus was late again.»
its sense in the lessons: In science and maths, «typically» means «usually, in most cases but not all»: «A typical spider has eight legs», «typically about 20 children in a class». In reports and exam questions it shows a general pattern. In everyday talk it can sound fed-up: «Typically, it rained on sports day.» Phrases: «typically between», «typically British», «typically late».
examples from the lessons: A cat typically sleeps for more than twelve hours a day. | Summers in Australia are typically hot and dry. | Typically, our school bus arrives at quarter to nine. | It was a typically Irish welcome, with tea and biscuits. | Typically, my brother left his dirty socks on the floor again. | A trip to the coast typically takes two hours. | Bananas typically grow in hot, wet countries.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelt with «-ally»: typically (not «typicly»). Say «TIP-ik-lee». From «typical». In maths, «typically» does not mean «always»: there can be exceptions. «Typically» is close to «usually» but sounds more formal; for a moan it shows the speaker expected something bad.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An ulcer is a sore place on the skin or inside the body where the surface has broken down; it is slow to heal and can hurt. 2) A mouth ulcer is a small, painful white or yellow spot inside your mouth. 3) A stomach ulcer is a sore in the lining of the stomach.
its sense in the lessons: In health and science lessons, ulcers show what happens when the body's lining gets damaged; mouth ulcers are common and harmless, while stomach ulcers need a doctor. In everyday life children say «I've got a mouth ulcer, it stings when I eat crisps.» Phrases: «a mouth ulcer», «a stomach ulcer», «leg ulcer».
examples from the lessons: I have a mouth ulcer, so orange juice really stings. | Mouth ulcers usually heal on their own in a week or two. | Grandad's doctor treated his stomach ulcer with medicine. | The nurse put a dressing on the ulcer on Gran's leg. | Biting your cheek by accident can cause an ulcer. | Salty crisps make my ulcer hurt.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable, «an ulcer» (starts with a vowel sound, UL-ser). Myth: stomach ulcers were long thought to come only from worry and spicy food; scientists found that most are caused by a germ (bacteria) called H. pylori, and they won a Nobel Prize in 2005 for it. An ulcer that does not heal should be shown to a doctor.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unacceptable means not good enough or not allowed, so it cannot be accepted. 2) Unacceptable behaviour is behaviour that is wrong and must stop, like bullying or hitting.
its sense in the lessons: In school and safety rules, «unacceptable» is a strong word used by teachers and parents: «Swearing at a teacher is unacceptable.» In news and politics, leaders call things unacceptable to show strong disapproval. In maths and science, «an unacceptable answer» or «an unacceptable error» is one that is too far off. Phrases: «totally unacceptable», «completely unacceptable», «unacceptable behaviour».
examples from the lessons: Bullying is unacceptable in our school. | The head teacher said the mess in the toilets was unacceptable. | Being rude to the dinner ladies is unacceptable. | The shop said a torn receipt was unacceptable. | The water in the old pipes had unacceptable levels of lead. | The judge called the driver's speed unacceptable. | An answer with no working is unacceptable in this test.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: acceptable. Prefix «un-» means not. Spelt with «cc»: un-ac-cept-able. Do not confuse «accept» (agree to take) with «except» (but not). Formal and strong in tone: adults use it when they are serious.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unaccustomed to something means not used to it, because you have not done it or felt it often: «unaccustomed to the cold». 2) (formal) Unaccustomed also means unusual or not normal for someone: «He spoke with unaccustomed anger.»
its sense in the lessons: In stories, the word shows a character in a new place or situation, struggling a little: a city child unaccustomed to farm life. In everyday speech people more often say «not used to». Phrases: «unaccustomed to», «with unaccustomed ...».
examples from the lessons: The children from Florida were unaccustomed to snow. | Unaccustomed to waking so early, Leo yawned all morning. | My eyes were unaccustomed to the dark cave. | Gran, unaccustomed to phones, pressed every button. | She spoke with unaccustomed sharpness, so we knew she was upset. | Being unaccustomed to the heat, the visitors stayed in the shade.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually followed by «to» + noun or «-ing»: «unaccustomed to walking», not «to walk». Spelt with «cc»: un-ac-CUS-tomed. Opposite: accustomed (used to). It sounds more formal than «not used to».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unacquainted with something means not knowing about it or not having met it: «unacquainted with the rules». 2) Unacquainted people have not met each other before.
its sense in the lessons: It appears in stories and formal writing, often in older books: a stranger unacquainted with the town, a reader unacquainted with a word. In everyday talk people say «didn't know» or «hadn't met». Phrases: «unacquainted with».
examples from the lessons: The new boy was unacquainted with the school's rules. | Many people are unacquainted with this old card game. | The two families were unacquainted until the street party. | Being unacquainted with the forest, we kept to the path. | The visitor seemed unacquainted with British money. | I was unacquainted with the word, so I looked it up.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Followed by «with»: «unacquainted with the area». Spelt with «cq»: un-ac-QUAINT-ed. Opposite: acquainted. Formal; «not familiar with» means nearly the same.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To uncurl means to open out or straighten from a curled shape: a hedgehog uncurls when it feels safe. 2) To uncurl something means to straighten it out, like uncurling your fingers or a rolled-up poster.
its sense in the lessons: In science and nature lessons, animals uncurl (hedgehogs, woodlice, caterpillars) and plants uncurl (fern leaves in spring). In stories, a cat uncurls from sleep and stretches. Phrases: «uncurl slowly», «uncurl your fingers», «uncurl from a ball».
examples from the lessons: The hedgehog uncurled when the dog went away. | Fern leaves uncurl in spring like little green springs. | The cat uncurled and stretched in the sunshine. | Slowly uncurl your fingers to show what you are holding. | We uncurled the old map and pinned it on the wall. | A woodlouse rolls into a ball and uncurls when it feels safe.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: uncurled, uncurling. Can be used with or without an object: «the cat uncurled» / «she uncurled the poster». Opposite: curl up. «Un-» here means to reverse an action, like in «untie», «undo».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Undecided means not yet having made up your mind: «I'm undecided about which club to join.» 2) Undecided also means not yet settled or fixed: «The date of the trip is still undecided.» 3) An undecided game or match has not been won yet.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, votes, surveys and class elections have «undecided» people who have not chosen yet; in maths survey tables there is often a column for «undecided». In stories it shows a character thinking things over. Phrases: «still undecided», «undecided voters», «undecided about».
examples from the lessons: I'm still undecided about what to wear to the party. | In our class vote, 12 said yes, 9 said no and 4 were undecided. | The winner of the baking contest is still undecided. | Mum was undecided between the blue and the green car. | Undecided voters can change who wins an election. | The match was undecided until the last minute.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective. Followed by «about» or «whether»: «undecided about the trip», «undecided whether to go». In survey maths, the undecided are a separate group: if 30 children were asked and 12 said yes and 9 said no, then 30 − 12 − 9 = 9 were undecided. Opposite: decided, sure.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To undercharge means to ask someone to pay less than the real or correct price, often by mistake. 2) To undercharge for your work means to ask too little money for it.
its sense in the lessons: In maths problems on money, shopping and change, undercharging means the bill was too small: the difference between the correct price and the price charged tells you how much was missed. In everyday life, honest customers tell the shop when they have been undercharged. Phrases: «undercharge someone by £2», «be undercharged».
examples from the lessons: The cashier undercharged us by three dollars, so Dad went back to pay. | If a shop undercharges you, it is honest to tell them. | The café undercharged for the cakes because the price label was wrong. | My cousin undercharges for her babysitting — she should ask for more. | The bill should be £18, but we were charged £15, so we were undercharged by £3. | The new till kept undercharging for apples.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: undercharged. Opposite: overcharge. Maths: undercharged amount = correct price − price paid, e.g. correct £20, charged £17 → undercharged by £3. Usually followed by «by» + amount or «for» + thing.

part of speech: verb (underestimate, underestimates, underestimated, underestimating); noun (an underestimate, underestimates)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To underestimate means to guess that an amount, size or time is smaller than it really is: «I underestimated how long the walk would take.» 2) To underestimate a person means to think they are less clever, strong or able than they really are. 3) An underestimate (noun) is a guess that is too low.
its sense in the lessons: In maths lessons on estimating and rounding, an underestimate is an estimate lower than the true answer; rounding down often gives one. In stories and sport, a strong team underestimates a small team and loses — a classic lesson. Phrases: «never underestimate», «underestimate someone», «a slight underestimate», «underestimate the danger».
examples from the lessons: I underestimated how many sweets were in the jar: I said 50 and there were 72. | Never underestimate a small dog! | The champions underestimated our team and lost 2–1. | Rounding 48 and 37 down to 40 and 30 gives an underestimate of their sum. | People often underestimate how cold the sea is in spring. | Don't underestimate the danger of swimming in a river. | 200 is an underestimate; the real number is 230.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb stress: un-der-ES-ti-mate (last syllable «-mate»); noun: un-der-ES-ti-mut. Opposite: overestimate. Maths: an underestimate is less than the exact answer; rounding every number down gives an underestimate of a sum. Not the same as «underrate», which is only about people's or things' quality, though they overlap.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Undergrowth is the bushes, ferns, small plants and tangled stems that grow thickly under the trees in a wood or forest.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on habitats and forest layers, the undergrowth (or understorey and shrub layer) is home to insects, birds, mice and other animals. In stories, animals and people hide or rustle in the undergrowth, which tells the reader about secrets and danger. Phrases: «in the undergrowth», «thick undergrowth», «rustling in the undergrowth», «push through the undergrowth».
examples from the lessons: Something rustled in the undergrowth. | The rabbit vanished into the undergrowth. | We pushed our way through the thick undergrowth. | Many beetles and spiders live in the forest undergrowth. | The fox hid in the undergrowth until the dogs had gone. | Brambles in the undergrowth scratched our legs.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «the undergrowth», «thick undergrowth», not «undergrowths». One word. Similar words: «underbrush» (mainly US), «scrub», «bushes».

part of speech: noun (underpants — plural only; a pair of underpants)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Underpants are a piece of underwear worn under trousers or a skirt, covering the bottom and the private parts. 2) In the UK «underpants» are usually men's or boys' pants; in the US the word is used for anyone's.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and funny stories («Captain Underpants», «Aliens Love Underpants»), underpants make children laugh. In health and safety lessons on the body, pupils learn that the parts covered by underpants are private — the «pants rule» in the UK. Phrases: «a pair of underpants», «clean underpants».
examples from the lessons: Don't forget to pack clean underpants for the school trip. | Grandad buys a new pair of underpants every Christmas. | Captain Underpants is a superhero in a funny book series. | The underpants rule says your private parts belong to you. | My little brother ran into the garden in his underpants. | Socks and underpants go in the top drawer.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural noun: «my underpants are clean», not «is». Count them with «a pair of»: «two pairs of underpants». UK: «pants» means underpants; US: «pants» means trousers — a common trap between British and American English. Short form: «undies» (informal).

meaning for a pupil: 1) To understate means to say that something is smaller, less important or less serious than it really is. 2) Understated (adjective) also means simple and quiet in style, not showy: «an understated dress».
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons, «understatement» is a figure of speech: saying less than you mean, often for humour («It's a bit wet» in a flood); it is a well-known feature of British humour. In science and news, understating danger or numbers can mislead people. Phrases: «understate the problem», «to say it was hard would be to understate it».
examples from the lessons: He understated how hurt he was, so no one took him to the nurse. | «A bit chilly» understates it — it's freezing! | The report understated the number of people affected by the flood. | Don't understate the danger of thin ice. | Her clothes were simple and understated. | Calling the storm «breezy» was a huge understatement.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: understated. Noun: an understatement. Opposite: overstate, exaggerate. Understatement is not lying when everyone knows the real size; it is a way of being funny or modest.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Undisputed means accepted by everyone, so no one argues about it: «the undisputed champion». 2) It also means certainly true and not questioned: «an undisputed fact».
its sense in the lessons: In sport and news it describes clear winners and leaders: «the undisputed world champion». In history and science, an undisputed fact is one all experts agree on, unlike disputed or contested points. Phrases: «undisputed champion», «undisputed king of», «undisputed fact».
examples from the lessons: She is the undisputed chess champion of our school. | It is an undisputed fact that the Earth goes round the Sun. | The lion is the undisputed king of the pride. | Our cat is the undisputed boss of the house. | The boxer became the undisputed world champion. | His talent for drawing is undisputed.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective. Stress: un-dis-PYOO-tid. Opposite: disputed (argued about). «Indisputable» means «cannot be disputed»; «undisputed» means «is not disputed» — very close.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) Unhinged means mentally unbalanced, acting in a wild, crazy or frightening way. 2) (slang) Online, «unhinged» is used jokingly for very weird or over-the-top behaviour: «That video is unhinged.» 3) Literally, an unhinged door has been taken off its hinges.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, an unhinged villain is wild and unpredictable. In slang among young people, it means funny and extreme. In safety and kindness lessons, pupils should know that calling real people with mental illness «unhinged» can be hurtful. Phrases: «completely unhinged», «a bit unhinged», «unhinged behaviour».
examples from the lessons: The villain in the film was completely unhinged. | (slang) My little brother's dancing is absolutely unhinged. | (slang) «That cat video is so unhinged, I can't stop laughing.» | Dad unhinged the cupboard door to paint it. | The door hung unhinged after the storm. | After weeks alone, the sailor in the story seemed unhinged.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective from the verb «unhinge». Informal and can be unkind about real people's mental health; better to say «unwell» or «acting strangely» about real people. Say «un-HINJD».

meaning for a pupil: 1) UNICEF is the part of the United Nations that works to help children around the world, giving them food, clean water, vaccines, schooling and protection. 2) The letters first stood for «United Nations International Children's Emergency Fund»; today its name is the United Nations Children's Fund, but the old letters are kept.
its sense in the lessons: In lessons on human rights, citizenship and the world, UNICEF comes up with the Convention on the Rights of the Child (1989) and its Rights Respecting Schools award in the UK. In everyday life, schools raise money for UNICEF with charity days. Phrases: «UNICEF works with», «a UNICEF report», «support UNICEF».
examples from the lessons: UNICEF helps children in more than 190 countries and territories. | Our school raised £300 for UNICEF on Day for Change. | UNICEF sends vaccines to children who need them. | After the earthquake, UNICEF brought clean water to families. | UNICEF was set up in 1946, just after the Second World War. | Our class learnt about children's rights from a UNICEF poster.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It is a name (of an organization), usually written in capitals: UNICEF. Say «YOO-ni-sef». It is an acronym — read as one word, not letter by letter. It is part of the United Nations, not a government of any one country.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unidentified means not known or not recognised: no one knows yet who or what it is. 2) An unidentified flying object (UFO) is something seen in the sky that people cannot explain.
its sense in the lessons: In news and police reports, «an unidentified man» means his name is not known. In science, unidentified species or objects are waiting to be named or explained. In stories and films, UFOs and unidentified creatures make mystery. Phrases: «unidentified flying object», «an unidentified person», «for unidentified reasons».
examples from the lessons: An unidentified man was seen near the shop. | The scientists found an unidentified insect in the rainforest. | A UFO is an unidentified flying object. | The lost-property box has an unidentified blue jumper. | The police are trying to find the unidentified driver. | Most unidentified lights in the sky turn out to be planes or satellites.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective. Stress: un-eye-DEN-ti-fied. Myth: «unidentified flying object» does not mean «alien spaceship»; it just means nobody has explained it yet, and most are later found to be ordinary things like balloons, planes or planets.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unimpeded means not blocked or slowed down; free to move or happen: «an unimpeded view». 2) (formal) It describes things that go on without anything getting in the way.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography it describes flow: water flowing unimpeded, light passing unimpeded through glass. In formal writing and exam texts, «unimpeded progress», «unimpeded access». In everyday speech people say «with nothing in the way». Phrases: «an unimpeded view», «flow unimpeded», «unimpeded access».
examples from the lessons: From the hilltop we had an unimpeded view of the sea. | The river flowed unimpeded after the fallen tree was removed. | Light passes unimpeded through clear glass. | The ambulance drove unimpeded down the empty road. | Wheelchair users need unimpeded access to the building. | The ball rolled unimpeded into the goal.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal word. Stress: un-im-PEE-did. From «impede» (to block or slow down). Often used after a verb like an adverb: «move unimpeded».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Uninformed means not knowing the facts about something: «an uninformed guess». 2) An uninformed opinion or choice is one made without enough knowledge.
its sense in the lessons: In lessons on news, science and checking facts, pupils learn the difference between an informed opinion (based on facts) and an uninformed one. In everyday life, «Don't make uninformed decisions» means find out first. Phrases: «uninformed about», «an uninformed guess», «uninformed opinion».
examples from the lessons: It was an uninformed guess, because I hadn't read the question. | Many people were uninformed about the new bus timetable. | Don't share uninformed opinions online — check the facts first. | The visitors were uninformed about the danger of the tides. | An uninformed choice can cost you money. | Reading the label means you are not uninformed about what you eat.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective. Not the same as «misinformed» (given wrong facts): uninformed means you do not have the facts at all. Opposite: informed, well-informed. Usually «uninformed about» something.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To unite means to join together to make one group or one thing: «The two clubs united.» 2) To unite people means to bring them together so they work for the same goal. 3) United (adjective) means joined together or agreeing.
its sense in the lessons: In history and citizenship lessons, countries unite (the United Kingdom, the United States, the United Nations); in sport and stories, people unite against a danger. In maths, «unite» is not used, but the idea of joining groups (union of sets) is related. Phrases: «unite against», «unite behind», «unite to do», «united we stand».
examples from the lessons: The whole town united to clean up after the flood. | The two small schools united to make one bigger school. | England, Scotland and Wales were united under one Parliament in 1707. | Music can unite people from different countries. | The class united behind their captain. | Our team is united and ready to play. | «United we stand, divided we fall» is an old saying.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: united, uniting (drop the «e» before «-ing»). Stress: yoo-NITE. Noun: unity, union. Many names use «United»: the United Kingdom (England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland), the United States, Manchester United. Opposite: divide, split.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unmown means not cut by a mower: unmown grass has been left to grow long.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on habitats and wildlife, unmown patches of lawn or verge let wildflowers, bees and butterflies thrive («No Mow May» in the UK). In stories, an unmown lawn can show that a house is empty or neglected. Phrases: «unmown grass», «an unmown meadow», «leave a patch unmown».
examples from the lessons: We left a corner of the school field unmown for the bees. | The unmown grass came up to my knees. | Daisies and clover flowered in the unmown verge. | The empty house had an unmown, weedy garden. | Grasshoppers jumped through the unmown meadow. | During No Mow May, many lawns stay unmown.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective from «mow» (mow, mowed, mown/mowed). Say «un-MOAN». Do not confuse «mown» with «moan» (to complain) — they sound the same.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Unobjectionable means not likely to upset or annoy anyone; acceptable, though often not exciting.
its sense in the lessons: It appears in formal writing, reviews and reports: «an unobjectionable choice», «unobjectionable language». In everyday speech people say «fine», «OK» or «harmless». It tells the reader that nobody could complain, but sometimes that something is a bit dull. Phrases: «perfectly unobjectionable».
examples from the lessons: The film was unobjectionable, with no rude words or scary scenes. | The teacher chose an unobjectionable song for the assembly. | Plain toast is an unobjectionable breakfast for a sick child. | His comments were polite and unobjectionable. | The new rule seemed unobjectionable, so everyone agreed. | The food was unobjectionable but not very tasty.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Long formal word: un-ob-JEK-shun-a-bul. From «object» (verb, ob-JEKT: to say you disagree). Opposite: objectionable (offensive, unpleasant).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unpalatable food or drink tastes unpleasant. 2) An unpalatable fact or idea is unpleasant and hard to accept: «the unpalatable truth».
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on animals, some insects taste unpalatable so birds learn not to eat them (bright colours warn of this). In news and history, leaders face unpalatable choices. In stories, an unpalatable truth is one a character does not want to hear. Phrases: «unpalatable truth», «unpalatable choice».
examples from the lessons: The hospital food was cold and unpalatable. | Monarch butterflies are unpalatable to birds. | The unpalatable truth was that we had lost every match. | The medicine was unpalatable, so Mum mixed it with juice. | The council faced an unpalatable choice between closing the library and the pool. | Burnt porridge is completely unpalatable.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal word. Stress: un-PAL-a-ta-bul. «Palate» is the roof of your mouth (and your sense of taste); do not confuse with «palette» (paints) or «pallet» (wooden platform). Opposite: palatable.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unplanned means not planned or expected; it happened without being arranged first.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, unplanned stops, trips or costs happen; in safety lessons, planning for the unplanned (a first aid kit, a phone) is wise. In maths word problems, an unplanned cost changes the total: a family must pay for something they did not budget for. Phrases: «an unplanned stop», «unplanned costs», «completely unplanned».
examples from the lessons: We made an unplanned stop at the beach because the sun came out. | The fire drill was unplanned, so it felt real. | The car repair was an unplanned cost. | Our picnic turned into an unplanned water fight. | The baby's early arrival was unplanned. | Some of the best adventures are unplanned.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective. Double «n»: unplanned (plan → planned). In money problems, unplanned costs are added to the planned ones: planned £40 + unplanned £15 = £55 spent. Opposite: planned.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unresolved means not yet settled, solved or answered: an unresolved problem or argument is still going on.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, unresolved problems keep the reader turning pages, and a cliffhanger leaves things unresolved until the next book. In science and maths, an unresolved question has no answer yet. In everyday life, unresolved arguments between friends can make people unhappy. Phrases: «remain unresolved», «unresolved issues», «an unresolved mystery».
examples from the lessons: The mystery of the missing cake remained unresolved. | The argument between the two friends is still unresolved. | The book ends with the main problem unresolved, so we want the sequel. | Some questions in science are still unresolved. | The teacher helped us sort out our unresolved disagreement. | The court case is unresolved.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective. From «resolve» (to settle, to solve). Opposite: resolved, settled, solved. Common pattern: «remain unresolved».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unrivalled means better than all the others, with nothing equal to it: «an unrivalled view», «unrivalled skill».
its sense in the lessons: In adverts, travel books and sports reports, «unrivalled» praises something as the best. In history, an unrivalled empire or champion had no equal at its time. Phrases: «unrivalled view», «unrivalled knowledge», «unrivalled success».
examples from the lessons: The tower gives an unrivalled view of the whole city. | Her skill on the football pitch is unrivalled in our year. | For many years the Roman army was unrivalled. | The museum has an unrivalled collection of dinosaur bones. | Grandma's knowledge of birds is unrivalled. | The advert promised «unrivalled comfort».
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: UK, Ireland, Australia and New Zealand «unrivalled» (double l); US «unrivaled» (one l); Canada uses both. From «rival» (someone you compete with). Adverts often exaggerate: «unrivalled» there is a claim, not a proven fact.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Untrained means not taught or practised in a skill or job: «an untrained helper». 2) An untrained animal has not been taught to behave or obey: «an untrained puppy». 3) An untrained eye or ear cannot notice what an expert can.
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons, untrained people should not do dangerous jobs (electrical work, diving rescues); call trained helpers. In everyday life, untrained puppies chew and jump. In science and art, «to the untrained eye» means to someone who is not an expert. Phrases: «to the untrained eye», «untrained staff», «untrained dog».
examples from the lessons: An untrained puppy will chew your shoes. | To the untrained eye, the two birds look the same. | Untrained people should not climb into a sewer to rescue someone. | The new helpers were untrained, so the coach showed them what to do. | My voice is untrained, but I love singing. | It is dangerous for untrained divers to go into caves.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective. Opposite: trained, skilled. Common phrase: «to the untrained eye/ear».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unverifiable means impossible to check or prove true or false: «an unverifiable claim».
its sense in the lessons: In lessons on news, the internet and fake news, pupils learn to be careful with unverifiable claims: a story with no source, no evidence and no way to check. In science, a good idea must be testable; an unverifiable idea cannot be tested. Phrases: «unverifiable claims», «unverifiable rumours».
examples from the lessons: The post made an unverifiable claim that eating carrots lets you see in the dark. | Rumours on social media are often unverifiable. | The story about the ghost in the library is unverifiable. | Good reporters do not print unverifiable facts as true. | His boast that he once met the Queen was unverifiable. | Scientists prefer ideas that can be tested, not unverifiable ones.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Long word: un-VER-i-fy-a-bul. From «verify» (to check that something is true). Unverifiable does not mean false: it means we cannot check it. Opposite: verifiable.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To unwind means to relax after being busy, tired or worried: «I unwind by reading.» 2) To unwind something means to undo it from a roll or coil, like unwinding a ball of wool or a hosepipe.
its sense in the lessons: In health and wellbeing lessons, ways to unwind include sport, music, reading and time outdoors. In everyday life, parents unwind after work. In craft and science lessons, you unwind thread, string or wire. Phrases: «unwind after school», «time to unwind», «unwind the hose».
examples from the lessons: After a busy day, I like to unwind with a book. | Dad unwinds by going for a run. | We unwound the hose to water the garden. | The kite string unwound as the kite flew higher. | A warm bath helps me unwind before bed. | The cat unwound the ball of wool all over the floor.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular past: unwound (say «un-WOUND», rhymes with «found»), not «unwinded». Say «un-WINED» (like «wind» a clock), not like «wind» the breeze. Opposite of the second sense: wind up.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unworthy means not deserving something, especially something good: «I felt unworthy of the prize.» 2) Unworthy of someone means not good enough for their character: «That mean comment is unworthy of you.» 3) (church) In church language, people speak of being unworthy before God, meaning they need God's mercy.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, a hero feels unworthy at first and then proves themselves; in fairy tales, only the worthy can pull out the sword. In church, prayers before communion include words about being unworthy. In everyday talk, «that's unworthy of you» is a gentle telling-off. Phrases: «unworthy of», «feel unworthy», «unworthy of attention».
examples from the lessons: The young knight felt unworthy to hold the magic sword. | That rude remark is unworthy of you. | The prize went to a team that some said was unworthy of it. | The old story said only the pure in heart could lift the stone; the unworthy failed. | (church) In some services, people pray, «Lord, I am not worthy to receive you.» | The rumour was unworthy of a reply.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective. Usually followed by «of»: «unworthy of praise». Opposite: worthy. Say «un-WUR-thee» with the soft «th» as in «the».

part of speech: verb (upgrade, upgrades, upgraded, upgrading); noun (an upgrade, upgrades)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To upgrade something means to make it better, newer or more powerful, like upgrading a computer or a phone. 2) An upgrade is a better or newer version, or the change that makes it better. 3) To be upgraded on a plane or in a hotel means to be moved to a better seat or room. 4) To upgrade a storm or warning means to raise its level.
its sense in the lessons: In computing lessons and games, you install upgrades and updates; in games, you upgrade your character or tools. In everyday life, families upgrade phones and kitchens; weather reports upgrade storms to hurricanes. Phrases: «upgrade to», «a free upgrade», «software upgrade».
examples from the lessons: Dad upgraded the laptop so it runs faster. | In the game, you can upgrade your sword with gold coins. | We got a free upgrade to a bigger hotel room. | The storm was upgraded to a hurricane. | The school is upgrading the playground with new climbing frames. | The new phone is a big upgrade on my old one. | The upgrade cost £50.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb stress: up-GRADE; noun stress: UP-grade. Regular: upgraded. Opposite: downgrade. «Upgrade» (a better version) and «update» (latest changes or news) overlap but are not the same. In money problems, an upgrade usually adds to the cost: basic £100 + upgrade £30 = £130.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Uplifted means feeling happier, more hopeful or encouraged: «I felt uplifted by the music.» 2) Uplifted also means raised up: «uplifted hands», «uplifted faces». 3) In geography, uplifted rocks have been pushed upwards by forces in the Earth.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and church, people feel uplifted by songs, prayers or kind words; in church and the Bible, uplifted hands are a sign of prayer or praise. In geography and science, mountains form when land is uplifted. Phrases: «feel uplifted», «uplifted hands», «uplifting music».
examples from the lessons: We all felt uplifted after the choir sang. | The crowd's uplifted faces watched the fireworks. | (church) The people prayed with uplifted hands. | The Himalayas were uplifted when India pushed into Asia. | Her kind letter left me feeling uplifted. | Sea shells were found on top of the uplifted rocks.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Uplifted» is how you feel; «uplifting» is what makes you feel it: «an uplifting song made me feel uplifted». Similar trap: «bored/boring», «excited/exciting». Stress: up-LIF-tid.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Urgently means very quickly, because something is important and must be done right now: «We need help urgently.»
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons, emergencies need urgent action: call 999 (UK), 911 (US, Canada), 000 (Australia) or 111 (New Zealand), 112 or 999 (Ireland). In news, charities urgently need donations or blood. In stories, a character speaks urgently to show danger. Phrases: «urgently needed», «need something urgently», «speak urgently».
examples from the lessons: The hospital urgently needs blood donors. | «Come quickly!» she said urgently. | The roof leak must be fixed urgently before it rains again. | The lost hiker urgently needed water. | We urgently packed our bags when the flood warning came. | The head teacher urgently called all the parents.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from «urgent». Say «UR-jent-lee». «Urgent» means it must be done now; «important» means it matters, but not always right now — a useful difference when planning.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Vascular means to do with the tubes that carry blood in animals (blood vessels: arteries, veins and capillaries). 2) In plants, vascular means having tubes (xylem and phloem) that carry water and food through the plant.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on the body and on plants, «vascular» names the transport systems: the vascular system in humans (heart, blood vessels) and vascular plants (ferns, trees, flowers) versus non-vascular plants (mosses). In hospitals, vascular surgeons operate on blood vessels. Phrases: «vascular system», «vascular plants», «vascular bundle».
examples from the lessons: Your vascular system carries blood all round your body. | Trees are vascular plants with tubes that carry water up from the roots. | Mosses are non-vascular, so they stay small and grow in damp places. | We saw the vascular bundles in a celery stick dyed with red ink. | Grandad saw a vascular surgeon about the veins in his legs. | Exercise keeps your heart and vascular system healthy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Science word: VAS-kyoo-lur. From Latin «vasculum», a small vessel. Non-vascular plants (mosses, liverworts) have no such tubes. Celery in coloured water is a classic experiment to see vascular tubes.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Veal is the meat from a young calf (a baby cow), used as food.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, veal appears on restaurant menus in dishes like Wiener schnitzel or veal escalopes. In lessons on food and farming, some people choose not to eat veal because of how young calves are kept, and farming rules have changed to improve their welfare. Phrases: «veal cutlet», «veal escalope», «roast veal».
examples from the lessons: Wiener schnitzel is made from thin slices of veal. | The restaurant served veal with mushrooms. | Veal is paler and softer than beef. | Some families do not eat veal for animal welfare reasons. | The cookbook had a recipe for veal stew. | Veal comes from calves, and beef comes from older cattle.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «some veal», not «a veal». The animal is a calf (plural calves); the meat is veal — like pig/pork, cow/beef, sheep/mutton or lamb. The word came into English from old French. Do not confuse with «veil» (cloth over the face) — similar sound.

part of speech: noun (French; le veau, les veaux) — not an English word
meaning for a pupil: 1) (French) «Veau» is the French word for a calf (a baby cow), and also for veal, the meat of a calf. 2) It sounds like «voh» to an English ear (rhymes with «go», with a «v»). 3) It is not an English word; English took «veal» from the old French form of this word.
its sense in the lessons: In French lessons on food and farm animals, «le veau» appears on menus («blanquette de veau», a veal stew) and in lists like «la vache» (cow), «le veau» (calf), «le taureau» (bull). It tells an English reader something is French cooking or a French farm. «Veau» also appears in «ris de veau» (calf sweetbreads) on French menus.
examples from the lessons: In French, «le veau» means «the calf». | The French menu said «blanquette de veau» — a creamy veal stew. | «Veau» sounds like «voh». | In our French farm song, «la vache et le veau» means «the cow and the calf». | English «veal» comes from the old French word that became «veau». | My aunt in Paris ordered «escalope de veau».
note for the reader of a maths problem: French, not English. Masculine: «le veau»; plural «les veaux» (say «lay voh» — the «x» is silent). The «-eau» spelling in French says «oh», as in «gâteau», «château», «bureau». Do not confuse «veau» with «vaut» (is worth) or «vos» (your), which can sound alike.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Vehement means showing very strong feeling, especially when arguing or disagreeing: «a vehement protest». 2) A vehement person speaks or acts with great force and passion.
its sense in the lessons: In news and history, people make vehement protests or denials. In stories, a vehement character argues angrily or passionately. In everyday speech people say «strong», «fierce» or «furious». Phrases: «vehement protest», «vehement denial», «vehement opposition».
examples from the lessons: She was vehement that she had not broken the window. | There was vehement opposition to closing the library. | The two teams argued in vehement voices about the penalty. | His denial was so vehement that we believed him. | The villagers made a vehement protest against the new road. | My little brother is vehement that broccoli is poisonous.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say «VEE-uh-ment»; the «h» is silent. Adverb: vehemently («she vehemently denied it»). Noun: vehemence. It is about the strength of feeling, not about being right.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Velvety means soft and smooth like velvet cloth: «velvety petals». 2) A velvety voice or taste is smooth, deep and rich.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and descriptive writing, «velvety» is a sensory word for touch (moss, a puppy's ears, rose petals), sight (a velvety night sky) or taste (velvety hot chocolate). In science, some leaves, antlers and caterpillars have velvety hairs. Phrases: «velvety soft», «velvety petals», «velvety voice».
examples from the lessons: The rose petals felt velvety under my fingers. | The deer's new antlers were covered in velvety skin. | The night sky was velvety black. | The hot chocolate was rich and velvety. | Moss grows like a velvety carpet on the rocks. | The singer had a deep, velvety voice. | Our puppy's ears are velvety soft.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective from «velvet» + «-y». Say «VEL-vi-tee». Good word for descriptive writing instead of plain «soft».

part of speech: noun (a venture, ventures); verb (venture, ventures, ventured, venturing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To venture means to go somewhere that may be unknown, risky or a bit dangerous: «We ventured into the cave.» 2) To venture an opinion or a guess means to say it carefully, even though you are not sure. 3) A venture (noun) is a new project or business with some risk: «a business venture». 4) A venture can also be a risky journey or adventure.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, characters venture into dark forests, out into storms or beyond the walls; it shows bravery and danger. In money and business lessons, a venture is a new business that might make or lose money. Phrases: «venture out», «venture into», «venture a guess», «a joint venture», «nothing ventured, nothing gained».
examples from the lessons: The children ventured into the dark woods. | We didn't venture out in the snowstorm. | «Is it Paris?» she ventured. | Can I venture a guess? | Their cake stall was a successful business venture. | Mum's new café is an exciting venture. | Nothing ventured, nothing gained!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: ventured, venturing. «Adventure» comes from the same root. In money problems, a venture can make a profit (money in more than money out) or a loss. Say «VEN-cher».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A vertebra is one of the small bones that are linked together to make the backbone (spine). 2) The vertebrae protect the spinal cord, the bundle of nerves that carries messages between the brain and the body.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on the skeleton, the spine is made of vertebrae; animals with backbones are vertebrates (fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds, mammals) and animals without are invertebrates (insects, worms, jellyfish). Humans usually have 33 vertebrae (some join together). Phrases: «a broken vertebra», «neck vertebrae», «vertebrates and invertebrates».
examples from the lessons: The spine is made of many small bones, each called a vertebra. | A giraffe has seven vertebrae in its neck — the same number as a human. | The doctor said he had cracked a vertebra in the fall. | Snakes have hundreds of vertebrae. | Fish are vertebrates because they have a backbone of vertebrae. | We felt the bumps of our vertebrae down our backs.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular plural: vertebrae (say «VUR-te-bray» or «VUR-te-bree»), not «vertebras». Fact for maths and quizzes: a human has 7 neck vertebrae, as does a giraffe — a giraffe's are just much longer. Safety: a person who may have hurt their back or neck should not be moved until help comes.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A vestige is a small part or trace that is left of something that used to be bigger or used to exist: «the last vestiges of the castle». 2) In science, a vestigial body part is one that has lost most of its old use, like the tiny leg bones inside some whales.
its sense in the lessons: In history, vestiges of old walls or customs show what the past was like. In science lessons on evolution, vestigial parts (the human tailbone, whale hip bones) are evidence of change over time. In formal writing, «not a vestige of» means «not even a little». Phrases: «the last vestiges», «a vestige of», «vestigial organ».
examples from the lessons: Only a vestige of the Roman wall is left in the town. | There was not a vestige of food left after the party. | The human tailbone is a vestige of a tail our distant ancestors had. | The last vestiges of snow melted in April. | Some whales have vestiges of back-leg bones inside their bodies. | The custom is a vestige of an old harvest festival.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: vestige, vestiges. Say «VES-tij». Adjective: vestigial (ves-TIJ-ee-ul). Myth: the appendix was long called useless, but scientists now think it does have some uses, so «vestigial» does not mean «totally useless».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A veteran is a person who has served in the armed forces, especially someone who fought in a war. 2) A veteran is also someone who has done a job or activity for a long time and has much experience: «a veteran teacher». 3) (adjective) Veteran means old and experienced, or (of cars) very old: «a veteran car».
its sense in the lessons: In history and citizenship lessons, veterans are remembered on Remembrance Day (UK, Canada, 11 November), Veterans Day (US, 11 November) and Anzac Day (Australia and New Zealand, 25 April). In everyday life and sport, a veteran is someone with long experience. Phrases: «war veteran», «a veteran of», «veteran player».
examples from the lessons: Great-grandpa was a veteran of the Second World War. | Veterans marched past the war memorial on Remembrance Sunday. | On Anzac Day, we listened to a veteran speak at school. | Mrs Hall is a veteran teacher with thirty years in the classroom. | The veteran goalkeeper played his last match. | A veteran car rally drove through our village.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a veteran, veterans. Say «VET-er-un» or «VET-run». Informal US short form: «vet» — but in the UK «vet» usually means an animal doctor (veterinarian), a common trap. Veteran is about long experience, not only about old age.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Vibrato is a quick, small wobble up and down in the pitch of a note, made by a singer or a player of a string or wind instrument to make the sound warmer and richer.
its sense in the lessons: In music lessons, singers and violin, cello or flute players learn vibrato; it tells the listener the note is alive and expressive. In science, it links to sound, pitch and vibration. Phrases: «sing with vibrato», «a wide vibrato», «too much vibrato».
examples from the lessons: The opera singer's voice had a lovely vibrato. | My violin teacher showed me how to rock my finger for vibrato. | Too much vibrato can make a song sound wobbly. | The flute player added vibrato to the long note. | Choir boys often sing with little or no vibrato. | You can hear the vibrato when the singer holds a note.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable: «with vibrato». It is an Italian music word; say «vi-BRAH-toh». Do not confuse with «tremolo», a fast repeating of one note or a change in loudness. Related: vibrate, vibration.

part of speech: noun (a vicuna, vicunas; also spelt vicuña)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A vicuna is a wild South American animal related to the llama and alpaca; it is small, slim and light brown, and lives high in the Andes mountains. 2) Vicuna also means the very fine, soft, expensive wool or cloth made from this animal's fleece.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and science lessons on South America and mountain animals, the vicuna shows adaptation to cold and thin air. In history, the Inca protected vicunas; later they were hunted nearly to extinction for wool, and now they are protected again. Phrases: «vicuna wool», «herds of vicunas».
examples from the lessons: A herd of vicunas grazed on the high, cold grassland. | The vicuna is a wild cousin of the llama. | Vicuna wool is one of the softest and most expensive wools in the world. | The vicuna is the national animal of Peru and is on its coat of arms. | Vicunas have thick, soft coats to keep warm in the Andes. | Hunting nearly wiped out the vicuna, but now it is protected.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: vicunas. Spanish spelling: vicuña (say «vi-KOON-ya»); English often writes it without the wavy line. Do not confuse with the llama and alpaca (tame) or the guanaco (wild, bigger).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A vista is a beautiful, wide view, especially a long one seen between hills, trees or buildings. 2) (formal) A vista can also mean a range of future possibilities: «Reading opens new vistas.»
its sense in the lessons: In stories and descriptive writing, vistas describe landscapes from hilltops and mountains. In geography and travel, «sweeping vistas» of valleys and coasts. In formal speech, «opening up new vistas» means giving new chances. Phrases: «a stunning vista», «sweeping vistas», «open up new vistas».
examples from the lessons: From the top of the hill we saw a wonderful vista of fields and rivers. | The train passed through sweeping mountain vistas. | The window framed a vista of the sea. | Learning to read opened up whole new vistas for Gran. | The photographer captured the vista at sunset. | The path ended at a vista over the lake.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: vista, vistas. It comes from Italian and Spanish, meaning «view». Rather literary; in everyday speech, «view» is more common.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Vividly means very clearly and in a lively way, so you can almost see, feel or remember it: «I vividly remember my first day at school.» 2) Vividly coloured means with very bright, strong colours.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons, writers describe scenes vividly using strong verbs, adjectives and the senses; teachers praise writing that «vividly describes» a setting. In science, vividly coloured animals (poison dart frogs, wasps) often warn predators. Phrases: «vividly remember», «vividly describe», «vividly coloured».
examples from the lessons: I vividly remember the day we got our puppy. | The author describes the stormy sea vividly. | Poison dart frogs are vividly coloured to warn birds. | She vividly imagined the dragon flying over the school. | The parrot's feathers were vividly red and blue. | Grandad vividly told us about the big snow of his childhood.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from «vivid» (bright, clear). Say «VIV-id-lee». Good word for story writing and book reviews.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In science, a volatile liquid turns into a gas (evaporates) very easily, like petrol or nail-polish remover. 2) A volatile situation can change suddenly and become dangerous or violent. 3) A volatile person has sudden changes of mood and loses their temper easily. 4) (money) Volatile prices go up and down quickly and unpredictably.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on evaporation and safety, volatile liquids must be kept closed and away from flames, because their gas can catch fire. In news and history, «a volatile region» is one where fighting may start. In money lessons, volatile prices (fuel, crypto, shares) are risky. Phrases: «highly volatile», «a volatile situation», «volatile temper», «volatile prices».
examples from the lessons: Petrol is volatile, so its smell spreads quickly. | Keep volatile liquids away from flames. | The situation at the border is volatile. | The giant in the story had a volatile temper. | Fuel prices have been volatile this year. | Nail-polish remover is volatile and evaporates fast.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say «VOL-a-tile» (UK, rhymes with «tile») or «VOL-a-tul» (US). Volatile does not mean «poisonous» or «explosive» by itself, though many volatile liquids are flammable. Opposite (science): non-volatile, stable; (person): calm, steady.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Volcanically means because of volcanoes or in the way of a volcano: «volcanically active», «formed volcanically».
its sense in the lessons: In geography and science lessons, «volcanically active» places (Iceland, Hawaii, Japan, New Zealand's North Island) still have eruptions or hot springs. Islands and rocks can be formed volcanically. Phrases: «volcanically active», «volcanically formed».
examples from the lessons: Iceland is volcanically active, with hot springs and geysers. | The Hawaiian islands were formed volcanically. | Volcanically active areas often have earthquakes too. | The rock here was formed volcanically millions of years ago. | Rotorua in New Zealand is a volcanically active town that smells of sulphur. | Mount Etna is one of the most volcanically active mountains in Europe.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from «volcanic» + «-ally» (not «volcanicly»). Say «vol-KAN-ik-lee». Mostly used in science and geography.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A wafer is a very thin, light, crisp biscuit, often eaten with ice cream or with cream between layers. 2) (church) In many churches, a wafer is a thin, round piece of special bread given at Holy Communion. 3) A wafer is any very thin slice: a wafer of silicon in computer chips. 4) Wafer-thin means extremely thin.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, wafers come with ice cream (a «99» with a wafer in the UK, ice cream wafers) or as chocolate wafer bars. In church lessons, the communion wafer (also called the host in Catholic churches) is bread that Christians believe recalls or becomes the body of Jesus, depending on their church. In science and technology, chips are made on silicon wafers. Phrases: «wafer-thin», «ice cream wafer», «communion wafer».
examples from the lessons: I had a strawberry ice cream with two wafers. | The chocolate wafer bar snapped in half. | (church) At Mass, the priest gave each person a small round wafer. | The ham was sliced wafer-thin. | Computer chips are made on thin silicon wafers. | Gran keeps pink wafers in the biscuit tin.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a wafer, wafers. Say «WAY-fer». Do not confuse with «waver» (to be unsteady or unsure) — they sound similar. Different churches believe different things about the communion wafer; say «Catholics believe…», «many Protestants believe…».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Wakefulness is the state of being awake. 2) Wakefulness also means being unable to sleep when you want to.
its sense in the lessons: In science and health lessons on sleep, the body moves between sleep and wakefulness during a day; light and screens can cause wakefulness at night. In stories, a character's wakefulness at night shows worry or excitement. Phrases: «periods of wakefulness», «wakefulness at night».
examples from the lessons: Coffee can cause wakefulness at night. | Babies have short periods of wakefulness between sleeps. | The night before the trip, excitement kept me in a state of wakefulness. | Bright screens before bed can lead to wakefulness. | Owls are in their wakefulness at night and sleep by day. | The doctor asked Gran about her wakefulness in the early morning.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. From «wakeful» (awake, not able to sleep) + «-ness». Formal word; everyday talk says «being awake» or «not being able to sleep».

part of speech: verb (wallop, wallops, walloped, walloping); noun (a wallop, wallops)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) To wallop means to hit something or someone very hard. 2) (informal) A wallop is a hard hit, or the loud noise of a heavy thing falling. 3) (informal, sport) To wallop a team means to beat them by a lot. 4) (UK slang, old) Wallop is also an old jokey word for beer.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday talk and comics, «wallop» is a sound word (like «thud») and a strong, funny verb. In sport reports, a team gets walloped 6–0. In safety and kindness lessons, walloping a person is hitting and is not OK. Phrases: «pack a wallop» (be very powerful), «give it a wallop», «walloped by».
examples from the lessons: The ball walloped against the window. | Down came the sack of potatoes with a wallop. | Our team got walloped 7–0. | He gave the stuck door a wallop and it opened. | That chilli sauce packs a real wallop! | In the cartoon, the giant walloped the robot.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal. Regular verb: walloped, walloping. Adjective: walloping (very big: «a walloping great dog», UK informal). Hitting people is wrong and can be against the law; this word in stories is often comic.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A wanderer is a person or animal that travels from place to place with no fixed home or no clear plan. 2) A wanderer can also be someone who likes to roam and explore.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, poems and old tales, wanderers are travellers, knights, pilgrims or lonely figures on the road; the word gives a feeling of freedom or loneliness. In science, «planet» comes from a Greek word meaning «wanderer», because planets move across the night sky against the stars. Phrases: «a lonely wanderer», «the wanderer returns».
examples from the lessons: The old wanderer slept under the stars. | Our cat is a wanderer and visits every garden on the street. | The ancient Greeks called the planets «wanderers». | The wanderer told stories in every village he passed. | Albatrosses are great wanderers of the southern oceans. | In the poem, a lonely wanderer walks across the hills.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: wanderer, wanderers. From «wander» (to walk around slowly without a plan). Do not confuse «wander» (roam) with «wonder» (think about, be amazed) — different spelling and sound: WON-der vs WUN-der. Wolverhampton Wanderers is a football club (a name).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A watercourse is any channel that water flows along, like a river, stream, brook, ditch or canal.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons on rivers and the water cycle, watercourses carry rainwater to the sea; maps show them as blue lines. In safety and environment lessons, polluting a watercourse harms fish and is against the law. Phrases: «a natural watercourse», «along the watercourse», «pollution of watercourses».
examples from the lessons: A small watercourse runs along the bottom of the field. | Farmers must not let chemicals get into watercourses. | The map shows every watercourse as a thin blue line. | Willows grow along the banks of the watercourse. | After heavy rain, the dry watercourse filled with water. | Australian creeks can be dry watercourses for much of the year.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word. Countable. A rather formal or technical word used in geography, law and maps; everyday talk says «stream», «river», «creek» (US, Australia, New Zealand) or «burn» (Scotland).

part of speech: noun (waterfowl — plural same; a waterfowl rarely)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Waterfowl are birds that swim and live on or near water, especially ducks, geese and swans.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on birds and habitats, waterfowl have webbed feet, waterproof feathers and flat beaks; many migrate. In everyday life, families feed or watch waterfowl in parks and wetlands. Phrases: «wild waterfowl», «waterfowl reserve».
examples from the lessons: Ducks, geese and swans are waterfowl. | The wetland reserve is home to thousands of waterfowl. | Waterfowl have oily feathers that keep them dry. | Many waterfowl fly south for the winter. | Please don't feed bread to the waterfowl in the park — oats or seeds are better. | We counted the waterfowl on the lake for our science project.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural is usually the same: «many waterfowl». Usually used for the group; «a waterfowl» is rare. Wading birds like herons are usually called «waterbirds», not waterfowl. Bread is not good food for ducks — a common habit to avoid.

part of speech: adjective (weary, wearier, weariest); verb (weary, wearies, wearied, wearying)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Weary means very tired, especially after a lot of work or a long journey. 2) Weary of something means bored or fed up with it after too much of it: «weary of the rain». 3) To weary (verb) means to make or become tired: «The long walk wearied us.» 4) (Bible) In the Bible, Jesus says, «Come to me, all you who are weary,» offering rest.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, weary travellers, soldiers and heroes rest after long journeys; the word gives a slow, tired feeling. In church, the Bible verse «Come to me, all you who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest» (Matthew 11:28) is often read. Phrases: «weary of», «a weary sigh», «bone-weary», «world-weary».
examples from the lessons: After the long hike, we were weary and hungry. | The weary travellers stopped at the inn. | I'm weary of eating the same lunch every day. | She gave a weary sigh and sat down. | Mum looked weary after her night shift. | (Bible) «Come to me, all you who are weary,» Jesus said. | The long speech wearied the audience.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say «WEER-ee» (rhymes with «cheery»). Do not confuse with «wary» (careful, watchful: WAIR-ee) or «worry». Comparative: wearier, weariest. Adverb: wearily. Noun: weariness.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A weightlifter is a person who lifts heavy weights, especially a barbell, as a sport or to get stronger.
its sense in the lessons: In PE and sport, weightlifting is an Olympic sport with lifts called the snatch and the clean and jerk. In maths problems, weightlifters lift kilograms and you add the plates: the bar plus the discs on each side. In health lessons, children learn safe exercise; heavy lifting needs a trained coach. Phrases: «Olympic weightlifter», «a strong weightlifter».
