examples from the lessons: The weightlifter raised the heavy bar above her head. | Olympic weightlifters compete in different weight classes. | The weightlifter chalked his hands before the lift. | A weightlifter lifted 100 kg: a 20 kg bar plus 40 kg on each side. | My uncle is a weightlifter and goes to the gym every day. | The circus strongman was a famous weightlifter.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word. Countable. Maths: total weight = bar + plates on both sides, e.g. 20 kg + 2 × 25 kg = 70 kg. Children should not lift heavy weights without a trained coach.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A wether is a male sheep (or goat) that has been castrated, so it cannot become a father; farmers keep wethers for wool or meat.
its sense in the lessons: In farming lessons and old country stories, «wether» is one of the words for sheep: ewe (female), ram (male), lamb (young), wether (castrated male). The word «bellwether» comes from a wether wearing a bell that led the flock; today a «bellwether» is something that shows which way things are going. Phrases: «a flock of wethers», «bellwether».
examples from the lessons: The farmer kept the wethers for their wool. | A ewe is a female sheep, a ram is a male, and a wether is a castrated male. | The old shepherd hung a bell on the leading wether. | Wethers are usually calmer than rams. | The wethers grazed on the hillside. | This town is a bellwether: whoever wins here often wins the election.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Say «WETH-er», with the soft «th» as in «the». Homophone trap: «wether» (sheep), «weather» (rain, sun), «whether» (if) — all sound the same. A rare farming word.

part of speech: verb (whimper, whimpers, whimpered, whimpering); noun (a whimper, whimpers)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To whimper means to make small, weak crying sounds because you are scared, hurt or sad. 2) A whimper is such a small, quiet cry. 3) «Not with a bang but a whimper» means ending quietly and weakly, not in a big way.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, puppies, babies and frightened characters whimper; the word tells the reader someone is scared or in pain but trying to be quiet. In everyday life, a whimpering dog may be hurt or lonely. Phrases: «whimper softly», «without a whimper» (without complaining).
examples from the lessons: The puppy whimpered at the door. | The little boy whimpered when he grazed his knee. | We heard a whimper from under the bed. | The lost kitten was whimpering in the rain. | She had the injection without a whimper. | The storm ended not with a bang but a whimper.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: whimpered. The «wh» is said like «w». A whimper is quieter than a sob or a wail. «Without a whimper» = without complaining.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Wickedness is being very bad, cruel or evil. 2) (church, Bible) In the Bible and church, wickedness means sin and doing evil against God and other people.
its sense in the lessons: In fairy tales and stories, the wickedness of witches, stepmothers and villains is punished in the end. In church and Bible lessons, the prophets spoke out against wickedness, and Christians believe God forgives those who turn away from it. In ethics lessons, pupils think about what makes an act wicked. Phrases: «the wickedness of», «turn from wickedness».
examples from the lessons: The witch's wickedness was finally punished. | The story is about good beating wickedness. | (Bible) In the story of Noah, God saw great wickedness on the earth. | Hurting animals for fun is pure wickedness. | (church) The vicar spoke about turning away from wickedness. | The king was famous for his cruelty and wickedness.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. From «wicked» + «-ness». Trap: in slang, «wicked» can mean «great» («That skateboard is wicked!»), but «wickedness» always means real evil. Strong, rather old-fashioned word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Widespread means found in many places or among many people: «widespread flooding», «a widespread belief».
its sense in the lessons: In geography and science, widespread species live in many countries; widespread rain or snow covers a big area on the weather map. In news and history, widespread illness, damage or protest affects many people. In lessons on myths, «a widespread myth» is something many people wrongly believe. Phrases: «widespread damage», «widespread support», «a widespread myth».
examples from the lessons: The storm caused widespread damage across the country. | Robins are widespread in Britain and Ireland. | There was widespread excitement about the new playground. | It is a widespread myth that goldfish only remember things for three seconds. | Widespread snow closed many schools. | The idea has widespread support among parents.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word: widespread. Adjective, usually before a noun or after «is». Similar: common, extensive. In surveys, «widespread» suggests a large part of the group, but not everyone.

part of speech: verb (wilt, wilts, wilted, wilting); old verb form (thou wilt)
meaning for a pupil: 1) When a plant wilts, it droops and becomes soft and floppy, usually because it needs water or is too hot. 2) When a person wilts, they become tired and weak, especially in heat. 3) (old, Bible) «Thou wilt» is an old way of saying «you will», used in old Bibles and poems.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on plants, wilting shows a plant has lost water; watering makes it stand up again because water fills its cells. In everyday life, people wilt in hot weather. In church and old texts (the King James Bible), «thou wilt» means «you will» or «you want to». Phrases: «wilt in the heat», «a wilted lettuce», «not your will but thine» in prayers.
examples from the lessons: The flowers wilted because I forgot to water them. | We wilted in the hot sun at sports day. | A wilted lettuce goes crisp again in cold water. | The plant wilts in the afternoon and recovers in the evening. | The football team wilted in the second half. | (Bible, old) «If thou wilt, thou canst make me clean,» said the man to Jesus.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: wilted. «Thou wilt» is an old form of «will» used only in old texts. Science: wilting happens because the plant's cells lose water and go soft; it is a sign, not always death.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Wit is the ability to say clever and funny things quickly. 2) A wit is a person who is clever and funny with words. 3) Wits (plural) are your ability to think clearly and quickly: «keep your wits about you». 4) (old) «To wit» is an old, formal way of saying «that is to say» or «namely».
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons, writers and characters show wit through puns, jokes and quick answers; Oscar Wilde was a famous wit. In safety lessons, «keep your wits about you» means stay alert. In olympiad and puzzle work, wit means quick, clever thinking. Phrases: «quick wit», «at your wits' end» (so worried you don't know what to do), «scared out of your wits», «battle of wits», «live on your wits».
examples from the lessons: Her quick wit made the whole class laugh. | Oscar Wilde was a famous wit. | Keep your wits about you when crossing busy roads. | Mum was at her wits' end when the dog ran away. | The ghost story scared me out of my wits. | The puzzle was a real battle of wits. | (old, formal) There were three winners, to wit: Ava, Ben and Chloe.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Wit» (cleverness, uncountable) vs «wits» (your mind, plural). Apostrophe: «at your wits' end» (plural wits). Adjective: witty (funny and clever). «Witless» means stupid. Not the same as «with»: wit has no «h».

meaning for a pupil: 1) The withers are the highest point of a horse's back, the ridge between its shoulder blades; horses are measured to the withers. 2) «Withers» is also the form of the verb «wither»: a plant withers when it dries up and dies.
its sense in the lessons: In riding and farm life, horses and ponies are measured in «hands» from the ground to the withers (one hand = 4 inches, about 10 cm). In science, a plant that withers is drying out. In stories, «withers» (verb) describes plants, hope or old age fading. Phrases: «height at the withers», «withers away».
examples from the lessons: The pony is 13 hands high at the withers. | The saddle should not press on the horse's withers. | The vet felt the withers of the horse to check for pain. | Without rain, the grass withers and turns brown. | A flower withers if you leave it out of water. | My pony is 12 hands at the withers, so 12 × 4 = 48 inches tall.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Horse sense: plural only, «the withers». Maths: horse height in hands — 1 hand = 4 inches; a pony of 14.2 hands is 14 × 4 + 2 = 58 inches (the number after the dot is inches, not tenths). Verb: wither, withers, withered, withering.

part of speech: verb form (withhold, withholds, withheld, withholding); noun (withholding — money, law)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Withholding means keeping something back and not giving it, when it was expected: «withholding information». 2) (money) In some countries, especially the US, «withholding» is tax taken from your pay before you get it.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and police shows, withholding the truth or evidence is a kind of dishonesty. In everyday life and money, parents might be withholding pocket money as a punishment; workers' pay slips show tax withheld. In law, withholding evidence from police can be a crime. Phrases: «withholding information», «withholding payment», «withholding tax».
examples from the lessons: The witness was accused of withholding information from the police. | The builders are withholding the keys until the bill is paid. | Mum is withholding my pocket money until I tidy my room. | Withholding the truth can be a kind of lie. | The shop is withholding payment because the order was wrong. | Dad's pay slip shows how much tax was withheld.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Withhold» is irregular: withhold, withheld, withheld (like «hold, held»). Double «h»: with-hold. Maths: pay after withholding = gross pay − tax withheld, e.g. $500 − $80 = $420.

part of speech: proper noun (Worcestershire — a county); noun (Worcestershire sauce)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Worcestershire is a county in the West Midlands of England; its main city is Worcester. 2) Worcestershire sauce is a dark, tangy, spicy sauce first made in Worcester, used on food and in cooking.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons, Worcestershire is one of the English counties, with the River Severn and the Malvern Hills. In everyday life and cooking, Worcestershire sauce goes in stews, cheese on toast and a Caesar salad. The name is a famous spelling and pronunciation puzzle for children and visitors. Phrases: «Worcestershire sauce», «in Worcestershire».
examples from the lessons: Worcestershire is a county in the middle of England. | Dad shakes Worcestershire sauce onto his cheese on toast. | My cousins live in a village in Worcestershire. | The River Severn flows through Worcestershire. | Worcestershire sauce was first made in Worcester in the 1830s. | Nobody in our class could spell Worcestershire!
note for the reader of a maths problem: A name: write it with a capital W. Say «WUSS-ter-sher» (UK) or «WUSS-ter-sheer» (US) — not «wor-ces-ter-shire». Many English place names lose letters in speech: Leicester («LES-ter»), Gloucester («GLOSS-ter»). «-shire» means county.

part of speech: noun (wrack — mostly uncountable); verb (wrack — variant of rack)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Wrack is seaweed, especially the brown seaweed that grows on rocks or is washed up on the beach (bladder wrack, toothed wrack). 2) «Wrack and ruin» (also «rack and ruin») means a state of falling to pieces from neglect. 3) Wrack is sometimes used as a spelling of «rack» in «wracked with pain» (tormented by).
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on seashores and rock pools, bladder wrack has air bubbles that help it float in the water. In stories, an old house goes to wrack and ruin. «Wracked with guilt» or «nerve-wracking» describe strong worry or pain. Phrases: «bladder wrack», «wrack and ruin», «wracked with pain», «nerve-wracking».
examples from the lessons: We popped the air bubbles on the bladder wrack in the rock pool. | The tide left a line of wrack along the beach. | The old farmhouse went to wrack and ruin. | She was wracked with worry when her cat went missing. | Crabs hide under the wet wrack on the rocks. | The spelling test was nerve-wracking.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say «rak», the «w» is silent, like «wreck» and «write». «Rack» and «wrack» are both used in «racked/wracked with pain» and «nerve-racking/nerve-wracking»; many style guides prefer «rack» there. Do not confuse with «wreck» (a ruined ship or car).

part of speech: noun (a yoke, yokes); verb (yoke, yokes, yoked, yoking)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A yoke is a wooden bar fixed across the necks of two animals, usually oxen, so they can pull a plough or cart together. 2) A yoke is also a bar across a person's shoulders for carrying two buckets. 3) To yoke (verb) means to join animals with a yoke, or to join two things together. 4) (formal, Bible) A yoke is something that controls people or is a heavy burden: «the yoke of slavery». 5) (Ireland, slang) A «yoke» is any thing or gadget whose name you can't remember.
its sense in the lessons: In history and farming lessons, oxen were yoked to plough fields. In the Bible and church, Jesus says, «My yoke is easy and my burden is light» (Matthew 11:30), meaning following him is not crushing. In history lessons, nations threw off the yoke of an empire. In Irish speech, «Pass me that yoke» is everyday slang. Phrases: «under the yoke of», «throw off the yoke», «yoked together».
examples from the lessons: The farmer put the yoke on the two oxen. | The milkmaid carried two pails on a wooden yoke. | The people threw off the yoke of the cruel king. | (Bible) Jesus said, «My yoke is easy and my burden is light.» | The two horses were yoked together to pull the cart. | (Ireland, slang) «Where's the yoke for the telly?» Dad asked, meaning the remote.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: yoke, yokes. Homophone trap: «yoke» (wooden bar) and «yolk» (the yellow middle of an egg) sound the same, «yoke». The Irish slang sense is informal and friendly.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A zither is a musical instrument with many strings stretched over a flat wooden box; you lay it on a table or your lap and pluck the strings with your fingers or a pick.
its sense in the lessons: In music lessons on string instruments around the world, the zither is found in Austria and Germany (folk music); related zithers include the Chinese guzheng, the Japanese koto and the Finnish kantele. It belongs to the string family because sound comes from vibrating strings. Phrases: «play the zither», «zither music».
examples from the lessons: The man in the Austrian café played the zither. | A zither has dozens of strings over a flat box. | The Chinese guzheng is a kind of zither. | You pluck the zither strings with your fingers. | The film «The Third Man» has famous zither music. | We heard a zither at the folk festival.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Say «ZITH-er» with the «th» as in «this». Science: shorter, tighter or thinner strings give higher notes. It is not a guitar: it has no neck.

part of speech: noun (an abacus; plural abacuses or abaci)
meaning for a pupil: 1) An abacus is a frame with rows of beads that slide along wires or rods, used for counting and doing sums. 2) In buildings, an abacus is the flat slab on top of a column (architecture word).
its sense in the lessons: In maths lessons, the abacus helps children see place value: each row is a place (ones, tens, hundreds), and moving beads shows adding, taking away and carrying. In history, abacuses were used in ancient Mesopotamia, Greece, Rome and China; the Chinese suanpan and Japanese soroban are still used. Phrases: «count on an abacus», «move the beads».
examples from the lessons: We used an abacus to add 27 and 15. | On the abacus, the top row shows hundreds and the bottom row shows ones. | Some children in Japan learn very fast mental maths with a soroban abacus. | The abacus was used long before calculators. | Move three beads to the left to add three. | My little brother counts the coloured beads on his toy abacus.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: abacuses (most common) or abaci (formal). Say «AB-a-kus», stress on the first syllable. Maths: on a place-value abacus, each bead on the tens rod is worth 10, so 3 beads on tens and 4 on ones = 34; ten beads on one row are swapped for one bead on the next row up (carrying).

meaning for a pupil: 1) To abate means to become less strong or less in amount: «The storm abated.» 2) (formal, law) To abate something means to make it less or put an end to it: «abate the noise».
its sense in the lessons: In stories and weather reports, storms, winds, floods and pain abate; the word tells the reader the danger is passing. In formal writing and exams, it is a stiff word for «die down». In law, a council can order a nuisance (noise, smoke) to be abated. Phrases: «the storm abated», «show no signs of abating», «unabated» (still as strong).
examples from the lessons: We waited in the hut until the storm abated. | The floods began to abate after three days. | Her fever abated during the night. | The noise from the party showed no signs of abating. | When the wind abated, the boats sailed out again. | The fighting continued unabated.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: abated, abating. Formal; in everyday talk say «die down», «ease off». Opposite: increase, grow. «Unabated» means not getting weaker.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Abdication is when a king, queen or other ruler gives up the throne of their own free will. 2) (formal) Abdication of a duty or responsibility means failing to do what you should do, as if giving it up.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, the famous abdication in Britain is that of King Edward VIII in 1936, who gave up the throne to marry Wallis Simpson, an American divorcee; his brother became George VI. Other monarchs have abdicated too, like Queen Beatrix of the Netherlands (2013). In formal speech, «an abdication of responsibility» is a strong criticism. Phrases: «the abdication crisis», «abdication of responsibility».
examples from the lessons: The abdication of Edward VIII shocked Britain in 1936. | After the king's abdication, his brother was crowned. | The queen announced her abdication on television. | Leaving the little ones alone was an abdication of responsibility. | The history book has a whole chapter on the abdication crisis. | Her abdication let her son become king.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Verb: abdicate (abdicated, abdicating). Say «ab-di-KAY-shun». A ruler who is forced off the throne is «deposed» or «overthrown»; abdication means they give it up themselves (though sometimes under pressure).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Ablaze means burning strongly, on fire: «The barn was ablaze.» 2) Ablaze with light or colour means shining very brightly: «The sky was ablaze with fireworks.» 3) Ablaze with a feeling means full of strong feeling: «eyes ablaze with anger».
its sense in the lessons: In news and stories, «ablaze» describes fires (a house, a forest, a ship) and tells the reader of danger; in fire safety lessons, if a building is ablaze, get out, stay out and call the fire brigade. In descriptive writing, a garden «ablaze with colour» or a city «ablaze with lights» is beautiful. Phrases: «set ablaze», «ablaze with».
examples from the lessons: The old barn was ablaze by the time the firefighters arrived. | Lightning set the forest ablaze. | The sky was ablaze with fireworks on Bonfire Night. | In autumn the trees are ablaze with red and gold. | Her eyes were ablaze with excitement. | The city was ablaze with Christmas lights.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually after a verb: «the house was ablaze», not «an ablaze house». Say «a-BLAZE». Fire safety: never go back into a burning building.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To abound means to exist in large numbers or amounts: «Rabbits abound in these fields.» 2) To abound in or with something means to have lots of it: «The river abounds with fish.»
its sense in the lessons: In geography and science, it describes places rich in plants, animals or resources. In formal writing and exams, «Examples abound» means there are many examples. In stories, «rumours abounded» means people were saying lots of things. Phrases: «abound in», «abound with», «rumours abound».
examples from the lessons: Wildflowers abound in the meadow in June. | The Great Barrier Reef abounds with colourful fish. | Rumours abounded about the new teacher. | Stories about the old castle abound in the village. | Mistakes abound in his homework. | Opportunities abound for children who love sport here.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: abounded. Formal word; in everyday talk say «there are lots of». Adjective: abundant (plentiful); noun: abundance.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Abracadabra is a magic word said by magicians when they do a trick, as if it makes the magic happen. 2) (informal) Abracadabra also means words that sound clever or mysterious but make no sense.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, shows and children's magic tricks, «Abracadabra!» is said with a wave of a wand before a rabbit comes out of a hat. In history, it was once written on charms in ancient Rome to protect against illness; it is a very old word. In everyday life, «it's all abracadabra to me» means I don't understand it. Phrases: «say abracadabra».
examples from the lessons: «Abracadabra!» said the magician, and the coin vanished. | My little sister waved her wand and shouted «Abracadabra!» | At the party the magician pulled a rabbit from his hat after saying abracadabra. | Long ago, people wrote abracadabra on charms to keep sickness away. | The instructions were pure abracadabra to Grandad. | Saying abracadabra didn't make my homework disappear!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Not a real spell: magic tricks work by skill and clever hiding, not by words. Say «ab-ra-ka-DAB-ra». Nobody is sure where the word comes from.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To abrade means to scrape or wear away the surface of something by rubbing: «The rough rope abraded his hands.»
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography lessons on erosion, rocks are abraded by sand, pebbles and ice carried in wind, rivers, waves and glaciers (abrasion). In first aid, an abraded knee is a graze. In technology, sandpaper abrades wood to make it smooth. Phrases: «abraded skin», «abraded by sand».
examples from the lessons: Wind full of sand abrades the rocks in the desert. | The rough rope abraded his hands. | Pebbles carried by the river abrade the riverbed. | She fell off her bike and abraded her knee. | Sandpaper abrades the wood until it is smooth. | Glaciers abrade the rock beneath them, leaving scratches.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: abraded. Noun: abrasion (a graze, or the wearing away of rock). Adjective: abrasive (rough; also rude and harsh about a person). Formal and scientific; everyday words are «scrape», «graze», «rub».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Abreast means side by side, facing the same way: «three abreast». 2) Abreast of something means level with it: «The car drew abreast of the bus.» 3) To keep abreast of news or changes means to stay up to date with them.
its sense in the lessons: In road safety lessons, cyclists are advised when to ride in single file and when two abreast is allowed (e.g. the UK Highway Code). In PE and marching, pupils walk two abreast. In formal speech, «keep abreast of» means keep informed. Phrases: «two abreast», «draw abreast», «keep abreast of».
examples from the lessons: We walked to the museum two abreast. | The cyclists rode three abreast and blocked the lane. | The runner drew abreast of the leader on the last lap. | Dad reads the news to keep abreast of what's happening. | The ships sailed abreast across the bay. | Teachers keep abreast of new ideas in teaching.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb. Say «a-BREST». «Two abreast» = two side by side: a group of 20 walking two abreast makes 10 rows (20 ÷ 2). «Keep abreast of» is formal.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) To abscise means for a plant to drop a leaf, flower or fruit by forming a special layer of cells where it joins the stem. 2) (formal) To abscise also means to cut something off.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on plants and seasons, trees abscise their leaves in autumn: a layer of cells (the abscission layer) forms at the bottom of the leaf stalk, and the leaf falls. It is a rare, technical word; everyday English says «drop» or «shed». Phrases: «abscise leaves», «abscission layer».
examples from the lessons: In autumn, oak and maple trees abscise their leaves. | The plant abscises flowers that were not pollinated. | A corky layer forms before the leaf is abscised. | Some trees abscise small fruits when it is too dry. | Scientists study how plants decide when to abscise their leaves. | Evergreen trees abscise old needles a few at a time.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Rare technical word. Say «ab-SIZE». Noun: abscission (ab-SIZH-un). Not to be confused with «abscess» (a painful swelling full of pus) or «scissors», though «-scis-» comes from the same Latin root meaning «cut».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To abscond means to leave secretly and suddenly, especially to escape from somewhere or to avoid being caught. 2) To abscond with something means to run away with money or things that are not yours.
its sense in the lessons: In news and police reports, prisoners or thieves abscond; a treasurer may abscond with club funds. In stories, it is a dramatic, formal word for running off. In everyday talk, children say «run off» or «do a runner» (UK informal). Phrases: «abscond with», «abscond from».
examples from the lessons: The thief absconded with the cash box. | Two prisoners absconded from the open prison. | The club treasurer absconded with all the money. | (jokey) Our dog absconded with the Sunday roast. | The man absconded before the police arrived. | The puppy absconded with my sock.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: absconded. Formal and serious; often used jokingly about pets and small thefts. Say «ab-SKOND».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Abstemious means eating and drinking very little, especially not much rich food or alcohol; holding yourself back from pleasures.
its sense in the lessons: In formal writing, history and religious stories, monks, saints and some famous people lived abstemious lives. In health lessons, the word links to self-control and moderation. In church life, fasting in Lent is an abstemious practice. Phrases: «an abstemious life», «abstemious habits».
examples from the lessons: The old monk lived an abstemious life of bread and water. | Grandad is abstemious and never drinks alcohol. | She was abstemious at the party and had only one small cake. | During Lent some Christians are more abstemious and give up treats. | The athlete kept to an abstemious diet before the race. | He was too abstemious to have a second helping.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal. Say «ab-STEE-mee-us». Fun fact: «abstemious» and «facetious» contain all five vowels a, e, i, o, u in order — a favourite puzzle and olympiad fact. Related: abstain (choose not to do or have something).

meaning for a pupil: 1) An abutment is a strong structure of stone, concrete or brick at each end of a bridge or arch that holds it up and takes its weight. 2) An abutment is also the place where two things touch or join.
its sense in the lessons: In science and technology lessons on bridges and structures, abutments at each end push back against the forces of an arch bridge so it does not spread apart; pupils build bridges and learn about forces. Phrases: «bridge abutment», «stone abutments».
examples from the lessons: The stone abutments hold up both ends of the bridge. | Floodwater damaged the abutment, so the bridge was closed. | An arch pushes outwards, so it needs strong abutments. | In our bridge project, we used blocks as abutments. | The old Roman bridge still rests on its original abutments. | Engineers checked the abutments for cracks.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Say «a-BUT-ment». From the verb «abut» (to touch along an edge: «our garden abuts the park»). Technical word in building and engineering.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (music) An accompaniment is music played to support a singer or another instrument, like piano music behind a song. 2) An accompaniment is something that goes well with something else, especially food: «Chips are a good accompaniment to fish.» 3) «To the accompaniment of» means while a sound is going on: «to the accompaniment of cheers».
its sense in the lessons: In music lessons, the melody is the tune and the accompaniment supports it (chords, rhythm); a pianist accompanies the choir. In cooking and menus, sauces and side dishes are accompaniments. In stories, things happen «to the accompaniment of» thunder or laughter. Phrases: «piano accompaniment», «without accompaniment» (a cappella), «to the accompaniment of».
examples from the lessons: The choir sang with a piano accompaniment. | Our teacher played the guitar accompaniment while we sang. | Gravy is the perfect accompaniment to roast beef. | The team walked out to the accompaniment of loud cheers. | She sang without accompaniment, all alone. | Rice is a tasty accompaniment to curry.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Long spelling: ac-com-pan-i-ment (the «y» of «accompany» changes to «i»). Verb: accompany; a person who plays it is an accompanist. Singing «a cappella» means without instrumental accompaniment.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An accomplice is a person who helps someone else do something wrong or commit a crime.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, detective books and the news, the thief has an accomplice who keeps watch or drives the car. In law, an accomplice can also be punished. In ethics and friendship lessons, being someone's accomplice in teasing or cheating makes you part of it. Phrases: «an accomplice in», «his accomplice».
examples from the lessons: The robber's accomplice waited in the getaway car. | The police arrested the thief and his accomplice. | I won't be your accomplice in hiding Mum's birthday cake. | Laughing along with a bully can make you an accomplice. | (jokey) The dog was my accomplice in the great biscuit raid. | The detective guessed that the butler had an accomplice.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Say «a-KOM-plis». Do not confuse with «accomplish» (to succeed in doing something). An accomplice is a helper in wrongdoing; for a helper in good things say «partner» or «helper».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Accountability means being responsible for what you do and being ready to explain it and accept the results: «taking accountability for a mistake». 2) (formal) In government and work, accountability means that people in charge must explain their decisions to others and can be held to blame.
its sense in the lessons: In ethics and citizenship lessons, accountability is part of fairness: leaders answer to voters, schools to inspectors, children to their families. In everyday life, owning up to a mistake shows accountability. Phrases: «take accountability», «hold someone to account», «accountability for».
examples from the lessons: Owning up to breaking the vase showed real accountability. | Voters want accountability from their leaders. | Our class has a rota so there is accountability for tidying up. | The coach talked about accountability: everyone is responsible for the team. | The report called for more accountability in the council. | Taking accountability means saying sorry and fixing things.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. From «accountable» (responsible, able to be asked to explain). Formal; everyday talk says «owning up», «taking responsibility». Not about money, though it comes from the same word as «account».

meaning for a pupil: 1) An accountant is a person whose job is to keep and check the money records of a business or person, work out taxes and give advice about money.
its sense in the lessons: In money and careers lessons, accountants keep track of income (money in) and expenses (money out), and check that the numbers add up. In everyday life, families and small businesses use an accountant at tax time. Phrases: «a chartered accountant» (UK), «a certified public accountant / CPA» (US), «see an accountant».
examples from the lessons: My aunt is an accountant and loves working with numbers. | The accountant checked that the shop's money added up. | Dad sees an accountant once a year about his taxes. | An accountant needs to be good at maths and careful. | The club's accountant showed that we made a profit of £200. | She trained to be an accountant after university.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable, «an accountant». Double «c»: ac-coun-tant. Maths: accountants work with profit = money in − money out. The work is called accountancy (UK) or accounting (US).

meaning for a pupil: 1) In grammar, the accusative (or accusative case) is the form of a noun or pronoun used when it is the object of a verb, the one the action is done to. 2) In English we see it only in pronouns: «me, him, her, us, them, whom» (for example, «She saw him»).
its sense in the lessons: In grammar and language lessons (English, Latin, German, Russian, Ukrainian), pupils learn that many languages change word endings for the accusative; in German, «der Hund» (the dog) becomes «den Hund» when it is the object. In English, «He saw me» (not «He saw I») shows the same idea. Phrases: «in the accusative», «accusative case».
examples from the lessons: In «The dog bit him», «him» is in the accusative. | In German, «der» changes to «den» in the accusative. | Latin nouns have different endings in the accusative. | «Whom» is the accusative form of «who». | Our language teacher drew a table of nominative and accusative pronouns. | In Ukrainian the accusative of «книга» (book) is «книгу».
note for the reader of a maths problem: Grammar word. Say «a-KYOO-za-tiv». English grammar books often call it the «object case» or «objective». Partner: the nominative (the subject form: I, he, she, we, they). It has nothing to do with accusing anyone, though it comes from the same Latin word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An accuser is a person who says that someone else has done something wrong or committed a crime. 2) (Bible) In the Bible, «the accuser» is a name for Satan, who accuses people before God.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, courtroom scenes and history, the accuser faces the accused (the person blamed); a fair trial lets both sides speak. In church and Bible lessons, the Book of Revelation calls Satan «the accuser». Phrases: «face your accuser», «the accuser and the accused».
examples from the lessons: The accuser told the judge what she had seen. | In a fair trial, the accused can answer the accuser. | The boy's accusers said he had taken the ball. | It turned out that the accuser had lied. | (Bible) Revelation calls Satan «the accuser of our brothers». | The accuser pointed at the empty biscuit tin and then at me.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. From «accuse» + «-er». Opposite in a case: the accused (the person blamed). Being accused is not the same as being guilty: in law a person is innocent until proven guilty.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To accustom yourself to something means to get used to it: «It took a week to accustom myself to the new school.» 2) Accustomed to (adjective) means used to: «I'm accustomed to early mornings.» 3) (formal) Accustomed also means usual: «She sat in her accustomed seat.»
its sense in the lessons: In stories and formal writing, characters become accustomed to new places, the dark, the cold or a new family. In science, eyes become accustomed to the dark (they adjust). Phrases: «accustom yourself to», «become accustomed to», «grow accustomed to».
examples from the lessons: It took me a few days to accustom myself to the new timetable. | Our eyes slowly became accustomed to the dark. | The puppy soon grew accustomed to its new home. | Grandpa sat in his accustomed chair by the fire. | The family from Spain became accustomed to the rain in Scotland. | She is accustomed to getting up at six.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb, usually used with «yourself» or in «accustomed to». After «to», use a noun or «-ing»: «accustomed to waking up», not «to wake up». Double «c»: ac-cus-tom. Opposite: unaccustomed. Everyday words: «get used to», «used to».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) The acme is the highest point of something: the peak of success, skill or perfection: «the acme of good manners». 2) Acme is also a name used by many businesses, and is the joke company in Road Runner cartoons.
its sense in the lessons: In formal writing and old books, «the acme of» means the very best example. In cartoons, Wile E. Coyote buys gadgets from the ACME company, which always fail — a funny name everyone knows. Phrases: «the acme of», «at the acme of his career».
examples from the lessons: The castle was the acme of medieval building. | Her performance was the acme of her career. | The cake was the acme of perfection. | Wile E. Coyote's ACME rocket blew up again. | Many old shops were called «Acme» so they would come first in phone books. | Winning the cup was the acme of the team's season.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; usually «the acme of». Say «AK-mee». From Greek, meaning «point» or «peak». Similar: peak, height, pinnacle. Do not confuse with «acne» (spots) — one letter different.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Acne is a skin condition that causes spots, blackheads and pimples, especially on the face, back and chest; it is very common in teenagers.
its sense in the lessons: In health lessons on puberty and growing up, acne is explained as the result of changes in hormones that make the skin produce more oil, which can block pores. In everyday life, many teenagers have acne and can get help from a doctor or pharmacist; kindness matters, because teasing about spots hurts. Phrases: «have acne», «acne cream», «teenage acne».
examples from the lessons: Lots of teenagers get acne during puberty. | My older brother uses a cream for his acne. | Acne is not caused by being dirty. | The doctor gave my cousin medicine for her acne. | Washing your face gently twice a day can help with acne. | Never tease someone about their acne.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «he has acne», not «an acne». Say «AK-nee». Myths: acne is not caused by dirty skin and is not catching; chocolate is not proven to cause it. Do not squeeze spots — it can leave scars. Do not confuse with «acme» (peak).

part of speech: noun (acoustics — plural for a room; uncountable for the science)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The acoustics of a room or building are the way sound travels and is heard in it: good acoustics mean music and speech sound clear. 2) Acoustics is the science of sound: how it is made, how it travels and how we hear it.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on sound, pupils learn that hard surfaces reflect sound (echoes) and soft ones (curtains, carpets) absorb it; that is why halls and theatres are built with care. In music, concert halls are praised for their acoustics. Phrases: «good acoustics», «poor acoustics», «the acoustics of the hall».
examples from the lessons: The cathedral has amazing acoustics, so the choir sounds beautiful. | The school hall has poor acoustics; it's hard to hear at the back. | Acoustics is the science of sound. | Soft curtains improve the acoustics of a room. | The Sydney Opera House was designed with special attention to acoustics. | In the empty gym, the acoustics made our voices echo.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Grammar trap: about a place it is plural — «The acoustics are good»; as the name of a science it is singular — «Acoustics is a branch of physics». Say «a-KOO-stiks». Adjective: acoustic (as in an acoustic guitar, which is not electric).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To acquiesce means to agree to something quietly, or to accept it without arguing, even if you are not keen: «She acquiesced to the plan.»
its sense in the lessons: In formal writing, history and exam texts, people acquiesce to rules, demands or decisions. In stories, a character acquiesces with a sigh. In everyday talk people say «go along with», «give in», «agree». Phrases: «acquiesce in», «acquiesce to».
examples from the lessons: After a long argument, Dad acquiesced and let us stay up late. | The king acquiesced to the barons' demands. | She acquiesced with a nod, though she didn't really agree. | My brother acquiesced in the plan to share the bike. | The council acquiesced to the parents' request for a crossing. | The cat acquiesced to being picked up — for once.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal, tricky spelling: ac-qui-esce (with «cq» and «sce»). Say «ak-wee-ESS». Followed by «in» or «to». Acquiescing is quiet agreement; it is weaker than wholehearted agreement.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Acquiescence is the act of accepting or agreeing to something quietly, without protest, even if you are not keen.
its sense in the lessons: In history and formal writing, «the acquiescence of the people» means they did not resist a ruler or law. In ethics lessons, pupils think about when silent acquiescence to unfairness is wrong and when speaking up matters. Phrases: «with the acquiescence of», «silent acquiescence», «nod of acquiescence».
examples from the lessons: He gave a nod of acquiescence. | The plan went ahead with the acquiescence of the parents. | Silent acquiescence can let bullying continue. | The teacher took our silence as acquiescence. | Her acquiescence surprised everyone, because she usually argued. | The new rule was accepted with grumbling acquiescence.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Say «ak-wee-ESS-ence». Spelling: ac-qui-es-cence (with «cq» and «sc»). Verb: acquiesce. Adjective: acquiescent. Acquiescence is not enthusiastic agreement — it is going along with something.

part of speech: adjective (activated); verb form, the past of «activate» (activate, activates, activated, activating)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Switched on or made to start working: an activated alarm or card is now working. 2) (science) Made ready to act or react, like activated charcoal, which is treated so it soaks up more stuff. 3) Started or called into action: a plan, a team or a body's defences can be activated.
its sense in the lessons: In science it describes something set off, like a switch, a sensor, a chemical or the immune system; in everyday life cards, phones and alarms are activated; in safety talk alarms and sprinklers are activated by smoke or heat; in stories a trap or a robot «activated» means something is about to happen. Phrases: «activated by», «voice-activated», «motion-activated», «activated charcoal».
examples from the lessons: The fire alarm was activated by burnt toast. | Mum activated her new bank card by phone. | The motion-activated light came on when the fox walked past. | Once the robot was activated, its eyes glowed blue. | Activated charcoal is used in some water filters. | The rescue team was activated after the storm. | Our class tablets were activated with the school's code. | The trap was activated when the explorer stepped on the stone.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Used as a past form («the alarm was activated») and as an adjective («an activated card»). Opposite: deactivated. Spelling: activate + d = activated. Do not confuse with «active» (doing things) — activated means it has been switched on.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To give something as a reason or proof in an argument: to adduce evidence is to bring it forward to support what you say.
its sense in the lessons: A stiff, formal word met in law, essays, exam answers and old books; in everyday talk people say «give», «point to» or «bring up» instead. In a story, a lawyer or professor may «adduce» facts. Phrases: «adduce evidence», «adduce reasons», «adduce examples».
examples from the lessons: The lawyer adduced new evidence in court. | In her essay she adduced three reasons for saving the woods. | Scientists must adduce data to back up their claims. | He could adduce no proof that the dog ate his homework. | The teacher asked us to adduce examples from the text. | Several facts were adduced to show the bridge was unsafe.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A formal verb; pupils can use «give» or «present». Do not confuse with «deduce» (work something out) or «induce» (cause or persuade). Past: adduced.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Well enough, enough for what is needed, but not especially well. 2) In a way that is suitable or sufficient for a job.
its sense in the lessons: Used in school reports and rules («adequately prepared»), in science («adequately heated»), and in safety («adequately protected», «adequately supervised»). It means «enough», not «excellent». Phrases: «adequately prepared», «adequately explained», «not adequately».
examples from the lessons: The room was adequately heated, though not cosy. | Make sure you are adequately dressed for the snow. | The plants were not adequately watered, so they drooped. | She answered the question adequately but forgot the units. | The bridge was not adequately checked before the storm. | Children must be adequately supervised near the pool. | Explain your method adequately so the marker can follow it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb of «adequate» (enough). Opposite: inadequately. It does not mean «very well» — a teacher's «adequately» is a middle grade. Spelling: adequate + ly.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) Made of or about body fat: adipose tissue is the fat stored in the body. 2) (formal) Fatty.
its sense in the lessons: Used in biology and medicine lessons about the body: adipose tissue stores energy, keeps us warm and cushions organs. Rarely heard in everyday talk. Phrase: «adipose tissue», «adipose cells».
examples from the lessons: Adipose tissue stores energy for later. | Seals have thick adipose layers to keep warm in icy water. | Under the microscope, adipose cells look like round bubbles. | Bears build up adipose tissue before winter. | Our science sheet labelled the adipose layer under the skin. | Adipose tissue also protects the kidneys like a cushion.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A science word; say «fat» in everyday talk. Body fat is not all bad — some is needed for health. Do not confuse with «adapt» or «adopt».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (a name) A boy's name common in India, from Sanskrit, often taken to mean «the sun». 2) (Hindu belief) In Hindu tradition, the Adityas are a group of gods, and Aditya is a name for the sun god Surya. 3) The name of India's space probe Aditya-L1 that studies the Sun.
its sense in the lessons: Met as a person's name in class lists and stories, and in lessons on Hinduism or space. It is a name, not an ordinary English word.
examples from the lessons: Aditya sits next to me in maths. | Aditya's grandma told us a story from India. | In Hindu tradition, Aditya is a name for the sun. | Aditya-L1 is an Indian spacecraft that watches the Sun. | Aditya scored the winning goal at lunch. | Our teacher asked Aditya to read the poem aloud.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A proper name, so it takes a capital letter: Aditya. Said roughly «a-DIT-ya». Not an English word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (law, formal) The official decision made by a judge or another person in charge after hearing both sides. 2) The act of judging a contest, such as a music, dance or debate competition.
its sense in the lessons: Heard in law and in competitions (eisteddfods, music festivals, debating). In stories, an «adjudication» settles a dispute. Phrases: «under adjudication», «the adjudication panel», «final adjudication».
examples from the lessons: The adjudication of the singing contest took an hour. | After the adjudication, our choir came second. | The dispute went to adjudication. | The adjudication panel praised her poem. | The judge's adjudication ended the long argument. | At the dance festival, adjudications were read out at the end.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable and uncountable. Verb: adjudicate; person: adjudicator. Formal word; in everyday talk say «judging» or «decision».

part of speech: noun (adobe — uncountable for the material; adobes for bricks); proper noun (Adobe, a company)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Mud mixed with straw and dried in the sun to make bricks. 2) A building made of these sun-dried bricks, common in dry places like the south-western USA and Mexico. 3) (a name) Adobe is a software company that makes programs such as Photoshop and the PDF reader.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and history lessons it describes homes of Pueblo peoples and desert towns; in science, adobe keeps houses cool by day and warm at night. In computing, «Adobe» is a company name. Phrases: «adobe brick», «adobe house», «adobe walls».
examples from the lessons: The adobe house stayed cool in the desert heat. | Pueblo people built homes from adobe. | We made tiny adobe bricks from mud and straw in class. | Adobe walls are very thick. | Rain can wear away adobe over time. | Dad opened the file in Adobe Reader. | The old mission church is made of adobe.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Said «a-DOE-bee». Material sense is uncountable («built of adobe»); the company name has a capital A. Not the same as «abode» (home) — letters swapped.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The time of life between being a child and being an adult, roughly the teenage years. 2) An early stage of growth of something, like a country or an idea.
its sense in the lessons: Used in health and science lessons about growing up and puberty, and in stories about teenagers. Phrases: «in adolescence», «during adolescence», «early adolescence».
examples from the lessons: Adolescence is when children grow into adults. | Many changes happen to the body during adolescence. | My uncle says adolescence was his noisiest time. | The book follows a girl through her adolescence. | In early adolescence, sleep needs stay high. | Our health lesson talked about feelings in adolescence.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable. Person: an adolescent. Spelling trap: «sc» in the middle — adole-SC-ence. Starts at about 10–13 and ends at about 18–19 or later.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Someone who loves or admires someone or something very much. 2) (church, old use) Someone who worships.
its sense in the lessons: Rare in everyday speech; found in stories, poems and old books. People more often say «fan» or «admirer».
examples from the lessons: The singer waved to her adorers. | He was a great adorer of cats. | The prince had many adorers at court. | She is a true adorer of chocolate cake. | In the old hymn, the adorers knelt in prayer. | The puppy had a crowd of adorers at the park.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «adore». Formal or old-fashioned; «fan» is the everyday word. Plural: adorers.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Very skilful and clever with the hands or body. 2) Clever and quick at dealing with people or difficult situations.
its sense in the lessons: A book and exam word; in stories it praises a nimble thief, a juggler or a smooth talker. Phrases: «adroit at», «an adroit move», «adroit handling».
examples from the lessons: The juggler was adroit with five balls. | She gave an adroit answer to the tricky question. | The cat made an adroit leap onto the fence. | He is adroit at fixing bikes. | The captain's adroit steering saved the boat. | With adroit fingers she tied the knot.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb: adroitly. Opposite: clumsy, maladroit. Said «a-DROYT».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Progress or improvement in something, such as science or medicine. 2) Moving up to a better job or position; promotion. 3) Helping something move forward.
its sense in the lessons: Used in history and science lessons («advancements in technology»), in talk about jobs («career advancement»). Phrases: «advancement of science», «chances for advancement».
examples from the lessons: The printing press led to the advancement of learning. | Medical advancements have saved many lives. | She worked hard for advancement at her job. | Space travel was a great advancement. | The club is for the advancement of young musicians. | Each advancement in phones made them smaller.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable and uncountable. Related: advance (verb and noun). «Advance» and «advancement» often mean the same; «advance» is more common for progress.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (UK, Australia, old use) A small airfield where planes take off and land, without a big airport building.
its sense in the lessons: Heard in history stories about early flying and war, and in the UK, Australia and New Zealand for small local airfields. In the USA people say «airfield» or «airport».
examples from the lessons: The little plane landed at the country aerodrome. | In the war, pilots flew from an aerodrome in Kent. | Grandad worked at the local aerodrome. | We watched gliders at the aerodrome. | The aerodrome had just one grass runway. | Old maps show an aerodrome where the park is now.
note for the reader of a maths problem: British spelling; the American form «airdrome» is rare. Not the same as a big airport.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An event or happening: the party was a noisy affair. 2) affairs: things you deal with, business or matters, like money affairs or world affairs. 3) A matter that concerns someone: «That's my affair» means it is my business, not yours. 4) A secret romantic relationship between two people when one or both are married to someone else.
its sense in the lessons: In news and social studies: «current affairs», «foreign affairs», «Minister for Foreign Affairs». In stories and everyday talk: «a family affair», «a quiet affair». The romantic sense comes up in grown-up stories and news. Phrases: «current affairs», «state of affairs», «put your affairs in order».
examples from the lessons: The wedding was a small family affair. | We watch current affairs on Friday mornings. | The Minister of Foreign Affairs met other leaders. | What I do at lunch is my own affair. | The whole affair was over in ten minutes. | That's a sorry state of affairs! | Grandpa sorted out his money affairs. | In the story, a royal affair caused a scandal.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; plural «affairs» often means business or matters. Do not confuse with «affect» or «a fair» (a fun fair).

part of speech: verb (affiliate, affiliates, affiliated, affiliating); noun (an affiliate, affiliates)
meaning for a pupil: 1) verb: To join or connect officially with a larger group or organisation. 2) noun: A smaller group, company or person that is officially connected to a bigger one.
its sense in the lessons: Used about clubs, schools, TV channels and companies: a local station is an affiliate of a national network; a club is affiliated to a league. Phrases: «affiliated with/to», «an affiliate of».
examples from the lessons: Our football club is affiliated to the county league. | The local TV station is an affiliate of a big network. | The school is affiliated with the university. | The two charities decided to affiliate. | He is not affiliated with any party. | Each affiliate sends a member to the meeting.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb said «a-FIL-ee-ate», noun often «a-FIL-ee-it». UK often «affiliated to», US «affiliated with». Noun of the action: affiliation.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An official connection with a group, club, party or organisation. 2) The feeling of belonging to a group or the group you belong to.
its sense in the lessons: Used in civics («political affiliation»), religion («religious affiliation»), and on forms. Phrases: «in affiliation with», «party affiliation».
examples from the lessons: The club has an affiliation with the national body. | Her political affiliation was not mentioned. | The census asks about religious affiliation. | The school's affiliation with the museum gives us free trips. | He listed his university affiliation in the paper. | Team shirts show your affiliation.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. From the verb «affiliate». A formal word; everyday: «link», «connection».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A natural liking for or feeling of understanding with someone or something. 2) A close likeness or connection between things. 3) (science) A tendency of substances to join or react with each other.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday and story use, a person «has an affinity for» animals or music. In science, chemicals have an affinity. Phrases: «an affinity for/with», «feel an affinity».
examples from the lessons: She has a real affinity for horses. | I felt an affinity with the lonely boy in the book. | There is an affinity between the two languages. | Water has an affinity for salt, which dissolves in it. | He had an affinity with numbers from a young age. | The two artists share an affinity of style.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable and uncountable; usually «affinity for» or «affinity with». Formal, but common in writing. Do not confuse with «infinity».

part of speech: verb (affix, affixes, affixed, affixing); noun (an affix, affixes)
meaning for a pupil: 1) noun (grammar): A letter group added to a word to change its meaning: a prefix at the start (un-, re-) or a suffix at the end (-ful, -ness). 2) verb (formal): To stick, fix or attach something to something else.
its sense in the lessons: In English and grammar lessons, affixes make new words: un + happy, kind + ness. The formal verb appears on forms and instructions: «affix a stamp». Phrases: «affix a label», «affix a photo».
examples from the lessons: «Un-» and «-ful» are both affixes. | Add an affix to «help» to make «helpful». | Affix a stamp to the envelope. | Please affix your photo here. | The notice was affixed to the door. | In «replay», the affix «re-» means again.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun said «AF-fix», verb «a-FIX». Prefix and suffix are kinds of affix. The verb is formal; say «stick» in everyday talk.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To cause pain, suffering or trouble to someone or something. 2) (often passive) To be afflicted with an illness or problem is to suffer from it.
its sense in the lessons: Formal; met in news, history and stories: diseases, droughts and floods afflict people. Phrases: «afflicted with/by», «afflict a region».
examples from the lessons: Floods afflicted the town every spring. | The plague afflicted much of Europe. | He was afflicted with a terrible cough. | Hunger afflicts millions of people. | The old tree was afflicted by a fungus. | Shyness afflicted her as a child.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: affliction. Used mostly about illness and trouble. Do not confuse with «inflict» (to make someone suffer something: «inflict pain on»).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A list of things to be talked about or done at a meeting. 2) Things someone plans or wants to do: «What's on the agenda today?» 3) A secret aim or plan: a «hidden agenda».
its sense in the lessons: Used in school councils and meetings, in news and politics. Phrases: «on the agenda», «top of the agenda», «hidden agenda», «set the agenda».
examples from the lessons: The first item on the agenda is the school trip. | What's on the agenda for Saturday? | The class council wrote an agenda. | Saving water is high on the agenda. | I think he has a hidden agenda. | The meeting followed the agenda closely. | Lunch is next on the agenda!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; plural «agendas». It comes from Latin and was once plural, but now it is singular in English. In some countries (France, Spain) «agenda» means a diary — a false friend.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To make someone feel worried, nervous or upset. 2) To shake or stir a liquid hard. 3) To argue or campaign publicly to make a change happen.
its sense in the lessons: In science, agitate means shake or stir (washing machines agitate clothes). In history and civics, people agitate for rights. In stories, a character is agitated. Phrases: «agitate for/against».
examples from the lessons: The loud noise agitated the dog. | Agitate the jar to mix the paint. | Workers agitated for better pay. | Don't agitate your sister before bed. | The washing machine agitates the clothes. | Women agitated for the vote.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: agitation; person: agitator. Past: agitated. Formal compared with «upset» or «shake».

part of speech: adjective (agitated, more agitated, most agitated); past of «agitate»
meaning for a pupil: 1) Worried, nervous and upset, unable to keep calm. 2) Shaken or stirred, as a liquid.
its sense in the lessons: In stories it shows a character's feelings: pacing, fidgeting, talking fast. In science it can describe a stirred liquid. Phrases: «get agitated», «agitated about».
examples from the lessons: She grew agitated when the bus was late. | The horse was agitated by the storm. | Grandad gets agitated when he loses his glasses. | He paced up and down, looking agitated. | The agitated water bubbled in the beaker. | Try to calm the agitated puppy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective used for feelings; similar to «anxious», «upset», «worked up». Opposite: calm.

part of speech: verb form (agitating), the -ing form of «agitate»; adjective (agitating — rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Making someone worried or upset. 2) Shaking or stirring a liquid. 3) Campaigning loudly for a change.
its sense in the lessons: Used in history («agitating for reform»), in science («keep agitating the mixture»), and in stories. Phrases: «agitating for».
examples from the lessons: They were agitating for cleaner rivers. | Keep agitating the mixture until it is smooth. | The waiting was agitating for everyone. | Protesters were agitating outside. | The tumble dryer is agitating the clothes. | Stop agitating your brother!
note for the reader of a maths problem: The -ing form of agitate. «Agitating for» something means pushing for it publicly.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Very great pain of the body. 2) Very great worry or sadness of the mind. 3) (informal) Something very annoying or hard: «The waiting was agony!»
its sense in the lessons: In stories and medicine it shows strong pain; in everyday talk people exaggerate («Maths homework is agony»). Phrases: «in agony», «agony aunt» (UK: someone who answers readers' problems in a magazine), «the agony of waiting».
examples from the lessons: He was in agony after breaking his arm. | Waiting for the results was agony. | The agony of losing the final stayed with her. | Call for help if someone is in agony. | My new shoes were agony on the long walk. | The magazine has an agony aunt.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable. Adjective: agonising (UK) / agonizing (US). Stronger than «pain».

meaning for a pupil: 1) About farming, farmland or the people who work on the land.
its sense in the lessons: Used in history and geography: an agrarian society lives mainly by farming. Phrases: «agrarian society», «agrarian reform», «agrarian economy».
examples from the lessons: Long ago, most of Europe was an agrarian society. | Agrarian life follows the seasons. | The country moved from an agrarian economy to factories. | Agrarian reform gave land to farmers. | Many agrarian villages had a market day. | In agrarian times, children helped with the harvest.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal word; everyday: «farming». Opposite in history: industrial.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a pleasant, nice way. 2) In a friendly, willing way.
its sense in the lessons: Used in stories and polite speech: «agreeably surprised» means pleasantly surprised. Phrases: «agreeably surprised», «agreeably warm».
examples from the lessons: The water was agreeably warm. | She smiled agreeably at the visitors. | We were agreeably surprised by the test results. | The room was agreeably quiet. | He nodded agreeably and passed the salt. | The day passed agreeably at the beach.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «agreeable». Not the same as «in agreement»; it means pleasantly. Spelling: agreeab-ly (drop the e).

meaning for a pupil: 1) The movement of air from one place to another, for example through a room, a machine or around a wing.
its sense in the lessons: In science and design lessons: airflow around a plane wing gives lift; airflow cools computers and keeps rooms fresh. In safety, good airflow (ventilation) stops fumes building up. Phrases: «good airflow», «block the airflow».
examples from the lessons: Open a window to improve the airflow. | Don't block the airflow to the laptop fan. | Airflow over the wing helps the plane lift. | We tested airflow with streamers in a wind tunnel. | The fridge needs airflow at the back. | Good airflow keeps the classroom fresh.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable. One word. Related: ventilation, draught (UK) / draft (US).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Similar to or like something: «akin to» means much the same as. 2) (old use) Related by family.
its sense in the lessons: Used in writing and explanations to compare: «a feeling akin to fear». Almost always in «akin to».
examples from the lessons: A dolphin's clicks are akin to a language. | The feeling was akin to joy. | Lions are akin to house cats. | Her voice was akin to a whisper. | Riding a bike is akin to swimming: once learned, never forgotten. | This game is akin to chess.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Used after a verb, not before a noun: «It is akin to…», not «an akin thing». Formal-ish; everyday: «like», «similar to».

meaning for a pupil: 1) adjective: From or about Alaska, the largest state of the USA, in the far north-west of North America. 2) noun: A person who lives in or comes from Alaska.
its sense in the lessons: Used in geography lessons and nature stories: Alaskan bears, salmon, glaciers, the Alaskan Malamute dog. Phrases: «Alaskan wilderness», «Alaskan Malamute».
examples from the lessons: Alaskan winters are long and dark. | The Alaskan brown bear catches salmon. | An Alaskan Malamute pulled the sled. | My pen pal is an Alaskan. | Alaskan glaciers are melting faster. | Many Alaskan towns can only be reached by plane.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always a capital A: Alaskan. Alaska became a US state in 1959; the USA bought it from Russia in 1867.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (medicine) A loss of the ability to read, usually after damage to the brain, for example from a stroke, in someone who could read before. 2) (a name) Alexia is a girl's name.
its sense in the lessons: Met in science or health talk about the brain, and as a person's name in class lists and stories. It is not the same as dyslexia.
examples from the lessons: After her stroke, Grandma had alexia for a while. | Alexia means a person who could read loses that skill. | Alexia is in my netball team. | Doctors helped him relearn reading after alexia. | Alexia read her story to the class. | Alexia is rare compared with dyslexia.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Medical word is uncountable; the name takes a capital A. Do not mix up with dyslexia, which is a lifelong difference in learning to read.

part of speech: adjective (Algonquian); noun (Algonquian — the language family; Algonquians — the peoples)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A large family of Native American and First Nations languages of North America, including Cree, Ojibwe, Mi'kmaq and Blackfoot. 2) Describing the peoples who speak these languages.
its sense in the lessons: Used in history, geography and language lessons about Canada and the USA. Many English words came from Algonquian languages: moose, skunk, raccoon, moccasin.
examples from the lessons: Cree is an Algonquian language. | The word «moose» comes from an Algonquian language. | Algonquian peoples lived across a huge area of North America. | We learned Algonquian place names in Canada. | Ojibwe and Mi'kmaq are Algonquian too. | Many Algonquian languages are still spoken today.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital A. Not the same as «Algonquin», one people within the family. Said «al-GONG-kwee-an».

meaning for a pupil: 1) To make pain, a problem or suffering less bad or easier to bear.
its sense in the lessons: Formal; met in health, news and essays: medicine alleviates pain, aid alleviates hunger. Phrases: «alleviate pain», «alleviate poverty», «alleviate boredom».
examples from the lessons: This cream alleviates itching. | Planting trees can alleviate flooding. | Food parcels alleviated hunger in the town. | A cool cloth alleviated her headache. | Music alleviated the boredom of the long drive. | The new road alleviated traffic jams.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: alleviation. It makes things less bad, not gone completely. Everyday words: ease, relieve.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A narrow path or lane between or behind buildings.
its sense in the lessons: In stories alleyways are often dark, secret or spooky; in safety lessons children are told to avoid dark alleyways alone. Also a short cut in towns.
examples from the lessons: We took the alleyway behind the shops. | The cat disappeared down the alleyway. | Stay on the main road, not in dark alleyways. | The bins are kept in the alleyway. | The detective followed footprints into the alleyway. | Our street has an alleyway to the park.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Same as «alley». In northern England you may hear «ginnel» or «snicket»; in Scotland «close» or «wynd».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A book published every year with a calendar and facts like sunrise times, tides, the moon's phases and weather predictions. 2) A yearly book of facts and figures about a subject, like sport or a country.
its sense in the lessons: In history, farmers used almanacs to plan planting; Benjamin Franklin wrote «Poor Richard's Almanack». Today almanacs list records and facts. Phrases: «farmer's almanac», «sports almanac».
examples from the lessons: Grandpa checks the almanac for the full moon. | The almanac lists sunrise times for every day. | Benjamin Franklin published a famous almanac. | The football almanac has every score since 1888. | Farmers used almanacs to decide when to plant. | Old almanacs gave weather guesses, not always right.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Old spelling: almanack. Weather predictions in almanacs are not reliable science.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In the order of the letters of the alphabet, from A to Z.
its sense in the lessons: Used in school for ordering names, words in a dictionary, books on shelves, and in computing (sorting). Phrases: «arranged alphabetically», «sort alphabetically».
examples from the lessons: The class list is sorted alphabetically. | Put these words alphabetically: dog, cat, ant. | Library books are shelved alphabetically by author. | A dictionary is arranged alphabetically. | Line up alphabetically by first name. | The computer sorted the files alphabetically.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «alphabet». When two words start with the same letter, look at the second letter (cat before cow). Reverse order is Z to A.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a way that causes great surprise. 2) Very, extremely: «amazingly fast». 3) Used to say something is surprising: «Amazingly, nobody was hurt».
its sense in the lessons: Very common in everyday talk and stories for strong praise or surprise. Phrases: «amazingly good», «amazingly enough».
examples from the lessons: She runs amazingly fast. | Amazingly, the cake didn't burn. | The view was amazingly beautiful. | Amazingly enough, the dog found its way home. | He did amazingly well in the spelling test. | The ant can carry amazingly heavy loads for its size.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «amazing». Overusing it weakens writing; try «remarkably», «surprisingly», «incredibly».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal, medicine) Walking or moving about on foot.
its sense in the lessons: Used by doctors and nurses: after an operation, early ambulation (getting up and walking) helps recovery. Rare in everyday talk.
examples from the lessons: The nurse helped with Grandad's ambulation after surgery. | Early ambulation helps patients heal. | The crutches assist ambulation. | Ambulation was slow after her knee operation. | The physio checked his ambulation in the corridor. | Ambulation means walking.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Related: ambulatory (able to walk). Not connected in meaning to «ambulance», though both come from Latin for walking.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Useful or pleasant things and services in a place, like parks, shops, toilets, a pool or Wi-Fi. 2) (UK, informal) «Public amenities» can mean public toilets.
its sense in the lessons: Used in geography (town amenities), estate agents' adverts and holiday reviews. Phrases: «local amenities», «basic amenities», «close to amenities».
examples from the lessons: The campsite has good amenities: showers and a shop. | Our town needs more amenities for teenagers. | The hotel's amenities include a pool. | Basic amenities like clean water matter most. | The flat is close to local amenities. | The park's amenities include swings and a café.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly used in the plural. Said «a-MEE-ni-teez» (UK also «a-MEN-»). Formal-ish word for facilities.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The main working language of Ethiopia, written in its own script called Ge'ez (Fidel). 2) adjective: About that language.
its sense in the lessons: Met in geography and language lessons about Africa. It is a Semitic language, related to Arabic and Hebrew, with its own alphabet of syllables.
examples from the lessons: Amharic is spoken by millions in Ethiopia. | Amharic uses its own beautiful script. | My friend's mum speaks Amharic at home. | «Selam» is a greeting in Amharic. | Amharic letters stand for whole syllables. | We saw an Amharic sign in the café.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital A. Said «am-HAR-ik». Not an English word but the name of a language.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Friendly, pleasant and easy to like.
its sense in the lessons: In stories it describes a kind, cheerful character; in reports «an amiable chat». Phrases: «an amiable person», «amiable mood».
examples from the lessons: The amiable shopkeeper gave us free sweets. | Our new neighbour seems amiable. | They had an amiable chat over tea. | The giant was amiable, not scary. | She was amiable to everyone in class. | The dog has an amiable nature.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb: amiably. Similar to «friendly», «good-natured». Do not confuse with «amicable» (friendly agreement between groups, «an amicable settlement»).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Making a sound or signal louder or stronger. 2) (formal) Adding more detail to explain something better.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about sound and electricity: speakers and amplifiers give amplification. In English, «amplification» of a point means explaining it more. Phrases: «sound amplification», «needs amplification».
examples from the lessons: The concert used powerful amplification. | A guitar amplifier gives amplification to the strings' sound. | Hearing aids work by amplification. | Your answer needs more amplification. | A cupped hand gives a little amplification to your voice. | The microphone's amplification made her voice boom.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: amplify; machine: amplifier (informal «amp»). Uncountable mostly.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) The size of a wave: how high it rises from its middle line. In sound, bigger amplitude means louder; in light, brighter. 2) (formal) Large size or plenty.
its sense in the lessons: In science and maths, amplitude is half the distance from the top of a wave to its bottom. In sound lessons it is linked to loudness; pitch is linked to frequency. Phrases: «high amplitude», «amplitude of a wave».
examples from the lessons: A loud sound has a big amplitude. | Draw a wave with a small amplitude. | The earthquake's waves had a huge amplitude. | Amplitude is measured from the middle line to the top. | Turning up the volume increases the amplitude. | The amplitude of the swing got smaller as it slowed down.
note for the reader of a maths problem: For numbers: amplitude = (highest point − lowest point) ÷ 2. Trap: amplitude is loudness, not pitch (pitch is frequency).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (medicine) Using medicine so a person feels no pain during an operation, either by putting them to sleep (general) or numbing one part (local). 2) A loss of feeling in the body.
its sense in the lessons: Heard in hospital and dentist stories and health lessons. Phrases: «under anaesthesia», «general anaesthesia», «local anaesthesia».
examples from the lessons: She had her tonsils out under anaesthesia. | The dentist used local anaesthesia, so my tooth went numb. | Anaesthesia was first used in surgery in the 1840s. | General anaesthesia puts you into a deep sleep. | An anaesthetist watches you during anaesthesia. | After anaesthesia, you may feel sleepy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK: anaesthesia, anaesthetic; US: anesthesia, anesthetic. Uncountable. Said «an-is-THEE-zee-a».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Similar in some way, so that it can be compared: «analogous to» something.
its sense in the lessons: Used in science, maths and essays to make comparisons: a heart is analogous to a pump. In biology, analogous parts do the same job but evolved differently, like bird and insect wings.
examples from the lessons: The heart is analogous to a pump. | A school is analogous to a small town. | Bird wings and bat wings do analogous jobs. | This problem is analogous to the one we did yesterday. | Electricity in a wire is analogous to water in a pipe. | The two stories have analogous endings.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Said «a-NAL-a-gus». Noun: analogy. Formal; everyday: «similar», «like».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person whose job is to study information closely to understand it or find problems, like a data analyst or sports analyst. 2) A psychoanalyst, a kind of therapist (mostly US use).
its sense in the lessons: Heard in news, sport and business: «football analysts», «weather analysts». Phrases: «data analyst», «financial analyst».
examples from the lessons: The football analyst explained the goal. | A data analyst studies numbers on a computer. | My aunt works as a weather analyst. | Analysts think prices will rise. | The analyst found mistakes in the report. | Spies were studied by intelligence analysts.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: analyst (y), from «analyse» (UK) / «analyze» (US). Noun of the activity: analysis.
