meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who believes there should be no government or rulers and people should organise themselves freely. 2) (loose use) A person who wants to break rules and cause chaos.
its sense in the lessons: Met in history and politics lessons and in stories. Different anarchists had very different ideas; most were peaceful thinkers, a few used violence. Phrases: «anarchist ideas».
examples from the lessons: The anarchist wrote books about life without government. | Some anarchists set up communities in Spain. | He called himself an anarchist, but he still paid his bus fare. | Anarchist ideas spread in the 1800s. | The rebel in the story was a wild anarchist. | Not every anarchist believes in violence.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Related: anarchy (no government, often meaning chaos), anarchism. Do not assume all anarchists are violent — that is a myth.

part of speech: fragment; Scots word (ane); suffix (-ane in chemistry)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (Scots) «Ane» is the Scots word for «one»: «ane o them» means one of them. 2) (science) «-ane» is an ending in chemistry names of some gases and fuels: methane, propane, butane, octane. 3) As a word alone it is not standard English.
its sense in the lessons: Met in Scottish poems and songs (Robert Burns) and in science lessons naming fuels. On its own it is a fragment, not a common English word.
examples from the lessons: In Scots, «ane» means one. | «Ane day» is Scots for one day. | Methane ends in «-ane». | Propane and butane are camping gas fuels ending in -ane. | Burns wrote «ane» in his poems. | My Scottish nan counts «ane, twa, three».
note for the reader of a maths problem: Not an English word on its own. As a chemistry ending it is written «-ane». Do not confuse with «and» or «one».

part of speech: fragment; Mandarin pinyin (áng / àng); Tagalog word (ang); surname (Ang)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (Mandarin, pinyin) «ang» is a sound in Mandarin Chinese, as in «áng» (昂, to raise the head). It sounds like «ahng» to an English ear and is not an English word. 2) (Tagalog) «Ang» is the Filipino word for «the». 3) (a name) Ang is a surname in Southeast Asia, like the film director Ang Lee.
its sense in the lessons: Met in language lessons on Chinese or Filipino, or as part of a name. It is a fragment, not an English word.
examples from the lessons: In pinyin, «ang» rhymes roughly with «long» without the l. | «Ang bahay» means «the house» in Tagalog. | Ang Lee is a famous film director. | Our Mandarin teacher practised «ang» and «an». | My friend's surname is Ang. | «Ang» on its own is not an English word.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Not English. In pinyin, tone marks change the meaning; without them the word is unclear. As a name it takes a capital A.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (church) A Catholic prayer remembering that, Christians believe, the angel Gabriel told Mary she would be the mother of Jesus; it is said in the morning, at noon and in the evening. 2) (church) The bell rung to call people to say this prayer.
its sense in the lessons: Met in lessons on church life, in Irish life (RTÉ rings the Angelus bell on radio and TV at noon and 6 pm), and in the famous painting «The Angelus» by Millet. Phrases: «the Angelus bell», «say the Angelus».
examples from the lessons: The Angelus bell rang at noon. | Grandma stops to say the Angelus at six. | In Ireland the Angelus is broadcast on TV. | Millet painted farmers praying the Angelus in a field. | The church rings the Angelus three times a day. | We learned the words of the Angelus in RE.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually «the Angelus», with a capital A. Latin word for «angel» begins the prayer. Said «AN-je-lus».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Having sharp corners or angles. 2) (of a person or face) Thin, with bones showing clearly. 3) (maths, science) About angles or measured by an angle, like angular speed.
its sense in the lessons: In art and maths, angular shapes have corners, not curves. In stories, an «angular face» is thin and bony. In science, «angular» measures turning. Phrases: «angular shape», «angular face», «angular velocity».
examples from the lessons: The building had an angular, modern shape. | Triangles are angular; circles are not. | The witch had an angular face and long fingers. | Angular speed tells how fast something spins. | The crystals were sharp and angular. | His handwriting was tall and angular.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: rounded, curved. From «angle». Not about «angels».

meaning for a pupil: 1) verb: To make drawings or models seem to move in a film or cartoon. 2) verb: To make something more lively or interesting. 3) adjective: Alive, living (opposite: inanimate).
its sense in the lessons: In art and computing lessons, pupils animate characters frame by frame; in science, animate things are living, inanimate are not. Phrases: «animate a cartoon», «animated film», «animate and inanimate».
examples from the lessons: We animated a dancing robot in computing. | A smile animated her whole face. | Plants and animals are animate; rocks are inanimate. | It takes many drawings to animate one second. | His stories animated the boring lesson. | Clay figures were animated for the film.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb said «AN-i-mate», adjective «AN-i-mit». Noun: animation; adjective «animated» also means lively.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Destroyed completely. 2) (informal) Beaten very badly in a game or contest. 3) (slang) Very drunk or very tired.
its sense in the lessons: In history and science (matter and antimatter annihilate), «annihilated» means wiped out. In sport talk, a team got annihilated. Phrases: «completely annihilated».
examples from the lessons: The town was annihilated in the war. | Our team got annihilated 10–0. | In the game, the dragon annihilated the castle. | Antimatter and matter are annihilated when they meet. | I'm annihilated after that cross-country run. | The bug spray annihilated the ants.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Said «a-NIGH-a-lay-tid». Spelling: double n, single l. Strong word; «beaten» or «destroyed» are milder.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Having to explain your actions to someone and take responsibility: «answerable to» someone. 2) Able to be answered.
its sense in the lessons: Used in civics and work: a government is answerable to the people; a pupil is answerable to the teacher. Phrases: «answerable to», «answerable for».
examples from the lessons: The head teacher is answerable to the governors. | You are answerable for your own behaviour. | Is that question answerable? | Police must be answerable to the public. | The captain is answerable for the team's kit. | Some riddles aren't answerable at all.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Means responsible, not «able to talk». «Answerable to» a person, «answerable for» a thing.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The main enemy or opponent of the hero in a story, play or film (opposite: protagonist). 2) A person who strongly opposes someone. 3) (science) A muscle or chemical that works against another.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons, you name the protagonist (hero) and the antagonist (villain or opponent). In biology, muscles work in antagonistic pairs (biceps and triceps).
examples from the lessons: The wolf is the antagonist in Little Red Riding Hood. | Every good story needs an antagonist. | The two scientists were bitter antagonists. | The triceps is the antagonist of the biceps. | The antagonist tries to stop the hero. | Name the antagonist in the novel.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: antagonistic; verb: antagonise (UK) / antagonize (US). The antagonist need not be evil — it just works against the hero.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A small bird of the tropical forests of Central and South America; some kinds follow army ants to catch the insects fleeing from them.
its sense in the lessons: Met in nature books and science lessons on rainforests and food chains. Antbirds mostly eat insects, not ants.
examples from the lessons: Antbirds follow army ants through the forest. | The antbird snapped up a fleeing cricket. | There are over 200 kinds of antbird. | We saw a picture of an antbird in our rainforest book. | Antbirds live in Central and South America. | The antbird's song rang through the trees.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; one word. Despite the name, most antbirds do not eat ants — a common trap.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Being earlier in time than something else. 2) (formal, science) Being at the front.
its sense in the lessons: A very rare formal word met in grammar, law and science. In everyday talk people say «coming first» or «being earlier».
examples from the lessons: The anteriority of the first event was clear. | Grammar books mention anteriority in the past perfect. | The judge looked at the anteriority of the claims. | Anteriority means coming before. | In the body, anteriority means being towards the front. | The book argued for the anteriority of the older map.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. From «anterior» (in front, earlier). Opposite: posteriority. Rare — pupils can say «coming first».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (weather) About an anticyclone: an area of high air pressure that usually brings calm, settled weather.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons on weather: anticyclonic weather is dry and calm, sunny in summer, frosty or foggy in winter. Phrases: «anticyclonic conditions», «anticyclonic gloom».
examples from the lessons: Anticyclonic weather brought a week of sunshine. | Winter anticyclonic conditions can bring fog and frost. | The weather map showed an anticyclonic system. | Winds blow gently in anticyclonic weather. | Anticyclonic gloom means grey, still days. | The forecaster said it would stay anticyclonic.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: cyclonic (low pressure, often wet and windy). In the Northern Hemisphere winds turn clockwise around an anticyclone.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Killing or stopping the growth of tiny living things (microbes) such as bacteria, viruses or fungi. 2) noun: A medicine or substance that does this.
its sense in the lessons: In science and health lessons: antibiotics are antimicrobials; soaps and sprays may be antimicrobial. Phrases: «antimicrobial resistance», «antimicrobial soap».
examples from the lessons: Antimicrobial wipes clean the tables. | Antibiotics are a kind of antimicrobial. | Overusing antimicrobials can make germs resistant. | Honey has some antimicrobial power. | Hospitals use antimicrobial gels. | Copper has antimicrobial properties.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Myth: antibiotics do not work on viruses like colds. «Antimicrobial» is broader than «antibiotic».

meaning for a pupil: 1) The top or pointed tip of something, like a mountain or a triangle. 2) The highest point of success. 3) (maths) The point of a cone or pyramid opposite the base.
its sense in the lessons: In maths lessons, the apex is the top vertex of a pyramid or cone. In science, an «apex predator» is at the top of a food chain. Phrases: «apex predator», «at the apex of».
examples from the lessons: The climbers reached the apex of the mountain. | A square-based pyramid has one apex. | Lions are apex predators. | She was at the apex of her career. | Label the apex of the cone. | The roof slopes up to an apex.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: apexes or apices. In maths, apex is a special vertex.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Very shocking and unpleasant. 2) (informal) Very bad: «appalling weather», «appalling handwriting».
its sense in the lessons: Common in UK everyday talk and news for strong disapproval. Phrases: «appalling conditions», «appalling behaviour».
examples from the lessons: The weather was appalling on sports day. | The animals lived in appalling conditions. | His handwriting is appalling! | That was appalling behaviour. | The traffic was appalling this morning. | The food at the camp was appalling.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «appal» (UK) / «appall» (US). Adverb: appallingly. Double p, double l.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) A name or title given to someone or something. 2) A protected name for where a wine or food comes from, like Champagne.
its sense in the lessons: Rare formal word in books and food labels. Everyday: «name», «title».
examples from the lessons: «The Iron Lady» was an appellation given to Margaret Thatcher. | The cheese has its own appellation. | He was known by the appellation «Big Tom». | The wine label shows its appellation. | Kings often had appellations like «the Great». | Use the right appellation when you write to the mayor.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Formal. Related to «appeal» only in its old Latin root.

meaning for a pupil: 1) How far something can be used for or fits a particular case or situation.
its sense in the lessons: Used in science, maths and law: a rule's applicability to a problem. Phrases: «general applicability», «applicability to».
examples from the lessons: We tested the applicability of the rule to bigger numbers. | The law's applicability to children was unclear. | This method has wide applicability. | Check the formula's applicability before using it. | The study had little applicability outside the lab. | The safety rule has applicability in every classroom.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. From «applicable» (fitting, relevant). Formal; everyday: «whether it fits».

meaning for a pupil: 1) To be thankful for something: «I appreciate your help». 2) To understand how good or valuable something is and enjoy it. 3) To understand a situation fully: «I appreciate it's hard». 4) (money) To go up in value.
its sense in the lessons: Common in polite speech and letters; in art and music lessons we «appreciate» works; in money and maths, things that appreciate gain value (opposite: depreciate). Phrases: «I'd appreciate it if…», «much appreciated».
examples from the lessons: I really appreciate your help. | We learned to appreciate classical music. | I appreciate that you're tired, but please finish. | Houses often appreciate over time. | Your card was much appreciated. | She appreciates a good joke. | I'd appreciate it if you shut the door.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Said «a-PREE-shee-ate». In money problems, appreciate = increase in value; depreciate = decrease.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Thanks or gratitude for something. 2) Understanding and enjoying how good something is. 3) Understanding of a situation. 4) (money) A rise in value.
its sense in the lessons: In school, «art appreciation», «music appreciation»; in polite talk, «a token of our appreciation»; in money, appreciation of houses or coins. Phrases: «in appreciation of», «show appreciation».
examples from the lessons: We gave the caretaker flowers in appreciation. | She has a deep appreciation of nature. | The class showed their appreciation with applause. | Music appreciation is on Wednesdays. | There's been an appreciation in house prices. | He has no appreciation of how hard it was.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly uncountable. In maths, appreciation is an increase, often given as a percentage.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A value or answer that is close to the exact one but not exactly right. 2) Something that is like something else but not exactly the same.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, an approximation is a rounded or estimated number: π ≈ 3.14. In science, measurements are approximations. Phrases: «a rough approximation», «a good approximation».
examples from the lessons: 3.14 is an approximation of pi. | Give an approximation to the nearest ten. | My drawing is an approximation of the castle. | 1,000 is a rough approximation of 987. | The map is only an approximation of the coast. | Scientists gave an approximation of the dinosaur's weight.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Symbol for «approximately equal to»: ≈. In maths problems, an approximation is good for checking but the exact answer may be wanted.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who settles an argument or decides who is right. 2) A person who has great power to decide what is good, like in fashion or taste.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and news: the referee is the arbiter of the game; magazines are arbiters of fashion. Phrases: «final arbiter», «arbiter of taste».
examples from the lessons: The referee is the final arbiter on the pitch. | Mum acted as arbiter in our argument. | The court is the arbiter in disputes. | The magazine was the arbiter of style. | A fair arbiter listens to both sides. | Let the teacher be the arbiter.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Similar: judge, referee, arbitrator. Formal.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Without a real reason or plan, by chance or by a choice that is not fair.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, you can choose a number arbitrarily (any number). In everyday talk, rules made arbitrarily seem unfair. Phrases: «chosen arbitrarily».
examples from the lessons: He picked a card arbitrarily. | Choose a starting number arbitrarily. | The rules seemed to change arbitrarily. | The teams were split arbitrarily. | Prices were set arbitrarily. | Pick any point arbitrarily on the line.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Said «AR-bi-trer-i-lee» (UK «ar-bi-TRAIR-i-lee»). In maths, «arbitrary» means any one at all, with no special choice.

meaning for a pupil: 1) About archaeology: the study of the past by digging up and studying old objects, buildings and bones.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons: archaeological digs, sites, finds. Phrases: «archaeological site», «archaeological dig», «archaeological evidence».
examples from the lessons: Stonehenge is a famous archaeological site. | They found Roman coins on an archaeological dig. | Archaeological evidence shows people lived here 5,000 years ago. | We visited an archaeological museum. | The farmer's field became an archaeological treasure. | Archaeological work must be done slowly and carefully.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: archae-ological (UK and most writing); US sometimes «archeological». Said «ar-kee-o-LOJ-i-kal».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A group of islands close together in the sea.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons: Japan, Indonesia, the Philippines, the Hebrides, the Galápagos are archipelagos. Phrases: «a chain of islands».
examples from the lessons: Indonesia is the biggest archipelago in the world. | The Galápagos archipelago has giant tortoises. | We sailed around the archipelago. | Britain and Ireland are part of an archipelago. | The Philippines is an archipelago of over 7,000 islands. | Draw the archipelago on your map.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Said «ar-ki-PEL-a-go». Plural: archipelagos.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who argues, either one who quarrels a lot or one who gives reasons for an opinion.
its sense in the lessons: Rare word; in debates, a «good arguer» makes a strong case. Everyday talk prefers «debater» or saying someone «argues a lot».
examples from the lessons: She's a fierce arguer in debate club. | My brother is a terrible arguer — he just shouts. | A good arguer listens first. | The arguer gave three reasons. | Both arguers shook hands afterwards. | He's a born arguer.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «argue» + -er (the e drops). Not a common word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) About arithmetic: adding, subtracting, multiplying and dividing numbers.
its sense in the lessons: In maths lessons and puzzles: arithmetical skills, an arithmetical mistake, an arithmetical sequence (numbers going up by the same amount). Phrases: «arithmetical error», «arithmetical progression».
examples from the lessons: I made an arithmetical mistake in the sum. | 2, 5, 8, 11 is an arithmetical sequence. | Quick arithmetical skills help in shops. | The puzzle needs only arithmetical steps. | Check your arithmetical working. | An arithmetical slip cost me a mark.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Same as «arithmetic» used as an adjective. In an arithmetical (arithmetic) sequence, the same number is added each time — the common difference.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Behaving as if you are better or more important than other people.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, arrogant characters often learn a lesson (the hare in «The Tortoise and the Hare»). In PSHE, arrogance is contrasted with confidence. Phrases: «arrogant attitude».
examples from the lessons: The arrogant hare stopped for a nap. | Don't be arrogant about winning. | The arrogant king ignored good advice. | She's confident, not arrogant. | His arrogant smile annoyed the team. | Being arrogant can lose you friends.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: arrogance; adverb: arrogantly. Not the same as confident: confident people believe in themselves without looking down on others.

part of speech: noun (artefact, artefacts) — UK spelling; US: artifact
meaning for a pupil: 1) An object made by people long ago, such as a tool, pot or jewel, that tells us about the past. 2) Any object made by people. 3) (science, computing) A mistake or strange mark in a picture or result caused by the method or machine, not by the real thing.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, artefacts are clues about how people lived; museums display artefacts. In science and computing, an artefact is a false mark in data. Phrases: «ancient artefacts», «museum artefacts».
examples from the lessons: The museum has artefacts from ancient Egypt. | We handled Viking artefacts in class. | A broken pot is a useful artefact for historians. | Each group described one artefact. | The blur in the photo was an artefact of the camera. | Artefacts must be handled with gloves.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK: artefact; US: artifact. Countable.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A clever trick used to fool people. 2) Clever skill, or a way of doing things that is not natural.
its sense in the lessons: Found in stories about tricksters and in literature talk. Phrases: «by artifice», «without artifice» (honest, natural).
examples from the lessons: The fox won by artifice, not strength. | She spoke simply, without artifice. | The magician's artifice amazed us. | Odysseus used artifice to get into Troy. | Stage make-up is a kind of artifice. | The plan was full of artifice.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Related: artificial (not natural). Formal; everyday: «trick».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A vegetable with long green, white or purple stalks with pointed tips, eaten cooked. 2) The plant it grows from.
its sense in the lessons: In food and science lessons about plants and healthy eating. A funny fact: asparagus can make some people's wee smell. Phrases: «asparagus spears», «a bunch of asparagus».
examples from the lessons: We had asparagus with our dinner. | Asparagus spears grow up from the soil. | Grandad grows asparagus in his garden. | The asparagus season is in late spring. | I tried asparagus soup at school. | Snap off the woody ends of the asparagus.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «some asparagus», «spears of asparagus». Said «a-SPA-ra-gus».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (money) Things a person or company owns that are worth money, like a house, savings or machines. 2) A useful quality, skill or person: «She is an asset to the team». 3) (computing) Files like pictures and sounds used in a game or app.
its sense in the lessons: In money lessons, assets are what you own and debts are what you owe. In everyday talk, a kind pupil is «an asset to the class». In game design, assets are images and sounds. Phrases: «a great asset», «assets and debts».
examples from the lessons: The company's assets include three factories. | Her kindness is one of her best assets. | He's a real asset to the football team. | We added sound assets to our game. | A house is a big asset. | They had to sell their assets to pay the debt.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. In maths/money: net worth = assets − debts (liabilities). Opposite in money: liabilities.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To take in and understand new information fully. 2) To become part of a new group or country, taking on its ways (or to make someone do so). 3) (science) To take in food or nutrients and make them part of the body.
its sense in the lessons: In history and civics, immigrants assimilate (sometimes by choice, sometimes forced, which is often unfair); in science, plants assimilate carbon; in learning, you assimilate facts. Phrases: «assimilate into», «assimilate information».
examples from the lessons: It takes time to assimilate so many new facts. | The family assimilated into life in Canada. | Plants assimilate carbon dioxide. | She quickly assimilated the rules of cricket. | Forcing people to assimilate can harm their culture. | The body assimilates vitamins from food.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: assimilation. Double s. In history, forced assimilation (for example of Indigenous children) is a serious wrong.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A mixture of different kinds of things.
its sense in the lessons: Used for sweets, shapes, tools and people. In maths problems, an assortment of coloured beads may come before a probability question. Phrases: «an assortment of», «a wide assortment».
examples from the lessons: She brought an assortment of biscuits. | The box held an assortment of crayons. | There was an odd assortment of people at the bus stop. | The shop sells an assortment of hats. | Pick one sweet from the assortment. | An assortment of shells lay on the beach.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; «an assortment of» + plural noun. Similar: mixture, variety, selection.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To tell someone firmly that something is true, so they stop worrying. 2) To make sure something happens: «Practice assures success.»
its sense in the lessons: Used in polite and formal talk: «I assure you…», «Rest assured». In stories, characters assure each other. Phrases: «I can assure you», «rest assured».
examples from the lessons: I assure you the dog is friendly. | The pilot assured us the flight was safe. | Rest assured, we will find your bag. | She assured her mum she'd be home by six. | Hard work assured their victory. | He assured the teacher it wouldn't happen again.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Traps: assure (tell someone to calm them), ensure (make certain), insure (buy insurance). You assure a person: «I assured her».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (space) A pattern of stars that people recognise but which is not one of the 88 official constellations, like the Plough (Big Dipper). 2) A group of three asterisks (⁂) used in printing.
its sense in the lessons: In space lessons: the Plough (UK) or Big Dipper (US) is an asterism inside Ursa Major; the Southern Cross area and the Summer Triangle are other examples. Phrases: «a famous asterism».
examples from the lessons: The Big Dipper is an asterism, not a constellation. | The Summer Triangle is an asterism of three bright stars. | We spotted the Plough asterism from the garden. | An asterism can include stars from several constellations. | Ancient sailors used asterisms to find north. | The book used an asterism to split the chapter.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Trap: a constellation is an official sky area; an asterism is a familiar star pattern.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a way that causes great surprise. 2) Very, extremely: «astonishingly fast».
its sense in the lessons: Used in stories, reports and nature facts to show great surprise. Phrases: «astonishingly, …», «astonishingly well».
examples from the lessons: Astonishingly, the cat survived the fall. | The cheetah is astonishingly fast. | She did astonishingly well in her exam. | The ice was astonishingly thick. | Astonishingly, nobody noticed the elephant. | The seed grew astonishingly quickly.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «astonishing». Stronger than «surprisingly».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Clothes, especially for a special event: «formal attire». 2) verb (formal, old use): To dress someone.
its sense in the lessons: Seen on party invitations, school dress codes and in old stories. Everyday: «clothes». Phrases: «formal attire», «smart attire», «attired in».
examples from the lessons: The invitation said «formal attire». | The knight was attired in shining armour. | Sports attire must be worn in PE. | Her attire was perfect for the wedding. | Beach attire is not allowed in the restaurant. | The guests arrived in fancy attire.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «his attire», not «an attire». Formal.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (UK, Ireland) A vegetable with smooth, shiny, dark purple skin and soft white flesh; in the USA, Canada and Australia it is called eggplant. 2) A dark purple colour. 3) (rude, adult slang) a rude word grown-ups use; not for school.
its sense in the lessons: In food lessons and cooking: moussaka, ratatouille and baba ghanoush use aubergine.
examples from the lessons: We roasted aubergine for dinner. | Moussaka is made with aubergine. | My nan grows aubergines in her greenhouse. | Her coat was a lovely aubergine colour. | In America they call it eggplant. | Aubergine soaks up a lot of oil.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK/Ireland: aubergine (from French); US/Canada/Australia/NZ: eggplant. Said «OH-ber-zheen». Countable for the vegetable, uncountable as food.

meaning for a pupil: 1) About hearing or the ears.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about the ear and brain: the auditory nerve carries sound signals to the brain. In learning, some people talk of «auditory learners», but the idea of fixed learning styles is a myth. Phrases: «auditory nerve», «auditory system».
examples from the lessons: The auditory nerve sends signals to the brain. | Owls have excellent auditory senses. | The test checks auditory skills. | Loud music can harm the auditory system. | An auditory clue is a sound clue. | Bats rely on auditory signals to find food.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Related: audio, audience, audible. Myth: «learning styles» (visual, auditory) are not supported by good evidence.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) The outer part of the ear that you can see, also called the pinna. 2) (science, old use) A small pouch-like part of the heart's upper chambers (atria).
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about the ear and heart. Phrases: «the auricle of the ear».
examples from the lessons: The auricle collects sound waves. | Label the auricle on the ear diagram. | Rabbits can turn their auricles. | Each atrium of the heart has a small auricle. | The auricle is made of cartilage. | Earrings go through the auricle.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Said «OR-i-kul». Do not confuse with «oracle» (a wise source of answers) — they sound alike.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (medicine) To listen to sounds inside the body, like the heart and lungs, usually with a stethoscope.
its sense in the lessons: A doctor's word; in everyday talk people say «listen to your chest». Noun: auscultation.
examples from the lessons: The doctor auscultated my chest. | Nurses learn to auscultate the heart. | She auscultated his lungs for a wheeze. | To auscultate, you need a quiet room. | The vet auscultated the dog's heart. | Auscultate means to listen with a stethoscope.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Said «AWS-kul-tate». A technical word; children can say «listen with a stethoscope».

meaning for a pupil: 1) To prove that something is real or genuine, not fake. 2) (computing) To check someone's identity, for example with a password or fingerprint, before letting them in.
its sense in the lessons: In computing and online safety: apps authenticate you with passwords, codes or fingerprints (two-factor authentication). In history and art, experts authenticate old paintings and coins. Phrases: «two-factor authentication».
examples from the lessons: Experts authenticated the old painting. | Use your fingerprint to authenticate. | The website sent a code to authenticate me. | Never share the code you get to authenticate your account. | The museum authenticated the Roman coin. | The letter was authenticated by its signature.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: authentication. Online safety: a real company never asks you to read out an authentication code.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The right of a group, region or country to govern itself. 2) Being able to make your own choices and act independently.
its sense in the lessons: In civics and history: some regions have autonomy within a country (Scotland, Greenland). In growing up and ethics: children gain autonomy. In technology: self-driving cars have autonomy. Phrases: «a degree of autonomy».
examples from the lessons: Greenland has autonomy within Denmark. | Teenagers want more autonomy. | The robot has autonomy to choose its path. | Scotland has autonomy over its schools. | Giving pupils autonomy helps them learn. | The region fought for autonomy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Adjective: autonomous. Said «aw-TON-o-mee».

meaning for a pupil: 1) About autumn, or typical of autumn, like falling leaves, cool air and orange colours.
its sense in the lessons: Used in descriptive writing, poems and weather reports. In science, the autumnal equinox is around 22–23 September in the Northern Hemisphere. Phrases: «autumnal colours», «autumnal equinox».
examples from the lessons: The trees were full of autumnal colours. | There was an autumnal chill in the air. | The autumnal equinox has equal day and night. | We wrote autumnal poems about leaves. | An autumnal mist covered the field. | Her jumper was a warm autumnal orange.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Said «aw-TUM-nal» — the n is heard here, though silent in «autumn». In the USA «fall» is common for autumn.

meaning for a pupil: 1) adjective: Giving extra help or support: an auxiliary engine is a backup. 2) noun (grammar): A helping verb, like be, have or do, used with another verb: «She IS running», «I HAVE eaten». 3) noun: A helper or extra worker, like a nursing auxiliary.
its sense in the lessons: In grammar lessons, auxiliary verbs make tenses, questions and negatives; modal verbs (can, will, must) are also auxiliaries. In everyday life, auxiliary staff and auxiliary power help. Phrases: «auxiliary verb», «auxiliary power».
examples from the lessons: In «I am eating», «am» is the auxiliary verb. | The ship used its auxiliary engine. | «Do» is the auxiliary in «Do you like it?». | She works as a nursing auxiliary. | The hospital has auxiliary power if the lights go out. | Underline the auxiliary verbs.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: auxil-i-ary. Said «awg-ZIL-ya-ree».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Not liking something or strongly against it: «averse to» something. 2) «Not averse to» means quite happy to (a polite, slightly joking way to say you like it).
its sense in the lessons: Used in formal talk and writing: «risk-averse» people avoid risks. Phrases: «averse to», «not averse to», «risk-averse».
examples from the lessons: He's averse to getting up early. | I'm not averse to a second slice of cake! | The cat is averse to water. | Some people are risk-averse with money. | She was averse to the idea of camping. | Grandpa isn't averse to a joke.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: «averse» (disliking) vs «adverse» (harmful, bad: «adverse weather»). Used after verbs: «He is averse to…».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Stopping something bad from happening. 2) Turning your eyes or face away.
its sense in the lessons: Used in news and stories: «averting disaster», «averting her eyes». Phrases: «averting a crisis».
examples from the lessons: The pilot's quick thinking was key to averting a crash. | She kept averting her eyes from the scary film. | Averting a flood meant building a wall. | They succeeded in averting a strike. | Averting his gaze, he said sorry. | Firefighters worked all night, averting disaster.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: avert, averted. Do not confuse with «avert» and «advert» (an advertisement).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Flying aircraft, and everything to do with building, running and flying planes.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons (the Wright brothers, Amelia Earhart), in science (how planes fly) and jobs (pilots, engineers). Phrases: «aviation history», «civil aviation», «aviation fuel».
examples from the lessons: The Wright brothers started modern aviation in 1903. | Amelia Earhart was a hero of aviation. | My uncle works in aviation. | The museum has an aviation section. | Aviation fuel is very flammable. | Safety rules in aviation are very strict.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Person: aviator (old-fashioned for pilot).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) A thin, stiff bristle growing from the seed head of some grasses and grains, like barley and wheat.
its sense in the lessons: In science and farming: awns give barley its whiskery look; they can catch on animals' fur and help spread seeds. Safety: grass awns can get stuck in dogs' ears and paws.
examples from the lessons: Barley has long awns. | The awns on the wheat looked like whiskers. | A grass awn got stuck in the dog's paw. | Some awns help seeds dig into the ground. | Look at the awns with a magnifying glass. | The field shimmered as wind moved the awns.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Rare word; sounds like «on» in many accents.

meaning for a pupil: 1) About an axis: the line around which something turns or which runs through its middle.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography: Earth's axial tilt (about 23.5°) causes the seasons. In maths, axial symmetry is reflection symmetry about a line. Phrases: «axial tilt», «axial rotation».
examples from the lessons: Earth's axial tilt gives us seasons. | The fan has axial blades. | A butterfly shape shows axial symmetry. | Axial rotation of Earth causes day and night. | The planet's axial spin takes 24 hours. | Draw the axial line of symmetry.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «axis» (plural: axes). Myth trap: seasons come from axial tilt, not from Earth being closer to the Sun.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A pain in your back.
its sense in the lessons: In health lessons and everyday life: carrying a heavy school bag or sitting badly can give backache. Phrases: «have backache» (UK), «have a backache» (US).
examples from the lessons: Carrying my heavy bag gave me backache. | Grandma has a backache after gardening. | Lift with your knees to avoid backache. | Sitting badly can cause backache. | Dad's backache got better with rest. | A good chair helps prevent backache.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK often uncountable: «I've got backache»; US often countable: «a backache». One word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Light placed behind something, like the light behind a phone or laptop screen, or behind a person in a photo or play.
its sense in the lessons: In computing and photography lessons: screens use backlighting; in photos, backlighting makes outlines glow. Phrases: «screen backlighting», «keyboard backlighting».
examples from the lessons: Turn down the backlighting to save battery. | Backlighting made her hair glow in the photo. | The keyboard has backlighting for the dark. | Stage backlighting showed the dancers' shapes. | Strong backlighting can make faces look dark. | The old e-reader had no backlighting.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Verb: backlight (backlit).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) A virus that infects and kills bacteria; often shortened to «phage».
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on microbes: phages look like tiny space landers; scientists study them as a way to fight bacteria that antibiotics cannot kill. They do not infect people.
examples from the lessons: A bacteriophage attacks only bacteria. | The bacteriophage looks like a tiny lunar lander. | Phages could help when antibiotics fail. | Scientists found bacteriophages in river water. | A bacteriophage injects its DNA into a bacterium. | Our science poster showed a bacteriophage.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Said «bak-TEER-ee-o-fayj». Plural: bacteriophages. Short form: phage.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Another spelling of «baguette»: a long, thin loaf of French bread. 2) Another spelling of «baguette» for a small gem cut in a long rectangle shape.
its sense in the lessons: Mostly spelled «baguette»; «baguet» appears in some menus, older texts and jewellery. Same meaning, same sound.
examples from the lessons: We bought a baguet for the picnic. | The ring had two small baguet diamonds. | Slice the baguet into thin pieces. | A warm baguet smells lovely. | The bakery sells baguets every morning. | She tore off a piece of baguet.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The usual spelling is «baguette» (from French). Said «ba-GET».

part of speech: noun (bail, bails); verb (bail, bails, bailed, bailing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) noun (law): Money paid to a court so a person accused of a crime can stay out of prison until the trial; «on bail» means released this way. 2) verb: To scoop water out of a boat with a bucket (UK also spelled «bale»). 3) noun (cricket): One of the two small wooden pieces resting on top of the stumps. 4) «bail out»: to help someone out of trouble, often with money; or to jump out of a plane by parachute. 5) (slang) To leave suddenly, or to not turn up: «I'm gonna bail», «He bailed on us».
its sense in the lessons: Heard in news and crime stories (law), sailing and survival stories (bailing water), cricket lessons in the UK, Australia and NZ, and teen talk (bail = leave). Phrases: «on bail», «bail out», «bail on someone».
examples from the lessons: He was released on bail. | We bailed water out of the leaking boat. | The ball knocked off a bail — out! | The bank was bailed out by the government. | The pilot bailed out before the crash. | It's late, I'm gonna bail. (slang) | She bailed on the party at the last minute. (slang) | Grab the bucket and help me bail!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Homophone: «bale» (a bundle of hay); British English also uses «bale out» for boats and planes. «Bail» in law is money that is given back if the person comes to court.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person's area of skill, interest or responsibility: «Maths is her bailiwick». 2) (UK, law) The area ruled by a bailiff; today Jersey and Guernsey in the Channel Islands are each called a Bailiwick.
its sense in the lessons: Used in jokey or formal talk about who is in charge of what; in geography, the Bailiwick of Jersey and the Bailiwick of Guernsey. Phrases: «outside my bailiwick».
examples from the lessons: Fixing computers is Dad's bailiwick. | Jersey is a Bailiwick, not part of the UK. | Sorry, that's outside my bailiwick. | The garden is Grandma's bailiwick. | Guernsey and its islands form a Bailiwick. | Planning the trip is my bailiwick this year.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Old-fashioned or jokey; everyday: «area», «job», «thing». Capital B when naming Jersey or Guernsey.

part of speech: noun (balsam, balsams; balsam is often uncountable)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A sweet-smelling sticky oil or resin that comes from certain trees and is used in creams and medicines. 2) A soothing cream or ointment, like a balm. 3) A tree that gives this resin, such as the balsam fir. 4) A garden plant with bright flowers whose seed pods burst open when touched (also called impatiens or busy Lizzie).
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life the word appears on labels of lip balms, cough sweets and hair conditioners; in stories it suggests a calm, healing smell. In science lessons on plants it is a tree resin or a flower with exploding seed pods. Phrases: balsam fir, Himalayan balsam (a weed by rivers in the UK), Peru balsam.
examples from the lessons: Grandma rubs balsam on her sore knees. | The Christmas tree was a balsam fir that smelled lovely. | The cough sweets taste of balsam and honey. | Himalayan balsam grows thickly along the river bank. | When I touched the balsam pod, it popped and threw out its seeds. | The shop sells balsam shampoo. | Pine and balsam scents filled the cabin.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable for plants (two balsams), usually uncountable for the oil. Do not confuse with «balm» (a soothing cream) or «balsamic» (balsamic vinegar is from grapes, not from balsam). Stress on the first syllable: BAWL-sum.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (UK, informal) A sausage. 2) (informal) A firework that makes a loud bang. 3) (UK, informal) An old car in bad condition that often makes noises. 4) (slang) A really good, exciting song, usually loud and catchy.
its sense in the lessons: A very British everyday word: «bangers and mash» is a classic school-dinner and pub meal. On Bonfire Night children are warned that bangers are dangerous and should only be lit by adults. In slang, teenagers call a great song «an absolute banger». In stories an «old banger» is a cheap, rattling car.
examples from the lessons: We had bangers and mash for tea. | Dad's old banger broke down on the motorway again. | The neighbours set off bangers at midnight and the dog hid. | Never hold a banger in your hand after it is lit. | This new song is an absolute banger! | The school canteen serves veggie bangers on Fridays. | Uncle Pete drove a rusty banger with no radio.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one banger, two bangers. Mostly UK and Australian/NZ use for «sausage». The «song» sense is slang; in formal writing say «a hit song». Fireworks called bangers are banned for sale to children in many places.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To send someone away from a country or place as a punishment and forbid them to come back. 2) To get rid of something completely, such as a feeling or a thought. 3) To order someone to leave a place, often as a joke.
its sense in the lessons: In history and fairy tales kings banish traitors, and wizards banish evil spirits. In everyday life we «banish» boredom, worries or germs. Phrases: banish someone from, banish the thought, banished to his room.
examples from the lessons: The king banished the knight from the kingdom. | Napoleon was banished to the island of Elba. | A warm drink can banish the winter chills. | Mum banished the dog to the garden for stealing the sausages. | She tried to banish her fears before the test. | In the story the witch was banished forever. | "Banish that thought!" said the teacher with a smile.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: banished. The noun is «banishment». Similar: exile (formal, for countries), expel (from school or a group). «Banish» is stronger than just «send away»: it means you are not allowed back.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A wheelbarrow: a small cart with one wheel at the front and two handles, pushed by hand. 2) (UK) A small cart with two wheels used by street sellers to sell fruit and other goods (a market barrow). 3) (history) A large mound of earth built long ago over a grave.
its sense in the lessons: In gardening and building, a barrow carries soil, bricks and leaves. In UK history lessons, ancient barrows are burial mounds from the Stone Age and Bronze Age. Phrases: wheelbarrow, barrow boy (a street trader), long barrow, round barrow.
examples from the lessons: Grandad filled the barrow with weeds. | Can you push the barrow of bricks to the shed? | The fruit seller shouted from his barrow in the market. | We visited an old long barrow on the hill near Avebury. | Archaeologists found tools inside the barrow. | The barrow tipped over and the sand spilled out.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: barrows. Do not confuse with «borrow» (to take something and give it back) or «burrow» (an animal's hole). Barrow is also part of place names, like Barrow-in-Furness in England.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (a name) A boy's or man's name, short for Bartholomew or Bartlett; the best-known Bart is Bart Simpson, a cartoon boy. 2) BART (USA, abbreviation) Bay Area Rapid Transit, the train system around San Francisco. 3) Bart. (UK, abbreviation) Short for «baronet», a title written after a man's name.
its sense in the lessons: It is not an ordinary English word; it is almost always a name, so it is written with a capital B. In stories it is a character's name; in San Francisco, BART is the local train.
examples from the lessons: Bart Simpson is always getting into trouble. | My cousin Bart plays football. | We took BART from the airport into the city. | The letter was addressed to Sir John Smith, Bart. | Bart is short for Bartholomew.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Write with a capital letter: Bart. As a train system it is written in capitals: BART. There is no common word «bart» in lower case.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A long, loose coat made of soft towelling or cotton, worn before or after a bath or shower. 2) (US) Any dressing gown worn around the house.
its sense in the lessons: An everyday home word: people wear a bathrobe in the morning, at swimming pools and in hotels. In stories a character in a bathrobe is often just out of bed or relaxing. Phrases: a fluffy bathrobe, wrapped in a bathrobe.
examples from the lessons: Dad came downstairs in his bathrobe. | The hotel gave us white fluffy bathrobes. | She wrapped herself in a bathrobe after her shower. | Hang your bathrobe on the hook behind the door. | Grandpa answered the door in his bathrobe and slippers. | I got a bathrobe with a hood for my birthday.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: bathrobes. In the UK people often say «dressing gown»; «robe» is a shorter US word. One word, not «bath robe».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (USA) A BB is a small round metal pellet fired from an air gun called a BB gun. 2) (texting, slang) «bb» is short for «baby», a pet name, or for «bye bye». 3) (school, pencils) On pencils, BB means very soft and dark (more B means softer). 4) (other uses) BB can stand for many things, like «bed and breakfast» in some ads, or Big Brother.
its sense in the lessons: Not a real word but letters. Safety: BB guns can injure eyes and are not toys; children should never point one at anyone. In texts and gaming chat, «bb» means bye bye or babe. Art lessons mention 2B, BB and HB pencils.
examples from the lessons: My uncle keeps his BB gun locked in a cupboard. | A BB can hurt someone's eye, so never aim at people. | "gtg bb" means "got to go, bye bye". | The art teacher gave us soft BB pencils for shading. | He texted "miss you bb" to his girlfriend.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always say the letters separately: bee-bee. Usually written in capitals except in texting. Do not use «bb» in school writing; write «bye» or «baby» in full.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Small, round and shiny, like a bead; used mostly about eyes. 2) (informal) Watching very closely and suspiciously, as in «a beady eye».
its sense in the lessons: In stories, birds, rats and villains have beady eyes; it makes a creature seem sharp, alert and a bit sneaky. Phrase: keep a beady eye on (watch carefully, often a teacher or parent).
examples from the lessons: The crow watched us with its beady black eyes. | The teacher kept a beady eye on the back row. | The rat stared out from the hole with beady eyes. | Grandma has a beady eye for mess. | The doll had little beady eyes made of glass. | Keep a beady eye on your bag at the station.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative beadier, superlative beadiest. Mostly used with «eye» or «eyes». It is a little unkind to say a person has beady eyes.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The binturong, a furry animal from the forests of South and Southeast Asia with a long tail it can grip with; it is neither a bear nor a cat. 2) (sometimes) Another name for the red panda. 3) (US, old informal) A strong, fierce or very lively person.
its sense in the lessons: In science and zoo visits the bearcat is a good example that animal names can mislead: it is related to civets. Bearcats are said to smell like buttered popcorn. Some US sports teams are called the Bearcats.
examples from the lessons: The bearcat curled its long tail around the branch. | A bearcat smells a bit like popcorn. | We saw a bearcat sleeping at the zoo. | Despite its name, a bearcat is not a bear. | The Cincinnati Bearcats won the match. | Bearcats eat fruit and small animals.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: bearcats. Trap: the name does not mean it is a bear or a cat. Its proper name is binturong.

part of speech: noun (a bedside, bedsides); adjective (bedside, as in bedside table)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The area next to a bed. 2) Used before a noun for things kept next to a bed: a bedside table, bedside lamp. 3) Being at someone's bedside means staying with someone who is ill in bed.
its sense in the lessons: Everyday home word for furniture. In stories families gather at the bedside of a sick person. Phrases: bedside table, bedside lamp, at her bedside, bedside manner (how kindly a doctor talks to patients).
examples from the lessons: I keep a book on my bedside table. | Switch off the bedside lamp, please. | Mum sat at my bedside when I had a fever. | The family gathered at Grandad's bedside in the hospital. | The doctor has a gentle bedside manner. | My alarm clock is on the bedside cabinet.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly used before another noun. In the UK, «bedside cabinet»; in the US, «nightstand» means a bedside table. One word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The yellow wax that honeybees make to build their honeycomb. 2) This wax used to make candles, polish, crayons and lip balm. 3) (US, informal) In «none of your beeswax», a playful way to say «none of your business».
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about bees, workers make wax from glands on their bodies and build hexagon-shaped cells. In everyday life: beeswax candles, wood polish, wax wraps for sandwiches. The jokey phrase is common among US children.
examples from the lessons: Bees build their honeycomb out of beeswax. | We made candles from beeswax in craft club. | Mum polishes the old table with beeswax. | "What's in the box?" "None of your beeswax!" | My sandwich is wrapped in a beeswax wrap instead of plastic. | Beeswax melts if you leave it in the sun.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: some beeswax, not «a beeswax». One word. «None of your beeswax» is cheeky; don't say it to a teacher.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (a name) Ludwig van Beethoven (1770–1827), a German composer, one of the most famous in history; he kept writing music even after he became deaf.
its sense in the lessons: In music lessons children hear his Fifth Symphony (da-da-da-DUM), «Für Elise» and the «Ode to Joy». His story is told as an example of not giving up. Beethoven is also the name of a St Bernard dog in a family film.
examples from the lessons: Beethoven wrote nine symphonies. | I'm learning «Für Elise» by Beethoven on the piano. | Beethoven went deaf but kept composing. | The orchestra played Beethoven's Fifth. | Our class listened to the «Ode to Joy» by Beethoven. | In the film, Beethoven is a huge, messy dog.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A name, so write it with a capital B. Say BAY-toe-ven. The «van» in his name is Dutch-style, not German «von».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Coming or happening later than it should have.
its sense in the lessons: Most often in «belated birthday wishes» or «a belated thank-you» when you forgot or were late. In stories, a belated apology or realisation comes too late to help. Related adverb: belatedly.
examples from the lessons: Happy belated birthday, Gran! | I sent her a belated thank-you card. | He made a belated attempt to tidy his room before Mum came home. | The team got a belated goal in the last minute. | She belatedly realised she had left her lunch at home. | Sorry for the belated reply.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Not used for people: a belated card, not «a belated boy» (say «a late boy»). Adverb: belatedly. Similar: late, overdue.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Loved very much: a beloved pet, a beloved teacher. 2) (noun, old or poetic) A person who is loved, especially a sweetheart. 3) (church, Bible) Used for people dear to God or to each other, as in «dearly beloved» at the start of a wedding.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and news, «beloved» shows strong love or popularity: a beloved family dog, a beloved children's author. At weddings and funerals people hear «dearly beloved» or «beloved wife and mother» on gravestones.
examples from the lessons: Our beloved cat lived to be eighteen. | The beloved old teacher retired this year. | Dearly beloved, we are gathered here today… | He wrote poems to his beloved. | The gravestone said "beloved father and grandfather". | Paddington is a beloved children's character.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Said bee-LUV-id before a noun (my beloved dog) and often bee-LUVD after a verb (he was beloved by all). The noun sense sounds old-fashioned or romantic.

part of speech: verb, past form of besiege (besiege, besieges, besieged, besieging); adjective (besieged)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Surrounded by an army that is trying to capture a town or castle. 2) Surrounded or crowded by many people who want something, such as reporters or fans. 3) Bothered by a great many requests, questions or problems.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons castles and cities were besieged for months until food ran out. In news and everyday speech a famous person is «besieged by fans» and a shop is «besieged by shoppers» on sale day.
examples from the lessons: The castle was besieged for six months. | The besieged town ran out of food. | The footballer was besieged by fans asking for autographs. | The teacher was besieged with questions about the trip. | Troy was besieged by the Greeks for ten years. | The helpline was besieged with calls after the storm.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: «ie» – besiege, siege. Often in the passive: «be besieged by/with». Related noun: siege. Do not confuse with «beseech» (to beg).

part of speech: verb, -ing form of besiege (besiege, besieges, besieged, besieging); adjective (besieging)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Surrounding a town, castle or fort with an army to make it give up. 2) Crowding round someone or something, or sending lots of requests.
its sense in the lessons: History: the besieging army camps outside the walls, cuts off food and water and waits. In everyday speech: «fans besieging the stars' hotel». Phrase: the besieging army/forces.
examples from the lessons: The besieging army dug trenches around the walls. | Reporters were besieging the hotel. | The besieging soldiers built catapults. | Children were besieging the ice-cream van. | The besieging forces finally gave up and went home.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: besieging (drop the final «e» of besiege before -ing). «Besieging» is the attackers; «besieged» is the people inside.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To be a sign of something; to show that something is true or is going to happen.
its sense in the lessons: A stiff, old-fashioned word found in classic stories and exam texts: dark clouds betoken a storm; a smile betokens friendship. In everyday talk people say «be a sign of» or «show».
examples from the lessons: Dark clouds betokened a storm. | His silence betokened anger. | The gift betokened her thanks. | Red sky at night is said to betoken fine weather. | The empty streets betokened that something was wrong.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal and rare. Regular verb: betokened. Everyday words: show, mean, be a sign of.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Happening twice a year.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, a biannual check-up at the dentist or a biannual school newsletter comes twice a year. In maths problems it means 2 times in 12 months, usually about every 6 months.
examples from the lessons: We have a biannual dentist check-up. | The school holds a biannual book fair, in spring and autumn. | The magazine is biannual, so there are two issues a year. | The garden club meets biannually. | Our biannual car service is due next month.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Big trap: «biannual» = twice a year; «biennial» = once every two years. Many people mix them up, so writers often say «twice a year» to be clear. In a maths problem: 3 years of a biannual event = 6 times.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Short for bicarbonate of soda (also called baking soda or sodium bicarbonate), a white powder used in cooking and cleaning. 2) (science) A chemical salt containing the group HCO3; in the body it helps keep blood at the right acid level.
its sense in the lessons: In cooking, bicarbonate of soda makes cakes rise because it gives off carbon dioxide bubbles. In science lessons it fizzes with vinegar in the classic «volcano» experiment. It is also used to clean and remove smells, and to ease indigestion.
examples from the lessons: Add a teaspoon of bicarbonate of soda to the cake mix. | We mixed bicarbonate and vinegar to make our volcano erupt. | Bicarbonate of soda can clean a dirty oven. | The fizz is carbon dioxide gas made by the bicarbonate. | Mum keeps a box of bicarbonate in the fridge to stop smells. | Baking soda is another name for bicarbonate of soda.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable in cooking. UK: bicarbonate of soda or «bicarb»; US: baking soda. Do not confuse with baking powder, which already contains an acid. Do not eat it by the spoonful.

part of speech: noun (bidding, often uncountable; biddings rare); verb, -ing form of bid (bid, bids, bid, bidding)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Offering money for something at an auction. 2) (old-fashioned) A command or request: «do someone's bidding» means to do what they tell you. 3) (verb) Making an offer, or (formal, old) saying something to someone, as in «bidding goodnight». 4) (card games) Saying how many tricks you think you can win.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, a servant or a magical creature does its master's bidding. In everyday life and on websites, bidding happens at auctions and on eBay. Phrases: at someone's bidding, bidding war, open the bidding.
examples from the lessons: The bidding for the painting started at one hundred pounds. | The genie did his master's bidding. | Two people were bidding for the same bike online. | The dog came at his bidding. | She was bidding everyone goodnight. | A bidding war pushed the price up.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: double «d» – bidding. Past of bid for auctions is «bid»; in the old «say» sense it can be «bade». Maths: in an auction the highest bid wins.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A two-piece swimsuit for women and girls, with a top and bottoms. 2) Bikini Atoll, a group of islands in the Pacific Ocean where the USA tested nuclear bombs; the swimsuit was named after it.
its sense in the lessons: Everyday beach and swimming-pool word. In history lessons, Bikini Atoll is linked to nuclear tests in the 1940s and 1950s. Phrase: bikini top, bikini bottoms.
examples from the lessons: She wore a stripy bikini at the beach. | My sister packed two bikinis for the holiday. | I lost my bikini bottoms in the waves! | Some people prefer a one-piece swimsuit to a bikini. | Bikini Atoll is in the Marshall Islands. | Don't forget sun cream if you wear a bikini.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: bikinis. «Bikini bottoms» is plural, like trousers.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (politics, formal) Involving two sides, groups or countries, as in a bilateral agreement. 2) (science, medicine) Having to do with both sides of the body, as in bilateral symmetry.
its sense in the lessons: In politics and news, a bilateral treaty or meeting is between two countries. In science, animals like humans and butterflies have bilateral symmetry: the left and right halves are mirror images. In maths, that is a line of symmetry down the middle.
examples from the lessons: The two countries signed a bilateral trade deal. | Humans have bilateral symmetry. | A butterfly's wings show bilateral symmetry. | The prime ministers held bilateral talks. | The doctor said the infection was bilateral, in both ears. | A starfish does not have bilateral symmetry; it has five-way symmetry.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Bi-» means two; «lateral» means side. Compare: unilateral (one side), multilateral (many sides). Formal word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Coming as number one billion in order (1,000,000,000th). 2) One of a billion equal parts of something: 1/1,000,000,000.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, ordinal and fraction words. A nanometre is a billionth of a metre and a nanosecond is a billionth of a second. In news, «the billionth visitor» or «the billionth phone sold».
examples from the lessons: A nanosecond is a billionth of a second. | The company celebrated its billionth customer. | The world's billionth person was born in the 1800s. | Write one billionth as a fraction: 1/1,000,000,000. | Atoms are smaller than a billionth of a metre across.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Maths: a billion today means 1,000,000,000 (a thousand million) in the UK, USA and elsewhere; an old British meaning was a million million. A billionth = 1 ÷ 1,000,000,000 = 0.000000001.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Made of two different metals joined together. 2) (money, history) Using both gold and silver as the basis of money.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons a bimetallic strip is two metals stuck together; when heated, one expands more than the other, so the strip bends. It is used in thermostats, fire alarms and kettles that switch off. The £2 coin and the 1-euro coin are bimetallic (two colours).
examples from the lessons: A bimetallic strip bends when it gets hot. | The kettle switches off because of a bimetallic strip inside. | The £2 coin is bimetallic, silver in the middle and gold on the edge. | Brass expands more than iron, so the bimetallic strip curves. | Thermostats often use bimetallic strips.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Bi-» means two. Pronounced bye-meh-TAL-ik. Mostly found in science lessons.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Having or being body parts that are electronic or mechanical and work like real ones, often better. 2) (informal) Super-strong or with powers beyond normal.
its sense in the lessons: In science and news, bionic arms, hands and eyes help people who have lost a limb or their sight. In TV and stories, bionic heroes run faster and see further. It mixes «biology» and «electronic».
examples from the lessons: She has a bionic hand that she controls with her arm muscles. | Scientists are building bionic eyes for blind people. | In the old TV show, the bionic man could run at 60 miles per hour. | My grandad joked that his new knee was bionic. | A bionic leg helped the athlete run again.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced bye-ON-ik. Not every artificial limb is bionic; «bionic» usually means it has electronics and motors. Real bionic parts are helpful but not super-powered.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) All the parts of the Earth where living things exist, from deep in the sea to high in the air, together with all the life there. 2) A large closed building made to hold living things and copy natural habitats (for example Biosphere 2 in Arizona). 3) (UNESCO) A biosphere reserve: a protected area where people and nature live together.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and science lessons, the Earth is described in spheres: atmosphere (air), hydrosphere (water), lithosphere (rock) and biosphere (life). Pollution and climate change affect the whole biosphere.
examples from the lessons: The biosphere includes oceans, forests, soil and air. | Plants and animals together make up the biosphere. | Scientists lived inside Biosphere 2 for two years. | The biosphere is only a thin layer around the Earth. | Pollution harms the whole biosphere. | The area is protected as a UNESCO biosphere reserve.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually «the biosphere». «Bio-» means life, «sphere» means ball. Compare atmosphere, hydrosphere, lithosphere.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The place, town or house where a person was born. 2) The place where something started or was first made or done.
its sense in the lessons: In history and English lessons we visit the birthplaces of famous people, like Shakespeare's birthplace in Stratford-upon-Avon. In everyday forms you may be asked your «place of birth». Phrase: the birthplace of football, of jazz, of democracy.
examples from the lessons: Stratford-upon-Avon is Shakespeare's birthplace. | My dad's birthplace is a small village in Ireland. | Ancient Greece is called the birthplace of democracy. | New Orleans is said to be the birthplace of jazz. | We visited the house that was Lincoln's birthplace. | Write your name and birthplace on the form.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word. Countable: birthplaces. On forms, «place of birth» is more common.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (maths) To cut or divide something into two equal parts. 2) To cut across or through something, dividing it into two parts, not always equal.
its sense in the lessons: In geometry lessons, you bisect a line or an angle with a compass and ruler: a perpendicular bisector cuts a line in half at a right angle; an angle bisector cuts an angle into two equal angles. In geography, a road or river bisects a town.
examples from the lessons: Use your compass to bisect the angle. | The line bisects the square into two rectangles. | A river bisects the city. | If you bisect a 90 degree angle, each part is 45 degrees. | The motorway bisects the farm. | Bisect the line AB and mark the midpoint.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Maths: bisecting gives two EQUAL halves: bisect 10 cm → 5 cm and 5 cm; bisect 60° → 30° and 30°. «Bi-» means two, «sect» means cut. Noun: bisection; a line that bisects is a bisector.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (maths) The act of dividing something into two equal parts. 2) (maths, computing) A method of finding an answer by halving a range again and again, as in the bisection method or a binary search.
its sense in the lessons: In geometry lessons: the bisection of an angle or a line with a compass. In maths and coding, the bisection method guesses the middle of a range and keeps the half where the answer must be, like the game «guess my number between 1 and 100».
examples from the lessons: The bisection of the angle gave two angles of 35 degrees. | We learnt the bisection of a line with a compass. | Bisection finds the number in just a few guesses. | Guess 50, then 25, then 37: that is bisection. | The bisection of the circle makes two semicircles.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Maths: each bisection halves the range: 100 → 50 → 25 → 13 ... so about 7 halvings find any number from 1 to 100. Verb: bisect.

part of speech: noun (a bivouac, bivouacs); verb (bivouac, bivouacs, bivouacked, bivouacking)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A simple, temporary camp, often without a tent, made by soldiers or mountain climbers. 2) (verb) To camp outside for the night in such a camp. 3) A bivvy (bivvy bag), a small waterproof shelter for one person.
its sense in the lessons: In scouting, Duke of Edinburgh and outdoor-education trips, children learn to make a bivouac shelter from branches or a tarp. In history and adventure stories, soldiers bivouac in fields before a battle. Safety: keep warm and dry, never light fires under a tarp.
examples from the lessons: We built a bivouac out of sticks and leaves in the woods. | The climbers bivouacked on a ledge halfway up the mountain. | The soldiers set up a bivouac by the river. | Our scout group slept in bivouacs for one night. | He carries a bivvy bag in case he gets stuck on the hills. | The bivouac kept out most of the rain.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: past and -ing forms add «k»: bivouacked, bivouacking. Say BIV-oo-ak. Informal short form: bivvy (UK).

part of speech: verb, -ing form of blacken (blacken, blackens, blackened, blackening); noun (blackening)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Becoming black or darker, or making something black or dark. 2) Damaging someone's good name by saying bad things about them (blackening their name). 3) (noun) The process or result of something going black, like burnt toast or rotting fruit.
its sense in the lessons: In science, soot and smoke blacken things; in stories, «the sky was blackening» means a storm is coming. In cooking, blackening is a way of cooking fish or meat with spices in a very hot pan (Cajun style). «Blackening his name» means spreading bad stories about someone.
examples from the lessons: The sky was blackening before the storm. | The smoke is blackening the walls. | Bananas start blackening in the fridge. | He was accused of blackening his rival's name. | The chef was blackening the fish with spices. | Frost caused blackening of the plant's leaves.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Base verb: blacken (add -en). Related: blackened (adjective, as in blackened toast).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (US, informal) A feeling of being bored, tired, fed up or slightly sad, without a clear reason. 2) (informal) The plural of «blah», as in blah blah blah: boring or empty talk.
its sense in the lessons: Used in US everyday talk, especially about winter: «the winter blahs», «a case of the blahs». In comics and stories «blah, blah, blah» stands for talk that is boring or not worth repeating.
examples from the lessons: I've got the Monday morning blahs. | The winter blahs make everyone grumpy. | A walk in the sunshine can cure the blahs. | All his blahs about football bored me. | She had a case of the blahs after the holidays ended.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal; mostly American. Usually «the blahs». Not used in formal writing. If someone has the blahs for a long time, they should talk to a grown-up or a doctor.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Not responsible for something bad that happened; not guilty. 2) Never doing anything wrong; innocent and good.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and news, «he was completely blameless» clears someone's name. In everyday life we say it when someone was not at fault in an accident or argument. Phrase: lead a blameless life.
examples from the lessons: The driver was blameless; the other car went through the red light. | The dog was blameless – the cat broke the vase! | She led a blameless life. | Nobody is entirely blameless in this argument. | The report said the teacher was blameless.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «-less» means without, so «blameless» means without blame. Opposite: to blame, guilty, at fault.

part of speech: verb, -ing form of blare (blare, blares, blared, blaring); adjective (blaring)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Making a very loud, harsh, unpleasant noise. 2) (adjective) Very loud: blaring music, blaring horns.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and everyday life: blaring music next door, blaring sirens of ambulances and fire engines, blaring car horns in traffic. It tells the reader the noise is too loud or alarming. Safety: blaring alarms mean you must leave the building calmly.
examples from the lessons: Music was blaring from my brother's room. | The fire alarm was blaring, so we lined up outside. | Sirens blaring, the ambulance raced past. | The TV was blaring all evening. | Car horns were blaring in the traffic jam. | Turn down that blaring radio!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Base verb: blare. «Blaring» is stronger than «loud»; it suggests unpleasant noise. Often used with music, horns, sirens, alarms, TV.

part of speech: noun (a blaze, blazes); verb (blaze, blazes, blazed, blazing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A large, strong fire that burns brightly, often one that is dangerous. 2) A very bright light or colour: a blaze of colour. 3) (verb) To burn brightly and strongly. 4) A white stripe down the face of a horse or other animal, or a mark cut on a tree to show a path. 5) (verb) In «blaze a trail»: to be the first to do something new.
its sense in the lessons: In news and safety lessons, firefighters «tackle a blaze»; children learn fire safety. In stories, «the fire blazed in the hearth» is cosy. Phrases: blaze of glory, blaze a trail, guns blazing, What the blazes? (old, mild exclamation).
examples from the lessons: Firefighters fought the blaze for hours. | The fire blazed in the fireplace. | The garden was a blaze of colour in summer. | The horse has a white blaze on its nose. | She blazed a trail for women in science. | The sun blazed down on the beach. | What the blazes is going on here?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable as a fire: two blazes. «Blazing» means very bright or very hot. «What the blazes» is old-fashioned and mild. Do not confuse with «blazer», a school jacket.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Burning brightly and strongly. 2) Very hot or bright: blazing sun, blazing heat. 3) (informal) Very angry, or very strong: a blazing row. 4) Very fast: at blazing speed.
its sense in the lessons: In stories: a blazing fire, a blazing house, a blazing summer day. In weather and safety talk: wear sun cream on a blazing hot day. «A blazing row» (UK) is a very angry, loud argument.
examples from the lessons: We toasted marshmallows over the blazing fire. | It was a blazing hot day, so we stayed in the shade. | The firefighters rescued the cat from the blazing barn. | Mum and Dad had a blazing row about money. | The car drove off at blazing speed. | Her eyes were blazing with anger.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Blazing hot» = extremely hot. Base verb: blaze. Do not confuse with «blazer» (jacket).

part of speech: verb (bloat, bloats, bloated, bloating); noun (bloat, uncountable)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To swell up and become bigger than normal, usually with air, gas or liquid. 2) (noun) A swollen feeling in the stomach, or a disease of cows and sheep when their stomachs fill with gas. 3) (computing, informal) Too much extra stuff making something big and slow, as in software bloat.
its sense in the lessons: In health and everyday life, eating too fast or drinking fizzy drinks can bloat your tummy. In computing, «bloatware» slows a phone down. In stories, «bloated» describes something swollen and unpleasant.
examples from the lessons: Fizzy drinks make my tummy bloat. | Cows can get bloat if they eat too much wet clover. | The dead fish had bloated in the water. | Too many apps cause bloat on your phone. | Beans sometimes make people feel bloated.
note for the reader of a maths problem: More common as the adjective «bloated». Regular verb.

part of speech: adjective (bloated); verb, past form of bloat
meaning for a pupil: 1) Swollen and bigger than normal because of air, gas or liquid. 2) Feeling uncomfortably full after eating or drinking. 3) Too big, with too much in it (a bloated budget, bloated software).
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life after a big Christmas dinner people say «I feel bloated». In stories, a bloated body or toad is swollen and ugly. In news, a «bloated government» means too big and wasteful.
examples from the lessons: I feel so bloated after that pizza. | A bloated frog sat on the lily pad. | The dog looked bloated, so we took it to the vet. | The game is bloated with adverts. | My stomach felt bloated after the fizzy drink.
