note for the reader of a maths problem: Often after «feel» or «look». A sudden, very bloated, hard tummy in a dog is an emergency for the vet.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A large dog with a very good sense of smell, long droopy ears and loose wrinkled skin, used to follow the trail of people or animals. 2) (informal) A person, like a detective, who is very good at finding things out.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and police work, bloodhounds track missing people or escaped prisoners. In science, they are an example of how good a dog's nose is: much better than a human's. Phrase: sniff out like a bloodhound.
examples from the lessons: The bloodhound followed the scent through the woods. | Police used bloodhounds to find the lost hiker. | Bloodhounds have long, floppy ears. | Our detective sniffed out clues like a bloodhound. | A bloodhound's nose can follow a trail days old.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: bloodhounds. The name does not mean they like blood; «blood» once meant a pure-bred dog.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An animal that sucks blood, such as a leech, a mosquito, a tick or a vampire bat. 2) (informal, rude) A person who takes money from others or uses them unfairly. 3) (stories) A vampire.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about animals and food chains, bloodsuckers feed on the blood of other animals. In everyday speech, people may call greedy landlords or loan sharks «bloodsuckers» as an insult. Safety: check for ticks after walks in long grass.
examples from the lessons: Mosquitoes are tiny bloodsuckers. | A leech is a bloodsucker that lives in ponds. | Vampire bats are bloodsuckers. | He called the greedy landlord a bloodsucker. | In the story, the bloodsucker came out only at night. | Ticks are bloodsuckers, so check your legs after hiking.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word. Calling a person a bloodsucker is an insult.

part of speech: adjective (blooming); verb, -ing form of bloom (bloom, blooms, bloomed, blooming); adverb (blooming, UK informal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Having flowers that are open; flowering. 2) Healthy, happy and full of life: looking blooming. 3) (UK, informal, mild) A mild word used to show annoyance or for emphasis, like a gentle swear word: «that blooming dog!» 4) Growing and doing well (a blooming business, a blooming friendship).
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, plants are blooming in spring. In UK everyday talk grandparents say «blooming heck!» or «it's blooming freezing» instead of a ruder word. In stories, a blooming girl or garden is healthy and beautiful.
examples from the lessons: The roses are blooming in the garden. | The cherry trees are blooming early this year. | That blooming cat has knocked over the plant again! | It's blooming freezing out here! | You look blooming after your holiday. | Their friendship was blooming.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The UK mild exclamation is polite enough for most people, though some teachers may not like it. Similar mild words: flipping, blinking. Base verb: bloom.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (UK, informal) To cry noisily, often in a way that seems babyish.
its sense in the lessons: Used in British school stories and everyday speech, often a bit unkindly: «stop blubbing». It is a short form of «blubber». In stories it can show a character teasing someone.
examples from the lessons: He started to blub when his ice cream fell on the floor. | Stop blubbing and tell me what happened. | I nearly blubbed at the end of the film. | The little boy was blubbing because he lost his teddy. | Don't blub – it's only a scratch.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal and a bit mean; better say «cry». Double «b» in blubbed, blubbing. Related: blubber (to cry; also the fat of whales).

meaning for a pupil: 1) The state of being blurry: not sharp or clear, so you cannot see the edges or details well. 2) Unclear vision, when things look fuzzy to your eyes. 3) A lack of clearness in ideas or memories.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on light and eyes, blurriness happens when an image is out of focus; glasses or lenses can fix it. In photos, blurriness comes from moving the camera. Health: sudden blurriness of vision should be checked by a doctor.
examples from the lessons: The blurriness in the photo was because I moved. | Glasses fixed the blurriness of his eyesight. | Tell an adult if you notice blurriness when reading. | The blurriness of the picture made it hard to see the bird. | After swimming, I had some blurriness in my eyes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. From blurry + -ness (y changes to i). Related: blur, blurry, blurred.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Having a certain kind of body, used after another word: able-bodied, full-bodied, big-bodied. 2) (rare, verb past) From «body forth», to give a shape to an idea (old, literary).
its sense in the lessons: Almost always in compound words: an able-bodied person (fit and healthy), a full-bodied flavour (strong and rich), a slim-bodied insect. In slang, «got bodied» means badly beaten in a game or argument.
examples from the lessons: Every able-bodied man helped to fight the fire. | The coffee has a full-bodied taste. | A long-bodied dog like a dachshund. | The beetle is round-bodied and shiny. | (slang) We got bodied in the final, 5–0.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Rarely used alone; usually with a hyphen: able-bodied, full-bodied. Use «disabled» and «non-disabled» respectfully; «able-bodied» is common but some people prefer «non-disabled».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (Scotland, northern England) Pretty or attractive. 2) (UK) Healthy-looking, especially a plump, healthy baby.
its sense in the lessons: A Scottish and northern English word heard in songs like «My Bonnie Lies over the Ocean» and in everyday talk: «a bonny wee lass», «a bonny baby». In stories it gives a Scottish feeling.
examples from the lessons: What a bonny baby! | She's a bonny wee lass. | The bonny banks of Loch Lomond. | It's a bonny day for a walk. | Grandma says I'm looking bonny today.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Also spelt «bonnie». Comparative bonnier, bonniest. Mostly Scottish/northern; in the rest of the world people say pretty or lovely.

part of speech: verb (boogie, boogies, boogied, boogieing); noun (a boogie, boogies)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) To dance to fast pop music, especially in a fun, energetic way. 2) (noun) A dance, or a style of fast blues piano music (boogie-woogie). 3) (informal) To move fast or leave: «we need to boogie».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and at school discos, children «boogie on down». In music lessons, boogie-woogie is a 1930s-40s piano style. A boogie board is a short surfboard you lie on. «Bogey» (nose) is a different word.
examples from the lessons: Let's boogie at the school disco! | Grandpa boogied in the kitchen. | She plays boogie-woogie on the piano. | We rented boogie boards at the beach. | It's late – we need to boogie! | The whole class got up to boogie.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: boogieing (keep the «e»). Informal. Do not confuse with «bogey/booger» (snot) or «bogeyman».

part of speech: noun (a boomerang, boomerangs); verb (boomerang, boomerangs, boomeranged, boomeranging)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A curved, flat piece of wood that comes back to you when you throw it the right way, first made by Aboriginal Australians. 2) (verb) To come back to the place it started; to have the opposite effect from what was intended, often hurting the person who did it.
its sense in the lessons: In Australian history and culture lessons, boomerangs were used for hunting, sport and ceremonies by Aboriginal peoples, and not all of them return. In science, a boomerang returns because of spinning and air flow (lift). In stories, a mean plan «boomerangs» on the bully.
examples from the lessons: He threw the boomerang and it flew back to him. | Aboriginal hunters used boomerangs for thousands of years. | His trick boomeranged and he got into trouble himself. | Not all boomerangs come back. | Throwing a boomerang takes practice. | The rumour boomeranged back to her.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Safety: throw boomerangs only in big open spaces, away from people. Trap: only some types return; hunting boomerangs often do not.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Something that is very helpful and makes life better. 2) (old) A favour or request someone asks.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and news: «the new library is a boon to the village». In old stories, a hero asks the king for a boon. Phrase: a boon companion (an old phrase for a close friend).
examples from the lessons: The new bus route is a boon for the school. | The rain was a boon to the farmers. | Calculators are a boon for long sums. | The knight asked the queen for a boon. | Free Wi-Fi is a real boon on holiday.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a boon, boons. Opposite: a burden, a curse, a drawback. Often «a boon to/for».

part of speech: noun (a name; Bordeaux; bordeaux for the wine, bordeaux colour)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (a name) Bordeaux, a big city in south-west France, on the river Garonne. 2) A red or white wine made in the area around Bordeaux (often «claret» in the UK). 3) A deep red colour like that wine.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons, Bordeaux is a French port city famous for wine. Grown-ups talk about Bordeaux wine at dinner. In French it is said bor-DOH; the «x» and «eau» are not said as in English.
examples from the lessons: Bordeaux is in the south-west of France. | We stopped in Bordeaux on our holiday. | Dad ordered a glass of Bordeaux with dinner. | Her coat is a rich bordeaux colour. | The grapes for Bordeaux wine grow along the river.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually written with a capital B. Sounds like bor-DOH. It is a French place name used in English. Wine is only for adults.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The land near a border between two countries or regions. 2) A state or area between two things that is not clearly one or the other.
its sense in the lessons: In history and geography, borderlands such as the Scottish Borders were places of raids and battles. In stories, a borderland is wild and dangerous. As an idea: «the borderland between sleep and waking».
examples from the lessons: Raiders crossed the borderlands between England and Scotland. | The borderland was full of castles. | The village lies in the borderland between two countries. | Dreams happen in the borderland between sleep and waking. | Many languages are spoken in the borderlands.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Often plural: the borderlands. Similar: frontier, border region.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (adjective) Only just on one side of a line between two groups or results, so it is hard to decide which: a borderline pass. 2) (noun) A line that marks a border. 3) (medicine) Close to being an illness or problem but not quite.
its sense in the lessons: In school, a borderline mark is just at the pass mark, so the teacher must decide. In everyday life, «that's borderline rude» means almost rude. In health, «borderline high blood pressure».
examples from the lessons: His test score was borderline, so he might need to retake it. | That joke was borderline mean. | She was a borderline case for the team. | The doctor said Grandad's sugar levels are borderline. | Draw a borderline between the two fields.
note for the reader of a maths problem: In maths terms, borderline means very close to the cut-off number: if the pass mark is 50 and you get 49 or 51, that's borderline. One word.

part of speech: noun (a borrowing, borrowings; borrowing uncountable); verb, -ing form of borrow (borrow, borrows, borrowed, borrowing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Taking something that belongs to someone else, with their permission, and giving it back later. 2) (money) Getting money from a bank or person that must be paid back, often with extra (interest). 3) (language) A word taken from another language, like «café» from French or «kangaroo» from an Aboriginal language. 4) (maths, old) In subtraction, «borrowing» means taking ten from the next column (also called regrouping or exchanging).
its sense in the lessons: In school, borrowing books from the library. In maths subtraction, children learn borrowing (exchanging): 52 − 17, borrow a ten so 12 − 7 = 5. In English lessons, English has many borrowings from French, Latin, Norse and Hindi. In money lessons, borrowing costs extra because of interest.
examples from the lessons: I'm borrowing my sister's bike today. | Borrowing books from the library is free. | In 42 − 18 you need borrowing from the tens. | «Pyjamas» is a borrowing from Hindi/Urdu. | The country's borrowing is very high. | Thanks for borrowing me your pen – oops, I mean lending!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: you «borrow FROM» someone, they «lend TO» you. «Can I borrow your pen?», not «Can you borrow me your pen?» (lend). Maths: in UK schools «exchanging» or «regrouping» is now often used instead of «borrowing».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who comes from or lives in Boston, a big city in Massachusetts, USA. 2) (adjective) Having to do with Boston or its people, such as the Boston accent.
its sense in the lessons: In US history lessons, Bostonians took part in the Boston Tea Party (1773) before the American Revolution. A Bostonian accent often drops the «r» sounds: «pahk the cah».
examples from the lessons: My pen pal is a Bostonian. | Bostonians love their baseball team, the Red Sox. | The Bostonian accent is easy to recognise. | Angry Bostonians threw tea into the harbour. | She is a proud Bostonian.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Written with a capital B. Boston is also a small town in Lincolnshire, England, after which the US city was named.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person whose job is to stand at the door of a club or bar, check who comes in and remove people who cause trouble. 2) (cricket) A fast ball bowled so that it bounces high, near the batter's head. 3) Something that bounces, like a baby bouncer (a seat or swing that bounces a baby).
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and stories, bouncers are big and tough-looking. In cricket lessons and on TV, «a bouncer» is a short, fast ball. Parents use a baby bouncer to keep a baby happy.
examples from the lessons: The bouncer would not let the boys into the club. | The bowler sent down a fast bouncer. | My baby sister loves her bouncer. | The bouncer checked everyone's ID. | The batter ducked under the bouncer.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. A more formal word for the door job is «door supervisor» or «security».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A shady, pleasant place in a garden or wood, under trees or climbing plants. 2) (poetic, old) A private room or bedroom, especially a lady's. 3) The display made by a bowerbird.
its sense in the lessons: In poems and old stories, lovers meet in a rose bower. In science, the male bowerbird of Australia and New Guinea builds a bower and decorates it with blue things to attract a female.
examples from the lessons: They rested in a bower of roses. | The bowerbird decorated its bower with blue bottle tops. | The princess sat in her bower. | Ivy made a green bower over the bench. | The garden had a shady bower for reading.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Rhymes with «flower». Old-fashioned and poetic in most senses.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The time in a person's life when he is a boy, from birth until he becomes a young man. 2) The state of being a boy.
its sense in the lessons: In history and stories, writers describe a famous man's boyhood: where he grew up and what he did. Phrases: boyhood home, boyhood dream, boyhood friend.
examples from the lessons: He spent his boyhood on a farm. | Dad still talks about his boyhood in Belfast. | Becoming a pilot was his boyhood dream. | We visited Mark Twain's boyhood home. | They had been friends since boyhood.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable. Compare girlhood, childhood. «-hood» means a time or state, as in childhood, adulthood.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal, rude) Stupid; not thinking at all. 2) Having no brain, as in some simple animals.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday speech, «brainless» is an insult. In science, jellyfish and sponges have no brain, so they are brainless animals, yet they still survive. In stories, a brainless plan is a silly one.
examples from the lessons: That was a brainless thing to do! | Jellyfish are brainless but they can still sting. | The scarecrow thought he was brainless. | Don't be brainless – put your helmet on. | The film was fun but brainless.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Calling a person brainless is unkind. A sponge truly has no brain; a jellyfish has a nerve net instead.

part of speech: verb (brainstorm, brainstorms, brainstormed, brainstorming); noun (a brainstorm, brainstorms)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (verb) To think of lots of ideas quickly, in a group or alone, writing them all down before choosing the best. 2) (noun) A session of doing this. 3) (noun, UK, informal) A moment of confusion when you suddenly cannot think. 4) (noun, US, informal) A sudden clever idea.
its sense in the lessons: In school, before writing a story, children brainstorm ideas in a mind map or spider diagram. In work and science projects, teams brainstorm solutions. Phrase: brainstorm ideas.
examples from the lessons: Let's brainstorm ideas for our story. | We brainstormed names for the class pet. | Our group did a brainstorm on the board. | I had a brainstorm and forgot my own phone number. | She had a brainstorm: why not sell lemonade? | Brainstorm all the words you know about the sea.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word. In brainstorming, all ideas are accepted at first; you choose later.

part of speech: noun (brainstorming, uncountable); verb, -ing form of brainstorm
meaning for a pupil: 1) A way of finding ideas where people say every idea that comes to mind, quickly and without judging, then choose the best ones.
its sense in the lessons: A school and work method: before writing, planning a project or solving a problem, the class does brainstorming on the board or on sticky notes. Rules: no idea is silly, write everything, build on others' ideas.
examples from the lessons: Brainstorming helped us plan our science fair project. | We spent ten minutes brainstorming words for the poem. | In brainstorming, every idea counts. | Our team is brainstorming ways to save water. | Brainstorming works better when everyone takes a turn.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable as a noun: «some brainstorming». Related: mind map, spider diagram.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The person in a family who earns the money that the family lives on.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday adult life and stories about families, the breadwinner goes out to work. Today in many families both parents are breadwinners, or a mum is the main one. «Bread» here means money and food.
examples from the lessons: Mum is the main breadwinner in our house. | When Dad lost his job, Gran became the breadwinner. | Both my parents are breadwinners. | In the story, the eldest son had to become the breadwinner. | Being the only breadwinner can be stressful.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word. It does not mean someone wins bread in a contest. Any family member can be the breadwinner.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An escape from a prison or other place by force. 2) A sudden start or spread of something, like spots on the skin (an acne breakout). 3) (adjective) Suddenly very successful: a breakout star, breakout hit. 4) A breakout room or group: a small group split off from a bigger meeting or class.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and news: a prison breakout. In everyday life, teenagers get spot breakouts. In online lessons and meetings, teachers send pupils to breakout rooms. In entertainment, a breakout star suddenly becomes famous.
examples from the lessons: The prisoners planned a breakout. | I had a breakout of spots before the party. | This was the singer's breakout hit. | The teacher put us in breakout rooms on the video call. | The hens made a breakout through the fence!
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word as a noun; the verb is two words: «break out» (fire broke out, he broke out of jail).

meaning for a pupil: 1) With a fresh wind blowing: a breezy day. 2) Cheerful, relaxed and confident, sometimes too relaxed: a breezy manner.
its sense in the lessons: In weather reports and science: breezy means windy but not stormy; good for flying kites and drying washing. In stories, a breezy character is happy-go-lucky.
examples from the lessons: It's a breezy day, perfect for flying a kite. | The beach was breezy and cool. | She gave a breezy wave and walked off. | His breezy answer annoyed the teacher. | Take a jacket – it's breezy outside.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative breezier, breeziest. A breeze is a gentle wind; a gale is very strong. «Easy-breezy» (informal) means very easy.

part of speech: verb (brew, brews, brewed, brewing); noun (a brew, brews)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To make beer by soaking, boiling and fermenting grain. 2) To make tea or coffee by mixing it with hot water. 3) (noun, UK, informal) A cup of tea: «fancy a brew?» 4) (verb) Of something bad, to be about to happen: a storm is brewing, trouble is brewing. 5) (noun) A mixture, especially a strange one, like a witch's brew.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday UK and Irish talk, «put a brew on» means make a cup of tea. In stories, witches stir a brew in a cauldron, and trouble brews before a fight. In science, brewing uses yeast to turn sugar into alcohol and gas.
examples from the lessons: Gran brewed a pot of tea. | Fancy a brew? I'll put the kettle on. | The witches stirred their bubbling brew. | Dark clouds showed a storm was brewing. | I could tell trouble was brewing in the playground. | Monks used to brew beer in the abbey.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: brewed. «A brew» meaning tea is UK/Ireland/Australia informal. Beer is for adults only.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A factory or building where beer is made. 2) A company that makes beer.
its sense in the lessons: In history and local studies, towns grew around breweries. In science, a brewery is an example of using yeast and fermentation. Children may see brewery horses at shows in the UK.
examples from the lessons: The old brewery is now a museum. | You could smell malt near the brewery. | Shire horses used to pull carts for the brewery. | The town's biggest employer is a brewery. | Breweries use huge metal tanks.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: breweries (y → ies). Stress on the first syllable: BROO-er-ee.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Giving or offering money, gifts or favours to someone so they will do something dishonest or unfair for you. 2) (informal, humorous) Offering a treat to get someone to do something, as parents sometimes do.
its sense in the lessons: In law, news and ethics lessons, bribery is a crime: officials, referees or judges must not accept bribes. In everyday family life it is used jokingly: «a bit of bribery with chocolate got the kids to tidy up».
examples from the lessons: Bribery is against the law. | The official went to prison for bribery. | Mum used a little bribery to get us to eat our sprouts. | The referee was accused of bribery. | Bribery makes things unfair for honest people.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Related: bribe (noun and verb, a bribe), to bribe someone. Bribery is a serious crime even if the gift seems small.

part of speech: noun (a bridle, bridles); verb (bridle, bridles, bridled, bridling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The straps, metal bit and reins put on a horse's head to control it. 2) (verb) To put a bridle on a horse. 3) (verb) To show sudden anger or offence, often by pulling your head up: «she bridled at the remark». 4) (verb) To control or hold back something, like your temper.
its sense in the lessons: In riding lessons and stories about horses, you put on the saddle and bridle. In stories, a character bridles when insulted. A bridleway (UK) is a path for horses, walkers and bikes.
examples from the lessons: She put the bridle on the pony. | The horse shook its head against the bridle. | He bridled at being called a baby. | Hold the reins of the bridle gently. | We rode along a bridleway through the forest.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Do not confuse with «bridal» (about a bride, a wedding) – they sound the same.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The edge of a cliff, a steep place or water. 2) The point where something very good or very bad is about to happen: on the brink of war, on the brink of a discovery.
its sense in the lessons: In history and news: on the brink of war, the brink of collapse. In science stories: on the brink of a breakthrough. In nature lessons, animals «on the brink of extinction» are almost gone. Phrase: on the brink of, pull back from the brink.
examples from the lessons: The tiger is on the brink of extinction. | The two countries were on the brink of war. | We stood at the brink of the cliff. | She was on the brink of tears. | Scientists are on the brink of a great discovery. | The team was on the brink of winning the cup.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually «the brink of». Similar: verge, edge. Safety: keep away from the brink of cliffs and quarries.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Covered with short, stiff hairs. 2) Stiff and rough like bristles. 3) (informal) Easily annoyed or quick to get angry.
its sense in the lessons: In science, hedgehogs, pigs and some caterpillars are bristly. In everyday life, Dad's chin is bristly before he shaves. In stories, a bristly old man may be grumpy.
examples from the lessons: Dad's chin is bristly in the morning. | A hedgehog's back is bristly. | The new brush is very bristly. | The caterpillar had bristly hairs – don't touch it! | The headteacher was a bit bristly today.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative bristlier, bristliest. Some bristly caterpillars cause itchy rashes.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (UK, Australia, NZ, informal) An umbrella.
its sense in the lessons: Common in British and Australian everyday talk: «Take your brolly, it's going to rain!» Short for umbrella.
examples from the lessons: Don't forget your brolly! | My brolly blew inside out in the wind. | Gran never leaves home without a brolly. | Can I share your brolly? | I left my brolly on the bus.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: brollies. Informal; in formal writing use «umbrella». Not used much in the US.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A cruel, violent or rough person. 2) (old) A big, strong animal, especially a wild one. 3) (adjective) Using only strength, not thinking: brute force, brute strength. 4) (informal) Something big and hard to manage: «this box is a brute to carry».
its sense in the lessons: In stories, the villain or a bully is a brute. In science and computing, «brute force» means trying every possibility, for example trying every password or every number. Phrases: brute force, brute strength, you brute!
examples from the lessons: The brute pushed everyone out of his way. | He opened the door by brute force. | The bear was a huge brute. | Don't be such a brute to your brother! | Trying every combination of the lock is a brute-force method. | This suitcase is a brute to lift.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Related: brutal, brutality. In maths puzzles, a brute-force method checks every case one by one.

part of speech: adjective (bubbly, bubblier, bubbliest); noun (bubbly, uncountable, informal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Full of bubbles: bubbly water, bubbly bath. 2) Lively, cheerful and full of energy: a bubbly personality. 3) (noun, informal) Champagne or another sparkling wine.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: bubbly drinks and bubbly bath foam. In stories and school reports, a bubbly girl or boy is chatty and happy. Grown-ups drink a glass of bubbly at weddings and New Year.
examples from the lessons: My sister has a bubbly personality. | The bath was warm and bubbly. | The lemonade was nice and bubbly. | They opened a bottle of bubbly to celebrate. | Our new teacher is really bubbly. | Boil the jam until it's bubbly.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative bubblier, bubbliest. «Bubbly» as champagne is for adults.

part of speech: noun (a buffer, buffers); verb (buffer, buffers, buffered, buffering)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Something that protects one thing from another or softens a hit or shock. 2) Springs or pads on the end of a train or at the end of a railway track that soften a crash. 3) (computing) An area of memory where data is stored for a short time; «buffering» is when a video waits to load. 4) (science) A solution that keeps acidity (pH) from changing much. 5) (UK, informal) An old-fashioned man, often silly: «an old buffer».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, children see «buffering...» when videos stop. In geography, a buffer zone keeps two sides or a wild area apart. In science, buffers keep blood or ponds at a steady pH. Phrase: buffer zone, act as a buffer.
examples from the lessons: The video keeps buffering. | The train hit the buffers at the end of the line. | Trees act as a buffer against wind and noise. | The UN keeps a buffer zone between the two armies. | Savings are a buffer against hard times. | The old buffer next door tells long stories.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. «Buffering» as a verb is usually about videos and internet.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Swelling out in round lumps; bulging.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, a monster has bulgy eyes; a bulgy bag is too full. Informal, a bit funny.
examples from the lessons: The frog stared at me with bulgy eyes. | My school bag is all bulgy with books. | The alien had a bulgy green head. | His pockets were bulgy with conkers. | The goldfish has bulgy eyes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal; more standard: bulging. Comparative bulgier.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A public show, mainly in Spain, Portugal, southern France and parts of Latin America, in which people fight a bull in a ring; in most bullfights the bull is killed.
its sense in the lessons: In culture and ethics lessons, bullfighting is a tradition that many people see as cruel to animals; it is banned in some places and many people protest against it. Related: bullfighter, matador, bullring.
examples from the lessons: A bullfight takes place in a ring called a bullring. | Many people think bullfights are cruel. | The matador waved a red cape at the bull in the bullfight. | Some towns have banned bullfights. | We learnt about the debate over bullfights in Spain.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word. Countable: bullfights. Myth: bulls are not angered by the red colour; they react to the cape's movement, because bulls cannot see red well.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A very large frog, especially the North American bullfrog, with a deep, loud call that sounds like a bull or a cow mooing.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on life cycles and habitats, bullfrogs grow from big tadpoles and eat insects, fish and even small birds. In some countries they are an invasive species that harms local frogs.
examples from the lessons: The bullfrog croaked loudly from the pond. | A bullfrog can eat a small bird. | Bullfrog tadpoles can take two years to grow up. | We heard bullfrogs calling at night by the lake. | The bullfrog jumped into the water with a splash.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word. Plural bullfrogs. Only males make the loud call.

part of speech: noun (a bung, bungs); verb (bung, bungs, bunged, bunging)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A stopper or plug that closes a hole in a barrel, bottle or sink. 2) (verb, UK, informal) To put or throw something somewhere quickly and carelessly: «just bung it in the bag». 3) (verb) To block something up: «my nose is all bunged up». 4) (noun, UK, slang) A bribe: money given secretly to get an unfair advantage. 5) (Australia, informal) «Go bung» means break down or stop working.
its sense in the lessons: Very common in British and Australian everyday speech: «bung the kettle on», «bung it in the oven». With a cold, your nose is bunged up. In news, a «bung» is a secret payment, especially in sport.
examples from the lessons: Bung your coat on the chair. | Can you bung the pizza in the oven? | My nose is all bunged up with a cold. | Put the bung back in the barrel. | The football agent was accused of taking a bung. | The old telly's gone bung again (Australia).
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal in senses 2–5. Regular verb: bunged. In formal writing say put, throw, block, bribe.

part of speech: noun (a bungee, bungees); verb (bungee, bungees, bungeed, bungeeing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A long, stretchy rope or cord; bungee jumping is jumping from a high place with such a cord tied to your ankles so you bounce up and down. 2) A bungee cord (elastic strap with hooks) used to hold things on a bike rack or roof rack.
its sense in the lessons: In adventure stories and holidays, New Zealand is famous for bungee jumping from bridges. In science, it shows stored elastic energy: the cord stretches and pulls you back. In everyday life, a bungee strap holds luggage on.
examples from the lessons: My uncle went bungee jumping in New Zealand. | The bungee cord stretched and pulled her back up. | Use a bungee to hold the bag on the bike rack. | Bungee jumpers must be weighed first for safety. | I'd be too scared to bungee off a bridge!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Also spelt «bungy». Safety: bungee straps can snap back and hurt eyes; bungee jumping is only done with trained staff and age limits.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science, body) A small bag of fluid in the body, usually near a joint like the knee or elbow, that stops bones, muscles and tendons from rubbing. 2) (a name) Bursa, a big city in north-west Turkey.
its sense in the lessons: In science and health lessons, a bursa acts like a cushion. If it gets swollen and sore, it is called bursitis, for example «housemaid's knee». Bursa in Turkey is a famous old city.
examples from the lessons: A bursa helps your knee move smoothly. | The footballer hurt the bursa in his elbow. | Too much kneeling can swell the bursa in your knee. | We flew to Bursa to visit relatives. | The doctor said Grandma's sore shoulder was a swollen bursa.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: bursae (BUR-see) or bursas. Related: bursitis (swollen bursa). The city is written with a capital B.

part of speech: noun (bustle, uncountable; a bustle, bustles for the dress part); verb (bustle, bustles, bustled, bustling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (noun) Busy, noisy activity with lots of people moving about: the hustle and bustle of the city. 2) (verb) To move around quickly and busily. 3) (history) A pad or frame worn under the back of a long skirt in the 1800s to make it puff out.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, a busy market or a station is full of bustle; a mum or a cook «bustles about» the kitchen. In history lessons on Victorian clothes, women wore bustles. Phrase: hustle and bustle.
examples from the lessons: I love the hustle and bustle of the market. | Grandma bustled about the kitchen making tea. | Nurses bustled in and out of the ward. | Victorian ladies wore bustles under their dresses. | The town was bustling with tourists. | The station was full of bustle at rush hour.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The «t» is silent: BUSS-ul. Adjective: bustling (a bustling town).

part of speech: adjective (butch, butcher, butchest – rare); noun (a butch – slang)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) Looking or acting tough, strong and traditionally manly. 2) (slang) A word some people use for a lesbian woman who dresses or acts in a traditionally masculine way; it can be a proud self-description, but used by others it can be rude or hurtful. 3) (a name) Butch is also a nickname, as in the cowboy Butch Cassidy.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday talk, «a butch dog» or «a butch name» is tough-sounding. In stories and old westerns, Butch Cassidy was an American outlaw. Be careful: using it about a person can be teasing or unkind.
examples from the lessons: That bulldog looks very butch. | He tried to look butch in his leather jacket. | Butch Cassidy was a famous train robber. | "Rex is a butch name for a puppy," laughed Dad. | Don't call people names to tease them.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal. Do not use it to tease people about how they look. «Butcher» (meat seller) is a different word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A small plant with a flat rosette of sticky, pale green leaves and purple, violet or yellow flowers; it catches and eats small insects.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on plants and adaptations, butterwort is a carnivorous plant like the sundew and Venus flytrap. It grows in bogs and wet rocks, where the soil has few nutrients, so it gets food from insects. The leaves feel greasy like butter.
examples from the lessons: The butterwort caught a tiny fly on its sticky leaf. | Butterworts grow in wet, boggy places. | The butterwort has pretty violet flowers. | We saw butterwort on our trip to the Scottish hills. | Some people keep butterworts to catch fungus gnats.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. «Wort» is an old word for plant (as in St John's wort). Not related to butter except the greasy feel.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (adjective) From a time long ago; past: a bygone age, bygone days. 2) (noun, plural) Things from the past. 3) In «let bygones be bygones»: to forget old arguments and be friends again.
its sense in the lessons: In history and stories, «a bygone era» means olden times, like Victorian days. In everyday family life, «let bygones be bygones» is said after a quarrel.
examples from the lessons: The museum shows life in a bygone age. | Steam trains remind Grandad of bygone days. | Let's let bygones be bygones and be friends. | The village still has the charm of a bygone era. | They talked about bygones all evening.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Let bygones be bygones» is a set phrase. One word.

part of speech: abbreviation (ca, ca., Ca, CA); also French word (ça)
meaning for a pupil: 1) ca. or c. (from Latin «circa») means «about» or «around», used with dates and numbers: ca. 1500. 2) Ca (science) the chemical symbol for calcium. 3) CA (USA) short for California; also for Canada in internet addresses (.ca). 4) (French) «ça» means «that» or «it», as in «Ça va?» (How are you?); English speakers hear it as «sa». Not an English word.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, «ca. 1066» means about that year. In science, Ca is calcium, found in bones, milk and chalk. On addresses, CA means California. Canadian websites end in .ca. In French lessons, «Ça va?» means «How are you?».
examples from the lessons: The vase was made ca. 300 BC. | Ca is the symbol for calcium on the periodic table. | Her address was Los Angeles, CA. | Canadian websites end with .ca. | "Ça va?" "Ça va bien, merci!" | The castle was built ca. 1200.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Not a word but short forms. «ca.» with dates means approximately: «ca. 1500» could be a few years either side. In chemistry the symbol is Ca (capital C, small a). French ça has a little hook (cedilla) under the c.

part of speech: verb (cackle, cackles, cackled, cackling); noun (a cackle, cackles)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The loud, harsh sound a hen or goose makes. 2) (verb) To laugh in a loud, harsh, high way, often unpleasantly. 3) (noun) Such a laugh. 4) (UK, informal) Silly talk: «cut the cackle» means stop chatting and get to the point.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, witches and villains cackle when their plan works. On farms, hens cackle after laying an egg. It tells the reader a laugh sounds mean or wild.
examples from the lessons: The witch gave a wicked cackle. | The hens cackled in the farmyard. | The villain cackled with delight. | My aunt has a loud cackle of a laugh. | Cut the cackle and get on with your work! | The goose cackled at us as we walked past.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: cackled. A cackle is harsher than a giggle or a chuckle.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A pink powder made from zinc oxide with a little iron oxide, used in a lotion to soothe itchy or sore skin. 2) (old, science) An old name for zinc ores.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and health, calamine lotion is put on itchy chickenpox spots, insect bites, nettle stings and mild sunburn. It dries into a pink, chalky layer.
examples from the lessons: Mum dabbed calamine lotion on my chickenpox spots. | Calamine helps stop nettle stings itching. | The calamine left pink patches all over my legs. | Keep calamine lotion in the first-aid kit. | Shake the calamine bottle before you use it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable; usually in «calamine lotion». For outside use only, never drink it.

part of speech: verb, past form of calibrate (calibrate, calibrates, calibrated, calibrating); adjective (calibrated)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) Checked and adjusted so that it measures exactly right. 2) Marked with a scale of numbers for measuring: a calibrated cylinder. 3) Carefully planned or adjusted for a purpose: a carefully calibrated answer.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, measuring cylinders, thermometers and scales are calibrated. Before an experiment, you check that a balance reads 0 when empty. In everyday life, a calibrated oven or tyre gauge gives correct numbers.
examples from the lessons: The thermometer was calibrated in ice water at 0 °C. | Use a calibrated measuring cylinder to measure 50 ml. | The scales were calibrated before the weigh-in. | The engineers calibrated the sensors on the robot. | Her words were carefully calibrated not to upset anyone.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: calibration. Maths and science: a badly calibrated scale that reads 2 g too heavy will make every reading 2 g too much, so you subtract 2.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person whose job is to operate a camera for films or television.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and media lessons, the cameraman films the news, sport or a film. A more neutral word for anyone doing the job is «camera operator», since many are women.
examples from the lessons: The cameraman filmed the football match. | The reporter and her cameraman went to the flood. | The cameraman ran backwards to keep the runner in the shot. | Wave to the cameraman! | My aunt works as a camera operator on wildlife films.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: cameramen. Gender-neutral: camera operator, camera person.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (rare in English) A low, strong truck or cart used to carry heavy things, especially in the army. 2) (French and Spanish) «camion» (French) and «camión» (Spanish) mean a lorry or truck; French says it ka-mee-ON with a nasal end.
its sense in the lessons: Rare in English; you meet it in old military history texts. In French lessons, «un camion» is a lorry; in Spanish, «un camión» is a truck, and in Mexico also a bus.
examples from the lessons: (French) Le camion est rouge – the lorry is red. | A camion carried the cannons to the front. | In Mexico, people say «camión» for a bus. | The soldiers loaded the camion with supplies. | "Camion" is the French word for a truck.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly not used in everyday English; say lorry (UK) or truck (US).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) Short for camouflage: clothes or patterns in greens and browns that help you blend into the background. 2) (adjective) Having that pattern: camo trousers, camo jacket.
its sense in the lessons: In fashion and everyday life, camo trousers and caps are popular. In science, «camouflage» (camo) is how animals like chameleons hide. In video games, players unlock camo skins.
examples from the lessons: He wore camo trousers to the paintball party. | I got a camo backpack for school. | The soldiers were in full camo. | Chameleons are masters of camo. | My camo skin in the game is gold.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal short form of camouflage. Say KAM-oh.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who works hard to change something in society or politics, for example to protect the environment or to change a law. 2) A person who takes part in a political campaign or an election campaign. 3) (old) A soldier who has fought in many campaigns: «an old campaigner» (also someone with lots of experience).
its sense in the lessons: In news and citizenship lessons: climate campaigners, animal-rights campaigners, campaigners for children's safety. Greta Thunberg and Malala Yousafzai are famous young campaigners. Phrase: an old campaigner.
examples from the lessons: Campaigners want a new zebra crossing outside school. | The young campaigner spoke at the United Nations. | Environmental campaigners planted a thousand trees. | Campaigners handed in a petition to the council. | Grandad is an old campaigner at chess tournaments.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Spelling: campaign has a silent «g»: kam-PAYN-er.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Being a candidate in an election, or trying to be chosen for a job or position.
its sense in the lessons: In politics and news: «she announced her candidacy for president». In school elections, pupils announce their candidacy for school council. UK English also uses «candidature».
examples from the lessons: She announced her candidacy for class president. | His candidacy for mayor surprised everyone. | The party supported her candidacy. | He withdrew his candidacy after the scandal. | Write a speech to support your candidacy for school council.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: candidacies. Formal. Related: candidate (the person), stand for/run for election.

part of speech: adjective (candied); verb, past form of candy (candy, candies, candied, candying)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Cooked in sugar syrup to preserve it and make it sweet: candied peel, candied fruit. 2) (rare) Too sweet or flattering in words.
its sense in the lessons: In cooking and festivals: candied peel goes in Christmas cake, candied apples (toffee apples) at fairs and Halloween, candied yams at US Thanksgiving. In science, sugar stops germs growing, so candied fruit lasts a long time.
examples from the lessons: Gran puts candied peel in the Christmas pudding. | We had candied apples at the fair. | Candied cherries decorate the cake. | Candied yams are a Thanksgiving dish. | Candied ginger is sweet and spicy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: candy → candied (y → ied). Too many candied treats are bad for teeth.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The soft light from a candle or candles.
its sense in the lessons: In history and stories, people read and worked by candlelight before electricity. In everyday life: a candlelight dinner, a candlelight vigil to remember people. In church, carol services by candlelight at Christmas.
examples from the lessons: We did our homework by candlelight during the power cut. | People used to read by candlelight. | The church looked lovely in the candlelight. | They held a candlelight vigil for the victims. | Mum and Dad had a candlelight dinner.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word; uncountable. Safety: never leave candles burning unwatched; keep them away from curtains.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A holder for a candle, with a hole or spike on top. 2) (money, charts) A candlestick chart shows prices going up and down with bars that look like candles.
its sense in the lessons: In history and stories, people carried candlesticks to bed. In the board game Cluedo, the candlestick is one of the weapons. Nursery rhyme: «Jack be nimble, Jack be quick, Jack jump over the candlestick.» In churches, tall candlesticks stand on the altar.
examples from the lessons: Grandma polished the silver candlesticks. | Jack jumped over the candlestick. | It was Colonel Mustard with the candlestick in the library! | Two brass candlesticks stood on the altar. | She carried a candlestick up the dark stairs.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word. Countable: candlesticks.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The quality of being honest, open and saying what you really think, even if it is not nice to hear.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and news, people speak with candour about difficult things. In ethics lessons, candour is honesty and openness; a good friend may show candour about your mistakes.
examples from the lessons: She spoke with surprising candour about her mistakes. | I appreciate your candour. | The coach's candour helped the team improve. | He answered every question with candour. | Children often speak with complete candour.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK spelling: candour; US spelling: candor. Adjective: candid. Uncountable.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To write a letter as a capital (A, B, C) or start a word with a capital letter. 2) To use a situation to get an advantage: «capitalise on a mistake». 3) (money) To provide money (capital) for a business.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons, you capitalise the first word of a sentence, names, days, months, «I» and places. In sport and stories, a team capitalises on the other team's mistakes. Phrase: capitalise on.
examples from the lessons: Remember to capitalise the first word of every sentence. | Capitalise names like London and Monday. | Our team capitalised on their mistake and scored. | She capitalised on her success to start a shop. | Don't capitalise the whole word – it looks like shouting.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK spelling: capitalise; US spelling: capitalize. Use «capitalise on» for taking advantage.

part of speech: adjective (capped); verb, past form of cap (cap, caps, capped, capping)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Covered at the top: snow-capped mountains. 2) Having a top limit put on it: prices are capped at £5. 3) (UK, sport) Chosen to play for your national team: capped for England. 4) (teeth) Covered with an artificial crown by a dentist.
its sense in the lessons: In geography, snow-capped peaks. In money and news, capped prices or bills mean they cannot go above a limit. In UK sport, a player «capped 50 times» has played 50 international matches. In maths problems, «capped at 10» means the most it can be is 10.
examples from the lessons: We saw snow-capped mountains in the Alps. | Bus fares are capped at £2. | He was capped for Wales at the age of nineteen. | The dentist capped my broken tooth. | Screen time is capped at one hour a day in our house. | The pen was capped so it would not dry out.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double «p»: capped, capping. Maths: if a cost is capped at 10, then 12 becomes 10; values under 10 stay the same.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A large bird of prey from the Americas, related to falcons, with long legs and often a bare red or orange face; it walks on the ground and eats dead animals as well as live prey.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on birds of prey and food chains, caracaras are scavengers and hunters. Pronounced kar-ah-KAR-ah.
examples from the lessons: The caracara was eating a dead fish on the beach. | A crested caracara has a black cap and red face. | Caracaras walk on the ground more than other falcons. | We saw a caracara in Florida. | The caracara is a clever bird.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Despite its looks it is a kind of falcon, not an eagle or vulture.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A plant related to the carrot whose small, curved, brown seeds are used as a spice. 2) The seeds of this plant, with a warm, slightly liquorice-like taste.
its sense in the lessons: In cooking and history lessons, caraway seeds go in rye bread, seed cake, sauerkraut and cheeses. In science, they are actually small dry fruits.
examples from the lessons: Rye bread often has caraway seeds in it. | Gran's seed cake is made with caraway. | Caraway tastes a little like aniseed. | The sauerkraut was flavoured with caraway. | We grew caraway in the herb garden.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «caraway seeds». Said KAR-a-way.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Adding carbon dioxide gas to a drink so that it becomes fizzy. 2) The fizziness of a drink. 3) (science) A chemical reaction with carbon dioxide, for example when concrete or limestone react with CO2.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, fizzy drinks have carbonation: the gas is pushed in under pressure and bubbles out when you open the bottle. A shaken bottle sprays because the gas escapes fast. Flat lemonade has lost its carbonation.
examples from the lessons: The carbonation makes cola fizzy. | Our lemonade went flat because it lost its carbonation. | Carbonation happens when carbon dioxide dissolves in water. | Shaking the bottle releases the carbonation quickly. | Cold drinks keep their carbonation longer than warm ones.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Verb: carbonate; adjective: carbonated (carbonated water). Science: more gas stays dissolved in cold water, so warm drinks go flat faster.

part of speech: verb (carbonise, carbonises, carbonised, carbonising); US spelling: carbonize
meaning for a pupil: 1) To turn something into carbon or charcoal by heating it strongly, usually without much air. 2) (science) To change dead plants slowly into coal or into a black carbon layer over a very long time. 3) (cooking, joking) To burn food so badly that it goes black and hard.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons it comes up with coal, charcoal and fossils: plants carbonise when heat and pressure act on them for millions of years. In the kitchen it is a joking way to say toast or sausages are burnt to a crisp. It tells the reader that something has turned black and hard because of heat. Often in «carbonised remains», «carbonised wood», «carbonised seeds».
examples from the lessons: Charcoal is made by carbonising wood in a kiln with little air. | Over millions of years the buried ferns were carbonised into coal. | Dad left the toast in too long and carbonised it. | Archaeologists found carbonised grain in the old Roman oven. | If you heat sugar too long, it starts to carbonise and smell bitter. | The fossil leaf was a thin carbonised film on the rock. | Don't carbonise the marshmallows, just toast them golden.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: carbonised, carbonising. UK, Australia, NZ, Ireland often spell it with -ise; the USA and Canada use carbonize. Do not confuse with «carbonate» (to add fizzy carbon dioxide gas to a drink) — carbonated lemonade is fizzy, not burnt.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (medicine) To do with both the heart and the lungs together. 2) Used mainly in «cardiopulmonary resuscitation» (CPR): pushing on the chest and giving rescue breaths to someone whose heart has stopped.
its sense in the lessons: It is a long medical word built from «cardio» (heart) and «pulmonary» (lungs). Pupils meet it in first-aid and safety lessons, mostly through the short form CPR. It tells the reader that the heart and lungs are working together, for example when blood picks up oxygen in the lungs and the heart pumps it round the body. Phrases: «cardiopulmonary resuscitation», «cardiopulmonary system», «cardiopulmonary arrest».
examples from the lessons: CPR stands for cardiopulmonary resuscitation. | The lifeguard learned cardiopulmonary resuscitation on a dummy. | The heart and lungs together make the cardiopulmonary system. | Running every day keeps your cardiopulmonary health strong. | The first-aid poster showed the steps of cardiopulmonary resuscitation. | The doctor checked her cardiopulmonary fitness on a treadmill. | In an emergency, call 999 or 911 first, then start CPR if you have been trained.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It is an adjective only and has no plural. Say «car-dee-oh-PUL-mon-er-ee». Break it into parts: cardio = heart (as in cardiologist), pulmonary = lungs. Children should know the safety rule: call for help (999 or 112 in the UK and Ireland, 911 in the USA and Canada, 000 in Australia, 111 in New Zealand) before anything else.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An old word for a helmet, especially a knight's or soldier's metal helmet. 2) (animals) A hard bony or horny lump on the head or beak of some birds, such as the cassowary and the hornbill.
its sense in the lessons: It appears in history stories about knights and in nature lessons about birds. In a story it tells the reader that someone wears an old-fashioned metal helmet. In a nature book it describes the strange helmet-like crest on a cassowary's head or a hornbill's beak. It is a rare, rather old or technical word.
examples from the lessons: The knight lowered his shining casque before the joust. | The cassowary has a tall casque on top of its head. | Hornbills have a big casque on their beaks. | In the museum we saw a dented casque from a medieval battle. | Scientists think the cassowary's casque may help it with heat and sound. | The soldier's casque glinted in the sun. | The poem described a hero with a plumed casque.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a casque, two casques. Say «kask» — it sounds like «cask» (a wooden barrel), a homophone, so read the sentence to know which one is meant. Everyday English uses «helmet» instead.

part of speech: noun (cassia, uncountable as a spice; a cassia, cassias as a plant)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A spice made from the bark of a tree; it tastes and smells like cinnamon and is often sold as cinnamon. 2) A tree or bush with yellow flowers in warm countries; some kinds are grown in gardens and parks. 3) (Bible) A sweet-smelling spice mentioned in the Bible, used in holy oil and perfumes.
its sense in the lessons: In cooking and food lessons it explains where much «cinnamon» in shops really comes from. In geography and science it is a plant of warm places such as China, India and Australia. In Bible lessons it is one of the spices in the holy anointing oil. It tells the reader about a warm, sweet smell or a yellow-flowered tree.
examples from the lessons: Much of the cinnamon sold in supermarkets is actually cassia. | Cassia bark is thicker and rougher than true cinnamon. | Grandma's apple cake smelled of cassia and cloves. | Bright yellow cassia trees lined the street in the summer. | The Bible lists cassia among the spices for the holy oil. | Cassia comes from the bark of a tree that grows in southern China. | We crushed a stick of cassia in the science lesson to smell it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say «KASS-ee-uh». As a spice it is uncountable (some cassia); as a tree it is countable (cassias). Trap: cassia and true cinnamon are related but not the same plant; true cinnamon comes mostly from Sri Lanka.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A group in a society into which people are born, which in the past decided what work they did and whom they could marry; best known from the traditional system in India and Nepal. 2) Any fixed social class that is hard to move out of. 3) (science) A group of insects in a colony that do one kind of job, such as workers, soldiers or the queen in an ant or bee colony.
its sense in the lessons: In history and religion lessons it describes the old caste system linked to Hindu society in South Asia; today caste discrimination is against the law in India, though it still affects many lives. In science it describes the jobs in insect colonies. In stories it tells the reader that someone is held back or treated unfairly because of the group they were born into. Phrases: «caste system», «lower caste», «worker caste».
examples from the lessons: In India, discrimination because of caste is against the law. | The old caste system decided which jobs people could do. | Dr B. R. Ambedkar fought hard for people treated badly because of their caste. | In a beehive, the worker caste collects nectar and the queen lays eggs. | Termites have a soldier caste with big jaws to guard the nest. | In the story, the girl refused to accept that her caste decided her future. | Many people today marry across caste lines.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a caste, castes. Homophone trap: «cast» (actors in a play; a plaster cast on a broken arm) sounds the same as «caste». Talk about caste respectfully: it is about real people, and treating anyone as lower because of birth is unfair.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a relaxed, easy way, without seeming worried or careful. 2) Without thinking much or planning, as if it does not matter. 3) In clothes for everyday, not smart wear. 4) Now and then, not regularly or deeply (casually know someone).
its sense in the lessons: In stories it shows how a character acts — calmly, or pretending not to care («she said casually»), which often hints they are hiding something. In everyday life it describes clothes for weekends and non-uniform days. Phrases: «dressed casually», «said casually», «casually mentioned», «walked casually».
examples from the lessons: He casually strolled into the classroom ten minutes late. | "Oh, I won the race," she said casually, trying not to show off. | On mufti day we can dress casually instead of in uniform. | Mum casually mentioned that we were getting a puppy. | Don't treat safety rules casually; they protect you. | I only know him casually from football. | The cat lay casually on the warm windowsill. | He casually tossed the ball over the fence.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from «casual» + -ly; spelled with two l's (casual + ly). It describes how something is done. Trap: «casually» is not «causally» (to do with causes) — the letters u and a swap places.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) A substance that makes a chemical reaction go faster without being used up itself. 2) A person or event that makes a big change happen, or makes it happen sooner.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons it is the substance that speeds up a reaction, like enzymes in your body that help digest food, or the catalytic converter in a car. In history and stories it is the event that sets off big changes — «the catalyst for the war». It tells the reader that something started or sped up a change. Phrases: «a catalyst for change», «acted as a catalyst».
examples from the lessons: Enzymes in your saliva act as catalysts to break down food. | A catalyst speeds up a reaction but is not used up. | In the experiment, the catalyst made the hydrogen peroxide fizz quickly. | The new teacher was a catalyst for change in our school. | The storm was the catalyst that made the town build a stronger sea wall. | Rosa Parks's brave act became a catalyst for the bus boycott. | Platinum is a catalyst in a car's exhaust system.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a catalyst, catalysts. Say «KAT-uh-list». Adjective: catalytic (a catalytic converter). In science the key point: the catalyst is still there, unchanged, at the end of the reaction.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a way that causes terrible damage or disaster. 2) (everyday, exaggerating) Extremely badly, as when a plan goes completely wrong.
its sense in the lessons: In news and geography it describes floods, earthquakes or failures that cause huge damage. In everyday talk it is often used to exaggerate how badly something went («the cake failed catastrophically»). It tells the reader that the result was very, very bad. Phrases: «went catastrophically wrong», «failed catastrophically».
examples from the lessons: The dam failed catastrophically and the valley flooded. | Our class play went catastrophically wrong when the scenery fell down. | The bridge was catastrophically damaged in the earthquake. | My first try at baking bread failed catastrophically. | If the ice sheets melt, sea levels could rise catastrophically. | He catastrophically misjudged the jump and landed in the mud. | The rocket's engine failed catastrophically just after launch.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from «catastrophe» → «catastrophic» → «catastrophically» (note -ally). Say «kat-uh-STROF-ik-lee». In everyday speech it is often an exaggeration; in the news it can mean real loss of life, so think about who is listening.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Very clear and certain, with no doubt at all («a categorical no»). 2) (maths, formal) To do with categories or groups; categorical data is sorted into groups, not measured with numbers.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and the news it describes a firm, absolute answer or promise — «a categorical denial». In school maths and statistics, categorical data means things like favourite colour or type of pet, which go into a tally chart, bar chart or pie chart rather than being measured. It tells the reader there is no maybe. Adverb: «categorically».
examples from the lessons: The head teacher gave a categorical no to phones in class. | The minister issued a categorical denial of the story. | Favourite fruit is categorical data, but height is not. | We sorted the categorical data into a bar chart. | I can say with categorical certainty that I locked the door. | Dad was categorical: no screens after eight. | Eye colour is an example of categorical data.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective; adverb «categorically» («I categorically refuse»). In maths, categorical data (groups, names) is different from numerical data (measurements, counts); you can count how many are in each group but you cannot find the mean of colours.

part of speech: noun (a cauldron, cauldrons); US also caldron
meaning for a pupil: 1) A very large, deep metal pot for cooking over a fire, often shown in stories with witches. 2) A place or situation full of violent feelings or wild activity («a cauldron of noise»). 3) (sport) The large bowl in which the Olympic flame burns.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and fairy tales witches stir a bubbling cauldron of potion. In history lessons people cooked in cauldrons over open fires. In news and sport it describes a stadium full of noise or a tense situation. The Olympic cauldron is lit at the opening ceremony. It tells the reader about bubbling, heat or wild excitement.
examples from the lessons: The witch stirred her bubbling cauldron. | In Viking times, families cooked stew in an iron cauldron. | The Olympic cauldron was lit by a young athlete. | The stadium was a cauldron of noise when the goal went in. | Steam rose from the cauldron over the campfire. | In Macbeth, three witches chant around a cauldron. | The classroom was a cauldron of excitement before the holidays.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a cauldron, cauldrons. Say «KORL-drun». The US also writes «caldron». Witches with cauldrons are from stories and folk tales, not real life.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Causing something, acting as its cause («a causative factor», «the causative virus»). 2) (grammar) A form of a verb or sentence that shows someone makes something happen or has it done, like «I had my hair cut» or «She made him laugh».
its sense in the lessons: In science and health it names the cause of a disease or effect — «the causative agent». In grammar lessons, «causative» describes patterns with have/get/make/let: «We got the car fixed». It tells the reader who or what makes something happen. It is a formal word.
examples from the lessons: Scientists found the causative virus of the illness. | Smoking is a causative factor in many lung diseases. | "I had my bike repaired" is a causative sentence. | In the causative, the person doing the work is often not named. | "Make" is a causative verb in "Mum made me tidy my room". | The doctor explained the causative link between sugar and tooth decay. | We practised causatives: "I got my hair cut", "She had her eyes tested".
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal word. In grammar: «have/get + thing + past participle» (have it fixed) and «make/let + person + verb» (make him wait). Trap: a cause found together with an effect is not always causative — things can happen together by chance (correlation is not causation).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Carefully, so as to avoid danger or mistakes. 2) Slowly and not fully trusting something yet («cautiously hopeful»).
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons it describes how to cross roads, climb, or handle hot or sharp things. In stories it shows a character who is nervous or wary — creeping cautiously into a dark room. In the news, «cautiously optimistic» means hopeful but not sure. It tells the reader to expect care, slowness or doubt.
examples from the lessons: We crossed the busy road cautiously, looking both ways. | The cat cautiously sniffed the new food. | She cautiously opened the creaky door. | Hold the scissors cautiously, with the points down. | The doctors are cautiously hopeful that he will get better. | He stepped cautiously onto the frozen pond — a dangerous idea. | The deer moved cautiously out of the trees. | Cautiously, I lifted the lid of the mystery box.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from «cautious» + -ly; noun «caution». Spelling: c-a-u-t-i-o-u-s-l-y. Safety tip: never walk on frozen ponds or lakes, however cautiously.

part of speech: noun, a name (the Cayuga, Cayuga people; Cayuga Lake)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (a name) The Cayuga are a Native American (First Nations) people, one of the Six Nations of the Haudenosaunee (Iroquois) Confederacy, from what is now New York State and Ontario. 2) (a name) The Cayuga language spoken by that people. 3) (a name) Cayuga Lake, one of the Finger Lakes in New York State, and places named after it.
its sense in the lessons: It appears in history and geography lessons about North America, about the Haudenosaunee Confederacy and its Great Law of Peace, and on maps of New York State and Ontario. It is a proper name, so it starts with a capital letter in sentences.
examples from the lessons: The Cayuga are one of the Six Nations of the Haudenosaunee. | Many Cayuga people live today in Ontario, Canada, and in New York State. | Cayuga Lake is one of the long, thin Finger Lakes. | Only a few people still speak the Cayuga language fluently. | We read how the Cayuga joined the confederacy for peace. | Our map showed Cayuga Lake south of Lake Ontario.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A name, written «Cayuga» with a capital C. Say «kay-YOO-guh». Speak of the Cayuga as a living people today, not only in the past.

part of speech: noun (the cerebellum; plural cerebellums or cerebella)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) The part of the brain at the back, under the big main part, that controls balance, smooth movement and coordination.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on the body and the brain, it is the part that helps you ride a bike, walk without falling and catch a ball. It tells the reader about balance and coordination. Phrases: «the cerebellum controls balance», «damage to the cerebellum».
examples from the lessons: The cerebellum helps you keep your balance. | When you learn to juggle, your cerebellum is hard at work. | The cerebellum sits at the back of the head, below the cerebrum. | Gymnasts rely on their cerebellum for smooth movements. | A helmet protects your brain, including the cerebellum. | Our model brain had the cerebellum painted green. | Damage to the cerebellum can make walking wobbly.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say «serr-uh-BELL-um». It means «little brain» in Latin. Don't confuse it with the cerebrum, the large main part of the brain used for thinking. Plural is rare: cerebellums or cerebella.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A bright deep pinkish-red colour, like cherries.
its sense in the lessons: Used in art lessons and in descriptions of clothes, flowers and paint. It tells the reader the exact shade: brighter and pinker than plain red. It comes from the French word for cherry.
examples from the lessons: She wore a cerise dress to the party. | The cerise flowers stood out against the green leaves. | We mixed red and a little white and blue to get cerise. | Cerise is a bright cherry-pink colour. | His bike was painted cerise and silver. | The sunset turned the clouds cerise.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say «suh-REEZ». No plural as a colour. It comes from French «cerise» (cherry), but in English it means only the colour.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The act of officially proving that someone has passed a test or that something meets a standard. 2) An official document or award that shows this, like a certificate. 3) (films) The age rating given to a film or game (U, PG, 12A, 15, 18 in the UK; G, PG, PG-13, R in the USA).
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life it is how people show they are trained — lifeguards, electricians, first-aiders need certification. In school it appears with swimming awards, music grades and exams. For films it means the age rating. It tells the reader something has been officially checked. Phrases: «get certification», «safety certification», «film certification».
examples from the lessons: You need certification before you can work as a lifeguard. | The toy passed its safety certification. | The film got a PG certification, so we could watch it. | Mum is taking a course for her first-aid certification. | Organic food needs special certification. | The new bridge waited for certification before it opened. | My swimming certification says I can swim 100 metres.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun from «certify». «Certification» is the process or status; «certificate» is the actual paper you hold. Both can be used for the paper in everyday talk.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal, writing) Short for the Latin word «confer», meaning «compare»; it tells the reader to look at another thing and compare it with this one.
its sense in the lessons: It appears in dictionaries, textbooks and notes, often in brackets: «(cf. page 12)». It tells the reader: look at this other example too, it is similar or different in a useful way. Children mostly meet it in reference books. It is not said aloud as a word; people say «compare».
examples from the lessons: Rabbit (cf. hare) is a smaller animal with shorter ears. | The text says "cf. chapter 3" so I turned to chapter 3. | The dictionary wrote "cf. affect" next to "effect". | In the notes it said: warm-blooded, cf. cold-blooded. | Cf. means "compare", not "see also" exactly. | The teacher wrote "cf. last week's poem" on the board.
note for the reader of a maths problem: An abbreviation, not a word: written «cf.» with a full stop (period), often in lower case. Say it as «compare» when reading aloud. It is different from «e.g.» (for example) and «i.e.» (that is). It is not a short form of «confer» in its modern English meaning (to talk together or give an award).

meaning for a pupil: 1) The job of being the chair (chairman or chairwoman) of a meeting, committee or company. 2) The time during which someone has that job. 3) The skill of running a meeting well.
its sense in the lessons: In news and adult life it describes who leads a board or committee and for how long — «under her chairmanship». In school councils children may take turns to chair a meeting. It tells the reader who is in charge of the meeting and how well they run it. Phrases: «under the chairmanship of», «take over the chairmanship».
examples from the lessons: Under her chairmanship, the club raised a lot of money. | He was offered the chairmanship of the football club. | The chairmanship of the school council changes each term. | Good chairmanship means letting everyone speak. | During his chairmanship, the company grew quickly. | She stepped down from the chairmanship after ten years.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun with -ship (like friendship, leadership). Many people now prefer neutral words: «chair», «chairperson» and the job «chairing». It can be used for a woman too, but «chairwoman» or «chair» is common.

part of speech: verb (char, chars, charred, charring); noun (char, uncountable — burnt part; a char, chars — person, fish)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To burn something a little so the outside goes black. 2) (UK, old-fashioned) A cleaning woman paid to clean houses or offices (short for charwoman). 3) (UK, informal) Tea, as in «a cup of char». 4) A kind of fish related to trout and salmon that lives in cold lakes and seas (the Arctic char).
its sense in the lessons: In cooking it describes grilled or barbecued food with black marks; in science and history it describes burnt wood or remains. In old British stories «the char» is the woman who cleans. Older British people may say «a nice cup of char». In nature lessons the Arctic char is a cold-water fish. It tells the reader about burning, or an old-fashioned British word.
examples from the lessons: Char the peppers on the grill until the skins go black. | The forest fire charred hundreds of trees. | We found charred wood in the old fireplace. | Grandad asked for "a cup of char" with two sugars. | In the old story, the char scrubbed the floors every morning. | Arctic char live in very cold lakes. | The burnt toast was charred at the edges.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb doubles the r: charred, charring. «Char» for tea comes from the Chinese word «cha» (tea); it is British slang and a bit old-fashioned. Don't mix it up with «chart» or «chair».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who is very pleasant and attractive and makes people like them easily, sometimes to get what they want. 2) A person who charms animals, especially a snake charmer, who seems to make a snake «dance» to music.
its sense in the lessons: In stories a charmer is a likeable character — sometimes kind, sometimes a smooth talker who tricks others. People say a baby or a puppy is «a real charmer». In geography or stories about India and North Africa you may read about snake charmers. It tells the reader someone wins people over easily. Phrases: «a real charmer», «snake charmer».
examples from the lessons: My little brother is a real charmer; everyone gives him sweets. | The new puppy was a charmer and won the whole family over. | The fox in the fable was a smooth charmer who fooled the crow. | The snake charmer played a flute in front of a basket. | Be careful: a charmer online may be lying about who they are. | Grandpa was a charmer who could make anyone laugh.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a charmer, charmers. It can be praise or a warning, so read the tone. Myth: snakes cannot hear tunes the way we do; they follow the movement of the charmer's flute. Snake charming is now banned in some countries because it can hurt the snakes.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a slightly rude but often funny or playful way, showing a lack of respect (especially UK, Ireland, Australia, New Zealand). 2) In a bold, playful way, as in a cheeky grin.
its sense in the lessons: In stories it describes naughty, playful characters who answer back or grin. In real life a teacher might say a pupil answered «cheekily». It tells the reader the behaviour is a bit rude but often light-hearted. Phrases: «grinned cheekily», «answered cheekily».
