examples from the lessons: He grinned cheekily and stole the last biscuit. | "You're old, Grandad!" she said cheekily. | The monkey cheekily grabbed my sandwich. | He cheekily asked the head teacher for a longer break. | My sister winked cheekily at me across the table. | The puppy cheekily ran off with my sock.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from «cheeky» (y changes to i: cheekily). «Cheeky» is used much more in the UK, Ireland, Australia and New Zealand than in the USA, where people say «sassy» or «fresh». Being cheeky to adults can get you in trouble even if it is funny.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Rude but often playful or funny behaviour that shows a lack of respect. 2) Boldness, cheek, the nerve to ask for or do something.
its sense in the lessons: In school reports and stories it describes a child who answers back or plays around. It can be a telling-off word or a fond one. It tells the reader someone is being bold and a little rude. Similar: «cheek» («What a cheek!»).
examples from the lessons: The teacher would not put up with any more cheekiness. | His cheekiness made everyone laugh, even Mum. | I couldn't believe the cheekiness of the seagull stealing my chips. | Her cheekiness got her sent out of the room. | There was a twinkle of cheekiness in his eyes. | Grandma loved the cheekiness of her youngest grandchild.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: no plural, no «a». Spelling: cheeky → cheekiness (y changes to i). The short word «cheek» is often used the same way: «That's enough cheek from you!»

meaning for a pupil: 1) (UK, informal) Goodbye, said in a friendly, cheerful way. 2) (Australia, informal) A small red cocktail sausage, often served at children's parties (also called a little boy or saveloy in some places). 3) (a name) Cheerios is a brand of breakfast cereal shaped like little rings.
its sense in the lessons: In British and Irish talk, and in older stories, people wave and say «Cheerio!» when leaving. In Australia and parts of New Zealand, cheerios are little sausages eaten with tomato sauce at parties. It tells the reader someone is leaving happily, or names a party food. Similar: «bye», «cheers», «ta-ra».
examples from the lessons: Cheerio, see you tomorrow! called Gran from the door. | We said cheerio to our cousins at the station. | At the birthday party we ate cheerios with tomato sauce. | "Cheerio then!" said the postman as he left. | In the old film everyone said cheerio instead of goodbye. | I had a bowl of Cheerios for breakfast.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal, a bit old-fashioned in the UK but still heard. Spelled «cheerio» (not cheerioh). The cereal is «Cheerios» with a capital C because it is a brand name. Do not confuse with «cheers», which in the UK can mean thanks, goodbye, or what you say when clinking glasses.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Happy and friendly in a bright, lively way. 2) Making you feel happy, bright and pleasant (a cheery room, a cheery colour).
its sense in the lessons: In stories it describes friendly characters, voices and greetings — «a cheery wave». It also describes bright places and colours. It tells the reader the mood is light and happy. Phrases: «a cheery hello», «a cheery smile», «cheery news».
examples from the lessons: The bus driver gave us a cheery wave. | She has a cheery smile every morning. | Yellow curtains made the kitchen look cheery. | "Good morning!" he said in a cheery voice. | We sang a cheery song on the long car journey. | Despite the rain, everyone stayed cheery. | The card had a cheery picture of a sun.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative cheerier, superlative cheeriest. Adverb: cheerily. «Cheery» and «cheerful» mean nearly the same; «cheery» often describes a quick greeting or look.

part of speech: noun (a chequebook, chequebooks); US spelling: checkbook
meaning for a pupil: 1) (money) A small book of printed forms (cheques) that a bank gives to a customer; you write on a cheque to pay someone from your bank account. 2) (informal) Used to mean paying money to solve a problem, as in «chequebook journalism».
its sense in the lessons: In maths and money lessons it shows how adults used to pay before cards and phones: write the amount in numbers and words, sign it, and the bank moves the money. Fewer people use chequebooks now, but some still do for bills and gifts. Phrases: «write a cheque», «chequebook and pen».
examples from the lessons: Grandma took out her chequebook to pay the plumber. | A chequebook has cheques you tear out along the dotted line. | We practised writing a cheque in words and numbers. | Dad hardly ever uses his chequebook now; he pays by phone. | In the USA it is spelled "checkbook". | She keeps her chequebook in a safe drawer. | My birthday cheque came from Grandpa's chequebook.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK, Ireland, Canada, Australia and New Zealand spell it «cheque»; the USA uses «check», so «checkbook». Countable: chequebooks. Maths: the amount on a cheque is written twice, in figures (£25.50) and in words (twenty-five pounds and fifty pence), to stop mistakes and cheating.

part of speech: adjective (cherished); verb form (past of cherish: cherish, cherishes, cherished, cherishing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Loved, protected and cared for very much (a cherished toy). 2) Kept carefully in your mind and heart (a cherished memory, a cherished hope). 3) (verb) Past form of «cherish»: loved and looked after something precious.
its sense in the lessons: In stories it shows how much a character loves a person, a pet or an object — often something old with memories attached. In family and church life people speak of «cherished memories» of someone who has died. It tells the reader that something matters deeply. Phrases: «cherished memories», «a cherished possession», «cherished friend».
examples from the lessons: The teddy bear was her most cherished toy. | We have cherished memories of our holidays with Grandad. | He cherished the letter his father sent him. | The old photo is a cherished family treasure. | Freedom is a cherished right in many countries. | She cherished every moment with her new baby brother. | Our class cherished the oak tree in the playground.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb «cherish» is regular: cherished, cherishing. As an adjective it comes before a noun: «a cherished gift». It is stronger and warmer than «liked».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Looking after children, especially while their parents are at work. 2) The places and services that do this: nurseries, childminders, day care centres, after-school clubs.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday adult life parents arrange childcare — grandparents, a nursery, a childminder or an after-school club — and it can cost a lot of money. In the news, governments talk about childcare costs and free hours. It tells the reader who looks after the children. Phrases: «childcare costs», «free childcare», «childcare worker».
examples from the lessons: My little sister goes to childcare while Mum works. | Childcare can be very expensive for families. | Grandma helps with childcare on Fridays. | The after-school club offers childcare until six o'clock. | Some workplaces have childcare on site. | She is training to be a childcare worker. | The government promised more free childcare hours.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: no «a», no plural («some childcare», «childcare is»). Written as one word in the UK, often two words (child care) in the USA. In Australia and the USA it is often called «day care».

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a silly, immature way that is not right for someone's age (said of older children and adults, usually as criticism). 2) In a way like a child, simply and innocently (childishly happy).
its sense in the lessons: In stories it criticises a grown-up or older child who sulks, stamps or throws a tantrum. Sometimes it is kind, describing simple joy. It tells the reader someone is acting younger than they are. Similar: «immaturely»; opposite «maturely».
examples from the lessons: The two men argued childishly over a parking space. | He childishly refused to share the remote. | She stamped her foot childishly and stormed off. | Grandad laughed childishly at his own joke. | Stop behaving so childishly; you're twelve! | They were childishly excited about the snow.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from «childish». Trap: «childish» is usually negative (silly, immature), while «childlike» is positive (innocent, full of wonder). «Childlike wonder» is praise; «childish behaviour» is criticism.

part of speech: noun (a chine, chines); verb (chine, chines, chined, chining — cooking)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The backbone of an animal, or a joint of meat that includes part of the backbone. 2) A narrow ridge of land or a mountain ridge. 3) (UK, regional) A deep, narrow ravine cut by a stream through soft cliffs to the sea, especially on the Isle of Wight and in Dorset and Hampshire. 4) (cooking, verb) To cut through the backbone of a joint of meat to make it easier to carve.
its sense in the lessons: It is a rare word. In geography it appears in names of places on the south coast of England like Blackgang Chine and Shanklin Chine. In cooking books a butcher may «chine» a rack of lamb. It tells the reader about a backbone or a steep narrow valley.
examples from the lessons: We walked down Shanklin Chine to the beach on the Isle of Wight. | The butcher chined the pork so it was easy to carve. | A chine is a steep ravine cut into a soft cliff. | The stream had carved a deep chine through the sandstone. | The chef asked for a chine of beef. | Bournemouth has several chines leading to the sea.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a chine, chines. Say «chyne» (rhymes with fine). Not connected with the country China. Rare in everyday speech outside cooking and southern English place names.

part of speech: noun (chives, plural; a chive is rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A small herb with thin, hollow green leaves that taste like a mild onion, used chopped on food. 2) The plant that grows these leaves; it has round purple flowers.
its sense in the lessons: In cooking and gardening lessons pupils grow chives on a windowsill and snip them onto potatoes, eggs or soup. In science it is part of the onion family. It tells the reader about a fresh, oniony taste. Phrases: «chopped chives», «a bunch of chives», «sour cream and chives».
examples from the lessons: Sprinkle chopped chives on the baked potato. | We grew chives in a pot on the classroom windowsill. | Chives belong to the onion family. | Mum made scrambled eggs with chives. | The chives have pretty purple flowers in early summer. | Bees love the flowers of chives. | Use scissors to snip the chives.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually plural: «chives are» (like «onions»). Say «chyves». Chives taste milder than onions or garlic. Do not confuse with «chiefs» or «knives».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) A chemical compound made of chlorine joined with another element; the best known is sodium chloride, which is common table salt. 2) (science) The chloride ion, a chlorine atom with an extra electron, found dissolved in sea water and in our bodies.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons it explains what salt really is (sodium chloride) and what is dissolved in sea water. In health and swimming pools you may hear about chloride and chlorine. It tells the reader there is chlorine joined to something else. Phrases: «sodium chloride», «calcium chloride», «potassium chloride».
examples from the lessons: Table salt is sodium chloride. | Sea water contains a lot of sodium chloride. | Calcium chloride is spread on roads to melt ice. | Our blood has chloride in it, which the body needs. | We evaporated salt water and saw sodium chloride crystals form. | The label listed potassium chloride as an ingredient.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say «KLOR-ide». Trap: chloride is not the same as chlorine. Chlorine is a poisonous green gas used to clean pools; chloride is the much safer form found in salt. Chemical names ending in -ide often have two parts (sodium chloride, iron oxide).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (church) A boy who sings in a church or cathedral choir, usually wearing robes. 2) (informal) A person who looks very innocent and well-behaved, often said jokingly («he's no choirboy»).
its sense in the lessons: In church life and music lessons, choirboys sing high parts (treble) in cathedrals such as St Paul's or King's College, Cambridge, especially at Christmas services. In stories and everyday talk, «he looks like a choirboy» means he looks innocent, sometimes when he is not. Phrases: «cathedral choirboy», «no choirboy».
examples from the lessons: The choirboys sang carols at the cathedral on Christmas Eve. | My cousin became a choirboy at eight and practises every week. | The choirboy's voice rose high above the organ. | Choirboys often wear white robes over red cassocks. | He may look like a choirboy, but he's the cheekiest kid in class. | When his voice broke, he stopped being a choirboy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a choirboy, choirboys. Girls sing in choirs too: «choirgirl» or «chorister» (for both). «Choir» is said «KWY-er». The informal sense «no choirboy» means someone is not as good as they seem.

part of speech: verb form (chomp, chomps, chomped, chomping); adjective in «chomping at the bit»
meaning for a pupil: 1) Chewing or biting noisily and with big movements of the jaw. 2) In «chomping at the bit»: very eager and impatient to start something (from a horse biting on the metal bit in its mouth).
its sense in the lessons: In stories it gives a lively sound picture of someone or some animal eating — a horse chomping hay, a child chomping an apple. The phrase «chomping (or champing) at the bit» describes excitement and impatience before a race, a trip or a game. It tells the reader about noisy eating or eagerness.
examples from the lessons: The horse was chomping on a carrot. | My brother sat chomping crisps through the whole film. | The dog was chomping happily on its bone. | We were chomping at the bit to get into the swimming pool. | Stop chomping with your mouth open! | The caterpillar kept chomping through the leaves. | The team was chomping at the bit before kick-off.
note for the reader of a maths problem: -ing form of the regular verb «chomp». The older form of the idiom is «champing at the bit», but «chomping at the bit» is now more common. Chewing with your mouth open is thought rude at the table.

part of speech: a fragment or a name (Chon — not a common English word)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (a name) Chon is a surname and given name, for example a Korean surname (also written Jeon or Chun) and a name used in some other Asian and Hispanic families. 2) Not a common English word: it may be a fragment of a longer word cut off in a text.
its sense in the lessons: Children may meet it as part of a person's name in a story or class list. It does not carry an everyday English meaning on its own. If it appears alone in a text, check if it is a name or part of a broken word.
examples from the lessons: Mr Chon is our new music teacher. | The book was written by a Korean author called Chon. | "Chon" on the list was the start of a longer word cut off by the page. | Ji-ho Chon won the spelling bee. | We learned that Korean names put the family name first, as in Chon Ji-ho. | Ask the person how they like their name said.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A name gets a capital letter: «Chon». It is not an English dictionary word, and there is no plural. Its sound depends on the family: often «chon» or «jun». Nothing more should be invented about it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) To do with circulation, especially the movement of blood around the body by the heart, arteries, veins and capillaries. 2) To do with things moving in a circle or loop, like air or water moving round a system.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on the body, «the circulatory system» is the heart, blood vessels and blood, which carry oxygen and food to every cell and take away waste. Exercise and healthy food keep it strong. It tells the reader the topic is how blood flows. Phrases: «circulatory system», «circulatory problems».
examples from the lessons: The heart is the main organ of the circulatory system. | Our circulatory system carries oxygen to every part of the body. | We drew the circulatory system with red and blue arrows. | Exercise is good for your circulatory health. | Grandpa has circulatory problems, so his feet feel cold. | Arteries, veins and capillaries are all part of the circulatory system.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective only. Say «SUR-kyuh-luh-tree» (UK) or «SUR-kyuh-luh-tor-ee» (US). It comes from «circulate» (move round). Fact: blood is always red inside you; veins only look blue through the skin — a common myth says blood in veins is blue.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (language) A small mark like a little roof (^) written over a vowel in some languages, for example French «â, ê, î, ô, û» as in «forêt» or «hôpital». 2) (science, rare) Bending around something, used for some nerves and blood vessels.
its sense in the lessons: In French lessons the circumflex often shows that an «s» used to follow the vowel: «forêt» (forest), «hôpital» (hospital), «île» (isle). In English it appears only in borrowed words like «crème brûlée» or «rôle» (old spelling). It tells the reader about a little hat-shaped accent. Phrases: «circumflex accent».
examples from the lessons: In French, "forêt" has a circumflex on the e. | The circumflex looks like a tiny roof over the letter. | "Hôpital" has a circumflex where English has an s in "hospital". | We learned three French accents: acute, grave and circumflex. | On a keyboard you can type a circumflex with the ^ key. | The circumflex in "crème brûlée" sits on the u.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: circumflexes. Say «SUR-kum-flex». In maths and computing the ^ symbol on its own (called a caret) can mean «to the power of»: 2^3 = 8. English words normally do not use accents.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To find a clever way to avoid a rule, problem or difficulty, often in a way that is not quite fair. 2) (formal) To go around something that is in the way.
its sense in the lessons: In news and adult life it describes getting round rules or controls — «circumventing the law», «circumventing parental controls». In stories it shows a clever, sometimes sneaky character. It tells the reader someone avoided an obstacle instead of facing it. It is a stiff, formal word; everyday English says «get round» or «get around».
examples from the lessons: He tried to circumvent the rules by using his brother's account. | The engineers circumvented the problem with a new design. | The army circumvented the mountains by marching along the coast. | Circumventing school internet filters is against the rules. | She found a way to circumvent the traffic jam. | Good laws are hard to circumvent.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: circumvented, circumventing. Formal; «get round» is the everyday way to say it. Built from «circum» (around, as in circumference) + «vent» (come). Often suggests something sneaky.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A line of words quoted from a book, speech or writer (a quotation). 2) A reference that tells the reader exactly where information came from (author, title, page, website). 3) An official written statement praising someone, for example for bravery. 4) (law, US) An official order to appear in court or a ticket for breaking a rule, such as a parking ticket.
its sense in the lessons: In school writing and projects, giving a citation shows where your facts came from, so you are honest and not copying. Soldiers, firefighters and police may get a citation for bravery. In the USA a driver can get a «traffic citation». It tells the reader where words came from or that someone has been officially named.
examples from the lessons: Every fact in your project needs a citation. | The essay began with a citation from Martin Luther King Jr. | The firefighter received a citation for bravery. | The police officer gave the driver a citation for speeding. | The citation listed the author, the year and the page. | Copying without a citation is called plagiarism. | Scientists count how many citations their papers get.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a citation, citations. Verb: «cite» (to quote or mention a source). Homophone trap: «cite» sounds like «site» (a place, a website) and «sight» (seeing).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) All the citizens of a country, town or place, thought of as one group.
its sense in the lessons: It appears in history, politics and news writing — «an informed citizenry», «the citizenry of Athens». It tells the reader we mean the whole people, not one person. Everyday English says «the people» or «citizens».
examples from the lessons: Democracy needs an informed citizenry. | The citizenry of ancient Athens voted in the assembly. | The new law was welcomed by the citizenry. | The mayor spoke to the whole citizenry of the town. | A free press helps the citizenry know the truth. | The citizenry gathered in the square to celebrate.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal and uncountable; used with «the». Say «SIT-iz-en-ree». Ordinary speech uses «citizens» or «the people».

part of speech: verb (clack, clacks, clacked, clacking); noun (a clack, clacks)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To make a short, sharp sound like two hard things hitting each other. 2) The sound itself (the clack of heels, the clack of a keyboard). 3) (informal) To chatter loudly and on and on.
its sense in the lessons: In stories it is a sound word that helps the reader hear the scene — heels on a hard floor, knitting needles, an old typewriter, a train on the tracks. It tells the reader there is a sharp, repeated, hard sound. Similar: «click», «clatter».
examples from the lessons: Her shoes clacked on the stone floor. | We heard the clack of knitting needles. | The old typewriter clacked as Grandad typed. | The train clacked over the rails. | The stork clacked its long beak. | The castanets clacked in time to the music. | Keyboards were clacking all over the computer room.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: clacked, clacking. It is an onomatopoeic word — it sounds like the noise it names. Not the same as «clap» (hands) or «clank» (a heavy metal sound).

part of speech: adjective (clad); verb form (clad as an old past form of clothe; clad, clads, cladding — to cover a building)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal or literary) Wearing a certain kind of clothes («clad in armour», «a black-clad figure»). 2) Covered with a layer of some material («stone-clad», «ivy-clad»). 3) (building, verb) To cover a building's walls with a layer of material; the layer is called «cladding».
its sense in the lessons: In stories and poems it describes how people are dressed — «a knight clad in steel». In building and the news it describes walls covered with panels; the Grenfell Tower fire in London in 2017 led to rules about safe cladding. It tells the reader what someone or something is wrapped in. Often with «in»: «clad in».
examples from the lessons: The knight was clad in shining armour. | A figure clad in black stood at the gate. | The hills were clad in snow. | The house was clad in red brick. | Ivy-clad walls surrounded the old garden. | Workers are replacing unsafe cladding on the tower. | The children came clad in wellies and raincoats.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly used as an adjective after a noun or in compounds (snow-clad, steel-clad). It sounds old-fashioned or literary in the sense «dressed»; everyday English says «dressed in». «Cladding» is the noun for the covering on a building.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unpleasantly damp, cold and sticky to touch, especially skin. 2) (weather) Damp and heavy, warm and sticky (clammy air).
its sense in the lessons: In stories it shows fear or nerves — «clammy hands» before a test or a scary moment. In health and first-aid lessons, clammy pale skin can be a sign that someone is unwell or in shock, so tell an adult. In weather descriptions it means humid. It tells the reader about an unpleasant damp feeling.
examples from the lessons: My hands were clammy before the spelling test. | The cave walls felt cold and clammy. | It was a clammy, muggy day in August. | His forehead was pale and clammy, so the teacher called the nurse. | The frog felt clammy in my hands. | Wet socks are horribly clammy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative clammier, superlative clammiest. Not the same as «clumsy». In first aid, pale, cold and clammy skin with dizziness can be a warning sign — get an adult or call for help.

part of speech: verb (clang, clangs, clanged, clanging); noun (a clang, clangs)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To make a loud, ringing sound like metal being hit. 2) The loud metal sound itself. 3) In «clanger» (UK, informal): a silly, obvious mistake («drop a clanger»).
its sense in the lessons: In stories it is a sound word for gates, bells, pots, pans and prison doors — it makes the reader hear the scene. It tells the reader something metal has been hit or has shut heavily. Similar: «clank», «clash», «ding».
examples from the lessons: The iron gate clanged shut behind us. | The fire bell clanged loudly. | A pan fell with a clang on the kitchen floor. | The blacksmith's hammer clanged on the anvil. | The bin lid clanged in the wind. | We heard the clang of the school bell.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: clanged, clanging. It is onomatopoeia — the word sounds like the noise. «Clang» is a ringing sound; «clank» is a duller, heavier one.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The metal tongue or ball hanging inside a bell that hits it to make it ring (a clapper). 2) (UK, informal) In «like the clappers»: very fast or very hard («run like the clappers»). 3) A device that makes a clapping noise, for example to scare birds, or the clapperboard used when filming.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday British, Irish, Australian and New Zealand speech, «go like the clappers» means go extremely fast. In music and church life the clapper is what makes a bell ring. It tells the reader about bells or great speed.
examples from the lessons: We ran like the clappers to catch the bus. | The bell's clapper swung and struck the side. | The bell-ringers checked the clappers before Sunday service. | Grandad drove like the clappers to get us to the hospital in time. | The rain came down like the clappers. | A clapper scared the birds off the field.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Singular «clapper», plural «clappers»; the idiom always uses the plural: «like the clappers». It is informal British-style English and is not common in the USA. Not the same as «clapping» (hitting your hands together).

meaning for a pupil: 1) An explanation that makes something clearer or easier to understand. 2) (science, cooking) Making a liquid clear by removing bits from it (clarifying butter or water).
its sense in the lessons: In class you can «ask for clarification» when you don't understand the instructions — it is a polite way to say «Could you explain that again?». In news, an official may give a clarification after a confusing statement. It tells the reader something unclear is being made clear. Phrases: «ask for clarification», «for clarification», «seek clarification».
examples from the lessons: Can I ask for some clarification about the homework? | The teacher gave a quick clarification of the rules. | For clarification, the trip is on Friday, not Thursday. | The company issued a clarification after the mistake. | The question needed clarification before we could answer it. | Clarification of butter removes the milky bits.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From the verb «clarify» (y changes to i: clarification). Usually uncountable, but «a clarification» is fine for one statement. Asking for clarification is a smart thing to do, not a sign of being slow.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (music) A woodwind instrument shaped like a long black tube with keys and a single reed in the mouthpiece; it makes a smooth, warm sound.
its sense in the lessons: In music lessons pupils learn the families of instruments: the clarinet is in the woodwind family with the flute, oboe and bassoon. Many children learn it in school bands and orchestras, and it is used in jazz and classical music. Phrases: «play the clarinet», «clarinet lessons», «clarinet player» (clarinettist).
examples from the lessons: My sister plays the clarinet in the school band. | The clarinet has a single reed that vibrates. | I have my clarinet lesson on Tuesdays. | In "Peter and the Wolf", the clarinet plays the cat. | Clarinets are made of wood or plastic. | He practised his clarinet scales every evening. | A clarinet player is called a clarinettist.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a clarinet, clarinets. Say «klar-uh-NET». Even though some clarinets are plastic, it belongs to the woodwind family. Person: clarinettist (UK) or clarinetist (US). We say «play the clarinet» with «the».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) Stylish, elegant and of good quality, often looking expensive. 2) (informal) Behaving in a fair, polite and graceful way (a classy gesture). 3) (informal, sarcastic) Said of something rude or tasteless to mock it («Burping at the table — classy!»).
its sense in the lessons: In everyday talk and stories it praises clothes, restaurants, cars or behaviour. In sport, a «classy player» is very skilful, and a «classy move» is good sportsmanship. It can also be said sarcastically to mean the opposite. It tells the reader something has style or grace.
examples from the lessons: She wore a classy black dress to the wedding. | We had dinner in a classy restaurant for Mum's birthday. | That was a classy goal — so smooth! | Shaking hands with the losing team was a classy thing to do. | The hotel looked very classy with its golden lights. | "Wiping your nose on your sleeve? Classy," said my brother.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative classier, superlative classiest. Informal: avoid it in formal essays. Watch the tone: «Classy!» can be sarcasm meaning the opposite.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A strong fear of being in small, closed or crowded spaces, such as lifts, tunnels or cupboards. 2) (everyday) A feeling of being trapped or squeezed in, even without real fear.
its sense in the lessons: In health and wellbeing lessons it is an example of a phobia — a fear stronger than the danger. In stories it builds tension in caves, tunnels and lifts. People with claustrophobia may feel their heart racing and want to get out. Phrases: «suffer from claustrophobia», «a feeling of claustrophobia». Adjective: «claustrophobic».
examples from the lessons: Grandma has claustrophobia, so she always takes the stairs. | The narrow cave gave me a touch of claustrophobia. | People with claustrophobia can find MRI scans hard. | The crowded train carriage felt claustrophobic. | Breathing slowly can help with claustrophobia. | The story's tunnel scene was full of claustrophobia.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Say «klos-truh-FOH-bee-uh». From Latin «claustrum» (closed place) + Greek «phobia» (fear). Opposite fear: agoraphobia (fear of open or crowded public places). A phobia is real and not silly; do not tease people about it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) The collarbone: the long, thin bone between the top of the breastbone and the shoulder; you have one on each side.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on the skeleton it is one of the named bones. In sport and safety, a broken collarbone is a common injury from falling off a bike or horse onto an outstretched arm. It tells the reader about the bone at the front of the shoulder.
examples from the lessons: The clavicle is also called the collarbone. | She broke her clavicle when she fell off her bike. | You can feel your clavicle just below your neck. | We labelled the clavicle on our skeleton diagram. | Each person has two clavicles. | A broken clavicle usually heals in a sling.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a clavicle, clavicles. Say «KLAV-ik-ul». Everyday word: collarbone. In Latin «clavicula» means «little key», because of its shape.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To do with office work, such as typing, filing and keeping records (a clerical job, a clerical error). 2) (church) To do with the clergy — priests, vicars, ministers — and their work (a clerical collar).
its sense in the lessons: In everyday adult life, a «clerical worker» does office tasks, and a «clerical error» is a small mistake in writing or typing records, such as a wrong date. In church life, priests and ministers may wear a white «clerical collar» (dog collar). It tells the reader about offices or about clergy.
examples from the lessons: Mum does clerical work at the hospital. | The wrong date was just a clerical error. | The vicar wore a clerical collar. | A clerical mistake sent the parcel to the wrong house. | The school office needs a new clerical assistant. | Clerical robes are worn by priests during services.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective only. It comes from «cleric» (a member of the clergy) — in the past, priests were among the few people who could write, so «clerk» and «clerical» came to mean office work too. «Clerical error» is a fixed phrase meaning a small mistake in paperwork.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science, geography) To do with climate — the usual weather of a place over many years (climatic zones, climatic change).
its sense in the lessons: In geography and science lessons it describes the world's climate zones (tropical, desert, temperate, polar) and long-term changes in weather. In the news it appears with climate change. It tells the reader we are talking about patterns over years, not today's weather. Phrases: «climatic conditions», «climatic zones», «climatic change».
examples from the lessons: Penguins are adapted to cold climatic conditions. | The map showed the Earth's climatic zones. | Rainforests need warm, wet climatic conditions. | Scientists study climatic changes over thousands of years. | Different climatic regions grow different crops. | The Ice Age was a time of great climatic cooling.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective only. Trap: «climatic» (about climate) is often confused with «climactic» (about the climax, the most exciting moment). «A climatic zone» but «the climactic scene». Climate is the long-term pattern; weather is what happens today.

part of speech: noun (a climax, climaxes); verb (climax, climaxes, climaxed, climaxing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The most exciting, important or tense moment of a story, film, event or piece of music, usually near the end. 2) The highest point of something that has been building up (the climax of the season). 3) (verb) To reach that most exciting point.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons, story structure has a beginning, build-up, climax (the problem at its worst or the big moment), resolution and ending. In music and sport it is the big finale. It tells the reader the tension is at its peak. Phrases: «reach a climax», «build up to a climax», «the climax of the story».
examples from the lessons: In the climax of the story, the hero faces the dragon. | Our story plan had five parts, with the climax in the middle of the mountain. | The fireworks were the climax of the festival. | The music builds to a loud climax. | The match reached its climax in the last minute. | The film climaxes with a chase across the rooftops. | Plan your climax before you write the ending.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a climax, climaxes. Adjective: «climactic» (the climactic scene) — not «climatic», which is about weather. In story writing the climax comes before the resolution.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A flat board with a metal clip at the top that holds sheets of paper, so you can write while standing or walking. 2) (computers) The hidden place in a computer or phone that stores what you have copied or cut until you paste it.
its sense in the lessons: In school, clipboards are used on field trips, nature walks and surveys to make tally charts. In computing lessons, «copy to the clipboard» then «paste» moves text or pictures. In stories, a person with a clipboard is often an official or organiser. It tells the reader about writing on the move or copying and pasting.
examples from the lessons: Each group took a clipboard on the minibeast hunt. | We did a traffic survey with tally marks on our clipboards. | The coach held a clipboard with the team list. | Press Ctrl and C to copy the text to the clipboard. | The clipboard keeps only the last thing you copied. | A woman with a clipboard asked us questions about the park.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a clipboard, clipboards. Compound word: clip + board. Computing tip: be careful copying passwords — they may stay on the clipboard where others could paste them.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (gardening) A glass or plastic cover shaped like a bell or a small tunnel, put over young plants to protect them from cold and pests. 2) A close-fitting, bell-shaped woman's hat, popular in the 1920s. 3) (cooking) A dome-shaped cover put over a plate of food to keep it warm.
its sense in the lessons: In gardening and science lessons, a cloche works like a mini greenhouse: it traps warmth so seeds sprout earlier. In history and costume, flappers in the 1920s wore cloche hats. In posh restaurants and films the waiter lifts the silver cloche to show the food. It tells the reader about a bell-shaped cover.
examples from the lessons: We put a cloche over the lettuce seedlings to keep the frost off. | A plastic bottle cut in half makes a good cloche. | The waiter lifted the silver cloche with a flourish. | In the 1920s photo, she wore a little cloche hat. | The cloche traps heat like a tiny greenhouse. | Slugs couldn't get to the plants under the cloche.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a cloche, cloches. Say «klosh». It is the French word for «bell», used in English for these bell-shaped things. Not related to «clock», though the sound is a bit similar.

meaning for a pupil: 1) With no clouds at all; clear (a cloudless sky). 2) (literary) Calm and untroubled, without worries (cloudless happiness).
its sense in the lessons: In weather and stories it paints a picture of a perfect sunny day or a clear starry night. In science, cloudless nights are colder because heat escapes into space, so frost forms more easily. It tells the reader the sky is completely clear. Phrases: «a cloudless sky», «a cloudless day».
examples from the lessons: We lay on the grass under a cloudless blue sky. | On a cloudless night you can see thousands of stars. | It was a cloudless day, perfect for the beach. | Cloudless nights in winter often bring frost. | Wear sun cream on cloudless summer days. | The astronomers waited for a cloudless night.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective made with the suffix -less (without), like «careless», «endless». It does not change form. Science fact: clouds act like a blanket; without them, nights get colder.

part of speech: adjective (cloven); verb form (an old past participle of cleave: cleave, cleaved/cleft/clove, cleaved/cleft/cloven)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Split into two parts, especially a hoof divided into two toes («cloven hoof»), as on cows, sheep, goats, pigs and deer. 2) (old, literary) Split or cut apart by a strong blow.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on animals, cows, deer and goats have cloven hooves while horses have a single solid hoof. In old stories, folk tales and paintings the Devil is often shown with cloven hooves, so «showing the cloven hoof» once meant showing a wicked side. In the Bible, the food laws in Leviticus mention animals that «part the hoof» (have cloven hooves) and chew the cud. It tells the reader something is split in two.
examples from the lessons: Deer have cloven hooves. | The pig's cloven hoof left a two-part print in the mud. | Horses do not have cloven hooves; their hooves are solid. | In the story, the stranger's boots hid cloven hooves. | Sheep and goats are cloven-hoofed animals. | The Bible's food laws speak of animals with a divided hoof that chew the cud.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mainly used in «cloven hoof» / «cloven-hoofed». The verb «cleave» is old and odd: its past forms are cleaved, cleft or clove, and cloven or cleft. In modern English people say «split» instead.

part of speech: verb form (clump, clumps, clumped, clumping); noun (a clump, clumps)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Walking with slow, heavy, noisy steps (clumping up the stairs). 2) Gathering together into a tight group or lumps (wet flour clumping, trees clumping together). 3) (noun «clump») A group of plants growing close together, or a lump of something.
its sense in the lessons: In stories it is a sound and movement word: heavy boots clumping on wooden floors, a giant clumping through the forest. In cooking and science, things clump together into lumps — flour, wet sand, cat litter. It tells the reader about heavy steps or things sticking together in groups.
examples from the lessons: He came clumping down the stairs in his big boots. | The giant went clumping through the woods. | The wet sand kept clumping together. | Stir the flour well to stop it clumping. | Daffodils were growing in a clump by the gate. | The horses went clumping along the lane. | The cattle stood clumping together for warmth.
note for the reader of a maths problem: -ing form of the regular verb «clump». Similar sound words: «stomp», «clomp», «tramp». The noun «clump» is countable: a clump of grass, clumps of trees.

part of speech: verb (clutch, clutches, clutched, clutching); noun (a clutch, clutches); adjective (clutch — US slang)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To hold something tightly, often because you are afraid, in pain or don't want to lose it. 2) To try to grab something quickly («clutch at the rope»). 3) (noun) A pedal in a car (and a lever on a motorbike) used to change gears. 4) (noun) A group of eggs laid at one time by a bird, or a group of chicks; also a small group of things. 5) (noun) In «in someone's clutches»: in someone's power or control. 6) (slang, especially US) Very good at doing well in a tense, important moment («a clutch shot»). 7) (noun) A small handbag with no handle, held in the hand.
its sense in the lessons: In stories it shows fear or determination — clutching a teddy, clutching a ticket. The idiom «clutch at straws» means trying anything when there is little hope. In nature lessons a hen sits on a clutch of eggs. In driving, the clutch is pressed to change gear. In sport talk (especially in North America), a «clutch» player scores when it matters most. It tells the reader about holding tight, power or eggs.
examples from the lessons: She clutched her mum's hand in the dark corridor. | He was clutching a crumpled five-pound note. | The duck sat on a clutch of eight eggs. | Press the clutch before you change gear. | The princess was in the witch's clutches. | That last-second basket was so clutch! | He clutched his stomach and groaned. | Don't clutch at straws — just admit you forgot.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: clutches, clutched, clutching. Noun plural: clutches. Note the many meanings — read the sentence: eggs, cars, grip, bags or slang. «Clutch» as an adjective (a clutch player) is informal slang, mainly American.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To come together and join to form one larger thing or group. 2) (science) For drops, particles or bubbles to merge into one (raindrops coalesce in clouds).
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, tiny water droplets coalesce to make raindrops heavy enough to fall; dust and gas coalesced to make stars and planets. In history and news, groups or ideas coalesce into a movement or a plan. It tells the reader separate parts are becoming one. It is formal; everyday English says «join together» or «merge».
examples from the lessons: Tiny droplets coalesce into raindrops. | The planets formed when dust and rock coalesced around the young Sun. | Small groups coalesced into one big protest. | Our ideas slowly coalesced into a plan for the project. | Two puddles coalesced into one big pool. | The bubbles coalesced into a large one.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: coalesced, coalescing. Say «koh-uh-LESS». Formal word. It is not connected with «coal». Noun: coalescence.

part of speech: verb form (past of coalesce: coalesce, coalesces, coalesced, coalescing); adjective (coalesced)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Past form of «coalesce»: came together and joined into one bigger thing or group. 2) (adjective, science) Joined or merged together (coalesced droplets).
its sense in the lessons: Used in science to explain how stars, planets, raindrops and bubbles were formed, and in history to say how groups or ideas joined into one. It tells the reader that the joining has already happened.
examples from the lessons: The droplets coalesced into a big raindrop. | Gas and dust coalesced to form the Earth. | Over the summer, the friends coalesced into a band. | The scattered villages slowly coalesced into a town. | The two oil drops coalesced on the water. | Their different ideas coalesced into one clear plan.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past simple and past participle of «coalesce» (just add -d). Formal. Say «koh-uh-LEST». Everyday words: merged, joined together.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Rough and thick to touch, not smooth or fine (coarse sand, coarse cloth). 2) Made of big pieces or grains, not fine ones (coarse salt, coarsely chopped). 3) Rude, crude or vulgar in manners or language (coarse jokes). 4) (fishing, UK) «Coarse fishing» is fishing for freshwater fish other than salmon and trout.
its sense in the lessons: In science and art lessons it describes textures: coarse sandpaper, coarse grains of sand or soil. In cooking, «coarse» salt or «coarsely chopped» onion means big pieces. In stories it describes rude, rough people or language. It tells the reader about roughness, either of a surface or of manners.
examples from the lessons: Coarse sandpaper takes off a lot of wood quickly. | The beach had coarse yellow sand. | The donkey's fur felt coarse. | Grind the pepper coarse, not fine. | The pirate told coarse jokes that made the sailors laugh. | We sieved the soil to separate coarse and fine bits. | Grandad goes coarse fishing for carp.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative coarser, superlative coarsest; adverb coarsely. Homophone trap: «course» (a race course, a course of lessons, «of course») sounds exactly the same as «coarse». Coarse = rough; course = path, lessons or certainly.

part of speech: adjective (cocky, cockier, cockiest — informal); noun (a cocky, cockies — Australia, informal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) Too confident and sure of yourself in an annoying or rude way. 2) (Australia, informal) A cockatoo, the noisy crested parrot. 3) (Australia, informal) A farmer, especially a small farmer («a cow cocky»).
its sense in the lessons: In stories and sport it describes a show-off who is sure they will win, often before they lose. Coaches warn teams not to get cocky. In Australia, «cocky» is also a friendly name for a cockatoo or a farmer. It tells the reader someone thinks too much of themselves, or names an Australian bird or farmer.
examples from the lessons: He got cocky after winning and lost the next game. | Don't be so cocky — the test isn't marked yet. | The cocky hare stopped for a nap and the tortoise won. | A flock of cockies screeched in the gum trees. (Australia) | My uncle is a cocky with sheep and wheat. (Australia) | She gave a cocky grin as she crossed the finish line.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative cockier, superlative cockiest. Informal: avoid it in formal writing; formal words are «overconfident», «arrogant». Being confident is good; being cocky is too much.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Making someone do something by using force or threats, so they have no real choice. 2) (law) Pressure that is against the law, such as forcing someone to sign something or controlling someone by threats.
its sense in the lessons: In PSHE, safety and ethics lessons it is the opposite of free consent: no one should push you into doing something with threats or pressure, online or offline. In history and politics it describes rulers who used force instead of persuasion. It tells the reader a choice was not free. Phrases: «under coercion», «coercive control».
examples from the lessons: He only signed the paper under coercion. | Bullying can include coercion, like "Do this or else". | A promise made under coercion is not a free promise. | The king ruled by coercion, not by kindness. | If someone online pressures you, it is coercion — tell a trusted adult. | Persuasion uses reasons; coercion uses threats.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Verb: «coerce» (coerce, coerced, coercing). Say «koh-UR-shun». Trap: persuading with good reasons is not coercion; threatening or forcing is.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Of the same age, or existing at the same time as something else. 2) (noun, formal) A person or thing of the same age or time as another.
its sense in the lessons: It is a rare formal word used in history, archaeology and science writing: «the cave paintings are coeval with the first farms». It tells the reader two things belong to the same period. Everyday English says «from the same time» or «the same age».
examples from the lessons: The two castles are roughly coeval, both built around 1100. | The fossil is coeval with the dinosaurs. | Shakespeare's coevals included Christopher Marlowe. | Scientists think the rock layers are coeval. | These tools are coeval with the first farms in Britain. | The two ancient cities were coeval but far apart.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Very formal, rare. Say «koh-EE-vul». Similar words: «contemporary», «contemporaneous». Built from «co-» (together) + Latin «aevum» (age).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Clear, logical and convincing (a cogent argument, a cogent reason).
its sense in the lessons: In debating, persuasive writing and exams, a cogent argument gives clear reasons and evidence that make people agree. It tells the reader an argument is strong and makes sense. Everyday English says «convincing» or «strong».
examples from the lessons: She gave a cogent argument for a longer lunch break. | The lawyer's case was clear and cogent. | Use evidence to make your essay cogent. | He had no cogent reason for being late. | The scientist presented cogent evidence for her theory. | A cogent speech uses facts, not just feelings.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal. Say «KOH-junt». Adverb: cogently. Do not confuse with «cognitive» or «cog» (a tooth on a gear wheel).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science, formal) The mental processes of knowing, thinking, learning, remembering and understanding. 2) The ability to think and understand.
its sense in the lessons: In science and psychology it names everything your brain does to think — paying attention, remembering, solving problems, using language. Doctors may test the cognition of older people, and scientists study animal cognition in crows and chimps. It tells the reader we are talking about thinking. Adjective: «cognitive».
examples from the lessons: Sleep is important for good cognition. | Scientists study the cognition of clever animals like crows. | Puzzles and reading exercise your cognition. | Animal cognition experiments show dolphins recognise themselves in mirrors. | The doctor checked Grandma's cognition with memory questions. | Cognition includes attention, memory and reasoning.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Say «kog-NISH-un». Adjective: cognitive (cognitive skills). Related to «recognise» — both come from the Latin for «to know».

part of speech: noun (a col, cols); abbreviation (Col. — colonel; col. — column)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (geography) The lowest point on a ridge between two mountain peaks, often used as a pass to cross the mountains. 2) (abbreviation) Col. is short for Colonel, an army officer's rank. 3) (abbreviation) col. is short for column, in tables and newspapers.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons on mountains, a col is a dip between two peaks, and walkers and roads often cross there; in cycling races like the Tour de France, many mountain passes are called «Col» (Col du Tourmalet). In writing, «Col.» before a name means Colonel, and «col.» in a table means column. It tells the reader about a mountain pass or a short form.
examples from the lessons: We climbed up to the col between the two peaks. | The road crosses the mountains at a high col. | The cyclists raced over the Col du Tourmalet. | Col. Smith commanded the regiment. | Look at col. 3 in the table for the totals. | Snow often lies in the col until summer.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable as a mountain word: a col, cols. As an abbreviation it has a full stop: «Col.» (colonel, with a capital C before a name) and «col.» (column). «Colonel» is said «KER-nul», not «col-o-nel».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Made so that it can be folded up or pushed down into a smaller shape when not being used (a collapsible chair, a collapsible water bottle). 2) Likely or able to fall down or fold in (a collapsible steering column that folds in a crash for safety).
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life collapsible things save space: camping chairs, cups, umbrellas, crates. In design and technology lessons pupils may design collapsible structures. In car safety, some parts are made collapsible to absorb a crash. It tells the reader something folds or shrinks on purpose.
examples from the lessons: We took collapsible chairs to the beach. | My collapsible water bottle fits in my pocket. | The collapsible table folds flat against the wall. | Grandma has a collapsible walking stick. | In DT we designed a collapsible bridge. | The car's steering wheel is collapsible to protect the driver.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelled with -ible (not -able): collapsible. Comes from «collapse». Some dictionaries also accept «collapsable», but «collapsible» is the standard spelling.

part of speech: noun (cologne, uncountable; a cologne, colognes); a name (Cologne — a city)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A light perfume, often for men, also called eau de cologne. 2) (a name) Cologne is a large city on the River Rhine in western Germany, famous for its huge Gothic cathedral (Köln in German).
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life people splash on cologne before going out; in shops it is sold next to perfume. In geography and history, Cologne Cathedral took about 600 years to build and survived bombing in the Second World War. The perfume is named after the city where it was first made in the 1700s. It tells the reader about a smell or a place.
examples from the lessons: Dad wears a bit of cologne on special days. | The cologne smelled of lemons and wood. | Too much cologne can make people sneeze. | Cologne Cathedral has two enormous spires. | We took a boat trip on the Rhine at Cologne. | Eau de cologne was first made in Cologne.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say «kuh-LOHN». As a perfume it is often uncountable (some cologne); as a city it is a name with a capital C. In German the city is «Köln». Spraying cologne near eyes or flames is unsafe.

part of speech: noun (a colossus, colossi or colossuses); a name (the Colossus of Rhodes; Colossus — the computer)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A huge statue, much bigger than life size. 2) A person, company or thing that is enormously big, powerful or important («a colossus of science»). 3) (a name) The Colossus of Rhodes: a giant bronze statue of the sun god Helios in ancient Greece, one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World. 4) (a name) Colossus: one of the first electronic computers, built in Britain during the Second World War to help break German codes at Bletchley Park.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons the Colossus of Rhodes is one of the Seven Wonders; it fell in an earthquake about 2,200 years ago. In computing history, Colossus helped code-breakers. In sport and news, a «colossus» is a giant figure who dominates. It tells the reader something is enormous or hugely important.
examples from the lessons: The Colossus of Rhodes stood over thirty metres tall. | An earthquake toppled the Colossus. | The Colossus computer helped break secret codes in the war. | The goalkeeper was a colossus in defence. | The giant statue was a true colossus. | Some people call that company a colossus of technology.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural colossi («kuh-LOSS-eye») or colossuses. Adjective: colossal (huge). Myth: pictures often show the Colossus of Rhodes standing with legs across the harbour, but historians think that is unlikely.

part of speech: noun, a name (the Comanche, Comanche people; Comanche — the language)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (a name) The Comanche are a Native American people of the southern Great Plains (today mainly Oklahoma, USA), famous in history as expert horse riders. 2) (a name) The Comanche language, spoken by that people. 3) (a name) A name used for some places, vehicles and other things named after the Comanche.
its sense in the lessons: In history and geography lessons about the American West and Native American nations, the Comanche are known for their skill with horses and their large territory called Comanchería. In the Second World War, Comanche «code talkers» used their language to send secret messages for the US Army. It is a proper name, so it starts with a capital letter.
examples from the lessons: The Comanche were among the finest horse riders of the Great Plains. | Today the Comanche Nation has its headquarters in Oklahoma. | Comanche code talkers sent secret radio messages in the Second World War. | We read about the Comanche leader Quanah Parker. | The Comanche language is being taught to young people again. | The map showed the lands where the Comanche once lived.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A name, written with a capital C. Say «kuh-MAN-chee». Talk about the Comanche as a living nation today, not only in old Western films, which often showed Native peoples unfairly.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) To burn, or to catch fire, especially through a chemical reaction with oxygen. 2) (informal, joking) To get very angry or excited, as if about to burst into flames.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on burning, a fuel combusts when it reacts with oxygen and gives out heat and light; the fire triangle needs fuel, heat and oxygen. In safety, oily rags and hay can combust on their own if they get hot. In jokes, «I'll combust» means «I'm too excited or angry». Noun: combustion.
examples from the lessons: Petrol combusts inside a car engine. | Wood combusts when it gets hot enough and has oxygen. | Piles of damp hay can combust on their own. | Never leave oily rags in a heap; they can combust. | If I have to wait any longer, I'll combust! | The match combusted with a bright flash.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: combusted, combusting. Noun: combustion; adjective: combustible (able to burn). «Spontaneous combustion» means catching fire without a flame — it happens with hay and oily rags, but stories of people bursting into flames are a myth.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) To do with comets, the icy bodies that travel around the Sun and grow glowing tails when they come near it.
its sense in the lessons: In space lessons it describes comets' dust, tails, orbits and ice — «cometary dust», «cometary orbit». Meteor showers happen when the Earth passes through cometary dust. It tells the reader the subject is comets.
examples from the lessons: Meteor showers come from cometary dust. | The probe studied cometary ice up close. | A cometary orbit can be very long and stretched. | Scientists think cometary water may have reached the young Earth. | The telescope showed a faint cometary tail. | Halley's Comet has a cometary orbit of about 76 years.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective only, rare. Say «KOM-uh-tuh-ree». From «comet». Don't mix comets (icy, with tails) with asteroids (rocky) or meteors (streaks of light in the sky).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (money) A product or raw material that is bought and sold, such as wheat, oil, coffee, gold or copper. 2) Something useful or valuable that people want (time is a precious commodity).
its sense in the lessons: In geography and economics lessons, countries trade commodities; prices of commodities like oil and wheat go up and down and affect what we pay in shops. In everyday talk people say things like «patience is a rare commodity». It tells the reader we are talking about goods for trade or something valuable. Phrases: «commodity prices», «a precious commodity».
examples from the lessons: Coffee is one of the most traded commodities in the world. | Oil is an important commodity. | When commodity prices rise, food can cost more. | Water is a precious commodity in the desert. | Gold and silver are traded as commodities. | In the busy morning, time is a rare commodity.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a commodity, commodities (y changes to ies). Say «kuh-MOD-ih-tee». Not the same as «commode» (an old cabinet or a chair with a toilet pot).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Shared by all the people in a group or building (a communal kitchen, communal garden). 2) Done by or involving a group of people together (communal singing, a communal meal). 3) To do with different communities, sometimes groups who disagree (communal violence).
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life flats may have a communal garden or laundry; school trips may have communal showers and dormitories. In church life a communal meal brings people together. In history and news, «communal» can describe tensions between communities. It tells the reader something is shared or done together.
examples from the lessons: Our block of flats has a communal garden. | At camp we ate in a communal dining hall. | The communal fridge at work is always full. | The village had a communal well in the past. | Communal singing filled the church at Christmas. | Please keep the communal areas tidy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective only. Say «KOM-yoo-nul» (UK) or «kuh-MYOO-nul» (US). Comes from «common» and «community». It does not mean «communist».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Willing and happy to talk and share information with others. 2) To do with communication (communicative skills, a communicative approach to learning a language).
its sense in the lessons: In school reports, a communicative child talks and shares ideas easily; a shy child may be «not very communicative». In language lessons, the communicative approach means learning by talking in real situations. It tells the reader how much someone talks or how good they are at getting ideas across.
examples from the lessons: He's very communicative and always tells us about his day. | My teenage brother isn't very communicative in the mornings. | Our French lessons use a communicative approach with lots of talking. | Good leaders are communicative and clear. | Dolphins are highly communicative animals. | Babies become more communicative as they learn to babble.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say «kuh-MYOO-nih-kuh-tiv». Comes from «communicate». Opposite: uncommunicative. It describes a person's willingness, not only their skill.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (UK, Australia, informal) Short for «competition», especially one to win a prize (enter a comp). 2) (UK, informal) Short for «comprehensive school», a state secondary school for all abilities. 3) (informal) Short for «complimentary»: free tickets or items (comps). 4) (informal) Short for «composition» (in music or in art and writing), or «compilation». 5) (US, informal) Short for «compensation»: money paid to make up for a loss, like «workers' comp».
its sense in the lessons: It is a clipped, informal word, so its meaning depends on the setting: in Britain and Australia, «a comp» is often a sports or prize competition; parents may say they went to «the local comp» (school); at a theatre, «comps» are free tickets. It tells the reader a longer word has been shortened.
examples from the lessons: I entered a drawing comp and won a book voucher. | She's running in the swimming comp on Saturday. (Australia) | Mum went to the local comp in Leeds. | We got two comps for the show because Dad works there. | The band's new comp album has all their hits. | His dad got workers' comp after the accident. (US)
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal clipped form; avoid it in formal writing and say the full word. Plural: comps. Say «komp». Not a word on its own in exams: write «competition», «comprehensive school», «complimentary» or «compensation».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Pressing something together so it becomes tighter and smaller, with less space inside it. 2) (science) The squeezing of layers of sediment or soil by weight on top, which helps turn sediment into sedimentary rock.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on rocks, compaction and cementation turn layers of mud and sand into sedimentary rock over millions of years. In gardening and farming, soil compaction from heavy machines or feet makes it hard for roots and water to get in. Rubbish trucks use compaction to squeeze rubbish. It tells the reader things are being pressed tighter.
examples from the lessons: Compaction squeezes layers of sand into sandstone. | Heavy tractors cause soil compaction. | Rubbish lorries use compaction to fit more rubbish in. | We modelled compaction by pressing layers of clay together. | Roots struggle to grow in soil with too much compaction. | Road builders use rollers for compaction of gravel.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Verb: «compact» (to press tight). Not to be confused with «compact» as an adjective (small and neat) or a noun (a small make-up case, or an agreement).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Able to work together with something else without problems (a charger compatible with your phone). 2) (people) Able to live, work or get on together well because they are alike in some way. 3) (medicine) Suitable to be given or put into someone's body without harm (a compatible blood type).
its sense in the lessons: In computing and technology, a game or app may be compatible only with certain consoles or phones. In friendships, compatible people get on well. In science and health, blood donors must have a compatible blood type. It tells the reader things fit together and work. Opposite: incompatible.
examples from the lessons: Is this game compatible with my tablet? | The charger isn't compatible with the old phone. | My sister and I aren't very compatible on long car trips. | Blood for a transfusion must be a compatible type. | These two Lego sets are compatible, so you can mix them. | Their ideas were compatible, so they worked well together.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelled with -ible: compatible. Often used with «with». Opposite: incompatible. Noun: compatibility.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who complains a lot, often about small things. 2) A person who makes an official complaint.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and everyday life it describes someone who always grumbles about food, weather or rules — usually said as criticism. In adult life, a shop or council may deal with «the complainer» politely. It tells the reader someone grumbles or has made a complaint. Similar: «moaner», «whinger» (UK, Australia), «grump».
examples from the lessons: My cousin is a real complainer; nothing is ever good enough. | Don't be a complainer — try the new food. | The complainer wrote to the council about the noise. | Even the biggest complainers loved the school trip. | A complainer can spoil the fun for everyone. | The shop manager listened to the complainer patiently.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a complainer, complainers. Verb: complain; noun: complaint (the thing said). Informal similar words: moaner, whinger (UK, Australia, NZ), whiner (US). Complaining fairly about a real problem is fine and can fix things.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A friend or companion, especially someone who shares difficult work or danger with you, such as a fellow soldier (comrades in arms). 2) A fellow member of a socialist or communist party or trade union, used as a title («Comrade Petrov»), especially in the old Soviet Union.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons about wars, soldiers speak of their comrades who fought beside them; on Remembrance Day people remember fallen comrades. In history about the Soviet Union and other communist countries, «comrade» was the usual title instead of Mr or Mrs. In stories it shows loyalty and shared struggle. Phrases: «comrades in arms», «fallen comrades».
examples from the lessons: The old soldier remembered his comrades from the war. | They were comrades in arms through the long winter. | In the Soviet Union people called each other "Comrade". | On Remembrance Day we honour fallen comrades. | The explorers were loyal comrades on the icy journey. | "Well done, comrade!" he joked to his friend.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a comrade, comrades. Noun: comradeship (friendship in hard times). Today it can sound old-fashioned or political; in everyday talk people say «friend», «mate» or «teammate».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Short and clear, saying what is needed in few words without leaving out important things. 2) (of books) Shortened but still covering the main points (a concise dictionary).
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons teachers ask for concise answers and summaries — say it clearly in few words, no waffle. In science, a concise conclusion states the result simply. It tells the reader something is short but complete. Opposite: wordy, long-winded.
examples from the lessons: Write a concise summary of the story in three sentences. | Her answer was concise and correct. | Try to be concise in your science conclusion. | The concise dictionary fits in my school bag. | Good instructions are clear and concise. | His speech was concise, just two minutes long.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective; adverb concisely; noun concision or conciseness. Concise does not mean «too short»: it must still include the important points. Not the same as «precise» (exact).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Happening or existing at the same time (concurrent events). 2) (maths) Meeting at the same point (concurrent lines all pass through one point). 3) (law) In a court sentence, served at the same time as another rather than one after the other.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and timetables, concurrent activities happen at the same time — you cannot go to two concurrent clubs. In maths, three or more lines are concurrent if they all cross at one point. In computing, concurrent programs run at the same time. It tells the reader things overlap in time or meet in one place. Adverb: concurrently.
examples from the lessons: The two football matches were concurrent, so we could only watch one. | The festival had concurrent shows on three stages. | In geometry, concurrent lines meet at a single point. | The three medians of a triangle are concurrent. | The judge gave two concurrent sentences. | The computer can run concurrent tasks.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective; adverb concurrently. Maths note: «concurrent lines» meet at one point; «parallel lines» never meet. In timetables, concurrent means «at the same time», so you need to choose one.

part of speech: noun (a confidant, confidants); feminine also confidante
meaning for a pupil: 1) A person you trust and tell your secrets and private feelings to.
its sense in the lessons: In stories a character often has a confidant — a best friend, a grandparent, a teacher — who keeps their secrets. In wellbeing lessons pupils are encouraged to have a trusted adult to talk to. It tells the reader there is someone the character trusts deeply. Similar: «trusted friend».
examples from the lessons: Grandma was my closest confidant when I was little. | The king's confidant knew all his plans. | She became her sister's confidant after the move. | Everyone needs a confidant to share worries with. | In the story, the dog is the boy's only confidant. | A good confidant listens and keeps secrets safe — unless someone is in danger.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say «KON-fih-dant» or «kon-fih-DAHNT». «Confidante» (with an e) is sometimes used for a woman. Trap: «confidant» (a person) is not «confident» (sure of yourself). Safety: if a secret means someone is being hurt, tell a trusted adult even if it was told in confidence.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Keeping private information secret and only sharing it with people who are allowed to know it. 2) (law) A duty or agreement to keep information private, as doctors, lawyers and counsellors must.
its sense in the lessons: In adult life, doctors, nurses, school counsellors and banks keep information confidential. In PSHE lessons, pupils learn that school staff keep things private except when a child might be in danger — then they must tell people who can help. It tells the reader information is private and protected. Phrases: «patient confidentiality», «a confidentiality agreement», «in confidence».
examples from the lessons: Doctors must respect patient confidentiality. | The counsellor explained the rules about confidentiality. | Mum signed a confidentiality agreement at her new job. | Confidentiality means your records are not shown to strangers. | If you are in danger, a teacher must share the information to keep you safe. | The bank takes confidentiality seriously.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Adjective: confidential (private, secret). Say «kon-fih-den-shee-AL-ih-tee». Confidentiality has limits: staff must act to protect children's safety.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) A very large, destructive fire that spreads widely. 2) (formal) A big war or conflict.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons it describes great fires such as the Great Fire of London (1666) or the Great Chicago Fire (1871). In news and old writing, a «conflagration» can also mean a war that spreads. It tells the reader the fire or conflict is huge. Everyday English says «a huge fire» or «blaze».
examples from the lessons: The Great Fire of London was a terrible conflagration. | The conflagration destroyed hundreds of homes. | Firefighters battled the conflagration all night. | Dry bushland can turn a small spark into a conflagration. | Leaders feared the border fight would become a wider conflagration. | Only stone buildings survived the conflagration.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a conflagration, conflagrations. Formal. Say «kon-fluh-GRAY-shun». From Latin «flagrare» (to blaze), as in «flagrant».

meaning for a pupil: 1) To come together and form a group or crowd in one place. 2) (church) To gather for worship.
its sense in the lessons: In science and nature, animals congregate at waterholes or in flocks; in everyday life pupils congregate in the playground or at the school gate. In church life, people congregate for services, and the gathered people are called the «congregation». It tells the reader many people or animals are gathering. Formal; everyday words: «gather», «meet».
examples from the lessons: Pupils congregated around the noticeboard to see the results. | Starlings congregate in huge flocks in the evening. | People congregated in the square for the celebration. | Elephants congregate at the waterhole in the dry season. | The faithful congregated in the church for Easter. | Please don't congregate in the corridors.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: congregated, congregating. Noun: congregation (the people at a church service). It is more formal than «gather».

part of speech: abbreviation and noun (Conn. — Connecticut; the conn — on a ship)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (abbreviation) Conn. is an old short form of Connecticut, a state in the north-east of the USA (the postal code is CT). 2) (nautical) The conn is the control of a ship's steering and movement; the officer «with the conn» gives the orders to the helmsman. 3) (a name) A short name, such as part of Irish names like Conn (a legendary Irish king, Conn of the Hundred Battles).
its sense in the lessons: Children may meet «Conn.» in old addresses, maps and history books about the USA, and «the conn» in sea stories and films set on ships and submarines («You have the conn»). It tells the reader about a US state or who is steering a ship.
examples from the lessons: Hartford, Conn., is the capital of Connecticut. | "You have the conn," the captain told the officer. | The officer took the conn as the submarine dived. | Today letters to Connecticut use the code CT, not Conn. | In Irish legend, Conn of the Hundred Battles was a high king. | The old map wrote "Conn." beside the state.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As an abbreviation it has a capital and full stop: «Conn.». «The conn» is a sea word, not everyday English. Not a short form of «con» (a trick) or «cone».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A feeling or idea that a word suggests, in addition to its basic meaning. For example, «home» means a place to live, but it suggests warmth and safety.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons, pupils study how writers choose words for their connotations: «slim» has good connotations, «skinny» can sound negative, though both mean thin. In poetry and persuasive writing, connotations shape how readers feel. It tells the reader to think beyond the dictionary meaning. Opposite term: denotation (the plain, literal meaning).
examples from the lessons: The word "home" has connotations of warmth and safety. | "Stubborn" and "determined" have different connotations. | Red can have connotations of danger or of love. | The poet chose words with dark connotations to create fear. | "Cheap" can have negative connotations, while "good value" sounds positive. | Discuss the connotations of the word "storm" in the poem.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a connotation, connotations. Verb: connote. Denotation = what a word literally means; connotation = what it suggests. Connotations can differ between countries and people.

part of speech: verb form (conquer, conquers, conquered, conquering); adjective (conquering)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Taking control of a country or people by force, especially in war. 2) Succeeding in beating or overcoming a difficult problem or fear (conquering a fear of heights). 3) Climbing a difficult mountain to the top. 4) (adjective) Having won, victorious (the conquering hero).
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons it describes empires such as the Romans conquering Britain or the Normans conquering England in 1066. In everyday life and wellbeing, «conquering your fears» means overcoming them bravely. In stories, «the conquering hero» returns home in triumph. It tells the reader about winning, by force or by effort.
