examples from the lessons: The Romans were conquering lands all around the Mediterranean. | William the Conqueror led the Normans in conquering England in 1066. | She is conquering her fear of the dark. | The climbers celebrated conquering the mountain. | The crowds cheered the conquering hero. | Conquering a hard maths problem feels great.
note for the reader of a maths problem: -ing form of the regular verb «conquer». Spelling: c-o-n-q-u-e-r. Noun: conquest; person: conqueror. Say «KONG-ker-ing». In history, conquest often meant great suffering for the people who were conquered.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Agreement among all or most people in a group. 2) (science) The general view of most experts after studying the evidence (the scientific consensus).
its sense in the lessons: In class discussions and school councils, a group may «reach a consensus» on a decision. In science lessons, the scientific consensus is that the Earth is warming because of human activity and that vaccines are safe and effective. In news, «there is no consensus» means people disagree. It tells the reader most people agree. Phrases: «reach a consensus», «general consensus», «build a consensus».
examples from the lessons: The class reached a consensus to visit the zoo. | There is a strong scientific consensus about climate change. | After a long chat, the family came to a consensus on pizza. | The council could not reach a consensus. | A consensus does not always mean everyone agrees completely. | The general consensus was that the play was brilliant.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelled with an s in the middle: c-o-n-s-e-n-s-u-s (not «concensus»). «General consensus» is common but slightly repetitive. A consensus can still be wrong; in science it is based on evidence and can change with new evidence.

part of speech: noun (a conservatoire, conservatoires); US often conservatory
meaning for a pupil: 1) (music) A college where people study music, singing, dance or drama to a very high level, often to become professional performers.
its sense in the lessons: In music lessons and stories, talented young players hope to study at a conservatoire, such as the Royal Northern College of Music, the Royal Conservatoire of Scotland or the Paris Conservatoire. Some conservatoires have junior departments for children on Saturdays. It tells the reader about serious music training.
examples from the lessons: My cousin plays the cello at the junior conservatoire on Saturdays. | She auditioned for a place at the conservatoire. | The Paris Conservatoire is famous for its musicians. | Students at the conservatoire practise for hours each day. | He hopes to study singing at a conservatoire. | The conservatoire's orchestra gave a free concert.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Say «kon-SUR-vuh-twah». In the USA, a music college is usually called a «conservatory», but in the UK «conservatory» more often means a glass room added to a house.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Comfort given to someone who is sad or disappointed. 2) A person or thing that gives comfort in a bad situation («It's some consolation that...»). 3) (sport) A small prize or match for those who did not win, as in «consolation prize» or «consolation goal».
its sense in the lessons: In stories and everyday life, friends offer consolation after a loss or disappointment. In sport and competitions, a «consolation prize» is given to someone who didn't win, and a «consolation goal» is scored by a team that is losing badly. In church life, prayer and hymns can bring consolation in grief. It tells the reader someone is being comforted.
examples from the lessons: She hugged her friend in consolation. | We lost the final, but got a consolation prize. | United scored a consolation goal in the last minute. | It was some consolation that the rain stopped for the picnic. | His dog was a great consolation after Grandpa died. | Many people find consolation in prayer.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: console (stress on the second syllable: kun-SOLE). Do not confuse with «console» (stress on first: KON-sole), the games machine or control panel. «A consolation prize» is a fixed phrase.

part of speech: noun (a constable, constables); a name (John Constable)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (UK, Ireland, Australia, NZ, Canada) A police officer of the lowest rank; often written PC (police constable), as in «PC Smith». 2) (history) An important officer in a medieval castle or a royal court (the Constable of the Tower of London). 3) (US) A local law officer in some small towns. 4) (a name) John Constable was an English painter famous for landscapes like «The Hay Wain» (1821).
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and safety lessons, a police constable might visit school to talk about road safety or online safety. In history, castles had a constable in charge when the lord was away. In art lessons, Constable's paintings show the English countryside. It tells the reader about a police officer, a castle officer or the painter.
examples from the lessons: PC Jones came to talk to us about bike safety. | The constable directed the traffic after the crash. | The Constable of the castle guarded it for the king. | We copied John Constable's painting of a hay cart in a river. | Police constables patrol the town centre. | The chief constable leads a whole police force in Britain.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a constable, constables. Say «KUN-stuh-bul». «Chief Constable» is the head of a UK police force, not the lowest rank. If you are lost or in danger, a police officer is someone you can ask for help.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (law, politics) In a way that follows or is allowed by a country's constitution (its main set of laws and rules). 2) In a way that comes from someone's natural body or character («constitutionally unable to sit still»).
its sense in the lessons: In history and citizenship lessons, a law can be «constitutionally» allowed or not; in the USA the Supreme Court decides if laws are constitutional. In everyday writing, it can jokingly describe someone's nature: «He is constitutionally unable to be on time.» It tells the reader something is about the constitution or about a person's nature.
examples from the lessons: The President was constitutionally elected. | The court decided the law was not constitutionally valid. | Ireland's constitution can only be changed by a vote of the people. | The new rule was constitutionally questioned. | My brother is constitutionally unable to keep his room tidy. | Some people are constitutionally strong and rarely get ill.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from «constitutional» from «constitution». Long word: con-sti-TOO-shun-ul-ee. The UK has no single written constitution, unlike the USA, Ireland, Canada and Australia.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Something that limits or controls what you can do (time constraints, money constraints). 2) (maths, design) A condition or rule that an answer or design must follow. 3) Holding back your feelings or actions; a lack of freedom.
its sense in the lessons: In design and technology, a design brief has constraints: budget, size, materials. In maths, a problem's constraints are the rules the answer must obey (whole numbers only, under 10). In everyday life, families have time and money constraints. It tells the reader there is a limit. Phrases: «time constraints», «under constraint», «budget constraints».
examples from the lessons: Because of time constraints, we could only visit one museum. | The constraint was that the bridge must hold 1 kg. | Money constraints mean we can't go abroad this year. | In the puzzle, the constraint is that each number is used once. | A design brief lists all the constraints. | He spoke without constraint about his feelings.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable when meaning a limit: constraints. Verb: constrain. In maths word problems, constraints narrow down the possible answers: e.g. «both numbers are even and add up to 10» rules out 3 + 7.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A substance that makes something dirty, impure, harmful or poisonous, such as germs, chemicals or dirt in water, food, air or soil.
its sense in the lessons: In science and health lessons, contaminants such as bacteria, lead, oil or plastics can get into drinking water, food or the environment. Water companies test for contaminants to keep tap water safe. It tells the reader something unwanted and harmful is present.
examples from the lessons: The water was tested for contaminants. | Bacteria are a common contaminant in raw chicken. | Microplastics are a contaminant in the oceans. | The filter removes contaminants from the water. | Lead used to be a contaminant in old water pipes. | Factories must stop contaminants getting into rivers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a contaminant, contaminants. Same family: contaminate (verb), contamination (noun for the process or state), contaminated (adjective).

meaning for a pupil: 1) To make something dirty, impure or harmful by adding something bad to it, such as germs, poison or chemicals. 2) (science) To spoil an experiment or sample by letting something unwanted get in. 3) To have a bad influence on something (contaminate someone's thinking).
its sense in the lessons: In science, cooking and food-safety lessons: do not let raw meat contaminate other food — use separate boards and wash your hands. In environment lessons, oil spills and sewage contaminate rivers and seas. In experiments, dirty equipment can contaminate results. It tells the reader something clean has been spoiled.
examples from the lessons: Raw chicken can contaminate other food with bacteria. | Wash your hands so you don't contaminate the food. | An oil spill contaminated the beach. | Sewage contaminated the river after the storm. | Don't touch the sample or you'll contaminate it. | Chemicals from the old factory contaminated the soil.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: contaminated, contaminating. Food safety: keep raw meat away from ready-to-eat food, use separate chopping boards, and wash hands after touching raw meat. Opposite: purify, decontaminate.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The state of being made dirty, impure or harmful by something unwanted (water contamination). 2) The act or process of contaminating something. 3) (science) Unwanted material spoiling a sample or experiment.
its sense in the lessons: In health, science and news, contamination of water, food or air can make people ill; «cross-contamination» in kitchens spreads germs from raw to cooked food. In environment lessons, radioactive or chemical contamination can last a long time. It tells the reader there is something harmful where it shouldn't be.
examples from the lessons: The water company found contamination in the reservoir. | Cross-contamination happens when raw meat touches cooked food. | Food labels warn about contamination with nuts. | Scientists wear gloves to avoid contamination. | Radioactive contamination stayed near Chernobyl for many years. | The beach was closed because of sewage contamination.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: no «a», no plural. Verb: contaminate. «Cross-contamination» is an important food-safety word: allergens (like nuts) can also cross-contaminate food, which is dangerous for people with allergies.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) At the same time as something else happened, or during the same period.
its sense in the lessons: In history and law, a note written contemporaneously is written at the time of the events, which makes it more reliable evidence than one written later. It tells the reader two things happened in the same period. Everyday English says «at the same time».
examples from the lessons: The diary was written contemporaneously with the events. | Two inventors worked on the telephone contemporaneously. | The police officer made notes contemporaneously. | The two kingdoms grew contemporaneously. | Historians trust sources written contemporaneously more than later ones. | The songs were recorded contemporaneously in London and New York.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Very formal. Adverb from «contemporaneous» (existing at the same time). Say «kon-tem-puh-RAY-nee-us-lee». Related words: contemporary, coeval, concurrent. In history, sources made at the time are usually primary sources.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Contempt is the feeling that someone or something is worthless and does not deserve any respect. 2) (law) Contempt of court is the crime of disobeying a court or being rude to a judge.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, contempt tells the reader a character looks down on someone, often shown by a sneer, a cold voice or turning away; it is stronger than dislike. Phrases: «with contempt», «hold someone in contempt», «beneath contempt» (so bad it does not even deserve contempt), «familiarity breeds contempt» (a saying: knowing something too well can make you stop respecting it), «contempt of court».
examples from the lessons: The queen looked at the beggar with contempt. | She spoke to the new boy with open contempt, and the teacher stopped her. | Bullying someone for being poor is beneath contempt. | The villain laughed with contempt at the hero's tiny sword. | The man was jailed for contempt of court after shouting at the judge. | Treat people with respect, not contempt, even when you disagree. | His contempt for the rules got the whole team disqualified.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: say «contempt», not «a contempt» or «contempts». Adjectives: contemptuous (showing contempt: a contemptuous look) and contemptible (deserving contempt: a contemptible lie) — they are easy to mix up. Opposite: respect, admiration.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Contiguous things touch each other or share a border, with no gap between them. 2) (formal) Contiguous also means next to each other in a row or in time, one straight after another.
its sense in the lessons: In geography, «the contiguous United States» means the 48 states that touch each other, leaving out Alaska and Hawaii. In maths and computing it describes blocks, squares or numbers that sit side by side without gaps. It is an exam and textbook word; in everyday talk people say «touching», «next to» or «joined».
examples from the lessons: The contiguous United States are the 48 states that join together on the map. | France and Spain are contiguous countries. | Colour in four contiguous squares on the grid to make a line. | The two gardens are contiguous, so the dog runs from one to the other. | The farm is made of three contiguous fields. | The class read five contiguous pages without stopping.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal word; everyday words are «touching», «adjacent», «neighbouring». Noun: contiguity. In a maths problem, contiguous squares or numbers come one after another with nothing missing (for example 4, 5, 6).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Contradictory statements or ideas cannot both be true because they say opposite things. 2) A contradictory person often says the opposite of what others say, or of what they themselves said before.
its sense in the lessons: In detective stories, contradictory stories from witnesses show someone is lying or mistaken. In science, contradictory results mean an experiment must be checked again. In logic and maths puzzles, two contradictory clues cannot both hold, so one must be false. Phrases: «contradictory evidence», «contradictory messages», «contradictory advice».
examples from the lessons: The two witnesses gave contradictory accounts of the crash. | «It is raining» and «it is not raining» are contradictory statements. | Mum and Dad gave me contradictory instructions about bedtime. | The experiment gave contradictory results, so we repeated it. | The rules on the sign were contradictory: «Keep left» and «Keep right». | His contradictory answers made the detective suspicious. | The puzzle has two contradictory clues, so one of the twins must be lying.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: contradict (to say the opposite); noun: contradiction. Contradictory does not just mean «different»: two different opinions can both be partly right, but contradictory statements cannot both be true at the same time.

part of speech: noun (contradistinction — usually uncountable, mostly in «in contradistinction to»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Contradistinction is telling two things apart by showing how they are opposite or different.
its sense in the lessons: A stiff, formal word used in books and essays, almost always in the phrase «in contradistinction to», which means «as opposed to» or «unlike». In school it may appear in exam texts; in your own writing «unlike» or «in contrast to» is clearer.
examples from the lessons: Mammals feed their babies milk, in contradistinction to reptiles, which do not. | The essay described day, in contradistinction to night. | Facts, in contradistinction to opinions, can be checked. | The writer drew a contradistinction between bravery and foolishness. | Living things, in contradistinction to rocks, grow and reproduce. | In contradistinction to his noisy brother, Tom was very quiet.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal and rare. Simpler choices: «unlike», «as opposed to», «in contrast to». Do not confuse it with contradiction (saying the opposite of something).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (medicine) A contusion is a bruise: an injury where the skin is not broken but blood leaks under it, making a dark mark.
its sense in the lessons: It is the doctor's word for a bruise and appears in hospital reports, first-aid books and news («he suffered a contusion»). In science lessons about the body it explains why bruises change colour as they heal. Phrases: «a bone contusion», «cuts and contusions», «minor contusions».
examples from the lessons: The doctor said the dark mark on my knee was only a contusion. | The footballer suffered a contusion after the hard tackle. | The X-ray showed no broken bone, just a contusion. | She had a few cuts and contusions after falling off her bike. | Put ice on a contusion to stop it swelling. | A contusion turns purple, then green, then yellow as it heals.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one contusion, two contusions. Everyday word: bruise. Not the same as concussion (an injury to the brain after a knock on the head) — the two words sound alike.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Convalescence is the time when someone slowly gets their strength back after an illness or operation.
its sense in the lessons: Used in stories and history (soldiers and patients in convalescent homes), and by doctors and in letters about someone who has been ill. It tells the reader the illness is over but the person is still weak and must rest. Phrases: «a long convalescence», «during his convalescence», «a period of convalescence».
examples from the lessons: After the operation, Grandpa needed six weeks of convalescence. | During her convalescence she read every book in the house. | The doctor said a quiet convalescence by the sea would help. | In the old story, the soldier spent his convalescence in a country hospital. | Convalescence after flu can take a week or two. | His convalescence was slow, but he was back at school by spring.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: convalesce (to get better slowly); adjective and noun: convalescent (a convalescent patient; a convalescent home). Spelling trap: «-scence», with sc.

meaning for a pupil: 1) When lines, roads or rivers converge, they move towards each other and meet at one point. 2) When people converge on a place, they come to it from different directions. 3) When ideas or opinions converge, they become more alike. 4) (maths) A series or sequence converges when it gets closer and closer to one fixed number.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and art, converging lines meet at a point, like railway tracks in a drawing with perspective. In science, light rays converge after passing through a magnifying glass (a converging lens). In news and stories, crowds «converge on» a square or a stadium. Opposite: diverge.
examples from the lessons: The two roads converge just before the bridge. | Railway lines seem to converge in the distance. | Fans converged on the stadium from all over the city. | A magnifying glass makes rays of sunlight converge on one spot. | Police cars converged on the bank after the alarm rang. | Our ideas converged, and we agreed on one plan. | The sums 1/2 + 1/4 + 1/8 + ... converge on 1.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: converged, converging. Noun: convergence. Opposite: diverge (to move apart). In maths, «converges to 1» means the answers get as close to 1 as you like, though each sum alone may never reach it exactly.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A converter is a machine or device that changes something from one form into another, such as electricity, signals or files. 2) A converter is a tool or chart that changes amounts from one unit or currency into another. 3) (cars) A catalytic converter is a part of a car's exhaust that makes the gases less poisonous.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life you meet plug converters for travel abroad, video and file converters on computers and unit converters on phones (inches to centimetres, pounds to kilograms, dollars to euros). In science, a solar panel is a converter of light energy into electrical energy.
examples from the lessons: We packed a plug converter for our trip to Ireland. | Use the unit converter to change 10 miles into kilometres. | A solar panel is a converter of sunlight into electricity. | The website has a currency converter for pounds and dollars. | Dad installed a converter so the old TV can get digital channels. | The car failed its test because the catalytic converter was broken. | I used a file converter to turn my photo into a smaller picture.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Also spelt convertor (less common). Verb: convert. A plug adapter only changes the shape of the plug; a voltage converter also changes the electricity — using the wrong one can damage a device, so ask an adult.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To convince someone is to make them believe that something is true. 2) To convince someone to do something is to persuade them to do it. 3) Convinced (adjective) means completely sure.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, characters try to convince others with arguments, proof or tricks; in persuasive writing at school you try to convince the reader. In safety lessons: strangers and scammers may try to convince you to share passwords or go somewhere — stop and tell an adult. Phrases: «convince someone of something», «convince someone to do», «I'm convinced that», «not convinced».
examples from the lessons: I convinced Mum that I had finished my homework. | She convinced her brother to share his sweets. | The detective was convinced the butler was lying. | Write a letter to convince the head teacher to have a longer break. | The scientist showed the photos to convince people the comet was real. | Don't let anyone convince you to keep a secret that makes you feel unsafe. | I'm not convinced this answer is right; let's check it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Adjective: convincing (a convincing excuse = easy to believe); unconvincing is the opposite. Noun: conviction (strong belief; also, in law, being found guilty). Convince is mostly about belief; persuade is mostly about action, but they overlap.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Convulsive movements are sudden, violent shakes of the body that a person cannot control. 2) Convulsive laughter or sobbing is so strong that the whole body shakes.
its sense in the lessons: In medicine and first aid, convulsive seizures happen in some illnesses like epilepsy or a very high fever; the safety rule is to keep the person safe, not hold them down, and call an adult or emergency help. In stories, «convulsive sobs» or «convulsive laughter» show very strong feeling.
examples from the lessons: The baby had a convulsive fit during a high fever, so they called an ambulance. | He shook with convulsive laughter at the joke. | She cried with convulsive sobs at the funeral. | A convulsive seizure can last a minute or two. | The dog's convulsive shaking worried the vet. | His convulsive cough kept the whole family awake.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: convulsion (a sudden violent shake; «convulsions» in plural for a fit). Verb: convulse. In first aid, never put anything in the mouth of someone having a seizure.

part of speech: noun (a cooler, coolers); adjective (cooler — the comparative of cool)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Cooler means more cool: a little colder, or (slang) more stylish or exciting. 2) A cooler is a box or bag that keeps food and drinks cold, especially on picnics (also «cool box» in the UK, «esky» in Australia). 3) A cooler is a machine or part that cools something, like a water cooler or a computer fan. 4) (slang, old) The cooler is prison or a cell.
its sense in the lessons: In science and weather, «cooler» compares temperatures: cooler in the shade, cooler at night. In everyday talk, «cooler» compares how fashionable things are. On a picnic or a trip to the beach, the cooler holds the drinks. In older films, «put in the cooler» means locked up.
examples from the lessons: It is cooler in the shade than in the sun. | Tomorrow will be cooler, about 15 degrees. | Pack the sandwiches and juice in the cooler. | We chatted by the water cooler at the sports centre. | Your new trainers are way cooler than mine. | The computer needs a better cooler or it gets too hot. | In the old film, the gangster spent a night in the cooler.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative: cool, cooler, coolest. As a noun it is countable: two coolers. In a maths problem, «5 degrees cooler» means subtract 5 from the temperature. In the UK the box is usually a «cool box» or «cool bag».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Cooperation is working together with other people to reach the same goal. 2) Cooperation is being helpful and doing what you are asked, for example with the police or a teacher.
its sense in the lessons: In school, cooperation is a key part of group work, team sports and class projects. In science, many animals show cooperation, like ants in a colony or wolves hunting in a pack. Between countries, cooperation means sharing work, like the International Space Station. Phrases: «in cooperation with», «thank you for your cooperation», «international cooperation».
examples from the lessons: The project was finished thanks to the cooperation of the whole class. | Ants survive by cooperation: each one has a job. | Thank you for your cooperation, said the sign at the airport. | The space station was built in cooperation with many countries. | Good cooperation helped our team win the relay. | The police asked for the public's cooperation in finding the lost dog.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: no «a» and no plural. Also spelt co-operation (often in the UK). Verb: cooperate; adjective: cooperative. Opposite: competition (working against each other) or refusal to help.

part of speech: noun (a coordinate, coordinates); verb (coordinate, coordinates, coordinated, coordinating)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (maths) Coordinates are a pair of numbers, like (3, 5), that show exactly where a point is on a grid or graph. 2) (geography) Coordinates are numbers of latitude and longitude that give a place on the Earth. 3) To coordinate is to organise people or things so they work well together. 4) To coordinate your body is to make your arms, legs and eyes move together smoothly.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, the first coordinate is along (x, across) and the second is up (y): «along the corridor, up the stairs». On maps and GPS, coordinates find any place. In PE, coordination matters for catching and dancing. In clubs, someone coordinates the rota or the event. Phrases: «x-coordinate», «y-coordinate», «grid coordinates», «colour-coordinated».
examples from the lessons: Plot the point with coordinates (4, 2) on the grid. | The x-coordinate comes first, then the y-coordinate. | The ship sent its coordinates when it called for help. | Mrs Brown coordinates the school fair every year. | Juggling helps you coordinate your hands and eyes. | Her socks are coordinated with her hat. | The pirate map gave the coordinates of the treasure: B7.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced «co-OR-din-ate» for both noun and verb (the noun's end often sounds like «-nit», the verb's like «-nate»). Nouns: coordination, coordinator. In maths, the order matters: (2, 5) and (5, 2) are different points. Also spelt co-ordinate in the UK.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) A copepod is a tiny animal with a hard shell and many legs, a relative of crabs and shrimps, that lives in the sea and in fresh water.
its sense in the lessons: Copepods are part of plankton, so they appear in science lessons about food chains in the ocean: they eat tiny plants (algae) and are eaten by fish, whales and other animals. Some are smaller than a grain of rice; there are many thousands of kinds.
examples from the lessons: A copepod is so small you need a microscope to see its legs. | Copepods eat tiny algae and are eaten by small fish. | Billions of copepods drift in the ocean as plankton. | We found copepods in a jar of pond water. | Copepods are crustaceans, like crabs and lobsters. | Without copepods, many ocean food chains would collapse.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one copepod, many copepods. Pronounced «KOH-puh-pod». The «-pod» part comes from Greek for «foot», as in tripod and octopus-like words.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Copiously means in very large amounts, much more than usual.
its sense in the lessons: Used in books and reports about rain, tears, blood, sweat or notes: «it rained copiously», «she wept copiously», «he took notes copiously». It tells the reader there was a great deal of something. Everyday words are «a lot», «heavily», «loads of».
examples from the lessons: It rained copiously all weekend, and the river flooded. | She wept copiously at the end of the film. | The runner sweated copiously in the heat. | He took notes copiously during the science talk. | Water the seedlings copiously after planting. | The wound bled copiously, so they pressed a clean cloth on it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: copious (copious notes, copious rain). It is about amount, not about copying — do not confuse it with «copy».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A cordless device works without being plugged into the wall by a wire, usually because it has a battery.
its sense in the lessons: Used for everyday machines at home and in DIY: a cordless phone, cordless drill, cordless vacuum cleaner, cordless kettle (whose base is plugged in). It tells you that you can carry it around, but it must be charged.
examples from the lessons: Grandma still has a cordless phone in the hall. | Dad used a cordless drill to put up the shelf. | The cordless vacuum needs charging every night. | A cordless kettle lifts off its base so you can pour easily. | Cordless headphones use Bluetooth instead of a wire. | We took the cordless speaker into the garden.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Cord» here means an electric wire (in the UK often called a lead or flex). Do not confuse cord with chord (notes played together in music).

part of speech: noun, a name (Córdoba — a city; a córdoba, córdobas — money)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (a name) Córdoba is a historic city in southern Spain, famous for its great mosque-cathedral (the Mezquita). 2) (a name) Córdoba is also a big city in Argentina. 3) (money) The córdoba is the money of Nicaragua.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, Córdoba in Spain was one of the largest and most learned cities in Europe about a thousand years ago, when it was ruled by Muslims; Muslims, Christians and Jews lived there. In geography, the Argentine Córdoba is that country's second-largest city. It is a Spanish name, not an English word.
examples from the lessons: Córdoba is a city in the south of Spain. | The great mosque of Córdoba later became a cathedral. | Córdoba in Argentina has a famous old university. | The price was 50 córdobas in the market in Nicaragua. | About a thousand years ago Córdoba had huge libraries. | We visited Córdoba and Seville on our holiday.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Written with a capital C and an accent (Córdoba) in careful writing; pronounced «KOR-do-ba». There is also an English word «cordovan», a kind of leather first made in Córdoba.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A corporal is a soldier with a low rank, above a private, who is in charge of a small group of soldiers. 2) (formal) Corporal (adjective) means to do with the body.
its sense in the lessons: In history and war stories, corporals lead small groups of soldiers. The adjective mostly appears in «corporal punishment»: punishing someone by hitting them, which used to happen in schools and is now banned in schools in the UK, Ireland, New Zealand, Canada and most of Australia, and in many US states. Phrases: «Corporal Smith» (as a title), «corporal punishment».
examples from the lessons: Corporal Jones led his section across the field. | A corporal is in charge of a few soldiers. | In Victorian schools, corporal punishment with a cane was common. | Corporal punishment is not allowed in schools in the UK. | The private saluted the corporal. | My great-grandad was a corporal in the war.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a title it takes a capital: Corporal Lee. Not to be confused with «corporate» (to do with companies) or «corporeal» (having a body, not a spirit). Corporal punishment means hitting, not other punishments like detention.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Corroboration is extra evidence or information that shows that a statement or idea is true.
its sense in the lessons: Used in law, detective stories, journalism and science: a good reporter or scientist looks for corroboration before believing a claim. In lessons about checking news online, corroboration means finding the same fact in other reliable sources. Phrases: «without corroboration», «independent corroboration», «in corroboration of».
examples from the lessons: The witness's story needed corroboration from another person. | The detective found a receipt in corroboration of the alibi. | Without corroboration, the rumour should not be shared. | The photo provided corroboration that the comet was real. | Scientists repeated the test to get corroboration of the result. | Check two good sources for corroboration before you believe a claim online.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: corroborate (to support with evidence). Uncountable. Simpler words: proof, support, confirmation. Corroboration supports a claim but does not always prove it completely.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Corrosion is the slow damage of metal or stone by water, air or chemicals, such as iron turning to rust. 2) Corrosion can be any slow wearing away or destruction of something.
its sense in the lessons: In science, corrosion is a chemical change: iron reacts with water and oxygen to form rust; salt water speeds it up, so cars and piers by the sea corrode faster. People stop corrosion with paint, oil, grease or by coating iron with zinc (galvanising). Phrases: «signs of corrosion», «protect against corrosion».
examples from the lessons: Corrosion has eaten holes in the old metal gate. | Salt on winter roads speeds up corrosion of cars. | Paint protects the bridge from corrosion. | In our experiment, the iron nail in salty water showed the most corrosion. | Gold does not suffer from corrosion, so it stays shiny. | The battery leaked, and corrosion ruined the remote control.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Verb: corrode; adjective: corrosive (a corrosive acid — safety: these burn skin, so never touch them). Rust is corrosion of iron and steel only; other metals corrode in other colours, like green on copper.

part of speech: adjective (corrupted); verb (corrupt, corrupts, corrupted, corrupting — corrupted is the past form)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (computing) A corrupted file or piece of data has been damaged, so it cannot open or works wrongly. 2) Corrupted means made dishonest or morally bad, especially by money or power. 3) A corrupted word or text has been changed from its original form, often by mistake.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday computer use: «the file is corrupted» means it is broken; keep backups. In stories and history, a hero or ruler can be corrupted by power or greed. In language lessons, many place names are corrupted forms of older words. Phrases: «a corrupted file», «corrupted by power», «corrupted data».
examples from the lessons: My game save got corrupted, and I lost all my progress. | The photos were corrupted when the memory card was pulled out. | In the story, the good king was corrupted by greed. | Power corrupted the leader, and he began to lie. | The name of the town is a corrupted form of an old Viking word. | A virus corrupted files on the school computer.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective corrupt (a corrupt official = dishonest, takes bribes) is the usual adjective for people; corrupted is used for files and for something that has been changed for the worse. Nouns: corruption.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) Cortisol is a hormone, a chemical messenger made by the body, that helps it deal with stress and controls energy, sleep and waking.
its sense in the lessons: In science and health lessons, cortisol is sometimes called «the stress hormone»: it rises when you are scared or worried and helps the body react, then should fall again. It is normally highest in the morning to help you wake up. Sleep, exercise and calm breathing help keep it healthy.
examples from the lessons: Cortisol helps your body wake up in the morning. | When you feel stressed before a test, your cortisol goes up. | Cortisol is made by small glands above the kidneys. | Doctors can measure cortisol with a blood test. | Exercise and sleep help keep cortisol levels healthy. | Cortisol and adrenaline both help the body react to danger.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Pronounced «KOR-ti-zol». «Stress hormone» is a nickname; cortisol is not bad in itself — the body needs it every day; trouble comes only if it stays too high or too low for a long time.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A cosmonaut is an astronaut from Russia or, in the past, from the Soviet Union.
its sense in the lessons: In history and science lessons: Yuri Gagarin, a Soviet cosmonaut, was the first person in space in 1961, and Valentina Tereshkova was the first woman in space in 1963. Different countries use different words: astronaut (USA, Europe and most countries), cosmonaut (Russia), taikonaut (often for China).
examples from the lessons: Yuri Gagarin was the first cosmonaut to orbit the Earth. | Valentina Tereshkova was the first woman cosmonaut. | The cosmonaut floated inside the space station. | Cosmonauts and astronauts work together on the International Space Station. | The cosmonaut trained for years before her flight. | Our class wrote questions for a retired cosmonaut.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. «Cosmos» means space or the universe; «naut» means sailor — so a cosmonaut is a «space sailor», like astronaut is a «star sailor».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A cougar is a large wild cat of North and South America, with brown fur and a long tail; it is also called a puma or mountain lion. 2) (rude, adult slang) a rude word grown-ups use; not for school.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography, cougars are top predators in mountains and forests of the Americas, from Canada to Chile; they hunt deer and are mostly shy of people. Safety in cougar country: stay in a group, keep small children close, and never run from one — stand tall and make noise.
examples from the lessons: The cougar crept silently through the rocks. | A cougar is also called a puma or a mountain lion. | Cougars hunt deer in the mountains of Canada. | The sign in the park said: «Cougar country — keep children close». | A cougar can leap higher than a basketball hoop. | We saw a cougar at the zoo, sleeping in the sun.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one cougar, two cougars. Cougar, puma and mountain lion are all the same animal; it is not a lion and does not roar.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A counterpart is a person or thing that has the same job or place as another, but in a different group, country or situation.
its sense in the lessons: Used in news and history: the Prime Minister meets his or her counterparts (other leaders); a head teacher meets counterparts from other schools. In science, it compares matching things: the human arm and its counterpart, the bird's wing. Phrases: «his French counterpart», «a digital counterpart».
examples from the lessons: The British Prime Minister met her Canadian counterpart. | Our class captain chatted with her counterpart from the visiting school. | The bird's wing is the counterpart of the human arm. | The e-book is the digital counterpart of the paper book. | The US president spoke with his counterpart in Japan. | Our school's head teacher wrote to her counterpart in Australia.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Counterpart means «the matching one elsewhere», not «the opposite one»: an opponent is someone against you, a counterpart is someone like you on another side.

part of speech: noun (a covering, coverings); verb form (covering — the -ing form of cover)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A covering is a layer of something that lies on or over something else. 2) A covering is something you use to cover or protect something, such as a sheet, lid or curtain. 3) Covering (verb) means putting something over, hiding, protecting, dealing with a topic, or doing someone else's job for a while.
its sense in the lessons: In weather and nature: «a light covering of snow», «a covering of fur». At home: floor coverings (carpets, rugs), wall coverings. In school: «covering a topic» means teaching it; a «cover teacher» is covering for someone who is away. Phrases: «a thin covering», «covering for someone» (also: hiding someone's mistake), «covering up».
examples from the lessons: There was a light covering of snow on the playground. | Animals in the Arctic have a thick covering of fur. | Put a covering over the paint pots so they don't dry out. | Mr Lee is covering our class while Mrs Day is ill. | We are covering fractions this week. | The skin is the body's covering. | Never keep covering for a friend who is in danger — tell an adult.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable as a noun: coverings. «Covering for» someone can be kind (doing their job) or dishonest (hiding what they did) — the sentence tells you which. «Cover-up» is hiding the truth.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Covert means secret or hidden, done so that people do not notice. 2) A covert is a thick bush or small wood where wild animals hide.
its sense in the lessons: In spy stories and news, a covert operation is a secret mission. In science of animals, birds and deer hide in coverts. Opposite: overt (done openly). Phrases: «covert operation», «covert action», «covert glance».
examples from the lessons: The spies went on a covert mission behind enemy lines. | She gave him a covert glance across the classroom. | The police did covert surveillance on the gang. | The fox ran into the covert to hide from the hounds. | Covert bullying, like leaving someone out on purpose, is still bullying. | The army planned a covert rescue.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced «KOH-vert» (also «KUV-ert», especially in the UK). Opposite: overt. Do not confuse with «cover» (noun/verb) or «convert» (to change).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A cowshed is a farm building where cows are kept, fed or milked, especially in winter.
its sense in the lessons: In farm stories, nursery books and lessons on where food comes from: cows shelter, eat hay and are milked in the cowshed or milking parlour. In stories, a messy room is sometimes compared to a cowshed.
examples from the lessons: The farmer led the cows into the cowshed before the storm. | The cowshed smelled of hay and milk. | In winter the cows stay in the cowshed. | We saw the calves in the cowshed on our school trip. | Your bedroom looks like a cowshed! said Mum. | The old cowshed has been turned into a holiday cottage.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. One word (cowshed); some write cow shed. Similar buildings: barn (for hay or animals), byre (old or Scottish word for cowshed), stable (for horses).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) Crabby means grumpy and easily annoyed, in a bad mood.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday talk and stories, a crabby person snaps at others, often because they are tired, hungry or unwell («crabby» after a long trip). It is a mild, friendly-sounding word, used a lot in the USA and Canada; in the UK people also say «grumpy», «ratty» or «cranky». Phrases: «feeling crabby», «a crabby old man».
examples from the lessons: The baby gets crabby when she is tired. | Dad is always crabby before his morning coffee. | Don't be so crabby — it's only a game! | I was crabby because I hadn't had lunch. | The crabby neighbour shouted at us to keep the ball out of his garden. | After the long car ride, everyone was hot and crabby.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative crabbier, superlative crabbiest. It is not about crabs, though it comes from the idea of a crab's pinching, bad-tempered way. Similar: grumpy, cranky, grouchy, ratty (UK).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A craftsperson is someone who makes things skilfully by hand, such as pots, furniture, jewellery or baskets.
its sense in the lessons: A gender-neutral word for craftsman or craftswoman, used in museums, fairs and history lessons about medieval guilds, apprentices and trades. It tells the reader the person is skilled and careful. Phrases: «a skilled craftsperson», «local craftspeople».
examples from the lessons: A craftsperson carved the wooden chair by hand. | The craft fair is full of local craftspeople. | In the Middle Ages, a young apprentice learned from a craftsperson. | The potter is a craftsperson who makes bowls on a wheel. | It takes years of practice to become a skilled craftsperson. | The museum showed tools used by craftspeople long ago.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural is usually craftspeople. Related: craftsman, craftswoman, craft, craftsmanship (the skill shown in the work), crafty (which means cunning — a trap!).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A crankshaft is a long metal rod in an engine that turns the up-and-down movement of the pistons into turning (spinning) movement that drives the wheels.
its sense in the lessons: In science and design technology, the crankshaft is an example of a mechanism that changes one kind of motion into another, like the pedals and crank of a bicycle. Cars, motorbikes, boats and old steam engines use crankshafts.
examples from the lessons: The pistons push the crankshaft round. | A broken crankshaft means the engine cannot work. | A bicycle's pedals turn a crank, a little like a crankshaft. | The mechanic showed us the crankshaft inside the old engine. | In D&T we built a model with a crankshaft that made a toy bird flap. | Steam engines used a crankshaft to turn their wheels.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. A «crank» is a handle or arm bent at a right angle that you turn; a «shaft» is a long rod. Crank also has an informal meaning: a strange person with odd ideas.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Credibility is the quality of being believed and trusted.
its sense in the lessons: In lessons on news and the internet: the credibility of a source depends on who wrote it, whether facts can be checked and whether other good sources agree. In stories, a liar loses credibility; a witness's credibility matters in court. Phrases: «lose credibility», «damage your credibility», «a credibility problem».
examples from the lessons: The website had no author or date, so its credibility was low. | After lying twice, he lost all credibility. | The scientist's careful work gave her great credibility. | Spelling mistakes can hurt the credibility of a letter. | The witness's credibility was questioned in court. | Check the credibility of a source before you use it in your project.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Adjective: credible. Opposite: lack of credibility, incredibility (rare). Do not mix with «credit» (money, or praise).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Credible means believable, able to be trusted as true. 2) A credible person, plan or threat is serious and likely to be real or to succeed.
its sense in the lessons: In research, a credible source is one you can trust (a good encyclopedia, a science organisation). In stories and stories you write, a credible plot or character feels real. In news: «a credible threat» means the danger is real and taken seriously. Opposite: incredible (which now usually means «amazing»).
examples from the lessons: The scientist gave a credible explanation for the strange lights. | Is that website a credible source? | His excuse about the dog eating his homework was not very credible. | The team made a credible effort to win. | Police said the threat was credible and closed the road. | Make your characters credible so the reader believes in them.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: incredible today mostly means «amazing», not just «not believable». Do not confuse credible (believable) with creditable (deserving praise) or gullible (too easy to fool).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Creditable means deserving praise, good enough to be respected, though often not the very best. 2) (money, rare) Able to be added to an account as credit.
its sense in the lessons: Used in sports reports and school reports: «a creditable third place», «a creditable effort» — it tells the reader the result was good and honourable, especially given the difficulties. Rather formal.
examples from the lessons: The team finished a creditable third in the league. | She gave a creditable performance in her first concert. | Getting 70 per cent in a hard test is a creditable result. | Helping the new pupil was a creditable thing to do. | The small school made a creditable effort against the champions. | His creditable behaviour earned him a merit certificate.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: creditable (deserving praise) is not credible (believable). Opposite: discreditable (shameful). Related: credit (praise; also money).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (money) Creditworthiness is how safe a bank or shop thinks it is to lend money to a person or company, based on whether they usually pay back what they owe.
its sense in the lessons: An adult money word seen by children in talk about loans, mortgages and credit cards: banks check creditworthiness before lending. A «credit score» is a number that measures it. Paying bills on time builds it; missed payments damage it.
examples from the lessons: The bank checked Dad's creditworthiness before giving the mortgage. | Paying bills on time improves your creditworthiness. | A company's creditworthiness affects how much it can borrow. | Missing loan payments harmed her creditworthiness. | Lenders use a credit score to judge creditworthiness. | Good creditworthiness can mean lower interest on a loan.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Adjective: creditworthy. Here «credit» means borrowing money that you must pay back, usually with interest — not praise.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (money) A creditworthy person or company is thought safe to lend money to, because they are likely to pay it back.
its sense in the lessons: An adult money word: banks lend more easily, and more cheaply, to creditworthy customers. A child may hear it in talk about loans, credit cards and buying a house.
examples from the lessons: The bank decided the family was creditworthy and gave them a loan. | You become creditworthy by paying debts on time. | Shops only offer «buy now, pay later» to creditworthy customers. | The company was no longer creditworthy after it lost money. | Being creditworthy helps adults rent a flat. | Lenders check whether a business is creditworthy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Also written credit-worthy. Noun: creditworthiness. Opposite: not creditworthy, a bad credit risk.

part of speech: adjective (cretaceous; Cretaceous with a capital as a name)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) The Cretaceous is the last period of the age of dinosaurs, from about 145 to 66 million years ago. 2) (science) Cretaceous (small c) means made of chalk or like chalk.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about dinosaurs and fossils: Tyrannosaurus rex and Triceratops lived in the Cretaceous; it ended when a huge asteroid hit the Earth and most dinosaurs died out. The period is named after chalk (Latin «creta»), because chalk rocks like the White Cliffs of Dover formed then. Phrases: «the Cretaceous period», «Late Cretaceous».
examples from the lessons: Tyrannosaurus rex lived in the Late Cretaceous period. | The Cretaceous ended about 66 million years ago. | An asteroid strike at the end of the Cretaceous wiped out most dinosaurs. | The White Cliffs of Dover are made of Cretaceous chalk. | The first flowering plants spread during the Cretaceous. | We found a Cretaceous fossil shell on the beach.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced «krih-TAY-shus». Order of dinosaur periods: Triassic, Jurassic, Cretaceous. Myth: dinosaurs did not all live at the same time — T. rex lived closer in time to us than to Stegosaurus (a Jurassic dinosaur).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A cricketer is a person who plays cricket, a bat-and-ball game played by two teams of eleven.
its sense in the lessons: Cricket is very popular in the UK, Australia, New Zealand, India, Pakistan, the West Indies and South Africa, and played in Ireland and Canada too. Cricketers can be batters, bowlers, fielders or wicketkeepers; an all-rounder is good at both batting and bowling. Phrases: «a professional cricketer», «a young cricketer».
examples from the lessons: My cousin wants to be a professional cricketer. | The cricketer hit the ball for six. | Women cricketers play for England and Australia in the Ashes. | Every cricketer on the team wore white. | The young cricketer practised bowling in the nets. | A good cricketer needs patience and quick reactions.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Not about the insect «cricket». The word for the game's player is cricketer, not «cricket player» (though that is understood).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Crispy food is hard and dry on the outside, and breaks with a pleasant crunch when you bite it.
its sense in the lessons: Used about food in everyday life, cooking lessons and menus: crispy bacon, crispy chips, crispy duck, crispy batter. In science of cooking, food goes crispy when water is driven out by heat. Leaves can also be called crispy in autumn.
examples from the lessons: I like my toast nice and crispy. | The chips were golden and crispy. | Fry the bacon until it is crispy. | The autumn leaves were crispy under our feet. | The roast potatoes had crispy edges. | Keep the biscuits in a tin so they stay crispy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative crispier, superlative crispiest. Similar: crisp (more often used for fresh apples, lettuce, cold air or paper: a crisp apple). In the UK «crisps» are thin potato slices in packets (US: chips).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) A crocodilian is any animal in the crocodile family group: crocodiles, alligators, caimans and gharials. 2) Crocodilian (adjective) means like a crocodile or to do with crocodiles.
its sense in the lessons: In science, crocodilians are large reptiles with armoured skin, strong jaws and long tails that live in rivers and swamps of warm countries; they are close relatives of birds and of dinosaurs. In Australia, saltwater crocodiles live in the north — safety: obey crocodile warning signs and never swim where they live. In stories, a crocodilian grin is a wide, scary smile.
examples from the lessons: Alligators and crocodiles are both crocodilians. | Crocodilians lay eggs in nests on land. | Crocodilians have been around since the time of the dinosaurs. | The gharial is a crocodilian with a long, thin snout. | The villain gave a crocodilian smile. | In Northern Australia, signs warn swimmers about crocodilians in the rivers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable as a noun. Pronounced «krok-uh-DIL-ee-an». Myth: crocodiles do not really cry over their prey; «crocodile tears» means pretend sadness.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A croquette is a small roll or ball of mashed potato, meat, fish or vegetables, covered in breadcrumbs and fried.
its sense in the lessons: A food word from French, seen on menus and in school dinners and frozen food: potato croquettes, chicken croquettes, fish croquettes. In Spain they are called croquetas, a popular tapa.
examples from the lessons: We had potato croquettes with our roast dinner. | The croquettes were crispy outside and soft inside. | Mum made fish croquettes from leftover salmon. | In Spain we tried ham croquettes as tapas. | The school menu had vegetable croquettes on Friday. | Let the croquettes cool a bit — the middle is very hot.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Pronounced «kroh-KET». From French «croquer» (to crunch). Safety: the inside can stay hotter than the outside.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Crossness is the feeling or state of being cross, that is, annoyed or a bit angry.
its sense in the lessons: A mostly British word, used in stories and in talk with children: «cross» means annoyed, and crossness is that mood. It tells the reader someone is irritated, not furious. Phrases: «with a hint of crossness», «her crossness passed».
examples from the lessons: Her crossness disappeared when she saw the birthday cake. | There was a note of crossness in Dad's voice. | He tried to hide his crossness about losing the game. | The teacher's crossness was clear from her frown. | Tiredness often turns into crossness at the end of the day. | Grandma's crossness never lasted long.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Adjective: cross (UK: «Mum was cross with me»). Note: cross also means a shape like + or ×, and to go over (cross the road) — unrelated to crossness.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Cruelly means in a cruel way, causing pain or suffering on purpose or without caring. 2) Cruelly can also mean in a way that seems very unfair or unlucky.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, it describes how villains treat others: «cruelly mocked», «cruelly beaten». In sports and news, it describes bad luck: «cruelly injured just before the final». In lessons on kindness and animal care, treating people or animals cruelly is wrong and may be against the law.
examples from the lessons: The wicked stepmother treated Cinderella cruelly. | The puppy had been cruelly abandoned by the roadside. | The other children laughed cruelly at his mistake. | She was cruelly injured a week before the race. | It is against the law to treat animals cruelly. | The team was cruelly beaten by a goal in the last second.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: cruel + ly = cruelly (double l). Adjective: cruel; noun: cruelty. If someone treats you or an animal cruelly, tell a trusted adult.

part of speech: noun (a crusade, crusades); verb (crusade, crusades, crusaded, crusading)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (history, church) The Crusades were wars from about 1095 to 1291 in which Christian armies from Europe fought mainly to take control of Jerusalem and the Holy Land. 2) A crusade is a long, strong effort to change something that people believe is wrong. 3) To crusade is to work hard and publicly for a cause.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, the Crusades involve knights, Richard the Lionheart and Saladin; many people on all sides died, and today historians see the wars as violent and complicated, remembered differently by Christians, Muslims and Jews. In everyday life and news, a crusade is a campaign: a crusade against litter or for clean water. Phrases: «a crusade against», «on a crusade», «the First Crusade».
examples from the lessons: The First Crusade began in 1096. | Richard the Lionheart fought in the Third Crusade. | Thousands died in the Crusades on all sides. | Our class started a crusade against plastic litter. | She crusaded for safer crossings near schools. | Grandad is on a crusade to get everyone to recycle. | The crusaders built castles in the Holy Land.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun for a person: crusader. Capital C for the historical wars (the Crusades). Today some people avoid «crusade» for campaigns because of the violent history, so «campaign» is often a better choice.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Crushingly means very strongly or in a way that is overwhelming, so you feel defeated or flattened. 2) Crushingly is used before adjectives like «boring», «disappointing» or «obvious» to mean «extremely».
its sense in the lessons: Used in sports reports and stories: «crushingly defeated» (beaten by a lot), «crushingly disappointing» (very upsetting). It tells the reader the feeling or result was overwhelming.
examples from the lessons: Our team was crushingly defeated, 9–0. | The ending of the film was crushingly sad. | The long speech was crushingly boring. | It was crushingly obvious that he had eaten the cake. | The news was crushingly disappointing for the fans. | The heat was crushingly heavy in the afternoon.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: crushing (a crushing defeat). Verb: crush. In a sports problem, «crushingly beaten» means a big difference in score.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Cuban means from Cuba, an island country in the Caribbean Sea, south of Florida. 2) A Cuban is a person from Cuba.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and history, Cuba's capital is Havana; people there speak Spanish. Cuban music (salsa, son), dance, food and old cars are famous. History lessons mention the Cuban Missile Crisis of 1962, when the USA and the Soviet Union came close to nuclear war. Always written with a capital C.
examples from the lessons: Havana is the Cuban capital. | My friend's grandma is Cuban, and she speaks Spanish. | We danced to Cuban music at the party. | The Cuban Missile Crisis happened in 1962. | Cuban sandwiches are popular in Miami. | Many Cubans live in Florida.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always a capital C: Cuban. Pronounced «KYOO-ban». Plural: Cubans.

part of speech: noun (a cuff, cuffs); verb (cuff, cuffs, cuffed, cuffing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A cuff is the end part of a sleeve, around the wrist. 2) (US) A cuff is a turned-up fold at the bottom of a trouser leg (UK: turn-up). 3) Cuffs (informal) are handcuffs, and to cuff someone is to put handcuffs on them. 4) To cuff someone is to hit them lightly with an open hand; a cuff is such a light hit. 5) A cuff is a band put round the arm to measure blood pressure.
its sense in the lessons: In clothes, a shirt cuff may have a button or a cufflink. In crime stories, police «cuff» a suspect. In older stories, a «cuff round the ear» was a light slap (hitting children is wrong and is banned in many places). Phrases: «off the cuff» (said without preparing), «on the cuff» (US, on credit).
examples from the lessons: The cuffs of my school shirt are dirty. | He rolled up his cuffs to wash his hands. | The police cuffed the thief and put him in the car. | In the old story, the boy got a cuff round the ear. | She gave a funny speech off the cuff, without notes. | The nurse put a cuff on Grandma's arm to check her blood pressure. | His jeans had wide cuffs at the bottom.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: cuffs. Regular verb: cuffed. «Off the cuff» means unprepared, not «off the sleeve». Cufflinks are small fasteners for shirt cuffs.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To culminate is to reach the highest or final point of something, often after a long time or many steps.
its sense in the lessons: A formal word used in history, sport and stories: «the year culminated in a big concert», «the war culminated in a great battle». It tells the reader what the ending or climax was. Usually followed by «in» or «with».
examples from the lessons: The school year culminated in a big summer show. | Weeks of training culminated in winning the cup. | The adventure culminated with the dragon's defeat. | The protests culminated in a new law. | Our science project culminated in a trip to the museum. | Years of hard work culminated in her first book.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Noun: culmination (the high point). Formal; simpler: «end in», «lead up to», «reach a climax». Use «culminate in/with», not «culminate to».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal, law) Culpability is being to blame for something wrong or bad.
its sense in the lessons: A stiff word used in law, news and serious discussions of right and wrong: courts decide a person's culpability; in ethics lessons we ask how much someone is to blame if they did not mean the harm. Phrases: «accept culpability», «deny culpability», «moral culpability».
examples from the lessons: The court had to decide the driver's culpability for the crash. | The company denied any culpability for the oil spill. | He accepted culpability and apologised. | Being a child can reduce a person's culpability in law. | The inquiry looked at the culpability of the officials. | Culpability is greater when harm is done on purpose.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Adjective: culpable (to blame). Everyday words: blame, guilt, fault. Related: culprit.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A culprit is the person who has done something wrong or committed a crime. 2) A culprit is the cause of a problem.
its sense in the lessons: In detective stories and at school («Who broke the window? Find the culprit!»). In science and health, «the culprit» is the cause: «sugar is the culprit for tooth decay». Phrases: «the real culprit», «the main culprit», «the guilty culprit».
examples from the lessons: The teacher found the culprit who drew on the wall. | The detective finally named the culprit. | The dog was the culprit — there were crumbs on its nose! | Too much sugar is the main culprit in tooth decay. | The culprit for the flood was a blocked drain. | The police are still looking for the culprits.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Pronounced «KUL-prit». «Guilty culprit» repeats the idea; «culprit» already means the guilty one. Do not call someone a culprit before you know they did it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Cumulative means increasing by adding one amount to another over time, so the total keeps growing.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, a cumulative total (running total) adds each new number to all the earlier ones. In science and health, cumulative effects build up slowly, like damage from too much sun or the benefit of daily practice. In school, a cumulative test covers everything learned so far. Phrases: «cumulative total», «cumulative effect», «cumulative frequency».
examples from the lessons: The cumulative total of rainfall for the week was 40 mm. | Saving £2 a week has a cumulative effect: £104 in a year. | Too much sun has a cumulative effect on your skin. | The cumulative score after three rounds was 75 points. | Our final exam is cumulative, so revise everything. | A cumulative tale, like «The House that Jack Built», adds a new line each time.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced «KYOO-myoo-luh-tiv». In a maths problem, «cumulative» means keep adding: after days with 3, 5 and 2, the cumulative totals are 3, 8 and 10. Adverb: cumulatively.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Cumulatively means taken all together, with each new amount added to the ones before.
its sense in the lessons: Used in maths, science and reports: «cumulatively, the team scored 200 goals», «small savings, cumulatively, make a big difference». It tells the reader to think of the total built up over time.
examples from the lessons: Cumulatively, we raised £500 over the whole term. | Each mistake was small, but cumulatively they cost us the game. | Cumulatively, the rain over the week flooded the field. | The planets' small pulls, cumulatively, change the comet's path. | Reading ten minutes a day adds up cumulatively to hours of reading. | Cumulatively, the class has walked 1,000 km this year.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: cumulative. In maths, «cumulatively» means add all the parts together.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Cunning means clever at tricking people or getting what you want, often in a sly or dishonest way. 2) A cunning plan or idea is clever and well thought out. 3) Cunning (noun) is the skill of tricking or deceiving people. 4) (US, old informal) Cunning can mean cute: a cunning little puppy.
its sense in the lessons: In fairy tales and fables, the fox is cunning (it tricks the crow into dropping the cheese). In stories it can be a warning sign about a character or praise for a clever hero. Phrases: «a cunning plan», «as cunning as a fox», «use cunning».
examples from the lessons: The cunning fox tricked the crow into dropping her cheese. | I have a cunning plan to win the treasure hunt. | The thief used cunning to get past the guards. | Odysseus was famous for his cunning in the Trojan horse story. | The cunning cat waited until we left the kitchen. | Scammers can be very cunning, so never share your password.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable as a noun. Similar: sly, crafty, wily, clever. «Cunning» is not always bad: a hero can have a cunning plan.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A curfew is a rule that says people must be indoors or at home by a certain time, especially at night. 2) A curfew is the time by which a child or teenager must be home, set by their parents. 3) (history) In the Middle Ages, the curfew was a bell rung in the evening telling people to put out their fires.
its sense in the lessons: In family life, teenagers often have a curfew («be home by 9»). In news and history, governments may set a curfew during a war, riots or an emergency. It tells the reader there is a deadline for being off the streets. Phrases: «break a curfew», «impose a curfew», «a 10 o'clock curfew», «after curfew».
examples from the lessons: My big sister's curfew is ten o'clock on Saturdays. | The army set a curfew, and nobody could go out after dark. | He broke his curfew and was grounded for a week. | The campers had to be in their tents by curfew. | During the storm, the town had a night-time curfew. | In medieval towns, a bell rang for curfew.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Pronounced «KUR-fyoo». From old French «cover fire» (covre-feu). In a time problem, a 9:30 curfew means you must be home at or before 9:30.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Curvature is how much something curves or bends. 2) (medicine) A curvature of the spine is when the backbone bends sideways or too much.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography, you can see the curvature of the Earth from a high plane or from space — evidence that the Earth is round. In maths, curvature describes how sharply a curve bends: a small circle has more curvature than a big one. Phrases: «the curvature of the Earth», «curvature of the spine».
examples from the lessons: From the top of the mountain we could almost see the curvature of the Earth. | Ships disappear bottom first because of the Earth's curvature. | The curvature of the bridge makes it strong. | A small circle has a greater curvature than a large one. | The doctor checked her back for any curvature of the spine. | The lens's curvature bends the light.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable; «a curvature» for a particular bend. Related: curve, curved, curvy. Myth: from a normal plane the curve is hard to see clearly; ships vanishing over the horizon show it better.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A cygnet is a young swan.
its sense in the lessons: In nature lessons and stories like «The Ugly Duckling», where the grey, clumsy bird turns out to be a cygnet that grows into a beautiful white swan. Cygnets are grey or brown and fluffy; they often ride on their parents' backs. Family words: cob (male swan), pen (female swan).
examples from the lessons: Five grey cygnets swam behind their mother. | The ugly duckling was really a cygnet. | Cygnets sometimes ride on the swan's back. | Don't go near the cygnets — the parents will protect them fiercely. | By winter the cygnets were almost as big as their parents. | We watched the cygnets hatch on the river bank.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Pronounced «SIG-nit». Homophone: signet (a signet ring, with a seal on it). Swan family: cob (male), pen (female), cygnet (young).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Cylindrical means shaped like a cylinder: a long round shape with two flat circles at its ends, like a tin can or a tube.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, cylindrical objects are 3D shapes with two circular faces and one curved surface; you can find their volume (area of the circle × height). In everyday life: tins, pipes, candles, drums, toilet-roll tubes are cylindrical. In science: a test tube is almost cylindrical.
examples from the lessons: A tin of beans is cylindrical. | The tower was tall and cylindrical. | Roll the paper into a cylindrical shape. | A cylindrical container holds more if it is wider. | Many batteries are cylindrical. | The candle is cylindrical, with a circle on each end.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced «sih-LIN-dri-kul». Noun: cylinder. In maths, a cylinder has 3 faces (2 flat circles, 1 curved), 2 edges and no vertices; its volume = π × radius × radius × height.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (a name) Cyril is a man's first name. 2) (a name, church) Saint Cyril was a Christian missionary of the 800s who, with his brother Methodius, brought the Christian faith and writing to Slavic peoples.
its sense in the lessons: As a name it was popular in Britain in the early 1900s and is less common now. In history, Saint Cyril is honoured by many churches; the Cyrillic alphabet, used for Ukrainian, Russian, Bulgarian and other languages, is named after him, though it was probably made by his followers.
examples from the lessons: Cyril is my great-grandad's name. | Saint Cyril and his brother Methodius were missionaries. | The Cyrillic alphabet is named after Saint Cyril. | Uncle Cyril told us stories about the war. | Ukrainian is written in Cyrillic letters. | The book was by an author called Cyril.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A name, so it takes a capital C: Cyril. Pronounced «SIR-il». Adjective: Cyrillic (the alphabet).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) A cytokine is a tiny protein that cells send out as a message, especially to control the body's immune system when fighting germs.
its sense in the lessons: A science and medicine word: when you catch a cold, cells release cytokines that call immune cells to fight the infection; they can also cause fever and tiredness, which is part of how the body fights back. Children may hear it in news about illnesses and vaccines.
examples from the lessons: Cytokines tell white blood cells where to go. | When you have flu, cytokines help cause the fever. | Scientists study cytokines to make new medicines. | Cytokines are messages sent from one cell to another. | Some cytokines calm the immune system down. | Too many cytokines at once can make a person very ill.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable, mostly plural: cytokines. Pronounced «SY-toh-kine». «Cyto» means cell; «kine» means movement.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Dah is the long sound or long signal in Morse code, written as a dash (−); the short one is «dit». 2) (informal) «Dah» is a sound people say, as in «ta-dah!», when showing something proudly; it can also be a spelling of «duh» meaning «that's obvious». 3) (a name) Dah is not an English word in other uses; it may be a part of a name or a word in another language.
its sense in the lessons: In science and history lessons on communication, Morse code uses dits and dahs: the letter A is «dit-dah» (·−), and SOS is «dit-dit-dit, dah-dah-dah, dit-dit-dit». In play, «Ta-dah!» announces a magic trick.
examples from the lessons: In Morse code, the letter A is dit-dah. | SOS is three dits, three dahs and three dits. | Ta-dah! said the magician, pulling out a rabbit. | Hold the button longer for a dah than for a dit. | «Is water wet?» «Dah, of course!» | We tapped out dahs and dits on the desk.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A sound word, not a common word on its own. «Dah» and «dit» are spoken names for dash and dot. Spellings of the show-off sound: «ta-da», «ta-dah», «tada».

part of speech: noun (dahl — uncountable; also dal, dhal); a name (Dahl)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Dahl (also dal or dhal) is a South Asian dish of split lentils, peas or beans cooked with spices into a thick stew, or the dried split pulses themselves. 2) (a name) Roald Dahl is a famous children's author who wrote «Charlie and the Chocolate Factory», «Matilda» and «The BFG».
its sense in the lessons: In food lessons and everyday meals, dahl is common in Indian, Pakistani, Bangladeshi and Sri Lankan cooking, eaten with rice or flatbread; it is healthy and full of protein. In English lessons, Roald Dahl's books are read in schools across the UK and beyond, and 13 September is celebrated as Roald Dahl Day.
examples from the lessons: We had dahl and rice for dinner. | Red lentil dahl is quick to cook. | Dahl is full of protein and fibre. | Roald Dahl wrote «Matilda». | Our class read a Roald Dahl book every term. | Grandma adds cumin and garlic to her dahl.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The food is usually uncountable. Spellings vary: dal, daal, dhal, dahl — all the same dish. The author's name has a capital D. Pronounced «dahl» (rhymes with «doll» in many accents).

meaning for a pupil: 1) To dampen something is to make it a little wet. 2) To dampen a feeling is to make it weaker or less happy. 3) To dampen a sound or a movement is to make it quieter or smaller.
its sense in the lessons: In cooking and art, you dampen a cloth or paper. In stories, «the rain dampened our spirits» means people felt less cheerful. In science and music, materials dampen sound or vibration. Phrases: «dampen someone's spirits», «dampen enthusiasm», «put a damper on» (spoil the mood).
examples from the lessons: Dampen the cloth before you wipe the table. | The rain did not dampen our spirits at sports day. | The bad news dampened everyone's excitement. | Thick curtains dampen the noise from the street. | Dampen the soil before you plant the seeds. | Nothing could dampen her joy on her birthday.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Adjective: damp (slightly wet). Similar: moisten (wet), weaken, deaden (sound). A «damper» is a thing that dampens: a part of a piano or chimney, or something that spoils fun («put a damper on it»).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Dappled means marked with spots or patches of different colours or shades. 2) Dappled light or shade is a pattern of light and shadow, for example under trees.
