its sense in the lessons: A descriptive word loved in stories and poems: «dappled sunlight» falls through leaves; a «dappled grey» horse has spotted fur. In art lessons, it describes how light breaks into patches. It helps the reader picture a soft, spotted pattern.
examples from the lessons: We sat in the dappled shade of the oak tree. | The dappled sunlight danced on the path. | The pony was dappled grey. | A fawn has a dappled coat that hides it in the woods. | The painter showed the dappled light on the river. | The forest floor was dappled with gold.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: dapple (to mark with spots); usually seen as «dappled». Similar: spotted, mottled, speckled.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A daredevil is a person who does dangerous, exciting things, often to show off or to entertain people. 2) Daredevil (adjective) describes risky, bold actions: a daredevil jump.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, films, circuses and stunt shows, daredevils walk tightropes, jump motorbikes over buses or do wild skateboard tricks. In safety lessons: stunts are done by trained people with safety gear — do not copy them at home or online «challenges».
examples from the lessons: The daredevil rode his motorbike over twenty cars. | My little brother is a daredevil on the climbing frame. | The crowd gasped at the daredevil's tightrope walk. | Don't try daredevil tricks you see online. | She made a daredevil jump from the high board. | Stunt performers are daredevils with lots of training.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Written as one word. Similar: risk-taker, stuntman, stuntwoman. «Dare» means to be brave enough to do something.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A dartboard is a round board, divided into numbered sections, at which you throw darts in the game of darts.
its sense in the lessons: Common in pubs, games rooms and homes in the UK, Ireland, Australia and elsewhere. In maths, a dartboard gives practice in adding, doubling and trebling: the outer ring doubles a score, the inner ring trebles it, and the centre is the bull's-eye. Safety: darts are sharp — only throw when no one is near the board.
examples from the lessons: We hung a dartboard in the garage. | The dartboard has numbers from 1 to 20 around the edge. | Hitting the outer ring of the dartboard doubles your score. | Hitting the treble 20 gives 60 points. | The bull's-eye is the centre of the dartboard. | Magnetic dartboards are safer for children.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; one word. In a maths problem, a «double 5» = 10 and a «treble 5» = 15; the outer bull = 25 and the bull's-eye = 50 points; the highest score with three darts is 180.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To deactivate something is to turn it off or stop it from working. 2) To deactivate an account is to close it or pause it so it cannot be used.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and computing: deactivate an alarm, deactivate a social media account. In action stories, heroes deactivate bombs or traps. In science, heat can deactivate some substances, like germs or enzymes. Opposite: activate.
examples from the lessons: Mum deactivated the burglar alarm when we got home. | The agent had ten seconds to deactivate the bomb. | You can deactivate your account in the settings. | The robot was deactivated for the night. | Cooking deactivates many germs in food. | Don't deactivate the smoke alarm — it keeps you safe.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Noun: deactivation. Prefix «de-» means undo, as in defrost, decode. Opposite: activate.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A deafening noise is extremely loud, so loud you can hardly hear anything else. 2) (idiom) A deafening silence is a silence that is very noticeable, for example when people refuse to answer.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, deafening noises are thunder, cheering crowds, explosions or music: they tell the reader the sound is overwhelming. In science and health, very loud sounds (measured in decibels) can damage hearing — use ear defenders. Phrases: «a deafening roar», «deafening applause», «deafening silence».
examples from the lessons: The thunder was deafening. | The crowd's cheer was deafening when we scored. | The music at the concert was deafening, so we wore earplugs. | After the teacher's question there was a deafening silence. | The fire alarm made a deafening ring. | A jet engine is deafening up close.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective from the verb deafen (to make deaf). Use it for sounds, not for people. A deafening silence is a figure of speech: the silence itself is not loud.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A dealer is a person or business that buys and sells a particular kind of thing, such as cars, art or antiques. 2) In card games, the dealer is the person who hands out the cards. 3) A drug dealer is a person who sells illegal drugs.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: car dealers, art dealers, antique dealers. In card games at home and school: «Who's the dealer?» In safety lessons: drug dealers break the law and may target young people; say no and tell a trusted adult.
examples from the lessons: Dad bought our car from a dealer. | The dealer shuffled the cards and dealt five each. | The art dealer sold the painting for a lot of money. | It's your turn to be the dealer. | Never take anything from a drug dealer — tell an adult. | The antique dealer said the clock was 200 years old.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Verb: deal, past dealt (pronounced «delt»). Related: dealership (a car dealer's shop).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) A decapod is a crustacean with ten legs, such as a crab, lobster, shrimp, prawn or crayfish.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about animal groups: decapods belong to the crustaceans, which belong to the arthropods (animals with jointed legs and a hard outer skeleton). Two of the ten legs are often big claws (pincers).
examples from the lessons: A crab is a decapod because it has ten legs. | Lobsters and prawns are decapods too. | The front two legs of many decapods are claws. | Decapods have a hard shell called an exoskeleton. | We counted the legs to prove the crayfish was a decapod. | Some squids are also called decapods because they have ten arms.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. «Deca» means ten; «pod» means foot. Note: in older books, squids were also called decapods (ten arms), so the word has two scientific uses.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A deceitful person often lies or tricks people to make them believe things that are not true. 2) A deceitful action or word is meant to trick someone.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, deceitful characters (like the wolf in «Little Red Riding Hood») use lies to get what they want; the reader learns not to trust them. In lessons on honesty and online safety, deceitful messages and scams try to fool you. Phrases: «deceitful behaviour», «a deceitful smile».
examples from the lessons: The deceitful fox pretended to be the hen's friend. | It was deceitful to copy his homework and say it was yours. | The scam email was deceitful: it pretended to come from a bank. | She was hurt by her friend's deceitful words. | The villain hid his deceitful plan behind a smile. | Being deceitful can break people's trust.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: «ei» after c (deceit, deceive). Noun: deceit; verb: deceive. Opposite: honest, truthful.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A deceiver is a person who deceives, that is, tricks people into believing something false.
its sense in the lessons: Used in stories, fables and the Bible (the devil is sometimes called «the deceiver»). In everyday talk people say liar, cheat or trickster. It warns the reader not to trust that character.
examples from the lessons: The deceiver promised gold but gave only stones. | In the fable, the fox was a clever deceiver. | Christians believe the devil is «the great deceiver». | The online deceiver pretended to be a child. | The queen soon discovered the deceiver's lies. | A deceiver hides the truth to get what they want.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Verb: deceive (deceives, deceived). Spelling: «ei» after c. Similar: liar, cheat, trickster, fraud.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) Deceleration is slowing down; the rate at which something's speed gets smaller.
its sense in the lessons: In science, deceleration is the opposite of acceleration: when a car brakes or a ball rolls to a stop, it decelerates; friction and air resistance cause deceleration. In maths and physics, it can be measured in metres per second per second (m/s²). Seatbelts protect you during sudden deceleration in a crash.
examples from the lessons: The car's deceleration was quick when the driver braked. | Friction causes the deceleration of the rolling ball. | A parachute causes a big deceleration. | Seatbelts protect you during sudden deceleration. | The rocket's deceleration let it land gently. | We measured the trolley's deceleration on the carpet.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: decelerate. Opposite: acceleration. In a maths problem, a deceleration of 2 m/s every second means the speed drops by 2 each second (from 10 to 8, 6, 4…).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) A decibel is a unit for measuring how loud a sound is.
its sense in the lessons: In science, sounds are measured in decibels: whispering is about 30 dB, normal talk about 60 dB, a busy road about 80 dB, a rock concert over 100 dB. Long exposure above about 85 dB can damage hearing — wear ear protection and keep headphones at safe volume.
examples from the lessons: A whisper is about 30 decibels. | The concert reached 110 decibels. | Sounds above 85 decibels can harm your hearing over time. | We measured the playground noise in decibels with an app. | The teacher's whistle was very high in decibels. | Lower the volume on your headphones to keep the decibels down.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Short form: dB. Maths trap: the decibel scale is not like a ruler — adding 10 dB means about ten times more sound energy and sounds roughly twice as loud, so 80 dB is much more than «a bit» louder than 70 dB.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Decipherment is working out the meaning of a code, secret message or old writing that is hard to read.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, the decipherment of Egyptian hieroglyphs using the Rosetta Stone (by Jean-François Champollion in 1822) and the code-breaking work at Bletchley Park are famous examples. In puzzles and olympiads, decipherment means solving a code or an unknown script step by step.
examples from the lessons: The decipherment of hieroglyphs took many years. | The Rosetta Stone helped with the decipherment of Egyptian writing. | The code-breakers worked on the decipherment of secret messages. | Some ancient scripts still wait for decipherment. | Our puzzle club practised decipherment of simple codes. | The decipherment of the old letter revealed a hidden treasure map.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: decipher (to work out). Similar: decoding, deciphering. It applies to codes and hard writing, not to ordinary reading.

part of speech: noun (a decoy, decoys); verb (decoy, decoys, decoyed, decoying)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A decoy is a person or thing used to trick someone and lead them away or into a trap. 2) A decoy is a model of a bird, such as a wooden duck, used by hunters to attract real birds. 3) To decoy someone is to trick them in this way.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, games and war history, decoys distract enemies: fake tanks, dummy soldiers. In nature, some animals act as decoys (a bird pretends to have a broken wing to lead a fox away from its nest). In sport, a decoy runner draws defenders away.
examples from the lessons: The duck decoy floated on the pond. | The army used inflatable tanks as decoys. | One friend acted as a decoy while the others hid the present. | The mother bird pretended to be hurt as a decoy. | The striker made a decoy run to draw the defender. | The spy was decoyed into a trap.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: decoys. Regular verb: decoyed. Pronounced «DEE-koy» (noun), «dih-KOY» (verb, sometimes).

part of speech: adjective (dedicated, more dedicated); verb form (dedicate, dedicates, dedicated, dedicating)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A dedicated person works very hard at something because they care about it a lot. 2) Dedicated equipment or a place is used only for one particular purpose. 3) To dedicate a book, song or building to someone is to say it is in their honour. 4) (church) A dedicated church or chapel has been given to God or named after a saint in a ceremony.
its sense in the lessons: In school and sport, a dedicated pupil or coach works hard and keeps going. In everyday life: «a dedicated cycle lane» is only for bikes. Books often start with «Dedicated to my mother». Churches are dedicated to saints. Phrases: «dedicated to», «a dedicated fan».
examples from the lessons: She is a dedicated swimmer who trains every morning. | Our teacher is dedicated to helping every child. | The town built a dedicated lane for bikes. | The book is dedicated to the author's grandmother. | The church is dedicated to Saint Patrick. | The park was dedicated to the soldiers who died in the war. | He is a dedicated fan of his football team.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Followed by «to»: dedicated to music. Noun: dedication. Similar: committed, devoted, hard-working.

part of speech: verb form (deepen, deepens, deepened, deepening); noun (a deepening — rare); adjective
meaning for a pupil: 1) Deepening means becoming or making something deeper, so it goes further down. 2) Deepening means becoming stronger, more serious or more intense, like a feeling, a problem or a colour. 3) A deepening sound or voice becomes lower.
its sense in the lessons: In geography, rivers deepen their valleys over time. In stories and news: «a deepening mystery», «deepening friendship», «a deepening crisis», «the deepening dusk». In science, the sea gets deeper further from the shore.
examples from the lessons: The river is deepening its channel every year. | There was a deepening mystery about the missing key. | Their deepening friendship lasted for years. | The sky turned a deepening blue at sunset. | News reports spoke of a deepening crisis. | The workers were deepening the harbour for bigger ships.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: deepen (regular). Adjective: deep; noun: depth. «Deepening» can be good (friendship) or bad (crisis) — the noun after it tells you which.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal, law, logic) Defeasible means able to be cancelled or overturned, for example a right, a contract or a conclusion that may be undone by new facts.
its sense in the lessons: A rare scholarly word. In law, a defeasible right can be taken away if a condition happens. In logic and thinking skills, a defeasible conclusion is a good guess that new evidence could overturn: «Birds fly, so Tweety flies» — unless we learn Tweety is a penguin. It reminds us that many everyday conclusions are «true unless shown otherwise».
examples from the lessons: «Tweety is a bird, so Tweety flies» is a defeasible conclusion. | The judge said the agreement was defeasible. | Most everyday reasoning is defeasible: new facts can change our minds. | The family's right to the land was defeasible if they stopped farming it. | A scientist's theory is defeasible if a better experiment shows it wrong. | The rule is defeasible: there are exceptions.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Very formal and rare. Opposite: indefeasible (cannot be taken away). Pronounced «dih-FEE-zuh-bul». Not related to «defeat» in meaning, though the two words share an old root.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Defiantly means in a way that shows you refuse to obey or are openly standing up against someone or something.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, characters act defiantly against bullies, tyrants or rules: «she lifted her chin defiantly». It can show bravery (standing up to unfairness) or rudeness (refusing to do as asked), depending on the story. Phrases: «stare defiantly», «answer defiantly».
examples from the lessons: The boy folded his arms and stared defiantly at the bully. | «I won't go!» she said defiantly. | The little flag waved defiantly in the storm. | The prisoners sang defiantly in their cells. | He defiantly refused to tidy his room. | The tree stood defiantly after the hurricane.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: defiant; noun: defiance; verb: defy. Spelling trap: defiantly (refusing) is often confused with definitely (surely) — check the letters: defi-ANT-ly vs defin-ITE-ly.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Definite means clear, sure and fixed, with no doubt. 2) A definite plan, date or answer has been decided. 3) (grammar) The definite article is the word «the».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: «Is it definite that we're going?» In grammar lessons, «the» is the definite article (pointing to one particular thing), while «a/an» are indefinite articles. In maths, «a definite answer» is one exact number. Phrases: «a definite yes», «nothing definite yet».
examples from the lessons: Is the trip definite, or might it be cancelled? | We need a definite answer by Friday. | There's a definite smell of burning in here! | «The» is called the definite article. | She gave a definite «no». | Nothing is definite yet, but we may move house. | There is a definite improvement in your handwriting.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: definite (not «definate»); remember «finite» inside it. Adverb: definitely. Opposite: indefinite (not fixed). Do not confuse with definitive (final and most complete).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Deforestation is the cutting down or burning of large areas of forest, so the trees are gone and the land is used for something else.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and science, deforestation is a big world problem: forests like the Amazon rainforest are cleared for farms, cattle, palm oil, mining or wood. It destroys animals' homes (habitats), causes soil erosion and floods, and adds carbon dioxide to the air, making climate change worse. Solutions: replanting (reforestation), protecting forests, recycled paper and buying sustainable wood.
examples from the lessons: Deforestation destroys the homes of orangutans. | The Amazon rainforest is shrinking because of deforestation. | Deforestation adds carbon dioxide to the air. | After deforestation, rain washes the soil away. | Our class wrote letters about stopping deforestation. | Planting trees helps undo deforestation.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Verb: deforest. Opposite: reforestation, afforestation (planting new forests). Prefix «de-» means taking away.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Deformation is a change in the shape of something, for example when it is bent, squashed or stretched. 2) A deformation is a part of something that has become the wrong shape.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on forces, deformation happens when a force pushes or pulls: a spring stretches, a ball squashes, plasticine bends. Elastic deformation goes back to its shape (a spring); plastic deformation stays changed (bent metal). In geography, rocks deform in mountains and earthquakes.
examples from the lessons: Squeezing a sponge causes deformation. | The car's bumper showed deformation after the crash. | A spring returns to its shape after deformation. | The heat caused deformation of the plastic bottle. | Great forces cause the deformation of rock layers into folds. | We measured the deformation of the elastic band with different weights.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable and uncountable. Verb: deform. Do not confuse with deformity (a body part shaped unusually).

part of speech: adjective (deformed); verb form (deform, deforms, deformed, deforming)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Deformed means having a shape that has been changed or twisted, so it is not the usual or proper shape. 2) To deform something (verb) is to change its shape by force or heat.
its sense in the lessons: In science, materials are deformed by forces (a deformed spring). In history and medicine, it can describe a body part shaped differently; today people say «a limb difference» or «a different shape» to be kind and respectful. In stories, monsters are sometimes described as deformed — a description that should not be used to mock real people.
examples from the lessons: The plastic ruler was deformed by the heat. | The car's door was deformed in the crash. | Too much force deformed the spring, and it didn't spring back. | The old tree had a deformed, twisted trunk. | The fruit was deformed but still tasted good. | Never call a person deformed — it is hurtful.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Noun: deformation (for objects), deformity (for bodies). Using «deformed» about a person is unkind; prefer respectful words like «has a limb difference».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A deformity is a part of the body that has an unusual or twisted shape, from birth or after illness or injury.
its sense in the lessons: Used in medicine and history (doctors treat deformities with operations or special shoes and braces). In lessons on kindness and disability, people with a deformity deserve respect; many prefer words like «difference» or «condition». In older stories, deformity is sometimes wrongly used to show a character is evil — a myth.
examples from the lessons: The surgeon corrected the deformity in the baby's foot. | A clubfoot is a deformity that can be treated. | She was born with a hand deformity but plays the piano brilliantly. | The illness left him with a deformity of the spine. | Making fun of someone's deformity is cruel. | Doctors now treat many deformities in early childhood.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: deformities. Myth: in old stories, an unusual body shows a bad person — this is false and unfair. Kind language: «a difference», «a condition».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (medicine) A delusional person firmly believes things that are not true, even when shown clear proof, often because of an illness. 2) (informal) Delusional means having very unrealistic hopes or ideas about yourself or a situation.
its sense in the lessons: In medicine and mental health, delusions can be a symptom of illness, and the person needs care and kindness, not mockery. In everyday talk and banter, «You're delusional!» is said jokingly to someone who thinks their team will win everything. Phrases: «delusional thinking», «completely delusional».
examples from the lessons: The doctor said the patient was delusional and needed treatment. | You're delusional if you think we'll win 10–0! | The delusional king believed he could fly. | He was delusional about how good his singing was. | Illness can make a person delusional, so they need help. | It's delusional to think you can pass without revising.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: delusion (a false belief). Do not confuse with illusion (a false impression of the eyes or mind, like a magic trick). Calling someone delusional can be hurtful if they are really ill.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To demarcate something is to mark or set its edges or limits clearly.
its sense in the lessons: A formal word for boundaries in geography, sport and maps: lines demarcate the pitch, fences demarcate a field, and treaties demarcate borders between countries. In everyday talk people say «mark out» or «separate».
examples from the lessons: White lines demarcate the football pitch. | Cones demarcate the area for the race. | The treaty demarcated the border between the two countries. | Hedges demarcate the fields on the farm. | The teacher used tape to demarcate the reading corner. | A rope demarcated the safe area for spectators.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Noun: demarcation (a demarcation line). Formal: simpler words are mark, mark out, separate.

part of speech: noun (demeanour — usually uncountable; US spelling demeanor)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Someone's demeanour is the way they look and behave, which shows their mood or character.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, a character's demeanour (calm, nervous, cheerful, cold) helps the reader understand them without being told directly. In school reports and formal speech, it describes how someone carries themselves. Phrases: «a calm demeanour», «a friendly demeanour», «change of demeanour».
examples from the lessons: She kept a calm demeanour during the exam. | His cheerful demeanour made everyone smile. | The detective noticed the man's nervous demeanour. | The judge had a serious demeanour. | Her demeanour changed when she heard the good news. | The new teacher's friendly demeanour put us at ease.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK, Ireland, Australia, NZ and Canada spell it demeanour; the US spells it demeanor. Formal; simpler: manner, behaviour.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A demographic is a group of people with something in common, such as age or where they live, especially when studied or targeted by sellers. 2) Demographics are facts and numbers about a population: how many people, how old, where they live and so on. 3) Demographic (adjective) means to do with the study of populations.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and maths, demographic data shows population changes, birth and death rates and ages, often in graphs and population pyramids. In business and media, companies aim adverts at a demographic, like teenagers. Phrases: «demographic change», «the target demographic».
examples from the lessons: Children under ten are the target demographic for this cartoon. | The census gives demographic information about the country. | Our town's demographics show more older people than before. | We drew a graph of demographic data in geography. | Demographic change means fewer children in some villages. | Adverts are made for a particular demographic.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable as a noun. Noun for the study: demography. In maths problems, demographics come as percentages and charts — check what the whole (100%) refers to.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (church, Bible) A demon is an evil spirit; Christians believe demons are fallen angels who oppose God. 2) In myths, legends and games, a demon is a wicked monster or spirit. 3) (informal) A demon is a person who does something with great energy or skill: a demon at chess. 4) Demons can also mean a person's inner troubles or bad memories.
its sense in the lessons: In Bible stories, Jesus drives demons out of people; in religious education, beliefs about demons are said as «Christians believe» or «some people believe». In fantasy stories and video games, demons are monsters. In everyday talk, «a speed demon» drives very fast, and «fighting your demons» means battling worries or bad habits.
examples from the lessons: In the Bible, Jesus cast out demons. | Christians believe demons are fallen angels. | The hero fought a fire demon in the video game. | My little sister is a demon at chess! | Grandad called the fast driver a speed demon. | He spoke about the demons he faced after the war.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: demons. Adjective: demonic. Similar: devil, fiend. The Greek «daimon» once meant a spirit that could be good or bad.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal, money) To denominate an amount or a price is to state it in a particular currency or unit. 2) (formal) To denominate something is to give it a name.
its sense in the lessons: A formal money word in news and economics: «prices are denominated in dollars». Children more often meet the related words denomination (the value of a coin or note, like a £5 note; or a Christian group such as Methodists or Catholics) and denominator (the bottom number of a fraction).
examples from the lessons: Oil prices are denominated in US dollars. | The prize was denominated in euros. | The loan was denominated in pounds. | Old Latin books denominate the river by another name. | Many international prices are denominated in dollars. | The cost was denominated in both currencies.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal and rare. Related: denomination (a coin's value; a church group), denominator (fraction's bottom number: in 3/4 the denominator is 4). In money problems, «denominated in pounds» means the amount is counted in pounds.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To depress someone is to make them feel very sad and without hope. 2) (formal) To depress a button, key or pedal is to press it down. 3) (money) To depress prices, trade or wages is to make them lower or less active.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday talk, «the rainy weather depresses me» means it makes me feel low. In instructions: «depress the brake pedal». In economics and news, a bad year depresses sales. Adjectives: depressed (feeling very low; also, an illness called depression that needs care) and depressing (making you sad).
examples from the lessons: Grey, rainy days depress me. | Depress the button to start the machine. | The bad news depressed the whole team. | The driver depressed the clutch. | The storm depressed sales at the seaside shops. | Losing every game started to depress him.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Nouns: depression, depressant. Depression is a real illness, not just feeling a bit sad; if someone feels hopeless for a long time, they should talk to a trusted adult or doctor.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Derivable means able to be worked out, obtained or traced from something else.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and logic, a result is derivable if you can work it out step by step from known facts or rules. In language lessons, words are derivable from roots («happiness» is derivable from «happy»). In science, a value may be derivable from measurements.
examples from the lessons: The answer is derivable from the facts in the puzzle. | «Happiness» is derivable from «happy». | The area of a triangle is derivable from the area of a rectangle. | The total is derivable if you know the price and the number. | Every step of the proof must be derivable from the step before. | Is this rule derivable from the others?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: derive; noun: derivation. Formal: simpler «can be worked out». In maths problems, «derivable» means you can calculate it from the given numbers.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) Dermal means to do with the skin.
its sense in the lessons: A science and medicine word: dermal cells, dermal layers, dermal patches (medicine stuck on the skin) and dermal fillers (adult cosmetic treatments). The dermis is the thick layer of skin under the top layer (epidermis). It tells the reader that something is about or on the skin.
examples from the lessons: The dermal layer of skin has blood vessels and nerves. | The cream is for dermal use only — don't swallow it. | A nicotine patch is a dermal patch. | Scientists studied dermal cells under the microscope. | Some animals breathe partly through dermal surfaces. | Sun can cause dermal damage.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Related: dermis, epidermis, dermatology (the study of skin), dermatologist (skin doctor). «Derma» is Greek for skin.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (medicine) Dermatitis is a condition where the skin becomes red, itchy, sore or swollen, often because something irritates it or the body reacts to it.
its sense in the lessons: In health lessons and everyday life: contact dermatitis can come from soaps, plants or metals; eczema is a common type. It is not catching. Doctors treat it with creams and by avoiding the cause. Phrases: «contact dermatitis», «a flare-up of dermatitis».
examples from the lessons: The new soap gave me dermatitis on my hands. | Dermatitis made her skin red and itchy. | The doctor gave him cream for his dermatitis. | Dermatitis is not catching, so you can still hold hands. | Some people get dermatitis from nickel in jewellery. | Eczema is a kind of dermatitis.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. «-itis» means swelling or inflammation, as in tonsillitis and appendicitis. Myth: dermatitis is not caused by being dirty and you cannot catch it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To desalt something is to remove salt from it, such as seawater or salty food.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography, desalting (desalination) turns seawater into drinking water, important in dry countries such as parts of Australia and the Middle East. In cooking, salted fish or ham is soaked in water to desalt it.
examples from the lessons: The plant desalts seawater to make drinking water. | Soak the salty fish overnight to desalt it. | Boiling and catching the steam can desalt water. | Some dry countries desalt sea water for their cities. | We desalted salty water in a science experiment using evaporation. | Desalted water must still be clean to drink safely.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. The more common word is desalinate; noun: desalination. In our experiment, the salt stays behind when the water evaporates.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To desiccate something is to remove all the water from it so it becomes completely dry. 2) Desiccated (adjective) means completely dried out; desiccated coconut is dried, shredded coconut for baking.
its sense in the lessons: In cooking, desiccated coconut goes into cakes and biscuits. In science, a desiccator dries chemicals, and little packets of silica gel desiccate new shoes and bags (safety: do not eat them). In nature, deserts and drought desiccate plants and soil.
examples from the lessons: Sprinkle desiccated coconut on top of the cake. | The hot wind desiccated the crops. | Silica gel packets desiccate the air in a shoe box. | The desiccated leaves crumbled in my hand. | Egyptians desiccated bodies with salt to make mummies. | Drought desiccates the soil until it cracks.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: one s, two c's — desiccate. Regular verb. Noun: desiccation. The silica gel packets say «do not eat»: they are not food.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Desirable means worth having or wanting; good, useful or attractive. 2) (formal) Desirable means advisable or a good idea.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: a desirable house, a desirable job. In job adverts and school tasks: «experience is desirable but not essential» means it helps but is not required. In science and ethics: a desirable outcome is a good result. Opposite: undesirable.
examples from the lessons: A garden is desirable when you have a dog. | It is desirable to arrive ten minutes early. | Good teamwork is a desirable skill. | The house is in a very desirable area. | The advert said French was desirable but not essential. | A healthy breakfast is desirable before a long day.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: desire + able = desirable (drop the e). Noun: desirability. «Desirable» in job adverts means nice to have, «essential» means you must have it.

part of speech: verb (despatch, despatches, despatched, despatching); noun (despatch, a despatch)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To despatch something is to send it off, especially a parcel, letter or message. 2) To despatch someone is to send them somewhere to do a job. 3) (formal) To despatch a task is to do it quickly; (old) to despatch someone can mean to kill them. 4) A despatch is a sending, or an official report or message, for example from a war.
its sense in the lessons: Despatch is a British spelling of dispatch. In shops and online orders: «your order has been despatched». In history and war stories: soldiers «mentioned in despatches» were praised in official reports. Phrases: «with despatch» (quickly), «despatch rider» (a messenger on a motorbike).
examples from the lessons: Your parcel was despatched this morning. | The ambulance was despatched to the accident. | The general sent a despatch to London. | She despatched her homework in ten minutes. | In the old story, the knight despatched the dragon. | Despatch riders carried messages in the war.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Same as dispatch (more common today, especially in the US). Regular verb. Plural noun: despatches. Both spellings are correct.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Detachable means able to be removed and put back again.
its sense in the lessons: Used in everyday life about clothes and things: a detachable hood, detachable collar, detachable keyboard, detachable shower head. It tells you the part comes off and can be fitted again.
examples from the lessons: My coat has a detachable hood. | The laptop has a detachable keyboard. | The car seat has a detachable cover for washing. | The pencil case has a detachable pocket. | Some backpacks have detachable straps. | The toy robot has detachable arms.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: detach (to take off); opposite: attach. Opposite adjective: fixed, permanent. Spelling: detach + able.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Determinate means fixed, exact and clearly limited, not vague. 2) (science) A determinate plant, like some tomato plants, grows to a fixed size and then stops.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and science, a determinate quantity has one exact value; a determinate answer can be worked out exactly. In gardening, determinate tomatoes are bushy and ripen together. In law, a determinate sentence is for a fixed time. Opposite: indeterminate.
examples from the lessons: The problem has a determinate answer: 12. | The prisoner got a determinate sentence of five years. | Determinate tomato plants stop growing at about one metre. | The recipe gives a determinate amount of flour. | The number of people at the party was determinate, so we bought exactly enough cake. | Some puzzles have more than one answer and are not determinate.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal and rare. Pronounced «dih-TER-min-it». Opposite: indeterminate. Do not confuse with determined (a determined person will not give up). In maths, «determinate» means only one exact answer.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To make a bomb or explosive go off on purpose. 2) To explode suddenly with a loud bang.
its sense in the lessons: Used in stories about wars, mines and fireworks, in science about chemical reactions, and in news about bomb squads making old bombs safe; tells the reader something is blowing up on purpose; phrases: «detonate a bomb», «remotely detonated», «controlled explosion».
examples from the lessons: The bomb squad detonated the old shell in an empty field. | The fireworks detonated high above the river. | Engineers detonate explosives to knock down old towers. | The mine did not detonate, so the soldiers marked it with a flag. | In the film, the hero cut the red wire before the bomb could detonate. | Scientists showed how a tiny spark can detonate a gas cloud. | A wartime bomb found on a building site in London was safely detonated.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: detonated, detonating. Noun: detonation; the device that sets off a bomb is a detonator. Safety: never touch an old shell or strange metal object; tell an adult and call the police. Do not confuse with «decimate» or «devastate».

part of speech: verb (devastate, devastates, devastated, devastating); adjective forms: devastated, devastating
meaning for a pupil: 1) To destroy or badly damage a place, so little is left. 2) To make someone feel terribly shocked and sad. 3) (informal) devastating can also mean extremely strong or impressive, as in «a devastating goal».
its sense in the lessons: In geography and history it describes storms, floods, fires and wars that ruin towns and farms; in stories it shows a character's deep grief; phrases: «devastated by the news», «a devastating fire», «left devastated».
examples from the lessons: The hurricane devastated the little island town. | Bushfires devastated huge areas of forest in Australia. | Mia was devastated when her old dog died. | The flood devastated the farmers' crops. | The news of the factory closing devastated the whole village. | The team was devastated after losing in the last minute. | She hit a devastating shot into the top corner. | The war devastated the city, but people rebuilt it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. «Devastated» (feeling) and «devastating» (causing it): I was devastated; the news was devastating. Noun: devastation (uncountable). Stronger than «upset» or «damaged»; do not use it for small things unless joking.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person or company that writes computer programs, apps or games. 2) A person or company that buys land and builds houses, shops or offices on it. 3) A chemical used to make photos appear on old-style film or paper. 4) Someone who develops or works out a new idea or product.
its sense in the lessons: In computing lessons a developer is a programmer who builds apps and websites; in towns a property developer plans new housing; in old photography the developer liquid brought pictures out; phrases: «software developer», «game developer», «property developer», «web developer».
examples from the lessons: My aunt is a game developer and makes puzzle games. | The developer fixed the bug in the app. | A developer wants to build new houses on the old football field. | Web developers make websites work on phones and computers. | In the darkroom, Grandad dipped the paper in developer and a picture appeared. | The village protested against the developer's plans. | Developers test their code many times before it is released. | The developer of the vaccine worked for years.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: a developer, two developers. From the verb develop (no «e» at the end: develop, not «develope»). In apps, «developer mode» or «dev» is short for developer.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A tiny one-celled living thing, a kind of algae, that lives in water and has a glassy shell made of silica. 2) (science) diatoms make a large part of the oxygen we breathe and are food for many sea animals.
its sense in the lessons: In science and biology lessons diatoms appear in food chains, plankton, microscopes and oxygen; their shells pile up on the sea floor and form diatomaceous earth used in filters and toothpaste; phrases: «diatoms under the microscope», «plankton and diatoms».
examples from the lessons: Under the microscope, the diatom looked like a tiny glass jewel. | Diatoms float in oceans, lakes and rivers. | Diatoms make oxygen using sunlight, like plants. | Small sea creatures eat diatoms. | Our class drew different diatom shapes: circles, boats and stars. | Old diatom shells pile up on the sea floor over millions of years. | Scientists study diatoms to learn how clean a river is.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one diatom, many diatoms. Pronounced DIE-a-tom. Too small to see without a microscope. They are not animals and not exactly plants; they are algae (protists).

meaning for a pupil: 1) To become wider or bigger, especially an opening in the body. 2) The pupils of your eyes dilate (get bigger) in the dark so more light can come in. 3) (medicine) A doctor may use drops to dilate your pupils to look inside your eyes. 4) (formal, rare) To talk or write at length about something.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about the eye: pupils dilate in dim light and shrink in bright light; in health topics blood vessels dilate when you are hot; in maths «dilation» means making a shape bigger or smaller by a scale factor; phrases: «dilated pupils», «blood vessels dilate».
examples from the lessons: Your pupils dilate when you walk into a dark room. | The optician put drops in my eyes to dilate them. | When you are hot, blood vessels in your skin dilate. | Cat's eyes dilate into big black circles at night. | Watch a friend's eyes dilate when you turn off the light. | The nurse checked whether the patient's pupils were dilated. | The opposite of dilate is constrict.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: dilated, dilating. Noun: dilation (also dilatation). In maths, a dilation is an enlargement: a scale factor of 2 makes every length twice as long; a scale factor of 1/2 makes it half. Opposite: constrict or contract.

part of speech: noun (dill, uncountable; a dill, dills in Australian slang)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A herb with soft feathery leaves and a fresh taste, used in cooking, especially with fish, potatoes and pickles. 2) (Australia, NZ, informal) A silly or foolish person; a mild, friendly insult.
its sense in the lessons: In cooking and gardening lessons dill is a herb grown from seeds; in food it flavours dill pickles and salmon; in Australian talk calling someone «a dill» is like calling them a twit; phrases: «dill pickle», «fresh dill», «you dill!».
examples from the lessons: Mum sprinkled chopped dill on the potatoes. | I love crunchy dill pickles in my burger. | We grew dill in a pot on the windowsill. | Dill seeds smell a bit like aniseed. | (Australia) «You left your lunch on the bus, you dill!» laughed Jack. | (Australia) Don't be a dill, put your hat on in the sun. | Grandma makes salmon with dill sauce.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The herb is uncountable: some dill, not «a dill». The slang sense is countable (a dill) and mild, used among friends. A «dill pickle» is a cucumber pickled with dill.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The act of making a liquid weaker or thinner by adding water or another liquid. 2) A liquid that has been made weaker this way. 3) The weakening of something, like an idea, power or share.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on mixtures and solutions, dilution means adding solvent so the solution is less concentrated; in cooking and cleaning you dilute squash or bleach; in safety, labels give the right dilution; phrases: «the dilution of squash», «one part to ten parts water».
examples from the lessons: Dilution makes the orange squash less sweet. | We tested how dilution changes the colour of food dye. | The label says the right dilution is one cap to five litres of water. | Dilution with lots of water makes a spill less harmful. | Each dilution was paler than the last one. | Too much dilution and the paint becomes runny. | Rain causes the dilution of salt in the rock pool.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From the verb dilute. In maths, a dilution ratio 1:4 means 1 part concentrate to 4 parts water, so 5 parts in all; the concentrate is 1/5 of the mix. Do not confuse with «delusion» (a false belief) or «dilation» (getting wider).

part of speech: verb (past and past participle of dim: dim, dims, dimmed, dimming); adjective (dimmed lights)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Made less bright: the lights were dimmed. 2) Became less bright by itself. 3) Made a feeling, hope or memory weaker. 4) (on a car) dimmed or dipped headlights point lower so they do not dazzle other drivers.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and stories, dimmed lights show the start of a film, a quiet bedtime or a sad mood; hopes can be dimmed by bad news; in science, a dimmed lamp gives less light energy; phrases: «the lights dimmed», «dimmed hopes».
examples from the lessons: The lights dimmed and the film began. | Dad dimmed the lamp so the baby could sleep. | The stars dimmed as the clouds rolled in. | Her hopes dimmed when it started to rain on sports day. | The screen dimmed to save battery. | The theatre went quiet as the lights dimmed. | Time had dimmed his memory of the old house.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double the m: dim → dimmed, dimming (short vowel + one consonant). Adjective dim also means a bit stupid (informal, rude: «a bit dim»). Do not confuse with «damned».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A loud, long, unpleasant noise, often from many sounds together. 2) (verb, rare: din, dins, dinned, dinning) To din something into someone means to make them learn it by repeating it again and again.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and everyday life a din is the noise of a busy playground, a building site or a crowded canteen; it tells the reader the place is noisy and hard to think in; phrases: «make a din», «above the din», «what a din!», «din it into someone».
examples from the lessons: The children made a terrible din in the dining hall. | We could hardly hear the teacher above the din. | What a din! Turn that music down! | The din of the traffic kept me awake. | The parrots made a great din at dawn. | Mum dinned it into us to look both ways before crossing. | The din of hammers came from next door.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually «a din» or «the din»; no plural in normal use. Short and old word. Not the same as «dinner»; and «din-dins» is baby talk for dinner.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The state of being dirty: covered in mud, dust or germs. 2) Being unfair or dishonest, as in a dirty trick (less common).
its sense in the lessons: In health and hygiene lessons dirtiness of hands or kitchens spreads germs; in stories it shows a messy or poor place; phrases: «the dirtiness of the water», «because of its dirtiness».
examples from the lessons: The dirtiness of the river worried the scientists. | We were shocked by the dirtiness of the old shed. | Dirtiness in a kitchen can make people ill. | The dirtiness of my football kit made Mum groan. | The inspector wrote about the dirtiness of the toilets. | Washing your hands removes dirtiness you cannot even see. | Some people did not like the dirtiness of the game.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: no plural. Built from dirty + ness (y changes to i). More common words: dirt, filth, mess. Opposite: cleanliness or cleanness.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To turn off a feature or machine so it does not work, for example in an app or a phone. 2) To stop something or someone from working properly, often by damaging it. 3) To cause someone to have a disability, through injury or illness.
its sense in the lessons: In computing lessons you disable a setting, sound or notifications; in safety, an alarm or a car can be disabled; in health topics an accident can disable a person; the adjective «disabled» names people with disabilities; phrases: «disable notifications», «disable the alarm», «disabled access».
examples from the lessons: Ask an adult to disable in-app purchases on the tablet. | The engineer disabled the alarm while he fixed it. | You can disable the sound in the game settings. | The storm disabled the power lines. | A bad fall disabled him for many months. | The thief tried to disable the camera. | Please do not disable the safety lock.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: disabled, disabling. Opposite: enable. Polite words: «disabled people» or «people with disabilities»; avoid old rude words like «cripple». A disabled toilet or parking space is for disabled people, not anyone.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The feeling that something or someone is bad, wrong or not acceptable. 2) Showing this feeling by a look, a word or a sound.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, a frown, a «tut» or a shake of the head shows a character's disapproval; in everyday life parents and teachers show disapproval of rude behaviour; phrases: «shake your head in disapproval», «a look of disapproval», «to show disapproval of».
examples from the lessons: Mrs Patel shook her head in disapproval. | Grandma tutted in disapproval when I put my feet on the table. | There was a murmur of disapproval from the crowd. | The coach's face showed his disapproval. | The plan met with disapproval from the parents. | She gave the noisy boys a look of disapproval. | The cat stared at the wet dog with clear disapproval.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: no plural. From disapprove; opposite: approval. «Disapproval of» something (not «disapproval to»).

meaning for a pupil: 1) To think that something or someone is bad or wrong. 2) To refuse to agree to a plan or request officially (less common; usually «reject»).
its sense in the lessons: In stories adults disapprove of mess, rudeness or late nights; it tells the reader a character dislikes what another is doing; phrases: «disapprove of», «a disapproving look», «strongly disapprove».
examples from the lessons: My dad disapproves of eating in front of the telly. | Many people disapprove of littering. | She gave me a disapproving look. | The head teacher disapproved of the new haircut rule. | Do you approve or disapprove of school uniform? | The council disapproved the plans for the car park. | Our dog disapproves of baths.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Use «disapprove of» + thing: «I disapprove of bullying». Adjective: disapproving. Noun: disapproval. Opposite: approve.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A change in the usual colour of something, often to a worse colour. 2) A spot or patch where the colour has changed, like a stain or a bruise.
its sense in the lessons: In science and everyday life, discoloration shows rust, mould, sun damage, a stain on teeth or a bruise on skin; it is often a sign of a problem; phrases: «discoloration of the teeth», «a yellow discoloration».
examples from the lessons: The dentist noticed some discoloration on my tooth. | Sunlight caused discoloration of the curtains. | There was a brown discoloration on the ceiling from the leak. | Rust leaves a red discoloration on metal. | The bruise left a purple discoloration on his knee. | Discoloration of leaves can mean a plant is ill. | We cleaned the discoloration from the bath.
note for the reader of a maths problem: This is the US spelling (also used often in the UK); the UK spelling is «discolouration». Verb: discolour (UK) / discolor (US).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A change in the usual colour of something, often to a worse colour. 2) A spot or patch where the colour has changed, like a stain or a mark.
its sense in the lessons: In UK, Irish, Australian and NZ writing, the same word as «discoloration»; used for stains on teeth, walls, fabric and leaves; often a sign of damage, mould or illness; phrases: «discolouration of the water», «slight discolouration».
examples from the lessons: There was a slight discolouration on the old photo. | The water came out with a brown discolouration. | Tea can cause discolouration of the teeth. | Damp left a grey discolouration on the wall. | The doctor looked at the discolouration on her skin. | Yellow discolouration on leaves can mean too much water. | Bleach caused discolouration on my jeans.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK spelling with «ou»; US spelling «discoloration». Same meaning. Verb: discolour; adjective: discoloured.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) A feeling of embarrassment and unease, when someone is confused or made to look foolish. 2) (old) Defeat or failure of a plan.
its sense in the lessons: Found in classic books and formal writing to show a character feeling awkward and embarrassed, often to the amusement of others; phrases: «to his discomfiture», «much to her discomfiture».
examples from the lessons: To his discomfiture, everyone laughed at his mistake. | She could not hide her discomfiture when the teacher read her note aloud. | Much to the bully's discomfiture, nobody joined in. | The villain's discomfiture made the audience cheer. | He blushed red with discomfiture. | The spelling bee winner enjoyed her rival's discomfiture a little too much.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal and rare; everyday words: embarrassment, awkwardness. Do not confuse with «discomfort» (a bit of pain or unease). Uncountable.

part of speech: verb (past and past participle of discredit: discredit, discredits, discredited, discrediting); adjective (a discredited idea)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Shown to be false or not to be believed: a discredited theory. 2) Made to lose people's trust or respect.
its sense in the lessons: In science and history, a discredited idea is one that evidence has shown to be wrong; in news, a person can be discredited by lies or scandals; it tells the reader not to trust it; phrases: «a discredited theory», «discredited by the evidence».
examples from the lessons: The old idea that the Sun goes round the Earth was discredited long ago. | The fake study was discredited by other scientists. | The cheat was discredited and lost his medal. | Rumours tried to discredit the new captain, but they were lies. | That diet myth has been completely discredited. | His story was discredited when the video was found. | A discredited source should not be used in your project.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Noun: discredit («bring discredit on»). In research and fact-checking: a discredited claim is one shown false, not just one people dislike.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Carefully and quietly, so that other people do not notice or are not embarrassed. 2) In a way that keeps a secret or private matter private.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and everyday manners, people act discreetly to avoid embarrassing others, like passing a note or telling a friend their zip is open; phrases: «discreetly left the room», «discreetly mentioned».
examples from the lessons: She discreetly told him there was spinach in his teeth. | The waiter discreetly put the bill on the table. | Dad discreetly wiped a tear from his eye. | Please leave discreetly if you need the toilet during the show. | The detective discreetly followed the man. | The teacher discreetly helped Sam with his shoelaces. | He discreetly checked his phone under the table.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From discreet (careful, private). Trap: «discreet» (careful) and «discrete» (separate) sound the same but are different words. Adverb form: discreetly (double e).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A difference between two things that should be the same, such as two numbers, accounts or stories. 2) A mismatch that shows something may be wrong.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and science, a discrepancy is a difference between expected and measured results; in detective stories, discrepancies in what people say reveal a lie; in money, between the till and the receipts; phrases: «a discrepancy between», «explain the discrepancy».
examples from the lessons: There was a discrepancy between the two thermometers. | The detective spotted a discrepancy in the witness's story. | We found a discrepancy of £2 in the cake sale money. | Can you explain the discrepancy between your answer and mine? | The discrepancy was caused by a typo. | Scientists noticed a discrepancy in the data. | The register showed 28 pupils, but there were 27: a discrepancy of one.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: discrepancies (y → ies). In maths, the discrepancy is found by subtracting: if one count is 30 and the other is 27, the discrepancy is 3. Formal word; simpler: difference, mismatch.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Separate and distinct; made of parts that are clearly apart from each other. 2) (maths) Discrete data can only take certain values, usually whole numbers that you count, like the number of pets.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and statistics, discrete data are counted (shoes, goals, children) while continuous data are measured (height, time); in science, discrete steps or parts; phrases: «discrete data», «discrete steps», «discrete parts».
examples from the lessons: The number of goals in a match is discrete data. | Height is continuous, but the number of children in a class is discrete. | The project has three discrete stages. | Shoe sizes are discrete: you cannot buy size 4.37. | The tablet split the job into discrete tasks. | Draw a bar chart with gaps for discrete data. | The puzzle had discrete pieces that fitted together.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Homophone trap: «discrete» (separate) vs «discreet» (careful, tactful). Tip: in «discrete» the «t» separates the two «e»s, just as the word means separate. Maths: discrete values are countable, usually whole numbers; bar charts for discrete data have gaps.

part of speech: noun (a discus, discuses or disci — rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A heavy flat round disc that athletes throw as far as they can. 2) The sport or event of throwing this disc, called «the discus».
its sense in the lessons: In PE and sports days, the discus is a field event in athletics and the Olympics; in history, ancient Greek athletes threw the discus, as in the famous statue «The Discus Thrower»; phrases: «throw the discus», «discus thrower», «the discus event».
examples from the lessons: She won the discus at the county championships. | The discus flew over thirty metres. | You spin round before you throw the discus. | Ancient Greeks threw the discus at the Olympic Games. | Stand well back when someone is throwing the discus. | Our school has a plastic discus for practice. | The discus thrower held the disc flat in her hand.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: discuses (most common). Safety: never walk in front of the throwing area. Do not confuse with «discuss» (talk about, double s) or «disc/disk».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Very bad, shameful, and deserving strong disapproval. 2) Shocking in a way that makes people feel ashamed for whoever did it.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and real life, adults call bad behaviour, cheating, mess or unfair treatment «disgraceful»; it tells the reader the speaker is very cross and shocked; phrases: «a disgraceful way to behave», «absolutely disgraceful», «it's disgraceful that…».
examples from the lessons: Throwing litter in the river is disgraceful. | «Your bedroom is disgraceful!» said Mum. | The referee called the foul disgraceful. | It is disgraceful that some children have no warm coat. | The players' behaviour after the match was disgraceful. | Grandpa thought the price of a coffee was disgraceful. | The newspaper called the broken promise disgraceful.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb: disgracefully. Noun: disgrace («It's a disgrace!»). Strong word; stronger than «naughty» or «bad». Spelling: disgrace + ful (one l).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Not wanting to do something; unwilling. 2) (formal) Not in the mood to do something, often because you are tired or lazy.
its sense in the lessons: In books and formal writing it shows a character who would rather not do something; in everyday talk people say «I don't feel like it» instead; phrases: «disinclined to help», «feel disinclined to».
examples from the lessons: After the long walk, I felt disinclined to do my homework. | The cat was disinclined to leave the warm radiator. | He was disinclined to believe the strange story. | The king seemed disinclined to listen. | On rainy Sundays, I am disinclined to get out of bed. | The shopkeeper was disinclined to give a refund.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually followed by «to» + verb: disinclined to go. Opposite: inclined (willing). Formal; everyday: unwilling, not keen.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A chemical liquid or spray that kills germs and bacteria on surfaces. 2) As an adjective: used to kill germs, as in disinfectant wipes.
its sense in the lessons: In health, hygiene and science lessons, disinfectant cleans kitchens, toilets and hospital floors and stops illness spreading; in safety, it is poisonous to drink and must be kept away from small children; phrases: «spray with disinfectant», «hand disinfectant», «disinfectant wipes».
examples from the lessons: The caretaker mopped the floor with disinfectant. | The hospital smelled of disinfectant. | Use disinfectant wipes to clean the table. | Never drink disinfectant: it is poisonous. | Mum keeps the disinfectant on a high shelf. | The nurse put disinfectant on my cut knee. | Disinfectant kills most germs in seconds.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable when you mean types or bottles, uncountable as a substance. Verb: disinfect. Safety: never mix cleaning products (like bleach and other cleaners), as dangerous gases can form. Disinfectant is for surfaces, antiseptic is for skin.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To break into many small pieces and fall apart. 2) To become weaker and stop working as a whole, like a team, plan or friendship.
its sense in the lessons: In science, rocks, meteors and old paper disintegrate; in space, a meteor disintegrates as it burns in the air; in stories, a group or plan can disintegrate; phrases: «disintegrate into pieces», «slowly disintegrating».
examples from the lessons: The old book was so dry that it disintegrated in my hands. | The meteor disintegrated in the atmosphere. | Wet paper soon disintegrates. | The sandcastle disintegrated when the wave hit it. | Their friendship disintegrated after the argument. | Leaves disintegrate on the forest floor and make soil. | The rocket disintegrated in a flash of light.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Noun: disintegration. Similar: crumble, fall apart, break up. Opposite: come together, integrate.

part of speech: verb (past and past participle of dislocate: dislocate, dislocates, dislocated, dislocating); adjective (a dislocated shoulder)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Pushed out of its normal place, especially a bone pushed out of its joint. 2) Moved from its usual place or broken up so it does not work smoothly, like dislocated plans or people forced from home.
its sense in the lessons: In health and first aid lessons, a dislocated shoulder, finger or knee is a painful injury that needs a doctor; in history and news, «dislocated» people have been forced out of their homes; phrases: «a dislocated shoulder», «dislocated his finger».
examples from the lessons: He dislocated his shoulder playing rugby. | The doctor put the dislocated finger back in place. | A dislocated knee is very painful. | She fell off the trampoline and dislocated her elbow. | Do not try to push a dislocated joint back yourself; get help. | The war left thousands of families dislocated. | The goalkeeper's dislocated thumb kept him out for weeks.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Noun: dislocation. First aid: keep the injured part still, call an adult or ambulance. Not the same as a broken bone (fracture), though both need a doctor.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An injury where a bone is pushed out of its normal place at a joint. 2) A serious disturbance where things or people are moved from where they should be, like families forced from home or businesses disrupted.
its sense in the lessons: In health and first aid, a dislocation is treated at hospital; in history, geography and economics, war, floods or factories closing cause dislocation of people and work; phrases: «a shoulder dislocation», «social dislocation».
examples from the lessons: The X-ray showed a dislocation of the shoulder. | A dislocation needs a doctor to put it back. | Floods caused great dislocation in the town. | The war brought dislocation to millions of people. | The hip dislocation took months to heal. | Gymnasts warm up to avoid a dislocation. | The strike caused dislocation to train services.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable for injuries (two dislocations); uncountable for the general disturbance. Verb: dislocate.

part of speech: verb (past and past participle of dismantle: dismantle, dismantles, dismantled, dismantling); adjective
meaning for a pupil: 1) Taken apart piece by piece. 2) Ended or got rid of step by step, like a system, law or organisation.
its sense in the lessons: In D&T and everyday life, people dismantle a tent, a bed or a machine to move or fix it; in history, unfair systems like apartheid were dismantled; phrases: «dismantled the tent», «dismantled the system».
examples from the lessons: We dismantled the tent and packed it in the car. | Dad dismantled my old bed before we moved house. | The engineer dismantled the engine to find the problem. | The fairground rides were dismantled overnight. | The robot was dismantled and its parts reused. | Apartheid in South Africa was dismantled in the early 1990s. | The Berlin Wall was dismantled after 1989.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb (drop e: dismantling). Opposite: assemble, put together, build. Safety: do not dismantle electrical things that are plugged in.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To make someone confused about where they are or which way to go. 2) To make someone confused and unable to think clearly.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and safety lessons, fog, darkness, spinning or a bang on the head can disorient someone; in science, some animals become disoriented by bright city lights; phrases: «feel disoriented», «disorienting experience».
examples from the lessons: The thick fog disoriented the walkers. | After spinning round, I felt disoriented. | Bright lights can disorient baby turtles on the beach. | The loud noise disoriented the dog. | The new school building was big and disorienting. | Waking in a strange room can disorient you. | The cave was so dark that we were quickly disoriented.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly US; UK English also uses «disorientate» (disorientated). Both are correct. Noun: disorientation. Safety: if lost, stay put and call for help.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To make a feeling, fear, doubt or false belief go away. 2) (less common) To drive away or scatter something, like fog or clouds.
its sense in the lessons: In science and fact-checking, people dispel myths with evidence; in stories, a kind word dispels fear; phrases: «dispel a myth», «dispel fears», «dispel rumours».
examples from the lessons: The scientist dispelled the myth that goldfish have a three-second memory. | Her smile dispelled my worries. | The sun soon dispelled the morning mist. | The teacher tried to dispel rumours about the school closing. | Turning on the light dispelled our fear of the dark. | The facts dispelled any doubt. | We wrote a leaflet to dispel common myths about bats.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double l in past forms: dispelled, dispelling. Spelling trap: only one «l» in dispel. Used with myths, fears, doubts, rumours, not with physical objects (you do not «dispel» a ball).

meaning for a pupil: 1) To fail to please someone or to give them what they wanted. 2) dissatisfied (adjective): not happy with something because it is not good enough.
its sense in the lessons: Mostly used as the adjective «dissatisfied» in everyday life and reviews: customers, players or pupils dissatisfied with a result or service; phrases: «dissatisfied with», «a dissatisfied customer».
examples from the lessons: The ending of the film dissatisfied many viewers. | She was dissatisfied with her painting and started again. | A dissatisfied customer asked for a refund. | Poor service dissatisfies shoppers. | The coach was dissatisfied with the team's effort. | If you are dissatisfied, write a polite complaint. | The cold dinner dissatisfied everyone.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: double s (dis + satisfy). y → ies/ied: dissatisfies, dissatisfied. Noun: dissatisfaction. The verb form is rare; «dissatisfied» is common. Compare «unsatisfied» (not yet fulfilled).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Not the same; different from each other. 2) «Not dissimilar» means quite similar.
its sense in the lessons: In science and maths, dissimilar things are compared and contrasted; in maths, dissimilar shapes do not have the same proportions; in English, «not dissimilar» is a polite way of saying alike; phrases: «dissimilar to», «not dissimilar».
examples from the lessons: The two sisters are very dissimilar: one is loud, one is quiet. | A bat and a bird are dissimilar in many ways. | The twins wore dissimilar hats so we could tell them apart. | Her answer was not dissimilar to mine. | Dissimilar triangles have different angles. | The two rocks look dissimilar under the microscope.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double s. Followed by «to» or «from». Opposite: similar. More formal than «different».

part of speech: verb (past and past participle of dissipate: dissipate, dissipates, dissipated, dissipating); adjective (a dissipated person)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Disappeared slowly by spreading out, like fog, smoke, heat or a crowd. 2) Wasted, like money or energy. 3) (old, formal) dissipated person: someone who has spent their life on drinking and wild living.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on energy, heat is dissipated (spread out and wasted) into the surroundings; in weather, fog and storms dissipate; in stories, anger or fear dissipates; phrases: «the fog dissipated», «energy dissipated as heat».
examples from the lessons: The fog dissipated by midday. | Most of the energy was dissipated as heat. | Her anger dissipated when he said sorry. | The crowd dissipated after the concert. | The storm dissipated before it reached the coast. | The smell of burnt toast slowly dissipated. | He dissipated his prize money on sweets and comics.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Noun: dissipation. Double s, single p. In physics: energy is never destroyed; dissipated energy is spread out into the surroundings, usually as heat or sound, and is hard to use.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To persuade someone not to do something. 2) To talk someone out of a plan or idea.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and everyday life, friends and parents dissuade someone from a risky or foolish plan; in safety, signs try to dissuade people from swimming in dangerous water; phrases: «dissuade someone from doing».
examples from the lessons: I tried to dissuade my brother from jumping into the cold lake. | Nothing could dissuade her from entering the race. | The warning signs dissuade people from climbing the cliffs. | Mum dissuaded me from cutting my own fringe. | The teacher dissuaded him from giving up. | Rain did not dissuade the fans from coming.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pattern: dissuade someone from doing something. Opposite: persuade. Pronounced dis-SWADE. Double s.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science, medicine) Further away from the centre of the body or the point where something is attached. 2) Opposite of proximal (closer to the centre).
its sense in the lessons: Used in biology, medicine and anatomy: the fingertips are distal to the elbow; doctors describe injuries this way; in geography, sometimes for areas far from a source; phrases: «distal end», «distal part of the arm».
examples from the lessons: Your fingers are distal to your wrist. | The distal end of the bone is near the knee. | The doctor said the break was in the distal part of the arm. | In the diagram, label the distal and proximal ends. | Your toes are the most distal part of your leg. | The distal tip of the leaf was brown.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Science word; opposite: proximal. «Distal to» = further from the body's centre than. Related to distant.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To swell out or stretch because of pressure from inside. 2) distended (adjective): swollen and puffed out.
its sense in the lessons: In science and health, a stomach or balloon distends when filled with gas or liquid; in news about hunger, children with distended bellies may be badly fed; phrases: «a distended stomach», «distend with gas».
examples from the lessons: The balloon distended as we blew air into it. | After the big meal, his tummy felt distended. | Starving children can have distended bellies. | The snake's body distended as it swallowed the egg. | The vet felt the dog's distended belly. | Water made the sponge distend.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Noun: distension (UK also distention). Medical and formal word; simpler: swell, bloat.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To make a liquid pure by heating it into steam (vapour) and cooling the steam back into liquid. 2) To make a drink like whisky this way. 3) To take the most important parts of an idea or text and put them in a short form.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons distillation separates a liquid from a mixture, such as getting pure water from salty water; in everyday life distilled water goes in irons; in writing, you distil a long story into a summary; phrases: «distilled water», «distil the main points».
examples from the lessons: We distilled salty water to get pure water. | Distilled water is used in car batteries and irons. | Whisky is distilled in Scotland and Ireland. | Can you distill the story into one sentence? | The steam cooled in the tube and became distilled water. | The teacher helped us distill our ideas into a poster. | Perfumes are made by distilling flowers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: US spelling «distill»; UK spelling «distil» (distils), but both have distilled, distilling. Noun: distillation; a place that makes spirits is a distillery. Science: distillation works because liquids boil at different temperatures; water boils at 100 °C.

part of speech: verb (past and past participle of distort: distort, distorts, distorted, distorting); adjective
meaning for a pupil: 1) Twisted or changed out of its normal shape. 2) (sound, picture) Changed so that it is unclear or not true to the original, like a crackly sound or a wobbly reflection. 3) Changed so that it gives a false idea, like distorted facts.
its sense in the lessons: In science, lenses, water and curved mirrors make distorted images; in music, distorted guitar sound is deliberate; in media literacy, facts can be distorted to mislead; phrases: «a distorted reflection», «distorted facts», «distorted sound».
examples from the lessons: The fun-house mirror made my face look distorted. | The speaker crackled and the music was distorted. | A straw in water looks bent and distorted. | The newspaper distorted what the mayor had said. | Heat made the plastic ruler distorted. | Her voice sounded distorted on the bad phone line. | A distorted map can make some countries look bigger than they are.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Noun: distortion. In maths and maps: map projections distort size or shape (Greenland looks far bigger than it is). In news: a distorted story is partly true but twisted.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The act of making something more varied by adding different kinds of things. 2) (money, business) Spreading money, work or products across many different areas to reduce risk.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and economics, a farm or town that relies on one product may need diversification; in science, the diversification of species means new kinds evolving over time; phrases: «diversification of crops», «diversification of the economy».
examples from the lessons: Diversification helped the farm survive when wheat prices fell. | The town's diversification brought new jobs in tourism and technology. | Scientists study the diversification of dinosaurs. | Diversification means not putting all your eggs in one basket. | The museum's diversification included new art and science rooms. | Crop diversification protects farmers from bad weather.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable, formal. Verb: diversify. In money: diversification lowers risk because if one thing loses value, others may not.

part of speech: verb (past and past participle of diversify); adjective (a diversified business)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Made more varied; spread across many different kinds of things. 2) (business, money) Having many different products, jobs or investments instead of just one.
its sense in the lessons: In economics and geography, a diversified economy or farm does many things; in biology, species diversified over time; phrases: «a diversified economy», «diversified into».
