examples from the lessons: The farm diversified into cheese-making and holiday cottages. | A diversified diet includes many different foods. | Mammals diversified after the dinosaurs died out. | The company diversified from toys into video games. | A diversified economy is less hit when one industry fails. | Our school club has diversified: it now does chess, coding and drama.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From diversify: y → i + ed. Adjective use: «a diversified portfolio». «Diversified into» + new area.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To make something more varied or to start doing more different kinds of things. 2) (money, business) To spread money or work across different areas so as not to depend on one thing. 3) (biology) To develop into many different kinds over time.
its sense in the lessons: In geography, economics and money lessons, farms, towns and companies diversify to reduce risk; in science, living things diversify through evolution; phrases: «diversify into», «diversify your diet», «diversify your savings».
examples from the lessons: Farmers diversify by growing different crops. | The library wants to diversify its books. | Try to diversify your diet with more fruit and vegetables. | The company decided to diversify into electric bikes. | Over millions of years, birds diversified into thousands of species. | The town needed to diversify after the mine closed.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb forms: diversifies, diversified, diversifying. Noun: diversification. Related: diverse, diversity.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Quiet, calm and easy to control or teach. 2) (animals) Gentle and not likely to bite or fight.
its sense in the lessons: In science about animals, docile breeds like guinea pigs or some cows are easy to handle; in stories it can describe a gentle animal or person who does what they are told, sometimes too much; phrases: «a docile animal», «docile and gentle».
examples from the lessons: The old horse was docile and let the children ride him. | Guinea pigs are usually docile pets. | The farmer chose a docile breed of sheep. | The tiger looked docile, but it was still dangerous. | Manatees are large but docile animals. | He was docile at school but wild at home.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced DOH-sile (UK) or DOSS-ul (US). Noun: docility. Safety: even docile animals can bite if scared. Sometimes it is a criticism of people (too obedient).

part of speech: noun (a doggie, doggies); also spelled doggy
meaning for a pupil: 1) A child's word for a dog, especially a small or cute one. 2) doggy bag: a bag for taking home food you did not finish at a restaurant. 3) doggy paddle (or doggie paddle): a simple way of swimming, paddling with your hands like a dog.
its sense in the lessons: Used in baby talk, picture books and family talk; in swimming lessons doggy paddle is the first stroke many children learn; phrases: «nice doggie», «doggy bag», «doggy paddle».
examples from the lessons: Look at the little doggie in the window! | The toddler pointed and said, «Doggie!» | We asked for a doggy bag for the leftover pizza. | I can only swim doggy paddle so far. | The doggie wagged its tail at us. | My baby cousin hugged her toy doggie. | Don't pat a doggie without asking the owner first.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Childish or cute word; for older pupils just «dog». Spelled doggie or doggy; plural doggies. Safety: always ask before touching someone's dog.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To have power or control over someone or something. 2) To be the biggest, strongest or most important part of something. 3) (sport) To play much better than the other team for most of a game. 4) To be the tallest or most noticeable thing in a place.
its sense in the lessons: In history, empires dominated other lands; in sport, a team dominates a match; in science, a dominant gene shows in the child; in everyday life, one topic can dominate the news or a conversation; phrases: «dominate the game», «dominate the skyline».
examples from the lessons: The castle dominated the little town. | Our team dominated the match but still lost 1–0. | One loud boy tried to dominate the group. | The story of the flood dominated the news. | Rome dominated much of Europe for centuries. | Bright red dominates the painting. | Lions dominate the African grassland food chain.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Adjective: dominant; noun: domination, dominance. Pronounced DOM-in-ate. In genetics, a dominant trait shows even if only one parent passes it on.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A small flat rectangular tile with spots (0 to 6) on each half, used in a game. 2) dominoes: the game played with these tiles. 3) domino effect: when one event causes a chain of other events, like a line of falling dominoes.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, dominoes are used for counting, adding and pairs; in science and everyday life, toppling domino chains show chain reactions; in history and news, the «domino effect» describes one change leading to many; phrases: «play dominoes», «domino effect», «fall like dominoes».
examples from the lessons: Grandpa and I play dominoes after tea. | We set up 500 dominoes and knocked them all down. | Add the spots on each domino to find the total. | One late bus caused a domino effect, and everyone was late. | A full domino set has 28 tiles. | The dominoes fell one after the other. | Match the domino ends with the same number.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: dominoes (with e). Maths: a double-six set has 28 dominoes, and the spots on the whole set add up to 168. The game name is plural: «Dominoes is fun».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (slang) A person who seems silly, awkward or uncool, often because they are very keen on something. 2) (slang, friendly) Used jokingly between friends to mean a lovable goof.
its sense in the lessons: Used in American and Canadian school talk, films and cartoons; can be a mean insult or a friendly tease; similar to nerd, dweeb or geek; phrases: «what a dork», «don't be a dork», «dorky glasses».
examples from the lessons: (slang) «You're such a dork,» laughed Emma when I fell off my chair. | (slang) He wore a dorky hat with a propeller on top. | (slang) I don't care if people think I'm a dork; I love maths. | (slang) Calling someone a dork just to hurt them is unkind. | (slang) My dad did a dorky dance at the wedding. | (slang) The main character in the film is a lovable dork.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Slang; mostly US and Canada. Can hurt feelings when used to mock someone; think about how it sounds. Similar words: nerd, geek, dweeb, goof.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) Short for dormitory: a big bedroom with many beds, for example at a boarding school, camp or hostel. 2) (US) A building at a college where students live.
its sense in the lessons: In boarding school stories (like many British school books) children share a dorm; in school trips and camps pupils sleep in dorms; in US college life students live in dorms; phrases: «the girls' dorm», «dorm room», «lights out in the dorm».
examples from the lessons: On the school trip, eight of us shared a dorm. | The boys had a midnight feast in the dorm. | My cousin lives in a college dorm in Boston. | Lights out in the dorm was at nine o'clock. | The camp had four dorms and a big dining hall. | We decorated our dorm with posters.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Short (clipped) form of dormitory. Countable: dorms. In US English «dorm» often means a whole building; in UK English it is usually one big room.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science, anatomy) The back or upper surface of a body part, like the back of the hand or the top of the foot or tongue. 2) (science) The back of an animal.
its sense in the lessons: Used in biology, medicine and anatomy diagrams; related to «dorsal» as in the dorsal fin of a shark; a pupil meets it mostly in science or in a doctor's notes; phrases: «dorsum of the hand», «dorsum of the foot».
examples from the lessons: The doctor looked at the dorsum of my hand. | The dorsum of the foot is the top side. | The fish has a spiny dorsum. | Label the dorsum and the belly side on the diagram. | The dorsum of the tongue helps us taste food. | A frog has a green dorsum and a pale belly.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: dorsa (Latin). Technical word; everyday word: back. Related adjective: dorsal (e.g. dorsal fin). Opposite side: ventral.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Something or someone that doubles an amount or size. 2) (games and sport) A move or score that counts twice, or a player who scores twice. 3) (horse racing, betting) A bet on two races where you only win if both win (usually called a «double»).
its sense in the lessons: Not a common word; used in maths puzzles for a machine or rule that doubles numbers, in board games and quizzes for bonus squares, and in technical talk for devices that double voltage or frequency; phrases: «score doubler», «a doubler question».
examples from the lessons: In our function machine, the doubler turns 5 into 10. | The quiz had a doubler round where points counted twice. | Land on the doubler square and your coins double! | The engineer built a voltage doubler. | If you put 7 into the doubler, what comes out? | The doubler round helped our team win.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. In maths: a doubler multiplies by 2, so 3 → 6, 12 → 24; doing it twice multiplies by 4. Rare word; usually say «double» or «times two».

part of speech: adjective (drab, drabber, drabbest); noun (drab, uncountable — a dull brownish colour, rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Dull and boring, with no bright colours or interest. 2) Grey or brownish in colour. 3) (of life or a place) Without fun or excitement.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, drab clothes, rooms or towns create a sad or boring mood; in science, some female birds are drab so they can hide on the nest; phrases: «drab and grey», «a drab little room», «drab colours».
examples from the lessons: The classroom looked drab until we put up our paintings. | The female duck is drab brown, but the male is bright green. | She wore a drab grey coat. | The town looked drab in the winter rain. | Our new wallpaper turned a drab room into a happy one. | He wanted to escape his drab, boring life. | Drab feathers help birds hide from foxes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparatives: drabber, drabbest (double b). Opposite: bright, colourful, cheerful. Noun: drabness.

part of speech: verb (drawl, drawls, drawled, drawling); noun (a drawl)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To speak slowly, stretching out the vowel sounds. 2) A slow way of speaking with long vowel sounds, often typical of a region, like a Southern drawl in the USA.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, «drawled» is used as a speech verb to show a lazy, relaxed, bored or cocky way of talking; in talk about accents, a drawl belongs to some regions; phrases: «a Southern drawl», «a lazy drawl», «he drawled».
examples from the lessons: «Well, howdy, folks,» the cowboy drawled. | She spoke with a slow Texas drawl. | «I'm sooo bored,» drawled my sister. | His Australian drawl made everyone smile. | The cat yawned, and the boy drawled, «Time for bed.» | You can hear a drawl when people stretch their words.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: drawled. Do not confuse with «draw» or «drool». In writing, it is a good alternative to «said» when someone talks slowly.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A low, strong cart without sides, pulled by horses, used to carry heavy loads like barrels of beer. 2) (Australia, old) Any cart or wagon for carrying goods.
its sense in the lessons: In history and classic stories, drays and dray horses carried barrels from breweries through city streets; today some breweries still keep dray horses for shows; phrases: «a dray horse», «brewer's dray».
examples from the lessons: A big dray horse pulled the barrels through the town. | In Victorian London, drays rattled over the cobbles. | The brewery shows its drays at the county fair. | The barrels were loaded onto the dray. | Shire horses are often used as dray horses. | In old Australia, drays carried wool to the ports.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: drays. Old-fashioned word, mostly in history. Dray horses are large, strong breeds like Shires and Clydesdales.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Very bad or unpleasant. 2) Causing fear or great shock; terrible. 3) (informal) Used to make something stronger: a dreadful mess.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday British talk «dreadful» is a common word for bad weather, food or behaviour; in stories it describes frightening events; phrases: «a dreadful mistake», «I feel dreadful», «dreadful weather», «the dreadful news».
examples from the lessons: The weather was dreadful, so sports day was cancelled. | I made a dreadful mistake on my test. | There was a dreadful accident on the motorway. | «What a dreadful thing to say!» gasped Grandma. | I feel dreadful; I think I have flu. | The food at the café was dreadful. | The dreadful storm blew trees down.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb: dreadfully (often means «very»: «dreadfully sorry»). Spelled with -ful (one l). Similar: awful, terrible, horrible. From dread (great fear).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Without dreams. 2) (of sleep) Very deep and peaceful.
its sense in the lessons: Found in stories and poems to describe deep, restful sleep after a long day; phrases: «a dreamless sleep», «fell into a dreamless sleep».
examples from the lessons: After the long hike, I fell into a deep, dreamless sleep. | The night was quiet and dreamless. | The baby slept a dreamless sleep. | She woke from a dreamless sleep feeling fresh. | Some nights are dreamless; others are full of strange dreams. | The cat lay in a dreamless sleep by the fire.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Built from dream + less (without). Almost always used with «sleep». Scientists think we all dream, but we often do not remember it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Looking or seeming as if you are thinking about other things and not paying attention. 2) Soft, gentle and pleasant, like something in a dream. 3) (informal) Very attractive or wonderful.
its sense in the lessons: In stories a dreamy character gazes out of the window or forgets things; music and colours can be dreamy (soft and calm); in teen talk «dreamy» can mean good-looking; phrases: «a dreamy look», «dreamy music».
examples from the lessons: Lily had a dreamy look on her face during maths. | The music was soft and dreamy. | He is a dreamy boy who loves stories. | The sunset made the sky a dreamy pink. | (informal) «The new singer is so dreamy,» sighed my sister. | The ice-cream was dreamy and smooth. | Stop being dreamy and pack your bag!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparatives: dreamier, dreamiest. Adverb: dreamily. Noun: dreaminess.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a funny way that seems serious, with a straight face (dry humour). 2) In a dry way, without water or wetness (rare).
its sense in the lessons: In stories it is a speech adverb: someone says something drily when they make a quiet joke or a sarcastic remark; in British humour, dry wit is common; phrases: «said drily», «remarked drily».
examples from the lessons: «Oh, brilliant,» said Dad drily, as the rain came down on our picnic. | «Lovely weather for ducks,» Grandpa remarked drily. | She smiled drily at his excuse. | «I'm sure the homework ate itself,» the teacher said drily. | He answered drily, without a smile. | The comedian spoke drily, which made it even funnier.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Also spelled «dryly» (more common in US English). From dry. Dry humour means jokes told in a calm, serious voice.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A kind of small to medium meat-eating dinosaur with feathers and a big curved claw on each foot, like Velociraptor. 2) A member of the dinosaur family Dromaeosauridae, known as «raptors».
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about dinosaurs and evolution, dromaeosaurs show that birds are related to dinosaurs, because they had feathers; they appear in books, museums and films (as «raptors»); phrases: «feathered dromaeosaur», «dromaeosaur claw».
examples from the lessons: Velociraptor was a dromaeosaur about the size of a turkey. | Dromaeosaurs had feathers like birds. | The museum showed a dromaeosaur's curved toe claw. | Scientists think dromaeosaurs were fast and clever hunters. | Microraptor was a tiny dromaeosaur with four wings. | Dromaeosaur fossils have been found in Mongolia and North America.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced DROH-mee-oh-sore. Name means «running lizard». Trap: real Velociraptors were much smaller than in the films and had feathers. Plural: dromaeosaurs.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A small tube, usually glass or plastic, with a rubber bulb at the top, used to take up a liquid and let it out drop by drop. 2) (informal) Someone who drops something, as in a name-dropper (someone who boasts about famous people they know).
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, a dropper (or pipette) adds small amounts of liquid in experiments; in health, medicine or eye drops come with a dropper; phrases: «a dropper bottle», «eye dropper», «name-dropper».
examples from the lessons: Use the dropper to add three drops of food colouring. | The nurse gave the baby medicine with a dropper. | We put iodine on the potato with a dropper. | Squeeze the bulb gently, or the dropper will squirt. | Eye drops come in a little dropper bottle. | Count each drop from the dropper carefully.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. In science, a «pipette» is a more exact tool; in maths and science, if each drop is 0.05 ml, then 20 drops make 1 ml.

part of speech: verb (past and past participle of drug: drug, drugs, drugged, drugging); adjective
meaning for a pupil: 1) Given a drug, often secretly or against your will, to make you sleepy or unable to act. 2) Feeling sleepy, slow or confused because of medicine or another drug. 3) (of food or drink) Having a drug secretly put in it.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and films villains drug a guard's drink to sneak past; in health and safety lessons, never accept drinks from strangers and tell an adult if someone acts drugged; in medicine, animals at the vet may be drugged to keep them calm; phrases: «a drugged drink», «felt drugged».
examples from the lessons: In the story, the guard was drugged and fell asleep. | After the operation, I felt drugged and sleepy. | The vet drugged the lion so it could be moved safely. | The poisoned apple in the fairy tale was drugged. | Never drink something if you do not know who made it. | The spy realised his tea had been drugged.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double g: drug → drugged, drugging. Safety: secretly drugging someone is a serious crime. Medicines are drugs too, but only take them as an adult or doctor says.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The sound of a drum being hit, or a steady rhythm of such sounds. 2) A steady, repeated message or warning that keeps coming, like «a drumbeat of bad news».
its sense in the lessons: In music lessons the drumbeat keeps the rhythm and the beat; in history, drumbeats led soldiers marching; in stories it builds tension; in news it means something repeated again and again; phrases: «a steady drumbeat», «the drumbeat of war».
examples from the lessons: The band marched to a steady drumbeat. | I could feel the drumbeat in my chest. | We clapped along to the drumbeat. | The soldiers moved in time with the drumbeat. | Far away in the jungle, a drumbeat began. | There was a constant drumbeat of complaints about the noise.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word: drumbeat. Countable. In music, count the drumbeats: «1, 2, 3, 4» in 4/4 time.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Drunk, or often drunk: affected by too much alcohol. 2) Caused by or happening when people are drunk, like drunken shouting. 3) (in names of things) Swaying or crooked as if drunk, as in «a drunken sailor».
its sense in the lessons: In stories, history and news it describes behaviour caused by alcohol, often noisy or dangerous; in health lessons, it is linked with the dangers of alcohol; in songs, like the old sea song «What shall we do with the drunken sailor?»; phrases: «drunken behaviour», «drunken singing».
examples from the lessons: Drunken shouting woke us up in the night. | The police stopped the drunken driver. | Sailors sang about a drunken sailor. | The story had a drunken pirate who fell asleep on the deck. | Drunken behaviour at football matches is not allowed. | The old fence leaned at a drunken angle.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Used before a noun: «a drunken man» (but «the man was drunk»). Safety: alcohol is not for children; a drunk person should never drive. Old past participle of drink is «drunk», not «drunken».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Having two parts, uses or sides; double. 2) dual nationality / dual citizenship: being a citizen of two countries at the same time. 3) (maths) In some topics, dual means a matching partner shape or idea (for example, a cube and an octahedron are duals).
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: dual carriageway (a road with two lanes each way, UK), dual-language books, dual controls in a learner car; in maths and geography; phrases: «dual carriageway», «dual citizenship», «dual purpose».
examples from the lessons: My cousin has dual citizenship: Irish and Australian. | This book is dual-language, English on one page and French on the other. | Driving schools use cars with dual controls. | The road becomes a dual carriageway after the roundabout. | This tool has a dual purpose: a torch and a whistle. | The game has a dual-screen mode.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Homophone trap: dual (two) vs duel (a fight between two people). Tip: «dual» has «a» like «a pair». Not used about people (do not say «dual twins»).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who is from Dublin, the capital city of Ireland, or who lives there. 2) «Dubliners» is also the name of a famous book of stories by James Joyce (1914) and of an Irish folk band, The Dubliners.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and everyday Irish life, a Dubliner is someone from Dublin; in literature, the book «Dubliners»; phrases: «a true Dubliner», «born a Dubliner».
examples from the lessons: My granny is a proud Dubliner. | Dubliners are famous for their sense of humour. | As a Dubliner, he knew every street in the city centre. | The Dubliners sang old Irish folk songs. | Lots of Dubliners walk along the River Liffey. | James Joyce wrote a book called «Dubliners».
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital D in normal writing: Dubliner (a proper noun). Ending -er means a person from a place, like Londoner or New Yorker. Dublin is in Ireland, not in the UK.

part of speech: noun (a duct, ducts); verb (duct, ducts, ducted — rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A pipe or tube that carries air, water, cables or other things inside a building. 2) (body) A tube in the body that carries liquids, like a tear duct. 3) duct tape: very strong sticky cloth tape.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about the body, tear ducts carry tears and other ducts carry fluids; in buildings, air ducts carry heating and air conditioning; in films, heroes crawl through air ducts; phrases: «air duct», «tear duct», «duct tape».
examples from the lessons: Warm air comes through a duct in the floor. | Tears drain from your eyes through tiny tear ducts. | The spy crawled through the air duct. | Dad fixed the broken hose with duct tape. | Mice were living in the heating duct. | Engineers cleaned the ducts in the school roof.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Pronounced «dukt». «Duct tape» is also called «duck tape» informally (and Duck Tape is a brand). Safety: real air ducts are dangerous to crawl in.

part of speech: noun (a dud, duds); adjective (a dud battery)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) Something that does not work properly or is useless, like a firework that does not go off or a dead battery. 2) (informal) A person or thing that fails or disappoints. 3) duds (US, informal, old): clothes. 4) (military) A bomb or shell that did not explode.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, a dud battery, light bulb or firework; in safety lessons, a «dud» firework must never be picked up because it may still go off; in stories, a disappointing plan or present; phrases: «a dud firework», «turned out to be a dud».
examples from the lessons: The last firework was a dud. | This battery is a dud; let's try another. | The new phone turned out to be a dud. | Never go back to a dud firework: it might explode. | (informal) The film was a dud, and nobody went to see it. | One of the eggs was a dud and did not hatch. | (US, old informal) He put on his best duds for the party.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal. Safety: wait at least 30 minutes and let an adult deal with a dud firework or unexploded bomb.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (medicine) A condition in which a person or animal grows much shorter than usual, often because of their genes. 2) (science) In biology, «island dwarfism» is when animals on islands become small over many generations.
its sense in the lessons: In health lessons, dwarfism is a medical condition, not an illness to laugh at; many people with dwarfism prefer «little people» or «people of short stature»; in science, island dwarfism produced tiny elephants and hippos; phrases: «a person with dwarfism», «island dwarfism».
examples from the lessons: Dwarfism is a medical condition that affects how tall a person grows. | People with dwarfism live full lives as actors, doctors, teachers and athletes. | Island dwarfism made some ancient elephants as small as ponies. | Some breeds of dog have a kind of dwarfism. | Our class learned that dwarfism is often caused by genes. | It is unkind to make jokes about someone's height.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Respectful words: «person with dwarfism», «little person», «person of short stature»; avoid «midget», which many find offensive. «Dwarf» is fine for stars and fairy tales (and plural dwarfs or dwarves).

meaning for a pupil: 1) To become smaller, fewer or weaker little by little until there is very little left. 2) dwindling (adjective): getting smaller.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and science, dwindling numbers of animals, water or forests show a problem; in maths stories, supplies dwindle as they are used; in stories, hope or light dwindles; phrases: «dwindling numbers», «dwindle away», «dwindling supplies».
examples from the lessons: Our supply of biscuits dwindled during the camping trip. | The number of tigers in the wild has dwindled. | The crowd dwindled as it got dark. | Their hope dwindled as the hours passed. | Our savings dwindled after the holiday. | The river dwindled to a tiny stream in summer.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Similar: shrink, decrease, fade. Opposite: grow, increase. In maths: if 20 sweets dwindle by 3 each day, after 5 days 5 are left.

part of speech: verb (present participle of dye: dye, dyes, dyed, dyeing); noun (dyeing, uncountable)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Changing the colour of something, like hair, cloth or wool, by soaking it in a colouring liquid called dye. 2) The craft or job of colouring cloth and wool.
its sense in the lessons: In art, D&T and history lessons, dyeing cloth with plants like onion skins or beetroot; in everyday life, dyeing hair or Easter eggs; phrases: «tie-dyeing», «dyeing my hair», «dyeing eggs».
examples from the lessons: We are dyeing T-shirts with tie-dye in art club. | My sister is dyeing her hair blue. | In the past, dyeing cloth purple was very expensive. | We tried dyeing eggs with onion skins. | Wear gloves when dyeing, or your hands will change colour too. | The factory specialises in dyeing wool.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: dye → dyeing (keeps the e) vs die → dying (end of life). «Dyeing my hair» is colouring; «dying» means about to die.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A soft, warm cover for one ear; usually a pair of these joined by a band over the head, called earmuffs. 2) Ear defenders: hard earmuffs that protect ears from loud noise.
its sense in the lessons: In winter clothes topics, earmuffs keep ears warm; in safety lessons, ear defenders (earmuffs) protect hearing near loud machines or fireworks; phrases: «a pair of earmuffs», «fluffy earmuffs».
examples from the lessons: I wear fluffy earmuffs when it snows. | The builder wore earmuffs to block the noise of the drill. | Grandma knitted me a pair of earmuffs. | My little brother wore earmuffs at the fireworks show. | Her pink earmuffs matched her mittens. | Put your earmuffs on, it's freezing!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually plural: earmuffs, «a pair of earmuffs». One word. Safety: loud noise can damage hearing forever; protect your ears.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a serious and sincere way, really meaning what you say or do. 2) Trying hard and with great care.
its sense in the lessons: In stories it is a speech adverb that shows a character being sincere and serious; in everyday life, people earnestly promise or hope; phrases: «said earnestly», «earnestly hoped», «work earnestly».
examples from the lessons: «I promise I'll tidy my room,» said Tom earnestly. | She earnestly hoped her lost cat would come home. | The children listened earnestly to the firefighter. | He worked earnestly on his science project. | «Please believe me,» she said earnestly. | They earnestly asked for help.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From earnest (serious). «In earnest» means seriously or properly: «The rain started in earnest.» Not related to the name Ernest, though «The Importance of Being Earnest» plays on both.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Towards the east or in the east: an easterly direction. 2) (of wind) Blowing from the east. 3) (noun) A wind that comes from the east.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and weather lessons, an easterly wind blows FROM the east towards the west; compass directions and maps; phrases: «an easterly wind», «in an easterly direction», «the trade winds, or easterlies».
examples from the lessons: A cold easterly wind blew across the field. | We walked in an easterly direction towards the sunrise. | The ship sailed on an easterly course. | The easterlies near the equator are called trade winds. | The weather forecast says a strong easterly will bring snow. | Our school is on the easterly side of the town.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: a wind is named after where it comes FROM; an easterly wind blows from east to west. Similar: northerly, southerly, westerly. In UK weather, cold easterlies often come from Siberia («the Beast from the East»).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Short for electrocardiogram: a medical test that records the electrical signals of the heart as a wavy line. 2) The machine that does this test (electrocardiograph).
its sense in the lessons: In health and science lessons about the heart, an ECG shows how the heart beats; in hospitals and TV dramas, the ECG line beeping on a screen shows a patient's heartbeat; phrases: «have an ECG», «ECG machine».
examples from the lessons: The doctor gave Grandad an ECG to check his heart. | Sticky pads are put on your chest for an ECG. | The ECG showed a normal heartbeat. | An ECG does not hurt at all. | On the screen, the ECG line went up and down with each beat. | Nurses read the ECG to see if the heart was beating normally.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Written in capitals: ECG; said «ee-see-gee», so «an ECG». In the USA also called EKG (from the German spelling). Do not confuse with EEG (brain waves).

meaning for a pupil: 1) An official order or rule given by a king, emperor, government or other ruler. 2) (informal) Any strict order from someone in charge.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, kings and emperors issued edicts (for example the Edict of Milan in 313 allowed Christians to worship freely in the Roman Empire); in stories, a cruel king's edict; jokingly, a parent's edict; phrases: «issue an edict», «by royal edict».
examples from the lessons: The emperor issued an edict that all people must pay a new tax. | The Edict of Milan in 313 gave Christians freedom to worship. | By royal edict, the forest belonged to the king. | Mum's new edict: no phones at the table! | The people refused to obey the unfair edict. | The edict was read out in the town square.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: edicts. Pronounced EE-dikt. Formal and old-fashioned; today «law», «order», «decree».

part of speech: noun (an Edmontosaurus, Edmontosauruses; also Edmontosaurus as the genus name)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A large plant-eating duck-billed dinosaur (a hadrosaur) that lived in North America near the end of the age of dinosaurs, about 68 to 66 million years ago. 2) Named after Edmonton in Alberta, Canada, where the first fossils were found.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons and museums about dinosaurs, Edmontosaurus was a common herbivore that lived in herds and was hunted by Tyrannosaurus rex; some fossils even show skin; phrases: «a herd of Edmontosaurus», «duck-billed dinosaur».
examples from the lessons: Edmontosaurus had a flat beak like a duck. | Edmontosaurus ate plants with hundreds of grinding teeth. | A T. rex bite mark was found on an Edmontosaurus bone. | Herds of Edmontosaurus roamed Canada and the USA. | Edmontosaurus could grow up to 12 metres long. | The museum had a mummified Edmontosaurus with skin prints.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Scientific names start with a capital letter and are often written in italics: Edmontosaurus. Pronounced ed-MON-toh-SORE-us. «-saurus» means lizard.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (a name) Edo is the old name of the city of Tokyo in Japan, before 1868. 2) (a name) The Edo period (1603–1868) was a time in Japanese history when shoguns ruled from Edo. 3) (a name) Edo is also a people and a language of southern Nigeria, around Benin City, and a state in Nigeria.
its sense in the lessons: In history and geography lessons, «Edo» appears in topics about Japan (samurai, shoguns, woodblock prints) and about Nigeria (the Kingdom of Benin and the Benin Bronzes); it is not an ordinary English word; phrases: «Edo period», «Edo Japan», «Edo State».
examples from the lessons: Tokyo was called Edo until 1868. | Samurai lived in the Edo period. | Hokusai made his famous wave print in the Edo period. | The Edo people live in southern Nigeria. | The Benin Bronzes were made by Edo artists. | We made a timeline of Edo Japan.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A proper noun: write Edo with a capital E. Pronounced EH-doh. Not an English word with a general meaning.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person whose job is to teach or educate people, like a teacher, tutor or lecturer. 2) (formal) Someone who is an expert in education or helps plan how children learn.
its sense in the lessons: In formal writing and news, «educators» means teachers and others working in schools; in museums and zoos, an «educator» runs learning sessions; phrases: «a museum educator», «parents and educators».
examples from the lessons: My mum is an educator at the science museum. | Educators met to talk about reading in schools. | Maria Montessori was a famous educator from Italy. | The zoo educator showed us a snake. | Parents and educators want children to be safe online. | A good educator makes learning fun.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. More formal than «teacher». From educate; noun education. Pronounced ED-yoo-kay-tor.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Short for electroencephalogram: a medical test that records the electrical activity of the brain as wavy lines. 2) The machine that does this test.
its sense in the lessons: In health and science lessons about the brain, an EEG shows brain waves; doctors use it to study sleep and conditions such as epilepsy; small metal discs are put on the head; phrases: «have an EEG», «EEG test».
examples from the lessons: The doctor did an EEG to look at my brain waves. | During an EEG, little sensors are stuck on your head. | An EEG does not hurt. | Scientists use EEGs to study sleep. | The EEG showed the brain waves while she was asleep. | The EEG helped doctors understand his seizures.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Written in capitals: EEG; said «ee-ee-gee», so «an EEG». Do not confuse with ECG (heart). The long word: electroencephalogram (e-lek-tro-en-SEF-a-lo-gram).

meaning for a pupil: 1) The bubbles of gas that rise in a liquid, as in fizzy drinks or when a tablet dissolves. 2) Lively, cheerful and excited behaviour.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on reactions, effervescence (fizzing) is a sign that a gas is being made, for example when vinegar meets bicarbonate of soda; in stories, a character's effervescence means bubbly energy; phrases: «effervescence shows a gas is made».
examples from the lessons: We saw effervescence when the tablet dropped into the water. | Effervescence is a sign of a chemical reaction. | The lemonade lost its effervescence when left open. | Her effervescence made the party fun. | Vinegar and baking soda cause strong effervescence. | The effervescence was carbon dioxide gas escaping.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Pronounced eff-er-VESS-ence. Everyday word: fizz, fizzing. In chemistry: the bubbles in fizzy drinks are carbon dioxide.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (of a liquid) Giving off bubbles of gas; fizzy. 2) (of a person) Lively, cheerful and full of energy.
its sense in the lessons: In science and health, effervescent tablets fizz when dropped in water; in stories, an effervescent character is bubbly and enthusiastic; phrases: «an effervescent tablet», «an effervescent personality».
examples from the lessons: Mum dropped an effervescent vitamin tablet into the glass. | Fizzy drinks are effervescent. | Our new teacher has an effervescent personality. | The effervescent mixture bubbled over the beaker. | She gave an effervescent laugh. | The bath bomb is effervescent and fizzes in water.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced eff-er-VESS-ent. Spelling: double f, -scent. Noun: effervescence. Simple word: fizzy (for drinks), bubbly (for people).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal, often mocking) A very clever person who is interested in study and ideas, sometimes seen as out of touch with real life. 2) (informal, friendly) A brainy person, a «brainbox».
its sense in the lessons: Used in everyday talk, cartoons and the UK TV quiz show «Eggheads»; can be a gentle tease or an insult about being too clever; phrases: «a bunch of eggheads», «egghead scientists».
examples from the lessons: (informal) My brother is a real egghead who reads encyclopaedias for fun. | (informal) The eggheads at the university solved the puzzle. | The quiz show «Eggheads» has a team of very clever people. | (informal) Don't call him an egghead just because he likes maths. | (informal) The film's hero is a shy egghead who saves the day. | (informal) «Ask the egghead in our class,» joked Sam, pointing at Priya.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal; can be unkind. Similar: brainbox, boffin (UK), nerd, geek. One word.

part of speech: adjective; noun (the eightieth, an eightieth); ordinal number (80th)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The ordinal number for 80: coming after the seventy-ninth and before the eighty-first. 2) One of 80 equal parts of something (1/80).
its sense in the lessons: In maths, ordinal numbers show order in a line or list; in everyday life, an eightieth birthday is a big celebration; phrases: «eightieth birthday», «the eightieth anniversary», «one eightieth».
examples from the lessons: Granny had a big party for her eightieth birthday. | He finished in eightieth place out of 200 runners. | This year is the eightieth anniversary of our school. | One eightieth of 160 is 2. | The eightieth page of my book has a map. | Written in figures, eightieth is 80th.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: eight + ieth (the y of eighty changes to i): eightieth. Maths: an eightieth = 1/80 = 0.0125. Ordinal: 80th; cardinal: eighty.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Being killed or badly hurt by an electric shock. 2) (law, US history) A way of executing a criminal using the electric chair, used in some US states.
its sense in the lessons: In science and safety lessons, electrocution is the danger of touching live wires, using electrical things near water, or climbing pylons; phrases: «risk of electrocution», «danger of electrocution».
examples from the lessons: Never fly a kite near power lines because of the risk of electrocution. | Water and electricity together can cause electrocution. | The sign on the pylon warned of danger of electrocution. | The electrician turned off the power to avoid electrocution. | Many birds die by electrocution on power lines. | Never poke anything into a socket.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: electrocute (electrocuted). Strictly, electrocution means killed, but people often use it for a bad shock. Safety: stay away from substations, railway lines and fallen power cables; call an adult and 999 / 911 / 000 / 111.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) A liquid or paste that lets electricity pass through it because it has ions (charged particles) in it, as in a battery. 2) (health) Salts in your body and in sports drinks, like sodium and potassium, that help your muscles and nerves work.
its sense in the lessons: In chemistry lessons, electrolytes are used in electrolysis and batteries; in health and sport, after sweating or being ill you may need to replace electrolytes with drinks; phrases: «electrolyte drink», «battery electrolyte».
examples from the lessons: Salty water is an electrolyte, so it conducts electricity. | Sports drinks contain electrolytes. | The battery's electrolyte lets the current flow. | When you have a tummy bug, the doctor may suggest an electrolyte drink. | We used salt water as the electrolyte in our experiment. | Pure water is a poor electrolyte.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Pronounced e-LEK-tro-lite. Related: electrolysis (splitting a compound with electricity). Safety: battery electrolytes can be acid and burn skin.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To lift something up to a higher position. 2) To give someone a higher rank or importance. 3) To make something better or improve it, like a mood or a dish.
its sense in the lessons: In first aid, you elevate (raise) an injured leg or arm to reduce swelling or bleeding; in geography, «elevation» means height above sea level; in stories, someone is elevated to a higher job; phrases: «elevate your leg», «elevated position», «elevate your mood».
examples from the lessons: Elevate your sprained ankle on a cushion. | The nurse told him to elevate his arm to stop the bleeding. | The house stands on an elevated spot above the river. | Music can elevate your mood. | She was elevated to captain of the team. | The train runs on an elevated track above the street.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Noun: elevation (height above sea level). US: elevator = UK: lift. First aid: RICE = Rest, Ice, Compression, Elevation.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Removing or getting rid of something completely. 2) (sport, games, shows) Being knocked out of a competition. 3) (maths, logic) Solving a problem by ruling out wrong answers one by one (process of elimination).
its sense in the lessons: In maths and logic puzzles you use the process of elimination; in sport and TV shows, rounds have eliminations; in health and science, the body gets rid of waste; phrases: «process of elimination», «elimination round», «the elimination of disease».
examples from the lessons: By a process of elimination, we found who took the cake. | Our team lost in the elimination round. | The elimination of smallpox was a great success for science. | The quiz had a different elimination each week. | Cross off wrong answers: that is elimination. | The elimination of plastic straws helps the sea.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From eliminate. In maths: if three options are wrong, elimination tells you the fourth is right. In algebra, the «elimination method» removes a variable from equations.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To make something longer, or to become longer. 2) elongated (adjective): long and thin, longer than usual.
its sense in the lessons: In science, cells, shadows and shapes elongate; in art, elongated figures look tall and thin; in maths, an elongated shape is stretched in one direction; phrases: «elongated shadows», «an elongated shape».
examples from the lessons: Our shadows elongate as the sun goes down. | A giraffe has an elongated neck. | The cell elongates before it splits. | The artist painted elongated faces. | Stretch the dough to elongate it. | An ellipse is like an elongated circle.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Noun: elongation. Pronounced EE-long-gate. Similar: stretch, lengthen.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Being set free from slavery or from strict control by others. 2) Getting equal rights and freedoms, for example for women or a group of people.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons: the Emancipation Proclamation (1863) by Abraham Lincoln declared enslaved people in the Confederate states free; the abolition of slavery in the British Empire (1833–1834); women's emancipation and the vote; phrases: «the emancipation of slaves», «women's emancipation».
examples from the lessons: The Emancipation Proclamation was signed by Abraham Lincoln in 1863. | Emancipation meant that enslaved people were free. | The fight for women's emancipation included the right to vote. | Many people celebrate Emancipation Day. | Frederick Douglass spoke out for emancipation. | Catholic emancipation in Britain and Ireland came in 1829.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Verb: emancipate. Pronounced e-man-si-PAY-shun. Formal history word; simpler: freedom, liberation.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To make something more beautiful by adding decorations. 2) To add extra details to a story to make it more exciting, often ones that are not true.
its sense in the lessons: In art and D&T, you embellish a card or bag with sequins and ribbons; in English and storytelling, you can embellish a story with details, but in real reports adding untrue details is dishonest; phrases: «embellish the truth», «embellished with gold».
examples from the lessons: We embellished our cards with glitter and stars. | The queen's dress was embellished with pearls. | Grandpa likes to embellish his fishing stories. | Don't embellish the facts in a news report. | She embellished her poem with lovely describing words. | The book cover was embellished with gold letters.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: embellishes, embellished. Noun: embellishment. When telling the truth matters, embellishing is close to lying.

part of speech: verb (past and past participle of embody: embody, embodies, embodied, embodying); adjective
meaning for a pupil: 1) Showed or represented an idea or quality clearly, as a perfect example. 2) Included as part of something, like rules embodied in a law. 3) (science, formal) Having a body; in AI and robots, «embodied» means having a body that acts in the real world.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and history, a hero embodies courage or a leader embodies hope; in law and RE, values are embodied in rules; in science, an embodied robot can move and sense; phrases: «embodied the spirit of», «embodied in».
examples from the lessons: The firefighter embodied courage. | Our school's values are embodied in five simple rules. | The robot is an embodied AI that walks around the lab. | For many, Nelson Mandela embodied forgiveness. | The team embodied the spirit of fair play. | His kind smile embodied his gentle nature.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From embody: y → ied (embodied, embodies). Noun: embodiment («She is the embodiment of kindness»). Christians believe that in Jesus God became embodied as a man (the Incarnation).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (medicine) A medicine or substance that makes a person vomit (be sick). 2) Making someone sick, as an adjective.
its sense in the lessons: In medicine and history, emetics were once used against poisoning, but doctors now rarely use them; in safety lessons, never make someone sick after swallowing poison unless a doctor says so; in stories, an emetic may appear in old medicine; phrases: «an emetic drug».
examples from the lessons: In the old days, doctors gave an emetic to poison victims. | Salty water was once used as an emetic. | The vet gave the dog an emetic after it ate chocolate. | Some plants are emetic and make animals sick. | Today, doctors rarely use emetics. | If someone swallows something poisonous, call for help at once.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun. Pronounced e-MET-ik. Safety: do not make yourself or others sick after swallowing poison; ring the emergency number or a poison helpline.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who leaves their own country to live in another country.
its sense in the lessons: In history and geography lessons, emigrants leave home because of poverty, war or for new chances, such as Irish emigrants in the Great Famine of the 1840s or British emigrants to Australia; phrases: «Irish emigrants», «emigrants to America».
examples from the lessons: Many Irish emigrants sailed to America during the famine. | My great-grandparents were emigrants from Italy. | The emigrants waved goodbye to their village. | Emigrants often send money home to their families. | Ships full of emigrants arrived in New York. | Ten-pound Poms were British emigrants to Australia.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: an emigrant LEAVES a country (exit = e), an immigrant COMES INTO a country (in = im). The same person is both: an emigrant from Ireland and an immigrant to Canada. Verb: emigrate.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A small face made from keyboard symbols, like :-) or :(, used in messages to show a feeling. 2) (informal) An emoji: a little picture showing a face or thing.
its sense in the lessons: In computing and online safety lessons, emoticons add feeling to messages; they help show if someone is joking, but can be misunderstood; phrases: «add an emoticon», «a smiley emoticon».
examples from the lessons: She ended her message with a smiley emoticon :-). | Emoticons were invented before emojis. | Turn your head sideways to see the emoticon's face. | A wink emoticon ;-) shows that you are joking. | Don't use too many emoticons in a formal email. | The emoticon :( shows that you are sad.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Made from «emotion» + «icon». Strictly, emoticons are made of keyboard characters; emojis are small pictures. The first known emoticon :-) was suggested in 1982.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To show that something is especially important. 2) To say a word or sound more strongly. 3) To make something more noticeable, like a line or a colour.
its sense in the lessons: In English, you emphasise key points in writing with bold, underlining or words like «especially»; in speaking, you stress a word; in art, colour can emphasise a shape; phrases: «emphasise the point», «emphasise the importance of».
examples from the lessons: The teacher emphasised the importance of checking our answers. | Underline the words you want to emphasise. | She emphasised the word «never». | Bright colours emphasise the eyes in the painting. | The firefighter emphasised: get out, stay out, call 999. | He emphasised that the test was only for practice.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK spelling «emphasise»; US spelling «emphasize». Noun: emphasis (plural emphases). Do not say «emphasise on»: say «emphasise the point» or «put emphasis on».

meaning for a pupil: 1) The state of having nothing or nobody inside. 2) A sad feeling that something is missing in your life, or that nothing matters.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, the emptiness of a house or a desert sets a lonely mood; in talk about feelings, emptiness can come with grief or sadness, and it helps to talk to someone; in religion and philosophy, some traditions speak of emptiness as calm; phrases: «a feeling of emptiness», «the emptiness of space».
examples from the lessons: The emptiness of the classroom after school felt strange. | After her friend moved away, she felt a deep emptiness. | Astronauts look out at the emptiness of space. | The emptiness of the desert stretched for miles. | The house echoed with emptiness. | If you feel emptiness for a long time, tell a grown-up you trust.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Built from empty + ness (y → i). Opposite: fullness. Feelings of emptiness are worth sharing with a trusted adult.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (law) The act of making a bill into law, or the law itself. 2) Acting out a story or event, like a re-enactment of a battle.
its sense in the lessons: In citizenship lessons, the enactment of a law happens when parliament passes it and it is signed; in history, a re-enactment brings the past to life; in drama, acting out a scene; phrases: «the enactment of the law», «a historical re-enactment».
examples from the lessons: The enactment of the new law took many months. | We watched a re-enactment of the Battle of Hastings. | Our class did an enactment of the Nativity story. | The Parliament voted for the enactment of the bill. | The enactment made school compulsory for all children. | Each enactment is written down in the law books.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: enact. «Re-enactment» = acting a past event again. Formal word; simpler: passing (of a law), acting out.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A place where a group of people, like soldiers, refugees or travellers, set up tents or shelters for a time. 2) A camp, especially a large or temporary one.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, Roman and army encampments; in news, refugee encampments after war or disaster; in stories, an encampment by a fire; phrases: «a military encampment», «refugee encampment».
examples from the lessons: The Roman soldiers built an encampment by the river. | The refugees lived in a large encampment for months. | The scouts set up an encampment in the woods. | Smoke rose from the encampment at night. | Archaeologists found the remains of an ancient encampment. | Protesters made an encampment outside the building.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Formal word for camp. Verb: encamp (to set up camp).

meaning for a pupil: 1) To cover or surround something completely, as if in a case or box. 2) To put something inside a hard protective cover.
its sense in the lessons: In science and history, fossils or insects get encased in rock, ice or amber; in D&T and everyday life, wires are encased in plastic, a broken arm in plaster; phrases: «encased in ice», «encased in plaster», «encased in amber».
examples from the lessons: The insect was encased in amber millions of years ago. | Snow encased the car overnight. | His broken leg was encased in plaster. | The wires are encased in plastic for safety. | The chocolate egg was encased in shiny foil. | Builders encase the steel in concrete.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb (drop e: encasing). Similar: enclose, cover, wrap. Spelling: en + case.

part of speech: verb (past and past participle of encase); adjective (encased in)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Completely covered or surrounded by something hard or protective. 2) Put inside a case or shell.
its sense in the lessons: In science and stories, things encased in ice, amber, rock or metal are protected or trapped; in health, a broken arm encased in plaster; phrases: «encased in ice», «encased in amber», «encased in armour».
examples from the lessons: The mammoth was encased in ice for thousands of years. | The knight was encased in shining armour. | Her phone was encased in a tough rubber cover. | The fossil fish was encased in stone. | The bridge was encased in scaffolding. | His arm was encased in a bright blue cast.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past form of encase; usually followed by «in». Similar: covered, wrapped, sealed.

part of speech: verb (present participle of encircle: encircle, encircles, encircled, encircling); adjective (the encircling hills)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Forming a circle around something; surrounding it on all sides. 2) Moving around something in a circle.
its sense in the lessons: In geography, encircling hills or walls surround a town; in history, armies encircled a city in a siege; in maths and art, drawing a ring around something; in stories, the encircling dark adds danger; phrases: «the encircling hills», «encircling the city».
examples from the lessons: The encircling mountains protected the valley. | The children made a ring, encircling the maypole. | Wolves were encircling the camp. | A wall encircling the old town kept enemies out. | The moat encircling the castle was full of water. | Clouds were encircling the mountain top.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From encircle; drop e before -ing. Similar: surrounding, ringing. Noun: encirclement.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Slowly going into a place, time or right that belongs to someone else, a little at a time. 2) (law) Building or using land beyond your boundary onto someone else's land. 3) (nature) The sea, a desert or towns slowly spreading over land.
its sense in the lessons: In geography, coastal erosion and desert encroachment take land; in science, towns encroach on animals' habitats; in law and citizenship, encroachment on rights; in American football, a foul called encroachment; phrases: «encroachment on», «the encroachment of the sea».
examples from the lessons: The encroachment of the sea is eating away the cliffs. | Towns' encroachment on forests leaves animals with less space. | The neighbour's new fence was an encroachment on our garden. | Desert encroachment makes farming harder. | People protested against the encroachment on their rights. | Rising water caused the encroachment of salt into farmland.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: encroach («encroach on»). Pronounced en-KROHCH-ment. Formal word; simpler: creeping in, taking over.

part of speech: noun (encryption; uncountable, sometimes an encryption, encryptions)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Encryption is turning a message or data into a secret code so that only someone with the right key can read it. 2) An encryption is one particular way or system of doing this.
its sense in the lessons: In computing and online-safety lessons, encryption is what keeps passwords, bank details and private chats safe as they travel across the internet; the padlock in a web browser means the connection uses encryption. In history lessons it links to codes and code-breaking, such as the Enigma machine. Phrases: «end-to-end encryption», «strong encryption», «break the encryption», «encryption key».
examples from the lessons: Encryption scrambles your message so nobody else can read it. | The padlock icon shows the website uses encryption. | Our chat app has end-to-end encryption. | During the war, code-breakers tried to crack the enemy's encryption. | Without the key, the encrypted file looks like nonsense. | Banks use strong encryption to protect your money. | We made a simple encryption by moving each letter three places along the alphabet.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly uncountable: «use encryption», not «an encryption», unless you mean one type of it. Verb: encrypt (encrypts, encrypted, encrypting); opposite: decryption, decrypt. Encryption is not the same as a password: the password may unlock the key, but encryption is the scrambling itself.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Endangerment is putting someone or something in danger. 2) (law) Endangerment is the crime of acting so carelessly that you put another person, especially a child, at serious risk, as in «child endangerment» or «reckless endangerment».
its sense in the lessons: A rare, formal word met in news, law and nature reports; in science it can describe how a species becomes endangered. In stories and the news it tells the reader that someone's careless choices put others at risk, even if nobody was hurt. Phrases: «child endangerment», «reckless endangerment», «endangerment of wildlife».
examples from the lessons: The driver was charged with reckless endangerment. | Leaving a toddler alone in a hot car is child endangerment. | Pollution has led to the endangerment of many river fish. | The report warned about the endangerment of rare birds. | The judge said the man's actions caused the endangerment of everyone on the bus. | Cutting down the forest increases the endangerment of orangutans.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable, formal. Built from «endanger» (to put in danger) + «-ment». Everyday speech usually says «putting people in danger» instead. Do not confuse with «endangered» (an adjective: an endangered species is at risk of dying out).

part of speech: adjective (endowed); verb past form of endow (endow, endows, endowed, endowing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) If a person is endowed with something, they naturally have a good quality or ability: «endowed with great patience». 2) If a school, hospital or college is endowed, someone has given it a large sum of money that keeps paying for it. 3) (adult slang) a rude use about the body grown-ups make; not for school.
its sense in the lessons: In history and reading lessons you meet it in old-fashioned or formal writing: «Nature had endowed her with a quick mind». Old colleges and charities were «endowed» by rich people, so they still have money today. The US Declaration of Independence says people are «endowed by their Creator with certain unalienable Rights». Phrases: «endowed with», «well endowed (school/college)», «an endowed chair (a paid professor's post)».
examples from the lessons: She was endowed with a beautiful singing voice. | The old school was endowed by a rich merchant in 1600. | The museum is well endowed, so it can buy new paintings. | Cats are endowed with very sharp hearing. | The Declaration says people are endowed with certain rights. | The hospital was endowed by a family who wanted to help the poor.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually with «with»: endowed with talent. Formal word; everyday speech says «she has a gift for» or «was given money». Noun: endowment (money given to keep an organisation going). Avoid the phrase «well endowed» about people, as it can be a rude joke.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A rule, law or agreement that is enforceable can really be made to happen: people can be made to obey it, and there is a way to punish or stop those who break it. 2) (law) A contract is enforceable if a court will make the people in it keep their promises.
its sense in the lessons: In citizenship and law lessons it separates rules that only sound good from rules that can actually be checked and backed up. In everyday life, parents and teachers learn that a rule must be enforceable to work: «No phones at dinner» is easier to check than «Be nicer». Phrases: «legally enforceable», «an enforceable contract», «not enforceable».
examples from the lessons: A rule is only useful if it is enforceable. | A promise made in a playground game is not legally enforceable. | The teacher made the rule enforceable by collecting phones at the door. | Is a ban on running in the corridor enforceable? | The contract is enforceable, so both sides must keep it. | A law against littering is hard to enforce on an empty beach, so it is barely enforceable there.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Built from «enforce» (make people obey) + «-able». Opposite: unenforceable. Spelling: keep the e after c (enforce-able), because «c» before «a» would sound like k otherwise.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To engender a feeling or situation is to cause it or make it begin: «Kindness engenders trust». 2) (old use) To engender a child is to father it; this sense is found only in very old books.
its sense in the lessons: A formal, exam-style word for «cause» or «create», used mostly about feelings and attitudes, not about physical things. In essays and reports you might write that a policy «engendered anger» or a teacher «engendered a love of reading». Phrases: «engender trust», «engender fear», «engender respect».
examples from the lessons: Fair rules engender respect in the class. | His rude jokes engendered a lot of anger. | The coach's praise engendered confidence in the team. | Rumours can engender fear in a small town. | Good teamwork engenders friendship. | The new law engendered a long debate in Parliament.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; in speech say «cause» or «create». It is followed by an abstract noun (trust, fear, hope), not by a thing like «a cake». Not related to the word «gender» in meaning, though they share an old root meaning «to produce».

part of speech: adjective (engrossing; more engrossing, most engrossing); verb -ing form of engross (engross, engrosses, engrossed, engrossing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Something engrossing is so interesting that it holds all your attention and you forget what is around you. 2) As a verb form, engrossing means taking up someone's whole attention.
its sense in the lessons: In reading and book reviews it is a strong word of praise: an engrossing story is one you cannot put down. Related: if you are engrossed in something, you are so busy with it that you do not notice anything else, which in safety talk can be risky (engrossed in a phone while crossing a road). Phrases: «an engrossing book», «engrossing story», «engrossed in».
examples from the lessons: The book was so engrossing that I read it in one night. | It was an engrossing match right up to the last minute. | She found the science documentary engrossing. | He was engrossed in his game and didn't hear his mum. | The puzzle was engrossing, and the whole class went quiet. | Don't get engrossed in your phone while crossing the street.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Engrossing» describes the thing; «engrossed» describes the person: «an engrossing book», «I was engrossed». Spelling: double s. Similar words: gripping, absorbing, fascinating.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To engulf something is to cover or surround it completely, like a wave, flames or fog swallowing it up. 2) If a feeling engulfs you, it suddenly fills you completely: «Panic engulfed him».
its sense in the lessons: In geography and science it describes floods, lava, sandstorms or fire covering an area; in biology, a white blood cell can engulf a germ to destroy it. In stories it creates a dramatic picture of something being swallowed or overwhelmed. Phrases: «engulfed in flames», «engulfed by the sea», «engulfed by fear».
examples from the lessons: Flames engulfed the old barn. | A huge wave engulfed the sandcastle. | Thick fog engulfed the town overnight. | Lava from the volcano engulfed the village. | A wave of sadness engulfed her when her dog died. | White blood cells engulf germs and destroy them. | The crowd engulfed the singer as she left the stage.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: engulfed, engulfing. Often passive: «engulfed in/by». Stronger than «cover»: it means completely surrounded or swallowed.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To enjoin someone to do something is to order or strongly urge them to do it. 2) (law) To enjoin someone from doing something, especially in the USA, is for a court to forbid them to do it with an official order (an injunction).
its sense in the lessons: An old-fashioned or legal word, found in religious texts, formal rules and law reports. In the Bible and church writing, people are enjoined to love, pray or forgive. In news it means a court has stopped someone: «The company was enjoined from selling the toy». Phrases: «enjoin someone to do», «enjoin someone from doing», «enjoin silence».
examples from the lessons: The rules enjoin all pupils to wear their uniform properly. | The scriptures enjoin believers to love their neighbours. | The judge enjoined the factory from dumping waste in the river. | Her parents enjoined her to be careful on the trip. | The captain enjoined silence on deck. | The court enjoined the company from using the name.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Confusing: «enjoin to» means order, but «enjoin from» (US law) means forbid. Very formal; in speech say «tell», «order» or «ban». Noun: injunction (a court order).

part of speech: verb -ing form of enjoin (enjoin, enjoins, enjoined, enjoining); noun (the enjoining — rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Enjoining is ordering or strongly urging someone to do something (formal). 2) (law) Enjoining is a court forbidding someone to do something by an official order.
its sense in the lessons: See «enjoin». It appears in formal reports, law news and religious writing, usually in the present participle: «a sign enjoining visitors to keep off the grass». Phrases: «enjoining someone to», «a court enjoining».
examples from the lessons: The poster was enjoining everyone to wash their hands. | The preacher spent the sermon enjoining us to forgive. | A court is enjoining the firm from building on the field. | Signs enjoining silence hung in the library. | The headteacher's letter, enjoining parents to read with their children, went home on Friday. | The judge is considering enjoining the sale.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The -ing form of «enjoin»; keep the single n before -ing. Very formal; in speech say «telling», «urging» or «banning».

part of speech: verb -ing form of enlist (enlist, enlists, enlisted, enlisting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Enlisting is joining the army, navy or air force, or signing someone up for them. 2) Enlisting someone's help is asking for and getting their help or support for a job.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, many young men were enlisting in 1914 at the start of the First World War, some lying about their age. In everyday life, enlisting help means getting others to join in: «enlisting friends to clean the beach». Phrases: «enlisting in the army», «enlisting the help of», «enlisting volunteers».
examples from the lessons: Thousands of young men were enlisting in 1914. | He is thinking about enlisting in the navy after school. | We are enlisting the help of parents for the school fair. | The teacher is enlisting volunteers to plant trees. | By enlisting her older brother, she finished the model in time. | Posters encouraged people to go enlisting at the town hall.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «enlist» (en- + list: to put your name on the list). Past: enlisted. Noun: enlistment. «Enlist in» the army; «enlist someone's help».

part of speech: adjective (enraged; more enraged, most enraged); verb past form of enrage (enrage, enrages, enraged, enraging)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Enraged means extremely angry, full of rage. 2) As a verb form, enraged means made someone extremely angry.
its sense in the lessons: A strong feeling word in stories and news, much stronger than «cross» or «annoyed». In reading lessons, it tells the reader a character has lost their temper and may do something wild; in nature writing, an enraged animal (a bull, a bear) is dangerous. Phrases: «enraged by», «enraged at», «an enraged crowd».
examples from the lessons: The giant was enraged when he found his gold gone. | The unfair decision enraged the fans. | An enraged bull charged at the fence. | She was enraged by the rude comments. | The news of the cancelled trip enraged the whole class. | Keep away from an enraged dog.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Enraged» describes the angry person; «enraging» describes what causes it: «an enraging decision». Scale of anger: annoyed < cross < angry < furious ≈ enraged.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Enthusiasm is a strong feeling of excitement and interest in something, and wanting to do it. 2) An enthusiasm (countable) is a hobby or interest that you love: «Dinosaurs are his great enthusiasm».
its sense in the lessons: In school reports, teachers praise pupils who show enthusiasm for learning; in sports, the coach likes enthusiasm in training. In stories, enthusiasm shows a character is eager and keen. Phrases: «with enthusiasm», «full of enthusiasm», «show enthusiasm», «lose your enthusiasm», «enthusiasm for».
examples from the lessons: She joined the choir with great enthusiasm. | The class showed lots of enthusiasm for the science project. | His enthusiasm for football never fades. | After the rain started, we lost our enthusiasm for the picnic. | The teacher's enthusiasm made maths fun. | Painting is one of Grandad's many enthusiasms. | The crowd cheered with enthusiasm.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable: «a lot of enthusiasm», not «many enthusiasms» (unless you mean hobbies). Preposition: enthusiasm for something. Adjective: enthusiastic; person: enthusiast. Spelling: enthUsiasm.

meaning for a pupil: 1) If you do something enthusiastically, you do it with excitement, eagerness and lots of energy. 2) It can also mean warmly and strongly in favour: «The plan was enthusiastically received».
its sense in the lessons: Used in reports, stories and descriptions to show how keenly someone acts: clapping, agreeing, joining in. In a school report: «She takes part enthusiastically in every lesson». Phrases: «nodded enthusiastically», «clapped enthusiastically», «enthusiastically welcomed».
examples from the lessons: The children clapped enthusiastically after the play. | He nodded enthusiastically when asked if he wanted cake. | She takes part enthusiastically in every PE lesson. | The new playground was enthusiastically welcomed. | The dog wagged its tail enthusiastically. | They enthusiastically cleaned the beach all morning.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: ends in -ically (enthusiastic + ally), not «enthusiasticly». Adjective: enthusiastic; noun: enthusiasm.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An entity is something that exists as a separate, single thing with its own identity, such as a company, a country or a living being. 2) (formal) In law and business, an entity is an organisation treated as one unit, such as «a legal entity». 3) In computing and stories, an entity can be any object or being: a character in a game, or a mysterious creature or ghost.
its sense in the lessons: A formal, general word used when you want to talk about «a thing» without saying exactly what kind. In science and philosophy it means anything that exists. In computing, game characters and objects are called entities. In spooky stories, «an entity» is an unknown being. Phrases: «a separate entity», «a legal entity», «a single entity».
examples from the lessons: The school and the nursery are separate entities. | A company is a legal entity, like a person in the eyes of the law. | Each country is an independent entity. | In the game, every monster is an entity with its own health points. | The ghost story was about a strange entity in the attic. | The team works together as a single entity.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: entities (y → ies). Countable: an entity. Formal; in everyday speech say «thing», «body» or «organisation».

meaning for a pupil: 1) An epiphyte is a plant that grows on another plant, usually a tree, for support, but does not take food from it; it gets water and nutrients from the air, rain and bits of rubbish.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on rainforests and plant adaptations, epiphytes like many orchids, bromeliads, mosses and ferns live high on tree branches to reach sunlight. It is a good example of a plant that uses another without harming it (unlike a parasite). Phrases: «epiphytic plants», «epiphytes in the rainforest canopy».
examples from the lessons: An orchid growing on a tree branch is an epiphyte. | Epiphytes live high in the rainforest to get more light. | Moss on an oak tree is a kind of epiphyte. | Bromeliads are epiphytes that hold water in their leaves. | An epiphyte does not steal food from its tree. | Tiny frogs lay eggs in pools inside epiphytes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say it «EP-ih-fite». Plural: epiphytes. Adjective: epiphytic. Trap: an epiphyte is not a parasite; mistletoe is a parasite because it takes food from the tree, but an orchid is an epiphyte.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (Bible, church) An Epistle is one of the letters in the New Testament written by early Christian leaders such as Paul, Peter and John to churches or people. 2) (formal or humorous) An epistle is a long, formal letter.
its sense in the lessons: In church and RE lessons, the Epistles are read aloud in services, and part of the service is called «the Epistle» reading. Examples are the Epistle to the Romans and the First Epistle of John. In everyday talk, calling a letter «an epistle» is a joke meaning it is very long or serious. Phrases: «the Epistles of Paul», «the Epistle reading».
examples from the lessons: Paul wrote an epistle to the church in Rome. | In church today we heard a reading from the Epistle to the Corinthians. | The New Testament contains many epistles. | Christians believe the Epistles teach how to live as followers of Jesus. | Grandma sent me a three-page epistle about her holiday. | The Epistle reading comes before the Gospel.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say it «ih-PISS-ul»; the t is silent. Capitalised for a Bible book: the Epistle to the Romans. Adjective: epistolary (written as letters, as in a novel told through letters).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Equine means to do with horses or like a horse: «equine vet», «equine flu». 2) (rare noun) An equine is a horse or an animal of the horse family, such as a donkey or zebra.
its sense in the lessons: Used in science, farming and vet talk about horses: equine health, equine centres, equine therapy. In biology, the horse family (horses, donkeys, zebras) is called the equines. In descriptions, an «equine face» is long, like a horse's. Phrases: «equine vet», «equine centre», «equine therapy».
examples from the lessons: She wants to be an equine vet when she grows up. | The riding school is also an equine rescue centre. | Equine flu stopped the horse races for a week. | Zebras and donkeys are equine animals. | The farm offers equine therapy for children. | The statue had a proud equine head.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say it «EK-wine». From Latin equus, horse. Related words: equestrian (to do with horse riding). Compare: canine (dogs), feline (cats), bovine (cows).

meaning for a pupil: 1) The erection of a building, statue or tent is the act of building it or putting it up. 2) (formal) An erection can be a building or structure itself, especially one that is not liked. 3) (adult, body word) a word grown-ups use about the body; not for school.
its sense in the lessons: In history and building topics, it is a formal word for putting something up: «the erection of a wall», «the erection of the statue in 1890». Everyday speech usually says «putting up» or «building». Phrases: «the erection of a monument», «erection of scaffolding».
