examples from the lessons: The erection of the new bridge took two years. | Workers began the erection of the tents for the festival. | A sign announced the erection of a statue in the park. | The erection of the castle walls kept invaders out. | Planning permission is needed for the erection of a garden wall. | The erection of scaffolding blocked the pavement.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; from the verb «erect» (to build, put up). In everyday writing, prefer «building» or «putting up» to avoid giggles. Countable when it means a structure.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal, medical) Eructation is the scientific word for burping: letting air or gas from the stomach come up and out through the mouth.
its sense in the lessons: A very formal or medical word; doctors and science books use it, but at home people say «burp» or «belch». Writers sometimes use it as a joke, because a long fancy word for a burp sounds funny. In science, it is linked to digestion and fizzy drinks. Phrases: «eructation after meals».
examples from the lessons: Eructation is the medical word for a burp. | Fizzy drinks can cause eructation. | Cows release a lot of gas by eructation. | The doctor asked if he had any eructation after eating. | «Pardon my eructation,» said Dad, making everyone laugh. | Babies need help with eructation after feeding.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable in general, countable for single burps. Verb: eruct (rare). Everyday words: burp, belch. Say «excuse me» after a burp in company.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Espresso is a strong, dark coffee made by forcing very hot water through finely ground coffee beans. 2) An espresso is one small cup of this coffee.
its sense in the lessons: Mostly in grown-up everyday life: cafés, kitchens, coffee machines. It is the base of many coffee drinks such as cappuccino and latte. In science and health lessons, it is an example of a drink with lots of caffeine, which is not good for children. Phrases: «a shot of espresso», «double espresso», «espresso machine».
examples from the lessons: Dad orders an espresso after lunch. | The café has a shiny new espresso machine. | A cappuccino is espresso with frothy milk. | An espresso comes in a very small cup. | Espresso has a lot of caffeine, so it's not for kids. | Mum asked for a double espresso to wake up.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Italian word for «pressed out». Plural: espressos. Common mistake: «expresso» with an x is wrong in careful spelling. Say «es-PRESS-oh».

meaning for a pupil: 1) An estimation is a careful guess of a number or amount, made without counting or measuring exactly. 2) Estimation is the skill or act of making such guesses. 3) (formal) Your estimation of someone is your opinion of them: «She went up in my estimation».
its sense in the lessons: In maths, estimation means rounding numbers to check whether an answer is sensible, or guessing how many sweets are in a jar or how long a line is. In science, you estimate before measuring. In everyday life, «go up / down in someone's estimation» means they think better or worse of you. Phrases: «a rough estimation», «in my estimation», «go up in someone's estimation».
examples from the lessons: My estimation was 50 sweets, and there were 47. | Use estimation to check your answer: 298 + 403 is about 700. | Estimation is useful when you don't have a ruler. | A rough estimation of the crowd was ten thousand people. | In my estimation, the film was too long. | He went up in my estimation when he helped the new boy. | Our estimation of the journey time was wrong because of traffic.
note for the reader of a maths problem: In maths, an estimation is not the exact answer; the sign ≈ means «approximately». Round first (298 ≈ 300) and then calculate. «Estimate» (noun and verb) is more common: «make an estimate». Countable or uncountable.

part of speech: adjective (etched); verb past form of etch (etch, etches, etched, etching)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Etched means cut or scratched into a hard surface like glass, metal or stone, often with acid or a sharp tool, to make a picture or words. 2) If something is etched on your memory or face, it stays there clearly and does not go away: «The day was etched in my memory».
its sense in the lessons: In art lessons, etching is a printmaking method where a picture is cut into a metal plate with acid. In stories, «worry was etched on his face» shows strong feelings that are easy to see. Phrases: «etched in glass», «etched in my memory», «etched on her face».
examples from the lessons: Their names were etched on the silver trophy. | The window had a pattern etched into the glass. | The artist etched a picture onto a copper plate. | That holiday is etched in my memory forever. | Fear was etched on the boy's face. | Old graffiti was etched into the stone wall.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past form adds -ed: etch → etched. Noun: etching (a picture made this way). «Etched in / on your memory» is a fixed phrase meaning you will never forget it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (a name) Etna, or Mount Etna, is a large, active volcano on the island of Sicily in southern Italy; it is the highest active volcano in Europe outside the Caucasus.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons on volcanoes and Italy, Etna is a famous example of an active volcano that often erupts, while people still farm and live on its slopes because the volcanic soil is very rich. Phrases: «Mount Etna», «Etna erupted».
examples from the lessons: Mount Etna is on the island of Sicily. | Etna erupts quite often, sending lava down its sides. | Farmers grow grapes and oranges on Etna's rich soil. | We watched a video of Etna glowing at night. | Etna is one of the most active volcanoes in the world. | Ash from Etna closed the airport for a day.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A name, written with a capital E. Not an ordinary English word. Height is about 3,300 metres, but it changes with eruptions.

part of speech: adjective (Etruscan); noun (an Etruscan, Etruscans; the Etruscan language)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The Etruscans were an ancient people who lived in central Italy, in an area called Etruria (roughly modern Tuscany), before and during the early days of Rome. 2) Etruscan means belonging to these people, their art or their language. 3) Etruscan is also the name of their language, which used an alphabet like the Greek one and is still only partly understood.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons about ancient Rome, the Etruscans come up as the neighbours who ruled Rome for a time and taught the Romans things such as arches, gladiator games and parts of the alphabet. Their painted tombs and bronze statues are famous in museums. Phrases: «Etruscan tombs», «Etruscan kings», «the Etruscan alphabet».
examples from the lessons: The Etruscans lived in Italy before the Romans became powerful. | We saw an Etruscan vase in the museum. | Some early kings of Rome were Etruscans. | Etruscan tombs are painted with scenes of feasts and music. | Experts can read Etruscan letters but understand only some of the words. | The Romans learnt a lot from Etruscan builders.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A name of a people: written with a capital E. Plural: Etruscans. Say «ih-TRUS-kun».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Etymological means to do with etymology, the history of where words come from and how their meanings and forms have changed.
its sense in the lessons: In English and spelling lessons, an etymological explanation tells you why a word is spelled the way it is, for example the silent b in «doubt» was added because of the Latin word «dubitare». Dictionaries often have an etymological note at the end of an entry. Phrases: «etymological dictionary», «etymological roots», «etymological note».
examples from the lessons: The etymological dictionary shows that «sandwich» comes from a person's name. | An etymological link connects «tele» in telephone and television. | Our teacher gave an etymological reason for the silent k in «knight». | The book has etymological notes for every word. | Many science words have Greek etymological roots. | There is no etymological connection between «island» and «isle», even though they look alike.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb: etymologically. Do not confuse with «entomological», which is about insects. Say «et-ih-muh-LOJ-ih-kul».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Etymology is the study of where words come from and how they have changed over time. 2) The etymology of a word is its own history: which language it came from and what it meant before.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons, knowing the etymology of a word helps with spelling and meaning: «bicycle» has «bi» (two) and «cycle» (wheel) from Greek and Latin. Many English words come from Latin, Greek, French, Old Norse and Old English. Phrases: «the etymology of», «folk etymology» (a popular but wrong story about a word's origin).
examples from the lessons: The etymology of «breakfast» is «breaking your fast» after the night. | I love etymology because every word has a story. | «Dinosaur» has a Greek etymology meaning «terrible lizard». | The dictionary gives the etymology at the end of each entry. | Etymology shows that «hello» and «hallo» are related. | Some funny stories about word origins are false etymologies.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: etymologies. Do not confuse with «entomology», the study of insects (remember: insects have six legs, and «ent» like «ant»). Many famous word-origin stories (for example that «posh» means «port out, starboard home») are myths.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To evaluate something is to judge how good, useful or successful it is, after thinking about it carefully. 2) In maths, to evaluate an expression is to work out its value as a number: «Evaluate 3 × (4 + 2)».
its sense in the lessons: In school, pupils evaluate their own work, a design in DT or an experiment in science, saying what went well and what could be better. In maths it is an instruction word: find the number. In reading, you evaluate a source to see whether it is reliable. Phrases: «evaluate your work», «evaluate the evidence», «evaluate the expression».
examples from the lessons: Evaluate your model bridge: did it hold the weight? | Evaluate 5 + 3 × 2 (the answer is 11). | The teacher evaluated our stories and gave feedback. | Scientists evaluate the results of an experiment carefully. | We need to evaluate which website gives true facts. | Evaluate the expression 2a when a = 7. | Doctors evaluate a patient before choosing a treatment.
note for the reader of a maths problem: In maths, «evaluate» means «work out the value», so remember the order of operations (brackets, then × and ÷, then + and −). Noun: evaluation. Not the same as «estimate»: to evaluate you work it out properly.

meaning for a pupil: 1) If someone is evasive, they avoid giving a clear, direct answer, often because they are hiding something. 2) Evasive action is a quick movement to avoid danger, such as swerving or ducking.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and the news, an evasive answer is a clue that a character or politician may be hiding the truth. In safety talk, a driver or pilot «takes evasive action» to avoid a crash. In nature, animals use evasive moves to escape predators. Phrases: «an evasive answer», «be evasive about», «take evasive action».
examples from the lessons: When I asked who ate the cake, my brother was very evasive. | The minister gave an evasive answer to the question. | The pilot took evasive action to avoid the birds. | The rabbit made evasive zigzags to escape the fox. | Stop being evasive and tell me what happened! | Her evasive reply made the detective suspicious.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: evade (to avoid); noun: evasion. Adverb: evasively. Trap: «tax evasion» (illegal, hiding money) is different from «tax avoidance» (using legal tricks).

part of speech: adjective (everlasting); noun (an everlasting — a kind of flower)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Everlasting means lasting for ever, never ending. 2) (informal) Everlasting can also mean going on far too long and boring: «his everlasting complaints». 3) (church, Bible) In Christian prayers and the Bible, God and eternal life are called everlasting: «everlasting life». 4) An everlasting (noun) is a flower that keeps its shape and colour when dried.
its sense in the lessons: In church, hymns and Bible lessons, «everlasting» often appears: «God is everlasting», «life everlasting»; Christians believe in everlasting life with God. In stories and fairy tales, there are everlasting gobstoppers, everlasting love or an everlasting winter. In everyday speech, people use it to complain about something that never stops. Phrases: «everlasting life», «everlasting love», «for ever and ever».
examples from the lessons: Christians believe that God's love is everlasting. | The witch cast a spell of everlasting winter. | In the story, the sweet was an everlasting gobstopper. | I'm tired of my sister's everlasting questions! | The hymn spoke of life everlasting. | Nothing on Earth is truly everlasting. | Mum dried some everlastings for a vase.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Built from «ever» + «lasting». Similar words: eternal, endless, permanent. In science, very little is truly everlasting: even mountains wear away and stars burn out.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Exactitude is the quality of being completely exact, correct and careful about small details.
its sense in the lessons: A formal word for exactness or precision, used in science, maths and careful work: measuring with exactitude, describing events with exactitude. In stories it describes a careful character, like a watchmaker or a detective. Phrases: «with exactitude», «scientific exactitude».
examples from the lessons: The scientist measured the liquid with great exactitude. | We can't say with exactitude when the castle was built. | The watchmaker worked with exactitude. | Maps need exactitude, or ships may get lost. | The detective described the room with exactitude. | Exam markers check answers with exactitude.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable, formal. Everyday words: exactness, accuracy, precision. In maths, an exact answer is not rounded: 1/3 is exact, 0.33 is only approximate.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Something exchangeable can be swapped or traded for something else. 2) In shops, goods that are exchangeable can be taken back and changed for a different item, size or colour.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, shops print «exchangeable within 28 days» on receipts. In money lessons, coins are exchangeable for other currency at a bank. In maths and science, things that are exchangeable can be swapped without changing the result, like the numbers in 3 + 4 = 4 + 3. Phrases: «exchangeable for», «exchangeable but not refundable».
examples from the lessons: The shoes are exchangeable if they don't fit. | Sale items are not exchangeable. | Tokens are exchangeable for prizes at the arcade. | Pounds are exchangeable for euros at the bank. | In addition, the two numbers are exchangeable: 2 + 5 = 5 + 2. | These parts are exchangeable between the two toy cars.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Built from «exchange» + «-able»; keep the e after g (exchangeable) so g stays soft. «Exchangeable» (you can swap it) is not the same as «refundable» (you get your money back). Maths word for swappable order: commutative.

part of speech: verb -ing form of excrete (excrete, excretes, excreted, excreting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Excreting is getting rid of waste from the body, such as urine (wee), faeces (poo) or sweat. 2) In plants and other living things, excreting means pushing out waste materials they do not need.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, excretion is one of the life processes of living things (MRS GREN: movement, respiration, sensitivity, growth, reproduction, excretion, nutrition). Kidneys excrete waste in urine; skin excretes sweat; lungs get rid of carbon dioxide. Phrases: «excreting waste», «excreting through the kidneys».
examples from the lessons: The kidneys are always excreting waste in urine. | All living things need excreting as a life process. | Fish are excreting ammonia into the water. | Plants get rid of oxygen as waste through their leaves, a kind of excreting. | Sweat is a way of excreting water and salt. | The body is excreting the medicine through the kidneys.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Science word; noun: excretion. Do not confuse with «secrete» (to make and release something useful, like saliva) or with «egestion» (getting rid of undigested food). Spelling: excrete (one t), excreting (drop the e).

meaning for a pupil: 1) An execution is the killing of a person as an official punishment for a crime, decided by a court or ruler. 2) The execution of a plan, task or skill is the doing or carrying out of it, and how well it is done: «Great idea, poor execution». 3) (law, computing) Execution can mean carrying out a will or legal order, or a computer running a program.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, executions such as those of Anne Boleyn or Charles I are part of the story of kings and laws; many countries, including the UK, Canada, Australia, New Zealand and Ireland, no longer use the death penalty, while some US states still do. In sport, art and gymnastics, judges mark the execution of a move. In coding, «execution» is when the computer runs your program. Phrases: «the execution of a plan», «public execution», «carry out an execution».
examples from the lessons: Charles I's execution took place in London in 1649. | Many countries have banned execution as a punishment. | The plan was clever, but the execution was messy. | The gymnast scored high marks for execution. | The program stops execution when it finds an error. | The lawyer was in charge of the execution of the will.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Sensitive topic: speak calmly and factually. Verb: execute (executes, executed, executing). Person who carries out executions: executioner. Do not confuse with «executive» (a manager in a company).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Something exhaustive is complete and thorough, covering every part or every possibility. 2) In maths, an exhaustive list or search tries all the possible cases.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and logic, an «exhaustive search» or «exhaustive list» means you have checked every possibility, for example listing all the ways to make 10p. In science and history, an exhaustive study leaves nothing out. Phrases: «an exhaustive list», «an exhaustive search», «exhaustive research».
examples from the lessons: The police made an exhaustive search of the woods. | This is not an exhaustive list, just some examples. | We made an exhaustive list of all the ways to make 5 with two dice. | The book is an exhaustive guide to British birds. | After exhaustive tests, the medicine was approved. | Her answer was exhaustive and covered every point.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: «exhaustive» means complete, not tiring; tiring is «exhausting». An exhaustive search can be exhausting! Adverb: exhaustively.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) An exhortation is a strong, serious request or speech that urges people to do something. 2) (church) In some church services, an exhortation is a short talk encouraging the people to live well or to prepare for prayer or communion.
its sense in the lessons: Found in formal writing, history and religion: a general gives an exhortation to the troops before battle; a preacher gives an exhortation to the congregation. In everyday life, a coach's or parent's «exhortations» are their repeated urgings. Phrases: «an exhortation to», «despite all exhortations».
examples from the lessons: The general's exhortation filled the soldiers with courage. | Despite the teacher's exhortations, nobody tidied up. | The preacher ended with an exhortation to love one another. | Posters carried exhortations to save water. | The coach shouted exhortations from the side of the pitch. | Paul's letters are full of exhortations to be kind and patient.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal. Verb: exhort (to urge strongly). Say «eg-zor-TAY-shun»; the h is silent.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Existential means to do with existence, especially the big questions about why we exist and what life means. 2) An existential threat or danger is one that could end something completely, such as a species, a country or the world. 3) (informal) An «existential crisis» is a time when someone worries deeply about the meaning of their life, often used jokingly.
its sense in the lessons: In philosophy and big-questions lessons, existential questions are «Why am I here?» and «What is the point of life?». In the news, climate change or a war may be called an existential threat. Young people sometimes joke about having an existential crisis over small things. Phrases: «existential questions», «existential threat», «existential crisis».
examples from the lessons: Asking «Why do we exist?» is an existential question. | Some scientists call climate change an existential threat. | My brother had an existential crisis when he turned eighteen. | Losing its forest is an existential danger for the orangutan. | Philosophers have argued about existential ideas for centuries. | «I'm having an existential crisis about which cereal to choose,» joked Mum.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal word. Related: exist, existence; existentialism (a philosophy of the 1900s). In grammar, «there is / there are» is called an existential sentence.

part of speech: verb past form of exonerate (exonerate, exonerates, exonerated, exonerating); adjective (exonerated)
meaning for a pupil: 1) If someone is exonerated, they are officially shown or declared not guilty of something they were blamed or accused of. 2) More generally, it means freed from blame.
its sense in the lessons: In law and news reports, a prisoner may be exonerated by new evidence such as DNA, after years in prison. In stories and detective tales, the innocent suspect is exonerated at the end. In everyday life, a pupil can be exonerated when the real culprit owns up. Phrases: «exonerated of», «fully exonerated», «exonerated by DNA evidence».
examples from the lessons: The man was exonerated after DNA proved he was innocent. | The inquiry exonerated the nurse of any blame. | When the real thief confessed, Sam was exonerated. | She was fully exonerated by the court. | The video exonerated the goalkeeper. | In the story, the detective exonerated the butler.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal. Noun: exoneration. Usually «exonerated of» something or «exonerated by» evidence. Similar: cleared, acquitted (found not guilty at trial).

meaning for a pupil: 1) An exoskeleton is a hard outer covering that supports and protects the body of animals such as insects, spiders, crabs and lobsters, instead of bones inside. 2) A robotic exoskeleton is a machine suit worn on the outside of the body to help a person walk or lift heavy things.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on animals, invertebrates with an exoskeleton (insects, crustaceans, spiders) are compared with vertebrates that have an endoskeleton (bones inside). An animal must shed or moult its exoskeleton to grow. In technology news, exoskeleton suits help people with injured legs walk again. Phrases: «shed its exoskeleton», «a robotic exoskeleton».
examples from the lessons: A beetle's exoskeleton is hard and shiny. | Crabs moult their exoskeleton as they grow. | We have an endoskeleton, but insects have an exoskeleton. | The exoskeleton protects the spider's soft body. | A robotic exoskeleton helped the man walk again. | We found the empty exoskeleton of a cicada on a tree.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Exo-» means outside; «endo-» means inside. Plural: exoskeletons. Trap: snails have a shell, but it is usually not called an exoskeleton in school.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Exotic means coming from or belonging to a faraway country, especially a hot one, and seeming unusual and exciting. 2) Exotic can mean very unusual and colourful, not ordinary. 3) (science) An exotic species is a plant or animal brought into a place where it does not naturally live.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and food lessons, exotic fruits (mango, papaya, dragon fruit) and exotic animals are compared with local ones. In science and nature, exotic or invasive species, like rabbits in Australia or grey squirrels in Britain, can harm native wildlife. Be careful: calling people «exotic» can sound unkind, as if they are strange. Phrases: «exotic fruit», «exotic pets», «exotic places».
examples from the lessons: We tried exotic fruits like lychees and passion fruit. | Parrots are exotic birds from warm countries. | The holiday brochure showed exotic beaches. | Keeping exotic pets like snakes needs special care. | Rabbits were an exotic species in Australia and spread everywhere. | Her costume was bright and exotic.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposites: native, local, ordinary. «Exotic» depends on where you are: a kangaroo is exotic in Ireland but ordinary in Australia. Avoid using it to describe people.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal, medical) Expectoration is coughing up and spitting out mucus (phlegm) from the chest and throat. 2) More generally, it is a formal word for spitting.
its sense in the lessons: A medical word used by doctors when someone has a chest infection or a cold. Old signs in buses and stations once said «No expectoration» to stop people spitting, which spreads germs. In health lessons, it links to germs, coughs and hygiene. Phrases: «cough with expectoration», «medicine to help expectoration».
examples from the lessons: The doctor asked about his cough and expectoration. | Some cough syrups help with expectoration. | An old tram sign said «Expectoration forbidden». | Expectoration in public spreads germs. | Catch coughs in a tissue to avoid spreading what comes up with expectoration. | Expectoration is a fancy word for spitting.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal or medical; everyday words: coughing up, spitting. Verb: expectorate. Medicine that helps you cough up mucus is called an expectorant.

part of speech: verb -ing form of expel (expel, expels, expelled, expelling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Expelling someone is officially making them leave a school, club or country because of bad behaviour. 2) Expelling something is forcing it out, such as air from the lungs or gas from an engine.
its sense in the lessons: In school life, expelling a pupil is the most serious punishment, worse than being suspended or excluded for a few days. In science, the lungs are expelling air when you breathe out; a volcano is expelling lava and ash. In history, rulers expelled groups of people from countries. Phrases: «expelling air», «expelling a pupil», «expelling from the country».
examples from the lessons: The school is expelling him for bullying. | When you breathe out, you are expelling air from your lungs. | The volcano was expelling ash for days. | A rocket moves by expelling hot gas backwards. | The club is expelling members who cheat. | Whales blow by expelling air through their blowholes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: double l in expelled and expelling (expel → expelling). Noun: expulsion. In the UK, «excluded» is the official school word; «expelled» is common in speech.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Experimentation is the process of trying out experiments to test ideas and find things out. 2) It can also mean trying new and different ways of doing things to see what works.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, experimentation is at the heart of the scientific method: ask a question, predict, test fairly, measure and conclude. In art, cooking and music, experimentation means trying new ideas boldly. In ethics, animal experimentation is a topic people argue about. Phrases: «scientific experimentation», «animal experimentation», «through experimentation».
examples from the lessons: Through experimentation, we found which paper towel soaked up the most water. | Science moves forward through careful experimentation. | The chef loves experimentation with new flavours. | People disagree about animal experimentation. | The band's new album shows a lot of experimentation. | Experimentation taught her that the plant grew best near the window.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Related: experiment (noun: an experiment; verb: experiment with). A fair test changes only one thing at a time.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Extensively means a lot, widely, or over a large area or many places. 2) It can also mean in great detail and thoroughly.
its sense in the lessons: In reports, news and science writing: «The area was extensively damaged by the flood», «She has travelled extensively». In research, a topic «extensively studied» has had lots of work done on it. Phrases: «travelled extensively», «extensively damaged», «extensively used».
examples from the lessons: The village was extensively flooded after the storm. | She has travelled extensively in Asia. | The book was extensively researched. | Plastic is used extensively in packaging. | Bees have been studied extensively by scientists. | The old house was extensively repaired.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: extensive (large, wide-ranging). Spelling: extensive + ly. Similar: widely, greatly, thoroughly.

part of speech: verb past form of exterminate (exterminate, exterminates, exterminated, exterminating); adjective (exterminated)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Exterminated means killed completely, so that a whole group of animals, insects or pests is destroyed. 2) In history, it can describe the mass killing of a group of people, which is one of the worst crimes.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, pests like rats, cockroaches or termites are exterminated by pest-control workers (exterminators). In history lessons, the word is used about the Holocaust and other genocides, when the Nazis tried to exterminate the Jews of Europe; it should be used seriously and respectfully. In science fiction, the Daleks in «Doctor Who» famously shout «Exterminate!». Phrases: «exterminated pests», «completely exterminated».
examples from the lessons: The termites in the shed were exterminated. | The dodo was hunted until it was exterminated. | Millions of people were exterminated in the Holocaust. | Wolves were exterminated from Britain hundreds of years ago. | The council exterminated the rats near the bins. | In the film, the robots wanted every human exterminated.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Serious word; when speaking about people, use it only for real historical facts. Noun: extermination; person: exterminator. Similar: wipe out, destroy, eradicate.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To extirpate something is to destroy it completely, pulling it out by the roots. 2) (science) A species is extirpated from an area when it dies out there but still lives elsewhere. 3) (medical) To extirpate can mean to remove an organ or growth completely by surgery.
its sense in the lessons: A rare, formal word. In nature and conservation, wolves were extirpated from Britain, but they still live in Canada; bears were extirpated in many places. In history and formal writing, people tried to extirpate ideas, diseases or crimes. Phrases: «extirpate a disease», «extirpated from the region».
examples from the lessons: The government tried to extirpate the disease completely. | Beavers were extirpated from England but have now returned. | Gardeners try to extirpate weeds by the roots. | The king vowed to extirpate all rebels. | The species is extirpated from Ireland but still lives in Scotland. | The surgeon extirpated the growth.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Very formal; everyday speech says «wipe out» or «root out». Say «EK-ster-pate». Noun: extirpation. Difference: extinct = gone everywhere; extirpated = gone from one area only.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To extrude something is to push or squeeze it out through a small opening, often to give it a shape, like toothpaste from a tube. 2) In industry and technology, to extrude plastic, metal or pasta is to force it through a shaped hole to make long pieces.
its sense in the lessons: In design and technology, plastic pipes, window frames and pasta are made by extrusion, and 3D printers extrude melted plastic in thin lines. In geography and science, volcanoes extrude lava onto the surface (extrusive rock). In maths, «extrude» is used in 3D drawing software to turn a 2D shape into a prism. Phrases: «extrude plastic», «extruded lava», «extrude a shape».
examples from the lessons: The 3D printer extrudes hot plastic to build the model. | Pasta machines extrude dough into spaghetti. | The volcano extruded thick lava. | Squeeze the tube to extrude a line of glue. | In the drawing program, extrude a square to make a cube. | Factories extrude aluminium to make window frames.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: extrusion. Adjective: extrusive (rocks formed from lava on the surface). Opposite idea: intrude (push in). In maths: extruding a 2D shape makes a prism with that shape as its cross-section.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Faintness is a weak, dizzy feeling as if you might faint (pass out). 2) Faintness is also the quality of being faint: hard to see, hear or smell because it is very weak, like the faintness of a star or a sound.
its sense in the lessons: In health and safety lessons, faintness can come from heat, not eating, standing still too long or the sight of blood; first aid says sit or lie down and raise the legs. In science, faintness describes dim light or quiet sounds. In stories, it shows a character is weak or shocked. Phrases: «a feeling of faintness», «the faintness of the light».
examples from the lessons: After running in the heat, she felt a wave of faintness. | Tell an adult if you have faintness or dizziness. | The faintness of the star made it hard to see. | Because of the faintness of the writing, we could barely read the letter. | Faintness can come from skipping breakfast. | He sat down when faintness came over him.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. From «faint» (adjective: weak, pale; verb: to pass out). Do not confuse with «feint» (a pretend move in sport or fencing) or «faint-hearted» (not brave).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Falsification is changing facts, documents, evidence or results in a dishonest way so that they show something untrue. 2) (science, philosophy) Falsification is showing that an idea or theory is false by testing it, which is an important part of how science works.
its sense in the lessons: In law and honesty lessons, falsification of documents, exam results or accounts is cheating and can be a crime. In science, Karl Popper argued that a good theory must be testable so it could be proved false (falsifiability). In history, rulers sometimes used falsification of records as propaganda. Phrases: «falsification of evidence», «falsification of records», «data falsification».
examples from the lessons: The company was fined for falsification of its accounts. | Falsification of exam results is serious cheating. | The scientist lost her job for falsification of data. | Old photos were edited in a falsification of history. | One black swan was enough for the falsification of «all swans are white». | The police found falsification of the passport.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: falsify (falsifies, falsified). Adjective: false. In science, finding evidence that disagrees with a theory is a good thing, not cheating; falsifying results is cheating.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Familiarity is knowing something well because you have seen, heard or done it many times: «familiarity with the rules». 2) Familiarity is a friendly, relaxed way of behaving with someone, as if you know them well. 3) (formal) Too much familiarity is behaving too casually or rudely with someone you do not know well.
its sense in the lessons: In school, familiarity with times tables or a story helps you work faster. In everyday life, the familiarity of home makes us feel safe. The saying «Familiarity breeds contempt» means that when you know something too well you may stop respecting it. Phrases: «familiarity with», «a sense of familiarity», «familiarity breeds contempt».
examples from the lessons: Her familiarity with the town helped us find the café. | Practice gives you familiarity with the times tables. | There was a comforting familiarity about Grandma's kitchen. | The new teacher was surprised by the pupils' familiarity with her first name. | Familiarity with the rules makes the game more fun. | «Familiarity breeds contempt,» said Dad when we got bored with the toy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable; «familiarity with something». Adjective: familiar (familiar to someone, familiar with something). Spelling: familiar + ity.

part of speech: verb past form of fancy (fancy, fancies, fancied, fancying); adjective (fancied)
meaning for a pupil: 1) If you fancied something, you wanted or liked the idea of it (mainly UK): «I fancied a cup of tea». 2) (informal, UK) If you fancied someone, you found them attractive and had a crush on them. 3) (old or formal) Fancied can mean imagined or believed, sometimes wrongly: «He fancied he heard a noise». 4) In sport and racing, a fancied team or horse is one people think will win.
its sense in the lessons: In UK, Irish, Australian and New Zealand everyday speech, «fancy» is very common for wanting: «Fancy a game?». In playground talk, «he fancied her» means he had a crush. In older books, «she fancied herself a princess» means she imagined or thought she was. Phrases: «fancied a…», «fancied himself as», «the fancied team».
examples from the lessons: I fancied pizza for dinner, so we ordered one. | She fancied a walk on the beach. | In Year 6 he fancied a girl in his class. | The fancied team lost in the first round. | He fancied he saw a ghost on the stairs. | She fancied herself as a great singer. | Did you fancy any of the cakes?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: fancy → fancied, fancies (y → i). «Fancy» also means decorated or posh (fancy dress, a fancy hotel). «Fancied himself» can mean he was proud or vain. American English says «I'd like» or «I feel like» more than «I fancy».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A fanfare is a short, loud, exciting tune played on trumpets or other brass instruments to announce someone important or the start of something. 2) Fanfare (uncountable) is a lot of excitement, publicity and showy celebration around something.
its sense in the lessons: In music lessons and history, fanfares announce kings, queens and ceremonies. In everyday life and news, a new phone or film may be launched «with much fanfare», or something may happen «without fanfare», quietly. Phrases: «a fanfare of trumpets», «with great fanfare», «without fanfare».
examples from the lessons: A fanfare of trumpets announced the queen. | The film opened with a loud fanfare. | The new park opened with great fanfare. | He retired quietly, without any fanfare. | Our school band played a fanfare at sports day. | The game was launched with a lot of fanfare online.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable for the tune (a fanfare), uncountable for the fuss (much fanfare). Comes from French. Say «FAN-fair».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) Fantastic means extremely good, wonderful: «a fantastic party». 2) Fantastic means strange and imaginary, like something from a fantasy story: «fantastic creatures». 3) (informal) A fantastic amount is very large: «a fantastic sum of money».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and school, teachers say «Fantastic work!» as praise. In reading lessons, fantastic beasts and fantastic worlds belong to fantasy stories, not real life. Phrases: «fantastic!», «a fantastic time», «fantastic beasts».
examples from the lessons: We had a fantastic time at the beach. | Fantastic work on your story! | The book is full of fantastic creatures like dragons and griffins. | The view from the mountain was fantastic. | He told a fantastic tale about flying to the moon. | The prize was a fantastic amount of money.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Used a lot in speech; in careful writing, choose a more exact word (excellent, imaginative). Adverb: fantastically. Related: fantasy (imaginary stories). Old sense «imaginary» is still used in stories.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A farce is a funny play or film full of silly situations, mix-ups, chases and people hiding in cupboards. 2) (informal) A farce is a situation that is so badly organised or unfair that it is ridiculous: «The sports day was a farce».
its sense in the lessons: In drama and English lessons, farce is a type of comedy with fast action and unlikely events. In everyday life and news, people complain that a meeting, a match or a trial was «a farce» when it went badly. Phrases: «a complete farce», «turn into a farce».
examples from the lessons: We watched a farce where everyone kept slamming doors. | The match was a farce because the referee didn't turn up. | The school trip turned into a farce when the bus broke down. | The play is a farce full of mistaken identities. | Calling that a fair vote is a farce! | Farce is one of the oldest kinds of comedy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: farcical. Say «farss». It is a strong criticism when used about real events.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (rude, slang) Fatso is an insulting name for a fat person.
its sense in the lessons: It is a rude word used in bullying and name-calling; in stories, a bully may shout it. In lessons on kindness and health, it is an example of hurtful body-shaming: people come in many shapes and sizes, and calling names hurts. Sometimes friends use it as a joke nickname, but it can still upset people. Phrases: none that are kind.
examples from the lessons: The bully shouted «fatso» at him, and he went red. | Calling someone fatso is unkind and can hurt for a long time. | In the story, the boy who was called fatso became the hero. | Our class rule is no name-calling, like «fatso» or «weirdo». | She told a teacher when they kept calling her fatso. | Never call anyone fatso, even as a joke.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Rude and hurtful; do not use it. Plural: fatsos. If someone calls you names, tell a trusted adult.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Favoritism is unfairly treating one person or group better than others, because you like them more, not because they deserve it.
its sense in the lessons: In school and family life, children notice favoritism when a teacher always picks the same pupil or a parent seems to prefer one child. In citizenship, favoritism in jobs or government is unfair and can be corruption. In stories, a parent's favoritism often causes jealousy between brothers and sisters, like Jacob giving Joseph the special coat in the Bible. Phrases: «show favoritism», «accused of favoritism».
examples from the lessons: The coach was accused of favoritism because his son always played. | It's favoritism if the teacher only picks her friends' children. | Jacob's favoritism towards Joseph made his brothers jealous. | Parents try not to show favoritism. | Favoritism in hiring is unfair to good workers. | «That's favoritism!» my brother shouted when I got the bigger slice.
note for the reader of a maths problem: American spelling: favoritism; UK, Ireland, Australia, New Zealand and Canada usually write favouritism. Uncountable. Related: favourite / favorite, «teacher's pet».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Fearsome means very frightening to look at or meet, because it is big, strong or dangerous. 2) It can also mean very impressive or hard to deal with: «a fearsome reputation».
its sense in the lessons: In stories and nature lessons, fearsome creatures such as sharks, T. rex and dragons are described with this word. In sport, a fearsome team or player is one others are scared to play. Phrases: «a fearsome reputation», «fearsome teeth», «a fearsome warrior».
examples from the lessons: The T. rex had fearsome teeth. | The knight faced a fearsome dragon. | Vikings were fearsome warriors. | Our netball team has a fearsome reputation. | The storm made a fearsome noise. | The tiger looked fearsome but was asleep.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Built from «fear» + «-some» (like «troublesome»). Similar: frightening, terrifying, formidable. Describes the frightening thing, not the scared person.

part of speech: adjective (federated); verb past form of federate (federate, federates, federated, federating)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Federated describes states, groups or organisations that have joined together under one central government or body while still keeping some power of their own. 2) In schools in England, a federation is when two or more schools share one governing body and often one head teacher; such schools are federated.
its sense in the lessons: In history and citizenship lessons, the USA, Canada, Australia and Germany are federations of states or provinces. The Federated States of Micronesia is a country of islands. In computing, a federated system shares work between separate computers. Phrases: «federated states», «federated schools».
examples from the lessons: Australia's colonies federated in 1901 to form one country. | Our school is federated with the infant school down the road. | The Federated States of Micronesia is in the Pacific Ocean. | The clubs federated to make one big league. | In a federated country, each state makes some of its own laws. | Canada's provinces are part of a federal system.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Related: federal (adjective, as in «federal government»), federation (noun). In a federation, power is shared between the centre and the parts.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Festivities (usually plural) are the parties, music, food and fun events held to celebrate something. 2) Festivity (uncountable) is the happy, joyful feeling of a celebration.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and religious education, festivities happen at Christmas, Easter, Diwali, Eid, Hanukkah, Chinese New Year, weddings and birthdays. In the news and in stories, it tells the reader there is celebration and joy. Phrases: «the festivities», «Christmas festivities», «join in the festivities», «an air of festivity».
examples from the lessons: The town's Christmas festivities started with a lantern parade. | We joined in the Diwali festivities at school. | There was an air of festivity in the street. | The wedding festivities lasted all day. | After the festivities, we helped clean up. | New Year's Eve festivities ended with fireworks.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually plural: the festivities. Related: festival, festive. Spelling: festivity, festivities (y → ies).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Feudalism was the system in medieval Europe in which the king gave land to lords in return for loyalty and soldiers, and peasants (serfs) worked the lords' land in return for protection and a place to live.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons about the Middle Ages, especially after William the Conqueror's Norman Conquest of 1066, feudalism is drawn as a pyramid: king at the top, then barons and bishops, then knights, then peasants at the bottom. Similar systems existed in Japan. It explains why lords had castles, knights fought and peasants had few rights. Phrases: «the feudal system», «feudal lord».
examples from the lessons: Feudalism came to England with the Normans in 1066. | Under feudalism, peasants worked the lord's land. | The feudal pyramid had the king at the top. | Knights promised to fight for their lord under feudalism. | Feudalism slowly ended after the Black Death. | Japan also had a kind of feudalism with samurai.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Adjective: feudal. Say «FYOO-dul-izm». Historians today argue the picture of a neat pyramid is too simple, but it is a useful model for learning.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The fibula is the thinner of the two long bones in the lower leg, on the outside, next to the larger shin bone (tibia). 2) (history) A fibula is also an ancient brooch or pin used to fasten clothes, as worn by Romans and Celts.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on the skeleton, the fibula and tibia are the two bones between knee and ankle; the fibula helps support the ankle. In history and museums, Roman fibulae are pins found by archaeologists. Phrases: «a broken fibula», «tibia and fibula».
examples from the lessons: The fibula is the thin bone on the outside of your lower leg. | He broke his fibula playing football. | The tibia and fibula sit side by side. | Archaeologists found a Roman fibula in the field. | Your fibula connects to your ankle. | The skeleton model shows the fibula clearly.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: fibulae (Latin) or fibulas. Say «FIB-yoo-luh». Trap: the bigger shin bone is the tibia, not the fibula. Trick: «fibula» is the «little fib», the smaller one.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Fiendish means very cruel or wicked, like a fiend (a devil or evil spirit). 2) (informal) Fiendish means extremely clever, complicated or difficult: «a fiendish puzzle».
its sense in the lessons: In stories, a villain makes a fiendish plan. In puzzles and maths, a fiendish sudoku or riddle is very hard, so it is often used for olympiad or challenge questions. Phrases: «a fiendish plan», «fiendishly difficult», «fiendish puzzle».
examples from the lessons: The villain had a fiendish plan to steal the crown jewels. | This sudoku is fiendish! | The maths challenge had a fiendish final question. | The witch gave a fiendish laugh. | The maze was fiendishly difficult. | The detective uncovered a fiendish trick.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «fiend» (a devil, or a person who loves something: «a football fiend»). Adverb: fiendishly. Say «FEEN-dish».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A fife is a small, high-sounding flute without keys, played mainly in military marching bands, often with drums. 2) (a name) Fife is a region in eastern Scotland, between the Firth of Forth and the Firth of Tay; St Andrews is in Fife.
its sense in the lessons: In music and history lessons, fife and drum bands marched with armies, such as in the American Revolution. In geography of Scotland, Fife is a council area and historic «Kingdom of Fife». Phrases: «fife and drum», «the Kingdom of Fife».
examples from the lessons: The boy played a fife in the marching band. | A fife sounds higher than a flute. | Fife and drum music led the soldiers. | St Andrews is a famous town in Fife. | We went camping on the coast of Fife. | Our music teacher showed us a wooden fife.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Rhymes with «life». As a place name it takes a capital F.

part of speech: adjective (Filipino); noun (a Filipino, Filipinos; a Filipina for a woman; the Filipino language)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Filipino means from or belonging to the Philippines, a country of more than seven thousand islands in South-East Asia. 2) A Filipino is a person from the Philippines. 3) Filipino is also the national language of the Philippines, based mostly on Tagalog; English is also widely spoken there.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons, the Philippines is an island nation in the Pacific; Filipino food (adobo, lumpia), festivals and people appear in lessons on cultures. Many Filipino nurses and carers work in the UK, Ireland, the USA, Canada and Australia. Phrases: «Filipino food», «the Filipino language», «Filipino family».
examples from the lessons: My friend's mum is Filipino. | We tried Filipino food at the festival. | Filipino is the national language of the Philippines. | Many Filipinos speak both Filipino and English. | The Filipino team won the dance competition. | A Filipino nurse looked after my grandad.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A name of a people: written with a capital F. Spelling trap: the country is Philippines (Ph, double p, single l), but the people are Filipino (F, single p, single l). Filipina is often used for a woman.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The finale is the last part of a show, concert, piece of music or event, usually the most exciting part. 2) A season finale is the last episode of a TV series' season.
its sense in the lessons: In music lessons, the finale is the last movement of a symphony. At school shows, the whole cast sings in the finale. In everyday life, fireworks are often the grand finale. Phrases: «the grand finale», «season finale», «as a finale».
examples from the lessons: The fireworks were the grand finale of the night. | Everyone came on stage for the finale. | The season finale ended with a cliffhanger. | The orchestra played the finale loudly. | As a finale, the magician made the rabbit vanish. | The finale of our school play had a big song.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From Italian. Say «fih-NAH-lee». Trap: do not confuse with «final» (the last game in a competition) or «finally».

part of speech: verb (fingerspell, fingerspells, fingerspelled or fingerspelt, fingerspelling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To fingerspell is to spell out a word letter by letter using hand shapes in sign language, for example a name or a word that has no sign.
its sense in the lessons: In lessons about deafness and sign language (British Sign Language, American Sign Language, Auslan, Irish Sign Language, New Zealand Sign Language), pupils learn to fingerspell their names. BSL uses two hands for fingerspelling, ASL uses one. Phrases: «fingerspell your name», «the fingerspelling alphabet».
examples from the lessons: We learnt to fingerspell our names in BSL. | She fingerspelled the name of her town. | In ASL you fingerspell with one hand. | Can you fingerspell «cat»? | Names are often fingerspelt because they have no sign. | Our class practised fingerspelling every morning.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: fingerspelled (US) or fingerspelt (UK). Noun: fingerspelling. Sign languages are full languages, not just fingerspelling; most words have their own signs.

part of speech: noun (a fink, finks); verb (fink, finks, finked, finking — fink on someone)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (US, slang, old-fashioned) A fink is a person who tells on others to the police or people in charge; a snitch or tattletale. 2) (US, slang) A fink is an unpleasant, untrustworthy person. 3) (US, slang) To fink on someone is to tell on them. 4) (old, US) A fink was also a strike-breaker who worked when others were on strike.
its sense in the lessons: Mostly found in old American films, comics and stories, where gangsters or kids call someone a fink. It is a mild insult. Everyday modern words are «snitch», «grass» (UK) or «tattletale» (US). Phrases: «fink on someone», «you rat fink».
examples from the lessons: «Don't be a fink and tell the teacher!» | He finked on his friends to the police. | In the old film, the gangster called him a rat fink. | Nobody trusted him after he was a fink. | «You little fink!» shouted her brother. | Telling an adult about bullying is right, not being a fink.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Slang and old-fashioned. Remember: telling a trusted adult when someone is hurt or in danger is the right thing, not snitching.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Finnish means from or belonging to Finland, a country in northern Europe. 2) Finnish is the main language of Finland; it is not related to English or Swedish but belongs to the Uralic family with Estonian and Hungarian.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons, Finland is a land of forests and lakes, with saunas and the Northern Lights, and Lapland, where some people say Father Christmas lives. Finnish schools are often discussed because they start formal lessons at age seven. In language lessons, Finnish is famous for long words and many cases (word endings). Phrases: «the Finnish language», «a Finnish sauna».
examples from the lessons: Finnish people love saunas. | She speaks Finnish and English. | Finnish has very long words with many endings. | We read about Finnish schools in class. | Moomins come from Finnish stories by Tove Jansson. | The Finnish flag is a blue cross on white.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A name: written with a capital F. Person: a Finn (Finns). Trap: «Finnish» (from Finland) sounds like «finish» (to end) but has double n.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A fireman is a person whose job is to put out fires and rescue people; today the usual word is firefighter, because both men and women do this job. 2) (old) A fireman was also a worker who kept the fire burning in a steam engine or ship's boiler.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and safety lessons, firefighters visit schools to teach fire safety: smoke alarms, stop-drop-and-roll, and calling 999, 911, 000 or 111 (depending on country). In history, steam-train firemen shovelled coal. Phrases: «Fireman Sam», «fireman's lift» (a way of carrying a person over your shoulders).
examples from the lessons: The fireman rescued a cat from the tree. | Today we say firefighter, because women do the job too. | Fireman Sam is a children's TV show. | A fireman shovelled coal into the steam engine. | The fireman showed us how to check a smoke alarm. | In PE we learned a fireman's lift.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: firemen. Modern, neutral word: firefighter. Emergency numbers: 999 (UK, Ireland also 112), 911 (USA, Canada), 000 (Australia), 111 (New Zealand).

part of speech: noun (a fishmonger, fishmongers; the fishmonger's = the shop)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A fishmonger is a person who sells fresh fish and seafood, often in a shop or at a market stall. 2) The fishmonger's is the shop where fish is sold.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life (mainly UK, Ireland, Australia and New Zealand), the fishmonger cleans and cuts fish for customers. In history and stories, fishmongers worked at busy markets like Billingsgate in London. Similar words: butcher (meat), greengrocer (fruit and vegetables), ironmonger (tools). Phrases: «at the fishmonger's», «the fishmonger's slab».
examples from the lessons: We bought fresh salmon from the fishmonger. | The fishmonger cleaned the fish for us. | Mum went to the fishmonger's on Friday. | The fishmonger's slab was covered in ice. | Fishmongers sell crabs, prawns and mussels too. | The old market was full of shouting fishmongers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Monger» is an old word for seller (ironmonger, cheesemonger). «Scaremonger» and «warmonger» mean people who spread fear or want war. American English more often says «fish seller» or «fish market».

part of speech: verb (fizzle, fizzles, fizzled, fizzling); noun (a fizzle — informal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To fizzle is to make a soft hissing, spitting sound, like a sparkler or a fizzy drink. 2) (informal) If something fizzles out, it slowly ends in a weak, disappointing way after a good start. 3) (informal noun) A fizzle is a disappointing failure.
its sense in the lessons: In science, fizzling happens when a gas escapes from a liquid or when a fuse burns. In everyday life and stories, plans, storms, friendships and excitement can «fizzle out». Phrases: «fizzle out», «end in a fizzle».
examples from the lessons: The sparkler fizzled in the rain. | The firework fizzled and didn't go off. | Our plan to build a treehouse fizzled out after a week. | The storm fizzled out before it reached the coast. | The party was a bit of a fizzle. | The sausages fizzled in the pan.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: fizzled, fizzling. «Fizzle out» is the most common phrase. Related: fizz, fizzy.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A flange is a flat rim or edge that sticks out around a pipe, wheel or metal part, used to make it stronger, hold it in place or join it to something else. 2) On a train wheel, the flange is the raised inside edge that keeps the wheel on the rail.
its sense in the lessons: A technical word used in engineering, plumbing and design and technology. Pipes are joined by bolting their flanges together; train wheels stay on the track because of their flanges. Phrases: «pipe flange», «wheel flange».
examples from the lessons: The plumber bolted the two pipe flanges together. | The flange on a train wheel stops it slipping off the rails. | The shelf bracket has a flange for the screws. | Check that the flange is flat before tightening. | A tin can's rim is a kind of flange. | The engineer measured the flange carefully.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Say «flanj». Technical word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science, medical) Flexion is bending a joint so that the angle between the bones gets smaller, like bending your elbow or knee. 2) (grammar, rare) Flexion can mean changing the ending of a word to show its grammar (more often called inflection).
its sense in the lessons: In PE and science lessons on muscles and joints, flexion is the opposite of extension (straightening). The biceps causes flexion of the elbow. Physiotherapists measure flexion after an injury. Phrases: «knee flexion», «flexion and extension».
examples from the lessons: Bending your elbow is flexion. | Flexion and extension work like a hinge. | After his injury, he could only manage a little knee flexion. | The biceps muscle causes flexion of the arm. | Stretches improve flexion of the hips. | The physio measured the flexion of her ankle.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK also spells it «flection» in old books. Related verb: flex (to bend). Opposite: extension.

part of speech: verb (flinch, flinches, flinched, flinching); noun (a flinch)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To flinch is to make a small, quick movement backwards or away because of pain, fear or surprise. 2) Not to flinch from something means to face it bravely without avoiding it.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, a character flinches when a door slams or someone raises a hand, showing fear. In everyday life, children may flinch at an injection. In sport, a brave goalkeeper does not flinch. Phrases: «without flinching», «didn't flinch», «flinch from a task».
examples from the lessons: She flinched when the nurse gave her the injection. | He didn't flinch when the ball flew at him. | The dog flinched at the sound of fireworks. | She faced the bully without flinching. | He gave a little flinch when I touched the bruise. | The firefighter never flinched from danger.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: flinched. Noun: a flinch. Similar: wince (a face of pain), recoil.

part of speech: verb (flit, flits, flitted, flitting); noun (a flit — UK, Scotland)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To flit is to move or fly quickly and lightly from one place to another, like a butterfly or a bird. 2) If a thought or expression flits across your mind or face, it is there for a very short moment. 3) (Scotland, northern England) To flit, or do a flit, is to move house; a «moonlight flit» is leaving secretly at night, often to avoid paying debts.
its sense in the lessons: In nature writing and poems, butterflies, bats and birds flit about. In stories, a smile flits across a face. A person who flits from one hobby to another never stays with one. Phrases: «flit about», «flit from… to…», «moonlight flit».
examples from the lessons: Butterflies flitted between the flowers. | A bat flitted past the window. | A smile flitted across her face. | He flits from one hobby to another. | A strange thought flitted through my mind. | The family did a moonlight flit and left no address.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: double t in flitted, flitting. Short, light, quick movement; compare «float» (slow) and «dart» (fast and sharp).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Floral means made of flowers or decorated with patterns of flowers. 2) Floral can also describe a smell like flowers.
its sense in the lessons: In art and design, floral patterns appear on dresses, curtains and wallpaper. In everyday life, floral displays decorate weddings and funerals. In science, «floral parts» are the parts of a flower (petals, stamens, carpels). Phrases: «floral dress», «floral tribute», «floral scent».
examples from the lessons: She wore a floral dress to the party. | The church had floral displays for the wedding. | People left floral tributes at the memorial. | The soap has a floral smell. | Grandma's teacups have a floral pattern. | Petals are one of the floral parts we studied.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective only. Related: flora (the plants of an area; «flora and fauna» = plants and animals), florist (a person who sells flowers).

part of speech: noun (a flyer, flyers; also spelled flier)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A flyer is a small printed sheet of paper advertising an event, shop or service, handed out or put through letterboxes. 2) A flyer is a person or thing that flies, such as a pilot, a passenger who flies often, or a bird. 3) (informal) In sport, a flyer is a very fast start, or a very fast runner or player.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and design lessons, pupils make flyers for school fairs or cake sales. In stories, «frequent flyers» travel on planes a lot. In athletics, a «flying start» or «a flyer» is a very quick start. Phrases: «hand out flyers», «frequent flyer», «get off to a flyer».
examples from the lessons: We handed out flyers for the school fair. | A flyer for a pizza shop came through the letterbox. | Design a flyer to advertise your club. | Amelia Earhart was a famous flyer. | Swifts are amazing flyers that hardly ever land. | The team got off to a flyer and scored in the first minute.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: flyer is more common in the UK; flier is also used in the US. Plural: flyers. Related: fly, flight.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Fodder is food such as hay, straw or grain given to farm animals like cows, horses and sheep. 2) (informal) Fodder is material that is easily used for a particular purpose, often without much thought: «gossip fodder», «fodder for jokes». 3) «Cannon fodder» means soldiers treated as if their lives do not matter.
its sense in the lessons: In farming and geography lessons, farmers store fodder for winter. In everyday life and the news, a silly event becomes «fodder for comedians». In history, especially the First World War, «cannon fodder» describes soldiers sent to die in great numbers. Phrases: «animal fodder», «cannon fodder», «fodder for».
examples from the lessons: The farmer stores fodder in the barn for winter. | Hay is the main fodder for horses. | The mistake became fodder for jokes online. | The celebrity's outfit was fodder for gossip. | Many soldiers in 1916 were treated as cannon fodder. | Turnips are grown as winter fodder.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «some fodder», not «a fodder». Similar: feed, forage. Rhymes with «odder».

part of speech: noun (a fontanelle, fontanelles; US spelling fontanel)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A fontanelle is a soft spot on a baby's head where the bones of the skull have not yet joined together. It closes as the baby grows, usually by about 18 months to 2 years.
its sense in the lessons: In science and family-life lessons about babies and growing up, the fontanelle shows that a baby's skull is made of separate plates that can move a little at birth and then grow together. Parents are told to be gentle with a baby's head. Phrases: «the soft spot», «the fontanelle closes».
examples from the lessons: A newborn baby has a soft fontanelle on top of its head. | The fontanelle lets the baby's skull grow. | Be gentle with the baby's head because of the fontanelle. | The nurse checked the baby's fontanelle. | The fontanelle closes by about the age of two. | Everyday people call the fontanelle the soft spot.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK spelling: fontanelle; US: fontanel. Say «fon-tuh-NEL». Myth: touching it gently does not hurt the baby; there is a tough layer under the skin.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Foolishness is silly or unwise behaviour or thinking, without good sense. 2) Foolishness can also mean nonsense: «Stop this foolishness!».
its sense in the lessons: In stories, fables and the Bible, foolishness is often contrasted with wisdom (the wise man built his house on the rock, the foolish man on the sand). In everyday life, parents say «That's enough foolishness». In safety lessons, foolishness like playing near railway lines can be dangerous. Phrases: «sheer foolishness», «stop this foolishness».
examples from the lessons: It was foolishness to swim in the river alone. | «Enough of this foolishness!» said the teacher. | The fable shows the foolishness of the greedy dog. | The Bible compares wisdom with foolishness. | He regretted his foolishness later. | Running across the road without looking is pure foolishness.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Adjective: foolish; noun: fool (a foolish person); April Fool's Day is 1 April. Similar: silliness, stupidity (ruder).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A forager is an animal that searches for food, such as a bee looking for nectar or a squirrel looking for nuts. 2) A forager is a person who gathers wild food like berries, mushrooms and plants. 3) (history) Hunter-gatherers were foragers who lived by hunting animals and collecting wild plants before farming.
its sense in the lessons: In science, bees are called foragers when they collect nectar and pollen. In history lessons about the Stone Age, people were foragers before farming began. In everyday life, foragers pick blackberries; safety rule: never eat wild mushrooms or berries unless an expert adult says they are safe. Phrases: «a forager bee», «hunter-gatherers and foragers».
examples from the lessons: Forager bees bring nectar back to the hive. | Stone Age people were hunters and foragers. | The forager filled her basket with blackberries. | Squirrels are busy foragers in autumn. | A good forager knows which plants are poisonous. | Ants send out foragers to find crumbs.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: forage (forages, foraged, foraging). Noun: forage also means food for animals. Safety: never eat wild food without checking with an expert adult.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (golf) «Fore!» is a shout golfers use to warn people that a ball is flying towards them. 2) To come to the fore means to become important or noticed: «New stars came to the fore». 3) (ships) Fore means at or towards the front of a ship: «fore and aft» means front and back. 4) Fore- is also a prefix meaning before or front: forehead, foresee, forecast.
its sense in the lessons: In sport (golf), shouting «Fore!» is a safety warning. In everyday news, an issue «comes to the fore». On ships and in pirate stories, the fore is the front (the bow). In spelling lessons, the prefix «fore-» helps you understand words like forearm and forefather. Phrases: «come to the fore», «to the fore», «fore and aft».
examples from the lessons: The golfer shouted «Fore!» as the ball flew towards the crowd. | Kindness came to the fore during the floods. | The sailors ran fore and aft. | She brought the problem to the fore at the meeting. | The cabin is in the fore part of the ship. | Forearm, forehead and forecast all start with fore-.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Homophones: fore, four (4) and for. «Fore-» (before, front) is different from «for-» (as in forget, forgive). Trap: «forego» and «forgo» are often confused.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A forecourt is an open area in front of a building, such as a petrol station, hotel, shop or church. 2) In tennis and similar sports, the forecourt is the part of the court nearest the net.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life (mainly UK, Ireland, Australia, New Zealand), the forecourt of a petrol station is where the pumps are; safety rules there say no smoking and no phones. In sport, players step into the forecourt to hit volleys. Phrases: «petrol station forecourt», «on the forecourt».
examples from the lessons: We parked on the forecourt of the petrol station. | No smoking is allowed on the forecourt. | Children were playing on the church forecourt. | The hotel forecourt was full of taxis. | She moved into the forecourt to hit a volley. | The car dealer had shiny cars lined up on the forecourt.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Built from «fore» (front) + «court» (yard). Countable.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Your forefinger is the finger next to your thumb, the one you usually point with; it is also called the index finger or first finger.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, people point, press buttons and beckon with their forefinger. In science lessons on the hand, the fingers are thumb, forefinger (index), middle, ring and little finger (pinkie). In stories, a teacher may wag a forefinger to tell someone off. Phrases: «between thumb and forefinger», «wag a forefinger».
examples from the lessons: She pointed at the map with her forefinger. | Hold the pencil between your thumb and forefinger. | The teacher wagged her forefinger at us. | He pressed the button with his forefinger. | Your forefinger is also called your index finger. | The baby grabbed my forefinger.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Also: index finger, first finger, pointer finger (US). Plural: forefingers.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A forelock is a lock (bunch) of hair that grows just above the forehead, on a person or a horse. 2) «To tug your forelock» (UK, old) means to show too much respect to someone rich or powerful, as servants once did.
its sense in the lessons: In horse care, the forelock is the part of the mane that falls between a horse's ears onto its face. In history and stories, poor workers «tugged their forelocks» to the lord. The phrase «take time by the forelock» means to act quickly while there is a chance. Phrases: «tug your forelock», «brush the forelock».
examples from the lessons: She brushed her pony's forelock. | A long forelock fell over his eyes. | The horse's forelock blew in the wind. | In old times, farm workers tugged their forelocks to the squire. | Plait the forelock before the show. | His forelock was always messy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Built from «fore» (front) + «lock» (of hair). Do not confuse with «forearm» or a door lock.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A forerunner is a person or thing that came before another and led the way for it: «The abacus was a forerunner of the calculator». 2) A forerunner can be a sign that something is about to happen.
its sense in the lessons: In history and technology lessons, forerunners show how inventions grew: Babbage's engines were forerunners of computers; the penny-farthing was a forerunner of the modern bicycle. In the Bible and church, John the Baptist is called the forerunner of Jesus. Phrases: «a forerunner of», «the forerunner to».
examples from the lessons: The abacus was a forerunner of the calculator. | The gramophone was a forerunner of today's music players. | Christians call John the Baptist the forerunner of Jesus. | Dark clouds are often the forerunner of a storm. | This early plane was a forerunner of the jumbo jet. | The Romans' roads were forerunners of modern motorways.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Similar: predecessor, ancestor, pioneer. Plural: forerunners.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To foresee something is to know or guess that it will happen before it does.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, planning means trying to foresee problems (rain on sports day, traffic jams). In safety lessons, a risk assessment means foreseeing dangers. In stories, fortune-tellers and prophets claim to foresee the future. Phrases: «foresee a problem», «could not have foreseen», «as far as I can foresee».
examples from the lessons: Nobody could foresee the storm. | Do you foresee any problems with the plan? | The teacher foresaw that the trip would be muddy and told us to bring boots. | In the story, the witch foresaw the king's fall. | We couldn't have foreseen the road being closed. | Good planners foresee what might go wrong.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular: foresee, foresaw, foreseen (like see, saw, seen). Adjective: foreseeable («in the foreseeable future» = as far ahead as we can guess). Noun: foresight. Spelling: fore- (before), not «forsee».

part of speech: adjective (former); noun (the former; a former — in technology)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Former means earlier, from before but not now: «the former head teacher», «a former champion». 2) The former means the first of two things just mentioned; the second is «the latter». 3) (UK schools, old) A form is a class, and some schools call a pupil «a sixth-former».
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, «former colonies» and «former presidents» are common. In writing and reading comprehension, «the former… the latter» helps compare two things without repeating them. In design technology, a former is a frame or mould something is shaped around. Phrases: «former pupil», «in former times», «the former and the latter».
examples from the lessons: Our former teacher came to visit. | He is a former Olympic champion. | Tea and coffee? I prefer the former, so tea please. | Kenya is a former British colony. | The castle is a shadow of its former self. | In former times, children worked in factories. | My sister is a sixth-former.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «The former» = first of two; «the latter» = second. Use only with two things; for more, say «the first» and «the last». Adverb: formerly. Do not confuse with «formal» or «farmer».

meaning for a pupil: 1) To formulate a plan, idea or rule is to think it out carefully and put it together in detail. 2) To formulate something is to express it clearly in words or symbols. 3) To formulate a medicine, food or product is to make it from a particular mixture.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, pupils formulate a question and a hypothesis (a prediction) before an experiment. In maths, you formulate an equation from a word problem. In everyday life and business, companies formulate plans or new products like shampoos. Phrases: «formulate a plan», «formulate a hypothesis», «formulate a question».
examples from the lessons: Formulate a hypothesis before you start the experiment. | The team formulated a plan to raise money for the trip. | She took a moment to formulate her answer. | Can you formulate the word problem as an equation? | The cream is formulated for sensitive skin. | Scientists formulate rules from many observations.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal. Noun: formulation. Related: formula (plural: formulae or formulas), a rule written in symbols such as A = l × w.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To fortify a place is to make it stronger against attack by building walls, towers or ditches. 2) To fortify yourself is to make yourself stronger or braver, for example with food, a drink or encouragement. 3) To fortify food is to add extra vitamins or minerals to it: «fortified cereal».
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, castles, towns and hill forts were fortified with walls, moats and gates. In science and healthy-eating lessons, cereals and milk are fortified with vitamins and iron. In stories, a hero «fortified himself with a cup of tea». Phrases: «a fortified town», «fortified with vitamins», «fortify yourself».
