examples from the lessons: The Normans fortified the town with stone walls. | The castle was fortified with a moat and drawbridge. | This cereal is fortified with iron and vitamins. | She fortified herself with a big breakfast before the race. | The soldiers fortified the hill. | Fortified foods help people get enough vitamin D.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: fortify → fortifies, fortified (y → i). Nouns: fortification, fort, fortress. «Fortified wine» is wine with extra alcohol added.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Fossilisation is the very slow process, over thousands or millions of years, by which the remains or traces of a living thing are turned into a fossil, usually in rock. 2) (figurative) Fossilisation is when ideas, habits or a language stop changing and become fixed.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on rocks, evolution and dinosaurs, fossilisation is explained step by step: an animal dies, is buried quickly in mud or sand, the soft parts rot, minerals slowly replace the bones, and layers of rock press down. Mary Anning found famous fossils in Lyme Regis. Phrases: «the process of fossilisation», «conditions for fossilisation».
examples from the lessons: Fossilisation takes millions of years. | Only a few dead animals ever go through fossilisation. | Quick burial in mud helps fossilisation. | Shells are often found because they survive fossilisation well. | We drew a comic strip of the stages of fossilisation. | Teeth and bones are the parts most likely to survive fossilisation.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK, Australian, New Zealand and Irish spelling: fossilisation; US and Canada: fossilization. Verb: fossilise / fossilize. Myth: most living things never become fossils; fossilisation is rare.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Foxy means sly and clever at tricking people, like the fox in fables. 2) Foxy means like a fox in looks, colour or smell, for example reddish-brown. 3) (adult slang) a word grown-ups use; not for school.
its sense in the lessons: In fables and stories, the fox is often cunning, so a «foxy» character is sly (Mr Fox, Reynard). In nature, a foxy smell or reddish colour comes from foxes. Phrases: «a foxy grin», «foxy red».
examples from the lessons: The foxy old man tricked everyone in the village. | The fox in the fable was foxy and clever. | The dog had a foxy reddish coat. | There was a foxy smell near the bins. | He gave a foxy grin when he won the game. | Don't trust the foxy salesman in the story.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparison: foxier, foxiest. In stories for children, use it for sly or fox-like.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (maths) Fractional means in the form of a fraction, or to do with fractions: «a fractional number», «fractional parts». 2) Fractional means very small: «a fractional increase», «a fractional delay».
its sense in the lessons: In maths, fractional amounts are parts of a whole, like 3/4 or 1/2; fractional answers are not whole numbers. In science and sport, a fractional difference is very tiny, like a hundredth of a second in a race. Phrases: «fractional part», «fractional difference», «fractional increase».
examples from the lessons: A half is a fractional amount. | Give your answer in fractional form, like 2/3. | The winner was faster by a fractional amount. | Prices had a fractional rise this month. | 3.75 has a whole part of 3 and a fractional part of 0.75. | There was a fractional pause before she answered.
note for the reader of a maths problem: In maths problems, «fractional» means not a whole number: 7 ÷ 2 = 3½ is a fractional answer. The «fractional part» of a decimal is the bit after the point. Adverb: fractionally (very slightly).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Fragmentation is the breaking of something into small pieces. 2) Fragmentation is when a group, country, habitat or system splits into many smaller, separate parts.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography, habitat fragmentation happens when roads, farms and towns cut forests into small patches, which harms animals. In history, the fragmentation of empires led to many small states. In computing, file fragmentation slows down old hard drives. Phrases: «habitat fragmentation», «the fragmentation of», «fragmentation of rock».
examples from the lessons: Habitat fragmentation makes it hard for animals to find mates. | Frost causes fragmentation of rocks. | After the war came the fragmentation of the empire. | The bomb's fragmentation scattered metal pieces. | Hedgehogs suffer from fragmentation of gardens by high fences. | Fragmentation of the team happened after the argument.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Related: fragment (a small piece; verb: to break into pieces), fragmented. Say «frag-men-TAY-shun».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Frantic means very worried, scared or upset, so that you cannot think calmly. 2) Frantic means done very quickly and wildly, with lots of rushing: «a frantic search».
its sense in the lessons: In stories and news, a frantic parent searches for a lost child; a frantic rush happens before a deadline or the school bus leaves. In safety lessons, staying calm is better than being frantic. Phrases: «frantic with worry», «a frantic search», «a frantic rush».
examples from the lessons: She was frantic with worry when her cat went missing. | There was a frantic rush to finish the homework. | The dog barked frantically at the door. | After a frantic search, we found the keys in the fridge. | The last minutes of the match were frantic. | Don't get frantic; take a deep breath.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb: frantically. Similar: panicky, desperate, hectic. Opposite: calm.

part of speech: verb (fray, frays, frayed, fraying); noun (the fray)
meaning for a pupil: 1) If cloth or rope frays, its threads come loose at the edge and it starts to wear out. 2) If someone's nerves or temper fray, they become tense and start to get annoyed. 3) The fray is a fight, argument or competition: «join the fray», «enter the fray».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, jeans, shoelaces and ropes fray with use; in safety, a frayed rope or electric cable is dangerous and should be replaced. In stories and news, people «jump into the fray» of an argument or battle. Phrases: «frayed edges», «tempers frayed», «join the fray», «above the fray».
examples from the lessons: The edges of my jeans have started to fray. | Never use a frayed electric cable. | Tempers frayed as the long car journey went on. | Another team entered the fray in the second half. | The knight rode into the fray. | Her nerves were frayed before the exam.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: frayed. «Frayed» describes worn cloth or tired, edgy nerves. «Stay above the fray» means do not get involved in an argument.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) Freaky means strange and a bit scary or weird: «a freaky noise». 2) (informal) Freaky can mean very unusual and surprising: «a freaky coincidence». 3) (adult slang) a word grown-ups use; not for school.
its sense in the lessons: Common in children's and teen talk, films and spooky stories: freaky houses, freaky masks, freaky dreams. «Freaky Friday» is a famous film about a mother and daughter swapping bodies. Phrases: «that's freaky», «a freaky coincidence».
examples from the lessons: That old house is really freaky at night. | It's freaky that we both have the same birthday. | The mask in the shop window looked freaky. | I had a freaky dream about talking cats. | There was a freaky noise in the attic. | The weather has been freaky this week.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal; in formal writing use «strange», «eerie» or «unusual». Related: freak (noun; informal verb «freak out» = panic or get very upset).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A fresco is a painting made on a wall or ceiling while the plaster is still wet, so the colours become part of the wall. 2) Fresco is the method of painting this way.
its sense in the lessons: In art and history lessons, famous frescoes include Michelangelo's paintings on the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel in Rome and ancient frescoes in Pompeii and Minoan Crete. Many church walls in Europe have frescoes of Bible stories. Phrases: «paint in fresco», «a ceiling fresco».
examples from the lessons: Michelangelo painted the frescoes in the Sistine Chapel. | The church walls are covered in old frescoes. | Frescoes in Pompeii show scenes of Roman life. | The artist had to work fast before the plaster dried. | We made a pretend fresco with plaster in art class. | The fresco showed angels and saints.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From Italian «fresco» = fresh (wet plaster). Plural: frescoes or frescos. Say «FRESS-koh». Not to be confused with «al fresco» (eating outdoors).

part of speech: adjective (Frisian); noun (a Frisian, Frisians; the Frisian language; a Frisian cow or horse)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Frisian means from or belonging to Friesland or the Frisian Islands, a region along the North Sea coast in the Netherlands and Germany. 2) Frisian is the language spoken there; it is the closest living language to English. 3) A Frisian (or Friesian) is also a breed of black-and-white dairy cow, or a black horse breed.
its sense in the lessons: In language and history lessons, Frisian is interesting because it is English's closest relative; a saying goes «Bread, butter and green cheese is good English and good Frisian». In farming, black-and-white Friesian cows (Holstein-Friesians) give lots of milk. Phrases: «the Frisian language», «Frisian Islands», «Friesian cow».
examples from the lessons: Frisian is spoken in the north of the Netherlands. | Frisian is the closest language to English. | The Frisian Islands lie in the North Sea. | The farm has a herd of black-and-white Friesian cows. | A Frisian horse is tall, black and shiny. | Old English and Frisian were once very similar.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A name: written with a capital F. For cows, the spelling Friesian is more common; for the language, Frisian. Say «FRIZH-un» or «FREE-zhun».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Fruity means tasting or smelling strongly of fruit. 2) A fruity voice is deep, rich and warm. 3) (UK, informal) Fruity can mean a bit cheeky or rude, as in a «fruity joke». 4) (old, offensive slang) An unkind word once used to mock people; do not use.
its sense in the lessons: In food and science lessons on taste and smell, fruity flavours come from fruit or fruit-like chemicals. In stories, an actor or grandad may have a fruity laugh or voice. Phrases: «fruity flavour», «a fruity voice», «fruity smell».
examples from the lessons: This yoghurt has a fruity taste. | The shampoo smells fruity. | Grandpa has a deep, fruity laugh. | The drink was sweet and fruity. | Try the fruitiest smoothie on the menu. | The actor spoke in a rich, fruity voice.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparison: fruitier, fruitiest. Related: fruit, fruitful (producing good results, not «full of fruit» in most uses).

part of speech: verb past form of fuel (fuel, fuels, fuelled, fuelling; US: fueled, fueling); adjective (-fuelled, as in «coal-fuelled»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Fuelled means given fuel such as petrol, gas, coal or wood, so that it can work or burn: «a plane fuelled for take-off». 2) Fuelled means made stronger or bigger, especially feelings, ideas or fights: «Anger was fuelled by rumours». 3) As part of a word, «-fuelled» tells what something runs on: «diesel-fuelled», «coffee-fuelled».
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography, power stations are coal-fuelled, gas-fuelled or nuclear, and burning fossil fuels adds carbon dioxide to the air. In the news and stories, rumours fuel fear and arguments. In everyday life, a good breakfast «fuels» you for the day. Phrases: «fuelled by», «fuelled up», «fuelled the fire».
examples from the lessons: The rocket was fuelled and ready to launch. | The fire was fuelled by dry leaves. | Rumours fuelled the argument. | The old power station was coal-fuelled. | We fuelled up with pancakes before the hike. | Her success was fuelled by hard work. | The car was fuelled at the petrol station.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK, Ireland, Australia, New Zealand spell it fuelled, fuelling (double l); US and often Canada spell fueled, fueling. «Add fuel to the fire» means make a bad situation worse.

part of speech: adjective (fumbling, more fumbling); verb form (fumble, fumbles, fumbled, fumbling); noun (fumbling, a fumbling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Using your hands in a clumsy, unsure way, so you drop things or cannot do a job neatly. 2) Searching for something awkwardly, for example in a pocket or in the dark. 3) Speaking or acting in a nervous, unsure way, without finding the right words. 4) (sport) Dropping or failing to hold a ball you should have caught, especially in American football or cricket.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, «fumbling» shows that a character is nervous, cold, in a hurry or in the dark: «fumbling with the keys» builds tension before a door opens. In sport it marks a mistake. In everyday life it describes clumsy hands, for example with buttons in gloves. Phrases: fumbling for the light switch, fumbling with buttons, fumbling for words, a fumbling attempt.
examples from the lessons: She was fumbling with her keys while the rain poured down. | He went fumbling for the light switch in the dark hall. | My fingers were so cold that I kept fumbling with my coat buttons. | Tom gave a fumbling answer because he had not done the reading. | The goalkeeper's fumbling let the ball slip into the net. | Fumbling in her bag, Gran finally found her glasses. | After some fumbling, the new boy managed to open his locker. | The quarterback's fumbling cost the team the game.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It is the -ing form of the verb «fumble» (drop the e, add -ing). As an adjective it goes before a noun: a fumbling start. Do not confuse with «tumbling» (falling over and over) or «mumbling» (speaking unclearly), although someone can be fumbling and mumbling at once. «Fumbling for words» means struggling to speak, not using your hands.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Working properly and able to do its job: a functional lift goes up and down. 2) Made to be useful and practical rather than pretty: a functional kitchen has what you need and no decorations. 3) (maths) To do with functions, rules that turn each input number into one output number. 4) (formal) Having a job or role inside a system: the heart is a functional part of the body.
its sense in the lessons: In science and design lessons «functional» means «does the job», and pupils are asked to make a product that is both functional and attractive. In maths it links to functions (input-output machines). In everyday life it is used for working machines and plain, practical things. Phrases: fully functional, functional design, functional clothing, still functional.
examples from the lessons: The old printer is slow, but it is still functional. | Our design must be functional as well as good-looking. | The school canteen has plain, functional tables. | After the storm, only one lift was functional. | Wellies are functional rather than fashionable. | The robot we built in class is now fully functional! | A function machine turns each input into one output. | Each part of a flower has a functional role.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective formed from «function» + -al. Opposite: non-functional, broken, or decorative. «Functional» does not mean «fun»; the first letters are the same but the meanings are not. Do not mix it up with «fictional» (made up, from stories).

part of speech: verb (fundraise, fundraises, fundraised, fundraising); noun form fundraising, fundraiser (a fundraiser, fundraisers)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To collect money for a charity, a school or a good cause, often by holding events. 2) To ask people or organisations to give money to support a project.
its sense in the lessons: Schools fundraise with bake sales, sponsored walks, fun runs, raffles and non-uniform days, and children often help. In stories and news it shows a community working together for a cause. In maths problems, fundraising questions ask you to add up money raised, find totals, or work out how much more is needed to reach a target. Phrases: fundraise for charity, a fundraising event, reach the target.
examples from the lessons: Our class is going to fundraise for the animal shelter. | We fundraised £250 with a cake sale. | The PTA fundraises every year for new books. | My cousin is fundraising by running a half marathon. | They need to fundraise $500 to pay for the school trip. | Kids in Canada often fundraise by selling chocolate bars. | If we have raised £180 of a £300 target, we still need to fundraise £120. | The scouts fundraised by washing cars on Saturday.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually written as one word (fundraise), sometimes «fund-raise». The person is a «fundraiser», and an event is also «a fundraiser». In maths: money fundraised is added to a total; «target minus amount raised» gives how much is still needed. The money goes to the cause, not to the people collecting it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An outdoor show with rides, games, stalls and sweets that people pay to enjoy, often travelling from town to town. 2) (UK, Australia) The usual word for what Americans call a carnival or a fair.
its sense in the lessons: In stories a funfair is a place of excitement, bright lights, candyfloss and sometimes danger or getting lost. In everyday life children go with family or friends and spend pocket money. In maths, funfair problems use ride prices, tokens and change. Safety: stay with your adult, agree a meeting point, and follow the height rules on rides. Phrases: go to the funfair, funfair rides, the funfair is in town.
examples from the lessons: The funfair comes to our park every summer. | I won a goldfish at the funfair! | We rode the dodgems and the big wheel at the funfair. | Each ride at the funfair costs £2, so four rides cost £8. | Stay together at the funfair so nobody gets lost. | The funfair lights glowed across the dark field. | In America they usually call it a carnival or a county fair. | Mum bought candyfloss at the funfair.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: a funfair, two funfairs. One word, not «fun fair», in British English (both spellings appear). In the US «carnival» or «fair» is more common; in the UK «carnival» usually means a street parade. A «fair» can also mean an event for selling things (a book fair, a craft fair), with no rides.

part of speech: adjective (furred); verb form, past of fur (fur, furs, furred, furring)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Covered with fur, or with a coat of soft hair: a furred animal. 2) Lined or trimmed with fur, like a furred hood. 3) (UK) Coated with a crusty layer, like a kettle furred with limescale or pipes furred up inside. 4) (of a tongue) Covered with a whitish coating when you are ill.
its sense in the lessons: In science, «furred» animals are mammals with fur that keeps them warm. In everyday British life a kettle «gets furred up» in hard-water areas because of limescale. In stories it describes animals, coats and cosy clothes. Phrases: furred up, a thick-furred coat, a furred tongue.
examples from the lessons: The fox is a furred animal with a bushy tail. | Her parka has a furred hood for the cold. | Our kettle is furred up with limescale. | Arctic hares are thickly furred to survive the winter. | The old pipes had furred inside and the water ran slowly. | When I had flu, my tongue felt furred. | Polar bears are furred even on the soles of their feet. | Mammals are furred, but birds are feathered.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: double r before -ed (fur → furred, furring). Pronounced like «furd». Not the same as «fared» (got on) or «feared». «Furry» is the more common everyday adjective: a furry kitten.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Being hard to please, especially about food, clothes or how things are done. 2) Worrying too much about small details. 3) Having too much decoration, so something looks busy and fiddly.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life «fussiness» usually means fussy eating, refusing foods. In stories it shows a character who is picky or anxious about small things. In art and design it criticises too many decorations. Phrases: fussiness about food, a fussy eater, without fussiness.
examples from the lessons: My little brother's fussiness about food drives Mum mad. | The cat's fussiness means it only eats one brand. | Her fussiness about tidy desks helps our group stay organised. | The teacher said the poster had too much fussiness and needed fewer colours. | Dad's fussiness over the car makes him wash it every Sunday. | Fussiness at dinner can mean missing out on new tastes. | Grandpa laughs at his own fussiness about the remote control.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «his fussiness», not «a fussiness». Made from «fussy» (y → i + -ness). Similar words: pickiness, being choosy. It is not always bad: careful fussiness can stop mistakes.

part of speech: noun (a gag, gags); verb (gag, gags, gagged, gagging)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (noun) A joke or a funny trick, especially by a comedian: a running gag. 2) (verb) To feel as if you are going to be sick, with your throat tightening: the smell made me gag. 3) (noun) A piece of cloth put over or in someone's mouth to stop them talking or shouting. 4) (verb) To stop someone from speaking freely, for example a newspaper: a gagging order. 5) (informal) «Gagging for something» (UK slang) means wanting it very much: I'm gagging for a drink.
its sense in the lessons: In stories a gag can be a joke, or a sign of danger when a villain gags a captive. In everyday life children «gag» on food they dislike or at bad smells. In news and law, a gagging order stops people publicly talking about something. Phrases: a running gag, sight gag, gag reflex, gagging order, gagging for it (avoid this one: it can sound rude).
examples from the lessons: The comedian's best gag was about a talking dog. | The smell from the bin made me gag. | The running gag in the cartoon is that the dog never gets the ball. | The robbers had tied a gag around the guard's mouth. | Some people gag when the dentist checks their back teeth. | The judge gave a gagging order so the newspapers could not print the names. | After footy training I was gagging for a cold drink. | Dad's old gags make us groan every Christmas.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: double g before -ed and -ing (gagged, gagging). «Gag reflex» is the body's automatic way of stopping you choking. In the UK, «gagging for it» can have an adult meaning; it is better avoided. A «gag» (joke) is not the same as a «gaggle» (a group of geese).

meaning for a pupil: 1) To do with a galaxy, a huge group of stars, gas and dust held together by gravity, such as our Milky Way. 2) (informal) Enormous, huge in size or importance: a galactic mess.
its sense in the lessons: In science and space lessons «galactic» is used for things across or inside a galaxy: the galactic centre, a galactic year. In science fiction stories it appears in names like «Galactic Empire» or «galactic war». As slang it exaggerates size. Phrases: the galactic centre, intergalactic travel, galactic scale.
examples from the lessons: The Sun goes around the galactic centre once every 230 million years or so. | Our science topic is about galactic shapes, like spirals. | In the film, a galactic war breaks out between two planets. | There is a black hole at the galactic centre. | My bedroom was a galactic mess after the sleepover. | Intergalactic space is the gap between galaxies. | The game lets you build a galactic empire.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «galaxy» (y changes to «-actic»). «Intergalactic» = between galaxies; «galactic» = within or about a galaxy. The Milky Way is our galaxy; it is not the same as the Solar System, which is tiny by comparison.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Great bravery, especially in battle or danger. 2) Polite, kind behaviour from a man towards women, such as opening doors or offering a seat (old-fashioned).
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons and old stories «gallantry» describes soldiers, knights and rescuers who acted bravely; medals «for gallantry» honour courage. In old-fashioned stories it also means good manners towards ladies. Phrases: an award for gallantry, acts of gallantry, gallantry medal.
examples from the lessons: The firefighter got a medal for gallantry. | The knight was famous for his gallantry in battle. | Acts of gallantry during the war are remembered on Anzac Day. | In the old novel, the captain showed gallantry by giving up his seat. | The lifeboat crew's gallantry saved six sailors. | The Victoria Cross is Britain's highest award for gallantry.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «his gallantry», «great gallantry». Adjective: gallant (a gallant knight). Spelling: two l's, then -antry. Not the same as «gallery» (a room for pictures). The second, polite-to-women sense sounds old-fashioned today.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An adult male goose. 2) (informal, UK, Australia) A quick look: have a gander at this.
its sense in the lessons: In farm and nature lessons, the gander is the male goose, the goose is the female, and goslings are the young. In everyday British and Australian talk, «take a gander» means «have a look». There is also a saying: «what's good for the goose is good for the gander» means a rule must be fair to both people. Phrases: have a gander, take a gander.
examples from the lessons: The gander hissed and chased us away from the goslings. | A goose lays the eggs, and the gander guards the nest. | Come and have a gander at my new bike! | Mum took a gander at the menu and ordered chips. | The farmer keeps one gander and six geese. | «What's good for the goose is good for the gander,» said Dad, so I could stay up late too. | Have a gander out the window, it's snowing!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural ganders. Male goose = gander; female = goose; young = gosling; a group on the ground = a gaggle. «Gander» (look) is informal; do not use it in formal writing. Not related to «gender», although they sound alike.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A large white seabird with black wing tips and a yellowish head that dives from high up into the sea to catch fish. 2) (UK, informal) A greedy person who eats a lot, very fast.
its sense in the lessons: In science and nature lessons gannets are studied as diving seabirds that nest in huge colonies on cliffs and islands, for example around Britain, Ireland, New Zealand and Canada. In everyday British talk, calling someone a gannet is a jokey way of saying they eat greedily. Phrases: a gannet colony, you greedy gannet.
examples from the lessons: A gannet can dive into the sea at almost 100 kilometres per hour. | Thousands of gannets nest on Bass Rock in Scotland. | We watched gannets plunge into the waves to catch mackerel. | You ate all the biscuits, you gannet! | My brother is a real gannet at birthday parties. | New Zealand has a big gannet colony at Cape Kidnappers. | The gannet's air sacs protect it when it hits the water.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: g-a-n-n-e-t, double n, single t. Plural: gannets. The «greedy person» sense is mild teasing, not a swear word, but it is still a bit rude to say to someone. It is a myth that gannets go blind from diving; their eyes are protected.

part of speech: verb (gape, gapes, gaped, gaping); noun (a gape, gapes)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To stare with your mouth wide open, because you are surprised or amazed. 2) To be or become wide open: a hole gaped in the wall. 3) (noun) A wide-open mouth or a wide opening; in birds, the width of the open beak.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, characters «gape» when they are shocked or astonished, and a «gaping hole» or «gaping wound» is a big, frightening opening. In science, the gape of a bird or snake is how wide it can open its mouth. Phrases: gape at, a gaping hole, gaping mouth, stand gaping.
examples from the lessons: We gaped at the giant whale skeleton in the museum. | The children gaped when the magician vanished. | A huge hole gaped in the road after the flood. | Don't just stand there gaping, help me! | The baby birds gaped, waiting for worms. | A snake's gape lets it swallow an egg whole. | There was a gaping hole in the fence where the cow got out.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: gaped (one p); -ing: gaping. Pronounced to rhyme with «tape». Do not confuse with «gasp» (a quick breath in) or «gap» (a space). «Gawp» (UK) is a similar informal word for staring rudely.

part of speech: noun (a garrison, garrisons); verb (garrison, garrisons, garrisoned, garrisoning)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A group of soldiers living in a town or fort to guard it. 2) The fort, castle or town where these soldiers live. 3) (verb) To put soldiers in a place to guard it.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons garrisons appear with castles, Roman forts on Hadrian's Wall, and towns during wars and sieges. In stories a garrison defends a fortress against attackers. Phrases: a garrison town, the garrison surrendered, to garrison a fort.
examples from the lessons: The Romans kept a garrison at every fort along Hadrian's Wall. | The castle's garrison held out for three months. | Gibraltar was a British garrison town for centuries. | The king garrisoned the town with 500 soldiers. | When food ran out, the garrison surrendered. | A small garrison guarded the bridge.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: a garrison, two garrisons. Verb past: garrisoned. Spelling: double r, single s. A garrison is a group; you do not say «a garrison» for one soldier.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Thick, soft and wobbly like jelly. 2) Made of or containing gelatine, the clear substance used to set jelly.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons «gelatinous» describes frogspawn, jellyfish, some fungi, slime and the layer around seeds such as chia. In cooking it describes stock that sets when cold. In stories it describes slimy monsters or blobs. Phrases: gelatinous mass, gelatinous texture.
examples from the lessons: Frogspawn is a gelatinous mass of eggs. | The jellyfish's body is soft and gelatinous. | Chia seeds turn gelatinous when you soak them in water. | The monster was a gelatinous green blob. | Cold gravy can turn gelatinous in the fridge. | Some mushrooms have a gelatinous cap. | We made slime with a gelatinous, wobbly texture.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stress: ge-LAT-in-ous. Spelling: gelatin (US) or gelatine (UK), but the adjective is always «gelatinous». Gelatine usually comes from animals, so many vegetarians avoid gelatinous sweets made with it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (grammar) The form of a noun or pronoun that shows who owns something or what it belongs to: in English, «the dog's bone», «Sam's coat», «the roof of the house». 2) In languages like Latin, German or Ukrainian, a special case ending used for owning and for «of».
its sense in the lessons: In grammar lessons English pupils usually call it «possessive» or the possessive apostrophe; «genitive» is the older grammar word used in foreign-language lessons and language olympiads. Knowing the genitive helps with Latin, German, Ukrainian and Russian, where the ending of the word changes. Phrases: the genitive case, genitive plural, genitive ending.
examples from the lessons: In «the cat's tail», «cat's» is in the genitive. | Latin uses a genitive ending: «Marci» means «of Marcus». | The genitive plural of «children» is «children's». | In German, «des Mannes» is genitive: «of the man». | The olympiad puzzle asked us to find the genitive ending. | «Whose» is the genitive form of «who».
note for the reader of a maths problem: In English the genitive is shown by 's (singular: the girl's) or s' (plural ending in s: the girls'), or by «of». Possessive pronouns (my, your, his, its) have no apostrophe: «its» (belonging to it) is not «it's» (it is). Stress: GEN-i-tiv.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Being real and not fake: the genuineness of a painting or a coin. 2) Being honest and sincere, really meaning what you say or feel.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life people check the genuineness of money, signatures and products; in stories experts test whether treasure or a will is real. In ethics and friendship lessons it means a person is honest and not putting on an act. Phrases: doubt the genuineness of, test its genuineness.
examples from the lessons: The museum checked the genuineness of the old map. | Everyone could feel the genuineness of her thank-you speech. | Banks check the genuineness of banknotes with special lights. | I liked the genuineness of his apology. | Experts doubted the genuineness of the dinosaur egg. | Genuineness matters more than fancy words.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Made from «genuine» + -ness. Pronounced JEN-yoo-in-ness. Synonyms: authenticity, sincerity, realness. Opposite: fakeness, falseness.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To do with geology, the science of the Earth's rocks, soil, layers and how they formed and changed. 2) To do with very long stretches of Earth's history, millions of years long: geological time.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography lessons it appears in rock cycle work, fossils, volcanoes and maps: a geological map shows which rocks are where. «Geological time» shows that mountains and canyons take millions of years to form. Phrases: geological time, geological map, geological survey, geological feature.
examples from the lessons: The Grand Canyon is a famous geological feature. | A geological map shows the rocks under the ground. | Fossils help scientists understand geological time. | The Giant's Causeway in Ireland is a geological wonder of basalt columns. | In geological terms, humans arrived only a moment ago. | The geological survey found coal under the hills. | Rocks form layers over geological ages.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stress: jee-uh-LOJ-ik-ul. From «geology» (geo = earth, -logy = study). A geologist is the scientist. «Geographical» is different: it is about places, maps, countries and people as well as land.

meaning for a pupil: 1) From or to do with Ghana, a country in West Africa. 2) (noun) A person from Ghana.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and culture lessons Ghanaian topics include its capital Accra, cocoa farming, kente cloth, jollof rice, highlife music, and independence in 1957 (the first in sub-Saharan Africa to break free from colonial rule). Many Ghanaian families live in the UK, the USA and Canada. Phrases: Ghanaian food, Ghanaian culture, a Ghanaian-British family.
examples from the lessons: My friend Kwame's family is Ghanaian. | Ghanaian kente cloth has bright woven patterns. | We tasted Ghanaian jollof rice at the culture fair. | Many Ghanaians speak English as well as Twi or Ewe. | Ghanaian farmers grow lots of the world's cocoa. | A Ghanaian storyteller told us about Anansi the spider.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always with a capital G: Ghanaian. Spelling: Ghana + ian (Ghanaian, not «Ghanian»). Pronounced gah-NAY-un. Ghana's official language is English.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Like a ghost or to do with ghosts: pale, faint, strange and scary. 2) Faint and hard to see or hear, as if not quite real: a ghostly shape in the fog.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, especially spooky ones and at Halloween, «ghostly» builds a creepy mood: ghostly figures, ghostly voices, ghostly white. In descriptive writing lessons it is a good word for mist, moonlight and echoes. Phrases: a ghostly figure, a ghostly whisper, ghostly pale.
examples from the lessons: A ghostly figure drifted across the old hall. | We heard a ghostly moan from the attic, but it was just the wind. | The moon gave the garden a ghostly glow. | Her face looked ghostly pale after the fright. | Ghostly shapes of ships appeared out of the fog. | The tale was full of ghostly whispers. | Using «ghostly» made my Halloween story spookier.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It looks like an adverb (-ly) but it is an adjective: «a ghostly sound», not «he walked ghostly». Spelling: gh at the start, silent h. Ghosts are a part of stories and beliefs; science has never shown that they exist.

part of speech: noun, a name (Gilbert); noun (a gilbert — science unit, rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (a name) A boy's or man's first name, or a surname. 2) (science, rare) An old unit used to measure magnetic force.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and history it is a name, for example Gilbert in «Anne of Green Gables» (Canada), or W. S. Gilbert of the comic operas «Gilbert and Sullivan». The Gilbert Islands are part of Kiribati in the Pacific. Usually written with a capital G.
examples from the lessons: Gilbert Blythe teased Anne in «Anne of Green Gables». | My great-grandad was called Gilbert. | Gilbert and Sullivan wrote funny songs and operas. | The Gilbert Islands are in the Pacific Ocean. | Gilbert is in my class this year.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a name it always takes a capital letter. Pronounced GIL-bert, with a hard g as in «gift». Only use the unit sense in old science books.

part of speech: adjective (gilded); verb form, past of gild (gild, gilds, gilded, gilding)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Covered with a thin layer of gold or gold-coloured paint. 2) Looking rich and fancy, sometimes only on the outside: a gilded life. 3) (phrase) «A gilded cage» means a comfortable, rich life where you are not free.
its sense in the lessons: In history and art lessons gilded frames, crowns, church domes and palace ceilings show wealth and power. In stories «gilded» shows luxury or hints that something only looks good. In US history the «Gilded Age» (about 1870–1900) was a time of great riches for some and poverty for many. Phrases: gilded frame, gilded cage, the Gilded Age.
examples from the lessons: The portrait hung in a gilded frame. | The palace had gilded ceilings and huge mirrors. | The princess lived in a gilded cage and longed to go outside. | The church dome is gilded and shines in the sun. | Autumn leaves gilded the park with gold. | The Gilded Age was a time of millionaires and factories in America.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: gild, gilded. Homophone trap: «gild» (cover with gold) and «guild» (a group of workers) sound the same. «Gilded» does not mean solid gold, only a thin layer. Saying «to gild the lily» means to spoil something already beautiful by adding more.

part of speech: noun, a name (Gladstone); noun (a Gladstone bag, Gladstone bags)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (a name) William Ewart Gladstone, a British Prime Minister four times in the 1800s. 2) A Gladstone bag: an old-fashioned leather travelling bag that opens wide into two halves, like a doctor's bag. 3) (a name) Gladstone is also a place name, for example a city in Queensland, Australia.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons Gladstone appears with Queen Victoria and his rival Disraeli. In old stories a doctor or traveller carries a Gladstone bag. Usually with a capital G.
examples from the lessons: William Gladstone was Prime Minister four times. | The doctor opened his Gladstone bag and took out a stethoscope. | Gladstone and Disraeli argued in Parliament. | Gladstone is a port city in Queensland. | Grandad's old Gladstone bag is in the attic.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital G as a name and usually in «Gladstone bag». Pronounced GLAD-stun. It is not a kind of stone.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Covered with glitter, tiny shiny bits that sparkle. 2) Shining with lots of small flashes of light: glittery snow. 3) Showy and glamorous, full of bright lights and fame.
its sense in the lessons: In art and crafts lessons children make glittery cards and decorations. In stories it describes snow, stars, party clothes and treasure. In science, glitter is often tiny plastic, so many schools now use eco-friendly glitter. Phrases: glittery card, glittery dress, glittery nail polish.
examples from the lessons: We made glittery Christmas cards in class. | Her glittery shoes sparkled on the stage. | The snow looked glittery in the morning sun. | The glittery glue got all over my hands. | Hollywood is a glittery world of film stars. | My sister painted her nails a glittery purple. | Some schools have banned plastic glitter to protect the sea.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective from «glitter» + -y. Similar: sparkly, shiny. Comparative: glitterier is rare; «more glittery» is common. Saying: «All that glitters is not gold» means something shiny is not always valuable.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Very beautiful and wonderful to see or feel: a glorious sunset. 2) (of weather) Bright, sunny and warm: a glorious day. 3) Bringing great fame, honour and praise: a glorious victory. 4) (informal) Very enjoyable: we had a glorious time.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday British and Irish talk «glorious weather» is a happy remark about sunshine. In history and poetry it describes famous victories and brave deeds; in stories and descriptive writing it is a strong word for beauty. Phrases: glorious sunshine, a glorious day, glorious victory, the Glorious Twelfth.
examples from the lessons: What a glorious sunny day for the beach! | The sunset over the sea was glorious. | The team won a glorious victory in the final. | We had a glorious time at Gran's farm. | The gardens are glorious in spring. | The poem tells of glorious deeds by brave knights. | The weather forecast promised glorious sunshine for sports day.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective from «glory» (y → i + -ous). Adverb: gloriously. Strong word: use it for really great things, or it loses its power. Do not mix with «glamorous» (stylish and attractive).

part of speech: noun (gloss, glosses); verb (gloss, glosses, glossed, glossing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A smooth shine on a surface: the gloss on a new car. 2) Gloss paint: shiny paint used on doors and wood. 3) A make-up product that makes lips shiny: lip gloss. 4) A short explanation of a word or phrase, often written in the margin or in a glossary. 5) (verb) «Gloss over» means to talk about a problem quickly so people do not notice it.
its sense in the lessons: In art and DIY, gloss paint is shiny and easy to wipe, unlike matt paint. In reading and language lessons a gloss explains a hard word; a glossary is a list of them at the back of a book. In everyday talk, «glossing over» a mistake means hiding it by not talking about it. Phrases: gloss paint, lip gloss, high gloss, gloss over.
examples from the lessons: Dad painted the door with white gloss. | The horse's coat had a lovely gloss after brushing. | My sister wears strawberry lip gloss. | The book gives a gloss for each hard word. | The coach glossed over our mistakes and praised our effort. | Photos can be printed in gloss or matt. | Don't gloss over the problem, tell me what really happened.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: glosses. Uncountable when it means shine: «the gloss on the floor». Opposite of gloss paint is matt (UK) / matte (US). «Glossy» is the adjective: a glossy magazine. «Glossary» is a list of glosses (word meanings).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Twisted, rough and full of knots, like an old tree trunk or branch. 2) (of hands or fingers) Bent and knobbly, often from old age or hard work.
its sense in the lessons: In stories «gnarled» trees create a spooky or ancient mood in forests; gnarled hands show an old or hard-working character, like a wise old woman or farmer. In descriptive writing lessons it is a strong, vivid adjective. Phrases: gnarled oak, gnarled roots, gnarled hands.
examples from the lessons: A gnarled old oak stood by the gate. | The witch pointed a gnarled finger at the children. | The gnarled roots made it hard to walk along the path. | Grandad's gnarled hands still mend fishing nets. | Gnarled olive trees can live for hundreds of years. | The wind had twisted the tree into a gnarled shape.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Silent g: pronounced «narld». Related noun: gnarl (a knot in wood). Do not confuse with «gnawed» (chewed), also with a silent g. «Gnarly» in surfer slang (US, Australia) can mean «great» or «dangerous».

meaning for a pupil: 1) The area right in front of the goal, between the goalposts, in football (soccer), hockey and similar games.
its sense in the lessons: In PE lessons and match reports «goalmouth» describes where the action is close to the goal: a goalmouth scramble is a messy fight for the ball in front of the goal. Phrases: goalmouth scramble, in the goalmouth, goalmouth action.
examples from the lessons: There was a goalmouth scramble and Ellie scored. | The goalkeeper cleared the ball out of the goalmouth. | The muddy goalmouth made it hard to dive. | The ball bounced around the goalmouth before going in. | Commentators love exciting goalmouth action. | Defenders must guard the goalmouth at corners.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word: goal + mouth. Plural: goalmouths. It is not a mouth: it is an opening, like the «mouth» of a river or a cave.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person whose job is to look after a group of goats, usually taking them out to graze in the hills.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, fairy tales and Bible lessons goatherds and shepherds live simple lives looking after animals; in «Heidi» the goatherd Peter takes the goats up the Alps. In history and geography it shows farming in mountains. Phrases: a young goatherd, the goatherd's hut.
examples from the lessons: Peter the goatherd led the goats up the mountain. | The goatherd whistled to bring the goats home. | In the story, the goatherd found a lost princess. | A goatherd in Greece showed us his flock. | The goatherd slept in a small stone hut. | The lonely goatherd sang in the hills.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word: goat + herd. Pronounced GOHT-herd. «Herd» here means a person who looks after animals, as in shepherd (a sheep herd). Not to be confused with «goat herd» (two words: a group of goats).

meaning for a pupil: 1) The skin of a goat, often made into leather. 2) Something made from goat leather, such as a bag, drum, or a container for water or wine.
its sense in the lessons: In history and Bible lessons goatskin bottles carried water and wine; in music, many drums such as the djembe have goatskin tops. In art and design it is a soft leather for gloves and book covers. Phrases: goatskin drum, goatskin bag, goatskin leather.
examples from the lessons: The djembe drum has a goatskin top. | Travellers carried water in goatskin bags. | Her gloves are made of soft goatskin. | In the Bible story, Jacob wore goatskin on his arms. | The old book is bound in goatskin. | Goatskin is thinner than cowhide.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word: goat + skin. Usually uncountable when it means the material (made of goatskin), countable for one skin or bag (two goatskins). Vegetarians and vegans may avoid goatskin products.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Soft, sticky and wet: gooey chocolate cake. 2) (informal) Too sweet and sentimental, full of soppy feelings: a gooey love song.
its sense in the lessons: In cooking and everyday life «gooey» is a happy word for melted cheese, brownies and marshmallows. In science it describes sticky substances like slime and glue. In stories it can describe something icky, or soppy romantic moments. Phrases: gooey brownies, gooey slime, go all gooey.
examples from the lessons: The brownies were warm and gooey in the middle. | My hands got gooey making slime. | The pizza had gooey melted cheese. | Gran went all gooey when she saw the puppy. | Toasted marshmallows are gooey inside. | The film was too gooey for my brother.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative: gooier, gooiest (y → i). From «goo», a sticky substance. Similar: sticky, squishy. «Go all gooey» (informal) means to become soft and emotional.

part of speech: adjective (goofy, goofier, goofiest); noun, a name (Goofy)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) Silly, clumsy and funny in a harmless way. 2) (informal) Having big, sticking-out front teeth: a goofy grin. 3) (a name) Goofy, the tall, clumsy Disney cartoon dog. 4) (surfing, skateboarding) Goofy-footed: riding with the right foot forward.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday North American, Australian and British talk, «goofy» is a friendly word for being silly or making a funny face. In stories it describes a fun, clumsy character. In skateboarding and surfing, «goofy» or «regular» tells which foot is in front. Phrases: a goofy grin, goofy dance, goofy-footed.
examples from the lessons: My dad does a goofy dance at weddings. | She made a goofy face for the class photo. | Goofy and Mickey went fishing in the cartoon. | We laughed at his goofy jokes all day. | I skate goofy, with my right foot forward. | The puppy is goofy and keeps tripping over its ears.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal: avoid in formal writing. Comparative: goofier, goofiest. Usually not mean, but «goofy teeth» can hurt someone's feelings. The verb «goof» or «goof up» means to make a silly mistake (US).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A small, round, sour green or reddish fruit with fine hairs and stripes that grows on a prickly bush. 2) (UK, informal) «Play gooseberry» means to be the third person with a couple who want to be alone. 3) Cape gooseberry: a different small orange fruit in a papery case.
its sense in the lessons: In gardening and food lessons gooseberries are a traditional British fruit used in pies, jam and «gooseberry fool». In everyday British talk, being «a gooseberry» means feeling left out with a couple. Phrases: gooseberry jam, gooseberry bush, play gooseberry.
examples from the lessons: We picked gooseberries from Grandad's prickly bush. | Gooseberries are very sour unless you cook them with sugar. | Mum made a gooseberry crumble. | I didn't want to play gooseberry, so I left my sister and her boyfriend alone. | Cape gooseberries are orange and sweet. | The gooseberry bush scratched my arms.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: gooseberries (y → ies). Pronounced GOOZ-buh-ree (UK) or GOOS-berry. It has nothing to do with geese. Old joke for small children: babies were «found under a gooseberry bush», which is not true.

meaning for a pupil: 1) GOP: short for «Grand Old Party», a nickname for the Republican Party, one of the two main political parties in the United States. 2) Not an English word on its own in lower case; it appears in news as GOP.
its sense in the lessons: In politics and news lessons about the USA, «GOP» appears in headlines: «GOP candidates», «the GOP majority in the Senate». The other main party is the Democratic Party. Its symbol is an elephant; the Democrats' is a donkey. Phrases: the GOP, GOP leaders, GOP voters.
examples from the lessons: The GOP is another name for the Republican Party. | News headlines often say «GOP» to save space. | The GOP's symbol is an elephant. | Abraham Lincoln was the first Republican president. | GOP and Democratic leaders argued about the new law.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always written in capitals: GOP, said as letters «G-O-P». It is about American politics only. The «Grand Old Party» nickname is from the 1800s. Teachers ask us to say what each party says in its own words, fairly.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A small North American burrowing animal with large cheek pouches, which digs tunnels and eats plant roots (pocket gopher). 2) (US, Canada) A name also used for ground squirrels. 3) (informal) A person who runs small errands for others («go for» this, «go for» that), also spelled gofer.
its sense in the lessons: In science and nature lessons in the USA and Canada, gophers are burrowing rodents that can damage gardens and crops. The University of Minnesota's team is the Golden Gophers. In computing, the Go programming language has a gopher mascot. Phrases: gopher hole, pocket gopher.
examples from the lessons: A gopher dug tunnels all over the farmer's field. | Gophers carry food in pouches in their cheeks. | Watch out for gopher holes when you run on the prairie. | The film studio hired a gopher to fetch coffee. | The Go language's mascot is a cute blue gopher. | In Canada, people call ground squirrels gophers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: gophers. «ph» sounds like f: GOH-fer. The errand-runner sense is often spelled «gofer». Gophers are not moles: moles eat insects, gophers eat plants.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Very beautiful or attractive. 2) Very pleasant or enjoyable: gorgeous weather, a gorgeous cake. 3) (informal, UK) A friendly way to address someone: «Hello, gorgeous!»
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life it is an enthusiastic word for lovely views, food, clothes, babies and pets. In stories it describes beautiful places and people. In descriptive writing it is a stronger word than «pretty» or «nice». Phrases: gorgeous view, absolutely gorgeous, look gorgeous.
examples from the lessons: What a gorgeous view of the mountains! | The bride looked gorgeous in her dress. | We had gorgeous weather at the beach. | This chocolate cake is absolutely gorgeous. | Look at that gorgeous puppy! | The autumn colours in Canada are gorgeous. | Gran calls everyone «gorgeous» when she says hello.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: g-o-r-g-e-o-u-s (the e before -ous keeps the g soft: GOR-jus). Adverb: gorgeously. Calling a stranger «gorgeous» can feel too personal; it is mostly said by family and friends.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To do with a government, the group of people who run a country, state or area and make its laws and decisions.
its sense in the lessons: In citizenship and politics lessons it appears in phrases like governmental departments, governmental decisions and non-governmental organisations (NGOs) such as charities that are not run by the state. Phrases: governmental agency, governmental policy, non-governmental organisation.
examples from the lessons: The new park is a governmental project. | The Red Cross is a non-governmental organisation. | Governmental decisions affect schools and hospitals. | The report came from a governmental agency. | Some charities work without governmental money. | Teachers explained the difference between governmental and local council jobs.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal word; in everyday speech people usually say «government» as an adjective: government money. Spelling: remember the n in «governMENTal» (gover-n-ment). NGO = non-governmental organisation.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who studies grammar, the rules of how words and sentences are built in a language, or who writes books about it. 2) (informal) Someone who cares a lot about correct grammar.
its sense in the lessons: In language lessons and olympiads grammarians are the experts who describe languages, such as the ancient Indian grammarian Pāṇini or writers of school grammar books. In everyday life a «grammar fan» corrects others' mistakes. Phrases: a strict grammarian, ancient grammarians.
examples from the lessons: Pāṇini was an ancient grammarian who described Sanskrit. | A grammarian would say «fewer apples», not «less apples». | The grammarian wrote a big book about English verbs. | My aunt is a real grammarian and corrects every text. | Grammarians study how languages change over time. | Not every grammarian agrees about split infinitives.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: grammarians. Stress: gruh-MAIR-ee-un. Spelling: grammar ends in -ar, not -er. Modern grammarians mostly describe how people really speak rather than give strict rules; dialects have their own grammar too.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An old machine for playing music from records, flat discs with grooves, often with a big horn to make the sound louder.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons gramophones show how people listened to music before radio, cassettes, CDs and streaming. In old stories families gather round the gramophone. Thomas Edison invented the phonograph, and Emile Berliner the gramophone with flat discs. Phrases: wind up the gramophone, a gramophone record.
examples from the lessons: Great-grandma danced to music on the gramophone. | You had to wind up the gramophone by hand. | The museum has a gramophone with a huge brass horn. | Gramophone records were made of shellac and broke easily. | In the film, an old gramophone played in the empty house. | The gramophone came before the record player.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: gramophones. «ph» sounds like f: GRAM-uh-fone. In American English «phonograph» is the more common old word; modern word: record player or turntable.

part of speech: adjective (granulated); verb form, past of granulate
meaning for a pupil: 1) In the form of small grains: granulated sugar. 2) (verb, science) Made into small grains or having a grainy surface.
its sense in the lessons: In cooking and maths recipe problems, granulated sugar is ordinary white sugar with small crystals, different from icing sugar and caster sugar. In science it describes substances broken into grains. Phrases: granulated sugar, granulated coffee.
examples from the lessons: The recipe needs 200 grams of granulated sugar. | Granulated sugar has bigger crystals than caster sugar. | If 1 cake needs 150 g of granulated sugar, 3 cakes need 450 g. | We sprinkled granulated sugar on the pancakes. | Instant coffee is often granulated. | The salt was granulated, not in big rocks.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced GRAN-yoo-lay-tid. From «granule» (a small grain). In maths recipe questions, multiply the amount of each ingredient by the number of batches.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A feeling of pleasure or satisfaction when you get what you want. 2) Something that gives pleasure. 3) «Instant gratification» means wanting pleasure right now, not waiting for it; «delayed gratification» means waiting for a bigger reward later.
its sense in the lessons: In PSHE and ethics lessons delayed gratification is an important idea: saving pocket money, studying now for later success, or the famous «marshmallow test» where children wait for a second sweet. In everyday life screens and snacks give instant gratification. Phrases: instant gratification, delayed gratification, a sense of gratification.
examples from the lessons: Saving for a bike teaches delayed gratification. | Games give instant gratification, but reading pays off later. | She felt deep gratification when her painting won a prize. | In the marshmallow test, some children waited for two sweets. | Gratification can come from helping others too. | He wanted instant gratification and ate the cake before dinner.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Long word: grat-i-fi-CAY-shun. Verb: gratify (to please). Adjective: gratifying. Do not confuse with «gratitude» (thankfulness) or «graffiti» (writing on walls). Fairly formal.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Without a good reason, in a way that is unnecessary and often unkind or shocking: gratuitously rude. 2) (formal, old) Free of charge, without payment.
its sense in the lessons: In reviews of films and books, «gratuitously violent» means there is more violence than the story needs. In ethics lessons it describes harm done for no reason, which makes it worse. Phrases: gratuitously cruel, gratuitously violent, gratuitously rude.
examples from the lessons: The villain was gratuitously cruel to the animals. | The review said the film was gratuitously violent. | He was gratuitously rude to the waiter for no reason. | Don't use gratuitously long words in your essay. | Some games are criticised for being gratuitously gory.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb of «gratuitous». Stress: gruh-TYOO-it-us-lee. Not linked to «gratitude». The «free of charge» sense is rare now; «gratuity» (a tip) keeps that idea.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An imaginary, mischievous little creature blamed for things going wrong with machines. 2) (informal) An unknown small fault that makes a machine or computer break down: there's a gremlin in the system.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and films (like «Gremlins») gremlins are naughty creatures. In everyday life adults joke that «gremlins» broke the printer or the Wi-Fi. The idea started with pilots in the Royal Air Force in the 1920s–1940s, blaming plane faults on gremlins. Phrases: a gremlin in the works, technical gremlins.
examples from the lessons: Dad blamed the gremlins when the computer crashed. | There's a gremlin in the printer again. | In the story, a green gremlin hid inside the plane. | Technical gremlins delayed the school play's lights. | Pilots used to joke that gremlins chewed the wires. | The engineers hunted the gremlin for hours.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a gremlin, gremlins. Gremlins are not real; «a gremlin» in machines is a way of saying «an unknown fault». Not the same as goblins, though both are small mischievous creatures in stories.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A sweet red syrup, traditionally made from pomegranate juice, used to flavour and colour drinks.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life grenadine is added to lemonade or orange juice to make red, layered drinks, such as a «Shirley Temple». In cooking or science lessons the layered drink shows density: the heavy syrup sinks to the bottom. Phrases: a splash of grenadine, grenadine syrup.
examples from the lessons: The waiter added a splash of grenadine to my lemonade. | Grenadine is a sweet red syrup. | It sank to the bottom of the glass because it is heavier. | A Shirley Temple is ginger ale with grenadine and a cherry. | Our science demo used grenadine to show layers. | Grenadine was first made from pomegranates.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Pronounced GREN-uh-deen. It comes from the French word for pomegranate («grenade»). Not related to «grenade» (a small bomb), even though the words are cousins. Many shop brands now use other fruit flavours and colouring.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Very serious and harmful: a grievous mistake. 2) (formal) Causing great sadness or pain: a grievous loss. 3) (law, UK) «Grievous bodily harm» (GBH) is a serious crime of badly hurting someone.
its sense in the lessons: In history, Bible and old stories it marks serious wrongs, sins and losses. In UK news and law, GBH is a serious assault. In everyday speech it is rare and sounds formal or old-fashioned. Phrases: a grievous error, grievous loss, grievous bodily harm.
examples from the lessons: The general made a grievous mistake and lost the battle. | The death of the queen was a grievous loss to the country. | The man was charged with grievous bodily harm. | «I have sinned grievously,» said the knight in the story. | A grievous wound needs a doctor straight away. | Forgetting her birthday was not a grievous crime.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced GREE-vus (two syllables). A very common mistake is «GREE-vee-us» or spelling it «grievious»: there is no i before -ous. Related: grief, grieve, grievance.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Very seriously or badly: grievously wounded. 2) (formal) In a way that causes great sorrow or harm: grievously wronged.
its sense in the lessons: In history, war stories and the Bible it describes serious wounds, sins and wrongs. In news it appears in reports of serious injuries. In everyday speech people usually say «badly» or «seriously» instead. Phrases: grievously wounded, grievously mistaken, grievously hurt.
examples from the lessons: The soldier was grievously wounded in the battle. | «You are grievously mistaken,» said the old judge. | The village suffered grievously in the flood. | The king felt he had been grievously wronged. | Two climbers were grievously injured in the fall.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb of «grievous». Pronounced GREE-vus-lee, three syllables; not «grievious-ly». Formal and old-fashioned; for school writing «seriously» is often clearer.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In West Africa, a traditional storyteller, singer, poet and historian who keeps the history of families and peoples alive by telling it aloud, often with music.
its sense in the lessons: In history, music and culture lessons about West Africa (Mali, Senegal, The Gambia, Guinea), griots show how history was passed down by memory and speech, not only in books. They often play the kora, a harp-like instrument, and tell the story of Sundiata Keita, founder of the Mali Empire. Phrases: a griot's song, the griot tradition.
examples from the lessons: The griot told the story of Sundiata Keita. | Griots remember the history of whole families. | The griot played the kora while he sang. | In Mali, griots are still honoured today. | Our class learned how griots keep history alive by speaking it. | The book was written by a griot's grandson.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: griots. Pronounced GREE-oh (the t is silent, from French) or GREE-ot. Other local names include jali or jeli. It is a respected role, often passed from parent to child.

part of speech: noun (a grouping, groupings); verb form (group, groups, grouped, grouping)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A set of people or things that are put together because they are alike or work together. 2) The act of putting things into groups. 3) (maths) Putting numbers or objects into equal groups to help count, multiply or divide; also using brackets to group parts of a calculation.
its sense in the lessons: In maths lessons grouping helps with multiplication (3 groups of 4 = 12), division (sharing into groups) and place value (grouping into tens). In science, grouping or classifying animals and materials by features is a key skill. In class, teachers arrange pupils in groupings for tasks. In politics a grouping is a set of parties or countries working together. Phrases: grouping in tens, ability grouping, a political grouping.
examples from the lessons: We used grouping to count the beads in tens. | 20 sweets shared by grouping into 5s gives 4 groups. | In science we did a grouping of animals by what they eat. | The teacher changed the table groupings this week. | Brackets show the grouping in 2 × (3 + 4). | A new grouping of countries agreed to work together on climate. | Grouping words by their spelling patterns helps me learn them.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a grouping, groupings. In maths, «grouping» for division means: how many groups of a given size fit into a number, e.g. 12 ÷ 3 = 4 groups of 3. Brackets change the grouping and so the answer: (2 + 3) × 4 = 20, but 2 + 3 × 4 = 14.

part of speech: noun (a groyne, groynes); US spelling groin
meaning for a pupil: 1) A low wall or fence of wood, stone or concrete built out from a beach into the sea to stop the sand and pebbles being washed away.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons on coasts (UK, Ireland, Australia, New Zealand), groynes are a kind of «hard engineering» that stops longshore drift, the way waves move sand along the coast. Beaches with groynes have more sand on one side. Phrases: wooden groynes, coastal defences, longshore drift.
examples from the lessons: Wooden groynes stretch down the beach at Brighton. | Groynes trap sand carried by longshore drift. | We sat on a groyne and ate our picnic. | Sand piles up on one side of each groyne. | The council built new groynes to protect the coast. | In our geography test we had to label the groynes on a diagram.
note for the reader of a maths problem: British spelling: groyne. American spelling: groin, which is also the word for the top of the inside leg, so the British spelling avoids a mix-up. Rhymes with «coin». Safety: do not climb on slippery groynes when the tide is coming in.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Rather dirty, usually from mud, sweat or touching things. 2) (informal) Not quite honest or decent: a grubby little trick.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life «grubby» describes children's hands, knees, clothes and old books; adults say «wash those grubby hands before dinner». In hygiene lessons it reminds us to wash hands to remove germs. In stories it can describe a dishonest deal or a poor, dirty place. Phrases: grubby hands, grubby little fingers, grubby clothes.
examples from the lessons: Wash your grubby hands before you eat! | His school shirt was grubby after playtime. | The library book had grubby fingerprints on it. | The grubbiest kid on the team scored the winning goal. | The car was grubby after the muddy road. | It was a grubby trick to cheat in the quiz.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative: grubbier, grubbiest (y → i). From «grub» (dirt, or an insect larva). Milder than «filthy». Informal word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A wild South American animal like a small, slim llama, with a light brown woolly coat, living in the Andes mountains and Patagonia.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography lessons about South America, guanacos appear with llamas, alpacas and vicuñas, all in the camel family. Llamas were bred from wild guanacos long ago. They live in herds in dry grasslands and high mountains. Phrases: a herd of guanacos, wild guanacos.
examples from the lessons: A guanaco is a wild cousin of the llama. | We saw a herd of guanacos in Patagonia. | Guanacos can live in very dry places. | Llamas were tamed from guanacos thousands of years ago. | The guanaco spat when the tourist came too close. | Guanacos have thick wool to keep warm in the Andes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: guanacos. Pronounced gwah-NAH-koh. Comes from the Quechua language. Llama and alpaca are tame; guanaco and vicuña are wild.

meaning for a pupil: 1) From or to do with Guatemala, a country in Central America, south of Mexico. 2) (noun) A person from Guatemala.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and culture lessons Guatemalan topics include the ancient Maya cities such as Tikal, volcanoes, colourful woven textiles, coffee and worry dolls. Many Guatemalans speak Spanish and many speak Maya languages. Phrases: Guatemalan coffee, Guatemalan worry dolls, Guatemalan textiles.
examples from the lessons: Guatemalan worry dolls are tiny dolls you tell your worries to. | Tikal is an ancient Maya city in the Guatemalan rainforest. | Mum buys Guatemalan coffee. | Many Guatemalans speak a Maya language as well as Spanish. | The Guatemalan flag has a quetzal bird on it. | My friend's family is Guatemalan-American.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always capital G. Pronounced gwah-tuh-MAH-lun. Spelling: Guatemala + n. The quetzal is both the national bird and the money of Guatemala.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who guesses, who gives an answer without knowing for sure. 2) In tests and games, a rule or player that picks an answer without really knowing, for example always choosing the longest option.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and quizzes, a «good guesser» uses estimation and clues; a random guesser often gets it wrong. In school testing a «guesser» is the score you would get by pure luck, which a real answer should beat. Phrases: a good guesser, a lucky guesser, a wild guesser.
examples from the lessons: She is a great guesser at riddles. | A lucky guesser might get one in four answers right on a quiz. | The longest-answer guesser is the score to beat. | In the game, the guesser has to find the hidden word. | Dad is a terrible guesser of people's ages. | Be a smart guesser: estimate first, then check.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: guessers. From «guess» + -er. In maths, a sensible guess is called an estimate; checking it with a calculation is good practice. With 4 options, pure guessing gets about 1 in 4 (25%) right on average.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Finding an answer by guessing, without enough facts or careful working out.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and science lessons teachers say «show your working, not guesswork»: answers need reasons, measurements or calculations. In everyday life weather, cooking without a recipe or finding your way without a map may involve guesswork. Phrases: pure guesswork, a lot of guesswork, take the guesswork out of.
examples from the lessons: My answer was pure guesswork, but it was right! | A recipe takes the guesswork out of baking. | Science uses evidence, not guesswork. | Without a map, finding the path was guesswork. | The teacher said, «I want calculations, not guesswork.» | Weather forecasts used to involve much more guesswork.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «a lot of guesswork», not «a guesswork». One word. Different from an estimate, which is a sensible guess based on facts.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A book that gives information to visitors about a place, such as a city, country, museum or castle, with maps, history and tips.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life families take guidebooks on holiday; in geography lessons pupils may write their own guidebook to their town. In stories a guidebook helps travellers find hidden places. Phrases: a travel guidebook, according to the guidebook.
examples from the lessons: The guidebook said the castle opens at ten. | We wrote a guidebook to our town for visitors. | According to the guidebook, the museum is free. | Mum read the guidebook on the plane to Dublin. | The guidebook had a map of the old city. | Nowadays many people use apps instead of guidebooks.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word: guide + book. Plural: guidebooks. Spelling: «guide» has a silent u (g-u-i-d-e). A «guide» can also be a person who shows you around.

meaning for a pupil: 1) From or to do with Guinea, a country in West Africa. 2) (noun) A person from Guinea. 3) Sometimes used for Equatorial Guinea or Guinea-Bissau, which are different countries (more exactly: Equatoguinean, Bissau-Guinean).
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons Guinea is known for its rivers (the Niger and Senegal start there), bauxite mining, and French as an official language. Guinean music has famous griots and kora players. Phrases: Guinean music, a Guinean village.
examples from the lessons: The Guinean capital is Conakry. | Guinean griots play the kora. | Our football coach is Guinean. | The River Niger starts in the Guinean highlands. | Many Guineans speak French as well as local languages.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always capital G. Pronounced GIN-ee-un. Do not confuse Guinea (West Africa) with Papua New Guinea (in Oceania), Guinea-Bissau or Equatorial Guinea; a person from Papua New Guinea is a Papua New Guinean. A «guinea pig» is a pet from South America, not from Guinea.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To do with a gyroscope, a spinning wheel or disc that keeps steady and resists being tipped over. 2) Behaving like a gyroscope: steady because it spins.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on forces, gyroscopic effects help explain why a spinning top stays up, why a moving bicycle is easier to balance, and how spinning helps a frisbee fly straight. Phones, drones and planes use gyroscopic sensors to know which way they are tilted. Phrases: gyroscopic effect, gyroscopic stability, gyroscopic sensor.
examples from the lessons: A spinning top stays upright because of the gyroscopic effect. | My phone has a gyroscopic sensor that knows when I turn it. | The drone uses gyroscopic sensors to stay level. | Spinning wheels give a bike some gyroscopic stability. | A frisbee flies straighter because of its gyroscopic spin. | Satellites use gyroscopic wheels to point the right way.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced jy-ruh-SKOP-ik (soft g, like «giant»). From «gyroscope» (gyro = circle, turning). A common myth says bikes stay up only because of gyroscopic effects; in fact steering and the shape of the bike matter even more.

part of speech: noun (a hackney, hackneys); adjective hackneyed; noun, a name (Hackney)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (a name) Hackney, a borough (area) in East London. 2) A hackney carriage: the official name for a taxi in the UK, especially a black cab. 3) A breed of horse or pony with a high-stepping trot, once used to pull carriages. 4) «Hackneyed» means used so often it has become boring: a hackneyed phrase.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday British life and law, «hackney carriage» is written on licensed taxis. In history lessons hackney coaches were horse-drawn cabs for hire. In writing lessons teachers warn against hackneyed phrases (clichés) like «it was all a dream». Phrases: hackney carriage, a hackneyed phrase, the London Borough of Hackney.
examples from the lessons: My cousin lives in Hackney in East London. | The sign on the black cab said «Hackney Carriage». | Hackney ponies lift their legs high when they trot. | In Victorian times you could hire a hackney coach. | «Once upon a time» is a hackneyed opening for a story. | The writer avoided hackneyed phrases.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital H for the place name. Pronounced HACK-nee. «Hackneyed» is the adjective for overused words; it is linked to hired horses that were overworked.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) The red substance in red blood cells that carries oxygen from the lungs around the body and gives blood its red colour.
its sense in the lessons: In science and health lessons haemoglobin explains why blood is red and how oxygen gets to the muscles; it contains iron, so iron-rich foods (beans, spinach, red meat) help keep it healthy. Doctors measure haemoglobin in blood tests; too little can cause anaemia, making people tired and pale. Phrases: haemoglobin levels, low haemoglobin.
examples from the lessons: Haemoglobin carries oxygen around the body. | Blood is red because of haemoglobin. | Haemoglobin needs iron, so eat your beans and greens. | The doctor checked her haemoglobin with a blood test. | Low haemoglobin can make you feel tired. | Haemoglobin picks up oxygen in the lungs and drops it off in the muscles.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. British spelling haemoglobin (ae), American hemoglobin (e). Pronounced HEE-muh-gloh-bin. «Haemo-» / «hemo-» means blood. Myth: blood inside veins is not blue; it is always red, only darker when it has less oxygen.

part of speech: noun (a haemorrhage, haemorrhages); verb (haemorrhage, haemorrhages, haemorrhaged, haemorrhaging); US hemorrhage
meaning for a pupil: 1) (medicine) A lot of bleeding from a broken blood vessel, inside or outside the body; a serious emergency. 2) (verb) To bleed heavily. 3) (informal, money) To lose a lot of something very fast: the club is haemorrhaging money.
its sense in the lessons: In health and first-aid lessons a haemorrhage means serious bleeding: call 999 / 911 / 000 / 112 and press on the wound. In news, a brain haemorrhage is a kind of stroke. In business news it describes losing money or people quickly. Phrases: brain haemorrhage, internal haemorrhage, haemorrhaging money.
examples from the lessons: The footballer was rushed to hospital with an internal haemorrhage. | A brain haemorrhage is a medical emergency. | Press firmly on a wound to slow a haemorrhage. | The shop was haemorrhaging money and had to close. | Doctors stopped the haemorrhage during the operation. | The team was haemorrhaging players to bigger clubs.
