note for the reader of a maths problem: Hard spelling: h-a-e-m-o-r-r-h-a-g-e (UK) or h-e-m-o-r-r-h-a-g-e (US): double r, then h. Pronounced HEM-uh-rij. Safety: heavy bleeding always needs an adult and emergency help.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) The way someone's hair is cut and styled, especially a special or fancy style.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life «hairdo» is a friendly, slightly old-fashioned word for a hairstyle, often for weddings, parties or school photos. In stories it can show a character's personality or be funny when the wind ruins it. Phrases: a new hairdo, a fancy hairdo.
examples from the lessons: Mum got a new hairdo for the wedding. | The wind wrecked Auntie's hairdo. | My sister's hairdo has plaits and ribbons. | Look at the funny hairdos in Grandad's old photos! | The singer is famous for her big hairdo. | I want a short hairdo for the summer.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: hairdos. Informal. Similar: hairstyle, haircut. A «hairdresser» does a hairdo; a «barber» cuts mostly men's and boys' hair.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A very large flat fish that lives in cold northern seas, such as the North Atlantic and North Pacific, eaten as food.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about sea life, halibut are flatfish: both eyes are on one side of the head and they lie on the sea floor. In food, halibut is a white fish, served grilled, in fish and chips or fish pie. In Canada and Alaska halibut fishing is important. Phrases: halibut steak, Atlantic halibut.
examples from the lessons: A halibut has both eyes on one side of its head. | Halibut can grow longer than a grown-up person. | We had grilled halibut for dinner. | Fishermen in Alaska caught a huge halibut. | Atlantic halibut are now protected because of overfishing. | Young halibut swim upright, then one eye moves across.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural usually «halibut» (like sheep), sometimes «halibuts». Pronounced HAL-i-but. It is a fish, not a mammal; do not mix it with «habit».

meaning for a pupil: 1) To see, hear or feel things that are not really there, for example because of high fever, illness, lack of sleep or drugs. 2) (computing, informal) Of an AI chatbot: to make up facts that sound true but are false.
its sense in the lessons: In health lessons it is linked to fever, illness and the dangers of drugs. In science of the brain it shows that our senses can be fooled. In computing lessons, «AI hallucinates» means a chatbot invented an answer, so we must check facts. Phrases: start to hallucinate, the AI hallucinated a source.
examples from the lessons: With a very high fever, some people hallucinate. | The lost explorer was so thirsty he hallucinated a lake. | After three nights without sleep, he began to hallucinate. | The chatbot hallucinated a book that doesn't exist. | Am I hallucinating, or is that a kangaroo in the garden? | Drugs can make people hallucinate and are dangerous.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced huh-LOO-si-nate. Noun: hallucination. Spelling: double l, one c. Seeing a mirage in the desert is a real light effect, not always a hallucination. Always tell an adult if someone is seeing things that are not there.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) The big toe, the first and largest toe of the foot; in birds, the toe that points backwards.
its sense in the lessons: In science and anatomy lessons, «hallux» is the scientific Latin name for the big toe. In bird science, the hallux helps birds grip branches when perching. Doctors use it in words like «hallux valgus» (a bunion). Phrases: the hallux, a bird's hallux.
examples from the lessons: The hallux is the scientific name for your big toe. | A perching bird uses its hallux to grip the branch. | The doctor said the bunion was on her hallux. | Your hallux helps you balance when you walk. | Apes have a hallux that can grab like a thumb.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: halluces (rare). Pronounced HAL-uks. It is a science word; in everyday speech say «big toe».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) One of the two tiny knob-shaped organs on flies and mosquitoes, in place of a back pair of wings, which help them balance and steer while flying.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about insects, halteres explain why flies are such good fliers: the halteres beat with the wings and sense turning, a bit like a living gyroscope. Most insects have four wings; true flies have two wings and two halteres. Phrases: a fly's halteres.
examples from the lessons: Flies have halteres instead of a second pair of wings. | The halteres help a fly keep its balance. | Under the microscope we saw the tiny halteres. | Mosquitoes have halteres too. | Halteres work a bit like a gyroscope.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually used in the plural: halteres (hal-TEER-eez). Science word; not used in everyday talk. Halteres come from the Greek for weights held by jumpers.

part of speech: noun (a hamstring, hamstrings); verb (hamstring, hamstrings, hamstrung, hamstringing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) One of the strong tendons or muscles at the back of the thigh, above the knee. 2) (verb) To stop someone or something from working well: the team was hamstrung by injuries. 3) (verb, old) To cut an animal's hamstring so it cannot run.
its sense in the lessons: In PE and sports lessons the hamstrings are stretched in warm-ups; a «hamstring injury» or «pulled hamstring» is common in football, rugby and running. In news it describes plans that are held back by lack of money or rules. Phrases: pull a hamstring, hamstring stretch, hamstrung by.
examples from the lessons: Stretch your hamstrings before you run. | The striker pulled a hamstring and was off for a month. | Touch your toes to feel your hamstrings stretch. | The project was hamstrung by a lack of money. | Hamstring injuries are common in sprinters. | The physio taped up her sore hamstring.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past tense: hamstrung (also hamstringed, rarer). One word: ham + string. «Ham» is an old word for the back of the knee. In science, the hamstrings bend the knee, the opposite of the quadriceps.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (a name) The Hani are a people of southern China (Yunnan), Vietnam, Laos and Myanmar; their language is also called Hani. 2) (a name) Hani is a first name used in Arabic and some other languages, and a surname. 3) It is not an ordinary English word.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons the Hani people are famous for the Honghe Hani rice terraces in Yunnan, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, carved into mountain slopes over more than a thousand years. As a person's name it is written with a capital H. Phrases: Hani rice terraces, the Hani language.
examples from the lessons: The Hani rice terraces climb up the mountains like giant steps. | The Hani people have farmed these hills for centuries. | Hani is a language spoken in China and Vietnam. | Hani is in Year 5 at our school. | We saw photos of the Hani terraces filled with water.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital H. Pronounced HAH-nee. It is a name or the name of a people and language, not an English common word. Do not confuse with «honey» or «hanny».

part of speech: noun (hap, haps — old-fashioned); verb (hap, haps, happed, happing — old)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (old) Luck or chance, especially something that happens by chance. 2) (old) An event that happens; «haps» means things that happen. 3) (Scotland, northern England, dialect) To wrap up warmly; a «hap» is a warm shawl or blanket.
its sense in the lessons: In modern English «hap» is rarely used alone, but it is the root of common words: happen, happy, perhaps, mishap, haphazard, hapless. In old stories and the Bible-era English it means luck. In slang, «what's the haps?» (US) means «what's happening?». Phrases: by hap, what's the haps.
examples from the lessons: In old stories, «by hap» means «by chance». | «Happen» and «perhaps» both come from «hap». | A «mishap» is a small accident, a bit of bad hap. | Granny in Shetland happed the baby in a woolly shawl. | «What's the haps?» my cousin from California asked.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Old and dialect word; do not use in school essays except when explaining word roots. Word family: happen, happy, perhaps, mishap, haphazard (by chance, without a plan), hapless (unlucky). Not to be confused with «hip» or «hop».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Being unkind, strict or cruel: the harshness of the punishment. 2) Being rough and unpleasant to the senses: the harshness of a sound, a light or a taste. 3) Being very difficult to live in: the harshness of the desert or the Arctic winter.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and history it describes strict rulers, hard punishments and cruel words; in geography and science it describes extreme climates, like deserts and polar regions, where animals need special adaptations. In ethics lessons we compare harshness with fairness and kindness. Phrases: the harshness of winter, harshness of the climate, harshness of her words.
examples from the lessons: The harshness of the Arctic winter makes life hard for animals. | We were shocked by the harshness of the punishment. | The harshness in his voice made the little boy cry. | Camels are adapted to the harshness of the desert. | The bright light's harshness hurt my eyes. | She said sorry for the harshness of her words.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. From «harsh» + -ness. Opposites: gentleness, softness, kindness, mildness.

part of speech: noun (hash, hashes); verb (hash, hashes, hashed, hashing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The symbol # (also called hash sign, pound sign in the US, or number sign), used in hashtags and on phones. 2) A dish of chopped cooked meat and potatoes fried together: corned beef hash. 3) (informal) «Make a hash of something» means do it very badly. 4) (computing) A code made from data by a fixed rule, used to check files and passwords. 5) (slang) Short for hashish, an illegal drug made from cannabis. 6) (verb) «Hash out» means to discuss something until you agree.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life «press hash» on the phone means press #; #hashtags label posts online. In computing lessons, a hash turns a password into a scrambled code. In cooking, hash and hash browns (fried grated potato) are breakfast foods. In stories «made a hash of it» is a funny way to say «messed it up». Safety: drugs are illegal and harmful. Phrases: hash browns, make a hash of, hash out, hashtag.
examples from the lessons: Type your PIN and then press hash. | We had corned beef hash for tea. | I made a total hash of my spelling test. | Hash browns are my favourite breakfast. | Websites store a hash of your password, not the password itself. | The two captains hashed out the rules before the game. | The # symbol is called hash in the UK and pound sign in the US. | The police found hash, an illegal drug, in the car.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: hashes. In the UK # is «hash»; in the US it is often «pound sign» or «number sign»; in music ♯ is «sharp», a different symbol. Not related to «rash» or «harsh». The drug sense is slang: say «cannabis» in school writing.

part of speech: noun (a hassle, hassles — also uncountable); verb (hassle, hassles, hassled, hassling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) Something annoying and difficult that takes effort: getting the bus is such a hassle. 2) (informal) Trouble or arguing: I don't want any hassle. 3) (verb, informal) To keep annoying someone or asking them to do something: stop hassling me about my homework.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday talk «hassle» describes boring chores, queues, forms and travel problems, and nagging or pestering. In stories it shows a character being bothered or bullied. Safety: if someone keeps hassling you online or in the street, tell a trusted adult. Phrases: such a hassle, no hassle, hassle-free, hassle someone about.
examples from the lessons: Packing for the trip was a real hassle. | It's no hassle, I'll drive you to school. | Stop hassling your sister! | The older kids were hassling us for our sweets. | Online shopping is meant to be hassle-free. | Mum hassled me to tidy my room all weekend. | I don't want any hassle, I just want to play.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal word. Spelling: double s. Can be countable (a hassle) or uncountable (too much hassle). Being hassled repeatedly can be bullying or harassment, which is serious.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A small axe with a short handle, used with one hand to chop wood. 2) (idiom) «Bury the hatchet» means to stop arguing and make peace. 3) (idiom) «A hatchet job» means harsh, unfair criticism that tries to damage someone.
its sense in the lessons: In camping, survival stories (like «Hatchet» by Gary Paulsen) and history lessons a hatchet is a tool for chopping firewood and building shelters. Safety: hatchets are sharp tools only for adults or with close adult supervision. In everyday talk, friends «bury the hatchet» after a fight. Phrases: bury the hatchet, hatchet job, hatchet-faced.
examples from the lessons: Dad used a hatchet to chop kindling for the campfire. | In «Hatchet», a boy survives in the Canadian wilderness. | After a week of arguing, the twins finally buried the hatchet. | The newspaper did a hatchet job on the new mayor. | Always carry a hatchet with its blade covered. | The scouts learned how to use a hatchet safely.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: hatchets. Spelling: hat-chet. A hatchet is smaller than an axe and used with one hand. Not related to «hatch» (an egg hatching), although they look alike.

part of speech: noun (a hatter, hatters); a name (the Mad Hatter)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who makes or sells hats. 2) (idiom) «As mad as a hatter» means very crazy or silly. 3) (a name) The Mad Hatter, a character in «Alice's Adventures in Wonderland» by Lewis Carroll.
its sense in the lessons: In reading lessons the Mad Hatter hosts a crazy tea party in «Alice in Wonderland». In history, hatters once used mercury to make felt hats, which could make them ill and act strangely; this may explain the saying «mad as a hatter». Phrases: mad as a hatter, the Mad Hatter's tea party.
examples from the lessons: The Mad Hatter's tea party never ended. | A hatter made top hats for the gentlemen. | My uncle is as mad as a hatter, but very kind. | Old hatters often became ill from the mercury in their work. | The hatter measured my head for a new cap. | We dressed up as the Mad Hatter for World Book Day.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: hatters. Double t. «Mad as a hatter» is a jokey idiom; it is not kind to use «mad» about real mental illness. The work used to be dangerous because of mercury, a poison.

part of speech: noun (Hausa — the people, the language); adjective (Hausa)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (a name) The Hausa are a large people of West Africa, mainly in northern Nigeria and Niger. 2) The Hausa language, spoken by tens of millions of people in West Africa as a first or second language. 3) It is not an English word; it is the name of a people and their language.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and culture lessons about Nigeria and West Africa, Hausa is one of the most widely spoken African languages, used in markets and on radio across many countries. Hausa cities such as Kano have old walls and dye pits. Phrases: the Hausa language, Hausa traders.
examples from the lessons: Hausa is spoken by many millions of people in West Africa. | The Hausa people live mainly in northern Nigeria and Niger. | «Sannu» means «hello» in Hausa. | Kano is a famous Hausa city with ancient dye pits. | The BBC broadcasts news in Hausa.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always capital H. Pronounced HOW-suh. «Hausa» is both the people and the language. It is written in Latin letters today and sometimes in Arabic-based script (Ajami).

part of speech: adjective (haywire — used after a verb: go haywire)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) Out of control, not working properly, behaving wildly: the computer went haywire. 2) (informal) Of a person or plan: crazy or messed up.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life machines, phones, traffic lights and computers «go haywire» when they start doing strange things. In stories it builds funny or scary chaos. The word comes from wire used to tie hay bales, which got tangled easily. Phrases: go haywire, everything went haywire.
examples from the lessons: The traffic lights went haywire and everyone stopped. | My tablet went haywire after the update. | When the fire alarm went off, the whole school day went haywire. | The robot in the story went haywire and danced around the lab. | Our holiday plans went haywire when the flight was cancelled. | The compass went haywire near the magnet.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal; mostly in the phrase «go haywire». One word. It is not used before a noun («a haywire robot» is rare).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Not clear because of mist, smoke, dust or heat in the air: a hazy sky. 2) Not clear in your mind, vague: my memory of that day is hazy. 3) Not sure or confused: I'm a bit hazy about the rules.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and weather lessons, hazy days are caused by heat, dust, smoke from bushfires or pollution. In stories «hazy» describes summer heat, dreamy moments or blurry memories. Phrases: hazy sunshine, a hazy memory, hazy about the details.
examples from the lessons: It was a hot, hazy summer afternoon. | Smoke from the bushfires made the sky hazy. | My memory of my third birthday is very hazy. | I'm a bit hazy about how fractions work. | The mountains looked hazy in the distance. | The forecast is hazy sunshine for sports day.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative: hazier, haziest (y → i). From «haze». Similar: misty, foggy (fog is thicker and wetter). Not related to «lazy», although they rhyme.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The padded part at the top of a seat, for example in a car, plane or chair, that supports the back of your head.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and road safety lessons car headrests protect your neck in a crash and should be at the right height. On planes and buses some headrests have screens on the back. Phrases: adjust the headrest, car headrest.
examples from the lessons: Adjust the headrest so it is level with the top of your head. | My little brother kicked the back of Dad's headrest. | The headrest protects your neck if the car stops suddenly. | The plane seat had a screen in the headrest. | I fell asleep against the headrest.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word: head + rest. Plural: headrests. Safety: a headrest set too low does not protect your neck.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who hears or listens to something, especially a speech, a story or a sermon. 2) (language) In linguistics, the listener in a conversation, as opposed to the speaker.
its sense in the lessons: In language and grammar lessons, «speaker and hearer» describe both sides of talking: good writing and speech think about what the hearer already knows. In Bible and church language, Christians are told to be «doers of the word, and not hearers only». Phrases: the speaker and the hearer, hearers of the story.
examples from the lessons: The storyteller held all her hearers spellbound. | A good speaker thinks about what the hearer needs to know. | The Bible says to be «doers of the word, and not hearers only». | Every hearer laughed at the joke. | In a conversation, the hearer and speaker take turns.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: hearers. Slightly formal or old-fashioned; today people usually say «listener». Not «hearrer». Homophone-like trap: «here» and «hear» are different words; a hearer hears.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Loud, cheerful and friendly: a hearty laugh, a hearty welcome. 2) (of food) Large, warm and filling: a hearty breakfast, hearty soup. 3) Strong and healthy: hale and hearty. 4) Sincere and strongly felt: hearty thanks.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life «hearty» describes big meals after a cold walk, and loud, warm greetings. In stories it describes jolly characters like sailors, farmers or Father Christmas. Phrases: a hearty meal, hearty laugh, hale and hearty, hearty congratulations.
examples from the lessons: We had a hearty breakfast of porridge and eggs. | Grandad gave a hearty laugh at my joke. | The farmer gave us a hearty welcome. | Hearty soup is perfect on a cold winter day. | Great-gran is 95 and still hale and hearty. | The team gave hearty thanks to their coach.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative: heartier, heartiest. Adverb: heartily (eat heartily, laugh heartily). Different from «heartfelt» (deeply sincere) and from «hardy» (tough, able to survive hard conditions).

part of speech: adjective (heaving); verb form (heave, heaves, heaved / hove, heaving); noun (heaving)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Pulling, pushing or lifting something heavy with a lot of effort. 2) Rising and falling strongly: heaving waves, heaving shoulders when crying. 3) Trying to vomit, retching. 4) (UK, informal) Very crowded: the shop was heaving.
its sense in the lessons: In stories «heaving» describes stormy seas, tired sailors pulling ropes, sobbing shoulders or someone being sick. In everyday British talk a «heaving» place is packed with people. In PE and science, heaving is using force to lift or pull. Phrases: heaving with people, heaving seas, heaving a sigh.
examples from the lessons: The beach was heaving with people on the hot day. | The sailors were heaving on the ropes. | The heaving waves rocked the little boat. | Her shoulders were heaving as she cried. | He was heaving over the bucket after the boat trip. | Heaving a sigh, Mum picked up the toys again. | The pub garden was heaving after the match.
note for the reader of a maths problem: -ing form of «heave». Past: heaved (usually); «hove» is used for ships («hove into view»). «Heaving a sigh» means sighing deeply. «Heaving» (crowded) is informal British.

part of speech: noun (heckling — uncountable); verb form (heckle, heckles, heckled, heckling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Shouting rude remarks or questions to interrupt someone who is speaking or performing in public, such as a comedian or politician.
its sense in the lessons: In politics lessons heckling happens at rallies and in Parliament, where MPs shout «hear, hear» or jeer. In everyday life comedians deal with heckling. In citizenship and kindness lessons we learn to disagree politely without heckling. Phrases: face heckling, heckling from the crowd.
examples from the lessons: The comedian dealt with the heckling very cleverly. | There was loud heckling during the politician's speech. | Heckling the referee is not good sportsmanship. | In Parliament, heckling can get very noisy. | The teacher stopped the heckling in the school debate. | She kept calm despite the heckling.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable as a noun. A person who heckles is a «heckler». Spelling: heck-ling (drop the e of heckle). It is rude, and in some places like school assemblies it can get you in trouble.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A young female cow that has not yet had a calf (or has had only one).
its sense in the lessons: In farming and science lessons, cattle words are: calf (baby), heifer (young female), cow (adult female that has had calves), bullock or steer (young castrated male), bull (adult male). In the Bible, heifers appear in old sacrifices. Phrases: a young heifer, heifers in the field.
examples from the lessons: The heifer will have her first calf in spring. | Five heifers were grazing in the meadow. | A heifer becomes a cow after she has calves. | The farmer took his best heifer to the agricultural show. | In the Bible, a red heifer is mentioned in the book of Numbers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced HEF-er (the «ei» sounds like «e» in «bed»). Spelling trap: h-e-i-f-e-r. Plural: heifers. Calling a woman a heifer is a rude insult; do not do it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To do with Greece and the Greek people, language and culture, especially ancient Greece. 2) (history) To do with classical Greek civilisation before Alexander the Great (later times are called Hellenistic).
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons on ancient Greece, «Hellenic» is linked to Hellas, the Greeks' own name for their land. The modern country's official name is the Hellenic Republic. Phrases: Hellenic culture, the Hellenic Republic, Hellenic Navy.
examples from the lessons: Greece's official name is the Hellenic Republic. | The Olympics began as a Hellenic festival. | The museum has a hall of Hellenic statues. | Greeks call themselves Hellenes. | Hellenic myths tell of Zeus and the gods of Olympus.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital H. Pronounced heh-LEN-ik or heh-LEE-nik. «Hellenistic» refers to Greek culture spread after Alexander the Great. Nothing to do with «hell».

part of speech: noun (a helping, helpings); verb form (help, helps, helped, helping); adjective (helping)
meaning for a pupil: 1) An amount of food served to one person at one time: a second helping of pudding. 2) Giving help: helping others is kind. 3) (phrase) «A helping hand» means some help.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life «a second helping» means more food on your plate; in maths, helpings appear in sharing and fraction problems (8 helpings from 2 pizzas). In PSHE and stories, helping others is a key value. Phrases: a second helping, a helping hand, helping out, helping with.
examples from the lessons: Can I have a second helping of lasagne, please? | Thanks for giving me a helping hand with the boxes. | Helping at the food bank made me feel good. | Each helping of soup is 250 millilitres. | If one cake makes 8 helpings, 3 cakes make 24 helpings. | I'm helping Gran with her garden on Saturday. | She took a small helping because she wasn't hungry.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable (a helping, two helpings) when it means a portion. In maths, «helpings» = equal portions: total ÷ size of each helping = number of helpings. Similar words: portion, serving. Do not confuse «helping» (a portion) with «helper» (a person who helps).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) Eating only plants, such as grass, leaves, fruit and seeds.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on food chains, animals are herbivorous (plant-eaters), carnivorous (meat-eaters) or omnivorous (both). Cows, rabbits, elephants, koalas and many dinosaurs like Triceratops were herbivorous. Herbivores are primary consumers in a food chain. Phrases: herbivorous animals, herbivorous dinosaurs.
examples from the lessons: Rabbits are herbivorous animals. | Triceratops was a herbivorous dinosaur. | Herbivorous animals have flat teeth for grinding plants. | Koalas are herbivorous and eat only eucalyptus leaves. | In the food chain, herbivorous animals eat the producers. | Is a panda herbivorous? It mostly eats bamboo.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced her-BIV-uh-rus (in US English the h is often silent: er-BIV-or-us). Noun: herbivore. «A herbivorous» (UK) vs «an herbivorous» (US, when the h is silent). Pandas are mostly herbivorous but sometimes eat small animals.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (US, informal, rude) An insulting word for someone from the countryside, suggesting they are simple and old-fashioned. 2) (adjective, informal) Small, rural and old-fashioned: a hick town. 3) A short sound like a hiccup.
its sense in the lessons: In American stories and films «hick» is used by snobbish characters to look down on country people. In kindness lessons it is an example of a word that mocks people for where they live. Phrases: a hick town, country hick.
examples from the lessons: The city kids unkindly called him a hick. | They grew up in a small hick town in Kansas. | «Don't call people hicks,» said the teacher. | In the film, the «hick» farmer turned out to be the cleverest character. | Hick! went my little sister when she had hiccups.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal and insulting; mainly American. Similar unkind words: yokel, bumpkin, redneck. Using it about a real person is rude.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A North American tree of the walnut family, with hard nuts. 2) The very hard, strong wood of this tree, used for tool handles and drumsticks. 3) Smoke from hickory wood, used to flavour meat: hickory-smoked bacon.
its sense in the lessons: In science and nature lessons in the USA and Canada hickory trees provide nuts for squirrels and people. In everyday life «hickory-smoked» appears on barbecue food. In nursery rhymes: «Hickory, dickory, dock, the mouse ran up the clock». Phrases: hickory nuts, hickory-smoked, hickory stick.
examples from the lessons: «Hickory, dickory, dock, the mouse ran up the clock.» | Squirrels love to eat hickory nuts. | Axe handles are often made of hickory. | Dad's barbecue sauce has a hickory-smoked flavour. | Hickory wood is very hard and strong. | The pioneers used hickory to make wagon wheels.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: hickories. Uncountable when it means the wood (made of hickory). Pronounced HIK-uh-ree. Pecans are a kind of hickory nut.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A system where people or things are arranged in levels, from the most important or powerful at the top to the least at the bottom. 2) The people in charge of an organisation, such as a church or company. 3) (science, maths) Any ordering of things into levels, like groups inside groups.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons the feudal system is a hierarchy: king, barons, knights, peasants. In science, classification of living things is a hierarchy (kingdom, class, order, family, genus, species). In church life, «hierarchy» means bishops, priests and deacons. In maths, the order of operations is like a hierarchy. Phrases: at the top of the hierarchy, social hierarchy, a pecking order.
examples from the lessons: In the feudal hierarchy, the king was at the top. | Wolves in a pack have a hierarchy. | Living things are sorted in a hierarchy from kingdom to species. | The Catholic Church has a hierarchy of bishops and priests. | At school the hierarchy goes from the head teacher to the teachers and assistants. | Chickens have a hierarchy called a pecking order.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: hierarchies. Pronounced HY-uh-rar-kee. Spelling: hier-archy (i before e here). Adjective: hierarchical. Do not confuse with «hieroglyph» (Egyptian picture writing), which starts the same.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To do with Spanish-speaking countries and their people and culture, especially Latin America and Spain. 2) (US) Used for people in the USA whose families come from Spanish-speaking countries.
its sense in the lessons: In social studies and US census lessons, Hispanic Heritage Month (15 September to 15 October) celebrates Hispanic Americans. Many people prefer «Latino», «Latina», «Latinx/Latine» or naming their country, like Mexican American. Phrases: Hispanic culture, Hispanic Heritage Month, Hispanic Americans.
examples from the lessons: Hispanic Heritage Month starts in September. | Many Hispanic families speak both Spanish and English. | Our class learned about Hispanic artists like Frida Kahlo. | Hispanic Americans live in every US state. | The festival had Hispanic music and dancing. | Some people prefer to say «Latino» instead of «Hispanic».
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital H. «Hispanic» is about language (Spanish), «Latino» about Latin America; a Brazilian is Latino but not Hispanic (Brazil speaks Portuguese). It describes heritage, not race. It is polite to use the name people choose for themselves.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A thing that holds or supports something: a pencil holder, a cup holder. 2) A person who owns or has something official: a ticket holder, a passport holder, an account holder. 3) A person or team that currently has a title or record: the record holder, the title holder.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life holders keep things tidy (toothbrush holder, phone holder). In sport, the «holders» are the current champions and the «record holder» has the best result ever. In maths and money problems, «ticket holders» or «account holders» are counted or paid. Phrases: record holder, title holder, card holder, cup holder.
examples from the lessons: Put your pencils back in the pencil holder. | Only ticket holders may enter the stadium. | Usain Bolt is the world record holder for the 100 metres. | The car has a cup holder for my juice. | The holders were knocked out of the cup in the first round. | Every account holder gets a bank card. | The candle holder was made of glass.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a holder, holders. Often joined to another noun: cardholder, shareholder, householder, stakeholder (sometimes as one word). «Holder» is not «older».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) The root-like part at the bottom of seaweed that holds it tightly to rocks. 2) A clamp or hook that holds something firmly, for example to a workbench or wall. 3) (old) Something you can hold on to firmly.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on the seashore and kelp forests, the holdfast is not a real root: it only grips the rock and does not take in food. In woodwork, a holdfast clamps wood to the bench. Phrases: a kelp holdfast, a seaweed's holdfast.
examples from the lessons: The seaweed's holdfast stuck tightly to the rock. | A holdfast is not a root, because it does not take in water. | Storms can tear kelp from its holdfast. | The carpenter used a holdfast to clamp the wood to the bench. | Tiny crabs hide inside kelp holdfasts.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word: hold + fast («fast» here means firmly, as in «stuck fast»). Plural: holdfasts. A science and craft word, rarely used in everyday talk.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A breed of large black-and-white dairy cow (also called Holstein-Friesian or Friesian in the UK), famous for giving a lot of milk. 2) (a name) Holstein, a region in northern Germany, part of Schleswig-Holstein.
its sense in the lessons: In farming and science lessons, Holsteins are the most common dairy cows in the USA, Canada, the UK, Australia and New Zealand; the classic cartoon cow with black and white patches is a Holstein. Phrases: Holstein cows, Holstein-Friesian.
examples from the lessons: A Holstein cow can give over 30 litres of milk a day. | The black-and-white cows on the farm are Holsteins. | In the UK people often call them Friesians. | The breed came from Holstein in Germany and Friesland in the Netherlands. | Each Holstein has its own pattern of patches.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital H. Pronounced HOHL-styne or HOHL-steen. If one cow gives 30 litres a day, 10 cows give 300 litres: multiply. Not all black-and-white cows are Holsteins.

part of speech: noun (Homo — science); prefix homo- ; noun (homo — offensive slang)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) Homo, the genus (group) that includes humans and our extinct close relatives; our species is Homo sapiens, Latin for «wise human». 2) (prefix) homo- means «same», as in homophone (same sound), homogeneous (all the same kind). 3) (offensive) An old insulting word for a gay person; it is a hurtful slur and should not be used.
its sense in the lessons: In science and history lessons on human evolution, Homo sapiens, Homo neanderthalensis (Neanderthals) and Homo erectus are species of the genus Homo. In English lessons, homophones (there, their, they're) use the «same» prefix. In kindness lessons, the insult sense is an example of words that hurt people. Phrases: Homo sapiens, Homo erectus.
examples from the lessons: We are Homo sapiens, which means «wise human». | Homo erectus used fire and stone tools. | Neanderthals belong to the genus Homo too. | «Homophone» means two words with the same sound. | A homogeneous mixture looks the same all the way through. | The teacher explained that using «homo» as an insult is hurtful and not allowed.
note for the reader of a maths problem: In science, write Homo with a capital H and in italics: Homo sapiens. Latin «homo» (human) and Greek «homo-» (same) are different roots. The slang insult is offensive: never use it about anyone.

meaning for a pupil: 1) From or to do with Honduras, a country in Central America. 2) (noun) A person from Honduras.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and culture lessons Honduran topics include the Maya city of Copán, Caribbean coral reefs near the Bay Islands, bananas and coffee, and the Spanish language. Honduras was hit hard by Hurricane Mitch in 1998. Phrases: Honduran coffee, Honduran culture.
examples from the lessons: Copán is an ancient Maya city in Honduras. | Honduran coffee is grown in the mountains. | Our new classmate is Honduran and speaks Spanish. | The Honduran flag has five blue stars. | Many Hondurans live in the United States. | Divers love the Honduran reefs in the Caribbean.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital H. Pronounced hon-DOOR-un or hon-DYOOR-un. Spelling: Hondura + n (not «Hondurian»). Capital city: Tegucigalpa.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A climbing plant with sweet-smelling yellow, white or pink tube-shaped flowers that contain sweet nectar.
its sense in the lessons: In science and nature lessons honeysuckle is a climber that attracts bees, butterflies, moths and hummingbirds (in America) with its scent and nectar. Children sometimes suck the sweet nectar from the flowers. In poems and stories it is a symbol of summer evenings. Phrases: honeysuckle hedge, the scent of honeysuckle.
examples from the lessons: The honeysuckle smells sweetest in the evening. | Moths visit honeysuckle at night for nectar. | Honeysuckle climbed all over the garden fence. | We tasted the tiny drop of nectar in a honeysuckle flower. | Honeysuckle berries can be poisonous, so do not eat them. | The hedge was covered in pink honeysuckle.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word: honey + suckle. Uncountable for the plant in general, countable for kinds (honeysuckles). Safety: the flowers' nectar is harmless, but the berries of many honeysuckles are poisonous.

meaning for a pupil: 1) It is hoped that; if things go well: hopefully it won't rain tomorrow. 2) In a hopeful way, wishing for something: the dog looked at me hopefully.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday talk «hopefully» begins sentences about wishes for the future. In stories it describes a character's hopeful look or voice. In writing lessons, the second sense helps «show, don't tell». Phrases: hopefully not, hopefully soon.
examples from the lessons: Hopefully we'll win the match on Saturday. | The dog looked hopefully at my sandwich. | «Will it snow?» «Hopefully!» | Hopefully the bus won't be late. | She asked hopefully if she could stay up late. | Hopefully, my cold will be better by Monday.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Some old grammar books said «hopefully» must only mean «in a hopeful way»; today the meaning «it is hoped» is completely normal and accepted. Spelling: double l (hopeful + ly).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A feeling that nothing good will happen and that there is no point in trying. 2) The state of being completely without hope or chance of success.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and history lessons, hopelessness appears in hard times such as wars, famine or being lost, and characters often find hope again. In wellbeing and PSHE lessons, feelings of hopelessness are a sign to talk to a trusted adult, as help is always available. Phrases: a feeling of hopelessness, sense of hopelessness.
examples from the lessons: A feeling of hopelessness came over the lost climbers. | The story moves from hopelessness to joy. | The charity helps families out of hopelessness. | Talking to a friend helped her overcome her hopelessness. | The hopelessness of the situation made them cry, but then help arrived. | If you feel hopelessness for a long time, tell a grown-up you trust.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Built from hope + less + ness. Opposite: hope, hopefulness, optimism. If someone feels hopeless for a long time, it is important to get help from a parent, teacher, doctor or helpline like Childline.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A large container shaped like a funnel, which lets grain, coal, sand or food pour out at the bottom. 2) A person, animal or insect that hops, such as a grasshopper. 3) (informal) In compounds: someone who moves quickly from place to place, like a «bar-hopper» or «island-hopper». 4) (a name) Grace Hopper, a famous American computer scientist; Edward Hopper, a painter.
its sense in the lessons: In farming and machinery, grain and coal pour from hoppers into trucks. In computing lessons Grace Hopper wrote early programming languages and helped popularise the word «bug». In stories, hoppers can be frogs, kangaroos or insects. Phrases: grain hopper, in the hopper (US: waiting to be dealt with).
examples from the lessons: The farmer filled the hopper with grain. | Coal slid out of the hopper into the train. | Grace Hopper was a computer pioneer. | Kangaroos are amazing hoppers. | The bird feeder has a hopper that refills the tray. | My idea is in the hopper for next term.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: hoppers. Double p (hop + p + er). «Hopper» (hops) vs «hoper» (rare: someone who hopes).

part of speech: adjective (horrified); verb form, past of horrify (horrify, horrifies, horrified, horrifying)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Very shocked, upset and frightened by something terrible. 2) (informal) Very surprised and disapproving, often in a funny way: Mum was horrified by my messy room.
its sense in the lessons: In stories «horrified» shows strong feelings of shock and fear when a character sees something terrible. In everyday life it is used jokingly for small shocks. In writing lessons it is a stronger choice than «shocked» or «scared». Phrases: horrified by, horrified at, a horrified look.
examples from the lessons: She was horrified to see the dog run into the road. | We watched in horrified silence. | Mum was horrified by the state of my bedroom. | The villagers were horrified when the dragon appeared. | He gave a horrified gasp. | People around the world were horrified by the news of the earthquake.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past of «horrify» (y → i + ed). «Horrified» describes how a person feels; «horrifying» describes the thing that causes it: «a horrifying scene made me horrified». Similar: appalled, shocked, terrified.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (UK, Ireland) A long, bendy rubber or plastic tube for carrying water, used to water gardens or wash cars; in the US, Canada and Australia usually just «hose».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday British life a «hosepipe ban» is a rule against using hosepipes during a drought to save water. In science and geography it links to water saving. In summer, children play with hosepipes and sprinklers. Phrases: hosepipe ban, turn on the hosepipe.
examples from the lessons: Dad watered the tomatoes with the hosepipe. | There's a hosepipe ban because it hasn't rained for weeks. | We sprayed each other with the hosepipe on the hot day. | Coil up the hosepipe so nobody trips over it. | A hosepipe can use hundreds of litres of water an hour. | The car was washed with a bucket during the hosepipe ban.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word in British English. Plural: hosepipes. In American, Canadian and Australian English people usually say «hose» or «garden hose». In maths: if a hosepipe uses 10 litres a minute, 15 minutes uses 150 litres.

part of speech: verb (hospitalise, hospitalises, hospitalised, hospitalising); US spelling hospitalize
meaning for a pupil: 1) To send someone to hospital or keep them there for treatment because they are ill or injured.
its sense in the lessons: In news and health lessons it describes serious illness or accidents: «Three people were hospitalised after the crash». In safety lessons it shows why we follow rules about roads, water and fire. It is usually used in the passive: «was hospitalised». Phrases: be hospitalised with, hospitalised for a week.
examples from the lessons: Grandad was hospitalised with pneumonia. | Two cyclists were hospitalised after the accident. | Heatstroke can be bad enough to hospitalise someone. | She was hospitalised for three days. | Wear a helmet: bad falls hospitalise many riders each year. | The flu outbreak hospitalised several elderly people.
note for the reader of a maths problem: British spelling: hospitalise; American and often Canadian: hospitalize. Both are correct. Noun: hospitalisation. Usually passive: «was hospitalised». More formal than «taken to hospital».

part of speech: noun (a hotdog, hotdogs; also written hot dog); verb (hotdog, hotdogs, hotdogged, hotdogging — informal, mainly US); interjection (hot dog! — old-fashioned US)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A hot sausage, usually a frankfurter, served in a long soft bread roll, often with ketchup or mustard. 2) (informal, mainly US) A person who shows off, especially in a sport, doing risky or flashy tricks. 3) (informal, US) To hotdog is to show off with daring tricks, for example on skis, a skateboard or a surfboard. 4) (old-fashioned US) «Hot dog!» is a happy shout meaning «great!»
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life it is a quick food sold at sports games, fairs, barbecues and street stands; in stories it sets a scene of a ballgame, a fair or a picnic. In maths word problems hotdogs are things to count, price and share («each hotdog costs $3»). The show-off sense appears in sports stories. Phrases: a hotdog stand, hotdog bun, hotdog with everything, a hotdog vendor.
examples from the lessons: We bought two hotdogs at the baseball game. | Dad put ketchup and mustard on my hotdog. | The hotdog stand at the fair had a long queue. | If one hotdog costs $3, how much do four hotdogs cost? | Grandpa sliced the hotdog so the baby would not choke. | Stop hotdogging on the slopes and ski safely! | He is a bit of a hotdog on the skateboard, always doing tricks for the crowd. | «Hot dog! We won!» shouted Uncle Joe.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: one hotdog, two hotdogs. Spelled «hotdog» or «hot dog»; both are fine. It contains no dog meat — the name is an old joke about the sausage's shape and German «dachshund sausages». In the UK and Australia people also say «frankfurter» or «sausage in a bun»; in Australia a «hot dog» is sometimes called a «hotdog» or «frank». Safety: cut hotdogs into small pieces for little children, as round slices can cause choking. In maths, a hotdog problem is usually a multiplication or money problem.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Not able to leave your home, usually because you are ill, very old, disabled or looking after someone. 2) Stuck indoors for a while because of bad weather, an injury or rules such as a lockdown.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life the word comes up when talking about elderly grandparents, neighbours who need help with shopping, or people recovering from an operation. Charities and churches visit housebound people and bring meals or library books. In stories it shows a character who is lonely or cut off from the world. Phrases: housebound elderly, become housebound, housebound for weeks.
examples from the lessons: My great-grandmother is housebound, so we visit her every Sunday. | The snowstorm left the whole village housebound for three days. | After breaking his leg, Tom was housebound and very bored. | Our class wrote cards for housebound people in the town. | The library delivers books to housebound readers. | Being housebound can make someone feel lonely, so a phone call helps. | Mum does the shopping for our housebound neighbour.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It is an adjective: «she is housebound», «housebound people». It does not mean «bound for the house» (going home); it means held at home. Compare «bedridden» (cannot get out of bed) — stronger than housebound. Be kind with the word: it describes a situation, not who the person is.

part of speech: verb, past form of «huddle» (huddle, huddles, huddled, huddling); adjective (huddled)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Crowded closely together in a group, often to keep warm, feel safe or talk secretly. 2) Curled up or hunched, with arms and legs pulled close to the body, often because of cold or fear. 3) (adjective) Pressed close together: huddled houses, huddled sheep.
its sense in the lessons: In stories «huddled» paints a picture of cold, fear or secrecy: children huddled under a blanket during a storm, penguins huddled against the wind. In science lessons animals huddle to save body heat (emperor penguins are a famous example). In sport, a team huddles to plan a play. Phrases: huddled together, huddled around (a fire, a phone), huddled up, huddled in a corner.
examples from the lessons: The children huddled together under the blanket while the thunder roared. | Emperor penguins huddled in a big group to keep warm. | We huddled around the campfire telling stories. | The puppy lay huddled in the corner, shaking. | The team huddled to plan the last play of the game. | She sat huddled in her coat at the bus stop. | Sheep were huddled against the stone wall in the snow. | The friends huddled over the map, whispering.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Huddled» is the past tense and past participle of «huddle»; a «huddle» (noun) is a close group: «the players went into a huddle». Spelling: double d. Do not confuse with «hurdled» (jumped over a hurdle). In science: huddling reduces the surface of each body exposed to the cold, so animals lose less heat.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Very big, heavy and bulky, often in a clumsy or slightly frightening way. 2) Used of things too: a hulking building, a hulking old ship.
its sense in the lessons: In stories «hulking» describes a giant, a monster, a big bully, a huge machine or a dark building — it tells the reader the thing is large and heavy and maybe a bit threatening or awkward. It is a describing word for size and weight, not for kindness. Phrases: a hulking figure, a hulking great (UK informal), hulking shape.
examples from the lessons: A hulking figure stood in the doorway of the cave. | The hulking tractor rumbled down the lane. | Despite his hulking size, the giant was gentle with the children. | A hulking old warehouse stood by the river. | The dog was a hulking Saint Bernard with a soft heart. | A hulking great lorry blocked the road (UK). | The hulking robot in the film could hardly fit through the door.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It is an adjective, used before a noun: «a hulking man», rarely «he was hulking». Related noun: a «hulk» is a big clumsy person or thing, or the shell of an old ship. «The Hulk» is a comic-book superhero (a name). Saying a real person is «hulking» can sound rude; better to say «tall» or «strong».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Having a shape or features like a human being: a head, two arms, two legs, walking upright. 2) (noun) A robot, alien or creature that looks like a person. 3) (science) A word for early human-like species in old books; scientists today usually say «hominin» or «hominid».
its sense in the lessons: In science and technology lessons, humanoid robots are robots built in the shape of a person so they can use stairs, tools and doors made for humans. In science fiction stories humanoid aliens are aliens that look roughly like people. Phrases: humanoid robot, humanoid alien, humanoid form, humanoid shape.
examples from the lessons: The museum had a humanoid robot that could wave and shake hands. | In the film, the aliens were humanoid, with two arms and two legs. | Engineers build humanoid robots so they can walk up stairs like we do. | The statue had a humanoid shape but the head of a bird. | A humanoid robot fell over when it tried to kick a ball. | Our class drew humanoid aliens for the space story. | Not every robot is humanoid; a robot vacuum is shaped like a disc.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Humanoid» means «like a human», not a real human; «-oid» means «like» (as in «asteroid» = like a star). Countable noun: a humanoid, two humanoids. Do not confuse with «human» or «humane» (kind). A robot that looks extremely real is often called an «android».

meaning for a pupil: 1) The amount of water vapour (invisible water in gas form) in the air. 2) The damp, sticky, heavy feeling of air that holds a lot of water vapour, as on a hot muggy day.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography humidity is part of weather and climate: it is measured with a hygrometer and is often given as «relative humidity» in percent — how full of water vapour the air is compared with the most it can hold at that temperature. High humidity makes hot days feel hotter because sweat dries slowly. Weather forecasts give humidity, and it matters for plants, rainforests, deserts and bathrooms. Phrases: high humidity, low humidity, relative humidity, humidity level.
examples from the lessons: The humidity in the rainforest is very high, so everything feels damp. | Deserts usually have low humidity. | The weather app says the humidity is 85 percent today. | High humidity makes it hard for sweat to dry, so we feel hot and sticky. | We measured the humidity in the classroom with a hygrometer. | Bread goes mouldy faster when the humidity is high. | My hair goes frizzy in the humidity. | Florida summers are famous for their heat and humidity.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «the humidity is high», not «humidities» in everyday use. Adjective: «humid» (a humid day). In maths and science, relative humidity is a percentage from 0% (completely dry) to 100% (air holds all the water vapour it can; dew or fog may form). It is not the same as rainfall: air can be humid without rain. Opposite feeling: dry air.

part of speech: adjective (hydrated, well hydrated); verb, past form of «hydrate» (hydrate, hydrates, hydrated, hydrating)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Having enough water in your body; not thirsty or dried out. 2) (verb, past) Given water or moisture: hydrated skin, hydrated plants. 3) (chemistry) Joined with water molecules in its structure, as in «hydrated copper sulphate», a blue crystal.
its sense in the lessons: In health and PE lessons «stay hydrated» means drink enough water, especially in hot weather and during sport. In science, hydrated crystals contain water; heating them drives the water off (blue copper sulphate turns white). On skincare bottles «hydrated» means moist. Phrases: stay hydrated, keep hydrated, well hydrated, hydrated salt.
examples from the lessons: Remember to stay hydrated on sports day. | Drink water before, during and after football to keep hydrated. | When you are well hydrated, your pee is pale yellow. | The nurse made sure the sick child stayed hydrated. | The cream keeps your skin hydrated in winter. | Blue hydrated copper sulphate turns white when you heat it. | Camels can go for days without water and still stay hydrated longer than us.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: «dehydrated» (not enough water). «Hydr-» comes from Greek for water (hydrant, hydroelectric). A safety point: thirst, headache, tiredness and dark urine can be signs you need more water. Myth: everyone needs exactly eight glasses a day — needs depend on age, weather and activity, and food also contains water.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Taking in enough water so that your body works well. 2) Putting water or moisture into something, such as skin, soil or a dry substance. 3) (chemistry) A reaction in which water joins with another substance.
its sense in the lessons: In health, PE and sport, hydration means drinking enough; sports drinks and water bottles are sold for hydration. In science, hydration is when water combines with a substance; cement sets by hydration. Gardeners talk about soil hydration. Phrases: good hydration, hydration pack, hydration station, stay on top of your hydration.
examples from the lessons: Good hydration helps your brain think clearly in tests. | The race had hydration stations with cups of water every mile. | Hydration is extra important on hot days. | The coach talked to us about hydration before the match. | This lotion is for skin hydration. | Concrete hardens through a chemical reaction called hydration. | Fruit like watermelon helps with hydration because it is mostly water.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «hydration», not «a hydration» in everyday use. Verb: «hydrate»; adjective: «hydrated»; opposite: «dehydration». Do not confuse with «hydrogen» (a gas) or «hydraulic» (moved by liquid pressure), though all share «hydr-» = water.

part of speech: adjective (hydraulic); noun «hydraulics» (uncountable — the science, or the hydraulic parts of a machine)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Worked by the pressure of a liquid, usually oil or water, pushed through pipes. 2) To do with moving water, for example in dams, canals and pipes: hydraulic engineering. 3) (of cement) Able to set hard under water.
its sense in the lessons: In science and design-technology lessons, hydraulic systems show how a small push on liquid in a narrow pipe can make a big force in a wide pipe — this is how car brakes, diggers, car lifts and dentists' chairs work. Children build hydraulic models with syringes and water. Phrases: hydraulic lift, hydraulic brakes, hydraulic arm, hydraulic press, hydraulic pump.
examples from the lessons: The digger's hydraulic arm lifted the heavy rocks. | We made a hydraulic robot arm using syringes and coloured water. | The mechanic raised the car on a hydraulic lift. | Cars stop using hydraulic brakes. | The dentist's chair moves up with a hydraulic pump. | A hydraulic press can squash a can flat. | The engineer studied hydraulics to design the dam.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Hydraulic» is an adjective; «hydraulics» is the noun for the subject. Compare «pneumatic» — worked by air or gas pressure instead of liquid. The idea: liquids are very hard to squash, so pressure passes through them. In maths/science, pressure = force ÷ area, so a bigger piston gets a bigger force from the same pressure.

part of speech: adjective (hygienic, more hygienic, most hygienic); adverb «hygienically»
meaning for a pupil: 1) Clean and free of germs, so it is unlikely to spread illness. 2) Helping to keep things clean and healthy: a hygienic way of storing food.
its sense in the lessons: In health, science and food-tech lessons, hygienic habits stop germs spreading: washing hands, covering sneezes, keeping kitchens clean, storing food properly. Hospitals, kitchens and bathrooms must be hygienic. Phrases: hygienic conditions, it is not hygienic to…, a hygienic kitchen, more hygienic.
examples from the lessons: It is not hygienic to share a toothbrush. | The school kitchen must be kept hygienic. | Washing your hands with soap is the most hygienic thing to do before eating. | Paper towels can be more hygienic than a shared cloth towel. | The nurse put on gloves to keep things hygienic. | Licking the spoon and putting it back in the jar is not hygienic! | Cats are quite hygienic animals and wash themselves a lot.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: «hygienic» has «-gie-»: h-y-g-i-e-n-i-c. Noun: «hygiene» (personal hygiene). Opposite: «unhygienic». «Hygienic» is about germs and cleanliness, not about tidiness: a messy room can be hygienic and a neat one can have germs.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A dental hygienist: a trained health worker who cleans people's teeth, removes hard tartar and teaches how to brush and floss. 2) Less often, any expert on hygiene and health, such as an occupational hygienist who checks workplaces are safe and clean.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, children meet a hygienist at the dentist's: the hygienist scrapes and polishes the teeth and shows how to brush properly. In stories about jobs it is a health career. Phrases: dental hygienist, see the hygienist, the hygienist's chair.
examples from the lessons: The hygienist cleaned my teeth and made them shiny. | The hygienist showed me how to floss between my teeth. | Mum has an appointment with the dental hygienist. | My aunt trained for three years to become a hygienist. | The hygienist said I should brush for two minutes, twice a day. | A hygienist works alongside the dentist.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a hygienist, two hygienists. Spelling like «hygiene»: h-y-g-i-e-n-i-s-t. A hygienist is not a dentist: dentists fill and pull teeth; hygienists mostly clean and prevent decay.

part of speech: noun (hype — uncountable); verb (hype, hypes, hyped, hyping; often «hype up»); adjective (informal: hyped, hyped up)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Lots of excited advertising or talk that makes something seem better or more important than it really is. 2) (verb) To make a big fuss about something to get people excited: they hyped the new game. 3) (slang) Hyped or hyped up means very excited: «I'm so hyped for the holidays!» 4) (slang, adjective) «Hype» can mean exciting or great: «that song is hype».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and media lessons, hype is about adverts, trailers and social media that make a film, toy, game or trainer seem amazing. Children learn to ask whether something lives up to the hype. In slang, «hyped» is a common way to say «excited». Phrases: the hype around…, believe the hype, live up to the hype, hype up, hype man.
examples from the lessons: There was so much hype about the new phone that people queued all night. | The film did not live up to the hype. | Don't believe the hype; read real reviews first. | The coach hyped up the team before the final. | I'm so hyped for the school trip tomorrow! | The advert hyped the toy as «the best ever». | That new song is hype! (slang) | Our media lesson showed how hype can make us want things we don't need.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a noun «hype» is uncountable: «a lot of hype», not «hypes». «Hyped» (excited) is informal slang, not for formal writing. Do not confuse with «hyper» (overactive, too energetic: «the kids are hyper after cake») or «hypo» (short for low blood sugar). Hype is a kind of persuasion; being able to spot it is part of media literacy.

meaning for a pupil: 1) So upset, frightened or excited that you cannot control your feelings, for example screaming or crying wildly. 2) (informal) Extremely funny: «the film was hysterical». 3) Laughing so much you cannot stop: hysterical laughter.
its sense in the lessons: In stories «hysterical» shows a character who has lost control — panicking, sobbing or shrieking — or, in a funny scene, people helpless with laughter. In everyday speech children often use it to mean «really funny». In safety lessons: in an emergency, try to stay calm and not get hysterical. Phrases: become hysterical, hysterical laughter, absolutely hysterical, in hysterics.
examples from the lessons: The joke was so hysterical that I fell off my chair. | She became hysterical when she saw the spider. | We were in hysterics watching the cat chase its tail. | Stay calm in a fire drill; getting hysterical makes things worse. | The crowd went hysterical when the band came on stage. | The toddler was hysterical because he lost his teddy. | Dad told a hysterical story about his first day at work.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Two opposite feelings: very upset OR very funny — the sentence tells you which. «Hysterical» about a person who is upset can sound dismissive or unkind, so be careful using it about someone. The old idea that women are «hysterical» by nature is a myth and the word's history is unfair to women. Noun: «in hysterics» (laughing or crying uncontrollably).

part of speech: abbreviation, noun (ICU — the ICU, ICUs; usually written in capitals)
meaning for a pupil: 1) ICU stands for «intensive care unit»: the part of a hospital where very ill or badly hurt patients get constant care and special machines to help them breathe and keep their heart working. 2) (texting, informal) «icu» can be read as «I see you».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life you hear «in ICU» or «in the ICU» when someone is very seriously ill, in news reports and hospital dramas. Doctors and nurses watch ICU patients day and night. Related: PICU (paediatric ICU, for children), NICU (neonatal ICU, for new babies). In the UK it is also called «intensive care» or «ITU».
examples from the lessons: Grandad was moved to the ICU after his operation. | The ICU nurses checked on him every few minutes. | Babies born very early may spend weeks in the NICU. | The news said the injured driver was in ICU. | Only two visitors at a time are allowed in the ICU. | My aunt is an ICU doctor. | The patient got better and left the ICU for an ordinary ward.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say each letter: «I-C-U». Write it in capitals: ICU. Being in the ICU means someone is very ill, but many patients get better and go home. In texting, «icu» meaning «I see you» is playful slang, not the hospital sense.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Able to be recognised or named: you can tell who or what it is. 2) Able to be picked out as separate and definite: an identifiable pattern, an identifiable cause.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, children make plants, animals, rocks or leaves identifiable using keys and features. In safety and online-safety lessons, «personally identifiable information» is anything that tells strangers who or where you are — name, school, address — so keep it private. Lost property should be identifiable with your name in it. Phrases: easily identifiable, clearly identifiable, identifiable by, personally identifiable.
examples from the lessons: Put your name in your coat so it is easily identifiable. | The bird was identifiable by its bright red chest. | Don't post anything that makes you identifiable, like your school uniform. | In the photo, the faces were not identifiable. | There was no identifiable reason why the plant died. | Fingerprints make a person identifiable. | The rock was identifiable as granite from its speckled crystals.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: identif-i-able (keep the i from «identify» and add «-able»; the y changes to i). Verb: «identify»; noun: «identification» (ID). Opposite: «unidentifiable». Pronounced eye-DEN-ti-fy-a-ble.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A name, number, label or sign that shows exactly who or what something is. 2) (computing) A name given to something in a program, such as a variable or function name, so the computer can tell them apart.
its sense in the lessons: In computing lessons, identifiers are the names you give variables, like «score» or «lives»; they usually cannot have spaces or start with a number. In everyday life, a barcode, a passport number, a username or a pupil number is an identifier. In science, features of a plant can act as identifiers. Phrases: unique identifier, user identifier, a variable identifier.
examples from the lessons: Each library book has a barcode as its identifier. | In Scratch we used «score» as the identifier for our variable. | Your username is an identifier, but your password must stay secret. | A unique identifier means no two things share it. | The spots on its back are a good identifier for this ladybird. | The program gave an error because the identifier had a space in it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun. Verb: «identify»; «identifier» is the thing that identifies. A unique identifier belongs to just one thing; a name like «Sam» is not unique, but a passport number is. In programming, identifiers are case sensitive in many languages: «Score» and «score» can be different.

part of speech: verb (idolise, idolises, idolised, idolising; US spelling idolize)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To admire or love someone very much, often too much, as if they were perfect — a star, a sports player or an older brother or sister. 2) (religion) Literally, to treat something as an idol to worship; Jews, Christians and Muslims teach that worshipping idols is wrong.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life children idolise footballers, singers, YouTubers or older siblings. In PSHE lessons pupils talk about role models and remember that no one is perfect. In stories, a character who idolises someone may learn that the hero has flaws. Phrases: idolise someone, idolised by fans, a hero he idolised.
examples from the lessons: My little brother idolises his favourite footballer and copies his haircut. | She idolised her big sister and followed her everywhere. | Millions of fans idolise the singer. | It's fine to admire people, but don't idolise them; everyone makes mistakes. | As a boy he idolised the astronauts on the Moon. | The Bible warns against idolising things like money.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK spelling «idolise», US «idolize»; both are correct. Noun: «idol» (a person who is idolised, or a statue worshipped as a god). Do not confuse «idol» with «idle» (lazy, not working) — they sound the same.

part of speech: noun (an igniter, igniters; also spelled ignitor)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A device or part that starts a fire or makes a fuel catch light, such as the clicker on a gas cooker or barbecue. 2) A small substance or charge that sets off a bigger burning, as in rockets and fireworks.
its sense in the lessons: In science and safety lessons, an igniter is what gives the spark or heat to start burning: gas hobs, boilers, lighters, rocket motors. Safety: only adults should use igniters and lighters; never play with them. Phrases: spark igniter, gas igniter, the igniter is broken.
examples from the lessons: The igniter on the barbecue clicks and makes a spark. | Our gas cooker has an igniter, so we don't need matches. | The rocket's igniter lit the fuel and it whooshed into the sky. | The boiler would not start because the igniter was broken. | Never play with lighters or igniters. | The model rocket kit came with a small electric igniter.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: «ignite» (to catch or set on fire); noun: «ignition». Both spellings «igniter» and «ignitor» are used. In science: burning needs fuel, oxygen and heat — the igniter supplies the heat (the fire triangle).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Not knowing about something; lack of knowledge or information. 2) Rude or unfriendly behaviour that comes from not knowing or not caring how others feel (in UK English «ignorant» can also mean rude).
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and lessons, ignorance is simply not knowing yet — everyone is ignorant of many things, and learning cures it. In citizenship lessons, ignorance about other people can lead to unfairness and prejudice. Phrases: ignorance is bliss (it can be happier not to know), in ignorance of, out of ignorance, ignorance of the law is no excuse.
examples from the lessons: Ignorance about germs made illnesses spread in the past. | He said the wrong thing out of ignorance, not to be mean. | «Ignorance is bliss,» said Mum when I asked how much the dentist costs. | Learning about other cultures helps fight ignorance. | Ignorance of the rules is no excuse for cheating. | I admit my ignorance — I didn't know spiders aren't insects.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «ignorance», not «an ignorance». Adjective: «ignorant»; verb «ignore» means something different — to deliberately not pay attention. Not knowing something is not the same as being stupid; calling someone «ignorant» is usually rude. In law, «ignorance of the law is no excuse» means you must follow a law even if you did not know it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Not real, though it seems real; based on an illusion. 2) (formal) Seeming true or possible but actually false: an illusory hope, an illusory advantage.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on light and the brain, optical illusions show illusory movement, size or colour. In formal writing and exams, «illusory» says something only appears to be so. Phrases: illusory movement, an illusory sense of safety, prove illusory.
examples from the lessons: The moving pattern was illusory; the picture was not really moving. | The lake in the desert was illusory — it was a mirage. | His lead in the race proved illusory when he tripped. | The feeling of safety in a car without seatbelts is illusory. | Magicians create illusory effects to fool our eyes. | In art we made an illusory 3D cube on flat paper.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal word; in everyday speech people say «not real» or «fake». Noun: «illusion». Do not confuse «illusion» (false impression) with «allusion» (hint at something) or «delusion» (a strong false belief). Pronounced ih-LOO-suh-ree.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Perfectly clean and tidy, with no dirt or mess at all. 2) Without any mistake; perfect: an immaculate performance. 3) (church) Without sin: Catholic Christians believe in the «Immaculate Conception», that Mary, the mother of Jesus, was free of original sin from the start of her life.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life it describes a spotless room, uniform or car, or a perfect piece of work. In sport and music, an immaculate performance has no errors. In church lessons it appears in the Catholic feast of the Immaculate Conception (8 December). Phrases: immaculately dressed, in immaculate condition, immaculate handwriting.
examples from the lessons: Grandma's kitchen is always immaculate. | His uniform was immaculate on the first day of school. | The second-hand bike was in immaculate condition. | The gymnast gave an immaculate performance and scored ten. | Her handwriting is immaculate. | Catholics celebrate the Immaculate Conception on 8 December. | After an hour of tidying, my room looked immaculate — for one day.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: double m, one c at the start, «-late» at the end: i-m-m-a-c-u-l-a-t-e. A common confusion: the «Immaculate Conception» is about Mary being free from sin, not about the birth of Jesus (that is the «Virgin Birth»).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Behaving in a silly or childish way that is not right for your age. 2) Not being fully grown or developed yet, as with a young animal, plant or fruit.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and PSHE, adults may point out immaturity when someone giggles at the wrong time or sulks. In science, immaturity is a stage of growth: an immature frog is a tadpole, an immature fruit is unripe. Phrases: a sign of immaturity, emotional immaturity, the immaturity of the plant.
examples from the lessons: Laughing when someone falls over shows immaturity. | The teacher said his rude joke was a sign of immaturity. | Because of the bird's immaturity, its feathers were still grey. | The immaturity of the apples meant they were sour. | Everyone shows some immaturity sometimes; we learn as we grow. | The coach worried about the young team's immaturity under pressure.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Adjective: «immature»; opposite: «maturity», «mature». Being a child is not immaturity — the word means acting younger than you are. Pronounced im-uh-CHOOR-i-tee or im-uh-TYOOR-i-tee.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Very soon; about to happen at any moment. 2) (formal) Used in news and official speech for something expected almost immediately: «the report is due imminently».
its sense in the lessons: In news and formal announcements it says an event is coming very soon: a storm, an arrival, a decision. In stories it builds tension — danger is near. Phrases: expected imminently, due imminently, arriving imminently.
examples from the lessons: The baby is expected imminently, so Dad keeps his phone on. | The storm is due to hit the coast imminently. | The train is arriving imminently at platform two. | The results will be announced imminently. | The volcano was not imminently going to erupt, the scientists said. | Our new puppy is arriving imminently!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: «imminent» (an imminent storm). Do not confuse with «eminent» (famous and respected) or «immanent» (present inside something — a rare religious word). «Imminently» usually goes with good or bad events coming soon; everyday talk prefers «any minute now».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Not moving at all; perfectly still. 2) Not able to move or be moved, for example because of an injury, illness or because something is fixed in place.
its sense in the lessons: In science, some living things are immobile, like plants and barnacles, which stay in one place. In stories a frightened character stands immobile, frozen with fear. In health, a person with a broken leg may be immobile for weeks. Phrases: stand immobile, lie immobile, completely immobile.
examples from the lessons: The cat sat immobile, watching the mouse hole. | After the accident he was immobile for a month. | Plants are immobile, so they can't run from danger. | The statue-like guard stood immobile at the palace gate. | The heavy wardrobe was immobile; we couldn't shift it. | In musical statues you must stay immobile when the music stops.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: «mobile» (able to move). Nouns: «immobility». Verb: «immobilise» (to stop something moving). Pronounced ih-MOH-bile (UK) or ih-MOH-bul (US).

part of speech: verb (immobilise, immobilises, immobilised, immobilising; US spelling immobilize)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To stop someone or something from moving or working. 2) (first aid) To keep an injured body part still, for example with a splint or sling, so it does not get worse. 3) To stop a vehicle from being started, as with a car alarm or wheel clamp.
its sense in the lessons: In first-aid and safety lessons, you immobilise a broken arm with a sling and do not move someone who may have a neck injury. In science stories, a spider's venom immobilises its prey. In everyday life cars have immobilisers to stop thieves. Phrases: immobilise the injury, immobilise the prey, immobilise a car.
examples from the lessons: The first-aider used a sling to immobilise my broken arm. | The spider's bite immobilises the fly. | Snow and ice immobilised the whole town. | The car has a device that immobilises the engine if it's stolen. | Don't move someone who might have hurt their neck; paramedics will immobilise it. | The cold immobilised the lizard until the sun warmed it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK «immobilise», US «immobilize». Noun: «immobilisation»; a car's anti-theft device is an «immobiliser». Related adjective «immobile».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Being fair and not taking sides; treating everyone in the same way. 2) (formal) In news, law and sport, the rule that a judge, referee, reporter or teacher must not favour one person or group.
its sense in the lessons: In citizenship and media lessons, impartiality is why the BBC and other public broadcasters must give both sides of a story, why judges must not judge friends' cases, and why referees must be neutral. In school, a teacher marking fairly shows impartiality. Phrases: show impartiality, strict impartiality, keep impartiality.
