examples from the lessons: The referee's impartiality was questioned after the penalty. | Judges must show impartiality in court. | The news channel promised impartiality in its election coverage. | Our teacher marked the stories blind to keep her impartiality. | Impartiality means treating your best friend and a stranger the same in a game. | A judge who knows the person on trial may step aside to protect impartiality.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Adjective «impartial»; opposite «partiality» or «bias». «Impartial» does not mean «partly»: it comes from not being «partial» (favouring one part or side).

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a fair way, without favouring anyone or taking sides. 2) (formal) Judging only on facts and rules, not on who people are.
its sense in the lessons: Used of referees, judges, teachers, reporters and anyone who must decide fairly: «the jury must listen impartially». In citizenship lessons, it describes how courts and elections should work. Phrases: act impartially, judge impartially, report impartially.
examples from the lessons: The referee must judge the match impartially. | Our class captain shared the jobs out impartially. | The reporter tried to describe both sides impartially. | The judge listened impartially to everyone. | Teachers should mark work impartially. | Choose the winner impartially, not just your friend.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb of «impartial». Sound and spelling: im-PAR-shuh-lee. Opposite idea: «with bias», «unfairly».

meaning for a pupil: 1) So slowly or slightly that you cannot notice it happening. 2) In a way too small to see, hear or feel.
its sense in the lessons: In science, many changes happen imperceptibly: plants grow, the hour hand moves, mountains wear down, continents drift. In stories, light fades imperceptibly at dusk or a character nods imperceptibly — so small that others hardly see it. Phrases: change imperceptibly, nod imperceptibly, imperceptibly slowly.
examples from the lessons: The hour hand moves imperceptibly round the clock. | Day turned imperceptibly into night. | She nodded imperceptibly to show she agreed. | The glacier moves imperceptibly, only a little each day. | My little sister is growing imperceptibly taller. | The temperature dropped imperceptibly through the evening.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective «imperceptible» (not able to be noticed); opposite «perceptibly», «noticeably». Root: «perceive» = notice. Spelling: im-per-cep-ti-bly.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To copy the voice, look or way of moving of someone, usually to make people laugh. 2) To pretend to be another person in order to trick people, which can be a crime, for example pretending to be a police officer.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life comedians impersonate famous people, and children impersonate teachers in the playground. In online-safety lessons, scammers may impersonate a bank, a friend or a company in a message — so check before trusting. In law, impersonating a police officer is illegal. Phrases: impersonate a voice, impersonate a celebrity, impersonate a police officer.
examples from the lessons: He can impersonate the head teacher's voice perfectly. | The comedian impersonated the Prime Minister. | A scammer impersonated my aunt's bank in a text message. | It is a crime to impersonate a police officer. | My sister impersonated a robot in the school play. | Someone impersonated my friend online, so we reported the account.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: «impersonation»; person: «impersonator». Impersonating for fun is fine if it is kind; impersonating to deceive is fraud. Online safety: a message that sounds like someone you know may be an impersonation — check by another route.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A funny copy of someone's voice, way of speaking or actions. 2) Pretending to be someone else to trick people, which can be a crime.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: a comedian's impersonations; a child's impersonation of a grumpy cat. In online safety and law: impersonation of a bank, a company or an official is used in scams and phishing. Phrases: do an impersonation of, a brilliant impersonation, identity impersonation.
examples from the lessons: She does a brilliant impersonation of our dog barking. | The class laughed at his impersonation of a pirate. | The fake email was an impersonation of a real company. | Impersonation of a police officer is a crime. | The comedian's impersonations of famous singers were amazing. | We learned how to spot impersonation in online messages.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable for each act («two impersonations») and uncountable for the general idea. Verb «impersonate». An impression is the same as a funny impersonation: «do an impression».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Not letting water, air or anything else pass through: an impervious material. 2) Not affected or bothered by something: impervious to criticism, impervious to the cold.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography, impervious (or impermeable) rocks and materials do not let water soak in: clay, plastic, concrete; this causes puddles and floods. In stories, a character impervious to teasing or danger is not hurt or moved by it. Phrases: impervious to water, impervious to pain, impervious to criticism, impervious surface.
examples from the lessons: Plastic is impervious to water, so it makes a good raincoat. | Concrete roads are impervious, so rain runs off into drains. | We tested which materials were impervious in our science lesson. | She seemed impervious to the cold in just a T-shirt. | The superhero was impervious to bullets. | He was impervious to their teasing and just smiled.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually followed by «to»: «impervious to water». Similar: «impermeable», «waterproof». Opposite: «permeable», «porous». In real life no one is completely impervious to hurt; the word describes how it looks.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Hard to believe; not likely to be true. 2) Not reasonable or realistic: an implausible plan.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons pupils judge whether a story's events are plausible or implausible; in history and science they check whether a claim fits the evidence. In everyday life, an implausible excuse is one nobody believes. Phrases: an implausible excuse, an implausible story, it seems implausible that.
examples from the lessons: «The dog ate my homework» is an implausible excuse. | It is implausible that a snail could win a race against a horse. | The film's ending was so implausible that we laughed. | The detective found the man's story implausible. | Your plan to dig to Australia is a bit implausible. | It seems implausible, but it's true: a bee can't see the colour red.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: «plausible» (believable). «Implausible» does not mean «impossible»: an implausible thing could happen but probably did not. In probability words: impossible < unlikely/implausible < possible < likely < certain.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To show or suggest that someone is involved in something wrong, such as a crime. 2) (formal) To show that something is a cause or part of a problem: smoking is implicated in many illnesses. 3) (formal, rare) To imply or suggest something.
its sense in the lessons: In detective stories, a clue or a witness implicates a suspect. In science and health news, a germ or habit is «implicated» in an illness when evidence links them. Phrases: be implicated in, implicate someone in a crime, evidence implicates.
examples from the lessons: The muddy footprints implicated the dog in the broken vase mystery. | The letter implicated the butler in the theft. | Scientists implicated a virus in the outbreak. | He refused to say anything that might implicate his friends. | Sugar is implicated in tooth decay. | The detective found no evidence to implicate the gardener.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually used with «in»: «implicated in the crime». Noun: «implication» — which also means a hidden meaning or a likely result. Being implicated is not the same as being proved guilty.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Bringing goods into a country from another country to sell or use. 2) Something that has been brought in from somewhere else, such as a plant, animal or custom.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and history lessons, importation of tea, spices, cotton or grain shows trade between countries; some importations, like rabbits in Australia or cane toads, caused big problems. Laws control the importation of animals, plants and weapons. Phrases: importation of goods, ban the importation, an importation from abroad.
examples from the lessons: The importation of tea from China made it popular in Britain. | Australia has strict rules on the importation of fruit and plants. | The rabbit was an importation that spread across Australia. | The government banned the importation of ivory. | Halloween costumes became popular partly as an importation from America. | Importation costs make foreign goods more expensive.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly formal; everyday speech uses «importing» or «imports». Verb «import»; opposite «exportation», «export». In maths and economics: imports are goods coming in, exports are goods going out.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The quality of being impossible or almost impossible to do in practice. 2) (formal) Something that cannot be done because of real-world limits like cost, time or difficulty.
its sense in the lessons: A stiff, formal word in reports, law and exams: «the impracticability of the plan» means the plan cannot really be carried out. Children rarely say it; in plain words it is «it just won't work». Phrases: the impracticability of, owing to its impracticability.
examples from the lessons: The council dropped the bridge plan because of its impracticability. | The impracticability of moving the whole school in one day was obvious. | Owing to the impracticability of the trip, it was cancelled. | The report explained the impracticability of building on the marsh. | My teacher pointed out the impracticability of feeding a hundred pets. | Everyone could see the impracticability of a swimming pool on the roof.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Long formal word: im-prac-ti-ca-bil-i-ty. Adjective «impracticable». Compare «impracticality» (being not sensible or useful), a close but different idea.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Impossible to do or carry out in practice, even if it sounds good. 2) (of a road or path) Impossible to use or travel on: the road was impracticable after the flood.
its sense in the lessons: Used in formal writing, reports and history about plans that cannot be carried out because of cost, time, danger or difficulty. Phrases: an impracticable plan, prove impracticable, impracticable in practice.
examples from the lessons: The plan to build a tunnel to the island proved impracticable. | Walking across the desert in a day is impracticable. | The flooded road was impracticable for cars. | The idea was clever but impracticable. | It was impracticable to count every grain of sand. | Carrying all the books home at once was impracticable, so we took two trips.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: «impracticable» = cannot be done; «impractical» = could be done but not sensible or useful (high heels for hiking are impractical). Many people mix them up. Formal word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Not sensible or useful in real life; hard to use or do. 2) Describing a person who is not good at everyday practical tasks or who has unrealistic ideas.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: impractical shoes, clothes, gifts or plans. In design-technology lessons, pupils test whether a design is practical or impractical to use. Phrases: totally impractical, impractical for, impractical idea.
examples from the lessons: White trainers are impractical for a muddy field trip. | A glass lunchbox is impractical for a school bag. | His idea was fun but impractical. | Long dresses are impractical for climbing trees. | Grandad says I'm impractical because I can't fix my bike. | It would be impractical to walk to school in the snow, so we took the bus.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: «practical». Trap: «impractical» (not sensible) vs «impracticable» (cannot be done at all). In US English «impractical» is common for both.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Not exact or accurate; rough or vague. 2) Not clearly expressed: imprecise instructions.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and science, an imprecise measurement is not exact enough (measuring a pencil with steps, not a ruler). Estimates are imprecise on purpose. In writing, imprecise instructions confuse the reader. Phrases: imprecise measurement, imprecise language, rather imprecise.
examples from the lessons: Measuring with your hand span is imprecise. | «About a hundred» is an imprecise answer; the exact answer is 97. | The instructions were imprecise, so we built the model wrong. | Old maps were imprecise about the size of countries. | Use a ruler; guessing is too imprecise. | His description of the thief was imprecise.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: «precise». In maths, precise means exact detail (3.14159) and accurate means close to the true value; an imprecise answer can still be roughly right (π ≈ 3). Estimates and rounding make numbers deliberately imprecise.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To soak or fill something completely with a substance: wood impregnated with oil. 2) (biology) To make a female animal pregnant, so that a baby starts to grow inside her.
its sense in the lessons: In science and design-technology lessons, materials are impregnated with chemicals to make them waterproof, fireproof or longer-lasting (fence posts soaked in preservative). In biology about animals, it means fertilising so that young will grow. Phrases: impregnated with, impregnate wood.
examples from the lessons: The fence posts were impregnated with a chemical to stop them rotting. | The cloth was impregnated with wax to make it waterproof. | The bandage is impregnated with antiseptic. | The air was impregnated with the smell of smoke. | Farmers keep the bull separate until they want the cows impregnated. | The matches are impregnated with a chemical that helps them light.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The «soak/fill» sense is the one met most in school and science. Noun: «impregnation». The adjective «pregnant» is related to the second sense only. Pronounced IM-preg-nate.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A performer who copies the voices and ways of famous people for entertainment. 2) (art) An Impressionist is one of a group of painters in France in the late 1800s, such as Claude Monet and Pierre-Auguste Renoir, who painted light and colour quickly in short brushstrokes to show a moment as it looked. 3) (adjective) In this style: Impressionist paintings; also used for some music, like Debussy's.
its sense in the lessons: In art lessons, children copy Impressionist paintings of water lilies, gardens, boats and sunsets and use dabs of colour. In everyday life, an impressionist on TV does funny celebrity voices. Phrases: French Impressionists, Impressionist painting, a TV impressionist.
examples from the lessons: Monet was a famous Impressionist who painted water lilies. | We painted sunflowers in an Impressionist style with short dabs. | The Impressionists liked to paint outdoors to catch the light. | The impressionist did the voices of five famous footballers. | Impressionist paintings look blurry up close and clear from far away. | My uncle is a great impressionist; he sounds just like our grandad.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The art movement is often written with a capital I: «Impressionism», «the Impressionists». The name came from Monet's painting «Impression, Sunrise» (1872), and a critic first used it as a joke. A performer who copies voices «does impressions».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Not likely to happen or to be true. 2) Strange and surprising: an improbable friendship between a cat and a duck.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, probability words go from impossible to certain; «improbable» means unlikely, close to the impossible end. In stories, an improbable event surprises the reader. Phrases: highly improbable, it is improbable that, an improbable winner.
examples from the lessons: It is improbable that it will snow in July in London. | Rolling a six ten times in a row is highly improbable. | The underdog team won an improbable victory. | The dog and the rabbit had an improbable friendship. | It's improbable but not impossible. | Getting every answer right by guessing is very improbable.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: «probable». In maths probability: improbable means a probability near 0 but not 0; impossible = 0, certain = 1. Similar: «unlikely».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Behaviour that is not right, honest or acceptable, especially for someone in an important job. 2) (formal) A small wrong or rude act that breaks the rules of good behaviour.
its sense in the lessons: In news and formal speech, a politician, official or business is accused of «financial impropriety» when they handle money dishonestly. In old-fashioned stories, it means bad manners. Phrases: financial impropriety, no impropriety, accused of impropriety, the appearance of impropriety.
examples from the lessons: The official was accused of financial impropriety. | An inquiry found no impropriety in how the money was spent. | The judge stepped away to avoid any appearance of impropriety. | In old novels, being alone with a stranger was seen as an impropriety. | The club's treasurer was cleared of impropriety. | The coach was careful to avoid any impropriety in choosing the team.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal word. Adjective: «improper»; opposite: «propriety». Pronounced im-pruh-PRY-uh-tee. Being accused of impropriety does not mean being proved guilty.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Making something up on the spot, without a script or plan — in music, drama or speech. 2) Using whatever you have to solve a problem quickly when you lack the proper things. 3) A piece of music, drama or speech made up in the moment.
its sense in the lessons: In drama lessons, improvisation (often «improv») means acting a scene without lines; in music, jazz players improvise solos. In everyday life and outdoor survival, improvisation means using a jumper as a pillow or a stick as a splint. Phrases: improv, drama improvisation, jazz improvisation, a bit of improvisation.
examples from the lessons: In drama we did an improvisation about getting lost at the zoo. | Jazz musicians are famous for improvisation. | When the tent pole broke, Dad's improvisation was a long branch. | The speech was pure improvisation; she had no notes. | Improv games help you think quickly. | Our band's best song started as an improvisation.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: «improvise». Short form «improv» (informal, especially US). Countable when it is one piece; uncountable for the skill. Spelling: improvis-ation, not «improvization» in the UK; US also uses improvisation.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Suddenly and without stopping to think first. 2) Following a strong sudden wish or feeling, often in a way you may regret.
its sense in the lessons: In PSHE and stories, acting impulsively — grabbing, shouting, buying on a whim — is contrasted with «stop, think, then act». In money lessons, buying impulsively can waste pocket money; shops place sweets near tills because people buy impulsively. Phrases: act impulsively, buy impulsively, impulsively decide.
examples from the lessons: He impulsively jumped into the pool with his clothes on. | She impulsively spent all her pocket money on sweets. | Don't act impulsively when you're angry; count to ten. | I impulsively hugged my friend when we won. | Shops put treats near the tills so people buy them impulsively. | He answered impulsively and got the sum wrong.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective «impulsive»; noun «impulse» (a sudden urge). An «impulse buy» is something bought without planning. Acting impulsively is not always bad — a kind hug can be impulsive — but for safety and money it pays to think first.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Mixed with other substances, so not pure or clean: impure water, impure gold. 2) (religion, old-fashioned) Morally or spiritually unclean, as in old rules of worship.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, impure substances are mixtures; pupils filter, evaporate or distil to remove impurities and make salt or clean water. In history and religious lessons, «impure» appears in old rules about what made people clean or unclean for worship. Phrases: impure water, impure metal, an impure sample.
examples from the lessons: Muddy river water is impure, so we filtered it. | Rock salt is impure; we dissolved it and filtered out the sand. | Impure gold is mixed with other metals. | The chemist tested whether the sample was pure or impure. | Old laws in the Bible describe things that made people impure. | Drinking impure water can make you ill.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: «pure». In chemistry, «pure» means only one substance; everyday «pure» can mean natural — orange juice labelled «pure» is still a mixture. Noun «impurities» = the unwanted bits mixed in.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To say that something, usually bad, is caused by or belongs to someone: to impute blame. 2) (maths and statistics) To fill in a missing value in data with an estimated one.
its sense in the lessons: A stiff exam and legal word: «they imputed the failure to poor planning». In data and statistics, imputing means guessing a missing number from the others, for example using the average. Phrases: impute blame, impute motives, impute missing values.
examples from the lessons: It is unfair to impute bad motives to someone without proof. | The report imputed the delay to the bad weather. | The scientist imputed the missing temperature using the average of the days before and after. | Don't impute the mistake to her; it was mine. | The judge refused to impute guilt without evidence. | The historian would not impute cruelty to the king without evidence.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal. Noun «imputation». Easier everyday words: «blame», «put down to». In data work, imputed values are estimates, not real measurements, and good reports say which ones were filled in.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A mistake or wrong fact in something said, written or measured. 2) Not being exact or correct; the amount by which a measurement is wrong.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and science, inaccuracy in measurement comes from rough tools or careless reading; pupils repeat measurements to reduce it. In history and media lessons, they look for inaccuracies in sources and news. Phrases: an inaccuracy in, full of inaccuracies, measurement inaccuracy.
examples from the lessons: The teacher found three inaccuracies in my history report. | The old map was full of inaccuracies. | We repeated the experiment to reduce inaccuracy. | The film had many historical inaccuracies. | The inaccuracy of the cheap scale was about ten grams. | Check facts carefully to avoid inaccuracies.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable for each mistake («inaccuracies»), uncountable for the general quality. Adjective «inaccurate»; opposite «accuracy». In maths, inaccuracy can be measured as the difference between your answer and the true value.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Not suitable or not right for a particular time, place or person. 2) (safety) Describing words, pictures, touching or messages that are wrong or unsafe for a child, which a child should tell a trusted adult about.
its sense in the lessons: In school, inappropriate behaviour breaks class rules (shouting in assembly, rude words). In online and personal-safety lessons, if anyone shows or sends something inappropriate, or touches you in a way that feels wrong, you say no and tell a trusted adult. In writing, an inappropriate word does not fit the register. Phrases: inappropriate behaviour, inappropriate language, inappropriate for children.
examples from the lessons: Wearing flip-flops on a mountain hike is inappropriate. | Rude jokes in assembly are inappropriate. | If someone sends you something inappropriate online, tell a trusted adult. | The film was rated inappropriate for young children. | Laughing at a funeral would be inappropriate. | Slang can be inappropriate in a formal letter.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: «appropriate». Spelling: one double p: «in-ap-pro-pri-ate». Safety: you are never in trouble for telling an adult about something inappropriate.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Not paying attention; not listening or watching carefully. 2) Not giving enough care or thought to someone's needs: an inattentive host.
its sense in the lessons: In school, an inattentive pupil misses instructions; in road safety, inattentive walking (looking at a phone) is dangerous. In stories, an inattentive guard lets the hero sneak past. Phrases: inattentive in class, inattentive driver, inattentive to detail.
examples from the lessons: The inattentive guard was asleep when the prisoner escaped. | Being inattentive near roads is dangerous. | I was inattentive and missed the homework instructions. | An inattentive driver can cause an accident. | The waiter was inattentive and forgot our drinks. | Tiredness can make you inattentive in lessons.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: «attentive». Being inattentive sometimes is normal; some people have ADHD, which makes paying attention harder — it is not laziness.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To swear a new leader into office at an official ceremony, such as a US president. 2) To open a new building, service or event officially for the first time. 3) (formal) To begin or start a new period or system.
its sense in the lessons: In history and citizenship lessons, US presidents are inaugurated on 20 January after an election. In everyday news, a mayor inaugurates a new bridge, library or hospital, often by cutting a ribbon. Phrases: be inaugurated as, inaugurate a new era, inauguration day.
examples from the lessons: The new president was inaugurated in Washington. | The mayor inaugurated the new library by cutting a ribbon. | The festival was inaugurated in 1950 and still runs today. | The invention of the steam train inaugurated a new age of travel. | Our school inaugurated its new playground with a party. | The first Australian Parliament was inaugurated in 1901.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: «inauguration» (Inauguration Day in the USA). Pronounced in-AW-gyuh-rate. In the UK, a monarch is «crowned» (coronation) rather than inaugurated.

part of speech: noun (inbreeding — uncountable); verb «inbreed» (inbreed, inbreeds, inbred, inbreeding)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (biology) Breeding between closely related animals or plants, such as brothers and sisters or parents and offspring. 2) The health problems that can come from this, because harmful hidden genes are more likely to show up.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on inheritance and conservation, inbreeding is a danger for small animal populations (cheetahs, rare zoo animals) and some dog breeds; zoos swap animals to avoid it. In history, some royal families married close relatives, which caused illnesses. Phrases: avoid inbreeding, inbreeding in dogs, signs of inbreeding.
examples from the lessons: Zoos swap animals with other zoos to avoid inbreeding. | Cheetahs are at risk because of inbreeding in small groups. | Some pedigree dog breeds have health problems from inbreeding. | Inbreeding makes it more likely that babies inherit illnesses. | Farmers bring in a new bull to stop inbreeding in their herd. | Some old royal families suffered from inbreeding.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Opposite: «outbreeding» or mixing genes from different families, which gives variety. Adjective «inbred». Calling a person «inbred» is a nasty insult; don't use it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) The light given off by something because it is very hot, like a glowing metal wire or lava. 2) (literary) A strong bright glow or a burning strong feeling.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on light and heat, old-fashioned light bulbs work by incandescence: electricity heats a thin wire until it glows white. The Sun, flames, red-hot coals and lava also shine by incandescence. In stories it describes brilliant light or passion. Phrases: incandescent bulb, the incandescence of lava.
examples from the lessons: An old light bulb shines by incandescence when its wire gets white-hot. | The incandescence of the lava lit up the night. | Red-hot iron in the blacksmith's fire shows incandescence. | LED bulbs don't use incandescence, so they waste less heat. | The candle flame glows by incandescence of tiny soot bits. | The incandescence of the sparkler lit up our faces on Bonfire Night.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective «incandescent» — which also means extremely angry in informal UK speech («incandescent with rage»). Not the same as «fluorescence» or «luminescence», which give light without great heat (glow sticks, fireflies).

meaning for a pupil: 1) To burn something completely until only ashes are left, especially rubbish or waste. 2) (informal) To destroy completely with great heat, as with lasers in stories.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and science lessons on waste, rubbish is buried in landfill, recycled or incinerated; some incinerators make electricity. Hospitals incinerate used medical waste. In sci-fi stories, a laser incinerates an alien ship. Phrases: incinerate waste, incinerated rubbish, incinerator.
examples from the lessons: The town incinerates its rubbish to make electricity. | Hospitals incinerate used needles safely. | The meteor was incinerated as it fell through the atmosphere. | In the film, the dragon incinerated the castle gates. | Burning plastic at home is dangerous; it should not be incinerated in a garden fire. | Garden waste is often composted rather than incinerated.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun «incineration»; machine: «incinerator». Stronger than «burn»: it means burnt completely to ash. Pronounced in-SIN-uh-rate.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Just beginning to happen or to show: an incipient cold, incipient baldness. 2) In an early stage, before it is fully grown or obvious.
its sense in the lessons: A formal word in medicine, science and books: an incipient storm, crack or illness is one just starting. In everyday speech people say «starting», «early», «beginning». Phrases: incipient signs, an incipient crack, at an incipient stage.
examples from the lessons: The doctor spotted an incipient infection and gave him medicine. | An incipient crack in the dam worried the engineers. | Grandad has incipient baldness, he jokes. | There were incipient signs of spring: tiny green buds. | The storm was still incipient, just a dark line of clouds. | The gardener caught the incipient disease before it spread to the other roses.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal. Pronounced in-SIP-ee-unt. Do not confuse with «insipid» (dull, tasteless).

part of speech: verb (incline, inclines, inclined, inclining); noun (an incline, inclines)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (noun) A slope: a hill or ramp that goes up or down. 2) (verb) To lean, tilt or bend something, for example to incline your head to show you agree. 3) (verb, formal) To tend to or want to: «I'm inclined to agree». 4) (verb, formal) To make someone want to do something: the warm day inclined us to swim.
its sense in the lessons: In science, an inclined plane (a ramp) is a simple machine that makes lifting easier — longer path, smaller force; pupils roll cars down inclines to test friction and speed. In maths, the incline of a line is its slope. In everyday speech, «I'm inclined to…» means «I'd rather…». Phrases: inclined plane, a steep incline, be inclined to, if you're so inclined.
examples from the lessons: We rolled toy cars down an incline to test which went furthest. | The road has a steep incline, so cyclists get off and push. | A ramp is an inclined plane that helps lift heavy things. | She inclined her head politely. | I'm inclined to believe him; he's usually honest. | The treadmill can be set to an incline to make walking harder. | If you're so inclined, you can do the bonus question.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stress: noun IN-cline, verb in-CLINE. Noun «inclination» = a slope or a liking. In maths, a steeper incline means a bigger gradient: rise ÷ run.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Not able to be squashed into a smaller space. 2) (science) Describing a substance whose volume stays nearly the same when you press on it, such as liquids and solids.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on states of matter, gases are compressible (air in a syringe squashes) but liquids and solids are almost incompressible, because their particles are already close together. This is why hydraulic machines use liquids. Phrases: almost incompressible, incompressible liquid.
examples from the lessons: Water is almost incompressible, so you can't squash it in a syringe. | Air is compressible, but bricks are incompressible. | Hydraulic brakes work because oil is nearly incompressible. | We pushed the plunger: the water stayed the same; it's incompressible. | Solids are incompressible because their particles are packed tight. | We squeezed a sealed bottle of water and found it almost incompressible.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: «compressible». Strictly, nothing is perfectly incompressible; liquids squash a tiny bit under huge pressure, so science says «nearly incompressible».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Not staying the same; changing in quality or behaviour: an inconsistent player. 2) Not agreeing or fitting together: two facts that are inconsistent with each other. 3) (formal) Not following the same rules each time: inconsistent marking.
its sense in the lessons: In science, results that are inconsistent vary a lot, so you repeat the test; in maths and logic, statements that cannot both be true are inconsistent. In detective stories, a suspect's story is inconsistent with the clues. In sport, an inconsistent team plays well one week and badly the next. Phrases: inconsistent with, inconsistent results, wildly inconsistent.
examples from the lessons: Our results were inconsistent, so we repeated the experiment. | His story was inconsistent with the footprints. | The team has been inconsistent all season. | The rules were applied in an inconsistent way, which felt unfair. | My handwriting is inconsistent: neat at first, messy at the end. | Saying «I never lie» and then lying is inconsistent.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Followed by «with»: «inconsistent with the facts». Opposite: «consistent». In maths, a set of equations with no solution is called inconsistent.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (literary) Changing often; not loyal or faithful: an inconstant friend. 2) Not steady; changing in amount or strength: an inconstant wind.
its sense in the lessons: Mostly found in old stories, poems and formal writing: the «inconstant moon» changes shape every night; an inconstant lover keeps changing whom they love. In everyday talk people say «changeable» or «unreliable». Phrases: an inconstant friend, inconstant weather.
examples from the lessons: The inconstant wind kept changing direction. | In the poem, the moon is called inconstant because it changes shape. | He was an inconstant friend who forgot us when someone new came along. | Spring weather in Ireland is inconstant: sun, then rain. | The candle's inconstant flame flickered. | The old song warned of an inconstant heart.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: «constant». Do not confuse with «inconsistent», which is the everyday word for not staying the same or not agreeing. «Inconstant» is old-fashioned and literary.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To include something as part of a bigger thing: incorporate ideas into a story. 2) To mix in: incorporate the butter into the flour. 3) (business, law) To make a company into a legal organisation; «Inc.» after a US company name means «Incorporated».
its sense in the lessons: In writing lessons, pupils incorporate feedback, quotes or new words into their work. In cooking, you incorporate ingredients gently. In maths projects, you incorporate a chart into a report. Phrases: incorporate into, incorporate ideas, incorporated company.
examples from the lessons: Try to incorporate three new adjectives into your story. | Gently incorporate the eggs into the cake mixture. | The new design incorporates a cup holder. | Our school play incorporated songs from around the world. | The town was incorporated in 1850. | The company's name ends in «Inc.», short for «Incorporated».
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually followed by «into» or «in». Noun «incorporation». Similar easier words: «include», «add», «mix in». «Inc.» (US) is like «Ltd» (UK, Australia, NZ).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Not being able to believe something; great surprise and disbelief. 2) The look or feeling of someone who thinks «that can't be true!»
its sense in the lessons: In stories, characters react with incredulity to shocking news or amazing events; it shows on their face (eyes wide, mouth open). In science, healthy incredulity means checking strange claims. Phrases: in incredulity, stare in incredulity, a look of incredulity.
examples from the lessons: She stared at the huge pumpkin in incredulity. | His face showed pure incredulity when he heard he had won. | The class listened with incredulity as the teacher said octopuses have three hearts. | «You did all your homework?» Mum asked with incredulity. | The news was met with incredulity. | «A whale is a mammal, not a fish?» he said with incredulity.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Adjective: «incredulous» (not believing); do not confuse with «incredible» (unbelievable, amazing). A person is incredulous; a story is incredible.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a way that cannot be cured or made better by medicine. 2) (informal, often playful) Completely and permanently, as a habit: incurably curious, incurably optimistic.
its sense in the lessons: In health and family-life lessons, someone «incurably ill» has an illness doctors cannot cure, though they can often make the person comfortable. In playful speech, «incurably» means «always and forever». Phrases: incurably ill, incurably romantic, incurably curious.
examples from the lessons: The hospice cares for people who are incurably ill. | Grandad is incurably cheerful, even in the rain. | My sister is incurably nosy. | Doctors could not cure the illness, but they helped him feel less pain. | She's incurably curious and asks a hundred questions a day. | My uncle is incurably late for everything.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective «incurable»; opposite «curable». Be gentle with the medical sense; incurable does not always mean someone will die soon — many people live long lives with incurable conditions that are managed.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A sudden attack on or invasion of a place, often short. 2) (formal) Coming into a place or area where you are not wanted or not expected: the incursion of sea water into a field.
its sense in the lessons: In history and news, an incursion is a raid across a border, such as Viking incursions into England or military incursions reported between countries. In geography and science, sea water or weeds make incursions into land or crops. Phrases: an incursion into, border incursion, Viking incursions.
examples from the lessons: Viking incursions terrified villages along the coast. | The army reported an incursion across the border. | The storm caused an incursion of sea water into the fields. | Rabbits made nightly incursions into our vegetable patch. | The news described the drone incursion as a serious threat. | Foxes made an incursion into the henhouse last night.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal word; usually followed by «into». Similar: «raid», «invasion» (bigger and longer). In news about wars, each side may describe the same event differently.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Without choosing carefully; at random or in a careless way. 2) Without caring who gets hurt or affected: bombs that kill indiscriminately.
its sense in the lessons: In health lessons, taking medicine or antibiotics indiscriminately is unsafe. In news about wars, weapons that harm people indiscriminately are condemned by international law. In stories, a careless giant smashes indiscriminately. Phrases: kill indiscriminately, use indiscriminately, spray indiscriminately.
examples from the lessons: The storm knocked down trees indiscriminately. | Using antibiotics indiscriminately helps germs become resistant. | The goat ate everything indiscriminately, even my socks. | International law forbids attacks that harm civilians indiscriminately. | He copied answers indiscriminately and got them all wrong. | Don't click on links indiscriminately; some are scams.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective «indiscriminate». Root «discriminate» = to tell apart or choose carefully (it also means to treat people unfairly). «Indiscriminately» = without telling apart.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) A slight illness, like a cold or upset stomach, that stops you doing something. 2) (formal) Unwillingness to do something.
its sense in the lessons: A stiff, formal or old-fashioned word, often in announcements: «due to the singer's indisposition, the show is cancelled». In everyday speech: «feeling poorly», «under the weather». Phrases: a slight indisposition, due to indisposition.
examples from the lessons: Due to a slight indisposition, the actor could not perform tonight. | The teacher's absence was explained as a brief indisposition. | In the old novel, the duchess suffered an indisposition and stayed in bed. | His indisposition to help was obvious. | The head teacher's indisposition meant the assembly was cancelled. | Owing to indisposition, Lady Mary sent her apologies.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective «indisposed» (slightly ill, or unwilling). Very formal; also used as a polite euphemism to avoid saying exactly what is wrong.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Not clear or sharp; hard to see, hear or remember clearly. 2) Blurred or faint: indistinct shapes in the fog.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, indistinct voices, shapes and footsteps build mystery or fear. In science, a picture under a microscope is indistinct until you focus. In speaking lessons, mumbling makes speech indistinct. Phrases: indistinct voices, an indistinct shape, an indistinct memory.
examples from the lessons: Indistinct voices came from behind the door. | An indistinct shape moved in the fog. | Turn the knob until the cell is no longer indistinct under the microscope. | My memory of being a baby is very indistinct. | He spoke so quietly his words were indistinct. | The old writing on the stone was indistinct.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: «distinct» (clear). Do not confuse with «extinct» (no longer living) or «instinct» (natural feeling).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Not able to be divided or separated into parts. 2) (maths) Not able to be divided exactly by a certain number without a remainder: 7 is indivisible by 2. 3) (formal) So closely joined that they act as one: «one nation… indivisible» in the US Pledge of Allegiance.
its sense in the lessons: In maths lessons, «indivisible by» means there is a remainder: 9 is indivisible by 4. A prime number is indivisible by any number except 1 and itself. In US schools children say «one nation under God, indivisible…» in the Pledge of Allegiance. In science, atoms were once thought indivisible. Phrases: indivisible by, one and indivisible.
examples from the lessons: Seven is indivisible by two; there is always one left over. | A prime number is indivisible except by one and itself. | The friends were indivisible; you never saw one without the other. | People once thought atoms were indivisible, but they have smaller parts. | «One nation, indivisible» is a line from the US Pledge of Allegiance. | Is 15 indivisible by 4? Yes, because 15 ÷ 4 leaves a remainder of 3.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: «divisible». Maths: «a is indivisible by b» = a ÷ b leaves a remainder. Careful: everything can be divided as a fraction (7 ÷ 2 = 3.5); «indivisible» in maths means not into whole numbers exactly.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Laziness; not wanting to work or make an effort. 2) A relaxed, slow, lazy state, as on a hot day.
its sense in the lessons: A literary and formal word, found in stories and old books: an idle character's indolence. In everyday talk people say «laziness». Phrases: a life of indolence, sheer indolence, summer indolence.
examples from the lessons: The king lived a life of indolence while his people worked. | His indolence meant the garden was full of weeds. | On the hot afternoon the cats lay in happy indolence. | The teacher blamed his poor marks on indolence. | The story warned against indolence and greed. | After a busy term, we enjoyed a week of indolence on the beach.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Adjective «indolent». Formal and judging; being tired or ill is not indolence.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To let yourself do or have something you enjoy, especially as a treat: indulge in chocolate. 2) To let someone have whatever they want, even when it's not good for them: to indulge a child. 3) To allow and go along with someone's interest or wish: indulge his curiosity. 4) (church, history) An «indulgence» in the medieval Catholic Church was a release from punishment for sin; selling them was one cause of the Reformation.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, «indulge» is about treats, cake and spoiling; in PSHE about healthy balance. In history lessons, Martin Luther in 1517 protested against the sale of indulgences. Phrases: indulge in, indulge yourself, indulge a whim, indulge someone.
examples from the lessons: On my birthday I indulged in a huge slice of cake. | Grandma indulges us with sweets when we visit. | Go on, indulge yourself — you've earned it. | Mum indulged my curiosity and let me take the clock apart. | Don't indulge the puppy every time it begs. | Martin Luther protested against the selling of indulgences.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Often «indulge in» + something. Adjective «indulgent» (too kind, spoiling). Indulging sometimes is fine; too much can be unhealthy. Spelling: i-n-d-u-l-g-e.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The change of a country or area from farming and handwork to factories, machines and big industry. 2) (history) In particular the Industrial Revolution in Britain from about 1760, which then spread to Europe, North America and the world.
its sense in the lessons: In history and geography lessons, industrialisation brought steam engines, factories, railways and growing cities, but also child labour, pollution and crowded housing. Today many countries are still industrialising. Phrases: rapid industrialisation, the age of industrialisation, effects of industrialisation.
examples from the lessons: Industrialisation changed Britain from farms to factories. | During industrialisation, many children worked long hours in mills. | Industrialisation made cities grow very fast. | Smoke from industrialisation polluted the air. | Railways spread across the country during industrialisation. | China went through rapid industrialisation in recent decades.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. UK «-isation», US «-ization». Verb «industrialise»; adjective «industrial». The opposite trend is «deindustrialisation», when factories close.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Not fit or safe to eat, because it is poisonous, rotten or not food at all. 2) (informal) Tasting so bad that you cannot eat it: the burnt toast was inedible.
its sense in the lessons: In science and outdoor-safety lessons, many wild berries and mushrooms are inedible or poisonous — never eat wild plants without an expert adult. In cooking stories, burnt food is «inedible». Phrases: completely inedible, inedible parts, inedible mushrooms.
examples from the lessons: Some wild mushrooms are inedible and even deadly. | The burnt pizza was inedible. | The peel of a banana is inedible for people, but goats eat it. | Plastic fruit is inedible — it's just for show. | The cake was so salty it was inedible. | Never eat berries in the woods; many are inedible.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: «edible» (safe to eat). Do not confuse with «indelible» (cannot be rubbed out, like an indelible pen). «Inedible» is stronger than «not tasty».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Too great to be measured or counted. 2) (formal) Extremely valuable or important: of inestimable value.
its sense in the lessons: A formal word in speeches and thank-you notes: «your help has been of inestimable value». In history, treasures and inventions may be called of inestimable worth. Phrases: of inestimable value, inestimable importance.
examples from the lessons: The ancient library was of inestimable value. | Her help has been of inestimable value to our school. | The invention of printing was of inestimable importance. | The crown jewels are of inestimable worth. | The damage from the fire was inestimable. | Grandma's stories are of inestimable value to our family.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal. Root: «estimate» = guess the size or value; «inestimable» = too big to estimate. Usually positive (great value).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Certain to happen; impossible to avoid or stop. 2) (informal) So usual or expected that everyone knows it will come: the inevitable rain on sports day.
its sense in the lessons: In science and maths, some outcomes are inevitable (the Sun will set; a dropped ball falls). In probability, an inevitable event is «certain». In stories, an inevitable ending is one the reader sees coming. In everyday humour: «the inevitable question: are we there yet?» Phrases: it was inevitable that, the inevitable, delay the inevitable.
examples from the lessons: It was inevitable that the ice cream would melt in the sun. | Getting older is inevitable. | With no revision, failing the test was almost inevitable. | On the long car trip came the inevitable question: «Are we there yet?» | Change is inevitable, so learn to adapt. | They delayed the inevitable by hiding the broken vase.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced in-EV-it-uh-bul. In maths probability, inevitable = certain = probability 1. Careful: many things people call inevitable are only likely.

part of speech: noun (infantry — uncountable; usually «the infantry»; with a singular or plural verb in UK English)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Soldiers who fight on foot, as opposed to soldiers on horses, in tanks, ships or planes. 2) The part of an army made up of these soldiers.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, infantry fought in battles from Roman legions to the trenches of the First World War; cavalry rode horses and artillery fired big guns. Phrases: infantry soldier, infantry regiment, light infantry.
examples from the lessons: Roman infantry fought in tight rows with shields. | The infantry marched for days to reach the battle. | My great-grandad served in the infantry in the Second World War. | In the past, cavalry rode horses while the infantry walked. | An infantry soldier carries a heavy pack. | Archers and infantry stood together at the Battle of Hastings.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: one soldier is «an infantryman» or «an infantry soldier». Do not confuse with «infant» (a baby) — though both come from Latin for «young», as young soldiers once fought on foot. Related: cavalry (horses), artillery (big guns).

part of speech: adjective (inflamed, more inflamed); verb, past form of «inflame» (inflame, inflames, inflamed, inflaming)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (body) Red, swollen, hot and sore, usually because of an injury or infection. 2) (feelings) Made much angrier or more excited: an inflamed crowd. 3) (verb) Made a bad situation worse: his words inflamed the argument.
its sense in the lessons: In science and health lessons, inflammation is the body's response to injury or germs — redness, heat, swelling and pain help healing. Doctors talk of inflamed tonsils, throats, joints or skin. In news and history, speeches can inflame anger. Phrases: inflamed skin, inflamed throat, inflamed tonsils, inflame tensions.
examples from the lessons: My throat was red and inflamed, so I stayed home. | The cut became inflamed, so we went to the doctor. | Her eyes were inflamed from hay fever. | The rude comment inflamed the argument. | The speech inflamed the angry crowd. | An inflamed appendix may need an operation.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun «inflammation»; adjective «inflammatory» (causing anger or swelling). Trap: «inflammable» means easily set on fire — the same as «flammable», not the opposite! Seek an adult or doctor if a wound gets more inflamed, hot or spreads red.

part of speech: adjective (inflected); verb, past form of «inflect» (inflect, inflects, inflected, inflecting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (grammar) Changed in form to show grammar, such as tense, number or person: «walked» is an inflected form of «walk». 2) (grammar) Describing a language that changes word endings a lot, like Latin, German or Ukrainian. 3) (voice) Changed in pitch, as a voice that goes up at the end of a question.
its sense in the lessons: In English and grammar lessons, inflected forms are the different forms of one word: cat/cats, run/ran/running, big/bigger/biggest. Learning French or Ukrainian, pupils see heavily inflected words with many endings. Phrases: inflected form, highly inflected language.
examples from the lessons: «Ran» is an inflected form of «run». | Latin is a highly inflected language with many word endings. | «Cats» is the inflected plural of «cat». | English is less inflected than German. | Her voice inflected upward at the end of the question. | In a dictionary, inflected forms are listed with the main word.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb «inflect»; noun «inflection» (UK also «inflexion»). Inflection keeps it the same word in a new form; derivation makes a new word (happy → happiness).

part of speech: noun (an inflection, inflections; UK also inflexion)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (grammar) A change in the form of a word, usually its ending, to show tense, number, person and so on: «-s», «-ed», «-ing», «-er», «-est». 2) The rise and fall of the voice when speaking: the inflection of a question. 3) (maths) A point of inflection is where a curve changes the way it bends.
its sense in the lessons: In grammar lessons, inflections are word endings that change meaning in grammar: walk → walks, walked, walking. In speaking and drama lessons, voice inflection shows feelings and questions. In higher maths, a curve's inflection point is where it switches from curving one way to the other. Phrases: verb inflection, voice inflection, point of inflection.
examples from the lessons: The «-ed» inflection shows that an action happened in the past. | Add the plural inflection «-s» to «dog» to get «dogs». | Her voice had a rising inflection, so I knew it was a question. | Read your poem with more inflection so it isn't boring. | English has fewer inflections than Latin. | The curve has a point of inflection in the middle.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: an inflection, many inflections. Spelling: «inflection» is usual; «inflexion» is an older UK spelling. Irregular forms like «ran» or «mice» are also inflected forms, but made without a regular ending.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (grammar) To do with inflection: changing the form of words to show grammar. 2) Describing endings or languages that work this way: inflectional endings, an inflectional language.
its sense in the lessons: In grammar lessons: English inflectional endings are -s (plural, he walks), -'s (possessive), -ed, -ing, -en, -er and -est. They change grammar but not the basic meaning or word class. Phrases: inflectional ending, inflectional morphology, inflectional suffix.
examples from the lessons: «-ing» is an inflectional ending. | Inflectional suffixes don't change the word class: «walk» and «walked» are both verbs. | Russian and Ukrainian have many inflectional endings. | The teacher listed English's eight inflectional endings. | «Happiness» uses a derivational suffix, not an inflectional one. | «Biggest» uses the inflectional ending «-est».
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective from «inflection». Contrast: inflectional suffixes (-s, -ed) keep the word in its class; derivational suffixes (-ness, -ly) can make a new word. A technical grammar word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The movement of water, air or other things flowing into a place: the inflow of a river into a lake. 2) The arrival of money, people or goods into a place: an inflow of visitors, cash inflow.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and science, rivers, pipes and air give inflow into lakes, reservoirs or rooms; outflow goes out. In maths problems, a tank with inflow and outflow fills or empties at the difference of the two rates. In money lessons, cash inflow is money coming in. Phrases: inflow and outflow, inflow of water, an inflow of tourists.
examples from the lessons: The inflow of river water filled the reservoir. | The bathtub's inflow was faster than its outflow, so it overflowed. | Summer brings an inflow of tourists to the beach town. | The shop had a big inflow of money at Christmas. | Warm air inflow made the room cosy. | If the inflow is 5 litres a minute and the outflow is 3, the tank gains 2 litres a minute.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: «outflow». In maths, net change = inflow − outflow. Stress: IN-flow.

part of speech: adjective (inflowing); also the -ing form of the rare verb «inflow»
meaning for a pupil: 1) Flowing in; coming into a place: inflowing water, inflowing air. 2) Arriving into a place in a stream: inflowing traffic, inflowing money.
its sense in the lessons: Used in geography and science about rivers, streams, tides and air coming into a lake, sea or room: «the inflowing streams feed the lake». In maths tank problems, the inflowing water fills the tank. Phrases: inflowing river, inflowing water, inflowing tide.
examples from the lessons: Several inflowing streams feed the lake. | The inflowing tide covered the sand. | Cold inflowing air came through the open window. | The inflowing water raised the level of the tank by 2 cm a minute. | The inflowing river brings mud into the bay. | Inflowing sea water made the river taste salty near its mouth.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly a technical, describing word; everyday English says «water flowing in». Opposite: «outflowing». Noun: «inflow».

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a relaxed, friendly, everyday way, not following strict rules or formal manners. 2) Unofficially; not as part of an official process: they agreed informally. 3) (language) Using casual words, slang or chatty style rather than formal language.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons, pupils learn when to write formally (letters to the council, reports) and informally (messages to friends, diaries); register matters. In everyday life, «dress informally» means casual clothes; «known informally as» gives a nickname. Phrases: speak informally, dress informally, known informally as, informally agreed.
examples from the lessons: You can write informally in a text to your friend. | We dressed informally for the class picnic. | The Houses of Parliament clock is informally known as Big Ben. | The teachers met informally in the staff room. | «Gonna» is how people say «going to» informally. | They informally agreed to swap stickers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective «informal»; opposite «formally». Informal does not mean wrong: «can't», «kids», «gonna» are fine in chat but usually not in exam writing. A big skill is matching your language to the situation.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Not happening often; rare. 2) Happening with long gaps in between: infrequent buses.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: infrequent buses in the countryside, infrequent visits from relatives abroad. In maths and data lessons, infrequent values appear few times in a tally or frequency table. In science, infrequent events like eclipses are worth waiting for. Phrases: infrequent visits, infrequent buses, an infrequent visitor.
examples from the lessons: Buses to our village are infrequent, only two a day. | Total eclipses are infrequent in any one place. | Our cousin from Canada is an infrequent visitor. | Snow is infrequent in Sydney. | In the tally chart, red cars were infrequent. | His infrequent mistakes were easy to fix.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: «frequent» (often). In maths, frequency means how many times something happens; an infrequent item has a low frequency. Similar: «rare», «occasional».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A drink made by soaking leaves, flowers or fruit in hot water, like herbal tea. 2) (medicine) Putting a liquid such as medicine or fluid slowly into a vein through a tube (a drip). 3) Adding something new that brings energy or change: an infusion of money, an infusion of new ideas.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: a mint, camomile or fruit infusion is like tea without tea leaves. In hospital, a patient may have an infusion of fluids or medicine. In science, making an infusion is a way of drawing flavour or colour out of plants into water. Phrases: herbal infusion, an infusion of cash, a saline infusion.
examples from the lessons: Grandma drinks a camomile infusion before bed. | We made an infusion of red cabbage to test acids and alkalis. | The nurse gave him an infusion of fluids through a drip. | The new players gave the team an infusion of energy. | A mint infusion is made by steeping leaves in hot water. | The school got an infusion of money to fix the roof.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb «infuse» (to steep, or to fill with a feeling: infused with hope). Countable for each drink or dose. Don't confuse «infusion» with «confusion» or «diffusion» (spreading out of particles).

meaning for a pupil: 1) As a basic, natural part of something that cannot be removed; by its very nature. 2) (formal) In itself, not because of something added from outside: inherently dangerous.
its sense in the lessons: In science and safety: fire is inherently dangerous; some sports are inherently risky, so we wear helmets. In ethics lessons: is a lie inherently wrong? In maths: some problems are inherently hard. Phrases: inherently dangerous, inherently good, inherently unfair.
examples from the lessons: Fire is inherently dangerous, so treat it with care. | Climbing is inherently risky, which is why we use ropes. | Nobody is inherently bad; people can learn and change. | Some games are inherently unfair because of their rules. | Mistakes aren't inherently bad; they help us learn. | Glass is inherently fragile.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective «inherent» (an inherent risk). Pronounced in-HEER-ent-lee or in-HAIR-ent-lee. Do not confuse with «inherit» (to receive from a parent or someone who has died).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Not likely to upset, annoy or offend anyone; harmless. 2) Pleasant but rather dull or ordinary: an inoffensive colour.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: an inoffensive joke, an inoffensive little animal, an inoffensive beige wall. In stories it can describe a quiet, harmless character, sometimes unfairly picked on. Phrases: quite inoffensive, perfectly inoffensive, a mild inoffensive man.
examples from the lessons: The joke was inoffensive, so everyone laughed. | Grass snakes are inoffensive and won't hurt you. | He was a quiet, inoffensive boy who never caused trouble. | They painted the room an inoffensive cream. | It's better to pick an inoffensive team name. | The puppy was inoffensive, just very excited.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: «offensive». «Inoffensive» can be praise (harmless) or mild criticism (boring).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Much more than is usual, reasonable or expected; too much. 2) Unreasonably large: an inordinate amount of time.
its sense in the lessons: Formal and in reports: «an inordinate amount of homework», «inordinate delays». Exam-style writing uses it to say «far too much». Phrases: an inordinate amount of, inordinate length, inordinately proud.
examples from the lessons: He spent an inordinate amount of time choosing a pencil. | The queue caused an inordinate delay. | She was inordinately proud of her sandcastle. | We received an inordinate number of emails about lost property. | The film was of inordinate length — almost four hours. | The cat spends an inordinate amount of time asleep.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal. Easier words: «excessive», «far too much», «huge». Pronounced in-OR-din-ut.

part of speech: verb (inquire, inquires, inquired, inquiring; UK also enquire)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To ask for information about something: inquire about the times of trains. 2) (formal) To ask someone something politely: «May I inquire your name?» 3) To investigate officially: inquire into an accident.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, people inquire at reception or the information desk. In science, «enquiry» or «inquiry» learning means asking questions and testing them. In news and law, officials inquire into accidents and complaints. Phrases: inquire about, inquire after someone (ask how they are), inquire into, inquire within (on shop signs).
examples from the lessons: Mum inquired about swimming lessons at the leisure centre. | «May I inquire where you are going?» asked the guard. | The sign said «Part-time job — inquire within». | The council will inquire into the playground accident. | Grandma always inquires after my health. | We inquired how long the train would take.
note for the reader of a maths problem: In the UK many use «enquire» for asking and «inquire» for official investigations; in the US «inquire» is used for both. Nouns: «inquiry», «enquiry». «Inquire» is more formal than «ask».

meaning for a pupil: 1) An animal or plant that eats mainly insects. 2) (science, older) A word once used for a group of small mammals like shrews, moles and hedgehogs.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on food chains and diets, animals are herbivores (eat plants), carnivores (eat meat), omnivores (eat both) and insectivores (eat insects). Examples: anteaters, bats, swallows, frogs, hedgehogs, Venus flytraps. Phrases: an insectivore, insectivorous plants.
examples from the lessons: Bats are insectivores; one bat can eat hundreds of midges in a night. | The hedgehog is an insectivore that hunts beetles and worms. | A Venus flytrap is an insectivore plant. | Anteaters are insectivores with long sticky tongues. | Swallows are insectivores that catch flies in the air. | Is a frog an insectivore or a carnivore? Both words can fit.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective «insectivorous». «-vore» means «eater»: herbivore, carnivore, omnivore. An insectivore is a kind of carnivore. Spiders and worms are not insects, but insectivores often eat them too.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Not noticing or caring about other people's feelings; saying or doing hurtful things. 2) Not able to feel or react to something: insensitive to pain, insensitive to light.
its sense in the lessons: In PSHE lessons, an insensitive comment (about someone's looks, family or loss) hurts even if it wasn't meant to. In science, a measuring device or body part may be insensitive to small changes. Phrases: an insensitive remark, insensitive to, culturally insensitive.
examples from the lessons: Laughing at her haircut was insensitive. | It was insensitive to talk about the party in front of the boy who wasn't invited. | Some fish are insensitive to cold water. | The old scales were insensitive to tiny weights. | I'm sorry; that was an insensitive thing to say. | Being insensitive to pain can be dangerous, because pain warns us.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: «sensitive». Usually followed by «to». Being insensitive is often by accident; saying sorry and listening helps.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Always together; such close friends that you can't keep them apart. 2) Impossible to separate: two ideas that are inseparable.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and everyday life, best friends, twins, or a child and a pet are «inseparable». In science, some mixtures or parts are not easy to separate. In grammar, an inseparable phrasal verb can't have its object in the middle («look after the baby», not «look the baby after»). Phrases: inseparable friends, inseparable from.
examples from the lessons: Mia and Zoe have been inseparable since nursery. | The boy and his dog were inseparable. | For many people, Christmas is inseparable from family. | The twins are inseparable and even finish each other's sentences. | Rights and responsibilities are inseparable. | «Look after» is an inseparable phrasal verb.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: «sep-a-rable» — «a» in the middle, as in «separate». Opposite: «separable».

part of speech: noun (an inset, insets); verb (inset, insets, inset, insetting); adjective (inset)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A small map, picture or box placed inside a bigger one, often in a corner. 2) A piece of different material sewn or set into something, like a panel in a dress. 3) (verb) To put something into a surface or a larger thing: a ring inset with a jewel.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons, maps often have an inset showing a small area in detail or where a place is in the country (for example Alaska and Hawaii on US maps). In newspapers and books, an inset photo or box adds extra information. In the UK, «INSET days» are teacher-training days when pupils have no school (from «in-service training»). Phrases: inset map, see inset, INSET day, inset with.
examples from the lessons: The inset map shows where the island is. | Look at the inset in the corner of the page. | Alaska is shown in an inset on many US maps. | The brooch was inset with tiny pearls. | We have an INSET day on Friday, so no school! | The magazine had an inset photo of the author.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past form is «inset», like «set». In the UK «INSET day» is written in capitals because it is an abbreviation. Stress: IN-set (noun), in-SET (verb).

part of speech: noun (insignia — plural or singular; also «insignias»; old singular «insigne»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A badge, sign or symbol that shows someone's rank, job, group or authority, like stripes on a uniform. 2) An emblem of an organisation, such as a club or army logo.
its sense in the lessons: In history and citizenship lessons, soldiers, police, scouts and pilots wear insignia showing rank and unit; kings and queens have royal insignia (crown, sceptre). In stories, insignia identify a spaceship's crew. Phrases: rank insignia, royal insignia, military insignia, insignia of office.
examples from the lessons: The pilot's jacket had the airline's insignia. | Police officers wear insignia showing their rank. | The crown and sceptre are royal insignia. | Our scout group has its own insignia on our badges. | Each Starfleet crew member wore the same insignia. | The general's insignia had four stars.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Grammar: «insignia» is used as both singular and plural today («this insignia», «these insignia»); «insignias» is also accepted. Pronounced in-SIG-nee-uh.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Demanding something firmly and not giving up. 2) Saying firmly again and again that something is true.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and everyday life, a character's insistence gets things done or causes arguments: «at my mum's insistence, I wore a coat». Phrases: at someone's insistence, insistence on, insistence that.
examples from the lessons: At Dad's insistence, we all wore helmets. | Her insistence on fairness made her a good captain. | Despite his insistence that he was innocent, he was blamed. | The teacher's insistence on neat work helped us improve. | At my insistence, we stopped for ice cream. | The family went to church every Sunday at Grandma's insistence.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb «insist» (insist on, insist that); adjective «insistent». Spelling: «-ence», not «-ance».

part of speech: adjective (insoluble; US also insolvable for problems)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) Not able to dissolve in a liquid, usually water: sand is insoluble in water. 2) Impossible to solve or answer: an insoluble problem.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on materials and mixtures, pupils test whether substances are soluble (salt, sugar) or insoluble (sand, chalk, oil); insoluble solids can be separated by filtering. In maths and stories, an insoluble puzzle has no solution. Phrases: insoluble in water, insoluble problem.
examples from the lessons: Sand is insoluble in water, so we can filter it out. | Salt is soluble, but chalk is insoluble. | Oil is insoluble in water and floats on top. | The mystery seemed insoluble until the detective found a clue. | Some maths puzzles are truly insoluble. | Insoluble fibre in food helps digestion.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: «soluble». In science, insoluble in water does not mean insoluble in everything: oil paint dissolves in white spirit. For problems, «unsolvable» is more common in everyday speech.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Happening immediately, with no delay at all. 2) (science) At one exact instant of time: instantaneous speed.
its sense in the lessons: In science, light from a nearby lamp seems to arrive instantaneously (it's very fast but not truly instant); in maths and physics, instantaneous speed is the speed at a single moment, like a speedometer reading, compared with average speed over a journey. In everyday life, messages and reactions can be instantaneous. Phrases: instantaneous reaction, almost instantaneous, instantaneous speed.
examples from the lessons: The reaction was instantaneous: the mixture fizzed straight away. | Text messages arrive almost instantaneously. | The speedometer shows your instantaneous speed. | When you flick the switch, the light seems instantaneous. | Her answer was instantaneous; she didn't need to think. | Death of the cells was instantaneous in the boiling water.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: in-stan-ta-ne-ous. Similar: «instant», «immediate». In science, average speed = distance ÷ time; instantaneous speed is the speed at one moment, which can be different.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who starts something, especially trouble such as a fight, argument or protest. 2) A person who causes an action or plan to begin: the instigator of the idea.
its sense in the lessons: In school and stories, the instigator is the one who started the trouble — «who was the instigator of the food fight?» In history lessons, instigators started revolts or protests. Phrases: the instigator of, chief instigator.
examples from the lessons: The teacher wanted to know who was the instigator of the snowball fight. | He was the instigator of the plan to build a treehouse. | The instigators of the riot were arrested. | She was the instigator of our class charity sale. | Don't be the instigator of unkind games. | In the story, the fox was the instigator of every trick in the farmyard.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb «instigate» (to start something); noun «instigation». Usually about starting trouble, but can be neutral.

part of speech: verb (instill, instills, instilled, instilling — US spelling; UK spelling instil, instils, instilled, instilling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To slowly put an idea, feeling or habit into someone's mind so it stays: instil good manners. 2) (medicine, rare) To put liquid in drop by drop, like eye drops.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and school, parents and teachers try to instil confidence, kindness, discipline or a love of reading in children. Coaches instil teamwork. Phrases: instil in/into someone, instil confidence, instil fear, instil a love of.
examples from the lessons: Our coach instilled confidence in the whole team. | Grandad instilled a love of fishing in me. | Good teachers instill curiosity. | The scary film instilled fear in my little brother. | Parents try to instill good manners in their children. | Practice instils good habits.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: US «instill», UK and Australia «instil» — both have «instilled», «instilling». Pattern: instil something in/into someone. Pronounced in-STILL.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Done naturally, without learning or thinking about it. 2) (science) Coming from instinct: behaviour an animal is born knowing, like a spider spinning a web.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, instinctive behaviour (birds migrating, babies sucking, turtles heading for the sea) is compared with learned behaviour (a dog learning tricks). In everyday life, an instinctive reaction is pulling your hand away from something hot. Phrases: instinctive reaction, instinctive behaviour, an instinctive feeling.
examples from the lessons: Pulling your hand from a hot pan is instinctive. | Baby turtles have an instinctive urge to crawl to the sea. | Spinning webs is instinctive for spiders; nobody teaches them. | She had an instinctive feeling that something was wrong. | Ducklings instinctively follow their mother. | He's an instinctive footballer who always knows where to run.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun «instinct». Opposite idea: «learned» behaviour. Note: some things we do quickly feel instinctive but were actually learned through practice, like riding a bike.

part of speech: verb, -ing form of «intensify» (intensify, intensifies, intensified, intensifying); adjective (intensifying)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Becoming stronger, greater or more extreme: an intensifying storm. 2) Making something stronger: intensifying the colour. 3) (grammar) An intensifying word (an intensifier) makes another word stronger, like «very», «really», «so», «totally».
its sense in the lessons: In geography and weather reports, storms and hurricanes are «intensifying» as winds grow stronger. In news, a conflict or debate may be intensifying. In grammar and writing lessons, intensifiers like «extremely» strengthen adjectives, but overusing them weakens writing. Phrases: an intensifying storm, intensifying heat, intensifying pressure.
examples from the lessons: The hurricane is intensifying as it moves over warm water. | The rain was intensifying, so we ran for shelter. | Adding more salt kept intensifying the flavour. | «Very» is an intensifying word. | The heat was intensifying through the afternoon. | Competition was intensifying in the final round.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb «intensify» changes y → i: intensifies, intensified; but keeps y before -ing: intensifying. Noun «intensity»; grammar term «intensifier».
