part of speech: verb (inter, inters, interred, interring; formal); prefix «inter-»; also a short name «Inter» (Inter Milan, a football club)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To bury a dead person in a grave or tomb. 2) (prefix «inter-») Between or among: international (between nations), interact, interval, internet. 3) (a name) «Inter» is the short name of Inter Milan (Internazionale), an Italian football club.
its sense in the lessons: In history, church and formal news, someone «was interred» in a cemetery, churchyard or abbey; it is a respectful word for buried. As a prefix «inter-» appears in many school words: international, interview, interrupt, intercity. Phrases: interred in, interred at, inter- (between).
examples from the lessons: The king was interred in Westminster Abbey. | Her ashes were interred in the family grave. | «Interact» means to act with each other. | An international match is a match between nations. | The soldiers were interred in a war cemetery in France. | Inter beat Juventus at the weekend.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: double r in «interred», «interring» (stress on -TER). Opposite: «disinter» (dig up), and the noun «interment». Do not confuse with «intern» (a trainee; or to imprison someone in wartime) or «inter-» with «intra-» (within: intranet).

part of speech: verb, past form of «interbreed» (interbreed, interbreeds, interbred, interbreeding)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (biology) Bred together: when two different kinds of animals or plants mate and have young. 2) (science) Had young with a different group, species or variety, mixing their genes.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on evolution and variation, scientists say Neanderthals and early modern humans interbred, so many people today carry a little Neanderthal DNA. Lions and tigers have interbred in zoos (ligers), and horses and donkeys have mules. Farmers have interbred plants and animals to get new varieties. Phrases: interbred with, have interbred.
examples from the lessons: Scientists found that Neanderthals and modern humans interbred long ago. | Horses and donkeys can be interbred to produce mules. | A liger is the young of a lion and tiger that interbred. | Wild wolves and dogs have sometimes interbred. | The farmer interbred two kinds of wheat to make a stronger one. | Species that have interbred share some genes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past tense and past participle are both «interbred» (like «bred»). Noun «interbreeding». Offspring of two different species, like mules, are often unable to have young themselves.

part of speech: noun (interment, interments); uncountable for the act, countable for one burial
meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Interment is the burying of a dead person's body in a grave or tomb. 2) (formal) An interment is one burial, the ceremony when a body is laid in the ground.
its sense in the lessons: A stiff, formal word heard at funerals, in newspapers, church notices and old stories; it tells the reader that someone has died and is being buried with respect. Phrases: «interment will follow», «private interment», «place of interment». In history lessons it appears with old graves and burial customs.
examples from the lessons: The interment took place in the village churchyard. | After the church service, the family went to the cemetery for the interment. | The notice said «Interment private, family only». | Archaeologists study the interment of ancient kings. | Grandad's interment was quiet and peaceful. | The Egyptians prepared bodies carefully before interment. | Flowers were laid on the grave after the interment.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: do not mix up «interment» (burial) with «internment» (locking people up, often in wartime) — one letter changes the meaning. Everyday word: burial. Not about «intern» (a trainee).

meaning for a pupil: 1) To intermingle is to mix together, so that the different parts are spread among each other. 2) When people intermingle, they mix and mingle in a group, talking with people they did not come with.
its sense in the lessons: Used in science for things that mix (smells, colours, liquids), in geography and history for peoples and cultures mixing, and in stories for crowds at a party. It tells the reader that things are no longer apart. Phrases: «intermingle with», «intermingled with».
examples from the lessons: The smells of bread and coffee intermingled in the kitchen. | At the party, the parents intermingled with the teachers. | In the river mouth, fresh water intermingles with salt water. | The two colours of paint intermingled into a swirl. | Many cultures intermingle in a big city like London or Toronto. | Laughter intermingled with the music. | At lunch the older and younger pupils intermingled on the field.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: intermingled, intermingling. Often with «with». A bit more formal than «mix» or «mingle»; means the same.

part of speech: noun (an intern, interns); verb (intern, interns, interned, interning)
meaning for a pupil: 1) An intern is a student or young person who works somewhere for a short time to learn the job, sometimes without pay. 2) (US) An intern is a young doctor who has just finished medical school and is training in a hospital. 3) To intern someone is to lock them up, usually in a camp, during a war, because they come from an enemy country.
its sense in the lessons: Everyday life and careers: «a summer intern», «an intern at the newspaper». In history lessons the verb is used for people held in camps in wartime (for example Japanese Americans in the Second World War). Phrases: «work as an intern», «an internship».
examples from the lessons: My cousin is an intern at a bank this summer. | The intern made tea and learned how the office works. | The young intern checked the patient's chart with the senior doctor. | She wants to be an intern at the zoo. | During the war, thousands of people were interned in camps. | The internship lasts six weeks. | The intern asked lots of good questions.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say «IN-tern» for the noun; the verb is often «in-TERN». The job is an «internship»; being locked up is «internment». Do not mix with «interment» (burial) or «internal» (inside).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Internationally means between or among different countries. 2) Internationally means all over the world, in many countries, not just one.
its sense in the lessons: Used in geography, news, sport and business: «known internationally», «internationally famous», «traded internationally». It tells the reader that something crosses borders. In science, units like the metre are agreed internationally.
examples from the lessons: She is an internationally famous singer. | The football match was shown internationally. | Scientists work together internationally to study the climate. | The metre is an internationally agreed unit. | This chocolate is sold internationally. | The charity helps children internationally. | Our school writes to pen pals internationally.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from «international» (+ -ly). Spelling: inter + national + ly, with «-ally». Opposite: nationally, locally.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Intertidal describes the strip of seashore that is under water at high tide and out in the air at low tide. 2) Intertidal plants and animals live in that strip and can survive both wet and dry times.
its sense in the lessons: A science and geography word for rock pools and beaches: «the intertidal zone». It tells the reader about creatures like crabs, limpets, barnacles and seaweed that cope with tides. Safety: tides come back in fast, so check tide times before exploring.
examples from the lessons: We studied the intertidal zone on our school trip to the beach. | Limpets cling to rocks in the intertidal area. | The intertidal zone is covered twice a day by the sea. | Barnacles are intertidal animals. | Rock pools form in the intertidal zone at low tide. | Intertidal creatures must survive heat, cold and waves. | Always check the tide before exploring intertidal rocks.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective only; not used for people. Built from «inter-» (between) + «tidal» (tides): between the high and low tide lines.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Intolerable means too bad, painful or annoying to put up with. 2) (formal) Intolerable behaviour is behaviour that will not be accepted at all.
its sense in the lessons: Used in stories for heat, noise, pain or unfairness that a character cannot bear; in school rules or news, «intolerable» means «will not be allowed». It tells the reader that a limit has been reached.
examples from the lessons: The heat in the tent was intolerable. | The noise from the building site became intolerable. | Bullying is intolerable at our school. | The pain in his tooth was almost intolerable. | The waiting felt intolerable. | The king's taxes were intolerable to the poor. | Living next to the motorway was intolerable for them.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: tolerable, bearable. Spelling ends «-able». Do not mix with «intolerant» (not accepting other people or a food).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Intolerant means not willing to accept people whose ideas, beliefs or ways are different from yours. 2) If you are intolerant of a food, your body cannot digest it well and it makes you feel ill. 3) Intolerant of something means unable to put up with it, like noise or cold.
its sense in the lessons: In citizenship and ethics lessons it names unkind, closed-minded attitudes; in health and science it is about foods: «lactose intolerant», «gluten intolerant». Phrases: «intolerant of», «be intolerant to».
examples from the lessons: My brother is lactose intolerant, so he drinks oat milk. | It is wrong to be intolerant of people from other religions. | Some plants are intolerant of frost. | The old man was intolerant of noise. | An intolerant person may refuse to listen to other views. | She found out she was gluten intolerant. | Our class talked about how to stand up to intolerant comments.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: intolerance. A food intolerance is not the same as an allergy: an allergy can be dangerous and fast; an intolerance usually upsets the tummy. Opposite: tolerant. Do not mix with «intolerable».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Intoxication is being drunk, or affected by alcohol or drugs so that you cannot think or move properly. 2) Intoxication can also mean being poisoned by a harmful substance. 3) (literary) Intoxication is a strong, exciting, dizzy feeling, as if you were drunk with joy.
its sense in the lessons: In health and safety lessons it names the danger of alcohol and drugs; in law and the news, «driving under intoxication»; in stories, «the intoxication of victory». It tells the reader that someone's mind is not clear.
examples from the lessons: Intoxication makes it dangerous to drive a car. | The doctor treated him for alcohol intoxication. | Water intoxication can happen if someone drinks far too much water too fast. | The team felt the intoxication of winning the cup. | Some plants can cause intoxication in pets. | Police tested the driver for intoxication. | Intoxication slows down a person's reactions.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: no «an». Verb: intoxicate; adjective: intoxicated (drunk, formal). Contains «toxic», meaning poisonous.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Intravenous means going into a vein, the tube that carries blood back to the heart. 2) An intravenous drip or injection gives medicine, food or fluid straight into the blood through a needle in a vein.
its sense in the lessons: A medical word heard in hospitals, on TV dramas and in science lessons about blood. It tells the reader that a patient needs medicine fast or cannot eat or drink. Phrases: «intravenous drip», «intravenous fluids», often shortened to «an IV».
examples from the lessons: The nurse gave her intravenous fluids. | He had an intravenous drip in his arm. | Intravenous medicine works quickly. | The patient was fed by intravenous feeding for a few days. | Doctors chose an intravenous antibiotic. | Intravenous means «into a vein». | The bag of intravenous fluid hung beside the bed.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Built from «intra-» (inside) + «venous» (of veins). Do not mix «intra-» (inside) with «inter-» (between). Short form: IV.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Intravenously means by putting something straight into a vein, usually with a needle or drip.
its sense in the lessons: Medical word: «given intravenously», «fed intravenously». In science and in hospital stories it tells the reader how medicine reaches the blood fast.
examples from the lessons: The medicine was given intravenously. | When she could not eat, she was fed intravenously. | Fluids were dripped intravenously into his arm. | Some vaccines are not given intravenously but into a muscle. | The vet gave the dog fluids intravenously. | Drugs given intravenously act quickly.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb of «intravenous». Opposite routes: by mouth (orally), into a muscle. Short: «by IV».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Intrinsically means by its own nature, in itself, not because of anything added from outside. 2) (formal) Intrinsically good or bad means good or bad deep down, in its very nature.
its sense in the lessons: A formal word used in ethics, exams and essays: «intrinsically valuable», «not intrinsically wrong». It tells the reader about the real nature of something, not its use or price. In maths a coin's intrinsic value is the metal, not the number on it.
examples from the lessons: Gold is not intrinsically useful, but people value it. | Playing games is not intrinsically bad. | Every person is intrinsically valuable. | The plan was intrinsically unfair. | Some things are intrinsically interesting, like volcanoes. | A paper banknote has almost no intrinsic value, but we agree it is worth money. | The problem is intrinsically hard.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: intrinsic. Opposite: extrinsically (from outside). Spelling: intrinsic + ally.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) An intro is an introduction, the start of a song, book, talk or video. 2) (informal) An intro is when you introduce one person to another.
its sense in the lessons: Clipped everyday talk: «the intro of the song», «skip the intro», «give me an intro». In school writing, use «introduction» in formal work. It tells the reader about the beginning part.
examples from the lessons: I love the guitar intro to that song. | Skip the intro and go to the game. | Can you give me an intro to your friend? | The video's intro was too long. | Write a short intro for your story. | The band played the intro twice.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Short for «introduction». Plural: intros. Informal; in essays write «introduction».

meaning for a pupil: 1) An invasive plant or animal spreads into a place where it does not belong and harms the plants and animals already living there. 2) An invasive illness, such as some cancers, spreads into other parts of the body. 3) An invasive medical test or operation goes inside the body, by cutting or putting something in. 4) Invasive questions or actions go too far into someone's private life.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography: «invasive species» like cane toads in Australia, grey squirrels in the UK, Japanese knotweed. In health: «non-invasive test». In everyday life: «invasive questions», privacy online. It tells the reader that something pushes in where it should not.
examples from the lessons: Cane toads are an invasive species in Australia. | Grey squirrels are invasive in Britain and push out red squirrels. | The doctor said the scan is non-invasive and will not hurt. | Asking how much money someone earns can feel invasive. | Japanese knotweed is an invasive plant that is hard to remove. | Invasive weeds choked the pond. | Some apps collect invasive amounts of data.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From the verb «invade». Opposite: non-invasive, native (for species). Pronounced in-VAY-siv.

part of speech: verb (invert, inverts, inverted, inverting); noun (an invert — rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To invert something is to turn it upside down. 2) To invert something is to swap it round so it goes the opposite way, back to front or in reverse order. 3) (maths) To invert a fraction is to turn it upside down, so 2/3 becomes 3/2.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, dividing by a fraction means «invert and multiply». In science, a lens can invert an image. In English grammar, questions invert the subject and verb («Is he…?»). «Inverted commas» are quotation marks (UK). It tells the reader that the order or direction has been flipped.
examples from the lessons: Invert the glass and the water will spill out. | To divide by 1/2, invert it and multiply by 2. | A pinhole camera inverts the picture. | In a question we invert «he is» to «is he». | Put the words in inverted commas. | The cake was inverted onto a plate. | Bats hang inverted from the cave roof.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular: inverted, inverting. Noun: inversion. «Inverted commas» (UK) = speech marks. Maths trap: inverting 4 (= 4/1) gives 1/4.

part of speech: verb form (-ing form of invest); noun (investing, uncountable)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (money) Investing is putting money into something, like a business, shares or property, hoping it will grow and bring back more money later. 2) Investing time or effort is spending it on something because you expect it to be worth it.
its sense in the lessons: Money lessons and adult life: «investing in shares», «investing for the future»; there is always a risk the money falls. Everyday: «investing time in practice». It tells the reader someone is giving now to gain later.
examples from the lessons: Mum is investing some money for my future. | Investing in shares can make or lose money. | He is investing a lot of time in learning the piano. | The council is investing in new playgrounds. | Investing early gives money more time to grow. | Our school is investing in new computers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Base verb: invest (invests, invested). Person: investor. Thing: investment. Prepositions: «invest in». Maths: if you invest £100 and it grows by 10%, you have £110.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (money) An investor is a person or company that puts money into a business, shares or property, hoping to make a profit.
its sense in the lessons: Money and business lessons, news and TV shows like «Dragons' Den» or «Shark Tank»: inventors ask investors for money. It tells the reader who is paying in and expects a share of profits.
examples from the lessons: The investor gave the company money to build a factory. | Investors hope their shares go up in value. | She pitched her idea to three investors. | The investor lost money when the shop closed. | Small investors put in a few pounds each. | Investors met to hear about the new app.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: investors. Spelling ends «-or». Related: invest, investment.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Invisibly means in a way that cannot be seen. 2) Invisibly can mean without people noticing, quietly in the background.
its sense in the lessons: Science: air and gases move invisibly; germs spread invisibly. Stories: a ghost or a spy moves invisibly. Everyday: helpers who work invisibly.
examples from the lessons: Germs spread invisibly from hand to hand. | The gas leaked invisibly into the room. | The magician's thread was invisibly thin. | Volunteers work invisibly to keep the park clean. | Radio waves travel invisibly through the air. | The cat slipped invisibly through the shadows.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb of «invisible» (-ible → -ibly). Opposite: visibly.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (church) An invocation is a prayer asking God, or in some religions a saint or spirit, for help or blessing, often at the start of a service. 2) An invocation is calling on something or someone for help or as an authority, like invoking a law. 3) (stories) In magic stories, an invocation is a spell said to call up a spirit.
its sense in the lessons: Church and religion lessons: the opening prayer of a service; old poems begin with an invocation to the Muse. Law and formal speech: «invocation of a rule». Fantasy stories: a wizard's invocation.
examples from the lessons: The service began with an invocation. | The minister said a short invocation before the meal. | Old Greek poems start with an invocation to the Muse. | The wizard spoke an invocation to call the dragon. | The invocation asked God to bless the new school. | The invocation of the rule ended the argument.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: invoke. Plural: invocations. Pronounced in-voh-KAY-shun.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To invoke a law, rule or right is to use it or point to it to support what you do. 2) (church) To invoke God or a saint is to pray and call on them for help. 3) To invoke a name or idea is to mention it to make people feel or remember something. 4) (computing) To invoke a program or function is to start it running.
its sense in the lessons: Formal and law language: «invoke a rule», «invoke the right to stay silent». In religion: «invoke God's help». In coding lessons: «invoke a function». In stories: «invoke spirits».
examples from the lessons: The captain invoked the rule that everyone must wear a helmet. | The priest invoked God's blessing. | The speech invoked the memory of the heroes. | Call the function to invoke it. | He invoked his right to see a lawyer. | The witch tried to invoke a spirit. | Mentioning the trip invoked happy memories.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular: invoked, invoking. Noun: invocation. Trap: «invoke» (call on) is different from «evoke» (bring a feeling to mind), though people mix them.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Involuntarily means without meaning to, without choosing to, as when your body does something by itself. 2) Involuntarily can mean against your will, when someone else forces it.
its sense in the lessons: Science: reflexes like blinking or sneezing happen involuntarily; the heart beats involuntarily. Stories: a character shivers or gasps involuntarily. Formal/adult: «involuntarily made redundant».
examples from the lessons: She blinked involuntarily when the ball came near. | He shivered involuntarily in the cold wind. | Your heart beats involuntarily, even when you sleep. | I laughed involuntarily at the silly face. | Some workers were involuntarily moved to another office. | He flinched involuntarily at the loud bang.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: involuntary. Opposite: voluntarily. Spelling: in + voluntar + ily.

meaning for a pupil: 1) IQ stands for «intelligence quotient», a score from a special test that tries to measure some kinds of thinking skills, like puzzles and patterns. The average score is set at 100.
its sense in the lessons: Heard in everyday talk and news: «a high IQ», «an IQ test». It tells the reader someone is called clever. Many scientists say an IQ score measures only some skills, not kindness, creativity or wisdom, and that scores can change with schooling.
examples from the lessons: The test gave an IQ score of 105. | An average IQ is about 100. | Having a high IQ does not make you a good friend. | Some people say IQ tests miss many kinds of talent. | She joked that her cat has a high IQ. | The doctor used an IQ test as one of many checks.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Written in capitals: IQ; said «eye-queue». «An IQ» (because it starts with a vowel sound). Myth: IQ is not fixed for life and is not the only kind of intelligence.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (a name) The Iroquois are a group of Native American nations, also called the Haudenosaunee, from what is now New York State and parts of Canada. 2) (a name) Iroquois also names their languages and their league of nations.
its sense in the lessons: History and social studies in the USA and Canada: the Iroquois Confederacy joined Mohawk, Oneida, Onondaga, Cayuga, Seneca and later Tuscarora nations. They lived in longhouses and grew corn, beans and squash. Many people today prefer their own name, Haudenosaunee.
examples from the lessons: The Iroquois lived in long wooden longhouses. | The Iroquois Confederacy joined six nations. | We read about the Iroquois in social studies. | The Iroquois grew corn, beans and squash, called the Three Sisters. | Many Iroquois people live in New York State and Ontario today. | The Haudenosaunee are also known as the Iroquois.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital letter: Iroquois. The «s» is silent: «IR-uh-kwoy». Plural is the same: the Iroquois. Their own name: Haudenosaunee.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) To irradiate something is to send rays, such as X-rays, gamma rays or ultraviolet light, onto or through it. 2) To irradiate food is to treat it with rays to kill germs so it keeps longer. 3) (literary) To irradiate is to light something up brightly.
its sense in the lessons: Science lessons about radiation and light; health: doctors irradiate cancer cells to kill them; food safety. In stories: «a smile irradiated her face». It tells the reader rays or light are shining on something.
examples from the lessons: Doctors irradiate tumours to destroy them. | Some spices are irradiated to kill germs. | The sun irradiates the Earth with light. | The scientist irradiated the seeds to see if they changed. | Sunlight irradiated the whole valley. | Irradiated food is not radioactive.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular: irradiated. Noun: irradiation. Myth: irradiated food does not become radioactive. Contains «radiate» (to send out rays).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Irredeemable means so bad that it cannot be saved, fixed or made better. 2) (money) An irredeemable voucher or bond cannot be swapped back for money.
its sense in the lessons: Formal word in stories and essays: «an irredeemable villain», «an irredeemable mess». In ethics talk, many people believe no person is truly irredeemable. Money: some vouchers are irredeemable for cash.
examples from the lessons: The villain in the story seemed irredeemable. | The burnt cake was irredeemable. | Our teacher said no pupil is irredeemable. | The gift card is irredeemable for cash. | After the storm, the old shed was irredeemable. | He made an irredeemable mistake.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Built from ir- (not) + redeem (save, buy back) + -able. Opposite: redeemable. Double «r» and double «e».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Irreparable means so badly damaged or harmed that it cannot be repaired or put right.
its sense in the lessons: Used for damage, harm, loss: «irreparable damage», «irreparable harm». In science and geography: damage to nature; in stories: a broken friendship. It tells the reader there is no going back.
examples from the lessons: The flood did irreparable damage to the old books. | Cutting down the forest caused irreparable harm. | The vase was irreparable after it fell. | Telling the secret did irreparable damage to their friendship. | Losing the old photos was an irreparable loss. | The engine was irreparable, so they bought a new one.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say «ih-REP-er-uh-bul», stress on «REP», not «repair-able». Opposite: reparable (rare), repairable.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Irrevocably means in a way that can never be changed, cancelled or taken back.
its sense in the lessons: Formal word in stories, history and law: «changed irrevocably», «irrevocably lost». It tells the reader that a moment is final.
examples from the lessons: The invention of the internet irrevocably changed the world. | Once the email was sent, it was irrevocably gone. | The old village was irrevocably lost under the new lake. | Their lives were irrevocably changed by the war. | The decision is irrevocably made. | Some species have been irrevocably wiped out.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: irrevocable (can't be revoked). Say «ih-REV-uh-kuh-blee». Spelling: double «r».

meaning for a pupil: 1) To irrigate land or crops is to bring water to them through pipes, channels or sprinklers so plants can grow. 2) (medical) To irrigate a wound or eye is to wash it out with a steady flow of water or liquid.
its sense in the lessons: Geography and science: farmers irrigate dry land; ancient Egyptians irrigated with the Nile. Health and first aid: irrigate an eye with clean water if something gets in it. It tells the reader water is being brought on purpose.
examples from the lessons: Farmers irrigate their fields in dry summers. | The ancient Egyptians irrigated land with water from the Nile. | Sprinklers irrigate the school field. | The nurse irrigated the cut with salt water. | Irrigate your eye with clean water if sand gets in it. | Canals were dug to irrigate the desert. | Irrigated crops grow even when it does not rain.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular: irrigated. Noun: irrigation. Double «r».

meaning for a pupil: 1) An islander is a person who lives on an island, or was born on one.
its sense in the lessons: Geography and stories: Pacific Islanders, Torres Strait Islanders in Australia, Channel Islanders, people of the Scottish islands. It tells the reader where someone lives and often about ferries, fishing and the sea.
examples from the lessons: The islanders take the ferry to the mainland. | Torres Strait Islanders are one of Australia's First Peoples. | The islanders welcomed the visitors. | She is a proud islander from Orkney. | The islanders fish and grow vegetables. | Pacific Islanders sailed great distances in canoes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Silent «s»: «EYE-lan-der». Plural: islanders. Capital letter in names like «Torres Strait Islander», «Pacific Islander».

meaning for a pupil: 1) An issuer is a person, company or government that gives out something official, like cards, tickets, passports, money or shares.
its sense in the lessons: Money and adult life: «the card issuer» is the bank behind a credit card; the government is the issuer of coins and passports. Formal word, used in instructions and small print.
examples from the lessons: The bank is the issuer of my mum's debit card. | Contact the card issuer if your card is lost. | The government is the issuer of passports. | The Royal Mint is the issuer of British coins. | The issuer of the gift card can tell you the balance. | The ticket issuer printed the date on each ticket.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From the verb «issue» (give out). Spelling: double «s».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Itinerant means travelling from place to place, often for work, instead of living in one place. 2) (formal) An itinerant is a person who travels about like this.
its sense in the lessons: History and stories: itinerant preachers, pedlars, tinkers, farm workers who moved with the harvest, travelling teachers or musicians. It tells the reader a person has no fixed home or moves for work.
examples from the lessons: An itinerant preacher rode from village to village. | Itinerant workers moved from farm to farm to pick fruit. | The itinerant musician played in a different town each night. | In old times, itinerant pedlars sold pots and ribbons. | The circus had an itinerant life. | Some teachers are itinerant and visit several schools.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say «eye-TIN-er-unt» or «ih-TIN-er-unt». Related: itinerary (a travel plan).

part of speech: noun (an IV, IVs); Roman numeral IV
meaning for a pupil: 1) IV is the Roman numeral for 4 (one before five: I before V). 2) (medical) An IV is a drip that gives fluid or medicine into a vein; short for «intravenous». 3) IV is used in names of kings, queens and popes for «the Fourth», like Henry IV.
its sense in the lessons: Maths and history: Roman numerals on clocks, chapters and kings' names. Hospitals and TV: «put on an IV». It tells the reader either a number (4) or a medical drip.
examples from the lessons: IV means 4 in Roman numerals. | King Henry IV ruled England. | The clock showed IV instead of 4. | The nurse put an IV in his arm. | Chapter IV begins on page 30. | VI is 6, but IV is 4, because the smaller number comes first.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Maths: I before V means subtract, so IV = 5 − 1 = 4; VI = 5 + 1 = 6. Some clocks write IIII. Medical «an IV» (vowel sound: «eye-vee»). Read Henry IV as «Henry the Fourth».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (old) Izzard is an old name for the letter Z, used in parts of Britain and America long ago. 2) (a name) Izzard is also a surname.
its sense in the lessons: Found in old books and word puzzles: «from A to izzard» meant «from start to finish», like «from A to Z». Not used today in everyday English; the letter is now called «zed» (UK, Australia, Canada, Ireland, New Zealand) or «zee» (USA).
examples from the lessons: In old books, «from A to izzard» means from beginning to end. | Izzard is an old name for the letter Z. | Today we say «zed» or «zee», not izzard. | The puzzle asked for the old name of Z: izzard. | He knew the subject from A to izzard.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Old-fashioned word; do not use it in your spelling of the alphabet today. As a surname it is a name, nothing more.

part of speech: verb (jeer, jeers, jeered, jeering); noun (a jeer, jeers)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To jeer is to shout or laugh at someone in a rude, mocking way to show you do not like them. 2) A jeer is a rude, mocking shout or remark.
its sense in the lessons: Stories and sport: crowds jeer at the other team or the referee. Citizenship and kindness lessons: jeering is a kind of bullying. It tells the reader that people are being unkind as a group. Phrases: «jeer at», «boos and jeers».
examples from the lessons: The crowd jeered at the referee. | It is unkind to jeer at someone who falls over. | The boos and jeers stopped when the band started. | The bullies jeered as he walked past. | The player ignored the jeers and scored. | Nobody should jeer at someone's clothes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular: jeered. Often with «at». Similar: mock, taunt, boo. Opposite: cheer.

part of speech: verb form (-ing form of jeer); adjective (jeering); noun (jeering, uncountable)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Jeering is shouting or laughing at someone in a rude, mocking way. 2) A jeering voice or crowd mocks someone.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, sport reports and kindness lessons. It tells the reader a crowd or person is mocking. Phrases: «jeering crowd», «a jeering laugh».
examples from the lessons: The jeering crowd made the player angry. | Stop jeering at your sister. | We heard jeering from the back of the hall. | His jeering laugh hurt her feelings. | The jeering stopped when the teacher came in. | Fans were warned that jeering is not allowed.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Base verb: jeer. Opposite: cheering.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (church) A Jesuit is a member of the Society of Jesus, a Roman Catholic order of priests and brothers founded by Saint Ignatius of Loyola in 1540. 2) (old, insult) In the past, «jesuitical» was used as an unfair insult for someone thought to be sly in argument.
its sense in the lessons: Religion and history lessons: Jesuits are known for schools and universities, missions around the world and science. Pope Francis was a Jesuit. Many schools and colleges in the USA, Ireland and Australia are Jesuit schools.
examples from the lessons: He goes to a Jesuit school. | The Jesuits were founded by Saint Ignatius of Loyola. | Jesuit missionaries travelled to China and South America. | Pope Francis was the first Jesuit pope. | Jesuit priests often work as teachers. | Some Jesuits were also scientists and astronomers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital letter: Jesuit. Plural: Jesuits. Say «JEZ-yoo-it». The old insult sense is unfair; avoid it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To jettison something is to throw it out of a ship, plane or spacecraft to make it lighter, often in an emergency. 2) To jettison an idea or plan is to drop it or give it up because it is not useful.
its sense in the lessons: Science and space lessons: rockets jettison empty fuel tanks. Stories: sailors jettison cargo in a storm. Everyday and formal: «jettison the plan».
examples from the lessons: The rocket jettisoned its empty boosters. | The sailors jettisoned the cargo to stop the ship sinking. | The pilot jettisoned fuel before landing. | We jettisoned our first idea and started again. | The balloonists jettisoned sandbags to rise higher. | The company jettisoned the old logo.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular: jettisoned (one «n»). Say «JET-ih-sun». Similar: dump, discard, ditch.

part of speech: noun (a jig, jigs); verb (jig, jigs, jigged, jigging)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A jig is a fast, lively folk dance, especially from Ireland and Scotland, or the music for it. 2) To jig is to dance or bounce up and down in a quick, happy way. 3) A jig is a tool that holds a piece of wood or metal in place while you cut or drill it. 4) (fishing) A jig is a type of fishing lure that is jerked up and down.
its sense in the lessons: Music and PE: Irish dancing and the Irish jig; St Patrick's Day. Design and technology: a jig for cutting. Phrases: «the jig is up» (informal: the trick has been found out).
examples from the lessons: We learned an Irish jig in PE. | The fiddler played a lively jig. | The children jigged about with excitement. | Dad used a jig to cut all the pieces the same size. | «The jig is up!» said the detective. | My uncle caught a fish with a jig. | She did a little jig when she won.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: jig, jigged, jigging (double «g»). «The jig is up» (US) / «the game is up» (UK) means a secret plan is discovered.

part of speech: noun (a jinx, jinxes); verb (jinx, jinxes, jinxed, jinxing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A jinx is a person or thing that people believe brings bad luck. 2) To jinx something is to bring bad luck to it, often (people joke) by talking about it too early. 3) (game) «Jinx!» is called out in a children's game when two people say the same word at the same time.
its sense in the lessons: Everyday talk and sport: «Don't say we'll win, you'll jinx it!» It tells the reader about superstition. Science: there is no proof that jinxes are real; it is a belief and a joke.
examples from the lessons: Don't say it's going to be sunny, you'll jinx it! | He thinks the number 13 is a jinx. | «Jinx!» we both shouted at once. | The team felt jinxed after losing five games. | Some sailors believed a cat on board was a jinx. | Saying the word does not really jinx anything.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: jinxes; verb forms jinxed, jinxing. It is a superstition, not a fact.

part of speech: noun (a jitter, the jitters); verb (jitter, jitters, jittered, jittering)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) The jitters are a nervous, shaky feeling, especially before something important. 2) To jitter is to make small, quick, shaky movements. 3) (computing) Jitter is small, unwanted wobbles in a signal or picture, or in the timing of data.
its sense in the lessons: Everyday: «pre-match jitters», «first-day jitters», «exam jitters». Science and computing: jitter in a video or a game connection. It tells the reader someone is nervous or something is shaking.
examples from the lessons: I had the jitters before my piano exam. | First-day jitters are normal at a new school. | The picture on the screen began to jitter. | Too much fizzy drink gives him the jitters. | The online game lagged because of jitter. | Her hands jittered as she held the trophy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually «the jitters» (plural, informal). Adjective: jittery (nervous). Regular verb.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Jocular means joking, funny and playful in a friendly way.
its sense in the lessons: Formal word in stories and reports: «a jocular remark», «a jocular uncle». It tells the reader someone is joking, not serious or nasty.
examples from the lessons: Grandpa was in a jocular mood at dinner. | The headteacher made a jocular comment about the rain. | His jocular manner made everyone relax. | It was a jocular letter full of puns. | She answered in a jocular tone. | The jocular coach always told jokes at practice.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say «JOK-yoo-ler». Formal; everyday words: jokey, playful, funny. Related: joke, jocularity.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Journalistic means to do with journalism, the work of collecting and writing the news for newspapers, websites, radio or TV. 2) Journalistic writing is written in the style of news: clear, short and based on facts.
its sense in the lessons: English and media lessons: writing a newspaper report in journalistic style (headline, who, what, when, where, why). Citizenship: journalistic rules like checking facts and hearing both sides.
examples from the lessons: We wrote a journalistic report on the school fair. | Journalistic writing uses short paragraphs. | Checking facts is an important journalistic rule. | She won a prize for journalistic work. | The article was journalistic, not a story. | Good journalistic practice means asking both sides.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «journalism», «journalist». Spelling: journal + ist + ic.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) Jovian means to do with the planet Jupiter. 2) (science) Jovian planets are the giant gas planets like Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune. 3) (old, literary) Jovian means like the Roman god Jupiter (Jove): grand, jolly and powerful.
its sense in the lessons: Space science: «Jovian moons» (Io, Europa, Ganymede, Callisto), «Jovian planets». Science fiction stories: «a Jovian» is an imagined being from Jupiter (not real).
examples from the lessons: Ganymede is the biggest Jovian moon. | The Jovian planets are huge and made mostly of gas. | Scientists study Jovian storms like the Great Red Spot. | Europa is a Jovian moon that may have an ocean under its ice. | In the old story, a Jovian visitor landed on Earth. | The probe sent back Jovian photos.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually with a capital: Jovian. From «Jove», another name for Jupiter. No real living beings are known on Jupiter.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Judicious means wise and sensible, showing good judgement.
its sense in the lessons: Formal word in exams, reports and stories: «a judicious choice», «judicious use of water». It tells the reader someone thought carefully before acting.
examples from the lessons: Making a judicious choice, she saved half her pocket money. | The judicious use of water helps in a drought. | It was judicious to wait until the storm passed. | The captain made a judicious decision. | A judicious editor cut the boring parts. | Use glue judiciously, not too much.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; everyday: wise, sensible. Do not mix with «judicial» (to do with judges and courts). Spelling ends «-cious».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Jumbo means very large, bigger than usual. 2) A jumbo, or jumbo jet, is a very big passenger plane, like the Boeing 747. 3) (a name) Jumbo was a famous huge elephant in the 1800s, shown at London Zoo and in an American circus.
its sense in the lessons: Everyday shopping: «jumbo pack», «jumbo crayons», «jumbo hot dog». Travel: «a jumbo jet». It tells the reader something is extra big.
examples from the lessons: We bought a jumbo pack of crayons. | The jumbo jet carried over 400 people. | He ate a jumbo hot dog at the fair. | Jumbo the elephant was famous long ago. | Our class made a jumbo birthday card. | The shop sells jumbo bags of popcorn.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: jumbos. Informal, mostly in adverts and talk. The word «jumbo» for big things comes from the elephant's name.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (law) A juror is one of the ordinary adult citizens on a jury, the group who listen to a trial in court and decide if the accused person is guilty or not guilty.
its sense in the lessons: Citizenship and law lessons: in the UK, the USA, Canada, Australia, New Zealand and Ireland, adults can be called to be jurors; they must be fair and listen to the evidence. It tells the reader about a trial.
examples from the lessons: Twelve jurors listened to the trial. | The juror took notes during the evidence. | Jurors must not talk about the case outside court. | Mum was called to be a juror. | The jurors decided the man was not guilty. | Each juror promised to be fair.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: jurors. The group is a «jury». Spelling ends «-or». Jurors are ordinary people, not lawyers.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Justly means fairly, in a way that is right and treats people equally. 2) Justly means rightly, with good reason, as in «justly proud».
its sense in the lessons: Ethics, citizenship and stories: «treat people justly», «justly punished», «justly famous». It tells the reader something is fair or deserved.
examples from the lessons: The judge treated everyone justly. | She was justly proud of her painting. | A good leader rules justly. | He was justly rewarded for his hard work. | The city is justly famous for its parks. | The teacher shared the sweets justly.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «just» (fair). Opposite: unjustly. Do not confuse with «just» meaning «only» or «a moment ago».

part of speech: noun (a Kazak, Kazaks; a kazak rug); adjective (Kazak)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (a name) Kazak is another spelling of Kazakh, a person from Kazakhstan or of the Kazakh people, or their language. 2) A Kazak (also Kazakh) rug is a thick, colourful woollen carpet with bold patterns, first made in the Caucasus region.
its sense in the lessons: Geography: the Kazakh people live mainly in Kazakhstan in Central Asia. Art and homes: «a Kazak rug». The usual modern spelling for the people is «Kazakh».
examples from the lessons: The Kazak people have a long history of horse riding. | Kazakhstan is the home of the Kazakh people. | Grandma has a red Kazak rug. | Many Kazaks speak both Kazakh and Russian. | The Kazak rug has bold geometric patterns. | We found Kazakhstan on the map in Central Asia.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital letter for the people. Modern spelling: Kazakh. Do not mix with «Cossack».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Keenly means eagerly, with a lot of interest. 2) Keenly means very strongly or deeply, as in «keenly felt». 3) Keenly means sharply and carefully, as in «watched keenly».
its sense in the lessons: Stories and reports: «keenly awaited», «keenly interested», «a keenly fought match». It tells the reader that feelings or attention are strong.
examples from the lessons: The children waited keenly for the results. | She keenly felt the loss of her dog. | The owl watched the field keenly. | It was a keenly fought football final. | He is keenly interested in dinosaurs. | The new book was keenly awaited.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «keen» (eager, sharp). «Keenly» goes before or after the verb.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A ketch is a sailing boat with two masts, a taller one at the front and a shorter one near the back.
its sense in the lessons: Stories about the sea, history and sailing lessons. It tells the reader what kind of boat is used. Not to be confused with old dialect «ketch» for «catch».
examples from the lessons: They sailed round the coast in a ketch. | A ketch has two masts. | The old fishing ketch was painted blue. | The pirates chased a small ketch. | We visited a ketch in the harbour museum. | The ketch caught the wind and sped away.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: ketches. In some old dialect speech, «ketch» means «catch» («ketch that ball») — that is not standard English.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Khaki is a dull yellow-brown or greenish-brown colour. 2) Khaki is a strong cotton cloth of this colour, used for army uniforms. 3) (US) Khakis are trousers made of this cloth.
its sense in the lessons: Art and clothes: «khaki shorts», «khaki trousers». History: soldiers in the First World War wore khaki so they were harder to see. It tells the reader the colour or kind of clothes.
examples from the lessons: Soldiers wore khaki uniforms. | Dad wore his khaki shorts on holiday. | Mix brown and green to make khaki. | He bought a pair of khakis for school. | Khaki is hard to spot among dry grass. | The explorer wore a khaki hat.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say «KAH-kee» (UK, Australia) or «KAK-ee» (US). Spelling: k-h-a-k-i. The word comes from Hindi/Urdu for «dust-coloured».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (a name) The Khanty are an Indigenous people who live in western Siberia, in Russia, near the Ob River. 2) (a name) Khanty is also the name of their language, related to Hungarian.
its sense in the lessons: Geography and culture lessons about peoples of the far north: many Khanty traditionally herd reindeer, fish and hunt. Their land is in the Khanty-Mansi region of Russia.
examples from the lessons: The Khanty live in western Siberia. | Some Khanty families still herd reindeer. | The Khanty language is distantly related to Hungarian. | The Khanty catch fish in the cold rivers. | We read a Khanty folk tale in class. | Oil drilling has changed Khanty land.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital letter: Khanty. Plural the same: the Khanty. Pronounced «KHAN-tee».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A kicker is a player who kicks the ball, especially in American football or rugby, to score points or kick it far. 2) (informal) The kicker is a surprising twist or extra fact at the end, often an unpleasant one. 3) (informal) A kicker is a person or animal that kicks.
its sense in the lessons: Sport: «the team's kicker», «goal kicker» in rugby and Australian football. Everyday: «And here's the kicker…» introduces a surprise. Stories: a donkey that is a kicker.
examples from the lessons: The kicker scored the winning goal in the last second. | The rugby team's best kicker took the conversion. | The trip was cancelled, and the kicker was we'd already packed. | Watch out, that horse is a kicker. | And here's the kicker: the treasure was fake! | The kicker practises every day.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: kickers. «The kicker» meaning «the surprising part» is informal.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) A killjoy is a person who spoils other people's fun, often by being grumpy or too strict.
its sense in the lessons: Everyday talk and stories: «Don't be such a killjoy!» It tells the reader someone is stopping fun, though sometimes the «killjoy» is just being sensible about safety.
examples from the lessons: Don't be a killjoy, come and play! | My brother called me a killjoy when I said it was bedtime. | The killjoy turned the music off. | He's not a killjoy, he's just worried about safety. | The old caretaker was a killjoy about ball games. | Nobody likes to be called a killjoy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: killjoys. Informal. Similar: spoilsport, wet blanket.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A kilt is a knee-length pleated skirt, usually of tartan cloth, worn traditionally by men and boys in Scotland, and also in Ireland, as part of Highland dress. 2) A kilt is a similar pleated skirt worn by girls or women.
its sense in the lessons: Culture and history: Scottish weddings, Highland games, bagpipers, Burns Night. It tells the reader about Scottish tradition. Each tartan pattern is often linked to a clan (family).
examples from the lessons: He wore a kilt to his cousin's wedding. | The piper wore a kilt and played the bagpipes. | Each clan has its own tartan for its kilt. | At the Highland Games, the strongmen wore kilts. | Her school uniform has a tartan kilt. | A kilt has deep pleats at the back.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: kilts. Men wearing kilts is normal in Scottish tradition; it is not a dress. A small bag worn in front is a «sporran».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (Scotland) A kirk is a church. 2) (Scotland, church) The Kirk is the Church of Scotland, the main Presbyterian church there. 3) (a name) Kirk is also a first name or surname, like Captain Kirk in «Star Trek».
its sense in the lessons: Scottish stories, songs and place names: «the village kirk», «Kirkcaldy», «Falkirk». Religion lessons: the Church of Scotland is called the Kirk. It tells the reader the setting is Scotland or northern England.
examples from the lessons: The family walked to the kirk on Sunday. | The Kirk is the Church of Scotland. | The old kirk had a stone bell tower. | Many Scottish towns have «kirk» in their name, like Falkirk. | They were married in the village kirk. | Captain Kirk is a character in Star Trek.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Scottish and northern English word; in standard English say «church». Capital «K» for the Church of Scotland and for the name.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A knighthood is the title and honour of being a knight, given in the UK by the king or queen to people for great service, so a man is called «Sir» (a woman gets a damehood, «Dame»). 2) (history) In the Middle Ages, knighthood was the rank of a knight, a trained soldier on horseback who served a lord.
its sense in the lessons: History: knights, castles, chivalry, being knighted with a sword touch on the shoulder. Today: famous people get knighthoods for work in sport, science, music or charity (for example Sir David Attenborough).
examples from the lessons: The famous scientist received a knighthood. | With his knighthood, he became Sir Tom. | In the Middle Ages, a squire trained for years to earn knighthood. | The king gave him a knighthood for bravery. | A woman gets a damehood, not a knighthood. | Knighthood was linked to rules of chivalry.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: knighthoods. Silent «k»: «NITE-hood». Verb: to knight someone.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Knowledgeable means knowing a lot about something, or about many things.
its sense in the lessons: School and everyday life: «a knowledgeable guide», «knowledgeable about dinosaurs». It tells the reader whom to ask. Phrase: «knowledgeable about».
examples from the lessons: Our museum guide was very knowledgeable. | She is knowledgeable about birds. | Ask Grandpa, he is knowledgeable about trains. | A knowledgeable shop assistant helped us. | He became knowledgeable by reading every day. | The quiz team was knowledgeable about history.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: keep the «e» after «g»: knowledge + able = knowledgeable. Silent «k». Say «NOL-ij-uh-bul».

part of speech: noun (a kohlrabi, kohlrabis; kohlrabi, uncountable as food)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Kohlrabi is a vegetable of the cabbage family with a round, swollen stem that grows just above the ground; you can eat it raw or cooked.
its sense in the lessons: Food, gardening and science lessons: kohlrabi is green or purple, tastes like mild cabbage or broccoli stem. It tells the reader about vegetables and healthy eating.
examples from the lessons: Kohlrabi looks a bit like a little alien. | We grew kohlrabi in the school garden. | Raw kohlrabi is crunchy and sweet. | Mum added kohlrabi to the soup. | Kohlrabi can be green or purple. | Kohlrabi is related to cabbage and broccoli.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say «kole-RAH-bee». Plural: kohlrabis or kohlrabi. From German «Kohl» (cabbage) + «Rübe» (turnip).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) kW stands for kilowatt, a unit of power equal to 1,000 watts. 2) kWh stands for kilowatt-hour, a unit of energy used on electricity bills.
its sense in the lessons: Science and everyday life: kettles, heaters and car engines are measured in kW; electricity bills count kWh. It tells the reader how much power a machine uses.
examples from the lessons: The kettle uses about 2 kW. | A small heater may be 1 kW. | Our electricity bill shows we used 300 kWh. | The electric car's motor is 150 kW. | 1 kW = 1,000 watts. | A 2 kW heater for 3 hours uses 6 kWh.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Correct writing: small «k», capital «W» (kW), because the watt is named after James Watt. Maths: kW × hours = kWh; e.g. 2 kW for 3 hours = 6 kWh. Do not mix kW (power) with kWh (energy).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (Australia) A kylie is a boomerang, especially a non-returning hunting boomerang, a curved throwing stick made by Aboriginal Australians. 2) (a name) Kylie is a girl's name, like the Australian singer Kylie Minogue.
its sense in the lessons: Australian history and culture: Aboriginal hunting tools. In everyday life it is most often heard as a first name.
examples from the lessons: The kylie spun through the air. | Aboriginal hunters used a kylie to hunt animals. | A kylie does not always come back like a returning boomerang. | We saw an old kylie at the museum. | Kylie is a popular name in Australia. | The kylie was carved from hard wood.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a name it has a capital: Kylie. The word comes from a Western Australian Aboriginal language.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To lacerate skin or flesh is to cut or tear it badly, leaving a jagged wound. 2) (literary) To lacerate someone's feelings is to hurt them deeply.
its sense in the lessons: First aid and health: «a lacerated hand», a laceration needs cleaning and maybe stitches. Stories and news reports about accidents. Formal word.
examples from the lessons: He lacerated his knee on the sharp rocks. | Broken glass can lacerate your feet. | The nurse cleaned the lacerated skin. | The thorns lacerated her arms. | The harsh words lacerated his feelings. | Wear gloves so the wire does not lacerate your hands.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular: lacerated. Noun: laceration (a deep cut). Say «LASS-er-ate».

part of speech: noun (lacquer, lacquers); verb (lacquer, lacquers, lacquered, lacquering)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Lacquer is a clear or coloured liquid that dries to a hard, shiny coat on wood or metal. 2) To lacquer something is to cover it with lacquer. 3) (UK, old) Hair lacquer is hairspray.
its sense in the lessons: Art and design and technology: lacquered boxes, especially Chinese and Japanese art. Everyday: furniture, nail varnish. It tells the reader something is shiny and protected.
examples from the lessons: The box was covered in red lacquer. | Japanese lacquer bowls are very beautiful. | Dad lacquered the wooden table. | Lacquer makes wood shiny and protects it. | The lacquer took a day to dry. | Open a window when using lacquer, because it smells strong.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say «LACK-er». Spelling: l-a-c-q-u-e-r. Safety: lacquer fumes can be harmful and it can burn.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) Lactase is an enzyme, a natural chemical in the body, that breaks down lactose, the sugar in milk, so it can be digested.
its sense in the lessons: Science and health lessons: people without enough lactase are lactose intolerant and may get tummy aches from milk. Lactase drops or pills can help. It tells the reader about digestion.
examples from the lessons: Lactase breaks down the sugar in milk. | People who make little lactase may get tummy aches from milk. | Babies make lots of lactase to digest their milk. | You can buy milk with lactase already added. | Many adults around the world make less lactase as they grow up. | Lactase is an enzyme in the small intestine.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: lactase (the enzyme, «-ase») vs lactose (the milk sugar, «-ose»). Enzyme names often end «-ase».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (religion) A lama is a teacher or monk in Tibetan Buddhism. 2) (a name) The Dalai Lama is the most famous lama, a spiritual leader of Tibetan Buddhists.
its sense in the lessons: Religion lessons: Tibetan Buddhism, monasteries, prayer wheels, Lhasa. Buddhists believe a lama guides people on the path to wisdom and kindness.
examples from the lessons: The lama taught the young monks. | The Dalai Lama is a well-known Buddhist leader. | Lamas live and study in monasteries in Tibet. | The lama spoke about kindness and peace. | Visitors bowed to the old lama. | A lama may wear red and yellow robes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Homophone trap: «lama» (Buddhist teacher, one «l») vs «llama» (the woolly animal from South America, double «l»).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Lanky means tall and thin in an awkward, long-legged way. 2) Lanky hair is long, straight and limp.
its sense in the lessons: Stories and descriptions of characters: «a lanky teenager», «lanky legs». It tells the reader what someone looks like; it can be a bit teasing, so be kind.
examples from the lessons: My lanky cousin can reach the top shelf. | The lanky boy ran with long strides. | Baby giraffes have lanky legs. | He grew lanky over the summer. | She is the lankiest girl in the class. | His hair was lanky after the swim.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative: lankier, lankiest (y → i). Commenting on someone's body can hurt; use it carefully.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A lanyard is a cord or strap worn round the neck to hold an ID card, keys or a whistle. 2) (sailing) A lanyard is a short rope on a ship used for tying or holding things.
its sense in the lessons: School and work: staff and visitors wear lanyards with ID badges; PE teachers have whistles on lanyards. Sailing stories. It tells the reader who someone is or what they carry.
examples from the lessons: The teacher wore her ID badge on a lanyard. | Visitors must wear a red lanyard. | The coach's whistle hung on a lanyard. | Sailors tied the bucket with a lanyard. | I keep my house key on a lanyard. | Our school trip lanyards had our names on them.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: lanyards. Spelling: l-a-n-y-a-r-d.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A lapdog is a small pet dog that likes to sit on people's laps. 2) (informal, insult) A lapdog is a person who always obeys a more powerful person without thinking.
its sense in the lessons: Everyday and stories: «a little lapdog». In news and politics, «lapdog» is an insult for someone who just does what a leader wants.
examples from the lessons: Grandma's lapdog sleeps on her knee. | A Pekingese is a typical lapdog. | The lapdog yapped at the postman. | People called the minister the president's lapdog. | My big dog thinks he is a lapdog. | Lapdogs were popular with rich ladies long ago.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: lapdogs. One word. The insult sense is rude about a person; use it with care.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (old, may offend) Lapp is an old name for the Sámi, the Indigenous people of the far north of Norway, Sweden, Finland and Russia. Many Sámi find the word «Lapp» offensive and prefer «Sámi».
its sense in the lessons: Geography and history: the Sámi herd reindeer, have their own languages and parliaments. The region is called Lapland. It tells the reader about the Arctic north; use «Sámi» for the people.
examples from the lessons: The Sámi were once called Lapps in old books. | Many Sámi prefer not to be called Lapps. | Lapland is in the far north of Finland. | Sámi families herd reindeer across the snow. | Our teacher said to use «Sámi», not «Lapp». | Old maps say «Lapp» but today we say Sámi.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Use «Sámi» (also «Saami»). «Lapland» is still a common place name. Capital letter.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (US) A Latino is a person in the USA whose family comes from Latin America, such as Mexico, Puerto Rico, Cuba or Colombia. 2) Latino describes their cultures, music and food.
its sense in the lessons: Social studies and everyday US life: Latino families, Latino music, Hispanic Heritage Month. Many people also use «Latina» for women, «Latinx» or «Latine» for everyone, and «Hispanic» for Spanish-speaking heritage.
examples from the lessons: Many Latino families live in California and Texas. | She is proud of her Latino heritage. | Latino music like salsa is great for dancing. | The book is about a Latino boy in Chicago. | Latina is often used for a girl or woman. | Our class celebrated Hispanic and Latino Heritage Month.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital letter: Latino. Plural: Latinos. «Latino» (from Latin America, any language) is not exactly the same as «Hispanic» (Spanish-speaking origin): Brazilians are Latino but not Hispanic.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A latte is a coffee drink made with espresso and lots of hot steamed milk, often with foam on top.
its sense in the lessons: Everyday life in cafés: adults order lattes; «oat latte», «chai latte», «matcha latte». It tells the reader about a café setting. Coffee has caffeine, which is not good for children in large amounts.
examples from the lessons: Mum ordered a latte and I had a hot chocolate. | The barista drew a heart in the latte foam. | A chai latte has spiced tea instead of coffee. | Dad likes his latte with oat milk. | The café sells lattes in three sizes. | He spilled his latte on the newspaper.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say «LAH-tay» (UK, US) or «LAT-tay». From Italian «caffè latte» (coffee with milk); in Italy «latte» alone just means milk.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) To leach is when water slowly washes chemicals or minerals out of soil, rock or another material. 2) To leach is when a substance slowly seeps out of something, like colour or chemicals from plastic.
its sense in the lessons: Science and geography: rain leaches nutrients from soil; chemicals leach into rivers. Everyday: colour leaches from clothes in the wash. It tells the reader about something slowly draining away.
examples from the lessons: Heavy rain leaches nutrients out of the soil. | Chemicals from the tip leached into the river. | Colour leached from the red sock into the white shirt. | Over years, salt leaches out of the rock. | Some plastics can leach chemicals into hot food. | The farmers added fertiliser because the soil was leached.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Homophone trap: «leach» (to seep out) vs «leech» (a blood-sucking worm). Regular: leached.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (money, law) Leased means rented under a written agreement for a fixed time, such as a house, car, office or land. 2) To have leased something out means to have let someone else use it in return for money.
its sense in the lessons: Adult life and money lessons: a leased car, a leased flat, land leased to a farmer. It tells the reader the user pays but does not own it.
examples from the lessons: The family leased a flat for two years. | The farmer leased the field to his neighbour. | Dad drives a leased car from his work. | The shop is in a leased building. | The council leased the old hall to a dance club. | They leased the boat for the summer.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Base: lease (a lease = the agreement). Say «leest». The person who owns and lets is the landlord or lessor; the one who pays is the tenant or lessee.

part of speech: noun (leavening, uncountable); verb form (-ing form of leaven)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Leavening is something added to dough or batter, like yeast, baking powder or baking soda, to make it rise and become light. 2) (literary) A leavening is a small amount of something, like humour, that makes something heavier or more serious better and lighter.
its sense in the lessons: Science and cooking: yeast makes gas bubbles that raise bread. Bible and church: unleavened bread (without yeast) at Passover; Jesus spoke of yeast (leaven) in parables. Stories: «a leavening of humour».
examples from the lessons: Yeast is the leavening in bread. | Baking powder is a leavening for cakes. | Matzah is bread made without leavening. | Without leavening, the cake came out flat. | His jokes gave a leavening of fun to the long meeting. | The class tested which leavening made the dough rise most.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say «LEV-en-ing». Base word: leaven. «Unleavened bread» = flat bread with no yeast.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) A lefty is a left-handed person. 2) (informal, politics) A lefty is a person with left-wing political views; sometimes said as a mild insult.
its sense in the lessons: Everyday and sport: a lefty pitcher in baseball, a lefty tennis player; about 1 in 10 people are left-handed. In politics talk, «lefty» can be teasing or rude.
examples from the lessons: My sister is a lefty and writes with her left hand. | The team needs a lefty pitcher. | Lefties sometimes need special scissors. | Uncle Pete called the reporter a lefty. | About one in ten people are lefties. | She is a lefty tennis player with a strong serve.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: lefties. Also spelled «leftie» (UK). Informal. Myth: left-handed people are not unlucky or less clever.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Legible writing or print is clear enough to be read easily.
its sense in the lessons: School: «Make your handwriting legible.» Everyday and safety: signs and labels must be legible. It tells the reader whether writing can be read.
examples from the lessons: Please make your handwriting legible. | The old letter was hardly legible. | Write your name legibly on the form. | The sign was legible from far away. | Doctors' notes are not always legible. | Use a dark pen so the answer is legible.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: illegible. Do not confuse with «eligible» (allowed or qualified).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (law) Legislative means to do with making laws. 2) The legislative branch of government is the part, such as Parliament or Congress, that makes laws.
its sense in the lessons: Citizenship and civics: the three branches of government are legislative (makes laws), executive (carries them out) and judicial (judges them). It tells the reader about law-making.
examples from the lessons: Congress is the legislative branch of the US government. | Parliament has legislative power in the UK. | The legislative process can take months. | A legislative assembly passed the new rule. | The legislative branch makes laws, and the courts explain them. | Our class held a pretend legislative debate.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say «LEJ-is-luh-tiv». Related: legislation (laws), legislator (a law-maker), legislature (the law-making body).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (law) A legislature is the group of elected people who make the laws of a country or state, such as a parliament, Congress or a state assembly.
its sense in the lessons: Civics and citizenship: the UK Parliament, the US Congress, the Australian Parliament, the Irish Oireachtas, Canadian provincial legislatures. It tells the reader who makes the laws.
examples from the lessons: The legislature voted on the new law. | Each US state has its own legislature. | The Scottish Parliament is a legislature. | Members of the legislature are elected. | The legislature debated school funding. | A bill must pass the legislature to become law.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: legislatures. Say «LEJ-is-lay-cher». The adjective is «legislative».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A legume is a plant that grows its seeds in pods, such as peas, beans, lentils, peanuts and clover. 2) Legumes are also the seeds or pods we eat from these plants.
its sense in the lessons: Science, food and farming: legumes are rich in protein and fibre; their roots hold tiny bacteria that add nitrogen to the soil, which helps farmers. It tells the reader about healthy food and plant science.
examples from the lessons: Peas and beans are legumes. | Legumes are a good source of protein. | Clover is a legume that makes soil richer. | Peanuts are legumes, not true nuts. | We cooked a soup with lots of legumes. | Farmers plant legumes to put nitrogen back into the soil.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: legumes. Say «LEG-yoom». Myth-buster: a peanut is a legume, not a nut.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Lemony means tasting or smelling of lemon, or being the pale yellow colour of a lemon.
its sense in the lessons: Food and cooking: «a lemony cake», «lemony smell». Art and description: «lemony yellow». It tells the reader about taste, smell or colour.
examples from the lessons: The cake had a lemony taste. | The kitchen smelled lemony after cleaning. | She painted the walls a lemony yellow. | This tea is fresh and lemony. | The fish came with a lemony sauce. | The lemony sweets made my mouth pucker.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal adjective. Also spelled «lemoney» (rare). No comparative needed usually.

part of speech: verb form (-ing form of lengthen); noun (a lengthening); adjective (lengthening)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Lengthening is making something longer, or becoming longer. 2) Lengthening shadows or days are slowly getting longer.
its sense in the lessons: Science and seasons: in spring the days are lengthening; at sunset shadows are lengthening. Sewing: lengthening trousers. In maths, lengthening a side changes the area. Stories: «lengthening shadows» shows evening.
examples from the lessons: The days are lengthening as spring comes. | Mum is lengthening my school skirt. | The shadows were lengthening as the sun went down. | The council is lengthening the cycle path. | Lengthening each side of a square makes its area bigger. | The queue kept lengthening.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Base verb: lengthen (length + en). Opposite: shortening. Maths: if each side of a square is doubled, the area becomes four times bigger.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Leniently means in a gentle, less strict way, giving a smaller punishment than expected.
its sense in the lessons: School rules, law and stories: «treated leniently», «marked leniently». It tells the reader that someone in charge was kind or soft.
examples from the lessons: The teacher treated the late pupils leniently. | The judge dealt leniently with the young driver. | The test was marked leniently. | Dad acted leniently because it was my birthday. | Rules about lunch were applied leniently on sports day. | He was punished leniently for his first mistake.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: lenient. Noun: leniency. Opposite: strictly, harshly. Say «LEE-nee-ent-lee».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) A letdown is a disappointment, something that was not as good as you hoped. 2) (verb phrase) To let someone down is to disappoint them by not doing what you promised.
its sense in the lessons: Everyday talk and stories: «The film was a letdown.» It tells the reader about disappointed hopes. Phrase: «What a letdown!»
examples from the lessons: The ending of the film was a real letdown. | After all the waiting, the fireworks were a letdown. | It was a letdown when the trip was cancelled. | Don't let your team down. | The new game was a letdown. | What a letdown — the pool was closed!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun is one word: «a letdown» (also «let-down»); the verb is two words: «let down», «let someone down». Plural: letdowns.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Lethargy is a heavy feeling of having no energy and not wanting to do anything.
its sense in the lessons: Health and science: lethargy can be a sign of illness, lack of sleep, poor food or not enough water. In stories: «a hot afternoon of lethargy». It tells the reader someone is very tired or sluggish.
examples from the lessons: After the flu, he felt lethargy for days. | Hot weather filled the class with lethargy. | Lethargy can be a sign that you need more sleep. | The vet said the dog's lethargy meant it was ill. | She shook off her lethargy and went for a run. | Too much screen time can lead to lethargy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: no «a». Adjective: lethargic. Say «LETH-er-jee».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Lexical means to do with words and their meanings, or with the vocabulary of a language.
its sense in the lessons: English and language lessons: «lexical words» (nouns, verbs, adjectives) carry meaning, while grammar words like «the» or «of» hold sentences together. Dictionaries and word studies. It tells the reader we are talking about vocabulary.
examples from the lessons: Nouns and verbs are lexical words. | A dictionary is a big lexical list. | The lesson was about lexical meaning. | We looked at the lexical differences between British and American English. | «Lift» and «elevator» are a lexical difference. | Lexical knowledge means knowing many words.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Related: lexicon (a vocabulary), lexicographer (a dictionary writer). Formal, mostly in language study.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A lexicographer is a person who writes or edits dictionaries.
its sense in the lessons: English lessons and history: Samuel Johnson wrote a famous English dictionary in 1755; Noah Webster wrote an American one in 1828. It tells the reader about people who collect words and their meanings.
examples from the lessons: A lexicographer writes dictionary entries. | Samuel Johnson was a famous lexicographer. | Noah Webster was an American lexicographer. | Lexicographers add new words like «emoji» to dictionaries. | The lexicographer studied how people really use the word. | She wants to be a lexicographer because she loves words.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say «lex-ih-KOG-ruh-fer». Plural: lexicographers. The work is «lexicography».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (a name) Lhasa is the main city of Tibet, high in the Himalayas, now under China's rule. 2) (a name) A Lhasa Apso is a small long-haired dog breed from Tibet.
its sense in the lessons: Geography and religion: Lhasa is one of the highest cities in the world, about 3,650 metres up; the Potala Palace was the home of the Dalai Lama. It is a holy city for Tibetan Buddhists.
examples from the lessons: Lhasa is the capital of Tibet. | The Potala Palace stands in Lhasa. | Lhasa is one of the highest cities on Earth. | Pilgrims walk to Lhasa to pray. | Our neighbour has a Lhasa Apso dog. | The air in Lhasa is thin because it is so high.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital letter: Lhasa. The «h» is silent: «LAH-suh».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Lidded means having a lid, a cover on top. 2) (literary) Lidded eyes are half-closed, with heavy eyelids, as if sleepy.
its sense in the lessons: Everyday: «a lidded box», «a lidded cup» for safety with hot drinks. Stories: «heavy-lidded eyes» show tiredness or calm.
examples from the lessons: Keep food in a lidded box. | Take your drink in a lidded cup on the bus. | The lidded jar kept the biscuits fresh. | The cat watched with lidded eyes. | Put rubbish in the lidded bin. | The lidded pot boiled faster.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «lid» + «-ded» (double «d»). Often in compounds: heavy-lidded.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) In lieu of something means instead of it.
its sense in the lessons: Formal and adult life: «time off in lieu» (TOIL) for extra hours worked, «payment in lieu of notice» when someone leaves a job. It tells the reader one thing replaces another.
examples from the lessons: We got a gift card in lieu of a prize. | Dad took a day off in lieu after working on Saturday. | In lieu of flowers, please give to charity. | She was paid in lieu of notice. | The school gave extra reading in lieu of homework. | He did chores in lieu of paying rent.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say «loo» (UK) or «loo/lyoo». Only used in «in lieu (of)». It comes from French «lieu» = place. Everyday: «instead of».
