meaning for a pupil: 1) Lifesaving means saving or able to save someone's life, like lifesaving medicine. 2) Lifesaving is the skill of rescuing people from drowning, taught in swimming and lifeguard classes.
its sense in the lessons: Health and safety: lifesaving skills, CPR, defibrillators; swimming badges; Surf Life Saving clubs in Australia and New Zealand. It tells the reader something can rescue people.
examples from the lessons: She learned lifesaving at the swimming pool. | The defibrillator is a lifesaving machine. | Vaccines are lifesaving. | He got a badge in lifesaving. | Learning CPR is a lifesaving skill. | The lifeguards did a lifesaving rescue.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Also written «life-saving». Related: lifeguard, lifesaver.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A ligature is a thread, string or band used to tie something tightly, especially by a doctor to tie off a blood vessel. 2) (writing) A ligature is two letters joined into one shape, like æ or œ, or «fi» in printed books. 3) (music) A ligature is a mark or clamp joining notes or holding a reed.
its sense in the lessons: Medicine and first aid history; typing and printing lessons (æ in «encyclopædia»); music: the clamp on a clarinet. Formal word.
examples from the lessons: The surgeon tied a ligature round the blood vessel. | «Æ» is a ligature of «a» and «e». | Old books use ligatures like «œ». | The clarinet's reed is held by a ligature. | Some fonts join «f» and «i» with a ligature. | The ligature stopped the bleeding.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: ligatures. Say «LIG-uh-cher». Related: ligament (in the body).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A lightbulb is a glass or plastic bulb that gives out light when electricity goes through it. 2) (informal) A «lightbulb moment» is a sudden moment when you understand something or have a great idea.
its sense in the lessons: Science: electric circuits, energy saving (LED bulbs use less energy than old filament bulbs); history: Thomas Edison and Joseph Swan. Cartoons: a lightbulb over someone's head means an idea. Safety: let bulbs cool before touching and switch off before changing.
examples from the lessons: The lightbulb in my bedroom has gone. | LED lightbulbs save energy. | Switch off before you change a lightbulb. | Edison and Swan both worked on the lightbulb. | I had a lightbulb moment and solved the puzzle. | In the circuit, the lightbulb lit up when we closed the switch.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Also «light bulb» (two words). Plural: lightbulbs. Myth: Edison did not invent the first bulb; many people worked on it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Lightweight means not heavy, weighing less than usual. 2) (sport) A lightweight is a boxer or other fighter in a lighter weight class. 3) (informal, insult) A lightweight is a person who is not important, serious or able to handle much, like someone who gets tired easily.
its sense in the lessons: Everyday: «a lightweight jacket», «lightweight bike». Sport: boxing and rowing weight classes. Talk: «Don't be a lightweight!» (teasing). Science: lightweight materials like aluminium.
examples from the lessons: This lightweight jacket is good for spring. | Aluminium is a lightweight metal. | He boxes as a lightweight. | Pack lightweight clothes for camping. | «You're such a lightweight!» she teased when he went to bed early. | The plane is built from lightweight materials.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word. Plural: lightweights. Opposite: heavyweight. As a teasing insult it is informal.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A lineage is the line of your ancestors, the family members who came before you, such as parents, grandparents and great-grandparents. 2) (science) A lineage is a line of living things that descend from a common ancestor.
its sense in the lessons: History and family studies: kings and queens and their lineage, family trees. Science: evolution and lineages of species. Bible: the lineage of Jesus in Matthew and Luke. It tells the reader where someone comes from.
examples from the lessons: The queen could trace her lineage back hundreds of years. | We drew a family tree to show our lineage. | Birds come from a lineage of dinosaurs. | The Bible gives the lineage of King David. | The horse had a famous lineage of champions. | Her lineage includes Irish and Italian ancestors.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say «LIN-ee-ij» (three parts), not «line-age». Plural: lineages.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To linger is to stay somewhere longer than usual or than needed, because you do not want to leave. 2) To linger is when a smell, feeling or illness stays for a long time. 3) To linger over something is to take your time with it.
its sense in the lessons: Stories: «she lingered at the gate». Everyday: smells and colds that linger. School: «Don't linger in the corridors.» It tells the reader something is slow to go away.
examples from the lessons: We lingered on the beach until sunset. | The smell of smoke lingered for days. | Don't linger in the corridor. | A cough can linger after a cold. | He lingered over his breakfast. | The happy memory lingered in her mind.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular: lingered, lingering. Adjective «lingering» (a lingering smell).

part of speech: noun (linguistics); uncountable, takes a singular verb
meaning for a pupil: 1) Linguistics is the scientific study of language: how sounds, words, grammar and meaning work, how languages change, and how people learn them.
its sense in the lessons: Language lessons and olympiad puzzles: linguists study patterns in languages they may not speak. It tells the reader about the science of language. University subject.
examples from the lessons: Linguistics is the study of language. | She wants to study linguistics at university. | Linguistics explains why «sheep» has no «-s» plural. | Language puzzles in the olympiad use linguistics. | Linguistics looks at sounds, words and grammar. | My aunt teaches linguistics.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Ends in «-s» but is singular: «Linguistics is fun». A person who studies it is a «linguist» (also: someone who speaks many languages). Adjective: linguistic.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A linnet is a small brown songbird of the finch family; the male has a pinkish-red chest and head in spring.
its sense in the lessons: Nature and science lessons in the UK and Ireland; old poems and songs mention linnets for their sweet song. It tells the reader about birds of hedges and heaths.
examples from the lessons: A linnet sang on the gorse bush. | The male linnet has a red chest in spring. | Linnets eat small seeds. | We spotted a flock of linnets on the farm. | Old poems compare a happy singer to a linnet. | The linnet is a kind of finch.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: linnets. Double «n».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Linseed is the seed of the flax plant, also called flaxseed. 2) Linseed oil is oil pressed from these seeds, used in paints and to protect wood, and (food-grade) in cooking.
its sense in the lessons: Art: artists mix oil paints with linseed oil; cricket bats are oiled with linseed oil. Food and health: linseed is added to bread and cereals. Science: flax also gives linen cloth. Safety: rags soaked in linseed oil can catch fire by themselves if crumpled up.
examples from the lessons: Linseed is the seed of the flax plant. | We oiled the cricket bat with linseed oil. | Artists thin oil paint with linseed oil. | Mum sprinkles linseed on her porridge. | Spread oily rags flat to dry, because linseed oil rags can catch fire. | Linen cloth is made from the same flax plant.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Also called flaxseed (US).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) To liquefy is to turn into a liquid, or to make a solid or gas become a liquid, often by heating or cooling or squeezing.
its sense in the lessons: Science lessons on states of matter: ice liquefies when it melts; gases can be liquefied by cooling and pressure (liquid nitrogen, LPG for barbecues). Cooking: a blender liquefies fruit. Earthquakes can liquefy wet soil.
examples from the lessons: Ice liquefies when it warms up. | Gases can be liquefied by cooling them. | Butter liquefies in a hot pan. | The blender liquefied the strawberries. | In an earthquake, wet sand can liquefy. | Liquefied gas is stored in metal tanks.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: «liquefy» with «e», not «liquify» (common mistake). Forms: liquefies, liquefied. Noun: liquefaction.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (church) A litany is a long prayer in which a leader says a line and the people answer with the same response each time, like «Lord, have mercy». 2) A litany is a long list of things, often complaints or problems, that seems to go on and on.
its sense in the lessons: Church lessons: the litany in Catholic, Anglican and Orthodox services. Everyday and news: «a litany of complaints», «a litany of mistakes». It tells the reader something is long and repeated.
examples from the lessons: The priest led the litany and the people answered. | In the litany, everyone repeated «Hear our prayer». | He gave a litany of excuses for being late. | The report listed a litany of problems. | My brother has a litany of complaints about broccoli. | The old church still sings the litany on Sundays.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: litanies (y → ies). Say «LIT-uh-nee».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Literacy is the ability to read and write. 2) Literacy is knowledge and skill in a certain area, such as computer literacy, money literacy or media literacy.
its sense in the lessons: School: «literacy lessons» (UK) for reading and writing; World Literacy Day; charities teach adults to read. Citizenship: media literacy helps you spot fake news. It tells the reader about skills for learning.
examples from the lessons: We have literacy every morning. | Literacy helps people get good jobs. | Our class learns media literacy to spot fake news. | Financial literacy means understanding money. | The charity improves literacy in poor areas. | Digital literacy means using computers safely and well.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Adjective: literate (able to read and write); opposite: illiteracy, illiterate. Related to «letter».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Very, very angry, so angry you can hardly keep calm. 2) (of skin) Dark blue-grey or purple, like the colour of a bad bruise. 3) (formal, old) Pale or ashen in the face, from shock or anger.
its sense in the lessons: In stories «livid» tells the reader a character is furious, much stronger than just «cross» or «annoyed»; it often comes before an argument or a punishment. Phrases: «absolutely livid», «livid with rage», «livid about something», «livid at someone». In science or first aid you may meet «a livid bruise», meaning dark purple. In everyday life a parent might be livid about a broken window.
examples from the lessons: Mum was livid when she saw mud all over the new carpet. | The coach was absolutely livid about the late kick-off. | Dad went livid when he heard someone had scratched the car. | She was livid with her brother for reading her diary. | A livid bruise spread across his knee after the fall. | The teacher looked livid, so the whole class went silent. | I was livid at myself for forgetting my lunch again. | The old story says his face turned livid with fear.
note for the reader of a maths problem: An adjective, used mostly after «be», «look», «go» («she went livid»). Mostly about strong anger in modern English; the colour sense (bruise purple) is the older meaning. People sometimes think it means «lively» because of «live» – it does not. Not a maths word.

part of speech: noun (a loanword, loanwords); also written «loan word»
meaning for a pupil: 1) A word one language has taken from another language and now uses as its own, like «pizza» from Italian or «kindergarten» from German. 2) (language study) Any borrowed word, studied to see where words came from.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons and spelling, loanwords explain odd spellings: «ballet» and «café» come from French, «tsunami» from Japanese, «kangaroo» from an Australian Aboriginal language (Guugu Yimithirr). English is full of loanwords from French, Latin, Norse, Greek and many more. Phrases: «a loanword from French», «borrowed into English». Knowing a word is a loanword helps you guess how it sounds and why it is spelt that way.
examples from the lessons: «Pyjamas» is a loanword from Hindi and Urdu. | «Shampoo» is a loanword from Hindi too. | Our teacher showed us that «chocolate» is a loanword from Spanish, which took it from Nahuatl. | Japanese has many English loanwords, like «aisu kuriimu» for ice cream. | «Safari» came into English as a loanword from Swahili. | Many loanwords keep their foreign spelling, such as «croissant». | We made a poster of loanwords and the countries they came from. | «Boomerang» is a loanword from an Aboriginal language of Australia.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one loanword, two loanwords. Can be written as one word or two («loan word»). The language does not give the word back – «loan» is just a picture word. Close words: «borrowing» (same idea), «calque» (a word translated part by part, like «skyscraper» in other languages). Not a maths word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Having lobes: rounded parts that stick out, like the parts of an oak leaf or of an ear. 2) (science) Divided into rounded sections, like a lung or the brain.
its sense in the lessons: In science «lobed» describes leaves (oak and maple leaves are lobed), organs (the lungs and liver are lobed) and some shapes in nature. It helps when you sort leaves in a nature study: lobed, toothed or smooth-edged. Phrases: «deeply lobed», «three-lobed», «lobed leaves».
examples from the lessons: An oak leaf is lobed, with round bumps along its edge. | We sorted our leaves into lobed and smooth ones. | The maple leaf on Canada's flag is lobed with sharp points. | The human brain is lobed, and each lobe has different jobs. | Some lobed leaves look a bit like a hand. | The scientist drew a three-lobed flower. | Ivy leaves are often lobed. | The lungs are lobed: the right lung has three lobes and the left has two.
note for the reader of a maths problem: An adjective made from the noun «lobe» (an earlobe, a lobe of the lung). Often used with a number: «three-lobed», «five-lobed». Do not confuse with «lobbed» (thrown high, from «lob»), which sounds almost the same. Not used in maths problems.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In or near the place where you are or where you live; nearby. 2) In one small part rather than everywhere, such as one spot on the body. 3) (business) Made, grown or sold in the nearby area, not brought from far away.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: «locally grown food», «shop locally», «known locally as …». In geography lessons it means in a small area, not the whole country. In science and health: «a locally painful knee», «local anaesthetic works locally». News says «locally» for things happening in your town. Phrases: «locally grown», «locally made», «locally known as», «act locally».
examples from the lessons: We buy our eggs locally from a farm down the road. | The hill is known locally as Witch's Hat. | Mum likes to shop locally to help small businesses. | The cream works locally, only where you rub it. | The storm caused flooding locally, but the rest of the country was dry. | Our school uses locally grown apples at lunch. | The festival is famous locally but few tourists have heard of it. | Think globally, act locally.
note for the reader of a maths problem: An adverb made from «local» + «-ly». Spelled with double l: «locally». It describes where something happens, not when. «Locally» does not mean «only cheap» or «small quality»; it just means nearby. Not usually a maths word, though in advanced maths «locally» means «in a small neighbourhood».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person whose job is cutting down trees and taking the logs away; a lumberjack. 2) (science, computers) A device or program that records information again and again over time, like temperatures or events. 3) (computers) A small program that writes a list (a log) of what happens on a computer.
its sense in the lessons: In history and geography, loggers are tied to forests, timber and saw mills in Canada, the USA, Australia and New Zealand, and to debates about cutting down rainforests. In science, a «data logger» records temperature, light or sound every few seconds for an experiment. In computing, a logger keeps a record of what a program did. Phrases: «data logger», «a logger's camp», «illegal loggers».
examples from the lessons: The logger cut the tall pine with a chainsaw. | Loggers in Canada once floated logs down the rivers. | We left a data logger in the classroom to record the temperature overnight. | The data logger showed it got coldest at 5 o'clock in the morning. | Illegal loggers are damaging parts of the Amazon rainforest. | A logger must wear a helmet and strong boots for safety. | The game has a logger that writes down every error. | The old loggers' hut is now a museum.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one logger, two loggers. From «log» + «-er». Other words for the job: «lumberjack» (North America), «timber worker», «forester» (looks after a forest, not always cutting). A «data logger» is a machine, not a person. Not a maths word, but data loggers produce tables and graphs used in maths and science.

part of speech: noun (lotto; a lotto game, lottos – rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A lottery game: people buy tickets with numbers, and if their numbers are drawn they win money. 2) A children's game like bingo, where you cover pictures or numbers on a card when they are called out.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, «Lotto» is the name of national lottery games in the UK, Ireland, Australia, New Zealand and parts of the USA and Canada. Adults talk about «winning the lotto». In maths, lotto is a great example of chance and probability: the chance of winning the top prize is tiny, like 1 in many millions. In stories a character who «wins the lotto» suddenly becomes rich. You must be an adult to play lotto for money.
examples from the lessons: Grandad buys a lotto ticket every Saturday. | If I won the lotto, I would buy a horse. | The chance of winning the lotto is less than one in ten million. | We played picture lotto at nursery and I covered the cat first. | Six numbers are drawn in the lotto each week. | Our maths teacher said lotto shows why unlikely events are very unlikely. | Nobody won the lotto jackpot, so it rolls over to next week. | Gambling, including lotto, is only for adults.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable («play lotto», «win the lotto»); often written with a capital as a game name («Lotto»). Same idea as «lottery». In maths problems it is about probability: more tickets give a slightly better chance, but the chance stays very small. Myth: picking «lucky» numbers does not change your chance.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Lowest; at the very bottom of a set of things. 2) (formal) The furthest down of several layers or levels.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography it appears for layers: «the lowermost layer of rock is the oldest». In instructions: «the lowermost shelf». It is a slightly formal or written word; in everyday speech people usually say «bottom» or «lowest». Opposite: «uppermost» or «topmost».
examples from the lessons: The lowermost layer of rock is usually the oldest. | Put the heavy books on the lowermost shelf. | The lowermost branch of the tree was easy to reach. | The lowermost step was covered in moss. | In the diagram, the lowermost line shows the coldest month. | Roots grow from the lowermost part of the stem. | Fish lived in the lowermost part of the tank. | The lowermost floor of the building is a car park.
note for the reader of a maths problem: An adjective with no «more» or «most» forms (it already means «most»). More formal than «lowest» or «bottom». Opposite: «uppermost». In maths, «lowermost» point of a graph = lowest point (the minimum).

meaning for a pupil: 1) To put oil, grease or another slippery stuff on parts of a machine so they move smoothly and do not rub or wear out. 2) (science, body) To keep a part of the body moist and slippery so it moves easily, as tears lubricate the eye. 3) (informal) To make something go more smoothly, like a talk or a deal.
its sense in the lessons: In science (forces) lubricating reduces friction: oil on a bike chain makes it easier to pedal. In everyday life: oiling a squeaky door hinge. In the body, joints are lubricated by fluid and eyes by tears. Phrases: «lubricate the chain», «well lubricated», «to lubricate the conversation» (informal). The noun is «lubricant», the action is «lubrication».
examples from the lessons: Dad lubricated my bike chain with oil. | Oil lubricates the engine so the parts do not grind. | Tears lubricate your eyes when you blink. | The squeaky gate stopped squeaking after we lubricated the hinges. | Our joints are lubricated by a special fluid. | In the friction experiment, we lubricated the ramp with soapy water and the block slid faster. | A little chat about football helped to lubricate the meeting. | Never lubricate brakes, or they will not grip.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: lubricated, lubricating. Related words: lubricant (the stuff), lubrication (the act). Science link: less friction, smoother movement, less heat and wear. Trap: lubricating brakes is dangerous – brakes need friction. Not a maths word.

part of speech: adjective (lumbering); also verb form of «lumber» (lumber, lumbers, lumbered, lumbering); noun (lumbering, the work of cutting timber – North America)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Moving slowly and heavily, in a clumsy way, like an elephant or a big tired bear. 2) (verb, -ing form) Walking or moving in a heavy, clumsy way: «the bear was lumbering along». 3) (North America) The work of cutting down trees and preparing wood (lumber) to sell.
its sense in the lessons: In stories «lumbering» paints a picture of size and heaviness: giants, trolls, dinosaurs, bears or old buses are lumbering. It tells the reader the creature is big and slow, maybe not very nimble. In history of Canada and the USA, lumbering was a big industry. Phrases: «a lumbering giant», «lumbering along», «lumbering towards us».
examples from the lessons: A lumbering giant stepped out of the forest. | The old bus came lumbering up the hill. | The bear was lumbering across the meadow. | Dinosaurs like Brachiosaurus were huge, lumbering animals. | The lumbering tractor held up all the traffic. | My big dog came lumbering in, covered in mud. | Lumbering was the main job in many Canadian towns in the 1800s. | The robot moved with a lumbering, clanking walk.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From the verb «lumber» (to move heavily). In the UK, «lumbered with» means stuck with a job nobody wants: «I got lumbered with the washing-up». Do not confuse with «lumber» in North America = sawn wood (UK «timber»). Not a maths word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) A person who behaves in a wild, silly or dangerous way: «He drives like a lunatic». 2) (adjective, informal) Very silly or crazy: «a lunatic idea». 3) (old, now offensive) An old word for a person with a serious mental illness; today it is hurtful to use it this way.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday speech people say «drives like a lunatic» or «a lunatic idea» to mean reckless or crazy. In history lessons you meet «lunatic asylum», an old name for a hospital for people with mental illness. Today we say «mental illness» and «psychiatric hospital» instead, because «lunatic» about real ill people is hurtful. The word comes from Latin «luna» (moon): people once wrongly believed the moon made people mad.
examples from the lessons: Some lunatic was driving at 80 miles an hour past the school! | Jumping off the shed roof was a lunatic idea. | The crowd went lunatic when the goal went in. | In Victorian times there were places called lunatic asylums. | Grandma says the price of petrol is lunatic. | He was running round the garden like a lunatic. | Today we say «a person with a mental illness», not «a lunatic». | Some people believed a full moon made people act like lunatics, but science has not shown this.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one lunatic, two lunatics. Informal and a bit rude when said about a person; never use it about people who are really ill. Myth: the full moon does not make people mad – studies have not found this. Related: «lunar» (about the moon), «lunacy» (madness, foolishness). Not a maths word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Shining softly and brightly, with a smooth glowing surface, like pearls, silk or healthy hair. 2) (science) Having lustre: the shiny look that metals and some minerals have when they are polished or freshly cut.
its sense in the lessons: In science (materials), metals are described as «lustrous» – shiny – which is one way to tell a metal from a non-metal. In geology, minerals are sorted by lustre: metallic, glassy, pearly, dull. In stories «lustrous» is a rich describing word for hair, fur, eyes or fabric. Phrases: «lustrous hair», «lustrous coat», «lustrous metal».
examples from the lessons: The horse had a lustrous black coat. | Gold is a lustrous metal that does not rust. | Her lustrous hair shone in the sunlight. | Metals are usually lustrous, hard and good conductors. | Freshly cut sodium is lustrous, but it soon goes dull in air. | The pearl was smooth and lustrous. | The cat's fur was thick and lustrous after a good brush. | We rubbed the old copper coin until it was lustrous again.
note for the reader of a maths problem: An adjective; the noun is «lustre» (UK, Australia) or «luster» (US). Not the same as «lusty» (strong, eager) or «lust» – different meanings. In science «lustrous» = shiny, a property of metals. Not a maths word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (usually plural «lyrics») The words of a song. 2) A short poem that shows the poet's own feelings, often one that could be sung. 3) (adjective) Expressing strong personal feelings, like a song: «lyric poetry».
its sense in the lessons: In music lessons you learn and write lyrics to tunes. In English lessons a lyric poem is a short poem about feelings, often in the first person («I»). Phrases: «song lyrics», «learn the lyrics», «write the lyrics», «a lyric poem». Lyrics are also covered by copyright, so you cannot copy someone's lyrics as your own.
examples from the lessons: I know all the lyrics to our school song. | She wrote the lyrics and her brother wrote the music. | The lyrics are printed inside the CD case. | Can you hear the lyrics, or is the music too loud? | A lyric is a short poem about the poet's feelings. | We wrote new lyrics for «Happy Birthday» about our teacher. | Some lyrics are hard to understand when people sing fast. | The song's lyrics tell a story about a lost dog.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: «a lyric» (one line or one poem) and «lyrics» (all the words of a song – we usually use the plural). Not the same as «lyrical» (adjective, beautiful and full of feeling). Spelling: l-y-r-i-c, with a y. From the Greek «lyre», an old stringed instrument. Not a maths word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Beautiful and full of feeling, like a song or a poem: «a lyrical description of the sea». 2) (music, poetry) Song-like, smooth and expressive. 3) (idiom) «wax lyrical» means to talk about something with great enthusiasm.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons, «lyrical» praises writing that sounds musical and expresses feelings. In music, a lyrical tune is smooth and singing. The phrase «wax lyrical about something» means to talk on and on happily about it. Do not confuse with «lyrics» (the words of a song).
examples from the lessons: The author's lyrical writing makes you see the hills. | The violin played a slow, lyrical tune. | Grandpa waxed lyrical about the football team he played for. | Her poem was gentle and lyrical. | The film had lyrical shots of the sea at sunset. | Mum always waxes lyrical about Irish soda bread. | The teacher called my description of autumn «quite lyrical». | A lyrical song is easy to sing along to.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective made from «lyric» + «-al». Adverb: «lyrically». «Wax» here is an old verb meaning «grow» or «become», not candle wax. Not a maths word.

part of speech: noun (a mace, maces; mace – the spice, uncountable); noun (Mace – a brand name of spray)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A heavy club with a metal head, often with spikes, used as a weapon by knights in the Middle Ages. 2) A decorated staff (a fancy stick) carried in ceremonies to show the power of a mayor, parliament or university. 3) A spice made from the red covering of the nutmeg seed. 4) (US) A spray that stings the eyes, used by some police; often called by the brand name Mace.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons a mace is a weapon of medieval knights. In citizenship lessons, the mace in the UK House of Commons, the Australian House of Representatives and other parliaments shows that Parliament is meeting; it is placed on the table during sittings. In cooking, mace is a spice used in cakes and sauces. Phrases: «the ceremonial mace», «a spiked mace», «a pinch of mace».
examples from the lessons: The knight swung his mace at the enemy shield. | The mace is carried into Parliament at the start of each day. | The mayor walked in behind a man carrying a silver mace. | Gran puts a pinch of mace in her Christmas cake. | Mace comes from the same fruit as nutmeg. | In the museum we saw a spiked iron mace. | Without the mace on the table, the House of Commons cannot do its business. | The university mace is used at graduation.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «A mace» (weapon or staff) is countable: two maces. Mace the spice is uncountable: «some mace». Spelled with c; sounds like «mace» rhymes with «face». Trap: «Mace» spray (a brand) is a different thing again. Not a maths word.

part of speech: noun (Madeira – a place; madeira – a wine; madeira cake)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (a place) Madeira is a group of islands in the Atlantic Ocean that belong to Portugal, famous for mountains, flowers and a warm climate. 2) A strong, sweet wine made on those islands. 3) (UK) Madeira cake: a plain, firm sponge cake, often eaten with a cup of tea.
its sense in the lessons: In geography Madeira is a Portuguese island group in the Atlantic, west of Morocco; its capital is Funchal, and the footballer Cristiano Ronaldo was born there. In British kitchens «madeira cake» is a simple yellow cake, good for decorating birthday cakes because it is firm. Its name comes from being served with Madeira wine long ago; the cake has no wine in it.
examples from the lessons: Madeira is a group of islands that belong to Portugal. | We went to Madeira on holiday and walked along the mountain paths. | Mum baked a madeira cake for the school cake sale. | A madeira cake is firm, so it is good for birthday cakes with icing. | Madeira wine is made on the islands. | Cristiano Ronaldo was born in Funchal, on Madeira. | The airport on Madeira is famous for its short runway. | Madeira means «wood» in Portuguese, because the island was covered in trees.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a place it takes a capital: Madeira. «Madeira cake» often written with a small m in recipes. Pronounced «ma-DEER-a». The cake does not contain wine. The wine is for adults only. In Portuguese «madeira» means «wood».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Made by magic or having magic powers, like in fairy tales: «a magical sword». 2) Wonderful and special, so lovely it feels like magic: «a magical evening».
its sense in the lessons: In stories, magical objects (wands, rings, cloaks) have special powers, and magical creatures (unicorns, dragons) live in imaginary worlds. In everyday life people say «magical» about a beautiful or exciting time: «Christmas morning felt magical». In science lessons, things that look magical (a rainbow, a magnet) have real explanations. Phrases: «magical powers», «a magical place», «magical thinking».
examples from the lessons: The witch had a magical cat that could talk. | The snowy forest looked magical in the moonlight. | The fairy gave her a magical ring. | Our trip to the beach was magical. | Magnets can seem magical, but they work by a force called magnetism. | In the book, the wardrobe is a magical door to another world. | The lights at the Christmas fair were magical. | «Magical thinking» means believing something will happen just because you wish it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective from «magic» + «-al». «Magic» is also an adjective: «a magic wand» and «a magical wand» are both fine; «magical» is used more for feelings («a magical day»). Adverb: «magically». Spelling: magic-al. Not a maths word, though «magic squares» are a maths puzzle.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (law) An official who acts as a judge in a local court, dealing with less serious crimes and some family or local matters. 2) (UK) A volunteer from the community, also called a Justice of the Peace (JP), who hears cases in a magistrates' court. 3) (history) In old Rome and other places, a person who held public power, like a mayor or governor.
its sense in the lessons: In citizenship lessons, magistrates are part of the justice system: in England and Wales most criminal cases start in a magistrates' court; in Australia and New Zealand magistrates also run local courts. Magistrates decide if someone is guilty of minor crimes and give punishments like fines. Phrases: «magistrates' court», «appear before a magistrate», «the magistrate fined him».
examples from the lessons: The man had to appear before a magistrate for speeding. | Magistrates in England are usually volunteers, not paid lawyers. | The magistrate fined her for dropping litter. | Most criminal cases start in the magistrates' court. | Our neighbour is a magistrate and sits in court twice a month. | The magistrate listened to both sides before deciding. | In ancient Rome, magistrates ran the city. | A magistrate can send serious cases to a higher court.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one magistrate, two magistrates. «Magistrates' court» has the apostrophe after the s. A magistrate is not always a trained lawyer (in the UK many are volunteers). Not the same as a «judge», who deals with bigger cases. Not a maths word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) A light, silvery-white metal and chemical element (symbol Mg, number 12) that burns with a very bright white flame. 2) (health) A mineral our bodies need, found in green vegetables, nuts and whole grains.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, burning magnesium ribbon makes a dazzling white light and white ash (magnesium oxide); you must not look straight at it. It is used in fireworks, flares and light metal parts (alloys) for bikes and cars. In health and food lessons, magnesium helps muscles and nerves work. Phrases: «magnesium ribbon», «magnesium oxide», «rich in magnesium».
examples from the lessons: Our teacher burned a strip of magnesium and it glowed bright white. | Do not look directly at burning magnesium. | Magnesium's symbol is Mg. | Spinach and almonds are rich in magnesium. | Fireworks use magnesium to make white sparks. | Some bike frames are made of a magnesium alloy because it is light. | When magnesium burns, it joins with oxygen to make magnesium oxide. | Sea water contains magnesium.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «some magnesium», not «a magnesium». Symbol Mg (not Ma or Mn – Mn is manganese, a different element). Spelling: mag-ne-sium. Safety: burning magnesium is very bright and hot; only teachers do this demo.

part of speech: noun (magnetisation, uncountable; magnetisations – rare); US spelling «magnetization»
meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) The process of making something into a magnet. 2) (science) How strongly something is magnetised, or the state of being magnetic.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on magnets you can magnetise an iron nail or a needle by stroking it with a magnet in one direction; this is magnetisation. Heating or hitting a magnet can destroy its magnetisation. It explains how compasses are made and how old computer disks stored data. Phrases: «the magnetisation of iron», «lose magnetisation».
examples from the lessons: Stroking a needle with a magnet causes magnetisation. | After magnetisation, the needle could pick up paper clips. | Dropping a magnet can weaken its magnetisation. | We tested the magnetisation by seeing how many pins the nail could hold. | The magnetisation of the steel lasted for weeks. | Heating a magnet strongly can destroy its magnetisation. | Electric currents can also cause magnetisation, like in an electromagnet. | Rocks keep a record of the Earth's magnetisation from long ago.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable in normal use. UK/Australia/NZ spelling «magnetisation», US/Canada spelling «magnetization» – both correct. Verb: magnetise (magnetize). Only some metals (iron, nickel, cobalt, steel) can be magnetised; aluminium, copper and gold cannot. Not a maths word, but magnetisation can be measured and compared in a fair test.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Making something look bigger than it really is, using a lens, microscope or zoom. 2) (science) How many times bigger something looks: «a magnification of ×10». 3) (formal) Making something seem more important or serious than it is.
its sense in the lessons: In science, microscopes and magnifying glasses have a magnification, written like «×40», meaning things look 40 times bigger. In maths, magnification links to scale and enlargement: a scale factor of 3 makes every length 3 times longer. In art and photography, zooming in is magnification. Phrases: «high magnification», «under magnification», «×100 magnification».
examples from the lessons: Under the microscope at ×100 magnification, we saw tiny cells. | The magnifying glass has a magnification of three times. | At low magnification you see the whole leaf. | Higher magnification shows more detail but a smaller area. | The photo of the fly was taken with strong magnification. | Magnification makes a 1 mm hair look 1 cm wide at ×10. | Binoculars give a magnification of about eight times. | Total magnification = eyepiece magnification × objective magnification.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable and uncountable. In numbers: magnification ×10 means the image is 10 times as long and 10 times as wide as the real thing (but not 10 times the area – area grows 100 times). To find a real size, divide the image size by the magnification. Verb: magnify. Not the same as «magnitude» (size, especially of earthquakes).

part of speech: noun (a mahatma, mahatmas; usually as a title: Mahatma)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A title meaning «great soul», given in India to a person who is very wise, good and respected. 2) (a name) Most often used for Mahatma Gandhi, the leader of India's peaceful struggle for freedom from British rule.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, «Mahatma» appears in the name Mahatma Gandhi (1869–1948), who led Indians in non-violent protest, like the Salt March of 1930, and inspired Martin Luther King Jr and Nelson Mandela. «Mahatma» is a title of respect, not his first name (that was Mohandas). Phrases: «Mahatma Gandhi», «the Mahatma».
examples from the lessons: Mahatma Gandhi led India's struggle for freedom without violence. | «Mahatma» means «great soul» in Sanskrit. | His real first name was Mohandas, and «Mahatma» was a title people gave him. | We read about the Mahatma's long walk to the sea to make salt. | Many people called Gandhi «the Mahatma» with deep respect. | Gandhi's birthday, 2 October, is a national holiday in India. | Martin Luther King Jr learned from the Mahatma's ideas about peaceful protest. | A mahatma is someone people see as very wise and good.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually written with a capital as a title: Mahatma Gandhi. A loanword from Sanskrit («maha» great + «atma» soul). Not his first name. Rarely used about anyone else in English. Not a maths word.

part of speech: noun (Malayalam, uncountable – the name of a language)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (a language) Malayalam is a language spoken by about 35 million people, mainly in the state of Kerala in south-west India. 2) The alphabet (script) used to write that language, with rounded letters.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and language lessons, Malayalam is one of the 22 official languages of India, part of the Dravidian family (like Tamil). People from Kerala live around the world, including the UK, the USA, Canada, Australia, New Zealand and Ireland, so classmates may speak Malayalam at home. The name «Malayalam» reads the same forwards and backwards in English letters – a palindrome.
examples from the lessons: My friend Anu speaks Malayalam with her grandparents. | Malayalam is the main language of Kerala in India. | Malayalam has its own script with curly letters. | «Malayalam» is a palindrome: it reads the same backwards. | There is a Malayalam film festival in our city. | Malayalam and Tamil are related languages. | We learned to say «hello» in Malayalam: «namaskaram». | Many nurses in Ireland come from Kerala and speak Malayalam.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always written with a capital M, because it is the name of a language. Pronounced roughly «MAL-a-YAH-lam». It is not an English word; it is a name. Do not confuse with «Malay» (a different language, spoken in Malaysia) – they are not related.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Wanting to do harm or evil to others; full of hate and spite. 2) (in stories) Seeming evil and threatening: «a malevolent stare».
its sense in the lessons: In stories, «malevolent» describes villains, witches, evil spirits or a dark, threatening atmosphere: «a malevolent grin». It tells the reader that someone wants to hurt others on purpose. It is a strong, slightly formal word, good for creative writing. Opposite: «benevolent» (kind, wanting to do good). Phrases: «a malevolent spirit», «malevolent eyes».
examples from the lessons: The malevolent witch wanted to poison the princess. | A malevolent grin spread across the villain's face. | The old house had a malevolent feeling, as if something was watching. | The dragon gave him a malevolent stare. | In the story, a malevolent spirit haunted the mill. | He wasn't malevolent, just careless. | The storm clouds looked malevolent and dark. | Benevolent kings help people; malevolent ones harm them.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective; noun «malevolence», adverb «malevolently». «Mal-» means bad (as in malfunction, malpractice); «bene-» means good (benevolent). Stronger than «mean» or «unkind». Not a maths word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) Able to be hammered, pressed or bent into a new shape without breaking, like gold, copper or clay. 2) Easily changed or influenced by other people: «young minds are malleable».
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on materials, «malleable» is a key property of metals: you can beat them into thin sheets (like aluminium foil or gold leaf). Non-metals are often brittle instead. In everyday talk, a malleable person is easy to persuade. Related science words: «ductile» (can be pulled into wires), «brittle» (breaks easily).
examples from the lessons: Gold is so malleable it can be hammered thinner than paper. | Metals are malleable, but glass is brittle. | Clay is malleable when it is wet. | Aluminium foil shows that aluminium is malleable. | A blacksmith heats iron to make it more malleable. | Plasticine is malleable, so you can shape it easily. | Young children's ideas can be quite malleable. | We tested which materials were malleable by gently hitting them with a hammer.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective; noun «malleability». Spelling: double l, «-able»: malleable. Opposite in science: brittle. Do not confuse with «mallet» (a hammer) – though both come from the same Latin word for hammer. Not a maths word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A hammer with a big head made of wood, rubber or plastic, used to hit things without damaging them. 2) A long-handled stick used to hit the ball in croquet or polo. 3) (music) A stick with a soft or hard head used to play a xylophone or drum.
its sense in the lessons: In design and technology lessons, a mallet is used to tap wood joints together or put tent pegs in. In sport, croquet and polo players use mallets. In music, xylophone and glockenspiel players use mallets. Safety: hold the mallet firmly and keep fingers clear.
examples from the lessons: Dad used a rubber mallet to knock in the tent pegs. | The carpenter tapped the joint with a wooden mallet. | In croquet you hit the ball with a long mallet. | I played the xylophone with two soft mallets. | Polo players swing their mallets while riding horses. | Use the mallet, not a metal hammer, so the wood isn't dented. | The judge in a cartoon bangs a little mallet called a gavel. | Keep your fingers away when someone is using the mallet.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one mallet, two mallets. Spelling: double l, -et. A judge's small hammer is called a «gavel». Do not confuse with «malt» or «mullet». Not a maths word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (law) When a doctor, lawyer or other professional does their job very badly or carelessly, and someone is harmed because of it. 2) (formal) Wrong or dishonest behaviour in a job, such as cheating in exams or misusing money.
its sense in the lessons: In news and adult life, «medical malpractice» means a doctor's serious mistake that harms a patient, and the patient may take them to court. In schools in the UK, «exam malpractice» means cheating in exams, like copying or having a phone in the exam room; it can cancel your results. Phrases: «medical malpractice», «exam malpractice», «sued for malpractice».
examples from the lessons: Taking a phone into an exam counts as malpractice. | The hospital investigated a case of malpractice. | The doctor was sued for malpractice after the wrong operation. | Exam malpractice can mean losing all your marks for that subject. | The lawyer was accused of malpractice for losing the client's money. | Our teacher read out the rules about exam malpractice. | Most doctors are very careful, and malpractice is rare. | Copying from a friend's paper is malpractice.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable: «some malpractice», «a case of malpractice». «Mal-» means bad. It is a formal word. Not the same as an ordinary mistake: malpractice means a professional did not take proper care. Not a maths word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) To do with mammals, or belonging to the group of animals called mammals. 2) (science) Having the features of a mammal, like hair or fur and feeding young on milk.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on classification, «mammalian» is a formal word for «of mammals»: «mammalian features» include hair, warm blood, and mothers feeding babies with milk. It is used in biology books and documentaries. Phrases: «mammalian species», «mammalian cells», «mammalian features».
examples from the lessons: Bats are the only mammalian animals that can truly fly. | Hair is a mammalian feature. | Whales have mammalian lungs and breathe air. | Scientists studied mammalian cells in the lab. | The platypus is a strange mammalian creature that lays eggs. | Our teeth are typically mammalian, with different shapes for different jobs. | Fossils show early mammalian ancestors lived alongside dinosaurs. | Most mammalian babies are born live, not from eggs.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective from «mammal». Pronounced «ma-MAY-lee-an». Trap: whales and dolphins are mammals, not fish; bats are mammals, not birds. Not a maths word.

part of speech: noun (manga, uncountable; also a manga, mangas)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Japanese comics and graphic novels, usually read from right to left, with a special drawing style (big eyes, speed lines). 2) The drawing style of these comics.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, manga are very popular with children and teenagers around the world; many libraries have a manga section. In art lessons pupils try drawing in manga style. Many manga become anime (Japanese cartoons). Some manga are for adults, so check the age rating. Phrases: «read manga», «a manga series», «manga-style drawing».
examples from the lessons: My cousin reads a new manga every week. | Manga books are read from right to left. | Our library has a whole shelf of manga. | In art we drew a cat in manga style with big shiny eyes. | Many popular cartoons started as manga. | She is saving up for the next volume of her manga series. | «Manga» is a Japanese loanword. | Check the age rating, because some manga are for adults.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable («I love manga»), but «a manga» for one book is also used; plural «manga» or «mangas». A loanword from Japanese. Do not confuse with «mango» (the fruit) or «anime» (animated films and shows). Not a maths word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A skin disease of dogs, foxes, cats and other animals, caused by tiny mites; it makes the fur fall out and the skin itchy and sore.
its sense in the lessons: In science and animal care, mange is caused by mites that burrow into skin. Foxes in towns in the UK often have mange, which is why some look bald and thin. Vets can treat it with medicine. The adjective «mangy» means suffering from mange, and in everyday talk «mangy» also means shabby or scruffy: «a mangy old coat».
examples from the lessons: The poor fox had mange and had lost most of its fur. | The vet gave our dog drops to cure his mange. | Mange is caused by tiny mites in the skin. | A dog with mange scratches all the time. | Animal rescue groups help foxes with mange. | Mange can spread between animals that are close together. | The stray cat's mange got better after treatment. | Grandad called his old jumper «mangy».
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Pronounced «maynj» (rhymes with «change»). Adjective: mangy. Not the same as the French «manger» (to eat). Sarcoptic mange in dogs can sometimes cause an itchy rash on people too, so wash hands after touching a sick animal. Not a maths word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To control or influence someone in a clever, unfair or dishonest way, to get what you want. 2) To handle, move or work something skilfully with your hands: «manipulate the controls». 3) To change information, numbers or pictures, sometimes to trick people: «manipulate a photo». 4) (science, medicine) To move or press a body part to treat it.
its sense in the lessons: In personal safety lessons, manipulating means tricking someone into doing what you want – a sign of an unhealthy friendship or of online grooming. In maths, you «manipulate» numbers or equations (rearrange them). In computing and art, people manipulate images. In media lessons, children learn that photos and statistics can be manipulated to mislead. Phrases: «manipulate someone into», «manipulate data», «manipulate objects».
examples from the lessons: He tried to manipulate his sister into doing his chores. | A real friend does not manipulate you with guilt. | The robot arm can manipulate tiny objects. | In maths we manipulated the equation to find x. | That photo has been manipulated to make the wave look bigger. | Toddlers learn to manipulate blocks and shapes. | Advertisers sometimes try to manipulate how we feel. | If someone online tries to manipulate you, tell a trusted adult.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: manipulated, manipulating. Nouns: manipulation, manipulator; adjective: manipulative (usually bad: a manipulative person). The «control people» sense is negative; the «handle skilfully» sense is neutral. In maths, manipulating an equation keeps it true as long as you do the same to both sides.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Controlling or influencing people in a clever and unfair way, so they do what you want. 2) Skilful handling or moving of something with the hands or a tool. 3) Changing information, numbers or pictures, sometimes to trick people. 4) (medicine) Moving or pressing body parts to treat them.
its sense in the lessons: In personal safety and friendship lessons, manipulation is a warning sign: guilt trips, threats, flattery or keeping secrets to control someone. In media literacy, «photo manipulation» and «data manipulation» can mislead. In maths, «algebraic manipulation» means rearranging expressions and equations. Phrases: «emotional manipulation», «photo manipulation», «algebraic manipulation».
examples from the lessons: Saying «If you were my friend you'd do it» can be a kind of manipulation. | Photo manipulation can make a fake picture look real. | Algebraic manipulation helped us solve for y. | Playing with clay improves children's manipulation of small objects. | The advert used clever manipulation of our feelings. | Data manipulation can make a graph tell a false story. | The physiotherapist used gentle manipulation on Dad's back. | Learning to spot manipulation keeps you safer online.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable and uncountable. Verb: manipulate; adjective: manipulative. Usually negative when about people, neutral when about hands, tools or maths. In maths problems, «manipulation» of an equation must keep both sides equal.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A model of a human body used to show clothes in a shop window. 2) (old-fashioned) A person whose job is to model clothes; a fashion model. 3) A model of a body used in art or for practising first aid (often called a «manikin»).
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, mannequins stand in shop windows wearing clothes for sale. In first aid lessons, you practise CPR on a training dummy (also called a manikin). In 2016 the «mannequin challenge» was a viral video game where people froze still like mannequins. Phrases: «a shop mannequin», «stand still like a mannequin».
examples from the lessons: The mannequin in the window wore a red winter coat. | We practised CPR on a mannequin in first aid class. | My brother stood so still he looked like a mannequin. | The shop staff changed the clothes on the mannequins every week. | An artist's mannequin is a small wooden figure with bendy joints. | The mannequin had no head, just a body. | In the spooky story, the mannequins came alive at night. | The mannequin challenge has everyone freeze in a pose.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one mannequin, two mannequins. Spelling is tricky: m-a-n-n-e-q-u-i-n (double n, -quin). Pronounced «MAN-i-kin». A variant spelling «manikin» is often used for medical training dummies. Not a maths word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (religion) A word, sound or short phrase repeated again and again in prayer or meditation, especially in Hinduism and Buddhism. 2) A saying or motto that a person or group repeats often because they believe it strongly: «Practice makes perfect is my mantra».
its sense in the lessons: In religious education, mantras are part of Hindu and Buddhist practice, such as the sound «Om». In everyday life, a mantra is a favourite slogan you repeat to keep going: «Never give up». In mindfulness lessons, children may repeat a calming phrase like a mantra. Phrases: «repeat a mantra», «my mantra is…», «the school's mantra».
examples from the lessons: Our coach's mantra is «Work hard, play fair». | Buddhists may repeat a mantra while meditating. | «Om» is a well-known mantra in Hinduism. | When I'm nervous, I say my mantra: «I can do this». | The school's mantra is «Be kind, be safe, be your best». | She repeated the mantra slowly to calm her breathing. | «Reduce, reuse, recycle» became the class mantra. | Some mantras are in the old language Sanskrit.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one mantra, two mantras. A loanword from Sanskrit. In everyday English it often just means a motto or slogan. Not the same as «mantis» (an insect). Not a maths word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A musical instrument made of a hollow ball or gourd filled with seeds, beads or small stones, with a handle; you shake it to make a rattling sound. Usually played in pairs.
its sense in the lessons: In music lessons, maracas are percussion instruments used to keep the beat, especially in Latin American music (from places like Cuba, Puerto Rico, Mexico, Venezuela). You can make your own maracas in class from plastic bottles or eggs filled with rice. Phrases: «shake the maracas», «a pair of maracas».
examples from the lessons: I shook the maracas in time to the song. | We made maracas from yogurt pots filled with rice. | A pair of maracas makes a lovely shaking rhythm. | Maracas are popular in Latin American music. | The baby loves the sound of the plastic maraca. | Shake the maracas softly for the quiet part. | Old maracas were made from dried gourds with seeds inside. | In the band, I play the maracas and my friend plays the drum.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one maraca, two maracas; usually used in the plural because they come in pairs. A loanword from Portuguese/Spanish, probably from a South American language. Not a maths word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who walks in a march, especially a protest march or a parade. 2) (history, UK) The Marcher Lords were powerful nobles who ruled the borderlands («the Marches») between England and Wales.
its sense in the lessons: In history and citizenship lessons, marchers take part in protests (like the civil rights marches in the USA or the suffragette marches in the UK) to show what they believe. In parades, marchers walk in step, like bands on Remembrance Day or St Patrick's Day. Phrases: «peace marchers», «protest marchers», «thousands of marchers».
examples from the lessons: Thousands of marchers walked through the city to protest. | The marchers carried banners and sang songs. | Civil rights marchers crossed the bridge at Selma in 1965. | The police closed the road so the marchers could pass. | Marchers in the St Patrick's Day parade wore green. | Each marcher held a candle for peace. | The Marcher Lords guarded the border with Wales. | Some marchers walked over 300 miles.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one marcher, two marchers. From «march» + «-er». Peaceful protest is a legal right in the UK, USA, Canada, Australia, New Zealand and Ireland, within rules. Not a maths word, though counting marchers is a classic estimation problem.

part of speech: noun (a mare, mares; mare – Latin «sea», plural «maria»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A female horse, donkey or zebra, especially an adult one. 2) (astronomy) A large, dark, flat area on the Moon, once thought to be a sea; plural «maria». 3) (UK slang, from «nightmare») A terrible or annoying situation: «It was a right mare getting here».
its sense in the lessons: In science and farm topics, a mare is a female horse; a male is a stallion, and a baby is a foal. In astronomy, the dark patches on the Moon are «maria», like the Sea of Tranquillity (Mare Tranquillitatis), where Apollo 11 landed. In UK slang, «a mare» or «a nightmare» is a really bad time. Phrases: «a mare and her foal», «having a mare» (UK slang: doing very badly).
examples from the lessons: The mare stood in the field with her new foal. | A female horse is called a mare. | Apollo 11 landed in a mare called the Sea of Tranquillity. | The dark patches on the Moon are called maria. | (slang, UK) The traffic was a total mare this morning. | (slang, UK) Our goalie had a mare and let in five goals. | The farmer has three mares and one stallion. | The grey mare jumped the fence easily.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one mare, two mares. The Moon sense is pronounced «MAH-ray», plural «maria». Do not confuse with «mayor» (a town leader, sounds the same in some accents) or «mere». The slang «mare» is short for «nightmare» – informal, not for writing tests.

part of speech: noun (Mari – a name of a people, a language and an ancient city); also a name
meaning for a pupil: 1) (a people) The Mari are a Finno-Ugric people who live mainly in the Mari El Republic in Russia, by the Volga river. 2) (a language) Mari is the language of that people, related to Finnish and Hungarian. 3) (history) Mari was an ancient city in what is now Syria, famous for clay tablets with old writing. 4) (a name) A girl's name in several countries, such as Estonia, Finland and Japan.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and history lessons Mari can appear as a people and language of Russia or as an ancient city on the Euphrates river in Syria, where archaeologists found thousands of clay tablets. As a name, it is a girl's name. It is not an ordinary English word. Do not confuse with «Mary» or «marry».
examples from the lessons: The Mari people have their own language and traditions. | Mari is related to Finnish. | Archaeologists found a royal palace at ancient Mari. | Clay tablets from Mari tell us about life 4,000 years ago. | My friend Mari comes from Estonia. | The Mari El Republic is in Russia. | Mari is a short name, often used in Finland and Japan. | The ruins of Mari are near the border of Syria and Iraq.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A name, so it is written with a capital M. Not an English common word. Different from «Mary» (a name), «marry» (to wed) and «merry» (happy), which sound similar in some accents.

part of speech: noun (a marinade, marinades); verb (marinade, marinades, marinaded, marinading – mostly UK)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A mixture of liquids like oil, vinegar, lemon juice, soy sauce, herbs and spices, in which food (meat, fish, tofu, vegetables) is soaked before cooking to add flavour or make it softer. 2) (verb, mostly UK) To soak food in such a mixture; also called «marinate».
its sense in the lessons: In cooking and food lessons, you make a marinade and leave chicken or vegetables in it for a while, in the fridge, before grilling or baking. The acid (lemon, vinegar, yogurt) can soften meat a little. Safety: keep raw meat marinade in the fridge and do not use it as a sauce unless it is boiled. Phrases: «leave in the marinade», «marinade overnight».
examples from the lessons: We made a marinade of lemon, garlic and olive oil. | Leave the chicken in the marinade for two hours. | The tofu soaked up the soy sauce marinade. | Dad's barbecue marinade has honey in it. | Keep meat in the marinade in the fridge, not on the table. | Throw away marinade that had raw meat in it, unless you boil it first. | The fish was marinaded in lime juice. | A yogurt marinade makes chicken soft and tasty.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The noun is «marinade»; the verb is usually «marinate» (marinate, marinated), though «marinade» as a verb is common in the UK. Countable: two marinades. Myth: marinades do not go deep into meat; most flavour stays near the surface. Not a maths word, but recipes use ratios (e.g. 3 parts oil to 1 part vinegar).

part of speech: noun (marmalade, uncountable; marmalades – kinds of marmalade)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A kind of jam made from oranges or other citrus fruits (like lemons or limes), with thin strips of peel in it. 2) (colour) An orange colour, often used for ginger cats: «a marmalade cat».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday British, Irish, Australian and New Zealand life, marmalade on toast is a traditional breakfast. Seville oranges, which are bitter, are used to make it in January. Paddington Bear loves marmalade sandwiches. A «marmalade cat» is an orange or ginger cat. Phrases: «orange marmalade», «marmalade on toast», «a marmalade cat».
examples from the lessons: I had toast and marmalade for breakfast. | Paddington Bear keeps a marmalade sandwich under his hat. | Gran makes marmalade from Seville oranges every January. | Our marmalade cat sleeps on the windowsill. | Lime marmalade is a bit sour. | Marmalade has thin strips of peel in it. | Can you pass the marmalade, please? | We weighed the sugar and oranges to make marmalade in class.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable: «some marmalade». In British use «marmalade» means citrus jam only; in many other languages similar words mean any jam – a false friend. Spelling: marm-a-lade. Not a maths word, but recipes use weights and ratios.

part of speech: noun (a marquee, marquees); adjective (marquee – US, informal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (UK, Australia, NZ, Ireland) A very large tent used for outdoor events like weddings, fairs and garden parties. 2) (US, Canada) A sign or roof over the entrance of a theatre or cinema, showing the names of shows and stars in lights. 3) (adjective, US) Most famous and important: «a marquee player».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life in the UK and Australia, a marquee is put up at weddings, school fêtes, cricket matches and agricultural shows. In the USA, the marquee is the lit-up sign outside a cinema. In sport, a «marquee signing» is a star player a club buys. Phrases: «put up a marquee», «under the marquee», «marquee player».
examples from the lessons: The school fête had a big white marquee for the cake stall. | When it rained, everyone crowded into the marquee. | The wedding party danced in a marquee in the garden. | The cinema marquee showed the name of the new film in lights. | The club's marquee signing scored in his first game. | It took ten people to put up the marquee. | The flower show was held in three marquees. | The marquee pegs were hammered deep into the grass.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one marquee, two marquees. Pronounced «mar-KEE». Spelling: m-a-r-q-u-e-e. Do not confuse with «marquis» (a noble title). British and American meanings differ. Not a maths word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A kitchen tool with a handle and a flat head with holes or a wavy wire, used to crush cooked potatoes or other food into a soft mush (a potato masher). 2) (old-fashioned slang) A man who made unwanted advances to women in public; this sense is old and rarely used now.
its sense in the lessons: In cooking lessons and at home, a potato masher is used to make mashed potatoes, mashed swede or mashed banana for baby food. Sometimes «masher» is a machine for crushing fruit or grain. In history, a German WWII grenade was nicknamed «potato masher» because of its shape. Phrases: «potato masher».
examples from the lessons: Pass me the potato masher, please. | Mum used the masher to make fluffy mashed potatoes. | We mashed the bananas with a masher for banana bread. | The masher has a wavy metal head. | Use the masher until there are no lumps left. | Our masher is made of plastic so it won't scratch the pan. | Grandad calls me the best potato masher in the family. | A masher crushes; a whisk mixes air in.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one masher, two mashers. From the verb «mash» (to crush into a soft mass). The old slang sense (a man pestering women) is outdated. Not a maths word.

part of speech: noun (a master, masters); verb (master, masters, mastered, mastering); adjective (master)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A man who has control over people, animals or a place: «the dog obeyed its master». 2) A person who is very skilled at something: «a chess master», «a master chef». 3) (verb) To learn something until you can do it very well: «master your times tables». 4) (verb) To control a feeling: «master your fear». 5) (UK, old-fashioned) A male teacher in a school: «the maths master». 6) (adjective) Main or most important: «the master bedroom», «the master copy». 7) A university degree after the first one: «a master's degree». 8) (history) A person who owned enslaved people or employed servants. 9) (old, polite) A title for a boy: «Master Tom Smith».
its sense in the lessons: In school, «master» as a verb is common: «master the skill», «master fractions». In history, «masters» and «servants», or slaveowners called masters, are part of lessons on the past. In stories, a dog's master, a sea captain called «the Master», and «Master» as a polite title for boys appear. «Master key» opens every lock; «master plan» is the main secret plan. Phrases: «master a skill», «Master's degree», «old masters» (great painters), «master and servant».
examples from the lessons: Once you master riding a bike, you never forget. | The dog sat at its master's feet. | It took me weeks to master the seven times table. | Our new teacher is a chess master. | The caretaker has a master key that opens every room. | She tried to master her fear of heights. | The villain had a master plan to steal the crown. | The letter was addressed to «Master James Brown». | In old schools the boys called their teachers «sir» or «master». | The museum has paintings by the old masters.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: mastered, mastering. Nouns: mastery, masterpiece. Female forms: «mistress» (old) – today «master» in skill senses is used for anyone, any gender («she's a master of disguise»). Some places now avoid «master» in computing (for example «main branch») because of its link to slavery. In maths, «master» a method means you can use it accurately every time.

part of speech: adjective (matt – UK; matte – US); noun (Matt – a name)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Not shiny; having a dull, flat surface: «matt paint», «a matt photo». 2) (a name) Matt is a boy's name, short for Matthew.
its sense in the lessons: In art and design lessons and at the paint shop, «matt» paint has no shine, while «gloss» is shiny and «satin» is in between. Photos can be printed matt or glossy. Make-up and screens can be matt too. As a name, Matt is very common in English-speaking countries.
examples from the lessons: We painted the walls with matt white paint. | Gloss paint is shiny, but matt paint is dull. | The photos came out matt, not glossy. | Matt paint hides bumps on the wall better. | My phone has a matt screen protector to stop glare. | Matt is my best friend in class. | The artist chose a matt finish for the poster. | A matt surface does not reflect light like a mirror.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK, Australia, NZ, Ireland usually spell it «matt»; the USA usually «matte»; both are correct. Do not confuse with «mat» (a small rug) or «mate» (friend). As a name it needs a capital: Matt. Not a maths word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Making something as big, high or great as possible: «the maximisation of profit». 2) (maths) Finding the largest possible value of something under some rules.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, maximisation problems ask, for example: what is the largest area of a field you can fence with 20 m of fence? (Answer: a 5 m by 5 m square gives 25 m².) In business and economics, «profit maximisation» means trying to earn as much money as possible. In science and engineering, people maximise efficiency or energy. It is a formal word. Opposite: «minimisation».
examples from the lessons: The maths puzzle was about maximisation of the rectangle's area. | Profit maximisation is the main goal of many companies. | Maximisation of space helped fit all the books on the shelves. | The engineers worked on the maximisation of the battery's life. | In this game, maximisation of your score means collecting every coin. | Maximisation and minimisation are two sides of optimisation. | The farmer planned for maximisation of his crop. | A square gives maximisation of area for a fixed perimeter of a rectangle.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Formal. UK/Australia/NZ spelling «maximisation», US/Canada «maximization». Verb: maximise/maximize; adjective: maximum. In maths problems, maximisation means find the greatest value allowed by the rules (the constraints) – not infinity.

part of speech: noun (mayo, uncountable – short for mayonnaise); noun (Mayo – a county in Ireland)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) Short for mayonnaise: a thick, creamy white sauce made from egg yolks, oil and lemon juice or vinegar, eaten with chips, sandwiches and salads. 2) (a place) Mayo is a county in the west of Ireland, known for its coast, mountains and Gaelic football.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, «mayo» is a common word in shops and cafés: «a chicken mayo sandwich», «chips and mayo». In geography, County Mayo is in Connacht in Ireland; its main town is Castlebar. Food safety: mayonnaise with raw egg should be kept cold.
examples from the lessons: Can I have mayo on my chips? | A chicken mayo sandwich is my favourite. | Mayo is made from eggs and oil. | Keep the mayo in the fridge after opening it. | In the Netherlands and Belgium, people often eat chips with mayo. | Our cousins live in County Mayo, in the west of Ireland. | Mayo play Gaelic football in green and red. | I like mayo, but my sister prefers ketchup.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal short form of «mayonnaise». Uncountable: «some mayo». The Irish county takes a capital: Mayo. Not a maths word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Having a clear meaning or making sense: «a meaningful sentence». 2) Important, serious or valuable to someone: «a meaningful friendship», «a meaningful job». 3) Showing a hidden feeling without words: «a meaningful look». 4) (maths, science) Big or real enough to matter, not just chance: «a meaningful difference».
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons a meaningful sentence makes sense; a jumble of words is not meaningful. In everyday life, a meaningful gift or chat is one that matters. In stories, «a meaningful look» tells the reader two characters share a secret thought. In science and maths, a «meaningful difference» means the result is big enough to trust, not just luck. Phrases: «meaningful look», «meaningful conversation», «make it meaningful».
examples from the lessons: Volunteering at the food bank felt really meaningful. | Mum gave Dad a meaningful look, and he stopped talking. | Put the words in order to make a meaningful sentence. | We had a meaningful talk about being kind. | A small difference of 1 cm is not meaningful when we measure with a ruler to the nearest cm. | Her grandfather's watch is very meaningful to her. | The teacher wants our feedback to be meaningful, not just «good job». | Meaningful work helps people feel proud.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective; adverb «meaningfully». Opposite: «meaningless». Spelling: meaning + ful (one l). In maths/science problems, a meaningful answer has sensible units and size – a 50 m tall child is not a meaningful answer.

meaning for a pupil: 1) By an amount that can be measured or noticed: «measurably better». 2) Clearly and noticeably, not just a tiny bit.
its sense in the lessons: In science, «measurably» means you can see the change with measurement: «the plant grew measurably in one week». In everyday life it means clearly or noticeably: «my reading has improved measurably». In reports and formal writing it is used to show evidence. Phrases: «measurably better», «measurably different».
examples from the lessons: The plant was measurably taller after a week in the sun. | Her running speed improved measurably over the term. | The air in the room was measurably warmer after the heater was on. | Washing hands measurably reduces germs. | The new road made the journey measurably shorter. | Our test scores went up measurably after extra practice. | The two balls were measurably different in weight. | The pond is measurably lower in summer.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from «measurable» + «-ly». Formal. Opposite: «immeasurably» (so much that it cannot be measured; often means «hugely»). In maths/science a measurable change must be bigger than the error of the measuring tool.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To get involved in someone else's business when you are not wanted, and often make things worse. 2) To touch or fiddle with something you should leave alone: «don't meddle with the wires».
its sense in the lessons: In stories, a meddler pokes their nose into other people's lives, like a nosy neighbour or a busybody aunt; meddling characters often cause trouble. In safety, «don't meddle with» electricity, gas or medicines. Phrases: «meddle in someone's affairs», «meddle with», «stop meddling». Famous line from cartoons: «those meddling kids» (Scooby-Doo).
examples from the lessons: Please don't meddle in our argument. | My little brother meddled with my model and broke it. | Never meddle with electric sockets. | The nosy neighbour always meddles in other people's business. | «I would have got away with it, if it weren't for you meddling kids!» | She meddled with the TV settings and now nothing works. | Grandma says it's best not to meddle. | Countries should not meddle in other countries' elections.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: meddled, meddling. Noun: meddler; adjective: meddlesome. Followed by «in» (affairs) or «with» (objects). Homophone: «medal» (a prize) – sounds the same, different meaning! Not a maths word.

part of speech: noun (meddling, uncountable); adjective (meddling); verb (-ing form of meddle)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (noun) The act of getting involved in other people's business when you are not wanted. 2) (adjective) Often interfering in other people's affairs: «a meddling neighbour». 3) (verb form) «-ing» form of «meddle»: «Stop meddling!»
its sense in the lessons: In stories, a meddling character (an aunt, a neighbour, a nosy fairy) causes problems by interfering. In history and news, «foreign meddling» means one country interfering in another's politics. In everyday life adults say «Stop meddling!» to children fiddling with things. Phrases: «a meddling busybody», «foreign meddling».
examples from the lessons: The meddling neighbour told everyone our news. | Her meddling made the problem worse. | Stop meddling with the thermostat! | The villain shouted about «meddling kids». | There were claims of foreign meddling in the election. | The meddling cat knocked the jigsaw off the table. | Thanks to his meddling, the surprise party was ruined. | Grandad hates meddling, so he lets us solve our own problems.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Form of «meddle». As a noun it is uncountable. Homophone trap: «medalling» (winning a medal, in sports talk) sounds similar. Spelling: double d, «-ling». Not a maths word.

part of speech: noun (Medusa – a name in Greek myth; a medusa, medusae or medusas – science)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (a name, Greek myth) Medusa was a monster, a Gorgon, with snakes for hair; anyone who looked at her face was turned to stone. The hero Perseus cut off her head. 2) (science) A medusa is the swimming, umbrella-shaped stage of a jellyfish or similar sea creature.
its sense in the lessons: In lessons on Greek myths, Medusa is one of the most famous monsters; Perseus defeated her by looking at her reflection in his shiny shield. Her image appears in art and on shields as a symbol of protection. In science lessons on sea life, jellyfish have a polyp stage (stuck to rocks) and a medusa stage (swimming bell). Phrases: «Medusa's head», «the medusa stage».
