examples from the lessons: Medusa had snakes instead of hair. | Anyone who looked at Medusa turned to stone. | Perseus used a mirror-shield so he would not look straight at Medusa. | In the myth, the winged horse Pegasus sprang from Medusa. | A jellyfish in its medusa stage swims by pulsing its bell. | The museum has an old coin with Medusa's face. | Medusae drift with the ocean currents. | Some later stories say Medusa was once a beautiful woman who was cursed.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a name it takes a capital: Medusa. In science the plural is «medusae» or «medusas». Pronounced «meh-DYOO-za». Myths are stories, not history. Not a maths word.

part of speech: noun (Meg – a name; a meg, megs – informal short for megabyte); verb (meg – UK football slang: nutmeg)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (a name) Meg is a girl's name, short for Margaret or Megan, like Meg in «Little Women». 2) (informal, computers) Short for megabyte: «a 5-meg file». 3) (UK, football slang) To kick the ball between an opponent's legs; short for «nutmeg».
its sense in the lessons: As a name, Meg appears in books (Meg March in «Little Women», «Meg and Mog»). In everyday computer talk, people say «megs» for megabytes, though in modern use gigabytes are more common. On the football pitch, children shout «megs!» when someone kicks the ball through another player's legs. It is informal, not for written tests.
examples from the lessons: Meg and Mog is a book about a witch and her cat. | My cousin Meg is learning to swim. | That photo is only two megs, so it will send quickly. | (slang, UK) He megged the defender and scored! | (slang) «Megs!» shouted everyone in the playground. | Meg is the oldest sister in «Little Women». | The game download was 300 megs. | A meg is about a million bytes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a name, capital M: Meg. «Meg» for megabyte is informal; the full word or «MB» is used in school. In maths, 1 megabyte = 1,000,000 bytes (or 1,048,576 bytes in the older computer counting). «Meg» (football) is short for «nutmeg», which is also a spice – different meaning.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A cone-shaped device you speak into to make your voice louder, so a crowd can hear you; modern ones use batteries and are electric. 2) (figurative) Something that helps a person spread their message widely.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, megaphones are used at sports days, protests, beaches, fire drills and on boats. In science, a simple cone megaphone directs sound waves forward, so the voice carries further. Safety: never shout into someone's ear with a megaphone, because very loud sound can damage hearing. Phrases: «speak through a megaphone», «megaphone diplomacy» (shouting messages publicly rather than talking).
examples from the lessons: The teacher used a megaphone at sports day. | The lifeguard shouted through a megaphone to the swimmers. | We made a megaphone from rolled-up card. | The protesters had a megaphone and a big banner. | The megaphone makes your voice louder in one direction. | During the fire drill, the head teacher used a megaphone. | Don't point a megaphone at anyone's ear. | Social media can be a megaphone for anyone's opinion.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one megaphone, two megaphones. «Mega-» means big; «-phone» means sound (as in telephone, microphone). Also called a «loudhailer» (UK) or «bullhorn» (US). Not a maths word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) Made of a membrane, or like a membrane: thin, soft and skin-like, often so thin you can almost see through it. 2) (science) Having thin skin-like parts, like a bat's or insect's wings.
its sense in the lessons: In science, «membranous» describes thin layers in plants and animals: bat wings, insect wings, the skin inside an eggshell, and membranes around cells. It is a formal biology word. Phrases: «membranous wings», «a membranous layer».
examples from the lessons: Bats have membranous wings stretched between their fingers. | Dragonflies have clear, membranous wings. | Inside the eggshell is a thin, membranous layer. | The frog's feet are joined by membranous webs. | The onion skin is thin and membranous. | Under the microscope we saw a membranous sheet of cells. | Some seeds have membranous wings to help them fly. | The pterosaur had large membranous wings.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective from «membrane». Pronounced «MEM-bra-nus». Formal science word. Not a maths word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Plural of «man»: adult male people. 2) People in general, in old-fashioned writing: «all men are created equal» (now many people prefer «people» or «everyone»). 3) Soldiers or workers under a leader: «the captain and his men». 4) Pieces in some board games: «chessmen», «the men in draughts».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: «men's toilets», «men and women», «men's football». In history texts you will meet «men» meaning all people, and «the king and his men». In maths problems: «3 men can paint a fence in 6 hours» – such problems are about rate of work. In games, draughts (checkers) pieces are called men. Phrases: «men and women», «the men's team», «one of the men».
examples from the lessons: Two men were fixing the road outside school. | The men's race starts at ten o'clock. | The captain led his men across the river. | «All men are created equal» is a famous line from 1776. | My dad plays in a men's football team on Sundays. | In draughts, each player starts with twelve men. | Men and women can both be nurses, pilots and engineers. | If 2 men can build a wall in 6 days, 4 men might do it in 3 days.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular plural: one man, two men (not «mans»). Possessive: «men's» (not «mens'»): «the men's room». Similarly woman → women. In maths work problems, more workers usually means less time (inverse proportion), if they work at the same rate.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A collection of wild or unusual animals kept to be shown to people, especially in the past (an early kind of zoo). 2) (informal) A mixed group of many different animals, or of strange and different people or things.
its sense in the lessons: In history, kings kept menageries, like the Royal Menagerie at the Tower of London (which had lions and a polar bear!). Today we have zoos, which also focus on care and saving species. In everyday talk, a family with lots of pets has «a menagerie». Phrases: «a menagerie of pets», «the royal menagerie».
examples from the lessons: The Tower of London once had a royal menagerie with lions. | Our house is a menagerie: two dogs, a cat, three rabbits and a snake. | The circus travelled with a menagerie of wild animals. | Grandma's garden is a menagerie of birds and squirrels. | The story is about a strange menagerie of creatures in a magic wood. | A menagerie was an early kind of zoo. | The class pets became a little menagerie. | The play had a menagerie of odd characters.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one menagerie, two menageries. Pronounced «meh-NAJ-er-ee». Spelling: m-e-n-a-g-e-r-i-e. A loanword from French. Not a maths word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science, health) The natural monthly bleeding from the womb (uterus) through the vagina that happens to girls and women, usually from puberty until about age 50; it is also called «having a period».
its sense in the lessons: In health and puberty lessons (PSHE, health education), menstruation is explained as a normal part of growing up: about once a month, the lining of the womb comes away as blood if there is no pregnancy. It usually begins between ages 8 and 16. Pads, tampons, period pants and menstrual cups are used. Schools in many places provide free period products. Phrases: «the menstrual cycle», «start menstruation», «period pain».
examples from the lessons: Menstruation is a normal part of puberty. | Our health lesson explained menstruation and the menstrual cycle. | Menstruation usually happens about once a month. | Most people call menstruation «having a period». | Some girls start menstruation at nine, others at fifteen – both are normal. | The school nurse has pads for anyone who needs them. | Menstruation stops during pregnancy. | It's fine to ask a parent or the school nurse questions about menstruation.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Adjective: menstrual. Verb: menstruate. Everyday word: «period». It is nothing to be ashamed of, and it is not an illness. Myths: you can swim, do sport and wash your hair during a period. In maths, the menstrual cycle is often about 28 days, but anywhere from about 21 to 35 days is normal.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The usual way a person or group thinks and feels about things; their attitude: «a winning mentality». 2) (formal) A person's mind or thinking ability.
its sense in the lessons: In sport and school, coaches talk about «a winning mentality», «a growth mentality» (believing you can get better with effort), or «a team mentality». It can also be negative: «a mob mentality» means people in a crowd doing things they would not do alone. Phrases: «a winning mentality», «herd mentality», «us-versus-them mentality».
examples from the lessons: Our coach says we need a winning mentality. | A growth mentality means believing you can learn hard things. | Mob mentality made the crowd start pushing. | Grandma has a «waste not, want not» mentality. | Her positive mentality helped her finish the race. | The team changed its mentality after the half-time talk. | Copying everyone else is called a herd mentality. | An «us versus them» mentality can lead to bullying.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one mentality, two mentalities. Not the same as «mental» (about the mind; also slang «crazy»). Related: mindset (very similar), attitude. Not a maths word.

part of speech: noun (a mentor, mentors); verb (mentor, mentors, mentored, mentoring)
meaning for a pupil: 1) An experienced and trusted person who helps and advises a younger or less experienced person over time. 2) (verb) To help and guide someone in this way. 3) (a name, Greek myth) Mentor was Odysseus's friend, who helped his son Telemachus – this is where the word comes from.
its sense in the lessons: In school, older pupils may mentor younger ones (a «buddy» or «peer mentor» scheme); new teachers have mentors too. In sport and jobs, a mentor helps you learn the ropes. In stories, a wise mentor guides the hero (like a wizard teaching a young apprentice). Phrases: «a peer mentor», «mentoring scheme», «my mentor».
examples from the lessons: My mentor in Year 6 helped me settle into school. | Our coach mentors the younger players. | In many stories, the hero has a wise old mentor. | She became a reading mentor for the infants. | A good mentor listens and gives honest advice. | The new teacher was mentored by an experienced colleague. | In the Odyssey, Mentor gave advice to young Telemachus. | Being a mentor helped him learn too.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one mentor, two mentors. Regular verb: mentored, mentoring. The person helped is a «mentee». Not the same as «menthol» or «mental». Not a maths word.

part of speech: noun (merchandise, uncountable; informal short form «merch»); verb (merchandise, merchandises, merchandised, merchandising)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Goods that are bought and sold, especially in shops. 2) Things like T-shirts, mugs and toys sold with the name or picture of a band, film, team or game on them; often called «merch». 3) (verb, business) To promote and sell goods, for example by how they are displayed.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, «merchandise» is the official stuff you can buy from a football club, film or band: shirts, scarves, posters. In maths, shops and merchandise appear in money problems (prices, discounts, profit). In business studies, merchandising is how shops arrange products to sell more. Phrases: «official merchandise», «band merch», «merchandise stall».
examples from the lessons: The club sells official merchandise at the stadium. | My sister bought band merch at the concert. | The shop's merchandise is on sale this week. | Film merchandise like toys and lunchboxes makes a lot of money. | All damaged merchandise must be returned to the store. | We set up a merchandise stall at the school fair. | The merchandise costs £8 each, so three items cost £24. | Shops put popular merchandise at eye level.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «a lot of merchandise», not «merchandises». Ends in -ise (both UK and US). Informal: «merch». Related: merchant (a person who sells), commerce. In maths problems, profit = selling price − cost of the merchandise.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Luckily; in a way that you are thankful for, because something bad was avoided or ended: «Mercifully, nobody was hurt». 2) In a kind and forgiving way, showing mercy: «the king acted mercifully».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday talk and stories, «mercifully» usually means «thank goodness»: «The test was mercifully short». It shows relief. The older sense means acting with mercy, like a judge or king who forgives. Phrases: «mercifully short», «mercifully, it stopped raining».
examples from the lessons: Mercifully, the rain stopped before the match. | The speech was mercifully short. | Mercifully, nobody was hurt in the crash. | The queen acted mercifully and set the prisoner free. | The long car journey mercifully ended at last. | Mercifully, I had remembered my coat. | The dentist was quick, mercifully. | The judge mercifully gave him a second chance.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from «merciful» + «-ly». Usually at the start of a sentence with a comma: «Mercifully, …». Related: mercy, merciful, merciless (with no mercy). Not a maths word.

part of speech: noun (a merino, merinos; merino – the wool, uncountable)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A breed of sheep with very fine, soft wool, first from Spain and now raised in large numbers in Australia and New Zealand. 2) The soft, warm wool from these sheep, or cloth made from it.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons on Australia and New Zealand, merino sheep and wool are an important part of farming history and trade. In everyday life, merino jumpers, socks and base layers are popular for keeping warm without itching. Phrases: «merino wool», «merino sheep», «a merino jumper».
examples from the lessons: Merino sheep have very soft wool. | Australia has millions of merino sheep. | My merino jumper is warm and doesn't itch. | Hikers often wear merino socks. | New Zealand farmers sell merino wool all around the world. | Merino sheep were first bred in Spain. | Shearing a merino sheep takes skill. | Merino wool keeps you warm even when it is a bit damp.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable for sheep (one merino, two merinos), uncountable for wool. Pronounced «meh-REE-no». A loanword from Spanish. Not a maths word, though wool weight and price problems may appear.

part of speech: noun (a merlin, merlins); noun (Merlin – a name)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A small, fast falcon (a bird of prey) found in Europe, Asia and North America, which hunts small birds. 2) (a name, legend) Merlin is the wise wizard in the stories of King Arthur, who guided and advised him.
its sense in the lessons: In nature studies, the merlin is one of the smallest falcons; it lives on moors and open land and catches birds in fast chases. In literature and legends, Merlin is the famous wizard of Camelot, who in many tellings helped Arthur become king and pull the sword from the stone. Phrases: «Merlin the wizard», «a merlin falcon».
examples from the lessons: A merlin is a small, fast falcon. | We saw a merlin chasing a pipit over the moor. | Merlin the wizard helped young Arthur. | In some stories Merlin lives backwards in time. | Merlins nest on the ground in heather. | The book tells how Merlin brought the stones of Stonehenge – but that is a legend, not history. | A merlin is smaller than a kestrel. | Merlin is often drawn with a long beard and a pointed hat.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The bird is «a merlin» (small m); the wizard is «Merlin» (capital M). Merlin the wizard is a character in legends; historians are not sure he ever existed. Not a maths word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Happy fun, laughter and enjoyment, especially when people are together celebrating. 2) Amusement: «his mistake caused much merriment».
its sense in the lessons: In stories and old-fashioned writing, merriment is the jolly fun at feasts, parties, Christmas and weddings. It tells the reader everyone is happy and laughing. In everyday speech it is a bit formal or playful. Phrases: «much merriment», «festive merriment», «eyes twinkling with merriment».
examples from the lessons: There was great merriment at the Christmas party. | The village feast was full of music and merriment. | Grandpa's eyes twinkled with merriment. | My silly hat caused much merriment. | The fair was a place of merriment and games. | Their merriment echoed down the street. | After the win, the team's merriment lasted all evening. | Robin Hood and his merry men lived with laughter and merriment.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «much merriment», not «a merriment». From «merry» + «-ment». Spelling: merr-i-ment (y changes to i). Not a maths word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (geography) A hill or mountain with steep sides and a large, flat top, found in dry places like the south-west USA and parts of Australia. 2) (Spanish) «Mesa» means «table» in Spanish; the hill is named for its table-like shape.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons on landforms, mesas form when soft rock around a hard cap of rock is worn away by wind and water (erosion). A smaller one is called a «butte». Famous mesas are in Arizona, Utah and New Mexico (for example Monument Valley). Phrases: «a flat-topped mesa», «mesa and butte».
examples from the lessons: A mesa is a hill with a flat top like a table. | We saw red mesas in the desert in Arizona. | Erosion slowly turned the plateau into mesas. | A butte is smaller and narrower than a mesa. | The old village was built on top of a mesa for safety. | «Mesa» means «table» in Spanish. | The cowboy rode past the tall mesa. | In Australia, flat-topped hills like mesas are sometimes called «jump-ups».
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one mesa, two mesas. Pronounced «MAY-sa». A loanword from Spanish. Order by size: plateau (largest) → mesa → butte (smallest). Not a maths word.

part of speech: noun (a mesquite, mesquites; mesquite – the wood, uncountable)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A spiny shrub or small tree of the pea family that grows in deserts and dry lands of the south-western USA and Mexico, with long seed pods. 2) The wood of this tree, used to give a smoky flavour to barbecued food.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and science lessons about deserts, mesquite is a desert survivor: its roots can go very deep (sometimes over 50 metres) to reach water. Native peoples ground its pods into flour. In cooking, «mesquite-grilled» food is cooked over mesquite wood. In Australia, mesquite was brought in and is now a harmful weed. Phrases: «mesquite tree», «mesquite smoke».
examples from the lessons: Mesquite trees grow in the deserts of Mexico and the USA. | Mesquite roots reach deep underground for water. | The barbecue was flavoured with mesquite wood. | Native Americans made flour from mesquite pods. | Cattle eat mesquite pods in dry seasons. | In Australia, mesquite is a weed that spreads quickly. | The desert road was lined with thorny mesquite. | Mesquite-smoked chicken has a strong flavour.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable for trees, uncountable for the wood. Pronounced «mes-KEET». A loanword from Spanish, from the Aztec language Nahuatl. Not a maths word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Very fast and sudden, especially a rise to fame or success: «a meteoric rise». 2) (science) To do with meteors or meteorites: «meteoric dust», «meteoric iron».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and news, «a meteoric rise» means someone became famous or successful very quickly, like a young singer or footballer. In science (space), meteoric material comes from space rocks; some ancient iron tools were made from meteoric iron. The picture: a meteor flashes across the sky very fast and bright. Phrases: «a meteoric rise», «meteoric iron».
examples from the lessons: The singer had a meteoric rise to fame. | The team's meteoric rise took them from the bottom league to the top in three years. | Tutankhamun had a dagger made of meteoric iron. | Scientists study meteoric dust collected from Antarctic ice. | Her career was meteoric. | Meteoric rock is different from Earth rock. | The app's meteoric success surprised everyone. | Some meteoric rises end just as fast.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective from «meteor». Usually used with «rise» or «success». Trap: a real meteor burns up quickly – but «a meteoric rise» means quick and bright, not «short-lived» (though people sometimes use it that way). Not about weather – that is «meteorological».

meaning for a pupil: 1) The science of the weather and the atmosphere: studying air, temperature, wind, clouds and rain to understand and predict the weather.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and science lessons, meteorology explains weather forecasts. Meteorologists use thermometers, rain gauges, barometers, weather balloons, satellites and computer models. National weather services include the Met Office (UK), Met Éireann (Ireland), the Bureau of Meteorology (Australia), MetService (New Zealand), Environment Canada and the National Weather Service (USA). Phrases: «study meteorology», «the Bureau of Meteorology».
examples from the lessons: Meteorology is the science of the weather. | A scientist who studies meteorology is a meteorologist. | Our class weather station is a small start in meteorology. | The Met Office uses meteorology to forecast storms. | Meteorology helps farmers know when to plant. | Satellites have changed meteorology a lot. | In Australia, the Bureau of Meteorology issues weather warnings. | Meteorology uses maths and computers to predict tomorrow's weather.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Trap: meteorology is about weather, NOT meteors – even though it comes from the same Greek word «meteoron» (thing high in the air). The study of meteors is part of astronomy. Adjective: meteorological. In maths, weather data gives averages, ranges and graphs.

part of speech: noun (a mews, mews – the same form for one and many); verb form (mews – of «mew»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (UK) A row of old stables in a small street or yard, often now turned into houses or flats; also the name of the little street: «a mews house». 2) (verb form) Third person of «mew»: the cat mews, meaning it makes a soft crying sound. 3) (old) A building where hunting hawks were kept, especially while they moulted.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday British life, mews houses are found in cities like London; they were built for horses and carriages behind big houses. Many street names end in «Mews». In stories, a kitten «mews» when it is hungry or lonely. Phrases: «a mews house», «a cobbled mews», «the kitten mews».
examples from the lessons: They live in a pretty mews house in London. | The mews used to be stables for horses. | The cobbled mews is closed to cars. | The tiny kitten mews for its mother. | Our address is 4 Stable Mews. | A mews was once where hawks were kept. | The kitten mewed and mewed until we fed it. | Many mews houses still have big old stable doors.
note for the reader of a maths problem: For the place, «mews» is the same for one or many: «a mews», «two mews» (though «mewses» is also seen). «Mews» (cat sound) also spelled «meows» or «miaows». Homophone: «muse» (to think deeply; or a goddess of the arts). Not a maths word.

part of speech: verb (miaou, miaous, miaoued, miaouing); noun (a miaou, miaous); interjection; also spelled «miaow» (UK) and «meow» (US)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The sound a cat makes. 2) (verb) To make this sound: «The cat miaoued at the door».
its sense in the lessons: In stories and early reading books, «miaou» is a sound word (onomatopoeia) for a cat's cry. It is an older or more French-looking spelling; «miaow» is common in the UK, Ireland, Australia and NZ, and «meow» in the USA and Canada. In French, cats say «miaou» too. Phrases: «miaou!», «miaoued loudly».
examples from the lessons: «Miaou!» said the little cat. | The cat miaoued at the back door to be let in. | Our kitten gives a tiny miaou when she is hungry. | In French books cats say «miaou». | «Miaou» is a word that sounds like the noise it names. | The cat's miaous woke me up at five o'clock. | I heard a sad miaou from the shed. | Dogs say «woof», cats say «miaou».
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spellings: miaou, miaow (UK), meow (US) – all mean the same. It is an example of onomatopoeia (a word that copies a sound). Pronounced «mee-OW». Not a maths word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A cloud of bad-smelling, unhealthy air, such as the smell from rotting things or a swamp. 2) (figurative) A heavy, unpleasant feeling that hangs over a place: «a miasma of gloom». 3) (history of science) The old wrong idea that diseases like cholera were caused by «bad air» (miasma), before germs were discovered.
its sense in the lessons: In history and science lessons, «miasma theory» was believed until the 1800s; John Snow's work on cholera in London in 1854 and later germ theory (Pasteur, Koch) showed diseases are spread by germs, not smells. In stories, a miasma hangs over swamps, dungeons or sad places. Phrases: «a miasma of smoke», «miasma theory».
examples from the lessons: A miasma rose from the rotting swamp. | People once blamed cholera on miasma, or bad air. | John Snow showed that dirty water, not miasma, spread cholera. | A miasma of cigarette smoke filled the old pub. | A miasma of sadness hung over the empty house. | Miasma theory was replaced by germ theory. | The dragon's cave was full of a foul miasma. | Florence Nightingale also believed in miasma, but her cleaning still saved lives.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one miasma, two miasmas. Pronounced «mee-AZ-ma» or «my-AZ-ma». Myth trap: bad smells do not cause diseases themselves; germs do (though rotting things can contain germs). Not a maths word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) To do with microbes: tiny living things like bacteria, fungi and some algae that can only be seen with a microscope. 2) Caused by microbes: «a microbial infection».
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, microbes can be helpful (making yogurt, bread, compost) or harmful (causing illness). «Microbial» appears in words like «antimicrobial» soap and «microbial growth» on old food. In health, handwashing reduces microbial spread. Phrases: «microbial life», «microbial growth», «antimicrobial».
examples from the lessons: Microbial life is found almost everywhere on Earth. | Mould on bread is a kind of microbial growth. | Yogurt is made by microbial action on milk. | Antimicrobial soap helps kill germs. | Scientists look for signs of microbial life on Mars. | Compost heaps are full of microbial activity. | Our gut has trillions of helpful microbial cells. | Cooking food properly kills most harmful microbial life.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective from «microbe». Pronounced «my-KROH-bee-al». «Micro-» means very small. Not all microbes are bad – most are harmless or helpful. Not a maths word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (maths) The point exactly halfway between two ends of a line segment, or halfway between two numbers. 2) The middle of a time, journey or event: «at the midpoint of the race».
its sense in the lessons: In maths, the midpoint of a line divides it into two equal parts; the midpoint of two numbers is their average: halfway between 4 and 10 is 7. On coordinate grids, the midpoint of (2, 4) and (6, 8) is (4, 6). In everyday life, «the midpoint of the term» or a journey. Phrases: «find the midpoint», «at the midpoint», «the midpoint between».
examples from the lessons: Mark the midpoint of the line with a dot. | The midpoint between 10 and 20 is 15. | We stopped for lunch at the midpoint of our journey. | The midpoint of a 12 cm line is 6 cm from each end. | At the midpoint of the race she was in third place. | Fold the paper to find its midpoint. | The midpoint of (0, 0) and (8, 4) is (4, 2). | Half-term is around the midpoint of the term.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one midpoint, two midpoints. In maths: midpoint of numbers a and b = (a + b) ÷ 2. For a line of length L, each half is L ÷ 2. Can be written «mid-point». Not the same as «median» (the middle value of a sorted list), though they can be equal.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) Moving regularly from one place to another, usually with the seasons, to find food, warmth or a place to breed: «migratory birds». 2) To do with migration: «migratory routes».
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography lessons, migratory animals include swallows, geese, Arctic terns, monarch butterflies, salmon, whales and wildebeest. They travel along migratory routes (flyways) every year. Some people also lead migratory lives, moving from place to place for work. Phrases: «migratory birds», «migratory route», «migratory species».
examples from the lessons: Swallows are migratory birds that fly to Africa for the winter. | The Arctic tern has the longest migratory journey of any animal. | Monarch butterflies are migratory insects in North America. | Humpback whales follow a migratory route along Australia's coast. | Salmon are migratory fish that return to their home river. | Migratory geese fly in a V shape. | Wetlands are important stopping places for migratory birds. | Some herders lead a migratory life with their animals.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective from «migrate». Noun: migration. A bird that stays all year is «resident», not migratory. Pronounced «MY-gra-tor-ee» or «my-GRAY-tor-ee». In maths, migration distance and speed problems: distance = speed × time.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (noun) A person born roughly between the early 1980s and the mid-1990s, who became an adult around the year 2000; also called Generation Y. 2) (adjective) To do with a millennium (a thousand years) or the year 2000: «millennial celebrations». 3) (adjective) To do with millennials: «millennial habits».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and the news, «millennials» are a generation, like Gen Z (born about 1997–2012) and Gen Alpha (born from about 2010 on). Many parents of today's children are millennials. Jokes and slang talk about millennial habits (avocado toast, side-parted hair). In history, «millennial» refers to the year 2000 or the passing of a thousand years. Phrases: «millennial generation», «a millennial parent».
examples from the lessons: My mum is a millennial, born in 1988. | Millennials grew up as the internet arrived. | There were millennial celebrations all over the world on 1 January 2000. | My cousin calls Dad's jokes «so millennial». | Millennials, Gen Z and Gen Alpha are different generations. | Some millennials remember dial-up internet. | The town planted a millennial oak tree in 2000. | The castle has stood for a millennial span – a whole thousand years.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable as a noun: one millennial, two millennials. Spelling: double l, double n: m-i-l-l-e-n-n-i-a-l. Related: millennium (1,000 years, plural millennia). Generation years are rough, not exact rules. In maths: «milli-»/«mille» link to 1,000 (a millennium is 1,000 years, a century 100).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (UK, Australia, NZ, Ireland) A kitchen machine that cuts meat or other food into very small pieces by pushing it through a plate with holes; in the US usually called a «meat grinder». 2) (informal, old) A person who walks with small fussy steps; this sense is rare and can be unkind.
its sense in the lessons: In cooking, a mincer turns beef into mince for burgers, shepherd's pie or spaghetti bolognese. Old hand mincers had a crank handle and were clamped to the table. Safety: never put fingers into a mincer; use the pusher. Phrases: «a hand mincer», «put the meat through the mincer».
examples from the lessons: Grandma's old mincer is clamped to the kitchen table. | Put the beef through the mincer to make mince. | The butcher has an electric mincer. | Never put your fingers into a mincer. | We used a mincer to make homemade burgers. | In America a mincer is called a meat grinder. | The mincer turns round and round when you crank the handle. | (idiom, UK) «I feel like I've been through the mincer» means «I feel worn out».
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one mincer, two mincers. From «mince» (to cut finely). British/Commonwealth word; American English says «grinder». Not a maths word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (music, UK, Australia, NZ, Ireland) A note that lasts for two beats in common time; in the US it is called a «half note». 2) (old measure) A tiny unit of liquid, about one drop. 3) (handwriting) A short downward stroke of the pen, as in the letters m, n, u and i.
its sense in the lessons: In music lessons, children learn note values: semibreve (4 beats), minim (2 beats), crotchet (1 beat), quaver (half a beat). A minim looks like a hollow oval with a stem. In maths and music together: two minims fill a 4/4 bar, or one minim equals two crotchets. Phrases: «a minim rest», «dotted minim» (3 beats).
examples from the lessons: A minim lasts for two beats. | Two minims fill one bar in 4/4 time. | A dotted minim lasts for three beats. | The minim looks like an empty circle with a stick. | In America, a minim is called a half note. | One minim equals two crotchets. | Hold the minim for two counts: «one, two». | The song ends on a long minim.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one minim, two minims. UK names vs US names: semibreve = whole note, minim = half note, crotchet = quarter note, quaver = eighth note. Maths: a dotted note is worth 1½ times the note (dotted minim = 2 + 1 = 3 beats). Do not confuse with «minimum».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (art, design, music) A style that uses very few, simple shapes, colours or notes, leaving out everything that is not needed. 2) (lifestyle) Living with fewer things and buying only what you really need.
its sense in the lessons: In art lessons, minimalist artworks may be just a few lines or blocks of one colour. In design, minimalism means clean, simple rooms and screens. In music, minimalism repeats simple patterns slowly changing (composers like Steve Reich, Philip Glass). In everyday life, some families choose minimalism to save money and have less clutter; it also links to caring for the environment. Phrases: «a love of minimalism», «minimalism in design».
examples from the lessons: Minimalism uses simple shapes and lots of empty space. | Our art teacher showed us minimalism with paintings of single squares. | The new library has a style of minimalism: white walls and plain shelves. | Minimalism in music repeats short patterns. | My aunt tried minimalism and gave away half her clothes. | Minimalism can help the planet by reducing waste. | Phone apps often use minimalism so they are easy to use. | Some people find minimalism calming; others find it boring.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Related: minimalist (person or adjective), minimal (very small). Comes from «minimum». Not about being «mini» or tiny in size; it is about simplicity. Not a maths word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (adjective) Very simple, using as few things, shapes or decorations as possible: «a minimalist bedroom». 2) (noun) An artist, designer or composer who works in the style of minimalism. 3) (noun) A person who chooses to live with very few possessions.
its sense in the lessons: In art and design lessons, a minimalist drawing or logo uses only what is needed. In everyday life, a minimalist home has few things; a minimalist packer brings a tiny bag. Phrases: «minimalist design», «a minimalist style», «minimalist living».
examples from the lessons: Her bedroom is minimalist: a bed, a desk and a plant. | The logo is minimalist, just a simple circle. | A minimalist artist might paint one line on a canvas. | My uncle is a minimalist and owns only 100 things. | The minimalist poster had three words and lots of white space. | We designed minimalist book covers in art. | The music was minimalist, repeating the same few notes. | Minimalist packing means only taking what you need.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable as a noun: one minimalist, two minimalists. Related: minimalism, minimal. Not a maths word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Making something as small as possible: «the minimisation of waste». 2) (maths) Finding the smallest possible value of something under some rules. 3) Making a problem seem less serious than it really is: «minimisation of bullying is harmful».
its sense in the lessons: In maths, minimisation problems ask for the smallest cost, distance or time: for example, the shortest path on a map. In science and the environment, «waste minimisation» means producing less rubbish. In safety and wellbeing, minimising a problem (saying «it's nothing» when someone is hurt) can stop people getting help. Phrases: «waste minimisation», «risk minimisation».
examples from the lessons: The school has a waste minimisation plan. | Risk minimisation means wearing a helmet when cycling. | The maths puzzle was about minimisation of the travel distance. | Minimisation of costs helped the club save money. | Saying «it's just teasing» can be a minimisation of bullying. | Engineers work on the minimisation of energy use. | Minimisation and maximisation are both kinds of optimisation. | The minimisation of plastic packaging is good for the oceans.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. UK/Australia/NZ «minimisation», US/Canada «minimization». Verb: minimise/minimize. In maths, minimisation means finding the least value allowed by the rules – not always zero.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (history) To do with the Minoans, an ancient Bronze Age civilisation on the Greek island of Crete, from about 3000 to 1100 BC. 2) (noun) A person from that civilisation.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons on Ancient Greece, the Minoans built great palaces like Knossos, painted colourful wall pictures (frescoes) of dolphins and bull-leaping, and traded by sea. Their name comes from the legendary King Minos, who in myth kept the Minotaur in a labyrinth. Their writing, Linear A, has still not been deciphered. Phrases: «Minoan civilisation», «Minoan palace», «Minoan art».
examples from the lessons: The Minoans lived on the island of Crete. | The Minoan palace of Knossos had hundreds of rooms. | Minoan frescoes show dolphins and young people leaping over bulls. | The Minoan civilisation is named after the legendary King Minos. | Nobody can yet read the Minoan writing called Linear A. | A huge volcanic eruption on Thera hurt Minoan trade. | Minoan sailors traded with Egypt. | The Minoans were one of the first great civilisations in Europe.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Written with a capital M because it comes from a name. Pronounced «mi-NOH-an». King Minos and the Minotaur are myths; the Minoan palaces are real archaeology. Not a maths word, but BC dates count backwards (3000 BC is earlier than 1100 BC).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To understand something wrongly; to misunderstand.
its sense in the lessons: It is a formal, rather rare word, used in careful writing and the exam voice. In everyday life we say «misunderstand» or «get the wrong idea». The noun «misapprehension» is more common: «under the misapprehension that…» means wrongly believing something. Phrases: «misapprehend the situation», «under a misapprehension».
examples from the lessons: He misapprehended the question and answered the wrong thing. | I think you have misapprehended what I meant. | The detective misapprehended the clue at first. | Do not misapprehend the instructions: read them twice. | She was under the misapprehension that the trip was on Friday. | The king misapprehended the messenger's words and grew angry. | It is easy to misapprehend a joke in a text message. | They misapprehended the map and took the wrong path.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: misapprehended. Formal; everyday words: «misunderstand», «get wrong». «Mis-» means wrongly; «apprehend» here means understand (it can also mean to arrest!). Noun: misapprehension. Not a maths word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A wrong idea or belief about something, often one that many people share because they misunderstood it.
its sense in the lessons: In science and maths lessons, teachers find and fix misconceptions, for example «heavier things fall faster» (in air without much drag they fall at nearly the same speed), «the Sun goes round the Earth», or «multiplying always makes a number bigger» (not with numbers less than 1, like × 0.5). In everyday life, there are misconceptions about animals, people and history. Phrases: «a common misconception», «clear up a misconception», «it's a misconception that…».
examples from the lessons: It is a common misconception that bats are blind. | A misconception is that summer happens because Earth is closer to the Sun – it is really because of Earth's tilt. | The teacher cleared up our misconception about fractions. | It's a misconception that goldfish only remember for three seconds. | Many people have misconceptions about wolves. | «Multiplying always makes bigger» is a maths misconception: 6 × 0.5 = 3. | We made a poster of science misconceptions. | Lightning can strike the same place twice – the opposite is a misconception.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one misconception, two misconceptions. Spelling: mis + conception (one s). Similar: myth, false belief, misunderstanding. In maths, misconceptions include: «the longer decimal is bigger» (0.25 < 0.3), «dividing always makes smaller» (6 ÷ 0.5 = 12).

part of speech: verb (miscount, miscounts, miscounted, miscounting); noun (a miscount, miscounts)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To count wrongly; to make a mistake when counting. 2) (noun) A wrong count, especially of votes: «There was a miscount in the election».
its sense in the lessons: In maths, miscounting is a common mistake: missing an object or counting one twice. Tips: touch or tick each object, count in groups. In elections, a miscount can lead to a recount. In sport, a referee may miscount the players or the seconds. Phrases: «miscount the votes», «a recount after a miscount».
examples from the lessons: I miscounted the sweets and gave myself one extra. | The teacher miscounted and thought someone was missing. | There was a miscount, so they counted the votes again. | Tick each one so you don't miscount. | She miscounted the stitches in her knitting. | If you miscount by one, the whole pattern goes wrong. | The referee miscounted the substitutes. | We miscounted the days until the holiday – it's actually ten!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: miscounted. Noun «a miscount» is countable. «Mis-» means wrongly. In maths problems, an «off by one» miscount is common: from 3 to 10 inclusive there are 8 numbers, not 7.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Great unhappiness or suffering, in body or mind. 2) Very poor and hard living conditions: «they lived in misery». 3) (UK, informal) A person who is always grumpy and complaining: «Don't be such a misery!» 4) (idioms) «make someone's life a misery» (keep upsetting them); «put an animal out of its misery» (kill it kindly to end its suffering); «put someone out of their misery» (tell them news they are anxious to hear).
its sense in the lessons: In stories, misery describes deep sadness, loss or hard lives, like Victorian children working in factories. In everyday life people use it for small troubles jokingly: «the misery of Monday mornings». In history, war and poverty caused great misery. Phrases: «a life of misery», «misery guts» (UK, informal grumpy person), «make life a misery».
examples from the lessons: The war brought misery to millions of people. | The bully made her life a misery. | Don't be such a misery – come and play! | Come on, put me out of my misery and tell me the score! | The flood left the town in misery. | Grandad calls my brother a «misery guts» when he sulks. | Toothache is pure misery. | Charity groups work to end the misery of hunger.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly uncountable, but «miseries» is used for different troubles. Adjective: miserable. Pronounced «MIZ-er-ee». Spelling: miser + y. A «miser» is a different word (someone who hates spending money). Not a maths word.

part of speech: noun (a mismatch, mismatches); verb (mismatch, mismatches, mismatched, mismatching)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A situation where two things do not fit together or do not match: «a mismatch between the picture and the words». 2) A contest where one side is much stronger than the other. 3) (verb) To put together things that do not match: «mismatched socks».
its sense in the lessons: In maths and science, a mismatch between your answer and the expected result tells you to check your working. In computing, «type mismatch» is an error. In sport, a mismatch is a one-sided game. In fashion, «mismatched socks» are worn on Odd Socks Day (Anti-Bullying Week in the UK) to celebrate being different. Phrases: «a mismatch between», «mismatched socks», «a total mismatch».
examples from the lessons: There is a mismatch between your answer and the total – check your sums. | I wore mismatched socks for Odd Socks Day. | The game was a mismatch: 10–0! | The colours were mismatched, a pink top with orange trousers. | A size mismatch means the lid won't fit the box. | The computer gave a «password mismatch» error. | There was a mismatch between what he said and what he did. | Mismatched shoes on the wrong feet made me trip.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: one mismatch, two mismatches. Regular verb: mismatched. In maths problems, a mismatch between the units (cm vs m) is a common trap – change to the same unit first.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A name or word that is wrong or misleading for the thing it describes.
its sense in the lessons: In science and everyday life, many names are misnomers: a jellyfish is not a fish, a starfish is not a fish, peanuts are not nuts (they are legumes), koala «bears» are not bears, and lead pencils contain graphite, not lead. Spotting misnomers is great for quizzes. Phrases: «a bit of a misnomer», «a well-known misnomer».
examples from the lessons: «Starfish» is a misnomer, because it is not a fish. | Calling a koala a «bear» is a misnomer – it is a marsupial. | «Lead pencil» is a misnomer: pencils contain graphite. | The «Tasmanian tiger» was a misnomer: it was a marsupial, not a cat. | Peanut is a misnomer; peanuts are legumes, like peas. | «Guinea pig» is a misnomer – they are not pigs and not from Guinea. | The «quiet carriage» was a misnomer that day. | Our teacher loves finding misnomers in English.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one misnomer, two misnomers. Pronounced «mis-NOH-mer». Not the same as a «misprint» or a «mispronunciation». «Mis-» = wrongly, «nomen» = name (Latin). Not a maths word.

part of speech: noun (a misprint, misprints); verb (misprint, misprints, misprinted, misprinting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A mistake in a printed text, such as a wrong letter, word or number. 2) (verb) To print something wrongly.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, misprints happen in newspapers, books, menus and timetables. In maths, a misprint in a question can make it impossible to solve – tell the teacher! Some misprinted stamps and coins are rare and worth a lot of money to collectors. Phrases: «a misprint in the book», «it must be a misprint».
examples from the lessons: There is a misprint on page 12: «teh» instead of «the». | The price on the menu was a misprint. | A misprint in the timetable made us miss the bus. | The question had a misprint, so the teacher fixed it on the board. | Some misprinted stamps are worth thousands of pounds. | The book's first edition had lots of misprints. | My name was misprinted on the certificate. | Is that a misprint, or does the recipe really need 100 eggs?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun; regular verb: misprinted. Not the same as a «typo» (typing mistake), but close; misprint is in the printed version. In maths problems, if a number seems silly (a 300 kg cat), check whether it is a misprint.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To say a word or a name in the wrong way, with the wrong sounds or the wrong stress.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons, many words are often mispronounced: «library» (lie-brer-ee, not lie-berry), «February», «specific» (not «pacific»). In everyday life, mispronouncing someone's name is easy to do, so it is kind to ask how to say it and to learn it. Readers often mispronounce words they only know from books, like «epitome». Phrases: «mispronounce a name», «a commonly mispronounced word».
examples from the lessons: Please tell me if I mispronounce your name. | Many people mispronounce «Wednesday». | He mispronounced «epitome» because he had only read it. | The newsreader mispronounced the name of the town. | It's okay to mispronounce words while you are learning a language. | My little brother mispronounces «spaghetti» as «pasghetti». | The teacher apologised for mispronouncing my surname. | Some words, like «colonel», are easy to mispronounce.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: mispronounced. Noun: mispronunciation – note the spelling changes: pronounce → pronunciation (no «o» after «n»). «Mis-» = wrongly. Not a maths word.

part of speech: verb (misquote, misquotes, misquoted, misquoting); noun (a misquote, misquotes)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To repeat someone's words wrongly, either by mistake or on purpose to change their meaning. 2) (noun) A wrong quotation.
its sense in the lessons: In English and history lessons, famous lines are often misquoted: «Elementary, my dear Watson» never appears exactly in the original Sherlock Holmes books; «Beam me up, Scotty» was never said exactly in Star Trek. In news and media literacy lessons, misquoting can spread false information, so check the original source. Phrases: «be misquoted», «a famous misquote».
examples from the lessons: The newspaper misquoted the head teacher. | «Play it again, Sam» is a famous misquote from the film «Casablanca». | Always check the original before you quote, so you don't misquote. | The politician said he had been misquoted. | She misquoted the poem, mixing up two lines. | Misquoting someone can change what they meant. | «Elementary, my dear Watson» is a misquote of the Holmes books. | The film poster misquoted a review to make it sound better.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: misquoted. The noun is «misquote» or «misquotation». Related: quote, quotation, quotation marks. In history, misquotes can stick for centuries. Not a maths word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To say or write something wrongly or falsely, such as facts or numbers, by mistake or on purpose.
its sense in the lessons: It is a formal word, often used in news, law and business: «the company misstated its profits» means it reported the wrong numbers. In school, if you misstate a fact in an essay, your argument may fall apart. Everyday words: «get wrong», «say wrongly». Phrases: «misstate the facts», «misstated figures».
examples from the lessons: The report misstated the number of pupils at the school. | He misstated the date of the battle in his essay. | The company misstated its profits and got into trouble. | Please check your notes so you don't misstate the facts. | The article misstated what the scientist had found. | She was careful not to misstate the rules of the game. | The sign misstated the opening times. | If you misstate a number in step one, every later answer will be wrong.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: misstated. Spelling: double s (mis + state). Noun: misstatement. Formal word, from the exam and news voice. In maths, a misstated number in a problem changes the answer.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Because of a mistake; wrongly: «He mistakenly took my bag». 2) Believing something that is not true: «Many people mistakenly think bulls hate red».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: «I mistakenly sent the message to the wrong person». In science lessons it is used to correct myths: «Some people mistakenly believe that…». In stories it shows a character made an honest error. Phrases: «mistakenly believe», «mistakenly think», «mistakenly took».
examples from the lessons: I mistakenly put salt in my tea instead of sugar. | Many people mistakenly believe that bulls hate the colour red; they react to movement. | She mistakenly got on the wrong bus. | The parcel was mistakenly delivered next door. | He mistakenly thought the test was tomorrow. | People once mistakenly thought the Earth was flat – in fact, educated people have known it is round for over 2,000 years. | The email was mistakenly sent to the whole school. | The goal was mistakenly ruled out by the referee.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from «mistaken» + «-ly». Means by mistake, not on purpose. Similar: wrongly, by mistake, in error. Not a maths word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A wrong translation from one language into another, where the meaning has been changed by mistake.
its sense in the lessons: In language lessons, mistranslations show why translating is hard: words can have more than one meaning, and idioms do not translate word for word. Funny mistranslations appear on menus and signs. Some famous claims are real mistranslations, others are myths. Phrases: «a funny mistranslation», «lost in translation».
examples from the lessons: The sign said «Slip carefully», a mistranslation of «Watch out, slippery». | The menu had a funny mistranslation: «fried ice». | A mistranslation can cause big misunderstandings between countries. | Idioms like «it's raining cats and dogs» often lead to mistranslations. | The teacher showed us mistranslations made by computer programs. | One word with two meanings can cause a mistranslation. | Mistranslations in instructions made building the bookshelf hard. | Translators check their work carefully to avoid mistranslation.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one mistranslation, two mistranslations. Verb: mistranslate. Related: translation, translator. «Mis-» means wrongly. Not a maths word.

part of speech: noun (a misunderstanding, misunderstandings); verb form (-ing form of «misunderstand»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A failure to understand something correctly: «There was a misunderstanding about the time». 2) A small disagreement or argument, often caused by not understanding each other: «We had a little misunderstanding».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, many arguments start from a misunderstanding: a text read in the wrong tone, a mixed-up time or place. In friendship lessons, children learn to clear up misunderstandings by asking and listening. In stories, misunderstandings drive funny plots. Phrases: «clear up a misunderstanding», «there's been a misunderstanding», «a misunderstanding about».
examples from the lessons: There must be a misunderstanding – I said three o'clock, not two. | We cleared up the misunderstanding by talking. | The whole argument was a misunderstanding. | A misunderstanding over the rules ended the game early. | Texts can lead to misunderstandings because you can't hear the voice. | The comedy is full of misunderstandings and mixed-up identities. | «Sorry, I think we had a misunderstanding.» | A misunderstanding in maths: he thought «product» meant add, not multiply.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one misunderstanding, two misunderstandings. Verb: misunderstand (past: misunderstood – irregular). Often a polite word for a small argument. In maths word problems, misunderstanding key words (sum, product, difference, quotient) is a common trap.

part of speech: noun (modelling, uncountable); verb form (-ing form of «model»: model, models, modelled, modelling – UK; modeled, modeling – US)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Making models: small copies of things, or shapes from clay, Plasticine or other materials. 2) The job of a fashion model: wearing clothes for photos or shows. 3) (science, maths) Making a simplified version or a set of rules (a model) that shows how something works, often on a computer, to predict things. 4) (behaviour) Showing others how to behave by doing it yourself: «modelling good manners».
its sense in the lessons: In art and design lessons, «clay modelling» and «model making». In science and geography, computer modelling predicts weather and climate. In maths, «modelling» turns a real problem into numbers and equations. Teachers talk about «modelling» a skill: showing you how first. Phrases: «clay modelling», «computer modelling», «role modelling», «a modelling agency».
examples from the lessons: We did clay modelling in art today. | Weather forecasts use computer modelling. | My cousin does modelling for a clothes catalogue. | The teacher is modelling how to set out a long division. | Modelling the Solar System with balls showed us the sizes of the planets. | Modelling kind behaviour helps younger children learn. | Maths modelling turns a word problem into an equation. | Dad spends weekends modelling a tiny railway.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK/Australia/NZ/Ireland spell it «modelling» (double l); the US spells it «modeling». Both are correct in their countries. Remember: every model is simpler than the real thing, so its predictions can be wrong. In maths, modelling means writing the problem as numbers, then checking the answer makes sense.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To a medium amount or degree; fairly but not very: «moderately hot», «moderately difficult». 2) In a sensible, controlled way, not too much: «eat moderately».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: «a moderately priced restaurant». In health lessons: exercise moderately, eat sugar moderately. In science and recipes: «heat moderately» means medium heat. In surveys and grades, «moderately» is the middle step between «slightly» and «very». Phrases: «moderately successful», «moderately difficult», «moderately warm».
examples from the lessons: The test was moderately difficult. | Heat the pan moderately, not on full. | The film was only moderately funny. | Exercise moderately every day. | It was a moderately warm day, about 18 °C. | The shoes were moderately priced. | Our team was moderately successful this season. | The river was moderately deep, up to my knees.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from «moderate» + «-ly». Similar: fairly, reasonably, quite. Opposite ideas: extremely, very, barely. Not a maths word, though in surveys «moderately» is often in the middle of a scale.

part of speech: adjective (modernised); verb form (past of «modernise»: modernise, modernises, modernised, modernising – UK; modernize, modernized – US)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Made modern; changed with new equipment, methods or ideas so it is up to date: «a modernised kitchen». 2) (verb, past) Past form of «modernise»: «They modernised the old school».
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, countries «modernised» with railways, factories and schools, for example Japan after 1868. In everyday life, old buildings, trains and kitchens are modernised. Phrases: «a newly modernised station», «fully modernised», «modernised version».
examples from the lessons: The station was modernised with lifts and new screens. | Our school library has been modernised. | Japan modernised quickly in the late 1800s. | Grandma's modernised kitchen has an induction hob. | The old fairy tale was modernised for the film. | The hospital was modernised last year. | The farm modernised its machines to save time. | The modernised version of the song uses electric guitars.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK/Australia/NZ/Ireland usually spell «modernised»; US/Canada «modernized». Both correct. Related: modern, modernisation. Not a maths word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) One separate part or unit that fits together with others to make a bigger whole, like a part of a machine or building. 2) (education) A unit of a course on one topic, often with its own lessons and test: «the fractions module». 3) (space) A separate part of a spacecraft: «the lunar module». 4) (computers) A separate part of a program that does one job.
its sense in the lessons: In school, courses are split into modules or units. In space history, the lunar module «Eagle» landed Apollo 11 on the Moon in 1969, and the International Space Station is built of modules. In technology and building, modular homes are made from modules. In coding, programmers split programs into modules. Phrases: «a learning module», «the lunar module», «modular design».
examples from the lessons: This term we start the module on fractions. | The lunar module landed on the Moon in 1969. | The space station is made from many modules joined together. | Each module ends with a short quiz. | The robot kit has a light-sensor module. | The house was built from factory-made modules. | Our science module is about forces. | A computer program can be split into modules.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one module, two modules. Adjective: modular. Pronounced «MOD-yool». Not the same as «model». In maths, «modulus» and «modular arithmetic» are related words used at higher levels (clock arithmetic).

meaning for a pupil: 1) To make something slightly wet: «moisten the cloth». 2) To become slightly wet: «her eyes moistened».
its sense in the lessons: In cooking, recipes say «moisten the flour with a little water». In art, you moisten paper or a paintbrush. In science, seeds need moistened soil to germinate. In stories, «her eyes moistened» shows a character is close to tears. Phrases: «moisten the edges», «moisten with water», «eyes moistened».
examples from the lessons: Moisten the edges of the pastry so they stick. | Moisten the sponge before wiping the board. | Seeds sprout in moistened cotton wool. | Grandpa's eyes moistened as he read the letter. | Moisten the stamp to stick it on – or use a self-stick stamp. | Use a damp cloth to moisten the clay. | Moisten the soil, but don't flood it. | The frog moistens its skin in the pond.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: moistened. The «t» is silent: «MOY-sen». Related: moist (slightly wet), moisture. Not a maths word.

part of speech: noun (Mojave – a name of a desert and a people); also spelled «Mohave»
meaning for a pupil: 1) (a place) The Mojave Desert is a hot, dry desert in the south-western USA, mostly in California and Nevada; Death Valley, one of the hottest places on Earth, is in it. 2) (a people) The Mojave are a Native American people who live along the Colorado River.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons on deserts, the Mojave is famous for Joshua trees, Death Valley (which once reached 56.7 °C in 1913) and tough desert animals like the desert tortoise. Las Vegas is at its edge. In history and culture, the Mojave people have lived by the Colorado River for a long time and farmed its floodplain. Phrases: «the Mojave Desert», «Mojave people».
examples from the lessons: The Mojave Desert is in the south-west of the USA. | Joshua trees grow in the Mojave Desert. | Death Valley is in the Mojave and is very hot. | The desert tortoise lives in the Mojave. | The Mojave people live along the Colorado River. | It hardly ever rains in the Mojave. | The Mojave gets very cold at night. | We watched a film about wildflowers blooming in the Mojave after rain.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A name, so always a capital M. Pronounced «mo-HAH-vee». Spelled «Mojave» or «Mohave». Not an English common word. In maths, desert temperatures are good for range problems (hot days, cold nights).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) To do with molecules: the tiny groups of atoms joined together that make up substances. 2) (science) Happening at the level of molecules: «molecular biology», «a molecular model».
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, a water molecule is H₂O (two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom). Molecular models use balls and sticks to show molecules. «Molecular biology» studies DNA and proteins; «molecular gastronomy» is science-style cooking. Phrases: «molecular structure», «molecular model», «molecular biology».
examples from the lessons: We built a molecular model of water with balls and sticks. | Molecular biology studies DNA. | The molecular structure of diamond makes it very hard. | Scientists use molecular tests to find viruses. | The chef makes «caviar» from juice with molecular cooking tricks. | Ice and water have the same molecules but a different molecular arrangement. | Molecular scientists study very, very tiny things. | The molecular formula of carbon dioxide is CO₂.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective from «molecule». Pronounced «mo-LEK-yoo-lar». Molecules are made of atoms; an atom is not a molecule (unless joined to others). In maths/science, a molecular formula counts atoms: H₂O means 2 hydrogen + 1 oxygen = 3 atoms.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal, mainly US) Mom; a child's word for their mother. 2) (informal, mainly US) Any mother, including an animal mother, as in "the momma bear". 3) (slang, US) Used in jokes beginning "Yo momma…", which tease someone about their mother.
its sense in the lessons: A warm, homely word heard in American stories, songs and films; it tells the reader the speaker is close to their mother or is from the southern USA. In science and nature talk, "momma bird" or "momma cat" simply means the mother animal. Phrases: "momma bear", "momma's boy" (a boy who relies on his mother a lot), "Yo momma" jokes (often unkind).
examples from the lessons: Momma, can I have a snack? | My momma picks me up from school on Fridays. | The momma bird brought worms back to the nest. | Don't go near the cubs, the momma bear will be close by. | She sang the song her momma used to sing. | He's a real momma's boy, he phones her every day. | "Momma said there'd be days like this," Grandpa laughed.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal; in writing for school use "mother" or "Mom" (US) / "Mum" (UK). Spellings vary: momma, mama, mamma; in the UK, Ireland, Australia and New Zealand people say "mum" or "mam". Capital M when used as a name: "Thanks, Momma." "Yo momma" jokes can be hurtful.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal, US and Canada) Mother; a small child's word for their mom. 2) (informal) Used about mothers in general, as in "mommy bloggers" or "new mommies".
its sense in the lessons: A word of little children and of parents talking to them; in a story it shows the speaker is young or the moment is tender or scared ("I want my mommy!"). Phrases: "mommy and me" classes (for a parent and a baby), "mommy blogger".
examples from the lessons: Mommy, I had a bad dream. | The toddler cried, "Mommy, look at me!" | My little sister calls Mom "Mommy". | The baby duck followed its mommy into the pond. | "I'm not a baby, I don't need my mommy," Max said bravely. | Mommy and Daddy are coming to the school play. | The lost boy kept asking for his mommy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: American and Canadian; the British, Irish, Australian and New Zealand word is "mummy" (which is also an Egyptian preserved body — a trap!). Plural "mommies". Capital M when used as a name. Older children usually switch to "Mom".

meaning for a pupil: 1) To do with monks or nuns and the places they live, monasteries and convents. 2) Very plain, quiet and simple, like a monk's life, with few things and little fun.
its sense in the lessons: Used in history (monastic life in the Middle Ages, monks copying books by hand), in church life (monastic vows of poverty, chastity and obedience) and in everyday life to describe a bare, quiet room or strict routine. Phrases: "monastic life", "monastic order", "monastic vows", "a monastic cell".
examples from the lessons: Monastic life in the Middle Ages followed a strict timetable of prayer and work. | The monks kept a monastic garden full of herbs. | Monastic orders like the Benedictines still exist today. | Many old books survived because monastic scribes copied them. | Her bedroom was almost monastic: a bed, a desk and nothing else. | He lives a monastic life, studying all day and never going out. | The island of Iona in Scotland had a famous monastic community.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective only; the place is a "monastery" (for monks) or "convent"/"nunnery" (for nuns). Monks are men, nuns are women, but "monastic" can describe both. Don't confuse with "monotonous" (boring and the same).

part of speech: adjective (monochrome); noun (a monochrome, monochromes; also uncountable: in monochrome)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Using only one colour or shades of one colour, especially black, white and grey. 2) (noun) A picture, photo or screen in black and white or in one colour. 3) Dull and without variety, as in "a monochrome town".
its sense in the lessons: In art lessons, a monochrome painting uses tints and shades of just one colour. In science and technology, old TVs and screens were monochrome. In everyday talk, "monochrome" outfits are all one colour. In stories it can describe a dull, grey place or mood.
examples from the lessons: Old photos are often monochrome, black and white. | For art we made a monochrome painting using only shades of blue. | Grandad's first TV was monochrome. | The film was shot in monochrome to look old-fashioned. | She wore a stylish monochrome outfit, all black. | The rainy town looked monochrome and sad. | A monochrome printer prints only in black.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From Greek "mono" (one) + "chroma" (colour). Uncountable phrase "in monochrome". Spelling "colour" in the UK, "color" in the US, but "monochrome" is the same everywhere. Not the same as "monotone" (one tone of voice or sound).

part of speech: noun (a montage, montages); verb (montage, montages, montaged, montaging — rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) In films and TV, a quick series of short clips put together to show time passing or many things happening. 2) A picture made by putting many photos or pieces together. 3) The skill of choosing and joining pieces of film or pictures.
its sense in the lessons: Used in media studies, art (making a photo montage for a project) and everyday talk about films ("the training montage"). In a story, "a montage" tells the reader that lots of time passed quickly. Phrases: "training montage", "photo montage", "a montage of".
examples from the lessons: The film showed a montage of the team training hard all winter. | For our end-of-year assembly we made a montage of class photos. | The artist made a montage from old magazine pictures. | A montage of holiday clips played at the party. | Every sports film seems to have a training montage. | The news ended with a montage of the best moments of the Games. | We learned how editors cut film to build a montage.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced "MON-tahzh" (from French). Countable: "a montage", "two montages". Similar to "collage" (pictures glued onto paper); a montage is more often photos or film clips.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To do with the Moors, the Muslim people from North Africa who ruled much of Spain and Portugal for hundreds of years in the Middle Ages. 2) In the style of Moorish art and buildings, with arches, tiles, patterns and courtyards. 3) (UK, informal, usually spelled "moreish") So tasty that you want more.
its sense in the lessons: Used in history and art lessons about Spain (the Alhambra in Granada is a famous Moorish palace), in geography and in travel. The everyday UK food sense is usually spelled "moreish", and people often mix the two up. Phrases: "Moorish architecture", "Moorish Spain".
examples from the lessons: The Alhambra in Granada is a beautiful Moorish palace. | Moorish buildings often have horseshoe-shaped arches. | The walls were covered in Moorish tiles with star patterns. | Moorish scholars brought new ideas in maths and science to Europe. | We learned about Moorish Spain in our history topic. | These crisps are really moreish, I can't stop eating them! (UK) | The courtyard had a Moorish fountain in the middle.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital M when it is about the Moors. Trap: "moreish" (tasty, UK) is a different word with a different spelling, but they sound the same. "Moor" (a person) is also different from "moor" (wild, open hilly land in the UK, like Dartmoor).

meaning for a pupil: 1) From or to do with Morocco, a country in north-west Africa. 2) (noun) A person from Morocco.
its sense in the lessons: Used in geography (Morocco is just south of Spain, across the Strait of Gibraltar), in food (Moroccan tagine, couscous, mint tea), in art (Moroccan tiles and lamps) and in everyday talk about people and holidays. Phrases: "Moroccan food", "Moroccan mint tea", "Moroccan-style".
examples from the lessons: We cooked a Moroccan tagine with chickpeas and apricots. | Our new neighbours are Moroccan. | Moroccan mint tea is poured from high up into small glasses. | The market sold colourful Moroccan lamps. | Many Moroccans speak Arabic, Berber languages and French. | The Moroccan team played brilliantly in the World Cup. | The capital of Morocco is Rabat, but the biggest city is Casablanca.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always a capital M. Spelling: double c, single r in the middle (Mo-ROCC-an). The country is "Morocco"; the people are "Moroccans".

meaning for a pupil: 1) (old-fashioned, literary) The next day; tomorrow. 2) (old-fashioned) The morning, as in the greeting "Good morrow!", meaning "Good morning". 3) (literary) The time just after an event, as in "on the morrow of the war".
its sense in the lessons: Found in old books, fairy tales, poems and the Bible; it tells the reader the story is set long ago or the speaker talks in an old-fashioned way. Phrases: "on the morrow" (the next day), "good morrow", "take no thought for the morrow" (Bible, do not worry about tomorrow).
examples from the lessons: We shall leave on the morrow, said the knight. | "Good morrow, sir!" called the innkeeper. | The king promised an answer on the morrow. | In the old story, the travellers rested and set off on the morrow. | "Take no thought for the morrow," the Bible verse says. | Who knows what the morrow will bring? | The wizard said the spell would end on the morrow.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Old-fashioned; in normal speech and writing say "tomorrow" or "the next day". Usually "the morrow", not "a morrow". Not the same as "marrow" (a big vegetable, or the soft inside of bones).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Covered with moss, the soft, green, low plant that grows on damp stones, trees and ground. 2) Like moss: soft, green and springy.
its sense in the lessons: Used in science (moss grows in damp, shady places, often on the north side of trees in the Northern Hemisphere, though this is not a reliable compass) and in stories to paint a quiet, old, damp place: mossy stones, mossy walls, a mossy forest floor. Safety: mossy rocks and steps are slippery.
examples from the lessons: The path through the woods was soft and mossy. | Be careful, those mossy rocks are slippery! | An old mossy wall ran round the garden. | The frog sat on a mossy log by the pond. | We found tiny insects living in the mossy bark. | The roof of the shed was green and mossy. | The fairy house was built on a mossy stump.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective from "moss" + "-y". Comparative "mossier", superlative "mossiest". Myth: moss does not always grow on the north side of trees, so it is not a safe way to find north.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A hotel by a road for people travelling by car, where you can usually park right outside your room.
its sense in the lessons: Common in the USA, Canada, Australia and New Zealand on road trips; it tells the reader the characters are travelling by car and staying somewhere simple and cheap. The word comes from "motor" + "hotel".
examples from the lessons: We stayed at a motel on our road trip across Canada. | The motel had a swimming pool and free breakfast. | Dad parked the car right outside our motel room. | There's a cheap motel just off the highway. | The motel sign flashed "VACANCY" in red. | We stopped at a motel in the outback for the night. | In Australia many small towns have one pub and one motel.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: "a motel", "two motels". A blend word: motor + hotel (like "brunch" = breakfast + lunch). Not the same as "model".

part of speech: verb form (present participle of motivate: motivate, motivates, motivated, motivating); adjective (motivating)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Making someone want to do something or try hard. 2) (adjective) Giving you energy and the wish to work or keep going. 3) Being the reason behind something, as in "the motivating idea".
its sense in the lessons: Used at school and in sport about what helps you try hard: stars, praise, goals, a good coach. In stories it explains why a character acts. Phrases: "motivating factor", "find it motivating", "motivating yourself".
examples from the lessons: The coach is great at motivating the team. | I find sticker charts really motivating. | Motivating yourself to do homework on a sunny day is hard. | Her speech was so motivating that we all signed up to help. | Money was the motivating factor for the thief. | Seeing my progress on the chart is motivating. | Our teacher is good at motivating children who find maths hard.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: drop the "e" of "motivate" before -ing (motivating). Related: "motivation" (noun), "motivated" (wanting to do it), "motive" (a reason, especially for a crime). Opposite: "demotivating" or "discouraging".

meaning for a pupil: 1) The wish or energy to do something and keep trying. 2) A reason for doing something. 3) (formal) Something that gives a reason or encourages action.
its sense in the lessons: Used at school ("Where's your motivation today?"), in sport, in science about why animals behave as they do, and in stories about a character's reasons for acting. Phrases: "lack of motivation", "lose motivation", "a strong motivation", "the motivation behind".
examples from the lessons: I lost my motivation to practise piano after the holidays. | Winning the cup was a big motivation for the team. | What was the villain's motivation for stealing the jewel? | Our teacher gives us stickers for motivation. | Hunger is a strong motivation for animals to hunt. | She has lots of motivation; she practises every day. | The motivation behind the new rule was to keep everyone safe.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable ("lots of motivation", not "lots of motivations") when it means the wish to do something; countable when it means a particular reason. Verb: "motivate"; adjective: "motivated". In police stories, "motive" is the usual word for the reason for a crime.
