part of speech: verb form (past participle of mow: mow, mows, mowed, mowing, mown/mowed); adjective (mown)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Cut short with a mower or a scythe, used about grass and hay. 2) (adjective) Freshly cut, as in "newly mown lawn". 3) (with "down", literary) Killed in large numbers, as in "mown down".
its sense in the lessons: Used in everyday life and stories about gardens, parks, sports fields and farms; "the smell of freshly mown grass" is a classic summer image. In history and war stories "mown down" means many people were shot or knocked down.
examples from the lessons: The grass has been mown, so we can play football. | I love the smell of freshly mown grass. | The cricket pitch was neatly mown in stripes. | The farmer had mown the hay and left it to dry. | Dad has mown the lawn every Saturday this summer. | The newly mown field was full of birds looking for insects. | In the battle, soldiers were mown down by machine guns.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past tense is "mowed" (He mowed the lawn). Past participle can be "mown" or "mowed" (has mown / has mowed). Homophone trap: "moan" (to complain) sounds the same as "mown".

part of speech: verb form (past tense and past participle of muddy: muddy, muddies, muddied, muddying); adjective (muddied)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Made dirty or covered with mud. 2) (figurative) Made something less clear or more confusing, as in "muddied the waters".
its sense in the lessons: Everyday: muddied boots, knees and football kits. In stories and news, "muddy the waters" means to make a situation more confusing, often on purpose. Phrases: "muddy the waters", "muddied boots".
examples from the lessons: The players came off the pitch with muddied knees. | My new trainers got muddied on the walk. | The stream was muddied after the heavy rain. | Leave your muddied wellies by the back door. | His long explanation only muddied the waters. | The cows had muddied the gate with their hooves. | The extra rules muddied things instead of making them clear.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: change "y" to "i" before -ed (muddy → muddied, muddies), but keep the "y" before -ing (muddying). "Muddy" is also an adjective: "muddy boots".

meaning for a pupil: 1) A large amount of wet mud sliding quickly down a hill or mountain, often after heavy rain. 2) (informal) A mudslide is also the name of a fun slippery slide in mud.
its sense in the lessons: Used in geography and science (natural hazards; rain loosens soil on steep slopes, especially where trees have been cut down) and in news about disasters. Safety: mudslides can bury roads and houses; people are warned to leave when heavy rain is coming.
examples from the lessons: After days of heavy rain, a mudslide blocked the mountain road. | Mudslides are more likely where trees have been cut down. | The village was evacuated because of the danger of mudslides. | In geography we learned how a mudslide happens. | A small mudslide covered the footpath in brown sludge. | Rescue teams searched for people after the mudslide. | Tree roots help hold the soil and prevent mudslides.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Similar words: "landslide" (rocks and soil sliding, wet or dry) and "mudflow". "Landslide" is also used for a big election win, but "mudslide" is not.

part of speech: verb form (past tense and past participle of muffle: muffle, muffles, muffled, muffling); adjective (muffled)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (adjective) Quiet and unclear because something is in the way, as in "a muffled voice". 2) Made a sound quieter by covering it. 3) Wrapped up warmly, as in "muffled up in scarves".
its sense in the lessons: Used in science (sound travels less well through soft materials, which absorb it) and a lot in stories to build mystery: "a muffled cry", "muffled footsteps", "muffled voices behind the door". Phrases: "muffled up", "a muffled sound".
examples from the lessons: I heard muffled voices from the next room. | Her answer was muffled because her face was in the pillow. | The snow muffled the sound of our footsteps. | There was a muffled thump in the attic. | We wrapped the alarm clock in a towel and its ring was muffled. | The children were muffled up in coats and scarves. | In science we tested which materials muffled sound best.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: double f. Adjective use is the most common ("a muffled shout"). Related: "muffler" (an old word for a scarf; in the US, the part of a car that makes the engine quieter).

part of speech: noun (mulch, mulches — usually uncountable); verb (mulch, mulches, mulched, mulching)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A layer of material such as bark, leaves, straw or compost spread on soil around plants. 2) (verb) To spread mulch on soil.
its sense in the lessons: Used in gardening and science about plants and soil: mulch keeps soil moist, keeps weeds down, and as it rots it adds nutrients. In a school garden, children might spread bark mulch. Phrases: "a layer of mulch", "bark mulch", "mulch the beds".
examples from the lessons: We put a layer of mulch round the tomato plants. | Mulch helps the soil stay damp in hot weather. | The school garden is mulched with wood chips. | Grandma mulched her roses with compost. | Worms love the leaves we use as mulch. | Mulch stops weeds from growing so fast. | Spread the mulch, but don't pile it against the stems.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable: "some mulch", "a layer of mulch". Rhymes with "gulch". Not the same as "much".

meaning for a pupil: 1) Made of many cells. Living things like animals, plants and most fungi are multicellular.
its sense in the lessons: A science word: in biology, living things are sorted into single-celled (unicellular), like bacteria, and multicellular, like humans, trees and mushrooms. In multicellular living things, different cells do different jobs (muscle cells, nerve cells, leaf cells).
examples from the lessons: Humans are multicellular organisms with trillions of cells. | A bacterium is single-celled, but a frog is multicellular. | Plants and animals are multicellular. | In multicellular life, cells share out the jobs. | Some seaweeds are multicellular and some are tiny single cells. | The first multicellular living things appeared long after bacteria. | Is a mushroom multicellular? Yes, it is made of many cells.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: "unicellular" or "single-celled". Prefix "multi-" means "many". Pronounced "mul-tee-SELL-yoo-lar". Adjective only.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Having or including people from many different cultures, countries, religions or backgrounds. 2) Showing or celebrating many cultures, as in "a multicultural festival".
its sense in the lessons: Used in citizenship, PSHE and everyday life about schools, cities and countries such as the UK, Canada and Australia where people of many backgrounds live together. Phrases: "multicultural society", "multicultural school", "multicultural day".
examples from the lessons: Our school is multicultural; we speak over twenty languages. | London, Toronto and Sydney are very multicultural cities. | On Multicultural Day we brought food from our families' countries. | Canada calls itself a multicultural country. | The festival had multicultural music and dance. | Living in a multicultural area helps you learn about other people. | A multicultural class can share many different festivals.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective; noun "multiculturalism" is the idea or policy of welcoming many cultures. Prefix "multi-" means "many". Not the same as "multilingual" (speaking many languages).

part of speech: adjective (multilingual; more multilingual); noun (a multilingual — rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Able to speak or use several languages. 2) Written in or using several languages, as in "a multilingual sign" or "a multilingual dictionary".
its sense in the lessons: Used in language lessons and everyday life: many children are multilingual, speaking one language at home and another at school. Airports, museums and hospitals use multilingual signs. Phrases: "multilingual family", "multilingual school".
examples from the lessons: My cousin is multilingual; she speaks English, Polish and Spanish. | The airport signs are multilingual. | Many children in Ireland are bilingual or multilingual. | Our school library has multilingual books. | Being multilingual can help you get a job abroad. | The museum gave us a multilingual guide. | Switzerland is a multilingual country with four official languages.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Bilingual means two languages, "trilingual" three, "multilingual" several or many. "Monolingual" means only one. "Lingual" comes from Latin "lingua" (tongue, language).

meaning for a pupil: 1) The process of preserving a dead body so that it does not rot, as the ancient Egyptians did. 2) The natural drying and preserving of a body in very dry, cold or boggy places.
its sense in the lessons: A favourite topic in history lessons on Ancient Egypt: the Egyptians removed organs, dried the body with a salt called natron, wrapped it in linen bandages and put it in a coffin, because they believed the body was needed in the afterlife. In science, natural mummification shows how dryness and cold stop decay.
examples from the lessons: Mummification in ancient Egypt could take about seventy days. | The Egyptians used natron salt in mummification. | We learned about mummification in our history topic. | Even cats and crocodiles were preserved by mummification. | Ötzi the Iceman shows natural mummification in ice. | Bog bodies found in Ireland and Denmark were preserved by natural mummification. | Ancient Egyptians believed mummification helped the dead in the afterlife.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Verb: "mummify" (mummifies, mummified). The body is "a mummy" (trap: in the UK "mummy" is also a child's word for mother). Myth: mummies do not come back to life; that is only in films.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who kills another person on purpose, against the law.
its sense in the lessons: Used in news, law, history and crime stories and mysteries ("Who is the murderer?"). In law a murderer is a person convicted of murder, which is a very serious crime punished with long prison sentences. Phrases: "convicted murderer", "mass murderer".
examples from the lessons: The detective finally worked out who the murderer was. | The murderer was sent to prison for life. | In the mystery book, the murderer was the gardener. | Police are still searching for the murderer. | Macbeth becomes a murderer because he wants to be king. | Calling someone a murderer without proof is very serious. | Killing in an accident does not make you a murderer.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Verb and noun "murder"; "murderous" (adjective). An old word for a woman murderer is "murderess". Note: killing by accident is not murder; in law it may be "manslaughter". A person is not called a murderer by the court until found guilty.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal, science) All the muscles of a body or of one part of the body, and the way they are arranged.
its sense in the lessons: A science and medical word used in biology and PE ("the musculature of the leg"), in art (drawing the musculature of a horse) and in describing athletes. In everyday talk people say "muscles".
examples from the lessons: The musculature of a cheetah is built for speed. | The poster showed the musculature of the human arm. | Gymnasts develop strong upper-body musculature. | The artist studied horse musculature to paint them well. | A snake's musculature lets it move without legs. | The doctor checked the musculature of his injured shoulder. | Our heart's musculature never rests.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; the everyday word is "muscles". Pronounced "MUS-kyuh-luh-cher". Spelling: musc-ul-ature, from "muscle".

part of speech: noun (mush — uncountable); verb (mush, mushes, mushed, mushing); interjection (Mush!)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A soft, wet, squashed mass of something, like overcooked food. 2) (informal) Silly, soppy talk or writing about love. 3) (interjection) A shout telling sled dogs to start or go faster; (verb) to travel with a dog sled. 4) (UK slang, old-fashioned) A way of calling a man, like "mate"; also slang for a person's face or mouth, as in "Shut your mush".
its sense in the lessons: Everyday: food turned to mush, brain turning to mush when tired. In stories about the Arctic, Alaska and Canada, "Mush!" sends the dogs running (the Iditarod race). In UK talk, "Oi, mush!" is a rough way to address a man. Phrases: "turn to mush", "my brain is mush".
examples from the lessons: The peas were boiled so long they turned to mush. | After the exam my brain felt like mush. | The banana at the bottom of my bag was mush. | "Mush!" shouted the musher, and the huskies ran. | They mushed across the snow for three days. | The film was all romantic mush. | "Oi, mush, you dropped your wallet!" (UK slang)
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly uncountable. Adjective: "mushy" (mushy peas are a British side dish). A "musher" drives a dog sled. The slang "mush" for a man or a face is old-fashioned and a bit rough.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A small, tough, half-wild horse of the western USA, descended from horses brought by the Spanish. 2) (with a capital M) The name of a famous American sports car, the Ford Mustang, and of a Second World War fighter plane, the P-51 Mustang.
its sense in the lessons: Used in history and nature lessons about the American West and in cowboy stories. Mustangs are "feral" horses: their ancestors were tame, but they live wild. In everyday talk, "a Mustang" is often the car.
examples from the lessons: Herds of wild mustangs still roam parts of Nevada. | The cowboy tamed a young mustang. | Mustangs came from horses the Spanish brought to America. | My uncle drives a red Mustang. | The mustang galloped across the plains with its mane flying. | We read a story about a girl and a wild mustang. | The P-51 Mustang was a famous fighter plane.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Lower case for the horse, capital M for the car and plane. From a Spanish word for stray animals. "Feral" means once tame, now wild.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a way that is strange and cannot be explained. 2) In a secretive way, keeping something hidden on purpose, as in "she smiled mysteriously".
its sense in the lessons: A favourite word in stories and mysteries: "the light mysteriously went out", "the key mysteriously disappeared". It tells the reader something strange is going on and makes them want to find out why. Phrases: "mysteriously disappeared", "mysteriously vanished".
examples from the lessons: My homework mysteriously disappeared from my desk. | The door creaked open mysteriously. | She smiled mysteriously and would not tell us the secret. | The cookies mysteriously vanished from the jar. | The lights in the old house mysteriously went off. | The ship mysteriously disappeared at sea. | "Wait and see," said Grandad mysteriously.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from "mysterious" + "-ly"; noun "mystery". Spelling: mys-te-ri-ous-ly (keep the "ou"). Often comes before the verb: "mysteriously disappeared".

meaning for a pupil: 1) A unit of length: one billionth of a metre (0.000000001 m). Symbol: nm.
its sense in the lessons: A science and maths word for very, very tiny things: atoms, molecules, viruses and the wavelength of light are measured in nanometres. Computer chips have parts only a few nanometres across. In maths: 1 metre = 1,000,000,000 nm; 1 millimetre = 1,000,000 nm.
examples from the lessons: A nanometre is a billion times smaller than a metre. | A human hair is about 80,000 nanometres wide. | Visible light has wavelengths of about 400 to 700 nanometres. | Some viruses are about 100 nanometres across. | Computer chips have tiny parts measured in nanometres. | Your fingernails grow about one nanometre every second. | We use nm as the symbol for nanometre.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK, Canada, Australia and NZ spelling "nanometre"; US spelling "nanometer". Symbol "nm" (not "nM", which is a chemistry unit). Prefix "nano-" means one billionth. In maths problems: divide nanometres by 1,000 to get micrometres, by 1,000,000 to get millimetres.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Being narrow; having little width from side to side. 2) Being limited or small in range, as in "narrowness of mind" (not open to other ideas).
its sense in the lessons: Used about roads, streets, bridges, boats and passages ("the narrowness of the lane"), and about ideas and attitudes when someone will not consider other views. In stories it often builds a tight, uncomfortable feeling.
examples from the lessons: The narrowness of the lane meant the bus could not get through. | We were surprised by the narrowness of the old staircase. | The narrowness of the gap made it hard to squeeze through. | Because of the river's narrowness, a bridge was easy to build. | Her narrowness of mind meant she never tried new food. | The narrowness of the win surprised everyone; it was only one point. | The cave's narrowness made us crawl.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. From "narrow" + "-ness". Opposite: "width", "breadth", "broadness". "A narrow win" means a win by a small amount.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To make a speech sound through the nose, letting air come out of the nose as well as the mouth.
its sense in the lessons: A word from phonics and language study: sounds like "m", "n" and "ng" are nasal, and French has nasalised vowels (as in "bon" and "vin"). People with a cold may sound less nasal because their nose is blocked.
examples from the lessons: French speakers nasalise the vowel in "bon". | Try to say "man" and notice how you nasalise the "a". | Some accents nasalise vowels before "m" and "n". | In French class we practised nasalised vowels. | When you hold your nose you cannot nasalise a sound. | Our teacher showed how "ng" is nasalised at the back of the mouth.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK spelling "nasalise"; US spelling "nasalize". Adjective "nasal" (to do with the nose). Mainly a specialist word for language study.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unkind, mean or spiteful behaviour. 2) Being very unpleasant, as in the nastiness of a smell or an illness.
its sense in the lessons: Used in stories, PSHE and everyday talk about bullying and unkind behaviour ("There's no need for nastiness") and to describe how bad something is.
examples from the lessons: There was no need for that nastiness; say sorry. | The nastiness of the comments online upset her. | We talked in class about how to stand up to nastiness. | The nastiness of the smell made us hold our noses. | Despite the nastiness of the bug, he was better in a week. | The villain's nastiness grew worse with every chapter. | Kindness can beat nastiness.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. From "nasty" + "-ness": the "y" changes to "i". Adjective "nasty", adverb "nastily".

meaning for a pupil: 1) (old-fashioned, literary) Nothing. 2) (mainly US) Zero, the number 0 (UK and others usually write "nought").
its sense in the lessons: Found in old books, poems, the Bible and phrases: "come to naught" (fail, come to nothing), "all for naught" (for nothing, wasted). It tells the reader that effort was wasted or a plan failed.
examples from the lessons: All their hard work came to naught when the rain washed the sandcastle away. | The knight's quest was all for naught. | "It is naught but a bad dream," said the wizard. | Their plans came to naught. | Without water, the seeds will grow to naught. | He cared naught for gold. | The final score was two to naught. (US)
note for the reader of a maths problem: Old-fashioned. Spelling trap: "naught" (nothing) and "nought" (zero, UK) are often mixed up; and "naughty" comes from "naught" but means badly behaved. Homophones in many accents: naught, nought.

part of speech: adjective (nauseating; more nauseating); verb form (present participle of nauseate: nauseate, nauseates, nauseated, nauseating)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Making you feel sick, as if you might vomit. 2) (informal) Very annoying or unpleasant, as in "nauseating showing-off".
its sense in the lessons: Used about smells, sights, motion (a nauseating boat trip) and in health; in everyday talk and stories it is used for something so unpleasant it makes you feel sick, even if not really. Phrases: "a nauseating smell".
examples from the lessons: The smell from the bin was nauseating. | The rollercoaster was so fast it was nauseating. | Reading in the car can be nauseating. | His bragging was nauseating. | The rotten eggs gave off a nauseating stink. | Some medicines have nauseating side effects. | The boat rocked in a nauseating way.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From "nausea" (feeling sick). Spelling: nau-se-at-ing. "Nauseous" means feeling sick ("I feel nauseous") in everyday use.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A Native American people of the south-western USA (Arizona, New Mexico, Utah), who call themselves the Diné. 2) Their language, Navajo, which is still spoken today. 3) (adjective) To do with the Navajo people, as in Navajo weaving.
its sense in the lessons: Used in US history, geography and social studies: the Navajo Nation is the largest Native American reservation by land. In the Second World War, Navajo Code Talkers used their language to send secret messages the enemy could not break. Navajo weaving and silver jewellery are famous.
examples from the lessons: The Navajo Nation spreads across Arizona, New Mexico and Utah. | Navajo Code Talkers helped the USA in the Second World War. | Many Navajo people still speak the Navajo language. | We looked at Navajo weaving in the museum. | The Navajo call themselves the Diné, meaning "the people". | Monument Valley lies on Navajo land. | The Long Walk of 1864 forced thousands of Navajo from their homeland.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always a capital N. Also spelled "Navaho" in older books. Plural "Navajo" or "Navajos". Pronounced "NAV-uh-ho" (the "j" sounds like "h").

meaning for a pupil: 1) The small hollow or bump in the middle of your tummy, left where the umbilical cord was joined before you were born; your belly button. 2) (figurative) The centre of something, as in "the navel of the world".
its sense in the lessons: Used in science and health (the umbilical cord carries food and oxygen from mother to baby) and in everyday talk, though children usually say "belly button". Phrases: "navel orange" (an orange with a little bump like a navel), "navel-gazing" (thinking too much about yourself).
examples from the lessons: Your navel is where the umbilical cord was. | Most people call the navel a belly button. | A navel orange has a small bump at one end. | Some people have an "innie" navel and some an "outie". | Mammals have navels, but birds hatched from eggs do not. | Stop navel-gazing and help us! | The yoga teacher told us to breathe into the navel.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Homophone trap: "naval" (to do with a navy and ships) sounds the same but is spelled with an "a". Countable.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Being close in distance. 2) Being close in time, as in "the nearness of the holidays". 3) Being close in a relationship or feeling.
its sense in the lessons: Used in everyday talk and stories about place, time and people: the nearness of the sea, the nearness of exams, a feeling of nearness to a friend.
examples from the lessons: The nearness of the school means I can walk there. | We loved the nearness of the beach. | The nearness of Christmas made everyone excited. | The nearness of the storm made the dog nervous. | She felt a nearness to her grandmother when she read her letters. | The nearness of the two planets made them look like one bright star. | The house's nearness to the motorway made it noisy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. From "near" + "-ness". Similar: "closeness", "proximity" (formal).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) Keeping young or baby-like features after growing up, in animals or people.
its sense in the lessons: A biology word: the axolotl, a Mexican salamander, keeps its feathery gills and stays in water all its life, a famous case of neoteny. Scientists say dogs show neoteny compared with wolves (floppy ears, playfulness), and humans have flat faces and big heads, like young apes.
examples from the lessons: The axolotl is a famous example of neoteny. | Neoteny means an animal keeps baby features as an adult. | Some scientists think puppy-like dogs show neoteny. | Our science teacher explained neoteny using salamanders. | Humans show some neoteny compared with chimpanzees. | Because of neoteny, the axolotl keeps its gills. | Neoteny can make adult animals look cute.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable, a specialist science word. Pronounced "nee-OT-uh-nee". From Greek "neo" (new, young). Adjective: "neotenous".

meaning for a pupil: 1) (UK, Australia, NZ) Nervous, jumpy and easily worried or frightened. 2) (US, informal) Bold and cheeky, daring to do things others would not.
its sense in the lessons: A word that means different things in different countries: in a British story, a "nervy" horse or child is jumpy; in an American story, a "nervy" kid is cheeky or brave. Used about sport ("a nervy finish") and everyday feelings.
examples from the lessons: I always feel a bit nervy before a test. (UK) | The horse was nervy and jumped at every noise. | It was a nervy last five minutes, but we held on to win. | The nervy kitten hid under the sofa. | That was a nervy thing to say to the principal! (US) | He gave a nervy laugh. | She was nervy on her first day at the new school.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK and US meanings differ: UK "nervy" = nervous; US "nervy" = bold or cheeky. Comparative "nervier", superlative "nerviest". Related: "nervous", "nerve" ("You've got a nerve!" = how rude/cheeky).

part of speech: noun (a nestling, nestlings); verb form (present participle of nestle: nestle, nestles, nestled, nestling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (noun) A baby bird too young to leave the nest. 2) (verb) Settling snugly and comfortably, as in "nestling under a blanket". 3) (verb) Lying in a sheltered place, as in "a village nestling in the valley".
its sense in the lessons: In science about birds: hatchling → nestling → fledgling, as the chick grows and learns to fly. In stories and descriptions, "nestling" paints a cosy or sheltered picture: a cottage nestling among the hills.
examples from the lessons: The nestlings opened their beaks wide for food. | A nestling has few feathers and cannot fly. | The village lay nestling in the green valley. | The puppy was nestling against its mother. | We watched the robin feed its nestlings. | The cottage stood nestling under tall trees. | If you find a nestling on the ground, ask an adult or a wildlife centre for help.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Two words with the same spelling: the noun (baby bird) and the -ing form of "nestle" (silent t: "NES-ling"). Bird stages: egg, hatchling, nestling, fledgling. Safety: do not pick up wild baby birds without advice.

part of speech: verb form (past tense and past participle of net: net, nets, netted, netting); adjective (netted)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Caught with a net. 2) (sport) Scored, especially a goal in football or hockey. 3) (money) Earned or gained as profit after costs, as in "netted £500". 4) (adjective) Covered with a net or a pattern like a net.
its sense in the lessons: Used in nature (fishermen netted fish), sport reports ("Smith netted twice"), money and maths (net profit = money left after costs) and gardening (netted fruit bushes to keep birds off).
examples from the lessons: The fishermen netted hundreds of fish. | She netted the winning goal in the last minute. | Our cake sale netted £85 for charity. | We netted a butterfly and then let it go. | The strawberries were netted to stop the birds eating them. | He netted a hat-trick on Saturday. | The pond was netted to keep the leaves out.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: double t before -ed and -ing (net, netted, netting). In maths and money, "net" amount = what is left after taking away costs; "gross" = before. So if a sale took £100 and cost £15, it netted £85.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) Névé: old, grainy snow on a glacier or high mountain that has partly melted and refrozen, on its way to becoming glacier ice. 2) It may also be a typing error for "never" or "nerve", or part of a name.
its sense in the lessons: A geography word about glaciers: fresh snow → névé (also called firn) → glacier ice. In English texts it is often written with an accent, névé, because it comes from French.
examples from the lessons: High on the mountain, the snow had turned to névé. | Névé is snow that is halfway to becoming ice. | The climbers crossed the hard névé early in the morning. | In geography we learned how snow becomes névé and then glacier ice. | Névé feels crunchy and grainy under your boots.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A borrowed French word, pronounced "nay-VAY". Also called "firn". If you see "neve" in a text, check whether it is a typo for "never".

meaning for a pupil: 1) New information about something that has just happened. 2) Reports of recent events on TV, radio, websites or in newspapers. 3) (the news) A programme that reports recent events. 4) (informal) Someone or something interesting or important, as in "That's news to me" (I didn't know).
its sense in the lessons: Used everywhere: "good news", "bad news", "the six o'clock news". In media lessons pupils learn to check news is true and to spot fake news. Phrases: "break the news" (tell someone bad news), "that's news to me", "no news is good news", "in the news", "fake news".
examples from the lessons: I have some good news: we're getting a puppy! | We watched the news after dinner. | Have you heard the news about our teacher? | The news is on at six o'clock. | She broke the news gently that the hamster had died. | "Mr Ellis is leaving?" "That's news to me!" | Not everything you read online is real news.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable, takes a singular verb: "The news is good" (not "are"). Say "a piece of news" or "some news", never "a news". Though it ends in "s", it is not a plural.

meaning for a pupil: 1) From or to do with Niger, a country in West Africa. 2) (noun) A person from Niger.
its sense in the lessons: Used in geography and news about Niger, a large, hot country mostly covered by the Sahara Desert, whose capital is Niamey. The River Niger flows through it.
examples from the lessons: A Nigerien family moved into our street. | Nigerien farmers grow millet in dry soil. | The Nigerien capital is Niamey. | Many Nigeriens speak French and Hausa. | The Nigerien desert has camel caravans. | We read about Nigerien schoolchildren in our geography book.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: Niger and Nigeria are different countries. A person from Niger is "Nigerien" (said "nee-ZHAIR-ee-en"); a person from Nigeria is "Nigerian". Always a capital N.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) A nightdress: a loose dress worn in bed, mostly by girls and women.
its sense in the lessons: A homely everyday word about bedtime, sleepovers and getting ready for bed. In stories, someone "in her nightie" has just got out of bed.
examples from the lessons: I put on my nightie and brushed my teeth. | She came downstairs in her nightie. | Gran gave me a pink nightie with stars on it. | Pack your nightie for the sleepover. | My nightie is too long; I trip on it. | Mum ran into the garden in her nightie when the alarm went off.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal, short for "nightgown" or "nightdress". Also spelled "nighty". Plural "nighties". Pyjamas (UK) / pajamas (US) are the top-and-trousers kind.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Able to move quickly, easily and lightly. 2) Quick and clever in thinking, as in "a nimble mind".
its sense in the lessons: Used in PE, nature and stories about animals and people: nimble goats, nimble fingers (good at fine work like knitting or piano). The nursery rhyme "Jack be nimble, Jack be quick". Phrases: "nimble fingers", "nimble-footed", "nimble mind".
examples from the lessons: The nimble goat climbed the steep rocks. | Jack be nimble, Jack be quick, Jack jump over the candlestick. | She has nimble fingers for playing the piano. | The nimble goalkeeper leapt to save the ball. | A squirrel is nimble on the thin branches. | The fox's nimble mind found a way out of the trap. | Gymnasts must be strong and nimble.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative "nimbler", superlative "nimblest". Adverb "nimbly" (not "nimblely"). Noun "nimbleness". Similar: agile, quick.

part of speech: verb form (present participle of nip: nip, nips, nipped, nipping)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Giving a quick, small bite or pinch. 2) (of cold) Biting or stinging, as in "a nipping wind". 3) (UK, Ireland, Australia, NZ, informal) Going somewhere quickly for a short time, as in "nipping out to the shop". 4) (with "in the bud") Stopping something before it grows bigger.
its sense in the lessons: Everyday: a puppy nipping fingers, a crab nipping toes; in British talk, "I'm just nipping to the loo". In stories, a nipping wind or frost tells the reader it is very cold. Phrases: "nip out", "nip in the bud", "nip and tuck" (very close, in a race).
examples from the lessons: The puppy keeps nipping at my socks. | I'm just nipping out to the corner shop. (UK) | A crab was nipping at his toe. | The nipping wind made our ears red. | Mum is nipping to the post office, back in five minutes. | Stop the teasing now and nip it in the bud. | The frost was nipping the young plants.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: double p before -ing and -ed (nip, nipping, nipped). Related adjective "nippy" (UK: cold, chilly; also quick). Not the same as "napping" (sleeping briefly).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A man who belongs to the nobility, the highest social class below the king or queen, with a title such as duke, earl, lord or count.
its sense in the lessons: Used in history (medieval kings, knights and noblemen; the barons who made King John agree to Magna Carta in 1215), in fairy tales and adventure stories. Noblemen often owned land and castles and had power over the people who worked their land.
examples from the lessons: A wealthy nobleman lived in the castle on the hill. | The king called his noblemen to a meeting. | The noblemen forced King John to sign Magna Carta. | In the story, a poor girl married a nobleman. | Noblemen rode to war with their knights. | A nobleman's sons were taught to ride and fight. | The French Revolution took power away from many noblemen.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural "noblemen" (not "noblemans"). Woman: "noblewoman". The class is "the nobility" or "the aristocracy". "Noble" also means good and honest ("a noble act"), which is a different sense.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A woman who belongs to the nobility, with a title such as duchess, countess or lady.
its sense in the lessons: Used in history and stories about kings, queens and castles; noblewomen ran large households and estates, and some, like Eleanor of Aquitaine, were very powerful.
examples from the lessons: The noblewoman wore a long silk gown. | A noblewoman ran the castle while her husband was at war. | Eleanor of Aquitaine was a powerful noblewoman and queen. | In the story, the noblewoman helped the poor villagers. | Noblewomen were often married for land and power, not love. | The portrait shows a noblewoman with her children. | She was born a noblewoman but chose to become a nun.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural "noblewomen" (the second syllable sounds like "WIM-in"). Man: "nobleman". Titles: duchess, countess, baroness, lady.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To suggest someone officially for a job, position or prize, as in "nominate her for class captain". 2) To choose or name someone for a job or duty, as in "nominate a leader". 3) To put forward a film, song or book for an award.
its sense in the lessons: Used at school (nominate a classmate for school council or student of the week), in politics and elections (parties nominate candidates), and in awards (nominated for an Oscar). Phrases: "nominate someone for", "be nominated", "nominated as".
examples from the lessons: I nominate Priya for class captain. | Our book was nominated for a prize. | Each team must nominate a leader. | The film was nominated for three Oscars. | You can't nominate yourself for the award. | The party nominated a new candidate for president. | Who did you nominate for kindness champion?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Noun "nomination"; a person nominated is a "nominee". Being nominated does not mean winning, only being chosen as a possible winner.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (grammar) The form of a noun or pronoun used for the subject of a sentence, the one doing the action. In English, "I, he, she, we, they" are nominative; "me, him, her, us, them" are not.
its sense in the lessons: A grammar word used when learning languages like Latin, German, Ukrainian or Russian, where nouns change their endings in different cases. In English, it explains why we say "She and I went" (nominative) but "Mum saw her and me".
examples from the lessons: He is the nominative form; "him" is not. | In "The cat sat", "the cat" is in the nominative case. | In German we learned the nominative and accusative cases. | Latin nouns change their endings: "puella" is nominative. | Use the nominative "I" when you are the subject: "Tom and I won". | Ukrainian has seven cases, starting with the nominative.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Also called the "subject case". Trap: say "My friend and I played" (nominative), not "My friend and me played". Not the same as "nominate".

meaning for a pupil: 1) To make something seem normal or ordinary, so people accept it, as in "normalise talking about feelings". 2) To return something to a normal state, as in "relations normalised". 3) (maths, science) To change numbers to a standard scale so they can be compared.
its sense in the lessons: Used in PSHE ("We want to normalise asking for help"; "Don't normalise bullying"), in news about countries making peace (normalise relations), and in science and data, where values are scaled so they can be compared fairly.
examples from the lessons: We should normalise talking about mental health. | Laughing at bullying normalises it, which is wrong. | After the storm, life slowly normalised. | The two countries agreed to normalise relations. | Scientists normalise the results so they can compare them. | Her temperature normalised after the medicine. | Some games normalise violence, critics say.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK, Australia, NZ spelling "normalise"; US and Canada "normalize". Noun "normalisation". "Normalise" can be good (normalise asking for help) or bad (normalise cruelty).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Being too interested in other people's private business; being nosy.
its sense in the lessons: An everyday word for prying behaviour: peeping at someone's diary, listening at doors, asking too many personal questions. In stories, a nosy neighbour's nosiness may uncover a mystery. Linked to safety and privacy online.
examples from the lessons: Her nosiness got her into trouble when she read her sister's diary. | Excuse my nosiness, but where did you get that coat? | The neighbour's nosiness was annoying. | Nosiness helped the detective solve the case. | "Stop your nosiness and mind your own business!" | The cat's nosiness led it into the cupboard. | Nosiness about other people's passwords is never okay.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. From "nosy" (also spelled "nosey") + "-ness": the "y" becomes "i". Phrase: "Mind your own business". "Nosy parker" (UK) is someone who is nosy.

part of speech: adjective (notable; more notable); noun (a notable, notables — formal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Worth noticing or important enough to be noticed. 2) Famous or well known, as in "a notable writer". 3) (noun, formal) An important or famous person.
its sense in the lessons: Used in history and news ("notable events", "notable people") and in school writing for something important. Phrases: "notable for", "a notable exception" (one that doesn't follow the pattern).
examples from the lessons: The town is notable for its old castle. | Marie Curie was a notable scientist. | There was a notable improvement in his reading. | Most birds can fly; the penguin is a notable exception. | The day's notable events were a fire drill and a visit from an author. | Many local notables came to the opening. | Her kindness was notable.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb "notably" (especially). Similar: "noteworthy", "remarkable". Not the same as "noticeable" (easy to see); "notable" means important or worth mentioning.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a way that is easy to see, hear or notice.
its sense in the lessons: Used in science (the plant grew noticeably taller), in everyday life and in stories to show a clear change. In comparisons it says the difference is big enough to see.
examples from the lessons: The days are noticeably shorter in winter. | She was noticeably taller after the summer. | The class was noticeably quieter after the warning. | The plant in sunlight grew noticeably faster. | He was noticeably nervous before his speech. | It's noticeably colder today. | My handwriting has noticeably improved.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: keep the "e" in "notice" before "-able" to keep the soft "c": notice-ably. Adjective "noticeable". In science write-ups, "noticeably" is weaker than giving numbers: say how much.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Existing only as an idea or estimate, not real or exact, as in "a notional sum". 2) (formal) Based on theory, not on facts or practice.
its sense in the lessons: Used in money, maths and economics (a notional value, a number used to compare or plan, not a real amount paid) and in formal writing. In everyday life it is a rarer word.
examples from the lessons: Each player gets a notional £100 in the game to spend. | The price is only notional; nobody has really paid it. | The rent was a notional one pound a year. | The map uses a notional line to divide the zones. | We worked out a notional budget for our class party. | The equator is a notional line round the Earth.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal. From "notion" (an idea). In maths problems, a notional amount is an imagined amount used for working out; treat it as the given number.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A sweet made of sugar or honey, egg whites and nuts, either white and chewy or brown and crunchy.
its sense in the lessons: An everyday food word: nougat is found in chocolate bars and sold at Christmas in many countries (French nougat from Montélimar, Italian torrone, Spanish turrón).
examples from the lessons: Grandma brought back nougat from France. | This chocolate bar has a chewy nougat centre. | Nougat is sticky, so brush your teeth after eating it. | The white nougat was full of almonds and pistachios. | We bought a slab of nougat at the Christmas market. | Too much nougat is bad for your teeth.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced "NOO-gah" (UK/US) or "NUG-et" (UK, informal). Usually uncountable ("some nougat"); countable for single sweets. Not the same as "nugget" (a lump of gold or chicken).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (UK, Ireland, Australia, NZ) The number zero, 0. 2) (literary) Nothing (more often spelled "naught").
its sense in the lessons: A maths word in British-style schools: "nought point five" (0.5), "ten has one ten and nought ones", and the game "noughts and crosses" (US: tic-tac-toe). In maths problems, nought means the value is zero.
examples from the lessons: Write a nought in the units column. | Nought point five is the same as a half. | Let's play noughts and crosses. | The temperature fell to nought degrees. | A million has six noughts. | Anything multiplied by nought is nought. | The score was three–nought. (UK sport usually says "three–nil")
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK word; Americans say "zero". In maths: adding nought changes nothing; multiplying by nought gives nought; you cannot divide by nought. Trap: "nought" (zero) vs "naught" (nothing).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Short for November, the eleventh month of the year.
its sense in the lessons: Used in dates, calendars and forms: "5 Nov" (Bonfire Night in the UK, also Guy Fawkes Night), "Nov 11" (Remembrance Day / Veterans Day). In school writing, write the month in full unless space is short.
examples from the lessons: My birthday is on 23 Nov. | Bonfire Night is on 5 Nov in the UK. | The calendar says "Nov" at the top. | Remembrance Day is on 11 Nov. | The trip is booked for Nov 14. | Fill in the date: Nov 2.
note for the reader of a maths problem: An abbreviation, not a word on its own; usually written with a capital N, often with a full stop in the US ("Nov."). November has 30 days. Month abbreviations: Jan, Feb, Mar, Apr, Aug, Sep/Sept, Oct, Nov, Dec.

meaning for a pupil: 1) At the present time, compared with the past.
its sense in the lessons: Used in history lessons and everyday talk to compare then and now: "In Victorian times children worked in factories; nowadays they go to school." It tells the reader a comparison with the past is being made.
examples from the lessons: Nowadays most people have a mobile phone. | Long ago people wrote letters; nowadays they send messages. | Children nowadays learn coding at school. | Nowadays we can watch films on a tablet. | "Kids nowadays!" Grandad grumbled with a smile. | Nowadays the castle is a museum. | Nowadays fewer children walk to school.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word, no space: "nowadays" (not "now a days"). Similar: "these days", "today". Usually at the start or end of the sentence.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Harmful or poisonous, especially gases, fumes and chemicals. 2) Very unpleasant, as in "a noxious smell". 3) (of plants) Harmful weeds that are a pest to farms, as in "noxious weeds" (Australia, US, Canada).
its sense in the lessons: Used in science and safety (noxious gases from cars, factories or fires can make people ill; never mix cleaning products because they can give off noxious fumes) and in stories about smells. In Australia and North America "noxious weeds" are plants landowners must control by law.
examples from the lessons: The factory let out noxious fumes. | Never mix bleach with other cleaners; it makes noxious gases. | A noxious smell came from the drain. | Some plants are listed as noxious weeds. | Car exhaust contains noxious gases. | The witch stirred a noxious green potion. | The firefighters wore masks against the noxious smoke.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; everyday words: "harmful", "poisonous", "toxic". Pronounced "NOK-shus". Safety: if you smell strong fumes, get to fresh air and tell an adult.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (games) Short for "non-player character": a character in a video game controlled by the computer, not by a player. 2) (slang, rude) An insult for a person who seems boring, follows the crowd or does not think for themselves.
its sense in the lessons: Used by gamers: shopkeepers, villagers and guards in games are often NPCs who repeat the same lines. Among teenagers, calling someone an "NPC" is an unkind insult. Phrases: "talk to the NPC", "NPC behaviour".
examples from the lessons: Talk to the NPC in the village to get your next quest. | The NPC kept saying the same line over and over. | In Minecraft, villagers are NPCs. | That NPC sells potions and swords. | "Stop acting like an NPC!" he said, which was mean. (slang) | Some NPCs in the game help you, others attack you.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say each letter: "en-pee-see"; "an NPC" (because "N" sounds like "en"). Plural "NPCs". The insult is unkind, like calling someone a robot.

meaning for a pupil: 1) "n't": the short form of "not" in contractions like "don't", "isn't", "can't", which may appear cut off as "nt". 2) (church, Bible) NT is short for the New Testament, the second part of the Christian Bible. 3) (Australia) NT is short for the Northern Territory, a part of Australia whose capital is Darwin. 4) (UK) The National Trust, a charity that looks after old houses, gardens and countryside.
its sense in the lessons: A fragment, not a word. In grammar lessons, "n't" stands for "not" in contractions: do + not = don't. In RE, NT means New Testament (the Gospels and letters about Jesus and the first Christians). In Australian geography, the NT contains Uluru.
examples from the lessons: Don't is short for "do not"; the "n't" means "not". | In RE we read the Gospels in the NT. | Uluru is in the NT, in the middle of Australia. | We went to an NT house with a huge garden. | The apostrophe in "isn't" replaces the "o" of "not". | Darwin is the capital of the NT.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Fragment and abbreviation, not a word on its own. In contractions the apostrophe goes where letters are missing: "did not" → "didn't" (not "did'nt"). Special forms: "can't" (cannot), "won't" (will not). OT = Old Testament.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A kind of sea slug, often brightly coloured, with no shell, that lives in the sea.
its sense in the lessons: A science word about sea life: nudibranchs live on reefs and rocks and come in amazing colours and patterns. Their bright colours warn predators they taste bad or are poisonous; some even store the stings of the animals they eat.
examples from the lessons: Divers love spotting colourful nudibranchs on the reef. | A nudibranch is a sea slug with no shell. | This nudibranch is bright purple with orange tips. | Nudibranchs' bright colours warn fish to stay away. | We saw a photo of a nudibranch in our ocean book. | Some nudibranchs eat jellyfish and keep their stings. | There are thousands of kinds of nudibranch.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced "NEW-dee-brank" ("ch" sounds like "k"). Means "naked gills" in Latin and Greek: their gills are on the outside. Plural "nudibranchs".

meaning for a pupil: 1) (maths) The way numbers are written, read and named, for example our place-value system with ten digits. 2) (formal) Counting or numbering things.
its sense in the lessons: A maths word: "systems of numeration" include our base-ten system, Roman numerals and ancient Egyptian and Mayan numbers. In numeration lessons pupils learn place value: ones, tens, hundreds, thousands.
examples from the lessons: Our system of numeration uses ten digits, 0 to 9. | Roman numeration uses letters like I, V, X and L. | The Maya had a numeration system based on twenty. | In numeration we learned to read big numbers like 4,056,000. | Place value is the key idea of numeration. | Babylonian numeration was based on sixty, which is why an hour has sixty minutes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly a formal or maths-textbook word. Related: "number", "numeral" (a written symbol for a number, like 7 or VII), "enumerate" (to list one by one).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (slang, unkind) A person who acts in a very silly, wild or crazy way. 2) (slang, can be friendly) A fun, daft person, as in "You're a total nutcase!" among friends.
its sense in the lessons: Used in informal talk and stories; it can be a joke between friends or an insult. It is unkind and hurtful to use about people with mental illness. In stories it shows the speaker is being rude or teasing.
examples from the lessons: You're a nutcase! laughed Tom as his friend jumped in the puddle. | Some nutcase drove the wrong way down the road. | My uncle is a lovable nutcase who dances everywhere. | Don't call people nutcases; it can hurt. | The dog went like a nutcase when it saw the ball. | Only a nutcase would swim in the sea in January!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal and slang; never use in school writing. Similar slang: "nutter" (UK), "nut", "loony", all unkind. Kind language: avoid using these words about people who are ill.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Doing what you are told by a parent, teacher, rule or owner. 2) (of animals) Trained to follow commands, as in "an obedient dog".
its sense in the lessons: Used at home, school and with pets ("dog obedience classes"). In stories and ethics lessons, being obedient is often good, but stories also ask when it is right to say no, for example if someone asks you to do something wrong or unsafe. In church life, obedience to God is one of the monastic vows.
examples from the lessons: Our dog is very obedient; he sits when told. | The obedient children lined up quietly. | Soldiers are trained to be obedient. | Being obedient doesn't mean doing something dangerous because someone says so. | The puppy became more obedient after training. | In the story, the obedient servant did everything the king asked. | Sheepdogs are clever and obedient.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: "disobedient". Noun "obedience"; verb "obey". Spelling: o-be-di-ent. Safety: you never have to obey a stranger or anyone asking you to keep a harmful secret.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (a name) The king of the fairies in old European folklore and stories. 2) (science) The second-largest moon of the planet Uranus.
its sense in the lessons: A name: Oberon appears in legends and in famous plays as the fairy king, husband of Titania. In astronomy, Oberon is a cold, icy, cratered moon of Uranus, discovered by William Herschel in 1787.
examples from the lessons: Oberon is the king of the fairies in the old stories. | Oberon and Titania quarrelled over a magic flower. | Oberon is one of the moons of Uranus. | William Herschel discovered Oberon with his telescope. | The moon Oberon is covered in craters.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A proper name, always with a capital O. Pronounced "OH-buh-ron". Uranus's moons are named after characters from English literature, like Titania and Miranda.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Unpleasant or offensive, so that people object to it.
its sense in the lessons: Used in formal or polite language: "objectionable behaviour", "objectionable language", "objectionable content" (for content online that is offensive or unsuitable). It tells the reader something is unacceptable.
examples from the lessons: His language was objectionable, so the referee sent him off. | The website removes objectionable content. | Some people found the joke objectionable. | There was an objectionable smell from the drains. | Their objectionable behaviour on the bus was reported to the school. | Is there anything objectionable in this film for young children?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal. From "object" (verb, "ob-JECT", to disagree) + "-ionable". Everyday words: "offensive", "nasty", "rude".

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Because a rule or law says you must; in a way that is required, not a choice.
its sense in the lessons: A stiff formal word used in rules, law and exam language: things that must be done "obligatorily" are compulsory. In everyday speech people say "you have to" or "it's compulsory".
examples from the lessons: Seatbelts must be worn obligatorily in cars. | In some countries, voting is done obligatorily. | Helmets are obligatorily worn on the building site. | The form must obligatorily be signed by a parent. | All visitors obligatorily sign in at the office. | Uniform is obligatorily worn in many UK schools.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal and rare; the adjective "obligatory" (compulsory, must be done) is far more common. Pronounced "ob-LIG-uh-tor-uh-lee" (UK) or "uh-blig-uh-TOR-uh-lee" (US). Opposite: "optionally", "voluntarily".

part of speech: verb form (past tense and past participle of obliterate: obliterate, obliterates, obliterated, obliterating); adjective (obliterated)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Destroyed completely so that nothing is left. 2) Covered or hidden so that it cannot be seen, as in "footprints obliterated by snow". 3) (informal) Beaten very badly in a game.
its sense in the lessons: Used in history and news (cities obliterated by bombs or volcanoes, like Pompeii), in science (asteroids obliterated by impact) and in stories. In sports talk it means a heavy defeat. Phrases: "completely obliterated", "obliterated from memory".
examples from the lessons: The town was obliterated by the volcano. | Snow obliterated our footprints. | The meteor was obliterated as it burned up in the atmosphere. | The old writing on the stone was nearly obliterated. | We got obliterated 10–0 in the final! (informal) | The flood obliterated the bridge. | Her sad memory was obliterated by the happy news.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Strong word: stronger than "destroyed". Spelling: ob-lit-er-at-ed (one "b", one "t" before "er"). Noun "obliteration".

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who plays the oboe, a woodwind instrument with a double reed.
its sense in the lessons: Used in music lessons and concerts: in an orchestra the oboist often plays the note "A" that all the other players tune to.
examples from the lessons: The oboist played the tuning note for the orchestra. | My sister wants to be an oboist. | The oboist practised the solo all week. | An oboist makes her own reeds from cane. | The duck's tune in "Peter and the Wolf" is played by the oboist. | The orchestra has two oboists.
note for the reader of a maths problem: An oboist (an, because it starts with a vowel sound). Pronounced "OH-boh-ist". The instrument is the "oboe". Other players: flautist, clarinettist, bassoonist.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A very rude or offensive word, especially a swear word. 2) Something shockingly offensive or rude. 3) Something morally shocking or wrong, as in "War is an obscenity" or "the obscenity of hunger in a rich world".
its sense in the lessons: Used in news, law and formal speech ("He shouted obscenities") and in ethics and politics to say something is deeply wrong. At school and in public, obscenities are not allowed. Phrases: "shout obscenities", "an obscenity".
examples from the lessons: The angry driver shouted obscenities out of the window. | Obscenities are not allowed in the school playground. | The referee sent off the player for using an obscenity. | The newspaper said wasting food while people starve is an obscenity. | The graffiti was full of obscenities, so the council cleaned it off. | Some people think huge bonuses are an obscenity.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable for single words ("obscenities"); uncountable for the quality. Adjective "obscene". Formal; everyday word: "swear word". Pronounced "ob-SEN-it-ee".

part of speech: adjective (obsessed; more obsessed); verb form (past tense and past participle of obsess: obsess, obsesses, obsessed, obsessing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Thinking about something or someone all the time, so it fills your mind. 2) (informal) Loving something very much, as in "I'm obsessed with this song". 3) (health) Troubled by thoughts that keep coming back and are hard to stop.
its sense in the lessons: Everyday and teenage talk: "obsessed with dinosaurs", "obsessed with football". In stories, an obsessed character cannot stop chasing a goal. In health talk, OCD (obsessive-compulsive disorder) is an illness, not just liking things tidy. Phrases: "obsessed with", "obsessed by".
examples from the lessons: My little brother is obsessed with dinosaurs. | I'm obsessed with this new song! | The detective was obsessed with solving the case. | She's obsessed with keeping her room tidy. | He became obsessed with winning and forgot to have fun. | Some people are obsessed with their phones. | The scientist was obsessed by one question.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually "obsessed with" (or "by"). Spelling: double s twice: o-b-s-e-s-s-e-d. Noun "obsession"; adjective "obsessive". Don't say "I'm so OCD" to mean tidy; OCD is a real illness.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To remove a need or a problem, so that something is no longer necessary, as in "This obviates the need for…".
its sense in the lessons: A stiff formal word used in exams, reports and official writing; it almost always comes in "obviate the need for". In everyday speech people say "avoid", "get rid of" or "means we don't need".
examples from the lessons: The new bridge obviates the need for a ferry. | Labelling the boxes obviated any confusion. | A good plan obviates the need for rushing. | Wearing a helmet does not obviate the need to ride carefully. | The calculator obviates the need for long division. | Online forms obviate the need for paper.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal and rare. Pronounced "OB-vee-ate". Do not confuse with "obvious" (easy to see); the two words are related in origin but mean different things.

part of speech: verb form (present participle of obviate: obviate, obviates, obviated, obviating)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Removing a need or problem, so that something is no longer necessary.
its sense in the lessons: A formal word used in reports and exam passages: "a system obviating the need for…". Everyday language would say "so we don't need" or "avoiding".
examples from the lessons: The new lift is obviating the need for stairs. | The plan aimed at obviating any delay. | The app saves time by obviating paperwork. | Solar panels are obviating the need for a generator. | By obviating the risk, the rule kept everyone safe. | Checking twice means obviating silly mistakes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; "-ing" form of "obviate" (drop the "e"). Almost always used with "the need for". Not related in meaning to "obvious".

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal, medicine) A blocking or closing of a tube, pipe or blood vessel. 2) (dentistry) The way your top and bottom teeth fit together when you bite. 3) (weather) An occluded front, where a cold front catches up with a warm front. 4) (science, astronomy) One object hiding another from view, as when the Moon passes in front of a star.
its sense in the lessons: A science and medical word: doctors talk about an occlusion in an artery; dentists and orthodontists (braces) check your occlusion; weather forecasters and geography lessons mention occlusions on weather maps; in astronomy it is like an eclipse.
examples from the lessons: The doctor found an occlusion in the blood vessel. | The dentist checked my occlusion to see how my teeth meet. | Braces can fix a bad occlusion. | The weather map showed an occlusion bringing rain. | An eclipse is a kind of occlusion of the Sun. | In video games, occlusion means hiding objects behind others.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal and technical. Verb "occlude" (to block). Pronounced "uh-KLOO-zhun". Everyday word: "blockage".

meaning for a pupil: 1) To do with a person's job or work. 2) Caused by or happening because of someone's work, as in "occupational injury".
its sense in the lessons: Used in health, safety and careers: "occupational hazard" (a danger that comes with a job), "occupational therapy" (help with everyday tasks after illness or injury, or for children who need support with skills like writing or dressing). Phrases: "occupational hazard", "occupational therapist", "occupational health".
examples from the lessons: Sunburn is an occupational hazard for lifeguards. | An occupational therapist helped my brother hold his pencil better. | Builders wear hard hats for occupational safety. | Getting paint on your clothes is an occupational hazard for artists. | The company has an occupational health nurse. | Back pain can be an occupational injury for nurses.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From "occupation" (a job). Spelling: double c, single p: oc-cu-pa-tion-al. Different from "occupied" (busy, or a seat taken).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) An animal with eight arms or legs, especially an octopus. 2) (science) A member of the group of sea animals that includes octopuses.
its sense in the lessons: A biology word used when sorting animals: octopuses are octopods; squid and cuttlefish have eight arms plus two longer tentacles, so they are not counted as octopods. Also used in science fiction for eight-legged robots or aliens.
examples from the lessons: An octopus is an octopod with eight arms. | Squid are not octopods because they have ten limbs. | The deep-sea dumbo octopus is a cute octopod. | Scientists study how octopods change colour. | The robot octopod walked on eight legs. | Octopods are very clever and can open jars.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Octo means eight (octagon, October was once the eighth month). In maths problems: 3 octopods have 3 × 8 = 24 arms. Spiders have eight legs but are called arachnids, not octopods.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A strange or unusual person, thing or event. 2) Being strange or unusual (uncountable).
its sense in the lessons: Used in stories, science and everyday talk: museums show oddities; nature has oddities like the platypus, a mammal that lays eggs. Phrases: "a bit of an oddity", "an oddity of nature".
examples from the lessons: The platypus is an oddity: a mammal that lays eggs. | The shop sold oddities like two-headed toy dragons. | It was an oddity that the clock ran backwards. | Among the plain houses, the purple one was an oddity. | In a class of football fans, the boy who loved opera was an oddity. | The oddity of the noise made us look around. | The museum's cabinet of oddities was my favourite room.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural "oddities". From "odd" (strange, and also not even). Odd numbers (1, 3, 5) have nothing to do with oddities, though they share the word "odd".

part of speech: noun (an odyssey, odysseys); proper noun (the Odyssey)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A long, exciting journey full of adventures and difficulties. 2) (the Odyssey, a name) An ancient Greek epic poem, said to be by Homer, about the hero Odysseus and his ten-year journey home after the Trojan War.
its sense in the lessons: Used in literature and history (myths, Greek legends: the Cyclops, the Sirens, Penelope waiting for Odysseus), and in everyday talk and stories for any long, eventful trip or experience ("Our journey to Granny's was a real odyssey").
examples from the lessons: The Odyssey tells how Odysseus sailed home from Troy. | Getting home in the snow was a three-day odyssey. | In the Odyssey, Odysseus tricks the Cyclops. | Our school trip turned into an odyssey when the coach broke down. | The film follows a dog's odyssey to find its family. | Learning to read was a long odyssey for him.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital O for the poem ("the Odyssey"), lower case for any long journey. Plural "odysseys". Spelling: o-d-y-s-s-e-y. Related: Ulysses is the Roman name for Odysseus.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) The sense of smell, or the act of smelling.
its sense in the lessons: A biology word about the senses: olfaction works when tiny particles in the air reach smell sensors in your nose. Dogs, sharks and bears have much stronger olfaction than humans. Smell is also linked to taste: when your nose is blocked, food tastes of less.
examples from the lessons: Dogs rely on olfaction far more than humans. | Olfaction is one of the five senses. | A cold can block olfaction and make food taste bland. | Sharks have strong olfaction for detecting blood in the water. | Scientists study olfaction to understand how memories link to smells. | Moths use olfaction to find flowers at night.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal science word; the everyday words are "smell" or "sense of smell". Adjective "olfactory" (as in "olfactory nerve"). Uncountable.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A sign or event that some people believe shows that something good or bad will happen in the future.
its sense in the lessons: Used in stories, myths and history (a comet seen as an omen before a battle; black cats and broken mirrors in superstitions). Science and most people today see omens as superstition, but they are common in stories to build suspense. Phrases: "a good omen", "a bad omen", "an omen of".
examples from the lessons: The sailors thought the storm was a bad omen. | Seeing a rainbow on the first day felt like a good omen. | In the story, a raven was an omen of trouble. | Some people think a black cat is an omen of bad luck. | Halley's Comet was seen as an omen before the Battle of Hastings in 1066. | Winning the first match was a good omen for the season.
note for the reader of a maths problem: An omen (an, before a vowel sound). Adjective "ominous" (threatening, as if something bad will happen). Omens are superstition, not science.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A Native American people, one of the Six Nations of the Haudenosaunee (Iroquois Confederacy), from what is now New York State; also their language. 2) (a name) Oneida Lake in New York State, and towns named after the people.
its sense in the lessons: Used in US history and social studies: the Oneida were one of the original five nations of the Haudenosaunee, with the Mohawk, Onondaga, Cayuga and Seneca. They sided with the Americans in the American Revolution and today have lands in New York and Wisconsin.
examples from the lessons: The Oneida are one of the Six Nations of the Haudenosaunee. | The Oneida helped the Americans during the Revolutionary War. | Oneida Lake is in New York State. | Many Oneida people live in Wisconsin today. | We learned about the Oneida in our Native American history unit.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A proper name, always with a capital O. Pronounced "oh-NYE-duh". The word means "people of the standing stone".

meaning for a pupil: 1) A Native American people of central New York State, one of the Six Nations of the Haudenosaunee (Iroquois Confederacy); also their language. 2) (a name) Onondaga Lake and Onondaga County, near Syracuse, New York.
its sense in the lessons: Used in US history and social studies: the Onondaga are known as the "keepers of the central fire" of the Haudenosaunee, where the Grand Council of chiefs meets. The Great Law of Peace is linked with them.
examples from the lessons: The Onondaga Nation hosts the Grand Council of the Haudenosaunee. | The Onondaga are called the keepers of the fire. | Onondaga Lake is near the city of Syracuse. | Onondaga is also the name of a language. | We read a legend told by Onondaga storytellers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A proper name, always a capital O. Pronounced "on-un-DAW-guh". The Six Nations: Mohawk, Oneida, Onondaga, Cayuga, Seneca and Tuscarora.

meaning for a pupil: 1) On the land, not at sea, as in "onshore wind farms". 2) (of wind) Blowing from the sea towards the land. 3) (money, business) Inside a country rather than abroad.
its sense in the lessons: Used in geography and science (onshore and offshore wind; an onshore breeze on a sunny afternoon at the beach), in energy (onshore wind turbines on hills) and in surfing reports (onshore wind makes waves messy). Phrases: "onshore wind", "come onshore".
examples from the lessons: Onshore wind farms are built on land. | An onshore breeze blew in from the sea in the afternoon. | The oil was brought onshore by pipeline. | Surfers don't like an onshore wind because it spoils the waves. | The storm moved onshore and caused flooding. | In geography we compared onshore and offshore wind energy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word. Opposite: "offshore" (out at sea, or from the land towards the sea). Trap: an "onshore wind" blows TO the land, an "offshore wind" blows FROM the land.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A kind of Chinese tea, partly oxidised, between green tea and black tea in taste and colour.
its sense in the lessons: An everyday food word: oolong is grown mostly in China (Fujian) and Taiwan, often served in small cups. In science, the leaves are left to react with air (oxidise) for some time, which changes the flavour and colour.
examples from the lessons: Grandpa drinks oolong tea after dinner. | Oolong is between green tea and black tea. | We tasted oolong at the Chinese New Year festival. | The tea shop sells a dozen kinds of oolong. | Oolong leaves are often rolled into small balls. | Oolong tea comes from China and Taiwan.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comes from Chinese "wulong", meaning "black dragon". Pronounced "OO-long". Usually uncountable ("some oolong"). Tea contains caffeine, like coffee.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To do with opera, plays where all or most of the words are sung, with an orchestra. 2) Very dramatic and over-the-top, as in "an operatic display of tears".
its sense in the lessons: Used in music lessons (operatic singers, operatic voices) and in everyday talk and stories for big, dramatic behaviour. Phrases: "operatic voice", "operatic singer", "operatic aria".
examples from the lessons: She has a powerful operatic voice. | The operatic singer hit the highest note perfectly. | Our school performed an operatic version of "Cinderella". | He gave an operatic sigh when told to tidy his room. | The film had operatic music in the big battle scene. | An aria is an operatic song for one singer.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From "opera" + "-tic". Pronounced "op-uh-RAT-ik". Opera singers sing classically; "soprano", "tenor", "bass" are voice types.

part of speech: adjective (oppressed); verb form (past tense and past participle of oppress: oppress, oppresses, oppressed, oppressing); noun (the oppressed)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Treated in a cruel and unfair way by people with power, and not given freedom or rights. 2) (feeling) Weighed down by worry or sadness, as in "oppressed by the heat". 3) (the oppressed) People who are treated unfairly by those in power.
its sense in the lessons: Used in history, citizenship and religious education: enslaved people, people under dictators and groups denied rights were oppressed; movements for civil rights fought against it. In the Bible, the Israelites in Egypt were oppressed and God led them out (the Exodus). Phrases: "the oppressed", "oppressed people", "feel oppressed".
examples from the lessons: The workers were oppressed by the cruel factory owner. | Martin Luther King Jr. spoke up for oppressed people. | In the Bible, the Israelites were oppressed in Egypt. | Many charities help the poor and the oppressed. | She felt oppressed by the heavy, hot air. | The king oppressed his people with high taxes. | In the story, the oppressed villagers rose up against the tyrant.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: double p and double s. Noun "oppression"; adjective "oppressive" (cruel and unfair; or uncomfortably hot: "oppressive heat"); person who does it: "oppressor". Not the same as "depressed" (very sad).

meaning for a pupil: 1) By speaking, not in writing, as in "answer orally". 2) (medicine) By mouth, as in "take this medicine orally".
its sense in the lessons: Used at school (oral tests, reading aloud, "present your project orally"), in history (stories passed down orally before writing, called oral tradition) and in health (medicine taken orally, by mouth, rather than by injection).
examples from the lessons: Please answer the questions orally, not in writing. | The old stories were passed down orally for hundreds of years. | Take two tablets orally with water. | We presented our science project orally to the class. | In the French test, part is done orally. | The vaccine can be given orally as drops.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From "oral" (to do with the mouth or speaking) + "-ly". Homophone trap: "aurally" (by hearing, to do with the ear) sounds the same. Medicine safety: only take medicine an adult gives you.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The skill of giving powerful, good speeches in public. 2) (church) A small chapel or room for private prayer; also a particular Catholic community and its church, like the London Oratory.
its sense in the lessons: Used in history, English and debating clubs: great speakers like Martin Luther King Jr. ("I have a dream") and Winston Churchill are famous for their oratory. In church life an oratory is a place set aside for prayer.
examples from the lessons: Martin Luther King Jr.'s oratory moved millions of people. | The debating club helps you improve your oratory. | Ancient Romans studied oratory at school. | The castle has a tiny oratory where the family prayed. | His oratory made the crowd cheer. | The Brompton Oratory is a large Catholic church in London.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable for the skill; countable for the chapel ("oratories"). A speaker is an "orator". Pronounced "OR-uh-tree" (UK) or "OR-uh-tor-ee" (US).

meaning for a pupil: 1) To do with an orchestra or written for an orchestra, a large group of musicians playing strings, woodwind, brass and percussion together.
its sense in the lessons: Used in music lessons and concerts: "orchestral music", "orchestral instruments", and film soundtracks. Phrases: "orchestral music", "orchestral version", "orchestral piece".
examples from the lessons: We listened to an orchestral piece by Beethoven. | The film has a great orchestral soundtrack. | Violins, flutes and drums are orchestral instruments. | The band released an orchestral version of their song. | The orchestral music grew loud as the hero arrived. | Our school has an orchestral club on Thursdays.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: "orchestra" + "-l": orch-es-tral; "ch" sounds like "k". Pronounced "or-KES-trul".

meaning for a pupil: 1) (maths) The y-coordinate of a point on a graph: how far up or down the point is from the x-axis.
its sense in the lessons: A maths word for graphs and coordinates: in the point (3, 5), 3 is the x-coordinate (abscissa) and 5 is the ordinate. In everyday school maths people mostly say "y-coordinate".
examples from the lessons: In the point (2, 7), the ordinate is 7. | The ordinate tells you how far up the point is. | Points on the x-axis have an ordinate of zero. | Read the ordinate from the vertical axis. | If the ordinate is negative, the point is below the x-axis. | The abscissa comes first, then the ordinate.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Technical maths word. Memory trick: x comes first ("along the corridor"), then y ("up the stairs"). The other coordinate is the "abscissa". Not the same as "ordinary" or "coordinate" as a whole pair.

part of speech: verb (orient, orients, oriented, orienting); noun (the Orient)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To find out or work out where you are or which way you are facing, as in "orient yourself with a map". 2) To turn or place something to face a certain way, as in "oriented north". 3) To aim something at a particular group or purpose, as in "a course oriented to beginners". 4) (the Orient, old-fashioned) The countries of East Asia.
its sense in the lessons: Used in geography and outdoor education (orienteering, using a compass to orient a map), in maths (orientation of a shape), and in everyday life (a new pupil getting oriented at school). The noun "the Orient" is old-fashioned and now usually replaced by "East Asia" or "Asia".
