examples from the lessons: Use the compass to orient the map to north. | It took me a week to orient myself in the new school. | The house is oriented to face the sun. | The church is oriented east, as many old churches are. | The game is oriented towards young children. | Marco Polo travelled to the Orient. (old-fashioned)
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK also uses "orientate" (orientate, orientated) with the same meaning; both are correct. Noun "orientation". "The Orient" and "oriental" sound old-fashioned and can offend when used about people; say "East Asia" or name the country.

part of speech: adjective (oriental; Oriental); noun (an Oriental — old-fashioned, offensive)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (old-fashioned) From or to do with the countries of East Asia, like China, Japan and Korea. 2) Used in some fixed names for things, like "oriental rug" or "Oriental Shorthair" (a cat breed).
its sense in the lessons: Seen in old books and in names of objects and animals (oriental rugs, the oriental pratincole bird). Today, describing people as "Oriental" is old-fashioned and can be offensive; people prefer "Asian", "East Asian" or the country, such as "Chinese" or "Korean".
examples from the lessons: The museum had a room of oriental rugs. | Old maps called East Asia "the Orient". | In the old book, the market sold "oriental spices". | The Oriental Shorthair is a slim cat breed. | We say "East Asian food" rather than "oriental food" now. | Calling people "Oriental" is old-fashioned and can be hurtful.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Use with care: for people, say "Asian", "East Asian" or name the country. In US law the word was removed from federal laws in 2016. In names of objects it may still appear.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A health professional who checks and treats problems with how the eyes move and work together, such as a squint or a lazy eye.
its sense in the lessons: Used in health and everyday life in the UK, Ireland, Australia and other countries: children may see an orthoptist at an eye clinic for a squint (strabismus) or lazy eye (amblyopia), and may be given an eye patch or glasses.
examples from the lessons: The orthoptist checked how my eyes moved together. | My little brother sees an orthoptist about his squint. | The orthoptist gave her an eye patch to wear. | At the hospital eye clinic, we saw an orthoptist and then an eye doctor. | An orthoptist can test a baby's eyes too. | The school nurse sent me to an orthoptist after the eye test.
note for the reader of a maths problem: An orthoptist (an, before a vowel sound). Pronounced "or-THOP-tist". Other eye jobs: "optician" (makes and sells glasses), "optometrist" (tests eyesight), "ophthalmologist" (eye doctor and surgeon).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (computing) OS is short for "operating system", the main program that runs a computer or phone, like Windows, macOS, Android or iOS. 2) (UK) OS is short for Ordnance Survey, the national mapping agency of Great Britain; "OS maps" are detailed maps used for walking. 3) (Latin, medicine) "os" means bone (plural "ossa") or mouth (plural "ora") in Latin; also (French) "os" means bone. 4) (clothing) OS can mean "one size" or "oversized".
its sense in the lessons: A fragment and abbreviation, not an English word on its own. In computing lessons, pupils learn the OS runs the apps and hardware. In UK geography, OS maps teach grid references and map symbols.
examples from the lessons: My phone needs an OS update. | Android and iOS are mobile OSs. | We used an OS map on our Duke of Edinburgh walk. | OS maps show footpaths, churches and contour lines. | In Latin, "os" means bone. | The label on the hoodie said OS, meaning one size.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Abbreviation, usually capitals: "OS" (say "oh-ess"). Plural for operating systems: "OSs" or "OSes". In French, "os" (bone) is said "oss" for one and "oh" for many; it is not an English word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To swing or move back and forth regularly, like a pendulum. 2) To keep changing between two feelings, ideas or states, as in "oscillate between hope and fear". 3) (science) Of electric current or waves, to change direction or strength in a regular rhythm.
its sense in the lessons: Used in science (pendulums, springs, vibrations and sound waves oscillate; a fan that oscillates turns from side to side) and in stories or formal writing to show someone changing their mind back and forth.
examples from the lessons: A pendulum oscillates from side to side. | The fan oscillates so it cools the whole room. | Guitar strings oscillate when you pluck them. | His mood oscillated between happy and grumpy. | The price oscillated between £5 and £6 all week. | The spring oscillated up and down after we let go.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: double s, double l: os-cil-late. Pronounced "OS-il-ate". Noun "oscillation". Similar: "swing", "vibrate", "waver".

part of speech: verb form (present participle of oscillate: oscillate, oscillates, oscillated, oscillating); adjective (oscillating)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Swinging or moving back and forth regularly. 2) (adjective) Moving or turning from side to side, as in "an oscillating fan". 3) Changing back and forth between two states or feelings.
its sense in the lessons: Used in science (oscillating pendulums, waves, springs, oscillating current) and in everyday talk (oscillating fans, oscillating sprinklers in the garden). In stories it describes swaying or wavering.
examples from the lessons: An oscillating fan turns from side to side. | The oscillating sprinkler watered the whole lawn. | We timed the oscillating pendulum in science. | The pendulum kept oscillating for a long time. | The prices kept oscillating up and down. | The oscillating light on the lighthouse swept across the bay.
note for the reader of a maths problem: -ing form of "oscillate": drop the "e". Double s, double l.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A regular movement back and forth, like a pendulum swing. 2) (science) One full swing or vibration, from one side to the other and back. 3) A change back and forth between two states, feelings or opinions.
its sense in the lessons: A science word: we count oscillations of a pendulum to measure its period (the time for one full oscillation). Sound and light are oscillations (vibrations and waves). In maths problems: if a pendulum makes 30 oscillations in 60 seconds, one oscillation takes 60 ÷ 30 = 2 seconds.
examples from the lessons: We counted ten oscillations of the pendulum. | One oscillation means swinging there and back again. | Sound is made by the oscillation of air particles. | A longer pendulum has slower oscillations. | There was an oscillation in her mood all day. | The bridge's oscillation in the wind worried engineers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable when you count swings; uncountable for the general idea. In maths and science: frequency = number of oscillations per second (measured in hertz, Hz). Spelling: os-cil-la-tion.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To leave someone out of a group on purpose and refuse to talk to them or include them.
its sense in the lessons: Used in PSHE and stories about bullying and friendship: ostracising someone, shutting them out of games or chats, is a form of bullying that can really hurt. In history, ancient Athenians could "ostracise" (banish) a citizen by voting with pieces of pottery called ostraka.
examples from the lessons: The group ostracised her after she told the truth. | Ostracising someone from a game is a kind of bullying. | In ancient Athens, people voted to ostracise powerful citizens. | He felt ostracised when nobody let him sit with them. | We should never ostracise a new pupil. | The village ostracised the family for years.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK, Australia, NZ spelling "ostracise"; US and Canada "ostracize". Noun "ostracism". Pronounced "OS-truh-size". Kindness tip: invite someone who is left out.

part of speech: noun (an outflow, outflows; also uncountable); verb (outflow — rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Water, air or another substance flowing out of a place. 2) (money) Money going out of a bank, business or country. 3) The place or pipe where something flows out.
its sense in the lessons: Used in geography (the outflow of a lake into a river), science (outflow of air from a storm), money and maths (cash inflow and outflow, money coming in and going out) and in news about people leaving a country. In maths problems, outflow is the amount going out, taken away from the total.
examples from the lessons: The river is the outflow from the lake. | The outflow pipe takes the dirty water away. | A cold outflow of air came from the thunderstorm. | The bakery's money outflow was bigger than its money coming in. | The country saw a large outflow of workers. | If 50 litres flow in and the outflow is 20 litres, 30 litres remain.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable or uncountable. Opposite: "inflow". In maths: total change = inflow − outflow. One word, no hyphen.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A short trip out for fun, often with a group, such as a class going to a zoo or museum. 2) A walk or ride out of the house, even a small one. 3) A time when a player or team takes part in a game or race: "his first outing for the team". 4) The act of telling everyone a secret about someone, such as who they love, without their permission; this is unkind and can hurt.
its sense in the lessons: In school life a class outing is a trip away from the classroom, with permission slips, packed lunches and a teacher counting heads. In stories an outing often starts the adventure or goes wrong. In sport news "outing" means one appearance or game. Phrases: a school outing, a family outing, go on an outing, a day outing.
examples from the lessons: Our class outing to the science museum is on Friday. | Remember to bring your permission slip for the outing. | Grandad's Sunday outing is a walk to the park and back. | The family outing to the beach was ruined by rain. | It was the goalkeeper's first outing since his injury. | The teacher counted us twice before the outing began. | Telling everyone her secret was a cruel outing, and she cried.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: an outing, two outings. Not the same as "outting" (no such word). In UK English a school "trip" and a school "outing" mean much the same; in the USA "field trip" is common. In a maths problem about an outing, look for how many children, buses or tickets there are.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To last longer than something else: to keep going or keep working after the other has stopped. 2) To stay alive or stay in a contest longer than someone else.
its sense in the lessons: In stories a hero may outlast a storm or outlast an enemy by not giving up. In science, one battery can outlast another; in sport, a runner can outlast the others in a long race. It tells the reader about patience, strength or lasting quality. Often followed by an object: outlast the storm, outlast the others.
examples from the lessons: These new batteries outlast the cheap ones by hours. | The little boat outlasted the storm. | She outlasted every other speller in the spelling bee. | Good boots will outlast a pair of trainers. | The old oak tree has outlasted three houses on this street. | Can you outlast me in a staring contest? | The castle walls outlasted the long siege.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: outlast, outlasted. Made from out- ("more than") + last ("keep going"). It needs an object: you outlast something or someone. In maths, if toy A lasts 5 hours and toy B lasts 3 hours, toy A outlasts toy B by 2 hours (a difference, so subtract).

meaning for a pupil: 1) To go faster than someone or something, so that you get ahead. 2) To grow, rise or improve faster than something else: "Prices outpaced wages."
its sense in the lessons: In sport and races, a runner outpaces the others. In news and economics, one number outpaces another when it grows faster. In stories, a hero may outpace a chasing dog or a wave. It tells the reader who is quicker. Often: outpace the others, easily outpace.
examples from the lessons: The cheetah can outpace any other land animal. | Mia outpaced the boys on the last lap. | Our school's reading scores outpaced the rest of the town this year. | The fox outpaced the hounds and escaped. | Weeds can outpace the vegetables if you do not pull them. | The train easily outpaced the cars on the road beside it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: outpaced (one c, no extra e). It needs an object. In maths, if Sam runs 6 metres a second and Ali runs 5, Sam outpaces Ali by 1 metre every second; after 10 seconds Sam is 10 metres ahead.

part of speech: noun (outrage, outrages); verb (outrage, outrages, outraged, outraging)
meaning for a pupil: 1) noun: A very strong feeling of anger and shock because something seems deeply unfair or wrong. 2) noun: An act that is so cruel, wrong or shocking that it makes people very angry: "The attack was an outrage." 3) verb: To make people feel very angry and shocked.
its sense in the lessons: In the news "outrage" shows that many people are angry about something, such as an unfair rule or a cruel act. In stories it shows a character's strong anger at injustice. In everyday talk someone may say "It's an outrage!" a bit jokingly about small things. Phrases: public outrage, in outrage, cause outrage, express outrage, be outraged by.
examples from the lessons: There was outrage when the council closed the library. | "It's an outrage!" shouted Dad when the price of crisps went up again. | The fans were outraged by the referee's decision. | Burning the forest was an outrage against nature. | People wrote letters to show their outrage. | She gasped in outrage when her brother ate her birthday cake. | The cruel treatment of the animals outraged the whole village.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun "outrage" is usually uncountable for the feeling (much outrage) but countable for a single act (an outrage, outrages). Adjective: outrageous (very shocking, or very silly: an outrageous hat). It is not "out" + "rage" in meaning "rage outside"; it comes from old French and means "going beyond the limit".

meaning for a pupil: 1) To put or let too many people or things into a place, so it is too full. 2) (overcrowded, adjective) Too full of people or things to be comfortable or safe.
its sense in the lessons: Used about buses, trains, classrooms, cities, prisons, fish tanks and gardens. In science, overcrowded plants or animals compete for food, light and space and may get ill. In safety, an overcrowded place can be dangerous because people cannot move or get out. Often in the form "overcrowded".
examples from the lessons: Do not overcrowd the fish tank, or the fish will get sick. | The bus was so overcrowded that we had to stand. | If you overcrowd the seedlings, none of them will grow well. | The city became overcrowded as more people moved in. | Our classroom feels overcrowded when two classes share it. | Too many shops overcrowd the little high street.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb; the adjective "overcrowded" is used much more than the verb. Spelled as one word. In maths, a place is overcrowded when the number of people is more than the number it is made for: a lift for 8 people with 11 inside is 3 over the limit.

part of speech: noun (overcrowding, uncountable); also the -ing form of the verb overcrowd
meaning for a pupil: 1) The state of having too many people or things in one place, so that it is too full. 2) The act of putting too many people or things into a place.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and history lessons, overcrowding in cities, slums, ships and prisons leads to disease, poor living and unhappiness. In science, overcrowding of plants or animals means they fight for food, water and light. In safety talk, overcrowding at concerts or stations can cause crushes. Phrases: overcrowding in schools, cause overcrowding, reduce overcrowding.
examples from the lessons: Overcrowding in the old city spread disease quickly. | The zoo moved some monkeys to stop overcrowding. | Overcrowding on the trains is worst at rush hour. | The new school was built to end overcrowding in the old one. | Thinning out the carrots stops overcrowding. | Victorian families often lived in overcrowding, eight people in one room.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: you say "overcrowding", not "an overcrowding" or "overcrowdings". In maths, overcrowding means number of people > space or places; for example 40 pupils in a room for 30 is 10 too many, or one third more than planned.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To do something too much or use too much of something: "Don't overdo the salt." 2) To work or exercise too hard and get very tired: "Don't overdo it." 3) To cook food too long, so it is dry or burnt (usually "overdone").
its sense in the lessons: In health and sport lessons, "don't overdo it" means rest and do not push your body too hard. In cooking, overdone meat or vegetables are cooked too long. In writing, teachers warn you not to overdo exclamation marks or describing words. The phrase "overdo it" is very common.
examples from the lessons: Don't overdo it on your first day back after being ill. | The steak was overdone and as hard as a shoe. | She overdid the glitter, and now the whole card sparkles. | Try not to overdo the exclamation marks in your story!!! | I overdid the running and my legs ached all week. | A little perfume is nice, but don't overdo it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular like "do": overdo, overdoes, overdid, overdone. Do not confuse with "overdue" (late: an overdue library book). "Overdone" can mean cooked too long or done too much.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A ruler who has power over other rulers or lords, especially in the Middle Ages. 2) A person or group that controls others completely; often used jokingly: "our new robot overlords".
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons about the Middle Ages, a king or great lord was the overlord of smaller lords, who promised loyalty and soldiers in return for land (the feudal system). In stories and films, an evil overlord rules a land cruelly. In jokes, people say "our cat is the overlord of this house".
examples from the lessons: The king was overlord of all the barons in England. | Each knight promised to fight for his overlord. | In the game, you must defeat the dark overlord of the volcano. | The local lords paid taxes to their overlord. | "All hail the cat, overlord of the sofa!" laughed Mum. | The villagers feared the cruel overlord in the castle.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: an overlord, overlords. Mostly a history or story word; in real modern life people rarely say it seriously. Do not confuse with "landlord" (someone who rents a home to you).

meaning for a pupil: 1) To beat someone by being stronger, so they cannot fight back. 2) (of a feeling, smell or taste) To be so strong that it takes over: "The smell overpowered us." 3) (overpowering, adjective) Very strong, too strong.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, guards overpower a thief or a hero overpowers a monster. In cooking, a strong flavour like garlic can overpower the others. In everyday life an overpowering smell is too strong to bear. In games "overpowered" (slang "OP") means a character or item is too strong to be fair.
examples from the lessons: The guards overpowered the robber and took the bag. | The smell of fish overpowered the whole kitchen. | Too much chilli will overpower the taste of the soup. | She was overpowered by sleepiness and dropped her book. | The perfume in the shop was overpowering. | That sword is so overpowered that the game is too easy (slang: it's OP).
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: overpowered, overpowering. In gamer slang "OP" stands for "overpowered". Not the same as "empower" (to give someone power).

meaning for a pupil: 1) To think something or someone is better or more important than it really is. 2) (overrated, adjective) Not as good as people say: "That film is overrated."
its sense in the lessons: Mostly used in opinions and reviews: "That band is overrated." In discussions and persuasive writing it shows disagreement with popular opinion. It is an opinion word, so give reasons. Opposite: underrate, underrated.
examples from the lessons: In my opinion, that famous burger place is overrated. | People overrate how much fun a long car trip is. | Sleep is not overrated; you really need it. | Critics overrated the film, but the children found it boring. | Some say homework is overrated, but practice helps. | Is the new phone worth it, or just overrated?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb, most often used as the adjective "overrated". Opposite: underrated. When you say something is overrated, it is your opinion, not a fact; in a debate, back it up with reasons.

part of speech: adjective (overriding); also the -ing form of the verb override (override, overrides, overrode, overridden, overriding)
meaning for a pupil: 1) adjective: More important than anything else: "Safety is the overriding concern." 2) verb form: Cancelling or taking control of a decision, setting or machine, as in "overriding the alarm" or "overriding a rule".
its sense in the lessons: In formal writing and the news, "the overriding aim / concern / priority" means the most important one. In computing and machines, overriding a setting means taking manual control. In school rules, a teacher may be overriding an earlier decision. Phrases: overriding concern, overriding importance, overriding priority.
examples from the lessons: Safety is the overriding concern on a school trip. | Her overriding wish was to see her grandmother again. | The pilot was overriding the autopilot to land the plane. | Winning was not the overriding aim; having fun was. | The head teacher is overriding the old rule about phones. | Of overriding importance is that everyone gets home safely.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Overriding (most important) is quite formal. The verb is irregular: override, overrode, overridden. Do not confuse with "overwriting" (writing over something, like saving over a file).

part of speech: verb, past form of overshoot (overshoot, overshoots, overshot, overshooting); also the noun overshot (rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Went past a place, line or target by mistake, without stopping where you meant to. 2) Went over a planned amount, time or budget: "We overshot the budget." 3) (overshot wheel) A water wheel where the water falls onto the top of it.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life a driver overshoots a turning or a bus stop. In sport a ball overshoots the goal. In maths and science, overshooting means going past the target number or estimate; you then correct back. In history and technology, an overshot water wheel is turned by water poured onto its top.
examples from the lessons: We overshot the turning and had to drive back. | The rocket overshot the target by a few metres. | His throw overshot the basket completely. | We overshot our budget by five pounds at the fair. | The plane overshot the runway and stopped in the grass. | The mill used an overshot wheel, with water falling from above.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular: overshoot - overshot - overshot (not "overshooted"). Opposite: undershoot, undershot (stop short). In maths, if the target was 100 and you reached 108, you overshot by 8 (subtract the target from what you got).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A way of explaining something that makes it far too simple, so that important parts are left out and it becomes wrong or misleading. 2) The act of making something too simple.
its sense in the lessons: In science and history lessons, teachers say "that's an oversimplification" when an answer is too simple to be true, e.g. "the Romans were just cruel". It reminds pupils that real causes are often many. In debates, it warns against easy answers. Phrases: a bit of an oversimplification, a gross oversimplification.
examples from the lessons: Saying "plants eat soil" is an oversimplification. | It is an oversimplification to say the war started because of one shot. | "All dogs love bones" is an oversimplification. | The teacher said our poster was clear but an oversimplification. | Calling the weather "just hot or cold" is an oversimplification. | Some oversimplification helps beginners learn, but later you need the details.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: an oversimplification (starts with a vowel sound, so "an"). Verb: oversimplify; adjective: oversimplified. A simple explanation is fine; an oversimplification is one so simple that it misleads.

part of speech: adjective (overstated); also the past form of the verb overstate (overstate, overstates, overstated, overstating)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Said to be bigger, more important or worse than it really is; exaggerated. 2) verb: Said something in a way that made it seem bigger or more important than it truly was.
its sense in the lessons: In the news, science and history, "the danger was overstated" means it was not as big as people said. In persuasive writing pupils learn that overstated claims weaken an argument. Common phrase: "cannot be overstated" means something is extremely important: "The importance of sleep cannot be overstated."
examples from the lessons: The danger from the spider was overstated; it is harmless. | He overstated how many goals he scored. | The importance of washing your hands cannot be overstated. | The advert overstated how fast the toy car could go. | Reports of the storm damage were overstated. | She admitted she had overstated the problem.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: overstate, overstated. Opposite: understated, understate. "Cannot be overstated" is a compliment meaning "very, very important", not a criticism. In maths, if someone says 100 people came but only 60 did, the number was overstated by 40.

part of speech: adjective (overwhelming); also the -ing form of the verb overwhelm (overwhelm, overwhelms, overwhelmed, overwhelming)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Very great or strong, so that it is hard to deal with: "an overwhelming feeling of sadness". 2) Much bigger than the other side: "an overwhelming majority". 3) verb form: Being too much for someone, so they cannot cope.
its sense in the lessons: In wellbeing lessons, feelings or schoolwork can be overwhelming; the advice is to break tasks into small steps and talk to someone. In elections and votes, an overwhelming majority or win means by a very large amount. In stories, an army or wave may be overwhelming. Phrases: overwhelming majority, overwhelming evidence, feel overwhelmed.
examples from the lessons: The noise in the hall was overwhelming. | The class voted by an overwhelming majority for a pet hamster. | When homework feels overwhelming, start with one small task. | There was overwhelming evidence that the dog ate the cake. | The kindness of our neighbours was overwhelming. | The flood was overwhelming the town's defences. | She felt overwhelmed on her first day at the new school.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: overwhelming has "wh" and one m. "Overwhelmed" describes how a person feels; "overwhelming" describes the thing that causes it. In maths and voting, an overwhelming majority is far more than half, for example 27 votes out of 30.

part of speech: verb (overwork, overworks, overworked, overworking); noun (overwork, uncountable)
meaning for a pupil: 1) verb: To work too hard or too long, or to make someone do so. 2) noun: Too much work that makes someone tired or ill. 3) (overworked, adjective) Tired from too much work; also a word or phrase that is used so often it is boring ("an overworked word").
its sense in the lessons: In health and life lessons, overwork is a cause of tiredness and stress; people need rest. In history, children and workers in factories were overworked. In writing lessons, teachers call "nice" and "said" overworked words and ask for better ones.
examples from the lessons: The doctor said she was ill from overwork. | Don't overwork the horse; it needs a rest. | Factory children in the 1800s were badly overworked. | "Nice" is an overworked word; try "kind" or "lovely". | Dad overworks before holidays and then falls asleep on the beach. | Overworking your muscles can cause injury.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. The noun is uncountable: "from overwork", not "an overwork". In maths problems, overwork can mean hours above the normal: 50 hours instead of 40 is 10 hours extra.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A young owl, a baby owl. 2) A small kind of owl, such as the little owlets of Asia and Africa.
its sense in the lessons: In nature and science lessons, owlets hatch from eggs, are fluffy and white or grey, and are fed by their parents until they can fly. In stories and picture books, an owlet is a cute baby owl character. The ending -let means small, as in piglet and booklet.
examples from the lessons: Three fluffy owlets sat in the hollow tree. | The mother owl brought a mouse to her owlets. | The owlet fell out of the nest, but it was not hurt. | Owlets cannot fly until their feathers grow. | We watched the owlets on the nest camera at school. | In the story, the owlet was scared of the dark.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: an owlet (starts with a vowel sound, so "an"). The suffix -let means small (piglet, droplet, booklet). Do not touch owlets you find on the ground; tell an adult, as the parents may be nearby.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To add oxygen to something, such as water or blood. 2) (oxygenated, adjective) Containing oxygen: "oxygenated blood".
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, the lungs oxygenate the blood; oxygenated blood (bright red) goes from the heart to the body. Pond plants and air pumps oxygenate water for fish. Waterfalls and waves also oxygenate rivers. Phrases: oxygenate the blood, oxygenated water.
examples from the lessons: The lungs oxygenate the blood with every breath. | Pond weed helps to oxygenate the water. | A pump oxygenates the water in our class fish tank. | Oxygenated blood flows from the heart to the muscles. | Waterfalls oxygenate the river as the water splashes. | Exercise makes your heart pump oxygenated blood faster.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Oxygen + -ate. Opposite: deoxygenated (blood that has given up its oxygen and returns to the heart). Myth: blood inside you is never blue; it is darker red when it has less oxygen.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To make someone who is angry or upset become calm and quiet. 2) To bring peace to a place, often by force, ending fighting there.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life parents pacify a crying baby; teachers pacify an angry pupil. In history, armies "pacified" lands, which often meant they defeated people by force. A baby's dummy is called a "pacifier" in the USA. Phrases: pacify a baby, try to pacify.
examples from the lessons: Mum pacified the crying baby with a song. | He tried to pacify his sister by giving her his sweets. | Nothing could pacify the angry customer. | The dog was pacified with a biscuit. | The Roman army tried to pacify the rebel tribes. | A cuddle often pacifies a frightened child.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular spelling: pacify, pacifies, pacified (y changes to i). Related: pacifier (US for a baby's dummy), pacifist (someone against all war), Pacific Ocean (named "peaceful"). In history, "pacify" can hide violence, so read carefully.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The science that studies life from long ago, mostly through fossils of animals and plants, such as dinosaurs. 2) The study of how living things changed over millions of years.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on fossils and evolution, palaeontology tells us about dinosaurs, ancient sea creatures and early plants. A palaeontologist digs up fossils, cleans them and works out what the animal was like. Mary Anning, a fossil hunter from Lyme Regis in England, found famous fossils in the 1800s.
examples from the lessons: Palaeontology is the study of fossils. | She wants to study palaeontology and dig up dinosaurs. | Mary Anning made great discoveries for palaeontology. | Palaeontology tells us that sharks are older than trees. | The museum has a palaeontology room full of bones. | In palaeontology, a single tooth can tell you what an animal ate.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK spelling: palaeontology; US spelling: paleontology. Person: palaeontologist. Pronounced "pal-ee-on-TOL-uh-jee". Myth: palaeontologists do not study human history in old cities; that is archaeology. Dinosaurs and people never lived at the same time.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Nice enough to eat or drink; having a pleasant taste. 2) Acceptable or easy to agree with: "a more palatable idea".
its sense in the lessons: In cooking and health, palatable food tastes good enough to eat; medicine may be made palatable with sweet flavour. In formal writing and news, a palatable plan or choice is one people can accept. Opposite: unpalatable (nasty to eat or hard to accept).
examples from the lessons: The medicine was made palatable with strawberry flavour. | Adding honey made the porridge more palatable. | School dinners have become more palatable this year. | The new bedtime rule was more palatable when we got a story too. | The truth was not palatable, but he needed to hear it. | Some leaves are not palatable to caterpillars.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Rather formal. Comes from "palate" (the roof of the mouth, and the sense of taste). Do not mix up palate (mouth), palette (paints) and pallet (wooden platform).

meaning for a pupil: 1) The state of being pale: having a light colour or less colour than usual. 2) Lightness of a person's face when they are ill, tired or frightened.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, a character's paleness shows fear, shock or illness. In health, paleness of the skin can be a sign of being unwell, cold or low on iron. In art, paleness means a light, soft colour.
examples from the lessons: Her paleness worried the school nurse. | The paleness of the sky meant snow was coming. | He noticed the paleness of the ghostly figure. | After the flu, his paleness lasted a week. | The paleness of the wall made the room feel cool. | Fear showed in the sudden paleness of her face.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable noun. From "pale" (adjective: pale, paler, palest). Similar: pallor, which is more formal and used mostly for faces. Do not confuse "pale" with "pail" (a bucket).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A flat board or tray that an artist uses to hold and mix paints. 2) The set of colours used in a painting, a room, a design or a computer program: "a palette of blues and greens". 3) A range of things to choose from, such as sounds or flavours.
its sense in the lessons: In art lessons, you mix colours on a palette. In design and computing, a colour palette is the group of colours you choose from. In writing about art or food, "palette" can mean a range of colours or flavours (but taste itself is "palate").
examples from the lessons: Squeeze some red and white paint onto your palette. | She mixed pink on her palette. | The painting uses a palette of soft greens. | Pick a colour from the palette at the top of the screen. | Wash your palette before the paint dries. | The autumn trees showed a palette of red, orange and gold.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a palette, palettes. Homophone traps: palette (paints), palate (roof of the mouth, sense of taste), pallet (wooden platform for goods, or a straw bed). All three sound the same: "PAL-it".

meaning for a pupil: 1) One of the people who carry the coffin at a funeral. 2) A person who walks beside the coffin at a funeral as an honour.
its sense in the lessons: In life and church lessons about funerals, pallbearers are usually family members or close friends of the person who died; carrying the coffin is a sign of love and respect. Often there are six pallbearers. The "pall" is the cloth that covers a coffin.
examples from the lessons: Six pallbearers carried the coffin into the church. | Grandad's grandsons were his pallbearers. | Being a pallbearer is an honour. | The pallbearers walked slowly and carefully. | At the soldier's funeral, the pallbearers wore uniforms. | She asked her brothers to be pallbearers for their mum.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. One word. "Pall" here means the cloth over a coffin; it is not the same word as "pal" (friend). A sad, respectful word; speak gently about funerals.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A flat wooden or plastic platform on which goods are stacked so that a forklift truck can lift and move them. 2) A simple straw bed or thin mattress on the floor (old use, in stories). 3) A flat wooden tool used by potters (less common).
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and shops, goods arrive on pallets in lorries and warehouses. People also make garden furniture out of old pallets. In history stories, a poor person or prisoner sleeps on a pallet of straw.
examples from the lessons: The forklift lifted a pallet of bricks. | The lorry was full of pallets of tinned beans. | We built a bug hotel from an old pallet. | The prisoner slept on a pallet of straw. | Each pallet holds 40 boxes. | Mind your fingers near the wooden pallets.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: pallet, pallets. Homophones: palette (paints) and palate (roof of the mouth). In maths, pallets are about multiplication: if each pallet holds 40 boxes, 6 pallets hold 6 x 40 = 240 boxes.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unhealthy paleness of the face or skin, from illness, fear, shock or tiredness.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and descriptions, "pallor" is a strong, slightly formal word to show a character is ill, frightened or ghostly. Doctors and nurses notice pallor as a sign of illness or blood loss. Phrases: a deathly pallor, a sickly pallor.
examples from the lessons: His pallor showed he had not slept. | The patient's pallor worried the doctor. | A deathly pallor spread across her face when she saw the ghost. | After the long winter, his pallor was gone. | The vampire in the book had a strange pallor. | Her pallor faded as she drank some sweet tea.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable; formal and descriptive. Similar to "paleness". Spelling ends in -or, not -our (it is not "pallour").

meaning for a pupil: 1) A feeling that your heart is beating very fast, very hard or unevenly. 2) (informal, joking) "Palpitations" can mean strong nervous excitement or shock: "You nearly gave me palpitations!"
its sense in the lessons: In health lessons, palpitations can happen with fear, exercise, too much caffeine or illness; if they keep happening, see a doctor. In everyday talk, grown-ups joke "You gave me palpitations!" after a fright.
examples from the lessons: Too much coffee gave Mum palpitations. | She felt palpitations before going on stage. | The doctor checked his heart because of the palpitations. | "Don't jump out at me! You'll give me palpitations!" said Gran. | Palpitations after running usually settle when you rest. | The scary film gave me palpitations.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually plural: "palpitations". Pronounced "pal-pi-TAY-shuns". If someone has chest pain or feels faint with palpitations, tell an adult and get help.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A wide view of a large area of land, sea or sky. 2) A wide photograph or picture showing a whole scene from side to side. 3) A full overview of a topic or a period: "a panorama of history".
its sense in the lessons: In geography and trips, from a hill or tower you see a panorama of the town. On phones, the "panorama" mode takes a wide photo by turning slowly. In writing, a panorama is a wide description of a scene. Adjective: panoramic.
examples from the lessons: From the top of the hill there was a panorama of the whole city. | I took a panorama of the beach with my phone. | The castle tower gives a wonderful panorama of the valley. | The book gives a panorama of life in Victorian times. | Hold the phone still when you take a panorama. | The painting is a huge panorama of a battle.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a panorama, panoramas. Adjective: panoramic (a panoramic view). From Greek "pan" (all) + "horama" (view).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who jumps from an aircraft and floats down using a parachute.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about forces, a parachutist shows air resistance: the open parachute slows the fall by pushing against the air. In history, parachutists (paratroopers) were used in wars. In sport and charity events, people do parachute jumps or skydives.
examples from the lessons: The parachutist floated gently down to the field. | Air resistance slows the parachutist down. | The parachutist landed right in the middle of the target. | Our teacher was a parachutist for charity. | We made model parachutists from paper and string. | The parachutists jumped one after another from the plane.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Parachute + -ist. Also "skydiver" for people who fall a long way before opening the parachute. Science note: a parachute does not stop gravity; it increases air resistance so you fall slower.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A statement or idea that seems to contradict itself or seems impossible, but may still be true. 2) A situation that has two opposite facts that both seem to be true. 3) (logic) A puzzle where reasoning leads to an impossible answer, such as "This sentence is false."
its sense in the lessons: In maths, logic and philosophy, famous paradoxes like "This sentence is false" or the time-travel grandfather paradox make you think hard. In everyday life, "the paradox is..." points out something strange: "The more you rush, the slower you go." In olympiad puzzles, paradoxes test careful thinking.
examples from the lessons: This sentence is false is a famous paradox. | It's a paradox that the busiest people often have the most time to help. | The time machine story had a strange paradox. | "Less is more" sounds like a paradox. | Zeno's paradox says a runner can never catch a tortoise, but in real life he does. | It was a paradox: the more she tried to sleep, the more awake she felt.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: paradox, paradoxes. Adjective: paradoxical. A paradox is not just a contradiction; it is something that seems impossible yet makes you think. In maths, some paradoxes are solved with better ideas, such as infinite sums adding up to a finite number (1/2 + 1/4 + 1/8 + ... = 1).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Loss of the ability to move some or all of the body, usually because of injury or illness to the nerves. 2) A state of not being able to act, decide or work: "a paralysis of fear", "traffic paralysis".
its sense in the lessons: In health and science, paralysis happens when nerves or the spinal cord are damaged; many people with paralysis use wheelchairs and live full lives. In news, snow or strikes can cause paralysis of transport. In stories, a character may feel paralysis from fear.
examples from the lessons: After the accident he had paralysis in his legs. | Polio once caused paralysis in many children. | The snowstorm caused paralysis on the roads. | She stood in a paralysis of fear. | Some spiders' bites cause paralysis in insects. | Many athletes with paralysis compete in the Paralympics.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable. Verb: paralyse (UK), paralyze (US); adjective: paralysed / paralyzed. Speak respectfully: say "a person with paralysis", and remember that many disabled people live active lives.

part of speech: noun, plural of paramecium (a paramecium, paramecia); also "parameciums"
meaning for a pupil: 1) Paramecia are tiny one-celled living things that live in fresh water and are shaped like a slipper; they swim using tiny hairs called cilia.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about microscopes and microorganisms, paramecia are seen in pond water. They eat bacteria and move by beating their cilia. They show that a whole living thing can be just one cell.
examples from the lessons: We saw paramecia under the microscope. | Paramecia live in pond water. | Paramecia swim by waving tiny hairs called cilia. | One paramecium is too small to see with your eyes. | The paramecia ate the bacteria in the drop of water. | Paramecia are shaped a bit like a slipper.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Paramecia is plural; the singular is paramecium. Pronounced "pa-ruh-MEE-see-uh". They are single-celled organisms (protists), not animals or plants in the usual sense, and not bacteria.

meaning for a pupil: 1) adjective: Organised like an army, but not part of a country's official army. 2) noun: A group like this, or a member of it.
its sense in the lessons: In history and news, paramilitary groups have fought in places such as Northern Ireland during the Troubles, and in many wars; some police forces also have paramilitary units. The word warns that armed people are acting outside the normal army.
examples from the lessons: Paramilitary groups fought during the Troubles in Northern Ireland. | The police sent in a paramilitary unit. | The news reported attacks by paramilitaries. | They wore paramilitary uniforms but were not soldiers. | Peace agreements asked paramilitaries to give up their weapons. | The Good Friday Agreement of 1998 helped bring peace in Northern Ireland.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective and countable noun (paramilitaries). "Para-" here means "alongside" or "like". It is a serious news word; it is not the same as "paratrooper" (a soldier who jumps by parachute).

part of speech: adjective (paranoid; more paranoid, most paranoid); noun (a paranoid, rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (everyday) Too worried that people are against you, talking about you or trying to trick you, without good reason. 2) (medicine) Having an illness that makes a person have strong false beliefs that others want to harm them.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday talk, "Don't be paranoid" means "you are worrying too much that something bad is happening". In health lessons, being paranoid as an illness needs a doctor and kindness. In online safety, it's good to be careful, which is not the same as paranoid.
examples from the lessons: I'm paranoid that I left the oven on. | Don't be paranoid; they weren't laughing at you. | He became paranoid that someone was reading his diary. | It's sensible to be careful online, not paranoid. | She felt paranoid after the scary film and checked the locks twice. | The doctor helped the paranoid patient feel safe.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: paranoia. Pronounced "PA-ruh-noid". The everyday use is informal; be gentle with the medical use and do not call people "paranoid" as an insult.

part of speech: adjective (parched); also the past form of the verb parch (parch, parches, parched, parching)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Very dry because of heat and lack of rain: "parched fields". 2) (informal) Very thirsty: "I'm parched!" 3) (of food) Dried or roasted, as in "parched corn".
its sense in the lessons: In geography and science, parched land comes from drought; plants wilt and the soil cracks. In everyday talk, "I'm parched" means "I really need a drink". In stories, a parched desert traveller shows heat and danger.
examples from the lessons: After the long summer, the grass was parched. | "I'm parched! Can I have some water?" | The farmer looked sadly at his parched fields. | The desert sun parched the travellers' lips. | Rain finally fell on the parched earth. | Drink water often on hot days so you don't get parched.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly used as an adjective. "I'm parched" is informal, especially UK and Ireland. Stronger than "dry" or "thirsty".

meaning for a pupil: 1) adjective: From or connected with Paris, the capital city of France. 2) noun: A person who lives in Paris or comes from there.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and French lessons, Parisian things are from Paris: Parisian cafés, the Parisian Metro. In stories, a Parisian character may speak French and live near the Eiffel Tower or the River Seine.
examples from the lessons: She bought a book in a little Parisian shop. | Many Parisians ride the Metro to work. | The Parisian café sold warm croissants. | Our French teacher grew up as a Parisian. | The Eiffel Tower is the most famous Parisian landmark. | The film is set in a Parisian flat.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always written with a capital P in real use: Parisian. Pronounced "puh-RIZ-ee-un" in English. In French, a man from Paris is "un Parisien" and a woman "une Parisienne".

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To eat or drink something, usually offered to you: "partake of the feast". 2) (formal) To take part in an activity: "partake in the games". 3) (church) To receive communion, the bread and wine: "partake of the bread".
its sense in the lessons: A formal or old-fashioned word, found in stories, the Bible, church services and polite invitations. Christians speak of partaking of the bread and wine at communion. In everyday modern speech people say "join in" or "have some" instead.
examples from the lessons: Will you partake of some tea and cake? | All the villagers partook in the harvest festival. | The guests partook of a great feast. | At communion, Christians partake of the bread and wine. | He would not partake in the cruel game. | "Do partake," said the duchess, offering the biscuits.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular like "take": partake, partook, partaken. Usually "partake of" (food, drink) or "partake in" (an activity). Formal: in normal talk say "have", "eat" or "take part".

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unfair support for one person or side over another: "The referee showed partiality." 2) A special liking for something: "a partiality for chocolate".
its sense in the lessons: In school, sport and law, partiality is unfair: judges and referees must be impartial (not favouring anyone). In everyday or old-fashioned speech, "a partiality for" something means you really like it.
examples from the lessons: The referee was accused of partiality towards the home team. | A judge must avoid partiality. | Grandpa has a partiality for strong cheese. | The teacher showed no partiality and treated us all the same. | Her partiality for cats was well known. | Partiality in a contest is unfair to the other players.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable. Opposite: impartiality (being fair). Adjective: partial, which has two meanings: "unfair, favouring" and "liking" ("I'm partial to cake"), and also "not complete" ("a partial eclipse"). Do not mix up the meanings.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (grammar) A word or phrase that shows a part of a whole or an amount, such as "some of", "a piece of", "a slice of", "a glass of". 2) (French) The partitive article "du, de la, des" meaning "some": "du pain" means "some bread".
its sense in the lessons: In English grammar, partitive phrases let us count uncountable things: "a loaf of bread", "a cup of tea", "a piece of advice". In French lessons, the partitive article is used before food: "Je voudrais du fromage" (I'd like some cheese). In maths, partitive division means sharing into equal groups.
examples from the lessons: A slice of cake is a partitive phrase. | "Some of the children" uses a partitive. | In French, "de la confiture" means "some jam" (a partitive). | Use a partitive like "a piece of" with uncountable nouns: a piece of information. | "A bar of chocolate" is a partitive phrase. | In partitive division, 12 sweets shared among 3 children gives 4 each.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A grammar term for older pupils. Common English partitives: a piece of, a bit of, a slice of, a cup of, a glass of, a bottle of, some of, most of. In maths, "partitive division" means sharing a total into a known number of groups (12 / 3 = 4 in each group).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who passes by, usually in "passer-by" (plural passers-by): someone walking past a place. 2) (sport) A player who passes the ball, especially a good one: "a great passer". 3) Someone who passes a test or exam (rare).
its sense in the lessons: Most often seen inside "passer-by": in stories and news, a passer-by sees an accident or helps someone. In sport commentary, a good passer gives accurate passes to teammates.
examples from the lessons: A passer-by called an ambulance. | Passers-by stopped to watch the street performer. | She is the best passer in our netball team. | The quarterback is a brilliant passer. | A kind passer-by found my lost glove. | No passers-by noticed the tiny kitten.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The plural of "passer-by" is "passers-by" (the s goes on "passer"). "Passer" alone is mostly used in sport. Do not confuse with "pastor" (a church minister).

meaning for a pupil: 1) With very strong feeling or enthusiasm: "She spoke passionately about animals." 2) Very much, deeply: "He passionately believes in fairness." 3) With strong love (in stories and songs).
its sense in the lessons: In persuasive writing and speeches, speaking passionately shows that someone really cares. In stories it shows strong emotion: love, anger, or belief. Phrases: speak passionately, care passionately, believe passionately, argue passionately.
examples from the lessons: She spoke passionately about saving the rainforest. | He passionately believes that every child should read. | The fans cheered passionately for their team. | Gran passionately loves her garden. | The class argued passionately about school uniforms. | The singer sang passionately, with her eyes closed.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from "passionate" (adjective) and "passion" (noun). Spelling: passion + ate + ly, with double s. In church, "the Passion" means the suffering and death of Jesus, as Christians believe.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Something you enjoy doing in your free time, such as a hobby, game or sport.
its sense in the lessons: In school writing about yourself, you list your favourite pastimes. In history lessons, you learn about pastimes from long ago, like hopscotch, marbles or archery. Cricket and baseball are called national pastimes in England and the USA.
examples from the lessons: Reading is my favourite pastime. | Fishing is a popular pastime in Ireland. | Baseball is called America's national pastime. | Victorian children's pastimes included hoops and marbles. | Grandma's pastime is knitting. | Drawing comics is a fun pastime on rainy days.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: pastime has only one s and one t (not "pasttime" or "passtime"), even though it means passing the time. Countable: a pastime, pastimes.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Like a father or to do with being a father: caring and protective. 2) Related through your father: "my paternal grandmother" is your father's mother.
its sense in the lessons: In family trees, paternal relatives are on your father's side; maternal relatives are on your mother's side. In science, some animals show paternal care, like male seahorses carrying the eggs. In stories, a paternal teacher or king cares for others like a father.
examples from the lessons: My paternal grandparents live in Scotland. | Male seahorses show amazing paternal care. | The old captain had a paternal feeling for his young crew. | Paternal leave lets dads stay at home with a new baby. | My paternal aunt is my dad's sister. | Emperor penguin fathers are very paternal; they keep the egg warm.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite side: maternal (mother's side). Noun: paternity (being a father; paternity leave). Paternal is an adjective; you cannot say "a paternal" as a noun.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The man who is the head of a family or tribe, often the oldest. 2) (Bible) One of the great early fathers of the people of Israel: Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. 3) (church) A bishop of the highest rank in some churches, such as the Orthodox Churches.
its sense in the lessons: In history and family stories, the patriarch is the head of the family. In Bible lessons, the patriarchs are Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, whose stories are in the book of Genesis. In church life, the Ecumenical Patriarch of Constantinople and the Patriarch of Moscow lead Orthodox churches.
examples from the lessons: Grandpa is the patriarch of our big family. | Abraham is called the first patriarch in the Bible. | The patriarch blessed his twelve sons. | The Patriarch led the Orthodox service. | In the story, the old patriarch ruled the farm with a stern voice. | Jacob was a patriarch whose sons became the twelve tribes of Israel.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Pronounced "PAY-tree-ark". Related: patriarchy (a society where men hold most power). Opposite in family sense: matriarch (the woman who leads a family).

meaning for a pupil: 1) noun: In ancient Rome, a member of the old, rich and noble families. 2) noun: A rich, upper-class person. 3) adjective: Belonging to or like the upper class; proud and elegant in manner.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons on Ancient Rome, patricians were the noble families and plebeians were the ordinary people; at first only patricians could hold top jobs. In descriptions, a patrician face or voice looks or sounds upper-class.
examples from the lessons: In Ancient Rome, patricians were rich landowners. | The plebeians argued with the patricians for more rights. | He spoke with a patrician voice. | The patrician family owned a huge villa. | A patrician wore a toga with a purple stripe. | The old lady had a patrician air about her.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun and adjective. Opposite in Rome: plebeian (pleb). Pronounced "puh-TRISH-un". Not connected with the name Patrick in meaning, though both come from Latin "pater" (father).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Loving your country and feeling proud of it, and wanting to help it. 2) Showing love of your country, such as patriotic songs, flags or colours.
its sense in the lessons: In history and citizenship lessons, patriotic feelings unite people, especially in hard times; but too much can turn into hating others, so pupils learn the difference between patriotism and nationalism. On national days, people sing patriotic songs and wave flags (the Fourth of July, Anzac Day, Canada Day, St Patrick's Day).
examples from the lessons: She felt patriotic when the national anthem played. | The streets were full of patriotic flags. | Ukrainians sang patriotic songs to keep up their spirits. | It is patriotic to help your community. | The soldiers were praised for their patriotic courage. | We wore patriotic colours for Canada Day.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: patriotism; person: a patriot. Pronounced "pay-tree-OT-ik" (UK) or "pay-tree-OT-ik" / "pat-ree-OT-ik". Loving your country does not mean thinking other countries are bad.

part of speech: adjective (patronising; more patronising); also the -ing form of the verb patronise (patronise, patronises, patronised, patronising); US spelling patronizing
meaning for a pupil: 1) Talking to someone or treating them as if they were less clever or less important than you, in a kind-seeming but rude way. 2) verb form: Being a regular customer of a shop or business (formal).
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and wellbeing lessons, a patronising tone sounds like "Oh, well done, sweetie" said to a grown person, or talking down to children. It hurts because it seems friendly but shows no respect. In writing, it describes a character who looks down on others.
examples from the lessons: Don't be patronising; I can tie my own shoes! | His patronising smile made her angry. | The waiter's patronising voice annoyed Grandad. | She explained it slowly in a patronising way. | Speaking to the new girl as if she were a baby was patronising. | Many families have been patronising the corner shop for years.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK spelling: patronising; US: patronizing. Verb: patronise. The second meaning (being a customer) is formal and old-fashioned. Opposite in attitude: respectful.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A building beside a sports field, especially a cricket ground, where players change and rest. 2) A light building or large tent used at fairs, shows and exhibitions. 3) A decorative building in a park or garden for shelter, like a summerhouse. 4) One of several buildings that make up a hospital or exhibition.
its sense in the lessons: In sport (UK, Australia, NZ, Ireland), the cricket pavilion is where players change and have tea; a batter who is out walks back "to the pavilion". At fairs and world exhibitions, each country may have a pavilion. In parks, a bandstand or tea pavilion.
examples from the lessons: The cricketers had tea in the pavilion. | He was out and walked back to the pavilion. | Each country had its own pavilion at the World Fair. | We sheltered from the rain in the park pavilion. | The Royal Pavilion in Brighton looks like an Indian palace. | The flower show had a huge pavilion full of roses.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a pavilion, pavilions. Spelling: one l, then "-ion" after "pavil-". Pronounced "puh-VIL-yun".

meaning for a pupil: 1) A female peafowl. She is mostly brown and grey, without the huge colourful tail of the male peacock.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on animals and adaptation, the peahen's dull colours help her hide while sitting on her eggs; the male peacock shows off his bright tail to attract her. People often say "peacock" for both, but the female is a peahen. The babies are called peachicks.
examples from the lessons: The peahen sat quietly on her eggs. | Peahens are brown, so they are hard to spot. | The peacock spread his tail to impress the peahen. | We saw a peahen and three peachicks at the zoo. | A peahen does not have a long, colourful tail. | The peahen called loudly to her chicks.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a peahen, peahens. Male: peacock; female: peahen; both together: peafowl; babies: peachicks. Myth: not all "peacocks" are male; that word is often used wrongly for both.

meaning for a pupil: 1) All the peasants of a country taken together: the poor farm workers and small farmers, especially in the past.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons on the Middle Ages, the Russian Empire and other times, the peasantry made up most of the people and worked the land for lords. Revolts by the peasantry (such as the Peasants' Revolt of 1381 in England) are taught. In Ukraine's history, the peasantry suffered terribly in the Holodomor famine of 1932-33.
examples from the lessons: The peasantry worked the lord's fields. | Most of the people in medieval England belonged to the peasantry. | The peasantry rose up in the Peasants' Revolt of 1381. | Heavy taxes made life hard for the peasantry. | The king feared the anger of the peasantry. | The Holodomor caused the deaths of millions of the Ukrainian peasantry.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable and used with "the". From "peasant" (one person). In modern English, calling someone a "peasant" is a rude joke meaning they are low or uncool; do not use it as an insult.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A natural substance in fruits, especially apples and lemons, that makes jam and jelly set (go thick and firm).
its sense in the lessons: In cooking and science, pectin is a kind of fibre found in fruit cell walls; when jam is boiled with sugar and acid, pectin makes it set. Some fruits like strawberries have little pectin, so people add pectin or lemon juice. It is also healthy fibre.
examples from the lessons: Apples contain lots of pectin. | Add pectin so the strawberry jam will set. | Pectin makes jelly wobbly but firm. | Lemon juice helps the pectin in jam to work. | Pectin is found in the skins and cores of fruit. | Gummy sweets can be made with pectin instead of gelatine.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Pronounced "PEK-tin". Pectin comes from plants, so vegetarians can eat sweets made with pectin; gelatine comes from animals.

part of speech: adjective (pectoral); noun (a pectoral, pectorals; informal pecs)
meaning for a pupil: 1) adjective: Of or on the chest: "pectoral muscles". 2) noun: The pectoral muscles of the chest, often called "pecs" (informal). 3) (pectoral fin) One of the pair of fins on the sides of a fish, just behind the head. 4) (church) A pectoral cross is a cross worn on the chest by bishops.
its sense in the lessons: In science and PE, pectoral muscles move your arms and shoulders; push-ups make them stronger. In biology, fish use pectoral fins to steer and stop. In church life, bishops wear a pectoral cross on a chain. Gym slang: "pecs".
examples from the lessons: Push-ups build your pectoral muscles. | The fish used its pectoral fins to turn. | Sharks have big pectoral fins. | The bishop wore a gold pectoral cross. | "Look at my pecs!" joked my uncle at the beach. | Swimming works the pectorals and the shoulders.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective and noun. "Pecs" is informal slang. Pronounced "PEK-tuh-rul". Fish have pectoral fins (sides) and a dorsal fin (back).

part of speech: noun (a pediatrician, pediatricians); UK spelling paediatrician
meaning for a pupil: 1) A doctor who specially looks after babies, children and teenagers.
its sense in the lessons: In health lessons and everyday life, a pediatrician checks how children grow, gives vaccinations and treats children's illnesses. In the USA, children often see a pediatrician for check-ups; in the UK, a family GP sees children and sends them to a paediatrician at the hospital if needed.
examples from the lessons: The pediatrician checked the baby's weight. | My little brother sees a pediatrician every year. | A pediatrician is a doctor for children. | The paediatrician said I was growing well. | The pediatrician listened to my chest with a stethoscope. | She wants to be a paediatrician when she grows up.
note for the reader of a maths problem: US spelling: pediatrician; UK, Ireland, Australia, NZ: paediatrician. Pronounced "pee-dee-uh-TRISH-un". Related: pediatrics / paediatrics (the medicine of children). Do not confuse with podiatrist (a foot doctor).

part of speech: noun (a pelt, pelts); verb (pelt, pelts, pelted, pelting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) noun: The skin of an animal with the fur or hair still on it. 2) verb: To throw many things at someone or something quickly: "pelt with snowballs". 3) verb: (of rain or hail) To fall very hard: "It's pelting down." 4) verb: (informal) To run very fast: "He pelted down the road." 5) (at full pelt) As fast as possible.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons about fur traders in Canada and North America, beaver pelts were traded. In stories and the playground, children pelt each other with snowballs. In weather talk (UK, Ireland, Australia), "it's pelting down" means heavy rain. "At full pelt" means at top speed.
examples from the lessons: They pelted each other with snowballs. | It was pelting down with rain all day. | Fur traders sold beaver pelts. | He pelted down the hill at full pelt. | The crowd pelted the stage with flowers. | Hail pelted against the windows. | The fox had a thick red pelt.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun; regular verb (pelted). "It's pelting down" is informal. Note: cruelly throwing things at people or animals is wrong; snowball fights only with friends who agree.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Of or near the pelvis, the bowl-shaped group of bones at the bottom of your body that joins your spine to your legs. 2) (pelvic fin) One of a pair of fins on the underside of a fish.
its sense in the lessons: In science and health lessons, the pelvic bones (hips) support your body and protect organs; the legs join the pelvis at the hip joints. In biology, fish have pelvic fins underneath. Physiotherapists talk about pelvic muscles and pelvic floor exercises.
examples from the lessons: The pelvic bones hold up the top half of your body. | Your thigh bone fits into a socket in the pelvic bone. | The fish has small pelvic fins underneath. | X-rays showed a pelvic injury after the fall. | The skeleton's pelvic bones look like a butterfly. | Some snakes still have tiny pelvic bones from their ancestors.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective only. Noun: pelvis (plural pelvises or pelves). Pronounced "PEL-vik".

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a way that can be noticed or seen, even if only a little: "It grew perceptibly colder."
its sense in the lessons: In formal writing, science reports and stories, "perceptibly" describes a change you can just notice. Its opposite "imperceptibly" means so slowly or slightly that you cannot notice it. Often with change words: perceptibly colder, perceptibly louder, perceptibly faster.
examples from the lessons: It grew perceptibly darker as the clouds came. | Her voice shook perceptibly. | The plant had grown perceptibly in one week. | He relaxed perceptibly when the test was over. | The water level rose perceptibly during the storm. | The train slowed perceptibly before the station.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal adverb. From "perceptible" (able to be noticed) and "perceive" (to notice). Opposite: imperceptibly. In science, a perceptible change is one you can measure or see.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The state of being perfect, with no faults at all. 2) Something or someone that is perfect, an ideal example: "The cake was perfection." 3) The act of making something perfect: "the perfection of a skill".
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and wellbeing lessons, chasing perfection can make people stressed; it's fine to make mistakes and learn. In cooking and sport, "cooked to perfection" or "played to perfection" means done very well. In church, Christians believe God is perfect, and some speak of God's perfection.
examples from the lessons: The chips were cooked to perfection. | Nobody can reach perfection, so do your best. | The gymnast's routine was close to perfection. | Practice helps, but perfection is not the goal. | "This lemonade is perfection!" said Mum. | He spent years on the perfection of his magic trick.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Adjective: perfect; verb: to perfect (pronounced "per-FEKT"). Person who wants everything perfect: a perfectionist. In maths, a "perfect number" (like 6 = 1 + 2 + 3) is a special number equal to the sum of its smaller factors.

meaning for a pupil: 1) noun: A magazine or journal that comes out regularly, such as every week, month or three months. 2) adjective: Happening again and again at regular times (usually "periodic").
its sense in the lessons: In libraries and research, periodicals are magazines and journals, kept on special shelves. Scientists publish discoveries in periodicals. As an adjective, it means repeated at times: periodical checks.
examples from the lessons: The library keeps science periodicals on the top shelf. | My aunt writes for a gardening periodical. | Children's periodicals like comics come out weekly. | The museum has old periodicals from the 1800s. | The machine needs periodical checks. | She looked up the article in a medical periodical.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun. "Periodic" (adjective) is more common for "happening regularly" (the periodic table of elements is a chemistry chart). Both come from "period" (a length of time).

meaning for a pupil: 1) To spread through every part of something: "The smell of bread permeated the house." 2) (science) To pass through a material or a membrane: "Water permeates the soil."
its sense in the lessons: In science, liquids and gases permeate materials like soil, rock and cloth; a permeable rock lets water through, an impermeable one does not. In stories, a smell, feeling or idea permeates a place: "Fear permeated the village." Formal word.
examples from the lessons: The smell of baking permeated the whole street. | Rainwater permeates the sandy soil quickly. | A feeling of excitement permeated the school before the holidays. | Damp permeated the walls of the old house. | Music permeated every corner of the hall. | Ink permeated the paper towel in our experiment.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Related: permeable (lets liquid through: sand, sponge), impermeable (does not: plastic, clay). Pronounced "PUR-mee-ate".

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To do something wrong, harmful or illegal, such as a crime or a trick.
its sense in the lessons: In news, law and history, crimes, frauds and attacks are "perpetrated"; the person who did it is the perpetrator. It is a formal, serious word. In mystery stories, detectives find out who perpetrated the crime. Sometimes used jokingly: "Who perpetrated this terrible pun?"
examples from the lessons: The police found who perpetrated the robbery. | Crimes perpetrated during wars must be investigated. | The trick was perpetrated by two clever boys. | "Who perpetrated this mess?" asked Dad. | The fraud was perpetrated over many years. | History remembers those who perpetrated great cruelty.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal regular verb. Person: perpetrator. Trap: do not confuse with "perpetuate" (to make something carry on). Perpetrate = commit a bad act; perpetuate = keep it going.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To make something continue for a long time, often something bad like a myth, an unfair idea or a problem. 2) To keep a memory or name alive: "The statue perpetuates his memory."
its sense in the lessons: In school discussions, "perpetuate a stereotype" means keep an unfair idea going by repeating it; "perpetuate a myth" means keep spreading a false story. In history, monuments perpetuate the memory of people and events. Formal word.
examples from the lessons: Jokes like that perpetuate unkind stereotypes. | The film perpetuates the myth that bats are blind. | Sharing fake news perpetuates lies. | The scholarship perpetuates the memory of a kind teacher. | Poverty can perpetuate itself from parents to children. | We must not perpetuate unfair rules.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal regular verb. Trap: "perpetuate" (keep going) vs "perpetrate" (commit a crime). Related: perpetual (lasting for ever). Myth check: bats are not blind.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To keep trying to do something even when it is difficult or you fail at first, and not give up.
its sense in the lessons: In school, perseverance is a learning value: you persevere with a hard maths problem, a new instrument or a spelling list. In stories, heroes persevere through trouble. Often "persevere with" something or "persevere in" doing it. Similar: keep going, don't give up, stick at it.
examples from the lessons: If you persevere with your reading, it will get easier. | She failed her swimming test twice but persevered. | The explorers persevered through snow and ice. | Persevere with the puzzle; you're nearly there. | He persevered and finally learned to ride a bike. | Scientists persevere through many failed experiments.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Spelling trap: persevere (not "perservere"). Pronounced "pur-suh-VEER". Noun: perseverance; adjective: persevering. Mars rover "Perseverance" landed in 2021.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (writing) To describe a thing, animal or idea as if it were a person, with human feelings or actions: "The wind howled angrily." 2) To be a perfect example of a quality: "She personifies kindness."
its sense in the lessons: In English and poetry lessons, personification is a figure of speech: "The sun smiled down", "The trees whispered". Pupils learn to spot and use it. In everyday speech, "he personifies patience" means he is the best example of being patient.
examples from the lessons: Poets often personify the moon as a lady. | In "the angry storm", the writer personifies the weather. | Grandma personifies kindness. | Can you personify the sea in your poem? | The cartoon personifies the vegetables as funny characters. | Old stories personify death as a figure in a cloak.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular spelling: personifies, personified (y to i). Noun: personification. Do not mix up with simile (using "like" or "as") or metaphor (saying one thing is another).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Worry or anxiety; being upset: "She showed no perturbation." 2) (science) A small change or disturbance in the movement or state of something, such as a planet's orbit being pulled by another planet.
its sense in the lessons: In science and astronomy, perturbations in Uranus's orbit led astronomers to discover Neptune in 1846. In maths and physics, a perturbation is a small push or change. In old-fashioned stories, it means worry.
examples from the lessons: Small perturbations in Uranus's orbit helped find Neptune. | He listened without any sign of perturbation. | The spacecraft corrected for perturbations in its path. | A tiny perturbation can change the weather a lot. | Her perturbation grew as the dog did not come home. | Scientists measured the perturbation caused by the moon.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal. Verb: perturb (to worry); adjective: perturbed (worried), unperturbed (calm). In science it means a small disturbance, not a big crash.

part of speech: verb (pervert, perverts, perverted, perverting); noun (a pervert, perverts)
meaning for a pupil: 1) verb: To change something so that it is used wrongly or for a bad purpose: "pervert the truth". 2) verb (law): "Pervert the course of justice" means to try to stop the police or courts finding the truth, for example by lying or hiding evidence; this is a crime. 3) noun: (rude, adult slang) a rude word grown-ups use; not for school.
its sense in the lessons: In law and the news, "perverting the course of justice" is a serious crime in the UK, Ireland and Australia. In formal writing, to pervert something good means to twist it into something bad. The noun is an adult insult and not for school.
examples from the lessons: He was charged with perverting the course of justice. | Lying to the police can pervert the course of justice. | They perverted the rules to get their own way. | The villain perverted the wizard's gift into a curse. | Do not pervert the truth to win an argument.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stress: verb "per-VERT", noun "PER-vert". Adjective "perverse" means stubbornly unreasonable, doing the opposite of what is sensible (a perverse choice). The noun is rude; do not call people this.

part of speech: noun (pes, plural pedes) (science, Latin); also an abbreviation or fragment
meaning for a pupil: 1) (anatomy, Latin) The foot, or the foot part of an animal's back leg; used by scientists, as in "pes planus" (flat foot). 2) (fragment) Often a piece of a bigger word or a plural of PE written as "PEs" (physical education lessons).
its sense in the lessons: Mostly met in science books describing skeletons and animals' feet, or in medical names like "pes planus" (flat feet) and "pes cavus" (high arch). It is Latin, not an everyday English word. In school texts "PEs" may be a typing of PE lessons.
