examples from the lessons: In Latin, "pes" means foot. | Doctors call flat feet "pes planus". | The dinosaur's pes had three big toes. | The scientist measured the length of the fossil pes. | The word "pedal" comes from Latin "pes, pedis", foot. | Our timetable lists two PEs a week.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Latin word: pes (singular), pedes (plural). Pronounced "pays" or "pez". English words from it: pedal, pedestrian, centipede (hundred feet). It is not a normal English word on its own.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (old or formal) A deadly disease that spreads quickly through many people, such as the plague. 2) (Bible) One of the disasters sent as punishment or warning, as in the plagues of Egypt; the rider "Pestilence" of the Book of Revelation. 3) Something that is very harmful or annoying (old use).
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, the Black Death of 1347-1351 was a pestilence that killed huge numbers of people in Europe. In Bible lessons and old stories, pestilence goes together with famine and war. The modern word is "epidemic" or "pandemic".
examples from the lessons: The pestilence swept through the town in 1665. | In the Bible, pestilence and famine are warnings. | The Black Death was a terrible pestilence. | People fled the city to escape the pestilence. | Rats and fleas helped spread the pestilence. | Old prayers asked God to keep people safe from pestilence.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Old-fashioned and formal; modern words: plague, epidemic, pandemic. Related: pest, pesticide. Pronounced "PES-ti-lunce".

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) The process by which a dead plant or animal slowly turns into stone over a very long time, as minerals replace it: petrified wood. 2) Being so frightened that you cannot move (usually "petrified").
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on fossils and rocks, petrification turns wood into stone, as in the Petrified Forest in Arizona. In stories, a monster like Medusa causes petrification, turning people to stone. In everyday talk, "I was petrified" means very scared.
examples from the lessons: Petrification turned the ancient tree into stone. | The fossil shows petrification of the bones. | Petrification takes millions of years. | In the myth, Medusa's stare caused petrification. | We saw petrified wood that looked like a log but was stone. | Minerals in water cause petrification.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Verb: petrify; adjective: petrified (turned to stone, or very scared). Spelled petrification, not "petrifaction" (an older variant is "petrifaction", also correct).

part of speech: noun (a phage, phages); short for bacteriophage
meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) A tiny virus that attacks and kills bacteria, not people. 2) (fragment) A word ending meaning "eater", as in "macrophage" (a white blood cell that eats germs).
its sense in the lessons: In science and medicine, phages look like tiny space landers; they inject their genes into bacteria. Doctors are testing phage therapy to fight bacteria that antibiotics cannot kill. The ending "-phage" means "eat" in Greek.
examples from the lessons: A phage is a virus that infects bacteria. | Phages look like tiny moon landers. | Scientists use phages to fight resistant bacteria. | Phages are harmless to human cells. | A macrophage is a white blood cell that eats germs. | There are more phages on Earth than stars in the sky, scientists estimate.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Pronounced "FAYJ". Full name: bacteriophage. Related Greek words: -phagy, sarcophagus (originally "flesh-eater"). It is a science word, not everyday English.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (language) The smallest unit of sound in a language that can change the meaning of a word, such as /c/, /a/, /t/ in "cat"; changing /c/ to /h/ gives "hat".
its sense in the lessons: In phonics lessons, children split words into phonemes ("sh-i-p" has 3 phonemes) and match them to letters or groups of letters (graphemes). English has about 44 phonemes but only 26 letters. Phrases: segment phonemes, blend phonemes.
examples from the lessons: Ship has three phonemes: sh-i-p. | The word "cat" has three phonemes. | Change one phoneme in "pin" to get "pan". | English has about 44 phonemes. | The letters "igh" make one phoneme in "night". | Robots learn to recognise phonemes in speech.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Pronounced "FOH-neem". A phoneme is a sound; a grapheme is the letter or letters that write it. Number of phonemes is not the same as number of letters: "night" has 5 letters but 3 phonemes (n-igh-t).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Connected with the sounds of speech. 2) Written in a way that shows exactly how a word sounds: "a phonetic spelling". 3) (phonetic alphabet) A set of symbols where each one stands for one sound (IPA), or the list of code words like Alpha, Bravo, Charlie used on radios.
its sense in the lessons: In English and language lessons, a phonetic spelling like "fone" for "phone" shows sound, not correct spelling. Dictionaries use phonetic symbols to show pronunciation. Pilots, police and soldiers use the phonetic alphabet (Alfa, Bravo, Charlie...) so letters are not misheard.
examples from the lessons: Spanish spelling is more phonetic than English. | The dictionary gives a phonetic guide to say the word. | "Skool" is a phonetic spelling of "school". | Pilots use the phonetic alphabet: Alpha, Bravo, Charlie. | "K" is "Kilo" in the phonetic alphabet. | Some sounds have no letter, so we use phonetic symbols.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective. Noun: phonetics (the study of speech sounds; takes a singular verb: "Phonetics is..."). Note the irony: "phonetic" is not spelled phonetically (it starts with ph, not f).

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a way that matches the sounds of speech: "Spell it phonetically" means write it the way it sounds. 2) To do with the sounds of words, not their meaning.
its sense in the lessons: In phonics and spelling lessons, young children often spell words phonetically ("bcoz" for "because"); teachers then show the correct spelling. Reading a word phonetically means sounding it out. Some words (yacht, colonel) cannot be read phonetically.
examples from the lessons: She spelled "because" phonetically as "bcoz". | Sound the word out phonetically: c-a-t. | "Colonel" is not spelled phonetically at all. | Young children write phonetically at first. | Read the nonsense words phonetically. | Finnish is written almost exactly phonetically.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from phonetic. Spelling: phonetic + ally (not "phoneticly"). Spelling phonetically in tests is usually marked wrong if the real spelling is different.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (chemistry) Containing phosphorus, especially in "phosphoric acid", a chemical used in fertilisers, rust remover and some fizzy drinks like cola. 2) Glowing like phosphorus (old, rare).
its sense in the lessons: In chemistry and health lessons, phosphoric acid gives cola its sharp taste and can harm tooth enamel if you drink too much. Farmers use fertilisers made from phosphoric acid to help plants grow.
examples from the lessons: Cola contains phosphoric acid. | Phosphoric acid can remove rust from metal. | Too many fizzy drinks with phosphoric acid can damage teeth. | Fertiliser factories use phosphoric acid. | The label lists phosphoric acid as an ingredient. | Phosphoric acid is made from phosphorus.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective, mostly in "phosphoric acid". Pronounced "fos-FOR-ik". Related: phosphorus (a chemical element that glows), phosphate. Safety: acids can burn; never mix chemicals at home.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A scientist who studies physics: the science of matter, energy, forces, light, sound, electricity and how the universe works.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, famous physicists include Isaac Newton (gravity), Marie Curie (radioactivity), Albert Einstein (relativity) and Stephen Hawking (black holes). Physicists work in labs, universities, space agencies and hospitals.
examples from the lessons: Isaac Newton was a famous physicist. | Marie Curie was both a physicist and a chemist. | The physicist explained how rainbows form. | She wants to be a physicist and study black holes. | Physicists built the huge machine to smash atoms. | A physicist helped design the hospital's scanner.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Pronounced "FIZ-i-sist". Not to be confused with "physician" (a medical doctor) or "physique" (body shape). Physics is uncountable and takes a singular verb: "Physics is fun."

meaning for a pupil: 1) The size and shape of a person's body, especially how strong and muscly it is.
its sense in the lessons: In sport, PE and descriptions in stories, physique tells you about someone's body build: a strong physique, a slim physique. Health lessons teach that every body is different and that being healthy matters more than a certain physique.
examples from the lessons: The swimmer has a powerful physique. | The rugby player's physique was huge and strong. | Each athlete's physique suits their sport. | The giant in the story had a frightening physique. | Exercise can change your physique over time. | Don't compare your physique with photos online, which are often edited.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Pronounced "fi-ZEEK" (from French). Do not confuse with physics or physician.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Very pretty, like a picture or a postcard, especially an old village or a countryside view. 2) (of language) Vivid and colourful, full of interesting description.
its sense in the lessons: In geography, travel and descriptive writing, picturesque villages, harbours and valleys are charming places tourists like to visit. Writers use it to paint a scene for the reader. Similar: pretty, scenic, charming.
examples from the lessons: We stayed in a picturesque fishing village. | The cottage by the river was picturesque. | The Cotswolds are full of picturesque villages. | The harbour looked picturesque at sunset. | Grandad has a picturesque way of telling stories. | The train ran through picturesque mountains.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: picturesque ends in -esque (like "grotesque"). Pronounced "pik-chuh-RESK". Adjective only.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To make a hole in or through something with a sharp point: "The needle pierced the cloth." 2) To have a hole made in a body part to wear jewellery: "She had her ears pierced." 3) (of light, sound or cold) To suddenly go through something: "A scream pierced the silence." 4) (piercing, adjective) Very loud and high, very sharp, or very cold; piercing eyes seem to look right through you.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, ear piercing is common; hygiene and permission matter. In stories, an arrow pierces armour, light pierces the darkness, a cry pierces the night. In science, sharp objects pierce materials because the force is on a tiny area (high pressure).
examples from the lessons: The arrow pierced the target. | She got her ears pierced for her birthday. | A whistle pierced the air. | Sunlight pierced the clouds. | A thorn pierced his finger. | The wind was piercing on the hill. | Her piercing blue eyes stared at me.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb; spelling "ie" (i before e). Noun: piercing (a hole for jewellery, or the jewellery). Safety: sharp objects can pierce skin; carry scissors pointing down.

part of speech: noun (a pigeonhole, pigeonholes); verb (pigeonhole, pigeonholes, pigeonholed, pigeonholing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) noun: One of a set of small open boxes in a wall or desk where letters and papers are put for each person. 2) verb: To decide too quickly that someone or something belongs to one simple type, unfairly: "Don't pigeonhole people." 3) verb: To put something aside and ignore it (old use).
its sense in the lessons: In schools and offices, teachers have pigeonholes in the staff room for letters. In discussions about fairness, pigeonholing people means putting them in a box, like "girls are bad at maths", which is unfair. Similar: label, stereotype.
examples from the lessons: Leave the note in Mr Jones's pigeonhole. | Each teacher has a pigeonhole in the staff room. | Don't pigeonhole him as just a footballer; he loves poetry too. | She hated being pigeonholed as the shy one. | The letters were sorted into pigeonholes. | Pigeons once lived in holes like these in dovecotes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word (sometimes "pigeon-hole"). Regular verb. Spelling: pigeon has "eo" (pi-geon).

meaning for a pupil: 1) The natural colour of skin, hair, eyes, leaves or other living things, caused by pigments (coloured substances). 2) Coloured spots or patches on skin.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, melanin is the pigment that gives skin, hair and eyes their colour; more melanin means darker skin. Leaves are green because of chlorophyll. Animals' pigmentation can help camouflage. Difference in skin pigmentation is natural and says nothing about a person's worth.
examples from the lessons: Skin pigmentation comes from melanin. | The frog's bright pigmentation warns that it is poisonous. | Albino animals lack pigmentation. | Sun can cause dark pigmentation spots on skin. | Autumn leaves change pigmentation as chlorophyll breaks down. | Human skin pigmentation varies, and all of it is normal.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. From pigment (a colouring substance). Albinism means little or no pigment; people with albinism need extra sun protection.

part of speech: verb (pinpoint, pinpoints, pinpointed, pinpointing); noun (a pinpoint, pinpoints); adjective (pinpoint)
meaning for a pupil: 1) verb: To find or show the exact place, cause or time of something. 2) noun: A very small dot or point, like the point of a pin: "a pinpoint of light". 3) adjective: Very exact: "pinpoint accuracy".
its sense in the lessons: In geography and maps, you pinpoint a town on a map using grid references or coordinates. In science and detective stories, you pinpoint the cause of a problem. In sport, a pinpoint pass is very accurate.
examples from the lessons: Can you pinpoint London on the map? | The doctor pinpointed the cause of the pain. | GPS can pinpoint your position. | A pinpoint of light shone in the dark cave. | The darts player threw with pinpoint accuracy. | It's hard to pinpoint exactly when the problem started.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. One word. In maths and maps, to pinpoint means to give exact coordinates, such as (3, 5).

part of speech: noun (a pioneer, pioneers); verb (pioneer, pioneers, pioneered, pioneering)
meaning for a pupil: 1) noun: One of the first people to explore or settle in a new land. 2) noun: One of the first people to do something new, such as in science or art: "a pioneer of flight". 3) verb: To be the first to do, invent or use something. 4) (pioneering, adjective) New and leading the way.
its sense in the lessons: In history, pioneers settled the American West and parts of Canada and Australia, often on land where Indigenous peoples already lived. In science and technology, pioneers like the Wright brothers (flight) or Ada Lovelace (programming) lead the way. In plants, pioneer species are the first to grow on bare ground.
examples from the lessons: Pioneers travelled west in covered wagons. | Ada Lovelace was a pioneer of computer programming. | The hospital pioneered a new heart operation. | Marie Curie did pioneering work on radioactivity. | Lichens are pioneer plants on bare rock. | The settlers were called pioneers, though Indigenous people already lived there.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun; regular verb. Pronounced "pie-uh-NEER". In history, remember that "new" land for pioneers was often home to other people already.

part of speech: noun (a pipette, pipettes); verb (pipette, pipettes, pipetted, pipetting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) noun: A thin glass or plastic tube used in science to measure or move small amounts of liquid, drop by drop. 2) verb: To move liquid with a pipette.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, a pipette (or dropper) adds a few drops of indicator or water exactly. Squeeze the bulb, dip it, then release to suck up liquid; squeeze gently to let out drops. Accurate measuring makes a fair test.
examples from the lessons: Use the pipette to add three drops of iodine. | She pipetted the liquid into the test tube. | A pipette helps you measure small amounts. | Squeeze the pipette gently to let out one drop. | The scientist used a plastic pipette. | Wash the pipette before using another liquid.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Spelling: pipette, with double t and -ette (as in "cassette"). Pronounced "pi-PET". US also "pipet". In maths and science, measure in millilitres (ml): 1 ml is about 20 drops.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The pipes in a building, machine or system, taken all together, such as for water, gas or heating.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, plumbers fix pipework under sinks or in the central heating. In science and technology, pipework carries water, gas or oil. Leaks or frozen pipework in winter are common problems; that is why pipes are lagged (wrapped) to keep them warm.
examples from the lessons: The plumber checked the pipework under the sink. | Old pipework in the house was made of lead. | Frozen pipework can burst in winter. | The factory's pipework carries steam. | The boiler has a lot of pipework around it. | The pipework was painted red to show it carries hot water.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: "the pipework", not "a pipework". Made of pipe + work, like "ironwork" or "brickwork".

meaning for a pupil: 1) A hidden danger or difficulty that is easy to miss: "the pitfalls of online shopping". 2) (old) A pit dug and covered so that animals or enemies fall into it, a trap.
its sense in the lessons: In school, teachers warn about common pitfalls in maths (forgetting to carry the one) or in writing. In online safety, pitfalls include scams and fake websites. In history, pitfall traps were used for hunting. Phrases: avoid the pitfalls, common pitfalls.
examples from the lessons: A common pitfall is forgetting the units in your answer. | Learn the pitfalls of sharing photos online. | The guide explains how to avoid the pitfalls of camping. | Hunters dug pitfalls to catch animals. | One pitfall in subtraction is taking the smaller digit from the larger. | Every new job has its pitfalls.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; usually plural "pitfalls". One word. In maths it means a typical mistake; for example, in 52 - 17, a pitfall is writing 45 instead of 35 by subtracting 2 from 7.

part of speech: adjective (pituitary); noun (the pituitary, short for the pituitary gland)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) The pituitary gland is a small gland, about the size of a pea, under the brain; it makes hormones that control growth and many other body processes.
its sense in the lessons: In science and health lessons about hormones, the pituitary gland is often called the "master gland" because it tells other glands what to do. It controls growth: too much or too little growth hormone changes how tall someone grows.
examples from the lessons: The pituitary gland is about the size of a pea. | The pituitary makes growth hormone. | Doctors checked her pituitary gland. | The pituitary is called the master gland. | The pituitary sits just below the brain. | Hormones from the pituitary travel in the blood.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced "pi-TYOO-i-tree". Usually in "pituitary gland". A gland is an organ that makes chemicals (hormones) for the body.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A large card or board with a message written on it, carried at a protest or march, or put up in public.
its sense in the lessons: In citizenship and history lessons, protesters, marchers and suffragettes carried placards with slogans. In news, people hold placards at demonstrations. Schools make placards for climate strikes or charity events.
examples from the lessons: The protesters carried placards saying "Save our park". | Suffragettes held placards asking for votes for women. | We made placards for the class march about litter. | The placard was written in big red letters. | Fans held up placards for their favourite player. | Police asked them to lower their placards.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Pronounced "PLA-kard". Similar: sign, banner, poster. Do not confuse with "placate" (to calm someone).

meaning for a pupil: 1) To make someone feel less angry or upset, often by giving them something or saying something kind.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and stories, people placate an angry friend, a crying child or an upset customer. In history and myths, people tried to placate gods with gifts. Similar: calm, soothe, pacify.
examples from the lessons: She tried to placate her brother with a biscuit. | The shop gave a free gift to placate the angry customer. | Nothing could placate the furious teacher. | Ancient people offered gifts to placate their gods. | He apologised to placate his friend. | The manager placated the fans with free tickets.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Pronounced "pluh-KATE" (UK) or "PLAY-kate" (US). Adjective: placatory. Similar to pacify.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To do with the placenta, the organ that grows inside a mother during pregnancy to give the baby food and oxygen. 2) (placental mammals) Mammals whose babies grow inside the mother with a placenta, such as humans, dogs, cats and whales.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on animal groups, placental mammals are compared with marsupials (kangaroos, koalas), whose babies grow in a pouch, and monotremes (platypus), which lay eggs. Most mammals are placental. In Australia and NZ, this contrast is a common topic.
examples from the lessons: Humans are placental mammals. | Kangaroos are marsupials, not placentals. | Whales and bats are placental mammals. | The placental blood carries food to the baby. | Australia has many marsupials but also placental mammals like dingoes. | Most mammals on Earth are placental.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective (also a noun in science). Noun: placenta (plural placentas or placentae). Pronounced "pluh-SEN-tul".

meaning for a pupil: 1) A strong, emotional request for something: "a plea for help". 2) (law) What a person says in court when accused of a crime: "guilty" or "not guilty". 3) An excuse or reason given: "on the plea that he was ill".
its sense in the lessons: In stories and news, a plea for help, peace or money shows someone in need. In law lessons and courtroom stories, the accused enters a plea of guilty or not guilty; a "plea bargain" (US) is a deal for a shorter sentence. Phrases: a plea for help, make a plea, enter a plea.
examples from the lessons: The charity made a plea for warm blankets. | The puppy's eyes were a silent plea for food. | He entered a plea of not guilty. | The family made a plea for their lost cat to be found. | Her plea for more time was accepted. | The police issued a plea for witnesses.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a plea, pleas. Verb: plead (pleaded; in US also pled). Do not confuse with "please" or "plee" (no such word).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person or thing that pleases others. 2) (people-pleaser) Someone who always tries to make others happy, even when it is bad for themselves, and finds it hard to say no. 3) (crowd-pleaser) Something that lots of people enjoy, like a popular song or dish.
its sense in the lessons: In wellbeing lessons, being a people-pleaser can mean you hide your own feelings; it's fine to say no politely. In everyday talk, a crowd-pleaser is a popular film, song or food at a party.
examples from the lessons: Pizza is always a crowd-pleaser at parties. | She is a people-pleaser and can't say no. | That song was a real crowd-pleaser. | Being a people-pleaser can make you tired. | The magic show was a big pleaser with the little ones. | It's kind to help, but you don't have to be a people-pleaser.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Mostly used in compounds: people-pleaser, crowd-pleaser. From "please" + -er.

part of speech: verb (plod, plods, plodded, plodding); noun (a plod; the plod, UK slang)
meaning for a pupil: 1) verb: To walk slowly and heavily, as if tired: "We plodded through the mud." 2) verb: To work slowly and steadily at something boring or hard: "plod on with homework". 3) noun: A slow, heavy walk. 4) noun (UK slang, "plod" or "PC Plod"): the police or a police officer; a bit mocking.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, characters plod through snow or mud when tired. In school, "plod on" means keep working steadily. In UK slang, "the plod" is the police, from PC Plod in the Noddy books; it is cheeky, not polite.
examples from the lessons: We plodded home through the rain. | The tired horse plodded up the hill. | I plodded on with my maths until it was done. | The elephant plodded slowly across the plain. | "Watch out, here comes the plod!" (UK slang) | After a long plod, we reached the top.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb, double d: plodded, plodding. Similar: trudge, lumber. The slang "the plod" is cheeky; do not say it to a police officer.

part of speech: adjective (plodding); also the -ing form of plod (plod, plods, plodded, plodding)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Walking slowly and heavily. 2) Working slowly and steadily but without much excitement or skill. 3) (of a story or film) Slow and dull.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, plodding footsteps show tiredness or a heavy creature. In reviews, a plodding film or book is slow and boring. Describing a person as plodding can be unkind, but a plodding worker can also be steady and reliable, like the tortoise.
examples from the lessons: We heard plodding footsteps on the stairs. | The plodding donkey carried the bags. | The film had a plodding story. | Plodding along, the tortoise won the race. | His plodding style got the job done. | The plodding pace made the walk last forever.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double d. Can be a description or the verb form: "He is plodding home." Similar: trudging, lumbering.

part of speech: verb (plonk, plonks, plonked, plonking); noun (plonk, uncountable; a plonk)
meaning for a pupil: 1) verb (informal, UK, Australia, NZ): To put something down heavily or carelessly: "Plonk your bag there." 2) verb (informal): To sit down heavily: "He plonked himself on the sofa." 3) noun (informal, UK, Australia): Cheap wine. 4) noun: A dull, heavy sound, like a single piano note: "plonk!"
its sense in the lessons: In everyday British, Irish and Australian talk, "plonk it down" means just put it there, without care. Grown-ups call cheap wine "plonk". In music and stories, "plonk" can be the sound of a key or something dropping.
examples from the lessons: Just plonk your coat on the chair. | She plonked herself down next to me. | Dad plonked the shopping on the table. | They had a bottle of cheap plonk with dinner. | The little boy plonked out a tune on the piano. | Don't plonk that heavy box on my toe!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal. Regular verb. US English often says "plunk" instead. The wine sense is slang for adults.

part of speech: verb, past form of plot (plot, plots, plotted, plotting); adjective (plotted)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (maths, maps) Marked points on a graph, grid or map: "We plotted the points." 2) Secretly planned something, usually bad: "They plotted to steal the crown." 3) Planned the story of a book or film: "a well-plotted mystery". 4) (plotted plant) Planted in a pot (rare; usually "potted").
its sense in the lessons: In maths, you plot coordinates like (2, 3) on a grid and join them to make a line graph; in science you plot results. In history, Guy Fawkes and others plotted to blow up Parliament in 1605 (the Gunpowder Plot). In English lessons, a well-plotted story has events that fit together.
examples from the lessons: We plotted the points (1, 2) and (3, 4) on the grid. | The temperatures were plotted on a line graph. | The pirates plotted to take the ship. | Guy Fawkes plotted to blow up Parliament. | The captain plotted a course on the map. | The mystery is cleverly plotted. | She plotted her revenge on her brother for weeks.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double t: plot, plotted, plotting. In maths, when plotting (x, y), go across first (x), then up (y): "along the corridor, then up the stairs".

meaning for a pupil: 1) A clever trick or plan used to get an advantage or to make someone do something.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, games and advertising, a ploy is a sneaky plan: a "free gift" can be a ploy to make you buy more. In sport, a ploy is a tactic to fool the other side. Media literacy lessons teach children to spot marketing ploys.
examples from the lessons: The "free" toy was a ploy to get us to buy more cereal. | Pretending to be ill was a ploy to miss the test. | The team used a clever ploy to win the ball. | The fox's ploy was to flatter the crow. | Adverts use ploys to make you want things. | His ploy didn't work; Mum saw through it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Short, informal-neutral word. Similar: trick, tactic, scheme. In shop maths, a "buy 3 for the price of 2" offer only saves money if you actually need 3.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (voting) More votes than any other single person or party, but not more than half of all votes. 2) A large number or variety of things: "a plurality of opinions". 3) (grammar) The state of being plural, more than one.
its sense in the lessons: In citizenship lessons on elections, a plurality wins in "first past the post" systems (UK, US, Canada): the candidate with the most votes wins even without a majority. In discussions, "plurality" means many different views living side by side.
examples from the lessons: She won with a plurality, but not a majority. | A plurality of the class voted for pizza. | The town has a plurality of languages and cultures. | In first past the post, a plurality is enough to win. | The plurality of nouns is shown by adding -s. | Democracy needs a plurality of voices.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly uncountable or "a plurality". Maths: with 3 candidates getting 40%, 35% and 25%, the first has a plurality (most votes) but not a majority (more than 50%). In UK English "relative majority" means the same.

meaning for a pupil: 1) adjective: Rich, comfortable and expensive-looking: "a plush hotel". 2) noun: A soft fabric with a thick, furry surface, used for soft toys, cushions and seats. 3) (plush toy) A soft cuddly toy.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, plush means luxurious: plush seats in a cinema or a plush car. Soft toys are called plush toys or plushies. In stories, a plush room shows wealth.
examples from the lessons: The hotel had plush red carpets. | My teddy is made of soft plush. | We sat on plush seats at the theatre. | She won a plush toy at the fair. | The rich family lived in a plush house. | The cinema has new plush recliners.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective and uncountable noun. Informal: a "plushie" is a soft toy. In shop maths, plush toys are often sold by size: small, medium, large.

part of speech: adjective (plushy, plushier, plushiest); noun (a plushy, plushies), usually spelled plushie
meaning for a pupil: 1) adjective (informal): Rich and comfortable-looking, like plush; luxurious. 2) noun (informal): A soft, cuddly toy, usually spelled "plushie".
its sense in the lessons: In everyday and children's talk, plushies are cuddly toys collected and won at fairs. As an adjective it means fancy and expensive, sometimes a bit too much.
examples from the lessons: She has a shelf full of plushies. | The waiting room was plushy and quiet. | I won a unicorn plushy at the fair. | The plushy cushions were very soft. | My little brother sleeps with his dinosaur plushy. | The hotel lobby was a bit too plushy for us.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal. The noun is usually spelled "plushie" (plural plushies). Comparative: plushier, plushiest (y to i).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A card game in which players bet money or chips on whose cards are best, often bluffing (pretending). 2) A metal rod used to move burning wood or coal in a fireplace. 3) Someone who pokes (rare). 4) (poker face) A face that shows no feelings.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, a poker is kept by an open fire with other fireside tools. Poker the card game is a betting game for adults; betting money is gambling and not for children. "Poker face" means hiding your feelings, useful in games. In maths, poker hands are a famous probability topic.
examples from the lessons: Gran stirred the fire with the poker. | Never play with the hot poker. | The grown-ups played poker with chips. | He kept a poker face while he lied about the cake. | A poker is made of iron. | In poker, a "flush" is five cards of the same suit.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Card game is uncountable ("play poker"); the fire tool is countable (a poker, pokers). Safety: a poker gets very hot. Gambling for money is for adults only and can cause harm.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A serious disease caused by a virus that attacks the nerves and can cause paralysis, especially in children. It can be prevented by a vaccine.
its sense in the lessons: In history and health lessons, polio once paralysed many thousands of children each year. Vaccines developed by Jonas Salk (1955) and Albert Sabin made it rare; the world has almost wiped it out. Franklin D. Roosevelt, a US president, had polio.
examples from the lessons: Poliomyelitis is usually called polio. | The polio vaccine has saved millions of children. | Jonas Salk made the first polio vaccine. | Poliomyelitis can cause paralysis in the legs. | Today polio is very rare thanks to vaccination. | President Roosevelt used a wheelchair after he had polio.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Pronounced "poh-lee-oh-my-uh-LIE-tis". Short form: polio. "Myelitis" means swelling of the spinal cord.

part of speech: noun (a polka, polkas); verb (polka, polkas, polkaed, polkaing — rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A lively, bouncy dance for couples that started in Central Europe in the 1800s, with quick hopping steps. 2) The music played for this dance, usually with two beats in a bar. 3) (as in «polka dots») a pattern of round dots of the same size spread evenly over cloth. 4) (verb, rare) To dance a polka.
its sense in the lessons: In music and PE lessons a polka is a fast, happy folk dance; in art and clothes «polka dots» are the even round spots on a dress, a tie or a mug. In stories it tells the reader there is a cheerful party or village dance. Phrases: «dance a polka», «polka music», «polka dots», «polka-dot dress».
examples from the lessons: At the school ceilidh we learned to dance the polka. | The band played a polka and everyone started hopping round the hall. | A polka has two beats in each bar, so it is easy to clap along. | My nan's favourite dress is red with white polka dots. | Ladybirds look like they are wearing polka dots. | The accordion player squeezed out a jolly polka. | In art we printed polka dots with the ends of pencils. | Grandad and Gran polkaed round the kitchen at Christmas.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: a polka, two polkas. «Polka dot» is usually two words, with a hyphen before a noun: a polka-dot scarf. The verb is rare and old-fashioned. Say POL-ka (UK) or POLE-ka (US). Polka dots are a pattern of circles, not a dance, even though they share the name.

part of speech: noun (a polytechnic, polytechnics); adjective (polytechnic — teaching many technical subjects)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A college that teaches many practical and technical subjects, like engineering, building, computing and design, often to older students and adults. 2) (UK) A kind of college that existed until 1992, when most polytechnics became universities. 3) (adjective) Teaching many arts and sciences, especially technical ones: a polytechnic school.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday talk it is a place to learn a skilled job or a technical degree; «poly» is a short name for it in the UK, New Zealand and elsewhere. In history lessons it tells you about how colleges changed. Phrases: «go to the polytechnic», «polytechnic institute», «the local poly».
examples from the lessons: My uncle studied engineering at a polytechnic. | In New Zealand some colleges were called polytechnics for many years. | The polytechnic teaches plumbing, cooking and computer design. | In 1992 most British polytechnics became universities. | Mum went to the poly to train as a nurse. | Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute is a famous college in the USA. | A polytechnic is good for people who like hands-on learning.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one polytechnic, two polytechnics. «Poly» is the informal short form (UK, NZ). From Greek «poly» (many) and «techne» (art, skill). Do not mix up with «polygon» (a shape with many sides); both start with «poly» meaning many.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A very small, fluffy dog with a fox-like face, pointed ears and a thick fur coat, often orange or cream. 2) A person from Pomerania, a region by the Baltic Sea that is now in Poland and Germany. 3) (adjective) Coming from Pomerania.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life it is usually the name of a dog breed, often called a «Pom»; in geography and history lessons it names the people and land of Pomerania. In stories a Pomeranian is often a pampered little lap dog that yaps at strangers. Phrases: «a pet Pomeranian», «a Pomeranian puppy».
examples from the lessons: Our neighbour has a Pomeranian that looks like a tiny lion. | The Pomeranian barked at the postman from behind the window. | A Pomeranian puppy can fit in two hands. | Pomeranians need their thick fur brushed often. | Queen Victoria kept Pomeranians and made the breed popular. | Pomerania is a region by the Baltic Sea, and its people are Pomeranians. | My cousin calls her dog a Pom for short.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually written with a capital P, because it comes from a place name, but the dictionary lists it in lower case. Plural: Pomeranians. Short form: Pom (careful: in Australia and New Zealand «Pom» or «Pommy» is also slang for an English person, which can sound rude). It is a toy breed, not a puppy that stays small by itself — it is small when fully grown.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (party popper) A small paper tube you pull with a string so it goes bang and shoots out curly paper streamers. 2) (UK, Ireland) A press stud: a small metal or plastic fastener in two halves that snap together on clothes, also called a snap fastener. 3) A machine or pan for making popcorn: a popcorn popper. 4) Anything or anyone that pops, such as a fishing lure that pops on the water. 5) (poppers, adult slang) a drug sniffed from small bottles; dangerous and not for children.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life party poppers go off at birthdays and New Year; baby clothes and coats often close with poppers in the UK. In science a popper can show a small chemical or air «bang». Phrases: «party popper», «do up the poppers», «popcorn popper».
examples from the lessons: We pulled the party poppers when the clock struck midnight. | Bits of streamer from the poppers landed in the cake. | The baby's sleepsuit has poppers all the way down the legs. | Can you do up the poppers on my coat? | Dad made popcorn in the old popcorn popper. | Party poppers are loud, so cover your ears if you do not like bangs. | Point a party popper upwards, never at someone's face.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a popper, poppers. In the USA people say «snaps» or «snap fasteners» more than «poppers». Safety: party poppers contain a tiny explosive charge; never point them at eyes. The drug sense is plural («poppers») and is for adults to know about, not for school.

part of speech: adjective (poppin', informal form of popping); verb form (poppin' = popping)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (slang) Exciting, lively and busy, full of people and fun: «The party is poppin'.» 2) (slang) Looking great or bright and standing out: «Those colours are poppin'.» 3) (slang greeting) «What's poppin'?» means «What's happening? How are you?» 4) Just a spoken way of writing «popping», the -ing form of «pop» (bursting, going quickly somewhere).
its sense in the lessons: In real speech and songs young people use it to praise something lively or stylish. In stories it tells the reader the character speaks in casual slang. The apostrophe shows a dropped g. Phrases: «what's poppin'?», «the place is poppin'», «poppin' off».
examples from the lessons: What's poppin', guys? | The skate park was poppin' on Saturday. | Her new trainers are poppin' with that neon green. | I'm just poppin' to the shops, back in five. | The corn kept poppin' in the pan. | The bakery was poppin' the morning they gave away free doughnuts. | Those stickers really make your folder poppin'.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal spelling of «popping»; in neat writing and exams write «popping». The apostrophe stands for the missing g (poppin'). Slang words change fast and can sound odd if overused or used by adults trying to sound young.

part of speech: verb (popularise, popularises, popularised, popularising; US popularize)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To make something liked or known by many people: «The film popularised skateboarding.» 2) To explain a hard subject, like science or history, in a simple way so ordinary people can understand and enjoy it.
its sense in the lessons: In history and science lessons we read that someone «popularised» an idea, game or food, meaning they made it spread. In everyday life TV presenters and authors popularise science. Phrases: «popularise science», «popularised by», «help to popularise».
examples from the lessons: The Beatles helped to popularise long hair for boys in the 1960s. | That TV show popularised baking at home. | David Attenborough popularised nature programmes. | Who popularised the game of Minecraft at our school? | Writers like him popularise maths with fun puzzles. | Tea was popularised in England in the 1600s. | Social media can popularise a dance in just a few days.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK spelling: popularise; US spelling: popularize (both fine; keep one spelling in a piece of work). Noun: popularisation. To popularise does not mean to invent; the thing usually existed before and became well known.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To be a sign or warning that something important, often bad, is going to happen: «Dark clouds portend a storm.» 2) (formal) To mean or point to something in the future.
its sense in the lessons: It is a stiff, bookish word for «be a sign of». In stories and old tales it tells the reader that trouble is coming — a black cat, a comet, a strange silence «portends» disaster. In science lessons we say the signs «suggest» rather than «portend». Phrases: «portend trouble», «portend disaster», «portend change».
examples from the lessons: The howling wind seemed to portend a terrible night. | In old stories a comet in the sky portended war. | Falling sales may portend hard times for the shop. | The sudden quiet in the forest portended danger. | People once believed that a red sky portended bad weather. | Nobody knew what the strange letter portended.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal and literary; in everyday talk say «be a sign of» or «mean». Noun: portent (a sign of the future); adjective: portentous. Many «omens» in stories are superstitions, not science: a black cat does not really portend bad luck.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The way someone or something is shown or described in a picture, film, play or book: «a funny portrayal of a teacher». 2) An actor's performance of a character: «his portrayal of the king». 3) The act of describing something in a certain way, true or unfair.
its sense in the lessons: In English and media lessons we judge a «portrayal»: is it fair, true, kind or one-sided? In everyday life reviews talk about an actor's portrayal. Phrases: «the portrayal of», «a realistic portrayal», «an unfair portrayal», «a moving portrayal».
examples from the lessons: Her portrayal of the Wicked Witch scared the little ones. | The book gives a true portrayal of life in a coal-mining town. | Some people think the film's portrayal of farmers is unfair. | We compared two portrayals of Robin Hood. | The painting is a portrayal of the queen as a young girl. | His portrayal of a nervous pupil made us laugh. | Old cartoons often had hurtful portrayals of other peoples.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a portrayal, portrayals. Verb: portray (portray, portrays, portrayed). Do not confuse with «portrait», which is a picture of a person; a portrayal can be in words, film or acting too.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To write a date on a cheque or document that is later than the day you write it, so it only counts from that later day. 2) (formal) To happen or exist after something else: «These houses postdate the castle.»
its sense in the lessons: In money and grown-up life a postdated cheque cannot be cashed until its date. In history and science (dating rocks or objects) it means «come after». It is the opposite of «predate». Phrases: «postdate a cheque», «a postdated cheque», «postdate the war».
examples from the lessons: Dad postdated the cheque to the first of next month. | The bank will not pay a postdated cheque before its date. | The town's library postdates the church by two hundred years. | These cave paintings postdate the oldest ones found in Spain. | If something postdates another thing, it came later. | The coins in the hoard postdate the Roman invasion.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: predate (to come before; also to date earlier). Sometimes spelled «post-date». Traps: postdate has nothing to do with the post (mail); «post» here is Latin for «after». On a timeline, the thing that postdates sits further to the right (later).

part of speech: interjection (pow!); noun (POW, POWs — abbreviation); noun (a pow — rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A word for the sound of a punch, a bang or a small explosion, used in comics and cartoons: «Pow! Biff! Bang!» 2) (POW, abbreviation) A prisoner of war: a soldier captured and held by the enemy during a war. 3) (informal) A word to show something sudden and exciting happened: «And then, pow, the lights went out.»
its sense in the lessons: In comics it is a sound word (onomatopoeia) that makes action feel loud. In history lessons POW camps held captured soldiers in the World Wars. Phrases: «pow!», «POW camp», «a former POW».
examples from the lessons: In the comic, the hero's fist went «Pow!» | Write some sound words like «pow», «crash» and «boom». | My great-grandad was a POW in the Second World War. | The POWs were sent home when the war ended. | We were walking along and, pow, it started pouring with rain. | The fireworks went pow, pow, pow over the river.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a sound word it is often written in capitals with an exclamation mark: POW! As the abbreviation it is written POW (plural POWs) and read as letters, P-O-W. Pow is an onomatopoeia, a word that sounds like what it means.

part of speech: noun (a name: Powhatan — a person, a people and a place)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (a name) Powhatan was the leader of a large group of Algonquian-speaking Native American tribes in what is now Virginia, USA, around 1600; he was the father of Pocahontas. 2) (a name) The Powhatan are the Native American people of that union of tribes, and their language. 3) (a name) A county and some places in Virginia are named Powhatan.
its sense in the lessons: In US history lessons it comes up with the English settlement of Jamestown (1607) and the story of Pocahontas. It is a name, not an ordinary English word. Phrases: «Chief Powhatan», «the Powhatan people», «the Powhatan Confederacy».
examples from the lessons: Powhatan led many tribes in the land the English called Virginia. | Pocahontas was the daughter of Powhatan. | The Powhatan people grew corn, beans and squash. | English settlers at Jamestown traded with the Powhatan. | Today Powhatan descendants still live in Virginia. | Our history book has a map of the Powhatan lands.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always written with a capital P. Pronounced roughly POW-uh-tan. His own name is often given as Wahunsenacawh; «Powhatan» was also the name of his home town and his people. Many Disney-style stories about this time are not accurate history.

part of speech: noun (a precipitant, precipitants); adjective (precipitant — formal, rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) A substance that you add to a liquid to make a solid form and come out of it (a precipitate). 2) (formal) Something that causes an event to happen suddenly, a trigger: «Stress was the precipitant of the argument.» 3) (formal, rare adjective) Done too quickly, without thinking; rushed.
its sense in the lessons: In chemistry lessons a precipitant is added to a solution so cloudy solid bits appear. In medicine and formal writing it means the trigger of something. In stories it is rare. Phrases: «add a precipitant», «the precipitant of», «a precipitant decision» (rare).
examples from the lessons: The teacher added a precipitant and the clear liquid went cloudy. | Salt can act as a precipitant in some experiments. | The heavy rain was the precipitant of the landslide. | Doctors looked for the precipitant of her asthma attack. | His precipitant decision to quit surprised everyone. | A precipitant makes the solid «fall out» of the solution.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: a precipitant, precipitants. Related words: precipitate (the solid that forms; also to cause suddenly), precipitation (rain, snow and hail, or forming a solid). Easily confused with «precipitate»; the precipitant is what you add, the precipitate is what forms.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Something that came before a later thing and led to it or helped it develop: «The abacus was a precursor of the calculator.» 2) A sign or event that comes before something else: «a precursor to a storm». 3) (science) A substance from which another substance is made in a chemical reaction or in the body.
its sense in the lessons: In history and technology lessons we trace precursors: older inventions, animals or ideas that came first. In science a precursor is a starting chemical. Phrases: «a precursor of», «a precursor to», «an early precursor».
examples from the lessons: The penny-farthing was a precursor of the modern bicycle. | Telegrams were a precursor to text messages. | Some dinosaurs were precursors of birds. | Dark clouds were the precursor to a big storm. | The Greek Olympics were a precursor of today's Games. | In plants, some chemicals are precursors of colours in leaves. | The first computer games were simple precursors of the games we play now.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a precursor, precursors. Use «precursor of» or «precursor to». It is formal; in everyday talk you can say «forerunner» or «early version». From Latin for «a runner who goes ahead».

meaning for a pupil: 1) To exist or happen earlier than something else: «Dinosaurs predate humans by millions of years.» 2) To write a date on a document that is earlier than the real day (also «backdate»). 3) (science, of animals) To hunt and eat other animals as prey (a related word: predator).
its sense in the lessons: In history and science timelines it means «come before». In nature lessons «predate on» means an animal hunts others. It is the opposite of «postdate». Phrases: «predate by», «long predate», «predate on».
examples from the lessons: Stonehenge predates the pyramids of Giza in some of its parts. | The oak tree predates every house in our street. | Fossils show that sharks predate dinosaurs. | Owls predate on mice and voles. | Some stories of King Arthur predate the castles they mention. | Dad predated the form by mistake, so he had to fill in a new one.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: postdate. Also spelled «pre-date». Do not confuse with «predator» (an animal that hunts). On a timeline, what predates something sits further to the left (earlier). The sense «to hunt» is used mainly by scientists.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Able to be guessed or known before it happens: «Tides are predictable.» 2) Always doing the same thing, so you know what will happen; sometimes boring: «a predictable ending».
its sense in the lessons: In maths and science predictable patterns let you say what comes next (number sequences, tides, the seasons). In stories a predictable plot is one where you guess the ending. In everyday life a predictable routine helps people feel safe. Phrases: «a predictable pattern», «utterly predictable», «predictable results».
examples from the lessons: The number pattern 2, 4, 6, 8 is predictable. | The film was so predictable that I guessed the ending. | Babies like a predictable bedtime routine. | Sunrise times are predictable for every day of the year. | Our dog is predictable: he always barks at the bin lorry. | Weather is not always predictable, so take a coat. | Coin tosses are not predictable; each one is a 50-50 chance.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: unpredictable. Noun: predictability; adverb: predictably. Calling a person or story «predictable» can be a mild criticism. In maths, a predictable pattern has a rule you can use to find the next number.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The state of being more in number or more common than others: «a predominance of girls in the choir». 2) The state of having the most power or influence: «the predominance of one team in the league».
its sense in the lessons: In maths and geography «predominance» describes which group is biggest in a set of data; in history it describes which country or group had the most power. It is a formal word. Phrases: «a predominance of», «the predominance of», «in predominance».
examples from the lessons: The class survey showed a predominance of dog owners over cat owners. | There is a predominance of pine trees in this forest. | The predominance of rain in the west makes it very green. | Rome's predominance in the Mediterranean lasted for centuries. | The garden has a predominance of red and yellow flowers. | In the pie chart, the predominance of blue shows that most children chose swimming.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable, but used with «a»: «a predominance of». Adjective: predominant; adverb: predominantly. Formal; simpler words are «most», «the majority». In data, predominance means the biggest share, not always more than half.

meaning for a pupil: 1) If possible; it would be better if: «Come early, preferably before nine.» 2) In a way that is chosen or liked more than other ways.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and instructions it marks the best choice when there are several: «Use a pencil, preferably a sharp one.» In recipes and safety notes it tells you what is ideal but not required. Phrases: «preferably not», «preferably before», «preferably in».
examples from the lessons: Bring a drink, preferably water, not fizzy pop. | Write your answer in pen, preferably black. | We need a helper, preferably someone tall. | Go to bed early, preferably by eight. | Keep the medicine somewhere cool, preferably in the fridge. | Plant the seeds in spring, preferably on a dry day. | «Shall I bring my brother?» «Preferably not.»
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: preferably (one r after the f, then -ably). Stress on the first syllable: PREF-er-a-bly. It shows a wish, not a rule: something preferable is better, not must-have. Related: prefer, preference, preferable.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) In a way that gives one person or thing better treatment than others: «Members are served preferentially.» 2) (science, formal) More often or more strongly than other choices: «Bees preferentially visit blue flowers.»
its sense in the lessons: In science reports it means «more likely to» or «by choice». In fairness and rules talk it warns that someone gets special treatment. Phrases: «treated preferentially», «preferentially chosen», «preferentially absorb».
examples from the lessons: Some shops treat loyal customers preferentially. | The plant preferentially grows towards the light. | Water preferentially flows down the steepest slope. | It is unfair if the teacher marks friends preferentially. | Mosquitoes preferentially bite some people more than others. | Older passengers are seated preferentially on this bus.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal and long; in everyday talk say «by choice», «more often» or «first». Related: prefer, preference, preferential (adjective: preferential treatment). Not the same as «preferably», which means «if possible».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Too early; before the usual or proper time: «The baby was born prematurely.» 2) Before you have enough facts or before you are ready: «Don't celebrate prematurely.»
its sense in the lessons: In health and science it describes babies born early, leaves falling early, or hair going grey early. In sport and stories it warns about cheering or acting too soon. Phrases: «born prematurely», «prematurely grey», «end prematurely», «celebrate prematurely».
examples from the lessons: My cousin was born prematurely and spent weeks in hospital. | The match ended prematurely because of the storm. | The striker celebrated prematurely and the goal was disallowed. | His hair went prematurely grey when he was thirty. | The flowers opened prematurely in the warm February. | Don't judge the book prematurely; read to the end. | The firework went off prematurely, so everyone stepped back.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: premature (a premature baby); in Australia and the UK a premature baby is often called a «prem» or «preemie» (US). Spelling: pre-mature-ly. Too early, not too late — opposite of «belatedly».

meaning for a pupil: 1) One of the teeth between the pointed canine teeth and the big flat molars at the back of the mouth; premolars have two points and help crush food. 2) (adjective) To do with these teeth.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about teeth we learn incisors cut, canines tear, premolars and molars crush and grind. Adults have eight premolars; children's milk teeth have no premolars. Phrases: «upper premolar», «lower premolar», «premolars and molars».
examples from the lessons: Premolars sit between your canines and your molars. | An adult has eight premolars, two on each side of each jaw. | The dentist said my premolar needs a filling. | Premolars help to crush food before you swallow. | Children's milk teeth include molars but no premolars. | Sometimes premolars are taken out to make room before braces.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a premolar, premolars. In the USA they are also called «bicuspids» (two points). Count for maths: 8 premolars in a full set of 32 adult teeth (8 incisors, 4 canines, 8 premolars, 12 molars). Myth: children's back milk teeth are molars, not premolars.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A state of thinking about one thing so much that you hardly notice other things: «In his preoccupation, he missed the bus.» 2) Something that fills your mind all the time, a worry or strong interest: «Football is his main preoccupation.»
its sense in the lessons: In stories it shows a character lost in thought or worried; in everyday life it names what someone cares about most. Phrases: «a preoccupation with», «main preoccupation», «lost in preoccupation».
examples from the lessons: Her preoccupation with the test made her forget her lunch. | Winning the cup was the team's only preoccupation. | Dad's main preoccupation is paying the bills. | His preoccupation with his phone annoyed his gran. | The writer's great preoccupation was the sea. | In her preoccupation she walked straight past her friend.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable when it means a thing that fills your mind (preoccupations); uncountable when it means the state. Use «with»: a preoccupation with money. Adjective: preoccupied; verb: preoccupy. Not about «occupation» (a job), though it shares the root.

part of speech: adjective; verb form (past of preoccupy: preoccupy, preoccupies, preoccupied, preoccupying)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Thinking so much about one thing, often a worry, that you do not notice what is around you: «She looked preoccupied.» 2) (verb, past) Filled someone's mind: «The problem preoccupied him all week.»
its sense in the lessons: In stories it shows a character who is distracted or worried, so they miss clues or ignore friends. In everyday life a preoccupied parent may not hear you. Phrases: «preoccupied with», «seem preoccupied», «too preoccupied to».
examples from the lessons: Mum seemed preoccupied and did not hear my question. | He was too preoccupied with his game to eat dinner. | The detective was preoccupied with the missing key. | She stared out of the window, preoccupied. | Money worries preoccupied the family all winter. | I was so preoccupied that I put the milk in the cupboard.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Use «preoccupied with» (not «about»). It is close to «distracted» and «absorbed». Noun: preoccupation. Spelling: double c, single p in the middle: pre-oc-cu-pied.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A special right that belongs to a person or group because of who they are or their job: «It is the judge's prerogative to decide.» 2) (law, UK history) Royal prerogative: powers that belong to the king or queen and the government acting for them. 3) (everyday, a bit formal) Your own choice that nobody else can make for you: «It's your prerogative to change your mind.»
its sense in the lessons: In history and citizenship lessons it explains powers of kings, presidents or judges. In everyday talk people say «It's my prerogative» to mean «it is my right to choose». Phrases: «royal prerogative», «the prerogative of», «it's your prerogative».
examples from the lessons: In the past, starting a war was the king's prerogative. | It is the referee's prerogative to stop the match. | Choosing the class trip is the head teacher's prerogative. | «It's my prerogative to change my mind,» said my sister. | The royal prerogative is now mostly used by government ministers. | Parents have the prerogative to choose their children's school.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a prerogative, prerogatives. Spelling trap: pre-ROG-a-tive, not «perogative». It is a formal word; simpler: «right», «special power», «choice».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Something you believe is true without proof: «the presumption that he was at home». 2) (law) An idea a court treats as true until proved otherwise: «the presumption of innocence». 3) Rude, too-confident behaviour, doing something you have no right to do: «What presumption, to sit in the head's chair!»
its sense in the lessons: In maths and science, presumptions must be checked; in law «innocent until proven guilty» is the presumption of innocence. In stories it can describe a cheeky or arrogant character. Phrases: «the presumption of innocence», «on the presumption that», «a fair presumption».
examples from the lessons: Our plan was based on the presumption that it would not rain. | In court there is a presumption of innocence. | The presumption that all spiders are dangerous is wrong. | She acted on the presumption that her friend had the tickets. | His presumption in reading my diary made me cross. | That was a reasonable presumption, but it turned out false. | Scientists test presumptions with experiments.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable for a belief (presumptions); uncountable for rude boldness. Verb: presume; adjective: presumptuous (too bold), presumable. Close to «assumption»; a presumption is usually a little stronger, based on some reason.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To take something for granted as true before you start: «The plan presupposes that everyone will help.» 2) (formal) To need something to be true or to exist first: «Reading presupposes knowing the letters.»
its sense in the lessons: In maths and logic it points to the hidden starting idea of a question or argument. In reasoning and olympiad puzzles it helps you spot a trick question: «When did you stop cheating?» presupposes that you cheated. Phrases: «presuppose that», «presupposes knowledge of».
examples from the lessons: The question «Who broke the vase?» presupposes that somebody broke it. | Long division presupposes that you know your times tables. | His plan presupposes that the bus will be on time. | The story presupposes that dragons can talk. | Good teamwork presupposes trust. | Don't presuppose the answer before you check the facts.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal. Noun: presupposition. In logic, a loaded question presupposes something that may be false; you can answer by questioning the presupposition. Similar to «assume», but «presuppose» is about what must already be true for something else to make sense.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A false reason given to hide the real reason for doing something: «He called on the pretext of borrowing sugar, but really he wanted to see the puppy.» 2) An excuse used to start something, like a fight or a war.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and history lessons a pretext reveals hidden motives: a villain or a country uses a pretext to do what it wanted all along. In online safety, scammers use pretexts (a fake parcel, a fake prize) to get your details. Phrases: «on the pretext of», «under the pretext that», «a pretext for».
examples from the lessons: She went to the kitchen on the pretext of getting water, but really she wanted biscuits. | The invaders used a small border fight as a pretext for war. | The scammer phoned on the pretext of checking the bank account. | He made up a pretext to leave the party early. | Asking for directions was just a pretext to start talking. | Never give your password, whatever pretext someone gives.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a pretext, pretexts. Use «on/under the pretext of» + noun or -ing. Stress: PRE-text. A pretext is always false or hiding something; an honest reason is not a pretext. Not related to «text» messages in meaning.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Common or widespread in a place or at a time: «Colds are prevalent in winter.» 2) (formal) Most common, strongest among others.
its sense in the lessons: In science and health lessons it describes how common an illness, animal or habit is; in geography, which plants or winds are common in a region. Phrases: «prevalent in», «prevalent among», «widely prevalent».
examples from the lessons: Head lice are prevalent in primary schools. | Malaria is prevalent in some hot, wet countries. | The prevalent wind here blows from the west. | Smartphones are prevalent among teenagers. | Kangaroos are prevalent in many parts of Australia. | Bullying online is more prevalent than many adults think.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: prevalence (how common something is; in maths and health surveys it can be a percentage). Formal; simpler: «common», «widespread». Note «prevailing wind» and «prevalent wind» are both used; «prevailing» is more usual for wind.

part of speech: adjective (more primitive, most primitive); noun (a primitive, primitives — rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Very simple and basic, not advanced: «a primitive tool made of stone». 2) Belonging to an early stage of development, long ago: «primitive life forms». 3) (art) A painter or style that is simple and untrained-looking on purpose or by nature. 4) (old, now hurtful) Once used about peoples or cultures thought to be «less advanced»; today this is seen as unfair and rude.
its sense in the lessons: In history and science lessons it describes early tools, cells or animals; in everyday life it means basic: «The campsite toilets were primitive.» In computing a «primitive» is a basic building block. Phrases: «primitive tools», «primitive life», «primitive conditions».
examples from the lessons: Early humans made primitive tools from flint. | Bacteria are among the most primitive living things. | The hut was primitive, with no water or electricity. | His first robot was primitive but it could move forward. | Primitive fish had no jaws. | We camped in primitive conditions on the island. | Calling another people «primitive» is unfair; their ways are just different.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb: primitively. Be careful: using «primitive» about real living peoples or cultures is old-fashioned and hurtful. In science «primitive» means early or simple in form, not «worse».

part of speech: verb (prise, prises, prised, prising; US pry); noun (prise — rare, leverage)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (UK, Ireland, Australia, NZ) To force something open or apart, often by pushing a tool into a gap and levering: «She prised the lid off the tin with a coin.» 2) To get something out of someone with effort: «I finally prised the secret out of him.»
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and science (levers) you prise open tins and shells; in stories, characters prise open doors or prise out secrets. Phrases: «prise open», «prise off», «prise out of», «prise apart».
examples from the lessons: Dad prised the paint tin open with a screwdriver. | The bird prised the mussel shell apart. | He prised the stone out of his boot. | We prised the truth out of my little brother. | Use a spoon to prise the lid off, not your teeth. | The burglars tried to prise the window open.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK spelling is «prise»; American English uses «pry» (pry open). Do not confuse with «prize» (a reward), which sounds the same; the noun «prise» (a grip or lever) is rare. Prising uses the idea of a lever from science lessons.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Shaped like a prism: a solid with two matching ends and flat sides. 2) Splitting white light into the colours of the rainbow, as a glass prism does; shining with many colours: «prismatic colours». 3) Using a prism: «a prismatic compass».
its sense in the lessons: In maths lessons prismatic shapes are prisms like a Toblerone box; in science, prismatic colours show how light splits into a spectrum. In stories it describes rainbow sparkles. Phrases: «prismatic colours», «prismatic compass», «prismatic crystals».
examples from the lessons: Sunlight through the crystal made prismatic colours on the wall. | Some crystals grow in prismatic shapes. | A prismatic compass helps you take exact bearings. | The soap bubble shimmered with prismatic light. | A triangular prism is a prismatic solid with two triangle ends. | The fountain spray looked prismatic in the sun.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective from «prism». In maths, a prism has the same cross-section all along its length; its volume = area of the end × length. Rainbow colours: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To announce something officially and publicly: «The king proclaimed a holiday.» 2) To say something proudly or strongly so everyone knows: «She proclaimed she was the best speller.» 3) To show something clearly: «His smile proclaimed his joy.» 4) (church, Bible) To announce or preach a message, like the good news.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons kings, queens and governments proclaim laws and new rulers. In everyday life people proclaim opinions loudly. In church, preachers «proclaim the Gospel». Phrases: «proclaim independence», «proclaimed king», «proclaim the news».
examples from the lessons: In 1776 the American colonies proclaimed their independence. | The herald proclaimed the new king in the market square. | Tom proclaimed that he would never eat broccoli. | The banners proclaimed «Welcome Home!» | Christians proclaim the message of Jesus in churches and on the streets. | The poster proclaimed a big sale.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: proclamation (an official announcement). Proclaiming is louder and more official than «saying» or «announcing». Spelling: pro-claim (one c, ai).

meaning for a pupil: 1) How much work, goods or results someone or something produces in a certain time: «Productivity rose when the new machines came.» 2) The quality of being productive, getting a lot done. 3) (science) How much plant or animal life a place produces, like a field or a lake.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and money lessons productivity compares output with time or workers: more done per hour means higher productivity. In everyday life it is about using time well. In geography a farm's productivity is how much food it grows. Phrases: «high productivity», «boost productivity», «productivity per hour».
examples from the lessons: The factory's productivity doubled with new robots. | Short breaks can improve your productivity when you study. | Good soil increases the productivity of the farm. | My productivity drops when I'm tired. | The ocean near the coast has high productivity because of plankton. | Workers asked for more pay because productivity had gone up.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: no plural. Adjective: productive. Maths: productivity = output ÷ input (for example, 60 toys made in 3 hours = 20 toys per hour). Being busy is not the same as being productive.

meaning for a pupil: 1) As a job for money, not just as a hobby: «She sings professionally.» 2) In a skilled, careful, polite way, as a good worker should: «He handled the angry customer professionally.» 3) By an expert: «The photos were professionally taken.»
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life it tells you whether someone does something as their paid job, or does it to a high standard. In careers lessons pupils hear about playing sport or drawing professionally. Phrases: «play professionally», «professionally trained», «behave professionally», «professionally made».
examples from the lessons: My uncle plays football professionally in Scotland. | The nurse spoke to us calmly and professionally. | Our school photos were taken professionally. | She wants to dance professionally when she grows up. | The kitchen was professionally cleaned after the flood. | Even when the crowd booed, the referee acted professionally.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: professional; noun: a professional (a pro), profession. Spelling: one f, double s: pro-fes-sion-al-ly (two l's). Opposite in sense 1: as an amateur; in sense 2: unprofessionally.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Very deeply or greatly: «profoundly grateful», «profoundly changed». 2) (health) Very severely, especially about hearing: «profoundly deaf» means hearing very little or nothing. 3) In a wise, deep-thinking way: «He spoke profoundly about life.»
its sense in the lessons: In stories it shows strong feelings or big changes; in health and inclusion lessons «profoundly deaf» is a respectful term. Phrases: «profoundly moved», «profoundly affected», «profoundly deaf», «profoundly different».
examples from the lessons: The war profoundly changed the town. | We were profoundly grateful for the neighbours' help. | My friend is profoundly deaf and uses sign language. | The film moved her profoundly. | Inventing the wheel profoundly affected how people lived. | The two cats are profoundly different in character.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: profound (deep, very great, wise); noun: profundity. Formal; simpler: «deeply», «greatly», «very». Spelling: pro-found-ly.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Coming or given in very large amounts, pouring out: «profuse bleeding», «profuse sweating». 2) Given very freely and many times: «profuse apologies», «profuse thanks». 3) Growing thickly and in great numbers: «profuse flowers».
its sense in the lessons: In health and first aid it warns that a lot of blood or sweat is coming out; in stories it shows someone thanking or apologising again and again. Phrases: «profuse apologies», «profuse thanks», «profuse bleeding».
examples from the lessons: He made profuse apologies for breaking the window. | Profuse bleeding needs firm pressure and a grown-up to call for help. | The roses grew in profuse bunches over the wall. | After the race she was covered in profuse sweat. | The visitors gave profuse thanks for the meal. | The tree has profuse white blossom in spring.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb: profusely (thank someone profusely, bleed profusely); noun: profusion (a profusion of flowers). Formal; simpler: «a lot of», «plenty of». First aid: call 999 (UK), 911 (US, Canada), 000 (Australia), 111 (NZ), 112/999 (Ireland) for heavy bleeding.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) A person or animal from whom others are descended, an ancestor: «the progenitor of the family». 2) (formal) A person or thing that starts a movement, idea or style; a founder or first model: «the progenitor of rock music». 3) (science) A cell or living thing that later things develop from.
its sense in the lessons: In history and family-tree work it names the first ancestor; in science (evolution, cells) it names the starting form. In stories it gives a grand, old-fashioned feel. Phrases: «the progenitor of», «a common progenitor».
examples from the lessons: He was the progenitor of a long line of farmers. | The wolf is the progenitor of all pet dogs. | Some call that band the progenitor of punk music. | Scientists study progenitor cells that grow into blood cells. | Adam is called the progenitor of humankind in the Bible. | The Wright brothers' plane was the progenitor of every modern aircraft.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: progenitor, progenitors. Formal; simpler: «ancestor», «forefather», «founder». The «progeny» are the children or descendants, the opposite end of the family tree.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Moving forward or developing step by step from one stage to another: «the progression from caterpillar to butterfly». 2) (maths) A sequence of numbers that follow a rule, like 3, 6, 9, 12 (an arithmetic progression) or 2, 4, 8, 16 (a geometric progression). 3) (music) A series of chords played one after another: «a chord progression». 4) Getting better or worse over time, as in an illness or in skill.
its sense in the lessons: In school maths, a progression is a number pattern with a steady rule; in science it describes the stages of growth; in sport and learning it shows getting better. Phrases: «arithmetic progression», «geometric progression», «chord progression», «natural progression».
examples from the lessons: The numbers 5, 10, 15, 20 form an arithmetic progression. | In a geometric progression you multiply by the same number each time. | We watched the progression from tadpole to frog. | Moving from swimming lessons to the team was a natural progression. | The guitar song uses a simple chord progression. | Doctors try to slow the progression of the disease. | Our reading books show a progression from easy to hard.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable in maths and music (a progression, progressions). Verb: progress; adjective: progressive.
