Maths: in an arithmetic progression each term = previous term + the same difference (3, 7, 11: +4); in a geometric progression each term = previous term × the same ratio (3, 6, 12: ×2).

part of speech: noun (a promenade, promenades); verb (promenade, promenades, promenaded, promenading)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (UK, Australia, NZ, Ireland) A wide path by the sea for walking along, often called «the prom». 2) A slow, relaxed walk in a public place, to enjoy yourself or to be seen. 3) (verb) To walk slowly and grandly in public. 4) (US, old) A formal dance; the US school «prom» gets its name from this. 5) (dance) A move in square dancing where partners walk round the circle together.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday British seaside life the prom is where you eat chips and ice cream; in history and stories ladies and gentlemen «promenaded» in parks. In music, the BBC «Proms» are concerts named after promenade concerts. Phrases: «along the promenade», «on the prom», «promenade deck».
examples from the lessons: We walked along the promenade eating ice cream. | Brighton has a long promenade by the beach. | Victorian families liked to promenade on Sunday afternoons. | The ship's promenade deck had deckchairs. | Huge waves crashed over the promenade in the storm. | In square dancing, «Promenade!» means walk round with your partner. | The American high school prom takes its name from «promenade».
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a promenade, promenades. Short form: prom (UK: seafront; US: school dance). Pronounced prom-uh-NAHD (UK) or prom-uh-NAYD (US). Safety: keep away from the edge of the promenade in stormy weather.

part of speech: noun (prominence, uncountable; a prominence — a raised part)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Being well known or important: «She rose to prominence as a singer.» 2) Being easy to see or notice: «The story was given prominence on the front page.» 3) A part that sticks out or up, like a hill or a bump. 4) (science) A huge loop of glowing gas rising from the surface of the Sun (a solar prominence).
its sense in the lessons: In history and news, people «rise to prominence»; in geography it means a raised piece of land; in space science a solar prominence is a giant arc of hot gas. Phrases: «rise to prominence», «give prominence to», «gain prominence», «solar prominence».
examples from the lessons: She rose to prominence after winning the talent show. | The newspaper gave the school play great prominence. | The castle stands on a rocky prominence above the town. | A solar prominence can be bigger than the whole Earth. | The bump of the nose bone is a small prominence. | Recycling has gained prominence in recent years.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly uncountable for importance; countable for a raised part (prominences). Adjective: prominent; adverb: prominently. Do not confuse with «promise» or «permanence».

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a place or way that is easy to see or notice: «The sign was prominently displayed.» 2) In an important way, playing a big part: «She figures prominently in the story.»
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and safety notices must be displayed prominently; in history and stories a person who «features prominently» is important. Phrases: «prominently displayed», «feature prominently», «figure prominently».
examples from the lessons: The fire exit sign is prominently displayed above the door. | His name features prominently in the history book. | The trophy sits prominently on the head's desk. | Our class picture was prominently placed in the hall. | Dogs feature prominently in her stories. | Put the price prominently on the label.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: prominent; noun: prominence. Spelling: prom-i-nent-ly (i after m). Simpler words: «clearly», «where everyone can see», «importantly».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (law, formal) The person to whom a promise is made; the one who will receive what was promised. The person who makes the promise is the «promisor».
its sense in the lessons: It is a legal word found in contracts and law books; in everyday life we just say «the person you promised». In ethics lessons it helps talk about who is owed a promise. Phrases: «the promisor and the promisee».
examples from the lessons: If I promise to give you my bike, you are the promisee. | The promisee can ask a court for help if a contract is broken. | In the contract, the shop is the promisor and the customer is the promisee. | A promisee trusts that the promise will be kept. | Lawyers use the word promisee, but children just say «the one I promised».
note for the reader of a maths problem: Rare and legal. The ending -ee marks the person who receives (like employee, trainee, payee); -or or -er marks the person who does (promisor, employer). Stress: prom-i-SEE.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A high point of land or rock that sticks out into the sea or a lake; a headland. 2) (science, body) A part of the body that sticks out, a bump on a bone.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons it is a coastal landform shaped by waves; in stories castles and lighthouses often stand on a promontory. Phrases: «a rocky promontory», «on the promontory», «a promontory overlooking the sea».
examples from the lessons: The lighthouse stands on a rocky promontory. | We walked out to the end of the promontory to watch seals. | Waves slowly wear away the soft rock around a promontory. | Tintagel Castle was built on a promontory in Cornwall. | From the promontory we could see both bays. | The ruined fort stood on a promontory high above the sea.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: promontory, promontories (y becomes ies). Similar words: headland, cape, point. Stress: PROM-on-tree (UK), PROM-on-tor-ee (US).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Made or used to advertise something and help it sell: «promotional posters», «a promotional video». 2) To do with getting a better job or a higher position: «promotional prospects». 3) (sport) To do with moving up to a higher league.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and media lessons it marks adverts, free samples and special offers, things made to persuade you to buy. Learning to spot promotional content keeps you a smart shopper. Phrases: «promotional material», «promotional offer», «promotional video», «promotional tour».
examples from the lessons: The shop gave out promotional pens with its name on. | That «review» was really a promotional video paid for by the company. | We got a promotional offer: two pizzas for the price of one. | The band went on a promotional tour for their new album. | Promotional leaflets came through the letterbox. | Influencers must say when a post is promotional.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Related: promote (verb), promotion (noun: an advert campaign, a better job, or moving up a league). Media tip: «promotional» means someone wants you to buy or like something, so check the facts.

part of speech: verb form (past of promulgate: promulgate, promulgates, promulgated, promulgating); adjective (promulgated) — formal
meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal, law) Made a new law or rule official by announcing it publicly: «The new law was promulgated in May.» 2) (formal) Spread an idea or belief widely among people: «The ideas were promulgated through books and sermons.»
its sense in the lessons: A stiff word from law, government and history: rulers promulgate laws and decrees, and movements promulgate ideas. In church history, popes and councils promulgated teachings. Phrases: «promulgate a law», «promulgated by», «widely promulgated».
examples from the lessons: The emperor promulgated a new set of laws. | The rules were promulgated on the school website. | His ideas were promulgated by his students. | The constitution was promulgated after the war. | Rumours promulgated online are not always true. | The council promulgated a ban on fireworks in the park.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; simpler words: «announced», «made official», «spread». Noun: promulgation. Stress: PROM-ul-gate-ed. Do not confuse with «promoted».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) A natural habit of behaving in a certain way, a tendency: «a propensity to tell jokes», «a propensity for getting lost».
its sense in the lessons: In stories and reports it describes someone's typical behaviour; in science it can describe how likely something is to happen. Phrases: «a propensity to», «a propensity for».
examples from the lessons: My dog has a propensity to chew socks. | She has a propensity for getting into trouble. | Some metals have a propensity to rust. | His propensity to exaggerate made people doubt him. | Cats have a propensity for sleeping in sunny spots. | This rope has a propensity to tangle.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: propensity, propensities. Use «a propensity to + verb» or «a propensity for + noun/-ing». Formal; simpler: «tendency», «habit». Not the same as «property» or «prosperity».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A statement that something will happen in the future, especially one made by someone believed to have special knowledge: «The witch's prophecy came true.» 2) (Bible, church) A message that Christians and Jews believe comes from God, given through a prophet, sometimes about the future and often about how people should live. 3) The power or act of saying what will happen in the future.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and myths prophecies drive the plot (a chosen one, a curse, a hero's fate). In religious education, the books of the prophets in the Bible contain prophecies; Christians believe some Old Testament prophecies point to Jesus. In science we make «predictions» with evidence, not prophecies. Phrases: «a prophecy came true», «fulfil a prophecy», «self-fulfilling prophecy».
examples from the lessons: The old prophecy said a girl from the village would save the kingdom. | The prophecy came true at the end of the book. | Isaiah's prophecies are read in church at Christmas. | Christians believe Jesus fulfilled the prophecies of the prophets. | Saying «I'll fail» can become a self-fulfilling prophecy. | The fortune teller's prophecy was just a guess. | In the myth, the king tried to escape the prophecy but could not.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun «prophecy» (ends -cy, sounds like «see») versus verb «prophesy» (ends -sy, sounds like «sigh»): the prophet prophesied a prophecy. Plural: prophecies. A self-fulfilling prophecy comes true because people believe it. A scientific prediction is based on evidence and can be tested.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a way that keeps the same ratio, so that when one amount changes, the other changes by the same scale: «If you double the recipe, increase everything proportionally.» 2) Fairly and in the right size compared with something else: «Punishments should be given proportionally.»
its sense in the lessons: In maths, cooking, maps and science, things that change proportionally keep the same ratio. In fairness and law it means not too much and not too little. Phrases: «increase proportionally», «proportionally more», «shared proportionally».
examples from the lessons: If you double the cake recipe, add all the ingredients proportionally. | The map shrinks the whole country proportionally. | The prize money was shared proportionally to how much each person paid. | Big dogs eat proportionally more than small dogs. | When you resize a photo, keep the sides proportionally the same. | The punishment should be proportionally fair to what was done.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: proportional; noun: proportion. Maths: if y is proportional to x, y = k × x, so doubling x doubles y (2 pens cost £3, so 4 pens cost £6). «Proportionally» is the same as «in proportion».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Lying flat on the ground with your face down: «He lay prostrate on the floor.» 2) (verb) To prostrate yourself: to lie face down, especially to worship, pray or show great respect or obedience. 3) Completely exhausted, weak or overcome: «prostrate with grief», «prostrate with heat».
its sense in the lessons: In religious education people prostrate themselves in prayer (Muslims in sujood, some Christian ceremonies, Bible stories of people bowing down to God or kings). In stories it shows someone collapsed or overcome by feeling. Phrases: «lie prostrate», «prostrate oneself», «prostrate with grief».
examples from the lessons: The tired runner lay prostrate on the grass. | In the Bible story, the brothers prostrated themselves before Joseph. | Muslims prostrate themselves during their prayers. | She was prostrate with grief after her dog died. | The heat left us almost prostrate. | The soldier fell prostrate before the king.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: «prostrate» (lying flat) has an r after the t; «prostate» (no second r) is a gland in men's bodies — a different word. Prostrate means face down; lying on your back is «supine».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A country or area that is controlled and protected by a stronger country, while keeping some of its own rulers: «Brunei was a British protectorate.» 2) The relationship of such protection and control. 3) (history, UK) The Protectorate: the time from 1653 to 1659 when Oliver Cromwell and then his son ruled England, Scotland and Ireland as «Lord Protector».
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons it comes up with empires: Britain, France and other powers ran protectorates in Africa, Asia and the Pacific. Phrases: «a British protectorate», «become a protectorate», «the Protectorate».
examples from the lessons: Many countries in Africa were once protectorates of European powers. | The Solomon Islands were a British protectorate until independence. | Oliver Cromwell ruled during the Protectorate. | A protectorate keeps its own leader but a stronger country controls its defence. | The island became a protectorate after the treaty. | Our history topic compared colonies and protectorates.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: protectorate, protectorates; capital P for Cromwell's Protectorate. Related: protector, protect. A protectorate is not the same as a colony, though in practice the stronger country often held the real power.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The official rules of correct behaviour on formal occasions, for example when meeting a king or a president: «royal protocol». 2) A set of steps that must be followed in a certain situation, like a plan for safety or medicine: «the school's fire protocol». 3) (computers) A set of rules computers use to send and receive information: «Internet protocol». 4) (law) An extra agreement added to a treaty between countries.
its sense in the lessons: In computing lessons protocols (like HTTP and IP) let computers talk; in science and safety a protocol is the exact method to follow; in history and news it is formal manners. Phrases: «follow protocol», «break protocol», «safety protocol», «internet protocol».
examples from the lessons: The doctors followed the protocol for treating burns. | Our school has a protocol for when someone has an allergic reaction. | The prince broke protocol by hugging the crowd. | Web pages travel using the HTTP protocol. | Under royal protocol, you wait for the queen to speak first. | The science protocol says to wear goggles during the experiment.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable for a set of steps (protocols); uncountable for formal manners. IP stands for Internet Protocol; HTTP for HyperText Transfer Protocol. Stress: PRO-to-col.

part of speech: adjective; verb form (protrude, protrudes, protruded, protruding)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Sticking out from a surface or edge: «a nail protruding from the wall», «protruding teeth». 2) (verb) Sticking out beyond the rest.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday safety it warns about things that stick out and can hurt you (nails, branches, rocks); in science it describes body parts or landforms; in stories it gives a vivid picture. Phrases: «protruding from», «protruding eyes», «protruding rocks».
examples from the lessons: Careful, there's a nail protruding from that plank. | The frog has big protruding eyes. | A branch was protruding into the path. | Protruding rocks made the river dangerous for boats. | His wallet was protruding from his back pocket. | Some fish have protruding jaws for catching food.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: protrude; noun: protrusion. Use «protruding from» or «protruding out of». Safety: tell a grown-up about protruding nails or broken edges in the playground.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science, formal) To do with puberty, the time, usually between about 8 and 16, when a child's body slowly changes into an adult's body: «pubertal changes», «pubertal growth spurt».
its sense in the lessons: In health and RSE lessons it describes normal changes that happen to everyone as they grow up, like a growth spurt, body hair and voice changes. It is a doctor's word; everyday speech just says «puberty» or «growing up». Phrases: «pubertal growth spurt», «pubertal changes», «pubertal age».
examples from the lessons: The pubertal growth spurt can make you grow several centimetres in a year. | Pubertal changes happen at different ages for different children. | The doctor checked whether the boy was at a pubertal stage yet. | Feeling moody can be part of normal pubertal changes. | Health lessons explain pubertal changes so nobody is scared. | Pubertal growth often starts earlier in girls than in boys.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: puberty (PEW-ber-tee). It is normal and happens to everyone at their own speed; there is no «right» age. If you have questions, ask a parent, school nurse or doctor.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Attention from newspapers, TV, the internet and the public: «The rescue got a lot of publicity.» 2) The work of getting people to notice something, like adverts, posters and interviews: «The publicity for the film was everywhere.»
its sense in the lessons: In media lessons it explains how events, products and people become known; in everyday life it is the posters and adverts around us. Phrases: «good publicity», «bad publicity», «a publicity stunt», «get publicity».
examples from the lessons: The school fair got good publicity in the local paper. | The singer's new song had huge publicity. | Climbing the tower was just a publicity stunt. | The company got bad publicity after the toy broke easily. | We made posters for publicity for the bake sale. | «There's no such thing as bad publicity,» some people say, but that is not always true.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «a lot of publicity», not «publicities». Related: public, publicise (UK)/publicize (US), publicist. A «publicity stunt» is something done mainly to get attention.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A company or person that prepares books, magazines, newspapers, music or games and makes them available for people to buy or read. 2) (computers) A program or person that puts something online for others to see.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons the publisher's name is on a book's spine and title page and is used in references; in everyday life publishers choose and sell books. Phrases: «the publisher of», «a children's publisher», «find a publisher».
examples from the lessons: The publisher's name is on the spine of the book. | Penguin is a famous publisher. | She sent her story to a publisher, hoping it would be printed. | The game publisher released a new update. | In our book review, write the author, title and publisher. | The newspaper's publisher decided to print a special edition.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: publisher, publishers. Verb: publish; noun: publication. The author writes the book; the publisher edits, prints and sells it; the printer only prints it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A pufferfish: a fish that can blow itself up into a ball, often covered in spikes, to scare away enemies; many are poisonous to eat. 2) (UK, Australia, NZ) An inhaler, a small device that puffs medicine into your lungs, used for asthma. 3) A puffer jacket: a warm, padded coat with puffy stuffed sections. 4) (old) A small steam boat or train that puffs smoke; a person who puffs.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons pufferfish show animal defences; in health and safety a «puffer» means an asthma inhaler, which pupils with asthma must have at school. In everyday life a puffer jacket keeps you warm in winter. Phrases: «puffer fish», «blue puffer», «puffer jacket».
examples from the lessons: The puffer blew itself up into a spiky ball. | Puffers are poisonous, so never eat one you catch. | Jack uses his blue puffer when his asthma gets bad. | Take your puffer on the school trip, just in case. | My new puffer jacket is so warm. | The old steam puffer chugged up the Scottish coast.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: puffer, puffers. «Pufferfish» is often one word. In the USA people say «inhaler» more than «puffer». Safety: a reliever puffer (often blue) is for asthma attacks; tell a teacher at once if a friend cannot breathe properly.

part of speech: noun (pul, puls or puli — rare); fragment
meaning for a pupil: 1) A small coin of Afghanistan: 100 puls make one afghani; today it is hardly used. 2) (Persian, Dari) The word for «money» in Persian and Dari; it is not an English word. 3) Often just a misspelling or cut-off piece of «pull» or a name.
its sense in the lessons: It is not a normal English word. It can turn up in maths puzzles about world money, or in a text as a typing slip for «pull». Honest entry: if you see «pul», check whether «pull» was meant.
examples from the lessons: One afghani is worth one hundred puls. | The old coin in the museum was an Afghan pul. | In Persian, «pul» means money. | The sign said «PUL» but someone had rubbed off the last L of «PULL». | Pul coins are so small in value that people rarely use them.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural forms vary: puls or puli. In English text «pul» is most often a typo for «pull» (to move something towards you). Maths: 1 afghani = 100 pul, like 1 pound = 100 pence.

part of speech: verb form (past of pulverise: pulverise, pulverises, pulverised, pulverising; US pulverize, pulverized); adjective (pulverised)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Crushed into powder or tiny pieces: «pulverised rock», «pulverised coal». 2) (informal) Beaten very heavily in a game or fight: «Our team got pulverised 7–0.» 3) Completely destroyed: «The old building was pulverised by the wrecking ball.»
its sense in the lessons: In science and cooking it describes grinding solids into powder (rock, chalk, spices); in sport reports it is a strong, playful word for a huge defeat. Phrases: «pulverised into dust», «pulverised rock», «got pulverised».
examples from the lessons: The miners pulverised the rock to get the gold out. | We pulverised chalk to make paint powder. | The pestle pulverised the spices in the bowl. | Our football team got pulverised by the champions. | The glacier pulverised the stones into fine sand. | The old car was pulverised in the crusher.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK spelling: pulverised; US: pulverized. Noun: pulverisation. Science: crushing a solid into powder does not change what it is made of; it is a physical change, not a chemical one, and the powder dissolves faster because it has more surface.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The last line or words of a joke, which make it funny: «Wait for the punchline!» 2) The surprising or important ending of a story, speech or advert.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons and everyday fun it is the payoff of a joke; comedians practise timing the punchline. In writing, a strong ending is sometimes called the punchline. Phrases: «deliver the punchline», «forget the punchline», «get the punchline».
examples from the lessons: He forgot the punchline, so nobody laughed. | The punchline of the joke is «Lettuce in, it's cold out here!» | Wait for it, the punchline is coming. | She delivered the punchline perfectly and the whole class laughed. | I didn't get the punchline until my sister explained it. | The story's punchline was that the ghost was the dog all along.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: punchline, punchlines. Also written «punch line» or «punch-line». Do not give away the punchline before the joke is told. «Get the punchline» means understand why it is funny.

meaning for a pupil: 1) At exactly the right time, not late: «The train left punctually at nine.» 2) Regularly on time, every time: «She pays her bills punctually.»
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and school it describes good habits: arriving and handing in work on time. In maths word problems «punctually» tells you there is no delay, so the time is exact. Phrases: «arrive punctually», «start punctually», «punctually at».
examples from the lessons: Lessons start punctually at nine o'clock. | The bus arrived punctually, so we were not late. | Please hand in your homework punctually. | Grandad always arrives punctually for Sunday lunch. | The concert began punctually at seven. | Swiss trains are famous for running punctually.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: punctual; noun: punctuality. Spelling: punc-tu-al-ly (double l). Maths: «arrived punctually at 3:15» means exactly 3:15, no minutes early or late. Not related to punctuation except through Latin «punctum» (a point).

meaning for a pupil: 1) That can be punished by law or by rules: «Stealing is a punishable offence.» 2) (law) That carries a particular punishment: «punishable by a fine».
its sense in the lessons: In citizenship, law and safety lessons it tells you something is against the rules and has a penalty. On signs: «Dropping litter is punishable by a fine.» Phrases: «punishable by», «a punishable offence», «punishable by law».
examples from the lessons: Dropping litter here is punishable by a £100 fine. | Cheating in the exam is punishable by disqualification. | Bullying is punishable under school rules. | In some countries, chewing gum on the train is punishable. | Pulling the emergency cord without reason is punishable by law. | Hacking into someone's account is a punishable crime.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually followed by «by»: punishable by a fine. Related: punish, punishment. «A punishable offence» means a crime or rule-break that can bring a penalty; it does not mean the punishment will always happen.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) To do with a pupa, the resting stage in an insect's life between larva and adult, when it changes shape inside a case or cocoon: «the pupal stage».
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on life cycles it names the third stage of complete metamorphosis: egg, larva, pupa, adult. A butterfly's pupa is called a chrysalis. Phrases: «pupal stage», «pupal case», «pupal skin».
examples from the lessons: The caterpillar entered its pupal stage and hung still for two weeks. | A butterfly's pupal case is called a chrysalis. | The beetle came out of its pupal skin. | During the pupal stage the insect's body completely changes. | We kept the pupal cases in a jar to watch them hatch. | Mosquitoes have a pupal stage in water.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: pupa (plural pupae or pupas). Pronounced PEW-pul. Not to do with «pupil» (a school child or the black part of the eye), though both come from Latin words for small children and dolls. Life cycle order: egg → larva → pupa → adult.

part of speech: verb (purge, purges, purged, purging); noun (a purge, purges)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To get rid of people, things or ideas that are not wanted, often harshly: «The ruler purged his enemies from the army.» 2) (history) A purge: a time when a government or leader removes or punishes lots of people, sometimes killing them, as in the purges under Stalin. 3) To clean out completely: «purge the pipes», «purge old files from the computer». 4) (church) To make free from sin or guilt; to cleanse the soul. 5) (old, medicine) To empty the bowels with strong medicine.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons it describes cruel removals of people by dictators; in computing and everyday life it means a big clear-out; in religion it means cleansing from sin. Phrases: «purge of», «a political purge», «purge the system».
examples from the lessons: In the 1930s Stalin's purges killed and imprisoned huge numbers of people. | I purged all the old photos from my tablet. | The plumber purged the air from the radiators. | The new king purged the palace of his brother's friends. | In the story, the hero tried to purge his guilt by helping others. | Mum had a big purge of the toy cupboard.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: a purge, purges. Related: purgatory (in Catholic belief, a state of cleansing after death), purification. In history, «purge» usually means something violent and unjust; in a tidy-up it is light.

part of speech: noun (purification, uncountable; a purification — a ritual)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Making something clean and pure by removing dirt or harmful things: «water purification». 2) (church, religion) Making a person or place spiritually clean, often with a ceremony; for example, the Bible's laws of purification, or washing before prayer in many faiths. 3) (science) Separating a pure substance from a mixture.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography lessons water purification makes water safe to drink (filtering, boiling, chlorine). In religious education many faiths have purification rituals; in church the Feast of the Purification (Candlemas, 2 February) remembers Mary taking baby Jesus to the Temple. Phrases: «water purification», «air purification», «purification tablets», «rites of purification».
examples from the lessons: Water purification removes germs so the water is safe to drink. | Hikers carry purification tablets for stream water. | The factory has an air purification system. | Candlemas is also called the Feast of the Purification. | Muslims wash in a set way for purification before prayer. | We learned about purification by filtering muddy water in science.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly uncountable. Verb: purify; adjective: pure. Science: filtering removes bits you can see, boiling kills germs, but neither removes all dissolved chemicals. Never drink river water without purifying it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To make something pure by removing dirt, germs or harmful things: «Boil the water to purify it.» 2) (religion, church) To make someone spiritually clean, free from sin or guilt: «Christians believe God can purify people's hearts.» 3) (science) To separate a substance from a mixture so it is pure.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons we purify water by filtering, boiling or evaporating; in everyday life air purifiers clean the air indoors; in religious education people purify themselves by washing, prayer or fasting. Phrases: «purify water», «purify the air», «purify the heart».
examples from the lessons: We purified muddy water with sand and charcoal filters. | Boiling water for one minute helps to purify it. | Plants help to purify the air in a room. | In the Bible, people washed to purify themselves before worship. | Scientists purified the salt by evaporating the water. | The tablets purify water from streams.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: purify, purifies, purified (y changes to i before -es and -ed), purifying (keeps y). Nouns: purification, purity. Purifying water by boiling kills germs but does not remove salt or poison.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal, children's) A cat, especially a friendly pet cat: «Here, pussycat!» 2) (informal) A gentle, kind person who seems tough but is soft and easy to like: «He looks scary but he's a pussycat really.»
its sense in the lessons: In nursery rhymes and children's stories it is a cosy word for a cat: «The Owl and the Pussycat went to sea» (Edward Lear) and «Pussycat, pussycat, where have you been?» In everyday talk it describes someone softer than they look. Phrases: «a big pussycat», «pussycat, pussycat».
examples from the lessons: The Owl and the Pussycat went to sea in a beautiful pea-green boat. | «Pussycat, pussycat, where have you been?» «I've been to London to visit the Queen.» | Our pussycat sleeps on the radiator. | The big rugby player is a total pussycat with his little sister. | The baby pointed and said «pussycat!» | The guard dog turned out to be a pussycat.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: pussycat, pussycats; also «pussy-cat» or «puss». It is a babyish or cosy word; in school writing use «cat». Short form «puss» is fine (Puss in Boots), but the short form «pussy» also has a rude adult meaning, so say «pussycat», «puss» or «cat».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A question, problem or mystery that is hard to understand or solve: «That riddle is a real puzzler.» 2) A person who enjoys doing puzzles, like crosswords or sudoku.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and olympiad lessons a puzzler is a tricky problem that needs clever thinking; in everyday life it is anything that confuses you; in stories a mystery can be «a puzzler» for the detective. Phrases: «a real puzzler», «a bit of a puzzler», «keen puzzler».
examples from the lessons: Here's a puzzler: what has keys but can't open locks? | Question 10 on the maths test was a real puzzler. | Why the cat kept hiding the socks was a puzzler. | Grandma is a keen puzzler who does the crossword every day. | The missing biscuits were a puzzler until we found crumbs on the dog. | The teacher gives us a Friday puzzler to solve in pairs.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: puzzler, puzzlers. Informal and friendly. Related: puzzle (noun and verb), puzzled (confused), puzzling (confusing). The answer to the keys riddle is «a piano».

meaning for a pupil: 1) To do with fireworks: «a pyrotechnic display». 2) (pyrotechnics, noun) A fireworks show, or the skill of making and setting off fireworks. 3) (figurative) Very brilliant, dazzling and showy, especially in music, speech or skill: «pyrotechnic guitar playing».
its sense in the lessons: In science and safety lessons pyrotechnics explain how chemicals make coloured light and bangs; in everyday life it is a fancy word for a fireworks show; in reviews it praises dazzling skill. Phrases: «pyrotechnic display», «pyrotechnic show», «verbal pyrotechnics».
examples from the lessons: The pyrotechnic display lit up the whole bay. | Pyrotechnic experts set off the fireworks safely from a barge. | Different metals give pyrotechnic colours: copper makes blue, strontium makes red. | The guitarist's pyrotechnic solo amazed the crowd. | Only trained people should handle pyrotechnic devices. | The film ended with pyrotechnics over the castle.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun «pyrotechnics» is usually plural. From Greek «pyr» (fire), as in «pyromaniac» and «pyre». Safety: fireworks are explosives; follow the Firework Code, keep back, never go back to a lit firework.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Often arguing or ready to start a quarrel; easily angry with others: «a quarrelsome neighbour».
its sense in the lessons: In stories it describes grumpy characters who pick fights; in everyday life and PSHE lessons it helps talk about getting along. Phrases: «a quarrelsome child», «in a quarrelsome mood».
examples from the lessons: The two quarrelsome brothers argued all the way to the beach. | The quarrelsome goose chased everyone round the farmyard. | When he is tired he gets quarrelsome. | Our neighbour is quarrelsome about where we park. | The quarrelsome kings went to war over a tiny island. | Try not to be quarrelsome; listen first.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Related: quarrel (noun and verb: quarrel, quarrelled, quarrelling in UK; quarreled, quarreling in US). The ending -some means «tending to» (like tiresome, troublesome). Opposite: easy-going, peaceable.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A verse or stanza of a poem with four lines, often with a rhyme pattern like ABAB or AABB.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons on poetry pupils count lines and spot rhyme schemes; many nursery rhymes, hymns and ballads are made of quatrains. Phrases: «write a quatrain», «a rhyming quatrain», «the first quatrain».
examples from the lessons: A quatrain is a stanza with four lines. | «Twinkle, twinkle, little star» starts with a quatrain. | Write a quatrain about the sea with the rhyme scheme AABB. | Each verse of the hymn is a quatrain. | The poem has three quatrains and a couplet at the end. | In the quatrain, lines 1 and 3 rhyme, and so do lines 2 and 4.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: quatrain, quatrains. Pronounced KWOT-rain. Poetry words for line counts: couplet (2), tercet (3), quatrain (4), quintain or cinquain (5). From French «quatre» (four).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A stone or concrete platform along the edge of water in a harbour, where boats stop to load and unload: «The fishing boats tied up at the quay.»
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons quays are part of ports and harbours; in everyday life and stories people walk along the quay to watch boats. Phrases: «on the quay», «along the quay», «quayside».
examples from the lessons: The ferry waited at the quay. | Fishermen unloaded their catch on the quay. | We ate chips on the quay and watched the boats. | Stand back from the edge of the quay. | Old warehouses line the quayside. | The tall ship was moored at the quay for the festival.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Sounds exactly like «key» (KEE) — a homophone; also like «cay» (a small island). Countable: quay, quays. Similar words: wharf, dock, pier, jetty (a pier sticks out into the sea; a quay runs along the shore). Safety: quays have no railings; do not run near the edge.

part of speech: noun (a quest, quests); verb (quest, quests, quested, questing — literary)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A long search or journey to find or get something important: «a quest for the lost treasure». 2) A strong effort to achieve something: «the quest for a cure». 3) (games) A mission or task in a video game or story that the player must complete. 4) (verb, literary) To search for something.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, myths and legends heroes go on quests (King Arthur's knights and the Holy Grail); in games a quest is a mission; in science and news people are on a quest for answers. Phrases: «go on a quest», «the quest for», «a side quest».
examples from the lessons: The knights set out on a quest to find the Holy Grail. | Frodo's quest was to destroy the ring. | Scientists continue their quest for a cure for cancer. | I finished three side quests in the game today. | Our quest to find the lost remote took all afternoon. | Her quest for a gold medal took years of training.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: quest, quests. Use «a quest for» + thing or «a quest to» + verb. The verb is old-fashioned and literary. Related to «question» and «request» (all from Latin «quaerere», to seek).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Being fast in movement: «the quickness of a cat». 2) Being clever and fast in thinking or understanding: «quickness of mind». 3) Being easily stirred, especially to anger: «quickness of temper».
its sense in the lessons: In PE and stories it describes speed and reflexes; in school, quickness of mind helps with mental maths; in describing people, «quickness of temper» means getting angry fast. Phrases: «quickness of mind», «quickness of hand», «with great quickness».
examples from the lessons: The goalkeeper's quickness saved the penalty. | Her quickness at mental maths amazed the class. | The magician's quickness of hand fooled us all. | A cheetah's quickness helps it catch prey. | His quickness of temper got him into trouble. | Quickness is useful, but checking your answers matters too.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: no plural. Related: quick, quickly, quicken. In everyday talk «speed» is more common; «quickness» often describes a person's skill. «The quick and the dead» is an old Bible phrase where «quick» means «living».

part of speech: verb (quieten, quietens, quietened, quietening; often «quieten down») — UK, Ireland, Australia, NZ
meaning for a pupil: 1) To become quiet or calmer: «The class quietened when the head came in.» 2) To make someone or something quiet or calm: «She quietened the crying baby.» 3) To make worries or fears less strong: «quieten your fears».
its sense in the lessons: In school and everyday life teachers ask a class to quieten down; in stories, quietening shows calm after noise or panic. Phrases: «quieten down», «quieten a crowd», «things quietened».
examples from the lessons: Quieten down, everyone, the film is starting. | The wind quietened after midnight. | Dad sang to quieten the baby. | The streets quietened when the shops closed. | Taking deep breaths can quieten your worries. | The crowd quietened as the singer walked on stage.
note for the reader of a maths problem: British and Commonwealth word; American English usually says «quiet down» (quiet as a verb). Spelling: quieten, quietened (no double n). Do not confuse «quiet» (no noise) with «quite» (fairly).

part of speech: noun (a quince, quinces; quince — the fruit as food)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A hard, yellow fruit shaped like a big pear, very sour and hard when raw but sweet and pink when cooked; used for jam, jelly and paste. 2) The small tree that grows this fruit. 3) (ornamental quince, Japanese quince) A garden bush with bright red or pink flowers in spring.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday cooking quinces are made into jelly or membrillo (quince paste, eaten with cheese). In poetry, «The Owl and the Pussycat» «dined on mince, and slices of quince». Phrases: «quince jelly», «quince jam», «quince tree».
examples from the lessons: The Owl and the Pussycat dined on mince and slices of quince. | Gran makes quince jelly every autumn. | A raw quince is too hard and sour to eat. | Cooked quince turns a lovely pink colour. | Our quince tree is heavy with yellow fruit. | The word «marmalade» comes from a Portuguese word for quince jam.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable for the fruit or tree (quinces); uncountable as food. Quinces smell sweet even when raw. «Marmalade» was first made from quince (Portuguese «marmelo»), not oranges.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A strange or unusual habit or way of behaving: «One of her quirks is wearing odd socks.» 2) A strange thing that happens by chance: «By a quirk of fate, they were born on the same day.» 3) A sudden twist or turn, like a quick curl in handwriting.
its sense in the lessons: In stories quirks make characters memorable and real; in everyday life it is a kind word for odd habits; in science and history «a quirk of history» explains odd facts. Phrases: «a quirk of fate», «a quirk of history», «little quirks».
examples from the lessons: One of Dad's quirks is eating cereal for dinner. | By a quirk of fate, the two lost friends sat next to each other on the train. | The house has some quirks, like a door that opens by itself. | Every pet has its little quirks. | English spelling is full of quirks. | A quirk of the rules let the team play an extra match.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: quirk, quirks. Adjective: quirky (odd in a fun way). A quirk is usually harmless and a bit charming, not a bad fault.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A track or ground where races are held, especially horse races, with stands for people to watch: «Aintree racecourse». 2) Any course for racing, such as for cars or runners.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life in the UK, Ireland, Australia and New Zealand racecourses host horse racing like the Grand National or the Melbourne Cup. In maths, a racecourse can give lap and distance problems. Phrases: «at the racecourse», «racecourse track», «a day at the racecourse».
examples from the lessons: Thousands of people went to the racecourse for the Grand National. | The horses galloped round the racecourse. | Flemington racecourse in Melbourne hosts the Melbourne Cup. | The school fun run was held on the old racecourse. | The racecourse is a mile and a half around. | The car park at the racecourse was full.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. American English often says «racetrack» or «track». Gambling on races is for adults only. Maths: if a racecourse is 2 km round, 3 laps = 6 km.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person, animal or machine that takes part in races: «a racing car driver is a racer». 2) A car, bike, boat or horse built or trained for racing: «a racer bike». 3) (US) A kind of fast snake, like the black racer.
its sense in the lessons: In sport and stories it names competitors in races; in everyday life it can be a toy or a bike. In science, some animals are named racers because they move fast. Phrases: «a fast racer», «a cycle racer», «racer bike», «go-kart racer».
examples from the lessons: The racers lined up at the starting line. | Lewis Hamilton is a famous racing car racer. | My brother got a red racer bike for his birthday. | The snail was the slowest racer in our garden race. | The black racer is a fast, harmless snake in North America. | Each racer must wear a helmet.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: racer, racers. Related: race, racing. Careful: «racer» (someone who races) has nothing to do with «racist» or «race» meaning a group of people.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To do with race, the old idea of grouping people by skin colour, family background or where their ancestors came from: «racial equality», «racial prejudice». 2) Happening between groups that people see as different races: «racial tension», «racial discrimination».
its sense in the lessons: In history and citizenship lessons it appears in topics like the civil rights movement, apartheid and laws against discrimination. Scientists now say all humans are one species and «races» are not clear biological groups, but racism and its harm are real. Phrases: «racial equality», «racial discrimination», «racial justice», «racial abuse».
examples from the lessons: Martin Luther King Jr worked for racial equality in the USA. | Racial discrimination is against the law in the UK. | Apartheid in South Africa was a system of racial separation. | Racial abuse at football matches is reported to the police. | Our school celebrates racial and cultural diversity. | Rosa Parks protested against racial segregation on buses.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb: racially (racially mixed, racially abused). Related: race, racism, racist. Treating people worse because of their race is unfair and, in many countries, illegal; tell a trusted adult if it happens. Not connected to «racing».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Spreading out from a centre, like the spokes of a wheel or the rays of the sun: «a radial pattern». 2) (maths) To do with the radius of a circle. 3) (science, body) To do with the radius bone in the forearm: «the radial artery», used to feel your pulse at the wrist. 4) (noun) A radial tyre, a kind of car tyre; or a road leading out from a city centre.
its sense in the lessons: In maths it links to the radius and circles; in science and PE you find your radial pulse at the wrist; in nature, starfish and flowers have radial symmetry. Phrases: «radial symmetry», «radial pulse», «radial roads», «radial tyres».
examples from the lessons: A starfish has radial symmetry, with arms spreading from the middle. | Find your radial pulse on the thumb side of your wrist. | The city's radial roads lead out like spokes. | A spider's web has radial threads and spiral threads. | Daisies show a radial pattern of petals. | The mechanic fitted four new radials to the car.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Related: radius (plural radii), radiate, radiation. Maths: the radius goes from the centre of a circle to its edge; the diameter is twice the radius. Radial symmetry means you can cut it in many ways through the centre and get matching parts.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) A kind of carbon, called carbon-14, that is slightly radioactive and slowly breaks down over thousands of years. 2) (adjective) Using carbon-14 to find out how old something is: «radiocarbon dating».
its sense in the lessons: In science and history lessons radiocarbon dating tells how old once-living things are (wood, bone, cloth), up to about 50,000 years. All living things take in carbon-14; after they die it slowly disappears, so scientists measure what is left. Phrases: «radiocarbon dating», «radiocarbon age», «radiocarbon test».
examples from the lessons: Radiocarbon dating showed the wooden boat was 3,000 years old. | Scientists used radiocarbon to date the bones in the cave. | Radiocarbon dating only works on things that were once alive. | The Shroud of Turin was tested by radiocarbon dating in 1988. | You cannot use radiocarbon to date dinosaur bones; they are far too old. | Half of the radiocarbon in a sample breaks down in about 5,730 years.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Also called carbon-14 or C-14. Maths: its half-life is about 5,730 years, so after 5,730 years half is left, after 11,460 years a quarter is left. Myth: radiocarbon dates dinosaurs — false; dinosaurs are tens of millions of years old, so other methods are used on rocks.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (medicine, science) To do with X-ray pictures and other images of the inside of the body or objects: «a radiographic image of the knee». 2) Made using X-rays: «a radiographic test of a metal pipe».
its sense in the lessons: In health and science lessons it is the hospital word for X-ray pictures; radiographers take them. Engineers also use radiographic tests to find cracks in metal. Phrases: «radiographic image», «radiographic examination», «radiographic evidence».
examples from the lessons: The radiographic image showed a small crack in the bone. | The dentist took radiographic pictures of my teeth. | Engineers did a radiographic check of the bridge's welds. | Radiographic evidence showed the statue had a hidden metal rod inside. | A radiographer is trained to take radiographic images safely. | The vet looked at radiographic pictures of the dog's leg.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Related: radiograph (an X-ray picture), radiography, radiographer (the person who takes X-rays), radiologist (the doctor who reads them). X-rays are used only when needed, and staff wear protection because too many X-rays can harm the body.

part of speech: noun (abbreviation: RAF — the Royal Air Force)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (abbreviation) The RAF: the Royal Air Force, the air force of the United Kingdom, founded in 1918. 2) (Australia, NZ, Canada) RAAF, RNZAF and RCAF are the Royal Australian, New Zealand and Canadian Air Forces, named in the same way.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons the RAF is famous for the Battle of Britain in 1940; in everyday life it appears at air shows (the Red Arrows) and in careers talks. Phrases: «in the RAF», «RAF pilot», «RAF base», «the Red Arrows of the RAF».
examples from the lessons: My great-grandad flew Spitfires in the RAF. | The RAF won the Battle of Britain in 1940. | The Red Arrows are the RAF's display team. | There is an RAF base near our town. | She joined the RAF as an engineer. | Winston Churchill praised the RAF pilots as «the few».
note for the reader of a maths problem: Written in capitals: RAF. Said as letters (R-A-F) or sometimes as one word «raff». Use «the»: the RAF. It is an abbreviation, not an ordinary word. Founded on 1 April 1918, it is the oldest independent air force in the world.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Old and torn, with holes and loose threads: «a ragged coat». 2) Wearing old, torn clothes: «a ragged child». 3) Rough and uneven at the edges, not smooth: «a ragged coastline», «ragged clouds». 4) Not well together; untidy, uneven or tired: «a ragged performance», «ragged breathing». 5) (verb form) Past of «rag» (to tease): «They ragged him about his hat.» (UK, old-fashioned)
its sense in the lessons: In stories ragged clothes show poverty or a long hard journey (Victorian street children); in geography a ragged coastline has many bays and points; in sport a ragged team plays badly. Phrases: «ragged clothes», «ragged edges», «run ragged» (made very tired).
examples from the lessons: The poor boy in the story wore a ragged coat. | Tear the paper slowly or the edge will be ragged. | Norway has a ragged coastline full of fjords. | The band gave a ragged performance after no practice. | Looking after twins runs Mum ragged. | His breathing was ragged after the race. | The scarecrow's ragged hat flapped in the wind.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced RAG-id (two syllables) as an adjective; but as the past of the verb «rag» it is one syllable, RAGD. «Run someone ragged» means make them very tired. Related: rag, rags. Not the same as «rugged» (rough and strong).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who owns or runs a ranch, a very large farm, mainly in the USA, Canada and Australia, where cattle, sheep or horses are raised. 2) (US) A ranch-style house: a long, low house on one floor.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons ranchers raise animals on wide grasslands; in stories and westerns ranchers ride horses and drive cattle. Phrases: «cattle rancher», «sheep rancher», «a rancher in Texas».
examples from the lessons: The rancher rode out to check his cattle. | Ranchers in Montana raise cattle on huge open lands. | In Australia a rancher is usually called a grazier or station owner. | The rancher fixed the fence before winter. | Ranchers need water for their animals in dry summers. | My uncle is a rancher in Alberta.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: rancher, ranchers. Related: ranch. In Australia people say «station» for a big farm and «grazier» or «pastoralist» for the farmer; in the UK and Ireland, «farmer» is used.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Smelling or tasting bad because it has gone off, especially fat, oil, butter, nuts or milk: «rancid butter». 2) (informal) Horrible or very unpleasant: «That joke was rancid.»
its sense in the lessons: In science and food lessons rancid fat shows food spoiling as fats react with air; in everyday life it tells you not to eat something; kids also use it as slang for «disgusting». Phrases: «go rancid», «turn rancid», «a rancid smell».
examples from the lessons: The butter had gone rancid in the heat. | Old cooking oil smells rancid. | Nuts can turn rancid if you keep them too long. | Throw that rancid milk away. | Ugh, your PE bag smells rancid! | Keep oil in a cool, dark place so it does not go rancid.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Use «go/turn rancid». Science: fats go rancid when they react with oxygen in the air (oxidation) or with water and germs; cold, dark and airtight storage slows it. Eating rancid food can make you feel ill.

part of speech: noun (a ranking, rankings); adjective (ranking); verb form (rank, ranks, ranked, ranking)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A position in a list that shows how good or important someone or something is compared with others: «a world ranking of 5». 2) (rankings) The list itself: «the tennis rankings», «school league rankings». 3) (adjective) Having a high or the highest position: «the ranking officer». 4) (verb) Putting things in order: «Ranking your favourite foods is fun.»
its sense in the lessons: In maths and data lessons ranking means putting items in order (1st, 2nd, 3rd) by size or score; in sport and news rankings compare players, teams and schools. Phrases: «world ranking», «top ranking», «ranking list», «ranking order».
examples from the lessons: She is ranked number one in the world rankings. | Ranking the planets by size, Jupiter comes first. | Our team rose in the league rankings after three wins. | The ranking officer gave the orders. | We did a ranking of our favourite books from 1 to 10. | Websites appear in a ranking when you search online.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: ranking, rankings. Maths: ranking puts data in order; a tie can share a ranking (joint 2nd). Ranking from smallest to largest is «ascending order»; largest to smallest is «descending order». Rank 1 is the top, so a lower rank number means a better place.

part of speech: adjective; verb form (rasp, rasps, rasped, rasping)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Harsh, rough and scratchy in sound: «a rasping voice», «a rasping cough». 2) (verb) Making a harsh, scraping sound, or rubbing with a rough tool: «rasping the wood smooth».
its sense in the lessons: In stories it describes rough voices of old men, villains, or someone ill; in science it describes sounds of friction; in design and technology a rasp is a rough file for wood. Phrases: «a rasping voice», «a rasping breath», «a rasping sound».
examples from the lessons: The old pirate spoke in a rasping voice. | I could hear a rasping cough from the next room. | The door opened with a rasping creak. | The carpenter was rasping the edges of the wood. | The cat's rough tongue made a rasping sound on my hand. | After shouting at the match, his voice was rasping.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Related: rasp (noun: a coarse file; verb: to scrape), raspy (informal adjective). Similar words: hoarse, croaky, grating. Rasping is not about raspberries.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal, US) A rattlesnake: a poisonous snake in the Americas that shakes the rattle on its tail to warn you. 2) Something that rattles, like a baby's rattle or a noisy old car or train. 3) (old, Australia/UK slang) A train, especially an old rattling one. 4) (informal, old) An excellent or very lively thing: «a rattler of a story».
its sense in the lessons: In nature and safety lessons in the USA and Canada rattlers warn with a buzzing tail; stay back. In stories and westerns rattlers hide in rocks. Phrases: «a western diamondback rattler», «watch out for rattlers».
examples from the lessons: The hiker froze when she heard the rattler's buzz. | Rattlers live in deserts and dry hills in the USA. | If you hear a rattler, back away slowly. | The old bus was a real rattler on the bumpy road. | Grandpa called the steam train «the old rattler». | A rattler shakes its tail to say «Keep away!»
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: rattler, rattlers. Informal; the proper name is rattlesnake. Safety: rattlesnake bites need hospital help at once; call 911 and keep the person still. Rattlesnakes live only in the Americas, not in the UK, Ireland, Australia or New Zealand.

part of speech: verb (ravage, ravages, ravaged, ravaging); noun (the ravages of — plural)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To damage or destroy something badly: «The storm ravaged the coast.» 2) (the ravages of) The very bad effects of something over time: «the ravages of war», «the ravages of time».
its sense in the lessons: In history and geography lessons wars, fires, floods, diseases and pests ravage lands; in stories it shows terrible destruction. Phrases: «ravaged by war», «ravaged by fire», «the ravages of time».
examples from the lessons: Bushfires ravaged huge areas of Australia. | The town was ravaged by war. | Locusts ravaged the farmers' crops. | The old castle shows the ravages of time. | A terrible disease ravaged Europe in the 1300s. | The hurricane ravaged the islands.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The noun is almost always plural: «the ravages of». Do not confuse «ravage» (destroy) with «ravish» or «ravenous» (very hungry). Stress: RAV-ij.

part of speech: verb (rave, raves, raved, raving); noun (a rave, raves); adjective (rave — rave reviews)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To talk with great excitement and praise about something you like: «She raved about the film.» 2) To talk wildly or angrily, as if not thinking clearly: «He was raving about aliens.» 3) (noun) A big party with loud electronic dance music, often all night, mainly for adults. 4) (adjective) Full of praise: «The show got rave reviews.» 5) (UK slang, old) «Raving mad» means completely crazy; «a raver» is someone who goes to raves or loves partying.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life people rave about food, games and books; in reviews «rave reviews» means critics loved it; in stories raving characters seem angry or confused. Phrases: «rave about», «rave reviews», «stark raving mad», «go to a rave».
examples from the lessons: Everyone is raving about the new burger place. | The play got rave reviews in the papers. | He was raving about how unfair the referee was. | My older cousin went to a rave and danced till morning. | Mum raved about the view from the top of the hill. | The storm made the sea rave against the rocks. | «Stark raving mad» is an old way of saying completely crazy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun (a rave, raves). «Rave about» or «rave over» = praise loudly. Raves are adult events; they are often noisy and late at night. Do not confuse with «raven» (a large black bird).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A deep, narrow valley with steep sides, usually cut by a stream or river over a long time.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons ravines show erosion by water; in stories heroes cross ravines on rope bridges or fall into them. Phrases: «a deep ravine», «the bottom of the ravine», «cross the ravine».
examples from the lessons: A rope bridge crossed the deep ravine. | The stream has cut a ravine through the rock over thousands of years. | The goat climbed down the side of the ravine. | Stay on the path; the ravine edge is dangerous. | In the story, the dragon lived at the bottom of a ravine. | Ferns grew in the damp shade of the ravine.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: ravine, ravines. Pronounced ruh-VEEN. Size order of valleys: gully (small), ravine (bigger), gorge or canyon (very large and deep). Not related to «raven» or «ravenous».

meaning for a pupil: 1) To make something work or become active again after it was stopped or switched off: «reactivate your account». 2) (science) To start a chemical, a volcano, a virus or a process working again.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday computing you reactivate accounts or alarms; in science volcanoes and germs can reactivate; in health, the chickenpox virus can reactivate later as shingles. Phrases: «reactivate an account», «reactivate the alarm», «reactivated volcano».
examples from the lessons: Mum reactivated the burglar alarm before we left. | You must reactivate your library card every year. | Scientists think the volcano could reactivate. | The chickenpox virus can reactivate years later as shingles. | Click the link to reactivate your account. | Adding water reactivated the dried yeast.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Prefix re- means «again»: re + activate. Noun: reactivation. Online safety: be careful of scam emails asking you to «reactivate your account» with a link; check with an adult.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science, chemistry) How easily and how strongly a substance takes part in chemical reactions: «Potassium has high reactivity.» 2) (science, psychology) How strongly a person or body reacts to something, such as stress or an allergy trigger.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons metals are put in a «reactivity series» from most reactive (potassium, sodium) to least (gold, platinum); this explains why gold does not rust and why sodium fizzes in water. Phrases: «reactivity series», «high reactivity», «low reactivity».
examples from the lessons: Potassium is at the top of the reactivity series. | Gold has very low reactivity, so it stays shiny for centuries. | We tested the reactivity of metals in acid. | Sodium's high reactivity makes it fizz and dart about on water. | Iron's reactivity with water and air makes it rust. | Some children have high reactivity to pollen.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Adjective: reactive; opposite: unreactive (inert). A handy reactivity order: potassium, sodium, calcium, magnesium, aluminium, (carbon), zinc, iron, (hydrogen), copper, silver, gold. Safety: very reactive metals are handled only by teachers.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To put things back into a straight line or the correct position: «realign the wheels of a car». 2) To change your plans, ideas or friendships to fit a new situation: «The country realigned itself with its neighbours.»
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and technology it is used for car wheels, teeth with braces and pictures on a page; in history and news it describes countries and groups changing sides. Phrases: «realign the wheels», «realign with», «realign priorities».
examples from the lessons: The mechanic realigned the car's wheels. | Braces slowly realign your teeth. | We realigned the chairs into neat rows. | After the election some parties realigned with each other. | The team realigned its goals after losing the first game. | Realign the ruler with the edge of the paper.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Prefix re- means «again». Noun: realignment. Spelling: re-align (the g is silent: ree-uh-LINE).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Seeing and accepting things as they really are and dealing with them sensibly: «a sense of realism». 2) (art, literature) Showing people and things as they really are, in a true-to-life way: «The painting's realism is amazing.» 3) (art history) Realism: an art and writing movement of the 1800s that showed ordinary everyday life honestly.
its sense in the lessons: In art and English lessons realism means life-like pictures and believable stories; in everyday life it means being sensible about what can be done. In video games, realism means graphics that look real. Phrases: «a sense of realism», «with great realism», «realism and hope».
examples from the lessons: The realism of the painting made the fruit look real enough to eat. | The film's realism made the war scenes hard to watch. | Some realism is needed: we can't build a pool by Friday. | The game's realism is amazing; the rain looks real. | Writers like Dickens used realism to show the lives of the poor. | Hope is good, but mix it with realism.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Related: real, realist, realistic, reality. Opposites in art: fantasy, abstract art. Being realistic is different from being negative; it means seeing the facts clearly.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To cut and gather a crop, like wheat, from a field: «Farmers reap the corn in late summer.» 2) To get something good (or bad) as a result of what you have done: «reap the rewards», «reap the benefits». 3) (Bible) «You reap what you sow»: what you do now decides what will happen to you later (Galatians 6:7).
its sense in the lessons: In history and farming lessons reaping is harvest work, once done with sickles and scythes; in everyday life and morals people «reap the rewards» of hard work. In church the harvest festival gives thanks for what is reaped. Phrases: «reap the rewards», «reap the benefits», «reap what you sow», «reap a harvest».
examples from the lessons: In the past, whole families helped reap the wheat by hand. | If you practise every day, you will reap the rewards. | You reap what you sow, so be kind. | The farmers reaped a good harvest this year. | The school reaped the benefits of its new library. | The Grim Reaper is a made-up figure of death carrying a scythe.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: reap, reaped. Related: reaper (a person or machine that reaps; «the Grim Reaper» is a symbol of death in stories). Opposite pair: sow (plant seeds) and reap (harvest). Do not confuse with «rip» or «leap».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Changing the order, position or plan of things: «a rearrangement of the furniture». 2) A changed plan, time or date: «a rearrangement of the match». 3) (music) A new version of a piece of music for different instruments or voices. 4) (maths, science) Putting the parts of a number, formula or molecule in a different order; in maths, a different order of the same items.
its sense in the lessons: In maths lessons rearrangement means changing a formula (rearrange a = b + c into b = a − c) or counting different orders of items. In everyday life it means moving furniture or changing a timetable. Phrases: «a rearrangement of», «furniture rearrangement», «date rearrangement».
examples from the lessons: The classroom rearrangement gave us more space for reading. | After the rearrangement, the match is on Tuesday. | The band played a rock rearrangement of an old carol. | «Listen» and «silent» are rearrangements of the same letters. | Rearrangement of the formula helps us find the missing value. | There are six rearrangements of the letters A, B and C.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable or uncountable. Verb: rearrange. Maths: n different items have n! (n factorial) orders: 3 items → 3 × 2 × 1 = 6; letters that rearrange into a new word make an anagram. Spelling: re-arrange-ment (double r).

part of speech: verb (recapture, recaptures, recaptured, recapturing); noun (recapture, a recapture)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To catch again a person or animal that escaped: «The zookeepers recaptured the lion.» 2) To take back a place that an enemy had taken: «The army recaptured the town.» 3) To bring back a feeling or memory, or to show it again: «The film recaptures the magic of childhood.» 4) (noun) The act of catching or taking something again.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons armies recapture forts and cities; in news and stories prisoners or animals are recaptured; in art and writing, works recapture moods of the past. Phrases: «recapture the town», «recapture the magic», «recapture the lead».
examples from the lessons: The escaped parrot was recaptured in the park. | The army recaptured the fort after a long siege. | Police recaptured the prisoner the next day. | We went back to the beach to recapture that summer feeling. | The team recaptured the lead in the last minute. | Ukraine recaptured many towns that had been occupied.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Prefix re- means «again». Regular verb: recapture, recaptured. Also used in sport for taking back a lead or a title.

part of speech: adjective; verb form (recline, reclines, reclined, reclining)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Leaning or lying back in a relaxed way: «a reclining figure». 2) (of seats) Able to tip back: «a reclining chair», «reclining seats on a plane». 3) (verb) Lying back or leaning back.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life reclining seats are on coaches, planes and sofas; in art lessons a «reclining figure» is a statue or painting of a person lying back (Henry Moore's sculptures). Phrases: «reclining seat», «reclining chair», «a reclining figure», «reclining Buddha».
examples from the lessons: Grandad fell asleep in his reclining chair. | The coach had reclining seats for the long trip. | Henry Moore made big statues of reclining figures. | The cat was reclining on the warm windowsill. | In Thailand there is a huge reclining Buddha statue. | Please put your reclining seat upright for landing.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: recline; noun: recliner (a chair that leans back). Politeness: check behind you before reclining your seat on a plane or coach. Not the same as «declining» (going down, saying no).

meaning for a pupil: 1) To remember something from the past, often with effort: «I don't recollect his name.» 2) (re-collect, with a hyphen) To collect or gather again: «re-collect the worksheets». 3) (formal) To calm yourself or get your thoughts together: «She paused to recollect herself.»
its sense in the lessons: In stories and history (witness accounts, memoirs) characters recollect events; in everyday life it is a slightly formal way of saying «remember». Phrases: «as far as I can recollect», «recollect seeing», «recollect oneself».
examples from the lessons: I can't recollect where I put my keys. | Grandma recollects the day the war ended. | As far as I can recollect, we met at the zoo. | Do you recollect seeing a red car? | He tried to recollect the words of the poem. | The witness could not recollect the man's face.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: recollection (a memory). Use «recollect + noun» or «recollect + -ing»: recollect meeting him. More formal than «remember». Note: «re-collect» with a hyphen means gather again and has a different stress (ree-col-LECT).

meaning for a pupil: 1) To change something back into what it was before, or into another form again. 2) To change a building or machine back to its old use. 3) To bring someone back to a belief or religion they had left.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and science it means changing units or forms again, for example turning centimetres into metres and then back to check an answer. In everyday life people reconvert a garage back into a room or a file back into its first format. It tells the reader that a change is being undone or repeated. Phrases: «reconvert to», «reconvert into», «reconvert back».
examples from the lessons: We converted 3 metres into centimetres and then reconverted it to check. | Dad wants to reconvert the playroom into a garage. | The old church was reconverted from a shop into a place of worship. | Can you reconvert the photo into the old file type? | The ice melted and the water was frozen again, so it was reconverted into ice. | Some machines can reconvert heat into electricity. | After the war the factory was reconverted to make cars again.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: reconverted, reconverting. «re-» means «again» or «back». In maths, reconverting does not change the amount: 300 cm reconverted is still 3 m. Not a very common word; «convert back» is said more often.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Able to be got back after being lost, deleted or stolen. 2) (of a person or an illness) Able to get better. 3) (money) Able to be paid back or claimed back.
its sense in the lessons: In computing and everyday life it often describes lost files, photos or money: «the file is recoverable» means there is still hope. In stories it tells the reader that the situation is not hopeless. In science and the environment, «recoverable oil» is oil that can be taken out of the ground. Phrases: «fully recoverable», «not recoverable», «recoverable from».
examples from the lessons: Don't panic, the deleted homework is recoverable from the bin folder. | The doctor said the damage to his knee was recoverable. | Only half of the lost money was recoverable. | Is the data on this broken phone recoverable? | The ship sank so deep that it was not recoverable. | The costs of the trip are recoverable if it is cancelled. | Most mistakes in a draft are easily recoverable.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Built from «recover» + «-able» (able to be recovered). Opposite: «unrecoverable» or «irrecoverable». Used about things more than people. It is an adjective, so it comes after «is» or before a noun: «a recoverable file».

meaning for a pupil: 1) To make something again so that it is like it was before. 2) To copy or act out a past event, scene or picture. 3) (less common, pronounced «REK-ree-ate») To relax and enjoy yourself; this sense is usually spelt «re-create» the other way round, so see notes.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons classes recreate old houses, meals or battles to understand the past. In science you recreate an experiment to check that the result was right. In art you can recreate a famous painting. In stories it means bringing back something lost. Phrases: «recreate a scene», «recreate the experiment», «recreate from memory».
examples from the lessons: We recreated a Roman kitchen in the classroom. | Can you recreate the drawing from memory? | Scientists recreated the experiment and got the same result. | The film recreates life in a Victorian school. | I lost my password list and had to recreate it. | Let's recreate the photo we took when we were little. | The museum recreated a dinosaur skeleton from bones and casts.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: recreated. Pronounced «ree-kree-ATE» for «make again». Related noun: «recreation», which usually means fun and free time (pronounced «rek-ree-AY-shun»), not «making again» — a common trap. In science, recreating an experiment is how results are checked.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Made of straight lines. 2) Moving in a straight line. 3) (maths) A rectilinear shape has only straight sides, often with right angles, like an L-shape or a rectangle.
its sense in the lessons: In maths it describes compound shapes made of rectangles, for example «find the area of this rectilinear shape» — you split it into rectangles and add the areas. In science «rectilinear motion» is movement in a straight line. It tells the reader that there are no curves. Phrases: «rectilinear shape», «rectilinear figure», «rectilinear motion».
examples from the lessons: Find the perimeter of the rectilinear shape. | An L-shape is a rectilinear shape. | Split the rectilinear shape into two rectangles. | A circle is not rectilinear because it is curved. | The car moved in rectilinear motion along the straight road. | The new library has a rectilinear design with flat walls and square corners. | Draw a rectilinear shape with six sides.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal and mostly a maths word. Comes from Latin «rectus» (straight) + «linea» (line). Maths problems: to find the area, split into rectangles and add; for the perimeter, add every side, and work out missing sides by subtracting lengths. It does not mean «rectangle» only.

part of speech: adjective (recumbent); noun (a recumbent, recumbents — a recumbent bicycle)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Lying down, especially on your back or leaning back. 2) A recumbent bicycle or bike is one you ride sitting back in a low seat with your legs in front. 3) (noun) A short name for a recumbent bicycle.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and old books it describes someone lying down to rest. In sport and everyday life it names a special low bike or exercise bike with a back rest. In art and history it describes statues of people lying down on tombs. Phrases: «recumbent position», «recumbent bike», «recumbent figure».
examples from the lessons: The cat lay recumbent in the sun. | My grandad uses a recumbent exercise bike at the gym. | The statue shows a recumbent knight on top of his tomb. | She rides a recumbent to school and it looks very low. | The patient stayed in a recumbent position after the operation. | A recumbent bike is easier on your back. | The lions were recumbent under the tree.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal word; in everyday speech say «lying down». Not the same as «incumbent» (the person now holding a job). Pronounced «ri-KUM-bent».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Getting better and stronger after an illness, injury or tiring time. 2) Getting back something lost, such as energy or money (less common).
its sense in the lessons: In health lessons it is the time after illness or an operation when the body heals. In sport it is rest after hard training. In stories it tells the reader that a character needs time to heal. Phrases: «a period of recuperation», «time for recuperation», «rest and recuperation» (often shortened to R and R).
