examples from the lessons: After the operation she needed six weeks of recuperation. | Sleep helps the body's recuperation. | The footballer went home for recuperation. | Grandma's recuperation was slow but steady. | A week at the seaside was perfect for recuperation. | Muscles need recuperation after hard exercise. | The soldiers were sent away for rest and recuperation.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «a long recuperation» is possible, but no plural. Verb: «recuperate» (recuperated). Formal; in everyday speech people say «getting better» or «recovery».

meaning for a pupil: 1) To become red or redder. 2) (of a person's face) To blush because you are embarrassed, shy or angry. 3) To make something red.
its sense in the lessons: In stories it often tells the reader that a character is embarrassed or angry: «his face reddened». In science and nature it describes leaves in autumn, a sky at sunset, or skin that is sunburnt or sore. Phrases: «redden with anger», «redden with embarrassment», «the sky reddened».
examples from the lessons: Her cheeks reddened when the teacher read out her poem. | The leaves redden in autumn. | His face reddened with anger. | The sky reddened as the sun went down. | My nose reddens in the cold. | The rash began to redden and itch, so we called the doctor. | Tomatoes redden as they ripen.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: reddened, reddening; note the double «d». A rash or skin that keeps reddening and swelling can need a doctor. «Blush» is a near synonym for faces.

part of speech: verb, past form of «redeem» (redeem, redeems, redeemed, redeeming); adjective (redeemed)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Exchanged a voucher, coupon or points for something. 2) Made up for a bad thing or a mistake, so that someone or something seems good again. 3) (church) Christians believe that Jesus redeemed people, meaning he saved them from sin and its punishment. 4) Paid back money, or got back something left with a pawnbroker or lender.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life you redeem vouchers, tickets and loyalty points. In stories a character who is «redeemed» does something good that makes up for past wrongs — often the turning point of the story. In church and the Bible «the redeemed» are people Christians believe are saved by God. Phrases: «redeemed himself», «redeemed a voucher», «redeemed by».
examples from the lessons: I redeemed my book token at the shop. | He missed a penalty but redeemed himself with a goal later. | Christians believe that Jesus redeemed the world. | The coupon can be redeemed for a free drink. | The film's great ending redeemed the boring start. | She redeemed her grandad's watch from the pawnshop. | The villain was redeemed when he saved the children.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past form and past participle of «redeem». Noun: «redemption». «Redeem yourself» means to make up for a mistake. A coupon that «cannot be redeemed for cash» means you cannot swap it for money.

part of speech: verb (redeposit, redeposits, redeposited, redepositing); noun (a redeposit, redeposits)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To put money back into a bank or account. 2) (science) To drop or lay down material, like sand or mud, again in a new place. 3) (noun) Money or material put down again.
its sense in the lessons: In money lessons it means paying money back in after taking it out. In geography and science, rivers and the sea pick up sand and stones and redeposit them somewhere else, building beaches and deltas. Phrases: «redeposit the money», «redeposit sediment».
examples from the lessons: I took out ten pounds and then redeposited it. | The river picks up mud and redeposits it at the bend. | Waves redeposit sand further along the beach. | Mum redeposited the cheque after the bank lost it. | The wind redeposited the dust on the windowsill. | Glaciers carried rocks and redeposited them far away.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: redeposited. «re-» means «again». In maths problems, redepositing money adds it back: if you had 50 dollars, took out 20 and redeposited 20, you have 50 again. A rare word; «put back in» is more common.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person with red or orange-red hair. 2) The name of some birds or animals with red heads, such as the redhead duck in North America.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and stories it describes how someone looks. It is mostly friendly, but teasing people about red hair (calling them «ginger» meanly in the UK) can be bullying. In science, red hair comes from genes passed down from parents. Phrases: «a natural redhead», «a fiery redhead» (a stereotype).
examples from the lessons: My cousin is a redhead with lots of freckles. | Anne of Green Gables is a famous redhead in books. | Redheads can get sunburnt easily, so they need sun cream. | The baby was born a redhead like her dad. | Both of my brothers are redheads. | A redhead duck was swimming on the pond.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a redhead, two redheads. Written as one word. Myth: redheads do not have «fiery tempers» — hair colour does not decide your temper. In the UK «ginger» is common and can be used kindly or unkindly.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Finding something again that had been lost, forgotten or hidden. 2) Enjoying or noticing something again after a long time, such as a hobby or a writer.
its sense in the lessons: In history and science it tells how lost cities, animals or old ideas were found again, like an animal thought extinct being seen again. In everyday life it can mean finding an old toy or hobby again. Phrases: «the rediscovery of», «a rediscovery of».
examples from the lessons: The rediscovery of the lost city made world news. | Scientists were thrilled by the rediscovery of a frog thought to be extinct. | Clearing the attic led to the rediscovery of my old teddy. | Mendel's ideas about genes were forgotten until their rediscovery in 1900. | Her summer was a rediscovery of reading. | The rediscovery of the shipwreck helped historians.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: rediscoveries (y changes to ies). Verb: «rediscover». «re-» means «again»: it is only a rediscovery if someone knew about it before.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To make an effort, a feeling or an action much stronger or greater. 2) (in the card game bridge) To double again a bid that has already been doubled.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and news it shows people trying even harder: «the rescuers redoubled their efforts». In school a teacher might say to redouble your effort before a test. It does not usually mean exactly «times two» — it means «a lot more». Phrases: «redouble your efforts», «redoubled their search».
examples from the lessons: The team redoubled their efforts in the second half. | After the storm, the rescuers redoubled their search. | The rain redoubled and we ran for shelter. | The teacher told us to redouble our practice before the concert. | Her fear redoubled when the lights went out. | Police have redoubled patrols near the school.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: redoubled. Mostly used with «efforts». In maths it is not a number word; do not multiply by 2 or 4 because of it. Pronounced «ree-DUB-ul».

part of speech: verb (redraft, redrafts, redrafted, redrafting); noun (a redraft, redrafts)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To write a piece of writing again, making it better. 2) (noun) A new, improved version of a piece of writing.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons redrafting is a key step in writing: plan, draft, edit, redraft, publish. You fix spelling, add better words, change the order and improve the ending. In adult life laws, letters and plans are redrafted. Phrases: «redraft your story», «a first redraft».
examples from the lessons: Please redraft your story using the teacher's comments. | I redrafted my letter three times. | The redraft is much clearer than the first draft. | We redrafted the class rules together. | When you redraft, check your full stops and capital letters. | The council redrafted its plan after people complained.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: redrafted. Synonyms: revise, rewrite. A draft is a first try; a redraft is a later try. UK spelling «draft»; «draught» is a cold air current or a game piece — a trap.

part of speech: noun (a regent, regents); adjective after a noun (Prince Regent)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who rules a country for a king or queen who is too young, ill or away. 2) (US) A member of a board that runs a university or schools. 3) The Regency was the time in Britain (1811–1820) when the future George IV ruled as Prince Regent.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons it explains who held power when a king was a child, for example Lady Jane Grey's time or young kings in the Middle Ages. In stories and fantasy a regent may be good or may try to steal the throne. Place names like Regent Street and Regent's Park in London come from the Prince Regent. Phrases: «act as regent», «the Prince Regent».
examples from the lessons: The king was only six, so his uncle ruled as regent. | The regent made decisions until the prince grew up. | In the story the wicked regent wanted the crown for himself. | Regent's Park in London is named after the Prince Regent. | Her mother was regent while she was a baby queen. | A board of regents runs the state university.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: regents. Capital letter when it is a title: Prince Regent. A regent is not the real monarch; the power is borrowed.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A set plan of diet, exercise, medicine or care that someone follows to stay healthy or get better. 2) (formal) A strict system of rules or routine.
its sense in the lessons: In health lessons and doctors' talk it names a plan like «take this tablet twice a day for a week». In sport it is a training plan. It tells the reader that something is done regularly and carefully. Phrases: «a strict regimen», «a training regimen», «a medicine regimen», «stick to a regimen».
examples from the lessons: The doctor gave Grandad a new medicine regimen. | The swimmer followed a strict training regimen. | My skin care regimen is just soap and water. | The puppy has a feeding regimen of three meals a day. | It is important to finish the whole antibiotics regimen. | Her daily regimen includes a walk and stretches.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal word. Do not confuse with «regiment» (a group of soldiers) or «regime» (a government or system of rule, often strict). Pronounced «REJ-i-men». Always follow a medicine regimen exactly as the doctor says.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Going back to an earlier, worse or less developed state. 2) (maths, statistics) A way of finding the line or rule that best fits data, to see how one thing changes with another. 3) (psychology) When a person, often a child, starts acting younger than their age, for example after a shock. 4) (computing) A bug where something that used to work stops working.
its sense in the lessons: In science and maths for older pupils «regression line» or «line of best fit» shows the trend on a scatter graph. In everyday life and health it can describe an illness coming back or a child going back to babyish habits, like a toddler wetting the bed again when a new baby arrives. Phrases: «regression to», «linear regression», «a regression in».
examples from the lessons: After the new baby came, my little brother showed some regression and wanted a bottle again. | The doctor was worried about a regression in her health. | We drew a regression line through the points on the graph. | The new update caused a regression, and the game crashed again. | Scientists used regression to see how height changes with age. | Sleep regression is when a baby suddenly sleeps badly again.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable in the technical senses. Verb: «regress». Opposite: «progression» or «progress». In maths, a regression line is a best guess of the trend, not an exact rule; points do not all sit on it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To make something stronger, especially by adding material or support. 2) To make an idea, feeling or habit stronger. 3) To send more soldiers, police or helpers to make a group stronger. 4) (learning) To repeat or reward something so that it is learnt better.
its sense in the lessons: In science and design technology, concrete is reinforced with steel rods, and paper bridges with folded strips. In school, practice reinforces learning and praise reinforces good behaviour. In history and stories armies are reinforced. Phrases: «reinforced concrete», «reinforce the message», «reinforce a lesson», «reinforce good behaviour».
examples from the lessons: The builders reinforced the wall with steel bars. | Doing practice questions reinforces what you learnt. | Fold the card to reinforce the bridge. | Praise reinforces kind behaviour. | More firefighters arrived to reinforce the team. | The photo reinforced the idea that the castle was haunted. | Reinforced glass is hard to break.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: reinforced. Noun: «reinforcement» and «reinforcements» (extra soldiers). Pronounced «ree-in-FORCE». In science, a reinforced structure can hold a bigger load before it breaks.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To finally agree to something after first saying no; to become less strict. 2) (of weather, pain or pressure) To become less strong.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and family life it tells the reader that a parent, teacher or ruler changed their mind and gave in: «Mum finally relented and let us stay up». In weather reports the rain or wind relents. Phrases: «finally relented», «refused to relent», «the rain relented».
examples from the lessons: Dad said no at first, but then he relented and bought the ice cream. | The teacher relented and gave us five more minutes. | The storm did not relent all night. | The king refused to relent and the prisoner stayed in jail. | When the heat relented, we went outside. | She begged until her big sister relented.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: relented. Adjective: «relentless» means never stopping or giving up — the opposite feeling. Not the same as «lent» or «Lent».

part of speech: verb (reload, reloads, reloaded, reloading); noun (a reload, reloads)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To load something again, such as a gun, a lorry or a dishwasher. 2) (computing) To open a web page or program again so that it shows the newest version; also called refresh. 3) To put more money or credit on a card again.
its sense in the lessons: In computing and everyday life you reload a page that is stuck or slow. In games characters reload weapons. In everyday life you reload a travel card or a printer with paper. Phrases: «reload the page», «reload a card», «hit reload».
examples from the lessons: The page froze, so I reloaded it. | Click reload to see the new scores. | The lorry was reloaded with boxes. | Mum reloaded my bus card with ten dollars. | In the game you have to reload before the next level. | Reload the printer with paper, please. | The washing machine was reloaded with towels.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: reloaded. Noun: «a reload». In maths, reloading a card adds money: 5 pounds left + 10 pounds reload = 15 pounds.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Not wanting to do something, so that you do it slowly or unwillingly. 2) (science) How much a material resists a magnetic field (a technical sense).
its sense in the lessons: In stories it shows a character's feelings: «with great reluctance, he handed over the ball». In everyday life it describes not wanting to go to bed, eat vegetables or say sorry. Phrases: «with reluctance», «a reluctance to», «show reluctance».
examples from the lessons: With great reluctance, I turned off the game. | Her reluctance to go to the dentist was obvious. | He agreed, but with some reluctance. | The dog showed reluctance to get into the bath. | There was a reluctance among the players to change the rules. | Despite her reluctance, she joined the choir and loved it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: «reluctant»; adverb: «reluctantly». Followed by «to + verb»: «a reluctance to leave». Opposite: eagerness, willingness.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (old or literary) To tear something into pieces violently. 2) To break a silence or the air with a loud sound. 3) (literary) To cause great sadness or pain to someone's heart.
its sense in the lessons: Mostly found in old stories, poems, the Bible and fantasy books. In the Bible people «rent their clothes», tearing them to show great sorrow. «Heart-rending» means very sad. Phrases: «rend apart», «rend the air», «heart-rending», «rent their clothes».
examples from the lessons: The giant rent the tree in two. | A scream rent the silence. | In the Bible, Jacob rent his clothes when he heard the bad news. | It was a heart-rending story about a lost puppy. | The storm threatened to rend the sails. | The war rent the country apart.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular verb: rend, rent, rent. Trap: «rent» is also the money paid to live in a house — a different word. Today «tear» is used instead of «rend»; «heart-rending» is still common.

part of speech: noun (a rendezvous, rendezvous — plural spelt the same); verb (rendezvous, rendezvouses, rendezvoused, rendezvousing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A meeting at an agreed time and place. 2) The place where people agree to meet. 3) (verb) To meet at an agreed time and place. 4) (space) When two spacecraft meet and line up in space.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, adventures and spy books a rendezvous is a secret meeting place. In everyday life and safety, families agree a rendezvous point in case they get lost at a fair or a fire drill. In science and news it describes spacecraft meeting the space station. Phrases: «rendezvous point», «a secret rendezvous», «rendezvous with».
examples from the lessons: If we get separated, our rendezvous is the big clock. | The spies had a secret rendezvous at midnight. | The fire assembly point is our rendezvous in a drill. | The capsule made a rendezvous with the space station. | We rendezvoused with Grandma at the station. | The boats will rendezvous near the island.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Borrowed from French («present yourselves»). Pronounced «RON-day-voo»; the z and s are silent. Plural spelt the same but the s is said: «RON-day-vooz». Agreeing a meeting point is a good safety habit in crowds.

part of speech: verb (repeal, repeals, repealed, repealing); noun (a repeal, repeals)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (law) To officially end a law so that it no longer counts. 2) (noun) The act of ending a law.
its sense in the lessons: In history and citizenship lessons laws are repealed by a parliament or congress, for example laws that were unfair. In news it tells the reader a rule has been cancelled. Phrases: «repeal a law», «the repeal of».
examples from the lessons: Parliament voted to repeal the old law. | The Corn Laws were repealed in Britain in 1846. | In the USA, Prohibition was ended by the repeal of a law in 1933. | People marched to ask for the unfair tax to be repealed. | The repeal of the rule means you can now ride bikes in the park. | Only lawmakers can repeal a law, not the police.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: repealed. Mostly about laws, not school rules (you «scrap» or «change» those). Not the same as «appeal» (asking for a decision to be changed) or «repel» (push away).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Filling something up again after it has been used or emptied. 2) The new supply that fills it up.
its sense in the lessons: In science and nature it describes water refilling a lake or underground store after rain, or the body replacing lost water. In everyday life shops replenish shelves and you replenish a pencil case. Phrases: «replenishment of stocks», «water replenishment».
examples from the lessons: Rain brings replenishment to the reservoir. | The shop waits for the replenishment of its milk supplies. | After the race, our bodies need replenishment of water and salts. | The ship stopped at the port for replenishment. | Replenishment of the forest takes many years after a fire. | The class store cupboard needs replenishment of glue sticks.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; verb: «replenish». In maths it means adding back: a tank with 20 litres left and 80 litres of replenishment holds 100 litres.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Making an exact copy of something. 2) (science) Doing an experiment again to see whether you get the same result. 3) (biology) The way cells copy their DNA or viruses make copies of themselves.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons replication is how we test that a result is true: if other people repeat the experiment and get the same answer, we trust it more. In biology it explains how cells and viruses copy themselves. Phrases: «replication of results», «DNA replication».
examples from the lessons: We did three replications of the experiment to be sure. | Replication helps scientists check that results are not a fluke. | Before a cell divides, DNA replication makes a copy. | The museum's dinosaur is a replication, not a real fossil. | Viruses spread by replication inside cells. | Without replication, one strange result is not enough.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: «replicate». Noun «replica» means a copy of an object. In maths and science, more replications usually give a more reliable average.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A place where things are stored or kept safe. 2) (computing) A place where files or code are stored, often online; programmers say «repo» for short. 3) A person or book that holds a lot of knowledge.
its sense in the lessons: In computing lessons a code repository stores a project's files and history. In everyday life a museum or library is a repository of objects and books. In stories a wise old person might be «a repository of knowledge». Phrases: «a repository of», «code repository».
examples from the lessons: The library is a repository of old maps. | The programmers keep their code in an online repository. | Grandma is a repository of family stories. | The museum is a repository for ancient coins. | Upload your project to the class repository. | The old cave was a repository for treasure.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: repositories. Formal; everyday words are «store» or «storeroom». «Repo» is short in computing; «repo» also means taking back things bought on credit (US).

part of speech: verb (repost, reposts, reposted, reposting); noun (a repost, reposts)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To post something online again, especially something someone else posted. 2) (noun) A post shared again. 3) To send a letter again.
its sense in the lessons: In online safety and digital lessons pupils learn to think before they repost: reposting a rumour or someone's photo can spread lies or hurt someone. Phrases: «repost a video», «repost without permission».
examples from the lessons: She reposted the funny cat video. | Don't repost photos of your friends without asking them. | The fake news story got thousands of reposts. | He reposted his drawing because nobody saw it the first time. | Check the facts before you repost. | The letter came back, so we reposted it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: reposted. Not the same as «riposte» (a quick clever answer, or a counter-attack in fencing). A repost spreads a message further, so you share responsibility for it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To do with having young or making new living things. 2) To do with copying or reproducing something, such as pictures.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons it is used in «reproductive system» (the body parts that let living things have young) and «reproductive parts of a flower» (stamen, carpel). It is a scientific, neutral word. Phrases: «reproductive system», «reproductive organs», «reproductive cycle».
examples from the lessons: The stamen and carpel are the reproductive parts of a flower. | We learnt about the life cycle and the reproductive system in science. | Frogs have a reproductive cycle that starts with frogspawn. | Bees help the reproductive process of plants by carrying pollen. | Mammals and birds have different reproductive systems. | The reproductive season for many birds is spring.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Built from «reproduce» + «-ive». Noun: «reproduction». A science word used plainly in lessons; there is nothing rude about it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To refuse to accept or support something; to say firmly that it is wrong or not true. 2) (formal, law) To refuse to keep an agreement or pay a debt. 3) (old) To say you will have nothing more to do with someone.
its sense in the lessons: Found in news, history and the stiff exam voice: a leader repudiates a claim or a treaty. In stories it shows strong rejection. Phrases: «repudiate a claim», «repudiate the treaty», «firmly repudiated».
examples from the lessons: The minister repudiated the rumours. | She repudiated the claim that she had cheated. | The country repudiated the treaty and war began. | The company repudiated the deal at the last minute. | The scientist repudiated his old theory when new evidence appeared. | He repudiated any link with the gang.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal (exam voice); simpler words are «reject» or «deny». Regular verb: repudiated. Noun: «repudiation». Pronounced «ri-PEW-dee-ate».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Very unpleasant, making you feel sick or disgusted. 2) (science) Pushing away, as with the force between two like magnetic poles; this sense is rare in school, where «repel» is used.
its sense in the lessons: In stories it describes horrible monsters, smells or behaviour. In everyday life children use it for food or slime they hate. Calling a person repulsive is hurtful. In science «repulsive force» is a push between magnets. Phrases: «a repulsive smell», «utterly repulsive».
examples from the lessons: The bin smelt repulsive after a week in the sun. | The witch had a repulsive laugh. | Bullying is repulsive behaviour. | I find cold rice pudding repulsive. | Like poles of magnets feel a repulsive force. | The troll's cave was full of repulsive slime.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Strong word; «disgusting» is similar. Verb: «repel»; noun: «repulsion». Avoid using it about people's looks — it is unkind.

part of speech: verb (reread, rereads, reread, rereading); noun (a reread, rereads)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To read something again. 2) (noun) A second or later reading of a book.
its sense in the lessons: In reading and English lessons rereading is a strategy: reread a sentence that does not make sense, reread a question before you answer, and reread your own writing to edit it. In maths, rereading the problem helps you find the numbers that matter. Phrases: «reread the question», «reread the text».
examples from the lessons: Always reread the question before you start. | I reread my favourite book every summer. | If a sentence is confusing, reread it slowly. | She reread the letter three times. | Reread your story and check the spelling. | Harry Potter is worth a reread.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular: reread, reread, reread (spelt the same, but the past is said «ree-RED»). Sometimes spelt «re-read» in the UK. A key exam habit: many maths mistakes come from not rereading the question.

part of speech: noun (a rerun, reruns); verb (rerun, reruns, reran, rerunning)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (noun) A TV programme or film shown again. 2) (verb) To run a race, a test or a program again. 3) (noun) Something that happens again in the same way.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life reruns are repeats on TV. In science and computing you rerun an experiment or a program to check it. In sport a race is rerun after a false start. Phrases: «a rerun of», «rerun the race», «rerun the test».
examples from the lessons: The channel is showing reruns of an old cartoon. | The race was rerun after a false start. | Rerun the program and see if the bug is gone. | We reran the experiment and got the same result. | The final was a rerun of last year's match. | I watched a rerun of my favourite show.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular: rerun, reran, rerun, rerunning (double «n»). UK people often say «repeat» for a TV rerun. In science, rerunning checks that a result is reliable.

part of speech: verb (resent, resents, resented, resenting); also the past form of «resend» (re-sent)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To feel angry and hurt about something you think is unfair, often for a long time. 2) To feel bitter towards a person because of what they did or have. 3) (spelling sense, often written «re-sent») Sent again, as the past of «resend».
its sense in the lessons: In stories it shows hidden feelings: a stepsister resents Cinderella, a child resents a new rule. In personal and social education it helps pupils name the feeling and talk about it instead of letting it grow. Phrases: «resent being told», «resent someone for», «deeply resent».
examples from the lessons: He resented being picked last for the team. | Cinderella's stepsisters resented her kindness. | I resent having to do all the washing-up. | Don't resent your brother for winning; congratulate him. | She resented the new rule about phones. | The email bounced back, so I re-sent it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced «ri-ZENT» for the feeling, but «ree-SENT» for «sent again» — a homograph trap. Regular verb: resented. Noun: «resentment»; adjective: «resentful». Followed by «-ing»: «resent doing».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Feeling angry and bitter because you think you were treated unfairly. 2) Showing that feeling, for example in a look or words.
its sense in the lessons: In stories it describes how a character feels inside, often after being left out or blamed. In feelings lessons it is one of the «hidden anger» words; talking about it helps. Phrases: «resentful of», «resentful about», «feel resentful».
examples from the lessons: She felt resentful when her sister got a bigger present. | The resentful giant would not share his garden. | He gave a resentful look and walked off. | Try not to stay resentful; talk to the person. | The workers were resentful about the low pay. | The cat seemed resentful of the new puppy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb: «resentfully». Noun: «resentment». Used with «of» or «about». Close to «bitter»; stronger than «annoyed».

meaning for a pupil: 1) To move people to a new place to live, often after war, disaster or danger. 2) To settle down or get comfortable again. 3) To make a place lived in again.
its sense in the lessons: In geography, history and news it is about refugees and families moved to new homes, for example after floods or war. In everyday life a baby or a pet resettles after waking up. Phrases: «resettle refugees», «resettled in», «resettle into».
examples from the lessons: The families were resettled in a safe town after the flood. | Many refugees from Ukraine were resettled in other countries. | The baby woke, then resettled and fell asleep. | After the move, it took our cat weeks to resettle. | The island was resettled a hundred years later. | The village was resettled away from the river.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: resettled. Noun: «resettlement». Usually about groups of people moving because they must, not by choice.

part of speech: verb, -ing form of «resonate» (resonate, resonates, resonated, resonating); adjective (resonating)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Making a deep, clear sound that continues or echoes. 2) (science) Vibrating strongly because of a sound or vibration at the same frequency. 3) Meaning a lot to someone because it matches their feelings or experience.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on sound, a guitar body or a glass is resonating when it vibrates with a note. In music it describes rich, ringing sounds. In everyday talk a story or message is «resonating with» people when they feel it is true for them. Phrases: «resonating with», «resonating sound».
examples from the lessons: The bell's sound kept resonating through the hall. | The glass started resonating when she sang a high note. | The guitar's hollow body is resonating, which makes it loud. | Her speech about kindness was resonating with the whole class. | The drum was resonating long after he hit it. | The story is resonating with children all over the world.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Form of «resonate». Noun: «resonance». Myth: a singer can only break a glass in rare cases with a very loud, exact note — most singing cannot.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A short rest or break from something hard, painful or unpleasant. 2) (care) A short break for someone who looks after an ill or disabled person, when someone else takes over; called respite care. 3) (law, old) A delay given before a punishment.
its sense in the lessons: In stories it is a calm moment between dangers. In everyday life it means a break from rain, heat, noise or work. In family life «respite care» helps young carers and parents rest. Phrases: «a brief respite», «respite from», «without respite», «respite care».
examples from the lessons: The shade gave us a respite from the hot sun. | The rain stopped for a short respite. | The weekend was a respite from tests. | His little sister goes to respite care once a month so the family can rest. | The soldiers fought without respite. | Lunch break is a welcome respite.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced «RES-pite» or «RES-pit». Often with «from». Countable or uncountable. Formal-ish; «break» is the everyday word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Saying or writing something again, often in different or clearer words. 2) A new or changed version of a statement, such as a rule or account.
its sense in the lessons: In English and maths lessons restating a question in your own words helps you understand it; a good essay conclusion includes a restatement of the main point. In law and business, rules and money figures can be restated. Phrases: «a restatement of», «restatement of the question».
examples from the lessons: Your conclusion should include a restatement of your opinion. | Start your answer with a restatement of the question. | The teacher's restatement of the rule made it clearer. | The company issued a restatement of last year's figures. | His speech was just a restatement of what he said before. | A restatement in simple words helps younger children.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: «restate». In maths, restating a word problem in numbers («how much more» = subtract) is a useful step. A restatement should not change the meaning.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Calm and peaceful, helping you to relax. 2) Giving good rest, such as restful sleep.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and health lessons it describes places, music or habits that help you relax and sleep. In stories it sets a quiet mood. Phrases: «a restful night», «a restful holiday», «restful colours».
examples from the lessons: We had a restful day at the beach. | Soft music is restful before bed. | Pale blue is a restful colour for a bedroom. | After a restful night's sleep I felt great. | The garden is a restful place to read. | Screens before bed can make sleep less restful.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb: «restfully». Opposite: «restless» (cannot keep still or relax) — trap: «restless» does not mean «full of rest». «Rest» + «-ful».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Bringing someone back to life or to consciousness when their heart or breathing has stopped. 2) Bringing an idea, plan or business back into use.
its sense in the lessons: In first aid and safety lessons it is the life-saving help called CPR (cardiopulmonary resuscitation): calling the emergency number (999, 911, 000, 111 in NZ, 112) and pressing hard and fast in the middle of the chest. In hospital dramas «Resus» is the emergency room. Phrases: «mouth-to-mouth resuscitation», «cardiopulmonary resuscitation», «attempt resuscitation».
examples from the lessons: The lifeguard started resuscitation on the swimmer. | We learnt the steps of resuscitation in a first-aid class. | Quick resuscitation can save a life. | The ambulance crew continued resuscitation on the way to hospital. | CPR stands for cardiopulmonary resuscitation. | The old festival needed resuscitation after years of decline.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Verb: «resuscitate». Hard spelling: re-sus-ci-ta-tion. Pronounced «ri-SUS-i-TAY-shun». Safety: always call for help first or get an adult; an AED (defibrillator) machine can talk you through it.

part of speech: verb (retort, retorts, retorted, retorting); noun (a retort, retorts)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To answer quickly and sharply, often in an angry or clever way. 2) (noun) A quick, sharp or clever reply. 3) (science, old) A glass container with a long bent neck used for heating and distilling liquids.
its sense in the lessons: In stories it is a speech verb instead of «said»: «"Not likely!" she retorted». It tells the reader the answer was quick and cheeky or angry. In history of science pictures of old laboratories show retorts. Phrases: «retorted angrily», «a witty retort».
examples from the lessons: «You started it!» he retorted. | She had a clever retort for every joke. | «I'm not scared,» retorted the mouse. | The alchemist heated the liquid in a glass retort. | His rude retort got him in trouble. | When teased, she retorted with a smile.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: retorted. Good «said» alternative in story writing, but only for sharp replies. Pronounced «ri-TORT».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Copying or looking like the style of the past, especially the 1950s to 1990s. 2) (informal) Old-fashioned in a fun or cool way. 3) As a prefix «retro-» means «backwards», as in «retrograde» or «retrospective».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life it describes clothes, games, music and furniture that look old on purpose, like retro video games or a retro diner. In design and art lessons it is a style word. Phrases: «retro style», «retro games», «go retro».
examples from the lessons: Dad loves playing retro video games. | The café has a cool retro look. | She wore retro sunglasses from the 1970s. | Retro sweets are sold in old-fashioned jars. | Vinyl records are retro but popular again. | The new phone has a retro design.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Does not change form: «more retro» is possible in speech. Informal. Not the same as «antique» (really old, usually over 100 years). «Retro» things can be brand new but look old.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Going backwards, or getting worse instead of better. 2) (science, astronomy) Moving in the direction opposite to the usual one; for example, a planet seeming to move backwards across the night sky. 3) (medicine) «Retrograde amnesia» is losing memories from before an injury.
its sense in the lessons: In science and astronomy it describes «retrograde motion»: planets like Mars seem to go backwards for a while because Earth overtakes them. In news and history «a retrograde step» is a change that makes things worse. In astrology people talk of «Mercury in retrograde», which is not science. Phrases: «a retrograde step», «retrograde motion», «in retrograde».
examples from the lessons: Closing the library would be a retrograde step. | Mars shows retrograde motion in the night sky. | Venus spins in a retrograde direction, opposite to most planets. | After the fall, he had retrograde amnesia and forgot the morning. | Some moons orbit in a retrograde way. | Going back to the old rules felt retrograde.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal. Myth: planets do not really turn round; it only looks that way from Earth. Claims that «Mercury retrograde» causes bad luck are astrology, not science. Opposite: «progressive».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Thinking back about past events or about your own past. 2) Looking back to judge something after it has happened.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and reflection lessons it is the act of looking back on what happened and what you learnt. The phrase «in retrospect» (thinking back now) is far more common. Phrases: «a moment of retrospection», «in retrospection», «in retrospect».
examples from the lessons: At the end of the year we had a time of retrospection about what we learnt. | In retrospection, the trip was great fun despite the rain. | Grandad's stories are full of retrospection. | Retrospection helps you see your mistakes clearly. | The diary was written in quiet retrospection. | In retrospect, I should have studied more.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal and uncountable. Adjective: «retrospective». Everyday speech uses «looking back» or «in retrospect». Opposite idea: «anticipation» (looking forward).

part of speech: noun (a revelation, revelations); proper noun (Revelation — a book of the Bible)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A surprising fact that is made known, often a secret. 2) The act of making something known. 3) Something or someone surprisingly good: «the new player was a revelation». 4) (church) Christians and other believers say God shows truth to people by revelation. 5) (Bible) Revelation, the last book of the New Testament, full of visions about the end of the world.
its sense in the lessons: In stories a revelation is a big twist: a secret is uncovered. In news it is a fact that comes out. In church and Bible lessons, the Book of Revelation (not «Revelations») is the final book, written by John. Phrases: «a shocking revelation», «come as a revelation», «the Book of Revelation».
examples from the lessons: The revelation that the butler was the thief shocked everyone. | The new goalkeeper was a revelation this season. | Learning to swim was a revelation for her. | Christians believe the Bible is God's revelation. | The Book of Revelation describes a new heaven and a new earth. | The diary contained some surprising revelations.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: revelations. Verb: «reveal». The Bible book is called «Revelation», singular; saying «Revelations» is a common mistake. Capital letter for the book.

part of speech: verb, -ing form of «revert» (revert, reverts, reverted, reverting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Going back to an earlier state, habit or way of behaving. 2) (law) Property going back to its former owner. 3) (computing) Undoing changes and going back to an earlier version.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life it describes going back to old habits, such as reverting to bad spelling over the holidays. In computing it means undoing changes to a document or code. In science, wild-bred animals or plants reverting to their wild form. Phrases: «reverting to», «reverting back».
examples from the lessons: After the holidays, he kept reverting to his old messy handwriting. | The school is reverting to the old timetable. | The garden is reverting to wild grass. | I'm reverting the document to yesterday's version. | Without practice, she was reverting to bad habits. | The land is reverting to the farmer after the lease ends.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Form of «revert»; always with «to». «Revert back» repeats itself, but people say it. In business English «I will revert» means «I will reply» — this is Indian and some business English, not usual in UK/US.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To officially cancel a law, permission, licence or decision. 2) (cards) To fail to follow suit when you could, breaking a rule.
its sense in the lessons: In law and adult life a driving licence or passport can be revoked. In school, privileges can be revoked for bad behaviour. Phrases: «revoke a licence», «revoke permission», «revoke a ban».
examples from the lessons: The judge revoked his driving licence. | The school revoked our right to play football at lunch for a week. | The country revoked the old law. | Her visa was revoked when she broke the rules. | The king revoked his order and freed the prisoner. | You can revoke an app's permission to use your camera.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: revoked. Noun: «revocation». Formal; «cancel» or «take away» are everyday. Very close to «repeal», but «repeal» is used for laws by a parliament.

part of speech: noun (rhesus, rhesuses — also «rhesus monkey»); adjective (rhesus — in «rhesus factor»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A rhesus monkey (rhesus macaque) is a small brown monkey from Asia with a reddish face. 2) (science, medicine) The rhesus factor (Rh) is a protein on red blood cells; blood is called Rh-positive if it has it and Rh-negative if not.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on blood groups, «rhesus positive» and «rhesus negative» explain the plus or minus in blood types like O+ and A−. In nature lessons rhesus monkeys live in India, China and nearby, often in cities and temples. The rhesus factor was named after experiments with these monkeys. Phrases: «rhesus monkey», «rhesus positive», «rhesus negative».
examples from the lessons: Rhesus monkeys live in large groups in India. | My blood group is O rhesus positive. | The plus in A+ means rhesus positive. | A rhesus macaque stole a banana from a tourist. | Rhesus monkeys were sent into space in the early days of rockets. | Doctors check the rhesus factor before giving blood.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced «REE-sus». Hard spelling: r-h-e-s-u-s. Rh is the short form. Most people are rhesus positive.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A large bush with big leathery green leaves that stay all year and big bunches of bright flowers, often pink, purple, red or white. 2) (UK) In some places it is a weed that spreads and shades out native plants.
its sense in the lessons: In science and nature lessons it is an example of an evergreen flowering shrub. In parks and gardens it blooms in spring. Safety: its leaves and flowers are poisonous if eaten, to people and pets. Its name is Greek for «rose tree». Phrases: «rhododendron bush», «rhododendron flowers».
examples from the lessons: The rhododendron in the park is covered in pink flowers. | Bees visit the rhododendron in spring. | Do not eat rhododendron leaves; they are poisonous. | Wild rhododendron is spreading in the Scottish woods. | The rhododendron is the national flower of Nepal. | We hid behind the big rhododendron during hide-and-seek.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Hard spelling: r-h-o-d-o-d-e-n-d-r-o-n, with a silent «h» after the first «r». Pronounced «roh-duh-DEN-drun». Plural: rhododendrons. Azaleas are close relatives.

meaning for a pupil: 1) With a regular repeated beat or pattern. 2) In a way that has to do with rhythm in music or poetry.
its sense in the lessons: In music and PE lessons children clap, march or dance rhythmically. In poetry it describes lines with a steady beat. In science, the heart beats rhythmically and waves hit the beach rhythmically. Phrases: «move rhythmically», «clap rhythmically», «breathe rhythmically».
examples from the lessons: We clapped rhythmically to the song. | The waves splashed rhythmically on the shore. | Her heart beat rhythmically under the doctor's stethoscope. | The rowers pulled rhythmically together. | Breathe slowly and rhythmically to calm down. | The poem is rhythmically strong, with a beat like a drum.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Hard spelling: r-h-y-t-h-m-i-c-a-l-l-y (no vowel letter between «rh» and «thm», and double «l»). Adjective: «rhythmic» or «rhythmical»; noun: «rhythm».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A common wild plant with long narrow leaves that have strong lines (ribs) and a dark brown flower head on a tall stalk.
its sense in the lessons: In nature walks and science lessons in the UK, Ireland, Australia and New Zealand it is a common lawn and roadside weed. Children play a game called «soldiers» or «conkers with plantains», flicking the heads off each other's stalks. Phrases: «ribwort plantain».
examples from the lessons: Ribwort grows in the field behind the school. | We played soldiers with ribwort stalks. | The leaves of ribwort have long lines like ribs. | Ribwort plantain is a food plant for some caterpillars. | Count how many ribwort plants are in the quadrat. | Ribwort flowers have tiny white stamens round the head.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable or uncountable. «-wort» is an old word for plant (also in «St John's wort»). Not the same as the «plantain» fruit, which is like a banana — a trap.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Being morally good, honest and fair; doing what is right. 2) (church, Bible) Being right with God; Christians believe that people are made righteous by God's grace through faith. 3) (sometimes) Being too sure you are better than others (see «self-righteousness»).
its sense in the lessons: In Bible and church lessons it is a key word: «Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness» (Matthew 5). In ethics lessons it means acting with justice and fairness. In stories a hero fights for righteousness. Phrases: «paths of righteousness», «self-righteousness».
examples from the lessons: The psalm says, «He guides me in paths of righteousness.» | The judge was known for her righteousness and fairness. | Christians believe righteousness comes as a gift from God. | Martin Luther King spoke of justice and righteousness flowing like a river. | The knight fought for truth and righteousness. | His self-righteousness annoyed everyone.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Adjective: «righteous». Spelling trap: righ-teous-ness (the «t» sounds like «ch»: «RYE-chus-ness»). «Self-righteous» is negative: acting as if you are morally better than others.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Noisy, wild and out of control, like a riot. 2) Full of fun, loud laughter and wild energy: «a riotous party». 3) (of colour or plants) Very bright, rich or growing wildly.
its sense in the lessons: In news and history it describes violent crowds. In stories and everyday life it often means wild fun: a riotous birthday party or a riotous comedy. In nature writing, a garden can be «a riot of colour». Phrases: «riotous laughter», «riotous behaviour», «a riotous time».
examples from the lessons: The clown show ended in riotous laughter. | The crowd became riotous after the match. | We had a riotous time at the sleepover. | The garden was riotous with colour in June. | Riotous behaviour on the bus is dangerous. | The story is a riotous adventure with pirates and pies.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «riot». Adverb: «riotously». In UK law, «riotous assembly» was an old crime. Context tells you if it is good fun or real danger.

part of speech: verb, past form of «ripen» (ripen, ripens, ripened, ripening); adjective (ripened)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Became ripe: fruit or grain grew ready to eat or harvest. 2) Made something ripe. 3) (of ideas, plans, cheese) Developed fully over time.
its sense in the lessons: In science and nature lessons it describes fruit changing colour, getting softer and sweeter. In everyday life green bananas ripened on the windowsill. Old phrases: «the time was ripe» means the right moment had come. Phrases: «sun-ripened», «ripened on the vine».
examples from the lessons: The tomatoes ripened in the greenhouse. | The bananas ripened faster in a paper bag. | Sun-ripened strawberries taste the sweetest. | By August the wheat had ripened. | The cheese ripened in a cave for months. | Her plan ripened slowly over the summer.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past form of «ripen». Fact: some fruits like bananas, avocados and pears keep ripening after picking; others, like strawberries and grapes, do not. Ethylene gas from bananas speeds up ripening of nearby fruit.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who gets up from bed at a certain time: «an early riser», «a late riser». 2) The upright part of each step on a staircase, between one tread and the next. 3) A low platform or stage block that makes people stand higher, as for a choir. 4) A pipe going upwards in a building.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life «early riser» describes someone who wakes up early. In design and maths, stairs have risers and treads; the riser height tells how high each step is. In school concerts choirs stand on risers. Phrases: «early riser», «late riser», «choir risers».
examples from the lessons: Grandma is an early riser and gets up at five. | I'm a late riser at weekends. | Each stair riser is 18 centimetres high. | The choir stood on risers so everyone could be seen. | The water riser pipe runs up the building for the firefighters. | If there are 12 steps with 20 cm risers, the stairs are 240 cm high.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: risers. In maths problems with stairs: total height = number of steps × riser height. Comes from «rise».

part of speech: adjective (Romani); noun (Romani — the language; a Romani, the Romani — the people)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The Romani (also spelt Romany) are a people whose ancestors came from India about a thousand years ago and who now live in many countries, especially in Europe and the Americas. 2) Romani is also the language of these people, related to languages of India. 3) (adjective) To do with the Romani people or language.
its sense in the lessons: In history, geography and citizenship lessons the Romani people are an ethnic group with rich traditions of music, crafts and family life; many have suffered unfair treatment, including in the Holocaust. In the UK and Ireland, Gypsy, Roma and Traveller pupils are named in school records. The word «gypsy» is seen as rude by some and used with pride by others. Phrases: «Romani people», «Romani language», «Romani music».
examples from the lessons: The Romani people have lived in Europe for centuries. | Romani music influenced flamenco and jazz. | Our class learnt a few words of Romani. | Many Romani families were killed in the Holocaust. | Romani Day is celebrated on 8 April. | She is proud of her Romani heritage.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually written with a capital: Romani. Also «Roma» and «Romany». Not related to Romania or Rome, despite the similar sound — a common confusion. Avoid using «gypsy» as an insult; respect what people call themselves.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Romansh is a language spoken by a small number of people in south-east Switzerland, in the canton of Graubünden. 2) It is one of Switzerland's four national languages, with German, French and Italian. 3) (adjective) To do with this language or its speakers.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and language lessons it is an example of a small language that comes from Latin, like French, Italian and Spanish. Fewer than 1 in 100 Swiss people speak it as a main language. Phrases: «Romansh speakers», «in Romansh».
examples from the lessons: Romansh is one of the four national languages of Switzerland. | Only about sixty thousand people speak Romansh. | Romansh comes from the Latin spoken by Roman soldiers. | Some Swiss road signs are in Romansh. | «Bun di» means «good day» in Romansh. | Schools in some Swiss valleys teach in Romansh.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Written with a capital: Romansh (also spelt Romansch or Rumantsch). Not the same as «Romani» or «Romanian». It is a real language, not a dialect of Italian.

part of speech: noun (a romeo, romeos — informal); proper noun (Romeo — a name)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (a name) Romeo is a boy's name; the most famous Romeo is the young lover in Shakespeare's play «Romeo and Juliet». 2) (informal) A young man who flirts a lot or acts like a romantic lover: «he thinks he's a real Romeo». 3) In the radio spelling alphabet (NATO), «Romeo» stands for the letter R.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and everyday life it is used for a boy who is very romantic. In the spelling alphabet used by pilots, police and soldiers, R is said as «Romeo» so it is not misheard. Phrases: «a real Romeo», «Romeo and Juliet», «Romeo, Romeo, wherefore art thou Romeo».
examples from the lessons: In the spelling alphabet, R is «Romeo». | «Romeo and Juliet» is a sad love story by Shakespeare. | He's a bit of a Romeo, always giving girls flowers. | The pilot spelt R-A-Y as «Romeo, Alpha, Yankee». | Romeo is a popular boy's name in Italy. | Our cat is called Romeo.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually with a capital letter. Trap: «wherefore art thou Romeo» means «why are you Romeo?» (why are you from the enemy family), not «where are you». Calling someone «a Romeo» is light teasing.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (church) A string of beads used by Catholic Christians to count prayers. 2) (church) The set of prayers said with these beads, including the Hail Mary and the Lord's Prayer. 3) (rare, old) A rose garden.
its sense in the lessons: In church and religious education lessons Catholics pray the rosary, moving a bead with each prayer and thinking about events in the lives of Jesus and Mary. Some other faiths use prayer beads too, such as Muslims and Buddhists. Phrases: «say the rosary», «pray the rosary», «rosary beads».
examples from the lessons: Granny says the rosary every evening. | The rosary has five groups of ten beads, called decades. | She held her rosary beads during the service. | Catholics pray the rosary to think about Jesus's life. | The rosary was a gift for his First Holy Communion. | Muslims use prayer beads called misbaha, which are like a rosary.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: rosaries. Catholics believe the rosary is a prayer, not a lucky charm, so wearing it as jewellery can upset some people. From Latin «rosarium», rose garden.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Pink or pinkish-red, like a rose, especially of cheeks or skin. 2) Hopeful and likely to be good: «a rosy future». 3) (in phrases) «Ring a Ring o' Roses» and «everything's rosy» mean things are fine.
its sense in the lessons: In stories it describes healthy faces («rosy cheeks» from cold or exercise) or sunsets. In everyday talk and news it means hopeful: «the future looks rosy». «Look at the world through rose-tinted (rose-coloured) glasses» means seeing only the good. Phrases: «rosy cheeks», «a rosy picture», «not all rosy».
examples from the lessons: She came in from the snow with rosy cheeks. | The sky turned rosy at dawn. | The future looks rosy for our team. | Things are not all rosy at the factory. | The baby has rosy little toes. | He painted a rosy picture of the holiday, but it rained all week.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative: rosier, rosiest (y changes to i). «Everything's rosy» is informal and can be said with sarcasm. Myth: «Ring a Ring o' Roses» is often said to be about the plague, but historians find no evidence for that.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Almost round, but not quite a perfect circle or ball. 2) (of a number) Roughly a round number.
its sense in the lessons: In science and maths lessons it describes shapes found in nature that are nearly round, like pebbles, seeds or leaves. In everyday life it describes faces, buns or tables. «-ish» means «a bit» or «roughly». Phrases: «a roundish shape», «roundish leaves».
examples from the lessons: The beetle has a roundish body. | We found a smooth roundish pebble on the beach. | Draw a roundish blob for the head. | The leaves are roundish with wavy edges. | Let's meet at roundish five o'clock — about then. | Potatoes come in roundish and long shapes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal. «-ish» can go on many words: greenish, smallish, sevenish. In maths, a roundish shape is not a circle, so you cannot use circle formulas exactly.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Very simple and basic, not developed much. 2) Knowing only the first, simplest parts of something: «rudimentary French». 3) (biology) Small and not fully developed, such as a part of a body that no longer has much use.
its sense in the lessons: In history and design lessons it describes simple early tools, shelters or machines. In everyday life it describes basic skills. In science, some animals have rudimentary wings or eyes that hardly work, like an ostrich's wings that cannot fly. Phrases: «rudimentary knowledge», «rudimentary tools», «rudimentary shelter».
examples from the lessons: The cavemen used rudimentary stone tools. | I only have a rudimentary knowledge of French. | They built a rudimentary shelter from branches. | Penguins' wings are not rudimentary; they use them to swim. | The first computers were rudimentary compared with phones today. | Some snakes have rudimentary back legs, tiny bumps inside the body.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal word; «basic» or «simple» is everyday. Comes from «rudiments», the first basic things you learn. Not linked to «rude».

meaning for a pupil: 1) To think deeply about something for a long time. 2) (negative) To keep going over the same worries again and again. 3) (science) Of cows, sheep and goats: to bring food back up from the stomach and chew it again, called chewing the cud.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, animals that ruminate (ruminants) have a stomach with four parts and chew the cud. In stories and reflection lessons it describes a character deep in thought. In mental health it names worry that goes round in circles; talking to someone helps. Phrases: «ruminate on», «ruminate about».
examples from the lessons: The cows lay in the field, ruminating. | He ruminated on the riddle all evening. | Try not to ruminate about one bad mark. | Sheep and goats ruminate their food. | She ruminated over whether to tell the truth. | The old wizard ruminated by the fire.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal for thinking. Regular verb: ruminated. Noun: «rumination»; animal noun: «ruminant». Used with «on», «about» or «over».

meaning for a pupil: 1) The back end of an animal's body, above the back legs. 2) (food) A cut of meat from this part: «rump steak». 3) (informal, jokey) A person's bottom. 4) A small leftover part of something bigger, such as a group or parliament after most have left.
its sense in the lessons: In nature and farm lessons it names a body part of horses, cows and birds. In food it is a steak. In history, the «Rump Parliament» (1648–1653) was what was left of the English Parliament after many members were thrown out. Phrases: «rump steak», «the rump of».
examples from the lessons: The horse has a white patch on its rump. | Dad cooked rump steak for dinner. | The robin has an orange chest and a brown rump. | «Get off your rump and help,» joked Grandad. | Only a rump of the club was left after the arguments. | The Rump Parliament ruled England after the Civil War.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: rumps. Meaning 3 is jokey, not rude. Not the same as «rumpus» (a noisy fuss).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Written in runes, the letters used by Germanic peoples such as the Vikings and Anglo-Saxons before the Latin alphabet. 2) Mysterious or magical, like old runes (literary).
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons about Vikings and Anglo-Saxons, runic stones and runic inscriptions show names and messages carved in wood or stone. In fantasy stories runic marks are often magical. Phrases: «runic alphabet», «runic inscription», «runic stone».
examples from the lessons: The museum has a runic stone from Viking times. | The Vikings' runic alphabet is called the futhark. | We wrote our names in runic letters. | The sword had a runic inscription on the blade. | In the fantasy book, the door was covered in glowing runic symbols. | Runic letters are made of straight lines because they were easy to carve.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «rune». Fact: runes were mostly used for everyday writing, names and memorials; the idea that they were mainly magic is a modern myth, though some charms existed.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A small animal of the weasel family that lives in the forests of Russia and northern Asia, with soft dark brown fur. 2) The fur of this animal, which was once very expensive. 3) (literary, heraldry) Black: «sable» is the word for black on coats of arms.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography lessons it is an animal of the taiga forest. In history, sable fur was a sign of wealth for kings and nobles. In art, fine paintbrushes were made from sable hair. Phrases: «sable fur», «sable brush».
examples from the lessons: A sable is a small furry animal like a weasel. | The tsar wore a coat trimmed with sable. | Artists use soft sable brushes for watercolours. | Sables live in the cold forests of Siberia. | The knight's shield showed a sable lion on gold. | The sable's thick fur keeps it warm in winter.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: sables. Pronounced «SAY-bul». Many people today think wearing real fur is cruel; synthetic brushes are common now.

part of speech: noun (sabotage; uncountable); verb (sabotage, sabotages, sabotaged, sabotaging)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Damaging or destroying something on purpose, especially machines, roads or plans, to stop an enemy or rival. 2) (verb) To damage something on purpose. 3) To secretly spoil someone's plan or chance.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, resistance fighters in World War II sabotaged railways and factories. In everyday life a person can «sabotage» a game or a group project by spoiling it on purpose. In stories it is a villain's trick. Phrases: «act of sabotage», «sabotage someone's plans», «self-sabotage».
examples from the lessons: The spies planned sabotage on the bridge. | Someone sabotaged our sandcastle while we were swimming. | Don't sabotage the group project by not doing your part. | The train crash was caused by sabotage, not an accident. | She thought her rival had sabotaged her bike. | Staying up late before a test is self-sabotage.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced «SAB-uh-tahzh». From French. Regular verb: sabotaged. Myth: it is often said the word comes from workers throwing wooden shoes (sabots) into machines; that story is probably made up. Damaging property on purpose is a crime.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To make someone feel sad. 2) (old) To become sad.
its sense in the lessons: In news and formal talk «we are saddened to hear» is a polite way to say people are very sad, often after a death or disaster. In stories it shows feelings. Phrases: «deeply saddened», «saddened to hear», «it saddens me».
examples from the lessons: We were saddened to hear that our teacher was leaving. | It saddens me when people drop litter. | The news of the fire saddened the whole town. | The school was deeply saddened by the loss of a pupil. | Her tears saddened her little brother. | The end of the film saddened everyone.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: saddened (double «d»). Often passive: «be saddened by». Formal-ish; «make sad» is everyday.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (French) «Salade» is the French word for salad or for lettuce. It sounds like «sa-LAD» to an English ear. It is not an English word, though it appears on menus in English-speaking places.
its sense in the lessons: Heard in French lessons and seen on café menus: «salade niçoise» (a salad with tuna, egg, olives and green beans from Nice), «salade verte» (green salad). In French, «quelle salade!» can also mean «what a mess!» (informal). Phrases: «une salade», «salade de fruits» (fruit salad).
examples from the lessons: In French, «une salade» means a salad. | I ordered a salade niçoise at the café. | «Salade de fruits» means fruit salad. | The menu said «salade verte», which is a green salad. | My French teacher asked, «Tu aimes la salade?» | In France, people often eat salade after the main course.
note for the reader of a maths problem: French, feminine: «la salade», «une salade». The final «e» is silent. The English word is «salad» — do not add an «e» in English spelling.

part of speech: noun (samba, sambas); verb (samba, sambas, sambaed, sambaing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A fast, lively dance from Brazil. 2) The music for this dance, with strong drum rhythms. 3) (verb) To dance the samba.
its sense in the lessons: In music and PE lessons children play samba rhythms on drums like the surdo and shakers, and learn about the carnival in Rio de Janeiro. In geography it is part of Brazilian culture, which grew from African traditions. Phrases: «samba band», «samba school», «dance the samba».
examples from the lessons: We played samba drums in music class. | At the carnival in Rio, samba schools parade through the streets. | The crowd danced the samba all night. | Samba music came from the African-Brazilian community. | Our samba band played at the school fair. | They sambaed across the stage.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: sambas. Verb past: sambaed (rare). A «samba school» in Brazil is a community group that prepares for carnival, not an ordinary school.

part of speech: noun (a samurai, samurai — plural usually the same)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A member of the warrior class in old Japan who served a lord and fought with swords and bows. 2) The samurai as a class of people in Japanese history.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons the samurai lived in Japan from about the 12th century until the 1870s, when their class was ended. They followed a code of honour, later called bushido, valuing loyalty and courage. In films, games and stories they are famous sword fighters. Phrases: «samurai sword», «samurai warrior», «samurai armour».
examples from the lessons: The samurai wore armour made of small plates laced together. | A samurai had to be loyal to his lord. | Samurai swords are called katana. | The museum has a samurai helmet with horns. | Samurai also studied poetry and tea ceremony. | Japan ended the samurai class in the 1870s.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural is usually «samurai», though «samurais» is sometimes seen. Myth: not all samurai were men only with swords; bows were their first weapon, and a few women warriors fought too. Pronounced «SAM-oo-rye».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (US, Canada) A box or pit filled with sand for children to play in; in the UK and Australia it is called a sandpit. 2) (computing) A safe, closed space where a program can run without harming the rest of the computer. 3) (games) A sandbox game lets players build and explore freely, like Minecraft.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life little children play in the sandbox at the park. In computing and online safety lessons, a sandbox keeps unknown programs from damaging files. In gaming, «sandbox mode» means free play without strict goals. Phrases: «play in the sandbox», «sandbox game», «sandbox mode».
examples from the lessons: The toddlers built castles in the sandbox. | Minecraft is a famous sandbox game. | The new app runs in a sandbox, so it cannot change your files. | Cover the sandbox at night so cats don't use it. | We tried the code in a sandbox first. | In sandbox mode you can build anything you like.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: sandboxes. UK, Australia, New Zealand: «sandpit». Hygiene: wash your hands after playing in shared sand.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A strong wind in a desert that lifts and carries clouds of sand through the air. 2) (figurative) A wild confusing rush of something.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and science lessons sandstorms happen in deserts like the Sahara and in Australia's outback; they can block out the sun, damage crops and make breathing hard. In stories they are a danger for travellers and explorers. Safety: stay indoors, close windows, cover your nose and mouth. Phrases: «caught in a sandstorm», «a sandstorm blew up».
examples from the lessons: The camels lay down when the sandstorm came. | A huge sandstorm turned the sky orange. | Stay indoors during a sandstorm and close the windows. | Sandstorms can carry Sahara dust all the way to Britain. | The explorers waited in their tent until the sandstorm passed. | Even on Mars there are giant sandstorms, called dust storms.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: sandstorms. One word. Close to «dust storm» (finer dust, can happen outside deserts). Fact: dust from the Sahara sometimes falls with rain in the UK and colours cars orange.

part of speech: (Latin) adjective in the name Homo sapiens; noun (informal, Sapiens — short for Homo sapiens)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (Latin) «Sapiens» means «wise» or «knowing»; it is the second part of the scientific name of modern humans, Homo sapiens, meaning «wise human». 2) (informal) Used alone to mean modern humans: «early sapiens». It is not an ordinary English word.
its sense in the lessons: In science and history lessons Homo sapiens are modern humans, who appeared in Africa about 300,000 years ago. Other kinds of humans, such as Neanderthals, are named Homo neanderthalensis. Phrases: «Homo sapiens», «early Homo sapiens».
examples from the lessons: Humans belong to the species Homo sapiens. | «Sapiens» is Latin for wise. | Homo sapiens first lived in Africa. | Neanderthals lived at the same time as early Homo sapiens. | Scientific names like Homo sapiens are written in italics. | The museum shows a skull of an early sapiens.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Latin. The «s» at the end is not a plural; «Homo sapiens» is both singular and plural. Write «Homo» with a capital and «sapiens» with a small letter. Pronounced «SAP-ee-enz».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A young tree with a thin trunk. 2) (literary) A young person, especially a slim young man.
its sense in the lessons: In science and nature lessons saplings grow from seeds and become trees; schools plant saplings on tree-planting days. In stories a sapling stands for youth and new life. Phrases: «plant a sapling», «oak sapling».
examples from the lessons: We planted an oak sapling in the school garden. | The sapling was tied to a stick so the wind would not bend it. | Deer eat the bark of young saplings. | In ten years the sapling will be a big tree. | The storm snapped the little sapling. | Each class planted a sapling for Arbor Day.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: saplings. Smaller than a tree, bigger than a seedling. In maths problems: if 30 saplings are planted in 5 equal rows, there are 6 in each row.

part of speech: noun (sass; uncountable); verb (sass, sasses, sassed, sassing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal, mainly US) Cheeky, rude talk, especially to a parent or teacher; back talk. 2) (verb, informal) To talk back cheekily to someone. 3) (informal, praise) Bold, lively confidence and style: «she's got sass».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday family life an adult may say «Don't give me any sass!» when a child answers back. In stories it shows a cheeky, confident character. In the UK people more often say «cheek» or «lip». Phrases: «give someone sass», «don't sass me», «full of sass».
examples from the lessons: «Don't sass your mother,» said Dad. | That's enough sass, young lady. | The puppy has a lot of sass for such a tiny dog. | He sassed the teacher and got a detention. | The singer performed with style and sass. | I didn't mean to give you sass.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal, mostly American. Adjective: «sassy». UK equivalent: «cheek» («don't give me cheek»). Being sassy can be fun, but sassing adults can be seen as rude.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a way that is good enough or acceptable. 2) In a way that meets a rule or a need.
its sense in the lessons: In school reports «working satisfactorily» means doing well enough, not excellent. In everyday life and the formal voice it means a job was done properly. In maths, a problem is «solved satisfactorily» when the answer is checked. Phrases: «completed satisfactorily», «progressing satisfactorily», «answer satisfactorily».
examples from the lessons: The patient is recovering satisfactorily. | He completed the course satisfactorily. | The plumber fixed the leak satisfactorily. | Your homework was done satisfactorily, but try harder on spelling. | The question was not answered satisfactorily. | Things are going satisfactorily at the new school.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Long spelling: sat-is-fac-to-ri-ly. Adjective: «satisfactory». In reports «satisfactory» is middle, below «good». Opposite: «unsatisfactorily».

meaning for a pupil: 1) To make something completely wet, soaked through. 2) (science) To make a liquid hold as much of a substance as it can, so no more dissolves. 3) To fill something so full of a thing that no more can fit, like a market full of products.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons a saturated solution is one where no more salt or sugar will dissolve; extra stays at the bottom. In geography, saturated ground causes flooding because rain cannot soak in. In everyday life rain saturates your clothes. Phrases: «saturated with», «saturated solution», «saturated fat».
examples from the lessons: The rain saturated my coat. | Stir in sugar until the water is saturated. | The ground was saturated, so the field flooded. | The town is saturated with coffee shops. | Saturated fat is found in butter and cheese. | The sponge was saturated and dripping.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: saturated. Noun: «saturation». In science, warm water can usually hold more dissolved solid before it is saturated than cold water. In food labels, «saturated fat» is a type of fat to eat less of.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A factory or building where logs are cut into planks and boards by machine saws.
its sense in the lessons: In history and geography lessons sawmills grew up beside rivers in Canada, New Zealand, Australia and the US, using water power at first. In everyday life wood for houses and furniture comes from sawmills. In safety talk sawmills are dangerous places with big blades. Phrases: «work at the sawmill», «old sawmill».
examples from the lessons: The logs were floated down the river to the sawmill. | Grandad worked at the sawmill for forty years. | The old sawmill used a water wheel. | Sawdust from the sawmill is used for animal bedding. | The village grew up around the sawmill. | Children must never go near the saws in a sawmill.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: sawmills. One word. «Saw» (the tool) + «mill». In maths problems: if a sawmill cuts 1 log into 8 planks, 25 logs give 200 planks.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A small, very sharp knife used by surgeons in operations. 2) A similar sharp knife used in science, art or crafts for precise cutting.
its sense in the lessons: In science and health lessons surgeons use scalpels to make clean, careful cuts. In design and technology older pupils may use a craft knife or scalpel with a safety mat and supervision. In stories it appears in hospital scenes. Phrases: «surgeon's scalpel», «scalpel blade».
examples from the lessons: The surgeon asked for a scalpel. | A scalpel is sharper than a kitchen knife. | Only adults should use a scalpel in the art room. | The scientist cut the leaf with a scalpel. | Each scalpel blade is used once and then thrown away safely. | The nurse counted the scalpels after the operation.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: scalpels. Pronounced «SKAL-pul». Safety: scalpel blades go in a sharps bin, never the normal rubbish.

part of speech: noun (a scapegoat, scapegoats); verb (scapegoat, scapegoats, scapegoated, scapegoating)
