meaning for a pupil: 1) A person or group blamed for something bad that is not really their fault, often so others escape blame. 2) (Bible) In the Old Testament (Leviticus 16), on the Day of Atonement the priest put the people's sins on a goat and sent it into the desert. 3) (verb) To unfairly blame someone this way.
its sense in the lessons: In ethics, history and anti-bullying lessons, scapegoating is unfair: in history whole groups, such as Jews in Nazi Germany, were wrongly blamed for a country's problems. In everyday life a child can be made the scapegoat for a broken window. Phrases: «make someone a scapegoat», «used as a scapegoat».
examples from the lessons: The new boy was made the scapegoat for the broken window. | Don't scapegoat your sister for your mess. | In history, minorities were often used as scapegoats. | In the Bible the scapegoat carried the people's sins into the wilderness. | The coach became the scapegoat when the team lost. | Scapegoating someone is a kind of bullying.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: scapegoats. One word. Verb: «scapegoat», and «scapegoating» for the act. Not the same as «escape goat».

part of speech: adjective (scarred); verb, past form of «scar» (scar, scars, scarred, scarring)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Having scars, marks left on the skin after a wound heals. 2) Marked or damaged on the surface, such as land or a table. 3) Hurt deeply in the mind or feelings by a bad experience.
its sense in the lessons: In science and health lessons skin heals and can leave a scar. In stories and history it describes battle wounds or a land scarred by war or mining. In feelings and family life, a person can be «emotionally scarred». Phrases: «scarred for life» (often jokey), «badly scarred», «scarred by».
examples from the lessons: His knee was scarred from falling off his bike. | The hillside was scarred by the old quarry. | The war scarred the whole town. | She was scarred by the dog bite and is now scared of dogs. | «I watched that scary film and I'm scarred for life!» he joked. | The old desk is scarred with names and scratches.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double «r»: scar, scarred, scarring. Trap: «scared» (afraid, one «r») is a different word — very common spelling mix-up.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) A person who is forgetful, disorganised and cannot keep their mind on one thing.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and stories it is a gentle, often affectionate word for someone who keeps losing things or forgetting. It can be kind teasing, but saying it too often can hurt. Adjective: «scatterbrained». Phrases: «a bit of a scatterbrain», «you scatterbrain».
examples from the lessons: I'm such a scatterbrain — I left my lunch at home again. | Grandpa calls me a scatterbrain when I lose my glasses. | The scatterbrain professor forgot where he parked. | Don't be a scatterbrain: pack your bag the night before. | She's a lovely scatterbrain who always forgets birthdays. | Lists help a scatterbrain stay organised.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal. Countable: scatterbrains. One word. Often used kindly about yourself. Forgetfulness can sometimes be part of ADHD, which is not a fault.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Doubt about whether something is true or will work. 2) The habit of not believing things until there is good evidence. 3) (philosophy) The idea that we cannot be sure of some or any knowledge.
its sense in the lessons: In science and media lessons healthy scepticism means checking facts and asking «how do we know?» before believing a claim, an advert or something online. In stories a sceptical character doubts magic or ghosts. Phrases: «healthy scepticism», «treated with scepticism», «scepticism about».
examples from the lessons: The claim was met with scepticism. | A good scientist uses scepticism and checks the evidence. | She viewed the advert with scepticism. | Healthy scepticism helps you spot fake news. | His scepticism about ghosts disappeared when the door creaked. | Philosophers argue about scepticism and what we can really know.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK spelling: scepticism; US spelling: skepticism. Pronounced «SKEP-ti-sizm» (the «c» sounds like «k»). Adjective: «sceptical» / «skeptical». Scepticism is not the same as refusing all evidence.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (old-fashioned) A person who goes or went to the same school as you; a schoolmate.
its sense in the lessons: Found mostly in old books, letters and history: Victorian stories mention schoolfellows. Today people say «classmate», «schoolmate» or «school friend». Phrases: «an old schoolfellow».
examples from the lessons: Grandad met an old schoolfellow at the shop. | In the story, Tom's schoolfellows teased him. | The two schoolfellows wrote letters for fifty years. | Charles Dickens wrote about cruel schoolmasters and frightened schoolfellows. | She invited her schoolfellows to tea. | They were schoolfellows at a boarding school.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Old-fashioned. Countable: schoolfellows. Modern words: schoolmate, classmate.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person whose job is teaching children in a school.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and stories it names a teacher's job, often in a village or small school. In jobs lessons it is a career that needs training. Phrases: «a primary schoolteacher», «retired schoolteacher».
examples from the lessons: My aunt is a schoolteacher in Dublin. | The village schoolteacher taught all ages in one room. | Schoolteachers mark a lot of homework. | He wants to be a schoolteacher when he grows up. | The old schoolteacher remembered every pupil's name. | A schoolteacher needs patience and kindness.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: schoolteachers. One word (sometimes «school teacher»). In everyday speech «teacher» is more common.

part of speech: noun (a screening, screenings); verb, -ing form of «screen» (screen, screens, screened, screening)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A showing of a film or TV programme. 2) (health) A medical test given to many people to find illnesses early, before they cause problems. 3) Checking people or things to see if they are suitable or safe, such as bags at an airport. 4) (verb form) Hiding or protecting with a screen.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life cinemas have screenings, and schools may hold a film screening. In health lessons, babies have hearing screening and children have eye screening at school. In safety, airports use security screening. Phrases: «a film screening», «health screening», «security screening», «eye screening».
examples from the lessons: The school held a screening of the film for charity. | All children have eye screening in their first year at school. | Security screening at the airport took ages. | The trees are screening the garden from the road. | There were two screenings of the movie that evening. | Screening helps doctors find illnesses early.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: screenings. Medical screening does not mean you are ill; it checks healthy people. «Screen time» is time spent on devices — a different idea.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) Extremely tasty and delicious. 2) (informal) Very attractive or delightful.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and stories, especially Roald Dahl's books, it describes yummy food: «a scrumptious cake». It shows enjoyment and is fun to say. Phrases: «scrumptious food», «absolutely scrumptious».
examples from the lessons: This chocolate cake is scrumptious! | Willy Wonka made scrumptious sweets. | Grandma's apple pie is simply scrumptious. | We had a scrumptious picnic in the park. | The café sells scrumptious pancakes. | «Scrumptious!» said the giant, licking his lips.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal; a fun word for «delicious». Spelling trap: s-c-r-u-m-p-t-i-o-u-s (the «t» sounds like «sh»). Adverb: «scrumptiously».

meaning for a pupil: 1) An artist who makes sculptures — figures or shapes carved from stone or wood, or made from clay, metal or other materials.
its sense in the lessons: In art lessons pupils learn about sculptors such as Michelangelo, Barbara Hepworth and Henry Moore. In history famous statues tell us about the past. Phrases: «a famous sculptor», «the sculptor carved».
examples from the lessons: Michelangelo was a sculptor and a painter. | The sculptor carved a bear from a tree trunk. | Barbara Hepworth was a British sculptor who made smooth shapes with holes. | Our class visited a sculptor's studio. | The sculptor shaped the clay with her hands. | A sculptor made the statue in the town square.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: sculptors. Spelling: -or, not -er. The work is a «sculpture»; the verb is «sculpt». Do not mix up «sculptor» (person) and «sculpture» (object).

part of speech: verb, past form of «sear» (sear, sears, seared, searing); adjective (seared)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Burnt or scorched the surface of something with strong heat. 2) (cooking) Cooked the outside of meat or fish quickly in a very hot pan. 3) Caused a sharp, burning pain or a strong lasting feeling: «the memory was seared into her mind».
its sense in the lessons: In cooking it describes meat browned on the outside. In science and nature it describes land or plants burnt by the sun or fire. In stories it shows strong memories or pain. Phrases: «pan-seared», «seared into my memory», «seared by the sun».
examples from the lessons: Dad seared the steak in a hot pan. | The sun seared the grass brown. | The image of the fire was seared into his memory. | Pan-seared salmon is crispy outside. | Pain seared through his ankle when he fell. | The desert wind seared their faces.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past form of «sear». Not the same as «sheared» (cut, as sheep's wool) or «seer» (a person who sees the future). Safety: hot pans can burn you; ask an adult.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a way that depends on or changes with the seasons of the year. 2) At certain seasons only.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography lessons animals migrate seasonally, and rivers flood seasonally. In everyday life shops sell things seasonally, and people eat food that is grown seasonally. In maths and news, figures can be «seasonally adjusted» to remove changes caused by seasons. Phrases: «seasonally adjusted», «seasonally available».
examples from the lessons: Many birds move seasonally between countries. | We try to eat seasonally and buy local strawberries in summer. | The river floods seasonally after heavy rain. | Some shops open only seasonally, in the holidays. | The weather changes seasonally. | Unemployment figures are seasonally adjusted.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: «seasonal». In maths and news, «seasonally adjusted» numbers have the usual seasonal ups and downs taken out so that trends are easier to see. Remember the seasons are opposite in the Southern Hemisphere.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Towards the sea, away from the land.
its sense in the lessons: In geography, sailing and stories it gives a direction: the tide flows seawards, a ship heads seawards. In safety talk at the beach, a rip current can carry swimmers seawards. Phrases: «drift seawards», «look seawards», «face seawards».
examples from the lessons: The tide was flowing seawards. | The boat drifted seawards in the strong wind. | From the cliff we looked seawards. | Rip currents can pull swimmers seawards; swim parallel to the shore to escape. | The river runs seawards through the town. | The house faces seawards.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Seawards» is mostly UK; «seaward» works in both UK and US. Opposite: «landwards» or «inland». «-wards» means «in the direction of», as in «homewards» or «backwards».

meaning for a pupil: 1) The belief that religion should be kept separate from government, public schools and laws. 2) A way of living or thinking that is not based on religion.
its sense in the lessons: In religious education, citizenship and history lessons secularism explains why, for example, the USA and France keep church and state apart, while the UK has an official church (the Church of England) but many secular laws. A secular state lets people of any faith or none live freely. Phrases: «secularism and religion», «a secular state».
examples from the lessons: France has strong rules of secularism in its schools. | Secularism means the government does not favour any religion. | Some people support secularism; others want religion in public life. | The USA's founders wrote secularism into the constitution by separating church and state. | Secularism does not mean being against religion. | Our class debated secularism in schools.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Adjective: «secular» (not religious). Trap: secularism is about how a country is run, and secular people can still respect faith. A «secularist» supports it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Involving a lot of sitting and little exercise. 2) (of people or animals) Staying in one place, not moving around or migrating.
its sense in the lessons: In health and PE lessons a sedentary lifestyle — sitting too long with screens — is linked to weaker muscles and health problems; children are advised to be active for about 60 minutes a day. In science and history, sedentary animals stay in one area, and sedentary people settle in villages instead of wandering. Phrases: «sedentary lifestyle», «sedentary job».
examples from the lessons: A sedentary lifestyle is bad for your heart. | Sitting at a desk all day is a sedentary job. | Get up and stretch to break up sedentary time. | When farming began, people became sedentary and built villages. | Some birds are sedentary and stay all winter. | Too much gaming can make you sedentary.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal. Pronounced «SED-un-tree» or «SED-un-terr-ee». Opposite: «active». Similar root to «sedate» and «sediment» (Latin «sedere», to sit).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A grass-like plant that grows in wet places such as marshes, ponds and riverbanks. Its stems are often triangular.
its sense in the lessons: In science and nature lessons sedges are part of wetland habitats, giving shelter to insects and birds. A rhyme helps tell them apart: «sedges have edges, rushes are round, grasses are hollow». Phrases: «sedge warbler», «sedge grass».
examples from the lessons: Sedge grows thickly around the pond. | Sedges have three-sided stems. | A sedge warbler sang from the reeds. | We found frogspawn among the sedge. | Ducks nest in the sedge by the river. | Feel the stem: if it has edges, it is a sedge.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable or uncountable. Not the same as «hedge». Remember: «sedges have edges».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A small plant with thick fleshy leaves that store water; also called stonecrop. Many sedums have star-shaped flowers and grow on rocks, walls and roofs.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons sedum is an example of a succulent plant adapted to dry places. In everyday life and design, «green roofs» are often covered in sedum because it needs little soil and water. Bees and butterflies love its flowers. Phrases: «sedum roof», «sedum plant».
examples from the lessons: The bus shelter has a sedum roof. | Sedum leaves are thick so they can store water. | Butterflies landed on the pink sedum flowers. | We planted sedum in the rock garden. | Sedum is a succulent, like a cactus. | Sedum can grow on old stone walls.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced «SEE-dum». Plural: sedums. Also called «stonecrop».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A machine that measures and records how much the ground shakes during an earthquake.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and science lessons seismographs show earthquakes as zigzag lines on paper or a screen; bigger zigzags mean stronger shaking. Scientists use them to find where an earthquake happened and how strong it was. Phrases: «seismograph reading», «recorded on a seismograph».
examples from the lessons: The seismograph drew big zigzag lines during the earthquake. | Scientists in New Zealand watch seismographs day and night. | A seismograph can detect earthquakes on the other side of the world. | We made a model seismograph with a pen and a moving strip of paper. | The seismograph showed small shakes before the volcano erupted. | Seismograph records help warn people about tsunamis.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced «SIZE-muh-graf». «Seismo-» means earthquake, «-graph» means writing or drawing. The record is a «seismogram»; the science is «seismology». Earthquake strength is given on the moment magnitude scale; each step up means much more energy (about 32 times more).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Shaped like half a circle.
its sense in the lessons: In maths it describes shapes and arcs; to find the area of a semicircular shape, find the area of the whole circle and halve it. In science, the «semicircular canals» in the inner ear help you balance. In everyday life it describes windows, tables or rows of chairs. Phrases: «semicircular shape», «semicircular canals», «semicircular arch».
examples from the lessons: We sat in a semicircular row around the teacher. | The church has a semicircular window over the door. | Find the area of the semicircular garden. | The semicircular canals in your ear help you keep your balance. | Romans built semicircular arches. | The rainbow made a semicircular shape across the sky.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Semi-» means half. Maths: area of a semicircle = half of π × radius × radius; the perimeter of a semicircle is half the circumference plus the diameter (the straight edge) — a common trap is forgetting the diameter.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A material, such as silicon, that lets electricity flow through it better than an insulator but not as well as a metal, and whose flow can be controlled. 2) A device or chip made from such material, used in computers and phones.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on electricity, materials are conductors (metals), insulators (plastic, rubber) and semiconductors in between. In technology and news, semiconductors (chips) are inside phones, cars and computers; countries like Taiwan, South Korea and the USA make many of them. Phrases: «semiconductor chip», «semiconductor industry».
examples from the lessons: Silicon is the most common semiconductor. | Every phone contains tiny semiconductor chips. | A semiconductor conducts electricity better than rubber but worse than copper. | Solar panels use semiconductors to turn light into electricity. | There was a shortage of semiconductors, so car factories slowed down. | LED lights are made with semiconductors.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: semiconductors. «Semi-» means half or partly. Silicon Valley in California is named after the semiconductor silicon. Not the same as a «superconductor», which carries electricity with no resistance at all.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Very exciting and surprising, causing great interest. 2) (informal) Extremely good: «you look sensational». 3) (of news) Made to shock or excite people more than the facts deserve.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and sport it means amazing: «a sensational goal». In media lessons sensational headlines exaggerate to grab attention, so readers should check the real facts. Phrases: «a sensational win», «sensational news», «sensational headlines».
examples from the lessons: She scored a sensational goal from the halfway line. | The magician gave a sensational show. | You look sensational in that costume! | The newspaper printed a sensational story that turned out to be false. | It was a sensational comeback after being three goals down. | Be careful with sensational headlines online.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb: «sensationally». Noun: «sensation». «Sensationalism» is reporting that exaggerates. Context shows whether it is praise or criticism.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Full of tender feelings like love, sadness or longing, especially about the past: a sentimental person is easily moved. 2) Kept or valued for the memories it brings, not for money: a thing has sentimental value. 3) (critical) Too soft and sugary in feeling, making you sad or happy in a way that seems overdone or not real.
its sense in the lessons: In stories it tells the reader a character is soft-hearted, missing someone or thinking of old times; in English lessons pupils learn it can be praise (warm) or criticism (soppy). Everyday phrases: «sentimental value», «get sentimental», «a sentimental song», «for sentimental reasons». In money talk an old toy may be worth little in pounds or dollars but have huge sentimental value.
examples from the lessons: Grandad gets sentimental when he looks at old photos. | This old teddy has sentimental value, so please don't throw it away. | Mum kept my first shoes for sentimental reasons. | The film was too sentimental for my brother, who said it was soppy. | She sang a sentimental song about her home town. | Don't get all sentimental on me, it's only a sleepover! | The ring isn't expensive, but it means a lot to me. It's sentimental. | Our teacher said the poem was moving without being sentimental.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective only; noun «sentiment», «sentimentality»; adverb «sentimentally». «Sentimental value» means value in feelings, not price — in a maths problem it adds nothing to the cost. Don't confuse with «sensitive» (easily hurt or quick to notice) or «sensible» (wise, practical).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Something that keeps two things apart or divides one thing into parts, such as a line, a wall or a sheet. 2) A machine that splits a mixture into its parts, for example cream from milk or oil from water. 3) (computing, writing) A symbol such as a comma, a full stop, a slash or a space that shows where one item ends and the next begins. 4) (maths) The symbol used to split groups of digits or the whole part from the decimal part, like the point in 3.5.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on mixtures pupils meet separators that use sieves, magnets or spinning; in maths and computing a separator is the mark between items in a list or the decimal point. In everyday life plastic separators sit between biscuits in a packet, eggs in a tray or files in a folder. Phrases: «a decimal separator», «a thousands separator», «a page separator».
examples from the lessons: Put a cardboard separator between the layers of cups so they don't break. | A cream separator spins milk very fast so the cream comes out. | In the list «red, blue, green» the comma is the separator. | In the UK and USA the decimal separator is a dot, but in France it is a comma. | The folder has coloured separators for each subject. | We used a magnet as a separator to pull iron filings out of the sand. | Type a space as the separator between the numbers. | The farmer's separator splits the grain from the chaff.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one separator, two separators. Spelling trap: it is «separ-a-tor» with an «a» in the middle, like «separate» (remember «there is a rat in separate»). In numbers: 1,000 uses a comma as a thousands separator in the UK and USA; 1.5 uses a point as the decimal separator; other countries swap them, so 1.000 may mean one thousand.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (medicine) A very serious illness that happens when the body's fight against an infection goes wrong and starts to harm its own organs. 2) (older use) Any poisoning of the body by germs from a wound or infection.
its sense in the lessons: In health and science lessons sepsis shows why cuts should be kept clean and why a very ill person needs a doctor quickly. Health posters say «Think sepsis» and list warning signs such as very fast breathing, mottled or bluish skin, confusion and feeling worse than ever before. It is an emergency: call 999, 911, 000 or 111 as advice says. In stories it may explain why a character in the past died from a small wound.
examples from the lessons: Sepsis can start from a small cut that gets badly infected. | The nurse said sepsis is an emergency and needs treatment fast. | Doctors gave him antibiotics to fight the sepsis. | Before germs were understood, many soldiers died of sepsis after battles. | Keep a scrape clean so it does not get infected. | If someone is very ill, confused and breathing fast, an adult should ask a doctor about sepsis. | Florence Nightingale's clean hospitals helped cut deaths from infection. | She spent a week in hospital with sepsis but made a full recovery.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable; adjective «septic». Sounds like «SEP-sis». It is not a germ itself and you cannot «catch» sepsis from someone; it is the body's reaction to an infection. Myth: it only happens to very old people — anyone can get it, but early treatment helps most people recover.

part of speech: adjective (septic); noun (Australia, slang: a septic, septics)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (of a wound or body part) Infected with germs so it becomes red, swollen, painful and full of pus. 2) A septic tank is an underground tank where waste from toilets is broken down by bacteria, used by homes not joined to the main sewers. 3) (Australia, UK, slang) A septic is an American; it comes from rhyming slang «septic tank» = «Yank». It can sound mocking.
its sense in the lessons: In health lessons «go septic» warns pupils to clean cuts and splinters; in science and geography septic tanks show how countryside homes deal with waste. In Australian talk «a septic» or «seppo» is a jokey, sometimes rude word for an American. Phrases: «go septic», «a septic finger», «a septic tank».
examples from the lessons: Clean that cut, or it might go septic. | His toe went septic after he stood on a rusty nail. | The farmhouse has a septic tank instead of a sewer pipe. | A truck comes every few years to empty the septic tank. | The doctor gave her cream for a septic insect bite. | (Australia, slang) "Who's the bloke with the accent?" "Some septic on holiday." | Wash your hands before you touch a blister so it doesn't turn septic.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Septic» goes with «sepsis». Opposite: «antiseptic» (stopping germs), as in antiseptic cream. Do not confuse with «sceptic» (UK spelling of skeptic, a doubter), which sounds like «SKEP-tic». The slang sense is not polite to say to an American.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Coming one after another in a fixed order. 2) Done step by step, finishing one step before starting the next. 3) (maths, computing) Following a sequence or pattern, like numbers that go up by one each time.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, sequential numbers are like 4, 5, 6, 7; in computing, sequential steps are carried out in order, which is the first idea of a program. In stories and history, sequential events are told in time order. Everyday use: tickets with sequential numbers, sequential instructions in a recipe. Phrases: «in sequential order», «sequential steps», «sequentially numbered».
examples from the lessons: The pages are numbered in sequential order. | Our coding lesson showed that a computer follows sequential instructions. | The raffle tickets had sequential numbers from 101 to 150. | Put the pictures of the story in sequential order. | The recipe gives sequential steps: mix, pour, then bake. | The house numbers on our street are not sequential, which confuses the postman. | We read the chapters sequentially, not jumping ahead.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective; noun «sequence». It means «in order», not just «many». In a maths problem «sequential numbers» usually means consecutive whole numbers (each one more than the last): three sequential numbers add to 3 times the middle one, e.g. 6+7+8=21.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A slim wild cat of African grasslands, with long legs, very large ears and a golden coat with black spots and stripes. It leaps high to catch birds and rodents.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on animals and habitats the serval shows how body shape fits a way of hunting: big ears hear rodents underground and long legs let it jump over tall grass. In stories it is an African wild cat, not a pet. Some people keep servals illegally or in special permits, which wildlife groups warn is bad for the animal.
examples from the lessons: The serval has the longest legs for its size of any cat. | A serval can leap high into the air to catch a bird. | Its huge ears help the serval hear mice under the grass. | We saw a serval at the wildlife park in Kent. | Servals live in the grasslands of Africa near water. | The serval's coat has black spots on gold, a bit like a cheetah's. | A serval is a wild animal and does not make a good house pet.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one serval, two servals. Say «SER-vul». Not the same as a cheetah or leopard, though its spots look alike; it is much smaller, about the size of a big house cat but taller.

part of speech: noun (sesame, sesame seeds — the plant and seeds); exclamation (open sesame)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A plant grown in warm countries for its small flat seeds. 2) The tiny cream or black seeds of that plant, eaten on bread and in food and pressed to make sesame oil. 3) «Open sesame!» — the magic words that open the robbers' cave in the story «Ali Baba and the Forty Thieves»; jokingly, any easy way to get something you want.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life sesame seeds sit on burger buns, bagels and in tahini and hummus; on food labels sesame is listed as an allergen, so safety lessons teach pupils to read labels if a friend is allergic. In stories «Open sesame!» opens magic doors; people say it jokingly when a door opens by itself or when a good grade is «an open sesame» to a good school.
examples from the lessons: My burger bun is covered in sesame seeds. | Hummus is made with chickpeas and tahini, a sesame paste. | Ella is allergic to sesame, so we check the labels. | Grandma fries the vegetables in sesame oil. | Ali Baba said "Open sesame!" and the rock door slid open. | The automatic door opened and Leo shouted, "Open sesame!" | Black sesame seeds are used in some Chinese desserts. | The bakery's sesame bagels sell out first.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say «SESS-uh-mee» (three syllables). Uncountable as food (some sesame), countable as seeds (sesame seeds). Sesame is one of the main food allergens in the UK, USA, Canada, Australia and New Zealand; an allergic person must avoid even tiny amounts.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The system of underground pipes and drains that carries dirty water and toilet waste away from homes and buildings. 2) The work of taking away and dealing with that waste. 3) (sometimes, loosely) The waste itself, more often called sewage.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and science lessons sewerage is part of how towns stay healthy: clean water comes in, dirty water goes out through sewers to treatment works. History lessons link it to the Great Stink of London in 1858 and Joseph Bazalgette's sewers, which helped stop cholera. Phrases: «a sewerage system», «sewerage charges», «water and sewerage».
examples from the lessons: Our town's sewerage system was built over a hundred years ago. | The water bill includes a charge for sewerage. | Before proper sewerage, cities smelled terrible and diseases spread. | Workers are fixing the sewerage pipes under the main road. | Joseph Bazalgette designed London's sewerage system. | Good sewerage keeps rivers cleaner and people healthier. | The new houses must be joined to the sewerage network.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Trap: «sewerage» is mainly the pipes and system; «sewage» is the dirty water and waste itself; «a sewer» is one pipe. Do not confuse «sewer» (SOO-er, a drain) with «sewer» (SOH-er, a person who sews).

part of speech: noun (a shaker, shakers); Shaker (a member of a religious group)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A container with small holes in the lid for shaking out salt, pepper, sugar or other powder. 2) A container you shake to mix drinks, such as a protein or milkshake shaker. 3) A musical instrument filled with beads or seeds that rattles when shaken, like a maraca or egg shaker. 4) A Shaker is a member of a small Christian group in the USA, famous for simple handmade furniture and for shaking or dancing in worship. 5) In «movers and shakers», important people who make things happen.
its sense in the lessons: In music lessons young pupils play egg shakers and maracas to keep the beat; in the kitchen salt and pepper shakers sit on the table. In history and religion lessons the Shakers show a group that lived simply and made plain, careful furniture. Phrases: «salt shaker», «pepper shaker», «movers and shakers», «Shaker style».
examples from the lessons: Can you pass the salt shaker, please? | Our class played egg shakers along with the song. | The pepper shaker is empty again. | Dad mixes his protein drink in a plastic shaker. | The Shakers made simple wooden chairs that are still copied today. | She is one of the movers and shakers in our town, always starting new projects. | We made shakers by putting rice in yoghurt pots and taping them shut. | The shaker rattles like rain.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. In the UK a salt shaker is often called a «salt cellar», in the USA a «salt shaker». «Shaker» with a capital S is the religious group or the style of furniture. Comes from the verb «shake».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A sharp, broken piece of glass, pottery, metal or ice. 2) (archaeology) A broken piece of old pottery found in the ground, also called a potsherd. 3) (figurative) A small sharp bit of something, like «a shard of light» or «a shard of memory».
its sense in the lessons: In safety lessons shards warn that broken glass must be swept up by an adult and wrapped before going in the bin. In history and archaeology lessons pottery shards help experts learn how people lived long ago. In stories shards make a scene feel sharp and dangerous. The Shard is also a very tall pointed skyscraper in London, named for looking like a glass shard.
examples from the lessons: A shard of glass lay on the kitchen floor after the cup broke. | Don't touch the shards — let me sweep them up. | The archaeologists found Roman pottery shards in the field. | A shard of ice fell from the gutter. | A shard of sunlight came through the gap in the curtains. | From the top of the Shard you can see all of London. | Wrap the broken shards in newspaper before you throw them away.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a shard, shards. Usually used about hard, brittle things that break, not about soft things like paper. Safety: never pick up glass shards with bare hands.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An electric tool with small moving blades for cutting hair close to the skin, usually on the face or legs. 2) (old-fashioned, informal) «A young shaver» is a boy or young lad. 3) A person who shaves.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life a shaver is part of a grown-up's bathroom kit; safety lessons say children should not play with shavers or razors because the blades are sharp. In older stories an adult may call a boy «a young shaver». Phrases: «an electric shaver», «a shaver socket» (a special bathroom plug in the UK).
examples from the lessons: Dad uses an electric shaver every morning. | The bathroom has a special socket for the shaver. | Grandpa bought a new shaver because the old one was blunt. | Please don't use my shaver to cut the doll's hair! | (old-fashioned) "Come here, you young shaver," said the old farmer with a smile. | The shaver buzzes loudly. | Mum charges her shaver overnight.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. A «shaver» is usually electric; a «razor» is often a hand blade, though people mix the words. Comes from «shave» (shave, shaves, shaved, shaving).

part of speech: noun (a sheath, sheaths — say «sheeths» or «sheethz»); verb related: sheathe
meaning for a pupil: 1) A close-fitting cover for the blade of a knife, sword or dagger. 2) (science) A covering around part of a plant or animal, such as the leaf sheath of grass or the sheath around a nerve. 3) A protective covering around a cable or wire. 4) A close-fitting, simple dress.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons and adventure stories, a knight pulls his sword from its sheath; in safety lessons a sheath shows a knife should be covered when carried by an adult. In science, a sheath is a wrapping layer, such as the myelin sheath that helps nerve messages travel fast. Phrases: «in its sheath», «a knife sheath», «a sheath of leaves».
examples from the lessons: The knight drew his sword from its sheath. | Put the camping knife back in its sheath when you finish. | The cable has a plastic sheath to keep the wires safe. | A leaf sheath wraps around the stem of the grass. | The dagger had a sheath made of leather. | Nerves have a fatty sheath that speeds up messages. | The actor wore a long silver sheath dress to the film awards.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun «sheath» (ends in -th as in «thin»), verb «sheathe» (ends in -the as in «breathe»): you sheathe a sword in its sheath. Plural «sheaths».

part of speech: verb (sheathe, sheathes, sheathed, sheathing — past form); adjective (sheathed)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Past form of «sheathe»: put a knife or sword back into its cover. 2) (adjective) Covered or wrapped in a close-fitting layer, as in «steel-sheathed» or «sheathed in ice». 3) (of a cat's claws) Pulled back in, not showing.
its sense in the lessons: In stories «he sheathed his sword» means the fight is over or he chose peace. In science and design «sheathed» describes things wrapped in a protective layer, like cables sheathed in plastic or a ship's hull sheathed in copper. Cats keep their claws sheathed when they walk so they stay sharp.
examples from the lessons: The knight sheathed his sword and bowed. | The old ship was sheathed in copper to protect it from worms. | The branches were sheathed in ice after the freezing rain. | The cat's claws stayed sheathed while it played gently. | The wires are sheathed in rubber so they are safe to touch. | She sheathed the knife before handing it back. | The tower is sheathed in glass that shines in the sun.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: sheathe, sheathed. Say the «th» softly, as in «breathe». Do not mix up with the noun «sheath». «Unsheathed» means taken out of its cover, ready to use.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The quality of being shiny: how bright, smooth and gleaming a surface looks when light falls on it. 2) (science) How much a material reflects light, used when we sort materials by their properties.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on materials, pupils test shininess to sort metals from other materials (metals are usually shiny) and learn that smooth surfaces reflect more light. In art and computer drawing, shininess is how glossy something is. In everyday life, adverts boast about the shininess of hair, cars and shoes.
examples from the lessons: We sorted the materials by hardness and shininess. | The shininess of the spoon showed it was made of metal. | Polishing the shoes brought back their shininess. | The advert promised shininess for your hair. | Foil has more shininess than paper. | The game lets you change the shininess of the car. | Over time the coin lost its shininess and turned dull.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable; from «shiny» (y changes to i before «-ness»: shiny → shininess). Opposite ideas: dullness, matt. Spelling trap: one «n» after «shi», then «-iness».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person whose job is designing or building ships. 2) A company that builds ships.
its sense in the lessons: In history and geography lessons shipbuilders show how port towns such as Belfast (where the Titanic was built), Glasgow on the Clyde and Newcastle grew rich and how jobs changed when shipyards closed. In technology lessons pupils learn about hulls, floating and steel. Related words: shipyard, shipbuilding, dock.
examples from the lessons: The Titanic was built by shipbuilders in Belfast. | My great-grandad was a shipbuilder on the River Clyde. | Shipbuilders use huge cranes to lift steel plates. | The shipbuilder is making a new ferry for the islands. | Viking shipbuilders made long, fast boats from wood. | Thousands of shipbuilders lost their jobs when the yard closed.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; one word, no hyphen. The work is «shipbuilding»; the place is a «shipyard».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person or company that sends goods from one place to another, by sea, air, road or rail. 2) (informal, fans) A person who likes the idea of two characters in a story or show being a couple and supports that pairing.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and business lessons shippers move goods around the world in containers; in everyday life a shipper sends parcels bought online. Among young fans online, a «shipper» is someone who «ships» two characters, from «relationship». Phrases: «a freight shipper», «the shipper pays the cost».
examples from the lessons: The shipper sent the parcel by air. | Big shippers carry toys from factories to shops across the ocean. | The shipper charges more for heavy boxes. | The company is the largest shipper of bananas. | (informal) Half the fans are shippers who want the two heroes to fall in love. | The shipper lost my package, so they sent a new one.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Note «shipper» sends things but does not have to use a ship; in the USA «ship» just means «send». The fan sense comes from the verb «to ship» (to want two characters together).

meaning for a pupil: 1) To steal things from a shop by hiding them and leaving without paying.
its sense in the lessons: In citizenship and safety lessons shoplifting is a crime: stealing even a sweet is still stealing, shops have cameras and security guards, and someone caught may be reported to the police. In stories it can show a character under pressure from friends or in need. Signs say «Shoplifters will be prosecuted».
examples from the lessons: Taking a chocolate bar without paying is shoplifting. | The guard saw a man try to shoplift a phone case. | Never let anyone pressure you to shoplift. | He was caught shoplifting and his parents were called. | The shop has cameras to stop people shoplifting. | She was too honest to shoplift, even when her friends dared her. | The sign said, "Shoplifters will be prosecuted."
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Person: «a shoplifter»; act: «shoplifting» (uncountable). It is a form of theft in the UK, USA, Canada, Australia, New Zealand and Ireland. Age does not make it allowed.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who shouts a lot or speaks very loudly. 2) A loud person who gets angry quickly and yells when cross.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and family lessons «a shouter» describes a parent, coach or teacher who yells; pupils learn that some people shout when stressed and that it is fine to tell a trusted adult if shouting at home feels scary. In sport, a shouter on the sideline cheers or complains loudly.
examples from the lessons: Our coach is a shouter, but he's kind really. | Mum isn't a shouter; she goes quiet when she's cross. | The shouter in the crowd yelled at the referee. | My little brother is the loudest shouter in the house. | The shouters at the front of the protest held big signs. | If an adult is a shouter and it frightens you, talk to someone you trust.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; from «shout». Informal word, not often in formal writing. Opposite: a quiet or calm person.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Skill at entertaining a crowd and getting attention, by doing things in a bold, exciting or dramatic way.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, sport and the arts, showmanship describes performers who don't just do something well but make it fun to watch, like a footballer doing tricks or a magician with a big cape. In English lessons it can be praise (great entertainment) or criticism (showing off more than being good). Phrases: «a bit of showmanship», «pure showmanship».
examples from the lessons: The magician's showmanship had the whole hall gasping. | His goal celebration was pure showmanship. | The circus ringmaster was famous for his showmanship. | Good showmanship can make even a science demo exciting. | She plays well, but she needs less showmanship and more teamwork. | P. T. Barnum was known for his showmanship and his tall tales.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. From «showman» + «-ship». Not about «ships». Used of anyone, man or woman.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Clever at understanding people and situations and at making good, practical decisions, especially about money or business. 2) (of a guess or choice) Wise and likely to be right.
its sense in the lessons: In stories a shrewd character spots tricks, makes clever deals and is hard to fool, like a shrewd shopkeeper or detective. In money lessons a shrewd buyer compares prices. It is mostly praise but can hint at being a bit sly. Phrases: «a shrewd guess», «a shrewd move», «a shrewd businesswoman».
examples from the lessons: The shrewd shopkeeper knew the coin was fake. | That was a shrewd move — you saved half your pocket money. | Grandma is shrewd; you can't fool her with a story. | I made a shrewd guess that the answer was 12, and I was right. | A shrewd buyer checks the price per gram, not just the price. | The detective gave the suspect a shrewd look. | He shrewdly kept some money back for later.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective; noun «shrewdness». Rhymes with «food». Not the same as «shrew», a tiny mouse-like animal (and an old insulting word for a bad-tempered woman). In maths word problems a «shrewd shopper» usually picks the better deal (lowest unit price).

part of speech: verb (shriek, shrieks, shrieked, shrieking — past form)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Past form of «shriek»: gave a sudden, very high, loud cry, out of fear, pain, excitement or laughter. 2) Said something in a high, loud voice. 3) (of things) Made a high, sharp noise, like brakes, wind or a whistle.
its sense in the lessons: In stories «shrieked» is a strong speaking verb that tells the reader a character is frightened, shocked or wildly excited — stronger than «shouted» or «said». Teachers suggest it in creative writing instead of «said». Phrases: «shrieked with laughter», «shrieked in terror».
examples from the lessons: She shrieked when the spider ran across her foot. | The children shrieked with laughter at the clown. | "Get out of my room!" my sister shrieked. | The brakes shrieked as the bus stopped. | The wind shrieked around the old house all night. | Everyone shrieked as the roller coaster dropped. | The parrot shrieked whenever the doorbell rang.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: shriek → shrieked. Spelling: «ie» (i before e). Similar words: screamed, squealed, screeched; «shrieked» is often higher and sharper. Noun: «a shriek».

part of speech: adjective (shrunken); old past participle of shrink (shrink, shrank, shrunk/shrunken)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Having become smaller than before, often in a way that looks wrinkled, dried or weak. 2) (of numbers or amounts) Made smaller, reduced.
its sense in the lessons: In stories a shrunken figure is an old or ill person who looks small and frail, or a magic spell has made someone tiny; in science, a dried fruit is a shrunken grape. In everyday life clothes washed too hot come out shrunken. In history and museum talk «shrunken heads» were made by a few peoples long ago, which can be mentioned in museums.
examples from the lessons: My jumper came out of the wash all shrunken. | The old man looked shrunken in the big armchair. | A raisin is a shrunken, dried grape. | The shrunken lake left boats stuck in the mud. | In the story, the witch's spell left the prince shrunken to the size of a thumb. | The shrunken budget meant fewer school trips.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly used as an adjective before a noun: «a shrunken apple». As the verb's past participle people usually say «shrunk»: «My jeans have shrunk». Past simple is «shrank»: «The jumper shrank».

part of speech: noun (si — music note); abbreviation (SI); Spanish/Italian word (sí, si)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (music) The seventh note of the do-re-mi scale in some countries, now usually called «ti» in English (do, re, mi, fa, so, la, ti). 2) SI (science) — short for the International System of Units (from French «Système international»), the metric units scientists use, like metres, kilograms and seconds. 3) (Spanish, Italian) «sí» means «yes» in Spanish and «si» means «if» or «yes» in other languages; it is not an English word.
its sense in the lessons: In music lessons «si» may appear in older or foreign do-re-mi scales; in science lessons «SI units» are the standard units for measuring. In language lessons and on the street pupils may hear «¡Sí!» from Spanish speakers, sounding like English «see». Si is also a nickname, short for Simon (a name).
examples from the lessons: In some countries they sing "do, re, mi, fa, sol, la, si." | In English we usually sing "ti" instead of "si". | The SI unit of length is the metre. | Write your answer in SI units: metres, kilograms or seconds. | "¿Quieres pizza?" "¡Sí!" — that means "Yes!" in Spanish. | Si, short for Simon, is in my football team.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «si» alone is not an everyday English word. «SI» is written in capitals for the units. Spanish «sí» (yes) has an accent; Spanish «si» without the accent means «if». In maths and science «SI units» means metres (m), kilograms (kg), seconds (s), amperes (A), kelvin (K), moles (mol), candelas (cd).

meaning for a pupil: 1) To make someone feel shocked, disgusted or very upset, as if they might be sick. 2) To start to become ill. 3) «Sicken of» something (old-fashioned) — to become tired of it.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and news «it sickens me» shows strong disgust at cruelty or unfairness; «sickening» describes a horrible crash, sound or smell. Older stories say an animal or child «began to sicken» before falling ill. In everyday talk «a sickening goal» means a very disappointing one for the losing team.
examples from the lessons: The cruelty to the dog sickened everyone who saw it. | The calf began to sicken and would not eat. | It sickens me when people drop litter in the park. | There was a sickening crash as the car hit the wall. | The smell of rotten eggs sickened us. | After a week of rain, we sickened of staying indoors. | We lost to a sickening goal in the last minute.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Adjective «sickening» (very unpleasant). It is stronger than «annoy». Not the same as «to be sick» (to vomit) or «to feel sick».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Often ill, weak or not healthy. 2) Looking pale or unhealthy. 3) (of taste or smell) Too sweet in a way that makes you feel a bit sick. 4) (of colour or light) Pale and unpleasant, like a sickly yellow. 5) (of feelings) Too sweet or sentimental.
its sense in the lessons: In stories a sickly child or plant is weak and often ill, especially in history before modern medicine. In everyday life «sickly sweet» describes sweets, perfume or a cake with too much icing. In art and descriptions «a sickly green» is an ugly pale colour.
examples from the lessons: She was a sickly baby but grew into a strong girl. | The plant looked sickly because it had no sunlight. | The cake was sickly sweet with so much icing. | The room smelled of sickly perfume. | The walls were painted a sickly yellow. | He looked pale and sickly after the flu. | The film had a sickly happy ending.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective, though it ends in -ly (not an adverb). Comparative «sicklier», superlative «sickliest». Do not mix up with «sickle», a curved blade for cutting crops.

part of speech: noun (a silicate, silicates; silicate as a substance)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) A mineral or compound made of silicon and oxygen, often with metals; most rocks, sand and clay are made of silicates. 2) A material made from such compounds, as in some glass, cement and paint.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography lessons on rocks, pupils learn that the Earth's crust is mostly silicate minerals such as quartz, feldspar and mica, and that glass is made from silica sand. Chemistry for older pupils names silicates as salts of silicic acid.
examples from the lessons: Most of the rocks in the Earth's crust are silicates. | Quartz is a silicate mineral found in sand. | Clay is made of tiny silicate grains. | The Moon's surface is covered in grey silicate dust. | Some glues and paints contain silicates. | Mica is a silicate that splits into thin shiny sheets.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable for kinds (silicates), uncountable for the stuff. Say «SIL-ih-kate». Related: silicon (an element, Si), silica (silicon dioxide, as in sand), silicone (a rubbery man-made material). Don't mix these up.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (geology, older term) The lower layer of the Earth's crust, under the oceans and below the continents, made of heavy rock rich in silicon and magnesium (si + ma). 2) (a name) Sima is a given name in several countries, for example in Iran, Croatia and Czechia.
its sense in the lessons: In older geography books, pupils meet «sial» (the lighter rock of the continents) and «sima» (the heavier rock below and under the oceans), helping explain why continents «float». Modern books usually say «oceanic crust» instead. As a name it is just a person's name.
examples from the lessons: Sima is the heavier layer of rock under the ocean floor. | The old textbook showed sial on top of sima. | Basalt is a rock typical of the sima. | The word sima comes from silicon and magnesium. | Sima is a girl in my class. | Under the continents, the lighter sial rests on the heavier sima.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Rare, technical word; most modern school books use «oceanic crust» and «basalt». Not a common English word in daily life. As a name it starts with a capital letter.

part of speech: verb (simmer, simmers, simmered, simmering — -ing form); adjective (simmering)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Cooking gently in liquid that is just below boiling, with small bubbles. 2) (of feelings) Growing slowly inside someone without fully showing yet, like anger or excitement. 3) (of a problem or argument) Continuing quietly and likely to grow worse. 4) «Simmering down» — becoming calmer after being angry or excited.
its sense in the lessons: In cooking and science, simmering is gentle heating below 100 °C at sea level, used for soups and sauces; safety lessons remind pupils to keep pan handles turned in. In stories simmering anger shows a character close to exploding. In news, «simmering tensions» describes a dispute that has not yet become a fight.
examples from the lessons: The soup is simmering on the stove. | Let the sauce keep simmering for ten minutes. | She was simmering with anger but said nothing. | There were simmering tensions between the two teams. | "Simmer down!" said the teacher when we got too loud. | Leave the pan simmering, not boiling hard. | The simmering argument finally boiled over at lunch.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb; doubled «m» already in «simmer». Simmering is gentler than boiling: small, slow bubbles. «Boil over» (literally and figuratively) is what happens after things simmer too long.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The act of making something simpler or easier to understand or do. 2) An explanation or version that leaves out details to be easier, sometimes so much that it is no longer quite right. 3) (maths) Making an expression or fraction simpler, like turning 4/8 into 1/2.
its sense in the lessons: In maths lessons simplification means cancelling fractions, collecting like terms or reducing ratios to lowest terms. In science and history teachers say «this is a simplification» when a model is easier than the full truth (like the atom as tiny balls). Phrases: «an oversimplification», «a useful simplification».
examples from the lessons: Simplification of 6/9 gives 2/3. | Saying the Earth is a perfect ball is a simplification. | The new rules are a simplification of the old ones. | That's an oversimplification — the war had many causes. | Simplification of 2x + 3x gives 5x. | The teacher made a simplification so younger children could follow. | Simplification of the instructions made the game easier to learn.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable and uncountable. From «simplify» (y changes to i). In maths, simplification never changes the value: 4/8 and 1/2 are equal; you divide top and bottom by the same number.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Being honest and meaning what you say or feel; not pretending. 2) Real and true feeling shown in words or actions.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and ethics lessons sincerity shows a character is trustworthy and that an apology or thank-you is real, not just polite words. Letters end «Yours sincerely» in the UK (or «Sincerely» in the USA). Phrases: «in all sincerity», «with sincerity», «doubt someone's sincerity».
examples from the lessons: I could hear the sincerity in her apology. | He spoke with such sincerity that everyone believed him. | In all sincerity, I think you did brilliantly. | Some people doubted the politician's sincerity. | A thank-you card is nicer when it is written with sincerity. | Her sincerity made her a good friend.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable; adjective «sincere», adverb «sincerely». Spelling trap: «sincerity» drops the final e of «sincere». In UK letter rules: «Dear Mr Smith … Yours sincerely» when you know the name.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who rides a skateboard, a short board on four small wheels, often doing tricks.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life skateboarders use skate parks, ramps and pavements; safety lessons say to wear a helmet and pads and not ride on busy roads. Skateboarding has been an Olympic sport since 2021, and some Olympic skateboarders were children. Tricks have names like «ollie» and «kickflip».
examples from the lessons: The skateboarder jumped over the low wall. | Skateboarders practise in the park after school. | Wear a helmet if you want to be a skateboarder. | The youngest skateboarder at the Olympics was only 12. | A skateboarder zoomed past us down the hill. | The skateboarder fell, got up and tried the trick again.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; one word. Also «skater» or (slang) «sk8er». Sport is «skateboarding».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A book of plain, often thick, paper for drawing sketches and quick pictures. 2) A collection of a person's sketches or quick notes.
its sense in the lessons: In art lessons pupils keep a sketchbook to practise drawing, collect ideas and test colours; teachers look in it to see progress. In everyday life artists carry sketchbooks to draw outside. Phrases: «sketchbook page», «keep a sketchbook».
examples from the lessons: I drew our cat in my sketchbook. | Bring your sketchbooks to the art lesson. | Her sketchbook is full of drawings of birds. | Leonardo da Vinci filled his notebooks with sketches. | The teacher asked us to glue leaf rubbings into our sketchbooks. | I take a small sketchbook on holiday.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; one word (sometimes «sketch book»). Not lined like an exercise book.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Not complete or detailed; giving only the main points. 2) Drawn or done quickly and roughly, like a sketch. 3) (informal, slang) Seeming a bit dodgy, untrustworthy or unsafe.
its sense in the lessons: In school, «sketchy notes» or «a sketchy answer» lack detail, and «my memory is sketchy» means you don't remember well. Among young people «that's sketchy» means it feels shady or unsafe — useful in online safety: a sketchy link or website should not be clicked. In art, a sketchy drawing has quick loose lines.
examples from the lessons: My memory of the trip is a bit sketchy. | The report was too sketchy; add more detail. | Her drawing was sketchy, just a few quick lines. | (slang) That website looks sketchy — don't click it. | (slang) The guy selling cheap phones seemed sketchy. | We only have sketchy information about the storm. | (slang) The bridge looked really sketchy, so we didn't cross it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective; comparative «sketchier». The slang sense is very common in the USA, Canada and now the UK. Similar words: dodgy (UK), shady.

part of speech: adverb (skilfully — UK, Australia, NZ, Ireland; skillfully — USA)
meaning for a pupil: 1) In a way that shows skill and good ability; cleverly and well.
its sense in the lessons: In stories it describes how a character does something with expert hands or clever thinking: skilfully dribbling a ball, skilfully avoiding a question. In school reports it praises good work. It tells the reader the action was done well, not by luck.
examples from the lessons: She skilfully dribbled past three defenders. | The surgeon skilfully repaired the broken bone. | The baker skilfully decorated the cake. | He skilfully changed the subject when we asked about the broken window. | The story is skilfully written, with a twist at the end. | The pilot skilfully landed the plane in the wind.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: UK and Commonwealth «skilful, skilfully» (one l after «ski»); US «skillful, skillfully». Adjective: skilful; noun: skill.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A flat spoon or ladle with holes, used to lift things off the top of a liquid, like foam from soup. 2) A seabird that flies low and skims fish from the water's surface with its long lower beak. 3) A person or thing that skims, such as a stone that skips over water or a reader who reads quickly. 4) A device that removes oil, leaves or dirt from the surface of water, for example in a pool or after an oil spill. 5) (crime) A hidden device criminals fit to cash machines to steal card details.
its sense in the lessons: In cooking, a skimmer takes scum off jam or soup; in science and nature, skimmer birds and dragonflies (also called skimmers) live by water. In safety lessons on money, pupils learn that adults should cover the PIN and watch for skimmers on cash machines. In geography, skimmers clean up oil spills.
examples from the lessons: Grandma used a skimmer to take the foam off the jam. | The pool skimmer catches leaves before they sink. | A black skimmer flew low over the waves. | Ships used skimmers to clean up the oil spill. | Mum checks the cash machine for skimmers. | That flat stone is a great skimmer — it bounced five times!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; from «skim» (double m before -er). A skimming stone (UK) is a «skipping stone» in the USA.

part of speech: noun (a skipper, skippers); verb (skipper, skippers, skippered, skippering)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The captain of a ship or boat, especially a small one. 2) (informal, UK, Ireland, Australia, NZ) The captain of a sports team. 3) (informal) A friendly name for a boss or leader, like «Okay, skipper». 4) (verb) To be the captain of a boat or team. 5) A small butterfly that darts quickly from flower to flower. 6) A person who skips.
its sense in the lessons: In sport talk, especially cricket, rugby and football in the UK, Australia and New Zealand, the skipper is the team captain. In stories at sea the skipper gives orders. In nature lessons skippers are little brown or orange butterflies.
examples from the lessons: The skipper steered the fishing boat into the harbour. | Our skipper scored the winning try. | She skippered the netball team to victory. | "Aye, aye, skipper!" laughed the crew. | England's skipper lifted the trophy. | A tiny skipper butterfly landed on the thistle. | Dad calls his boss "skipper" as a joke.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; verb is regular (skippered). From Dutch «schipper» (shipman). Not just «a person who skips», though that is possible.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A large brown seabird of cold northern and southern seas that often chases other seabirds to make them drop or bring up their food, and attacks people who come near its nest.
its sense in the lessons: In science and nature lessons about seabirds and Antarctica, skuas show a «pirate» way of feeding called kleptoparasitism (stealing food). Visitors to Scottish islands such as Shetland are warned that great skuas, called «bonxies» locally, dive at people near their nests.
examples from the lessons: A skua chased the puffin until it dropped its fish. | Great skuas live on the islands of Shetland. | The skua swooped at our heads because we were near its nest. | In Antarctica, skuas steal penguin eggs. | Skuas are called the pirates of the sea. | The skua is brown and about the size of a big gull.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: skua, skuas. Say «SKYOO-uh». Local Scottish name for the great skua: «bonxie».

part of speech: verb (slash, slashes, slashed, slashing); noun (a slash, slashes)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To cut something with a long, quick, violent stroke of a blade. 2) To reduce prices, costs or numbers by a lot. 3) (noun) A long cut or a wild sweeping blow. 4) (noun) The sloping line symbol /, used in writing, fractions, dates and web addresses. 5) (UK, slang, rude-ish) «Have a slash» means go for a wee (urinate); it is crude and not for school.
its sense in the lessons: In maths the slash shows a fraction or division (3/4, 10/2); in dates in the UK 10/10/2026 means day/month/year, but in the USA it is month/day/year. In shops «prices slashed!» means big discounts. In stories slashing describes sword fights or ripped tyres. Phrases: «slash and burn» (clearing forest by cutting and burning, in geography).
examples from the lessons: Write three quarters as 3/4, with a slash. | The shop has slashed its prices by half. | The pirate slashed the rope with his sword. | Someone slashed the tyres on our car. | Type "and/or" with a slash between the words. | Farmers in some rainforests use slash-and-burn farming. | There was a long slash in the tent after the storm. | (UK slang, crude) "Back in a minute, I need a slash."
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb; plural «slashes». The symbol «/» is also called a forward slash or oblique; «\» is a backslash. In maths, a/b means a divided by b. A price «slashed by 50%» is halved.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A place where farm animals such as cows, pigs, sheep and chickens are killed for their meat. 2) (figurative) A place or event where many people are killed.
its sense in the lessons: In science, food and ethics lessons, slaughterhouses (also called abattoirs) are part of how meat reaches shops; pupils may discuss animal welfare rules and why some people choose to be vegetarian. In history and serious stories it can describe a battle. It is a serious word, not for jokes.
examples from the lessons: Cattle are taken to a slaughterhouse before their meat is sold. | Laws say animals must be treated without cruelty at the slaughterhouse. | The old slaughterhouse in town is now a museum. | Some people became vegetarian after learning about slaughterhouses. | Vets check the animals at the slaughterhouse. | In Kurt Vonnegut's novel, a slaughterhouse in Dresden gives the book its name.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Another word: «abattoir» (UK, Australia). Comes from «slaughter» (to kill animals for food, or to kill many people).

part of speech: adjective (Slavonic, also Slavic); noun (Slavonic — a language group or Church Slavonic)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To do with the Slavs, the peoples of central and eastern Europe such as Ukrainians, Poles, Czechs, Slovaks, Serbs, Croats, Bulgarians and Russians, or with their languages. 2) Old Church Slavonic is an old Slavic language used in church services and early books of Orthodox Christians. 3) Slavonia is also a region of Croatia; «Slavonian» describes it.
its sense in the lessons: In language and history lessons pupils learn that Ukrainian, Polish and Czech are Slavonic (Slavic) languages, related to each other like English is to German. In church history, Saints Cyril and Methodius created an alphabet for Old Church Slavonic in the 800s. In music, Dvořák wrote «Slavonic Dances».
examples from the lessons: Ukrainian and Polish are both Slavonic languages. | Dvořák's Slavonic Dances are lively pieces of music. | The priest read the prayers in Church Slavonic. | Many Slavonic languages use the Cyrillic alphabet. | My friend is learning a Slavonic language: Czech. | Slavonic peoples live across eastern and central Europe.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually written with a capital S. «Slavic» is more common in the USA, «Slavonic» in older British use. Do not confuse with «slave»; the history of the two words is debated, and calling Slavs «slaves» is offensive.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who gets up and walks about, or does other things, while still asleep.
its sense in the lessons: In science and health lessons sleepwalking is a sleep behaviour that is fairly common in children and usually stops as they grow up. Safety advice: gently guide a sleepwalker back to bed and keep doors and stairs safe. In stories a sleepwalker causes mystery or comedy. Myth: it is dangerous to wake a sleepwalker — it is not harmful, though they may be confused.
examples from the lessons: My little brother is a sleepwalker and once ended up in the kitchen. | The sleepwalker didn't remember anything in the morning. | Lead a sleepwalker gently back to bed. | Mum put a gate at the top of the stairs because I was a sleepwalker. | In the story, the sleepwalker wandered into the garden at midnight. | Many children are sleepwalkers for a while.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; one word. Verb: sleepwalk (sleepwalks, sleepwalked, sleepwalking). Also «sleepwalking» as a noun.

part of speech: noun (a sleigh, sleighs); verb (sleigh, sleighs, sleighed, sleighing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A large sledge pulled by horses, reindeer or dogs, for carrying people or goods over snow. 2) Father Christmas's or Santa Claus's sleigh, pulled by reindeer in Christmas stories. 3) (verb) To ride in a sleigh. 4) (slang) «Sleigh» is a joking Christmas spelling of slang «slay», meaning to do something brilliantly.
its sense in the lessons: In Christmas stories, songs («Jingle Bells», «Sleigh Ride») and cards Santa rides a sleigh with reindeer; in geography, sleighs are used in snowy places like Lapland, Canada and Alaska. In history, sleighs carried people across snow before cars.
examples from the lessons: Santa's sleigh is pulled by reindeer. | We rode in a horse-drawn sleigh in Lapland. | "Dashing through the snow, in a one-horse open sleigh…" | The sleigh bells jingled in the cold air. | They loaded wood onto the sleigh. | (slang, Christmas joke) "Your jumper looks great — you sleigh!"
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Sounds exactly like «slay» (to kill; in slang, to do brilliantly) — homophones. «eigh» says «ay» as in «eight». A smaller one for children is a «sledge» (UK) or «sled» (USA).

part of speech: adjective (sluggish, more sluggish, most sluggish); adverb sluggishly
meaning for a pupil: 1) Moving or working slowly, without energy. 2) (of a machine, body or computer) Slow to respond. 3) (of money, trade or the economy) Not growing much; slow. 4) (of a river) Flowing slowly.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life you feel sluggish when tired or after a big meal; a sluggish computer is slow. In geography a sluggish river flows slowly across flat land. In news «sluggish sales» or «a sluggish economy» means things are slow. Science: cold-blooded animals like lizards are sluggish when cold.
examples from the lessons: I feel sluggish after a big Sunday lunch. | The laptop is sluggish; it needs restarting. | Lizards are sluggish until the sun warms them. | The sluggish river wound slowly through the fields. | Toy sales were sluggish this year. | The sluggish traffic made us late for school.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective; from «slug» (the slow creature). Opposites: lively, brisk, quick.

part of speech: noun (slumber, slumbers); verb (slumber, slumbers, slumbered, slumbering)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (literary) Sleep. 2) (verb, literary) To sleep, often peacefully. 3) (figurative) A time of being quiet or inactive, like a volcano that has not erupted for years.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, poems and fairy tales slumber is a gentle, old-fashioned word for sleep — Sleeping Beauty falls into a deep slumber. In everyday talk, «slumber party» is a sleepover (USA). In science, a slumbering volcano is dormant.
examples from the lessons: The princess fell into a deep slumber. | The baby slumbered peacefully in her cot. | We had a slumber party with pillows and popcorn. | The dog was disturbed from its slumber by the doorbell. | The volcano has slumbered for a hundred years. | "Do not wake the dragon from its slumber," whispered the wizard.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Mostly literary; in normal talk say «sleep». «Slumber party» is American for a sleepover.

part of speech: adjective (slushy, slushier, slushiest); noun (a slushy, slushies — a drink)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Covered in or made of slush: half-melted, wet, dirty snow. 2) (informal) Soppy and too sentimental, like a soppy love story. 3) (noun, informal) A slushy (or slushie) is a frozen drink of crushed ice and sweet flavouring.
its sense in the lessons: In winter, slushy roads and pavements are slippery and wet, so safety talk warns to walk carefully. In shops and fairs, slushies are bright sugary ice drinks. In talk about films or books, «slushy» means soppy and over-sweet.
examples from the lessons: The snow turned slushy by lunchtime. | Watch out — the pavement is slushy and slippery. | I had a blue raspberry slushy at the cinema. | My sister loves slushy love songs. | The slushy road splashed our coats. | The film was too slushy for me.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective from «slush». The drink is spelled «slushy» or «slushie», plural «slushies». Too much slushy drink fast can give «brain freeze».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Fairly small; a bit small but not very.
its sense in the lessons: The ending «-ish» makes a word less exact: smallish, tallish, sevenish. In everyday talk it softens descriptions. In maths problems «smallish» is not a number; it gives no exact information.
examples from the lessons: We live in a smallish house near the park. | She has a smallish dog, about the size of a cat. | It was a smallish crowd, maybe fifty people. | Choose a smallish potato for the baby. | The school is smallish, with only one class per year. | The answer is a smallish number, somewhere under ten.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal; same meaning as «fairly small», «rather small». No comparative form is usually used.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (UK, informal, old-fashioned) A person or thing that is wonderful, very nice or very attractive: «She's a smasher». 2) A person or thing that smashes or breaks things, e.g. a can smasher or a record smasher.
its sense in the lessons: In British books and older family talk, «a smasher» is warm praise; grandparents may say «You're a little smasher». The plain sense appears in phrases like «record smasher» in sport or «Ball Smasher» as a toy or game name.
examples from the lessons: Thanks for the help, you're a smasher! | Grandad said the new puppy was a little smasher. | That goal was a real smasher! | The can smasher squashes tins for recycling. | She's a record smasher — she broke the school record three times. | "What a smasher of a day!" said Nan, looking at the blue sky.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Related British praise words: «smashing» (great), «brilliant». It is informal and a bit old-fashioned now.

part of speech: verb (smear, smears, smeared, smearing); noun (a smear, smears)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To spread something soft, sticky or oily over a surface, often messily. 2) (noun) A dirty mark made by something rubbed on a surface. 3) To make a mark blurry by rubbing, like smudging ink. 4) To spread false or unfair stories to damage someone's good name: «a smear campaign». 5) (medicine) A small sample of cells taken on a slide for testing; in the UK a «smear test» is a health check for grown-up women.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life you smear butter on toast or jam on your face; in art you smear paint with a finger. In science, a smear of cells on a slide is looked at under a microscope. In news and media lessons, a «smear» is a false attack on someone, linked to fake news and propaganda.
examples from the lessons: She smeared butter on her toast. | There was a smear of chocolate on his cheek. | Don't touch the wet paint, or you'll smear it. | The window was covered in greasy smears. | The politician said the story was a smear. | Mum went to the doctor for a routine smear test. | We put a smear of pond water on a slide and looked at it under the microscope.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb; noun countable. «Smear» and «smudge» are similar; smudging is usually ink or pencil. A «smear campaign» is not a cleaning plan; it is spreading lies about someone.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To take goods or people secretly and illegally into or out of a country, avoiding laws or taxes. 2) (informal) To take something secretly into or out of a place where it is not allowed: sneaking sweets into a cinema.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons smugglers in Cornwall and other coasts hid brandy, tea and tobacco to avoid taxes. In news, people-smuggling and drug-smuggling are serious crimes. In everyday jokes, children «smuggle» snacks into class or a pet into the house.
examples from the lessons: Smugglers used caves to hide barrels of brandy. | It is a crime to smuggle animals across borders. | He smuggled a torch into bed to read his book. | They tried to smuggle the puppy into the house. | Customs officers caught a man smuggling fake watches. | We smuggled a cake into the classroom for the teacher's surprise party.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb; double g. Person: «smuggler»; act: «smuggling». «Smuggle in» and «smuggle out» are common. Don't confuse with «snuggle» (cuddle up).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (USA, Canada, Australia) A soft sports shoe with a rubber sole, called a trainer in the UK. 2) A person who sneaks.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life in North America, «sneakers» are the shoes for PE and play; in the UK the word is «trainers», in Australia and New Zealand «sneakers» or «runners», in Ireland «runners». They are called sneakers because rubber soles are quiet so you can sneak about.
examples from the lessons: Put on your sneakers for gym class. | I got new sneakers with flashing lights. | My sneakers got muddy at the park. | In Britain they call sneakers "trainers." | He's a real sneaker — always creeping up behind you! | She tied her sneaker laces in a double knot.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually plural: a pair of sneakers. UK: trainers; Ireland: runners; old UK: plimsolls or pumps for simple canvas shoes.
