part of speech: noun (a snook, snooks); phrase (cock a snook)
meaning for a pupil: 1) «Cock a snook» (UK, old-fashioned) — to make a rude, mocking sign by putting your thumb on your nose and spreading your fingers; also to show open disrespect for someone or a rule. 2) A long, silvery fish of warm seas, caught for food and sport.
its sense in the lessons: In British writing, «cock a snook at» someone means to cheekily defy or mock them, like breaking a silly rule on purpose. Teachers may call the gesture rude. Anglers in the Caribbean and Florida fish for snook.
examples from the lessons: The cheeky boy cocked a snook at the bus driver. | The little shop cocked a snook at the big supermarket by giving everything away free. | Thumbing your nose — cocking a snook — is a rude gesture. | Dad caught a snook on his holiday in Florida. | The new band cocks a snook at old rules about music. | The pupils cocked a snook at the rain and played outside anyway.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Rare word; mostly heard in «cock a snook» (here «cock» means «tip up», not a rude word). Another phrase for the gesture: «thumb your nose». Not to be confused with «snooker», the game.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A warm, padded, waterproof outfit, all in one piece or as jacket and trousers, worn by children to play in the snow or cold.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life in Canada, the northern USA and other cold places, children wear snowsuits to school in winter; in safety lessons it shows how to keep warm and avoid frostbite. Babies wear snowsuits in pushchairs in cold weather (but not in car seats, because padding makes straps loose).
examples from the lessons: Put on your snowsuit before you go out to build a snowman. | My baby sister looks like a star in her pink snowsuit. | Canadian children wear snowsuits at recess in winter. | The snowsuit kept me dry when I rolled in the snow. | Take the snowsuit off in the car so the seat belt fits snugly. | I zipped up my snowsuit and ran out to go sledging.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; one word. Similar: ski suit, snow pants (USA), salopettes (UK, ski trousers with straps).

part of speech: verb (snuffle, snuffles, snuffled, snuffling — -ing form); adjective, noun (snuffling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Breathing noisily through the nose, as when you have a cold or are crying. 2) (of an animal) Sniffing about noisily, like a hedgehog or a pig looking for food. 3) (noun) The sound of this.
its sense in the lessons: In stories snuffling tells you a child is crying quietly or has a cold, or a small animal like a dog, pig or hedgehog is searching about. In nature writing hedgehogs are «snuffling» in the hedge at night.
examples from the lessons: The puppy was snuffling around the garden. | I heard a hedgehog snuffling in the leaves. | She lay in bed snuffling with a cold. | The pig went snuffling through the mud for food. | The little boy stopped crying and only kept snuffling. | We could hear snuffling under the shed.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: snuffle, snuffled. Similar: sniffling (a person with a cold or after crying), sniffing (smelling). «Snuffle» feels softer and more animal-like.

part of speech: verb (snuggle, snuggles, snuggled, snuggling); noun (a snuggle, snuggles)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To get into a warm, comfortable position, often close to someone or under a blanket. 2) To hold someone close and cuddle them. 3) (noun) A cuddle.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life children snuggle up with a book, a pet or a parent; in stories it shows warmth, safety and love. Phrases: «snuggle up», «snuggle down», «snuggle into».
examples from the lessons: We snuggled up under the blanket to watch a film. | The kittens snuggled together to keep warm. | Come and have a snuggle on the sofa. | She snuggled down in bed with her teddy. | The baby snuggled into Mum's arms. | On cold nights the dog snuggles at the end of my bed.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb; double g. Adjective: «snuggly». Similar: cuddle, nestle. Don't confuse with «smuggle».

part of speech: noun (a softy, softies — also spelled softie)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) A kind, gentle person who is easily moved or who can't be strict. 2) (informal, teasing) Someone thought too weak or scared, a wimp.
its sense in the lessons: In family talk «Dad's a big softy» means he is soft-hearted, maybe tough-looking but gentle and easy to persuade. Among children it can be a mild tease; teachers may remind them not to call others names. It is usually friendly.
examples from the lessons: Grandpa looks grumpy, but he's a big softy. | Don't be such a softy — the water's not that cold! | Mum's a softy and always lets us stay up a bit later. | The huge dog is a softy who's scared of cats. | Our coach is strict, but she's a softy at heart. | He pretends to be tough, but he cried at the film — what a softy!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; plural «softies». Spelled «softy» or «softie». Related: soft-hearted, «a soft touch» (easy to persuade).

part of speech: noun (soh — music; also spelled so, sol); abbreviation (SOH — maths)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (music) The fifth note of the do-re-mi (tonic sol-fa) scale: do, re, mi, fa, soh, la, ti, do. 2) (maths, SOH) The first part of SOH CAH TOA, a memory aid for trigonometry: Sine = Opposite ÷ Hypotenuse. 3) (informal) «SOH» short for «sense of humour», as in dating ads.
its sense in the lessons: In music lessons «soh» is the fifth note when singing do-re-mi; British books often spell it «soh», others «so» or «sol». In older pupils' maths, «SOH CAH TOA» helps remember sine, cosine and tangent. In «The Sound of Music» the song says «So, a needle pulling thread».
examples from the lessons: Sing up the scale: doh, ray, me, fah, soh, lah, te, doh. | Soh is the fifth note of the scale. | In "Do-Re-Mi", Maria sings that "so" is a needle pulling thread. | Remember SOH CAH TOA for your trigonometry test. | SOH: sine is opposite over hypotenuse. | Our choir warmed up by singing doh, me, soh, doh.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Not an everyday word on its own. Spellings vary: soh, so, sol. In maths, SOH means sin θ = opposite ÷ hypotenuse, e.g. opposite 3, hypotenuse 5 gives sin θ = 0.6.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Caring and anxious about someone's health, comfort or happiness; very attentive. 2) (formal) Eager or anxious to do something.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and formal writing a solicitous nurse, host or friend fusses kindly over someone. It is a «stiff exam voice» word for «caring» or «attentive». Phrases: «solicitous of», «solicitous about».
examples from the lessons: The nurse was solicitous, checking on us every hour. | He was solicitous about his grandmother's health. | The waiter was solicitous, refilling our water glasses. | She asked solicitously whether I was warm enough. | The host was solicitous of every guest's comfort. | Our neighbour was very solicitous when Mum was ill, bringing soup every day.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; say «suh-LISS-ih-tus». Noun: «solicitude». Related to «solicitor» (a lawyer in the UK) only in origin; they do not mean the same.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Standing together and supporting each other because you share the same goals, problems or feelings. 2) Support shown to a group in trouble by people who are not in it. 3) Solidarity (with a capital S) was a Polish trade union and freedom movement led by Lech Wałęsa from 1980.
its sense in the lessons: In citizenship and history lessons solidarity explains trade unions, protests and how people help each other — for example wearing a colour in solidarity with a friend, or countries showing solidarity with Ukraine. In stories it shows a group sticking together. Phrases: «in solidarity with», «show solidarity», «a sign of solidarity».
examples from the lessons: We wore odd socks in solidarity with children with Down syndrome. | The workers showed solidarity by striking together. | Many towns lit up in blue and yellow in solidarity with Ukraine. | Solidarity in Poland helped end communist rule. | Shaving their heads was an act of solidarity with their friend who had cancer. | The team felt real solidarity after the hard match.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. From «solid» (standing firm together). Not the same as «solitude» (being alone).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) The change of a liquid into a solid, such as water turning into ice or melted wax hardening. 2) (figurative) Becoming firmer or more fixed, like plans or opinions.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on states of matter, solidification is another word for freezing: the particles lose energy and lock into a fixed pattern. Lava's solidification makes igneous rocks; chocolate sets by solidification. Water freezes at 0 °C (32 °F).
examples from the lessons: Solidification happens when water turns to ice. | The lava cooled, and solidification made new rock. | Melted chocolate sets by solidification in the fridge. | Freezing is another name for solidification. | The solidification of candle wax happens quickly as it cools. | After much talking, there was a solidification of the plan.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable; from «solidify» (y → i + -cation). Opposite: melting (liquefaction is a different word for becoming liquid). For water, solidification and melting both happen at 0 °C.

part of speech: adjective (soluble; also less soluble, more soluble)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) Able to dissolve in a liquid, especially water, like sugar or salt. 2) (of a problem) Able to be solved.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on mixtures pupils test which substances are soluble (salt, sugar, coffee) and which are insoluble (sand, chalk); a soluble solid seems to disappear but is still there, and can be got back by evaporation. In everyday life, soluble tablets dissolve in water; soluble aspirin fizzes.
examples from the lessons: Sugar is soluble in water. | Sand is not soluble — it sinks to the bottom. | We tested which powders were soluble. | Mum dissolved a soluble tablet in a glass of water. | The puzzle looked hard, but it was soluble. | More sugar is soluble in hot tea than in cold tea.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: insoluble. Noun: solubility. Related verb: dissolve; solution (the mixture). Trap: dissolving is not melting — melting needs heat, dissolving needs a liquid. In maths-like science problems the mass is kept: 100 g water + 10 g salt makes 110 g of solution.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Sleepiness; the feeling of being drowsy and heavy, ready to fall asleep. 2) (literary) A sleepy, very quiet state of a place.
its sense in the lessons: A stiff, formal word: doctors write «somnolence» on reports, and novelists describe «the somnolence of a hot afternoon». In everyday talk people just say «sleepiness» or «drowsiness». Medicine labels may warn that a drug causes somnolence, meaning do not drive.
examples from the lessons: A warm room and a long talk filled the class with somnolence. | The medicine may cause somnolence, so don't operate machines. | The village lay in the somnolence of a summer afternoon. | The doctor noted the patient's somnolence. | After the big lunch, a pleasant somnolence crept over Grandad. | A strange somnolence fell over the castle in the fairy tale.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable; formal. Adjective: «somnolent». From Latin «somnus» (sleep), like «insomnia» (not being able to sleep).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal, old-fashioned) A friendly or slightly bossy way an older person speaks to a boy or young man: «Listen, sonny». 2) (a name) Sonny is also a nickname or first name.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and films an older character says «sonny» to a boy, sometimes warmly, sometimes to sound in charge («Now look here, sonny!»). It can sound patronising if said to a grown man. «Sonny Jim» is a British jokey version.
examples from the lessons: Off you go, sonny, and mind the road. | "Don't you talk back to me, sonny!" | The old fisherman said, "Want to hold the rod, sonny?" | "Sit down, Sonny Jim," laughed Grandad. | Sonny is the name of the dog next door. | "Here's your change, sonny," said the man at the market stall.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Used only when speaking to someone, not as «a sonny». Not the same as «sunny» (full of sunshine), though they sound alike — homophones.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A tall cereal grass grown in warm, dry countries, especially in Africa and Asia, for its grain, its sweet juice and animal feed. 2) The grain or syrup made from this plant.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and science lessons sorghum shows a crop that grows well in hot, dry places where wheat and rice struggle; it feeds millions of people in Africa and India. In the USA sorghum syrup is a sweetener; sorghum flour is gluten-free.
examples from the lessons: Sorghum grows well where there is little rain. | In Sudan many families eat porridge made from sorghum. | Farmers feed sorghum to cattle. | Sorghum flour is used in gluten-free bread. | We poured sorghum syrup on our pancakes in Tennessee. | Sorghum is one of the most important cereals in the world.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Say «SOR-gum» (the «h» is silent). A cereal like wheat, rice, maize and millet.

part of speech: adjective (sorrowful, more sorrowful, most sorrowful); adverb sorrowfully
meaning for a pupil: 1) Feeling or showing great sadness. 2) Causing sadness.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and poems «sorrowful» is a stronger, more literary word than «sad»: a sorrowful face, sorrowful music. In church, the Sorrowful Mysteries are prayers Catholics say about Jesus's suffering. Teachers suggest it in writing to show deep grief.
examples from the lessons: The puppy gave a sorrowful look when we left. | She sang a sorrowful song about a lost love. | It was a sorrowful day when our school closed. | He shook his head sorrowfully. | The sorrowful music made Mum cry. | Catholics pray the Sorrowful Mysteries of the rosary.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective from «sorrow» + «-ful» (one l). Similar: sad, mournful, grief-stricken. Opposite: joyful.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Deeply and well, of sleep: «sleep soundly». 2) Completely or heavily, of a defeat or punishment: «beaten soundly». 3) In a sensible, reliable or well-built way: «soundly made», «soundly argued».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life parents hope children «sleep soundly». In sport news a team «soundly beaten» lost by a lot. In science and essays a «soundly based» idea rests on good evidence.
examples from the lessons: The baby slept soundly all night. | Our team was soundly beaten 6–0. | The bridge was soundly built and lasted 200 years. | Her plan was soundly thought out. | He was soundly told off for lying. | After the long walk, we all slept soundly.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from «sound» (meaning healthy, solid, deep), not from «sound» (noise). «Safe and sound» means safe and unhurt.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A sharp, acid taste, like lemons or vinegar. 2) A bad-tempered, bitter or unfriendly mood or feeling.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on taste, sourness is one of the basic tastes (with sweet, salty, bitter and umami) and comes from acids. In stories, sourness of a character or a friendship shows bitterness or resentment.
examples from the lessons: The sourness of the lemon made my face screw up. | Add sugar to reduce the sourness of the rhubarb. | Our tongue can taste sourness, sweetness, saltiness, bitterness and umami. | There was a sourness between the two friends after the argument. | The milk had a sourness that told us it was off. | His sourness spoiled the party.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable; from «sour» + «-ness». Sour taste means acid; in science, acids taste sour (but never taste chemicals in the lab).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Soya beans, the seeds of a plant from East Asia that are rich in protein, used to make many foods. 2) Soy sauce, a dark salty sauce made from fermented soya beans, used in Chinese, Japanese and other cooking. 3) Made from soya: soy milk, soy yoghurt.
its sense in the lessons: In food and science lessons soy is an important plant protein; vegetarians and vegans eat tofu and soy milk. On food labels soy is a common allergen. In geography, huge areas of Brazil and the USA grow soya, sometimes linked to cutting down forests.
examples from the lessons: Can I have soy sauce with my sushi? | My cousin drinks soy milk because she can't have cow's milk. | Tofu is made from soy. | Soy is listed as an allergen on the label. | Most soya is fed to farm animals. | Dad marinated the chicken in soy and honey.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. US «soy», UK often «soya» (soya milk, soya beans). Allergy safety: someone allergic to soy must check labels.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person from Spain.
its sense in the lessons: In history and geography lessons, Spaniards such as Christopher Columbus's crews (though he was Italian) and later explorers sailed to the Americas; today Spaniards speak Spanish, Catalan, Basque and Galician. In everyday talk, «a Spaniard» means a Spanish person.
examples from the lessons: My football coach is a Spaniard from Valencia. | Rafael Nadal is a famous Spaniard who plays tennis. | The Spaniards built forts across Central and South America. | Two Spaniards and a Portuguese sailor joined the crew. | Many Spaniards eat dinner late in the evening. | The Spaniard on our team scored two goals.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always with a capital S. Adjective is «Spanish», not «Spaniard»: «a Spanish town», «the Spanish people». Do not confuse with «spaniel» (a dog breed, whose name comes from Spain too).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Using only a little of something; carefully and not wastefully.
its sense in the lessons: In cooking, «use salt sparingly» means only a pinch; in health, the food pyramid says to eat sugary foods sparingly. In science and art, use glue or paint sparingly. In everyday life, people use water sparingly in a drought.
examples from the lessons: Use the glue sparingly or it will make a mess. | Eat sweets sparingly. | Water was used sparingly during the drought. | Apply the cream sparingly to the rash. | The writer used capital letters sparingly. | She praised us sparingly, so her praise meant a lot.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from «sparing» (careful with amounts), from «spare». Opposite: generously, lavishly. In maths problems it may mean a smaller amount is used each time.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A sudden tightening of a muscle that you cannot control, which may hurt. 2) A sudden short burst of a feeling or action, like a spasm of coughing or of anger.
its sense in the lessons: In health and PE lessons a muscle spasm or cramp can happen when tired or not warmed up; stretching helps. In stories «a spasm of pain» or «a spasm of fear» shows a sudden strong feeling. Phrases: «back spasm», «go into spasm».
examples from the lessons: He felt a spasm in his leg near the end of the race. | A spasm of coughing stopped her from speaking. | Hiccups are spasms of the muscle under your lungs. | Gentle stretching can ease a muscle spasm. | A spasm of fear went through him when the light went out. | Her back went into spasm when she lifted the box.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Say «SPAZ-um». Adjective: spasmodic (happening in fits). Trap: the short word «spaz» or «spastic» used as an insult is very offensive to disabled people; never use it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A common kind of mint plant with pointed leaves and a fresh, sweet taste. 2) The flavour made from it, used in chewing gum, toothpaste and sweets.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life spearmint flavours gum and toothpaste; in science and gardening lessons it is a herb that spreads quickly. It is milder and sweeter than peppermint.
examples from the lessons: I like spearmint chewing gum. | Spearmint grows like crazy in the garden. | The toothpaste tastes of spearmint. | We added spearmint leaves to the lemonade. | Spearmint is sweeter than peppermint. | Grandma made spearmint tea for my sore tummy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable; one word. Named for its spear-shaped leaves.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Focusing on one particular subject, skill or job and becoming an expert in it. 2) The particular subject or area someone focuses on. 3) (science) The way a body part, cell or animal is adapted for one special job.
its sense in the lessons: In careers talk, doctors and scientists choose a specialisation, such as heart doctor or children's doctor. In science lessons, cell specialisation means red blood cells, nerve cells and muscle cells each have a special shape for their job. In history and economics, specialisation means people doing one job well and trading.
examples from the lessons: Her specialisation is children's medicine. | Red blood cells show specialisation: they carry oxygen. | Specialisation lets each worker do one job very well. | At university you choose a specialisation. | The hummingbird's long beak is a specialisation for drinking nectar. | Dr Lee's specialisation is volcanoes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK spelling with -s- (specialisation); US spelling «specialization». From «specialise/specialize». Not the same as «speciality».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A food or dish that a place, person or restaurant is famous for and makes very well. 2) A thing someone is especially good at or knows a lot about. 3) A special branch of study or work, such as a doctor's speciality.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life a café's speciality is its best dish; Cornish pasties are a speciality of Cornwall. In jokes about family, «Dad's speciality is burnt toast». In careers talk, a doctor's speciality is their area, like heart medicine.
examples from the lessons: Fish and chips is the speciality of the seaside café. | Pancakes are Grandma's speciality. | Haggis is a Scottish speciality. | Her speciality is drawing horses. | The doctor's speciality is skin problems. | Getting lost is my brother's speciality! | Pasta is a speciality of Italy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «specialities». UK: speciality (5 syllables); US: «specialty» (3 syllables: SPESH-ul-tee). «Specialisation» is more about choosing to focus.

part of speech: verb (specify, specifies, specified, specifying — past form); adjective (specified)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Past form of «specify»: said or stated clearly and exactly. 2) (adjective) Named or fixed clearly in advance, as in «at the specified time», «a specified amount».
its sense in the lessons: In maths and science, «the specified unit» means the exact unit the question asks for; instructions say «in the specified box». In everyday life, rules and forms give specified times, prices and sizes. Phrases: «unless otherwise specified», «as specified».
examples from the lessons: The question specified that we must answer in centimetres. | Arrive at the specified time, 9 o'clock. | Use the specified amount of flour: 200 g. | The rules specified that each team has five players. | Unless otherwise specified, round to one decimal place. | She specified that she wanted a blue bike, not a red one.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: specify → specified (y → i). «Specified» means exact and stated, not just «special». In maths word problems, use the specified unit or rounding, or your answer may be marked wrong.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To guess or form ideas about something when you don't have all the facts. 2) (money) To buy things like shares, land or currencies hoping to sell them later for more, with a risk of losing money.
its sense in the lessons: In history, science and reading lessons, pupils speculate (make guesses) about why something happened, then look for evidence; teachers say «don't just speculate, check». In news, people speculate about who will win or why something happened. In money lessons, speculating is risky investing.
examples from the lessons: Scientists speculate that there might be water on that planet. | Everyone speculated about who the new teacher would be. | Don't speculate — read the text and find the answer. | Newspapers speculated about why the singer quit. | People who speculate on shares can win or lose a lot of money. | We can only speculate about how the Stone Age people moved the stones.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Noun: speculation; adjective: speculative. Speculation is a guess, not a proven fact; a good answer says «we can only speculate» when there is no evidence.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An instrument in a car, bike, train or other vehicle that shows how fast it is going.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life a car's speedometer shows speed in miles per hour (UK and USA) or kilometres per hour (Canada, Australia, New Zealand, Ireland). In maths and science lessons, it links to speed = distance ÷ time; road safety lessons remind drivers to keep to speed limits.
examples from the lessons: The speedometer showed 30 miles per hour. | Dad checked the speedometer as we passed the school. | My bike has a little speedometer on the handlebars. | In Ireland, speedometers show kilometres per hour. | The needle on the speedometer went up as the train sped along. | The speedometer reads 0 when the car is parked.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Say «spee-DOM-ih-ter». A speedometer shows speed at this moment, not average speed. In maths: 60 mph means 60 miles in one hour; 1 mile ≈ 1.6 km.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A small wild plant with tiny bright blue flowers, often found in grass, lawns and hedges.
its sense in the lessons: In nature walks and science lessons about wildflowers in the UK and Ireland, speedwell is one of the easiest blue flowers to spot in spring. Its old name «bird's-eye» comes from the white centre.
examples from the lessons: Tiny blue speedwell flowers grew all over the lawn. | We found speedwell on our nature walk. | Speedwell flowers have four petals. | The bees visited the speedwell in the hedge. | Germander speedwell is a common British wildflower. | Speedwell flowers close up when it rains.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable for kinds. One word. The flower's Latin name is Veronica.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A kind of soft moss that grows in wet bogs and can hold huge amounts of water; it slowly turns into peat.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography lessons sphagnum moss builds peat bogs, which store a lot of carbon and help fight climate change; draining or digging bogs releases carbon. In history, sphagnum was used as wound dressing in the First World War because it soaks up liquid and slows germs. Gardeners use it for hanging baskets.
examples from the lessons: Sphagnum moss can hold many times its weight in water. | Peat bogs are made of old sphagnum. | In World War I, people collected sphagnum to dress wounds. | Bog bodies were preserved by sphagnum and peat. | Gardeners line baskets with sphagnum moss. | Protecting bogs with sphagnum helps store carbon.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Say «SFAG-num» (ph = f). Also called bog moss or peat moss.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A device or tool that splits something, like a log splitter or a cable splitter that lets one signal go to two machines. 2) (UK, informal) A person who leaves a group or party to form a new one. 3) (informal) In sorting and naming things, a splitter divides them into many small groups (opposite: a lumper). 4) (cricket, baseball) A type of throw or bowl that makes the ball drop or move.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life a headphone splitter lets two people listen to one device; a log splitter chops firewood. In science, «lumpers and splitters» argue about how many species there are. In politics news, «splitters» break away from a party.
examples from the lessons: We used a headphone splitter to share the music. | Grandad uses a log splitter to chop wood. | The TV splitter sends the signal to two rooms. | The splitters left the party and started their own. | Some scientists are lumpers; others are splitters who name many species. | He pitched a splitter and struck out the batter.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; from «split» (double t). In plumbing and electronics it's a common shop word.

part of speech: verb (splutter, splutters, spluttered, spluttering); noun (a splutter, splutters)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To speak quickly and with difficulty, making spitting sounds, because you are angry, shocked or embarrassed. 2) To cough or spit noisily, as when choking on food or water. 3) (of an engine or fire) To make a series of short, uneven popping noises.
its sense in the lessons: In stories «spluttered» shows a character is shocked or furious and can't speak smoothly. It also describes a choking cough or an old car engine starting badly. Phrases: «splutter into life», «spluttered with laughter».
examples from the lessons: But — but — that's not fair! he spluttered. | She spluttered when the water went up her nose. | The old car spluttered and stopped. | The candle spluttered in the wind. | I spluttered with laughter at the joke. | The engine spluttered into life.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb; double t. Similar: sputter (more common in the USA for engines), stammer (speaking with breaks).

part of speech: verb (spout, spouts, spouted, spouting — -ing form); noun (spouting — Australia, NZ)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (of a liquid) Pouring or shooting out in a strong stream, like water from a fountain or a whale's blowhole. 2) (informal, disapproving) Talking a lot, often boringly or without thinking, as in «spouting nonsense». 3) (Australia, New Zealand) Spouting is the gutter along the edge of a roof that collects rainwater.
its sense in the lessons: In science and nature, whales are seen spouting when they breathe out; volcanoes and geysers spout water or lava. In everyday talk «spouting off» means talking too much or showing off what you think. In Australia and New Zealand, people clean leaves out of the spouting.
examples from the lessons: The whale was spouting water high into the air. | Water came spouting out of the broken pipe. | He's always spouting nonsense about football. | Stop spouting off and listen! | The geyser was spouting every ten minutes. | (NZ) Dad climbed the ladder to clear the spouting.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. A «spout» is the part of a teapot or jug where liquid comes out. «Spout off» is informal and a bit rude about the speaker.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A tiny, wingless, six-legged animal that lives in soil and leaf litter and jumps by flicking a spring-like tail under its body.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about soil and minibeasts, springtails are among the most common tiny creatures, breaking down dead leaves and helping make soil. Pupils may find them with a magnifying glass or in a Tullgren funnel. They are harmless to people.
examples from the lessons: We found springtails in the leaf litter under the hedge. | A springtail jumps by flicking its tail. | Springtails help break down dead leaves. | You need a magnifying glass to see a springtail. | Thousands of springtails can live in one square metre of soil. | Springtails are not insects, though they look like them.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; one word. Scientists today usually class them as six-legged animals related to insects but not true insects.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A small magical creature like a fairy or elf in stories, often playful or mischievous. 2) (computing) A small picture or character that moves around in a computer game, such as in Scratch. 3) (science) A rare flash of red light high above a thunderstorm. 4) Sprite (with a capital S) is a lemon-lime fizzy drink brand.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, sprites are water or air spirits in myths and fairy tales; in coding lessons with Scratch, pupils program sprites (like the cat) to move, talk and react. In science, «red sprites» are a kind of upper-air lightning photographed from planes and space.
examples from the lessons: In Scratch, make the sprite move ten steps. | A water sprite lived in the river in the fairy tale. | Change your sprite's costume to make it look like it's walking. | The mischievous sprite hid the farmer's boots. | Red sprites flash high above thunderclouds. | Can I have a Sprite with my lunch?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Say to rhyme with «bright». Similar: fairy, pixie, elf. In Scratch, a sprite is any object on the stage besides the background.

part of speech: verb (stabilise, stabilises, stabilised, stabilising — -ing form); adjective (stabilising)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Making something steady and less likely to move, fall or change. 2) Becoming steady after a time of change, like prices, weather or a patient's health. 3) (adjective) Helping to keep something steady: «stabilising wheels», «stabilising effect».
its sense in the lessons: In science and technology lessons, a wide base or extra wheels stabilise a model; on bikes, stabilisers (UK; training wheels, USA) help young riders. In health news, a patient's condition is «stabilising» after an emergency. In money news, prices are stabilising after rises.
examples from the lessons: The doctors are stabilising the injured man. | His temperature is stabilising now. | Stabilising wheels help small children learn to ride. | The wide base is stabilising the tower so it won't topple. | Prices are slowly stabilising after a big jump. | The ship has fins for stabilising it in rough seas.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK spelling «stabilise, stabilising», US «stabilize, stabilizing». Noun: stabiliser/stabilizer, stability. Adjective «stable» (steady); opposite «unstable».

part of speech: verb (stagger, staggers, staggered, staggering); noun (a stagger)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To walk or move unsteadily, almost falling, because you are hurt, tired, dizzy or carrying something heavy. 2) To shock or amaze someone very much. 3) To arrange things so they do not all happen at the same time, like staggered lunch breaks or a staggered start in a race. 4) (noun) An unsteady walk.
its sense in the lessons: In stories a character staggers when hurt, exhausted or dizzy. In news and maths, big numbers «stagger» people (they are amazing). At school, lunch times and race starts are staggered so lanes are fair: runners on outer lanes start ahead because the outer track is longer.
examples from the lessons: He staggered under the weight of the heavy box. | The tired runner staggered over the finish line. | I was staggered by how much the trip cost. | Lunch breaks are staggered so the hall isn't too crowded. | In the 200 m race, the start is staggered. | She staggered out of the spinning teacups ride laughing.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb; double g. «Staggered» (adjective) means shocked or arranged at different times. «Staggering» (adjective) means amazing. In maths, staggered times means start times spaced out, e.g. groups every 10 minutes.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Very surprising and shocking, because it is so large or amazing. 2) (verb) Walking unsteadily, almost falling.
its sense in the lessons: In news, science and maths talk, «a staggering number» means a hugely large number, like the staggering distance to the stars. In stories it can mean walking unsteadily. Phrases: «a staggering amount», «staggering success».
examples from the lessons: The cost of the new stadium is staggering. | A staggering million people watched the parade. | The view from the mountain top was staggering. | He came staggering out of the smoke. | The Sun is a staggering 150 million kilometres from Earth. | Her success was staggering for someone so young.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective use is very common; the meaning is «amazing because so big». Similar: astonishing, astounding. In maths writing it gives feeling, not a number.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A set of stairs inside or outside a building, often with the walls or space around it.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and safety lessons, stairways are routes out of a building in a fire; lifts (elevators) should not be used. In stories and songs, a stairway can lead somewhere mysterious or symbolic, like «a stairway to the stars».
examples from the lessons: Use the stairway, not the lift, if there's a fire. | A narrow stairway led up to the attic. | The old castle had a spiral stairway. | Don't play on the stairway — someone might trip. | The stairway was lit with small lamps. | The emergency stairway is at the end of the corridor.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; one word. Similar: staircase, stairs, steps. Do not confuse «stair» with «stare» (to look hard) — homophones.

part of speech: noun (a stake, stakes — plural form); verb (stake, stakes, staked, staking)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Pointed wooden or metal posts pushed into the ground, for example to hold up plants or a tent. 2) Money or something valuable risked in a bet or game; «the stakes are high» means a lot can be won or lost. 3) A share in a business: «a stake in the company». 4) (verb) Third-person form of «stake»: risks something, or marks land with posts. 5) (history) A post at which people were once killed by burning, as in «burned at the stake».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, gardeners use stakes to support tomatoes and tents are fixed with stakes (also called pegs). In sport and games, «high stakes» means a match matters a lot. In history lessons, people accused of heresy or witchcraft were sometimes burned at the stake. In money talk, «a stake» is part ownership. Phrases: «at stake» (at risk), «high stakes», «stake a claim».
examples from the lessons: Push the stakes into the ground to hold the tent. | Tie the beans to the stakes so they grow straight. | The stakes are high: the winner goes to the final. | Our team's place in the league is at stake. | He staked all his sweets on winning the game. | Joan of Arc was burned at the stake in 1431. | She owns a stake in her family's bakery.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Homophone: «steaks» (pieces of meat) — «stakes» are posts or bets. «At stake» means at risk (not a meat!). In maths with money, «stake» is the amount bet.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Making things the same size, shape, quality or way of working, so they fit together or can be compared. 2) Agreeing on standard rules, units or spellings that everyone uses.
its sense in the lessons: In history and science lessons, standardisation of measures (metric units), time (railway time and time zones) and spelling (dictionaries like Johnson's in 1755) made life easier. In technology, standard plugs, USB-C chargers and paper sizes like A4 are examples. In maths, standard units let everyone compare answers.
examples from the lessons: Standardisation of units means a metre is the same everywhere. | Railway timetables led to the standardisation of time across Britain. | Standardisation of plugs means one charger fits many phones. | Dictionaries helped the standardisation of spelling. | Paper sizes such as A4 are the result of standardisation. | The factory brought in standardisation so all parts would fit.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK spelling «standardisation», US «standardization». From «standardise/standardize». Related: standard (a rule or level).

part of speech: verb (standardise, standardises, standardised, standardising — past form); adjective (standardised)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Past form of «standardise»: made things the same or fitted to one rule or standard. 2) (adjective) Done or made in the same way for everyone, so results can be compared: «a standardised test».
its sense in the lessons: In school, «standardised tests» such as SATs in England or state tests in the USA are the same for every pupil so results can be compared. In history, measures and spellings were standardised. In science, standardised units let experiments be repeated anywhere.
examples from the lessons: The test is standardised, so everyone answers the same questions. | Spelling was standardised in the 1700s and 1800s. | The parts are standardised so they fit any machine. | Standardised units help scientists share results. | Railway gauges were standardised so trains could travel across the country. | The forms were standardised to make them easier to fill in.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb; UK spelling «-ised», US «-ized» (standardized). A «standardised score» in tests is adjusted so different tests can be compared, e.g. 100 = average.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) Dust made in old stars and spread in space when they die; the atoms in our bodies were made inside stars long ago. 2) (literary) A magical, dreamy or romantic quality, like sparkle or charm.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on space, «we are made of stardust» is a true idea: elements such as carbon, oxygen and iron in our bodies were made inside stars. In stories and songs, stardust means magic, glitter and dreams.
examples from the lessons: The iron in your blood was made in stars — you are stardust! | The spacecraft collected stardust from a comet's tail. | The fairy sprinkled stardust over the sleeping town. | The singer had a bit of stardust about her. | Scientists study stardust to learn how stars make new elements. | The song says the night sky was full of stardust.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable; one word. A NASA mission called Stardust brought comet dust back to Earth in 2006.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who stares, looking at someone or something for a long time with fixed eyes.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and stories, «a starer» can make people uncomfortable; in kindness lessons, children learn that staring at people who look different can hurt, so it is better to smile or say hello. Rare word; people usually say «someone who stares».
examples from the lessons: The baby is a real starer — she watches everyone on the bus. | Don't be a starer; it's rude. | The starer at the window watched us all afternoon. | My cat is a starer; she sits and looks at the wall. | The starers on the platform watched the steam train pass. | Don't be a starer at the boy in the wheelchair; just say hello.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; rare. From «stare» (drop the e, add -er). Homophone trap: «stare» (look) vs «stair» (step).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Serious suffering or death caused by having little or no food for a long time. 2) (informal, exaggerated) Being very hungry: «I'm dying of starvation!» said jokingly before tea.
its sense in the lessons: In history and geography lessons, starvation happens in famines, sieges and wars, like the Irish Great Famine (1845–1852) or the Holodomor in Ukraine (1932–1933); in news, aid groups bring food to people facing starvation. In science, the body without food uses its fat and then muscle. In everyday jokes children exaggerate hunger. Phrases: «starvation wages» (very low pay), «die of starvation».
examples from the lessons: During the famine, many people died of starvation. | Aid agencies are working to prevent starvation in the war zone. | The Holodomor caused the starvation of millions of Ukrainians. | Animals in the snow can face starvation in a hard winter. | "Is tea ready? I'm dying of starvation!" | Using hunger and starvation as a weapon of war is against international law.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable; from «starve» (drop e, add -ation). Hunger is the feeling; starvation is the dangerous state. Jokey use is exaggeration, not literal.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Statues as a group: the statues in a place or collection. 2) The art of making statues.
its sense in the lessons: In museum visits and history or art lessons, «Roman statuary» means Roman statues together. Gardens of grand houses have «garden statuary». It is a stiff, formal word.
examples from the lessons: The museum has a fine collection of Greek statuary. | Garden statuary lined the path to the house. | The church was full of marble statuary. | The guidebook describes the palace's statuary. | Ancient statuary was often painted in bright colours. | The palace garden is famous for its statuary and fountains.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable; formal. Say «STATCH-oo-uh-ree». A single piece is «a statue». Myth: ancient Greek statues were plain white — many were painted.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (of a person, usually a woman) Tall, graceful and impressive, like a statue. 2) Very still, like a statue.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and descriptions, statuesque praises someone's tall, elegant figure and calm presence. It is a formal or literary word, often in descriptions of athletes, models or queens.
examples from the lessons: The statuesque queen stood at the top of the stairs. | The statuesque basketball player towered over us. | She stood statuesque and silent while the crowd cheered. | The heron waited in the water, statuesque. | The actress looked statuesque in a long gown. | The statuesque giraffe stood perfectly still under the tree.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say «statch-oo-ESK»; the «-esque» means «like» (as in «picturesque»). It is a compliment, not about being made of stone.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Being firm and not shaking or wobbling. 2) Being regular and even, without sudden changes. 3) Being calm, sensible and reliable.
its sense in the lessons: In PE and science, steadiness means balance: a steady hand in a hoop-and-wire game, steadiness on a balance beam. In stories, steadiness of a character means they are calm and trustworthy in a crisis. In maths and science graphs, steadiness means a steady rate, no jumps.
examples from the lessons: Holding the tray, the waiter showed great steadiness. | Surgeons need steadiness of hand. | Her steadiness in the crisis calmed everyone. | The steadiness of the rain meant the river rose slowly. | We admired the steadiness of the tightrope walker. | The graph shows the steadiness of the temperature all day.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable; from «steady» (y → i + -ness). Opposite: shakiness, unsteadiness.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A boat driven by a steam engine, often with a large paddle wheel, used especially on rivers in the 1800s.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, steamboats show the Industrial Revolution: they carried passengers and goods up and down rivers like the Mississippi. In film history, Mickey Mouse first appeared with sound in «Steamboat Willie» (1928). Today some steamboats run for tourists.
examples from the lessons: The steamboat puffed slowly up the Mississippi River. | Mark Twain once piloted steamboats. | Steamboats carried cotton and passengers in the 1800s. | Mickey Mouse first whistled in "Steamboat Willie." | We went on a steamboat trip on the lake. | The steamboat's paddle wheel churned the water.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; one word. A large one is a «steamship». Bigger idea: steam power changed transport (trains, ships, factories).

part of speech: noun (a steamroller, steamrollers); verb (steamroller, steamrollers, steamrollered, steamrollering)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A heavy machine with big, wide rollers that flattens roads; once powered by steam, now usually by diesel (often called a road roller). 2) (verb, informal) To force something through or defeat someone easily with great power, ignoring objections. 3) (noun, figurative) A force that crushes all opposition.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and children's books, steamrollers flatten new roads. In news and sport, a team «steamrollered» another means beat them easily; a leader «steamrollers» a plan through means forced it without listening.
examples from the lessons: The steamroller flattened the new road. | The cartoon cat was squashed flat by a steamroller. | The team steamrollered their opponents 8–0. | The boss steamrollered the plan through the meeting. | Old steamrollers puff smoke at the vintage show. | We watched the steamroller go slowly back and forth.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; one word. Past: steamrollered (or steamrolled in the USA). A modern machine is a road roller.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (history) An upright stone slab or pillar with writing or carvings on it, put up as a monument, gravestone or to record laws or events. 2) (science, botany) The central core of a plant's root or stem, which carries water and food.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons about ancient Egypt, Mesopotamia, the Maya and China, stelae recorded laws, victories and names of rulers; Hammurabi's law code is carved on a stele, and the Rosetta Stone is part of a stele. In older pupils' biology, the stele carries water through a root.
examples from the lessons: Hammurabi's laws were carved on a tall black stele. | The Rosetta Stone is a broken piece of a stele. | The Maya put up stelae to honour their kings. | The stele marks the grave of an ancient soldier. | We saw a carved stele in the British Museum. | The archaeologists cleaned the stele to read the old writing.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say «STEE-lee» (two syllables). Plural «stelae» (STEE-lee) or «steles». Do not mix up with «steel» (metal) or «steal» (take).

meaning for a pupil: 1) The woman who is married to (or the partner of) your father but is not your birth mother.
its sense in the lessons: In family lessons, stepmothers are part of stepfamilies or blended families, formed when a parent remarries after a divorce or a death. Many stepmothers are loving and kind. In fairy tales such as «Cinderella», «Snow White» and «Hansel and Gretel», the «wicked stepmother» is a stock villain — a story pattern, not the truth about real stepmothers.
examples from the lessons: My stepmother helps me with my homework. | Dad married my stepmother when I was six. | Cinderella's stepmother made her do all the chores. | I call my stepmother by her first name. | My stepmother and my mum both came to the school play. | Fairy tales often have a wicked stepmother, but mine is lovely.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; one word. Related: stepfather, stepparent, stepbrother, stepsister, stepchild, stepdaughter, stepson. A «half-sister» shares one parent with you; a «stepsister» shares no parent. Short informal forms: «stepmum» (UK), «stepmom» (USA).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Stiffness is being hard to bend or move, like a new board or a stiff collar. 2) Stiffness in the body is a tight, achy feeling in your muscles or joints, often after exercise or sleeping badly. 3) Stiffness in how someone acts is being too formal, cold or awkward, not relaxed. 4) (science) Stiffness is how strongly a material or spring resists being bent or stretched.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life you hear about stiffness in a sore neck, stiff legs after a long walk, or stiffness that goes away after stretching. In science and design, engineers test the stiffness of beams, rulers and springs. In stories, stiffness in a character's voice or manners tells the reader they are nervous, upset or very proper. Phrases: «muscle stiffness», «morning stiffness», «stiffness in the joints».
examples from the lessons: I felt some stiffness in my legs after the cross-country race. | Gentle stretching helps reduce stiffness. | Grandad's knees have a bit of stiffness in cold weather. | The stiffness of the cardboard made it hard to fold. | We measured the stiffness of three different rulers in science. | There was a stiffness in her voice when she said hello. | The stiffness of the new shoes gave me blisters. | After the long car ride, the stiffness in my back made me groan.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «some stiffness», not «a stiffness» (except «a stiffness in his manner»). From the adjective «stiff» + -ness. Do not confuse with «stuffiness» (an airless room or a blocked nose).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A stimulant is a substance that makes your body and brain more awake and active for a while, such as the caffeine in coffee, tea and cola. 2) Some stimulants are strong drugs, some used as medicine and some illegal, that can be harmful. 3) A stimulant can also be anything that gets something going or growing faster, like a stimulant to the economy or to the imagination.
its sense in the lessons: In health and science lessons, «stimulant» describes caffeine, nicotine and some medicines that speed up the heart and the nervous system. In safety talk, children learn that energy drinks contain stimulants and are not meant for children, and that illegal stimulants are dangerous. In sport, some stimulants are banned. Phrases: «a mild stimulant», «caffeine is a stimulant», «banned stimulants».
examples from the lessons: Caffeine is a stimulant found in coffee, tea and cola. | Energy drinks contain stimulants, so they are not for kids. | The doctor said the medicine is a mild stimulant. | Some athletes have been banned for taking stimulants. | A stimulant can make your heart beat faster. | Nicotine in cigarettes is a stimulant and is very addictive. | For Mum, a strong cup of tea is her morning stimulant. | The new park was a stimulant for local businesses.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: «a stimulant», «stimulants». The opposite kind of substance, which slows the body down, is a «depressant» or «sedative». Related words: «stimulate», «stimulating», «stimulus» (a different noun: a thing that causes a reaction).

part of speech: verb (past tense and past participle of stimulate: stimulate, stimulates, stimulated, stimulating); adjective (stimulated)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Stimulated is the past form of «stimulate»: made something more active, or made it start or grow. 2) If a person is stimulated, their mind is interested, excited and full of ideas. 3) (science) In the body, a nerve, muscle or sense is stimulated when something triggers it to react, like light stimulating the eye.
its sense in the lessons: In science, «stimulated» describes how nerves, cells or plants respond to light, heat, touch or chemicals. In school life, teachers want pupils to be stimulated, meaning curious and engaged. In money and news, spending can be «stimulated» by low prices. Phrases: «stimulated by», «well stimulated», «over-stimulated» (too much noise and excitement, often said of babies, pets or autistic children).
examples from the lessons: The trip to the museum stimulated our interest in dinosaurs. | Bright light stimulated the cells in the eye. | The toddler was over-stimulated by the noisy party and started crying. | Lower prices stimulated sales at the shop. | The story stimulated lots of questions from the class. | Warm weather stimulated the seeds to sprout. | I felt stimulated and full of ideas after the science fair.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: stimulate → stimulated. Used both actively («The film stimulated discussion») and passively («We were stimulated by the talk»). «Over-stimulated» means too much input, not «very clever». Do not confuse with «simulated» (copied or faked, as in a simulated flight).

part of speech: adjective (stimulating, more stimulating, most stimulating); verb (present participle of stimulate)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Stimulating means interesting and exciting in a way that makes you think and want to know more. 2) Stimulating can mean making something more active, like a drink stimulating your brain. 3) As a verb form, stimulating is what you are doing when you stimulate something: «They are stimulating growth».
its sense in the lessons: In school, teachers and reports praise «a stimulating lesson», «a stimulating classroom» or «stimulating books», meaning ones that make pupils curious. In science, «stimulating» describes what causes nerves, muscles or plants to react. Phrases: «a stimulating discussion», «intellectually stimulating», «stimulating environment».
examples from the lessons: It was a really stimulating science lesson about volcanoes. | Puzzles are a stimulating way to spend a rainy afternoon. | The teacher made the classroom bright and stimulating. | We had a stimulating discussion about whether robots can think. | Coffee has a stimulating effect on the brain. | Fertiliser works by stimulating plant growth. | Grandma finds crosswords stimulating. | The zoo gives the monkeys stimulating toys so they do not get bored.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As an adjective it means «interesting, thought-provoking», not «very fun» exactly. Comparative: «more stimulating». Opposite: «dull», «boring», «unstimulating».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A stinger is the sharp part on an insect or animal, such as a bee, wasp or scorpion, that it uses to sting. 2) A stinger can be an animal or plant that stings, like a stinging jellyfish (Australia) or a nettle. 3) (informal) A stinger is a painful hit, remark or ending, something that «stings».
its sense in the lessons: In science and nature lessons, children learn that bees, wasps, scorpions and stingrays have stingers for defence. In safety lessons, you learn to scrape out a bee stinger gently and to tell an adult. In Australia, «stingers» often means box jellyfish and other stinging jellyfish in the sea in summer. Phrases: «the bee's stinger», «stinger suit», «stinger season» (Australia).
examples from the lessons: A honeybee leaves its stinger in your skin. | Mum scraped the stinger out with a bank card. | A scorpion's stinger is at the end of its tail. | The stingray's stinger is on its tail. | We wore stinger suits when we swam at the beach in Queensland. | The wasp waved its stinger at us. | That last goal was a real stinger for the other team. | Only female bees and wasps have stingers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Myth: all bees die after stinging — only honeybees usually do, because their barbed stinger gets stuck; wasps and bumblebees can sting again. The word for the injury is «a sting», not «a stinger».

part of speech: noun (a stowaway, stowaways); verb (stow away, stows away, stowed away, stowing away)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A stowaway is a person who hides on a ship, plane, train or lorry to travel without paying or without being allowed. 2) To stow away (verb, two words) is to hide on a vehicle like that in order to travel secretly. 3) (playful) A stowaway can be an animal or thing that travelled by accident, like a spider in a box of bananas.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and adventure books, a stowaway hides in a ship's hold or a lifeboat and is discovered at sea. In history, some famous explorers' ships had stowaways. In safety and real life, stowing away is very dangerous and against the law. In news, animals such as snakes or frogs sometimes turn up as stowaways in luggage or fruit. Phrases: «a stowaway on board», «stow away on a ship».
examples from the lessons: The sailors found a stowaway hiding among the barrels. | In the story, the boy stowed away on a pirate ship. | A tiny frog was a stowaway in our bag of salad. | Stowing away on a plane is extremely dangerous. | The cat had stowed away in the removal van. | The captain made the stowaway work in the kitchen. | A spider was a stowaway in the box of bananas. | Some stowaways were found inside a lorry at the port.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The noun is one word «stowaway»; the verb is two words «stow away». «Stow» alone means to pack something away neatly («stow your bags under the seat»).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Strabismus is the medical name for a squint: when a person's two eyes do not point in the same direction at the same time, so one eye may turn in, out, up or down.
its sense in the lessons: In health and science lessons, strabismus is explained with how the two eyes work together to see depth. In everyday life, children with strabismus may wear glasses or an eye patch, or have eye exercises or a small operation. It is a common condition and nothing to tease anyone about. The everyday word is «squint» (UK) or «crossed eyes» / «lazy eye» (informal, not exactly the same).
examples from the lessons: The eye doctor said my little brother has strabismus. | Strabismus means the eyes point in different directions. | She wears an eye patch to help treat her strabismus. | Strabismus is often noticed when a child is a baby or toddler. | Glasses can help some children with strabismus. | Our class learned that strabismus can be treated.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Medical, formal word; uncountable. Do not confuse with «a squint» meaning narrowing your eyes in bright sun. «Lazy eye» (amblyopia) is a related but different problem, though they often go together. Pronounced «struh-BIZ-mus».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Straightforward means easy to understand or do, with no hidden difficulties: a straightforward question. 2) A straightforward person is honest and open and says what they mean.
its sense in the lessons: In maths, «a straightforward problem» is one with clear steps and no tricks. Teachers say «This part is straightforward» to calm the class. In everyday life you meet straightforward instructions, recipes and directions. In stories, a straightforward character is honest and plain-speaking. Phrases: «fairly straightforward», «perfectly straightforward», «not as straightforward as it looks».
examples from the lessons: The first question on the test was straightforward. | Building the shelf was more straightforward than we expected. | The recipe is straightforward: mix, pour and bake. | Gran is very straightforward; she always tells you the truth. | Finding the area of a rectangle is straightforward: multiply length by width. | It is not as straightforward as it looks. | The directions to the park were straightforward. | He gave a straightforward answer to a tricky question.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word, no hyphen. Usually «more straightforward», not «straightforwarder». Close words: «simple», «easy», «clear», «honest». In maths, a «straightforward» word problem often needs just one operation.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A streamer is a long, narrow strip of coloured paper or ribbon used to decorate for parties and celebrations. 2) A streamer is a person who streams live video online, for example playing video games while people watch. 3) A streamer can be a long flag or ribbon that streams out in the wind, such as on a kite or a bike handlebar.
its sense in the lessons: At birthdays, Christmas and other parties, people hang streamers from the ceiling. In children's online life, «a streamer» is someone who broadcasts live on sites such as YouTube or Twitch; online safety lessons teach that you never share personal details in a streamer's chat. Phrases: «party streamers», «paper streamers», «a gaming streamer», «a famous streamer».
examples from the lessons: We hung red and gold streamers for the party. | The bike had colourful streamers on the handlebars. | My cousin watches a gaming streamer every evening. | The streamer said hello to his viewers. | The kite had a long streamer for a tail. | Paper streamers fell from the ceiling at midnight. | She wants to be a streamer when she grows up. | Never tell a streamer's chat where you live.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Two very different senses: decorations, and an online broadcaster. Related verb: «to stream» (a video, or water flowing).

part of speech: noun (strep — uncountable, informal); short for streptococcus
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) Strep is short for streptococcus, a kind of bacteria that can cause illness. 2) Strep, or strep throat, is a sore throat caused by these bacteria, with fever and pain when swallowing, which doctors may treat with antibiotics.
its sense in the lessons: In health lessons and at the doctor's, especially in the USA and Canada, children hear «strep throat» and «a strep test», where a cotton swab is rubbed at the back of the throat. In the UK people often say «a throat infection» or «tonsillitis» instead. It is spread by coughs, sneezes and sharing cups, so hand-washing helps. Phrases: «strep throat», «a strep test», «Group A strep».
examples from the lessons: I had strep throat and missed two days of school. | The doctor did a quick strep test with a swab. | Strep is caused by bacteria, not a virus. | She took antibiotics for her strep. | Don't share water bottles if someone has strep. | The nurse said there was strep going around the class.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A clipped, informal word; the full scientific name is «streptococcus» (plural «streptococci»). Uncountable: «She has strep», not «a strep». A common cold is a virus; antibiotics do not cure viruses, but they can treat strep.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Strictness is being strict: making people follow rules exactly and not allowing bad behaviour. 2) Strictness can also mean being exact and precise, like the strictness of a rule or a meaning.
its sense in the lessons: In school life, pupils talk about the strictness of a teacher, a head teacher or school rules, like uniform or homework. In families, children compare the strictness of parents. In stories, strictness can show a character who is fair and firm or one who is harsh. Phrases: «the strictness of the rules», «strictness and kindness».
examples from the lessons: The new teacher was known for her strictness. | The strictness of the school uniform rules surprised us. | Dad's strictness about bedtime annoys my brother. | Her strictness came from wanting us to be safe. | The coach's strictness made the team work harder. | Some parents mix strictness with lots of kindness. | The strictness of the exam rules meant no phones at all.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable; from «strict» + -ness. Strictness is not the same as being unkind: a teacher can be strict and still caring.

part of speech: verb (present participle of strive: strive, strives, strove or strived, striven or strived, striving); noun (striving — uncountable, and strivings)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Striving means trying very hard for a long time to get or reach something: «She is striving to improve». 2) As a noun, striving is the effort of trying hard, or the things a person tries hard for.
its sense in the lessons: In school mottos, reports and assemblies you hear «striving for excellence», «always striving to do our best». In stories and history, striving describes people working hard against difficulties. Phrases: «striving for», «striving to», «striving towards a goal».
examples from the lessons: Our school motto is «Striving for excellence». | She is always striving to beat her best time. | The team kept striving even when they were losing. | Striving for a goal takes patience. | He is striving to learn his times tables by Friday. | The explorers were striving to reach the South Pole. | All that striving paid off when she won the prize.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Strive» is formal; everyday words are «try hard» or «work hard». Past: «strove» (traditional) or «strived»; past participle «striven» or «strived». Used with «for» + noun or «to» + verb.

part of speech: verb (strum, strums, strummed, strumming); noun (a strum, strums)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To strum is to play a guitar, ukulele or similar instrument by brushing your fingers or a pick across the strings. 2) A strum is one brush across the strings, or the sound it makes.
its sense in the lessons: In music lessons, children learn to strum chords on the ukulele or guitar and practise strumming patterns (down, down, up). In stories, a character strumming a guitar often sets a relaxed or dreamy mood. Phrases: «strum a chord», «strumming pattern», «strum along».
examples from the lessons: She strummed her ukulele and sang a song. | We learned to strum a C chord in music. | He was strumming his guitar by the campfire. | Down, down, up — that's the strumming pattern. | Strum gently, not too hard. | With one strum, the whole room went quiet. | Dad strums along when we sing in the car.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb; double the m: «strummed», «strumming». You «strum» strings with a sweep; you «pluck» one string at a time.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (a name) Stuart is a boy's first name and also a surname, used especially in Scotland, England and other English-speaking countries. 2) (history) The Stuarts were a royal family who ruled Scotland and then England, Scotland and Ireland from 1603 to 1714, including James I, Charles I, Charles II and Queen Anne.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, Stuart is a common first name or family name. In UK history lessons, «the Stuarts» or «Stuart times» is the period after the Tudors, with events such as the Gunpowder Plot (1605), the English Civil War, the Great Plague and the Great Fire of London (1666). Also spelled «Stewart» (the older Scottish spelling of the royal house). Phrases: «the Stuart kings», «Stuart England», «Mary, Queen of Scots, a Stuart».
examples from the lessons: My uncle's name is Stuart. | The Stuarts came after the Tudors. | James I was the first Stuart king of England. | The Great Fire of London happened in Stuart times. | We made a timeline of the Stuart monarchs. | Queen Anne was the last Stuart ruler.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always with a capital letter. Also spelled «Stewart» or «Steuart». As a name, it is not a common noun.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Stubble is the short, rough hairs that grow on a man's face when he has not shaved for a day or a few days. 2) Stubble is the short, stiff stalks left standing in a field after a crop like wheat has been cut.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, children notice Dad's stubble feeling scratchy. In farming and geography lessons, stubble is left in fields after the harvest, and some farmers plough it in. In stories, stubble on a character's chin often shows he is tired, busy or has not cared for himself. Phrases: «a bit of stubble», «designer stubble», «a stubble field».
examples from the lessons: Dad's stubble is scratchy when he kisses me goodnight. | After the harvest, the field was full of golden stubble. | The detective rubbed the stubble on his chin. | Some men keep a little stubble on purpose. | We walked carefully across the stubble in the field. | Birds were pecking for seeds among the stubble. | Grandpa had stubble after the camping trip.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «some stubble», not «a stubble». Adjective: «stubbly». Stubble is shorter than a «beard».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Stubbly means covered with short, rough hairs, like a man's chin when he has not shaved. 2) Stubbly can describe a field covered with short stalks left after a harvest.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and stories, a «stubbly chin» or «stubbly cheek» shows a man who has not shaved, often after a long trip or a hard night. In farming descriptions, stubbly fields appear after harvest time. Phrases: «a stubbly chin», «stubbly face».
examples from the lessons: Grandad's stubbly chin tickled my cheek. | After a week camping, Dad's face was stubbly. | The pirate captain had a stubbly face and a big hat. | We ran across the stubbly field. | His cheek felt stubbly and rough. | The cat would not sit on the stubbly grass.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «stubble» + -y. Comparison: «stubblier», «stubbliest» (rare). A describing word, not a noun.

part of speech: noun (stunting — uncountable); verb (present participle of stunt: stunt, stunts, stunted, stunting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Stunting is when something, especially a child or a plant, does not grow as tall or as well as it should, often because of poor food, illness or lack of light. 2) As a verb form, stunting means stopping or slowing something's growth or development. 3) Stunting can also mean doing stunts: daring tricks on bikes, skateboards, cars or planes.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography lessons, «stunting» is a word used by health workers and charities about children who did not get enough good food when very young, so they grow shorter than normal. In plant experiments, poor light or soil causes stunting. In sport and films, «stunting» means doing tricks. Phrases: «stunting growth», «child stunting».
examples from the lessons: Lack of sunlight caused stunting in our bean plants. | Charities work to reduce stunting in young children. | Smoking around children risks stunting their lung growth. | Bad food in early life can lead to stunting. | The cold winds were stunting the trees on the hill. | The bikers were stunting in the car park. | Our class graph showed stunting in the plants without water.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From the verb «stunt» (to stop growth) and also the noun «a stunt» (a daring trick). Uncountable as a health word. Stunting is about height and growth, not about being clever or not.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Stupidly means in a silly or unwise way, without thinking first: «I stupidly left my coat at school». 2) Stupidly can describe a dazed, blank way of doing something, like staring stupidly. 3) (informal) Stupidly can mean «extremely», as in «stupidly expensive» or «stupidly fast».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday talk, children often use «stupidly» to admit a small mistake about themselves. In stories, it shows a character making a bad choice. In slangy speech, «stupidly» works like «really» («that ride was stupidly fun»). Teachers remind pupils not to call other people stupid; saying «I stupidly forgot» about yourself is fine. Phrases: «stupidly expensive», «I stupidly forgot».
examples from the lessons: I stupidly forgot my PE kit again. | He stupidly ran into the road without looking. | She stared stupidly at the broken vase. | Those trainers are stupidly expensive. | The roller coaster was stupidly fast. | We stupidly left the back door open and the dog got out.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «stupid» + -ly. It can sound unkind about others, so it is gentler to use «foolishly» or «without thinking». The informal «stupidly expensive» means «very».

part of speech: noun (a sty, sties or styes); also spelled stye for the eye sense
meaning for a pupil: 1) A sty, or pigsty, is a pen or small building where pigs are kept. 2) (informal) A sty is a very dirty or messy place, like a messy bedroom. 3) A sty (also spelled stye) is a small, red, sore lump on the edge of the eyelid, caused by an infection.
its sense in the lessons: In farm and story books, pigs live in a sty. At home, parents may say «Your room is a pigsty!» meaning very messy. In health, a stye on the eyelid is common, usually harmless, and helped by a warm cloth and clean hands; do not squeeze it. Phrases: «a pig sty / pigsty», «like a pigsty», «a stye in my eye».
examples from the lessons: The pigs rolled in the mud in their sty. | Mum said my bedroom looked like a pigsty. | I had a sore stye on my eyelid. | The farmer cleaned out the sty every morning. | A warm cloth can help a stye get better. | Don't rub a stye or squeeze it. | The three little pigs never lived in a sty.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: «sties» (pens) or «styes» (eye lumps). The eye sense is often spelled «stye». Rhymes with «sky».

meaning for a pupil: 1) To subdivide is to divide something that has already been divided into even smaller parts. 2) (land, homes) To subdivide land is to split a big piece of land into smaller plots for houses (especially USA, Canada, Australia, New Zealand).
its sense in the lessons: In maths, you might divide a shape into halves, then subdivide each half into quarters, or subdivide a number line into tenths. In science, groups of animals are subdivided into smaller groups (classes, orders, families). In geography and everyday life, a «subdivision» is a new housing area made by subdividing land. Phrases: «subdivide into», «further subdivided».
examples from the lessons: We divided the square into four and then subdivided each part into four again. | Each centimetre on a ruler is subdivided into ten millimetres. | Animals are subdivided into smaller and smaller groups. | The farmer subdivided his land and sold it for houses. | The teacher subdivided our group into pairs. | The chapter is subdivided into short sections.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Sub-» means «under» or «smaller»; subdivide = divide again. In maths: if a whole is divided into 4 parts and each is subdivided into 3, there are 4 × 3 = 12 smaller parts. Noun: «subdivision».

meaning for a pupil: 1) To subdue is to get control over a person, group or country, usually by force: «The army subdued the rebels». 2) To subdue a feeling is to calm it or hold it back, like subduing your excitement or anger. 3) To subdue light, colour or sound is to make it softer or quieter.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, kings and armies «subdue» lands and peoples; the Romans subdued much of Britain. In stories, a hero may subdue a monster or a thief. In everyday and feelings talk, you might try to subdue your nerves before a test. Phrases: «subdue the enemy», «subdue a fire», «subdue a laugh».
examples from the lessons: The Romans subdued many tribes in Britain. | Police officers subdued the man who was shouting. | She tried to subdue her giggles in assembly. | Firefighters worked all night to subdue the flames. | The knight subdued the dragon in the end. | Dimmer lights subdued the bright room. | It took the vet two helpers to subdue the frightened horse.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: drop the final e before -ing: «subduing». Past «subdued», which is also an adjective with its own meaning (quiet and sad). Formal; in everyday speech people say «calm down» or «control».

part of speech: adjective (subdued, more subdued, most subdued); verb (past tense and past participle of subdue)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Subdued means quiet and a little sad or tired, not lively as usual: «You seem subdued today». 2) Subdued light, colours or sounds are soft and gentle, not bright or loud. 3) As a verb form, subdued means brought under control: «The rebels were subdued».
its sense in the lessons: In stories and feelings lessons, «subdued» is a good word to show a character is quietly unhappy, worried or tired. In art and design, «subdued colours» are soft and muted. In history, peoples and lands were «subdued» by armies. Phrases: «a subdued mood», «subdued lighting», «in a subdued voice».
examples from the lessons: Tom was very subdued after his dog got lost. | The class was subdued after the sad news. | The restaurant had subdued lighting. | She painted her bedroom in subdued colours. | He spoke in a subdued voice. | The rebellion was quickly subdued. | The crowd was subdued after their team lost.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As an adjective it is about mood or brightness, not about being beaten. Opposites: «lively», «cheerful», «bright», «loud».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To subjugate people or a country is to defeat them and take control so they must obey, often taking away their freedom. 2) (formal) To subjugate something is to make it less important than something else, like subjugating your own wishes to the needs of the group.
