its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, empires subjugated other peoples, and children learn about how colonised or enslaved peoples were treated unfairly and how many fought for freedom. In ethics talk, it describes unfair power over others. Phrases: «subjugated peoples», «subjugate a nation».
examples from the lessons: The empire tried to subjugate its neighbours. | Many peoples were subjugated by powerful empires in the past. | The rebels refused to be subjugated. | Laws were used to subjugate the poor in that story. | Our history topic looked at how nations were subjugated and how they won freedom. | No country should subjugate another.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal, strong word, harsher than «control». Noun: «subjugation». Close words: «conquer», «subdue», «oppress».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Subordination is being under someone else's control or authority, or putting someone or something in a lower, less important place. 2) (grammar) Subordination is joining a less important clause to a main clause with a word such as because, although, when or if, making a complex sentence.
its sense in the lessons: In English grammar lessons (UK KS2 and similar), pupils learn subordination: «I went home because it was raining» — «because it was raining» is a subordinate clause. In history and work life, subordination describes ranks, such as soldiers under officers. Phrases: «subordinating conjunction», «subordinate clause», «subordination to».
examples from the lessons: Using subordination makes our sentences longer and more interesting. | «Although» is a word that shows subordination. | In the army there is strict subordination of soldiers to officers. | The teacher marked my sentences for subordination and coordination. | «When the bell rang, we ran out» uses subordination. | In the old days, women's subordination to men was written into the law in many countries.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. In grammar, the opposite idea is «coordination» (joining equal clauses with and, but, or). Related: «subordinate» (adjective and noun: a less important clause, or a person lower in rank).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Subsidence is when the ground slowly sinks lower, which can crack buildings, roads and walls. 2) Subsidence can also mean a thing such as a flood, storm or feeling dying down.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and science lessons, subsidence is caused by old mines underneath, soil drying out, removal of groundwater or soft ground; it is part of studying how land changes. In everyday life in the UK, homeowners worry about subsidence cracks, and house insurance covers it. Phrases: «subsidence damage», «mining subsidence».
examples from the lessons: Subsidence caused big cracks in the wall of the old house. | The road was closed because of subsidence. | Old coal mines can cause subsidence above them. | Dry summers can shrink clay soil and lead to subsidence. | The surveyor checked the house for subsidence. | Pumping out too much groundwater can cause subsidence. | After the subsidence of the floodwater, people went home.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. From the verb «subside» (to sink or to die down). Pronounced «sub-SY-dence» or «SUB-sid-ence». Not the same as a landslide, which is fast and sideways.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Subsistence is having just enough food, water and money to stay alive, with nothing extra. 2) Subsistence farming is growing just enough food to feed your own family, not to sell. 3) (formal, money) Subsistence can mean money paid to cover basic living costs like meals when away for work.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons, pupils compare subsistence farming with commercial farming (growing to sell). In history, many poor families lived at subsistence level. In adult working life, «subsistence allowance» pays for meals and hotels on work trips. Phrases: «subsistence farming», «a subsistence level», «means of subsistence».
examples from the lessons: Many families in the past lived on subsistence farming. | Subsistence farmers grow food mainly to eat, not to sell. | Their wages were barely enough for subsistence. | In geography we compared subsistence and commercial farming. | Fishing was the village's means of subsistence. | Dad gets a subsistence allowance when he works away.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Related verb «subsist» (to stay alive with very little). Do not confuse with «substance» (material) or «assistance» (help).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) A substrate is the surface or material that something grows on or lives on, such as soil, sand, rock or a fish tank's gravel. 2) (science) In chemistry and biology, a substrate is the substance that an enzyme acts on and changes. 3) (technology) A substrate is a base layer that something else is built on, like the material under a computer chip.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about habitats, the substrate of a rock pool, stream or aquarium is what lives on the bottom. In biology, «enzymes break down substrates». In pet care, reptile and fish owners choose a safe substrate for the tank. Phrases: «on the substrate», «enzyme and substrate».
examples from the lessons: The stream's substrate was gravel and pebbles. | Mussels attach themselves to a rocky substrate. | We put sand as the substrate in the fish tank. | Mushrooms grow on a substrate of wood or straw. | Each enzyme works on its own substrate. | The gecko's tank needs a safe substrate.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable, science word. «Sub-» means «under»: the layer underneath. Not used in everyday chat.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Subsurface means lying or happening just below a surface, such as under the ground, the sea or the skin. 2) The subsurface is the layer under the surface.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and science, «subsurface water» is groundwater under the soil; scientists look for subsurface oceans on moons like Europa and Enceladus. In engineering, subsurface surveys check ground before building. Phrases: «subsurface water», «subsurface ocean», «subsurface layer».
examples from the lessons: Scientists think Europa has a subsurface ocean under its ice. | Subsurface water feeds the well. | The robot scanned the subsurface for old pipes. | Subsurface rock can be studied with drills. | The bruise was a subsurface injury under the skin. | Geologists mapped the subsurface before the tunnel was dug.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word. «Sub-» means «under». Mostly a science and technical word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) When a mother mammal suckles her baby, she feeds it with milk from her body. 2) When a baby animal suckles, it drinks milk from its mother.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on mammals and life cycles, children learn that all mammals suckle their young: cows, cats, whales, kangaroos (joeys in the pouch) and humans. In farm visits, you see lambs and piglets suckling. «Suckling» is also an old word for a baby still drinking its mother's milk. Phrases: «suckle her young», «a suckling pig».
examples from the lessons: The cow suckled her calf in the field. | Mammals suckle their young with milk. | The kittens suckled while the mother cat purred. | A joey suckles inside its mother's pouch. | Whales suckle their babies underwater. | The piglets pushed to suckle from the sow.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. A science word for feeding milk; for human babies people usually say «breastfeed». Feeding milk to young is one of the features that makes an animal a mammal.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (grammar) Suffixation is making a new word or a new form of a word by adding a suffix (a word ending) such as -ness, -ful, -ly, -ed or -s to the end of it.
its sense in the lessons: In English spelling and grammar lessons, pupils study suffixes: «kind» + «-ness» = «kindness», «hope» + «-ful» = «hopeful», «quick» + «-ly» = «quickly». Suffixation can change the word class (an adjective becomes a noun) and sometimes changes spelling (happy → happiness, run → running). Phrases: «suffixation and prefixation», «spelling rules for suffixation».
examples from the lessons: Suffixation turns «teach» into «teacher». | «Careless» is made by suffixation: care + less. | Our spelling list is all about suffixation with -ly. | Suffixation can change a verb into a noun, like «move» to «movement». | We learned that suffixation sometimes needs a spelling change, like «happy» to «happiness». | Prefixation adds to the front; suffixation adds to the end.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A linguistics word; teachers usually just say «adding a suffix». Watch spelling rules: drop the final e (hope → hoping), double the consonant (run → running), change y to i (happy → happier). Opposite place: «prefixation» (adding to the front: un-, re-, dis-).

meaning for a pupil: 1) If something is suggestive of something else, it makes you think of it or hints at it: «clouds suggestive of rain». 2) Suggestive can mean giving a clue or sign that something may be true: «The muddy boots were suggestive». 3) (rude, adult slang) a rude word grown-ups use; not for school.
its sense in the lessons: In reading and science, «suggestive» is a careful word for evidence that hints at something without proving it: «The results are suggestive but not certain». In art and stories, a suggestive picture or sound brings an idea to mind. Phrases: «suggestive of», «highly suggestive».
examples from the lessons: The dark clouds were suggestive of a storm. | The music was suggestive of the sea. | The footprints were suggestive, but they did not prove who took the cake. | The smell was suggestive of fresh bread. | The detective found several suggestive clues. | The early results are suggestive, so the scientists will test more.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually used with «of»: «suggestive of something». Related: «suggest», «suggestion». In science, «suggestive» means «hints at», not «proves».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Suitably means in a way that is right or proper for the situation: «suitably dressed for the rain». 2) Suitably can mean «as much as you would expect»: «She was suitably impressed».
its sense in the lessons: In school letters and instructions, you read «Pupils should come suitably dressed for outdoor learning» or «wear suitable shoes». In everyday life it means in the right way for the weather, place or event. Phrases: «suitably dressed», «suitably impressed», «suitably qualified».
examples from the lessons: Please come suitably dressed for the cold weather. | The children were suitably quiet in the library. | He was suitably impressed by my model volcano. | Make sure you are suitably dressed for PE. | The hall was suitably decorated for the party. | Only suitably trained adults can use the climbing wall.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «suitable» + -ly, dropping the final -le into -ly (suitable → suitably). Do not confuse with «sweetly». Opposite: «unsuitably».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A suite is a set of rooms that go together, especially in a hotel, like a bedroom with its own sitting room. 2) A suite is a set of matching furniture, such as a three-piece suite (a sofa and two armchairs) or a bathroom suite. 3) (music) A suite is a piece of music made of several shorter parts played one after another. 4) (computers) A suite is a set of programs that work together, like an office suite.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday UK life, families buy «a three-piece suite» or a «bathroom suite». In hotels, the «suite» is the big special room. In music lessons, children hear suites such as «The Nutcracker Suite» or «The Planets Suite». In school, the «ICT suite» or «computer suite» is the room with computers. Phrases: «hotel suite», «three-piece suite», «en-suite bathroom».
examples from the lessons: We stayed in a hotel suite with two bedrooms. | Mum and Dad bought a new three-piece suite. | Our class went to the ICT suite to type our stories. | We listened to «The Nutcracker Suite» in music. | The bedroom has an en-suite bathroom. | The new bathroom suite is white. | The office suite includes a word processor and spreadsheets.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced «sweet», like «sweet» (a homophone), but spelled «suite». Do not confuse with «suit» (clothes, pronounced «soot»). «En suite» (from French) means a bathroom joined to a bedroom.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A sunbather is a person who lies or sits in the sun, often at a beach or pool, to relax or get a tan.
its sense in the lessons: In beach scenes in stories and summer pictures, sunbathers lie on towels. In health and safety lessons (especially Australia and New Zealand: «Slip, Slop, Slap»), children learn that too much sun burns skin and can cause skin cancer, so sunbathers need sunscreen, hats and shade. Phrases: «sunbathers on the beach», «a lone sunbather».
examples from the lessons: The beach was crowded with sunbathers. | A seagull stole a sandwich from a sunbather. | The lifeguard told the sunbathers about the jellyfish. | Sunbathers should wear sunscreen and drink water. | One sunbather fell asleep and got sunburnt. | The lizard is a sunbather too, warming itself on a rock.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. From «sunbathe» (verb: sunbathe, sunbathed, sunbathing). Myth: «A tan is healthy» — a tan is actually skin damage from the sun.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A sundae is a dessert of ice cream topped with sauce, such as chocolate or strawberry, and often with whipped cream, nuts, sprinkles and a cherry, served in a tall glass or bowl.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, children order sundaes at ice-cream parlours, cafés and birthday treats. In maths word problems, sundaes appear in counting combinations («3 flavours and 2 toppings — how many different sundaes?»). In healthy-eating lessons, a sundae is a «sometimes» treat. Phrases: «an ice-cream sundae», «a hot fudge sundae», «build your own sundae».
examples from the lessons: I had a chocolate sundae with a cherry on top. | We made sundaes at Lily's party. | A hot fudge sundae is my favourite treat. | The café sells sundaes in tall glasses. | If there are 3 ice-cream flavours and 2 sauces, you can make 6 different sundaes. | My sundae had sprinkles, nuts and cream.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelled «sundae», not «Sunday», though it sounds the same (a homophone) and the name may come from «Sunday». Countable: «two sundaes». In combination problems, multiply the choices: flavours × toppings.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Sunni (Sunni Islam) is the largest branch, or group, of Islam; most Muslims in the world are Sunni. 2) A Sunni is a Muslim who belongs to this branch. 3) Sunni describes things belonging to this branch, such as Sunni mosques.
its sense in the lessons: In religious education lessons, pupils learn that Islam has two main branches, Sunni and Shia, which share the core beliefs (one God, the Prophet Muhammad, the Qur'an, the Five Pillars) but disagree about who should have led Muslims after the Prophet Muhammad died. In news, the words appear about countries in the Middle East. It should be spoken about with respect. Phrases: «Sunni Muslims», «Sunni and Shia».
examples from the lessons: Most Muslims in the world are Sunni. | Sunni and Shia Muslims both follow the Qur'an. | In RE we learned about the Sunni and Shia branches of Islam. | My friend's family are Sunni Muslims. | The Sunni mosque was full for Friday prayers. | Sunnis and Shias share many of the same beliefs.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always written with a capital letter. Pronounced «SOO-nee». Not the English word «sunny» (bright with sunshine), which sounds similar.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A sunshade is something that keeps the sun off you, like a big umbrella at the beach or over a garden table, or a canopy. 2) A sunshade can be a screen on a car or pram windscreen that blocks sunlight.
its sense in the lessons: In summer and sun-safety lessons (especially Australia and New Zealand), sunshades, hats and shade sails help protect skin. In everyday life, families put up sunshades at the beach or in the garden and use car sunshades to keep the car cool. Phrases: «a beach sunshade», «a car sunshade», «under the sunshade».
examples from the lessons: We sat under the sunshade to eat our lunch. | Dad put the sunshade up on the beach. | The pram has a sunshade for the baby. | A sunshade on the windscreen keeps the car cool. | The café has big sunshades over the tables. | The wind blew our sunshade over.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word, countable. Similar words: «parasol» (a small sun umbrella), «awning», «shade sail» (Australia).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Superficially means only on the surface or at first look, not deeply: «They look superficially alike». 2) Superficially can mean done quickly and carelessly, without real thought or care. 3) (medical) Superficially injured means hurt only on the skin, not deep inside.
its sense in the lessons: In reading and science lessons, «superficially similar» is used when two things look alike but are really different (a whale and a fish). In reports, a teacher may say work was done superficially, meaning without enough depth. In health, a superficial cut is shallow. Phrases: «superficially similar», «only superficially».
examples from the lessons: Bats and birds are superficially alike, but bats are mammals. | He read the chapter only superficially and missed the main point. | The driver was superficially injured, with just a few scratches. | The twins look superficially the same but act very differently. | The problem was fixed superficially, so it came back. | Superficially, the plan looked good.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «superficial» + -ly. «Super-» here means «above» (on the surface), not «very good». It is often a criticism: «superficial» = shallow.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Superiority is being better, stronger or higher in quality than others. 2) Superiority is also acting as if you are better than other people, which is unkind and annoying.
its sense in the lessons: In sport and history, a team or army may have «superiority» in numbers or skill. In PSHE and stories, a character with a «superiority complex» or an «air of superiority» looks down on others. In maths, superiority can be about one amount being bigger. Phrases: «a sense of superiority», «an air of superiority», «superiority in numbers», «air superiority».
examples from the lessons: Their team's superiority was clear by half-time. | She spoke with an air of superiority that upset her friends. | The army had superiority in numbers. | No group of people has superiority over another because of skin colour. | The new phone's superiority is its long battery life. | His sense of superiority made him hard to like.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. From «superior» (better, higher) + -ity. Opposite: «inferiority». «Superiority complex» means thinking you are better than everyone.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A superstar is an extremely famous and successful singer, actor, sports player or other performer. 2) (informal) A superstar is someone who is brilliant at something or who has done a great job: «You're a superstar for helping!»
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, children talk about pop superstars and football superstars. Teachers and parents say «You're a superstar!» as praise. In media lessons, pupils think about how superstars are shown in magazines and online and how photos may be edited. Phrases: «a pop superstar», «a football superstar», «become a superstar».
examples from the lessons: The singer became a superstar after her first album. | He is a football superstar who plays for England. | Thanks for tidying up — you're a superstar! | Many superstars started as ordinary kids. | The superstar signed autographs for her fans. | In our class, everyone is a superstar at something.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word, countable. Stronger than «star». Praise use («you're a superstar») is friendly and informal.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A superstitious person believes in luck or magic signs, like thinking black cats, broken mirrors or Friday the 13th bring bad luck. 2) Superstitious describes a belief or habit based on such ideas rather than on facts or science.
its sense in the lessons: In science and thinking lessons, pupils compare superstitious beliefs with evidence and testing. In sport, many players are superstitious and wear «lucky» socks. In history and stories, superstitious people feared witches or omens. Phrases: «a superstitious belief», «superstitious about».
examples from the lessons: Grandma is superstitious and never opens an umbrella indoors. | Some footballers are superstitious about their lucky boots. | Sailors used to be very superstitious. | He was superstitious about the number 13. | Knocking on wood is a superstitious habit. | Scientists test ideas instead of trusting superstitious beliefs. | I'm not superstitious, but I still kept my lucky pencil.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: «superstition». Spelling: -tious. Many hotels skip a 13th floor because of superstition, but the floor still exists — it is just numbered 14.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A supposition is an idea or belief that you think is true but have not proved: a guess based on some reasons. 2) Supposition is the act of supposing or guessing rather than knowing.
its sense in the lessons: In science, a supposition is like a hypothesis that needs testing. In stories, especially mysteries, detectives say «That's just supposition» meaning there is no proof yet. In maths and logic, you can make a supposition («Suppose x is 5») and work out what follows. Phrases: «pure supposition», «on the supposition that», «based on supposition».
examples from the lessons: That's just supposition — we need evidence. | The detective's supposition turned out to be right. | On the supposition that it will rain, we packed coats. | Her supposition was that the cat ate the fish. | Science turns suppositions into tested facts or throws them out. | The whole story was based on supposition.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal word. From the verb «suppose». Close words: «assumption», «guess», «hypothesis». Not the same as «a fact».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Supremacy is being the most powerful, the strongest or the best, with power over all others. 2) Supremacy can describe the idea that one group should have power over others, which is unfair and harmful, as in «white supremacy».
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, empires and navies fought for supremacy (Britain's naval supremacy, the space race). In sport, teams battle for supremacy. In citizenship lessons, pupils learn that ideas of racial supremacy are false and have caused great harm. Phrases: «battle for supremacy», «naval supremacy», «air supremacy».
examples from the lessons: The two teams fought for supremacy in the league. | Britain once had supremacy at sea. | The battle decided supremacy over the region. | Ideas of racial supremacy are wrong and dangerous. | The king wanted supremacy over the whole country. | The cats fought for supremacy of the garden.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. From «supreme» (highest). Pronounced «soo-PREM-a-see».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Surgically means by an operation done by a surgeon: «The tumour was surgically removed». 2) Surgically can mean very precisely and carefully, like a surgeon: «surgically precise».
its sense in the lessons: In health and science lessons, «surgically» describes operations in hospital, such as removing tonsils or an appendix. In news and sport, it means extremely precise. Phrases: «surgically removed», «surgically repaired», «surgical precision».
examples from the lessons: The doctor surgically removed her appendix. | His broken knee was surgically repaired. | The vet surgically removed a sock from the dog's stomach. | The pass was surgically accurate. | Some problems can be treated with medicine instead of surgically. | The splinter was too deep, so it was removed surgically.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «surgical» + -ly. Related: «surgery», «surgeon». In the UK, «surgery» also means a doctor's or dentist's office.

part of speech: noun (a surtitle, surtitles); verb (surtitle, surtitled — rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Surtitles are words shown on a screen above the stage at an opera or play, giving a translation of what is being sung or said in another language, or the words for people who cannot hear well.
its sense in the lessons: In music and drama lessons or on a theatre trip, pupils may see surtitles above the stage, for example when an opera is sung in Italian or German. They are like subtitles on a film, but above a stage. Phrases: «read the surtitles», «with English surtitles».
examples from the lessons: The opera was in Italian, but there were English surtitles. | We read the surtitles above the stage. | Surtitles help deaf audience members follow the play. | It was hard to watch the singers and read the surtitles at the same time. | The theatre shows surtitles on a long screen. | Without the surtitles, I would not have understood the story.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually plural: «surtitles». «Sur-» means «above» (from French). Compare «subtitles», which are at the bottom of a film or TV screen.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Surveillance is carefully watching a person, place or activity, often secretly, to check for crime or danger or to collect information. 2) Surveillance can mean the cameras and equipment used for watching, such as CCTV.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday UK life, there is CCTV surveillance in shops, stations and streets. In stories, police or spies keep a suspect «under surveillance». In citizenship and online safety lessons, pupils discuss privacy: who can watch us, and how apps and websites collect data. In health, «disease surveillance» means watching for outbreaks. Phrases: «under surveillance», «surveillance cameras», «CCTV surveillance».
examples from the lessons: The shop has surveillance cameras near the door. | The police kept the house under surveillance. | Spies use surveillance to gather secrets. | There is a lot of CCTV surveillance in big cities. | Doctors use surveillance to spot new flu outbreaks. | Some people worry that too much surveillance harms privacy. | The bird watchers' surveillance of the nest lasted weeks.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Spelling: double l, «-ance»: surveillance. From French «surveiller» (to watch over). Pronounced «sur-VAY-lance».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Suspiciously means in a way that shows you do not trust someone or something: «The dog sniffed the stranger suspiciously». 2) Suspiciously means in a way that makes other people think something is wrong or that someone has done something bad: «He was acting suspiciously». 3) (humour) Suspiciously can mean «surprisingly, in a way that makes you wonder»: «The room was suspiciously tidy».
its sense in the lessons: In stories and mysteries, characters look or act suspiciously, giving clues to the reader. In safety lessons, children learn to tell a trusted adult if someone is behaving suspiciously. In humour, «suspiciously quiet» means a parent thinks the children are up to something. Phrases: «act suspiciously», «look at someone suspiciously», «suspiciously quiet».
examples from the lessons: The cat looked at the new dog suspiciously. | A man was acting suspiciously near the bikes. | The kids were suspiciously quiet in the kitchen. | She eyed the green soup suspiciously. | Report any bag left suspiciously on the train. | My brother was suspiciously helpful today. | The detective noticed the butler smiling suspiciously.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «suspicious» + -ly. Two directions: being suspicious (not trusting) or seeming suspicious (making others distrust you). Noun: «suspicion».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A sweeper is a person whose job is to sweep, such as a street sweeper or road sweeper. 2) A sweeper is a machine or tool for sweeping, like a carpet sweeper or a street-cleaning truck. 3) (sport) In football, a sweeper is a defender who plays behind the other defenders to stop attacks. 4) (sport) In curling, a sweeper brushes the ice in front of the stone.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday town life, children see road-sweeper trucks and street sweepers. In PE and football, the sweeper is a position. In history stories, chimney sweeps (also called sweepers) were sometimes small children, which was cruel and was later banned. Phrases: «street sweeper», «road sweeper», «carpet sweeper».
examples from the lessons: The street sweeper cleaned up the leaves. | A big road sweeper drove past with its brushes spinning. | Nan uses a carpet sweeper on the rug. | He played as the sweeper in our football team. | The sweepers brushed the ice in front of the curling stone. | The sweeper came early to clean the market square.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. From «sweep» + -er. A «chimney sweep» is usually just called «a sweep», not «a sweeper».

meaning for a pupil: 1) To sweeten food or drink is to make it taste sweeter, for example by adding sugar, honey or fruit. 2) To sweeten something can mean to make it nicer or more pleasant: «The fresh air sweetened the room». 3) To sweeten a deal or offer is to make it more attractive, often by adding something extra.
its sense in the lessons: In cooking and healthy-eating lessons, pupils learn ways to sweeten food with fruit instead of lots of sugar, and read labels for «sweetened» drinks. In everyday and business talk, «to sweeten the deal» means adding a bonus. Phrases: «sweeten with honey», «sweeten the deal», «artificially sweetened».
examples from the lessons: We sweetened the porridge with banana. | Mum sweetens her tea with honey. | Many fizzy drinks are sweetened with lots of sugar. | Ripe apples can sweeten a crumble without extra sugar. | To sweeten the deal, the shop added free batteries. | Dad bought flowers to sweeten Mum's mood.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. «Unsweetened» means no sugar has been added. A «sweetener» is a substance used instead of sugar.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (old-fashioned) A sweetmeat is a sweet, candy or other small sweet treat like sugared fruit, nuts or marzipan. It has nothing to do with meat.
its sense in the lessons: In old stories, fairy tales and historical books, characters eat «sweetmeats» at feasts or buy them at fairs. In history lessons about Tudor or Victorian times, banquets ended with sweetmeats. Today people say «sweets» (UK), «candy» (USA) or «lollies» (Australia, New Zealand). Phrases: «a plate of sweetmeats».
examples from the lessons: The queen's banquet ended with sugared sweetmeats. | In the story, the witch tempted the children with sweetmeats. | Victorian children bought sweetmeats at the fair. | The tray held figs, nuts and other sweetmeats. | Sweetmeats were a rare treat for poor families long ago. | Grandad jokingly calls toffees «sweetmeats».
note for the reader of a maths problem: Old-fashioned. Trap: «meat» here is an old word for «food», so a sweetmeat is not meat. Countable.

part of speech: noun (a swoosh, swooshes); verb (swoosh, swooshes, swooshed, swooshing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A swoosh is the soft rushing sound of something moving fast through air or water. 2) To swoosh is to move quickly with that sound. 3) A swoosh is a curved tick-like shape or line, like a famous sports-shoe logo.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and comics, «swoosh» is a sound word (onomatopoeia) for a cape, a sword, a ball, a slide or a fast car. In English lessons, pupils collect sound words like swoosh, splash and bang. Phrases: «with a swoosh», «swoosh past», «swoosh down».
examples from the lessons: The ball went into the net with a swoosh. | The superhero's cape swooshed as he flew. | We swooshed down the water slide. | Swoosh! The bird dived into the lake. | The skier swooshed past us. | The logo is a white swoosh. | I heard the swoosh of the automatic doors.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Onomatopoeia (a word that sounds like what it means). Regular verb: «swooshed». Informal. Similar sound words: «whoosh», «swish».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Synchronisation is making things happen at exactly the same time or speed, like clocks showing the same time or dancers moving together. 2) (technology) Synchronisation, often called syncing, is keeping information the same on two devices, such as a phone and a computer.
its sense in the lessons: In PE, dance and swimming, «synchronisation» is moving in time together, as in synchronised swimming. In science and technology, devices sync their clocks and files. In film, sound synchronisation means the voices match the lips. Phrases: «in synchronisation», «synchronisation of clocks», «data synchronisation».
examples from the lessons: The dancers' synchronisation was perfect. | Synchronisation keeps the photos the same on my phone and tablet. | Synchronised swimmers practise their synchronisation for hours. | The film's sound synchronisation was off, so the voices were late. | Train timetables need synchronisation of station clocks. | Fireflies in some forests flash in synchronisation.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK spelling «synchronisation»; US spelling «synchronization». Informal short form: «sync» (or «synch»). Verb: «synchronise». Uncountable.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A tabby is a cat with a striped, swirled or spotted coat, often grey, brown or ginger, with an «M» shape on its forehead. 2) Tabby describes this kind of striped pattern: «a tabby kitten». 3) (old) A tabby can be a female cat.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and stories, tabby cats are very common pets, like Mog in the picture books. In science lessons on genetics and animals, children learn tabby is a coat pattern, not a breed. Phrases: «a tabby cat», «a ginger tabby», «a silver tabby».
examples from the lessons: Our tabby cat sleeps on the windowsill. | The tabby kitten had a white tip on its tail. | A ginger tabby followed us home. | Tabbies have an «M» shape on their foreheads. | Mog is a famous tabby in a picture book. | My tabby chases leaves in the garden.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; plural «tabbies». «Tabby» is a pattern, not a breed. Myth: all ginger cats are male — most are, but not all.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Tableware is all the things used for serving and eating a meal at a table: plates, bowls, cups, glasses, knives, forks and spoons.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and shops, «tableware» appears in kitchen departments. In design and technology or history lessons, pupils look at tableware from different times, like Roman pottery or Victorian china. In helping at home, children set the table with tableware. Phrases: «plastic tableware», «party tableware», «fine tableware».
examples from the lessons: The shop sells pretty tableware. | We used paper tableware at the picnic. | Roman tableware was found in the field. | Please put the tableware in the dishwasher. | The party tableware had dinosaurs on it. | Grandma keeps her best tableware for Christmas.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «some tableware», not «tablewares». Close words: «crockery» (plates, cups, bowls), «cutlery» (UK) or «silverware» (USA) for knives, forks and spoons.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To tabulate information is to arrange it in a table, in rows and columns, so it is easy to read and compare.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and science lessons, pupils tabulate results: they collect data from an experiment or survey and put it in a table before drawing a graph. Phrases: «tabulate the results», «tabulate the data».
examples from the lessons: We tabulated the results of our plant experiment. | Tabulate how many pets each pupil has. | The scientist tabulated the temperatures for each day. | First tabulate the data, then draw a bar chart. | The survey answers were tabulated by the computer. | She tabulated her pocket money spending in a notebook.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal school word; you can also say «put in a table». Noun: «tabulation». In maths, tabulating makes totals and differences easy to see: add the column to find the total.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Tailless means having no tail: a tailless animal, or an aircraft or kite built without a tail.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on animals and adaptation, pupils meet tailless animals such as frogs (adult), apes, Manx cats and koalas, and compare them with animals that use tails for balance. In stories, a lizard may lose its tail and become tailless for a while before it grows back. Phrases: «a tailless cat», «tailless amphibians».
examples from the lessons: Adult frogs are tailless, but tadpoles have tails. | The Manx cat is a famous tailless breed. | Apes are tailless, but most monkeys have tails. | The lizard ran off tailless after the cat grabbed it. | The kite was tailless and kept spinning. | Koalas are almost tailless.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «tail» + «-less» (without). Spelling: tail + less keeps both l's: «tailless». A trap: apes (gorillas, chimps) are tailless; monkeys usually have tails.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The takahe is a large, flightless bird from New Zealand, with blue-green feathers, a big red beak and red legs. It was thought to be extinct but was found again in 1948 and is now protected.
its sense in the lessons: In New Zealand schools and in science lessons on endangered animals and conservation, the takahe is a famous success story: rangers protect it on islands free of predators like stoats and rats. The name comes from the Māori language. Phrases: «the South Island takahe», «takahe conservation».
examples from the lessons: The takahe is a big bird that cannot fly. | Takahe live in New Zealand. | People thought the takahe was extinct until 1948. | We saw a takahe at a wildlife sanctuary. | Rangers protect takahe from stoats and rats. | The takahe has a bright red beak. | Our class made posters about saving the takahe.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A Māori word, often written «takahē» with a macron; pronounced roughly «TAH-kah-heh». Plural is often the same, «takahe». Do not confuse with the pukeko, a smaller relative that can fly.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The Taliban is a militant political and religious group in Afghanistan. It ruled most of Afghanistan from 1996 to 2001 and took power again in 2021. It is widely criticised, for example by the United Nations, for very harsh rules, especially stopping girls and women from going to secondary school, university and many jobs.
its sense in the lessons: In news and current-events lessons, «the Taliban» is mentioned in reports about Afghanistan, refugees and girls' education. Children may learn about Malala Yousafzai, a Pakistani schoolgirl who was shot by Taliban gunmen in 2012 for speaking up for girls' education, survived, and won the Nobel Peace Prize. Most Afghans and most Muslims are not part of the Taliban. Phrases: «the Taliban government», «under the Taliban».
examples from the lessons: The Taliban took control of Afghanistan in 2021. | Under the Taliban, many girls cannot go to secondary school. | Malala spoke out against the Taliban for girls' right to learn. | Many families left Afghanistan when the Taliban returned. | The news report was about the Taliban and women's rights. | The United Nations has criticised the Taliban's rules on girls.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always with a capital letter and usually «the Taliban». The word comes from Pashto and means «students». It is a group's name, not a word for all Afghans or all Muslims — saying so would be unfair and untrue.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A talkative person talks a lot, often in a friendly and chatty way.
its sense in the lessons: In school reports, teachers may write that a pupil is «talkative», sometimes as a gentle way of saying they chat too much in class. In stories, a talkative character might be a chatty parrot or a friend who never stops talking. Phrases: «a talkative child», «very talkative», «in a talkative mood».
examples from the lessons: My little sister is very talkative at dinner. | The parrot was so talkative it said hello to everyone. | He is shy at first but talkative with friends. | My report said I am «a little too talkative in class». | Grandpa gets talkative when he tells old stories. | The taxi driver was friendly and talkative.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Close words: «chatty» (informal), «gabby», «a chatterbox» (noun). Opposites: «quiet», «shy», «silent». It can be praise or a polite complaint, depending on context.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (history) A tallyman was a person who kept a tally, or count, of goods, such as bananas being loaded onto a ship, or votes. 2) (UK, old-fashioned) A tallyman was a door-to-door salesman who sold goods and collected the money in small weekly payments.
its sense in the lessons: In history and songs, the tallyman counted bunches of bananas being loaded in Jamaica, as in the famous «Banana Boat Song» («Come, Mister Tally Man, tally me banana»). In old UK stories about poor families, the tallyman came on Fridays to collect payments. Today, people more often say «counter» or «collector». Phrases: «the tallyman came round».
examples from the lessons: The tallyman counted every bunch of bananas. | «Come, Mister Tally Man, tally me banana», goes the old song. | In the 1930s, the tallyman called at Nan's house every Friday. | The tallyman wrote the numbers in his book. | Families paid the tallyman a little each week for their new coats. | At the dock, the tallyman checked each sack.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Old-fashioned. Plural «tallymen». A «tally» is a running count, often kept with marks in groups of five (four lines and one across), which helps in maths with counting data.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A tambourine is a musical instrument like a small round frame or hand drum with little metal discs (jingles) round the edge that jingle when you shake or hit it.
its sense in the lessons: In music lessons, tambourines are percussion instruments children shake and tap to keep the beat. They are used in school bands, folk music, church and gospel music and pop songs. Phrases: «shake a tambourine», «tap the tambourine», «play the tambourine».
examples from the lessons: I played the tambourine in the school concert. | Shake the tambourine on every beat. | The tambourine jingled when she hit it with her hand. | Our music box has drums, shakers and tambourines. | The band's singer danced with a tambourine. | Tap the tambourine softly, then shake it loudly.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. A percussion instrument (you hit or shake it). Spelling: tam-bou-rine.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Tameness is being tame: when an animal is gentle, used to people and not afraid of them. 2) Tameness can mean being dull, mild or not exciting enough: the tameness of a boring film.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on animals and in pet care, the tameness of an animal shows how used to humans it is. On remote islands, some birds show great tameness because they have never learned to fear people. In reviews and stories, «tameness» means something was too mild. Phrases: «the tameness of the birds».
examples from the lessons: The tameness of the robin surprised us — it ate from my hand. | Animals on the Galápagos Islands are famous for their tameness. | The hamster's tameness grew as we handled it gently. | Critics complained about the tameness of the ending. | The tameness of the deer in the park comes from being fed. | Tameness can be dangerous for wild animals near roads.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable; from «tame» + -ness. A tame animal is not the same as a «domesticated» one: a single wild animal can become tame, but domesticated animals (like dogs) were changed over many generations.

part of speech: noun (a tamer, tamers); adjective (comparative of tame: tame, tamer, tamest)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A tamer is a person who tames or trains wild animals, such as a lion tamer in an old-fashioned circus. 2) Tamer is the comparative of «tame»: more gentle and used to people. 3) Tamer can also mean milder or less exciting: «The second ride was tamer».
its sense in the lessons: In stories and history of circuses, «the lion tamer» appeared with a whip and chair; today many countries ban wild animals in circuses. In everyday talk, «tamer» compares things: a tamer roller coaster, a tamer joke. In science, foxes in a famous experiment became tamer over many generations. Phrases: «lion tamer», «much tamer», «a tamer version».
examples from the lessons: The lion tamer stepped into the cage. | This roller coaster is much tamer than the big one. | Our new kitten is getting tamer every day. | The horse tamer spoke softly to the wild horse. | The film for little children is a tamer version of the book. | Of the two squirrels, the grey one was tamer.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Two different words: the noun «a tamer» (person) and the adjective «tamer» (more tame). Adjective forms: tame, tamer, tamest.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Tangible means real and able to be touched: a tangible object. 2) Tangible means clear and definite enough to be seen or measured: tangible results, tangible proof.
its sense in the lessons: In school reports and news, «tangible progress» or «tangible results» means real changes you can see. In money and business, «tangible things» are physical things like buildings and machines. In science, evidence should be tangible. In stories, a feeling can be so strong it is almost «tangible», as if you could touch it. Phrases: «tangible evidence», «tangible results», «tangible benefits».
examples from the lessons: We need tangible proof, not just rumours. | The new playground is a tangible result of our fundraising. | Her reading made tangible progress this term. | The excitement in the hall was almost tangible. | A book is tangible, but a story in your head is not. | The detective wanted tangible evidence like fingerprints.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: «intangible» (cannot be touched, like ideas, feelings or skills). Formal word. Related to «touch» in Latin.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Tardiness is being late, especially arriving late to school, work or a meeting. 2) Tardiness can mean being slow to do something.
its sense in the lessons: In school, especially in the USA and Canada, «tardiness» is used for arriving late; there may be rules and «tardy slips». Teachers' reports may mention tardiness. In stories, it describes a character who is always late. Phrases: «tardiness policy», «excuse for tardiness».
examples from the lessons: The school sent a letter home about my tardiness. | Tardiness means missing the start of lessons. | Her tardiness made the whole team wait. | The teacher said tardiness must improve this term. | Traffic is no excuse for tardiness every day. | The coach does not accept tardiness at practice.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; uncountable. Everyday words: «lateness», «being late». From «tardy» + -ness (y changes to i).

part of speech: adjective (tardy, tardier, tardiest); noun (a tardy, tardies — US school slang)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Tardy means late, arriving after the right time: «Don't be tardy for class». 2) Tardy means slow to act or happen. 3) (USA, school) A tardy is a mark against you for arriving late, as in «I got three tardies».
its sense in the lessons: In US and Canadian schools, «tardy» is everyday school language: a «tardy bell» rings, late pupils get a «tardy slip» or «a tardy». In the UK and Australia, people mostly say «late». Phrases: «tardy slip», «tardy bell», «tardy for school».
examples from the lessons: If you are tardy, sign in at the office. | The tardy bell rang and the hall was empty. | I got a tardy because the bus broke down. | He was tardy three times this week. | The tardy reply came weeks after the letter. | Three tardies mean a detention at our school.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective forms: tardy, tardier, tardiest. Noun plural: «tardies». Mostly American in school use; in British English it sounds old-fashioned or formal.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Taro is a tropical plant grown for its large, starchy root (corm), which is cooked and eaten like a potato. Its big leaves are heart-shaped and can also be cooked. 2) Taro is also the food made from this root, and its purple-grey flavour in bubble tea and desserts.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and food lessons, taro is a staple food in the Pacific Islands (including for Māori and Pacific peoples in New Zealand, and in Hawaii, where it is made into poi), Asia and Africa. In everyday life, children may have taro bubble tea or taro chips. Safety: raw taro can irritate the mouth and throat — it must be cooked. Phrases: «taro root», «taro chips», «taro bubble tea».
examples from the lessons: Taro is an important food in the Pacific Islands. | In Hawaii, taro is mashed to make poi. | I tried purple taro bubble tea. | Taro must be cooked before you eat it. | The taro plant has huge heart-shaped leaves. | Mum fried some taro chips. | We learned that taro grows in wet, warm places.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced «TAH-roh» or «TAIR-oh». Not to be confused with «tarot» (cards for fortune-telling) — a homophone trap. Often uncountable as a food.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) Tartaric describes tartaric acid, a natural acid found in grapes, bananas and tamarinds; it is used in cooking, baking powder (as cream of tartar) and making wine.
its sense in the lessons: In science and cooking, tartaric acid is a safe food acid; cream of tartar (made from it) helps egg whites whip and is mixed with bicarbonate of soda in some baking powders and fizzy sherbet. In chemistry lessons on acids, it is an example of an acid in food. Phrases: «tartaric acid», «cream of tartar».
examples from the lessons: Tartaric acid is found in grapes. | Cream of tartar comes from tartaric acid. | Sherbet fizzes because the tartaric or citric acid meets the bicarbonate of soda. | Tartaric acid gives some sweets a sour taste. | We listed acids in food: citric, tartaric and malic. | Winemakers measure tartaric acid in grapes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Science word, almost always in «tartaric acid». Pronounced «tar-TAR-ik». Not related to «tartar sauce» or the tartar on teeth.

part of speech: noun (tat — uncountable, informal UK); verb (tat, tats, tatted, tatting — rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (UK, informal) Tat is cheap, tasteless or useless things, like junk sold at a fair: «The shop sells tourist tat». 2) Tit for tat means paying someone back in the same way for something bad they did to you. 3) (slang) Tat is short for tattoo. 4) (crafts) To tat is to make lace by tatting, using a small shuttle and thread.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday British talk, a parent may say «Don't spend your money on that tat». In stories and PSHE, «tit for tat» describes arguments where each side gets back at the other, which usually makes things worse. Phrases: «cheap tat», «tourist tat», «tit for tat».
examples from the lessons: Dad said the souvenir shop was full of tat. | Don't waste your pocket money on plastic tat. | It turned into a tit-for-tat argument about who pushed first. | My uncle has a dragon tat on his arm. | The jumble sale had some treasures among the tat. | Grandma taught me to tat lace with a shuttle.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal. «Tat» (junk) is uncountable: «a lot of tat». «Tit for tat» is a fixed phrase. Tatting is an old craft word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To teem with something is to be full of it, crowded with lots of living things moving about: «The pond teemed with tadpoles». 2) (UK, informal) When rain is teeming down, it is raining very heavily.
its sense in the lessons: In science and nature writing, rock pools, rainforests and ponds «teem with life». In stories, streets teem with people. In British weather talk, «It's teeming (down)» means heavy rain. Phrases: «teem with», «teeming with life», «teeming rain».
examples from the lessons: The rock pool was teeming with tiny crabs. | Rainforests teem with insects and birds. | It was teeming down, so we stayed inside. | The market teemed with shoppers. | The river teems with fish in spring. | A drop of pond water teems with microbes under the microscope.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Homophone trap: «teem» (to be full of) and «team» (a group that plays together) sound the same. «Teem» is almost always in the -ing form or with «with».

meaning for a pupil: 1) When a baby teethes, its first teeth are growing through the gums, which can make the baby sore, grumpy and dribbly.
its sense in the lessons: In family life, parents say «The baby is teething» and give teething rings or cold things to chew. «Teething problems» (idiom) means small problems when something new starts, like a new computer system or a new school. Phrases: «teething ring», «teething baby», «teething problems / troubles».
examples from the lessons: My baby brother is teething, so he cries a lot. | Babies usually start teething at around six months. | She chewed on a cold teething ring. | Teething can make babies dribble and have red cheeks. | The new website had a few teething problems. | Our puppy is teething and chews everything.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: the verb is «teethe» (with e, rhymes with «breathe»), the noun is «teeth» (plural of «tooth»). Regular verb: «teethed», «teething». The idiom «teething problems» means early problems, not teeth.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (music) The tempo is the speed of a piece of music: fast, slow or in between. 2) Tempo is the speed or pace at which something happens, like the tempo of a game or of life in a city.
its sense in the lessons: In music lessons, pupils learn tempo as one of the elements of music, with Italian words like allegro (fast), andante (walking pace) and largo (slow), and count beats per minute with a metronome. In sport, a team «raises the tempo» by playing faster. Phrases: «a fast tempo», «change of tempo», «up-tempo».
examples from the lessons: The song has a fast tempo. | We clapped along to keep the tempo. | The conductor set a slow tempo for the lullaby. | A metronome helps you keep a steady tempo. | The team raised the tempo in the second half. | Life in the city moves at a quick tempo.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: «tempos» in everyday English, «tempi» in music books (Italian plural). Tempo is speed; «rhythm» is the pattern of long and short sounds; «pitch» is how high or low.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A tenement is a large old building divided into many flats, especially one that was crowded and often poor, as in Glasgow, Edinburgh, Dublin or New York in the past. 2) (Scotland) A tenement is any block of flats several floors high with a shared stair (a close).
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons about the Victorian era and industrial cities, children learn about tenement families living in one or two rooms with shared toilets. In Scotland today, many people still live happily in old stone tenements. Phrases: «tenement building», «tenement flat», «tenement close».
examples from the lessons: Many families lived in crowded tenements in Victorian Glasgow. | Our great-great-grandparents had one room in a tenement. | The tenement had a shared toilet on each landing. | Gran grew up in a tenement flat in Edinburgh. | New York's tenements were full of new immigrants. | The old tenement has been turned into smart flats.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Not the same as «tenant» (a person who rents a home). Pronounced «TEN-uh-ment».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Tenfold means ten times as much or as many: «Sales grew tenfold». 2) As an adjective, tenfold means having ten times the size, or having ten parts: «a tenfold increase».
its sense in the lessons: In maths and science, «tenfold» is a word for multiplying by 10 and is used in news about growth: «a tenfold increase». In stories and the Bible, a reward may be repaid tenfold or a hundredfold. Phrases: «increase tenfold», «a tenfold rise», «repay tenfold».
examples from the lessons: The number of visitors grew tenfold: from 50 to 500. | There was a tenfold increase in bikes at school. | His kindness was repaid tenfold. | The price went up tenfold in ten years. | Under the microscope, the cell looked tenfold bigger. | A tenfold rise in rain caused floods.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Maths: «tenfold» = multiply by 10 (×10). «Increase tenfold» means the new amount is 10 times the old one (50 → 500), not old + 10. Similar: twofold (×2), threefold (×3), hundredfold (×100).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A terminator is someone or something that ends or destroys something. 2) (science) The terminator is the line on the Moon or a planet that divides the day side from the night side. 3) The Terminator is a famous action film robot (from the films starting in 1984), so people use the word for a tough, unstoppable robot or person. 4) (technology) A terminator is a part that marks or closes the end of a cable, line or piece of data.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about the Moon's phases, the terminator is the curved shadow line you can see through a telescope, where craters look sharpest. In everyday chat, «terminator» is used jokingly for a tough robot or a person who «gets rid of» things like pests. Phrases: «the lunar terminator», «pest terminator».
examples from the lessons: Look along the terminator to see the craters best. | The terminator moves across the Moon as its phases change. | In the film, the Terminator is a robot from the future. | Dad called himself the Spider Terminator. | The cable needs a terminator at the end. | Sunrise is happening wherever the terminator crosses the Earth.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. From «terminate» (to end). The science sense (day–night line) surprises many people.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Terminology is the set of special words and phrases used in a subject or job, like the terminology of science, football or music.
its sense in the lessons: In school, teachers ask pupils to «use the correct terminology», for example «numerator» and «denominator» in maths, or «photosynthesis» in science, or «noun» and «verb» in grammar. Phrases: «technical terminology», «scientific terminology», «correct terminology».
examples from the lessons: Use the correct terminology in your science write-up. | Football has its own terminology, like «offside» and «corner». | The doctor explained the medical terminology to Mum. | We made a glossary of maths terminology. | Music terminology includes words like «tempo» and «crescendo». | Computer terminology changes fast.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable. A single special word is «a term». Close words: «vocabulary», «jargon» (jargon often means words outsiders find hard to understand).

part of speech: verb (terrorise, terrorises, terrorised, terrorising; US terrorize)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To terrorise people is to frighten them very badly, again and again, often by threats or violence. 2) (humour) To terrorise can mean to playfully bother or chase, like a puppy terrorising the cat.
its sense in the lessons: In history and news, gangs, pirates or armies terrorised towns. In anti-bullying lessons, terrorising another child is bullying and must be reported. In stories, a monster or a dragon terrorises a village. Phrases: «terrorise a town», «terrorised by».
examples from the lessons: A dragon terrorised the village in the old tale. | Pirates terrorised ships along the coast. | Bullying means terrorising someone again and again — tell a teacher. | Our new kitten terrorises the dog. | The wolf terrorised the farm animals. | The gang terrorised the neighbourhood until the police came.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK spelling «terrorise», US «terrorize». Related: «terror», «terrorist» (someone who uses violence to frighten people for political aims). The playful sense is only for light jokes.

part of speech: noun (proper noun: Tết); also a letter name
meaning for a pupil: 1) Tết (Tet) is the Vietnamese Lunar New Year, the most important festival in Vietnam, celebrated in late January or February with family visits, special food, flowers and red envelopes of lucky money. It is a Vietnamese word, not an English one. 2) Tet is also the name of the ninth letter of the Hebrew alphabet (ט), also written «teth».
its sense in the lessons: In RE, geography and festivals lessons, children learn about Tết, like Chinese New Year (Lunar New Year) celebrated in Vietnam and by Vietnamese families in the USA, Australia, the UK and elsewhere. In history, the «Tet Offensive» (1968) was a major attack during the Vietnam War. Phrases: «Tết holiday», «celebrate Tết».
examples from the lessons: Linh's family celebrates Tết with sticky rice cakes. | Tết is the Vietnamese New Year. | Children get red envelopes with lucky money at Tết. | Houses are decorated with peach blossoms for Tết. | We learned about Tết and Chinese New Year in class. | The Tet Offensive was an important event in the Vietnam War.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Vietnamese: written «Tết», pronounced roughly «tet» to an English ear. Capital letter. Not an English word; «tête» in French (head) is different.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Textual means to do with a text, the actual written words of a book, poem or document. 2) Textual evidence is words or lines taken from a text to support what you say about it.
its sense in the lessons: In English and reading lessons, pupils are asked to give «textual evidence»: quote words from the story to prove a point («How do you know she is nervous? Find evidence in the text»). In history and Bible study, «textual» describes studying the exact words of old writings. Phrases: «textual evidence», «textual analysis», «textual details».
examples from the lessons: Use textual evidence to show how the character feels. | The teacher wanted a quote as textual evidence. | Textual clues tell us the story is set in winter. | Scholars compare old copies of the Bible for textual differences. | Our textual analysis looked at the poet's word choices. | There were small textual changes in the new edition.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A school and formal word. Related: «text», «context». Not the same as «textured» (about how a surface feels).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A therapist is a trained person who helps people get better from illness, injury or problems, often by treatment that is not drugs or surgery. 2) A therapist often means someone who helps with feelings and thoughts by talking, like a counsellor or psychologist. 3) Many therapists have a special kind: speech therapist, physiotherapist, occupational therapist, play therapist.
its sense in the lessons: In school and everyday life, children may see a speech therapist for talking and sounds, a physiotherapist after an injury, an occupational therapist for handwriting or daily skills, or a play therapist or counsellor for worries and big feelings. In PSHE lessons, pupils learn that seeing a therapist is normal and brave, like going to a doctor. Phrases: «speech therapist», «see a therapist», «family therapist».
examples from the lessons: I see a speech therapist on Tuesdays to practise my «r» sounds. | The therapist helped Dad walk again after his accident. | Talking to a therapist helped her with her worries. | My cousin's occupational therapist gave him a special pencil grip. | The play therapist used toys to help the boy talk about his feelings. | There is nothing embarrassing about seeing a therapist.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Related: «therapy». Trap: read it as «thera-pist», not «the rapist» — a well-known joke about word breaks.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A thesis is a long piece of writing based on research, written for a university degree, such as a PhD. 2) A thesis is the main idea or claim that a writer or speaker wants to prove: «My thesis is that school should start later».
its sense in the lessons: In English and essay writing, older pupils learn to write a «thesis statement»: one sentence that says what the essay will argue. In adult life, university students write a thesis at the end of their studies. Phrases: «thesis statement», «a PhD thesis», «to support a thesis».
examples from the lessons: My big sister is writing her thesis on bees. | Your thesis statement should come at the start of your essay. | His thesis is that dinosaurs were warm-blooded. | She spent three years on her PhD thesis. | The writer gives three reasons to support her thesis. | The professor read hundreds of theses.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: «theses» (pronounced «THEE-seez»). Formal word. Close words: «argument», «main claim». Opposite idea in debates: «antithesis».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Thinness is being thin: not thick, as with a thin sheet of paper or ice. 2) Thinness of a person or animal is having little fat on the body, sometimes because of illness or hunger. 3) Thinness can mean being weak or watery, or not having much in it: the thinness of a soup or of an excuse.
its sense in the lessons: In science and maths, thinness is measured as thickness (in mm). In health lessons, pupils learn that bodies come in many healthy shapes, and very great thinness can be a sign of illness; nobody should be teased about their body. In safety, the thinness of ice on ponds is a danger. Phrases: «the thinness of the ice», «extreme thinness».
examples from the lessons: The thinness of the ice made it dangerous to walk on. | We compared the thinness of different kinds of paper. | The vet was worried about the stray cat's thinness. | The thinness of the walls meant we could hear the neighbours. | His excuse had a thinness everyone noticed. | You can see light through a leaf because of its thinness.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. From «thin» + -ness (double n). Opposite: «thickness» (for objects), «fatness» (for bodies — but talking about bodies needs kindness).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A thistle is a wild plant with prickly leaves and stems and a round purple (sometimes yellow or white) flower head; its seeds float on fluffy down.
its sense in the lessons: In science and nature lessons, thistles show how plants protect themselves with prickles and spread seeds by the wind. In history and culture, the thistle is the national emblem of Scotland. Butterflies and goldfinches love thistles. Phrases: «thistle down», «the Scottish thistle», «prickly as a thistle».
examples from the lessons: I stung my hand on a prickly thistle. | The thistle is the symbol of Scotland. | Goldfinches eat thistle seeds. | Thistle down floated across the field. | Butterflies landed on the purple thistles. | Donkeys will sometimes eat thistles.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: silent t in the middle — «thistle», said «THISS-ul». Countable.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Thoughtless means not thinking about how your actions or words affect other people, often in a way that is unkind or rude. 2) Thoughtless can mean careless: done without thinking about what might happen.
its sense in the lessons: In PSHE and stories, a thoughtless comment can hurt someone's feelings even if it was not meant badly; characters learn to be more thoughtful. In safety, thoughtless actions, like leaving a toy on the stairs, can cause accidents. Phrases: «a thoughtless remark», «how thoughtless of me».
examples from the lessons: It was thoughtless of me to forget your birthday. | His thoughtless joke upset her. | Dropping litter is thoughtless. | Leaving the gate open was thoughtless — the dog got out. | I'm sorry, that was a thoughtless thing to say. | The thoughtless driver splashed everyone at the bus stop.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «thought» + «-less». Opposite: «thoughtful» (kind and caring, or thinking deeply). Noun: «thoughtlessness».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A thrifty person is careful with money and does not waste things: they save, reuse and buy only what they need.
its sense in the lessons: In money lessons, being thrifty means saving pocket money, comparing prices, mending things and buying second-hand. In the USA, a «thrift store» is a charity shop selling used items. In history, thrifty families in wartime «made do and mend». Phrases: «thrifty shopper», «thrifty habits».
examples from the lessons: Grandma is very thrifty and reuses wrapping paper. | Being thrifty helped us save for a holiday. | My thrifty brother saved all his birthday money. | We bought thrifty second-hand books for school. | Thrifty people turn off lights to save money. | During the war, families had to be thrifty.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Positive word, unlike «stingy» or «mean» (UK), which mean not wanting to share. Noun: «thrift». Forms: thriftier, thriftiest.

part of speech: adjective (throbbing); verb (present participle of throb: throb, throbs, throbbed, throbbing); noun (throbbing — uncountable)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A throbbing pain beats again and again, like a pulse: a throbbing headache or a throbbing thumb. 2) Throbbing describes a strong, steady beating sound or movement, like throbbing music or engines. 3) As a verb, throbbing is the -ing form of «throb», to beat strongly.
its sense in the lessons: In health and first aid, a throbbing finger after hitting it with a hammer, or a throbbing toothache, tells a nurse or doctor about the kind of pain. In stories, a throbbing heart shows fear or excitement, and throbbing music shows a loud party. Phrases: «a throbbing headache», «a throbbing pain», «heart throbbing».
examples from the lessons: I had a throbbing headache after the noisy party. | My thumb was throbbing after I shut it in the door. | The music was throbbing through the walls. | Her heart was throbbing with fear. | The engine gave a low throbbing hum. | Ice helped the throbbing in my ankle.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double b: throb → throbbed, throbbing. A «heartthrob» is a famous person many fans have a crush on.

part of speech: noun (a throttle, throttles); verb (throttle, throttles, throttled, throttling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A throttle is the control in a car, motorbike, boat or plane that changes how much fuel or power goes to the engine, so it goes faster or slower. 2) To throttle someone is to squeeze their throat so they cannot breathe; this is very dangerous and a serious crime. 3) (humour) «I could throttle him!» means you are very cross, not that you would really do it. 4) To throttle something is to slow it or limit it, like an internet company throttling a connection speed.
its sense in the lessons: In science and technology, the throttle controls engine power; pilots and drivers «open the throttle» to speed up and «go full throttle». In everyday chat, «full throttle» means doing something with all your energy. Safety: never put hands or anything around anyone's neck, even as a game. Phrases: «full throttle», «open the throttle», «throttle back».
examples from the lessons: The pilot opened the throttle and the plane sped down the runway. | We cycled full throttle down the hill. | Twist the throttle to make the motorbike go. | My phone's internet was throttled after I used all my data. | «I could throttle my brother for reading my diary!» Mum laughed. | Never squeeze someone's neck — it can throttle them.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: throttled, throttling. The joking «I could throttle you» is an idiom for being annoyed; the real act is violence.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A tiara is a small crown, often decorated with jewels, worn on the head by women and girls, like princesses and queens at special events. 2) (church, history) The papal tiara was a tall triple crown once worn by popes.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, girls may wear toy tiaras for dressing up, birthdays or weddings. In stories and history, princesses and queens wear tiaras at balls and royal events. Phrases: «a sparkly tiara», «wear a tiara», «a diamond tiara».
examples from the lessons: The princess wore a sparkly tiara. | I wore a plastic tiara to my birthday party. | The queen's diamond tiara is kept safe in a museum. | The bride had a small tiara in her hair. | The fairy costume came with a wand and a tiara. | Popes once wore a tall triple tiara.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Pronounced «tee-AR-uh». A tiara is smaller than a crown and usually sits at the front of the head.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A tic is a sudden movement or sound that a person makes again and again without meaning to, like blinking, shrugging, sniffing or clearing the throat. 2) A tic can be a habit in how someone talks or acts, like always saying «like» (a verbal tic).
its sense in the lessons: In health and PSHE lessons, children may learn that tics are common in childhood, often come and go, and can be part of Tourette's syndrome; people with tics cannot simply stop, so they should never be teased or copied. In writing, a «verbal tic» is a habit word. Phrases: «a nervous tic», «a verbal tic», «motor tic».
examples from the lessons: He has a tic that makes him blink a lot. | Tics are not something you can just stop. | My friend with Tourette's has vocal tics. | Her verbal tic is saying «basically» all the time. | The tic gets worse when he is tired or stressed. | We never laugh at someone's tic.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Homophone trap: «tic» (a twitch) and «tick» (a ✓ mark, a clock sound, or a small biting creature) sound the same.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A tiercel (also spelled tercel) is a male hawk or falcon, especially in falconry, the sport of training hawks to hunt.
its sense in the lessons: In falconry and nature books, «tiercel» is the old special word for the male bird, which is about a third smaller than the female (the name comes from the old word for «third»). Children may meet it in bird-of-prey displays, historical stories and old poems. Phrases: «a tiercel peregrine», «falcon and tiercel».
examples from the lessons: The falconer flew a tiercel peregrine at the show. | A tiercel is smaller than the female falcon. | The tiercel landed on the falconer's glove. | In the old poem, the knight kept a tiercel. | The female falcon is bigger than the tiercel. | The tiercel brought food to the nest.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Rare, specialist word. Also «tercel». Female hawks and falcons are usually larger than males — the opposite of many other birds.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A timekeeper is a person who keeps track of time in a game, race or event, often with a stopwatch, and says when time is up. 2) A good timekeeper is someone who is always on time: «She is an excellent timekeeper». 3) A timekeeper can also be a clock or watch, judged by how accurately it keeps time.
its sense in the lessons: In PE, sports days and debates, a pupil may be chosen as timekeeper to time races or speeches. In school reports and jobs, «a good timekeeper» means someone punctual. In maths, timekeepers record times in minutes, seconds and hundredths. Phrases: «official timekeeper», «good timekeeper», «poor timekeeper».
examples from the lessons: I was the timekeeper for the 100-metre race. | The timekeeper blew the whistle when time was up. | My teacher says I am a good timekeeper. | The old clock is still an accurate timekeeper. | The timekeeper recorded 14.5 seconds for Sam. | In group work, one person is the timekeeper.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word, countable. In time problems, the timekeeper subtracts start time from finish time to find how long something took.

part of speech: noun (a ting, tings); verb (ting, tings, tinged — rare, tinging)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A ting is a short, high, clear ringing sound, like a small bell or a spoon tapping a glass. 2) To ting is to make that sound. 3) (UK slang, from London and Jamaican speech) Ting means «thing»: «It's a whole ting», «a peng ting».
its sense in the lessons: In stories and poems, «ting» is a sound word (onomatopoeia), like the ting of a bicycle bell or a microwave. In UK youth slang, «ting» stands for «thing» and is part of Multicultural London English. Phrases: «ting!», «with a ting», «that's a ting» (slang).
examples from the lessons: The microwave went ting! | She tapped her glass — ting, ting — to make a speech. | The bike bell gave a cheerful ting. | (slang) «That new game is a whole ting, innit.» | (slang) «Grab your tings, we're leaving.» | A coin fell on the floor with a ting.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Sound word; informal. Slang «ting» = «thing» is very informal and not for written schoolwork. Do not confuse with «tinge» (a slight colour).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (a name) Titania is the queen of the fairies in Shakespeare's play «A Midsummer Night's Dream», the wife of Oberon. 2) (science) Titania is the largest moon of the planet Uranus, named after her. 3) (a name) Titania is also sometimes used as a girl's name.
its sense in the lessons: In English and drama, Titania appears in stories retold for children of «A Midsummer Night's Dream», where a magic flower makes her fall in love with Bottom, a man with a donkey's head. In science and space lessons, Titania is one of Uranus's moons, many of which are named after Shakespeare characters. Phrases: «Titania and Oberon», «Uranus's moon Titania».
examples from the lessons: Titania is the fairy queen in «A Midsummer Night's Dream». | Titania argues with Oberon, the fairy king. | Titania is the biggest moon of Uranus. | Voyager 2 took photos of Titania in 1986. | In our school play, Lily played Titania. | Many of Uranus's moons, like Titania and Miranda, have names from Shakespeare.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always with a capital letter. Pronounced «tih-TAH-nee-uh» or «tie-TAY-nee-uh». Not to be confused with «titanium» (a metal) or «Titan» (Saturn's biggest moon).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Tolerance is accepting and respecting people whose beliefs, ways of life or opinions are different from yours, even if you disagree. 2) Tolerance is being able to put up with something unpleasant, such as pain, heat or noise: «a low tolerance for cold». 3) (health) Tolerance is when the body gets used to a medicine or drug so it works less. 4) (maths, engineering) A tolerance is the small amount by which a measurement is allowed to be different from the exact size.
its sense in the lessons: In citizenship and British values lessons, «mutual respect and tolerance of those with different faiths and beliefs» is taught as an important value. In science and health, people have tolerance to heat, pain or a medicine. In design and technology, a part may have a tolerance of ±0.5 mm. Phrases: «tolerance and respect», «zero tolerance» (no bad behaviour allowed at all), «low tolerance for».
