examples from the lessons: Our school teaches tolerance and respect for all faiths. | The school has zero tolerance for bullying. | Desert plants have a high tolerance for heat. | I have a low tolerance for spicy food. | Some medicines stop working as well because the body builds up tolerance. | The bolt must be 20 mm, with a tolerance of 0.1 mm. | Tolerance means living kindly with people who are different.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly uncountable. Verb: «tolerate»; adjective: «tolerant». In maths, a tolerance of ±0.1 mm on 20 mm means any size from 19.9 mm to 20.1 mm is accepted. «Zero tolerance» means no exceptions.

part of speech: noun (a tonic, tonics; tonic — uncountable for the drink); adjective (tonic)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Tonic, or tonic water, is a fizzy drink with a slightly bitter taste. 2) A tonic is something that makes you feel better, stronger or happier: «The holiday was a real tonic». 3) In the past, a tonic was a medicine people believed would make them stronger. 4) (music) The tonic is the first and main note of a musical scale or key, the «home» note, like C in C major. 5) Hair tonic is a liquid put on hair.
its sense in the lessons: In music lessons, older pupils learn the tonic as «doh», the note a tune often ends on. In everyday life, adults say a walk, sunshine or good news is «a tonic». In history, Victorians bought tonics that often did not really work. Phrases: «a real tonic», «tonic water», «the tonic note».
examples from the lessons: The sunny weekend was a real tonic after the rainy week. | Grandad drinks tonic water with ice and lemon. | Seeing my friends again was just the tonic I needed. | In C major, the tonic is C. | The song ends on the tonic, so it sounds finished. | The old shop sold bottles of health tonic. | Tonic water glows under ultraviolet light because of the quinine in it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Different senses: a drink, a cheering thing, a music note. Not to be confused with «tectonic» (earth plates) or «sonic» (sound).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Tonsillitis is an illness where the tonsils, two lumps of soft tissue at the back of the throat, become infected and swollen, causing a sore throat, pain when swallowing and often a fever.
its sense in the lessons: In health lessons and everyday life, tonsillitis is common in children; it is usually caused by a virus, sometimes by bacteria such as strep. Rest, drinks and painkillers from an adult help, and a doctor may give antibiotics if it is bacterial. Some children who get it very often have their tonsils taken out (a tonsillectomy). Phrases: «a bout of tonsillitis», «have tonsillitis».
examples from the lessons: I was off school with tonsillitis. | Tonsillitis made it hurt to swallow. | The doctor looked at my tonsils with a light. | My sister had her tonsils out because she kept getting tonsillitis. | Ice lollies helped my sore throat when I had tonsillitis. | Tonsillitis is usually caused by a virus.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «She has tonsillitis». Spelling: tonsil + -itis (double l: tonsillitis). «-itis» means inflammation, like «appendicitis».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Topaz is a hard, clear gemstone, often golden-yellow, brown, blue or pink, used in jewellery. 2) A topaz is one jewel made of this stone. 3) Topaz is also a golden-yellow colour.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on rocks and minerals, topaz is number 8 on the Mohs scale of hardness (diamond is 10). In jewellery and stories, it is a precious birthstone (November). It appears in the Bible as one of the stones on the high priest's breastplate and in the walls of the heavenly city in Revelation. Phrases: «a topaz ring», «blue topaz».
examples from the lessons: Mum's ring has a golden topaz in it. | Topaz is harder than quartz. | Topaz is the birthstone for November. | The museum showed a huge blue topaz. | On the Mohs scale, topaz scores 8. | The cat's eyes were the colour of topaz.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural «topazes». Pronounced «TOH-paz». On the Mohs hardness scale (1–10), a mineral scratches any mineral with a lower number.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A topknot is hair tied in a knot or bun on the top of the head. 2) A topknot is a tuft of feathers or hair on top of the head of a bird or animal, like some ducks, chickens and dogs.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, children and adults wear topknots as a hairstyle; in many Sikh families, boys tie their long hair in a topknot (called a joora or patka) as part of their faith. Samurai warriors in Japan had a topknot. In nature, birds such as the crested duck have topknots. Phrases: «tie a topknot», «a messy topknot».
examples from the lessons: She tied her hair in a topknot for PE. | My Sikh friend wears his hair in a topknot under a patka. | The duck had a funny feathery topknot. | Samurai warriors wore a topknot. | The poodle had a bow on its topknot. | Dad has a little topknot now that his hair is long.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word, countable. The k is silent: «TOP-not».

meaning for a pupil: 1) The torso is the main part of the human body, not counting the head, arms and legs; the chest, stomach and back. 2) A torso is a statue of a body without a head, arms or legs, like many old Greek statues found broken.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, children label the torso on body diagrams and learn that it holds the heart, lungs, stomach and other organs. In art and history, museums display ancient torsos. In sport and PE, «twist your torso» is a stretch. Phrases: «upper torso», «twist your torso».
examples from the lessons: The heart and lungs are in the torso. | Twist your torso slowly from side to side. | The museum had a marble torso from ancient Greece. | We drew the torso, then added arms and legs. | The life jacket covers your whole torso. | A rash spread across his torso.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; plural «torsos». Close words: «trunk» (the body without limbs), «upper body».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Towelling is a thick, soft, absorbent cotton cloth with little loops, used to make towels, bathrobes and baby bibs. 2) A towelling can be a rub with a towel to dry yourself. 3) (old, informal) A towelling once meant a beating.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, beach robes, dressing gowns, nappies (in the past) and sweatbands are made of towelling. In design and technology lessons about fabrics, pupils test how absorbent towelling is compared with other cloths. Phrases: «towelling robe», «towelling socks».
examples from the lessons: My dressing gown is made of soft towelling. | Towelling soaks up water well. | We tested towelling, cotton and plastic to see which absorbed most water. | The baby's bib was white towelling. | Tennis players wear towelling wristbands to wipe sweat. | After the swim, Dad gave me a quick towelling.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK spelling «towelling» (double l), US «toweling». Uncountable as a fabric.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Traction is the grip that stops a wheel, shoe or tyre from slipping on a surface. 2) Traction is the pulling force used to move something along, like an engine pulling a train. 3) In hospital, traction is a set of weights and pulleys that gently pulls a broken bone or injured back into the right place. 4) (informal) An idea or plan gains traction when more and more people start to support it.
its sense in the lessons: In science it comes with friction and forces: rough surfaces give more traction, ice and wet leaves give less. In safety talk it explains grippy shoes, winter tyres and why cars skid. In everyday talk «gain traction», «get traction», «lose traction». In stories it tells the reader whether a character can move steadily or is slipping.
examples from the lessons: My trainers have good traction on the gym floor. | The car lost traction on the icy road and slid. | Put sand on the ice to give the wheels more traction. | Steam engines gave the traction that pulled the first trains. | After the fall, Grandad's leg was in traction for two weeks. | The idea of a longer lunch break gained traction with the whole class. | Mud gives bike tyres very little traction.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: say «good traction», not «a traction». Close to «grip» and linked to «friction» in science. Comes from Latin «trahere», to pull (like «tractor»).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Tragically means in a very sad way, usually because someone died or something terrible happened. 2) It can also introduce a sad fact: «Tragically, nobody survived.» 3) (informal, joking) People sometimes use it to make a small disappointment sound huge: «Tragically, the shop had run out of chocolate.»
its sense in the lessons: Used in history lessons, news and stories to mark a terrible event and a serious, sad tone. At the start of a sentence it warns the reader that bad news is coming. In jokes it shows exaggeration. Phrases: «tragically died», «tragically short life», «tragically, …».
examples from the lessons: The young explorer tragically died on the way home. | Tragically, the ship hit an iceberg and sank. | The famous singer's life was tragically short. | Many people were tragically hurt in the earthquake. | Tragically, the fire spread before help arrived. | Tragically, my sandwich fell face down in the mud. (joking) | Romeo and Juliet's story ends tragically.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formed from «tragic» + «-ally»; spell it with «-ally», not «-ly» («tragicly» is wrong). The noun is «tragedy». Used for real deaths and disasters it is serious, so do not use it jokingly about real sad events.

part of speech: noun (a trailer, trailers); verb (trailer, trailers, trailered, trailering — rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A trailer is a wheeled box or platform pulled behind a car, truck or tractor to carry things or animals. 2) A trailer is a short video showing bits of a film, show or game to make people want to watch it. 3) (US, Canada) A trailer is a caravan or a mobile home that people live or holiday in. 4) (verb, rare) To trailer something is to carry it on a trailer or to advertise it with a short clip.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: towing a boat or horses, and watching film trailers before a cinema film. In maths problems a truck and trailer may carry loads, so its weight is added to the truck's. In stories about the USA, a «trailer park» is a place where people live in mobile homes. Phrases: «horse trailer», «film trailer», «movie trailer», «trailer park».
examples from the lessons: Dad hooked the trailer onto the back of the car. | The horse stepped carefully into the trailer. | We watched the trailer for the new cartoon film. | The trailers before the movie lasted twenty minutes. | My cousin in Texas lives in a trailer near the lake. | The tractor pulled a trailer full of hay. | A truck weighs 3 tonnes and its trailer weighs 2 tonnes, so together they weigh 5 tonnes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: «a trailer», «two trailers». In the UK people say «caravan» for a holiday trailer; in the USA «trailer» or «RV». Comes from «trail», to drag behind. A film trailer comes before the film even though the word sounds like «after» – long ago they were shown after it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A trait is a quality that is part of someone's character, like being brave, shy or kind. 2) In science, a trait is a feature passed down from parents to children, such as eye colour or the shape of a leaf. 3) A trait can also be a typical feature of something, like a trait of a style of music.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons it comes with inheritance, genes and evolution: «inherited traits», «animals pass traits to their young». In English lessons pupils describe «character traits» of people in stories, backing each trait with evidence from the text. Phrases: «character trait», «personality trait», «family trait».
examples from the lessons: Kindness is Mia's best trait. | Brown eyes are a trait she got from her dad. | Write down three character traits of the wolf in the story. | Curly hair is a family trait in our house. | Giraffes passed on the trait of long necks. | Being stubborn is not always a bad trait. | Plants also inherit traits from their parent plants.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: «a trait», «traits». In British English it is often said «tray», in American English «trate» (with the t). Inherited traits come from parents; skills you learn, like riding a bike, are not inherited traits.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A trajectory is the curved path that a thrown, kicked or fired object follows through the air or space. 2) A trajectory is also the direction in which something develops over time, like the trajectory of a career or of prices.
its sense in the lessons: In science and maths it is the path of a ball, arrow or rocket, usually an arch shape called a parabola because gravity pulls it down. In space lessons rockets and probes follow trajectories to planets. In grown-up talk: «on an upward trajectory» means getting better or bigger. Phrases: «the ball's trajectory», «change trajectory», «on a trajectory».
examples from the lessons: The football followed a high trajectory into the net. | Scientists worked out the rocket's trajectory to Mars. | Gravity bends a ball's trajectory into a curve. | The arrow's trajectory was too low and it hit the ground. | Draw the trajectory of the paper plane on the graph. | The team's results are on an upward trajectory. | A strong wind changed the kite's trajectory.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; plural «trajectories» (y → ies). Stress on «-JEC-». A trajectory is a path, not a speed. A thrown ball's path is a curve (a parabola), not a straight line, because gravity pulls it down all the time.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Tranquillity is a calm, quiet, peaceful state, with no noise, hurry or worry. 2) Tranquillity can also mean a calm feeling inside a person.
its sense in the lessons: Used in descriptive writing to paint peaceful places: a lake at dawn, a garden, a library. It tells the reader the mood is calm and safe, often before something disturbs it. Phrases: «peace and tranquillity», «a sense of tranquillity», «the tranquillity of the countryside». The Moon has a «Sea of Tranquillity», where the first people landed in 1969.
examples from the lessons: We enjoyed the tranquillity of the lake at sunrise. | The library is a place of peace and tranquillity. | A dog's bark broke the tranquillity of the night. | Grandma loves the tranquillity of her garden. | The astronauts landed on the Sea of Tranquillity. | After the busy fair, the tranquillity of home felt lovely. | Breathing slowly can give you a sense of tranquillity.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. UK, Australia, NZ and Ireland spell it with double l: «tranquillity»; the US often writes «tranquility». The adjective is «tranquil». A formal, literary word; in everyday talk people say «peace and quiet».

part of speech: noun (a transaction, transactions — this is the plural)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Transactions are acts of buying, selling, paying or moving money, like paying at a till or moving money between bank accounts. 2) (formal) Transactions are dealings or exchanges between people or groups. 3) (formal) Transactions can also be the written record of what a society or meeting did, as in a scientific journal's title.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and money lessons, transactions appear in bank statements and shop problems: each transaction adds or takes away money. In everyday life: card transactions, online transactions, a «transaction fee». Banks keep a list of transactions so you can check where money went.
examples from the lessons: The shop made 300 transactions on Saturday. | Mum checked the transactions on her bank statement. | Every transaction at the till prints a receipt. | Some online transactions need a code sent to a phone. | In this game, record each transaction in your money table. | The bank charges a fee for some transactions. | Kim had £20, then made two transactions of £5 each, so £10 was left.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural of «transaction» (countable). In a money problem, a deposit adds money and a payment or withdrawal takes it away; add or subtract each transaction in order. «Transactions» of a society means its published reports – a formal, old use.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Transatlantic means crossing the Atlantic Ocean, such as a flight or voyage between Europe and America. 2) Transatlantic also means about or between the countries on both sides of the Atlantic, like the UK and the USA.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons: transatlantic voyages, the transatlantic slave trade (a terrible trade in enslaved African people), the first transatlantic flight and telegraph cable. In everyday life: «a transatlantic flight», «a transatlantic call». It tells the reader the trip or link spans a big ocean.
examples from the lessons: We took a transatlantic flight from London to New York. | The Titanic was on a transatlantic voyage when it sank. | The first transatlantic telephone cable was laid under the sea. | The transatlantic slave trade forced millions of Africans across the ocean. | My uncle has a transatlantic accent from living in both countries. | Charles Lindbergh made a famous solo transatlantic flight in 1927. | Transatlantic friendships are easier with video calls.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Trans-» means across. Usually written in lower case and as one word. It refers only to the Atlantic; crossing the Pacific is «transpacific».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Transferable means able to be moved or handed from one person, place or thing to another. 2) A transferable ticket or pass can be used by someone else, not only by the buyer. 3) Transferable skills are abilities you can use in many different jobs or subjects, like teamwork or clear writing.
its sense in the lessons: In school and careers talk: «transferable skills» such as problem-solving, communication and organisation. On tickets and passes the words «non-transferable» mean only the named person may use it. In science, energy is transferred, and things that can be passed on are transferable.
examples from the lessons: This bus pass is not transferable, so only you may use it. | Teamwork is a transferable skill you can use in any job. | Good spelling is transferable to every subject. | The concert ticket is transferable, so Gran can go instead. | Points in this game are transferable to your friend's account. | Learning to plan helps in maths and in art – it is transferable. | Some diseases are easily transferable between animals and people.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: «transferable» has one r before «-able» in most dictionaries, though «transferrable» is sometimes seen. Opposite: «non-transferable». Stress is usually on «-FER-».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A transformation is a big change in how someone or something looks, works or behaves. 2) In maths, a transformation is a way of moving or changing a shape on a grid: a translation (slide), reflection (flip), rotation (turn) or enlargement. 3) In science, a transformation is a change from one form to another, like a caterpillar becoming a butterfly.
its sense in the lessons: In maths it is key: after a transformation the new shape is called the image. In science it describes life cycles and energy changes. In stories, a character's transformation shows how they grew or changed, as in fairy tales where a frog becomes a prince. Phrases: «a complete transformation», «undergo a transformation».
examples from the lessons: The caterpillar's transformation into a butterfly takes about two weeks. | Reflect the triangle in the mirror line – that is a transformation. | Rotation, reflection and translation are all transformations. | The old shed had a total transformation into a playhouse. | In the story, the beast's transformation back into a prince happens at the end. | The town went through a big transformation when the factory closed. | Draw the image of the square after the transformation.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Verb: «transform». In maths, translations, reflections and rotations keep the shape's size and angles the same; only an enlargement changes the size. Do not confuse «translation» (maths slide) with translating words.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal, science) To translocate is to move something from one place to another, especially to move wild animals or plants to a new home to keep them safe. 2) (biology) In plants, to translocate is to carry food, such as sugar, through the stem from the leaves to other parts.
its sense in the lessons: Mainly in science and conservation: rangers translocate rhinos, kiwis or beavers to safer places so they can breed. In plant biology, sugars are translocated through tubes called phloem. A formal word; in everyday talk people say «move» or «relocate».
examples from the lessons: Rangers translocated twenty rhinos to a safer park. | Scientists plan to translocate the rare frogs to a new pond. | Kiwi chicks are sometimes translocated to islands without predators. | Plants translocate sugar from their leaves to their roots. | Beavers were translocated to Scotland to bring them back to the rivers. | The team must check the new home before they translocate the birds.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: «translocated», «translocating». The noun is «translocation». Formal and scientific; «relocate» is the more common everyday word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A transporter is a large vehicle that carries other vehicles or heavy loads, like a car transporter lorry. 2) A transporter is any person or thing that carries something from place to place. 3) In science fiction, a transporter is an imaginary machine that sends people instantly from one place to another. 4) (biology) A transporter is a tiny part of a cell wall that carries substances in or out of the cell.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: car transporters on motorways, tank transporters in the army. In science fiction stories like Star Trek: «beam me up» with a transporter. In science, transporter proteins move things across cell membranes. Phrases: «car transporter», «a transporter bridge».
examples from the lessons: A car transporter carried eight new cars down the motorway. | The army used a transporter to move the heavy tank. | In the film, the captain stepped into the transporter and vanished. | Bees are transporters of pollen from flower to flower. | The transporter bridge carries cars across the river on a hanging platform. | Cells have transporters that let sugar in.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: «a transporter», «transporters». Comes from «transport» + «-er» (a person or thing that does). A real-life instant transporter does not exist; it is only in stories.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A trapper is a person who catches wild animals in traps, especially for their fur. 2) A trapper can also be anyone whose job is to catch animals with traps, such as pests or animals for study.
its sense in the lessons: Mostly in history and stories about North America, Canada and the Wild West: fur trappers, the fur trade, log cabins. Today some trappers catch pests or catch animals for scientists to tag and release. It tells the reader about a hard, outdoor life in the wilderness.
examples from the lessons: The fur trapper set his traps along the frozen river. | Trappers sold beaver furs to traders in Canada. | The old trapper knew every track in the forest. | Scientists hired a trapper to catch and tag the foxes. | In the story, the trapper shared his cabin with a lost boy. | The trapper checked his traps every morning.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. From «trap» + «-er»; note the double p. A «trapper» catches animals; a «hunter» usually shoots them. Many people today think fur trapping is cruel, and some places ban it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (law) Treason is the crime of betraying your own country, for example by helping its enemies or trying to overthrow its ruler or government. 2) Treason can also mean any great betrayal of trust.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons: the Gunpowder Plot of 1605, when Guy Fawkes was caught and tried for treason; traitors in wartime. It tells the reader the crime is one of the most serious there is, and in the past it was punished by death. Phrases: «high treason», «commit treason», «charged with treason», «an act of treason».
examples from the lessons: Guy Fawkes was found guilty of treason. | Selling secrets to an enemy country is treason. | In the old days, treason was punished by death. | The knight was accused of treason against the king. | Bonfire Night remembers a plot that was treason. | Telling the other team our tactics felt like treason! (joking) | A person who commits treason is called a traitor.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «commit treason», not «a treason». Person: «traitor»; adjective: «treasonous». It is about betraying your country, not just breaking any law. «High treason» is the old legal name for the worst kind.

part of speech: verb (trickle, trickles, trickled, trickling); noun (a trickle, trickles)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To trickle is for a liquid to flow slowly in a thin line or small drops. 2) To trickle is also for people or things to come or go slowly, a few at a time. 3) A trickle is a thin slow flow of liquid. 4) A trickle is also a small number of people or things arriving slowly.
its sense in the lessons: In science: water trickling through soil or rocks, a stream as a trickle in summer. In everyday life: «trickle in», «trickle out» for people arriving or leaving slowly. In stories it makes the reader see small, slow movement: a trickle of blood, sweat or tears. Phrases: «trickle down», «a trickle of», «slow to a trickle».
examples from the lessons: A trickle of water ran down the window. | Sweat trickled down his face in the heat. | The pupils trickled into class after lunch. | In summer the river is only a trickle. | Sand trickled through her fingers. | Letters from fans came in at a trickle. | Rain trickled through the cracks in the roof.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: «trickled», «trickling» (drop the e). A trickle is slower and smaller than a stream or a flow; a «gush» is the opposite. Countable as a noun: «a trickle».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A trombone is a large brass musical instrument that you play by blowing into it and moving a long sliding tube in and out to change the notes.
its sense in the lessons: In music lessons it belongs to the brass family with the trumpet, horn and tuba; it plays low notes. In bands and orchestras the trombone player is a trombonist. The «sad trombone» sound (wah-wah-wah-waaah) is used in cartoons for a failure.
examples from the lessons: Leo plays the trombone in the school band. | The trombone's slide moves in and out to change the note. | Trombones belong to the brass family. | The jazz band had two trumpets and a trombone. | A sad trombone sound played when the cartoon cat fell over. | Ella practises the trombone every evening. | The trombone is longer than the trumpet and plays lower.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: «a trombone». Player: «trombonist». It uses a slide, not valves like a trumpet. Comes from Italian «tromba» (trumpet) + «-one» (big), so it means «big trumpet».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Trustworthiness is the quality of being trustworthy: honest, reliable and able to be trusted to do what is right. 2) Trustworthiness of information means how reliable and true it is, such as a source or a website.
its sense in the lessons: In ethics and citizenship lessons it is a core value along with honesty and respect. In research lessons pupils judge the trustworthiness of websites and news by checking who wrote it and whether other sources agree. In stories a character proves their trustworthiness by keeping a secret or a promise.
examples from the lessons: Keeping secrets shows trustworthiness. | The teacher praised Sam for his trustworthiness. | Check the trustworthiness of a website before you use it. | Trustworthiness matters a lot when you look after a pet for a neighbour. | A good friend's trustworthiness is worth more than gold. | We discussed the trustworthiness of the news story. | Her trustworthiness made her the perfect class treasurer.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Built from «trust» + «worthy» + «-ness»; note «worthi-» (y becomes i). Adjective: «trustworthy». Opposite: «untrustworthiness». Not the same as «trust»: you trust someone; their trustworthiness is the quality that makes trust sensible.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A tuner is a device that helps you tune a musical instrument by showing whether a note is too high, too low or just right. 2) A tuner is the part of a radio or TV that picks up a chosen station or channel. 3) A tuner is a person whose job is tuning instruments, especially pianos.
its sense in the lessons: In music lessons pupils use a clip-on tuner or an app before playing guitar, violin or ukulele. In science lessons about sound and waves, a radio tuner picks a frequency. In everyday life, a piano tuner visits to fix the sound of a piano.
examples from the lessons: Clip the tuner onto your guitar before you start. | The tuner showed my string was too low. | The piano tuner came to fix our old piano. | Turn the radio tuner to find the music station. | My violin teacher uses a tuner app on her phone. | A tuner helps you get each string exactly right.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. From the verb «tune» + «-r». Do not confuse with «tuna», the fish, which sounds similar.

part of speech: noun (the Tuscarora, a Tuscarora); proper noun, usually with a capital T
meaning for a pupil: 1) (a name) The Tuscarora are a Native American people who lived in what is now North Carolina and later moved north to New York and Ontario, Canada. 2) Tuscarora is also their language, which belongs to the Iroquoian family. 3) (a name) Tuscarora is also used as a place name for towns, a mountain area and a nation's reservation.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons about North America: the Tuscarora joined the Haudenosaunee (Iroquois) Confederacy in the 1720s, making it the Six Nations. It is a name, written with a capital letter.
examples from the lessons: The Tuscarora once lived in North Carolina. | The Tuscarora joined the Iroquois Confederacy and it became the Six Nations. | Some Tuscarora people live on a reservation in New York State. | Tuscarora is an Iroquoian language. | We read about the Tuscarora in our history project.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A proper noun: write it with a capital T. The plural is usually «Tuscarora» (the people). Spelling: tus-ca-RO-ra. It is a real people's name, so use it respectfully.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Typhoid is a serious illness caused by bacteria, caught from dirty water or food, which gives a high fever, stomach pain and weakness.
its sense in the lessons: In science and history lessons it shows why clean water, sewers and handwashing matter: in the past typhoid killed many people in crowded cities. Today it is treated with antibiotics and prevented with vaccines, which travellers sometimes get. Phrases: «typhoid fever», «a typhoid vaccine», «Typhoid Mary».
examples from the lessons: Typhoid spreads through dirty water and food. | Before travelling, Aunt Jo had a typhoid vaccine. | Clean drinking water stopped typhoid in many cities. | Typhoid gives people a very high fever. | Doctors treat typhoid with antibiotics. | Washing your hands helps stop typhoid spreading. | In Victorian times many children died of typhoid.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «he had typhoid», not «a typhoid». Do not confuse with «typhus», a different disease spread by lice, or with a «typhoon», a storm. «Typhoid Mary» was a cook who spread the disease without feeling ill.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Ugliness is the quality of being ugly or very unpleasant to look at. 2) Ugliness can also mean nastiness or cruelty in how people behave, like the ugliness of bullying or war.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and fairy tales, ugliness is often set against beauty (The Ugly Duckling, Beauty and the Beast) to teach that looks do not show who someone really is. In discussions it also describes nasty behaviour or hard truths. Phrases: «the ugliness of war», «beauty and ugliness».
examples from the lessons: The Ugly Duckling was teased for his ugliness. | Beauty is on the inside, so outward ugliness does not matter. | The book shows the ugliness of war. | The old car park's ugliness spoiled the view. | Bullying shows the ugliness in how people can treat others. | Belle looked past the Beast's ugliness and saw his kindness.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. From «ugly» + «-ness»; y becomes i. Calling a person ugly is unkind; in discussion, talk about things and actions instead.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Ultramarine is a bright, deep blue colour. 2) Ultramarine is also a blue pigment (colouring powder) for paint, first made by grinding a precious blue stone called lapis lazuli. 3) (adjective) Ultramarine describes something that has this deep blue colour.
its sense in the lessons: In art lessons it is a paint colour in the paint box, used for skies and seas. In history of art, real ultramarine was more costly than gold, so painters saved it for special things such as the Virgin Mary's robe in old church paintings. The name means «beyond the sea», because the stone came from far away across the sea.
examples from the lessons: I painted the sea with ultramarine. | The sky turned a deep ultramarine at dusk. | Mix ultramarine with white to make a pale blue. | Long ago, ultramarine paint cost more than gold. | She wore an ultramarine dress to the party. | Ultramarine was made from a blue stone called lapis lazuli.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable. Today most ultramarine paint is made artificially and is cheap. Do not confuse with «ultraviolet», light we cannot see.

part of speech: noun (an ump, umps) — informal short form
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal, mostly US and Canada) Ump is a short word for «umpire», the official who watches a game such as baseball, cricket or tennis and decides if the rules are kept.
its sense in the lessons: Heard in sports talk, especially baseball in North America: «Kill the ump!» is an old joking cry from angry fans. In cricket and tennis people more often say «umpire» in full, or «the umpie» (Australia). It tells the reader the speaker is a relaxed sports fan.
examples from the lessons: The ump called him out at third base. | Don't argue with the ump! | The ump yelled «Strike three!» | Our coach shook hands with the ump after the game. | Fans booed when the ump made a strange call. | My uncle is an ump for the kids' baseball league.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It is a clipped, informal form of «umpire»; write «umpire» in schoolwork. Baseball, cricket and tennis have umpires; football (soccer), rugby and basketball have referees («ref»).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unaddressed means not dealt with, solved or talked about yet, like an unaddressed problem. 2) An unaddressed letter or parcel has no address written on it.
its sense in the lessons: In formal and school talk: «the issue remains unaddressed» means nobody has fixed it yet. In everyday life an unaddressed envelope cannot be posted. In stories, unaddressed worries or problems often grow until a character faces them.
examples from the lessons: The broken swing is still unaddressed after a month. | The letter was unaddressed, so the post office sent it back. | Bullying that is left unaddressed can get worse. | Some questions remained unaddressed at the meeting. | Her worries went unaddressed until she told her teacher. | Please don't post an unaddressed envelope.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Un-» means not. Often in the pattern «go unaddressed» or «remain unaddressed». A rather formal word; in everyday speech people say «not sorted» or «ignored».

part of speech: adjective (unannounced); also used as an adverb
meaning for a pupil: 1) Unannounced means happening or arriving without anyone being told beforehand; unexpected and without warning.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: a guest turning up unannounced, a surprise test, an unannounced school inspection. In stories it creates surprise or tension when someone arrives without warning. Phrases: «turn up unannounced», «arrive unannounced», «an unannounced visit».
examples from the lessons: Grandma turned up unannounced with a cake. | The inspectors made an unannounced visit to the school. | We had an unannounced fire drill this morning. | The teacher gave an unannounced spelling test. | A fox walked into the garden unannounced. | The band played an unannounced song at the end of the show.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: double n – «un-» + «announced». Can follow a verb like an adverb: «she arrived unannounced».

part of speech: verb (unbalance, unbalances, unbalanced, unbalancing); noun (unbalance — uncountable, rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To unbalance something is to make it lose its balance, so it tips or wobbles. 2) To unbalance a situation is to make it unfair or uneven, such as giving one team many more good players. 3) (older use) To unbalance a person is to upset them so much that they cannot think clearly. 4) (noun, rare) Unbalance is a lack of balance; «imbalance» is the usual word.
its sense in the lessons: In science and PE: weight on one side can unbalance a seesaw or a gymnast. In maths, an equation is like a balance – adding to one side only unbalances it. In fairness talk: big differences can unbalance a game or a diet. Adjective «unbalanced» is common: «an unbalanced diet».
examples from the lessons: A big wave unbalanced the boat. | Don't lean too far or you'll unbalance the ladder. | Putting all the tall children on one team would unbalance the game. | If you add 3 to only one side, you unbalance the equation. | The heavy bag unbalanced my bike. | Eating only sweets gives you an unbalanced diet.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. The noun usually used is «imbalance», not «unbalance». In maths, keep an equation balanced by doing the same thing to both sides. Calling a person «unbalanced» (mentally) is unkind and old-fashioned.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Unbecoming behaviour is not suitable or proper for a person in a certain role, such as a teacher, officer or guest. 2) (old-fashioned) Unbecoming clothes or colours do not look nice on the person wearing them.
its sense in the lessons: Found in formal rules and older stories: «conduct unbecoming of an officer», «unbecoming of a young lady». It tells the reader someone behaved below the standard expected of them. In everyday talk people say «not right» or «doesn't suit you».
examples from the lessons: Shouting at the referee was unbecoming of a team captain. | The officer was punished for conduct unbecoming. | Grandma said the green hat was rather unbecoming. | Sulking after losing is unbecoming. | Such rude words are unbecoming in a library. | The old novel described a dress «most unbecoming».
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal or old-fashioned. Used with «of» or «to», or «for»: «unbecoming of a captain». It does not mean «not becoming» in the sense of «not turning into».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Uncapped means without a cap or lid on top, like an uncapped pen or bottle. 2) Uncapped means without an upper limit, such as uncapped prices or an uncapped number of players. 3) (sport, UK, Ireland, Australia) An uncapped player has never yet played for their national team.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: leaving a pen or glue uncapped makes it dry out. In money and news talk: «uncapped fees» can rise with no limit. In sports news: a «cap» is a match for your country, so an uncapped player is new to the national squad.
examples from the lessons: Don't leave the felt-tip uncapped or it will dry out. | The uncapped bottle spilt all over the bag. | The coach picked three uncapped players for England. | Some phone plans have uncapped data. | The glue stick dried out because it was left uncapped. | An uncapped player made her debut for Ireland today.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «cap» + «un-» + «-ed»; double p. In maths, «uncapped» means there is no maximum number. Opposite: «capped».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unchanging means staying the same all the time and never changing.
its sense in the lessons: In science: some laws of nature and the speed of light are unchanging. In descriptive writing: an unchanging landscape, an unchanging routine. In religious talk: Christians believe God's love is unchanging. It tells the reader that something is steady, reliable, or perhaps boring.
examples from the lessons: The desert looked unchanging for miles. | Her unchanging smile made everyone feel welcome. | The rules of chess are almost unchanging. | Every day followed the same unchanging routine. | Christians believe God's love is unchanging. | The stars seemed unchanging in the night sky.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective only. Close to «constant» and «permanent». In fact, many things that seem unchanging, like mountains and stars, change very slowly over millions of years.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unclaimed means not collected or asked for by the person it belongs to, like an unclaimed prize or bag. 2) Unclaimed land or money has nobody who owns it or asks for it.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and school: «lost property» is full of unclaimed coats; unclaimed prizes, unclaimed parcels. In history: explorers wrongly called land «unclaimed» even when people already lived there. Phrases: «unclaimed prize», «unclaimed baggage», «go unclaimed».
examples from the lessons: The lost property box is full of unclaimed jumpers. | The raffle prize went unclaimed. | Unclaimed parcels are sent back after two weeks. | An unclaimed suitcase went round and round the airport belt. | Unclaimed items will go to the charity shop on Friday. | The explorers said the land was unclaimed, but people already lived there.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Often in «go unclaimed» or «remain unclaimed». «Claim» means to ask for something as yours. Trap: «unclaimed» land in history was often already home to Indigenous people.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Uncommon means not happening or seen often; rare or unusual. 2) (old-fashioned) Uncommon can mean remarkable or very great, like «an uncommon talent».
its sense in the lessons: In science: uncommon animals, plants or diseases; in maths, uncommon events have a low probability. In everyday talk: «it's not uncommon» means it happens quite often. In stories it marks something special or surprising.
examples from the lessons: Snow is uncommon in Sydney. | It is not uncommon to feel nervous before a test. | The uncommon bird was spotted by only a few people. | Twins are less common than single babies, but not very uncommon. | She has an uncommon gift for music. | An uncommon name can be hard to spell.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: «common». «Not uncommon» is a double negative meaning «fairly common». In maths, an uncommon event is unlikely, but it can still happen. Comparatives: «more uncommon», «most uncommon».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Uncompleted means not finished; still waiting to be done or completed.
its sense in the lessons: In school: uncompleted homework, an uncompleted worksheet, uncompleted tasks. In news and everyday life: an uncompleted building or road. It tells the reader work was started but not finished. The more common word is «incomplete» or «unfinished».
examples from the lessons: Any uncompleted homework must be done by Friday. | The uncompleted bridge stood in the river for years. | Tick off each task and circle the uncompleted ones. | His uncompleted puzzle lay on the table. | The game saves your uncompleted levels. | The builders left the house uncompleted.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Close to «unfinished» and «incomplete». «Incomplete» often means missing parts; «uncompleted» stresses that the job was not finished.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unconditionally means completely, with no conditions, limits or «if»s attached. 2) To love someone unconditionally means to love them whatever they do or however they are.
its sense in the lessons: In family talk: parents love their children unconditionally. In church talk: Christians believe God loves people unconditionally. In history and law: an army may «surrender unconditionally», giving up with no terms. In maths and logic, a rule that holds «unconditionally» holds in every case.
examples from the lessons: Gran loves all her grandchildren unconditionally. | The army surrendered unconditionally in 1945. | A good dog loves you unconditionally. | Christians believe God loves every person unconditionally. | The school agreed unconditionally to the plan. | Friends who support you unconditionally are a treasure.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «unconditional» + «-ly»; spelling «-ally». A «condition» is an «if» part of a deal; unconditionally means there is none. Opposite: «conditionally».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Uncontrolled means not controlled or held back; going on in a wild or dangerous way. 2) Uncontrolled can mean not checked or managed by rules or people, like uncontrolled building.
its sense in the lessons: In safety talk: uncontrolled fires, uncontrolled bleeding, an uncontrolled car or dog. In science experiments, an uncontrolled variable is something you forgot to keep the same, which makes the test unfair. In stories it shows danger or strong feelings: «uncontrolled laughter», «uncontrolled anger».
examples from the lessons: The uncontrolled fire spread through the forest. | An uncontrolled dog chased the sheep. | Press on a cut to stop uncontrolled bleeding. | The car went into an uncontrolled skid. | We burst into uncontrolled giggles. | Uncontrolled variables make a science test unfair.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: double l before «-ed». A «controlled» experiment keeps all things the same except one; an uncontrolled one does not. Close to «out of control».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Undefined means not clearly explained, described or fixed, like an undefined plan. 2) Undefined means without a clear shape or outline. 3) (maths) A calculation is undefined when it has no meaning or answer, like dividing a number by zero. 4) (computing) A variable or value is undefined when it has not been given a value yet.
its sense in the lessons: Important in maths: «6 ÷ 0 is undefined», because no number times 0 gives 6. In computing lessons, «undefined» appears as an error when something has no value. In everyday talk: «an undefined role» means nobody said exactly what the job is.
examples from the lessons: Dividing a number by zero is undefined. | The shape had undefined edges in the fog. | Her job in the team was still undefined. | The program printed «undefined» because the box was empty. | The rules of the new game were undefined, so we argued. | The muscles were undefined under his baggy shirt.
note for the reader of a maths problem: In maths, «undefined» is not the same as 0: 0 ÷ 6 = 0, but 6 ÷ 0 is undefined. «Define» means to give the exact meaning. Opposite: «defined».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Undercover means working secretly, pretending to be someone else, to find out information, as police or spies do. 2) (adverb) To go undercover is to start working in this secret way. 3) (sometimes «under cover») Under cover means under a roof or shelter, out of the rain.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and crime shows: undercover police, undercover agents, undercover reporters. It tells the reader a character is hiding who they really are. In everyday life «under cover» (two words) means sheltered: «Keep your bike under cover».
examples from the lessons: The undercover officer pretended to be a builder. | The reporter went undercover to find out the truth. | In the film, the spy worked undercover for years. | An undercover inspector ate at the café. | Keep the logs under cover so they stay dry. | My cat went undercover under the bed when the hoover came out. (joking)
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually one word for secret work: «undercover», and two words for shelter: «under cover». It does not mean «under a blanket».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Underfur is the soft, thick, short fur close to the skin of some animals, under the longer outer hairs, which keeps them warm and dry.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about animal adaptations: sea otters, beavers, foxes and arctic animals have dense underfur that traps air for warmth. In history: the fur trade valued underfur for making felt hats. Close to «undercoat» used by dog owners.
examples from the lessons: Sea otters have thick underfur that keeps them warm in cold water. | The fox's underfur grows thicker in winter. | Beaver underfur was once used to make hats. | Brushing the dog removes loose underfur. | Air trapped in the underfur keeps the animal dry. | Arctic hares have soft underfur under their white coats.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Dog and cat owners usually say «undercoat». The long outer hairs are called «guard hairs».

meaning for a pupil: 1) An understatement is a way of saying something that makes it sound smaller, weaker or less important than it really is. 2) Understatement is the habit or style of speaking this way, often for humour or politeness.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons it is a figure of speech, the opposite of exaggeration (hyperbole); British humour is famous for it. In everyday talk: «That's an understatement!» means the truth is much bigger. In stories it shows a calm or funny character: calling a hurricane «a bit windy».
examples from the lessons: Saying the hurricane was «a bit windy» is an understatement. | «It's an understatement to say I was hungry – I was starving!» | British people are known for understatement. | The coach called our 10–0 win «not bad», which was an understatement. | Find the understatement in the poem. | To say the test was hard is an understatement.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: «overstatement» or «exaggeration». Not a lie: the speaker and listener both know the truth is bigger. «The understatement of the year» is a joking phrase.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Undue means more than is needed, right or sensible; too much. 2) (old use) Undue can also mean not yet owed or due to be paid.
its sense in the lessons: Common in formal and adult speech: «undue stress», «undue pressure», «without undue delay», «undue attention». In school rules: «do not cause undue noise». It tells the reader the amount is too great or unfair.
examples from the lessons: Try not to put undue pressure on yourself before the test. | The bus arrived without undue delay. | The loud phone drew undue attention to him. | Doctors said there was no cause for undue worry. | Don't place undue weight on one leg after the sprain. | The coach gave undue praise to only one player.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal. Do not confuse with «unduly» (adverb: «unduly worried») or with «overdue» (late). Sounds like «un-dew».

meaning for a pupil: 1) To undulate is to move up and down or side to side in smooth waves. 2) Land or a surface that undulates has a gentle wavy shape, with soft rises and dips.
its sense in the lessons: In geography: undulating hills and countryside. In science: snakes, eels and jellyfish undulate to move. In descriptive writing it gives a calm, flowing picture. The adjective «undulating» is the most common form.
examples from the lessons: The snake undulated across the sand. | The road undulated over gentle hills. | Seaweed undulates in the waves. | We walked through undulating farmland. | The flag undulated in the breeze. | A ribbon undulated behind the gymnast.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. From Latin «unda», a wave. Formal or descriptive; in everyday speech say «roll», «ripple» or «wave».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Undyed means not coloured with dye; still its natural colour, like undyed wool or cotton.
its sense in the lessons: In art, textiles and science lessons: natural fibres before dyeing, undyed yarn, eco-friendly clothes. It tells the reader a material is plain and natural. In shops: «undyed wool», «undyed cotton».
examples from the lessons: The sheep's wool was undyed and creamy white. | We bought undyed cotton bags to decorate in art. | Undyed yarn looks natural and soft. | Natural honey is undyed – its colour comes from the flowers. | Some people prefer undyed hair. | The class dipped undyed fabric into beetroot juice.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: «un-» + «dyed» (from «dye», colour), not «undied» (from «die»). «Dyed» and «died» sound the same – a homophone trap.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Uneasily means in a worried, nervous or uncomfortable way. 2) Uneasily can also mean awkwardly or not settled, like two things sitting uneasily together.
its sense in the lessons: In stories it shows a character feeling that something is wrong: looking around uneasily, laughing uneasily, shifting uneasily in a chair. It tells the reader to expect trouble or tension. Phrase: «sit uneasily with» means not to fit well together.
examples from the lessons: She looked around uneasily in the dark corridor. | He laughed uneasily at the strange joke. | The dog sniffed the air uneasily. | Tom shifted uneasily in his seat when the teacher asked who did it. | The two ideas sit uneasily together. | We waited uneasily for the test results.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «uneasy» + «-ly»; y becomes i: «uneasily». Opposite: «easily» only in the «comfortable» sense, so better «calmly» or «comfortably».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Uneducated means having had little or no schooling or education. 2) Uneducated can also describe speech, writing or guesses that show little knowledge.
its sense in the lessons: In history and social studies: in the past many children were uneducated because they had to work; today education is a right. Using it about a person's speech can be rude and snobbish, since dialects are not uneducated. Phrase: «an uneducated guess» (joking opposite of «an educated guess»).
examples from the lessons: In Victorian times many poor children were uneducated. | Free schools mean fewer people grow up uneducated. | Being uneducated is not the same as being unintelligent. | My first answer was just an uneducated guess. | Malala fought so girls would not stay uneducated. | Calling someone uneducated because of their accent is unfair.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: «educated». Be careful: calling people «uneducated» can be hurtful. Lack of schooling is often caused by poverty or unfair rules, not by the person.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unevenness is the state of not being flat, smooth or level, like bumps on a road. 2) Unevenness is also the state of not being equal or regular, like uneven sharing or uneven quality.
its sense in the lessons: In science and DT: the unevenness of a surface affects friction and how things roll. In maths and fairness talk: unevenness in groups or shares. In everyday talk: unevenness in someone's work means it is good in parts and weak in parts.
examples from the lessons: The unevenness of the path made me trip. | We sanded the wood to remove the unevenness. | The teacher noticed the unevenness of the teams. | The unevenness of the pavement is dangerous for prams. | There was some unevenness in her handwriting. | Unevenness in the floor made the marble roll to one corner.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. From «uneven» + «-ness»; note «nn». In maths, an uneven number usually means an odd number, but «unevenness» is not used about odd numbers.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unexpectedly means in a way that nobody expected or planned; as a surprise.
its sense in the lessons: In stories it signals a twist: «Unexpectedly, the door opened.» In everyday life: visitors arrive unexpectedly, weather changes unexpectedly. In science, a result can turn out unexpectedly, which leads to new questions. Phrases: «quite unexpectedly», «not unexpectedly» (which means «as expected»).
examples from the lessons: Unexpectedly, it started to snow in April. | Grandad arrived unexpectedly with presents. | The shy boy unexpectedly won the singing contest. | The experiment ended unexpectedly when the beaker cracked. | The bus stopped unexpectedly in the middle of the road. | Not unexpectedly, the team that trained hardest won.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «unexpected» + «-ly». «Not unexpectedly» is a double negative and means «as we expected». Often at the start of a sentence followed by a comma.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unfaithful means not loyal; breaking a promise or letting down someone who trusted you. 2) A husband, wife or partner is called unfaithful when they secretly start a love relationship with someone else, which breaks their promise to each other. 3) (formal) An unfaithful copy or translation does not match the original exactly.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, the Bible and old tales it marks betrayal: an unfaithful servant, an unfaithful friend. In family life seen by a child, it can be a reason why grown-ups split up; it is a grown-up matter and never the child's fault. In church talk: the Bible praises faithfulness and calls breaking promises to God unfaithful.
examples from the lessons: The unfaithful servant ran off with his master's money. | The king's unfaithful advisor sold secrets to the enemy. | In the parable, the unfaithful worker hid his money instead of using it. | Their parents split up because one of them had been unfaithful. | The film was an unfaithful version of the book – it changed the ending. | A dog is never unfaithful to its owner.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: «faithful». The noun is «unfaithfulness» or «infidelity». When grown-ups split up, it is never the children's fault.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unflattering means making someone or something look or seem worse than they really are, like an unflattering photo. 2) Unflattering words are honest but not kind or praising.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: unflattering photos, clothes, light or haircuts. In media lessons, newspapers can choose unflattering pictures to make someone look bad – a form of bias. In feedback, an unflattering review points out problems.
examples from the lessons: That photo of me with my eyes shut is so unflattering! | The newspaper used an unflattering picture of the mayor. | Bright yellow light can be unflattering. | The critic wrote an unflattering review of the play. | The baggy uniform was unflattering on everyone. | The diary gives an unflattering picture of the queen.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «flatter», to praise too much or make look good. Opposite: «flattering». It does not mean «not flat».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unforgettable means so special, exciting, beautiful or strange that you will remember it for a very long time.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday talk and writing for trips, holidays and events: «an unforgettable day». In persuasive writing and adverts: «an unforgettable experience». In stories it tells the reader the moment matters a lot.
examples from the lessons: The school trip to the zoo was unforgettable. | Seeing the northern lights was an unforgettable sight. | Our holiday in Ireland was unforgettable. | She gave an unforgettable speech at assembly. | The taste of Nan's apple pie is unforgettable. | It was an unforgettable match – we won in the last second.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: double t before «-able»: «unforgettable». Opposite: «forgettable». Adverts often overuse it, so in writing try to say why the day was unforgettable.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unfree means not free; not allowed to choose how you live, work or move, such as a slave, a serf or a prisoner. 2) (formal) Unfree can also describe a country or society where people lack basic rights and freedoms.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons: unfree labour, serfs in medieval times, enslaved people, convicts sent to Australia. In citizenship lessons: free and unfree countries, freedom of speech and voting. It is a formal, rather rare word; people usually say «not free».
examples from the lessons: Medieval serfs were unfree and could not leave their lord's land. | Enslaved people were unfree and forced to work without pay. | Convicts in early Australia were unfree workers. | In an unfree country people cannot say what they think. | Historians study unfree labour across the world. | The prisoners felt unfree behind the high walls.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal and uncommon. Opposite: «free». The noun is «unfreedom» (rare); usually «lack of freedom».

part of speech: adjective (unfrozen); past participle of «unfreeze» (unfreeze, unfreezes, unfroze, unfrozen, unfreezing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Unfrozen means no longer frozen; thawed, or never frozen at all. 2) (money, law) Unfrozen money or accounts can be used again after being blocked. 3) (computing) An unfrozen screen or app works again after it stopped responding.
its sense in the lessons: In science: ice and frozen water that has melted is unfrozen; states of matter and melting. In cooking safety: frozen meat must be fully unfrozen (defrosted) before cooking. In news: unfrozen bank accounts. In computing: an unfrozen game.
examples from the lessons: The pond is unfrozen again now spring has come. | Make sure the chicken is fully unfrozen before cooking. | The bank account was unfrozen after the mistake was fixed. | The computer finally unfroze and the game came back. | Some plants survive only in unfrozen soil. | The unfrozen peas went soft.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular verb: unfreeze – unfroze – unfrozen. In cooking people usually say «defrosted» or «thawed». Not the same as «melted» for food.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unglazed pottery or tiles have no shiny glassy coating (glaze) on the surface, so they look dull and feel rough. 2) An unglazed window or door has no glass in it.
its sense in the lessons: In art and pottery lessons: clay pots are fired unglazed (bisque), then painted with glaze and fired again to make them shiny and waterproof. In history: old houses with unglazed windows had shutters instead of glass. Plant pots of unglazed terracotta let water and air through.
examples from the lessons: Our clay pots came out of the kiln unglazed. | Unglazed pots soak up water. | The terracotta plant pot is unglazed. | We painted glaze on the unglazed bowl. | Medieval cottages had unglazed windows with wooden shutters. | Unglazed floor tiles are less slippery.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Glaze» means a shiny coat on pottery, or glass in a window («glazier» fits glass). In the UK «double glazing» means windows with two layers of glass.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Ungovernable means impossible to control or rule, like an ungovernable country, crowd or class. 2) Ungovernable feelings, like anger, are too strong to control.
its sense in the lessons: In history and news: a country or region becomes ungovernable after war or chaos, when the government cannot keep order. In stories: an ungovernable temper, ungovernable horses. It tells the reader things have gone beyond control.
examples from the lessons: After the war, the region became ungovernable. | The wild horse was ungovernable. | The class was ungovernable on the last day of term. | He had an ungovernable temper as a child. | Rebels made the province ungovernable. | The crowd grew ungovernable when the gates opened.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «govern» + «-able» with «un-». Formal. Close to «uncontrollable» and «unruly».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Ungrammatical means not following the rules of grammar of a language, like «She go to school yesterday.»
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons: spotting and correcting ungrammatical sentences in SPaG tests. Teachers note that many dialect forms («we was», «I ain't») follow their own rules and are not mistakes in the dialect, but they are counted as ungrammatical in Standard English. In linguistics, an ungrammatical sentence is marked with a star (*).
examples from the lessons: «Him and me goes to school» is ungrammatical in Standard English. | Circle the ungrammatical sentence. | The robot's sentences were ungrammatical and funny. | Poets sometimes write ungrammatical lines on purpose. | «We was» is usual in some dialects but ungrammatical in Standard English. | My little brother's speech is ungrammatical but cute.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: «grammatical». Spelling: «-mm-» and «-ical». «Ungrammatical» does not mean «meaningless»: «Me want cookie» is ungrammatical but clear.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unheated means without any heating, so it stays cold, like an unheated room, pool or greenhouse.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: an unheated garage, conservatory or outdoor pool. In science: unheated water stays at room temperature; experiments compare heated and unheated samples. In history and social studies: poor families in unheated homes in winter.
examples from the lessons: The unheated swimming pool was freezing. | We kept the apples in the unheated garage. | In the experiment we compared heated and unheated water. | The old church was unheated, so we wore coats. | Some families can't pay bills and live in unheated homes. | Seeds grew slowly in the unheated greenhouse.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: «heated». An adjective; it describes a place or thing, not a person.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To unhook something is to undo it from a hook or take a hook out of it, such as unhooking a fish or a coat. 2) To unhook a piece of clothing, like a bra or a dress, is to undo its small hooks. 3) To unhook a trailer or carriage is to separate it from the vehicle pulling it.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: unhook a coat, a gate, a trailer, a lead. In fishing: unhook a fish carefully and put it back. In stories it can show escape: unhooking a rope, a door latch.
examples from the lessons: Dad unhooked the trailer from the car. | Gently unhook the fish and put it back in the water. | Can you unhook my coat from the peg? | The farmer unhooked the gate to let the sheep through. | She unhooked the dog's lead at the park. | The train driver unhooked the last carriage.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Opposite: «hook» or «hook up». «Unhook» is a separate word, written without a space.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unhygienic means dirty in a way that can spread germs and illness.
its sense in the lessons: In science and health lessons: not washing hands, sharing cups, coughing without covering your mouth, dirty kitchens. It tells the reader there is a risk to health. In food safety: unhygienic conditions in a café can make people ill.
examples from the lessons: Licking your fingers after touching the bin is unhygienic. | Sharing a water bottle can be unhygienic. | The café was closed because the kitchen was unhygienic. | It is unhygienic to sneeze without covering your mouth. | Not washing your hands after the toilet is unhygienic. | Leaving food out with flies on it is unhygienic.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: «hygienic» has «-gie-» (hy-JEE-nic). Opposite: «hygienic». The noun is «hygiene».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unimaginably means to a degree that is so great, small or extreme that it is very hard or impossible to imagine.
its sense in the lessons: Used in science for huge or tiny numbers: unimaginably big distances in space, unimaginably small atoms, unimaginably long times. In history and stories: unimaginably cruel or brave. It tells the reader the size or strength goes beyond everyday experience.
examples from the lessons: Space is unimaginably big. | Atoms are unimaginably small. | The dinosaurs lived an unimaginably long time ago. | The heat inside the Sun is unimaginably fierce. | Life in the trenches was unimaginably hard. | The view from the top was unimaginably beautiful.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «unimaginable» + «-ly»: drop the «e» of «-able» and add «-y»: «unimaginably». Often used before an adjective.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Uninformative means giving little or no useful information.
its sense in the lessons: In school research and writing: an uninformative website, title, label, or answer. Teachers ask for informative writing, so an uninformative paragraph needs more facts. In science, a graph without labels is uninformative.
examples from the lessons: The sign just said «Danger» – very uninformative. | His answer «stuff happened» was uninformative. | A graph without labels is uninformative. | The website was colourful but uninformative. | The weather report was so short it was uninformative. | Give your project a title that is not uninformative.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: «informative». Formal; in everyday talk say «not helpful» or «doesn't tell you much».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Unintelligibility is the state of being impossible or very hard to understand, especially speech or writing that cannot be made out.
its sense in the lessons: A formal, long word used about speech, handwriting, radio signals and messages. In language and science talk: the unintelligibility of a noisy signal, or of two languages to each other's speakers. In everyday talk say «you can't make it out».
examples from the lessons: The unintelligibility of the old letter made it hard to read. | The radio message crackled into unintelligibility. | Mumbling leads to unintelligibility. | The unintelligibility of the code kept the secret safe. | Teachers complained about the unintelligibility of his handwriting. | Two dialects can drift towards unintelligibility over centuries.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable and very formal. Built from «intelligible» (able to be understood) + «un-» + «-ity». It has nothing to do with being unintelligent.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Uninteresting means not interesting; dull and boring, so it does not hold your attention.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons: avoid uninteresting openings and words like «nice» by using vivid vocabulary. In everyday talk: an uninteresting programme or day. It tells the reader something is plain or dull.
examples from the lessons: The book had an uninteresting start but got exciting. | Rainy days at home can feel uninteresting. | Try to make your story opening less uninteresting. | The museum was small but not uninteresting. | He found maths uninteresting until he met puzzles. | The plain grey wall looked uninteresting.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: «interesting». Do not confuse with «disinterested», which means fair and not taking sides, or «uninterested», which means not interested (a person).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Uniquely means in a way that is the only one of its kind, so nothing else is like it. 2) Uniquely can mean especially or particularly, like «uniquely suited».
its sense in the lessons: In science: fingerprints identify people uniquely; some animals live uniquely on one island. In maths: a number can be written uniquely as a product of primes. In persuasive writing: «uniquely designed».
examples from the lessons: Each person's fingerprints identify them uniquely. | Kangaroos are uniquely Australian. | The kiwi bird is uniquely found in New Zealand. | Every whole number above 1 can be written uniquely as a product of prime numbers. | She is uniquely good at solving riddles. | The cake was uniquely decorated for her birthday.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «unique», meaning one of a kind. Strictly, «unique» cannot be «very unique», but people say it. Sounds like «you-NEEK-lee».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unknowable means impossible to know or find out, even with study or tools.
its sense in the lessons: In science and philosophy lessons: some things may be unknowable, like what happened before the universe began, or what someone else truly feels. In stories it adds mystery. In everyday talk: «the future is unknowable».
examples from the lessons: The future is unknowable. | Some scientists think what happened before the Big Bang may be unknowable. | The ancient king's real thoughts are unknowable. | Without the missing page, the end of the story is unknowable. | Philosophers argue about what is unknowable. | The deep sea once seemed unknowable.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Different from «unknown»: unknown means not known yet; unknowable means it can never be known. Do not confuse.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unknowing means not knowing or not aware of what is happening, often of something important. 2) An unknowing helper does something without realising what it is part of.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and mysteries: an unknowing victim, an unknowing helper, unknowing of danger. In science: germs can be spread by unknowing carriers. It tells the reader a character does not know what the reader knows (dramatic irony). The adverb «unknowingly» is very common.
examples from the lessons: The unknowing guard let the thief into the castle. | She was unknowing of the surprise party. | Germs can be spread by unknowing people with no symptoms. | The unknowing fish swam towards the hook. | He unknowingly took the wrong bag home. | The cat sat unknowing on the remote control.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Close to «unaware» and «unwitting». The adverb is «unknowingly». Different from «unknown» (not known to others).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (rare) Unlogical means not logical; not following reason or sense. The usual word is «illogical».
its sense in the lessons: Pupils may meet it in children's speech or older texts, but in writing the correct everyday word is «illogical». In maths and reasoning lessons, an illogical (unlogical) argument jumps to a conclusion that does not follow.
examples from the lessons: That answer seems unlogical – please use «illogical» in your writing. | It is unlogical to wear a coat in a heatwave. | Her excuse sounded unlogical to the teacher. | The robot said the rule was unlogical. | It is illogical to think 0.5 is bigger than 0.75 just because the digits look different. | Spock would call that unlogical!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Rare and often called a mistake: use «illogical». Many adjectives starting with l take «il-»: illegal, illegible, illogical.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unloved means not loved or cared for by anyone. 2) Unloved things are not wanted, used or looked after, like an unloved old toy or building.
its sense in the lessons: In stories it shows sadness and loneliness: an unloved orphan, an unloved pet, as in Cinderella or Toy Story. In everyday life: an unloved park or house that needs care. In church talk: Christians believe no one is unloved by God.
examples from the lessons: The unloved toy sat at the bottom of the box. | In the story, the orphan felt unloved until she met her new family. | The rescue centre helps unloved animals. | The old cinema stood unloved for years. | No child should feel unloved. | Christians believe no one is unloved by God.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: «loved» or «beloved». A sad word; if someone feels unloved, telling a trusted adult can help.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To unmask someone is to take off their mask so you can see their face. 2) To unmask a person or plan is to show the truth about them, especially that they are a cheat, spy or criminal.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and cartoons: the villain is unmasked at the end (as in Scooby-Doo). In news: unmasking a fraud or a lie. It tells the reader the truth is finally coming out.
examples from the lessons: At the end, the kids unmasked the ghost – it was the caretaker! | The detective unmasked the thief. | The reporter unmasked the fake charity. | The superhero was never unmasked. | At midnight, everyone at the party unmasked. | The test unmasked a mistake in the plan.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Opposite: «mask». Noun: «unmasking». In the «reveal the truth» sense, close to «expose».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unmeasured means not measured; nobody has found its size, amount or value. 2) (literary) Unmeasured can mean without limit; too great to measure.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and science: unmeasured lengths, angles or amounts that need a ruler, protractor or scale. In science experiments every important thing should be measured; unmeasured results give weak evidence. In poetry: «unmeasured love».
examples from the lessons: Label the unmeasured angle «x». | Two sides of the triangle are still unmeasured. | The rainfall that day went unmeasured. | The scientist knew unmeasured guesses were not evidence. | The cook added an unmeasured pinch of salt. | The poem spoke of unmeasured joy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: «measured». In maths problems, an unmeasured side or angle is the one you must find. «Measured» can also mean calm («a measured voice»), but «unmeasured» is rarely used that way.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unnatural means not natural; made by people or different from what usually happens in nature. 2) Unnatural means strange, odd or not normal, like an unnatural silence or colour. 3) Unnatural behaviour is forced or false, not relaxed.
its sense in the lessons: In science: unnatural colours in food come from dyes; unnatural things are made by people (synthetic). In stories it signals something creepy: «an unnatural silence», «an unnatural glow». In drama lessons: an unnatural voice sounds forced.
examples from the lessons: The sweets were an unnatural bright green. | An unnatural silence fell over the forest. | Her smile in the photo looked unnatural. | Keeping a parrot alone all day is unnatural for it. | The lake glowed with an unnatural light. | Try to speak naturally – shouting every line sounds unnatural.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: double n – «un-» + «natural». Careful: «natural» does not always mean safe, and «unnatural» does not always mean bad.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unofficially means not in an official or formal way; not approved, announced or recorded by the people in charge. 2) Unofficially can mean privately or secretly, before something is officially said.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday and school life: «unofficially, he's team captain», unofficial records, nicknames. In news: «unofficially, sources say». It tells the reader something is true or accepted but not formally approved yet.
examples from the lessons: Unofficially, Mia is the class's best speller. | The race was unofficially timed with a phone. | He was unofficially in charge of the snacks. | Unofficially, the teacher said we'd get a longer break. | The hill is unofficially called Dragon's Back. | The record was set unofficially, so it doesn't count.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «unofficial» + «-ly»; double f. Opposite: «officially». An unofficial record usually does not count in a competition.
