meaning for a pupil: 1) Unpersuasive means not good at making people believe or agree with something; not convincing.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons: persuasive writing and debating need strong reasons and evidence; an argument without them is unpersuasive. In everyday life: an unpersuasive excuse. It tells the reader the argument did not work.
examples from the lessons: His excuse that the dog ate his homework was unpersuasive. | The advert was colourful but unpersuasive. | Give evidence, or your argument will be unpersuasive. | The judge found the story unpersuasive. | Shouting louder doesn't make an unpersuasive point stronger. | The team's case for no homework was unpersuasive.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: «persuasive». Close to «unconvincing», which is the more common word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unpigmented means without pigment, the natural colouring in skin, hair, eyes, plants or paint, so it looks white, pale or clear.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons: pigments like melanin colour skin and hair, and chlorophyll colours leaves; unpigmented parts look white or pale. Albino animals have unpigmented fur and pink eyes. In art: unpigmented paint base is clear.
examples from the lessons: Albino animals have unpigmented fur. | Some cave fish are unpigmented and nearly see-through. | The unpigmented part of the leaf is white. | A white streak of unpigmented hair ran through his fringe. | Mix the pigment into the unpigmented paint. | Unpigmented skin burns easily in the sun.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Scientific word. «Pigment» means colour substance. Unpigmented skin needs extra sun protection.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unploughed land has not been dug up and turned over with a plough, so it is still grass, stubble or wild ground. 2) Unploughed roads or paths have not had the snow cleared by a snowplough.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and farming lessons: unploughed fields, meadows and prairies keep soil and wildlife safe. In winter life in Canada and the northern USA: unploughed (unplowed) roads after a snowstorm. In history: settlers turning unploughed prairie into farms.
examples from the lessons: The unploughed meadow was full of wild flowers. | Rabbits live at the edge of the unploughed field. | After the blizzard, our street was still unploughed. | Settlers ploughed up miles of unploughed prairie. | Leaving strips unploughed helps bees and birds. | The bus could not drive up the unploughed hill.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK, Ireland, Australia, NZ spell «plough»; the US spells «plow». The «-ough» sounds like «ow» in «cow».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unpredictable means impossible to know or say beforehand what will happen. 2) An unpredictable person or animal behaves in ways you cannot guess, sometimes calm and sometimes not.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography: unpredictable weather, earthquakes and volcanoes. In maths and probability: a dice roll is unpredictable, but over many rolls we can predict patterns. In safety: unknown dogs and wild animals can be unpredictable, so ask before stroking. In stories, an unpredictable character keeps readers guessing.
examples from the lessons: British weather is unpredictable, so take a coat. | A dice roll is unpredictable. | Wild animals can be unpredictable – don't feed them. | The ending of the book was unpredictable. | Earthquakes are hard to predict, so they seem unpredictable. | My little sister's moods are unpredictable. | The match was unpredictable until the last minute.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: «predictable». In maths, one roll of a fair dice is unpredictable, but each number has a chance of 1 in 6. Noun: «unpredictability».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unprepared means not ready for something, because you did not get ready or did not expect it. 2) Unprepared can also describe things that have not been made ready, like unprepared food or ground.
its sense in the lessons: In school: unprepared for a test, without PE kit or pencil. In safety: being unprepared for bad weather or an emergency; first aid kits and fire drills help people be prepared. In stories, an unprepared character faces trouble. Phrase: «caught unprepared».
examples from the lessons: I was unprepared for the surprise spelling test. | The hikers were unprepared for the snow. | Don't come to PE unprepared – bring your kit. | The town was unprepared for the flood. | The teacher was not unprepared – she had a spare pencil for everyone. | He walked onto the stage unprepared and forgot his lines.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: «prepared» or «ready». Often with «for»: «unprepared for the test». Scouts' motto «Be prepared» is the opposite idea.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unreal means not real; imaginary or seeming like a dream. 2) Unreal can describe something so strange or shocking that it is hard to believe it is really happening. 3) (slang) Unreal means amazing, brilliant or excellent: «That goal was unreal!» 4) (slang) Unreal can also mean unfair or ridiculous: «The price is unreal.»
its sense in the lessons: In stories: an unreal world, dreams and fantasy. In everyday talk: «It felt unreal» about big news or events. In young people's slang, especially in Australia, NZ and the USA, «unreal» is strong praise. It tells the reader the speaker is amazed.
examples from the lessons: The dream felt unreal. | Winning the cup still feels unreal. | That skateboard trick was unreal! (slang) | Dragons are unreal creatures from stories. | The prices at the theme park were unreal. (slang) | The sunset was so bright it looked unreal. | «How was the concert?» «Unreal, mate!» (slang)
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: «real». In the slang senses it is informal; do not use it in formal writing. Spelling: «un-» + «real», one word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unrecorded means not written down, filmed or saved, so there is no record of it. 2) Unrecorded music or sound has not been recorded.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons: unrecorded history – much of the past, especially of ordinary people, was never written down, so historians use objects and oral history. In science: unrecorded results are lost evidence, so always write them down. In music: unrecorded songs.
examples from the lessons: Much of ancient history went unrecorded. | Write your results down so none go unrecorded. | The goal went unrecorded because nobody filmed it. | The band played an unrecorded song at the show. | Many women's stories from the past are unrecorded. | The temperature that morning was unrecorded.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: «recorded». Often in «go unrecorded». Unrecorded does not mean it did not happen.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Unremedied means not put right, cured or fixed; a problem or wrong that nobody has repaired.
its sense in the lessons: Formal word in law, reports and news: «the problem remains unremedied», an unremedied wrong or injustice. In everyday talk say «not fixed» or «not sorted». In ethics, unremedied wrongs leave people asking for justice.
examples from the lessons: The leak in the roof remained unremedied for months. | The unfairness went unremedied for years. | An unremedied mistake can cause bigger problems later. | The report listed the faults still unremedied. | The broken lift was unremedied, so people used the stairs. | The court said the wrong could not stay unremedied.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal and rare. From «remedy» (a cure, a fix); y becomes i: «remedied». Often in «remain unremedied» or «go unremedied».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) An unsaturated solution can still dissolve more of a substance, like water that can take more sugar or salt. 2) (food, science) Unsaturated fats are fats found mostly in plants and fish, like olive oil, that are usually liquid at room temperature and are healthier than saturated fats. 3) Unsaturated colours are pale or greyish, not strong.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on dissolving: keep adding salt until no more dissolves; before that, the solution is unsaturated, after that it is saturated. In health and food labels: «saturated fat» and «unsaturated fat». In art: unsaturated colours are dull or pastel.
examples from the lessons: The salt water was unsaturated, so more salt dissolved. | Keep stirring sugar in until the solution is no longer unsaturated. | Olive oil is high in unsaturated fat. | Nuts and fish contain unsaturated fats. | Read the label to compare saturated and unsaturated fat. | The old photo had unsaturated, faded colours.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: «saturated» (holding as much as it can). In food, both fats give energy; unsaturated fats are usually called healthier. Spelling: «sat-u-rat-ed».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Unserviceable means broken or worn out and no longer fit to use, like an unserviceable tyre or plane.
its sense in the lessons: Used in formal reports, the army, airlines, schools and councils: «the playground equipment is unserviceable». In everyday talk people say «broken», «useless» or «out of order».
examples from the lessons: The old bus was unserviceable and sent for scrap. | Two fire extinguishers were found unserviceable. | The plane was unserviceable, so the flight was cancelled. | The pump is unserviceable after the flood. | Unserviceable equipment must be labelled and taken away. | The rusty bike looked unserviceable.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal. Opposite: «serviceable» (usable). Spelling: keep the «e» before «-able»: «serviceable».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unshared means not shared with anyone else; kept by one person only, like an unshared secret, room or toy.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday and computing life: unshared files or folders that only you can see. In stories: an unshared secret or feeling that a character carries alone. In safety talk: some things, like passwords, should stay unshared.
examples from the lessons: Keep your password unshared. | She kept her worry unshared, which made it heavier. | The file is unshared, so only I can open it. | An unshared bedroom felt big after her brother moved out. | Unshared toys can cause arguments in the playroom. | His joy at the news went unshared because nobody was home.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: «shared». Some things are good to share (feelings with a trusted adult), and some are not (passwords).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unsocial means not wanting to be with other people, or not friendly in company. 2) (UK, Ireland, Australia) Unsocial hours are working hours at night, early morning or weekends, when most people are not at work.
its sense in the lessons: In family and money talk: nurses, police and bakers often work unsocial hours, sometimes for extra pay. In behaviour talk: «unsocial» is close to «unsociable». «Antisocial» is different: harmful to others.
examples from the lessons: Nurses often work unsocial hours. | Dad gets extra pay for unsocial hours on Sundays. | Our cat is unsocial and hides when guests come. | Bakers start at unsocial hours, like 4 in the morning. | Feeling unsocial sometimes is normal. | The night shift is unsocial but well paid.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Close to «unsociable» (not enjoying company). Do not mix with «antisocial», which means harming or annoying others, like vandalism. «Unsocial hours» is a fixed UK phrase.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unsound means not safe or strong; in bad condition, like an unsound building or bridge. 2) Unsound reasoning, ideas or advice are not based on good sense or facts; wrong or unreliable. 3) (law, old-fashioned) «Of unsound mind» means a person who is mentally ill and cannot make responsible decisions.
its sense in the lessons: In safety: an unsound wall, tree or ice can collapse. In maths and logic: an unsound argument gives a wrong conclusion. In law: «of unsound mind». It tells the reader something cannot be trusted.
examples from the lessons: The old bridge was unsound, so it was closed. | Don't climb that tree – the branch is unsound. | His argument was unsound because the facts were wrong. | The ice looked thick but was unsound. | The engineer said the walls were structurally unsound. | That plan is financially unsound – it costs more than we have.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: «sound» (safe, sensible). «Sound» here does not mean noise. «Of unsound mind» is an old legal phrase; today people say a person is unwell.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Untagged means without a tag or label, like an untagged suitcase or piece of clothing. 2) (computing, social media) An untagged photo or post has no name or label linked to it. 3) (science) An untagged animal has not been fitted with a tag for study. 4) (games) In the game of tag, an untagged player has not been caught.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: untagged bags at the airport, untagged clothes. In science: scientists tag birds, sharks or turtles to follow them; untagged ones cannot be tracked. In online safety: ask before tagging a friend in a photo; leaving them untagged respects their privacy. In the playground game «tag» or «it».
examples from the lessons: The untagged suitcase was left at the airport. | Please leave me untagged in that photo. | Scientists could not track the untagged sharks. | Only two players were still untagged at the end of the game. | Untagged lost property is hard to return. | The untagged cows were counted again.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: «tagged». Double g before «-ed». In online safety, it is kind to ask before you tag someone.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Untested means not yet tried, checked or proved to work. 2) An untested person has not yet shown what they can do in a hard situation.
its sense in the lessons: In science: an untested idea is only a hypothesis until an experiment tests it. In safety and medicine: untested medicines or products can be dangerous. In computing: untested code may have bugs. In sport and stories: an untested player or hero.
examples from the lessons: The new medicine is still untested. | An untested idea is only a guess. | Don't use untested climbing equipment. | The young goalkeeper was untested in big matches. | Our robot's code was untested, so it crashed. | The bridge design was untested in strong winds.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: «tested». In science, an idea becomes evidence only after it is tested fairly.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Untidiness is the state of being messy and not in order, like a room with things everywhere. 2) Untidiness can also mean messy work or appearance, like untidy handwriting or clothes.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday family life: arguments about untidiness in bedrooms. In school: untidiness in books and handwriting may lose marks for presentation. It tells the reader about a messy place or character.
examples from the lessons: Mum complained about the untidiness of my room. | The teacher marked down the untidiness of my work. | His untidiness drove his sister mad. | The untidiness of the garden showed nobody lived there. | Untidiness on the stairs can cause falls. | She tried to fix the untidiness of her hair before the photo.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. From «untidy» + «-ness»; y becomes i. Opposite: «tidiness». In safety, toys left on stairs are dangerous untidiness.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Untraceable means impossible to find, follow or trace, like an untraceable phone call, person or source. 2) An untraceable amount is so small it cannot be found or measured.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and detective shows: untraceable calls, letters, money or poisons. In online safety: anonymous accounts can seem untraceable but often are not. In science: untraceable amounts of a substance.
examples from the lessons: The kidnapper used an untraceable phone. | The thief vanished and was untraceable. | The missing ring seemed untraceable. | The money was sent in an untraceable way. | Police found that the letter was not untraceable after all. | Only untraceable amounts of the chemical were left.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: keep the «e» before «-able»: «untraceable» (c needs e to sound like s). Opposite: «traceable». Online, people are often traceable even when they think they are not.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Untruthfulness is the quality or habit of not telling the truth; being dishonest or lying. 2) Untruthfulness can also mean the falseness of a statement.
its sense in the lessons: In ethics and religion lessons: truthfulness is a value; untruthfulness breaks trust. In church talk: the Bible tells people not to bear false witness. In stories like «The Boy Who Cried Wolf», untruthfulness leads to nobody believing the boy.
examples from the lessons: His untruthfulness lost him his friends' trust. | The boy who cried wolf was punished for his untruthfulness. | The teacher was upset by the untruthfulness of the excuse. | Untruthfulness in adverts is against the law. | Christians believe untruthfulness harms the soul and others. | The judge noticed the untruthfulness of the witness.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable, formal. Everyday words: «lying», «dishonesty». Opposite: «truthfulness» or «honesty».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unwitting means not knowing or not aware of what you are doing or what is happening. 2) Unwitting can describe something done by accident, without meaning to, like an unwitting mistake.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and news: an unwitting helper, unwitting victim, unwitting accomplice who helps a crime without knowing. It tells the reader a character did not realise. Adverb «unwittingly» is common: «she unwittingly told the secret».
examples from the lessons: The postman was an unwitting helper in the robbery. | She made an unwitting mistake on the map. | The unwitting tourist bought a fake ticket. | He unwittingly gave away the surprise. | The cat was an unwitting star of the video. | Unwitting people can spread fake news.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From old «wit», meaning to know. Close to «unknowing», «unaware». Opposite: «witting» (rare), usually «knowing» or «deliberate».

meaning for a pupil: 1) To unwrap something is to take off the paper, plastic or cover that is around it. 2) (informal) To unwrap a secret or idea is to reveal or explain it.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: unwrapping presents on birthdays and Christmas, unwrapping sweets or a sandwich. In science and DT: unwrapping a parcel to see packaging. In stories and fairy tales: unwrapping a mysterious gift.
examples from the lessons: We unwrapped our presents on Christmas morning. | Unwrap the chocolate bar carefully. | The baby loved unwrapping paper more than the toy! | Don't unwrap your sandwich until lunchtime. | She slowly unwrapped the mysterious parcel. | The museum unwrapped the old map from its cloth.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double p before «-ed» and «-ing»: «unwrapped», «unwrapping». The «w» in «wrap» is silent.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unwritten means not written down; existing only in speech or memory. 2) An unwritten rule is one that everybody follows or knows, even though nobody wrote it down. 3) Unwritten can also mean not yet written, like an unwritten story or chapter.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: unwritten rules, like not taking the last biscuit or queuing politely. In history and law: the UK has an «unwritten constitution» (not one single document). In language lessons: some languages are unwritten, passed on by speaking.
examples from the lessons: It's an unwritten rule not to sit in Grandad's chair. | The UK is said to have an unwritten constitution. | Some languages are still unwritten. | The ending of the story is still unwritten. | Queuing at the bus stop is an unwritten rule. | The old songs were unwritten and passed on by singing.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From the irregular verb «write – wrote – written»; double t. Opposite: «written». An unwritten rule is real even though it has no paper.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An upheaval is a big, sudden change that causes confusion, disorder or worry, like moving house or a war. 2) (geology) An upheaval is a strong upward movement of the Earth's crust that pushes up land or rocks.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday and family life: moving house, changing schools, a new baby or divorce can cause upheaval. In history: revolutions and wars are political upheavals. In geography and science: mountains formed by upheavals in the Earth's crust. Phrases: «a time of upheaval», «great upheaval».
examples from the lessons: Moving to a new country was a big upheaval. | The war brought great upheaval to the town. | Building work caused upheaval in our kitchen for weeks. | The Industrial Revolution was a time of upheaval. | Mountains were formed by upheavals of the Earth's crust. | A new school can be an upheaval, but it gets easier.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Can be countable («an upheaval») or uncountable («a lot of upheaval»). From «heave», to lift with effort. Pronounced «up-HEE-val».

meaning for a pupil: 1) To uphold a rule, law or tradition is to support it and make sure it is kept. 2) (law) To uphold a decision is for a court or judge to say the earlier decision was correct and keep it. 3) (formal) To uphold a value is to defend it and live by it.
its sense in the lessons: In citizenship and law: police uphold the law; a court upholds or overturns a decision; a referee upholds the rules. In ethics and school values: upholding honesty and respect. In church talk: to uphold the faith or teachings.
examples from the lessons: Police officers uphold the law. | The referee upheld the decision after watching the video. | We promise to uphold the school rules. | The judge upheld the ban. | The knights swore to uphold justice. | Our family upholds the tradition of Sunday lunch together.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular: uphold – upheld – upheld. Opposite in law: «overturn». Formal; everyday words are «support», «keep».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Upholstery is the soft padding, springs and cloth or leather that cover sofas, armchairs and car seats. 2) Upholstery is also the craft or job of making and covering furniture in this way.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: spilling juice on the upholstery, cleaning car upholstery, choosing fabric. In DT lessons: materials like foam, fabric and leather. The worker is an «upholsterer».
examples from the lessons: Don't put muddy shoes on the upholstery! | The car's upholstery is grey cloth. | The cat scratched the sofa's upholstery. | Grandad learned upholstery and fixed old chairs. | We cleaned the juice stain off the upholstery. | The leather upholstery felt cold in winter.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Person: «upholsterer»; verb: «upholster». Spelling: «up-HOL-ster-y», no «d» after «up».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Upriver means towards the source of a river, against the flow of the water. 2) Upriver also means at a place further up the river from where you are.
its sense in the lessons: In geography: rivers flow from the source to the mouth, so going upriver means going towards the source, often uphill. In history and stories: explorers paddling upriver, salmon swimming upriver to lay eggs. Close to «upstream»; opposite «downriver».
examples from the lessons: Salmon swim upriver to lay their eggs. | The explorers paddled upriver for days. | The village is a mile upriver from the bridge. | Rowing upriver is harder than rowing down. | Pollution from a factory upriver killed the fish. | We took an upriver boat trip.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: «downriver». Similar to «upstream». Upriver means against the current, not always north: some rivers flow north.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal, science, medicine) Urination is the act of passing urine (wee) out of the body.
its sense in the lessons: Used in science lessons on the human body and in medicine: the kidneys clean the blood and make urine, which is stored in the bladder and released by urination. Doctors ask about it to check health. In everyday talk children say «going for a wee» or «peeing» (US).
examples from the lessons: Urination removes waste water from the body. | The kidneys make urine, and urination gets rid of it. | Drinking lots of water leads to more frequent urination. | The doctor asked about any pain during urination. | Animals use urination to mark their territory. | Babies can't control urination yet, so they wear nappies.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal and scientific. Verb: «urinate»; the liquid is «urine». Everyday words: «wee», «pee». A polite, medical word, not rude.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A utensil is a tool or object used in the kitchen or for eating, such as a spoon, fork, whisk or spatula. 2) A utensil can also be any useful tool for a job in the house.
its sense in the lessons: In cooking lessons and food technology: kitchen utensils, cooking utensils, and safety with knives and hot pans. In the USA, «utensils» often means knives, forks and spoons (cutlery in the UK). In history: Roman or Stone Age utensils found by archaeologists.
examples from the lessons: A whisk is a kitchen utensil. | Wash all utensils after cooking. | In the USA, people call knives and forks «utensils». | Archaeologists found Roman cooking utensils. | Hang the utensils on the hooks above the cooker. | Use a wooden utensil so you don't scratch the pan.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: «a utensil». Use «a», not «an», because it starts with a «you» sound. UK people usually say «cutlery» for knives, forks and spoons.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Utilisation is the act of using something, especially making practical or good use of it.
its sense in the lessons: A formal, stiff word used in reports, business, science and exams: «utilisation of resources», «energy utilisation». In everyday talk people simply say «use». Pupils meet it in formal texts and should understand it, but «use» is usually better in their own writing.
examples from the lessons: The utilisation of solar energy is growing. | The report looked at the utilisation of school space. | Good utilisation of time helps you finish the test. | Plants show efficient utilisation of sunlight. | The utilisation of the new library has doubled. | Better utilisation of water helps farms in dry years.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK, Ireland, Australia, NZ often spell «-isation»; the US and Canada spell «utilization». Verb: «utilise» / «utilize». Usually «use» is clearer and better style.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Utmost means greatest or most extreme, as much as possible: «of the utmost importance». 2) (noun) Your utmost is the most you can do: «do your utmost». 3) (old use) Utmost can mean farthest or most distant: «the utmost ends of the earth».
its sense in the lessons: In formal speech and writing: «of the utmost importance», «with the utmost care», «try your utmost». In stories and the Bible: «the utmost parts of the earth». It tells the reader something matters as much as it possibly can.
examples from the lessons: Handle the eggs with the utmost care. | Safety is of the utmost importance. | She did her utmost to win the race. | The secret must be kept with the utmost care. | He tried his utmost but still missed the bus. | The explorers sailed to the utmost ends of the earth.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal. Used only before a noun or in «do your utmost» / «try your utmost». Close to «uttermost» (older). It has no comparative.

part of speech: noun (Valhalla) — a name, usually with a capital V
meaning for a pupil: 1) (a name, Norse myth) Valhalla is the great hall in the old Norse (Viking) myths where the god Odin welcomed warriors who died bravely in battle. 2) (informal) Valhalla can mean a wonderful place of honour or a heaven for some group, like «a Valhalla for football fans».
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons about the Vikings: Vikings believed brave warriors chosen by the Valkyries feasted in Valhalla until the end of the world. In stories, films and games it appears often. Say «Vikings believed …», because it is a myth, not a real place.
examples from the lessons: Vikings believed fallen warriors went to Valhalla. | In Valhalla, the warriors feasted with Odin. | The Valkyries chose who would go to Valhalla. | We read Norse myths about Valhalla. | The stadium was a Valhalla for rugby fans. | The game ends with the hero entering Valhalla.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A proper name: write it with a capital V. Pronounced «val-HAL-a». From Old Norse «Valhöll», «hall of the slain». A myth from the Viking religion, not a real place.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Validly means in a way that is valid: officially correct, accepted by the rules or the law. 2) Validly means in a way that is logically sound, with reasons that really lead to the conclusion.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and logic: an argument is validly made when the conclusion follows from the facts. In law and voting: a validly signed form, validly cast votes. In science: a result is validly measured when the test is fair.
examples from the lessons: The votes were validly cast, so they all count. | The form must be validly signed by a parent. | Can you validly conclude that all cats are black from one black cat? No! | The test was validly done with fair rules. | Only validly bought tickets are accepted. | The passport was validly issued.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «valid» + «-ly». Opposite: «invalidly». In logic, «valid» means the reasoning works, even if a starting fact is wrong.

part of speech: verb (vaporise, vaporises, vaporised, vaporising); US spelling vaporize
meaning for a pupil: 1) To turn a liquid or a solid into a gas or vapour, usually by heating it. 2) To destroy something completely so that almost nothing is left, as with a ray or a huge blast in stories. 3) (informal) To disappear suddenly, as if into thin air.
its sense in the lessons: In science it names a change of state: water vaporises when it boils and becomes steam, and the gas spreads out into the air. Sweat cools you because it vaporises from your skin. In science fiction a laser or ray "vaporises" a rock or a ship, which tells the reader nothing is left. Related words: vapour, evaporate, vaporiser. Phrases: "vaporise into steam", "be vaporised by the blast".
examples from the lessons: When water boils, it vaporises and turns into steam. | The puddle vaporised in the hot sun by lunchtime. | In the film, the alien's ray vaporised the rock in a flash. | A drop of perfume vaporises quickly, so you can smell it across the room. | Our teacher heated the ice until it melted and then vaporised. | My pocket money seems to vaporise the moment I get to the shop. | Liquids vaporise faster when it is hot and windy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: vaporised in the past. UK and Australia often spell it "vaporise"; the USA spells it "vaporize"; both are correct. Vaporise and evaporate are close: evaporate is used for slow drying at the surface (a puddle), vaporise for any turning into gas, often fast or with heat. Do not confuse with "vapour" (the noun, the gas itself). In science, the mass of water does not vanish when it vaporises: it is still there as gas.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A slightly different form or version of something, such as a different spelling of a word or a different version of a game. 2) A new form of a virus or other living thing whose genes have changed a little, for example a Covid variant. 3) (adjective, formal) Different from the usual form.
its sense in the lessons: In spelling lessons a variant is another accepted way to write a word: "color" is the US variant of "colour". In games and puzzles a variant changes one rule. In science and the news, a variant is a changed form of a germ, which might spread faster. In maths, people may speak of a variant of a problem: the same problem with small changes. Phrases: "a variant of", "a new variant", "spelling variant".
examples from the lessons: Grey and "gray" are variants of the same word. | We played a variant of tag where you freeze when caught. | Scientists are watching a new variant of the flu virus. | This puzzle is a variant of the one we did yesterday, with bigger numbers. | Chess has many variants, and some use a round board. | The shop sells three variants of the toy car in different colours. | The new variant spread quickly through the town.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: a variant, two variants. A variant is not a completely different thing; it is the same thing changed a little. "Variant" and "variety" are related but not the same: a variety is a kind or a mix of many kinds. The verb "vary" means change; "variable" in maths is a letter that stands for a number that can change.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (medicine) The proper medical name for chickenpox, a common illness that gives an itchy rash of spots and blisters, mostly in children. 2) (medicine) The virus that causes it, called the varicella-zoster virus.
its sense in the lessons: You will mostly hear "chickenpox" in everyday life; doctors, nurses and vaccine leaflets use "varicella". It spreads easily from person to person. Many children are given a varicella vaccine, which helps protect them. The same virus can wake up years later in an adult and cause shingles (herpes zoster). Phrases: "varicella vaccine", "varicella-zoster virus".
examples from the lessons: Varicella is the doctor's word for chickenpox. | The leaflet said the varicella vaccine protects children from chickenpox. | My little brother had varicella and was covered in itchy spots. | The nurse wrote "varicella" on the school note. | Varicella spreads easily, so children stay home until the spots crust over. | The varicella virus can return years later as shingles.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: say "varicella", not "a varicella". Pronounced VARR-ih-SELL-uh. It has nothing to do with chickens: the name "chickenpox" is old and its origin is not certain. Do not scratch the spots, as they can scar. A doctor, not a pupil, decides if someone has it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Several different; of different kinds. 2) More than one; many separate ones.
its sense in the lessons: It tells the reader there are a number of different things, but does not say exactly how many. In school writing it is a useful word for listing kinds: "various animals", "various shapes". In maths problems "various" does not give a number, so you must find the number elsewhere in the question. Phrases: "for various reasons", "at various times", "in various ways", "various kinds of".
examples from the lessons: The shop sells various kinds of sweets. | We measured various objects in the classroom with a ruler. | She was late for various reasons. | The puzzle can be solved in various ways. | Various children brought in pets for show and tell. | The museum has various dinosaur bones from around the world. | We drew various shapes: circles, squares and triangles. | I have visited my nan at various times this year.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Various goes before a plural noun: various books, not various book. Do not use "of" straight after it in careful writing: say "various children", not "various of the children" (use "several of" instead). Do not confuse with "variety" (noun) and "vary" (verb). In maths, "various" never means a fixed number.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In different ways, or by different people at different times. 2) Used to show that something has been given several different names or descriptions.
its sense in the lessons: It is a written, slightly formal word. It often comes before "described as", "called" or "known as" to say that people use several different names or descriptions for the same thing. It warns the reader that people do not all agree.
examples from the lessons: The animal is variously called a cougar, a puma or a mountain lion. | The castle has been variously described as beautiful and gloomy. | The children were variously dressed as pirates, robots and fairies. | The old story is variously told in different villages. | His age was variously reported as nine and ten. | The colour was variously described as blue, green and teal.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from "various" plus -ly. It is mainly used in writing, not in everyday chat. It does not mean "very" or "a lot".

meaning for a pupil: 1) Very much; to a very great degree. 2) Over a very large area or amount.
its sense in the lessons: It makes a comparison or a description much stronger: "vastly bigger", "vastly different", "vastly improved". In maths and science it tells the reader the difference is very large, but it is not an exact number. Phrases: "vastly different", "vastly better", "vastly outnumbered".
examples from the lessons: The Sun is vastly bigger than the Earth. | My handwriting has vastly improved this term. | The two stories are vastly different. | The defenders were vastly outnumbered by the attackers. | A blue whale is vastly heavier than an elephant. | Life today is vastly different from life in the Middle Ages. | The new game is vastly better than the old one.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from "vast" (very large). It usually goes before an adjective or a verb like "improve", "increase" or "differ". In maths, "vastly bigger" tells you the difference is huge, but you still need the real numbers to calculate.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The quality of being extremely large, wide or huge. 2) A very large, empty area, such as a desert, an ocean or space.
its sense in the lessons: Used in stories, poems and science to make the reader feel how big and empty something is: the vastness of space, of the ocean, of the desert. It often makes a person feel small or lonely. Phrases: "the vastness of space", "in the vastness of".
examples from the lessons: The astronaut stared out at the vastness of space. | The vastness of the ocean made the little boat seem tiny. | We were amazed by the vastness of the desert. | In the vastness of the Australian outback, there was no house for miles. | The vastness of the library made it easy to get lost. | Scientists still cannot imagine the vastness of the universe.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly uncountable: "the vastness of", not "a vastness". It comes from "vast" plus -ness. It describes size, not a number.

part of speech: noun (a veil, veils); verb (veil, veils, veiled, veiling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A piece of thin cloth worn over the head or face, for example by a bride at a wedding or by some women for religious reasons. 2) Something that covers or hides something, like a veil of mist or a veil of secrecy. 3) (verb) To cover or hide something partly. 4) (church) The head covering worn by nuns, and the curtain in the Temple described in the Bible.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life you see a veil at weddings, where the bride may wear a white veil, and in some religions, where women cover their hair or face. In stories, "a veil of mist" or "a veil of darkness" tells the reader something is hidden. "Veiled" can mean hidden but hinted at: "a veiled threat". In church, when a woman becomes a nun, people say she "takes the veil". Phrases: "lift the veil", "a veil of secrecy", "a veiled threat", "take the veil".
examples from the lessons: The bride wore a long white veil. | A veil of mist covered the hills in the morning. | The nun wore a black veil over her hair. | My aunt lifted her veil to kiss the groom. | The plan was kept under a veil of secrecy. | His words were a veiled warning to stop. | Clouds veiled the moon, so the night was very dark. | Some Muslim women wear a veil as part of their faith.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: a veil, veils. Rhymes with "rail" and "male". Do not confuse with "vale" (a valley, old word), which sounds the same, or "vein" (a tube carrying blood). Respect: wearing a veil is a personal or religious choice and should not be mocked.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A building or arena with a steeply sloping oval track for bicycle racing.
its sense in the lessons: Used in sport, especially track cycling at the Olympics and big competitions. The track is banked (tilted) at the ends so that riders can go very fast around the bends without sliding off. Phrases: "at the velodrome", "the velodrome track".
examples from the lessons: The cyclists raced around the velodrome at great speed. | We watched the track cycling at the velodrome. | The velodrome track is steep at the corners. | The London velodrome was built for the 2012 Olympics. | My cousin trains at the velodrome every Saturday. | The crowd cheered as the riders crossed the line in the velodrome.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a velodrome. Pronounced VEL-oh-drome. "Velo-" comes from the French word for bicycle, "vélo", and "-drome" means a racecourse, like in "aerodrome" and "hippodrome".

meaning for a pupil: 1) A long, bitter quarrel between two families in which they keep taking revenge on each other, sometimes violently. 2) A long campaign by one person to harm or annoy another person they dislike.
its sense in the lessons: Used in stories, history and the news. It tells the reader that the anger is personal and goes on for a long time, often for no fair reason. The word came from Italian, where it means revenge. Phrases: "a vendetta against", "carry on a vendetta", "a personal vendetta".
examples from the lessons: The two families had a vendetta that lasted a hundred years. | He seemed to have a personal vendetta against the referee. | In the story, the vendetta ended when the children of both families became friends. | The teacher said it was not a vendetta; she was just being fair. | Old vendettas can make a village an unhappy place. | She dropped her vendetta and said sorry.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a vendetta, two vendettas. It comes from Italian. A vendetta is not just one argument; it is long and about getting even. Taking revenge usually makes problems worse, which is what many stories about vendettas teach.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who checks that something is true, correct or real. 2) (computing) A program or tool that checks automatically whether something is correct, such as a password, a document or the answer to a problem.
its sense in the lessons: Used in computing, science and official work. A fact verifier checks facts in news stories; an age verifier checks how old someone is before they use a website. In maths and computing, a verifier checks a proof or an answer. It comes from "verify" (to check that something is true).
examples from the lessons: The verifier checked that the signature was real. | A computer verifier checked all our answers in seconds. | Fact verifiers make sure the news report is true. | The website uses an age verifier before you can sign up. | A proof verifier can check that each step of a maths proof follows the rules. | The ticket verifier scanned my code at the gate.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a verifier, verifiers. Built from "verify" plus -er (y changes to i). Related words: verify, verification, verified. A verifier only checks; it does not create the answer.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) Describing a part of a body that is still there but has become small or useless over a very long time, such as the tiny leg bones inside some snakes. 2) (formal) Remaining as a small trace or bit of something that used to be bigger or more important.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about evolution, vestigial body parts are clues that living things changed over a long time. Examples often given are the tailbone in humans, the wings of birds that cannot fly (like the ostrich and kiwi), and leg bones in whales. Phrases: "a vestigial organ", "vestigial wings", "a vestigial tail".
examples from the lessons: Ostriches have vestigial wings that cannot lift them into the air. | Whales have small vestigial leg bones inside their bodies. | The human tailbone is often called a vestigial part. | The kiwi has tiny vestigial wings hidden under its feathers. | Scientists study vestigial organs to learn how animals changed. | Only a vestigial bit of the old castle wall is left.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective, from "vestige" (a small trace that remains). Pronounced vest-IJ-ee-ul. Myth trap: "vestigial" does not always mean completely useless; some vestigial parts, like the human appendix and tailbone, still have small uses. It is a science and formal word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To annoy, worry or upset someone, especially about small things. 2) (formal) To puzzle someone; a "vexed question" is one that is hard to answer and that people argue about.
its sense in the lessons: It is an old-fashioned or written word; in everyday speech people say "annoy" or "bother". You find it in classic stories, the Bible and poems. "Vexed" means annoyed; "vexing" means annoying. "A vexed question" is a hard, much-argued problem. Phrases: "vexed with someone", "a vexed question", "a vexing problem".
examples from the lessons: The noisy neighbours vexed my grandad. | She was vexed that her brother had eaten the last biscuit. | The missing piece of the puzzle vexed us all afternoon. | Do not vex your mother by being late. | Climate change is a vexed question that people argue about. | It was a vexing problem, but we solved it in the end. | The king was vexed when his orders were ignored.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: vex, vexes, vexed. The -es ending is because it ends in x. It is an older, more formal word: in a story it often shows the character is cross. "Vexed" is not as strong as "furious".

part of speech: verb, past form of vindicate (vindicate, vindicates, vindicated, vindicating); adjective (vindicated)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Shown to be right after other people doubted you or blamed you. 2) Cleared of blame or suspicion, so that people now know you did nothing wrong. 3) (adjective) Feeling happy and proud because you have been proved right.
its sense in the lessons: Used in stories, the news and law. It tells the reader that someone who was doubted, laughed at or wrongly blamed has been proved right or innocent. "I feel vindicated" means "I was right all along." Phrases: "be vindicated by", "feel vindicated", "fully vindicated".
examples from the lessons: When the lost money was found, Tom was vindicated. | The scientist was vindicated when the experiment worked. | She felt vindicated when the answer turned out to be the one she had said. | The new evidence vindicated the man who was wrongly accused. | Our team's plan was vindicated when we won the match. | Everyone laughed at his idea, but he was vindicated in the end.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Vindicated is the past of "vindicate"; the noun is "vindication". It is a formal word. Do not confuse with "vindictive", which means wanting to hurt someone for revenge; that is a very different meaning.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who plays the violin, a stringed musical instrument held under the chin and played with a bow.
its sense in the lessons: Used in music lessons and about orchestras and bands. A violinist can be a learner in a school orchestra or a famous professional. The leading violinist of an orchestra is called the leader (UK) or concertmaster (US). Phrases: "a famous violinist", "first violinist".
examples from the lessons: My sister is a violinist in the school orchestra. | The violinist played a sad tune on the street. | A violinist needs to practise every day. | The orchestra had twenty violinists. | The violinist tucked the violin under her chin and lifted the bow. | Mozart's father was a violinist and a music teacher.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a violinist. Built from "violin" plus -ist, like pianist and cellist. Someone who plays the fiddle in folk music may be called a fiddler, though the instrument is the same.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (computing) Made or seen on a computer or online, not in the real physical world, such as a virtual tour or a virtual classroom. 2) Almost completely something, though not officially or not quite: "a virtual stranger" is someone you hardly know. 3) (science) In optics, a virtual image is one that seems to be behind a mirror or lens but cannot be shown on a screen.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and school it often means online or computer-made: virtual reality (VR), a virtual museum visit, a virtual pet, virtual lessons from home. The second sense, "almost", is common in books and the news: "a virtual certainty" means almost certain. In physics lessons on mirrors, the image in a flat mirror is virtual. Phrases: "virtual reality", "a virtual tour", "a virtual certainty", "a virtual stranger".
examples from the lessons: We went on a virtual tour of the Natural History Museum. | During the snow days we had virtual lessons on the laptop. | In virtual reality you feel as if you are inside the game. | My virtual pet needs feeding every day in the app. | The new kid was a virtual stranger to us. | It is a virtual certainty that it will rain in Manchester this week. | The image you see in a mirror is a virtual image. | The traffic jam brought the town to a virtual standstill.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective; the adverb "virtually" usually means "almost" (virtually empty = almost empty), not "online". Safety: people you meet in a virtual world are still real people; never share personal details with strangers online. "Virtual" is not the same as "virtuous" (good and moral).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Very good and moral; behaving in an honest, kind and right way. 2) (humorous) Feeling pleased with yourself for doing something good or healthy, like eating salad. 3) A "virtuous circle" is a chain of good events, each one causing the next.
its sense in the lessons: Used in stories, fables, the Bible and ethics lessons to describe a good character, often the opposite of a wicked one. In everyday chat people use it jokingly: "I feel virtuous because I did my homework early." In economics and science, a "virtuous circle" is the good opposite of a "vicious circle". Phrases: "a virtuous life", "feel virtuous", "a virtuous circle".
examples from the lessons: The virtuous princess always told the truth. | In the fable, the virtuous farmer was rewarded for his kindness. | I felt very virtuous after tidying my room without being asked. | The Bible praises a virtuous person who is honest and kind. | Reading more makes you better at reading, which makes you read more: a virtuous circle. | She led a quiet and virtuous life.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective from "virtue" (a good quality, like honesty or courage); note the spelling: virtue drops the e and adds -ous. Opposite: wicked, immoral, sinful. Do not confuse with "virtual" (online or almost). The opposite of a virtuous circle is a vicious circle.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) How thick and sticky a liquid is, and how slowly it flows. 2) (science) How strongly a liquid or gas resists flowing; a high viscosity means it flows slowly.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons you compare liquids: honey, treacle and syrup have a high viscosity and pour slowly; water and juice have a low viscosity and pour quickly. Heating usually lowers the viscosity of a liquid, so warm honey runs faster. A common experiment is timing a marble falling through different liquids. Phrases: "high viscosity", "low viscosity", "measure the viscosity".
examples from the lessons: Honey has a higher viscosity than water. | We tested the viscosity of oil, syrup and water by timing how fast they ran down a slope. | Warm syrup has a lower viscosity, so it pours more easily. | Ketchup has a high viscosity, so it is hard to get out of the bottle. | Engine oil must have the right viscosity to work well. | The marble sank slowly because the liquid had a high viscosity.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly uncountable. Adjective: viscous (thick and sticky). Trap: viscosity is not the same as density; oil is less dense than water (it floats) but has a higher viscosity (it flows more slowly). In a results table, a longer time to flow means higher viscosity.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Extremely important or necessary; something you cannot do without. 2) Needed to stay alive, like the heart, lungs and brain, which are "vital organs". 3) Full of energy and life.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and school it means "very important": "It is vital that you listen to the safety rules." In science and health, vital organs keep the body alive, and nurses check "vital signs" such as heartbeat, breathing and temperature. In stories it can describe a lively, energetic person. Phrases: "vital for", "it is vital that", "vital organs", "vital signs", "play a vital role".
examples from the lessons: Water is vital for all living things. | It is vital that you wear a helmet when you ride a bike. | The heart and lungs are vital organs. | The nurse checked his vital signs. | Bees play a vital role in growing our food. | The goalkeeper made a vital save in the last minute. | Sleep is vital for a growing brain. | She was a bright and vital old lady who loved dancing.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective; adverb "vitally" (vitally important). It is stronger than "important". The plural noun "vitals" can mean the vital organs. It comes from the Latin word for life, like "vitamin" and "vitality".

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) Like glass, or made of glass: hard, shiny and often see-through. 2) (science) The vitreous humour (or vitreous body) is the clear jelly that fills the inside of the eyeball.
its sense in the lessons: A science and technical word. In lessons on the eye, the vitreous humour is the clear jelly that keeps the eye round and lets light pass to the back. In geology, a mineral with a glassy shine has a "vitreous lustre". In everyday life, "vitreous china" is the shiny material used for toilets and basins, and "vitreous enamel" covers old saucepans and signs.
examples from the lessons: The vitreous humour is a clear jelly inside the eye. | Quartz has a vitreous shine, like glass. | The toilet is made of vitreous china. | Light passes through the vitreous jelly to reach the back of the eye. | The old metal sign was coated in vitreous enamel. | The rock had a vitreous look where lava had cooled quickly.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced VIT-ree-us. It is a technical word; in everyday talk say "glassy". "Humour" in "vitreous humour" is an old word for a body fluid, not a joke.

meaning for a pupil: 1) By speaking out loudly and openly, so others clearly hear your opinion. 2) Using the voice, especially in singing.
its sense in the lessons: Vocally often goes with protest or support: if someone complains vocally, everyone knows how they feel. In music, it describes the singing part: "vocally, the song is hard." Phrases: "vocally opposed to", "vocally support", "very vocally".
examples from the lessons: The parents vocally opposed closing the playground. | Our class vocally supported the idea of a longer break. | The fans cheered vocally for their team. | Vocally, this song is very hard to sing. | She is quiet in class but vocally strong in the choir. | Some neighbours complained vocally about the noise.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from "vocal" (to do with the voice; also outspoken). Related: vocalist (a singer), vocal cords. Do not confuse "vocal" with "verbal" (using words) or "vocabulary".

meaning for a pupil: 1) A thin, light, see-through cloth made of cotton, silk or polyester, used for curtains, dresses and blouses.
its sense in the lessons: Used in clothes, sewing and home shopping. Voile curtains let light into a room but stop people from seeing in easily. The word comes from French, where it means "veil". Phrases: "voile curtains", "cotton voile".
examples from the lessons: We hung white voile curtains in the kitchen. | The summer dress was made of light cotton voile. | Sunlight shone softly through the voile. | Nan sewed a blouse from blue voile. | Voile is so thin you can almost see through it. | The shop sells voile by the metre.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: "some voile", "a metre of voile". Pronounced VOYL (rhymes with "boil") in English, or vwahl in the French way. It is related to "veil".

part of speech: verb (vouch, vouches, vouched, vouching), used as "vouch for"
meaning for a pupil: 1) To say that you know someone is honest, good or telling the truth, and you will take responsibility for that. 2) To say that something is true or good because you have seen or tried it yourself.
its sense in the lessons: It almost always comes as "vouch for". If a friend vouches for you, they put their own good name behind you. In stories, someone may refuse to vouch for a suspicious stranger. In everyday life, a teacher or a neighbour may vouch for a person who wants a job. Phrases: "vouch for someone", "I can vouch for that", "can't vouch for".
examples from the lessons: I can vouch for Sam; he would never steal. | The teacher vouched for her honesty. | I can vouch for this pizza place; it's brilliant. | Nobody could vouch for the stranger, so he was not let in. | Mum vouched for my story about the broken window. | I can't vouch for the weather tomorrow!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: vouch, vouches, vouched. Nearly always followed by "for". Rhymes with "couch" and "pouch". Related noun: voucher (a ticket you can swap for goods or money), which comes from the same root. Only vouch for someone you really know: it means you share the blame if they let people down.

part of speech: noun (wailing, uncountable); verb, -ing form of wail (wail, wails, wailed, wailing); adjective (wailing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A long, loud, high cry of pain, sadness or anger. 2) A long, high sound like a cry, such as a siren or the wind. 3) (informal) Complaining loudly and at length. 4) The Wailing Wall is a name for the Western Wall in Jerusalem, a holy place where Jewish people pray.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, wailing tells the reader that someone is very upset: a baby wailing in the night, mourners wailing at a funeral. It can also describe sounds: a wailing siren or the wind wailing in the chimney. The Western Wall in Jerusalem is a very holy place for Jewish people; "Wailing Wall" is an older name, and many prefer "Western Wall". Phrases: "wailing and crying", "a wailing siren", "the Wailing Wall".
examples from the lessons: The baby was wailing in the middle of the night. | We heard the wailing of a fire engine's siren. | The wind was wailing around the old house. | There was wailing and crying when the dog ran away. | Stop wailing about your homework and just start it! | People pray at the Western Wall, also called the Wailing Wall. | The ghost in the story made a terrible wailing sound.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Wail is a regular verb (wailed, wailing). Homophone trap: "wailing" sounds like "whaling" (hunting whales) and "Wales" sounds like "wails"; check the spelling by meaning. Wailing is louder and longer than crying or sobbing.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (UK) A short jacket with buttons and no sleeves, worn over a shirt and often under a suit jacket; in the USA and Canada it is called a vest.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, waistcoats are worn with smart suits, at weddings, and as part of some uniforms. In old stories and costumes, gentlemen wear waistcoats with a pocket watch. A "hi-vis waistcoat" or "high-visibility vest" is the bright yellow top for safety near roads. Phrases: "a three-piece suit" (jacket, trousers and waistcoat), "waistcoat pocket".
examples from the lessons: Dad wore a grey waistcoat to my cousin's wedding. | The White Rabbit took a watch out of his waistcoat pocket. | The page boy wore a little velvet waistcoat. | Our crossing guard wears a bright yellow safety waistcoat. | In the play, I wore a waistcoat and a top hat. | The waistcoat had six shiny buttons.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Pronounced WAIST-coat or, more traditionally, WESS-kut. False friend between countries: in the UK a "vest" is a vest worn under a shirt (a singlet in Australia and New Zealand), but in the USA a "vest" is a waistcoat. Spelling: waist (middle of the body), not "waste".

meaning for a pupil: 1) A very easy win in a game or contest, where the other side hardly fights back. 2) (sport) A win given to one side because the other side did not turn up or could not play.
its sense in the lessons: Used in sport, games and competitions, also in the news about elections. It tells the reader the contest was not close at all. Phrases: "it was a walkover", "win by a walkover", "no walkover".
examples from the lessons: The final was a walkover; we won 8–0. | The other team did not turn up, so we won by a walkover. | Don't expect a walkover; they are a strong side. | The spelling quiz was a walkover for Priya. | The election was a walkover for the popular mayor. | The tennis player got a walkover when her opponent was injured.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a walkover. Written as one word for the noun; the verb phrase is two words: "walk over" (to walk across, or to treat someone badly: "Don't let them walk all over you"). Similar words: easy win, a doddle (UK), a breeze, a cakewalk.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (India, informal) A person who does a particular job or is connected with a particular thing, as in chai-wallah (a tea seller) or rickshaw-wallah. 2) (old-fashioned UK slang) A person in charge of something, often said jokingly: "the computer wallah".
its sense in the lessons: The word comes from Hindi and Urdu and is common in Indian English and in British English from the time when Britain ruled India. In India it is part of everyday names for jobs: dabbawala (lunchbox delivery person), chai-wallah. In old British books it may be used jokingly. Some people find the old British use a little dated. Phrases: "chai-wallah", "the tech wallah".
examples from the lessons: The chai-wallah poured hot sweet tea at the station. | In Mumbai, dabbawalas deliver thousands of lunchboxes every day. | Ask the computer wallah to fix the printer. | The rickshaw-wallah pedalled us through the busy market. | Grandad called the man who sold ice cream "the ice-cream wallah". | The paper wallah threw the newspaper onto the step.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Also spelled "walla" or "wala" (dabbawala). Usually joined to another word with a hyphen. It is informal. Do not confuse with "wallaby" (an animal like a small kangaroo) or "wally" (a silly person).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (UK slang, mild) A silly or foolish person; a mild, often friendly insult. 2) (Scotland, informal) Made of china or porcelain, as in a "wally dug" (a china dog ornament) or a tiled "wally close" (entrance). 3) Wally is also a name, as in the books "Where's Wally?" (called "Where's Waldo?" in the USA and Canada).
its sense in the lessons: In UK playgrounds and comedy, "you wally!" is a gentle way of calling someone silly, often in fun. It is milder than words like "idiot". In the puzzle books, you search crowded pictures for Wally in his red-and-white striped jumper. Phrases: "you wally!", "a right wally", "feel like a wally".
examples from the lessons: Don't be a wally; put your coat on, it's freezing! | I felt like a right wally when I fell off the stage. | Dad, you wally, you've got your jumper on backwards! | We spent ages trying to find Wally in the busy beach picture. | My cousin called me a wally for losing my shoe. | Nan has a pair of wally dugs on her mantelpiece in Glasgow.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a wally, plural wallies (y changes to ies). It is mild slang, mostly British; still, it can hurt if said unkindly, so do not use it to bully. Capital W for the name and the book character. Not the same as "wallah" or "wallaby".

part of speech: noun (a waltz, waltzes); verb (waltz, waltzes, waltzed, waltzing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A smooth ballroom dance for two people who turn round and round together, with three beats in each bar of music. 2) A piece of music for this dance. 3) (verb) To dance a waltz. 4) (informal) To walk somewhere in a confident, casual way, sometimes rudely, as if nothing matters: "He waltzed in late." 5) (informal) To win or do something very easily: "She waltzed through the test."
its sense in the lessons: In music lessons, a waltz is counted "ONE-two-three, ONE-two-three": it is in 3/4 time. Famous waltzes include "The Blue Danube" by Johann Strauss. In stories, "waltzed in" shows a character is cheeky or too relaxed. Australians know the song "Waltzing Matilda", where "waltzing" means wandering the land with your swag (bedroll). Phrases: "waltz in", "waltz off with", "waltz through".
examples from the lessons: My grandparents danced a waltz at their wedding anniversary. | The band played a slow waltz. | We counted the waltz: one-two-three, one-two-three. | He waltzed into class ten minutes late without saying sorry. | She waltzed through the maths test in ten minutes. | The cat waltzed off with my sandwich! | We sang "Waltzing Matilda" in our Australia topic. | The prince and Cinderella waltzed around the ballroom.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: waltz has a t before the z. Plural and third person: waltzes. Regular verb: waltzed. In music maths, a waltz has 3 beats in a bar, so 4 bars have 12 beats.

part of speech: verb (wane, wanes, waned, waning); noun (on the wane)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) Of the Moon: to look smaller each night after the full moon, as less of its lit side faces the Earth. 2) To become weaker, smaller or less important little by little: interest, light or strength can wane.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on the Moon's phases, the Moon waxes (grows) from new moon to full moon, then wanes (shrinks) back. A "waning crescent" is the thin Moon before the new moon. In stories and the news, "his interest began to wane" means he became less interested. "On the wane" means getting weaker. Phrases: "wax and wane", "a waning moon", "on the wane", "interest waned".
examples from the lessons: After the full moon, the Moon begins to wane. | We drew the waning moon in our science diary. | As the evening went on, the light began to wane. | My interest in the film waned after half an hour. | The storm waned during the night. | The fashion for that toy is on the wane. | The Moon waxes and wanes about once a month.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: waned, waning. Opposite: wax (for the Moon), grow, increase. Homophone trap: "wane" sounds like "Wayne" (a name) and "wain" (an old word for a farm cart). The Moon does not really change size; only the part we see lit by the Sun changes.

part of speech: verb (warble, warbles, warbled, warbling); noun (a warble)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Of a bird: to sing with a sweet, trembling, changing sound. 2) Of a person: to sing in a high, wobbly voice, often said jokingly. 3) (noun) A warbling sound.
its sense in the lessons: Used in nature writing, stories and poems: birds warble in the trees in spring. It can be gently funny about people: "Grandad warbled an old song in the bath." Warblers are a group of small songbirds named after their song.
examples from the lessons: A little bird warbled in the hedge. | We heard blackbirds warbling at dawn. | Grandad warbled an old song while he made the tea. | The singer's voice warbled on the high notes. | The warble of the robin filled the garden. | My sister warbles along to every song on the radio.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: warbled, warbling. A warbler is a small songbird. "Warble" is gentler than "screech" or "squawk". Do not confuse with "wobble", though a warbling voice does wobble a little.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A small flat ring of metal, rubber or plastic put under a nut or a screw, or inside a tap, to make it tight or stop leaks. 2) (informal) A washing machine, or a dishwasher. 3) A person who washes things, as in "window washer" or "car washer". 4) (Australia, New Zealand) A small square cloth for washing your face, called a flannel in the UK and a washcloth in the USA.
its sense in the lessons: In design and technology lessons, washers spread the pressure of a nut or a bolt and stop it from loosening. A dripping tap often needs a new rubber washer. In everyday chat, people say "put it in the washer". In Australia, "grab a washer" means a face cloth. Phrases: "a rubber washer", "the washer and dryer", "window washer".
examples from the lessons: Dad fixed the dripping tap by changing the washer. | Put a washer under the nut before you tighten it. | My muddy football kit went straight into the washer. | The window washer cleaned the shop windows. | In Australia, Mum handed me a washer to wipe my face. | The kit came with ten screws and ten washers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a washer, washers. In Australia and New Zealand "washer" is the face cloth; in the UK "flannel"; in the USA "washcloth". Not the same as "washing" (the clothes to be washed).

meaning for a pupil: 1) An area of land that is empty, ruined or not used, such as land with rubble, weeds and rubbish. 2) A place or a time with nothing good or interesting in it: "a cultural wasteland".
its sense in the lessons: In stories and films, a wasteland is a bleak, dangerous place, often after a war or a disaster. In cities, children may see empty patches of wasteland where buildings were knocked down; these can hide dangers like broken glass, so they are not safe places to play. In geography it can describe land damaged by mining or factories. Phrases: "a barren wasteland", "an urban wasteland", "an icy wasteland".
examples from the lessons: The old factory site was a wasteland of broken bricks and weeds. | In the film, the heroes crossed a frozen wasteland. | The town turned the wasteland into a park with trees and a playground. | Do not play on the wasteland; there is broken glass there. | After the war, the city was a wasteland. | Grandad said Sunday afternoon telly used to be a wasteland.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually countable (a wasteland), but also used without "a" for land (an area of wasteland). One word. "Waste ground" means the same in the UK. "Waste" here means unused or spoiled, not rubbish only.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Paying careful attention to what is happening, so you notice any danger or problem.
its sense in the lessons: Used in stories, safety and everyday life. A watchful parent, teacher or lifeguard keeps an eye on children. In stories it suggests protection or suspicion. Phrases: "under the watchful eye of", "keep a watchful eye on", "stay watchful".
examples from the lessons: The lifeguard kept a watchful eye on the swimmers. | We built the den under the watchful eye of our teacher. | The mother bird was watchful as the cat came near. | Be watchful when you cross a busy road. | The watchful guard noticed the open gate. | Meerkats take turns to be watchful while the others feed.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective from "watch" plus -ful (with one l). Adverb: watchfully; noun: watchfulness. Similar: alert, careful, vigilant.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The line along the side of a ship or boat where the water reaches. 2) A line or mark showing how high water has come, for example on a wall after a flood, or on a beach.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on floating, the waterline shows how deep a boat sits in the water: the more weight it carries, the lower it floats and the higher the waterline climbs up its side. After floods, waterlines on buildings show how deep the flood was. Phrases: "below the waterline", "above the waterline".
examples from the lessons: The ship was painted red below the waterline. | When we added marbles to our foil boat, the waterline rose up its side. | A hole below the waterline can sink a ship. | You can still see the waterline on the walls from last year's flood. | The heavier the cargo, the lower the ship sits in the water. | We marked the waterline on our model boat with a pen.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; usually "the waterline". One word (sometimes "water line"). Ships have special marks (Plimsoll lines) to show the safe waterline when loaded.

part of speech: noun (a watermark, watermarks); verb (watermark, watermarks, watermarked)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A faint picture or pattern pressed into paper, which you can see when you hold it up to the light; banknotes have them to show they are real. 2) A faint logo or word put over a digital picture or document to show who owns it. 3) A mark showing how high water has reached, as in "high-water mark". 4) (verb) To put a watermark on paper or a picture.
its sense in the lessons: In money and maths lessons on coins and notes, the watermark is one of the security features that help stop forged money. Online, a watermark on a photo shows it belongs to someone and should not be copied without permission. Phrases: "hold it up to the light to see the watermark", "high-water mark".
examples from the lessons: Hold the banknote up to the light and you will see the watermark. | The photo had the photographer's name as a watermark. | The school watermarked the test papers with its logo. | A real banknote has a watermark; a fake one may not. | The flood left a dirty watermark on the wall. | Don't copy pictures with watermarks; they belong to someone else.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. One word. "High-water mark" also means the best or highest point of something ("the high-water mark of her career"). Copying a watermarked picture without permission can break copyright rules.

part of speech: noun (waterworks, plural form, used with a singular or plural verb)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A building or system that cleans water and sends it through pipes to people's homes. 2) (informal) Tears; "turn on the waterworks" means to start crying, often to get sympathy. 3) (UK, euphemism) The body's system for making and passing urine (wee): "trouble with the waterworks".
its sense in the lessons: In geography and history lessons, the waterworks of a town supply clean, safe drinking water. In everyday family talk, "here come the waterworks!" is said, sometimes unkindly, when someone starts to cry. Older people and doctors in the UK may say "the waterworks" politely instead of naming the bladder. Phrases: "turn on the waterworks", "the town waterworks".
examples from the lessons: The town's waterworks clean river water so we can drink it. | We visited the old Victorian waterworks on our school trip. | As soon as she lost the game, she turned on the waterworks. | Here come the waterworks; my little brother has dropped his ice cream. | Grandad went to the doctor about his waterworks. | A new waterworks was built to supply the growing city.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Ends in -s even when it means one building: "The waterworks is by the river" or "are by the river" are both heard. Teasing someone for crying ("turning on the waterworks") can be unkind; everyone cries sometimes.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A life-size model of a person made of wax, usually of a famous person. 2) (waxworks) A museum or exhibition of such models, such as Madame Tussauds in London.
its sense in the lessons: Used in everyday life and on trips: at a waxworks you can stand next to models of kings, queens, film stars and athletes. In stories, waxworks can be spooky because the figures look almost alive. Phrases: "a waxwork of", "the waxworks museum".
examples from the lessons: We had our photo taken with a waxwork of the Queen. | The waxwork looked so real I nearly said hello. | Madame Tussauds is a famous waxworks in London. | In the scary story, the waxworks came alive at midnight. | It takes months to make one waxwork. | The waxwork of the footballer was wearing his real shirt.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. "A waxworks" (with -s) can mean the whole museum, and it can take a singular verb: "The waxworks is closed on Monday." Wax melts when hot, so the figures are kept away from strong heat.

part of speech: noun (weaning, uncountable); verb, -ing form of wean (wean, weans, weaned, weaning)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Slowly getting a baby or a young animal used to eating food instead of drinking only its mother's milk (or formula). 2) Slowly helping someone to give up something they depend on or are used to: "weaning him off sweets". 3) (Scotland, noun "wean") A child; this is a different, Scots word.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on life cycles and mammals, weaning is the stage when young animals stop feeding on milk. Parents talk about weaning a baby onto mashed food around six months. In everyday life, "weaning off" means cutting down slowly, such as weaning off screens. Phrases: "wean off", "wean onto", "be weaned from".
examples from the lessons: The piglets are weaning now and eating from the trough. | Weaning a baby starts with soft, mashed food. | My baby sister was weaned onto mashed banana. | Puppies finish weaning at about eight weeks old. | Dad is weaning himself off sugar in his tea. | Mum is weaning us off screens before bedtime.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Wean is a regular verb (weaned, weaning). Weaning is slow and step by step, not sudden. In Scotland, "wean" (sounds like "wayn") also means a small child: "Get the weans to bed."

meaning for a pupil: 1) Making you feel tired, bored or fed up, especially because it goes on too long.
its sense in the lessons: A rather formal or literary word; in everyday talk people say "tiring", "boring" or "tedious". In stories it describes long journeys, dull jobs or someone who keeps complaining. Phrases: "a wearisome journey", "a wearisome task".
examples from the lessons: The long walk home in the rain was wearisome. | Copying out the same sentence twenty times was a wearisome task. | The knight began his wearisome journey across the mountains. | His endless complaining became wearisome. | Waiting in the queue all afternoon was wearisome for everyone. | The old woman found the stairs wearisome.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From "weary" (very tired) plus -some. Spelling: y changes to i. Pronounced WEER-ee-sum. Similar: tiresome, tedious. It does not mean "worrying".

part of speech: adjective (weepy, weepier, weepiest); noun (a weepy, weepies — informal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Ready to cry, or crying easily, often because you are tired or sad. 2) (informal) Of a film, book or song: sad and likely to make people cry. 3) (noun, informal) A sad film or story that makes people cry.
its sense in the lessons: Used in everyday family talk: "She's weepy because she's overtired." People call a sad film "a weepy" or "a real tear-jerker". It is a gentle, informal word.
