examples from the lessons: The baby gets weepy when she needs a nap. | I felt a bit weepy on the last day of school. | That film is such a weepy; bring tissues! | Mum always cries at weepy films. | The song is quite weepy, but beautiful. | Grandad went weepy when he saw the old photos.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative: weepier, weepiest. From "weep" (to cry; past "wept"). It is informal. Feeling weepy is normal and nothing to be ashamed of.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A man or boy from Wales, a country in the west of Great Britain, part of the United Kingdom.
its sense in the lessons: Used in history, geography and sport. A Welshwoman is a woman from Wales; together the people are "the Welsh" or "Welsh people". Many Welsh people speak Welsh (Cymraeg) as well as English. Phrases: "a proud Welshman", "a Welshman and an Irishman".
examples from the lessons: My grandad is a proud Welshman from Cardiff. | The Welshman scored the winning try for his rugby team. | The famous poet Dylan Thomas was a Welshman. | A Welshman, a Scotsman and an Englishman walked into a shop. | My teacher is a Welshman who speaks Welsh at home. | Two Welshmen sang in the choir.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always written with a capital W: Welshman. Plural: Welshmen. Many people now prefer "Welsh person" or "Welsh people" when speaking of everyone. Homophone trap: "Welsh" sounds like the verb "welch" or "welsh" (to fail to pay a debt), which some Welsh people find offensive; avoid that verb.

part of speech: adjective (whacking — informal UK, Australia); adverb (whacking — informal); noun (a whacking); verb, -ing form of whack (whack, whacks, whacked, whacking)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Hitting someone or something hard with a loud smack. 2) (noun, old-fashioned) A beating as a punishment. 3) (informal, UK and Australia) Very big: "a whacking great spider" or "a whacking bill".
its sense in the lessons: In stories it describes hitting: whacking a ball with a bat, whacking a pillow. "A whacking great..." in British and Australian chat means "a really huge...". In old stories, children were given "a whacking" as punishment; today hitting children is wrong and against the law in many countries, including Scotland, Wales and New Zealand. Phrases: "a whacking great", "a whacking fine".
examples from the lessons: She was whacking the ball over the fence. | There's a whacking great spider in the bath! | Dad got a whacking bill from the garage. | He kept whacking the old rug to get the dust out. | In the old story, the boy got a whacking for stealing apples. | That's a whacking big slice of cake. | The wind was whacking the shutters against the wall.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Whack is a regular verb (whacked, whacking). "Whacking" as an adjective is informal and almost always comes before "great" or "big". Do not confuse with "wacky" (crazy and funny). Hitting people is never okay.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A ship used for hunting whales. 2) A person who hunts whales, especially on such a ship. 3) A whaleboat, a long narrow rowing boat.
its sense in the lessons: Used in history and stories, such as "Moby-Dick". Whalers once hunted whales for oil, meat and bone. Today most countries have banned commercial whaling to protect whales, though a few countries still allow some. In history and geography lessons, places like Nantucket (USA) and Hobart (Australia) were whaling ports. Phrases: "an old whaler", "whaler's harpoon".
examples from the lessons: The old whaler sailed from Nantucket in 1840. | The whalers rowed out with their harpoons. | Today most countries protect whales from whalers. | In the museum we saw a whaler's harpoon. | Captain Ahab in "Moby-Dick" is a whaler. | The whaler came home after three years at sea.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a whaler, whalers. Homophone trap: "whaler" and "wailer" (someone wailing) sound alike. Whaling is the activity; a whaler is the ship or the person.

part of speech: verb (whine, whines, whined, whining); noun (a whine)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To complain in an annoying, high, unhappy voice, often about small things. 2) Of a dog or another animal: to make a long, high, sad sound. 3) Of a machine: to make a long, high, steady noise, like a drill or a jet engine. 4) (noun) The sound itself, or a complaint.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life parents say "Stop whining!" when children complain. In stories, a dog whines at the door to go out, and engines whine. Calling someone "a whiner" is a bit unkind. Phrases: "whine about", "stop whining", "the whine of an engine".
examples from the lessons: Stop whining and eat your carrots. | The dog whined at the door to go out. | My brother whines whenever it's his turn to wash up. | We heard the whine of the dentist's drill. | The jet engine gave a high whine. | "It's not fair," she whined. | The puppy gave a little whine when we left.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: whined, whining. Homophone trap: "whine" sounds like "wine" (a drink made from grapes); only "whine" has an h. In the USA "whine" is common for complaining; in the UK people also say "moan" or "whinge" (whinge is also used in Australia).

part of speech: verb (whirr, whirrs, whirred, whirring); noun (a whirr); US spelling whir
meaning for a pupil: 1) To make a soft, steady buzzing sound like something spinning fast, such as a fan, a camera or wings. 2) (noun) That sound. 3) To move fast with such a sound.
its sense in the lessons: It is a sound word (it sounds like the noise it names). In stories, machines, fans, wheels and hummingbird wings whirr. "My mind was whirring" means thoughts were spinning fast. Phrases: "whirr into life", "the whirr of the fan".
examples from the lessons: The fan whirred softly in the hot classroom. | We heard the whirr of the hummingbird's wings. | The old computer whirred into life. | The sewing machine whirred as Nan sewed. | My mind was whirring with ideas for the story. | The drone whirred over the playing field.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK spelling: whirr (double r); US spelling: whir. Past: whirred; -ing form: whirring (double r in both spellings). Do not confuse with "whirl" (to spin round fast) or "were".

meaning for a pupil: 1) One of the long stiff hairs that grow near the mouth of a cat, a mouse, a seal and many other animals, used to feel things. 2) (whiskers) Hair growing on a man's face. 3) (informal) A very small amount or distance: "by a whisker" means only just.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, whiskers help animals such as cats feel their way in the dark and judge if they can fit through a gap. In sport and everyday talk, "won by a whisker" means won by a tiny amount. Phrases: "by a whisker", "within a whisker of", "the cat's whiskers" (old-fashioned: the very best).
examples from the lessons: The cat's whiskers twitched as it smelled the fish. | Whiskers help a cat feel its way in the dark. | We won the race by a whisker. | She came within a whisker of beating the record. | Grandpa had grey whiskers on his chin. | The mouse cleaned its whiskers with its paws. | Seals use their whiskers to find fish in murky water.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a whisker, whiskers. "Whiskered" means having whiskers. Do not confuse with "whisky" (an alcoholic drink) or "whisk" (a kitchen tool). Never cut a cat's whiskers; it needs them.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The quality of being white, like snow, milk or a clean page. 2) Paleness of the skin, for example from being ill or frightened.
its sense in the lessons: In stories it describes snow, light, teeth or a pale face: "the whiteness of her face showed how scared she was." In science, white light contains all the colours of the rainbow. Phrases: "the whiteness of the snow", "dazzling whiteness".
examples from the lessons: The whiteness of the snow hurt our eyes. | The toothpaste advert promised whiteness. | I noticed the whiteness of his face after the fall. | The whiteness of the clouds was dazzling. | Polar bears blend in with the whiteness of the ice. | The page's whiteness made the drawing stand out.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: say "whiteness", not "a whiteness" (except in poems). From "white" plus -ness.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Almost white, or a little bit white; pale in colour.
its sense in the lessons: Used in science descriptions, nature notes and stories when something is not pure white: whitish flowers, a whitish sky, a whitish powder in an experiment. It helps describe exactly what you see. Phrases: "whitish grey", "a whitish powder".
examples from the lessons: The mushroom had a whitish cap. | A whitish powder was left after the water evaporated. | The sky was a whitish grey before the snow. | The caterpillar had whitish stripes. | His face went whitish with fear. | The rock had whitish lines of quartz in it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective from "white" plus -ish (the e is dropped). The ending -ish means "a bit, rather", as in greenish, smallish, tallish. Also spelled "whiteish", but "whitish" is the usual spelling.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (money) Selling goods in large amounts to shops and businesses, who then sell them on to customers at a higher price. 2) (adjective, money) To do with such selling: "wholesale prices". 3) Done on a very large scale, often too much and without care: "wholesale destruction". 4) (adverb) In large amounts, or completely.
its sense in the lessons: In money and business lessons, the chain goes: a factory makes goods, a wholesaler buys lots of them cheaply, a shop buys from the wholesaler, and you buy from the shop at the retail price. The difference between wholesale and retail prices is how shops make a profit. In the news, "wholesale" can also mean huge and sweeping, often bad: "wholesale changes", "wholesale destruction". Phrases: "buy wholesale", "wholesale price", "wholesale changes".
examples from the lessons: The shop buys its sweets wholesale and sells them one by one. | The wholesale price of a pen was 20p, and the shop sold it for 50p. | Grandad runs a wholesale fruit business. | The storm caused wholesale damage to the forest. | The new head teacher made wholesale changes to the timetable. | Buying wholesale is cheaper because you buy a lot at once.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: retail (selling to the public). A wholesaler is the business that sells wholesale. Maths: profit per item = retail price minus wholesale price; for example, bought at 20p and sold at 50p gives 30p profit per item. Wholesale prices are usually lower per item because you buy in bulk.

part of speech: noun (a winch, winches); verb (winch, winches, winched, winching)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A machine with a rope or a chain wound round a turning drum, used to lift or pull heavy things. 2) (verb) To lift or pull something with a winch. 3) (verb, Scotland, informal) To go out with someone as a boyfriend or girlfriend; a different, Scots sense.
its sense in the lessons: In science and design-technology lessons, a winch is a simple machine using a wheel and axle: turning a big handle makes it easier to lift a heavy load. In the news, rescue helicopters winch people to safety, and tow trucks winch cars out of ditches. Wells once used a winch to raise buckets of water. Phrases: "winch up", "winch to safety", "winch out".
examples from the lessons: The helicopter winched the climber to safety. | We built a winch from a cotton reel and a pencil. | The tow truck used its winch to pull the car out of the mud. | The sailors winched up the anchor. | An old winch lifted the bucket out of the well. | The bigger the handle on a winch, the easier it is to turn.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a winch, plural winches. Regular verb: winched. Do not confuse with "wench" (an old word for a young woman, now rude or old-fashioned) or "flinch". A winch is a type of wheel-and-axle simple machine.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An amount of money you get unexpectedly, such as a prize, a gift or money you find. 2) A fruit, especially an apple, that has been blown off a tree by the wind.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and money lessons, a windfall is lucky, unplanned money: a big win, an unexpected gift from a relative. Sensible people may save part of a windfall. In gardens and orchards, windfalls are apples lying on the ground; they are often used for cooking or juice. Phrases: "a windfall of", "an unexpected windfall".
examples from the lessons: Finding a £10 note in my old coat was a nice windfall. | The school got a windfall when a parent gave £1,000. | We collected windfalls under the apple tree to make a crumble. | Nan said I should save half of my birthday windfall. | Some windfalls were bruised, so we fed them to the horse. | The village used the windfall to fix the playground.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a windfall, windfalls. One word. A windfall is not something you earned or planned. In money problems, adding a windfall increases your total savings once; it is not a regular income.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Typical of winter: cold, snowy, icy or frosty. 2) (weather forecasts, UK) "Wintry showers" are showers of rain mixed with sleet or snow. 3) (of a smile or a manner) Cold and unfriendly.
its sense in the lessons: Used in weather forecasts, stories and geography. "Wintry weather" tells you to wrap up warmly and take care on icy paths. In stories, "a wintry smile" shows someone is not truly friendly. Phrases: "wintry weather", "wintry showers", "a wintry scene".
examples from the lessons: The forecast says there will be wintry showers tomorrow. | It was a wintry morning, and the car was covered in frost. | We painted a wintry scene with snowy trees. | Take care on the wintry roads. | The wind felt wintry even though it was only October. | She gave him a wintry smile and walked away.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: wintry (the e of winter is dropped); "wintery" is also seen but less common. Comparative: wintrier, wintriest. Opposite: summery.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Wanting or hoping for something. 2) "Wishful thinking" means believing that something is true or will happen only because you want it to, not because it is likely.
its sense in the lessons: Mostly heard in "wishful thinking": "Thinking there won't be homework this weekend is wishful thinking." It warns that a hope is not based on facts. In stories it can describe a hopeful look: "a wishful glance at the cake". Phrases: "wishful thinking", "a wishful look".
examples from the lessons: Hoping the test will be cancelled is just wishful thinking. | He gave a wishful look at the toy in the shop window. | Thinking our team will win 10–0 is wishful thinking. | "Maybe it'll snow on Christmas Day," she said in a wishful voice. | Believing the homework will do itself is wishful thinking. | The dog gave a wishful glance at my sandwich.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective from "wish" plus -ful (one l). Adverb: wishfully. In science and maths, wishful thinking is a trap: check the facts and evidence instead of believing what you want.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The use of magic powers, especially to do harm, as believed in stories and in many old beliefs. 2) (history) In the past, a crime people were wrongly accused of, as in the witch trials in Europe and in Salem, Massachusetts, in 1692. 3) (informal) Something so clever or surprising it seems like magic.
its sense in the lessons: In fairy tales and fantasy books, witches use witchcraft with spells, potions and broomsticks. In history lessons, many innocent people, mostly women, were accused of witchcraft, tried and even killed because of fear and rumours; it is a lesson about blaming people without evidence. The Bible forbids witchcraft, and Christians believe people should trust God, not spells. Some people today follow modern religions such as Wicca, which they call witchcraft or the Craft. Jokingly: "How did you fix that? It's witchcraft!" Phrases: "accused of witchcraft", "witchcraft and wizardry".
examples from the lessons: In the story, the old woman used witchcraft to turn the prince into a frog. | In 1692, people in Salem were wrongly accused of witchcraft. | Long ago, people blamed witchcraft for bad harvests. | The Bible warns against witchcraft. | Harry Potter goes to a school of witchcraft and wizardry. | Grandad called the new phone "pure witchcraft". | The witch trials show how fear and rumours can hurt innocent people.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: "witchcraft", not "a witchcraft". One word. Myth trap: there is no scientific evidence that spells or curses work. Historical accusations of witchcraft were based on fear and gossip, not facts.

part of speech: adjective (withering); verb, -ing form of wither (wither, withers, withered, withering)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Of a plant: drying up, shrinking and dying, for example because it has no water. 2) (adjective) A withering look or remark is very scornful and makes someone feel small and foolish. 3) (adjective) Extremely strong and damaging, like "withering heat" or "withering fire".
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on plants, leaves start withering when a plant lacks water or light. In stories, "she gave him a withering look" tells the reader she was very unimpressed and made him feel silly. Phrases: "a withering look", "withering criticism", "withering heat".
examples from the lessons: The flowers were withering because nobody had watered them. | Our bean plant in the dark cupboard was withering. | The teacher gave him a withering look when he walked in late. | The grass was withering in the summer heat. | Her withering comment made him go red. | The leaves are withering and turning brown in autumn.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Wither is a regular verb (withered, withering). Do not confuse with "whether" (if) or "weather" (rain and sun). A withering look does not hurt the body; it hurts feelings.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To be strong enough not to be damaged or broken by something, such as heat, cold, wind or weight. 2) To resist an attack or a pressure successfully.
its sense in the lessons: In science and design-technology lessons, you test materials to see what they can withstand: a bridge must withstand heavy loads, and a shelter must withstand wind and rain. In history and stories, a castle withstands a siege. Phrases: "withstand the heat", "withstand the weight", "withstand pressure".
examples from the lessons: Our paper bridge could withstand the weight of ten coins. | Oven gloves can withstand high temperatures. | The castle walls withstood the attack for months. | Houses in hurricane areas are built to withstand strong winds. | This jacket can withstand heavy rain. | Can your egg box withstand a fall from the table?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular verb like "stand": withstand, withstood, withstood. In a test, "it withstood 5 kg" means it held 5 kg without breaking. Similar: resist, endure, hold out against.

part of speech: noun (writing; a writing — rare; writings); verb, -ing form of write (write, writes, wrote, written, writing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The activity or skill of putting words on paper or a screen. 2) Words that are written: "There was writing on the wall." 3) A person's handwriting: "I can't read your writing." 4) Books, stories, poems or articles that someone has written; "writings" are someone's written works. 5) The job of being a writer.
its sense in the lessons: In school, "writing" is a whole subject: creative writing, persuasive writing, story writing, joined-up writing. Teachers mark your writing for ideas, spelling, punctuation and handwriting. "In writing" means written down, which makes it official: "Please put your request in writing." "The writing is on the wall" means trouble is clearly coming (from a story in the Bible, Daniel 5). Phrases: "in writing", "creative writing", "joined-up writing", "the writing is on the wall".
examples from the lessons: We did some creative writing about a dragon. | Your writing is much neater this term. | I can't read the writing on this old letter. | Please put your complaint in writing. | Roald Dahl's writing makes children laugh. | She is writing a story about her cat. | The writing on the board was too small to see. | After losing six games, the writing was on the wall for the team.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: one t (writing), but "written" has two t's. The w is silent. Uncountable in the activity sense: "Writing is fun." Past of write: wrote; past participle: written. Homophone trap: "write" sounds like "right" and "rite".

meaning for a pupil: 1) The Roman numeral for 16: X (10) + V (5) + I (1) = 16. 2) Used in names of kings and popes, as in Louis XVI (Louis the Sixteenth), a king of France.
its sense in the lessons: In maths lessons on Roman numerals, you add the letters from left to right when the bigger ones come first: XVI = 10 + 5 + 1 = 16. Roman numerals appear on clocks, in book chapters, in the names of kings and queens, and in years on films and buildings. Louis XVI was king of France at the time of the French Revolution and was executed in 1793.
examples from the lessons: XVI is the Roman numeral for 16. | We wrote our ages in Roman numerals; I am X and my sister is XVI. | Louis XVI was a king of France. | Chapter XVI of the book is the scariest. | XVI + IV = XX, because 16 + 4 = 20. | The old clock shows the hours in Roman numerals, but none goes up to XVI.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually written in capitals: XVI. With names, it is read as an ordinal: "Louis XVI" is "Louis the Sixteenth". It is not a word but a number. Trap: XIV is 14 (I before V means take away 1), while XVI is 16 (I after V means add 1).

part of speech: noun (a yacht, yachts); verb (yacht — rare; usually "go yachting")
meaning for a pupil: 1) A boat with sails, used for racing or for pleasure. 2) A large, expensive motor boat or ship, often owned by a very rich person, used for holidays or parties.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and sport, yachts race in regattas, and people go yachting or sailing for fun. In the news, rich people's huge "superyachts" are sometimes in the headlines. In science lessons on forces, a sailing yacht is pushed by the wind on its sails. Phrases: "go yachting", "a yacht race", "a luxury yacht".
examples from the lessons: We watched the yachts racing across the bay. | My uncle has a small yacht and takes us sailing in summer. | The film star arrived on a huge luxury yacht. | The wind filled the yacht's white sails. | The Sydney to Hobart yacht race starts on Boxing Day. | Yachts lined the harbour in Auckland, the "City of Sails".
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a yacht, yachts. Tricky spelling and sound: it is pronounced "yot" (rhymes with "hot"); the "ch" is silent. The word comes from Dutch. A person who sails a yacht is a yachtsman or yachtswoman, or simply a sailor.

part of speech: noun (Yana, a name); also part of words (-yana, Buddhism)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (a name) Yana is a girl's name, common in Ukraine, Russia, Bulgaria and other countries; in Ukrainian it is written Яна. 2) (Buddhism) In Sanskrit, "yana" means "vehicle" or "path", and appears in the names of branches of Buddhism, such as Mahayana and Vajrayana. 3) Yana is also the name of a river in Siberia, Russia.
its sense in the lessons: It is not an ordinary English word. In stories and class lists it is usually a girl's name, said "YAH-nuh". In religion lessons about Buddhism, you may see it inside longer words like Mahayana ("great vehicle"), meaning a way to reach enlightenment.
examples from the lessons: Yana is a new girl in our class from Ukraine. | Yana and I sit together at lunch. | Mahayana Buddhism is followed in China, Japan and Korea. | In Sanskrit, "yana" means "vehicle" or "path". | The Yana River flows north to the Arctic Ocean. | Yana wrote her name in Ukrainian letters: Яна.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a name it takes a capital letter: Yana. It is not an English word, and there is nothing else to invent about it. In Buddhist terms it is joined to another word (Mahayana, Vajrayana).

part of speech: adjective, determiner and adverb (yon — old-fashioned, dialect)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (old-fashioned or dialect) That, or those, over there: "yon hill" means "that hill over there". 2) (dialect, adverb) Yonder; over there.
its sense in the lessons: It is found in old poems, the Bible (older translations), fairy tales and in dialects of Scotland and the north of England. It makes language sound old or rural. "Hither and yon" means "here and there, in all directions". Related: "yonder" (over there), "beyond".
examples from the lessons: Who lives in yon castle? asked the traveller. | The shepherd pointed to yon hill. | "Fetch me yon bucket, lad," said the old farmer. | Leaves blew hither and yon in the wind. | In the poem, the knight rode towards yon dark tower. | Grandad from Yorkshire still says "yon" when he means "that".
note for the reader of a maths problem: Not used in modern standard English; in your own writing it will sound old-fashioned or like a dialect, which can be good for a character's voice. Do not confuse with "yawn" or with "yen" (Japanese money, or a strong wish).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) The point in the sky directly above your head. 2) The highest point a heavenly body such as the Sun reaches in the sky. 3) The time when something is most powerful or successful; the peak.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography lessons on the Sun, Moon and stars, the zenith is straight overhead; the opposite point, under your feet, is the nadir. Near the equator, the Sun can be at the zenith at noon on some days. In history, "at its zenith" means at its strongest: "The Roman Empire was at its zenith in the second century." Phrases: "at the zenith", "reach its zenith", "from zenith to nadir".
examples from the lessons: At noon the Sun was almost at its zenith. | The zenith is the point in the sky right above your head. | The Roman Empire reached its zenith about 1,900 years ago. | At the zenith of her career, she won three gold medals. | The star climbed slowly towards the zenith. | The opposite of the zenith is the nadir.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually "the zenith". Opposite: nadir (lowest point). Pronounced ZEN-ith (UK) or ZEE-nith (US). Myth trap: in the UK, Canada, Ireland, New Zealand and most of Australia and the USA, the Sun is never exactly at the zenith; it only gets directly overhead between the tropics.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (medicine) Short for herpes zoster, the medical name for shingles: a painful rash of blisters, usually in a stripe on one side of the body. 2) (medicine) Part of the name of the varicella-zoster virus, the virus that causes chickenpox and later can cause shingles.
its sense in the lessons: A doctors' word; in everyday life people say "shingles". Shingles mostly affects older adults: after someone has had chickenpox, the virus can sleep in the body for years and wake up later. There is a vaccine for older people. In science, it is an example of how some viruses can stay hidden in the body. Phrases: "herpes zoster", "varicella-zoster virus".
examples from the lessons: Zoster is the medical name for shingles. | Grandma had herpes zoster and her side was very sore. | The varicella-zoster virus causes both chickenpox and shingles. | The doctor offered Grandad a zoster vaccine. | Zoster usually appears as a stripe of blisters on one side of the body. | You can only get zoster if you have had chickenpox before.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Pronounced ZOS-ter. It is a medical word, and "zoster" alone is a shortened form. Shingles is not the same as roof shingles (flat tiles), which is a different meaning of the word. Only a doctor should say whether someone has it.

part of speech: noun (taffy, taffies; uncountable for the sweet); Taffy — a name
meaning for a pupil: 1) (US, Canada) A soft, chewy sweet made by boiling sugar or molasses and pulling it until it is shiny and stretchy; salt-water taffy is a famous kind. 2) (UK, old) Another word for toffee in some places. 3) (a name) Taffy is the little girl in two of Kipling's Just So Stories, «How the First Letter Was Written» and «How the Alphabet Was Made»; her full name is Taffimai Metallumai, which she says means «Small-person-without-any-manners-who-ought-to-be-spanked». 4) (UK, old, rude) An old nickname for a Welsh person; many Welsh people find it insulting, so do not use it.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life taffy is a seaside sweet in the USA and Canada, often sold at fairs and boardwalks. In «Reading children's books» Taffy is a clever, cheeky Stone-Age girl who draws a picture-letter for her mother and helps her father Tegumai invent the alphabet — the story is about how writing began. Phrases: «salt-water taffy», «taffy pull» (a party where people pull warm taffy).
examples from the lessons: We bought a bag of salt-water taffy on the boardwalk. | The taffy stuck to my teeth. | Grandma showed us how to pull taffy until it went pale and shiny. | Taffy drew a picture on birch bark to send a message to her mother. | Taffy and her daddy Tegumai made the first letters together. | Taffy was not very good at sitting still and being quiet. | In the story, nobody could read Taffy's picture properly, so there was a big muddle.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Taffy the sweet is uncountable («some taffy»), but «a taffy» or «taffies» can mean single pieces in the US. The girl's name starts with a capital letter. In the UK people usually say toffee, which is often harder. Do not call Welsh people «Taffy».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A woman whose job, in the past, was washing other people's clothes and sheets by hand, for money. 2) In The Wind in the Willows, Toad escapes from prison disguised as a washerwoman, wearing the gaoler's daughter's aunt's cotton dress, shawl and bonnet.
its sense in the lessons: Before washing machines, washing clothes was hard work: water was heated, clothes were scrubbed on a washboard, wrung through a mangle and hung to dry. Poorer women did this for richer families. In history lessons the word shows how people lived and worked in Victorian and Edwardian times. In the story, the disguise is funny because proud Toad has to pretend to be a hard-working woman, and he fails when a barge-woman asks him to wash her clothes and he cannot.
examples from the lessons: The washerwoman carried a big basket of sheets down to the river. | Toad dressed up as a washerwoman to get out of the prison. | The washerwoman's hands were red from the hot water and soap. | In Victorian times, many poor women worked as washerwomen. | The barge-woman laughed when she saw that the washerwoman could not wash a single shirt. | The gaoler's daughter's aunt was a washerwoman. | Old pictures show a washerwoman scrubbing clothes on a washboard.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural is washerwomen (like woman — women). It is an old-fashioned word; today we say a laundry worker or use a laundry or laundrette. Do not mix it up with a washing machine.

part of speech: noun (a gryphon, gryphons); also spelt griffin or griffon
meaning for a pupil: 1) A made-up creature from old stories, with the head, wings and front legs of an eagle and the body, back legs and tail of a lion. 2) In Alice in Wonderland, the Gryphon is a lazy, rough-talking creature who takes Alice to meet the Mock Turtle and tells her about their school under the sea.
its sense in the lessons: Gryphons are found in myths of ancient Greece and Persia and on coats of arms, flags and old buildings, where they stand for strength and watchfulness. It is not a real animal — no gryphon ever lived. In Alice, the Gryphon (drawn by John Tenniel) says «What fun!» and laughs at the Queen, and together with the Mock Turtle dances the Lobster Quadrille.
examples from the lessons: The Gryphon was asleep in the sun when the Queen found him. | A gryphon has an eagle's head and a lion's body. | The Gryphon and the Mock Turtle danced the Lobster Quadrille for Alice. | There is a stone gryphon over the door of the old bank. | In the fantasy game, the knight rode a gryphon through the sky. | The Gryphon told Alice that the lessons «lessen» from day to day. | Gryphons are made up, like dragons and unicorns.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Three spellings: gryphon, griffin, griffon; all mean the same creature (but a griffon is also a kind of dog and a kind of vulture). It is a myth, not a real animal.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (old) A dishonest man who tricks people; a rogue. 2) (cards) The jack in a pack of playing cards, the card with a young man's picture, between the ten and the queen. 3) (old) A boy or young male servant. 4) In Alice in Wonderland, the Knave of Hearts is put on trial for stealing the Queen's tarts.
its sense in the lessons: Knave is an old word found in fairy tales, nursery rhymes and old books: «The Queen of Hearts, she made some tarts… The Knave of Hearts, he stole the tarts». In card games, older people and British books may say knave for the jack. In stories it tells the reader that a character is not to be trusted. The trial of the Knave in Alice is very unfair — the King keeps wanting the verdict before the evidence.
examples from the lessons: The Knave of Hearts was accused of stealing the tarts. | «You knave!» shouted the king in the old play. | In this card game, the knave is worth ten points. | The knave carried the King's crown on a velvet cushion. | The wicked knave tricked the farmer out of his cow. | Alice did not think there was any proof against the Knave. | Put the knave of spades on the queen of hearts.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The k is silent: it sounds like «nave». Do not confuse with nave (the long middle part of a church). In cards, knave = jack (J). Old-fashioned word; today people say rogue or cheat.

part of speech: noun (croquet, uncountable); verb (croquet, croquets, croqueted, croqueting — rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A lawn game in which players hit wooden balls with long-handled wooden mallets through small metal hoops stuck in the grass. 2) (verb, rare) To knock another player's ball away by hitting your own ball against it.
its sense in the lessons: Croquet is played in gardens and clubs, especially in the UK, Ireland, New Zealand and Australia, often in summer. In Alice in Wonderland the Queen's croquet game is mad: the balls are live hedgehogs, the mallets are live flamingos and the hoops are soldiers bent over, and the Queen shouts «Off with his head!». Phrases: «a game of croquet», «croquet lawn», «croquet mallet».
examples from the lessons: We played croquet on Grandpa's lawn after lunch. | Alice's flamingo kept twisting round to look at her instead of hitting the hedgehog. | Hit the ball through the hoop with the mallet. | The croquet club meets every Saturday in summer. | The Queen played croquet with live hedgehogs. | It is hard to play croquet when the lawn is bumpy. | The soldiers had to bend over to be the croquet hoops.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Sounds like «CROH-kay»; the t is silent. It is uncountable: «a game of croquet», not «a croquet». Do not mix up with croquette (a fried roll of food) or cricket.

part of speech: noun (a djinn, djinns or djinn); also spelt jinn, jinni, genie
meaning for a pupil: 1) In Arab and Muslim stories and beliefs, a spirit made of smokeless fire that can be good or bad and can sometimes take the shape of people or animals. 2) A genie, like the magic spirit in a lamp in the story of Aladdin. 3) In the Just So Story «How the Camel Got His Hump», the Djinn in charge of All Deserts gives the lazy Camel a hump because he only says «Humph!» and will not work.
its sense in the lessons: Muslims believe that jinn are real beings created by God, mentioned in the Qur'an; in story books they are magic spirits who grant wishes or play tricks. In the Just So Stories the Djinn is a wise, powerful spirit who teaches the Camel a lesson about laziness: the Camel must now carry his own food in his hump so he can work three days without eating.
examples from the lessons: The Djinn rolled across the desert in a cloud of dust. | «Humph!» said the Camel, and the Djinn made his back puff up into a hump. | In the old tale, a djinn came out of the bottle. | The Djinn in charge of All Deserts was riding on a whirlwind. | Aladdin's genie is a kind of djinn. | Some people tell stories of djinn who live in empty places. | The Djinn said, «You've had three days off; now work.»
note for the reader of a maths problem: Sounds like «jin»; the d is silent. Plural can be djinns or djinn. Genie is the English form of the same word. Speak of Muslim beliefs respectfully: «Muslims believe in jinn».

part of speech: noun (a gaoler, gaolers); also spelt jailer, jailor
meaning for a pupil: 1) (UK, old spelling) A person whose job is to guard prisoners in a prison; a jailer or prison officer.
its sense in the lessons: Gaoler is the old British spelling of jailer, found in old books. In The Wind in the Willows, Toad is locked in a dungeon guarded by an old gaoler; the gaoler's kind daughter feels sorry for Toad and helps him escape dressed as her aunt, the washerwoman. Today we say prison officer.
examples from the lessons: The old gaoler jangled his keys outside Toad's cell. | The gaoler's daughter brought Toad hot buttered toast and tea. | The gaoler locked the heavy door and walked away. | Long ago the gaoler lived in a small house beside the gaol. | The gaoler counted the prisoners every evening. | In the story, the gaoler never noticed that Toad had gone. | The gaoler of the castle was a grumpy man with a lantern.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Sounds exactly like «jailer». The spelling gaol/gaoler is old British; in the USA and most modern writing it is jail/jailer. Today the job title is prison officer (UK) or correctional officer (US).

part of speech: noun (a wonderland, wonderlands); Wonderland — a name
meaning for a pupil: 1) A place full of wonderful, magical or beautiful things. 2) Wonderland is the strange dream world Alice falls into down the rabbit hole in Lewis Carroll's book Alice's Adventures in Wonderland (1865). 3) A place that is very beautiful at a certain time, such as «a winter wonderland» when everything is covered in snow.
its sense in the lessons: In Alice, Wonderland is a place where nothing follows normal rules: drinks make you shrink, a cat grins and vanishes, and the Queen wants to cut off everyone's head. At the end Alice wakes up and it was a dream. In everyday life people use the word for a place that seems too good or strange to be real. Phrases: «winter wonderland», «a toy wonderland», «Alice in Wonderland».
examples from the lessons: Alice fell down the rabbit hole into Wonderland. | After the snowstorm the garden was a winter wonderland. | The toy shop was a wonderland of lights and games. | In Wonderland, animals talk and argue with Alice. | The coral reef is an underwater wonderland of colour. | When Alice woke up, Wonderland was only a dream. | The book is often called «Alice in Wonderland» for short.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Write Wonderland with a capital W when it is Alice's world. Countable: a wonderland. The full title is Alice's Adventures in Wonderland.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (UK, Ireland, Australia, NZ) A thick, sticky, dark sweet syrup made when sugar is refined; black treacle is very dark, golden syrup is a light kind. Americans call it molasses. 2) Something too sweet or sentimental, like a soppy speech.
its sense in the lessons: Treacle is used in baking: treacle tart, gingerbread, parkin, sticky toffee pudding. In Alice in Wonderland, the Dormouse tells a story about three sisters who lived at the bottom of a treacle-well and drew treacle; Alice thinks it is nonsense. «Treacle-well» is a real old phrase for a healing spring. Phrases: «black treacle», «treacle tart», «as slow as treacle».
examples from the lessons: Harry Potter's favourite pudding is treacle tart. | Mum added a spoonful of black treacle to the gingerbread. | The three little sisters lived at the bottom of a treacle-well. | The mud was as thick as treacle. | Americans call treacle molasses. | My hands were sticky with treacle. | The Dormouse said the sisters were learning to draw treacle.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «some treacle», not «a treacle». In the UK golden syrup and treacle are related but not the same. In the US the word is molasses. A «treacly» film is too sweet and sentimental.

part of speech: adjective (ratty, rattier, rattiest); Ratty — a name
meaning for a pupil: 1) (UK, Australia, NZ, informal) Bad-tempered and easily annoyed; grumpy. 2) (US, informal) Shabby, old and torn, like a ratty old jumper. 3) Like a rat, or full of rats. 4) (a name) Ratty is the friendly nickname of the Water Rat in The Wind in the Willows, Mole's best friend, who loves «messing about in boats».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday British talk, «Don't be so ratty» means «Don't be grumpy». In the US, «ratty» clothes are worn out. In the Wind in the Willows, Ratty is kind, sensible, fond of poetry and the river; he is really a water vole, not a rat. The book teaches about friendship and the river bank.
examples from the lessons: Ratty took Mole for his first boat ride on the river. | I'm always ratty when I'm tired. | He wore a ratty old T-shirt to paint the fence. | «Believe me, my young friend,» said Ratty, «there is nothing half so much worth doing as messing about in boats.» | Don't get ratty with your little brother. | Ratty and Mole went to the Wild Wood to find Badger. | The dog chewed his toy until it was ratty.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparisons: rattier, rattiest. Note the two different senses in the UK (grumpy) and the US (shabby). Ratty in the book is a water vole; a common myth is that he is a rat.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A male servant in a grand house who wears a uniform, opens doors, serves food at table and carries messages. 2) In Alice in Wonderland, the Fish-Footman brings the Duchess an invitation from the Queen to play croquet, and the Frog-Footman takes it; both wear powdered wigs.
its sense in the lessons: Footmen worked in large houses and palaces in the past and still work at Buckingham Palace today. In history lessons they show how rich families lived with many servants. In Alice, the Frog-Footman sits outside the Duchess's door and talks nonsense, saying he will sit there «till tomorrow», which shows how silly rules and manners can be.
examples from the lessons: The footman opened the carriage door for the Queen. | The Fish-Footman handed over a letter almost as large as himself. | The Frog-Footman sat staring stupidly up at the sky. | In the big house, footmen served dinner in white gloves. | The footman bowed and carried in the silver tray. | Alice knocked, but the footman would not let her in. | The two footmen got their curls tangled together when they bowed.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural footmen. It is a job of the past (and of royal palaces), not a man who walks. Do not confuse with foot soldier.

part of speech: noun (a Parsee, Parsees); also spelt Parsi; adjective (Parsee)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A member of a community of Zoroastrians in India and Pakistan whose families came from Persia (Iran) more than a thousand years ago. 2) In the Just So Story «How the Rhinoceros Got His Skin», the Parsee is a man on an island in the Red Sea whose cake the Rhinoceros eats; to get even, the Parsee rubs cake-crumbs into the Rhinoceros's skin, which makes it itch so he rubs it into folds.
its sense in the lessons: The Parsis follow Zoroastrianism, one of the oldest religions, and many live in Mumbai. In the story, the Parsee wears a hat from which «the rays of the sun were reflected in more-than-oriental splendour»; the tale is a made-up explanation of why rhinos have baggy, folded skin — not a true one. Today «Parsi» is the usual spelling.
examples from the lessons: The Parsee baked a cake that was two feet across and three feet thick. | The Rhinoceros ate the Parsee's cake and went away. | The Parsee filled the Rhinoceros's skin with cake-crumbs. | Many Parsis live in the city of Mumbai in India. | Parsis follow the Zoroastrian religion. | The Parsee sang a little song as he climbed down from his palm tree. | Real rhinos have folded skin, but not because of cake crumbs.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Write with a capital P. Modern spelling Parsi, plural Parsis. Kipling's story is a «just so» explanation, not a true science fact.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A small, brightly coloured parrot from Australia, New Guinea and nearby islands, with a brush-tipped tongue for eating nectar and pollen from flowers. 2) In Alice in Wonderland, the Lory is a bird in the pool of tears who argues with Alice and says «I am older than you, and must know better».
its sense in the lessons: Lories and lorikeets (their smaller cousins) are real birds; rainbow lorikeets are common in Australian gardens. In Alice, the Lory may be a joke about Alice's sister Lorina; it gets cross and sulky after Alice will not believe it, showing a grown-up who thinks age alone makes you right.
examples from the lessons: A lory has a brush-like tongue for licking nectar. | The Lory sulked and said it was older than Alice. | We saw bright red and green lories at the bird park. | Rainbow lorikeets are a kind of lory found in Australia. | The Lory, the Duck and the Dodo all ran in the Caucus-race. | The lory drank sweet juice from the flowers. | Alice would not let the Lory win the argument just because it was older.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural lories (y — ies). Do not confuse with lorry (a truck in the UK) or lorikeet (a smaller kind).

part of speech: noun (a prickle, prickles); verb (prickle, prickles, prickled, prickling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A small sharp point on a plant or animal, like on a hedgehog, holly leaf or bramble. 2) A tingling or stinging feeling on your skin. 3) (verb) To give a stinging, tingling feeling: «The wool prickled my neck.» 4) (verb) When your skin or the back of your neck prickles, you feel fear or excitement.
its sense in the lessons: In science, prickles and spines protect plants and animals: a hedgehog rolls up and shows its prickles. In stories, «the hairs on the back of her neck prickled» tells the reader the character senses danger. Phrases: «a prickle of fear», «prickle with tears» (eyes stinging before crying).
examples from the lessons: The hedgehog's prickles kept the fox away. | My new jumper prickles. | I felt a prickle of fear when the door creaked. | Watch out for the prickles on the rose stem. | Her eyes prickled with tears. | Mole felt the back of his neck prickle in the Wild Wood. | Holly leaves have prickles on their edges.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Prickly is the adjective: «a prickly cactus», «a prickly person» (easily annoyed). Strictly, botanists say prickles grow on the skin of a stem (rose), while thorns and spines are changed branches or leaves, but in everyday talk they are mixed.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Too proud of yourself; thinking you are cleverer, better-looking or more important than you are.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, a conceited character often boasts and then gets a lesson. Toad in The Wind in the Willows is very conceited: he sings songs about how wonderful he is («The world has held great Heroes… but never a name to go down to fame compared with that of Toad!»). Kipling's Just So animals can be conceited too. The noun is conceit. Opposite: modest, humble.
examples from the lessons: Toad was so conceited that he wrote songs about himself. | She is clever but not at all conceited. | Don't be conceited just because you won. | The conceited peacock spread his tail for everyone to admire. | Badger told Toad to stop being so conceited. | It sounded conceited when he said he was the best player in the school. | Nobody likes a conceited winner.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The noun is conceit (also an old word for a clever idea in a poem). Similar words: vain, big-headed, arrogant, stuck-up (informal). Spelling: ei after c — conceited.

part of speech: verb (spank, spanks, spanked, spanking); noun (a spank, spanks); adjective (spanking — informal, see notes)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To hit someone, usually a child, on the bottom with an open hand as a punishment. 2) (noun) A slap on the bottom. 3) (rude, adult slang) a rude word grown-ups use; not for school.
its sense in the lessons: In the past many parents and schools spanked children. Today it is against the law to hit children in Scotland, Wales, Ireland, New Zealand and many other countries, and most experts say it does not help children behave. In the Just So Stories, Taffy's long name means «Small-person-without-any-manners-who-ought-to-be-spanked», which is a joke, but in real life children have a right not to be hit. If someone hurts you, tell a trusted adult. Informal «spanking» also means very good or fast: «a spanking new bike», «at a spanking pace».
examples from the lessons: In old stories, naughty children were often spanked. | It is now against the law to smack or spank children in Wales. | Taffy's name says she ought to be spanked, but her daddy loved her. | The horses trotted along at a spanking pace. | He rode a spanking new bicycle. | If an adult hurts you, tell a teacher you trust.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: spanked. Similar: smack (UK). «Spanking new» (informal) means brand new; «at a spanking pace» means fast. This is a safety word: hitting children is banned in many countries.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The wide, open grassland of southern Africa, with few trees, where animals like zebras, giraffes and antelope live.
its sense in the lessons: The word comes from Afrikaans and Dutch, meaning «field». In geography, the veld is the South African grassland (high veld and low veld), like the prairie in North America or the steppe in Asia. In the Just So Story «How the Leopard Got His Spots», the Giraffe and Zebra live on «the High Veldt» which is all sandy-yellow, until they move into the stripy, speckly shade of the forest.
examples from the lessons: Zebras and antelope graze on the veldt. | The Leopard lived on the High Veldt, which was sandy-yellow-brownish. | Long dry grass covered the veldt as far as we could see. | The veld is a kind of grassland in South Africa. | In the dry season, the veldt turns brown. | The Giraffe and the Zebra left the veldt for the forest.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Two spellings: veldt (old English spelling, used by Kipling) and veld (modern South African). The ending sounds like «felt». Similar words: savanna, prairie, steppe.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A dark prison room, often underground, in a castle. 2) (games) In video and board games, a set of dangerous rooms or tunnels to explore.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, castles had dungeons for prisoners. In The Wind in the Willows, Toad is sentenced to twenty years and thrown into «the remotest dungeon of the best-guarded keep of the stoutest castle in all the length and breadth of Merry England». In fairy tales a dungeon tells the reader that someone is trapped and needs rescue. Phrases: «locked in the dungeon», «dungeons and dragons».
examples from the lessons: The king threw the thief into the dungeon. | Toad lay in the dungeon and wept. | The dungeon was cold, damp and dark. | We visited a castle and saw the old dungeon. | In the game, you have to find the key to escape the dungeon. | The gaoler's daughter brought food down to the dungeon. | Many castle dungeons were really used as storerooms.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: d-u-n-g-e-o-n (the e keeps the g soft: «DUN-jun»). Myth: not every castle had a torture dungeon; many cellars were for storing food.

part of speech: noun (a gipsy, gipsies); also spelt gypsy, gypsies; adjective (gipsy)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (old, can be offensive) An old word for a member of the Romani people, who came to Europe from India long ago and many of whom lived and travelled in caravans. 2) In The Wind in the Willows, Toad sells the horse he has taken to a gipsy for six shillings and sixpence and a hot breakfast; Toad's caravan is a «gipsy caravan». 3) Used in some names, like the gipsy moth.
its sense in the lessons: Many Romani and Traveller people find the word «gypsy» rude, especially when used as an insult, so today it is better to say Roma, Romani people or Travellers. Some families do still call themselves Gypsies with pride. In old books like The Wind in the Willows the word is used as it was in Edwardian times, sometimes with unfair ideas; in lessons we name those ideas as wrong today. Romani people have their own language, Romani, and a long history in Europe, including persecution.
examples from the lessons: Toad sold the horse to a gipsy who was sitting by the road. | Toad's painted caravan was called a gipsy caravan. | Romani people came to Europe from India hundreds of years ago. | Today we say Roma or Travellers rather than gipsies. | The gipsy made a stew in a pot over the fire. | The gipsy moth has hairy caterpillars.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Two spellings: gipsy (old British) and gypsy. Plural gipsies/gypsies. Say Roma, Romani people or Travellers in your own writing. The word comes from «Egyptian», an old mistaken belief about where Romani people came from.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (old) A small sweet made of a seed or nut, such as aniseed, caraway or an almond, coated in hard sugar.
its sense in the lessons: Comfits were eaten in Tudor and Victorian times, like sugared almonds or sprinkles today. In Alice in Wonderland, after the Caucus-race the Dodo says everybody has won and must have prizes, and Alice hands round a box of comfits from her pocket, one each; she gets her own thimble back as her prize. The scene is a joke about silly rules where everyone wins.
examples from the lessons: Alice found a box of comfits in her pocket. | Each animal got one comfit as a prize. | The comfits were a little wet from the salt water. | A comfit is a seed or nut covered in sugar. | Sugared almonds are a kind of comfit. | The big birds complained they could not taste their comfits.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Old-fashioned word; today we say sugared almonds, sugar-coated sweets or sprinkles. Countable: a comfit, comfits. Do not confuse with confetti (paper pieces) or comfort.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A part of a river where the water is still or slow, away from the main current, often behind a bend or a weir. 2) A quiet place, such as a small town, where not much happens and new ideas arrive slowly.
its sense in the lessons: In The Wind in the Willows, Ratty and Mole row along the river and into quiet backwaters among the reeds and willows; one backwater leads to the weir where they meet the Piper at the Gates of Dawn and find little Portly. In geography, a backwater is calm, so mud settles and plants grow. In everyday talk, calling a town a backwater can be unkind, meaning it is dull or old-fashioned.
examples from the lessons: Ratty steered the boat into a quiet backwater. | Water lilies grew in the still backwater. | Ducks dabbled in the backwater, away from the strong current. | My uncle says his village is a sleepy backwater. | The backwater was full of reeds and dragonflies. | They tied up the boat in a little backwater for lunch. | Fish rest in backwaters when the river is in flood.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a backwater. It is one word. Calling a place a backwater is a judgement, sometimes rude.

part of speech: noun (a scull, sculls); verb (scull, sculls, sculled, sculling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) One of a pair of oars that one rower uses, one in each hand. 2) A light, narrow racing boat rowed with sculls. 3) (verb) To row a boat using a pair of sculls, or using one oar at the back of the boat moved from side to side. 4) (verb, Australia, NZ, informal) To drink a whole drink very quickly in one go (this is for grown-ups at parties).
its sense in the lessons: In The Wind in the Willows, Ratty sculls his little boat on the river and teaches Mole; when Mole grabs the sculls to show off, he turns the boat over. In sport, single sculls and double sculls are Olympic rowing races. Phrase: «scull a boat», «single sculls».
examples from the lessons: Ratty sculled gently up the river. | Mole snatched the sculls and fell in the water. | She won the single sculls race at the regatta. | Hold one scull in each hand and pull together. | The fisherman sculled with one oar at the back of the boat. | You need practice to scull in a straight line.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Scull sounds exactly like skull (the bones of the head) — homophones with different meanings. A scull is a small oar; a sculler is the rower.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A small square of cloth (or paper) you carry in your pocket to wipe your nose, eyes or face. 2) A square of cloth worn around the neck or head, like a scarf.
its sense in the lessons: For health, use a handkerchief or tissue when you sneeze or cough, then wash your hands (catch it, bin it, kill it). In old stories, people wave handkerchiefs to say goodbye, drop them as a signal, or tie things up in them. In Alice, the Walrus holds a pocket-handkerchief to his eyes while eating the oysters; Mole and Ratty wave handkerchiefs too. Short forms: hanky, hankie.
examples from the lessons: Use a handkerchief when you sneeze. | Grandma has handkerchiefs with her initials sewn in the corner. | The Walrus held his pocket-handkerchief before his streaming eyes. | She waved her handkerchief as the train left. | He wrapped the conkers in a handkerchief. | Can I borrow a tissue? I forgot my handkerchief. | The pirate wore a red handkerchief on his head.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: hand-ker-chief, with a silent d in speech («HANG-ker-chif»). Plural usually handkerchiefs. Informal: hanky.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An old dance for four couples standing in a square, done in several parts, popular in the 1800s. 2) The music for this dance. 3) (cards, old) A card game for four players.
its sense in the lessons: Quadrilles were danced at balls in Victorian times, like a square dance. In Alice in Wonderland, the Mock Turtle and the Gryphon dance the Lobster Quadrille for Alice, with the song «Will you walk a little faster? said a whiting to a snail». The name comes from Latin and French words for four (like quadrilateral).
examples from the lessons: The Mock Turtle and the Gryphon danced the Lobster Quadrille. | At the ball, four couples stood in a square for the quadrille. | «Will you, won't you, will you, won't you, will you join the dance?» | In a quadrille, each couple takes turns to move. | The band played a lively quadrille. | Lobsters are thrown out to sea in the middle of the Lobster Quadrille.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Sounds like «kwa-DRILL». «Quad-» means four: quadrilateral, quad bike, quadruple. Old-fashioned word.

part of speech: noun (awe, uncountable); verb (awe, awes, awed, awing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A strong feeling of wonder and respect, sometimes with a little fear, when you see something huge, beautiful or powerful. 2) (verb) To fill someone with awe: «The mountains awed us.» 3) (church) The deep respect and wonder people of faith feel before God; Christians speak of «awe and wonder».
its sense in the lessons: In science and RE lessons, «awe and wonder» describes the feeling of looking at stars, mountains or a newborn baby. In The Wind in the Willows, in the chapter «The Piper at the Gates of Dawn», Mole feels «a great Awe» when he and Ratty meet Pan, the Friend and Helper, on the island. Phrases: «in awe of», «stand in awe», «awe-inspiring», «awestruck».
examples from the lessons: We stood in awe at the edge of the Grand Canyon. | The little children were in awe of the big footballers. | Mole felt a great awe fall upon him. | The night sky filled her with awe. | The cathedral was awe-inspiring. | He was too awed to speak. | In assembly we talked about awe and wonder.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «filled with awe». Awe is the root of awful (once meaning «full of awe», now «very bad») and awesome (now «great» in slang). Homophones: awe / or / oar in many accents.

part of speech: noun (a cudgel, cudgels); verb (cudgel, cudgels, cudgelled or cudgeled, cudgelling or cudgeling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A short thick stick used as a weapon; a club. 2) (verb) To hit someone with a cudgel. 3) (phrase) «Cudgel your brains» means think very hard to remember something. 4) (phrase) «Take up the cudgels for someone» means defend them strongly in an argument.
its sense in the lessons: In The Wind in the Willows, Badger, Ratty, Mole and Toad arm themselves with cudgels and pistols to win back Toad Hall from the weasels and stoats. In old stories, robbers and guards carry cudgels. Hitting people is violence; in stories it shows a fight or danger.
examples from the lessons: Badger handed each friend a stout cudgel. | The robber waved a cudgel at the travellers. | Mole ran through the hall waving his cudgel. | I cudgelled my brains but could not remember her name. | She took up the cudgels for her little brother in the argument. | The guard carried a heavy cudgel.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK spelling cudgelled, cudgelling; US cudgeled, cudgeling. Old-fashioned word. Similar: club, stick, truncheon.

part of speech: noun (a parlour, parlours); US spelling parlor
meaning for a pupil: 1) (old) A sitting room in a house kept for receiving visitors or for the family to relax in. 2) A shop or business giving a certain service: an ice-cream parlour, a beauty parlour, a funeral parlour. 3) (farming) A milking parlour is the building where cows are milked.
its sense in the lessons: In old books, the parlour is the best room of a house. In The Wind in the Willows, Mole's little home, Mole End, has a parlour, and Badger's home and Toad Hall have fine rooms; the word shows a cosy, old-fashioned home. In modern life, an ice-cream parlour is a fun place to visit. A funeral parlour is where the body of a person who has died is looked after before a funeral. Phrases: «parlour game» (an indoor party game like charades).
examples from the lessons: We had sundaes at the ice-cream parlour. | Grandma's parlour had a piano and lace curtains. | The cows walk into the milking parlour twice a day. | We played parlour games at the Christmas party. | The visitors were shown into the parlour. | The funeral parlour was quiet and calm.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK/Ireland/Australia/NZ/Canada spelling parlour; US spelling parlor. Countable.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (US, Canada) Suspenders are straps that go over the shoulders to hold trousers up; British people call these braces. 2) (UK, Ireland, Australia) A suspender is an elastic strap that holds up a stocking or sock; suspender belts were worn by women and sock suspenders by men in the past.
its sense in the lessons: This word means different things in different countries — a famous trap. A US «suspenders» is a UK «braces». In the past, gentlemen wore sock suspenders under their trousers; in old books and photos you may see them. Usually used in the plural: «a pair of suspenders».
examples from the lessons: Grandpa wears red suspenders to hold up his jeans. | In Britain, those straps are called braces, not suspenders. | The clown's trousers fell down when his suspenders snapped. | Old-fashioned sock suspenders kept socks from slipping. | He clipped his suspenders to his trousers. | Firefighters wear suspenders on their heavy trousers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually plural: suspenders, «a pair of suspenders». UK braces = US suspenders. Don't confuse with suspend (to hang up, or to stop for a time) or suspense (waiting nervously).

part of speech: noun (a caucus, caucuses); verb (caucus, caucuses, caucused, caucusing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (politics) A meeting of members of a political party or group to choose candidates or decide what to do, especially in the USA. 2) A group of people inside an organisation who share the same interests. 3) (Alice) The Caucus-race in Alice in Wonderland is a silly race where everyone runs in a circle, starting and stopping when they like, and at the end the Dodo says «Everybody has won, and all must have prizes».
its sense in the lessons: In the US, the Iowa caucuses help choose presidential candidates. In New Zealand and Australia, a party caucus is its members of parliament meeting together. In Alice, Carroll is making fun of politics: the caucus-race goes nowhere and everybody wins, to dry the animals off after the pool of tears. Phrase: «everybody has won and all must have prizes».
examples from the lessons: The Dodo said the best way to get dry was a Caucus-race. | The party caucus met to choose a new leader. | In the Caucus-race, they ran round and round in a circle. | Iowa holds its caucus in winter. | Everybody won the Caucus-race, so everybody had a prize. | The caucus voted for the plan.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural caucuses. Sounds like «CAW-kus». Mostly a politics word in the US, Australia and NZ.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A young eagle, still a baby or chick. 2) In Alice in Wonderland, the Eaglet is a young bird in the pool of tears and the Caucus-race who tells the Dodo to «Speak English!» because it does not understand his long words.
its sense in the lessons: The ending -let means small, as in piglet, booklet, droplet. In science lessons, eaglets hatch from eggs in a big nest called an eyrie and are fed by both parents until they can fly. In Alice the Eaglet stands for Alice's sister Edith; the Dodo is Carroll himself.
examples from the lessons: The eaglet waited in the nest for its mother. | «Speak English!» said the Eaglet. | Eaglets are covered in soft grey down. | Two eaglets hatched in the eyrie this spring. | The eaglet flapped its wings for the first time. | The webcam shows the eaglets being fed.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Use «an eaglet» (starts with a vowel sound). Baby animal words: eaglet, owlet, duckling, cygnet, fawn, cub.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Places on exactly opposite sides of the Earth from each other. 2) (UK) The Antipodes is a name for Australia and New Zealand, because they are on the other side of the world from Britain.
its sense in the lessons: In geography, if you could dig a tunnel straight through the centre of the Earth, you would come out at your antipode; for most places in Europe that is in the ocean, near New Zealand. In Alice in Wonderland, as Alice falls she wonders if she will come out among «the Antipathies» — she mixes the word up with antipathies, meaning dislikes — and imagines people walking upside down.
examples from the lessons: New Zealand is close to the antipodes of Spain. | Alice wondered if she would fall right through the Earth to the Antipodes. | My cousins live in the Antipodes, in Melbourne. | An antipodean Christmas is in summer. | If you dig straight down from Britain, you come out in the sea near New Zealand. | People at the antipodes are not really upside down; gravity pulls everyone towards the centre of the Earth.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Sounds like «an-TIP-o-deez», four syllables. Usually plural with «the». Myth: people on the other side are not upside down — «down» always points to Earth's centre.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A small dried black grape without seeds, used in cakes, buns and puddings. 2) A small round berry that grows in bunches on a bush: blackcurrant, redcurrant, whitecurrant.
its sense in the lessons: In cooking, currants go in currant buns, Eccles cakes, spotted dick and Christmas pudding. In the nursery rhyme «Five currant buns in a baker's shop», and in maths problems with buns, currants can be counted. In Alice in Wonderland, Alice finds a little cake marked EAT ME «in currants». Blackcurrant juice is popular in the UK.
examples from the lessons: Five currant buns in a baker's shop, round and fat with a sugar on the top. | The cake had «EAT ME» written on it in currants. | We picked redcurrants in the garden. | Blackcurrants are full of vitamin C. | Put a handful of currants into the scone mixture. | Each bun has 8 currants; how many currants are in 5 buns?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Homophone trap: currant (fruit) and current (flow of water or electricity; or «now»). Currant has -ant like «ant in the cake».

part of speech: noun (a gaol, gaols); verb (gaol, gaols, gaoled, gaoling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (UK, old spelling) A prison; a jail. 2) (verb) To put someone in prison.
its sense in the lessons: Gaol is the old British spelling of jail; it sounds exactly the same. You see it in old books and on old buildings, and it is still used in Australia in names like «Old Melbourne Gaol». In The Wind in the Willows, Toad is sent to gaol for twenty years for stealing a motor-car, driving dangerously and cheeking the police; he escapes disguised as a washerwoman.
examples from the lessons: Toad was thrown into gaol. | The old gaol is now a museum. | He was gaoled for stealing horses. | The gaoler locked the gaol at night. | In the past, people could be sent to gaol for owing money. | We visited the Old Melbourne Gaol on a school trip.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: gaol is said «jail», not «goal». Do not mix up with goal (in football). Modern spelling everywhere is jail; prison is the formal word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A soldier of middle rank, above a corporal, who is in charge of a group of soldiers. 2) A police officer of the rank above a constable. 3) (in titles) Sergeant Major, Sergeant at Arms.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, a sergeant often gives orders, shouts drills or arrests people. In The Wind in the Willows, the policemen who catch Toad and the court are part of the story of the law. Phrases: «drill sergeant», «police sergeant», «Sergeant-at-Arms».
examples from the lessons: The sergeant shouted, «Left, right, left, right!» | Sergeant Jones is in charge of the local police station. | My grandad was a sergeant in the army. | The sergeant has three stripes on his sleeve. | The sergeant asked the witness some questions. | A police sergeant came to talk to our class about road safety.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: s-e-r-g-e-a-n-t; it sounds like «SAR-jent». Short form: Sgt.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A large wooden barrel, made of strips of wood held by metal hoops, used for holding wine, beer, water or other liquids. 2) The amount a cask holds.
its sense in the lessons: In stories about ships and pirates, casks hold fresh water, rum or gunpowder. Coopers are the craftspeople who make casks. In The Wind in the Willows, the Sea Rat tells of sailing on ships through ports full of wine and goods. In maths, casks may appear in volume and capacity problems.
examples from the lessons: The sailors rolled the casks onto the ship. | A cask of fresh water was kept on deck. | The cooper hammered the hoops round the cask. | The cellar was full of old wine casks. | Each cask holds 50 litres; how much do 4 casks hold? | The pirate sat on a cask of rum.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Similar: barrel, keg (smaller), tun (huge). Do not confuse with casket (a small box, or in the US a coffin) or mask.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A short, simple song or poem, often cheerful or funny.
its sense in the lessons: In The Wind in the Willows, Ratty makes up little songs, like «Ducks' Ditty» («All along the backwater, / Through the rushes tall, / Ducks are a-dabbling, / Up tails all!»). Toad sings boastful ditties about himself. In music lessons a ditty is an easy tune to learn.
examples from the lessons: Ratty sang his ducks' ditty. | She hummed a little ditty while she cooked. | The ducks did not like Ratty's ditty very much. | We learned a ditty about the days of the week. | Toad sang a conceited ditty about how clever he was. | The advert has a catchy ditty.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural ditties (y — ies). Slightly old-fashioned, friendly word.

part of speech: noun (a plop, plops); verb (plop, plops, plopped, plopping); adverb (plop)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The soft sound of something small dropping into water, like a pebble or a frog. 2) (verb) To fall or drop with this sound. 3) (verb, informal) To sit down or put something down heavily and carelessly: «She plopped down on the sofa.»
its sense in the lessons: Plop is an onomatopoeic word — it sounds like the noise it names (like splash, drip, buzz). In The Wind in the Willows, the river bank is full of small sounds like the plop of a water vole or a fish. In poetry and writing lessons it is used for sound effects. Phrase: «plop down».
examples from the lessons: The frog jumped into the pond with a plop. | A big raindrop plopped onto my nose. | He plopped his bag on the floor. | Something went plop in the dark river. | She plopped down on the beanbag. | Two ice cubes plopped into my drink. | We heard a plop as the water vole dived.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past plopped, -ing plopping (double p). It is an onomatopoeia. Compare: plop (small and soft), splash (bigger), sploosh (informal, big).

part of speech: verb, -ing form of murmur (murmuring); noun (a murmuring, murmurings); adjective (murmuring)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Saying something quietly and softly, so it is hard to hear. 2) Making a low, soft, continuous sound, like a stream, bees or the wind in leaves. 3) (noun) Murmurings are quiet complaints or rumours: «murmurings of unhappiness».
its sense in the lessons: In stories, a murmuring river or murmuring voices create a calm or secret mood. In The Wind in the Willows, the river is always murmuring and chattering, and the reeds whisper. In the Bible, the Israelites' «murmuring» in the desert means grumbling against Moses. Phrases: «murmuring stream», «murmuring voices».
examples from the lessons: The murmuring stream sent me to sleep. | We could hear voices murmuring behind the door. | Bees were murmuring in the lavender. | There were murmurings in class when the trip was cancelled. | The river went on murmuring through the night. | Mum sat murmuring a lullaby to the baby. | The crowd was murmuring before the show began.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: murmur + ing (one r at the end, no doubling). See murmur. Similar: whispering, muttering (more grumbly), humming.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who travels by sea, especially a sailor whose life and job is at sea.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, the Vikings, Phoenicians and Polynesians were great seafarers who crossed oceans. In The Wind in the Willows, the chapter «Wayfarers All» introduces the Sea Rat, a seafarer who tells Ratty wonderful stories of ports around the Mediterranean, and Ratty nearly leaves home to follow him. Phrase: «a seafaring nation», «seafaring life».
examples from the lessons: The Sea Rat was a seafarer who had sailed to many ports. | The Phoenicians were brave seafarers. | Seafarers once used the stars to find their way. | My great-grandfather was a seafarer all his life. | Polynesian seafarers sailed canoes across the Pacific. | The seafarer told tales of storms and strange lands.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Built like wayfarer (a traveller on foot): sea + farer (from old «fare», to travel). Similar: sailor, mariner, seaman.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who runs or works at a high level in a bank, deciding about loans and money. 2) (games) The player in charge of the bank in a game like Monopoly, who hands out and takes in money. 3) (UK, informal) Something certain to happen or win: «That team is a banker for the title.»
its sense in the lessons: In money lessons, a bank keeps people's savings safe and lends money; bankers decide who can borrow and how much interest to charge. In Monopoly, one player is the banker. In old stories, bankers are often rich and important. Phrases: «a bank manager» (more common for the person you meet at a branch).
examples from the lessons: The banker agreed to lend the family money for a house. | I'll be the banker in Monopoly. | Her mum is a banker in the city. | The banker counted out the notes. | Bankers had to explain why the bank lost so much money. | The banker gave each player 1,500 pounds to start.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. A bank clerk or teller serves customers; a banker usually means a senior person. In games maths, the banker adds and subtracts money.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The rules of polite behaviour in a society or group, such as how to greet people, eat at table or write a letter.
its sense in the lessons: In personal and social education, good etiquette means being polite: saying please and thank you, not talking with your mouth full, waiting your turn. There is also online etiquette (sometimes called netiquette). In Alice in Wonderland, the Mad Tea-Party breaks every rule of etiquette — the Hatter is rude, there is no room though the table is large, and Alice is told off for being «not invited». The Queen of Hearts cares about etiquette only for others. Phrases: «table etiquette», «court etiquette», «a breach of etiquette».
examples from the lessons: Good table etiquette means not reaching across the table. | Royal etiquette says you curtsey or bow to the Queen. | It is bad etiquette to type in capital letters online. | At the Mad Tea-Party, there was no etiquette at all. | Our teacher taught us the etiquette of writing a thank-you letter. | Shaking hands is good etiquette after a match.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. French origin: sounds like «ET-ee-ket». Do not mix up with a ticket. Netiquette = internet etiquette.

part of speech: noun (a golosh, goloshes); usual spelling galosh, galoshes
meaning for a pupil: 1) (old) A rubber shoe worn over an ordinary shoe to keep it dry in rain or snow; an overshoe.
its sense in the lessons: Golosh is an old British spelling of galosh, found in old books. In the past people put goloshes over their good shoes on wet days. Today children wear wellies (wellington boots) or rain boots instead. In the US, galoshes is still sometimes used for rubber boots.
examples from the lessons: Grandpa pulled on his goloshes before going out in the snow. | Put your goloshes on or your shoes will get muddy. | The old lady left her wet goloshes by the door. | Galoshes keep your shoes clean and dry. | In the 1900s, many people wore goloshes in winter. | He slipped his goloshes off in the hall.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually plural (a pair of goloshes). Modern spelling galoshes. Similar: overshoes, wellies (UK), gumboots (Australia, NZ), rain boots (US).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (old-fashioned, UK) Another spelling of hello, used to greet someone. 2) A way to show surprise: «Hullo, what's this?»
