its sense in the lessons: Hullo is common in old British books such as The Wind in the Willows and Winnie-the-Pooh; the animals greet each other with «Hullo!». It is the same word as hello and hallo. In stories, «Hullo, hullo!» often shows a cheerful character noticing something.
examples from the lessons: «Hullo, Mole!» called Ratty from the riverbank. | Hullo, what's this lying in the grass? | The boy waved and shouted, «Hullo, you fellows!» | She said hullo to everyone in the street. | «Hullo!» said the policeman. «What have we here?» | Old books use hullo where we write hello.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Same meaning as hello, hallo and hiya (informal). Old-fashioned in writing today; use hello in your own stories unless the voice is old-fashioned.

part of speech: adjective (ingenious, more ingenious, most ingenious); adverb (ingeniously); noun (ingenuity)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Very clever and inventive, especially at finding new ways to solve problems. 2) (of an idea or machine) Cleverly planned and made.
its sense in the lessons: In design and technology and science, an ingenious invention solves a problem in a new way, like the wheel or Velcro. In the Just So Stories, Taffy and her father Tegumai are ingenious: they invent letters from pictures and sounds. In Alice, the White Knight has many «ingenious» inventions that never work, which is a joke. Phrase: «an ingenious idea».
examples from the lessons: What an ingenious way to fix the bike! | Tegumai and Taffy found an ingenious way to write sounds. | The robot was an ingenious invention. | She built an ingenious trap to catch the sweet thief. | The escape plan was ingenious. | Leonardo da Vinci drew many ingenious machines.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: ingenious (clever) vs ingenuous (innocent, too trusting). The noun of ingenious is ingenuity, not «ingeniousness» (that is rare).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Belonging to the New Stone Age, the last part of the Stone Age, when people began farming, keeping animals, making pottery and polished stone tools, and living in villages; in Britain about 4000 to 2500 BC.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, the Neolithic is when Stonehenge's first stages and Skara Brae in Orkney were built. In the Just So Stories, Taffy and her father Tegumai Bopsulai are «Neolithic» people (Kipling says so), living by a river and inventing writing — though really writing was invented much later, in Mesopotamia and Egypt around 3200 BC. That is one of Kipling's made-up facts. Phrases: «Neolithic farmers», «Neolithic Age».
examples from the lessons: Neolithic people grew wheat and kept sheep. | Skara Brae is a Neolithic village in Orkney. | We made Neolithic pots out of clay at school. | Kipling calls Tegumai a Neolithic man. | Neolithic tools were polished stone axes. | The first stage of Stonehenge was built in Neolithic times. | Real writing came after the Neolithic.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually with a capital N. «Neo-» means new, «-lithic» means stone: New Stone Age. Order: Palaeolithic (Old), Mesolithic (Middle), Neolithic (New) Stone Age, then the Bronze Age.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The thick, tough outer skin of some fruits, like oranges, lemons and watermelons. 2) The hard outer layer of cheese or bacon. 3) The bark of a tree (old use).
its sense in the lessons: In cooking, lemon rind (also called zest when grated) gives flavour to cakes. You cut the rind off bacon or some cheeses before eating. In science, the rind protects the fruit inside. In stories, people throw away orange rinds or watermelon rinds after eating. Phrases: «orange rind», «cheese rind», «bacon rind».
examples from the lessons: Grate the lemon rind into the cake mix. | Don't eat the rind of the watermelon. | The cheese has a hard waxy rind. | He cut the rind off the bacon. | Orange rind smells sweet when you peel it. | The ants found the melon rinds in the bin.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Rind is used for thick skins; peel is the general word; zest is the coloured outer part of citrus rind; skin is used for thin coats like apples. Sounds like «rined» (rhymes with find).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A bag with a long strap, worn over the shoulder or on the back, used especially for carrying school books.
its sense in the lessons: In the UK, Ireland and Australia, satchels were the traditional leather school bags; today most pupils use backpacks or rucksacks. In stories and old poems, a schoolboy goes «with his satchel and shining morning face». The word gives an old-fashioned or school feeling.
examples from the lessons: She put her pencil case and reading book in her satchel. | My grandad had a brown leather satchel at school. | The postman's satchel was full of letters. | He swung his satchel over his shoulder and ran to school. | Don't forget your satchel! | The satchel was heavy with books.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Similar: schoolbag, rucksack, backpack, school bag. Spelling: s-a-t-c-h-e-l.

part of speech: fragment (shan, from shan't); also Shan — a name
meaning for a pupil: 1) A piece of the word «shan't», which means «shall not», as in «I shan't go». It is not a word by itself in English. 2) (a name) The Shan are a people of Myanmar (Burma) and nearby lands, with their own language; Shan State is in Myanmar.
its sense in the lessons: «Shan't» (shall + not) is mostly British and old-fashioned, used in old books like Alice in Wonderland and The Wind in the Willows: Alice says «I shan't be able!» as she grows tall. Today most people say «won't».
examples from the lessons: «I shan't!» shouted the cross little boy. | «I shan't be able to reach the key,» said Alice. | We shan't be long — wait here. | Shan't is short for shall not. | The Shan people live in the hills of Myanmar.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always written shan't with an apostrophe where the letters «ll no» are left out. «Shan» alone is just a fragment (or a name). Modern English: won't.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A large piece of soft cloth, often wool or silk, worn over the shoulders or head, or wrapped around a baby.
its sense in the lessons: Shawls keep people warm and are part of many traditional costumes. In The Wind in the Willows, Toad escapes from prison in the washerwoman's cotton print gown, shawl and black bonnet. In the past, babies were wrapped in shawls; in church, some women wear a shawl over the head. In stories, an old woman in a shawl is a common picture.
examples from the lessons: Grandma wrapped her shawl around her shoulders. | Toad pulled the shawl over his face and walked past the guards. | The baby was wrapped in a white knitted shawl. | She wore a colourful silk shawl to the wedding. | The prayer shawl is called a tallit in Jewish worship. | The wind blew her shawl off.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Similar: wrap, stole, scarf (smaller). Sounds like «shorl».

part of speech: adjective (submissive, more submissive, most submissive); adverb (submissively); noun (submission)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Willing to obey others and do what they want without arguing or standing up for yourself. 2) (animals) Showing by body language that you will not fight, like a dog rolling on its back.
its sense in the lessons: In science, animals show submissive behaviour to stronger animals to avoid fights: a puppy lies down, a wolf tucks its tail. In personal education, being too submissive can mean you do not stand up for yourself; being respectful is different from letting others push you around. If anyone pressures you to do something wrong or unsafe, you can say no and tell a trusted adult. In old stories, servants and children were expected to be submissive.
examples from the lessons: The puppy rolled over in a submissive way. | The younger wolf lowered its head to look submissive. | She was too submissive and always let others choose. | The captured knight bowed in a submissive way. | You can be polite without being submissive. | In the old story, the servant answered submissively.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposites: assertive, rebellious, dominant. Related verb: submit (to give in; also to hand in homework). Noun submission.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (UK) A short thick stick carried by police officers as a weapon; in the US it is called a nightstick or baton.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, Victorian police (Bobbies or Peelers) carried wooden truncheons and rattles or whistles. Today police carry batons. The word also appears in Punch and Judy shows.
examples from the lessons: The policeman tapped his truncheon against his hand. | Victorian police carried a wooden truncheon. | The museum has an old painted truncheon. | Mr Punch waved his stick like a truncheon. | Police today carry a baton, not a truncheon. | The guard held his truncheon ready.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. UK word, a little old-fashioned. Similar: baton, club, cudgel, nightstick (US).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (UK, old) A person who guards prisoners in a prison; a prison guard. 2) (old) A person who guards a gate or a building.
its sense in the lessons: In The Wind in the Willows, warders guard the castle where Toad is imprisoned. At the Tower of London, the famous Beefeaters are called Yeoman Warders. Today the job title is prison officer. In old stories, a warder with keys stands for being trapped.
examples from the lessons: The warder rattled his keys. | The Yeoman Warders guard the Tower of London. | Toad crept past the sleeping warder. | Every evening the warder locked the cells. | The warder at the gate asked who we were. | Old prisons had warders in dark uniforms.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Do not mix up with warden (a person in charge of a place — a prison warden, a traffic warden, a park warden) or ward (a hospital room). Similar: gaoler, jailer, guard.

part of speech: noun (whitewash, uncountable; a whitewash in sport); verb (whitewash, whitewashes, whitewashed, whitewashing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A white liquid made of lime or chalk and water, painted on walls and fences to make them white. 2) (verb) To paint with whitewash. 3) (verb) To hide the bad things someone has done so that they look innocent: «The report tried to whitewash the mistakes.» 4) (sport, informal) A win where the losers score nothing or lose every game: «a 5–0 whitewash».
its sense in the lessons: In history, farm buildings, cottages and fences were whitewashed. In The Wind in the Willows, Mole is spring-cleaning and whitewashing his little home with a brush and a pail when spring calls him and he flings the brush down, saying «Bother!» and «O blow!» and «Hang spring-cleaning!». In Tom Sawyer, Tom tricks his friends into whitewashing a fence for him. In news and history, «whitewash» means hiding the truth.
examples from the lessons: Mole was whitewashing his house when spring called him. | Tom Sawyer got his friends to whitewash the fence. | The farmer whitewashed the barn walls. | The report was called a whitewash because it hid the truth. | England beat them 5–0 — a total whitewash! | The old cottage was whitewashed every summer.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word. Uncountable for the paint, countable for the sports sense. The «hiding» sense is a judgement; be fair before using it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal, a little old-fashioned) Very; extremely: «awfully kind», «awfully sorry». 2) Very badly: «He behaved awfully.»
its sense in the lessons: In old British books like The Wind in the Willows and Alice, characters say «awfully» a lot: «awfully nice», «awfully sorry». In modern speech it is a polite, slightly posh way to say «very». Sense 2 (badly) is less common.
examples from the lessons: That's awfully kind of you. | I'm awfully sorry I'm late. | It's awfully cold today. | «This is awfully jolly!» said Tom. | She sang awfully, so everyone laughed. | Thank you awfully for the present.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Awfully usually means «very» (even with good words: «awfully nice»). Awful (adjective) means very bad. Spelling: awful + ly — two l's (awfully).

part of speech: noun (a blotch, blotches); verb (blotch, blotches, blotched, blotching)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A large, uneven mark or patch of colour, such as an ink stain or a red patch on the skin. 2) (verb) To mark with blotches.
its sense in the lessons: In art, a blotch of paint can be a mistake or part of a picture. On skin, red blotches can come from crying, heat, an allergy or an illness like a rash — if blotches spread or you feel ill, tell an adult. In old schools, pupils used blotting paper to stop ink blotches. In the Just So Stories, the Leopard and the Ethiopian get blotchy, spotty and stripy patterns so they can hide in the forest shade.
examples from the lessons: There was a big ink blotch on my page. | Her face came out in red blotches after the long run. | The leaf had brown blotches on it. | The giraffe's skin is covered in blotches. | Use blotting paper to stop the ink blotching. | The rash made blotches on his arms.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural blotches. Adjective blotchy. Similar: splodge (UK informal), stain, spot, patch, smudge.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A white, waxy substance with a strong, sharp smell, taken from the wood of the camphor tree or made in factories; it is used in some medicines and rubs, and once to keep moths away from clothes.
its sense in the lessons: In science, camphor is a chemical that turns straight from a solid to a gas (it sublimes), which is why its smell spreads. In the past, clothes were stored with camphor or mothballs. In old stories, a room or old clothes smelling of camphor tells the reader they have been put away for a long time. Safety: camphor is poisonous if swallowed, especially for small children.
examples from the lessons: The old trunk smelled of camphor. | Vapour rub has camphor and menthol in it. | Camphor is poisonous, so never eat it. | The camphor tree grows in Asia. | Grandma kept camphor in the wardrobe to stop moths. | The smell of camphor made my eyes water.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Sounds like «CAM-fer». Safety word: keep camphor products away from small children.

part of speech: noun (a chairman, chairmen); also chair, chairperson, chairwoman
meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who leads a meeting or a committee and keeps order, deciding who speaks. 2) The person in charge of the board of a company, club or organisation.
its sense in the lessons: In school councils and clubs, the chair runs the meeting, sticks to the agenda and lets everyone speak. In stories, the chairman bangs a hammer called a gavel and calls «Order, order!». Today many people say «chair» or «chairperson» so it fits anyone. In The Wind in the Willows, Badger acts as leader when the friends meet to plan.
examples from the lessons: The chairman asked everyone to sit down. | Our class chose Priya as chair of the school council. | The chairman of the football club gave a speech. | «Order, please!» said the chairman. | The chairwoman thanked everyone for coming. | The chairman counted the votes for each idea.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural chairmen. Neutral words: chair, chairperson. Do not confuse with a chair (furniture) — although «chair» is also used for the person.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A row of bushes, shrubs and small trees growing along the edge of a field or a country lane.
its sense in the lessons: Hedgerows are typical of the British and Irish countryside. In science, a hedgerow is a habitat: birds nest in it, hedgehogs and dormice hide in it, and blackberries, hawthorn and wild roses grow there. In The Wind in the Willows, the animals travel along country lanes between hedgerows, and Toad's caravan rolls past them. Many hedgerows were pulled up for bigger fields, and now people are planting them again.
examples from the lessons: Blackbirds nest in the hedgerow. | We picked blackberries from the hedgerow. | The hedgehog hid under the hedgerow. | The lane ran between tall hedgerows full of flowers. | Hedgerows give food and shelter to many animals. | We counted 12 kinds of plants in 30 metres of hedgerow.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word. Countable. Compare hedge (any line of bushes, including a garden hedge); hedgerow is the countryside kind.

part of speech: adjective (horrid, more horrid or horrider, most horrid or horridest)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Very unpleasant or nasty: «a horrid smell». 2) (of people) Unkind or mean: «Don't be horrid to your sister.» 3) (old) Causing horror; frightening.
its sense in the lessons: A common word in British children's books and in speech among children: «Horrid Henry» is a famous naughty character. In Alice and The Wind in the Willows, characters call things or people horrid when they are upset. In stories it tells you a character is mean or something is nasty.
examples from the lessons: That medicine tastes horrid. | Don't be horrid to the new girl. | It was a horrid, rainy day. | «You horrid creature!» cried Alice. | The weasels were horrid to Toad. | I had a horrid dream last night.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal and a bit childish or old-fashioned in UK speech. Similar: nasty, horrible, awful, mean. Horrid and horrible mean nearly the same.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A woman or girl servant who cleaned and tidied a house, made beds and lit fires, in the past.
its sense in the lessons: In Victorian and Edwardian times, many young women worked as housemaids in big houses, working long hours for low pay. In Alice in Wonderland, the White Rabbit mistakes Alice for his housemaid, Mary Ann, and sends her to fetch his gloves and fan; she then grows huge inside his house. In history lessons the word shows life «below stairs».
examples from the lessons: The White Rabbit thought Alice was his housemaid. | The housemaid got up at five to light the fires. | Mary Ann, the Rabbit's housemaid, was nowhere to be seen. | Housemaids had very little free time. | The housemaid polished the silver every Friday. | In the big house there were three housemaids and a cook.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. A job of the past; today we say cleaner or housekeeper. Similar: maid, servant, maidservant.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (old, rare) Greatness in amount or size. 2) (phrase, UK) «Much of a muchness» means nearly the same, with little difference: «The two shops are much of a muchness.»
its sense in the lessons: In Alice in Wonderland, at the Mad Tea-Party the Dormouse talks of drawing «all manner of things — everything that begins with an M — such as mouse-traps, and the moon, and memory, and muchness — you know you say things are "much of a muchness"». It is a joke: you cannot draw «muchness». Today the word is used almost only in the phrase.
examples from the lessons: The two films were much of a muchness. | «Did you ever see such a thing as a drawing of a muchness?» asked the Dormouse. | Both pizzas are much of a muchness, so pick either. | These tents are much of a muchness — buy the cheaper one. | The Dormouse listed things beginning with M, like muchness. | The teams were much of a muchness, so the match was close.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Used almost only in «much of a muchness» (UK, informal). Uncountable.

part of speech: adjective (splendid, more splendid, most splendid); adverb (splendidly)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Very beautiful, grand and impressive: «a splendid palace». 2) (UK, a little old-fashioned) Very good; excellent: «What a splendid idea!»
its sense in the lessons: In The Wind in the Willows, Toad uses «splendid» all the time about himself, his house and his motor-cars. In old-style British speech, «Splendid!» means «Great!». In descriptive writing, splendid can describe a grand building, costume or view.
examples from the lessons: What a splendid idea! | The palace had a splendid golden gate. | Toad said Toad Hall was the most splendid house on the river. | We had a splendid day at the beach. | The peacock spread its splendid tail. | «Splendid!» said the teacher. «Full marks.»
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun splendour (UK) / splendor (US). Similar: magnificent, grand, superb, excellent.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Short trousers fastened just below the knee, worn by men in the past and today for horse riding (riding breeches). 2) (informal, old) Trousers.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, Tudor, Stuart and Georgian men wore breeches with long stockings; boys were «breeched» (put into breeches) when they were about 5–7. Riders wear tight riding breeches. In The Wind in the Willows, Toad dresses up in fine clothes; in pictures of old times, gentlemen and servants wear breeches. Phrase: «too big for your breeches» (or britches) means too proud of yourself.
examples from the lessons: The king wore velvet breeches and white stockings. | She pulled on her riding breeches before her lesson. | Pirates wore loose breeches. | He's getting too big for his breeches since he won. | The footman wore breeches and buckled shoes. | Breeches stop just below the knee.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always plural: «a pair of breeches». Sounds like «BRITCH-iz», not «BREE-chiz». US informal spelling britches.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A short sword with a slightly curved blade and one sharp edge, used by sailors and pirates in the past.
its sense in the lessons: In stories about pirates and sea battles, a pirate waves a cutlass. In The Wind in the Willows, Ratty lays out weapons for each friend before the battle for Toad Hall; in pirate tales like Treasure Island, cutlasses are everywhere. Real swords are dangerous weapons, not toys.
examples from the lessons: The pirate drew his cutlass. | Sailors in the navy once carried cutlasses. | The captain held a cutlass in one hand and a lantern in the other. | The museum has an old naval cutlass. | «Hand over the treasure!» growled the pirate, waving his cutlass. | A cutlass is shorter than most swords.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural cutlasses. Similar: sabre, sword, scimitar (strongly curved).

part of speech: noun (despair, uncountable); verb (despair, despairs, despaired, despairing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The feeling of having lost all hope. 2) (verb) To lose hope: «Don't despair — we'll find your cat.» 3) (phrase) «Drive someone to despair» or «be the despair of someone» means make them feel hopeless and worried.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, despair is the low point before something changes: Toad in his dungeon «flung himself at full length on the floor, and shed bitter tears, and abandoned himself to dark despair». In PSHE, if you feel hopeless, it is important to talk to someone you trust. Christians believe that God's love gives hope even in despair. Phrases: «in despair», «despair of».
examples from the lessons: Toad lay in his dungeon in despair. | Don't despair — you can try again tomorrow. | She shook her head in despair at the mess. | The teacher despaired of ever getting the class quiet. | After the storm, the farmers were in despair. | His messy room is the despair of his mum.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable noun. Adjective despairing; related word desperate. «Despair of» means «lose hope about». Spelling: des-pair.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A very large African antelope with spiral horns on both males and females, light brown colour and a hanging fold of skin on the throat; it is the largest antelope in the world.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on African grasslands, elands graze on the savanna and veld with zebras and giraffes. In the Just So Story «How the Leopard Got His Spots», the Leopard and the Ethiopian hunt the Giraffe, the Zebra, the Eland and the Kudu on the High Veldt; the animals escape into the forest and change colour. Kipling's story is not real science.
examples from the lessons: The eland is the biggest kind of antelope. | Elands can jump very high for such large animals. | The Eland and the Kudu ran into the forest. | A herd of eland grazed on the veldt. | Both male and female elands have twisted horns. | The eland has a fold of skin hanging from its neck.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Use «an eland» (vowel sound). Plural elands or eland (like deer). Sounds like «EE-land».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A cover made of cloth or leather worn over the ankle and lower leg, to keep out mud, snow or stones. 2) (old) Leather leggings once worn by bishops, soldiers and gentlemen.
its sense in the lessons: Walkers and hikers wear gaiters to stop mud and snow getting into their boots. In old stories and pictures, country gentlemen and old soldiers wear leather gaiters buttoned up the side; in The Wind in the Willows, Toad's chauffeur-style motoring outfit includes boots and gaiters. A «neck gaiter» is a tube of cloth worn around the neck in winter.
examples from the lessons: Put your gaiters on — the path is muddy. | The old gamekeeper wore leather gaiters. | Snow got into her boots because she forgot her gaiters. | I wear a neck gaiter when skiing. | The bishop in the old picture wore black gaiters. | Gaiters fasten with a strap under the boot.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually plural: a pair of gaiters. Similar: leggings, spats (short, over the shoe).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A tall pipe for smoking tobacco, in which the smoke passes through water in a jar before being breathed in through a long tube; also called a water pipe or shisha.
its sense in the lessons: In Alice in Wonderland, the blue Caterpillar sits on a mushroom smoking a long hookah and asks Alice «Who are you?». Hookahs come from India, Persia and the Middle East. Health and safety: smoking a hookah is not safe — it is as harmful as smoking cigarettes and it is illegal to sell tobacco to children.
examples from the lessons: The Caterpillar was quietly smoking a long hookah. | «Who are you?» said the Caterpillar, taking the hookah out of its mouth. | Hookah smoke is harmful to your lungs. | In the old picture, the man sat with his hookah. | Shisha is another name for hookah smoking. | The Caterpillar's hookah stood on top of the mushroom.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Sounds like «HOOK-ah». Safety: hookah smoking is not safer than cigarettes.

part of speech: noun (a murmur, murmurs); verb (murmur, murmurs, murmured, murmuring)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A soft, low sound of voices, or of water, wind or bees, that goes on and on. 2) (verb) To say something very quietly. 3) A quiet complaint: «They paid without a murmur.» 4) (medicine) A heart murmur is an extra sound a doctor hears in the heartbeat; many are harmless.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, a murmur sets a quiet, gentle mood, or shows a crowd reacting: «a murmur of surprise ran round the room». In The Wind in the Willows, the river murmurs and the reeds whisper. Phrases: «without a murmur» (without complaining), «a murmur of agreement».
examples from the lessons: A murmur of excitement ran through the audience. | «Goodnight,» she murmured sleepily. | We heard the murmur of the stream. | He did his chores without a murmur. | The doctor heard a small heart murmur, but said it was nothing to worry about. | The murmur of bees filled the garden.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: m-u-r-m-u-r; past murmured, -ing murmuring (no double r). Similar: mutter (grumbly), whisper (with breath), mumble (unclear).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A long, warm coat worn over other clothes in cold weather.
its sense in the lessons: In old books and pictures, gentlemen wear heavy overcoats in winter; in The Wind in the Willows, the animals bundle up in coats and mufflers, and Toad wears a motoring overcoat with goggles and cap. In everyday life, «overcoat» is a bit old-fashioned; people say coat or winter coat.
examples from the lessons: Dad buttoned up his overcoat against the snow. | Toad put on his goggles, cap and overcoat for driving. | Hang your overcoat in the hall. | The detective wore a long grey overcoat. | It was so cold that he wore an overcoat over two jumpers. | The overcoat came down to his knees.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Use «an overcoat» (vowel sound). Compound of over + coat. Similar: greatcoat (army), raincoat, mac (UK), parka.

part of speech: adjective (satiable); in Kipling, «'satiable» short for insatiable
meaning for a pupil: 1) (rare) Able to be satisfied or filled. 2) (Just So Stories) In «The Elephant's Child», Kipling writes «'satiable curtiosity», meaning «insatiable curiosity» — a curiosity that can never be satisfied; the Elephant's Child keeps asking questions.
its sense in the lessons: In «The Elephant's Child», the young elephant is «full of 'satiable curtiosity» and asks everyone questions, like «What does the Crocodile have for dinner?»; he gets spanked for it, but in the end his long trunk (pulled long by the Crocodile) helps him. The story praises curiosity. The real word for never satisfied is insatiable; satiable alone is rare.
examples from the lessons: The Elephant's Child was full of 'satiable curtiosity. | He asked the Kolokolo Bird about the Crocodile because of his 'satiable curtiosity. | Her curiosity was insatiable — she never stopped asking why. | A small appetite is easily satiable. | Kipling made up the word «curtiosity» on purpose. | Scientists need an insatiable curiosity.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Rare in normal English. Opposite in meaning: insatiable (never satisfied), the common word. «Satiate» means fill completely; «sate» is the short form. Kipling's «'satiable curtiosity» is playful spelling, not standard.

part of speech: adjective (snobbish, more snobbish, most snobbish); noun (snob, snobbery)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Thinking you are better than other people because you are richer, posher or more educated, and looking down on them.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, a snobbish character turns their nose up at others. In The Wind in the Willows, Toad can be snobbish about his grand house and money, though he is friendly too. In PSHE, being snobbish is unkind; everyone deserves respect whatever their family's money or accent. Phrases: «a snobbish attitude», «food snob».
examples from the lessons: She was too snobbish to play with the village children. | Don't be snobbish about other people's clothes. | The snobbish lady said the tea-shop was not good enough. | Toad was a little snobbish about his motor-car. | He made a snobbish remark about her accent. | The new kid thought we were snobbish, but we were just shy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: a snob; snobbery. Informal similar: posh, stuck-up, toffee-nosed (UK). Opposite: down-to-earth, humble.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A thin, pointed stick used in hand spinning to twist wool or other fibres into thread. 2) A rod or pin in a machine that turns round, or around which something turns. 3) (adjective form spindly) Long and thin, like spindly legs.
its sense in the lessons: In history, people spun yarn with a spindle before spinning wheels and mills. In the fairy tale Sleeping Beauty, the princess pricks her finger on a spindle and falls asleep for a hundred years. In science and DT, a spindle is a turning part of a machine. A «spindle tree» is a hedgerow tree whose wood was used for spindles.
examples from the lessons: The princess pricked her finger on the spindle. | The woman twisted the wool onto her spindle. | The spinning wheel has a spindle that turns very fast. | Spiders have long, spindly legs. | The door handle fell off its spindle. | Before mills, all thread was made with a spindle.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Adjective spindly (long and thin, weak-looking).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Not signed; with no name written on it: «an unsigned letter». 2) (music, sport) Not having a contract with a record company or a team: «an unsigned band». 3) (maths, computing) An unsigned number has no plus or minus sign and is never negative.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, an unsigned letter or note is anonymous — you don't know who wrote it. In school, an unsigned permission slip means the trip is not allowed until a parent signs. In computing, an unsigned whole number can only be 0 or positive. In Alice in Wonderland, at the trial the White Rabbit reads a letter «not signed at the end», and the King says that makes it worse — a silly kind of logic.
examples from the lessons: The letter was unsigned, so we don't know who sent it. | Your permission slip is still unsigned. | The King said an unsigned letter proved the Knave meant mischief. | The band is still unsigned but plays every weekend. | An unsigned number cannot be negative. | Don't sign up for anything online without asking an adult.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Prefix un- = not: unsigned = not signed. In maths/computing, «unsigned» means without a + or − sign, so the value is zero or positive.

part of speech: adjective (wretched, more wretched, most wretched); adverb (wretchedly); noun (wretch)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Very unhappy, ill or miserable: «I felt wretched with flu.» 2) Very poor or bad in quality: «They lived in wretched huts.» 3) (informal, annoyed) Used to show you are cross with something: «This wretched computer won't work!»
its sense in the lessons: In stories, a wretched character is suffering — Toad feels wretched in his dungeon, and poor people in old books live in wretched conditions. In sense 3 it is a mild, annoyed word, not a swear word. In the Bible and old hymns, «a wretch like me» (Amazing Grace) means a sinful, unhappy person whom Christians believe God saves.
examples from the lessons: Toad felt wretched in his cold cell. | The wretched dog has eaten my homework! | The refugees lived in wretched tents. | I felt wretched after staying up so late. | «Amazing grace, how sweet the sound, that saved a wretch like me.» | Mole felt wretched when he lost his way in the Wild Wood.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Sounds like «RETCH-id», two syllables; the w is silent. A wretch is a miserable or bad person.

part of speech: noun (a beheading, beheadings); verb, -ing form of behead (behead, beheads, beheaded, beheading)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Cutting off someone's head as a punishment; an execution. 2) (verb) Cutting off the head of a person or animal.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, Anne Boleyn and Charles I were beheaded; in Tudor England the axe was used, in the French Revolution the guillotine. In Alice in Wonderland, the Queen of Hearts shouts «Off with his head!» all the time, but the King quietly pardons everyone and nobody is actually beheaded — the Cheshire Cat even has no body to cut its head from. Beheading is a terrible, real punishment from history, not a joke in real life.
examples from the lessons: Henry VIII ordered the beheading of two of his wives. | «Off with her head!» shouted the Queen. | The executioner said you can't behead a cat with no body. | Charles I was beheaded in 1649. | Nobody was really beheaded in Wonderland. | Beheadings once took place in front of crowds at the Tower of London.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb behead (be + head): beheaded, beheading. Similar: decapitate (formal), execution (any killing as a legal punishment).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Covered in blotches; marked with uneven patches of colour.
its sense in the lessons: Skin can go blotchy after crying, running, cold, or with a rash or allergy. Old paintwork and dyed cloth can be blotchy. In the Just So Stories, Kipling's Leopard gets his spots from the Ethiopian's fingertips, and the forest is «speckly, spotty, patchy-blatchy» with shadows — Kipling plays with such words.
examples from the lessons: Her face was blotchy from crying. | The paint dried blotchy because it was too thin. | His skin went red and blotchy in the cold wind. | The forest shade was stripy and blotchy. | The old map was blotchy with water stains. | A blotchy rash can be a sign of illness — tell an adult.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparisons blotchier, blotchiest. Similar: patchy, spotty, mottled.

part of speech: adjective (crimson); noun (crimson, uncountable); verb (crimson — rare, to go red)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A deep, strong red colour with a little blue in it. 2) (verb, rare) To turn deep red, as when blushing.
its sense in the lessons: In art, crimson is one of the reds, deeper than scarlet. In stories, a face turning crimson shows embarrassment or anger; a crimson sky shows sunset. In Alice in Wonderland, the gardeners paint the white roses red because the Queen wanted red ones. Phrases: «go crimson», «crimson with rage».
examples from the lessons: The sky turned crimson at sunset. | Toad went crimson with rage. | She wore a crimson velvet dress. | The crimson roses filled the garden. | His cheeks went crimson when everyone laughed. | Mix red with a little blue to get crimson.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Similar reds: scarlet (bright, orange-red), maroon (dark brown-red), ruby, cherry. Blushing: «go red/crimson/scarlet».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Very; extremely: «I'm dreadfully sorry.» 2) Very badly: «The team played dreadfully.»
its sense in the lessons: In old British books such as Alice in Wonderland, «dreadfully» is often used for «very»: Alice was «dreadfully puzzled» and «dreadfully frightened». It sounds polite and a little old-fashioned. In everyday talk «dreadfully» can also mean in a very bad way.
examples from the lessons: I'm dreadfully sorry about the window. | Alice was dreadfully puzzled by the Hatter's remark. | The play went dreadfully — everyone forgot their lines. | It was dreadfully cold in the castle. | She missed her family dreadfully. | Mole was dreadfully frightened in the Wild Wood.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb of dreadful (very bad; terrible). Spelling: dreadful + ly — two l's. Similar: awfully, terribly, very.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A long, narrow, flat-bottomed boat with a high point at each end, rowed by one person standing at the back with one oar, used on the canals of Venice in Italy. 2) A cabin hanging from a cable that carries people up a mountain (a cable car). 3) A basket or cabin hanging under a hot-air balloon or airship. 4) (shops) A free-standing set of shelves in a supermarket.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons on Italy, gondolas are a famous sight of Venice, a city built on water, rowed by gondoliers. In The Wind in the Willows, the Sea Rat tells Ratty about Venice, with «gondolas» and lanterns on the canals. In ski resorts, gondolas take skiers up the mountain.
examples from the lessons: We rode in a gondola along the canals of Venice. | The gondolier sang as he rowed. | We took the gondola up to the top of the mountain. | The Sea Rat talked of gondolas and lamps in Venice. | The hot-air balloon's gondola was made of wicker. | The gondola swayed gently in the wind.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. The rower is a gondolier. Stress on the first syllable: «GON-do-la».

part of speech: noun (loosestrife, uncountable; a loosestrife, loosestrifes for kinds)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A tall wild plant that grows by rivers, ponds and in damp places; purple loosestrife has spikes of bright purple-pink flowers, and yellow loosestrife has yellow flowers.
its sense in the lessons: In The Wind in the Willows, the riverbank in summer is full of wild flowers: «Purple loosestrife arrived early, shaking luxuriant tangled locks along the edge of the mirror», in the chapter «The Piper at the Gates of Dawn». In science, loosestrife is a habitat for bees and butterflies; in North America purple loosestrife came from Europe and is an invasive weed that crowds out native plants.
examples from the lessons: Purple loosestrife grows along the riverbank. | Bees buzzed around the loosestrife. | The loosestrife was reflected in the still water. | In Canada, purple loosestrife is an invasive weed. | Yellow loosestrife is a different plant. | Grahame describes loosestrife, willow-herb and meadowsweet by the river.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word. Despite the name it has nothing to do with being «loose» or «strife» (fighting) — it is a plant name from old translations.

part of speech: noun (a mangle, mangles); verb (mangle, mangles, mangled, mangling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (noun) A machine with two rollers, turned by a handle, used in the past to squeeze water out of wet washing. 2) (verb) To crush, tear or damage something badly so it is out of shape. 3) (verb) To spoil words, music or a story by saying or doing them badly: «He mangled the French phrase.»
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, washing day before washing machines meant scrubbing, boiling and putting clothes through the mangle. In The Wind in the Willows, the washerwoman's world of tubs and mangles is part of Toad's disguise. Safety: machines can mangle fingers — keep hands away from moving parts. In stories, a mangled car or bike shows a bad crash.
examples from the lessons: Grandma used to put the sheets through the mangle. | Turn the handle and the mangle squeezes out the water. | The bike was mangled in the crash. | The dog mangled my slipper. | He mangled the words of the song. | Keep your fingers away from the rollers of the mangle.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb past mangled. Noun is old-fashioned; the verb is common. Similar: crush, wreck; for words: garble, murder (informal).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Belonging to Phoenicia, an ancient land of trading cities (like Tyre, Sidon and Byblos) on the coast of what is now Lebanon, about 1500–300 BC. 2) A person from Phoenicia. 3) The Phoenician alphabet was one of the first alphabets, with letters for sounds; Greek, Latin and our ABC came from it.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons on how writing began, the Phoenicians were great seafarers and traders who sailed the Mediterranean, founded Carthage and spread their alphabet; they also made a famous purple dye from sea snails. The Just So Stories tell a made-up tale of Taffy inventing letters; the real story goes through Egyptian signs, the Phoenician alphabet and the Greeks to the Romans.
examples from the lessons: The Phoenicians sailed all over the Mediterranean. | Our alphabet comes from the Phoenician alphabet. | Phoenician traders sold purple dye and cedar wood. | Carthage was a Phoenician city in North Africa. | The Phoenician letter aleph became the Greek alpha and our A. | Tyre was a rich Phoenician port.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Write with a capital P. Sounds like «fo-NEE-shun» or «fuh-NISH-un». The Phoenician alphabet had only consonants; the Greeks added vowels.

part of speech: adjective (ridiculous, more ridiculous, most ridiculous); adverb (ridiculously)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Very silly or unreasonable, so that people may laugh at it: «a ridiculous hat». 2) (informal) Extreme; amazing: «The price was ridiculous.»
its sense in the lessons: In Alice in Wonderland, almost everything is ridiculous — a Caucus-race where everyone wins, a trial where the sentence comes first. In The Wind in the Willows, Toad's boasting is ridiculous. In maths, a ridiculous answer (like a child 50 metres tall) tells you to check your working — always ask «does this answer make sense?».
examples from the lessons: That's a ridiculous excuse! | Toad looked ridiculous in the washerwoman's bonnet. | «Sentence first — verdict afterwards!» said the Queen. «Stuff and nonsense!» said Alice, because it was ridiculous. | The shoes were ridiculously expensive. | If your answer says a cat weighs 400 kg, it's ridiculous — check it. | He wore a ridiculous hat with a feather.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: ridiculous starts with «rid-», not «red-» (from ridicule). Similar: absurd, silly, ludicrous.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Made of steel, or grey and shiny like steel. 2) Hard, strong and determined; not showing soft feelings: «a steely stare», «steely determination».
its sense in the lessons: In stories, steely eyes or a steely voice show that a character is tough, cold or very determined — like a strict teacher or a hero who will not give up. In art and description, «steely grey» is a cold blue-grey colour of sky or sea.
examples from the lessons: She gave him a steely look and he stopped talking. | The sky was a steely grey before the storm. | With steely determination, she finished the race. | The captain spoke in a steely voice. | Badger had a steely glint in his eye before the battle. | The sea looked steely and cold.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparisons steelier, steeliest. Steely is usually about people's looks, voices and wills, or about colour.

part of speech: noun (a toady, toadies); verb (toady, toadies, toadied, toadying)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who flatters and obeys a powerful person too much, to get favours; a creep (informal). 2) (verb) To behave like this: «He toadied to the boss.» 3) (rare) Like a toad.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and history, toadies surround kings and bullies, agreeing with everything. The word comes from old travelling sellers' helpers who pretended to eat «poisonous» toads. In The Wind in the Willows, Toad is not a toady — he is the opposite: proud and boastful — but the weasels and stoats flatter him when it suits them. Phrases: «toady up to».
examples from the lessons: The bully's toadies laughed at all his jokes. | Stop toadying to the teacher. | The king was surrounded by toadies who never told him the truth. | He was such a toady that nobody trusted him. | She toadied to the rich lady in hope of a present.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural toadies; past toadied. Similar: crawler, creep, suck-up (US), teacher's pet, brown-noser (rude). Do not mix up with toad or Toad the character.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The Tudors were the family of kings and queens who ruled England from 1485 to 1603: Henry VII, Henry VIII, Edward VI, Mary I and Elizabeth I. 2) Belonging to that time: «Tudor houses», «Tudor clothes». 3) (building) A style of house with black wooden beams and white walls, or a modern copy of it (mock Tudor).
its sense in the lessons: A big topic in UK history lessons: Henry VIII and his six wives («divorced, beheaded, died, divorced, beheaded, survived»), the break with the Church of Rome, the Spanish Armada (1588), explorers, Shakespeare's early life, Tudor food and clothes. In The Wind in the Willows, old houses like Toad Hall belong to the past of «Merry England».
examples from the lessons: Henry VIII was a Tudor king. | Elizabeth I was the last of the Tudors. | We dressed up in Tudor costumes for history day. | Our street has mock Tudor houses with black beams. | Tudor sailors fought the Spanish Armada. | The Tudors ruled for 118 years, from 1485 to 1603.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always a capital T. Maths: from 1485 to 1603 is 1603 − 1485 = 118 years.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Not carrying a weapon. 2) Without the use of weapons: «unarmed combat».
its sense in the lessons: In news and history, unarmed people are those who cannot fight back, so attacking them is especially wrong. In the police in the UK, Ireland and New Zealand, most officers are unarmed (they do not carry guns). In stories, a hero facing a monster unarmed is in danger. In The Wind in the Willows, Mole goes into the Wild Wood alone and unarmed, and Ratty comes after him with pistols and a cudgel.
examples from the lessons: Most British police officers are unarmed. | Mole went into the Wild Wood alone and unarmed. | The soldiers did not shoot at the unarmed crowd. | Judo is a kind of unarmed self-defence. | The knight stood unarmed before the dragon. | The prisoners were unarmed.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Prefix un- = not: un + armed. Opposite: armed. Do not confuse with «disarmed» (had weapons taken away; or charmed).

meaning for a pupil: 1) To unwind or straighten something that was wound into rings, like a rope, a hose or a snake.
its sense in the lessons: In science and nature, snakes coil up to rest and uncoil to move or strike. In the Just So Story «The Elephant's Child», the Bi-Coloured-Python-Rock-Snake uncoils himself from the rock to help the Elephant's Child pull away from the Crocodile. On boats, sailors uncoil ropes.
examples from the lessons: The snake slowly uncoiled itself from the branch. | Uncoil the hose before you water the garden. | The Rock-Snake uncoiled himself and knotted his tail round a tree. | The sailor uncoiled the rope and threw it to the shore. | The spring uncoiled with a twang. | She uncoiled from the sofa and stretched.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Prefix un- = undo: coil (wind into rings) — uncoil (unwind). Past uncoiled.

part of speech: verb, -ing form of writhe (writhe, writhes, writhed, writhing); adjective (writhing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Twisting and turning the body, usually because of pain, or wriggling like a snake or worm. 2) Feeling very embarrassed or upset: «writhing with embarrassment».
its sense in the lessons: In stories, a character writhing on the ground is in great pain; snakes and worms writhe. In Alice in Wonderland, the Mock Turtle says that at school under the sea he learned «Reeling and Writhing» — a pun on reading and writing — and «the different branches of Arithmetic — Ambition, Distraction, Uglification, and Derision» (puns on addition, subtraction, multiplication and division). If someone is writhing in pain, get help from an adult fast.
examples from the lessons: The worm was writhing on the path. | The Mock Turtle learned Reeling and Writhing at school. | He lay writhing in pain after the fall. | The snake writhed as it slid across the sand. | She was writhing with embarrassment. | Call 999 (or 911, 112, 000, 111 in NZ) if someone is writhing in pain and badly hurt.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb writhe: writhed, writhing (drop the e). The w is silent: «RYE-thing». Pun: Reeling and Writhing = reading and writing.

part of speech: adjective (astute, more astute, most astute); adverb (astutely)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Clever at understanding people and situations quickly, and using that to your advantage; sharp and shrewd.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, an astute detective notices small clues; an astute businessperson spots a good deal. In the Just So Stories, some animals are astute, like the clever Cat who walks by himself and makes a bargain with the Woman. In exam and newspaper English, «an astute observation» means a sharp, wise remark.
examples from the lessons: That was an astute guess. | The astute detective noticed the mud on the boots. | Badger was an astute old animal who knew the weasels' tricks. | She made an astute choice and saved money. | An astute reader will spot the clue in chapter one. | The Cat was astute and made a clever bargain.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Use «an astute». Similar: shrewd, sharp, clever, canny. Slightly formal word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) Any member of the group of sea mammals that includes whales, dolphins and porpoises.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, cetaceans are mammals, not fish: they breathe air through a blowhole, are warm-blooded, give birth to live young and feed them milk. Some (baleen whales) filter tiny food through baleen plates; others (toothed whales, dolphins) have teeth. In the Just So Story «How the Whale Got His Throat», Kipling jokes that the Whale's throat was blocked by a grating made from a raft, so he can only eat very small fish — real baleen whales do eat tiny krill, but not because of a grating.
examples from the lessons: Whales, dolphins and porpoises are all cetaceans. | Cetaceans breathe air through a blowhole. | The blue whale is the biggest cetacean and the biggest animal ever. | A cetacean is a mammal, not a fish. | We saw cetaceans from the boat off the coast of New Zealand. | In the story, the Whale got a grating stuck in his throat.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Sounds like «sih-TAY-shun». Common myth: whales are fish — they are not. The word comes from Latin cetus, whale.

part of speech: noun (a chink, chinks); verb (chink, chinks, chinked, chinking)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A narrow crack or opening, as in a wall or door, that light can come through. 2) A light ringing sound, like coins or glasses knocking together. 3) (verb) To make this sound: «The coins chinked in his pocket.» 4) (phrase) «A chink in someone's armour» means a weak spot. 5) (rude, offensive) A very offensive word used against Chinese or East Asian people; never use it.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, light shining through a chink in the curtains or under a door, or spying through a chink in the fence, is common. In The Wind in the Willows, light through chinks in shutters can show someone is home. The sound sense goes with coins and glasses. Sense 5 is a racist insult — if you hear it, it is right to tell a teacher.
examples from the lessons: Sunlight came through a chink in the curtains. | The coins chinked in the money box. | We peeped through a chink in the fence. | The glasses chinked as they clinked them together. | His only chink in the armour is his weak left foot. | There was a chink of light under the door.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Senses 1–4 are ordinary English. Sense 5 is a racist slur: never call anyone this. Similar for sound: clink, jingle, tinkle.

part of speech: noun (a curtsey, curtseys); verb (curtsey, curtseys, curtseyed, curtseying); also spelt curtsy, curtsies, curtsied
meaning for a pupil: 1) A polite movement made by girls and women, bending the knees with one foot behind the other, to show respect, for example to a queen or at the end of a performance. 2) (verb) To make a curtsey.
its sense in the lessons: In history and in royal etiquette, women curtsey and men bow to the monarch. In ballet and dance shows, dancers curtsey at the end. In Alice in Wonderland, Alice tries to curtsey while she is falling down the rabbit hole — «fancy curtseying as you're falling through the air!» — and she curtseys to the Queen of Hearts. In old stories, servants curtsey to their masters.
examples from the lessons: Alice tried to curtsey as she fell. | The ballet dancers curtseyed to the audience. | She curtseyed to the Queen and the Queen smiled. | The maid bobbed a curtsey and left the room. | Bow or curtsey when the music stops. | Alice made a little curtsey to the Duchess.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Two spellings: curtsey (curtseys, curtseyed) and curtsy (curtsies, curtsied). Usually done by women and girls; men and boys bow. Comes from the word courtesy (politeness).

meaning for a pupil: 1) The skin of a deer, especially when made into soft leather for clothes, shoes or bags.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, Stone Age and Native American peoples used deerskin for clothes, moccasins and drums. In the Just So Stories, Taffy and her father Tegumai wear skins and bark and live like Neolithic people; Taffy's mother and her people use deerskin. Today deerskin leather is used for soft gloves.
examples from the lessons: The moccasins were made of soft deerskin. | Stone Age people sewed clothes from deerskin. | Tegumai wrapped himself in a deerskin. | Deerskin gloves are very soft and warm. | The drum was covered with a deerskin. | The hunter dried the deerskin in the sun.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Compound: deer + skin. Uncountable for the leather (some deerskin), countable for one whole skin (a deerskin). Similar: buckskin, suede.

part of speech: adjective (gleaming); verb, -ing form of gleam (gleam, gleams, gleamed, gleaming)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Shining brightly because clean, polished or wet: «gleaming shoes». 2) (verb) Giving out or reflecting a soft, bright light.
its sense in the lessons: In descriptive writing, gleaming makes a picture of something shiny and new: a gleaming car, gleaming teeth, gleaming eyes. In The Wind in the Willows, Toad's new motor-car is gleaming and splendid; the river gleams in the sun. Eyes «gleaming» can show excitement or a sly plan.
examples from the lessons: Toad stared at the gleaming motor-car. | Her shoes were gleaming after she polished them. | The river was gleaming in the sunlight. | The cat's eyes were gleaming in the dark. | The kitchen was gleaming after we cleaned it. | His teeth were gleaming white.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Gleam: gleamed, gleaming. Similar: shining, glinting (small flashes), glistening (wet), sparkling, glowing.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Of ancient Greece, or in the style of ancient Greece: «Grecian columns», «a Grecian urn». 2) (of looks, old) A «Grecian nose» is straight, in line with the forehead, like on Greek statues.
its sense in the lessons: In history and art lessons, ancient Greek temples, vases and statues inspired many later buildings with «Grecian» columns. Grecian is mostly used for art, buildings and faces; for the people and language we say Greek. In Alice in Wonderland, the Mock Turtle's Classics master was «an old crab» who taught «Laughing and Grief» (a pun on Latin and Greek).
examples from the lessons: The museum had a Grecian urn painted with dancers. | The bank has tall Grecian columns at the front. | She has a Grecian nose like a statue. | The Mock Turtle learned «Laughing and Grief» — Latin and Greek. | The garden had a little Grecian temple. | Grecian patterns run round the edge of the vase.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital G. Use Greek for people, language and food («Greek salad»); Grecian is mostly for style and art.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (of a voice) Low, deep and rough. 2) (of a person) Rather unfriendly or impatient in the way they speak, though maybe kind underneath.
its sense in the lessons: In the fairy tale «The Three Billy Goats Gruff», the goats outwit the troll under the bridge. In The Wind in the Willows, Badger is gruff: he speaks shortly and hates Society, but he is kind and wise and looks after Mole and Ratty in the snow. In stories, gruff tells the reader how someone sounds.
examples from the lessons: «Who's there?» said Badger in a gruff voice. | The Three Billy Goats Gruff crossed the bridge. | Grandpa sounds gruff, but he's really very kind. | The guard answered gruffly. | His voice was gruff from his cold. | «Come in, then,» said the gruff old man.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparisons gruffer, gruffest. Similar: rough, hoarse (sore throat), brusque (formal), grumpy.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The amount a hat can hold. 2) (informal) A large number: «He scored a hatful of goals.»
its sense in the lessons: The ending -ful makes measuring nouns: spoonful, handful, cupful, hatful. In Alice in Wonderland, the Hatter sells hats, and a hatful of something would be a funny measure. In sports news, «a hatful of goals» means lots of goals.
examples from the lessons: She picked a hatful of strawberries. | He scored a hatful of goals this season. | The magician pulled a hatful of ribbons out of the hat. | We collected a hatful of conkers. | A hatful of water spilled on the floor.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural hatfuls (not «hatsful»). Like spoonful — spoonfuls, handful — handfuls. In maths it is not an exact measure.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Without hope; in a way that shows you think things cannot get better. 2) Completely; very much (usually about something bad): «hopelessly lost», «hopelessly in love».
its sense in the lessons: In The Wind in the Willows, Mole is hopelessly lost in the Wild Wood in the snow until Ratty finds him. In stories, «hopelessly» shows how bad a situation feels; «hopelessly in love» is a common story phrase. Phrases: «hopelessly lost», «hopelessly outnumbered».
examples from the lessons: Mole was hopelessly lost in the Wild Wood. | The little army was hopelessly outnumbered. | She stared hopelessly at the broken vase. | I'm hopelessly bad at drawing horses. | The prince fell hopelessly in love. | The road was hopelessly blocked by snow.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: hope + less + ly. Adjective hopeless (no hope; or very bad at something: «hopeless at maths»).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person whose job is to look after a house: cleaning, cooking, shopping and running things for the family who live there. 2) In a big old house, the head servant in charge of the other women servants and the household stores. 3) A person who is good or bad at keeping their own home tidy and running: «She is a good housekeeper.»
its sense in the lessons: In stories set in old times (Victorian or Edwardian England) a big house has a housekeeper with keys at her belt who orders the maids about; in Alice the White Rabbit thinks Alice is his housemaid Mary Ann. In everyday life today a housekeeper may work in a hotel, cleaning rooms. Phrases: «a hotel housekeeper», «the housekeeper's room», «good housekeeping» (sensible care of a home or of money).
examples from the lessons: The housekeeper kept the keys to every cupboard in the old house. | Mrs Hudson was Sherlock Holmes's housekeeper. | My aunt works as a housekeeper in a big hotel by the sea. | The housekeeper rang a bell to call the family to dinner. | Gran says she was never much of a housekeeper, but she was a great cook. | In the story, the housekeeper heard a strange noise in the attic. | The housekeeper checked that every room was clean before the guests came.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one housekeeper, two housekeepers. A housekeeper is paid; a housewife or househusband looks after their own home without pay. Not the same as «housekeeping» (the work itself, also a word in computers for tidying files).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (UK) A hard, striped peppermint sweet, often black and white. 2) Nonsense or a trick meant to fool people: words that sound important but are false. 3) A person who pretends to be better, kinder or cleverer than they really are. 4) As a cry, «Humbug!» means «Rubbish! I don't believe it!» (old-fashioned).
its sense in the lessons: Most famous from Charles Dickens's A Christmas Carol, where mean old Scrooge says «Bah! Humbug!» about Christmas; so calling someone «a bit of a Scrooge» or saying «bah humbug» today means grumbling about fun. In the UK, humbugs are old-fashioned sweets sold in jars. In stories a humbug is a fraud or a show-off who is found out. Phrases: «bah, humbug», «a mint humbug».
examples from the lessons: Grandad bought a paper bag of mint humbugs at the sweet shop. | «Bah! Humbug!» growled Scrooge when his nephew wished him a merry Christmas. | The magic cure the man sold at the fair was pure humbug. | Don't be such a humbug about the party, Dad! | The humbug stuck to my teeth for ages. | He pretended to be a great explorer, but he was a humbug who had never left town. | My brother says «bah humbug» every time we put up the Christmas tree.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The sweet is countable (a humbug, humbugs); the nonsense sense is mostly uncountable («that's humbug»). The sweet is mostly British; in the USA the word is known mainly from Scrooge.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A kind of willow tree or bush that grows by rivers and wet ground, with long thin bendy shoots. 2) One of those long thin bendy willow shoots, used to weave baskets and fences.
its sense in the lessons: A river-bank word: in The Wind in the Willows the river is lined with osiers, rushes and willows where the Rat and the Mole row and where water animals hide. In crafts, osiers are cut and woven into baskets, hurdles and fish traps. It tells the reader the setting is a quiet English river. Phrases: «osier beds» (places where osiers are grown), «an osier basket».
examples from the lessons: The little boat slid in among the osiers by the bank. | Basket makers cut osiers in winter when the leaves have fallen. | A moorhen built her nest under the osiers. | The osier beds along the river were thick and green. | We wove a little fence from thin osiers in our school garden. | The wind rustled through the osiers as the Mole watched the water.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: an osier, osiers. Starts with a vowel sound, so «an osier». Said «OH-zee-er» (UK) or «OH-zher» (US). It is a kind of willow, not a separate kind of tree from willows.

part of speech: adjective (potted); verb form (past of «pot»: pot, pots, potted, potting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Growing in a pot: a potted plant lives in a flowerpot, not in the ground. 2) (food) Cooked meat or fish pressed into a small pot or jar and covered with fat or butter so it keeps: «potted shrimps», «potted meat». 3) Made short and simple: «a potted history» tells a long story in a few lines. 4) Past form of the verb «pot»: put a plant in a pot, or (snooker, pool) knock a ball into a pocket.
its sense in the lessons: In The Wind in the Willows the Rat packs a famous picnic basket with cold chicken, cold tongue, cold ham, cold beef, pickled gherkins, salad, French rolls, cress sandwiches, «potted meat», ginger beer, lemonade and soda water: potted meat was a spread for sandwiches. In the science classroom we grow potted plants and measure them. Phrases: «a potted plant», «potted meat», «a potted history/biography».
examples from the lessons: We put a potted plant on each windowsill in the classroom. | Mum bought a jar of potted shrimps at the seaside. | The Rat's basket was full of good things, including potted meat. | Our teacher gave us a potted history of the Romans in five minutes. | He potted the black ball and won the game of pool. | I potted the seedlings into bigger pots. | The potted geranium needs watering every few days.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «potted» has double t because «pot» is a short word ending in one vowel and one consonant: pot → potted, potting. Not the same as «spotted» (having spots).

part of speech: noun (a raja, rajas; also spelled rajah)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A king or prince in India or other parts of South and Southeast Asia in the past. 2) A title of honour for an Indian ruler or nobleman.
its sense in the lessons: Comes from Sanskrit «rājan», king; it is related to «Raj», the name for British rule in India (1858–1947), and «maharaja», great king. In old stories and adventure books a raja lives in a palace with elephants and jewels; such pictures are often made up or exaggerated. In history lessons rajas ruled many small Indian states under the British. Phrases: «the Raja of …», «maharaja», «rani» (a raja's wife or a queen).
examples from the lessons: The raja rode through the city on a painted elephant. | Many small kingdoms in India were ruled by a raja. | The raja's palace had marble halls and gardens with fountains. | In the old story, a poor boy brought the raja a clever gift. | The rani was the raja's wife. | Our history book showed a photo of a raja meeting British officers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a raja, rajas. Two spellings, «raja» and «rajah», both correct. Raja is also a person's name in South Asia; then it is «(a name)». Not to be confused with «Raj» (British rule of India).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Thought by people to be good, honest and proper in the way you live and behave. 2) Decent and good enough to be seen: «Put on something respectable for the wedding.» 3) Fairly good or fairly large, though not excellent: «a respectable score», «a respectable sum of money».
its sense in the lessons: In stories about Victorian and Edwardian England, being respectable mattered a lot: a respectable family had a clean house, went to church and behaved properly. In The Wind in the Willows Toad's wild driving and stealing a car make him far from respectable, and his friends try to make him behave. In school we may get «a respectable mark» in a test – not top, but good. Phrases: «perfectly respectable», «a respectable distance», «look respectable».
examples from the lessons: Comb your hair and look respectable for the photo. | They were a respectable family who never missed church on Sunday. | Our team scored a respectable 45 points. | The Badger said that a respectable animal does not drive cars into ponds. | She saved a respectable amount of money for her holiday. | Keep a respectable distance from the edge of the cliff. | His old coat was patched but still respectable.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Do not mix up with «respectful» (showing respect to others): a respectful pupil listens politely; a respectable person is respected by others. Ends in «-able», not «-ible».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A driver who drives selfishly and dangerously, too fast or taking up too much of the road so others cannot pass. 2) More loosely, anyone (also a cyclist) who acts as if the road belongs to them.
its sense in the lessons: In The Wind in the Willows Toad becomes a roadhog after he falls in love with motor cars: he drives wildly, crashes cars, and is called a «road-hog» and worse at his trial. Early motorists in the 1900s were often blamed for frightening horses and people. For safety lessons: a roadhog ignores other road users; good drivers share the road. A hog is a pig, so the word calls the driver greedy like a pig.
examples from the lessons: A roadhog in a big van zoomed past us on the narrow lane. | Toad was a terrible roadhog, crashing car after car. | Don't be a roadhog on your bike – let others pass on the path. | The newspaper called the speeding driver a dangerous roadhog. | Dad grumbled about the roadhog who wouldn't let him change lanes. | A roadhog frightened the horses and scattered the hens.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Written as one word, two words («road hog») or with a hyphen («road-hog»); all are fine. It is an insult, not a polite word.

part of speech: noun (a spanking, spankings); adjective (spanking); adverb (spanking new); verb form (of «spank»: spank, spanks, spanked, spanking)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A punishment by hitting a child's bottom with an open hand, done in the past by parents and some teachers. 2) (adjective, old-fashioned) Fast, lively and fine: «at a spanking pace», «a spanking breeze». 3) (adverb, informal) Very, used with «new»: «spanking new» means brand new and shiny.
its sense in the lessons: In the Just So Stories the Elephant's Child is spanked again and again by his tall aunts and uncles because of his «satiable curtiosity», until he gets his long trunk and spanks them back. Today hitting children is against the law in many countries, including Scotland, Wales, Ireland and New Zealand, and many people think it is wrong; stories from long ago show it as normal. «Spanking new» and «a spanking pace» are harmless everyday phrases.
examples from the lessons: In the old days a naughty child might get a spanking. | The Elephant's Child was spanked by all his relatives for asking questions. | The new bus was spanking new and smelled of paint. | The horses trotted along at a spanking pace. | A spanking breeze filled the sails of the little boat. | Smacking and spanking children is now banned in Scotland and Wales. | Our school has a spanking new gym.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable as a punishment («a spanking»). «Spanking new» means only «very new», nothing about hitting. The verb is «spank»; past «spanked».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A ship or boat driven by a steam engine; a steamship. 2) A pan or pot with holes in it that sits over boiling water to cook food in the steam. 3) A machine that uses steam to clean things or take creases out of clothes.
its sense in the lessons: In The Wind in the Willows a passing steamer makes waves on the river, and the Sea Rat tells of sailing on ships and steamers to far ports. In history, steamers carried people across oceans and along rivers from the 1800s. In cooking, a steamer cooks vegetables without boiling them in water, so more vitamins stay in. In science: water boils and turns to steam, and the steam carries heat. Phrases: «a paddle steamer», «river steamer», «steam vegetables in a steamer».
examples from the lessons: We sailed across the lake on an old paddle steamer. | The steamer blew its whistle as it left the harbour. | Mum cooks broccoli in a steamer so it stays green. | The waves from the steamer rocked the little rowing boat. | Thousands of people crossed the Atlantic on great steamers. | The dry cleaner used a steamer to smooth the wrinkled dress. | Be careful: steam from the steamer can burn your hand.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Safety: steam is hotter than it looks and can scald; open a steamer lid away from your face. In Australia «steamer» was once also an old slang word, but it is not used now.

part of speech: noun (victuals, usually plural; verb: victual, victuals, victualled, victualling – rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (old-fashioned) Food and drink, especially supplies of food for a journey or for many people. 2) (verb, rare) To supply a ship or an army with food.
its sense in the lessons: An old word found in old stories and in The Wind in the Willows, where the animals speak of food and drink in grand old ways; sailors and armies needed victuals for long voyages. It makes speech sound old or funny. Today «vittles» (the same word, spelled as said) is used jokingly in the USA, especially in cowboy talk.
examples from the lessons: The sailors loaded the ship with victuals for the long voyage. | «Fetch the victuals!» cried the hungry pirate. | The innkeeper brought plenty of good victuals to the table. | The army ran short of victuals in the cold winter. | Grandad jokingly calls his dinner «my vittles». | The travellers packed bread, cheese and other victuals for the road.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A big spelling trap: it is spelled «victuals» but said «VIT-ulz» – the c and the u are silent. Usually plural. Not used in everyday modern speech except as a joke.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A small sea fish of the cod family, with white flesh, found in the seas around Europe; it is eaten as food. 2) (also other fish called whiting in the USA and Australia) a name for several kinds of small white-fleshed sea fish. 3) Finely ground white chalk used for whitewash, paint and cleaning.
its sense in the lessons: In Alice's Adventures in Wonderland the Mock Turtle's song begins «"Will you walk a little faster?" said a whiting to a snail», and the Gryphon makes a joke that whitings are what boots and shoes are done with under the sea (playing on whitening shoes, cleaning them white). In Victorian England whiting was often served with its tail in its mouth. At the fish shop, whiting is a cheap fish for fish and chips in Australia.
examples from the lessons: We had fried whiting and chips at the seaside. | «Will you walk a little faster?» said a whiting to a snail. | The fisherman caught three whiting off the pier. | In Wonderland, the whiting does the boots and shoes under the sea. | King George whiting is a favourite fish in South Australia. | Old cottages were painted with whiting mixed with water.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The plural is usually the same: «three whiting», though «whitings» is also used (Alice uses «whitings»). Do not mix up with «whitening» (making something whiter).

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a sad, longing way, as when you wish for something you cannot have or something that is gone. 2) In a quietly thoughtful, dreamy way, with a little sadness.
its sense in the lessons: Stories use «wistfully» to show a feeling without saying it outright: a character who looks wistfully at a shop window wants the toy but cannot buy it. In The Wind in the Willows the Mole and the Rat feel the pull of home and of far-off lands, and the Rat gazes wistfully south after meeting the Sea Rat. Often with «look», «gaze», «smile», «sigh», «say». A good word for creative writing to show longing.
examples from the lessons: Tom looked wistfully at the bikes in the shop window. | The old sailor smiled wistfully as he talked about the sea. | «I wish summer could last forever,» she said wistfully. | The puppy gazed wistfully at the biscuit on the table. | Gran wistfully remembered her school days. | The Rat stared wistfully south, where the swallows had flown.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from the adjective «wistful» + «-ly». Spelled with one l in «wist-» and double l at the end: «wistfully». Not the same as «wishful» (based on wishing, like «wishful thinking»), though close.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The science that studies animals: their bodies, how they live, grow, behave and where they come from. 2) The animal life of a place: «the zoology of Australia» (formal).
its sense in the lessons: A school science word: zoology is one branch of biology; botany studies plants. A zoologist studies animals, maybe in a lab, a zoo or the wild. In lessons we classify animals (mammals, birds, reptiles, amphibians, fish, insects) – that is zoology. Stories like the Just So Stories give made-up reasons for animal features, and zoology gives the true ones (for example, how leopards really got spots through evolution).
examples from the lessons: Zoology is the study of animals. | My cousin is studying zoology at university. | We learned some zoology when we sorted animals into groups. | A zoology book explained how bats find their way in the dark. | She wants a job in zoology, working with gorillas. | Kipling's stories are fun, but zoology tells us how the camel really got its hump.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: no «a zoology». Said «zoo-OL-uh-jee» or «zoh-OL-uh-jee». Related words: zoologist (person), zoological (adjective), zoo (short for zoological garden). The ending «-ology» means «the study of».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (old-fashioned or literary) A word that shows sadness, sorrow or regret: «Alas, it was too late.» 2) (humorous) Used today in a joking way for small disappointments.
its sense in the lessons: Found in old stories, poems and fairy tales: «Alas! The prince was gone.» In The Wind in the Willows and Alice the word fits the grand, old-style storytelling voice. In modern writing it is often slightly funny: «Alas, the cake was all eaten.» It tells the reader something sad or disappointing has happened.
examples from the lessons: Alas, the ship sank before it reached the shore. | «Alas! I shall be too late!» cried the White Rabbit. | I wanted to go to the beach, but alas, it rained all day. | Alas, poor Toad was locked in the deepest dungeon. | Alas, there was no chocolate left in the box. | The knight looked for the dragon, but alas, it had flown away.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually at the start of a sentence, followed by a comma. Mostly in writing, rarely in everyday chat (except for a joke). Not a sound word like «ah»; it means sorrow.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Wet, dirty and messy, as when you have been out in rain or mud. 2) Looking untidy, worn out and sorry for yourself.
its sense in the lessons: In Alice's Adventures in Wonderland the birds and animals come out of the Pool of Tears a «queer-looking party», with draggled feathers and wet fur, and must get dry (hence the Caucus-race). Stories use «bedraggled» to show someone has had a hard time: a bedraggled cat after a storm. In everyday life: a bedraggled teddy, bedraggled flowers after rain.
