examples from the lessons: The kitten came in from the rain looking bedraggled. | After the storm, the garden flowers were bedraggled and bent. | The bedraggled hikers finally reached the hut. | The animals climbed out of the pool wet and bedraggled. | My old teddy is bedraggled but I still love him. | Toad arrived home bedraggled, muddy and very sorry for himself.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelled with double g and one l: «bedraggled» (be- + draggled). Used as an adjective.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The number of people or the amount of goods a boat can carry or is carrying. 2) (informal) A very large number or amount of something: «a boatload of homework».
its sense in the lessons: In history: boatloads of settlers, convicts or refugees crossing the sea. In maths problems: «Each boatload holds 12 people; how many boatloads for 60 people?» – a division problem, and you must round up if there is a remainder, because a part-full boat still has to make a trip. Informally it means «lots». Phrases: «a boatload of», «by the boatload».
examples from the lessons: A boatload of tourists arrived at the island. | The first boatloads of convicts reached Australia in 1788. | The ferry can take a boatload of 40 cars. | We got a boatload of presents for my birthday! | If each boatload holds 8 children, 30 children need 4 boatloads. | Fish were brought to the harbour by the boatload.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one boatload, two boatloads. Maths trap: 30 ÷ 8 = 3 remainder 6, so you need 4 boatloads, not 3. The informal «a boatload of» means «a lot of» and is not used in formal writing.

part of speech: noun (champagne – uncountable; a champagne, champagnes for kinds or glasses)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A sparkling (fizzy) white or pink wine made in the Champagne area of France, drunk at celebrations. 2) Loosely, any fizzy wine (though strictly only wine from Champagne may be called champagne). 3) A pale golden-cream colour.
its sense in the lessons: An adult drink with alcohol; children do not drink it. At weddings, New Year and big wins adults «pop the champagne» and make a toast. Racing drivers spray champagne after a win. In The Wind in the Willows Toad's grand life includes fine food and drink. In geography: Champagne is a region in north-east France. Phrases: «a glass of champagne», «pop the cork», «champagne lifestyle» (very rich living).
examples from the lessons: The grown-ups drank champagne at midnight on New Year's Eve. | The winner sprayed champagne over the crowd. | At the wedding, everyone raised a glass of champagne for a toast. | Champagne comes from a region of France with the same name. | We children had fizzy apple juice instead of champagne. | The bride's dress was a soft champagne colour.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It contains alcohol, which is not safe for children. Said «sham-PAYN» (from French, so «ch» sounds like «sh»). Usually uncountable. The region is written with a capital C: Champagne.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A tall wild plant with large hairy leaves and bell-shaped purple, pink or white flowers, growing in damp places by rivers and ditches. 2) The leaves or root of this plant, used in the past as a herbal medicine for bruises and broken bones, and by gardeners to feed the soil.
its sense in the lessons: A river-bank plant: in The Wind in the Willows the Mole and the Rat pass purple loosestrife, willow-herb and comfrey along the river, and the names paint a summer English bank. Gardeners make «comfrey tea» as plant food. Its old name «knitbone» came from the belief it helped bones heal. Safety: comfrey should not be eaten; it can harm the liver.
examples from the lessons: Comfrey grew thick along the edge of the stream. | Bees buzzed around the purple comfrey flowers. | Grandad soaks comfrey leaves in water to feed his tomatoes. | People once called comfrey «knitbone». | The Mole saw comfrey and willow-herb on the river bank. | Don't eat comfrey – it is not safe as food.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Said «KUM-free». Usually uncountable. Old herbal uses are history, not proven medicine; never eat wild plants without an adult who knows them.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A room with glass walls and a glass roof, built onto a house, where people sit in the sun and grow plants. 2) A large glass building in a park or garden for growing tender plants; a big greenhouse. 3) (also conservatoire) A school or college for training musicians, singers or actors.
its sense in the lessons: Many British, Irish and Australian homes have a conservatory at the back. In big old houses like Toad Hall a conservatory held palms, ferns and exotic flowers. In science, a conservatory works like a greenhouse: sunlight comes in through the glass and warms the air, which keeps plants growing. In the music sense: a gifted violinist may study at a conservatory.
examples from the lessons: We have breakfast in the conservatory when it's sunny. | The conservatory was full of orange trees and ferns. | It gets very hot in the conservatory in summer. | My piano teacher trained at a famous music conservatory. | The botanical gardens have a huge Victorian conservatory. | Dad grows chillies in the conservatory because it's warm there.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; plural «conservatories» (y → ies). Not the same as «conservative» or «conservation». In the USA the music sense is more common; in the UK the glass-room sense.

part of speech: adjective (consummate); verb (consummate, consummates, consummated, consummating – formal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (adjective, formal) Showing very great skill; perfect at something: «a consummate musician». 2) (adjective) Complete, total – used with a bad quality too: «a consummate liar». 3) (verb, formal) To complete or make perfect: «to consummate a deal».
its sense in the lessons: A grand word used in stories and reviews to praise great skill. In The Wind in the Willows Toad boasts of his own consummate cleverness when he escapes and tricks people. In exam writing it is a strong, formal word for «expert». The verb has a formal legal sense about marriage that is for adults; a pupil only needs «complete a deal».
examples from the lessons: She is a consummate artist who can draw anything. | The goalkeeper made the save with consummate ease. | Toad thought himself a consummate actor in his washerwoman disguise. | He was a consummate liar who fooled everybody. | The two companies consummated the deal last week. | The magician performed the trick with consummate skill.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Two pronunciations: the adjective is «kun-SUM-it» or «KON-suh-mit»; the verb is «KON-suh-mate». Formal; in everyday talk say «brilliant», «expert» or «total».

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a way that shows you are not sure about something, or do not quite believe it. 2) In a way that is uncertain or unlikely.
its sense in the lessons: Alice often speaks or looks «doubtfully» in Wonderland, because so many strange things are said to her. Stories use it to show a character is unsure without saying «I don't believe you»: «"Are you sure?" she asked doubtfully.» Often with «say», «look», «ask», «shake your head».
examples from the lessons: «Is this the right way?» asked Alice doubtfully. | Mum looked doubtfully at the burnt toast. | He doubtfully tasted the strange green soup. | «I suppose it might work,» she said doubtfully. | The Mole looked doubtfully at the wobbly boat. | The dog sniffed the new food doubtfully.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «doubt» + «-ful» + «-ly». The b in «doubt» is silent: «DOWT-ful-ee». Spelled with double l at the end.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Belonging to the time when Edward VII was king of the United Kingdom, from 1901 to 1910 (often stretched to 1914, before the First World War). 2) (noun) A person who lived in that time. 3) In a style typical of that time: clothes, houses, furniture.
its sense in the lessons: The Wind in the Willows (1908) is an Edwardian book: Toad's new motor cars, gramophones, picnics, steamers, gentlemen with servants and the gaol all belong to Edwardian England. In history lessons the Edwardian era follows the Victorian one. Edwardian houses often have bay windows and big gardens. Phrases: «Edwardian England», «the Edwardian era», «an Edwardian house».
examples from the lessons: Our school is in an old Edwardian building. | The Wind in the Willows was written in Edwardian times. | Edwardian ladies wore long dresses and huge hats. | The first cars appeared on Edwardian roads and scared horses. | We dressed up as Edwardians for history day. | The Edwardian era came after the Victorian era.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always a capital E because it comes from a name (Edward). The input is lower case only because of the word list. Do not confuse with «Elizabethan» or «Victorian».

meaning for a pupil: 1) All the plants that grow in a particular place or at a particular time. 2) The tiny living things, especially bacteria, that live in a part of the body: «gut flora». 3) (a name) Flora is a girl's name; Flora was also the Roman goddess of flowers.
its sense in the lessons: A science and geography word, often paired: «flora and fauna» means plants and animals of a place, like «the flora and fauna of Australia». In nature lessons we note the local flora on walks. Comes from Latin «flos», flower. In stories, Flora may be a girl's name.
examples from the lessons: The flora of the rainforest includes thousands of kinds of plants. | We studied the flora and fauna of the river bank. | Mountain flora must survive cold wind and snow. | The island has strange flora found nowhere else. | Healthy gut flora help you digest food. | Flora was the Roman goddess of flowers and spring.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable («the flora of Ireland»). Flora = plants; fauna = animals – an easy pair to mix up. As a name it takes a capital F.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Feeling that everything is spinning and you might fall; dizzy. 2) So happy and excited that you feel silly and cannot keep calm. 3) (old-fashioned) Silly and not serious: «a giddy girl». 4) Making you dizzy: «a giddy height».
its sense in the lessons: In Alice, after growing and shrinking, Alice feels giddy and confused; the word fits the dizzy world of Wonderland. In everyday life children feel giddy after spinning round or on a roundabout. Safety: if you feel giddy, sit down, so you do not fall; feeling giddy often can mean you need water, food or a doctor. Phrases: «giddy with excitement», «giddy heights», «My giddy aunt!» (old UK exclamation of surprise).
examples from the lessons: I felt giddy after spinning round and round. | We were giddy with excitement on the last day of school. | Looking down from the tower made me giddy. | «Being so many different sizes in a day is very confusing,» said Alice, feeling giddy. | Sit down if you feel giddy. | «My giddy aunt!» cried Gran when she saw the mess.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative «giddier», superlative «giddiest» (y → i). Close in meaning to «dizzy» but «giddy» can also mean happily excited.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An old weapon used from about the 1300s to the 1600s: a long wooden pole with an axe blade, a sharp spike on top and often a hook at the back. 2) Today a ceremonial weapon carried by some guards, for example the Swiss Guard at the Vatican.
its sense in the lessons: A history word for medieval and Tudor soldiers. In The Wind in the Willows, when Toad is sent to prison, he is led past guards and gaolers with halberds and pikes through a grim old castle to the dungeon – the old weapons make the scene feel ancient and frightening. A soldier with a halberd is a halberdier.
examples from the lessons: The guard at the castle gate held a long halberd. | The Swiss Guard still carry halberds at the Vatican. | Soldiers with halberds marched Toad down to the dungeon. | A halberd could chop, stab and hook a rider off his horse. | We saw a rusty halberd in the museum. | The knight ducked under the halberd's blade.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Said «HAL-berd». A weapon from the past; similar older weapons are the pike and the spear.

part of speech: noun (a hiccough, hiccoughs); verb (hiccough, hiccoughs, hiccoughed, hiccoughing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) An old spelling of «hiccup»: a sudden, sharp «hic» sound when a muscle under your lungs (the diaphragm) jerks and makes you breathe in. 2) (hiccoughs / hiccups) A short spell of these sounds one after another. 3) A small problem or delay: «a hiccough in our plans».
its sense in the lessons: The spelling «hiccough» is found in older books; today most people write «hiccup». In science, hiccups come from the diaphragm tightening suddenly; they usually stop by themselves. Myths say a fright cures them – not proven. Phrases: «have (the) hiccups», «a slight hiccough».
examples from the lessons: I got hiccoughs after drinking my fizzy drink too fast. | He hiccoughed all through the school assembly. | The old book spells hiccup as «hiccough». | My little brother tried to scare away my hiccoughs. | There was a small hiccough with the bus, but we arrived on time. | Hiccoughs happen when your diaphragm jerks.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: «hiccough» is said exactly like «hiccup» («HIK-up»), not like «cough». Prefer «hiccup» in your own writing. Plural: hiccoughs/hiccups.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (old-fashioned) To here; to this place: «Come hither» means «come here». 2) In the phrase «hither and thither» (or «hither and yon»): here and there, in many directions.
its sense in the lessons: An old word from fairy tales, the Bible and old stories, still alive in the phrase «hither and thither» – running about in all directions. The pair: hither (to here), thither (to there), whither (to where?). It makes speech sound old or grand, as in old-fashioned stories.
examples from the lessons: «Come hither, child,» said the old king. | The ants ran hither and thither when we lifted the stone. | Leaves blew hither and thither in the wind. | The servants hurried hither and thither preparing the feast. | «Bring the lantern hither!» called the captain. | The puppy dashed hither and thither around the garden.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Old-fashioned: in everyday speech say «here». Hither = to here, thither = to there, whither = to where. Do not confuse «whither» with «wither» (to dry up and die).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Rude and not showing proper respect, especially to an older person or someone in charge; cheeky. 2) (formal, old) Not relevant to what is being talked about.
its sense in the lessons: Grown-ups in Alice's Adventures in Wonderland often call Alice impertinent, and she calls the Hatter's remarks impertinent too: «"You shouldn't make personal remarks," Alice said; "it's very rude."» In old school stories teachers punish impertinent pupils. Today we would say «cheeky» or «rude». Phrases: «an impertinent question», «don't be impertinent».
examples from the lessons: «Don't be impertinent!» said the teacher. | It was impertinent to ask the old lady how old she was. | The Queen thought Alice was impertinent. | The impertinent parrot copied everything the captain said. | Asking how much money someone earns can be an impertinent question. | The boy gave an impertinent reply and was sent out.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Not the opposite of «pertinent» in everyday use: it mostly means «rude», not «irrelevant». Noun: impertinence. Close words: cheeky, rude, insolent.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Full of joy; very happy. 2) Causing great joy: «a joyous occasion».
its sense in the lessons: A warm, slightly literary word: stories, hymns and carols speak of joyous bells, joyous news, a joyous homecoming. In The Wind in the Willows there are joyous feasts and the joyous return of Toad Hall. In church, Christmas and Easter are joyous festivals. In writing it is stronger than «happy».
examples from the lessons: The joyous crowd cheered as the team came home. | Christmas bells rang out with a joyous sound. | It was a joyous day when our new baby sister came home. | The animals held a joyous banquet at Toad Hall. | The children sang a joyous song at the end of term. | Easter is a joyous festival for Christians.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Close to «joyful»; both are fine. Adverb: joyously. Not used about people's personality as much as «cheerful».

part of speech: noun (a koodoo, koodoos – Kipling's spelling of «kudu»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Kipling's spelling of kudu: a large African antelope; the male has long spiral (twisted) horns, and both have thin white stripes on a grey-brown body. 2) There are two kinds, the greater kudu and the lesser kudu.
its sense in the lessons: In the Just So Stories («How the Leopard Got His Spots») the Giraffe, the Zebra, the Eland and the Koodoo live on the sandy-yellow High Veldt and later hide in the stripy, blotchy shadows of the forest, and Kipling's spelling is «Koodoo». The true reason for their stripes is camouflage that helps them hide from predators, built over a long time by evolution, not a story. Today we write «kudu».
examples from the lessons: The koodoo hid among the stripy shadows of the forest. | A kudu has long twisted horns. | We saw a greater kudu at the safari park. | Kipling spelled kudu as «koodoo». | The kudu's thin white stripes help it hide among trees. | Lions and leopards hunt kudu in Africa.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Modern spelling is «kudu» («KOO-doo»); «koodoo» is old. Plural: kudus or kudu (same as singular).

part of speech: noun (a kris, krises; also «keris», «creese»); proper noun (Kris – a name)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A short dagger from Malaysia, Indonesia and nearby lands, often with a wavy blade, a traditional weapon and a work of art passed down in families. 2) (a name) Kris is a short form of names like Kristopher, Kristina or Kristen.
its sense in the lessons: In history and culture lessons on Southeast Asia, the kris is a treasured object, made by skilled smiths with patterned metal and carved handles; the Indonesian kris is on UNESCO's list of the world's intangible cultural heritage. In old adventure stories pirates and warriors carry krises. As a name, Kris is just a person's name.
examples from the lessons: The museum showed a kris with a wavy blade and a gold handle. | In Java, a family kris is passed from parents to children. | The smith folded the metal many times to make the kris. | My friend Kris is in my class. | The warrior in the old story carried a kris in his belt. | A kris is a dagger, not a toy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: plural «krises». Also spelled «keris» (Malay/Indonesian) and «creese» (old English). As a name it has a capital K. Not related to «Kris Kringle» (an American name for Santa Claus) except for the sound.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Moving slowly and lazily, without energy, often in a pleasant, relaxed way. 2) Weak and tired, without any wish to do things, maybe from heat or illness. 3) (of weather, days) Slow, warm and calm: «a languid summer afternoon».
its sense in the lessons: Story writers use «languid» for lazy summer scenes and for elegant, bored people. In The Wind in the Willows the summer river and lazy afternoons have a languid feel. A languid wave of the hand shows someone cannot be bothered. Opposite: energetic, brisk, lively.
examples from the lessons: The cat stretched in a languid way on the warm wall. | It was a languid summer afternoon, and nobody wanted to move. | She gave a languid wave from her deckchair. | The heat made everyone feel languid. | The river flowed slow and languid between the willows. | The bored prince spoke in a languid voice.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Said «LANG-gwid». Adverb: languidly. Related words: languish (become weak), languor (pleasant tiredness).

part of speech: noun (a mastermind, masterminds); verb (mastermind, masterminds, masterminded, masterminding)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A very clever person who plans something difficult, especially the person who plans a crime or a big scheme. 2) (verb) To plan and organise something difficult and clever. 3) (UK) Mastermind is a famous TV quiz show with a black chair.
its sense in the lessons: In detective stories the villain is often a criminal mastermind; heroes may mastermind a rescue. In The Wind in the Willows the Badger masterminds the plan to win back Toad Hall from the stoats and weasels through the secret tunnel. In school we may call a top quiz player «a mastermind».
examples from the lessons: The detective finally caught the mastermind behind the robbery. | Badger masterminded the attack on Toad Hall. | My sister masterminded a surprise party for Mum. | Who is the mastermind behind this clever trick? | She is a maths mastermind. | The mastermind of the plan stayed hidden in the shadows.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun; the verb is regular (masterminded). Often used about bad plans (crimes), but can be positive too.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (of hair) A dull light brown colour, like a mouse. 2) (of a person) Quiet, shy and not easily noticed. 3) Like a mouse or smelling of mice.
its sense in the lessons: Used in stories to describe looks and character: «a mousy little man». In Alice there are many mice; a «mousy» smell can mean mice live in a place. It can sound unkind when said about someone's hair or character, so be careful using it about real people.
examples from the lessons: She had mousy brown hair tied in a ponytail. | The new boy was mousy and hardly spoke. | The old shed had a mousy smell. | A mousy little clerk sat behind the desk. | Don't call people mousy – it can hurt their feelings. | The mousy kitten hid under the sofa.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Both «mousy» and «mousey» are correct. Comparative: mousier, mousiest. Can be unkind about a person.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A long, thin boat made to travel on the narrow canals of Britain, usually about 2 metres wide and up to 22 metres long. 2) Such a boat used as a floating home or for holidays.
its sense in the lessons: In history, narrowboats pulled by horses walking along the towpath carried coal and goods on canals in the 1700s and 1800s; families lived in a tiny cabin at the back, painted with roses and castles. In The Wind in the Willows Toad meets a barge-woman on the canal with her horse. Today many people live on narrowboats or hire them for holidays. Safety: canals have locks and deep water.
examples from the lessons: We spent a week on a narrowboat on the canal. | A horse once pulled the narrowboat along the towpath. | The narrowboat was painted with roses and castles. | My uncle lives on a narrowboat in London. | The narrowboat went slowly through the lock. | Narrowboats are only about two metres wide.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Written as one word or two («narrow boat»). Mostly a British word. Not the same as a barge, which is usually wider.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A puzzle in which pictures, letters, numbers or symbols stand for words or parts of words: a picture of an eye + a heart + a ewe = «I love you». 2) A coat of arms or design whose picture is a pun on a family's name.
its sense in the lessons: Rebuses are popular word puzzles in school and in puzzle books; they train thinking about sounds. «2 B or not 2 B». Lewis Carroll and Kipling loved word games; rebuses are a cousin of their puns. In history, early writing used rebus ideas: a picture for a sound helped turn pictures into letters.
examples from the lessons: Can you solve this rebus: a picture of a bee and a leaf means «belief»? | We made our own rebus puzzles in class. | «I C U» is a simple rebus. | The family's coat of arms was a rebus on their name. | Early writing used the rebus idea to spell sounds. | The rebus puzzle had a picture of a sun and a flower: sunflower.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: rebuses. Said «REE-bus». From Latin «rebus», «by things».

part of speech: noun (a rifle, rifles); verb (rifle, rifles, rifled, rifling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A long gun fired from the shoulder, with spiral grooves inside the barrel so the bullet spins and flies straight. 2) (verb) To search quickly and roughly through something, often to steal: «The burglar rifled through the drawers.» 3) (verb, sport) To hit or kick a ball very hard and straight: «He rifled the ball into the net.»
its sense in the lessons: Soldiers, hunters and farmers use rifles; in history the rifle changed wars. In stories, «rifled through» shows someone searching messily or secretly. Safety: real guns are never toys; if you find one, do not touch it, leave and tell an adult. In football or cricket reports, «rifled» means hit hard.
examples from the lessons: The soldier carried a rifle on his shoulder. | Someone had rifled through my schoolbag. | She rifled through the cupboard looking for her shoes. | The striker rifled the ball into the top corner. | Farmers in Australia may use a rifle to protect sheep from foxes. | Never touch a rifle or any gun; tell an adult straight away.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The noun is countable. «Rifle» (search) and «rifle» (gun) are the same spelling with different meanings. Do not confuse with «riffle» (to flick through pages quickly).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (adjective) Working or travelling on the sea; living by the sea and sailing: «a seafaring nation». 2) (noun) The life or work of sailors; travel by sea.
its sense in the lessons: In The Wind in the Willows the Sea Rat is a seafaring rat who tells the Water Rat wonderful tales of ports in Constantinople, Italy and Marseilles and almost tempts him to leave the river for a seafaring life. In history: the Vikings and Polynesians were great seafaring peoples. A seafarer is a sailor.
examples from the lessons: The Vikings were a seafaring people. | The Sea Rat told tales of his seafaring life. | Polynesian seafaring was so skilled they found islands across the Pacific. | My great-grandad came from a seafaring family. | Seafaring was hard and dangerous in old times. | The town has a long seafaring history.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective and noun with the same form. Related: seafarer (a sailor). Not a verb – we don't say «to seafare».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A tendon: a tough cord in the body that joins a muscle to a bone. 2) (sinews, literary) Strength or power: «the sinews of war» (money and supplies needed for war).
its sense in the lessons: In science, tendons (sinews) let muscles pull on bones so we can move; the Achilles tendon is at the back of the heel. Stories describe strong people with «muscle and sinew». In history, people used animal sinew as thread and bowstrings. Phrases: «strain every sinew» (try as hard as you possibly can).
examples from the lessons: The sinew joins the muscle to the bone. | He strained every sinew to win the race. | Native peoples used animal sinew to sew clothes. | The meat was tough and full of sinew. | The athlete's arms were all muscle and sinew. | The bowstring was made of twisted sinew.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Said «SIN-yoo». Adjective: sinewy (lean and strong). «Tendon» is the science word today.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A state like being half asleep or dreaming, when you are awake but do not notice what is around you. 2) A state when someone is deeply lost in thought, music or wonder and does not hear you. 3) (also trance music) A kind of fast electronic dance music.
its sense in the lessons: In The Wind in the Willows («The Piper at the Gates of Dawn») the Rat and the Mole hear wonderful piping and fall into a kind of trance of awe before the god Pan; then they forget it. In stories hypnotists and magicians put people «into a trance». In everyday life we say «He's in a trance» about someone daydreaming. Phrases: «in a trance», «fall into a trance».
examples from the lessons: She stared at the fire as if in a trance. | The music put the animals into a kind of trance. | «Wake up! You're in a trance!» laughed my friend. | The hypnotist claimed he could put people in a trance. | The Rat walked on in a trance, listening to the distant piping. | My brother watches cartoons like he's in a trance.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Related: entrance (verb «en-TRANCE» = to fill with wonder) is spelled like «entrance» (a way in) but said differently.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A large wheel turned by people or animals walking on steps or boards inside or around it, used in the past to grind corn or pump water. 2) A punishment in Victorian prisons where prisoners had to walk on such a wheel for hours. 3) (figurative, like «treadmill») Boring, tiring work that never seems to end.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons about old prisons, the treadwheel was hard labour for convicts from 1818 into the late 1800s: prisoners climbed endless steps, often doing no useful work. In The Wind in the Willows Toad fears hard punishment in gaol. Today «treadmill» is a running machine in a gym, and «a treadmill» also means dull, endless routine.
examples from the lessons: Prisoners in Victorian gaols had to walk on the treadwheel for hours. | The treadwheel turned the millstones to grind corn. | A donkey walked inside the treadwheel to lift water from the well. | Working in that factory felt like being on a treadwheel. | We saw a picture of an old prison treadwheel in our history book. | The treadwheel was a cruel and pointless punishment.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Close to «treadmill»; «treadmill» is the usual modern word (and also a gym machine). From «tread» = to step.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Belonging to a tribe – a group of families or communities who share ancestors, language, customs and often land, with their own leaders. 2) Showing strong loyalty to your own group and dislike of others: «tribal football fans».
its sense in the lessons: In history and geography lessons we learn about tribal peoples in Africa, the Americas, Asia and the Pacific; many Native American nations and Aboriginal and Māori groups prefer their own names («nation», «iwi», «mob»). «Tribal» can be used respectfully about traditions, but old books sometimes used it in a looking-down way, which is wrong. Phrases: «tribal lands», «tribal art», «tribal leaders».
examples from the lessons: The museum showed tribal art from many parts of Africa. | Tribal elders met to decide what to do. | Many tribal lands were taken by settlers in the past. | Football fans can be very tribal about their team. | The tribal dance told the story of the first people. | Māori groups called iwi have their own lands and leaders.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective only; the noun is «tribe». Be respectful: call peoples by their own names when you can, and avoid using «tribal» to mean «primitive» – that idea is wrong.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A large deep bowl with a lid, from which soup is served at the table. 2) A similar dish for serving vegetables or sauce.
its sense in the lessons: In Alice's Adventures in Wonderland the Mock Turtle sings «Beautiful Soup, so rich and green, / Waiting in a hot tureen!» – a funny song because mock turtle soup was a real Victorian dish. In grand houses and old stories, the soup tureen is carried in by a servant at a feast. Phrases: «a soup tureen».
examples from the lessons: The waiter carried a steaming tureen of soup to the table. | «Beautiful Soup, so rich and green, waiting in a hot tureen!» | Gran's best china tureen is only used at Christmas. | Lift the lid of the tureen carefully – it's hot. | The giant poured soup from the tureen into his bowl. | The tureen was painted with blue flowers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Said «tyoo-REEN» or «tuh-REEN». Not the same as «terrine» (a dish of pressed food), though they come from the same French word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (proper noun) One of the four historic provinces of Ireland, in the north; it has nine counties – six are in Northern Ireland (part of the UK) and three in the Republic of Ireland. 2) (noun, old-fashioned) A long, loose, heavy overcoat, often with a belt and a short cape, worn in Victorian and Edwardian times.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and history: Ireland's provinces are Ulster, Munster, Leinster and Connacht; people sometimes say «Ulster» to mean Northern Ireland, though that is not exact. In The Wind in the Willows Toad, as a motorist, dresses in the grand clothes of early drivers – goggles, cap, gaiters and an enormous overcoat – the kind of coat called an ulster. Phrases: «Ulster rugby», «the province of Ulster».
examples from the lessons: Donegal is part of Ulster but is in the Republic of Ireland. | Ulster is one of the four provinces of Ireland. | The traveller buttoned his heavy ulster against the wind. | Ulster Rugby play in Belfast. | Victorian gentlemen wore long ulsters in winter. | Six of Ulster's nine counties are in Northern Ireland.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The place has a capital U: Ulster. The coat is written lower case: an ulster. Ulster and Northern Ireland are not exactly the same; it is a sensitive topic for some people, so use names carefully.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To undo the laces of something, such as shoes, boots or a corset. 2) To loosen or open something by pulling out its laces.
its sense in the lessons: An everyday word: we unlace our boots after a muddy walk. In old stories, ladies' dresses and corsets were laced up tightly, and fainting characters had their stays unlaced. Phrases: «unlace your shoes/boots».
examples from the lessons: Unlace your football boots before you take them off. | She unlaced her skates and rubbed her cold feet. | The soldier sat down and unlaced his heavy boots. | My little brother can lace his shoes but not unlace the knots. | Toad unlaced his gaiters in front of the fire. | Unlacing wet boots is hard when your fingers are cold.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: unlaced, unlacing (drop the e before -ing). «Un-» means undoing: lace → unlace, tie → untie.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Great courage, especially in battle or danger. 2) (old) Worth or bravery shown in brave deeds.
its sense in the lessons: A grand old word found in stories about knights and heroes, and in war history: medals «for valour», like the Victoria Cross, which says «For Valour». In The Wind in the Willows the animals fight bravely to win back Toad Hall, and Toad boasts of his valour afterwards. Phrases: «acts of valour», «for valour», «discretion is the better part of valour» (it is wiser to be careful than to be brave in a foolish way – from Shakespeare's Falstaff).
examples from the lessons: The Victoria Cross is awarded «For Valour». | The knight was famous for his valour. | The firefighters showed great valour in saving the family. | «Discretion is the better part of valour,» said the Rat, and they ran away. | Many soldiers won medals for valour in the war. | Songs were sung about her valour.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK, Ireland, Australia, NZ, Canada spelling: valour; USA: valor. Uncountable. Adjective: valiant.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A position that gives you a good view or an advantage: «a vantage point» is a high or good place to watch from. 2) (formal) Advantage. 3) (tennis, old UK) Advantage after deuce.
its sense in the lessons: In geography fieldwork we choose a vantage point to draw a landscape. In stories a scout climbs to a vantage point to see the enemy coming; the Badger and the Mole spy on the weasels from a good vantage point. Phrases: «vantage point», «from this vantage».
examples from the lessons: From our vantage point on the hill we could see the whole town. | The owl watched from a vantage point in the oak tree. | Let's find a good vantage point to watch the parade. | From her vantage at the window, she saw everything. | The spy chose a vantage point behind the wall. | We climbed the tower for the best vantage point.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly used in «vantage point». Same root as «advantage». Uncountable in the formal sense.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Liking to try new, exciting and sometimes risky things; brave and curious. 2) Full of excitement and danger: «an adventurous journey». 3) New and bold, not the usual: «an adventurous menu».
its sense in the lessons: In The Wind in the Willows the shy Mole becomes adventurous when he leaves his spring-cleaning and goes to the river; Toad is too adventurous and gets into trouble. Alice is adventurous when she follows the White Rabbit. In everyday life: «Be adventurous – try a new food!» Safety: being adventurous is good, but think about danger and tell an adult where you are going.
examples from the lessons: The adventurous girl climbed to the top of the hill. | Mole felt adventurous and set off to see the river. | We had an adventurous holiday camping in the mountains. | Be adventurous and try the curry! | The explorers made an adventurous trip across the ice. | Toad was adventurous, but also very foolish.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «adventure» + «-ous». Opposite: cautious, timid. Adverb: adventurously.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A strong feeling of dislike for someone or something. 2) Something that a person strongly dislikes.
its sense in the lessons: A formal word. In Alice's Adventures in Wonderland, falling down the rabbit hole, Alice wonders if she will come out among «the Antipathies» – she means the Antipodes (people on the other side of the Earth, like Australia and New Zealand), and Carroll makes a joke by mixing up the two long words. In exam writing «antipathy» is a strong word for dislike. Phrases: «antipathy towards/to».
examples from the lessons: The cat has a deep antipathy towards the dog next door. | Alice thought she might come out among «the Antipathies». | There was a long antipathy between the two families. | I have an antipathy to cold porridge. | The Badger had a great antipathy to society and parties. | Her antipathy to spiders began when she was little.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Said «an-TIP-uh-thee». Plural: antipathies. Opposite: sympathy. Do not mix up with «antipodes» (places on the opposite side of the Earth), which is Alice's joke.

part of speech: noun (backsliding – uncountable); verb form (of «backslide»: backslide, backslides, backslid, backsliding)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Going back to bad old habits after you had been doing better. 2) (church) Falling away from faith or from living as a Christian after having been committed.
its sense in the lessons: In church language, a «backslider» is someone who has turned away from faith; preachers in the 1800s used the word often. In everyday life it means slipping back: after New Year's resolutions, backsliding into eating too many sweets. In The Wind in the Willows Toad promises to be good, then backslides as soon as he sees a motor car.
examples from the lessons: After a week of early nights, there was some backsliding at the weekend. | The preacher warned the people against backsliding. | Toad promised to change, but his backsliding began at once. | We must stop backsliding into old bad habits. | Christians believe God forgives the backsliding person who comes back. | My diet lasted two days before the backsliding started.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable as a noun. Verb past: «backslid». A person is «a backslider».

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a beautiful way; in a way that is very pleasant to see or hear. 2) Very well; with great skill: «She played beautifully.» 3) Perfectly, completely: «It worked beautifully.»
its sense in the lessons: A common praise word in school: «You've written that beautifully», «beautifully presented work». In stories: «The bird sang beautifully.» It can describe the way something is done, not just how it looks.
examples from the lessons: She sings beautifully. | Your handwriting is beautifully neat. | The garden was beautifully kept. | The plan worked beautifully. | The table was beautifully laid for the feast. | The sun set beautifully over the sea.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: beautiful + ly = «beautifully» with double l. The tricky vowels: b-e-a-u.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Painful, itchy red or purple swellings on the toes, fingers, ears or nose, caused when skin gets very cold and then warms up too fast. 2) A common winter complaint in old times, when houses were cold.
its sense in the lessons: In old stories children with chilblains sit by the fire in winter. In science, cold makes small blood vessels narrow; warming too quickly makes them swell and leak, causing chilblains. Safety and health: keep feet and hands warm and dry, wear socks and gloves, warm up slowly – not with your feet right on a heater. They usually heal on their own.
examples from the lessons: In the cold farmhouse, the children had chilblains on their toes. | Wear thick socks so you don't get chilblains. | Gran's chilblains itch every winter. | Don't warm cold feet too quickly by the fire, or you may get chilblains. | My fingers were swollen with chilblains after building the snowman. | Chilblains were common when houses had no heating.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually plural. Said «CHIL-blaynz». Not the same as frostbite, which is more serious freezing of the skin.

part of speech: noun (coaxing – uncountable); adjective (coaxing); verb form (of «coax»: coax, coaxes, coaxed, coaxing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Gently persuading someone to do something by being kind, patient and pleasant. 2) (adjective) Gentle and persuading: «a coaxing voice». 3) Getting something to work or move by careful, gentle handling: «coaxing a fire to light».
its sense in the lessons: In stories, characters coax shy animals out of hiding, or coax a friend to come along; the Rat coaxes the homesick Mole and the Badger coaxes Toad to give up cars. In everyday life: coaxing a cat out from under the bed with treats. Phrases: «with a bit of coaxing», «coax someone into/out of».
examples from the lessons: After a lot of coaxing, the kitten came out from under the sofa. | She spoke in a coaxing voice. | The Rat was coaxing the Mole to tell his trouble. | It took some coaxing to get my brother into the cold sea. | Dad was coaxing the old car to start. | With gentle coaxing, the shy pupil read her poem aloud.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Said «KOH-ksing». «Coax» rhymes with «hoax». Coaxing is gentle; forcing or bullying is not coaxing.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A large sea eel with grey or black skin, living in rocky places and wrecks in the sea around Europe and elsewhere; it can grow longer than a tall man. 2) Its flesh as food.
its sense in the lessons: In Alice's Adventures in Wonderland the Mock Turtle's teacher at the school in the sea was «an old conger-eel» who taught «Drawling, Stretching and Fainting in Coils» – Carroll's jokes on Drawing, Sketching and Painting in Oils. In nature lessons: congers are fish, not snakes; they hide in holes and come out at night to hunt. Safety: congers can bite hard.
examples from the lessons: A huge conger lived in the old shipwreck. | The divers saw a conger eel peeping from a hole in the rock. | The Mock Turtle's drawling-master was an old conger-eel. | Fishermen caught a conger as long as the boat. | A conger is a fish, not a snake. | Congers come out at night to hunt.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Said «KONG-ger». Usually called a «conger eel».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A small water bird, also called the little grebe, which dives under water to catch small fish and insects and often swims with only its head showing. 2) Old name used for some other small grebes.
its sense in the lessons: A river-bank bird: in The Wind in the Willows the river is busy with water birds, and a dabchick is one of the shy small divers the Rat would know. In nature lessons: grebes have lobed (not webbed) toes and build floating nests. It dives so quickly it seems to vanish.
examples from the lessons: A dabchick bobbed up near the reeds and dived again. | The little grebe is often called a dabchick. | Dabchicks build floating nests of weed. | We watched a dabchick diving for tiny fish. | The dabchick vanished under the water in a flash. | Two dabchicks trilled loudly on the pond.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Old country name; birdwatchers today say «little grebe».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A small valley or hollow, usually with trees and grass around it. 2) (a name) Dell is also a family name and a computer company name.
its sense in the lessons: A word from stories, poems and nursery rhymes: «The farmer's in his dell» (a playground singing game). Fairy tales put fairies and picnics in a woodland dell. In The Wind in the Willows the woods and river bank have hidden hollows and dells. It tells the reader of a quiet, sheltered, pretty place.
examples from the lessons: We had a picnic in a shady dell. | «The farmer's in his dell» is an old singing game. | Bluebells covered the floor of the dell. | The fox had a den in a hidden dell. | A little stream ran through the dell. | Children played in the dell until sunset.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Mostly in stories and poems; a «valley» is bigger.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (old-fashioned, unkind) A person who is slow to learn or thought to be stupid, especially a pupil. 2) In «dunce's cap» (dunce cap): a tall paper cone hat that pupils in old schools were made to wear as a punishment.
its sense in the lessons: In old school stories a pupil who got answers wrong was made to sit in the corner in a dunce's cap. Today this is seen as cruel; everyone learns at a different speed, and calling someone a dunce is unkind. Fun fact: the word comes from John Duns Scotus, a clever medieval thinker whose followers were later mocked as «Dunsmen».
examples from the lessons: In the old school, the dunce had to sit in the corner. | The teacher made him wear a dunce's cap. | Calling someone a dunce is unkind. | Toad acted like a dunce, but he thought he was clever. | «I'm such a dunce at maths!» she laughed – but she was wrong. | Today no teacher uses a dunce's cap.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. An insult; avoid using it about people. Rhymes with «once».

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a way that shows you really want to do or have something and are excited about it. 2) Keenly and with much interest: «We listened eagerly.»
its sense in the lessons: Stories use «eagerly» to show excitement: «She eagerly opened the present.» Alice eagerly follows the White Rabbit; the Mole eagerly learns about boats. Common phrases: «eagerly awaited», «eagerly waiting», «nodded eagerly».
examples from the lessons: The children eagerly waited for the bell. | The puppy eagerly wagged its tail. | Alice ran eagerly after the White Rabbit. | We eagerly opened the box of new books. | The film was eagerly awaited. | «Can I come?» asked the Mole eagerly.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «eager» + «-ly». Do not confuse «eagerly» (excitedly) with «anxiously» (worriedly).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Short for «Esquire»: a polite title written after a man's name, mostly in letters, in old-fashioned British style: «John Smith, Esq.». 2) (USA) Used after the name of a lawyer (man or woman).
its sense in the lessons: In The Wind in the Willows Toad is a gentleman, and letters would be addressed to «Toad, Esq., Toad Hall». In history, an esquire was a young man who served a knight (a squire), then a gentleman just below a knight. You write «Esq.» instead of «Mr», never both.
examples from the lessons: The letter was addressed to «Mr Toad, Esq.» – which is wrong, because you don't use both! | Write «James Brown, Esq.» on an old-style letter. | In the USA, «Esq.» after a name often means the person is a lawyer. | An esquire once carried a knight's shield. | The invitation said «Henry Wood, Esq.» | Old envelopes often show «Esq.» after a man's name.
note for the reader of a maths problem: It is an abbreviation, not a word you say; written with a capital E and often a full stop: «Esq.». Rule: «Mr John Smith» or «John Smith, Esq.», not both.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Foolishness; a very silly or unwise act or idea. 2) A strange decorative building, like a fake ruin or a tower, built in a big park or garden just for show. 3) (follies, plural) A show with dancing, songs and jokes (old theatre word).
its sense in the lessons: In The Wind in the Willows the Badger and Rat try to save Toad from his folly with motor cars. In stories, «the folly of greed» is a lesson. On country walks in Britain and Ireland you may see a folly tower on a hill. Phrases: «sheer folly», «the height of folly», «it would be folly to…».
examples from the lessons: It would be folly to swim in the sea during a storm. | Toad's folly with cars cost him a fortune. | There is a stone folly at the top of the hill. | Running away was sheer folly. | The rich lord built a folly that looked like a castle ruin. | Grandad says buying that old boat was his greatest folly.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: follies. Uncountable in the meaning «foolishness». Related word: fool, foolish.

part of speech: verb (frolic, frolics, frolicked, frolicking); noun (a frolic, frolics)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To play and run about in a happy, lively way. 2) (noun) Lively, happy play or a fun time.
its sense in the lessons: Used for young animals and children: lambs frolic in spring fields, puppies frolic on the beach. In The Wind in the Willows the animals frolic in the summer river. In stories, frolic shows carefree joy.
examples from the lessons: The lambs frolicked in the spring sunshine. | Puppies were frolicking on the sand. | The otters frolicked in the river. | After school we had a frolic in the snow. | Children frolicked in the paddling pool. | The kittens frolicked with a ball of wool.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: add a k before -ed and -ing: frolicked, frolicking (not «frolicing»). Same rule: picnic → picnicked, panic → panicked.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Smelling stale, damp and old, like a room shut up for a long time. 2) Old-fashioned and dull in ideas: «fusty old rules».
its sense in the lessons: Stories use «fusty» for attics, old libraries, cellars and closed-up houses; Mole's little home, shut all winter, might smell fusty when he returns. In everyday life: «Open the window, it's fusty in here!» Close words: musty, stuffy.
examples from the lessons: The old attic smelled fusty. | Open a window – it's fusty in here. | We found fusty old books in a trunk. | The museum was full of fusty glass cases. | The school had some fusty old rules nobody followed. | His coat smelled fusty after a year in the cupboard.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative: fustier, fustiest. Close in meaning to «musty».

part of speech: noun (a garibaldi, garibaldis); proper noun (Garibaldi – a name)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (UK) A flat rectangular biscuit with a layer of squashed currants inside, sometimes called a «squashed fly biscuit». 2) (a name) Giuseppe Garibaldi (1807–1882), an Italian general who fought to unite Italy; he was a hero in Victorian Britain. 3) A red blouse like the red shirts worn by his soldiers (old fashion).
its sense in the lessons: In The Wind in the Willows, the Rat looks at Mole's little home with its plaster statues of «Garibaldi, and the infant Samuel, and Queen Victoria» – popular ornaments in Victorian and Edwardian homes. In history lessons, Garibaldi and his «Redshirts» helped make Italy one country. The biscuit was named after him.
examples from the lessons: Can I have a garibaldi with my tea? | Children call garibaldis «squashed fly biscuits». | Mole's home had a statue of Garibaldi. | Garibaldi led his Redshirts to unite Italy. | The garibaldi biscuit is full of currants. | Many British streets and pubs are named after Garibaldi.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The biscuit is usually written lower case; the man's name has a capital G. Garibaldi is a real person – nothing invented about him here.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A thick glove with a long wide cuff covering the wrist, worn for work, riding or motoring. 2) A metal glove that was part of a knight's armour. 3) In phrases: «throw down the gauntlet» – challenge someone; «take up the gauntlet» – accept a challenge; «run the gauntlet» – face attacks or criticism from many people one after another.
its sense in the lessons: In The Wind in the Willows Toad's motoring outfit includes goggles, cap and gauntlets – early drivers wore them against cold and dirt. Knights threw down a gauntlet to challenge an enemy to a fight. «Run the gauntlet» comes from an old punishment of running between two rows of people hitting you. In science and safety: welders and gardeners wear gauntlets to protect their hands.
examples from the lessons: Toad pulled on his driving gauntlets and goggles. | The knight threw down his gauntlet as a challenge. | Wear gauntlets when you cut thorny roses. | Our teacher threw down the gauntlet: who could finish the puzzle first? | The new pupil had to run the gauntlet of questions in the playground. | The welder wore thick leather gauntlets.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Plural: gauntlets. Not the same as «gaunt» (very thin).

part of speech: adjective (gay, gayer, gayest); noun (a gay person – usually «gay people»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Describing a person, especially a man, who is romantically attracted to people of the same sex; women may also call themselves gay or lesbian. This is the usual meaning today and a respectful word. 2) (old-fashioned) Happy, merry and full of fun: «a gay laugh». 3) (old-fashioned) Bright and colourful: «gay flags». 4) (rude, offensive) Used by some as an insult meaning «bad» or «stupid» – this is hurtful and wrong.
its sense in the lessons: In old books like The Wind in the Willows and Alice, «gay» means merry and bright: Toad sings gay songs, and the river is gay with flowers; this is not about love. Today in everyday life the first meaning is the usual one: some families have two dads or two mums; gay people should be treated with respect. Saying «that's so gay» to mean «rubbish» is bullying language and schools stop it.
examples from the lessons: My uncle is gay and lives with his husband. | Some of my friends have two mums. | In the old song, the girls were «gay and bright». | The town was gay with flags for the festival. | Toad sang a gay little song as he drove along. | Using «gay» as an insult is unkind and not allowed in our school.
note for the reader of a maths problem: In books written before about 1960, «gay» usually means «merry» or «bright». Today it nearly always means sense 1. Never use it as an insult. Related word: LGBT.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Not paying attention to something, especially to a warning or danger; careless. 2) In «heedless of»: without thinking about: «heedless of the danger».
its sense in the lessons: In The Wind in the Willows Toad is heedless of his friends' warnings and drives too fast. Stories show heedless characters getting into trouble. Safety: being heedless near roads, water or fire is dangerous. Phrases: «heedless of the danger/warning», «heedless rush».
examples from the lessons: Heedless of the warning, Toad jumped into the car. | The boy ran heedless across the busy road. | She was heedless of the rain and kept playing. | Heedless spending soon emptied his piggy bank. | The puppy dashed heedless into the river. | Don't be heedless near the cliff edge.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «heed» (attention) + «-less» (without). Adverb: heedlessly. Opposite: heedful, careful.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal, old-fashioned) From now on; from this time into the future.
its sense in the lessons: A grand word for promises and announcements. In The Wind in the Willows, at the banquet, a changed Toad promises his friends to be modest: henceforward he will be a different Toad. In laws and old documents, «henceforth» starts a new rule. In everyday life we say «from now on».
examples from the lessons: Henceforward, all pupils must wear a hat outside. | «Henceforward I shall be a quiet and humble Toad!» he promised. | Henceforward the castle belonged to the young king. | Henceforth, the meeting will be on Mondays. | Henceforward we shall help each other. | The king declared that henceforward there would be no taxes on bread.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; in speech use «from now on». Same as «henceforth». Written as one word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A small furry plant-eating mammal of Africa and the Middle East, looking like a big guinea pig or rabbit without long ears; it lives among rocks or in trees. 2) Also called the «rock hyrax», «dassie» (South Africa) or «coney» (in the Bible).
its sense in the lessons: A science surprise: although it looks like a rodent, the hyrax's closest living relatives are elephants and sea cows – zoology shows this from its teeth, feet and DNA. In the Bible the «coneys» are called «a feeble folk» who make their homes in the rocks (Proverbs 30). Kipling's Just So Stories are set among African animals like these.
examples from the lessons: A hyrax was sunning itself on a warm rock. | The hyrax is a distant cousin of the elephant. | In South Africa the hyrax is called a dassie. | The Bible says the conies make their homes in the rocks. | Hyraxes live in groups and keep watch for eagles. | The hyrax has rubbery pads on its feet for gripping rocks.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: hyraxes (or, rarely, hyraces). Said «HY-raks». It is not a rodent, even though it looks like one.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a way that causes great shame or embarrassment in front of others; humiliatingly.
its sense in the lessons: In The Wind in the Willows Toad is often dumped ignominiously: thrown into the river by the barge-woman, falling into the mud, and finally hurled out of things he had boasted about. Stories use the word when a proud character suffers an embarrassing fall. Sports reports: «The team were ignominiously knocked out by a small club.»
examples from the lessons: The barge-woman threw Toad ignominiously into the canal. | The proud champion was ignominiously beaten in the first round. | The thief was ignominiously caught with his hand in the cake tin. | The villain fled ignominiously. | Our big plan ended ignominiously when the tent fell down. | The bully slipped ignominiously in the mud.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Long word: ig-no-MIN-ee-us-lee. From «ignominy» (public shame) → ignominious (adjective) → ignominiously (adverb).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Rude behaviour or words that show no respect, especially to an older person or someone in charge; cheek. 2) (an impertinence) A rude remark or act.
its sense in the lessons: In Alice's Adventures in Wonderland the creatures and royalty are offended by Alice's impertinence, though she is usually just honest. In old school stories teachers punished impertinence. Today we often say «cheek» or «rudeness». Phrases: «the impertinence of it!», «What impertinence!»
examples from the lessons: «What impertinence!» cried the Duchess. | The pupil was punished for his impertinence. | She had the impertinence to read my diary. | The Caterpillar's questions felt like an impertinence to Alice. | I'll have no impertinence from you, young man! | His impertinence shocked the old lady.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun from «impertinent». Mostly uncountable. Close: cheek (UK, informal), insolence (formal).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Done or made without planning or practice, on the spur of the moment: «an impromptu speech». 2) (noun, music) A short piece of music written to sound as if it were made up on the spot.
its sense in the lessons: In school: an impromptu talk is one you give without preparing; drama classes use impromptu acting (improvisation). In The Wind in the Willows Toad bursts into impromptu songs about himself. Phrases: «an impromptu party», «an impromptu performance».
examples from the lessons: We had an impromptu picnic in the park. | The class gave an impromptu concert for the head teacher. | Toad sang an impromptu song all about his own cleverness. | The teacher asked me to give an impromptu speech. | Schubert wrote famous impromptus for piano. | The street musician gave an impromptu show.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Said «im-PROMP-tyoo». Comes from Latin «in promptu» (in readiness). Close words: improvised, spontaneous, off the cuff.

part of speech: noun (a jaunt, jaunts); verb (jaunt, jaunts, jaunted, jaunting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A short trip or outing for fun. 2) (verb) To go on such a trip.
its sense in the lessons: In The Wind in the Willows Toad loves jaunts: first in a gypsy caravan along the open road, then in motor cars. In everyday life: «a jaunt to the seaside». It is a light, happy word for a short pleasure trip, not a hard journey.
examples from the lessons: We went on a jaunt to the beach on Sunday. | Toad planned a jaunt along the open road in his caravan. | The friends took a jaunt into town. | Grandma enjoys a jaunt in the countryside. | Our class jaunt to the zoo was great fun. | They jaunted off to France for the weekend.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Said «jawnt». Adjective «jaunty» means cheerful and confident.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A special uniform worn by servants of a great house or by members of a company or guild in the past. 2) The colours and design of a company's vehicles: «the airline's livery». 3) (livery stable / livery yard) A place where horses are kept and fed for their owners, or hired out, for payment.
its sense in the lessons: In Alice's Adventures in Wonderland the Fish-Footman and the Frog-Footman are «in livery», like footmen of a rich house; Alice thinks one is a fish because of his face. In history, rich families had servants in matching livery. Today buses, trains and planes have a livery of company colours. Phrases: «in livery», «livery stable».
examples from the lessons: The footman wore a smart livery with gold buttons. | Two footmen in livery stood at the door. | The trains have a new red and white livery. | The Fish-Footman was in livery, though he looked like a fish. | Grandad keeps his horse at a livery yard. | The servants' livery showed which family they worked for.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Plural: liveries. Not related to «liver» (the body organ) or «delivery».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A small piece of jewellery that opens like a tiny box, hung on a chain round the neck, holding a photo, a lock of hair or a keepsake.
its sense in the lessons: In stories lockets hold a picture of a loved one and often help solve a mystery: a lost child is recognised by her mother's locket. In everyday life, a locket can be a gift from a grandparent. Phrases: «a gold locket», «a heart-shaped locket».
examples from the lessons: Gran gave me a silver locket with Mum's photo inside. | She opened the locket to show a lock of baby hair. | The orphan was recognised by the locket round her neck. | A heart-shaped locket hung on a thin chain. | The detective found a broken locket on the floor. | He wore his father's locket for luck.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Not the same as «locker» (a cupboard that locks) or «lock».

meaning for a pupil: 1) So good that nothing or nobody is equal to it; without equal; the best.
its sense in the lessons: A grand, slightly old-fashioned word of praise. In The Wind in the Willows Toad boasts of his own matchless genius and «matchless» driving; the reader knows he is far from it, which makes it funny. In poems and adverts: «matchless beauty», «matchless skill».
examples from the lessons: The view from the mountain top was matchless. | Toad sang about his own matchless cleverness. | She played with matchless skill. | The castle had a matchless collection of paintings. | Their matchless courage saved the village. | The chef cooks matchless pies.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Nothing to do with matches (for lighting); it means «no match» = no equal. Close words: unequalled, unrivalled, peerless.

part of speech: verb form (past of «mellow»: mellow, mellows, mellowed, mellowing); adjective (mellowed)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Became softer, calmer and kinder with age or time: «Grandad has mellowed.» 2) (of colours, sounds, light) Became soft, warm and rich, not harsh. 3) (of fruit, wine, cheese) Became ripe, sweet and smooth.
its sense in the lessons: In The Wind in the Willows old houses and walls are mellowed by time, and the warm autumn light is mellow. In stories a grumpy character who has mellowed is easier to like. In everyday life: «My big sister has mellowed since she went to college.»
examples from the lessons: Grandad was strict, but he has mellowed with age. | The old brick wall had mellowed to a warm red. | The apples mellowed in the autumn sun. | The evening light mellowed into gold. | After a cup of tea, the cross teacher mellowed. | The cheese mellowed in the cellar for a year.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: mellow → mellowed. Opposite ideas: harsh, sharp, raw.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A small, long, thin animal of the weasel family with dark brown fur, living near rivers and lakes and good at swimming and hunting. 2) Its soft, shiny fur, made into expensive coats, or a coat made of it: «a mink coat».
its sense in the lessons: In nature lessons: the American mink escaped from fur farms in Britain and Ireland and now hunts water voles (like Ratty!) and birds, so it is a problem for river wildlife. Many people think killing animals for fur is cruel; fur farming is now banned in the UK and some other countries. The Wind in the Willows has stoats, weasels and ferrets of the same family.
examples from the lessons: A mink slipped into the river and swam away. | American mink hunt water voles along British rivers. | The rich lady wore a mink coat. | Fur farming of mink is banned in the UK. | Mink are good swimmers and divers. | The mink has a thick, dark brown coat.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: «mink» or «minks». Related to stoats, weasels, otters and ferrets (the mustelid family).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Laughter, fun and great happiness, especially among a group of people.
its sense in the lessons: A slightly old, literary word. In The Wind in the Willows the banquet and the Christmas carols at Mole End are full of mirth; in Alice the Hatter's tea party is anything but. Stories say «roars of mirth», «shaking with mirth». Today in speech we would say «laughter» or «fun».
examples from the lessons: The clown's tricks filled the room with mirth. | The children shook with mirth at Dad's joke. | There was much mirth and merriment at the feast. | His face was red with mirth. | The field-mice sang carols, and there was great mirth at Mole End. | Her mirth turned to tears when the puppy ran away.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: no «a mirth». Adjective: mirthful; «mirthless» means without joy («a mirthless laugh»).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A vertical (upright) bar of stone or wood that divides a window into two or more parts, especially in old churches and Tudor houses.
its sense in the lessons: A building and history word: Tudor and Elizabethan houses have «mullioned windows» with many small panes. In The Wind in the Willows Toad Hall and the old castle-gaol have such ancient windows, which make the buildings feel old and grand. In maths: mullions are often at equal spacing – a window 3 m wide with 2 mullions has 3 equal lights.
examples from the lessons: The old manor house had tall mullioned windows. | Moonlight shone between the stone mullions. | The church window was divided by three mullions. | Tudor houses often have mullions and leaded glass. | A mullion splits the window into narrow parts. | We drew the castle with its mullioned windows.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Adjective: mullioned. A vertical bar is a mullion; a horizontal one is a «transom».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Covered with small lumps or bumps; lumpy and knobbly to touch.
its sense in the lessons: A rare, playful word used by writers to describe texture, such as nubbly wool, nubbly tree bark or a nubbly animal skin; in the Just So Stories Kipling likes funny describing words like this. From «nub», a small lump. In science lessons on materials we describe textures: smooth, rough, bumpy, nubbly.
examples from the lessons: The old sweater was made of nubbly wool. | The crocodile's back felt nubbly. | Tree bark is rough and nubbly. | The toad's skin was dry and nubbly. | I like the nubbly cover of this notebook. | The rocks on the beach were nubbly with barnacles.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Rare and informal. Close words: knobbly, bumpy, lumpy.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A large mammal with very thick skin, such as an elephant, rhinoceros or hippopotamus. 2) (humorous) A big, heavy, clumsy person or thing.
its sense in the lessons: An old zoology word, now used mainly for fun or in writing; scientists no longer group these animals together, because elephants, rhinos and hippos are not closely related. In the Just So Stories the Elephant's Child and the Rhinoceros are Kipling's pachyderms, with funny made-up reasons for their trunks and skins. From Greek «pachys» (thick) + «derma» (skin).
examples from the lessons: The elephant is the most famous pachyderm. | The zoo's pachyderms were splashing in the mud. | The rhinoceros is a pachyderm with folds in its skin. | Scientists no longer use «pachyderm» as a real animal group. | The Elephant's Child was a curious little pachyderm. | Hippos and elephants are both called pachyderms.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Said «PAK-ee-derm». Countable. «Derm» (skin) also appears in «dermatologist» (skin doctor) and «epidermis».

part of speech: verb form (of «propel»: propel, propels, propelled, propelling); adjective (propelling, as in «propelling pencil»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Pushing or driving something forward. 2) (adjective, UK) A «propelling pencil» is a mechanical pencil in which the lead is pushed out by twisting or clicking. 3) Making someone do something or go somewhere: «Fear was propelling him on.»
its sense in the lessons: In science: an engine, oars, wings or a jet of water can propel a boat, a plane or a squid; Newton's third law – push backwards, go forwards. In The Wind in the Willows the Rat propels the boat with oars, and Toad's car is propelled by its engine. In maths class you might use a propelling pencil for neat graphs.
examples from the lessons: The oars were propelling the boat across the river. | A squid moves by propelling water out of its body. | The rocket is propelled by burning fuel. | Can I borrow your propelling pencil? | The crowd was propelling us towards the gate. | A propeller turns, propelling the ship forward.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double l before -ing and -ed: propelled, propelling. Related: propeller, propulsion.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (old-fashioned) Food, especially dry food for horses and farm animals, such as hay and oats. 2) (humorous) Food for people.
its sense in the lessons: An old word that sounds grand and funny; in The Wind in the Willows the animals talk about good provender for a trip, and the horse pulling Toad's caravan needs provender. Today used for fun: «Bring plenty of provender for the picnic!»
examples from the lessons: The farmer stored provender for the horses in the barn. | The caravan horse needed provender and water. | «Let's see what provender is in the basket!» said the Rat. | The army carried provender for the horses. | We packed plenty of provender for the long walk. | The stable boy gave the ponies their evening provender.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Old-fashioned: in everyday talk say «food» or «fodder».

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a dashing, stylish and confident way, often slightly careless or cheeky: «a hat worn rakishly to one side». 2) (old) In a way that shows wild, not respectable behaviour.
its sense in the lessons: In The Wind in the Willows Toad, when dressed up as a motorist or a dandy, might wear his cap rakishly on one side; it shows he thinks he looks very smart and bold. Stories use it for pirates, adventurers and show-offs. From «rake», an old word for a man who lived a wild, careless life.
examples from the lessons: He wore his cap rakishly tilted over one eye. | The pirate grinned rakishly. | Toad set his cap rakishly on his head. | The sailor's scarf was tied rakishly at his neck. | The car was painted rakishly in red and gold. | She wore her beret rakishly on one side.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from «rakish». Old-fashioned word. Not about garden rakes.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Wisdom and good judgement; the ability to understand things and make good decisions.
its sense in the lessons: A formal, grand word. In The Wind in the Willows the Badger is the wise animal whose sagacity the others trust. Fables praise the sagacity of the owl or the elephant. In exam writing, «sagacity» is a strong word for «wisdom».
examples from the lessons: The old Badger was known for his sagacity. | The judge showed great sagacity in her decision. | Owls are often shown as birds of sagacity. | It needed sagacity to solve the riddle. | The king listened to the sagacity of his advisers. | Her sagacity helped the team avoid a big mistake.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Adjective: sagacious. Close: wisdom, shrewdness. Related to «sage» (a wise person; also a herb – a different meaning).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Half a circle: a shape made by cutting a circle in half along its diameter. 2) Things arranged in a curved line like half a circle: «sit in a semicircle».
its sense in the lessons: Maths: a semicircle has a curved edge (half the circumference) and a straight edge (the diameter). Its area is half the circle's area: ½ × π × r². Its perimeter is half the circumference plus the diameter: πr + 2r. In class: «Sit in a semicircle on the carpet.» A protractor is a semicircle marked from 0° to 180°. In Alice, the animals sit in a ring for the Caucus-race.
examples from the lessons: Draw a semicircle with a compass. | The children sat in a semicircle around the teacher. | A protractor is shaped like a semicircle. | The area of a semicircle is half the area of the full circle. | A rainbow looks like a semicircle in the sky. | If the radius is 2 cm, the semicircle's curved edge is about 6.28 cm.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Semi-» means half. Countable. Maths trap: the perimeter is not just half the circumference – you must add the diameter.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Full of shadows; dark and hard to see in: «a shadowy corner». 2) Like a shadow: dim, faint and not clear: «a shadowy figure». 3) Mysterious and secret, not well known: «a shadowy organisation».
its sense in the lessons: In The Wind in the Willows the Wild Wood is shadowy and frightening; the Mole sees faces in the shadows. Stories use «shadowy» for mystery and danger. In science, a shadow forms when light is blocked by an object.
examples from the lessons: A shadowy figure crept along the alley. | The Mole hurried through the shadowy Wild Wood. | The old house had shadowy corners. | We could see shadowy shapes under the water. | The spy worked for a shadowy group. | The shadowy forest made the children nervous.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative: shadowier, shadowiest (y → i).

part of speech: adjective (sleek, sleeker, sleekest); verb (sleek, sleeks, sleeked, sleeking – rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (of hair or fur) Smooth, shiny and healthy-looking. 2) (of shapes, cars, boats) Having a smooth, elegant shape, often fast-looking. 3) (of people) Well-dressed and looking rich or too smooth.
its sense in the lessons: In The Wind in the Willows the Water Rat and the Otter have sleek fur from swimming; Toad's motor cars are sleek and shining. In science, sleek streamlined shapes cut through air or water with less drag, which is why dolphins, fish and fast cars are sleek.
examples from the lessons: The otter's fur was sleek and wet. | A sleek black cat sat on the wall. | The sleek new train sped past. | Dolphins have sleek bodies for fast swimming. | The horse's coat was sleek after brushing. | The Water Rat was sleek and brown.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative: sleeker, sleekest. Rhymes with «week». Do not confuse with «slick» (smooth and clever, sometimes slippery).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A path along the bank of a river or canal, where horses once walked pulling barges and boats with ropes. 2) Today, a path along a canal or river used for walking, running and cycling.
its sense in the lessons: In The Wind in the Willows Toad, escaping in a washerwoman's dress, meets a barge pulled by a horse on the towpath, then steals the horse. In history, towpaths helped move coal and goods before railways. Safety today: on a towpath cyclists should slow down and ring their bells; keep away from the edge – the water may be deep and cold.
examples from the lessons: We cycled along the canal towpath. | A horse once pulled the barge along the towpath. | Toad rode off on the barge-horse along the towpath. | Ring your bell when you pass walkers on the towpath. | The towpath was muddy after the rain. | Ducks waddled across the towpath.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. From «tow» (pull with a rope) + «path». «Tow» rhymes with «go».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Moving people or goods from one place to another. 2) A way of travelling or carrying things: cars, buses, trains, planes, ships. 3) (history) Sending convicts from Britain and Ireland to live and work far away, especially to Australia (1788–1868) and earlier to America, as a punishment.
its sense in the lessons: In the USA «transportation» is the everyday word; in the UK and Australia people more often say «transport». In history lessons, transportation of convicts founded Australian colonies; in The Wind in the Willows Toad's crimes might have earned harsh punishments. In science and geography: transportation is also the movement of rock and soil by rivers, wind and ice.
examples from the lessons: Public transportation includes buses and trains. | Many convicts were sentenced to transportation to Australia. | The river's transportation of sand builds up the beach. | The school organises transportation for the trip. | Bikes are a healthy kind of transportation. | Transportation to Australia could last fourteen years or for life.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. UK usage: «transport». Verb: transport. In geography, transportation is the middle stage: erosion, transportation, deposition.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Sad and full of longing for something you cannot have, or for something that is past. 2) Thoughtful and dreamy, with gentle sadness.
its sense in the lessons: A storytelling word for gentle sadness: a wistful look, smile, sigh or song. In The Wind in the Willows the Rat feels wistful as the birds fly south and the Sea Rat tempts him with tales of far lands. In creative writing it shows a feeling without crying. Phrases: «a wistful smile», «a wistful look».
