examples from the lessons: She gave a wistful smile as she waved goodbye. | The old man looked wistful as he spoke of his childhood. | The Rat felt wistful when the swallows talked of the south. | There was a wistful note in her voice. | The puppy gave a wistful look at the closed door. | The song was sweet and wistful.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb: wistfully. Not the same as «wishful» («wishful thinking» = believing what you wish were true).

part of speech: verb (abide, abides, abided or abode, abiding)
meaning for a pupil: 1) In «can't abide» / «cannot abide»: to dislike someone or something so much that you cannot put up with them. 2) In «abide by»: to obey or follow a rule, law or decision. 3) (old-fashioned, Bible) To live or stay somewhere; to remain: «Abide with me».
its sense in the lessons: In school: «Pupils must abide by the rules.» In everyday speech: «I can't abide cold tea.» In church and the Bible: the hymn «Abide with Me» (sung at football cup finals in England) and «Now abide faith, hope, love» (1 Corinthians 13). Old stories use «abide» for «stay». Phrases: «abide by», «can't abide», «law-abiding».
examples from the lessons: Everyone must abide by the rules of the game. | I can't abide people who are rude to waiters. | «Abide with me» is a famous hymn. | The players agreed to abide by the referee's decision. | The Badger could not abide parties. | A law-abiding citizen obeys the law.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: «abided» (modern) or «abode» (old). Mostly used in fixed phrases; in everyday speech say «stand» (I can't stand…) or «follow» (follow the rules). Adjective: abiding (lasting).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Very silly and not making sense; ridiculous. 2) So unreasonable it is laughable: «an absurd price».
its sense in the lessons: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland is full of the absurd: a cat that grins and vanishes, a tea party where it is always six o'clock, a trial where the verdict comes before the evidence. In maths, a question may have an absurd answer (like −3 people or 2.5 buses), which tells you to check your working. Phrases: «that's absurd», «utterly absurd», «the absurd».
examples from the lessons: It's absurd to wear a coat in this heat! | The Mad Hatter's riddle had an absurd answer – or none at all. | The price of the toy was absurd. | Alice thought the whole trial was absurd. | An answer of 2.5 buses is absurd – we need 3 buses. | His excuse was so absurd that everyone laughed.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Said «ab-SURD» or «ab-ZURD». Noun: absurdity. Adverb: absurdly. Maths: an absurd answer is a sign to check your working again.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A written sound like a small cough, made to get people's attention, to show you are about to speak, or to show you don't approve of something. 2) (humorous) Used in writing to point out a joke or a hint: «My birthday is next week, ahem.»
its sense in the lessons: In Alice's Adventures in Wonderland the Mouse, wanting to dry everyone, says «Ahem!» with an important air before reciting the driest thing he knows – a dull history lesson about William the Conqueror. In everyday life a teacher may say «Ahem» to make the class quiet.
examples from the lessons: «Ahem!» said the Mouse with an important air. | The teacher said «Ahem» and the class went quiet. | «Ahem, I think you're sitting in my seat.» | «Somebody (ahem) forgot to feed the cat.» | Dad cleared his throat: «Ahem! Dinner is ready.» | «Ahem!» coughed the butler at the door.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Said with a little throat-clearing sound: «uh-HEM». Not a real word with meaning on its own; it is a sound.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal or old) Clothing, especially clothes of a certain kind: «sports apparel». 2) (old) Fine clothes and dress for a special occasion.
its sense in the lessons: In shops and adverts, especially in the USA: «outdoor apparel», «children's apparel». In old stories and the Bible: «fine apparel», «gorgeous apparel». In The Wind in the Willows Toad's disguise as a washerwoman is very different from his grand motoring apparel. In everyday talk we say «clothes».
examples from the lessons: The shop sells sports apparel. | The king was dressed in rich apparel. | Rain apparel keeps you dry on camping trips. | Toad swapped his fine apparel for the washerwoman's dress. | The school apparel store sells uniforms. | «Wear suitable apparel for the hike,» said the notice.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: no «an apparel» or «apparels». Formal; everyday word: clothes. Do not confuse with «apparent» (clear, seeming).

part of speech: adjective (astonished); verb form (past of «astonish»: astonish, astonishes, astonished, astonishing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Very surprised, so much that you can hardly believe it. 2) (verb, past) Surprised someone very much: «The news astonished us.»
its sense in the lessons: Alice is astonished again and again in Wonderland: at a rabbit with a watch, at growing taller than a house, at the grinning cat. In stories, «astonished» is stronger than «surprised». In science lessons, results can astonish us when they go against what we expected. Phrases: «astonished at/by», «astonished to see».
examples from the lessons: Alice was astonished to see a rabbit take a watch out of its pocket. | We were astonished by the size of the dinosaur skeleton. | Mum was astonished when I tidied my room without being asked. | The crowd stared, astonished, at the magician. | The Mole was astonished by the river. | The results of the experiment astonished the class.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Astonished» describes the person who feels it; «astonishing» describes the thing that causes it: I was astonished; the trick was astonishing. Close words: amazed, astounded.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The covers on a bed: sheets, blankets, a duvet or quilt, and pillowcases.
its sense in the lessons: In stories children hide under the bedclothes with a torch to read, or pull the bedclothes over their heads when scared. In The Wind in the Willows Toad escapes from his bedroom by knotting his bedclothes into a rope and climbing out of the window – but never try this in real life, it is very dangerous.
examples from the lessons: She pulled the bedclothes over her head. | Toad tied his bedclothes together to make a rope. | The cat was asleep in a heap of bedclothes. | Mum changes the bedclothes every week. | The bedclothes were all tangled after the nightmare. | Never climb out of a window on bedclothes – it's dangerous.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural only: «the bedclothes are» (no «a bedclothe»). Today people often say «bedding» or «bed linen».

part of speech: adjective (billiard – as in «billiard table», «billiard room», «billiard ball»); noun (billiards – the game, uncountable)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Belonging to the game of billiards: a game played on a large table covered in green cloth, where players hit balls with a long stick called a cue. 2) (billiards) The game itself; snooker and pool are related games.
its sense in the lessons: In big houses like Toad Hall there was a billiard room; in The Wind in the Willows the weasels and stoats feast in Toad's house. In maths and science, billiard balls show angles of bouncing (the angle a ball hits the cushion equals the angle it bounces off) and how energy passes from one ball to another. Phrases: «billiard table», «billiard ball», «bald as a billiard ball».
examples from the lessons: The old house had a billiard room with a huge green table. | The billiard balls clicked together. | Grandad taught me to play billiards. | A billiard ball bounces off the cushion at the same angle it hits it. | The billiard cue was taller than me. | «He's as bald as a billiard ball!» laughed Dad.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Billiard» (no s) is used before a noun: «a billiard table». The game is «billiards», which takes a singular verb: «Billiards is fun.»

meaning for a pupil: 1) Slightly blue; having a little blue in its colour.
its sense in the lessons: In science and art: «bluish-green» water, «bluish light». In stories: lips turning bluish with cold, a bluish mist. First aid: bluish lips or skin can be a sign someone is too cold or not getting enough air – get adult help quickly.
examples from the lessons: The mountains looked bluish in the distance. | The sea was a bluish-green colour. | His lips were bluish with cold. | A bluish light glowed from the cave. | The egg had a bluish shell. | Ice can look bluish when it is very thick.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: «bluish» (drop the e) is more common than «blueish»; both are seen. The «-ish» ending means «a bit»: greenish, reddish.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Like a boy, or looking or behaving like a boy: «a boyish grin». 2) Young-looking and full of fun, said about a grown man: «He has a boyish face.»
its sense in the lessons: In The Wind in the Willows Toad's boyish excitement about new crazes makes him fun and foolish. In stories a «boyish grin» shows a cheeky, happy look. It can also describe a girl's short haircut or style («a boyish haircut»).
examples from the lessons: Grandad still has a boyish grin. | The teacher's boyish face made him look very young. | Toad clapped his hands with boyish excitement. | She had a short, boyish haircut. | His boyish enthusiasm for trains never faded. | The coach laughed with boyish delight when they won.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «boy» + «-ish». Same pattern: girlish, childish. Do not confuse with «childish», which is usually a criticism (silly).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Slightly brown; of a colour that is close to brown but not quite. 2) Brown mixed with another colour, as in brownish-green or brownish-red.
its sense in the lessons: Used in describing things in stories and in science (the colour of a leaf, a rock, soil, an animal's fur). The ending -ish means «a bit» or «rather»: brownish, greenish, tallish, smallish. Often joined to another colour: brownish-yellow, brownish-grey.
examples from the lessons: The pond water looked brownish after the rain. | The Water Rat's coat was a soft brownish colour. | The leaves turn brownish in autumn. | We found a brownish rock with white stripes. | Her eyes are brownish-green. | The old photo had gone brownish with age. | Mole saw a brownish shape moving among the reeds. | The bread was toasted until it was brownish on top.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective only; no plural. Spelled with -ish added to brown. -ish makes a colour less exact: brownish = «more or less brown». Do not confuse with «brownie» (a small cake, or a young Girl Guide).

part of speech: noun (the brunt — almost only in «bear the brunt», «take the brunt»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The worst part or the main force of something bad, such as an attack, a storm or blame. 2) To bear (or take) the brunt of something means to suffer the most from it.
its sense in the lessons: Almost always heard in the phrases «bear the brunt of», «take the brunt of», «the full brunt of». Used in news, history and stories when one person or place suffers most: the coast took the brunt of the storm. In stories it tells the reader who suffered most or who was blamed.
examples from the lessons: The small village bore the brunt of the storm. | The front of the car took the brunt of the crash. | Mum took the brunt of the work when Dad was ill. | The goalkeeper bore the brunt of the blame for the loss. | Our tent faced the brunt of the wind. | The soldiers at the front took the full brunt of the attack. | Toad's friends bore the brunt of his silly adventures. | The east side of the house takes the brunt of the weather.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable; always «the brunt», never «a brunt» and no plural. Used with «of»: the brunt of the storm. Not the same as «grunt» or «blunt».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A small plant with flowers like tiny daisies, white petals around a yellow middle, which has a sweet apple-like smell. 2) A drink (camomile tea) made from the dried flowers, often drunk to feel calm or sleepy. 3) In old times, a bitter medicine made from the plant.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life it is mostly camomile tea, which people drink at bedtime. In science and gardening it is a herb. In Alice in Wonderland the Duchess's line is a joke about tastes and tempers: Alice thinks pepper makes people hot-tempered, vinegar sour, camomile bitter and barley-sugar sweet-tempered. Peter Rabbit's mother also gives him camomile tea when he is ill.
examples from the lessons: Gran drinks a cup of camomile tea before bed. | Camomile flowers look like tiny daisies. | The garden smelled of camomile and mint. | Peter Rabbit was put to bed with camomile tea. | Alice said that camomile makes people bitter. | We dried camomile flowers for a science project. | Some people say camomile helps them relax. | The lawn was made of camomile instead of grass.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Two spellings: camomile (UK) and chamomile (USA and many others); both are right. Say «CAM-uh-mile». Uncountable when it is the plant or tea: some camomile. A herb tea is not real tea from the tea bush.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Of a boat: to turn over in the water so that the bottom is on top. 2) To make a boat turn over.
its sense in the lessons: Used in sailing, water safety and stories of the sea and rivers. Safety: if a small boat capsizes, stay with the boat and hold on, and always wear a life jacket. In The Wind in the Willows Mole grabs the oars, the boat capsizes, and the Rat has to pull him out of the river.
examples from the lessons: The little boat capsized in the strong wind. | Mole tried to row and capsized the boat. | If your canoe capsizes, hold on to it. | A big wave nearly capsized the ferry. | We practised what to do if the dinghy capsized. | Don't stand up in the boat or it will capsize. | Everyone was wearing life jackets when the raft capsized. | The children watched the toy boat capsize in the bath.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: capsized, capsizing (drop the e before -ing). Used for boats, not cars (a car «overturns» or «rolls over»). Spelled with -ize in both UK and US English.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In old times, a light carriage with two or four wheels, pulled by one horse, often with a folding hood. 2) (in «chaise longue») a long chair or sofa with a back at one end where you can put your legs up.
its sense in the lessons: Mostly found in old stories and history books about the days of horses and carriages. Today people mostly meet it in «chaise longue», a piece of furniture. In a story, a chaise tells the reader that the person is travelling the old way, by horse.
examples from the lessons: The doctor arrived in a small chaise pulled by a grey pony. | In the old story the lady rode to town in her chaise. | The chaise rattled along the country lane. | Grandma has a velvet chaise longue in her sitting room. | A chaise was cheaper than a big coach. | The horse stopped and the chaise tipped forward. | In history we drew a picture of a chaise. | He lay back on the chaise longue with a book.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say «shayz» (it comes from French, where it means «chair»). Plural: chaises. «Chaise longue» means «long chair» in French; in the USA people often say «chaise lounge».

part of speech: noun (a chanty, chanties) — another spelling of shanty
meaning for a pupil: 1) A song that sailors sang long ago while they worked together, pulling ropes or turning the capstan; also spelled «shanty» and «chantey». 2) Not the same word as «shanty» meaning a rough hut.
its sense in the lessons: Found in sea stories and music lessons. Sea chanties have a strong beat so that the sailors could pull at the same moment; one person sings a line and the crew answers. In The Wind in the Willows the Sea Rat talks of sailors' songs and ports.
examples from the lessons: The sailors sang a chanty as they pulled up the anchor. | In music we learned an old sea chanty. | One sailor sang the line and the others answered in the chanty. | The chanty helped them pull the rope together. | «What Shall We Do with the Drunken Sailor?» is a famous chanty. | The old seaman hummed a chanty while he mended the nets. | Our class sang chanties at the school concert.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spellings: chanty, chantey, shanty — the same sea song; «shanty» is commonest today. Plural: chanties. Say «SHAN-tee» (the «ch» sounds like «sh»). Do not mix up with «shanty» = a poor hut (shanty town).

part of speech: noun (conceit — uncountable in sense 1; a conceit, conceits in sense 2)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Thinking far too well of yourself; being too proud of how clever, good-looking or important you are. 2) (in poetry, formal) a clever, surprising comparison or idea.
its sense in the lessons: Used in stories and character studies to describe a vain, boastful person. It is the noun for «conceited». In The Wind in the Willows Toad is full of conceit: he boasts and sings songs about how wonderful he is. In lessons about values, conceit is the opposite of humility (being humble).
examples from the lessons: Toad's conceit grew with every song he sang about himself. | Her conceit made her hard to like. | He was clever, but without any conceit. | The hare's conceit made him lose the race. | «I'm the best,» he said, full of conceit. | The story warns against pride and conceit. | The poet used a clever conceit, comparing love to a compass.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable when it means pride: no «a» and no plural. Adjective: conceited (a conceited boy). Different from «concept» (an idea) and «deceit» (lying). Spelling rule: i before e except after c — conceit.

part of speech: noun (a countenance, countenances); verb (countenance, countenances, countenanced, countenancing — formal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal, old-fashioned) A person's face, or the look on it. 2) (verb, formal) To allow or approve of something, usually used in «not countenance»: the teacher would not countenance cheating. 3) (in «keep your countenance») to keep a calm, straight face and not laugh.
its sense in the lessons: Found in older books and the Bible («the Lord lift up his countenance upon thee» — a blessing asking God to look kindly on you). In stories it tells the reader about a face and mood: a cheerful countenance, a grim countenance. Alice often has trouble keeping her countenance when the creatures say silly things.
examples from the lessons: The old man had a kind countenance. | His countenance fell when he heard the news. | Alice could hardly keep her countenance when the Mock Turtle sang. | The headteacher would not countenance bullying. | The Badger's countenance was stern but kind. | «The Lord make his face shine upon you,» says the blessing in the Bible. | Her countenance brightened when she saw the letter. | Dad would never countenance lying.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Old-fashioned and formal; in everyday talk say «face» or «look». «His countenance fell» means he looked disappointed. As a verb it is almost always negative: «I will not countenance it.»

meaning for a pupil: 1) Clearly and without any doubt; very much: it was decidedly colder. 2) In a firm way, showing you have made up your mind: «No,» she said decidedly.
its sense in the lessons: Used in stories and formal writing to make a description stronger or to show someone is firm. Alice in Wonderland often uses it: Alice speaks decidedly when she is sure of herself. In a story it tells you the feeling is clear and certain.
examples from the lessons: It was decidedly colder this morning. | «I'm not going,» said Alice decidedly. | The new playground is decidedly better than the old one. | The Rat was decidedly cross with Toad. | The cake looked decidedly odd. | She shook her head decidedly. | This maths test was decidedly harder. | The weather was decidedly against a picnic.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb of «decided». Two meanings: «clearly/very» (decidedly better) and «firmly» (said decidedly). Not the same as «decisively», which means acting quickly and firmly to settle something.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Sad and without hope, often after a failure or a disappointment; low in spirits.
its sense in the lessons: Used in stories to tell the reader a character feels let down and sad: shoulders drooping, head hanging. Common in sports reports for the losing team. Mole is dejected when he cannot visit his old home; Toad is dejected in prison.
examples from the lessons: The team walked off the pitch looking dejected. | Toad sat dejected in his prison cell. | She felt dejected when she wasn't picked for the play. | The dejected puppy lay by the door. | After losing the spelling bee he looked dejected. | Mole followed the Rat in a dejected way. | Don't look so dejected, you can try again! | The dejected children walked home in the rain.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective; noun: dejection. Similar words: downcast, despondent, glum, gloomy. It comes from a Latin word meaning «thrown down».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Very much, so much it hurts: she desperately wanted a puppy. 2) In a wild way, because things are bad and there is little hope: he swam desperately for the shore. 3) Extremely, very badly: they were desperately poor; it was desperately cold.
its sense in the lessons: Used in stories to show great need, fear or effort. In news: people desperately need help after a flood. In The Wind in the Willows Toad desperately wants motor cars; Mole runs desperately through the Wild Wood.
examples from the lessons: I desperately need a drink of water. | The kitten clung desperately to the branch. | Mole ran desperately through the Wild Wood. | She desperately wanted to win. | The family were desperately poor. | He looked around desperately for his mum. | Toad desperately wanted a motor car. | We were desperately tired after the hike.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb of «desperate». Spelling trap: desp-E-rate (not desparate). Do not use it for small wishes in careful writing; it means a very strong need or a bad situation.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Very sad and without hope, feeling that things will not get better.
its sense in the lessons: Used in stories and reports to describe a deep, quiet sadness after something has gone wrong. Close to «dejected» and «hopeless». It tells the reader that a character has almost given up.
examples from the lessons: Mole grew despondent as the snow fell in the Wild Wood. | The despondent farmer looked at his flooded field. | She was despondent after failing the test. | Toad became despondent in the dark prison. | Don't be despondent — we can fix it. | The team was despondent after the fifth defeat. | He gave a despondent sigh.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective; noun: despondency. Spelling: despond-ENT. Similar: dejected, downcast, hopeless, low. Opposite: hopeful, cheerful.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Shy and not sure of yourself; not wanting to speak up or push yourself forward.
its sense in the lessons: Used in stories to describe a quiet, modest, unsure person. Mole is diffident at first with the grand Badger. In everyday life a diffident child might know the answer but not put a hand up.
examples from the lessons: The diffident boy rarely spoke in class. | Mole felt diffident in front of the great Badger. | She gave a diffident smile. | He was diffident about showing his drawing. | Don't be diffident — your idea is good! | The new girl was diffident on her first day. | In a diffident voice, he asked for help.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective; noun: diffidence. Opposite: confident (both come from Latin «to trust»; diffident = not trusting yourself). Don't confuse with «different».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Dark, dull and dirty-looking; not bright or clean: a dingy room. 2) Of colours: faded and dull, not fresh.
its sense in the lessons: Used in stories to set a gloomy scene: a dingy attic, a dingy cellar, a dingy street. It tells the reader a place is shabby and unpleasant. Toad's prison cell is dark and dingy.
examples from the lessons: The dingy room had one small window. | Toad was locked in a dingy dungeon. | Her white socks had gone dingy and grey. | We painted the dingy kitchen bright yellow. | The shop was dingy but full of treasures. | They walked down a dingy back street. | The curtains looked dingy and old. | A dingy light came through the dusty glass.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say «DIN-jee» (soft g). Do not confuse with «dinghy» (a small boat), said «DING-ee». Comparative: dingier, dingiest.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To make someone sad because something was not as good as they hoped, or did not happen. 2) To let someone down by not doing what they expected.
its sense in the lessons: A very common everyday word for feelings. Adjectives: disappointed (how you feel) and disappointing (what made you feel it). Phrases: «disappointed in someone», «disappointed with something», «I'm sorry to disappoint you». In stories it shows that hopes were not met.
examples from the lessons: The film disappointed me — the book was better. | I don't want to disappoint my team. | We were disappointed when the trip was cancelled. | The weather was disappointing. | Alice was disappointed to find the little door locked again. | Sorry to disappoint you, but there's no cake left. | His test score didn't disappoint his mum. | Toad disappointed his friends again and again.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: one s, two p's — dis-ap-point. I am disappointED (my feeling); the match was disappointING (the thing). Noun: disappointment.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A kind of small shark found in seas around Britain, Europe, North America and elsewhere, often with a spotted skin. 2) A name for some other fish, such as the bowfin of North American lakes.
its sense in the lessons: Used in science and nature lessons about the sea: the dogfish is a real shark, though small and harmless to people. It lays eggs in cases called «mermaid's purses» that wash up on beaches. In fish shops in Britain it is sometimes sold as «rock salmon» or «huss».
examples from the lessons: We saw a dogfish at the sea-life centre. | A dogfish is a small kind of shark. | The fisherman caught a spotted dogfish. | Dogfish eggs come in cases called mermaid's purses. | On the beach we found an empty dogfish egg case. | The dogfish swam slowly along the bottom of the tank. | In biology we looked at the skin of a dogfish. | Dogfish have rough skin like sandpaper.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural usually «dogfish» (same as singular), sometimes «dogfishes» for kinds. It is a fish, not a dog; the name may come from the way they hunt in packs.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A polite title written after a man's name in old letters and on envelopes, shortened to «Esq.»: John Smith, Esq. 2) In history, a young man of good family who served a knight and carried his shield; a squire. 3) (USA) A title used after the names of lawyers.
its sense in the lessons: Found in old books, letters and legal writing. On an envelope it shows respect for a gentleman. In Alice in Wonderland Alice, grown so tall her feet are far away, jokes about sending them a present addressed «Alice's Right Foot, Esq., Hearthrug, near the Fender» — a joke on grand letter addresses. In history lessons about knights, an esquire (squire) was a knight's helper on the way to becoming a knight.
examples from the lessons: The letter was addressed to «Thomas Brown, Esq.» | In the Middle Ages, an esquire carried the knight's shield. | The young esquire hoped to become a knight one day. | Old letters often wrote «Esq.» after a gentleman's name. | In the USA some lawyers write «Esq.» after their names. | The esquire helped his knight put on his armour.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Shortened to «Esq.» with a capital E. You use «Esq.» instead of «Mr», never both: «Mr John Smith» or «John Smith, Esq.» Old-fashioned today in Britain. Same word as «squire».

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a way that avoids giving a clear, direct answer or avoids doing something.
its sense in the lessons: Used in stories to show that a character is hiding something or does not want to say the truth: «Maybe,» he said evasively. Readers should notice: an evasive answer is a clue. From the verb «evade» (to escape or avoid).
examples from the lessons: «I might have seen it,» he said evasively. | Toad answered evasively when the Badger asked about the car. | She looked away and spoke evasively. | When asked who broke the vase, the twins answered evasively. | The politician replied evasively to the question. | «Oh, somewhere,» said the Cat evasively. | He shrugged evasively and changed the subject.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb of «evasive». Noun: evasion. Related verb: evade (evade a question, evade capture). It suggests the person is avoiding something on purpose.

part of speech: adjective (exasperating, more exasperating, most exasperating); also the -ing form of the verb exasperate
meaning for a pupil: 1) Very annoying, making you feel cross and impatient, often because it keeps happening.
its sense in the lessons: Used in stories and everyday life about people or things that try your patience. Alice finds the creatures of Wonderland exasperating, for example the Caterpillar's short answers. Toad is exasperating to his friends because he never learns.
examples from the lessons: The Caterpillar's short answers were exasperating. | It's exasperating when the bus is late again. | Toad was the most exasperating animal on the river. | My little brother can be exasperating! | This puzzle is exasperating — I can't solve it. | «How exasperating!» cried Alice. | The slow computer was exasperating. | It was exasperating to lose the same game three times.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: exasperate, exasperated (how you feel), exasperating (what causes it). Noun: exasperation. Stronger than «annoying».

meaning for a pupil: 1) An old or poetic spelling of «fairy»: a small magical creature in stories. 2) (old, poetic) The land of fairies, fairyland: «the realm of Faery». 3) (adjective) magical, of fairies.
its sense in the lessons: Found in poems, old tales and fantasy books, where the spelling makes things sound older and more mysterious. In The Wind in the Willows, Rat and Mole meet the Piper at the Gates of Dawn, a magical, almost fairy-like moment. In stories it tells the reader we are in a world of magic.
examples from the lessons: The old poem spoke of the land of Faery. | In the story a faery queen lived under the hill. | The poet wrote «faery» instead of «fairy». | The forest seemed like a faery place in the moonlight. | Faery folk were said to dance in rings. | The book used old spellings like «faery». | Children in the tale were stolen away to Faery.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Old or poetic spelling; the normal spelling today is «fairy». Plural: faeries. Say it like «fairy». Do not use it in ordinary writing unless you want an old, magical tone.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Weakly, without strength or energy. 2) In a poor, unconvincing way: he laughed feebly at the joke.
its sense in the lessons: Used in stories to show that someone is tired, ill, frightened or not sure: the kitten mewed feebly. Alice often speaks feebly when she is confused or afraid.
examples from the lessons: The baby bird chirped feebly. | «I'm not sure,» said Alice feebly. | He waved feebly from his hospital bed. | The torch shone feebly in the dark. | Mole tried feebly to push the door open. | She smiled feebly at the bad joke. | The old engine coughed feebly and stopped. | Toad protested feebly when the Badger scolded him.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb of «feeble» (weak). Spelling: feeble → feebly (drop -le, add -ly). Opposite: strongly, firmly.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) A person who tells fibs, small lies that are not very serious.
its sense in the lessons: A gentle, childish word, used at home and in the playground: «You fibber!» It is softer than «liar». In stories it can be playful. A fib is a small untrue thing; even small fibs can break trust.
examples from the lessons: «You're a fibber — you did eat the biscuit!» | My little sister is a terrible fibber. | Don't be a fibber; tell the truth. | Everyone knew he was a fibber. | «I'm not a fibber!» she cried. | The fibber said his dog had done his homework. | Toad was a boaster and a bit of a fibber.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal. From «fib» (fib, fibs, fibbed, fibbing). Double b: fibber. Softer and more childish than «liar».

part of speech: noun (fishing — uncountable); also the -ing form of the verb fish (fish, fishes, fished, fishing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Catching fish, as a hobby or as a job: go fishing. 2) (verb, informal) Trying to get something indirectly, such as information or praise: fishing for compliments. 3) Searching for something with your hand: she was fishing in her bag for her keys.
its sense in the lessons: Everyday: «go fishing», «fishing rod», «fishing boat», «fishing line», «fishing net». Geography and history: fishing towns and the fishing industry. In The Wind in the Willows the river animals fish, and the Otter knows the best places. Safety: wear a life jacket on boats and be careful of hooks.
examples from the lessons: Grandad takes me fishing on Saturdays. | The fishing boats came back with full nets. | She bought a new fishing rod. | Otter was out fishing on the river. | He was fishing in his pocket for a coin. | Stop fishing for compliments! | Fishing is an important job in Newfoundland. | Our town grew up as a fishing village.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a noun it is uncountable: «a lot of fishing», not «fishings». Phrases: go fishing, fishing trip. «Fishy» (adjective) means suspicious.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal, old) In a suitable or proper way; rightly.
its sense in the lessons: Found mainly in old books and the Bible («a word fitly spoken is like apples of gold», Proverbs 25:11). It tells the reader something is done in a way that fits the moment. In modern English we say «properly» or «aptly».
examples from the lessons: The story ends fitly with a feast. | A word fitly spoken is like apples of gold. | The hall was fitly decorated for the wedding. | He was fitly rewarded for his courage. | The old book said the king was fitly honoured. | The poem was fitly read at the end of the day.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Old-fashioned; from «fit» (suitable). Today use «properly», «suitably» or «aptly». Not about being physically fit.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A low stool or small padded seat for resting your feet on when you sit in a chair. 2) (Bible, figurative) something under someone's feet, showing power: «the earth is my footstool».
its sense in the lessons: Everyday furniture word in homes, especially older ones. In stories it often appears by the fire in a cosy room, like the Badger's kitchen. In the Bible God says «heaven is my throne and the earth is my footstool», meaning God is greater than the whole world.
examples from the lessons: Grandpa rested his feet on the footstool. | The cat slept on the footstool by the fire. | She sat on a footstool to read to the little ones. | Badger pulled up a footstool for Mole. | The footstool had a velvet top. | I stood on the footstool to reach the shelf. | «The earth is my footstool,» says the Bible.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Compound noun: foot + stool. Plural: footstools. Standing on a footstool to reach high things can be unsafe; ask for help.

part of speech: adjective (gallant, more gallant, most gallant); noun (a gallant, gallants — old)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Brave, especially in a fine, noble way: a gallant knight. 2) (of a man, old-fashioned) Very polite and kind to women. 3) (old) Grand and splendid to look at: a gallant ship. 4) (noun, old) a fashionable young man.
its sense in the lessons: Found in stories of knights, soldiers and heroes, and in history. «A gallant effort» means a brave try, even if it failed — common in sports reports. In The Wind in the Willows the friends make a gallant attack to win back Toad Hall from the weasels.
examples from the lessons: The gallant knight rode to save the village. | The team made a gallant effort but lost. | He held the door open in a gallant way. | The four friends made a gallant charge into Toad Hall. | The gallant soldiers did not run away. | Toad imagined himself as a gallant hero. | A gallant ship sailed into the harbour.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say «GAL-ant» for brave; «ga-LANT» sometimes for the polite-to-women sense (old). Noun: gallantry (bravery). Adverb: gallantly.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In stories from Arabia and the Middle East, a magic spirit, often living in a lamp or bottle, who must obey whoever sets it free and may grant wishes. 2) (informal) «the genie is out of the bottle» means something has happened that cannot be undone.
its sense in the lessons: Found in fairy tales, especially «Aladdin» from The Thousand and One Nights. The older Arabic word is «jinn» or «djinn»; in Kipling's Just So Stories, «How the Camel Got His Hump», the Djinn in charge of All Deserts gives the lazy Camel his hump. In stories a genie brings magic, wishes and often a lesson about wanting too much.
examples from the lessons: Aladdin rubbed the lamp and a genie appeared. | The genie said, «Your wish is my command.» | If you met a genie, what would you wish for? | The Djinn gave the Camel a hump for saying «Humph!» | The genie was trapped in the bottle for a thousand years. | Once the secret was out, the genie couldn't be put back in the bottle. | In the play, my friend dressed up as a genie.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say «JEE-nee». Plural: genies (or old genii). Related to Arabic «jinn/djinn». Genies are made-up, from stories; they are not real.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A small cucumber kept in vinegar, eaten as a pickle; in the USA and Canada usually called a «pickle». 2) The small cucumber itself, grown for pickling. 3) (UK, informal) «The Gherkin», a famous pickle-shaped tower in London.
its sense in the lessons: An everyday food word: gherkins go in burgers, sandwiches and salads. In maths and cooking, recipes may use gherkins. A nickname for a building shaped like one in the City of London.
examples from the lessons: I always take the gherkin out of my burger. | Mum chopped gherkins into the potato salad. | Gherkins taste sour and crunchy. | In America, a gherkin is just called a pickle. | We saw the Gherkin building on our trip to London. | A jar of gherkins stood on the picnic table. | Grandpa grows gherkins in his vegetable patch.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say «GUR-kin» (hard g). Plural: gherkins. The h is silent. UK: gherkin; USA/Canada: pickle (and «pickle» in the UK often means a chutney).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Very carefully and slowly, because you are afraid of hurting yourself or breaking something, or of what might happen.
its sense in the lessons: Used in stories to show caution: she stepped gingerly onto the ice. In everyday life and safety: moving gingerly over something slippery or touching something sore. Alice goes gingerly near strange creatures; Mole steps gingerly into the boat.
examples from the lessons: She stepped gingerly onto the frozen pond. | He touched his bruised knee gingerly. | Mole climbed gingerly into the boat. | Alice picked up the bottle gingerly. | The vet lifted the hurt puppy gingerly. | We walked gingerly across the wobbly bridge. | He gingerly opened the box to see what was inside.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Although it ends in -ly, it does not come from «ginger» the spice or hair colour. Say «JIN-jer-lee». Mostly an adverb.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (architecture, history) In the style of many churches and cathedrals built in Europe from about 1150 to 1500, with pointed arches, tall spires and big stained-glass windows. 2) (stories) Gothic stories are spooky tales with old castles, ghosts, dark nights and mystery. 3) Of the Goths, an old Germanic people, or their language. 4) (Goth, informal) a style of dress and music with black clothes and dark make-up.
its sense in the lessons: History and art lessons: Gothic cathedrals such as Notre-Dame in Paris and Westminster Abbey in London. Reading: a gothic novel or a gothic mood (crumbling house, storm, candlelight). Fonts: «Gothic» or blackletter writing in old books.
examples from the lessons: Westminster Abbey is built in the Gothic style. | Gothic windows have pointed tops. | The haunted castle in the story felt very gothic. | Her teenage cousin likes Goth music and black clothes. | We drew a Gothic cathedral with flying buttresses. | The old Bible was printed in Gothic letters. | The Goths were a people who fought against Rome.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually capital G for the building style and the people (Gothic, Goths); small g is often used for the spooky mood (a gothic tale). Not every old church is Gothic; round arches are Romanesque/Norman.

part of speech: noun (a gypsy, gypsies; also gipsy, gipsies); adjective (gypsy)
meaning for a pupil: 1) An old name for a person of the Romani people (Roma), whose ancestors came from India long ago and travelled through Europe; many Romani people still travel, many live in houses. 2) (in old books) anyone who lives a travelling life, moving in a caravan from place to place. 3) (adjective) of a travelling kind: a gypsy caravan.
its sense in the lessons: History and community lessons: Romani people have their own language and culture and have often been treated unfairly; many were killed in the Holocaust. In the UK «Gypsy, Roma and Traveller» communities use the word for themselves, but some people find «gypsy» hurtful, so «Romani» or «Roma» is safer. In The Wind in the Willows Toad's painted «gipsy caravan» is his new craze, and later he sells a horse to a gipsy.
examples from the lessons: Toad bought a bright yellow gipsy caravan. | The old gypsy caravans were painted red and gold. | Toad sold the barge-woman's horse to a gipsy. | Romani people, once called gypsies, have their own language. | In history we learned how Roma people were treated in the war. | The story told of travelling folk who lived in caravans. | Some families in Ireland and Britain are Travellers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spellings: gypsy (usual today) and gipsy (old, used in The Wind in the Willows). The word comes from «Egyptian», a wrong old belief about where they came from. Be careful: some people find «gypsy» rude; «Romani» or «Roma» is respectful. Do not use it as an insult. «Gyp» (to cheat) is offensive — avoid it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (old, formal, often plural) Clothes, especially special clothes worn for a job or ceremony.
its sense in the lessons: A very rare word found in old books, often for a joke because it sounds grand. In The Wind in the Willows Toad escapes from prison in the washerwoman's dress, and the old-fashioned words make his disguise sound funny.
examples from the lessons: The knight put on his habiliments for battle. | The actor wore the habiliments of a king. | Toad dressed in the washerwoman's habiliments. | «What strange habiliments!» laughed the Rat. | The priest's habiliments were white and gold. | The old book described the lady's fine habiliments.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Very formal and old-fashioned; in everyday English say «clothes». Usually plural. Say «ha-BIL-i-ment».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A rug laid on the floor in front of a fireplace.
its sense in the lessons: Found in stories of cosy homes, especially older British ones with open fires. In The Wind in the Willows the animals warm themselves on the hearthrug by Badger's fire. In Alice in Wonderland Alice, grown very tall, jokes about posting presents to her own foot: «Alice's Right Foot, Esq., Hearthrug, near the Fender». It tells the reader that a scene is warm, safe and homely.
examples from the lessons: The dog stretched out on the hearthrug. | The children sat on the hearthrug toasting bread. | Mole curled up on Badger's hearthrug. | The cat licked its paws on the hearthrug. | A spark jumped from the fire onto the hearthrug. | Grandma's hearthrug was red and soft.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Compound: hearth (the floor of a fireplace) + rug. Say «HARTH-rug»: hearth rhymes with «path», not with «earth». Safety: a fireguard stops sparks burning the rug.

part of speech: verb (heave, heaves, heaved, heaving; hove in sailing); noun (a heave, heaves)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To lift, pull or push something heavy with great effort: they heaved the box into the van. 2) To throw something heavy. 3) To rise and fall in a strong, steady way: the sea heaved; his chest heaved. 4) To heave a sigh: to sigh deeply. 5) To feel as if you are going to be sick; to retch. 6) (sailing) «heave to» = stop a ship; «hove into view» = came into sight. 7) (noun) a big pull or push: one more heave!
its sense in the lessons: Everyday: helping to lift things, «heave-ho!» when pulling together. Stories of the sea: «heave the anchor», «the ship hove to». PE and science: forces — heaving is pushing or pulling with a big force. «Heave a sigh of relief» shows a feeling ending.
examples from the lessons: They heaved the heavy suitcase into the car. | «One, two, three, heave!» | The sea heaved under the little boat. | She heaved a sigh of relief. | Mole heaved himself up the bank. | His shoulders heaved as he sobbed. | A ship hove into view on the horizon. | The smell made my stomach heave. | The Rat gave the boat a heave and it floated free.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: heaved (usual); «hove» only in sailing phrases. «Heave-ho» is a shout for pulling together. Bend your knees when lifting heavy things to protect your back.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A lively dance, often danced by one sailor, connected with sailors and the sea. 2) The music for this dance. 3) An old wind instrument made with a horn.
its sense in the lessons: Music and dance lessons; sea stories. The «Sailor's Hornpipe» is a famous tune. In Alice in Wonderland the Mock Turtle and the Gryphon dance the Lobster Quadrille, another dance of the sea. The Sea Rat in The Wind in the Willows comes from the world of sailors.
examples from the lessons: The sailors danced a hornpipe on deck. | We learned the Sailor's Hornpipe in music. | The fiddler played a fast hornpipe. | Irish dancers often dance hornpipes too. | The jolly sailor jumped up for a hornpipe. | The old instrument called a hornpipe was made from a cow's horn.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Compound: horn + pipe. Plural: hornpipes. A dance and a tune, also an old instrument.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A small, rounded hill or mound of earth, grass or snow; a hump in the ground. 2) A ridge in a field of ice.
its sense in the lessons: Geography and nature words for small lumps in the land. In The Wind in the Willows Mole and the Rat struggle through the snowy Wild Wood over hummocks and hollows before they find Badger's door. In stories hummocks make a landscape bumpy and good for hiding.
examples from the lessons: The rabbit hid behind a grassy hummock. | The marsh was full of mossy hummocks. | Mole stumbled over a hummock in the snow. | We sat on a hummock to eat our sandwiches. | Polar bears walk across the ice hummocks. | The children rolled down the little hummock.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: hummocks. Similar: mound, knoll, hillock, hump. Smaller than a hill.

part of speech: noun (a hurdle, hurdles); verb (hurdle, hurdles, hurdled, hurdling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (sport) Hurdles are a race in which runners jump over a row of light frames: the 100 metres hurdles. 2) A hurdle is one of those frames. 3) A problem or difficulty you must get past: the last hurdle before the holidays. 4) (old, farming) A movable fence panel of woven sticks, used to pen sheep. 5) (verb) to jump over something while running.
its sense in the lessons: PE and sports day: hurdles races; Olympics. Everyday figurative sense: «we've cleared the first hurdle». History and farming: wattle hurdles for sheep pens, as in old country scenes. In The Wind in the Willows the countryside has hedges and hurdles.
examples from the lessons: She won the girls' hurdles on sports day. | He knocked over the last hurdle. | Learning to read was a big hurdle for him. | We cleared the first hurdle and got the money for the trip. | The farmer moved the hurdles to make a new sheep pen. | The horse jumped the hurdles easily. | Our class practised hurdles in PE.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Hurdles» (plural) can name the race and takes a singular verb: «Hurdles is my best event.» Do not confuse with «huddle» (to crowd together). Verb: to hurdle a fence.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Not able or not willing to believe something; showing that you do not believe it: an incredulous look.
its sense in the lessons: Used in stories to show a character's surprise and disbelief: «You did WHAT?» she asked, incredulous. Alice is often incredulous at the strange rules of Wonderland. In reading, it describes a reaction, not a thing.
examples from the lessons: Alice gave the Hatter an incredulous look. | «A talking toad?» said the boy, incredulous. | The crowd was incredulous when the small team won. | She listened with an incredulous smile. | Mum was incredulous that I had tidied my room. | The Rat stared at Toad, incredulous. | He shook his head, incredulous.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Used for people and their looks or voices. Do not confuse with «incredible» (hard to believe — used for things): the story was incredible, so I was incredulous. Noun: incredulity. Adverb: incredulously.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Letting someone have or do what they want, even when it might not be good for them; too kind and not strict: indulgent parents. 2) Treating yourself to something pleasant: an indulgent chocolate cake.
its sense in the lessons: Used in stories and family life about grown-ups who spoil children or friends who forgive too easily. In The Wind in the Willows the Rat is often indulgent to Toad and Mole, and Badger is less so. Related: self-indulgent (doing too much of what you like).
examples from the lessons: Her indulgent grandparents let her stay up late. | The Rat smiled in an indulgent way at Mole's excitement. | An indulgent teacher might let the class skip homework. | We had an indulgent breakfast of pancakes and cream. | Toad's friends had been too indulgent with him. | The king was indulgent to his spoiled son.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: indulge (indulge a child, indulge in sweets). Noun: indulgence. In church history «indulgences» were pardons sold by some in the Middle Ages, which Martin Luther protested against.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A stand or tray on a desk that holds pots of ink, pens and sometimes sand or a pen-wiper, used in the days of dip pens.
its sense in the lessons: History word from school desks and offices before ballpoint pens. In Alice in Wonderland, at the trial, the Queen throws an inkstand at Bill the Lizard; when ink trickles down his face he can use it to write with his finger. It tells the reader of an old-fashioned desk or office.
examples from the lessons: The Queen threw an inkstand at the poor Lizard. | Grandpa's desk still has a brass inkstand. | Old school desks had a hole for the inkwell. | The clerk dipped his pen and put it back in the inkstand. | A silver inkstand stood on the king's desk. | In the museum we saw an inkstand with two glass pots.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Inkstand (the whole stand) is not quite the same as inkwell (the pot of ink set into a desk), but people often mix them. Plural: inkstands.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Always wanting more and never satisfied: an insatiable appetite; an insatiable curiosity.
its sense in the lessons: Used in stories and science (an insatiable predator) and about people who never stop wanting to know or have more. In Kipling's Just So Stories the Elephant's Child is «full of 'satiable curtiosity» — Kipling's playful way of saying insatiable curiosity: he asks so many questions that he goes to the great grey-green, greasy Limpopo River to find out what the Crocodile has for dinner.
examples from the lessons: The Elephant's Child had an insatiable curiosity. | Caterpillars have an insatiable appetite. | She has an insatiable love of books. | The dragon's hunger for gold was insatiable. | Toad had an insatiable craze for new things. | Babies seem to have an insatiable need for milk. | His thirst for knowledge was insatiable.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say «in-SAY-sha-bul». It means «cannot be satisfied» (in- = not, sati- = enough). Kipling's «'satiable curtiosity» is a joke spelling, not standard English.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Not able to be changed, cancelled or taken back once it is done: an irrevocable decision.
its sense in the lessons: Used in formal writing, law and serious moments in stories: an irrevocable step, an irrevocable promise. It tells the reader there is no going back. In life lessons: some choices, like hurtful words, can feel irrevocable, so think first.
examples from the lessons: The judge's decision was irrevocable. | Once the letter was posted, the choice felt irrevocable. | Cutting down the old tree was an irrevocable mistake. | The king made an irrevocable promise. | Some damage to nature is irrevocable. | He took the irrevocable step of leaving home.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say «ir-REV-uh-kuh-bul» (stress on REV), not «irre-VOKE-able». Formal. Opposite: revocable. Similar: final, permanent.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A short, close-fitting jacket without sleeves, often of leather, worn by men in the 1500s and 1600s. 2) A modern sleeveless jacket, especially a work or high-visibility one.
its sense in the lessons: History lessons about Tudor and Stuart clothes; costumes in plays and stories of olden days. In stories it tells the reader about a character's old-fashioned dress, such as a soldier or a woodman.
examples from the lessons: The Tudor man wore a leather jerkin over his shirt. | For the play I wore a brown jerkin and a hat. | The archers wore jerkins and carried longbows. | Builders wear bright yellow jerkins on site. | In the picture, the knave wears a red jerkin. | The woodcutter's jerkin was torn by brambles.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: jerkins. A historical clothing word; today «vest» (UK: «waistcoat» or «gilet») is used for similar clothes.

part of speech: verb (jostle, jostles, jostled, jostling); noun (a jostle)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To push and bump against people in a crowd. 2) To compete hard for something: players jostling for a place in the team.
its sense in the lessons: Everyday and safety: crowds jostle at the school gate or on the bus; take care on stairs. Stories: busy markets, crowds of animals. Figurative: teams jostling for first place. In Alice in Wonderland, the animals crowd and jostle around Alice after the Pool of Tears.
examples from the lessons: People jostled to get onto the train. | The animals jostled each other on the river bank. | Please don't jostle in the lunch queue. | The ducklings jostled for the bread. | Fans jostled to see the singer. | Three teams are jostling for the top spot. | I was jostled and dropped my ice cream.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Silent t: say «JOS-ul». Regular verb: jostled, jostling. Similar: shove, push, elbow, barge.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To move along in a clumsy, bouncing, loose way, like a big puppy or a rabbit.
its sense in the lessons: A fun descriptive word in stories about animals: dogs lollop, hares lollop, a big friendly creature lollops along. It paints a picture of floppy, happy movement. Kipling uses this kind of bounding movement for the Kangaroo in the Just So Stories, chased by Yellow-Dog Dingo.
examples from the lessons: The big puppy came lolloping across the garden. | The hare lolloped away over the field. | Rabbits lollop when they are not in a hurry. | The kangaroo lolloped across the plain. | A shaggy dog lolloped up to say hello. | The baby elephant lolloped behind its mother.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal. Spelled with one p in the past: lolloped, lolloping (stress on LOL). Similar: bound, lope, bounce.

part of speech: verb (mull, mulls, mulled, mulling); noun (Mull — a place name)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To mull over something: to think about it carefully for some time. 2) To heat wine, cider or juice with sugar and spices: mulled wine. 3) (a name) Mull is a large island off the west coast of Scotland; «mull» is also a Scottish word for a headland, as in the Mull of Kintyre.
its sense in the lessons: Everyday phrase: «Let me mull it over» — I need time to think. Winter and Christmas: mulled wine, mulled apple juice. Geography: the Isle of Mull in the Hebrides.
examples from the lessons: I'll mull it over and tell you tomorrow. | Mole mulled over the Rat's words. | She sat mulling over the maths problem. | Dad made mulled apple juice for the children. | The smell of mulled wine filled the market. | We went to the Isle of Mull to see puffins. | Don't mull too long — the bus is coming!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually «mull over» or «mull something over». Mulled wine contains alcohol and is for grown-ups; mulled juice is for children. Not the same as «mule» (an animal).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A brown, speckled bird that hunts moths at dusk and at night and makes a long, whirring, churring song. It sleeps on the ground or along a branch in the day, hidden by its camouflage.
its sense in the lessons: Science and nature: a great example of camouflage — its feathers look like bark and dead leaves. Nightjars come to Britain and Europe in summer from Africa. In North America related birds are the whip-poor-will and nighthawk. In stories, its strange churring makes a summer night feel mysterious.
examples from the lessons: We heard a nightjar churring on the heath. | A nightjar's feathers look just like dead leaves. | Nightjars catch moths in the dark. | The nightjar sat so still we nearly stepped on it. | In autumn the nightjars fly back to Africa. | The ranger took us on a walk to listen for nightjars.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Compound: night + jar (an old word for a harsh noise). Plural: nightjars. Old names: goatsucker (from a myth that it drank goats' milk — not true).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Oats that have been crushed or ground, used to make porridge, oatcakes and biscuits. 2) (USA, Canada) Hot porridge made from oats. 3) A pale greyish-brown colour, like oats: an oatmeal jumper.
its sense in the lessons: Everyday food word: oatmeal for breakfast, oatmeal cookies. In science and health: oats give slow energy and fibre. Colour words in shops: oatmeal carpet. Old stories of Scotland and the north of England mention oatmeal as a main food.
examples from the lessons: I eat a bowl of oatmeal before school. | Gran makes oatmeal cookies with raisins. | The Scots made oatcakes from oatmeal. | The sofa is an oatmeal colour. | Add milk to the oatmeal and stir. | Oatmeal keeps you full all morning.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: some oatmeal, a bowl of oatmeal. In the UK «porridge» is the cooked dish and «oatmeal» the ground oats; in North America «oatmeal» is used for both.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The state of being completely forgotten: the old song fell into oblivion. 2) The state of not knowing or noticing what is happening around you, as in deep sleep. 3) Being destroyed or wiped out completely.
its sense in the lessons: Used in stories, history and poems: famous names that «faded into oblivion», someone who «drank himself into oblivion». In everyday talk and sport: «the team was knocked into oblivion». It tells the reader something has disappeared or been forgotten.
examples from the lessons: The old castle had fallen into oblivion. | Many toys from long ago have passed into oblivion. | Tired out, Mole sank into the oblivion of sleep. | The tiny shop was saved from oblivion by the new owners. | The planet in the film was blasted into oblivion. | Her brave story should not be lost to oblivion.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable; no «an». Adjective: oblivious (not noticing): «He was oblivious to the rain.»

meaning for a pupil: 1) Cruel and unfair, keeping people down and taking away their freedom: an oppressive ruler. 2) Of weather: hot, heavy and airless, making you feel uncomfortable. 3) Making you feel worried, sad or weighed down: an oppressive silence.
its sense in the lessons: History and citizenship: oppressive kings, laws and governments; people fighting for freedom. Science and geography: oppressive heat before a thunderstorm. Stories: an oppressive silence in the Wild Wood.
examples from the lessons: The people rose up against the oppressive king. | The heat was oppressive before the storm broke. | Mole felt the oppressive silence of the Wild Wood. | Slavery was an oppressive and cruel system. | The air in the attic was hot and oppressive. | An oppressive feeling of dread filled the room.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: oppress (to treat cruelly). Noun: oppression; person: oppressor. Double p, double s.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To make someone or something seem less important by being more successful or noticeable: her sister overshadowed her. 2) To cast a shadow over something; to tower over it. 3) To make a happy time sadder: the rain overshadowed the party.
its sense in the lessons: Used in everyday talk, news and stories: one event overshadowing another, a tall building overshadowing a garden. In the Bible the Angel tells Mary that the power of God will «overshadow» her. In stories it shows rivalry or a darker mood.
examples from the lessons: The big oak overshadows our garden. | His win was overshadowed by an injury. | She felt overshadowed by her clever brother. | The tall flats overshadowed the little houses. | Worry about the test overshadowed the weekend. | Toad's boasting overshadowed the others' good work.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Compound: over + shadow. Regular verb. Often used in the passive: «was overshadowed by».

part of speech: noun (palaver — uncountable or a palaver, informal); verb (palaver — old)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal, UK) A lot of fuss and bother about something unimportant: what a palaver! 2) (old) Long talk or chatter. 3) (old) A long meeting or talk between groups of people, especially between traders and local people long ago.
its sense in the lessons: Everyday British talk: «What a palaver just to get a passport!» In older books and adventure stories, a palaver is a meeting to talk things over. It tells the reader there is too much talk and fuss.
examples from the lessons: What a palaver getting the dog into the car! | Mum said the school concert was a lot of palaver. | Stop all this palaver and get your shoes on! | The chiefs held a long palaver by the river. | There was a great palaver over who sat where. | It's too much palaver to bake bread every day.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal, mainly UK. Say «pa-LAH-ver». Comes from Portuguese «palavra» (word). Similar: fuss, carry-on, rigmarole.

part of speech: noun (parchment — uncountable; a parchment, parchments for a document)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A material for writing on, made long ago from the thin, dried skin of a sheep, goat or calf. 2) A document written on it: an old parchment. 3) Thick, stiff, yellowish paper made to look like it (parchment paper); also baking paper.
its sense in the lessons: History lessons: medieval books, charters and Magna Carta (1215) were written on parchment. Stories: treasure maps and old scrolls. In Alice in Wonderland the White Rabbit unrolls a parchment scroll to read out the accusation at the trial. Cooking: line the tin with baking parchment.
examples from the lessons: Magna Carta was written on parchment. | The White Rabbit unrolled the parchment scroll. | The pirate's map was drawn on old parchment. | Monks copied books onto parchment by hand. | Line the cake tin with baking parchment. | The old man's skin looked like parchment. | We made our certificates look like parchment.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable as a material (a sheet of parchment); countable for documents (old parchments). «Vellum» is fine parchment made from calfskin.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) An important or famous person. 2) A character in a play or story.
its sense in the lessons: Used in older stories and formal writing, sometimes with a smile, to make someone sound grand: «a very great personage». Alice meets many odd personages in Wonderland, such as the King and Queen of Hearts. Toad thinks of himself as an important personage.
examples from the lessons: A royal personage visited our town. | The Duchess was a very grand personage. | Toad imagined himself a famous personage. | Many great personages came to the wedding. | The play has only four personages. | The mayor was the most important personage at the fair.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal and a bit old-fashioned; in everyday English say «important person». Do not confuse with «personal» or «parsonage» (a priest's house).

part of speech: verb (pettifog, pettifogs, pettifogged, pettifogging — old, rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (old) To argue about small, unimportant details in a fussy way. 2) (old) To act as a petty, tricky lawyer who works on small, mean cases.
its sense in the lessons: Very rare; found in old books, mostly as «pettifogging» (fussy about tiny details) and «pettifogger» (a petty, tricky lawyer). In stories it describes a fussy, mean-minded person who argues about nothing, like the court in Alice's trial.
examples from the lessons: Stop pettifogging about the rules and let's play! | The pettifogging clerk counted every penny. | He was called a pettifogger by the angry judge. | The old lawyer would pettifog for hours over a comma. | Don't pettifog — the main idea is right.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Rare and old-fashioned. Commonest form: the adjective «pettifogging». Related to «petty» (small, unimportant).

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a cross, sulky, childish way, as when someone is easily annoyed about small things.
its sense in the lessons: Used in stories to describe how a character speaks or acts: «I don't care!» she said pettishly. Alice in Wonderland uses it for grumpy characters and for Alice herself when she is fed up. It tells the reader the character is behaving like a sulky child.
examples from the lessons: «I won't!» said the little boy pettishly. | The Duchess answered pettishly. | She tossed her head pettishly. | Toad kicked the stone pettishly. | «Oh, leave me alone,» he said pettishly. | The spoiled prince waved the servant away pettishly.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb of «pettish» (bad-tempered over small things). Related to «pet» in the old sense «a fit of sulking» («in a pet»). Similar: crossly, sulkily, peevishly.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Of a horse or other animal: having large patches of two colours, usually black and white. 2) (noun) A piebald horse or pony.
its sense in the lessons: Used in stories and about horses and ponies, and in nature lessons about animal colours. Gypsy and Traveller horses are often piebald or skewbald (brown and white). In stories it helps the reader picture an animal.
examples from the lessons: The children rode a piebald pony. | A piebald horse stood in the field. | Our cat is piebald, black and white. | The travellers' piebald horses grazed by the road. | She drew a piebald pony with big patches. | The circus had a piebald horse with a white face.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Piebald = black and white patches; skewbald = white with brown or another colour. Pie- comes from the magpie, a black and white bird.

part of speech: verb (pinion, pinions, pinioned, pinioning); noun (a pinion, pinions)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (verb) To hold or tie someone's arms tightly so they cannot move them. 2) (verb) To cut or tie a bird's wing feathers so it cannot fly. 3) (noun, poetic) A bird's wing, or the outer part of a wing. 4) (noun, machines) A small gear wheel with teeth that fits into a larger wheel or a toothed bar (rack and pinion).
its sense in the lessons: Stories: a prisoner is pinioned by guards. In The Wind in the Willows the policemen seize Toad and drag him off to prison. Science and design: a «rack and pinion» turns round movement into straight movement, as in a car's steering. Poetry: «on eagle's pinions».
examples from the lessons: The guards pinioned the thief's arms. | Toad was seized and pinioned by two policemen. | The eagle spread its pinions. | A rack and pinion moves the train up the mountain. | The swans' wings were pinioned so they could not fly away. | He was pinioned to the ground by the bigger boy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Not the same as «opinion». A pinion in a machine is the smaller of two gears.

part of speech: adjective (poky, pokier, pokiest — informal; also pokey)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) Of a room or house: small and cramped, with not enough space. 2) (USA, informal) Slow and dull. 3) (noun, USA slang, «the pokey») jail.
its sense in the lessons: Everyday talk about homes and rooms: «a poky little flat». In stories it tells the reader a place is tight and uncomfortable. In The Wind in the Willows Mole's home, Mole End, is small but cosy, and Mole worries the Rat will think it poky and shabby.
examples from the lessons: They lived in a poky little flat above the shop. | My bedroom is a bit poky. | The car was poky and slow. | Mole feared the Rat would think his house was poky. | It was hard to cook in the poky kitchen. | We squeezed into a poky little café.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal. Also spelled pokey (especially in the USA). Not the same as «pokey» meaning jail in American slang.

meaning for a pupil: 1) One of the long sloping beams of wood that hold up a roof. 2) (phrase) «packed to the rafters» = completely full of people or things.
its sense in the lessons: Building and design lessons about roofs. Stories: owls, bats and swallows nest in the rafters of barns; hams hang from the rafters of an old kitchen, as in Badger's house in The Wind in the Willows. «The hall was packed to the rafters» means very full. «The cheers shook the rafters.»
examples from the lessons: Swallows built a nest in the rafters of the barn. | Hams and bunches of herbs hung from the rafters. | The hall was packed to the rafters for the concert. | We could see the old wooden rafters in the attic. | An owl sat on a rafter, watching. | The builders fixed new rafters on the roof.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually plural: rafters. A roof «beam» lies flat or slopes; rafters slope from the ridge to the walls.

part of speech: adjective (reverberating); the -ing form of the verb reverberate (reverberate, reverberates, reverberated, reverberating)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Of a sound: echoing again and again, loudly, filling a space. 2) Having effects that go on spreading for a long time: the news is still reverberating.
its sense in the lessons: Science lessons on sound and echoes: sound bouncing off hard walls in halls, caves and tunnels. Stories: the reverberating boom of a drum or of thunder. In news: decisions that reverberate around the world.
examples from the lessons: The thunder was reverberating round the hills. | Our voices kept reverberating in the cave. | The drum's boom went reverberating through the hall. | The bell's reverberating sound made the birds fly up. | The news is still reverberating around the school. | A reverberating shout came from the tunnel.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: reverberate; noun: reverberation (an echo). It is a stronger, longer word for «echoing».

part of speech: noun (a Romany, Romanies; Romany — the language); adjective (Romany, also Romani)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A member of the Romani people (Roma), who came from India long ago and spread through Europe and the world; some travel, many live settled lives. 2) Their language, Romani (Romany), which is related to languages of India. 3) (adjective) of the Romani people: Romany culture, a Romany caravan.
its sense in the lessons: History and community lessons: Romani people have their own language, music and traditions, and have often been treated unfairly; many were murdered in the Holocaust. «Romani» or «Roma» is the respectful name; the older word «gypsy» can hurt. In old books, such as The Wind in the Willows, Romany life is linked with painted caravans and horses.
examples from the lessons: Romany families have travelled Europe for hundreds of years. | The Romany language is related to Hindi. | We listened to Romany music in class. | Romani people celebrate International Roma Day on 8 April. | Her grandmother was a Romany and spoke the language. | An old Romany caravan stood in the museum.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital R: Romany, Romani, Roma. Spellings Romany and Romani are both used; «Romani» is preferred by many today. Not the same as «Romania» (a country) or «Roman».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A very small stream or brook. 2) A small channel of running water, such as rain running down a path or gutter.
its sense in the lessons: Nature and geography words for water: smaller than a stream. In stories it gives a quiet, detailed picture of the countryside, like the ditches and little streams along the river bank in The Wind in the Willows.
examples from the lessons: A little runnel trickled down the hillside. | Rain made runnels in the sandy path. | We built a dam across the runnel. | Runnels of water ran off the roof. | The frog sat by a muddy runnel. | Sweat ran in runnels down his face.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: runnels. Smaller than a brook or stream; similar words: rill, rivulet, trickle.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Cheerful and hopeful about what will happen, even when things are hard. 2) (old, literary) Of a face: rosy, red. 3) (old, history) In old medicine, a person «ruled» by blood, thought to be cheerful.
its sense in the lessons: Formal and literary. Used in news and grown-up talk: «not very sanguine about our chances». In stories it describes an optimistic character, like Toad, who is always sure the next plan will work. History: old doctors believed in four «humours» — this was wrong.
examples from the lessons: Toad was sanguine about his chances of escape. | The coach was sanguine about the next match. | She is not sanguine about the weather for sports day. | He had a sanguine, rosy face. | Despite the rain, Dad remained sanguine. | The doctors were sanguine that she would recover.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; in everyday talk say «hopeful» or «optimistic». Say «SANG-gwin». It comes from Latin «sanguis» (blood). Trap: it does NOT mean bloody or bloodthirsty (that is «sanguinary»).

part of speech: verb (scrabble, scrabbles, scrabbled, scrabbling); noun (Scrabble — a game)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To scratch or grope about quickly with your hands or claws, looking for something or trying to hold on: he scrabbled in his pocket for a coin. 2) To struggle or hurry to get something. 3) (Scrabble, a name) a board game in which players make words with letter tiles and score points.
its sense in the lessons: Stories: animals scrabble at the earth; Mole scrabbles and digs his way up from his home in the first chapter of The Wind in the Willows; Alice scrabbles to keep hold. Everyday: playing Scrabble at home, a good game for spelling and maths (adding scores, double and triple word squares).
examples from the lessons: Mole scrabbled and scraped his way up to the sunlight. | The dog scrabbled at the door. | She scrabbled in her bag for her keys. | The kitten scrabbled up the curtain. | We played Scrabble after dinner. | «Quiz» on a triple word score earned lots of points in Scrabble. | He scrabbled for a handhold on the rocks.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double b. The game is a brand name, written with a capital S. Similar verbs: scramble, scratch, grope. Not the same as «scribble» (to write messily).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A sailor, especially one who is not an officer. 2) A person who is good at sailing a ship: a fine seaman.
its sense in the lessons: Used in history and sea stories, and in navies: «Able Seaman». In The Wind in the Willows the Sea Rat is a travelling seaman who tells the Water Rat of ports and sea voyages and almost tempts him to leave the river. In geography: sailors on cargo ships today.
examples from the lessons: The old seaman told stories of faraway ports. | The Sea Rat was a seafaring seaman. | Every seaman on board helped with the sails. | He was an Able Seaman in the Royal Navy. | The seamen pulled up the anchor. | A good seaman can read the weather.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: seamen. Today «sailor» or «seafarer» is more usual and includes women.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Curving and winding, with many bends, like a snake or a river. 2) Moving in a smooth, twisting, graceful way.
its sense in the lessons: Used in descriptive writing and geography (a sinuous river, a sinuous road). Science: snakes and eels move in sinuous waves. In The Wind in the Willows the river is described as a sleek, sinuous, full-bodied animal, chasing and chuckling, which enchants Mole.
examples from the lessons: The river was sinuous and full of bends. | The snake moved in a sinuous way. | A sinuous path wound up the mountain. | Mole had never seen such a sleek, sinuous river. | The dancer's arms made sinuous shapes. | Eels swim with sinuous movements.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say «SIN-yoo-us». Comes from Latin «sinus» (a curve). Not the same as «sinewy» (strong and muscly).

part of speech: noun (a sluice, sluices); verb (sluice, sluices, sluiced, sluicing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A gate or channel that controls how much water flows in a river, canal or mill stream (also called a sluice gate). 2) (verb) To wash something with lots of water: sluice down the yard. 3) (verb) Of water: to pour or rush out.
its sense in the lessons: Geography and science: sluices control floods and water levels on rivers and canals, and turn mill wheels. In The Wind in the Willows the river runs past weirs, mills and locks. Everyday: farmers sluice out a cowshed; rain sluices down the street.
examples from the lessons: The farmer opened the sluice to let water into the field. | Water rushed through the sluice gate. | They sluiced down the muddy yard with a hose. | Rain sluiced down the windows. | The miller closed the sluice to stop the wheel. | Engineers built sluices to stop the town flooding.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say «sloos». Silent ui sound: s-l-oo-s. Safety: sluices and weirs have very strong currents — never swim near them.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A building or room where meat or fish is hung and smoked over a slow fire to flavour it and keep it from going bad.
