its sense in the lessons: History and food science: smoking was a way to preserve food before fridges, using smoke and drying. Today smokehouses make smoked salmon, kippers and bacon. In farm and village stories it is one of the outbuildings.
examples from the lessons: The fish hung in the smokehouse for two days. | Grandpa's farm had an old wooden smokehouse. | Smoked salmon comes from a smokehouse. | The kippers were made in a smokehouse by the harbour. | Before fridges, many farms had a smokehouse. | The smokehouse smelled of oak smoke.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Compound: smoke + house. Plural: smokehouses.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Giving off little or no smoke when burned: smokeless fuel. 2) Without smoke: a smokeless sky. 3) (law, UK) A «smokeless zone» is an area where only fuels that make little smoke may be burned.
its sense in the lessons: Science and history: after the deadly London smog of 1952, Britain passed the Clean Air Act and made smokeless zones, so people burned smokeless coal. Everyday: «smokeless» fuels and stoves are better for the air. In the old days of steam, «smokeless» meant a very clean fire.
examples from the lessons: Our town is a smokeless zone. | Dad bought smokeless fuel for the stove. | Smokeless coal helped clean the air in cities. | The sky above the factory was smokeless at last. | Modern stoves are almost smokeless. | The cosy room had a bright, smokeless fire.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Suffix -less means «without»: smokeless = without smoke. «Smokeless tobacco» is chewed tobacco — it is still harmful.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Firm and loyal; not changing in what you believe or in who you support: a steadfast friend. 2) Firm and not moving: a steadfast gaze.
its sense in the lessons: Used in stories, poems, the Bible and talk about values. It praises loyalty and faithfulness. Hans Christian Andersen wrote «The Steadfast Tin Soldier». In the Bible, «steadfast love» is used for God's faithful love. In The Wind in the Willows Rat, Mole and Badger stay steadfast friends to Toad.
examples from the lessons: Rat was a steadfast friend to Mole. | The tin soldier stayed steadfast to the end. | She was steadfast in her belief that he was innocent. | The Psalms speak of God's steadfast love. | The dog waited, steadfast, by the door. | He gave her a steadfast look.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb: steadfastly. Old spelling: stedfast. Similar: loyal, faithful, unwavering. Opposite: fickle, wavering.

part of speech: adjective (stricken); old past participle of the verb strike
meaning for a pupil: 1) Badly affected by something bad, such as illness, sadness or disaster: a stricken ship, a grief-stricken family. 2) Showing great shock or pain: a stricken face. 3) (in compounds) panic-stricken, terror-stricken, poverty-stricken, grief-stricken.
its sense in the lessons: Used in news and stories about disasters and strong feelings: the stricken town after the earthquake, a stricken look. Compounds tell the reader what caused the suffering. Toad is «panic-stricken» when he thinks the police are coming.
examples from the lessons: Rescue boats went out to the stricken ship. | The grief-stricken family held each other. | Toad was panic-stricken at the sound of the police. | Aid was sent to the flood-stricken villages. | She gave him a stricken look. | The poverty-stricken children had no shoes. | The stricken plane landed safely.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Today the normal past form of strike is «struck»; «stricken» survives mostly as an adjective. «Struck by lightning», but «panic-stricken».

part of speech: verb (strive, strives, strove or strived, striven or strived, striving)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To try very hard to do or get something, over a long time: strive to do your best. 2) To struggle or fight against something.
its sense in the lessons: Common in school mottoes, assemblies and formal writing: «We strive for excellence.» In values lessons: striving means working hard and not giving up. In the Bible and hymns: strive to do good. In stories: heroes strive against danger.
examples from the lessons: We strive to be kind to everyone. | She strove to finish the race. | Our school motto is «Strive and Succeed». | The team strives to improve every week. | Mole strove to keep up with the Rat. | Scientists strive to find cures for diseases. | They strove against the storm all night.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular: strive, strove, striven (old) or strived (newer, especially in the USA). Formal; everyday word: «try hard». Noun: strife (fighting) is related but different in meaning.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a sulky way: quiet, cross and unwilling to be friendly because you are upset or did not get your way.
its sense in the lessons: Used in stories to show grumpy, childish moods. Alice in Wonderland: the Dormouse and other creatures often speak sulkily; Toad sulks when he cannot have his way. It tells the reader a character is upset but not shouting.
examples from the lessons: «I don't want to,» he said sulkily. | The Dormouse answered sulkily. | She sat sulkily in the corner. | Toad sulkily agreed to give up motor cars. | My brother sulkily put his toys away. | The cat walked off sulkily after its bath.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb of «sulky». Verb: sulk (sulk, sulked, sulking). Noun: a sulk («in a sulk»). Spelling: sulky → sulkily (y changes to i).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Without sunlight; dark or dull: a sunless day; the sunless depths of the sea. 2) Where the sun never reaches: a sunless cave.
its sense in the lessons: Science: the deep ocean is sunless, so no plants grow there; animals there make their own light. Poetry: Coleridge's «Kubla Khan» speaks of «caverns measureless to man / Down to a sunless sea». Stories: a sunless forest feels gloomy, like the Wild Wood in winter.
examples from the lessons: It was a cold, sunless day. | Strange fish live in the sunless deep sea. | The cave was damp and sunless. | Plants cannot grow in a sunless cellar. | The Wild Wood felt sunless and gloomy. | After a week of sunless weather, we longed for summer.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Suffix -less = without. Opposite: sunny, sunlit.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (literary, old) An area of short grass; a lawn or green field of turf.
its sense in the lessons: Found in poems and older stories describing the countryside: «a green sward». In The Wind in the Willows there are meadows and green banks by the river. In geography and farming, «sward» is used for the grass cover of a field.
examples from the lessons: The children ran across the green sward. | Sheep grazed on the sward by the river. | They spread a picnic on the sward. | The castle stood above a smooth sward. | Daisies dotted the sward. | The farmer checked the sward before letting the cows out.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Literary; everyday words: grass, lawn, turf. Say «swawd», rhyming with «ward»; the w is spoken, unlike in «sword».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Fairly tall; a bit taller than average.
its sense in the lessons: Used in describing people and things in stories and everyday life. The ending -ish means «a bit» or «rather»: tallish, smallish, brownish. It gives a rough, not exact, size.
examples from the lessons: He's a tallish boy with red hair. | A tallish tree stood by the gate. | The stranger was tallish and thin. | We need a tallish jar for the flowers. | My teacher is tallish. | A tallish heron waded in the shallows.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal; -ish makes the meaning less exact. Not used for exact measuring in maths: say the height in centimetres or inches instead.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A flash of lightning together with a crash of thunder. 2) Something sudden and shocking: the news came like a thunderbolt. 3) (myths) A bolt of lightning thrown as a weapon by a god, such as Zeus in Greek myths or Thor in Norse myths.
its sense in the lessons: Science: lightning is a giant spark of electricity; thunder is the sound it makes. Safety: in a storm stay indoors and away from tall trees. Myths: Zeus hurls thunderbolts. Stories: «like a thunderbolt» shows a big surprise.
examples from the lessons: A thunderbolt struck the old oak. | Zeus threw thunderbolts from Mount Olympus. | The news hit us like a thunderbolt. | Thor's hammer made thunder and lightning. | The thunderbolt lit up the whole sky. | Toad's arrest came like a thunderbolt to his friends.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Compound: thunder + bolt. Real lightning is not a solid object; «bolt» is just a picture. Myth: lightning never strikes the same place twice — false; tall buildings are struck many times.

part of speech: adjective (tinkling); noun (a tinkling); the -ing form of the verb tinkle (tinkle, tinkles, tinkled, tinkling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Making light, clear, ringing sounds, like a small bell or glass. 2) (noun) such a sound. 3) (informal, childish) Weeing (to tinkle).
its sense in the lessons: Descriptive writing: the tinkling of bells, a tinkling stream, tinkling laughter. Science: high, light sounds made by small vibrating objects. Music: a tinkling piano. At the end of Alice in Wonderland, Alice's sister dreams that the rattling teacups change to tinkling sheep-bells.
examples from the lessons: We heard the tinkling of a bell. | A tinkling stream ran through the wood. | Her tinkling laugh filled the room. | The ice was tinkling in the glasses. | The teacups changed to tinkling sheep-bells. | Wind chimes were tinkling in the breeze. | The little brook went tinkling over the stones.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Onomatopoeia: the word sounds like what it means. Verb: tinkle. «Give someone a tinkle» (old UK, informal) = phone them.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Betraying someone who trusts you; being disloyal or false. 2) Hidden danger: the treachery of thin ice.
its sense in the lessons: Stories, history and the Bible: Judas's treachery in betraying Jesus; traitors in history (the Gunpowder Plot). In The Wind in the Willows the weasels and stoats take Toad Hall while he is away. Values lessons: the opposite of loyalty and trust.
examples from the lessons: The king was shocked by the treachery of his own brother. | Judas's treachery is told in the Bible. | The weasels used treachery to seize Toad Hall. | Betraying a friend's secret is a kind of treachery. | Beware the treachery of the ice in spring. | The story is full of plots and treachery.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly uncountable. Adjective: treacherous (can mean disloyal, or dangerous: treacherous roads). Person: traitor. Opposite: loyalty.

part of speech: verb (twiddle, twiddles, twiddled, twiddling); noun (a twiddle)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To twist, turn or play with something with your fingers, often without thinking: twiddle a knob, twiddle your hair. 2) (phrase) «twiddle your thumbs» = to sit doing nothing, waiting, bored.
its sense in the lessons: Everyday: twiddling the dial on a radio, twiddling a pencil. «Twiddling our thumbs» = wasting time while waiting. In stories it shows nervousness or boredom.
examples from the lessons: Stop twiddling your hair! | He twiddled the knob to find the station. | We sat twiddling our thumbs while the bus was late. | She twiddled her pencil during the test. | Toad twiddled his thumbs, bored with the river. | Twiddle the dial to set the oven.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal. Regular verb. Similar: fiddle, twirl, twist.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The sum of two pennies in British money. 2) (old) A British coin worth two old pennies, used before 1971. 3) (informal, «not care twopence») to not care at all.
its sense in the lessons: Money and history lessons: before 1971 Britain had pounds, shillings and pence, with 12 pennies in a shilling. Today a 2p coin exists. In Mary Poppins the bird woman sells crumbs for «tuppence a bag». Maths: twopence = 2p; in old money, twopence was 2 of the 240 pennies in a pound.
examples from the lessons: The sweets cost twopence each. | «Feed the birds, tuppence a bag!» | I wouldn't give twopence for that old toy. | She found a twopence coin from 1930. | Twelve pennies made one shilling. | Two twopences make fourpence. | He didn't care twopence what they said.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say «TUP-pence». Often spelled «tuppence». Maths: twopence = 2 pence; old money: 12d = 1 shilling, 20 shillings = £1, so £1 = 240d. Today 100p = £1.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Not kind; not caring about other people's feelings or pain; hard-hearted. 2) (rare) Not able to feel anything physically, numb.
its sense in the lessons: Used in stories to describe cruel or cold characters: an unfeeling stepmother. Alice finds some Wonderland creatures unfeeling, such as the Queen who orders heads cut off. In The Wind in the Willows Toad calls the people who lock him up unfeeling. Values lessons: the opposite of empathy.
examples from the lessons: The unfeeling giant laughed at the crying child. | «How unfeeling of you!» cried Alice. | It was unfeeling to laugh at her fall. | The Queen was cold and unfeeling. | Toad complained that the world was unfeeling. | His fingers were unfeeling with cold.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Un- = not. Similar: heartless, cold, callous. Opposite: kind, caring, sympathetic.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal, mainly UK, old-fashioned) Too proud and full of yourself; acting as if you are better than others; uppity. 2) (cricket) A shot that goes up in the air and might be caught.
its sense in the lessons: Used in older British stories when someone gets above themselves: «Don't get uppish with me!» Toad gets uppish whenever things go well for him. In cricket commentary, an «uppish» shot is a risky one.
examples from the lessons: Toad became uppish after his escape. | «Don't you get uppish with me, young man!» | The new girl seemed a bit uppish at first. | His uppish manner annoyed the others. | The batsman played an uppish drive and was nearly caught. | Success made him uppish.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal and old-fashioned; more common today: «uppity», «snooty», «stuck-up».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Without success; in vain: he tried vainly to open the door. 2) (less common) In a vain, proud way about your looks or abilities.
its sense in the lessons: Used in stories about efforts that fail: Alice tries vainly to reach the key on the glass table. Common phrase: «in vain» (= with no result). In The Wind in the Willows Mole searches vainly for the path in the Wild Wood.
examples from the lessons: Alice tried vainly to reach the golden key. | He searched vainly for his lost glove. | Mole looked vainly for a way out of the wood. | The cat jumped vainly at the bird. | They waited vainly for the bus. | She vainly admired herself in every mirror.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «vain», which has two meanings: «useless» (in vain) and «too proud of your looks». Homophones: vain, vein (a blood tube), vane (a weathervane).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Wide, open grassland in southern Africa, with few trees, especially in South Africa.
its sense in the lessons: Geography: the veld is like the prairie in North America or the pampas in South America. Kipling's Just So Stories use the old spelling «veldt»: in «How the Leopard Got His Spots» the animals live on the sandy-yellow-brownish High Veldt before they move to the forest, and the Leopard and the Ethiopian follow them. Science: grassland animals such as zebra, antelope and lions.
examples from the lessons: Zebras graze on the African veld. | The Leopard hunted on the High Veldt. | The veld turned green after the rains. | Farmers keep cattle on the veld. | We read about the animals of the veld in geography. | The sun set over the wide, open veld.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say «felt» or «velt» (from Afrikaans/Dutch «field»). Old spelling: veldt, used by Kipling. Usually «the veld».

meaning for a pupil: 1) To be unsure and keep changing your mind; to hesitate: she wavered between the red and the blue. 2) To become weaker or less steady: his courage wavered. 3) To move or shake unsteadily: the candle flame wavered. 4) Of a voice: to shake.
its sense in the lessons: Used in stories to show doubt or fear: the hero's courage wavers. Everyday: wavering between choices. Values: «unwavering» loyalty. Science: a flame wavers in a draught. Toad's good promises always waver when he sees a motor car.
examples from the lessons: She wavered between the two puppies. | His voice wavered as he spoke. | Toad's good resolutions wavered at the sound of a horn. | The candle flame wavered in the wind. | Her courage never wavered. | He wavered at the edge of the diving board.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: wavered, wavering. Homophone trap: waver (to hesitate) and waiver (giving up a right, in law). Adjective: unwavering = steady, never doubting.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Without any purpose, plan or direction: they wandered aimlessly round town.
its sense in the lessons: Used in stories and everyday life about wandering, drifting or doing something with no goal. Alice wanders aimlessly in the wood. In The Wind in the Willows the boat drifts aimlessly down the river. In values lessons: having goals versus drifting.
examples from the lessons: We wandered aimlessly around the shops. | The boat drifted aimlessly on the river. | He kicked a stone aimlessly along the road. | Alice walked aimlessly through the wood. | The puppy ran aimlessly round the garden. | She flicked aimlessly through the magazine.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Built from aim + -less (without) + -ly. Adjective: aimless.

part of speech: noun (an alp, alps; the Alps — a name)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (the Alps, a name) The great range of high mountains in Europe, across France, Switzerland, Italy, Austria and others. 2) A high mountain, especially a snowy one. 3) In Switzerland, a high mountain meadow where cows graze in summer.
its sense in the lessons: Geography: the Alps include Mont Blanc and the Matterhorn; skiing, glaciers and mountain farming. History: Hannibal crossed the Alps with elephants. In stories it adds a sense of great height.
examples from the lessons: We went skiing in the Alps. | Mont Blanc is the highest peak in the Alps. | Hannibal crossed the Alps with elephants. | Cows graze on the alp in summer. | Snow lay on the alps all year. | Heidi lived with her grandfather in the Alps.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital A for the mountain range: the Alps. Adjective: Alpine (alpine flowers). The Southern Alps are in New Zealand; the Australian Alps in Australia.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a worried, nervous way: she waited anxiously for the results. 2) Wanting something very much and impatient for it: anxiously awaiting the holidays.
its sense in the lessons: Used often in stories to show worry: Alice looks anxiously around; the White Rabbit checks his watch anxiously. In everyday life: waiting anxiously for news. Health: if worry stops you sleeping or eating, talk to a grown-up you trust.
examples from the lessons: The White Rabbit looked anxiously at his watch. | We waited anxiously for the doctor. | She looked anxiously at the dark sky. | Alice asked anxiously, «Will I grow again?» | Mole peered anxiously into the Wild Wood. | The parents anxiously watched the rescue. | He checked his answers anxiously.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb of «anxious». Noun: anxiety. Spelling trap: anx-I-ous-ly.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Showing that you are thankful: an appreciative letter. 2) Enjoying and understanding the good qualities of something: an appreciative audience.
its sense in the lessons: Used in everyday life and values lessons: being appreciative means saying thank you and noticing what others do. Audiences give appreciative applause. In stories, it shows a polite, thankful character, like Mole enjoying Badger's supper.
examples from the lessons: We were very appreciative of your help. | The appreciative crowd clapped and cheered. | Mole was appreciative of Badger's warm kitchen. | She gave an appreciative smile. | Thank-you cards show you are appreciative. | The judges were appreciative of her painting.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say «a-PREE-shuh-tiv». Followed by «of»: appreciative of your help. Verb: appreciate; noun: appreciation.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (Scottish, dialect) Old. 2) In «Auld Lang Syne»: a Scottish song by Robert Burns, meaning «old long since», days long ago.
its sense in the lessons: A Scots word heard in songs, poems and in Scotland and Northern Ireland. «Auld Lang Syne» is sung at New Year (Hogmanay) all over the English-speaking world, holding hands in a circle. «Auld Reekie» («Old Smoky») is a nickname for Edinburgh.
examples from the lessons: We sang «Auld Lang Syne» at midnight. | «My auld granny lives in Aberdeen,» said Hamish. | Robert Burns wrote in Scots words like «auld». | The auld castle stood on the hill. | Edinburgh is called Auld Reekie. | Should auld acquaintance be forgot?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Scottish form of «old»; not used in standard English writing except in songs and Scots speech. Say «awld».

part of speech: noun (a baa, baas); verb (baa, baas, baaed, baaing); interjection
meaning for a pupil: 1) The sound a sheep or lamb makes. 2) (verb) To make this sound; to bleat.
its sense in the lessons: Early reading, nursery rhymes («Baa, Baa, Black Sheep») and farm visits. Science: animal sounds. In Alice's world, the sound of sheep-bells and bleating sheep belongs to the countryside she wakes up to.
examples from the lessons: «Baa, baa, black sheep, have you any wool?» | The lambs baaed for their mothers. | We heard a loud «baa» from the field. | The sheep went «baa» when the dog barked. | Little Tom can say «baa» like a sheep. | The baaing of sheep woke us early.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Onomatopoeia. Past: baaed. Not «bah» (which is a cross sound people make: «Bah! Humbug!»).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Of land: too poor to grow plants or crops; bare and empty: a barren desert. 2) (old, also Bible) Of a woman or animal: not able to have babies. 3) Of a plant or tree: not producing fruit. 4) Empty, giving no results: a barren argument.
its sense in the lessons: Geography and science: barren deserts, ice fields, rocky islands. In the Bible several women thought to be barren, like Sarah and Hannah, later have children, and Christians and Jews see this as God's blessing. Stories: barren land shows hardship.
examples from the lessons: Nothing grew on the barren hillside. | The Arctic tundra looks barren in winter. | The barren tree gave no apples. | In the Bible, Sarah was barren until she had Isaac. | After the fire, the land was barren. | The talks were long and barren.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double r. Today «unable to have children» is said kindly with «infertile»; «barren» for people is old-fashioned and can hurt. Opposite for land: fertile.

meaning for a pupil: 1) As much as a wheelbarrow will hold.
its sense in the lessons: Measuring words with -ful: a spoonful, a cupful, a barrowful. Gardening and farm work. In Alice in Wonderland, when Alice fills the White Rabbit's house, the creatures outside talk of fetching «a barrowful» of something and then throw pebbles in at the window, which turn into little cakes.
examples from the lessons: We moved three barrowfuls of soil. | «A barrowful will do, to begin with.» | «A barrowful of what?» thought Alice. | Dad tipped a barrowful of leaves onto the bonfire. | It took ten barrowfuls to fill the sandpit. | A barrowful of apples stood by the gate.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: barrowfuls (sometimes barrowsful). In maths, a «barrowful» is not an exact unit; give kilograms or litres for exact amounts.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To cry very loudly, like a baby. 2) To shout loudly and roughly. 3) (informal) «bawl someone out» = to tell them off angrily.
its sense in the lessons: Everyday: babies bawl; a coach bawls instructions. In Alice in Wonderland the Duchess's baby howls and sneezes. In stories it gives a loud, noisy picture.
examples from the lessons: The baby bawled all night. | «Get out!» bawled the cook. | The coach bawled at the players to run. | The little boy bawled when he dropped his ice cream. | Dad bawled me out for being late. | The Duchess's baby bawled and sneezed.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Homophone: ball. Regular verb: bawled, bawling. Similar: wail, howl, yell.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (old, formal) A bedroom, especially in a palace or a grand house.
its sense in the lessons: Found in old stories, fairy tales, the Bible and history about kings and queens: «the king's bedchamber». It gives the reader a grand, old-fashioned feeling. «Lady of the Bedchamber» is a title for a queen's helper.
examples from the lessons: The princess slept in a grand bedchamber. | The prince crept into the king's bedchamber. | Servants lit the fire in the queen's bedchamber. | In the old castle we saw the royal bedchamber. | The Lady of the Bedchamber helped the queen dress.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Old-fashioned; use «bedroom» in everyday English. Compound: bed + chamber (old word for room).

meaning for a pupil: 1) To cut off a person's head as a punishment or execution.
its sense in the lessons: History: Anne Boleyn and Charles I were beheaded; in the French Revolution the guillotine was used. In Alice in Wonderland the Queen of Hearts keeps shouting «Off with his head!», but the King quietly pardons everyone and no one is really beheaded. There is a funny argument about whether you can behead the Cheshire Cat, who has only a head.
examples from the lessons: Charles I was beheaded in 1649. | «Off with her head!» shouted the Queen. | The executioner said you can't behead a head with no body. | In history we learned that Anne Boleyn was beheaded. | Nobody was really beheaded in Wonderland. | The guillotine was used to behead people in France.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Noun: beheading. Be- + head (to take off the head). Today almost all countries have stopped this punishment.

part of speech: the -ing form of the verb behold (behold, beholds, beheld, beholding — old); noun (beholding — rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (old, literary) Looking at; seeing, especially something wonderful or surprising. 2) (Bible) «Behold» = look! see!
its sense in the lessons: Found in the Bible («Behold, I bring you good tidings of great joy»), poems, carols and old stories. «Beholder» is in the saying «Beauty is in the eye of the beholder». It tells the reader a sight is important or wondrous.
examples from the lessons: The shepherds stood beholding the angel. | Beholding the sea for the first time, she gasped. | «Behold, a virgin shall conceive,» says the Bible. | Mole stood beholding the river in wonder. | The crowd stood beholding the fireworks. | Beauty is in the eye of the beholder.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Old-fashioned; today say «looking at» or «seeing». Irregular: behold, beheld. Do not confuse with «beholden» (owing someone a favour).

part of speech: adjective (bewitched); past form of the verb bewitch (bewitch, bewitches, bewitched, bewitching)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Under a magic spell put on by a witch or wizard. 2) Charmed and delighted, as if by magic: bewitched by the music.
its sense in the lessons: Fairy tales: a princess or prince is bewitched and turned into a frog or put to sleep. Everyday and stories: being bewitched by something beautiful. In The Wind in the Willows Mole is bewitched by the river, and Toad seems bewitched by motor cars.
examples from the lessons: The princess was bewitched by the wicked witch. | The prince was bewitched into a frog. | Mole was bewitched by the sparkling river. | Toad stared at the motor car as if bewitched. | The audience was bewitched by her singing. | The cottage looked bewitched in the moonlight.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Witches and spells are from stories; they are not real. Adjective «bewitching» = very charming.

part of speech: adjective (blackish; no comparative forms in normal use)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Nearly black, or black with a little of another colour in it. 2) Rather dark and dirty-looking.
its sense in the lessons: A describing word for colour, used in science (the colour of a rock, a beetle or a bird), in art and in stories to paint a dark, gloomy picture. The ending «-ish» means «rather» or «a bit», as in greenish, reddish, smallish. In stories a blackish river, sky or wood often warns of danger or bad weather.
examples from the lessons: The beetle had a blackish shell with a green shine. | The pond water looked blackish under the trees. | Blackish clouds rolled in before the storm. | The burnt toast was blackish at the edges. | Some crows look blackish blue in the sun. | We tested the blackish mud and found it full of rotting leaves. | The Mole peered into the blackish depths of the Wild Wood.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Built from «black» + «-ish» (= rather, somewhat). It is an adjective only; say «a blackish stone», not «a blackish». Other colour words take the same ending: brownish, greyish (UK) / grayish (US), yellowish. «Blackish» is less than fully black.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Perfect happiness and calm joy. 2) Something that gives you great pleasure («This bath is bliss!»). 3) (church) In Christian writing, the perfect happiness of heaven that Christians believe God gives.
its sense in the lessons: A feeling word used in stories, poems and everyday talk to show someone is completely happy and relaxed. Phrases: «pure bliss», «sheer bliss», «wedded bliss», «ignorance is bliss» (it can feel easier not to know something bad). In The Wind in the Willows the Mole feels bliss on his first day on the river.
examples from the lessons: Lying on the warm sand was pure bliss. | After the long walk, a cup of hot chocolate was bliss. | The Mole sat in the boat in a state of bliss. | A day with no homework is bliss! | The baby slept in bliss after her feed. | «Ignorance is bliss,» said Dad when I asked about the bill. | The hymn spoke of the bliss of heaven.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: say «bliss», not «a bliss» or «blisses». Adjective: blissful; adverb: blissfully («blissfully unaware» = happily not knowing). Do not mix up with «blister» (a sore bubble on the skin).

part of speech: adjective (blithesome; more blithesome, most blithesome — old-fashioned)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (old-fashioned, literary) Cheerful, merry and light-hearted. 2) (literary) Carefree, not worried about anything.
its sense in the lessons: A rare old word met in poems and old children's books, not in modern talk. It paints a happy, bouncy character or mood. It comes from «blithe» (= cheerful) + «-some» (= full of), as in «handsome» or «lonesome».
examples from the lessons: The blithesome lark sang over the fields. | Toad set off in a blithesome mood, sure everything would go well. | The poem tells of a blithesome girl dancing on the green. | It was a blithesome spring morning. | In old books a blithesome heart means a happy one. | Grandma laughed at the old word and said, «Just say cheerful!»
note for the reader of a maths problem: Old-fashioned: in your own writing «cheerful», «merry» or «blithe» is more natural. Modern «blithe» can also mean «careless about something serious» («blithe disregard»), which is less positive than «blithesome».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A pupil who lives at a boarding school during term instead of going home each day. 2) A person who pays to live and eat meals in someone else's house. 3) A person who rides a skateboard, snowboard or surfboard (informal). 4) A person who climbs onto a ship to attack or take it over (old use, pirates).
its sense in the lessons: Common in school stories set in the UK and Ireland, where boarders and day pupils live different lives (dormitories, matron, house rules). In older stories families «take in boarders» to earn money. In pirate stories, boarders swing onto an enemy ship. Opposite of a boarder at school: a day pupil.
examples from the lessons: My cousin is a boarder at a school in Scotland. | The boarders sleep in a big dormitory. | Mrs Hughes took in a boarder to help pay the rent. | The boarder paid for his room and his meals every week. | The skate park was full of young boarders. | «Repel boarders!» shouted the captain as the pirates climbed up. | Day pupils go home at four, but boarders stay for supper.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Homophone trap: «boarder» (a person who boards) and «border» (the edge or line between countries) sound the same. Related: board (food and a room: «bed and board»), boarding school, boarding house.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A shed or building by a river or lake where boats are kept. 2) A building of a rowing club where boats and oars are stored.
its sense in the lessons: Found in stories about rivers and lakes, in holiday places and at rowing clubs. In The Wind in the Willows Toad Hall has a fine boathouse, and the Water Rat keeps his little blue-and-white boat by the river bank. A boathouse often stands half over the water so boats can slide in and out.
examples from the lessons: The boats were locked in the boathouse for the winter. | Toad showed them his boathouse full of boats he no longer used. | We found old oars and life jackets in the boathouse. | The rowing team carried their boat out of the boathouse. | Ducks nested under the boathouse floor. | The boathouse door opened straight onto the lake.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word: boathouse (boat + house). Plural «boathouses» is pronounced with a «z» sound in the middle of «-houses», like «houses».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (old-fashioned) A lady's small private sitting room or dressing room. 2) (literary) A pretty, private bedroom.
its sense in the lessons: An old word from French, met in Victorian and Edwardian stories and in grand houses, where a rich lady had her boudoir to write letters, dress and rest. It tells the reader the house is wealthy and old-fashioned.
examples from the lessons: The duchess received her friends in her boudoir. | The boudoir had pink curtains and a little writing desk. | In the old house we saw the lady's boudoir with its mirror and chair. | The maid brought tea up to her mistress's boudoir. | The story says the queen sat sulking in her boudoir. | Today most people would just say «bedroom» or «sitting room».
note for the reader of a maths problem: Borrowed from French; the «oir» sounds like «wah». Countable: a boudoir, two boudoirs. It is old-fashioned; do not use it for an ordinary modern bedroom except as a joke.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A long pole sticking out forward from the front (the bow) of a sailing ship. 2) The spar to which the ropes of the front sails are tied.
its sense in the lessons: A sailing word met in sea stories, pirate tales and The Wind in the Willows, where the Sea Rat tells of his voyages. Sailors climb out on the bowsprit to handle the front sails (the jibs). Useful in history lessons on sailing ships.
examples from the lessons: The ship's bowsprit pointed out over the waves. | A sailor sat astride the bowsprit, fixing a rope. | The figurehead was carved just under the bowsprit. | Spray flew over the bowsprit as the ship dived into a wave. | The Sea Rat spoke of ships with long bowsprits sailing south. | In our model ship the bowsprit is a thin stick of wood.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Bow» here rhymes with «cow» in the word «bow» of a ship, but in «bowsprit» most people say BOH. Bow = front of a ship; stern = back. Countable noun.

part of speech: noun (a brook, brooks); verb (brook, brooks, brooked, brooking — formal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A small stream of fresh water. 2) (formal, verb) To allow or put up with something, usually in the negative: «She would brook no argument» means she would not allow any argument.
its sense in the lessons: In nature lessons and stories a brook is a little stream running through fields and woods, smaller than a river. Poems often describe it «babbling». The verb sense is formal and found in older books: «brook no delay», «brook no interference». In The Wind in the Willows small brooks run down to the river.
examples from the lessons: We jumped across the little brook in the meadow. | The brook babbled over the stones. | Minnows swam in the clear brook. | Cows drank from the brook at the bottom of the field. | The water from the brook flows into the river. | The teacher would brook no talking during the test. | Grandad would brook no nonsense at the dinner table.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Size order: brook / stream / creek (US, Australia) are small; river is big. The verb is formal and almost always used with «no» or «not». Brook is also a surname and a girl's name (often spelt Brooke).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Small broken branches and twigs lying on the ground or cut from trees. 2) Thick, low undergrowth of small bushes and shrubs.
its sense in the lessons: In outdoor lessons and stories brushwood is what you gather to start a campfire or what makes a forest hard to walk through. Safety: dry brushwood catches fire quickly. In The Wind in the Willows the Mole stumbles through the brushwood of the Wild Wood.
examples from the lessons: We gathered brushwood to light the campfire. | The path was blocked with brushwood. | A rabbit hid under the brushwood. | Dry brushwood burns very fast, so be careful. | The farmer cleared the brushwood from the edge of the field. | The Mole pushed through the brushwood, frightened by the faces.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «some brushwood», «a pile of brushwood», not «a brushwood» or «brushwoods». Similar words: twigs, kindling, undergrowth, scrub.

part of speech: noun (Burton — a name); phrase «go for a burton» (UK slang)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (UK slang, «go for a burton») To be lost, broken, ruined or killed: «My holiday plans have gone for a burton.» 2) (a name) Burton is an English surname and a place name, such as the town of Burton upon Trent, famous for brewing beer.
its sense in the lessons: The phrase «gone for a burton» was RAF slang in the Second World War for a pilot who was killed, and now means jokingly that something is ruined or gone. Mostly heard in the UK, often from older people. As a name it gets a capital letter.
examples from the lessons: Our picnic went for a burton when the rain came. | «My new phone has gone for a burton,» said Mum after dropping it in the bath. | Grandad says his knees have gone for a burton. | The pilots said a lost friend had «gone for a burton». | Burton upon Trent is a town in the Midlands. | Mr Burton is our new teacher.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Only the phrase «go/gone for a burton» is common English slang; «a burton» on its own is not used. Written with a capital B as a name (Burton). Nobody knows for sure where the phrase came from; the old story that it means a pint of Burton beer is not proven.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a busy way: working hard and actively at something. 2) While being very occupied with a task.
its sense in the lessons: A how-word used in stories to show characters hard at work: bees, ants, cooks, the Rat packing a picnic basket. It often goes with verbs like work, write, chatter, bustle. Phrases: «busily engaged in», «busily at work».
examples from the lessons: The bees buzzed busily from flower to flower. | Mum was busily packing for the trip. | The pupils wrote busily until the bell rang. | The Rat busily packed the lunch basket. | Ants busily carried crumbs back to their nest. | The shop assistant was busily stacking shelves. | Everyone chatted busily before the show began.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formed from «busy» by changing y to i and adding «-ly»: busy → busily (like happy → happily). Pronounced BIZ-i-lee; the «u» in busy sounds like «i».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Cruel and not caring at all about other people's feelings or pain. 2) Showing no pity: «a callous remark».
its sense in the lessons: Used in stories, history and ethics lessons to describe a person who hurts others and does not care. It is a strong judging word: callous behaviour, callous disregard, callous indifference. Its opposite is kind, caring or compassionate.
examples from the lessons: It was callous to laugh when she fell over. | The callous man kicked the stray dog. | The villain made a callous joke about the people he had cheated. | Ignoring someone who needs help can be callous. | The judge called the crime cold and callous. | She was shocked by his callous words.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Homophone trap: «callous» (adjective, unkind) and «callus» (noun, a hard patch of skin on hands or feet) sound the same. Noun: callousness; adverb: callously.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A large, upright, turning drum on a ship or dock, turned by sailors pushing bars, used to wind in heavy ropes or the anchor chain. 2) A similar turning part on a machine, such as an old tape recorder.
its sense in the lessons: A sailing word met in sea stories, pirate tales and history lessons on ships. Sailors walked round and round pushing the capstan bars, often singing sea shanties to keep time. In The Wind in the Willows the Sea Rat tells of ships and harbours.
examples from the lessons: The sailors pushed the capstan to raise the anchor. | They sang a shanty as they walked round the capstan. | The heavy rope was wound around the capstan. | A capstan uses a lever to make pulling easier. | The old ship had a wooden capstan on deck. | We saw a capstan at the harbour museum.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Science link: the capstan bars act as levers, so a small push far from the middle gives a big pull on the rope. A windlass is a similar winding machine that turns on its side (horizontally).

part of speech: noun (chaff — uncountable); verb (chaff, chaffs, chaffed, chaffing — old-fashioned)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The dry husks (outer cases) of grain such as wheat, separated from the seeds when farmers thresh it. 2) Cut hay or straw used as animal food. 3) Something useless or worthless: «separate the wheat from the chaff» means keep the good and throw out the bad. 4) (old-fashioned) Friendly teasing; to chaff someone means to tease them in fun.
its sense in the lessons: In farming and history lessons chaff is what blows away when grain is winnowed. In the Bible the wicked are compared to chaff that the wind drives away. The phrase «sort the wheat from the chaff» is common in everyday talk about choosing the best. The teasing sense is old and appears in Victorian and Edwardian books.
examples from the lessons: The farmer threw the grain into the air and the wind blew the chaff away. | Horses eat chaff mixed with oats. | We must sort the wheat from the chaff in these ideas. | The psalm says the wicked are like chaff that the wind blows away. | The older boys chaffed him about his new hat. | Chaff from the threshing machine covered the barn floor.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «some chaff», not «a chaff». Do not mix up with «chafe» (to rub and make sore). The teasing sense is old-fashioned; today people say «tease» or «banter».

part of speech: verb (chivvy, chivvies, chivvied, chivvying; also spelt chivy)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (mainly UK, informal) To keep telling someone to hurry up or do something, in an annoying way. 2) To chase or hunt someone, or drive animals along.
its sense in the lessons: An everyday British word for nagging people to get moving: parents chivvy children to get dressed, teachers chivvy a class into line. In older stories (The Wind in the Willows) animals are chivvied and chased by others. Often followed by «along», «into» or «out of».
examples from the lessons: Mum chivvied us out of bed for school. | The teacher chivvied the class back inside after the bell. | The sheepdog chivvied the sheep through the gate. | Stop chivvying me, I'm nearly ready! | Dad chivvied everyone into the car. | In the story the weasels chivvied the poor rabbits.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mainly British. Past: chivvied (y → ie). Similar words: nag, hurry, hustle. Not rude, but it shows the person being chivvied may feel annoyed.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Limited or restricted: «a circumscribed life» is one with narrow limits. 2) (maths) Drawn around a shape so that it touches it: a circumscribed circle passes through every corner of a triangle or polygon.
its sense in the lessons: In geometry a circumscribed circle (circumcircle) goes round a shape through all its vertices; an inscribed circle sits inside touching each side. In formal writing «circumscribed» means kept within limits, by rules, money or illness.
examples from the lessons: The teacher drew a circle circumscribed about the triangle. | A circumscribed circle touches every corner of the square. | Her freedom was circumscribed by strict rules. | In the old days girls lived very circumscribed lives. | The king's power was circumscribed by the law. | Draw the circle that circumscribes the regular hexagon.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Built from Latin «circum» (around) + «scribe» (write, draw). In maths: circumscribed = drawn outside around a shape; inscribed = drawn inside. For a regular hexagon, the radius of the circumscribed circle equals the side length.

part of speech: adjective (clangorous; more clangorous, most clangorous — literary)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (literary) Making a loud, ringing, clanging noise, like bells or metal being struck. 2) Full of harsh, repeated loud sounds.
its sense in the lessons: A rare, poetic word for noise, used in stories to describe bells, metal gates, factories or a busy railway yard. It comes from «clangour», a loud continuous clanging. In everyday talk people say «clanging» or «noisy».
examples from the lessons: The clangorous church bells woke the whole village. | We heard the clangorous noise of the blacksmith's hammer. | The iron gates shut with a clangorous crash. | The clangorous shipyard rang with hammers all day. | Fire engines raced past with a clangorous alarm. | The poem describes the clangorous city streets.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Literary and rare. Spelling: «clangour» (UK) / «clangor» (US), but «clangorous» drops the «u» in both. Related: clang, clank, clatter.

part of speech: verb (coax, coaxes, coaxed, coaxing); noun (coax — short for coaxial cable, technical)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To persuade someone gently and patiently to do something. 2) To get something to work or move by careful, gentle effort: «coax the fire into life». 3) (technical, noun) A short form of «coaxial cable», a TV or aerial cable.
its sense in the lessons: Common in stories and everyday life: coaxing a shy cat out from under a bed, coaxing a younger child to eat vegetables. It shows kind, patient persuasion rather than force. Phrases: «coax out», «coax into», «coax a smile».
examples from the lessons: She coaxed the kitten out from under the sofa with some milk. | Dad coaxed the old car into starting. | We coaxed my little brother into trying the broccoli. | The Rat coaxed the Mole back to sleep. | He coaxed a smile from the crying baby. | Gran coaxed the fire back into life with dry sticks. | The TV aerial is joined with a coax cable.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced KOHKS, one syllable. Coax is gentle; «force» or «make» is not. Similar: persuade, sweet-talk, encourage.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A small edible shellfish with two ribbed, heart-shaped shells, found in sand on beaches. 2) (idiom) «It warms the cockles of my heart» means it makes me feel happy and loved. 3) A small light boat (also called a cockleshell).
its sense in the lessons: In science and seaside lessons cockles are molluscs that live buried in wet sand. The Irish song «Molly Malone» has «cockles and mussels, alive, alive-o». The heartwarming idiom is used in everyday British, Irish and Australian talk.
examples from the lessons: We found empty cockle shells on the beach. | Cockles bury themselves in wet sand. | Molly Malone sold cockles and mussels in Dublin. | Your kind letter warmed the cockles of my heart. | People in Wales still gather cockles at low tide. | The tiny cockle bobbed on the waves.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one cockle, two cockles. The idiom always uses the plural: «the cockles of your heart». A cockle is a mollusc, an animal without a backbone, like mussels and clams.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a way that is easy, useful or suitable for someone: «The shop is conveniently close.» 2) (said with doubt) At a time that suits someone a little too well, as if on purpose: «He conveniently forgot his homework.»
its sense in the lessons: Everyday word for places that are handy and for timing that helps you. In stories, the second sense is a hint that a character is pretending or lying: «she conveniently lost the letter». Phrases: «conveniently located», «conveniently placed», «conveniently forgot».
examples from the lessons: Our house is conveniently close to the school. | The bus stop is conveniently placed outside the library. | He conveniently forgot to tidy his room. | The plug was conveniently near the desk. | The answer was conveniently written on the back of the book. | My sister conveniently disappeared when it was time to wash up.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «convenient» + «-ly». Noun: convenience; opposite: inconveniently. Watch the tone: «conveniently forgot» usually means the speaker thinks it was not a real accident.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (church) A building where nuns live, pray and work together. 2) (church) A community of nuns. 3) A school run by nuns, often called a convent school.
its sense in the lessons: Seen in history lessons, stories set in Catholic or Anglican countries, and Ireland, where many schools were convent schools. Nuns are women who give their lives to God and take vows; Christians believe this is a calling. Monks live in a monastery; nuns live in a convent.
examples from the lessons: The nuns of the convent rise early to pray. | My grandma went to a convent school in Cork. | The old convent is now a museum. | Visitors could buy jam made by the sisters of the convent. | The convent garden had high stone walls. | In the story the girl was sent away to a convent.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Do not confuse with «convert» (to change, or a person who changes religion) or «covenant» (a solemn promise, in the Bible). Monastery = for monks; convent or nunnery = for nuns.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A small group of trees growing close together; a little wood. 2) A small wood where trees are regularly cut back so they regrow (also «coppice»).
its sense in the lessons: A countryside word common in British and Irish nature lessons, maps and stories. In The Wind in the Willows the river bank and fields are dotted with copses. Animals such as rabbits, foxes and pheasants shelter in a copse.
examples from the lessons: We had our picnic in the shade of a small copse. | A fox ran into the copse at the end of the field. | Bluebells grow in the copse every spring. | The map shows a copse beside the farm. | The pheasants hid in the copse. | We played hide-and-seek among the trees of the copse.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Do not confuse with «corpse» (a dead body); copse has no «r». Size: copse < wood < forest.

part of speech: noun (the Cotswolds — a place; Cotswold — a name and adjective)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (a name, a place) The Cotswolds are a range of gentle hills and pretty villages in south-central England, famous for honey-coloured stone houses and sheep. 2) (adjective, «Cotswold») From the Cotswolds: Cotswold stone, Cotswold sheep, Cotswold villages.
its sense in the lessons: Met in geography lessons on England, holiday talk and stories set in the English countryside. In the Middle Ages the Cotswolds grew rich on wool from Cotswold sheep, and the wool money built big churches. The area is an Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty (now called a National Landscape).
examples from the lessons: We went walking in the Cotswolds in the summer. | The cottages are built of golden Cotswold stone. | Cotswold sheep have long curly wool. | Medieval wool merchants grew rich in the Cotswolds. | The Cotswold villages have dry-stone walls and old churches. | Our class looked at the Cotswolds on the map of England.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A proper noun: always with a capital C. The hills are «the Cotswolds» (plural). «Wold» is an old word for open hilly country.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A plant that grows along the ground or climbs up walls, fences and trees, such as ivy. 2) A small bird that creeps up tree trunks looking for insects (a treecreeper). 3) (informal) A person who behaves in a creepy way, for example by watching people secretly. 4) (old-fashioned, plural) Soft shoes or a baby's one-piece suit (US, «creepers»).
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons creepers show how some plants climb towards the light using tendrils or little roots. In stories, creepers cover old houses, ruins and jungles. In The Wind in the Willows and the Just So Stories creepers grow over banks and trees.
examples from the lessons: Ivy is a creeper that climbs up walls. | The old house was covered in green creepers. | Monkeys swung on the creepers in the jungle. | A treecreeper ran up the oak trunk. | The creeper had tiny tendrils that gripped the fence. | «Don't be a creeper and read my diary!» said my sister.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun. Related: creep (verb: creep, crept), creepy (adjective: scary in a strange way). Similar plants: vine, climber.

part of speech: verb (crimp, crimps, crimped, crimping); noun (a crimp, crimps)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To press something into small folds or ridges, such as pastry edges or hair. 2) To squeeze two things together to join them, such as a metal end on a wire. 3) (noun) A small fold, wave or ridge. 4) (US, informal) «Put a crimp in» something means to spoil or limit it.
its sense in the lessons: In cooking you crimp the edge of a pie with a fork or your fingers to seal it. Hairdressers crimp hair into zigzag waves. Electricians crimp metal connectors onto wires. In the US «that put a crimp in our plans» means it got in the way.
examples from the lessons: Crimp the edges of the pie with a fork. | She crimped her hair for the party. | The electrician crimped the plug onto the wire. | The paper had little crimps along the edge. | The rain put a crimp in our beach day. | Gran showed me how to crimp a pasty.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: crimped. Adjective: crimped or crimpy. Do not confuse with «cramp» (a sudden pain in a muscle) or «scrimp» (to save money carefully).

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a way that shows you want to know or learn about something: «The cat sniffed the box curiously.» 2) Strangely or oddly: «The house was curiously quiet.» 3) (at the start of a sentence) «Curiously, …» means «It is strange that …».
its sense in the lessons: A how-word used often in stories to show a character looking or asking with interest, and to point out something odd. In Alice in Wonderland Alice looks about her curiously and famously says «Curiouser and curiouser!», a playful wrong form she made up when things got stranger and stranger.
examples from the lessons: Alice peeped curiously into the little door. | The puppy curiously sniffed the new toy. | The street was curiously empty that morning. | Curiously, nobody had heard the bell. | She looked curiously at the strange box. | The Mole asked curiously what lived in the Wild Wood.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «curious» + «-ly». Two senses: interested (looked curiously) and strangely (curiously quiet). Noun: curiosity. «Curiouser» is not correct English: it is Alice's joke from Lewis Carroll.

part of speech: adjective (dank, danker, dankest); (slang) dank = very good
meaning for a pupil: 1) Unpleasantly cold, wet and stale-smelling: «a dank cellar». 2) (slang, mostly US, young people) Excellent, cool.
its sense in the lessons: A setting word in stories for gloomy dungeons, caves, cellars and old tunnels; it tells the reader the place is uncomfortable and maybe frightening. Science link: dank places grow mould. The slang sense is used jokingly online and by teenagers.
examples from the lessons: The dungeon was dark and dank. | A dank smell came from the old cellar. | Moss grew on the dank walls of the tunnel. | The Mole's tunnels felt dank in winter. | The house was dank after the flood. | (slang) «That new game is dank!» said my cousin.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always about cold wetness, never pleasant (compare «damp», which is milder, and «moist»). The slang sense is very informal; do not use it in written work.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a tactful way, careful not to upset or offend people. 2) By means of diplomacy, the work of governments talking and agreeing with each other.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, answering diplomatically means saying the truth kindly: telling a friend you prefer another drawing without hurting them. In history and news, countries solve problems diplomatically through talks instead of war.
examples from the lessons: She diplomatically said the cake was «interesting». | The teacher dealt with the argument diplomatically. | The two countries settled the quarrel diplomatically. | Dad diplomatically changed the subject. | Badger answered Toad diplomatically, so as not to make him angry. | I diplomatically suggested we take turns.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «diplomatic» + «-ally». Related: diplomat (a person who represents a country), diplomacy. Similar: tactfully. Opposite: bluntly, rudely.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Very sad and gloomy, looking or sounding miserable. 2) Causing sadness: «doleful news».
its sense in the lessons: A feeling word in stories and poems. It paints sad faces, sad songs and sad sounds. In Alice in Wonderland the Mock Turtle sings in a doleful voice, and in The Wind in the Willows Toad is doleful in prison.
examples from the lessons: The puppy gave me a doleful look. | The Mock Turtle sang a doleful song. | Toad sat in his cell looking doleful. | A doleful bell rang across the valley. | He told the doleful story of his lost kite. | The rain made the day feel doleful.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb: dolefully. Similar: mournful, woeful, sorrowful. It sounds a little old-fashioned and literary.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a dreamy way, as if half asleep or thinking about something far away. 2) In a soft, gentle, pleasant way.
its sense in the lessons: Used in stories to show a character lost in thought, sleepy or happy, often looking out of a window or at the water. Alice at the start of Alice in Wonderland feels sleepy on the river bank, and the Mole gazes dreamily at the river.
examples from the lessons: She stared dreamily out of the classroom window. | The Mole gazed dreamily at the flowing water. | He smiled dreamily, thinking of the holidays. | Alice said dreamily, «Do cats eat bats?» | The music played dreamily in the background. | The cat stretched dreamily in the sun.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «dreamy» + «-ly» (y → i): dreamily. Teachers may say a pupil is «daydreaming» if they look out of the window dreamily.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Rather dark, as at dusk, the time when evening turns into night. 2) Dark or dim in colour: «dusky pink», «dusky blue». 3) (old, now offensive) Used in old books to describe people with dark skin; this use is hurtful today and should not be used.
its sense in the lessons: A describing word in nature lessons and stories for evening light, shadows and soft colours. Animals are named with it: the dusky dolphin, dusky shark. In older books, including some of Kipling's, words about skin colour are used in ways we now know are wrong.
examples from the lessons: The dusky sky was full of bats. | We walked home through the dusky lane. | She wore a dusky pink dress. | The dusky dolphin lives near New Zealand. | The room grew dusky as the sun went down. | Moths came out in the dusky garden.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «dusk» + «-y». Use it for light and colours. The old use about people's skin is racist today: if you read it in an old book, know it is an outdated way of speaking.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A British nobleman of high rank, below a marquess and above a viscount. 2) (history) In early England, a powerful lord who ruled a large area for the king.
its sense in the lessons: Met in history lessons on the Middle Ages, castles and kings, and in stories of the British upper class. An earl's wife is a countess. The ranks from top are: duke, marquess, earl, viscount, baron. Earl is also a man's name.
examples from the lessons: The earl lived in a huge castle. | Harold was Earl of Wessex before he became king. | An earl's wife is called a countess. | The Earl of Sandwich is said to have given the sandwich its name. | The earl owned all the land around the village. | Earl is also a first name, as in Earl Grey tea.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Use «an earl» (starts with a vowel sound). Capital E in titles: the Earl of Essex. There is no «earless»: the female equivalent is countess. The word came from Old English «eorl», a warrior or nobleman.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A long bank of earth or stone built to carry a road or railway, or to stop a river from flooding. 2) A raised wall or path along a river, such as the Thames Embankment in London.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and science lessons embankments are flood defences and transport works. In The Wind in the Willows Toad on the run hides near a railway embankment. Safety: railway embankments are dangerous places to play.
examples from the lessons: The train ran along a high embankment. | The river burst over the embankment in the flood. | We walked along the Thames Embankment in London. | Workers built an embankment to protect the town. | Never play on the railway embankment. | Grass and wild flowers grew on the steep embankment.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: an embankment, two embankments. Related: bank (the side of a river), dyke or levee (US) for flood banks.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Cut or carved into a hard surface such as metal, stone, glass or wood: «His name was engraved on the cup.» 2) (figurative) Fixed firmly in your memory: «The day is engraved on my mind.» 3) Printed from a cut metal plate (an engraving).
its sense in the lessons: Seen on trophies, rings, medals, gravestones and plaques. In history lessons, old pictures in books were often engravings. In stories something «engraved in his memory» will never be forgotten.
examples from the lessons: The winner's name was engraved on the trophy. | Her watch had a message engraved on the back. | The date was engraved on the stone. | The silver cup was engraved with the school badge. | That sunny day is engraved in my memory. | The old map was engraved on copper.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past form of «engrave» (regular). Noun: an engraving (a picture), an engraver (a person). Different from «printed» or «painted»: engraving cuts into the surface.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Filled with great delight and joy, so happy that you forget everything else. 2) Completely charmed or fascinated by something beautiful.
its sense in the lessons: A strong feeling word in stories: the Mole is enraptured by the river on his first day; audiences are enraptured by music. It is stronger than «pleased» or «delighted».
examples from the lessons: The children were enraptured by the puppet show. | The Mole was enraptured by the sparkling river. | She listened enraptured to the singer. | The crowd sat enraptured as the fireworks burst. | He gazed enraptured at the stars. | Toad was enraptured by the motor car.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Related: rapture (great joy), rapturous. Similar: delighted, thrilled, spellbound. Mostly literary.

part of speech: noun (an ermine, ermines; ermine — uncountable for the fur)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A stoat (a small, long-bodied animal of the weasel family) in its white winter coat, with a black tip to its tail. 2) The white fur of this animal, with black spots, worn on the robes of kings, queens, judges and lords.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons the ermine shows how some animals change colour with the seasons for camouflage in snow. In history and pictures of coronations, kings and peers wear ermine-trimmed robes as a sign of rank. In The Wind in the Willows stoats are the enemies of the riverbank animals.
examples from the lessons: The ermine turned white in winter to hide in the snow. | The king's robe was trimmed with ermine. | An ermine has a black tip to its tail all year round. | In summer the same animal is brown and is called a stoat. | The judges wore red robes with ermine collars. | Stoats and weasels took over Toad Hall.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Ermine» and «stoat» are the same animal; «ermine» is used for the white winter coat and the fur. Today most people think killing animals for fur is wrong, and many robes now use fake fur.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Extremely interested in something, so that you want to keep watching or learning about it. 2) Held still by something you cannot stop looking at, as if under a spell.
its sense in the lessons: A key school word: pupils are fascinated by dinosaurs, space or volcanoes. In stories, a character fascinated by something often follows it into adventure, like Toad fascinated by motor cars. Phrases: «fascinated by», «fascinated with».
examples from the lessons: I am fascinated by volcanoes. | The children watched the caterpillar, fascinated. | Toad was fascinated by the motor car. | She was fascinated with the stars and wanted to be an astronaut. | The cat sat fascinated by the goldfish. | We were fascinated to learn how bees make honey.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: «fascinated» describes the person who feels the interest; «fascinating» describes the thing that causes it. «I am fascinated» (not «I am fascinating», which means you are the interesting thing). Spelling: sc in the middle.

meaning for a pupil: 1) One of the front feet of an animal with four legs. 2) (sailing) The lowest front part of a ship's hull, where the keel meets the stem.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on animals: moles dig with their strong forefeet, horses stamp with a forefoot. In The Wind in the Willows the animals often use their forepaws and forefeet. Useful to describe how animals move and dig.
examples from the lessons: The mole digs with its broad forefeet. | The pony lifted one forefoot to be shod. | The dog put a forefoot on my knee. | A kangaroo's forefeet are small; its back feet are huge. | The rabbit cleaned its face with its forefeet. | The ship's forefoot cut through the water.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular plural: forefeet (like foot → feet). «Fore» means front; the back ones are hind feet. For dogs and cats people often say «front paws».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who is running away or hiding, especially from the police or from danger. 2) (adjective) Running away or escaping: «a fugitive slave». 3) (literary, adjective) Lasting only a short time, fleeting: «a fugitive smile».
its sense in the lessons: In stories, history and the news. In The Wind in the Willows Toad becomes a fugitive after escaping from prison, disguised as a washerwoman. In history lessons on slavery, fugitives escaped to freedom along the Underground Railroad. In the Bible, Cain is told he will be a fugitive and a wanderer.
examples from the lessons: The fugitive hid in the woods from the police. | Toad was now a fugitive, running from the law. | Fugitives from the war crossed the border. | Harriet Tubman helped fugitive slaves reach freedom. | The police caught the fugitive at the station. | A fugitive smile crossed her face.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Not the same as a refugee: a refugee flees danger to find safety and is not a criminal; «fugitive» often means running from the law. Comes from Latin «fugere», to flee.

part of speech: noun (a furrow, furrows); verb (furrow, furrows, furrowed, furrowing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A long narrow groove cut into the soil by a plough. 2) A deep line or wrinkle on the skin, especially the forehead. 3) (verb) To make lines on your forehead by frowning: «He furrowed his brow.» 4) (verb) To plough a field into grooves.
its sense in the lessons: In farming and history lessons fields are ploughed into straight furrows for planting seeds. In stories, a furrowed brow shows a character is worried or thinking hard. Proverb: «to plough a lonely furrow» means to work alone without help.
examples from the lessons: The farmer ploughed long straight furrows across the field. | Seeds were dropped into the furrows. | Gulls followed the plough to eat worms from the furrows. | She furrowed her brow over the hard sum. | Deep furrows lined the old man's face. | The Mole saw the furrows of the brown fields from the bank.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Rhymes with «borrow». Regular verb: furrowed. Do not confuse with «burrow» (an animal's hole) or «ferret».

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a happy, cheerful, lively way: «The children sang gaily.» 2) Brightly and colourfully: «gaily painted boats». 3) Carelessly, without thinking about the trouble it causes: «He gaily spent all the money.»
its sense in the lessons: A common word in older stories, songs and The Wind in the Willows, where the Water Rat's boat and Toad's caravan are «gaily painted» and animals chat gaily. It shows a light, happy mood or bright colours.
examples from the lessons: The children danced gaily round the maypole. | The canary-coloured caravan was gaily painted. | Flags fluttered gaily in the wind. | Toad sang gaily as he drove off. | She waved gaily from the train. | He gaily promised things he could not do.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «gay» in its older sense «happy, bright». The spelling is gaily, not «gayly». Today «gay» mostly means attracted to people of the same sex, but «gaily» keeps the old cheerful meaning.

part of speech: noun (a garfish; plural garfish or garfishes)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A long, thin fish with a narrow beak-like jaw full of sharp teeth. 2) (Australia, New Zealand) A similar slim fish called a halfbeak, popular for eating and fishing.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on sea life: garfish are fast hunters near the surface. In Australia «gar» are a common catch from jetties. Kipling's Just So Stories have sea creatures, and garfish appear in seaside fishing.
examples from the lessons: A garfish has a long pointed beak. | The garfish swam fast near the surface. | We caught garfish off the jetty in Adelaide. | Garfish have green bones, which surprises people. | The fisherman sold fresh garfish at the market. | A shoal of garfish flashed in the sunlight.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural is usually «garfish» (like «fish»). Often shortened to «gar». The «gar» in its name is an old word for a spear.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Tasting or smelling strongly of garlic. 2) Having breath that smells of garlic after eating it.
its sense in the lessons: An everyday food word for cooking at home or school. Garlicky dishes include garlic bread, some pasta sauces and many dishes from Italy, France, Spain and Asia. Someone may joke about «garlicky breath».
examples from the lessons: This garlic bread is lovely and garlicky. | The kitchen smelled garlicky after Dad cooked. | I don't like garlicky soup. | His breath was garlicky after lunch. | The sauce was too garlicky for my sister. | Gran makes a garlicky roast chicken.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: garlic + k + y (garlicky), because «garlicy» would be read with an «s» sound. Same rule: picnic → picnicking, panic → panicky.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Wearing gauntlets: thick gloves with wide cuffs that cover the wrist, or armoured gloves worn by knights. 2) (of a hand) Covered with such a glove.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons knights wore metal gauntlets. In The Wind in the Willows, early motorists like Toad dressed up in goggles, caps and gauntlets, so a «gauntleted hand» grips the steering wheel. Also seen in stories of bikers, falconers and fencers.
examples from the lessons: The knight raised his gauntleted fist. | Toad's gauntleted hands gripped the steering wheel. | The falconer held the hawk on his gauntleted arm. | The motorcyclist pulled off his gauntleted gloves. | A gauntleted hand knocked on the castle door. | The fencer saluted with a gauntleted hand.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «gauntlet» + «-ed». Idioms with gauntlet: «throw down the gauntlet» (challenge someone), «run the gauntlet» (go through a lot of attacks or criticism).

part of speech: verb (gleam, gleams, gleamed, gleaming); noun (a gleam, gleams)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To shine softly or brightly, often by reflecting light: «The polished car gleamed.» 2) (noun) A soft light or shine. 3) (noun) A small sign of a feeling or idea: «a gleam of hope», «a gleam in his eye».
its sense in the lessons: Used in stories to describe shining things (swords, water, eyes, clean floors) and hope. «A gleam in his eye» often means a character has a clever or mischievous idea. In The Wind in the Willows the river gleams and sparkles in the sun.
examples from the lessons: The river gleamed in the morning sun. | Her eyes gleamed with excitement. | The kitchen floor was gleaming after we cleaned it. | A gleam of light shone under the door. | There was a gleam of hope at last. | Toad had a naughty gleam in his eye.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Adjective: gleaming (gleaming white teeth). Similar: shine, glint (a quick small flash), glow (steady light without flame), glitter, sparkle.

part of speech: verb (glint, glints, glinted, glinting); noun (a glint, glints)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To give out a small, quick flash of light. 2) (noun) A short bright flash of reflected light. 3) (noun) A look in the eye showing a feeling such as anger, fun or a clever plan: «a glint in her eye».
its sense in the lessons: In stories glints of metal or eyes add tension: a knife glints in the dark, a villain's eyes glint. In science, glints are reflections of light from shiny surfaces such as water, glass and metal.
examples from the lessons: Something glinted in the grass – it was a coin! | The knight's sword glinted in the sun. | A glint of gold caught her eye. | The cat's eyes glinted in the torchlight. | He had a glint of mischief in his eye. | Sunlight glinted on the water.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: glinted. A glint is quicker and smaller than a gleam. Similar: sparkle, glimmer, flash.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A tropical fruit, round or pear-shaped, with green or yellow skin and pink or white sweet flesh full of small seeds. 2) The small tree that this fruit grows on.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography lessons on tropical plants and foods, and in stories set in hot countries such as India, Africa and the Caribbean. Guavas are rich in vitamin C. In Kipling's Just So Stories tropical fruits and trees fill the jungle.
examples from the lessons: I had guava juice for breakfast. | Guavas smell sweet when they are ripe. | The guava tree grows in hot countries. | Guavas have lots of vitamin C. | Gran made guava jam. | The monkey stole a guava from the tree.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced GWAH-va. Countable: a guava, three guavas.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) The act of living in a place: «The house was not fit for human habitation.» 2) (formal, literary) A house or home; a place where people live.
its sense in the lessons: Used in formal writing, law and older stories. A house «unfit for habitation» is too dangerous or dirty to live in. In history and geography, «signs of habitation» are clues that people once lived somewhere (fire marks, tools, walls). In The Wind in the Willows Badger's home under the Wild Wood was built on the ruins of an old human habitation.
examples from the lessons: The old cottage was unfit for human habitation. | There was no sign of habitation for miles. | Archaeologists found signs of early habitation in the cave. | Badger's home was built among the ruins of an ancient city. | Smoke from a chimney showed a habitation nearby. | The island has no human habitation.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal: in everyday talk say «home» or «house». Related: inhabit (to live in), inhabitant (a person who lives somewhere), habitat (the natural home of an animal or plant). Habitat is for animals and plants; habitation is for people.

part of speech: noun (a hartebeest; plural hartebeest or hartebeests)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A large African antelope with a long face, a sloping back and curved horns, living on grassy plains.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on African animals and the savanna food chain: hartebeest eat grass and are hunted by lions, leopards and hyenas. In Kipling's Just So Stories («How the Leopard Got His Spots») the Giraffe, the Zebra and the Eland live on the High Veldt with the hartebeest, and the Leopard hunts them.
examples from the lessons: The hartebeest grazed on the dry plain. | A lion crept towards a herd of hartebeest. | Hartebeest have long faces and curved horns. | In the Just So Story, the Leopard hunted on the High Veldt. | Hartebeest can run very fast to escape. | We saw a hartebeest at the safari park.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced HAR-tuh-beest. From Afrikaans «hartbees», old Dutch for «deer beast». Plural is often the same: two hartebeest.

part of speech: noun (a hoe, hoes); verb (hoe, hoes, hoed, hoeing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A garden tool with a long handle and a flat blade, used to cut weeds and loosen the soil. 2) (verb) To dig, weed or loosen soil with a hoe. 3) (rude, slang) A spelling of «ho», a very rude insulting word for a woman; not for school.
its sense in the lessons: In science and gardening lessons: a hoe keeps weeds down so vegetables can grow. Farmers in history hoed fields by hand. Pupils may hoe the school vegetable patch. In stories, a gardener leans on his hoe.
examples from the lessons: Grandad used a hoe to cut the weeds. | We hoed the vegetable patch at school. | Hoeing loosens the soil so water can sink in. | The farmer hoed between the rows of potatoes. | Leave the hoe in the shed when you finish. | The gardener rested on his hoe and smiled.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Homophone traps: «hoe» (garden tool), «ho» (rude slang), «whoa» (stop!). Verb forms: hoes, hoed, hoeing (keep the e).

meaning for a pupil: 1) The act of encouraging or stirring people up to do something bad, violent or against the law. 2) (law) The crime of urging people to commit a crime or violence: «incitement to violence», «incitement to hatred». 3) Something that pushes people to act; a cause or reason.
