its sense in the lessons: Seen in history lessons (riots, rebellions), the news and law. In the UK and many countries «incitement to racial hatred» is against the law. In ethics, it raises the question of whether the person who stirs others up is to blame for what they do.
examples from the lessons: He was arrested for incitement to violence. | Incitement to hatred is against the law. | The speech was an incitement to riot. | Posting threats online can be incitement. | The judge said the words were a clear incitement. | Shouting «Get him!» to a crowd can be incitement.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Related verb: incite (to stir up). Usually about bad actions. Do not confuse with «excitement» (a happy, eager feeling).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Having bad habits or faults that cannot be changed or corrected: «an incorrigible liar». 2) (playful) Always doing something naughty or silly that people half like: «You're incorrigible!»
its sense in the lessons: In The Wind in the Willows Toad is incorrigible: his friends try again and again to cure him of his craze for motor cars, but he goes back to it. Used for cheeky characters, naughty pets and old habits. Often said with a smile.
examples from the lessons: Toad was incorrigible; he always went back to motor cars. | My puppy is an incorrigible thief of socks. | Grandad is an incorrigible joker. | «You're incorrigible!» laughed Mum when I took another biscuit. | The teacher called him an incorrigible chatterbox. | She is an incorrigible optimist.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From in- (not) + corrigible (able to be corrected). Adverb: incorrigibly. Spelling: double r.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (South Africa) An important meeting or conference to discuss something, originally a gathering of Zulu or Xhosa people. 2) (Scouts) A large meeting of Scout leaders.
its sense in the lessons: A word from the Zulu and Xhosa languages, used in South African English and in Kipling's Just So Stories for a big gathering or talk. Today it is used for conferences and meetings in South Africa and in the Scout movement.
examples from the lessons: The chiefs held an indaba to settle the dispute. | The Scout leaders met at an international indaba. | The animals gathered for a great indaba. | The government called an indaba on water shortages. | Everyone had a say at the indaba. | In South Africa «indaba» can also mean «my business»: «That's your indaba!»
note for the reader of a maths problem: From Zulu «indaba» (matter, business, talk). Countable: an indaba, indabas. Mainly South African English.

part of speech: verb (jab, jabs, jabbed, jabbing); noun (a jab, jabs)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Poking or pushing something sharp or pointed quickly and hard: «He kept jabbing me with his pencil.» 2) (boxing) Throwing quick, short straight punches. 3) (noun, UK informal) A jab is an injection or vaccination: «the flu jab». 4) (figurative) Making sharp, unkind remarks at someone.
its sense in the lessons: Everyday word in the playground («Stop jabbing me!»), in sport (boxing) and in the UK, Ireland, Australia and New Zealand for vaccinations at the doctor's. In stories it adds sharp, quick action.
examples from the lessons: Stop jabbing me with your elbow! | He was jabbing at the buttons on the remote. | The boxer kept jabbing with his left hand. | I had my flu jab at school. | She was jabbing her finger at the map. | The Rat was jabbing the river bank with a stick.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double b: jab → jabbed, jabbing. «Jab» for an injection is informal (UK, Ireland, Australia); in the US people say «shot».

part of speech: noun (a jinni, jinn; also djinn, genie)
meaning for a pupil: 1) In Arabic and Muslim tradition, a spirit made of fire, invisible to people, which can be good or bad. 2) (stories) A magic spirit, often living in a lamp or bottle, who can grant wishes; usually called a genie.
its sense in the lessons: Met in the Arabian Nights (Aladdin) and in Kipling's Just So Stories: in «How the Camel Got His Hump» the Djinn in charge of All Deserts gives the lazy Camel his hump. Muslims believe jinn are real beings created by God; in stories they are magical characters.
examples from the lessons: The jinni came out of the bottle in a puff of smoke. | The Djinn gave the Camel a hump for being lazy. | In the story the jinni granted three wishes. | Aladdin's genie lived in a lamp. | Muslims believe that God created the jinn from fire. | The fisherman was scared of the angry jinni.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spellings vary: jinni, jinnee, djinni, djinn, genie. «Jinn» is often the plural. «Genie» is the usual word in English stories. Pronounced JIN-ee.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (a name, a place) Lancaster is a city in north-west England, the county town of Lancashire. 2) (history) The House of Lancaster was a royal family of England, whose sign was the red rose; it fought the House of York in the Wars of the Roses. 3) (history) The Lancaster was a famous British bomber plane of the Second World War. 4) (a name) A surname.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons: the Wars of the Roses (1455–1487) were between Lancaster (red rose) and York (white rose), ended by Henry Tudor. Geography: Lancaster has a castle and a university. Burt Lancaster was an American film actor.
examples from the lessons: Lancaster is a city in Lancashire. | The red rose was the badge of the House of Lancaster. | Henry VII united Lancaster and York. | We visited Lancaster Castle on our trip. | The Lancaster bomber had four engines. | Mrs Lancaster is our neighbour.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always written with a capital L. Pronounced LAN-kuh-ster. Lancashire is the county; Lancaster is its city.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (old-fashioned) A woman whose job is to wash and iron clothes and sheets for other people.
its sense in the lessons: Met in history lessons on Victorian and Edwardian times, when many poor women worked as laundresses or washerwomen. In The Wind in the Willows Toad escapes from prison disguised as a washerwoman, the gaoler's daughter's aunt, and later has to try washing clothes and makes a mess of it.
examples from the lessons: The laundress washed the sheets in a big tub. | In Victorian times many women worked as laundresses. | Toad dressed up as a washerwoman to escape. | The laundress ironed the shirts with a heavy iron. | The laundress worked long hours for little money. | The hotel once had its own laundress.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Old-fashioned: today we say «laundry worker». A male laundry worker was a laundryman. Related: laundry, launder. Plural: laundresses.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a lazy way, without effort or energy: «He lazily picked up a pen.» 2) Slowly and gently, in a relaxed way: «The river flowed lazily.»
its sense in the lessons: In stories, lazily often paints warm, relaxed summer scenes: the river drifts lazily, a cat stretches lazily, the Rat and Mole lie lazily in the boat. It can also criticise someone for not trying hard.
examples from the lessons: The river flowed lazily past the meadow. | The cat stretched lazily in the sun. | The Rat and the Mole drifted lazily downstream. | He lazily copied the answer without thinking. | Smoke rose lazily from the chimney. | We spent the morning lazily in our pyjamas.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «lazy» + «-ly» (y → i). The first sense is critical; the second is often pleasant and positive.

part of speech: noun (libel — uncountable; a libel, libels); verb (libel, libels, libelled, libelling — UK; libeled, libeling — US)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (law) A false written or published statement that damages a person's good name. 2) (verb) To publish something false that harms someone's reputation.
its sense in the lessons: In law and the news: people sue newspapers for libel. It is linked to honesty and ethics: saying untrue harmful things about someone is wrong and can be against the law. Libel is written (or in print, online, on TV); slander is spoken.
examples from the lessons: The singer sued the newspaper for libel. | Writing lies about someone online can be libel. | The judge said the article was a libel. | He was accused of libelling his neighbour. | Truth is a defence against libel. | The paper had to pay a large sum for the libel.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Do not confuse with «label» (a tag with information) or «liable» (responsible by law). Libel = written; slander = spoken; both are called defamation. UK spelling doubles l: libelled.

part of speech: adjective (lighthearted / light-hearted; more lighthearted, most lighthearted)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Cheerful and free from worry. 2) Not serious; meant to be fun: «a lighthearted film».
its sense in the lessons: Used in stories for happy moods and in everyday talk for jokes, shows and articles that are not serious. At school, a lighthearted quiz is just for fun. The Wind in the Willows begins with the Mole running off lighthearted on a spring day.
examples from the lessons: The Mole felt lighthearted as he ran across the meadow. | We watched a lighthearted comedy. | It was just a lighthearted joke. | The end of term felt lighthearted and happy. | Her lighthearted laugh filled the room. | The newspaper had a lighthearted story about a dog on a skateboard.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: light-hearted (UK, often hyphenated) or lighthearted (US). Adverb: lightheartedly. Opposite: heavy-hearted, serious.

part of speech: noun (macaroni — uncountable; old: a macaroni, macaronies)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A kind of pasta in short, curved tubes. 2) (history, 18th century) A young man who wore very fancy, showy clothes and a big wig, copying the fashions of Europe.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday cooking: macaroni cheese (UK) or mac and cheese (US). In history and music lessons: the old song «Yankee Doodle» says he «stuck a feather in his cap and called it macaroni» — meaning he thought a feather made him a fine, fashionable gentleman; British soldiers sang it to mock the Americans.
examples from the lessons: We had macaroni cheese for dinner. | Macaroni is made from wheat flour and water. | Boil the macaroni for ten minutes. | Yankee Doodle «stuck a feather in his cap and called it macaroni». | In the 1770s a macaroni wore a huge wig. | We made a necklace by threading dry macaroni.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable as food: «some macaroni», not «a macaroni». Ends in -i, from Italian «maccheroni».

meaning for a pupil: 1) The funny mistake of using a word that sounds like the right word but means something quite different: «He's the pineapple of politeness» instead of «pinnacle».
its sense in the lessons: A language lesson word. It comes from Mrs Malaprop, a character in Sheridan's play «The Rivals» (1775), who kept mixing up words. Malapropisms make people laugh in stories, comedy and real life. In Alice in Wonderland, Carroll's characters play with words in a similar way (the Mock Turtle studies «Reeling and Writhing» instead of Reading and Writing, which is a pun).
examples from the lessons: Saying «for all intensive purposes» instead of «for all intents and purposes» is a malapropism. | Grandad's malapropisms make us laugh. | «He's the pineapple of politeness» is a famous malapropism. | The comedian used lots of malapropisms. | Our teacher asked us to spot the malapropism in the sentence. | «Dance a flamingo» instead of «flamenco» is a malapropism.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A malapropism is a mistake (the speaker means the real word); a pun is a joke made on purpose. Pronounced MAL-uh-prop-izm.

part of speech: adjective (marvellous — UK, Ireland, Australia, New Zealand; marvelous — US; more marvellous, most marvellous)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Extremely good, wonderful: «a marvellous day». 2) (old use) Causing great wonder or surprise; amazing.
its sense in the lessons: A happy word in stories and everyday British talk, a little old-fashioned or posh. In The Wind in the Willows Toad calls everything «marvellous» when he is excited, and Alice finds marvellous things in Wonderland.
examples from the lessons: We had a marvellous time at the seaside. | «What a marvellous idea!» said Gran. | The view from the hill was marvellous. | Toad thought the motor car was the most marvellous thing in the world. | The magician did marvellous tricks. | You did a marvellous job on your painting.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: UK marvellous (double l), US marvelous (one l). From «marvel» (a wonderful thing; to wonder at). Similar: wonderful, splendid, fantastic.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Showing great skill: «a masterful performance». 2) Strong, sure and in control, liking to give orders: «a masterful manner».
its sense in the lessons: In sports, music and art lessons a masterful performance is excellent. In stories a masterful character takes charge; in The Wind in the Willows Badger is masterful when he takes charge of Toad, and Toad likes to think of himself as a masterful driver.
examples from the lessons: The pianist gave a masterful performance. | Badger spoke in a masterful voice and Toad obeyed. | She scored a masterful goal. | The captain had a masterful way of giving orders. | The book is a masterful story of friendship. | Toad imagined himself a masterful motorist.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Two senses: very skilful, and bossy/commanding. Some people use «masterly» only for skilful and «masterful» for commanding, but both are used for skill today. Adverb: masterfully.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A very large, strong dog with a short coat, a big head and loose skin round the face, kept as a guard dog.
its sense in the lessons: Met in stories as a guard dog at gates, farms and castles, and in science lessons on dog breeds. The English Mastiff is one of the heaviest dog breeds.
examples from the lessons: The mastiff guarded the farm gate. | A mastiff can weigh more than a grown man. | The mastiff barked in a deep voice. | Despite its size, our neighbour's mastiff is very gentle. | The castle was guarded by two mastiffs. | The mastiff drooled on my shoe.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: mastiffs. Breeds include the English Mastiff, Bullmastiff and Tibetan Mastiff.

part of speech: adjective (meagre — UK, Ireland, Australia, NZ; meager — US; more meagre, most meagre)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Small in amount, not enough: «a meagre meal», «meagre wages». 2) (old) Thin, lean.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons on poverty, war and workhouses, people lived on meagre food and meagre pay. In stories it shows hardship: In maths word problems, a meagre amount is a small one.
examples from the lessons: The prisoners ate a meagre meal of bread and water. | They lived on a meagre wage. | We had a meagre harvest after the dry summer. | His meagre savings were not enough for a bike. | The soup was meagre and thin. | In the war, families had meagre rations.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: meagre (UK) / meager (US). Pronounced MEE-guh. Similar: scant, scanty, small. Opposite: plentiful, generous.

part of speech: adjective (menacing; more menacing, most menacing); verb (menace, menaces, menaced, menacing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Seeming likely to cause harm; threatening: «a menacing look». 2) (verb) Threatening or putting someone or something in danger.
its sense in the lessons: In stories this word builds fear: menacing clouds, a menacing growl, menacing faces in the Wild Wood. In everyday safety talk, a menacing dog or stranger means: get away and tell an adult.
examples from the lessons: The dog gave a menacing growl. | Menacing clouds gathered over the hills. | The Mole saw menacing faces in the Wild Wood. | The bully gave him a menacing look. | The weasels came forward with menacing sticks. | A menacing silence fell over the room.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «menace» (a threat or danger, or an annoying person: «Dennis the Menace»). Similar: threatening, sinister, frightening.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (literary) Very muddy and boggy; full of mire (deep, sticky mud).
its sense in the lessons: A rare word in poems, old books and the Bible («He brought me up out of a horrible pit, out of the miry clay», Psalm 40). In stories it describes swampy, muddy paths where feet and wheels get stuck.
examples from the lessons: The cart got stuck on the miry road. | We squelched through the miry field. | The psalm says God lifted him out of the miry clay. | The miry lane was hard to walk in after the rain. | The horses struggled through the miry ground. | Toad's car splashed through a miry puddle.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «mire» (deep mud, a bog) + «-y». Pronounced MY-ree. Everyday words: muddy, boggy. «Stuck in the mire» can mean stuck in a difficult situation.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Very large and frightening, like a monster: «a monstrous wave». 2) Very wrong, cruel or shocking: «a monstrous lie». 3) Ugly and strange in shape.
its sense in the lessons: In stories monstrous creatures and waves bring danger. In ethics and history lessons, a monstrous crime is extremely wicked. In Alice in Wonderland Alice grows to a monstrous size.
examples from the lessons: A monstrous wave crashed over the boat. | It was a monstrous lie. | Alice grew to a monstrous size in the little house. | The giant had monstrous hands. | The ogre built a monstrous wall round his castle. | The cruelty of the slave trade was monstrous.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «monster» + «-ous»; spelling drops the e: monstrous, not «monsterous». Adverb: monstrously.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A small piece or bite of food. 2) A small amount of anything: «not a morsel of sense».
its sense in the lessons: In stories hungry characters search for a morsel to eat; animals snatch tasty morsels. In everyday talk «a tasty morsel» is a small delicious bite. In The Wind in the Willows the animals share every morsel at their feasts.
examples from the lessons: The bird pecked up every morsel of bread. | The hungry boy had not eaten a morsel all day. | Rat offered Mole a tasty morsel from the picnic. | The dog waited for a morsel to fall from the table. | There was not a morsel left on the plate. | She did not have a morsel of fear.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a morsel, morsels. Similar: bite, scrap, crumb, titbit (UK) / tidbit (US).

part of speech: adjective (noisome; more noisome, most noisome — formal, literary)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (literary) Having a very nasty smell: «a noisome swamp». 2) (old) Harmful or very unpleasant.
its sense in the lessons: A rare literary word for disgusting places in stories: dungeons, sewers, rubbish tips. In the Bible (Psalm 91) God protects from «the noisome pestilence» (a harmful disease).
examples from the lessons: A noisome smell came from the drain. | The prisoners lay in a noisome dungeon. | Flies buzzed over the noisome rubbish. | The psalm speaks of the noisome pestilence. | The pond had become a noisome swamp. | We held our noses near the noisome bins.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Trap: «noisome» has nothing to do with noise! It comes from an old word «noy» (annoy). It means smelly or harmful, not loud.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Slowness to understand things; not noticing what is obvious. 2) (maths, rare) The quality of being an obtuse angle, wider than a right angle. 3) Bluntness, not being sharp or pointed.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, a character's obtuseness annoys others because he will not «get» a hint; in The Wind in the Willows Toad's friends despair at his obtuseness about his own foolishness. In maths, «obtuse» is the everyday word: an obtuse angle is between 90° and 180°.
examples from the lessons: Her obtuseness made the joke fall flat. | Badger sighed at Toad's obtuseness. | His obtuseness about the hints was annoying. | The teacher explained the obtuseness of the angle by comparing it with a right angle. | Was it real obtuseness, or was he pretending not to understand? | The obtuseness of the old knife made it useless for cutting.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «obtuse» + «-ness». In maths use «obtuse angle»: acute < 90°, right = 90°, obtuse between 90° and 180°, reflex > 180°. Calling a person obtuse is rude.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A smooth, greasy cream rubbed on the skin to heal cuts, burns, rashes or sore places. 2) (Bible, church) Oil or perfumed oil used for anointing, as in the Bible story where a woman pours precious ointment on Jesus's head.
its sense in the lessons: In health and first-aid lessons: put antiseptic ointment on a clean cut. Safety: only use medicine an adult gives you. Idiom: «a fly in the ointment» means one small thing that spoils something good.
examples from the lessons: Mum put some ointment on my grazed knee. | The doctor gave me an ointment for the rash. | Rub the ointment in gently. | The only fly in the ointment was the rain. | In the Bible a woman poured precious ointment on Jesus. | Keep the ointment out of your eyes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Can be countable (different ointments) or uncountable (some ointment). Similar: cream, salve, balm, lotion (thinner).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A sudden, strong burst of a feeling or action that you cannot control: «a paroxysm of laughter», «a paroxysm of rage». 2) (medicine) A sudden attack or worsening of an illness, such as a fit of coughing.
its sense in the lessons: In stories this word shows a character overcome: Toad has paroxysms of joy and rage in The Wind in the Willows. In medicine, whooping cough causes paroxysms of coughing.
examples from the lessons: The children fell into paroxysms of laughter. | Toad flew into a paroxysm of rage. | A paroxysm of coughing shook the old man. | She was seized by a paroxysm of fear. | The joke sent the class into paroxysms. | Whooping cough brings paroxysms of coughing.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced PA-rok-sizm. Usually followed by «of». Similar: fit, outburst, spasm.

part of speech: noun (a Parsi, Parsis; also Parsee); adjective (Parsi)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (a name of a people) A member of a community in India whose ancestors came from Persia (Iran) over a thousand years ago and who follow the Zoroastrian religion. 2) (adjective) Belonging to this community.
its sense in the lessons: In Kipling's Just So Stories, «How the Rhinoceros Got His Skin» tells of a Parsee man with a hat that shone in the sun, who lived on an uninhabited island in the Red Sea and got his revenge on the rude Rhinoceros with cake crumbs. In geography and religion lessons, Parsis live mostly around Mumbai and are known for their fire temples.
examples from the lessons: The Parsee in the Just So Story had a hat that shone in the sun. | The Parsee filled the Rhinoceros's skin with cake crumbs. | Parsis follow the Zoroastrian faith. | The Parsi community lives mostly in Mumbai. | Freddie Mercury's family were Parsis. | A sacred fire burns in the Parsi temple.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Written with a capital P: Parsi or Parsee (the older spelling Kipling used). Their religion is Zoroastrianism, one of the oldest religions that worship one God.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Having or showing very strong feelings, such as love, anger or excitement. 2) Very keen on or interested in something: «passionate about football».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday talk and school reports: a pupil passionate about science or reading. In stories passionate speeches and arguments show strong feeling. Toad is passionate about each new craze — boats, caravans, then motor cars.
examples from the lessons: She is passionate about protecting animals. | He gave a passionate speech about saving the rainforest. | Toad was passionate about every new hobby. | The fans were passionate supporters of their team. | My teacher is passionate about poetry. | They had a passionate argument about the rules.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «passion» + «-ate». Adverb: passionately. «Passionate about» (not «passionate for»).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (UK, old-fashioned) The amount of something you could buy for one penny: «a pennyworth of sweets». 2) (idiom) «Put in your two pennyworth» (UK) or «two cents' worth» (US) means to give your opinion. 3) A small amount.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons and older British stories, children bought a pennyworth of sweets, milk or bread. Pronounced PEN-ee-wurth or «PEN-uth». Today the idiom about giving your opinion is common: «Can I put in my two pennyworth?»
examples from the lessons: She bought a pennyworth of toffees. | In 1900 a pennyworth of milk was a big jug. | Everyone wanted to add their two pennyworth to the argument. | The boy spent his last penny on a pennyworth of sherbet. | Not a pennyworth of difference! | Grandad remembers buying a pennyworth of chips.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Old-fashioned word; also written «penn'orth». In maths, «a pennyworth» means whatever 1p buys; if one sweet costs a halfpenny, a pennyworth is 2 sweets.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Cheerful, lively and full of energy. 2) Standing up straight and bright: «perky ears».
its sense in the lessons: An everyday word for happy, lively people, pets and moods. After a rest, someone feels perky again. Puppies with perky ears, perky birds hopping about. Phrase: «perk up» means to become more cheerful.
examples from the lessons: You look very perky this morning! | The puppy had perky ears. | A perky robin hopped across the lawn. | After a nap Grandma felt perky again. | The flowers looked perky after the rain. | She gave a perky little wave.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative: perkier, perkiest. Related: perk up (become more cheerful). Different from «perk» (a bonus or extra benefit of a job).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Calm, peaceful and not easily upset or excited: «a placid horse». 2) (of water) Still and smooth: «a placid lake».
its sense in the lessons: In stories: placid animals (cows, old horses), placid ponds and rivers in calm scenes. In everyday talk, a placid baby rarely cries.
examples from the lessons: The old horse was placid and gentle. | The lake was placid in the early morning. | Our baby is very placid. | Cows grazed placidly in the meadow. | The river flowed placid and slow. | He has a placid nature and never shouts.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb: placidly. Similar: calm, tranquil, serene. Opposite: excitable, stormy.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Sounding sad, like someone complaining or crying softly: «a plaintive cry». 2) Sad and gentle, asking for pity.
its sense in the lessons: In stories this word describes sad sounds: a plaintive cry of a lost kitten, a plaintive song, a plaintive voice. In The Wind in the Willows the Mole's plaintive cry when he smells his old home makes the Rat turn back.
examples from the lessons: The lost kitten gave a plaintive mew. | We heard the plaintive cry of a seagull. | «Ratty, please come back!» came the Mole's plaintive call. | She sang a plaintive song about home. | The dog gave a plaintive whine at the door. | His plaintive voice made us feel sorry for him.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced PLAIN-tiv. Related to «complain». Not the same as «plaintiff» (in law, the person who brings a case to court).

part of speech: verb (plumb, plumbs, plumbed, plumbing); adverb (plumb — informal); noun (a plumb, plumb line); adjective (plumb)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (verb) To fit water pipes in a building: «plumb in a washing machine». 2) (noun) A weight on a string (a plumb line or plumb bob) used to check that something is exactly vertical or to measure depth. 3) (adjective) Exactly vertical, perfectly upright. 4) (verb) To measure the depth of water; «plumb the depths» means reach the deepest or worst point. 5) (informal, adverb, mainly US) Completely or exactly: «plumb crazy», «plumb in the middle».
its sense in the lessons: In science and DT lessons, a plumb line shows the true vertical because gravity pulls the weight straight down. Builders use it for walls. Sailors once used a weighted line to plumb the depth. Plumbers fit pipes. In everyday talk: «plumb the depths of despair».
examples from the lessons: The builder used a plumb line to check the wall. | The wall is not plumb; it leans. | Dad plumbed in the new dishwasher. | Sailors plumbed the depth of the river. | Gravity pulls the plumb bob straight down. | «You're plumb crazy!» said the cowboy. | The ball landed plumb in the middle of the target.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The «b» is silent: say PLUM. Homophone trap: «plum» (the fruit). Plumber, plumbing come from Latin «plumbum», lead, because old pipes were made of lead (chemical symbol Pb).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Acting too important and too serious, using grand words to show off. 2) (of speech or writing) Full of big, showy words.
its sense in the lessons: A judging word in stories for self-important characters: Toad is pompous and boastful in The Wind in the Willows, and the Duchess and the King of Hearts are pompous in Alice in Wonderland. Pupils may notice pompous language in old speeches.
examples from the lessons: Toad made a pompous speech about how clever he was. | The pompous mayor talked for an hour. | He wrote in a pompous style full of long words. | Don't be so pompous! | The pompous butler looked down his nose at us. | The King made a pompous announcement at the trial.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb: pompously. Noun: pomposity. Related: pomp (grand show and ceremony). Similar: self-important, conceited, stuck-up.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A heavy grid of iron or wooden bars that slides down in grooves to close a castle gateway.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons on medieval castles: the portcullis was dropped to stop attackers, with «murder holes» above the gateway. The portcullis is also a symbol of the UK Parliament. Used in adventure stories and games.
examples from the lessons: The guards lowered the portcullis to keep out the enemy. | The portcullis crashed down just behind the knight. | We saw the old portcullis at the castle. | The portcullis was raised with chains and a winch. | A portcullis appears on the badge of Parliament. | Arrows flew through the bars of the portcullis.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced port-CULL-is. Plural: portcullises. From old French for «sliding door».

meaning for a pupil: 1) To be in charge of a meeting, ceremony, court or event: «The judge presided over the trial.» 2) To be in control of a situation or period: «He presided over a time of peace.»
its sense in the lessons: In law and civics lessons: a judge presides over a court; a chairperson presides over a meeting. In Alice in Wonderland the King of Hearts presides over the trial of the Knave of Hearts, with the Queen shouting «Off with his head!» In church, a priest or minister may preside at communion.
examples from the lessons: The judge presided over the trial. | The head teacher presided at the prize-giving. | The King of Hearts presided over the trial in Wonderland. | The mayor presided over the meeting. | The priest presided at the wedding. | Gran presided over the Christmas dinner table.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually followed by «over» or «at». Related: president (the person who presides), presidency. Regular verb: presided.

part of speech: noun (a punchayet, punchayets; modern spelling panchayat)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (India) A village council, traditionally of five elders, that settles disputes and runs local affairs. 2) (Kipling, Just So Stories) A meeting or council of animals to decide a matter.
its sense in the lessons: From Hindi «panch» (five). Kipling, who grew up in India, uses Indian words in the Just So Stories and The Jungle Book. In geography and civics lessons on India, the panchayat is still the local village government.
examples from the lessons: The punchayet met under the big tree to decide. | The village panchayat settled the quarrel over water. | In the story, the animals held a punchayet. | The elders of the punchayet listened to both sides. | Today India has thousands of elected panchayats. | Kipling uses old Indian words like «punchayet».
note for the reader of a maths problem: The usual modern spelling is «panchayat». It is a word from India, not general English.

part of speech: adjective (queer, queerer, queerest); noun (a queer — offensive); verb (queer — informal)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (old-fashioned) Strange or odd: «a queer noise», «I feel queer» (unwell). 2) (identity) Used by some people to describe themselves as lesbian, gay, bisexual or not fitting usual ideas of gender; this use is accepted by many today. 3) (offensive) For a long time it was used as an insult against gay people, and it can still hurt when used to mock someone. 4) (UK, informal, old) «Queer someone's pitch» means to spoil their plans.
its sense in the lessons: In old books like Alice in Wonderland and The Wind in the Willows, «queer» simply means strange: Alice meets «a queer-looking party», and the animals hear queer sounds in the Wild Wood. Readers today should understand this old meaning. In modern life, be careful: only use it about people in the way they choose, never as an insult.
examples from the lessons: «What a queer thing!» said Alice. | They were a queer-looking party on the bank. | The Mole heard a queer whistling in the Wild Wood. | I feel a bit queer after that ride. | It was a queer, foggy day. | Some people describe themselves as queer, and we respect the words people choose for themselves.
note for the reader of a maths problem: In old stories it means «strange»; in modern use it is about identity and can be hurtful if used as an insult. Old phrase: «queer as Dick's hatband» (very odd).

part of speech: verb (quiver, quivers, quivered, quivering); noun (a quiver, quivers)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To shake slightly and quickly: «Her lip quivered.» 2) (noun) A slight trembling movement or sound. 3) (noun) A case for carrying arrows, worn on the back or hip.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, quivering shows fear, cold or strong feeling (a quivering lip before crying, quivering whiskers). In history lessons, archers such as Robin Hood carried arrows in a quiver. In science, a plucked string quivers to make sound.
examples from the lessons: Her lip quivered as she tried not to cry. | The Mole's whiskers quivered with excitement. | Robin Hood pulled an arrow from his quiver. | The leaves quivered in the breeze. | A quiver of fear ran down his back. | The plucked string quivered and hummed.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: quivered. Similar: tremble, shiver, shudder. The arrow case is also a quiver: «a quiver of arrows».

part of speech: verb (ramble, rambles, rambled, rambling); noun (a ramble, rambles)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To walk for pleasure in the countryside, often without a fixed route. 2) (noun) A long walk in the countryside. 3) To talk or write for a long time in a confused way, wandering off the point. 4) (of plants) To grow and spread in all directions: «rambling roses».
its sense in the lessons: In UK, Irish and New Zealand outdoor life, people go on rambles and join ramblers' clubs. The countryside code tells ramblers to close gates. In school, teachers ask pupils not to ramble in their writing but to stay on the point. In The Wind in the Willows the Mole and Rat enjoy rambles along the river.
examples from the lessons: We went for a ramble across the hills. | The Mole and the Rat rambled along the river bank. | Grandpa tends to ramble on about the old days. | Don't ramble — answer the question. | Roses rambled over the cottage wall. | The ramblers stopped for lunch by a stream.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Related: rambler (a walker; a climbing rose), rambling (long and confused; or spreading). «Ramble on» = talk too long. Similar: hike (longer, harder), stroll (short and slow).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) A result or consequence of an action or decision, often one that is complicated or not expected. 2) (formal) A branch, or one of many branches of something, like a tree or river.
its sense in the lessons: In ethics and history lessons: thinking about the ramifications of a choice means thinking about all the results, near and far. In the news: the ramifications of a new law. Formal word, seen in exam and adult writing.
examples from the lessons: We need to think about the ramifications of this decision. | The war had ramifications all over the world. | Cutting down the forest had serious ramifications for the animals. | Toad never considered the ramifications of his wild driving. | The ramifications of the new rule were not clear. | Every lie has ramifications.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually in the plural: ramifications. Formal: in everyday talk say «results» or «consequences». From Latin «ramus», a branch.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Bitter, deep anger or hatred that lasts a long time after someone has hurt you.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and history, old quarrels leave rancour between families or countries. In ethics and church lessons, forgiving means letting go of rancour. Phrase: «without rancour» means calmly, without bitterness.
examples from the lessons: There was no rancour between the two friends after the argument. | The old feud left a lot of rancour. | She spoke without rancour about the past. | Rancour between the countries lasted for years. | Forgiveness can wash away rancour. | Toad bore no rancour once his friends had saved Toad Hall.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «rancour», not «a rancour». Spelling UK rancour, US rancor; adjective rancorous (no «u» in either). Similar: resentment, bitterness, spite.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Full of great joy and excitement: «rapturous applause». 2) Showing extreme delight.
its sense in the lessons: Used in stories and reports of concerts and sports: a rapturous welcome, rapturous cheers. Toad imagines rapturous crowds cheering him. Related to «rapture», very great joy.
examples from the lessons: The band got a rapturous welcome. | The audience burst into rapturous applause. | Toad dreamed of rapturous crowds cheering his name. | The winning team got a rapturous reception at home. | She gave a rapturous cry when she saw the puppy. | Their rapturous faces said it all.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb: rapturously. Related: rapture, enraptured. Similar: ecstatic, overjoyed, delighted.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who cuts and gathers a crop such as wheat (old-fashioned). 2) A machine that cuts grain. 3) «The Grim Reaper» is a picture of death as a skeleton in a black cloak carrying a scythe.
its sense in the lessons: In farming history: reapers cut wheat with sickles and scythes at harvest; later the reaping machine (McCormick's reaper) did the work. In the Bible, «you reap what you sow» means your actions bring their results. The Grim Reaper appears in stories and Halloween costumes.
examples from the lessons: The reapers worked in the field all day. | The old reaper was pulled by horses. | A reaping machine cuts wheat faster than people. | The Grim Reaper carries a scythe. | Harvest songs were sung by the reapers. | The Bible says that whatever we sow, we will reap.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «reap» (to cut and gather a crop). «Reap» also means to get a result: «reap the benefits». The Grim Reaper is a symbol, not a real person.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) A quick reply, especially a clever, sharp or rude one.
its sense in the lessons: In stories this word describes witty or sharp answers in an argument. In Alice in Wonderland Alice and the creatures exchange rejoinders (the Hatter and the March Hare at the tea party), and in The Wind in the Willows Toad gives cheeky rejoinders.
examples from the lessons: She had a quick rejoinder for every insult. | «That's not my fault!» came the sharp rejoinder. | The Hatter's rude rejoinder made Alice angry. | He could not think of a rejoinder. | Toad's rejoinder made the others laugh. | Her rejoinder was short and clever.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal: everyday words are reply, answer, comeback (informal). Similar: retort, riposte.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Quick, witty conversation in which people make clever, funny replies to each other.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and comedy, repartee shows clever, lively characters (the Mad Hatter's tea party is full of nonsense repartee). Writers and comedians are admired for their repartee.
examples from the lessons: The friends enjoyed a bit of witty repartee. | The show was full of quick repartee. | The Mad Hatter's tea party is full of strange repartee. | Her clever repartee made everyone laugh. | He was good at repartee and never lost an argument. | The banter and repartee went on all evening.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «some repartee», not «a repartee». From French; pronounced rep-ar-TEE. Similar: banter, wit.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A small gun (a pistol) with a turning cylinder holding several bullets.
its sense in the lessons: Met in history (Wild West, wars), detective stories and The Wind in the Willows, where Badger and the friends take weapons — pistols, cudgels and swords — to win back Toad Hall from the weasels. Safety: real guns are dangerous; if you ever see one, do not touch it, move away and tell an adult.
examples from the lessons: The cowboy carried a revolver on his belt. | A revolver holds six bullets in a turning cylinder. | The detective found a revolver in the drawer. | Badger armed the friends with pistols and cudgels. | If you find a gun, don't touch it — tell an adult. | Police in some countries carry revolvers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «revolve» (to turn round), because the cylinder turns. Countable. Different from a rifle (long gun) and a pistol (a general word for a hand gun).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A long, curly lock of hair hanging down in a spiral.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and old pictures, especially of Victorian girls. In Alice in Wonderland Alice worries she has turned into Ada, «for her hair goes in such long ringlets, and mine doesn't go in ringlets at all». Hairdressers make ringlets with curling tongs.
examples from the lessons: Her hair hung in golden ringlets. | Alice said Ada's hair went in long ringlets, but hers did not. | The doll had shiny brown ringlets. | Mum made ringlets in my hair for the wedding. | Victorian girls often wore their hair in ringlets. | A ringlet fell over her eye.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually plural: ringlets. Similar: curl, lock, tress.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) A noisy fuss, quarrel or commotion. 2) (US, Australia, NZ) «Rumpus room»: a family playroom.
its sense in the lessons: Everyday informal word for a noisy row or uproar. In stories, characters cause a rumpus: Toad causes a terrible rumpus wherever he goes, and the Queen of Hearts' croquet game is a rumpus. In Australia and New Zealand many houses have a rumpus room.
examples from the lessons: The dogs caused a rumpus in the garden. | There was a rumpus when the teacher left the room. | Toad's arrival always caused a rumpus. | We played games in the rumpus room. | What's all this rumpus about? | The news caused a rumpus in the village.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal. Plural: rumpuses. Similar: commotion, uproar, fuss, din, ruckus.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (old-fashioned) A wicked, dishonest person who cheats or does bad things to others.
its sense in the lessons: A villain word in older stories, plays and cartoons: «You scoundrel!» In The Wind in the Willows the weasels and stoats who seize Toad Hall are called villains and scoundrels; when Toad steals the car, the magistrate calls him an incorrigible rogue and a hardened ruffian.
examples from the lessons: «You scoundrel!» shouted the captain. | The scoundrel stole the old lady's purse. | The weasels were a gang of scoundrels. | The story is about a scoundrel who cheats a whole town. | He was a charming scoundrel. | The scoundrel ran off with the money.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Old-fashioned: today people say «crook», «villain» or «rogue». It is an insult, but not a swear word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a way that should make someone feel ashamed; very badly or unfairly: «They were shamefully treated.» 2) Showing shame.
its sense in the lessons: In history and ethics lessons, people who were shamefully treated suffered great unfairness. In stories, a character who behaved shamefully must feel sorry and put things right; Toad behaves shamefully and later promises to change.
examples from the lessons: The poor workers were shamefully treated. | The ducks were shamefully neglected by their owner. | Toad behaved shamefully at the trial. | He shamefully lied to his best friend. | The old church had been shamefully left to fall down. | She hung her head shamefully.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «shameful» + «-ly». Related: shame, ashamed, shameless (with no shame). Opposite: honourably.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A small, roughly built hut or shack made from scrap materials. 2) A sea shanty: a song sailors sang together while working, to keep time when pulling ropes. 3) «Shanty town»: an area of very poor homes made of scrap, at the edge of a city.
its sense in the lessons: In music and history lessons, sea shanties («Drunken Sailor», «Wellerman») were sung on sailing ships while turning the capstan or hauling ropes. In geography lessons on cities and poverty, shanty towns grow where people cannot afford proper housing.
examples from the lessons: The sailors sang a shanty as they hauled the ropes. | We sang «Drunken Sailor» in music class. | The family lived in a shanty made of tin sheets. | Shanty towns grow at the edges of many big cities. | The old fisherman knew every sea shanty. | The shanty had no running water.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: shanties (y → ies). «Chanty» or «chantey» is an older spelling of the song sense. Both meanings are different words with the same spelling.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A shipmate is a person who sails on the same ship as you, especially another sailor in the crew. 2) (old, friendly) Sailors sometimes call any fellow sailor «shipmate» as a friendly way of speaking to him.
its sense in the lessons: In sea stories and pirate tales a shipmate is someone you share work, danger and food with on a voyage, so the word tells the reader of loyalty and trust between sailors. In The Wind in the Willows the Sea Rat talks of his old voyages and the men he sailed with. Phrases: «old shipmate», «my shipmates».
examples from the lessons: The two old sailors had been shipmates for twenty years. | «Ahoy there, shipmate!» called the man on the dock. | Long John Silver pretended to be a good shipmate to the boys. | On the school trip to the tall ship, every pupil had a shipmate to work with. | The Sea Rat told stories of his shipmates in faraway ports. | She waved goodbye to her shipmates when the cruise ended. | A good shipmate shares the work and keeps watch.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one shipmate, two shipmates. Made of «ship» + «mate» (friend). Mostly used in stories and by sailors; on land we say «classmate» or «teammate» for the same idea.

part of speech: verb (shunt, shunts, shunted, shunting); noun (a shunt, shunts)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To shunt something is to push or move it to one side, often roughly. 2) To shunt a train or railway carriage is to move it from one track to another. 3) To shunt a person is to send them somewhere less important because you do not want them in the way. 4) (noun, UK informal) A shunt is a small car crash where one car bumps into the back of another. 5) (noun, medicine) A shunt is a small tube doctors put in the body to carry fluid from one place to another.
its sense in the lessons: On the railway, small engines shunt wagons into sidings; in The Wind in the Willows Toad's adventures run through railways and engines. In everyday talk «shunted aside» or «shunted off» means someone was pushed out of the way unfairly. In science, a shunt in electricity is a path that lets current go around something.
examples from the lessons: The little engine shunted the coal wagons into the siding. | The new boy felt he had been shunted to the back of the class. | Dad had a shunt in the car park, but nobody was hurt. | The workers shunted the heavy boxes along the floor. | The old carriages were shunted onto a side track. | Doctors fitted a shunt to drain the fluid. | Don't let the little ones be shunted aside in the game.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: shunt, shunted. Often with «aside», «off», «onto», «into». The car-crash noun is mostly British. Do not mix up with «shun» (to keep away from someone on purpose).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Silvery means shiny and grey-white, like silver. 2) A silvery sound is high, clear and pleasant, like a little bell. 3) Silvery hair is grey or white and shining.
its sense in the lessons: Writers use «silvery» for moonlight, water, fish and frost to make a picture soft and beautiful. In The Wind in the Willows the river and the moonlight are often silvery and magical. In science, metals such as aluminium and tin are described as silvery.
examples from the lessons: The moon cast a silvery light on the river. | Small silvery fish darted under the bridge. | Grandma has beautiful silvery hair. | We heard the silvery sound of a little bell. | Aluminium is a light, silvery metal. | The frost made the grass look silvery in the morning. | The fairy had a silvery voice.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective made from «silver» + «-y». It describes colour or sound; it does not mean the thing is made of silver. A silvery spoon may be steel.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Singularly means very, unusually or especially, often in a surprising way. 2) Singularly can also mean one at a time, separately, though «singly» is more common for this.
its sense in the lessons: Mostly found in old books and formal writing: «a singularly ugly hat», «singularly unhelpful». Old-fashioned narrators in Alice and The Wind in the Willows use such words for a grand or funny tone. In maths, «singular» means one (singular and plural), but «singularly» almost always means «very».
examples from the lessons: It was a singularly cold morning for June. | The Mole found the Wild Wood singularly unfriendly. | He was singularly unlucky with the weather on his holidays. | The answer was singularly clear. | Toad was singularly pleased with himself. | That was a singularly bad idea.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «singular» (single, unusual). Formal and rather old-fashioned; in everyday speech say «very», «really» or «unusually». It does not mean «sadly» or «alone».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal, playful) To skedaddle is to run away quickly, often because you are frightened or caught. 2) (informal) To leave a place in a hurry.
its sense in the lessons: A funny, lively word used in stories and in family talk: «Now skedaddle, all of you!» It tells the reader the escape is fast and a little comic. It came into English in the USA in the 1860s and is used in the UK, Australia and elsewhere too.
examples from the lessons: When the farmer shouted, the boys skedaddled over the fence. | «Skedaddle! Your dinner's getting cold,» said Mum. | The mice skedaddled when the cat came in. | We'd better skedaddle before the rain starts. | The weasels skedaddled when Badger burst into the hall. | The thief skedaddled with the cake.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: skedaddled, skedaddling. Informal; not for formal essays — there use «flee» or «run away». Spelling: double d.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A sloe is a small, round, dark blue-black fruit of the blackthorn bush, very sour when raw. 2) The blackthorn bush itself is sometimes called a sloe.
its sense in the lessons: Sloes grow wild in hedges in Britain and Ireland and ripen in autumn. People use them to make jam and sloe gin (a grown-up drink). In nature lessons, the blackthorn is one of the first hedges to flower white in spring. «Sloe-eyed» in old books means having dark, beautiful eyes.
examples from the lessons: We found sloes in the hedge on our autumn walk. | Sloes are too sour to eat straight from the bush. | The blackthorn has white flowers in spring and sloes in autumn. | Birds eat the sloes in winter. | Grandad makes sloe jelly every October. | The sloes looked like tiny dark plums.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one sloe, two sloes. Sounds the same as «slow» — a homophone; do not mix them up. Do not eat wild berries unless an adult says they are safe.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Smartly means in a neat, tidy and good-looking way, especially about clothes. 2) Smartly means quickly and sharply. 3) Smartly can mean cleverly.
its sense in the lessons: In school, pupils are asked to dress smartly for photos or concerts. In stories «stepped smartly» or «turned smartly» shows quick, brisk movement, often soldier-like. «He rapped smartly on the door» means a quick, firm knock. In The Wind in the Willows animals often step or reply smartly.
examples from the lessons: Everyone came to the wedding smartly dressed. | The soldier turned smartly and marched away. | She rapped smartly on the door. | Please walk smartly, we are late. | He answered the question smartly. | Toad stepped smartly into the motor car. | The waiter was smartly dressed in black and white.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «smart». In British English «smart» often means neat and well-dressed; in American English it more often means clever. «Smartly» can also mean «quickly», so read the sentence to see which.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Smilingly means while smiling, in a smiling and friendly way.
its sense in the lessons: A story word that tells the reader the person is happy, friendly or politely pleased while speaking or acting. Sometimes a character answers «smilingly» while hiding what they really feel.
examples from the lessons: The teacher smilingly handed out the prizes. | «Of course you may,» she said smilingly. | The Rat smilingly shook his head. | The shopkeeper smilingly waved goodbye. | He nodded smilingly at the baby. | The Cheshire Cat looked smilingly down from the tree.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from «smiling» + «-ly». Rather bookish; in speech we say «with a smile». Spelling: smile → smiling (drop the e) → smilingly.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A softhearted person is kind, gentle and easily feels sorry for others. 2) Sometimes it means too kind, so that the person is easy to persuade.
its sense in the lessons: In stories a softhearted character helps the weak, forgives easily or cannot say no. It is usually praise, but «too softhearted» can mean someone is easily tricked. The opposite is «hard-hearted».
examples from the lessons: Grandma is so softhearted that she feeds every stray cat. | The softhearted giant let the children go. | Don't be softhearted — he's only pretending to cry. | Mole was softhearted and could not bear to see anyone sad. | The softhearted judge gave him a second chance. | She was too softhearted to win the argument.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Also written «soft-hearted». Opposite: «hard-hearted». Noun: «softheartedness». It is not about the real heart in your body.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Solemnly means in a very serious way, without smiling or joking. 2) Solemnly can mean in a formal, important way, as in a promise or ceremony.
its sense in the lessons: Used for serious moments: promises, oaths, funerals, church services and prize-givings. «I solemnly swear» begins an oath in court. In Alice, creatures often speak very solemnly about silly things, which makes the reader laugh.
examples from the lessons: The judge spoke solemnly to the court. | «I solemnly promise to look after the puppy,» said Jack. | The Mock Turtle sighed solemnly. | The children walked solemnly into the church. | He solemnly shook hands with each of us. | The flag was solemnly lowered.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «solemn» (the n is silent: SOL-em). Spelling of the adverb: solemnly — keep the n. Not the same as «sadly», though solemn moments may be sad.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Stoutly means bravely, firmly and strongly, without giving in. 2) Stoutly built means made strong and thick.
its sense in the lessons: In old stories characters «stoutly deny» or «stoutly defend» something: they say it firmly and will not change their minds. In The Wind in the Willows the animals defend their home stoutly. A «stoutly made» door or boot is strong and solid.
examples from the lessons: Toad stoutly denied that he had taken the car. | The soldiers stoutly defended the castle. | The gate was stoutly made of oak. | She stoutly refused to give up. | He stoutly believed his team would win. | The little dog barked stoutly at the fox.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «stout», which means strong, brave, or (of a person) rather fat. «Stoutly» almost always means firmly or strongly, not fat. Old-fashioned; in speech say «firmly».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Suet is hard white fat from around the kidneys of cows and sheep, used in cooking. 2) Vegetable suet is a similar fat made from plants.
its sense in the lessons: In British and Irish cooking suet makes dumplings, Christmas pudding, mince pies and steamed puddings. Bird lovers put suet balls out in winter to feed birds. In The Wind in the Willows and old stories, suet puddings are hearty country food.
examples from the lessons: Mum adds suet to the dumplings for the stew. | We hung a suet ball in the garden for the birds. | Christmas pudding is made with suet and dried fruit. | Vegetarians use vegetable suet. | The old cook made a big suet pudding. | Blue tits love pecking at suet in winter.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «some suet», not «a suet» (but «a suet pudding», «suet balls»). Pronounced SOO-it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Sullenly means in a bad-tempered, silent and unfriendly way, as when someone is sulking. 2) Sullenly can describe dark, gloomy weather or water.
its sense in the lessons: A story word that tells the reader a character is angry or unhappy but will not say so. «He answered sullenly» shows a grudging, grumpy reply. Dark clouds or a river can move sullenly, which makes the mood gloomy.
examples from the lessons: The boy stared sullenly at his plate. | «I don't care,» she muttered sullenly. | The weasels sullenly handed back the keys. | The river flowed sullenly under grey skies. | He sat sullenly in the corner all afternoon. | The prisoner answered sullenly.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «sullen» + «-ly». Sullen is about silent bad mood; «sulky» is close. Not the same as «sadly».

part of speech: verb (sup, sups, supped, supping); noun (a sup); interjection («'sup» — slang)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (old or northern UK) To sup is to drink something a little at a time, or to sip. 2) (old) To sup is to eat supper, the evening meal. 3) (noun) A sup is a small mouthful of a drink. 4) (slang, «'sup» or «sup») A short way of saying «What's up?» as a greeting.
its sense in the lessons: In old stories and the Bible people «sup» with friends, meaning eat the evening meal together. In the north of England and Ireland «sup» still means to drink («sup your tea»). Young people text «sup?» meaning «hi, how are you?».
examples from the lessons: The travellers supped with the farmer and his wife. | Have a sup of tea before you go. | He supped his soup slowly. | «Sup, mate?» said the older boy. | The Rat and Mole supped by the fire. | Take just a sup, it's very hot.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: supped, supping (double p). The greeting «'sup» is very informal slang; do not use in writing at school. Related to «supper» and «soup».

part of speech: verb (swagger, swaggers, swaggered, swaggering); noun (swagger — uncountable)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To swagger is to walk or behave in a very proud, showy way, as if you think you are better than others. 2) (noun) Swagger is that proud, showy way of walking or behaving. 3) (informal) Swagger can mean confident style that others admire.
its sense in the lessons: In The Wind in the Willows Toad swaggers and boasts after his escapes; the word tells the reader he is vain and showing off. Pirates and bullies swagger in stories. «Swag» in modern slang comes from this word and means cool style.
examples from the lessons: Toad swaggered down the road, singing about himself. | The new captain walked with a swagger. | Pirates swaggered through the town. | He swaggered into class as if he owned it. | She had the swagger of a champion. | The bully swaggered up to the little ones.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: swaggered, swaggering (double g). Usually a criticism. Do not mix up with «stagger» (to walk unsteadily, nearly falling).

part of speech: noun (a swathe, swathes); verb (swathe, swathes, swathed, swathing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A swathe is a long, wide strip or area of land, crops or something else. 2) To swathe something is to wrap it up in cloth or bandages. 3) A swathe can be a large part of a group: «a swathe of the country».
its sense in the lessons: In nature and geography writing, «a swathe of forest» means a big strip of it. When grass or corn is cut with a scythe, each cut row is a swathe. «Cut a swathe through» means to move through and knock things down. In stories a hurt person is «swathed in bandages» or a baby «swathed in blankets».
examples from the lessons: The fire burned a wide swathe of forest. | The baby was swathed in a warm blanket. | His arm was swathed in bandages. | The farmer cut the hay in long swathes. | A swathe of bluebells covered the wood. | Snow fell across a huge swathe of Canada.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Also spelt «swath» (especially in the US) for the strip meaning. Rhymes with «bathe». Regular verb: swathed.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) The syrinx is the voice organ of a bird, deep in its chest where the windpipe splits; it lets birds sing. 2) A syrinx is a set of panpipes, a simple instrument of reed tubes of different lengths that you blow across. 3) (Greek myth) Syrinx was a nymph who, running from the god Pan, was turned into reeds, from which Pan made his pipes.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, birds sing with the syrinx, not with vocal cords like people. In The Wind in the Willows, in «The Piper at the Gates of Dawn», Rat and Mole hear the music of Pan's pipes on an island. The word «syringe» comes from the same Greek word for a tube or pipe.
examples from the lessons: A songbird makes its song with its syrinx. | Some birds can sing two notes at once using their syrinx. | The shepherd played a tune on his syrinx. | Pan made his pipes from the reeds that had been Syrinx. | Rat and Mole heard the far-off music of the pipes. | A syrinx is made of reeds of different lengths.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced SIRR-inks. Plural «syrinxes» or «syringes». In the myth it is a name, so it gets a capital letter: Syrinx.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A tactful person is careful to say and do things in a way that does not upset or hurt others. 2) A tactful remark or action is kind and careful about other people's feelings.
its sense in the lessons: In PSHE and everyday life being tactful means telling the truth kindly, choosing the right moment and words. In Alice, many creatures are very untactful and rude, which makes the story funny. Opposite: tactless.
examples from the lessons: It was tactful of you not to mention her haircut. | The teacher gave tactful advice about the story. | Mole was too tactful to laugh at Toad. | Try to be tactful when you tell him he lost. | She made a tactful excuse and left. | A tactful friend knows when to stay quiet.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: tact (uncountable). Adverb: tactfully. Opposite: tactless. Being tactful is not the same as lying; it is choosing kind words.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A tamarisk is a shrub or small tree with feathery leaves and small pink or white flowers that grows well in dry, salty places such as seasides and deserts.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and science, tamarisks grow in deserts, by salt lakes and on coasts; their long roots find water deep underground. In the Bible, Abraham planted a tamarisk tree at Beersheba. In some places, such as parts of the USA and Australia, tamarisk is a weed that spreads and drinks river water.
examples from the lessons: A tamarisk grew by the seaside path. | Tamarisks can live in salty sand. | The tamarisk's pink flowers look like feathers. | Abraham planted a tamarisk tree at Beersheba. | The camel rested in the shade of a tamarisk. | Farmers in Australia try to stop the tamarisk spreading.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: tamarisks. Pronounced TAM-a-risk.

part of speech: noun (thatch — usually uncountable; a thatch); verb (thatch, thatches, thatched, thatching)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Thatch is a roof covering made of straw, reeds or similar dried plants laid thickly. 2) To thatch a roof is to cover it with thatch. 3) (informal) A thatch of hair is a thick, untidy mass of hair.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, many old cottages in England, Ireland and elsewhere had thatched roofs; people in Iron Age roundhouses used thatch too. A thatcher is a person who thatches roofs. Thatch keeps rain out because water runs down the steep straw.
examples from the lessons: The cottage had a roof of golden thatch. | The thatcher thatched the roof with reeds. | Birds were nesting in the thatch. | Iron Age roundhouses were covered with thatch. | He had a thick thatch of red hair. | A thatched roof needs replacing every few decades.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: thatched («a thatched cottage»). Person: thatcher. Ends in -tch; plural verb form «thatches».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Timidly means in a shy, nervous, frightened way, without confidence.
its sense in the lessons: A story word for a character who is shy or scared: «she asked timidly». In Alice, Alice often speaks timidly to strange creatures; in The Wind in the Willows Mole is timid at first in the Wild Wood. It helps the reader feel the character's nervousness.
examples from the lessons: The new girl timidly raised her hand. | «May I come in?» asked Mole timidly. | The deer timidly stepped out of the wood. | Alice timidly began to explain. | He knocked timidly on the head teacher's door. | The puppy timidly sniffed my hand.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «timid» + «-ly». Noun: timidity. Opposite: boldly, confidently.

part of speech: verb (titter, titters, tittered, tittering); noun (a titter, titters)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To titter is to laugh quietly in a nervous, silly or slightly rude way, often trying not to. 2) (noun) A titter is such a little laugh.
its sense in the lessons: In class, a titter often goes round the room when something embarrassing happens. In stories it shows people laughing behind their hands, sometimes unkindly. Similar words: giggle, snigger, chuckle.
examples from the lessons: A titter ran round the class when the teacher's chair squeaked. | The girls tittered behind their books. | There was a nervous titter from the audience. | Don't titter, it's rude. | The guests tittered when Toad fell over. | He heard a titter from the back row.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: tittered, tittering (double t at the end). A titter is quieter and sillier than a laugh; a snigger is more unkind; a chuckle is warmer.

part of speech: verb (toil, toils, toiled, toiling); noun (toil — uncountable; toils)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To toil is to work very hard for a long time, usually at tiring work. 2) To toil can mean to move slowly and with great effort: «toil up a hill». 3) (noun) Toil is hard, tiring work. 4) (old) Toils, plural, are nets or traps: «caught in the toils».
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, people toiled in fields, mines and factories. In the Bible, God tells Adam he will toil for his food, and Jesus says the lilies of the field «toil not». In The Wind in the Willows the washerwoman and the bargewoman toil hard. Phrases: «toil and trouble», «years of toil».
examples from the lessons: The farmers toiled in the fields all day. | We toiled up the steep hill with our backpacks. | Children once toiled in factories and mines. | After years of toil he built his own house. | «Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow; they toil not.» | The ants toiled to carry the crumbs home.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: toiled. Formal or storybook word; in speech say «work hard». Noun is usually uncountable.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A trestle is a frame with legs, often a beam on two pairs of sloping legs, used to hold up a table top or plank. 2) A trestle table is a long table made of a board on trestles, easy to fold away. 3) A trestle is also a framework of beams that holds up a railway bridge.
its sense in the lessons: At school fairs, harvest suppers and jumble sales, food is laid on trestle tables. In The Wind in the Willows, a feast is laid on trestle tables. In engineering, trestle bridges carry railways across valleys, especially in North America.
examples from the lessons: We set out the cakes on trestle tables in the hall. | The painter stood on a plank between two trestles. | The old train crossed a wooden trestle bridge. | Fold the trestles away after the fair. | The banquet was laid on long trestle tables. | Dad built a workbench on two trestles.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Pronounced TRESS-ul (the t is silent).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A turnip is a round root vegetable with white flesh and a white and purple skin. 2) (UK informal, old) Calling someone a turnip means they are stupid.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons a turnip is a root that stores food for the plant. In history, Turnip Townshend grew turnips to feed cattle in winter. In Scotland and the north of England «turnip» or «neep» may mean the bigger yellow swede. Stories like «The Enormous Turnip» are read in infant classes. In Ireland and Scotland people carved turnips as lanterns at Halloween before pumpkins.
examples from the lessons: Grandad grows turnips in his garden. | The Enormous Turnip was too big to pull up. | We had mashed turnip with our dinner. | Sheep eat turnips in winter. | Children carved scary faces in turnips for Halloween. | A turnip is a root vegetable.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: turnips. «Swede» (UK) = «rutabaga» (US) is a different, yellow vegetable, though people mix them up.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (church) Unction is the act of anointing someone with holy oil as a sign of God's blessing, for example for the sick. 2) (formal, disapproving) Unction is a way of talking that is too smooth, oily and falsely serious or polite.
its sense in the lessons: In church, «the anointing of the sick», once called «extreme unction», is a sacrament in which a priest anoints a sick or dying person with oil; Catholics and some other Christians believe it brings God's strength and comfort. In the Bible, kings and priests were anointed with oil. In old books a person who speaks «with unction» seems greasy and insincere.
examples from the lessons: The priest gave unction to the dying man. | Kings were anointed with holy oil, a kind of unction. | He spoke with great unction about his own goodness. | The anointing of the sick was once called extreme unction. | The salesman's unction made us distrust him. | Christians believe the oil is a sign of God's care.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Adjective: «unctuous» (oily, too smooth) is used more today than «unction» for the second sense.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Undecorated means plain, with no decorations or ornaments. 2) (of a soldier) Undecorated means not given any medals.
its sense in the lessons: In art and DT lessons, an undecorated pot or cake is the plain version before you add patterns. In history, a soldier who was never given a medal is undecorated.
examples from the lessons: The cake was still undecorated when the guests arrived. | We painted the undecorated clay pots. | The church walls were plain and undecorated. | The Christmas tree stood undecorated in the corner. | He was a brave but undecorated soldier. | An undecorated room can look bare.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Made of «un-» (not) + «decorated». Opposite: decorated.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Undoubtedly means certainly, without any doubt; it is sure to be true.
its sense in the lessons: Used to say something is definitely true: «She is undoubtedly the best player.» In essays it shows a strong opinion or a known fact. In stories, a boastful character like Toad says he is «undoubtedly» the cleverest, which the reader may doubt.
examples from the lessons: She is undoubtedly the fastest runner in the school. | It will undoubtedly rain tomorrow. | Toad was undoubtedly the richest animal on the river. | Undoubtedly, this is the best pizza I've had. | The dog was undoubtedly hungry. | Exercise is undoubtedly good for you.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The b is silent: un-DOUT-ed-lee. Spelling: doubt → doubted → undoubtedly. Similar: certainly, definitely, no doubt.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unguarded means not watched or protected by anyone. 2) An unguarded moment or remark is one when you are not careful and say or show something you meant to keep secret.
its sense in the lessons: In safety talk, an unguarded fire or pool is dangerous because nobody is watching. In sport, an unguarded player or goal is free and open. In stories, a character lets slip a secret «in an unguarded moment». In The Wind in the Willows Toad escapes when the gate is unguarded.
examples from the lessons: Never leave a fire unguarded. | The goal was unguarded and he scored easily. | Toad slipped past the unguarded gate. | In an unguarded moment, she told us her secret. | The castle was left unguarded at night. | The bags were unguarded on the train.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Made of «un-» + «guarded». The «u» after g is silent: un-GAR-did.

part of speech: adjective; past form of the verb «unlace» (unlace, unlaces, unlaced, unlacing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Unlaced means with the laces undone or taken out. 2) As a verb, to unlace something is to undo its laces.
its sense in the lessons: Children are told to tie their shoes because unlaced shoes can make you trip. In old stories, ladies unlaced their tight corsets, and soldiers unlaced their boots after a long march.
examples from the lessons: Your shoes are unlaced — tie them before you fall! | He unlaced his boots and rubbed his feet. | She ran out with her trainers unlaced. | The skater unlaced her skates. | Toad unlaced his heavy boots by the fire. | An unlaced boot slipped off in the mud.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Unlace» is a regular verb: unlaced. Opposite: laced, laced up. «Untied» is more common for shoes.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Upland is high land, hills or high ground away from the sea. 2) (adjective) Upland describes things in or of high land: upland farms, upland birds.
its sense in the lessons: In geography, uplands are areas of hills and mountains, such as the Scottish Highlands or the Pennines; the land below is the lowland. Upland weather is colder and wetter, and farms there keep sheep more than crops. In The Wind in the Willows the animals look up from the river to the uplands and the far hills.
examples from the lessons: Sheep graze on the uplands. | The upland farms are small and windy. | Curlews nest on upland moors. | Scotland has large areas of upland. | The river starts in the uplands and flows to the sea. | Upland streams are fast and cold.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Often plural: «the uplands». Opposite: lowland(s). Stress on «up»: UP-lund.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Uproar is a lot of loud, confused noise and excitement from many people. 2) An uproar is a public storm of anger or protest about something.
its sense in the lessons: In class, «the room was in uproar» means everyone was shouting and out of order. In news, «an uproar over the new rules» means many people are angry. In Alice the courtroom and the Queen's croquet game end in uproar; in The Wind in the Willows the battle in Toad Hall is an uproar.
examples from the lessons: The classroom was in uproar when the hamster escaped. | There was an uproar when the referee gave the penalty. | The court was in an uproar. | The plan to close the library caused an uproar. | The crowd went into uproar at the goal. | The banquet in Toad Hall ended in uproar.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Phrases: «in uproar», «cause an uproar». Adjective: uproarious (very noisy, or very funny). It has nothing to do with a lion's roar, though it sounds like it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Valerian is a tall wild plant with small sweet-smelling pink or white flowers that grows by rivers and in damp places. 2) Valerian is also a medicine made from the root of this plant, which some people take to help them sleep.
its sense in the lessons: In The Wind in the Willows the river banks are full of wild flowers such as willow-herb and meadowsweet; valerian grows in such places too. Red valerian grows on old walls and cliffs in Britain. Cats are attracted to the smell of valerian root, a bit like catnip.
examples from the lessons: Pink valerian grew along the river bank. | Red valerian sprouted from the old castle wall. | Butterflies visit valerian flowers. | Some adults take valerian to help them sleep. | Our cat rolled in the valerian. | The root of valerian smells very strong.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced va-LEER-ee-un. Herbal medicines should be taken only with an adult's say-so.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal, old) Valorous means very brave, especially in battle.
its sense in the lessons: A grand storybook word for heroes and knights: «a valorous knight». Toad in The Wind in the Willows likes to think of himself as valorous. It comes from «valour» (bravery).
examples from the lessons: The valorous knight rode out to fight the dragon. | The soldiers were honoured for their valorous deeds. | Toad sang about his own valorous adventures. | She was valorous in the face of danger. | The poem praises a valorous king. | The little mouse made a valorous stand against the cat.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; in speech say «brave». Noun: valour (UK) / valor (US). Not about «value», though they look alike.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A valuation is an expert's decision about how much money something is worth. 2) Valuation can mean how much you think something or someone is worth in a general way.
its sense in the lessons: In money matters, before a house is sold or a mortgage is given, a surveyor makes a valuation. An antique expert gives a valuation of an old vase. In maths word problems, a valuation is a number of pounds or dollars that something is worth, not what it was sold for.
