examples from the lessons: The expert gave a valuation of £500 for the old clock. | The bank needed a valuation of the house. | Grandma's ring had a high valuation. | We had the painting valued, and the valuation surprised us. | His own valuation of his skill was too high. | The valuation of the company went up.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Verb: value, valued. A valuation is an estimate of worth; the actual price paid can be higher or lower.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal, literary) Verdant means green and full of growing plants and grass.
its sense in the lessons: A describing word for poems and stories: «verdant meadows», «verdant hills». It paints a fresh, rich, green picture, as of the river banks in spring in The Wind in the Willows. In geography, wet climates such as Ireland's make the land verdant.
examples from the lessons: The cows grazed in verdant fields. | After the rain, the valley was verdant and fresh. | Ireland is famous for its verdant hills. | The river banks were verdant in spring. | The garden became verdant again in May. | The poet described the verdant forest.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; in speech say «green» or «lush». From an old French word for green (vert). Noun: verdure (green plants).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A vigil is a time when you stay awake, especially at night, to watch over someone or something or to pray. 2) A vigil is a quiet gathering of people to remember someone or to show they care about something, often with candles. 3) (church) A vigil is a service on the evening before a holy day, such as the Easter Vigil.
its sense in the lessons: In church life, Christians keep a vigil of prayer, for example on Holy Saturday night (the Easter Vigil). Families may keep a vigil at a sick person's bed. After a sad event, people hold a candlelit vigil. In The Wind in the Willows Rat and Mole keep watch through the night looking for little Portly.
examples from the lessons: The family kept a vigil by Grandad's bed. | People held a candlelit vigil for the victims. | The Easter Vigil is held on Saturday night. | The soldiers kept vigil at the gate. | Rat and Mole kept vigil all night by the river. | She kept a long vigil waiting for news.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Phrase: «keep (a) vigil». Adjective: vigilant (watchful). Related: vigilance.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Vigour is great strength, energy and enthusiasm in the body or the mind. 2) Vigour can describe healthy, strong growth of plants.
its sense in the lessons: In PE and health, exercise gives you vigour. In stories, a character works «with vigour», meaning hard and with energy, as Badger does when he starts to fight. In gardening, a plant grows with vigour when it is healthy.
examples from the lessons: He scrubbed the floor with great vigour. | The old man still had the vigour of a young one. | The team played with new vigour after half-time. | The roses grew with vigour after the rain. | She argued with vigour for her idea. | The Rat rowed with vigour.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Spelling: vigour (UK, Canada, Australia, NZ, Ireland), vigor (US). Adjective: vigorous (no u in either spelling). Adverb: vigorously.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A waif is a homeless, neglected child or animal, often thin and with nobody to care for it. 2) (informal) A waif is a very thin, pale, delicate-looking person.
its sense in the lessons: In Victorian stories and history, waifs were poor orphans living on the streets, like the children Dr Barnardo helped. The phrase «waifs and strays» means homeless children or lost animals. In The Wind in the Willows Rat and Mole search for the lost baby otter, a little waif. The word makes the reader feel pity.
examples from the lessons: The kind woman took in the little waif. | Victorian cities had many waifs living on the streets. | «Waifs and strays» are lost children or animals. | The kitten was a thin little waif when we found it. | The story is about a waif who finds a home. | She looked like a waif in her big coat.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Sounds like «waive» (to give up a right) — a homophone. Do not mix up with «wife».

meaning for a pupil: 1) The waterside is the land along the edge of a river, lake or sea. 2) (adjective) Waterside describes things found by the water: a waterside cafe, waterside plants.
its sense in the lessons: The Wind in the Willows is set mostly by the waterside, where Rat lives in his hole in the bank. In science, waterside plants such as reeds and willows like wet soil. In safety lessons, children are told to be careful at the waterside, because banks can be slippery.
examples from the lessons: We had a picnic at the waterside. | Ducks and moorhens live along the waterside. | The Rat's house was right at the waterside. | Waterside paths can be slippery. | They ate at a waterside cafe by the harbour. | Willows grow well by the waterside.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually «the waterside» or used before a noun. Safety: never play near deep water without an adult.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (literary, old) A wayfarer is a traveller who goes on foot, walking from place to place.
its sense in the lessons: An old storybook word for walkers on long journeys. In The Wind in the Willows the chapter «Wayfarers All» tells of the Sea Rat, a wanderer who tempts Rat to leave home and travel. In church hymns, life is sometimes called a journey, and the faithful are wayfarers. Phrase: «weary wayfarer».
examples from the lessons: The weary wayfarer stopped at the inn for the night. | «Wayfarers All» is a chapter about the call to travel. | The wayfarer asked the farmer the way to town. | Pilgrims and wayfarers walked the old road. | The Sea Rat was a wayfarer who had seen many lands. | The cottage gave shelter to wayfarers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. From «way» (road) + «fare» (to travel). Verb-like adjective: «wayfaring». Modern words: traveller, walker, hiker.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (old) A wench was a girl or young woman, especially a servant girl or a country girl. 2) (now insulting) Today the word is old-fashioned and often rude when said to a woman.
its sense in the lessons: Found in old stories, ballads, plays and historical tales: «a serving wench at the inn». It tells the reader the story is set long ago. In The Wind in the Willows and similar books the word belongs to an older, rougher kind of speech. Today you should not call anyone a wench.
examples from the lessons: The serving wench brought ale to the travellers. | In the old ballad, a country wench milked the cows. | The pirate shouted for the kitchen wench. | The play is set in a tavern with a busy wench. | «Wench» is an old word you meet in historical stories. | Calling a woman a wench today is rude.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: wenches. Old-fashioned and disrespectful now; use it only when reading or quoting old texts.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (a name) Winchester is a historic city in Hampshire in the south of England, once the capital of the Saxon kings, with a great cathedral. 2) A Winchester is a kind of repeating rifle made by the American Winchester company from the 1860s, famous in the Wild West. 3) (a name) Winchester is also a surname and the name of towns in the USA and elsewhere.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons, Winchester was King Alfred's capital, and a famous round table said to be King Arthur's hangs there. Winchester College is an old English school. In Westerns, cowboys carry a Winchester rifle. Since it is a name, it usually takes a capital W.
examples from the lessons: King Alfred's statue stands in Winchester. | Winchester Cathedral is one of the longest in Europe. | The cowboy kept his Winchester by the door. | Winchester was once the capital of England. | We visited Winchester on our school trip. | The round table in Winchester Great Hall is very old.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A proper noun: write Winchester with a capital letter. Pronounced WIN-chess-ter. Guns are dangerous and are only for trained adults.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal, rude) A windbag is a person who talks too much, usually about boring or unimportant things, or boasts endlessly. 2) (old) A windbag is the bag of a bagpipe that holds the air.
its sense in the lessons: A teasing word in stories and everyday talk. In The Wind in the Willows Toad could be called a windbag because he boasts and talks about himself without stopping. Politicians are sometimes mocked as windbags.
examples from the lessons: Uncle Bert is a real windbag — he talks for hours. | «Be quiet, you old windbag!» | The speech was so long that people called him a windbag. | Toad was a windbag who never stopped boasting. | Nobody wanted to sit next to the windbag at dinner. | The piper squeezed the windbag under his arm.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Informal and a bit rude; don't call a teacher or visitor a windbag. Similar: chatterbox (gentler), bore, show-off.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To accomplish something is to succeed in doing it, especially after hard work. 2) (adjective «accomplished») Accomplished means very skilled: an accomplished pianist.
its sense in the lessons: In school reports and goals, «what did you accomplish this term?» means what did you manage to do. In stories, heroes accomplish tasks or quests. «Mission accomplished» means the job is done. In maths, «the task is accomplished» means solved.
examples from the lessons: She accomplished her goal of swimming a length. | We accomplished a lot in one afternoon. | The knight accomplished his quest. | It took months to accomplish the job. | He is an accomplished violinist. | What do you hope to accomplish this year? | Mission accomplished — the cake is baked!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: accomplished. Noun: accomplishment. Pronounced a-KUM-plish. Similar: achieve, complete, manage.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal, often funny) Accoutrements are the extra things, clothes or equipment you have or carry for a particular activity or job. 2) Accoutrements can mean the things that usually go with something: the accoutrements of wealth.
its sense in the lessons: An old, grand word used for a soldier's belts and pouches or for a traveller's gear. In The Wind in the Willows Toad's caravan and motoring outfits come with lots of accoutrements, and the word makes his fuss over equipment funny. In everyday life, «all the accoutrements» means all the bits and pieces.
examples from the lessons: The soldier checked his accoutrements before the march. | Toad bought every accoutrement for motoring. | The camping trip needed all sorts of accoutrements. | A big house with all the accoutrements of wealth. | She packed her painting accoutrements. | The knight's accoutrements gleamed in the sun.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually plural. Spelt «accoutrement» (UK) or «accouterment» (US). Pronounced a-KOO-tra-ment. From French. Simpler words: equipment, gear, kit.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An adviser is a person whose job is to give advice, especially to help someone make decisions. 2) An adviser can be anyone who gives you advice.
its sense in the lessons: In government, the Prime Minister or President has advisers. At school, a careers adviser or a teacher adviser helps pupils choose. In money matters, a financial adviser helps people with savings. In fairy tales, kings have wise (or wicked) advisers.
examples from the lessons: The king's adviser told him to make peace. | The careers adviser came to talk to us. | My older sister is my best adviser. | The President met his advisers. | A financial adviser helps with savings. | The wicked adviser tricked the young prince.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Also spelt «advisor»; both are correct. Advice is the noun for what is given (uncountable: «some advice»); advise is the verb.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An alder is a tree of the birch family that grows by rivers and in wet ground, with roundish leaves and small cones and catkins.
its sense in the lessons: In science and nature, alders like wet soil; their roots help hold river banks together, and they make little woody cones that stay on all winter. In The Wind in the Willows the river is lined with willows and alders. Alder wood does not rot easily under water, so it was used for posts and piers, and Venice stands partly on alder.
examples from the lessons: Alders grow along the river bank. | The alder has small brown cones like tiny pine cones. | Siskins feed on alder seeds in winter. | The Rat tied his boat to an old alder. | Alder wood lasts well in water. | Catkins hang from the alder in early spring.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Do not mix up with «elder», another tree (with white flowers and black berries), or with «older».

meaning for a pupil: 1) An antimacassar is a small cloth, often lacy, put over the back or arms of a chair or sofa to keep it clean.
its sense in the lessons: In Victorian and Edwardian times men put Macassar oil on their hair, which stained chairs; the cloth was «anti» (against) the Macassar oil. In history lessons about Victorian homes and in old books, the word shows an old-fashioned, tidy parlour. Trains and planes still sometimes have them on headrests.
examples from the lessons: Grandma's armchair had a lace antimacassar. | Antimacassars kept hair oil off the chairs. | The Victorian parlour was full of antimacassars and ornaments. | The train seats had white antimacassars. | She crocheted an antimacassar for the sofa. | The word comes from Macassar hair oil.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. A long word: an-ti-ma-CASS-ar. Old-fashioned; today people may say «chair back cover».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (old) An apothecary was a person who made and sold medicines, like a chemist or pharmacist today. 2) (old) An apothecary also gave simple medical advice and treatment.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons about the Middle Ages, Tudor and Victorian times, the apothecary mixed herbs, powders and potions in a shop with jars. In stories, the apothecary sells cures and sometimes poisons. Today his job is done by a pharmacist (UK: chemist; US: drugstore).
examples from the lessons: The apothecary mixed a potion of herbs. | In Tudor times you went to the apothecary for medicine. | Rows of jars lined the apothecary's shop. | The apothecary weighed the powder carefully. | Today a pharmacist does the job of an apothecary. | The story's villain bought poison from an apothecary.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: apothecaries (y → ies). Pronounced a-POTH-e-ka-ree. Old-fashioned word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To apprise someone of something is to tell them about it or inform them.
its sense in the lessons: Used in formal letters, reports and the stiff exam voice: «Please keep me apprised of any changes» means «please keep telling me». In old stories, a servant apprises the king of news.
examples from the lessons: Please apprise me of any changes to the timetable. | The captain was apprised of the danger. | The head teacher apprised parents of the new rules. | Keep me apprised of your progress. | Badger apprised the others of the weasels' plan. | We were not apprised of the decision.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; in speech say «tell» or «let know». Pattern: apprise someone OF something. Do not confuse with «appraise» (to judge the value or quality of something).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Artful means clever at getting what you want, especially by tricking people; crafty. 2) Artful can mean done with skill and cleverness.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, an artful character is cunning, like the Artful Dodger, the young pickpocket in Oliver Twist. In The Wind in the Willows the weasels and stoats can be artful, and so can Toad in his disguises. It can be praise («an artful design») but more often warns of trickery.
examples from the lessons: The Artful Dodger was a clever young thief. | The fox was artful and fooled the hens. | Toad made an artful escape dressed as a washerwoman. | It was an artful way to get extra pudding. | She made an artful arrangement of flowers. | Don't trust him — he's very artful.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb: artfully. Similar: crafty, cunning, sly, wily. Not the same as «artistic», though both come from «art».

meaning for a pupil: 1) To look askance at something or someone is to look at them with doubt, suspicion or disapproval. 2) (old) Askance means sideways, out of the corner of your eye.
its sense in the lessons: Used in stories and formal writing: «the neighbours looked askance at Toad's new motor car» means they did not approve. It shows that people doubt or distrust something without saying so.
examples from the lessons: The old ladies looked askance at the noisy children. | The teacher looked askance at his excuse. | Badger looked askance at Toad's new hobby. | People looked askance at the strange visitor. | She glanced askance at the plate of snails. | The cat eyed the dog askance.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Almost always in «look askance at». Pronounced a-SKANSS. Formal and literary.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An ass is a donkey, an animal like a small horse with long ears. 2) (rude, informal) Calling someone an ass means they are being stupid or silly. 3) (rude, US) Ass is a rude word for your bottom, the part you sit on.
its sense in the lessons: In the Bible, Jesus rides into Jerusalem on an ass on Palm Sunday, and Balaam's ass speaks to him. In fables, the ass is often foolish. In old British books «Don't be an ass!» is a mild telling-off between friends, used by Toad's friends about him. The American bottom sense is rude and not for school.
examples from the lessons: The farmer loaded the ass with sacks of grain. | Jesus rode into Jerusalem on an ass. | Balaam's ass saw the angel before he did. | «Don't be such an ass!» said Rat to Toad. | In the fable, the ass wore a lion's skin. | He made an ass of himself at the party.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: asses. Phrase: «make an ass of yourself» (behave stupidly). The UK rude word for bottom is spelled «arse»; both are rude. For the animal, «donkey» is the everyday word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To assail someone is to attack them violently. 2) To be assailed by doubts, worries, smells or questions is to have them come at you strongly from all sides.
its sense in the lessons: In history and stories, armies assail a castle. In everyday writing, «assailed by a terrible smell» or «assailed by questions from reporters». In The Wind in the Willows Mole is assailed by fear in the Wild Wood and later by the smell of his old home.
examples from the lessons: The castle was assailed by enemy troops. | Mole was assailed by the smell of his old home. | She was assailed by doubts before the exam. | Reporters assailed the footballer with questions. | Strange noises assailed them in the dark wood. | The ship was assailed by storms.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: assailed. Noun for the attacker: assailant. Formal; simpler words: attack, hit, bother.

part of speech: adjective; present participle of «astonish» (astonish, astonishes, astonished, astonishing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Astonishing means so surprising that it is hard to believe; amazing.
its sense in the lessons: Used for very surprising facts, events and sights: «an astonishing discovery». In science, «it is astonishing that a tiny seed grows into an oak». In Alice everything that happens is astonishing to Alice. In maths, a result may be «astonishing» when the numbers are much bigger than expected.
examples from the lessons: It is astonishing how fast a cheetah runs. | Alice saw an astonishing sight: a cat with a grin and no body. | The magician did an astonishing trick. | An astonishing number of people came. | The blue whale is astonishing in size. | It's astonishing that you finished so quickly!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb: astonishingly. Stronger than «surprising»; similar to «amazing», «astounding». «Astonished» describes the person who feels it; «astonishing» describes the thing that causes it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Astonishment is a feeling of very great surprise.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, characters stare, gasp or freeze in astonishment. Phrases: «to my astonishment», «in astonishment», «stare in astonishment». In Alice, Alice is often filled with astonishment at Wonderland.
examples from the lessons: To my astonishment, the cat began to talk. | The crowd gasped in astonishment. | Mole stared in astonishment at Rat's boat. | Much to our astonishment, we won the cup. | Her eyes widened in astonishment. | He shook his head in astonishment.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «great astonishment», not «an astonishment». Verb: astonish.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (old, literary) Athwart means across, from one side to the other of something. 2) (sailing) Athwart means across a ship, from side to side. 3) (old) Athwart can mean against, opposite to.
its sense in the lessons: Found in old stories and sea writing: «the fallen tree lay athwart the path», «a beam of sunlight fell athwart the room». In The Wind in the Willows the Sea Rat's sea talk and the river scenes use such old words. «Athwartships» means across the ship.
examples from the lessons: A fallen tree lay athwart the path. | A beam of sunlight fell athwart the floor. | The boat drifted athwart the stream. | The sailors stretched a rope athwart the deck. | Dark clouds lay athwart the sky. | The log jammed athwart the river.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Old-fashioned; today say «across». Pronounced a-THWORT.

part of speech: noun (an ax, axes); verb (ax, axes, axed, axing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) An ax is a tool with a heavy metal blade on a long handle, used for chopping wood. 2) (informal) To ax something is to cancel it or cut it; to ax a worker is to fire them.
its sense in the lessons: «Ax» is the American spelling; British, Irish, Canadian, Australian and NZ English usually write «axe». In history, Vikings fought with battle-axes. In news, «the show was axed» means cancelled. Safety: axes are very sharp and only for trained adults.
examples from the lessons: The lumberjack swung his ax at the tree. | George Washington's story tells of a cherry tree and an ax. | The TV show was axed after one season. | Dad chopped firewood with an ax. | The firefighter broke down the door with an ax. | Hundreds of jobs were axed at the factory.
note for the reader of a maths problem: US spelling «ax»; elsewhere «axe». Plural: axes (pronounced like the plural of «axis», but «axes» of a graph is a different word). Past: axed.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal, UK) Baccy is short for tobacco, the dried leaves people smoke in pipes and cigarettes.
its sense in the lessons: A homely, old-fashioned word heard from old men, sailors and countrymen in British stories. In The Wind in the Willows the animals and the Sea Rat might talk of their pipes and baccy. Health: smoking tobacco causes serious illness.
examples from the lessons: Grandad kept his baccy in a tin. | The old sailor filled his pipe with baccy. | «Got any baccy?» asked the tramp. | The shop sold sweets and baccy. | He ran out of baccy and grumbled. | Baccy is slang for tobacco.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal shortening of «tobacco»; also «backy». Uncountable. Smoking is harmful to health and not for children.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Banishment is being sent away from your country or home as a punishment and not allowed to come back. 2) Banishment can mean getting rid of something completely.
its sense in the lessons: In history, kings punished enemies with banishment; in the Bible, Adam and Eve's banishment from the Garden of Eden. In stories, a prince is banished from the kingdom. In everyday talk, «banishment to your bedroom» is a joke.
examples from the lessons: The king sentenced the traitor to banishment. | Napoleon's banishment to St Helena lasted until his death. | Adam and Eve's banishment from Eden is told in Genesis. | The Queen of Hearts threatened banishment and beheading. | After banishment he could never return home. | The banishment of mobile phones from class pleased the teacher.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: banish, banished. Similar: exile. Usually uncountable.

part of speech: adjective; verb (bankrupt, bankrupts, bankrupted, bankrupting); noun (a bankrupt)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (money, law) A person or company that is bankrupt cannot pay their debts, and a court takes control of what they own to pay the people they owe. 2) To bankrupt someone is to make them bankrupt. 3) (informal) Bankrupt of something means having none of it left: bankrupt of ideas.
its sense in the lessons: In money lessons, a business goes bankrupt when it owes more than it can ever pay back. In stories, a rich man may go bankrupt and lose his house. Toad spends so wildly on cars that his friends fear for his money. In Monopoly, a player who cannot pay is bankrupt and out of the game.
examples from the lessons: The shop went bankrupt and closed. | His spending nearly bankrupted the family. | In Monopoly, you lose when you go bankrupt. | The company was declared bankrupt by the court. | The war left the country bankrupt. | The writer felt bankrupt of ideas.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: bankruptcy. Phrase: «go bankrupt». In maths, being bankrupt means your debts (what you owe) are bigger than what you own and can pay.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (old) A bard was a poet and singer who told stories in verse, especially in old Celtic lands such as Wales, Ireland and Scotland. 2) (literary) A bard is any poet. 3) «The Bard» means William Shakespeare.
its sense in the lessons: In history, bards kept the stories and family histories of chiefs, singing them with a harp. In Wales the Eisteddfod still crowns a bard. In stories and games a bard is a musician-storyteller. People call Shakespeare «the Bard of Avon».
examples from the lessons: The bard sang of the great deeds of the king. | Welsh bards compete at the Eisteddfod. | Shakespeare is called the Bard of Avon. | The bard played his harp by the fire. | Robert Burns is Scotland's national bard. | Toad thought himself a great bard and wrote songs about himself.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Do not mix up with «barred» (blocked), which sounds the same in some accents.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A bargewoman is a woman who lives on or steers a barge, a long flat-bottomed boat that carries goods on canals and rivers.
its sense in the lessons: In The Wind in the Willows, Toad, dressed as a washerwoman, gets a lift from a large bargewoman with a horse-drawn barge; when she finds he is a toad she throws him into the water, and he steals her horse. In history lessons about canals, whole families lived and worked on barges.
examples from the lessons: The bargewoman steered the barge along the canal. | Toad pretended to be a washerwoman to the bargewoman. | The bargewoman's horse pulled the barge on the towpath. | Furious, the bargewoman threw Toad into the river. | Canal families, bargemen and bargewomen, lived on their boats. | The bargewoman laughed at Toad's poor washing.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: bargewomen. Man: bargeman or bargee. A rare compound word.

part of speech: noun (a barrack, usually plural: barracks); verb (barrack, barracks, barracked, barracking)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Barracks are a large building or group of buildings where soldiers live. 2) (UK, Ireland) To barrack someone is to shout rude or mocking things at them while they are speaking or playing. 3) (Australia, NZ) To barrack for a team is to cheer for and support it.
its sense in the lessons: In history, soldiers lived in barracks; the plural «barracks» can mean one building or many. At sports matches in Britain, a crowd may barrack a player or referee. In Australia, «Who do you barrack for?» means «Which footy team do you support?».
examples from the lessons: The soldiers marched back to the barracks. | The army barracks were by the river. | The crowd barracked the referee. | Don't barrack the speaker; let him finish. | (Australia) I barrack for Collingwood. | The old barracks are now a museum.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Barracks» can be singular or plural: «a barracks», «the barracks are». Verb: barracked. Note the two different verb meanings in Britain and Australia.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To beautify something is to make it more beautiful.
its sense in the lessons: In community projects, people beautify a town with flowers and murals. «Beautify the school garden» means make it look nicer. In stories, a character beautifies herself before a ball.
examples from the lessons: The volunteers beautified the park with flower beds. | We beautified the classroom with our paintings. | The town plants tulips to beautify its streets. | She beautified the old box with shells. | Toad wanted to beautify Toad Hall. | Murals beautified the grey wall.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: y → ies, ied (beautifies, beautified), but beautifying keeps y. Noun: beautification.

part of speech: verb (beset, besets, beset, besetting) — mostly passive «be beset by/with»
meaning for a pupil: 1) To be beset by problems, dangers or worries is to have many of them troubling you from all sides. 2) (old) To beset someone is to surround and attack them.
its sense in the lessons: Used in stories and news: «the journey was beset by problems», «beset with dangers». In The Wind in the Willows Mole in the Wild Wood is beset by fears; in old tales, travellers are beset by robbers.
examples from the lessons: The expedition was beset by storms. | Mole felt beset by eyes and whispers in the Wild Wood. | The team has been beset by injuries. | Travellers were beset by robbers on the old road. | The project was beset with problems from the start. | She was beset by doubts.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular: past and past participle are «beset» (no -ed). Doubles t: besetting. Formal.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Bloodthirsty means eager to kill or hurt people, or enjoying violence. 2) A bloodthirsty story or film has a lot of killing and violence in it.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, pirates, tyrants and monsters are bloodthirsty; the Queen of Hearts in Alice shouts «Off with his head!» all the time and seems bloodthirsty, though nobody is actually executed. In The Wind in the Willows the weasels are feared as bloodthirsty, and the Just So Stories mention fierce, hungry animals.
examples from the lessons: The pirates were a bloodthirsty crew. | The bloodthirsty Queen kept shouting «Off with their heads!» | Sharks are not as bloodthirsty as films show. | Grandad told us a bloodthirsty tale of battles. | The tyrant was bloodthirsty and cruel. | Some old fairy tales are rather bloodthirsty.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative: bloodthirstier. A myth: animals that hunt are not «bloodthirsty» or wicked — they hunt to eat.

part of speech: adjective; present participle of «bluster» (bluster, blusters, blustered, blustering)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Blustering means talking in a loud, boastful or angry way, often to hide that you are wrong or scared. 2) Blustering wind is strong and gusty.
its sense in the lessons: In The Wind in the Willows Toad is blustering when he boasts and argues, and his friends see through it. In stories, a blustering bully or king makes noise but has little real power. In weather, a blustering March wind blows hard in gusts.
examples from the lessons: Toad was blustering about his driving skill. | The blustering wind banged the gate. | The blustering man shouted but did nothing. | Under his blustering, he was afraid. | A blustering March day. | «Nonsense!» said the Duke, blustering.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: bluster («all bluster» = all noise, no action). Adjective: blustery (of weather). Regular verb.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Boisterously means in a noisy, lively, energetic way, full of rough fun.
its sense in the lessons: In school, children playing boisterously may be told to calm down. In stories, puppies, crowds and parties behave boisterously. In The Wind in the Willows the field mice sing and Toad celebrates boisterously.
examples from the lessons: The children played boisterously in the playground. | The puppies tumbled boisterously over each other. | The crowd sang boisterously. | Toad laughed boisterously at his own joke. | The wind blew boisterously round the house. | The boys boisterously burst into the room.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «boisterous» + «-ly». Pronounced BOY-stuh-russ-lee. Not unkind, but loud and rough.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A burly person is big, strong and heavily built.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, burly men are guards, policemen, sailors or blacksmiths. In The Wind in the Willows the policemen who arrest Toad and the gaoler are burly. The word gives the reader a picture of size and strength, not fatness.
examples from the lessons: A burly policeman grabbed Toad by the collar. | The burly blacksmith lifted the anvil. | Two burly men carried the piano. | The bouncer was tall and burly. | A burly farmer opened the gate. | He had grown into a burly teenager.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative: burlier, burliest. Similar: brawny, strapping, hefty. Usually about men.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A canoeist is a person who paddles a canoe.
its sense in the lessons: In PE, outdoor activities and Scouts, canoeists learn to paddle and stay safe on rivers and lakes. In The Wind in the Willows Rat is a skilled boatman on the river. Safety: canoeists wear life jackets and helmets.
examples from the lessons: The canoeist paddled across the lake. | All canoeists must wear a life jacket. | A canoeist raced through the rapids. | Canoeists camped by the river. | She became a canoeist at the Olympics. | The canoeist waved to the walkers on the bank.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: canoe + ist (keep the e: canoeist). Verb: canoe, canoed, canoeing.

part of speech: verb (caress, caresses, caressed, caressing); noun (a caress, caresses)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To caress someone or something is to touch or stroke them gently and lovingly. 2) (noun) A caress is a gentle, loving touch. 3) (literary) Wind or water caresses something when it touches it softly.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, a mother caresses her baby's head, a child caresses a pet. Poets say the breeze caresses the face. It shows tenderness. In The Wind in the Willows the river seems to caress the boat and the bank.
examples from the lessons: She caressed the kitten's soft fur. | The mother caressed her baby's cheek. | A gentle breeze caressed our faces. | The water caressed the side of the boat. | He gave the horse a caress on the nose. | The waves caressed the sand.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double s: caresses, caressed. Stress on the second part: ka-RESS. Gentle and loving; touches should always be welcome.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (old) A casquet is an old spelling of «casket», a small box for jewels or treasure. 2) (old) A casquet can also be a light helmet, like a «casque». 3) (a name) The Casquets are dangerous rocks with a lighthouse in the English Channel near Alderney.
its sense in the lessons: A rare word found in old books, poems and sea stories. A casquet of jewels is a treasure chest; sailors feared the Casquets rocks. Today we say «casket» for the box and «helmet» for the head covering.
examples from the lessons: The princess kept her rings in a silver casquet. | The knight wore a light casquet on his head. | Many ships were wrecked on the Casquets. | The pirates opened the casquet and found gold. | A casquet is an old word for a little jewel box. | The lighthouse on the Casquets warns ships.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Rare and old; pronounced KASS-kit or KASS-kay. Modern forms: casket (box), casque (helmet). In the USA «casket» also means a coffin.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Chaotic means in a state of complete confusion and disorder, with no plan or control. 2) (science) A chaotic system is one where tiny changes at the start lead to huge, unpredictable differences later, like the weather.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, a chaotic morning or classroom has everyone rushing and nothing in order. In Alice, the Mad Hatter's tea party and the Caucus-race are chaotic. In science, weather is chaotic, which is why forecasts beyond a week or two are hard.
examples from the lessons: The first day of term was chaotic. | The kitchen was chaotic after the party. | The Mad Hatter's tea party was completely chaotic. | Traffic was chaotic after the snow. | Weather is a chaotic system. | Our chaotic game of football had no rules at all.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: chaos (pronounced KAY-oss). Adjective: chaotic (kay-OT-ik). Adverb: chaotically. The ch sounds like k.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Cheerless means gloomy, dull and without anything to make you happy or comfortable.
its sense in the lessons: Writers use it for cold rooms, grey days and sad places. In The Wind in the Willows, Toad's cell in the dungeon is cheerless, and the Wild Wood in winter is cold and cheerless; the warm, bright homes of Badger and Mole are the opposite.
examples from the lessons: It was a cold, cheerless day in November. | The prison cell was dark and cheerless. | The empty house felt cheerless. | They ate a cheerless supper of dry bread. | The Wild Wood was cheerless in the snow. | A fire made the cheerless room warm again.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «cheer» + «-less» (without). Opposite: cheerful, cosy.

part of speech: verb (chirrup, chirrups, chirruped, chirruping); noun (a chirrup, chirrups)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To chirrup is to make a series of short, high sounds, like a bird or an insect; to chirp. 2) A person chirrups when they talk in a bright, cheerful, high voice. 3) (noun) A chirrup is such a sound.
its sense in the lessons: In nature, sparrows chirrup and crickets chirrup on summer nights. In stories, a cheerful character «chirruped happily». In The Wind in the Willows the birds and the field mice chirrup by the river.
examples from the lessons: The sparrows chirruped in the hedge. | We heard the chirrup of crickets. | «Good morning!» she chirruped. | The baby bird chirruped for food. | The grasshoppers chirruped in the long grass. | A robin chirruped on the fence.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: chirruped, chirruping (one p is usual). Similar: chirp, cheep, twitter.

part of speech: verb (churr, churrs, churred, churring); noun (a churr)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To churr is to make a low, long, trilling or whirring sound, like a nightjar, a grasshopper or a partridge. 2) (noun) A churr is that sound.
its sense in the lessons: In nature study, the nightjar's churr on summer evenings is a famous sound of heaths in Britain. Grasshoppers and some insects churr too. Writers use it in country scenes like those of The Wind in the Willows.
examples from the lessons: The nightjar churred on the heath at dusk. | We heard the churr of a grasshopper. | A partridge churred in the field. | The insects churred in the warm evening. | The churring went on all night. | Listen for the nightjar's long churr.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: churred, churring (double r). Also spelt «chirr». Sounds like the noise itself.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A comforter is a person or thing that comforts someone who is sad or worried. 2) (US) A comforter is a thick, warm quilt for a bed. 3) (UK, old) A comforter was a long woollen scarf. 4) (UK, old) A comforter was a baby's dummy (US: pacifier). 5) (Bible, church) The Comforter is a name for the Holy Spirit in some Bible translations; Christians believe God's Spirit comforts and helps them.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, a friend acts as a comforter in sad times. In The Wind in the Willows the animals wrap up in warm things in winter. In church, John's Gospel says Jesus promised to send «the Comforter». Phrase from the Bible: «Job's comforters», friends who make you feel worse.
examples from the lessons: Grandma was a great comforter when I was sad. | In America, I sleep under a fluffy comforter. | He wound his woollen comforter round his neck. | The baby sucked on his comforter. | Jesus promised his disciples the Comforter. | Job's friends were poor comforters.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Note the different meanings in the USA (quilt) and in old British English (scarf, dummy). Capital C for the Holy Spirit.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A commotion is a lot of sudden noise, confusion and excitement.
its sense in the lessons: In class or stories, «What's all this commotion?» means «Why is everyone so noisy?». In Alice, the Duchess's kitchen and the trial are full of commotion. In The Wind in the Willows Toad causes a commotion wherever he goes.
examples from the lessons: There was a commotion in the corridor. | What is all this commotion about? | The fox caused a commotion in the henhouse. | A commotion broke out when the dog ran on the pitch. | Toad's motor car made a commotion in the village. | We heard a commotion outside.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: «a commotion». Phrase: «cause a commotion». Similar: fuss, uproar, hullabaloo.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To comport yourself is to behave in a particular way. 2) (formal) To comport with something is to agree with it or suit it.
its sense in the lessons: A stiff, formal word: «He comported himself with dignity» means he behaved well and calmly. In old stories, people are told how to comport themselves at court or in church.
examples from the lessons: She comported herself with great dignity at the funeral. | Pupils must comport themselves well on the trip. | Toad did not comport himself like a gentleman. | His words do not comport with his actions. | The knight comported himself bravely. | Try to comport yourself sensibly.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; in speech say «behave». Usually with «yourself/himself». Noun: comportment.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Composedly means in a calm, steady way, with your feelings under control.
its sense in the lessons: A story word for a character who stays calm when things are frightening or upsetting. In Alice, Alice answers the strange creatures composedly to show she is not afraid. Related: composed (calm), composure (calmness).
examples from the lessons: She answered the judge composedly. | Despite the noise, he sat composedly in his chair. | Alice replied composedly, though she was puzzled. | The pilot spoke composedly to the passengers. | The cat sat composedly washing its face. | He composedly folded his napkin.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced kom-POH-zid-lee (four syllables). Bookish; in speech say «calmly».

part of speech: adjective; past form of «confound» (confound, confounds, confounded, confounding)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Confounded means very puzzled or confused. 2) (old-fashioned, mild swearing) Confounded is used to show annoyance, meaning «annoying» or «wretched»: «this confounded rain». 3) To confound someone is to surprise and confuse them; to confound a plan or prediction is to prove it wrong.
its sense in the lessons: In old books and The Wind in the Willows, gentlemen like Toad say «confounded» as a mild swear word: «that confounded policeman!». In science and news, a result can confound the experts, meaning it goes against what they expected. «Confound it!» was an old way of saying «Bother!».
examples from the lessons: The puzzle left everyone confounded. | «That confounded motor car!» shouted the old man. | The result confounded the experts. | Confound it, I've lost my keys! | Toad cursed the confounded washerwoman's dress. | The magician's trick confounded the audience.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. The mild-swearing sense is old-fashioned and only in old books or for fun today.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Consonantal means to do with consonants, or made of consonants.
its sense in the lessons: In English and phonics lessons, consonants are sounds like b, t, m, s, made by blocking the air with lips, tongue or teeth; vowels are open sounds. «Consonantal sounds» or a «consonantal cluster» like «str» in «street». Some writing systems, such as Hebrew and Arabic, are consonantal: they mostly write only consonants.
examples from the lessons: «Str» is a consonantal cluster. | Hebrew uses a mostly consonantal alphabet. | The word «rhythm» is very consonantal. | We practised consonantal sounds in phonics. | Welsh has some unusual consonantal sounds, like «ll». | A consonantal sound blocks the air for a moment.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «consonant» + «-al». Opposite: vocalic (about vowels). Technical word for language study.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (UK, Ireland, formal) A constabulary is the police force of an area.
its sense in the lessons: In Britain many police forces once had «Constabulary» in their names, like «Lancashire Constabulary». In The Wind in the Willows Toad is arrested and taken before the court by the police, and stories call the local police the constabulary. In Ireland, the old Royal Irish Constabulary existed before 1922.
examples from the lessons: The local constabulary searched the woods. | He was a constable in the county constabulary. | Toad was a terror to the constabulary. | The constabulary was called to the riot. | The Royal Irish Constabulary was disbanded in 1922. | The constabulary put out a warning about scams.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: constabularies. Related: constable (a police officer, often of the lowest rank). Pronounced kon-STAB-yoo-luh-ree.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Contemptuously means in a way that shows you think someone or something is worthless or does not deserve respect.
its sense in the lessons: A story word that shows a character's scorn: «she looked at him contemptuously». In The Wind in the Willows the weasels and the bargewoman treat Toad contemptuously; in Alice, the Caterpillar asks «Who are you?» contemptuously.
examples from the lessons: The Caterpillar looked at Alice contemptuously. | «You?» he laughed contemptuously. | She tossed the cheap ring away contemptuously. | The cat contemptuously ignored the dog. | The bargewoman spoke contemptuously to Toad. | He waved the idea away contemptuously.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «contempt» (noun) and «contemptuous» (adjective). Do not confuse with «contemptible» (deserving contempt). Showing contempt to people is unkind.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (old) A corsair was a pirate, especially one from North Africa (the Barbary corsairs) who attacked ships in the Mediterranean. 2) A corsair was also a pirate ship.
its sense in the lessons: In history and sea stories, Barbary corsairs captured ships and sometimes raided coasts, even as far as Ireland and Cornwall, to take people as slaves. In The Wind in the Willows the Sea Rat tells of his voyages in the Mediterranean, a sea once full of corsairs. Pirate stories use «corsair» for a dashing pirate.
examples from the lessons: The corsairs attacked the merchant ship. | Barbary corsairs raided Baltimore in Ireland in 1631. | The corsair raised a black flag. | The Mediterranean was once full of corsairs. | The captain escaped from the corsairs. | A corsair ship sailed into the harbour.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Pronounced KOR-sair. Similar: pirate, buccaneer, privateer.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (old) A corselet was a piece of armour that covered the body, chest and back. 2) A corselet is a tight piece of women's underwear that covers the body (also corselette). 3) (science) The corselet is the hard chest part (thorax) of an insect.
its sense in the lessons: In history and stories about knights and soldiers, a corselet of steel or leather protects the chest. In The Wind in the Willows the animals arm themselves with swords and pistols for the battle of Toad Hall. Today the word is rare.
examples from the lessons: The soldier wore a corselet of steel. | The knight buckled on his corselet. | A leather corselet protected his chest. | The beetle's shiny corselet gleamed. | The museum has a corselet from the Civil War. | He took off his corselet after the battle.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Pronounced KORSS-lit. Also spelt «corslet».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Crafty means clever at getting what you want by tricks and secret plans; sly. 2) (informal) Crafty can mean liking or good at making crafts by hand.
its sense in the lessons: In fables and stories, the fox is crafty: it tricks the crow into dropping her cheese. In The Wind in the Willows the weasels and stoats are crafty, and Toad makes crafty escapes. In the Just So Stories animals use crafty tricks. «A crafty look» suggests someone is planning something.
examples from the lessons: The crafty fox tricked the crow. | He gave a crafty smile. | Toad made a crafty plan to escape. | The crafty weasels took over Toad Hall. | That was a crafty way to win the game! | Gran is very crafty — she knits and sews everything.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative: craftier, craftiest. Adverb: craftily. Similar: cunning, sly, wily, artful.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To crave something is to want it very strongly, so that it is hard to think about anything else. 2) (old, formal) To crave something is to ask for it humbly: «I crave your pardon».
its sense in the lessons: In health lessons, people may crave sugar or salty food; a craving is a strong wish. In stories, a lonely character craves friendship, a proud one craves attention. In old stories and the Bible, a person «craves» a favour from a king.
examples from the lessons: After the long walk, I craved a cold drink. | Toad craved excitement and fast cars. | Babies crave attention and comfort. | «I crave your pardon, my lord.» | She craved a quiet moment alone. | Some people crave chocolate when they are tired.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Noun: a craving. Stronger than «want» or «would like».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal, mainly US) A critter is any creature or animal, especially a small one. 2) (informal) A critter can be a person, said in a joking or fond way.
its sense in the lessons: A friendly American word heard in cartoons, westerns and from farmers: «Some critter's been in the bins». In Canada and the US people speak of woodland critters like raccoons and skunks. It comes from «creature».
examples from the lessons: Some critter dug up the vegetable patch. | The woods are full of little critters. | Squirrels and chipmunks are cute critters. | «You poor critter,» said the farmer to the lamb. | We found a slimy critter under the rock. | The kids collected critters in jars and let them go.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal; in school writing use «creature» or «animal». Plural: critters.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A crumpet is a round, flat, soft bread cake with small holes on top, toasted and eaten hot with butter. 2) (rude, adult slang) a rude word grown-ups use; not for school.
its sense in the lessons: In Britain, Ireland, Australia and NZ, crumpets with butter and jam or honey are a classic winter tea-time treat. In The Wind in the Willows the animals enjoy hot buttered toast and cosy teas by the fire, the kind of food crumpets belong to. In Canada and the US the English muffin is a similar thing.
examples from the lessons: We toasted crumpets by the fire. | Butter melts into the little holes in a crumpet. | Grandma serves crumpets and tea on Sundays. | A packet of crumpets costs £1.20; how much do 3 packets cost? | I like my crumpet with honey. | Hot crumpets are perfect on a cold day.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: crumpets. Not the same as a muffin or a pikelet, though similar.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (old) A cur is a dog of no special breed, especially a bad-tempered or dirty one. 2) (old, insulting) Calling a man a cur means he is mean, cowardly or worthless.
its sense in the lessons: In old stories and Shakespeare-free classics, curs are snapping village dogs, and «You cur!» is a hero's insult to a villain. In The Wind in the Willows and Alice, old-fashioned insults like this make the speech sound grand or angry. In Alice, the Mouse's tale tells of a dog called Fury who is like a cruel cur.
examples from the lessons: A mangy cur barked at the beggar. | «Out of my way, you cowardly cur!» | The village curs chased the cart. | The cur snarled and showed its teeth. | Only a cur would hit someone smaller. | Fury, the dog in the Mouse's tale, acts as judge and jury.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: curs. Old-fashioned; today «mongrel» (mixed-breed dog). As an insult it is rude. Sounds like «cur» in «curtain» (rhymes with «fur»).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Curtly means in a short, rude, unfriendly way, using very few words.
its sense in the lessons: A story word showing that a character is cold, annoyed or impatient: «"No," she said curtly.» In Alice, many creatures answer Alice curtly; in The Wind in the Willows the Badger can be curt with Toad. In everyday life, a curt reply can hurt feelings.
examples from the lessons: «No,» he said curtly, and shut the door. | The clerk curtly told us to wait. | The Caterpillar answered Alice curtly. | She nodded curtly and walked away. | He curtly refused to help. | The letter was curtly written.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «curt» (short and rude) + «-ly». Not the same as «shortly», which means «soon».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Darkly means in a threatening, mysterious or gloomy way. 2) Darkly can mean with dark colours or in the dark. 3) Darkly funny means funny about sad or frightening things.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, someone who «hints darkly» or «mutters darkly» suggests danger or bad news without saying it plainly. In The Wind in the Willows the Badger speaks darkly of the Wild Wood. In the Bible (1 Corinthians), «through a glass, darkly» means seeing things dimly, not clearly yet.
examples from the lessons: «Something terrible will happen,» he said darkly. | The sky glowed darkly before the storm. | Rat hinted darkly at the dangers of the Wild Wood. | The film was darkly funny. | Her eyes were darkly shaded. | «For now we see through a glass, darkly.»
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «dark» + «-ly». Usually about tone or mood, not just about light.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Decently means in a polite, fair and respectable way that people think is right. 2) Decently can mean well enough or fairly well: «decently paid». 3) Decently can mean wearing enough clothes, not showing too much.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life, «treat people decently» means fairly and kindly. In money matters, a job that pays decently pays enough to live on. In stories, a character is «decently dressed» for church or a visit. In The Wind in the Willows Badger insists that Toad behave decently.
examples from the lessons: Please treat everyone decently. | She did decently in the test. | The workers wanted to be decently paid. | Are you decently dressed? We have visitors. | He behaved decently after losing. | The town looked after its poor decently.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «decent» (pronounced DEE-sent). Do not confuse with «descent» (going down) or «dissent» (disagreement).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A delicacy is a special, unusual or expensive food that people think is very tasty. 2) Delicacy is the quality of being fine, light or easily broken. 3) Delicacy is care and tact in dealing with a difficult or embarrassing matter.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and food lessons, each country has delicacies: snails in France, haggis in Scotland, pavlova in Australia and NZ. In stories, a feast is full of delicacies; in The Wind in the Willows the picnic basket and the banquets are full of them. «A matter of some delicacy» means one to handle carefully.
examples from the lessons: Snails are a delicacy in France. | The picnic basket was full of delicacies. | Lace is admired for its delicacy. | She handled the argument with delicacy. | Fresh crab is a seaside delicacy. | The feast had delicacies from every land.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable for foods (delicacies); uncountable for fineness and tact. Adjective: delicate.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Desperation is the feeling of having almost no hope, which makes you willing to try anything, even something risky.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, characters act «in desperation» or «out of desperation», trying a last wild idea. In The Wind in the Willows Toad in desperation escapes from prison dressed as a washerwoman. In everyday life, «in desperation I asked my little brother» means you had no better choice.
examples from the lessons: In desperation, the lost boy shouted for help. | Out of desperation, Toad dressed up as a washerwoman. | There was desperation in her voice. | The hungry fox raided the bins in desperation. | In desperation, he tried the last key. | The team played with desperation in the final minutes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. From «desperate». Phrases: «in desperation», «out of desperation». Do not confuse with «despair» (giving up hope completely), though they are close.

part of speech: adjective; past form of «despise» (despise, despises, despised, despising)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To despise someone or something is to dislike them very strongly and think they are worthless. 2) (adjective) Despised means hated and looked down on by others.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, a villain is despised by everyone; in the Bible, Isaiah speaks of one who was «despised and rejected», which Christians believe describes Jesus. In The Wind in the Willows the weasels and stoats are despised by the river animals, and Toad is despised by the bargewoman. In history, some groups were wrongly despised because of who they were.
examples from the lessons: The cruel king was despised by his people. | She despised cheating of every kind. | «He is despised and rejected of men.» | The despised weasels took over Toad Hall. | Toad felt despised by the whole world. | Don't let anyone be despised for being different.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: despised. Stronger than «dislike» or «hate»; it adds looking down on someone. Despising people is unkind.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Despondency is a feeling of low spirits and lost hope, being very sad and unwilling to try.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, a character falls into despondency after a failure; in The Wind in the Willows Toad sinks into deep despondency in his dungeon until the gaoler's daughter cheers him. In The Pilgrim's Progress, Christian falls into the «Slough of Despond», a bog of despair. In everyday life, talking to someone helps fight despondency.
examples from the lessons: Toad sank into despondency in his dark cell. | After losing the final, the team was full of despondency. | A kind word lifted her despondency. | The rain added to our despondency. | In his despondency he refused to eat. | Christian fell into the Slough of Despond.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Adjective: despondent. Similar: gloom, despair, low spirits. If sadness lasts a long time, talk to a trusted adult.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Very hateful; so bad or nasty that people strongly dislike it. 2) Of a person: behaving so cruelly or meanly that others cannot stand them.
its sense in the lessons: A strong, rather formal word for something you hate, stronger than «nasty» or «horrible». In stories it tells the reader that a character or deed is truly wicked, and that the speaker is very angry or disgusted. Often in «a detestable habit», «detestable behaviour», «a detestable man». In old children's books grown-ups and animals use it in proud, angry speeches.
examples from the lessons: Bullying younger children is a detestable thing to do. | The villain in the story was a detestable man who stole from the poor. | My brother has the detestable habit of reading my diary. | «What a detestable smell!» cried Aunt Mary as she opened the fridge. | Cheating in a test is detestable because it is unfair to everyone else. | The Queen thought the game was going detestably, and said so. | Leaving litter on the beach is a detestable way to treat nature.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective; the adverb is «detestably», the verb is «detest» (to hate) and the noun «detestation». Stress on the second syllable: de-TEST-a-ble. It is a strong word; in everyday talk people more often say «horrible» or «awful». Do not confuse with «delectable», which means delicious.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Great love and loyalty to someone or something. 2) Giving a lot of time and effort to a job, hobby or cause. 3) (church) Prayer and worship; «devotions» are short prayers or a time of prayer.
its sense in the lessons: It praises someone for faithful love or hard work: «devotion to duty», «devotion to her family», «with great devotion». In stories it shows loyalty, like a dog's devotion to its owner or a friend who never gives up. In church life «daily devotions» means a short time of Bible reading and prayer; Christians believe devotion to God shows in prayer and in kindness.
examples from the lessons: The dog's devotion to the old shepherd was famous in the village. | Her devotion to the violin meant she practised every single day. | The nurses were thanked for their devotion during the hard winter. | Grandma reads a psalm in her morning devotions. | Mole's devotion to his friend Rat grew stronger after the adventure in the Wild Wood. | The team showed real devotion by training in the rain. | A mother's devotion to her baby is a kind of love that does not count the cost.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun; mostly uncountable («great devotion»), but «devotions» (plural) means prayers. The verb is «devote» (devote time to something) and the adjective «devoted» (a devoted friend). Follow it with «to»: devotion to someone, not «devotion for».

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a way that is shameful and very bad, so that people disapprove strongly. 2) (as an intensifier) Shockingly; far too much, as in «disgracefully late» or «disgracefully dirty».
its sense in the lessons: It tells the reader that someone behaved badly enough to be ashamed of it, or that something is shockingly poor. Common in «behave disgracefully», «disgracefully rude», «disgracefully late». In stories grown-ups say it when they scold; Toad in The Wind in the Willows is told more than once that he has behaved disgracefully.
examples from the lessons: The fans behaved disgracefully and threw bottles on the pitch. | You have been disgracefully rude to your grandmother. | The bus was disgracefully late again this morning. | The old park was disgracefully neglected, with weeds everywhere. | Badger told Toad that he had behaved disgracefully with his motor-cars. | The workers were disgracefully paid for such hard work. | Our classroom was left disgracefully messy after the party.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from the adjective «disgraceful» and the noun «disgrace». Spelling: disgrace + ful + ly, with one l in -ful and two l's in -fully. It is a strong word of blame; use it when something is really shameful, not just a little wrong.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A cloth used for washing or wiping dishes, cups and pans. 2) (informal, UK) Sometimes also a cloth for drying dishes, usually called a tea towel.
its sense in the lessons: An everyday kitchen word. In lessons about the home and hygiene it reminds pupils that damp cloths can grow germs, so they should be washed and dried often. In stories a dishcloth often shows a busy, plain kitchen or a servant's hard work.
examples from the lessons: Wring out the dishcloth after you wash up. | Mum wiped the table with a damp dishcloth. | The dishcloth smelled sour, so Dad put it in the washing machine. | Granny hung the dishcloth over the tap to dry. | In the busy kitchen the cook threw a dishcloth over her shoulder. | Germs grow fast in a wet dishcloth, so change it often. | I knitted a cotton dishcloth in craft club.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: a dishcloth, two dishcloths. Written as one word. In the UK a cloth for drying dishes is a «tea towel», in the USA a «dish towel»; «dishcloth» is mainly for washing. «Dishrag» is another word for it, common in the USA.

part of speech: adjective (dispirited, more dispirited, most dispirited); verb form (dispirit, dispirits, dispirited, dispiriting — less common)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Having lost hope and energy; feeling down and discouraged. 2) Showing that feeling, as in a dispirited voice or a dispirited team.
its sense in the lessons: It describes how people feel after failure, bad news or a long struggle: they stop trying hard and look gloomy. In stories it tells the reader a character is close to giving up, often just before help or a new idea comes. Opposite: «cheerful», «encouraged», «in high spirits».
examples from the lessons: The team walked off the pitch looking dispirited after losing 5–0. | After three rainy days, the campers were tired and dispirited. | Mole felt lost and dispirited in the dark Wild Wood. | She gave a dispirited sigh and closed her maths book. | Don't be dispirited by one bad mark; you can try again. | The dispirited soldiers trudged back through the mud. | A kind word can cheer up a dispirited friend.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective formed like a past form of «dispirit» (to make someone lose heart). Its opposite in feeling is «in good spirits». Similar words: discouraged, downhearted, crestfallen. Do not confuse with «spirited», which means lively and brave.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The state of having a bad name; being thought badly of by people. 2) (formal) Loss of the respect a person, group or activity used to have.
its sense in the lessons: A formal word, used mostly in the phrase «bring something into disrepute» (make it look bad) and «fall into disrepute». In sport and school rules it means behaviour that shames the club or school. In stories a family or a house that has «fallen into disrepute» is no longer respected.
examples from the lessons: Cheating brought the whole game into disrepute. | The player was fined for bringing the club into disrepute. | The old inn had fallen into disrepute because of the fights there. | The school rules say pupils must not bring the school into disrepute. | After the scandal, the circus fell into disrepute. | Toad's wild driving brought the name of Toad Hall into disrepute. | Some old cures have fallen into disrepute because scientists showed they do not work.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable noun, no «a» and no plural. Almost always in «into disrepute» or «in disrepute». Formal, typical of rules and news reports. Related: «reputation» (what people think of you), «disreputable» (having a bad name). Stress: dis-re-PUTE.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Causing pain, worry or sadness; upsetting. 2) Full of trouble and suffering.
its sense in the lessons: A rare, slightly old-fashioned word; today people usually say «distressing». It describes a sight, piece of news or time that hurts people's feelings. In old books it may describe hard times, a sad cry or a painful journey.
examples from the lessons: It was a distressful sight to see the flooded houses. | The ship's crew had a long, distressful voyage through the storm. | The news of the accident was distressful for the whole town. | The lost puppy gave a distressful whine. | Moving away from all her friends was a distressful time for Ella. | The old poem tells of distressful days of war and hunger.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective; in modern English «distressing» is much more common, and «distressed» describes the person who feels upset. «Distress» is the noun (a ship in distress = in danger). Spelling: double s twice — distre-ss-ful.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a stubborn, determined way; going on and not giving up, even when it is hard.
its sense in the lessons: It praises perseverance: someone works or walks doggedly on despite tiredness, rain or failure. Common in «doggedly determined», «doggedly refused», «worked doggedly». It is a good word for describing scientists, explorers, athletes and pupils who keep trying.
examples from the lessons: Ben worked doggedly at his long division until he got it right. | The explorers trudged doggedly through the snow. | Mole doggedly followed the path even though the wood frightened him. | She doggedly refused to give up her seat on the team. | The tortoise plodded doggedly on and won the race. | The rescue workers dug doggedly through the night. | He practised his spellings doggedly every evening.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from the adjective «dogged» (pronounced DOG-id, two syllables), meaning stubborn and determined. It comes from the way a dog holds on and will not let go. Not rude and not about dogs today; it is a compliment.

part of speech: adjective; verb form (draggle, draggles, draggled, draggling — old-fashioned)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Wet, muddy and untidy, especially after being dragged through mud or rain. 2) Hanging limp and dirty, like the bottom of a long skirt or a bird's wet feathers.
its sense in the lessons: An old-fashioned, picture-making word found in older children's books, as in «draggled and dirty». It shows a character who has been through rain, mud or a river and looks a mess. In Alice in Wonderland the creatures come out of the Pool of Tears «a queer-looking party» with draggled feathers and fur clinging close; the word fits that scene.
examples from the lessons: The birds climbed out of the pool with draggled feathers. | After the storm, the cat came home wet and draggled. | Her long skirt was draggled with mud from the lane. | Toad looked a draggled sight after falling into the river. | The draggled flag hung from its pole in the rain. | We came back from the muddy walk tired and draggled.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Old-fashioned; today people say «bedraggled», which means the same and is far more common. The verb «draggle» means to make wet and dirty by dragging. Do not confuse with «dragged».

part of speech: adjective (draughty, draughtier, draughtiest); US spelling drafty
meaning for a pupil: 1) Of a room or building: having cold air blowing through it from gaps round windows and doors.
its sense in the lessons: An everyday home word, especially for old houses, castles, halls and classrooms in winter. In science lessons on heat, a draughty room loses warm air, and draught excluders and insulation stop it. In stories a draughty old house or castle feels cold, lonely or creepy.
examples from the lessons: The old castle was dark and draughty. | Close the door, it's draughty in here! | Grandpa put a sausage-shaped draught excluder by the draughty door. | The village hall is so draughty that we keep our coats on. | Badger's house was warm and snug, not draughty at all. | Draughty windows let heat escape and waste energy. | The tent was draughty, so we wore woolly hats to sleep.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK spelling «draughty», US spelling «drafty»; pronounced DRAHF-tee. From «draught» (a current of cold air). «Draughts» is also the UK name of the board game (US «checkers»). Comparative: draughtier, draughtiest.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Strange, soft or unreal, as if it were happening in a dream. 2) Very beautiful and peaceful, like something you might dream of.
its sense in the lessons: A describing word for scenes in stories and poems: mist, moonlight, music or odd events that do not feel real. Alice's adventures have a dreamlike feel, and in the end we learn that they were a dream. In The Wind in the Willows the chapter «The Piper at the Gates of Dawn» is dreamlike and magical.
examples from the lessons: The misty lake at dawn looked dreamlike. | Everything in Wonderland happened in a strange, dreamlike way. | The music had a slow, dreamlike sound. | Walking through the field of bluebells was a dreamlike experience. | Rat and Mole felt a dreamlike calm on the island at dawn. | The painting shows a dreamlike garden with floating clocks. | Snow falling at night makes the town look dreamlike.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective, one word: dream + like. Similar: dreamy, unreal, magical. It describes things, not usually people (a person who is half asleep is «dreamy», not «dreamlike»).

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a doubtful way, showing you are not sure something is true, good or safe. 2) In a way that is not quite honest or that people suspect.
its sense in the lessons: It shows a character's doubt: someone looks, asks or answers dubiously when they don't believe or trust what they hear. Common with «look», «say», «eye», «sniff». In stories it often comes when a strange plan is suggested, for example when Mole or Rat look dubiously at Toad's latest craze.
examples from the lessons: Mia looked dubiously at the green soup. | «Are you sure this is the right way?» asked Dad dubiously. | The cat sniffed the new food dubiously and walked away. | Rat eyed Toad's shiny new cart dubiously. | Alice looked dubiously at the bottle marked «DRINK ME». | He was dubiously quiet when Mum asked who had eaten the cake. | The teacher dubiously accepted the excuse about the dog eating the homework.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from «dubious» (doubtful; or not to be trusted). Pronounced DYOO-bee-us-lee. Similar: doubtfully, uncertainly, warily. «Dubious» can describe the person who doubts or the thing that is doubtful (a dubious excuse).

part of speech: noun (a duplicate, duplicates); verb (duplicate, duplicates, duplicated, duplicating); adjective (duplicate)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (noun) An exact copy of something, such as a key or a document. 2) (verb) To make an exact copy of something. 3) (verb) To do something again that has already been done, wasting effort. 4) (adjective) Exactly the same as another; made as a copy.
its sense in the lessons: Used for keys, cards, files, photos and paperwork: «a duplicate key», «in duplicate» (in two copies). In computing and data work, «duplicates» are repeated items that should be removed. In maths and science, experiments are duplicated (done twice) to check the results. In card collecting, «duplicates» or «swaps» are spare copies.
examples from the lessons: Dad had a duplicate key made for the shed. | I have three duplicates of this football card, so I'll swap them. | The form must be filled in in duplicate. | Delete the duplicate photos to save space. | Scientists duplicated the experiment to check the result. | Let's not duplicate work: you do the poster and I'll do the speech. | The printer duplicated the page by mistake. | Remove the duplicate numbers from the list 4, 7, 4, 9 and you get 4, 7, 9.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The noun and adjective are pronounced DYOO-pli-kut; the verb is DYOO-pli-kayt. «In duplicate» = two copies. Related: «duplication». In maths and data, «duplicates» are repeated values; counting a list «without duplicates» means counting each value once.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A cloth for wiping dust off furniture and shelves. 2) A board duster or board rubber: a pad used to wipe a chalkboard or whiteboard clean. 3) (US, Australia) A long, light coat worn to keep dust off, especially by riders. 4) A light housecoat.
its sense in the lessons: An everyday word from cleaning and from the classroom: teachers use a board duster. Phrases: «feather duster», «give the shelves a going-over with a duster». In old stories maids carry dusters; in Westerns cowboys wear dusters.
examples from the lessons: Mum gave me a yellow duster to polish the table. | The teacher wiped the board with a duster. | Grandma uses a feather duster on the high shelves. | Mole spring-cleaned his house with brooms and dusters until his back ached. | The cowboy wore a long brown duster. | Shake the duster outside so the dust doesn't fly back in. | The board duster was full of chalk.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a duster, dusters. From «dust» + -er (a thing that removes dust). In the UK «duster» usually means the cloth; in the USA «dust cloth» or «dust rag» is common, and «duster» more often means the coat or a feather duster. A «crop duster» is a plane that sprays crops.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A strong wish to do or have something, full of energy and interest. 2) Keenness; being impatient to start.
its sense in the lessons: It describes a happy, excited desire: «in her eagerness to help», «eagerness to learn». In school reports teachers praise «eagerness to learn». In stories eagerness often makes a character rush and make mistakes, like Toad's eagerness for every new craze or the Elephant's Child's eagerness to know what the Crocodile has for dinner.
examples from the lessons: In his eagerness to see the puppies, Sam ran ahead. | The class showed great eagerness to learn about volcanoes. | In her eagerness she knocked over the paint pot. | The Elephant's Child asked his questions with endless eagerness. | Mole's eagerness to see the river made him forget his spring-cleaning. | The dog wagged its tail with eagerness when it heard the lead. | Her eagerness to help made her the teacher's favourite helper.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable noun from the adjective «eager»; the adverb is «eagerly». Often followed by «to + verb» (eagerness to win) or «for + noun» (eagerness for news). Do not confuse «eager» (keen, wanting) with «anxious» (worried), though people sometimes use «anxious to» for eager.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Of this world and this life, not of heaven. 2) (informal, with no, any or why) At all; possible, as in «no earthly use» or «why on earth». 3) Of the planet Earth, as opposed to space.
its sense in the lessons: In church language «earthly» is contrasted with «heavenly»: Christians believe earthly riches pass away but heavenly treasure lasts. In everyday talk it strengthens a question or a «no»: «no earthly reason», «not an earthly chance». In science fiction «earthly» means from Earth.
examples from the lessons: There's no earthly reason why you can't finish your homework now. | Why on earth did you paint the cat blue? | He gave away his earthly possessions and became a monk. | Christians believe that earthly life is not the end. | That old bike is no earthly use to anyone. | The Bible says not to store up treasures on earth but in heaven. | The alien had never tasted earthly food. | She hasn't an earthly chance of winning.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective; it is used before nouns (earthly life), and in the strengthening sense only with «no», «any», «not» or questions. Opposite in religious use: «heavenly». Do not confuse with «earthy» (smelling of soil; plain and down-to-earth). «Why on earth» is the common phrase.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Nervous, tense and easily annoyed. 2) (informal) Bold, new and a bit shocking, especially in art, music, fashion or comedy.
