its sense in the lessons: It describes a mood: before a test, at night in a creepy place, or when people are worried. The second sense is used about films, clothes and jokes that push limits. In stories an edgy character snaps at others or jumps at noises.
examples from the lessons: Everyone felt edgy before the big match. | The dog was edgy during the fireworks. | Dad gets edgy when he's hungry. | Mole was edgy in the Wild Wood, jumping at every rustle. | The band has an edgy new sound. | Her edgy haircut was half pink and half black. | Don't be so edgy; it's only a practice test.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective from «edge»: if you are «on edge» you are nervous, and «edgy» means the same. Comparative edgier, superlative edgiest. The second sense is informal and often a compliment; the first is not.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Able to speak or write well, clearly and movingly, so that people are persuaded or touched. 2) (of a look, silence or gesture) Showing a feeling clearly without words.
its sense in the lessons: A praising word for speakers, speeches and writing, used in English and history lessons (an eloquent speech, an eloquent writer). Sense 2 is common in stories: «an eloquent silence», «an eloquent look» tells the reader what someone feels without them saying it.
examples from the lessons: Martin Luther King gave eloquent speeches about freedom. | Our class captain made an eloquent speech at assembly. | Her silence was more eloquent than any words. | The Water Rat spoke eloquently about the joys of the river. | The dog gave me an eloquent look at its empty bowl. | She wrote an eloquent letter to the council about saving the library. | You don't need long words to be eloquent; you need clear ones.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective; the adverb is «eloquently» and the noun «eloquence». Stress on the first syllable: EL-o-kwent. Opposite: «inarticulate». Not the same as «talkative» — someone can talk a lot without being eloquent.

part of speech: adjective; verb form (emancipate, emancipates, emancipated, emancipating)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Freed from slavery. 2) Freed from rules, control or limits that kept someone down, such as old rules about what women could do. 3) (law) Of a young person: legally free from their parents' control before adulthood (rare).
its sense in the lessons: Mostly a history word: enslaved people were emancipated, for example in the British Empire after 1833 and in the USA through the Emancipation Proclamation of 1863 and the 13th Amendment of 1865. It is also used about women gaining rights, like the vote. In everyday speech «emancipated» can mean independent and free-thinking.
examples from the lessons: Millions of enslaved people were emancipated in the USA in the 1860s. | The emancipated workers built their own schools and churches. | Lincoln's Emancipation Proclamation was signed in 1863. | Women felt more emancipated after they won the right to vote. | The emancipated slaves celebrated with songs of freedom. | Our history lesson was about how the slaves were emancipated in the British colonies.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb «emancipate» (to set free), noun «emancipation». Pronounced ee-MAN-si-pay-tid. It is a formal, serious word; for a pet escaping you would just say «set free». It tells about legal or social freedom, not just getting out of a room.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Without ever stopping or ending; for what seems forever. 2) Very much, without limit, as in «endlessly patient».
its sense in the lessons: Often used in stories with a slight exaggeration: «talked endlessly», «the road stretched endlessly». In maths, numbers go on endlessly (there is no biggest number), and some decimals like 1/3 = 0.333… go on endlessly.
examples from the lessons: My little sister talks endlessly about dinosaurs. | The desert stretched endlessly in every direction. | Toad boasted endlessly about his motor-car. | The numbers go on endlessly; you can always add one more. | One third written as a decimal is 0.333..., with threes going on endlessly. | Our teacher is endlessly patient with us. | The rain fell endlessly all weekend. | The Elephant's Child asked questions endlessly.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from «endless» (without end). Often an exaggeration in everyday talk: it just means «for a very long time». In maths, «endlessly» or «infinitely» is literally true for number lines and repeating decimals.

meaning for a pupil: 1) For ever, without beginning or end. 2) (informal) Always; very often, as in «eternally late». 3) (very strongly) Greatly, as in «I'll be eternally grateful».
its sense in the lessons: In church language God is described as eternal, and Christians believe in eternal life. In everyday speech «eternally grateful» is a common, warm exaggeration meaning very grateful. It can also describe things that seem never to change, like «eternally cheerful».
examples from the lessons: I'll be eternally grateful for your help. | Christians believe God lives eternally. | My brother is eternally losing his football boots. | The snow on the mountaintop seems eternally white. | The Mad Hatter and the March Hare were eternally having tea, because for them it was always six o'clock. | Grandpa is eternally cheerful, even in the rain. | The poem says the stars shine eternally.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from «eternal» (lasting for ever); the noun is «eternity». Pronounced ee-TER-na-lee. In everyday use it is usually an exaggeration; strictly, only things that never end are eternal.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Extremely well; in a way that is of the very best quality.
its sense in the lessons: A praising word used by teachers and in reports: «You have done excellently». It describes how well something is done, performed or made. Less common than «very well», so it sounds a little formal or teacher-like.
examples from the lessons: You did excellently in your spelling test. | The choir sang excellently at the concert. | The cake was excellently made. | The team played excellently in the second half. | «That is excellently argued,» said the judge. | Our school play went excellently.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from «excellent»; the noun is «excellence». Spelling: double l after the e: ex-cel-lent-ly. Do not say «more excellently» much; «excellent» already means the very best.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In an excited way; full of eager, happy energy or strong feeling.
its sense in the lessons: A common story word showing how characters speak or move when they are thrilled or worked up: «said excitedly», «jumped up and down excitedly», «chattered excitedly». It helps readers hear the voice. It can also show nervous excitement in a frightening moment.
examples from the lessons: «We're going to the seaside!» she shouted excitedly. | The children chattered excitedly about the school trip. | The puppy wagged its tail excitedly. | Toad danced excitedly around the yellow cart. | Alice ran excitedly after the White Rabbit. | The fans waved their flags excitedly. | He opened his birthday present excitedly.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from «excited»; related words: excite, exciting, excitement. Remember: you are «excited» (your feeling); a thing is «exciting» (it causes the feeling). Spelling: ex-cit-ed-ly, with one t.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Extremely painful. 2) (informal) Terribly embarrassing, boring or awkward, so that you can hardly bear it.
its sense in the lessons: Sense 1 is used for real pain (an excruciating toothache, broken bone). Sense 2 is a common exaggeration in everyday talk: «excruciating embarrassment», «an excruciating speech». In safety lessons, excruciating pain is a reason to get help quickly.
examples from the lessons: The pain in his broken leg was excruciating. | She had an excruciating toothache all night. | The wait for the test results was excruciating. | It was excruciating when Dad danced at my party. | The speech was so long and boring it was excruciating. | Stinging nettles can be painful, but a wasp sting can be excruciating.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective; pronounced ex-KROO-shee-ay-ting. It comes from Latin for «torture» or «cross». It is a strong word; save it for very bad pain or very bad embarrassment. The adverb is «excruciatingly».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Extremely painfully. 2) (informal) Extremely, in a way that is hard to bear, as in «excruciatingly slow» or «excruciatingly embarrassing».
its sense in the lessons: Usually it strengthens another adjective: «excruciatingly painful», «excruciatingly boring», «excruciatingly funny» (so funny it hurts). In stories it tells the reader that something was almost unbearable.
examples from the lessons: The cut was excruciatingly painful. | The queue moved excruciatingly slowly. | The film was excruciatingly boring. | It was excruciatingly embarrassing when my phone rang in assembly. | The comedian was excruciatingly funny. | The last minutes before the bell went excruciatingly slowly.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from «excruciating». It almost always comes before another adjective or adverb as a strong intensifier. Pronounced ex-KROO-shee-ay-ting-lee.

part of speech: adjective; verb form (exhilarate, exhilarates, exhilarated, exhilarating)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Making you feel very happy, excited and full of energy. 2) Thrilling in a fast, fresh or slightly scary way, like a ride, a race or a cold wind.
its sense in the lessons: Used for experiences: a roller coaster, sledging, swimming in cold sea, a win in the last minute. In stories it shows joy and freedom, like Toad's first exhilarating ride in a motor-car or Mole's first day on the river.
examples from the lessons: The roller coaster was exhilarating! | Sledging down the big hill was an exhilarating feeling. | Toad found speed exhilarating and could think of nothing else. | We had an exhilarating walk along the cliffs in the wind. | Scoring the winning goal was exhilarating. | The cold sea was exhilarating once we got used to it. | Mole felt exhilarated as the boat slid down the river.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective; the person feels «exhilarated», the thing is «exhilarating». Noun: exhilaration. Spelling trap: ex-hil-a-rat-ing, with a silent h and «a» after the l (not «exhilerating»). Similar: thrilling, exciting.

part of speech: noun (exploitation, exploitations — the plural is rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Treating people unfairly to get something from them, for example making them work hard for very little pay. 2) Using natural resources such as coal, oil or forests to make money or energy. 3) Making the most of a chance or a situation.
its sense in the lessons: In history and citizenship lessons it is used about child labour, slavery and very low wages. In geography it means using land, minerals and fish, sometimes too much (over-exploitation). In safety lessons it is a warning: no one should use children for money or work.
examples from the lessons: Child labour in Victorian factories was a cruel kind of exploitation. | The exploitation of coal made Britain rich but polluted the air. | Over-exploitation of the sea has left fewer fish. | Fair trade aims to stop the exploitation of farmers. | Laws protect children from exploitation. | The workers protested against their exploitation by the mill owners.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly uncountable. Verb: «exploit» (ex-PLOIT, to use unfairly or to make use of); noun «an exploit» (EX-ploit) means a brave or daring deed — a different meaning! «Exploitation» is usually negative about people and neutral or negative about resources.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The magical, imaginary land where fairies live in stories. 2) A place so beautiful, sparkling or magical that it seems unreal.
its sense in the lessons: A story and everyday word: «like fairyland» describes a garden full of lights, a snowy forest or a decorated town at Christmas. Alice in Wonderland is not called fairyland, but it is a magical dream-land of the same kind, and Alice even says she is «in the middle of a fairy-tale» now.
examples from the lessons: In the old story, the girl was carried off to fairyland. | The garden with all its lanterns looked like fairyland. | The snowy forest was a fairyland of white. | Alice felt she was living in a kind of fairyland. | The town square becomes a fairyland at Christmas. | My little brother thinks the bottom of the garden is fairyland.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Written as one word. Usually without «a» when it means the magic land («in fairyland»), but «a fairyland of lights» is fine. Related: fairy, fairy tale, fairy-tale (adjective). Fairies are imaginary; there is no real fairyland.

part of speech: verb form (fan, fans, fanned, fanning) — past tense and past participle of «fan»
meaning for a pupil: 1) Moved air towards something or someone with a fan or with your hand, to cool it down. 2) Made a fire burn more strongly by blowing air on it. 3) (fanned out) Spread out from one point in the shape of an open fan. 4) Made a feeling stronger, as in «fanned the flames» of anger.
its sense in the lessons: Everyday and story word: «she fanned herself», «fanned the flames», «the searchers fanned out». In Alice in Wonderland Alice fans herself with the White Rabbit's fan and starts to shrink. In science, air fanned onto a fire brings oxygen and makes it burn hotter.
examples from the lessons: Alice fanned herself with the White Rabbit's fan and began to shrink. | Grandma fanned her face in the heat. | He fanned the campfire until it blazed. | The search party fanned out across the field. | The peacock fanned its beautiful tail. | Angry words only fanned the quarrel. | The cards were fanned out on the table.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «fan» doubles the n: fanned, fanning. «Fanned out» = spread in a fan shape. Safety: fanning a fire makes it bigger, so never fan a fire indoors. The noun «fan» also means a keen supporter (a football fan) — not related to this verb's meaning.

part of speech: adjective; verb form (fascinate, fascinates, fascinated, fascinating)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Extremely interesting, so that you want to keep looking, listening or learning.
its sense in the lessons: A common word in school and everyday talk: «a fascinating fact», «a fascinating book». Teachers use it to make topics exciting; in stories it shows a character can't look away. The person feels «fascinated by» something.
examples from the lessons: Volcanoes are fascinating. | Did you know octopuses have three hearts? Isn't that fascinating? | The museum had a fascinating dinosaur display. | Mole found the river fascinating and could watch it for hours. | Alice found the Caterpillar rude but fascinating. | I read a fascinating book about space. | It's fascinating to watch ants carry food.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective; the thing is «fascinating», the person is «fascinated». Noun: fascination. Spelling: fa-sc-inating, with «sc» (the c is silent). Stronger than «interesting».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Not afraid of anything; very brave. 2) Ready to face danger or say difficult things without hesitating.
its sense in the lessons: A praising word for heroes, explorers, rescuers and animals. In stories a fearless character faces danger, but stories also show that being fearless is different from being careless; real courage is being afraid and doing the right thing anyway.
examples from the lessons: The fearless firefighter ran into the burning house. | Our cat is fearless and chases dogs. | Badger was fearless in the Wild Wood. | The fearless explorer crossed the ice. | She was fearless on the climbing wall. | Being brave doesn't mean being fearless; it means doing it even when you're scared. | The fearless little bird defended its nest.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: fear + -less (without fear). Adverb: fearlessly; noun: fearlessness. Opposite: fearful, timid. Safety trap: «fearless» is not the same as «reckless» — doing dangerous things without thinking is not brave.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Fancy, expensive or very smart clothes and jewellery worn for a special occasion. 2) Bright, showy decoration.
its sense in the lessons: A story word for people dressed up for parties, weddings and balls: «in all their finery», «in their Sunday finery». It can be gently mocking when someone shows off. In The Wind in the Willows Toad loves dressing up, and in old tales animals like the peacock show off their finery.
examples from the lessons: The guests arrived at the wedding in all their finery. | The Queen of Hearts came in all her royal finery. | The peacock strutted about showing off its finery. | On Sunday the family went to church in their finery. | Toad paraded in his new motoring finery: goggles, cap and gaiters. | The town was decked in flags and finery for the festival.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: no «a», no plural («in their finery»). Pronounced FY-ner-ee. From «fine» (beautiful, smart). Mostly found in stories and descriptions, slightly old-fashioned or humorous.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The part of a steam engine, boiler or stove where the fire burns. 2) (US, old) A box on a street with an alarm to call firefighters.
its sense in the lessons: A history and technology word: in steam trains the fireman shovels coal into the firebox to heat water and make steam. In The Wind in the Willows Toad escapes on a steam train and helps the engine driver, feeding the furnace — the firebox — with coal.
examples from the lessons: The fireman shovelled coal into the firebox. | The firebox glowed red and hot. | Steam engines boil water using heat from the firebox. | Toad helped stoke the engine's firebox as the train raced through the night. | Never touch the firebox of a wood stove; it is very hot. | The old engine's firebox had to be cleaned of ash every day.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a firebox, fireboxes. One word. In science, it shows how burning fuel makes heat that turns water into steam, which pushes the pistons. Not the same as a «fireplace» in a room, though both hold a fire.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The area right next to a fireplace, where people sit to keep warm. 2) (figurative) Home and family life, cosy and safe. 3) (adjective) Happening by the fire at home, as in «a fireside chat» or «fireside stories».
its sense in the lessons: A warm, cosy story word: sitting by the fireside means comfort, home and safety after cold or danger. In The Wind in the Willows Mole and Rat sit by the fireside in Badger's kitchen and in Mole End, and the fireside stands for home. «Fireside chat» was also the name of friendly radio talks by US President Franklin Roosevelt.
examples from the lessons: The cat slept on the rug by the fireside. | Grandpa told us stories at the fireside. | Badger's kitchen had a big, friendly fireside. | After the snowy walk, we warmed our toes by the fireside. | The President gave a fireside chat on the radio. | In winter the family gathered round the fireside to read.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word. Usually «the fireside» or «by the fireside». As an adjective it means cosy and homely. Safety note: keep a fireguard in front of an open fire, especially with small children and pets.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (old or trade word) A polecat, or its fur; also called a fitchew. 2) (Bible, old) A kind of plant grown for seeds, a vetch or similar, mentioned as «fitches» in old English Bibles. 3) A long-handled brush used by painters and signwriters.
its sense in the lessons: A rare word. In nature lessons the polecat (a wild animal of the weasel family) may be called a fitch, and its fur «fitch fur». In the King James Bible, Isaiah talks of farmers sowing and beating out «fitches». Painters know a «fitch» as a thin brush for fine work.
examples from the lessons: The polecat, or fitch, hunts rabbits at night. | Grandma's old coat had a fitch fur collar. | The farmer in the Bible beat out his fitches with a staff. | The painter used a fitch to reach into the corner. | A fitch is related to the weasel and the ferret.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a fitch, fitches. Rare and old-fashioned in most senses. Not the same as «fetch» (to go and get). The polecat's other old name is «fitchew»; the ferret is a tame kind of polecat.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Small broken pieces or splinters, as in «smashed to flinders». 2) (a name) Matthew Flinders, an English navigator who sailed round Australia in 1801–1803; many places are named after him, such as the Flinders Ranges and Flinders Street in Melbourne.
its sense in the lessons: The phrase «in flinders» or «to flinders» is an old way of saying smashed to bits; it appears in older stories about wrecks and crashes. In Australian geography and history, Flinders is a famous name.
examples from the lessons: The boat hit the rocks and was smashed to flinders. | The old chair broke into flinders. | Matthew Flinders was the first to sail all the way round Australia. | We went walking in the Flinders Ranges in South Australia. | The car crash left the cart in flinders. | Flinders Street Station is in the centre of Melbourne.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Old-fashioned; today people say «smithereens» or «splinters». Used in the plural only («to flinders»). As a name, it takes a capital F.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Done by using force or violence, against someone's will. 2) Strong and convincing, as in «a forcible argument».
its sense in the lessons: Used in law, history and news: «forcible entry» (breaking in), «forcibly removed». In stories it shows that someone was made to do something against their will. In safety lessons, nobody may use force on your body; that is wrong and should be reported.
examples from the lessons: The police made a forcible entry into the house. | The men were forcibly removed from the meeting. | Toad was forcibly taken to his bedroom by his friends. | There was no sign of forcible entry, so the door had been unlocked. | She made a forcible case for a new playground. | The farmers were forcibly moved off their land.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective; adverb «forcibly». Do not confuse with «forceful» (strong and confident, usually about a person or speech, not violent). «Forcible entry» is a legal phrase meaning getting in by breaking a door or window.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The main sail on the front mast of a ship. 2) On a small sailing boat, the sail in front of the mast, such as a jib.
its sense in the lessons: A sailing word found in sea stories and on boating trips. In The Wind in the Willows the Sea Rat tells of his voyages, and Rat dreams of sailing away; sea stories are full of words like foresail, mainsail and rigging.
examples from the lessons: The sailors hoisted the foresail as the wind rose. | The foresail filled with wind and the boat leapt forward. | In a storm they took down the foresail. | The Sea Rat told of ships with patched foresails sailing south. | Our dinghy has a mainsail and a small foresail. | Pull the rope to tighten the foresail.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Sailors often say it as FOR-sl. «Fore» means front (as in forehead, foreground); the back of a ship is «aft». Related: mainsail, topsail, jib, mast.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The part of a beach between the high-tide line and the low-tide line, covered by the sea at high tide. 2) The land along the edge of a sea, lake or river.
its sense in the lessons: A geography word about tides and coasts: the foreshore is uncovered at low tide and covered at high tide, so it is a place of rock pools and also of danger if the tide comes in quickly. In Australia and New Zealand «foreshore» is used for parks and walkways along the water.
examples from the lessons: At low tide we explored the rock pools on the foreshore. | The foreshore is covered by the sea twice a day. | Check the tide times before walking on the foreshore. | The Thames foreshore in London is full of old clay pipes and pottery. | We had a picnic on the foreshore at Darwin. | Crabs scuttled across the wet foreshore.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually «the foreshore». Safety: the tide can come in fast and cut you off, so always know when the tide turns. «Shore» is the land at the edge of water; «fore» means front.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To leave someone and stop helping or caring for them; to abandon. 2) To give up something you used to have or do.
its sense in the lessons: A formal, old-fashioned word found in the Bible, hymns, poems and old stories: «I will never leave you nor forsake you». Christians believe God does not forsake people. Jesus' cry on the cross, «My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?», comes from Psalm 22. In everyday life people say «abandon», «leave» or «give up».
examples from the lessons: The Bible says, «I will never leave thee, nor forsake thee.» | He would not forsake his friends in danger. | The village was forsaken, with every house empty. | She forsook her comfortable life to help the poor. | Toad promised to forsake motor-cars for ever, but he didn't keep his promise. | Don't forsake your old friends when you make new ones. | The forsaken puppy was found by the roadside.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular verb: forsake – forsook – forsaken (like take – took – taken). «Forsaken» is also an adjective: lonely, abandoned. Formal and old-fashioned; in everyday speech use «leave» or «give up». «Godforsaken» describes a lonely, miserable place.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (old-fashioned, mainly UK) Very; extremely, as in «frightfully kind» or «frightfully sorry». 2) In a frightening or terrible way.
its sense in the lessons: Sense 1 is a posh, old-fashioned British way of talking, common in older children's books: «frightfully good», «frightfully sorry». Toad in The Wind in the Willows talks like this. Sense 2 is rarer: «frightfully injured».
examples from the lessons: «Frightfully sorry, old chap!» said Toad. | It was frightfully kind of you to come. | The water was frightfully cold. | The town was frightfully damaged in the storm. | «That's frightfully clever,» said the duchess. | I'm frightfully tired after the long walk.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from «frightful» (terrible, shocking). In sense 1 it just means «very» and is not about fear; it sounds upper-class and old-fashioned. Similar: awfully, terribly, dreadfully — all can mean simply «very».

part of speech: adjective; verb form (furrow, furrows, furrowed, furrowing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Of a field: having long, narrow trenches cut by a plough. 2) Of a forehead or brow: wrinkled with deep lines, showing worry, anger or hard thinking.
its sense in the lessons: Sense 1 is a farming and geography word: a ploughed field is furrowed, ready for seeds. Sense 2 is a story word: «a furrowed brow» or «he furrowed his brow» shows a character puzzling or worrying; Badger often looks thoughtful with a furrowed brow.
examples from the lessons: The tractor left the field neatly furrowed. | Seeds were dropped into the furrowed soil. | Grandpa's furrowed brow showed he was worried. | She furrowed her brow over the difficult sum. | Badger furrowed his brow and thought about how to save Toad Hall. | The old farmer's face was furrowed with age. | The waves made furrows in the sand.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From the noun «furrow» (a long groove in a field, or a deep wrinkle). Common phrase: «a furrowed brow». Similar words for faces: frown, wrinkled, knitted (knitted brows).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Having a gable or gables: the pointed, triangle-shaped part of a wall under the two sloping sides of a roof.
its sense in the lessons: A building and history word: «a gabled roof», «a gabled house». In maths lessons, a gable is a triangle on top of a rectangle; children draw gabled houses all the time. In stories old gabled houses and inns often look cosy or mysterious.
examples from the lessons: We live in a red brick house with a gabled roof. | The old inn had three gabled windows facing the street. | Toad Hall was a fine old house with gables and chimneys. | The gabled end of the barn faced the road. | Draw a gabled house: a rectangle with a triangle on top. | The street was lined with tall gabled houses.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective from the noun «gable» (GAY-bl). Pronounced GAY-buld. A gable is the triangle shape of wall between two roof slopes; a «hipped» roof slopes on all four sides and has no gables.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A unit for measuring liquids. A UK (imperial) gallon is about 4.55 litres; a US gallon is about 3.79 litres. 2) (informal, plural) A very large amount, as in «gallons of tea».
its sense in the lessons: A maths and measurement word: in imperial units, 1 gallon = 4 quarts = 8 pints. The USA still uses gallons for milk and petrol (gas); the UK sells fuel in litres but people still talk of «miles per gallon». In everyday talk «gallons» is an exaggeration for lots of liquid.
examples from the lessons: We bought a gallon of milk at the store. | One gallon is 8 pints. | The car does 40 miles per gallon. | A bath holds about 20 gallons of water. | If 1 gallon is 8 pints, then 3 gallons is 24 pints. | He drank gallons of lemonade at the party. | The fish tank holds ten gallons.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Abbreviation: gal. Trap in maths problems: UK and US gallons are different sizes (UK 4.546 L, US 3.785 L); use the one the question gives. Conversions: 1 gallon = 4 quarts = 8 pints; in the US, 1 gallon = 128 fluid ounces.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A movable bridge or ramp for walking between a ship and the land. 2) (UK) A passage between rows of seats, in a theatre, bus or plane; in the US an aisle. 3) (interjection, informal) «Gangway!» means «Move out of the way, I'm coming through!»
its sense in the lessons: Used at ports and on ships, and in the UK for passages in cinemas and theatres. In stories sailors run up the gangway, and people shout «Gangway!» when carrying something big. In safety lessons, gangways must be kept clear so people can get out in an emergency.
examples from the lessons: The passengers walked up the gangway onto the ship. | Please keep the gangways clear. | «Gangway!» shouted the porter, pushing a trolley of bags. | The sailors pulled up the gangway and the ship set sail. | The Sea Rat strode down the gangway into the port. | Don't leave your bag in the gangway on the bus.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. In US English the passage between seats is «aisle». «Gangway!» as a shout is informal and friendly but urgent. Also «gangplank» for a simple board between ship and shore.

part of speech: verb (garner, garners, garnered, garnering); noun (a garner — old)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To collect or gain something, such as support, praise, votes or information. 2) (old) To gather and store grain. 3) (noun, old) A granary: a building for storing grain.
its sense in the lessons: Mostly a formal word in news and essays: «the idea garnered support», «the film garnered praise». In old texts and the Bible, grain is gathered «into the garner». It sounds bookish; everyday speech uses «get» or «gather».
examples from the lessons: The petition garnered over a thousand signatures. | Her painting garnered praise from all the judges. | The scientists garnered evidence from many experiments. | The farmer garnered the wheat before the rain. | The Bible says he will gather his wheat into the garner. | The campaign garnered support from parents and teachers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal or old-fashioned. Regular verb: garnered. Not to be confused with «garnish» (to decorate food). Simpler words: gather, get, win, collect.

part of speech: verb form (gas, gases/gasses, gassed, gassing); noun (gassing, gassings)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal, UK, old-fashioned) Chatting or talking for a long time about not very important things; also boasting. 2) Poisoning or killing with gas; an attack with poison gas. 3) (US, informal) Filling a car with petrol, as in «gassing up».
its sense in the lessons: Sense 1 is old-fashioned chatty English: «stop gassing and get on with it». Sense 2 is a serious history word: poison gas was used in the First World War, and the Nazis murdered millions in gas chambers in the Holocaust. Sense 3 is American everyday talk.
examples from the lessons: Stop gassing and finish your homework! | The two old friends sat gassing over a cup of tea all afternoon. | Toad was gassing on about his adventures again. | Soldiers wore masks to protect them from gassing in the First World War. | We stopped to gas up the car on the way to Grandma's. | Rat was tired of Toad's endless gassing.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb «gas» doubles the s: gassed, gassing. Sense 2 is very serious and sad; take care using it. Plural of the noun «gas» is «gases». «Gas» in the USA also means petrol.

part of speech: noun (a gavel, gavels); verb (gavel, gavels, gavelled/gaveled, gavelling/gaveling — rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A small wooden hammer that a judge, auctioneer or chairperson bangs to get attention, keep order or show that something is decided or sold.
its sense in the lessons: A law, court and auction word. In US courts a judge bangs a gavel; in British courts judges do not actually use gavels, but auctioneers do. «Going, going, gone!» — bang of the gavel — means sold. In Alice in Wonderland the King of Hearts is the judge at the trial of the Knave, though Carroll's court is noisy and silly.
examples from the lessons: The judge banged the gavel and shouted, «Order in court!» | The auctioneer struck the gavel: «Sold to the lady in red!» | Our class president used a gavel to start the meeting. | The gavel came down and the painting was sold. | In the school mock trial, Tom held the gavel. | The chairwoman tapped her gavel for silence.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Pronounced GAV-ul. Myth: English judges don't use gavels — that is mostly American and on TV. «The gavel came down» means a decision was made.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The skill of a general in leading an army and planning battles. 2) Clever leadership and planning of any big task.
its sense in the lessons: A history word for military leaders like Wellington or Napoleon. In The Wind in the Willows Badger, Rat, Mole and Toad plan the attack to win back Toad Hall from the stoats and weasels, and Rat organises everything like a general: that is generalship.
examples from the lessons: Wellington's generalship won the Battle of Waterloo. | Napoleon was famous for his generalship. | Rat showed fine generalship in planning the attack on Toad Hall. | Good generalship means caring for your soldiers and planning well. | Her generalship of the school fair made it a great success. | The battle was lost through poor generalship.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. From «general» (an army leader) + -ship (skill or state, as in leadership, friendship). Formal and a bit old-fashioned outside history.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Very bad, horrible or unpleasant. 2) Shocking and frightening, like something terrible to see. 3) Very pale and ill-looking, like a ghost. 4) (informal, UK) Awful, as in «a ghastly mistake», «ghastly weather».
its sense in the lessons: A strong descriptive word, both in scary stories (a ghastly face, a ghastly scream) and in everyday British talk (ghastly food, ghastly weather). It tells readers that something is dreadful or that someone looks deathly pale.
examples from the lessons: The school dinner was ghastly. | We had ghastly weather on holiday. | A ghastly scream came from the cellar. | He looked ghastly after being seasick. | I've made a ghastly mistake! | Toad thought the prison food was ghastly. | The weasels let out a ghastly howl as the friends burst in.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective; comparative ghastlier, superlative ghastliest. Pronounced GAHST-lee (UK) or GAST-lee (US); the h is silent. It looks like an adverb (-ly) but is an adjective. Linked in meaning to «ghost» (both from an old word for spirit).

part of speech: noun (a glimpse, glimpses); verb (glimpse, glimpses, glimpsed, glimpsing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (noun) A very quick look at something, so you see it only for a moment or only a part of it. 2) (verb) To see something for a moment, often by chance. 3) (noun) A short experience that shows you what something is like, as in «a glimpse of the future».
its sense in the lessons: Common in stories: «caught a glimpse of», «glimpsed a figure in the mist». It builds mystery, because the character (and the reader) see only a little. In history and science, a find can give «a glimpse into» how people lived long ago.
examples from the lessons: I caught a glimpse of the fox before it ran into the bushes. | Alice glimpsed the White Rabbit hurrying down a long passage. | We got a glimpse of the Queen as her car went past. | Through the trees Mole glimpsed the lights of a house. | The Roman coins give us a glimpse into life long ago. | She glimpsed a shooting star. | The museum offers a glimpse of life in a Victorian school.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: a glimpse; «catch a glimpse of» is the most common phrase. Regular verb: glimpsed. Do not confuse with «glance», which is the act of looking quickly; a glimpse is what you manage to see.

part of speech: verb form (glint, glints, glinted, glinting); adjective (glinting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Giving out small, quick flashes of light, especially reflected light from metal, glass, water or eyes. 2) (of eyes) Shining with a feeling, such as mischief, anger or fun.
its sense in the lessons: A picture-making story word: glinting swords, glinting water, glinting eyes. It helps the reader see sunlight catching something. In stories glinting eyes often show a clever or wicked plan, like the weasels' eyes glinting in the dark Wild Wood.
examples from the lessons: The sun was glinting on the river. | Mole saw little eyes glinting at him from the dark holes. | His glasses were glinting in the light. | The knight's sword was glinting in the sun. | Her eyes were glinting with mischief. | Coins were glinting at the bottom of the fountain.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Present participle of «glint»; noun «a glint» (a glint of gold, a glint in his eye). Similar: gleam, glitter, sparkle, twinkle. «Glint» is short and sharp; «gleam» is softer and steadier.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Darkness or near-darkness, as in a dim room or a dark wood. 2) A feeling of sadness and hopelessness. 3) (in phrases) «Doom and gloom» means talk that everything will go badly.
its sense in the lessons: In stories it sets a dark, sad or scary mood: «in the gloom of the forest». It also describes how people feel after bad news. «All doom and gloom» is a common everyday phrase. Mole loses his way in the gloom of the Wild Wood as the snow falls.
examples from the lessons: Mole stumbled through the gloom of the Wild Wood. | We could hardly see in the gloom of the cellar. | A feeling of gloom fell over the team after the defeat. | Stop the doom and gloom; it's not that bad! | Her smile lit up the gloom of the hospital ward. | The long winter gloom made everyone tired. | Out of the gloom came the friendly light of Badger's door.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: no «a», no plural. Adjective: gloomy; adverb: gloomily. Two meanings, darkness and sadness, often go together in stories.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a sad, hopeless or miserable way. 2) In a dark, dim way (rarer).
its sense in the lessons: Shows a character's low mood: «said gloomily», «stared gloomily out of the window». In The Wind in the Willows, Toad sometimes sits gloomily in his prison cell before he cheers himself up with a boastful song.
examples from the lessons: «We'll never win,» said Tom gloomily. | She stared gloomily at the rain. | Toad sat gloomily in his cell, thinking of Toad Hall. | Eeyore-like, the donkey looked gloomily at his thistles. | The clouds hung gloomily over the hills. | He gloomily packed his bag for the long trip.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from «gloomy». Spelling: gloomy → gloomily (y changes to i). Opposite: cheerfully, brightly.

part of speech: noun (a glug, glugs); verb (glug, glugs, glugged, glugging) — informal
meaning for a pupil: 1) (noun) The gurgling sound liquid makes when it is poured out of a bottle. 2) (noun, informal) An amount poured quickly, as in «a glug of oil». 3) (verb) To drink or pour something quickly and noisily.
its sense in the lessons: An informal, sound word (onomatopoeia): the word sounds like the noise it names. Used in recipes on TV («a good glug of olive oil») and in funny writing. In English lessons it is a good example of onomatopoeia, like splash, fizz and drip.
examples from the lessons: Add a glug of olive oil to the pan. | The water went glug, glug, glug down the plughole. | He glugged his orange juice in one go. | Don't glug your drink; sip it. | The bottle made a glug as she poured the milk. | «Glug» is an onomatopoeia, like «splash» and «buzz».
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal. Verb doubles the g: glugged, glugging. A «glug» is not an exact measure; in maths recipes use millilitres instead.

part of speech: verb form (go, goes, went, gone, going); noun (the going, goings); adjective (going)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (verb form) Moving or travelling somewhere; leaving. 2) (going to + verb) Used to talk about the future or a plan, as in «I'm going to read». 3) (noun) How easy or hard it is to move or make progress, as in «the going was hard». 4) (adjective) Working, available or usual now, as in «the going rate», «the best one going». 5) (in phrases) «Going, going, gone!» at an auction; «get going» = start; «keep going» = don't stop; «comings and goings» = people arriving and leaving.
its sense in the lessons: One of the most common words in English. In school it is used for plans («What are you going to do?») and for perseverance («keep going»). In maths, «going up in twos» means counting 2, 4, 6. Informally «gonna» is how «going to» sounds in fast speech. In stories, «while the going is good» means leave while you still can.
examples from the lessons: I'm going to the park. | We are going to have a test on Friday. | Keep going — you're nearly at the top! | The going was hard through the deep snow. | «Going, going, gone!» said the auctioneer. | The numbers are going up in fives: 5, 10, 15, 20. | Toad was always going somewhere in a hurry. | Let's get going before it rains. | There were comings and goings at the house all night.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Going to» + verb = future plan or prediction (It's going to rain). Spoken quickly, it sounds like «gonna», but write «going to» in school. Past of go is «went», past participle «gone». «Going» on its own can also mean leaving: «I must be going».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Moving in a smooth, light and beautiful way. 2) Having a beautiful, elegant shape. 3) Polite and kind, especially when things are difficult, as in «a graceful loser».
its sense in the lessons: Used for dancers, swans, cats, horses and buildings. In PE and dance it describes smooth movement. Sense 3 is about good manners: a «graceful» winner or loser is kind and fair. In stories swans and grebes glide gracefully on the river.
examples from the lessons: The ballet dancer was very graceful. | Swans are graceful birds on the water. | The cat made a graceful leap onto the wall. | She was graceful in defeat and shook hands with the winner. | The bridge has graceful curves. | The Water Rat rowed with graceful, easy strokes. | Deer are graceful runners.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective; adverb gracefully, noun grace. Opposite: clumsy, awkward. Spelling: grace + ful (one l). Do not confuse with «gracious», which means kind and polite (more about manners than movement).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) Grandfather; a friendly name for your grandad. 2) (informal, sometimes cheeky) A way of talking to or about any old man.
its sense in the lessons: A friendly family word, especially in the USA, Canada and Australia; in the UK people more often say «Grandad» or «Grandpa». Used in speech and informal writing; when talking to a stranger it can be rude.
examples from the lessons: Gramps took me fishing at the lake. | «Hi, Gramps!» shouted Lily as she ran to hug him. | My gramps tells the funniest stories. | We baked a cake for Gramps's birthday. | Gramps fell asleep in his armchair after lunch. | Calling a stranger «gramps» is cheeky.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal. Used like a name, with a capital G when you call someone: «Thanks, Gramps!» Other words: grandfather (formal), grandad, grandpa, granddad, pop, pops; grandmothers are gran, granny, nan, nana, grandma.

part of speech: verb (grapple, grapples, grappled, grappling); noun (a grapple — rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To fight with someone by holding and struggling with them. 2) (grapple with) To work hard to understand or deal with a difficult problem. 3) (noun) A hook used to grab or hold something, also called a grappling hook.
its sense in the lessons: Sense 2 is common in school and news: «grapple with fractions», «the town is grappling with floods». Sense 1 is used for wrestling and fights in stories, like Toad grappling with the barge-woman.
examples from the lessons: The two wrestlers grappled on the mat. | Pupils grappled with the tricky word problem. | The police officer grappled with the thief. | Scientists are grappling with the problem of climate change. | Toad grappled with the barge-woman, but she was too strong for him. | The pirates threw grappling hooks onto the ship.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: grappled, grappling. «Grapple with» is the main pattern. A «grappling hook» has several hooks on a rope, used to climb or catch hold of ships.

part of speech: adjective; verb form (gratify, gratifies, gratified, gratifying)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Pleased and satisfied, especially because something has gone well or people have praised you. 2) (verb form) Having had a wish or need satisfied.
its sense in the lessons: A formal word for being pleased: «gratified to hear», «gratified by the result». In stories it often shows pride or vanity, like Toad, gratified by praise, puffing himself up.
examples from the lessons: She was gratified by her excellent report. | The teacher was gratified to see everyone working hard. | Toad was gratified to hear the crowd cheering his name. | The scientist was gratified when the experiment worked. | We were gratified by the many letters of thanks. | He looked gratified when the judge praised his cake.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; in everyday talk «pleased». Verb «gratify» (y → i: gratifies, gratified). Adjective «gratifying» (a gratifying result). Related to «gratitude» and «grateful», but «gratified» means pleased, not thankful.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A diving water bird with lobed toes and a sharp beak, found on lakes and rivers; the great crested grebe has fancy head feathers.
its sense in the lessons: A nature word for river and lake birds in the UK, Ireland, North America, Australia and New Zealand. Great crested grebes are famous for their courtship «dance», in which the pair rise up breast to breast and shake their heads. Birds like grebes, coots and moorhens live on the river bank of The Wind in the Willows.
examples from the lessons: A great crested grebe dived under the water and came up with a fish. | Grebes carry their chicks on their backs. | We watched two grebes doing their courtship dance. | The little grebe is also called a dabchick. | Grebes build floating nests of reeds. | There were ducks, coots and a grebe on the lake.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a grebe, grebes. Pronounced GREEB. Grebes are not ducks: their feet have lobes, not webs, and they rarely walk on land. A young great crested grebe has a striped head.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A room where soldiers or guards on duty stay, often near a gate. 2) A room in a castle or barracks where prisoners are kept for a short time.
its sense in the lessons: A castle, army and prison word. In The Wind in the Willows Toad is dragged through the gloomy castle-prison, past guardrooms full of soldiers, to the deepest dungeon. In history lessons on castles, the guardroom is usually beside the gatehouse.
examples from the lessons: The soldiers rested in the guardroom by the castle gate. | Toad was dragged past the guardroom to the dungeon. | The guard went back to the guardroom to warm his hands. | The prisoner was kept in the guardroom overnight. | We visited the old guardroom at the Tower of London. | Keys hung on a hook in the guardroom.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable, one word. Related: guardhouse, gatehouse, barracks. «On guard» means watching; «off guard» means not ready.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The tube that food goes down from the mouth to the stomach; the oesophagus. 2) The throat.
its sense in the lessons: A science and story word. In science, food goes down the gullet (oesophagus) by muscle squeezes. In Kipling's Just So Story «How the Whale got his Throat», the sailor fixes a grating in the Whale's throat, so after that the Whale can only swallow very small fish; the story is a made-up explanation, not real science.
examples from the lessons: Food passes down the gullet to the stomach. | A fishbone got stuck in his gullet. | The pelican swallowed the fish whole down its gullet. | The Whale's throat, or gullet, was blocked by a grating in Kipling's story. | The heron gulped the frog into its gullet. | Muscles in the gullet push food down even if you are upside down.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. The science word is «oesophagus» (UK) or «esophagus» (US). Do not confuse the gullet (food pipe) with the windpipe (trachea, for air). Real whales: baleen whales do have small throats, but not because of any grating — Kipling made that up.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Generously; in large amounts, as in «paid handsomely» or «rewarded handsomely». 2) Clearly and well; by a big margin, as in «won handsomely». 3) In a good-looking, fine or elegant way.
its sense in the lessons: Mostly used about money and winning: «handsomely paid», «handsomely rewarded», «beat them handsomely». In stories a hero is «handsomely rewarded» by a king. Sense 3 is used for things that are finely dressed or made.
examples from the lessons: The finder of the lost dog was handsomely rewarded. | Our team won handsomely, 6–0. | The house was handsomely decorated for Christmas. | The workers were handsomely paid for the hard job. | The king rewarded the brave knight handsomely. | Toad tipped the waiter handsomely to show off.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from «handsome». Note that «handsome» is used for men's good looks, but «handsomely» usually means «generously» or «by a lot», not about looks. «Handsome reward» = a big reward.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To keep annoying, upsetting, threatening or bothering someone again and again. 2) To make repeated small attacks on an enemy.
its sense in the lessons: A serious word in safety and citizenship lessons: harassing someone online or in person is bullying and can be against the law. Children should tell a trusted adult if someone harasses them. In history, soldiers harass an enemy army with small attacks.
examples from the lessons: It is wrong to harass people online. | The boys were told off for harassing the younger children. | Tell a teacher if anyone harasses you.. | Small groups of soldiers harassed the enemy's supply wagons. | She felt harassed by the constant phone calls.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: one r, double s — harass (not «harrass»). Two pronunciations: HA-rus or ha-RASS. Noun: harassment. «Harassed» can also mean stressed and tired (a harassed mum).

meaning for a pupil: 1) The hip, bottom and top of the leg of a person or animal. 2) A back leg and hip of an animal as meat, as in «a haunch of venison».
its sense in the lessons: Used when animals or people sit back on their legs: «sat back on its haunches», «squatted on his haunches». In stories a dog, rabbit or hare sits on its haunches to look around; Kipling's animals often do. In old feasts, a haunch of venison (deer meat) was roasted.
examples from the lessons: The dog sat back on its haunches and begged. | The hare sat up on its haunches and listened. | He squatted on his haunches to look at the beetle. | The cook roasted a haunch of venison for the feast. | Badger sat on his haunches by the fire. | The lion crouched on its haunches, ready to spring.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; usually in the plural «haunches». Pronounced HAWNCH. Common phrase: «sit (back) on your haunches» = squat with your bottom near your heels.

part of speech: verb (hearken, hearkens, hearkened, hearkening); also spelled harken
meaning for a pupil: 1) (old-fashioned) To listen carefully. 2) (hearken back to) To go back to or remind people of something from the past.
its sense in the lessons: An old, poetic word found in the Bible, old stories and songs: «Hearken unto me». Kipling's Just So Stories use the old storyteller's style («Hear and attend and listen»), close to «hearken». Today «hark back» or «hearken back» means to recall the past.
examples from the lessons: «Hearken, children, to my tale,» said the old storyteller. | The Bible says, «Hearken unto me, O my people.» | The design hearkens back to the old Victorian style. | They would not hearken to the warning and the boat sank. | The song «Hark! the herald angels sing» uses the short form «hark». | Hearken to the wind in the trees.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Old-fashioned; today say «listen». Pronounced HAR-kun (the e is silent). US spelling «harken» also used. «Hark!» is a shorter old word meaning «Listen!» «Hearken unto» = listen to (old Bible English).

meaning for a pupil: 1) With a lot of energy, warmth and enjoyment, as in «laughed heartily» or «ate heartily». 2) Completely; very much, as in «heartily sick of» or «heartily agree».
its sense in the lessons: Common in stories and everyday speech: «laughed heartily», «ate heartily», «welcomed us heartily». «Heartily sick of something» means really tired of it. Badger and Rat eat heartily after their adventures in The Wind in the Willows.
examples from the lessons: The friends ate heartily after the long walk. | Grandpa laughed heartily at the joke. | We were heartily welcomed by our hosts. | I am heartily sick of this rain! | I heartily agree with you. | Mole and Rat ate heartily in Badger's warm kitchen.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from «hearty» (y → i). Pronounced HAR-ti-lee. It is about energy and warmth, not about the heart organ. «Heartily» in «heartily sick of» is a strong «very».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Warmth, friendliness and cheerful energy. 2) Strength and good health. 3) (of food) Being large, filling and satisfying.
its sense in the lessons: Describes a cheerful, loud, friendly manner (the heartiness of a greeting), sometimes a bit too much; or a big, filling meal. In stories a hearty character like Toad greets friends with great heartiness.
examples from the lessons: He greeted us with great heartiness. | The heartiness of the stew warmed us up. | Her heartiness made the new pupils feel welcome. | Toad's heartiness was a little too loud for Rat. | The old sailor was full of heartiness and good humour. | The farmer's heartiness came from hard work in the open air.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. From «hearty» (y → i + ness). Similar: warmth, cheerfulness, enthusiasm.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Your deepest feelings of love and sympathy. 2) (in the phrase «tug at/pull at someone's heartstrings») To make someone feel very sorry, sad or loving.
its sense in the lessons: Almost always used in «tug at the heartstrings» or «pull at the heartstrings»: a sad film, a lost puppy or a charity advert does this. In The Wind in the Willows, when Mole smells his old home, the call of it tugs at his heartstrings until he weeps.
examples from the lessons: The film about the lost puppy tugged at our heartstrings. | Charity adverts often pull at your heartstrings. | The smell of his old home tugged at Mole's heartstrings. | The orphan's story pulled at everyone's heartstrings. | The song about home tugs at my heartstrings every time. | Her letter touched my heartstrings.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural noun, one word. Used figuratively; heartstrings are not real parts of the heart. Writers also say «it plucked at his heartstrings».

part of speech: verb form (heave, heaves, heaved, heaving — sailors also use hove); noun (plural of heave; the heaves)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (verb) Lifts, pulls or throws something heavy with great effort. 2) (verb) Rises and falls strongly, like the sea or someone's chest when breathing hard. 3) (verb, with sigh) «Heaves a sigh» means lets out a big, deep sigh. 4) (verb) Tries to be sick; retches. 5) (noun) Big efforts to pull or lift; «the heaves» (informal) means retching.
its sense in the lessons: Used in stories and everyday life: «he heaves the sack onto his back», «she heaves a sigh of relief», «the sea heaves». In PE, team games like tug-of-war use «Heave!» for a big pull. Sailors shout «Heave ho!»
examples from the lessons: He heaves the heavy box onto the shelf. | The sea heaves and rolls in the storm. | Mum heaves a sigh of relief when we get home. | The barge-woman heaves Toad into the canal. | «One, two, three — heave!» shouted the tug-of-war captain. | After the fairground ride, Sam gets the heaves. | His chest heaves as he finishes the race.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Third-person form of «heave»: he heaves, she heaves. Past: heaved (usually); «hove» is used by sailors («hove into view» = came into sight). Sense 4 is about feeling sick; say «retching» in science.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Without being able to help yourself or do anything about a situation. 2) Without being able to stop, as in «laughed helplessly».
its sense in the lessons: Common in stories: a character watches helplessly as something goes wrong, or laughs helplessly at a joke. It shows that someone has no power in a moment, which builds tension or sympathy.
examples from the lessons: We watched helplessly as the balloon floated away. | The kitten mewed helplessly at the top of the tree. | Toad struggled helplessly in the water. | The children laughed helplessly at the clown. | Alice cried helplessly in the Pool of Tears. | The boat drifted helplessly towards the weir.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from «helpless» (help + less = without help). Noun: helplessness. «Laughed helplessly» means could not stop laughing, not that they were sad.

part of speech: noun (a hem, hems); verb (hem, hems, hemmed, hemming); interjection (hem, ahem)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (noun) The edge of a piece of cloth, folded over and sewn so it does not fray, such as the bottom of a skirt or trousers. 2) (verb) To sew a hem on something. 3) (verb, hem in) To surround someone or something so they cannot move or escape. 4) (interjection) «Hem!» or «Ahem!» is a little cough to get attention or show doubt. 5) (in «hem and haw») To hesitate and not decide.
its sense in the lessons: In sewing and textiles lessons pupils hem a piece of fabric. In stories people are «hemmed in» by enemies, crowds or mountains. In Alice in Wonderland the Mouse begins his «driest» story with «Ahem!» as a small cough before speaking.
examples from the lessons: Mum took up the hem of my school trousers. | We learned to hem a napkin in textiles class. | The sheep were hemmed in by the fence. | Toad felt hemmed in by the weasels on every side. | «Ahem!» said the Mouse, with an important air. | The skirt's hem was muddy from the field. | Stop hemming and hawing and choose a flavour!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb doubles the m: hemmed, hemming. «Hem in» = surround and trap. «Hem and haw» (US «hem and haw», UK more often «hum and haw») = hesitate. «Ahem» is how the throat-clearing sound is written.

part of speech: noun (a herald, heralds); verb (herald, heralds, heralded, heralding)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (noun) In the past, an official who carried messages and made announcements for a king or queen. 2) (noun) A sign that something is coming, as in «the herald of spring». 3) (verb) To be a sign that something is about to happen. 4) (verb) To announce or welcome something loudly and publicly. 5) Part of many newspaper names, such as «The Herald».
its sense in the lessons: In history, heralds announced news and organised coats of arms. In Alice in Wonderland the White Rabbit acts as herald at the trial, blowing a trumpet and reading out the charge. In church life the carol «Hark! the herald angels sing» calls the angels heralds of Jesus' birth. In nature lessons, snowdrops herald the coming of spring.
examples from the lessons: The herald blew his trumpet and read the king's message. | The White Rabbit, acting as herald, read out the accusation. | Snowdrops herald the start of spring. | «Hark! the herald angels sing.» | Dark clouds heralded the storm. | The invention of the steam engine heralded a new age. | My grandad reads the Herald every morning.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun; regular verb (heralded). Pronounced HE-ruld. «Heraldry» is the study of coats of arms. In sense 3 the subject is the sign, not a person: «Swallows herald summer».

part of speech: verb form (herald, heralds, heralded, heralding) — past tense and past participle; adjective (heralded)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Was a sign that something was coming. 2) Announced loudly or welcomed publicly. 3) (adjective, much-heralded) Talked about with great excitement before it happened.
its sense in the lessons: Used in history and news: «the invention heralded a new age», «the much-heralded new stadium». In stories trumpets heralded the arrival of the king or queen, as when the Queen of Hearts came to the croquet ground with her procession.
examples from the lessons: Trumpets heralded the arrival of the King and Queen of Hearts. | The first swallows heralded the summer. | The steam train heralded a new age of travel. | The much-heralded film turned out to be boring. | A loud crack of thunder heralded the storm. | The arrival of the internet heralded great changes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past form of «herald». «Much-heralded» = widely talked about in advance; it can sound slightly ironic if the thing disappoints. Similar: announced, signalled, foreshadowed.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) From now on; after this time. 2) (formal, law) In this document from this point on, as in «hereafter called the Buyer». 3) (noun, the hereafter) Life after death.
its sense in the lessons: A formal word in legal papers and old writing. In church life «the hereafter» means life after death; Christians believe in eternal life with God after death. In everyday speech people say «from now on» instead.
examples from the lessons: Hereafter, all homework must be handed in on Monday. | The Royal Society for the Protection of Birds, hereafter called the RSPB, was founded in 1889. | Many religions teach about the hereafter. | Christians believe that the hereafter is life with God. | «Hereafter you shall be called the Elephant's Child no more,» the storyteller might say. | The contract says the house, hereafter «the property», is sold.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal or old-fashioned; one word. In essays, «hereafter» is used to give a short name for something: «the United Nations (hereafter UN)». Related old words: hereby, herein, heretofore.

part of speech: verb form (hew, hews, hewed, hewn or hewed, hewing) — past participle of «hew»; adjective
meaning for a pupil: 1) Cut or chopped with an axe, pick or other sharp tool, especially wood or stone. 2) (adjective) Shaped roughly by cutting, as in «rough-hewn».
its sense in the lessons: A history and story word: «hewn from rock», «a rough-hewn table», «hand-hewn beams». It describes old buildings, castles, caves and furniture. Badger's underground home in The Wind in the Willows has rooms and passages, and old stone homes may be hewn from the rock.
examples from the lessons: The steps were hewn out of solid rock. | The cottage had a rough-hewn wooden table. | Stone for the cathedral was hewn from a nearby quarry. | Miners hewed coal deep underground. | The ancient tomb was hewn into the cliff. | The beams were hand-hewn by carpenters long ago.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Irregular past participle: hew – hewed – hewn (or hewed). Pronounced HYOON. Old-fashioned; today «cut» or «carved». Homophone trap: «hewn» sounds like «Hune»; «hew» sounds like «hue» (a colour) and «Hugh» (a name).

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a very ugly, horrible or frightening way. 2) (informal) Extremely, in a bad way, as in «hideously expensive» or «hideously embarrassing».
its sense in the lessons: Used in scary and funny stories: «grinned hideously», «hideously ugly». In everyday talk, «hideously» strengthens a complaint: «hideously expensive», «hideously early». It tells the reader something is very unpleasant.
examples from the lessons: The monster grinned hideously in the dark. | The old house had been hideously painted orange and purple. | The trainers were hideously expensive. | It was hideously early when the alarm rang. | The Duchess was hideously ugly in the old pictures of Alice. | The weasels laughed hideously at Toad's misfortune.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from «hideous» (very ugly or horrible). Pronounced HID-ee-us-lee. Not connected with «hide» (to keep out of sight) in meaning.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Arranged in levels or ranks, from the top to the bottom, with each level more important or powerful than the one below. 2) (science) Arranged in groups inside bigger groups, like a family tree.
its sense in the lessons: In history and citizenship, feudal society was hierarchical (king, lords, knights, peasants). In science, living things are sorted in a hierarchical way (kingdom, class, order, family, genus, species). In computing, folders inside folders are hierarchical. Schools and armies are hierarchical too.
examples from the lessons: The army is a hierarchical organisation, with generals at the top. | Medieval society was hierarchical: the king, then the lords, then the peasants. | Living things are classified in a hierarchical system. | Folders on a computer are arranged in a hierarchical way. | In the hierarchical world of Wonderland, the King and Queen of Hearts rule the cards. | A family tree is a hierarchical diagram.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective from «hierarchy» (HY-er-ar-kee). Pronounced hy-er-AR-ki-kul. Spelling trap: «hier» (not «heir» or «higher»). In maths and science, a tree diagram is a good picture of something hierarchical.

part of speech: noun (a homebody, homebodies) — informal, mainly US
meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who likes staying at home more than going out.
its sense in the lessons: A friendly, informal word for someone who loves home comforts. In The Wind in the Willows Mole and Badger are homebodies who love their snug houses, while Toad always rushes about and Rat dreams of the sea. In the UK people may say «home-lover» or «stay-at-home».
examples from the lessons: My grandad is a homebody who loves his armchair. | I'm a bit of a homebody; I'd rather read than go to a party. | Badger was a homebody who didn't like visitors much. | Cats are often homebodies. | She was a homebody until she joined the hiking club. | Mole was a homebody at heart, and he longed for Mole End.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a homebody, homebodies (y → ies). Informal, mostly American. Not an insult; it just describes a preference. Opposite: socialite, party animal, globetrotter.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Coming home after being away for a long time. 2) (US, Canada) A yearly celebration at a school or college with a football game and a dance, welcoming former pupils back.
its sense in the lessons: A warm, emotional story word: soldiers, sailors and travellers return home. In The Wind in the Willows, the chapter «Dulce Domum» is Mole's homecoming to Mole End at Christmas, and the last chapter, «The Return of Ulysses», is Toad's homecoming to Toad Hall. In the USA, homecoming is a big school event.
examples from the lessons: The family planned a party for the soldier's homecoming. | Mole's homecoming to his little house was a happy, tearful night. | Toad's homecoming meant fighting the weasels. | The homecoming game is the biggest match of the year at our high school. | The sailors had a joyful homecoming. | Ulysses' homecoming took ten long years.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. One word. Pronounced HOME-kum-ing. In the UK the school sense is rare; it is mostly American and Canadian. «Homecoming queen» and «homecoming dance» are US school traditions.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The work of looking after a home: cleaning, cooking, shopping and paying bills. 2) (in hotels and hospitals) The department that cleans the rooms. 3) Money set aside for running a home («the housekeeping»). 4) (informal) Small tidy-up jobs in an organisation, such as updating files or checking dates.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and lessons about the home it covers all the jobs that keep a house running. In stories, Mole takes pride in his housekeeping, and Rat is a good housekeeper. Sense 4 is used at meetings: «a few housekeeping notes before we start».
examples from the lessons: Housekeeping takes a lot of time in a big family. | Ring housekeeping and ask for more towels. | Mum keeps the housekeeping money in a jar. | Mole was proud of his tidy housekeeping. | Before the assembly, the head did some housekeeping: lost property and the bus times. | Learning housekeeping skills helps you live on your own.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: no «a», no plural. A «housekeeper» is a person paid to run a house. Everyone in a home can share the housekeeping, not only one person.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a sulky, annoyed and offended way.
its sense in the lessons: Shows a character is cross because their feelings or pride are hurt: «said huffily», «walked off huffily». Alice's creatures in Wonderland are always taking offence and answering huffily, like the Mouse and the Caterpillar.
examples from the lessons: «Fine, I'll play by myself,» she said huffily. | The Mouse swam off huffily when Alice mentioned her cat. | He folded his arms huffily. | The cat stalked off huffily when we laughed at it. | «I'm not talking to you,» said Toad huffily. | She huffily slammed the door.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from «huffy». Related: «in a huff» = in a bad mood because you feel insulted. Similar: sulkily, crossly, grumpily.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Easily offended; quick to sulk. 2) Sulky and annoyed because your feelings are hurt.
its sense in the lessons: An informal everyday word: «Don't get huffy». In Alice in Wonderland many creatures are huffy, taking offence at Alice's harmless words. In stories, a huffy character goes off in a sulk.
examples from the lessons: Don't get huffy just because you lost the game. | My sister gets huffy when we tease her. | The Caterpillar was very huffy with Alice. | He's in a huffy mood today. | Toad got huffy when his friends laughed at him. | The huffy cat refused to come in.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal; comparative huffier, superlative huffiest. Related: «in a huff», «huff and puff» (to complain loudly; also the Big Bad Wolf's huffing and puffing).

part of speech: noun (a hunch, hunches); verb (hunch, hunches, hunched, hunching)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (noun) A feeling that something is true, even though you have no proof. 2) (verb) To bend your back and shoulders forward and up, often from cold, tiredness or worry. 3) (noun, old) A hump or lump.
its sense in the lessons: Sense 1 is common in detective stories and everyday talk: «I had a hunch», «follow your hunch». In science a hunch must be tested with an experiment before it is accepted. Sense 2 describes body position: «hunched over his desk», «hunched against the cold». Mole hunched himself up in a hollow tree in the Wild Wood.
examples from the lessons: I had a hunch it would rain, so I took an umbrella. | The detective followed his hunch and found the thief. | He hunched over his book, reading. | The old man hunched his shoulders against the wind. | Mole hunched himself up in the hollow of a tree. | Scientists test their hunches with careful experiments. | Don't hunch over your desk; sit up straight.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun countable: a hunch, hunches. Verb: hunched, hunching. A «hunchback» is an old, now hurtful word for someone with a curved spine; say «a curved spine» instead. A hunch is a guess, not proof.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Very stupid or silly; making no sense.
its sense in the lessons: An informal, quite rude word for an idea, act or remark, not a polite way to describe a person. In stories characters call each other's plans idiotic when they argue, and Toad's schemes are often called idiotic by his friends.
examples from the lessons: That was an idiotic thing to do! | Jumping off the shed was an idiotic idea. | Rat thought Toad's plan to drive again was idiotic. | Stop asking idiotic questions and listen. | The Mad Hatter gave idiotic answers to every question. | It's idiotic to leave the gate open with the dog in the garden.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective from «idiot». Adverb: idiotically. It can hurt feelings, so describe the action, not the person («that was a silly idea», not «you are an idiot»). The old use of «idiot» for people with learning difficulties is now offensive.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Extremely; very much, to a great degree.
its sense in the lessons: Used to make an adjective or verb very strong: «immensely proud», «immensely popular», «enjoyed it immensely». Common in formal and story writing; in everyday talk «really» or «very».
examples from the lessons: I enjoyed the film immensely. | She was immensely proud of her brother. | The book is immensely popular with children. | The stars are immensely far away. | Toad was immensely rich and immensely boastful. | The trip helped us immensely.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from «immense» (very big). Spelling: imm-ense-ly, double m. Similar: enormously, hugely, tremendously.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal, old) To shut someone up in a prison or a closed place, as if behind walls. 2) To shut yourself away from other people.
its sense in the lessons: A rare, bookish word for being imprisoned or shut away: «immured in a dungeon». In The Wind in the Willows Toad is immured in the deepest dungeon of the oldest castle in England for stealing a motor-car. In history stories, people were sometimes walled up as punishment.
examples from the lessons: Toad was immured in the darkest dungeon of the castle. | The prisoner was immured in a tiny cell. | The writer immured herself in her room to finish her book. | In the legend, the princess was immured in a tower. | He felt immured in the dull office all day.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal and rare; pronounced i-MYOOR. From Latin «murus», wall (compare «mural», a wall painting). Today say «lock up», «imprison» or «shut away».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A feeling of being annoyed because you have to wait or because something is slow. 2) A strong wish for something to happen soon; eagerness. 3) Being easily irritated by people or mistakes.
its sense in the lessons: A common word in stories and school: «waited with impatience», «a sigh of impatience», «impatience to begin». In stories Toad is full of impatience for new adventures, and the Queen of Hearts shows her impatience by shouting «Off with her head!»
examples from the lessons: She tapped her foot with impatience. | The children's impatience grew as the bus was late. | Toad's impatience to drive again could not be stopped. | The Queen of Hearts had no patience at all, only impatience. | In his impatience, he opened the oven too soon and the cake sank. | The teacher showed no impatience with our questions.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Adjective: impatient; adverb: impatiently. Opposite: patience. Prefix «im-» means «not», as in impossible, impolite.

part of speech: verb form (impel, impels, impelled, impelling) — past tense and past participle; adjective
meaning for a pupil: 1) Made to feel that you must do something; driven by a strong feeling or need. 2) Pushed or driven forward by a force.
its sense in the lessons: A formal word, often in «felt impelled to»: «I felt impelled to speak up». In stories it shows a strong inner urge, like Mole impelled by the call of his old home, or Rat impelled by the Sea Rat's tales to go south. In science, an object can be impelled forward by a force.
examples from the lessons: She felt impelled to tell the truth. | Mole was impelled by a strong longing to find his old home. | Curiosity impelled the Elephant's Child to ask about the Crocodile. | The boat was impelled forward by the wind. | He felt impelled to help the lost child. | Rat was nearly impelled to follow the Sea Rat south.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb «impel» doubles the l: impelled, impelling. Formal; everyday words: drive, push, urge. Do not confuse with «compelled» (forced, often by others or by rules) or «expelled» (sent out).

meaning for a pupil: 1) So small, slight or slow that it cannot be seen, heard or felt.
its sense in the lessons: A science and story word: «an imperceptible movement», «imperceptible change». In science some changes, like the hour hand moving or plants growing, are imperceptible from second to second but clear over time. In stories it shows something very subtle, like an imperceptible nod.
examples from the lessons: The change in the river's level was almost imperceptible. | She gave an imperceptible nod. | The hour hand moves at an imperceptible speed. | Continents drift at an imperceptible rate, a few centimetres a year. | The Cheshire Cat faded away by imperceptible degrees until only its grin was left. | There was an imperceptible tremor before the earthquake.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective; adverb imperceptibly. Prefix «im-» = not, «perceptible» = able to be noticed. Spelling: -ible, not -able. Opposite: perceptible, noticeable.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a proud, bossy way, like someone who expects to be obeyed at once.
its sense in the lessons: Used for characters who give orders like a king or queen. The Queen of Hearts in Alice in Wonderland speaks imperiously all the time, and Toad orders people about imperiously when he feels grand. It shows arrogance and power.
examples from the lessons: «Off with her head!» shouted the Queen imperiously. | The cat looked at us imperiously, waiting for its dinner. | Toad imperiously ordered the servants to bring his car. | She waved her hand imperiously to show we should leave. | The duchess rang the bell imperiously. | «Bring me my crown,» said the king imperiously.
