note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from «imperious» (bossy and proud). Related to «imperial» and «emperor». Pronounced im-PEER-ee-us-lee. Similar: commandingly, haughtily, bossily.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To beg someone very strongly and emotionally to do something.
its sense in the lessons: A strong, formal word for begging, often in stories: «I implore you», «implored him to stop». It shows that a character is desperate. In The Wind in the Willows, Toad's friends implore him to give up motor-cars; in the Just So Stories the Elephant's Child implores his relatives to tell him what the Crocodile eats.
examples from the lessons: «Please, I implore you, let me go!» cried the prisoner. | She implored her parents to let her keep the puppy. | Rat implored Toad to give up motor-cars. | The Elephant's Child implored his relatives to answer his question. | He implored the referee to change his decision. | The villagers implored the king for help.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: implored, imploring. Pattern: implore someone to do something. Adjective «imploring» (an imploring look). Similar: beg, plead, beseech (old).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Not being careful or sensible; doing things without thinking about the risks. 2) An unwise act.
its sense in the lessons: A formal word for careless foolishness, often with money or danger. In The Wind in the Willows Toad's imprudence with motor-cars brings him into trouble, prison and loss of his home. In safety and money lessons, prudence (care) is the opposite.
examples from the lessons: Spending all his pocket money on day one was an act of imprudence. | Toad's imprudence led him straight to prison. | Swimming alone in the sea was pure imprudence. | The judge spoke of the young man's imprudence. | The family's imprudence with money left them in debt. | We learned from our imprudence and packed raincoats next time.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly uncountable. Adjective: imprudent; opposite: prudence, prudent (careful, sensible). Formal; everyday words: carelessness, foolishness, recklessness.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Without care; carelessly, without thinking about danger or consequences.
its sense in the lessons: A formal story word showing that a character acts or speaks rashly and gets into trouble: «incautiously leaned over the edge», «spoke incautiously». In Alice in Wonderland, Alice incautiously mentions her cat Dinah to the Mouse and the birds, who all run away.
examples from the lessons: Alice incautiously mentioned her cat to the Mouse. | He leaned incautiously over the side of the boat and fell in. | Toad incautiously boasted to the gaoler's daughter. | The fox crept incautiously into the farmyard. | She incautiously told everyone the secret. | Never cross the road incautiously.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from «incautious» (not cautious). Prefix «in-» = not. Similar: carelessly, rashly. Opposite: cautiously, carefully.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In an angry, offended way, because you think something is unfair or insulting.
its sense in the lessons: A very common word in children's classics: «said Alice indignantly», «Toad replied indignantly». It shows a character feels wronged and is protesting. Alice speaks indignantly many times in Wonderland when the creatures are rude to her.
examples from the lessons: «I'm not a serpent!» said Alice indignantly. | «I didn't do it!» Tom replied indignantly. | Toad indignantly denied that he had stolen the car. | The cat looked indignantly at the dog in its basket. | She indignantly pointed out that it was her turn. | «Who are you calling silly?» asked the Mock Turtle indignantly.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from «indignant»; noun «indignation». Similar: crossly, angrily, resentfully. «Indignant» means angry about unfairness, not just angry.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal, euphemism) Slightly ill, so not able to come or work. 2) (formal) Not willing to do something, as in «indisposed to help».
its sense in the lessons: A polite, formal way of saying someone is ill or unavailable: «The singer is indisposed tonight». It is often a euphemism, so the reason is kept private. In old stories servants say «Her Ladyship is indisposed». Sense 2 is rare and very formal.
examples from the lessons: The head teacher is indisposed today, so the deputy will take assembly. | The opera singer was indisposed, and her understudy sang instead. | «Mr Toad is indisposed and cannot see visitors,» said the butler. | Grandma felt indisposed after the long journey. | He was indisposed to lend us his bike. | The captain was indisposed with a cold.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal and polite. Noun: indisposition. Not the same as «disposed» (willing). Everyday: unwell, poorly (UK), sick (US). «Indisposed» hides the details, so it is used for privacy.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Hard-working; always busy and putting in steady effort.
its sense in the lessons: A praising word for people and animals: ants, bees and beavers are called industrious. In school reports, «industrious» praises a pupil who works steadily. In stories it contrasts with lazy characters, like the busy Mole spring-cleaning versus idle Toad. Note: «industrial» (about factories) is a different word.
examples from the lessons: Ants are industrious little creatures. | Our teacher wrote that I am an industrious pupil. | The industrious beavers built a dam across the stream. | Mole was industrious, spring-cleaning his little home. | The industrious baker was up at four every morning. | The fable of the ant and the grasshopper praises the industrious ant.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective from «industry» in its old meaning of hard work. Adverb: industriously; noun: industriousness. Trap: «industrial» means to do with factories and industry; «industrious» means hard-working.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who gives information to someone else, for example to a researcher or reporter. 2) A person who secretly gives the police information about crimes; an informer.
its sense in the lessons: In science and language research, an informant is someone who answers questions about their language, customs or experiences. In detective stories, an informant (or «grass», «snitch» in slang) secretly tells the police. In news, a journalist may protect an informant's name.
examples from the lessons: The scientist interviewed local informants about the old customs. | The police received a tip from an informant. | The reporter would not name her informant. | In the Wild Wood, the weasels had an informant who told them Toad's plans. | Language researchers record informants speaking their language. | The detective met his informant in the café.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: an informant (use «an» before the vowel sound). Similar: informer (usually for police), source. Slang words (grass, snitch, nark) are rude or unkind.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In the middle; between two levels, stages or places. 2) Not a beginner but not yet an expert, as in «an intermediate swimmer». 3) (noun) A person at a middle level; in chemistry, a substance made in the middle of a reaction.
its sense in the lessons: Used in school and clubs for levels: «beginner, intermediate, advanced». In maths, «intermediate steps» are the working between the question and the answer, and the UK «Intermediate Maths Challenge» is an olympiad competition for older pupils. In science, a chrysalis is the intermediate stage between caterpillar and butterfly.
examples from the lessons: I'm in the intermediate swimming group. | Show the intermediate steps in your working. | The chrysalis is an intermediate stage between caterpillar and butterfly. | The book is for intermediate learners of French. | Grey is an intermediate colour between black and white. | Between 3 and 7, the intermediate whole numbers are 4, 5 and 6. | She is no longer a beginner; she's an intermediate.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced in-ter-MEE-dee-ut. «An intermediate» (an, before a vowel sound). In maths, «intermediate» numbers are those between two given numbers; be careful whether the ends are included. Do not confuse with «intermediary» (a person who helps two sides talk).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Too strong to be beaten or defeated by anyone. 2) So firm that nothing can shake it, as in «invincible hope» or «invincible courage».
its sense in the lessons: In stories it tells the reader that a hero, army or monster seems impossible to beat, and often the story then shows a weakness after all. In history lessons armies and ships were called invincible, like the Spanish Armada of 1588, which was still defeated. In everyday talk people say they «feel invincible» when they are very confident, which can be a safety trap (no one is invincible on a bike without a helmet). Phrases: «feel invincible», «seem invincible», «an invincible team».
examples from the lessons: The team won every match and seemed invincible. | Superman is almost invincible, but kryptonite makes him weak. | The Spanish Armada was called invincible, yet it was beaten in 1588. | After his first win, Toad felt invincible behind the wheel. | Wearing her new boots, she felt invincible on the climbing frame. | No one is invincible, so always wear a helmet. | Their invincible hope kept them going through the long winter.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective only; the noun is «invincibility». Spelling: -ible, not -able. The opposite «vincible» is very rare; say «beatable». Trap: feeling invincible is not being invincible, which is why teenagers are warned about risks.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A man who was born in Ireland or whose family and home are Irish.
its sense in the lessons: Used in history, geography and stories to say where a man comes from; in old jokes «an Englishman, an Irishman and a Scotsman» is a common start, though jokes that mock a nation can be unkind. Today people often say «an Irish man» or «a man from Ireland»; for a woman «Irishwoman», for everyone «the Irish» or «Irish people».
examples from the lessons: The famous writer Oscar Wilde was an Irishman. | An Irishman ran the little shop on the corner. | My grandad is an Irishman from County Cork. | The Irishmen sang loudly after the rugby match. | Saint Patrick was not born an Irishman but became the saint of Ireland. | The story begins with an Englishman, an Irishman and a Scotsman on a train.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always written with a capital I. Plural: Irishmen (not Irishmans). Usually no capital M in the middle. Jokes about «the stupid Irishman» are old prejudice, not truth.

part of speech: noun (a jailer, jailers); also spelled gaoler (UK, old)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A person whose job is to look after the prisoners in a jail and keep them locked in.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and history lessons the jailer holds the keys, brings food and guards the cells. In The Wind in the Willows Toad is locked in a dungeon, and the gaoler's daughter, who feels sorry for him, helps him escape dressed as a washerwoman. Today the job is called «prison officer» or «correctional officer» (USA).
examples from the lessons: The jailer turned the big iron key in the lock. | Toad escaped with the help of the gaoler's daughter. | The jailer brought the prisoners bread and water. | In the Bible, Paul and Silas sang in prison and the jailer listened. | Today a jailer is usually called a prison officer. | The jailer fell asleep, and the hero crept out.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Gaoler» is the old British spelling and is said exactly like «jailer». Also spelled «jailor». Do not confuse with «jail» (the place) and «jailbird» (a prisoner, informal).

part of speech: noun (a jib, jibs); verb (jib, jibs, jibbed, jibbing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A triangle-shaped sail at the front of a sailing boat. 2) The long arm of a crane that sticks out and holds the hook. 3) To jib (at something) means to refuse to do it or be unwilling, like a horse that stops and will not go on.
its sense in the lessons: Used in sailing, boats and the river and sea stories; the Water Rat and the Sea Rat talk of boats and sails. In building sites the jib of a crane swings over the street. The verb is a bit old-fashioned and appears in older books: «he jibbed at paying». Phrase: «the cut of his jib» (old, how someone looks or seems, from the shape of a ship's sail).
examples from the lessons: The sailor raised the jib, and the boat turned into the wind. | The jib flapped in the breeze. | The crane's jib swung slowly over the building site. | The horse jibbed at the gate and would not go through. | He jibbed at paying so much for a ticket. | Grandad said he liked the cut of her jib.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Do not confuse with «gibe» or «jibe» (to mock, or in sailing to swing the sail across). Past: jibbed, with double b. «Cut of your jib» is an idiom, not about cutting.

part of speech: fragment or old spelling of «jig» (no standard English word «jigg»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Not a standard English word: it is an old or misspelt form of «jig», a lively dance or the music for it. 2) It may also be part of a word that was cut off, such as «jiggle» or «jiggery-pokery».
its sense in the lessons: In old books and songs you may see «jigg» for «jig»; read it as «jig»: a quick, bouncy dance, often Irish or Scottish, or the tune for it. «To jig» means to dance or bounce about quickly.
examples from the lessons: (Old spelling) They danced a merry jigg at the fair. | (Modern spelling) The fiddler played an Irish jig. | The children jigged up and down with excitement. | She learned to dance a jig for the festival. | «Jiggle» means to move something quickly from side to side. | The puppy jiggled with joy at the door.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Write «jig» today; «jigg» is not used. A jig is also a tool that holds work steady in a workshop, and a jigsaw is a puzzle or a saw.

part of speech: noun (a jimmy, jimmies); verb (jimmy, jimmies, jimmied, jimmying); name (Jimmy)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (a name) Jimmy is a short, friendly form of the name James. 2) (USA) A short metal bar with a flat end, used to force open doors or windows; in the UK it is called a «jemmy». 3) To jimmy a door or window means to force it open with a bar or tool. 4) (Scotland, informal) «Jimmy» is a friendly or cheeky way to call a man you do not know. 5) (USA) «Jimmies» are tiny coloured sugar sprinkles on ice cream.
its sense in the lessons: In crime stories a burglar jimmies a window, so the word tells the reader something is being broken into. At home you might jimmy open a stuck lid. In Scotland you may hear «Hey, Jimmy!» to any man. In New England, ice cream comes «with jimmies».
examples from the lessons: My cousin Jimmy is coming for tea. | The burglar used a jimmy to force the back door. | Dad jimmied open the paint tin with a screwdriver. | The window had been jimmied in the night. | (Scotland, informal) «Mind your step there, Jimmy!» | (USA) I'd like a vanilla cone with chocolate jimmies, please.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Capital J for the name. UK spelling of the bar is «jemmy». Past: jimmied; -ing form: jimmying. Forcing a lock that is not yours is a crime.

part of speech: verb (joggle, joggles, joggled, joggling); noun (a joggle, joggles)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To shake or move something with small quick jerks. 2) To bounce up and down gently, like a car on a bumpy road. 3) A joggle is a small shake or jolt.
its sense in the lessons: An old-fashioned, cosy word in stories: a cart joggles along a country lane, as in The Wind in the Willows, where the caravan rolls along the lanes. In everyday talk «jiggle» or «jog» is more common. In maths and science it is not used.
examples from the lessons: The pony cart joggled along the stony lane. | Don't joggle the table while I'm writing. | The baby laughed as Dad joggled her on his knee. | The jelly joggled on the plate. | The caravan gave a joggle as it went over a root. | Her bag joggled against her side as she ran.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Do not confuse with «juggle» (to keep throwing and catching things). Past: joggled; -ing form: joggling (drop the e). «Joggling» is also a sport: juggling while jogging.

part of speech: verb (jot, jots, jotted, jotting; usually «jot down»); noun (a jot)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To jot something down means to write it quickly in a few words. 2) A jot is a very tiny amount, used mostly in «not a jot» meaning «not at all».
its sense in the lessons: At school pupils jot down ideas, notes or working before writing properly; a «jotter» (UK, Scotland) is a rough notebook. In older stories and the Bible «not one jot» means not the smallest bit. Phrases: «jot down», «not a jot», «not care a jot».
examples from the lessons: Jot down your ideas before you start the story. | I jotted her phone number on my hand. | Jot your working in the margin. | He didn't care a jot about the rain. | The Mole hadn't a jot of fear left once he saw the Rat. | Please jot a quick note to say where you've gone. | «Jottings» are short notes written quickly.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: jotted, with double t. «Jot» comes from iota, the smallest Greek letter. Not a jot = nothing at all.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a very happy, glad way, full of joy.
its sense in the lessons: Used in stories to show how a character does something: they shout, sing or run joyfully. In church and Christmas songs people sing joyfully. It tells the reader the feeling is strong and happy, more than «happily».
examples from the lessons: The dog leapt joyfully at the door. | The children ran joyfully into the sea. | The bells rang joyfully on Christmas morning. | Mole cried joyfully when he smelled his old home. | She joyfully opened her birthday present. | The crowd cheered joyfully when the team scored.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «joy» + «-ful» + «-ly»: one l in joyful, two l in joyfully. Opposite: sadly, sorrowfully.

part of speech: noun (a kiddy, kiddies); adjective (kiddy, informal); also spelled kiddie
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) A small child. 2) (informal, adjective) Made for small children, as in «kiddy rides» or «the kiddy pool».
its sense in the lessons: A friendly, sometimes babyish word grown-ups use for little children. Older children may feel it is babyish: «That's a kiddy film!» Also in «kiddy-winkies» (playful).
examples from the lessons: The kiddies queued for the fairground rides. | We splashed in the kiddy pool. | Don't give me that kiddy cup, I'm nine! | The shop has a kiddy corner with toys. | The teacher read a story to the kiddies in Reception. | That cartoon is too kiddy for my big brother.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: kiddies. Both «kiddy» and «kiddie» are correct. Informal; in writing say «young children».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Needing a lot of hard work, effort and time. 2) (of writing or speech) Slow and heavy, showing too much effort.
its sense in the lessons: Used in history (building pyramids or castles was laborious), science and maths (counting one by one is laborious, so we use multiplication). In stories it tells the reader a task is long and tiring.
examples from the lessons: Copying the whole book by hand was laborious work. | Digging the tunnel was slow and laborious. | Adding 7 forty times is laborious, so use 7 × 40 instead. | The Mole's laborious spring-cleaning made his arms ache. | Before washing machines, washing clothes was laborious. | His laborious handwriting took ages.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comes from «labour». Spelled without u even in the UK: laborious, not labourious. Adverb: laboriously.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Loud crying and sad words because of grief or loss. 2) (Bible) Lamentations is a book of the Bible: sad poems about the fall of Jerusalem.
its sense in the lessons: A formal, old-fashioned word in stories, poems and the Bible: it tells the reader there is deep sorrow, often loud. In The Wind in the Willows Toad breaks into lamentations in his dungeon. Everyday words: crying, wailing.
examples from the lessons: There was weeping and lamentation in the city. | Toad flung himself down in bitter lamentation. | The lamentations of the mourners filled the church. | The Book of Lamentations is in the Old Testament. | Her lamentations over the broken vase went on all day. | The poem is a lamentation for a lost friend.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From the verb «lament» (to mourn) + -ation. Stress: la-men-TAY-shun. Often humorous today for too much complaining.

part of speech: verb (laze, lazes, lazed, lazing; often «laze about», «laze around»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To relax and do nothing much, in a lazy, pleasant way.
its sense in the lessons: Used in everyday life about holidays and weekends; in The Wind in the Willows the Rat loves to laze on the river bank in summer. It is not always bad: lazing is resting, while «lazy» means not wanting to work when you should. Phrases: «laze about», «laze around», «laze in the sun».
examples from the lessons: We lazed on the beach all afternoon. | Don't laze about, there's work to do! | The cat lazed in the sun on the windowsill. | On Sunday mornings Dad likes to laze in bed. | The Rat and the Mole lazed in the boat. | We spent a lazy day lazing by the river.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: lazed; -ing form: lazing. Related: lazy (adjective), laziness (noun). Not «laze» = «laser».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who teaches students at a university or college, often by giving talks called lectures. 2) Anyone who gives a talk to an audience.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life a university teacher; in the UK «lecturer» is a job title below «professor». In the USA such people are often called professors. In stories, «lecturing» someone also means telling them off at length.
examples from the lessons: My aunt is a lecturer in chemistry at the university. | The lecturer showed slides of the planets. | The students took notes while the lecturer spoke. | A visiting lecturer talked about whales. | Mum said, «Stop lecturing me, I'm not one of your students!» | He became a lecturer after finishing his PhD.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «lecture» + «-r». «Lecture» also means a long telling-off. Lecturer = person; lecture = the talk.

meaning for a pupil: 1) With no light at all; completely dark.
its sense in the lessons: A literary word in stories and science: deep caves and the deep ocean are lightless, so animals there may be blind or make their own light. It tells the reader a place is dark and often frightening.
examples from the lessons: The miners worked in lightless tunnels. | Deep in the ocean is a lightless world. | The Mole's underground home was lightless at night. | Fish in lightless caves often have no eyes. | The lightless windows showed the house was empty. | A black hole is so strong that it seems lightless.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Light + -less (without). More common words: dark, unlit, pitch-dark.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A big passenger ship that sailed across oceans on regular routes, like the Titanic (an ocean liner). 2) Something put inside another thing to line or protect it, like a bin liner (UK, a bin bag) or a nappy liner. 3) Eyeliner: make-up drawn along the eyelids. 4) In baseball and cricket, a ball hit hard and low (a line drive).
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons the Titanic was an ocean liner that sank in 1912. At home you put a liner in the bin. In art, a fine-liner is a pen with a thin tip. Phrases: «ocean liner», «cruise liner», «bin liner», «one-liner» (a short joke).
examples from the lessons: The Titanic was the biggest liner of its day. | We waved at the cruise liner leaving the harbour. | Put a new liner in the kitchen bin. | Draw the outline with a black fine-liner. | My sister put on eyeliner before the party. | The comedian told a funny one-liner.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: liners. Do not confuse with «lighter» or «line». A «one-liner» is a joke in one sentence.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a way that shows you want something very much, often something you cannot have.
its sense in the lessons: In stories it tells the reader about a character's wish: they look longingly at food, a toy, or home. Mole looks longingly towards his old home in The Wind in the Willows; Alice looks longingly at the lovely garden through the tiny door.
examples from the lessons: The puppy looked longingly at the sausages. | Alice gazed longingly at the garden through the little door. | She stared longingly at the bike in the shop window. | Mole sniffed the air longingly as he remembered his home. | He looked longingly out of the window at the snow. | The Rat listened longingly to the Sea Rat's tales.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «long» (to wish strongly) + -ing + -ly. Not about length.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Talking a lot; very chatty.
its sense in the lessons: A grand, formal word; it appears in exams, older books and as a joke. In stories it tells the reader a character never stops talking, like Toad boasting. Everyday words: chatty, talkative.
examples from the lessons: Our loquacious neighbour talked for an hour. | The parrot was very loquacious. | Toad grew loquacious as he described his motor-car. | The usually quiet boy was loquacious after his win. | A loquacious guide told us every detail of the castle. | Don't be loquacious in a test answer; be brief.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say: lo-KWAY-shus. Noun: loquacity. Opposite: taciturn, quiet.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A small, round, orange-yellow fruit with a sweet, slightly sour taste and big brown seeds. 2) The evergreen tree that it grows on.
its sense in the lessons: Used in food and science (plants) lessons. Loquats come from China and grow in warm places such as Australia, New Zealand, California and Mediterranean countries.
examples from the lessons: We picked loquats from the tree in Nan's garden. | A loquat looks a bit like an apricot. | Don't eat the loquat seeds. | The loquat tree stays green all winter. | In Sydney many back gardens have a loquat tree. | She made loquat jam.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say: LOH-kwot. Plural: loquats. The seeds are not to be eaten: they can be harmful.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a faithful way, staying on someone's side and not letting them down.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, a friend, dog or servant acts loyally; the Rat, Mole and Badger loyally help Toad even when he is foolish. In sport, fans support their team loyally.
examples from the lessons: The dog waited loyally by the door every day. | Badger loyally stood by Toad. | The fans loyally cheered even when the team lost. | She loyally kept her friend's secret. | The knight served the king loyally. | He loyally visited his grandad every Sunday.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: loyal; noun: loyalty. Spelling: two l's at the end, loyally.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Very grand, beautiful and impressive, like a king or queen.
its sense in the lessons: Used in geography and stories for mountains, eagles, lions, ships and old buildings; it tells the reader something fills you with wonder.
examples from the lessons: The eagle spread its majestic wings. | We gazed up at the majestic mountains. | The majestic stag stood still in the forest. | The ship looked majestic with all its sails up. | The lion is often called a majestic animal. | Badger walked into the room in a majestic way.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «majesty» (the greatness of a king). Adverb: majestically.

part of speech: adjective (mangled); verb, past of «mangle» (mangle, mangles, mangled, mangling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Badly crushed, twisted or torn so that it is spoilt. 2) (of words or music) Spoilt by being said or played very badly. 3) (old) Pressed through a mangle, a machine with rollers that squeezed water out of washing.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and news, a mangled car or bike tells the reader there was a bad crash. In everyday talk you can mangle a song or a foreign word. History: in Victorian times washing was pushed through a mangle. Alice mangles poems: her «How doth the little crocodile» comes out wrong.
examples from the lessons: The bike was mangled after the crash. | The dog left a mangled slipper. | Alice mangled the poem, and the words came out all wrong. | He mangled the French phrase, and the waiter laughed. | Grandma remembers mangling the washing on Mondays. | The storm left mangled trees along the road.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mangle the verb is unrelated to «mango». Present: mangle; -ing form: mangling.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a wonderful, excellent way. 2) Very, extremely (a bit old-fashioned), as in «marvellously happy».
its sense in the lessons: A warm, enthusiastic word in British stories and speech; Toad often says things are «marvellous». It tells the reader something went really well.
examples from the lessons: The plan worked marvellously. | The children behaved marvellously at the wedding. | She sang marvellously in the concert. | Everything went marvellously well. | The garden looked marvellously green after the rain. | Toad thought he drove marvellously.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK: marvellously (double l); USA: marvelously (single l). From «marvel» (a wonder).

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a quiet, gentle way, without arguing or fighting back.
its sense in the lessons: In stories it shows a character gives in or obeys without a word, sometimes too easily. Alice sometimes answers meekly when the creatures are rude. In the Bible, «Blessed are the meek» means people who are gentle and humble.
examples from the lessons: «Yes, Miss,» he said meekly. | The puppy sat meekly when told off. | Alice answered meekly, «I—I hardly know, sir.» | She meekly handed over her sweets. | Toad meekly followed Badger into the room. | He meekly agreed to tidy his room.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «meek» (gentle, humble). Meekly does not mean weak: it can be gentle on purpose.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A deep, quiet sadness that lasts a while. 2) (adjective) Sad, or making you feel sad, as in «a melancholy song».
its sense in the lessons: A literary word for a gentle, thoughtful sadness. In Alice in Wonderland the Mock Turtle is very melancholy, sighing and sobbing as he tells his story. Poems and music can be melancholy.
examples from the lessons: The Mock Turtle sang in a melancholy voice. | A melancholy tune played on the radio. | Rain on the window gave her a feeling of melancholy. | He was in a melancholy mood after his friend moved away. | The empty house looked melancholy in the fog. | Autumn can make some people melancholy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say: MEL-an-kol-ee. No «-ic» or «-y» to add: it is both noun and adjective. Do not confuse with «melon».

meaning for a pupil: 1) The thirteenth letter of the Hebrew alphabet, written מ. 2) A short form of «memory» or «member» in notes (mem.), or a cut-off part of «memo» or «memsahib». 3) (old, India) Short for «memsahib», a word servants in British India used for a European lady.
its sense in the lessons: In Bible studies the Hebrew letters (aleph, beth ... mem ...) head the parts of Psalm 119. In computer talk «mem» can mean memory. In old stories about British India, a «mem» or «memsahib» was a European lady.
examples from the lessons: Mem is the thirteenth letter of the Hebrew alphabet. | Psalm 119 has a part headed «Mem». | (note) mem. = member of the club. | In the old story the servant said, «The Mem-sahib is resting.» | The computer showed «mem: 8 GB». | Each part of Psalm 119 begins with the next Hebrew letter.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Not a full English word on its own; check what it stands for. «Mum» and «mam» are different words for mother.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a happy, cheerful, jolly way. 2) Carelessly, without thinking about trouble, as in «He merrily ignored the warning».
its sense in the lessons: Common in songs, carols and stories: «Row, row, row your boat, gently down the stream, merrily, merrily, merrily, merrily, life is but a dream.» «Ding dong merrily on high» is a Christmas carol. It tells the reader things are cheerful.
examples from the lessons: The fire crackled merrily. | The children sang merrily in the snow. | Row, row, row your boat, merrily down the stream. | The Rat sculled merrily along the river. | The bells rang merrily on Christmas morning. | He merrily ate the last cake, not knowing it was mine.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «merry» + «-ly»: y changes to i: merrily. Opposite: sadly, gloomily.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A bit of bad luck or an unlucky accident, often a small one. 2) (law, UK) «Death by misadventure» means a death caused by an accident during a risky but legal activity.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, a character's misadventures are funny or unlucky events, like Toad's misadventures with motor-cars and horses. The law sense is used in British courts.
examples from the lessons: The book tells of Toad's many misadventures. | After a few misadventures, we finally found the campsite. | Getting lost in the woods was quite a misadventure. | The holiday was full of small misadventures. | (law, UK) The coroner said the death was by misadventure. | Alice's misadventures in Wonderland kept going wrong.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mis- (badly) + adventure. Usually milder than «disaster».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) A wrong idea or a misunderstanding about something.
its sense in the lessons: A formal word; common in «under the misapprehension that...». In science lessons it is like a misconception: for example the misapprehension that heavy things fall faster. In stories it tells the reader a character believes something false.
examples from the lessons: He was under the misapprehension that the shop was open. | Many people have the misapprehension that bats are blind. | Let me correct a misapprehension: the Moon has no light of its own. | Toad was under the misapprehension that he was a great driver. | The letter cleared up the misapprehension. | Alice was under the misapprehension that she could still say her lessons.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say: mis-ap-ri-HEN-shun. Everyday words: misunderstanding, mistake.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A thick, dark, sticky syrup made when sugar is taken from sugar cane or sugar beet.
its sense in the lessons: Used in cooking (gingerbread, toffee, baked beans) and history (molasses was part of the slave trade across the Atlantic). In the USA «slow as molasses (in January)» means very slow. In the UK it is called black treacle. In Alice in Wonderland the Dormouse's three sisters live at the bottom of a treacle well.
examples from the lessons: Grandma uses molasses in her gingerbread. | Molasses is thick and dark brown. | You're as slow as molasses this morning! | In the UK, people often say black treacle instead of molasses. | Molasses was shipped from the Caribbean to make rum. | In 1919 a molasses flood swept through Boston.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «some molasses», not «a molasses». It ends in -es but is not plural: «Molasses is sticky.»

meaning for a pupil: 1) Very important, with big effects on the future.
its sense in the lessons: Used in history lessons for great events (the Moon landing was a momentous event) and in stories when a big decision is made.
examples from the lessons: The first Moon landing was a momentous day. | It was a momentous decision to move to Australia. | Winning the war was a momentous event. | The opening of the first railway was momentous. | Starting secondary school feels like a momentous step. | Mole's first trip on the river was momentous for him.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Not about «a moment» of time: momentous = very important. «Momentary» means lasting a moment. Noun: momentousness.

part of speech: noun (a mooring, moorings); verb form of «moor» (moor, moors, moored, mooring)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A place where a boat is tied up, often with a rope to a post or buoy. 2) Moorings are the ropes, chains and anchors that hold a boat in place. 3) «Mooring» is also the -ing form of «to moor», tying a boat up. 4) (figurative) Losing your moorings means losing the things that keep you steady.
its sense in the lessons: In river and sea stories, especially The Wind in the Willows, the Rat's boat is tied up at its mooring. On canals and harbours boats have moorings.
examples from the lessons: The Rat tied the boat to its mooring. | The boats bobbed at their moorings in the harbour. | They were mooring the boat for the night. | The storm tore the yacht from its moorings. | We found a mooring near the lock. | Without his friends, he felt he had lost his moorings.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «moor» (to tie up a boat). «A moor» is also a wild open hill land; different meaning.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Having a hidden spiritual meaning that is hard to explain, beyond the everyday world. 2) Strange, magical and full of wonder.
its sense in the lessons: In religion and stories: a mystical experience, a mystical light. In The Wind in the Willows the chapter «The Piper at the Gates of Dawn» is mystical: Rat and Mole meet the god Pan on an island and feel awe.
examples from the lessons: The forest at dawn felt mystical. | Rat and Mole had a mystical meeting on the island. | Some Christians tell of mystical experiences in prayer. | The old stone circle has a mystical feel. | The music sounded mystical and far away. | The story is full of mystical creatures.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Related: mystic, mystery, mysticism. Trap: mystical things are not proven by science; say «some people believe».

meaning for a pupil: 1) The telling of a story, especially by a narrator. 2) The spoken words that explain what is happening in a film, show or play.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons pupils learn first-person narration (I, we) and third-person narration (he, she, they). Documentaries have a narration.
examples from the lessons: The story is told in first-person narration. | Who does the narration in the nature film? | Her narration was clear and lively. | The play had narration between the scenes. | Alice in Wonderland uses third-person narration. | Record your narration over the slides.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Narrate = tell; narrator = the teller; narrative = the story.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Not taking proper care, so that something bad may happen. 2) (law) Failing to take the care that the law expects, which can lead to paying for harm.
its sense in the lessons: Used in safety, law and news: a driver's negligence caused a crash; negligence by a company. In stories it tells the reader someone was careless and to blame.
examples from the lessons: The accident was caused by negligence. | Leaving the gate open was negligence. | (law) The company was found guilty of negligence. | Toad's negligence wrecked another motor-car. | Medical negligence means a doctor did not take proper care. | Owners must avoid negligence with dangerous dogs.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: negligent. Do not confuse with «negligible» (too small to matter) or «neglect».

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a worried, slightly afraid way.
its sense in the lessons: Common in stories to show a character's feelings: they laugh, look, or speak nervously. It tells the reader they feel anxious.
examples from the lessons: She smiled nervously at her new class. | He waited nervously outside the head's office. | Alice nervously looked round for the White Rabbit. | The Mole nervously entered the Wild Wood. | The cat sniffed the dog nervously. | He laughed nervously before the test.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «nervous» + -ly. Not about the nerves of the body.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The state of being new or fresh. 2) The feeling that something is unfamiliar.
its sense in the lessons: Used in stories and everyday talk: the newness of a car, a school, a season. It tells the reader things are fresh or strange.
examples from the lessons: The newness of the school made her shy. | I love the newness of spring. | The newness of the bike soon wore off. | Mole was excited by the newness of the river. | The smell of newness filled the shop. | He liked the newness of his school shoes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: New + -ness. Uncountable.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (church) Another word for Christmas, used in songs and on cards. 2) A Christmas carol. 3) (a name) Noel is a name for boys, Noelle for girls.
its sense in the lessons: Used at Christmas: «The First Noel» is a famous carol. In The Wind in the Willows the field mice sing a carol at Mole's door. In French «Noël» means Christmas.
examples from the lessons: We sang «The First Noel» at church. | The card said «Noel» in gold letters. | (French) In France people say «Joyeux Noël». | My uncle Noel was born on Christmas Day. | The choir sang noels in the square. | Noel, Noel, born is the King of Israel.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From French «Noël». Often with a capital N. Do not confuse with «no».

meaning for a pupil: 1) The hard outer shell of a nut. 2) «In a nutshell» means in very few words, said briefly.
its sense in the lessons: The idiom is common in school: «in a nutshell, plants need light, water and air». It helps sum up.
examples from the lessons: The squirrel cracked the nutshell. | In a nutshell, we lost because we were slow. | The walnut's nutshell is hard. | In a nutshell, the mean is the total divided by how many numbers there are. | Explain your story in a nutshell. | The nutshells lay all over the floor.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: nutshells. «In a nutshell» is fixed.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A poem that praises or speaks to someone or something, often in a grand, serious style. 2) (playful) Anything made to celebrate something: «an ode to pizza».
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons pupils read odes such as Keats's «To Autumn» and «Ode to a Nightingale», and may write their own odes to the sea or to a pet. In music, «Ode to Joy» is the famous tune from Beethoven's Ninth Symphony, today the anthem of Europe. Phrase: «an ode to».
examples from the lessons: The poet wrote an ode to the sea. | We read Keats's «Ode to a Nightingale» in class. | Our class wrote funny odes to chocolate. | «Ode to Joy» is played at big European events. | The song is an ode to summer holidays. | Write an ode that praises your favourite place.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «An ode», not «a ode». Homophone: «owed» (past of owe: «I owed him £2»).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Complete and total, with no doubt: «an outright winner», «an outright lie». 2) (adverb) Openly and directly: «She told him outright». 3) (adverb) Completely, at once: «He was killed outright»; «They bought the house outright» (paid all of it at once).
its sense in the lessons: In sport an outright winner wins clearly; in money talk to buy something outright means to pay the full price at once, with no loan. In stories it tells the reader something is plain and total. Phrases: «laugh outright», «refuse outright», «win outright».
examples from the lessons: She was the outright winner of the race. | That's an outright lie! | He refused outright to eat the sprouts. | Alice laughed outright at the Gryphon. | (money) They paid for the car outright. | Ask her outright if she took it. | The team won the cup outright.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stress: OUT-right (adjective), out-RIGHT (adverb) is also heard. In maths «outright» can mean the full price paid in one go.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A rubber or plastic shoe worn over an ordinary shoe to keep it dry or clean.
its sense in the lessons: In older stories and cold places (Canada) people wore overshoes or galoshes in snow and mud. Today hospitals and building sites use plastic overshoes to keep floors clean.
examples from the lessons: He pulled on his overshoes before going out in the snow. | Visitors must wear blue plastic overshoes in the lab. | Grandad's overshoes stood by the door. | The overshoes kept her school shoes dry. | Galoshes are a kind of overshoe. | In the old days, people left their overshoes in the hall.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually plural: overshoes. Similar words: galoshes, wellingtons.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To sleep longer than you meant to, so that you wake up late.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday school life, oversleeping makes you late. It is common in stories and excuses.
examples from the lessons: I overslept and missed the bus. | Don't oversleep on the day of the trip! | He always oversleeps on Mondays. | Set two alarms so you won't oversleep. | The Dormouse seemed to oversleep all the time. | She overslept and had to run to school.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: overslept (not oversleeped). Do not confuse with «sleep over» (stay the night at a friend's house).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A show or procession where people dress up and act out scenes from history or stories. 2) A beauty contest (especially USA). 3) A grand, colourful display.
its sense in the lessons: At school a nativity pageant tells the Christmas story; towns hold historical pageants. In the USA beauty pageants are competitions.
examples from the lessons: Our school put on a pageant about the Romans. | The nativity pageant had shepherds and kings. | The town pageant marched through the streets. | She entered a beauty pageant. | The pageant of autumn colours was beautiful..
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say: PAJ-unt. Plural: pageants. Also «pageantry» (grand display).

part of speech: noun (a paling, palings); verb form of «pale» (pale, pales, paled, paling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A pointed wooden stake that is part of a fence. 2) A fence made of such stakes (palings). 3) «Paling» is also the -ing form of «to pale», to become pale or less bright.
its sense in the lessons: In older stories and The Wind in the Willows, fences of palings surround gardens and fields. In Australia, a «paling fence» is a common wooden garden fence.
examples from the lessons: The cat climbed over the palings. | (Australia) Dad fixed the paling fence. | Her face was paling with fear. | The sky was paling as dawn came. | The Mole squeezed through a gap in the palings. | A paling had fallen in the storm.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «pale» (a stake). Also the phrase «beyond the pale» (outside the limits of what is acceptable).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A sudden sharp pain or feeling. 2) A sudden strong feeling, like a pang of guilt or a pang of hunger.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, a pang of sadness or envy tells the reader a character's feelings changed suddenly. Common phrases: «hunger pangs», «a pang of guilt», «a pang of regret».
examples from the lessons: She felt a pang of guilt. | Hunger pangs woke him up. | Mole felt a pang when he smelled his old home. | A pang of envy hit her when she saw the bike. | He felt a pang of sadness at leaving. | The pangs of hunger made him grumpy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: pangs. Sudden, short feeling.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A plump brown bird that lives on the ground in fields and is sometimes hunted for food.
its sense in the lessons: Famous in the carol «The Twelve Days of Christmas»: «a partridge in a pear tree». In science, a game bird.
examples from the lessons: A partridge ran across the field. | «A partridge in a pear tree!» we sang. | The partridges hid in the long grass. | Partridges lay many eggs. | The farmer saw a flock of partridges. | Partridges are game birds.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: partridges. Not to be confused with pheasant.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a fatherly way: kind, caring or protective, like a father. 2) On the father's side of a family.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, a character may speak paternally to a younger one; Badger acts paternally to Toad and Mole. In family trees, «paternally» means through the father.
examples from the lessons: Badger spoke paternally to the young animals. | He smiled paternally at the children. | She is related to them paternally. | The coach put his arm paternally round the boy. | The old Rat looked paternally at the Mole. | Paternally, her family came from Ireland.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: maternally (mother's side). From «paternal».

part of speech: noun (a peal, peals); verb (peal, peals, pealed, pealing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The loud ringing sound of bells. 2) A loud sound, such as a peal of thunder or a peal of laughter. 3) To ring loudly.
its sense in the lessons: In church, bells peal for weddings, Sundays and Christmas; at Christmas in The Wind in the Willows the field mice come carol-singing to Mole's door. In stories, a peal of laughter tells the reader someone laughs joyfully.
examples from the lessons: The church bells pealed for the wedding. | A peal of thunder shook the house. | Peals of laughter came from the playground. | The bells rang out a joyful peal. | The doorbell pealed loudly. | The bells pealed at midnight on New Year's Eve.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Homophone: «peel» (the skin of fruit). Peal = sound; peel = skin.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a strange or odd way. 2) Especially or particularly, as in «peculiarly difficult». 3) Belonging only to one group or place, as in «peculiarly British».
its sense in the lessons: In stories it tells the reader something is not normal: in Wonderland everything behaves peculiarly, and Alice says things are getting «curiouser and curiouser». In everyday talk, «peculiarly British» means typical of Britain only.
examples from the lessons: The cat was behaving peculiarly before the storm. | It was a peculiarly hot day for April. | Alice thought the Duchess behaved most peculiarly. | Queuing politely is said to be peculiarly British. | He was peculiarly quiet at dinner. | The milk smelled peculiarly sour.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «peculiar» (strange; or belonging to one only). Trap: peculiar does not always mean bad, sometimes just «special to».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Feeling truly sorry for something wrong you did, and wanting to put it right. 2) (church) Sorrow for sin; Christians believe that God forgives those who turn back to him with true penitence.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, Toad shows penitence and promises to reform, but forgets it quickly. In church, Lent is a season of penitence, and confession is a sign of it. In ethics lessons, penitence is different from just being caught.
examples from the lessons: After his promise, Toad's penitence lasted only a day. | (church) Lent is a time of prayer and penitence. | Her penitence was real: she apologised and paid for the vase. | He hung his head in penitence. | (church) Christians believe God welcomes true penitence. | Tears of penitence ran down his face.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: penitent. Similar: repentance, remorse. Opposite: pride, defiance.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Having no money at all; very poor.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, a penniless character starts with nothing or loses everything: Toad escapes from prison penniless, without even his coat. In history lessons, many poor families were penniless in hard times. In maths problems, someone who spends all their money is left penniless: they have 0.
examples from the lessons: He was penniless after losing his job. | Toad escaped from prison penniless. | The penniless orphan slept under a bridge. | They arrived in the new country penniless but hopeful. | She spent all her money and was left penniless: £0. | The penniless inventor later became rich.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «penny» + «-less»: y changes to i. Opposite: rich, wealthy.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Tasting hot and spicy, full of pepper. 2) Quick to get angry; bad-tempered.
its sense in the lessons: In cooking, peppery food is spicy; rocket and watercress taste peppery. In Alice in Wonderland the Duchess's kitchen is full of pepper, so everyone sneezes, and the Duchess is peppery in temper too. In stories, «a peppery old colonel» shouts a lot.
examples from the lessons: The soup was very peppery. | In the Duchess's kitchen there was far too much pepper. | Rocket leaves have a peppery taste. | The peppery old man shouted at the boys. | This sauce is too peppery for the baby. | Watercress tastes slightly peppery.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «pepper» + «-y». Peppery temper = gets cross easily.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Great danger. 2) Something that is dangerous, a risk.
its sense in the lessons: In stories characters are «in peril» or face «perils»; Mole is in peril in the Wild Wood in the snow. In safety: «at your peril» means at your own risk, so be careful. Phrases: «in peril», «at your peril», «the perils of».
examples from the lessons: The ship was in peril in the storm. | Mole was in great peril in the Wild Wood. | Ignore the lifeguard's warning at your peril. | The book warns of the perils of the sea. | The firefighters saved the family from peril. | Toad learned the perils of fast cars.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: perilous. Plural: perils. Formal; everyday word: danger.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A small red spot on the skin, sometimes with yellow pus in the middle.
its sense in the lessons: In health lessons about growing up, teenagers often get pimples because their skin makes more oil. Washing gently and not squeezing them helps. «Goose pimples» are the little bumps on your skin when you are cold or scared.
examples from the lessons: A pimple appeared on his nose. | Teenagers often get pimples. | Don't squeeze your pimples or they get worse. | She had goose pimples in the cold wind. | Washing your face helps keep pimples away. | He worried about a pimple before the school photo.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: pimples. Similar: spot (UK), zit (slang). Goose pimples = goosebumps.

part of speech: noun (a pinecone, pinecones; also written pine cone)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The hard, woody, scaly case on a pine tree that holds the tree's seeds.
its sense in the lessons: In science, pinecones protect the seeds; in dry weather the scales open and seeds fall out, and in damp weather they close. That is why people use them to «forecast» the weather. In crafts, pinecones make bird feeders.
examples from the lessons: We collected pinecones in the forest. | The pinecone opened in the warm sun. | Squirrels pull seeds out of pinecones. | We made a bird feeder from a pinecone and peanut butter. | The pinecone closed when it got damp. | Pinecones lay all over the forest floor.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pine cone or pinecone both fine. Plural: pinecones. Fir and spruce trees have cones too.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a way that makes people feel pity, very sadly.
its sense in the lessons: In stories it tells the reader a character is in great distress: Alice cries in the pool of tears; Toad weeps in his dungeon; a puppy whines piteously.
examples from the lessons: The puppy whined piteously at the door. | Toad wept piteously in his dungeon. | The kitten mewed piteously in the rain. | The lost lamb bleated piteously. | The baby cried piteously all night. | He begged piteously for help.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «piteous». Similar: pitifully.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a way that makes people feel pity. 2) Disappointingly, very: «pitifully small», «pitifully few».
its sense in the lessons: In stories it shows misery; in everyday talk «pitifully small» means far too small. In maths problems, «pitifully few» means very few.
examples from the lessons: The stray dog was pitifully thin. | The kitten cried pitifully. | Only a pitifully small crowd came. | He sobbed pitifully when his toy broke. | The house was pitifully cold. | There were pitifully few apples left.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «pitiful». Two l's: pitifully.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a calm, peaceful way, without getting excited or upset.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, animals graze placidly or a river flows placidly. It tells the reader all is calm.
examples from the lessons: The cows grazed placidly in the meadow. | The river flowed placidly past the Rat's house. | She smiled placidly at the fuss. | The cat sat placidly in the window. | The old horse stood placidly by the gate. | The baby slept placidly through the noise.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «placid». Opposite: wildly, angrily.

part of speech: verb (plead, pleads, pleaded (UK) or pled (US), pleading)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To ask for something in a strong, emotional way; to beg. 2) (law) To say in court whether you are guilty or not guilty. 3) To give something as an excuse: «He pleaded a headache».
its sense in the lessons: In stories characters plead for mercy; Toad pleads with Badger. In law, defendants «plead guilty» or «plead not guilty».
examples from the lessons: He pleaded with his mum for a puppy. | (law) The man pleaded not guilty. | She pleaded for more time to finish. | Toad pleaded for mercy. | He pleaded a headache to miss PE. | «Please let me go!» she pleaded.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: pleaded (UK) or pled (US). Noun: plea.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (old, formal) A drink, especially an alcoholic drink. 2) (old) The act of drinking.
its sense in the lessons: An old word in older books, often used for comedy: long potations at an inn. Today say «drink».
examples from the lessons: After his long potations, the squire fell asleep. | The innkeeper served potations to the travellers. | The old book describes great potations at the feast. | Potations of ale were common in the Middle Ages. | The men grew noisy after their potations. | Avoid strong potations, said the doctor.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Old word; not «potato».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Like powder: fine, dry and soft. 2) Covered with powder.
its sense in the lessons: In science, flour and chalk are powdery solids. Skiers love powdery snow.
examples from the lessons: The snow was soft and powdery. | Flour is a powdery solid. | The moth's wings were powdery. | Chalk leaves a powdery mark. | The powdery sand blew in the wind. | Skiers love powdery snow.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «powder» + «-y».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Without the power or strength to do something. 2) Unable to help or act.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, a character feels powerless; in history, powerless people had no vote; in science, a device is powerless without electricity.
examples from the lessons: The people felt powerless against the king. | The radio was powerless without batteries. | He was powerless to stop the flood. | Toad was powerless in the dungeon. | She felt powerless to help. | Without votes, women were powerless.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «power» + «-less».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) The slow turning of the axis of a spinning object, such as a spinning top or the Earth, so that the axis traces a circle. 2) (science) The slow change in the direction of Earth's axis, taking about 26,000 years for one circle.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, a spinning top wobbles in a circle: that is precession. Earth's axis also precesses slowly, so the North Star changes over thousands of years.
examples from the lessons: A spinning top shows precession when it wobbles. | Because of precession, Polaris will not always be the North Star. | Precession of the Earth's axis takes about 26,000 years. | The gyroscope's precession was slow. | Scientists measure precession with telescopes. | Precession changes which stars we see at the pole.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Not «procession» (a line of people walking). Verb: precess.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (USA) A district of a city that has its own police station; also the police station itself. 2) (UK) A shopping area where cars are not allowed (a shopping precinct). 3) The area around a building, often enclosed, like a cathedral precinct. 4) (USA) A voting district.
its sense in the lessons: In American police stories, detectives work at «the 9th precinct». In Britain, families shop in the precinct.
examples from the lessons: The officer works at the 12th precinct. | We met in the shopping precinct. | The cathedral precincts were quiet. | (USA) Voters went to their precinct to vote. | The precinct was closed to cars. | No running in the school precincts.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: precincts. Meaning differs by country.

meaning for a pupil: 1) As you would guess or expect; probably.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and everyday talk, it shows something is likely but not certain. In science, it marks a guess.
examples from the lessons: Presumably the bus will be late in this snow. | The Rabbit was presumably late again. | Presumably you've done your homework? | The door was open, presumably left by the cat. | The tracks were presumably made by a fox. | Presumably they will come after lunch.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «presume». Not certain: «probably».

part of speech: verb (prod, prods, prodded, prodding); noun (a prod, prods)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To poke someone or something with a finger, a stick or another pointed thing. 2) To push or remind someone to do something they are slow to do. 3) (noun) A poke, or a reminder.
its sense in the lessons: In stories characters prod each other to wake up or pay attention; in everyday life parents prod children to do homework; a doctor prods your tummy to check where it hurts. Phrases: «give someone a prod», «prod at».
examples from the lessons: He prodded the fire with a stick. | Stop prodding me with your pencil! | She gave her brother a prod to wake him up. | Mum had to prod me to tidy my room. | The doctor prodded my tummy gently. | The Hatter and the March Hare kept trying to wake the sleepy Dormouse. | The farmer prodded the cows towards the gate.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: prodded, with double d. Similar: poke, nudge.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To hold something out to someone so that they can take it; to offer. 2) (formal) To offer advice, help or an explanation.
its sense in the lessons: A formal word in older stories and polite writing: to proffer a hand, a gift, a plate, an apology. Everyday word: offer.
examples from the lessons: He proffered his hand in friendship. | She proffered a cup of tea to the visitor. | The waiter proffered the menu. | The Rat proffered a sandwich to the hungry Mole. | He proffered his advice, but nobody listened. | The boy proffered an apology for the broken window.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: proffered (one r before -ed: proffered). Say: PROF-er.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A formal or official statement, often one that announces a decision. 2) A statement made in a grand way, as if it must be obeyed.
its sense in the lessons: In history and news, kings, judges and governments make pronouncements. In stories, a grand pronouncement can be funny: the Queen of Hearts's «Off with her head!» is a famous pronouncement.
examples from the lessons: The king made a pronouncement from the palace balcony. | The Queen of Hearts' pronouncement was: «Off with her head!» | The head teacher's pronouncement about mobile phones surprised us. | The judge's pronouncement was final. | Toad made grand pronouncements about his own cleverness. | The pronouncement was printed in all the newspapers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «pronounce» (to say officially, or to say a word's sounds). Spelling trap: pronouncement keeps the «ou», but pronunciation drops it.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) To put forward an idea, theory or question for people to think about.
its sense in the lessons: A formal word used in history of science and exams: scientists propound theories, philosophers propound ideas, people propound riddles.
examples from the lessons: Darwin propounded the theory of evolution by natural selection. | The professor propounded a new idea about dinosaurs. | She propounded a plan to the school council. | The Hatter propounded a riddle that had no answer. | He propounded a theory about the stars. | The question was propounded at the meeting.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; everyday words: put forward, suggest, propose.

part of speech: noun (prosecution, uncountable; the prosecution; a prosecution)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (law) Taking someone to court and charging them with a crime. 2) (law) «The prosecution» is the lawyer or team trying to prove that the accused person is guilty. 3) (formal) Carrying on with something, as in «the prosecution of a war».
its sense in the lessons: In court the prosecution tries to prove guilt, and the defence argues for the accused. In Alice in Wonderland the trial of the Knave of Hearts, accused of stealing the tarts, is a funny, unfair trial. In The Wind in the Willows Toad is prosecuted and sent to prison for twenty years.
examples from the lessons: The prosecution showed the evidence to the jury. | He faced prosecution for shoplifting. | The prosecution called its first witness. | Toad was prosecuted for stealing a motor-car. | The case was dropped, so there was no prosecution. | The defence argued against the prosecution.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: prosecute; the lawyer: prosecutor. Do not confuse with «persecution» (cruel treatment of people because of who they are).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person or animal that keeps someone or something safe from harm. 2) A thing that protects, such as a screen protector, gum shield or shin protectors. 3) (history) Lord Protector was the title of Oliver Cromwell, who ruled England, Scotland and Ireland in the 1650s.
its sense in the lessons: In stories the protector guards the weak: Badger looks after the younger animals of the wood. In sports and safety, protectors stop injuries. In history lessons, Cromwell as Lord Protector.
examples from the lessons: The dog is a loyal protector of the family. | Badger was a protector to the younger animals. | Wear knee protectors when you skate. | Put a protector on your phone screen. | Oliver Cromwell became Lord Protector in 1653. | The lioness is a fierce protector of her cubs.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Ends in -or, not -er. Verb: protect; noun: protection.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Where something comes from; its origin. 2) The record of where an object such as a painting or ancient vase has been and who has owned it.
its sense in the lessons: In history and museums, provenance helps prove an object is real and was not stolen. In food, shops label the provenance of meat and fruit.
examples from the lessons: The museum checked the painting's provenance. | The provenance of the old vase is unknown. | We buy food of local provenance. | Experts traced the coin's provenance to Roman Britain. | Without a provenance, the statue might be stolen. | The label shows the provenance of the apples.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say: PROV-en-unss. Formal; everyday word: origin.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Soft, wet and squashy, like pulp (the soft inside of fruit). 2) (of stories) Cheap, exciting and not very well written, like old «pulp» magazines.
its sense in the lessons: In cooking, pulpy fruit is soft and mushy; orange juice «with bits» is pulpy. In science, wood is made into pulp to make paper.
examples from the lessons: The peaches were soft and pulpy. | I like pulpy orange juice. | The paper turned pulpy in the rain. | Mash the bananas until pulpy. | The tomatoes were overripe and pulpy. | He reads pulpy adventure stories.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «pulp» + «-y». Comparative: pulpier.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Complaining in a whining, annoyed voice.
its sense in the lessons: A literary word in stories for a moaning character or voice: a querulous old man, a querulous child who is tired. It tells the reader the character complains a lot.
examples from the lessons: The querulous old man complained about the noise. | Her voice became querulous when she was tired. | The child grew querulous on the long car journey. | «Are we nearly there?» came a querulous voice. | He made a querulous remark about the food. | The querulous customer wanted his money back.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say: KWER-yoo-lus. Similar: whiny, grumbling. Not «quarrelsome» (always arguing), though close.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (old, Bible) Clothing, especially fine clothes.
its sense in the lessons: An old word in the Bible and old poems and stories. In the King James Bible: «Take no thought for your life... nor yet for your body, what ye shall put on. Is not the life more than meat, and the body than raiment?» Today say «clothes».
examples from the lessons: The king was dressed in fine raiment. | (Bible) His raiment was white as snow. | The angels shone in bright raiment. | Rich raiment hung in the queen's wardrobe. | (Bible) Is not the body more than raiment? | They wore raiment of silk and gold.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Old word; everyday word: clothes. Uncountable.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A storm with heavy rain, often with strong wind.
its sense in the lessons: In weather and geography lessons, rainstorms can cause floods. Safety: stay indoors, keep away from rivers and flooded roads.
examples from the lessons: The rainstorm flooded the street. | We sheltered from the rainstorm under a bridge. | A rainstorm hit the town at night. | The rainstorm stopped the football match. | Never walk through floodwater after a rainstorm. | After the rainstorm there was a rainbow.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: rainstorms. Similar: downpour, cloudburst.

meaning for a pupil: 1) So interested in something that you notice nothing else, as in «rapt attention». 2) Filled with deep joy or wonder, carried away by a feeling.
its sense in the lessons: In stories it tells the reader a character is spellbound: children listen with rapt attention to a story. In The Wind in the Willows, in «The Piper at the Gates of Dawn», the Rat stands rapt, listening to the far-off music of Pan's pipes, and Mole is rapt with awe. At school, teachers hope for rapt attention. Phrases: «rapt attention», «listen rapt», «rapt in thought».
examples from the lessons: The children listened with rapt attention to the story. | The Rat stood rapt, hearing the music of the pipes. | She watched the fireworks with a rapt face. | He was rapt in thought and did not hear the bell. | The audience sat rapt as the magician worked. | Mole gazed in rapt wonder at the Friend on the island. | The baby was rapt, watching the fish in the tank.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Homophones: «wrapped» (covered in paper) and «rapped» (knocked, or did rap music) sound the same. Not «rapped attention». Related noun: rapture.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A feeling of great joy and delight. 2) «In raptures» or «go into raptures» means very excited and pleased about something. 3) (church) For some Christians, especially in the USA, «the Rapture» is a belief that Christ will take believers up to heaven at the end of time; many other Christians do not hold this belief.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, a character's rapture shows overwhelming happiness: Toad goes into raptures over motor-cars, crying «Poop-poop!»; Mole is in raptures at his first day on the river. Poems speak of rapture at beauty.
examples from the lessons: Toad went into raptures over the motor-car. | The Mole gazed at the river in rapture. | She was in raptures about her new puppy. | The crowd cheered with rapture when the band came on. | Rapture filled her heart as she saw the sea. | He listened to the music in silent rapture. | (church) Some Christians believe in the Rapture; others do not.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: rapturous («rapturous applause»). Do not confuse with «rupture» (a burst or break).

part of speech: noun (a realisation, realisations; also uncountable); US spelling realization
meaning for a pupil: 1) The moment when you suddenly understand or become aware of something. 2) (formal) Making a plan or dream come true: «the realisation of her dream».
its sense in the lessons: In stories, a character's realisation is a turning point: Toad's sudden realisation that he must change; Alice's realisation that the cards are «nothing but a pack of cards». In maths, the realisation that a pattern repeats helps solve a problem. Phrases: «come to the realisation», «a sudden realisation», «the realisation dawned».
examples from the lessons: The realisation that she had left her bag on the bus hit her. | Slowly the realisation dawned that we were lost. | Alice came to the realisation that they were only a pack of cards. | The trip was the realisation of a lifelong dream. | His realisation that 9 × 9 is 81 helped him finish the puzzle. | With a sudden realisation, Mole knew it was his old home.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK: realisation (or realization); USA: realization. Verb: realise / realize. The z spelling is also accepted in the UK (Oxford spelling).

part of speech: verb, past and past participle of «recognize» (recognize, recognizes, recognized, recognizing); adjective (recognized); UK spelling usually recognised
meaning for a pupil: 1) Knew who someone was or what something was because you had seen or heard it before. 2) Accepted or admitted that something is true: «He recognized his mistake». 3) (adjective) Officially accepted, as in «a recognized qualification» or «a recognized country». 4) Showed thanks for or praised someone's work: «She was recognized for her bravery».
its sense in the lessons: In stories, characters recognize old friends or voices; in history, countries are recognized by others; at school, pupils are recognized for good work.
examples from the lessons: I recognized my teacher in the supermarket. | Mole recognized the smell of his old home at once. | She recognized her mistake and said sorry. | The firefighter was recognized for his courage. | It is a recognized school subject. | Nobody recognized Toad in the washerwoman's clothes. | He recognized the song after two notes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: US spelling -ize; UK usually -ise: recognised. Say: REK-ug-nized. Do not drop the g: not «reconized».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Unfortunate and something you wish had not happened; deserving regret.
its sense in the lessons: A slightly formal word used in news, by leaders and in school letters: «a regrettable incident». In stories it softens bad news or makes a character sound pompous.
examples from the lessons: It is regrettable that the trip was cancelled. | There was a regrettable accident in the playground. | The head called the fight «a regrettable incident». | It's regrettable that so few people came. | Losing the map was a regrettable mistake. | Badger said Toad's behaviour was most regrettable.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling: double t: regrettable. Do not confuse with «regretful» (feeling sorry yourself). Adverb: regrettably.

part of speech: noun (a rein, reins); verb (rein, reins, reined, reining; usually «rein in»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Reins are the long straps fixed to a horse's bit, used by the rider or driver to guide it. 2) (figurative) Control: «take the reins» (take charge), «give free rein» (let someone do as they like), «keep a tight rein on» (control closely). 3) To rein in means to slow a horse down, or to control or limit something. 4) Reins (UK) are also straps put on a toddler to keep them safe.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, a horse's reins; Toad takes the reins of the caravan and the horse. In everyday life, a new captain «takes the reins». Safety: toddler reins near roads.
examples from the lessons: She held the reins tightly as the pony trotted. | Toad seized the reins and the horse bolted. | He reined in his horse at the gate. | The new head took the reins of the school. | The teacher gave us free rein to design the poster. | Mum kept a tight rein on our pocket money. | The toddler wore reins on the busy street.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Homophones: «rain» (water from clouds) and «reign» (to rule as a king). Rein = straps, rain = weather, reign = rule. «Free rein», not «free reign».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Feeling sorry for something wrong you have done and wanting to change. 2) (church) Sorry for sins; Christians believe God forgives the repentant.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, Toad is repentant for a while, and then is boastful again. In the Bible, the repentant thief on the cross.
examples from the lessons: The boy looked repentant after breaking the window. | Toad was repentant, but not for long. | She wrote a repentant letter. | (Bible) Jesus forgave the repentant thief. | The repentant dog lowered its ears. | He was truly repentant and paid for the damage.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: repent; noun: repentance. Opposite: unrepentant.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a way that shows you are disappointed with someone or blame them.
its sense in the lessons: In stories characters look or speak reproachfully: the Rat speaks reproachfully to Toad. It shows quiet disapproval.
examples from the lessons: Mum looked at me reproachfully. | «You promised!» she said reproachfully. | The dog looked reproachfully at its empty bowl. | The Rat spoke reproachfully to Toad. | He glanced reproachfully at his little brother. | The teacher shook her head reproachfully.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «reproach» (blame). Not angry, but disappointed.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) What people generally think of someone or something; reputation.
its sense in the lessons: Phrases: «of good repute», «of ill repute» (with a bad name), «by repute».
examples from the lessons: He was a doctor of good repute. | The inn was a place of ill repute. | By repute, the Wild Wood was dangerous. | A family of high repute lived in the hall. | She knew him only by repute. | The shop has a repute for fair prices.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; everyday word: reputation. Adjective: reputed (said to be).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Firmly decided about what to do and not giving up, even when it is hard. 2) Showing determination, as in «a resolute look».
its sense in the lessons: In stories a resolute hero keeps going; in history, resolute leaders stood firm in hard times. Badger is resolute that Toad must change his ways. At school, a resolute effort means you keep trying. Similar: determined, firm, steadfast.
examples from the lessons: She was resolute: she would finish the race. | The resolute explorers kept walking through the snow. | Badger was resolute that Toad must give up motor-cars. | He gave a resolute shake of the head. | With resolute effort, he learned his times tables. | The villagers made a resolute stand against the plan to cut the trees. | Her face was calm and resolute.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say: REZ-uh-loot. Adverb: resolutely; noun: resolve or resolution (a New Year's resolution is a firm plan). Opposite: irresolute, hesitant.
