meaning for a pupil: 1) Good at finding quick, clever ways to deal with problems, using whatever is around.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, a resourceful character escapes or survives by being clever: Robinson Crusoe builds what he needs; in the Just So Stories the clever creatures find tricks. At school and in Scouts and Guides, being resourceful is praised. In safety, a resourceful person keeps calm and thinks.
examples from the lessons: The resourceful girl made a raft from barrels. | Be resourceful: use what you have in the box. | Robinson Crusoe was resourceful on his island. | The resourceful Mole found the door scraper in the snow. | Without a ruler, the resourceful boy measured with a book. | Our resourceful teacher made a game from bottle tops.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: resourcefulness. From «resource» (something useful you can draw on).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A statement saying that something you said or printed before was wrong, taking it back. 2) (science) Pulling something back in or out of sight, like a cat pulling in its claws or a plane pulling up its wheels.
its sense in the lessons: In news, a newspaper prints a retraction when it got a story wrong. In science lessons, cats have retractable claws, and retraction keeps them sharp. In science, a paper with mistakes may get a retraction, so honest checking matters.
examples from the lessons: The newspaper printed a retraction and an apology. | He demanded a retraction of the unfair story. | After the retraction, everyone knew the rumour was false. | Retraction of a cat's claws keeps them sharp. | Retraction of the plane's wheels happens just after take-off. | The scientists issued a retraction when they found a mistake.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: retract (take back, pull in). Adjective: retractable. Do not confuse with «subtraction».

part of speech: verb (revisit, revisits, revisited, revisiting); noun (a revisit, rare)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To go back to a place you have been to before. 2) To look at or think about a subject again, often to change or improve it.
its sense in the lessons: At school, teachers revisit topics such as fractions so that pupils remember them. In stories, a character revisits an old home: Mole goes back to Mole End at Christmas. In writing, you revisit a draft to improve it.
examples from the lessons: We revisited the beach where we played as babies. | Let's revisit fractions before the test. | Mole revisited his old home on a winter night. | She revisited her story and made the ending better. | The team will revisit the plan next week. | Every summer we revisit Grandma's farm.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past: revisited (one t). Re- = again + visit.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Being full of something good: rich colour, sound, taste or detail. 2) Being very full of goodness for growing, as in the richness of the soil. 3) (rare) Being wealthy; usually we say «wealth».
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography, the richness of soil helps crops grow, and «species richness» means how many kinds of living things live in a place. In art and music, richness of colour or sound. In cooking, the richness of a cake means it is full of butter and sugar.
examples from the lessons: The richness of the chocolate cake made me feel full. | The richness of the soil helps the farmer's crops. | The rainforest has a great richness of wildlife. | We admired the richness of the colours in the painting. | The richness of his voice filled the hall. | Shakespeare added to the richness of English.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «rich» + «-ness». Uncountable. For money, say «wealth».

part of speech: noun (a rick, ricks); verb (rick, ricks, ricked, ricking); name (Rick)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A big stack of hay, straw or corn built in a field or farmyard, often with a pointed thatched top to keep the rain out. 2) (UK, informal) To rick your neck or back means to twist or strain it a little, so it hurts. 3) (a name) Rick, a short form of Richard, Eric or Frederick.
its sense in the lessons: In old country stories and history, ricks stood in the farmyards before modern bales: field mice and harvest mice lived in ricks. In The Wind in the Willows the countryside of fields and farms has hay and corn stacked after harvest. In everyday British talk you «rick your neck» sleeping badly.
examples from the lessons: The farmer built a tall rick of hay. | Mice made nests in the corn rick. | The rick was thatched to keep out the rain. | I ricked my neck sleeping on the train. | Rick is my uncle's name. | Long ago, ricks stood in every farmyard after harvest.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Also called a hayrick or haystack. Do not confuse with «wreck» or «brick». Past: ricked.

part of speech: noun (rigging, uncountable); verb, -ing form of «rig» (rig, rigs, rigged, rigging)
meaning for a pupil: 1) All the ropes, wires and chains that hold up a ship's masts and work the sails. 2) Cheating to fix the result of something in advance, as in «vote rigging» or «match rigging». 3) Putting up equipment, like rigging lights for a show.
its sense in the lessons: In sea stories and history, sailors climb the rigging to set the sails; the Sea Rat in The Wind in the Willows tells of ships and voyages. In citizenship lessons, rigging an election is cheating and is against the law.
examples from the lessons: The sailors climbed the rigging to the top of the mast. | The wind howled through the rigging. | (law) Vote rigging means cheating in an election. | They accused the referee of rigging the match. | The crew were rigging the lights for the school play. | Old ships had miles of rigging.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «rig». Uncountable for the ropes. The second sense is always bad: rigging = cheating.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a very careful, thorough and exact way, checking every detail. 2) Strictly, without making exceptions.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons, a fair test must be done rigorously: same conditions, repeated measurements. In maths, proving something rigorously means every step follows. In everyday life, rules may be rigorously followed.
examples from the lessons: New medicines are rigorously tested before people use them. | Check your working rigorously, line by line. | The rules of the competition were rigorously enforced. | Scientists rigorously recorded every result. | She trained rigorously for the swimming gala. | The kitchen is rigorously cleaned every night.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «rigorous» (thorough, strict). Noun: rigour (UK) or rigor (US). Say: RIG-er-us-lee.

part of speech: noun (a roach, roaches; for the fish the plural is often roach)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (USA, Canada, informal) A cockroach: a flat brown insect that runs fast and lives in dirty kitchens and warm places. 2) A small silver freshwater fish with reddish eyes and fins, common in rivers, lakes and canals in Britain and Europe. 3) (slang) The end of a cannabis cigarette; drug slang, not a word for school.
its sense in the lessons: In North America «roaches» is the everyday word for cockroaches, pests that spread germs, so keeping food covered and kitchens clean is a health lesson. In Britain and Ireland a roach is a fish that anglers catch in rivers and canals, the kind of fish that swims in the river in The Wind in the Willows. Cockroaches are also a science fact: they are very tough insects with six legs.
examples from the lessons: (USA) We saw a roach run under the fridge. | Keep food in boxes so roaches don't get in. | Grandad caught a roach in the canal. | The roach has a silver body and red eyes. | Roach and perch swam in the clear river. | Cockroaches, or roaches, have six legs like all insects. | The exterminator came to get rid of the roaches.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Short for cockroach in North America; in the UK say cockroach for the insect. Plural for the insect: roaches; for the fish: roach or roaches. The myth that cockroaches would be the only survivors of anything is exaggerated.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A dishonest person who cheats or tricks people. 2) (playful) A naughty but likeable person, often a child: «You little rogue!» 3) (adjective) Behaving differently from the rest and causing trouble or danger, as in «a rogue wave», «a rogue elephant», «a rogue trader».
its sense in the lessons: In stories rogues are tricksters and villains; Toad is called a rogue and a ruffian when he steals the motor-car. In geography and the sea, a rogue wave is a sudden giant wave. In everyday talk grandparents call a cheeky child «a lovable rogue». Phrases: «rogue wave», «rogue trader», «go rogue» (stop following orders), «rogues' gallery».
examples from the lessons: The rogue sold fake watches at the market. | Toad was called a rogue and a ruffian by the court. | «You little rogue, you've eaten my biscuit!» laughed Nan. | A rogue wave knocked the sailors off their feet. | The rogue elephant was dangerous to the villages. | In the game, one robot goes rogue. | He was a charming rogue who always owed money.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say: ROHG; the -ue is silent. Plural: rogues. Adjective form for people: roguish (cheeky). Not «rouge» (red make-up).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A rough, violent or lawless person, especially a man or a boy who causes trouble.
its sense in the lessons: An old-fashioned word in stories and history: highwaymen, pirates and street gangs are ruffians. In The Wind in the Willows the stoats and weasels who take over Toad Hall are called ruffians, and Toad himself is called a ruffian by the court. Today grandparents use it half-jokingly for noisy boys.
examples from the lessons: A gang of ruffians stopped the coach on the road. | The weasels and stoats were a band of ruffians. | «You young ruffians, get off my lawn!» shouted the old man. | The magistrate called Toad a hardened ruffian. | Ruffians attacked travellers in the Middle Ages. | The pirates were cruel ruffians.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: ruffians. Adjective: ruffianly (rare). Do not confuse with «ruffle» (to mess up hair or feathers).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Very cruel and violent behaviour. 2) Fierce wildness, as in the savagery of a storm or a wild animal attack.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons about wars, savagery means great cruelty. In nature films, the savagery of a predator's attack. In stories it tells the reader something is shocking and brutal. Note: in old books «savage» was used as an insulting word for people of other cultures; today we know that was wrong and unkind.
examples from the lessons: The savagery of the battle shocked everyone. | The storm hit the coast with savagery. | The lion attacked with sudden savagery. | People were horrified by the savagery of the crime. | The book shows the savagery of war. | The weasels fought with savagery, but Badger's band won.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «savage» + «-ry». Uncountable. Old books calling whole peoples «savages» show a wrong, racist idea that is not accepted today.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A book used for lessons at school, such as a textbook or exercise book.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and older stories: children carry their schoolbooks in a satchel. In stories from long ago, schoolbooks were few and precious. Alice tries to remember what she learned from her lessons and schoolbooks, but it all comes out wrong.
examples from the lessons: She packed her schoolbooks into her bag. | His schoolbooks were full of doodles. | Grandad still has his old schoolbooks from 1960. | Don't forget your schoolbooks on Monday. | In the past, children shared schoolbooks. | The facts in old schoolbooks are sometimes out of date.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word: schoolbook (also «school book»). Plural: schoolbooks. Similar: textbook (for learning a subject), exercise book (for writing in).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A room where children are taught, especially in an old school or a big house.
its sense in the lessons: In older stories and history, rich families had a schoolroom at home where a governess taught the children; village schools had one schoolroom for all ages. Today we say «classroom». Alice thinks of her lessons and the schoolroom when she tries to say her tables.
examples from the lessons: The old schoolroom had a big black stove. | In Victorian times, all ages learned in one schoolroom. | The governess taught the children in the schoolroom upstairs. | We visited a Victorian schoolroom at the museum. | Slates and chalk lay on the schoolroom desks. | The schoolroom smelled of ink and wood.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: schoolrooms. Today the usual word is classroom.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Showing that you think someone or something is worthless, silly or not good enough. 2) A scornful look, laugh or voice is one that mocks or looks down on someone.
its sense in the lessons: A feelings and character word in stories: it tells the reader a character feels superior and does not respect someone. Writers pair it with a look, laugh, voice or glance: «a scornful laugh», «scornful of». In Alice in Wonderland many creatures are scornful of Alice, like the Caterpillar who asks «You! Who are you?» in a scornful tone; in The Wind in the Willows the weasels are scornful of the animals of the river bank until Badger returns. In everyday life being scornful hurts people and is a kind of rudeness.
examples from the lessons: She gave a scornful laugh when he said he could beat her at chess. | «You call that a sandcastle?» said Tom in a scornful voice. | The Caterpillar looked at Alice in a scornful way. | Don't be scornful of other people's ideas; listen first. | The older girls were scornful of the little ones' game. | He was scornful of anyone who supported the other football team. | Her scornful glance made him feel very small.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective; the noun is «scorn» and the adverb «scornfully». «Scornful of something» means looking down on it. Do not mix up with «scorn» used as a verb: «She scorned the offer». Opposite: respectful, admiring.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who rows a boat using two oars, one in each hand, called sculls. 2) A small light rowing boat made for sculling, often used in races.
its sense in the lessons: A sport and river word. In The Wind in the Willows the Water Rat sculls his little boat on the river, and Mole longs to learn; Rat is a skilled sculler, and Mole's first try at sculling ends with him tipping the boat over. In real life scullers race on rivers like the Thames and in the Olympics (single sculls, double sculls). Safety: anyone in a rowing boat should wear a life jacket and never stand up suddenly.
examples from the lessons: The sculler pulled hard on both oars and the boat shot forward. | Ratty was a fine sculler and never splashed. | Mole wanted to be a sculler too, but he grabbed the oars too soon. | My aunt is a sculler in a rowing club. | The single sculler won the gold medal. | Early in the morning the scullers were already out on the lake. | Two scullers glided past under the bridge.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun, plural «scullers». From the verb «scull» (to row with two oars, or with one oar over the back of the boat). Do not confuse with «skull» (the bone of the head) — same sound, different spelling and meaning. A rower who uses one oar with both hands is just called a rower, not a sculler.

part of speech: noun (a selvedge, selvedges); also spelt selvage
meaning for a pupil: 1) The edge of a piece of woven cloth, made so that it does not fray or unravel. 2) More widely, an edge or border strip of something, like the edge of a piece of land.
its sense in the lessons: A sewing and craft word. When you buy cloth from a roll, the two long sides have selvedges, firmer and sometimes with printed letters or little holes. In sewing lessons you cut patterns along the grain, parallel to the selvedge. In old books it can mean a narrow border of land or the edge of a thing.
examples from the lessons: The selvedge of the cloth had the maker's name printed on it. | Pin the pattern so the arrow runs along the selvedge. | The selvedge stops the cloth from fraying. | Grandma cut off the selvedge before sewing the quilt. | The denim had a neat red stripe on its selvedge. | Weavers make a tight selvedge on each side of the loom.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun. British spelling «selvedge», American spelling usually «selvage»; both say SEL-vij. Only the long sides of a roll of fabric have a selvedge; the cut ends do not.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a worn-out, old and untidy way: shabbily dressed means wearing old, faded, worn clothes. 2) In an unfair, mean or unkind way: to treat someone shabbily is to treat them badly.
its sense in the lessons: A describing word in stories: it shows a poor or careless look («shabbily dressed», «a shabbily furnished room»), or a mean way of behaving («they treated him shabbily»). In The Wind in the Willows Toad, escaping from prison, is dressed in the washerwoman's shabby clothes. In everyday talk «treat someone shabbily» means be unfair to someone who deserved better.
examples from the lessons: The old man was shabbily dressed but very polite. | They lived in a shabbily furnished flat above the shop. | The team treated their loyal goalkeeper shabbily. | I think you behaved rather shabbily towards your friend. | The shabbily painted gate creaked in the wind. | Toad, shabbily dressed as a washerwoman, hurried to the station.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from the adjective «shabby» (shabbier, shabbiest); noun «shabbiness». Spelling: shabby → shabbily (y changes to i). The second meaning is about behaviour, not clothes.

part of speech: noun (on shipboard); adjective (shipboard life, a shipboard party)
meaning for a pupil: 1) On shipboard means on or aboard a ship. 2) As an adjective, shipboard describes things that happen or are used on a ship: shipboard life, a shipboard romance, shipboard computers.
its sense in the lessons: A travel and sea word. Stories of voyages talk about shipboard life: sleeping in bunks or hammocks, meals in the galley, fire and lifeboat drills. In The Wind in the Willows the Sea Rat tells of his shipboard life and voyages to faraway ports. «On shipboard» is a little old-fashioned; today people say «on board» or «aboard».
examples from the lessons: Shipboard life was hard for the young sailors. | They held a shipboard concert on the last night of the voyage. | Everyone on shipboard must know where the lifeboats are. | The Sea Rat told stories of shipboard adventures. | Shipboard radar helps the captain see in fog. | The passengers grew bored with shipboard food.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly used before a noun as an adjective. «On shipboard» is older; prefer «on board» or «aboard» in your own writing. Not to be confused with «shipyard» (where ships are built).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Very bright, big or colourful so that people notice it, sometimes too much. 2) Done to make people admire you rather than for a real purpose: a showy trick, a showy way of playing.
its sense in the lessons: A describing word that can praise («showy flowers» in a garden) or criticise («a showy car», «too showy»). In stories it tells the reader that a person likes to be looked at — Toad in The Wind in the Willows loves showy things: a gaudy caravan, fast motor cars and loud clothes. In gardening, showy flowers have large bright petals that attract bees.
examples from the lessons: Sunflowers are showy flowers. | His showy red car was parked outside the school. | She did a showy cartwheel just to impress everyone. | The footballer's showy trick lost the ball. | The peacock spread its showy tail. | Toad loved showy clothes and loud horns. | I prefer a simple cake to a showy one.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative «showier», superlative «showiest»; adverb «showily»; noun «showiness». Often slightly negative: it hints at showing off. Related: «show-off» (a person who shows off).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Being silly: behaving in a foolish, funny or not serious way. 2) A silly act or silly talk.
its sense in the lessons: A behaviour word. Teachers say «That's enough silliness» to settle a class. In Alice in Wonderland the Mad Hatter's tea party and the Mock Turtle's lessons are full of silliness that is also clever nonsense. In stories silliness can be playful and happy or annoying and unsafe.
examples from the lessons: That's enough silliness — please sit down. | The party was full of giggles and silliness. | I laughed at the silliness of the joke. | Alice was tired of the silliness at the tea party. | Their silliness on the climbing frame was dangerous. | A bit of silliness after a hard test is fine.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable noun: say «a lot of silliness», not «silliness-es». From the adjective «silly». Silliness is not always bad — it can mean harmless fun.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Being simple and easy to understand or do. 2) Being plain, without decoration or extras. 3) An honest, plain way of living or thinking.
its sense in the lessons: A word for ideas, designs and ways of life. In maths and science, simplicity is valued: a simple rule that explains a lot. In art and design, simplicity means plain lines and few colours. In stories it can describe a quiet country life, like Mole's simple home in The Wind in the Willows. Phrase: «for simplicity» or «for the sake of simplicity» means to make things easier.
examples from the lessons: The simplicity of the game made it great for little children. | I love the simplicity of a plain white room. | For simplicity, round the numbers to the nearest ten. | The beauty of the answer was its simplicity. | They enjoyed the simplicity of life on the farm. | The instructions were written with great simplicity.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable. From «simple». Spelling: -icity at the end (simplicity, not simpleness). «For simplicity» in maths: you may round or leave out details to make the problem easier, but the answer is then approximate.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A wooden or plastic bottle-shaped piece that players try to knock down with a ball. 2) Skittles is the game played with them, an older cousin of ten-pin bowling. 3) (UK, informal) «Bowl over like skittles» or «knocked down like skittles» means many things falling quickly.
its sense in the lessons: A game word. Children play skittles in the garden or at a school fair; it is good for counting how many fell and how many stand. In The Wind in the Willows the animals and people of the old world play skittles in inns. Phrase: «Life is not all beer and skittles» (UK, old) means life is not all fun.
examples from the lessons: We set up nine skittles at the end of the hall. | Sam knocked down six skittles with one ball. | Let's play skittles in the garden! | The bowling ball scattered the skittles. | The wind knocked the bins over like skittles. | Life isn't all beer and skittles, said Grandad.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun; the game «skittles» takes a singular verb: «Skittles is fun.» In maths: if there are 9 skittles and 6 fall, 9 − 6 = 3 are left standing. «Skittles» is also a brand of sweets; that is a name.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To make something less tight, or to become less tight: slacken a rope. 2) To become slower, weaker or less busy: the pace slackened, the rain slackened.
its sense in the lessons: An action word in boating, sailing and climbing (slacken the rope, slacken the sail) and in describing change (the wind slackened, the traffic slackened). In The Wind in the Willows, when Rat stops rowing, the boat's pace slackens and they drift. Safety: never slacken a safety rope someone is relying on.
examples from the lessons: Slacken the rope a little so the knot comes undone. | The rain slackened and we went out to play. | Near the finish line, the runner did not slacken his pace. | The sail slackened when the wind dropped. | Traffic slackens after rush hour. | Don't slacken your effort before the test.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: slackened, slackening. From «slack» (loose). Opposite: tighten, quicken. «Slack off» is informal for working less hard.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A kind of comedy with funny falls, crashes, chases, custard pies and silly fights where nobody is really hurt. 2) As an adjective: slapstick humour, a slapstick film.
its sense in the lessons: A word for humour in films, plays and pantomimes. Clowns, Charlie Chaplin, Laurel and Hardy and many cartoons use slapstick. Toad's crashes with motor cars and his flight from the barge-woman in The Wind in the Willows read like slapstick. The name comes from a real stick of two flat pieces of wood that made a loud slap on stage without hurting.
examples from the lessons: The pantomime was full of slapstick. | The clown slipped on a banana skin — classic slapstick. | My little brother laughs at slapstick cartoons. | Slapstick comedy doesn't need words. | The film had lots of slapstick chases. | Don't copy slapstick stunts at home; real falls hurt.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable. Safety note: in slapstick the falls are planned by trained actors; in real life such falls cause injuries.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a clever, secret way, often to trick someone. 2) In a playful, knowing way, as if sharing a secret joke: she smiled slyly.
its sense in the lessons: A describing word in stories that tells the reader a character is cunning or teasing. Foxes and weasels act slyly in animal stories; in The Wind in the Willows the weasels and stoats slyly take over Toad Hall. In the Just So Stories animals often trick each other slyly. It can be friendly («winked slyly») or not («slyly stole»).
examples from the lessons: The fox looked slyly at the hens. | She slyly took the last biscuit when no one was looking. | He grinned slyly, knowing the answer. | The weasels slyly crept into Toad Hall. | Grandpa slyly slipped me a coin. | The cat slyly watched the bird from under the bush.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from «sly» (slyer/slier, slyest/sliest). Spelling: «slyly» is now usual. Noun: «slyness». «On the sly» means secretly.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who walks in their sleep; a sleepwalker.
its sense in the lessons: A science and health word, also used in stories and older books. Sleepwalking is common in children and usually harmless; most grow out of it. Safety: gently guide a sleepwalker back to bed, keep doors and stairs safe. Writers sometimes say someone moved «like a somnambulist» — slowly, not really aware. The word comes from Latin somnus (sleep) and ambulare (to walk).
examples from the lessons: The somnambulist walked down the stairs with her eyes open. | My cousin is a somnambulist and once woke up in the kitchen. | Doctors say you should gently lead a somnambulist back to bed. | He moved through the morning like a somnambulist. | Somnambulists don't remember walking in their sleep. | The story was about a somnambulist who walked on the roof.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun. Everyday word: sleepwalker. Myth: it is not dangerous to wake a sleepwalker, though they may be confused; the danger is in falling or tripping. Related: somnambulism (sleepwalking).

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a calm, gentle way that makes someone feel less upset, worried or in pain.
its sense in the lessons: A feelings word in stories and real life: parents speak soothingly to a crying baby, a nurse soothingly tells a child it will be alright. In The Wind in the Willows Rat talks soothingly to Mole when he is frightened or homesick. It also describes sounds and touches: water lapped soothingly, music played soothingly.
examples from the lessons: Mum spoke soothingly to the crying baby. | «There, there,» said Ratty soothingly. | The river murmured soothingly in the dark. | The vet stroked the frightened dog soothingly. | The cream felt soothingly cool on my sunburn. | She hummed soothingly until he fell asleep.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from «soothing», from the verb «soothe» (soothe, soothed). Spelling: sooth-ing-ly, keep the -th-. Opposite: harshly, roughly.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a very sad way, full of sorrow or grief.
its sense in the lessons: A feelings word in stories, more serious than «sadly». In Alice in Wonderland the Mock Turtle sighs and sings sorrowfully about his schooldays. In The Wind in the Willows Mole looks sorrowfully at his little home when he finds it again. It tells the reader a character feels deep sadness, often about a loss.
examples from the lessons: The Mock Turtle sighed sorrowfully. | «My kitten is gone,» she said sorrowfully. | He looked sorrowfully at the broken vase. | The dog waited sorrowfully at the door. | They sorrowfully said goodbye at the airport. | The old man shook his head sorrowfully.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from «sorrowful», from the noun «sorrow». A bit formal or literary; in speech people say «sadly».

meaning for a pupil: 1) So interested or amazed by something that you cannot look away or think of anything else. 2) In fairy tales: held under a magic spell.
its sense in the lessons: A feelings word for strong attention: an audience is spellbound by a great story or show. In The Wind in the Willows, in «The Piper at the Gates of Dawn», Rat and Mole are spellbound by the music they hear on the river. Phrase: «hold someone spellbound».
examples from the lessons: The children sat spellbound as the storyteller spoke. | We watched the fireworks spellbound. | The magician held the audience spellbound. | Rat and Mole stood spellbound by the strange music. | In the tale, the princess was spellbound for a hundred years. | I was spellbound by the whale swimming beside the boat.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective, usually after the verb: «they were spellbound». It comes from «spell» + «bound» (tied). Same in all forms.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Very well; excellently. 2) In a grand, rich and beautiful way: splendidly dressed.
its sense in the lessons: A praise word. Teachers say «You did splendidly!» Toad in The Wind in the Willows describes himself and his plans as splendid; in old books people are splendidly dressed for a ball. It is a little old-fashioned and very British in feeling.
examples from the lessons: You did splendidly in the race! | The hall was splendidly decorated for the party. | The plan worked splendidly. | The king was splendidly dressed in gold. | Everything is going splendidly, thank you. | The roses grew splendidly this summer.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from «splendid»; noun «splendour» (UK) or «splendor» (US). Common in British speech; Americans often say «great» or «really well».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A short time when you do a lot of something you enjoy, without holding back: a shopping spree, a spending spree. 2) A wild time of fun. 3) (serious, news) a spree of crimes means many crimes one after another.
its sense in the lessons: A word for doing too much at once. In everyday life: a shopping spree, a chocolate spree. In The Wind in the Willows Toad goes on a spree of buying motor cars and crashing them. In money lessons a spending spree can empty your savings fast.
examples from the lessons: Mum went on a shopping spree in the sales. | He spent all his pocket money in one spree. | Toad's motor-car spree ended in court. | The kids had a cake-baking spree on Saturday. | After the spending spree, there was no money left for the bills. | The team went on a scoring spree in the second half.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun. Usually «go on a spree». In money problems «spree» means spending lots quickly — check how much is left.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a strict, serious and unsmiling way, often when someone has done wrong.
its sense in the lessons: A voice and face word in stories and school: a teacher looks sternly over her glasses; a parent speaks sternly. In The Wind in the Willows Badger speaks sternly to Toad about his motor cars; in Alice in Wonderland the Queen of Hearts and the Duchess speak sternly. It tells the reader there is trouble.
examples from the lessons: «Sit down,» said the teacher sternly. | Badger looked sternly at Toad. | Dad sternly reminded us to look both ways. | The judge spoke sternly to the thief. | She frowned sternly at the muddy boots. | The sign sternly warned: No Swimming.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from «stern» (sterner, sternest). Do not confuse with the noun «stern», the back part of a boat (Rat sat in the stern).

part of speech: adjective (stifled); past form of the verb stifle (stifle, stifles, stifled, stifling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Held back so it is not heard or seen: a stifled laugh, a stifled yawn, a stifled cry. 2) Unable to breathe well because the air is hot or stuffy. 3) Stopped from growing or being free: stifled ideas.
its sense in the lessons: A feelings and sound word in stories: a stifled giggle in class tells the reader someone is trying not to laugh. In Alice in Wonderland the guinea pigs in court are «suppressed» — stuffed into a bag — for cheering. In science and health, stifling heat makes breathing hard. Safety: never cover someone's nose and mouth.
examples from the lessons: She gave a stifled giggle during the assembly. | I heard a stifled cry from the cupboard. | He stifled a yawn as the speech went on. | We felt stifled in the hot, crowded bus. | A stifled sob came from the next room. | Too many rules stifled their ideas.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «Stifled» is the past form and an adjective; «stifling» means very hot and stuffy (a stifling day). Regular verb.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A clever plan or trick to get what you want or to fool an enemy.
its sense in the lessons: A word for plans in stories, games and history. In The Wind in the Willows Badger's stratagem is to enter Toad Hall by the secret tunnel while the weasels feast; Toad uses many stratagems to escape prison. The Trojan Horse was a famous stratagem in Greek legend. In chess and sport, a stratagem is a smart plan.
examples from the lessons: The secret tunnel was Badger's stratagem. | The Trojan Horse was a famous stratagem. | Toad's stratagem was to dress as a washerwoman. | The fox used a stratagem to get the cheese. | Her chess stratagem surprised her older brother. | The general thought of a stratagem to cross the river.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun, a bit formal. Spelling: strat-a-gem (not -egy). Related but different: «strategy» (a long plan); a stratagem is one clever trick.

part of speech: verb (strew, strews, strewed, strewn or strewed, strewing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To scatter things untidily over a surface. 2) To be lying scattered over a place: leaves strewed the path.
its sense in the lessons: A describing verb for messy or scattered scenes: toys strewn across the floor, petals strewn at a wedding, rubbish strewn on the beach. In The Wind in the Willows the weasels leave Toad Hall strewn with mess after their feasting. Common phrase: «strewn with».
examples from the lessons: Toys were strewn all over the bedroom floor. | The flower girl strewed petals along the aisle. | Leaves strewed the path after the storm. | The beach was strewn with seaweed and shells. | Don't strew your clothes on the stairs. | The kitchen was strewn with crumbs and plates.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past participle usually «strewn» («was strewn with»). Similar: scatter. Old form: «strow».

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a way that refuses to change your mind or do what others want. 2) Of things: in a way that is hard to move, change or get rid of: a stain stubbornly stays.
its sense in the lessons: A character word in stories: Toad stubbornly refuses to give up motor cars; donkeys and mules are said to be stubborn. In science and everyday life, a stubbornly stuck lid or a stubbornly high temperature will not change easily.
examples from the lessons: He stubbornly refused to eat his peas. | The donkey stubbornly sat down in the road. | Toad stubbornly promised nothing. | The stain stubbornly stayed on my shirt. | She stubbornly kept trying until the puzzle was done. | The jar lid was stubbornly stuck.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from «stubborn»; noun «stubbornness» (double n). Can be good (refusing to give up) or bad (refusing to listen).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Able to bend and move easily: a supple body, supple joints. 2) Soft and bending without cracking: supple leather, a supple branch.
its sense in the lessons: A body and materials word. In PE, stretching keeps muscles supple; gymnasts and dancers are very supple. In science, materials like rubber and willow twigs are supple. In The Wind in the Willows, the supple willow branches bend over the river.
examples from the lessons: Gymnasts are very supple. | Stretching every day keeps your body supple. | Willow twigs are supple enough to weave baskets. | The old leather boots were still soft and supple. | Cats are supple and can squeeze through gaps. | Oil keeps the saddle supple.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective; comparative «suppler», superlative «supplest»; noun «suppleness». Similar: flexible, bendy. Opposite: stiff, rigid.

part of speech: adjective (swaggering); form of the verb swagger (swagger, swaggers, swaggered, swaggering)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Walking or behaving in a proud, show-off way, as if you are very important. 2) Too confident and boastful.
its sense in the lessons: A character word: it tells the reader someone is proud and showing off. Toad in The Wind in the Willows is the classic swaggering character — swaggering in his motor-car goggles and boasting songs. Pirates and bullies are often described as swaggering in stories.
examples from the lessons: Toad came swaggering down the drive in his goggles. | The swaggering pirate laughed at the crew. | He walked in with a swaggering grin. | The team's swaggering captain lost the match. | I don't like his swaggering way of talking. | The cockerel strutted about, swaggering.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From the verb «swagger» (regular). Noun «swagger»: «He walked with a swagger.» Similar: strutting, boastful. Do not confuse with «staggering» (walking unsteadily, or amazing).

meaning for a pupil: 1) From that place; from there. 2) From that time; after that. 3) For that reason; therefore.
its sense in the lessons: An old word met in classic books, the Bible and old maps or directions: «They went to London, and thence to Dover.» In modern talk people say «from there». In maths proofs very old texts write «thence» for «so».
examples from the lessons: They sailed to France and thence to Spain. | Go to the old oak and thence turn left. | He moved to Leeds and thence to Scotland. | From the Wild Wood the path led thence to Badger's house. | The river runs down to the town and thence to the sea. | We stayed a week in Paris, thence by train to Rome.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Old-fashioned and formal; do not use it in everyday writing. Related old words: hence (from here), whence (from where). «From thence» is a common old phrase though strictly «thence» already means «from there».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Near that place. 2) Near that number, amount or time: «ten o'clock or thereabouts» means about ten.
its sense in the lessons: A word for guesses and estimates. In maths it signals an approximate answer: «a hundred or thereabouts». In everyday talk and in stories: «He lives in Oxford or thereabouts.»
examples from the lessons: The party starts at six or thereabouts. | There were fifty people or thereabouts. | He lives in Dublin or somewhere thereabouts. | It costs £10 or thereabouts. | The treasure is buried by the old tree or thereabouts. | She's eight or thereabouts.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Almost always after «or»: «or thereabouts». In maths it means the number is approximate, not exact.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Used to introduce the third point in a list of reasons or steps, after «firstly» and «secondly».
its sense in the lessons: A writing and speaking word for organising ideas. In persuasive writing and speeches pupils use «firstly, secondly, thirdly, finally». In The Wind in the Willows and other classics characters like Badger or Toad list points in a speech this way.
examples from the lessons: Firstly, wash your hands; secondly, get the bowl; thirdly, add the flour. | Thirdly, recycling saves energy. | Thirdly, and most importantly, be kind. | Toad said firstly he was clever, secondly he was rich, and thirdly he was handsome. | Thirdly, check your answer. | Thirdly, we need more trees in the playground.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb. Some people prefer «first, second, third» without -ly; both are correct. Spelling: third + ly.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To beat or shake cut wheat, oats or other grain to separate the seeds from the stalks and husks. 2) To move about wildly, thrashing arms or legs (old or less common; usually «thrash»).
its sense in the lessons: A farming and history word. Long ago farmers threshed grain by beating it with a flail on the barn floor; later steam threshing machines came round to farms; today combine harvesters cut and thresh at once. In The Wind in the Willows the countryside around has fields and barns where grain is threshed. Related: «threshold» — the old floor-board at a doorway.
examples from the lessons: The farmers threshed the wheat in the barn. | A combine harvester cuts and threshes the grain. | Long ago, people threshed oats with a flail. | The threshing machine was noisy and dusty. | After threshing, the straw was stacked. | We saw how grain was threshed at the farm museum.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. Related noun «thresher». Do not confuse with «thrash» (to hit hard or to move wildly), though in old books they overlap.

meaning for a pupil: 1) News or information, especially important news. 2) In Christmas songs and the Bible: «good tidings» means good news.
its sense in the lessons: An old-fashioned and literary word. You meet it in Christmas carols («Good tidings we bring to you and your kin», «O tidings of comfort and joy»), in the Bible (the angel brings «good tidings of great joy» to the shepherds), and in old stories where messengers bring tidings. In The Wind in the Willows the animals pass tidings along the river bank.
examples from the lessons: The messenger brought tidings from the king. | Good tidings we bring to you and your kin! | The angel brought good tidings to the shepherds. | We waited anxiously for tidings of the lost ship. | Glad tidings! The baby has arrived. | The Rat brought tidings of Toad's latest crash.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural noun with plural verb: «The tidings were good.» Old-fashioned; today say «news». Not related to sea tides.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A clock or watch; any instrument for measuring time.
its sense in the lessons: A slightly formal or old word for clocks and watches. In Alice in Wonderland the White Rabbit takes a watch out of his waistcoat pocket, and the Mad Hatter's watch tells the day of the month, not the hour. In science, sundials, hourglasses and water clocks are early timepieces. Phrase: in shops and adverts «a fine timepiece».
examples from the lessons: Grandad's gold timepiece still ticks. | The White Rabbit looked at his timepiece and ran. | A sundial is an ancient timepiece. | The museum shows timepieces from long ago. | The Hatter's timepiece told the day, not the hour. | Ships needed a very accurate timepiece to find their way.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun, plural «timepieces». Everyday words: clock, watch.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Very hot and dry: a torrid summer, torrid desert. 2) Full of strong, difficult feelings or troubles: a torrid time means a very hard time.
its sense in the lessons: A weather and geography word: the old name «torrid zone» meant the hot lands between the tropics. In news and sport: «The team had a torrid afternoon» means they had a terrible time. Writers also use it for passionate love stories, a grown-up sense.
examples from the lessons: The explorers crossed the torrid desert. | It was a torrid summer with no rain. | Old maps call the hot lands near the equator the torrid zone. | The goalkeeper had a torrid afternoon. | The camels plodded on in the torrid heat. | We had a torrid time moving house.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective, a little formal. In sport and news (UK) «a torrid time» = a very bad time. Do not confuse with «horrid» or «torrent» (a rushing stream).

part of speech: noun (a tot, tots); verb (tot up, tots up, totted up, totting up)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A very small child, a toddler. 2) A small amount of an alcoholic drink, like a tot of rum (old, sailors). 3) (UK) tot up: to add up numbers to find a total.
its sense in the lessons: An everyday word: «tiny tots» classes for toddlers, «a play area for tots». In sea stories sailors got a daily tot of rum. In maths at home: «Let's tot up the shopping» means add it up. In The Wind in the Willows field-mice carollers are small and young, like tots.
examples from the lessons: The tiny tots played in the sandpit. | The swimming class is for tots under three. | Let's tot up how much we spent. | Sailors once got a tot of rum every day. | She totted up the scores at the end. | The park has a safe area for tots.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun «tots». Verb «tot up» is British and informal: totted, totting (double t). In maths «tot up» = add up to find the total.

part of speech: adjective (tousled); from the verb tousle (tousle, tousles, tousled, tousling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Untidy and messy, especially of hair: tousled hair looks as if you have just woken up.
its sense in the lessons: A describing word for appearance in stories: a child with tousled hair just out of bed, a boy tousled by the wind. Grown-ups sometimes tousle a child's hair as a kind gesture.
examples from the lessons: He came down to breakfast with tousled hair. | The wind left her hair tousled. | Dad tousled my hair and smiled. | A tousled puppy jumped out of the box. | She looked tousled after the long trip. | His tousled curls stuck out everywhere.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly used about hair. Say TOW-zuld: the first part sounds like «cow». Similar: messy, ruffled, untidy.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Very great in size, amount or strength; huge: a tremendous noise. 2) (informal) Very good; excellent: a tremendous goal, a tremendous time.
its sense in the lessons: A strong describing word in stories and speech. Toad in The Wind in the Willows loves big words and calls his own adventures tremendous. In science, volcanoes release tremendous energy; in sport, a tremendous effort. In maths it never gives an exact number — it only says «very big».
examples from the lessons: There was a tremendous crash of thunder. | You've made tremendous progress in reading! | The elephant was a tremendous size. | We had a tremendous time at the beach. | A volcano gives out tremendous heat. | The crowd gave a tremendous cheer. | It was a tremendous goal from the halfway line.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective; adverb «tremendously». Spelling: tremend-ous (not -ious). It is a feeling word, not a number word.

part of speech: verb (trespass, trespasses, trespassed, trespassing); noun (a trespass, trespasses)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To go onto someone's land or into a building without permission. 2) (Bible, church, old) A wrong or sin; to trespass means to do wrong. 3) (formal) To trespass on someone's time or kindness means to take more than you should.
its sense in the lessons: A law, safety and Bible word. Signs say «No Trespassing» or «Trespassers Will Be Prosecuted». Railway lines, farms and building sites are dangerous; trespassing there can kill. In The Wind in the Willows the weasels and stoats trespass in Toad Hall and take it over. In the Lord's Prayer, said in many churches, Christians ask «forgive us our trespasses, as we forgive those who trespass against us».
examples from the lessons: Don't trespass on the railway line — it's very dangerous. | The sign said: No trespassing. | The farmer caught boys trespassing in his field. | The weasels trespassed in Toad Hall. | «Forgive us our trespasses,» the congregation prayed. | I don't want to trespass on your kindness. | Trespassers will be prosecuted.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb; noun «trespasser». In the Lord's Prayer some churches say «debts» or «sins» instead of «trespasses». «Trespass on» = enter without permission; «trespass against» (old) = do wrong to.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Something small and unimportant. 2) Being unimportant or not serious.
its sense in the lessons: A word for unimportant things. Grown-ups say «Let's not argue over trivialities.» In Alice in Wonderland the King and Queen fuss over trivialities like who stole the tarts while making no sense. In quizzes, «trivia» are small facts — a related word.
examples from the lessons: Don't waste time on trivialities. | They argued over a triviality. | The meeting got stuck on trivialities. | She was surprised by the triviality of his complaint. | The court spent hours on trivialities like the Hatter's hat. | Forget the trivialities and look at the big picture.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable when it means a small thing (trivialities), uncountable for the quality. From «trivial». Related: «trivia» (bits of fun knowledge).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Causing trouble, worry or difficulty; annoying or hard to deal with.
its sense in the lessons: A describing word for people, animals, problems and things: a troublesome cough, a troublesome knee, a troublesome neighbour. In The Wind in the Willows Toad is a troublesome friend whose crazes worry Badger, Rat and Mole. In maths, a troublesome question is a hard one.
examples from the lessons: That troublesome cough kept me awake. | The troublesome puppy chewed my shoes. | Toad was a troublesome friend. | The last sum was the most troublesome. | Weeds are troublesome in the garden. | The troublesome wind kept blowing my kite away.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective formed with -some (like «tiresome», «awesome»). Similar: annoying, difficult.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who plays the trumpet. 2) A soldier or herald who sounds signals on a trumpet. 3) Trumpeter is the name of some animals with trumpet-like calls: the trumpeter swan.
its sense in the lessons: A music, history and nature word. In bands and orchestras trumpeters play bright, loud parts. In history, trumpeters sounded signals in battles and announced kings. In Alice in Wonderland the White Rabbit acts as herald and blows a trumpet in the court before reading the accusation. In science, the trumpeter swan of North America is the largest waterfowl there.
examples from the lessons: The trumpeter played a fanfare at the start. | The White Rabbit blew three blasts on his trumpet, like a herald's trumpeter. | My sister is a trumpeter in the school band. | The trumpeter sounded the call to battle. | We saw trumpeter swans on the lake in Canada. | The trumpeters stood on the castle wall.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun, plural «trumpeters». From «trumpet» + -er.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Rude and impolite; not showing good manners.
its sense in the lessons: A manners word, a bit formal and old-fashioned. In Alice in Wonderland Alice often thinks the creatures are uncivil — the Caterpillar, the Hatter, the Duchess — while Alice tells the Hatter that making personal remarks is very rude, and the March Hare says it was not very civil of her to sit down without being invited. In everyday life being uncivil means not being polite.
examples from the lessons: It was uncivil of him not to say thank you. | Alice thought the Caterpillar very uncivil. | Please don't be uncivil to our guests. | The shopkeeper gave an uncivil reply. | «That's very uncivil,» said the Duchess. | Being uncivil online is still being rude.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective; opposite «civil» (polite). Noun «incivility» (note in-, not un-). Formal; in speech people say «rude».

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a way that does not feel comfortable for your body: sitting uncomfortably. 2) In an embarrassed or worried way: laughing uncomfortably. 3) Too much, so it worries you: uncomfortably hot, uncomfortably close.
its sense in the lessons: A body and feelings word. In stories it tells the reader a character feels awkward or uneasy: Alice, grown huge, sits uncomfortably squashed in the White Rabbit's house. In safety and science: uncomfortably hot weather can cause heatstroke — drink water and find shade.
examples from the lessons: Alice sat uncomfortably with her arm out of the window. | He shifted uncomfortably in his seat. | It was uncomfortably hot in the classroom. | The dog came uncomfortably close to the edge. | She laughed uncomfortably at the joke. | The shoes pinched uncomfortably.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from «uncomfortable». Spelling: un-com-fort-ab-ly (drop the e of -able, add -ly).

meaning for a pupil: 1) The state of being unconscious: not awake and not able to notice anything, for example after a bad fall or fainting.
its sense in the lessons: A health and first-aid word. If someone falls into unconsciousness, call 999 (UK, Ireland 112/999), 911 (USA, Canada) or 000 (Australia), 111 (New Zealand), check breathing and put them in the recovery position if you have been taught. In stories a character slips into unconsciousness after a blow or a fall.
examples from the lessons: The blow to his head caused unconsciousness. | First aiders check for breathing in cases of unconsciousness. | She slipped into unconsciousness after the fall. | Fainting is a short period of unconsciousness. | The doctor asked how long the unconsciousness lasted. | He drifted out of unconsciousness and opened his eyes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable noun. From «unconscious». Spelling: double s in «-ness» after «-ous». Sleep is not unconsciousness in the medical sense: a sleeping person can be woken easily.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Rude, rough and without good manners; behaving in a way that is not polite or refined.
its sense in the lessons: A manners word. In stories, a rough character who burps loudly, talks with his mouth full or shouts is called uncouth. In The Wind in the Willows the weasels and stoats are uncouth guests in Toad Hall. It is a judgement about behaviour, not about how rich someone is.
examples from the lessons: It is uncouth to talk with your mouth full. | The uncouth guests shouted and threw food. | His uncouth jokes upset the visitors. | The weasels' uncouth songs echoed round Toad Hall. | Don't be uncouth — say please. | She was shocked by his uncouth manners.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective. Say un-KOOTH. The opposite «couth» exists but is rare and jokey.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Making you look silly or embarrassed; not calm, proper or serious.
its sense in the lessons: A feelings word in stories: falling in a puddle or crawling through a hedge is undignified. Toad in The Wind in the Willows hates undignified moments, like being thrown into the canal by the barge-woman. Alice feels undignified when she grows and shrinks.
examples from the lessons: Slipping on the ice was very undignified. | Toad was thrown into the water in a most undignified way. | The cat made an undignified leap and missed. | It's undignified to sulk in public. | The judge's wig fell off in an undignified moment. | He climbed out in an undignified scramble.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective; opposite «dignified»; noun «dignity». Spelling: un-dig-ni-fied.

part of speech: verb (undress, undresses, undressed, undressing); noun (in a state of undress)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To take off your clothes, or to take someone's clothes off (like a baby or doll). 2) (noun, formal or jokey) «in a state of undress» means not fully dressed.
its sense in the lessons: An everyday word for bedtime, bath time and PE: «Undress for your bath», «Get undressed for bed». Privacy and safety: your body is private; you get changed in private spaces, and no one should make you undress or take photos — tell a trusted adult if this happens.
examples from the lessons: Undress and get into your pyjamas. | Mum undressed the baby for the bath. | We undressed quickly in the changing room. | The doctor asked him to undress to the waist. | He got undressed and jumped into bed. | She answered the door in a state of undress.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. «Get undressed» is more common in speech than «undress». Opposite: dress, get dressed.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Without a label: an unlabelled jar or bottle. 2) Not named or marked, like an unlabelled diagram.
its sense in the lessons: A science, safety and maths word. In science lessons, always label diagrams and axes; an unlabelled graph loses marks. Safety: never drink or taste anything from an unlabelled bottle — it could be poison or bleach. In Alice in Wonderland Alice drinks from a bottle only after checking it is not marked «poison» — it was labelled «DRINK ME».
examples from the lessons: Never drink from an unlabelled bottle. | The jars in the cupboard were unlabelled. | You lose marks for an unlabelled graph. | Label the unlabelled parts of the flower. | An unlabelled box arrived at the door. | Alice checked the bottle was not marked poison.
note for the reader of a maths problem: British spelling «unlabelled» (double l); American «unlabeled». In maths and science, unlabelled axes make a graph impossible to read.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Not thinking about something or not paying attention to it; forgetting it.
its sense in the lessons: A formal or literary word. In stories: «unmindful of the danger, he ran on» means he did not think about the danger. Toad is often unmindful of his friends' warnings. Usually followed by «of».
examples from the lessons: Unmindful of the rain, the children kept playing. | He ran on, unmindful of the danger. | Toad was unmindful of Badger's warnings. | She was unmindful of the time and missed the bus. | They chatted, unmindful of the people waiting. | Never be unmindful of road safety.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective, usually «unmindful of». Formal; in speech say «not thinking about» or «forgetting».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Accepted by everyone as true or right, with no doubt. 2) Not asked questions; not checked.
its sense in the lessons: A word for facts, rules and leaders. «Her talent was unquestioned» means everybody agrees. In science, ideas should not stay unquestioned — scientists test them. In Alice in Wonderland the Queen of Hearts' orders go unquestioned until Alice says «Nonsense!».
examples from the lessons: His honesty was unquestioned. | She was the unquestioned champion. | The Queen's orders went unquestioned. | In science, no idea should be unquestioned. | The rules went unquestioned for years. | The witness left unquestioned.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective, from «question». Related: «unquestionable» (cannot be doubted), «unquestionably» (certainly).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Thinking about other people's needs and happy to share or help, not only thinking of yourself.
its sense in the lessons: A character and values word. In ethics lessons and stories, unselfish acts are praised: sharing lunch, letting a younger child go first. In The Wind in the Willows Rat is unselfish when he takes Mole home though he wants to get back. In team games an unselfish player passes the ball.
examples from the lessons: It was unselfish of her to share her sweets. | An unselfish player passes to a teammate in a better place. | Ratty was unselfish and turned back for Mole. | He made an unselfish choice to help his sister. | Volunteers do unselfish work. | Be unselfish and let others have a turn.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective; adverb «unselfishly»; noun «unselfishness». Opposite: selfish. Similar: generous, kind.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Of a place: still natural and beautiful, not damaged by building, pollution or crowds. 2) Of a person: still nice and natural, not made selfish by money or fame.
its sense in the lessons: A geography and nature word: an unspoilt beach, an unspoilt valley, unspoilt countryside. In The Wind in the Willows the River Bank is unspoilt countryside; the Wild Wood is wild. In ethics and geography lessons people discuss how to keep places unspoilt.
examples from the lessons: We found an unspoilt beach with no rubbish at all. | The valley is unspoilt by roads or houses. | Despite being famous, she was unspoilt and kind. | Let's keep the countryside unspoilt. | The River Bank was quiet and unspoilt. | The island's forests are still unspoilt.
note for the reader of a maths problem: British prefers «unspoilt», American «unspoiled»; both are correct. Opposite: spoilt/spoiled, damaged.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Not known about or not guessed: an unsuspected talent. 2) Not thought to be guilty: he went unsuspected.
its sense in the lessons: A word in stories and mysteries: an unsuspected secret passage, an unsuspected danger, an unsuspected thief. In The Wind in the Willows the secret tunnel into Toad Hall is unsuspected by the weasels. In science, an unsuspected result can lead to a discovery.
examples from the lessons: She had an unsuspected talent for singing. | An unsuspected danger lay beneath the ice. | The secret tunnel was unsuspected by the weasels. | The real thief went unsuspected for weeks. | The test showed an unsuspected problem. | They found an unsuspected room behind the shelves.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective. Related: «unsuspecting» (not expecting anything, trusting): an unsuspecting victim — do not mix them up.

part of speech: verb form of vanish (vanish, vanishes, vanished, vanishing); adjective (a vanishing act, vanishing species); noun (the vanishing of …)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Disappearing suddenly or completely, so you cannot see it any more. 2) Becoming fewer or smaller until almost gone: vanishing forests. 3) In art and maths: the vanishing point is where parallel lines in a perspective drawing seem to meet.
its sense in the lessons: A story, science and art word. In Alice in Wonderland the Cheshire Cat keeps vanishing, sometimes slowly, beginning with the tail and ending with the grin, which stays after the rest has gone. Magicians do vanishing tricks. In science and geography: vanishing habitats and species are in danger. In art lessons you draw roads and railway lines meeting at a vanishing point.
examples from the lessons: The Cheshire Cat began vanishing, starting with its tail. | The magician did a vanishing trick with a coin. | The sun was vanishing behind the hills. | Rainforests are vanishing because of logging. | Draw the road narrowing to a vanishing point. | Every time I buy biscuits they keep vanishing! | The ship was vanishing over the horizon.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From the regular verb «vanish». Similar: disappearing. «Do a vanishing act» (informal) = leave suddenly when needed.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Being too proud of how you look or what you can do; caring too much about being admired. 2) (Bible, old) Something worthless or empty; «vanity of vanities, all is vanity» (Ecclesiastes) means everything in this life passes away. 3) A vanity or vanity unit is a cupboard under a bathroom basin, or a dressing table.
its sense in the lessons: A character and values word. Toad in The Wind in the Willows is full of vanity — he sings songs praising himself («The world has held great Heroes … but never a name to go down to fame compared with that of Toad!»). In fables like the crow and the fox, vanity makes the crow drop the cheese. In the Bible, the book of Ecclesiastes uses «vanity» for things that do not last. In homes, a bathroom «vanity» is a piece of furniture.
examples from the lessons: Toad's vanity got him into trouble again and again. | The crow's vanity made it open its beak and drop the cheese. | It's not vanity to brush your hair. | «Vanity of vanities, all is vanity,» says the preacher in Ecclesiastes. | Her vanity made her look in every mirror. | The new bathroom has a white vanity with two drawers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable in the first meaning; countable «vanities» for things. Adjective: «vain». Phrase «vanity project» = something done mainly to look important.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Talking a lot, quickly and easily, often with feeling. 2) Of speech: long, fast and full of words.
its sense in the lessons: A formal describing word for talkers. Toad in The Wind in the Willows is voluble — he never stops talking about himself. In Alice in Wonderland the Duchess and the Mock Turtle can be voluble. It tells the reader someone talks a great deal.
examples from the lessons: Toad was voluble about his new motor car. | My voluble aunt told us every detail of her holiday. | The voluble guide never stopped talking. | She became voluble when she was excited. | He gave a voluble explanation that no one could follow. | The parrot was voluble all morning.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective, formal; adverb «volubly». Say VOL-yoo-bul. Similar: talkative, chatty. Not related to «volume» in meaning, though the root is shared (rolling).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal, old) To give or tell something kindly, as a favour, or as if from a high position: he vouchsafed no answer. 2) (church, old prayers) To grant: «Vouchsafe, O Lord, to keep us this day without sin.»
its sense in the lessons: An old and formal word met in classic books and old prayers. In stories it often appears with «no»: «she vouchsafed no reply» means she gave no answer at all, often proudly. In Alice in Wonderland the Caterpillar hardly vouchsafes Alice any answers. Old Anglican prayers like the Te Deum use it for God granting things.
examples from the lessons: The Caterpillar vouchsafed no reply. | He vouchsafed only a nod. | «Vouchsafe, O Lord, to keep us this day without sin.» | She did not vouchsafe a single word about her trip. | The king vouchsafed his blessing. | The cat vouchsafed us one glance and walked away.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb, formal and old. Say vouch-SAFE. In modern speech say «give» or «tell».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A board with ridges on it, once used for scrubbing clothes when washing them by hand. 2) A washboard used as a musical instrument, played by scraping it, in skiffle and folk music. 3) (informal) Washboard stomach: very flat, strong stomach muscles. 4) A bumpy dirt road with ridges is called washboard road (North America).
its sense in the lessons: A history and everyday word. Before washing machines, people scrubbed clothes on a washboard in a tub. In The Wind in the Willows Toad escapes prison dressed as a washerwoman and later has to wash clothes on a barge — and is no good at it. In music, washboards are played in skiffle and jug bands.
examples from the lessons: Grandma's grandma scrubbed shirts on a washboard. | Toad tried to wash the clothes but splashed everywhere. | The skiffle band had a guitar and a washboard. | The museum had an old tin washboard. | The dirt road was like a washboard. | He scraped the washboard with thimbles on his fingers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun, plural «washboards». Compound of «wash» + «board».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (Canada, US) A room with toilets and washbasins; a toilet or restroom. 2) A room for washing, or for laundry in some buildings.
its sense in the lessons: An everyday word, especially in Canada: «May I go to the washroom?» In the UK people say «toilet» or «loo», in the US «bathroom» or «restroom», in Australia «toilet» or «loo». Hygiene: wash your hands with soap after using the washroom.
examples from the lessons: May I please go to the washroom? | The washrooms are down the hall on the left. | Wash your hands after using the washroom. | The camp had a washroom with showers. | The school is cleaning the washrooms today. | Is there a washroom at the station?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun. Mainly Canadian English; other words: toilet, loo (UK, Ireland, Australia, NZ), bathroom, restroom (US).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Travelling, especially on foot from place to place: a wayfaring man. 2) The act of travelling on foot (old).
its sense in the lessons: An old and poetic word. In The Wind in the Willows chapter «Wayfarers All», the Sea Rat, a wayfaring rat, tells Water Rat about faraway ports and almost tempts him to leave the river; Mole has to hold him back. Old songs talk of «a poor wayfaring stranger». A wayfarer is a traveller. The wayfaring tree is a real English shrub growing by old paths.
examples from the lessons: The wayfaring Sea Rat told stories of distant lands. | «Wayfarers All» is a chapter in The Wind in the Willows. | The wayfaring man rested by the road. | Swallows feel the wayfaring urge in autumn. | The old song tells of a wayfaring stranger. | The wayfaring tree grows along chalky lanes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Old-fashioned; noun for the person: «wayfarer». Today say «travelling».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person whose job is to make and repair wooden wheels, for carts, wagons and carriages.
its sense in the lessons: A history and job word. Before cars, every village needed a wheelwright, together with the blacksmith who fitted iron tyres on the wheels. In The Wind in the Willows Toad's caravan and the carts of the countryside were made by craftsmen like wheelwrights. Surnames like Wright and Wainwright come from old jobs like this.
examples from the lessons: The wheelwright fixed the broken cart wheel. | The village once had a wheelwright and a blacksmith. | A wheelwright shaped the wooden spokes. | We watched a wheelwright at the heritage museum. | His great-great-grandfather was a wheelwright. | The wheelwright and the smith fitted the iron rim.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun. «-wright» means a maker (playwright, shipwright); it is not «write» or «right». Say WEEL-rite.

part of speech: adjective (whitewashed); past form of whitewash (whitewash, whitewashes, whitewashed, whitewashing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Painted with whitewash, a cheap white paint of lime and water used on walls. 2) (figurative) Covered up: a whitewashed report hides mistakes or wrongdoing. 3) (sport, UK informal) to be whitewashed means to lose every game in a series.
its sense in the lessons: A house, history and news word. The very first scene of The Wind in the Willows: Mole is spring-cleaning, whitewashing his little home, until he throws down his brush and says «Hang spring-cleaning!» Country cottages and farm walls are often whitewashed. In news, «whitewash» means hiding the truth. In Tom Sawyer, Tom tricks his friends into whitewashing a fence.
examples from the lessons: Mole was whitewashing the walls of his home. | The cottage had whitewashed walls and a red door. | Tom Sawyer got his friends to whitewash the fence. | The report was whitewashed to hide the mistakes. | England were whitewashed 5–0 in the series. | The whitewashed houses shone in the sun.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. In maths sport problems «whitewashed 5–0» means one side won every game. Figurative sense means covering up, which is dishonest.

meaning for a pupil: 1) With all your heart; completely and sincerely, without any doubt.
its sense in the lessons: A feelings and values word: «I agree wholeheartedly», «They supported the plan wholeheartedly». Badger, Rat and Mole help Toad wholeheartedly once he changes his ways. In school, «throw yourself into it wholeheartedly» means give it your full effort.
examples from the lessons: I wholeheartedly agree with you. | She threw herself wholeheartedly into the play. | The class wholeheartedly supported the charity. | He apologised wholeheartedly. | They laughed wholeheartedly at the joke. | The friends wholeheartedly welcomed Toad home.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from «wholehearted». Spelling: whole-heart-ed-ly, written as one word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A gentle, sad feeling of longing for something you miss or cannot have.
its sense in the lessons: A feelings word in stories. In The Wind in the Willows Mole is full of wistfulness when he smells his old home in the snow, and Rat when he hears the Sea Rat's tales. Alice looks with wistfulness at the lovely garden through the tiny door. It is softer than grief and mixed with fond memory.
examples from the lessons: There was wistfulness in her voice as she talked about her old school. | Mole felt wistfulness for his little home. | Alice looked with wistfulness at the garden. | He watched the boats with wistfulness. | A wistfulness came over Grandma as she looked at the photos. | The song was full of wistfulness.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable noun. From «wistful» (adjective), adverb «wistfully». Similar: longing, yearning, nostalgia.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (literary) Amazing and wonderful; causing wonder.
its sense in the lessons: A story and poetry word, used in fairy tales, hymns and old books: «wondrous sights», «a wondrous story». Alice's Wonderland is full of wondrous creatures. In the Bible and hymns, God's «wondrous works» are praised. In science, nature's wondrous patterns (snowflakes, rainbows) can be explained and still amaze.
examples from the lessons: They saw wondrous sights in the deep sea. | Alice had a wondrous dream. | The hymn praised God's wondrous works. | A wondrous rainbow stretched across the sky. | The museum is full of wondrous things. | Every snowflake is a wondrous pattern.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective, literary. Spelling: wondr-ous (no e). In everyday speech say «wonderful» or «amazing».

part of speech: adjective (worthy, worthier, worthiest); noun (a worthy, worthies — old or jokey)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Deserving respect, praise or attention: a worthy winner. 2) Worthy of something means deserving it: worthy of a prize. 3) Good and useful, but sometimes a bit dull: a worthy cause, a worthy book. 4) (noun, old or jokey) An important person: the local worthies.
its sense in the lessons: A values word. Charities are «worthy causes»; a deserving champion is «a worthy winner». In stories, heroes prove themselves worthy. In church and the Bible: «Worthy is the Lamb» — Christians praise Jesus as worthy. Also part of compound words: trustworthy, praiseworthy, newsworthy, seaworthy (a boat safe to sail — Toad's friends hope his boats are seaworthy).
examples from the lessons: She was a worthy winner of the race. | The story is worthy of a prize. | We raised money for a worthy cause. | «Worthy is the Lamb,» sang the choir. | Prove yourself worthy of their trust. | The town's worthies met in the hall. | Is the old boat still seaworthy?
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative «worthier», superlative «worthiest»; noun «worthiness». «Worthy of» + noun. Compounds with -worthy mean «deserving» or «fit for».

part of speech: noun (a wrench, wrenches); verb (wrench, wrenches, wrenched, wrenching)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (tool) A metal tool for gripping and turning nuts and bolts; in the UK it is usually called a spanner. 2) (verb) To pull or twist something suddenly and hard: wrench the door open. 3) To injure a joint by twisting it: wrench your ankle. 4) A sad feeling when you have to leave someone or something: leaving home was a wrench.
its sense in the lessons: A tool, action and feelings word. In design and technology lessons you use a wrench or spanner. In stories: a door is wrenched open, a toy wrenched from someone's hands. In The Wind in the Willows it is a wrench for Mole and Rat to leave the river, and for Toad to give up his motor cars. Safety: if you wrench your ankle, rest, ice and raise it, and tell an adult.
examples from the lessons: Pass me the wrench so I can tighten the bolt. | He wrenched the lid off the jar. | She wrenched her ankle playing netball. | Leaving the old house was a real wrench. | The wind wrenched the umbrella from my hand. | Dad used a wrench to fix the bike.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. In the UK «spanner» is the usual word for the tool; «wrench» is American (in the UK a wrench is an adjustable or pipe wrench). Similar verbs: twist, yank.

part of speech: adverb and adjective (yonder — old or dialect); pronoun (yonder, very old)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Over there; at some distance but within sight: the hill yonder. 2) That … over there: yonder tree.
its sense in the lessons: An old and country word. You meet it in old books, poems, songs, the Bible and cowboy films: «over yonder», «the wild blue yonder» (the open sky). In The Wind in the Willows and other classics, country folk point to «yonder» farm or wood. Still heard in parts of the southern USA and rural Britain and Ireland.
examples from the lessons: See yonder hill? Our cottage is just behind it. | The farmer pointed to the wood yonder. | «Who lives in yonder house?» asked the traveller. | They rode off into the wild blue yonder. | The river bends over yonder. | Yonder stands the old mill.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Old-fashioned or dialect; in everyday writing say «over there» or «that one over there». Often «over yonder».

meaning for a pupil: 1) An abyss is a very deep hole or gap in the ground, so deep it seems to have no bottom. 2) (literary) An abyss is a terrible situation or a huge difference that seems impossible to cross. 3) (science) The abyss is the deepest, darkest part of the ocean.
its sense in the lessons: Old stories and adventure tales use «abyss» for scary drops in mountains or under the sea. Scientists call the deep sea floor the abyssal zone, where it is cold and dark and strange fish live. Phrases: «stare into the abyss», «on the edge of an abyss».
examples from the lessons: The climbers looked down into the dark abyss. | A rope bridge hung over the abyss. | Strange glowing fish live in the abyss of the ocean. | Alice wondered if she was falling into a bottomless abyss. | The country was close to the abyss of war. | No light reaches the abyss at the bottom of the sea. | The dragon's cave opened onto a black abyss.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced «a-BISS». Plural abysses. Adjective abysmal means «very bad» (an abysmal score), and abyssal means «of the deep sea». Do not confuse with «abbess» (the head of a convent of nuns).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Agility is being able to move quickly, easily and lightly. 2) Agility (of mind) is being able to think quickly and cleverly.
its sense in the lessons: In PE and sport, agility means quick changes of direction, balance and speed. Animals like cats, squirrels and monkeys are famous for agility. Dog agility is a sport where dogs run through tunnels and over jumps. Phrases: «agility training», «mental agility».
