examples from the lessons: The cat jumped onto the fence with great agility. | We did agility drills in PE, running between cones. | Squirrels show amazing agility in the trees. | Our dog won a prize in an agility contest. | The goalkeeper needs agility to save the ball. | Puzzles help your mental agility. | Monkeys swing through branches with agility.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: no «an agility». Adjective: agile («an agile cat»). Opposite: clumsiness.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (a name) Anna is a girl's name. 2) (old, India) An anna was an old coin of India and nearby lands; sixteen annas made one rupee.
its sense in the lessons: As a name it is common in English and in many languages. In old books about India (like Kipling's) prices are given in annas and rupees, which no longer exist as coins in that form.
examples from the lessons: Anna is in my class. | Anna and her brother walk to school together. | The old merchant sold the mangoes for two annas. | Sixteen annas made one rupee. | In Kipling's day a few annas bought a meal. | The anna is no longer used today.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a name, it is written with a capital A. As a coin, plural annas. Maths: if 16 annas = 1 rupee, then 8 annas = half a rupee.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An artisan is a skilled worker who makes things by hand, such as a carpenter, potter or weaver. 2) (adjective) Artisan bread, cheese and so on are made by hand in small amounts, in a traditional way.
its sense in the lessons: History lessons talk about medieval artisans in guilds: blacksmiths, shoemakers, masons. Today shops label food «artisan» to show it is handmade.
examples from the lessons: The artisan carved a beautiful wooden chair. | In medieval towns artisans belonged to guilds. | Potters and glassblowers are artisans. | We bought artisan bread at the market. | The artisan taught his apprentice for seven years. | Local artisans sell crafts at the fair.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced «AR-ti-zan» (UK also «ar-ti-ZAN»). Not the same as «artist», though artisans can be artistic.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Astray means away from the right path or place, lost. 2) To go astray or be led astray means to do wrong things, often because someone tempted you.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, travellers go astray in the woods and letters go astray in the post. In the Bible and church, the lost sheep «went astray», and people «led astray» start behaving badly. Phrases: «go astray», «lead astray».
examples from the lessons: The letter went astray in the post. | We went astray in the Wild Wood. | Toad's friends were afraid he would be led astray. | The shepherd went to look for the sheep that had gone astray. | Don't let anyone lead you astray. | One of my gloves has gone astray.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Used after verbs like go and lead, not before a noun.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (a name) Ben is a boy's name, short for Benjamin. 2) (Scotland) A ben is a mountain or high peak, used in names like Ben Nevis. 3) (Scotland, old) The ben is the inner room of a small cottage («but and ben»).
its sense in the lessons: Ben Nevis in Scotland is the highest mountain in the UK (1,345 m). Big Ben is the famous great bell of the clock tower at the Houses of Parliament in London, and people use the name for the tower too.
examples from the lessons: Ben is my best friend. | Ben Nevis is the highest mountain in Britain. | Big Ben chimes every hour. | We climbed a ben in the Highlands. | Ben and Lily walked to school. | The Scottish cottage had a but and a ben.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a name it has a capital B. Big Ben is really the bell's name, though people use it for the whole tower (the Elizabeth Tower).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Benign means kind, gentle and not harmful. 2) (medicine) A benign lump or tumour is not cancer and does not spread.
its sense in the lessons: Formal word used in descriptions of people and in medicine: «The doctor said the lump was benign» is good news. In stories, a benign smile is a kind one.
examples from the lessons: The old man gave a benign smile. | The doctor said the lump was benign, so we were relieved. | The weather was benign all week. | Badger looked at Mole with a benign expression. | Most spiders in Britain are benign to people.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced «bi-NINE» (the g is silent). Opposite: malignant (harmful; medicine: cancer that spreads).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Brisk means quick and energetic («a brisk walk»). 2) Brisk weather is cold and fresh. 3) A brisk manner is quick and businesslike, sometimes a bit short. 4) Brisk business or trade is busy, with lots of buying and selling.
its sense in the lessons: Health lessons recommend a brisk walk every day for exercise. Stories describe brisk winds, brisk talkers and brisk trade at markets.
examples from the lessons: We went for a brisk walk after lunch. | It was a brisk autumn morning. | The nurse was kind but brisk. | Ice cream sales were brisk on the hot day. | Rat rowed at a brisk pace. | A brisk wind blew off the sea.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb: briskly. Comparative brisker, superlative briskest.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A small musical instrument of two shell-shaped pieces of hard wood (or plastic), held in the hand and clicked together to make a sharp rhythm, used especially in Spanish dancing and flamenco.
its sense in the lessons: In music lessons castanets are a percussion instrument: you hit them to keep the beat. In stories they bring a picture of Spain and flamenco dancers. Phrases: a pair of castanets, click the castanets.
examples from the lessons: The dancer clicked her castanets as she spun. | We played castanets in the music lesson. | Castanets are percussion instruments. | Click, clack went the castanets. | He kept the beat with a pair of castanets. | Castanets are often used in Spanish music. | My little sister loves the castanets in the music box.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually plural: castanets, "a pair of castanets"; one half is a castanet. Stress: cas-ta-NETS. They belong to the percussion family, like drums and tambourines.

part of speech: verb (cheep, cheeps, cheeped, cheeping); noun (a cheep, cheeps)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (of a young bird) To make a short, high, weak sound. 2) A short high sound made by a young bird. 3) (informal) A tiny sound from anyone: "Not a cheep out of you!" means be quiet.
its sense in the lessons: In nature stories baby birds cheep in the nest for food. In everyday talk "not a cheep" means not a single sound or complaint. Similar sound words: chirp, tweet, peep, chirrup.
examples from the lessons: The baby birds cheeped for food. | We heard a tiny cheep from the hedge. | The chicks were cheeping in the box. | The sparrows cheeped on the windowsill. | I don't want to hear a cheep out of you till morning! | Every cheep meant the nest was still busy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Homophone: "cheap" (low in price). Cheep is a bird sound; cheap is about money. Trap in spelling tests!

meaning for a pupil: 1) (history, church) All the Christian people and Christian countries of the world, thought of together. 2) (old) The parts of the world where Christianity was the main religion, especially Europe in the Middle Ages.
its sense in the lessons: In history and religion lessons: in the Middle Ages Europeans often thought of themselves as "Christendom", led by kings and the Church. In old stories "the finest in all Christendom" means the finest anywhere.
examples from the lessons: In the Middle Ages, most of Europe was called Christendom. | The king wanted to be the richest ruler in Christendom. | Pilgrims came from all over Christendom. | It was the finest castle in all Christendom. | Christians believe they are one family across Christendom. | The crusades were wars between Christendom and Muslim lands.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually written with a capital C. Uncountable: no plural. Say: KRIS-en-dum (the t is silent). An old, grand word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (church) To do with a congregation: the people who gather in a church for worship. 2) (church) Congregational churches are Protestant churches where each local church runs itself, with its members choosing their own minister.
its sense in the lessons: In religion lessons: congregational singing is when the whole church sings together, not just the choir. Congregationalists began in England and helped found New England in America (the Pilgrims).
examples from the lessons: The congregational singing filled the chapel. | Our village has a Congregational church. | In Congregational churches, the members choose their minister. | The hymn was sung by the whole congregation — congregational singing. | The Pilgrims of the Mayflower founded congregational churches. | The congregational meeting decided to repair the roof.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From "congregation". With a capital C when it names the church tradition. Say: kong-gruh-GAY-shun-ul.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An open space with no roof, surrounded by walls or buildings, inside a castle, house, school, inn or palace.
its sense in the lessons: In history and stories courtyards are inside castles and palaces; carts arrive at the inn courtyard. Many schools have a courtyard for break time or a garden. Phrases: in the courtyard, the castle courtyard.
examples from the lessons: We ate lunch in the school courtyard. | The knights rode into the castle courtyard. | The inn's courtyard was full of carriages. | A fountain stood in the middle of the courtyard. | Toad's motor car stood in the courtyard of the inn. | Children played games in the sunny courtyard.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Compound of court + yard. Similar: quad (UK school or college), patio, yard.

part of speech: adjective (crude, cruder, crudest); noun (crude — crude oil)
meaning for a pupil: 1) In a natural state, not yet made pure or processed: crude oil. 2) Simple and roughly made, without much skill: a crude raft. 3) Rude and rough in a vulgar way: crude jokes. 4) (maths, science) Rough, not exact: a crude estimate. 5) (noun) Short for crude oil.
its sense in the lessons: In science and geography: crude oil from the ground is refined into petrol, diesel and plastics. In history, early tools were crude. In everyday talk a crude joke is rude. In maths a crude estimate is a quick rough guess.
examples from the lessons: Crude oil is pumped from under the sea. | We built a crude shelter from branches. | The caveman's tools were crude but useful. | Don't tell crude jokes in class. | That's only a crude estimate of the answer. | The price of crude went up.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative: cruder, crudest. Adverb: crudely. Maths: a crude estimate is approximate, not exact.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) The process of crystals forming, for example when a salty or sugary solution cools or the water evaporates. 2) The way an idea or plan becomes clear and definite.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons: dissolve salt or sugar in warm water, leave it, and the water evaporates — crystals grow (crystallisation). It is a way to get a solid back from a solution, a separation method. Snowflakes and frost also form by crystallisation.
examples from the lessons: We watched the crystallisation of salt in a dish. | Crystallisation separates salt from salty water. | Honey can turn hard by crystallisation. | Snowflakes form by crystallisation of water vapour. | Slow crystallisation makes bigger crystals. | The meeting led to the crystallisation of our plan.
note for the reader of a maths problem: UK spelling -isation, US -ization. Verb: crystallise / crystallize. Uncountable. Note the double l: crystal-l-isation.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Not doing what you are told by a parent, teacher or person in charge; refusing to obey.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, disobedient children or animals get into trouble (Peter Rabbit, Toad). In everyday life and school: following safety rules matters. Opposite: obedient. In the Just So Stories the Elephant's Child's curiosity gets him into trouble.
examples from the lessons: The disobedient puppy chewed my shoes. | Toad was disobedient and vain. | The disobedient boy went near the river. | It is disobedient to ignore the fire alarm. | The children were punished for being disobedient. | A disobedient dog may run into the road.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Noun: disobedience. Verb: disobey. Prefix dis- means "not". Spelling: dis-o-bed-i-ent.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who does experiments, especially in science. 2) A person who likes trying new things to see what happens.
its sense in the lessons: Science lessons: the experimenter plans a fair test, changes one variable, measures and records results; a good experimenter keeps everything else the same. In stories, a curious character can be a bold experimenter — Alice experiments by eating and drinking to change size.
examples from the lessons: The experimenter measured the water every hour. | A good experimenter changes only one thing at a time. | Alice became an experimenter with the little cakes. | The experimenter wrote the results in a table. | Benjamin Franklin was a famous experimenter with electricity. | Be a careful experimenter and wear safety goggles.
note for the reader of a maths problem: «an experimenter» (vowel sound). From experiment + -er. Also spelled «experimentor» rarely, but -er is standard. Related: experiment (noun and verb), experimental.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To let a liquid or smell come out slowly, as a plant oozes sap or skin gives off sweat. 2) To show a feeling or quality strongly, as in «she exuded confidence».
its sense in the lessons: Science: trees exude sap or resin (amber is fossilised resin); some plants exude sticky stuff to trap insects. Everyday and stories: a person exudes confidence, charm or warmth; Toad exudes pride.
examples from the lessons: The pine tree exuded sticky resin. | Toad exuded pride as he drove past. | The cheese exuded a strong smell. | Our new teacher exudes calm. | The cut stem exuded white milky sap. | The champion exuded confidence before the race.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced ig-ZYOOD. Regular verb. Similar: ooze, give off, radiate. Usually not used about sudden, fast flows.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A tall pole on which a flag is flown; a flagpole.
its sense in the lessons: Everyday: schools, castles, town halls and ships have flagstaffs. In The Wind in the Willows, Toad Hall has a flagstaff. Also Flagstaff, a city in Arizona, USA, where Pluto was discovered in 1930 (a name).
examples from the lessons: The flag fluttered on top of the flagstaff. | They raised the flag up the flagstaff every morning. | Toad Hall's flagstaff stood on the roof. | Lightning struck the tall flagstaff. | Pluto was discovered at an observatory in Flagstaff, Arizona. | The flag was lowered to half-mast on the flagstaff.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Same as «flagpole». A «staff» here is a pole or stick. «Half-mast» means the flag is lowered halfway, to show sadness when someone important has died.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (UK) A building made mostly of glass where plants are grown, kept warm by the sun; a greenhouse. 2) (UK, slang, old) A military prison.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons a glasshouse (greenhouse) traps the sun's heat so tomatoes and tender plants grow well; the idea helps explain the «greenhouse effect». Proverb: «People who live in glass houses shouldn't throw stones» — don't criticise others for faults you have yourself.
examples from the lessons: The tomatoes are ripening in the glasshouse. | Kew Gardens has a huge Victorian glasshouse full of palm trees. | It is warm inside the glasshouse even in winter. | We grew seedlings in a little glasshouse at school. | People who live in glass houses shouldn't throw stones. | The gardener opened the glasshouse windows on a hot day.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. «Glasshouse» is mostly British; «greenhouse» is used everywhere. The proverb is usually written as two words: «glass houses».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A narrow, deep valley, especially in Scotland or Ireland, often with a stream at the bottom. 2) Glen is also a man's name (a name).
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons about Scotland and Ireland, glens are valleys carved by rivers and glaciers (Glen Coe, the Glens of Antrim). The word appears in place names and Scottish songs and stories.
examples from the lessons: We camped by a stream at the bottom of the glen. | Glen Coe is a famous glen in the Scottish Highlands. | Mist filled the glen in the morning. | Deer were grazing in the quiet glen. | A glacier carved out the glen long ago. | My uncle Glen lives in Canada.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Comes from Scottish Gaelic «gleann». Similar: valley, dale (northern England), vale.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who makes jewellery, cups, plates or other objects out of gold. 2) In history, goldsmiths also kept people's gold safe and lent money, which helped start the first banks.
its sense in the lessons: In history and art lessons goldsmiths made crowns, coins and church treasures (like the Anglo-Saxon gold of Sutton Hoo). In money lessons goldsmiths' receipts were an early form of paper money in London.
examples from the lessons: The goldsmith made a ring for the king. | A goldsmith melts gold and hammers it into shape. | In medieval London goldsmiths had shops on Cheapside. | The museum showed cups made by a famous goldsmith. | Goldsmiths in the 1600s kept merchants' gold in strong rooms. | My cousin is training to be a goldsmith.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. «Smith» means a maker who works metal: blacksmith (iron), silversmith (silver), goldsmith (gold).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who rows or steers a gondola in Venice, standing at the back and pushing with one long oar.
its sense in the lessons: Gondoliers are a famous sight in Venice, often in striped shirts and straw hats; some sing to their passengers. There is a comic opera called «The Gondoliers».
examples from the lessons: The gondolier pushed the boat away from the steps. | Our gondolier wore a striped shirt and a straw hat. | Gondoliers train for years to steer through the narrow canals. | The gondolier called out before turning the corner. | She dreams of being the first gondolier in her family. | The gondolier sang an Italian song.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Stress on the last syllable: «gon-do-LEER». Countable.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A grid or screen of metal bars or wires across a window, door, opening or vent, to protect it or let air through. 2) The metal grid at the front of a car that lets air reach the engine.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life you see grilles on shop windows, drains, air vents, speakers and the fronts of cars; in old buildings a small grille in a door lets people look or talk through. Safety: never poke fingers or sticks through a grille.
examples from the lessons: The bank window had a strong metal grille. | Air comes out of the grille in the ceiling. | The car's shiny grille had a badge in the middle. | The nun spoke to visitors through a grille. | Leaves blocked the drain grille. | The speaker's grille protects the parts inside.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Homophone: «grill» (to cook under heat; the part of an oven). Grille with an -e is the screen of bars.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Dirt that has built up in a thick, sticky or black layer on a surface or skin: «the grime on the windows». 2) (music) Grime is a style of fast rap music that started in London around 2002.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life grime is the dirt you scrub off old windows, ovens or hands after mending a bike. In stories about Victorian cities it shows smoke, soot and poverty. Adjective: grimy.
examples from the lessons: The windows were black with grime. | He scrubbed the grime off his hands. | Years of grime covered the old painting. | Victorian chimney sweeps were covered in soot and grime. | The cleaner wiped away the grime from the oven. | My cousin listens to grime and drill music.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: «a lot of grime», not «grimes». Adjective: grimy. Don't confuse with «crime» or «grim» (serious, gloomy).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who owns or runs a shop that sells food and things for the home, such as tea, sugar, tins and cleaning things. 2) «The grocer's» (UK) or «the grocery store» (US) is the shop itself.
its sense in the lessons: In history and stories (old village life, The Wind in the Willows) the grocer was the corner shop owner who weighed out sugar and tea. In maths problems the grocer sells apples by the kilo and gives change. Today most people shop in supermarkets.
examples from the lessons: Mum sent me to the grocer's for a pint of milk. | The grocer weighed out a pound of sugar. | A grocer sells apples at 40p each; how much do 5 apples cost? | Our local grocer knows everyone's name. | The grocer stacked oranges in a neat pyramid. | In the old days the grocer delivered food by bicycle.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. «Greengrocer» (UK) sells fruit and vegetables. «Groceries» = the food you buy. The shop is «the grocer's» with an apostrophe.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A small warship with big guns, used especially on rivers or near the coast. 2) «Gunboat diplomacy» means a strong country forcing weaker ones to agree by threatening to use its navy or army.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons about the British Empire and the 1800s, gunboats patrolled rivers in China and Africa, and «gunboat diplomacy» describes bullying by powerful countries.
examples from the lessons: A gunboat sailed up the river. | The navy sent two gunboats to guard the harbour. | The gunboat's guns pointed at the shore. | Historians call this «gunboat diplomacy». | Gunboats were used in the Opium Wars in China. | The model gunboat had tiny cannons.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; one word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a way that cannot be repaired, mended or put right. 2) So badly that it cannot be undone.
its sense in the lessons: In science and nature lessons: damage to a habitat can be irreparable. In stories a friendship or a vase can be irreparably broken. Phrases: «irreparably damaged», «irreparably harmed».
examples from the lessons: The precious vase was irreparably broken. | Pollution can irreparably damage a river. | The old car was irreparably smashed. | Their friendship was not irreparably hurt; they made up. | Too much sun can irreparably harm your eyes. | The storm irreparably damaged the ancient tree.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronunciation: ir-REP-a-ra-bly (stress on «rep», not «pair»). Opposite: «reparable» (rare); everyday: «can be fixed».

part of speech: noun (ivy, ivies; uncountable for the plant in general); also a name (Ivy)
meaning for a pupil: 1) An evergreen climbing plant with dark shiny leaves that grows up walls and trees. 2) (poison ivy, North America) A different plant whose leaves give an itchy rash. 3) (Ivy League, USA) A group of old famous universities. 4) (a name) Ivy is a girl's name.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons: ivy is a climber; its berries are food for birds in winter but poisonous to people. At Christmas, «The Holly and the Ivy» carol. In stories old houses are «covered in ivy». Phrases: «ivy-covered walls», «poison ivy», «Ivy League».
examples from the lessons: Ivy climbed all over the old castle wall. | Birds eat ivy berries in winter. | Don't eat ivy berries; they are poisonous to people. | We sang «The Holly and the Ivy» at the Christmas concert. | In Canada we learn: leaves of three, let it be — that's poison ivy. | The Badger's house had an ivy-covered entrance. | My great-gran was called Ivy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Poison ivy (North America) is not a true ivy. Ivy does not usually kill healthy trees, a common myth; it uses them for support. Plural «ivies» is rare (kinds of ivy).

part of speech: noun (a jack, jacks); verb (jack, jacks, jacked, jacking — jack up, jack in); also a name (Jack)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A tool for lifting a heavy thing, like a car, a little way off the ground. 2) (cards) A playing card with a picture of a young man, between the ten and the queen; also called the knave. 3) (electric) A socket where you plug in a lead, like a headphone jack. 4) (games) jacks — a children's game of picking up small metal pieces while bouncing a ball; in bowls, the small white ball. 5) (ship) A small flag on a ship, as in the Union Jack, the UK flag. 6) (a name) Jack, a boy's name, often a nickname for John; in fairy tales Jack is a brave clever boy. 7) (verb, informal) jack up = lift with a jack or raise prices; (UK slang) jack in = give up; (slang) jack = steal («he jacked my bike»). 8) (male animal) A male donkey or hare is a jack.
its sense in the lessons: In fairy tales: «Jack and the Beanstalk», «Jack and Jill». Sayings: «jack of all trades» (someone who can do many jobs), «hit the jackpot», «jack-in-the-box». In Alice, the Knave (Jack) of Hearts stole the tarts. In safety: never go under a car held only by a jack. Phrases: «car jack», «headphone jack», «Union Jack», «jack it in».
examples from the lessons: Dad used a jack to lift the car and change the tyre. | The Jack of Hearts stole the tarts. | Plug your headphones into the jack. | Jack climbed the beanstalk. | We played jacks on the playground. | The Union Jack is the flag of the United Kingdom. | He was fed up and jacked in his job (UK slang). | The shop jacked up the price of sweets. | A jack-in-the-box popped up and made the baby laugh. | My uncle is a jack of all trades.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Jack (name) has a capital letter. «Jack» and «knave» name the same card. The game «jacks» is plural. Slang «jack» = steal is rude-ish street talk; «jack all» (UK slang) = nothing.

part of speech: noun (Khmer — a people and a language); adjective (Khmer)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The main people of Cambodia in South-East Asia. 2) The language of Cambodia, with its own alphabet. 3) (adjective) To do with the Khmer people, their language or their old empire, which built Angkor Wat. 4) (history) The Khmer Rouge: a cruel government that ruled Cambodia from 1975 to 1979 and killed very many people.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and history lessons about Asia: the Khmer Empire built the huge temple of Angkor Wat. In world languages lessons: Khmer has one of the longest alphabets in the world. Phrases: «the Khmer Empire», «Khmer script», «Khmer Rouge».
examples from the lessons: Most people in Cambodia speak Khmer. | Angkor Wat was built by the Khmer Empire. | Khmer script has curly letters. | My classmate's family is Khmer and they celebrate Khmer New Year in April. | The Khmer Rouge caused terrible suffering in the 1970s. | We tasted Khmer food at the festival.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Pronounced «kuh-MEER» or «kmeye» in English. Always a capital: Khmer. Not the same as «Hmong» or «Thai».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (church) The ordinary members of a church who are not priests, ministers or clergy. 2) People who are not experts in a subject.
its sense in the lessons: In church life lessons: the clergy (priests, vicars, ministers) lead services; the laity are the ordinary churchgoers, who can also read the Bible aloud, sing and help. Adjective: «lay» (a lay reader, a lay preacher). Phrases: «the clergy and the laity».
examples from the lessons: The bishop met with the clergy and the laity. | Members of the laity read the Bible readings on Sunday. | My grandmother is a lay reader, one of the laity who helps lead services. | The laity helped organise the church fete. | Science books for the laity explain things simply. | Both clergy and laity sang in the choir.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually «the laity», treated as plural or singular. A «layman» or «layperson» is one member. Pronounced LAY-i-tee. Not about «laying» anything.

part of speech: noun (Leo — a constellation, star sign and name)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (space) A group of stars, a constellation, said to look like a lion. 2) (star signs) The fifth sign of the zodiac, for birthdays from about 23 July to 22 August. 3) (a name) Leo, a boy's name meaning «lion» in Latin; many popes were called Leo. 4) (Latin) leo = lion.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons on space: Leo is a constellation seen in spring in the Northern Hemisphere, with the bright star Regulus. Star signs (astrology) are not science: the stars do not decide your character. Phrases: «the constellation Leo», «I'm a Leo».
examples from the lessons: We found the constellation Leo in the spring sky. | Regulus is the brightest star in Leo. | My birthday is in August, so my star sign is Leo. | Leo is the Latin word for lion. | My friend Leo plays football with me. | Star signs like Leo are fun, but they are not science.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always a capital: Leo. Constellations are real patterns of stars; astrology (horoscopes) is a belief, not proved by science.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To do with a mother or being a mother; motherly. 2) (family) Related through your mother («maternal grandmother» = your mum's mother). 3) (health) To do with women having babies («maternal health»).
its sense in the lessons: In family trees and science lessons: maternal and paternal sides of the family; maternal care in animals (a hen sitting on eggs). In health: maternity leave, maternity ward. Phrases: «maternal instinct», «maternal grandfather».
examples from the lessons: My maternal grandmother is my mum's mum. | Hens show strong maternal care. | She felt maternal towards the little kitten. | Elephants have strong maternal bonds. | The maternity ward is where babies are born. | My maternal uncle lives in Ireland.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite for fathers: «paternal». Related: «maternity», «mother», Latin «mater». In family-tree puzzles, «maternal» tells you which side.

part of speech: noun (max — informal, short for maximum); adjective; verb (max out, maxes, maxed, maxing); also a name (Max)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) Short for «maximum»: the biggest amount possible. 2) (informal, adverb) At most («It'll take ten minutes max»). 3) (verb, informal) max out = use up to the limit («maxed out the card»). 4) (slang) «to the max» = completely. 5) (a name) Max, a boy's name (short for Maximilian or Maxwell). 6) (maths, computing) max — the largest value in a set.
its sense in the lessons: In maths and computing: «max» and «min» find the largest and smallest numbers. Everyday: «ten minutes max». On cookers and games: turn it up to max. Phrases: «to the max», «max out», «at the max».
examples from the lessons: I'll be ten minutes, max. | Turn the volume up to max! | The max score is 100 points. | Find the max of 4, 9 and 7 — it's 9. | He maxed out his phone's storage. | We partied to the max. | My dog is called Max.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal; in exam writing use «maximum». In maths «max» = the greatest value, «min» = the smallest. «Max» as a name has a capital.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The Mesozoic is a long stretch of Earth's history, from about 252 million to 66 million years ago, often called the Age of Dinosaurs. 2) Belonging to that time: Mesozoic rocks, Mesozoic reptiles.
its sense in the lessons: Used in science lessons about fossils, dinosaurs and the timeline of life on Earth. It is split into three periods: the Triassic, the Jurassic and the Cretaceous. It ended when an asteroid hit Earth and most dinosaurs died out. Phrases: the Mesozoic era, Mesozoic fossils.
examples from the lessons: Dinosaurs lived in the Mesozoic. | The Mesozoic era had three periods. | Our class made a timeline of the Mesozoic along the corridor wall. | The first birds appeared in the Mesozoic. | Mesozoic rocks on the Jurassic Coast are full of ammonites. | Flowering plants spread near the end of the Mesozoic. | Humans did not live in the Mesozoic at all.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually written with a capital M: the Mesozoic. Say «mez-oh-ZOH-ik». Myth trap: cartoons show cavemen with dinosaurs, but the Mesozoic ended about 66 million years before the first humans. In timeline sums: 252 − 66 = 186 million years long.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A stone by the side of a road showing how many miles it is to a town. 2) An important event or step in someone's life or in a project, like a first word or a 100th birthday.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: «a big milestone» for a baby's first steps, starting school, a team's 1000th goal. In history: Roman roads had milestones. In stories, a traveller counts the milestones to see how far he has come. Phrases: reach a milestone, an important milestone, mark a milestone.
examples from the lessons: The old milestone said «London 12 miles». | Walking was a big milestone for my baby brother. | Our school reached a milestone: 500 books read! | Toad sped past milestone after milestone in his motor car. | Losing your first tooth is a milestone. | The Romans put milestones along their roads. | Finishing the project was an important milestone for the class.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a milestone, two milestones. The road sense is old and literal; the «important step» sense is now the common one. Not the same as «millstone» (a heavy stone for grinding grain; «a millstone round your neck» is a burden).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A scientist who studies minerals — the natural solid materials such as quartz, salt and gold that make up rocks.
its sense in the lessons: Used in science lessons about rocks and crystals and in careers talk. A mineralogist tests a mineral's hardness, colour, streak and crystal shape. Related words: mineral, mineralogy (the science), geologist (who studies rocks and the Earth as a whole).
examples from the lessons: A mineralogist looked at the shiny crystal under a lens. | My aunt is a mineralogist at the museum. | The mineralogist said the «gold» was really fool's gold. | Mineralogists use a scale of hardness from 1 to 10. | I want to be a mineralogist when I grow up. | The mineralogist scratched the rock to test it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Say «min-er-AL-o-jist» (the stress moves from MIN-eral). Spelling: mineral + -ogist (not «minerologist»). A geologist studies the whole Earth; a mineralogist studies minerals.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Not boasting about yourself or your skills, even when you are good. 2) Dressing or behaving in a way that does not draw attention to your body, often for reasons of religion or custom. 3) Being small or not much: the modesty of their home.
its sense in the lessons: In PSHE and stories, modesty is a good quality: a modest winner says «the team did well». In religion lessons, many faiths teach modesty in clothes. Opposite: boastfulness, vanity, arrogance. Phrase: «false modesty» — pretending to be humble to get praise.
examples from the lessons: Despite her modesty, she was the best player. | «It was nothing,» he said with modesty. | Toad had no modesty at all — he sang songs about himself. | Some people wear long clothes for modesty. | His modesty made everyone like him. | The prize-winner thanked her teachers with great modesty. | False modesty is fishing for compliments.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Adjective: modest (a modest girl; a modest house = a small, plain house). Not the same as shyness: a modest person may be confident but does not boast.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Thrown or done with the arm raised above the shoulder: an overarm throw, an overarm bowl.
its sense in the lessons: In PE: an overarm throw goes further; in cricket, bowlers bowl overarm; in swimming, front crawl uses overarm strokes. Opposite: underarm.
examples from the lessons: Throw the ball overarm. | In cricket you must bowl overarm. | His overarm throw reached the far end. | Swim front crawl with an overarm stroke. | Practise your overarm throw at playtime. | Little ones throw underarm, older children overarm.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite: underarm. US often says «overhand». One word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) A way of living in which one living thing (the parasite) lives on or inside another (the host) and takes food from it, harming it.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about food chains and relationships: fleas, ticks, tapeworms and mistletoe show parasitism. Compare mutualism (both gain) and commensalism (one gains, the other is not harmed). The cuckoo laying eggs in other birds' nests is called brood parasitism.
examples from the lessons: Fleas on a dog are an example of parasitism. | We learned about parasitism in science. | The cuckoo's tricks are a kind of parasitism. | Mistletoe lives by parasitism on trees. | Parasitism harms the host. | Ticks live by parasitism and can spread disease.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Parasite (the creature), parasitic (adjective), parasitism (the way of life). Say «PA-ra-sigh-tizm».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A long, pale cream root vegetable, shaped like a carrot, with a sweet taste when cooked.
its sense in the lessons: In cooking: roast parsnips with Sunday dinner or Christmas dinner (UK, Ireland). In science/gardening: a root vegetable grown underground; frost makes it sweeter. Old saying: «Fine words butter no parsnips» (talk alone does not get things done).
examples from the lessons: We had roast parsnips with our chicken. | A parsnip looks like a white carrot. | Grandad grows parsnips in his allotment. | Parsnips taste sweeter after a frost. | Fine words butter no parsnips. | Mum made parsnip soup.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Spelling: pars-nip. Trap: the wild parsnip plant's sap can burn skin in the sun — don't pick wild plants.

meaning for a pupil: 1) From or belonging to Peru, a country in South America. 2) A person from Peru.
its sense in the lessons: In geography: Peruvians speak Spanish, and many speak Quechua or Aymara; Machu Picchu, the Andes and the Amazon are in Peru. In stories: Paddington Bear comes from «darkest Peru». Peruvian food includes potatoes (first grown there) and quinoa.
examples from the lessons: Paddington is a Peruvian bear. | Machu Picchu is an Inca city in the Peruvian Andes. | Our Peruvian classmate taught us some Spanish. | Llamas live in the Peruvian mountains. | Peruvian farmers grow many kinds of potatoes. | Peruvians celebrate Independence Day in July.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always capital P. Country: Peru; people: Peruvians.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Small and unimportant: petty problems. 2) Caring too much about small things in a mean way: «Don't be so petty!» 3) Minor, less serious: petty crime, petty theft. 4) Small, for daily use: petty cash.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday speech: «That's so petty!» = making a fuss about something tiny, being mean. In law: petty theft (stealing small things). In money: petty cash is a small amount kept for small costs. In history: petty kings ruled small lands.
examples from the lessons: Don't be petty — share the crayons. | They had a petty argument about who sat where. | Shoplifting a sweet is still petty theft. | The office keeps petty cash in a tin. | Toad thought rules were petty. | It's petty to stay cross about a game.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative: pettier, pettiest. From French petit (small). «Being petty» is a common teenage word.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To do with philosophy — thinking deeply about big questions like what is true, right or real. 2) Calm and accepting when something bad happens: «He was philosophical about losing.»
its sense in the lessons: In school: philosophy for children (P4C) asks philosophical questions — «Is it ever OK to lie?» In stories: Rat or Badger may be philosophical, accepting things calmly. Phrase: be philosophical about something.
examples from the lessons: «Do animals think?» is a philosophical question. | He was philosophical about missing the bus. | We had a philosophical chat about friendship. | Badger took the news philosophically. | The book has a philosophical feel. | Alice's Cheshire Cat makes philosophical jokes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From philosophy. Spelling: ph- at the start and in the middle sounds f: phil-o-SOF-ical.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who travels to a holy place for religious reasons. 2) (history, US) The Pilgrims (Pilgrim Fathers) were English settlers who sailed to America on the Mayflower in 1620. 3) Anyone on a long journey with a purpose.
its sense in the lessons: In religion lessons: pilgrims go to Jerusalem, Mecca (Hajj), Lourdes, Santiago de Compostela, Canterbury. In history: Chaucer's Canterbury Tales tell of pilgrims; Thanksgiving in the US remembers the Pilgrims. Phrases: pilgrim route, «The Pilgrim's Progress» (a famous Christian story by Bunyan).
examples from the lessons: Pilgrims walked to Canterbury Cathedral. | Muslim pilgrims travel to Mecca for Hajj. | The Pilgrims landed at Plymouth Rock in 1620. | A pilgrim carried a staff and a shell. | Christians believe pilgrimage brings them closer to God. | The pilgrims sang as they walked.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Related: pilgrimage (the journey). «The Pilgrims» (US history) with capital P.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A long line of pipes that carries oil, gas or water over long distances. 2) «In the pipeline»: being planned or prepared, coming soon.
its sense in the lessons: In geography: oil and gas pipelines cross countries and seas. In everyday talk: «A new playground is in the pipeline.» In computing, a pipeline is a series of steps that data passes through.
examples from the lessons: The pipeline carries gas across the sea. | A new swimming pool is in the pipeline. | Water flows through the pipeline to the city. | Workers checked the pipeline for leaks. | Big changes are in the pipeline at school. | The oil pipeline is hundreds of miles long.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. One word. Phrase: «in the pipeline» = coming soon.

meaning for a pupil: 1) As much as a pocket can hold.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and rhymes: «a pocketful of rye» in «Sing a Song of Sixpence». In everyday life: a pocketful of sweets, conkers or coins.
examples from the lessons: He had a pocketful of conkers. | Sing a song of sixpence, a pocket full of rye. | She came home with a pocketful of shells. | I found a pocketful of coins in my coat. | Rat brought a pocketful of biscuits. | The boy had a pocketful of marbles.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Plural: pocketfuls (common) or pocketsful. One word, single l at the end.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A piece of low, flat land taken back from the sea or a lake and protected by dykes (walls of earth), mainly in the Netherlands.
its sense in the lessons: In geography lessons: the Dutch built polders by building dykes and pumping water out, once with windmills, now with pumps. About a quarter of the Netherlands is below sea level. Farms and towns stand on polders.
examples from the lessons: Much of Holland is made of polders. | Windmills pumped water out of the polders. | The polder is below sea level. | Farmers grow tulips on the polders. | A dyke protects the polder from the sea. | We cycled across a flat Dutch polder.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A Dutch word used in English. Countable. Related: dyke (dike in US), reclaimed land.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An official who keeps records, especially of births, marriages and deaths. 2) (school, university) The person in charge of student records and admissions. 3) (UK, medicine) A hospital doctor in training to become a consultant (a senior specialist).
its sense in the lessons: In citizenship lessons and adult life: in the UK, a baby's birth must be registered with the registrar, and couples can be married by a registrar at a register office instead of in church. In hospitals, «the registrar will see you» means a fairly senior doctor. Phrases: «register office», «the registrar of births, marriages and deaths».
examples from the lessons: Mum and Dad took my baby sister's birth certificate from the registrar. | My aunt was married by a registrar at the town hall. | The university registrar keeps all the students' records. | The registrar checked the names before the wedding. | A registrar came to look at Grandpa's X-ray. | When someone dies, the family tells the registrar.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun; ends in «-ar» (not «-er»). Stress: REJ-is-trar or rej-is-TRAR. «Register office» (often called «registry office») is where the registrar works.

part of speech: verb (relearn, relearns, relearned or relearnt, relearning)
meaning for a pupil: 1) To learn something again that you have forgotten or lost. 2) To learn a new or better way of doing something you already did.
its sense in the lessons: In school, children relearn things after holidays (like times tables). After an accident or illness, people may relearn how to walk or talk with help from therapists. In stories, a character who relearns something shows change and growth. Phrases: «relearn how to», «have to relearn».
examples from the lessons: After the summer, I had to relearn my nine times table. | Grandpa relearned how to walk after his operation. | Alice tried to relearn her lessons, but the words came out wrong. | We relearned the song for the concert. | It is hard to relearn spelling if you learnt it wrong. | After the hospital, she slowly relearnt to write.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular in US (relearned); UK also «relearnt». «re-» means «again» (redo, rewrite, revisit).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A deep, painful feeling of being sorry and guilty for something wrong you have done. 2) (idiom) «Without remorse»: cruelly, without feeling sorry.
its sense in the lessons: In ethics and church lessons, remorse is the first step to saying sorry, making things right and being forgiven; Christians speak of repentance, which includes remorse and turning away from wrong. In law, judges sometimes take into account whether someone shows remorse. In stories, Toad shows remorse after his crimes — though it does not last long! Phrases: «feel remorse», «show remorse», «full of remorse», «without remorse».
examples from the lessons: He felt deep remorse after hitting his little sister. | Toad was full of remorse — for at least five minutes. | The thief showed no remorse in court. | Remorse made her go back and say sorry. | The villain laughed without remorse. | True remorse means trying to put things right.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable noun (never «a remorse»). Adjective: remorseful (feeling sorry); remorseless (cruel, without pity — also «never stopping»: the remorseless rain). Similar: guilt, regret (regret is milder).

part of speech: noun (retrospect — mainly in the phrase «in retrospect»)
meaning for a pupil: 1) «In retrospect»: when you think about something afterwards, looking back on it, often seeing it differently.
its sense in the lessons: A useful phrase in writing and reflection: «In retrospect, I should have revised more.» In history lessons, historians look at events in retrospect and can see causes that people at the time could not. In ethics, looking back in retrospect helps us learn from mistakes. Phrases: «in retrospect», «with hindsight» (similar).
examples from the lessons: In retrospect, it was a mistake to leave my coat at home. | In retrospect, the plan was too risky. | Toad's adventures seemed funny only in retrospect. | Looking back in retrospect, the war could have been avoided. | In retrospect, the test was easier than I thought. | The trip, in retrospect, was the best day of the year.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable noun, almost always in «in retrospect». «Retro-» means backwards (retro fashion = from the past). Adjective: retrospective (looking back; also an art show of an artist's past work). Similar: hindsight.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Made of silk. 2) Soft, smooth and shiny like silk: «silken hair», «a silken voice».
its sense in the lessons: A literary, poetic word in stories and fairy tales: a princess's silken dress, the Rat's silken fur, the river's silken surface. In everyday speech people more often say «silk» or «silky».
examples from the lessons: The princess wore a silken gown. | Her hair was long and silken. | The river slid by with a silken sound. | The cat's fur felt silken under my hand. | He spoke in a soft, silken voice. | A silken thread hung from the spider's web. | The king sat on silken cushions.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Old-fashioned, literary form; «silky» is the everyday word. Do not add -er/-est; say «more silken».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A Knight Templar: a member of a religious order of knights founded about 1119 to protect Christian pilgrims travelling to Jerusalem. 2) (UK law) A lawyer who works in the Temple, an area of law courts and offices in London.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons about the Crusades, the Templars were famous fighting monks; they became rich and were shut down in 1312. Many legends and myths about Templar treasure are made up. Phrases: «the Knights Templar», «Templar church».
examples from the lessons: The Knights Templar guarded pilgrims on the road. | The Templars wore white cloaks with red crosses. | The Templar order was ended in 1312. | We visited an old Templar church in London. | Stories of Templar treasure are mostly legends. | A Templar took vows like a monk. | The Templars built castles in the Holy Land.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually with a capital: «Templar». Be careful: many «Templar secrets» in films are myths, not history.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A male cat; also a tomcat. 2) The male of some other animals, such as a turkey. 3) (a name) Tom is a boy's name, short for Thomas.
its sense in the lessons: In nature lessons, a male cat is a tom, a female is a queen, a baby is a kitten. «Tom Thumb», «Tom Kitten», «Tom Sawyer» are famous story characters. Phrases: «tomcat», «tom turkey», «peeping Tom» (someone who spies).
examples from the lessons: The tom fought with the cat next door. | Our tomcat comes home every morning. | A male turkey is called a tom. | Tom is my best friend. | Tom Thumb was no bigger than his father's thumb. | The old tom slept on the wall. | Toms often roam far from home.
note for the reader of a maths problem: As a name, write «Tom» with a capital. Female cat = queen; male = tom.

part of speech: noun (Tupi — a name of a people and language); adjective (Tupi)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (a name) The Tupi are Indigenous peoples of Brazil, who lived along the Atlantic coast when Europeans arrived. 2) Tupi is also their family of languages; many words, like jaguar, piranha, toucan and tapioca, came into English from Tupi through Portuguese.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and history lessons about Brazil and the Amazon. In word lessons it explains where animal names come from: jaguar, toucan, cashew, petunia. Kipling's Just So Stories mention the Amazon and its animals, such as the Jaguar.
examples from the lessons: The word «jaguar» comes from the Tupi language. | The Tupi lived in villages along the coast of Brazil. | Many Brazilian place names are Tupi words. | «Toucan» came into English from Tupi through Portuguese. | Tupi people grew cassava for food. | Some Tupi words are still used in Brazilian Portuguese.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A proper name: write it with a capital T. Sometimes spelled Tupí. Not an English word itself; it is the name of a people and their languages.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To unpick is to take out the stitches of sewing or knitting carefully, one by one. 2) (figurative) To take apart a problem, plan or argument carefully to understand it or undo it.
its sense in the lessons: In textiles and sewing lessons: if you make a mistake, unpick the stitches with a seam ripper. In maths and reading lessons: «Let's unpick this question» = look at each part. Phrases: unpick a seam, unpick a problem.
examples from the lessons: I sewed it wrong, so I had to unpick the seam. | Use the seam ripper to unpick the stitches. | Nan unpicked the old jumper to reuse the wool. | Let's unpick this word problem step by step. | The detective unpicked the story bit by bit. | It took an hour to unpick the knots.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular: unpicked. Mainly UK; US often «take out stitches» or «rip out». Figurative use is common in British classrooms.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To uproot is to pull a plant or tree out of the ground with its roots. 2) To make people leave their home and move to a new place (The war uprooted many families). 3) To get rid of something completely (to uproot a bad habit).
its sense in the lessons: In science and gardening: storms uproot trees; uproot weeds. In history and geography lessons about refugees: people uprooted by war. Phrases: uprooted trees, uproot a family.
examples from the lessons: The storm uprooted the old oak. | Pull the weeds up — uproot them completely. | The war uprooted thousands of families. | Moving to another country uprooted our lives. | Pigs uproot plants with their snouts. | The elephant uprooted a small tree.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular: uprooted. up + root.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Thin and bending easily, then springing back (a whippy stick, whippy branches). 2) (of cream, ice cream) Soft and fluffy, whipped (UK informal «a Mr Whippy» = soft-serve ice cream).
its sense in the lessons: In nature and science lessons: flexible materials; willow twigs are whippy. In everyday life: a whippy fishing rod, a whippy aerial. Phrases: whippy stick, whippy branch.
examples from the lessons: Willow branches are long and whippy. | The fishing rod was light and whippy. | He cut a whippy stick from the hedge. | The whippy branches flicked back in my face. | We got a whippy ice cream from the van. | Bamboo is strong and whippy.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparatives: whippier, whippiest. From «whip».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Completely sincere and enthusiastic, with no doubts (wholehearted support, a wholehearted thank you).
its sense in the lessons: In school: giving wholehearted effort; a wholehearted apology. In church: Christians speak of loving God wholeheartedly. Phrases: wholehearted support, wholehearted agreement.
examples from the lessons: She gave the plan her wholehearted support. | Thank you for your wholehearted effort. | It was a wholehearted apology. | The class gave a wholehearted cheer. | We are in wholehearted agreement. | Rat welcomed Mole with wholehearted kindness.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word (also «whole-hearted»). Adverb: wholeheartedly. Opposite: half-hearted.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (church) An abbot is the man in charge of an abbey, a community of monks who live, pray and work together. 2) (history) In the Middle Ages an abbot could also be a powerful landowner, as important as a lord.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons about monasteries, castles and the Middle Ages, the abbot runs the abbey, keeps its rules and looks after its lands and money; in stories he is often wise, sometimes greedy or strict. The woman who leads a community of nuns is an abbess. Phrases: the abbot of the abbey, Father Abbot.
examples from the lessons: The abbot rang the bell for morning prayers. | Every monk in the abbey obeyed the abbot. | The old abbot welcomed the tired travellers and gave them bread. | In 1539 King Henry VIII closed the abbeys and the abbots lost their lands. | Our class visited the ruins of an abbey where an abbot once lived. | The abbot wrote down the rules the monks had to follow. | In the story, a greedy abbot hid the gold under the chapel floor.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: one abbot, two abbots. Use «an»: an abbot. Spelling: two b's, one t at the end. The female form is abbess. Do not mix up abbot (the leader) with abbey (the building and community): the abbot lives in the abbey. A monk is any member; the abbot is the head.

part of speech: adjective (acquainted — usually after a verb: be acquainted, get acquainted); also the past form of the verb acquaint (acquaint, acquaints, acquainted, acquainting)
meaning for a pupil: 1) If you are acquainted with someone, you know them a little, because you have met them, but they are not a close friend. 2) If you are acquainted with something, such as a book, a rule or a place, you know about it because you have read it, seen it or used it. 3) (formal) To get acquainted means to meet and start to know each other.
its sense in the lessons: It tells the reader how well people know each other: «acquainted» is less than friends. In formal writing and old stories people are «acquainted» or «introduced». At school: «Get acquainted with the rules before the test.» Phrases: be acquainted with, get acquainted, become acquainted, well acquainted with, acquaint yourself with.
examples from the lessons: Are you two acquainted, or shall I introduce you? | I am acquainted with her brother, but I don't know her. | The new pupils spent the first day getting acquainted. | Please get acquainted with the fire drill before Monday. | Grandad is well acquainted with every path in these woods. | We were only slightly acquainted, so I was surprised she remembered my name. | Mr Bennet was acquainted with half the families in the village. | Before the experiment, acquaint yourself with the safety rules.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Always followed by «with»: acquainted with someone or something, not «acquainted to». Spelling: acq- (a, c, q): acquainted. Being acquainted is weaker than being friends. The noun is acquaintance: a person you know a little. «Get acquainted» is a bit formal; in everyday speech people say «get to know each other».

meaning for a pupil: 1) An aura is a special feeling or quality that seems to surround a person or place, like an air of calm, mystery or importance. 2) In pictures and stories, an aura is a soft glow of light around someone or something. 3) (medicine) Some people with migraines or epilepsy get an aura: strange lights, tingles or feelings just before the headache or the fit starts.
its sense in the lessons: In stories it tells the reader how a character or place feels to others: an aura of mystery, power, calm or danger. In art it is the glow around saints or magical beings. Some people believe everyone has a coloured aura that only special people can see; science has found no evidence for this. Phrases: an aura of mystery, an aura of calm, an aura about her.
examples from the lessons: The old house had an aura of mystery. | The head teacher had an aura of calm, even when the fire alarm went off. | In the painting, a golden aura glows around the angel. | The champion walked onto the court with an aura of confidence. | There was an aura of excitement in the hall before the show. | Before her migraine starts, Mum sees an aura of flashing zigzags. | The wizard's staff was surrounded by a blue aura.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: an aura, auras. Use «an»: an aura. Usually «an aura of» + a quality: an aura of mystery. Myth: «aura readers» say people give off coloured light; there is no scientific proof of this. Do not confuse with «oral» (spoken or about the mouth), which sounds a bit similar.

part of speech: noun (a bobble, bobbles); verb (bobble, bobbles, bobbled, bobbling)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (UK) A bobble is a small soft ball of wool on top of a woolly hat or on the end of a string; a bobble hat has one. 2) A bobble is also a tiny ball of fluff that forms on an old jumper or blanket after a lot of wear (also called a pill). 3) (verb) To bobble means to bounce or move up and down unsteadily, like a ball on bumpy ground. 4) (US, sport) To bobble the ball means to fumble it, to fail to catch or hold it cleanly.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life it comes in winter clothing (bobble hat) and in clothes that look old (a bobbly jumper). In sport commentary a ball bobbles on a bumpy pitch, and in American baseball and football a player bobbles a catch. Phrases: bobble hat, bobble on top, the ball bobbled.
examples from the lessons: Grandma knitted me a red hat with a big bobble on top. | My old jumper is covered in little bobbles. | Put on your bobble hat, it's freezing outside. | The ball bobbled over the bumpy grass and the goalie missed it. | The shortstop bobbled the ball and the runner reached first base. | The toy boat bobbled on the waves. | She uses a little shaver to take the bobbles off her cardigan.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: a bobble, bobbles. Verb past form: bobbled (double b, then -le, drop e: bobbling). Adjective: bobbly (a bobbly jumper). In the US a hat bobble is usually called a pom-pom, and a hat with one a knit cap or beanie with a pom-pom. Do not confuse with «bubble» (a ball of air in liquid) or «bauble» (a shiny decoration).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Bumpiness is how bumpy something is: how many lumps, holes or rough parts a surface has. 2) Bumpiness is also the feeling of being shaken up and down, like on a rough road, a bumpy flight or a choppy boat ride.
its sense in the lessons: In science and maths it describes how rough or smooth a surface is, for example when testing how far a toy car rolls on carpet, sand or a smooth floor (more bumpiness means more friction). In everyday life it describes rough journeys. Phrases: the bumpiness of the road, a bit of bumpiness.
examples from the lessons: The bumpiness of the old track made the bike rattle. | The pilot said to expect some bumpiness during the flight. | We measured how the bumpiness of the surface changed how far the car rolled. | The bumpiness of the lane made Dad drive very slowly. | Sandpaper has more bumpiness than glass, so there is more friction. | The baby slept through all the bumpiness of the bus ride.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: no plural, no «a» (say «some bumpiness» or «the bumpiness»). Made from bumpy + -ness; the y changes to i: bumpiness. Opposite: smoothness. On planes the proper word for bumpiness is turbulence.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) A canard is a false story or rumour that many people repeat and believe, especially one spread on purpose. 2) (aircraft) A canard is a small extra wing near the front of a plane, in front of the main wings. 3) (French) In French, «canard» is the ordinary word for a duck; in English it is not used for the bird.
its sense in the lessons: In news and history lessons it means a lie or myth that keeps going round, for example an old rumour about a person or group. It warns the reader that the story is false. Phrases: an old canard, a tired canard, repeat a canard.
examples from the lessons: The idea that we use only ten percent of our brains is an old canard. | The newspaper had to apologise for spreading the canard. | The teacher said that story about the king was a canard. | That plane has small canards in front of its main wings. | In Paris, Dad ordered «canard», which turned out to be duck. | Don't repeat that canard about goldfish having a three-second memory.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a canard, canards. Said «ka-NARD» or «KAN-ard». A formal, bookish word; in everyday talk say «a myth», «a rumour» or «a lie». It comes from French «canard» (duck); old French had a saying about «half-selling a duck», meaning cheating.

part of speech: noun (cardamom — uncountable as a spice; a cardamom pod, cardamom pods)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Cardamom is a sweet, strongly scented spice made from the small green or black seed pods of a plant in the ginger family. 2) The cardamom plant is the tall tropical plant that these pods grow on, mostly in India, Sri Lanka and Guatemala.
its sense in the lessons: In cooking it flavours curries, rice, Indian sweets, chai tea, Scandinavian buns and Arabic coffee. In geography and history lessons it is one of the spices traders carried along the spice routes. Phrases: cardamom pods, ground cardamom, a pinch of cardamom.
examples from the lessons: Mum crushed three cardamom pods for the rice. | The cinnamon and cardamom buns smelled wonderful. | Chai tea is spiced with cardamom, ginger and cloves. | Cardamom is one of the most expensive spices in the world. | Traders brought cardamom from India to Europe by ship. | Add a pinch of ground cardamom to the biscuit dough.
note for the reader of a maths problem: The spice is uncountable (some cardamom), but the pods are countable (two cardamom pods). Spelling: cardamom (ends -mom); «cardamon» is a common variant, but cardamom is the standard spelling. Said «KAR-da-mum».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Comical means funny, especially in a silly or odd way that makes people laugh, often without meaning to. 2) Comical can also mean so silly or badly done that it is almost a joke.
its sense in the lessons: In stories it tells the reader that a sight or situation is funny: a comical hat, a comical fall, a comical face. It often describes something that is not trying to be funny but is. Phrases: comical sight, look comical, a comical mistake, almost comical.
examples from the lessons: The puppy looked comical in its tiny raincoat. | Grandad pulled a comical face and the baby giggled. | It was a comical sight: the clown slipping on a banana skin. | The penguins waddled along in a comical line. | His excuse was so bad it was almost comical. | The cat's comical leap into the box made us all laugh.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective; adverb: comically (comically large shoes). «Comical» and «comic» are close: a comic is also a noun (a comic book, a comedian), but «comical» is only an adjective. Comical often means funny without meaning to be, while «a comedy» is meant to be funny.

part of speech: noun (condemnation — mostly uncountable; a condemnation, condemnations)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Condemnation is strong public disapproval: saying clearly that something is very wrong or bad. 2) (law) Condemnation is the act of a court sentencing someone to a punishment. 3) Condemnation of a building is an official decision that it is unsafe and must not be used.
its sense in the lessons: In news and history lessons leaders and countries make a «condemnation» of a war, an attack or cruelty. In stories it shows harsh judgement. Phrases: strong condemnation, widespread condemnation, condemnation of the attack, a statement of condemnation.
examples from the lessons: The attack drew condemnation from leaders around the world. | The head teacher's condemnation of the bullying was very clear. | There was strong condemnation of the cruelty to the animals. | After the flood, the condemnation of the old bridge meant nobody could cross it. | The prisoner waited in silence for his condemnation. | The judge's words were a condemnation of the whole plan.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Made from the verb condemn (ends in a silent n: con-DEM) + -ation: condemnation, where the n is now heard (con-dem-NAY-shun). Usually «condemnation of» something. Do not confuse with «condensation» (water drops forming on a cold surface): they look and sound alike.

part of speech: adjective (deadpan); adverb (deadpan); noun (deadpan — uncountable); verb (deadpan, deadpans, deadpanned, deadpanning)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Deadpan describes a way of telling a joke or saying something funny with a completely serious, blank face and flat voice, as if you do not know it is funny. 2) (verb) To deadpan means to say something in this serious, expressionless way. 3) A deadpan face or look is one that shows no feeling at all.
its sense in the lessons: In lessons on humour, hyperbole and understatement it is a key style: the speaker says something silly or huge as if it is perfectly ordinary, and that makes it funnier. British humour often uses it. It tells the reader the speaker is joking even though they look serious. Phrases: deadpan humour, a deadpan face, deadpan delivery, said deadpan.
examples from the lessons: «Oh, it's only a little rain,» Dad said deadpan, as water poured through the roof. | Her deadpan jokes make the whole class laugh. | He kept a deadpan face while the teacher read out his funny poem. | «I'm thrilled,» she deadpanned, looking at the pile of homework. | The comedian's deadpan delivery made the joke twice as funny. | British comedy often uses deadpan humour. | Try telling the joke deadpan, without smiling.
note for the reader of a maths problem: One word, no hyphen. Past form doubles the n: deadpanned, deadpanning. Deadpan is not the same as being rude or sad: the speaker is joking but hides it. It often goes with understatement: calling a huge storm «a bit breezy» in a deadpan voice.

part of speech: noun (disparagement — mostly uncountable; a disparagement, disparagements)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Disparagement is saying that someone or something is not good or not important, in an unkind or scornful way; putting it down. 2) A disparagement is one remark like that.
its sense in the lessons: In lessons on language and argument it is the opposite of praise: «downplaying» someone's work or calling it worthless. In stories it shows a mean or proud character. Phrases: words of disparagement, without disparagement, disparagement of others.
examples from the lessons: The rival team's coach spoke with disparagement about our players. | Her disparagement of his painting hurt his feelings. | The critic's review was full of disparagement. | «Only a little school play,» he said, with a hint of disparagement. | Good sports players avoid the disparagement of their opponents. | She ignored the disparagement and kept practising.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal word; everyday words are «putting down», «running down», «belittling». Verb: disparage (disparages, disparaged, disparaging); adjective: disparaging (a disparaging remark). Do not confuse with «disparity» (a big difference between things) or «despair» (losing all hope).

part of speech: adjective (displeasing, more displeasing, most displeasing); also the -ing form of the verb displease (displease, displeases, displeased, displeasing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Displeasing means not nice or not pleasant; making you feel annoyed, uncomfortable or unhappy. 2) (verb) Displeasing someone means making them annoyed or unhappy.
its sense in the lessons: A formal or old-fashioned word, common in classic stories and polite speech: something is «displeasing to the eye/ear» or «displeasing to the king». It is a softer, more polite way of saying «unpleasant» or «I don't like it» — a kind of understatement. Phrases: displeasing to the eye, displeasing to the ear, afraid of displeasing.
examples from the lessons: The sour smell was displeasing. | The ugly new wall was displeasing to the eye. | The squeaky violin made a displeasing sound. | The servant was afraid of displeasing the queen. | She found the cold, grey room rather displeasing. | Displeasing your coach by being late is a bad idea.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formed from dis- + pleasing. Everyday words: unpleasant, nasty, horrible. The past form displeased is common as an adjective: «Mum was displeased» (annoyed). Opposite: pleasing.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To downplay something means to make it seem smaller, less important or less serious than it really is. 2) Downplaying your own success means talking about it modestly, so you do not seem to show off.
its sense in the lessons: In lessons on hyperbole and understatement, downplaying is the opposite of exaggerating: saying «it's just a scratch» about a deep cut. In the news, leaders sometimes downplay a problem, and readers should ask whether it is worse than they say. In safety: never downplay an injury or a danger; tell an adult. Phrases: downplay the danger, downplay the problem, downplay your role.
examples from the lessons: He downplayed his injury, but his ankle was badly swollen. | «It was nothing,» she said, downplaying her prize. | The company tried to downplay the size of the oil spill. | Don't downplay a bad headache; tell the nurse. | The team captain downplayed her part in the win. | Understatement is a way of downplaying something on purpose for effect. | The mayor downplayed the flood risk, and many people were not ready.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb: downplayed, downplaying. One word, no hyphen. Opposite: exaggerate, overstate, play up. Downplaying can be modest and kind (about your own success) or dishonest (hiding how bad a danger is). Similar: play down («play down the problem»).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Eternity is time that goes on for ever, with no end. 2) (church) Christians and many other believers use eternity for the life after death that they believe never ends, with God. 3) (informal, hyperbole) An eternity is a very long time, or a time that feels very long: «I waited an eternity for the bus.»
its sense in the lessons: In religious education it means endless time and life after death («for all eternity»). In everyday talk and lessons on hyperbole it is a favourite exaggeration for a long, boring wait. In maths, eternity is like infinity for time: it never finishes. Phrases: for all eternity, an eternity, what seemed like an eternity, eternity ring.
examples from the lessons: The queue for the rollercoaster took an eternity. | Five minutes before the bell can feel like an eternity. | Christians believe that God is from eternity to eternity. | The ancient Egyptians wanted the pharaoh's body to last for eternity. | After what seemed like an eternity, the lost dog came home. | The prince promised to love her for all eternity. | Waiting for my test results felt like an eternity.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Mostly uncountable, but with «an» in the hyperbole sense: an eternity. Adjective: eternal (eternal life); adverb: eternally. Said «ih-TER-nih-tee». «An eternity» in everyday speech is an exaggeration: it might mean ten minutes, so it does not give a real number of hours.

part of speech: noun (a gazillion, gazillions); adjective-like number word (a gazillion stars) — informal
meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal, hyperbole) A gazillion is a made-up, huge number used to say «very, very many»; it is not a real number. 2) Gazillions means an enormous amount, more than anyone could count.
its sense in the lessons: In lessons on hyperbole it is a typical exaggeration: «I've told you a gazillion times!» It tells the reader that there are a lot, not an exact amount. Children also say zillion, bazillion, squillion, umpteen. In maths it is not a real number like million or billion. Phrases: a gazillion times, gazillions of, a gazillion and one.
examples from the lessons: I've asked you a gazillion times to tidy your room! | There were gazillions of ants on the picnic blanket. | She has a gazillion stickers in her collection. | The sky had a gazillion stars that night. | «How many questions are on the test?» «About a gazillion.» | The phone game has gazillions of players.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal; do not use it in serious writing or for a maths answer. A gazillion is NOT a real number: a million is 1,000,000 and a billion is 1,000,000,000, but a gazillion has no value. Other made-up words like it: zillion, jillion, bazillion, squillion. In a word problem, «a gazillion» is exaggeration and gives no number to calculate with.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Gusty weather has wind that blows in sudden strong bursts, then drops, then blows hard again. 2) (rare) Gusty can describe a sudden loud burst of laughter, a sigh or a feeling.
its sense in the lessons: In weather forecasts and geography lessons «gusty winds» warn of sudden strong blows that can knock things over, so take care on bikes, near trees and at the beach. In stories it sets a wild or stormy scene. Phrases: gusty winds, a gusty day, gusty showers.
examples from the lessons: It's a gusty day, so hold on to your umbrella. | Gusty winds blew the bins over in the night. | The forecast says gusty showers this afternoon. | Flying a kite is fun on a gusty afternoon. | The ferry was cancelled because of gusty conditions. | A gusty breeze rattled the windows. | On gusty days, the teacher doesn't let us use the climbing frame.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Comparative: gustier, gustiest (y changes to i). The noun is gust (a gust of wind = one sudden blow). A gusty wind is different from a steady wind: it keeps changing strength. Weather reports often give «gusts up to 60 mph», meaning the strongest bursts reach that speed, not the usual wind speed.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A hindrance is something or someone that makes it harder for you to do something or slows you down. 2) Hindrance is the act of getting in the way.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life and stories: a heavy bag, a bad leg, or a little brother who «helps» can be a hindrance. The phrase «more of a hindrance than a help» is a gentle, funny way of saying someone made things worse. Phrases: a hindrance to, more of a hindrance than a help, without hindrance.
examples from the lessons: My long scarf was a hindrance when I tried to climb the tree. | The puppy was more of a hindrance than a help in the garden. | The heavy rain was a hindrance to the rescue workers. | Not knowing the language can be a hindrance when you travel. | The ships passed through the canal without hindrance. | Noise in the classroom is a hindrance to learning.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelling trap: hindrance, NOT «hinderance»; the e of hinder drops. Verb: hinder (hinders, hindered, hindering) = to slow down or get in the way. Use «a»: a hindrance. Opposite: a help.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Hyperbolic language exaggerates on purpose, making things sound much bigger, better or worse than they really are, like «I'm so hungry I could eat a horse.» 2) (maths) Hyperbolic means to do with a hyperbola, a special open curve with two separate branches.
its sense in the lessons: In English lessons on hyperbole and understatement it describes exaggerated sentences used for effect or fun, not to trick. In adverts and news, readers should notice hyperbolic claims («the best ever!»). In higher maths there are hyperbolic curves and functions. Phrases: hyperbolic language, a hyperbolic claim, hyperbolic praise.
examples from the lessons: «This bag weighs a ton» is a hyperbolic way of saying it is heavy. | The advert made hyperbolic claims about the miracle shampoo. | Her hyperbolic story said the spider was the size of a dinner plate. | We underlined all the hyperbolic phrases in the poem. | He gave hyperbolic praise: «the greatest sandwich in history». | A hyperbola is a curve, and things to do with it are called hyperbolic.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Said «hy-per-BOL-ik»; the noun hyperbole is said «hy-PER-bo-lee» (four parts, not «hyper-bowl»). Adverb: hyperbolically. Opposite in style: understated (using understatement, or litotes). Hyperbole is not lying: everyone knows it is exaggerated.
