meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) An infirmity is a physical or mental weakness or illness, especially one that comes with old age. 2) Infirmity is the state of being weak or ill for a long time.
its sense in the lessons: A formal or old-fashioned word in history, classic stories and the Bible («the infirmities of age»). Today people more often say «illness», «disability» or «frailty». It tells the reader that a character is weak, ill or very old. Phrases: the infirmities of old age, illness and infirmity.
examples from the lessons: Grandad never complained about the infirmities of old age. | The old king's infirmity meant his son ruled for him. | The hospital was built for the sick and those in infirmity. | Despite her infirmity, she walked to church every Sunday. | In the Bible, Jesus is described as healing many infirmities. | The almshouse was for poor people who could no longer work because of infirmity.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; a doctor would say illness or condition. The adjective is infirm (weak from age or illness). An infirmary is an old word for a hospital or a sick room in a school. Be respectful: do not use «infirm» as an insult.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An insider is a person who belongs to a group, club, company or organisation and so knows how it works and what is happening inside it. 2) Insider information is secret knowledge that only people inside a group have.
its sense in the lessons: In news and history lessons «insiders» are the people who know secrets; in detective stories the thief may be «an insider» who worked at the bank. In money and law, «insider trading» is using secret company information to buy or sell shares, which is a crime. Phrases: an insider's view, an insider job, insider tips, insider trading.
examples from the lessons: The police think the robbery was an inside job, done by an insider. | Grandad was a football insider: he knew all the players. | A theatre insider told us how the scenery is moved. | The book gives an insider's view of life in the palace. | New pupils can feel like outsiders until they make friends and become insiders. | Using insider information to buy shares is against the law.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: an insider, insiders. Use «an». Opposite: outsider (someone who does not belong or is not part of the group). «An inside job» means a crime done with help from someone inside.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Litotes is a kind of understatement where you say something by saying that its opposite is not true, like «not bad» meaning «good» or «not a small problem» meaning «a big problem». 2) It is a figure of speech, a way of using words for a special effect.
its sense in the lessons: In lessons on hyperbole and understatement, litotes is a cousin of understatement: «She's not unfriendly» means she is fairly friendly; «It's not the worst idea» means it is quite good. It is very common in British and Irish speech and in old poems such as Beowulf. It can sound modest, polite, ironic or dry. Phrases: an example of litotes, using litotes.
examples from the lessons: «Not bad at all,» said Dad, which is litotes for «very good». | «He's no fool» is an example of litotes. | Saying a hurricane is «not exactly a light breeze» uses litotes. | We found three examples of litotes in the poem. | «I wasn't unhappy with my mark» means I was pleased. | Old English poets loved litotes, like «that was no small gift».
note for the reader of a maths problem: Said «LY-toe-teez» or «ly-TOE-teez» (four sounds, the final -es says «eez»). It is the same word for one example or many. Litotes uses a double negative on purpose: «not unkind» = kind (a bit). The opposite figure of speech is hyperbole (big exaggeration).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Lovingly means in a way that shows love and care. 2) Lovingly also means very carefully and gently, with great attention, because you care about doing something well.
its sense in the lessons: In stories it tells the reader how a character feels: a mother looks lovingly at her baby; Grandad lovingly fixes an old clock. It often describes careful handwork. Phrases: look lovingly at, lovingly made, lovingly restored, lovingly cared for.
examples from the lessons: Mum looked lovingly at the new baby. | The cake was lovingly decorated by Gran. | The old train was lovingly restored by volunteers. | He lovingly stroked the cat's soft fur. | She wrapped each present lovingly. | The garden is lovingly cared for by the whole street.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from loving + -ly. Spelling: lovingly (drop the e of love before -ing). Adjective: loving (a loving family).

part of speech: adjective (mad, madder, maddest); noun (madder — uncountable; a madder plant)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Madder is the comparative of mad: more angry. 2) (informal, mostly UK) Madder means more crazy, silly or wild. 3) Madder is a plant with roots that give a red dye, and the red colour made from it, used for thousands of years to dye cloth.
its sense in the lessons: Mostly it is the -er form of mad in everyday speech: «He got madder and madder.» In US English mad usually means angry; in UK English mad usually means crazy or silly («mad about football» = loves it). In history and art lessons madder is a natural red dye, used for British soldiers' red coats and old paintings. Phrases: madder and madder, madder than ever, madder red, rose madder.
examples from the lessons: The longer she waited, the madder she got. | That's an even madder idea than the last one! | Dad got madder when the car still wouldn't start. | Madder roots were boiled to make red dye. | The painter used rose madder for the sunset. | The soldiers' coats were dyed with madder.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Double d in madder and maddest (short vowel + one consonant). Mad has two senses: angry (especially US) and crazy (especially UK); be careful, «mad» can be unkind when used about people with mental illness. As a plant and colour, madder is an uncountable noun.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Mono is short for monophonic: sound recorded or played through one channel, so it comes from one speaker and not left and right like stereo. 2) (US, informal, medicine) Mono is short for mononucleosis, an illness caused by a virus that makes you very tired with a sore throat and swollen glands (in the UK called glandular fever). 3) Mono- at the start of a word means one or single, as in monorail, monologue, monochrome, monotone. 4) (informal) Mono can be short for monochrome (one colour, or black and white).
its sense in the lessons: In science and music lessons it is the opposite of stereo. In maths and science, the prefix mono- means one (a monomer, a monoplane). In health it is the «kissing disease» passed through spit. Phrases: in mono, mono sound, have mono.
examples from the lessons: Old records were recorded in mono. | Switch the headphones to mono if one ear doesn't work. | My cousin had mono and missed three weeks of school. | A monorail runs on just one rail. | A monologue is a speech by one person. | Don't share drinks: mono spreads through spit. | The photo looks great in mono.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A clipped word: say what it is short for. «Mono» (sound) is the opposite of stereo (two channels). The prefix mono- = 1, bi- = 2, tri- = 3, poly- = many: a monoplane has one pair of wings, a biplane two. The illness is called glandular fever in the UK and Australia.

part of speech: noun (a muff, muffs); verb (muff, muffs, muffed, muffing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A muff is a soft tube of fur or warm cloth that you put both hands into from each end to keep them warm, worn in old times. 2) Ear muffs are two soft pads joined by a band that keep your ears warm or block out loud noise. 3) (verb, informal) To muff something means to do it badly or miss it, especially to drop a catch or spoil a chance. 4) (rude, adult slang) a rude word grown-ups use; not for school.
its sense in the lessons: In history and old stories, ladies carry fur muffs in winter. In safety, ear muffs protect hearing near loud machines or at fireworks. In sport and everyday talk «muff it» means to mess up a chance. Phrases: ear muffs, muff a catch, muff it, muff your lines.
examples from the lessons: In the old painting, the lady carries a fur muff. | Wear ear muffs when you use the loud drill. | Grandma's muff kept her hands warm on the sleigh ride. | The fielder muffed an easy catch. | I muffed my lines in the school play. | Don't muff your chance to score!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: a muff, muffs; usually «ear muffs» (also earmuffs). Verb past: muffed, muffing (double f). The verb sense is informal; a cleaner everyday word is «fumble» or «mess up».

part of speech: adjective (ossified); also the past form of the verb ossify (ossify, ossifies, ossified, ossifying)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (science) Ossified means turned into bone: soft cartilage that has hardened into bone, as happens in a growing child's skeleton. 2) (formal) Ossified describes ideas, rules or groups that have become fixed, stiff and unable to change, like old dry bones.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about the human body, a baby's skeleton is partly soft cartilage that slowly becomes ossified as the child grows. In history and argument it describes old-fashioned systems that never change: «an ossified government». Phrases: became ossified, ossified ideas, ossified rules.
examples from the lessons: A baby's skull is not fully ossified, so it has soft spots. | As children grow, cartilage in the bones becomes ossified. | The old club had ossified rules that nobody dared to change. | The teacher said the empire's government had become ossified and slow. | The X-ray showed which bones had ossified. | Some ideas grow ossified if nobody questions them.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From Latin «os» = bone. Verb ossify: ossifies, ossified (y changes to i). Noun: ossification. The second sense is figurative and formal. Do not confuse with «fossilised», which means preserved in rock; but both can be used for ideas that are stuck in the past.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (formal) Pertinent means closely connected to the subject being talked about, and useful for it; relevant.
its sense in the lessons: In school and exam writing pupils are asked to give «pertinent details» or «pertinent evidence»: facts that really answer the question. In meetings and courts a pertinent question goes straight to the point. Phrases: pertinent to, a pertinent question, pertinent facts, pertinent information.
examples from the lessons: That's a very pertinent question. | Only include facts pertinent to the topic. | The detective noticed one pertinent detail: the muddy boots. | Choose the quotation most pertinent to the question. | Is that pertinent to our science project, or is it off topic? | The judge asked the witness for any pertinent information.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Formal; everyday word: relevant. Used with «to»: pertinent to the question. Noun: pertinence. Opposite: irrelevant (or impertinent in an old sense; today impertinent means rude and cheeky to an older person).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Pleasantly means in a nice, enjoyable or friendly way. 2) Pleasantly also means to a nice degree: «pleasantly warm» is warm in a comfortable way.
its sense in the lessons: In stories it describes friendly smiles, nice weather and good surprises. Often used in «pleasantly surprised», which is a modest, understated way of saying you liked something more than you expected. Phrases: pleasantly surprised, smile pleasantly, pleasantly warm, pleasantly cool.
examples from the lessons: She smiled pleasantly at the new neighbours. | The water was pleasantly warm. | I was pleasantly surprised by my test mark. | A pleasantly cool breeze came off the sea. | The afternoon passed pleasantly in the garden. | He talked pleasantly with the shopkeeper.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adverb from pleasant + -ly. Spelling: pleas-ANT-ly (pleasant, not «plesent»). «Pleasantly surprised» often means «happier than expected», a kind of mild understatement.

part of speech: noun (rationing — uncountable); also the -ing form of the verb ration (ration, rations, rationed, rationing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (history) Rationing is a system in which the government limits how much food, fuel or clothes each person may have, because there is not enough for everyone, as in Britain during and after the Second World War. 2) Rationing is any sharing out of something in small fixed amounts so it lasts, for example water on a boat or sweets in a holiday.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons about the Second World War, families had ration books with coupons for butter, sugar, meat, eggs and sweets; sweet rationing in Britain ended in 1953. In maths, rationing problems share a total equally: 20 biscuits rationed over 5 days is 4 a day. In survival and safety it means making supplies last. Phrases: wartime rationing, food rationing, water rationing, ration book, rationing ended.
examples from the lessons: During the war, rationing meant each person got only a small amount of butter a week. | Sweet rationing ended in Britain in 1953. | The sailors began rationing their water when the wind dropped. | We're rationing the chocolate so it lasts all holiday. | Gran still remembers her ration book. | In the drought there was water rationing, so no hosepipes. | If 30 sweets are rationed over 10 days, each day gets 3.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable noun. The verb ration (rations, rationed, rationing) is regular. A ration is one fixed share. Said «RASH-un-ing» (UK and US); some Americans say «RAY-shun-ing». Maths: rationing usually means total ÷ number of days or people = the share each one gets.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A sackful is the amount that one sack holds, or a whole sack full of something. 2) (informal, hyperbole) A sackful can mean a large amount of something, like a sackful of letters or presents.
its sense in the lessons: In stories Father Christmas carries a sackful of presents; farmers and millers carry sackfuls of grain, potatoes or flour. In maths a sackful is a unit: «Each sackful weighs 25 kg.» Phrases: a sackful of, sackfuls of.
examples from the lessons: Santa carried a sackful of presents down the chimney. | The farmer sold ten sackfuls of potatoes. | The miller ground a sackful of wheat into flour. | We got a sackful of fan letters after the show. | Each sackful of sand weighs 20 kilograms. | The children collected a sackful of conkers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a sackful, plural usually sackfuls. One l at the end: -ful, not -full. Maths: «3 sackfuls of 25 kg» = 3 × 25 = 75 kg.

part of speech: noun (a sire, sires; Sire — a title); verb (sire, sires, sired, siring)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (old-fashioned) Sire was a way of speaking to a king, like «Your Majesty»: «Yes, sire.» 2) The sire of an animal, especially a horse or dog, is its father. 3) (verb) To sire means to be the father of a young animal (or, in old writing, of a child). 4) (old-fashioned) Sire was also an old word for a lord or a father.
its sense in the lessons: In fairy tales and historical stories, servants and knights say «sire» to the king. In farming, horse racing and dog breeding, the sire is the father and the dam is the mother. Phrases: «Yes, sire», the sire of the foal, sired by.
examples from the lessons: «Your horse is ready, sire,» said the stable boy. | «Forgive me, sire,» the knight said, bowing to the king. | The famous racehorse sired many champion foals. | The puppy's sire was a prize-winning sheepdog. | The farmer chose a strong bull to sire the calves. | In the old tale, the prince's sire was a wise king.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Said like «sigh-er» (one or two beats). Do not confuse with «sir» (polite word for any man) — «sire» is only for kings or very old style. Animal parents: sire = father, dam = mother. Regular verb: sired, siring.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In someone's stead means in their place, instead of them. 2) To stand someone in good stead means to be very useful to them later. 3) (old) Stead was an old word for a place or a farm, which survives in place names and the word homestead.
its sense in the lessons: Mostly found in fixed phrases and old or formal writing. «Instead» is made from «in» + «stead». «Practising your times tables will stand you in good stead» means it will help you later. Phrases: in his stead, in her stead, stand you in good stead.
examples from the lessons: The captain was ill, so his deputy led the team in his stead. | Learning to swim will stand you in good stead. | The king could not come, so he sent his son in his stead. | Good manners will always stand you in good stead. | Reading every day stood her in good stead for the exam. | The settlers built a homestead on the prairie.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Not used on its own in everyday speech; use «instead» or «in place of». Same root as «instead», «homestead» and «steadfast». Do not confuse with «steed» (an old word for a horse).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Steepness is how steep something is: how sharply a slope, hill, road or roof goes up or down. 2) (maths) In maths the steepness of a line is measured by its gradient or slope: how far it goes up for every step across.
its sense in the lessons: In geography it describes hills and mountains (steepness is shown by contour lines that are close together on a map). In science, a ramp's steepness changes how fast a toy car rolls. In maths a steeper line on a graph shows something changing faster. Phrases: the steepness of the hill, the steepness of the slope.
examples from the lessons: The steepness of the hill made us get off our bikes and push. | On a map, close contour lines show great steepness. | We changed the steepness of the ramp and timed the car. | The steepness of the roof lets snow slide off. | The steepness of the line on the graph shows how fast the plant grew. | Grandad was worried about the steepness of the steps.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable: no «a», no plural. From steep + -ness. In maths: gradient = rise ÷ run (how far up ÷ how far across); a bigger number means a steeper line. A steeper slope is harder to climb but quicker to roll down.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A thoroughfare is a main road or street through a town or city, used by a lot of traffic and people. 2) A thoroughfare is also any route or passage that people go through from one place to another.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and local history it names the busy main roads of a town. On signs «No thoroughfare» means you may not go through: it is a private road or a dead end. Phrases: a busy thoroughfare, main thoroughfare, no thoroughfare.
examples from the lessons: Oxford Street is a busy London thoroughfare. | The old market square was the town's main thoroughfare. | The sign on the gate said «No thoroughfare». | The alley is a popular thoroughfare for pupils walking to school. | Cross the busy thoroughfare only at the lights. | Horses and carts once filled the city's thoroughfares.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable. Spelling: thorough + fare: tho-rough-fare. «Thorough» here keeps its old meaning «through». «No thoroughfare» on a sign means no way through, not «no fare to pay».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A transcription is a written copy of something that was spoken, recorded or written somewhere else. 2) Transcription is the act of writing down speech or copying a text. 3) (language) A phonetic transcription writes how words sound using special symbols, like in a dictionary. 4) (music) A transcription is a piece of music rewritten for different instruments. 5) (science) In biology, transcription is the copying of information from DNA in a cell.
its sense in the lessons: In lessons it is how interviews, speeches and old documents are written down; dictionaries give a transcription showing pronunciation. In history, scholars make transcriptions of old handwriting. Phrases: a transcription of the interview, phonetic transcription, make a transcription.
examples from the lessons: The teacher gave us a transcription of the radio interview. | Read the transcription of the king's speech. | The dictionary shows the transcription of every word in special symbols. | Volunteers made a transcription of the old diaries. | The band played a transcription of a piano piece for guitars. | In cells, transcription copies a message from DNA.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Verb: transcribe (transcribes, transcribed, transcribing). Note: transcribe has a b, transcription has a p. Do not confuse with «translation» (changing words into another language): a transcription keeps the same language.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To unfasten something means to open it or undo it, such as a button, buckle, belt, seat belt, clasp or lock. 2) Unfasten also means to come undone: «The strap unfastened.»
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life you unfasten your coat, shoes or bag; in safety: never unfasten your seat belt while the car or plane is moving, and wait until the sign is off. Phrases: unfasten your seat belt, unfasten the buckle, unfasten the straps.
examples from the lessons: Please do not unfasten your seat belt until the plane has stopped. | She unfastened her coat in the warm classroom. | He unfastened the gate and let the dog in. | Can you help me unfasten this necklace? | The baby learnt to unfasten the straps of his pushchair. | Unfasten the buckles of your helmet before you take it off.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Regular verb. The t is silent: «un-FAH-sen» (UK) or «un-FAS-en» (US), like «fasten». Same meaning as «undo». Opposite: fasten, do up.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Untranslatable describes a word or phrase that has no exact match in another language, so it cannot be translated easily without a long explanation or losing some meaning.
its sense in the lessons: In language lessons, French, Mandarin and Ukrainian classes and lessons on jokes and wordplay, pupils learn that some words, puns and jokes are untranslatable: the meaning can be explained, but the fun or feeling may be lost. Famous examples are Danish «hygge» (cosy togetherness) or Portuguese «saudade» (a sad longing). Phrases: untranslatable word, almost untranslatable, an untranslatable pun.
examples from the lessons: Some jokes are untranslatable because they are based on puns. | «Hygge» is often called an untranslatable Danish word. | The poem's rhymes are almost untranslatable. | The teacher said the Ukrainian word was untranslatable, then explained it in a sentence. | Every language has a few untranslatable words. | The author's wordplay was untranslatable, so the translator added notes.
note for the reader of a maths problem: un- + translate + -able; drop the e of translate: translatable. Myth: «untranslatable» rarely means no meaning can be given; usually it means there is no single matching word, and a phrase is needed instead.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Ventriloquism is the skill of speaking without moving your lips, so the voice seems to come from somewhere else, usually a puppet or dummy on your knee.
its sense in the lessons: In stories, fairs and talent shows a ventriloquist makes a dummy seem to talk. In science lessons it shows how our brains guess where a sound comes from by what we see. Phrases: a ventriloquism act, ventriloquism show.
examples from the lessons: She won the talent show with her ventriloquism act. | Ventriloquism takes lots of practice in front of a mirror. | In ventriloquism, sounds like b and p are the hardest to say without moving your lips. | The ventriloquism made it seem as if the dummy was singing. | Long ago, ventriloquism was used to make people think spirits were speaking. | We watched a ventriloquism show at the seaside.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. The person is a ventriloquist; the puppet is a dummy. Said «ven-TRIL-o-kwiz-um». From Latin for «speaking from the belly», but the voice really comes from the throat and mouth. Ventriloquists cannot actually throw their voice; it is a trick of attention.

part of speech: noun (a wad, wads); verb (wad, wads, wadded, wadding)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A wad is a thick soft lump or roll of material, such as cotton wool, paper or chewing gum. 2) A wad of money or paper is a thick bundle of banknotes or sheets. 3) (verb) To wad something means to press it into a soft lump: «He wadded up the paper.»
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life: a wad of tissues, a wad of gum under a desk, a wad of cash in a film robbery. In stories a «wad of notes» tells the reader someone is rich or is paying a bribe. Phrases: a wad of cash, a wad of paper, wad up, a wad of gum.
examples from the lessons: The nurse pressed a wad of cotton wool on my cut. | Someone left a wad of gum under the desk. | The robber pulled out a thick wad of banknotes. | He wadded up the paper and threw it in the bin. | She had a wad of homework sheets to mark. | Stuff a wad of newspaper in your wet shoes to dry them.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a wad, wads. Verb past: wadded, wadding (double d). «Wadding» is also soft padding material. Do not confuse with «wade» (walk through water).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A worrier is a person who worries a lot, often about small things or things that may never happen.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and lessons on feelings, a worrier is a character who is anxious and keeps thinking about what could go wrong. Worry is normal, and it helps to tell someone you trust. Phrases: a born worrier, a bit of a worrier, a natural worrier, a big worrier.
examples from the lessons: My little brother is a real worrier; he checks his bag five times. | Mum is a bit of a worrier when we go camping. | Worriers often feel better after they talk about their fears. | Grandad calls himself a born worrier. | The worrier in the story was sure the bridge would fall down. | Don't be such a worrier; we'll get there on time.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable: a worrier, worriers. From worry + -er; the y changes to i: worrier. Spelling: two r's, then -ier. Do not confuse with «warrior» (a fighter): they look alike.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Wriggly describes something that twists and turns its body a lot, like a worm or a fish. 2) Wriggly also describes a person, especially a child, who cannot keep still. 3) A wriggly line is wavy, with lots of little bends.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons about minibeasts, worms and caterpillars are wriggly. At home and in class, a wriggly toddler or pupil cannot sit still. In art and writing, a wriggly line shows movement. Phrases: wriggly worms, a wriggly toddler, a wriggly line.
examples from the lessons: We found three wriggly worms under the stone. | The wriggly baby wouldn't stay still for the photo. | The fish was so wriggly I couldn't hold it. | Draw a wriggly line under the spelling mistake. | Tadpoles are tiny wriggly creatures. | The class was wriggly after lunch.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From the verb wriggle (wriggles, wriggled, wriggling) + -y: drop the e. Comparative: wrigglier, wriggliest. The w is silent: «RIG-lee». Also spelled the same in all English-speaking countries.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Something put in the wrong time, especially in a story or picture, like a wristwatch on a Roman soldier. 2) A person, custom or thing that seems old-fashioned and belongs to an earlier time.
its sense in the lessons: In history and reading lessons, spotting an anachronism means noticing that something could not have existed then; it tells the reader a writer or film-maker made a mistake or is playing a joke. Phrases: «a glaring anachronism», «a bit of an anachronism», «spot the anachronism».
examples from the lessons: The film showed a knight with a mobile phone, which is a funny anachronism. | Can you spot the anachronism in this picture of ancient Egypt? | A clock striking in Julius Caesar's Rome is an anachronism, because such clocks did not exist yet. | Some people think writing cheques is an anachronism now that we pay by phone. | Grandad says the old red phone box is a lovely anachronism. | Our teacher hid three anachronisms in the story about the Vikings. | A dinosaur next to cavemen is a famous anachronism in cartoons. | The steam train in the medieval story was an anachronism.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun; plural «anachronisms». Adjective «anachronistic». Pronounced a-NAK-ro-nism. Do not confuse with «acronym» (a word made from first letters, like NASA). Dinosaurs and people never lived at the same time, so cartoons showing them together are anachronisms, not history.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A comparison that explains one thing by showing how it is like another, for example saying the heart is like a pump. 2) (school, olympiad) A puzzle of the form «A is to B as C is to D», like «hot is to cold as up is to down». 3) A likeness between two things in some way.
its sense in the lessons: In science an analogy helps explain something hard with something familiar (electricity flowing like water in pipes). In English and reasoning tests, analogies are word puzzles where you find the same link between two pairs. Phrases: «draw an analogy», «by analogy», «a good analogy», «an analogy between».
examples from the lessons: The teacher used the analogy of a pump to explain how the heart works. | Bird is to nest as bee is to hive — can you finish the analogy? | Comparing the eye to a camera is a common analogy. | By analogy with «sing, sang», some children say «bring, brang», but it is «brought». | There is an analogy between a city and an ant colony: both need workers and roads. | Our olympiad paper had ten analogy questions. | Every analogy breaks down somewhere: the heart is not really made of metal. | Hand is to glove as foot is to sock.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; plural «analogies» (y changes to ies). Adjective «analogous» (similar). An analogy shows likeness in one way, not that things are the same — a trap in arguments. In «A is to B as C is to D», find the link between A and B first, then apply the same link to C.

meaning for a pupil: 1) Anyway; used to go back to the main point or to say something is true whatever happened: «Anyhow, we got home safely.» 2) In spite of something: «It was raining, but we went anyhow.» 3) (informal) Carelessly, in no order: «clothes thrown down anyhow».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday speech and stories «anyhow» moves the talk on or shows a decision does not change. Phrases: «anyhow, …», «do it anyhow», «just anyhow».
examples from the lessons: Anyhow, that's enough about my holiday — how was yours? | The shop was shut, but we didn't need milk anyhow. | She was tired, but she finished her homework anyhow. | He threw his school bag down anyhow and ran outside. | I don't know how it got broken; anyhow, we need a new one. | It's too late to go swimming anyhow. | The books were piled up anyhow on the floor.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Means almost the same as «anyway», which is more common. Not «anyhows». Do not mix up with «any how» written as two words (rare). It changes nothing in the numbers of a maths problem.

meaning for a pupil: 1) An alcoholic drink for adults, made from grain (usually barley) and hops, fizzy and often golden or brown; it is not for children. 2) A glass, can or bottle of this drink: «He ordered a beer.» 3) In some drink names that have no alcohol, like «root beer» or «ginger beer», which children can drink.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and adult-life lessons beer appears at pubs, barbecues and sports matches; grown-ups may drink it, and the law says children must not buy or drink it. Drinking too much makes people drunk and is unsafe for driving. Phrases: «a pint of beer», «beer garden» (outdoor area of a pub), «ginger beer», «root beer».
examples from the lessons: Dad had one beer at the barbecue and then switched to water. | Beer is made from barley, water, hops and yeast. | You must be an adult to buy beer. | Ginger beer is a fizzy soft drink that children can have. | Root beer is popular in the USA and has no alcohol. | The pub has a beer garden with a play area. | People should never drive after drinking beer. | In the story, the farmer brewed beer in a big wooden barrel.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable as a drink («some beer»), countable as a serving («two beers»). It contains alcohol, which is harmful to children's growing bodies. «Ginger beer» and «root beer» are usually soft drinks despite the name — a trap. Do not confuse with «bier» (a stand for a coffin), which sounds the same.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who boasts: someone who talks too proudly about what they have or can do, often making it bigger than it really is.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and lessons on hyperbole, a boaster exaggerates to look important, and the story often shows him being caught out, as in fables. Related: «boast», «boastful», «show-off», «big-head» (UK informal), «bragger».
examples from the lessons: Nobody believed the boaster who said he could run faster than a car. | Toad was a terrible boaster in «The Wind in the Willows». | Don't be a boaster — let your work speak for itself. | The boaster said he had a hundred pets, but he only had a goldfish. | In the fable, the boaster bragged about jumping far, and the town asked him to show them. | A boaster often uses words like «the best ever» and «millions». | My cousin is a bit of a boaster about his football goals.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; plural «boasters». Verb «boast (boasts, boasted)», adjective «boastful». More common words: «show-off», «bragger». A boaster's numbers are often exaggerated, so in a problem do not trust them as exact.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a way that is typical of a particular person or thing; as they usually do: «Characteristically, Grandma brought cake.» 2) In a way that shows a special feature of something: «The leaves are characteristically heart-shaped.»
its sense in the lessons: In stories it tells the reader that a character acted just as you would expect from them. In science it describes the typical features used to recognise a plant, animal or material. Related: «characteristic» (a typical feature), «typically».
examples from the lessons: Characteristically, Toad crashed the car on his first day. | The cat characteristically ignored us when we came home. | Holly leaves are characteristically spiky. | She answered characteristically fast, with her hand up first. | Characteristically for a cheetah, it sprinted and then rested. | He was characteristically late for the bus. | The weather was characteristically wet for a Manchester spring.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Long word: char-ac-ter-IS-tic-al-ly (ends in «-ally», not «-aly»). Opposite: «uncharacteristically» (not like them at all). Means the same as «typically» but more formal.

part of speech: noun (a clop, clops); verb (clop, clops, clopped, clopping)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (noun) The hollow knocking sound of a horse's hooves on a hard road. 2) (verb) To walk making that sound, like a horse on cobbles, or a person in hard heavy shoes.
its sense in the lessons: In stories it is an onomatopoeia — a word that sounds like what it means — telling the reader a horse is coming. Often doubled: «clip-clop», «clop, clop, clop».
examples from the lessons: Clip-clop, clip-clop went the pony down the lane. | We heard the clop of hooves outside the window. | The horse clopped slowly across the cobbled square. | My little sister clopped around in Mum's high heels. | Clop, clop — the milk cart came round the corner. | The donkey's hooves clopped on the stones. | In the poem, the clop of the horse woke the village.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past form «clopped», «-ing» form «clopping» (double p). An example of onomatopoeia, like «buzz» and «splash». «Clip-clop» is the most common form in children's books.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The time in the early morning when light first appears in the sky; dawn.
its sense in the lessons: In stories daybreak marks the start of a journey or the end of a long night; in science it links to sunrise and the Earth turning. Phrases: «at daybreak», «before daybreak», «from daybreak till dusk».
examples from the lessons: We set off at daybreak to catch the early ferry. | The rooster crows at daybreak. | The soldiers waited until daybreak to cross the river. | Farmers often work from daybreak till dusk. | By daybreak the snow had covered the whole garden. | Birds sing loudest just before daybreak, in the dawn chorus. | Daybreak comes earlier in summer than in winter.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable, usually with «at»: «at daybreak». Means the same as «dawn» and «first light»; opposite «dusk», «nightfall». Daybreak is a little before sunrise, when the sky already lightens but the Sun is not yet up.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (computers) To find and fix the mistakes (bugs) in a computer program. 2) To find and fix problems in any plan or machine. 3) (rare) To remove insects or hidden listening devices from a place.
its sense in the lessons: In coding lessons debugging means running the program, seeing what goes wrong, finding the line with the mistake and fixing it — step by step. Phrases: «debug the code», «a debugging tool», «debug your program».
examples from the lessons: Our robot kept turning left, so we had to debug the program. | Debugging means finding the mistake and fixing it. | It took me ten minutes to debug my Scratch game. | The teacher showed us how to debug by testing one step at a time. | Good programmers spend lots of time debugging. | We debugged our plan for the school fair after the first test run. | The spy movie showed agents debugging a hotel room.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past form «debugged», «-ing» form «debugging» (double g). Noun «a bug» = a mistake in a program. A famous story says the word «bug» came from a moth found in an early computer, but people already used «bug» for faults before that — a common myth.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (a name of a country) From or connected with the Dominican Republic, a country in the Caribbean sharing an island with Haiti; also a person from there. 2) (a name of a country) From or connected with Dominica, a small different island country in the Caribbean. 3) (church) A Dominican is a friar or nun of the Dominican Order, a Catholic religious order started by Saint Dominic in the 1200s.
its sense in the lessons: It is a proper adjective and name, so it is normally written with a capital D. In geography it names people from these Caribbean countries; in church history it names an order of preaching friars. Phrases: «the Dominican Republic», «a Dominican friar».
examples from the lessons: The Dominican Republic is on the island of Hispaniola. | Many famous baseball players are Dominican. | Dominica and the Dominican Republic are two different countries. | A Dominican friar wears a white habit with a black cloak. | Our neighbour is Dominican and speaks Spanish at home. | The Dominicans were founded to preach and teach.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A proper noun and adjective, written «Dominican» with a capital D. Do not confuse the Dominican Republic (Spanish-speaking, large) with Dominica (English-speaking, small island). Friars of the Dominican Order are sometimes called «Black Friars».

meaning for a pupil: 1) The state of understanding something clearly after it was puzzling; gaining knowledge. 2) (history) The Enlightenment: a time in Europe in the 1700s when thinkers said people should use reason, science and evidence and question old ideas. 3) (religion) In Buddhism, a state of perfect understanding and peace that Buddhists believe the Buddha reached.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons the Enlightenment is the age of scientists and thinkers like Isaac Newton, Voltaire and Benjamin Franklin, and of ideas about rights and freedom. In everyday speech it means finally understanding. Phrases: «the Age of Enlightenment», «seek enlightenment», «for your enlightenment» (humorous).
examples from the lessons: After the teacher's diagram, I felt a moment of enlightenment. | The Enlightenment was a time of new ideas about science and freedom. | Thinkers of the Enlightenment said people should question kings. | Buddhists believe the Buddha reached enlightenment under a tree. | The library was built for the enlightenment of the townspeople. | For your enlightenment, the answer is on page twelve. | Many ideas in the American Declaration of Independence came from the Enlightenment.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. The history period is written with a capital E and «the»: «the Enlightenment». Verb «enlighten» (to explain, to make clear); adjective «enlightened». It has nothing to do with lamps or light bulbs, though it comes from «light» as in «seeing clearly».

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person, team or animal that enters a competition, race or exam. 2) A person who joins a school, job or profession as a newcomer.
its sense in the lessons: In olympiads, races and contests an entrant is one who takes part. In maths problems the number of entrants is how many people take part. Phrases: «each entrant», «new entrants», «the youngest entrant».
examples from the lessons: There were forty entrants in the spelling bee. | Each entrant gets a number to pin on their shirt. | The youngest entrant in the race was only seven. | All entrants must hand in their poems by Friday. | The cake competition had more entrants than last year. | New entrants to the school get a buddy for the first week. | If each of 12 entrants pays £2, the prize fund is £24.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; plural «entrants». Do not confuse with «entrance» (a way in, a door). Related verb «enter», noun «entry». In maths, «entrants» are the people counted, not the prizes or places.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (law, home) To force someone to leave the house or land they live in, usually by law because they did not pay rent or broke the rules. 2) To make someone or something leave a place: «The cuckoo chick evicts the other eggs from the nest.»
its sense in the lessons: In adult-life lessons eviction is a serious problem for families who cannot pay their rent; the landlord must follow the law. In nature lessons animals can be evicted from nests or burrows. Phrases: «be evicted», «evict the tenants», «an eviction notice».
examples from the lessons: The family was evicted when they could not pay the rent. | A landlord cannot evict tenants without following the law. | The cuckoo chick evicts the other eggs from the nest. | The squirrels were evicted from the loft by the pest controller. | They got a letter warning that they might be evicted. | Badger never evicted anyone from his warm home in the Wild Wood. | Being evicted can be very hard for children who must change school.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past form «evicted». Noun «eviction». Usually passive: «they were evicted». In many countries charities and councils help families who are threatened with eviction.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a funny or strange way: «He walked funnily after the long ride.» 2) Mainly in «funnily enough»: used to say something is surprising or a strange coincidence.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday speech «funnily enough» introduces a surprise or coincidence; in stories it signals an unexpected twist. Phrases: «funnily enough».
examples from the lessons: Funnily enough, my teacher has the same birthday as me. | The clown walked funnily in his huge shoes. | Funnily enough, I was just thinking about you. | My leg felt funnily heavy after sitting on it. | Funnily enough, the dog ate the carrot but not the meat. | She spoke funnily because she had a cold.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Spelt with double n and «-ily»: funny → funnily. «Funnily enough» does not mean something is a joke; it means it is surprising or a coincidence.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) To talk a lot, quickly and often about unimportant things; to chatter. 2) (informal, noun) Chatty talk. 3) (informal) «the gift of the gab» (UK) or «the gift of gab» (US): the ability to talk easily and persuade people.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday talk and stories «gab» describes chatter between friends. «Gift of the gab» is said of salespeople, presenters and charming characters. Related: «chatter», «natter» (UK), «yak».
examples from the lessons: The girls gabbed on the phone for an hour. | Stop gabbing and finish your work! | My uncle has the gift of the gab — he can sell anything. | Grandma loves a good gab with her neighbour. | They were gabbing so much that they missed their bus stop. | Toad had the gift of the gab and talked his way out of trouble.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal; not for formal writing. Past form «gabbed», «-ing» form «gabbing». Adjective «gabby» (talkative). Do not confuse with «grab».

meaning for a pupil: 1) An opening in a wall or fence that can be closed with a gate; an entrance. 2) A place you pass through to reach another place: «Dover is the gateway to France.» 3) Something that leads to something bigger: «Reading is a gateway to learning.» 4) (computers) A device that connects one computer network to another.
its sense in the lessons: In geography a city can be called the gateway to a region; in stories gateways are often magical openings to other worlds. Phrases: «the gateway to», «stand in the gateway».
examples from the lessons: The cows came through the gateway into the field. | St Louis is called the Gateway to the West, with its famous arch. | The old castle gateway had a heavy wooden door. | In the story, the wardrobe was a gateway to another world. | Learning to read is a gateway to every other subject. | Don't block the gateway with your bike. | The computer connects to the internet through a gateway.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; plural «gateways». A «gate» is the moving door; a «gateway» is the opening (and the gate). Often «the gateway to» + a place or an idea.

meaning for a pupil: 1) GMT stands for Greenwich Mean Time: the time at the Prime Meridian in Greenwich, London, used as the starting point for the world's time zones. 2) The time used in the UK in winter (in summer the UK uses British Summer Time, one hour ahead of GMT).
its sense in the lessons: In geography and time lessons GMT is the zero point for time zones: places to the east are ahead, places to the west are behind. Phrases: «GMT+1», «GMT-5», «at 9 pm GMT».
examples from the lessons: GMT stands for Greenwich Mean Time. | New York is five hours behind GMT in winter. | The match starts at 3 pm GMT. | In summer the UK clocks go forward to BST, one hour ahead of GMT. | Paris is at GMT+1 in winter. | At the Royal Observatory in Greenwich you can stand on the line where GMT is measured. | If it is noon GMT, it is 7 am in New York (in winter).
note for the reader of a maths problem: An abbreviation, written in capitals: GMT. Not an English word on its own. Scientists today mostly use UTC (Coordinated Universal Time), which is almost the same. In maths problems: «GMT+3» means add 3 hours to GMT; «GMT−5» means take away 5 hours.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who often grumbles: someone who complains in a low, unhappy voice about small things.
its sense in the lessons: In stories a grumbler is a moaning character who is never happy, often shown in a funny way. Related: «moaner», «whinger» (UK, Australia), «complainer», «grouch».
examples from the lessons: Uncle Bob is a real grumbler about the weather. | Don't be a grumbler — we'll have fun even if it rains. | The old grumbler in the story complained about every child in the street. | Every team has a grumbler who hates early practice. | The grumbler moaned that the soup was too hot, then too cold. | Mole was no grumbler; he got on with the spring cleaning.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; plural «grumblers». From the verb «grumble (grumbles, grumbled)». Informal synonyms: «moaner», «whinger» (UK), «grouch» (US).

meaning for a pupil: 1) (a name) Hogg is a surname, a family name used in Scotland and England, for example the Scottish writer James Hogg. 2) (spelling) It is not the ordinary word «hog» (a pig), which has one g.
its sense in the lessons: In lessons it appears only as somebody's name. Nothing else is known about the person from the word itself.
examples from the lessons: Mrs Hogg is our new class teacher. | James Hogg was a Scottish poet called «the Ettrick Shepherd». | The letter was signed «T. Hogg». | Is it Hogg with two g's? Yes, H-O-G-G.
note for the reader of a maths problem: A name, written with a capital H. Not an English common word. Do not confuse with «hog» (a pig, or to keep something greedily for yourself).

meaning for a pupil: 1) Lack of the skill or ability needed to do a job properly; doing something badly because you do not know how.
its sense in the lessons: In stories and news it explains why things went wrong — a careless worker, a bungling villain. In adult-life lessons people can lose jobs for incompetence. Phrases: «sheer incompetence», «through incompetence», «gross incompetence» (formal).
examples from the lessons: The bridge fell down because of the builder's incompetence. | The robbers' incompetence made the story funny. | Toad's incompetence at driving caused many crashes. | She was angry at the incompetence of the company that lost her parcel. | Losing the keys three times was pure incompetence. | The coach was blamed for the team's incompetence.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable. Adjective «incompetent», opposite «competent» and «competence». It means lack of skill, not lack of effort — a lazy expert is not incompetent. Strong word; can be rude to say to a person.

meaning for a pupil: 1) In a way that causes trouble or difficulty, or at a bad time: «The bus broke down inconveniently in the rain.»
its sense in the lessons: In stories it shows bad luck in timing or place. Often «inconveniently placed», «inconveniently timed».
examples from the lessons: The shop is inconveniently far from the station. | It started raining inconveniently just as we left. | The plug was inconveniently placed behind the sofa. | Inconveniently, my pencil broke during the test. | The dentist appointment was inconveniently timed during football practice. | The bridge was inconveniently closed for repairs.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Opposite «conveniently». Adjective «inconvenient», noun «inconvenience». Spelt in-con-VEN-ient-ly.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A place where two or more roads meet or cross; a crossroads or junction. 2) (maths) The point or line where two lines or shapes cross. 3) (maths) In sets and Venn diagrams, the part where two sets overlap: the things that belong to both.
its sense in the lessons: In road safety, intersections are where you must stop, look and cross carefully. In maths, the intersection of two lines is a point; in a Venn diagram, it is the middle where circles overlap. Phrases: «at the intersection», «the point of intersection», «busy intersection».
examples from the lessons: Wait for the green man at the busy intersection. | Turn left at the next intersection. | The two lines meet at the point of intersection. | In the Venn diagram, children who like cats and dogs go in the intersection. | The intersection of the sets {1, 2, 3} and {2, 3, 4} is {2, 3}. | There is a traffic light at every intersection on our street. | Two straight lines that cross have exactly one intersection.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; plural «intersections». Verb «intersect». In the UK people often say «junction» or «crossroads» for a road intersection. In maths sets, the intersection is the overlap («and»), not putting everything together (that is the «union»).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person, army or group that sets people or a place free from enemies, slavery or prison.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons liberators free countries or people, like the armies that freed towns in the Second World War or Simón Bolívar, «the Liberator» of several South American countries. Phrases: «hailed as a liberator», «the Liberator».
examples from the lessons: The town welcomed the soldiers as liberators. | Simón Bolívar is called «the Liberator» in South America. | Abraham Lincoln is remembered as a liberator of enslaved people. | In the story, the hero was a liberator who opened the prison gates. | People threw flowers to the liberators. | The liberators of the concentration camps found terrible things.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; plural «liberators». Verb «liberate», noun «liberation». Some people called «liberators» by one side were seen as invaders by the other — a history trap to watch for.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The soft, pale, legless young form (larva) of a fly, which hatches from an egg and feeds on rotting food or dead animals. 2) (old-fashioned, insult) A rude name for a worthless person.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons maggots are part of a fly's life cycle: egg, larva (maggot), pupa, adult fly. They clean up nature by eating rotting things. Anglers use them as bait; doctors sometimes use clean maggots to clean wounds. Phrases: «crawling with maggots».
examples from the lessons: The rubbish bin was crawling with maggots in the hot weather. | A maggot turns into a pupa and then into a fly. | Grandad uses maggots as bait when he goes fishing. | Maggots help break down dead animals. | Doctors sometimes use special clean maggots to clean wounds. | We learnt about the life cycle of a fly: egg, maggot, pupa, fly. | The old apple had a maggot inside.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; plural «maggots». A maggot is a larva, not a worm — a common mistake. Caterpillars are the larvae of butterflies and moths; maggots are the larvae of flies.

meaning for a pupil: 1) The time between two events: «in the meantime» means while you wait for something else to happen. 2) (adverb) Meanwhile; at the same time.
its sense in the lessons: In stories «in the meantime» moves to what was happening elsewhere or while waiting. In everyday life it tells someone what to do while they wait. Phrases: «in the meantime», «for the meantime» (for now).
examples from the lessons: Dinner will be ready in an hour; in the meantime, do your homework. | The doctor is coming. In the meantime, keep the ice on your knee. | Meantime, Ratty was rowing up the river. | The new library opens in May; for the meantime, use the mobile library. | In the meantime, the snow kept falling. | We waited for the bus and in the meantime ate our sandwiches.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Most often in «in the meantime». Means the same as «meanwhile». Written as one word. In time problems it is the gap between two events.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person or thing that has the same name as another. 2) A person or thing named after someone: «The ship was named after the queen, its namesake.»
its sense in the lessons: In stories and history, a namesake shares a name with a famous person or place; things are often named after people. Phrases: «his namesake», «a famous namesake».
examples from the lessons: I met my namesake — another girl called Ruby Brown! | The town of Washington is named after George Washington, its namesake. | My grandad is my namesake; we are both called Thomas. | The new ship is a namesake of an old one sunk in the war. | Prince Charles's namesake, King Charles I, lived in the 1600s. | The bakery's namesake was the founder's grandmother.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; plural «namesakes». It can mean either the person who has the same name or the one the thing was named after — read carefully which. One word, not «name sake».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Too active; working, moving or doing more than is normal or healthy. 2) (body) An organ that works too hard, like an overactive thyroid.
its sense in the lessons: Used about imagination («an overactive imagination» — imagining scary or unlikely things), bodies and machines. Often a gentle way of saying someone is imagining things. Phrases: «an overactive imagination», «an overactive bladder».
examples from the lessons: You have an overactive imagination — there is no monster under the bed. | The puppy was overactive after eating cake crumbs. | An overactive gland can make the heart beat fast. | My brother's overactive brain keeps him awake at night. | The detective said the witness had an overactive imagination. | An overactive volcano had to be watched closely.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Prefix «over-» means «too much». Opposite: «underactive». Also spelt «over-active». Not the same as «hyperactive», which is often used about children who cannot sit still.

meaning for a pupil: 1) To cook food for too long, so it becomes dry, hard, burnt or mushy. 2) (informal) To overdo something, like telling a story with too much drama: «He overcooked the ending.»
its sense in the lessons: In cooking and everyday life it means the food is spoilt by too much heat. In writing or sport (UK informal) it means trying too hard or exaggerating. Phrases: «overcooked vegetables», «overcook the pasta».
examples from the lessons: Don't overcook the pasta or it will go soggy. | The steak was overcooked and tough. | Mum overcooked the cake and the edges were black. | Overcooked broccoli loses its bright green colour. | The writer overcooked the drama with too many explosions. | If you overcook an egg, the yolk turns grey-green.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past form «overcooked». Opposite «undercook» (cooked too little), which can be unsafe for chicken and eggs. Prefix «over-» means «too much».

meaning for a pupil: 1) Bigger than the normal size; very large. 2) Too big for its purpose, like an oversized coat on a small child.
its sense in the lessons: In fashion «oversized» clothes are made big on purpose; in stories it can be funny or show someone is too small for something. In hyperbole lessons it is a plain way to say «very big». Phrases: «oversized jumper», «oversized luggage».
examples from the lessons: She wore an oversized jumper that came down to her knees. | Oversized luggage costs extra on the plane. | The clown had oversized shoes. | The cat sat in an oversized box. | The giant in the story carried an oversized spoon. | Oversized hoodies are fashionable at our school.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Also «outsized». Opposite «undersized». Prefix «over-» means «too much». It describes size only, not weight.

part of speech: noun (a quaver, quavers); verb (quaver, quavers, quavered, quavering)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (music, UK) A note that lasts half a beat in common time — half as long as a crotchet; in the USA it is called an eighth note. 2) (verb) When a voice quavers, it shakes because the person is afraid, nervous, old or upset. 3) (noun) A shake or tremble in the voice.
its sense in the lessons: In music lessons a quaver is drawn as a filled-in note with a stem and one flag (tail); two or more quavers are often joined by a beam. Two quavers equal one crotchet. In stories a quavering voice shows fear or sadness. Also «Quavers» is a UK crisp brand.
examples from the lessons: A quaver lasts half as long as a crotchet. | Two quavers make one beat in 4/4 time. | Her voice quavered as she said goodbye. | «Is anyone there?» he asked with a quaver in his voice. | In America a quaver is called an eighth note. | The quavers were joined together with a beam. | The old man's voice quavered as he sang. | A semibreve equals eight quavers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; plural «quavers». Past form «quavered». UK names: semibreve (4 beats), minim (2), crotchet (1), quaver (1/2), semiquaver (1/4). US names: whole, half, quarter, eighth, sixteenth note. Maths: 1 semibreve = 2 minims = 4 crotchets = 8 quavers.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (music, UK) The longest common note: it lasts four beats in 4/4 time, as long as two minims or four crotchets; in the USA it is called a whole note.
its sense in the lessons: In music lessons a semibreve is drawn as an open oval with no stem. It fills a whole bar of 4/4 time. Note values form a halving pattern, useful for fractions in maths.
examples from the lessons: A semibreve lasts for four beats. | In America a semibreve is called a whole note. | One semibreve fills a whole bar in 4/4 time. | A semibreve looks like an empty oval with no stem. | Two minims make one semibreve. | Hold the semibreve until I count to four. | A semibreve is as long as eight quavers.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; plural «semibreves». «Semi-» here does not mean «small»: it is a «half» of the old «breve», a note now rarely used. Maths: 1 semibreve = 2 minims = 4 crotchets = 8 quavers = 16 semiquavers. A whole-bar rest looks different (a small block hanging below a line).

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person who shoots a gun, arrow or ball. 2) (sport) A player who shoots at goal, for example in netball or basketball, where the shooter is the player allowed to score. 3) (informal) A gun. 4) A video game where players shoot things («a shooter game»). 5) (slang) A small glass of strong alcoholic drink drunk quickly — for adults.
its sense in the lessons: In news, a «shooter» is someone who fired a gun and hurt people — a serious, frightening word. In netball (UK, Australia, NZ) the Goal Shooter is a position. In games, «first-person shooter» is a type. Phrases: «sharp shooter», «straight shooter» (an honest person), «goal shooter».
examples from the lessons: She plays Goal Shooter in the netball team. | He is the best three-point shooter on the basketball team. | The police caught the shooter quickly. | My uncle is a straight shooter — he always tells the truth. | That video game is a shooter, rated for adults. | The archer was a sharp shooter who hit the middle every time. | In the Western film, the shooter rode into town.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; plural «shooters». «Straight shooter» (informal) is praise: an honest person. If you ever hear shots or see someone with a gun, get away, hide and tell an adult or call 999/911/000/111. Many shooter games have age ratings above primary-school age.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) A very small amount of something: «a smidge of butter». 2) (informal) A little bit, slightly: «a smidge too long».
its sense in the lessons: In everyday talk and lessons on downplaying (understatement), «a smidge» makes something sound tiny. People sometimes say «a smidge» about something that is not really small, as a joke or to sound modest. Related: «smidgen», «tad», «touch», «pinch», «a bit».
examples from the lessons: Can I have just a smidge of ketchup? | The skirt is a smidge too long. | Add a smidge of salt to the soup. | I'm a smidge tired after the walk. | «Just a smidge of cake,» said Dad, taking a huge slice. | Move the picture a smidge to the left.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal; mostly in «a smidge (of)». Short for «smidgen». It has no exact size — in a maths problem «a smidge» is not a number. Often used to downplay: «a smidge late» may mean quite late.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A person whose job is to record or control the sound for films, television, radio, concerts or plays.
its sense in the lessons: In stories about film-making and theatre the soundman holds the microphone or works the sound desk. Today people often say «sound engineer», «sound technician» or «sound person» so it fits women as well as men.
examples from the lessons: The soundman held a long microphone above the actors. | At the concert the soundman made the guitars louder. | The soundman asked everyone to be quiet before filming. | Our school play had a soundman at the back of the hall. | The soundman checked the microphones: «One, two, one, two.» | The news crew had a cameraman and a soundman.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable; plural «soundmen» (not «soundmans»). Also written «sound man». Neutral words: «sound engineer», «sound technician».

meaning for a pupil: 1) The season of spring, between winter and summer, when plants start to grow, flowers bloom and many baby animals are born.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons springtime brings longer days, warmer weather, buds, blossom, frogspawn and lambs. In stories it often means new beginnings and hope. Spring is March to May in the northern half of the world (UK, USA, Canada, Ireland) and September to November in the southern half (Australia, New Zealand).
examples from the lessons: In springtime the lambs play in the fields. | Mole felt the springtime calling him out of his hole. | Daffodils bloom in springtime. | Birds build their nests in springtime. | In Australia springtime starts in September. | We planted beans in the springtime. | Springtime is when frogs lay frogspawn in ponds.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Uncountable, usually «in springtime» or «in the springtime». Means the same as «spring», but sounds softer and more poetic. Remember seasons are opposite in the two halves of the Earth.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) A small amount; a little: «a tad of milk». 2) (informal) «a tad» + adjective or adverb means «slightly, a little»: «a tad cold». 3) (old, US) A small child, especially a boy.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday talk and lessons on downplaying, «a tad» softens what you say so it sounds polite or modest: «It's a tad expensive» may mean it is very expensive. Related: «a smidge», «a touch», «a bit», «slightly».
examples from the lessons: The soup is a tad salty. | Could you turn the music down a tad? | I'm a tad nervous about the test. | «A tad late» said the teacher, when we were twenty minutes late. | Pass me a tad more sugar, please. | The jacket is a tad big, but you'll grow into it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal; almost always «a tad». It is not an exact amount — in maths problems it gives no number. Often used for understatement (making something sound smaller than it is). Not the same as «tadpole».

meaning for a pupil: 1) (informal) Very small; tiny. 2) In «teeny-weeny» or «teeny-tiny» (informal, childish): extremely small.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday talk, stories and baby talk «teeny» makes something sound very small or cute. In lessons on downplaying, «a teeny problem» can hide a big one. Related: «tiny», «wee» (Scotland, Ireland), «itsy-bitsy».
examples from the lessons: Look at the teeny little ladybird! | I only want a teeny piece of cake. | The mouse had teeny pink paws. | «It's a teeny scratch,» she said, but it was bleeding a lot — tell an adult. | The baby wore teeny socks. | There was a teeny-weeny spider in the bath. | That's a teeny bit unfair!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Informal. Comparative «teenier», superlative «teeniest». Do not confuse with «teen» (13–19 years old) or «teenage». Means «very small», not an exact size.

part of speech: adjective; noun (a thirtieth, thirtieths); ordinal number (30th)
meaning for a pupil: 1) Coming next after the twenty-ninth in order; number 30 in a line or list (30th). 2) (fraction) One of thirty equal parts of something: one thirtieth = 1/30.
its sense in the lessons: In maths it is an ordinal number (place in order) and also a fraction. In everyday life it appears in dates («the thirtieth of June») and birthdays. Phrases: «thirtieth birthday», «on the thirtieth».
examples from the lessons: My birthday is on the thirtieth of April. | Mum is having a party for her thirtieth birthday. | He finished thirtieth out of fifty runners. | One thirtieth of 90 is 3. | June has thirty days, so the thirtieth is the last day. | February never has a thirtieth day. | Each child got a thirtieth of the pizza — a very thin slice!
note for the reader of a maths problem: Written 30th. Spelling: «thirty» → «thirtieth» (y changes to ie). Fractions: 1/30 is one thirtieth; 7/30 is seven thirtieths. To find a thirtieth of a number, divide by 30. Not the same as «thirteenth» (13th).

meaning for a pupil: 1) To make something ugly or uglier.
its sense in the lessons: A rare, slightly playful word, used in stories and complaints about buildings or places spoilt by ugly changes. Opposite: «beautify». In computing, «uglify» also means squashing program code so it is shorter and hard to read.
examples from the lessons: The huge car park uglified the village green. | Graffiti uglified the old bridge. | «Don't uglify your homework with scribbles,» said the teacher. | The witch tried to uglify the princess with a spell. | Some people think the new tower block uglifies the skyline. | The programmer used a tool to uglify the code.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Past form «uglified», third person «uglifies» (y changes to ie). Rare and informal-sounding; more common: «spoil», «make ugly». Opposite «beautify».

part of speech: verb (-ing form of weigh); noun (weighing, weighings)
meaning for a pupil: 1) The -ing form of «weigh»: measuring how heavy something is: «She is weighing the flour.» 2) Having a certain weight: «a parcel weighing 2 kilograms». 3) Thinking carefully about something before deciding: «weighing up the choices». 4) (noun) The act of measuring weight: «the weighing of the babies».
its sense in the lessons: In maths and science, weighing means using scales to find mass in grams and kilograms. In everyday life «weighing up» means comparing good and bad points before choosing. Phrases: «weighing scales», «weighing up», «weighing on my mind» (worrying me), «weighing in at» (sport).
examples from the lessons: We are weighing the apples on the kitchen scales. | A bag weighing 5 kg is too heavy for me. | She is weighing up whether to join the choir or the football club. | The test has been weighing on my mind all week. | The boxer was weighing in at 70 kilograms. | Weighing the ingredients carefully makes a better cake. | Hmm, I'm still weighing it up.
note for the reader of a maths problem: From «weigh (weighs, weighed, weighing)». Noun «weight». Silent «gh»: say WAY-ing. Homophone trap: «weigh» sounds like «way». In maths, «weighing 300 g» gives the mass of each item; total mass = number × that mass.

part of speech: noun (a whiff, whiffs); verb (whiff, whiffs, whiffed, whiffing)
meaning for a pupil: 1) (noun) A short smell, often brief or faint: «a whiff of smoke». 2) (noun) A slight sign or hint of something: «a whiff of danger». 3) (verb, UK informal) To smell bad: «Your trainers whiff!» 4) (US, sport) To swing at a ball and miss it completely.
its sense in the lessons: In stories a whiff warns or tempts — a whiff of smoke means fire, a whiff of cooking means dinner is near. In safety lessons a whiff of gas or smoke means tell an adult and get out. Phrases: «catch a whiff of», «get a whiff of», «a whiff of scandal».
examples from the lessons: I caught a whiff of fresh bread from the bakery. | There's a whiff of smoke — tell an adult now! | Your football socks really whiff! | The dog got a whiff of the fox and ran off. | A whiff of danger made the explorers stop. | Mole caught a whiff of his old home and longed to go back. | The batter whiffed the ball and was out.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun; plural «whiffs». Past form of verb «whiffed». Adjective «whiffy» (UK informal: smelly). A whiff is short and slight, not a strong lasting smell. If you smell gas at home, leave and call the emergency gas number.

meaning for a pupil: 1) (old, formal) An old past form of «work», meaning made, shaped or caused: «The storm wrought great damage.» 2) In «wrought iron»: iron that has been heated and hammered into shape, used for gates, railings and fences. 3) In «wrought up» or «overwrought»: very upset, nervous or worked up.
its sense in the lessons: In history and old books «wrought» describes what was made or caused («What hath God wrought» — the first long-distance telegraph message, 1844). In everyday life you see «wrought-iron gates». Phrases: «wrought iron», «wrought havoc» (caused great damage), «finely wrought» (skilfully made).
examples from the lessons: The park has beautiful wrought-iron gates. | The flood wrought havoc in the town. | The blacksmith wrought the iron into a horseshoe. | The finely wrought silver cup was in the museum. | She was all wrought up before the concert. | War wrought great changes in people's lives. | «What hath God wrought» was the first message sent by Morse code over a long line.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Old-fashioned and formal; today we say «made» or «caused». Not the past of «wreak», though people often say «wrought havoc» and «wreaked havoc» — both are used. Pronounced RAWT, rhymes with «caught». «Wrought iron» is different from «cast iron», which is poured into moulds.

part of speech: noun (an armoury, armouries; US spelling armory, armories)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A place where weapons and armour are kept, such as a room in a castle or a building used by an army. 2) A collection of weapons that a person, army or country has. 3) A set of skills, tools or ideas that someone can use to deal with a problem, like weapons ready for a fight. 4) (US) A building where soldiers, such as the National Guard, meet and train; some old ones are now used for sports or events.
its sense in the lessons: In history lessons the armoury is the store of swords, shields, helmets and later guns in a castle, fort or ship; museums such as the Royal Armouries in Leeds and the Tower of London show old armour. In stories a hero may break into the armoury to arm the castle's defenders. In everyday talk and writing the word is often used in a picture-like way: «the teacher's armoury of tricks», «a striker with a full armoury of shots», «another weapon in our armoury against germs». Phrases: «in the armoury», «a weapon in someone's armoury», «a whole armoury of».
examples from the lessons: The knights ran down to the armoury to fetch their swords and shields. | The castle armoury held hundreds of spears and helmets. | On our school trip we saw old suits of armour in the Tower of London armoury. | The army's armoury includes tanks, ships and planes. | Patience is the best tool in a teacher's armoury. | The goalkeeper has a whole armoury of saves. | Soap and hot water are a strong weapon in our armoury against germs. | In our town the old armory is now a basketball hall.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: one armoury, two armouries. «Armoury» is the UK, Irish, Australian, New Zealand and Canadian spelling; «armory» is the US spelling — both mean the same. Do not mix it up with «armour/armor», which is the metal covering a knight wears; the armoury is where armour and weapons are kept. Stress on the first part: AR-muh-ree.

meaning for a pupil: 1) A thin, clear, shiny sheet material that is used for wrapping things such as flowers, sweets, gifts and food. 2) Coloured cellophane: thin see-through sheets in bright colours used in crafts, for example to make stained-glass windows or coloured lenses.
its sense in the lessons: In everyday life cellophane is the crinkly see-through wrapping around a bunch of flowers, a box of chocolates or a gift basket. In science lessons it is an example of a transparent material: light passes through it, and coloured cellophane lets only some colours through, so looking through red cellophane makes the world look red. In art and craft it is used for lanterns, windows and filters. Cellophane is made from cellulose, the stuff of plant cell walls, usually from wood pulp. Phrases: «wrapped in cellophane», «a cellophane wrapper», «red cellophane».
examples from the lessons: The roses came wrapped in shiny cellophane. | Mum tore the cellophane off the new box of crayons. | We made a lantern with orange cellophane over the holes. | Look through the blue cellophane and everything turns blue. | Cellophane is transparent, so light can pass through it. | The sweets were twisted up in little cellophane wrappers. | The cellophane crackled when I squeezed the parcel. | Our class made stained-glass windows from black card and coloured cellophane.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Usually uncountable: «some cellophane», «a sheet of cellophane», not «a cellophane» (but «a cellophane wrapper/bag» is fine). Trap: people often call any clear plastic wrap «cellophane», but true cellophane is made from wood cellulose, not from oil like most plastic film and cling film; real cellophane can rot away (biodegrade) much more easily than plastic. It began as a trade name in the early 1900s. Say: SEL-uh-fayn.

part of speech: noun (a conifer, conifers); adjective form coniferous (a coniferous forest)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A tree or bush that grows its seeds in cones and usually has thin needle-like or small scaly leaves, such as a pine, fir, spruce, cedar, yew or cypress. 2) Most conifers are evergreen: they keep their leaves all year round, so they stay green in winter.
its sense in the lessons: In science lessons conifers are one of the big groups of plants: they make seeds but no flowers or fruit, and the seeds sit between the woody scales of a cone. Huge coniferous forests (the taiga) cover the cold north of Canada, Scandinavia and Russia; coniferous trees cope well with snow because their narrow needles and sloping shape let the snow slide off. Christmas trees are conifers. Some of the tallest and oldest living things are conifers: coast redwoods in California and bristlecone pines. In gardens people plant conifers as hedges. Phrases: «a coniferous forest», «conifer needles», «conifer cones».
examples from the lessons: A pine tree is a conifer because it grows cones. | Conifers stay green all winter. | We collected pine cones under the conifers in the park. | Our Christmas tree is a conifer called a Norway spruce. | The coniferous forests of Canada stretch for thousands of kilometres. | Squirrels eat the seeds hidden in conifer cones. | The needles of a conifer are really thin leaves. | The tallest tree in the world is a conifer, a coast redwood.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: one conifer, many conifers; the adjective is «coniferous». Trap: not every conifer is evergreen — the larch drops its needles every autumn. Also not every evergreen is a conifer: holly and many eucalyptus trees are evergreen but have flowers, not cones. The opposite group in lessons is «broadleaf» or «deciduous» trees like oak and maple. Say: KON-ih-fer.

part of speech: noun (a diamondback, diamondbacks); also used before another noun (a diamondback rattlesnake, a diamondback terrapin)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A diamondback rattlesnake: a large, very venomous American rattlesnake with a pattern of diamond shapes along its back and a rattle on its tail. 2) A diamondback terrapin: a small turtle with diamond-shaped patterns on its shell that lives in salty marshes along the east coast of the USA. 3) Any animal with diamond shapes on its back, for example the diamondback moth, a small pest of cabbages.
its sense in the lessons: In science and nature lessons the eastern and western diamondback rattlesnakes are examples of venomous reptiles of North America: they shake the rattle on their tail as a warning, and their pattern helps them hide (camouflage).
