Safety lesson: if you hear a rattle on a trail, stand still, then slowly back away; never touch or poke a snake, and a bite needs emergency help at once. The diamondback terrapin is studied as an animal that lives in brackish water, where rivers meet the sea. In stories set in deserts or the American Southwest a diamondback is often the danger on the path. Phrases: «a western diamondback», «an eastern diamondback», «diamondback terrapin».
examples from the lessons: A diamondback rattlesnake lay coiled in the shade of a rock. | The diamondback shook its rattle to warn the hikers away. | Diamondbacks are the largest rattlesnakes in North America. | The ranger told us to back away slowly from the diamondback. | A diamondback terrapin was sunning itself on the muddy bank. | The terrapin's shell has a pattern like little diamonds. | Diamondback moth caterpillars had eaten holes in the cabbages. | In the zoo's reptile house we saw a western diamondback behind thick glass.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable noun: one diamondback, two diamondbacks; one word, no hyphen. On its own it usually means the rattlesnake; for the turtle or moth people add «terrapin» or «moth». The «diamonds» are only a pattern of shapes, not jewels. Myth: you cannot tell a rattlesnake's exact age by counting its rattle segments, because it adds a new one each time it sheds its skin, and pieces can break off.

part of speech: noun (an engraving, engravings; engraving — the craft, uncountable); verb form of engrave (engrave, engraves, engraved, engraving)
meaning for a pupil: 1) A picture made by cutting lines into a metal plate or block of wood, then covering it with ink and pressing paper onto it to print the picture. 2) Words, names or patterns cut into a hard surface such as metal, glass, stone or wood. 3) The art or job of cutting designs into hard surfaces. 4) The act of cutting a design into something (part of the verb «engrave»: «She is engraving a name on the cup»).
its sense in the lessons: In history and art lessons old books and newspapers were often illustrated with engravings, because before photographs could be printed, engraving was a way to copy the same picture many times. Banknotes and stamps are still made with very fine engravings that are hard to copy. In everyday life you see engraving on trophies, medals, rings, watches and gravestones, where names and dates are cut into the metal or stone. In stories an engraving on a ring or a sword can be a clue. Phrases: «an engraving of», «the engraving on the trophy», «wood engraving».
examples from the lessons: The old book had an engraving of a sailing ship on every page. | The engraving on the cup says «Champions». | Gran's ring has tiny engraving inside it. | Thomas Bewick made famous wood engravings of birds. | The man in the shop is engraving my name on the medal. | Banknotes have fine engravings to stop people copying them. | The engraving on the old gravestone was worn and hard to read. | In art we tried a kind of engraving by scratching pictures into a foam tile and printing it.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Countable when it means a picture or the words cut in («two engravings»); uncountable when it means the craft («she studies engraving»). It is also the «-ing» form of the verb «engrave», which needs an object: you engrave a name on (or into) something. Do not confuse it with «etching», a similar printmaking method that uses acid to bite the lines into the metal instead of cutting them by hand. Say: in-GRAY-ving.

part of speech: adjective (muggy, muggier, muggiest); noun form mugginess
meaning for a pupil: 1) Muggy weather is warm, damp and still, with heavy, sticky air that makes you feel hot and tired. 2) (informal) A room or place that feels close and stuffy, with warm, damp air and no fresh breeze.
its sense in the lessons: In geography and science lessons muggy weather means high humidity: a lot of water vapour in warm air, so sweat dries slowly and people feel hotter than the thermometer shows. Muggy days often come before a thunderstorm in summer, and are common in places like Florida, Queensland and Hong Kong. In everyday life people say «It's so muggy today» or «a muggy night» when it is hard to sleep. Safety: on muggy days drink plenty of water and rest in the shade, because the body cools down less easily. Phrases: «hot and muggy», «warm and muggy», «a muggy afternoon».
examples from the lessons: It's really muggy today, so my shirt is sticking to my back. | The air felt warm and muggy before the thunderstorm. | We couldn't sleep on that muggy summer night. | Open a window, it's muggy in this classroom. | Muggy weather means there is lots of water vapour in the air. | Brisbane can be very hot and muggy in January. | After the rain the jungle was muggy and full of insects. | It was the muggiest day of the summer holidays.
note for the reader of a maths problem: Adjective: muggy, muggier, muggiest; the noun is «mugginess». It is about warm, wet air — cold damp weather is called «damp» or «raw», not muggy. Trap: it has nothing to do with a mug (a cup) or with «mugging» (robbing someone in the street). Close words: humid, sticky, sultry, close.
